Leroy Irvis wrote presidents of Penn State, Temple, and Pitt to inform them of the efforts of House democrats to allocate funds to counteract PA Governor Thornburgh's 10 percent funding cuts in grants to non-preferred institutions. Irvis says the Governor's budget is unbalanced, relying too heavily on increasing fees and action by the PA Liquor Control Board. As the process begun by the Governor is irrevocable, the Legislature must approve legislation to raise revenue for the institutions.

headline: New transportation attitude needed, PennDot chief says
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation held its PA Transportation Conference in which Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson urged the audience to consider cooperative efforts for saving energy; gains in mass transit, car pooling, imroved fuel efficiency and the choice between funding road maintainence or damage caused by inefficient roads. Larson said PA is working for federal funding and called on Governor Thornburgh to achieve funding stability.

headline: ‘Stings’ on CETA’s municipal jobs
abstract: The Federal Government’s Comprehensive Employment Training Act (CETA) has been used to help cities like Philadelphia and Chester maintain municipal services.  But in the process it has also been making it tougher for both cities to cope with their depleted finances.

headline: Legislative Race Who's Who: At Least 5 New Faces to Win
abstract: The article names each of the candidates running in the Legislative PA House and Senate districts comprising Westmoreland, Cambria, Fayette, Washington, Allegheny, Beaver, and Butler. A short background of candidates is provided, including former occupation and age.

headline: Warped Thinking
abstract: The editors attack a liberal editorial in the Philadelphia Inquirer which accused Republicans of being "unaware of the misery of hopelessness." Contrary to liberal opinion, Republicans, who are also black, Hispanic, middle class, and union members, are well aware of that misery. The difference between the two parties is that Republicans want to solve the problems on a personal level rather than in a massive government program.

headline: LD Board id Told of Precautions for TMI Cleanup
abstract: Lower Dauphin School Board members are hoping that the venting of krypton 85 gas at the Three Mile Island site will not occur until after school ends in June.  The Board and Superintendent wrote letters to the Board of Education and to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh hoping for a delay because of predicted absences during the venting process.

headline: NONE
abstract: Joke about the lack of competition in the trucking industry

headline: ‘Why Aren’t They Out Arresting Kids Who Steal Cars?’
abstract: This cartoon depicts that all the congressmen are worried about the Federal Bureau of Inspection’s ‘sting’ operation.

headline: Legislative Race Who's Who: At Least 5 New Faces to Win
abstract: The article names each of the candidates running in the PA House and Senate districts comprising Westmoreland, Cambria, Fayette, Washington, Allegheny, Beaver, and Butler. A short background of candidates is provided, including former occupation and age.

headline: Watching for the worst on the campaign trails
abstract: This article introduces the missions and jobs of Secret Service to protect presidential candidates from potential assassins.

headline: Library funding a disgrace
abstract: The editorial board finds the current level of funding for the Reading Public Library, less than the cost of going to a movie and buying a small popcorn, is disgraceful. The state of PA ranks 15th in the country for financial support for each person who uses the library. It is particularly galling to the editors that 50 percent of book borrowers are from out of county. More people outside the city use the library and take advantage of the funding than those who live in the city.

headline: Once a Year
abstract: Currently, Pennsylvania residents must have their cars inspected twice a year.  State Representative Bill Steward is proposing legislation to reduce this to once a year.  The editorial supports this saying that it will not diminish safety or repair bills.

headline: 165th Legislative District
abstract: Incumbent to the PA House seat Mary Ann Arty is being challenged by independent Frani Battista in the 165th Legislative District.

headline: Legislators Face Busy Schedules
abstract: State lawmakers face some controversial issues.  And it is likely that partisan bickering could slow down the legislative process to a crawl, especially before the April 22 primary election.  Among the pending issues are divorce reform, revision of the unemployment compensation law, a general state budget, and funding for PennDOT.

headline: Weidner's roots were in local government
abstract: PA Rep. Marvin D. Weidner served in the House for 14 years. Those who knew him described his path from borough tax collector and county treasurer, to member of the House Local Government Committee, to Chairman of the Committee. Weinder oversaw recoding and revision of local government laws in the state legislature. He was active in the PA Local Government Commission. Weidner's proposed revisions to the PA Ethics law and delay of a sales tax bill were efforts to protect local governments.

headline: Olson to direct vocational education
abstract: Jerry C. Olsen, who was fired by the school board as Superintendent, will begin work as the director of the Bureau of Vocational Education with attendance at a Middle States Assembly. PA Secretary of Education Robert Scanlon is pleased to have Olsen on board. Olsen will also head the PA Fire School and Manpower training programs sponsored by the federal and state government.

headline: Overweight
abstract: The editorial board feels it is essential that Governor Thornburgh's administration follow through on promises to improve efforts to get overweight trucks off the road, if public support and money is to be obtained for highway repairs many feel are caused by the trucks. Thus far, that effort is hampered by a federal mandate supporting truckers interests and the malfunction of portable weighing stations. The concerns of the PA Department of Transportation are not reflected by the General Assembly granting higher weight allowances to the trucking industry.

headline: 2 Candidates Must Resign Court Jobs
abstract: David Lane, a court spokesman, said two Philadelphia Traffic Court employes, running for political office must resign their posts or withdraw as candidates.  The two employes are Joseph Diorio and Robert V. Jacobs.

headline: Legislators listed by party
abstract: A list of PA House members and their party affiliations is provided. Incumbents are denoted by an "x."

headline: Weisberg Want's Piccola's Seat in 104th
abstract: Democrat and former director of the PA Bureau of Consumer Protection is challenging 2 term incumbent Republican Jeffrey Piccola for the 104th District house seat. Though the two have much in common in terms of career and family life, Weisberg charges Piccola is often absent from the Legislature, a non-participant in much of floor debate, and has different ideas on some legislative issues. Weisberg cites his record with the Consumer Protection Bureau to convince potential constituents that he is for them.

headline: PSEA Hit List
abstract: Murrysville Representative Lee Taddonio is one the PA State Education Association hit list because he wants to put a lid on state spending.  The teacher’s union is saying that it wants more tax spending for higher wages.

headline: Pa. delays installation of new Platt bridge deck
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation announced a delay in plans to re-deck the George C. Platt Memorial Bridge, due to Federal Highway Administration funds restrictions imposed by President Carter. 90 percent of the construction costs are eligible for Federal coverage. The plan is to close the bridge for two years, though the job could be done in four if the bridge were only partially closed, PennDOT spokesman Robert Rowland responded to a request from Philadelphia Mayor Green's administration.

headline: 2 lawmakers trade shots over free-mail privileges
abstract: Two Western Pennsylvania lawmakers are taking shots at each other over charges that one is taking advantage of free House mailing privileges to take a shot at higher political office.  PA Representative H. William DeWeese DeGreene says that PA Representative Roger Raymond Fischer has used the advantage beyond his own district.

headline: Legislators Play with Fire
abstract: The PA Legislature continues to tempt fate when it comes to the regulation of elderly boarding homes, which have wholly inadequate fire protection systems and unsafe conditions.  In fact, members of the House Health and Welfare Committee voted against significant reforms of boarding homes.  The drive for these reforms has been left principally in the hands of Gov. Richard Thornburgh who tends not in favor of the reforms.

headline: Welcome Back, Congressmen.
abstract: A political cartoon depicts a fat duck in a suit, smoking a cigar and on crutches, bursting through a doorway, the door off its hinges. A policemen looks in inquiringly. A female receptionist pens at her desk, next to which sits a very small duck who remarks, "He didn't get much done as a healthy duck!" The duck is reading a newspaper headlined "Jobs Vacant" and "Help Wanted." The caption reads, "welcome back Congressman."

headline: PSEA Push
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Education Association is attempting to force the Legislature to increase its 44 percent funding to school districts by 6 percent to shoulder half of the burden. PSEA President James Angle said the PSEA will lobby Governor Dick Thornburgh, who has a history of working for 50 percent state funding of schools. Angle said the effort was not to shift the burden of funding from local to state, but rather to equalize an unfair tax pattern.

headline: Panel will study electrifying rails in state corridor
abstract: A five - member panel of the state Senate is to be named to study the economic possibilities of electrifying the Harrisburg - Pittsburgh rail corridor as a major step towards easing PA’s dependence on imported oil.

headline: 2 Set Out Vying for a Mystery Job
abstract: Former Dauphin County District Attorney LeRoy Zimmerman is campaigning against PA Senator Michael O'Pake for PA attorney general, a position for the duties of which were just now announced as PA Governor Thornburgh signed into effect election provisions, mediated by creation of a General Counsel who may supercede the attorney general in civil suits. O'Pake disagreed with the provision for general counsel, though Zimmerman agreed with its ameliorating status.

headline: Legislature Should Not Bend
abstract: The state Constitution requires bills to spend at least three days in each chamber before they can be passed.  This allows for debate and public feedback.  State legislature tried to pass a budget in a shorter period of time.  Such a precedent could override the important system of checks and balances.

headline: Welder Real Loser With 2-party Name
abstract: Carter Reagan, a Texan welder with an unfortunate name given this year's election, hopes jokes will die down now that elections are over. His friends had no sympathy and only made things worse for him when he told them he was undecided. Carter Reagan received no sympathy from owners of the Nixon Ford Motor Company down the block.

headline: PSU, Temple Seek More State cash as Tuitions Climb
abstract: Annual tuition will be hiked by at least $75 at the PA State University and $200 at Temple University next September to combat inflation.

headline: Pardon Me, Boy…
abstract: This editorial expresses the cheers for the new train, "The Pennsylvanian."  Although some persons argue that tax money would be better spent on other mass-transit projects, this editorial argues that "The Pennsylvanian" is a noble experiment which should be given a chance to work.

headline: 21st District Senate Candidates level charges at each other
abstract: Though Republican Tim Shaffer and Democrat Jim Ross for PA Senate agreed on issues such as voting against gun control legislation and state gasoline taxes in a debate sponsored by the League of Women Voters and the Chamber of Commerce. However candidates accused one another of misquoting and taking credit for achievements not their own as charges and counter-charges were exchanged ranging from auto-emissions testing to services for senior citizens. Candidates for the PA House Jim Burd and Ron Painter were in agreement on many issues.

headline: Let the House Decide the Election
abstract: A woman for Kentucky has decided to take political pundits to heart. She will vote John Anderson for President in an attempt to throw the election to the House of Representatives, where she is confident politicians much more knowledgeable and skilled than she, will elect the proper man for the job out of all three candidates.

headline: What are Cuban facts?
abstract: A black American writes the editors, asking if the public view of the Cuban riots is being intentionally distorted by the media. It certainly seems suspicious.

headline: Renovations are approved for Clarion
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has approved $1.8 million for building renovations at Clarion State College.

headline: Pay now, or pay more later
abstract: This editorial supports a swap proposed by Governor Thornburgh to the legislature: the current 11-cents-per-gallon gas tax would go down to 5 cents, while the 6 percent sales tax would be applied to gasoline.

headline: 24 leaders rip Bulletin OIC stories
abstract: Executive director of the Philadelphia Urban Coalition John Bowser, joined by other community leaders, denounced the Bulletin's coverage of mismanagement, tax delinquencies, and statistics by the Opportunities Industrial Centers, a nonprofit founded by Reverend Leon H. Sullivan. The program receives less in federal funds than other agencies, Bowser argued. Criag Ammerman, the Bulletin's executive director said the Bulletin would correct its reports if contrary evidence was presented.

headline: Letters: Details missing on firing
abstract: The writer of this letter discusses the unsuccessful efforts of PA Representative Micozzle and Senator Loeper to reinstate Thomas Martinicchio to his PennDOT position, but also notes that the public has not be made aware of why he was fired to begin with.  The writer requests more information on this situation from state officials.

headline: What to expect
abstract: The author attempts to predict what President elect Ronald Reagan will do as President based on his history as Governor of California and his campaign promises.  The author cites tax cuts, anti-corruption, making Social Security financially solvent, and other issues.

headline: Scanlon Is Due at Hamilton
abstract: Robert Scanlon, PA Secretary of Education, as part of his weekly visits to classrooms to see how teaching can be improved, will be the guest speaker at Hamilton Elementary School for the first student achievement assembly to be held this term.

headline: Penn State Researcher’s Idea to Combat Confusion: Nonsense Symbols Work on State Highways in Tests
abstract: Doctor Richard Olsen of PA University argues nonsense symbols - pictures unrelated to destination - should be removed from highway routes.

headline: 3 ARE FOUND GUILTY IN PATRONAGE FRAUD
abstract: Defendents in "the ghost-workers trial," Peter Camiel, Commissioner of the PA Turnpike Authority and former chairman of the Democratic City Committee, PA Senator Vincent Fumo, and Thomas Nolan, former PA Senator and Senate majority leader, were convicted on charges of mail fraud. According to their testimony, in an effort to get re-elected, they paid persons to run copying machines, election campaigns, and sometimes not work at all, with money that was supposed to be used by the State Legislature. The convictions are expected to be appealed in Federal District Court under Judge Clifford Scott.

headline: Lewis Must Catch Flaherty to Chase Dream
abstract: Craig Lewis doesn’t think he would win the Democratic nomination for retiring U.S. Senator Richard Schweiker’s seat if the election were held tomorrow.  But with eight other candidates competing for a crack at apparent shoo-in Flaherty, it may just be another year of paying his dues.

headline: What's in a name? For GOP's Dwyer, overcoming Treasurer Casey's name is everything
abstract: PA Senator Budd Dywer has a number of obstacles to overcome for PA Auditor General against Robert E. Casey, most formidable being the name of his opponent, whom voters confuse with the former gubernatorial candidate and PA Auditor General Robert P. Casey. Dwyer has neither the funds nor the time to explain this discrepancy to voters. Dwyer claims E. Casey has mismanaged funds and cannot claim responsibility for tax savings for voters, as his department was a caretaker of other government funds.

headline: School Integration Plan Is Approved
abstract: A plan that responds to a state Human Relations Commission order and will integrate 40 of PA’s 77 public schools was approved by an unlikely alliance of board members after they spent three hours making last - minute alternations.

headline: PennDOT Announces Cutbacks
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation announced $100 million in cutbacks as it struggles to meet the pressures of inflated petroleum prices. PA Governor Thornburgh proposed a so-called "SWAP" tax on gasoline, a replacement of the current 11 cent tax, to a 5 cent flat tax and 6 percent sales tax. PA Senate Majority Leader Henry Hager was not surprised by the cutbacks. Unfortunately, the reduced budget will disqualify the state to receive federal matching funds.

headline: 3 Candidates to Speak to AFL-CIO
abstract: Three presidential hopefuls, Ronald Reagan, U.S. Senator Edward M. Kennedy, and George Bush will address the PA AFL-CIO convention next week.

headline: Lewis, Schweiker, Haig Cabinet picks
abstract: Three prominent Pennsylvanians are among the choices of President-elect Ronald Reagan for his new Cabinet, Republican sources report. They are retiring US Senator Richard Schweiker as Secretary of Health and Human Services, PA Republican Chairman Drew Lewis as Transportation Secretary, and former NATO Commander General Alexander Haig Jr. for Secretary of State.

headline: When you can see the convention on TV
abstract: The newspaper provides a listing of what channels will carry coverage of the Democratic National Convention, including dates and times for tonight and tomorrow.

headline: School-Aid Pitch
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Education Association is going to try to hold the PA Legislature and Governor Thornburgh to providing schools with half of their funding. The PSEA says enough can be squeezed out of the budget for education by rearranging priorities in the existing budget. However, in reality, there will be either higher state taxes or higher local taxes, and higher real estate taxes either way.

headline: PennDOT Awards Area Road Pacts
abstract: PennDOT has awarded contracts totaling $1,194,023 for area highway construction projects slated to begin in the spring.  $78,259 to Silver Springs Construction Co. Inc. of Mechanicsburgh, $903,796 to Kimbob Inc. of Harrisburg, $69,558 to Kohler Signal Co. of Lemoyne, and $142,410 to Winder Services Inc. of Reading.  One-fourth of the cost of each projects will be paid by the local community and the remainder will come from federal aid funds.

headline: 3 Co-Defendeants Cut from Lederer's Abscam Trial
abstract: US Representative Raymond Lederer will face charges of bribery and conspiracy by the Federal Bureau of Investigation alone as the court waits to hear the verdict on appeals by three co-defendants, Camden Mayor Angelo Errichetti, Philadelphia City Councilman Louis Johnson and Philadelphia attorney Howard Criden, convicted in the Michael "Ozzie" Myers case. The appeals are expected to take more than a year working their way to the US Supreme Court.

headline: Lewis: He decides quickly, and acts
abstract: Andrew D. Lewis, PA campaign manager for President Ford, was nominated by President-elect Ronald Reagan to serve as Secretary of Transportation. A court-appointed trustee who guided Reading Railroad out of bankruptcy, friends expect Lewis to make a quick study of the transportation agency's operations. Lewis is thought to have gained Reagan's attention for refusing to switch sides at the request of US Senator Richard Schweiker in 1976. Reagan admires loyalty.

headline: While Ford Maneuvers, Reagan Fumes
abstract: The long - smoldering resentment that Ronald Reagan privately has displayed toward Gerald R. Ford’s possible entry into the Republican presidential race boiled over into public view.

headline: School-code changes being studied
abstract: PA Education Secretary Robert Scanlon explains costs associated with revising the school code. Revising the code grants more power to local districts and streamline sections interpreted and defined differently throughout the code. Given that the measure has passed the House, Scanlon is optimistic. The House recalled several proposals in the legislation, however Scanlon is pleased the legislation went through. This will mark the first time the PA Senate has addressed the issue.

headline: PennDOT Crew Back
abstract: Some 70 to 80 PennDOT workers who had walked off the job Friday as a protest to the unfairly reassignment of an employee returned Monday under a court injunction ordering them back to work.

headline: 3 on council have records subpoenaed
abstract: Campaign records for 1979 have been subpoenaed for the three city councilmen, Council President George X. Schwartz, Majority Leader Harry P. Jannotti and Councilman Louis C. Johanson, implicated in the Federal Bureau of Investigation "sting" operation, an action providing the first hard evidence that a federal grand jury has begun work here on the Abscam scandal.

headline: OIC: An unfulfilled dream
abstract: The Reverend Leon H. Sullivan, founder of Opportunities for Industrial Centers, a nonprofit agency providing job training for minorities, has never been on the agency's payroll, though executive director Elton Jolly admitted Sullivan recieves vouchers for services rendered, and that the agency covers his travel expenses while on OIC business. Sullivan is a paid pastor of Zion Baptist Church and serves on the board of several corporations, including General Motors, for pay.

headline: Who Will Be Reagan's Running Mate?
abstract: This piece, written by an astrologer, discusses Ronald Reagan needing only 48 more Republican delegates to secure the Republican nomination for President, and that attention will soon shift to the selection of his running mate, the Vice Presidential candidate.  The article continues to find linkages between the astrological comparison between Reagan and the candidates for Vice President to find lasting and important relationships.

headline: Schools, rumors, fear in U. Darby
abstract: Even before Upper Darby school officials announced their plans to close four elementary schools last month, the rumors had begun to circulate.

headline: PennDOT gets gree light to purchase 1,000 buses
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed SB 381, authorizing the PA Department of Transportation to purchase 1000 buses for use by 16 local mass transit agencies, including the Harrisburg Capital Area Transit system. Upon receipt of the buses, each agency will reimburse the state 3.3 percent of the total cost of the $128 million project. Thornburgh said the approach will allow for the purchase of buses at the lowest possible cost as well as meet common transit needs.

headline: 4 High Pennsylvania Democrats Indicted: Camiel, Fumo, Scarcelli, Nolan accused of fraud
abstract: Philadelphia's former Democratic boss, Peter J. Camiel, his patronage chief, PA Aenator Vincent J. Fumo and two other important PA Democrats were indicted by a federal grand jury yesterday on charges of defrauding the state.  The cost to the taxpayers was more than $225,000.

headline: Lottery case lawyer files dismissal motion
abstract: A defense lawyer has filed a motion in the Common Pleas Court of Dauphin County to dismiss the Pennsylvania lottery scandal from court, alleging the state should never have brought the charges in Dauphin County and does not set forth a crime. Attorney William Costopoulos said defense attorneys of fellow defendants would most likley follow suit. Among the six defendents accused of fixing the PA lottery on April 24 is Edward Plevel, suspended lottery bureau district manager.

headline: Why group homes
abstract: A resident writes that an earlier editorial blaming conditions at Pennhurst on the PA Department of Public Welfare and the Office of the Special Master incorrectly excludes the governor and legislature from blame. Both are content with the status quo, despite findings by the Federal Court and Third Circuit Court of Appeals. Considering individual needs in the right to choose, which Judge Broderick ordered, will result in individuals being locally placed in a community home rather an institution like Pennhurst.

headline:
Spanish teacher sponsors relative
Ex-refugee aids Gap Cubans
abstract: Lebanon Valley College faculty member, Dr. Angela Aguirre, recently discovered her 21-year-old niece at Fort Indiantown Gap.  Aguirre studies Pineyro and agrees with his support of Cuban freedom.

headline: PennDot Planning Pothold Assault On Area's 'Burma Road,' Route 51
abstract: After years of roads crumbling in winter from heavy traffic and water accumulation underneath the roads, PennDot has finally alotted $7.8 million in a contract with Trumbull Corporation to add drainage piping and reconstruct the roads to better facilitate runoff. Jefferson Borough recently filed a suit naming PennDot as a defendant, claiming that water from a nearby shopping mall has flooded a local creek and is costing the borough money in repairs. In the drainage plan with Trumbull, PennDot engineers admitted they do not think the creek can handle an increase in the amount of runoff.

headline: 8 named in FBI probe - 9th person linked to bribery case
abstract: A 9th member of Congress may be involved in political corruption according to the investigation of FBI while the 8 names have already become public.

headline: Lottery Decides Candidate Audits
abstract: After the April 22 primary, the Department of Sate will hold a lottery, the random drawing of 10% of all statewide primary candidates for independent auditing of their campaign expenses.  This audit will performed by Coopers & Lybrand.

headline: Why Ronald Reagan Will Be The Next President
abstract: This opinion gives a special report argues that consistently underrated by his opponents, Ronald Reagan is the Republican nominee most likely to win over hardcore Democratic voters.

headline: The merger act isn't working
abstract: A resident of Swarthmore resents the editors' opinion that residents should not protest the School Board's plan to close their community school. The resident cites statistics from the PA Department of Education, Bureau of Planning and Educational Statistics, available from the Pennsylvania Economy League, that show the 1968 Reorganization Act has failed. Reorganization has led to greater inequity between districts. If the school were in one of the wealthier districts, editors would not hold the same opinion.

headline: Potholes end erosion on Route 51 are targets of PennDot's $7.8 million rehabilitation project
abstract: A photograph depicts a car driving down the road from the vantage point of the shoulder.

headline: A black party? Not included, but cheering still
abstract: A citizen writes to the editor that we should support black political unity. In absence of it, there are only angry, terrified sects. She would much rather they have power and confidence than become isolated, bitter, and vengeful.

headline: Lottery Scandal Didn't Lead to Resignation, Says Cohen
abstract: Secretary of Revenue Howard Cohen's resignation was announced by PA Governor Thornburgh along  with grand jury findings that an April 24th lottery drawing was rigged. The timing sparked speculation that Cohen, who was responsible for the bureau of state lotteries, was responsible for the rigging, though he denied any relationship. As secretary, Cohen said he brought integrity back to the Bureau in addition to restructuring and eliminating jobs to make the Bureau more efficient.

headline: Why Some Black Voters Pick Reagan
abstract: Columnist Mr. Raspberry tells of a friend he knows who is voting for Presidential candidate Ronald Reagan. A rarity among black voters, this voter says she has other friends, including a Congress of Racial Equality Member, who are going to vote the same way. The friend believes Jimmy Carter has only treated her people with pity, perpetuating a crippling welfare cycle. She would have voted for US Sen. Edward Kennedy had he won the primary.

headline: Vote Down Teacher Residency Bill
abstract: This editorial argues that the decision on whether teachers of a school district must reside in that district is one which should be made by the district’s school board and not by the General Assembly.

headline: Potholes Forever
abstract: This editorial criticized PA Department of Transportation because there are always potholes on Pittsburgh’s roads.

headline: A circus
abstract: Foreign correspondents, including chairman of the European Broadcasting Union, Vittorio Boni, were on hand to cover the GOP Convention. Their reactions however were shock and distaste. Many, covering their first US political convention, noted the difference between American and European politics.

headline: Luck of draw puts Schuylkill man atop ballot
abstract: For the Republican U.S. Senate nomination, Bertasavage, Schuylkill County, may draw a substantial number of votes on Election Day, because he was placed at the top of the ballot, and that position is usually good for 100,000 votes from people who tend to vote for the No. 1 candidate.  This article also illustrates several arguments made by Bertasavage.

headline: Widely Known Names Blur 14th District Race
abstract: For the Democratic race for Congress in the 14th District, Bill Coyne is the only candidate with political experience, but he faces the biggest problem.  He accuses his two competitors of trying to confuse the voters by capitalizing on their names, which are well-known names of former or current officials.  Similar situation also happens in the 18th, 20th, 22nd and 25th District.

headline: WANTED: A State Librarian
abstract: This letter argues that the PA State Library merits attention in order to provide the lifelong learning.

headline: Reaction is favorable: Photo licenses clicking along
abstract: PA’s controversial photo license program for drivers is clicking away at a statewide pace of 150,000 renewals a month while legislative critics mull fresh attempts to kill it.  The state Transportation Department survey shows 91% favorable to the program.

headline: A gutsy pledge for a ‘pol’ to make
abstract: This editorial argues that Delaware County Councilman Harold Haabestad’s pledge is commendable.  Haabestad says that in his campaign for a U.S. Senate seat he will not accept contributions from anyone doing business with his county.

headline: Major Shift Underway
abstract: The editorial board sees the landslide Republican victories at both the federal and state levels as a positive mandate for conservatism from voters demanding a return to fiscal stability and military strength. Though the board doubts the party registration of voters will change, it expects conservatism is here to stay for a while, and hopes that in PA legislators in Harrisburg can get down to solving serious problems created by decades of Democratic control.

headline: With Connally out of the race, Shuster will back GOP’s choice
abstract: U.S. Representative Bud Shuster of Bedford County says "1980 should be a Republican year and I look forward to vigorously supporting the nominee of our party."

headline: We must fight move designed to destroy education of Blacks
abstract: The editorial board notes that blood, sweat, and tears are required to help expand and protect affirmative action in every field, especially education. It is unfair, according to the board, that white schools receive less pressure from the government to desegregate than black schools. The students at Cheyney State College in PA filed in federal district court against the US Department of Education and the Commonwealth for skewed "desegregation" policies negatively affecting their school welfare.

headline: Rebuilding El cars adds extra years to track life
abstract: A Southeastern PA Transit Authority plan to spend $5 million in order to renovate 50 cars on its Market-Frankford line aims to extend the life of the cars by about 8 years. SEPTA has received funds for the project from the federal Urban Mass Transit Administration and the PA Department of Transportation. SEPTA has applied for an additional federal grant to allow the renovation of another 20 cars and more efficient repair equipment.

headline: A new regional partnership
abstract: Editors encourage the work of US Rep. from PA Robert W. Edgar, in leading the Northeast-Midwest Congressional Coalition to determine the impact of the recession on the regions. In the past, such studies have been called divisive, however the editors believe it is necessary to determine how past policies have been biased against different regions, and how policies might be changed to bring all regions onto a more equal footing. The Coalition will present its findings to each Presidential candidate for them to offer a posed response.

headline: Marks, DiCarlo await official count
abstract: Claims are being made by both candidates in the 24th US House Congressional District of PA that encompasses Mercer, Crawford, and Erie Counties. Democrat David DiCarlo, appears to be slightly behind incumbent Republican Marks, however DiCarlo's aides allege errors in counting were made. Both candidates plan to challenge results of the Erie County Elections Office when they are released.

headline: 'Wolf packs' label dehumanizing
abstract: A citizen agrees with Pamela Smith's recent article pointing out racist undertones in labeling black teenage gangs 'wolf packs.' She believes the economy, inflation, and unemployment are causing the rise in crimes by teens. Most disturbing is the recent return of Councilman Harry Jannotti to City Council, despite having blatantly committed crimes. The real wolf-pack is the crowd of 'right-wingers' around President-elect Ronald Reagan.

headline: $11.8 Billion Plan Faces June 30 Deadline      Budget Agony Time Hangs
abstract: State Congress is debating Gov. Thornburgh’s proposed budget.  Specifically, there is disagreement concerning funding for highway improvement, for the General Fund, and for a pay increase for state judges.  Also, Senate approved an environmental bill that would track hazardous waste from the chemical plant to its disposal site.

headline: Refusing breath test urged as drunk-driving evidence
abstract: State Rep. E. Raymond Lynch has introduced a bill that would allow a motorist's refusal to take a breathalyzer test to be used against him as evidence in a drunk-driving case.  Other bills have also been introduced recently includes bills relating to tax exemption, election forms, corrections workers, residential facilities, finance charges, and mortgage prepayments.

headline: A Reagan Revolution, Perhaps, but Not and Ideological Mandate
abstract: A columnist points out that despite Ronald Reagan's election to the presidency and the changeover in Senate majority, Reagan's win is not much compared to the margins of victory of those gone before him. The columnist cannot understand how this message conveys an ideological mandate. Voters, looking for change, can now look to Reagan, who has the chance to start fresh with the economy and American hostage situation in Iran.

headline: Maureen Reagan, daughter of the Republican presidential candidate, addresses press conference at Wilkes-Barre Scranton International Airport.
abstract: A photograph of Maureen Reagan, the daughter of Republican presidential candidate Ronald Reagan, captures her address during a press conference at the Wilkes-Barre International Airport. With her are US Senator for PA John Heinz, Lieutenant Governor William Scranton and US Senator for PA Richard Schweiker. The group barn-stormed the state today drumming up last minute support for the GOP ticket.

headline: York County hires accounting firm to recover federal - program funds
abstract: David M. Griffith and Associates, a Chicago accounting firm was hired by York County commissioners to recover funds which the county has spent in connection with administering federal programs.

headline: 17 legislators seek role in auto emissions suits
abstract: Seventeen state lawmakers opposed to an auto emissions inspection program asked federal court to allow them to intervene in lawsuits.  They hope to protect the interests of Pennsylvania motorists.

headline: Responsibility to commuters
abstract: This editorial argues that Westmoreland County Commissioners and the Westmoreland County Transit Authority always don’t have courage to meet their responsibilities to the commuting public.

headline: A wealth of good impressions as Thornburgh enters limelight
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh is a moderate on some issues and more conservative on others than he appeared in his 1978 campaign against Pittsburgh Mayor Pete Flaherty. Thornburgh stands by the GOP Presidential candidate Ronald Reagan, and his goal to lower taxes through less government. But after Three Mile Island, he is not supportive of nuclear energy. His most conservative aim is to cut the state's welfare rolls, legislation for which is locked in the PA Senate after passing the House.

headline: Maureen Reagan, daughter of the Republican presidential candidate, addresses press conference at Wilkes-Barre Scranton International Airport.
abstract: A photograph of Maureen Reagan, the daughter of Republican presidential candidate Ronald Reagan, captures her address during a press conference at the Wilkes-Barre International Airport. With her are US Senator John Heinz, Lieutenant Governor William Scranton and US Senator Richard Schweiker. The group barn-stormed the state today drumming up last minute support for the GOP ticket.

headline: York County Vote Machine Is Defective
abstract: Three voting machines in a northern York County township were impounded by the county Elections Board during the balloting on April 22 after one of the machines was found to be defective.

headline: Thornburgh Signs Rail Network Bill
abstract: Governor Thornburg (PA) signed a bill to replace the Liquor Control Board identification system with photo drivers licenses from Ohio, Indiana, Michigan, Illinois, West Virginia and Kentucky. Thornburgh also vetoed a bill relating to prisoner visits and passed bills relating to: taxes collected through sales, beer importing, physician licensing, and historic district ordnances

headline: 4 firms sue to block new water limits
abstract: Four Montgomery County food processing companies filed suit in federal court, claiming the new water regulations stipulated by the Delaware River Basin Commission are unconstitutional and invalid. The suit alleges the metering of water is arbitrarily defined and would cause economic adverse affects for the companies. DRBC spokesman Dawes Thompson declined comment until the commissioners have read the suit. A hearing will be held January 15th under US District Judge Charles Weiner.

headline: Roses and Thorns
abstract: This article discusses things which have been going well (white roses) and those that have not (thorns).  Roses currently are York's designation as the Outstanding City of the year for the annual statewide conference on urban economic development, York Area Transportation Authority sayings its busses are making proper stops at Delco Plaza and AMP Inc's plans to build two more plants in York County.  Thorns are Police Chief Norman Lippy's plans to restrict parking at the intersection of Susquehanna Trail and Cemetery Roads in Strinestown and the Pennsylvania legislature taking $560,000 out of the state police account for other purposes.

headline: Abolition - 200th anniversary to be marked
abstract: On March 1, 1780, 200 years ago tomorrow, PA became the first state to legislate the abolition of slavery.  The legislation was proposed by George Bryan.  There will be a ceremony tomorrow in Independence Square in Philadelphia.

headline: Meese, Baker get key Reagan posts
abstract: President-elect Ronald Reagan appointed aide and chief of staff during his term as Governor of California, Edwin Meese, and James Baker III, campaign manager for President Ford and George Bush, to be two of his White House advisers. Reagan will visit Washington to meet with economic advisers to discuss tax cuts and a pledge to cut the federal budget by 2 percent. The Heritage Foundation recommends Reagan phase out the Department of Energy in favor of nuclear research.

headline: Zemprelli faces challenge from freshman legislator
abstract: With less than three weeks to go before the April 22 primary election, PA Senate Majority Leader Edward P. Zemprelli appears to be the only key legislator facing a serious challenge.  He is being opposed by PA Senator Robb Austin, a freshman legislator.

headline: A Look at ‘Acid Rain’
abstract: There is an increasing interest these days in the environmental threats posed by "acid rain."  The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency held the nation’s first interstate "summit conference" on acid rain, and Lieutenant governor William Scranton also has spoken of the frustration.

headline: Season near to fix roads
abstract: This editorial argues that since spring is approaching, it is a good season for PA Department of Transportation to repair the lamentable roads.

headline: About this voter's guide
abstract: The Voter's Guide was prepared by the joint efforts of the League of Women Voters, Allegheny County Council, and the League of Women Voter's Education Fund. The nonpartisan organization attempts to promote political awareness and responsibility. Biographical material for the guide was supplied by candidates including occupation, education, training, and experienced for the positions of US Congress Representative, PA Senate and House Representative, PA attorney general, auditor general, and treasurer.

headline: Merry Endorsed
abstract: The editorial board endorses Jim Merry, former Linesville Borough council president, leader of the community's senior citizens housing development group, and secretary of the Crawford County Industrial Authority,  for representation of the 5th district in the General Assembly. The board believes Merry's credentials and trusted status as a businessman make him a good candidate.

headline: Zemprelli hits Street switch to GOP, hints at 'opportunism'
abstract: Democrats unable to identify philosophical differences between their party and claims of support for the poor made by now Republican PA Senator-elect Milton Street, surmise his switch from Democrats is for personal gain. Street is promised chairmanship of the Housing and Urban Affairs Committee. He argues the Republicans are more apt to support blacks, though Democrats say he is trying to obtain support to run against Democratic US Senator William Gray in the next election year.,

headline: South St. property in legal limbo
abstract: State Representative Frank Salvatore's (Republican- Philadelphia) amendment prevented the sale of two pieces of expensive real estate in Queen Village. The amendment prevents the sale of the property for profit reasons. The Urban Community Alternatives Inc. from Society Hill said they could not purchase the property since the money could not be raised.

headline: Acid - rain is raised in coal bill
abstract: Environmental groups are vowing to defeat President Carter’s $10 billion program to convert utilities to coal, because the proposal does not impose the safeguards they consider essential to protect against a growing acid - rain problem.

headline: Sending a clear message
abstract: The editorial board encourages Secretary of Transportation Thomas Larson and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to show the Legislature they mean business during the next term. To meet the needs of the financially ailing Department of Transportation, Thornburgh proposed a 5 percent flat tax with a six percent sales tax on gas, replacing an 11 cent flat tax. However, the Legislature refused to grant the proposal allocating an additional $100 million to the Department before the end of its term.

headline: About this voter's guide
abstract: The Voter's Guide was prepared by the League of Women Voters, Allegheny County Council, and the League of Women Voter's Education Fund. The nonpartisan LWV organization attempts to promote political awareness and responsibility. Biographical material for the guide was supplied by candidates including occupation, education, training, and experience for US Congress, the PA Legislature, PA attorney general, auditor general, and treasurer.

headline: Mezvinsky Asks Labor’s Support
abstract: Area union officials applauded but did not endorse Edward Mezvinsky yesterday as he brought his campaign for the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senator to Western PA.

headline: City flood project may fall victim to bickering
abstract: The $86.1 million Harrisburg flood control project, which the House of Representatives plans to take up this week as part of a huge works bill, may again become the innocent victim of those in the Carter administration, environmental groups and Congress itself who want to reform the way federal water resources improvements are funded.

headline: Protecting the homeowner
abstract: PA Senator H. Craig Lewis introduced legislation to fix PA tax-sale law that allows houses to be sold for back taxes, no matter what the amount. County officials who collected taxes rejected to the work involved and persuaded the Pa House members to strip the notification provision from the bill. The new bill before the legislation includes a notice to tax payers 10 days before tax sale.

headline: Bear Cub Killing Helps Only Hunters
abstract: A citizen argues that legalizing an illegal act as an answer to continued violation of law is not the best way to deal with violations. By legalizing bear cub hunting in PA, a state with more bear hunters than there are cubs, the state is ensuring that bears don't stand a chance!

headline: SEPTA fix-up put near billion
abstract: South Eastern PA Transit Authority officials hope to establish a benchmark for federal funding after new general manager David Gunn stopped the practice of making a wish list budget and order staffers to think more realistically. 80 percent of the funds for SEPTA's plans to advance, renovate or acquire capital is expected to come from the federal Urban Mass Transportation Administration over the next six years. Supplemental funds will come from the state and local governments.

headline: Abrupt Switch on Senate Race - Governor Backs Open Primary
abstract: In an abrupt about - face, Thornburgh decided to switch and join the state Grand Old Party in providing for an open primary April 22 for U.S. senator.

headline: Missing Reagan frustrates a debate
abstract: Ronald Reagan, the pollster's favorite in Iowa's Republican precinct, was absent in the debate.  However, since the Iowa competition is primarily a test of organizational strength and old loyalties, it is not likely to be markedly altered by Reagan's no-show at the debate.  While the other 5 candidates didn't have much to debate with each other, Anderson was the only one to condemn Reagan's positions and to risk sharp, direct criticism of the fellow debaters.

headline: Harrisburg flood-control project survives 'merit test' on House floor
abstract: Maneuvering by U.S. Rep. Allen Ertel, D-Montoursville, helps pave the way for the Harrisburg flood-control project to survive a 'merit test' on the House floor, helping to assure that floodwall protection for South Harrisburg could be placed on the Corps of Engineers construction list this year.

headline: Senate Oks bill to help facilitate second mortgages
abstract: The PA Senate approved a bill that will allow first time homeowners to apply for a second mortgage wihtout having to go through the same bank or savings institution that holds the first mortgage. Senator Michael Schaefer (Democrat-Allegheny) was the prime sponsor of the bill.

headline: Better Than Nothing
abstract: Although the system to be provided by the Lanscaster County commissioners to monitor emissions from the nuclear plants is not convinced the right one, there is assurance in the fact they are grappling with the problem.

headline: SEPTA isn't entirely to blame; To The Editor
abstract: A Southeastern PA Transit Authority rider directs commuters to complain to elected federal and state officials, not to one another. To the resident, the $300 million commuter tunnel seems like a waste of money--SEPTA could have bought a lot of buses, trains, and hired police to keep the service clean and orderly for that amount of money. On the other hand, Washington has paid more attention to acquiring nuclear bombs than funding mass transit.

headline: Abscam and The Delaware Valley
abstract: This editorial argues that PA’s justice system should grind forward, after several Philadelphia public officials have been "stung" by the Federal Bureau of Investigation scam, to make them pay price for undermining public confidence on government.

headline: Moorhead Faces Struggle Against Coyne
abstract: William S. Moorhead was so magic that wan one in each of the last 11 congressional elections.  This year, though, the magic is in danger of losing its powers.  Tired of running at 56, he has passed the baton to his son, William Moorhead III.  But his son is regarded as a long shot in his race against City Councilman William Coyne for the Democratic nomination.  This article also describes the campaigns in other four congressional districts in Allegheny County.

headline: House Advances City Flood Project
abstract: The U.S. House approved a water resources bill that would allow about $4 billion worth of public works projects and studies.  A Harrisburg flood control proposal would get $71.3 million in federal money to be matched by $14.8 million in state and local funds if Congress and the state later appropriate the money.

headline: The commuter tunnel: boom
abstract: The Center City Rail Tunnel is under construction to connect Penn Central and Reading Railroads so trains can connect directly into one another to eliminate delays from switching between the two terminals. Crtiics say the money being put into the new station is needed for repairs of other transit services. Others say the project could be a catalyst to start funding necessary repairs.

headline: Abortion Battler Blind To History
abstract: The author feels that state representative Gregg Cunningham is misguided in his understanding of the principles of the Constitution.  The author is reacting to Cunningham's involvement in a showing of an anti-abortion film.  She feels by not promoting contraceptives, he is keeping women slaves to children.

headline: For student aid: Know what to do, when to do it, how to do it right
abstract: null

headline: How oil costs drive landlords to abandon all hope
abstract: The article interviews several landlords who all state that high heat oil costs are not allowing them to make any profit on rentals.  They fear that abandonment may be the only solution and that cases of abandonment will increase as oil prices continue to rise.

headline: SEPTA Strike Grinds to a Halt: Guv Gets Credit for Contract
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh was credited for making suggestions and helping the transit worker's 19-day strike against Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority's city transit division come to an end. The deal involved SEPTA dropping the need for part-time employees and reducing the pay raise from 16 percent to 14.5 percent over the two years of the new contract.

headline: Sen. Lewis files suit in attempt to get pay data on state attorneys
abstract: The minority chairman of the PA state Senate Appropriations Committee filed suit in Commonwealth Court in an attempt to force General Counsel Jay Walden to release the names and salaries of state attorneys. PA Senator H Craig Lewis said Waldman Gov. Dick Thornburgh's top legal adviser refused repeated requests to provide the information. The Thornburgh administration said such information was available to Lewis from other sources.

headline: Private Liquor Stores in Pa.? Local Legislators Divided: Only Two Fully Support Thornburgh Plan
abstract: Lancaster County's state legislators are divided on whether to support or not Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal to reform the Liquor Control Board. The governor's proposal would allow privately-owned retail liquor stores, while the state would retain the wholesale system, replacing the three-member Board with a five-member Board, and expanding state wholesale warehouses from the present five to 10 or 13. The bill was introduced in the state Senate.

headline: Giles to Assume Council Office
abstract: The April 21st non-legislative session of the Harrisburg City Council will involve the administration of the oath of office to Robert E. Giles, who was named last week to serve out the unexpired term of former Council Vice President Wesly Plummer. At the session, the council will also discuss the roles of the three remaining Harrisburg Parking Authority, amid a recent controversy concerning the operation of the municipal parking system.

headline: State Reapportionment Drawing Near for Pols
abstract: The potentially acrimonious process of redrawing the political landscape of the city and state, known as reapportionment, began yesterday. A state commission with redefining the state 203 state and 50 PA Senate seats met in Harrisburg and voted to officially accept data from the 1980 census. Because of the population decrease the state will lose two of its US House seats.

headline: Abortion fight
abstract: The handwriting is on the wall for Pittsburgh's abortion clinics is on the wall. They are actively trying to raised money to keep abortion legal. A numbers of pro-choice candidates lost this past November. The President is against abortion. Anti-abortion legislation is close to passing, and things look bleak for pro-choicers.

headline: Free Education
abstract: Simplest way to solve the schools' problems is to assess an extra charge on those deriving the greatest benefit, the parents of the children attending the schools. The Author suggest public schools should no longer be free.

headline: Huge coal-shipping terminal to be built in Port Richmond
abstract: A coal-shipping terminal to be built in the Port Richmond section of Philadelphia could funnel up to $200 million a year into the region's economy, according to Green Administration estimates.  Plans for the terminal, to be located on a 130-acre site covering much of the rail yards in Port Richmond, were to be announced by Mayor Green and officials of Atlantis Terminal Corporation, a New York-based company which has leased the grounds from Conrail.

headline: SEPTA Strike Grinds to a Halt: SEPTA Forgives Us Our Transpasses
abstract: The March Transpasses from Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, not used during the strike, can be presented at several locations for a $17 credit on an April Transpass, or can be mailed directly to SEPTA for a $17 refund. April passes are on sale for $30, instead of the usual $32, because the strike continued into the first two days of the month

headline: Senate panel Oks revised crimes codes
abstract: The fundamentalist Moral Majority and American Civil Liberties Union are opposing a significant rewrite of the federal criminal code. The U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee approved the revisions on Wednesday and sent the measure to the full Senate. Some of the major revisions are elimination of parole for federal offenders and a more uniform system for sentencing on many criminal offenses. The revised criminal code was produced by a coalition of liberal Democrats and conservative Republicans.

headline: 'Product Liability' Bill Ok'd by House Insurance Group
abstract: A PA state House committee approved a compromise bill that would limit consumers' abilities to sue manufacturers over defective goods. The committee approved the measure despite complaints from a business spokesman that it had been watered down it no longer gave manufacturers much protection against frivolous lawsuits by consumers.

headline: Glancey and Smith Running Head to Head in Heated Race; The heated see-saw battle of the Third Congressional District between Joe Smith and David Glancey has become a crucial test of Mayor Green's political effectiveness.
abstract: Non-partisan organized labor is emerging as the bridge between voters in the Third Congressional District and "Republican" candidate Joseph Smith, the long-time Democratic state senator from Kensington.  City labor leaders are said to be bent on sending a message to Mayor Bill Green and other skeptics about labor's clout in Philadelphia and Smith has been tapped as their vehicle.  Organized labor is upset with the Green Administration for pushing Senator Lynch onto the side of Green's long-time aide and ally, Democratic City Chairman David Glancey.

headline: State Redistricting Delayed Until 1982
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislation has put off the subject of congressional reapportionment until next year.  The article provides further detail about why legislators have decided to postpone the reapportionment.

headline: Abortion foes rake 2 senators
abstract: 10,000 protestors from PA marched in Washington, D.C. to support an anti-abortion amendment.  US Senators John Heinz and Arlen Spector were confronted by protestors and tried to handle the situation diplomatically even though they disagreed with the protestors

headline: Freedom of expression Suffers in Harrisburg
abstract: For an agency that oversees how students are taught how to write, the PA Education Department's pen keep getting in trouble. Most recently it was the gag order issued by PA Education Secretary Robert Scanlon against presidents of state-owned colleges that provoked a public furor. PA Governor Dick Thornburgh likes to have control over what everyone in the state government is saying.

headline: If you want to testify, here's what to say
abstract: Hearings on the Susquehanna nuclear power plant will begin at 9a.m. and are schedule for every Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday in October. Individuals not in designated interview groups will be given two chances to give comments which must be limited to five minutes or less.

headline: SEPTA strike had no winners
abstract: The author argues that there are no real winners in the Transit Workers Union's 19 day strike against the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority. The strike cost the strikers in pay, the city of Philadelphia in wage tax revenues, and the stores in lost sales. He ends by assuring that the poor riding public inconvenienced by the strike will soon be asked to pay 75 cents for riding the transit system.

headline: Sentence Guidelines Face Double-Barrel Challenge
abstract: The House and the Senate moved similarly to set aside initial proposals of the state Sentencing Commission and direct a resubmission of new standards before the end of the year. Unless rejected by both of these, the guidelines, which take into consideration a number of factors in fixing minimum sentences, will take effect on July 23.

headline: Protection Taxes
abstract: Taxes aimed at preventing people from hurting themselves aren't working. People still drink booze, smoke, and gamble despite increasing financial penalties imposed by government. Prohibition via taxation and regulation continues, however, government uses guilt feelings and self-righteousness as a lever to gain revenue. The government should not try to protect people from themselves and let people govern themselves.

headline: Glancey boosts Smith supporter
abstract: Democratic ward leaders will meet to choose a candidate for the 4th District State Senate seat vacant by the election of PA Senator Joseph Smith to Congress in July. Democratic City Committee chairman David Glancey and other sources predict their choice will be Nicholas Stampone leader of the 41st ward for the past 17 years and committeeman for 33 years.

headline: State to mark 300th Anniversary Quietly: Its Taste for Big Parties Tempered by Economic Squeeze
abstract: The state Historical and Museum Commission will celebrate Pennsylvania's 300th anniversary with a small ceremony to be attended by Governor Thornburgh.  There will be no large parties due to a reduced state budget.  England gave William Penn the charter for Pennsylvania in 1681 as payment for a debt.  The article outlines various events planned to commemorate the anniversary

headline: Abortion Hearing Draws a Crowd
abstract: A standing room only crowd of some 200 abortion advocates and opponents packed a House committee hearing on proposed legislation aimed at making abortions difficult to obtain for all PA women. The legislation is the strictest introduced in any state and tries to thwart as much as possible Roe vs. Wade.

headline: Funds OK'd for school's conversion
abstract: The PA Housing Finance Agency has approved $5,240,000 in financing for converting the Edison Junior High School into a rent-subsidized apartment building for families and the elderly.

headline: Ignore Bills, Say Customers of Met-Ed's
abstract: A group of Metropolitan Edison Company's customers are encouraging non payment of their utilities bills to protest rate hikes as a result of the Three Mile Island nuclear accident.  Metropolitan Edison owns the Three Mile Island nuclear plant and is partially responsible for clean-up costs.

headline: SEPTA ties fare hike to good service
abstract: At the first in a series of public hearings, Southeastern PA Transportation Authority's general manager promised better service in return for the higher fares that the transit authority hopes will be in effect July 1. SEPTA is seeking to raise the base fare 5 cents, to 70 cents, and to eliminate student discounts, which now are 30 cents. Although the proposals are expected to draw sharp criticism in the city, officials faced little opposition last night in the Chester County hearing.

headline: Sentence Guides Proposed
abstract: The State Sentencing Commission proposed stricter guidelines for sentencing criminals based on a report that cited disparities in sentencing between counties.  Unless it is vetoed by the state legislature, it will go into effect automatically.

headline: Public is high on the idea
abstract: Pennsylvania residents like Governor Thornburgh's proposal to do away with state controled liquor stores.  The article interviews citizens in Philadelphia as to why they don't like the current State Stores.

headline: Glancey wraps it up with Kennedy rally; Smith does it quietly
abstract: US Senator Edward Kennedy gave a rousing conclusion to David B Glancey's congressional campaign, telling a rally that the Philadelphia Democrat was needed in Washington to help fight the budget and tax-cut proposals of the Reagan Administration. The polls will open tomorrow.

headline: State Top Court Bid Announced
abstract: State Representative William Hutchinson (R-Schuylkill County) has announced his candidacy for one of two seats available on the state Supreme Court.

headline: Abortion Measure Is Vetoed
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh vetoed the toughest anti-abortion legislation in the country. The governor's action is almost certain to lead to attempts by anti-abortion legislators for an override of the veto, but the bill itself, Senate Bill 742, in its passage through the House and Senate had fewer supporters than are necessary to win a veto fight.  The article goes further into detail about Thornburgh's veto message.

headline: Get politics out of school
abstract: Two Harrisburg school board members, representing both major political parties, have come to the conclusion that partisan politics does not belong in education.  School board president Miles Thomas, Republican, and member John Hope, Democrat, recently witnessed their board agonize through 24 ballots before Thomas was finally selected as president of the board.  Political infighting played a huge part in the impasse.  The article goes into further detail about how the school needs to separate from politics.

headline: In one western Pennsylvania town, talk's not cheap
abstract: Pennsylvania's Public Utility Commission granted the latest increase in rates in Big Run despite a history of woeful phone service in the area.  The rates on minimum monthly charges for a private line have been increasing rapidly, even though the commission found the services to be inadequate.  Citizens Utilities, the telephone company used by the commission, says that it is that high because Big Run Phone serves an area of 60 square miles; but cities 10 miles away do not suffer from price gouging like Big Run.

headline: SEPTA: Let's go back to square one
abstract: The mass transit system in the Philadelphia area needs radical new solutions to its problem.  In 1963, it was thought that a public authority and public ownership would liberate the region from the problems of separate companies, undercapitalization, and mismanagement.  However, the creation of Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority has not improved the situation one iota.

headline: Sentencing: Guidelines Still Inappropriate
abstract: The editors oppose new sentencing guidelines, designed to create uniformity among judges, based on the fact that it takes away a judge's ability to sentence based on circumstances.  They urge lawmakers to reject the guidelines.

headline: Record Keeping for the Government
abstract: United States Senator John East introduced legislation that would place a three year limit on record keeping requirements that federal agencies can impose on private citizens and a similar limit on the power of federal agencies to bring civil actions for nonwillful violations of agency rules. The introduction of this legislation is a result of the numerous complaints from small business owners.

headline: Glancy and Smith Running Head to Head in Heated Race; The heated see-saw battle fo the Third Congressional District between Joe Smith and David Glancey has become a crucial test of Mayor Green's political effectiveness.
abstract: Non-partisan organized labor is emerging as the bridge between voters in the Third Congressional District and "Republican" candidate Joseph Smith, the long-time Democratic state senator from Kensington.  City labor leaders are said to be bent on sending a message to Mayor Bill Green and other skeptics about labor's clout in Philadelphia and Smith has been tapped as their vehicle.  Organized labor is upset with the Green Administration for pushing Senator Lynch onto the side of Green's long-time aide and ally, Democratic City Chairman David Glancey.

headline: State Worker Total Declines As Pay Rises
abstract: The Governor Annual Work Force Report showed that the number of state employees has been declining since 1975, while salaries and benefits have increased.  The article details the report.

headline: Abortion opponents win test vote
abstract: The PA State House rejected an amendment to a bill that would water down legislation that would make it more difficult for a woman to get an abortion.  The bill requires that there is a 24 hour waiting period before an abortion is performed, that a minor have the consent of both parents before having an abortion, and reports of all abortions be made to the state Health Department within 15 days of the procedure.  The article details several other restrictions in the bill.

headline: Good time
abstract: State Representative Joe Petrarca has submitted a measure to allow the state to use off-track betting as a revenue base to provide aid for schools, at a time when school taxes are about at the limit of taxpayers' willingness or ability to pay them. Petrarca predicts that within five years the state could realize annual revenues of $905 million. The editorial recommends state legislators and the governor to give every consideration possible for the bill.

headline: Industrial-Strength Cleanup: Utility Groups Sees 'Some Financial Support' on TMI-2, Doesn't Say How much
abstract: An industry task force report prompted the board of the Edison Electric Institute to recognize the need for the industry's commitment to some financial support for the decontamination cleanup of Three Mile Island's Unit 2. However, a suggestion by PA Public Utility Commission that a reasonable industry contribution was imminent was dismissed by the EEI board. The task force gives six recommendations for the board to accept, and suggests federal assistance would be difficult and require legislation.

headline: SEPTA's New Buses
abstract: The editorial praises SEPTA (transportation system) for buying 298 new buses from General Motors rather than Grumman, which they feel has inferior buses.

headline: Serious crime increases in state
abstract: Serious crime in PA during the first half of 1981 topped last year's record levels by 3.1 percent. Murders increased by 11.4 percent. Rapes by 4. Robberies were also up by 16.4 percent. Vehicle theft and arson were down though.

headline: Reform vital for no-fault auto law
abstract: The editors support proposed automobile insurance legislation that would reduce the amount of benefits accident victims could receive from insurance companies.  The editors feel that many have abused the current insurance law to get benefits they didn't deserve, which costs everyone money in higher rates.

headline: Goehringer Commits Hersey: GOP Candidate Zap Establishment
abstract: Fred Goehringer is conducting an unorthodox campaign, so unorthodox that he may soon be offered a job in the Reagan cabinet, or a free vacation in Hawaii, just to get him out of town.  He seems to be campaigning against the Bipartisan Establishment in Pittsburgh, a stratagem no other Republican candidate for mayor has ever dared to pursue.

headline: State's lawmakers expedite redistricting
abstract: PA lawmakers tired of waiting for a plan from Washington, have started looking for ways to reapportion the state's congressional districts and eliminate two of the 25 seats. In Washington, the state's congressmen have been busy redrawing their district lines so a plan they all like can be sent to the Legislature. The PA state Senate leadership is growing impatient waiting for a plan and has begun working on its own version.

headline: Abortions: Its foes and supporters square off
abstract: A "New Right" coalition comprised of socially conservative legislators, backed by fundamentalist Christians, members of the Moral Majority, a variety of anti-abortion groups, and the Roman Catholic Church is flexing its muscles within Washington. The group's mission is to save the American family from a downhill slide into amorality and immorality. This coalition is attacking sex education in schools, birth control for minors, and the right to abortion within the US. In the short run the New Right hopes to decimate federal funding of sex education curricula and contraceptive counseling to minors. In the long run the coalition's ultimate goal is to ban all abortions through a constitutional amendment.

headline: Goodling bill seeks refugee clarification
abstract: US Representative William Goodling (R-Pa), introduced a bill that would consolidate federal aid programs to local school districts and make it clear any legally admitted alien would qualify a school for assistance. The new legislation would repeal four existing laws dealing with refugees and granting state and local schools varying levels of assistance, and merge their functions into one program.

headline: Injunction Denied in Mined Bond Cuts
abstract: Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court Judge John MacPhail refused to grant an injunction against the state's $1000 per acre reduction in the amount of strip mine operators must post as bond for land reclamation. MacPhail ruled against five environmental groups stating that Clifford Jones did not break pollution or strip mining laws in lowering the bond rate from $4000 to $3000 per acre, effective August 1.

headline: SEPTA's subsidies
abstract: The two major problems that SEPTA faces are the structure of the agency and the operational efficiencies of the system. Since it is not a part of any government is faces a lack of support. It also faces productivity losses and increased expenditures due to labor. They have to improve efficiency to help keep it alive.

headline: Shoplifting arrests are up 10%
abstract: Shoplifting arrests are on the rise at major-city center department stores in Pennsylvanian after falling off steadily since 1977. The increase in shoplifting incidences is thought to be an extension of increased inflation and a creeping unemployment rate within these demographic areas.

headline: Restaurant raided over back taxes
abstract: State Department of Revenue closed a French restaurant in Center City Philadelphia and seized its liquor license for its alleged failure to remit $23,000 in sales and personal income taxes. The license was restored 4 hours later when the owner of LaCamargue made a payment of $11,000 and made arrangements to pay the remainder and future taxes on time. The move is part of a three-month crackdown on delinquent taxpayers by the State Attorney General and the Revenue Secretary.

headline: Good Team At Work
abstract: Residents of Westmoreland should be pleased to see the bipartisan team of Republican Jess Stairs and Democrat Amos Hutchinson at work in Harrisburg. They are pushing for reconstruction of the electric chair, and now they have joined forces to provide low-interest to fire and ambulance companies through a $10 billion fire bond issue that needs to be approved by the state Senate to go on the ballot.

headline: States, Cities Lick Budget Wounds
abstract: Governors and mayors are joining forces in a common effort to protect their states and cities against the next round of Reagan budget cuts.  The beginnings of a new coalition between the states and local officials may be the most significant achievement of the annual meeting of the National Governors' Association.  Jotted by a 25 percent reduction in federal aid as a result of President Reagan's $35 billion cut from 1982 spending, the governors are worried about what they could lose in the $73 billion in cuts the administration is looking for in the next two years.

headline: After state cuts funding, will abortion rate change?
abstract: On September 24, members of the House were pressured to answer whether to pass a bill cutting off state funds for nearly all Medicaid abortions.  State funds went to pay for about 10,000 Medicaid abortions in 1979, so the bill cutting off that money will save 10,000 lives.  The House passed the bill, which Governor Thornburgh signed into law December 19.  After months of legal challenges, with the cutoff of funds for Medicaid abortions finally scheduled to go into effect in a few days, the best available evidence indicates that it will neither save the lives of most fetuses carried by poor women nor result in large numbers of illegal, unsafe abortions.

headline: Governor won't help schools
abstract: Governor Thornburgh and the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce called for the Philadelphia school district to cut their spending to avoid a deficit and school shutdown.  They said that no public or private money would be used to help the district, which is now $73 million in debt.  The Chamber ruled out lending any more money to the district, as it would just plunge them further into debt.  The governor feels the district has mismanaged their funds and needs to reduce excess spending and keep better records.

headline: Interior Dept. to let Centralia fire burn
abstract: The US Interior Department decided it was best to let Centralia's underground mine fire continue, while the only help expected is the relocation of 26 families most directly affected by the fire. Further complication in the story came when businessmen representing a coal company offered $30 million for anthracite rights under the town.

headline: SEPTA's subsidies: Money covers inefficiency, intead of users' fares
abstract: The two major problems that Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority faces are (a) the structure of the agency and (b) the operational efficiencies of the system.

headline: Six Hostages Freed Unhurt After 5 Days
abstract: Seven prisoners, holding hostages at Graterford Prison, released six hostages and surrendered, ending the five day stand off that started with a failed escape attempt.  The article details the events of the hostage takeover.

headline: Revitalized Chamber is needed
abstract: The editors feel that the Erie Area Chamber of Commerce needs to be revitalized to generate more tourism and port development in the area.  They also feel the Chamber must do a good job in promoting the new convention center.

headline: GOP City Council Hopeful to Skip Campaign Opener
abstract: As Allegheny County Republicans kick off their campaign today with a picnic at South Park Stanley Fineburg, GOP candidate for city council will be flying to Florida for vacation. His plans for council are discussed. He may spend up to $10,000 of his own money to make up for lost time.

headline: Steel Valley classes resume for 2 weeks; Teachers back for 2 weeks
abstract: Teachers in the Steel Valley School District have agreed to return to classes for 2 weeks, temporarily ending an 11 week strike.  The agreement states that the teachers must stay for 2 weeks and give 1 week notice if they plan to strike again.  The strike stems from disagreement on salaries, layoffs and teacher freedom from reprisal.

headline: And the Angels Sing…
abstract: A question and answer column. In this column writers asks Chuck Stone questions concerning the Graterford situation, black women being paid to have babies out of wedlock and basic equal rights. Chuck Stone answers in terse few word sentences resembling an insult.

headline: Hager asks funds for study of school board's complaint
abstract: A long-standing complaint by school boards that costs mandated by the state and federal governments are a major cause of spiraling education taxes would be studied under a resolution introduced to the Senate. It would be a $35,000 fund for a 8 to 9 month study of the problem by the problem by the PA Economy League. The School Boards Association is proposing several different plans including a year of home rule with regard the PA state School Code.

headline: Investors Back GPU Executives
