abstract: General Public Utilities stockholders at the annual meeting gave their corporate officers a vote of confidence, by electing nine directors to the board, approving a board proposal to enlarge its number, and rebuff two resolutions committing the company against nuclear power. Stockholders, who have lost $800 million in dividends since the Three Mile Island accident caused a corporate cash drain, listened to GPU chairman William Kuhns blame state utility commissions and the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

headline: Some Of State gas Stations To Take Break
abstract: About a third of the service stations in Pennsylvania will be closed on Labor day, and the West Penn Motor Club has advised motorists planning to travel to fill up the Saturday or Sunday before.  The club also said Turnpike construction will be curtailed through the holiday period and all stations on the superhighway will operate around the clock with no purchase restrictions.  Fuel prices are up about 20 percent from last Labor Day, but the latest Wet Penn survey shows there has been a price decrease of about 3 cents per gallon since July.  The survey showed current average per-gallon fuel prices in the Pittsburgh area at $1.34 for regular; $1.388 for unleaded; $1.458 for premium unleaded and $1.327 for diesel.

headline: Something's Rotten In The County Jail
abstract: (6 pages) The Board of Prison Inspectors of Allegheny County are being sued by the Neighborhood Legal Services on behalf of the inmates of the Allegheny County Jail, citing that the conditions in the jail are unconstitutional.  The article details the descriptions from former inmates of the horrible conditions there and the lack of action by the Board of Prison Inspectors.  It also outlines Jere Krakoff's investigation of the jail.

headline: Runaway firms give Phila. A thrashing with Sunbelt
abstract: Like much of the Northeast, the Philadelphia are has suffered a steady loss of jobs to the Sunbelt region in recent years. The article presents examples of companies that have already moved away from the region, and some who are contemplating such moves. Some companies can't work with local unions, and therefore prefer to relocate.

headline: GOP Congress Redistricting Spares 3 Area Dems
abstract: Three area congressmen have reason to be pleased with the latest Republican plan to reapportion the state's congressional districts. They are all Democrats. Coyne, Murphy, and Atkinson get to keep their seats, despite the fact that the Republicans are trying to redistrict so that Democrats are at a disadvantage.

headline: Suburban papers join the AM rush
abstract: The rush to be first paper of the day to hit the newsstands has caught on in the Philadelphia suburbs, where three daily newspapers have switched from afternoon to morning publication schedules. When an evening papers switches to morning delivery, life is not all rosy sunrises. One such paper reports that a local sanitation truck crew, not accustomed to curbside piles of newspapers awaiting delivery, scooped up some stacks and hauled them off.

headline: Another barrage
abstract: The author responds to a press release by the People Concerned for the Unborn Child (PCUC) that identified Women's Health Services annual income.  The author states that the PCUC is attempting to cast a negative light on the clinic and lists the positive services that the clinic provides to women.  The author also urges lawmakers not to pass the Abortion Control Act, which the author believes would endanger pregnant women seeking an abortion.

headline: Hearing on injunction is delayed
abstract: A court hearing on the Philadelphia School District's request for an injunction against teachers strike was postponed until Wednesday at the request of the striking union's attorney. School district administrators reluctantly agreed to accept teaching assignments at seven schools for high school seniors and one for handicapped students that the district plans to open next week. City council also probably won't pass any of the proposed tax increases.

headline: Itkin wants strip mine bonds increased
abstract: Charging that the PA Department of Environmental Resources is letting the coal companies off easy state Rep Ivan Itkin has introduced legislation that would strip the department of its authority to set rates for surface-mines bonds. It would impose a minimum rate of $4,000 per acre at strip mines, replacing the current rate of $3,000. Strip-mine operators are required to post bonds so that money is available to cover the cost of reclaiming their mines if they fail to do so. If an operator properly reclaims a mine, the bond money is returned.

headline: Speed War Cuts Deaths
abstract: Pennsylvania received $992,000 in federal Highway Safety funds, with $185,000 spent by PA's Department of Transportation and $800,000 going toward the State Police for 55 miles-per-hour enforcement last year. The lower speed hasn't cut the number of accidents, but it has cut their severity.

headline: Spare other babies the pain
abstract: Author believes the six month period given to mothers giving up their children for adoption to relinquish their rights should be shorten to three weeks and the child would be in the care of the adoption agency in this period. The Hazler story shows that the current system does not work.

headline: Sees auto insurance bill great cause for concern
abstract: The author wants to stress to readers the threat of a new Auto Insurance Bill being debated on the state House floor.  The author states that bill would put restrictions on accident victims to be compensated for pain and suffering, and it will not lower insurance rates.  The author urges readers to call their representatives and ask them to vote against the bill.

headline: GOP Congress Redistricting Spares 3 Area Dems
abstract: Three area congressmen have reason to be pleased with the latest Republican plan to reapportion the state's congressional districts. They are all democrats. The fact says a lot about the complexity of the struggle that is the beginning to unfold between Washington and Harrisburg.

headline: Street Car Ride Derailed
abstract: State Senator Milton Street (R-Philadelphia) has admitted driving a car for more than a year with a suspended license, and having more than $1,000 in outstanding speeding tickets. But he denies being behind the wheel when it was stopped by a PA state trooper on the PA turnpike. The state police department has several warrant's for the senator's arrest, but has been legally advised that they cannot be served while Street is in Harrisburg or en route to or from the capital.

headline: Anti-Abortion Bill
abstract: The editorial hopes for defeat of a proposed bill to define life as beginning at the moment of conception. Hearings began on April 27 for the bill sponsored by US Senator Jesse Helms (R-NC) and US Representative Henry Hyde (R-IL). The editorial calls for responses to the proposed legislation.

headline: Hearts, minds and a merger
abstract: The editorial explains that in September, the General Braddock School District will be combined with four predominantly white districts, due to US District Judge Gerald Weber's refusal to stay his order. The editorial argues for redistricting, that PA is under constitutional mandate to provide equal educational opportunity, and that parents should realize that this is not currently happening.

headline: Jones To The PUC?
abstract: Governor Dick Thronburgh appears close to success in filling a vacancy on the state Public Utility Commissino, which has not been up to full strength for 20 months.  To join the two Democrats and two Republicans now on the commission, he nominated Clifford L. Jones, the secretary of the Department of Environmental Resources, to a 10-year term.

headline: Squeeze on fired controllers tightens
abstract: The government says they were fired for good because of the strike by the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization. Other employers won't touch the former controllers for fear they'll leave if allowed to go back to the control towers. They are becoming dependent on their wives and loans from relatives.

headline: Sprague asks halt to probe of his actions in Boyle case
abstract: Richard A. Sprague petitioned the Washington County, Pennsylvania, Court of Common Pleas to prevent the county district attorney from investigating his actions as special prosecutor in the murder trials of W. A. (Tony) Boyle.  In a six-hour hearing before Common Pleas President Judge Charles G. Sweet, Sprague requested that the state attorney general probe an allegation made against him by county District Attorney Herman J. Bigi.  Bigi's office is investigating Sprague's handling of the prosecution of Boyle, the former United Mine Workers president, for the 1969 slaying of union dissident Joseph A. (Jock) Yablonski, his wife and daughter.

headline: Senate Oks chiropractic care as insurance cost
abstract: The PA Senate has endorsed a measure that would authorize chiropractic care as an allowable expense for auto insurance. Other matters of Senate business are also discussed such ascensions, mileage rates for state officials, and nominations by the governor.

headline: GOP Control No Guarantee of Unity
abstract: Author opines that now that Republicans dominate both house of the General Assembly, Governor Dick Thornburgh may not have as easy a time getting his agenda through the legislature as one would think.  He outlines the Governor's proposals including a percentage based gas tax and welfare and education reform

headline: Street pays up, decides speeding tickets aren't funny
abstract: State Senator Milton t. Street (R-Philadelphia) has regretted his press remarks that seemed to make fun of the law, and has paid $889 to settle fines for having his driver's license suspended. He's also drawn more consternation from fellow state Republicans for the remarks than from the publicity about an allegedly improperly awarded grant to a north Philadelphia group founded by the Senator. Republicans intend to have committee hearings on the grant matter.

headline: Anti-Abortion Bill Up To Governor
abstract: The Friend bill is aimed at discouraging women from having abortion, which is now up to Governor Dick Thornburgh to decide if the bill becomes law.  The article continues to provide pros and cons to the bill provided by different Pennsylvania legislators.

headline: Historical house cleaning
abstract: The state's Historical and Museum Commission, which is charged with maintenance of 48 sites and 12 museums, is sorting out its holdings and even considering selling off a few sites.  There is also a plan to make existing sites more self-sufficient and increase public involvement in them.  The different priorities arose following a management study commissioned by the Thornburgh administration.  The commission realized it was holding on to a "Fibber McGee's close" of items instead of a worthwhile historical collection.

headline: Lawmakers Back to Work on TMI, Budget, Defense
abstract: Pennsylvania congressmen return to Capitol Hill this week to refine the budget cuts passed earlier in the summer, consider changes in the Clean Air Act and develop a cleanup plan for the damaged Three Mile Island nuclear plant.

headline: State Is Urged To Reconsider Airport
abstract: Capital City Airport has asked the state not to eliminate state-paid police and fire protection. They said the states decision may impact the long-range viability of the airport.  Some accuse Governor Thornburgh of dragging his feet on negotiations between the two.

headline: State leaders offer prayers
abstract: The attempted assassination of President Reagan made several Pennsylvania lawmakers demand stricter gun laws and offer their prayers.  The article quotes several lawmakers on their reactions to the assassination attempt.

headline: Senators back keeping system: State Stores plan prepared
abstract: State senators are backing a plan to keep the current state liquor store system in place, with some changes.  The changes include; sales and merchandising modernization, credit card availability, and special sales.  Republicans hope to introduce the new bill after the election break.

headline: GOP County Director Joins Schweiker Staff
abstract: James Byrnes has resigned as executive director of the Republican County Committee to become deputy director of advisory committees for US Human Services Secretary Richard Schweiker. Succeeding Byrnes is political consultant Larry Dunn. He recently was the successful campaign manager for Common Pleas Judge William Standish, who won both the Republican and Democratic nominations for a 10-year term on the bench.

headline: Street's Deciding Vote Sends Liquor Bill to Senate
abstract: PA Senator T. Milton Street launched a tirade against labor unions in general and then cast the deciding vote to send PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's private liquor store plan to the Senate floor. His anger was directed at officials of public-employee unions.

headline: Anti-abortion forces in U.S. Senate standing by with two approaches
abstract: Anti-abortion forces in the Pennsylvania Senate are operating on two fronts, the "human life" bill and a states' rights constitutional amendment.  The dispute has divided the anti-abortion community.  The article further explains the dispute.

headline: How college students and parents scamper for aid
abstract: Vendor Steve Savva said that he found just what he was looking for- the busiest spot on the Temple University campus when he parked Steve's Lunch Truck right in front of the student financial aid office last week. His boom last week was a side effect of the Reagan administration's recent reduction in spending for education and aid to college students and their families.

headline: Limerick evacuation plan revealed: Under '12 hours' needed, report says
abstract: A report commissioned by the Philadelphia Electric Company reported that it would take less than 12 hours to evacuate the 173,000 people living within 10 miles of the Limerick nuclear plant in case of an undesired event. The study is needed to get a license from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to operate Limerick, which is scheduled to begin operation in 1985. Local officials said the 11 hours and 15 minutes evacuation time was not realistic.

headline: State motorists want action on highway funding proposals
abstract: Officials of motor clubs were in the state capitol to reflect concern on the state's lack of highway repair funding. The PA American Automobile Association presented several issues to the state Legislature. The editorial argues the proposals, which include a tax on gasoline sales, cutting inspections to once annually, eliminating the proposed auto emission inspection, and other measures, represent an acceptable compromise to rescue PA's road system.

headline: State plans to rebuild Western Pen
abstract: Pennsylvania is making plans to rebuild Western Penitentiary at a cost of $18 to $19 million.  A bill providing the money has been passed by a House-Senate conference committee and is awaiting confirmation by the full House.  The article gives brief detail about the bill and commentary from the State Bureau of Prison.

headline: Small Business's Turn for Relief from Red Tape
abstract: After a flurry of gripes, Washington, D.C. promises a break from time-consuming forms, costly rules, and meddlesome inspectors. The US Commerce Department has grown tired of complaints from small businesses and now the federal government will begin relaxing some of the restrictions small businesses are claiming cost them money.

headline: GOP delay could hurt Bloom
abstract: Governor Thornburgh angers Senate Republican leaders by waiting until two weeks ago to nominate Robert Bloom for the post of revenue secretary when the position has been vacant for almost a year. Pennsylvania State Constitution states that nominees must be submitted within 90 days of a vacancy. Democrats state that they are likely to vote against Bloom since they feel that Thornburgh has violated this 90-day mandate.

headline: Street's example
abstract: The precedent PA Senator T Milton Street may have set in the opening of the Cleveland Elementary School could soon prove to be another example of cutting your nose off to spite your face. When one considers how the present proposed budget cuts with its eliminations of staff and programs that directly affect Mr. Street's constituents and the laying off of a high percentage of young black teachers from a system repeatedly denounced for being predominantly white. Isn't it time we stop settling for second rate education for the sake of political careers?

headline: Anti-abortion group reveals clinic's revenues, doctors' salaries
abstract: People Concerned for the Unborn Child obtained income levels for doctors of Women's Health Services Incorporated, a tax-exempt non-profit clinic that specializes in women's health issues such as unwanted pregnancies. Members of People Concerned for the Unborn Child state they received such information from the Internal Revenue Service through the Freedom of Information Act.

headline: How inept teachers thrive in the district
abstract: On February 11, 1980, the Board of Education did something truly unusual.  It fired a teacher.  The board did not mince words when it dismissed elementary teacher Dorothy Ellis.  She had refused to prepare lesson plans or to take advice on classroom control.  It said, concluding that she was one effective as a teacher.  In other organizations, that would have been the end of Dorothy Ellis.  But not in the Philadelphia school system.  Within weeks after the board had fired her, Ellis was back on the school system payroll and back in the classroom, this time as a substitute teacher.

headline: Oil company here swaps assets, picks up new sources of energy
abstract: Sun Company has adopted an aggressive strategy to balance its refining capacity and crude oil supplies. Long viewed as cash rich but oil poor, Sun has recently swapped dollars for oil in the ground, by spending $2.9 billion in the last two years to acquire new oil, gas and coal properties.

headline: State Police Offer Forum On truck Law Enforcement
abstract: A group of truckers met in Breezewood with representatives of the PA State Police and the PA Department of Transportation on April 6 to discuss the enforcement of trucking regulations. The truckers are making a statewide effort to organize and lobby for legislative reform that would increase tolerance on weight limits and cut excessive safety regulations, which they say are forcing many drivers into bankruptcy. The Police and PennDOT representatives recommended they go to the legislature.

headline: State proceeds with welfare cuts after legal roadblock is removed
abstract: A U.S. Circuit Court imposed a stay on an injunction that blocked the Pennsylvania Public Welfare Department from making cuts.  The stay will now allow welfare officials to review their programs and make cuts, since the Reagan Administration has reduced funding for state welfare programs.

headline: Small town: 'Sure' to liquor reform
abstract: An informal survey of 600 residents of the primarily Christain town of Dauphin found that they would support Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal to abolish state liquor stores in favor of private ones.  The residents favor free enterprise and don't feel that privatizing the store would lead to more alcohol abuse.

headline: GOP Gets Election Funding
abstract: State Senate Republicians have raised over $50,000 to regain control of the senate.   The article details who dontated and what events were held.

headline: Strong, Prosperous U.S. Wanted, Shuster Finds
abstract: null

headline: Anti-abortion group's listing seen misleading
abstract: A state administrative judge has recommended that a listing for a Philadelphia anti-abortion agency be removed from Bell Telephone's white pages. State Public Utility Commission law judge Sheldon Farber said in an opinion that the listing, "Abortion, Birth Control and Pregnancy Testing Clinic," which is run by Save Our Unborn Lives deliberately misleads and deceives the public. Before the listing can be eliminated, the full PUC must approve.

headline: How one city school came to be opened
abstract: State Senator Milton Street began talking with teachers on the picket lines and with others who crossed them, asking the teachers if they thought a school could be opened in the middle of the bitter labor struggle that was keeping 213,000 children out of their classrooms.  Street discusses his results with Superintendent Micael P. Marcase and they both assessed that several hundred teachers wanted to cross the picket line and teach.  Marcase opened one school in his North Philadelphia legislative district.  Street and Marcase encouraged parents to send their children to schools and ensured safety to the teachers while they were on duty.

headline: Long-term stress study sought
abstract: Dr. Evenlyn Bromet, director of a major study on the mental health effects of the Three Mile Island nuclear accident, would like to continue to the study.  She has already received funding to continue it for three more years, but would like it to go on for 5-7 years.  The article details the findings of the study so far: that women and workers near the plant have higher levels of stress and anxiety.

headline: State roads: 1 death every 4 hours
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) stated that in 1980 2,062 died in traffic accidents.  Several interest groups were interviewed about the pain and suffering caused by the death of a loved one in a car accident.

headline: State Senate Okays Shared-Custody Bill
abstract: The state Senate has given unanimous approval to a "shared custody" bill aimed at giving divorced fathers more access to and legal control over their children. The bill was sent to the state House. Other Senate actions included an approval of a compromise extending state income tax rates for two years, and a bill abolishing the Lottery Commission.

headline: Some random thoughts
abstract: Kathryn Fourhman, the York County coroner, has been crusading for years to get the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board to crack down on drunk driving by cracking down on tavern owners who sell liquor illegally.  Now, instead of pointing her finger at the state, she is waving it also in the direction of local officials.  Both the state Liquor Control Board and local police have the power to make arrests.  But the state agency rarely asks for undercover help from local police.  The Liquor Control Board should take advantage of the local police agencies.  Local police unquestionably have more expertise on the taverns likely to be violating state liquor laws.  It would save a lot of time.  And it might even save the life of a drunk driver.

headline: GOP Governors Split on Reagan Cut
abstract: null

headline: Suit seeks Abscam funds back
abstract: The U.S. federal government filed suit to collect $61,900 from four Philadelphia men convicted in the FBI's Abscam probe into political corruption. Former City Council President George Schwartz received $30,000, former City Councilmen Louis Johanson received $25,000, Councilman Harry Jannotti received $10,000 and Johanson's former law partner Howard Criden received $5,000.

headline: Assuring Black Stake In
abstract: Winning promises that developers of Downtown's Renaissance II projects would see 15 percent minority participation was the Pittsburgh National Association for the Advancement of Colored People's first step in providing minority-owned firms a fair share of the building-boom pie.  Monitoring those agreements is proving to be just as time and energy consuming for their volunteers.  The Oxford Development Company is building a 46-story office complex on Grant Street at a cost of $100 million.  Minorities, with their subcontracts totaling $1.8 million, are getting 1.8 percent of the work.  Since the combined investment in the four projects is $365 million, a 15 percent share would give minorities - blacks, Hispanics, and women - work worth $54.75 million.

headline: Improving higher education in Erie
abstract: Gannon University has record enrollment this school year. Penn State's Behrend College will expand its graduate program with an emphasis on high-technology fields directly related to Erie business and industry.

headline: May Finalize $25 Million Settlement: Hearing on TMI Suit
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission study made use of seven separate polls, each basing its conclusions on data gathered from a relatively small percentage of actual population.  The study found that only one in five evacuees actually lost pay because of the accident, most about $110.   Factoring out expenses covered by insurance, the total estimated personal losses for the evacuees from the 0-15 mile ring amounted to an average of $105 for every person who left.  Business faced a dual problem: loss of customers in addition to the loss of a portion of the labor force.

headline: State subsidy hike cushions Beaver Falls rail link
abstract: Each workday, about 250 people ride the train to Pittsburgh and Lake Erie commuter train to Pittsburgh and back. These fares only make up only 17% of what it costs to operate the train. Taxpayers and the railroad have to make up the rest. Each passenger is subsidized $1,375. Indications are that passengers will have to make up 30% of costs.

headline: State should allow TV in court
abstract: The author urges Pennsylvania to allow TV and radio broadcasts of criminal court trials in the wake of a Supreme Court Ruling that it was up to the states to decide whether or not to allow television and radio in courtrooms.  The author argues that TV and radio are part of the media and should be allowed to cover trials as newspapers and photographers are

headline: Squeeze on fired controllers tightens
abstract: null

headline: GOP Split on Fumo, Camiel
abstract: Last October 1980, Turnpike Commissioner Peter Camiel, Pennsylvania state Senator Vincent Fumo and former Pennsylvania state Senator Thomas Nolan were charged with found guilty of fraud by a federal court jury of causing persons to be placed n the legislative payroll who labored only for the Democratic Party in Philadelphia. US Judge Clifford Green, set aside these fraud convictions based on a legal technicality. In any event, US Senate Republican leaders almost fell over themselves accommodating Senator Fumo, while Governor Thornburgh moved to block Camiel's reinstatement on the ground's that Judge Green's decision was being appealed.

headline: Summer jobless pay OK'd for 3,300 laid off by schools
abstract: A hearing ruled against the Philadelphia School District in its challenge of some $3 million in summer unemployment compensation paid teachers who were rehired in the fall after being laid off in the spring.  The district informed 3,300 Philadelphia Federation of Teachers union members that they had been laid off as part of its effort to reduce n impending $223 million deficit.  The article goes over in brief detail the court cases.

headline: 'Back to Bigotry'
abstract: The editorial argues against US Congressman Bob Walker introducing legislation to amend the Civil Rights Act of 1964, by outlawing hiring and admissions quotas based on sex or race in corporations and colleges. The editorial also argues that Walker is preoccupied with other problems than those important for his 16th District, such as the Three Mile Island cleanup.

headline: In the suburbs, small enrollments close school doors
abstract: In October the Tredyfrin- Easttown Board of School Director announced that it would close the Poali School because of the district's declining enrollment. Parents are furious and searching for answers. It may be the beginning of a trend all over the country due to declining family size.

headline: Meeting secret on mine fire at Centralia
abstract: A state-federal meeting on the long-burning Centralia mine fire will closed to reporters and residents.  The article discusses specifics of an $850,000 borehole drilling program, what is intended to be discusses at the meeting, and potential answers to the fire problem.

headline: State told to speed air cleanup: Car-exhaust plan ordered by June 1
abstract: US District Judge Louis Bechtle ordered PA to establish an auto-emission inspection program without further delay. The PA Department of Transportation had asked the judge to delay the start of the program, saying the instrument's needed to properly test cars for illegal emissions were not yet available. The judge disagreed and the state must file a plan for implementation of the program by June 1. He will hold a hearing on the plan June 10.

headline: State still contesting Pennhurst
abstract: PA officials have ordered state lawyers to pursue all possible appeal processes to fight a US Supreme Court justice's decision to uphold a $10,000-a-day fine for not funding an overseer for the Pennhurst Center. Justice William Brennan rejected state's request to issue an indefinite stay of an earlier court order to fund the institution which houses mentally retarded residents.

headline: State asks voters to float water bonds
abstract: PA voters November 3 will decide the future of a proposed $300 million bond issue to provide low-interest loans for water projects. It is intended that money from the selling the tax-exempt bonds would be loaned out at the same rate the state pays, probably about 12 percent.

headline: GOP to plot Dem Congressmen
abstract: Leaders of PA's 25 member delegation to the House sent two couriers to Harrisburg last week. Their mission was to ask the state legislators to grant the congressman a little consideration. Because of populations shifts two of PA's congressional districts must be eliminated.

headline: Sunrise For 'Sunset'
abstract: "Sunset" legislation in Pennsylvania has finally emerged into the public eye.  Under the sunset law signed by Governor Dick Thornburgh, periodic reviews are to be conducted of 76 state commissions, boards and other agencies to determine if they are still performing necessary services.  The article goes further into detail about the sunset law.

headline: Back to court: Judges want school desegregation re-argued
abstract: A 12 year legal battle over desegregation in the Pittsburgh public school, ending in 1980 with a busing plan, is now being re-argued at the order of the judges on the Commonwealth Court.  The article details the lengthy legal battle.

headline: Lack of Legal Notice Scuttles School Bids
abstract: Due to the city school district forgetting to follow legal notification procedures, the school board will reject bids for the purchase of Davis School in Squirrel Hill. Notification of the sale needed to be advertised in the "Pittsburgh Legal Journal." Not all is lost---the district may end up making profit from this mistake as interest rates may decrease in the next months thereby attracting more buyers.

headline: Met Ed advised on bankruptcy: PUC turns down bulk of rate hike
abstract: The Public Utility Commission (PUC) reduced the rate increase to Metropolitan Edison Company, which owns the Three Mile Island Nuclear Plant.  The company was crippled by the nuclear accident there in 1979 and the Public Utility Commission states that they don't need an increase in funds because only reactor number 2 was damaged and reactor 1 is still usable.   The Nuclear Regulatory Commission will not allow reactor 1 to be used.  The recommendation by the Public Utility Commission could force Metropolitian Edison into bankruptcy.

headline: State transit building evacuated 2nd time
abstract: Employees inside the PA state Transportation and Safety Building were evacuated for the second time in 12 hours after smoke was mysteriously spotted seeping from a floor opening. The incident was very similar to a problem the night before when police spotted a smoking manhole. Within 20 minutes a manhole 30 yards north of the first exploded. They did not have an exact cause.

headline: Statewide raiders seek illegal-betting evidence
abstract: State and federa linvestigators conducted one of the biggest gambling raids in Pennsylvania history to smash an organized crime ring.  Coordinated raids were held in nine counties as a result of a six month long investigation.  There were no immediate arrests.  The article lists some of the places that were raided.

headline: State Charges Toyota 'Price Fix'
abstract: The state Justice Department filed suit against 48 Pennsylvania Toyota dealerships for inflating the retail price of a "protective package" applied to cars they sold.  They state that the package was worth much less than the $500 customers were forced to pay for it.  Similar suits have been filed in other states

headline: GOP's Plan: Seize Control Of House
abstract: The editorial explains that assuming the Republicans gain control of the US House of Representatives and maintain their Senate majority in the 1982 election, this would give the GOP control of both chambers of Congress and the White House. Also, PA loses two seats, one once held by Democratic Representative Raymond Lederer, recently convicted in the Abscam scandal, and the other in Western PA, where two districts represented by Democratic congressmen will be merged.

headline: Sunset to be legislative priority
abstract: State House Representative Samuel E. Hayes, Jr -R- plans to introduce Sunset legislation on the House floor.  The legislation would authorize a review of state agencies to ensure that they are accomplishing their goals.  The newspaper supports his proposed legislation.

headline: Black heroism in area is recalled
abstract: The article recalls heroism by blacks in the area.  In 1720 a slave named Hercules saved the life of his owner, John Harris, Sr., father of Harrisburg's founder.  After 1825, there were many confrontations between slave owners and blacks who wanted to free runaway slaves. Many Pennsylvanians set up schools and churches for African Americans and helped assist runaway slaves.  The article outlines the history of blacks in Harrisburg from the 1700s to desegregation in 1971.

headline: Lashing At Lobbies
abstract: Governor Thornburgh lashed out against the Pennsylvania State Education Association (PSEA), stating that they were practicing unfair lobbying techniques.  PSEA is upset by Governor Thornburgh's proposed budget plans in education, stating that they need more than what the Governor intends to increase.

headline: Met-Ed owes no taxes, so rate bid can be cut, witness says
abstract: The Public Utility Commission (PUC) claims that Metropolitan Edison will not owe any taxes due to the 1979 Three Mile Island nuclear accident clean up.  Therefore, it cannot ask for a $76.5 million rate increase.  The article furthers outlines Metropolitan Edison's financial status and other information about Three Mile Island

headline: State weighing in against trucks
abstract: As a nation we have responded to the potential oil shortage and high cost of gasoline by down-sizing out autos. The same factors have caused the trucking industry to maximize its cargo load to economize in delivering our goods and products over the highways. Speeding regulations and weigh restrictions are the only short term solution, but some want separate highways.

headline: Student advisers want themselves legalized
abstract: null

headline: State Faces Union Vote Versus Popular Vote
abstract: Long lines are a method for liquor stores to spark private ownership.  Recently, as the Thornburgh plan to dismantle the state's antiquated liquor retailing system lay mortally wounded in a Senate committee, people stood in a long line in a state store, trying to buy a bottle of wine.  There are few store owners who would allow their operations to get so gummed up that patrons would have to wait in long lines to buy their wares.  But state liquor store employees have no incentive to sell their products.  They get no commissions and no praise from the boss because the boss is a large, cold, impersonal bureaucracy.

headline: Gov. bills jeopardized by Stockman
abstract: null

headline: Survey of state leaders shows: Financing State Services Top 1981 Issue
abstract: The Council of State Governments did a survey of state governors and legislators as to the top five legislative concerns of 1981.  Financing state services was the biggest concern, followed by fiscal affairs, labor issues and environmental problems.  The article lists the results of the survey by state.

headline: Braddock merger foes go to top court
abstract: Opponents of the court-ordered merger of five east suburban school districts asked the US Supreme Court to give them time to fight the consolidation. In a petition addressed to Justice William J. Brennan Jr., the state and all of the involved school district except General Braddock asked that merger now underway be postponed until their appeals can be heard. On April 28 it was ordered that the five districts be merged as a means to desegregate the mostly black General Braddock schools.

headline: Legislators study special ed funding plan
abstract: The legislative staffs of the PA House and Senate Education committees are studying a proposal by the PA Department of Education for formula-type funding for special education. Monies now sent to intermediate units would be rerouted to individual school districts based on a weighted funding formula operated on a credit basis.

headline: Minnich wonders if we can 'afford' nuclear
abstract: John E. Minnich, Dauphin County Commission chairman addressed the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), stating that he feels the government cannot afford to use nuclear power if it cannot afford to clean up after an accident.  His statements were made in regard to the federal government not allocating enough money to clean up the nuclear waste after the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant accident.  He also stated that the government does not see nuclear waste as a threat to health and safety.

headline: The Parkway Limited
abstract: Looking back at the golden days of rail-road, rail supporters now argue if trains were available and fast, commuters would leave their autos and board trains to get to work. Commuters between Greensburg and Pittsburgh have the opportunity to use the trains, but no more of the 2,000 the train can hold use it. If more people don't use it the service it is going to have to be closed.

headline: The Best Way to Beat the Rap is to Beat It
abstract: There is no one to get juveniles who do not show up to court. Family Court has not served a bench warrant for years. Even if it did arrest juveniles, it has no where to put them. In many ways it operates on the fringes of the legal system. The DA's office uses it as training for staffers.

headline: State Junk Mail
abstract: The State Commerce Department, set up to promote Pennsylvania as a good place for business, recently sent out a mass mailing to business at a cost of $30,500.  The mailings were filled with pieces of red tape to symbolize how Governor Thornburgh has cut through the red tape to make Pennsylvania a business friendly place.  The author feels this money was wasted.

headline: Gov. bills jeopardized by Stockman
abstract: Reagan's economic plan is designed for the rich, and while PA Governor Thornburgh will try to see it continues on the state level he will have difficulty getting things passed with black leaders calling against them.

headline: Taxpayers face bill for fatter pensions
abstract: At the time when Congress is considering cutting Social Security, PA lawmakers are trying to liberalize state and local government pensions which are inflated beyond the limits of fiscal responsibility. The latest proposal has to do be approved by the voters. A retired worker receives whatever pension he worked during his productive years, rarely does he get an cost of living increase. The Legislature did this but employees weren't happy with that alone. They also want surviving spouses to have a cost-of-living increase.

headline: Cancer rates higher among blacks than whites- doctor
abstract: A higher percentage of blacks than whites are dying of cancer. Cancer deaths are increasing 20 percent faster among blacks than whites. The only permanent solution is an improved economic status for black people. Their nutritional habits are not as good because they cannot afford the same quality of food.

headline: Leonard criticizes plan to audit school district
abstract: City Controller Thomas Leonard criticized Governor Dick Thornburgh's requirement that the city and state jointly audit Philadelphia's school district as a condition for the state's advance of $80 million in subsidies to the schools. Leonard said his office had conducted several audits earlier, but that resulting recommendations were never implemented. He blamed the school board, Superintendent Michael Marcase for doing nothing, and city Mayor Green and Thornburgh for not insisting that reforms be implemented.

headline: N.J. nuke to ship fuel across Pa.
abstract: Reactor fuel from New Jersey will be shipped across the Pennsylvania Turnpike to Ohio, but officials say it will not pose a health hazard to residents.  The shipment will be in a safe containment and heavily guarded by police.  The article details the shipping route.

headline: Still Here
abstract: The editorial rebuts PA Department of Transportation's director Thomas Larsen's remark that the PA pothole is extinct. The author lists several potholes that exist on different roads in the Alle-Kiski Valley.

headline: The Commonwealth vs. the pathologist
abstract: The trial of Cyril Wecht begins tomorrow, in which he is accused of using his position of Allegheny County coroner for his own personal gain.  He is accused of using county facilities and staff to make $140,000 worth of tissue examinations for his own pathology laboratory.  Wecht says that it was a teaching program for the staff.  The article details the charges against Wecht and his reaction to them.

headline: State Pushes Image Abroad
abstract: The state Commerce Department set up branch offices in London, Paris, and Frankfurt to promote Pennsylvanian products and attracts tourists and industry.

headline: House Willl Act on Sunset Bill:  Sunset Bill To Get Day In House
abstract: The House State Government Committee aproved House Bill 105, called Sunset legislation, which would bring up 76 agencies for scrutiny and possible elimination.  The bill would put statutory agencies up for review every six years based on performance and fininancial compliance.  The Senate has not passed the bill yet.

headline: Teacher layoffs a major focus in Pa. school pacts
abstract: Teacher contracts expired in 24 school districts over the summer. Eight of those districts have still not adopted new contracts or reached tentative settlements. Now the threat of a strike looms over these districts. Districts are rushing to prevent this, but some say its inevitable.

headline: Card-carrying white male
abstract: Opinion piece in which the author calls pictures on drivers licenses a form of racism and also calls Governor Dick Thornburgh a racist.

headline: Loan Crackdown:  Senate Unit Votes to Put Clout Behind Collection of Student Debts.
abstract: The state Senate approved a bill that would allow the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) to pursue loan defaulter by suspending the current six year statute of limitations for student loans.  The article outlines the proposed legislation.

headline: N-accident evacuee plan taps South Park
abstract: In a forum to discuss the state of nuclear evacuation preparedness, a plan was presented to evacuate Beaver County residents to Allegheny County's South Park, in the case of a nuclear accident at the Beaver Valley Power Station at Shippingport. Allegheny County is preparing its evacuation plans, to be finished by the end of June.

headline: Strike talks, train service are on today; SEPTA talks set to resume today
abstract: Negotiators are set to resume talks with Philadelphia's striking mass transit workers.  The Common Pleas Court ruled that commuter rail service would be able to continue by postponing a ruling on whether striking SEPTA workers can protest at Conrail stations.  The article details the Court's decision to postpone and the obstacle to resolving the strike.

headline: The DA needs to call in the plumbers
abstract: There are leaks in the District Attorney's office that need to be replaced so that people will not know who is about to be arrested and they flee. Rendell needs to hire a plumber to fix said leaks.

headline: State store
abstract: Tarentum residents are not about to panic about it, but it does seem about time they get their state liquor store back. The PA State Liquor Control Board closed theirs when the lease ran out. There were plenty of choices for other sites but they haven't made any effort to pick one.

headline: Invested state pension fund yields 9.8 percent in income
abstract: The State Employees' Retirement Board has accepted a report by A. G. Becker Company of Chicago on the 1980 investment performance of the $3 billion pension fund. The report showed the fund earned 9.8 percent income, a sharp increase in the market value of the fund in contrast to a year of declining value in the fund's large bond portfolio.

headline: Teacher Talks Make Headway
abstract: A late night negotiating session this past Tuesday brought the schools district and Philadelphia Federation of Teachers as close to an agreement on a contract as the two sides have been since the strike ended on October 27. However no settlement is imminent says both sides.

headline: Carolina Settles Integration Suit on Universities: NAACP Must Approve Agreement with U.S.
abstract: The Reagan Administration agreed with North Carolina to end an 11-year-old civil rights battle in an arrangement that helps black colleges but does not penalize white colleges. The agreement provides for increased funds to the state's predominantly black colleges and the creation of 29 new programs that will attract more white students. However, the agreement does not demand that predominantly white colleges should remove like programs in an effort to avoid duplication, thus deterring white students to attend the black colleges. The university system's board unanimously agreed on the agreement however, this does not end the matter until the NAACP consents to the agreement as they were the group that originally brought up the suit leading to government involvement.

headline: Logan classes canceled after parents' protest
abstract: Logan Elementary School in North Philadelphia was closed after protesting parents, led by state Representative Milton Street, blocked the entrances so teachers could not get in.  They are protesting because the school refuses to transfer eight teachers that the group feels are incompetent.  A judge ordered an injunction to keep the protests away from the entrances, but Rep. Street says that they will not obey the judge's orders.  The article details the protest.

headline: N-Energy Supported - Quietly
abstract: Friends and Family of TMI (Three Mile Island) stood by while thousands protested nuclear energy in the wake of the TMI accident in 1979.  The group supports their right to demonstrate, but also a healthy mix of nuclear and coal energies, and feels that nuclear energy should not be banned.

headline: SWAP, SWITCH, And Pennies
abstract: The editorial argues that although PA Department of Transportation and Westmoreland County will get more money, their troubles surrounding highway maintenance and construction are far from over. The SWAP tax proposed by Governor Dick Thornburgh and the SWITCH tax proposed by state House Representative Jim Manderino, regardless of whether right or wrong, are being defeated by both parties. The editorial calls for the problems to be solved without playing politics.

headline: The doctor says of the Phillies: 'These guys lied'
abstract: Unofficial Phillies team physician, Dr. Patrick Mazza was charged with illegally prescriping amphetamines to several people on the baseball team.  Dr. Mazza maintains that the Phillies requested these drugs and the team let him down by not testifying to that matter.  The article outlines the details of the hearing.

headline: State Stores: A Telling Comparison
abstract: The authors are angry over Pennsylvania's ranking as the least efficient state in running state-owned liquor stores.  They compare the system to other states and wonder how long it will be until the legislature does something to either improve or abolish the system.

headline: Governor Offers Mayor Election Good Wishes
abstract: Governor Thornburgh sent a letter to Harrisburg Mayor Paul E. Doutrich Jr. to convey his good wishes as the mayor faces a re-election campaign.  The letter also stated that the Governor has enjoyed working with the mayor over the years.

headline: Teachers' contract advancing; Proposal may go to council today
abstract: A proposed contract for Philadelphia teachers might be presented to the City Council after the Board of Education meets with the School Superintendent Michael P. Marcase and James R. Melinson, the district's labor negotiator.  The article goes further into detail on the advances of the Philadelphia teacher's contract negotiations.

headline: Changing the guard, not goals, at NOW
abstract: President of the National Organization of Women (NOW) in Pennsylvania, Bridget Whitley delivered and extemporaneous congratulatory speech to the new President, Sara Clavez. She sat surrounded by friends wondering how the winning platform was different than hers. Clavez stated that NOW's statewide priorities would not change which includes securing enough votes to ratify the Equal Rights Amendment, lobbying to prevent passage of the Abortion Control Act now before the legislature, securing the rights of homosexuals and ending racial discrimination.

headline: Many Oppose Special Ed Standards
abstract: Parents of students and advocacy groups have opposed new special education standards that the state Education Department is trying to implement, which would streamline programs and save the Department over $30 million. Both the majority and minority chairmen of the state House Education Committee are pushing a bill that would give the Legislature veto power over standards proposed by the Education Department.

headline: New brew for gasohol; Firm develops enzyme to make alcohol from trees
abstract: General Electric Corporation and a Univeristy of Pennsylvania biochemistry professor are banking on an enzyme to bring them success with a new kind of brew; a wood-based alcohol that could be used in gasohol, the gasoline-alcohol mixture used to replace some of the foreign oil in America's gas tanks.  The corporation will strive for the next two years at the University City Science Center and Institute in West Philadelphia to refine and commercialize a fermentation process that has been used in the laboratory to turn wood into alcohol.

headline: Tax Panel Plan May TRIP Up SWAP
abstract: Governor Thornbugh's Tax Commission has come up with an alternative to his SWAP (Sustain the War Against Potholes) gasoline tax.  TRIP (Transportation Rehabilitation and Improvement Program), proposed by the Tax Commission would raise gasoline and vehicle registration fees.

headline: The girls get the dirtiest deal of all
abstract: PA maximum security juvenile facilities for boys are crowded, those for girls are worse because there is only one. They believe an additional 50 beds will have to be added immediately and 150-200 in the near future. The PA Department of Public Welfare is now considering making a 44-bed unit of two unused buildings at Byberry. There is not a facility for mentally-disturbed girls at all.

headline: State to Seek Disaster Loans For Drought
abstract: Governor Thornburgh asked the Small Business Administration for low-cost disaster loans for 50 Pennsylvania counties in anticipation of a worsening drought.  The money will be used to prepare alternate water sources.  The request comes in the wake of the declared water emergency in the Delaware River Basin in which all non-essential water use has been banned.

headline: Governor To Address United Way
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh will be speaking at the annual meeting of the Tri-County United Way.  The article details the Governor's success as Chairman of the State Employees Combined Appeal (SECA).

headline: Teachers in Norwin, Sto-Rox districts resume negotiations
abstract: Striking teachers in the school districts Sto-Rox and Norwin will meet with negotiators to discuss contracts.  The article details the history of negotiations between teachers and the school districts.

headline: Chinese professor named to U.S. advisory unit
abstract: Education Secretary T.H. Bell appointed Nathan Mao, a Shippensburg State College English professor, to serve on the National Advisory Council on Ethnic Heritage Studies.  Mao, who also worked as an interpreter for Governor Thornburgh on his trip to China, hopes to dispel stereo types about Asian Americans.

headline: Military Tuition
abstract: PA doesn't give in-state tuition to the military even though 39 others states do. The Commonwealth has about 10,700 Service persons stationed here. When these Service persons want to take additional course work at a public college, they are considered as out-of-staters and are not afforded in-state tuition rates.

headline: New Jersey, Pennsylvania Should Buy GPU's Three Mile Island Site, Study Says
abstract: A study for New Jersey utility regulators recommends that the state and PA buy the crippled Three Mile Island nuclear power plant. The study, made for the NJ Board of Public Utilities, recommends the two states organize a regional  power authority to buy, clean up and eventually run the facility, now owned by a NJ-based company with NJ and PA subsidiaries.

headline: The peaks and valleys of city driving
abstract: Since streets have been repaved potholes have been replaced by depressed manholes. Many motorists think these are just as dangerous as the potholes. City halls should increase employees so that they can take these complaints. To many complaints are falling into he cracks and leading to bad situations.

headline: The Inside Story: Unlocking the Rage
abstract: The article is a narrative by Chuck Stone of his experience meeting with the hostage takers at Graterford Prison.  His descriptions include his attempts at negotiations with the leader, Joseph Bowen, and how angry Bowen was at the world.

headline: Statewide Mob Probe Revealed
abstract: A statewide grand jury is expected to return presentments against alleged operators of a $300-$400 million statewide gambling operation in what law enforcement sources have described as the largest case of its kind in PA history.

headline: Governor to push reforms
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's thoughts aren't on his chances of getting re-elected, yet. Instead he is trying to garner legislative support for a series of reforms. He wants to pass welfare reform, eliminate state liquor sales, implement although crime package, and restart of the highway program.

headline: Teachers on strike in 6 Pa. districts
abstract: Teachers in six PA school districts were on strike in contract disputes that affected 16,600 students. About 190 members of the Pottsville walked out. In suburban Johnstown 123 teachers walked out. In Westmoreland county teachers in the Normin School District set up picket lines on what would have been the first day of classes. Teachers in Beaver County staged the first strike in the county. In Harmony School District 33 teachers continued to strike.

headline: City 1975 equal employment program falls short; 1975 affirmative action promise: 'City isn't proud of its efforts'
abstract: Statistics from 1975 to 1979 show that white male city employees make more than black males and females and white females, despite a non-discrimination policy.  The city's goal is to have their employment reflect Pittsburgh's labor market but less than one per cent of the city jobs are held by blacks and white women combined. In Pittsburgh's labor market it is 54 percent.  White male city workers also have higher pay than the other groups.  US District Judge Gerald Weber ruled that police officers be promoted by a racial-sexual quota system.

headline: Most hail new Montco school head but others decry loss of CETA jobs
abstract: Students and faulty leaders at Montgomery County Community College say they are optimistic about the selection of Doctor Edmond A. Watters 3d as the school's second president.  Watters, who has served as dean of academic affairs at the 7,500 student college in Blue Bell since May 18, was chose by the school's board of trustees last week.  He takes office August 31, succeeding Doctor LeRoy R. Brendlinger, who has served as president of the college since it opened in 1966.  Brendlinger said last march that he would retire by June 30, or when a new president had been selected.

headline: No headline
abstract: Picture of curator Donald Hoff looking at footprints on slabs of rock unearthed at nuclear plant site.

headline: The Pothole Hotline
abstract: The editors feel that the pothole hotline, provided by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT), provides taxpayers with an outlet for their complaints.  They support the hotline and what it hopes to achieve.

headline: The lifers' leader: A lobbyist with a sense of urgency
abstract: Robert Edwards, a convicted murderer and president of the Lifers Association of Pennsylvania, is lobbying lawmakers to ease restrictions on parole for those serving life sentences.  He feels that Governor Thornburgh does not pardon lifers for political reasons.  The article details his views on how the parole system should work.

headline: The banks should pay their fair share
abstract: The editors believe that Pennsylvania's Supreme Court decision to exempt commerical banks from paying two Philadelphia taxes is unfair.  They feel that the banks should be treated like other industries and pay their fair share.

headline: Governor: Dennis Chargers Bad Rap. Won't Fire Community Affairs Chief
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh said allegations against PA Department of Community Affairs Secretary Shirley Dennis were a "bad rep", that he would not fire her, but pledged cooperation in a probe of a federally-funded contract awarded by her department. The contract provided funds to the North Philadelphia Block Corporation, which hired welfare recipients to insulate poor homes. But Philadelphia District Attorney said employees would be charged with welfare fraud, after continuing to receive welfare checks during their employment with the NPBC.

headline: Teachers on strike in 6 Pa. districts
abstract: Teachers in six Pennsylvania school districts, five in the western part of the state, were on strike due to contract disputes that affected 16,000 students.  About 190 members of the Pottsville Area Education Association in Schuylkill County walked out, affecting about 3,500 students in 10 schools.  The teachers have refused to buedge from a fact finder's recommendation of salary increases of $1,500 and $1,550 in a two-year contract.  The school district offered a three-year pact with raises of $1,250, $1,250, and $1,300.

headline: City Blacks: 2 centuries of setbacks, progress
abstract: Three pictures with captions. The first is of Martin Delany, a physician, founded schools and churches for blacks after the Civil War. The second is of the Loendi Literary and Social Club for men, a gathering place for the elite "Old Pittsburghers". The third is of a black worker in 1936. The city was built by workmen from many places.

headline: Most seniors register
abstract: Nearly all of the city's high seniors registered at seven strikebound schools scheduled to open today. The schools will reopen as planned because Common Pleas Court judges decided not to issue an immediate ruling on a suit filed by Philadelphia administrators. Students seemed to be unfazed by the angry striking teachers.

headline: No More Giveaway At TMI
abstract: The author argues against the federal giveaway of funds to fix the Three Mile Island plant, because the costs to taxpayers and consumers is too much. Instead, he believes that it is time for the free market to decide the true cost of making electricity through atomic energy, and that by cutting funds we can see whether the nuclear energy industry can make it on its own.

headline: Thornburgh at Midterm - Part 2:  PennDOT's Performance Getting Mixed Reviews
abstract: The author assesses Governor Thornburgh's job of improving the PA Transportation Department.  The author states that the Governor did a good job in appointing Thomas Larson as its secretary and that the management has improved.  There are some critics of this also and a debate is outlined

headline: The Moody Blues
abstract: Thirty angry men, mostly police, had come together at the request of one of Frank Rizzo's close associates to talk about the state of things in the Philadelphia Police Department. They have complaints about the commissioner, the mayor, the paperwork, and the disciplinary harassment.

headline: The Homespun Pleasures Of Lancaster County
abstract: Lancaster County has 941 square miles of rich, rolling farmland with small towns that look like sets for a Civil War movie.  There are several interesting, entertaining, and delicious things to experience in the historic community of Lancaster County.

headline: Governors at home in '84
abstract: The author feels that there may be a massive movement of governors into national politics through the Senate races.  There are 11 Republican senators whose term expires in 1986 in states where Democratic governors also will be finishing their current terms that year.  The piece goes further into detail about specific governors that are contemplating on running the Senate races.

headline: Teachers ponder precedent...  ...prposed by a mayor 'alone'
abstract: null

headline: End to the old rhetoric: The new black leadership will not look toward Washington
abstract: The New York Times proclaims that blacks are not as cheered up by President Reagan as whites are.  Indeed, the word is that the Reagan presidency has made blacks quite gloomy about their personal futures and that of the nation.

headline: Murray reelected as teacher union boss
abstract: John Murray defeated John Ryan to be elected president of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers (PFT).  The article interviews Murray on how it feels to have won.

headline: No steam ahead, Downtown companies fear
abstract: The state Public Utilities Commission (PUC) will hear the case of the financially failing Allegheny County Steam Heating Co. (ACSH), a subsidy of Duquesne Light.  PUC recently ordered Duquesne Light to cut all funding for ACSH, but downtown businesses fear it will be too costly for them to convert to gas if ACSH is dissolved.  The article details the possible actions PUC may take.

headline: The System: No solution
abstract: Although the long Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority strike ended, in part due to Governor Dick Thornburg's intervention, the crisis only gets the transit system rolling again. This does not alter the long-term financial dilemma confronting the Authority and the rest of the nation's urban mass transit systems. Fares will have to be raised again, and another solution may involve some form of regional tax.

headline: The NRC: A bad case of sunburn
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Common Cause are locked in a dispute the US District Judge Edward Curran now threatens could send the five NRC commissioners to jail on contempt-of-court charges. The issue is whether the NRC may hold private meetings when it makes decisions on the agency's budget.

headline: The state has no business in the liquor business
abstract: The editorial states the reasons why the state should not control liquor sales in Pennsylvania.  The authors support Governor Thornburgh's initiative to make liquor store ownership private.

headline: Governors Meet As Best They Can
abstract: Only three of the eight members of the Coalition of Northeastern Governors attended a coalition in Saratoga Springs.  The three members could vote on none of the recommendations made during the two day session because it lacked a quorum.  The article provides more details of the coalition.

headline: Teachers Union Lists Primary Picks
abstract: The Pittsburgh Federation of Teachers, a politically powerful teachers' union, has released a list of candidates it is supporting in the May 19 primary. With two exceptions, it has decided to support the Democratic Party's slate.

headline: EX-JAYCEES
abstract: The editorial argues that community service should not have any sexual requirements, and agrees with the Pittsburgh Jaycees decision to accept women. Their decision has resulted in being expelled from the national organization, and have had to rename the group the United Junior Citizens Organization of America. The editorial adds that the group has contributed substantially to the community with many service projects.

headline: Negative
abstract: The disruption of the school strike is arousing disenchantment in children's education. These strikes are going to have a negative affect on our children. The author of the letter writes that after the strike is over teachers have to cram information into students in less time than the material should be and they do not learn it.

headline: Northeast Hit by Coal Shortages: Northeast Short of Coal as State Anthracite Fields Idle
abstract: Increased demands for anthracite coal have caused a shortage of coal to heat homes. Pennsylvania does have available athracite coal, but it is currently not being mined.  The article details the history of athracite coal in Pennsylvania. The State Commerce Department stated that they would increase production.

headline: Thornburgh pumps wholesale gas tax
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has traded his SWAP gasoline tax for a newer model, a 3.5% tax on the whole price of all motor fuels sold in PA, which he hopes will get better mileage in the PA Legislature. Republicans believe it will go over better because it is a tax on companies not consumers. The companies will of course pass it on to the public. They want a large part of the revenue to go to local road maintenance.

headline: The state's crackdown on crime
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has surged against organized crime with grand jury recommendations that 51 people be charged with conspiracy and bookmaking.  Some of the suspects have been fingered by the Pennsylvania Crime Commission as having ties with organized crime; in fact, some are believed to be among the top gambling figures in the United States.  The pinch on illegal gambling could well be a pinch on illegal drug traffic as well.  Drugs are the number one money-maker for organized crime and gambling is second.  The state grand jury's achievement would not have been possible without wiretapping.  The idea of listening in on other people's conversations is odious, and there is strong inclination to prohibit such police activity, even with court approval.

headline: There's method in muddiness
abstract: The editors cite a passage from a bank promissory note to illustrate how confusing technical language can be to regular people.  The support attempts in the legislature to pass a law that would outlaw fine print, Latin phrases, double negatives, and archaic English phrases in contracts.  The outline "Plain-English" measures in other states.

headline: Governor's meeting with President Reagan
abstract: An April 21st governor's meeting with President Reagan at the White House is depicted in this photograph including the president, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, and the governors of Ohio, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, and Alabama. They discussed ways to promote public support for the Reagan budget.

headline: Teachers vote 'yes' on strike
abstract: The teachers answered Philadelphia Mayor Green's call to sacrifice with a resounding 'No' drawing the lines for a strike next week. The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers voted to not to return to school unless the contract the PFT signed with the School District is observed. Green stepped into the middle of the crisis saying he would support a 10% tax increase if several conditions were met.

headline: Fast Lane to Success?  Parents Use Deseg to Duck School Crime, Drugs
abstract: The last in a series of articles called "The State of Black Philadelphia."  The article details the stories of a black parent who wants her children to go to a white school to avoid crime and drugs. The article questions wether desegeration is the answer to inner city school problems.

headline: New college loans OK'd; Thornburgh signs bill allowing parents to borrow
abstract: null

headline: Nothing has changed
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has indentified eight nuclear reactors among them the undamaged Unit 1 at Three Mile Island, as vulnerable to cracks the could permit radiation to leak. The problem lies in the steel housings of fuel rods that are weakened by a bombardment of radioactive particles.

headline: Thornburgh seeks to bar Camiel return to Pa. post
abstract: The Thornburgh Administration asked the Pennsylvania state attorney general to seek an injunction barring Pennsylvania Turnpike Commissioner Peter Camiel from voting on the commission or receiving more than $18,000 in back pay yesterday. Camiel was acquitted Tuesday by US District Judge Clifford Scott Green of charges that he padded the state payroll with ghost employees, even though Camiel was found guilty by a jury in May 1980. Camiel's acquittal resulted from a legal technicality rather than a finding of innocence. Even if Camiel is reinstated as commissioner, the governor has the right to suspend a commissioner for acts of misconduct that may fall short of an indictable offense.

headline: The Times That Try Men's Souls
abstract: The article discusses a recent murder of a Philadelphia police officer and how a black journalist was accused.  The article provides further details about the witnesses at scene of the murder and the racial controversies brought to the attention of the media.

headline: Thornburgh: Scrap State Stores:  Governor to unveil plan to scrap State Stores for private franchises
abstract: Governor Thornburgh proposed to close 725 state liquor stores to allow private franchises to sell wine and spirits.  The proposal is meant to stop corruption within the Liquor Control Board (LCB) which has had a monopoly on alcohol sales since Prohibition.  The article outlines the specific changes the Governor seeks.

headline: Governors will be living it up during Atlantic City conference
abstract: The 73rd annual Governors Conference is held in Atlantic City and the governors will get to live it up in high style. The article lists the amenities each governor and their families will be provided while at the conference. Discussions are reported to entail talk about the Reagan administration's budget cuts and how the states will be able to maintain their programs with a 25% federal budget cut.

headline: Ted warms up pols for Glancey
abstract: US Senator Edward Kennedy and local politicians brought a message of get out the vote to supporters of David Glancey. Glancey and three others are running for 3rd Congressional District. Some say this is a referendum on Philadelphia Mayor Green's performance.

headline: Feminist quits in row over abortion ruling
abstract: Anne L. Lang resigned from her job as director of the state's Bureau of Management Services when Governor Thornburgh signed a bill banning the use of federal Medicaid money to fund abortions for poor women in Pennsylvania. Ms. Lang is a feminist and was once an officer for the National Organization for Women.  The article details her career in the Thornbugh administration.

headline: No fat left
abstract: The author responds to Governor Thornburgh's statements that school districts need to "cut the fat" from their budget.  The author states that they've cut so much in recent years that there's nothing left to cut, and that Governor Thornburgh should keep his campaign promise to increase funding to schools.  The author urges taxpayers to be outraged and contact their representatives.

headline: N-planning cost put squarely on utility
abstract: The US Supreme Court refused to block a ruling barring a utility from charging customers for $60 million in planning and preliminary work on four nuclear power plants never completed. The justices rejected a request from the Cleveland Electric Illuminating Co. that they delay an Ohio Supreme Court ruling that found costs associated with the unfinished plants not an allowable ratemaking expense.

headline: Thornburgh signs gas-tax measure
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed legislation enacting a $1.3 billion Motor License Fund budget for 1981-82 and a 3.5% tax on gasoline in order to raise $192 million for Pennsylvania highway construction and maintenance. The tax is to be levied against oil company revenues, although Democrats express the view that motorists should expect a 3-4 cent increase at the gas pump. Thornburgh delineates that local jurisdictions will be able to offset expenditures in their own budgets which will help hold the line on local property tax increases through this piece of legislation.

headline: These Angels Don't Fear to Tread
abstract: The writer of the opinion column comments on the recently graduated first class of Angels, a group of 61 volunteers that will protect Philadelphia's subways from criminals. A 50 percent decrease in subway crimes in three months was predicted by the founder of the New York chapter of Guardian Angels, Curtis Sliwa. Philadelphia Police Department has welcomed and recognized the group and agreed on cooperation.

headline: Thornburgh's liquor plan
abstract: The editorial argues Governor Dick Thornburgh's plan to license retailers in the sale of liquor, but keep the wholesale operation with the state, would not provide consumers with significant reduction in prices, and would be unacceptable to retailers. It suggests that neither the legislators nor the taxpayers are likely to accept the new proposal.

headline: Greater Pitt Hails Strike Settlement
abstract: A tentative national settlement in the air controller' dispute brought relief to travelers at the Greater Pittsburgh  Airport. Controllers had been on strike previously, but as of the publish date, a full shift of controllers appeared, ready to work. The Federal Aviation Administration stressed that a tentative agreement had been reached in Washington DC as of 5 a.m. that morning. Controllers back at work stressed that this should not appear as a sign of weakness on the part of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization.

headline: Testimony Continues in 666-Fix, Stagehand Accuses TV Emcee
abstract: Former stagehand, Joseph Bock, accused of rigging the Pennsylvania lottery, testified at a preliminary hearing that Nick Perry, the announcer for the nightly Daily Number drawing at WTAE-TV in Pittsburgh, had approached him about rigging the drawing.  He used phony weighted balls to bring up the numbers 6-6-6 for a $3.5 million payoff.  At the end of the hearing, District jUstice Mary Cross ruled the state had proven it had a sufficient case to warrant a Dauphin County Common Pleas Court trial.

headline: Film on 3 women miners digs below the surface of Pa. town
abstract: "We Dig Coal" documents Mrs. McCusker's death and the working lives of herself and her two co-workers, Mrs.. Carson and Bernice Dombroski.  It briefly covers the federal sex-discrimination suit filed by Mrs. McCusker and three other women.  The suit produced jobs for the four women through an out-of-court settlement.  The central issue of the documentary is attitudes concerning women in the mines.

headline: Not Marcase, but teachers' union incurs council's wrath this time out
abstract: Both the Schools Superintendent Michael Marcase and the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers' president John Murray testified at Philadelphia's City Council chambers. The heated debate is over the school district, on the brink of insolvency, and one of the council's ideas is to reduce the teaching staff to fill the $223 million budget gap.

headline: N-Power Has State Divide
abstract: A Harris survey released Monday revealed that Pennsylvanians oppose nuclear energy partly because of Three Mile Island, but still would favor building more nuclear power plants if it meant lower electric bills. The survey was commissioned by the Pennsylvania Governor's Energy Council.

headline: Thoughts on auto inspections
abstract: The editors opine that Governor Thornburgh's proposal to reduce car inspections from twice a year to once annually is a bad idea. They feel that drivers need them twice a year to make sure their cars are safe and would otherwise put off routine maintence if the inspection were only yearly.

headline: They are dinosaur prints
abstract: Footprints of dinosaurs, coelophyses, were found in Montgomery County. They are suspected to be 180 million to 200 years old. Only two men in the US can properly identify the footprints, and pictures will be sent to one of them for confirmation.

headline: Track's value
abstract: The editors feel that the Fairview race track, for horse races, is important to the Erie economy.  The cite employment and increased revenue from taxes as way the track is valuable, and urge lawmakers to renew the license for the track next year.

headline: Green: Schools Hang on Tax Rise
abstract: Mayor green sought to slow the rush to a school strike with a cool-headed speech calling for a 10 percent property tax hike.  And while teachers' union president John P. Murray said he was surprised by the non-combative tone of Green's remarks, he vowed once again to lead a strike a week from now unless laid-off teachers.  Green also pledged to try to float a bond issue for the financially devastated schools, but he conditioned his support on concessions Murray and others said would be extremely difficult to extract.

headline: Thank you, Mr. Congressman!!
abstract: Editorial believes people ought to be thanking their congressmen because they performed meritorious service in the budget battle to keep rural electric cooperative program alive, let alone sound and healthy.

headline: Foes of Abortion Scored on 'Pernicious' Move
abstract: Conservative Pennsylvania House members plan to circumvent the committee system to promote anti-abortion legislation that was tabled back in October. Prime movers of the "Abortion Control Act" made known their intention to gut a bill which will be on the House calendar next week and use it as the vehicle to bring the abortion issue before the House for a vote. Pro-choice supporters call this tactic pernicious and state that conservatives should be appalled for attempting to slip one past Pennsylvania voters in such an obscure manner. This indicates that the bill did not have the necessary support to have the piece of legislation passed in the a normal manner to begin with.

headline: Not More Paperwork
