abstract: The editors discuss current education reform proposals.  They disagree with a legislative proposal to require teachers and administrators to complete evaluation forms.  The also agree with the Pennsylvania State Education Association's (PSEA) opposition to a proposal to require a master's degree for teaching certification.

headline: NRC aide fears safety setbacks in atomic 'rush'
abstract: Nuclear Regulatory Commission member Victor Gulinsky told the American Society of Newspaper Editors that the fervor to cut back federal regulations, combined with pressure on utilities to get nuclear plants on-line, could reverse safety improvements made since the Three Mile Island. But a former executive director of the Union of Concerned Scientists challenged Gulinsky's judgment that the NRC had improved nuclear safety.

headline: Time is running out
abstract: Commuters will not be able to purchase tickets at the Yardley train stop after Friday.  Conrail is closing the ticket office at this and other lightly used stations in an effort to trim operating costs.  Passengers who get on a Yardley will be able to buy tickets on board without having to pay the additional 50 cents usually required for this service.  But closing the ticket office also means the passengers will have to stand outside to wait for the train.  Conrail says it needs at least $99 million to continue to run the 13 commuter lines which carry 124,000 riders daily. Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority says it has only $93 million to give.  Unless the money is forthcoming, Conrail says all commuter trains in Philadelphia and the surrounding counties will come to a dead stop.

headline: This mafia stuff is getting serious
abstract: The editorial explains that the PA Crime Commission is conducting a preliminary investigation on the infiltration of organized crime in taverns and bars. The report is expected soon after public hearings in September. The editorial argues Pennsylvanians should know what businesses are corrupt so that they can decide whether to continue patronizing them.

headline: Two bills to remove ceilings on credit-card, loan interest offered
abstract: Legislation that would remove interest rate ceilings on credit cards and small consumer loans was introduced in the state Senate.  The legislation would not affect consumers current interest rates if passed.  Retailer lobbies have been actively pressing for the passage of the bill.

headline: Green's long, lingering decisions have both friends, foes fuming
abstract: Article inventories Philadelphia Mayor Green's inability to make snap decisions. The only snap decision Green is of record making was turning the fountain back on for Hallahan High School's students for the last day of school. This decision contradicted his water conservation mandate. The result of this decision had negative ramifications and as a result it is unlikely Green can be prodded into making quicker decisions in the future.

headline: The '82 race just might be between Lewis and Lewis
abstract: Lewis verses Lewis is going to be a probable match up of candidates in the 1982 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election.  One is Montgomery County Republican Drew Lewis, President Reagan's secretary of transportation.  The other is Democrat H. Craig Lewis, Bucks County state senator for the 6th District.  Neither Lewis has had success in statewide campaigns, but if the picture being painted by political insiders becomes a reality in the fall of 1982 the race might be between Lewis and Lewis.

headline: null
abstract: Editorial cartoon has a white older man sitting behind a desk with a black man in front of him holding an envelope and a piece of paper that has "3 cent RAISE" written on it.  The black man says, " This's right on time...for the cost-of-livin' ten years ago!"

headline: For blacks, the struggle of '81 is one from '65
abstract: An important section of the Voting Rights Act, a part that places counties with a history of voter discrimination under close federal scrutiny, is due to expire in August 1982. Black officials in the south are alarmed that one-time segregationist Strom Thurmont (R-South Carolina) is now chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee and has announced his opposition to a bill that would extend the law for 10 years. A series of congressional hearings on the proposed extensions is scheduled to start next month.

headline: Nothing Special
abstract: Philadelphia's public schools are now in their fifth teacher's strike in eleven years. And this strike could be longer than any other. That's because the schools are deeper in debt than before and for the first time, the teachers' contract has to be reopened. A lot of people are to blame for this mess, especially the School Board. Students learn a lot from these strikes, so we must try to be diplomatic.

headline: NRC Denies Request To Start Up TMI-1
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) denied General Public Utilities Corp's (GPU) request to restart the Unit 1 at the Three Mile Island (TMI) Nuclear Power Plant.  GPU asked the board to allow the unit to operate before a board provides recommendations and a decision on allowing the unit to restart.  An accident at Unit 2 in 1978 has dictated that the power plant not be treated as other power plants that haven't had accidents.  The articles details other ruling by NRC.

headline: Tolls Make State Turnpike Road to Riches
abstract: The PA turnpike has accumulated a $125 million bankroll, its largest in history. The profits made may soon be enough to sustain an aggressive maintenance program and to pay off its bonded indebtedness. At the same time, Pennsylvania's Department of Transportation (PennDOT) has much less money, and the governor is struggling to find a way to fund the much needed repairs on state highways. The author contends that this has created a political struggle between democrats and republicans as to how to solve PennDOT's problems while keeping the Turnpike the best maintained highway in the Commonwealth.

headline: Thornburgh-Rendell plan
abstract: The editorial agrees with Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposals to get tough on criminals by building more prison cells and stiffer sentences, but argues that the solution is not putting more people in prisons. Instead, he proposes that the justice system has an obligation to try rehabilitation.

headline: Two in area tied to gaming probe
abstract: Victor Restagno and Philip Ebright are among 51 reputed professional gamblers recommended to PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman by the state wide grand jury to face charges of conspiracy and bookmaking. They are all tied in a loosely connected network of gambling.

headline: Gubernatorial hopefuls hunt for headline prominence
abstract: The lure of the state's highest elected office has the state's highest elected office has the gubernatorial candidates out looking for headlines even though two still won't say definitely they're running, and the Primary election is over six months away. PA Governor Thornburgh has been touring a variety of small towns throughout the state. Al Benedict and James Lloyd have also been campaigning around the state.

headline: The Available Democrat
abstract: PA Auditor General Al Benedict may run for governor next year, but his department is being investigated by the grand jury. There have been allegations of making or forced political contributions from employees of the AG's department.

headline: null
abstract: Editorial cartoon illustrates a scene that appears to be from inside a space ship (called Voyager II) with an older man sitting behind a control panel saying, "They claim we've violated Libyan airspace!". There is a large window in front of him showing Saturn with fighter planes circling around that are about to hit Voyager II.

headline: Governor names city man to his Hispanic Council
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh appointed nine people to the Governor's Council on Hispanic Community. Min. J. de Collingwood, the council executive director, spoke on the importance of encouraging local governments and school districts to develop bicultural programs to ensure equal opportunities and treatment for Hispanics.

headline: Optimism over governor's aid offer disappears
abstract: Governor Thornburgh pledged $36 million in extra state funds to help alleviate a teachers' strike in Philadelphia.  However, since his pledge the strike has continued for over a month with no state funds allocated.  The article details the school district's deficit problems.

headline: NRC Finds 15 Nuclear Plants 'Below Average'
abstract: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission's first national survey comparing the performance of the country's operating atomic power plants lists 15 below average in areas such as management control, maintenance, radiation and fire protection and overall compliance with operating regulations.

headline: Transit official for battle over funds: Official braces for a battle over transit
abstract: Transit operators are concerned by statements made by the US Transportation Secretary-desginate, Drew Lewis, that the federal government should gradually reduce mass transit subsidies.  Cities and counties would not be able to make up for the lost subsidies and there is fear that it would cripple mass transit.

headline: Throwing book at criminals
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell held a conference stating his views on the guidelines the Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing is proposing.  He wants tougher sentencing guidelines for violent crime repeaters.

headline: U.S. eyes 1st Pa. rate hike
abstract: In response to First Pennsylvania Bank's decision to increase interest rates on credit cards from 15 to 19.8 per cent, state Representative Charles P. Laughlin stated that he would seek a restraining order to prevent the bank from doing so.  The U.S. Comptroller of the Currency, however, stated that the bank acted within the law in raising rates.  The article details the legality of the bank's actions.

headline: Guidelines for the school nominating panel
abstract: One of the most important groups assembled by Philadelphia Mayor Green is the 13-member nominating panel that currently is deliberating on recommendations to the mayor to fill vacancies on the Philadelphia Board of Education. Race, sex, ethnicity, and political and philosophical considerations are concerns.

headline: The better of two redistricting plans
abstract: In this letter to he editor the writer discusses the pros and cons of each of the two redistricting plans. On November 6, the Joint Committee on Congressional Reapportionment heard testimony on Pittsburgh's congressional redistricting plans. The O'Connell plan combines 10 congressional districts  and places 10 incumbents into the runoffs. The Zemprelli plan only combines 4 districts and this is achieved in a bipartisan manner.

headline: null
abstract: Picture with the caption, "HOUSE VISITOR -- Jill Ann Shafer of York, Miss Pennsylvania, tries out the gavel during a visit to the state House of Representatives Tuesday.  She was accorded honors."

headline: House defers debate on bill on abortions
abstract: null

headline: Our Ideas: The Arrogance of the PSEA
abstract: The editors feel that the Pennsylvania State Education Association (PSEA) has become too arrogant in their criticism of Governor Thornburgh's education policy.  The editors cite PSEA statement that they got Governor Thornburgh elected and feel that it is a very pompous thing to say, since individual citizens decide upon their elected officials, not one specific lobbying group.  They are pleased that the Governor has stood up to their criticism.

headline: NRC Reorganizes, Implements Position To Speed Up Licensing of New Reactors
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) announced plans to reorganize to speed the process of licensing for new reactors.  The new deputy director of the NRC will be Victor Stello.  The article details the reorganization and who will be filling what positions.

headline: Travelers set record in city
abstract: In 1980, a record number of travelers went through the Pittsburgh International Airport, Greyhound and Trailways bus stations.The article sites statistics that show that Pittsburgh's transportation industry is growing.

headline: To join or not to join
abstract: Officials of four Lower Bucks municipalities soon will revive their discussions on a proposal to create a consolidated police department. The state Department of Community Affairs gave positive results in a feasibility study and the townships are commissioning a second study. The editorial argues the joint department would improve law enforcement, but too much time studying the concept might lead to its death.

headline: U.S. Shipbuilders Sinking Fast
abstract: Out in the yards of the Sun Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Company beside the Delaware River, helmeted workers are building a vast monument to the decline of an American industry.  It is a 640-foot ocean-going freighter that Sun Ship is constructing for Waterman Steamship Corporation.  Still unnamed, it is known as hull number 680, the 680th in a line of ships that began in 1916.  There will be no hull number 681.  Sun Ship , a subsidiary of the Sun Company,  is giving up the business after 65 years, sunk by a vanishing market for United States tax operating loss of $62 million in 1980.

headline: Gypsy Moth Republicans And By-Election
abstract: On June 25, 1981, in the midst of the well-publicized national budget debate, the votes of the 4th district in Ohio wne to he polls to choose a success to the late Republican congressman Tennyson Guyer, and the result was a near deadhead between State Representative Michael Oxley, Republican, and State Representative Dale Locker, Democrat.  Oxley led by a few hundred votes, and was expected to win the recount.  These by-elections are not precise barometers, because they tend to exaggerate the shift agains the party in the White House.  The Gypsy Moths, counter-named for the troublesome caterpillars, now turning to moths, who have been eating up the leaves of millions of acres of New England trees, are the Northeastern and Great Lakes Republicans.

headline: The Careys of Albany
abstract: First Lady of New York is featured since her husband is running for re-election. Her daily life is detailed along with her personal history.

headline: …but it's place of livelihood
abstract: Tax relief is a common goal that is complicated. A bill for tax relief would cost Philadelphia an estimated yearly revenue loss of $47 million to $57 million. The burden would only be shifted to local taxes instead and the opinion suggests the bill be stopped.

headline: House defers debate on bill on abortions
abstract: Abortion legislation was postponed until after the Thanksgiving recess, because of bad weather and inordinate debate on a mandatory-sentencing bill. The abortion bill includes a 24-hour cooling off period for a woman seeking an abortion. It would also require that females under 18 obtain parental consent and that doctors try to save fetuses deemed capable of survival outside the mother's womb.

headline: Pa. law allows teachers to pick their residency
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed into law a bill that abolishes the Philadelphia School District's residency requirement. It allows all current school district employees to live outside the city without losing their jobs. However, teachers hired in the future will be subject to residency requirements. This caveat to the no-residency requirement for new teachers was codified not law in order to prevent the loss of the city's tax base.

headline: NRC ruled in contempt for meeting in secret
abstract: Members of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission are in contempt of court for holding a budget meeting in private despite a court order that it be made public, says a federal judge. They can purge themselves by releasing a transcript of their meeting to the public.

headline: Trimming service at PAT
abstract: The editorial argues that Allegheny County has failed to find a way to finance the Port Authority Transit system. This week PAT announced service cuts by deleting mostly after-midnight bus-runs. This is in response to the Regan administration's threat to cut some $15 million in operating subsidies. PAT believes the cuts will not cause much inconvenience to commuters, as opposed to the other alternative of fare increases.

headline: Today's kids sewed the seeds of its downfall, Lancaster firm says
abstract: American Seed Co. has gone out of business, overwhelmed by the dishonestly of grade-school children. It is a sad end for a company that introduced generations of the nation's youth to the ways of free enterprise. In ads featured in every in every juvenile publication held its offer: Sell packs of garden seeds and split the proceeds with the company or win prizes. Instead kids pocketed all the money.

headline: U.S. Steel oil bid 'bad politics'?
abstract: U.S. Steel's decision to place a bid of $6.4 billion on Marathon Oil Company receives much criticism as the bid is seen as good economics but bad public relations. Many critics believe that U.S. Steel should have used the investment to hone its competitive edge especially with foreign steelmakers instead of buying an oil company.

headline: Has eye on governorship, Scranton says
abstract: null

headline: The city GOP seizes the day
abstract: The Democratic party of Philadelphia is frozen in a moment of transition. Their creed is ancient: Mayors come and go, reform movements ebb and flow, but ward leaders are forever. It is a posture that creates a window of opportunity for the routed oldtimers. The infighting has caused the other party to seek a way to overcome. Republicans are connecting with Democrats on the outs to join forces.

headline: 5-county SEPTA tax urged
abstract: A state tax study recommended several changes in the state's tax structure including, a state income tax to finance SEPTA, and an increase in the state income tax.  The article details the report done by the State Tax Commission, appointed by Governor Thornburgh.

headline: House Panel Right on Abortion Bill
abstract: The Health and Welfare Committee of the PA state House of Representatives has held public hearings to solicit testimony on the proposed Abortion Control Act of 1981. These proposals are contrary not only to the US Constitution, but to the state constitution as well.

headline: Postponing the crisis: Business as usual for city schools
abstract: The editorial argues that the Philadelphia School Board will not be able to find the $223 million difference between what they say they need and what is available, and although the system has major budgetary and other problems, Governor Dick Thornburgh has bailed them out with enough money to keep the school system open through June. In the view of the editorial, the requirement for the school system to undergo a strict audit is not enough.

headline: NRC staff report:  TMI cleanup to take seven years
abstract: The Nuclear Regulartory Commission state that the damage from the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear accident does not pose any health threats to residents, but will take seven more years to clean up.  They also stated that the water decontamination unit installed by the Metropolitan Edison Co. will not work to the commissions standards.  The article details the workings of the unit any health dangers to workers.

headline: Turnpike Board to sell 3 plazas
abstract: The Turnpike Commission will sell three abandoned service plazas at auction next month. Closed two years ago, the plazas formerly served as restaurants and service stations. Sales will be conducted by a Philadelphia auctioneer on each site and high bids are subject to commission approval.

headline: Toughened Jail Sentence Guide Is Still 'Softer' Than Local Courts
abstract: The Commission on Sentencing has rewritten some it's guidelines making them tougher on criminals.  There is criticism that the guidelines on some sentences are too soft on criminals.  Lancaster county judges already have stricter sentencing in place.  The article details the new sentencing guidelines, which the General Assembly must still approve

headline: Want a liquor license? Be ready to shell out; Soaring prices for liquor licenses give rise to criticism
abstract: In Abingtown Township, where the Willow Grove Mall is being developed, state liquor licenses now cost $75,000 or $80,000, and the price is heading up.  From the sound of it , the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board is making a fortune from the sale of licenses, which are defined in the state liquor code "personal prvilege(s) granted by the board."  But the Liquor Control Board does not make a cent from these sales.  The same code that allows the board to grant such "personal privileges" ensures a severe shortage of licenses - and thus a tremendous demand for them - in many parts of Pennsylvania, particularly the suburbs of Philadelphia.  And having created the demand, the liquor code allows private entrepreneurs to sell their state licenses for as much as they can get.

headline: Hearings on US Aid Will Wait
abstract: House Republican leaders beat back a Democratic bid to hold immediate public hearings on the Thornburgh administration's plans to deal with block grants proposed by President Reagan.

headline: The Consumer Party
abstract: The editors endorsed the Consumer Party and all of its candidates because of their stance on crime in the Philadelphia.  They urge the party to take steps to become a more viable force with broad base political support.

headline: A budget proposal that spells austerity for many in Pennsylvania
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's proposed budget cuts spending in most state agencies.  Some feel that this will lead to higher local taxes. The article details his proposed budget and what the most controversial aspects are.  The author feels that the most needed services are being cut, but there are increases for law enforcement and business development.

headline: House vote on abortion delayed
abstract: The PA House of Representatives postponed for two weeks a scheduled vote on a tough anti-abortion bill. The discussion of mandatory sentences for violent crimes ran longer than expected. It would require a woman to wait 24 hours before she could obtain an abortion.

headline: Pa. plan to change special ed program draws fire
abstract: Education Secretary Robert Scanlon's proposal to reduce funding for special education and gifted classes is drawing criticism from teachers, school administrators and parents.  They feel the proposal will cause the district to increase taxes to fund the programs.  The article details the proposal and peoples' criticisms.

headline: NRC: Beaver nuclear plant is poorly run
abstract: Dusquesne Light Co's nuclear power plant in Shippingport is the worst run of the nation's 50 operating nuclear facilities says a survey by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has found. Fifteen of the plants were found below average.

headline: Turnpike commissioner quits
abstract: Ray Bollinger quit his job as Pennsylvania Turnpike Commissioner after Governor Thornburgh vetoed a bill that would increase his salary.  The Governor must now appoint someone else to the position.

headline: Tougher jail sentences
abstract: The editors opine that since the guidelines for tougher sentencing will take effect in three months unless the legislature votes it down, they should allow the guidelines to go through.  They feel that since mandatory sentencing is already in place for first degree murder, it should also be in place for crimes committed more often, like violent crimes and burglary.  District Attorney Ed Rendell also supports the guidelines.

headline: Wants No-Layoff Clause Removed: Governor Firm on Liquor Pact
abstract: The Thornburgh administration refused to budge from its insistence that a no-layoff clause must be removed from a contract with liquor store clerks before the proposal is acceptable.  Robert C. Wilburn, secretary of Budget and Administration, stated that if the no-layoff clause was retained, it would impede transition to a private liquor retail system.  The article continues to provide information about the Pennsylvania Governor Richard Thornburgh's thoughts on the clause and the views of his administration.

headline: Heinz & Specter Show Is ... Well, Interesting
abstract: US Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter from PA are taping a series of monthly television interview shows with political personalities. The show, entitled "Senator's report to PA", in its first episode featured Vice President George Bush and Democrat Ernest Hollings from South Carolina.

headline: The Daily Number
abstract: The graph depicts what the winner of the PA Lottery might get, depending on the amount and type of bet placed. The author explains that there are many ways to play, and the Daily Number has proved a most attractive lure to heavy participation.

headline: A CHALLENGE TO THE GOP'S NEW GRASS-ROOTS POWER
abstract: Mayors and governors of both political parties are slashing budgets in hopes that President Reagan's promised 'American economic renaissance' materializes soon. If it does not, Democrats are threatening on turning next year's election into a referendum on Reagan's economic policies which can undo impressive GOP political gains at the grassrootslevel. Because of Reagan's program to reduce the size and role of government is beginning to have dramatic impact on states and municipalities, the distinction between purely local concerns and national issues is blurring. Governor Richard Thornburgh is mentioned as he only received a 53% majority in the 1978 elections. With Thornburgh's across the board spending cuts winning little public acceptance, such federal spending cuts can hit closer to home.

headline: House votes to block forced busing orders
abstract: The House easily passed legislation yesterday aimed at halting court-ordered busing of school children for desegregation purposes. Former President Carter vetoed a bill containing the proposal last year, President Reagan is on the record as opposed to court-ordered busing.

headline: Pening school: Just a beginning
abstract: When the school money problem is finally solved, the school system will still continue to sink into oblivion. Until we have six new school board members and a new superintendent no amount of money will make our schools better.

headline: Nuclear Damage at Diablo
abstract: The facts are not all in yet about the situation at the Diablo Canyon nuclear reactor. Opposition to Diablo Canyon stems from its proximity to an active earthquake fault and it may not be able to withstand an earthquake, but the Nuclear Regulatory Commission are already being slammed for this error.

headline: Turnpike repairs approved
abstract: On April 22, the PA Turnpike Commission approved a $2.1 million resurfacing of a 10.7 mile stretch of the toll road between the Pittsburgh and Irwin interchanges in Allegheny and Westmoreland counties, and a $6.8 million reconstruction of 10.5 miles of the Northeast Extension in Montgomery, Bucks and Lehigh counties. The Commission also expects to have a record-breaking travel increase this coming summer.

headline: Trooper 'fun'
abstract: PA state troopers are more interested in speeders and spending tax dollars than they are stopping crime. Authors wishes they spent their time more wisely trying to protect the public from dangerous criminals.

headline: Welfare For Horses?
abstract: The editors opine that with the current shortfalls in revenue for the state, the state legislature should not pass a bill that would give a tax break to the horse racing industry and allow telephone bets.  The editors urge the Governor to veto the bill should it be passed by the House.

headline: Heinz press aide leaving job
abstract: US Senator John Heinz's press secretary, David Murray is leaving the Senator's office to pursue other job prospects in his home state of New Jersey.

headline: The Governors' Gamble
abstract: Governors will be holding their annual meeting next week in Atlantic City. The governors won some and lost some and their dollar losses far outweighed their winnings. Under the Carter administration 1982 budget plan, federal aid would have been $100 billion, not enough to keep pace with inflation but still an increase from the previous year. Under the Reagan administration, the budget adopted last week will be for only $88 billion. Although the states lost considerable funds, they did retain more control over how and where to spend the budgeted money. The Reagan budget thus reverses, if only modestly, the recent drift in federal-state relations. Over the last decade, states gained an increasing share of federal revenues, but at the expense of a considerable greater number of restrictions on the use of that money. At the moment this is a moral victory for the governors.

headline: Budget gets mixed reviews
abstract: null

headline: Human life amendment
abstract: The major fault with the Human Life Amendment is that it would substitute the Moral Majority's dictate for a woman's right to make a personal choice. They want to tell women what to do. Planned Parenthood points out the problems with the amendment. The editorial wants religious people to not impose their beliefs on other when it comes to abortion.

headline: Penn law dean to head to U. of Iowa
abstract: James O. Freedman, dean of the University of Pennsylvania Law School was named president of the University of Iowa yesterday. Freedman stated that the opportunity of leading a major university was too big a professional challenge to turn down. Freedman also is the chairman of the Pennsylvania State Reapportionment Commission. He received his bachelor’s degree from Harvard, then his law degree from Yale Law School. He also served as a clerk under Thurgood Marshall, the US Supreme Court Justice.

headline: Nuclear plant out of service
abstract: The Beaver Valley Station Unit 1 of Duquesne Light Company's nuclear facility at Shippingport remained out of service after a May 2 minor release of radioactive steam. The Beaver County nuclear plant release was below the allowable 10 percent, and will remain out of service while it is repaired.

headline: Turnpike travelers offered doughnut, safety break
abstract: Some drivers stopped at the Highspire service plaza to munch a doughnut and watch a film and slideshow, part of a safety program sponsored by the state police, PA Motor Truck Association and Turnpike Commission. Those who did not stop got a PMTA radar speed check. They read pamphlets and watched a film that taught them how to share the road better.

headline: Two Testify Perry Asked Aid, 'Heavy Bets' on 4-6 Combos
abstract: Brothers Peter and Jack Maragos, both longtime business associates of lottery-trial defendant Nick Perry, testified Friday that Perry asked them to join in fixing the PA Daily Number game and place "heavy bets" on 4-6 number combinations. The two are key witnesses in the trial against Perry and Edward Plevel, which face charges of perjury, theft, conspiracy and rigging a publicly exhibited contest as a result of the 6-6-6 drawing.

headline: We'll drink to that
abstract: The editors support Governor Thornburgh's proposal to privatize state-owned liquor stores.  They feel that everyone can support this proposal and hope that it is passed.

headline: Heinz spurts into 1982 campaign
abstract: US Senator  John Heinz is starting to campaign even though no one has said they would are intending to run against him. He hasn't done anything to make voters want to kick him out.

headline: The Hanging Judge as Hero
abstract: The editorial analyzes the toughness of Judge James McDermott, also known as "The Hanging Judge", arguing that his good reputation as a tough sentencer will help him in the election run for state Supreme Court Judge.

headline: BUREAUCRATS: RE-READ LAST YEAR'S ELECTION RESULTS
abstract: The editorial argues that President Regan's budget policies are being distorted by liberals and bureaucrats. The president is trying to live up to his campaign promises to return to the local level the right to decide how much is spent for what, whereas the Manpower Programs and the management of the Economic Development Council of Northeastern Pennsylvania, for example, are trying to arouse public opinion against Reagan's proposals. The editorial argues it's because they're afraid of losing their bureaucrat jobs.

headline: Justice has two standards
abstract: The author opines that blacks cannot be assured fairness in the Philadelphia judicial system.  The author states that very few judges or police officers are black and feels that there is institutional racism within the judical system because of this.

headline: Penn shuts its museum after 3d theft
abstract: The University Museum at the University of Pennsylvania will be closed until Tuesday while new security measures are being installed. Three items have been stolen from the museum in the past few months. The most recent item was an Indian necklace. Previously a Japanese porcelain horse and a 455 year old gold saw were stolen. None of the items have been recovered.

headline: Nuclear power industry is in a fight for survival
abstract: The announcement by Boston Edison Company said it planned to scrap the proposed Pilgrim II nuclear power plant underscores the deepseated problems that threaten the survival of the nation's power industry, because of costly delays and uncertain over regulatory requirements.  Once heralded as the cheapest, cleanest, safest way to generate electricity, nuclear power is the victim of fears generated by Three Mile Island, political opposition, regulatory miasma, high interest rates and an uncertain demand for electricity.  The expected licensing of California's Diablo Canyon nuclear plant is unlikely to ease this situation.  No new nuclear power plants have been ordered in four years; nearly three dozen have been canceled in that time.

headline: Two rail lines hang in there
abstract: The editorial argues that the last minute extension of a scheduled termination for Southeastern PA Transportation Authority's train between Pottstown and Pottsville is a good victory for commuters. The extra two months and state subsidies will give the state General Assembly more time to consider further subsidies.

headline: US Crime Surging Again
abstract: Besides a 9.4 percent rise in its crime index, the FBI's September 10 report on lawbreaking noted these developments in 1980. Since 1976 daytime burglaries of homes rose 32 percent, street robberies 45 percent, and bank holdups 71 percent. Handguns were used in 50 percent of all murders. Seventy percent of those arrested were under 25.

headline: What's at stake today
abstract: For 134 of the 205 years since the republic was founded here, The Bulletin has been respected and independent voice in Philadelphia.  Over those 134 years, The Bulletin set a standard of conservative, reliable journalism for the 16 other Philadelphia dailies which were once published here.  The Bulletin's eight craft unions must decide if they will continue the fight of keeping the newspaper running.

headline: Heinz, Specter Star In TV Trek
abstract: US Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter, both moderate GOP Republicans, have started a new half-hour TV show named "Your Senators Report to PA". The show is being filmed in the taxpayer-supported studios of the US Capitol, and the senators are solely responsible for the content. The first show featured Vice President George Bush and the second one US Senator Fritz Hollings (D-South Carolina). TV stations in six of the state's seven broadcast markets have agreed to carry the show.

headline: The irony of politics and a new challenge
abstract: The editorial analyzes Philadelphia Republican Jim McDermott, candidate for PA Supreme Court, and his recent visit to Scranton, PA. The editorial acknowledges McDermott's wisdom and past electoral run difficulties.

headline: Caliguiri asks tax hikes; Cut in services part of package
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Caliguiri asked City Council for tax increases to fight inflation.  The mayor also announced that he plans to reorganize city government to make it more effective, and reduce funding for non-essential services.  The mayor stated several reasons for the cuts including; decreased federal funding, the decline in the housing market, and the major league baseball strike.

headline: Key anti-abortion clause loses
abstract: Pennsylvania legislation making it more difficult for women to obtain abortions in Pennsylvania headed to the House for approval after a vote deleted one of the most restrictive provisions.  Pennsylvania Representative Stephen Friend was the prime sponsor of the bill.  Pennsylvania Representative Michael M. Dawida's amendment removes provisions that would have permitted virtually any citizen to go to court to request an order halting an abortion sought under the law.  The article provides further detail about the bill and all of the key provisions it has included.

headline: Pennsylvania teachers are being taught to do their LEAST for discipline
abstract: The LEAST program teaches teachers how to do as little as possible to maintain control. Any time you create a disruption in responding to misbehavior, you lose teaching time. L stands for leave it alone, E for end the disruption directly, A for attend more fully to the reasons behind disruption. S for spell out directions to the student. T stands for track students misbehavior.

headline: Nuclear Power: Safe and Sound?
abstract: Letter to editor suggesting the Post is biased against nuclear power and is working against the administration's analysis. Nuclear power is still the most economical way to expand our electricity supplies.

headline: Two views on rail reductions
abstract: Two letters to the editor about Southeastern PA Transit  Authority. The first believes SEPTA's proposed commuter rail service cutbacks are the first steps of a long-overdue restricting plan, but don't go far enough. The second is upset that SEPTA is focusing on providing transportation.

headline: Vests for the police
abstract: The editorial argues that police officers in Philadelphia face dangers and should be protected by supporting Mayor Green's proposal to supply all officers with bullet-proof vests. He calls for Philadelphians to contribute to a special Police Fund to supply the officers with the vests, as a way of thanking them for the job of putting their lives in danger.

headline: Where the Action Is
abstract: Last week the state and federal law enforcement agencies cracked down on illegal gambling in three states, with PA having its biggest gambling bust in history. One conclusion is that legal gambling, which is prevalent in all three states, is not a deterrent to illegal gambling. Proponents of legal gambling argue that in this way the state can benefit the Commonwealth, while the editorial argues that less gambling is needed.

headline: Here's one scenario for reapportionment
abstract: The editorial presents his theory on how the redrawing of the congressional district lines in PA will occur. Philadelphia is in danger of losing one of its four congressional districts unless one or two present districts spill over into the suburbs.

headline: The Miracle Worker of North Frazier Street
abstract: Falaka Fattah is the founder and director of the House of Umoja, a youth organization that is unorthodox and successful against juvenile crime. It stresses personal pride and economic development with minimum state and federal help.

headline: Capital budget measure passes Senate, 44-0
abstract: The PA  Senate approved legislation outlining $127 million in public construction projects for the 1981-1982 fiscal year with almost half to be used for educational facilities. It is more than double PA Governor Thornburgh's original recommendation of $57 million.

headline: Lesbian sues to get back recreation job
abstract: A gay rights activist went to federal court in an attempt to force the City of Philadelphia to rehire her as supervisor of a neighborhood recreation center, a post she quit under pressure in 1974. Patricia Hill left her job after making a television appearance asking for justice for gays. When she tried to get rehired, she was refused because she is a lesbian. The city denies this.

headline: Pennsylvania's Press
abstract: The author feels that Governor Thornburgh should revoke the gag order issued by Pennsylvania Secretary of Education, Robert Scanlon, who outlined procedures for state college and university presidents when talking about legislation affecting their institutions.  The author feels this is censorship.

headline: Nuclear Power's New Dilemma
abstract: Safety rules and malfunctions in nuclear power plants combine to hurt profits and in some cases push up customer bills. They are failing at their promise of cheap reliable power. On average nuclear plants are shut down one out of every eight days they should be running.

headline: U.S. Oks funds to ease Parkway snarl
abstract: The Federal Highway Administration allocated $10.8 million in funds to reduce traffic problems while the Parkway East is reconstructed.  The article outlines the plans to reduce congestion until the project is completed in November 1982, including Commuter Rail Service, extended bus service, van pools and Park-n-Ride Lots.

headline: Zimmerman Proposed 2nd Grand Jury
abstract: Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman hopes to intensify efforts against crime by nearly tripling the number of prosecutors in his office and by empanelling a second state grand jury. The creation of a second grand jury could be used by district attorneys when they share jurisdiction with the attorney general.

headline: Why A Nice County Is in the Liquor Business
abstract: The author, a Montgomery County official, argues for maintaining the county's Liquor Control Department, for the goals of moderating the use of alcohol, providing some convenience to citizens, and receiving revenues. If the county got rid of the control, then it would have to raise taxes to account for its loss, or cut the budget. The author does agree that there are management problems with the DLC that need to be fixed, and says the county is committed to implementing a reorganization plan that will bring better order and operations.

headline: High court choice seen as crucial
abstract: The article outlines the details of the election for Pennsylvania's Supreme Court.  It talks about the four candidates and their various views on the current court system and the changes they'd like to make.  It also outlines a controversy regarding one of the current Supreme Court Justices, Rolf Larsen, and his ties to candidate Robert Colville.  He is actively politicking, which is against ethical standards for a judge.

headline: The Monster
abstract: It's called the "three headed monster." the mis-shaped figure is the referendum on the November ballot to decide the make-up of Pittsburgh City Council. Voters will have three "yes" or "no" choices. Elect council at large, elect council by district, or elect seven members by district and two at large.

headline: Cashing in on preferential treatment
abstract: A very timely booklet shows business and industry how they can win government contracts. The government is putting a renewed emphasis on granting regions of high unemployment preference in the award of government contracts. And with the Maybank amendment requiring awards to lowest bidders repealed, some of the huge US Defense Department outlay is being targeted to labor surplus areas. This is the first time PA will have a preference in competing for Defense Department contracts.

headline: Letters to the editor: The end of the 15-percent solution
abstract: The author talks about the "15 per cent" compensation from the Civil Rights movement, that African Americans should be entitled to 15 per cent of what they were previously denied.  The author lambastes black leaders as lazy and complacent and states that there is no leadership among black youth.  The author also feels that the black community is not standing up to "the man" and are not be proactive about starting businesses.

headline: Phase out the school-tax burden
abstract: The author feels that the recent findings by the Pennsylvania Tax Commission ignore the burden that the school tax puts on home owners.  The author cites several studies showing the problems with the school tax.

headline: Nuclear Regulatory Agency Chief Assails 'Failure in Plants' Safety
abstract: Nunzio J. Palladino, chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) stated that many nuclear facilities have terrible quality assurance programs.  The NCR found problems at several plants around the country.  The article details the specific problems at the plants.

headline: US 'Blackmails' State on Emissions
abstract: A bill to halt the auto-emissions inspections had been passed by our legislators and sent on to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, but the governor considered the inspections unnecessary, costly and a burden to the public. It was then learned if the bill was signed PA would lose $400 million in federal highway money.

headline: Zimmerman Taps Guida As Special Prosecutor
abstract: PA State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman made Richard Guida head of the special prosecution section to coordinate enforcement activities with local law enforcement agencies. There will be more individuals hired to the special prosecution section and as of now there is no fixed budget. Guida's position involves handling requests from district attorneys from the mid-sized to small counties that seek prosecutorial assistance in handling cases.

headline: Why can't we have true no-fault law?
abstract: Op-ed discusses the deficiencies in Pennsylvania's no-fault insurance protection law. The piece expands into a laundry list of the law's shortcomings such as: failure to eliminate auto accident liability lawsuits and equitably distributing the cost of insurance protection by mandating every PA driver obtain liability insurance.

headline: High Court Hopeful Touts Experience
abstract: Philadelphia Judge James McDermott, running for the state supreme court, lambasted his opponents for not having any bench experience as a judge, stating that experience is a necessity for any candidate.  The article details Mr. McDermott's career as a judge.

headline: The ONLY candidate with the Governor's nomination
abstract: An advertisement depicts a drawing of Reed McCormick, who is running for Centre County Judge. The ad states that he has received nomination from the Governor, received bipartisan recommendation from the county Judicial Nominating Committee, and approved by the State Senate Judiciary Committee, and also calls for a vote to elect McCormick.

headline: Coalition to Battle Reagan Budget
abstract: A newly formed statewide coalition said it will fight a battle against President Reagan's proposed budget. The coalition of 32 diverse organizations believe the poor and working people will be the most affected. The US House is beginning debate on the budget.

headline: Letters to the editor; Abortion bill: God's law involved, too
abstract: Three letters to the editor discussing the Abortion Control Act and three different views on abortion.  One that says abortion is a woman's choice, another with freedom to choose is not a good excuse to kill an unborn child, and another is that states the Internal Revenue Service must consider the fetus to be a dependent and deserves a deduction.

headline: Phila. Teachers ordered back
abstract: A Common Pleas Court judge ordered striking Philadelphia teachers to return to their classrooms on Monday. Schools Superintendent Michael Marcase said the district would announce tomorrow when students are expected to return to school.

headline: Nuclear-plant foes in Midwest win big victory
abstract: Construction of the controversial Bailly nuclear power plant on the shore of Lake Michigan has been abandoned with the announcement by the Northern Indiana Public Service Company that it is scrapping its $1,8 billion project, ending a 10-year battle and marking a major victory for anti-nuclear forces.  Edmund A. Schroer, chairman of the utility, said that the project was being terminated because "it is evident that completion of the projection in 1989 is no longer achievable, because of continuing delays associated with the construction-permit extension proceedings and problems with the design.  Schroer said delaying the target date a year, to 1990, would cost an additional $161 million; a year later, the overrun would total $324 million.

headline: US Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis press conference
abstract: The photograph is of a news conference with US Transportation Secretary, with the caption: "Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis discusses the future of the Conrail system during a press conference at the Barclay in Philadelphia. He is with New Jersey Governor Brendan Byrne, New York Governor Hugh Carey, and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: War on porn: Philadelphia's legal battle is likely to last for years
abstract: District Attorney Edward Rendell arrested 16 alleged pornographers in response to a new obscenity rule in Pennsylvania.  They are owners of adult stores and movie houses, which the State wants to be shut down.  The alleged pornographers will see the case to the Supreme Court and cite the First Amendment as their defense.  Some feel that adult stores are tied to organized crime.

headline: Wine sale decontrol urged
abstract: Democratic senator says he introduce legislation to allow table wine to be sold in supermarkets, grocery stores and delicatessens as a first step in abolishing the state liquor store. The bill would allow stores that sell $5,000 worth of food per month to obtain a license from the state to sell table wines, those containing 14 percent alcohol or less.

headline: High court reinstates winners of Phila. Judicial primary
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has instated the winners of the disputed May 19 Philadelphia Democratic judicial primary. The high court said the majority of the justices were convinced an "inadvertent" voting-machine error did not affect the result of the primary within the meaning of Section 1772 of the Election Code.

headline: The Real Point
abstract: The editorial explains state Senator Milton Street's weatherization program and how its welfare workers were collecting additional salaries. Since then, Street held a press conference in his brother's Philadelphia City Council office. He excluded an I Team Reporter, and his brother shoved and pushed him down. Later Street was caught driving with a revoked license. The editorial argues the real point is that Street's program wasted tax dollars, and that the only way to know if some important people knew about it is through a full investigation by Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Commerce's burget cut of almost 33 pct. bared by secretary
abstract: Commerce Secretary Geoffrey Stengel announced at a Senate Budget hearing that the Commerce Department's budget would be cut by one third. Stengel said that he supported Governor Thornburgh's budget proposal.  The article details the programs that would be cut and the events at the hearing.

headline: Letters to the editor; An endeavor to protect human life
abstract: Five different letters to the editor that do not approve of the way the abortion bill is coming through the Pennsylvania Senate.

headline: Phila. Teachers strikes: No school 5 times in last 10 years
abstract: Graph showing the number of days of school missed due to teacher strikes in the past 10 years.

headline: Nuke Development
abstract: The editorial argues the Three Mile Island story isn't over. In the next week or so, the fate of the managing company will be determined by a government torn between pro and anti-nuke forces - one side wants its head and the other fears the alternatives that bankruptcy creates.  Editorial says that TMI could lie at the base of a national energy disaster or it could open the door to reason and progress.

headline: War on potholes gets dirty
abstract: Some country roads in Westmoreland County are getting a unique anti-pothole treatment. They've been turned into plain dirt roads. The PA Department of Transportation has stripped off the old pocket surface leaving motorists a dirt base. All roads have been coated with stone chips and doused with oil to keep down the dust.

headline: Wecht's trial delayed
abstract: A trial against Cyril Wecht, a coroner from 1970 to 1980 and now a county commissioner, included a former coroner's office employee testimony that the morgue technicians were giving higher priority to tissue testing for Wecht's private lab than the normal county autopsy work. Wecht's defense, however, established that private work was essential to their training, and that all work for the county was usually completed on time. Wecht is charged with theft of services based on his use of county employees on the private tests.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: Man in bed and alarm goes off saying "the preceding has been a test of the emergency broadcast system.  In the event of a real nuclear attack, you will, unfortunately, be dead…"

headline: Hill Workers Health Service Fate Argued
abstract: State Senator George W. Gekas stated that through communications with Health Secretary H. Arnold Muller, he may be able to prevent the loss of the Employee Health Service for Capitol Hill workers.  The program was slated to be cut as part of Governor Thornburgh's budget proposal.

headline: The Redistricting Game
abstract: The author opines that the redistricting of Pennsylvania will be contraversial.  The author explains the debate between Democrats and Republicans over the issue of redistricting and cites historical events to show the contraversy.

headline: Dial-a-Bet Easy Winner In Senate
abstract: The PA State Senate approved a bill that would give tax breaks to race tracks that allow betting by telephone.  The bill also provides for an extended racing season, and allows "simulcast" between Pennsylvania tracks.  The history of the bill is detailed.

headline: Medicaid abortions go to court
abstract: Supreme Court Justice Roy Wilkinson Jr. correctly delayed cutting off state funds for Medicaid abortions.  Wilkinson refused to overturn Commonwealth Court Judge John A MacPhail's ruling giving poor women at least until October to get Medicaid abortions.  Governor Thornburgh last December signed into law a bill that prohibited the use of Medicaid funds for abortions except when: a mother's life is at stake,  or rape or incest victim promptly reports it.  Medicaid funds are now used to pay for abortions in cases where mother's health is at state and her income is less than $3,600 a year.  The Commonwealth Court will hear arguments next month from the Women's Law Project that the law denies equal protection to poor women.  The Supreme Court could hear the appeal in October.

headline: Philadelphia's teachers must help
abstract: Station gives message to teacher: Instead of holding a pep rally tonight to close schools, why don't you talk about how to keep them open? Philadelphia Mayor Green offered a tax increase for the schools. He tied it to cuts by the school board, more money from the state, ad to sacrifices on your part. Teachers should move to compromise as well.

headline: Oil to coal
abstract: The editors opine that coverting from oil to coal fired plants, as proposed by U.S. Senator John Heinz, will be too costly for the environment to be efficient

headline: Wholesale tax on fuel is acceptable
abstract: For better than a year the governor and the legislators have been pushing and tugging over how best to get more money for the PA Department of Transportation. The House would keep the 11-cent gas tax and create a 3.5 percent wholesale tax which is expected to yield $192 million for highway repairs. The editorial believes this is a good way to fund PennDOT.

headline: What did Boyle probe really find?
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman's office has completed a limited, five-week investigation of the handling of the Yablonski murder case. It concludes that no one misbehaved, but does not address should former United Mine Workers President WA Boyle have been convicted of murdering his union rival? The evidence suggests he did not.

headline: $1 tax would aid ailing Vietnam vets
abstract: A proposed pair of bills would require Pennsylvania residents to pay a one dollar tax to help cover the medical expenses of Vietnam veterans suffering from exposure to herbicides, such as Agent Orange, used during the conflict.  The tax would be for one year only and would go to the Vietnam Veterans Herbicide Assistance Fund.

headline: Hispanic chosen for judgeship:  3 others named to Common Pleas
abstract: Governor Thornburgh chose Nelson Diaz, a Puerto Rican civil rights leader, to fill a vacancy on the Philadelphia Common Pleas Court.  Thornburgh also made three other nominations to fill vacancies; John Braxton, Victor DiNubile, and Joseph Bongiovanni.  The article details the candidates histories.

headline: Thornburgh Backs Scranton For Lt. Gov.
abstract: The cartoon depicts Governor Dick Thornburgh wearing an election pin with the words "THORNBURGH BACKS SCRANTON FOR LT. GOV". The word Thornburgh is in much larger font than the rest of the caption.

headline: Does state tax report have some loose ends?
abstract: The Tax Commission's report may serve as a blueprint for tax reform or prove to be worthless.  A source close to the Commission said that they are taking political realities into account when drafting their report.  The article details the draft's recommendations and why they are not feasible.

headline: NAACP vows to find black judge candidate
abstract: President of the Pittsburgh branch of the NAACP, Harvey Adams, vowed to find a black candidate for the Allegheny Common Pleas Court with or without the support of the Democratic county committee.  City ward leaders recommended four white candidates for the position, Bernard Novak, John Musmanno, Samuel Kamin, and Bernard Mcginley.  Adams feels that City Magistrate Walter Little has more credentials.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: "School executives discuss proposed legislation on self-rule."

headline: Opposes Restart of TMI Unit 1
abstract: The author feels that the only way to avoid another nuclear accident is to get rid of nuclear power.  The author feels that it is neither safe nor cheap and opposes restarting Three Mile Island's (TMI) nuclear plant.  The author urges reader to call Governor Thornburgh to express their opposition.

headline: With a view to '82
abstract: The picture depicts Governor Dick Thornburgh being present when Southeastern PA Transportation Authority Chairman David Girard-diCarlo and union president DiClerico announced an end to the transit strike.

headline: What teen-agers think about drugs nationally
abstract: Graphs of how teenagers felt about drugs in 1975, 1977, and 1980.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon depicts two men in a boxing ring.  One is standing up and on his arm it states "Ron the Ripper," depicting Ronald Reagan.  The other is on the ground, twisted in knots, and reads "AWACS Sale Foes."

headline: Honoring America
abstract: Photograph of R. Budd Dwyer and his family saying the pledge of allegiance at his inaugural ceremonies

headline: VA is urged to buy Bucks hospital
abstract: U.S. Representative James Coyne of Pennsylvania asks the Veteran's Administration to consider buying a lower Bucks County hospital for use a veterans hospital rather than buying the Delaware Valley Medical Center. Converting the Bucks County Hospital will cost approximately $2 million while buying the land and building the Delaware Valley Medical Center will cost approximately $75 million. Locating a Veterans Hospital in Bucks County is more convenient for veterans to drive to and is closer to a very large veteran population.

headline: Each of us bore $921 tax burden in Pennsylvania
abstract: Pennsylvania's per capita state and local tax burden was $921 in fiscal year 1979, slightly lower than the national average, but higher than West Virginia and Ohio.

headline: New Pro-Abortion Tack: Cheaper Than Welfare, Backers Feel
abstract: Some pro-abortion forces in Pennsylvania have stated that it is cheaper to fund abortions for women who want them, rather than have more people on welfare.  This month, Pennsylvania is expected to make it illegal to use Medicaid funds to get an abortion, while the US Senate and President Reagan are pushing for a constitutional amendment to ban abortion.  The article outlines the pro-abortion groups economic argument for keeping abortions legal and their oppositions comments.

headline: Picketing teachers arrested
abstract: For the second year in a row, a teacher's strike will delay the start of classes for Philadelphia's public school students. Fewer than 300 of the districts teachers showed up yesterday for work. About 600 teachers picketed the school district's administration building.

headline: Opposes Start-up of TMI's Unit 1
abstract: Letter to the editor against the reopening of Unit 1 at Three Mile Island, because it has been inactive for two years. They call for people to write the governor to stop it.

headline: You can dial-pothole-repair now
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation now has a hotline to report potholes.  The article gives the phone numbers, information on how the hotline works, and how potholes form.

headline: Where to go for help
abstract: A list of places to go for help if addicted to meth.

headline: Fight for copter unit to continue
abstract: State representative William F. Goodling is attempting to save the helicopter maintenance mission, which the army wants to transfer to Corpus Christi, Texas.  The transfer would mean the loss of 481 civilian jobs.  The article details Goodling's speech to the West Shore Chamber of Commerce.

headline: Horning In Again
abstract: The columnist explains that Governor Dick Thornburgh has secretly handed leasing rights of a state-owned museum at Penn's Landing to a private outfit, while Philadelphia's Mayor Green was hoping to use it extensively in next year's 300th Birthday celebrations for the city. This comes in addition to the governor's horning in on the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority settlement. The author also offers information on the food purchases for the Governor's mansion.

headline: The Scene: Traffic: Wonder if the I-Team got it on tape?
abstract: The author explains that state Senator Milton Street was stopped by a state trooper on the PA turnpike. The trooper was unable to arrest the senator for driving with a suspended license and unpaid traffic violations, due to a provision against arresting lawmakers on their way to a legislative session. The senator claims his aide was driving the car. They were on the way to a hearing of the Senate Committee for Law and Justice.

headline: Education, court boost urged
abstract: The ranking Democrat on the state House Appropriations Committee proposed a shift of the $127 million in Governor Dick Thornburgh's 1981-82 spending plan to give extra funds to education and county courts. Representative Max Pievsky said the reductions would provide another $50 million for local school districts, and also free up money for county courts, local sewage-facility  grants, child-welfare programs, and county environmental health grants.

headline: NOW petitions to stop anti-abortion effort
abstract: The National Organization for Women (NOW) is petitioning against a proposed constitutional amendment banning abortions called the Human Life Amendment.  NOW Vice President Carol McCullough stated that the proposed amendment would define birth control methods as murder as well as abortions.

headline: Program to resolve strike problems among teachers runs into hurdle
abstract: Philadelphia school board member Herman Mattleman suggests sending human relations specialists to schools to try to moderate differences between teachers who were on the picket lines and those who crossed the picket line during the 50 day strike that ended October 28. Leaders of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers refused to participate unless the board exonerated 53 Philadelphia Federation of Teachers' members charged with criminal contempt during the strike.

headline: Our business in Philadelphia
abstract: The author opines that state-sponsored renovation of Philadelphia's coal loading Pier 124 is being poorly managed at the expense of all of Pennsylvania and that Governor Dick Thornburgh, the state legislature and Philadelphia's City Hall are to blame for the deficiencies.

headline: null
abstract: Costs of operating PA's 36 rape crisis centers and 56 domestic violence centers might be paid by those found guilty of certain crimes. A bill would impose a $10 cost on persons found guilty of serious crimes. The bill is modeled after the PA state Crime Victims Compensation Fund.

headline: Woes befall two doctors who crossed Scaife
abstract: Two doctors, William Monsour and Murdoch head, seem to have been targeted by Richard Scaife through IRS investigations and federal court indictments. Scaife, a conservative who has contributed millions to political institutions, has allegedly used his high connections to start the investigations.

headline: Gap Guard commander nominated for promotion
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has announced the nomination of PA National Guard Brigadier General Frank H. Smoker Jr. to the rank of major general. The nomination requires confirmation by the state senate. Smoker, 55, of Anville, will continue to serve as commander of the PANG headquarters at Fort Indiatown gap, a post he has held since 1978.

headline: House election set in Delco today
abstract: A special election will be held in Delaware County to fill the PA House seat of PA Republican Representative Arthur F. Earley, who died in June. Four candidates are running for the remainder of Earley's term, which expires at the end of 1982.

headline: The shame of the schools: The patronage game; It's not what you know, but who you know
abstract: It must have been a hellish day for Superintendent of Schools Michael P. Marcase.  The second school strike of the year, a strike by maintenance workers, was in a third day of near round-the-clock negotiations.  The mayor of Philadelphia was on a tear, demanding resignations from the entire school board as a prelude to firing the superintendent himself.  And with the schools shut down and the strike costing $600,000 a day in lost state subsidies, Marcase made a hard decision that afternoon to lay off nearly all the district's 26,000 employees.

headline: Equal Amounts Targeted For Legislature, Judicary
abstract: Governor Thronburgh's proposed budget has equal amounts for the state legislature and judiciary. The article details amounts to several departments.

headline: Omnibus Law
abstract: The Omnibus Anti-Abortion Package now being considered impedes a woman's right to choose. The impregnating man will be notified. No abortion may be performed unless doctor certifies it is necessary. Doctor must provide woman with photos of aborted fetuses. Health insurance policies cannot cover abortions. A woman must be told there are unknown risks to the procedure. She may be dragged into court by any person who decides she may violate this law.

headline: Protests Violate Law, New District Warned
abstract: Teachers and administrators who actively protest implementation of the court-ordered merger of five east suburban school districts could be held in contempt of court.  And parents who picket the federal courthouse could also receive fines and jail terms because federal law prohibits obstruction of civil rights orders.  Those warnings surfaced when United States District Judge Gerald Weber met with attorneys representing black parents in the former General Braddock schools and the new east suburban school district that came into existence this year.

headline: Outburst erupts on Limerick: Critics disrupt annual meeting
abstract: A few angry shareholders of the Philadelphia Electric Company disrupted the meeting after being denied the opportunity to comment on three proposals. The first proposal was to halt construction of the Limerick nuclear power plant, while the other two were about re-electing the company's 12 directors and reappointing Coopers and Lybrand for another one-year term. The outburst ended quickly.

headline: Anne Alpern's contributions
abstract: Anne X. Alpern, who recently died, is remembered for her public service.  She was the first woman judge on the state Supreme Court and also served as city solicitor and an Allegheny County judge.

headline: Wolf Packer Tells of Campus Killing
abstract: A pack of ten teenagers brutally beat and robbed Douglas Huffman, who died the next day from his injuries. Arthur Rudd, one of the youths on trial for murder and robbery, testified that the group had gone looking for someone to rob when they saw to young white men.  Three approached them from the front and three from the back.  One of them hit Douglas Huffman and he fell to the sidewalk and didn't get up.

headline: GE to lay off 200 due to military contract problems
abstract: 200 employees at General Electric (GE) will be laid off due to loss or delay of major Navy and Air Force contracts.  The plant in Philadelphia does research and development for re-entry weapons systems.

headline: House Oks letting teachers in Phila. Live outside district
abstract: A bill that would allow Philadelphia School District employees to live outside the city limits was approved. Opponents said it would destroy the city's tax base and eventually result in layoffs of teachers. The bill exempts current employees.

headline: The state plans its own birthday party
abstract: The article details the history of Pennsylvania and of its' founder William Penn.  It then notes that a celebration will be held to commemorate the 300th birthday

headline: Ertel explains tax-cut flip-flop
abstract: Representative Allen Ertel of Montoursville completed his flip-flop cycle of voting on Reagan's tax cut bill. On July 29, he voted against it, later that day he voted for it and on August 4th he voted against it. The article details Ertel's rationale throughout the voting process. This bill was passed with an overwhelming majority and afforded the oil industry $11 billion in tax credits.

headline: Once a radical, always a foe? Some think so
abstract: Editorialist asks "What would happen to those revolutionaries after they graduated from college?" He refers to what used to be considered radicals. This editorial focuses on Mitch Crane, once a marcher of civil rights and against the Vietnam War to a newly elected district justice of Chester County.

headline: PSEA backs strikers in Beaver
abstract: Striking teachers in the Beaver Area and Monaca school districts got support from Nancy Noonan, vice president of the PA State Education Association, for "fighting for all the right kind of things." the two school districts are on strike with talks to end the strike continuing.

headline: Potassium iodide due for TMI area
abstract: The state Department of Health's emergency management coordinator said they have plans to have a stockpile of a blocking agent for radioactive iodine available by June. Julia Cox said potassium iodide solution would be distributed to three groups that would be among the last to evacuate the Three Mile Island area in the event of a nuclear accident: on-site personnel, emergency workers and institutionalized persons. The inexpensive drug prevents the human thyroid from absorbing the radioactive iodine, thus lowering the chances of getting thyroid cancer.

headline: $10,000-a-day fine restored in Pennhurst
abstract: A US Supreme Court justice reinstated a $10,000-a-day contempt-of-court fine against PA Welfare Secretary Helen O'Bannon in a dispute over the Pennhurst Center for mentally retarded. Justice William Brennan Jr. reversed a temporary stay issued two weeks ago, and denied other requests to halt the transfer of residents from the huge Chester County institution to smaller, community facilities.

headline: Wrong way: Guidelines are too low for rape
abstract: The author opines that the new sentencing guidelines proposed by the PA Commission on Sentencing are too lenient to adequately punish sex offenders.  The author outlines the multiple effects rape victims suffer from and calls on the state to have harsher sentencing guidelines.

headline: Heinz bid to refit USS Iowa ok'd
abstract: The U.S. Senate has approved a bill by U.S. Senator John Heinz of Pennsylvania to reactivate the battleship USS Iowa, which is moored in the Philadelphia Navy Yard.  Proponents of the bill state that refitting old ship is cheaper and quicker than building new ones.

headline: House panel votes 10-2 for ousting Lederer
abstract: The US House Ethics Committee recommended on Tuesday, April 28, that Representative Raymond F. Lederer, convicted in the Abscam bribery scandal, be expelled from Congress. It is speculated that Lederer, serving his third term in Congress, is keeping his seat in the hope that a federal judge will rule soon on whether FBI agents overstepped constitutional bounds in the investigation of a $50,000 bribe he accepted from an undercover agent.

headline: The state plans its own birthday party
abstract: To mark Pennsylvania's 300 birthday, the state is planning a modest celebration called "A Celebration of Friends."  The article briefly details the history of Pennsylvania and William Penn.

headline: Fiscal anguish for many in Thronburgh budget plan
abstract: The author opines that many special interest groups will face "fiscal anguish" due to Governor Thornburgh proposed budget that will cut funding to almost all agencies.  The author states a recent survey that shows that many states are going through this "fiscal anguish"  because most state are loath to raise taxes.

headline: Outspoken Harvey Adams pushes for equality
abstract: Harvey Adams says black leaders exist in Pittsburgh even if blacks don't know who they are. 15 percent of blacks recognize Harvey as someone who is trying to help them. He claims the press isn't paying enough attention to blacks affairs. He admits that the civil rights leaders have been very quiet lately.

headline: PSEA is 'disappointed' with budget reaction
abstract: A teleconference sponsored by the National Education Association on Monday, April 6, failed to attract 6 of the 7 education-related organizations invited. The PA State Education Association was disappointed with the lack of concern of organizations about Reagan's proposed $195 million budget cuts affecting PA. The teleconference linked Pennsylvania and 33 other states with a panel of educators and government officials in Washington.

headline: PE's Pot $25 Light; You'll Ante
abstract: The Public Utility Commission (PUC) stated that Philadelphia Electric Company (PE) customers failed to pay $10.6 million in charges, which the company writes off as uncollectable debt.  PE then passes that debt on to paying customers in the form of higher rates.  The article details PUC's findings on unpaid utility bills.

headline: $123 million for prison cells OK'd
abstract: The Pennsylvania senate sent Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh his legislation authorizing $123 million for 2,860 new prison cells, a key part of his anti-crime package.  The article gives more details about Pennsylvania prisons, Thornburgh's anti-crime package, and plans for the construction of the new prison cells.

headline: Zimmerman Answers Big-Spending Charge
abstract: The author, state Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman, responds to an editorial that suggested the newly created Office of Attorney General in PA is spending too much money to restructure the office space. He contends in his state House and Senate appropriations committee testimony that the $900,000 needed is an estimate by the Department of General Services, that it involves basic restructuring, that it is part of the original budget request of $21.1 million, and the extra space will be for the added legal and support staff for the recently expanded responsibilities mandated by the Legislature.

headline: Heinz, Specter Vote 'No'
abstract: Pennsylvania Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter both voted against selling aircraft equipment to Saudi Arabia due to the fact that they have not followed U.S. Peace Initiatives in the Middle East.

headline: House vote on abortion bill delayed
abstract: The United States House of Representatives postponed a scheduled vote on a tough anti-abortion bill for two weeks. United States Representative Stephen Freind, a sponsor of the bill states that he will be responsible for bringing up the measure December 8 after the Thanksgiving holiday.

headline: The State's Birthday
abstract: Governor Thornburgh will issue a proclamation to celebrate the state's 300th birthday.  Ceremonies will be kept low-key in light of the tightened state budget.  The article details the history of the state.

headline: From Harrisburg
abstract: The state legislature is delaying a decision on the state budget. Instead, they're concentrating on revenues, giving Governor Dick Thornburgh an extension of high income tax rates he requested, and sparring over ways to raise money needed for highway, bridge construction, and repairs. A major reasoncited is that legislators are awaiting signals about what their constituents want.

headline: Parental right to know of abortions upheld
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled that states require parental notification when teen-age daughters seek abortions.  The article details the requirements of the ruling.  It also details another Supreme Court case that ruled that statutory rape laws are valid even if they only punish males.

headline: PSEA may be on collision course with sponsor of tax-shift move
abstract: The PA State Education Association and the sponsor of legislation replacing the school property tax with a local personal income tax may be on a collision course. The powerful lobbying group says it'll support the legislation, but only if its rewritten to its liking. The group wants the legislation to include a provision mandating an increase in the state's basic education subsidy to 50 percent of local budgets.

headline: Photograph
abstract: "George Kunder in the TMI control room, where he spent 10 tense, sleepless days in March 1979."

headline: $50 million spent on delinquents - Is system working?
abstract: Taxpayers in PA are spending $50 million a year to support detention centers, camps and schools for the state's juvenile delinquents. The article reviews some of the measures taken to expand services, and some opinions of those in the system.

headline: ... Corner isn't good enough
abstract: The author states that Pennsylvania's senior citizen population is growing and predicts that by 2035 a quarter of the population will be elderly.  The author feels that measures need to be taken now to support the elderly population of the future.  The author rebuke the State Senate for defeating a bill that would have created a "Silver-Haired Legislature" to deal with the state's elderly concerns.

headline: Helicopter union not giving up
