abstract: The president of the union representing helicopter maintenance employees at the New Cumberland Army Depot said the group plans to continue to fight the Army's proposal to transfer the mission to Corpus Christi, Texas.  Donald Giffin, president of Local 2004 of the American Federation of Government Employees, said the Army's decision has had a devastating effect on employees and their families, adding that the loss of the 481 civilian jobs will adversely effect the central Pennsylvania economy.

headline: Housing policy stripped of bond-buying wording
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has deleted a proposal to use state pension funds to buy government bonds from its new housing policy, saying that the inclusion in the original was an editing error.  The article details how the error was made.

headline: They're friends, but Rendell and Cannon are ready for a battle
abstract: The article analyzes the race for the Philadelphia District Attorney's office in the May 19 primary. The candidates are incumbent Edward G. Rendell and Republican challenger William T. Cannon, who consider each other as friends.

headline: Gallery II gets go ahead
abstract: Channel 10's concern with Gallery II trash, security, and parking is appropriate but premature. Our immediate concern must the jobs. We will spend $67.4 million of public funds to create approximately 1,964 jobs at a cost of over $34,000 each with no guarantee the jobs will go to unemployed Philadelphians. City government must make sure to jobs go to the jobless.

headline: Phila. Payment for altar overturned
abstract: The US Supreme Court refused to let the city of Philadelphia spend $204,569 of taxpayers' money for a huge outdoor altar used by Pope John Paul II during a visit to the city in the fall of 1979. The Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia, which had offered to pay for the platform from the start, and insists on paying for the costs. Several Philadelphia residents and church groups successfully challenged the expenditure in lower courts, citing the First Amendment's prohibition on governmentally supported religion.

headline: Pupil Moves Not Equal, Board Says
abstract: Author writes that open enrollment policies for elementary schools is an institutionalized way of preserving the status quo---segregation. Open enrollment was discontinued the previous year because of the desegregation plan for elementary schools, however, it has been reinstated this fall to allow elementary students to attend any school in the city as long as their race improves the balance of the new school. Data showed that it was black children requesting the transfers only. Superintendent Wallace states the reason for the transfer requests were educationally-based and not racial.

headline: Photograph
abstract: "GPU's Henry Hukill stands in front of a TMI cooling tower"

headline: 2 racket informers to tell all
abstract: Two federal informers wearing bullet-proof and surrounded by US marshals were sentence to a maximum of 20 years in prison after they pleaded guilty to federal racketeering charges for their roles in four contract killings. They will testify against seven other men charged with contract killing as part of their plea bargain. They are under heavy security and their location is a secret.

headline: 24 accused of double dipping: All worked for Street's agency
abstract: 24 people were charged with illegally accepting welfare payments while they were employed by a federal jobs program supervised by the North Philadelphia Block Development Corporation, a nonprofit organization founded by state Senator Milton Street (R-Philadelphia). District Attorney Edward Rendell is also investigating Senator Street, Yvonne Hipp, and other supervisory employees of the corporation.

headline: Help for 'Agent Orange' victims
abstract: PA Vietnam War veterans who were or may have been exposed to "Agent Orange" may some receive some assistance from state government. They have received very little from the US Veterans Administration. Agent Orange was used as a defoliant during the war. Many US troops were exposed to the chemical.

headline: How area's senators voted
abstract: The article goes into brief detail about how Philadelphia legislators voted on different bills and laws.

headline: Things Are Moving In Western State
abstract: The brief article states that striking teachers in the school districts Sto-Rox and Norwin will meet with negotiators to discuss contracts.

headline: Go west, south?  Let's think twice
abstract: The editors feel that one of the proposals of the report of President Carter's Commission for a National Agenda for the Eighties is unacceptable.  The proposal suggests that cities in the Northeast and Northcentral parts of the U.S. are going to fail and that residents there should relocate to the South and West.  They don't believe additional people will find employment opportunities and feel federal aid should be targeted more appropriately.

headline: Philadelphia Battle Over All-Male Clubs
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council recently moved to penalize any private clubs that exlude women as members.  The article interviews numerous people who are both for and against including women in private clubs.

headline: Quick budget passage tied to school funding
abstract: Republican lawmakers disagreed over the commitment to the state's affluent school districts as they quickly passed Governor Dick Thornburgh's 1981-1982 general fund budget. The disagreement came over the 'hold harmless clause', an $11.7 million cost that must be appropriated in new money or taken out of the $50 million increase in basic instruction aid proposed by the governor.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph of a man walking through an industrial complex, presumably at the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear power plant.

headline: 4 Cons Holding 38 At State Pen
abstract: Four convicts took 38 hostages after a failed escape attempt at Graterford State Prison.  One of the leaders is Joseph Bowen, convicted of murdering a prison guard in 1971.  The article details what little is known about the current situation.

headline: 44 groups lose status as charities
abstract: The state Commission on Charitable Organizations has ordered 44 charitable organizations to stop soliciting funds in PA. By state law, all charities are required to renew their registration annually with the state in an effort to ensure Pennsylvanians that money collected by charities is used in a proper manner.

headline: In National Commander's Speech Here; Legion Stresses Agent Orange Woe
abstract: The American Legion will not accept a bureaucratic, business-as-usual approach to solving Agent Orange problem according to National Commander Jack W. Flynt.  Flynt was in Harrisburg as a keynote speaker for the mini convention and Membership Roundup of the Pennsylvania Department of The American Legion.  In speaking of his meetings with the Vietnam Verterans Congressional Caucus, he signaled out for praise Representative Allen Ertel, as well as two other Pennslyvania congressmen, Representative Donald Bailey and Representative P. Murtha.  He declared that the nation has a duty to take care of the Vietnam veterans.

headline: How They Voted In Congress
abstract: The article lists how area (Ohio, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia) U.S. Senators voted on key bills over the past week.  The House was not in session.

headline: This May Hurt a Little; Anxiety, and some surprises, as the extent of Reagan's revolution sinks in
abstract: null

headline: GOP Adds Governor's Cuts to Bill
abstract: Republicans in the state legislature added Governor Thornburgh's recommended 1% across the board budget cut to a Senate bill.  School districts and vocational education will be exempt from the cuts. The budget cuts are detailed.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: PA State Representative Stephen Friend, who supports an anti-abortion bill in the state House.

headline: Report Bowne to quit as director of museum
abstract: James DeHart Bowne, director of the Everhart Museum since 1978 and embroiled in controversy with Museum Association of Scranton for most of that time, is resigning his position. He will become executive director of the Greenville County Museum of Art Sept. 1.

headline: Plentiful supply': Water will flow at Point Pleasant
abstract: The author feels that the anti-nuclear lobby is thwarting the Delaware River Basin Commission's Commission attempts to start building the Point Pleasant Pumping Station.  The author feels the anti-nuclear lobby is wrong on several environmental points and outlines them in the article.

headline: 40 Atlanta children in Pa. camp
abstract: null

headline: 500 march to protest U.S. plan to cut funds
abstract: 500 Marchers streamed through Center City Philadelphia to protest Reagan administration plans to reduce federal financing of social services in this city by $278 million. The demonstrators ranged from elected officials to single women supporting families on welfare, and represented over 150 civic groups.

headline: Navy official says Phila. Shipyard did 'reasonable job' on the Guam
abstract: Admiral Thomas B. Hayward, chief of naval operations, told U.S. Representative G. William Whitehurst (R- Va.) that the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard did a "reasonable job" on overhauling the attack ship, Guam.  Hayward said that there were problems with the work on the ship, but that many of them were to be expected because the Navy had changed the package of work to be performed and also ordered the ship in servie five months earlier than planned.  Whitehurst represents an area near the Newport News Shipyard and Draydock Company, a private company that is Philadelphia's rival for millions of dollars in aircraft-carrier overhaul work.

headline: In Abscam six years for Criden
abstract: Philadelphia lawyer Howard Criden, convicted as a bagman in an Abscam political corruption case, has been sentenced to six years in prison and fined $40,000.

headline: Thornburgh Outlines 5 Major Plans for the Fall
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has his eye on five major legislative problems for fall, including a $300 million bond issue to help solve water problems, a welfare reform package, a crime package, a tax reform package, and state Liquor Control Board reform.

headline: Governor ask 1% cut in spending
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh proposed a 1% reduction in state spending that would total $50 million to $70 million this fiscal year. This is needed to make up for lost state revenue resulting from President Reagan's recently enacted tax-cut package. The Welfare Department will be heavily impacted.

headline: Pitt Objects to Inclusion In Pa Desegregation Plan
abstract: The Universtiy of Pittsburgh administrators feel that the university should be excluded from the desegregation plan sought by the federal Department of Education.  They feel that because they have their own affirmative action plan they should not have to be included in the government's.  The federal plan, instituted in 1974, was found to be in violation by the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: Ruining Philadelphia education
abstract: Editorial against striking Philadelphia teachers, that claims they care more about their contracts than their jobs. It claims the teacher's union is ruining the Philadelphia education System.

headline: Power play?
abstract: The article analyzes the economics of electric utilities. It recommends that investors should watch not only balance sheets and Wall Street ratings, but also election results and political appointments.

headline: 7 jurors selected for Narducci trial
abstract: Seven jurors were selected for the federal racketeering and conspiracy trial of alleged organized crime figure Frank "Chickie" Narducci and an associate. The two were indicted last year on charges that they bribed two police officers in return for protection for a South Philadelphia card game. The trial will be held in the US District Court of eastern PA, and most of the prosecution's case will center on the taped meeting conversations of the undercover officers with Narducci and Anthony Rossano.

headline: A Limping Monster
abstract: The editorial argues that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's welfare reform package created a problem by forcing 68,000 people off welfare rolls without having jobs for those people. The state Legislature has come up with a solution under which recipients would work at government jobs, and would force the Public Welfare Department to set up the program. The editorial argues that a state-run program like the federal Works Progress Administration of the depression years would help.

headline: none
abstract: Editorial Cartoon: Reagan appears to have been knocked down and sitting on the ground with a small airplane near his right hand.  There is a short older gentleman that is standing on him, holding Reagan's tie so that they are nose to nose.  Reagan is saying, " It's OK, Menachem... You want F-16s, you got 'em"

headline: In limbo: Myers keeps busy and waits
abstract: As the Philadelphia's First District Representative to the US Congress, Michael Myers was expelled from Congress after the federal Abscam investigation, and defeated for re-election by an independent. As he awaits the court' decisions in the investigation, he is using his carpentry tools and skills in Philadelphia in the meantime.

headline: Thornburgh plays the hero
abstract: Within a week's time, Governor Dick Thornburgh has helped both Centralia residents and Philadelphia area commuters. He agreed for the state to a plan to buy up 25 houses threatened by an underground mine fire, and also helped the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority and the striking Transport Workers Union reach a deal to end the strike. The author argue some people believe he's a master politician, while others say he is just a great public-relations person.

headline: Governor Extends Two Taxes
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed into law a measure extending for two years the current rates of the state's personal and corporate income taxes. Meanwhile, the state Senate Judiciary Committee approved and sent the Senate two bills that would shield conversations between counselors and victims at rape and domestic violence crisis centers. Also, the full state Senate unanimously approved three judges.

headline: Politicians get failing grade in survey of community; Prime issues listed: Politicians get failing grade in survey of Black community
abstract: The response from over 90 percent of the 400 community and grassroots organizations, civil rights, civic, social and human service groups, and individual activists responding to a recent "Tribune" questionnaire regarding the general conditions of the Black community was poor, as in complete failure.  The respondents pointed out that elected officials are: not responsive to the Black community, most of them are unknown and not visible to the community, not enough of them feel obligated to their constituents, most of them maintain extremely poor relationships with the community, and do not encourage community input, they should do less bickering, solve more problems, and hold more meetings with the community.

headline: Scanlon offers plan to change teacher training
abstract: State Education Secretary Robert Scanlon announced changes to the way Pennsylvania trains its teachers.  The proposal, which must still be approved by the state Board of Education, includes an extra year of schooling to learn pedagogy, licenses that would have to be renewed every five years, and raising admissions criteria for education schools in universities.

headline: President urged to make taxpayers fund TMI cleanup
abstract: The Nuclear Safety Oversight Committee in Washington made a recommendation to President Reagan that the $1 billion cost associated with the clean up after the Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Plant accident in 1978, be paid by taxpayers.  The debate centers around the Pennsylvania Public Utilities Commission's decision to allow a substantial rate increase for General Public Utilities, which owns power plant.

headline: 7 sites weighed for new prison
abstract: Pittsburgh city officials who are opposed to converting the C. Howard Marcy Center into a prison convinced state officials to look at seven other alternatives, which are in less populated areas of Allegheny County

headline: A reformed welfare-reform bill
abstract: A letter from state representative Samuel Hayes which details the legislative procedure involved in attempting to pass a welfare reform bill and why a new bill was drafted.  He states that the new bill contains all the provisions of the old one with some changes and hopes that it will be passed.

headline: Specter proposes Agent Orange relief
abstract: Vietnam veterans who were victims of Agent Orange could get compensation from the federal government under legislation introduced by Pennsylvania Senator Arlen Specter.  The article goes further into detail about the legislation and a limit history behind Agent Orange.

headline: Is an election any way to select our judges
abstract: The editorial argues that state court judges should not be elected by popular vote, and that the public could care less about the current judgeship race. Instead, the editorial thinks that a solution could be to rely on life-time appointments in the same ways as the federal judiciary.

headline: Thornburgh seeks crime, welfare action
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh announced his agenda for the new state legislative session, renewing his calls for action on crime, welfare reform and a new-look liquor store operation. He will be pushing these three things as his big ticket items.

headline: Governor Eyes Sale Of Medical Buildings
abstract: The Thornburgh Administration looks to sell 16 property lots in order to fill an estimated $15 million gap in the state budget. The list of property lots are mainly unused or underused medical buildings. These lots were presented at a House-Senate panel on Thursday.

headline: Poll finds blacks not optimistic
abstract: The 1981 PA Poll, commissioned by the Post-Gazette and done by the Gallup Organization, found that Pittsburgh blacks are generally pessimistic about the opportunities available to them, and that those available in Pittsburgh are not as good as in other cities.  They express less confidence in the ability of the government to solve the city problems as do the white residents. But blacks do have confidence in the job done by Mayor Richard Caliguiri. 406 black adults were interviewed by phone between March 31 and April 14.

headline: Scanlon, congressman discuss U.S. cuts
abstract: Pennsylvania Education Secretary Robert Scanlon were scheduled to meet with the United States chairman of the House select subcommittee on education to discuss federal funding cutbacks for Pennsylvania's special education programs. Congressman, United States Representative Austin Murphy wants to know how Scanlon plans to deal with future changes to the budget.

headline: Prices stabilize for fuel oil, gasoline
abstract: Pennsylvanians paid the same average prices for fuel oil, electricity and gasoline in December as they did in September, but they paid more for natural gas and anthracite, according to the Governor's Energy Council. The council provides further detail about the stable pricing.

headline: A 'beast' nobody can tame
abstract: Methamphetamine takes a greater toll on the human body than any of the other 'recreational chemicals.' It has become the drug of choice for thousands in the Philadelphia area. Police consider it a huge problem. One part of the problem is how easy it is to make and relatively cheap aside from one chemical.

headline: A temporary reprieve from Thornfare
abstract: Federal Judge Joseph Lord ruled that the Department of Health and Human Services acted improperly, violating its own procedures in the Aid to Families with Dependent Children cuts. This decision blocks Pennsylvania's planned cuts in welfare benefits. This decision will have national implications as welfare rights groups elsewhere contest federal cuts. This ruling also catches the Pennsylvania State Legislature at a crucial moment as it is weighing both the Aid to Families' cuts and Thornfare IV, which eliminates benefits to 63,000 of the working poor and cut them for 44,000 more. This time around Thornfare will purge 68,000 recipients from the General Assistance rolls.

headline: State Congressmen Send Protest On Proposed Abandonment of Fort
abstract: The Pennsylvania congressional delegation said that army abandonment of Fort Indiantown Gap near Annville would be a misguided, miscalculated and ineffectual attempt to save money. The Army estimated that realigning the fort would save $300 million annually, although a General Accounting Office report stated that the 700 jobs that would be lost would cost more than predicted savings.

headline: Is this project really needed?
abstract: PA Department Secretary Walter Baran announced the work schedule for construction of a new parking garage and office building behind the main Capitol, for renovation of a former state museum into new offices for the governor and for repairs to the 75-year-main Capitol. Total cost of the projects is to exceed $32 million, but because the work is being financed, the ultimate cost to taxpayers will be at least several times that amount.

headline: Thornburgh sees 'more' in less federal funds
abstract: Governor Thronburgh stated that he can accept President Reagan's cuts in federal funding for states, if states are given more "flexibility" in spending the funds.  The author opines that no matter what the state still has less money and must cut programs.

headline: Governor mixes eggs and taxes
abstract: On May 5, Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a bill extending the state's personal and corporate net income taxes for two more years, cooked a 350-egg omelet with state Senate President Pro Tempore Henry Hager to proclaim PA Egg Month, attended the ceremony to award the second annual Distinguished PA Artist Award, and the Hazlett Memorial Awards for Excellence in the arts.

headline: Pro-choice
abstract: The whole debate on the moral issues of abortion does not belong in politics. The author thought that was out of it when Roe vs. Wade was decided and should stay that way.

headline: School aid bill vetoed
abstract: null

headline: Problems still stall US nuclear power
abstract: Editorial defends nuclear energy with facts, attack congressmen for standing up against it, and blames congress for the industry's problems.

headline: A Breakdown of Justice
abstract: When Municipal Court Judge Lynwood Blount failed to show up for an Saturday morning assigned arraignment shift. Blount gave advance notice of being unable to comply with the shift, yet no replacement was found. If judges cannot comply with assigned arraignment shifts then criminals are able to go free due to a 6 hour arraignment rule. The Municipal Court has no weekend standby judges in the summer, although the standby system is set to resume in September. Officials should take responsibility and create more than a standby system within the criminal justice system to guarantee that criminals do not go free.

headline: An Inspiring Example
abstract: Retired Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart has dedicated his time to tape recording a law text book for blind students.

headline: State VFW Delegates Feel Women Can Man the Front
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of the Veterans of Foreign Wars states that women should be able to fill combat roles in times of war. This statement came after a resolution was voted down by the 62nd annual convention of veterans organization. Governor Thornburgh is severely criticized for misstating the degree to which Pennsylvania state really aids veterans and researches veterans issues. Reference is made to the Reagan administration closing down many Veterans Affairs hospitals.

headline: It's End of Era for Mayors, Players
abstract: The United States Conference of Mayors was held in Louisville, Kentucky this past week. It is an event in which important mayors get together to discuss respective issues. The columnist compares mayors to baseball players in this article. Baseball players were able to obtain unimaginable salary spikes through their union just as mayors were able to obtain large amounts of federal grants and aid through their lobbying efforts. Over the past 20 years, both gropes enjoyed increased autonomy which is threatened by President Reagan's budget cuts and proposal to transfer domestic programs out of Washington. Mayors fear this transition as they will now be in competition for funds with governors of the same state.

headline: Thornburgh sets Friday as statewide 'History Day'
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has officially designated Friday, May 15, as "History Day". In celebration, a statewide competition of exhibits, performances and papers by students grades six through 12 will be held that day in the Grantville Holiday Inn. The day-long event is coordinated by the PA Historical and Museum Commission. Finalists from 30 states will be selected at the National History Day competition.

headline: Governor seeks 1% appropriations cut
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh called for a 1 percent across-the-board reduction in state general fun appropriations and subsidy payments this year- to adjust the budget to the impact of $267 million in the federal budget and business tax cuts in PA. He proposed a two-year phase-in at the state level of the new federal accelerated depreciation schedule for business investment, which, he said would give business in PA a $51 million state tax incentive for investment this year, and an additional $107 million or more next year.

headline: Races clash at a Phila. high school
abstract: University City High School was plagued with racial troubles between black and Asian students that forced administrators to dismiss classes early.  The early dismissal came after two stabbings and after lunchroom brawls.  The article provides details about the racial troubles and what the school plans on doing to solve the problems.

headline: School blues: Lawsuits won't teach kids
abstract: Although the city and school districts have been passed, the editorial argues that the problems over school financing in the city and school district of Philadelphia will go on for months. The editorial suggests the need for the school board and Superintendent of Schools Michael Marcase resign and allow city Mayor Green to appoint a new board, which would then name a new superintendent. By making the schools part of the city government, It would make the mayor accountable for their performance and funding.

headline: Public Funds:  Synfuels are too a big risk
abstract: Letter to the Editor in response to a series of articles entitled "Energy anarchy." Author opines that the newspaper's researchers overlooked the fact that the expenses involved in getting oil from coal would exceed the current conventionall method of getting oil.  He states that synthetic fuels are more costly than oil and states his arguments why.

headline: A death that causes real light
abstract: Athanasios Stamatis Magos, a friend of the author, died and the media tied his death with the Greek mob. Ethnic prejudice has caused Greeks to be lumped together. There are plenty of law-abiding Greeks. He laments his friend's death and speaks of his great qualities and the discrimination he had to face. His death has put it in perspective.

headline: Bill to trim welfare rolls is back on House floor
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's welfare reform bill, which would stop benefits for "able-bodied" persons receiving cash payments, was on the state House floor again, after Republicans rejected having public hearings on the bill.  The article outlines the details of the bill and discusses its pros and cons.

headline: Submarine Standoff
abstract: The taxpayers may not get stuck with paying for some of General Dynamics' submarine-building mistakes.  The company had submitted a claim for $18.9 million to cover the cost of correcting problems caused by using defective steel and making improper welds on an attack submarine.  It also said more claims were coming to cover similar problems on other subs and indicated the total could reach $100 million.  Navy Secretary, John Lehman, expressed an extreme distaste for the company's mistakes, and he warned General Dynamics it faced the loss of future submarine contracts.  Now the company not only has backed down on the cliams, but has also agreed to speed up work on seven giant Trident submarines whose construction had been far behind schedule.

headline: It's laurel for hardy at state's 300th  fest
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and the PA Legislature join together to celebrate the 300th birthday anniversary of the state, even though it was raining.

headline: Thornburgh vs. Heinz
abstract: null

headline: Governor: Let's cut spending by 1 percent, lop 1,100 jobs
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh called for a 1 percent, across the board cut in state spending and elimination of 1,100 state jobs to ease the impact on the state of $267 million in federal budget cuts and business tax breaks. He stated he wanted to give the Reagan budget a chance to work and did not want to replace federal cuts with increased state spending.

headline: Rape agency fears cut in city funding
abstract: Women Organized Against Rape (WOAR) is worried that they will lose their funding for education and prevention programs so Philadelphia City Council can fund programs within the school district. The article details the expenses and states that events are being held for Rape Prevention Week.

headline: School Board Extravagance
abstract: The editorial claims the members of Pittsburgh's Board of Education have wasted taxpayers' money. He argues that with nearly 10% more students, outside districts in the county provide equal, if not better education with nearly 20% fewer employees, and the employee ratio in these districts is nearly 35% more cost-efficient than Pittsburgh. He calls for people to express their concerns to the school district.

headline: PUC boss urges public input on TMI
abstract: At a Lebanon Valley Chamber of Commerce meeting, the chairman of the state Public Utility Commission urged individuals and organizations to get involved in the advocacy efforts to expedite the cleanup of the crippled nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island. Susan Shanaman proposed the cleanup, which is estimated to be at more than $1 billion, be financed by a federal grant, and that timely removal of the nuclear-waste materials is paramount as costs are increasing.

headline: A first for justice
abstract: Nelson Diaz added another first to his long list of achievements as a community leader and lawyer when he was sworn as Philadelphia Common Pleas Court judge, the first Hispanic in PA history. He is only 34 but has demonstrated he is committed to justice for all.

headline: Breaking the poverty chain
abstract: Breaking the poverty chain that keeps several Pittsburgh blacks on the welfare and unemployment rolls is getting growing attention from public service agencies and cooperating employers.  Children whose parents are poorly educated, unemployed or working in low-paid, unskilled jobs do not learn at home how to get started and how to get ahead in the job market.  Urban Youth Action is one of the longest-running attempts to avoid the unemployment syndrome by teaching Pittsburgh teenagers about the world of work.

headline: The Unthinkable!
abstract: The unthinkable of Nuclear War and Lancaster County brings Elizabethtown College professors Donald B. Krybill and John P. Ranck to believe the best way to reduce the arms race is to begin at the grassroots and have prepared  study under that name.  The Federal Emergency Management Agency lists all of Lancaster County west of a line running one mile east of the city as a "high risk area."  The article continues to provide further details on the study.

headline: Legislators: Earley a Man of Courage
abstract: State and county officials attended the funeral of PA state Representative Arthur Earley yesterday and remembered the only black Republican to serve in the state House of Representatives as a man of insight and courage. PA Governor Thornburgh gave the eulogy.

headline: Thornburgh, top Dems trade wheeling, dealing charges
abstract: Republican Governor Dick Thornburgh and his Democratic political opponents are spicing up the usual summer lull with attacks directed at each other's apparent political wheeling and dealing.  Each side is trying to paint the other as political opportunities out to protect and reward their legions.  It is something the attackers hope to parlay into support in next year's election.  The latest round occurred when Thornburgh aides released a July 15 letter to the governor from Senate Democratic floor leader Edward Zemprelli of Allegheny County.  It concerned a deal Zemprelli put forth, one that would preserve Democratic control of the turnpike.

headline: Governors assured on grants
abstract: In a meeting, President Reagan assured 19 of the nation's governors that he will push hard for federal block grants so the states can take over most social programs. This help would be given to governors in support for the administration's budget cuts. The block grants would replace up to 200 federal categorical grants being phased out.

headline: Report From the Front: Vandals strike again in Delaware County
abstract: Patricia Bailey experienced a racial incident when vandals burned a cross on her front lawn and threw a hatchet through her window.  There have been 36 similar incidents in Delaware County in the last 6 years.

headline: School Leaders: End Government Intrusion
abstract: The Pennsylvania School Boards Association stated that they support legislation that gives school district more local control over schools' operations at their 85th annual convention.  Topics at the convention included teacher strikes, tax reform, and other legislation that would affect school districts.  The article details the topics at the convention.

headline: PUC chief exects $4 Duquesne rate hike
abstract: Duquesne Light Co asked for a $113 million annual rate increase, but will probably not get more that $70, said the Public Utility Commission chairman, Susan Shanaman.  That means utility bills for customers would go up about $4.

headline: A gun-control bill that even hunters can endorse
abstract: Legislation introduced contemporaneously, in both the House and the Senate at Harrisburg, House Bill 1804 and Senate Bill 1081 should enlist their approval.  Governor Dick Thornburgh and a Democratic Philadelphia district attorney, Ed Rendell, are working in tandem for the type of "gun control" that sprotsmen will support.  The legislation calls for mandatory minimum five-year prison sentences for certain crimes and also appropriates money to construct nearly 3,000 new prison beds, which will be needed once the legislation becomes a reality.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: The cartoon depicts a large machine lableled 'Welfare Reform' with a large gear labeled 'Pennsylvania General Assembly Model 81.'  A man depicting Governor Thornburgh is turning a hand crank saying "I just can't seem to get it started."

headline: Walgren Fights Defense Call For More Brass
abstract: U.S. Representative Doug Walgren questioned why the House Armed Services Committee endorsed a bill that would create six more assistant secretaries in the Department of Defense.  He feels it is hypocritical of the Reagan Administration to make so many budget cuts, then add high level, high paying positions.

headline: Jackpot:  A behind-the-scenes report about whay really happened when a bunch of amateurs figured out how to fix the Daily Number
abstract: The 7 page articles details the events of the April 24th, 1980 rigging to the Pennsylvania daily lottery.

headline: Thornburgh's TMI plan criticized by Democrat
abstract: null

headline: Governors attack Reagan's economics
abstract: Democratic governors launched their first full-scale attack on Reagan's economic program. The budget approved by US Congress last week cuts federal aid to state and local governments by as much as 35% below current levels when inflation is considered. Governors concluded their meeting by adopting a resolution that suggests Washington take over Medicaid and welfare programs.

headline: Sen. Lewis Is Criticized by Black Leaders For Seeking Suspension of DCA's Dennis
abstract: Statewide black leaders said allegations that state Community Affairs Secretary Shirley Dennis acted improperly on a federal home insulation contract  constituted a racist attack. The criticism was directed at state Senator H. Craig Lewis (D-Bucks), who has suggested Governor Dick Thornburgh fire or suspend Mrs. Dennis for alleged improper action in pushing the contract after it was disapproved by federal officials. Thornbugh saw no impropriety and suggested the charges were politically motivated.

headline: School openings delayed for talks
abstract: Philadelphia School District officials said they will postpone opening six elementary schools in effort to facilitate meaningful negotiations with the Teacher's Federation. The district will continue operations at 9 schools already opened.

headline: PUC hears PE's value questioned: Broker says firm should end Limerick to aid financial health
abstract: A Philadelphia stockbroker testified at the state's Public Utility Commission hearings that Philadelphia Electric Company is a poor investment risk. Sam Folin, testifying on behalf of consumer organizations seeking to halt construction of the Limerick nuclear plant, was challenged by PE's lawyer, who asked that his statements be thrown out. The PUC Judge, holding hearings to determine whether the utility should be permitted to complete the plant, said he would later rule whether to admit Folin's testimony.

headline: A new breed of urban gang
abstract: The author opines that the Guardian Angels, a volunteer town-watch group, may not be as good as they seem.  The author is hesitant to allow them to patrol the city's subway system and mentions that most of them are black or Hispanic, wear military style berets, and are tax-exempt from public donations.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: The cartoon depicts an officer in uniform pulling someone from the water in front of the Statue of Liberty.  In the water there is a sinking boat that says "Haitians" on the side.

headline: Bell asks record increase on rates
abstract: Bell telephone of Pennsylvania will ask for a record $425 million rate increase which will be aimed at basic residential service.  The article continues to provide details on how Bell intends to raise their rates.

headline: Jacobs aims to end GOP losing streak
abstract: Mary Jane Jacobs is one of four candidates for City Council in the May 19 special election to fill the vacancy created by the election of William Coyne to Congress. She hopes to be the first Republican elected to City Council in 43 years.

headline: Thornburgh-Scranton Rift Has GOP Worried
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton's decision to break away from Governor Dick Thornburgh's team plan and finance his own course for the May 1982 primary election campaign appears to be confined to a political debate. But there's the danger that if their disagreement continues, it could spill over and affect coordinating decisions in governmental matters, as well as party fund-raising and elections.

headline: Governor's Proposed Budget to 'Do More With Less'
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburg's proposed budget for 1981-82 will be about $12 billion and emphasize combating street crime by not cutting the State Police budget.  The proposed budget is not expected to raise taxes, though they will not decrease.  All departments will experience some spending cuts.

headline: Sentences for 'Plowshares Eight' indicate cost of dissent runs high
abstract: Contrasts the sentences given in two protesting incidents. One was the 1972 Valley Forge 1,000-person protest and the second was the 1980 King of Prussia protest which was significantly smaller in size. Both incidents were geographically close to one another, however the first incident was more violent and large in scale while the second was not. It questions why the second protest scene received stiffer sentences for less damage than did the first.

headline: School summit: Progress, or more song and dance?
abstract: A meeting on the financial situation of the Philadelphia school system will be held in an attempt to reach a compromise. The teachers union, school superintendent Michael Marcase, Mayor William Green, Philadelphia City Council, PA governor, and the school board are the main actors involved in the dispute over financial problems and relevant program cuts. Governor Dick Thornburgh released state funds to get the schools through the rest of the year, but warned there would be an audit aimed at tightening future spending.

headline: PUC Oks Utility Refunds
abstract: The Public Utility Commission ruled that Duquesne Light Company owes its customers $19.9 million in refunds to its 547, 000 customers of Allegheny and Beaver counties. Customers paid for a nuclear power plant and for replacement power at the same time, essentially paying for the electricity they used once twice. The power plant was shut down for five months.

headline: A NEW JUVENILE CENTER
abstract: The entire state of Pennsylvania only has 235 spaces for the delinquents in its maximum security centers.  Sixty-eight of those are at Cornwells Heights in Bucks County.  It serves not only Philadelphia, but all of Eastern Pennsylvania.  For months now Cornwells Heights has been overcrowded and has not taken new admissions.  And that backs up on the local County detention centers which can not transfer their inmates who belong in maximum security.  And with no room in the overcrowded detention centers, a lot of bad kids are out breaking into homes and mugging our elderly.

headline: Cartoon:  Permanent Fixture?
abstract: The cartoon depicts a large man in front of the Governor's office whose shirt says "Welfare Reform."  His feet are being nailed to the floor by a donkey with a sign that says "Demo Liberals."  A barrel of nails is labeled "Delaying Tactics."

headline: Letters to the editor; Costly ads
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania should not be able to get away with a huge rate increase.  The author rants about how it is unfair to inflate the rates.

headline: Jacobson In Governor's Race Again
abstract: Article backgrounds Alvin Joseph Jacobson, a perennial candidate for governor. In 1978, he acquired only 10,000 votes. When he ran for president last year he only received 4,900 and will most likely receive a low percentage of votes this time around.

headline: Thou Shale Not Fourch by Essoin
abstract: The cartoon depicts a construction site at the State Capitol.  A sign reads "$26 million extension of house offices - commonwealth of PA General Services Dept. Sec. Walter Baran - Your Tax Dollars at Work."  A man in a suit depicting a lawmaker says to a man in a hard hat depicting a tax payer, "It is very badly needed - sometimes we are here two or three days a week."

headline: GOVERNORS TIGHTEN BUDGETS
abstract: The article summarizes each governor's state of the state, budget, and other major messages in 1981. State governors are pinching pennies in budgets presented in 1981, cutting back payrolls, and services wherever possible.

headline: State asks court to stop school merger
abstract: The state joined four east suburban school districts in fighting the court-ordered desegregation of the General Braddock School District. State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman announced that his office had filed an appeal with the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia seeking to overturn the desegregation order.

headline: School Surveys
abstract: The editorial argues that the Superintendent and board of Pittsburgh Public Schools should be given time to improve the school system. They have rightly taken the first step of collecting research about the schools, and in order to improve the system, they need to know how much trouble there is.

headline: PUC suspends UGI increase
abstract: The PA state Public Utility Commission suspended for investigation the $20.9 million base-rate increase sought by UGI Corp. It will raise the average customer rates by $50 annually. It will raise revenue by 7.7%.

headline: A QUESTION OF JUSTICE/ Send them a message: No wolves on the streets
abstract: Wolf-pack attacks claimed the life of Douglas Huffman, a graduate student at Penn's Wharton School.  Due to peer pressure and poor judgment, two teenagers beat Douglas Huffman to death.  There's no joy in handing life sentences, mandatory for convictions of second-degree murder, to two youngsters.  But in this case a strong message had to be sent.

headline: City Attorney Ready to Climb Above Disability
abstract: In an attempt to make a statement about the abilities of the disabled, on the 4th of July Charles O'Brien, 11 other handicapped people and 12 climbers will attempt to reach the peak of Mount Rainier in Washington state. The Harrisburg Attorney, with one leg amputated below the knee, is taking part in an expedition that has been chosen by the Reagan administration as the major project of the International Year of Disabled Persons.

headline: MANIFEST DESTINY
abstract: Novelist James Michener presents past American space exploration of space, and predicts the importance of America's upcoming launch of space shuttle Columbia from Cape Canaveral. He argues the launch inaugurates a new radical era of space exploration and that the entire space program depends on what happens.

headline: Job Selling:  Will Washington Buy The Idea?
abstract: The author wonders whether reports that jobs in the Pennsylvania government can be bought and sold are just  a new spirit of free enterprise coming from the White House.  The article uses a fictitious, humorous interview to make is point sarcastically.

headline: Three councilwomen saw light, instead of darkness
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh succeeded in getting negotiations off the ground in the teacher strike. Now the city government is aligned to work with the teachers to reach a deal. Three councilwomen changed their positions making it all come together.

headline: Group fights corporate tax-limit bill
abstract: A coalition of public employee and social service groups said they would fight a bill in Pennsylvania that will not sufficiently limit the amount of money corporations could deduct from their state net-income tax under President Reagan's plan to stimulate the economy. PA State Senator Vincent Fumo stated that he would attempt to amend the President's bill with a provision that would reduce the amount of revenue lost.

headline: State Court Blocks Cut on Abortion
abstract: Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court Judge John MacPhail blocked implementation of a law which would cut off state funding for most abortions for poor women as it would have caused immediate and irreparable harm to pregnant women who are receiving the funds for abortions. This law was signed by Governor Thornburgh in December 1980, and scheduled to take effect August 16.

headline: School Tax Reform Bill Risky, Unfair
abstract: null

headline: PUC wants higher insulation levels
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission asked Commonwealth Court to stay its ruling that reversed an order by the regulatory agency for minimum insulation standards as a precondition to electric service hookups. At issue is the PUC's March 1980 approval of PA Power & Light Co.'s minimum insulation standards which new houses and other buildings, regardless of how heated, had to meet to qualify for electric service. The PUC claims there is no precedent by a higher tribunal to guide its decision.

headline: A tougher stance may be an answer to juvenile crime
abstract: The juvenile system in Bucks County needs to be fixed, because money is being spent unwisely. One out of every 24 children has a serious run in with the law every year. It costs Bucks County $2 million a year with half paid directly by taxes.

headline: Civil War Spawned Visiting Nurses
abstract: The Fruit and Flower Mission, continues its philanthropic work with Christmas just around the corner. This organization distributes funds to the needy through the Visitors Nurse Association of Allegheny County. The Fruit and Flower Mission originated during the Civil War where transient soldiers were fed.

headline: Attracted by Arnold Palmer: Japanese Manufacturer To Build Plant in York
abstract: The state Commerce Department announced a Japanese manufacturer will locate its first United States plan in York, and quoted the firm's president as saying he was attracted to Pennsylvania by an advertisement featuring golfer Arnold Palmer.  The Japan Automatic Machine Company, of Tokyo, purchased 3.3 acres of land in the York City Industrial Park and made a total initial investment of $900,000.  The maker of automatic crimping machinery to be used by the electronics industry said it would begin construction of its plant in March, with production slated for late 1982.

headline: Judge Morrison's Unit Sets Opening
abstract: A Citizens Committee for Judge Clarence Morrison will open its campaign headquarters in the Uptown Shopping Center on Saturday. PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, who appointed Morrison to vacancy on the county bench last year is scheduled to cut ribbon at the ceremonies.

headline: Three in Cabinet Posts Nominated by Governor
abstract: Governor Thornburgh nominated three men to fill vacancies in his Cabinet.  Peter S. Duncan for the Department of Environmental Resources, Barry H. Stern as secretary of Labor and Industry, and Robert K. Bloom as secretary of Revenue.  All are now serving in an acting capacity and must be confirmed by the state Senate.  The article details their respective histories.

headline: Guv to Seek $12B Budget, No Tax Cuts
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's proposed budget will be over $12 billion, including spending cuts with no general tax increase.  There will be cuts in almost every department except the State Police.  Most taxes will stay the same.

headline: State House To Debate Abortion Bill
abstract: The state House is set to debate a bill that would discourage women from getting abortions.  The bill is very controversial with several interest groups opposed to it.  The article details lawmakers expectations of the bill passage.

headline: School tax reform bill risky, unfair
abstract: PA Senate bill 1085 would allow school districts to substitute wage tax revenue for property tax money. The editorial believes it is too risky for school districts already reeling under the effects of federal cutbacks and inflation. They believe there must be a better way to fund schools.

headline: Quakers urge nuclear power halt
abstract: The Quaker author of the letter to the editor, representing the North Branch Friends Meeting, points out the concerns the organization has about the licensing of PA Power and Light's Susquehanna nuclear power plant near Berwick. They urge that construction be halted on the reactors, and that people's overall role in increasing energy efficiency be examined.

headline: Abortion Advice Curb Clears Panel
abstract: A Pennsylvania House-Senate conference committee added a compromise provision to a bill that would authorize the state to spend $2.2 billion in federal funds, $4.6 million of which is earmarked for family planning.  The article goes over the conference in further detail and the appropriations for family planning.

headline: Conferees Near OK on SS Bill
abstract: Democrats and Republicans attended a conference to come to an agreement on a stopgap bill that would restore minimum Social Security benefits to 3 million Americans.  The article details the history of the bill in both the U.S. House and Senate.

headline: Bill Seeks to Mandate 15% Down, 25-Month Payback: Target Japanese Care via Tight Credit Terms - Ertel
abstract: U.S. Congressman Allen Ertel proposed a bill that would tighten credit on Americans who buy Japanese cars.  The bill, if passed, will require a 15 per cent down payment and only 25 months to repay a car loan on a Japanese car.  The bill is aimed at increasing sales of American made cars, which would have no credit restrictions.

headline: Judge mulls suit of 666 drawer
abstract: A lawyer for Edward Plevel, convicted of rigging the state lottery numbers to be 6-6-6, stated that the woman who physically drew the numbers, Violet Lowery, has no right to sue his client.  Lowery, who was not convicted of any crime on the grounds of being an innocent bystander, is suing Plevel for emotional distress due to being constantly hounded by the media.  The court is still deciding whether or not to throw out Lowery suit.

headline: Three vying for seat on Commonwealth Court
abstract: The third statewide court race on the primary election ballet, for one seat on Commonwealth Court, does not seem crowded in comparison with the contests for Superior Court and the Supreme Court. Two of the three candidates for nomination to Commonwealth Court are cross-filed on the Republican and Democratic ballots.

headline: Gypsy Moths Feel Reagan is up a Tree Without their Vote
abstract: For new budget cuts to pass Northeast GOP moderates need a lot of persuading. They call themselves the Gypsy Moths, and if he cannot gain their approval his budget cuts will not  go through Congress. They want more military cuts and to repeal tax breaks.

headline: State Reaction Mixed To Pennhurst Decision
abstract: The April 20th US Supreme Court ruling that a 1975 Congressional act does not give mentally retarded persons the right to be treated in community-based programs was received with mixed reactions in PA. While Susan Reider Earson, spokeswoman for the PA Association for Retarded Citizens, was disappointed and said the Bill of Rights was important, State Welfare Secretary Helen O'Bannon said the ruling was an important legal victory for PA. The battle was over Pennhurst State School and Hospital near Philadelphia, and its alleged violation of resident's rights by segregation.

headline: Schools bar some impaired foster children, groups say
abstract: Child-welfare advocates filed a complaint against the state Department of Education, accusing school districts in the state of refusing to admit some foster-care children who are mentally or physically handicapped or who speak a foreign language.  The administrative complaint was filed at the federal Office for Civil Rights, region 3.  The welfare groups contended that a 70 year old clause in the Pennsylvania Public School Code is being used by school districts to deny admittance to children with special educational needs whose natural parents live in one school district but whose foster parents live in another.

headline: Radiated water shifted in Unit 2 for cleanup start
abstract: Engineers at Three Mile Island completed the transfer of 15,000 gallons of highly radioactive water into Unit 2 fuel-handling building today in preparation for the start of a major step in the Unit 2 cleanup. The water was drawn from the basement by a pump and flowed through a hose inserted through the wall of the containment building. The water was deposited in a holding tank in the adjacent fuel handling building. The entire operation is sealed t prevent the escape of radiation.

headline: Adoptive law
abstract: Letter to the editor clarifying misleading information about adoption. PA adoption agencies do not give birth parents six months to change their minds. It allows private attorneys or adoption agencies 30 days to petition the court. Both parents must appear and consent to the adoption and the child can the child can remain in the adoptive home with out fear of change.

headline: Controversy rages over 'workfare' for welfare
abstract: Pennsylvania Representative Terry L. Punt understands his system to make welfare recipients work to earn their bimonthly welfare checks.  The concept is called, workfare, which is where welfare recipients in Pennsylvania would be required to pick up trash, sweep floors, answer telephones, type letters, or do other tasks that fall under the heading of public service.  The article goes further into detail about the workfare process.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: The cartoon depicts the inside of a state liquor store.  Two clerks are talking.  One says "How much longer do we have to be nice to people?"  The other says, "Just till the private store bill fails."

headline: Judge rejects teachers' suit
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Harry A Takiff threw out a lawsuit by Philadelphia's public school teachers, ruling that the Board of Education did not violate its contract commitments when it laid off 3,500 district employees. In rejecting arguments by the 21,000 members Philadelphia Federation of Teachers could not be held to contract agreements which depended on funding from another legislative body.

headline: THROW THE BULLET AWAY
abstract: Transport Workers Union president Dominick DiClerico said he was willing to bite the bullet if the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority conceded on its demands to hire part-timers. The editorial argues that DiClerico should accept SEPTA's already fair terms, because the strike is hurting SEPTA workers and the residents of the city of Philadelphia.

headline: Higher-Interest Bill Faces Battle; Consumers To Fight Higher-Interest Bill
abstract: Consumer labor groups are organizing an effort to block enactment of a bill that would significantly hike interest rates in Pennsylvania.  The bill, passed by the Senate and is pending in the House, has strong support from bankers, retailers, and Thornburgh administration officials who contend that present usury limits are too low.  Failure of the House to approve the bill prior to the summer recess has given opponents several months to map strategy for an all-out lobbying effort.

headline: The Dreaded Complication
abstract: Cover story states that abortions remain one of the major ethical controversies of our time but has become one of the most common medical procedures performed within the US. The focus of the article is on the small number of abortions performed relatively late in the pregnancy where the result is a live baby.

headline: Schools boards' new chief
abstract: Joseph Oravitz has been named as the new executive director of the Pennsylvania Schools Boards Association. He will assume the post June 30, 1982.

headline: Radioactive Mice Scurry at A-Plant
abstract: Management of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant, which had an accident in 1979, has found radioacitve mice droppongs.  This could mean that the mice themselves are also radioactive.  Experts, however, say that rodent bites will not transmit radiation because the doses are so small

headline: After 14 arsons in one month, fear, anger spread like wildfire
abstract: There have been 14 arsons in one month all of them within half a block of Main Street. When the library was burned down fear of arson changed to anger.

headline: Countian named delegate to national conference on aging
abstract: N. Eugene Shoemaker, a 71 year old local man, was invited to attend the White House Conference on Aging.  96 other Pennsylvanians will be attending the conference also.  The article details Mr. Shoemaker's career and the history of the conference.

headline: Embargo Background
abstract: The Soviet grain embargo was begun in response to the invasion of Afghanistan by Soviet troops. President Carter ordered the suspension of grain sales, except for 8 million tons per year of corn and wheat. The embargo went into effect January 7, 1980, and covered grain and other foods like seeds, meat, poultry products, certain animal fats, soybeans, technology industrial items, and in February fertilizer was added to the list.

headline: Judge Taylor Garners Races in Huntingdon
abstract: According to unofficial tabulations of the May 19 voting, incumbent Newton Taylor won both party nominations for Common Pleas Court judge in Huntingdon County. Both him and Morris Terrizzi, the former judge, are Republicans and were cross-filed.

headline: Top court Oks legislative redistricting
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld the final plan of the Legislative Reapportionment Commission, and noted that the equality of population the five member panel achieved among the 203 state House and 50 Senate districts is closer to the one person, one vote principle than previous reapportionment plans.  The article goes further into detail about the redistricting plans.

headline: House handles key legislation
abstract: The House shot out three major pieces of legislation, including a $6.8 billion general state budget. The decisions were made largely behind closed doors.  One was a gas tax measure which would impose a 3.5% wholesale tax on all transportation-related petroleum products sold in PA to raise $192 million to repair roads.

headline: The future is worrisome to minority firms
abstract: Two threats are causing minority entrepreneurs in Philadelphia and elsewhere to be worried about the future. The first is the sickly economy with its high interest rates and threat of recession. The other is the budget-cutting efforts of the Reagan administration, which has threatened to curtail the scope of programs that have traditionally been the sources of financial support for minority business enterprises. An example are the loans and contract programs administered by the Small Business Administration.

headline: Services Reverses Decision
abstract: According to an opinion by state Representative Don Snyder (134th Legislative District), hundreds of thousands of tax dollars were saved when the state Department of General Services reversed its decision to close the Allentown distribution center for surplus federal food. The decision would have affected 87 school districts and state institutions in a five-county area. He gives credit to Mr. Fred Polish, Supervisor of Food Services of East Penn School  District, and his fellow school officials for standing up for the local taxpayers.

headline: Radioactive waste from TMI is trucked to Coast for burial
abstract: Almost a ton of radioactive material is being trucked across 10 states, the first waste from the Three Mile Island nuclear power accident headed for burial at a disposal site. It is the first of 22 such shipments, of which the Nuclear Regulatory Commission claims is a safe transportation method.

headline: Airport regains fire protection
abstract: PA has reached an agreement with the Fairview Twp. Volunteer Fire Department for fire protection. In March the firefighters claimed they would no longer answer calls at the airport because of the state's unwillingness to provide the department with what it considered adequate compensation. They will receive an even $10,000 a year and respond to any fire at the airport but not in-fight or on-ground emergencies.

headline: County nun delegate to conference
abstract: Sister Irma Catharine Leicht has been selected a one of Pennsylvania's delegates to the 1981 White House Conference on Aging.  The article details her life and describes the events that will be held at the conference

headline: Ertek seeks auto-import credit curbs
abstract: U.S. Congressman Allen Ertel proposed a bill that would tighten credit on Americans who buy Japanese cars.  The bill, if passed, will require a 15 per cent down payment and only 25 months to repay a car loan on a Japanese car.  The bill is aimed at increasing sales of American made cars, which would have no credit restrictions.

headline: Judge Who Used Taxpayer$
abstract: Pennsylvania Judge David Savitt, administrator of Philadelphia's Court of Common Pleas, is responsible for overseeing the court's $40 million budget and 2,000 employees alongside guarding against misuse of court property. However, a check on Savitt's campaign records shows that he used a city car to campaign throughout the state, gave leftover campaign funds to his wife and son, and members of the judge's staff helped him campaign. Savitt denies that he did anything to violate state law or statute.

headline: Top level federal pensions
abstract: 250 state and local Pennsylvania government employers, representing about 125,000 employees have or are threatening to pull out of Social Security. And why shouldn't they when the average pension in the federal retirement system is $959.39 per month, more than triple that of Social Security. The author wonders why, if the Reagan administration wanted to cut the federal budget, doesn't cut government pension benefits back to a level equal to those available in the private-sector pension plans and then include all government workers in Social Security?

headline: In Bucks, Goldwater assails labor and backs AWACS sale
abstract: US Senator Barry Goldwater said that union leaders were partly to blame for problems for problems in the American economy. Union leadership has spent too many years worrying about everything except how a man is going to get along. Goldwater said that Reagan's program would create up to 13 million jobs in the next five years.

headline: Thornburgh Should Veto 'Inquisition'; Governor Should Sign Abortion Bill; State Abortion Bill Is Bad Act By Men
abstract: Three letters to the editor with opinions on Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh's abortion bill.

headline: Special ed funding changes unveiled
abstract: Education officials unveiled a plan to counter the states controversial state funding formula for special education.  This plan would give school districts the option to teach special needs children, contract out to private institutions, or send them to an intermediate unit.  This plan would be used to replace the states plan for larger class sizes, which is unacceptable to the education community.

headline: Reagan Leaning To Easing Rules For Atom Power
abstract: The Reagan Administration's long-awaited policy on nuclear power, to be announced next month, will specify the President's intention to move expeditiously but wisely to remove governmental barriers to the wider use of nuclear energy, according to a draft of his statement.  According to the draft, which an aide said would essentially make up the final statement, Reagan will call for these policy changes: obstacles to the construction of the current generation of nuclear reactors would be removed, the breeder reactor would be developed, and the ban on the commercial reprocessing of spent reactor fuel would be lifted.

headline: Angels graduate to the subways
abstract: After a graduation ceremony, the newly-created Guardian Angels began patrols last night, promising to cut crime in half within three months. Unarmed except for martial-arts training, the self-appointed guardians of the city's subway system have made Philadelphia the 10th city to have an active chapter.

headline: Critics think formal attire inappropriate for Schweiker
abstract: Richard Schweiker says he didn't mean to be criticized for posing in fancy dress for a magazine cover, but the Welfare chief says never intends to do it again. The Washington post seized on the picture as a symbol of Reagan officials' appetite for extravagance at a time when they are pruning Social Security and the welfare rolls.

headline: State among foreign trade leaders
abstract: Tokyo, Frankfurt, Mexico City, Paris, London are Pennsylvania industry's windows to the world, international trade centers where the state spends $437,000 in taxpayers' money to help commonwealth companies get lucrative contracts.  Thirty-three states, most in recent years, maintain foreighn offices so they can compete for economic opportunitys, such as a Japanese car manufacturer looking to open a United States plant, or a country like Korea looking to buy coal.  Pennsylvania is among the leaders, selling, accoring to one estimate, $7 billion to $8 billion of goods yearly around the globe.  And the commonwealth in the first three-quarters of 1980 led its 49 competitors for foreign manufacturing industry investments, landing 27 companies.

headline: Jumping on the 'sunset' bandwagon might not be the best move
abstract: The author opines that the 'sunset' laws, which allow state agencies to be periodically evaluated for efficiency and perhaps terminated, is not the answer to the state's problems.  The author feels that this will create legislative 'bargining' to keep agencies and will do more harm than good.

headline: Turmoil
abstract: The editors detail the political in-fighting of the Democratic Party and wonder how the party can still function.  They site several feuds within the party including, Democratic commissioners, the sheriff and coroner, and the district attorney.

headline: Income Tax
abstract: Business analyst Frank Witgen states shifting the burden of taxation from landowners to wage earners will become a disincentive to work. Disproportionally effecting middle and low income families.

headline: Thornburgh: 'Cool, With Class'
abstract: The author describes an incident where Governor Thornburgh was confronted by student protesters.  The author feels that the Governor handled the situation with poise and class by acknowledging there right to protest.  The author states that although he does not agree with many of the Governor's policies, he thinks he is a very likeable guy.

headline: State Alleges College Fraud
abstract: A press conference was held on alleged welfare fraud by Montgomery County Community College.  State Auditor General Al Benedict claims that the college misused $364,064 that should have gone to train people who receive welfare.  The college claims that it used the funds to train nurses and the college could be able to use state funds as it sees appropriate.

headline: Reagan's NRC: Change is coming
abstract: The article is an interview with Victor Gilinsky, a member of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).  The NRC is charged with deciding what to do with the Three Mile Island (TMI) Nuclear Power Plant, which had a partial meltdown in 1978.  They must deal with nuclear waste disposal and decontamination.  The company that owns TMI, GPU Nuclear Group (formerly Metropolitan Edison) stated that it would welcome any help from NCR with clean up.

headline: ANOTHER POINT OF VIEW
abstract: Although recent KYW Newsradio editorials have supported strict gun controls, in this broadcast Arnold Solis Cohen, of center city Philadelphia, argues that he is not a gun nut, but that more laws will never deter criminals from obtaining guns illegally. His suggestion, instead, is for mandatory psychological screening and completion of a course of instruction in firearm safety.

headline: Cutting deeper into food benefits:  Women, children stand to lose under new state order
abstract: The state had to repay the federal government $7.4 million due to a miscalculation of how many clients would be enrolled in the Women, Infants and Children Program (WIC).  WIC provides funds to purchase essential food for low income women with children who have nutritional defeciencies.  Because of the miscalculation, WIC has had to cut back almost 25,000 of the people they serve, causing severe hardship for some.  The article describes the cutbacks effects in individual counties

headline: Bush attacks Castro, defends Reagan policy
abstract: Vice President George Bush, speaking at Duquesne University yesterday, strongly defended administration policies toward El Salvador and all of Latin America. Bush said the worst offender of human rights in the hemisphere was not El Salvador but Fidel Castro's government in Cuba. Demonstrators from the Thomas Merton Center gathered outside the university to protest.

headline: Jury shown tape of Lederer taking $50,000 in bag
abstract: U.S. Representative Raymond F. Lederer (D-PA) is accused of taking a $50,000 bribe in return for proposing a private bill.  The jury in the trial was shown a video tape of him taking the money.  The men who asked for the favor were federal agents in charge of an investigation of corruption in Congress.  Lederer maintains that it was entrapment

headline: TV stagehand fourth to plead guilty to fixing Daily Number lottery draw
abstract: Fred Luman, a WTAE-TV stagehand pleaded guilty to helping fix the lottery's daily number game by switching the ping pong balls used.  He also agreed to testify against former announcer Nick Perry.  The article details the scandal.

headline: Letters to the editor; Help for industry
abstract: William Perkins's "An Unwise Tax Break for Business" article stated several obvious misconceptions.  The letter criticizes Perkins for not even considering the loss of taxes and jobs that would result from the state's decision to disallow the accelerated-depreciation allowance.

headline: Time flies for the ERA; ERA time nearly out, O'Bannon tells group
abstract: The Equal Rights Amendment supporters in Harrisburg joined those in nearly 200 cities across the nation in "countdown rallies" representing the beginning of the final year's campaign to ratify the amenment.  Thirty-five states have ratified since 1972, three more are needed by June 30, 1982.  Pennsylvania, an early ratifier of the federal amendment, is celebrating the 10th anniversary of its own equal rights amendment.

headline: State backs school merger delay
abstract: The state Department of Education is attempting to delay a US District court-ordered merger of four east suburban school districts with the General Braddock School District. According to the judge, the Swissvale, Turtle Creek, Churchill and Edgewood districts are to be merged into a 9,000-student district by this fall because it is the only way to desegregate the 68 percent black Braddock district. The Education Department, school districts, and students are all fighting the order.

headline: Recommended: A 12 pct. Increase in PE customers' bills
abstract: An administrative law judge recommended that the Philadelphia Electric Co. should be allowed to collect additional revenues by raising customers' electric bills by 12%.   The judge gave his recommendation to the Public Utility Commission (PUC).

headline: Art thefts: Latest growth business in city and the world
abstract: The growing trend toward investment in art has not escaped the attention of culture vultures with larceny in their hearts.  Art thieves are burglarizing museums, galleries, churches, historic sites and private collections worldwide at an increasing rate.  And Philadelphia has not been ignored.  Some criminals are selective: They can tell a Picasso from a Pissaro, a Rembrandt from a Reubens.

headline: Democrats KO money for welfare
abstract: The state Legislature adjourned for two weeks after defeating a $50.5 million money bill which included funds for welfare recipients, Governor Dick Thornburgh's counsel general's office, and control of gypsy moths. The appropriations bill was defeated in the House vote.

headline: Demand Reagan Pull Out Translators: Colombian Captors Threaten To Kill Local Missonary
abstract: A group of Marxist terrorists in Colombia, called Operation National Sovereignty, kidnapped Chester Bitterman III and threatened to kill him if his organization, Wycliffe Bible Translators, doesn’t leave the country.  The terrorist group feels that the Wycliffe organization threatens their indigenous way of life and plunders their resources.

headline: Justice Flaherty For Governor?
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice John Flaherty stated that he may run for resign from the court and run for Governor again the incumbent, Dick Thornburgh.  Flaherty stated that Democratic leaders are pressuring him to run.

headline: Two in Franklin County Seek GOP Treasurer Nod
abstract: In Franklin County, the only county-wide battles of any consequence are the tax collector and district justice races. Two candidates are seeking the Republican Nomination for county treasurer to oppose the incumbent Democrat who's not being challenged in the primary. There's also a Republican contest there for jury commissioner. Five Republicans are vying for the tax collector nomination in Hamilton Township. Other townships in Franklin County also have interesting judicial and tax collector races.

headline: Levy on income would replace nuisance taxes
abstract: The state House of Representatives Finance Committee voted to abolish local nuisance and earned income taxes, allowing local officials to impose a personal income tax if there is a dollar-for-dollar reduction in other taxes. The package of bills was sent to the House floor. Earlier this month, the state Senate Finance Committee approved its version of tax reform, which would abolish school property taxes, and replace them with new local personal income tax and an increase in the state income tax.

headline: Tough abortion bill proposed
abstract: A bipartisan coalition in the House of Representatives introduced a four-bill package that is intended to make Pennsylvania the most difficult state in the nation to get an abortion on demand.  The package of bills is aimed at large-scale abortion mills that operate on an entrepreneurial, profit-motive basis and are concerned not with health care but with killing babies for profit.  The national Abortion Rights Action League called the anti-abortion initiative "pure harassment of Pennsylvania women and their right to medically safe abortion procedures."  Some of the restrictive features of the abortion-control bill are: a 72-hour waiting period after the initial request for an abortion, and minors still supported by parents must get parental  or court consent.

headline: State Education Dept. learns some distasteful media lessons
abstract: For an agency that oversees how students are taught how to write, the PA Education Department's pen keeps getting it in trouble. Most recently it was the gag order issued by Education Secretary Robert Scanion against presidents of state-owned colleges that provoked a public furor and continues to do so. Even though the Department held hearings on special education changes their minds were already made up. A memo said that the presidents were not allowed to publicly oppose any legislative stances taken by the administration. This got him into a lot of trouble with Democratic lawmakers.

headline: Record PE rate increase supported by PUC judge
abstract: null

headline: Attorney-general designate: Smith's priorities sound familiar
abstract: The author opines that William French Smith, President Reagan's choice for attorney general, doesn't understand the majority of crimes committed are the jurisdiction of state and local authorities and very few are federal.  There is little the Justice Department can do to combat street crime and the author fears that if Smith is confirmed, there will be less of an emphasis on combating organized crime

headline: Dissension among delegates marks the start of conference on aging
abstract: The White House Conference on aging, which seeks to resolve issues facing senior citizens, found dissension among the delegates as to the ground rules state by the Reagan Administration.  Many delegates found the voting system among the delegates unfair.  The article details the dissent at the conference.

headline: Gray ask Reagan to Bar S. African Team
