abstract: US Representative William Gray urged President Ronald Reagan to block the US State Department from granting visas to the national rugby team of South Africa. He claims it is an insult to American of conscience especially black Americans.

headline: Kauffman testifies in probe of fellow jurist Larsen
abstract: Supreme Court Justice Bruce W. Kauffman was called to testify in the state's investigation of Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen.  Larsen is being investigated on charges of violating the state's prohibition on politicking by judges.  The article details the charges.

headline: Two Pennsylvania areas make the 'metropolitan' list
abstract: PA has lost 66,000 residents in the past decade, but the State College and Sharon have grown to become two of the 36 newest metropolitan areas acceding to the 1980 census. The 1980 census said that 75 percent of all Americans live in metropolitan areas.

headline: Local Taxation: Unending Dialogue
abstract: There are discussions in the state Legislature about reforming tax laws.  The article discusses specific taxes (income tax, property tax, occupational tax), there problems, and how they might be addressed

headline: Two sponsors to tone down abortion bill
abstract: The sponsors of a four bill anti-abortion package are backing amendments that would tone down some of their proposals. At a press conference they said reduce their 72 hour waiting period for women seeking abortions to 24 hours. They will also eliminate that the woman has to notify their partner and exempt minors pregnant with their fathers baby from having to get his approval for the procedure.

headline: State Kills Changes in Special Ed
abstract: State Education Secretary Robert Scanlon withdrew a set of proposed changes in special education standards that would have increased the size of classes for the handicapped and reduced the number of classroom aides. Although the changes could have saved $30 to $60 million, during hearings thousands of parents, teachers, and school administrators had complained the revisions would alter the quality of education for the state's handicapped students.

headline: Record PE rate increase supported by PUC judge
abstract: A Public Utilities Commission (PUC) Judge recommended that Philadelphia Electric be granted a $201 million annual rate increase.  If the PUC adopts the recommendation, customers would see a rate hike of about 12 per cent.  The recommendation is meant to keep Philadelphia Electric from going into bankruptcy.

headline: Bad Conduct
abstract: William Robinson, executive director of the Allegheny Prison, drove a government car onto some railroad tracks and got stuck between the rails and the car was totaled. He had consumed a few drinks before. He was fired and then got into a fight with the Swissvale Police. His actions reflected poorly on his position and should have known better.

headline: Elderly forced to walk: A one-hour hike to market
abstract: Rennie Cohen, director of the Center for Older Adults Northwest, stated that senior citizens were being adversely affected by the transit strike.  Some senior citizens are having to walk an hour each way to get groceries.  The article also states that taxis are not doing well because people are just avoiding going downtown, when the used to use mass transit.  That article details citizens daily commute without the transit system.

headline: How one hostage got through; By cultivating his rage, pride
abstract: Michael Metrinko was held hostage in Iran for over 14 months and recently released. The article is an interview with him detailing his prison experience and how he survived it.

headline: Knock out funds
abstract: Some government programs have proved their worth but some caused more problems than they solve. PA Family Planning falls into this category. Letter writes about why Family Planning should not gain its funding back.

headline: Two Pennsylvania Schwenkfelders in Reagan's Cabinet
abstract: Richard Schultz Schweiker, Reagan's choice for secretary of health and human services, and Lindsay "Drew" Lewis, Reagan's choice for transportation secretary are both Schwenkfelders- members of one of the world's smallest organized churches.  Both men are from Pennsylvania.  The article outlines what the religion is.

headline: Local view:  Area economists can't agree on 'mess'
abstract: The article interviews several local economists on President Reagan's statements that the U.S. economy is a "mess."  Most agreed the the economy is not good due to high inflation, high taxation and decreased productivity.

headline: Urges opposition to anti-abortion bill
abstract: Letter to the editor speaks out against the anti-abortion bill. She is worried it will eventually lead to birth control becoming illegal, having to tell father about an abortion, death certificates being issued for a fetus, and other things endangering women's health.

headline: State school funding not easy
abstract: Funding of public schools is hot debate in the PA General Assembly. The Reagan administration plans sharp cuts in federal aid to education. Some estimate 700,000 teachers will be laid by September. School districts have been raising property taxes to counter the decline.

headline: Reopen TMI Restart Case, Judge Orders
abstract: A judge considering the proposed restart of the undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island on Friday ordered the case reopened because of a cheating scandal involving technicians who would operate the reactor. Also, officials at the plant reported an increase in the rate of leakage of water from the cooling system of the damaged reactor, but said there was no release of radioactivity.

headline: Beg for a pardon? He will not
abstract: The opinion author argues George Senn, a man convicted for a shooting incident in 1964, should get a pardon for protecting the lives of 3 girls and a boy while shooting the alleged attackers. But the governor, his lieutenant governor, the state Board of Pardons, and the Delaware County judge who presided at the trial say they won't give him a pardon unless he admits to the wrongdoing and is sorry for what he did.

headline: 'Enormous' profit on state aid to Pinehill Center is charged
abstract: The state Welfare Department will investigate allegations that the stockholders of a Philadelphia center for the mentally retarded made a profit by improperly collecting nearly $1 million in state funds. Auditor General Al Benedict made the accusations Tuesday, after state auditors found that the Pinehill Rehabilitation Center was paid an excess in consulting fees, rent, unbudgeted director's fees and non-reimbursable costs.

headline: Phila. Iranian student sees easier life with hostage release
abstract: Article interviews two Iranian college students on their thoughts of the release of US hostages in Iran. Both have very different views on the subject

headline: 'Knowledge, Trade-Off' Issues Facing Wecht Jury
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Cyril Wecht is accused of using three county morgue employees to process specimens for his private firm. On May 18 he will be judged by a jury of seven men and five women. Judge Robert Walker will instruct them on applying the law, and the concepts of knowledge and trade-off will play an important part in the decisions.

headline: U.S. attorney selection panel begins interviewing 7 nominees
abstract: The long-awaited selection of a permanent United States attorney for Western Pennsylvania will begin at Duquesne University where a  merit selection panel will interview prospective nominees.  At least seven Republican lawyers from Allegheny and Butler counties, including current court-appointed United States Attorney J. Alan Johnson, are expected to be received by the seven-member bipartisan panel  in Room 710 of Rockwell Hall.

headline: Money to burn
abstract: At a time when President Reagan is leading the charge for tightening the belt on federal spending, individual states seem to be taking the ball and running in the opposite direction.  Two obvious examples of a state's spendthrift policy struck close to home in the last few weeks.  And in both cases, the tax payer was on the receiving end of the blows.  In one case, the state Department of Transportation rejected two low bids on 130 dump trucks in favor of one that cost the taxpayers $456,000 more than the low.  Also, the taxpayers were asked to swallow a state policy that will cost them between $18,000 and $27,000 in unnecessary finance charges for the purchase of vehicles for Somerset County's Mental Health-Mental Retardation and Children and Youth Services.

headline: Women's Athletics Aided By Philadelphia Ruling
abstract: A federal judge in Philadelphia ruled that sex discrimination laws apply to schools even if federal funds are not earmarked for athletics.  The judge found that Temple University's athletic programs are subject to Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972.  The article outlines other schools' issues with Title IX

headline: State University System In Bill Receives Backing
abstract: When Dick Thornburgh ran for governor in 1978 he stated that establishing a university system for the state of PA would be a priority. Now legislation for such a system has received backing and is due for discussion by the Senate Education Committee on December 7. 13 state-owned colleges and Indiana University of Pennsylvania would comprise this new state university system which features an administrative separation of the state colleges from the U.S. Department of Education and instead would be administered by the State System of Higher Education.

headline: Reopened Strip Mine Pleases DER
abstract: Greensburg mining company, Adam Eidemiller, Incorporated, abandoned an eastern Fayette County strip mine after beginning initial blasting to uncover coal seams. As a result, Clarksburg Coal Co. of Indiana has assumed responsibility for the abandoned sites in the area. The Department of Environmental Resources is pleased as Clark Coal is treating acid mine drainage, replacing soil in the mining areas and planting vegetation while tax payers remain unburdened by reclamation costs. The issue at hand, are shortcoming in strip mining regulation. The DER was able to privately work out with the coal industry new mining regulations as follows: Coal operators would now have to pay $50 per acre for new mining sites. This will provide for a $1 million per year reclamation fund.

headline: Better Justice; A New Verdict of Guilty
abstract: The M'Naghten rule states that a person is not guilty because of insanity, if at the time he committed the offense, he could not know the nature of his act or understand right from wrong owing to some defect or disease of the mind.  It has saved several mental incompetents, including a person named M'Naghten.  The article continues stating how this rule has helped the judicial system.

headline: Food Stamp Changes In Works
abstract: With the changes resulting from the Thornburgh administration's revision of public assistance eligibility, nearly 13,000 Pennsylvanians are expected to lose all food stamp benefits and approximately 271,000 people currently receiving food stamps will face a $2-$3 reduction.

headline: President in Philly; Favors Trade to Aid Third World
abstract: President Reagan came to Philadelphia to talk about Third World Development. he was only briefly interrupted by anti-war protesters.  His speech mostly involved instituting a free market trade system for Third World countries.  The article details his speech and visit to Philadelphia, and also interviews the anti-war demonstrators.

headline: Labor leaders endorse Smith for U.S. House
abstract: A group of local labor leaders endorsed state Senator Joseph Smith in the July 21 special election for the United States House seat in the Third District.  Smith opposed Democrat David Glancy in the race to fill the seat vacated by Raymond F. Lederer.

headline: U.S. court issues back-to-work order
abstract: United States District Judge Gustave Diamond issued a temporary restraining order directing air traffic controllers at three Western Pennsylvania airports to return to work at 7 A.M. today.  United States marshals began serving papers last night on striking controllers from Greater Pittsburgh International, Allegheny County, and Erie International airports.  Until then, the federal government was rushing 30 trained military personnel to Greater Pitt for temporary assignment as air traffic controllers.

headline: MY VOICE/ Graham Finney; Federal cuts felt locally
abstract: What the New Deal and the Great Society did for Washington over 50 years ago, the Reagan Administration promises to do for Harrisburg in a single budget burst.  With our attention riveted on the big economic picture in Washington, few of people have been asking how these changes will actually work, once they are in the federal system.  Since the Congress barely knows what program it has killed or cut or folded in block grants, there is room to argue that it is still too early to get excited.

headline: Whites' population loss far exceeds blacks'
abstract: Philadelphia lost more than 20 per cent of its white population between 1970 and 1980, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.  Consequently, blacks account for 33.5 per cent of the city's population.  The article details other Census Bureau statistics about Philadelphia's population.

headline: The agony and the ecstasy of teaching
abstract: Teacher explains his troubles with teaching and lacking control in the classroom. He joined a union to help protect his rights. He is about to be laid off, but has realized real teachers aren't in the career for the money or status.

headline: Rush to judgment
abstract: Dormont's Molly Rush is a committed idealist who believes that what other would call nuclear deterrence is murder in slow motion.  Rush clearly feels that she and others of the same view are morally permitted, even obligated, to interfere with the stockpiling of nuclear weapons, even if it entails violating the law.  Part of a mature view of civil disobedience is a recognition that one must accept the consequences of violating what one believes to be an unjust law.  For that reason, supporters of Rush and other peace activists who were sentenced for vandalism at a General Electric Company plant in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, cannot object to their being imprisoned for their lawbreaking.

headline: Bill ensures rape victims' confidentiality; bill targets countersuits from rapists
abstract: State Representative Ronald Cowell will introduce a bill making conversations between rape victims and their counselors confidential.  The problem is that victims will not seek help if they know their conversations will be released to the courts.  Additionally, confidentiality rules would keeps rapists from counter-suing their victims.

headline: Gives Views On System
abstract: A question and answer article. The question asks: If Governor Thornburgh offered you the post of secretary of public welfare, what would you do? The author answers by saying that the secretary of welfare position at either the federal or state level is the most thankless job and the most difficult job to do right.

headline: President plans major Phila. Speech
abstract: President Reagan is to visit Philadelphia to deliver a major foreign policy address to the World Affairs Council. The exact topic is unknown.

headline: Labor-industry chief approved; Nomination of Barry Stern is heading for Senate vote
abstract: A state Senate committee recommended Barry Stern to be Labor and Industry secretary.  The recommendation must now be voted on in the state Senate.  Democrats are opposed to Stern's recommendation, stating that the department has been used for political payoffs. The article details the Democrats opposition.

headline: Unacceptable judicial selection
abstract: The author opines that Governor Dick Thornburgh has not entirely kept his promise to take politics out of judicial appoints.  Though he has set up a merit based system, his nomination of Stephen J. McEwen is based on political ties and not merit and that he should nominate Phyllis W. Beck instead.

headline: No state cuts
abstract: The author of the opinion piece agrees with PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal on holding the line on taxes, even though local governments will be forced to increase taxes. But he argues that the governor's proposed budget cut in education would be better if he also proposed to cut costs in other state programs.

headline: Whose rights?
abstract: Your editorials of September 30 and October 1 civil rights issue of the '80s/ Abortion and the law" were Blatantly ignorant. While you extol the virtues of abortion, you conveniently fail to mention that rape and incest account for only 2 percent of all pregnancies.  The author of the letter writes that Bill 1725-28 is saving the lives of babies.

headline: Strike Splits Black Teachers
abstract: About 300 black teachers met last night to decide their role in the teachers' strike amid pressures from two sides- black union militants who oppose crossing picket lines and black community residents who want their children back in school. The meeting was called by the original Black Teachers and School Employees Caucus.

headline: Salem plant not the first for Bechtel
abstract: Bechtel Power Corp., prime contractor for the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station, has designed or built about half of the nation's nuclear reactors and has done the clean up on TMI. Little is known about it since it is privately owned.

headline: Bill exempting rape counselors' testimony advances
abstract: A state House-Senate conference committee approved a bill that grants rape counselors legal immunity from having to turn over their files in rape trials.  The bill is meant to protect the privacy of rape victims.  It must still be voted on in both the state House and Senate.  The article details the pros and cons of the bill.

headline: Golden Keystone Plan Sponsored For Elderly
abstract: A bill sponsored by state representative Jess Stairs (R) would give senior citizens discounts at retail stores, called the "Golden Keystone" system.  Participation by stores would be voluntary.

headline: Scaife: the South African connection
abstract: The article suggests an important western Pennsylvanian with federal connections, Richard Scaife, is involved with John McGoff and a South African propaganda scandal that forced the resignation of that country's president. The scandal involved a loan of the South African government to McGoff to buy his chain of newspapers, of which Scaife is a board member, to provide a positive perspective on that country. The sale never happened. South Africa has minerals considered of strategic interest for the conservative US administration and politicians. Conservatives have reinforced the perception that President Reagan and/or Scaife forces are hankering for a change in US policy toward South Africa.

headline: Laborites See Governor Delaborizing Government
abstract: Top state labor leaders charges that Governor Thornburgh is trying to eliminate labor representatives from state boards and commissions.  The sentiments were used by democrats to attack republicans.

headline: Under the Dome:  GOP shifts gears on ethics unit
abstract: The state Senate decided to keep its Ethics and Offical Conduct Committee in the unfunded, part-time status.  Republicans defeated the measure to change its status, arguing that the costs would be too much.

headline: No Tax is Temporary
abstract: The editorial argues that by tacking a tax measure on another bill already passed by the state House and likely to be passed, the Republican senators have reaffirmed the truth that a temporary tax is never temporary. The income tax additions were temporary, but Governor Dick Thornburgh said he needed the money, and Republican senators obliged.

headline: Why face abortion's issues? Because life's no fairy tale
abstract: The media's worrying over Princess Diana's fetus has given rise to the question of abortion especially since the abortion-control bill is being discussed right now. The author claims it punishes evil or sinful women who happen to have an unwanted pregnancy. He worries that they will soon want birth and death certificates for fetuses.

headline: Student Aid Cuts Bite Middle Class
abstract: If cutbacks in state and federal student aid become reality, many families will suffer bigger cuts in their children's college tuitions. The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency does not have enough money to match inflation, and is keeping the income cutoff the same for a third year in a row, which means many students will lose their grants once their parents' adjusted income rises above $25,000.

headline: Scranton Sees Coal Industry Peril In High-Cost Black Lung Insurance
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III said that PA's coal industry could be bankrupted from a proposed change in black lung protection insurance. The comments came as the state Insurance Commission continued its review of the way the coal industry pays black lung insurance premiums. The change proposed by the Coal mine Compensating Rating Bureau would mean a 376 percent increase in premiums paid by anthracite producers.

headline: Bill would create state Corrections Dept.
abstract: Senator D. Michael Fisber (R) proposed a bill that would create a Cabinet-level Department of Corrections that would mandate better medical and food services for prisoners.  The bill was endorsed by Governor Thornburgh.  The article outlines the details of the bill, including the provision of an exclusion of official visitors for 72 hours during emergencies.

headline: GOP presses plan to trim welfare rolls
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's proposal to reduce the number of people on the welfare rolls will be debated on the House floor.  The proposal would cut 68,000 people from the welfare rolls.  The article details the actions among Republicans and Democrats regarding the debate on public welfare.

headline: Thanks Given that 52 Are Free:  Governor, City Worshipers Rejoice
abstract: Governor Thornburgh publicly gave thanks to God that 52 of the American hostages in Iran had been released at a Presbyterian Church service.  The article outlines the details of the ceremony.

headline: Larsen called to Wecht hearing
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen was subpoenaed to testify in the pre-hearing against county Commissioner Cyril Wecht.  Mr. Wecht is accused of using his former position as county cororner for private gain between 1970-1980.  Mr. Wecht claims the charges are a political conspiracy aimed against him and accused Justice Larsen as being bias toward him.

headline: Union critics harm state, Thornburgh aide charges
abstract: Secretary of the Department of Labor and Industry, Charles Lieberth, was upset by statements from top labor leaders that Governor Thronburgh is eliminating labor supports from state positions.  He feels that public statements like this will not help to attrack business and industry to Pennsylvania.

headline: NRC chiefs ruled in contempt for secret budget hearings
abstract: A federal judge held the five members of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission on contempt for violating his order that the agency open its budget meetings to the public. They can clear themselves by releasing, within ten days, a transcript of a closed budget meeting.

headline: null
abstract: Cartoon that has to very similar pills and says, " New State Game: Try to pick the real drug or the look-alike drug."

headline: Takiff selects accountant to monitor schools
abstract: Common Pleas Court Judge Harry A. Takiff named Donald Rappaport, a general partner in the Philadelphia Office of Price Waterhouse and Company, to over see the operation of the Philadelphia public school system during this current financial crisis.  He will not start until Commonwealth Court answers an appeal filed by Philadelphia School District officials of Takiff's decision to name a conservator to deal with the district's $223 million deficit.  Rappaport said he understood that as conservator, he would give Takiff advice on school district finances and that Takiff would direct the school system to follow it, if he thought it was appropriate.  School district attorneys have argued that Takiff has no statutory authority to appoint someone to head the school system.

headline: Seminary Reaffirms Opposition to TMI
abstract: The faculty of Lancaster Theological Seminary has issued a statement in opposition to nuclear power plants, based on the accident at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in 1979.  The article prints a text of their statement.

headline: Black Day for New Judge
abstract: Governor Thornburgh nominated Phyllis Beck for judgeship of the Pennsylvania Superior Court. She is the first woman to sit on the bench in the court's 86 year history.

headline: Gov. Proposes Taking 68,000 Off Of Welfare
abstract: Governor Thornburgh is proposing to take all "able-bodied" people off welfare.  State senator Richard A. Snyder supports the proposal, which the governor has not officially introduced, but feels it could be much stricter.  The proposal is controversial and the Governor scaled back an original proposal to reduce the number of people taken off welfare

headline: U.S. bans pencils to Cambodia; Mennonites can't export gift kits
abstract: The U.S. Commerce Department refused the Mennonite Central Committee (MCC) from sending gift bags with pencils and rules to children in Cambodia, based on the fact that the U.S. does not recognize Cambodia and doesn't want the gift bags being construded as development aid from the United States.   The MCC plans to fight the ban.

headline: Lawmakers need pension reminders
abstract: PA's voters voted a firm 'no' on November 3 when the issue of increasing state pension benefits was put before them. The writer wonders if this message will reach Harrisburg, PA or not and he speculates that it will not unless lawmakers are constantly reminded of it. Few legislators are willing to vote against the bill of increased benefits for 'widows' with ballot approval as a constitutional amendment in the House passed 183-10.

headline: Unions plan to signal Green
abstract: Feeling more and more threatened by the city and school board's firm stand against the teachers in the 31 day strike, organized labor is looking for ways to pressure Philadelphia Mayor Green. The unions have considered a general strike designed to paralyze much of the city.

headline: Our Readers Write; An Opportunity Lost
abstract: The Patriot's article entitled "Skirting Deficit" with regard to tax breaks for corporations in Pennsylvania needs some clarification.  The article, written by Vincent J. Fumo (Pennsylvania Senator), continues to discuss how the article needs further clarity.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon depicting two school children sitting on top of school books. The binding of the books read "English, History, Literature, Reading, and Mathematics." Next to the schoolchildren is a picture of a drug pusher sitting atop a trash can with a wine bottle and a sign that reads "Home Sweet Home." The caption above this cartoon says: "Get high on life with these...NOT with this." The first portion of the sentence is situated above the children and the second portion of the sentence points to the pusher.

headline: Tax credits are a threat to all schools
abstract: The author looks at President Reagan's proposed tuition tax credit bills for parents who send their children to private schools.  The author feels that these tax credits would ruin public education and states that they are unconstitutional if passed.  The article details the author's argument.

headline: She knows the problem lives on
abstract: Stumping the state and country on a self-proclaimed crusade, Susan Shanaman is trying to rekindle what she sees as a waning public interest inn the continuing problems with Three Mile Island.  And, to hear her tell it, the time for solutions is running out.  Mrs. Shanaman, chairman of the state public Utilities Commission, has been closely associated with nuclear plan accident since her confirmation to the commission in the fall of 1979. While a partial clean-up of the damaged nuclear reactor's core and contaminated water has been progressing with funds from a $300 million insurance policy held by the General Public Utilities Company, Mrs. Shanaman said the money will barely scratch the surface of what will be needed to render thee facility harmless.

headline: Bribe probe suspect is held again
abstract: A 19-year-old robbery suspect who was freed by a municipal court judge allegedly in exchange for a $1,060 bribe, has been charged with another robbery.

headline: House vote on welfare purge delayed
abstract: State House Republicans have postponed a vote on Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposed welfare purge because they lacked sufficient votes. Legislative leaders are trying to remove a Democratic amendment gutting the Thornburgh bill, which would strip cash grants from 68,000 able-bodied welfare recipients.

headline: null
abstract: A warm collection of statuary is used in an attempt to offset the cold, hard lines of the Youth Study Center building

headline: Lawyer hints of surprises in lottery fix
abstract: District Justice Mary E. Cross ordered Pittsburgh television emcee Nick Perry and Edward Plevel, suspended state lottery bureau district manager, to appear in Dauphin County Court to answer charges that they conspired with six others in the rigging of the April 24 Lottery drawing.  Perry's lawyer, Tom Livingston, hinted to reporters that he believed that others, apparently so far unidentified were involved in the lottery fix.

headline: United Way
abstract: Photograph with the caption: Governor Dick Thornburgh meets with United Way of PA officials at the organization's annual meeting Wednesday at the Penn Harris Motor Inn. The photograph is of Lucy M. Sayre, United Way president, R. Max Mills, chairman of the government relations committee, and Bernard Hyman, executive director, alongside Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Pa. Dems say budget to lift local taxes
abstract: State Democrats claim that Governor Thornburgh's proposed budget only avoids a tax increase because it shifts money away from programs in municipalities and school districts.  They claim that costs will increase for schools and local governments which will in turn increase local property taxes.  The article also outlines the Governor's proposed gasoline tax to fund the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: 6 Months Added On Locust Mt. Closing Order
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh modified his closing order on Locust Mountain State General Hospital, extending the date by six months to Dec. 31, to allow Shenandoah area residents to consider options for creating an alternative health care facility. After State Senator James Rhoades, residents and officials of Schuykill County talked with the governor, he made the decision on the privately built but partly state subsidized hospital, which has more than a $500,000 deficit for this fiscal year. Possible alternatives are turning the hospital into a nursing home and using part of the building for acute and emergency care.

headline: Taxpayers pick up the tab for traveling school talks
abstract: Negotiations in the stalemated Philadelphia public school teachers' strike escalated this week. Before they broke off, representatives of the Philadelphia School district and the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers had spent the time since last Friday moving negotiations through three different high-priced center-city hotels. All of it on the taxpayer bill.

headline: Shippingport A-Plant the Worst, NRC Says
abstract: The Beaver Valley Nuclear power plant in Shippingport has the poorest performance record of the nation's 50 operating atomic plants, according to a Nuclear Regulatory Commission report. 14 other plants were reported below average. Repairs and maintenance have required the plant to be shut down for extended periods.

headline: Broadcaster Faces Trespass Charge
abstract: WCAU reporter Jack Reilly was arrested after he was barred from Graterford State Prison while trying to cover a hostage crisis there.  He was arrested three days after the crisis when he returned to the prison to cover a story unrelated to the crisis.

headline: 'Human services' group seeks ways to cope
abstract: A group of 20 community leaders announced that they had formed a human services consortium to explore ways to cope with the Reagan administration's budget and tax cuts. It could cost Philadelphia non-profits at least $110 million in 1982.

headline: null
abstract: Cartoon of a torture chamber that reads "would the next senator who needs persuasion on the AWACS deal please step forward."

headline: Learning about 'William Penn's Legacy'
abstract: A commemoration of the founding of Pennsylvania 300 years ago will be held to inform the public about William Penn and the history of Pennsylvania.  The article details the act ivies planned for the event.

headline: Vignola hiring not improper
abstract: Letter to the editor stating that a recent article on civil service posts in the city commissioners' office insinuates impropriety and requires clarification. A person cannot be appointed to a civil service position. An individual who possesses specific qualifications for a particular position may be temporarily placed in that position for not more than 90 days. During that period City Personnel Department administers a test for all qualified persons. These positions will reduce political influence in the election process.

headline: Pa. senators protest Reagan's budget cuts
abstract: Pennsylvania's U.S. Senators are upset by President Reagan's proposed budget cuts.  They feel the cuts will disproportionally hurt the Northeast and Midwest as opposed to other regions of the country.

headline: A way to cut busing costs
abstract: The editors feel that busing takes up too much of district school budgets and offer some solutions to reduce the costs including; eliminating busing for students in grades 9-12 and have all the students walk to school.

headline: Teachers criticize right-wing tactics
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Education Association (PSEA) lambasted the radical right at their semi-annual conference.  They feel that the right is bashing public schools and trying to get rid of them.  The article details their complaints about the right.

headline: Small towns study ways to make waterfalls generate power, cash
abstract: Five neighboring communities near Bald Eagle Creek in north-central PA formed a regional planning commission to solve their common problems. The commission decided to look into building a federally-funded hydroelectric plant at the Sayers Dam that would net the municipalities an income of $100,000 a year. The commission is seeking further studies, but is hampered by the Reagan administration's budget cuts.

headline: Bucks judges seek high court ruling
abstract: Bucks county judges ask the PA Supreme Court to decide whether they can have additional funding after the County Commission refused their demands.  The judges asked the Supreme Court to vacate the county's decision and hold a hearing on the Bucks County court budget

headline: Investigations Have Started
abstract: The editorial explains that in the state Senator Milton Street's Weatherization program situation, Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell has charged 24 of the people who worked in the program with welfare fraud. He's also investigating Street and others involved. The editorial also presents some of the views of those who wrote to him, saying he will forward them on to Governor Dick Thornburgh, and update the audience on what the governor does or does not do.

headline: null
abstract: Cartoon with a sign that says "Welcome to Centralia" with the caption Eventually it will burnout- US Interior Secretary James Watt

headline: Lederer constituents have mixed emotions
abstract: The resignation of US House Representative Raymond F. Lederer (D-PA) has left constituents with mixed emotions and opened the door for candidates eager to replace him, despite chances his district will be eliminated through reapportionment. Lederer was convicted in the FBI's Abscam investigation, and said he will resign May 5 rather than risk a House vote to expel him. Governor Dick Thornburgh must set a date for a special election to fill Lederer's seat.

headline: Voter turnout low, may be less than 50%
abstract: Voter turn out was so slow this afternoon that it's likely that less than 50 per cent of people voted.  Average voter turn out during an off election year is usually about 61 per cent.  The article details the races so far.

headline: Pennsylvanians Gird for Battle Over budget Woes
abstract: The article describes the budget problems in Pennsylvania and Governor Thornburgh's attempts to deal with them.  He believes in cutting the budget and tax cuts which will allow private enterprise to take over.  The article details his plans in depth including federal reductions and needed legislation.

headline: Allegheny General picks new director
abstract: Allegheny General Hospital chose John H. Westerman to be the new director of the hospital.  The article details Westerman's history and career.

headline: Teachers criticize state plan
abstract: The Allegheny Intermediate Unit (AIU) Education Association criticized Education Secretary Robert Scanlon's plan to have money for AIU go directly to the school school district rather than to AIU.  AIU deals with handicapped and gifted children

headline: Solar cells spark interest
abstract: The research into solar power through photovoltaic cells is growing, although the Reagan administration's budget cuts would put a hold on more development. Although too costly for homeowners, the technology is being explored by many companies and is starting to expand in Europe and Japan, and could lead to a reduction in the national dependence on foreign oil.

headline: Building more prisons no way to fight crime
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh has been talking as if adding more prison cells will solve the issue of rising crime. The opinion author believes that this will eventually lead to even more criminals. Both the state and federal levels are calling for more prisons. If money is taken away from welfare to prisons it will cause more desperate crime and more prisoners for those cells.

headline: Justices uphold Pa. fine
abstract: PA officials must continue paying a $10,000 daily fine for defying a judge's ruling to speed up the release and relocation of the mentally disabled residents of the PennHurst Center, the US Supreme court decided. The PA Welfare Department claims it cannot spend any more money to comply with the court order.

headline: null
abstract: Striking up a conversation with band leader Fred Warring is PA Senator John Heinz. Warring, who recently celebrated his 65th year in show business, was on Capitol Hill in Washington to receive yet another tribute.

headline: Lederer Resigns as 3rd District Rep
abstract: US Representative Raymond Lederer (D-PA), involved in an FBI's Abscam investigation of bribery, announced he would give up his US House seat May 5, 15 months after his conviction. PA Governor will have to set the date for a special election to fill the remaining year-and-a-half of Lederer's term.

headline: Voters Figure to Keep Leonard in Control
abstract: Thomas A. Leonard retained his position of Philadelphia City Controller, beating Charles Bush and Lee Frissell in yesterday's election.  The article details the campaign between the three and Leonard's history.

headline: PSEA says state budget will cost $3 million here
abstract: Residents of Armstrong County will pay more in property taxes in 1981-82 under the Governor's proposal to under fund schools, according to the PA State Education Association. Under the subsidy law, the state is required to pay 50 percent of all costs of basic instruction in the local school districts, but Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal calls for a 41.5 percent state share.

headline: Bad Prescription
abstract: A suggested cutback in state mental health and mental retardation facilities by Governor Thornburgh is considered a bad idea by the author, who states a lack of medical facilities to care for the patients and an increased cost to tax payers.

headline: Teachers hit Thornburgh education budget
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposed budget increases education subsidies by $50 million, but teacher union officials feel this is not enough.  Because of inflation, the officials feel that the state is decreasing its role in funding education and placing more of a burden on tax payers through local property taxes.  Governor Thoronburgh increased funding for university education by 5.4 percent

headline: Spare us TMI bill, customers ask
abstract: Utility customers have asked an administrative law judge to spare them from shouldering any of the cost of cleaning up the Three Mile Island nuclear plant. They claim they are not to be held responsible for the accident.

headline: Can Press Suit on More 'Yard Time'; State Prisoners Exercise rights, Win Legal Battle
abstract: Eleven maximum security inmates won a Commonwealth Court decision allowing them to continue their legal battle for more exercise time.  The inmates of B-block at Huntingdon state Prison sued the state, complaining they were entitled to at least two hours daily in the exercise yard.  Instead, they said they are getting only about 10 minutes a day.  The court overruled arguments by the Bureau of Corrections that the decision about exercise time is discretionary and not subject to a court order known as mandamus.  In their suit, the inmates are asking Commonwealth Court to issue a mandamus order, directing prison officials to comply with the two-hour minimum outlined in state law.

headline: Legal unit may curtail class-action suits
abstract: PA Legal Services, which faces a funding crisis, will likely curtail the number of controversial class-action suits its affiliates file. Future decisions on class-action suits will be made in Harrisburg. And negotiations will be encouraged as an alternative to filing suit.  The new guidelines for the 20 poverty-lawyer units in the state resulted from a year-long project.

headline: null
abstract: A photograph of Nicholas Stampone of Philadelphia taking oath of office in the special election of the state Senate seat of Joseph Smith. The caption state: "Sworn In: Nicholas Stampone, left, of Philadelphia, takes oath of office Monday in the Capitol after having won a special election for the state Senate seat of Joseph Smith, who was elected to Congress. The oath is administered by Commonwealth Court President Judge James Crumlish as Lt. Gov. William Scranton III watches."

headline: Legislative shuffling
abstract: The editorial argues that as PA legislators are redistricting state assembly seats, Bucks County should benefit from the process. It is expected to have an additional House seat, which the editorial argues could mean better representation and more political clout in Harrisburg. Conversely, Philadelphia, which has experienced a population decrease, should lose a seat.

headline: Voting 'Very Light' Here
abstract: A low turnout was reported as PA voters nominated candidates for seven appellate court seats, hundreds of local court seats and thousands of county and municipal offices, including mayor of Pittsburgh. The polls opened at 7 a.m. and will close at 8 p.m. The major battle in Pittsburgh features Mayor Richard Caliguiri's drive to seize the Republican nomination from GOP candidate Fred Goehringer.

headline: Reaganomics criticized at governors' meet
abstract: The governors of Pennsylvania, New York, and New Jersey met to discuss the regional economy.  The governor's made recommendations about how to improve the economy and were worried that President Reagan's economic plans will only send the region into a deeper recession.  The article details the events of the conference and the recommendations.

headline: Blue Cross to follow Blue Shield in seeking '65-special' rate hike
abstract: Blue Cross of Greater Philadelphia will file for what could be a whopper of a rate increase for the 344,604 area elderly residents who subscribe to its 65-special plan. PA Blue Shield has asked for a 28 percent increase. They are sold as supplements to Medicare.

headline: Teachers mass at N. Philadelphia school
abstract: In the greatest display of zeal so far in the month-long school strike, more than 1,000 teachers, joined by leaders of some of the city's biggest labor unions, disrupted the school day at North Philadelphia high school yesterday morning before marching to City Hall where they demanded to see Philadelphia Mayor Green. The board of education decided not to ask for a postponement of a court order requiring the teachers to return to work on Monday.

headline: Specter Hits Big Oil's Energy Diversification
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter (R. Pa.) criticized the tendency of oil companies to buy up coal and other natural resource companies, which he says drives up prices and reduces competition.  He urged the federal government to enforce antitrust laws .

headline: Can't prevent all suicides, prison officials says
abstract: Coroner Sanford Edberg said the state has legal and moral obligations to monitor prisoners who have suicidal tendencies or need medical care. It is impossible to prevent a prisoner from committing suicide if they really want to do it.

headline: Letters To The Editor: Why Our State Has A Welfare Mess
abstract: The author believes that the welfare problem is based on fraud that does not have harsh penalties in the court system.  The author believes that many people simply don't want to work and will continue to accept benefits as long as they're offered.

headline: null
abstract: Editorial cartoon, which has a large airplane that has "THORNBURGH CAMPAIGN" written on the side of it and "GREEN CRITCHLOW" on the nose of the airplane.  One of the pilots says to the other, "OK BILL- START THE ENGINES."

headline: Legislators favor 'restraining' courts
abstract: U.S. Attorney General William French Smith warned the federal courts on October 29 about "constitutionally dubious and unwise intrusions upon the legislative domain." On the same day the House State Government Committee released for a floor vote a bill which challenges a federal court consent decree requiring the state police to hire and promote racial quotas. The report-out of HB 1822 represents the third time this year that the House will have considered legislation to challenge federal court actions viewed by critics as intruding into the constitutional responsibilities of the Legislature.

headline: Walker's district may absorb all of Lebanon Co.
abstract: If PA's upcoming congressional reappointment follows lines recommended to legislative leaders this week, US Representative Robert Walker's 16th District will include all of Lebanon County, take in two Dauphin County townships, Derry and Conewago, and shift into Chester County's southwest corner, to the Oxford area. Details of the proposed plan were approved by a majority of the Commonwealth's 25-member congressional delegation.

headline: Reagan's Style: Concentrating on the 'Big Picture'
abstract: Looks at President Reagan's negotiating style. Reagan's approach is to look at the big picture while letting subordinates handle the necessary legislative horse trading. Therefore, Reagan chose to capitalize on his popularity and speech-making ability by addressing the nation on budget reductions and tax relief rather than social security issues.

headline: Britain ponders easing of mental patient law
abstract: The British government is thinking about changing a law that allow mental patients to be held without recourse to the law.  The change stems from a man who was denied his right to challenge his detention and later died.

headline: Teachers poised to strike today
abstract: Philadelphia Federation of Teachers seeing no hope of averting a school strike that picket lines would go up at 5 a.m. The official start of staff preparation for classes that are scheduled to begin Thursday.

headline: Spreading the Cost Of Atomic Cleanup
abstract: The author responses to a letter about who should pay for the Three Mile Island (TMI) Nuclear Power Plant cleanup after an accident in 1978.  The author feels that the parent company of TMI cannot afford to pay for the entire cleanup and so the federal government must step in to help.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Depicts three criminals writing a letter.  The letter states: "Dear Senator, Our group wants you to know know that you should vote against the governers [sic] plan for more prison cells in our fair state!"

headline: Local officials learn about new block grant program
abstract: The wheels of the new state block grant program are in motion, but no one's quite sure of what impact the Reagan administration’s  new program will have on social and human services.  Members of Governor Thornburgh's Council on Human Development met to establish clear lines of information on the Reagan Administration's planned block grant procedure.  A contingent of 14 Armstrong County representatives were among an audience of more than 250 persons who listened as the seven member panel outlined the basic procedure of the block grant proposal.

headline: (Cartoon) "You're On, Ron. . . Don't Muff It Like the Last Guy"
abstract: Cartoon depicting a stage with an empty spotlight and Ronald Regean on the side of the stage.

headline: Legislators return, GOP takes control
abstract: Republicans took control of the state General Assembly for the first time in 13 years.  Governor Dick Thornburgh is set to address the General Assembly and will stress the need to avoid a tax increase and push the legislature to vote for a percentage tax on gas.  Legislators are expected to elect Senator Henry Hager (R-Lycoming), as president pro tempore, while Representative Matthew Ryan (R-Delaware) is expected to be selected as speaker of the House.

headline: Walter Williams Wants to Overthrow the Welfare State
abstract: A group of black Conservatives met in a conference arranged by Dr. Henry Lucas, the first black member of the Republican National Committee, and formed the Coalition for Social Change. Walter Williams, the coalition's chairman for the economic advisory board espouses his views on welfare and socio-economic advancement. Among some of his views are that minimum wage results in fewer jobs for black teenagers, thus minimum wage should not be sought and that civil rights organizations are outdated, chained to liberals and labor unions and detached from the needs of their constituency.

headline: Recession deepens; state's job losses cited
abstract: The Commerce Department reported that spending on new construction fell 1.7 per cent in October, after steadily declining for the past eight months.  Most economist agree that the country is in a recession and cite problems with job loss.  The article outlines the statistics for both private business and government agencies.

headline: County proves thefts from Kane patients
abstract: Allegheny County Police are investigating thefts from the private accounts of patients at the John J. Kane Hospital. A routine audit of the elderly's accounts in the long-term care facility found that funds were taken between December 1980 and February 1981.

headline: The district will open 7 more schools
abstract: Philadelphia School District has already opened 9 schools despite the teachers strike will open 7 more next week. The school district also modified its request for an injunction to halt the strike, dropping the contention that the walkout is endangering the health and welfare of the community.

headline: State energy policy
abstract: The editorial board writes that it requires careful planning to ensure ample energy for the future. PA has already planned for the next 25 years. PA Governor Thornburgh has placed energy conservation, regeneration and development high on his list or priorities. He wants this plan to be an insurance policy against being caught short with regard to energy supplies.

headline: Casting judgment on the court
abstract: Earlier this year, Dragonetti single-handedly convinced the Legislature to pass a bill abolishing the centuries old ban against countersuits when a person feels he's been wrongly sued but was not imprisoned or had not suffered a loss of property as a result of such a suit.  Dragonetti had filed a countersuit against Girard Bank, which had named him a suit to reclaim a bad debt from a textile machinery firm.  He claimed he had been wrongfully sued because he only did public relations work for the firm and was not an officer or employee.

headline: Local Social Consciousness
abstract: The author opines that local communities do not want to help the less fortunate, despite President Reagan's and Governor Thornburgh's urging that welfare should be dealt with at a local level.  The author feels that people just don't car about their neighbors anymore.

headline: "Your Ship, Captain"
abstract: Cartoon depicts Ronald Reagan waist deep in water in a sailor's uniform with a ship's steering wheel.  It implies that his ship is sinking.

headline: Let the election stand; Errors were not decisive
abstract: A panel of three suburban judges, sitting as a special tribunal to hear a Philadelphia election dispute, has overreacted to errors in voting machine labeling by ruling 2-1 that the election results for Common Pleas Court in the Democratic primary on May 19 should be thrown out.  The 11 Democratic candidates who won nominations in the race will appeal to the Supreme Court, which should overrule and let the election stand.

headline: Ward leaders endorse Jamieson
abstract: Former Philadelphia Common Pleas president judge D. Donald Jamieson was elected chairman of Philadelphia's Republican Party.  He took over for William A. Meehan, who stepped down to become dputy prothonotary for Common Pleas Court, and appointed Joseph Duda to be the party's executive director.

headline: Regional income tax vs. sales tax
abstract: The author details the merits of the Pennsylvania Tax Commission's recommendation of a 0.2 per cent surcharge on the income tax versus a sales tax increase.  The taxes are needed to support SEPTA, and the author feels that the surcharge tax is better for the state

headline: Debate
abstract: Abortion is a matter for a woman and her doctor to resolve. Moralists and politicians have no place in this matter. The clinical influence of health professionals is largely ignored.

headline: The final test: A failure of leadership
abstract: In November 1978, the principal of Huey Elementary School, Donald Rouse, was charged with pilfering $3,500 from the candy fund, money that the children raised through candy sales to pay for extra equipment and special programs. Rouse admitted taking the money after an audit turned up the shortage, but he said he'd planned to use it "as a loan and replace the monies as the need arose."

headline: State must learn when not to regulate utilities
abstract: Price controls not only led the public into a dependency on imported oil, they were also responsible for the natural gas shortages in the winter of 1977 and gasoline shortage in the summer of 1979.  The article goes into detail about how regulating utilities does not always help the state.

headline: Cell doors closing on so many prisoners
abstract: Lawyer Robert Landis contends that two events show a crisis of the prison systems of Philadelphia and PA. The first is the state Legislature disapproval of the PA Commission on Sentencing's proposed guidelines for criminal courts, and the second is a specific ruling that overcrowding of prisons in Philadelphia, a problem at the national level as well, violates prisoner's rights. The only recent initiatives for reform of the system have come from the private sector, but the author questions whether the business leaders should take on additional public responsibility when political leaders falter.

headline: Manderino Upset About Business
abstract: State Representative Jim Manderino feels that Gov. Thornburgh is helping business at the expense of welfare programs.  The editors feel Representative Manderino is missing the point that businesses employ people and innately  promote social welfare.  The editors agree with Gov. Thornburghs decision to subsidize the railroads and lambaste Representative Manderino for his "socialistic" ideas.

headline: 11 Phila. Common Pleas
abstract: 27 candidates running for a judgeship on the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas are briefly reviewed. The judges will serve in the trial division, family court division, or the orphans court division. The term is for 10 years and the annual salary between $55,000 and $57,500.

headline: Letters to the editor: Sky-high state pensions not common
abstract: Much has been written recently about the State Employees Retirement System. Invariably the articles cite those examples in which a person will have more income after retirment than while working.  Or they focus on the $50,000 a year retiree.  As of the end of 1980, the number of retirees and beneficiaries totaled 48,783, with an average montly retirment benefit of $352.  A little arithmetic will show that for every retiree receiving $4,100 a month, a sizable number would have to be receiving less than the #352 average to balance the figure out.

headline: Watch out when block grants fall
abstract: A quiet battle is under way in Washington over the form future federal aid should take when being distributed to state and local governments and non-profits groups. Administration forces would like to provide lump sums to the states in the form of block grants, because they believe it would restore a balanced form of federalism. US Senator Arlen Specter thinks this makes sense.

headline: Rep. Atkinson Gets Informed Oval Office 'Wooing'
abstract: The White House granted Aliquippa US Representative Gene Atkinson a semi-private Oval Office meeting, in an attempt to win over the PA Democrat during a US House budget vote this week. Atkinson used the situation to voice his concerns over President Reagan's administration's proposed liquidation of Conrail.

headline: Flu bugs will have less bite
abstract: PA Health Department officials are expecting a return of three influenza viruses that dominated the commonwealth's flu season last year, but are predicting a milder outbreak. They are anticipating the same viruses as last year so they don't expect to see very much flu.

headline: The people united: We can keep the schools open
abstract: The city's school system is about to fail again.  Judge Harr A. Takiff's appointment of a conservator might be helpful, but it is clear that the Board of Education, the Philadelphia federation of Teachers and city and state administrators are preparing to defend their positions rather than work towards reasonable solutions.  It is time for parents of public school children and all interested taxpayers to step forward and demand better treatment.  If schools are closed on September 10, thereafter insist on a continuing share in their management.  To help offset the devastating effects of a strike, parents must demand that Superintendent Michael Marcase keep schools unlocked and staffed with sufficient custodial and secretarial help to allow volunteers to set up daycare operations.

headline: Steam pip cracks in 'good' reactor dim TMI's hopes
abstract: The undamaged reactor at the Three Miles Island nuclear plant could restart by next March if newly discovered stem pip cracks are sealed quickly, reports the Nuclear Regulatory Commission staff.  The article continues to explain Nuclear Regulatory Commission's plan and optimism in opening the reactor.

headline: Charges At Jail House Rock Cambria Court; Judge Urges Profe Into Use of Inmates' Money
abstract: In a highly unusual move, a Common Please Court judge here is urging a grand jury investigation into allegations that the warden of the Cambria County Jail has been involved in a number of questionable practices, including the misuse of a special inmates' funds and using the inmates to work on his home.  Judge Caram J. Abood's call for an investigation came after the district attorney's office announced it would not seek any criminal prosecutions in the case, which has rocked Cambria County.  Normally, grand jury investigations are initiated by prosecutors rather than judges, but Abood said he felt compelled to speak out because of the serious nature of the charges.

headline: Measure Would Take 'Employables' Off Rolls:  Carlisle Legal Aid Agency Hits Welfare Reform Bill
abstract: A bill introduced in the state house that would deny public assistance to anyone who is "employable" drew criticism from Legal Services, Inc. of Carlisle.  Legal Services says this bill would take "employable" people off welfare before they are able to find a job and thus, create more unemployment and poverty.

headline: 11 Phila. Common Pleas: LWV
abstract: The reviews of court candidates was compiled by the League of Women Voters of Philadelphia and by local leagues in several counties. The material was submitted by candidates, who were asked to fill out a questionnaire. The purpose of the LWV is to promote active and informed participation of citizens in government.

headline: Lewis firm on air dismissals
abstract: Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis states that only a court order could force the US government to hire back the 12,000 air traffic controllers slated to lose their jobs due to their week-long illegal walkout. He emphasizes that the government still considers the strike by the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization to be over and will now mover to rebuild the system.

headline: Welcome Civic Center pledge
abstract: The editors agree with Governor Thornburgh's commitment to see the completion of the Erie Civic Center.  They are also impressed with gasoline tax proposal and the privatizing of state liquor stores.  They congratulate the governor on his work.

headline: Repayment of bonds 'fairer way' sought in Pennsylvanian's bill
abstract: U.S. Representative James Coyne introduced legislation that would require the U.S. Treasury to repay long term government bonds in dollars equal to the value of the note, accounting for inflation.  The article gives an example of how the legislation would work.  Coyne states that investors would earn more interest if bonds were calculated in this way.

headline: Health Secretary Seeks Approval Of State Projects
abstract: State Health Secretary Dr. H. Arnold Muller called for the US Department of Health and Human Services to approve seven health projects. The projects include a new phone system for the Harrisburg Hospital, and additional beds for the proposed Attleboro Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in York, both projects previously approved by regional health planning agencies.

headline: Thornburgh attacks PSEA as unethical
abstract: Governor Thornburgh  lashed out against the Pennsylvania State Education Association (PSEA) for what he called unethical lobbying for higher school subsidies.  PSEA's plans to meet with the legislature was called a "shadow government of special interest" by the Governor.  He also named other groups he believes are acting unethically.

headline: Stockman Opposes Met-Ed Aid
abstract: At a meeting with a group of House members, Budget Director David Stockman opposes federal aid for the cleanup of Three Mile Island Unit 2. Stockman said he will study a proposal to partially fund the decontamination and costs of future nuclear accidents through an insurance fund financed by utilities, but believes the operator of Unit 2, Metropolitan Edison Company, should pick up the cost, even if it means bankruptcy.

headline: Chesco unit sued over sewer costs
abstract: Two Devon homeowners contended in a lawsuit filed in Chester County Court that they were among more than 2,000 customers who were being overcharged by a total of more than $500,000 for municipal sewer service. The suit alleged that the Easttown Township Municipal Authority had illegally overpaid Lisbon Contractors $534,108.35.

headline: Medicaid sterilization system faulted
abstract: Amid the Reagan administration's attack on federal regulations, a non-profit health group says one kind of paperwork should be preserved: reports designed to protect low-income patients from undergoing coerced or hasty sterilization.  Citing previously unreleased federal audits of Medicaid programs, the Health Research Group said 10 states including Pennsylvania have distressingly failed to comply with seven-year-old safeguards for patients.  In Pennsylvania's case, the Health Research Group's findings were limited to lax or improper reporting, rather than actual abuse of patients' rights.

headline: 19 Splits
abstract: The state constitution demands that legislative districts be compact and contiguous that they be nearly as equal in population as practicable, and no municipality shall be divided unless absolutely necessary. They knew local government would suffer from divided representation. Surely the commission can see the results of its narrow results and change the division.

headline: Lewis to push Scranton
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III has planned a major fundraiser on September 23,  for is campaign for Republican Nomination to a second term. US Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis will be attending and campaigning for Scranton.

headline: Wenger Farm Bill Is Been Signed by Gov.
abstract: null

headline: Sagging housing costs make dent
abstract: Inflation at both the local and national levels slowed dramatically last month, showing the effects of a downturn in home purchases. US Labor Department said that the Consumer Price Index, which measures prices of most goods and services, rose .4 percent last month, down from increases of 1.2 in Sept. and .8 percent in Aug. In Philadelphia price rose just .1 percent last month. It was the lowest one-month increase in three years.

headline: House votes bill to replace coroner
abstract: The Pennsylvania House voted to replace the Allegheny County coroner with an appointed medical examiner, in order to remove the position from politics.  The Senate will vote on it next.  The article outlines the details of the bill and its pros and cons.

headline: The wet cement is hardening
abstract: The opposing sides in the Erie school contract (Pennsylvania) dispute are backed into a bargaining corner over health insurance coverage. The 14,000 public school students have missed 16 days of school since Tuesday. By this time in the bargaining process, parties to the dispute will be approaching the point where it will be impossible to meet Pennsylvania's 180-day requirement for a full school year. Rationale for the dispute occurred when the school board signed a two year contract for Alpha Health Care coverage for the 800 teachers in the school system. The change in coverage from Pennsylvania Blue Cross Blue Shield to Alpha was a contract violation and constituted a lockout.

headline: Stop Delaying TMI Clean-up
abstract: The author of the letter argues against the litigation on the General Public Utility and how it's delaying the clean-up of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant, threatening to sue if it can be proven that his tax money is being spent on the litigation. The writer argues the delaying tactics are far more dangerous than the actual burn-out.

headline: Children Adrift/The foster-care system: Part 3: Children's aid group denies adoption bid
abstract: Note:  This is third in a continuing series on foster care in Philadelphia. The article chronicles "Dwight" and teenager in the foster care system, who was going to be adopted until the state turned the potential parent down, stating that Dwight was not ready for a permanent home.  The article details the potential parent's quest to adopt Dwight and the systems attempts to block the adoption.

headline: No welfare checks will go out Monday
abstract: No state welfare checks will be mailed on Monday. PA's Welfare Department is out of money to pay cash grants and the General Assembly has delayed action on a deficiency appropriations bill to fund the cash grant program. It will not affect the state's food stamp and medical assistance programs.

headline: 1981 PNPA Convention
abstract: Convention schedule and guests are highlighted.

headline: Lewis turning over memo on Dennis
abstract: State Senator H. Craig Lewis said he would turn over to state and federal prosecutors a memorandum dated November 20, another supposed piece of evidence backing his claim that state Community Affairs Secretary Shirley Dennis had rushed through a federally funded weatherization contract without proper approval and documentation. The memo from Greg Landis, fiscal officer in the department's Bureau of Community Energy, expressing concern to the chief of the bureau's fiscal management section, will be turned over to the state Attorney General and a US Attorney. The senator had previously supplied both with documents indicating Dennis signed the contract before her counsel, comptroller, and bureau director put their signatures on it.

headline: Westmoreland
abstract: In the May 19 primary election, five of 12 judge candidates remained in Westmoreland County. The party lineup in November will now list Robert Garland and Robert Rial on the Republican ballot against Donetta Ambrose and Bernard Scherer on the Democratic ballot, with Judge Dan Ackerman, appointed by Governor Dick Thornburgh, on both ballots.

headline: Sen. Street's records sought in tax case
abstract: The tax returns of PA Senator T Milton Street were ordered subpoenaed by PA's Attorney General in a new effort to collect $31,559 in state sales taxes and interest owed by the former street vendor. Street cannot be held criminally liable because of the statute of limitations has run out. The tax bill has doubled, because of interest and penalties for failure to pay up in time.

headline: Kane Hospital May Need Private Donations
abstract: Private donations may be necessary to help Allegheny county shoulder its $42 million burden of replacing Kane Hospital. The county failed to convince the PA Welfare Department to hike its $22,000 per bed limit on construction costs.

headline: Thornburgh heats fight with PSEA
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh, in a meeting yesterday with Pittsburgh local township officials, warned the officials that they would be pressured to raise taxes from special interest lobbyists. He was making reference to the Pennsylvania State Education Association's campaign to obtain 50 percent state financing of basic instruction for local school districts. While the PSEA has accused the governor of reneging on his 1978 election campaign promise, the governor defended himself as not being on an anti-PSEA crusade. He is battling a small clique in the PSEA that is aggressively campaigning, in his view, to feather the nest of its leaders more than trying to help local education.

headline: Strip Mine Fee
abstract: Pennsylvania coal operators will now have to pay $50 per acre for surface mining permits. This is supposed to raise $1 million for land restoration as the state has up to 25,000 acres of new land and restripping of old land started each year. The trade-off is that the Department of Environmental Resources is lowering the bonding rate from $4000 to $3000 an acre, with a minimum of $10,000 bond that any of the 1000 operators must initially take and forfeit if they do not clean up after their mining. The Thornburgh Package of 1980 was another advance, with its stipulations for pre-mining and public notification, the minimum $10,000 bonding and identification of coal company management to avoid the fly-by-night operators.

headline: City gangs quiet, but old tensions remain
abstract: 30 to 40 teenagers a year used to die due to gang violence. Pressure from the community and increased efforts by the city resulted in a drop in gang violence to only 2 in 1980 and 1 in 1981. Tensions are still there and teens are still joining them.

headline: Not all the poor are on welfare
abstract: The author explains that after being exposed to low-income neighborhoods in Philadelphia, he realizes that the Reagan Administration's notion that social services are extraneous and provided to people who are lazy and inept is an insult to Philadelphia's and America's poor. He argues that there is an unawareness of a large number of poor families, and that a significant number of low-income Americans who deserve and need assistance are choosing not to take any.

headline: 2 in western Pa. win nomination for high court
abstract: Common  Please Court Judge Salvatore Farino and District Attorney Robert Colville, both of Allegheny County, won the Democratic nominations for the state Supreme Court. State Representative William Hutchinson of Schuylkill County and law-and-order Judge James McDermott of Philadelphia won the Gop nominations.

headline: Lieberth gets job charting block grants; Lieberth gets block-grants post
abstract: null

headline: Why no one can win this one... and why part-timers should be hired
abstract: The editors opine why the Philadelphia mass transit strike has no winners because many people have had to spend more money to get to work, the strikers are not being paid, and the strike has only made government officials angry,  The editors feel the answer to the strike is to hire more part time employees to defer costs and union influence.

headline: Senate GOP snubs Thornburgh on tax
abstract: PA State Senate Republicans approved a bill to postpone business tax breaks until 1983.  Governor Thornburgh had wanted the tax breaks to take effect this year.  The article details the various bills that will be voted on both in the House and the Senate.

headline: Lab directors send work to own firm
abstract: In just 13 years Clinical Pathology Facility Incorporated has grown from a small operation with a handful of employees to one of the biggest and most respected laboratories based in this region.  It is a business that even the most astute entrepreneur would be pressed to imitate.  The laboratory handles work that is too complex, uncommon, or expensive for hospital laboratories to complete and since the mid-1970s the facility has fulfilled a role as an important resource for many Western Pennsylvania hospitals.

headline: Thornburgh Hit In Special-Ed Fight
abstract: The author cites three items that were not reported in an article about a meeting regarding Governor Thornburgh's Special Education changes; thanking the organizer, Ronald Wegert, that only two of the nine special education centers in Allegheny County were represented at the meeting, and that the Governor's proposal is only an attempt to shift the tax burden from the state to local communities.

headline: Suit involves intricate procedures:  TMI claimants face delays
abstract: Settlement of the Three Mile Island class action law suit will be delayed.  The claimants claim to have suffered losses from businesses closed down and families moved due to the nuclear accident at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in 1979

headline: Clemency For Cons A Thing Of Christmas Past
abstract: The State Bureau of Corrections stated that judges are no longer reducing the jail terms of those convicted of minor crimes so that they can be home for Christmas.  The reason judges are no longer reducing sentences for Christmas is because of public pressure to not seem lenient on criminals.  The article details how the judges and parole board work to reduce jail terms.

headline: Open letter to Governor
abstract: The author suggests that Governor Thornburgh employ the 90,000 people he wants to take of welfare, by the cultivation of alcohol through vegetable matter.  The author believes that the need for alcohol as fuel and cleaning fluid is unending.

headline: 27 Governors Seek Democrats' Gains
abstract: The Democratic Governors Conference raised $104,000, its first claim to any operating funds, from a $500-a-couple brunch at the Sands Horel in Atlantic City, the idea of looking to Democratic state organizations for leadership appeared to have gained support among national party spokesmen. This event was supposed to lace the responsibility for leading a democratic comeback squarely on the democratic governors' shoulders since the Democrats lost both the White House and the Senate.

headline: Life for a riverfront tomb
abstract: The Penn's Landing Museum built by the state as a gift to Philadelphia for the nation's Bicentennial in 1976, was never given to the city and has stood vacant five years with no state funding for operations. Now it looks as though it will be opened at last for Philadelphia's Tercentennial in 1982. Better late than never.

headline: Wilburn: PHEAA Pushed for West Shore Site Over Downtown
abstract: PA State Budget and Administration Secretary Robert Wilburn has accused the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency of aggressively pursuing a West Shore site for future headquarters when a number of downtown Harrisburg alternatives may have been as feasible. Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration wants PHEAA to be in Harrisburg. The agency's director, Kenneth Reeher, claims it will save taxpayer's money if it purchases the Liebman site on the West Shore, rather than rent the available office buildings in downtown Harrisburg.

headline: Specter Hears Budget Concerns
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter invited several community leaders and officials to discuss concerns about budget cuts that were proposed by President Reagan.  Teacher, miners and labor leaders attended to voice there concerns

headline: Legislator sees little hope to save Locust Mountain
abstract: Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court refuses to issue an order saving Locust Mountain State Hospital. Representative Edward Lucyk states his dismay and said that they have more or less exhausted every piece of legal recourse. Judge John MacPhail stated that the parties seeking to save the hospital had not proved that the state's closure of the facility will cause immediate and irreparable harm.

headline: Thornburgh Socks Pupils, Taxpayers
abstract: The author of the letter, Deer Lakes Area School Board president Thomas DeMartini, pleads for Governor Dick Thornburgh to reconsider his budget for education, which he contends does not consider children the nation's greatest asset. He argues for a state income-tax increase or a tax on refinery production as a viable revenue alternative to raising property taxes or gutting the schools of valuable programs.

headline: TMI Rally Gains Labor's Support
abstract: Doctor Sternglass, a University of Pittsburgh radiology professor, joined a panel of organizers pushing for a heavy turnout Saturday at a Capitol rally marking the second anniversary of the Three Mile Island accident. The professor believes radiation has likely caused more infant deaths, a claim denied by the state's Health Department which says there is no relation between the accident and infant deaths. Eleven labor unions are expected to participate in the rally.

headline: Closing loopholes in jail sentences
