abstract: The editorial argues that it seems like Governor Dick Thornburgh wants to get tough with convicted criminals by closing the loopholes in sentencing procedures. In a proposal that will be submitted to the legislature, he proposes replacing the current parole system with fixed, firm sentences so that a sentence given is a sentence served, and the building of an additional 2,500 jail cells to prevent overcrowding.

headline: Our Ideas:  We're Overtaxed for Welfare
abstract: The editors state that Pennsylvania spends more per person on welfare than any other state and feel that eligibility guidelines need to be changed.  The editors support Governor Thornburgh's proposal to take 68,000 "employable" people off welfare and lambaste democratics for not supporting it.

headline: 3 Penna. men are charged with bribery
abstract: A borough councilman from Exeter, PA. and two other Luzerne County men were arrested Friday and charged with trying to bribe a Wyoming area School Board member. These three men offered school board member, Walter Placek, assurances that his wife would not lose her job at the count nursing home is he would provide a key vote to fire the superintendent and other school officials.

headline: Lights---action---Dick Thornburgh!
abstract: Briefly recounts Thornburgh's busy travel plans that indicate he will be running for reelection.

headline: Wilkinson is confirmed for Supreme Court seat
abstract: Judge Roy Wilkinson, Jr. was confirmed by the state Senate for a seat on the Supreme Court.  The article details the partisan dispute over his nomination by Governor Thornburgh.

headline: State Acts to Wield Budget Ax
abstract: The Thornburgh administration is searching to find spending areas in which more than $100 million can be cut from the current budget in order to adjust to anticipated reductions in federal dollars to the state.  James Wiggins, a spokesman for Governor dick Thornburgh said between $70 million and $100 million may be lost to the state through accelerated depreciation allowances to businesses whose state taxes are geared to federal levies paid.

headline: Letters to the editor; Shifting costs
abstract: The article "Insurance Urged for Mental Ills and Alcoholism" distorts the impression regarding the probable effects of House Bill 665, by reporting only the insurance industry's projections.  The actual estimates indicate that the real value of additional resources that will be devoted to the services will be only a dollar and seventy-five cents per person.

headline: Thornburgh wields bat in education ball game
abstract: The article details detail two of Governor Thornburgh's education proposals.  One would alter how special education is funded in the state, the other would require teachers to have an extra year of college to become licensed.  The article discusses the pros and cons of each.

headline: TMI Repairs: A Study of Delays, Confusion, Red Tape and Turmoil
abstract: The article outlines the status of the Three Mile Island nuclear reactor complex two years after a nuclear accident there.  Decomtamination of radioactive material is still not completely done yet.  The time schedule to do this has been pushed back due to rising costs and lack of funds.  There is clear agency or group that is in charge, causing confusion.  The article details a study of the problems there.

headline: Columnist Ends a Siege
abstract: The mediation of Philadelphia Daily News columnist Chuck Stone helped to peacefully end a five day hostage situation at Graterford State Prison.  The takeover happened after a failed escape attempt and was led by convict Joseph Bowen.

headline: Overpriced food, poor press job cited by conferees on aging
abstract: Conferees at the White House Conference on Aging, state that the food at the conference was overpriced and the lines for the buffets were too long.  The article details conferees complaints ranging from two hour waits for food and having to paid $1.50 for a glass of water.

headline: 3 seeking election to state courts
abstract: Editorial supports three Lehigh County judges who are seeking election to the three Pennsylvania courts.  Maxwell E. Davidson for the State Supreme Court, Donald E. Wieand for the State Superior Court, and Madaline Palladino for State Commonwealth Court.

headline: OIC faces prove of U.S. in renting itself buildings
abstract: The US Department of Education is taking the Opportunities Industrialization Centers of America (OIC) to court. The department contends that the money was improperly spent because the Philadelphia OIC, an affiliate of the national organization, used the funds to pay rent on buildings it had received for free, then sold for $1 to its own subsidiary. The OIC, which already owes the US Department of Labor $1.7 million, says the funds were properly spent.

headline: Wilt Becomes Senator, Giving GOP Control
abstract: Republican Roy Wilt, a veteran state House member, was sworn in April 21st as a member of the PA Senate, replacing Budd Dwyer, who resigned to become state treasurer. The move gives Republicans an uncontested majority of 26 votes and allows the party to make an effort to prevent a rollback in the state personal income tax and corporate net income tax rates. Without the legislation, Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration says it will have to cut $230 million from the governor's $7.6 billion general fund spending blueprint.

headline: State economy static; employment climbs
abstract: The Pennsylvania Business Survey stated that jobs climbed to 5.1 million in Pennsylvania.  The increases were seen in the manufacturing sector.  The article details other findings of the group.

headline: Lloyd's paid-prescription plan fails again
abstract: PA State Senator James Lloyd's proposal to fund a paid-prescription program for the elderly failed for the second time in the Appropriations Committee.  Under his proposal, people over age 65 would only have to pay four dollars per prescription, with the state paying the rest of the cost.  His proposal would be paid for with lottery revenues.

headline: Transfer 8 Teachers, Street Demands
abstract: State Senator Milton Street told the school district that eight teachers must be transferred from Logan Elementary School based on Street's and the Logan Home and School Association's belief that they are incompetent.  Tensions between Logan teachers and parents are intense due to a 50 day teacher strike in which the parents helped non-striking teachers cross the picket line.

headline: TMI staff laxity cited by the NRC
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission found that the Three Mile Island nuclear plant was in violation of regulations at the time  1979 nuclear accident.  They cited the company that owns the plant, Metropolitan Edison, with failure to have on-site data evalutation and failure to train personnell on the behavior of a nuclear plant.  The article details the specific failures

headline: Commissioner Dunn Congratulates New Midstate Troopers
abstract: Photograph with caption saying: "State Police Commissioner Daniel F. Dunn shakes hands with Trooper John R. Brown of Middletown during graduation ceremonies for 36 troopers at the Pennsylvania State Polic Academy in Hershey.  With them are Trooper Michael P. Reiley of Gettsburgh, Pwinner of the Revolver Markmanship Award, and Trooper John K. Thierwechter of Chambersburgh, winner of the American Legion Award.

headline: Pa. starts using its new clout on boarding homes
abstract: The newly formed Personal Care Boarding Home unit of the Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare is trying to close down poorly maintained, dirty and unsafe boarding homes.  A law passed last year requires the Department of Public Welfare to inspect and regulate personal care boarding homes. The article cites the example of a boarding home in Altoona nick-named "Petticoat Junction" and other national examples of boarding home tragedies.

headline: 3 seeking election to state high court fail to detail funds
abstract: Three of the six candidates seeking election to the state Supreme Court in the May 19 primary election have declined to submit statements of their financial interests to the state Ethics Commission. State law does not require candidates and public officials to state annual incomes, only to detail sources of income over $500 for 1980. The remaining 19 candidates for seven vacancies on all three courts filed returns.

headline: Local Democratic Plan Adopted; New City Voting District Takes in Parts of 3 Twps.
abstract: Spilling into its suburbs for the first time, Lancaster city's newly redefined state House district the 96th, now will include portions of Lancaster Manheim and East Lampeter townships.  Some of the added areas have been surrounded by the city district for the past two decades or more, and their inclusion constitutes not only a bowing to logic, but a "victory" for local Democrats.  It was the city Democrats' plan, presented to the state Reapportionment Commission in July, that Chairman James O. Freedman adopted when the plan was unveiled in Harrisburg.

headline: Workfare
abstract: The cartoon depicts a 'Welfare Club' office with a voice coming from the inside saying: "We need a volunteer to go out and see if the 'workfare' bill has passed yet." The building has a sign that reads: "Hear Sen. Street: how to avoid paying fines", referring to State Senator Milton Street (R-Philadelphia).

headline: State Revenue Dept. deluged by tax returns
abstract: The state Department of Revenue received about 250,000 last-minute personal income tax returns on Wednesday, April 15. Another 600,000 pieces of mail would be received by Monday, April 20. Just as quickly as the Revenue Deparment received the money, the Treasury Department had it invested, mostly in loans to banks backed by federal treasury notes.

headline: Manor's Future
abstract: Westmoreland County Commissioner Bob Miller has moderated his call to sell the Manor, the region's major geriatrics center, to a management study.  This is far wiser course, but one has to wonder if he does not already suspect the results of such a study.  Miller apparently believes the place is being mismanaged although he is a part of the management.  Manor Administrator Emory DiDonato naturally feels the unit is being operated properly, although he admits cutbacks are possible.  Westmoreland County is contributing #3.2 million to a $13.7 million budget.  This is more than most counties pay in Pennsylvania.

headline: Tuition Protest
abstract: The photograph has a picture of students presenting garbage can lids to Governor Thornburgh aid Alan Rabinowitz to "keep a lid" on state college tution prices.

headline: TMI targets purification for Sept. 1
abstract: Processing of highly radioactive water standing in the basement of the Three Mile Island Unit 2 containment building for 2.5 years is expected to being about September 1.  The submerged demineralizer system, the $10 million treatment plant built to handle the task, is shut down for fine-tuning and modifications after successfully processing 100,000 gallons of moderately radioactive water.  Spokesman states they are hoping to begin moving the fist batch of water from the reactor building to holding tanks the last week of August, but the actual processing is slated to begin September 1.

headline: Computer Crime Hits Midstate
abstract: Computer crimes, the fastest spreading among white-collar crimes, is arriving in Midstate PA. From what area prosecutors can remember, a man from Mechanicsburg will be the first person to be arraigned for crimes involving a computer. The attorney general wants to increase efforts to combat white-collar crime, asking the General Assembly to increase the department's budget. This type of crime is difficult to fight, but can be done with an increased budget and new state laws.

headline: Panel OKs tentative welfare cuts agreement
abstract: A Republican-dominated conference committee has reached an agreement on a bill that cuts over 100,000 people off welfare and makes many of those remaining on the rolls work for their benefits. The article continues to discuss how the welfare program might plan to cut people from receiving aid.

headline: 3 State Agency Heads Named
abstract: Governor Thornburgh nominated three men to fill vacancies in his Cabinet.  Peter S. Duncan for the Department of Environmental Resources, Barry H. Stern as secretary of Labor and Industry, and Robert K. Bloom as secretary of Revenue.  All are now serving in an acting capacity and must be confirmed by the state Senate.  The article details their respective histories.

headline: Lone Montco race shifts voter focus to local contests
abstract: Because there are no exciting elections in Montgomery County this year, focus has shifted to local township and borough elections.  The article details several local races that may be interesting.

headline: Wrong move for Colville
abstract: The editors feel that Allegheny County District Attorney Bob Colville should not have sought election to the state Supreme Court.  They feel he is underqualified serve as a state Supreme Court Judge, although he already announced his candidacy.  They feel it also solidifies County Commissioner Cyril Wecht's claims that Mr. Colville's attempts to prosecute him are a political conspiracy

headline: State tax revenues fall short; Dip $52.9 million below estimates
abstract: The PA Revenue Department reported that tax revenue was lagging $52.9 million below estimated figures.  Economists attribute the shortfall to a sluggish state economy.  This news adds to Governor Thornburgh current budget deficits caused by President Reagan's tax-cut package.  Thornburgh has proposed a 1 per cent across the board budget cut in response to the deficits.

headline: No Rush on Trauma Care
abstract: The editors look at the two sides over the debate of designating hospitals as trauma care centers.  They call for an unbiased assessment of the current quality of care in Lancaster hospitals before rushing to designate trauma care centers.

headline: Tuition raised for Pitt students; Pitt students to pay more for tuition
abstract: University of Pittsburgh undergraduates will pay at least $180 more in tuition next year and students in the most popular programs will pay even more.  Medical students will face the largest tuition hike in the school's history when tuition jumps by 17 percent, which is necessary because the state Legislature has not increase funding to the School of Medicine since 1972.

headline: TMI Worker Hurt in Fall
abstract: Gary Aughinbaugh was hurt after falling off a 12 foot scaffold in a contaminated area of Three Mile Island's nuclear facility.

headline: Council hears Angels' leader bid for recognition by Phila.
abstract: Leader of the Guardian Angels, a town-watch group, Curtis Sliwa asked the Philadelphia city council for help in recruiting people to help them patrol the subway system.  The group of volunteers attempts to prevent crime by getting involved with anyone that appears to be in danger.  They asked the city to provide background checks on any would-be volunteers.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph of Dolly Tunney, who attended the White House Conference on Aging.

headline: 3d Congressional District: Elect David Glancey
abstract: null

headline: 'Long-Term Solution' Is Part of the Problem
abstract: The author opines that a "long-term solution" to the Philadelphia teachers' strike was part of the reason why they were never able to reach a settle.  The author feels that the union, school district and city all had different ideas on what a long-term solution meant.  The author analyzes the negotiations between the groups.

headline: 'Yes' on retention of Nix
abstract: The editors cite a Pennsylvania law that once a judge is elected, a referendum can be held after his or her term to see if voter's want the judge to be retained.  The editors urge voters to retain Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Robert Nix, Jr., and outline his strengths.

headline: State won UC victory but it wasn't cost-free
abstract: This article examines the US Congress' tightening on spending for dozens of programs by passing the reconciliation bill achieving $35 billion in savings over what might have been spent in 1982. Although it was to be a savings bill, the Reagan administration was forced to accept several increases in spending to satisfy various legislators. This looks at the industrialized states, with Pennsylvania as a focus, who have UC funds out of balance, over borrowed, and the repayment program that Pennsylvania now faces. The final UC agreement included a freeze on the penalty tax, giving Pennsylvania a decade or so to pay back UC funds without being penalized. To maintain the freeze Pennsylvania would have to keep up its tax effort on employers and maintain solvency by not raising benefits without raising taxes.

headline: Nursing Home Suit Asks Closing Delay
abstract: The Bethel Park and Convalescent and Nursing Home, run by Vivian Zaleta, has been ordered to shut down due to violations of Health Department regulations.  The families of the patients there are asking for a delay in the closure so they have more time to relocate their family members.  They hope that during the delay someone else will purchase the facility so they don't have to move their family members.

headline: What kind of savings?
abstract: They may have to close down the Neumann School in Frankford for problem children, despite being successful at turning around children. The federal budget cuts cut its entire budget and it does not know where it will get funding.

headline: TMI's financial fallout will need cleaning up, too
abstract: The article details the financial aftermath following the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear accident, how much the federal government is responsible for paying for the clean up and how much TMI's parent company, Metropolitan Edison, is.  The article states that Metropolitan Edison does not have the money to pay for the clean  up, which is causing clean up to go slower.

headline: County Must Represent Its Inmates
abstract: The Commonwealth Court ruled that the public defender in a county must represent an indigent inmate during state parole revocation hearings. The prison in Camp Hill conducts many hearings and the county commissioner Nelson A. Punt said that it would be a financial strain on Cumberland County, as they will have to hire two more full time public defenders.  Critics of the ruling state that it will but undue financial burden on counties in which state correctional facilities are located.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph of William Coombs, who attended the White House Conference on Aging.

headline: 4 Candidates Make Their Cases For Terms On State's Top Court
abstract: The article is comprised of four columns, each one dedicated to one of the four candidates for Supreme Court Justice.  They outline the candidates histories and views.  The candidates are; Bob Colville, Sal Farino, William Hutchinson, and James McDermott.

headline: Lots of candidates and bleary eyes
abstract: PA voters will be confronted with another big ballot when they go to the polls for the municipal election November 3,1981. They will be picking local governments and 7 state judges, vote on retention of other judges, and voice their opinion on five questions relating to bond issues and constitutional amendments.

headline: Yo, Plato
abstract: The School District of Philadelphia is financially so far in the hole it hasn't seen daylight in years. The teacher's union contract has been so etched on because nobody has the money to pay for what they promised. The Philadelphia City Council has to try and make all sides happy, but so far has blown it.

headline: Strong, Prosperous US Wanted, Shuster Finds
abstract: Despite the lashings of big labor, the lamentations of the liberal establishment  over the administration's policy known as Reaganomics, US Rep. Bud Shuster says there is a clear demand for a fiscally sound America. He performed a survey of his district and they supported the economic plan. 89.3% favored cutting spending. Those polled also wanted more benefits.

headline: Of sentencing, clinics and vacancies
abstract: The state House of Representatives voted to reject guidelines for uniform sentencing of criminals, prepared by a special commission on sentencing after almost two years of deliberation. Also, the state Health Department has decided to stop providing special health care facilities for state employees in Harrisburg, although the House has appropriated $100,000 to keep the clinics running. Finally, Republican Roy Wilt has been elected to fill the Senate seat vacated by R. Budd Dwyer, who became the state treasurer.

headline: What Philadelphia needs now is six school board resignations
abstract: The editors feel that six of the remaining board members of the Philadelphia school board should resign.  The district in is debt $73 million.  The editors feel that since the public has lost confidence in these board members, they should resign

headline: TMI's steam, whistling noise called unharmful
abstract: Residents near the Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Plant were told that steam and a whistling noise coming from the plant's boiler were not radioactive.

headline: Crime and the commonwealth
abstract: The editorial argues that Governor Dick Thornburgh and the state legislature talk tough about crime and criminals, but haven't focused very closely on the implications of such talk. The governor has now proposed tougher sentences and called for the creation of new state prison cells. But the editorial questions whether the legislature will recognize that increased toughness on criminals has a price tag, and whether they will approve the money for building more cells.

headline: Poor nations can aid selves, Reagan says
abstract: President Reagan said a propaganda campaign has been launched that would have the world believe the capitalist US is the cause of world hunger and poverty. But he rejected that idea and said the best way for poor countries to achieve prosperity is through free nations boosting their private investment and international trade.

headline: 6 linked to auditor general job-buying scandal
abstract: At least five Pittsburgh-area employees of the Auditor General's Department credited their jobs or promotions to fees paid to a mystery job broker identified as Samuel D. Peters, of Brookline.  Peters was named by John Clark, chief investigator for the Auditor General's Department, and Annette Reiff, director of departmental communications.  The two officials called a press conference to clarify what Reiff said was confusion in the wake of the recent suicide of Lloyd Hickman, who was one of the employees who told Clark he got paid $5,000 for his job and said the broker was Peters.  The statewide investigating grand jury recommended Hickman be prosecuted for perjury because he gave different information in his appearance before the panel; two days later, he was found dead.

headline: Lottery proposed to bail out schools
abstract: State Republican William Rieger (D-Philadelphia) has introduced a bill that would create a Philadelphia Sports Betting Lottery to help fund the city's financially troubled school system. Governor Dick Thornburgh agreed to advance $80 million is subsidies to keep the city's schools running for the remainder of the school year, but additional revenue would be needed next year.

headline: You don't give at some offices
abstract: A staffer in state Senator Milton Street's office has been suspended for raising money for Street to compensate for traffic fines and pay state income taxes. The editorial explains that state senator's offices are not to be used to raise funds for senator's private use. The editorial argues that Senator Street is misusing the PA Senate, and that this is a problem for the Republican Party he represents.

headline: Sworn to House, Smith to vote for Democrats' tax-cut proposal
abstract: After being sworn in as the newest House member, Representative Joseph Smith, promptly declared that he will vote for the Democratic tax-cut proposal offered as an alternative to President Reagan's plan.

headline: Our Readers Write:  Generic Drug Law Violation Overblown
abstract: Letter to the editor from a Rite Aid pharmacist complains that the press has unfairly given Rite Aid a bad name for a minor violation in PA's 1976 Generic Drug Act that requires pharmacist to inform customers that the can get generic, cheaper prescriptions instead of the name brands.

headline: 300 flee chlorine fumes
abstract: About 300 residents were evacuated for several hours early yesterday (August 16, 1981) when a cloud of toxic chlorine fumes swept through their neighborhood, according to fire officials.  The fumes were created by a fire in a nearby barn, where 500 pounds of chlorine was sorted, according to officials of the Franklin County Volunteer Fire Company.  A portion of the Letterkenny Army Depot was also evacuated. Six persons were treated at Chambersburg Hospital and later released after they inhaled the fumes.  Fire officials said the fire broke out at about 1 A.M.  Residents were allowed to return to their homes at about 7 A.M.  The chlorine was used in cleaning swimming pools.

headline: U.S Pledges Aid for 3 Mile Island
abstract: The Reagan administration asked the U.S. Congress for a $123 million appropriation for waste disposal and research costs associated with the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear accident in 1979.  The article details how the administration decided to fund the cleanup.

headline: Crime Breakers Series (Part 1): Citizens Can Do Something About Crime
abstract: The editorial introduces a series of live reports that will run for two weeks, showing how citizens can make a difference in reducing crime. The editorial calls for people to watch so that they can make a difference. Although not all actions will be adopted, the goal is to press these programs on public officials and all people.

headline: Proposed budget slashes aid to retarded
abstract: State public welfare officials say the $12.6 budget cut the welfare budget by $34.2 million and it will hurt the mentally retarded. County welfares will have to shoulder a bigger burden.

headline: 6 school districts still seek contracts
abstract: Six school districts in Allegheny County are approaching the beginning of the school year without teacher contracts.  Both parties at Baldwin-Whitehall held a negotiation session that continued into the late afternoon without a settlement.  Talks are expected to resume shortly.  A spokesman for the Pennsylvania State Education Association said the two parties have inched closer to an agreement.

headline: Lottery Returns $16 Million to LV Economy
abstract: For the fifth consecutive year, the PA Lottery has reported a significant growth in sales receipts from its seven games and subsequent increases in prizes awarded, commissions paid out to retailers and banks, and benefits to the elderly in the form of property tax and rent rebates and inflation dividends. The 1979-1980 fiscal year provided more than $16 million for the local economy of Lehigh and Northampton counties.

headline: Young Blood
abstract: Pennsylvania State Senator James Lloyd Jr., plans to formally announce his candidacy for Pennsylvania. Governor January 2, 1982 for the Democratic nomination in the May primaries. If he does run and win he will be the second youngest governor. Skeptics believe that Lloyd is not running for governor but for something smaller in order to establish his identity around Pennsylvania in order to serve some future political ambition. Lloyd refutes this by discussing the progress he has already made toward his campaign. His platform will focus on economic development and integrity in government.

headline: Tax Panel Proposes Changes For State
abstract: The article details the major recommendations for changes in state in local taxes, presented to Governor Thornburgh by the Pennsylvania Tax Commission.  The article covers state, local, highway, mass transit, and business taxes.

headline: Pa. dental associations accused of fixing fees
abstract: The Pennsylvania Dental Association is being charged with conspiring to fix fees for services reimbursed by insurance companies.  The charges also allege that they tried to keep dentists from using two insurance plans because their reimbursement fees were too low.  The article details the accusations.

headline: A cancellation
abstract: A nuclear plant dangerously close to a major population center gets canceled through the efforts of local citizens against higher electric rates, local citizens against nuclear dangers, environmental groups, and local government. That's what could happen with Limerick here.

headline: U.S. aid for TMI is urged
abstract: A congressional study says that the federal government should help to pay for cleaning up the contaminated nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island.  General Public Utilities Corporation customers could pay for the entire cleanup, but an approach that spreads the burden would be more equitable, the General Accounting Office reported.  The General Accounting Office, the investigative arm of Congress, said in its report that it made more sense to have the federal government, as well as customers, General Public Utilities Company stockholders, the federal government and other electric utilities, share in cleaning up the Pennsylvania reactor.

headline: Crime Check; Limiting Liability; Painting the Town
abstract: Recent Federal Bureau Investigations statistics show that Pittsburgh is still a relatively non-violent place to live, at least in comparison with the largest metropolitan areas in the country.  In 1980, there were 30,399 reports of violent criers in Pittsburgh or 72 reports per 1,000 people.  Pennsylvania state residents who have been injured by defective products may find their abilities to sue for damages severely limited.  Senate Bill 784 contains provisions that would drastically alter a consumer's opportunity to take legal action against a product manufacturer.  Bob Qualters will be moving the Forbes Street Bridge a few blocks north over the summer.  Sometime over the summer, Qualters will begin work on a three-story mural of street-level views of Pittsburgh.

headline: Q. Who pays daily fine of $10,000? A. Pa.
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh has a choice. He must spend either $300,000 or $65,000 per month of taxpayers' money for the court-appointed monitors of the return of Pennhurst residents for the institution to small, supervised community homes for people with mental disabilities. The governor has chosen to pay a penalty of $10,000 per day in fines, $300,000 a month, rather than comply with federal court order. Before the PA Department of Public Welfare has paid out court costs without legislative approval, so they should now.

headline: 666 trial: Ex-stagehand implicates Perry, Plevel
abstract: In front of a Dauphin County Common Pleas Court jury, former television stagehand Fred Luman implicated Nick Perry and Edward Plevel in the state lottery fix trial, and that greed was the undoing of the scheme. The Daily Number drawing was fixed, and resulted in a record payout of $3.5 million, but too many people played heavily on the number, raising suspicions about the drawing.

headline: Lottery Swindlers Get Terms
abstract: Fred Luman and Joseph Bock were both sentenced for 1 to 5 years by Judge William Lipsitt for fixing the Pennsylvania lottery.  The article continues to provide details about the case and sentencing.

headline: A new champion's view of old buildings: Let them be; New fighter sets sights on old buildings
abstract: Larry Tise, 37, a former minister, recently took office as executive director of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission and as the state historic preservation officer.  He is an extremist that believes that all old buildings, particularly districts of old buildings, whether they are historic or not, deserve to be saved.  He feels that historic preservation is a fundamentally conservative movement which, in recent years, has leaned heavily on government regulations.

headline: Tax Plan Introduced By Walker
abstract: U.S. Representative Robert Walker from the 16th district introduced a Republican supply-side anti-recession package in the U.S. House of Representatives which calls for the 1982 and 1983 tax cuts to be moved from July and January. The next round of income tax cuts are presumed to have little positive effect on the economy if they are delayed another nine months. Thus, to achieve a balanced federal budget by 1984, Walker along with 19 co-sponsors introduced legislation to initiate the tax cuts earlier.

headline: Parents of retarded vow to fight Pennhurst decision
abstract: The US Supreme Court on April 20 overturned a federal district judge's ruling ordering the transfer of 1,000 mentally retarded persons from the state-operated Pennhurst Mental Retardation Center in Chester County. This saved the hospital from immediate closing, a goal sought by the PA Association for Retarded Citizens, who prefer community alternatives to such institutions. At a news conference, three parents of retarded children vowed to continue fighting against institutionalization.

headline: A little upstaging on car emissions?
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz held a press conference on car emissions the day after Governor Thornburgh released his proposal for yearly auto inspections.  The Senator feels they could have had a joint press confernce, had he known of the announcement, though he reitierated that he and the Governor are good friends and work well together.

headline: U.S. aid promised for TMI
abstract: Governor Thornburgh announced that the federal government has committed $27 million towards clean up of the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant after an accident there in 1979.

headline: 'Crime hysteria' ends at jail door at $20,000 per prisoner
abstract: The author argues that the biggest ill that afflicts society is the growth in violent crimes, but that none of the ills defy more than the efforts to find a cure. Mentioning a US Department of Justice's report on the difficulty of finding easy answers, the author also points out that several common proposals, such as more prisons to reduce overcrowding, do not seem to offer easy solutions to the current problems.

headline: Rotunda sleep-over protests welfare purge
abstract: A small group of welfare activists slept overnight in the Capitol Rotunda after setting up an employment office to protest legislation which would remove an estimated 65,000 people from Pennsylvania's welfare rolls.  The article goes over the "workfare" program that Pennsylvania has developed and comments from Pennsylvania legislators.

headline: After Bartle ruling, state hires his firm to represent agency
abstract: null

headline: Lower Court Ruling Called 'Confusing'
abstract: The article has excerpts from the Commonwealth Court's ruling on the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers' appeal of the two Common Pleas Court decisions to stop the teachers' strike.

headline: Agency Hopes for Final OR on Capitol Excavation Soon
abstract: The PA Department of General Services expects to have final approval on plans for excavation work on the Capitol Extension, the first of three projects on the hill expected to cost $32 million. Groundbreaking is still set for November 16. The first project is a parking lot for 800 spaces. The other projects are renovation of the Capitol Building and rehabilitation of the old Museum Building as an office for the Governor.

headline: Tax-system scandal
abstract: The non-payment of real estate taxes on undeveloped property is a continuing and scandalous flaw in the tax system.  The legal remedies - tax liens on tax-delinquent property or a sheriff's sale to recover money for governmental coffers - simply do not work in many cases in terms of reaping sufficient money. The terms of the revenue return are useless if no one wants to buy the property because the taxes owed are woth more than the value of the land.  The result, as a recent Post-Gazette survey showed, is that many property owners just do not bother to pay, knowing that it is not worth the hassle for taxing bodies to force the issue.

headline: Pennhurst ruling leaves retarded in legal limbo
abstract: The editorial contends that the recent US Supreme Court decision, overturning a US Court decision forcing the state to relocate many residents of the Pennhurst Center for the Retarded in Chester County, is sort of a victory and sort of a defeat. It allows the state more time to deal with the problem, but that after a series of investigations in the mid-1970s over ill treatment of the patients and the subsequent improvement of conditions, there is a need for the state to provide community-based facilities. As a recent Temple University study has shown, they can thrive and grow in this setting, and the editorial argues the mentally retarded have the right to decent treatment, to dignity and to opportunity.

headline: A move forward for TMI
abstract: The article details the steps to move forward with clean up at the site of the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear accident.  The plans include cost-sharing between the state and federal government and General Public Utilities, owner of TMI.  The article outlines how the cost-sharing plan will work.

headline: UGI owes ratepayers $2 million, PUC says
abstract: PA state Public Utility Commission's Bureau of Audits charged that UGI Corp. owes over $2 million to its ratepayers because of a shortfall in refunds on money collected from customers as far back as November 1971. $1.5 million of that involved refunds to Valley Forge-based gas utility from its pipeline supplier.

headline: Crime is the major issue in statewide judicial races
abstract: The article discusses the candidates and issues involved in the judicial elections and states that the major issues is the perception that crime has increased because the courts are too lenient.  The article lists the candidates and details some of their histories.

headline: Senate lets welfare bill languish: Cuts may occur Sunday anyway
abstract: Governor Thornburgh stated that he may implement welfare cuts in order to comply with President Reagan's welfare reforms, even if the legislature as not passed the appropriate legislation yet.  The article details the proposed legislation's history in the state legislature.

headline: After Tuesday, Back to Square One
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Bill Green was spanked by voters when Joseph Smith won his old congressional seat. He is blaming unpopular fiscal decisions, but the author claims it is more than that. He no longer respects ward leaders.

headline: Maier ensures 2 aides get civil service posts
abstract: When Eugene Maier resigned as chairman of the city commissioners 12 days ago to run for a judgeship, he left behind a legacy that included more than just his legendary battles with fellow Commissioner Margaret Tartaglione. He also left two of his top deputies protected in newly created civil service pots that were approved by Philadelphia Mayor Green only one day before Maier was endorsed by the Democratic City Committee for a spot on the Common Pleas Court bench.

headline: An uphill fight to buy park land wins support
abstract: Despite opposition from the Reagan Administration, a House-Senate conference committee has approved funds to buy approximately 300 acres of largely undeveloped land adjacent to the Valley Forge National Park. A comprised total of $4 million for the Valley Forge acquisition instead of the original request of $9 million to buy 700 acres of land should be approved this week. Unless the President of the United States vetoes the bill, which is part of a general Interior Department appropriations bill, the $4 million should be made available to the National Park Service for purchasing next year.

headline: The Sixties defended: Blame for crime lies elsewhere
abstract: The author of the letter to the editor argues against a recent op-ed column that claimed the 1960s is to blame for the current crime epidemic. Instead, he argues that it is a lack of real employment opportunities for the young and alternatives to crime that is the problem. He adds that local initiatives are required.

headline: Pennhurst ruling: Yes but
abstract: The editorial welcomes the US Supreme Court's ruling that PA need not close down its facility for mentally retarded persons at Pennhurst, overturning lower court decisions that keeping persons at the facility violated their right to be placed in the least restrictive surroundings possible. However, the editorial argues that the ruling is worrisome because it could take the pressure off state and local officials to develop facilities so that more such persons could be returned to their home communities.

headline: A Winter's Tale
abstract: About six weeks ago, US Secretary of the Interior James Watt was planning a flying visit to Centralia, but he never did. The town is in desperate need for assistance, but the government is ignoring them. The non stop underground fire is releasing toxic gases into the town that could kill people.

headline: Unit 1 outage hits Met-Ed customers
abstract: Metropolitan Edison Co.'s (Met-Ed) customer pay $60 more per year for electricity than other places, due to the continued outage of Three Mile Island (TMI) Unit 1.  There was a nuclear accident at TMI in 1979 and the Nuclear Regulatory Committee (NRC) has not allowed the facility to run since then.  The article details the company's financial problems.

headline: Crime Remedies
abstract: It's ironic that President Reagan wants longer prison sentences for prisoners, but will not fund new prisons to store them in. He has declared an epidemic of violent crime. Judges are having to released prisoners early because there is not enough room to hold them all, but Reagan doesn't seem to notice.

headline: State bill would pit poor against poor
abstract: The state's Senate Finance Committee discussed a bill that would provide tax credits to businesses that hire general assistance recipients. The author argues that it will give advantage to the welfare recipient over the person who is unemployed and not collecting welfare. The author says the problem points to a potential downfall of using the tax credit as the bond to cure the problems of escalating welfare rolls and a lack of jobs.

headline: Air controllers' strike; A test of government itself
abstract: For striking United States air traffic controllers, it is distressing, at best.  As their strike ground into its third week, hope for support from controllers' unions in other countries had deteriorated into little more than mild token gestures, largely perfunctory, from the labor movement: picket line appearances here, speeches there - but no drawing together of anything faintly suggesting a hard, solid line.  That virtual vacuum of effective support looks increasingly like a failure of strategic judgment by the leaders of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization and its militant membership.  Not only has organized support not materialized, but every indication, including public opinion polls, is that the strikers have little significant public sympathy.  The strike is indisputably illegal.

headline: Majority Do Care
abstract: President of the League of Women Voters replies to Rick Prescott who wants the opportunity to vote for none of the above as the answer to voter apathy. She makes the point that voter turnout in PA is already 20% higher than nationally. She doubts that people will turn out to vote to leave the position vacant because none of the candidates are suitable.

headline: Avoiding Water Crisis
abstract: Discusses that the U.S. and Pennsylvania do not need another crisis but is in fact on the brink of another one. This looming crisis is a water crisis. Examples include the state's 2400 community water systems that need replacing. The bond issue is a solution that will keep the initial cost to consumers down. Editorialist urges readers to vote "yes" on the upcoming referendum.

headline: The tax man puts 'clergypersons' on their honor
abstract: State Revenue Secretary revoked the tax status held by clergy as employees of a church or congregation and changed it to an independent contractor.  The article outlines what tax rules churches and congregations should follow to comply with tax laws.  Clergy must be "on their honor" in declaring their status on their taxes.

headline: Phila. Blue Cross seeks 51% rise in rate for elderly
abstract: Blue Cross of Greater Philadelphia asked the PA Insurance Department for permission to raise rates for most senior citizens in its 65-Special plan by 51 percent on January 1. If granted in full the rate increase would raise the cost to each of 243,218 individual Philadelphia-area subscribers in the plan, which covers costs not paid for by federal Medicare coverage from $11.05 to $16.65 a month. The increases would raise $19.8 million annually.

headline: Acid Spill Routs 200 in Middletown
abstract: null

headline: Utilities are told: Put up or shut up
abstract: The nation's privately-owned electric utilities have a good opportunity to show if there is unity among such giants on the subject of nuclear energy. Now they are being asked to donate money to clean up TMI. If they decline critics say they don't care about the public.

headline: Crime rise 'not fault of courts'
abstract: Samuel Roberts, senior associate justice of the state Supreme court, speaking at the 85th annual meeting of the PA Bar Association, said it is disturbing to see the public and some lawyers blame the courts for the steadily increasing crime rate. Also speaking, the president of PBA, closing out his term, voiced strong opposition to the dismantling of the legal services program for indigent clients.

headline: State welfare checks delayed again
abstract: The mailing of checks for about 80,000 state welfare recipients was delayed for a second time as state officials appealed a federal court order to send them out even though there is no money to back the payments. Republican leaders said they have devised a strategy that could provide the needed $43 million in welfare funds. A judge ordered the checks be sent out anyway even though there was not enough money in the bank to cover them. At the center of the debate is a rider to the bill that would give the PA Office of General Counsel $150,000 to hire six more attorneys.

headline: All about Larsen: Gutsy justice nurses political roots
abstract: The article examines the personal and political roots, the judicial rulings and the financial dealings of State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen. His politicking is under investigation by the state Judicial Inquiry and Review Board. Justice Larsen, a Democrat, ran successfully in the 1977 campaign for the Supreme Court.

headline: Make Teacher Pact Talks Public
abstract: The editorial argues that PA's public employees negotiation act 195 has created many problems, including the fact that one out of four teachers' strike in the US have occurred in PA. The editorial agrees with some of the current legislature's proposals, including making all last contract offers by public employees and management available to the public. Other measures could also help avoid the September and October school closedowns.

headline: Capitol Project to Start Nov. 16
abstract: Groundbreaking will held November 16, 1981 for an addition to the Capitol that will provide office and parking space for House members and staff, state officials. It will be the first of three Capitol Hill projects expected to cost more than $32 million.

headline: The Word From Home
abstract: After the US Congress' Easter recess, lawmakers returned to Capitol Hill with their constituents' message to cut government spending but not to cut taxes if it means a big federal deficit. The fate of Reagan's administration hinges on persuading Americans that steep tax cuts and budget cuts are vital to reviving the economy.

headline: Problems do exist---but is the living arrangement at fault?
abstract: Discusses whether mishaps are more likely in an institutional or community setting for the mentally and physically retarded. Pennsylvania state Senator Edward Howard, a critic of community living arrangements for the mentally retarded states that the mentally handicapped should not have the same right to be "raped, robbed or mugged". Much of the argument against the deinstitutionalization of the mentally retarded focuses on who should be held accountable for the negative repercussions when a mentally handicapped individual is hurt or taken advantage of.

headline: Action on coal-mining regulations is tabled by environmental board
abstract: The Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court issued an order prohibiting the state Environmental Resources Department (DER) from enacting regulations adopted by the Environmental Quality Board to update the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act.  The order was issued after petitions were filed by several industrial associations.

headline: Utilities at odds over system for splitting costs
abstract: The electric current that is activated when a Philadelphia Electric Co. customer flicks a switch might not have been generated by PE. It could have been produced by any of the other 10 electric companies that are members of the PA New Jersey Maryland Interconnection. The companies pool their operations as if they all belong to a single system to save money.

headline: Crime system 'frustrates' victims; State poll on youth offenses tallied
abstract: Dr. Donald W. Hinrichs, a professor at Gettysburg College, presented his findings of a study on the victims of juvenile crime.  His study found that most victims do not understand the juvenile justice system.  The article details the outcomes of his study.

headline: State's inaction delays welfare
abstract: Failure of the PA Legislature to enact a $43.2 million deficiency appropriation means that 10 percent of Dauphin County's 16,200 welfare recipients will be going without their semi-monthly cash grants each day of the delay. None of the 2,446 recipients in Lebanon County will receive their expected grants and unless the crisis is resolved Cumberland County's 2,580 recipients won't be paid. The controversy over the money is wrapped up in political maneuvering on whether the governor's general counsel should receive an additional $150,000 to hire six lawyers has taken precedence over the needs of the recipients. The Legislature has long been aware that welfare cash grant funds were running out.

headline: Alleged election fraud probed by U.S. grand jury
abstract: An alleged election-fraud scheme in involving six Delaware County men, including two Republican Party leaders, is under investigation by a federal grand jury, according to the Philadelphia Bulletin.  Named by the Bulletin as subjects of a probe into bribery, election fraud and conspiracy are Nicholas F. Catania, Anthony R. Semeraro, Charles Sexton, Peter J. O'Keefe, Leroy Fratterola, and Don Fratterola.  The six allegedly used financial promises and the possibility of a "no-show state job" arranged by state Auditor General Al Benedict to convince Democrat Richard T. Burke to challenge Republican Thomas Lynch in the Democratic primary for country controller.

headline: Man of the Year:  Out of the Past, Fresh Choices for the Future; Invoking old values, Ronald Reagan must make them work in the '80s
abstract: Article starts by describing the attendance of Ronald Reagan at the National Review's 25th anniversary party.  The article then outlines his rise in politics from a Barry Goldwater supporter to California Governor to President of the US.  The article also outlines President Reagan's qualities and characteristics that led him to the presidency, along with his biographical and historical information.

headline: Carrying the ball for water bond
abstract: A campaign has been launched to seek voter approval of a $300 million water projects bond issue at the November 3 general election in Pennsylvania.  Spearheading the campaign as honorary chairman of a Vote Yes for Water Committee is Rockey Bleier, the former Pittsburgh Steeler who stressed the importance of the bond issue in kickoff statement.

headline: Theories Change, but problem doesn't: Little work for young blacks
abstract: Discusses the swelling army of unemployed young, black adults within Philadelphia. This part of the population has been steadily increasing over the past two decades. The PA state Department of Employment Security estimates that the unemployment rate among young black adults was 37%.

headline: Shenandoah state hospital slated to close
abstract: The Public Welfare Department announced plans to close the Locust Mountain State General Hospital in Shenahdoah, citing that the technology there is out of date and it's too costly to operate effectively.

headline: Adirondack Lakes Dying, Acid Rain Suits Pushed
abstract: Robert Abrams, New York's attorney general, is suing five Midwestern power plants over the acid rain produced by them that is acidifying the Adirondack mountain lakes. New York is appealing the US Environmental Protection Agency's decision to allow for increases in emissions from these plants. But great difficulty lies in tracing acid pollution to a particular coal-burning plant, and the science is not precise. Officials in Maine and Canada share the same problem of acid rain.

headline: Utilities back US public aiding TMI cost
abstract: Electricity customers throughout the county might have to pay to help complete the cleanup of the crippled Three Mile Island nuclear plant under a plan unanimously adopted yesterday by the nation's biggest electric-utility trade association.

headline: DA drops sex case against Hayes
abstract: Rape and other sexual assault charges against former PA Representative David S Hayes were dropped by the district attorney's office. A trial in May resulted in a hung jury on the charges, though Hayes was convicted of corruption the morals of a mirror.

headline: Street aide faces 3 welfare charges
abstract: Yvonne Hipp, the administrative aide who ran PA \ Senator Milton Street's controversial weatherization program, is expected to be charged with welfare fraud. Street claims they are really after him not her.

headline: Allegheny Commissioner Seeks Nod; Democrats Delaying Endorsement
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Cyril Wecht's bid for the Democratic endorsement for United States Senate is meeting guarded reaction from party leaders desperate for a strong ticket to unseat entrenched Republican opponents.  The article provides further details about Wecht and the Democrats options for endorsements.

headline: March 31 set for election for Dwyers's Senate seat
abstract: Lt. Gov. Willliam Scranton set March 31st as the day for a special election to fill the House Senate seat of R. Budd Dwyer, who resigner to become state treasurer.  He chose the date to assure the district has representation as soon as possible.

headline: Cold, dry fact: Drought is for real
abstract: The Delaware River Basin Commission (DRBC) declared a water-supply emergency and ordered a ban on nonessential water uses throughout the region.  Due to the crisis, governors of all four of the basin states- PA, NJ, NY, DE- gathered to veto a proposed dam project.  The article gives suggestions on how to conserve water

headline: Complaint by Lancaster Residents; PP&L Charged With Illegal Costs
abstract: Hearing could begin on a complaint filed by Lancaster residents who allege their utility bills include costs related to an unfinished nuclear plant.  The complaint alleges the Pennsylvania Power and Light Company is illegally charging customers for costs related to the Susquehanna nuclear station now under construction.  The article goes further into detail about the complaint.

headline: Specter saves tobacco supports
abstract: The editorial board says it was PA Senator Specter who saved tobacco supports. Arlen Specter voted to save tobacco supports, but not school lunches or aid to the needy. It is already a $1 billion industry that is a killer.

headline: Another Home Is Pulled Down In Centralia
abstract: Another Centralia, PA home was demolished Tuesday. This is the fourth of a slated 27 in the local area. Residents are saddened and sickened to witness such an event. The homes are to be razed through a joint state-federal plan to relocate 27 families threatened by an underground mine fire. Families residing in this 16 acre area were subject to noxious fumes from the underground mine fire.

headline: Utilities battle NRC over $15 million in fees
abstract: More than 30 electric utilities owe the Nuclear Regulatory Commission over $15 million fees, but many are contending they shouldn't have to pay because the fees apply to federal review work on nuclear plant construction permit applications that were later withdrawn. The dispute, pitting the Reagan administration's rigorous user-fee policy against an economically depressed industry, will probably end up in federal court.

headline: Dealing with the stigma of rape
abstract: Article stresses the need for compassion in courtrooms and counselling when dealing with victims of rape.  Defense lawyers must show more compassion when making rape cousellors testify.

headline: Street Corp. Issued Edict
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry has told state Senator Milton Street's North Philadelphia Block Development Corporation to straighten out its financial records or return $180,000 in job training funds. But Labor Department spokesman conceded that getting the cash back will be difficult legally. The Department awarded the federal grant money to hire welfare recipients to weatherize old homes, and a day before its April 19 audit, the corporation's financial records were stolen.

headline: An admirable appointment
abstract: President Reagan has nominated Faith Ryan Whittlesey to be ambassador to Switzerland. Beyond proper parochial pride, she is a political leader in Delaware County and formidable force in the PA Republican Party, there is ground for substantial satisfaction in the appointment.

headline: Mayor Green could use a St. Jude
abstract: Bill Green is at the crossroads of what was once a promising political career. Young Willie had it all- looks the chemistry, the soft con. He could have gone all the way to the top, but young Willie ended up in the wrong place at the wrong place. Young Willie is a big city mayor in Philadelphia and big city mayors in modern America usually end up in the 10-cent seats.

headline: Conservation is needed, not just superficial fixes
abstract: The author opines that in order for residents to seriously conserve water, the administration must stop water-wasteful plans like the Point Pleasant water diversiton plan and the Tocks Island dam proposal.

headline: Completing Limerick will save PE customers money, consultants say
abstract: Testifying at Public Utility Commission hearings on the future of the Limerick nuclear plant, Wirtshafter and Feldman considered that finishing the plant would save Philadelphia Electric Company customers money in the long run. Both work at the Energy Center of the University of PA. There would be less money saved, they acknowledged, if the plant was abandoned. But a PE attorney questioned their assertions.

headline: State delays decision on hospital building
abstract: Plans for a new building at Canonsburg General Hospital have been delayed by state health officials in order to hear additional arguments for and against the new building.  Some are worried about the cost of the new building.

headline: Authority approves condemnation action
abstract: The West Hills Area Water Pollution Control Authority has approved a resolution to bring condemnation proceedings against some 90 properties whose rights of way are needed for the Authority's planned sewer system. The Authority also voted to begin condemnation proceedings against four property sites the Authority must purchase for the system's sewage treatment plant and three of four pump stations.

headline: withdrawn Permit Fees Are Protested by 30 N-Utilities
abstract: Many of the more than 30 electric utilities owing the Nuclear Regulatory Commission more than $15 million in fees are contending they shouldn't have to pay because the fees apply to the federal review work on nuclear plant construction permit applications that are later withdrawn. The dispute will most likely end up in federal court. The NRC problems began to surface last year after the number of utilities abandoning nuclear plants in various stages of planning.

headline: Death row
abstract: It took prison officials three days to check on George Hayes and find him dead. This is inexcusable and reveals a weakness in the monitoring of inmates that should be remedied. His mental illness was ignored and should have been noticed before he committed suicide.

headline: The impact: 11,000 families to lose welfare, N.J. says
abstract: More than 11,000 New Jersey families will lose welfare benefits and 7,000 families will be cut from food stamps as a result of the Reagan administration's budget cuts, according to figures released by Timothy Carden, the state's human services commissioner.  In addition, Carden said, welfare disbursements to more than 10,000 families will be reduced, and all food stamp benefits will be cut.  The welfare cuts will affect families that receive federal assistance under the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program to supplement their earned income.  Benefits for the 127,000 New Jersey families that live entirely on welfare assistance will not be affected, Carden said, because the state alone determines the level of payments to those families.

headline: An Eye for an I
abstract: The picture depicts state Senator Milton Street speaking to reporters before entering the District Attorney's office to back up his challenge to KYW-TV's I-Team to document their charges of fraud and mismanagement at a weatherization program run by a community group Street founded. The I-Team did not show up, and instead his aide spent time reviewing a criminal complaint against a state welfare worker accused of giving confidential information to the I-Team.

headline: Mayor Says Governor Offers Scant Aid Hope
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Paul Doutrich Jr. met on April 10 with Governor Dick Thornburgh to request an increase in funds for the city, which faces a revenue shortfall and the prospect of scores of layoffs. Although the governor was willing to review the city's report, it will not provide monetary aid.

headline: DER seeks catchy slogan for water-project bonds
abstract: State Environmental Resources Secretary Cliffor Jones is searching for a catchy slogan, welcoming public suggestions, to generate support for the administration's plans to place a $300 million water-projects bond issue on the November ballot. A committee will also be organized to raise private funds to publicize and advertise the aim of the projected referendum. Legislation, announced by Governor Dick Thornburgh and legislative leaders, will be introduced to protect water resources.

headline: Congress may restore cut in state synfuel program
abstract: Pennsylvania Congressmen John Murtha and Joseph McDade expect that six proposed synthetic fuel plants will not be build unless Congress resurrects them.  President Reagan wants to abandon the plans due to budget cuts.  The plants were designed to buttress Pennsylvania's sagging coal industry.

headline: State delays decision on hospital building
abstract: State health officials have asked for extra time to decide whether or not plans for a new Cannonsburg General Hospital building can begin.

headline: AUTO EMISSION POLITICS
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Richard Thornburgh has shown much better common sense and much less desire to play political games than most of the would-be populists in the legislature who blindly supported a bill to prohibit the state from enforcing federal air pollution regulations.  The proposal to prohibit the use of state funds for enforcement of auto emission standards received strong support from the legislators who realized that the great majority of motorists in the state oppose the emissions of federally required emission tests and strict rules of enforcement.  In the voting to ban the use of state funds, these same legislators refused to admit that they were cutting off their noses to spite their own face.

headline: Was 'Scare' Overblown?- Analysis:  Anthracite Coal Demand Outstripping Supply
abstract: The author cites numerous sources to show that a predicted anthracite coal shortage was not accurate and that officials and departments overreacted.

headline: Decision-Making: 15 Plus 1,312 Equals 50
abstract: Committee of 15 was a group convened by the Pennsylvania Joint Council on Criminal Justice, a private non-profit group that had received a federal grant to study juvenile crime in the state.  The committee's 108 page report reveals a lot about how decisions are made about juvenile justice in Pennsylvania.  By sampling approximately 1 percent of the state's juvenile cases, the committee tried to determine how many juveniles  should be placed in a secure facility in any one year.  It came up with an initial figure of 1,312.  But the report never made clear that the statistical study was only capable of determining that the number of additional spaces needed actual ranged somewhere between zero and 3,000.

headline: Thornburgh asks end of free day-care
abstract: In order to absorb President Reagan's federal cutbacks, the Thornburgh administration has proposed the elimination of free day care for poor families. Some 8,000 families who have a gross monthly income of less than half the PA median would have to pay $5 a week for the first child in day care. Currently thy have to pay nothing.

headline: AN INSIDER'S GUIDE TO THE 1981 POLITICAL MACHINE
abstract: The author presents the different candidates in Philadelphia's upcoming Municipal Primary Election, to be held May 19. The city controller, district attorney and 25 judicial candidates will be selected by each party that day. The author suggests that political power will pass once again into the hands of the professionals who know how to use it, because although many will vote, the results of the election will actually be determined by the committeemen that work the city's polling places and divisions.

headline: McDermott wins seat on top Pa. court
abstract: Former Common Pleas Judge James T. McDermott was elected to a ten year term on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.  The article details the race for state Supreme Court and other judicial elections.

headline: DER Slated To Review Creek Plan
abstract: County commissioners have notified the state Department of Environmental Resources that they are interested in helping the Department of Environmental Resources get a feel for developing countywide storm water management plans.  Cumberland, Erie and Allegheny counties have been chosen by the department as target zones fo the experiment.

headline: Congressman charges TMI 'hidden cost'
abstract: Few people realize the financial drain that the accident at Three Mile Island has on electric utility companies and their customers across the country. TMI will cost the industry $550 million through the end of this year. This does not even cover the future costs of hundreds of millions of dollars. The sooner it is cleaned up the less interest will accrue.

headline: State Oks 55% Hike In Blue Cross Rates
abstract: Subscribers of Blue Cross of Western Pennsylvania will see an increase in their rates.  The state Insurance Department said that about 80,000 Western Pennsylvanians will pay 55.3 percent more each month for individual major medical coverage.  Insurance Commissioner Michael Browne said the new rates will generate an additional $1.3 million annually for Blue Cross.  The article goes further into detail about the rate increase for Blue Cross.

headline: Bell customers pay for wasteful practices
abstract: Workers were hired at Bell to destroy expensive equipment and sell it as scrap, but it was brand new. The entire event was a middle-management blunder. They have admitted to $747,416 in equipment and labor overcharges, but some say that's only part of it. It could exceed $4 million in sheer wastefulness in PA, because they are so lax in their auditing practices.

headline: Washington scene
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) says that after the 1979 accident at Three Mile Island, licensing processes for nuclear power plants are becoming increasingly more predictable. Due to the accident manpower had to be sifted from licensing to analysis of the factors contributing to the accident.

headline: Defense lawyer hits sentence guidelines
abstract: Proposed guidelines for sentencing criminals are too restrictive and possibly unconstitutional says veteran defense lawyer, Arthur Goldberg, to the PA state Sentencing Commission. Goldberg states that the guidelines which are to be submitted to the State Legislature in early January 1982 in effect state that judges do not have the ability or the courage to do the job for which they were elected.

headline: Under the budget ax, legal services look to cut costs
abstract: The agencies that provide legal help to the poor the Philadelphia's suburban counties are struggling with the questions of what offices they should close and which clients they should refuse because of reduced funding. They failed to get the PA General Assembly to restore a cut that had been made in state financing of local legal services programs.

headline: Another sad example
abstract: Last week it became known  to the public for the first time that PA's lawmakers have received a $2,500 boost in their expense accounts, a tidy raise from $7,500 year to $10,000. Some lawmakers claim it was a mistake and came about without some members knowing it. PA legislators have not approved the money yet so checks cannot be mailed.

headline: McKeesport Tosses Out Old Guard
abstract: Incumbents had a hard time retaining their seats in the heavily Democratic cities of McKeesport, Duquesne, and Clairton. Only one incumbent McKeesport councilman, Joseph Graziano, will be on the November ballots. James Haughey and Samuel Vidnovic are assured of seats in November because no Republicans filed. Incumbents Gerald Boyle and Thomas O'Neil were defeated.

headline: Disaster declared for 5 countries
abstract: President Reagan declared a major disaster in five storm-damaged counties in northwestern PA. The Presidential action permits of federal funds for disaster aid in stricken areas of Clarion, Crawford, Jefferson, Mercer and Venango counties. One person is missing, presumed drowned. An estimated 391 dwellings and at least 40 businesses were destroyed by the flood.

headline: Conservation could fatten PE revenues, hearing told
abstract: At a hearing of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission yesterday, an expert testified on behalf of consumer groups that a conservation plan would benefit the Philadelphia Electric Company. Cynthia Praul, a policy and program specialist at the California Energy Commission, said that the company could improve its financial position and its customers could save on their utility bills if it embarked on an aggressive program to promote conservation.

headline: State psychiatrists leave because of low pay
abstract: PA's psychiatrists earn lower salaries than do similar workers in other states, the main reason for which many are leaving the state to go elsewhere. Other reasons given are low morale. The 10,000 mental hospital patients are not left in good attendance, according to the state's mental health system critics.

headline: Bittersweet Experience
abstract: Although the dangers they face from the 19-year old Centralia mine fire are clear to most of them, many residents find leaving their home a bittersweet experience. They have to move because of gas and subsidence dangers.

headline: Water ban, si; surcharge no
abstract: The editoral comments on a letter from a reader who feels the water ban in unnecessary and the surcharge by Metopolitan Edison to stockpile coal is wrong.  The editors feel that the water ban is necessary and state their reasons, but feel agree with the reader that the surcharge is wrong.

headline: Deliquent father program works
abstract: The article outlines a program aimed at tracking down fathers who are court ordered to pay child support and simply disappear.  The program was launched in PA in 1975 in conjunction with the Department of Health and Human Services, the Internal Revenue Service and the Social Security Administration.

headline: Theft of records won't hinder welfare probe of Street
abstract: Auditors of the state Department of Labor and Industry, attempting to examine the financial records from the offices of the North Philadelphia Block Development Corporation, found the documents had been stolen. The community agency, administered by state Senator T. Milton Street, is under investigation by the state Department of Public Welfare for allegations of welfare fraud. A televised news report said the employees of the community agency were illegally collecting welfare while on the program payroll, and that the program was mismanaged.

headline: Are they Sacred Cows?
abstract: State Representative Italo Cappabianca (D-Erie) wants to know why Governor Thornburgh is willing to get rid of the Liquor Control Commission and the Turnpike Commission, but remains silent on the Public Utilities Commission and the Milk Board.  Cappabianca feels that the PUC and the Milk Board have become spokesmen for the special interests.

headline: METROPOLITAN; Deals are all business for Errichetti
abstract: The six-year term in a federal prison and the $40,000 fine Angelo J. Errichetti received August 13 were about the harshest penalties handed down in the Abscam corruption case.  The article goes further into detail about Errichetti and the reasons why he landed in prison.

headline: Disaster tag sought in the state
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh asked President Reagan to declare five storm damaged counties in northwestern PA a "major disaster area."  Unusually heavy rains resulted serious flash flooding. He said the initial survey estimate damage in the area at $22 million.

headline: Consider Halt to Berwick Nuclear Facility Work, PP & L Urged
abstract: Pennsylvania Power and Light Company should consider halting work on its Berwick nuclear plants to avoid rate increases that could run as high as 40 percent.  Susquehanna Alliance said its own just-completed study found that the plant's net costs to ratepayers over 10 years will range from $900 million to $2.9 billion.  Individual rates could increase 30 to 40 percent.  In contrast, stopping construction and selling off plant equipment would cost the company about $1.2 billion in lost investment.  Ratepayers and stockholders should share the cost.  An accident similar to the one that occurred at Three Mile Island could cost ratepayers and stockholders $4.4 billion to $5.9 billion.

headline: Study Set On Cancer In Town
abstract: Dr. Donald Reid, deputy health secretary for public health programs, said a task force will be set up to study the cancer rate in the borough of Nanty Glo in western PA. The town has an unusually high rate of cancer cases, almost twice the statewide rate for 1978.

headline: Car Emission Tests Begin May 1
abstract: U.S. District Court Judge Louis Bechtle ruled that motorists in the Pittsburgh and Philadelphia areas must have state-instituted auto emissions inspections tests aimed at clearing up air pollution by May 1, 1982. Bechtle rejected a postponement of said testing for January 1, 1983. The Thornburgh Administration stated it would appeal such a federal order. Motorists will have to pay to have their cars inspected, and if they fail the inspection they should expect to pay between $18-$35 to have it repaired. Bechtle ordered that approximately 800 additional inspection stations should be in operation by May 1982.

headline: Watt must not strip away federal mining program
abstract: Interior Secretary of the federal office of Surface Mining, James Watt believes that the states should incur the responsibility of upholding coal mining regulations. However, the US Supreme Court's decision says otherwise. This victory for citizen groups is considered largely hollow as Mr. Watt is administering the federal surface mining program out of existence. Watt has proposed a relaxation of enforcement standards that will allow states to submit surface mining regulatory programs for federal approval later or on an ad-hoc basis.

headline: Democrats put noose on judgeship names
abstract: State Senate Democrats have filed a petition with Republican Lt. Governor William Scranton III, Senate president, requiring a Senate vote within five legislative days on 16 judgeship nominees. Republicans have delayed the confirmation vote in the face of continuing Democratic policy to block Republican nominees. The action puts the Republican majority in a no-win situation, unless they agree on a deal with Democrats.

headline: Thornburgh plan for aged wins few friends
abstract: Article details Governor Thornburgh's plan to use a projected $300 million originating from state lottery surplus to fund an Older Pennsylvanians' Inflation Needs program. Support for this plan is thought to be split down bi-partisan lines and many senior citizens were hostile toward the new program. The governor stated that instead of the bureaucracy deciding where the money should be spent it will be up to each senior citizen to make tat decision.

headline: Area pals to clash?
abstract: Columnist Ed Wellejus reports on Lou Tullio's fundraiser at the Hilton. State Treasurer Budd Dwyer responded to Wellejus' question about the possibility of state treasurer and state auditor Al Benedict being in a political battle some day, to which Dwyer responded in affirmation. The columnist also reports on other events at the Hilton dinner.

headline: Miller is named coordinator of Bike/Hikes for retarded
abstract: Stanley A. Miller, commissioner of the state Bureau of Professional and Occupational Affairs, has been named coordinator of the 1981 Bike/Hikes for the Retarded, according to Barbara Edmiston, director of the Retarded Citizens Association of Dauphin County. The event is scheduled for April 12.

headline: Editorial Reply #4R81-06 - Redevelopment Committee
abstract: William J. Doyle, Chairman of the Regional Port Development Committee, states his goals and methods for bringing a regional Port Redevelopment Program to the tri-state region in one year.

headline: Construction Dates Extended For PP&L's Berwick Plant
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has approved the extension of construction permits for Pennsylvania Power and Light's (PP&L) nuclear power plant near Berwick.

headline: Thornburgh Plans to Host HMO Meeting
abstract: The Hershey Convention Center will be host to the second Annual Governor's Conference on Health Maintenance Organizations. Governor Dick Thornburgh will host a reception and deliver the keynote address.

headline: Car emission tests still in court
