abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh requested a US District Court Judge to postpone from Friday, May 1, until January 1, 1983, the start-up date for implementation of a vehicle emission inspection and maintenance program in 12 PA counties. The state and the US Environmental Protection Agency have reached an agreement on the postponement, but haven't been able to agree on an education program, which the governor is trying to remove from the entire program.

headline: Way open to restart unscathed TMI unit; TMI may go on-line
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued an order that could lead to reopening the undamaged reactor at the Three Mile Island power plant sometime in November, even as challenges to the restart continue.  By a 3-2 vote, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission directed that a separate panel hear any appeals from the decision of the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board on the restart.  The board completed nine months of hearings in July on the question of whether the undamaged reactor could reopen.

headline: Dilemma
abstract: The author opines that having stricter sentencing guidelines will require criminals to spend more time in prison.  The author states that this will lead to more overcrowding in prisons and eventually the need to spend more money on additional cells

headline: Thornfare: final chapter
abstract: Two years after the proposal was first proposed, Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh in enroute to victory in his effort to remove some 63,000 from the state's General Assistance rolls.  Intervening events in the welfare area have reduced the Thornburgh initiative to something of a footnote.  The article continues to discuss Thornburgh's initiatives towards his proposals and the General assistance programs.

headline: As Phila. goes, so don't go the state's voters
abstract: Philadelphia elections were overshadowed by a teachers' strike and a hostage crisis at Graterford State Prison.  The author feels that the Republican Party has a long way to go in the city if it wants to get power.  The author analyzes several Philadelphia elections and their outcomes.

headline: Milton street, One Way
abstract: The cartoon depicts a city street named Milton Street with a One Way arrow pointing downwards, in reference to state Senator T. Milton Street.

headline: Federal Control
abstract: The state should reject all proposals to take over control of locks and dams on PA rivers. The US Army Corps of Engineers is discussing proposals to turn Locks on the Allegheny River to the commonwealth. It is an example of the misguided priorities of the federal government.

headline: Consumer advocate UGI agree on rate
abstract: PA state Consumer Advocate Walter Cohen has agreed to settle a $21-million rate dispute involving UGI Corp allowing the gas utility to receive an average 4 percent rate increase from its 200,000 customers. In a statement issued yesterday, Cohen said he agreed to the settlement, which will give UGI an added $11.5 million in annual revenue, because it was less than the 10 percent rate increase originally sought by UGI last April. The settlement is expected to become effective in November.

headline: TMI harm seen as mental only
abstract: A top PA state health official said an analysis of 12 health-related research studies shows the Three Mile Island nuclear accident had no physical health effects on area residents. He did say the accident caused some mental health stress. Health officials abandoned a study on possible chromosome damage from low-level radiation because they felt it would not be worth the money.

headline: Centralia Mine Fire
abstract: In the northeast part of PA there's a little town called Centralia. Nineteen years ago a local dump began to burn. It ignited a mine fire, which has been burning since 1962. Last winter toxic gases began seeping into the homes of the town's residents. Someone should take responsibility for this and help these residents.

headline: Ways are sought to spur coal production
abstract: At a Pittsburgh hearing on the nation's coal industry problems, US Energy Department director of anthracite division Jerry Pell gave credit to the resurgence in interest of anthracite as an alternative to dependence on foreign oil, and argued the demand for anthracite already exceeds the supply. While the larger bituminous industry has problems of overproduction, he indicated that anthracite should be regarded as an important path toward energy independence in the highly oil-dependent northeast.

headline: Dirty money law needed
abstract: The editorial agrees with the state Crime Commission's recommendation that lawmakers consider a bill allowing the state to seize all money and assets used in and acquired from the illegal drug trade. An estimated $60 billion in dirty money is being invested in business ventures in the US this year, and the editorial argues that some progress can be made with strict enforcement of such law. However, caution is urged in that reputable business leaders should be consulted to avoid too strict measures that might negatively affect good businesses.

headline: Two Cuts Must be Restored
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare failed to obtain its $43.2 million supplementary appropriation from legislature. As a result the DPW was unable to send out public assistance checks to almost 800,000 needy families legally. Two weeks later, a House-Senate Committee slashed $1.1 million of a previously approved $2.2 million for legal services to the poor. The editorial ponders whether this series of events is by design or coincidence but concludes that the legislature has demonstrated the fallacy of the Reagan administration's argument that the states can be trusted to pick up the tab for legal services if Washington abandons the responsibility. Two important programs were cut: legal services and family planning.

headline: Assembly redistricting upheld
abstract: A divided Pennsylvania Supreme Court narrowly upheld the state's legislative reapportionment plan, casting aside complaints that the plan is racially gerrymandered and needlessly divides communities.  The plan was written by the state's bi-partisan Legislative Reapportionment commission.  The article goes into further detail about the reapportionment plan.

headline: Misleading ad
abstract: The author replies to a letter stating that Rep. William Klingaman refused to return phone calls aimed at him in radio ads.  The author states that the phone number given was to the anti-abortion organization, not to the legislature.  The author accuses the ads of hiding information.

headline: Fee to aid mine-site restorations
abstract: The PA Environmental Quality Board voted to impose a $50-an-acre fee on strip mine coal operators to create a $1million fund for restoring abandoned mines. At the same time, the state prepared to reduce those operators' bond charges from $4,000 an acre to $3,000 next month. An operator forfeits the bond if he fails to restore land that he has mined.

headline: Control utility expansion to curb future rates
abstract: The author raises questions about what can be done about the utility rate increases approves by the Pennsylvania Public Utilities Commission (PUC).  The author states that unnecessary growth, such as building power plants where there is no need, is what is driving rates up.  The author feels that PUC should be asking the utility companies whether rate increases are really necessary and urges public discussion on the topic.

headline: Tragic surgery cases probed at Einstein
abstract: State health investigators are trying to determine why one woman died and another lapsed into a coma after a minor surgery at Albert Einstein Medical Center. William Walker, director of the PA Bureau of Hospitals, said that although officials at the medical center at York and Tabor Roads had not requested the state probe, investigators had been sent to the hospital after news reports of the incidents.

headline: Centre Company Will Begin Cleanup of Toxic Wastes
abstract: After nearly a decade, the PA state Department of Environmental resources has been promised by the Ruetgers-Nease chemical Co of Centre County that the firm will begin required cleanup operation of soil and water contaminated by toxic pesticides.

headline: Weaseling on gasoline tax
abstract: The writer is furious that Pennsylvania lawmakers feel they can escape culpability for the results of their actions. The example used was Governor Thornburgh's 3.5% Oil Company Franchise Tax, which is essentially a 3.5% tax on each dollar of taxable revenue generated by oil companies operating in Pennsylvania from the sale of motor fuel. The author states that the general public is not as blind as lawmakers would like to believe as this 3.5% tax translates to a 2-3 cent increase per gallon at the gas pump. This allows lawmakers to escape criticism and culpability as oil companies can be blamed for the price increase at the pump.

headline: Drunken drivers targeted: Victims' relatives seek mandatory jail sentences
abstract: Article illustrates current penalties slated for drunk driving offenders which include probation and at times, community service. Mothers Against Drunken Drivers met in Washington, DC to testify at a congressional hearing on a U.S. House bill that would mandate set penalties for drunk drivers. Such penalties include massive fines, license suspension, community service and jail time. A letter was signed by more than 300 senators and congressmen and delivered to President Reagan on Friday asking him to appoint a national commission on drunken driving.

headline: Welfare Changes:  A Fair Plan Is Offered
abstract: When Governor Thornburgh announced his plans for welfare reform, the editors disagreed with it.  Now, however, they see his new reforms as a step in the right direction and urge lawmakers to adopt it. The Governors plan calls for "able-bodied" individuals to get off welfare.  The editors feel this is in line with the idea off temporary assistance.

headline: Atkinson asks to keep same committee seats
abstract: U.S. Representative Eugene Atkinson of Pennsylvania officially resigned from the House Democratic caucus, but intends to keep the committee seats that were assigned to him.  The article reprints his resignation letter.

headline: Monaco Team
abstract: A vote for change was experienced in the city of Lower Burrell, with Dennis Kowalski and Don Kinosz as the two newcomers to city council, new Mayor and incumbent councilman John Monaco, new councilmen David Hanna and incumbent councilman Bernie Kubiak elected in the May 19 primary election.

headline: For the benefit of hiker, US tramples a dream
abstract: Reverand Charles Evans Jr bought land atop Blue Mountain with the Appalachian Trail going through it, but hasn't been able to build much there because of a feud with the National Park Service over federal efforts to protect the trail from development. Over the last three years the park service has acquired 424 different properties along the trail.

headline: Cry for coal:  Northeast states turn to Penna. To fight shortage
abstract: Energy officials from New England are asking Pennsylvania to produce more anthracite coal due to a shortage in the Northeast.  The shortage was caused by an unanticipated rise in demand.  Anthracite coal is used mainly for home heating.

headline: We Can Do Without A Medical Examiner
abstract: The author feels that there is no need to replace the position of coroner with a medical examiner.  The author thinks that the current coroner in Allegheny County, Dr. Sanford Edberg is doing a good job of reaching out to the public.

headline: City: EPA water-pollution report outdated
abstract: A claim by the federal Environmental Protection Agency that the city may have a water pollution problem has come as a revelation to officials here. City Water Director Richard Cosentino said he has not had a chance to review the EPA report mailed to Mayor Caliguiri 11 days ago.

headline: Weighing the risks: An 'accident' at Salem plant to put emergency plan to test
abstract: A morning alert from a higher than normal radioactive level in the Salem I Nuclear Generating Station caught many people by surprise. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission informed the leak was fixed, and did not mind the ensuing communication problems. But the NRC will mind this coming Wednesday, April 8, when the operator, Public Service Electric and Gas, conducts the nation's first full-scale emergency drill under new federal guidelines instituted after the Three Mile Island accident.

headline: Enough time
abstract: PA's adoption laws should be changed. Why should adoptive parents, feed, clothe and love a child for six months while the natural mother is deciding if she wants her child? The natural mother has nine months to decide while she's pregnant. Adoption law is written unfairly in favor of the mother.

headline: Welfare Checks Delayed by State Squabble
abstract: A state House and Senate fight over funds for the Office of General Counsel will mean late assistance checks for some of the state's 850,000 welfare recipients. The holdup results from a legislative snag for the bill authorizing $43.2 million to fund the Welfare Department through June 30. The Senate inserted $150,000 in the appropriation to allow the governor's general counsel to hire six more lawyers for his staff.

headline: Atkinson shakes up alignment
abstract: The article details the strange tails of Congressmen in Pennsylvania's 25th District.  Most recently, Eugene Atkinson left the Democrats to join the Republican party.  The article analyzes what this means for both Republicans and democrats.

headline: Money talks, especially in politics
abstract: Special interests groups have become more prevalent in the PA State Legislature, channeling money to elect certain candidates sympathetic to their causes.  The article lists what how much representatives are getting from each PAC (political action committee) and what special interests groups want in Lehigh Valley.

headline: From Harrisburg
abstract: Last week at the polls Pennsylvanians took two major steps toward long-term health and prosperity with decisive margins of 64 and 70 percent the electorate approved bond issues of $300 million for loans to improve water systems, dams and ports; and $15 for loans to finance life-saving equipment for volunteer ambulance companies.

headline: Did Coal Industry Steamroller State?
abstract: The author states that she agrees with the newspapers articles on strip-mining in the state and wonders if the coal industry hasn't steamroller the state administration into complacency.  The author urges the newspaper to continue writing such articles.

headline: Who will play God for the dying? Mercy killing guidelines lacking
abstract: The article details two stories of people caring for the elderly.  They state that watching them suffer is awful and one woman stands accused of killing her invalid mother.  The article questions who should decide if someone's death is so imminent, they should be killed out of mercy.  The article also explores the history of mercy killing through the medical and religious communities.

headline: Clean up sports
abstract: Sports people must be held responsible for their conduct: on the field because they are performers and off the field because they are symbols. Officials need to clean up the sports picture.

headline: Witness: Scrapping 1 Limerick unit would be no savings over coal
abstract: Raymond Czahar, a computer expert with the California Public Utility Commission, testified in behalf of state Consumer Advocate Walter Cohen yesterday in PA Public Utility hearings on the unfinished plant in Limerick Township. He said that consumers would not pay substantially more over 20 years if both nuclear reactors were completed than if one unit were scrapped and coal-fired plants substituted for it. The PUC investigation was prompted by Cohen's suit questioning Philadelphia Electric Company's judgment in deciding to build the plant and subsequent orders for construction delays that escalated costs.

headline: Epidemic of thefts putting art world on alert
abstract: Authorities say the black market for stolen paintings like Trumbull is enormous, amounting to millions of dollars a year. Though they say the money involved in the thefts may be second only to that of narcotics traffic as a criminal activity, there are no precise figures.

headline: Welfare cutbacks seen as victory for Thornburgh
abstract: The welfare policies of Ronald Reagan and Richard Thornburgh are combined in a bill that will go before the House, which eliminates or reduces the benefits received by an estimated 165,00 persons.  The Thornburgh part of the bill would take away benefits of about 58,000 General Assistance recipients who are classified as physically and mentally able to work.  The article goes further into specific detail about the bill.

headline: Attorneys for 2 in Lottery Case Argue for New Trials
abstract: Attorneys for two people charged in rigging the state lottery, Nick Perry and Edward Plevel, argued that their clients should have new trials because there was no legal grounds for them being tried in Dauphin County Court.  The attorneys feel that the trials should have been held in the county where the crimes occurred, in this case, Philadelphia and Allegheny Counties.  The article details the crimes and the legal proceedings.

headline: Mortgage buy to help economy
abstract: The PA State Employees' Retirement Board says it has agreed to buy a $25 million conventional mortgage pass-through security from its investment adviser, Philadelphia Saving Fund Society. The firm was hired to provide investment advice and administrative support services for the pension fund's $365 million mortgage portfolio. It’s the first time the fund has ventured into conventional mortgages that are not government-insured.

headline: Gettysburg again, this time on film
abstract: Hollywood film maker Elmo Williams is seeking permission from the Park Service to make a film about the Battle at Gettysburg on location at one of the battlefield cites.  The article details the plan for filming the movie and how the public might react to it.

headline: Don't Restart Unit 1 at TMI
abstract: The author does not want reactor #1 to be restarted at the Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Plant, after the accident that happened there.  The author cites the human error factor and worries that another accident could happen if reactor #1 is started again.

headline: null
abstract: Cartoon caption reads, "Sure it'll be rough, but together we can do it - and here with some inspirational words is your friend and mine, Caspar Weinberger!"

headline: Congress Confronts Storage Problem
abstract: The US has so far failed to solve one of modern man's most pernicious problems: Safe and permanent disposal of nuclear waste. The US Department of Energy predicts utility companies will begin to exhaust their in-site storage capacity by 1986. About 75 million gallons of high level reprocessed waste already are stored in government facilities in the states of Washington, Idaho, and South Carolina and at a commercial site at West Valley, NY. Congress will state debating the issue when they return from their break.

headline: Would Be First Since TMI Accident: Nuclear Power Increase Likely
abstract: For the first time since the March 28, 1979, accident at Three Mile Island, the amount of electricity being generated annually by United States nuclear power plants is expected to increase.  In a report issued by the United States Department of Energy's Energy Information Administration, it is pregenerated electricity in 1981 will increase by 7.8 percent when compared with 1980.  Domestic nuclear power plants are expected to churn out 270.71 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity this year, compared to 251.12 billion bilowatt-hours of electricty last year, according to the Energy Information Administration's Short Term Energy Outlook.  The report said nuclear energy production began falling since the accident at Three Mile Island because of extened shutdowns across the country.

headline: Excessive Inheritance Taxes
abstract: The editors feel that Pennsylvania needs to reduce its Inheritance Tax levies, which are at a flat of 6 and 15 per cent.  They feel Pennsylvania is out of line with the rest of the country and that the tax is only hurting "the little guy."

headline: Welfare cuts approved by Pa. House; Would stop benefits for about 70,000
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh's bill that would purge an estimated 70,000 welfare recipients from the state's general-assistance rolls was approved by the Pennsylvania state House.  The article provides information about the bill being passed and it's anticipated effects on Pennsylvanians.

headline: Available, If, Rendell Says
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Edward G. Rendell indicated that he would become available for the race of Pennsylvania state governor, if state party leaders were to make him a tempting offer.  Rendell provided his conditions in detail.

headline: Mortgage buy to help economy
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Employees' Retirement Board has agreed to buy a $25 million conventional mortgage pass-through security from its investment adviser, the Philadelphia Saving Fund Society. The security is backed by a pool of residential mortgages on Pennsylvania homes. This agreement marks the first time the $3.3 billion retirement fund has ventured into conventional mortgages that are not government-insured.

headline: Goal of Landowners: Preserve Penn's Creek
abstract: null

headline: Electricity from coal
abstract: The author argues that the costs to General Public Utilities Corp (GPU) and its customers continues to rise, even though the Three Mile Island nuclear plant (TMI), has not produced any electricity since an accident there in 1979.  The author feels that reliance on coal powered electric would be more cost effective than nuclear.

headline: null
abstract: Photograph, caption states, "Dick Solly and his wife, Barbara, pick beans on their farm in Ivyland, Bucks County.  Speculators have shied away from buying such farmland."

headline: Congress expects users to share TMI cleanup cost, Minnich warns
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioner John Minnich stated that Congress will refuse to provide any federal funds for the cleanup of the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear accident unless utility customers chip in.

headline: York mayor, 3 others join panel on TMI
abstract: The Mayor of York is among four persons appointed to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Advisory panel on Three Mile Island. They join 8 others to make the panel a full 12 people. It advises the commission on major activities involved in the cleanup.

headline: Ex-Employee Sues Agency
abstract: Former state Health Department employee Martha Smith filed a sexual harassment lawsuit against the department in US Middle District Court, alleging that she was demoted from her job as public health behavioral research associate to program administratior because she spurned the sexual advances of Dr. George Tokuhata, director of the Bureau of Program Evaluation.

headline: Welfare defended as necessary
abstract: The author argues that Joanna Ehrhart, a recent recipient of the PA State Lottery prize, is wrong in pointing out that welfare recipients are people too lazy to work. He agrees with what she said about tax dollars funding welfare recipients, but he argues that many families need assistance to avoid becoming homeless, hungry, and without health care, and that they don't live better than those who work.

headline: Back to Tinicum!
abstract: Brewster Hopps was not amused about the delay of the 75th anniversary of the current PA state Capitol, because PA Governor Dick Thornburgh had other commitments and President Reagan was indisposed. The delay makes Hopps miss his deadline on his article comparing the current capitol to the first capitol.

headline: Ms. Hipp, Street honeymoon but she's divorced from job
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Senate voted that Yvonne Hipp be suspended from her state Senate job due to welfare fraud. Hipp will receive no pay and was not present to hear the case. Hipp is on her honeymoon with Pennsylvania State Senator T. Milton Street. Hipp is currently the executive adviser to a Senate committee that Street chairs. The new welfare rule which indicts Hipp does not mention Hipp personally but was clearly fashioned to apply to her situation. Hipp and street are to be notified when they return from their honeymoon.

headline: Greensburg gets recreation grant
abstract: Greensburg was awarded a $25,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Interior for the development of six recreational sites.

headline: Gambling on Limerick's fate
abstract: Editorial discusses the changes that have occurred in the thinking of the public about the construction of Limerick Nuclear Power plant along the Schuylkill in Montgomery County and the fact that the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission has said that it will hold Limerick to stricter standards that usual due to its location within 30 miles of millions of people.  Editorial notes that there are high stakes in this power plant - $1.5 billion has already been spent - and that the public will have to pay the costs if the NRC postpones a decision to grant an operating license to the plant.

headline: $1.99 milk is in store for some: Board Oks rise of 12 cents a gallon
abstract: The PA Milk Board ordered a rise of $0.12 per gallon of milk and cream in some counties.  This comes in a wake of increases and there are more increases expected in the future.

headline: Continued aid push for Centralia urged
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh should continue to seek federal aid to fight the 19-year-old underground mine fire in Centralia. The report from the governor's mine fire task force says federal funds are needed to fight the gasspewing fire burning unchecked in coal mines beneath the Columbia County town of 1,100. The total excavation could cost $90 million.

headline: null
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh gets the feel of the heavy machinery during a visit to the Parkway East construction project.

headline: Expert tips off seniors on con games
abstract: Pa. secretary of aging, Gorham Black, Jr.  Addressed seniors in Carlisle to warn them of scams.  He advised them to always ask for identification, never talk about personal finances and don't hesitate to call the police if you think you're being scammed.

headline: Welfare reform is possible
abstract: The author contends that Governor Dick Thornburgh and other state officials are going through the same problems and pressures as their national counterparts, regarding how to reduce welfare budgets while retaining benefits for the truly needy. This appears to be technically feasible, but the question is whether reform is politically possible as well.

headline: Back-door pension grab
abstract: PA Senator Edward Howard of Doylestown is sponsoring legislation that will help the state earn higher interest from its employee pension fund investments. Present laws restrict how the state's pension funds can be invested and the $3 billion in it is only earning about 6 percent interest. Under Howard's bill, the state will be able to pursue a more aggressive investment policy and may be able to increase its earnings to more than 13 percent.

headline: Mstate Democrats Elect Mezvinsky
abstract: A relative newcomer to Pennsylvania, Edward Mezvinsky, became the Democratic choice to head the party's state committee until next June.  Mezvinsky, 44, was selected to fill the unexpired term of Alex Debreczeni, who resigned effective August 13, 1981, midway through his second two-year term.  To win, the ex-congressman from Iowa beat back an effort by William Feucthenberger, 51, former Cumberland County chairman, who was sole opposition posed at the committee's meeting in the Embers.

headline: Group seeks a referendum on Bucks water project
abstract: Bucks County Commission was asked to include a question on the fall election ballot regarding the proposed Point Pleasant pumping-station project, a $35 million project which would divert up to 95 million gallons of Delaware River water daily. Commissioners want to stick to their votes approving the project earlier this year. The project has been in the planning stages since 1969. People believe the project will lead to an explosion of growth and development in central and upper Bucks County.

headline: Duquesne rate refund ordered
abstract: The Public Utilities Commission (PUC) voted to give Duquesne Light Co. customers a refund, which will not exceed eight dollars per customer, but the exact amount has not been determined yet.  The article details the explanation of the refund.

headline: Agriculture needs to be involved: Sec Block Speaks to Farmers In Harrisburg
abstract: US Secretary of Agriculture John R. Block spoke before a fundraising banquet of the PA Farmer's Association in Harrisburg, hours after the Soviet grain embargo had been lifted. He told farmers that agriculture needs to be involved in the political process. He also gave credit to President Reagan and the importance he gives to agricultural trade.

headline: Corporate dogma on pollution
abstract: A letter to the editor roasts a previous op-ed piece from David Anderson of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation entitled 'Reforming the Clean Air Act.' This writer states that Anderson's litany of facts illustrating that enforcing the Clean Air Act will contribute to a downturn in the economy is nothing but a smokescreen. The writer continues that Anderson's facts were not backed up by evidence and counters his argument with tests published by the Environmental Protection Agency. This writer is a blatant supporter of upholding the Clean Air Act and allowing states the responsibility to enforce them.

headline: null
abstract: Picture of the Moore-Rishel Covered Bridge

headline: Ex-policeman pleads guilty of extortion
abstract: Norman G. Bonneville, former assistant police chief, plead guilty to accepting bribes, following an investigation into the Harrisburg Police Bureau.  The article details the charges against Bonneville and talks about the investigation.

headline: Welfare: Reform gives way to cuts
abstract: The article covers the debate over Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh's "welfare reform" program. It also provides further explanation of the reformed program and what cutbacks are involved.

headline: Bad time for judge appointees
abstract: (Gannett News Service)  The author opines that the reason for Democrats in the Legislature blocking the confirmation of Judge Roy Wilkinson to the state Supreme Court is not based on his merits.  The author claims that the redistricting committee formed due to the 1980 census would become more Republican if Judge Wilkinson were confirmed.

headline: Municipal Pension Help Eyed;  State to Get New Municipal Pension Aid Plan
abstract: Legislation aimed at increasing pension funds of many Pennsylvania cities is expected to be introduced in the State Senate.  The legislations would set up a pension recovery fund and a municipal pension commission to study the situation.  This is scaled sown from the original legislation proposed by State Senator H. Craig Lewis (D).  The article outlines the specifics of the legislation

headline: Heinz hopes to speed lock and dam projects
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz has plans to expedite $430 million to rehabilite several locks and dams.  The projects are in critical need of repair and are hurting Pennsylvania's industries.  The article details the dams and locks to be repaired.

headline: Dye test will track TMI flow
abstract: A red fluorescent dye will be put into the Susquehanna River to track river currents 18 miles downstream from Three Mile Island. The test is aimed at determining whether the plant's monitoring stations are in effective locations. Meanwhile, technicians completed minor adjustments at the TMI Unit 2 cameras in preparation for a full entry later in April.

headline: Area drought still lingering despite rains
abstract: Although with above-normal rains this month and in February, this winter's drought problems still remain and have meant a loss for many farmers. The continuing deficit has forced counties in two states to remain on standby rationing.

headline: Dead-end to nuclear wasteland
abstract: The editor states that storage of nuclear waste is a problem for the nation and that the US Congress is not doing anything to address the problem.  He feels that there should be more places to store low level waste due the cost involved in shipping it.  He cites Three Mile Island as an example throughout the editorial

headline: $5.113 Billion to Rebuild or Replace:  1 of 4 Bridges in State Deficient, Study Shows
abstract: One of every four bridges in Pennsylvania is in need of repair or replacement according to a highway study requested by the Pennsylvania Highway Information Association.  The cost of fixing these bridge would be over $15 billion, so a 15 year plan was recommended.  The 15 year plan, however, does not cover bridges that may become defective within the next 15 years.  The article lists the locations of the bridges that are deficient.

headline: Far From Flashy, He Gets the Job Dunn
abstract: This narrative article acts as a biography for Daniel Dunn, the state of Pennsylvania's top law enforcement officer. Dunn was working for the FBI in Pittsburgh in the late 1960s when he ran a background check on an obscure young lawyer who is now his boss, Governor Dick Thornburgh. Dunn is typically a low key, behind-the-scenes type of man that does not enjoy receiving media publicity. However, when the Daily Numbers lottery drawing was rigged on April 24, 1980 he was hands-on and very active in attaining grand jury indictments for the offenders.

headline: What's a woman with no skills to do?
abstract: Recounts the pasts of several women who have been abused or deserted by their husbands and asks what a woman who never had to make a decision or work outside of the home supposed to do after divorce? The editorial explains the purpose and success that the Displaced Homemakers Program of the West Chester YWCA has had in training women how to support themselves and emerge from the vicious cycle that is welfare. This program was cut due to federal budget cuts and explains that it is more affordable to stay on welfare for these women than get a low-paying job that requires no skills.

headline: Baker contract may violate rule
abstract: In what appears to be a violation of a two-month old state Ethics Commission ruling, the Beaver County commissioner awarded Michal Baker Jr. Incorporated a $2,500 engineering contract without prior public notice.  The Ethics Commission wrote in a June 24th opinion that Baker may not contract with the Beaver County if the contract is valued at more than $500 unless the contract is awarded in an open and public process.  One of three criteria the commission listed to define the public process is prior public notice.  No notice was given before Beaver County commissioners' meeting that the county intended to award Baker a $2,500 contract to inspect Bray's Run Dam.

headline: Myers gets jail, fine for Abscam
abstract: Former Representative Michael Myers, the first Congressman thrown out of the House of Representatives since the Civil War, was sentenced today to three years in prison and fined $20,000 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Abscam political corruption investigation.  United States District Judge George Pratt imposed the sentence on Mayers, a Democrat from Pennsylvania.  In total, six defendants were sentenced for their convictions for bribery and conspiracy in the Federal Bureau of Investigation's "Arab Scam" sting operation in which agents posed as representatives of wealthy Arabs seeking political favors.

headline: Historic Preservation Input Sought in Area
abstract: The public is invited to provide input to a comprehensive state historic preservation plan to protect and revitalize older and historic buildings throughout the Commonwealth. Members of the PA state Bureau of Historic Preservation will conduct a series of meetings throughout the state this month.

headline: Emergency drill staged at TMI plant
abstract: The federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission observed a Three Mile Island nuclear reactor simulation of a nuclear emergency. The General Public Utilities, which owns the plant, hopes to persuade the NRC to allow the restart of TMI's undamaged reactor. Several hundred TMI workers, 20 state agencies and many emergency management workers took part in the drill to test their readiness to cope with another accident.

headline: Choice pork: Hog is in her heaven at Penna. Farm Show
abstract: Calvin H. Lazarus breed the winning hog, Ms. Elite at the Farm Show in Harrisburg, where farmers bring their livestock and crops for competition.

headline: Del. Senate approves 2 changes in bottle law
abstract: Delaware state Senate voted 11-9 to delete a portion of the state's "bottle law" which slated enactment of said law until Pennsylvania and Maryland state legislatures passed similar laws. The bottle law is a 5 cent deposit on soda and beer containers.

headline: . . . And a PAT plan
abstract: The Port Authority Transit (PAT) is facing a deficit due to federal funds being withdrawn from their budget.  The editors discuss two ways to supplement the revenues that will be lost; a county tax, and a gasoline tax.  The editors feel these are not good solutions for Pittsburgh and urge leaders to devise a plan to fund PAT.

headline: Father suspects murder at Haverford State Hospital: Cause of death: 'Pending'
abstract: Bill Broderick was strangled by his own sock at the Haverford State Hospital.  Investigators don’t know if it was murder or suicide.  The article details the facts surrounding the death and Broderick's life.

headline: White Mills Man Named Delegate to DC Aging Session
abstract: Governor Thornburgh chose 96 Pennsylvanians to act as delegates for the 1981 White House Conference on Aging.  The article details the act ivies of the Conference and states that local man Earl R. Reardon will be a delegate.

headline: Bar rates Shiomos 'unqualified'; Involvement in Abscam case cited
abstract: The Philadelphia Bar Association has rate Judge Thomas N. Shiomas as 'unqualified' to be retained on the Common Pleas Court due to his brief involvement in the Abscam investigation.  The article details Shiomas' career and also includes the ratings of other judges.

headline: Myerstown Attorney Nominated
abstract: Robert J. Eby, a Myerstown attorney, was nominated by Governor Thornburgh to fill a judgeship on the Lebanon County Court of Common Pleas.  The article details Mr. Eby's past career.

headline: Land-sale plan defended as 'fairer'
abstract: Pennsylvania Democrats are in a frenzy over Governor Thornburgh's lump land-sale plan as it will invite "land grabs" by people who have favors owed to them. Existing piecemeal approaches toward surplus state real property has led to conveyances for less than fair consideration. Governor Thornburgh needs $15 million from the land sales in order to complete the funding of the $6.8 billion general appropriation bill for education, welfare and health programs throughout the state. The proposed Surplus Land Disposition Act requires the General Services Department to conduct an annual survey of all the holdings of each state agency.

headline: Energy policy may boost rents; Landlords could act under state plan for conservation
abstract: Landlords of rental properties may be forced soon to upgrade these properties and make them energy efficient.  Under the proposal in the revised and final Pennsylvania Energy Policy prepared by the Governor's Energy Council, the owners of rental housing would be able to increase rents to pay for the upgrading.  Implementing the policy should not add to the cost of government.  The council's proposal stresses he need for greater use of Pennsylvania's coal directly and through extraction of synthetic fuels.  The state would set up a $30 million fund to finance low-interest residential conservation and solar home improvement loans through the sale of revenue bonds.

headline: Court order apparently ignored; Milk-pricing activity is 'as usual'
abstract: The Milk Marketing Board is continuing their sales even though a Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court order to change the way it sets milk prices.  The price order was passed to equalize retail milk prices in a new 20-county area.  The article provides further information about the court's orders and more details about the pricing of milk.

headline: DER Rewriting Federal Clean Air Act Statement
abstract: Pennsylvania environmental organizations vocal response directed at the Department of Environmental Resources has led the department to rewrite its third draft of a policy statement on the federal Clean Air Act.  Reagan is expected to sign the steel "stretch-out" legislation, which would extend for up to three years on a case-by-case basis the environmental deadlines mandated by the Clean Air act for steel companies. This fourth draft of the policy statement for the Clean Air Act would clear up unambiguous clauses non-comprehensible to laymen, have a stronger statement on acid rain and take a stronger stand in favor of protecting health by endorsing national ambient air standards.

headline: 1.3 million drivers got photo IDs in '80
abstract: The state Transportation Department stated that more than 1.3 million drivers got new driver's licenses with photo IDs on them in 1980.  They state that there are pleased with this

headline: Finding some fault with the no-fault divorce law in Pennsylvania
abstract: The new 'no-fault' law signed by Governor Dick Thornburgh that went into effect July of 1980 was designed to end an antiquated system of justice in PA that required proof of fault to obtain a divorce. Although it appeared simple, it has set up a complex web of conflicting local court rules that produce unanticipated courtroom scenarios.
Editorial briefly outlines new construction projects in Pittsburgh to take place in 1981 and optimistically predicates a transformation for Pittsburgh

headline: Bear in the air
abstract: PA state troopers have been using aerial police to track speeders. It started in 1978, and now the state has 6 helicopters and 1 airplane. A federal grant will allow the purchase of another plane.

headline: Natale cites past posts in judgeship try
abstract: Sebastian D. Natale is running for Dauphin County Common Please judge in the May 19 primary election. Serving previously as US commissioner and magistrate for the US Middle District Court in Harrisburg, Natale also worked as arbitrator in labor-management disputes. But what draws the interest of most voters is criminal law, he concedes, and agrees with Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposed mandatory sentence guidelines.

headline: New Ohio River locks advance
abstract: A $300 million modernization and relocation plan for the Gallispolis Locks and Dams on the Ohio River advanced an important step. The US Army Corps of Engineers' Board of Engineers for Rivers and Harbors have approved the plan to cut a channel through the middle of the dangerous river bend and construct two new locks for barge traffic.

headline: Summit on TMI Cleanup Proposed by Thornburgh
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh proposed a summit meeting with the state's entire congressional delegation to build a consensus on a cost-sharing plan for the cleanup of Three Mile Island.  Thornburgh outlined the preliminaries of his proposal to United States Representative Allen Ertel.  The article continues to explain Thornburgh's proposal.

headline: Dairy supports are a form of welfare
abstract: It costs the US government about $2 billion this fiscal year to maintain dairy price supports. Lately dairy farmers have not been following the rules of supply and demand and raising prices when there is not enough demand and way too much supply. Since that did not work for more profits they have asked for 7% more in price supports, yet they complain about urban welfare.

headline: DER to Challenge Rulling Won by State Coal Firms
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources(DER) stated that it would challenge a Commonwealth court ruling that prohibits DER from enforcing new rules on coal mines to prevent pollution.  There is some confusion over which rules the DER is allowed to enforce.

headline: 2 Truck Stops in Tax Fight Allowed to Reopen
abstract: Two trucks stops in Cumberland and Northumberland counties have been allowed to reopen after being shut down by state officials for more than two weeks amid allegations that they diverted $2.7 million in state diesel fuel taxes to an out-of-state account.

headline: Fire & Rescue Loans
abstract: The editors endorse a referendum that will be on the election ballot to expand a loan program for volunteer emergency services.  The article details the program and urges voters to support it.

headline: 2 ask veto of bill tied to renewal
abstract: State Representatives Thomas Murphy and Michael Dawida have asked Governor Thornburgh to veto a bill that would allow bond financing for residential rehabilitation in all of Allegheny County.  They argue that the bill would slow the rejuvenation of older, deteriorated cities and towns.

headline: Behind the diplomacy, bad blood:
abstract: The editorial argues that Philadelphia's mayor's efforts to bring Governor Dick Thornburgh into a school funding problem with the city Board of Education were shaped by the tensions between the two during the settlement last week of the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority's worker's strike. The Mayor wrote a letter requesting the cash shortfall be used as leverage to force the board members to resign. The editorial suspects the public pressure on the governor reflects the bitterness that City Hall officials feel toward the way the governor moved to bring the 19-day strike to an end.

headline: Need for state licensing
abstract: null

headline: Not written in water
abstract: The editors opine that now that the state water bond issue has been approved by voters, the state Legislature should follow the proposals that the "Vote Yes for Water" campaign committee set forth.  These include safeguarding and upgrading water supplies, dam safety and flood control projects, and strengthen port facilities.

headline: Supreme Court delays TMI ruling, giving Congress time to define law
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court decided to postpone consideration of a Three Mile Island case while Congress considers legislation that would resolve the dispute in favor of the government and the utilities yesterday. At issue is the 1980 ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission was required to hold a hearing on any change in nuclear-plant licenses whenever interested parties request one. Last week the House passed a bill that would allow the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to amend nuclear-plant licenses without hearings for two years.

headline: Farmers called better off Incorporated farms ruled out by PFA
abstract: The Director of the Pennsylvania Farm Association, Richard Dennison, states that farmers are better off avoiding incorporation despite federal tax breaks. Pennsylvania's culture is the family-owned farm he says. Moreover, incorporation is a more complicated way to go. This article details such complications.

headline: DOE to Help Bury 'Hot' TMI Material
abstract: The federal government has agreed to help owners of the damaged Three Mile Island nuclear plant bury or get rid of all the facility's radioactively contaminated equipment.  The "hot" equipment will be dangerous for 50,000 years.  In a memorandum of understanding, the Department of Energy and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission say they will assume responsibility for burying all of the Middletown, Pennsylvania, plants radioactively contaminated equipment in a government nuclear burial ground.  Some of the equipment first will be studied in a special Department of Energy research program to determine the best methods of packing it.

headline: 4 Roads Open To PAT In Fare-Zone Riddle
abstract: Officials of Allegheny County's mass transit system have four alternative courses of action after a Common Pleas Court order directing them to change the Port Authority Transit's system of zones and fares. They can either comply with Judge Silvestri's mandate to roll back fares to 60 cents, transfer charges to 10 cents and eliminate all promotional and pass programs, or appeal to the courts to gain a delay or reversal of the order, be denied such an appeal and then attempt to comply with the order, or continue the present zone and fare structure and risk being held in contempt of court.

headline: Firemen sounded warnings of flood
abstract: There was no formal warning when the flood hit, but the makeshift system of firefighters going door to door worked just fine. Neighbors went about the business of waking the other neighbors. There was only one person missing out of what could have been a deadly situation.

headline: At Large:  City of Chester is down, and you can expect a long count
abstract: The author feels that with the decision of Sun Ship to pull 3,100 from the city of Chester, the city will die economically.  He wonders if Governor Thronburgh can make them change their minds.  He cites stories from residents who feel the loss of jobs will make things even worse for them

headline: Benedict Aide Says Job Branch Ripe For Scam
abstract: A former campaign aide now in charge of state Auditor General Al Benedict's personnel bureau considers himself a likely suspect in the state grand jury probe into sales of jobs and  promotions within the department.  Russell J. Biggica, director of the auditor general's bureau of personnel, is none of a small circle of top-ranking officials in the auditor general's department who are under the shadow of the grand jury investigation.  The probe links a Brookline power broker who sold promises of state jobs and promotions to the department.  At least five employees have admitted they paid for their jobs; as many as 29 others in the department's Pittsburgh office have been targeted for investigation.

headline: Negotiations Set To Resume Today
abstract: Negotiations between the Philadelphia School District and the teachers' union will resume in the hopes of ending a fifty day strike.  The article details the history of the negotiations so far and talks about the possibility of other unions joining the strike to support the teachers.

headline: Panel Oks plan to divert water to Bucks, Montco
abstract: The Delaware River Basin Committee approved a water project that will divert water from the Delaware River for use in Bucks and Montgomery Counties.  The article details the project and states that the Environmental Protection Agency was at first against the project, but now they are not.  The project has been opposed by environementalists.

headline: SWAP Traded
abstract: There is not a whole lot of difference between the Thornburgh administration's SWAP tax on gasoline and 3.5% franchise tax on motor fuel producers which has passed the PA state House of Representatives. One way or another, the motorist is going to be paying the tax every time he buys gas. The franchise tax is far more subtle. The editorial board writes that PA Governor Thornburgh never could have guessed how much gas prices would have increased during his campaign.

headline: Farmers Told To Control The Source
abstract: Royal Palmer, export consultant for the Pennsylvania Agriculture Producers International, Inc., expressed his concerns with American Agriculture policy to the Adams County Farmers Associations.  Some problems he has are with containers for shipment, the price of butter, and encouraging more exports to the Middle East.

headline: Drilling Dilemma
abstract: The Citizens Advisory Council of Pennsylvania, created by the Pennsylvania state legislature to monitor and advise the Department of Environmental Resources states that tougher drilling regulations are needed as well as tougher enforcement in order to protect the land and water where gas and oil exploration occurs. Currently, due to the lack of legislation concerned with protecting Pennsylvania's land, stream and population, companies involved with oil and gas exploration within Northwestern Pennsylvania are cutting corners in order to make more profit. The Department of Environmental Resources has largely overlooked this are as it is in a remote area with low inhabitance. However, the damage coming from oil exploration is negatively impacting rural areas.

headline: 5 Hurt In Accidents Involving PAT Buses
abstract: The Pittsburgh Port Authority has had a wave of accidents, so the article goes into detail about the accidents and what happened.

headline: Firm ordered: Pay PennDOT
abstract: The Chicago-based Peabody-Magnaflux Corporation has 10 days to pay $30,834 to the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation and, in return, the state will drop 148 criminal charges of theft by deception and deceptive business practices that had been lodged against the testing company.  A consent order was approved by Common Pleas Judge Henry R. Smith Jr.  The order also says that Peabody-Magnaflux will cooperate fully with the state attorney general in the pending investigation of possible violations of the laws of Pennsylvania by present and former officials of Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: Boarding home progress
abstract: Four Lower Bucks County boarding homes were among the first 11 in the Philadelphia area to be licensed by the state of PA during ceremonies at the state official in Philadelphia. The issuance of licenses marks a significant milestone in a longstanding campaign to ensure safe and adequate living conditions for the estimated 60,000 to 100,000 PA who reside in personal-care boarding homes.

headline: Benedict aide tied to job-selling racket
abstract: The statewide investigating grand jury has charged that a Pittsburgh supervisor in the PA Auditor General's Department collected more than $90,000 for more than 20 jobs or promotions in a jobs-for-sale racket in the department. Attorney General LeRoy S Zimmerman said today conspiracy charges will be filed against Nicholas Saittis, a $22,690-a-year supervisor in the PA Bureau of Liquor.

headline: New King of the Hill-Altoona
abstract: In Harrisburg, PA the legislative show has been dominated for years by two heavyweights: Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. However, as more people have moved out of the cities and increasingly outward into the suburbs and countryside and unlikely contender has emerged...Altoona.

headline: Photograph: Mothers' Row
abstract: Photograph of two mothers at a dedication of a statue to honor the dead of World War II.

headline: Task Force Sees TMI Draft Bill
abstract: A draft bill in the US Senate would create a national insurance pool to cover costs of nuclear disasters and cover the Three Mile Island nuclear accident for $262 million.  The article explains exactly how much General Public Utilities, the owner of the Three Mile Island Nuclear plant, would be responsible for.  It also outlines the coverage amounts for other industries in the event of a technological disaster.

headline: Governor tells farmers they have a friend in him
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh attended the opening of the 65th annual Pennsylvania Farm Show where he promised to continue promoting legislation to keep the state's agricultural industry growing.  He and his wife toured the exposition.

headline: Drought alert looms for some areas
abstract: R. Timothy Weston, Pennsylvania's representative on the Delaware River Basin Commission, stated that decreasing water supplies are expected to bring an official drought warning soon.  The drought warning would mean a 15 per cent reduction in water supplies for New York and New Jersey.  Though Weston stated that Philadelphia will not be affected because it already conserves a lot of water.  The article discusses the implications of the imminent drought warning in depth.

headline: A new tax drafted on gasoline
abstract: State House Majority Leader Samuel Hayes Jr. (R-Blair) is drafting a bill that would levy a "franchise tax" of around 3.5 percent on gasoline sold in the state for transportation purposes, raising about $192 million a year. The tax would replace Governor Dick Thornburgh's SWAP, a proposal for tax-increase at the pump. The plan money would go toward fixing PA Department of Transportation's treasury problems, but it would hurt Mayor William Green's tax proposal for the city of Philadelphia.

headline: Free legal aid threatened, says lawyer
abstract: Robert Berkowitz, lawyer for the Neighborhood Legal Services Association (NLSA) fears that free legal aid for the poor will be terminated by President Reagan.   The Reagan Administration also wants to cut funding for senior citizens to get free legal help.  The article details the proposals to cut aid.

headline: 'Bogus bids' linked to $29,390 rehab grant
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Community Affairs awarded a $29,390 grant to a Harrisburg non-profit corporation which submitted what one Department of Community Affairs staff member called "bogus" construction estimates for a housing rehabilitation project.  The article goes further into detail about the grant dispersment.

headline: Benedict asks his subordinates to give to political fund
abstract: Auditor General, Al Benedict, whose office is already under investigation for possible campaign fund abuse, is again soliciting political contributions from his subordinates. A letter was sent out under the 'Friends of Al Benedict' letterhead urging workers to join the '500 Club.' To join, workers are asked to voluntarily donate $500 to be used to retire the remaining $80,000 debt from the 1980 campaign so that Benedict can remain a viable alternative to the present administration in Harrisburg. The letters were sent out October 6, approximately 20 days before Supreme Court Chief Justice Henry O'Brien approved the empanelling of a grand jury which will pursue basic allegations of job-selling, liquor franchise promises and making.

headline: New lottery millionaire may come from W. Pa.
abstract: Four of five finalists of the Big 50 lottery game are from western Pennsylvania. The millionaire drawing is scheduled for July 10, and the winner will receive $50,000 a year for life.

headline: Photograph: Up Front
abstract: Photograph of Governor Thornburgh and veterans during a dedication of a statue to the dead of World War II.

headline: TEED OFF/ Whose Public Utility Commission is this?; Just an innocent little game of golf
abstract: For years Pennsylvania consumer advocates have lambasted the Public Utility Commission as political puppets whose knees jerk whenever the big utilities yank the strings.  When Public Utility Commissioner James H. Cawley plays golf with top Bell Telephone officials at Merion Golf Club, as The Bulletin's Janet Novack revealed he did last week, he makes it virtually impossible for the Public Utility Commission or the utilities to avoid such unsavory characterizations.  The Bell people were not merely company executives.  They were the company officials who deal with rates and regulations.  An rates and regulations are matters over which Cawley and his fellow commissioners hold power.

headline: Letters to the editor; Disgusted
abstract: The "Hare Raid" article should have included people finding a more humane solution to their problem than by clubbing rabbits to death.  The "Unwed Mothers Keeping Babies" article glamorizes young girls getting pregnant and getting free handouts.

headline: Drought emergency is declared in region
abstract: The Delaware River Basin Commision (DRBC) declared a water emergency and banned the use of all nonessential water use.  The DRBC has four member states, including Pennsylvania.  The Commission is worried the next summer will be even worse and want to prepare the public for such an event.

headline: A SEPTA board leader writes off rail takeover
abstract: SEPTA board vice chairman Judith Harris stated that she does not expected SEPTA to take over the commuter rail system.  She also stated that it would be too expensive to take over Conrail's contract, which expires in December, but if they did have the funds they would have to cut several stops and routes.

headline: Full-Court Press
abstract: Opinion piece in which the author expresses the need for the PA senate to confirm Judge Roy Wilkinson as a State Supreme Court Justice.  He cites the slow speed of the courts and the need for another Justice.  He outlines Judge Wilkinson career and accomplishments.

headline: Bond specifics unknown
abstract: The Fayette County Democrat's, William Lincoln, problem is he wants electorate to support the proposed $300 million bond issue to aid water and port projects, but he fears the voting will more likely be done out of ignorance than enlightenment. No one really knows at this point exactly what the people will be getting should they approve the bond issue. Legislators will have water projects in their districts desperately needing funds and any vote against may be interpreted as opposition to aid rather than a desire to not be stampeded. No one knows the punishment for failing to repay a loan.

headline: Benedict election ran $91,000 in debt
abstract: Auditor General Al Benedict is asking his employees to make a contribution to reduce his $91,00 debt from his recent campaign.  The article details the going-ons of politicians, including: state Treasure Budd Dwyer has already begun fundraising for his next campaign, a publicity stunt at the Three Mile Island (TMI) Nuclear plant, Bill Wewer becoming the new executive director of the Pennsylvania Historical Commission, Julius McCoy is taking a leave of absence form his job at PennDOT while he runs for mayor, and a scandal involving TMI and the National Inquirer.

headline: New Plan Saves County Senate Seats
abstract: Democratic and Republican negotiators have reached a tentative agreement on a reapportionment plan that will preserve all seven of Allegheny county's senate seats even though there have been heavy population losses within Allegheny county. Therefore, the new reapportionment plan maintains seats for the county's three "city" and four "suburban" senators. The three city senators are: Eugene Scanlon, James Romanelli, and Leonard Bodack. The four suburban senators are: Edward Early, Michael Fisher, Edward Zemprelli, and Frank Pecora.

headline: Port unit rebuffs Thornburgh in filling key post
abstract: The Delaware River Port Authority voted to hire Raymond G. Heinzelmann as director of its World Trade Division, over Governor Thornburgh's recommendation of Raymond Wittig.  The article details the importance of the position, as well as Mr. Heinzelmann's career.

headline: The Effects of TMI
abstract: The accident at Three Mile Island had a profound effect on the public.  It has affected the future of every nuclear plant under construction.  The article continues to discuss the effects of the Three Mile Island accident.

headline: Local Mushroom Industry
abstract: This editorial broadcast seeks to incite constituent interest in the mushroom agri-business. While there are many decent and credible mushroom farmers/packers, there are many who still pollute streams, torch workers barracks, and underpay immigrants. An editorialist wants Governor Thornburgh to appoint a special investigating team to get the bottom of the mushroom agri-business so that botulism poisoning and exploitation does not occur any longer.

headline: Drought relief
abstract: The author of this letter, state Senator Jeanette Reibman, writes that she is disappointed with the federal government's rejection of Governor Dick Thornburgh's petition for aid to water companies affected by the drought, as well as disappointed with the Senate's defeat of her proposal to provide state loans to aid drought-stricken communities. But points out to the encouraging news that New Jersey has approved drought-relief projects and hopes PA will soon follow suit and enact legislation to provide voter referendum proposing $100 million for loans to conserve water by upgrading water supply systems.

headline: A simple (?) transaction
abstract: The state Senate joined the House in approving a bill transferring 1.68 acres of land in Bensalem Township from the state Welfare Department to the PA Turnpike Commission. The move will allow for the much-needed construction work at the turnpike's Route 1 Interchange. The exit ramps will be widened to allow for less rush-hour vehicle pileup in the traveling lanes of the turnpike. The editorial argues the legislature took 6 months, too long, to make the decision.

headline: Fund raiser for state police keeps 69%
abstract: Barry Arno, a fund raiser, kept 69% of $375,000 raised for a Pa. state police union.  The action is not illegal because of the deal he signed with the union, but there will still be an investigation.  Normally, fund raiser take 10-15% of the money raised.  Mr. Arno has been pled guilty to running a phony charity last year.

headline: Bringing city alive at night
abstract: The author feels that Erie should institute a campaign, such as the on used in Buffalo, NY, to draw people downtown at night to shop and use entertainment facilities.  The author state the fear of being unsafe should be stymied by increased police patrols.

headline: Benedict Fires Deputy Counsel
abstract: Auditor General Al Benedict has fired Washington County Democratic Chairman Michael Hanna as a deputy counsel. Hanna was dismissed May 29. Hanna's press secretary stated that Hanna's dismissal had nothing to do with the grand jury investigation into allegations of job selling in Benedict's department.

headline: New redistricting plan in county set for panel
abstract: An apparent compromise redistricting plan for state House seats in Allegheny County will be presented to the state Reapportionment Commission on Thursday.  The plan is an altered version of what became known as the Cyril Wecht proposal.  Wecht, Democratic chairman in Allegheny County, had been pushing a plan that caused some party leaders to rebel.  Nevertheless, two of Wecht's targets still would be running against severe odds. Democrat Michael M. Dawida, who represents the 26th District, would be running against Robert P. Horgos, also a Democrat, representing the 36th District.  Dawida still would have a chance because he is a tremendous campaigner, but the odds would be against him because most of Horgos' district would remain intact.

headline: Recreation- Demand is accelerating
abstract: When Art Buchwald suggested that joggers be licensed, he was recognizing what a growth industry recreation has become. Camping sites at state parks were sold out Memorial Weekend. Even PA Governor Thornburgh acknowledges public demand for recreation are accelerating in his PA Recreation Plan. It does not get into economics though. The issue is how to provide better facilities, better maintain them, and handle increased usage.

headline: The industry's view; Breeder reactor: Worthy plan
abstract: The position take in a recent editorial placed the Clinch River Breeder Reactor Project is in a context that could be misunderstood and overlooks some important facts.  The consensus of expert opinion, in the United States and worldwide, is that he would be foolish to turn our backs on a virtually inexhaustible source of energy such as the breeder.  Not only do public opinion surveys bear this out, but also the activities of various countries in the field of nuclear development bear this out.  The Clinch River project is at the forefront of breeder technology.  This is why the national Rural Electric Cooperative Association, representing rural electric systems in 46 states, believes the Clinch River project is vital to America's energy future.

headline: Mauling spurs suit
abstract: The parents of a 2 year old Detroit boy who was killed earlier this month by a pet wolf are suing the owner, keeper, seller, and breeder of the animal.

headline: Easing Auto Rules
abstract: The editorial argues that the Reagan administration's proposals for the relaxation or elimination of 34 environmental and safety regulations on carmakers might not cause significant damage to the environment or to the cause of safety. The editorial approves of the government not burdening the industry with unnecessary and expensive design regulations, but does not think the government should try to guarantee profits for American automakers by removing competition from foreign imports.

headline: A solution for PennDOT?
abstract: Afraid to support another tax bill after Governor Dick Thornburgh's unpopular gasoline tax, state House Republicans are not disclosing what they view as a favorable tax that would help solve PA Department of Transportation's money problems. The measure would replace the gasoline tax with a franchise tax on companies that sell gasoline and other petroleum transportation products wholesale.

headline: Funds earmarked for special grand jury in Montgomery Co.
abstract: Montgomery County, PA commissioners tentatively approved funds for a proposed investigating grand jury. The commissioners' action was taken during a hearing on the proposed 1982 budget for the district attorney's office, tentatively approved at $1.8 million. The grand jury would cost the county no more than $25,000 because it will be staffed primarily by members in the DA's office.

headline: City Parking Authority to Renew Offer to State
abstract: Harrisburg Parking Authority intends to renew its offer to the commonwealth to provide up to 519 parking spaces within the municipal system to accommodate state cars which will be displaced next fall when work begins on an addition to the Capitol.

headline: Bensalem Twp. Teachers on strike as contract talks are broken off
abstract: Teachers in Bensalem Township went on strike after negotiations between the union and the school district broke off at 3am with no further talks scheduled. Teachers worked last week under the terms of their old contract with the district while bargaining continued between the two sides. The main unresolved issue is wages.

headline: New State House seat in
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislative Reapportionment Commission, charged earlier this year with the task of drawing new legislative boundaries in the state, announced its plans for local redistricting that will create a new state House seat from portions of Adams, Cumberland and York Counties, according to state Representative Kenneth J. Cole.  The new house seat, which will be known as the 199th State House District, will include Berwick, Hamilton, Latimore and Reading Townships, and the boroughs of Abbottstown, East Berlin and York Springs in Adams County.

headline: Reviving The 'Ditch'
abstract: The editorial explains that there is a revival of the idea to build a river-canal link between Pittsburgh and Lake Erie. But it argues that the price tag, which was over $1 billion in the 1960s, would probably be at least $2.5 billion today. Proponents expect the federal government to fund the project. The editorial argues that old waterways remain in a dismal state of disrepair, such as the locks and dams along the Ohio River, and that it does not make sense to talk about building new ones.

headline: Thornburgh asks Mobil to roll back price hike
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh called on Mobil Oil Corp to roll back its recent 4-cent-a-gallon price hike that was prompted by PA's new oil franchise tax. They did similarly in New York and the governor believes they should do the same for PA.

headline: Milk Board
abstract: The city is in court fighting to overturn last March's milk price increase. The three cents a gallon hike costs people in Western PA an extra five million dollars a year. Getting rid of the Milk Board would be a more direct route of solving the problem.

headline: Editorial/Opinion
abstract: A cartoon featuring a sign "Welcome to Centralia." in a hilly and rocky location. The sign is half-burned with one of the sign posts completely burned through. The caption underneath the cartoon says, ' "Eventually, it will burn out!"---U.S. Interior Secretary James Watt.'

headline: After Yellow auction today, cabs still will be scarce
abstract: Yellow Cab Co of Philadelphia goes on the auction block today, and the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce is convinced the change of ownership is good news. Yellow has been operating under federal Bankruptcy Court protection for the last three years. They claim its nothing person, but the company hasn't been providing the city of its needs. The city only has 850 cabs when its supposed to have 1400 cabs.

headline: Gay cons transferring here for trysts?
abstract: The Philadelphia sheriff's office suspects homosexual inmates at Dallas State Prison are arranging to testify as witnesses in city trials in order to transfer temporarily to the less restrictive city prison system, where sexual trysts might be possible. The sheriff's office yesterday refused to honor subpoenas for nine prisoners called to testify at the trial of a Dallas inmate charged with assaulting a deputy sheriff while in Philadelphia.

headline: Celebrities Abound:  Pittsburgh Opens Convention Center With Big Flourish
abstract: Governor Thornburgh cut the ribbon to open the David L. Lawerence Convention Center in Pittsburgh.  Many celebrities were present at the ceremonies, designed to bring attention to the Center in the hopes that businesses from all over the U.S. will want to rent it for their events.

headline: Bid to Move Lottery Fix Trial Fails
abstract: Dauphin County Judge William Lipssitt ruled on Friday, April 3, that two defendants in the alleged million dollar fix of the Pennsylvania Daily Number game cannot have their trial moved to another county and tried separately on the charges. Defendants Nick Perry and Edward Plevel had requested that their charges to be separated, that they be separated as defendants, and that the trial be held in another county.

headline: Nixed
abstract: Robert Gleason was voted down 25-24 for a seat on the PA Turnpike Commission. Gleason was nominated by Governor Thornburgh and as is typical as of late, Democrats voted down Gleason's potential incumbency in a continuation of its cold war against the administration over nominations.

headline: Saving Lifeguards
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources backed away from a controversial proposal which would have permitted the operation of public pools and beaches in PA without lifeguards. The editorial argues it is a sensible and welcome decision, recognizing that there was a large opposition to the idea.

headline: U.S. knows N-plant saboteur, won't prosecute
abstract: The U.S. attorney for Western Pennsylvania, J. Alan Johnson, reports he knows who sabotaged the valves at the nuclear power plant in Shippenport, Beaver County. However, he is not going to prosecute since there is not enough evidence for a criminal prosecution. He states that the saboteur is no longer in a position to interfere with the safe operation of the facility.

headline: Milk Zooms
abstract: Milk prices have begun raising rapidly in area stores. Supermarkets were having a price war, but because of profit losses it had to go back to above costs.

headline: End near in wait for water; Counties to sign pact
abstract: After 13 years of planning, Bucks and Montgomery counties are ready to sign an agreement to build a water treatment plant and to send water to a nuclear power plant.  One of the causes of the delay was a pending lawsuit in U.S. District Court to block the project.  The project will decrease taxes for Bucks county residents

headline: Airport Report: Local Officials Doubt HIA Will Be Self-Supporting in Near Future; PEL Cites HIA Deficit Operation
abstract: null

headline: Gekas' bill proposes a judicial center for Capitol Complex
abstract: State Senator George W. Gekas filed a bill to establish a Pennsylvania Judical Center in the Capitol Complex.  The Center would house the state Supreme and Superior courts and possibly Commonwealth Court.

headline: City Threatens Refugees'; Landlord With Power Cutoff
abstract: City housing officials have threatened to cut electric power to four ramshackled apartment buildings on the Boulevard of the Allies on July 22, 1981, unless Doctor Le Phuoc Sang replaces wiring hazardous to his Vietnamese refugee tenants.  Sang was fined $523 by City Housing Court on Friday or city and county code violations, and the landlord faces still more charges by the county Health Department.

headline: Big Pension
abstract: The editors opine that the legislatures' pensions are too big.  They site former representative H. Jack Seltzer as being too large.  They feel that the State Employees' Retirement Board should have their budget cut.

headline: Nixon: The Unraveling of a Paradox Wrapped in an Enigma
abstract: States that the presidency enormously magnified and dramatized the paradoxes that were implicit in Richard Nixon's character from the earliest presidential years. Brief examples include: a candidate while in Miami Beach in 1968 promised truth in government and brought us untruth; a Quaker president who ordered more bombs dropped than any man in history; his quest to win the most electoral votes but stated that nobody is a friend of ours; the supreme anti-communist who nevertheless established friendly relations with the largest bloc of Communists.

headline: Selling the land slide
abstract: Despite criticism of a recent administration-sponsored land-sales law, it is an effective way for the Commonwealth finally to obtain revenue from state property which has become surplus or otherwise unprofitable.  Governor Thornburgh has said that the primary function of the land sales would be to bring the budget into line because some $15 million was anticipated to be raised from the land sales, should they be authorized. The bill requires state agencies to make inventories of their surplus land by July 1 of each year.

headline: Thornburgh Tours City, Amazed by Progress; TMI Re-Start Will Come Only After Safety Assured, Gov. Says
abstract: null

headline: Mushrooms recalled
abstract: The Food and Drug Administration said unbranded cans of mushrooms sold in New York and PA may be contaminated with botulin toxin and should be returned to the place of purchase. About 2,400 cans are believed to be in the stores. No reports of death or illness have been received, but the FDA advised consumers not to eat the mushrooms.

headline: Erie is heading for water crisis
abstract: The consultant's report on Erie's water system made the dire prediction that if local public officials allow the Erie Water Bureau to flounder along with an aging distribution system and perennial financial deficits, it will ultimately lead to a major public water service crisis that will be extremely costly to overcome. Erie has to be able to supply water if Erie wants more jobs and industry.

headline: AMP asks review on airport services
