abstract: Capital City Airport has asked the state not to eliminate state-paid police and fire protection. They said the states decision may impact the long-range viability of the airport.  Some accuse Governor Thornburgh of dragging his feet on negotiations between the two.

headline: George Bird Murder
abstract: A radio broadcaster rallies for public support to make the Philadelphia District Attorney, the courts and parents to put away the druggies, pushers and hoodlums that thrive in West Philadelphia. The murder of a likeable neighborhood man incites this rally cry. George Bird resisted robbery by eight neighborhood thugs and as a result they beat him to death.

headline: City's economic picture darkens
abstract: The worst of the job were behind us they said. Weak manufacturing companies had pretty well been shaken out in the 1970's, they claimed. And with a sounder base of businesses dealing in service and knowledge, they boasted, the Philadelphia economy appeared to be matching or even outpacing the nation during the short recession of 1980. Now the economic news has shifted when the region lost 15,800 jobs during the year ended July 1.

headline: Black Pols Push for School Solution
abstract: A group of black elected officials expressed their concern over the apparent lack of progress in resolving the city's public school crisis, and said they feared "a long and crippling strike."  They then met with Mayor Green in his office, but the only public result of all the activity was a promise that the mayor and the other politicians would meet again.  Meanwhile, a Common Pleas Court hearing on the School District's effort to break its contract with the teachers' union ended without a ruling.  The black officials' statement said the issue of the system's stability transcended race, even though the district's enrollment is 70 percent black.

headline: NJ prosecutors: Abscam 'besmirched' Del Tufo
abstract: Two former New Jersey attorneys general and a top state law enforcement official have publicly declared that former US Attorney Robert J. Del Tufo was treated unfairly by a federal judge who criticized him for moving too slowly during the FBI Abscam investigation.

headline: Spend to save Valley Forge
abstract: This opinion piece urges public awareness regarding the appropriation of 700 acres of prime land adjacent to the Valley Forge National Historical Park. The Interior Department asked for $45 million to acquire additional lands to add to the national park system, however, those funds can only be used in an emergency. The writer illustrates that the additional acreage adjacent to Valley Forge is an emergency as it is prime for strip mall and residential development.

headline: Thornburgh's challenge to use of nuclear energy
abstract: Soon PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will go to Washington hoping to bell the cost-cutting cats in the White House and secure a long-term commitment of federal funds for the clean-up of the damaged and potentially dangerous nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island. Thornburgh has been putting together the pieces of how to pay for completion of the TMI clean up. The owners have used 2/3 of the insurance money of just the first phase. The insurance money will only go so far, and government has to step in.

headline: Navy Bands to Perform
abstract: Remarks by Governor Dick Thornburgh and a performance by the US Naval Academy's Concert Band will highlight opening ceremonies of the 1981 PA State Farm Show in Harrisburg.

headline: Fines asked against state for defying exhaust order
abstract: The Delaware Valley Citizens Council for Clean Air asked that fines be imposed against Pennsylvania for defying a judge's order to start an automobile-emissions inspection program in 12 counties.  The article details the court order.

headline: Amtrak snubs cuts, urges more runs
abstract: A study by Amtrak and the Federal Railroad Administration, requested by Congress, and released Friday April 10, details possible expansion of high-speed passenger train service between major population centers. This comes despite the Reagan Administration's proposals to trim its budget from $718 to $613 million next year, and its opposition to Amtrak's corridor expansion.

headline: Getting at Agee, not the press
abstract: People like Philip Agee, who has been going around exposing identities of CIA agents, ought to be prevented from trying to dismantle US intelligence operations, because we need a law for that. That law should not muzzle the press when it reports mistakes in the intelligence field. A House bill will punish people like Agee.

headline: City's Elderly Protest Condos
abstract: Nine busloads of senior citizens from six Philadelphia apartment houses protested at the State Capitol Building against condominium conversions, pressuring lawmakers to support bills that would make condo conversions more difficult. A press release by the group blamed the condo conversion trend on greedy real estate speculators from Chicago.

headline: Block grants to the states: fallout from a Reagan brainstorm
abstract: The opinion author explains that a national debate is emerging over the Reagan administration's plans to combine 80-some separate grant-in-aid programs into five large block grants, and then allow the state governments to divide what's left in the grants. The author argues that it has led mayors, interest groups and congressional skeptics to question whether states will deliver social services without strong and detailed instruction from Washington. But governors, including PA's Dick Thornburgh, and state legislators believe the block grants would permit them to deliver services more economically and with less regulation.

headline: No Distance Runners in 4th District
abstract: The article states that neither candidate running for the state senate seat vacated by U.S. Representative Joseph Smith has long term political goals.  Nicholas Stampone and Charles Keeler are running for the seat, but its term will only be for one year.  After that, the 4th district will be absorbed by other districts.

headline: Water Bill Needs Governor's Backing for Passage, Kury Says
abstract: Former state Senator Franklin L. Kury stated that the proposed water resources management bill pass without tougher language and the strong support of Governor Thornburgh.  The article details Kury's opinions on how to improve the bill.

headline: Thoughts on TMI tomorrow
abstract: The author took a media tour of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant, which had an accident in 1979, sponsored by General Public Utilities (GPU).  The author discusses who he feels should pay for the clean up of the site, and what GPU should do next.

headline: Pa. naturalist warns food prices may soar out of consumers' reach
abstract: Robert Rodale, a naturalist, states that increases energy costs are pushing the cost of food up.  He has created the Cornucopia project to promote a sustainable food system.  The article outilnes his and his family's history and his business, Rodale Press, which publishes Mother Earth and Organic Gardening.

headline: 'Firm commitment' to seek $123 million; Reagan sets TMI aid figure
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh state that the Reagan Administration has pledged $123 million to cleanup Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear facility, after an accident there in 1979.  The article details a cost-sharing plans and what needs to be done in the ways of cleanup.

headline: Another Railroad That's on the Ropes
abstract: US Transportation Secretary Lewis believes Conrail's (Consolidated Rail Corporation) railroad lines, will never become more than marginally profitable, and therefore wants Congress to revoke the workers' guaranteed-pay law, cut away commuter-hauling routes, and for a new company to operate the high-cost freight terminals along the Northeast Corridor. After this, he believes that other railroads would be interested in buying Conrail's tracks. Washington has invested 3.3 billion dollars in rehabilitation of the lines, but will need at least another $342 million in federal help to become self-sustaining.

headline: Governor picks 7 to review siege at Graterford Prison
abstract: Governor Thornburgh announced the creation of a seven member panel to review the events and conditions surrounding the recent hostage crisis at the Graterford Prison in Montgomery County, PA. Thornburgh promised to set up this panel on November 2 after six employees who had been held hostage were released unharmed.

headline: City's housing projects: A place to call home
abstract: A feature on the history and restoration of housing projects in Philadelphia. The families who live there are highlighted.

headline: Board Votes to Hire 200 New Teachers
abstract: Coming off of a 50 day teachers' strike provoked by 3,500 layoffs, and facing a deficit of $70 million, the Board of Education decided to hire 200 new teachers yesterday. The Commonwealth Court order that ended the strike October 27 also canceled the layoffs. About 2,700 of the layoffs were teachers but 77 of them didn't return. Additionally, another 200 to 400 teachers left the district after summer vacation and the strike. The district's legal department is seeking to fill some of these vacancies by transferring teachers from the music, counseling, library and bilingual special programs which had been eliminated by the layoffs but then restored with the court order. The vacancies created by the transfer would not be filled.

headline: No equality in reapportionment plan
abstract: If the purpose of reapportionment is to insure equal voter representation, the proposed legislative reapportionment plan has failed. The flagrant disregard for municipal boundaries by the commission because many citizens to lose their impact. Voter confusion is common, when districts cut across municipalities. Author sees no equality in the plan.

headline: Water Loans? Yes
abstract: The editors urge readers to vote yes on the "Water Project Loan Referendum," which involves a $300 million bond issue for water projects, such as rehabilitating reservoirs and pipelines.

headline: Tiny Ohio River town seeks big power plant
abstract: Potter Township in Beaver County wants to build a $100 million hydroelectric power plant on the Montgomery Dam.  If Potter wins the permit from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, it will be the smallest municipality to build such a plant, but it has competition from several large utility companies

headline: Preserving state farmland
abstract: Pennsylvania has lost 50 percent of its farmland since the turn of the century, according to state agricultural officials.  Less than half of the land now farmed in the state is prime farmland and much of this prime land is vulnerable to development because it is near major urban areas.  Preserving farmland is one of the more popular issues of the day.

headline: Fish Commission under attack
abstract: State representative Carmel Sirianni charged that the Fish Commission hasn't been paying its 39 cents per acre in lieu of taxes to local governments.  The commission officials stated that they'd have to check.  The money is supposed to be divided up by local governments.

headline: Arnie tees off on promoting PennDOT
abstract: In an effort to illustrate the state's commitment to making the state transportation system one of the best, Arnold Palmer, Western PA's most popular golfer, was in Pittsburgh to promote the system. Also present at the new Sewickley Bridge project was state Transportation Secretary, Commerce Secretary, and Governor Dick Thornburgh, who said it's important that residents recognize PennDOT's work favorably.

headline: Governor's Foe Pushes For Names
abstract: Pennsylvania State Senator Craig Lewis, a leading critic of the Thornburgh Administration, is asking the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court to expedite lawsuit hearing Lewis filed last month. The lawsuit brought against Governor Dick Thornburgh and Jay Waldman, Thornburgh's general counsel, resulted when the administration refused to supply the names of lawyers it has employed. The Thornburgh Administration claims that the case should be dismissed for Lewis' lack of merit as he did not exhaust all other means to obtain the aforementioned information before filing suit.

headline: City's revival is a team effort...
abstract: The author notes that the Philadelphia area was at one time an important industrial site, but that times are changing.  The author lays out several ways he feels the city can be revived including; exploiting comparative advantages in the health area, fix problems with the school districts, and encourage leadership from the business community.

headline: Boondoggling up and down
abstract: Although the Capitol building switched from manual to push button elevators several years ago, up until recently the elevator operators were still on the payroll at taxpayers expense.  The author feels that finally cutting the needless jobs was good, but worries about the unnecessary spending in government.

headline: No fights or feuds and not much fun in Bucks contests
abstract: The candidates in the race to fill three county judgeships in Bucks County have agreed to run a high-level campaign with no mudslinging. The rest of the ballot focuses on nominations for six county offices ranging from sheriff to jury commissioner.

headline: Wormleysburg Legion statue dedicated to WW II sailors
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh gave the keynote address at a dedication presented by the Pennsylvania Department of the American Legion in Wormleysburg.  The statue was dedicated to Navy sailors who lost their lives during World War II.  The article details the events at the dedication.

headline: TMI Aftermath:  A Cost Question
abstract: Ratepayers of General Public Utilities Corp. (GPU) see rate increases to pay for the maintenance of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant after the nuclear accident in 1979.   Rates are six times higher than prior to the accident.  The article explains the causes and effects of the rate increases.

headline: Protectionism not the cure for disappearing farmland
abstract: The author of the letter to the editor writes that the editorial on Pennsylvania's farmland is mistakenly calling on protectionism. He argues that protectionism won't work, and that PA cannot spend the money it uses to buy agricultural products from other states on its own products, and that it is cheaper to buy from other states. He offers alternatives to improve PA's agriculture efficiency, such as through subsidies, tax breaks, and other government programs. He also argues that non-economic elements, such as tradition and beauty of the state's farms, cannot be easily evaluated.

headline: Fish Ladders; Restoring a Lost Resource
abstract: A proposal before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission would require the owners of four hydroelectric dams along the river to install fish ladders or elevators to permit shad, herring, eels and other anadromous fish to detour the damns and pass from the sea to the upper parts of the river to spawn.  The article goes further into detail about the need for these ladders, the costs and the construction plans.

headline: AT LONG LAST
abstract: Immediately after signing a new 3.5 percent wholesale gasoline tax into law, Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh held a press conference and announced his promised plans of construction would begin on the Blue Route n 1982 and the $234 million highway would be completed in 1987.

headline: Grand Jury Focuses on Con Man
abstract: A grand jury probe concerning influence peddling in the state auditor general’s office focuses on con man Samuel “Sonny” Peters. Five Pittsburgh men were conned into taking part in buying franchises in a proposed private liquor store system. Lloyd Hickman committed suicide Friday, July 31, 1981 after a grand jury accused him of lying about having paid to get his $20,000 a year job. Peters reportedly told potential franchisees that paying $25,000 a store prior to the private liquor store system bill was passed would pay an additional $80,000 once the bill was signed.

headline: Council approves bill requiring sprinklers and smoke detectors
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council approved a bill that would require smoke detectors and sprinklers systems in all high-rise buildings.  The bill also mandates that fire drills be held at least once every two months.

headline: Both Parties Nominate Blair's Judge Behrens
abstract: Voters in Blair County re-elected incumbent Judge Richard Behrens to a 10-year term on the Court of Common Pleas. He easily won over challenger William Haberstroh. Both contenders cross-filed, so the winner automatically was nominated to the bench. The district justice contest in northern Blair County was decided late Wednesday, May 20, when Bellwood Police Chief Gregory Ciaccio and John Greene were declared winners.

headline: No headline
abstract: County Commissioner Tom Foerster agrees that a county lottery could work at cross purposes to the state lottery. So officials are talking about licensing other games and devices of chance. We think the voters need to know just what sort of devices the gambling proponents have in mind. Nobody really knows at this point.

headline: $10,000 Pay Raise For Council Backed
abstract: Jim O'Malley, a member of the Pittsburgh City Council writes in response to an earlier November 11 article entitled "$10,000 Pay Raise is Not Enough." He states that city council members should be subject to the same pay increases as people in other professions…no more, no less. The $10,000 pay raise over the course of the next 4.5 years is actually a loss of $9,000 for city council members if they were in a different profession.

headline: TMI cleanup fuels funding proposals
abstract: Several proposals have been brought forth on the state and local levels to fund the clean up at the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant, where an accident occurred in 1978 and still has not been cleaned up.  The article outlines several of the proposals

headline: Sexy professor lures gypsy moth; some people have 'it' some don't
abstract: Alan Cameron, a professor at Penn State, has realized his body gives off the same sex-attractant as female gypsy moths. The US Department of Agriculture are planning to recreate this and confuse the gypsy moths so they cannot mate.

headline: Getting GRIP again
abstract: Conservation minded Pittsburghers will welcome the news that the Group for Recycling in Pennsylvania is opening a used-newspaper collection center after its absence for more than a year. The group will collect newspapers at Carnegie Mellon's Skibo Hall parking lot on the last Sunday of every month.

headline: Auto Inspections Hit
abstract: An Edinboro man writes that Pennsylvania should have inspections on a motorist's own volition. He states this will work well and has worked well for many states as there are three categories of passenger cars on the road: 1)new looking cars; 2) well-kept older cars; 3) "sick-looking clunkers." The premise underlying the writer's assumption that motorist's will be accountable and responsible to have their cars inspected on their own volition by their preferred garage, rather than mandated, is because people want their cars to stay in good shape. He goes further stating that random highway inspection sites should come to terms with being able to be initiated within minutes as a means of weeding out the "bad apples from the good."

headline: Grand Jury Indicts 13 in Three Cases
abstract: The statewide grand jury recommended charges against 13 persons in separate cases involving alleged $500,000 food stamp fraud, theft of $212,000 in long-distance phone calls and rigging of electric meters.

headline: Coyne, Specter Pause, Reflect and Celebrate
abstract: Two newcomers to Congress, US Representative William J. Coyne (D-PA) and Senator Arlen Specter (R-Pa.) celebrate the 97th opening of Congress and agree that revitalization of urban areas in the Northeast is necessary

headline: Bring Courts 'Home' to Harrisburg
abstract: With Harrisburg rearranging and expanding government buildings a hall of justice should be added fro PA's three appellate courts. It would end the traveling game they currently have, and there is space right in the Forum building.

headline: No Support for Two on Court Nets Thornburgh Lawyers' Ire
abstract: PA Bar Association President David Fawcett plans to publicly criticize Governor Dick Thornburgh for not supporting the election bids of two men he appointed to interim terms on the state Superior Court. Democrat Judges Richard DiSalle and Donald Wieand, who were installed on the state's second-highest court by Thornburgh's decision, are not currently being supported by the Republican governor for the May 19 primary elections.

headline: '76 Green campaign group missed a filing deadline
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Green's 1976 Senate campaign failed to file the required semiannual financial report which reports until all revenues have been accounted for until the commission has approved the settlement of all debts. Campaign officials assumed they had fulfilled their obligations when they submitted the debt settlement plan.

headline: TMI killer? A harsh debate, a decades-long wait
abstract: George Tokuhata, head of the PA Health Department's Division of Epidemiological Research, is in a storm of public suspicion and opinion over Three Mile Island. He presides over the studies that will determine if anyone was hurt or killed at the nuclear power plant. Proof will only come from the ongoing health surveys of the exposed population.

headline: State Farmers: Make Budget Trimming Evenly
abstract: The Pennsylvania Farmers Association met with Congress in Washington to talk about President Reagan's budget cuts.  They are willing to accept cuts as long as they do not disproportionally affect farmers.  The article details the government price support plan and the cuts that may affect farmers.

headline: Getting GRIP again
abstract: Conservation-minded Pittsburghers should welcome the news that Group for Recycling in PA is opening a used-newspaper collection center Sunday after the absence of one for more than a year. GRIP will collect newspapers at Carnegie Mellon's Skibo Hall parking lot. They also are accepting donations.

headline: Bayfront highway top Erie need
abstract: The editors state that a new report on the development of the Erie area stresses the importance of a bayfront highway.  They also not that strong support for the highway has come from the mayor, and the Erie Conference on Community Development.  The editors comment on other aspects of the report and hope that the report will be used as a guide for the future.

headline: Grand Jury Names Midstaters as Part of Gaming Ring
abstract: Eight midstaters were among 51 persons named by a statewide grand jury as part of a loosely connected network of gamblers operating in five states. They will be charged shortly with conspiracy and bookmarking. They found three major operations that worked loosely with each other.

headline: Crowds Jam Center for Opening
abstract: Over 12,000 people attended the opening ceremonies for the new David L. Lawrence Convention Center in Pittsburgh.  Governor Thornbugh cut the ribbon on the new project.  The article outlines the celebration and interviews several people about the center.

headline: Bringing In Bucks Via U.S. Lottery
abstract: Letter wanting a national lottery system with tax-free prizes to boost revenue for the federal government

headline: Northeast Lawmakers Cry 'Foul'
abstract: On the proposed Reagan administration budget cuts, northeastern US lawmakers feel that their industrial states bear more of the burden of the proposed cuts. US Senator John Heinz (R-PA) is opposed to the Federal Railway proposal to sell Conrail, but agrees with the proposed 10% tax cut that would benefit PA.

headline: After a year, how is Green doing?  Most agree city's less divided, well managed; some see lack of vision
abstract: Article outlines William J. Green's first year as Philadelphia mayor.  Both sides agree that he has managed the city well, but some point to things he has not done.  Article looks at the areas of Finance, Race, Education, Leadership, Openness, Politics and Goals

headline: TMI official plays down tests for operators
abstract: Nuclear reactor operators at the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant can be judged competent even if they fail the federal licensing test and company examinations. However, operators cannot work until they pass the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing test. This comes to light as reactor operators were accused of cheating on the licensing test. This hearing that resulted from such allegations will help the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board decide whether General Public Utilities can safely restart the Unit 1 reactor. Three Mile Island was the site of the nation's worst commercial nuclear accident in March 1979. The undamaged Unit 1 reactor was ordered closed after the accident had crippled the adjacent Unit 2 reactor.

headline: State ponders law to reduce manufacturers product liability
abstract: A poultry farmer with about 80,000 diseased chickens in his care brought suit against several companies which had supplied contaminated feed. Instead of waiting for the verdict, the 10 defendants said the farmer owes $345,000 in damages. This represents product liability. Business groups feel the law is to in the favor of product consumers and have been trying to change the law. They want to limit how long people can bring suit to 12 years for consumers and 30 years for nonconsumers.

headline: Goddard is critical of proposals to change the Clean Air Act
abstract: Maurice Goddard, who retired in 1979 after 25 years as the state's environmental protector, sharply criticized proposals to amend the Clean Air Act saying it would lead to more pollution. He also criticized officials for doing little to reduce acid rain.

headline: Before the monopoly; A competitive port rail system
abstract: In a letter to the editor, the author outlines in detail the history of a competitive rail system in Pennsylvania.  The author feels that editors comments for improving the rail system facilities are important, without redeveloping the transportation systems those improvement will be meaningless.

headline: Graterford inmates hold 38 after foiled escape try
abstract: Inmates at Graterford State Prison are holding 38 people hostage in the prison kitchen after a failed escape attempt.  Negotiators have reached the inmates and they asked for medical attention for one of the hostages with diabetes.  The article details the negotiation attempts and what is known of the current situation.

headline: Fire Alarms
abstract: The failure of an alarm system in a high rise downtown building during a fire last week, makes the editors ask the city to do more to ensure citizens' safety in high rise buildings.  They suggest unannounced random tests to ensure all alarms are working.

headline: Bureaucrats Better Off, Area Legislator Is Told
abstract: State Representative John Kennedy surveyed people in his district on their perception of the differences between state and private employees.  The majority of the respondents stated that they feel state employees make more money and have more benefits than private ones.  The article details the results of the survey and Kennedy's thoughts on it.

headline: Now He's Councilman White
abstract: State Representative John White, Jr., won the City Councilman election, beating Andrew Coates and Max Weiner in the special election.  He will be filling the seat left by Louis Johanson, who was sentenced to three years in prison on bribery charges.  The article details White's campaign.

headline: Assessors
abstract: The biggest complaint heard from Allegheny County taxpayers is about the unfair property assessments. The editorial claims that changes have been made in past few years to improve the assessor's office, but more can be done. The editorial argues that keeping assessment employees out of politics is a good idea, but that a further suggestion is that Commissioners should prohibit all political activity of committee people.

headline: TMI pool cleanup is next
abstract: (4 page article) The GPU Nuclear Power Group, who own the Three Mile Island plant, plan to clean the water in the radioactive pools at plant, following the nuclear accident in 1979.  The article details in depth the methods that will be used to clean the water and the effects of the accidents.

headline: What others say
abstract: A Pennsylvania state senator from Indiana proposed to raise money for homeless animals through a small tax on pet food.  The tax money would finance shelters for stray animals.  The article provides further details on how the tax would be implemented and help animal shelters.  It also discusses how animal shelters currently survive.

headline: Good bill
abstract: The editors state their support of US Sen. John Heinz's bill that would give an extension of three years to steel mills in complying with the Environmental Protection Agency's clean air laws.  They state their support of cleaner air, but feel an extension would help increase jobs in the Pittsburgh area

headline: Beyond the call of pothole duty
abstract: The author opines that porholes give people something in common to talk about.  The author details the trials of Ed Bucha, who answers the calls of the newly opened Pennsylvania Transportation Department "Pothole Hotline."

headline: Graterford siege is over
abstract: Two pictures grace this full front page of the Philadelphia Tribune. The photograph on the left is of a black male talking on a pay phone. The caption beneath the left photograph states: "Sen. Milton Street was frustrated by Thornburgh's office as a representative tells him he cannot enter Graterford Prison to talk with captors." The photograph on the right depicts two men. In the left side of this photograph there is the profile of a black male dialing a rotary pay phone and the back of a man with a turban and long beard watching the black man dial the phone. The caption beneath this photograph states: "Khalid Muhammad also talked with Thornburgh representatives to assure that he could resolve the hostage crisis instantly. He, too, was turned back."

headline: Governor Praises HamTech at Dedication
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh praised the efforts of government and business leaders that led to the transformation of the vacant Hess's department store building into the new home for Hamilton Technology Incorporated at a ribbon-cutting ceremony.  Thornburgh stated that the HamTech project represents his administration's two highest goals of economic development and community conservation.

headline: By the Numbers
abstract: The Borough of Steelton currently included in its entirety within the confines of the 106th district in the state House is served in two by the proposed new district lines. Running lines through townships is not new, but threatens identity of voters. The lines drawn seem to have not paid any attention to historical arrangements or associations of people.

headline: Now, River Basin Panel May Get Down to Business
abstract: Former state Revenue Department Secretary Warren M. Depuy is now a federal representative of the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, which will bring the Commission to a full quorum.  The article details Depuy's career and history.

headline: Caliguiri Dubbed 'Commuter Bandit'
abstract: When Mayor Richard Caliguiri pressed the PA House Finance Committee for the right to tax suburbanites who work in Pittsburgh he earned the title 'commuter bandit,' which is indicative of a 1960s armed bank robber that prowled Pittsburgh's streets. Specifically, Caliguiri wants the Legislature to give cities the right to levy a 0.25 percent tax on suburbanite wages.

headline: Local Control of Airports Urged
abstract: State Representative Benjamin Wilson writes to the editor explaining that an April 24 editorial needs to include the fact that 50 percent of the aviation fuels tax monies collected is going toward the losses incurred at both Capitol City and Harrisburg International Airport, which already have significant annual losses. The cost-cutting measures must begin somewhere, starting with fire and police, a fringe benefit. He suggests that what's really needed is for local control of the state-owned airports, an option that has general public consensus.

headline: Why are Countians Paying Highest Milk Prices Ever?
abstract: The state Milk Marketing Board has raised the minimum price of milk to an all-time high of $2.04 per gallon in Lancaster County and most central PA food stores.  The Milk Marketing Board says that prices are higher in Lancaster County than elsewhere because it costs more to produce and process the milk in the county's smaller dairies than it does in larger, cost-efficient dairies that serve the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh areas.  Editorial feels that the Milk Marketing Board is the reason for the higher prices.

headline: Governor gets TMI cleanup backing
abstract: Governor Thornburgh appealed to some of his National Governors'' Association colleagues for support of his cost-sharing plan for the cleanup of the Three Mile Island nuclear accident and came away delighted by the response.  Thornburgh took his proposal before the National Governors' Association Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Protection, asking only for a critique of its merits, but won an unqualified endorsement.

headline: BOUND FOR DISASTER
abstract: Photograph depicts Richard Fasy, Southeastern PA Transportation Authority's safety systems director, saying "If we had to report (to the National Transportation Safety Board) every accident a trolley was in, we would have to hire someone full time just to report them."

headline: Group Homes / Bethel Park
abstract: The editorial agrees with the State Commonwealth Court's decision to allow the Wesley Institute to start a group home for delinquent children in Bethel Park. The editorial argues that by having a treatment in a home instead of an institution, with friends and families nearby to help, makes returning to the community easier. He also affirms that the home will be well staffed and secure, and that many steps taken will ease residents' concern.

headline: Hello, No. 5
abstract: Philadelphia is now the fifth largest city instead of the fourth. Houston has taken the fourth place now based on the 1980 census.

headline: Caliguiri Election Hopes Built On Renaissance II
abstract: The article details the mayoral race between incumbent Richard Caliguiri and Fred Goehringer.  The article discusses the candidates views on Renaissance II, taxes, and affirmative action.

headline: Nullify those back-door pay raises
abstract: The back-door pay raise the US Senate authorized for lawmakers was voted only hours before President Reagan took to the television networks to urge the public to back his newest recommendations for additional cuts in federal spending. The proposal can still be nullified in conference committee and should be.

headline: City Council Balks At Setting Pay Cap
abstract: null

headline: Mass transit systems must be maintained
abstract: Words of praise for SEPTA are as few and far between as stops on a holiday bus schedule. Now its foreclosure is imminent. The goals of promoting mass transit have been misplaced. When fares are raised riders decrease. The federal government may come to the rescue, but locals will still have to hold down costs.

headline: null
abstract: Caption above the cartoon reads, "Only on Friday'n'payday...never on Monday." Below is a man wearing a hat that says, "$Bread$ Winner," punching his ticket while looking at the bulletin board that states, "Monday's message: Be HAPPY you have a job."  Below is another cartoon of two men on a street corner and the caption above them reads, "Crime's so bad these days...even my shadow carries a gun."

headline: Governor is put on spot on auto-emissions tests
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh is back in the middle of a tug-of-war over auto emissions tests in PA. The governor must decide whether t obey a federal court order requiring him to set up the tests by May or a new state law prohibiting him from spending state dollars for that purpose.

headline: Bound for Disaster: How thousands of bus, trolley and train riders risk pain and injury on SEPTA, an unsafe, unsound system
abstract: An Philadelphia Inquirer's study that included interviews with officials and employers and a review of 13 years' worth of statistical data, court records and government reports concluded that Southeastern PA Transit Authority has been heading toward collapse, both mechanically and financially, for more than a decade. With an increasingly old and ill-maintained float of buses, trolleys, and trains, and a lack of money for new units and better management, the study reports the transit system is unsafe and unsound.

headline: Growing fake drug trade leads Phila. Firm t sue
abstract: A year ago a company began advertising weight reducing pills that contain caffeine, not real amphetamines. Companies are now getting cracked down on for selling false claims.

headline: Housing for elderly OK'd in lower Burrell
abstract: The PA Housing Finance Agency has approved a $4.4 million loan for construction of a housing project for the elderly in Westmoreland County. The proposed eight-story building will contain 125 one-bedroom apartments.

headline: Caliguiri favored in Democratic race
abstract: Incumbent Pittsburgh city mayor Richard Caliguiri will most likely win the Democratic nomination for mayor, but his bid for the Republican nod was less assured. Caliguiri has very little opposition from the other four Democratic candidates, but has a stiffer resistance from Fred Goehringer, who has the Republican party's endorsement.

headline: Office plaza awaits 'go' at Capitol
abstract: The construction go-ahead is expected this week for a long-envisioned plaza-type addition to the main Capitol Building, extending between the terraces of the North Office Building and South Office Building.

headline: City council balks at setting pay cap
abstract: Council yesterday quickly defeated a proposal to keep salaries from going beyond the $27,500 that five members have been receiving for the past two years. The other four members have been paid $22,500 for the past four years. Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri has proposed they receive a $10,000 a year raise. No council member is entirely happy with the system, which has resulted in council members' having to defend large raises before the public.

headline: Mayor Optimistic Cannonsburg Can Save Fort Pitt Bridge Works
abstract: Cannonsburg Mayor Jack Passante feels that if citizens contribute funds the Fort Pitt Bridge Works can be reopened.  Even though the cost to reopen the plant is about $2.5 million, he feels that they can raise enough funds to do it.

headline: 2 big locals OK strike of liquor stores
abstract: About 3,500 liquor store employees across Pennsylvania have been working without a contract since June, and are now planning on going on strike.  The employees have been resisting a plan proposed by Governor Dick Thornburgh to convert the state stores to private enterprise.  Thornburgh recently rejected a state fact-finder's report that would have ensured the clerks' jobs if private owners take over.

headline: Governors Declare Regional Water Shortage
abstract: The governors in the three state Delaware River Basin Committee declared a ban on all nonessential water use due to a drought that his affecting the region.  The piece sets out steps to take to decrease water usage in order to avoid a more serious drought in the summer

headline: Break Deadlock On Road Projects
abstract: Erie Conference President Carl J. Schlemmer urged Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis to break the deadlock on several key Erie highway projects that have been halted for a long time.  The article outlines the projects that have been stalled.

headline: Gun Laws Disarm The Wrong People
abstract: The author writes to refute an article blaming the handgun for crime in America.  The author opines that anyone who has the intent to harm can get a gun regardless of laws.  The author feels that the Kennedy-Rodino gun bill will only disarm law abiding citizens and make them defenseless.

headline: Housing For Elderly OK'd In Lower Burrell
abstract: The Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency has approved a $4.4 million construction loan for a housing project for the elderly in Westmoreland County. The apartments will be located at Route 56 in Lower Burrell.

headline: Caliguiri Rides The Renaissance: 'Hanging Judges' Rope in the Voters
abstract: The author believes that the two major issues behind the upcoming elections are crime and judicial leniency, and Renaissance II.  The author feels all the judges will be tougher on crime and that Pittsburgh Mayor Caliguiri will be re-elected.  The piece details the author's predictions in the election.

headline: Official's ouster urged in dispute over a contract
abstract: Democratic members of the state's Senate Appropriations Committee called yesterday for the suspension or dismissal of Community Affairs secretary  Shirley Dennis for her role in awarding a contract to the North Philadelphia Block Development Corporation, an organization founded by state Senator T. Milton Street. State Senator H. Craig Lewis wrote a letter of request based on an investigation by Senate Democrats that indicated that Dennis misled the governor and violated federal guidelines. The US inspector general's office called on the state to return the amount disbursed, while Street, Dennis and Governor Dick Thornburgh denied the contract was a political payoff.

headline: City Council Oks property tax refunds
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council gave approval for $1.3 million in real estate tax refunds and is expected to refund $7 million.  The biggest beneficiaries of the tax refunds are big corporations such as U.S. Steel.  The article details the specifics of the tax refund.

headline: Moore Wants Legislation To Finish Rt. 15 Project
abstract: State Senator William J. Moore (R-33) is seeking to secure adequate funding for construction that would widen a 15-mile stretch of Route 15 from Hunterstown to the Maryland line in Adams County. The senator is prepared to introduce an amendment to the state highway capital funds budget that would provide state seed money that is necessary for the project to gain federal funding assistance.

headline: 2d-class treatment alleged: Nonstriking air traffic folk
abstract: On August 6, the Inquirer published a story under the heading, "A 2d air union wants to be counted."  In this story Federal Aviation Administration spokesman Fred Farrar was quoted as saying, "We're talking about two separate unions, the air traffic controllers and the flight service specialists, and National Association of Air Traffic Specialists is not in the news simply because it is not part of the controversy," Farrar said.

headline: Gypsy moth on move again, posing threat to foliage Western Pa.
abstract: Millions of dollars has been spent trying to wipe out the gypsy moth.  Spraying does not eradicate the gypsy moth it merely keeps them away from people.  There are only two parasites that will destroy the gypsy moth caterpillars, but the only problem is that it takes so long for them to populate to take care of the gypsy moths.

headline: Break it up
abstract: The author of the letter attacks state Representative Brian Clark's plan to turn over the PA Department of Transportation's functions to the Turnpike Commission. Although he agrees with the current problems with PennDOT, the author offers a plan to break up the Department as an alternative. He also suggests that legislators attack the problem of PennDOT, rather than laying it on another smoothly efficient state organization.

headline: Handgun Control 1
abstract: The editorial argues that the attempt to kill President Reagan should help the attempt to outlaw handguns. He points to the criminal use of handguns, their ease of acquire and conceal, the national increase in number of handgun-related deaths as reasons to end easy handgun procurement.

headline: How Home-Lot Prices Compare
abstract: New figures on land values show that it's not construction costs alone the inflate the prices of new homes across the US. Graph shows different costs per square foot by state.

headline: Caliguiri Track: Erase Top Foe With Write-In
abstract: Five Democrats and one Republican are running for Pittsburgh mayor in Tuesday, May 19th's primary, but the main event is Mayor Richard Caliguiri's effort to win the Republican nomination over GOP candidate Fred Goehringer with write-in votes. Goehringer also is appealing for Democratic write-ins, but his chances in this regard are remote.

headline: OK Expected For Redistricting Cuts To County;  Approval Expected For Redistricting Plan
abstract: The Pittsburgh and Philadelphia areas and the Democratic Party are the big losers in a legislative reapportionment plan slated for primary approval.  The plan, drafted by a bipartisan commission, calls for eliminating three House seats in Allegheny County and one Senate seat and five House seats in Philadelphia.  One new senatorial district and eight new House districts would be created in other parts of Pennsylvania which gained the population that the two major urban areas lost.  Political observers generally agreed that the plan, still subject to revision, favors Republicans because the population shifted to areas where the Government of the People is strong.

headline: Civic Center
abstract: Gus Pulakos, author of a letter to Governor Dick Thornburgh, argues that the money designated for the Memorial Civic Center should have gone toward Erie's water department. He argues that mayors should support as a priority the water, police, fire and street departments, but that civic centers are liabilities and burdens on the taxpayers.

headline: Motorists smile through opening day Parkway jam
abstract: Motorists were pleased with the reopening of the inbound lanes of the Squirrel Hill Tunnel, despite a ten minute jam caused by a ribbon cutting ceremony which Governor Thornburgh attended.  The article details the ceremony and continuing plans for road improvements in Pittsburgh

headline: 4,500 layoffs make for holiday of little cheer in Bucks County
abstract: About 2,700 United States Steel employees have been laid off at the Fairless Work plant, the biggest employer in Bucks County and about 1,800 more have received notice that their jobs will end in the next few weeks.  The article continues to describe the hardships that are anticipated for their holiday season.

headline: Gypsy moth spray questioned
abstract: Attorney representing hundreds of families who were injured when another chemical they were told was harmless was sprayed in Vietnam. The chemical was Agent Orange. The attorney believes this causes enough doubt to question spraying for gypsy moths.

headline: Bucks commuter feels ripped off by Conrail
abstract: Letter to the editor calls for Governor Dick Thornburgh and the Southe East PA Transit Authority to stop supporting Conrail.  Author complains that the recent SEPTA fare hikes are because Conrail is mismanaged and does not provide commuter rail service in the Northeast rail corridor.

headline: Hayes denies sex charges, says he's not gay
abstract: David Hayes, an Erie County Republican who resigned his state House of Representatives seat, is charged with rape, involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, corrupting the morals of a minor and indecent assault. He testified on his own behalf and denied having sex with a  17-year old male, who accused the former lawmaker of raping him during a drug-laced  homosexual orgy.

headline: Lewis backing change to bill on tax breaks
abstract: State Senator Craig Lewis backs a change in a bill that would give an estimated $56 million in tax breaks to Pennsylvania corporations.  Lewis feels that the state is in such a fiscal dilemma that they can not afford to lose the revenue from the taxes.  The article details the bill and the fiscal problems the state is facing.

headline: Caliguiri's Renaissance II a shield
abstract: The article details the Pittsburgh mayoral race between Mayor Caliguiri and Fred Goehringer.  Caliguiri is running on a "Renaissance II" platform of restoring Pittsburgh.  His opponent feels that this will not help Pittsburgh

headline: One who is learning: Education continued in strike
abstract: The author is a student involved in an organization called Students for Opening Schools.  The author states that the students want to return to school and continue learning, despite the Philadelphia teachers' strike.  The author chronicles her perception of the adults involved in the negotiations and states that she has learned that they behave more childishly than children.  She suggests that the students should run the city.

headline: Council leans to tax increase
abstract: As more than 500 parents, students, and teachers booed and applauded from the gallery, the Philadelphia City Council approved a resolution stating that it would consider increasing taxes as a part of a long-term plan t aid the Philadelphia School District. It is the first indictor that council members are willing to increase taxes.

headline: New era hailed in trolley-depot dedication
abstract: A new depot is opening for trolleys in Philadelphia. The depot is the city's first transit-maintenance building built since the Frankford Bus Depot in 1955, 13 years before the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority began in 1968. As officials heralded the $23 million structure, they called it a key to SEPTA's program for upgrading its decaying fleet of vehicles.

headline: 75 protest merger plan at Northeast job center
abstract: 75 people protested the threatened closing of an unemployment office in northeast Philadelphia.  State Representative John M. Perzel told the protesters that the building was in such bad shape the office had to be merged with another office.

headline: Gypsy Moth Traps Don't Help Much, Entomologist Says
abstract: David Shetlar, a Penn State University entomologist, says traps involving alluring smells and sticky paper are not effective products to eliminate the gypsy moth. Instead, he believes the best way to fight caterpillars is to spray with chemical insecticide, which kills on contact and also poisons foliage they eat. The spray made from Bacillus thuringiensis is very effective early in the season when caterpillars are small.

headline: Cleveland stop is proposed for Amtrak 'Pennsylvanian'
abstract: Ohio transportation officials are proposing a stop in Cleveland, Ohio for Amtrak's "Pennsylvanian," which operates daily between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  Officials say there may be federal funds available for the project.  The article outlines the route and times the proposed project would be available.

headline: Head-shop law
abstract: The author opines that a law passed by Governor Thornburgh banning any equipment intended to prepare or consume illegal drugs, will be overturned by the state Supreme Court. The reason is because the equipment can be used for perfectly legal purposes also.  The author agrees with the governor's efforts, but feels that society should be going after those who sell drugs.

headline: Lewis presses to hear tape on project
abstract: PA Senator Craig Lewis says PA Community Affairs Secretary Shirley Dennis is refusing to let him hear a tape recording of a meeting where controversial weatherization project was discussed. At issue is a 1979 state contract to Street's organization to weatherize 128 homes with $107,000 in federal funds. Lewis contends the contract was awarded improperly.

headline: Campaign for Johanson's seat: Short and low-key
abstract: The election campaign for the councilman seat vacated by Louis Johanson, who was convicted of bribery charges in the Abscam scandal, has been very low key.  Three candidates, Andrew Coates, Jr., Max Weiner, and John White, Jr. have not had any face to face debates.  The article details the candidates and the campaign.

headline: Only State Races: 23 Run For 7 Court Seats
abstract: Twenty-three candidates are seeking nomination for seven seats on the state's three highest courts in the May 19 primary election. Profiled are the six candidates for state Supreme Court, a job that carries a 10-year term and an annual salary of $64,500.

headline: County Audit Reveals Growth Of Local Government
abstract: Bedford County Auditors completed an audit of $4.7 million that passed through the county government in 1980. They found that the books did balance. In less than 10 years, the county's budget has gone from approximately $1 million to topping $4 million. The growth has been steady, much of it due to the addition of programs and offices.

headline: New lanes on I-83 span open Friday
abstract: The new widen section of the South Bridge will get a baptism by tire Friday morning. The change is part of a $65.9 million reconstruction project that will ultimately widen the span from four lanes to six and rebuild five interchanges over a 2 1/2 mile stretch.

headline: Always Can Cope, Striking Miners Say
abstract: As this year's strike by the nation's 160,000 United Mine Workers moves into its second week, striking miners say they always find ways to cope with payless days head. Even though it is difficult, families have saved some money for basic living expenses, while cutting back on entertainment expenses.

headline: Gypsy Moth: The Traveling Strip Show
abstract: The gypsy moth, originally brought to the US around 1869 for a failed investigation into improving silk production, escaped and spread rapidly, and is now considered the most destructive defoliating insect in the northeastern part of the US. The caterpillar stage is the most damaging, feeding on many types of trees. Many states and the federal government have attempted to diminish the population of gypsy moths, and one way is by setting up traps to attract males through aroma.

headline: Buddy system paying off on Parkway
abstract: The article details new traffic patterns in Pittsburgh during the Parkway East construction.  It states that commuters are now car-pooling more, creating a decrease of cars on the road.

headline: Heinz Renews Merit Plan To Select U.S. Attorneys
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz plans to use a special merit selection panel to choose a successor to the U.S. attorney post in Pittsburgh.  There were allegations that the senator had been having private interviews instead of using the merit system.

headline: Phila.'s image problem and the firm that got away
abstract: Like much of the Northeast, the Philadelphia area has suffered a steady loss of industrial jobs to the Sunbelt region in recent years. Polychrome Corporation of Yonkers, New York, is a large corporation that was attempting to setup operations in Philadelphia's industrial park. But citizen's and a City Councilman's opposition to the plant caused it to move instead to North Carolina. The author believes that Philadelphia has an image problem.

headline: Capitol Complex fire, explosion linked to underground circuit
abstract: PA Power and Light Co said the failure of an electric circuit caused an underground fire in the Capitol Complex. However the short circuit was not enough to cause the explosion that blew off a manhole cover on North Sixth Street.

headline: O'Pake to Ethics Panel: Rule on PHFA-Bartle Tie
abstract: null

headline: County Fudged Insulation Work Files
abstract: Administrators of the Allegheny County Weatherization Program, stung by charges of excessive delays and mismanagement, fudged their performance records to increase the number of completed jobs. Several homeowners were asked to sign statements indicating that insulation work on their houses was finished even though it was not. The county Health Department then used the signed statements to support inflated statistics submitted to the state agency that oversees the program.

headline: New tax key to X-way future; PennDOT official stresses need for SWAP tax
abstract: PA Department of Transportation deputy secretary of planning Harvey Haack said that the only way the Allegheny Valley Express Way would be finished is if Governor Dick Thornburgh's SWAP gasoline tax is approved.  PennDOT is delaying the project because they don't have enough money in their budget.  The SWAP tax plan, which would cut six cents from the flat 11-cent-a-gallon tax on gasoline and replace it with a 6% sales tax, has met stiff opposition in the General Assembly.

headline: Another Point Of View
abstract: Roger Tauss, chairman of the union's strike committee, offers his point of view, arguing that the union does not oppose testing for mechanics from the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority, but that the problem is SEPTA's insistence on written tests instead of performance tests. He argues the written form doesn't test repair skills, and are culturally biased. As for part-time, he argues that SEPTA wants them for flexibility to cut service to the public.

headline: Heinz pushes plan to delay clean air law for steel
abstract: An proposed amendment to the federal Clean Air Act would extend the deadlines for steel companies to comply.  Pennsylvania Senator John Heinz supports the amendment and held a press conference at U.S. Steel's Fairless Works in Falls Township

headline: Buses To Replace 'Parkway Limited'
abstract: PennDot will sponsor express bus service between downtown Pittsburgh and Westmoreland County starting Monday as part of its alternative transportation commitment for the Parkway East construction. It will provide two inbound and two outbound rush-hour trips each weekday from the Greensburg area and from the Jeannette-Manor-Irwin area. The buses will replace the experimental commuter train service, Parkway Limited, which became to expensive to operate due to a drop in commuters.

headline: Heros in the Hostage Siege
abstract: The article is a narrative by Chuck Stone of his experience meeting with the hostage takers at Graterford Prison.  His descriptions include his attempts at negotiations with the leader, Joseph Bowen, and his coordination with local law enforcement officers in ending the siege.

headline: Public housing threatened by Reagan cuts
abstract: A workshop concluded that a proposal by the Reagan administration and the US Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide no more than 85.5 percent of the operating funds needed by local housing officials will affect the maintenance and rehabilitation of existing units. HUD estimates the $165 millions shortage could grow to $200 million with the increased heating costs. The information was provided at a Pittsburgh workshop sponsored by local housing officials.

headline: Capitol Rededication Monday
abstract: There will be a rededication ceremony of the State Capital Building to commemorate its 75th anniversary.  Kermit Roosevelt, grandson of President Theodore Roosevelt will take part in the ceremony, as well as State Representative Joseph Pitts and Governor Thornburgh.  The article list the planned activities of the ceremony.

headline: OTHER VOICES: Teachers ponder precedent...proposed by a mayor 'alone'
abstract: The current school crisis drama is being played out in an atmosphere more bitter than any that can be remembered in the past 15 years.  Somehow, this confrontation between the teachers' union on the one side and the mayor and the media on the other side is being fueled by events that occurred earlier this summer outside the Philadelphia School District.  Two views of mayor Green's efforts to prevent a teachers' strike.

headline: County population down 9.7%, city drops 18.5%
abstract: New census data shows that Allegheny county's population fell 9.7% in the last decade and the city of Pittsburgh dropped 18.5%.  The article details other census information as well.

headline: New train to DC carries some old charm
abstract: A train called the Capitol may take a little longer to get from Pittsburgh to Washington, D.C., but it could help people avoid the traffic. It has a complete menu, two coach cars and two sleeper cars.

headline: Battle Over Budget Hits Rail Retirees
abstract: The Reagan Administration is proposing to cut benefits for railroad retirees, stating that they should not get both Social Security and railroad benefits.  The article interviews a railroad retiree from Johnstown, PA.  The article details how the railroad trust functions in conjunction with Social Security.

headline: Heinz Tries To Block EPA Auto Test Funds
abstract: Pennsylvania Senator, John Heinz, lands to introduce an amendment to an appropriations bill that would stop the Environmental Protection Agency from forcing Pennsylvania and several other states to start auto emission testing. The Heinz amendment is almost identical to a proposal defeated by a narrow margin in the House of representatives earlier this month. Heinz will try to attach the amendment to a House appropriations bill for the Department of Interior.

headline: But for SEPTA the big picture is horrible and getting worse
abstract: SEPTA has hired a consultant who will provide them with plans to transport commuters should the current rail system fail.  The plan consists of car-pooling and other measures.  The rail system has funding problems.  The article details the choices and options the SEPTA officials face.

headline: Hickton to stand trial on bribery charge
abstract: Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman rejected a request to place former district attorney in a rehabilitation program instead of standing trial for bribery and obstruction of justice.  The article outlines the details of the case.

headline: Sale of tax-exempt home loan bonds OK'd; Home-loan bond sale approved
abstract: Governor Thornburgh authorized a dozen urban governments and the state Housing Finance Agency to sell $430 million in tax-exempt revenue bonds for reduced rate home mortgages.  Issuance of such bonds would allow the agencies to offer mortgages to first-time buyers at a 12 percent interest rate, which is four to five pointes below current levels.  It also would allow home repair loans of up to $15,000.  the governor's proclamation allows Pittsburgh to proceed this week with the sale of $11 million in revenue bonds for home repair loans.  Although Pittsburgh has made three previous issues totaling $60 million, a new and restrictive federal law posed the prospect of limiting the city's new issue between $6 million and $7 million.

headline: Capitol: Home to governors, ghosts, greed, glory
abstract: A history of the Capitol is given. Nineteen governors have lived there and at least one of them haunts the building. The details of the construction and decorations are given. The capitol also violates up to 50 fire codes.

headline: OUR IDEAS: Redistricting Favors the GOP
abstract: Just as the nationwide shift of population from cities to rural and suburban areas favors the Republican Party nationally, so the movement of Pennsylvania residents from predominantly Democratic Philadelphia and Allegheny County to Lancaster and other predominantly Republican areas favors the state Government of the People.  Republicans already control both houses of the Pennsylvania General Assembly.  The preliminary redistricting plan released by the Pennsylvania Reapportionment Commission would reinforce the Government of the People's hold on the House and Senate.

headline: Editorial #81-03- State Budget Proposal
abstract: The editors opine that Governor Thornburgh's proposed budget, which cuts funding for almost all agencies, will translate into higher property taxes to fund education.  The editors urge listeners to write to their representatives to change the education portion of the budget so that education doesn't need to rely solely on property taxes.

headline: No Turnpike police on CB channel
abstract: PA state troopers are not paying attention to distress calls for stranded motorists, but instead they are pulling people over for speeding. They are not there for the safety of drivers at all.

headline: Bill to curb layoffs is introduced
abstract: State Representative David R. Wright introduced a bill that would allow employers to temporarily augment scaled-back wages with unemployment compensation to avoid or delay layoffs.  The bill would help to curb layoffs during seasonal slumps or poor economic conciliations.  The plan is already enacted in California.

headline: Itkin Wants Strip Mine Bonds Increased
abstract: Pennsylvania State Representative Ivan Itkin has introduced legislation that strips the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources of its authority to set rates for surface-mine bonds. The legislation would impose a minimum rate of $4,000 per acre at strip mines. Strip-mine operators are required to post such bonds so that the money is available to cover the cost of reclaiming their mines if they fail to do so.

headline: Camiel Ordered Reinstated Now
abstract: President Judge James Crumlish of Commonwealth Court revoked Governor Dick Thornburgh's suspension of Peter Camiel, in effect since May 21, 1980, as a member of the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission and ordered the governor and the commission to reinstate Camiel immediately. This includes providing Camiel with almost 18 months of back pay.

headline: Hickton to stand trial on bribery charges
abstract: Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman ordered that former district attorney John J. Hickton stand trial for bribery.  The charges state that Hickman offered district attorney Robert Colville political and financial support if he could convince a grand jury not to recommend criminal charges against Dr. Cyril Wecht, county commissioner and former coroner.

headline: Senate acts on aid for jobless
abstract: The United States Senate approved a measure that places a two year freeze on a scheduled federal tax increase on employers in Pennsylvania. The increase was earmarked to help repay the state's $1.5 billion trust fund debt to the federal government. This measure was introduced by Pennsylvania Senator John Heinz  in order to provide relief to employers who have had to shoulder an increasing share of the burden restoring Pennsylvania's unemployment fund to financial health. This is after state political leaders' concern that businesses may move their operations to other states rather than pay the higher tax in Pennsylvania.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: The cartoon depicts a man at a post office looking a sign with Santa Claus on it.  The sign reads "Mail awfully early & save big bucks*  *Postage rates go through the roof effective Nov.1.  Ho-ho-ho-ho-ho-et.-etc."

headline: Our Voice:  Save the Navy Yard hostages
abstract: 63 skilled laborers were hired to work in the Navy Shipyard to rebuild ships, but were let go recently when President Reagan ordered a freeze on all federal jobs.  The editorial urges senators and represenative to push for a waiver to President Reagan's job freeze so that these laborers can go back to work

headline: ERIE POLITICS: GOP Day Is Coming
abstract: Clifford J. Welsh, a top flight Government of the People tactician in Erie for nearly 30 years, thinks a major opportunity for the Republicans party will occur when Mayor Louis Tullio leaves City Hall.  He agreed that Tullio has won the respect of a lot of Republicans and his presence as chief executive makes it difficult to transform the local situation.

headline: Not justified
abstract: Governor Thornburgh is on target in charging the recent gasoline tax increase by Mobil Oil Corporation is not justified and should be lowered.  The governor pointed to the action Mobil took in New York State, where they raised its gasoline price by three cents per gallon in reaction to a new state oil tax.  Three days later it was announced it was cutting the price increase to 1.3 cents per gallon because the company would end up absorbing some of the cost of the tax.  That is the exact contention the governor made when Mobil and several other oil companies increased their wholesale prices in Pennsylvania by about four cents per gallon immediately after Pennsylvania enacted an oil franchise levy.

headline: Bucks Plant Steels Itself for Layoffs
abstract: Workers at US Steel Corp.'s Fairless Works are facing either substantial employee cutbacks next month or a shutdown of the plant for November because of a skimpy workload. No exact figures could be presented.

headline: Judge Oks Settlement Worth $5 Million to communities; Communities Win Ruling on Lawsuit
abstract: United States Middle District Court Judge malcom Muir issued an order approving a settlement of a class-action suit which is expected to result in 123 municipalities and sewer authorities receiving more than $5 million.  Two other courts still must act, and Muir's order is technically buject to appeal, but lawyers involved in the case say they anticipate no snags.  Under the order, the state Department of Environmental Resources and the United Stated Environmental Protection Agency each will pay about half of the settlement.

headline: Can Amtrak Survive The Budget Cutters?
abstract: Congress is considering whether to follow President Reagan's lead to cut subsidies to the National Railroad Passenger Corporation (Amtrak). The Reagan administration is asking Congress to vote $613 million in subsidies for the year beginning October 1, rather than the $970 million recommended by former President Carter. Amtrak says that the proposed cut would mean a loss of passenger service in 36 states, and would restrict service to the Northeast Corridor that links Boston, New York City, Philadelphia, and Washington.

headline: High court lifts license of lawyer in cheating claim
abstract: The PA state Supreme Court suspended a Pittsburgh lawyer's license to practice following a client's complaint that he was cheated out of $28,000 of a workmen's compensation award. Lawyer John M Grubor reportedly told his client that two robbers stole most of the money from him at gunpoint, but the court's Disciplinary Board found his story 'utterly incredible.'

headline: Senate committee clears two bills to put teeth in condominium law
abstract: Two bills that would declare a statewide 18-month moratorium on condominium conversions and offer special protection for elderly and handicapped tenants were approved by a PA state Senate committee. It would grant a lifetime lease to any lease to any tenant 62 years old or older and blind or disabled person who has lived in the apartment building for at least three years.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Two guys at a desk.  Sing on the wall says "Reagan Transition HQ Employment Office."  One guy says to the other guy, "You certainly have impeccable credentials: Harvard MBA, Corporate whiz, team player, conservative, Nancy Reagan likes your looks"

headline: Pa. auditor: State's books a mess
abstract: PA Auditor General, Al Benedict, released an audit of the state treasury finding that the treasury has been unable to reconcile its books and has a difference of $31 million dollars.  He charged former state treasurer Robert E. Casey with failing to address the huge problem.  Mr. Casey stated that it was a problem inheirited from previous treasurers.  Current treasure R. Budd Dwyer says he wishes he would have known about this prior to taking office.  Mr. Benedict says no criminal charges have been filed, but that it is impossible to know whether money was stolen due to the bad accounting practices.

headline: Forgotten Pledge
abstract: The author calls for Governor Thornburgh to make good on his campaign  pledge to do away with school and property taxes as unconstitutional.

headline: Now Catching for PennDot
abstract: Article looks at the importance of runaway truck escape ramps on Pennsylvania parkways and expressways. Faulty brakes are not the main reason that tractor-trailers become out of control; much of it has to do with overloading the trailer, driver carelessness and the hilly topography of Western PA.

headline: Bulletin asks its unions for concessions
abstract: The Bulletin will publish its last edition August 16th unless its unions agree to a package of concessions that are needed to reverse growing losses. The Bulletin's president and publisher N.S. Hayden said that this is a necessary first step in a plan to save the newspaper. Losses in the last 18 months have exceeded $23.7 million.

headline: Judge Won't Stall Emission Testing
abstract: Under an order by US District Judge Louis Bechtle, state officials need to come up with a plan to set up an auto emission inspection program by June 10. The state had agreed to make the inspections mandatory, but recently the state and the Environmental Protection Agency had asked the court to delay start-up until January 1, 1983. Under the plan, garages would set fees for inspections, and motorists would also have to pay for repairs, if necessary.

headline: Can't Get There From Here
abstract: The state of the nation's mass-transit systems can be described as a crisis. Furthermore, the Reagan Administration plans to phase out federal operating subsidies to the systems by 1985. The question remains of who will pay for mass transit. The article argues that for them to keep running, they will need help from everyone - concessions from labor unions, better management, higher fares, more state funding and belt-tightening across the systems.

headline: Hospital Change To Prison Eyed By Governor
abstract: In an announcement on April 8, Governor Dick Thornburgh said the state wants to convert the closed Retreat State Hospital into a 250-bed prison for northeastern PA at a cost of $13.3 million. The governor said the conversion of the empty hospital represents a potential minimum cost solution to the overcrowding of prisons in northeastern PA.

headline: Senate Oks financing for low-interest loans
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate has approved legislation authorizing the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency to issue tax-exempt bonds to finance low-interest mortgages for low-income families.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: US Senator Helms surrounded by lobbyists saying " Good work, Jesse- save that government aid for folks who are truly needy."

headline: Pa. hired bottom 2 of 7 law firms; Survey: 5 others more experienced; 2 law firms hired by Pa. ranked behind 5 others
abstract: The two law firms that Pennsylvania state Governor Thornburgh appointed earlier this year as bond co-counsel to the Pennsylvania House Finance Agency were rated behind five other state firms in September on the basis of experience in handling municipal bonds, a survey given to the Pennsylvania House Finance Agency board last year shows.  The survey was obtained from agency sources after it was disclosed earlier this week that one of the firms hired by Thornburgh's general council in March to serve as Pennsylvania House Finance Agency bond counsel was Rose, Schmidt, Dixon, Hasley, Whyte and Hardesty of Pittsburgh.

headline: Funding cuts would end Appalachian agency
abstract: President Reagan's proposal to cut funding to the Appalachian Regional Commission (ARC) will ultimately eliminate the organizations, says the organization.  The article details what they do and how the cuts will affect them.

headline: OK pact, TWU tells members: But no talks are set up in strike at Red Arrow
abstract: The leaders of local 234, Transport Workers Union, urged workers of Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) to ratify the tentative labor contract reached last week. After the union meeting, union workers appeared to be happy with the proposed pact. If the workers vote for the pact this Friday, April 10, they will end the 20-day transit strike. Meanwhile, the suburban Red Arrow lines entered its fifth day of strikes with no talks scheduled.

headline: Closing is final, Sun says:  Shipyard layoff decision is called 'irreversible'
abstract: Sun Ship, Incorporated President Robert H. Campbell said that his decision to layoff over 3,000 people and stop building ships will not be changed.  Several PA senators and Governor Dick Thornburgh have asked that the company take back their decision.

headline: Keystone State sets Proud Tradition
abstract: National Hunting and Fishing Day will be observed Saturday especially in PA. PA has the highest number of hunting tradition and activities. The theme this year is A Day for Years to Come.

headline: CAT, York will share new buses; CAT will get 5 buses under pooled purchases
abstract: null

headline: Hostage Drama Ends
abstract: Seven prisoners, holding hostages at Graterford Prison, released six hostages and surrendered, ending the five day stand off that started with a failed escape attempt.  The article details the events of the hostage takeover, as well as the negotiations.

headline: Shamokin Area Shot in Arm; Praise Heaped on Steam Plant Upstate That Burns Coal Waste
abstract: A dedication was held at the Shamokin Area Industrial Park for a new steam plant that will be fired by a waste product of coal.  Many are optimistic that the plant will help the area economically.  The article describes how the plant works and reactions to the new industry.

headline: Case near end, Street requests a jury trial
abstract: State Senator Milton Street's (R-Philadelphia) disorderly-conduct trial, in which he is charged with engaging in a melee during an April 1980 City Council debate on Abscam prosecutions, was nearly completed on May 20, when the legislator demanded to have the case heard before a jury. Street and Franklin Moses are charged with an array of misdemeanor offenses centering on simple assault. Judge Melvin Levy denied the motion, and the trial continues before Levy.

headline: Pa. Senate rejects 5 for judgeships
abstract: State Senate Democrats rejected five of Governor Dick Thornburgh's 14 judicial nominations, including - as promised - that of Commonwealth Court Judge Roy Wilkinson Jr. to an unexpired term on the state Supreme Court.  The five nominations were tabled on a Repbulican motion - a move that will allow the Senate to reconsider them when it reconvenes January 26.

headline: Good things
abstract: The editors point out two good things about Erie County's economy.   First, the job loss has stopped, and second, the local labor force has expanded.  Otherwise, the economy has stayed the same between the second and third quarters.  The editors feel the county is holding their own in the national market.

headline: Once Strong Highway Fun Has Deficit
abstract: In 1980 the Highway Trust Fund, which gets its revenues from the federal gasoline tax, had less money for highway construction and maintenance.  The reason for the decline is a drop in gasoline sales due to high prices.  States are also having problems getting revenue from their gas taxes.  Gov. Thornburgh has asked to convert the 11 cents state tax to a percentage tax.

headline: Coal Industry Rejects New Proposals by Union
abstract: Contract talks were delayed another three days after the coal industry rejected new union proposals in the first resumption of bargaining since 160,000 United Mine Workers struck the nation's coalfields March 27.
