No quick breakthrough in the negotiations is expected despite the scheduling of another round of talks for Friday, April 17. The strike has an impact on related industries and the economy.

headline: Laurels and barbs
abstract: The author approves the Richland School District superintendent for calming fears about asbestos in ceilings in a middle school, but disapproves of the Public Utility Commission for delaying a decision on the proposed Penelec-Met Ed managerial merger. Also disapproves of the General Public Utilities chairman William Kuhns dismissal of possible nuclear accidents like the one at Three Mile Island, and of those trying to make a big deal about how one American greeted Prince Charles when he arrived in the US.

headline: Caught in a bureaucratic web
abstract: The editorial argues against the bureaucracy that has prevented residents of 16 houses in Northeast Philadelphia from selling their homes because of their condemnation by the PA Department of Transportation. Since PennDOT's plans for road construction are no longer in the plans, the editorial argues that the state should prevent a repetition by changing its procedures and laws to prohibit tying up property after public works projects have been abandoned.

headline: House Rejects Sentence Rules
abstract: The state House rejected the PA Sentencing Commission guidelines for a more uniform punishment for similar crimes committed anywhere in the state. The rejection will not take effect unless the Senate adopts another resolution before April 24. Otherwise, they will go into effect on July 23.

headline: Smoke alarms
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council has approved and Pittsburgh Mayor Alighieri has signed into law a strict new fire and building code will require smoke alarms or other fie detection devices to be installed in every building in the city. Some worry to is no way to enforce it.

headline: Chester asks congressmen to helo get shipbuilding jobs
abstract: A meeting of public officials and business representative in the city of Chester are trying asking U.S. Senators and Congressment to put pressure on the shippbuilding industry not to lay off 3,100 in the Chester area.

headline: Pa. Senate sees voters deciding pension issue
abstract: A bill allowing state's voters to decide increases in pension benefits currently paid to public employees should be extended to the spouse if the employee dies was passed by the Senate yesterday. The bill passed easily but had loud opposition from Republican Edward Howard. Howard states that the bill should be tied up until after a study commission initiates and completes research concerning public employee retirement. Howard states that the slated benefits would go beyond those afforded to any private employee, would burden the taxpayer, and would expand other benefits like medical insurance.

headline: Green gets the message
abstract: By making Bill Green the major issue for the seat he once held Joseph Smith understood one basic concept Green in no longer a part of those neighborhoods. Green's budget cutting wisdom is not filtering down to row-houses. It is a tough realization for the Green people.

headline: Once-a-Year Auto Inspections Inadequate
abstract: The author opines that Governor Thornburgh's proposal to reduce auto inspections from twice a year to yearly is not supported by adequate evidence.  The author cites a survey of 14,000 Pennsylvanians who stated they wanted yearly inspections because for conveyance and because they felt they were getting ripped off by mechanics.  The author feels that the Governor's proposal is not geared toward safety and preventative maintenance.

headline: Contract is rejected by miners
abstract: Pennsylvania coal miners, joining a nationwide trend, rejected a proposed contract that would have allowed them to return to work this week.  Nearly 160,000 union members have been on strike since Friday March 27, and according to the United Mine Workers union headquarters in Washington, the vote so far is 2-1 against the pact.

headline: Legislators spout hot air on emissions
abstract: State lawmakers are trying to block the implementation of the federally mandated auto-emission inspector program, but they are actually doing much. Nothing they could do could take precedence over a federal statute. The program is unpopular with car owners, but there's nothing the state can do.

headline: Child auto-seats bill OK'd by Senate unit
abstract: A PA Senate panel has approved legislation requiring PA parents to place small children is safety seats when transporting them in the family car. Parents failing to provide restraints could be fined $25. It applies to children 4 or younger who weigh less than 40 pounds.

headline: House rejects sentencing plan
abstract: The House voted 157 to 37 for a resolution that tells the Pennsylvania Sentencing Commission to come up with harsher minimum prison terms for criminals within six months, effectively rejecting the commission's current proposed measures. The resolution was sent to the Senate, which has its own version and will possibly vote on it next week. Unless both reject the commission's report, the new sentences will take effect on July 23.

headline: Standing up for squatters: Activists tangle with city over housing
abstract: The Inner City Organizing Network (ICON) has been placing the homeless in vacant buildings, much to the chagrin of state officials.  Some believe that when ICON takes over a vacant building, that building should have been restored.  Housing officials feel its unfair to give house to the person occupying the house, rather than someone willing to pay for it.  The article details ICON's activities.

headline: Chester Mayor Fears Unrest in Wake of Cuts
abstract: Chester Mayor Joseph Battle has told federal authorities that he is concerned about possible civil unrest this winter if poor residents experience fuel and food shortages because of sharp federal budget cuts. He is already working on soup kitchens and warming centers for winter.

headline: Pa. sets example for ERA
abstract: Sally Ringland comes from a state the not only has its own Equal Rights Amendment but has also ratified the national ERA amendment to the constitution. She is now trying to convince other states of how well the PA state ERA works and how it does not cause the problems some claim it might.

headline: Home rule voting unwisely delayed
abstract: It is regrettable the Allentown Government Study Commission has decided to delay placing the proposed new city charter referendum on the ballot until the spring primary elections.  The seven-member panel organized in May 1980 and immediately ruled out placing a recommendation on last November's ballot.  Now it has voted 6-1 not to put it on this November's ballot.

headline: Open and closed on the Schuylkill: It's a state of being
abstract: The Schuylkill Expressway may be closed for a while in late 1983 for some long overdue construction on the dilapidated 20.7 mile stretch of road. If the entire expressway is shut down it will take 18 months to get the entire reconstruction job complete.

headline: Disagrees with us
abstract: Wendell Young III, Secretary-Treasurer of the United Food and Commercial Workers, complains that a Delaware County Daily Times' editorial is based on beliefs and not on convincing evidence, shown by a lack of basic information. Mr. Young's letter attacks the editorial's support of the Governor's plan to scrap the State Stores.

headline: Loggers Get Some Tips on Protecting 'Penn's Woods'
abstract: Pennsylvania loggers will soon receive an education pamphlet published by the Pennsylvania Forestry Association with guidelines on for timber harvesting.  The guidelines are voluntary.  The article outlines some of the guidelines.

headline: College joins lawsuit to halt the Blue Route; Chester mayor calls action by Swarthmore 'anti-poor'
abstract: Swarthmore College joined a suit by Marple and Radnor townships to halt construction of Interstate Route 476, the Midcounty Expressway.  The article goes into further detail about the expressway and the suit.

headline: How State Shortchanges Crime Victims
abstract: The state has realized more than $3 million in profits in the past five years from a fund meant to help the thousands of victims of violent crime each year in Pennsylvania. The state's Crime Victim's Compensation Board has paid out only $2.4 million to 1,100 victims, out of a total of more than $6 million collected through a $10 fine levied on those who are convicted or plead guilty to committing a violent crime. The original sponsors were unaware of the profits, and declared the bill was not intended to provide a surplus. While an average of half of all those who apply are rejected because of severe restrictions on who is eligible under the law, the state has quietly used the surplus for general expenses.

headline: Tenants criticize Montco programs
abstract: A group of Pottstown residents asked Montgomery County Commission for emergency housing.  189 tenants of landlord Thomas Lord say they have been living in deplorable conditions without heat, electricity or water.  Lord confirmed that the buildings were without utilities, stating that he just didn't have enough money for them because the tenants owe him back rent.

headline: Choices for Common Pleas
abstract: The editorial explains that the May 19 primary election for Allegheny County Common Pleas Court is notable for several reasons. One is that the race for the four seats has attracted a large number of young candidates, and another is that there is an increased interest of women in judicial office. The newspaper endorses four of these candidates: Raymond Novak, Marcella Hanson, Grace Harris, and William Standish.

headline: Pa. wants you; 580 volunteers are needed to fill positions on draft boards
abstract: null

headline: House Oks High Penalty On Wage Tax
abstract: The Pennsylvania House has passed legislation to make it more expensive for Pittsburgh residents and businesses to be delinquent in paying school taxes.  Under the bills, the school district could charge the going Federal Reserve Discount.  The article goes further into detail about the higher interest charges and the taxes.

headline: Our opinoin:  Roads and taxes
abstract: The editors feel that the condition for the roads in Pennsylvania are unacceptable and something must be done to fix them.  They support Governor Thornburgh's proposal of a gasoline tax with a three cent limit as a way to fund the repairs.

headline: Does Sun Ship sale mean jobs?
abstract: Sun Company has finally found a new buyer for its Sun Ship Incorporated subsidiary which marks a welcome opening for the holiday season in Chester, Pennsylvania. Residents of Chester took the news hard when they found out a year ago the Sun Ship, the backbone of this industrial city for 65 years was getting out of shipbuilding.

headline: Magnanimous State Lets Boy Off Hook
abstract: The state said it has decided to write off a $90 medical bill charged to the mother of a boy who nearly fell into the underground mine fire in Centralia. The Office of the Attorney General said it has sent a letter to Florence Domboski telling her she has enough other debts that the bill will be canceled.

headline: Commuters gear up for Parkway work; Thousands face months of Parkway East work
abstract: The Department of Transportation has started the Parkway East reconstruction in Pittsburgh to alleviate traffic congestion.  However, until the project is completed there will be more traffic.  The article outlines the project and suggests other routes, including car pooling and a commuter train.

headline: Imbalances cited in Law Day talk
abstract: In preparation for today's Dauphin County Bar Association's annual Law Day luncheon, state Supreme Court Justice Robert Nix Jr. agreed in a telephone interview that the courts must be responsive to the society they serve, but that they are not beyond accountability. Nevertheless, he says they must step in when the will of the majority is clearly in opposition to the dictates of morality.

headline: Thornburgh: Create jobs here
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh called for the creation of more jobs in PA, rejecting the notion that the Northeast must accept the inevitable migration of jobs and people to the Sun Belt. He noted that last year 419,000 Pennsylvanians were out of work. He singled out revitalization of highways, housing, railroads and water resources as instrumental in stimulating new jobs.

headline: City Mayors Yearn for the Old Federalism
abstract: The nation's mayors are disturbed by President Reagan's talk about a "new federalism" in which Reagan proposes to reduce the flow of funds from the federal government and giving state government's control over what is left. This jeopardizes many local cities and mayors as relations between governors and mayors have never been naturally allied. Many cities receive 15-20% of their budget from the federal government and these funds go toward repairing streets, hiring law enforcement and mass transit. Many mayors feel Reagan is out to destroy the special local-federal relationship that has emerged and flourished since WWII, which parallels the Federal-state relationship due to his demand for budget cuts.

headline: Pa. workers must list holding, court told
abstract: State Attorney General Harvey Bartle III told the State Supreme Court that governor has powers to request personal financial information from state employees based on the constitution.  This was his argument in court dealing with an lawsuit brought by the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME).  A ruling has not been made in the case yet

headline: House panel expected to OK tax plan
abstract: The Pennsylvania House is expected to pass a bill that would allow local school districts to replace property taxes with a maximum 3.5 per cent income tax.  The Senate has already passed a similar bill.  The article details the pros and cons of the bill.

headline: PA Senate passes $8.1 billion budget
abstract: The PA Senate passed the state's $8.1 billion 1982 budget, including a new wholesale transportation-fuel tax that could add 2 cents a gallon to gasoline prices and deep cuts in social service programs.  PennDOT has a new $1.2 million spending program.

headline: Eaton plant union calls for protest
abstract: Local 1717, International Association of Machinists, the union representing production workers at Eaton Corporation's plant in Northeast Philadelphia, said yesterday it will seek a 15-minute citywide work stoppage by union workers to protest area plant closings. The union is seeking the support of labor unions, clergymen, and civic leaders to put a halt to the wave of plant closings during the past several years in Philadelphia.

headline: Mandatory Luzerne County water cuts eyed
abstract: A PA Gas And Water Company official says 80,000 Luzerne County customers could face mandatory conservation if depleted reservoirs are not recharged.  The reservoirs have been depleted due to drought conditions affecting much of Eastern PA.  The two major water storage facilities, the Watres and Chenery reservoirs, have dropped to 33% and 28% of capacity, respectively, the lowest levels since the drought of 1930-31.

headline: Conrail funds hinge on reducing losses
abstract: Meeting with Governor Dick Thornburgh and others representing the Coalition of Northeast Governors, US Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis made an offer to provide an additional $1.5 billion to Conrail to help the financially strapped Northeast rail freight giant. The help is conditional on ultimately getting the government out of the railroad business.

headline: In custody cases, a knowledge gap
abstract: Article explains the effects that shuffling a child among and between biological, foster and adoptive parents has upon a child. A child loses the ability to trust and form emotional attachments, these children cannot give or receive love later in life and is ill-prepared to plan for long-term future events. Knowing this garden-variety type of information leads to the question: why do courts keep shuffling the children around? The author states it is partially because judges and lawyers were not introduced to interdisciplinary studies in college, like many students are today.

headline: Unglamorous Tasks
abstract: Pittsburgh's Renaissance II project needs to look not only into updating buildings and the like, but also looking at the underpinnings and substructures of what of which renewal effort rests. If these underpinnings such as: roads, bridges, parking, and the locks and dams on the rivers are ignored, they will be even more expensive in the future.

headline: City's Richest Workers Get 14% Raise
abstract: Although they are the highest paid employees on the city payroll, court reporters assigned to Philadelphia's Common Pleas Court have received a pay increase averaging 14.6% from the PA Supreme Court. The raise will add more than $500,000 to the court's budget, which must be paid by the city and has not been appropriated. Despite the increase, the court reporters' organization has hired lawyer Mark Mendel to press their demands for an even bigger raise.

headline: Pa., NJ. Among only 8 states reporting measles cases
abstract: Pennsylvania and New Jersey were among the few states to report measles cases in the first half of this year. More than 92 percent of America's counties were measles free.

headline: House to work on Pa. tax reform
abstract: The state House will begin working on a Senate bill that would allow local school districts to replace their funding source from property taxes to a local income tax.  The article discusses the pros and cons of switching the funding source.

headline: '76 Green campaign group missed a filing deadline
abstract: Mayro Green's 1976 Senate campaign committee has failed to file the required semiannual financial disclosure report, according to the Federal Elections Commisssion.  A commission spokesman said it in Washington that campaign committees for all federal candidates are required to continue filing the twice-a-year reports until all revenues have been accounted for and until the commission has approved the settlement of all outstanding debts.  The spokesman also said that the committee for Green's unsuccessful 1976 Senate race had submitted a plan for settlement of its final debts but thtat because the commission had not yet approved the plan, the committee was still required to file the disclosure report due July 31.

headline: FOP moves to control disputed health agency
abstract: Rank-and-file members of Lodge 5 of the Fraternal Order of Police are seeking to take control of a controversial health and welfare affiliate of their union whose funds have been reduced by Philadelphia Mayor Green's administration. The proposal, made April 7, was that the executive board take control of Police Health Administration, a non-profit that administers dental, optical and prescription programs for city police officers.

headline: Migration to Sun Belt Not a Solution
abstract: Editorial says that a proposal by a presidential commission to encourage citizens to migrate to the Sun Belt States would cause more problems than it would solve, increasing pollution and putting a strain on the southern states.

headline: Conrail Is Finally on the Tracks To Profitability, Its Chief Says
abstract: The article outlines an interview with the chief operating officer of Conrail and his ideas on the future of Contrail.

headline: In vote for mandatory sentencing PA house shoots down the liberals
abstract: Crime and punishment in PA is likely to become a little more grim due to mandatory sentencing. A mandatory 5 years will be given to certain types of violent crime. It cannot be described as lenient. If passed it will be the toughest anti-crime law in the country.

headline: Working on it
abstract: A letter written by State Senator Edwin Holl states that he agrees with the newspapers article about homes for the retired and recently introduced a bill to protect the eldery by requiring financial disclosure of the people or corporations who run retirement homes.

headline: City's top choice to host Democrats
abstract: Philadelphia is likely to be chosen as the site of the Democrats' 1982 mid-term convention, because defaults have left it almost alone in consideration.

headline: Panel to draw new political lines this week
abstract: State lawmakers have reason to feel nervous as the boundaries of the state of Pennsylvania’s 203 House and 50 Senate districts are being redrawn to reflect population change from the 1980 census. Chairman of the Pennsylvania Reapportionment Commission decreed that a comprehensive redistricting plan should be on the table by August 17. If parties to redistricting are unable to come to an agreement of as many issues as possible, Freedmen would cast the deciding vote. Republicans are happy about the reapportionment as it would be the largely Democratic bases in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia that would lose seats, not the Republicans. Democrats counter that they are not worried as they hold a commanding edge in statewide voter registrations.

headline: Landmark tax-shift bill OK'd
abstract: The state senate passed legislation giving school districts the choice of switching their revenue source from property taxes to a local income tax.  A change in the bill, giving school districts a choice, is what allowed it to pass.  The article weighs the pros and cons of the legislation.

headline: 90 days for planning of reapportionment may begin May 12
abstract: The 90-day period provided for the once-a-decade Legislative Reapportionment Commission to prepare a preliminary plan for redistricting the 203 state House and 50 Senate districts could begin May 12. That will happen only if Richard Campbell, executive director of the Legislative Data Processing Center, can submit good census data on that date's meeting of the five-member reapportionment panel, given that there are problems measuring some districts.

headline: General strike puts labor leaders in no-win situation
abstract: The article details how strikes in America are generally avoided because they put labor unions in no-win situations.  Historians point out that general strikes are only used in America in times of great labor and economic strife.  The article outlines strategies to avoid strikes by Philadelphia labor unions.

headline: Mineral Rights May Ground Airport Plans
abstract: A lawsuit pending in Common Pleas Court has raised doubts about the ownership of mineral rights on thousands of acres of airport property, including the area of a proposed $200 million to $300 million Midfield Terminal. If Allegheny County is forced to purchase mineral rights before building on the land, the cost of the project could soar.

headline: Conrail needs 'rehabilitation, not capital punishment'
abstract: US Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis argues that Conrail, the Consolidated Railroad Corporation, has cost the public treasury too much, and has not and probably will not become self-sufficient, relying instead on large federal subsidies. Therefore, the Reagan administration's private sector proposal is to give shippers and commuters a better service at a greatly reduced cost to taxpayers. This can be done, he argues, by selling off Conrail's assets to private carriers.

headline: In vote for mandatory sentencing Pa. House shoots down the liberal
abstract: The Pennsylvania State House of Representatives approved a key portion of Governor Thornburgh's anti-crime package. Thornburgh's anti crime package is considered one of the toughest state anti crime legislation in the nation's history. The Thornburgh bill requires judges to impose mandatory minimum five year jail terms to those who use a gun to commit crimes such as rape, robbery, assault, kidnapping and arson.

headline: $750,000 earmarked to try to attract, save jobs in state
abstract: With a $750,000 advertising and promotion budget, PA is one of the big spenders in an increasingly desperate battle among the states to attract new industries and retain those they already have. A study prepared by the Council of State Governments does not evaluate the effectiveness of Madison Avenue techniques, but it suggests the states who do advertise feel justified.

headline: Cleaning up a mess
abstract: On one point most people are agreed better way of running the Philadelphia public schools must be devised. Legislation is currently proposing that the board be elected instead of appointed. The PA General Assembly also has to amend the 1963 home rule law.

headline: Panel: Election coverage must go beyond hoopla
abstract: A decline in voter interest and in confidence in the news media may be the fault of politicians and reporters, three news media representatives said during a panel discussion with the nation's lieutenant governors.  Speaking before the 20th annual National Conference of Lieutenant Governors, Haynes Johnson, a national correspondent for the Washington Post, said that reporters needed to focus more attention on new trends and attitudes among American voters.  He said that the news media too often focused all of their attention on breaking news stories, but failed to go behind the scenes and report on the events leading up to the story.

headline: Leonard campaigning for now and the future
abstract: On March 6, 1975 an unknown 28-year-old lawyer named Thomas A Leonard got a phone call from one Frank L Rizzo, the mayor of Philadelphia. He promised to make him a star. He offered him a chance to register wills. Now he is a rising star in city politics. He was elected controller two years ago,

headline: A beginning
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Paul Doutrich and Pat Brinkley, a clerk in the city Administration Office, kick off Employ the Handicapped Week at City Hall.

headline: Grounded: Fired controllers swap condolences at picnic
abstract: Fired air traffic controllers met at Roosevelt Park, near the Philadelphia airport, counting down the seconds until President Reagan's deadline officially firing the striking air traffic controllers. Even though the spirit of this meeting was one of camaraderie and bravado it was simply masking their tears. Many of these men are out of $20,000-$40,000 a year government jobs and held in contempt of numerous federal courts. So, they held a picnic.

headline: Most Accidental Poisoning Victims Are Children; Over 1 Million Cases A Year
abstract: Each year, over 1 million children are injured or killed by accidental poisonings from common household items such as drugs, soaps, detergents, disinfectants, and noxious fumes.  Governor Thornburgh is trying to raise awareness of the problem by proclaiming March 15-21 as Poison Prevention Week in Pennsylvania.

headline: Conrail seeks to cut 26 Pa. lines
abstract: Conrail, a federally subsidized railroad, delivered to Congress a report calling for a cut in 26 of its Pennsylvania lines. The report that cites the lines that Conrail considers unprofitable was made public by US Representative James Nelligan (R-PA). The Interstate Commerce Commission will have to approve such action.

headline: Inmates at Graterford Give Out 12 Demands
abstract: Chuck Stone, a Philadelphia Daily News columnist met with four convicts holding nine hostages at Graterford State Prison and was given a list of demands.  The article details Mr. Stone's experience in the prison, but does not list the 12 "negotiations."

headline: 2 brothers given probation, fines in 'fix' of lottery
abstract: Peter K. and Jack K. Maragos, brothers, were sentenced by Dauphin County Court to five years probation and fines of $25,000 on top of the $40,000 restitution they owe, for rigging the Pennsylvania State Lottery's nightly drawing.  Others are also implicated in the crime.  The article details the scandal.

headline: 'Clear-language' order stalled
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's executive to order to have state agencies write their regulations in "simple, clear and concise language" had been stalled by the Director of the Pennsylvania Bulletin and Code, Gary Hoffman.  He states that executive orders must be reviewed by the attorney general.  The article details other officials dismay at the hold up.

headline: Penn[s]ylvania budget-time rites
abstract: The article describes how the state legislature holds budget hearings.  It details the process and talks about the political bickering and rivalary the goes on between the Republicans and Democrats.

headline: Letters to the editor; City Council's Christmas gift to itself
abstract: The generous gift exchange that City Council voted for the taxpayers to give council members a $10,000 pay raise and give Mayor Caliguiri a $12,000 pay raise, while council gives the public a $49 million tax package that will raise real estate and wage levies.  The article expresses the author's hope that the public will remember

headline: A fine bit of leadership
abstract: Block grants, according to the latest study, appear to be working.  Block grants are those that the federal government gives to a country or community to use as it will.  These block grants are slowly replacing rants given to pay for a specific purpose or project.  In fact, if President Reagan has his way, all federal grants to help countries pay for human services will eventually go to each county in one lump block grant.

headline: Gulf orders cutbacks at Phila. plant
abstract: The Gulf Oil Company will reduce the work force at its Philadelphia refinery and operate at its present rate of 60 to 65 percent of capacity over the next five years, reported a company spokesman.  Gulf spokesman John R. Galloway said the company does not yet know how great the reduction in the labor force will be, but added that it would not be major cutbacks.  Some workers will be offered transfers, others may take early retirement and still others will be laid off.

headline: Nation's Water Is Bountiful, But Supplies Are Squandered
abstract: Despite repeated reported water shortages in the US, experts believe that the US is endowed with water supplies that should be adequate to support the nation for generations. However, experts say that due to squander through poor management and inefficient use to such a degree that water is running short in many areas. The solution to the water problem is not technological ultimately but rather economic and political in nature.

headline: Council's grandstanding didn't help SEPTA's riders
abstract: Members of the Philadelphia City Council unanimously supported the striking SEPTA workers and their leader, Dominic DiClerico.  The article considers the pros and cons of this approach by the City Council, and the details of the union negotiations.

headline: Inmates Feared for Their Lives
abstract: The article provides a narrative of inmates, and government officials concerns during the Graterford State Prison hostage siege, where four inmates took thirty eight hostages after a failed escape attempt.

headline: 3 bulls propose recording of sales of gold and silver
abstract: Three bills proposed in the legislature are designed to make sellers of precious metals keep detailed lists of every purchase they make.  The bills were introduced after a rise in jewlery theft.  The three bills differ slightly.

headline: Close the schools
abstract: Letter to the editor claims teachers are more interested in striking than teaching. Author would like to use this opportunity to fire all the teachers and close public schools.

headline: Pension-benefit rebuke
abstract: Sixty-two percent of Pennsylvania voters voted "no" to a referendum extending cost-of-living adjustments to surviving spouses of state and municipal pensioners despite the question conditioning that such increases were actuarially sound. The voters' message is clear to the Thornburgh Administration: it should be committed to pension reform immediately. Even after a full year of exhaustive hearings on the subject and a plethora of sensible conclusions resulting from these hearings, the Thornburgh Administration is recasting a new committee to begin a new study of the topic.

headline: Mayor's pay upheld, but D.A.'s is cut
abstract: PA's Commonwealth Court approved salary raises for Philadelphia's City Mayor Green and members of the City Council. But the court rejected raises for the District Attorney, sheriff, register of wills and three city commissioners. The court's 5-2 ruling stemmed from a suit filed by several community groups to challenge the raises.

headline: A Justice Dissents
abstract: Justice Bruce Kauffman decided not to seek another term on the State Supreme Court after not receiving support from either the Democratic or Republican parties.  He was appointed to the Supreme Court by Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Gunfire Hits Tank at Non-Union State Coal Site
abstract: Gunfire hit an oil tank on Thursday, April 16, at a non-union PA coal mining company that has continued operating during the walkout by some 160,000 United Mine Workers. As the walkout entered its 22nd day, some mining companies posted armed guards and police increased patrols in Eastern coalfields. There is doubt that an agreement between the UMW and the Bituminous Coal Operators Association can be reached soon. Other incidents reported in Kentucky and West Virginia, while coalfields in Indiana, Utah, and Ohio were reported quiet.

headline: New DER chief sees industrial waste as major problem of '80s
abstract: Acting Pennsylvania State Secretary of Environmental Resources, Peter Duncan, states that disposal of industrial waste will be the issue of the 1980s. Duncan highlights the need for the state of Pennsylvania to hire responsible contractors and insists on performance bonds for contractors. Duncan attests to his adamancy in beginning a public information campaign for citizens and municipal governments about the risks of doing nothing to reduce industrial waste in the state.

headline: Decide on the State Gas Tax
abstract: The author calls on the legislature to decide how they will fund repairing Pennsylvania’s  roads.  The author supports governor Thornburgh's proposed percentage increase in the gasoline tax.  The author wants the legislature to either adopt the governor's plan or come up with their own.

headline: Inmates prepared for 'real battle'
abstract: A five day hostage crisis at Graterford Prison ended, after the inmates tried to build a barricade of potatoes and onions to hide behind.  Some of the hostages that survived the ordeal stated that they felt sympathetic to the leader, Joseph Bowen, who was serving a life sentence for killing three police officers.  The article describes the ordeal.

headline: 35 in city are carrying coverage: Federal crime insurance available
abstract: The Federal Crime Insurance program provides protection for residents and businesses against burglary and theft.  Policyholders are encouraged to install minimum security devices, such as deadbolt locks, and pay a premium.  Pennsylvania director of urban-property insurance stated that most policyholders in Pennsylvania are in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, primarily in inner-city areas.  The article outlines the program details, costs, and provides information on becoming part of the program.

headline: Coleman was warned dinner had ethical risks
abstract: Before a testimonial dinner during Philadelphia Council President Joseph Coleman received a $9,850 gold watch, Philadelphia City Solicitor Alan Davis warned him that such appearances of impropriety could pose serious legal and ethical risks. He went ahead anyway.

headline: Pensions In State In Trouble
abstract: Community Affairs Secretary, Shirley M. Dennis, estimated that municipial pension systems are underfunded by more than $2 billion.  She asked lawmakers to establish a commission, and refrain from increasing pension benefits

headline: Mayor's second-term goal: Reorganize
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Caliguiri is attempting to reorganize most city departments in his second term.  The mayor wants the city to be more fiscally sound and is seeking a broader tax base.  The article details some proposed tax reform ideas.

headline: A matter of ethics: Justice Larsen and friends
abstract: PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen's conduct is under investigation by the state Judicial Inquiry and Review Board. The examination, extended over 5 months, show that Larsen has taken official actions that appear to have favored his friends, political allies, and his expressed political intentions. The Philadelphia Inquirer has learned of and is reporting several of these actions.

headline: Heinz Bill Gives Family Deportation Reprieve
abstract: A Jenkintown , PA family will be allowed to remain in the U.S. rather than be deported to Canada, until the Senate Judiciary Committee acts on a bill designed to make them legal residents. Senator John Heinz III introduced a private bill that would give the Jenkintown family permanent resident status.

headline: Nurseries, pools ask relaxed water rules
abstract: State nursery and swimming pool industries asked the Pennsylvania Management Agency to relax its regulations on water, in light of the ongoing drought in the Delaware River Basin.  They fear that if the restrictions on water use continue, it will bankrupt 146 businesses, causing more Pennsylvanians to lose their jobs.

headline: Don't abandon Conrail
abstract: The editors feel that the Reagan Administration's decision to end federal financial support for the Conrail railroad system will hurt the Northeast United States.  The editors feel that industry will suffer because Conrail will not be able to continue their service without subsidies.  The editorial details their argument for keeping federal financial support for Conrail.

headline: Inmates rig 'escape' into driver's seat
abstract: Five inmates of the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill will be in the drivers seat as they begin an eight-week course to teach them to be "nomads of the highway."  They will be joined by an equal number of "outsiders" who are clients of Susquehanna Employment and Training Corporation, which is picking up the $25,250 tab for the program.  And when graduation ceremonies take place September 25, the trainees will have learned far more than a trade.

headline: A harness racing track is up to voters
abstract: The primary election on May 19 in Allegheny County will feature a public referendum on a horse-racing plant. If approved, developers would start plans to build a racetrack possibly in Monroeville, generating jobs and revenues. Although many Democrats and Republicans favor the proposition, it faces opposition from Monroeville officials, local ministers, and citizen groups.

headline: Commonwealth is model for 'order in the court'
abstract: Three candidates, including one incumbent, are running for the Democratic and Republican nominations for state Commonwealth Court in the May 19 primary election. Unlike the problems with the state supreme and superior courts, the candidates are left without any burning issue, as the Commonwealth Court has an admirable track record of the lowest backlog.

headline: Perry maintains 666 innocence
abstract: Former Pittsburgh TV host Nick Perry, facing up to 66 years in prison for the 666 state lottery fix, has denied any wrongdoing. Perry was convicted along with state lottery district manager Edward Plevel for a scheme in which weighted ping pong balls were used to collect some $1.4 million in winnings.

headline: New 3.5% local income tax proposed to replace school realty tax
abstract: Legislation that would replace school property taxes with a local personal income tax was resurrected by the Senate Finance Committee in a version Republican Leaders believe will be palpable to their members. It gives school districts the option of abolishing their present property and nuisance taxes and replacing them with a personal income tax of up to .5 percent plus a business tax.

headline: A not-so-quiet campaign to get McEwen a judgeship
abstract: Labor union officials are and a lobbyist from the Pennsylvania Insurance Federation are lobbying state senators on behalf of judicial nominee Stephen J. McEwen, Jr., former Delaware County district attorney.  It is rare for special interest groups to lobby for a specific judicial nominee.  The article details the career of Mr. McEwen as a district attorney and many believe his nomination by Governor Thornburgh was part of a political deal.

headline: Help for the Jobless
abstract: The editorial notes that Eastern Pennsylvania has recently lost a lot of jobs.  They support the initiative of state senators James Lloyd and Philip Price to encourage businesses to hire employees off the welfare rolls in return for a tax credit.

headline: Our Voice:  Let Manhattan tap the Hudson
abstract: Editorial states that now that the governors of four states have declared a drought in the region and banned certain uses of water for conservation reasons; they need to look at the use of their water by New York City.  They propose looking for more "lasting" solutions.

headline: Edberg calls for river safety
abstract: Coroner Sanford Edberg called for legislation requiring all boaters to pass a safe-boating test. This came as a result of a boating accident that swept six people over an Ohio River dam, killing them on June 13. The Dashfields Dam, where the aforementioned accident took place has been the scene of eight out of ten dam deaths in Allegheny County in the past six years. His recommendations were the boating safety test and large noticeable warning signs hanging from the Sewickley Bridge.

headline: It's enough to make you sick- if you can afford it
abstract: Opinion where the author would rather be killed getting mugged than having to deal with the ordeal of getting old. He doesn't think he can afford the medical costs and thinks by time he gets there he will already have to deal with overwhelming crime.

headline: A poor bet
abstract: A bill that would give substantial tax breaks to PA's horse racing tracks has come out of the Legislature. The editorial does not believe this is a good bet for the state. It will only benefit the race track owners. They don't like that is allows call-in bets.

headline: Commuters' wage-tax cut would harm entire region
abstract: The Finance Committee of the PA House of Representatives voted to send to the House floor a bill which would force a bill which would force Philadelphia to reduce from 4.31 percent to 2.9 percent the wage taxes paid commuters who work in Philadelphia but live outside it. While the scheme is clearly attractive to suburban PA, New Jersey and Delaware residents and especially so in time of intense public consciousness of the burdens of taxation at every level, it would be unwise and self-defeating for it to become law.

headline: Perry, Plevel guilty in '666'
abstract: The lottery-fix trial concluded May 20 in Dauphin County Court with the conviction of co-defendants Nick Perry and Edward Plevel on 15 counts related to the April 24, 1980, drawing of the PA Daily Number. The contest had a record payout by the state of more than $3 million as the fixed number 6-6-6 appeared in the lottery machines at the Pittsburgh televised drawing. The 12 person jury found Perry guilty of 10 charges and Plevel guilty of five charges.

headline: New taxes are sought for schools
abstract: While Philadelphia teachers walked the picket lines for the third day yesterday, members of City Council introduced a dozen different tax plans aimed at solving the financial problems of the school district. There is a proposal for a 10 percent real estate tax increase on the table.

headline: A pension sweetener sours for legislators
abstract: Governor Thornburgh proposed an unrecedented 1 percent across the board cut in state spending to meet the impact of federal budget cuts this year as two state representatives circulated a proposal to increase, by 73 percent, to the pension benefits for many legislators.  The smaller pension group consists of 144 of the 203 representatives and 20 of the 50 senators.  They would receive upon retirement a pesnion package equal to that of all other state employees.  The reason that legislators deserve higher pension benefits than other state employees is because legislators are subject to defeat in elections every two or four years, which means their careers are not as long as nonelective state employees.

headline: Inflation takes  3,000 face layoffs at 2 Budd plants
abstract: As many as 3,000 workers at two Budd Co. plants in Philadelphia may be out of work by the end of next week. Budd refused to confirm the numbers of layoffs. Heavy cutbacks in customers' orders are the cause of some of the layoffs, along with a strike preventing work at another plant.

headline: Pa. to probe Phila. Incinerator pollution
abstract: A PA House subcommittee began two days of hearings in Philadelphia into allegations of air and water pollution problems at the city's Northwest Incinerator. The city, which does not presently have a permit from the PA Department of Environmental Resources, received a letter from DER claiming that the groundwater is being polluted by the incinerator residue.

headline: Economic Relief
abstract: Editorial expressing the need to build the Blue Route, an expressway that would link Interstate 95 to the PA Turnpike.  The author suggests that this would offset the jobs lost by the decision of Sun Ship to stop building ships in the city of Chester and lay off over 3,100 people.  They call for the mayor, governor and all elected officials to support the Blue Route project

headline: Judge frees Street in driving case
abstract: PA state Senator T Milton Street was acquitted by a district justice of a charge of driving while his license was under suspension. The state was unable to approve that he was formally notified that his license had been suspended before the incident. Street said he expects to be acquitted on the other two 1980 incidents. He was also formally served with a subpoena asking for income tax and business records and his testimony.

newspaper: News of Delaware County – Drexel Hill/Upper Darby Edition
headline: Abolishing the State Stores
abstract: The author opines that Governor Thornburgh's proposal to abolish state owned liquor stores is a good idea.  The author states the State Senator Dick Tilghman (R) also supports the Governor's proposal, who stated that the state liquor commission is rife with corruption.

headline: Confirm Wilkinson
abstract: The editors state that Judge Roy Wilkinson should be confirmed to fill a vacancy on the state Supreme Court.  They state that democrats had intially held up the confirmation, but now that they have agreed on a member to fill the Reapportionment Committee, Judge Wilkinson should be confirmed.

headline: PFT Found Guilty of Contempt
abstract: Ruling that the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers was guilty of civil contempt, Common Pleas Court Judge Edward Bradley fined the union $10,000 for each day its members fail to obey court-imposed restrictions on mass picketing and a court order that they return to their jobs.

headline: No tax increase
abstract: Letter to the editor against increasing property taxes for the schools.

headline: A pension sweetener sours for legislators
abstract: Two PA state representatives quietly circulated a proposal to increase by 73 the comparatively generous pension benefits for many legislators. The amendment did not get added, because House members were not in favor of it.

headline: Inflation takes a dramatic pause
abstract: As many as 3,000 workers at two Budd Company plants in Philadelphia may be out of work by the end of next week. Company officials refuse to confirm the exact date when the lay-offs will occur but they could confirm that the reasons for the lay-offs at the two plants were for two very different reasons. At the Bustleton rail car plant most of the employees will be furloughed because their main supplier is on strike. The Nicetown plant makes auto parts for the auto industry which is in the worst slumps of the last 20 years.

headline: Pennsylvania Town Lives With Fire That Won't Stop
abstract: The residents of the town of Centralia, PA, are suffering from the hazardous fumes and other dangers associated with underground mine fires. The county, state, and federal agencies are discussing what to do, but the secretary of the Interior and Governor Dick Thornburgh have agreed on a $1 million emergency relief program under which 26 homes will be bought and the owners relocated. Failed solutions in the past have led experts to agree the only sure solution is to remove all 109 homes.

headline: Ed Bellock Challenged By District Road Woes
abstract: Ed Bellock was using a pocket calculator to do a quick calculation the other day.  With 15 Pennsylvania Department of Transportation crews laying eight tons of patch each day, or a total of 120 tons, Bellock figured it will take 108 workdays to finish patching roads in Westmoreland County.  The work is half finished, but the first snow flurries will probably fly before the work is complete.  For Bellock, Pennsylvania Department of Transportation maintenance manager for Westmoreland County, it is a schedule he must keep.  The roads he has charge of rank as some of the worst in the state and Bellock was hand-picked by the Thornburgh administration to make the county a showcase of road improvements.

headline: Judge, 4 others again found to be innocent of land fraud
abstract: Suspended Wayne County Judge Robert Conway and four other defendants have been found innocent of federal conspiracy and fraud charges in connection with the development of recreation area. A federal judge deliberated more than seven hours before handing down the decision. It was the third time the defendants have been cleared of indictments in the case.

headline: Alice in Booze-Land
abstract: The author talks about a state Senate meeting discussing the possibility of privatizing state liquor stores. Several Senators felt that privatizing the state stores would increase the efficiency of service for customers, but, the author feels their desire to but many restrictions on proposed alleged stores negates their capitalist position on privatizations.

headline: Congress lets ARC survive another year
abstract: The Appalachian Regional Commission and the Economic Development Administration will survive at least one more year under an agreement reached by House and Senate conferees. It provides $290 million for EDA and $215 million for ARC. Both sums are less than last year, but is still considered a victory, since President Reagan had sought to do away with the programs. In the past, PA has received more money than any of the other 13 states in the program.

headline: Phila. Bar Rates Shiomos Unfit
abstract: The Philadelphia Bar Association has rate Judge Thomas N. Shiomas as 'unqualified' to be retained on the Common Pleas Court due to his brief involvement in the Abscam investigation.  The article details Shiomas' career and also includes the ratings of other judges.

headline: Phila. Will review port leases, seek ads
abstract: City Representative Richard Doran stated that Philadelphia plans to review the leases of the two major containment terminals in order to make the port more competitive.  Mayor Green agreed with the decision and stated that they will keep all private companies informed of the city's plans

headline: A storm gathers
abstract: Joe Smith's angry campaign for Ray Lederer's old congressional seat in Tuesday's election has cause a storm from other politicians. Everyone is ripping apart the others, but are putting it aside for long enough up on Green's candidate for Congressman Dave Glancey. The election will be like a referendum of sorts for which side will win.

headline: It should stay open: Sun Ship: A union perspective
abstract: The author is refuting the remarks of the president of Sun Ship, Robert Campbell on why he decided to stop building ships.  Robert Campbell cited labor problems, absenteeism and low productivity.  The author states that there were no labor problems and that absenteeism and low productivity were the fault of the top management.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph of Centralia residents who had to be relocated due to the ongoing underground mine-fire.

headline: Editorial: GovernorL auto inspections/liquor stores
abstract: The editors applaud Governor Thornburgh's proposals to reduce the number of auto inspections from two to one per year and elimate state liquor stores in favor of private ownership.  The feel these changes will better serve Pennsylvanians.

headline: Judges who make their own rules
abstract: Judges at Family Court, shielded from public accountability by a wall of secrecy, are able to do almost anything they please. Judges have been ducking out of court early, plea-bargaining with defendants, allowing attorneys to ignore court orders, and handing out probation indiscriminately. The privacy is for children to not have their troubles follow them into adulthood, but is being abused by the court.

headline: Antitrust subcommittee is a thing of the past
abstract: The U.S. Senate decided to drop the Senate Antitrust Subcommittee.  U.S. Hugh Scott has tried to introduce antitrust improvement acts, but they have been defeated.  Judiciary Committee Chairman Strom Thurmond believes that antitrust legislation belongs in the Judiciary Committee.  Many U.S. Senators tried to get Senator Thurmond to reconsider, but he refused.

headline: Congressional trips can be helpful
abstract: Former US Representative from Pittsburgh, William Moorhead, defends congressional trips as extremely helpful. He benefited by seeing things first hand and representing America to foreign leaders well.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: Barry Stern, recommended as Labor and Industry secretary.

headline: Porthole- Committee of 70 report:  Stirs port controversy
abstract: The Committee of 70's study on the governance of the Ports of Philadelphia is questioned by this article.  It states that the harsh criticisms found by the study may be a result of hard economic times and "questionable research methods."  They state that the study has good ideas but can't be funded.  The article interviews mulptiple people involved with the ports

headline: A string on aid to schools
abstract: Philadelphia City Council President Joseph E. Coleman stated that the city will not approve the transfer of $30 million to the school district until an agreement is reached with the Philadelphia federation of Teachers (PFT), who have been on strike for over a month.  The article details the talks between city council and the school district.

headline: Judge orders coal miners back to work
abstract: A US District Court order 571 striking coal miners at US Steel's Cumberland Mine to return to work, ending a four day strike. Several other mines are still on strike.  The strike was started when six miners were fired and not given proper notice.

headline: Price of Good Intentions
abstract: The author sets out the Environmental Protection Agency's plan for a federal auto inspection program has good intentions at heart, but will cost tax payers millions in constant inspections.

headline: Explains vote
abstract: In his letter, PA lawmaker Brian D. Clark responds to Governor Dick Thornburgh and PA Department of Transportation Secretary William Green's accusations of him stalling the completion of the Allegheny Valley Expressway. He argues that the reason for his voting against state legislature bills as mentioned by Green is that the governor had attached two controversial measures he did not agree with. The first involved increasing the maximum truck weights that would worsen road conditions, and the second forcing his constituents to pay higher taxes without any hope that their road problems would be solved.

headline: Judicial candidates express views on salaries, TV in courtrooms
abstract: The newspaper interviews seven of the 14 candidates running for Superior Court nominations. The questions address the candidate's views on television cameras in the courtroom, judge salaries, and sentencing guidelines.

headline: Bets High on 6s, 4s, Druggist Testifies
abstract: Sanford Darling, who operates a pharmacy in Hazelwood, testified under a grant of immunity at the lottery rigging trial of Pittsburgh television personality Nick Perry and district lottery manager Edward Plevel. They are accused of taking part in a conspiracy to rig the April 24, 1980, Daily Number drawing in an attempt to defraud the state of $1.2 million.

headline: Congressman can get letters electronically
abstract: Pennsylvania Congressman James Coyne opened his office to direct computer mail for the first time yesterday. Coyne says that now constituents will be able to hook his computer keyboard to a TV and write his letter to his congressman right away. Coyne, also a former instructor at the Wharton School of Business and a computer buff, believes using this system will revolutionize the idea of voter contact.

headline: Pigeons Hold Lead In Capitol Battle
abstract: Governor Thornburgh has hired a private contractor to trap pigeons at the state capitol, which cause a nuisance to the legislators.  The article outlines the various ways they have tried to deal with the pigeon problem in the past, from poisoning them to having snipers shoot them.

headline: School Finance Bill Focuses On Wage Tax
abstract: Proposed legislation that would shift local school financing from property owners to income earners is being debated.  The article details the ramifications of the new tax and supporters say it would be more equitable.

headline: A victory for inertia
abstract: The editorial comments on the May 19 primary election that only attracted a third of the registered voters. It argues that those who won should be careful not too claim too much of a mandate, and the Democratic organization's power shouldn't be exaggerated, either locally or statewide.

headline: Labor leans to citywide strike
abstract: A call by the city's striking teachers for a citywide general strike October 28 received the moral support last night of the Philadelphia Regional of the AFL-CIO. In a voice vote, the council adopted a motion to show solidarity with the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers.

headline: Provides loans to upgrade systems; Bleier carries ball for water-bond issue
abstract: Former professional football star Rocky Bleier has joined a new team -a group trying to persuade voters to support a proposed $300 million water projects bone issue.  Bleier, a former Pittsburgh Steeler running back and now a television sportscaster in Pittsburgh, helped the Vote Yes For Water Committee kick off its statewide public relations campaign.  As honorary chairman of the group, Bleier told a small crowd of interested officials in the Capitol Rotunda the bond issue was needed because water is an increasingly scarce resource.

headline: Fatal crash sparks protest over 'death trap' bridge
abstract: A fatal car accident occurred less than two weeks ago, which was the ninth accident at the Route 372 bridge in as many years and the second in five years to claim a life.  The string of accidents and recent death have shocked and angered the people of Valley Township.  Residents of the community of about 4,000 said they have had enough of the "death trap" bridge and want action from the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: Judicial guidelines defended by Gekas
abstract: State Senator George W. Gekas stated that if changes to judicial sentencing guidelines are not enacted, judges will be limited in their discretion through legislative means.  He stated that legislative guidelines would be much tougher than the proposed judicial ones, and that he is concerned about rising crime.

headline: Bill would let stores sell table wines only
abstract: PA state Senator James R Kelley said he will introduce legislation to permit the sale of table wines in super markets, grocery stores, and delicatessens. Table wines typically have 12 percent alcohol by volume o less.

headline: Congressman can get letters electronically
abstract: Using a system that could revolutionize the idea of voter contact, receiving letters electronically. Someday soon he expects to zip responses right back to his constituents. Constituents who don't own computers can go to any of his offices and tap out messages there.

headline: Politics At The Morgue:  Voters Love It
abstract: The author discuss the race between Coroner Sandy Edberg and Dr. Joshua Perper.  The author feels that they have both wrongly assumed that the voters want to get rid of the coroner position.  The author analyzes both candidates election strategies and comments on them.

headline: Sen. Street joins fray over taxes; Battle over Phila. Taxes moves into the Senate
abstract: State Senator T. Milton Street introduced legislation that would freeze Philadelphia's assessments until the city sould reassess its 560,000 properties.  This is to reform the inequities of Philadelphia's real estate tax assessments.  Philadelphia has a special status in that they can raise property taxes without reassessing property value.  The article details that a heated debate is expected.

headline: A Whole Lot of Heat Over a Lukewarm Issue
abstract: Reapportionment is deal to the hearts of legislators and other assorted politicians and politician watchers like Hack, and when people have an interest in a subject they can make it interesting.

headline: Miners, Coal Operators Are Still Deadlocked
abstract: Following Friday, April 17's failed attempt to end the 23-day old coal strike, it was uncertain when talks would resume between the United Mine Workers and the industry. Each day it continues, it takes a toll on the miners and some related industries.

headline: Radioactive waste plans irk officials in W. Va.
abstract: West Virginia's Northern Panhandle is worried about PA's talk on moving radioactive material to a site near Weirton, W.Va., and also about Ohio's proposal for a hazardous waste disposal plant on the Ohio River. Officials in different W.Va. counties are concerned with the potential hazardous effect to their people.

headline: Fawn Bridge
abstract: The editors opine that repairing Fawn Bridge on Bull Creek Road is a political move by Governor Thornburgh to get support for SWAP tax that would raise the price of gasoline.  The editors urge readers to remember the Governor's "game" when they vote.

headline: Judicial Lottery: Again the Thundering Herd
abstract: The editorial argues that the statewide judgeship elections in this May's primary are like a horse race, for voters and candidates themselves. Of the 22 names, 21 are cross-filed on the Democratic and Republican ballots. One idea is to let the PA governor choose the judges, as the president does with federal judges, by having a bipartisan commission recommend 3 to 10 names, and the governor picking one. That name could be submitted to the State Senate for confirmation.

headline: Bills Would Curb 'Hot' Metal Mart; Sales Curbs on Precious Metals Backed
abstract: Law enforcement official support proposed legislation to tighten the controls over the selling and buying of precious metals.  The senate held hearings on a package of bills that would control the traffic in gold and silver jewelry.  The bills were proposed in response to an increase in property crimes last year and would require jewelers to fingerprint or photograph sellers.  The article outlines other details of the bills and the dealers responses to them.

headline: Conservative Legal Briefs On High Court Hopefuls
abstract: Candidates for the state Supreme, Superior and Commonwealth courts in the primary elections on May 19 are conservative and talking hard on crime. The toughest are the six candidates for the Supreme Court position, which has a 10-year term and an annual salary of $64,500. The article briefly reviews candidates William Hutchinson, James McDermott, Maxwell Davison, Sal Farino, Joseph Glancey, and Robert Colville.

headline: Powers to Eliminate 76 State Agencies: House Oks 'Sunset' Measure
abstract: The state House approved a measure, the "Sunset" bill, that would give lawmakers the power to eliminate 76 agencies, boards, commissions and departments.  The legislation establishes a department that would audit agencies for performance and report them to the House and Senate.  Several agencies could be affected by the bill if it passes.

headline: Speculators feed on backlogged bureaucracy
abstract: The editorial argues that in Philadelphia, property speculators are taking advantage of the city tax collection system's backlog. The bureaucracy in different city departments allows for the lack of action against tax delinquents. The city is taking steps toward computerization, streamlining sheriff's sale processes, and placing pressure through proposed legislation to require registration of absentee property owners.

headline: A Woman Sits on the High Court
abstract: The swearing in of Sandra Day O'Connor as the 102nd Justice of the US Supreme Court is a historic and politic milestone. It marks the beginning of true full representation of women in the judicial branch of government. She was voted for the position with a Senate vote of 99 to 0.

headline: New radiation data hints N-plant staffs need more safety
abstract: The beliefs of Dr. Edward Radford, director of the University of Pittsburgh's Center for Environmental Epidemiology, that the radiation limits set in federal guidelines are too low were confirmed by the findings of the journal Science. The new calculations indicate nuclear plant workers are in more danger than they think, and according to Dr. Radford, so are workers exposed too radiation in other industries.

headline: Radioactive Water Spilled
abstract: About 1,500 gallons of radioactive water was spilled inside the H.B. Robinson nuclear power plant in South Carolina.  No workers were exposed to it and it did not leak outside the plant.

headline: Final vote on toll-road bill delayed: House calendar crowds out plan
abstract: A $1 billion bill that would have the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission complete six western Pennsylvania highways as toll roads has gone back to committee because of a crowded, end-of-session House calendar.  After being rushed through the Transportation Committee, the bill had been on the verge of a final vote June 24, 1981, but action was suddenly postponed when lawmakers said they needed more time to study the bill.  Under the bill, the Turnpike Commission would float bond issues totally about $1 billion to finance the roadways.  Tolls from the highways would pay for the bonds.

headline: Judiciary gag order is denied by O'Brien
abstract: Pennsylvania Chief Justice Henry X. O'Brien defended a letter in which he said state judges should first clear it with the state Supreme Court before discussing bills with lawmakers.  The article continues to provide comments from O'Brien justifying his actions and views from other politicians in Pennsylvania with opposing views.

headline: Bingo bill
abstract: Governor Thornburgh should not have any difficulty signing the bill legalizing bingo.  The bill approved by the state House and Senate would legalize bingo games operated by charitable, non-profit groups.  It would require non-profit organizations to purchase a bingo liense for $100, limit to $250 the prize in any one game, expect in jackpot contests in which the purse cannot exceed $2,000.  No licensed organization could pay out more than $4,000 in any one day.  A special $50 license will be offered to senior citizens wanting to play bingo among themselves for non-profit.

headline: Despite Commissioners' Pressure Coroner Race Goes On
abstract: Politics have entered the coroners' race despite candidates promises to remove politics from the morgue. Legislation is now being proposed that will remove the office of coroner from elective politics. County Commissioners have written a public statement supporting the bill.

headline: Preliminary Reapportionment Plan
abstract: Maps showing the new redistricting of the PA state Senate and House seats.

headline: Supports Stauffer Bill
abstract: The Taxpayers Association of Lackawanna County is supporting PA Senators John Staufer's bill, which would reform school financing in PA. This will take the heavy burden from property taxes and distribute it through income tax. The Chamber of Commerce is the bill for selfish reasons and doing nothing for Scranton.

headline: Abscam FBI agent admits Lederer didn't ask money
abstract: A Federal Bureau of Investigations agent that gave a $50,000 bribe to US Representative Raymond Lederer (D-PA) admitted in court that Mr. Lederer never specifically asked for the money.  The FBI Agent said that the money was mentioned in a previous meeting with the middleman, Camden New Jersey Mayor Angelo Errichetti.  Lederer is accused of accepting the bribe in return for promising to introduce private immigration bills on behalf of two supposed Arab sheiks.  The defense is claiming entrapment.

headline: No Journal today as deal is rejected
abstract: The Philadelphia Journal announced that it would not publish after two unions rejected contract concessions that the company said would be necessary to keep the morning tabloid alive.  The article goes further into detail about the newspaper's executives, unions, and what is anticipated to happen afterwards.

headline: Rains didn't end water shortage, authorities warn
abstract: Authorities from the Delaware River Basin Committee stated that, although rains during the week helped, the water emergency and drought are not over yet.  State and local officials are continuing to urge residents to conserve water.

headline: Fort Pitt: New train rolls on in
abstract: Under an agreement with the state Department of Transportation, Amtrak began running The Fort Pitt, the third new train line started in Pittsburgh within the past year, connecting the city with Altoona and Johnstown. The western PA train line is another response to increases in demand and in ridership in lines such as the Pennsylvanian that connects Pittsburgh to Philadelphia.

headline: Justice panels proposes more prison beds, fewer inmates
abstract: The Philadelphia Criminal Justice Coordinating Commission has developed a plan to reduce to populations of adult and juvenile and detention facilities. The adult bed capacity will be increased by 763 and the average population will be cut by 188. Also an additional 44 beds for juveniles will be added.

headline: Bingo games legalized; doubling of inmates OK'd
abstract: null

headline: Contracts Up In Air For 60 School Districts
abstract: While six school districts in Allegheny County and 54 others in Western Pennsylvania remain without teacher contracts as the fall term approaches, one Beaver County school district in a tactical move already has decided to delay the start of classes until October 12.  The Aliquippa School District, which was crippled by a bitter nine-week strike three years ago, decided in April to give students a longer summer vacation in hopes the later start of classes will head off any teachers' strike this fall.

headline: Primary politics blossoms in spring
abstract: The author gives a summary of political figure's actions before the May 19 primary election. He describes the political re-entry of former Bucks County commissioner George Metzger, the publicity achieved by State Senator H. Craig Lewis (D-6), the Democratic party leader's unusual welcoming of intraparty battles in the Bucks County two row office races, and his political industriousness award for Republican state Senator Stewart J. Greenleaf for greeting constituents door-to-door and listening to their complaints.

headline: Tax board defies freeze, boosts assessments
abstract: Philadelphia's tax board has certified new assessments for 1981 despite a City Council ordinance mandating an assessment freeze for up to 3 years.  The new assessments are expected to raise property taxes for residents.  Residents were urged not to pay the higher taxes until the dispute has been settled in court.

headline: Accountant Probe Ends; Cops Baffled
abstract: The investigation into John S. Bell, former chief accountant who allegedly caused a $1.4 million loss from the Allegheny County treasury ended due to no leads.  The article details the investigation.

headline: No retreat on UC reforms
abstract: The editors feel that the problems with Pennsylvania's Unemployment Compensation (UC) fund lie within the generous benefit system it has.  They urge lawmakers to increase employer UC taxes and reject a bill that would allow retired people receiving pensions to "double dip" into the UC fund.

headline: Relocation may be a solution
abstract: The article presents both sides of the debate between relocating the borough of Centralia due to mine fire risks, or letting it stay where it is despite the risk.  Some suggest putting it to a referendum of the residents.

headline: Gas tax approved at all-night session
abstract: The PA state House approved in rapid-fire fashion three pieces of budget-related legislation. GOP leaders also pushed a gas-tax measure aimed at funding road repairs and a $1.2 million PA Transportation Department budget. Republicans provided most of the votes for the bills.

headline: Justice Says State Judges Should Be Appointed
abstract: Justice Bruce Kauffman, ending a two year interim term on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, says there is room for improvement in Pennsylvania's appeals judiciary system.  The article goes into detail about Kauffman's political biography and his reason to believe the court could do better.

headline: Bingo!  It's Up to Gov
abstract: A bill making bingo legal cleared the state Legislature and is on its way to Governor Thornburgh for his signature.  Representative Edward Burns, who introduced the bill, said the Internal Revenue Service has begun to tax the proceeds of illegal gambling operations, including charities like churches.  Associations wishing to conduct bingo games must be licensed by the county treasurer's office and they cannot pay out more than $4,000 in prizes in a 24-hour period or operate more than two days a week.

headline: Control of Pa. Senate, redistricting hinge on election in northwest
abstract: A special election in Meadville to replace Budd Dwyer, who stepped down in his post as state representative to be state Treasurer, has caused a lot of prominent politicians to visit the area.  The election will determine which party controls the state Congress.  The article details the election campaigns.

headline: Primary probe puts Delco GOP on the defensive
abstract: A federal investigation by a grand jury in Philadelphia has turned an expected Republican sweep in the fall elections in Delaware County into a question mark. One of the Republican candidates has been indicted so far. Several others are under investigation in an alleged scheme to manipulate the Democratic party primary for the county controller nomination.

headline: The city wins in Jersey
abstract: In a unanimous decision, the New Jersey Supreme Court upheld the right of Philadelphia to collect from a New Jersey resident not only the city wage tax but penalties owed for late payment. The court ordered a woman who worked at the Frankford Arsenal from 1967 to 1974 to pay a penalty of $2400 for not filing city wage tax returns. Previous court decisions have also upheld the right of the city to collect the wage tax from New Jersey residents.

headline: 'Accused' Replies
abstract: State Representative James R. Kelly responds in a letter to the editor to Lowman S. Henry's accusation that he and other democrats have acted 'childish' in their unwillingness to confirm Judge Roy Wilkinson as a Supreme Court Judge.

headline: No Strike
abstract: The cartoon depicts a catcher receiving the baseball in the center, while the umpire, with the letters N.L.R.B. indicating the National Labor Relations Board, inscribed on his chest, calling out "No Strike!"

headline: Reservoir Of Concern
abstract: Several people are willing to forgo the economic benefits of the mine.  IN addition to trout Unlimited, a number of organizations have publicly stated their opposition: local Kiwanis and Rotary clubs, the Philipsburg Association of Commerce, Philipsburg Borough Council and the governments of nearby boroughs and townships.  Also opposed are the state Fish Commission and the Keystone Water Company, which operates the reservoir.  The dispute centers on what effect mining would have on water flowing into Clover Run, a small stream that flows into Cold Stream, which flows into the reservoir. The proposed mine site is a combination of wooded hillsides, unreclaimed strip mines and abandoned deep mines.  Polluted water draining from old mines now flows away from Clover Run.

headline: Gas Tax Hike on Rough Road
abstract: Lawmakers told the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) that they could not support a gasoline because of the poor condition that the roads are currently in.  Lawmakers said they would not be able to justify additional taxes to the voters.

headline: JUSTIFIED?
abstract: A criminal jury recently convicted a Lincoln Place dentist of voluntary manslaughter.  Doctor John Wahrenberger shot an eighteen year old burglar escaping from his home, the victim had been one of three intruders.  Wahrenberger feels he is innocent, since he was protecting his property and defending his life.  However, the victim's body was fifty feet away from the house.  Under the state's new "Deadly Force" law, the doctor has a hard time justifying his actions.  To use deadly force the doctor had to show he felt his life was threatened and that nothing less than deadly force could have saved him.  Also, the intruder had to be in the house when shot.  The law does not take into account a normal, human response to strong emotions, so changing it would help.

headline: Bingo!  There's trouble
abstract: The editor's feel that Governor Thornburgh's statement that the new law legalizing bingo is good, but not ideal.  The editors feel that the law ends the hypocrisy of having something illegal, but it not being enforced, but they also feel the law creates too many loopholes.  They think that if the Governor did not like the bill, he should have sent it back to the legislature.

headline: Corruption Probe Cites Pa. Auditor
abstract: Lloyd Hickman, a low level employee of the state Auditor General’s Department, was the first person accused of wrongdoing by the grand jury probing alleged corruption within the state agency. It is recommended that Hickman be indicted for perjury during his grand jury testimony the prior month. Hickman lied when he denied paying an unnamed man a $5,000 down payment for a $20, 636 field auditor job. He also lied when he denied participating in a scheme with the same unnamed man to exact $25,000 from his wife’s physician, Dr. James Brooks in exchange for the guarantee that the physician would receive a liquor store franchise if the state turned over its State Store monopoly to private enterprise. Brooks testified that he did pay $25,000 to the unnamed man.

headline: Probe O'Pake, Waldman asks
