abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh's general counsel asked the state Ethics Commission to investigate possible violations of the Ethics Act by Pennsylvania Senator Michael O'Pake.  O'Pake asked the commission to investigate whether former Attorney General Harvey Bartley III violated the Ethics Act.  General Counsel Jay Waldman asked the commission to investigate whether O'Pake's district office charged constituents for services the state renders for free.  The article goes further into detail about Waldman's probes into O'Pake's practices.

headline: The need for reassessment
abstract: This article examines what is wrong with the current assessment system as it pertains to the Erie County Board of Assessment Appeals within Pennsylvania. This comes after the Board's unanimous decision to approve a general agreement with General Electric that would reduce the company's assessed valuation from the present $42 million to $7.75 million. The article goes further to state that Pennsylvania does not in comparison with other states unduly rely on the property tax. Reassessing the Board of Assessment Appeals could come if the Pennsylvania General Assembly would pass Senate Bill 609 which would make available to taxpayers needed information to judge the fairness of their assessment and give them an impartial procedure to challenge any unfairness.

headline: Act 195 must be changed
abstract: Editorial that questions the scope of Act 195, the state law that gives teachers and other state employees the right to collective bargain and strike.  The author uses the example of the Neshaminy teachers strike, which has been going on for a long time.  Act 195 is supposed to define what is bargainable, but the author believes that the act is too vague and is contributing to the ongoing strike in Neshaminy

headline: Nuclear Power
abstract: The author, a local union leader, contends that the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers believes its members have a right to refuse to work in any cancerous cesspool, when there is reason to believe it is dangerous to their health and life. He argues that due to its dangerous contaminants, nuclear power should be stopped, and that the fight begins at Three Mile Island, where a local problem signifies global disaster.

headline: Residents of Centralia see mine-fire action
abstract: Residents of Centralia, Pennsylvania demonstrated against an underground mine-fire that has been burning for twenty years.  Local officials say that they need state and federal support before anything can be done to put out the fire.  The fire has already erupted above ground in two places.  The article outlines what lawmakers have promised to do.

headline: Gasoline tax fuss
abstract: For more than two years, the Pennsylvania legislature refused to approve a change in the gasoline formula, proposed by Governor Thornburgh, because it would have meant drivers would pay more at the pump.  While at the same time, the state's bridges and highways were rapidly deteriorating at an alarming rate and funds were inadequate for their needed repairs.  The Thornburgh administration took a new approach, aiming its tax increase efforts at a highly visible and appearing target: Big Oil.  Instead of the 3.5 percent tax staying on the oil company, it was passed back onto the consumer.  Yet the oil companies can deduct less than half of the state tax on their federal income taxes and are not about to absorb any money to assure that Pennsylvania has smoother roads.

headline: Juvenile program claims better results without using prison
abstract: With a unique program that stresses rehabilitation and not prison for first time juvenile offenders. Bucks County spends less on juvenile justice than any other PA county but get better results a study has found. Bucks County opened the Youth Services Agency in 1975 as a clearing house for first time offenders. The hallmark of the YSA approach to juvenile justice is to start with first offenders and keep them out of the courts and treat them through community organizations.

headline: Brothers Accuse Perry Of 666 Fix Conspiracy
abstract: Peter and Jack Maragos, two business associates of Pittsburgh TV personality Nick Perry, have testified that Perry was part of a conspiracy to rig the Daily Number drawing April 24, 1980. Perry and Edward Plevel, former district lottery manager, are charged with participating in an alleged lottery fix that left insiders holding $1.2 million in winning tickets when the number 666 was drawn.

headline: Cotillion Ball's Ready to Roll
abstract: null

headline: Progress reported in Norwin teacher talks
abstract: The pace of negotiations in the long strike by teachers in the Norwin School District has stepped up. Both sides hope to head off a prolonged court battle. A hearing into a taxpayers' suit aimed at pushing the stalled talks off dead center had been scheduled to go into the third day of testimony before Westmoreland County Common Pleas Court Judge Joseph Hudock, but the session was called off.

headline: The readers' forum; Tax bills opposed
abstract: The author opposed the so-called "new" Stauffer Bills which would give school districts the option to switch from property tax funding to personal income tax funding.  The author feels that it will have problems with collection and monitoring.  The author instead favors a combination of property and income taxes to fund school districts.

headline: Act 195 'restores pride,' PSEA's Angle says
abstract: Jacque Angle, President of the Pennsylvania State Education Association (PSEA), lashed out at school board associations and the media for misrepresenting the positive effects collective bargaining, given to teachers by Act 195, has for teachers.  He stated that it helps improve class size, discipline and curriculum.  He also stated that the cause of the recent teachers strike in Philadelphia was due to the need for improved working conditions, not raises or benefits.

headline: PA UNEMPLOYMENT FUND
abstract: The editorial argues that although the state is doing all it can to help put the PA Unemployment Fund on a fiscally sound basis, it is the individual fraud and deception on the part of its recipients that is one of the more serious problems. The editorial calls for honest citizens to report the system cheaters to the Bureau of Unemployment Compensation.

headline: Right-to-know now a reality
abstract: Regulations that require businesses and industries in Philadelphia to regulate the presence of a wide variety of toxic materials used in the workplace and emitted into the air.  By October, lists of those on-site materials will be available to the public, and by February data on emissions will be available.  This comprehensive right-to-know program, approved by the City Council last January, is the result of a cooperative effort instituted by the Delaware Valley Toxics Coalition, a public interest organization comprised of environmental, labor and neighborhood groups.  In conjunction with the coalition, the Green administration assembled a far-reaching enforcement package that will regulate the use and storage of 491 toxic materials and the release of 99 chemicals into the air.

headline: Gasoline up 3 to 4 cents due to state tax; Gasoline up 3 to 4 cents a gallon
abstract: State motor fuels tax will drive prices up again by 3 to 4 cents a gallon.  The new tax, a 3.5 percent figure which will be levied on the wholesale prices of gasoline, diesel fuel and kerosene, will mean consumers will pay more at the pump, despite hopes by the Thornburgh administration and some legislators that an increase would not be forthcoming.  Governor Thornburgh and other state officials had hoped the oil companies would not pass the full tax onto their dealers, since a portion of it can be written off on the companies' federal taxes.

headline: Lancaster County's Crime Rate Drops to 3r Lowest in Nation
abstract: The Lancaster city and county metropolitan area has the third lowest crime rate in the US. It was sixth place last year. Other low and high crime areas are highlighted.

headline: Brown lauds no-fault 'reform' bill as Democrats object to measure
abstract: Insurance Commissioner Michael Browne said that a Thornburgh-administration backed bill to "reform" the state no-fault insurance law could save PA consumers as much as $166 million a year in annual automobile insurance premiums. House Democrats contended the bill offer very little to consumers.

headline: County To Appeal Late-Tax Ruling
abstract: Allegheny County plans to appeal a ruling that they are responsible for $1.2 million of late fees and interest for taxes not paid former chief accountant John S. Bell.  The County contends that they should not be held accountable for the irresponsible actions of an individual.  Bell simply stopped paying the state tax that comes out of county worker's paychecks, but was not accused of wrongdoing, as he did not try to steal the money.

headline: Prosecutor, defender debate fairness of Abscam probe
abstract: Lawyer John J. Duffy and Justice Department Official Irving Nathan debated the fairness of the role of the Federal Bureau of Investigation agents in the Abscam scandal, in which undercover FBI agents offered bribes to politicians and then later arrested them for taking the bribes.

headline: The whys and wherefores of Caliguiri's budget
abstract: Mayor Caliguiri $223.7 million budget submitted to City Council increases the real estate, wage, parking, business privilege, mercantile, water and deed transfer taxes. Caliguiri's budget is approximately $36 million more than the previous year. In addition to the higher taxes are reductions in some services.

headline: After 50 Years of Humiliation- GOP Decision: A Mayor Candidate?
abstract: The article details the Republican Party's failure to have a republican mayor in Pittsburgh.  It notes the failed candidacies of Bill Crehan, John Tabor, Tom Livingston and Joe Cosetti.  The author feels that with the backing of Repubican national committeewoman, Elsie Hillman and other high level politicians, the Republicans might have a chance to have a republican mayor in office.

headline: Pa. cuts funds for OIC: OIC programs lose $1 million in Pa. funds
abstract: PA cut off $1 million in funding to the Opportunities Industrialization Centers, Inc (OIC) due to the results of two audits and a finding of mismanagment and poor performance.  OIC is a job training program for former offenders.

headline: Rivers, Streams Nearing Record Lows in Drought
abstract: Drought is threatened in the Susquehanna River Basin, which supplies Lancaster with water, but it is slightly less serious than the drought facing the Delaware River Basin due to more rainfall and a lower population in the areas.  The article details the flows of the two basins and stresses the need for conservation to prepare residents for a summer drought

headline: Get tipsy driver off road, law asks
abstract: Congressmen, Allen Ertel and Michael Barnes were in Harrisburg today for a hearing on proposed federal legislation that stresses the need for a more workable National Driver Registration. This is intended to track repeat drunk drivers and prevent them from obtaining drivers licenses.

headline: Larsen investments chronicle rise to prosperity
abstract: Article chronicles Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen's rise in prosperity. Larsen's real estate holdings are valued at close to $1 million dollars, and he has held thousands of dollars' worth of securities.  Larsen has currently filed suit against two Pittsburgh brokerage houses because of money that he says he has lost and the article indicates that he is likely to lose both cases.

headline: Casino watchdogs keeping secrets
abstract: New Jersey's Casino Control Commission, a commission mandated through referendum, asked the Legislature to let it meet in secret to discuss administrative matters. Four months after the request, lawmakers are still ignoring the request. As a result the commissioners have held several meetings in secret. They claim they have to transgressed the letter or spirit of the law.

headline: Court issues back-to-work order
abstract: Common Pleas President Judge Edward Bradley's ordered striking teachers to return to work Monday. The executive board of the teachers' union is to meet tonight to decide on a response to that order. He struck down the contract as terminated because the district did not get money it was supposed to.

headline: Public campaigning funding
abstract: A Philadelphia Democratic senator said the alleged political ties between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and legal counsel hired  by the administration for the PA Housing Finance Agency are the strongest case for public funding of elections. A public funding mechanism to eliminate a potential conflict of interest when Thornburgh's general counsel hired two other firms connoted to Thornburgh to replace existing counsel for PHFA. A bill co-sponsored by Lloyd would establish a system intended to reduce the impact of large contributions on a statewide campaign.

headline: Vote Scheduled On Tax Reform
abstract: The state House Finance Committee has scheduled a vote for April 29 on a tax reform package that would give local governments the option of reducing their property taxes. The five-bill package would abolish local nuisance taxes for counties, municipalities and school districts. It would give local officials the authority to implement a local personal income tax and business taxes.

headline: Scanlon gag of state colleges abuse of power
abstract: The head of the PA Department of Education, Dr. Robert Scanlon, is behaving in an authoritarian and un-American manner. He has issued a secret memorandum which gags the presidents of PA's 14 state-owned colleges from commenting on legislation that affects those colleges. Editorial calls for the gag to be lifted for free flow of information.

headline: Pa. set Striking Example in '80, Led U.S. in Walkouts
abstract: Pennsylvania continued to have the highest number of strikes in the nation in 1980, but the days lost during those strikes declined significantly, the government said.  Alvin Margulis, regional commissioner of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistic, said the number of lost days due to strikes and lockouts declined to 2.2 million in Pennsylvania during 1980, lowest in 14 years.  Unlike 1979, most of the state's lost work days occurred in non-manufacturing industries, mostly due to Philadelphia's lengthy teachers' strike.

headline: Saving the Barriers
abstract: There's a hidden benefit in the recently enacted budget bill. It will restrict the federal government's role in developing coastal barrier islands. No building should ever have been allowed on these fragile strips of land running along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. The islands form a protective chain of shifting sand for the mainland. They provide habitat for a large variety of animals, birds, and marine life.

headline: Give the kids a break
abstract: The editorial explains that Southeastern PA Transportation Authority's arguments for raising the fares of Philadelphia high school students from 30 to 70 cents are not good enough. The editorial argues that those subsidies should not be eliminated. But it proposes to eliminate those for SEPTA's employees, who currently ride for free, claiming this would make up for the $1.7 million SEPTA says it will pick up through full student fares.

headline: Lawyers' jury 'strikes' assailed
abstract: Lawyers in criminal trials waste money and time when they exercise their options to "strike" prospective jurors for any reason or for no reason at all.  That is the conclusion of state Senator D. Michael Fisher and District Attorney Robert Colville.  They stated in a joint news conference that the practice, called peremptory challenging, should be eliminated.  Fisher said he will introduce legislation next month aimed at doing away with peremptory challenges in criminal trials.  The proposal will not affect trials in the civil divisions of the state's Common Pleas courts.

headline: Caliguiri suggests business program for arms contracts
abstract: Mayor Caliguiri says he will suggest city planners set up a training program to teach small businesses how to compete more effectively for military contracts.  And Republican Mayor Frank Fischl says he sees production of uniforms for the military as a means of revising the town's stagnant garment trades.

headline: Court lets stand Bellis' conviction
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has reversed a lower court and affirmed the 1977 misconduct conviction of former City Council majority leader Isadore H. Bellis for accepting $9,000 from an architect who received city contracts worth $180,000. The court rejected Bellis' contention that under state law he could not be tried for both the statutory crime of misfeasance, malfeasance and nonfeasance in the office.  The article goes further into detail about the case.

headline: Public servant should show concern for citizens
abstract: In November, we face a decision on a choice for tax collector for Upper Southampton Township. Since this is an elected office, it seems to us that the office holder is a public servant and should be available to serve the citizens of our township. This is not the case of tax collector, Agnes Douglas. She does not do her job and people do not have proper tax records.

headline: Wage Earner Tax Hearing In Coraopolis
abstract: The Pennsylvania public will get a chance to comment on legislation that would allow school districts to replace real estate tax with a levy on wage earners. Testimony will be taken from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on November 30 at the Ramada Inn in Coraopolis. This Coraopolis location is one of five that will be used for state-wide testimonies. Opposition to such a bill has come from business, labor and civic groups.

headline: School board eligibility bill OK'd in House
abstract: The PA state House overwhelmingly approved a bill to permit PA state Civil Service employees to serve on school boards. It would modify the existing prohibition against Civil Service employees taking active part in political campaigns.

headline: Pennsylvania Manufacturers Rediscover Politics
abstract: Both parties in the state senate are trying to restore the financial solvency of the Unemployment Compensation Fund.  Organized labor is against the measure due to expected cuts.  The article outlines the background of the PA Manufacturers Association within the state senate.

headline: Sewer Program
abstract: State Senate member Edward Zemprelli explains that Governor Dick Thornburgh has recommended abolishing a Sewer Subsidy Program that provides $14 million in state subsidies to municipal authorities to offset operation and maintenance of treatment plants. For this to happen, the General Assembly would have to repeal act 339. Zemprelli argues that the Governor is trying to put funding obligations solely on local authorities, but he believes the Governor's proposal should be opposed.

headline: GOP Leadership Sees Quick Approval
abstract: Republican leaders believe the PA Governor Thornburgh's $12.6 million budget will be approved next week. The tax measure included is a 3.5% wholesale tax on all transportation related petroleum products such as gasoline and motor oils sold in PA.

headline: Legal Aid: Reform, Not Disbandment
abstract: The editors opine that the Reagan Administration's proposal to do away with legal aid for the poor is wrong.  They feel that there are some problems with the system, but getting rid of it all together would be a huge blow to the American justice system.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon depicts 2 frames.  One frame has a picture of Hiroshima and reads "An american bomb did this in 1945."  The other has a picture of a run-down Detroit and reads "A japanese import did this in 1980.

headline: Court: some workers' expenses deductible
abstract: The state will lose about $24 million in revenues under a PA Supreme Court ruling that allows workers to claim state income tax deductions for expenses not reimbursed by their employers. Included deductions include costs of traveling away from home overnight, transportation from one site to another, costs of an office-in-home or office rental.

headline: Public workers, salaries increase, U.S. census says
abstract: The number of public employees is on the rise along with the total payroll for governmental workers despite politician promises to streamline the government. The US census bureau found an increase of 1.6% in a year, bringing the total to 16.2 million workers. Not surprisingly the total annual payroll was $19.9 billion, a 10.3% increase from the previous year. The largest number of federal employees is related to some aspect of the education division with national defense coming in a close second.

headline: A look at events of the past week
abstract: Spring is coming and the writers suggest attending the Philadelphia Flower Show.  Sen. Stewart Greenleaf proposed a bill in the legislature to improve rescue and emergency services on the Turnpike.  The National Republican Congresional Committee is planning to spend $2 million to promote President Reagan's budget and tax cut proposals.

headline: School Clouds
abstract: In Western Pennsylvania, the approach of the back-to-school season invariably stirs speculation over where teachers' strikes might occur.  With less than two weeks remaining before most schools are scheduled to reopen, 60 districts in this end of the state have failed to reach contracts with their teachers.  It has not helped that the state Legislature has adopted a see-no-evil attitude despite the flaws that have become evident since the Public Employee Relations Law took effect 11 years ago.  That law, for the first time, gave teachers and most other public workers in Pennsylvania power to bargain collectively and to strike.

headline: Pensioners get House bill aid
abstract: The state House approved a bill that would restore jobless benefits to pensioners furloughed from post-retirement jobs, but the Senate could add an amendment that would give employers a $136 million tax break as well.  The article details the history of the bill and its implications if passed.

headline: Some County Wells Are Going Dry As Groundwater Drops
abstract: The newspaper conducted a survey of the region and found that some wells are going dry due to the drought.  Some communities have asked residents to stop using non-essential water.  The article details the water situation in several boroughs and townships.

headline: GOP OKs SWAP tax substitute
abstract: The Republicans' substitute for the Sustained War Against Potholes tax proposed by Governor Dick Thornburgh, is a 3.5 percent oil company franchise tax on motor fuels which is expected to yield $129 million to the state and $63 million to local governments for maintenance of roads and bridges. A bill proposing such tax cleared the House Transportation Committee and was sent to the floor with the approval of the Thornburgh administration.

headline: Legislation on Mandatory Sentencing Gaining Support
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh, president of the state District Attorneys Association Frank Hazel, and Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell are supporting a PA Sentencing Commission plan for comprehensive sentencing legislation that would give judges specific directions on handing out felony sentences. Among the guidelines are 5-year mandatory prison sentences for persons convicted of using firearms during the commission of crimes, replacing the present parole system so that a sentence given is a sentence served, and authorization for the construction of 2,500 new prison cells.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon depicts a state liquor store with covered wagons surrounding it.  The caption reads, "Not that you've got 'em circled, here's a real challenge - find something I want!" The cartoon insinuates that the state liquor store system has no selection for customers.

headline: Crossroads politics: Teaching the bureaucracy to speak English
abstract: The author opines that Governor Thornburgh's executive order called "Improving Government Regulations" is an excellent step to reduce an increasingly unintelligible bureaucracy.  The order states that all regualtions will be drafted in clear, concise language, be organized in a logical sequence, explain things in non-technical terms, and use examples to illustrate points.

headline: Races for controller, Council, court enliven Delaware Co. primary
abstract: The League of Women Voters of Philadelphia and local leagues in different counties compiled a list of candidates for county, city, borough, and township offices in the May 19 primary elections. 23 of the Delaware county candidates are presented with their addresses, age, education background, employment, and the salary and term length of the office they're running for.

headline: ... Houston, El Paso ...
abstract: The photograph depicts Philadelphians Chuck and Nancy Wojciehowski and a worker in one of Chuck's Phoenix hoagie shops, with the caption: When the state of Arizona receives a request from out of state for job information, it sends back a questionnaire asking for background information. In the last two years, one of every 10 respondents has written from PA.

headline: School Negotiators Just an Issue Away
abstract: School District officials worked on trying to tally up the cost of what has been agreed on so far in contract negotiations with the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers.  The article goes further into detail about the contract negotiations and the district's budget.

headline: Phila. Extends OIC pact for 3 months
abstract: Philadelphia will contract with Opportunities Industrialization Centers, Inc. (OIC), a job training organization, for only three months rather than a full year.  Funding has also been cut to the organization.  The city is conducting an investigation into claims that OIC has exaggerated claims of success and maintains poor managerial records.

headline: State Car Exhaust Plan: Discrimination at its Best
abstract: The proposed auto-emissions inspection program is discriminating against residents of the highly populated areas of Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. The inspection program should apply to all residents of the state of Pennsylvania who own a vehicle.

headline: Investigate more
abstract: The author of this letter to the editor commends the newspaper on the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority article, yet argues that by running these stories next to the military's MX missile system articles, it has failed to draw connections between both. The author points to the massive military spending as reasons why the cities, mass transit systems and economy are failing. He argues the newspaper should investigate how more socially useful it would be to spend the $50 billion in urban mass transit.

headline: Letters to the editor:  Opposing ethics loopholes for lawyers
abstract: The author opines that the Commonwealth Court's ruling to exempt lawyers from the financial disclosure part of the Ethics Act is a bad idea and should be overruled by a higher court.  The author feels that all public officials should be subject to the same regulations concerning conflict of interest.

headline: City State Stores Rang Up $138 Million
abstract: An estimated $138 million was spent at Philadelphia's state liquor stores in fiscal year 1979-80.  The article notes that the school system and transportation system are facing deficits

headline: Cuts for Legal Services and Family Planning
abstract: The Family Planning Association of PA will receive no funds and the PA Legal Services Center will only receive half of what it did last year under the new state budget. The budget cuts were made during a late-night meeting that surprised leaders of the two agencies. They were originally supposed to receive the same amount as last year, but was changed at the last minute.

headline: 'Railroading' charged on pension bill
abstract: State Senator Edward Howard (R-Bucks) believes there is an effort to quickly move through the Legislature a provision for benefit increases to spouses of pensioners both in the state and municipal retirement systems. The comment was made after Senator Frank O'Connell (R-Luzerne) had scheduled his State Government Committee to consider House Bill 202. Howard is an outspoken opponent of the bill, which was approved earlier by the state House.

headline: A Day In The Life Of Saul Kohler--A Newspaper Editor
abstract: null

headline: Schweiker-Social Security: Raise taxes or curb benefits
abstract: Former PA Senator  Richard Sweiker appeared before the US Senate Finance Committee as a nominee for the head of the Department of Health and Human Services.  He was questioned on his stances toward funding Social Security.  He stated his recommendations for the Department of Health and Human Services.  The article also mentions President Ronald Reagan's other cabinet appointments and their plans.

headline: Phila. Seeks to save up to 500 CETA jobs
abstract: Jobs funded under the Comprehensive Employment and Training Act (CETA) have been cut nation-wide by $500 million. These funds are used to pay the salaries of about 1,350 city employees.  The article discusses possible solution to the loss of funds.

headline: State Government in Review:  Watch Water, Thornburgh Asks
abstract: (United Press International) The current drought that is facing PA is not expected to end in the next 90 days.  Governor Thrornburgh has called for residents to conserve water.  Governor Thornburgh also stated this week that the budget is nearing completion and he has no plans to increase taxes.  The article briefly outlines additional state news

headline: Governor backs plan for Vine St.
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh announced his support for a scaled down version of the Vine Street Expressway, raising hopes that construction on the project may begin in 1985. Under the plan an estimated $159 million would be spent to link the expressway and Interstate 95.

headline: Liability reform bill needed
abstract: Pennsylvania increasingly is getting the reputation for being a paradise for litigation in product liability cases. This can reportedly be resolved if the Pennsylvania state House this fall can follow the lead of the Senate in this area. The Senate passed a product liability reform bill prior to summer recess, making this the third consecutive session that one of the legislative chambers has passed a product bill. The lack of a product liability bill has created serious problems for Pennsylvania commerce, including: 1) increased prices on consumer and industrial goods; 2) Disincentives for making safety improvements and for the development of new products; 3) an increase in the number of product sellers attempting to do business without product liability coverage.

headline: Claims House Bill benefits insurance carriers
abstract: Letter to the editor believes something must be done to cut the high cost of auto insurance. He is not happy with current no-fault laws, and House Bill 1285 makes it all even worse, because it is in the interest of the insurance carriers.

headline: Cynical approach to endorsements
abstract: The editors are pleased by the Democratice State Committee's endorsement of State Superior Court Judge Donald Wieand, but are disappointed that they did not endorse Lehigh County Common Pleas Court Judge Maxwell Davison for State Supreme Court.

headline: Random Notes: Miller, Gerard Have Gripes to Settle with Thornburgh
abstract: Several pieces about political news in the region.  David B. Miller and Joseph M. Gerard are angry at Governor Thornburgh for his stance on federal patronage posts and trying to move the US attorney's office from Scranton to Harrisburg.  The article outlines other state political news

headline: A Pennsylvania Sketchbook
abstract: The book dedication is Governor Dick Thornburgh's invitation to enjoy "A PA Sketchbook", mentioning that each artist has made a personal expression of his experiences in PA. The piece features a picture of the Governor, as well as his signature.

headline: Scranton backers launch fund drive
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III's decision to run a separate re-election and fundraising campaign moved to Bucks County as Scranton scheduled a fundraising dinner at the Keystone Race Track for today. Governor Dick Thornburgh and his advisers believe he and Scranton should have a single re-election committee and a joint fund-raising campaign, and will continue trying to convince Scranton to do so. Scranton has declined to discuss his motivations.

headline: Photograph
abstract: "Sandra Weber, a deaf CERA worker, explains the operation of a teletype machine to other workers."

headline: State must act on water needs
abstract: The author details statistics on water, stating that there is actually very little clean fresh water available on earth.  The author calls on the state to reindustrialize to conserve water now so that in the future there is not competition for access to water.

headline: Governor 'Steals' Car Proposal
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh endorsed legislation that would reduce from twice a year to once a year safety inspections required of cars and small trucks in PA.  State Representative William Steward (D-Cambria County) is upset because he has been proposing such legislation for the past two years with no support from the administration.  When the governor finally decided to embrace the proposal, he threw his backing behind a bill just introduced by state Representative John Davies (R-Berks County).

headline: Litman indicted in medical bills fraud
abstract: S. David Litman and Irving M. Portnoy, lawyers, were indicted on charges that they defrauded insurance companies with inflated medical bills over a 29 year period to support personal injury claims.  The indictment states that they used false medical reports to increase the amounts of settlements from insurance companies, from which their fees were calculated.

headline: Commentary:  Legislators again facing bingo problem
abstract: The author states that lawmakers are worried about the IRS taxing the revenues of nonprofit organizations that sponsor bingo in states where it's illegal.  The author details the IRS law and chastizes the legislature for not enforcing the law that bingo is illegal in Pennsylvania.

headline: D.A. on verge of high-court bid
abstract: District Attorney Robert E. Colville will announce his candidacy for the state Supreme Court.  He is a democrat, but his ties to the party were severed when a grand jury investigation begin into the activies of ex-coroner Cyril Wecht, who is also the county chairman of the Democratic Party.  Wecht feels that charges against him were based on a vendetta.

headline: Rating Reagan's Cabinet
abstract: 131 Washington insiders provided informal report cards on Reagan 6-month-old cabinet. US Treasury Secretary is apparently the rising star. US Labor Secretary Raymond Donovan and US Energy Secretary James Edwards seem to be having trouble finding their footing. The entire cabinet receive a score of 6.4 out of 10. Each member is profiled with their assists and liabilities.

headline: Accents: Boy, they sure tawk weird
abstract: Columnist Clark DeLeon discusses a recent meeting with Governor Dick Thornburgh over regional accents. The governor sent a copy of a book called "How to Speak Pittsburghese" and a letter to the columnist written in the local accent.

headline: Scranton dances by himself
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton's decision to run alone if he seeks re-election in the 1982 primary triggered a response from Governor Dick Thornburgh's office, who feel they should run together. Scranton filed for the Scranton Lieutenant Governor Committee to begin raising campaign funds. He is reportedly frustrated at his lack of power.

headline: Plant closings called problem for everyone
abstract: Speakers at a seminar on the ethics of economic dislocation and plant closings spoke about the need for Corporate America to take the needs of the people into consideration. With a growing movement of companies going overseas and locals losing their jobs, the speakers talked about the growing problem and the neglect of the social consequences at enormous peril.

headline: State parks accepting bidds for cabins
abstract: The state Department of Envirnomental Resources is accepting applications for cabins and pavilions for the coming year.  Cabin-rental season is May 30- Sept. 8.  The article lists where applications can be filed.

headline: Green presents a plan to avoid a rail shutdown
abstract: Mayor Green of Philadelphia presented officials from the five-county region with his own plan to avert the shut down of the regions commuter trains.  The article provides details on how he intends to save the commuter trains in his plan.

headline: Long Siege Feared at Graterford
abstract: A three day hostage standoff is continuing, with convicted police killer Joseph Bowen as the ring leaders.  Officials stated that talks have been sporadic.  The article lists the other inmates holding hostages with Bowen.  The article details attempts at negotiations.

headline: Court upholds chiropractors for no-fault auto claims
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that chiropractic services may be considered medical services under the e PA no-fault automobile insurance law. For this to be true there must be no serious question that chiropractic expenses can be recovered under the allowable expenses component of basic loss benefits under the No-Fault Act.

headline: D.A. sees Street in fraud case: Says 20 workers may be charged
abstract: District Attorney Edward Rendell expected criminal charges of welfare fraud to be filed against at least 20 employees of a North Philadelphia home-weatherization program operated by state Senator Milton Street (R-Philadelphia). The workers were collecting welfare payments while employed by the federally funded program. Street, also under investigation, has said he would resign if the KYW report, which documented the case, proved to be accurate.

headline: Reagan cuts claim few U.S. jobs here
abstract: Reaganomics will have relatively little impact on the jobs of 15,000 federal employees in the Pittsburgh region.  About 100 will be displaced as a result of Reagan administration cutbacks, with the Department of Energy being the biggest loser.  The government will try to relocated displaced workers in other federal agencies, but few jobs are available in Pittsburgh.  Stanely Brem, the area administrator of the federal Office of Personnel Management, said that 15 people are registered in the agency's Displaced Employees Program, which is designed to help federal employees locate jobs in other agencies.

headline: At 22d and Latimer, residents say new plans for home threaten area; Pendergrass hopes to sell to TM group
abstract: Two weeks ago, neighbors first noticed the bright red-orange zoning notice on the old brick mansion, at Latimer and 22d Streets, owned by sultry soul singer Teddy Pendergrass.  Although Pendergrass lived in his 10-bedroom, luxury residence less than a year before moving on to a 34-room, $600,000 mansion in Gladwyne tow years ago, he held onto the property at 234 South 22d street as an investment.  That over turned out to be $300,000 from a California-based organization that teaches transcendental meditation in 60 cities, including Philadelphia, across the United States.

headline: Scranton Stance Angers Governor
abstract: Aides to Governor Dick Thornburgh are not happy with Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III deciding not to run as a team with Thornburgh for re-election in 1982. Scranton is believed to want to keep his primary campaign separate at the financial level only, and merge themes on Thornburgh-Scranton bumper stickers and other campaign regalia. The reason for Scranton's decision is not well understood, but the dispute gave public venting to a behind-the-scenes rift that has been developing between the two officials.

headline: Private Job unit Seeks Loosened SETCO Ties: While CETA Faces Federal Fund Cuts
abstract: The Comprehensive Employment and Training Act (CETA) is facing budget cuts while a private endeavor at reducing unemployment tries to loosen the ties to CETA which is administered by the Susquehanna Employment and Training Corporation (SETCO).  President Reagan has proposed eliminating CETA all together.   The article outlines the effect the cutbacks may possibly have.

headline: State Rejects Strip-Mine Plan Near Reservoir
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources denied a permit to a Clearfield County coal company to strip-mine near a reservoir that holds drinking water for citizens, stating that the application did not demonstrate adequate environmental protection. The decision is seen as a win for citizens groups who are concerned about the safety of the water.

headline: Heinz fights higher barge fees
abstract: United States Senator John Heinz is in the midst of one of his statewide tours, stopping along the way to criticize the Reagan administration's plan for increase in barge user taxes.  Heinz will try to block congressional action on the waterway proposal until a impact study is completely.  Heinz said if waterway tax increase are a good idea for barges fees, then irrigation fees are a good idea for those in western states because the canals were developed by a federal agency.

headline: 'Look-alike' drug sales ban eyed
abstract: null

headline: Dial-a-bet for horse races passes; bill goes to Thornburgh
abstract: An administration bill that would allow Pennsylvanians to place telephone bet to the tracks scored an easy victory in the House. People would have an account with money in it and only that money could be wagered by telephone.

headline: DA Challenger Wants to Delay Election
abstract: In the race for Philadelphia district attorney (DA), candidate William T. Cannon asked Common Please Court to order a investigation into the purchase of a bar by the DA's office, run by incumbent Edward Rendell.  Cannon says Rendell committed fraud by not presenting the bar to the Liquor Control Board.  Cannon then asked the Court to postpone the election until the results of the investigation are released.  The Court refused the request.

headline: Reagan fires air strikers
abstract: The Reagan administration began sending dismissal notices to striking air traffic controllers, promising that it was ready to manage the nation's airways without them. The 13,000 controllers who went on strike Monday morning have defied the back-to-work orders from the courts and administration. Reagan said on Monday that he would fire any controllers not back on the job by 11 a.m. August 5th.

headline: Atlantic City convention, there's status in name tags
abstract: This article discusses the color-coding status system of the name tags required to be worn at the Governor's Association meeting. Following this, much detail is given to the Republican versus Democrat governors basketball game in Atlantic City.

headline: Scranton: End of 'Federal Fix' Demands Creative Local Gov't.
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III told Lancaster County elected officials that it was time for competing government levels to bury the hatchet and come together to form a new partnership to meet the demands of the 'new federalism.' Scranton is referring to Reagan's actions in attempting to force states to be less reliant on a centralized government. His call was for a more imaginative and creative way to finance government services with a dwindling federal grant.

headline: Proposed Elimination of State Unemployment Tax Credit Hit
abstract: Two state Senators stated that they will not support the House's proposed legislation to impose $1.36 million in new unemployment taxes on businesses.  Supporters of the bill want the revenue to go to the repayment of $1.5 billion federal government loan to pay unemployment benefits.  The article details the bill.

headline: State Waste Sites Get Cleanup Priority
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) listed eight hazardous waste sites in Pennsylvania that are a top priority for clean up.  The article lists the sites.

headline: High-Speed Rail Link Envisioned
abstract: The High-Speed Intercity Rail Passenger Commission Act has been proposed in the state legislature to create a seven-member panel to consider technical, economic, financial and social aspects of building a non-Amtrak, for-profit rail network in PA connecting Philadelphia, Harrisburg and Pittsburgh.

headline: Magisterial district may be sacrificed
abstract: A recommendation to eliminate the smallest of Cambria county's 11 magisterial districts will come before the PA state Supreme Court for approval. President Judge H. Clifton McWilliams' proposal has merit as a cost saving measure and as a means to more evenly divide the remaining districts along population lines. The editorial asks why we should wait six years and spend $250,000.

headline: Dial-a-bet for horse races passes; bill goes to Thornburgh
abstract: An administration bill that would allow Pennsylvanians to place telephone bets to the state's horse-racing tracks scored an easy victory in the Pennsylvania State House yesterday. The bill won 158-34 and is now awaiting Governor Thornburgh's signature. The system differs from New York's in that Pennsylvania bettors would first have to deposit money in an account with the track and only that money could be wagered by telephone.

headline: DA ousted
abstract: In the May 19 primary election, Westmoreland County voters ousted District Attorney Al Nichols and nominated John Driscoll. But Democrat Driscoll will now have to run against Republican Gary Selway.

headline: Reapportionment knife
abstract: The southern half of the exisiting 17th Congressional District in Pennsylvania would be lopped off and lumped into a new midstate district most observers see as designed for Republican State Senator George W. Gekas.  Congressman Ertel's home of Lycoming county would be tacked onto a longer tier of northern counties, now the home of Representative William Clinger.  The hard political terms, Ertel would have 118,000 of his current constituentes in a combined district with 400,000 Pennsylvanians, most of whom are now served by Clinger.  If the blueprint being used by state legislators to reshape Pennsylvania's congressional seats for the 1982 elections weathers inevitable protests, the district will be more farflung.

headline: Capital Capers
abstract: The article reviews the happenings in the State Capital.  In the House, Representatives Manderino and Hayes got into an argument about rambling on the floor, while on the floor.  Philadelphia Phillies pitcher, Tug McGraw gave a rendition of "Casey at the Bat."  State Senator Craig Lewis referred to Governor Thornburgh's budget proposal as "voodoo economics."

headline: Senate OKs its version of 'sunset' bill
abstract: The PA Senate approved and sent to the state House its version of "sunset" legislation, which would require a legislative panel periodically assess some 70 state agencies and eliminate those deemed unnecessary. The Senate version would have the existing Legislative Budget and Finance committee do the work, while the House bill would set up a new Office of Legislative Auditor to review the agencies.

headline: Right-to-Work fund backs would-be union dropouts
abstract: The state's refusal to allow about 250 workers to withdraw from their unions at the end of the labor contract on June 30 has come under criticism from the Pennsylvania Right to Work Defense and Education Foundation Incorporated.  Albin W. Simokat, executive director, said he wrote to Governor Dick Thornburgh expressing shock that the commonwealth has agreed with the union in the interpretation of contract language.  Christ Zervanos, director of the state Bureau of Labor Relations, said the decision on withdrawing from unions was not a new practice.  Instead, he said, the rulings were made on a case-by-case basis, relying on the contract and previous judicial decisions.

headline: State's trout sticking program on schedule for season opening
abstract: The Pennsylvania Fish Commission (PFC) has started the state's trout stocking program without any problems.  Over 2 million trout will be moved into approved waters.  The article provides other news about the outdoors and fishing.

headline: Highway link
abstract: null

headline: Magistrate Charged in Sexual Bribery
abstract: Washington County district magistrate, Roland Checca, was charged with indecent exposure and sexual solicitation when he tried to get sexual favor from a female defendant in return for a dismissal of drunk driving charges.  The article details the charges.

headline: Don't let them raise rates 11 percent
abstract: The US Senate and the PA Legislature are about to change the interest rate ceilings on consumer loans. Supporters in the Senate say that eliminating the interest rate ceilings would make more credit available. They argue this will allow the free market to set the appropriate rates for interest rates. There seems to be few facts to support the position. A federal bill would end state regulation of rates.

headline: Dancing and singing under capitol dome marks Fumo's return
abstract: They were dancing and singing in the PA Capitol Rotunda after PA Senator Vincent Fumo was sworn in Monday for the second time since his federal mail fraud conviction was tossed out by trial judge.

headline: Reapportionment struggle is building at statehouse
abstract: Reapportionment will take place this year and the redistricting will be decided by a five member commission whose bias could be swayed by the State Supreme Court and the possible confirmation of Republican Roy Wilkinson.

headline: Capital Offense: How Washington Post And the Pulitzer Board Were Duped by Writer
abstract: The article explains about the Washington Post editorial on April 16 over one its reporters, Janet Cooke, who admitted that her Pulitzer Prize-winning article about an 8-year old heroin addict was a fabrication. Janet Cooke, a young black women from Toledo, Ohio, had also lied about her education background. Although the newspaper at first protected her and her article, it later retracted after an internal investigation of the piece. Bob Woodward, assistant managing editor of the metropolitan desk, felt embarrassed and negligent, and took responsibility for what happened.

headline: Senator adds new coat
abstract: Photograph depicts the Senate Democratic leader Edward Zemprelli, Allegheny, putting the final touches on a newly stained door and entrance leading to his state Capitol office Thursday. Zemprelli's hobby is wood finishing.

headline: Shipbuilding will be ended; 3,100 to lose jobs at Sun Ship yard in Chester
abstract: 3,100 workers will lose their jobs at the Sun Ship, Incorporated shipyard in Chester due to the company's decision to end new ship construction there, due to low productivity.  The decision is expected to have a severe impact on the region, including increased unemployment rates as the workers will have difficulties finding other work.  The article outlines the ripple effect the job loses will have throughout Delaware County

headline: Steps for the summer
abstract: The piece notes that there is a drought in the Delaware River Basin and states that if it continues it will only get worse in the summer.  They note to take steps to cut down on water usage such as turning off the tap when brushing your teeth and taking shorter showers.

headline: House Told of City Transit Woes
abstract: Thomas Larson of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) told the House Appropriations Committee of the problems that PennDOT is having and that it needs $1 billion dollars for next year.

headline: Man testifies in Hayes' rape trial
abstract: A man testified that on October 25, 1979, former state Representative David Hayes of Eerie County drugged him with laughing gas, marijuana and hashish and then raped him.  The trial of Hayes began before Common Pleas Judge Samuel Strauss and a jury of seven men and five women. He is charged with two counts of rape, two counts of involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, corrupting the morals of a minor and indecent assault.

headline: Gambling raids held in Pa., Del.
abstract: After a five month investigation, law enforcement officials raided eleven alleged gambling locations in Pennsylvania and Delware.  No arrests have been made yet, but Delaware Attorney General Richard Gebelein said the evidence should result in at least eight indictments.  One of them should be Matthew Whitaker, who was named in a 1970 Pennsylvania Crime Commission report on organized crime.

headline: Dark days ahead for W. PA town
abstract: Aliquippa may miss its $18,000 monthly light bill tomorrow and will lose power. They stop making the catch-up payments on the $55,000 balance until early next year, but still had to keep up with current payments.

headline: REAPPORTIONMENT: Eight new seats created in state House by legislative commission
abstract: Eight new seats have been created in the state House by the Legislative Reapportionment Commission.  The other new seats, under the statewide redistricting plan for the 203-member House adopted unanimously by the five-member panel, include one each in Lancaster County, Centre-Mifflin, Merks-Lehigh, Monroe, Bucks, Crawford-Mercer, and Westmoreland counties.  The panel took only five minutes to approve the preliminary plan for the House and Senate at its 10th public meeting before a crowded, standing-room audience in the Senate Majority Caucus Room.

headline: Chester Co. man in a top spot with Watt
abstract: John Robinson West holds the position under U.S. Interior Secretary John Watt. West is from Chester County, PA and admits to having this job opportunity essentially fall into his lap. While his interests lie more in the financial field and in national security matters, West states that his position now puts him in the hot spot of politics due to his boss's prodevelopment views of opening up government-owned land and water for energy development.

headline: Senator Harrison Williams Should Resign
abstract: Editorial believes PA Senator Harrison Williams be expelled from the Senate after being tied to the Abscam Scandals and refuses to resign.

headline: Solution must be a fair one
abstract: If the school district can fire over a 1,000 teachers this year despite contract agreements what protects the teachers who weren't fired? A sensible solution must be found to end their strike ad protect their jobs in the future. The writer of the opinion piece writes that the school board needs to stop thinking in the short term. But in the long term.

headline: Swimming pool filling Okd despite the drought
abstract: The State Emergency management Council has given approval to the private filling of swimming pools and the irrigation of plants in nurseries, despite the ongoing drought in the Delware River Basin.  Officials recently declared a ban on all unessential uses of water.

headline: How deep the bite?
abstract: The editorial argues that the PA legislature is attempting to fool the public by proposing taxes that they say are not taxes, but which will cost motorists as much or more than Governor Dick Thornburgh's tax proposal. Both types of taxes would help fund road improvements, and both would add costs to the fuel. The Republican proposal would not impose it at the pump, but rather on wholesale of transportation-related gas and oil.

headline: Mean Streets:  Why are we losing the war against crime?  A report from the trenches.
abstract: The article outlines the stories of crime from a victim, policeman, judge, professor, politician and prison warden.  Each details their accounts and views on crime

headline: Gambling Referendum
abstract: It looks like Allegheny Commissioners will not approve a gambling tax referendum. Eventually government sanctioned gambling could come to the county if the need for tax cash increases. The pressure towards it grows every year.

headline: Dark days ahead for W. Pa. town
abstract: null

headline: Reapportionment: Where the lines are drawn is a question of politics
abstract: Legislators of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania will be redrawing the congressional districts of Pennsylvania this week. In the past, partisan politics played as much of a role in locating district boundaries as rivers, mountains and county lines and this year is no exception. With the Republicans controlling both houses in Harrisburg, this means they also control congressional reapportionment.

headline: Dinosaur family out for walk?
abstract: The tracks unearthed last week by a construction worker at the Philadelphia Electric's Limerick nuclear power plant are said to belong to dinosaurs from approximately 190 million years ago. These prehistoric creatures were said to be five foot tall, three-toed creatures.

headline: Senior Citizens Who Drew 666 Daily Lottery Number Testifies
abstract: The drawing is of a courtroom. The caption mentions Violet Lowery of Pittsburgh testifying Tuesday, May 12, in Dauphin County Court that she drew the number 666 in the April 24, 1980 PA Daily Number game as a volunteer. The case involves two defendants, Edward Plevel and Nick Perry, accused of fixing the lottery.

headline: Specter, on visit to Indian family, pledges to seek amnesty for aliens
abstract: Stirred by the blight of a West Chester family of Indian immigrants fighting to remain in the United States, Pennsylvania Senator Arlen Specter said that he would introduce legislation to provide amnesty for some aliens living in the country.  However, Specter said he had not decided whether he would introduce a personal bill that, if passed, would save Shailesh and Premlata Patel and their three American-born children from deportation at the end of October.  No general legislation could be passed, however, in time to change the Patel's status before that deadline.

headline: Taking a stand
abstract: Harrisburg politicians made good on their promise to oppose the auto emissions testing program a federal judge has ordered for 12 Pennsylvania counties, including Bucks.  Under the terms of the court order, the testing program is to begin May 1, 1982.  The order would require once-a-year state inspection of all car exhaust systems.  The House and Senate both unanimously passed a bill to bar Pennsylvania Department of Transportation from spending any state funds to set up emissions testing.

headline: I love transit workers
abstract: The Cartoon depicts a Transport Worker's Union representative torturing a man representing Philadelphia, and telling him to repeat the words "I love transit workers"

headline: Milton Street acquitted of assault on policeman
abstract: State Senator Milton Street (R-Philadelphia) has been acquitted of assault charges, after taking the witness stand to deny kneeing a Philadelphia police officer in the groin during an April 10, 1980, melee in the City County chamber. Delaware County Judge Melvin Levy acquitted Street, as well as a supporter, Franklin Moses, of all charges.

headline: Drive to allow higher interest rates may stall out in House
abstract: The credit industry's drive to raise interest rates in the state may stall out in the PA House, due to labor's opposition and pre-election-year jitters. The bill would allow the cost of most types of consumer credit, including bank cards and department store charge, to rise by removing current state limits on interest rates.

headline: DAVID BRODER: Governors' Gamble' At Atlantic City
abstract: Those who follow the annual conferences of the National Governors Association from resort to resort are hopelessly addicted to the creation of dateline parables.  It was, therefore, dictated in advance that the theme of last week's meeting in the Resorts International casino-hotel would be " the governors' gamble."  And this year, for a change, the cliché fit extremely well.  The governors offered their some-time-partners in the federal government a deal, which was that they would take over the income-support programs and, in return, the governors would not excessively complain them dropping federal aid to education, transportation, and law-enforcement.

headline: Record keeping for the government
abstract: How long must businesses and private individuals hang on to records of transactions for the benefit of federal government agencies? The uncertainty over what records must be retained and for how long has led to clarifying legislation in Congress. Small business receive on average 4 forms every business day of the year. New legislation would place a three year limit on record keeping requirements.

headline: Don't count us out yet
abstract: Article establishes that "The Bulletin" is prepared to close August 16th if it cannot realize the savings of its losses to the Philadelphia Inquirer. It asks Bulletin employees and readers to help in its quest to boost revenue and advertising.

headline: Settlement: Was it close at hand?
abstract: After a fifty day long teachers' strike in Philadelphia, a court order put the teachers back to work and the kids back in school.  The article discusses the strike and rumors that a settlement between the union and the school district was near when the court order went into effect.

headline: State Names Rehabilitation Administrator
abstract: George C. Lowe, Jr. has been state director of vocational rehabilitation. The article details his previous work history.

headline: The Cost of Cleaning Up Our Environment
abstract: Taxpayer, Eric Nielsen, says that WCAU should stop making claims to clean up the environment without considering the costs to taxpayers.

headline: If you dig earthmovers, PennDOT welcomes you
abstract: In an effort to improve the reputation of its personnel, PA Department of Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson has scheduled two days of open houses at 51 of the department's county maintenance offices. PennDOT employees will show visitors around the offices, equipment sheds and yards, and will have state maps and PennDOT literature available.

headline: Montco restaurant is raided for back taxes
abstract: Sheriff's deputies from Montgomery County joined agents from the state Department of Revenue in conducting a raid June 2 on the Bagel Buffet Inc. restaurant at the Dreshertown Plaza shopping center. The state attorney general's office task force on delinquent taxes said the store's owners, Howard and Al Leibowitz, owe employer-withholding and sales taxes dating to 1978. The raid is part of two and a half month effort in Philadelphia that has netted the state $1.9 million in unpaid, back taxes.

headline: Ease Restrictions on Water, Schuylkill County Asks State
abstract: Based on the request of the county emergency management coordinator and county water providers, Schuylkill County commissioners will ask the PA Emergency Management Agency to suspend temporarily certain restrictions on water use in the county. In a similar move, the state Department of Environmental resources plans to ask PEMA to ease restrictions on swimming pools, car washes, and lawn watering in Schuylkill and 15 other counties.

headline: Decision delayed on Lederer case
abstract: The US House Ethics Committee members listened Thursday, April 9, to arguments for and against recommending expulsion from Congress of Representative Raymond Lederer (D., PA). Since only a few members attended, the decision was postponed until April 28. Lederer has been convicted of accepting a $50,000 bribe in the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) Abscam undercover investigation.

headline: Redistrict plan Okd, 3 seats out in county
abstract: The state reapportionment commission, clinging to its very strict population requirements, approved a final legislative redistricting plan that eliminates three Allegheny County House seats but retains all seven of it US Senate seats. It took the five-member commission less than a minute to approve a new legislative map which reflects the population changes of the past 10 years and continues to shift power from the cities to the suburbs.

headline: Ex-Traffic Court Boss Dead at 70
abstract: Former Traffic Court President, Judge Dominick Iannarelli, died of a heart attack at age 70.  The article details his lengthy career as a judge.

headline: Several Luzerne County Lawyers Are Trying the Old 'Sneak Play'
abstract: The article presents an analysis of five Luzerne County lawyers who are candidates vying for openings in the state's three courts. Candidates have mixed feeling as to the current selection process, some preferring the democratic election, and others favoring merit selection.

headline: State Store reform, not propaganda
abstract: A member of the United Food and Commercial Workers writes a letter to the editor regarding a past column that accused the United Food and Commercial Workers' conduct as nothing more than attempting to prevent change.

headline: The dangerous dumps found in Pa., N.J., Del.; N.J. home of 7 of nation's worst dump sites
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released a list of the most dangerous hazardous-waste sites in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware.  The article lists the sites and their locations.  The EPA is in negotiations with the states about how fund the clean up of these sites and stated that the list is a good start.

headline: It would be criminal to let communter lines fade away
abstract: In his financial report to the SEPTA board meeting, Treasurer George Miller stated that there was a twenty per cent loss in passengers on the commuter trains since it raised fares three months ago.  The editors feel that despite the Treasures statements regarding cuts to SEPTA, it would be premature to do so without further studies.

headline: More Cells, Stiffer Terms Proposed by Thornburgh
abstract: Faced with overcrowded prisons and rising crime, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh renewed his push for 2,700 additional cells and stiffer criminal sentences. The PA Legislature needs to authorized $85 million in bonds to pay for 2,205 new cells.

headline: Editorial Cartoon
abstract: Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board Inventory Control Office is pictured with several hundreds of  pieces of paper littering the entire office, all the papers have, "on order" or "out of stock," written on them.  There is a barrel that has "Senate Blend" stamped on it in the corner.  A man wearing a business suit is asking the old man in charge of the control office, "Where do you want me to put the computer?"

headline: Dem leader Hanna names heir apparent
abstract: Michael A. Hanna Sr. gave control of the Washington County Democratic Committee to Frank R. Mascara, chairman of the county commissioners, by naming Mascara vice-chairman of the party.  The article continues to provide  the reactions of Hanna naming Mascara as his heir.

headline: Redistricting Moves; State's 25 Congressmen Are Scrambling To Save Turf in Cutback to 23 Voting Areas
abstract: Pennsylvania Congressman Eugene Atkinson achieved some notational notoriety this year by voting with a band of southern Democrats to assure passage of both the budget and tax cut bills pushed by Republican President Ronald Reagan.  As the state legislature prepares to redraw congressional district lines.  Atkinson could have nothing but the memories if some of his Democratic colleagues in Washington had their way.  A map being circulated by Keystone delegation dean Joseph Gaydos would do this to Atkinson's district, which is made up largely of Lawrence, Beaver and Butler counties north of Pittsburgh.

headline: Fred Waring: Blending Business and Pleasure
abstract: The author interviewed musician Fred Waring about his long career in the industry and details his life. Mr. Waring works with the Young Pennsylvanias who sing and dance.

headline: Shapp Says Democrats Need a Primary Fight
abstract: Former Governor Milton J. Shapp told the Democratic State Committee that in order to gain visibility for their gubernatorial candidates, the Democrats need a fight in the primaries.  The article details Shapp's advice to the Democrats.

headline: State, US at odds over jobless pay
abstract: PA labor department officials expressed surprise at a letter being circulated on Capitol Hill that announces the cutoff of some $3 million in reimbursement for extended unemployment benefits paid this spring to the jobless in PA. The letter informs members of Congress that PA has failed to change its requirements for extended benefits to conform to 1980 amendments to federal law. The issue is more stringent requirements for recipients of unemployment compensation.

headline: Thornburgh offers relocation plan to Centralia
abstract: Together with the US Interior Department, Governor Dick Tornburgh unveiled a "sensitive and humane" plan to relocate families from the town of Centralia that live above an underground mine fire. The fire, burning since 1962, spews carbon monoxide and other noxious fumes into the homes, threatening families' health. The plan will not force anyone to sell their properties or move out of their homes, and will be voluntary.

headline: It's 'go' for Allegheny Valley missing link
abstract: Construction was virtually assured for the 3.7 mile missing link on the Allegheny Valley Expressway through East Deer, Tarentum and Harrison Township. Gov. Thornburgh announced the commitment of $22 million in state and federal funds for starting the $59 million job, which will open the four-lane divided highway nonstop between Blawnox and Kittanning Armstrong by late 1984.

headline: Mother's fight for children escalates
abstract: The Supreme Court agreed to decide whether parents can invoke a powerful federal court procedure to get their children back from state custody. They would rule on a PA woman's attempt to bring federal habeas corpus action to recover her children after exhausting her state level appeals.

headline: Even PhD find associate degree can be profitable
abstract: People with higher degrees are going back for associates in nursing, because there are lots of profitable jobs in that and other fields that only require an associates degree.

headline: Democrats Bolt to Put Screws to Mayor
abstract: Machinists Union leader, Norman Loudenslager, who worked with Democratic city Chairman David Glancey to elect Mayor Green in 1979, is just one of a large cadre of labor officials and Democratic party professionals who have bolted heir party in the convoluted rate for the 3rd Congressional District seat.

headline: Redistricting Plan Gives House Seven Seats
abstract: Picture with State Representative Samuel Hayes displaying a redistricting map, showing how the proposed reapportionment would add seven seats to the 203-member House.  The plan is the work of the Legislative Reapportionment Committee.

headline: Gen. Ike never faded tapes say
abstract: Dwight D. Eisenhower, former President and allied supreme commander during World War II, was never the general in retirement.  The National Park Service has compiled oral history tapes over the last decade as a record of the Eisenhower's' life at their Gettysburg farmhouse, which Mrs. Eisenhower often called the only real home they ever had.

headline: Shared Interest
abstract: Gorham Black Jr., PA Secretary of the PA Department of Aging, reviews listing of programs for older citizens with Alma Moody, president of the Uptown Senior Citizens Council.

headline: State's Miners Return
abstract: Striking anthracite miners from northeastern PA prepared to return to work after approving a new three-year contract that ended a 30-day strike against the hard coal industry. The miners, members of 43 United Mine Workers locals in the nine-county anthracite region, accepted the pact Sunday, May 31. Rejection of the pact would have dealt a serious blow to the revitalization of the anthracite industry.

headline: Thornburgh: Share cost of TMI clean up
abstract: null

headline: KEEP BRIDGE CAR POOLS
abstract: The Walt Whitman Bridge from New Jersey into Philadelphia sold a book of tickets to car pools for a month for only $4.00.  The Delaware Port Authority deliberately made the tickets so cheap to encourage carpooling to save energy.  Only a few people used the car pool tickets and they cost a lot to process.  So in September, the Port Authority is going to eliminate the big discount and make them the same price as regular commuter tickets.

headline: Municipal lawyers free of ethics act
abstract: The Commonwealth Court ruled that lawyers who are public employees are not required to provide financial disclosures as stated in the ethics act.  The Court ruled that the regulations were unconstitutional .

headline: Flat Out, He's Tired Of Rare Air
abstract: Stephen Levin, a Philadelphia Democrat, created House Bill 1766 due to his frustration of old-fashioned gas stations closing down and new self-service stations falling short of delivering the services/tools motorists require. Due to the increased price of gasoline service stations are steadily shutting down to the self-service gas stations that have cheaper gasoline for the very reason that there are no attendants to serve motorists. Thus, the 1766 bill is going to the House floor for a vote to have either free air or coin-operated air at gas stations for motorists.

headline: Democrats Score and Easy Win in City
abstract: The article details Philadelphia's elections, in which Democrats won all the seats.  The article notes the campaigns for district attorney, city council,  judicial races, and traffic court.

headline: Redistricting plan moving
abstract: A Republican compromise plan to redistrict the Pennsylvania congressional delegation in time for the May primary election began moving in the Pennsylvania House.  The redistricting involves a reduction of two seats.  The Democrats of Pennsylvania have maintained the ability to block the passing of the Republican plans.  The article continues to provide details about the two parties squabble over the redistricting plans in Pennsylvania.

headline: Governor's son to wed
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's son, John, will wed Sharon Kratz.  The brief article outlines the couple's college history.

headline: Shattered Jobless of Detroit
abstract: null

headline: Strike bans
abstract: An opinion piece that urges Pennsylvania state government to look into what causes satisfactory new contract terms for both sides of strikers before resorting to strike bans.

headline: Toxic Waste Dumping Hit
abstract: Despite a 1980 state law regulating hazardous wastes and a "strike force" to enforce it, illegal dumping of poisonous materials remains too high and will take another two years to bring under acceptable control, according to the chief of PA's Department of Environmental Resources. In other activities, the PA Environmental Council, the statewide citizens' lobbying group on environmental issues, decided last week to continue acting independently of DER and the private sector on waste matters.

headline: Keep the railroads
abstract: Representative Bud Shuster is worried about a report by President Reagan that may close Conrail.  He feels this could mean job loses in Altoona.

headline: My sister is mother of Rachael Marie
abstract: Author believes adoption takes a lot of time and considering how emotional the process is. She believes mothers should be able to either immediately give up rights of their babies or have the child put in foster care for six months, that way adoptive parents would not have to go to the uncertainty period.

headline: Foes Say Advocates Tried to Railroad It Through Panel: State Store Abolition Plan Suffers Another Setback
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's plan to dispose of the state store system took another hit as the State Law and Justice Committee erupted amid charges that the plan's supporters were attempting to railroad the issue to the floor.  In a meeting hastily called by State Senator Steward Greenleaf, committee chairman, the plan was amended into another bill and approved for floor consideration by a vote of 4-1.  Several arguments dispersed about whether the meeting was legitimately held, so further setbacks have occurred to Thornburgh's plan.

headline: Democrats stall judge's confirmation
abstract: State Senate Democrats delayed the confirmation of Republican Judge Roy Wilkinson Jr by witholding the required authorization to act on the appointment and giving strong indication that they will not supply the needed votes until after the formation of a commission to redistrict the Legislature.  Thirty-four votes are needed for confirmation; the Republicans only have 26.  Democrats object to immediate confirmation of Wilkinson because he would give the GOP a 4-3 majority on the Supreme Court, which settles all reapportionment disputes and decides issues that the reapportionment body cannot.

headline: Redistricting: How close is too close?
abstract: Representative Jim Merry made a good point in discussing the pending reapportionment plan for House and Senate districts in the state legislature.  Merry said it is a hsame to followpopulation counts so closely in legislative redistricting that there has been a lost of sight of county boundaries and traditional constituent representation areas.  The five-member state reapportionemnt commission, headed by Dr. James Freedman, dean of the University of Pennsylvania Law School, drew its proposed reapportionment map to the very tight specification that all legislative districts would be within half of one percentage point of the ideal average population.

headline: Guv's Son to Wed
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's son, John will wed Sharon Kratz.  The article details their college histories.

headline: Sheely Overrules Board's Decision
abstract: Cumberland County Judge Harold Sheely, while acknowledging that the county Election Board may have had reason in reversing its certification of the results of the Democratic primary for Silver Spring Twp. Supervisor, has ruled that the board didn't have the authority to do so. By reversing the board, Sheely cleared the way for John Rowland's name to be placed on the Democratic ballot in the General Election, creating a contest for the office.

headline: Sun Co's Unit to Discontinue It's Shipbuilding;  Loss Ridden Sun Ship Says It Isn't Efficient Enough In the Shrinking Market
abstract: Sun Ships, based in Pennsylvania, stopped it's shipbuilding operations after realizing that it was no longer effective due to the decrease in demand for new ships and a lack of technology.  Over 3,000 jobs will be lost in Chester, PA.

headline: Toxic-waste sites: Outcasts across the region
abstract: A third of an Amish town's population came out to oppose having a hazardous-waste landfill proposed for 285 acres in their town. The area desperately needs a site though. PA is the fourth largest generator of hazardous wastes, but can only deal with 20% produced. Whenever a new site is proposed, the community always objects.

headline: Larson Addresses Senate Appropriations Committee: Cut PennDOT in on General Fund, Secretary Urges
