abstract: State Transportation Secretary, Thomas D. Larson, told the Senate Appropriations Committee that his department should be funded through the general fund, rather than the motor license fund.  The article details Mr. Larson's speech to the committee.

headline: Mystery
abstract: Editorial questions why some attorneys and judges in the state are petitioning the Courts to relieve them of the requirement to disclose any source of outside side income.  Editorial says that perhaps the judges and attorneys are scared to let people know the sources of their outside income.

headline: Get the state out of state stores. . .
abstract: The author opines that it is time to support Governor Thornburgh's proposal to do away with state run liquor stores and have them be privately owned.  The author feels that in addition to better selection and lower prices, getting the state out of the liquoe business would reduce corruption.

headline: Democrats to make it official today: Phila. Gets meeting
abstract: The Democratic National Committee's executive committee meets today to formally select Philadelphia as host of the party's mini-convention next summer. The meeting is designed to get the party organized for the upcoming congressional elections.

headline: Reforms Too Strict?  Congress Waters Watergate Ethics
abstract: After the Nixon Watergate scandal, the U.S. Congress passed stricter codes of conduct for elected officials, but some present and former elected officials say the coes are overly refined, hard to understand and downright insulting.  The Senate Ethics Committee is studying changes which could eliminate everything in the code except financial disclosure.  The article includes the comments of several representatives and their views on the codes of conduct.

headline: Harrisburg Forest No. 43; John D. Witmer, Jr., GTC
abstract: A photograph depicting: Ralph Spearly, Supreme Tall Cedar; Governor Dick Thornburgh, signing the Tall Cedar Week Proclamation; Duane Goodhart, Supreme Director No. 3; John Witmer, Jr., Grand Tall Cedar; and Charles Trimmer, Treasurer. The caption beneath the photograph states, "Tall Cedars with the Governor of Pennsylvania."

headline: Sun Ship to turn to repairs in the hope of staying afloat
abstract: Sun Ship, based in Delaware County,  who recently announced that it would lay off some 3,100 workers and will go out of business, has decide to change strategies to try to stay afloat.  Sun Ship President, Robert H. Campbell, said that they would try to focus on repairing and rebuilding ships rather.  If the restructuring works, it may save the area from going further into economic decline.

headline: Toxin law could be better; Protecting pets and ourselves
abstract: The illness of former Mayor Frank Rizzo's dog from exposure to toxic chemicals is not a fluke or an isolated incident that easily can be dismissed.  The chemical culprit is just one of a host of pesticides that can cause serious illnesses that are used routinely.  The article continues to discuss what legislation should be added to protect people and pets from toxins.

headline: Letters:  Pa. should repair Orange St. bridge
abstract: The author is upset by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's (PennDOT) seemingly lack of concern about replacing an unsafe bridge in Media, Pa.

headline: New Program to Assist Elderly Victims of Crime
abstract: To alleviate the problems that deter senior citizens from reporting a crime and going through the court system, District Attorney Edwad G. Rendell initiated The Elderly Crime Assistance Program, and is supported by Common Pleas Judge Leon Katz. The program provides emotional support through volunteers, also senior citizens, who accompany them to court and offer peer counseling. The author argues it should allow police to apprehend more criminals as crime reporting increases.

headline: Golf-course licensing is redrafted by panel
abstract: A state Senate floor vote will be held to allow public golf courses to be granted liquor licenses outside of the quota law.  The article outlines the specific details of the bill and interviews several Senator on their thoughts on the bill.

headline: Democrats using new tactics to raise money
abstract: The Democratic Pennsylvania committee executive director, Sean Strub, stated that the Democrats are going to utilize a former beauty queen, political tomes and free lunches to fund-raise for their party.  The article goes further into detail about how the Democrats are planning on raising money for the 1982 year.

headline: Regan woos voters for Kean
abstract: The New Jersey election is widely regarded as the first national test of the President's programs. Polls taken in the state so far show Kean to be trailing Florio by six to eight percentage points. Registered Democrats outnumber registered Republicans in the state, which makes things difficult.

headline: It's a Rare Bird On Capitol Hill: Something Wise
abstract: A rare snowy owl has been seen on top of the Capitol building.  Public Utilities Commission, and avid bird watcher, Clifford Jones explains that the bird is usually seen in colder climates, but may have come here for the abundance of pigeons it can prey on.

headline: Talk of liquor strike makes busy season busier
abstract: Wendell Young, union leader of the 2,500 liquor store clerks, has threatened the strike if no progress has been made in contract negotiations with Pennsylvania.  The threat of strike is making the public nervous and making them stock up more during the holiday season, since they fear they will not be able to purchase liquor soon.

headline: Troubles hit EPA near TMI
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency has been charged with monitoring the environment around Three Mile Island and has been beset with equipment breakdowns and delays in analyzing samples.  The article goes further into detail about Middletown's office of Environmental Protection Agency's data on the samples, budget, and their plans for Three Mile Island.

headline: Letters: Cut Waste in PennDOT
abstract: The author opines that Governor Thornburgh should cut funds to the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) in his proposed budget, which cuts funding for almost all other agencies.  The author feels that PennDOT wastes public funds and cites examples.

headline: New trial asked for Murphy
abstract: An attorney for PA Senator William Murphy Jr., convicted last month of extortion, argued in US District Court that the federal government's key witness against Murphy may have been the one who committed the crime. Defense Attorney Victor Battaglia asked Judge Walter Stapleton to grant Murphy a new trial in light of news accounts that government witness Herbert Gregory Jr. bought a bar in February, four months after he declared bankruptcy. Another investigation found that Gregory has put down up to $18,000 in cash to buy the bar.

headline: Governnor porposes axing State Stores
abstract: Gov. Thronburgh proposed a plan to abolish all 725 state controlled liquor stores and have the sale of wine and spirits go through privately owned stores.  The proposal included the option of local governments to choose whether to have state and their zoning specifications.  Thronburgh stated that the Liquor Control Board has been marked by corruption and needs changed.  The proposal must first be passed by the Legislature

headline: Demos Pick Land to Run for Schwartz Seat
abstract: State Democratic ward leader Ann Land, former librarian of the state Senate, has been named as the party's candidate in the special election to choose a successor to George Schwartz of the 4th state House district. Schwartz, former Philadelphia City Council President in the 4th District, resigned from his post after being convicted of charges stemming from the Abscam investigation. The conviction was later overturned.

headline: Regulatory reform? No, it isn't
abstract: null

headline: Joan Specter Works Wonders In Marriage of 2 Career
abstract: Joan Specter is married to Pennsylvania's junior United States senator, a Philadelphia attorney who many Washington observers think is destined to become a power on Capital Hill.  In the pursuit of that political happiness, his wife is a definite asset.  The old saw about a good woman being behind every successful man seems too outdated to describe this tandem, but Mrs. Specter obviously takes her husband's career at least as seriously as her own.

headline: The end; The Journal officially folds after unions reject concessions
abstract: The Philadelphia Journal has decided to fold the paper, after union officials of the Newspaper Guild of Philadelphia and the Teamsters Local 628 rejected the company's request for a 12.5 percent wage cut and benefit concessions that would have totaled $275,000 per year.  The article continues to provide further commentary on the Journal's closing.

headline: 'Vested Interest' Cited in Fishing Creek Hearings: Landfill Perils 'Golden Years,' Retiree Says
abstract: Retiree Warren E. Berger stated that the proposal to put a landfill in the Fishing Creek Valley area will hurt his retirement plans.  He testified in front of the Environmental Hearing board that the noise from the landfill would be a nuisance and eventually the landfill would obscure his ability to see the sun rise.  Others testified about the danger to children and the environment

headline: Lewis' bid for transportation post has smooth sailing in committee
abstract: Drew Lewis should be confirmed as transportation secretary in the Reagan Administration.  He has had no problems going through the Senate confirmation hearings.  Drew Lewis once ran for governor of Pennsylvania

headline: No-Bid Contract Challenged
abstract: Kenneth L. Rotz is appealing a County Court Judge's ruling that Adams County Commissioners did not violate county code when they entered into a no-bid contract for weather proofing the County Courthouse.  The article details the appellant's rationale and the county's side of the story.

headline: Governor Boosts Liquor Plan
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh stated that he is still optimistic about his plan to privatize state liquor stores, even though the state Senate tabled the proposal.  In a speech to the Indiana County Chamber of Commerce, he pushed for his privatization plan and also talked about tax reform and education funding.  The article outlines the speech.

headline: Demos Score Easy Victories
abstract: Three quarters of Philadelphia city electorate chose to ignore the May 19 primary election. One surprise outcome of the vote was the rejection of a routine city government request to borrow money to fund the capital budget. The other important issue was the race for Common Pleas Court. And a number of disaffected Democrats had success in the special 4th Council District election to fill the unexpired term of former City Council President George Schwartz, who resigned after his conviction in the Abscame federal investigation case.

headline: Rehearing On Pension is Pushed
abstract: Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman asked the State Supreme Court to reconsider their decision to allow former House Speaker Herbert Fineman, convicted of obstruction of justice for accepting bribes, to receive his pension from the state.

headline: Levy to become 6 p.m. co-anchor with Larry Kane on Channel 10
abstract: Steve Levy, former Channel 6 sportscaster, will become Larry Kane's co-anchor at Channel 10 in Philadelphia.  The article details other news in TV and talk radio.

headline: The Skies Above And The Streets Below
abstract: Pittsburgh's City Council should be concerned with safety in the streets rather than safety in the skies. With one member abstaining, Council passed a resolution last week telling President Reagan that the skies above Pittsburgh have become so hazardous since striking air controllers were fired for breaking the law. This is the pitch that members of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization are pushing country-wide in an effort for the government to rehire them.

headline: Violations Hurt Land and Livelihoods:  Residents Scarred by Strip-Mine Abuse
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources (DER) is not doing enough to stop strip-mine abuses.  The article states that DER does not have enough inspectors to monitor the strip mines and that they have renewed licenses to companies who have violated environmental laws.  The article details the problems two local men have with their businesses because of the pollution.  Coal companies say they have to mine without permits or risk financial collapse.

headline: Lewis calls SWAP 'tax on a tax'
abstract: State Senator Craig Lewis says that motorists will be paying tax on their taxes if Governor Thornburgh's SWAP gasoline tax is passed.  The SWAP tax would be based on the average price of gasoline after federal and state taxes are included, thus making the SWAP actually tax other taxes.

headline: Now it's GOP's turn on state's US attorneys
abstract: Author relates story of the firing of US District Attorney David Marston in 1978 and alleges that he was fired because he was a Republican and that President Jimmy Carter had commit obstruction of justice.  The author then goes on state that merit is not considered when District attorneys are appointed and that now that there is a Republican president there will be more Republican District attorneys

headline: Governor Wants Private Sale, But. . . : Lawmankers Think Twice on Liquor Proposal
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's plan to abolish 725 state liquor stores and turn them over to private businesses is getting some dissent from the state legislature.  State representative Stanford I. Lehr ® is especially vocal in his opposition.  Several representatives voiced concern at the proposal, stating that the answer to corruption in the State Liquor Board is better management, not dismantling. The article interviews several representatives and their thoughts on the matter.

headline: Dems Do Little Courting for Common Pleas
abstract: Democratic City Committee Chairman David Glancey stated that the democrats can't lose the election for 12 seats on the Common Pleas Court.  The article details the candidates and their histories.

headline: Reilly named district attorney in Delaware County
abstract: John A. Reilly, a prosecutor, was named Delaware County's new district attorney.  The article continues to provide a short political biography on Reilly and an explanation on the office he will inherit.

headline: Limerick plant worker digs up ancient footprints
abstract: Officials at the Limerick nuclear power plant near Pottstown, PA in Montgomery County said a worker found what might be the footprints of an ancient lizard left in slabs of sandstone and preserved for approximately 190 million years. The prints are about 5 to 7 inches long, have three toe-like digits and were found about 20 feet below the surface. Twelve slabs were found with 16 distinct prints. The sandstone is said to be from the Triassic period, the first of the Mesozoic Era, when dinosaurs roamed the Earth.

headline: Turnpike staff to vote on tenative contract
abstract: The union representing employees of the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission reached an agreement on their contracts, which will be voted on by the union members.  The employees threatened a strike if their contracts were not renegotiated, but no details were released.

headline: Voters Will Approve Bond, Water Committee Predicts
abstract: Chairman of the Vote-Yes for Water Committee, George B. Wolff, stated that he was optimistic that voters will approve a $300 million water referendum that will change the way municipalities could borrow for water improvements.  The article details the water referendum.

headline: License word
abstract: Currently, Pennsylvania license automobiles with only numbers and letters in random order to identify vehicles.  With payment of a fee, Pennsylvanians can get a personalized license plate with words or numbers that they specify.  Proposal to extend that idea with all cars and trucks, which would make all license plates have some distinctive wording on it.  Almost all citizens would be able to actually remember their license plate without having to look it up.  It would be much easier to identify the vehicle if it were stolen since the license plate could be more easily spotted by both the police and the populace.

headline: Offer to Cons: No Punishment
abstract: Four inmates at Graterford Prison are holding 38 hostages, including three guards.  The article details the attempts at negotiations and states that no one so far has been hurt.

headline: Grand jury to return presentments
abstract: A statewide grand jury is expected to return presentments against alleged operators of a $300-$400 million state wide gambling operation in what law enforcement sources have described as the largest case of its kind in PA history.

headline: Dennis Coverup in Street Funding Probe?
abstract: In a memo date June 20, Jerry Astolfi, a former acting bureau official with the state's Department of Community Affairs, accepted most of the blame for allowing state Senator T. Milton Street's controversial weatherization program to be funded. However, it is believed he acted under pressure from DCA's Secretary Shirley Dennis, even though the state-administered federal aid to the North Philadelphia Block Development Corporation had not yet been approved by the US Department of Energy.

headline: Reins of power are now in hands of once-weak OMB
abstract: The Reagan administration has made the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) the clearinghouse for all new regulations, so that no major rule can be proposed or issued until the OMB is satisfied that the measure is necessary and is taking the lowest-cost approach. The change is most dramatically highlighted by the diesel rule that the administration wants to change so that more diesel-powered vehicles can be built.

headline: Looking Ahead
abstract: (Broadcast) Editorial in which they discuss the things that they feel need changed, like PA state liquor stores, car inspections, mass transit, and the gasoline tax.

headline: UMW Members OK contract
abstract: Members of the United Mine Workers union approved an end to the 72 day nationwide soft coal strike, which caused hardship them but not the US economy. The return  to work of 160,000 miners could delay by the threat of picket lines by UMW construction workers unhappy with contract language and the lack of their own agreement. The strike began with wildcat walkouts leading to shootings and isolated dynamiting.

headline: Walgren criticizes EPA on dump
abstract: U.S. Representative Doug Walgren (D) criticized the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for not notifying officials and residents in Indiana Township of the presence of toxic substances.  He called for an investigation into why federal officials knew of chemicals in Allegheny County but did not notify any local officials.

headline: Pa. attorney general blocks return of Camiel to turnpike commission
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General, Leroy Aimmerman, ruled yesterday that Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission Chairman Jack Greenblat had no authority to reinstate Peter Camiel to the commission or give him more than $18,000 in back pay. Camiel, former chairman of the Philadelphia Democratic Committee, was acquitted Tuesday on charges that he was padding the state payroll with employees that never sowed up for work. When Camiel was indicted in May 1980, Governor Thornburgh suspended him from the commission. Greenblat was corresponding with Thornburgh stating that he was going to reinstate Camiel. Zimmerman stated it would be illegal for Greenblat to do so.

headline: Off-hour bail service set to ease jail crowding
abstract: To hold down the population of the Bucks County Prison an official has volunteered to make himself and his deputies available every night and on weekends to process the release of prisoners on bail. The on-call system is being set up immediately to eliminate having people remain in the prison overnight or an entire weekend even though their release on bail has been approved by a judge.

headline: Hershey expects delectable year
abstract: Analysts have predicted a good year for Hershey Foods Corporation as the price of coca has remained constant and sugar prices have fallen. Although diversifying in recent years in other food areas, chocolate still accounts for 70 percent of its sales.

headline: DIASTERS
abstract: Philadelphia's teachers strike seems to be bringing out the worst in a lot of people.  Philadelphia's City Council's President Joe Coleman refused to consider any other plans for solving the school crisis except his own. Then the president lost control completely when Councilman Street went into his stump preaching act.  School Bard President Arthur Thomas is considering renewing Superintendent Marcase's contract.  Thomas is talking about creating a special committee of board members to grade Marcase.  The superintendent's contract expires this June.

headline: Reject Pension Grab in November
abstract: Even though the funding of pension funds for state employees and public school teachers are on a collision course to disaster, a move is underway to increase the already generous benefits paid by the funds.  The attempt can be sidetracked by the voters in November and should be.  The forecast of impending financial disaster is that the state Senator Edward L. Howard.  Howard claims the fiscal soundness of the two funds was strained by the generosity of a majority of members of the General Assembly in the 1970s.  They are among those who will be able to exercise Option 4 upon retirement, a provision which allows a retiree to withdraw in one lump sum the retiree's contribution to the fund with only a small reduction in the size of the monthly benefits to be paid to the retiree by the fund.

headline: Mr. Fixit for the Cities
abstract: The article analyzes the views of Felix Rohatyn, a millionaire capitalist who planned New York City's recovery from the edge of bankruptcy. Mr. Rohatyn is a widely sought after Democrat who wants to help other cities in crisis around the country with an industrial revolution-like program that includes a set of proposals such as special tax credits, a national gasoline tax, and expanded city tax bases.

headline: UMW, Coal Firms Move Closer to Accord But Friday Strike Still Appears Certain
abstract: The United Mine Workers union (UMW) and the coal industry are attempting negotiations to prevent a strike by Friday.  The article details the terms of the negotiations and the demands of the union.

headline: Waste guidelines too strict, DER told
abstract: Industry and business groups told the PA Department of Environmental Resources that its proposed guidelines for determining where hazardous chemical wastes can be disposed f in PA could effectively rule out every possible site in the commonwealth and damage the state's economy. Ecologists said the same guidelines may be too lax and need to be tightened up in some areas if the health of the state's citizens is to be protected.

headline: Pa. auto dealers protest high interest rates
abstract: Pennsylvania Independent Auto Dealers asked the U.S. Congress to force the Federal Reserve Board to lower interest rates, after 19 months of high interest rates aimed at deflecting inflation.  The group says that the high interest rates are forcing many dealerships out of business.

headline: O'Kicki still could get federal judgeship
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Joseph F. O'Kicki could be appointed to the federal district court for western PA, even though he's a Democrat and there is a new Republican adminstration.  A commission to select judges based on merit is still in place and US Senator Joseph Heinz wants it to be reorganized.  The article discusses the possibility of Judge O'Kicki being appointed.

headline: High spirits: State store profits soar
abstract: The PA state Liquor Control Board says net profits from state store operations in the first nine months of the fiscal year exceeded the previous year. It reported a net profit of $42.4 million compared to $34.7 million last year. Profits were up 22%, but sales were only up 6%.

headline: Disputed: Chamber raises questions on saving patronage jobs
abstract: The Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce criticized city officials for saving the jobs of 94 patronage workers on the school district payroll.  The employees, most of whom are assigned to the Board of Revision of Taxes, were among 3,000 laid off by the school district because of its budge deficit.  The Green administration and the City Council agreed early this month to use $1.6 million in city funds to keep them on the payroll.  Chamber chairman, Robert G. Wilder, would like the city to review the need for the employees and, if it determines that the jobs are necessary, should put them under civil service rules.

headline: Remap To Give GOP Edge In Congrss
abstract: State Senat Republican staffers hae drafted a reapportionment plan whose adoption conceivably could give the Republicans nearly a 2-to-1 control over Pennsylvania's congressional delegation.  The Republicans are not even ready to introduce this reapportionment, and it will likely be revised before being introduced officially. The draft plan would reduce the number of congressional districts in the state from 25 to 23, reflecting Pennsylvania's failure to keep pace with other parts of the nation in population growth.

headline: Newest Sculpture Has Critics Groaning
abstract: Pennsylvania state art critics discuss the monstrosity that is the new Benjamin Franklin statue placed on North Broad Street across from the Masonic Temple in Philadelphia. Critics state that the composition is poorly proportioned, ill-executed, and placed in a strange area. The statue depicts a young Benjamin Franklin at his printing press. The statue was a gift from the Freemasons of Pennsylvania, entitled "Benjamin Franklin Craftsman." The sculptor was done by Joe Brown, member of the Philadelphia Art Commission.

headline: Union chief says Street is a liar
abstract: Union President Wendell Young fired back at PA Senator Milton Street who had cast a key vote Tuesday for a bill the union opposes because he said Young and other union members had roughed up students trying to enter a school in his district. Young has denied any involvement in a scuffle at the school, and called a news conference at which he termed Young an absolute liar. During a meeting of the Senate Law and Justice Committee, Street cast the decisive vote to phase out the State Store system to the full Senate.

headline: Waste not, want not
abstract: Editorial says that New Yorkers need to conserve water or they will face a drought emergency when reservoir levels fall to 30% of capacity.  City Hall is urging New Yorkers to conserve water before they find themselves facing mandatory conservation measures that will entail real hardship and discomfort.

headline: Pa. gets $173 million to build, repair roads
abstract: Pennsylvania will receive an additional $173 million in federal funds this year to build new highways and to repair existing roads, Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis says.  The grant brings Pennsylvania's 1981 share of the $8.7 billion highway aid program to $513 million.  Only New York received a larger allocation in the second round of federal highway grants, collecting $183 million.

headline: On trial!
abstract: The editorial argues that Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal for minimum-five year sentences for persons convicted of using firearms during commission of crimes is similar to earlier experiences with sentences of less duration, with unimpressive results. The editorial hopes that the governor has measures in mind to force judges to apply the new law, which they refused to do with the earlier sentencing guidelines.

headline: High Usage Predicted Under Dial-A-Bet Law
abstract: Most horse racing tracks in Pennsylvania plan to use telephone betting and other provisions of a new law aimed to revitalizing the state's financially ailing horse racing industry.  Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh signed the measure which also gives thoroughbred and harness tracks a tax break, allows them to televise races held at other tracks, and permits extended racing seasons and special promotions.  The article goes further into detail about the new laws and their anticipated effects on Pennsylvania.

headline: Districts are for people, not polls
abstract: A lot of people and organizations are beginning to challenge the tentative congressional and state legislative districts that are supposed to reflect population changes shown in the 1980 census. They claim the map and being drawn for politicians not citizens.

headline: Remapping Plan Tribute to Dems?
abstract: Philadelphia's Democratic City Committee appears to have prevailed in the complex negotiations over the reapportionment of the city's state House districts.  Sources in both the Republican and Democratic Parties said the plan scheduled for adoption by the five-member Reapportionment Committee substantially followed the preliminary map drawn up by the city's Democratic leaders.  The city is losing five of its 34 state House seats because of the 15 percent drop in its population during the last decade.  Many politicians who saw their districts disappear in the new Democratic landscape desperately lobbied party heavyweights against the plan, apparently with little success.

headline: None
abstract: Broadcast recaps the success of the first ever Symphony Concerts in Point Park. It was the best received free public event in Pittsburgh and the broadcaster states that this should become an annual tradition.

headline: Woman's World Forum: Should teenagers be paid less than the minimum wage?
abstract: The idea of paying teenagers less than the minimum wage to counter youth unemployment, hotly debated for years, has gained new support from the Reagan administration.  Conservative Senator Orrin Hatch is sponsoring a bill, called the McDonald's amendment" by critics, which would allow employers to pay 16-19 year olds 75 percent of the minimum wage, with the stipulation that they pay the minimum after 6 months on the job and/or at age 20.  The minimum wage is now $3.35 an hour, up more than 46 percent since 1977.  The fast-food industry, biggest employer of teenagers in the country, is already exempt from paying the minimum wage to students.

headline: Water Bond
abstract: The editorial board writes that no other necessity of life is taken more for granted than pure water until it stops running out of the tap or it becomes undrinkable as a result of contamination. We have become shamefully wasteful in our care and use of water. We must pay for our past abuse. Water is infiltrated and hopelessly contaminated by the runoff of pesticides and herbicides from farms. The water systems have to be redone so that they are more protected and then not neglected once they are redone. The water resources bond issue on the November ballot will help address these issues.

headline: Pa. House approves annual car checks
abstract: The Pennsylvania State House passed a bill yesterday that would reduce the number of auto safety inspections from twice per year to once a year. The measure, proposed by Pennsylvania State Senator John Davies, had strong bipartisan support. For this reason, the fact that the semiannual inspection has been vocalized as a rip-off by consumer groups and advocates, and the Thornburgh Administration's full backing is presumably why this bill has passed the house currently rather than the several other previous attempts. Under this bill school buses, mass transit, and other public vehicles are required to undergo inspections semiannually while automobiles are required to undergo the inspection annually when registration is due.

headline: Our opinion: That common-law loophole
abstract: The recent Erie case involving the school teacher and the 14-year-old girl points up a glaring error in Pennsylvania's laws covering common-law marriage.  Under the current state statues, parents apparently have no recourse when  child 14 or over decides to enter into a common-law marriage.  The law allows parents to have common-law rites involving a child 13 or under annulled.  However, it does not appear to contain the same remedy when minor children above 14 are involved.  The way the law reads now, juvenile runaways could easily use the claim of a common-law marriage as a way out of going back home.  And adults sexually involved with teenagers could persuade them to commit themselves to a common-law marriage in order to avoid charges of corrupting the morals of a minor.

headline: Horse Track Bill May Gallop Through Senate
abstract: Legislation designed to revolutionize Pennsylvania's horse racing industry and have tracks serve as telephone 'bookies' will clear the Senate by October 1, 1981. PA Senator Frank O'Connel said they have the support of the Senate and Governor. The measure would make sweeping changes to benefit the horse racing industry, including longer racing seasons, lower taxes and telephone betting.

headline: Don’t let the politicians steal tomorrow's election
abstract: The editorial argues that in the May 19 primary elections, it will be a shame if professionals win, for several reasons. First, hand-picked candidates are not necessarily the best. Second, if not everyone shows up to vote, the political process is not represented by taxpayers. Third, most of candidates for the statewide judicial offices are cross-filed and almost guaranteed a win. Therefore, the editorial explains the importance of every registered voter's decision about the act of voting itself.

headline: Remember Ahab
abstract: Mitch Ruben attended school in Philadelphia, but the only attraction he has for Philadelphia is his $42,000 salary. The letter to the editor refers to no striking teachers as scabs and admittedly baits them. Remember Capt. Ahab. He baited, too, and caught something.

headline: On the Minds of Seniors
abstract: The article, based on seminars held by two state Senators, outlines the concerns of senior citizens and youth in Pennsylvania.  Their concerns include; the economy, jobs, welfare, the environment, transport, education, and the media.

headline: null
abstract: 'Survey said…' Roberta Waldman an adviser to the state Education Department's Student Advisory Council, receives the results of a school improvement survey conducted by Cotillion debutantes.

headline: Water bond issue is a good proposal
abstract: Generally it is best for people in community to handle their problems on their problems on their own rather than to look to others for help. However at times they are so widespread and so serious it demands a broader solution, like drought stricken water-systems. PA Governor Dick Thornburgh wants voters to decide if it will be handled at the state level.

headline: 'Pothole Hotline' Means 4,155 Calls - 2,607 Repairs
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) said that 4,155 people called their hotline to report potholes during its first two weeks of operation, which lead to 2,607 road repairs.  PennDOT officials say they've responded to 63 per cent of callers reports, but that snow has slowed down repairs.

headline: OUR VOICE; Making our prison system work
abstract: John Artis spent the past 14 years in prison for his part in one of New Jersey's killings, and is a prison success story.  Chief Justice Warren Burger thinks he knows why Artis is a success story and would like to recreate his success in other prisoners.  The article discusses Burger's plans to rework the prison system.

headline: House passes bingo bill - again
abstract: The state House passed along to the state Senate a bill allowing non-profit organizations to legally operate bingo games. The driving force is an effort by the U.S. Internal Revenue Service to tax proceeds from the games. It is believed the Senate will fulfill its role and do nothing beyond assigning it to a committee to meet a fate equivalent of death.

headline: Don't blame teachers
abstract: Teachers just want security at their jobs. How can be secure if the board wants to lay off 3.500 teachers at one time? Author doesn't blame taxpayers for being upset, but hopes they an sympathize with teachers.

headline: Remembering
abstract: The editorial argues that everyone is remembering that the strike against Southeastern PA Transportation Authority's Red Arrow division is still alive and well. The riders, the striking United Transport Workers Union, Governor Dick Thornburgh, and SEPTA are all affected by it. It argues that because just about everyone knows how critical the situation is, something should be expected to be done.

headline: Owls join football leaders, but without paying costs
abstract: Outlines Temple University's head football coach, Wayne Hardin's, football career. Discussion of Temple's wins and losses and Hardin's assignment to better the football team in order to become a peer competitor with powerhouse football teams like Pennsylvania State, Pittsburgh and West Virginia.

headline: A look at events of the past week
abstract: Lower Bucks schools opened on an unusually upbeat note this year. There was a degree of certainty to the opening of school this year that's been lacking in recent Septembers. The Centennial School District opened its doors proudly trumpeting recent improvements in student reading test scores.

headline: Water Conservation
abstract: The editors point that, while homeowners can do a lot to conserve water, the majority of water is used in irrigation and nuclear facilities.  They urge that home owners not be blamed for the water shortage.

headline: Panel approves Gleason for Turnpike post
abstract: Robert Gleason's nomination to the Turnpike Commission breezed through a Senate committee, but approved by the full Senate is not expected to come easily.

headline: Pa. braces for firestorm on open adoption records
abstract: A small legal notice published by the Pennsylvania Department of Health this week is focusing attention anew on one of the more emotional issues to cross any legislator's desk: the right of adoptees to obtain information about their biological parents.  Pennsylvania is one of the only three states that allows an adopted person over 18 to see his or her original birth certificate in all cases.  Now the state Health Department's Bureau of Vital Statistics is considering making an adoptee's search for his or her roots even easier.  It is offering to make the current addresses of those biological parents available to adoptees if the parents approve.  The public has 30 days to comment on the proposal.

headline: How my State Store plan would work
abstract: Letter to the editor from Governor Thornburgh clarifying a recent article about how his propsed dismantling of the State liquor store system would work.  He states that his proposal is not meant to get rid of the state liquor control all together, but to provide better consumer satisfaction in choices and prices of liquor.

headline: Don't use White to prove point, union boss warns
abstract: The threat of union leader Henry Nicholas to possibly knock off PA  Representative John White in his city council bid to prove the strength of Black trade unionists has hit a snag with Royal Sims, national vice president of the American Federation of Government Employees. Sims expressed support for Nicholas' position in backing the Philadelphia Federating of Teachers, but completely ruled out using White's candidacy to prove a point.

headline: Rep. Earley mourned; ranks of GOP thinned
abstract: PA House Republicans are worried about the impact on their thin majority in the House because f the sudden death of PA Representative Arthur Earley. They also hailed him as a an of principle who dealt well with the problems of his constituency in Chester City and parts of Eddystone. He died of a heart attack.

headline: PHOTOGRAPH
abstract: Photograph of New Jersey Governor Byrne with Doctor Walter H. Plosila, director of Pennsylvania Governor's Office of Policy and Planning.

headline: 10,000 pupils 'lost' during strike
abstract: Due to the 50 day teachers' strike the expected enrollment decline in Philadelphia public schools almost doubled to 9.5%. The initial decline in public school enrollment was thought to follow the national trend of falling school enrollment in general. However, no one can explain where some 9,000 students have gone as private school enrollment is seemingly not factored into the equation.

headline: Water troubles solved by blast at well's bottom
abstract: A dynamite blast at the bottom of a well restored water service to the residents of Walnutport after a rock slide stopped the supply from the well.  Drought and extreme cold are blamed for the closure of 3 other wells in that area.  This was the only functioning well there.

headline: Parking Unit Boss Eyes Salaried Job
abstract: Parking Authority Chairman Kenneth N. Garber is attempting to fire the current director, Francis J. Myers, Jr. and name himself to the position, stating that their views are not compatible.  The article interview Mr. Garber, and details his career.

headline: Pa. to act to east law on jail use; 1-per-cell statues is set for repeal
abstract: null

headline: Industry attracting ads show ingenuity among the states
abstract: States make it seem like every state is good for businesses to build their plants in from their advertising. PA was near the top spending $750,000 for promotion last year and this year again.

headline: Drastic reapportionment plan could pit Murtha, Shuster
abstract: Democratic Representative John P. Murtha of Cambria County and Republican Representative Bud Shuster of Bedford County could be battling each other next year for a seat in the United States House from the same district due to the reapportionment plan being considered by Republicans in the state Senate.  The reapportionment plan was developed by state Senator Frank O'Connell, chairman of the Senate's state Government Committee, which is handling the task of preparing a bill redrawing boundary lines for the state's congressional districts.

headline: Rep. Goodling is speaker for GOP dinner-dance
abstract: US Representative William Goodling will be the keynote speaker at the annual Cumberland County Republican dinner-dance. The Dave Stahl Big Band will begin at 7.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph:  The picture shows Rep. William F. Goodling, Lester Ginanni, Mike Greene, and Col. John P. Dreska at the West Shore Chamber of Commerce breakfast meeting.

headline: 10,800 seniors in class; district claims success
abstract: Twelth-grade pupils in the Philadelphia School District attended class for the first time since the strike began 17 days ago, taught by administrators who again ran gauntlets of jeering pickets.

headline: Water-Projects Bond Issue Support Committee is Aim
abstract: Representatives from more than 30 organizations have been invited to meet to form a committee supporting the PA Governor Thornburgh administration's proposed $300 million water-projects bond issue. It will provide loans mainly for water companies to make much-needed improvements to supply facilities.

headline: PAT rerouted
abstract: The editorial comments on Common Pleas Court Judge Silvestri ruling over Allegheny County's Port Transit Authority. It explains that the ruling, meant to keep the mass transit system in operation but also fix its fare and management problems, was a shock to commuters and to PAT. But it argues that the Judge has made good observations about the problems with the system, among them reasoning for rolling back fares and eliminating special passes.

headline: Panel to probe Larsen
abstract: After more than nine months of investigation, the PA state Judicial Inquiry and Review Board has decided to begin taking sworn testimony on allegations of misconduct involving PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen. They will b looking for misconduct in political activity, racial prejudice, and favoritism.

headline: Insurance Firm, Seniors' Groups End Close Ties
abstract: A newspaper expose apparently helped to break up a marriage of convenience between the nation's largest senior citizen organization and a major insurance company.  In 1977, it was reported that the American Association of Retired Persons was misusing its cut-rate mailing privilege to the advantage of the Colonial Penn Group, Incorporated, one of the leading insurers of the elderly.  Postal investigators are now in the process of deciding whether to bring suit against the old folks' organization for letting Colonial Penn advertise its policies in letters sent out by the association and its affiliated group, the National Retired Teachers Association, at the bargain rate accorded to non-profit institution.

headline: Edgar optimistic that Justice Dept. will reclaim Delco probe
abstract: United States Pennsylvania Representative Robert W. Edgar said that the United States Department of Justice would decide whether to reverse its order directing federal prosecutors to turn over a case of alleged political corruption in Delaware County to count prosecutors.  Edgar said he was optimistic that the case would be reclaimed by the United States Attorney's Office in Philadelphia.  The article goes further into detail about the case and the probability of opening the probe again.

headline: Rep. Lederer's Probe Delay Fails
abstract: Pennsylvania Representative Raymond F. Lederer, convicted of bribery charges in the Abscam scandal, failed to persuade the U.S. House ethics committee to postpone an investigation that could lead to his expulsion from the U.S. Congress.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: Nuzzio J. Palladino

headline: 138 teachers fired, staff shuffled in city schools
abstract: Extensive personnel changes in the city school district have enacted in an attempt to revitalize the blood and place more emphasis on student achievement and employee evaluations. School board embers approved the layoff of 134 teachers and the transfer of 75 administrators. The administrative changes will save the district $230,000 between now and Dec. 31 and another $675,000 in 1982. Class sizes and still within contract of 25 to 30, so nothing can be done about it.

headline: Watt turns back on Centralia
abstract: US Interior Secretary James G Watt has shown appalling insensitivity to the plight of the 1,100 inhabitants of Centralia, the PA town threatened with extinction by an underground coal mine fire. He claims the fire doesn't post a threat to health and safety and says it’s the state's responsibility. PA Governor Thornburgh has written a letter protesting his statements. Unfortunately it doesn't seem that Watt will change his tune. The editorial would like him to come see for himself the damage.

headline: Penna. gas-tax bill gains
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposed increase in the gasoline tax was approved by the state House Transportation Committee, but the measure will go to the full House and then the Senate. Under the bill, the current 11-cent-a-gallon tax would be replaced by a 6 percent sales tax and a flat 5-cent-a-gallon tax.

headline: Panel Wants Legislation to Ease Jailing of Violent Offenders
abstract: A special federal task force called for new legislation designed to crack down on violent crime by making it easier to put people in prison and harder for them to get out.  The eight-member task force on violent crime sent 64 recommendations to Attorney General William French Smith, who set up the panel in mid-April.  Although 49 recommendations called for new laws or spending, the group included a specific price tag for only one of them, a proposal for $2 billion in federal grants to states to build new prisons.  Former Attorney General Griffin B. Bell, co-chairman of the panel, estimated all the other recommendations together would cost less than $800 million.

headline: Insurance-scam case grows
abstract: More arrests are expected in a $750,000 insurance-fraud case which already has resulted in charges against seven persons in federal and state courts. David Shipman will be charged with overcharging the company's automobile insurance costumers.

headline: Dump at the right door
abstract: Opinion in favor of the teachers' union, because the city and the school board are violating the contract. Techniques of strikes are detailed and applied to the current strike.

headline: Rep. Yatron toppled as panel chairman
abstract: US representative Gus Yatron (D-PA) lost a secret vote of no confidence was stripped of his position as chairman of the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee.  Many feel that the move was politically motivated

headline: Photograph - Aliquippa: A city groping for the light
abstract: Photograph of a street in Aliquippa at night.  "The street lights will stay on - at least until Feb. 15 -  thanks to an early Christmas gift, but after that. . . "

headline: 5 years od teacher ed urged
abstract: The state Education Department recommended that teachers must first take five years of college and be licensed before they can teach.  This and other changes were announced by Education Secretary Robert Scanlon.

headline: What will we do about the next drought?
abstract: The editorial explains that the Delaware River Basin Commission provided good information and the people followed directions to make it through the drought season this year. But it argues that state emergency regulations varied widely among and within states. It suggests that regulations should cover all of the Delaware River Basin, all of the cities and towns on both sides.

headline: PennDOT Hiring Freeze Signals More Area Cuts
abstract: Local PA Department of Transportation maintenance personnel were informed of a statewide hiring freeze that in effect reduces the number of field positions in Bedford and Fulton counties by 12. The local office believes that overall funding for PennDOT will improve through the hoped-for passage of a gasoline tax, opening up more jobs within the agency. The latest reductions are to come about through attrition, not layoffs.

headline: Pardon George Senn
abstract: Letter responding to a column that George Senn deserves to be pardoned by Governor Thornburgh.  The author agrees

headline: Interest rate climbs on new car loans
abstract: The maximum interest rate on new car loans will rise again this month, according to the State Banking Secretary. The add-on rate translates into an annual rate of 17.08 percent, while the current annual rate is 16.25 percent.

headline: Election Day Rounds- and Revenge
abstract: There was no compassion among organizers in street warfare over who would succeed Raymond Lederer, who resign after he was caught in the FBI's Abscam net. The wisdom was that the candidate with the most workers on the street had the best chance of winning.

headline: Republicans' plan would eliminate Ertel's district
abstract: PA state Senate Republicans have fashioned a tentative statewide redistricting plan that includes a new Central PA district designed to eliminate the incumbent Democratic Allen Ertel in the 1982 elections. His home would be swifted into the top-heavy Republican 23rd district.

headline: Photographs
abstract: Photographs of Governors Edmund G. Brown, Jr (California), Albert H. Quie (Minnesota), and William O'Neill (Connecticut)

headline: 5 years of teacher ed urged
abstract: The state Education Department recommended that students go to college for five years before being licensed for teaching.  The fifth year of education would emphasize the training of students to become teachers.  They also want to make admission criteria stricter.

headline: 6 teams enter contaminated TMI building
abstract: 6 teams went into the Three Mile Island containment building at the damaged Unit 2 reactor to inspect the conditions and repair equipment that will be utilized in repairing the reactor.

headline: PennDOT lax
abstract: The editorial hopes that an investigation of road conditions on Route 56 in Allegheny Township will lead to an immediate correction of the dangerous traffic situation that led to the deaths of two people. Although the PA Department of Transportation should have investigated the consistent complaints from motorists, it has taken state Representatives Joseph Petrarca and Terry Van Horne's complaints to Governor Richard Thornburgh to prompt the order to investigate.

headline: Paying for using a gun
abstract: The editorial argues that the legislature should pass any one of the three current legislative bills, or agree on a compromise bill. These would do what the anti-gun control people want, which is to extend the length of the sentence added for the possession and actual use of the firearms during the commission of a crime.  The editorial also wants gun owners to act responsibly and accept some form of gun licensing.

headline: Interest-Rate Ceilings Kept
abstract: The state Senate rejected a bill that would remove interest-rate ceilings on credit cards and small consumer loans. The vote on the measure was 22-20, but Senate Republicans moved the proposal back into position for another vote. Opponents say the bill answers only to big bankers and is a nightmare for consumers, while bill supporters say lenders are losing money and fear they will force businesses to close and move to other states.

headline: Ethel Allen dies; was on City Council
abstract: Doctor Ethel Allen, 52, Philadelphia's first black councilwoman and once Pennsylvania's highest ranking black female official died at Albert Einstein Medical Center.  The article provides a short biography on Allen and her influence on Philadelphia.

headline: Republicans-for a change-favor debt-ceiling increase
abstract: (several notes on the happenings in Washington) Republicians in the U.S. Congress voted in favor to raise the debt ceiling.  The only Pennsylvanians invited to President Reagan's birthday party were Dick and Claire Schwelker.  The city of Philadelphia opened a lobbying office in D.C, run by Judith Winchester

headline: Raymond Gover Named Publisher
abstract: Raymond Gover, editor and publisher of the Saginaw News, was named as publisher of the Patriot, Evening News, and Sunday Patriot-News. He succeeds the late John Baum, who died on Wednesday.

headline: 50 Teachers Fired; Strike Fines Urged
abstract: The School District asked Common Pleas President Judge Edward J Bradley to fine striking teachers the equivalent of one day's pay for each day a striker stays off the job. The District also fired about 50 teachers who have been arrested on the picket lines. The new hard line against strikers came on the day the district was trying open schools for fourth graders.

headline: 8% to 9.5% Raises Recommended For Lawyers of PUC by Fact Finder
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission's unionized lawyers would receive salary increases ranging from 8 percent to 9.5 percent under recommendations of fact finder appointed to resolve a contract impasse.  Both parties to the issue, the Public Utility Commission and the Public Utility Commission Bar Association, have responded to the full report submitted by Walter H. Powell, named by the Bureau of Mediation to, work on the impasse.  The union represents 27 Public Utility Commission lawyers below the supervisory level.  In their negotiations, the lawyers had asked for an 18 percent salary increase, and a one-year contract, beginning July 1.  The Public Utility Commission had offered 5.5 percent in each year of a two-year contract.

headline: PennDOT Logic
abstract: The author opines that the state government does not want PennDOT to rebuilding a portion of Interstate 70, because they want a new portion built instead.  The new portion would cost more money, but would also get more money from the federal government

headline: Pennhurst patients ask fines for PA, counties
abstract: US District Judge Raymond Broderick was asked to fine the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia and three other counties a total of up to $88,000 a day for not complying with his order to provide homes in the community for 50 residents of Pennhurst Center. The request was made by lawyers for the PA Association of Retarded Citizens.

headline: Jury to deal out betting charges
abstract: Criminal charges are expected to be presented against as many as 25 sports betting figures allegedly involved in an interstate gambling ring when the statewide grand jury convenes its last session this week. It is also expected continue its probe of corruption in the state auditor general's office.

headline: Ethics
abstract: The editors feel that by making judges and lawyers exempt from the ethics rule, which requires financial disclosure to avoid conflicts of interest, the judicial system is not setting a good example.  They feel they should adhere to the ethics rules all other public employees must follow

headline: Restore a voice in Congress
abstract: The editorial discusses the resignation of Philadelphia's Third Congressional District US Representative Raymond Lederer, a day after the US House Ethics Committee voted to expel him. After the Abscam investigation, Lederer was hoping a judge would overturn the conviction, but it did not happen. Governor Dick Thornburgh must now schedule a special election to replace the Third District's seat.

headline: senator to narrate 'Tubby the Tube'
abstract: Senator George Gekas will narrate 'Tubby the Tuba' for the Hershey Symphony Orchestra's second annual children's concert.

headline: A day on the far side of the picket line
abstract: Striking teachers are getting aggressive and angry towards those crossing the picket lines, even going so far to slash tires and pouring acid on others cars.

headline: 83 Big Reasons to Buy Earplugs
abstract: Metropolitan Edison Company plans to install 83 giant sirens within 10 miles of Three Mile Island. The sirens are designed to be sounded for accidents at TMI and other emergency alerts. But the company's officials have given municipal offices the option of using the sirens for fire and local emergency calls as well. The sirens are rated at 125 decibels, and to avoid ear damage, will be placed atop 50-foot poles.

headline: PennDOT questioned
abstract: Letter to the editor questions the PA Department of Transportation's motives for seeking to cut its budget by $100 million.  The author feels there are too many high level positions getting paid too much.

headline: Pennsylvania joins fight to ease Harrisburg woe
abstract: PA state officials living in Harrisburg are being robbed and out of this they are joining the fight to stop crime in the City. The high crime rate, declining population, abandon housing, limited entertainment, and restricted city budgets paint a grim caricature. The issue has become a part of the mayoral campaign.

headline: Kansas oil firm to buy Sun refinery in Texas
abstract: The Sun Co said it had reached agreement in principle to sell its 60,000 barrel-a-day refinery on Corpus Christi to Koch Industries for $265 million in cash. Sun said the sale is subject to definitive agreement in 60 days.

headline: Ethics code upheld
abstract: The PA state Supreme Court's split decision was not the resounding endorsement of PA's three year old Ethics Code it should have been. But fortunately it upholds the financial-disclosure requirements for all local elected officials. Ever since the ethics law was passed in 1978 as part of a much need political reform package, local officials have been trying to skirt it. PA State Association of Township Supervisors filed a suit challenging the constitutionally of the code. The editorial wants the Ethics Code intact.

headline: Review Nolan Acquittal, Judge Asked
abstract: United States Attorney Peter Vaira has asked a federal judge to reconsider his acquittal of former state Senate Majority Leader Thomas M. Nolan and two other men on charges of putting "ghost" employees on the state payroll.  Nolan of Allegheny County, state Senator Vince J. Fumo, and former Philadelphia Democratic party chairman Peter Camiel were convicted of mail fraud last October 25.  United States District Judge Clifford S. Green overturned the verdicts August 3, ruling that government prosecutors had failed to prove their case.

headline: Sneezy, Grumpy Bashful, etc.; Thy Name Is Nick
abstract: The use of nicknames in the media are often reserved for the athletes and criminals, but only occassionally are they used for public figures.  When nicknames are used within this medium for a public figure, often a negative connotation is attacked and the reader is lead to assume that they are a crook or an alleged crook.  There is a rationale that leads to the assumption that nicknames and criminality go hand in hand.

headline: A new segregation: Talented students lured away
abstract: A natural outgrowth of a system that separates its good from its weak students is the relaxing of academic standards at the less favored schools. Student get high marks for merely trying hard, and students who flunk are still move along to keep up with their peers. No one denies this grade inflation.

headline: A Courageous Vote
abstract: In a non-binding referendum, residents of Centralia, the town which sits on top of a burning underground mine fire, voted two-to-one to dig up the fire. The vote means the borough will ask the US government to try to uncover the exact location of the fire, and increases the likelihood the town will have to be moved at a future date.

headline: Pennsylvania Dept. of Trans. Appointments to go to John A Pachuta and Bradley L Mallory
abstract: PA Transportation Department officials today announced the appointment of John Pachuta as director of the PA Bureau of Traffic Safety Operations and Bradley Mallory as director of the PA Bureau of Safety Programming and Analysis.

headline: Persistent ex-newsman seeks to have court correct error
abstract: Joseph Dragonetti, a persistent retired newsman, thinks a judge should correct his mistakes.  And Dragonetti, who took on the governor and the Legislature in his fight against the English Rule, now is going after Superior Court over just such a mistake.  Earlier this year, Dragonetti single-handedly convinced the Legislature to pass a bill abolishing the centuries old ban against countersuits when a person feels he's been wrongly sued but was not imprisoned or had not suffered a loss of property as a result of such a suit.  Dragonetti had filed a countersuit against Girard Bank, which had named him a suit to reclaim a bad debt from a textile machinery firm.  He claimed he had been wrongfully sued because he only did public relations work for the firm and was not an officer or employee.

headline: Law Enforcement
abstract: The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board (LCB) plans to bring charges against Philadelphia District Attorney, Ed Rendell for filing a phony name for a bar it had set up to run an anti-corruption sting.  The editors opine that the LCB's sudden interest in the case shows how absurd their licensing practices are and cost taxpayers.

headline: Ethics panel finds no evidence Bartle violated the law
abstract: The State Ethics Committee has cleared former Attorney General Harvey Bartle of any ethics violations.  The investigation was stemmed when Bartle, just prior to leaving his post as Attorney General, issues a legally binding opinion that the Governor could retain legal counsel for the Housing Finance Agency.  Shortly after he left his post and returned to a private law firm, Governor Thornburgh hired his law firm to represent the Housing Finance Agency.

headline: Reviving the spellbinder
abstract: Where are the silver-tongued orators of yesteryear, the spellbinders who could move legislatures and pack the visitors gallery? PA Representative Kenneth Brandt is trying to do something to revive the art of oratory. He has arranged a seminar on better speaking for about 40 Republicans representatives.

headline: State seeks perpetrators of hoax on 'vandalized' Capitol tree
abstract: Inept haulers were responsible for destroying a 35-foot blue spruce donated by a Cumberland County man for a Christmas tree on the Pennsylvania Capitol front.  The article continues in detail about Christmas tree being hauled away and what the capitol is planning to do about the situation.

headline: A sacrifice
abstract: Letter to the editor saying the teacher strike is not the end of public education in Philadelphia, but encourages people to enroll their children in private school to avoid these kinds of problems.

headline: A Met Ed tax bill may go unpaid
abstract: Metropolitan Edison Co (Met Ed). is refusing to pay a $23 million tax bill to the state until they receive a written decision from the state Public Utility Commission (PUC) on its request for a rate increase.  Met Ed fears they will have to file bankruptcy if the rate increase is not approved.

headline: Phila. Transit strike ended
abstract: A 19-day transit strike ended yesterday, Thursday April 2, after the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority and the local chapter of the Transport Workers Union reached an agreement. In the presence of Governor Dick Thornburgh, the deal was worked out by dropping the push for part-timers and lowering the increase in wages, measures SEPTA were looking to implement because of its current heavy debt. The workers will go back to work, but will have to vote on the one and a half percent reduction in wage increase.

headline: Phila. Gang warfare stirs fear of N.Y. mob takeover
abstract: According to the PA Crime Commission chairman Alvin Lewis presented its annual report to the state House-Senate Judiciary committees. He commented that a Philadelphia gangland war has opened a power vacuum that is attracting New York organized crime families.

headline: LCB
abstract: The editorial shares mail that they've received that supports Governor Thornburgh's proposal to eliminate state liquor stores.  The editorals also agree with the proposal.

headline: Ethics panel says state Sen. Kury can't go before PUC for year
abstract: The State Ethics Commission ruled that former state Senator Franklin L. Kury cannot practice law before the Public Utility Commission (PUC) for one year.  Because Kury was chairman of the Senate Consumer Affairs Committee, ethics law provides that cannot personally appear in front of the Public Utility Commission because of his association with it.  Kury plans to appeal the ruling, stating that he was never really associated with the PUC

headline: Rizzo, on the prowl is waiting for the time to pounce
abstract: Frank Rizzo is on the prowl for Philadelphia power and a chance to run the city once again that has been his life from his South Philadelphia boyhood, to his days as a beat cop, to his two terms as mayor.  Rizzo has decided that he plans another campaign for the mayoralty.  Peers say that he has gotten over any sense of defeat that he suffered in 1978 when his campaign to change the Home Rule Charter, a change that would have lifted the two term restriction on the mayor, was crushed by voters.

headline: Station Square
abstract: Picture of Station Square with the caption: "The shopping, restaurant, hotel and office complex called Station Square on the Southside is Scaife's favorite local charity."

headline: A superintendent's view of school funds
abstract: null

headline: A plan for TMI
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh has made a move toward answering the questions of who is going to pay to clean up Three Mile Island nuclear reactor and when the undamaged twin unit might return to service. He says it will return to service if an agreement to clean--up the other can be reached. He proposes the federal government and the nuclear industry each provide $31.7 million a year until 1986. PA will provide $5 million a year and NJ $2.5 million a year. He also wants General Public Utilities Corp., the owner, to provide $245 million.

headline: Philadelphia Rail System Imperiled by Lack of Funding
abstract: Without an emergency transfusion of public funds, this area's commuter-train service could die before next July. They faced the gradual elimination of federal operating subsidies, an important life-support aid for ailing transit systems here and throughout the rest of the country. About $47 million of the agency's budget was supposed to come from federal agencies.

headline: Phila. to link with PennDOT commuter, hopes to reduce errors in traffic court
abstract: There is good news for Philadelphia residents who have had to endure the Philadelphia Traffic Court's time-consuming searches, paperwork and mistakes such as undeserved license suspensions.  Within two weeks, the Philadelphia Traffic Court will become the first in the state to hook directly into the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation computer in Harrisburg.  Traffic Court President Judge Salvatore DeMeo said the move will increase efficiency and alleviate errors.

headline: Lebanon CofC is in favor of bill on UC conformity
abstract: The Lebanon Valley Chamber of Commerce has lent its support for state unemployment compensation conformity legislation which would meet a federal mandate in order to avoid the loss of about $600,000 in funding. While new federal regulations would reduce the unemployment taxes paid by PA business firm by less than $1 million the state stands to lose some $585 million in federal tax credits for business and $25 million in federal administrative funding.

headline: Excavation at Capitol Will Be Done at Night
abstract: Excavation work for the Harrisburg, PA Capitol Building extension project will occur between 7:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. in an effort to control noise and traffic confusion. This work is slated to begin January 4, 1982.

headline: Rumors of a '79 Green-Rizzo Deal Still haunt
abstract: In the spring of 197, Bill Green's opponents charged that Green had struck a deal with his enemy Frank Rizzo to win the support of Rizzo loyalists in the Democratic mayoral primary.  The article continues to provide further details about the deal and the reasons why its rumors still haunt him.

headline: They are dinosaur prints
abstract: Found just a few hundred yards from the Limerick nuclear power plant in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania were the footprints of what scientists confirmed as dinosaur footprints. The scientific name of the type of dinosaur is the coelophyses. This web-toed dinosaur could easily slosh through water and ate the predecessors of the toad.

headline: A superintendent's view on school funds
abstract: Superintendent defends himself and says he is not a pawn of school boards or teachers. He claims they don't understand the school subsidy system and more importantly the consequence of violating the principles of the subsidy system. He goes on to explain the system as simply as he can, concluding that Districts with low wealth-per-student will receive more state funding.

headline: About safety
abstract: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission requires time estimates for everyone living within 10 miles of Limerick to evacuate the area. If nuclear power is safe, why evacuate? The four million people of the Philadelphia area are not obliged to live with this omnipresent threat to their lives.

headline: Philadelphia Rail System Imperiled by Lack of Funds
abstract: null

headline: Philadelphia's Crime Watch to be Expanded to Include a Crime Watch
abstract: Philadelphia is trying to battle the trash and promote the clean block idea, where someone in the block organizes his or her neighbors to keep the block clean. The broadcast likes the idea and hopes neighborhoods take to the idea.

headline: Legal bingo questioned
abstract: Now that bingo has been legalized what benefits can be derived from the game for bingo fanatics: none. The law only enhances the county treasurer's cash register by 100 times the number of organizations involved. It was supposed to keep crime out of the bingo halls. It should have included rules of the game.

headline: Ex-LCB Chairman Seeks Cash
abstract: Former PA Liquor Control Board chairman Henry Kaplan has asked the state for workmen's compensation benefits because he claims his work problems triggered a stroke. The LCB is contesting the case.

headline: Runs in Sunbury Mayoral Primary: Ex-Con is Candidate
abstract: A convicted bank robber on parole and indignated over political corruption is running in the Republican primary for mayor of Sunbury. Robert Huffert is running against GOP candidate Daniel Filer, who was a drug abuse counselor at Lewisburg Federal Penitentiary while Huffert was an inmate, although the two never met.

headline: Tracy, Canyon take it on chin from papers
abstract: The Harrisburg Patriot-News' Saul Kohler, executive editor, announced on May 17 that the "Dick Tracy" and "Steve Canyon" cartoon strips would no longer run on the pages of the Harrisburg Patriot and Evening news. The decision was made because of Kohler believes the sole reason for their existence is violence, and the attempted assassinations of President Reagan and Pope John Paul II prompted the decision.

headline: A way out of schools crisis?  Phila. Finance chief looks at outside financial management of district
abstract: The Philadelphia School District could work itself out of its crisis from an impending deficit of as much as $223 million if financial management were taken away from the school administration, City Finance Director Edward G. DeSeve said.  In testimony before Common Please Court Judge Harry A Takiff, DeSeve spoke of successes in other cities where a panel outside the government was established to oversee municipal finances.

headline: Action Held a 'Cheap Shot'; Advocate Calls on PUC For $45 Million Refund
abstract: Consumer Advocate Walter Cohen called on the Public Utility Commission to refund within 60 days some $45 million he said was due for more than 1 million customers.  Cohen, in a letter to the commission, said $19.9 million in refunds should be made by the Duquesne Light Company, Pittsburgh; $13.9 million by National Fuel Gas Corporation, Erie; and about $10 million by the Pennsylvania Gas and Water Company, Wilkes-Barre.  But several commission members noted the Public Utility Commission was deadlocked on whether to order the refunds.

headline: Photograph
abstract: "Dominic DiClerico holds the bullet he says he will bite, if necessary, during contract negotiations in the transit strike."

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: "A family of a hostage drives away from the prison"

headline: Legal insurance as fringe benefit
abstract: Many of Philadelphia's firefighters would go to a single law firm for legal services, because they were free paid for by the city under their contract. Many were unsatisfied with the service. Now they can go to any of the 600 lawyers under the Prudential Insurance plan. They hope that group legal insurance will become the norm everywhere. It seems that more states are allowing it and congress even made it tax-deductible.

headline: Ex-Rep. Kelly, 2 Others Guilty in Abscam Trial
abstract: Former Florida congressman Richard Kelly was convicted of conspiracy and bribery in the Abscam undercover operation in which undercover FBI agents "set up" elected officials to see if they would accept bribes.  PA representative Raymond Lederer is the only one of seven that were convicted would is still serving in office.

headline: Should we limit the terms of Congress, Legislature?
abstract: It is only at PA state budget time that you will see live and in valor what one lawmaker likes to call the unholy alliance of state government. The author believes that bureaucrats, special interest groups, and legislators are at the center of this fight for self-perpetuation and if there were limited terms this problem would go away. She cites a poll where 2-1 people would like term limits.

headline: Up Front
abstract: The photograph has the caption: Up front at the annual membership meeting of the Greater Harrisburg Area YMCA Tuesday are Ginny Thornburgh, the state's first lady, speaker, and Carroll Sandnes, president.

headline: Abington Experiment Worth Watching
abstract: Regional school administrators no doubt will be watching with interest the effectiveness of a variation on a disciplining practice aborted by Abington Heights School District. Instead of punishing school behavior code violators by having them stay after school, high school offenders will be required to report to school Saturday mornings.

headline: Agency proposes cutback on nuclear-plant safeguards
abstract: The federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission, in an effort to reduce the backlog in nuclear plant licensing, is requesting authority to issue interim licenses, limit public comment, and reduce the authority of the agency's Atomic Safety and Licensing Review Board to raise safety issues. The editorial argues the NRC is sacrificing safety for speed, and has forgotten the lessons of the Three Mile Island, where safety issues were overlooked or ignored.

headline: Photograph
abstract: "Transit workers, representing about 10 percent of those on strike, attended a rally yesterday at Frankford Depot.  They backed union requests to stand firm."

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: "Daily News columnist Chuck Stone (left), who negotiated with hostage-takers, talks with officials and employees at the prison."

headline: Legalize bingo
abstract: If the state Senate approves a bill passed by the state House, and the governor signs it, bingo will be legalized in Pennsylvania. The editorial believes that illegality has made Pennsylvania bingo a game of charades, and argues that the most logical way to fend off the US Internal Revenue Service's tax crackdown threat as well as profiteering racketeers is to legalize the games.

headline: Ex-tax official caherged with taking bribes
abstract: John Bibbo, former Revenue Department supervisor, was charged with taking $15,000 in bribes from a beer distributor who owed $150,000 in back taxes.  Bibbo took the bribes from Joseph Galkowski.

headline: 'Single-issue voting' scuttles $23 million state fund bill
abstract: The Republican House Speaker and the House Democratic leader, in a clear abuse of power, acted contrary to the very purpose of representative government, and by doing so, they indirectly sent a message to Pennsylvanians that single issue politics has gone too far in the Pennsylvania Legislature.  House Bill 1290 was being voted on during this occasion, which contained about $23 million federal funds for a wide variety of state programs and agencies and $300,000 state appropriation to the Family Planning Association of Pennsylvania.  Both House Speakers decided to throw out the defeated vote count on the issue and vote again separately on the family planning money (which was defeated).

headline: Voices
abstract: The cartoon depicts a large chair that says "Walter" on it and very small Dan Rather sitting in it saying "Hi-I'm Dan Rather and this is the way it is."

headline: About those 'senior schools'
abstract: Letter to the editor commenting on the senior schools set up during the Philadelphia teacher strike. She believes that the people teaching are not following the approved curriculum and seniors will have to be retaught when teachers resume teaching.

headline: Anti Nukers Take on TMI Top Brass
