abstract: Three Mile Island Alert, Inc, a volunteer citizen group, protested the notion of restarting Three Mile Island's nuclear plant at a hearing with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).  The article details the hearing and those in attendance.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph of Transportation secretary Thomas Larson, who was appointed by Governor Thornburgh to study problems associated with drunk driving.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: "Dominick Iannarelli, retired judge"

headline: Legalized bingo makes sense
abstract: The author writes that bingo will soon be legalized in Pennsylvania. Legitimate and legal bingo games must abide by the following criteria: 1) the games must be run by a charitable or non-profit organization; 2) prizes may not exceed $2000 per game and $4000 per day; 3) no game employs can earn more than $50 per day; 4) the sponsor may not own the bingo equipment. These stipulations are necessary as organized crime has taken over this form of gambling in several states.

headline: Extending Welfare to State Employees
abstract: The editor argues that an amendment to a measure that started out as a welfare reform in PA has turned into a restriction on the governor's ability to administer state hospitals. The amendment, requested by a public employees' union, would allow the governor only to close hospitals with approval of the General Assembly.

headline: Smith may help GOP on conservative issues
abstract: The Republican party appears to have won yet more leverage in Congress with the election of Joseph Smith to fill House seat of former Representatitve Raymond Lederer. He still promises to sit with the Democrats, even thought he ran under the Republican banner and accepted contributions from the RNC. He is pro-life, but against Reagan's economic plan.

headline: What We've Done
abstract: Broadcast briefly goes over issues it has ranted about in the past and states whether these rants produced successful results or not. Issues are: Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority right to employ part-time workers; Mayor Green's attempt to fire Philadelphia's School Board; United Way's right to collect contributions for any legitimate charity; the need for Pennsylvania Boarding Home agency to hire more inspectors; increased security in Philadelphia's Suburban Station; and getting Pennsylvania out of the liquor business.

headline: AGAINST THE ODDS; She succeeds where public schools fail
abstract: null

headline: Anti-Limerick
abstract: Letter to the editor complaining about Philadelphia Electric Co and the completion of the Limerick nuclear power generator. They are not concern about the dangers, but instead their electric bill for the cost of repair if something did go wrong.

headline: Pike board, employees ruled subject to ethics law
abstract: The Commonwealth Court ruled that commissioners and employees of the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission are subject to the state ethics law, which would prohibit them from engaging in activities that are in conflict with public interest.  The law also requires disclosure of financial activities.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: "Dr. Donald W. Hinrichs.  Surveying crime victims"

headline: Legalizing bingo: the stakes are more than money
abstract: The bill to legalize bingo gambling in Pennsylvania would protect neighborhood parishes from unscrupulous entrepreneurs keep organized crime out of the game and save legitimate nonprofit groups from paying taxes on their bingo dollars.  The legislation would keep profitteers from organizing as nonprofit groups and running bingo games.  The argument of the bill's vagueness is still a concern for several Pennsylvania residents.

headline: Extension of pension benefits losing in early returns
abstract: Preliminary polls show that voters may have rejected an amendment to extend future pension benefits to the spouses of public pensioners that have died.  Other preliminary polls show voters approving a loans for water improvement rejects, emergency services funding, taxes on aviation fuels, and changes to the state constitution.

headline: Smith stuns Glancey for Congress
abstract: In a stunning blow to Philadelphia's Democratic establishment, PA state Sen. Joseph Smith was elected to Congress to fill the unexpired term of Raymond Lederer. Smith defeat Democrat David Glancey despite being outspent by 3 to 1. it was a fight of old versus new school politics.

headline: Why Frost Belt Outshines Sun Belt
abstract: Editorial opines that Governor Dick Thornburgh needs to point out the problems with the Sunshine Belt in the debate over moving more of the northern population south.

headline: Aid cutbacks, soaring tuitions could make colleges just for rich
abstract: College students and their families are struggling to pay for college. The Reagan administration is making things worse with cutbacks. Congress is also changing restrictions on loan eligibility making things even worse. Loans will only be able to families would make less than $30,000 a year.

headline: A-plant waste: Penna. To be a main street
abstract: Because most states will not accept shipments of nuclear waste from commercial power plants, few states have to worry about nuclear accidents. Pennsylvania is not among those worry-free states as it is predicted by the National Academy of Sciences that by the turn of the century approximately 9,000 shipments will cross into Pennsylvania en route to temporary storage facilities per year.

headline: Political animals won't play
abstract: The columnist writes that the Milton Shapp Administration from 1978-79 lost $415 million of Pennsylvania motorists' money. It did this by letting $415 million of unused federal funds originally slated for highway repair and construction go. To get the money back all the state had to do was put up matching funds varying from 10 to 25 percent of the amount sought. As a result of losing highway construction funds and highway/bridge maintenance overdue, Governor Thornburgh signed the Senate approved 3.5% tax on oil company gas revenues. This cost is then passed to the customer at the pump. The columnist questions where accountability should be placed for this mistake and concludes that no one really cares about political accountability anyhow.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph: "State troopers change shifts after spending a tense night inside Graterford Prison."  There is a hostage situation at the prison.

headline: Letter From the Editor
abstract: A writer sends a letter to the editor contrasting whether the Philadelphia school board or the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board was the most ineffectual. The writer's conclusion is that the Liquor Control Board is the most corrupt and ineffectual citing the Board's chairman as corrupt, thus permitting the state Liquor Control Board to take the title as the most evil of the two issues.

headline: Faces in the crowd
abstract: A photograph of a mysterious sign was one of many that greeted President Reagan during his short visit.

headline: Something's rotten in Harrisburg and in Washington
abstract: Vince Fumo was convicted of hiring people who were paid with taxpayers' money for work they did not perform. Fumo's conviction was overturned by a US Judge, last month, because they couldn't prove his guilt. Also the US Justice Department is just now getting around to asking for $186,000 in Abscam bribes back. Why did it take so long?

headline: Worth Waiting For
abstract: null

headline: Ann Witmer on Executive Board
abstract: Amy Witmer, press secretary and director of press and communications for the Pennsylvania State Department of Education, has been named to the executive board of directors of the Pennsylvania School Public Relations Association.

headline: Area faces a natural-gas crisis: PE, PGW say reserves won't stretch
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Co (PE) and Philadelphia Gas Work (PGW) reported that they have already used 60% of their reserves.  The have asked customers to reduce usage and switch to other fuels.  The shortage may mean stretching gas supplies through the winter by closing factories and schools.  The article cites multiple reasons for the shortage and possibilities for increasing supply.

headline: Politics ruined Pennsylvania roads
abstract: The author opines that the reason Pennsylvania roads are in such disrepair is due to politics.  The author gives his version of roadway politics being in the 1920s and believes that rural area interests are the problem with the current state of the roads.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph:" A bus carries the shackled hostage-takers away from Graterford; the inmates have asked to be taken to a federal facility."

headline: Letters to the Editor:  Liquor Reform Bid Is Halfway Step
abstract: Three letters to the editor dealing with Governor Thronburgh's proposed plan to do away with state-run liquor stores.  The authors all agree that the Liqour Control Board should be eliminated and that there should be private liquor stores.

headline: False Rumors
abstract: There are some false rumors on the street regarding the position of the Republican candidates on the race track issue. All Republicans candidates for municipal office and school directors are committed and obligated to support the wishes of the voters turned down the race track 4220 to 1790.

headline: State exempts judges from financial disclosure
abstract: The Commonwealth Court ruled that judges are exempt from financial disclosure required by the 1978 state Ethics Act based on constitutional grounds.  The article outlines the legal reasoning behind the Supreme Court's ruling.  The Ethics Act requires that public officials file an annual statement of financial affairs to ensure that they do not have conflicts of interest.

headline: Atlanta? What About YOUR Kids?
abstract: The author argues that Philadelphia's school system is educationally and financially bankrupt, and that the state will have to bail out the current budget's $73 million deficit. But the more worrisome fact is that parents and elected officials show little interest in fixing the problems.

headline: Arguments against plant are many
abstract: Nuclear power plants are not design to run forever. Based on current industry standards the PA Power and Light Co. will have to shut down Susquehanna Steam Electric Station sometime around 2020. The process called decommissioning, will not be simple. No ne knows what to do with an out of work power plant.

headline: Pothole-Dodging season Returns
abstract: The pot holes need to be fixed in Pittsburgh, because the problem is getting worse and costing drivers several dollars in car repairs.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph:" A jubilant Lorenso Alleyne, son of former hostage Lt. Alleyne"

headline: Licensing marriage counselors?
abstract: A United States Senate proposal requiring human service counselors to be licensed and have masters degrees was widely criticized in a Senate committee hearing. Witnesses to the hearing stating that quality of service would decline and services would become more expensive. The bill was sponsored by Senator Robert Jubelirer, Republican-Blair and he stated that he was only willing to compromise on the masters degree requirement.

headline: Farino seeks court rule changes
abstract: In the May 19 primary election, S. Louis Farino will be on the ballot as candidate for nomination to the state Supreme Court. Although a Democrat, he is well known around Pittsburgh as a judge on the Common Pleas court, and is cross-listed on both the Republican and Democratic ballots.

headline: Some gravy on his tie
abstract: The author contends that Milton Street, a state Senator who switched from Democrat to Republican, has been involved in a home-weatherization project scandal regarding a community group he founded, the North Philadelphia Block Development Corporation. It has been the target of a series of reports by the media, and the author argues that the state Senator is not as respectable as he is trying to make himself look.

headline: Bad listing
abstract: Teacher takes issue with the paper calling vocational students potential drop outs. Trades are very rewarding occupations.

headline: Atomic Power: Who Generates Delays?
abstract: In an otherwise perceptive editorial on the administration's draft nuclear power policy, the Journal states, "thanks to unceasing hearings, minute checks by novice government engineers and environmental lawsuits.  It takes 10 to 14 years for a nuclear plant to proceed from the drawing board to operation, about twice as long as in most other countries."  The fact is that licensing delay has very little to do with the length of United States nuclear construction times, which are actually not longer than most other countries.  The hearings themselves are conducted while construction is going on and this much maligned licensing process had yielded more nuclear power plant licenses than the rest of the free world combined.

headline: Potholes!
abstract: The Journal has sent off another batch of pothole complaints to City Hall as part of their contest in a continuing crusade to make streets safer. One reader wrote in to defend potholes because that's how he met his wife. Personal stories of potholes are given.

headline: Playing politics with judgeships
abstract: Back in 1980, Governor Dick Thornburgh selected John Rauhauser as the governor's nominee for the new sixth judgeship the state legislature authorized for York County.  The state Judiciary Committee unanimously approved the nomination.  After that, the Democrats in the Senate refused to supply the eight votes needed for the two-thirds majority approval that judicial nominees must receive.  Rather than have the Senate vote upon nominates and reject it, Thornburgh withdrew the nomination, along with the nominations of five other judicial candidates from other counties.

headline: Liquor store proposal contradictions
abstract: The author addresses a letter that his Managing Editor received from Governor Thornburgh's deputy press secretary, Steven Fink.  The author had written a previous column based on a pamphlet provided by the Governor's office about Governor Thornburgh's proposal to disban the state liquor store systema and give controll to private companies.  The author felt that the state was not giving them control if they still set prices.  Fink argued that he was wrong in his piece to say this and the author feels that Fink directly contradicted the Governor's office and asks the readers who they should believe.

headline: Federal Midstate Workers Laid Off
abstract: At least 200 Pennsylvania midstate federal employees were temporarily laid off on Monday, joining hundreds of thousands federal employees furloughed nationwide after President Ronald Reagan vetoed an emergency spending bill later revised to his satisfaction. Locally, the two largest employment sites, United States Navy Ships Parts Control Center and the New Cumberland Army Depot remained unaffected.

headline: Sound votes
abstract: In the May 19th primary election, Armstrong County voters approved a referendum to install punch card voting machines in the county. Allegheny County voters gave their approval by almost 2 to 1 for a harness race track, expected to be built near Monroeville.

headline: Bill To Force Student Borrowers To Pick Up Tab
abstract: The state Senate is proposing a bill that would allow the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) to pursue loan defaulter by suspending the current six year statute of limitations for student loans.  The article outlines the proposed legislation.

headline: Bad anniversary
abstract: The author of the letter to the editor argues that although the Three Mile Island reactor incident proved that nuclear reactors are not worth the risk, the Philadelphia Electric Company is applying for a license to operate the Limerick nuclear reactor. This is a bad day for all of humanity, and shows that people do not count and that money is our god. Limerick is, in effect, legal terrorism. In the absence of protection by our government, the author adds that people should use the same contempt and opposition to counter these efforts.

headline: PUC aborts bus fare hikes
abstract: The Public Utility Commission has changed its mind about a $1.5 million bus fare increase package that went into effect Saturday. The commission said it has ordered Greyhound Lines to immediately roll back the fares because it went too far on certain runs.

headline: Pol Worker is Aided Once Again
abstract: James M. King Jr., once acquitted on racketeering charges, now has as a constituent service staffer for Joseph Smith, who represents Philadelphia's 3rd District.  The article details King's career.

headline: Liquor talk is off, press told, then on
abstract: A meeting of businessmen interested in lobbying for PA Governor Thornburgh's plan to turn the state liquor stores over to private enterprise was held in Hershey after the press was told it had been called off. It resulted in an agreement to incorporate a broad-based coalition to lobby for Thornburgh's bill.

headline: Feisty strikers vow to survive
abstract: US District Court Judge Louis Pollack granted a government request to drop contempt proceedings against Local 246 pf the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization. Thanks to this judge, striking air traffic controllers in Philadelphia no longer have to worry about fines and other civil penalties for staying off the job. The catch is that these striking air traffic controllers do not have a ob to come back too. Upon hearing the news, the strikers were upbeat and confident that they were doing the right thing.

headline: Special election set in Glenolden
abstract: null

headline: Black groups push to end school strike
abstract: Pressure from blacks to end the school strike has become a major force in the dispute, which has kept the city's predominantly black student population out of school for 21 days. A black caucus of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers is being revived because the union is being too hard line on possible compromises.

headline: Bill would Let NRC Skirt Hearings
abstract: The US House of Representatives is scheduled to consider an Nuclear Regulatory Commission authorization bill that would nullify so-far-successful attempts in federal court by Steven Sholly of Mechanicsburg, PA to make the commission hold formal hearings almost any time there is public concern about a licensing decision. The District of Columbia district Court of Appeals ruled last year Sholly had been right in insisting that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission should have held a public hearing before allowing Metropolitan Edison Co. to vent krypton 85 gas from Three Mile Island.

headline: Rail Crisis Breakthrough
abstract: Two plans, Mayor Green's plan and the tax proposal, are brought up to save the rail crisis and they both depend on Pennsylvania providing an additional $3.1 million.  The article goes further into detail about the two plans and which one would be more cost effective.

headline: Police to monitor York County KKK rally Saturday
abstract: Local and state police will monitor the May 9 Ku Klux Klan rally in rural York County, but expect no trouble. Also, state Republican Ivan Itkin (D-Squirrel Hill) introduced legislation banning paramilitary training courses with the knowledge that they will be used to further a civil disorder.

headline: Maine May Shift State Liquor Store Outlets
abstract: Governor Brennan of Maine announced a proposal to close all but one of the state operated liquor stores there, so that private retailers can run the liquor stores.  The article details his plan.

headline: Firings To Get State Review
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman plans to review the firing of 12 Revenue Department supervisors and suspensions of 57 other employees for failing to file state income tax returns. The review will be conducted after Representative Max Pievsky (D-Philadelphia) urged Zimmerman to consider pressing charges against the employees.

headline: Specter fights cuts in mine inspections
abstract: Senator Arlen Spector says he will fight in the Senate Appropriations Committee to retain federal money for twice-a-year underground mine inspections.  The senator, a member of the appropriations panel, said a subcommittee vote last week to reduce inspections to once a year could make coal mines excessively dangerous.  The Senate subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services and Education voted over Specter's objections to cut coal mine inspection funds from $63 million to about $31 million.

headline: Budget cites boost cost of school lunch
abstract: When school opened this month in the Palisades School District in northeast Bucks County, school lunch prices had doubled to 90 cents. Like all public schools in PA participate in the National School Lunch Program. The reduction of federal subsidies has led to an increase of lunch prices.

headline: Bodack to reveal source of fake letter
abstract: PA Senator Leonard Bodack said he will give investigators the name of a Public Utility Commission staff member who gave him a fake letter aimed at tainting the nomination of Clifford Jones to the PUC. He claims the public has the right to know.

headline: Rail service ends: Can it return? Not finished
abstract: When the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority announced plans in April to discontinue railroad passenger service between Bethlehem and Lansdale and Pottsbill and Norristown, the problems loomed large.  First the General Assembly passed legislation providing $3.1 million in subsidies to support continuation of services between….not finished!

headline: Poverty, crime and prisons
abstract: A prisoner writes a letter to the editor, arguing that it is not the building of more prisons that will help solve crime, but rather solutions that target the underlying economic root of crime that will help. He argues that employment and job training offer the most promising and effective preventative measures.

headline: Mellon Bank chairman asks end to limits on branches
abstract: J. David Barnes, chairman and chief executive officer of Mellon National Corporation and Mellon Bank, renewed Mellon's call for statewide branch banking in PA. Although there's only a 50-50 chance that state legislature would enact this type of legislation this year, he was more optimistic that state Legislature would lift the ceilings on interest rates that may be charged on consumer loans, another goal of the banking industry.

headline: Foes Say State Job Revamp Spoils System
abstract: Governor Thronburgh propsed change to the Civil Service Commission is drawing criticism.  The proposal would take 250 jobs in senior management out of the Civil Service and allow politicians to hire their own managers.  Critics say this will lead to a "spoils system" within the commonwealth.

headline: Specter Hires Staff Director For District
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter appointed Yvonne O'Connor as his executive director for Western Pennsylvania.  The article briefly outlines Ms. O'Connors career

headline: Can the school district be put back together again?
abstract: The Philadelphia School district tends to break down a lot. This year 3,511 employees are being laid off and 12 schools closed. This years deficit is bigger than usual at $200 million, so this year it may not be able to tackle its problems. The state and city government are battling with the school board, decreasing chances of aid.

headline: Broke, bothered, but reprieved
abstract: The borough of Aliquippa is getting a reprieve from Duquesne Light Co., which it owes $60,000 for an overdo electric bill.  The electric company will not shut off power until February 15.  The borough is broke and unable to light Christmas lights in the town center.  Some employees are wondering if they will be paid or not.  The article analyzes Aliquippa's debt problems.

headline: Rail Station Project Assured More Funds
abstract: The Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority acted on a contract with the PA Department of Transportation to receive a grant of more than $1 million toward the renovation of Harrisburg's railroad station.  This will allow renovation to begin in the spring of 1982.

headline: Prison Overcrowding
abstract: In June, the Supreme Court ruled that it is not unconstitutional to house two in a cell designed for one.  Subsequently, the Pennsylvania State Legislature by rescinding the law which called for only one inmate per cell in a county prisons.  These are temporary safety valves for a festering situation the dilemma of sentences and inadequate prison facilities.  Legislators are passing stricter and mandatory sentences for criminals.  Consider New jersey action calling for minimum sentences for persons carrying a gun while committing a crime.

headline: Monroeville wants share of hotel tax
abstract: Several Monroeville hotel managers write to the editor that there seems to be a misunderstanding of the purpose of Hotel Tax Bill 333 now in the state House of Representatives. They argue that under this bill, the room tax collected would be returned to the municipality of Monroeville, which would then disperse it to the Convention and Visitors Bureau, a public authority, to be used solely for promoting the Monroeville area.

headline: For City Council
abstract: The editors endorse John White for Philadelphia City Councilman because he has shown an understanding of urban problems such as mass transit and the rights of tenants.

headline: Stae airs plan for top staff:  Would tak 300 from civil service
abstract: Governor Thornburgh proposed exempting 300 high-level positions from civil service classification.  This way, top government managers would be able to chose the people they'd like working for them from a larger pool of candidates and have the same goals.

headline: Chamber asks school to slash spending now
abstract: The Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce asked the school district to slash its spending programs by $70 million to prevent a deficit.  They did not comment on Mayor Green asking the entire Board of Education to step down.  The school board said that making those drastic cuts would violate many of the labor contracts that are already in place.

headline: Can Impasse Be Broken on TMI Cleanup?
abstract: Facing possible bankruptcy, legislators and the owners, regulators and creditors of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant are groping to break the impasse over who should pay for cleaning of the crippled reactor. General Public Utilities, Inc., the plant's owner, says it doesn't have the money to pay for cleanup, estimated to be between $1 and $1.3 billion. State regulators argue customers should not be forced to pay for cleanup costs.

headline: Rail takeover: SEPTA may have inside track
abstract: The author makes an analysis on SEPTA's ability to take over Conrail, now that suburban officials have announce that they will not give SEPTA additional funding.  The author feels that, at first glance, SEPTA would not have the funding to take over Conrail, but they might since they've been planning the take over for a long time.

headline: Prison stalemate continues:  Graterford standoff in third day
abstract: The article relates the third day of a standoff in Graterford State Prison.  Four inmates took hostages after a failed prison escape attempt.   The leader of the hostage-takers, Joseph Bowen, is serving a life sentence for murdering three law enforcement officers.  The article details what is known of the hostage situation.

headline: New State Guidelines Hold Allstate Hike to 17%
abstract: Owners of 470,000 cars insured by Allstate will be paying 17% more for coverage despite new state guidelines designed to keep down insurance rate increases. State Insurance Commissioner Michael Browne granted the increase following a rate request hearing in March. They were kept to that level because of new guidelines requiring insurance companies to report investment income as part of their income and loss statements.

headline: For state Supreme Court: Davison and McDermott
abstract: The editorial argues that the PA Supreme Court is or should be a source of national embarrassment because of its many problems. The opportunity is for PA voters in the May 19 primary to take a significant step toward correcting those failures. The editorial endorses Judges Maxwell Davison (Democrat) and James McDermott (Republican) as candidates for the state Supreme Court, because of their experience, knowledge, forcefulness and independence of spirit that is needed to restore the court's effectiveness.

headline: Stagehand again cites Perry, Plevel
abstract: The first major prosecution in the 666 lottery trial ended his testimony today, holding firm to his implication of Nick Perry and Edward Plevel in the alleged ringing of the April 24, 1980 drawing of the PA Daily Number game. Fred Luman, a former stagehand at a Pittsburgh TV station where the contest was broadcast, testified in a Dauphin County Court, and will be sentenced, as will Perry, former host of the nightly drawing, and Plevel, former lottery bureau district manager and security official.

headline: Chamber seeks easy way out for Marcase
abstract: Those who called for Schools Superintendent Michael Marcase are trying to find him another job possibly in the PA Department of Education. It will be much easier to move him out if he has somewhere nice to go.

headline: Centers Will Be Scrutinized
abstract: The US Department of Energy has a cost-accounting formula for the ten federally funded Regional Energy Information Centers in PA.  The centers use the formula to calculate engery cost effectiveness, yet it is impossible to know the future price of oil so the formula is not entirely accurate.  The article lists the PA depeartment that use the formula and how much oil they plan to save.

headline: Railroad station is charming, weary at 94, report says
abstract: The Historic Structures Report has a prescription for revitalizing the Amtrak station and transforming it into a modern inter modal transportation center. The 119 page report is estimated to cost $8.9 million. The first phase starting now will take 5 months and cost $239,800.

headline: Probation ordered in drug death; Ex-legislator accepts plea deal
abstract: null

headline: No reason
abstract: In the September 4 issue of the Post-Gazette was an article which mentioned that special-interest groups were thwarting the governor's effort to divest the state from the sale of alcoholic beverages and turn it over to private enterprise. There is not one justifiable reason for the state to divest itself of the state store system.

headline: For the teachers, victory is elusive
abstract: John Murray, president of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers (PFT) stated that they will not rest until the school districts honor their current contract, not negotiate a new one.  A court order made the teachers go back to work after a 50 day strike, postponing the issues leading up to the strike.

headline: state bar halts efforts to rate non-incumbents
abstract: The PA state Bar Association says it will not attempt to rate the nine non- incumbent candidates for state appellate courts in the November 3 election. He said members wanted something beyond the existing qualified and unqualified categories.

headline: Classes canceled for 2nd day today
abstract: Two proposals to fund Philadelphia public schools, both involving taxes increases, were introduced to city council as the third day of the teacher's strike postponed the start of classes for the city's 213,000 public school students.

headline: Centralia: Will it yield to fires below
abstract: Over 800 registered voters turned out for the town of Centralia's non-binding referendum to express their feelings about relocation. A fire started in an anthracite mine underneath the town, forcing the mine to close in 1962, and is now forcing the residents to decide whether to stay or leave.

headline: Reagan's transit chief holds some doors open
abstract: In his first visit to Philadelphia as administrator of the Urban Mass Transportation Administration Arthur E.Teele Jr delivered a message to the nation's mass transit officials that was a blend of sweet and sour. He drew a sharp distinction between federal transit subsidies for operating expenses and capital programs. There was a welcome hint of flexibility on that issue. There are still a lot of questions about how the administration will achieve its goals.

headline: Pro-Gun Law Bias Criticized
abstract: Pennsylvania Representative John White asked Pennsylvania state police why they did not consult more than just pro-gun groups when developing revisions to Pennsylvania's gun law. As the legislation is now written it would be more difficult to purchase, possess or to carry a firearm. It would create a situation where each of the 2,572 municipalities could write their own ordinances on owning, possessing or carrying a firearm within their boundaries.

headline: No-Fault Debate
abstract: The PA State House of Representatives convened on Monday with close to 50 proposed amendments for House Bill 1285 otherwise known as the no-fault insurance law. These amendments are designed to close loopholes in the this law which failed to live up to its promises in the past. Some of these promises include the end to spiraling automobile insurance costs. House Bill 1285 is vigorously supported by Governor Thornburgh and insurance companies and just as vigorously opposed by trial lawyers.

headline: Forms Judical Ticket
abstract: Senate Democrats blocked Governor Thornburgh's nominations for the Commonwealth court, Vincent A. Circillo and Stephen McEwen.  George Bloom, 105 years old, was made a life-long member of the state committee.

headline: state Democrats looking to chairman for rebound
abstract: During the State Committee election, Merzvinsky emerged as the compromise candidate of the party's east-west factions.  He was a favorite candidate supposedly because he has no enemies in the party.  But he should not be underrated.  During the 1980 United States Senate race in Pennsylvania, he impressed many one of the more articulate, savvy and well-versed candidates in the crowded battle.

headline: Clergy: Opening School Doesn't Solve Problems
abstract: Concerned Clergy, a group of Philadelphia ministers, stated that just because teachers were ordered back to work after a 50 day strike, the problems of keeping the schools open still remain.  The group feels that the city is insensitive to the needs of black children and wants to hold teachers accountable for their actions.

headline: 'Energy Week' to coincide with second TMI anniversary
abstract: American Energy Week' will coincide with the second anniversary of the Three Mile Island nuclear accident.  Many pro-nuclear and anti-nuclear groups are preparing for rallies and marches.  The article details the activities  of both sides, ranging from rallies, marches, "bill-burnings" and fairs.

headline: Refinery Tax Draws Opposition
abstract: Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson stated that he opposes taxing oil refineries in Pennsylvania.  He feels that a tax on refineries would reduce jobs in Pennsylvania and calls instead to institute Governor Thornburgh's plan to increase gasoline taxes.

headline: Put the Johns in jail
abstract: Editorial suggests arrests the men buying prostitutes to keep prostitution low in family areas. Other crimes follow the seedy transaction of sex for money, and it hurts whole neighborhoods.

headline: No-Fault Insurance Reform Bid Hits Stone Wall In Legislature
abstract: Opponents of the latest effort to reform Pennsylvania's no-fault auto insurance law have been able to steer the state House away from the issue. The Pennsylvania state House sent the bill to the Judiciary Committee for further consideration yesterday. This move is considered having a fox guarding the hen house since the committee is dominated by lawyers.

headline: Forums to air impact cuts
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's Human Resources Committee has scheduled public forums this month at six locations in the state to brief local government officials, human-service providers and citizens on the expected impact of federal budget cuts on human-service programs in PA.

headline: State Dems' Debreczeni steps down
abstract: null

headline: College Tuition: Military Deserves Resident Rate
abstract: Military personnel should be offered instate college tuition and scholarship aid as states party to Pennsylvania’s reciprocal scholarship aid agreements are. Ohio and New Jersey were some of the states privy to the reciprocal agreements. Moreover, Pennsylvania should adopt the policy that 39 other states have which extends residency status to military personnel and their families. Senator George Gekas (Republican) has proposed a bill doing just that. In it, military personnel that are residents of states other than Pennsylvania would receive in-state tuition just as Pennsylvanians in the military stationed in states other than Pennsylvania currently receive residency status.

headline: Ertel to offer TMI-cleanup bill without waiting for colleagues
abstract: State representative will introduce a bill to finance the cleanup from the Three Mile Island nuclear accident.  The article outlines the proposed bill and states what lawmakers are doing to deal with the cleanup.

headline: Rep. Shuster, Backer Of Reagan, Opposes Conrail Fund Cutoff
abstract: Rep. Bud Shuster (R- Pa.) stated that he opposes President Reagan's plan to stop federal funding for Conrail.  The article details the economic problems Conrail will have if funding is cut next year.

headline: Pyramid-scam operators face $250,000 fine
abstract: Operators of a pyramid scheme that fleeced several hundred people out of $650 each will be ordered to pay $250,000 in fines, stated Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman.  The article details how the scheme worked.

headline: Off-track betting not needed
abstract: Gamblers have seen how Atlantic City has suffered once the casinos came there, and it should stay out of PA. Their bill to allow off-track betting is useless. The paper wants the bill to be defeated, because PA doesn't need it.

headline: FRIDAY TALK
abstract: State Representative James Barber has been accused by his Democratic colleagues of siding with the enemy, Republican State Senator Milton Street.  But Barber does not try to hide his association with the outspoken and controversial senator.  As the senior Black member of the State House, Barber says his years of experience tell him that Street is the man to know if one wants to be in the know.  He points out that the former North Philadelphia activist is the only Black who sits in Republican caucuses.  Such a unique position can be used to provide Black Democrats, who want to stay in the know about their opposing party, with valuable and timely information.

headline: State fires wife of PSEA leader; politics charged
abstract: The state Department of Labor and Industry fired Valerie Preston, wife of the Pennsylvania State Education Association's (PSEA) director, one day after Governor Thornburgh accused PSEA of unfair lobbying practices.  Mrs. Preston feels that her husband's position in the union is the reason she got fired.  The Governor's office stated that there is no relation between her firing and the Governor's feud with PSEA.

headline: Thornburgh budget up to Legislature
abstract: Governor Thornburgh accounced his proposed budget, which is designed to "belt-tighten" to soften the impact of less federal funding.  Many departments will see cuts in their own budgets and some critics claim this will cause property taxes to increase.  The Governor does not propose any new taxes.  The legislature must approve the budget by July 1st.

headline: Committee of 70 Gives School District System a Flunking Grade
abstract: Calling the structure of the school district "reckless"  the Committee of Seventy urged that the school system be run like any other city department. In a 16 page report title "No School Today" the committee proposed that the school system be restricted according to sections of the City Charter that now don't apply to the school district. The report also proposed that the mayor be allowed to hire and fire superintendent.

headline: Expedite cleanup of TMI wastes
abstract: General Public Utilities stated that the clean up of the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear accident would take six to seven years.  The editors hope that it will be done as soon as possible and safely and that the federal government will assume some of the costs.

headline: Road Paved For Pothole Hotline
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) has established a telephone hotline to report potholes.  The article explains how it will work and what the numbers are.

headline: Rape Victim Privacy Bill Strengthened
abstract: A House Committee has strengthened a Senate bill designed to protect the confidentiality of rape crisis center records.  The Judiciary Committee has gutted State Senator Edward L. Howard's bill and inserted stronger language endorsed by rape counselors.  But the counselors have pushed for a bill co-sponsored by Representative John Alden and Representative Ronald Cowell, which grants counselors the same blanket privilege doctors and lawyers enjoy with their clients.

headline: On Grocery Store Operating Margins
abstract: PA Food Merchants Association President A.P. Vicks commends the editor for the fair and accurate report on the Senate Law and Justice Committee hearings related to Senate Bill 597. But he argues that his testimony on food market margins was misquoted, raising his concern that retail food merchants might interpret the number as a sign of him lowering their operating margins.

headline: Friday The 13th Lucky Number Day?
abstract: The worst luck a finalist could have in the 13th Big 50 Millionaire Drawing this Friday the 13th is to walk away with $10,000.

headline: State GOP Leaders Firm on Redistricting Proposal
abstract: Republican leaders of the PA Legislature came away from holding fast to their own plan and opposed to a bipartisan one devised by state delegation leaders for reapportioning the state congressional districts. They have to eliminate 2 seats because of the 1980 census results.

headline: Thornburgh Lobbies For State's Interests In D.C.
abstract: Governor Thornburgh was in D.C. as the new chairman of the Coalition of Northeastern Governors.  He said he supports the new Reagan administration and hopes he'll give the states a freer hand in fiscal policy.  He outlined his new state budget and called for more federal aid for transportation.

headline: Controversial blind teacher among those district lays off
abstract: Ceinwen King-Smith, the blind math teacher whose suspension by the city school district attracted national attention, was among the 138 teachers laid off. She was suspended after unsatisfactory ratings at Brashear High School and Latimer Middle School.

headline: Ex-TMI operator feared tought test
abstract: One of the two former Three Mile Island Unit I control room operators who cheated on federal examinations said he anticipated the tests would be difficult and he wanted to pass them to hold his license.  He told United States Investigators he expressed his concerns about passing the tests to his colleague prior to mock exams given about three weeks before the actual tests and was told not to worry.  The Nuclear Regulatory Commission ordered retesting of the remaining 34 Three Mile Island operators who too the exams.  Although a Nuclear Regulatory Commission probe detected no other substantiated evidence of cheating, the staff wants the retesting because others who know or may become aware of the rumors of cheating may feel the cheating was being condoned.

headline: Roads proposal panned: Bucks officials want expressway
abstract: The Bucks County Planning Commission will recommend to the county commissioners that they reject portions of long-range highway plans proposed by the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission. The decision reflects the concerns of commissioners and business people who are unhappy that the regional commission's Year 2000 Transportation Plan does not include a new Route 202 expressway in the county.

headline: Rape Victim Shield Law Pushed Again
abstract: State representative Ronald R. Cowell is planning to introduce legislation to make counselor’s notes from interviews with rape victims confidential.  The Supreme Court recently refused to grant confidential status to these notes.  The article outlines arguments both for and against confidentiality

headline: On Licensing
abstract: The proposed bill, as viewed by the public, is designed to protect the public against quack counselors, just as the licensing of a barber is designed to prevent the average Pennsylvanian from being scalped.  It is of interest that in Pennsylvania one does not require any formal training in order to hang out the professional's shingle in the areas of counseling.  Anybody can set himself up and purport to be skilled and knowledgeable in such delicate areas as marriage and family counseling.  The Senate Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure Committee is conducting public hearings on the proposed bill, seeking input from individuals and groups on the merits and demerits on the measure.

headline: Friend says he won't run for Congress
abstract: PA state Representative Stephen Friend announced he will not seek the seat held by US Representative Robert Edgar. He said family is more important to him. He said he will seek re-election the his PA House seat.

headline: State Government in Review: Spotlight Shines on $12.6 Billion Budget
abstract: The article reviews state government happenings.  The Governor unvieled his $12.6 billion budget proposal which will impose spending cuts for most agencies.  Governor Thornburgh also called for plans to reduce the number of "able bodied" people on welfare.  Education Secretary Robert Scanlon told school districts they would have to assume more fiscal responsibility.  Auditor General Al Benedict released an audit of the state treasury showing that the records were severely mismanaged.  The article lists multiple going-ons in the state government

headline: Thornburgh signs $7.2 billion budget
abstract: The state's new fiscal year began on July 1, 1981, when Governor Thornburgh signed bills authorizing expenditures of more than $12 billion.  Projected expenditures for fiscal 1981-1982 will be about 6 percent more than in 1980-1981.

headline: Deaf aid program
abstract: The author of the letter to state Senator Anthony Andrezeski explains that by providing his daughter with schooling in the Western PA School for the Deaf, she is getting a quality education and will be graduating with a 12th grade education. Had she stayed in the Erie program, he argues, she would have been handicapped for the rest of her life. He asks the senator to take a strong look at Dr. Scanlon's program and the quality education for handicapped children.

headline: Fired-Up at Met-Ed, 200 Anti-Nukes Burn $47,000 in Bills at Capitol Steps
abstract: Anti-nuclear protesters burned $47,000 worth of Metropolitan Edison electric bills on the state capitol steps.  The protesters are angry at rising rates due to the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear accident in 1979.  The article details the events at the protest.

headline: Rough Going for Road Funds
abstract: Declining motor fuel tax revenues are continuing to cause serious problems for state highway funds across the country. At least 40 states are seeking legislated solutions to highway construction and maintenance fund shortfalls. The article highlights the problems that many states, including PA, are facing, and the proposed solutions, as well as the proposals the federal government is considering.

headline: Rape:  Growing Nightmare/Part III: What drives assailants? The adventure, they say
abstract: The third of a series of articles on rape.  The article consists of four interviews with convicted rapists to find out their motivation for committing their crimes.  Most blamed alcohol and the thrill of the crime.  The article interviews a psychologist who offers explanations for their behavior and prospects for their rehabilitation

headline: One-sided
abstract: Letter to the editor that criticized the one-sided view point taken in the recent article by Donald Matusow, "Goliath would win product liabiltiy cases."  Within the letter it discusses how the Matusow's previous article was exaggerated and written towards extremely one side of the issue.

headline: 'Friends' Mark State's 300th at Penn Museum
abstract: Governor Thornburgh was the keynote speaker at Pennsylvania's 300th birthday party at the William Penn Museum.  The theme was "Celebration of Friends."  The article details Pennsylvania's history and the governor's speech.

headline: State Group Urges Resignation; Civil Rights Enforcer Rapped
abstract: The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission called for the immediate resignation of the nation's top civil rights enforcer.  The commission said that a published interview with William Bradford Reynolds, chief of the Civil Rights Division of the United States Justice Department, has "demonstrated his insensitivity to those American citizens whose rights he is responsible for protecting."  The article goes further into detail about Reynolds.

headline: Thornburgh Wins On Taxes, Budget
abstract: Two key Thornburgh Administration budget proposals have been passed through the General Assembly, which slash business taxes in 1983 and pare most state expenditures by 1 percent across the board.  The article goes further into detail about the two fiscal bills.

headline: District gets poor marks in survey of residents
abstract: The city's highest elected official has abandoned the public schools, and at no apparent political cost, is a sad testimony to the fact that in Philadelphia, the public has lost faith in the public schools.  A public opinion survey conducted by the Inquirer last spring found that Philadelphians are divorced from their school system.  Only one adult in five has children in the system, and the overall public believes the system is not doing a good job educating children.

headline: Governor backs energy policy
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh endorsed the state energy policy recommended by the Governor's Energy Council. He also announced a legislative package to implement the plan. It is for the next quarter of the century and beyond.

headline: Rumbling Toward Ruin; America's mass transit is a shambles, and no help is in sight
abstract: In this four page article, Time looks at America's mass transit system and the problems with it.  The article cites the Philadelphia transit workers strike, as well as problem in many other major cities.

headline: Rape: Growing Nightmare/Part IV- Decade of aid for victims: Change in laws, attitudes
abstract: Part 4 in a series of articles about rape.  Pittsburgh's first rape-crisis center was opened in 1972, following a night of twelve reported rapes when the Pittsburgh Pirates won the World Series and people celebrated in the street.  The article details the strides that rape-crisis centers have taken in the past.  The stress a change in attitude for the future from blaming the victim to understanding that it is a violent crime.

headline: One-Stop Buying of Liquor Urged
abstract: Letter wanting Pa. liquor laws to change so liqour, beer and groceries can be bought all at one place

headline: From Harrisburg
abstract: PA's legislators face issues that intensified since they adjourned for the summer late in June. School districts, local governments, and the state itself must all adjust to cutbacks in federal funds. School districts want either more state aid or authority to raise property taxes. Also PA Governor Thornburgh want to halt welfare cash grants to the able bodied.

headline: State Issues 'Naughty Word' list
abstract: The PA Department of Education has come out with a brochure listing a whole host of no-no's that should be expunged from human speech. Some of he words which are used every day have "hidden meanings" according to the brochure, and tend to be sexist racist or offensive to handicapped persons.

headline: Thornburgh, Heinz Feud Over Debt
abstract: US Senator John Heinz from PA and governor Dick Thornburgh are battling over legislation to give the state a break in paying its jobless benefit debt to the federal government. Continued state borrowing to pay jobless benefits through 1982 may push the debt up to $2 billion next year. Heinz added measures to a bill that the governor believes could scare businesses out of the state and deter new economic growth.

headline: District postpones opening of six struck schools
abstract: To demonstrate what they said was their intention to negotiate in good faith, Philadelphia School District officials postponed plans to open six elementary schools Monday. The decision was announced soon after the first formal negotiations in the nearly month old teachers strike had gotten under way at the Warwick Hotel in Center City.

headline: Governor's Aide Asks PUC Probe to Uncover Dirty tricks Source
abstract: A top aide to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has asked the head of the Public Utility Commission to determine if a staff member was responsible for a phony letter concerning PUC nominee Clifford Jones. Stafford cited a news report that quoted Bodack a saying a staff member of the PUC was the source of the letter, which portrayed Jones as friendly to utilities.

headline: Seems Like Old Times; PennDot Bungles Job
abstract: Former Governor Milton Shapp's Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is moving in the same direction of Governor Dick Thornburgh's Department of Transportation.  The letter continues to discuss how the administration might be different, but the projects are moving in the same direction.

headline: Rebuild Western Pen, State Conferees Say
abstract: A bill authorizing the rebuilding of Western Penitentiary is awaiting approval by Pennsylvania Legislature and Governor Thornburgh's signature.  The article provides further details about the bill and the construction plans for the penitentiary.

headline: Opinion:  Thornburgh's liquor plan deserves public backing
abstract: The author opines that the people of Pennsylvania need to support Governor Thornburgh's plan to abolish state owned liquor stores.  The author states the benefits of such a plan, including lower prices, more selection and increased revenue to the state.  The author also points out several opponents to the plan including state liquor store employees, "dry" organizations, and the owners of clubs and bars

headline: Frostbelt fights for $3 billion
abstract: Claudine Schneider is worried about losing her congressional seat next year as a Republican from a Democratic state. She helped organize a group to get $3.6 for gypsy moths in the frostbelt states. Republicans are not happy with the group.

headline: State judges
abstract: The editors list the candidates for supreme court judges.  They endorse William D. Hutchinson and Robert E. Colville due to their experience.  They also list the candidates for Superior court judge and endorse Donald Wieand, Richard DiSalle, Stephen McEwen, and Perry Shertz.

headline: Torrance Property Turnover Opposed
abstract: The state wants to sell 1,166 acres of land at Torrance State Hospital near Blairsville, but the proposal will be strongly opposed by at least one Westmoreland legislator. It includes three farms, 34 buildings, and two wooded tracts. PA Governor Dick Thornburgh wants to sell to help balance the state budget.

headline: Embarrassing
abstract: With teachers flouting the law how can children be expected to obey rules? They are already overpaid and shouldn't be paid anymore.

headline: Governor's Plan to Aid TMI Iced
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh lost his first battle to secure a substantial, long-term federal pledge toward the $1 billion TMI Unit 2 cleanup expenses as he testified before the House Energy Conservation and Power Subcommittee. All fronts are claiming they do not have to pay towards the clean up.

headline: SEPTA clears the track
abstract: Southeastern PA Transit Authority's top brass is taking over operation of its commuter rail lines, now in Conrail's hands. It is the only sensible choice according to the editorial. The roadbed to ultimate operation by SEPTA of the rail lines will be bumpy, but on the right track.

headline: Regulate camps
abstract: Letter to the editor supporting a house bill that would regulate summer camps. The only requirement currently is that camps with lakes and pools must have certified lifeguards.

headline: OUR IDEAS: A Bargain at the State Stores?
abstract: Senate Bill 597, the legislative expression of Governor Thornburgh's intention to get the state out of the retail liquor business, is having an effect on Pennsylvania's liquor stores, even though the bill is bottled up in the committee.  Within the last several months, state stores have been allowing vendors to place advertising displays in the stores.  They have experimented with layouts of merchandise.  And now, for the first time in its 48-year history, the Liquor Control Board is selling liquor and wine at discount.  Instead of using discounts passed along by liquor produceers to hike profits, the Liquor Control Board actually is giving consumers a break.

headline: Gallen Plan Would Take Plant From Ertel's District; Town Near TMI Question Reapportionment Wisdom
abstract: Pennsylvania Representative James J. Gallen proposed to sever five Dauphin County municipalities from the 17th congressional district represented by Democrat Allen E. Ertel and attach them to the 16th district of Republican Robert Walker.  This change would put Three Mile Island issues to Walker.  The article continues to provide details about the reactions of Pennsylvania legislators, the arguments between the two parties, and concerns of what happens to Three Mile Island.

headline: State Lawmaker Proposes Redistricting Plan
abstract: House State Government Chairman James Gallen introduced legislation that would eliminate two congressional seats held by Democrats.  The Legislature must reshape congressional districts before the 1982 election based on the data from the 1980 census.  The article details the proposal.

headline: Transport tax plan prepared: Regional levy for SEPTA included
abstract: The Pennsylvania Tax Commission will submit recommendations to Governor Thornburgh to improve the efficiency of the state tax system.  The report includes; a 0.25 per cent wage tax on non-residents, an increase in the state income tax, and a 0.2 per cent surcharge on income tax to fund SEPTA.

headline: Fed up
abstract: The public are fed up with the teacher's union, because they are the highest paid but the lowest scoring graduates. Why should taxpayers have to pay more for bad quality?

headline: GPU earnings reflect TMI-1 outage
abstract: As federal hearings into the restart of Three Mile Island Unit 1 proceed, the outage of the undamaged reactor continues to impact General Public Utilities Corporation's earnings, which declined 54 percent in the first quarter of 1981. PA's emergency Management Agency is discussing emergency preparedness plans at the hearings for the restart of Unit 1.

headline: SEPTA keeps line running
abstract: Two former subway operators ran nearly empty passenger trains on a suburban line again, despite another union demonstration during which two protesters were arrested as they scuffled with police. By early afternoon, union leaders agreed to stop trying to disrupt service between Newton, Bucks County, and the Fox Chase station in Northeast Philadelphia, pending a Bucks County Court hearing. The court will hear a South Eastern PA Transportation Authority motion seeking a court order to prevent any further mass picketing on the line.

headline: Religious leaders view death penalty
abstract: Last in a series of articles on the death penalty.  Elmo Smith was the last to die in the state's electric chair in 1962 for killing a schoolgirl.  The article outlines the views of religious leaders from different religions on the question of the death penalty

headline: Pa. drivers to pay more car insurance
abstract: More than a third of Pennsylvania's motorists will soon have to pay higher car insurance rates.  The increase will be in addition to the more than 15 percent of drivers whose rates are going up as a result of increases approved in July.  Insurance Commissioner Michael L. Brown, who approved the July increases, approved another $65.4 million increase.  The latest increase means Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company's 730,000 Pennsylvania policyholders' annual premiums will raise an average 9 percent on September 15.

headline: 'Gerrymandering' fears rise as state redistricting begins
abstract: The author details the history of the term 'gerrymandering' and worries that district reapportionment will end up in political gerrymandering.  The piece details the redistricting debate in the legislature.

headline: State Leaders Like Fun(ds):  Lawmakers Tap 'Extras' Funds
abstract: In 1980, state legislatures spent $188,409 in state funds for recreation, on top of the $7,500 personal spending account that each lawmaker gets.  The article details specific lawmakers spending public funds on such extravagent items as cigars, liquor, club memberships, and fancy restaurants

headline: What Reagan's cuts will do to culture in Phila.
abstract: Philadelphia's cultural institutions' programs will be cut by half, according to the proposed cuts by the Reagan administration. The city's cultural leaders, while acknowledging the nation's need for budget trimming, are privately saying that the loss of federal funds will be severely damaging, if not fatal to many of their programs.

headline: Fee of 5% Is Imposed; PHEAA Student Loans Cost More
abstract: Student borrowers who failed to have their college-aid loans approved through the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency before last weekend face a 5 percent federally imposed "discount" on any future application.  The federal government, which backs the loans given students by lending institutions, has ruled that any loan not approved by Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency and similar agencies in other states by midnight August 23 must pay the discount, which is, in reality, an added fee.  Qualifying students will now receive the amount of their loan less 5 percent, or $50 on ever $1,000 borrowed.

headline: GPU questioning reveals NRC split
abstract: Nuclear Regulatory Commission members clashed today over how harshly General Public Utilities officers should be questioned about their ability to safely restart Three Mile Island Unit 1. Commissioner Victor Gilinsky opened a day-long hearing by challenging whether GPU personnel has learned anything from the TMI Unit 2 nuclear accident. He said GPU officials have yet to clarify why state and federal officials were not promptly informed of abnormal Unit 2 conditions prior to the accident.

headline: SEPTA needs a regional tax
abstract: With South Eastern PA Transportation Authority about to feel deeply the federal cuts in mass transit subsidies and with the state, the city, and the four suburban counties all slated for wide-ranging reductions in federal funds covering a host of programs, it is essential that the make a regional tax to support SEPTA. With out such it will not be able to continue to serve the area.

headline: Rendell wants juvenile court open, repeaters tried as adults
abstract: District Attorney Edward Rendell has launched a drive to try repeat offenders 15 or over as adults and to open juvenile court to the public. A bill drafted by the DA's office to change the PA state Juvenile Act will be introduced in the legislature the week of October. 3. The DA's office now must petition Family Court, where proceedings are private for certification to adult court.

headline: Panel OKs Interest Rate Lift
abstract: The state Senate Banking and Insurance Committee approved a major bill that would remove the 15 percent interest-rate ceiling on credit cards and small consumer loans. The legislation was sponsored by Senate Republican Leader Robert Jubelirer, and is backed by powerful retailing and banking interests. Also, the Senate Youth and Aging Committee considered a bill that would permit those over age 62 with less than $15,000 annual income to defer payment on property tax increases.

headline: Get Out and Vote
abstract: A radio broadcast illustrating the importance of voting in the current election.

headline: State Lottery Sales Agents Enthusiastic About Game
abstract: Top PA Lottery sales agents seem to be benefiting from the sale of lottery tickets, which do not seem to have been highly affected by the 'fix' of the Daily Lottery in the Pittsburgh area. The article summarizes the enthusiasm of top sales agents in Lackawanna County. The Lottery profits benefit senior citizens.

headline: When a tax cut is not a tax cut at all
abstract: A Chester County legislator has been trying for 10 years to eliminate property taxes.  He seems to be gaining support, but there has been no rush to his side.  Senator John Stauffer's latest plan is to cut in half the real estate taxes paid to school districts, but this means the income taxes would go up.  If there is a 50 percent cut in property taxes for schools, then that would mean a 59 percent increase in state income taxes to make up the difference.  To the present 2.2 percent state income tax Senator Stauffer would add a locally imposed personal income tax that would average 1.3 percent statewide.

headline: Fewer teachers, not more money
abstract: In 1970, the Philadelphia School District was spending approximately $300 million to educate almost 65,000 more students than district has projected it will educate under $970 million budget for 1982. On average that $4,500 to educate each student. That's one employee for every nine students. The author would like less employees to save money.

headline: Grand jury probing for phony results on TMI safety tests
abstract: A federal grand jury in Harrisburg is investigating allegations that employees of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant deliberately falsified the results of required tests for months before the accident that crippled the PA reactor in March 1979. They are presenting evidence to the grand jury recommending seeking a perjury indictment against one TMI control room operator.

headline: SEPTA Offers Van Rides For Those Who Need Them
abstract: SEPTA is now offering a pilot program, Paratransit, in Philadelphia for individuals who are unable to use regular public transit.  The program would offer door-to-door van service, but requires advance reservations.

headline: Reworking 180-day rule
abstract: The editorial explains that the 180-day rule, whereby a person accused of a crime must go to trial within 180 days of his arrest or the charges against him will be dismissed, is a common target of the 23 candidates in PA's statewide judicial races in the upcoming primary elections. Many have suggested changes, but the editorial argues the best option is the one suggested by Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell. The idea is for the Supreme Court to change the rule to require immediate trial after 180 days instead of dismissing charges.

headline: Pacer plant criticized in study
abstract: null

headline: Get Uncle Sam out of the control towers
abstract: The unlawful walkout of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organizations has been in the news so long that the public is considering it a relatively minor inconvenience.  The controllers are probably hurting most, but they asked for it.  With the rest of the nation flinching under the cutbacks, the well-paid controllers tried to squeeze Uncle Sam for $10,000 a year in raises plus shorter work weeks and earlier retirement.  They only get sympathy from one another.  President Reagan and Secretary of transportation Drew Lewis had no choice but to fire the pack of them.

headline: State Marks Its Own Inaugural Rights
abstract: Inaugural ceremonies were held for three state-wide elected officials, Al Benedict as auditor general, LeRoy Zimmerman as attorney general, and R. Budd Dwyer as state treasurer.  The article highlights the events of the inaugurations as well as some history of the newly elected.

headline: 30 gather to protest plan to change legislative districts
abstract: A group of about 30 people gathered in the shadow of Independence Hall to protest a proposal to redraw Philadelphia's legislative districts. They claim if Philadelphia loses five of its seats, it will lead to less minority representation.

headline: Fire them
abstract: Letter to the editor from a teacher asking the school board to fire union teachers, because they are non-teaching teachers. More pay does not mean better teaching.

headline: Hampden Water Criticized by PUC on Lack of Service
abstract: The Public Utility Commission on Friday charged that the Hampden Twp. Water Co. is furnishing inadequate service to its 70 customers and is also operating in flagrant and total disregard of its responsibilities. Customers in higher elevations experienced outages and periods of low pressure after one of the system's two well pumps malfunctioned in mid-August. Other charges include failure to bill customers, failure to obtain water supply permit, and failure to keep proper financial records.

headline: SEPTA really may be nearing end of the line
abstract: This past week may have marked a turning point for SEPTA. Instead of wondering whether it has the money to keep the commuter trains running, the transit authority suddenly found itself fighting for its own existence. For the first time, some members of the five-county authority openly discussed the possibly of pulling out of the 13-year-old system.

headline: Rising Crime Filling Our Prisons; Is It The Fault of Penal System
abstract: The editorial argues that more prisons have not slowed the rise in violent crime in the US. Instead, a move for longer jail sentences is testing the penal system's ability to carry out legislative mandates for tougher punishment and the public's willingness to finance stiffer retribution.

headline: Pennsylvania State Store System
abstract: Author believes radio does not know fact from fiction when it comes to state liquor stores. The United Food and Commercial Workers believe the defeat of the Governor's proposal is proof that the General Assembly was able to see through the media hype and judge the issue on merits.

headline: Ghost Rising?
abstract: Opinion writer discusses Philadelphia politics and former Democratic state Senator Pete Camiel's battle to escape his ghost employee conviction in federal court. He also explains GOP district attorney candidate Bill Cannon and GOP City Chairman Don Jamieson being upset that Governor Dick Thornburgh went to Philadelphia to hold press conferences with Democratic incumbent Edward Rendell.

headline: State Opens New Office For Buying Needs Data
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh officiated at the opening of the state's Office for Procurement Information. It is the state's central office for businesses seeking data on all state agency requests for bids or proposals that involve expenditures of $5,000 or more.

headline: A worthy defeat
abstract: The House Health and Welfare Committee's vote this week to defeat the Abortion Control Act was an important victory for the privacy of PA women. The intrusive and ill-conceived bill sponsored by PA Representative Gregg Cunningham of Centre County was designed to humiliate woman who choose an abortion. It would have interfered with US Supreme Court decisions and was always inconsistent.

headline: For student aid: Know what to do, when to do it, how to do it
abstract: Every family has to bare its financial soul to the federal government when their child applies to college. They have to share their income, medical expenses, investments, securities. At the end of the test they are likely to be told their family can afford to pay $4,000 a year towards college, and only if colleges cost more than that will they receive aid. One of biggest challenges is conveying to students and parents the decreasing federal aid for college.

headline: Hearings on utility boosts totaling $318.6 million open Oct.1
abstract: State regulatory hearings into the $318.6 million combined rate case of Metropolitan Edison Co. and PA Electric Co. will open October 1 with two sessions devoted solely to public comment. They will try to accommodate requests for the consumers.

headline: SEPTA Strike Grinds to a Halt: 19-Day Walkout Is Over
abstract: The city's public transit system was working again today as a tentative settlement - forged with the help of Governor Dick Thornburgh - ended the 19-day strike of Transit Workers Union 234. The agreement came as Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority's management withdrew its demand to hire part-time workers and, in return, the union agreed to accept a 14.5 percent wage increase, down from the 16 percent offer on the table. The Union members are expected to vote on the compromise contract within 10 days, and SEPTA's board must also approve the contract.

headline: School blues: The grand jury 'clears' Marcase
abstract: A grand jury has 'cleared' Philadelphia schools superintendent Michael Marcase of wrongdoing in accepting appliances, furniture and work on his houses from a contractor doing work for the school district, but the editorial argues it is a serious offense and Marcase should resign. The editorial agrees with the grand jury recommendation that the state Legislature enact a law that would prevent school district employees involved in contracting or procurement from accepting all gratuities.

headline: Phila. Grabs tax debtors' bank funds
abstract: Philadelphia officials have seized the bank accounts of 126 Philadelphia Naval Yard workers who owe about $500,000 in city wage taxes. The seizures represent a fishing expedition launched to see if a total of 178 whom the city has won tax judgments have bank accounts in New Jersey or at the naval yard. They are trying to show that they mean business.

headline: Giles Named to Council
abstract: Robert E. Giles was named Tuesday, April 14, to City Council after a deadlocked council vote was broken by Harrisburg Mayor Paul Doutrich, Jr. Giles will fill the seat vacated March 31 by Wesley Plummer. The Republican,  seeking office for the first time, will be sworn in on Tuesday, April 21, and will serve a four-year term on the council.

headline: State pension funds: Capital that could fuel regional recoveries
abstract: The author argues that in these months of Reagan administration cutbacks, a California governor's task force presented an innovative way of opening up new sources of financing for such causes as local economic development, affordable housing and job-producing small businesses. The proposal is to invest state pension funds, which are growing at a fast rate, in mortgages, small businesses and other areas.

headline: Governor seeks to hold line on taxes
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh says his intention is to recommend no general tax increase when he presents the state budget for fiscal 1982-83 to the state Legislature.  Thornburgh has worked toward fiscal stability by cutting general state spending and eliminating some state positions.

headline: Fifteen years of local arts
abstract: The Greater Harrisburg Arts Festival celebrates its 15th year this Saturday. It will take place at the William Penn Memorial Museum.

headline: PUC argues on recovery of fuel costs
abstract: The Public Utility Commission yesterday postponed action on a motion that was supposed to remove the fixed energy cost rates used by utilities to recoup fuel costs from customers. This motion was introduced by Commissioner Michael Johnson and would have been the first step in abolishing the separate rates covering fuel and purchasing power.

headline: Children Services and Aleta
abstract: The State Welfare Department completed its inadequate and shabby investigation of Children Services, giving it a clean bill of health on its investigation of child abuse.  Full attention should have been placed on the Aleta Bailey case.  Her case was the one in question in the case of child abuse in which Children Services allowed her to return home after she was beat.  Later on she died.

headline: Convention Center Pros, Cons Aired
abstract: Nine meetings and numerous hours later, Mayor Stephen J. Lucasi’s proposal for a convention/exhibition center remains a numbers game.  The public was almost evenly divided on the issue.

headline: State's commerce chief announces June conference
abstract: State Commerce Secretary Geoffrey Stengel Jr. announced that the commonwealth and the US Small Business Administration will co-sponsor the Pennsylvania Small Business Procurement Opportunity Conference June 22-23 at the Farm Show Building

headline: Governors in Closed Meetings, Don't Take Official Stand on Balanced-Budget Move
abstract: The controversial subject is the proposed constitutional amendment aimed at requiring a balanced federal budget.  Whatever their individual feelings, the 44 state Chief executives attending the National Governors’ Association annual convention find the issue so touchy they held a closed-door meeting to discuss it.  They decided against taking an official position on the amendment, which has cleared the U.S. Senate and is expected to come before the house soon.

headline: Two State Congressmen vote for Industry's Clean-Air Compromise
abstract: Two Pennsylvania congressmen are emerging as possible swing votes as a House committee begins reconsideration of a controversial set of proposals to revamp the nation’s major air pollution laws.  The House Energy and Commerce Committee Representatives Douglas Walgren and Marc Marks voted in support of an amendment that is considered crucial to the industry backed coalition pushing for changes in the Clean Air Act.  Walgren and Marks previously have counted among lawmakers who generally opposed the changes, so their votes were viewed with alarm by committee members who favor strengthening environmental laws or oppose their weakening.

headline: Library must beg support
abstract: The Dauphin County library system relies heavily on revenue from its municipalities for funding.  The library system often has to beg for support from these municipalities.  Many are hopeful that a true county library system will someday be established, but until then it is the responsibility of municipalities to provide funding.

headline: Governor's budget nears ok
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's $13 billion state budget is nearly through, despite Democratic protests that it can't be funded without a tax increase.

headline: For the future
abstract: A new bill would help Philadelphia's public schools by giving the city government more control and responsibility. However, in the other bill that was recently passed, the amount of wage tax collected will reduce by nearly $60 million for those who live outside Philadelphia, but continue to work there.
