The authors urge that the tax savings bill is not passed as it would harm the future of the Delaware valley.

headline: PUC asks Contact by Utilities Before Cutting Delinquents' Service
abstract: The Public Utility Commission has reminded all utilities in the state that under a 3-year-old policy they are required to contact the commission before taking steps to terminate services of delinquent-bill customers during the winter heating season.

headline: Children-Youth Probe is Read in York County
abstract: Under the state's new Child Abuse Act, York Country commissioners read for the first time the report of an investigation of actions by the Children and Youth Services agency in the fatal beating of a 5-year-old girl.  Under the new act, The Children Youth Agency is able to share information about child abuse cases with the commissioners, law enforcement officials, educators, news media or the public.

headline: Cumberland may trim program
abstract: High interest rates may force Cumberland County Commissioners to scale down their ambitious building program.  The offered interest rate was 13.45%, well higher than the expected rate.  A new prison was to use more than half of the $11.7 million commissioners were expecting to borrow, and its necessity may make them go ahead with the project despite the rates.

headline: State's Grand Canyon is A Scenic Wilderness
abstract: Located in the center of the state’s rugged northern tier, the Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania serves as the main attraction of the tourism industry in Tioga County where forests outnumber fields and wild animals far outnumber people.  Several times a year, tourists wander off the marked trails and into the mountainous terrain surrounding the Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania.  And invariably, Gregory Sassaman, Superintendent of the Leonard Harrison and Colton Point State Parks, has to find them.

headline: Governors' Mansions: The Lineup Now
abstract: A map of the US shows 36 states that elected governors--34 of them Democratic for a gain of 9 by Democrats overall. Republicans gained 2 governors. Currently, there are 34 Democratic Governors and 16 Republicans.

headline: U.S House (Vote for one)
abstract: A question asks the candidates their views on whether they support legislation to change the Clean Air Act and, if so, how?

headline: TMI procedures not excellent
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a reader criticizes GPU Nuclear president Robert C. Arnold for claiming that Three Mile Island's procedures are excellent.  Arnold's statement overlooks the damaging evidence gathered during the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's hearings on operator cheating incidents, and also fails to acknowledge a court ruling that deemed the operations staff at Three Mile Isand inadequate.

headline: In Our Opinion: 'Jobs' Bill Just a Cruel Hoax
abstract: The $1 billion job creation bill approved in the U.S. House of Representatives and scheduled to meet certain deaths in the U.S. Senate is one of the best examples of pre-election politics at the expense of the taxpayers that has been attempted to date.  The bill is strongly opposed by the Reagan administration and should be. It is that very type of expense that brought the nation to its economic knees, dolling out unlimited dollars on fruitless programs which prepared no one for the truisms of life but merely handout money and deepened the deficit.  People in Pennsylvania are rightfully concerned about the high rate of unemployment, but most are not fooled by the proposal of a quick-fix jobs program.  Those who are truly interested in providing more jobs in the commonwealth should go after their legislators to do something about the staggering unemployment compensation fund debt.

headline: Future of block grants doubted
abstract: PA Representative Ron Cowell told special education program advocates that he does not believe Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal for education block grants will likely not receive legislative approval.  The proposed block grant program would replace 12 separate payments to school districts the state now gives.

headline: PUC is divided in its assessment of funding needs
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission split Thursday in its assessment of funds necessary to defend consumers against multi-million dollar rate requests by utilities. This year, the PUC has asked for an increase in the amount it gets from the state.

headline: Clarify language at hearings
abstract: Michael Tsoucalis, a member of the Upper Leacock Zoning Board, came up with a novel idea - define all the legal and technical terms being used.  The meeting of the board lasted over four hours and was filled with legal jargon.  By making these types of municipal hearings more accessible to all, these hearings can help to keep burdens off the courts.

headline: Despite slump, Pa. plans costly office building
abstract: Despite budget cutbacks and hard times, PA has begun a four-year plan to build an extra office building, complete with underground parking, to rehabilitate an old museum for the governor's use, and to correct fire and panic code violations in the 75-year-old main Capitol building at an estimated cost of $32 million.

headline: Statewide banking
abstract: The impact of the recently approved statewide banking law won't be seen immediately but it definitely assures of landmark changes and increased competition. The new rules will permit banks to expand anywhere within the state-in stages-over the next eight years.

headline: Governors Question Balanced Budget Bill
abstract: The debate over a constitutional amendment to balance the budget moved onto the agenda of the National Governors’ Association with a closed-session discussion of a draft resolution designed to derail the amendment pass by the Senate.  The draft resolution was scheduled for possible consideration by the governors at their primary session.  Meanwhile in Washington, the White House said that it did not view as a setback by the NGA executive council to recommend that the governors draft their own New Federalism program from scratch, rather than continue negotiations with the White House.

headline: U.S. Senate Race
abstract: Among the more interesting elections this year is for the US Senate seat currently held by John Heinz.  Since Alleghency County Commissioner Cyril Wecht has announced his candidacy for the Democrats for this spot, there does not seem to be any other Democratic condender.  Since both candidates are from Western Pennsylvania, and both are generally well-informed people, it should be a good election for the area regardless of who wins.

headline: A day on the Senate trail
abstract: A reporter follows Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Cyril Wecht and his Republican challenger, John Heinz, on the campaign trail for a day.

headline: Income 'index' on block
abstract: The current administration will consider withdrawing the protection from income tax "bracket creep" in the new tax, as part of its efforts to trim the budget deficit. According to the Treasury Secretary Donald Regan, the so-called "indexing" provisions would adjust tax brackets to stay even with inflation and this would cut down on federal revenues.

headline: Gag orders put Governor's 'Open Door' in doubt
abstract: State Education Secretary Robert Scanlon recently barred education officials from distributing public information to the state's largest union. He has also accused the union of misinterpreting and misrepresenting data on Governor Thornburgh's education budget for next year. This now raises questions about the Thornburgh administration's commitment to open government.

headline: PUC Suspends Cutback Plan
abstract: The Public Utility Commission indefinitely suspended a controversial request by PECO to cut back service to customers who don't pay their bills on time.  The Electric company wants to use devices called "service limiters" to cut back on power usage by delinquent customers.  These would provide only enough power to keep necessary appliances such as furnaces, lights and refrigerators operating.  The commissioners, expressed concern about the device's safety and its potential effectiveness in helping the company collect its overdue payments, which currently total about 250,000.

headline: Clemency's Not to Be Taken for Granted
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh pardoning power allows him to commute death sentences, to spare convicted criminals from prison and to reduce terms already being served, thus making inmates eligible for parole.  He can shorten the parole period, by commuting the original sentence.  He has only approved 16 percent of all of the recommendations for clemency handed to him by the pardons board.  Thornburgh grants clemency only in cases he considers “extraordinary.”

headline: Developers will Revise Renovation
abstract: Officials of National Development Corp. of Pittsburgh are planning on revising its plans for the renovation of the former downtown Boston store building in order to reduce the proposed leasing costs.  Possible tenants for the building include National Fuel Gas, Regional Clinical Laboratories of Northwestern Pennsylvania and the U.S. Postal Service.

headline: Statewide banking bill clears committee
abstract: The PA Senate Banking and Insurance Committee approved a bill that would liberalize Pennsylvania's bank branching rules immediately, and would allow unfettered state-wide banking in 8 years.  At present, banks are only allowed to open branches in their headquarters counties and neighboring counties.  Officials believe that smaller banks will become prime take-over targets of the large Pittsburgh and Philadelphia banks if the legislation passes.

headline: Governors say no to 'federalism'
abstract: President Ronald Reagan has indicated to the nation's governors that he is prepared to negotiate major changes in his New Federalism proposal, while witholding comment on the governor's specific objections.  Reagan renewed his pledge to ensure that states do not end up being financial winners or losers with the package.  In unofficial voting, the governors voted 36-5 in support of an alternative federalism plan that opposes the president's proposal that the states take over food stamps and Aid to Families with Dependent Children.  Both the governors and the White House expressed determination to continue negotiations in hope of reaching a compromise on a federalism plan that would sort out the responsibilities of federal, state, and local governments.

headline: U.S. withdrawal not in the cards
abstract: US Representative Bud Shuster advocates a reduction in US spending for the defense of Western Europe.  The editorial suggests that Rep. Shuster is wrong about pulling back in Europe, but right about having the Europeans pick up more of the share of the defense of Western Europe against the Soviet Union.

headline: Thornburgh Walks Out
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh claims that the format of Pennsylvania's annual NAACP conference was amended to try to force him into a debate with his Democratic opponent, U.S. Representative Allen Ertel.  For this reason, the governor abruptly left the conference after speaking--claiming that his speech was cut off and the rules were changed.

headline: Is a (shhhh!) tax increases due after the election?
abstract: There is a possibility of a new state tax after the November elections as the state will be short of money as of June 30. However, there is no talk of this currently.

headline: Good news for schools
abstract: Editorial: The paper believes that several changes need to take place to right Philadelphia's school system, and one good one has finally occurred with the resignation of superintendent Michael Marcase.  Other suggested changes include replacing board president Arthur Thomas.

headline: PUC to Mull Electric-Service Limiters: Philadelphia Utility Seeks OK of Devices
abstract: The electric utility industry is looking at a device that will limit the amount of electricity fed into homes of delinquent customers.  The PA Public Utility Commission is expected to act on a petition from Philadelphia Electric Co. to introduce the device in its service territory.  This is the first petition by a public utility in the state regarding the service limiter.

headline: Con-troversy: Underground Confinement Sparks Hunger Strike in PA.
abstract: Six inmates have begun a hunger strike to protest inhumane conditions at Dallas State Penitentiary.  They were striking to protest being confined to the underground section of the prison for an indefinite period without being told why.  The inmates also said they were being given half rations and were not allowed to shower or exercise as well as not being given clean clothing.

headline: Dream-Home Nightmare: Consumer tips are offered for avoiding house-buying headaches
abstract: Consumer tips are offered for avoiding house-buying headaches.

headline: Steel Output At Lowest in 44 Years
abstract: Domestic steel production dipped to its lowest levels in 44 years in June.  The output of raw tonnage was the worst in more than a decade.  The American Iron and Steel Institute reported June production totaled slightly more than 6 million tons, compared with about 6.7 million tons in May and more than 10.4 million tons in June 1981.

headline: Governors Snub New Federalism
abstract: The Republican Chairman of the National Governors Association declared Saturday that the months of negotiations between state executives and the White House have failed to resolve disagreements over President Reagan’s New Federalism plan.  The White House is left without the support of any organization of state and local officials for its plan to transfer $38.8 billion in federal programs to the state.

headline: Union's Leaders: No Strike
abstract: Leaders of Union Local 1201 representing public school district custodians and maintenance workers, voted against a strike in negotiations for a new contract. Union members await a ruling from Commonwealth Court on an appeal by the school against binding arbitration and the Court of Common Pleas, both of which found the district must grant workers a 10 percent pay raise. Chief district negotiator, J. William Jones, offered a 6 percent raise. Union leader William McDevitt refused.

headline: Supreme Court: Take your pick
abstract: Pennsylvania needs to scrap its current electoral system for judicial selection adopt a system that relies on gubernatioral nominations--rather than elections--for the appointment of judges to the Commonwealth, Superior and Supreme Courts.  Judges should not have to solicit campaign contributions and extol their virtues on TV ads, as these actions comprmise judicial integrity and impartiality.

headline: Job Bill Offers Relief
abstract: 9.8 percent of the workforce was unemployed as of July. Despite the fact the unemployment rate is at the highest it has ever been, very little is being done by the government.  President Reagan has successfully resisted virtually every proposal for government programs that would put people to work and provide them with an income.  He contends that government spending to stimulate the economy is responsible for the boom and bust cycle of the American economy.  If we resist the quick and easy solutions, he maintains, the nation will achieve a permanent and prosperous recovery.

headline: Goodling, others join education 'defenders'
abstract: Several Republicans on the US House Education and Labor Committee have broken ranks with the Reagan administration on its proposed cuts in education funds.  US Representative John Ashbrook complained that the administration is increasing defense funding at the expense of education funding.  Proposed cuts to special-needs children will reduce spending from $525 per child to $400 per child.

headline: PUC turns down CWIP charges; Limerick vote made them 'glad'
abstract: The Public Utility Commission has turned down the CWIP charges stating that the costs of major construction projects should not be placed into a utility's rate base unless it is useful for public service.

headline: Cops and consolidation
abstract: The rearranging of funding priorities at the federal and state level will place additional pressure on elected officials to consider consolidating municipal police agencies as a way to cut costs. This prediction comes in an article in Reports, a publication of the Pennsylvania Department of Community Affairs.

headline: 'Enterprise Areas' to Be Established: Pa. Would Give Priority in Aid
abstract: The Thornburgh administration plans to establish "enterprise development" areas in six Pennsylvania communities in a program that would move those communities to the top of the priority list at a number of state aid agencies.  The Enterprise Development Area Program was unveiled late last month by Governor Thornburgh and by Community Affairs Secretary Shirley M. Dennis, whose department will select the communities and oversee the coordination efforts that are the linchpin of the program.

headline: Steel, Union Must Work Together as Team
abstract: In these letters to the editors’ one person is responding to how people keep blaming Mr. Trautlein’s salary on why the steel industry is in the position that it is. This person believes that the union and the steel industry work as a team and not against one another before it is too late.  In the second letter, the person is extending their sincere thanks to all of the people who were so helpful when her husband suffered an injury at the Allentown Howard Johnson’s gas station on the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  The third letter was about reactionary comments generated by Guthsville II’s production of "Steambath" in Lehigh Valley.  In the last letter, the Leagues of Women Voters of the Bethlehem and Easton Areas thanked the Northampton County Council for the block grant awarded to them in the 1982 budget.

headline: Governors Soften Go-It-Alone Challenge
abstract: Leaders of the National Governors’ Association softened their go-it-alone challenge of the White House on New Federalism but several governors sought to confront Congress on budget balancing.  The outgoing chairman of the NGA, GOP Governor Richard Snelling, who originally wanted to bypass President Reagan and go direct to Congress with the governors’ plan to return to the states many programs now run from Washington, retreated to a "dual track" approach.  The essence of the resolution was that the governors would continue their long but so far fruitless negotiations with Reagan and prepare their own bill.

headline: Unjudicious
abstract: Cyril E. Sagan, who is running for U.S. Senate as a write-in candidate in the general election, appeared before Judge Maurice Cohill in U.S. District Court to request that he declare unconstitutional Pennsylvania’s aristocratic privilege of allowing judges to run for election on more than one party ticket, a so-called blue-ribbon committee of state judges and lawyers had the gall to suggest judges shouldn’t be elected at all.  They want a governor to appoint judges.

headline: Auto Emissions
abstract: A federal judge blocked Pennsylvania from receiving roughly 90 million dollars in federal highway monies until it implements an automobile emissions and inspection program.  Next month, the state will have its last chance to argue against the emissions program and the judge's decision.  If the state does not win its case, some legislators are proposing that the state forfeit highway money and refuse to participate in the emissions-and-inspection program.

headline: Jobless Pay Fund Heading Toward $2.3 Billion Debt
abstract: The unemployment compensation fund pays a maximum payment of $198 a week to a jobless person.  These payments have force Pennsylvania to borrow a total of $1.8 billion from the federal government.  Pennsylvania's federal debt will rise to $2.3 billion by January if something is not done yet to control this.  Legislation passed in 1981 was suppsed to trim benefits and increase unemployment taxes in such a way as to put a lid on Pennsylvania's federal debt.  However, this didn't work.  Now House Democratic Whip James Manderino wants Thornburgh to call a special session of the Legislature to take another crack at resolving the unemployment.

headline: Governor Cites 'Commitments': Student Loan Measure Signed
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed into law legislation that will make more state money available for new student loans despite his objections to changes in financial procedures.  The law allows the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency to sell up to $300 million in bonds annually to help finance the loans.  The measure was sponsored by PA Representative Stephen Friend.

headline: PUC will ponder PECO rate hike
abstract: The Public Utility Commission will begin debating on Philadelphia Electric Co.'s unprecedented $344.5 million annual rate hike request, which includes charges to finance construction work in progress.

headline: County to Prosecute Abuse Cases
abstract: There are at least 652,000 abused and neglected children in the United States.  Governor Richard Thornburgh signed legislation into law permitting police officers to view confidential child abuse cases.  Case workers must send police agencies copies of the abuse reports and the new legislation now gives law enforcement officers access to confidential abuse files without necessitating a court order.

headline: Ephrata Hub: Non-Taxing Recreation
abstract: The Ephrata Recreation Center, completed at a $1.5 million cost nearly four years ago without a dime of local, state, or federal tax money, has been a model for other Pennsylvania communities.  The center was a success from the start: some 6,000 people use its facilities in an average week.  The halfway mark has been reached in paying off the seven-year mortgage.  Officials of the state Department of Community Affairs praise the efforts of this northern Lancaster County community as “unique” and “exemplary,” while also cautioning would be imitators that it may be a tough act to follow.

headline: Steelworkers Push to Buy Firms' Unused Properties
abstract: A steelworkers’ activist group is urging area municipalities to create a public authority that would reclaim unused property from steel corporations.  The Tri-State Conference on Steel said it planned on asking the county to fund a study that would determine whether such a plan is feasible.  The authority, which would be called the Steel Valley Authority, would exercise the power of eminent domain over unused properties owned by a steel company.  It could legally force the owner to sell property to the authority, as long as the owner received a fair market price.

headline: Governor's State Game Appointee is Under Fire
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh nominated Robert S. Lichtenberger, who served with the PA Game Commission, to the Board, angering the PA Federation of Sportsmen's Clubs, which traditionally recommends nominees. The Federation may ask the nomination be withdrawn. The Lancaster County Republican Party would recommend a Lancaster County Jury Commissioner or a Mount Joy Borough Councilman. PA Senator Richard Snyder will study the nominee's background before confirmation.

headline: Upcoming election snags action on needed state legislation
abstract: Columnist discussing the behavior of state government in an election year.  Mentions that the budget and redistricting will be the most important issues facing the state legislature.

headline: How probe of AT&T was stifled
abstract: A state investigation of a peculiar arrangement saving AT&T up to 10 million dollars a year in Pennsylvania taxes was quietly thwarted under the supervision of a high-level tax official who is a friend of At&T's Pennsylvania tax lawyer.

headline: Jobless Rate Sticks at 9.8%
abstract: The nation’s unemployment rate stayed at 9.8 percent in August, but government labor analysts conceded that there’s nothing to indicate any imminent relief from high joblessness.  In Pittsburgh, more losses in both factory and non-factory jobs pushed the July unemployment total up six-tenths of a percentage point to 12.3 percent from 11.7 percent in June.  The August jobless rate for Pennsylvania eased from 10.8 percent of the workforce in July to 10.5 percent.

headline: Grading city schools
abstract: Although it is difficult to rate schools, a team of evaluators brought in to survey Pittsburgh's elementary schools were quite impressed and rate it between A+ to B-.

headline: Put 'waste' heat to use
abstract: The writer of this editorial discusses the use of waste heat generated by Pennsylvania Power and Light Company's Montour coal-fired plant near Washingtonville and how this practice will become commonplace.

headline: Couple Kill 40 Dogs In Obeying Court Rule
abstract: To comply with a court order to get rid of all but five of their 64 dogs, Donald and Frances Snyder began having the dogs put to sleep.  After putting 40 down, they were unable to kill anymore.  The couple decided to give away one of the animals and boarded 18 others in other homes or animal shelters.

headline: Ephrata's 'Dynamic' Rec Director A Bald-Headed Santa You'll Flip For
abstract: Tom Grater, Director of Recreation for 27 years in Ephrata, has developed a reputation as "a dynamic leader" who is committed to the Lancaster County community.  State officials in the Department of Community Affairs describe him as "a personality" and cite his drive behind the project to fund and build a new recreation center.

headline: The house that ulcers built
abstract: SmithKline has become the nation's most profitable pharmaceutical company because of a pill it invented to deal with ulcers.  Now, the company is runnning out of ways to spend its profits, after having built a new headquarters and bought two other companies to support its business.

headline: Governors wary of 'new federalism'
abstract: The winter meeting of the National Governors' Association became another chapter in the national debate over the merits of President Ronald Reagan's latest economic proposals.  But, with 36 of the nations 50 governors up for re-election this year, most are not forward-looking.  In that case, these proposals are not beneficial to re-election campaigns.  Most of the governors have already come out opposed to the proposed spending cuts.

headline: US Senate; Heinz unopposed, but running scared
abstract: Although US Senator John Heinz has no opponent in the Republican primary, he always anticipates the worst possible scenario and prepares for it. He has never lost an election.

headline: Law and order come to class
abstract: This article laments the fact that so little of today's secondary educational curriculum is devoted to the structure of law in society.  It is important that children are educated on this subject, as the administration of the legal system and its evolution will be the product of their future decisions; knowledge of the system and its procedures are necessary to make such collective decisions.

headline: LD Board to raise 2 taxes
abstract: The Lower Dauphin School Board tentatively approved a $10.1 million 1982-83 budget which includes a $6 million real estate tax increase and a $15 occupation assessment tax boost. The proposed plan would raise district taxes for the seventh time in 8 years.

headline: Hershey kids have a home
abstract: A team of students from the Milton Hershey School were taunted after a game for not having parents present to cheer them on. The school provides free tuition for children of single or no-parent homes.  It takes in about 100 students per year, out of about 4000 applications.  The trust that runs the school owns most of the Hershey Company, and provides the school with more than sufficient funding.

headline: Radiation Inspection Proposal is Aired
abstract: The Thornburgh administration is holding out for inspection legislation that would update the state’s involvement in control and inspection of radiation sources in Pennsylvania.  Representative James L. Wright is the sponsor of the HB 2612 which aims to protect commonwealth residents from unnecessary and harmful exposure resulting from improper use of radioactive materials, radiation sources and accidents involving nuclear power and radioactive material transportation.  Affected would be not only operators of nuclear plants, who would be paying a $150,000 annual fee per reactor, but also many persons now unlicensed by the state who handle X-ray and other machines that are a source of radiation.

headline: Court Tells Governor to Release Costs
abstract: A Commonwealth Court ruled that Governor Dick Thornburgh must release information requested by a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee on how much the state is spending for lawyers.  The court ruled 4-1 that the request by Senator Craig Lewis is not a political question as Thornburgh had contended.  Lewis’ suit was based on the PA Right-to-Know Act and the PA Administrative Code, which requires the governor to provide budgetary information to both the majority and minority chairman of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees.  While rejecting Lewis’ claim under the Right-to Know Act on technical grounds, the court concluded that the Administrative Code and the State Constitution required the release of the information.

headline: Federal Grant to Aid Employment Picture In Pottstown Area
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh announced a federal grant of nearly $3 million that will be combined with a previously announced $1 million state loan to aid in an expansion program by Knoll International, Inc. which will result in the creation of more than 400 new skilled jobs over the next three years in the Pottstown area.  This administration has been in the vanguard of supporting and encouraging the expansion of Pennsylvania’s growth oriented funds.  Knoll International is a prime example of how a small business could grow into a leader in its filed.  Knoll International’s East Greenville facility designs and manufactures office furniture.  U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development award Pottstown the Urban Development Action Grant, which it will use the funds to provide a loan to Knoll International.

headline: Thornburgh Sent Bill Raising Car-Loan Rates
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh must decide whether to sign legislation that would allow interest rates on auto loans to rise as high as 18 percent.  Republicans in the House and Senate compromised giving final approval to an amended bill that would raise the ceiling on auto loan rates.  The original legislation called for unlimited interest rates.

headline: Governors, by a Vote, Kill Call for Balanced Budget
abstract: By a single vote, the nation’s governors rejected a resolution calling for a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution.  Many argued that further restraint on federal spending was necessary and that a constitutional amendment was the best way to obtain it.

headline: US Senate; Sagan needs luck to male Senate race
abstract: Democrat Cyril Sagan believes that the only way wealthy Republican John Heinz can be beaten is to make a sharp contrast in who this man really is. He also says that he will use his own money to fund the campaign.

headline: Candidates push personal factors in EAST Shore campaigning
abstract: This article discusses several PA House races and focuses specifically on the 104th, 105th, 106th Legislative Districts.

headline: Legislators Call Hike in Operating Expenses Necessary
abstract: Legislators approved the 1982-83 budget for themselves that carried a 15 percent increase over the last year.  The boost is almost three times as large as the budget increase for all the rest of the state government.  Republicans, including 102 of them in the House and 26 of them in the Senate, were by themselves responsible for approving the $10.7 billion spending bill that included almost $64 million for the legislature.  Many representatives offended the boost because they say that it was necessary given the era of rising costs and inflated prices for materials.

headline: Higher education cuts: the tip of imprudence
abstract: Editorial:  President Ronald Reagan's recent proposed cuts in higher education spending are going to hurt the country's higher education system, according to 13 presidents of Philadelphia-area colleges.  The problem with their call is that it only addressed one part of the education cuts, other parts were much larger.

headline: Radiation leak hits New York N-Plant
abstract: A tube ruptured in a cooling system at the Ginna Nuclear Power Plant, emitting radioactive stream into the atmosphere and leaking thousands of gallons of water into the reactor's containment sump before the plant was stabilized.  The reactor shut down automatically and was doused with water to keep it from overheating.  Gary Sanborn, spokesperson for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission says that the plant is now stable, and that there was no damage to the reactor.

headline: Courts can Reduce Costs
abstract: Philadelphia’s courts spent $53 million during fiscal 1981.  A recent audit by City Controller Thomas A. Leonard’s office concluded that the budget practices of the Common Pleas and Municipal Courts “generally are a mess.”  Poor accounting has made it difficult to determine the total revenue collected.  The city could save $5.3 million annually with some simple changes in purchasing and management policies.

headline: Gov. Signs Housing Bill for Mid-Income Families
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has signed into law a multi-million-dollar subsidy program intended to reduce mortgage interest rates for middle-income families that want to purchase a home.  The program uses tax-exempt bonds to attract investors to put money into mortgages.

headline: Thornburgh to get bank growth bill
abstract: The PA House voted 118-70 to approve a bill that would allow PA's banks to expand their operations statewide.  The measure is backed by Governor Dick Thornburgh and is almost certain to be signed into law.  The bill would allow a bank holding company to gain control of up to 8 state banks throughout the next 8 years, after which time that limit would fall away.  The bill also allows banks to expand branch operations.  The bill was designed to intensify competition among banks.

headline: Governors: Federalism, Budget Linked
abstract: The nation's governors rejected a recent appeal by US President Ronald Reagan to consider the "new federalism" programs as being separate from budgetary concerns.  The governors believe that the proposed 1983 budget cuts are directly linked with the ability of the states to implement the "new federalism" policies.  The governors did not debate the merits of the defense budget nor the recent income tax cut.

headline: Vidmer Status is challenged
abstract: Commonwealth Court is expected to rule this week on whether Dick Vidmer is qualified to seek the Democratic nomination for state representation in the 26th legislative district. His candidacy has been challenged on the grounds that he has not lived in Pennsylvania for the required four years.

headline: House Seats: First Prize in November Vote
abstract: The 1982 congressional elections will determine whether Democrats will increase their power in a chamber they already control.  Expert analysts are predicting a Democratic gain of 40-45 seats--a gain that would, in all likelihood, make it nearly impossible for President Reagan to enact his economic agenda.

headline: Local officials react to budget proposal
abstract: Republican lawmaker Rudolph Dininni of Swatara Township says the economy may be the key to Governor Dick Thornburgh's success of getting his $13 billion budget proposal for the 1982-83 fiscal year.  One of the main areas of disagreement on Capitol Hill between the two parties is the amount of a budget balance at the end of the current fiscal year.  The Democrats, pointing to the lag in state-revenue collections, predict that the state could face a deficit by next January while Republicans believe that the economy and state revenues will pick up in the summer months.

headline: House Approves Increased Funds for 4 State-related Universities
abstract: The House and Senate gave final approval to a package of bills that provide $370 million for 41 institutions, including four state-related universities.  Now the bill goes Governor Dick Thornburgh for his approval.

headline: Rambo Hears Arguments on TMI Claims Case
abstract: Unless the owners and operators of Three Mile Island are made to pay damages for police and emergency services incurred after the nuclear accident, they will have no stake in preventing another occurrence.  Arnold Levin of Philadelphia made the statement in a hearing before U.S. Middle District Court Judge Sylvia H. Rambo on a request by the defendants to rule that they are not obligated to reimburse the state and municipalities for the extra money sent responding to the accident.  Susquehanna and Lower Swatara townships filed suit on behalf of all Pennsylvania municipalities within 100 miles of the Unit 2 reactor.  Attorney’s for the defendants General Public Utilities Corp., Metropolitan Edison Co., Jersey Central Power and Light Co., J. Ray McDermott & Co., and Catalytic Inc., have asked Rambo to rule in their favor without requiring that the case go to trial.  They contend that the defendants should not have to pay for the emergency and police services which governments are legally obligated to provide.

headline: Crime commission: trial by innuendo
abstract: In this editorial, the paper believes that recent accusations of mob involvement in the state liquor store business as made before the Pennsylvania Crime Commission is just another example of "trial by innuendo."  It notes that none of its reports of mob activity have resulted in any indictments.

headline: Governor's help asked in Midland
abstract: Governor Thornburgh and Nicholas DeBenedictis, executive director of the economic development committee of Thornburgh's cabinet, have both been asked by two legislators to become personally involved in discussions about the future of the Crucible plant in Midland.

headline: USS Predicts '82 Loss
abstract: U.S. Steel Corporation is predicting its first yearly loss in three years. It is also considering the permanent clusre of facilities in Homestead and Rankin, PA. The company's recently purchased Marathon Oil subsidiariy along with other subsidiaries continue to turn a profit however. The firm's Carnegie Pension Fund also sold half a million shares of the company's preferred stock.

headline: Great Debate: That Which Is Left Unsaid
abstract: It is doubtful that the average citizen is paying much attention to the ongoing debate between Governor Thornburgh and the Democratic Leadership in the Legislature on the financial condition of the state.  There are fundamental issues involved here that go to the heart of the operation of state government, the roles and responsibilities the state should assume vis-ŕ-vis local jurisdictions and school districts, and ultimately, to the pockets of taxpayers.

headline: Viewing Harrisburg: The 2 Largest Cities Still Rule State GOP
abstract: Martha Bell Schoeninger was re-elected chairman at the Republican State Committee meeting.  LeGree Daniels went from being Assistant Secretary to Secretary.  Dave Christopher from Allegheny County won vice chairmanship.  He promised committee members that with him in office, they would have fun.  He was nominated by Republican National Committeewoman Elsie Hillman of Pittsburgh and former Party Chairman George Bloom from Washington Country.  He received western votes as well as those from Philadelphia and its suburbs.

headline: null
abstract: This picture shows Governor Dick Thornburgh and L. Stanley Crane, chairman of Conrail, participating in ceremonies at Monday's opening of Philadelphia's modernized coal exporting facility.  Modernization of the pier is expected to triple the compan'y coal-exporting capacity.

headline: Look at the facts
abstract: In the battle of the rich-against-the-poor, the Democrats seem to be vouching for tax breaks that would benefit the rich, unlike the GOP which is supporting equal tax cuts for all citizens.

headline: How should school board be revamped?
abstract: A PA House committee listened to witnesses discuss ways to revamp the Philadelphia School Board.

headline: Readers' Forum: Questions for Congressman on Restart of TMI
abstract: A letter to the editor from an author concerned about the restart of Three Mile Island despite grievances by local, scientific, and regulatory agencies.

headline: Crime Doesn't Pay, But it Costs
abstract: There was a meeting between County Council and Erie County judges in Erie to discuss the finances for the upcoming year.  Judges emphasized their funding cannot be cut because they are operating with insufficient personnel and a tremendous work load.  County Executive Judy Lynch and council are going to be hard pressed to provide enough money to meet demands.  Erie County does not have a system whereby such small cases could be tired and save money.  If the defendant appeals his conviction, the county will have to pick up added costs.  The average taxpayer doesn’t realize the burden he or she is carrying in supporting the courts.  The courts are almost a government of itself in it is mandated by state government with all costs borne by counties.

headline: Homebuilding Crippled
abstract: The economic recession has crippled Pennsylvania’s homebuilding industry and has caused both a 52 percent unemployment rate and a drastic reduction in productivity, according to the president of the Pennsylvania Builders Association.  Annual housing production in the state has declined 51 percent over three years from a 1978 high of 58,400 units to 28,600 units last year.  The drop in production has created a 52 percent unemployment rate.

headline: Weirton Sales pitch
abstract: The Weirton division of the National Steel Corp. is facing financial difficulties and the company has offered to sell it to the employees. However, the editorial questions the economic feasibility of this, at least in the immediate future.

headline: Greater Johnstown students
abstract: Students and teachers appeared relieved to be back to their old routine after a long strike, columnist George Fattman observed.

headline: Vote on Two-Thirds Rule
abstract: Senate Republicans managed a narrow party-line vote to move legislation reducing the number of votes for confirmation (of appointments) from 34 to 26.  This came in the form of an amendment to a bill setting fixed terms of office.  Senate Democrats were against the amendment.

headline: Desegregation plan ahead
abstract: The Pittsburgh Post Gazaette commends the Pittsburgh Board of Public Education for approving a comprehensive racial desegregation plan and urges the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission to approve the plan.

headline: A Plant Accident Study Shows Worst Case Could be Worse Than Old NRC Estimates
abstract: A study shows that worst-case accident scenarios at nuclear power facilities, no matter how unlikely they are to occur, are far more catastrophic in terms of death and damage than the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has acknowledged.  U.S. Representative Edward J. Markey says the NRC is misleading the public and is not honest about what the worst case actually is.

headline: Make vendors accountable
abstract: A bill passed by the Pennsylvania House of Representatives and awaiting Senate action would require street vendors throughout the state to show evidence that they collect and pay the required sales taxes to the commonwealth.

headline: Independent SCUDdled
abstract: The State College and University Directors Board (SCUD) obtained information from the State Education Board before it proceeded with a $230 tuition hike. However, critics pointed out that the Education Department has been lobbying all along for the tuition hike and it could potentially be a conflict of interest.

headline: Record request: Bell rate hike hearings slated
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission voted to suspend a record rate increase by Bell of Pennsylvania while statewide hearings are held.  A judge has already approved part of the rate hike.

headline: Crime Down Statewide, up in city
abstract: The number of serious crimes committed in Pennsylvania has decreased by 1.5 percent from 1980 to 1981.  This is the first decrease in serious crime since 1977.  Murders were down 11 percent, motor vehicle theft dipped 11.4 percent and decreases were also recorded for 1981 for rape, burglary, arson and larceny-theft.  For Allegheny, Beaver, Washington and Westmoreland counties serious crime was down 2.5 percent in 1981 and would have decreased further except for a 2.7 percent increase in the city of Pittsburgh.  The figures may be linked to an increase in citizen involvement in recent years in the fight against crime.  Another reason could be because of the Neighborhood Watch program, in which residents watch for and report to police suspicious activity in their neighborhoods.

headline: Housing costs defy buyers; Most Americans still outside looking in
abstract: The Eighth-Annual Home Builders show is coming to a close today. This show proves that good homes are still being built all over the country. The next edition aims at publicizing the "affordability" of reasonably priced homes for Americans.

headline: What others say
abstract: Editorial originally in the Meadville Tribune, but reprinted in the Times Leader: While state leaders are thinking about privatizing liquor stores, the stores have also not caught on to using credit cards.  Consumer letters promote credit card use in State Stores by a 30-1 ratio.  The article suggests that accepting credit cards is an obvious first step to modernizing the liquor store system, and that crime would be reduced in these stores because they will have less cash on hand.

headline: Green and Murray Agree on New Teachers Contract
abstract: Mayor Green and School Superintendent Murray have agreed on a new teachers contract.  The contract provides for total salary increases of about 18 percent spread over the next three years and gives the school board power to make limited layoffs, primarily on a formula related to declining student enrollment.

headline: Vote rulingdue in Walgren suit
abstract: Judge Sylvia Rambo may rule today on a request by US Representative Doug Walgren to halt the entire state election process until congressional reapportionment is final.  The lawsuit, and others like it, asks the court to bar elections bureau officials from further action until the federal judiciary decides to remap the delegation.

headline: Robinson hits Reed for canceling snow-removal pact
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed cancelled a snow-removal contract with the state Department of Transportation and has drawn heavy criticism from City Council President William A. Robinson.  In cancelling the contract, the mayor trumped City Council's September 14th approval of the contract and may have hindered the city's snow-removal program in the process.

headline: Disenchanted Voters: What's the Use?
abstract: Pennsylvania voters from Mercer County express displeasure over the current political climate and the candidates running for office in 1982.  Voters complain about everything from Social Security to foreign policy.

headline: Moving in the right direction
abstract: Kenneth E. Brandt, state House representative from the 98th District, Lancaster County, spoke about a 14% reduction in real spending over the last 3 years, reduction of around 5000 jobs in the state work force, and other issues. He noted these from the governor's budget proposal.

headline: Institutions Get $370 Million; PAT Allotted Subway Funds
abstract: Government Dick Thornburgh approved $370 million in appropriations for state-related universities and other state-aided educational, medical, and cultural institutions.  He also signed a capital budget bill containing $6 million for improvements to the Pittsburgh State Office Building and $3.2 million for PAT.

headline: Report approves drilling for gas in Lake Erie
abstract: The US Army Corps of Engineers has concluded that the drilling for natural gas beneath Lake Erie would be little threat to the environment.

headline: Crime: tougher penalties sought
abstract: The PA Commission on Sentencing proposed a new get-tough set of guidelines for sentencing criminals.  If the guidelines are followed, it would increase the average minimum prison sentence by 49%.  Additional statistics showed that judges in rural areas gave stiffer sentences than those in urban areas.

headline: HRA Opposes State Takeover of Properties at 3rd, Market
abstract: The PA Department of General Services lacks the legal authority to assume ownership of Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority properties at Third and Market streets and HRA should be permitted to continue ownership of the properties, according to preliminary objections the authority has filled in Dauphin County Court.  The department offered the authority $788,000 for the properties, which are to be the site of the third state office building.  Authority officials replied that they must reclaim the combined $2.4 million HRA invested in the properties.  Because of the $1.6 million gap, the department exercised announced its intention to take the properties through the power of eminent domain unless the authority responded.

headline: 300 Viet Vets Gather Here, Hear of Official 'Headway'
abstract: U.S. Senator Alan Cranston of California told a convention of Vietnam Veterans in Philadelphia that although many wound from that war are gone, many of the deepest and most painful wounds remain yet to be healed.  The Ssenator told the United Vietnam Veterans Organization (UVVO) that an organization funded on the positiveness of the Vietnam veteran is an important factor in the final healing process.

headline: Grocer to Governor?  Native Son Lew Lehrman
abstract: Lew Lehrman grew up in Harrisburg and made a fortune by helping to take a local family grocery business and turning it into the giant Rite Aid drugstore chain.  Now he is running for the Governor of New York and appears to be the frontrunner to become the Republican Nominee in New York Primary on September 23.

headline: Where military dollars are spent
abstract: Graph reprinted from U.S. News & World Report: Graphs shows regions of the nations, with comparisons of population, defense spending, and military jobs.

headline: 1,200 hear Democrats tear into Thornburgh
abstract: At the Democratic City Committee's fall fund-raising dinner, several candidates criticized sharply the policies of the Thornburgh administration and urged voters to elect the governor's opponent, Congressman Allen Ertel.

headline: Unemployment Key as Voters Cast Ballots
abstract: The outcome of today's gubernatorial election in Pennsylvania will determine if the state's high unemployment rate produced a critical mass large enough to oust the Thornburgh administration.  Polling indicates that Governor Thornburgh will surmount criticism and beat U.S. Representative Alen Ertel, who blamed the governor for the state's economic woes.

headline: Nation's governors wary of tax-sharing proposal
abstract: State governors are wary of the Reagan administration plan to increase federal gas and excise taxes and to turn a share of the proceeds over to the states.  The governors fear that Federal increases on tobacco, alcohol, and cigarettes would preempt revenue sources they regard as their own.  States can already increase these taxes themselves, so they do not see a need for increased federal taxes just to be given back to them.

headline: It's a Reasonable Contract but Reforms must Follow
abstract: The three year contract agreed to by Mayor Green and Federation of Teachers President John P. Murray was unanimously recommended by the federation’s executive committee Sunday. It awaits approval of the federation membership and the Board of Education, and has the potential to help turn a deficit-ridden and poorly managed school system around.  Whatever its shortcomings, and they apparently include the need for long-term borrowing, the contract is preferable by far to a third costly school strike in three years that nobody wanted in the Philadelphia public schools.

headline: Restart poll gets support
abstract: Cumberland County and Dauphin County residents will take a "grass-roots" poll in May to gauge public sentiment regarding the restart of the undamaged Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear reactor.  Public support of including the poll on the ballot has been overwhelming.  There will be further meetings to discuss the language of the question on the ballot.

headline: Criminal control
abstract: In this letter to the editor the writer disputes a previous letter written in support of U.S. Congressman Bill Coyne's pro-gun stand.  Instead, the writer believes, Congressman Coyne should be support stricter gun-control laws and tougher sentencing,

headline: HUD Secretary grabs a quick sandwich
abstract: Photo:  Housing and Urban Development Secretary Samuel Pierce grabs a quick bite to eat during a whirlwind whistlestop visit in Aliquippa.

headline: 75, Protesting Nuclear War, March to G.E. Space Center
abstract: About 75 people began a 20-mile walk from Center City to the General Electric Space Center in Valley Forge to mark the 37th anniversary of the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and to protest General Electric’s part in the production of nuclear arms.  Brandywine Peace Community, a Media-based peace group organized the work.

headline: Hack's election analysis
abstract: A reporter's conversation with a political hack reveals the hack believes people are more inclined to believe in their idea of government rather than reality, given that government is so far away. The so called hack also attributes the slim margin of votes collected by PA Governor Thornburgh against Allen Ertel to lack of interest in the election overall. The John Heinz vs. Cyril Wecht vote seemed to center on bigger issues, at least in the public's perception.

headline: With the future birght, Scranton stays on team
abstract: Current Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III will not run for re-election, or in any other campaign in 1982, as some had speculated.  Scranton was noted as being frustrated by shoddy treatment by the Thornburgh administration.  It was speculated that he should run again, especially due to the rumor that Dick Thornburgh may be offered a federal posting.

headline: District: Kolter leads Atkinson
abstract: A Pittsburgh Post-Gazette poll shows State Representative Joseph P. Kolter far ahead of incumbent U.S. Representative Eugene V. Atkinson in the 4th Congressional District Race.  Atkinson made national headlines last year when he changed his party affiliation from Democrat to Republican.

headline: Self-Serve Victory
abstract: Allegheny Common Pleas Judge Stephen Zapalla ruled that a ban on self-service gasoline stations in Pittsburgh amounted to unwarranted interference in business by government.  Pittsburgh City Council originally imposed the ban in 1978, but now has 180 days to draw new regulations to govern the operation of self-service stations.

headline: No tax increases included
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, stressing unemployment, unveiled a $13 billion state budget with no tax increases and new block grants to school districts.  He announced an array of job creation programs designed to combat unemployment and turn the Commonwealth's economy around.

headline: Judge halts midyear rise in tuition
abstract: Commonwealth Court Judge David Craig issued a preliminary injunction barring Pennsylvania from imposing a $75 mid-year tuition increase on students in Pennsylvania's 13 state universities.  Judge Craig ruled that the Board of State College and University Directors voted improperly on the tuition increase because some of the members were not notified that they were able to participate in the vote by conference call, with only 8 of 13 members casting votes.  The Commonwealth Association of Students, which called the increase unfair and illegal, is seeking to demonstrate that students have a contract with the state once they pay tuition and that the state cannot unilaterally revise it once the semester begins.

headline: Rich want to restart TMI
abstract: Letter to the editor: Writer claims that "rich business people with their investments" want to restart Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear reactor.

headline: Crisis in the Courts
abstract: The Chief Justice of the US Supreme Court, Warren E. Burger, said in New York the other day that the courts of this country were being overwhelmed by legal conflict and that the American system of justice "may literally break down before the end of this century."  He points not only to the increasing number of cases dumped on the courts, but the increasing complexity of the cases, many of them raising wholly novel legal issues in a revolutionary technical age and putting new burdens on judges and juries with insufficient time to deal with them.

headline: It Was Genuine Praise
abstract: Rev. Joseph N. Kakalec, president of the Philadelphia Council of Neighborhood Organizations (PCNO) was honored by 600 people at the Franklin Plaza Hotel.  He is leaving for a one year sabbatical.  He has been an outspoken community and neighborhood activist for 10 years in Philadelphia.  Shirley M. Dennis, Secretary of the State Department of Community Affairs and Mistress of Ceremonies, and City Managing Director W. Wilson Goode both made tributes to Kakalec.

headline: Changes in arms policy?
abstract: Senator Gary Hart (D-Colo) has suggested reforms for the nation's military services, similar in proportions to that enacted by Adm. Sir John Fischer in the British Navy, in the early part of the century. His suggestions were published in the Sunday edition of the New York Times

headline: Halt actions on elections - Walgren
abstract: US Representative Doug Walgren asked a federal judge to halt nominating proceedings for all political offices on the May 18 ballot.  He believes the proceedings should be stopped because the state legislature was unable to draw new congressional districts after the state lost two seats in the 1980 census.  The State Senate rejected 7 redistricting plans before adjourning on February 11.

headline: Zimmerman names Head of Criminal investigation
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman on Thursday announced the appointment of Thomas F. Gallagher, formerly chief of Delaware County Criminal Investigation Division, to head the Bureau of Criminal Investigation.

headline: The Duplicitous, Divisive Mr. Gray
abstract: Congressman William Gray III is a duplicitous and divisive voice in the black community.  He first showed his proclivity for divisive politics by destroying the political legacy of Philadelphia's first black congressman, Robert Nix Sr.  Gray's divisive tactics have continued in his efforts to smear his congressional opponent, T. Milton Street, and his attempt to install his choices for ward leaders in four different ward elections.

headline: Why subsidize boarding houses?
abstract: A much under-publicized referendum on Tuesday's ballot asks Pennsylvania voters if state funds previously authorized for nursing homes should also be used for loans to repair, reconstruct and rehabilitate boarding homes.  This article urges voters to vote no on the referendum; anyone who owns a boarding home and charges residents fees for services rendered has an obligation to provide proper facilities.

headline: Official: Taxes to help budget gap
abstract: Charles Mebus, Deputy Revenue Secretary said that the general tax revenues would exceed official estimates for April and make a dent in the $110 million shortfall in collections to date.

headline: Keep College Tuition as is, board says
abstract: The Commonwealth Association of Students supported the State College Board and University Director's recommendation, concurrent with the PA Department of Education's recommendation, not to raise tuition fees next year. Department fiscal administrator John Godlewski expects colleges will have more funds available for the year if the governor and legislature agree. PA Higher Education Commissioner James Gallagher maintained the quality of all programs would be maintained.

headline: Robot Trends Where People Can't at Three Mile Island
abstract: A miniature robot found high levels of radiation but no apparent damage in two cubicles in an auxiliary building at Three Mile Island, GPU Nuclear Inc. officials said.  The cubicles contain filters that were used to purify water in the reactor coolant system and were heavily contaminated with radioactivity in the March 1979 accident.  The inspection was the first step toward removing the filters.

headline: Critics Seek Ways to Better Compensate Pennsylvania Crime Victims
abstract: Critics are seeking better ways to compensate Pennsylvania crime victims.  There have been several attempts at trying to pass legislation to help crime victims.

headline: Let the Pedestrian: Everywhere Downtown People are Giving that 'Last Full Measure' of Patience
abstract: The downtown area in Pittsburgh was undergoing construction, which was blocking pedestrians from getting to work, lunch, stores, and to exit out of the Gold Mud puddle.  The entire place was a mess.  It’s discouraging for all those who had their individual routine figured down to the half-minute or so.  They’ve all had to add more time in their schedules for the whims of cranes and high lifts and the people who drive them.

headline: 'Dense Pack' MX Missiles, Reagan Urges
abstract: President Ronald Reagan proposed to deploy the MX missile in a string of Wyoming silos, then invited the Soviet Union to take several joint steps to abate fears of an accidental nuclear war.

headline: Hand-wringing won't help the jobless
abstract: Columnist George Fattman calls out legislators who appear to have done nothing to help 5,000 plus Altoona-Johnstown residents who have run out of workers compensation benefits. A proposal to tax state imports, Fattman says, is not only just a short term fix, but also unconstitutional.

headline: Voters Pick Nominees in 10 States: 6 governors', 4 U.S. Senate Races on Ballots
abstract: New Jersey as well as nine other states held primary elections.  In the process, Republicans and Democrats chose their candidates for six governorships and four U.S. Senate seats, including on of each in both California and Ohio.

headline: Wecht Asks For Unity Among Democrats
abstract: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Cyril Wecht, speaking at the annual Democratic City Committee dinner, said it was time for Pennsylvania Democrats to unite and get out the vote.  He sharply criticized Democratic party members who support Senator Heinz and Governor Thornburgh, and said PA Democrats, who outnumber registered Republicans in the state by 750,000, should be embarrassed that both U.S. Senators, the governor, and both houses of the Legislature are Republicans.

headline: Referendum: Vote Yes
abstract: This article urges voters to vote yes to the "Personal Care Boarding Home Referendum," which will use previously authorized state funds to repair, reconstruct and rehabilitate boarding homes.  The program involves no new money, and will provide boarding home owners with the resources to upgrade their properties so they meet Pennsylvania's new, tougher saftey standards.

headline: Officials See a Deficit as Possible
abstract: Officials see a deficit as possible in the Pennsylvania state budget.  Wilburn and Richard A. Stafford, Governor Dick Thornburgh’s secretary for legislative affairs, have suggested that revenue could be raised by closing tax loopholes, creating a video-game tax and perhaps starting off-track betting.  All three measures would require the approval of the General Assembly.

headline: Lawmaker calls on Pa. to fund student loans
abstract: PA Representative Nicholas Maiale introduced a bill for state powers to finance a new, low-interest students loan program to help families deal with rising tuition costs.  The loans would be targeted at low-to-middle income families.  The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency would be allowed to float interest-free bonds to provide the money for the loans.

headline: Ruling: TMI Costs on Penna., Towns
abstract: U.S. District Judge Sylvia Rambo cut off efforts by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and more that 1,000 municipalities to recover overtime and other expenses brought on by the 1979 nuclear accident at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant.  The state and townships had contended that they spent more than $1.5 million because of the accident and should be reimbursed under the federal Price-Anderson Act, an industry-financed $560 million nuclear insurance pool.  Judge Rambo said that the Price-Anderson Act covers individual expenses arising from nuclear accidents and that Congress expressed no concern for governmental expenses in amending the bill 16 years ago.

headline: DA to drop charges on 41 teachers
abstract: The district attorney's office plans to drop the 41 remaining contempt of court cases against teachers arrested for violating a mass picketing injunction, during last fall's school strike. The step was being taken in order to unclog the courts.

headline: No Sale for Green's Housing Aid Plan
abstract: City Council and community groups gave the Green Administration’s “new direction” for next year’s proposed $63.1 million Community Development a lukewarm response.  The proposed program would make Community Development housing money available citywide for the first time, instead of limiting the federal money to 44 specific neighborhoods.  Green says that the new proposal is consistent with Council Bill 1029AA, which requires 75 percent of Community Development expenditures to benefit very-low and low-income families.  A preliminary review by the Council’s technical staff found the new proposal not in compliance with the spirit of Bill 1029AA.  Hispanics have been short-changed by the Community Development Program.

headline: Eastern States Conference Held: VFW Leader Vows to Push Agent Orange Fight
abstract: Legislation to provide compensation to Vietnam veterans who believe their health has been impaired by the chemical defoliant Agent Orange has little chance of passage in the lame-duck session of Congress, the Commander-in-Chief of the Veterans of Foreign Wars said.  Similar legislation will be introduced in January, according to James R. Currieo.

headline: Harry Jannotti should take leave - without pay
abstract: Philadelphia Councilman Harry Jannotti was recently convicted of bribery and extortion in the Abscam sting.  While he was awaiting conviction, Jannotti asked Council to take a paid leave of absence.  City Comptroller Tom Leonard, on the other hand, notes that Jannotti is paid to legislate, and if he is not doing that, then he should not be paid.  Editorial agrees and says that Jannotti should take an unpaid leave.

headline: Voters' turnout lowest in decades
abstract: The primary election voting in Allegheny County and the state has been the lowest in decades, with only about 30% of the registered electorate bothering to vote. One of the reasons for this includes the number of candidates nominated without any opposition.

headline: In memory of the rascal justice
abstract: A triangle of land was dedicated yesterday to Dr. Nicholas More, the first speaker of the Pennsylvania Provincial Assembly.  He was also the first chief justice of the state and one of five commissioners appointed by William Penn to govern the Pennsylvania colony.  Upper and Lower Moreland Townships, as well as the Society Hill section of Philadelphia, are named after him.

headline: TMI Owner Rips N-Reactor Firm
abstract: An attorney for General Public Utilities Corporation, the operator of Three Mile Island, argued in federal court that the maker of the plant's nuclear reactors--Babcock and Wilcox--knew about the saftey hazard that led to the nation's worst nuclear power accident, but failed to issue a warning because they feared a plant shutdown.  The trial will determine responsibility for the Three Mile Island accident and set a precedent for future nuclear-power cases.

headline: On jobs: how bad is bad?
abstract: This article discusses Penn State's Pennsylvania Business Survey in connection with current unemployment trends. The unemployment rate has reached 11.2% for the Commonwealth. However, the article discusses positive trends such as the fact that in each month of 1981, more Pennsylvanians held jobs than ever before.  It concludes by saying that it is time for constructive action and not panic.

headline: Legislator Urges Inquiry On Head Start Charges
abstract: Representative Bill Pendleton, has called for an investigation of recent allegations that the Community Action Pittsburgh, Inc. had mismanaged federal Head Start funds.  Funds were cut off after Federal officials accused the agency of programmatic, fiscal and administrative deficiencies.  This resulted in a loss of about $3 million in federal funds for Pittsburgh’s Head Start Program.  More than 1,000 disadvantaged children would be affected by the loss of funds.

headline: Scranton says oil glut won't last
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton III warned not to become complacent about energy conservation after the recent drop in gas prices. Scranton also mentioned that he would campaign in the November elections along with Governor Thornburgh, despite their current riff.

headline: Death Penalty Needs Test
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court outlawed the death penalty in 1972 because these did not sufficiently guarantee fair application.  Now the U.S. Supreme Court will look at the question of whether it is constitutional to execute a child before a sentence is carried out for murder.

headline: Pennsylvania's rural poor: Invisible, but they exist
abstract: This article describes the living conditions of poor people in the rural areas. There are more than a quarter of million of them in Pa. It also talks about the lack of representation of this group of people and grim outlook of their future.

headline: Ertel, Walker To Fight Gap Job Cuts, Shifts
abstract: Plans by the U.S. Army to transfer jobs from the Fort Indiantown Gap Base to Fort Mead in Maryland are being opposed by U.S. Representative Robert Walker. U.S. Representative Allen Ertel is joining Walker in appealing the Army's decision. Ertel disputes the cost savings the Army says it will achieve noting two General Accounting Office reports that say it will cost the Army money instead. U.S. Representative-elect George Gekas argues that the facility is vital for the country's defense and is seeking a seat on the U.S. House Armed Services Committee in order to better fight the decision.

headline: Heinz asks 90-day delay in Crucible shutdown
abstract: John Heinz, R-Pa, has asked New York-based Colt Industries Inc. to delay any planned shutdown of it financially troubled Crucible Steel Division plant in Midland, Beaver County, Pa., for at least 90 days.

headline: Votes in Congress
abstract: A list of how each member of the U.S. Congress from Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Virginia voted for the week ending today.

headline: null
abstract: A brand-new shiploader and coal-dumping facility are beginning operations on the Delaware River today.  The shiploader and coal-dumping facility, located at Pier 124 in Philadelphia, are expected to increase commercial activity and improve the coal business in both Philadelphia and the state.  A ceremony was held to dedicate the pier, and Philadelphia Mayor Green and Governor Thornburgh were on hand.

headline: Getting Tough on Steel
abstract: Although European steel producers agreed to reduce their exports to the United States, experts say that such a reduction will not solve the long-term ills of the beleaguered steel industry.  America's steel mills are only operating at 40 percent capacity and roughly 300,000 steel workers are unemployed; increased demand will not solve the problem of chronic under capacity.

headline: Pa. Sales-Tax Revenues off 8% in July
abstract: State revenues in July 1982 from sales and use taxes were $5.1 million about 8 percent less than had been expected.  However, the overall state general fund revenues from various taxes and payments totaled $316.4 million in July which was $4.1 million above the official estimates.  It is hard to speculate why there was a deficit.

headline: New Cheyney President Hopes to Expand Enrollment
abstract: Cheyney State College inaugurated its fifth president.  One objective of his tenure will be to increase enrollment at the predominantly black Delaware County institution from about 2,000 toward the neighborhood of 3,000.

headline: Self-Serve Gas Still Possible, Two City Councilmen Suggest
abstract: Jim O’Malley said there is a possibility that self-service gas pumps can be introduced in Pittsburgh before long.  O’Malley will introduce legislation “as soon as legally possible” to put self-service gas to a referendum, possibly on the May ballot next year.  O’Malley sponsored a bill the previous month to end the city’s ban against self-service gas sales.  It failed by a narrow 5-4 vote.  Ben Woods and Tom Flaherty both voted against the bill, but said they are willing to change their votes if divorcement legislation, which prohibits oil companies from the retail sale of their product, were enacted.  However, the city Home Rule Charter prohibits the bill from being re-introduced until the next calendar year.

headline: Depopulating Death Row
abstract: By the latest count of the NAACP’s Legal Defense and Education Fund there were 958 prisoners under death sentence as of June 20.  Some 80 others have had their sentences overturned but the states involved have been trying to reimpose them.

headline: PHFA bonds to aid purchasers of homes
abstract: The Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency has sold $100 million in tax-free revenue bonds, with the proceeds to be used by private lending institutions to provide mortgages on low-to-moderate priced homes at below-market interest rates. This was announced by Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Europe tries to export nuclear phobia to US
abstract: Two Europeans came to Philadelphia this weekend to spread the message of nuclear disarmament. This movement is spreading rapidly in Europe where large segments of the public oppose plans, spearheaded by the United States and supported by its allies, to deploy a new generation of nuclear missiles.

headline: Heinz, Wecht OK 2nd Debate
abstract: U.S. Senatorial candidates John Heinz and Cyril Wecht have agreed to debate on radio station WGSA in Lancaster in a warm-up for their televised confrontation in Philadelphia.

headline: Votes in Congress
abstract: This specific article lists how area members of Congress voted on key issues in the Senate and House in Harrisburg.

headline: Judge Grants Stay of N-Plant Order
abstract: Commonwealth Court President Judge James Crumlish stayed a Public Utility Commission order telling the Philadelphia Electric Company (PECO) to scrap or delay construction of a second reactor at Limerick nuclear power plant.  The full Commonwealth Court will hear oral arguments on December 14th to determine if PECO must stop construction at the Limerick site.

headline: The Saftey of Nuclear Energy
abstract: As the U.S. Supreme Court decides whether psychological harm to nearby residents must be considered before Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor is permitted to restart, we hope that members of the bench realize concerns about horrible accidents at nuclear plant sites are considerably overblown.  The possibility of a worst-case scenario accident occurring is 2 in one million--thus showing that nuclear energy is as safe as any other energy source available today.

headline: Pa. tinkers with data on unemployment; aides say figures stress good news
abstract: Recent reports from the state's 11 regional labor-market analysts have been revised by public-relations officials to soften or omit bad news about Pennsylvania's employment picture. The analysts have also been instructed to not discuss economic trends with the media without the approval of their supervisors at the state Department of Labor and Industry in Harrisburg. This is in direct contrast to the earlier policy where analysts had directly given reports to the media.

headline: New school budget: Education hangs in the balance
abstract: The Board of Education currently faces a potential $112 million deficit in 1982-83. It now faces the delicate question of how big a gap City Council will agree to finance. If too much is asked, there might be no increase at all, as was the case last year. On the other hand, if the board cuts its budget, it could lead to another strike.

headline: Senate tries to direct PUC
abstract: The Senate passed a resolution yesterday saying the Public Utility Commission (PUC) cannot permit utilities to recoup their investment in power plants before the plants are finished. This will affect the ruling that the PUC will have deliver in May on Philadelphia Electric Co.'s request to charge customers $100 million annually in order to cover investments on the unfinished Limerick power plant.

headline: Deputy District Attorney Discusses Sentencing Guidelines at Crime Clinic
abstract: Joseph H. Kleinfelter, Dauphin County Chief Deputy District Attorney for investigations talked with Dauphin County District Attorney Howard Stewart, Sergeant Albert A. Conrad, President of the Crime Clinic of Greater Harrisburg, and Judith E. Ferguson before speaking to the clinic on the state’s new mandatory sentencing act and new sentencing guidelines.

headline: Philadelphia Needs an Economic Strategy
abstract: A comprehensive strategy worked out by the city administration with business and labor, reviewed and ratified by agencies of the state and federal governments and then well communicated and marketed can immeasurably improve Philadelphia’s attractiveness as a center of commerce and trade.

headline: Governor presents first POW plates to 10 vets
abstract: New commemorative license plates for Prisoners of War (POWs) are presented to the first 10 recipients of the plate by Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Here's how they voted; In Harrisburg; In Congress
abstract: This article details the various bills passed in the House and Senate at Harrisburg. It also details the various bills passed by Congress in the House and Senate.

headline: Votes in Congress" Last Week's Tally in Key Eastern States
abstract: null

headline: Campaign posters
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a resident complains that Camp Hill police officers were removing Allen Ertel posters from borough telephone poles.  The reader accuses the department and police chief of selectively removing Democratic political posters.  In its defense, the police department says a Camp Hill ordinance prohibits the posting of campaign material on utility poles.

headline: Top court to weigh fears of residents on restart of TMI
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to decide whether "fears of recurring catastrophe" must be considered before production resumes at Three Mile Island--the site of the nation's worst nuclear reactor accident.
