headline: Panel Approves Spending Bill
abstract: A state House-Senate conference committee approved a $203.5 million spending bill containing federal revenue-sharing money and additional state funds for state agencies.  The bill was approved 4-1 and sent to the House and Senate for final votes.  The legislation includes $201.8 million in federal revenue-sharing money that was anticipated for the commonwealth’s $13 billion 1982-83 budget.

headline: Not Deaf to Handicapped
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled that a New York school district is not required to provide a deaf student with a sign-language interpreter.  Although the child was holding her own in class and was afforded numerous special services, her parents argued that she could not full-fill her maximum academic potential without an interpreter.  The ruling serves two important functions.  First, it affirms the basic principle that handicapped youngsters must not be denied a free education.  And second, it correctly explains that public schools-already operating under severe financial constraints-realistically can only be expected to offer programs that provide “some educational benefit” for the handicapped.

headline: Senator Scores TMI Cleanup Plan
abstract: State Senator Robert Mellow said last week's low level alert at Three Mile Island is another grim reminder that cleanup of the damanged plant is proceeding too slowly.  At the same time, he criticized Governor Dick Thornburgh's much-touted cost sharing plan to fund the cleanup.  State monies paying for the cleanup have come from windfall tax profits from customers having to paying higher taxes as a result of higher energy rates.

headline: Detectives Assigned Role in Child Abuse Probe
abstract: An amendment to Act 124, the state’s child abuse statute, has called on the Country Detective Bureau to investigate child abuse cases involving homicide, sexual abuse or exploitation, serious bodily injury and repeated physical injury.  The amendment will allow country commissioners to review child abuse files.   The Act previously required all cases of child abuse to be reported to child welfare agencies and prohibited them from turning the chases over to the police.

headline: Poverty hits home in rural areas of Penna.
abstract: Pennsylvania has the 5th largest rural population in the United States, and over 250,000 of those people are living below the poverty level.  In urban areas, where the poor are more concentrated, they are able to speak with a more unified voice.  However, distance between people in the rural areas keeps their plight quiet and many do not take advantage of assistance programs to which they are entitled.

headline: Herbicide veterans to get help
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed into law yesterday legislation to create a Vietnam Herbicide Information Commission which will provide information to Pennsylvania veterans who may have been exposed to Agent Orange and other herbicides during their military service.

headline: Hiding the Names of State's Lawyers
abstract: Senator H. Craig Lewis asked Governor Dick Thornburgh for the names, salaries, and hiring dates of the lawyers who work for the state at a cost of millions of dollars.  Even though a Commonwealth Court ruling that ordered Thornburgh to give Lewis what he wants, it may be a long time before the information is ever handed over.

headline: Vowing 'No Figurehead', Scranton announces bid
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III announced that he was going to stand for re-election this year. He praised the Thornburgh administration and also fielded questions about their relationship, saying that they were going to run as a team in the upcoming elections..

headline: Thornburgh winner by 111,000 votes
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thorngurgh beat U.S. Representative Alen Ertel by 111,000 votes.  The article also lists four House incumbents who won county races.

headline: Penna. Revenue Lagging
abstract: Declining tax revenue as a result of the struggling economy is projected to be almost two hundred million dollars less than originally thought. The situation is aggravated by higher than projected welfare and unemployment compensation payments. Governor Thornburgh's staff while acknowledging the situation insists they were not in error. Initial projections were based on figures as they were at the time, in fact a number of projections were reduced becaused they seemed too high. The state hopes to regain some money through seizing inactive bank accounts and money in accounts that lapsed because they did not use their full allotment. Because the state constitution prohibits the state from operating in the red, Governor Thornburgh will have to find some way to make up the difference.

headline: Now it can be told: old folks' gossip is a family treasure
abstract: Old people reminiscing is being encouraged as a form of oral history, and is being valued by folklorists as a way to preserve the past.  The Office of Folklife Programs at the Smithsonian Institution gathers and preserves stories older people tell.

headline: Shutdown of Indian Point 3 Extended By Tube Corrosion
abstract: The Power Authority of the State of New York said that the Indian Point 3 nuclear power plant will remain closed until at least the fall.  The reason is because of corrosion of steam-generator tubes.  X-rays revealed cracks as well as a hole in the steam generator.  Plant operators will propose solutions to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission so the tubes can be fixed.  If not, then they can be very harmful to the environment.

headline: Doomed Men: A Deadly Wait
abstract: PA's death row inmates have been moved from the general prison population to an isolated section of their respective prisons where their former privileges are curtailed. The state prison system argues it's a way to deal with overcrowding and ensure that prisoners with 'nothing to lose' can't escape. The American Civil Liberites Union (ACLU) claims that preventing prisoners from working, reducing their access to phone calls, and allowing them to exercise outdoors once a day is a violation of their rights, and they have filed suit accordingly.

headline: Reagan's plan hasn't reached Congress
abstract: Pennsylvania officials are looking into "Urban Enterprise Zones," a plan that President Ronald Reagan will be sending to Congress that would offer substantial tax benefits for businesses locating in economically depressed areas.  The City of Philadelphia has already identified its enterprise zones should the program become available, and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has offered state assistance in preparing applications.

headline: House Rejects MX Funds
abstract: The U.S. House voted to remove from a defense spending bill almost one billion dollars for the first five MX missiles. President Reagan called the vote "a grave mistake" and vowed to continue fighting for it while the Department of Defense was hopeful the funding could be approved in the U.S. Senate and then in a House-Senate conference bill. Critics, such as U.S. Representative Joseph P. Addabbo, believe it is too expensive and its basing system will not work. The article included a list of Western PA members of the U.S. House who voted for and against it.

headline: High court gets redistricting plea
abstract: State Senator Richard Tilghman has asked the PA Supreme Court to reconsider its approval of PA's new reapportionment plan because he said it is unconstitutional.  Tilghman said his district was divided into two parts with a gap of six-tenths of a mile between them, violating the constitutional requirement that districts be compact and contiguous.

headline: Wage tax cut bill may come to pass; city polls fear wage tax cut may come to pass
abstract: There is a possibility that the General Assembly will reduce the wage tax for commuters who live outside Philadelphia. In order to make up for this lost revenue, Senators Philip Price, R-Philadelphia and Henry Hager, R-Lycoming, are urging city officials to change the city's tax structure.

headline: Brightbill Outspends Foe
abstract: According to the latest data, Republican David Brightbill had spent more than his Democratic opponent, John Anspach, in the 48th Senatorial District race.  The article lists all of the campaign contributors for each candidate, as well as the monies spent, account balances, and contributors for several other statewide races.

headline: Defeated Street Not at a Loss for Words
abstract: PA State Senator Milton Street remained undaunted after losing to U.S. Representative William Gray by more than a 3 to 1 margin.  In fact, Senator Street announced his candidacy for Congress in the Spring of 1984 to campaign workers attending a post-election party.

headline: Reagan budget said to show large deficits through '84
abstract: The budget that President Ronald Reagan will be presenting to Congress on February 8 projects federal deficits for each year through 1984.  In the previous summer, however, President Reagan was projecting a balanced budget by 1984.  Administration projections also show that while there will be an economic recovery, unemployment rates are expected to stay high.  Gross National Product is also expected to remain flat.

headline: O'Pake bill allows colleges to offer deferred-payment plans
abstract: Senator Michael O' Pake introduced legislation that would allow public and private colleges and universities in Pennsylvania to offer deferred-payment plans for tuition, fees, and room and board.

headline: Sketch Shows How TMI Inspection Was Performed
abstract: Reporters were shown a 14-minute section of a videotape during a briefing regarding the incident that happened on Three Mile Island.  James Thiesing, project manager for Bechtel Corp., said 90 percent of the two-hour tape was murky because of the cloudy reactor coolant in which the camera was immersed during the taping.  The rubble that was viewed by the camera is believed to be the remains of the fuel assembly tubes that held uranium fuel inside the reactor.

headline: 'Double Celling' in Prisons
abstract: The population in Pennsylvania prisons increased by more than 14 percent in 1981.  Some 5,135 persons were incarcerated and the average length of sentence increased slightly from 26.5 months to 26.8 months.  The rise in the prison population caused corrections officials to double cell some prisoners at all institutions for the first time.  A report from the Bureau of Corrections shows a dramatic increase in violent incidents after double celling of prisoners.  Most lawmakers and taxpayers probably thought that legislative approved last year of the construction of 2,380 new prison cells would end the problem, but this is not as easy and cheap as one may think.

headline: Rebuttal: Debra Reed
abstract: Pittsburgh's group home ordinance was enacted in September 1980.  This law recognizes that we should accept group homes into our neighborhoods.  It also recognizes that we should preserve the residential character of our communities.  City Council must approve new group homes.  It must also approve established homes which did not legally exist before the ordiance was enacted.  The Whale's Take Home in Shadyside has never qualified for legal occupancy as a group home.

headline: Jumping on the nuke ban-wagon
abstract: Although Senator Arlen Specter has carefully stayed out of the spotlight, he turned it all around when he criticized President Reagan's policies on the nuclear weaponry.

headline: His excellency
abstract: The newspaper believes that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's new welfare bill is a bad one.

headline: Wage tax cut fails; But Sen. Street's vote keeps bill alive
abstract: Opponents of a bill that would reduce the wage tax for Pennsylvanians who commute to Philadelphia have won the battle in the Senate but lost a chance to win it, thanks to state Sen. Milton Street. The Republican said that his vote will get the bill out of the current deadlock.

headline: Would the real potholes stand up
abstract: Recently, Pennsylvania Democrats have criticized Governor Thornburgh's record on highway maintenance.  This criticism is ironic because highway maintenance is one of the areas in which the administration has made notable advances and achievements.

headline: Reagan policies/state impact
abstract: WILK radio, Wilkes-Barre, PA editorial: Immediate problems come from the sudden curtailment of federal grants and subsidies.  Reduced block grants replaced existing categorical grants and federal tax cuts.  Because state rates were tied to federal rates, this also cut into state revenues. The existance of these new block grants also has created a new state bureaucracy to decide how best to administer the grants.

headline: Open Philadelphia's Public Schools
abstract: In Philadelphia, the school board and the teachers union are negotiating again.  For the past two years, the Philadelphia school district has gone on strike.  The students can't afford another strike.  The strike will affect not just them but also the city and parents.

headline: 'Squeeze' on independence gas station dealers probed
abstract: The Governor's Energy Council is investigating charges that major oil companies are squeezing independent service station operators out of business in Pennsylvania. The allegations were raised during a Senate committee hearing on legislation that would require oil companies to sell off service stations they own.

headline: Drunk Driving Bill Is Signed
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed a drunk driving bill into law yesterday. It may be the toughtest such law in the country with first-time offenders being place in the general prison population, blood alcohol level being set at point one zero, and a new offense "homocide by vehicle" with a minimum three year sentence being created. While he is satisfied with the new blood alcohol limit, Thornburgh is concerned with the reliability of equipment used to make that determiniation as well as the mandatory minimum prison terms, which he believes should be a last rather than first resort, along with the possiblity of such offenders serving their terms in the general prison population rather than in separate minimum security prisons..

headline: Scranton Calls Centralia Fire 'Desperate'
abstract: Lieutenant William Scranton III said that the state would continue to press the federal government for aid to resolve the Centralia mine fire.  Scranton, in his first trip to the Columbia County community, toured the area affected by the mine.  The Lieutenant Governor said the Interior Department still refuses to discuss the Commonwealth’s request that the federal government fund 75 percent any future project to extinguish or abate the 20-year-old underground blaze.

headline: More jobs shaping up at Navy Yard? Navy may ship more jobs to city
abstract: Due to successful work on the USS Saratoga in Philadelphia, the Navy has announced plans for multi-billion dollar overhaul of four more careers. This is good news for the Philadelphia Navy Yard as it could mean lucrative contracts and jobs.

headline: Hochendoner weighs race for Congress
abstract: Dauphin County Minority Commissioner Lawrence J. Hochendoner confirmed that he is considering running for Congress from the 17th District in the May primary. Hochendoner also mentioned that his candidacy was being funded by Democratic leaders and political action committees.

headline: Wage Tax Cut Voted Down..But Not Out
abstract: The Senate rejected, but kept alive, a bill that would slash the Philadelphia wage tax from 4.3 to 2.9 percent for people who live in Pennsylvania suburban counties and work in the city.  It was the second time the Senate has defeated the bill, which was passed by the House in March.  It failed in the Senate on a 24-24 vote in April.  Proponents of the bill, primarily Republicans, claim it is unfair to force suburban Pennsylvania commuters to pay the full wage tax because they do not use city services.

headline: Death Penalty: Soceity's only Defense
abstract: Although the Civil Liberties Union wishes to abolish the death penalty, they and other opponents fail to consider the impact that the death penalty has on criminal activity.  It is our best defense against future crime and statistics bear this out; we need to start thinking about the true victims of "cruel and unusual punishment."

headline: Rep. Marks hits 'voodoo economics'
abstract: in a speech given today, Republican Representative Lincoln Marks called for an end to the "Reagonomics massacre" and castigated the President about his belief in Hooverism. The administrations refusal to re-evaluate its economic policies caused him to speak out.

headline: PA college students billed $75
abstract: State education officials approved an emergency $75 increase in tuition for students in PA state colleges to help offset unexpected, rising operating costs and to pay a fee for back pay to faculty.  The Commonwealth Association of Students is challenging the increase.

headline: Survey To Learn Who Will Be Left In The Cold
abstract: The Public Utility Commission (PUC) is trying to find out how many PA residents have had their heat disconnected between April and November. The PUC wants utilities to exercise restraint in disconnecting heat during the winter, including requiring them to meet with delinquent customers and negotiating repayment before doing so.

headline: Editorial: Child Abuse
abstract: This editorial looks at the new child abuse law that allows law enforcement agencies access without a court order to confidential case records in investigations of when it involves homicide, sexual abuse, serious bodily injury or abuse perpetrated by those who are not member of the child’s family was passed.  Credit should go to Governor Dick Thornburgh and Senator George W. Gekas of Harrisburg, who was the prime sponsor of the bill.

headline: Self Assessments
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners have a new plan to fix the property assessment process: do it yourself.  You fill out a card in which you answer basic questions about your home, you give your home an approximate value, then you turn in the card.  The plan requires legislative approval, but is believed to be a good plan.

headline: Navy's Cargo-Ship Contracts Give Boost to 3 Companies
abstract: The Navy has chosen three companies to provide as many as 13 cargo ships for military use, creating thousands of jobs, more than $800 million in modernization contracts and the difference between life and death for some troubled United States shipyards.  The awards went to Maersk Lines, General Dynamics Corp.’s Quincy, Mass., shipyard and Waterman Steamship Corp.

headline: Hotline Success
abstract: Pennsylvania Treasurer Budd Dwyer has been bragging about the success of the special government hotline to report waste.  Dwyer says a millions have been saved since he set up the telephone snitching system.  Most of the informants are "average citizens,"according to the treasurer.  A vast majority are not knowledgeable about government operations.  So one has to wonder what kind of reports we could get from insiders.

headline: Wait and see
abstract: A new bill is to be introduced in the House, marking another term to curb abortions in Pennsylvania. The governor rejected last year's bill because he saw many fatal conflicts with existing court rulings, prompting the draft of an entirely new bill. Although this bill makes sense, implementing it immediately will be tough due to present court challenges.

headline: TMI hearing to seek effects of cheating
abstract: At a November 9th hearing in Harrisburg, PA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) will be particularly interested in determining to what extent test cheating by Three Mile Island (TMI) reactor operators reflects upon the competence, attitude and integrity of General Public Utilities Nuclear Corporation.  The management competence question is one of three questions the NRC wants answered before they decide whether to restart the Unit 1 reactor of TMI.

headline: Among Phila. Voters, Gut Feelings and Indecision
abstract: This article gets the opinions of Philadelphia voters on the 1982 elections.  Most voters expressed frustration with state, local and national politicians and candidates.

headline: Revenues short by $58 million
abstract: The Thornburgh administration said yesterday that state revenues will be about $58 million below official estimates towards the end of fiscal year 1982. However, the spokesman said that this shortfall does not mean that the state will face a budget deficit.

headline: Posvar: More aid or more tuition
abstract: University of Pittsburgh Chancellor Wesley W. Posvar yesterday said that Pitt would probably have to raise its undergrad tuition by $88 to $118 per semester this fall, if Gov. Thornburgh's proposed 5.8 percent funding increase for the state-related university is adopted.

headline: Take a hard look at Med-Ed bills
abstract: Letter: The writer believes that York County legislators, both at the state and federal levels, have done nothing to keep their electric rates from going higher after the Three Mile Island accident, but have spent taxpayer dollars to prevent Metropolitan-Edison from going out of business.  The Public Utilities Commission also needs to be cleaned up.  It is clearly a partnership between the utilities and the companies.

headline: Editorial: Specter Has a Cure
abstract: The proposal that US Senator Arlen Specter put forth would limit the plea of insanity as a defense in criminal cases, by putting the burden of proof on the defense to show that the accused was in fact insane at the time of the crime.  In the Hinckley case, the judge instructed the jury that the prosecution had to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the would be assassin was sane when he fired the shots.  With expert witnesses for the prosecution saying Hinckley was sane and experts for the defense saying he was crazy as a loon, the jury found it impossible to say that the prosecution’s witnesses were right and the defense’s wrong.  After all, nobody really knows.

headline: Shadyside Group Wants Home for Boys Closed
abstract: The Shadyside Action Coalition called on City Council to close the Whale’s Tale, a group home for eight juvenile boys.  The coalition contend that the youths from the home are noisy, profane, and have come home in drunken stupors, ruining the neighborhood’s residential appeal.  The Whale’s Tale asked the city to approve their application for a “pre-existing use” as a group home.  They said the home should be permitted because it was in place prior to the passage in 1980 of a restrictive group home ordinance.

headline: 'No' to Vote on Freeze
abstract: The request for a referendum in Dauphin County regarding a freeze on development, testing, production, and deployment of nuclear weapons should have been surprising given the publicity surrounding the vote on the question of restarting Three Mile Island Unit 1.  Organizations, such as the Pennsylvania Campaign for Nuclear Weapons Freeze, would better serve their cause by concentrating their efforts in that direction.  Dauphin County Commissioner Norman P. Hetrick notes, placing the freeze question on the ballot could open the floodgates for a variety of issues.

headline: House bill 1824
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author suggests that HB 1824 would cut many services for special needs citizens.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh is believed to be trying to push this bill through the Senate for a vote.

headline: Waldman lawyer-hiring data is offered to Lewis
abstract: Counsel General Jay Waldman has informed PA Senator H. Craig Lewis that the Thornburgh Administration is prepared to turn over documents regarding state hiring of lawyers.  Sen. Lewis made the request 5 months ago.  The offer came 13 days before arguments before a Commonwealth court on a motion by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and Waldman to dismiss a suit filed by Lewis to overturn said documents.

headline: Vote yes for boarding homes
abstract: The Philadelphia Inquirer recommends a yes vote to the statewide ballot question.  The "Personal Care Boarding Home Improvement Referendum" will use 50 million dollars of previously authorized nursing-home funds to provide low-interest loans for the repair, rehabilitation and reconstruction of personal care boarding homes.

headline: Gray surges to a third House term
abstract: U.S. Representative William H. Gray won a third congressional term yesterday by defeating state Senator Milton Street.

headline: Save steelworkers
abstract: The Pittsburgh region has more than 2000 unemployed steel workers. These people are unsure of their future, with unemployment benefits fast running out. The government must step in to increase the unemployment benefits and ease the situation for the unemployed.

headline: Parents Put Out Over High Suspension Rate
abstract: Students in Philadelphia are being suspended at a rate three times the national average, according to a study conducted by the Parents Union for Public Schools.  The suspension rate for minority students is 18 percent, while the rate for whites is 10.8 percent and the gap is widening.  Schools with a low rate had parents that were active in school affairs and the emphasis of the school’s principal and staff was on instruction rather than control.  Schools with a high rate of suspension were characterized by an inactive Home and School Association, and suspensions used to establish standards or enforce control over students.  Suspensions were used to get the parent to come to school to talk about a student or as punishment for a repeated minor offense.

headline: Team To Study Psychological, Medical Effects Of TMI
abstract: A six million dollar Three Mile Island (TMI) Public Health Fund, taken from the twnety-five million dollar TMI settlement, will be established to protect those living and working near the damaged reactor. The fund will pay for research into the health effects of the TMI accident, health effects of low-level radiation exposure, improved monitoring of TMI facilities, improved accident preparedness at the plant, and a program to educate the public on lessons learned from the accident. It will be led by Dr. Karl Z. Morgan.

headline: Eight Graterford  guards hurt in melee
abstract: 8 guards at Graterford Prison were injured yesterday during a struggle with armed inmates, started when an inmate tried to carry a tray of food back to his cell.  When the struggle began, the rest of the prison was put on lock-down, but 35-50 inmates of cell block C refused to return.  An undecided number of inmates may be charged with additional crimes.

headline: Spectrum Prospers in Electronic Age
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton III was on hand when Spectrum Control Inc. announced the purchase of an old department store building to expand its services.  This will create 355 new jobs in Erie and Crawford countries.  It will create a new product that will enable manufacturers to meet new Federal Communications Commission emission standards.  Spectrum Control has applied for U.S. and worldwide patents for the connector.  Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority will provide a low-interest loan to the projects.

headline: Please for peace; In center city, a rally for nuclear disarmament
abstract: At about 11 am, about 200 people, demanding a halt to the nuclear arms race, stepped off the corner of Walnut and 18th Streets and conducted a peaceful march through the streets of the city to JFK Plaza.

headline: House Ignores Veto Threat, Oks Housing Bill
abstract: The House of Representatives ignored a veto threat and shouted its approval of a compromise $3 billion housing stimulus plan aimed at making it easier for low- and middle income Americans to buy new homes.  Under the legislation, the government would subsidize mortgage rates on new homes by up to 4 percentage points.  Homebuyers with family incomes of up to $30,000- $60,000 in high-cost areas would be eligible for the subsidies.  President Ronald Reagan opposes the plan on grounds it represents a budget-busting bailout of one industry.

headline: Walgren: Rostenkowski hid tax break
abstract: Rep. Doug Walgren, D-Mt, said that he and other members of Congress are being criticized for passing juicy tax breaks, when they had no idea what they were voting on. They allege that the chairman of the tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee, Dan Rostenkowski, doctored his remarks in the Congressional Record to make it appear that he told the House about tax breaks for Congress tucked away in a black-lung bill, last December.

headline: For state Assembly: James Greenwood…
abstract: The Bucks County Courier Times endorses incumbent state Representative Jim Greenwood for the 143rd Assembly District.  In his first two years, Representative Greenwood has shown his legislative practicality, his responsivness to constitutents, and an overall ability to get things done.

headline: Rocks wins three-way Fourth Senate District Race
abstract: M. Joseph Rocks, a Democratic state representative, beat incumbent Republican state Senator Philip Price Jr. in the race for the city's Fourth District Senate seat.  The Fourth District seat was considered crucial to both Democrats and Republicans, as both parties hoped to win control of the state Senate; Republicans controlled 26 of 50 Senate seats with 25 at stake in this election.

headline: School funding figures revised due to 'mistakes'
abstract: There was a revision in the budget figures for school funding due to "mistakes" which specifically involved the inclusion of $12 million in the 1981-82 budgets for vo-tech schools and the exclusion of $3 million for authority rentals. The new numbers show an increase for the various school districts.

headline: Parents, Teachers protest education funding plan
abstract: Around 100 teachers and parents rallied outside Governor Thornburgh's mansion, to protest his administration's spending proposal for education. The teacher's union has charged that Thornburgh's proposed $127 million education block grant is actually a front for under funding school districts.

headline: The only result remains fear
abstract: Employees have returned to work at the Ginna Nuclear Power Plant after a recent incident.  As was also the case with the Three Mile Island accident, the worst commercial nuclear accident in history, no one was harmed.  However, a resulting negative effect has been fear of "mental stress."

headline: Elderly shield; State senate passes stiff penalties for crimes against aged
abstract: For the first time, penalties with respect to crimes against the aged have been passed unanimously by the Senate. The legislation, sponsored by Sen. James J. Rhoades, R-Mahanoy City, now goes to the PA House of Representatives.

headline: Stadium
abstract: The City of Pittsburgh is considering a plan to take over the operation and maintenance of Three Rivers Stadium from the Pittsburgh Pirates.  If Council approves the proposal, then the stadium will get a complete overhaul.  The City is looking for ten year financial commitments, at $100,000 a year, from twelve corporations.  The taxpayers’ contribution will increase by $600,000 a year to $1.8 million.  The $600,000 increase will not be as bad since the City will generate more money for itself once it takes over the stadium.  The plan’s biggest criticism is the charge the Pirates are running out on the forty year lease they signed when the stadium opened.  The Pirates, however, feel the Stadium was constructed poorly.  The engineers and architects working on the Stadium have never said the job was done according to their specifications.  To avoid a drawn-out legal battle that either side could have lost, the City and the Pirates decided to negotiate, and rightly so.

headline: Recognition: Panel Recommends A Plaque to Honor City's Vietnam Vets
abstract: With the support of several veterans groups, the City Council Committee on Public Property in Philadelphia unanimously approved a bill to establish a plaque in City Hall courtyard memorializing those residents who served in the armed forces during the Vietnam era.  The hearing was timed to coincide with the convention of the United Vietnam Veterans Organization in Philadelphia.

headline: House Oks Early Retirement for Teachers
abstract: The House passed and sent to Governor Dick Thornburgh legislation that will allow some veteran teachers to take early retirements.  The bill could save school districts $72 million if the governor signs it.  It would give public school teachers who are at least 55 years old with 25 or more years’ experience a one-time option to retire this summer without loss of pension benefits.  Those with 25 years of service but between 50 and 55 years old could take early retirement, but their pension benefits would be reduced by 3 percent annually.

headline: Wecht Gets Apology in Philly
abstract: U.S. Senator Alan Cranston (D-CA) has apologized to Cyril Wecht for writing off Wecht’s U.S. Senate candidacy in a few offhand remarks to reporters.  He also emphasized that he is supporting various Democratic senatorial nominees including Wecht.

headline: Fear and Loathing in the Rust Bowl
abstract: In Beaver Falls, PA, Congressman Eugene Atkinson has become the scapegoat for Reaganomics and high unemployment.  Workers in this depressed steel town have labeled Atkinson a traitor and vowed to make him pay for their economic plight.  The most recent polls show Congressman Atkinson trailing 16 points behind his challenger, Joe Koltner.

headline: Republicans Win 3 on West Shore
abstract: Three incumbent Republicans--John Kennedy, Bruce I. Smith and Harold F. Mowery--won re-election in West Shore legislative races yesterday; Democrat John Broujos won in the newly created 199th legislative district.

headline: Schweiker Stumps for Tax Bill
abstract: Richard S. Schweiker, secretary of Health and Human Services, launched a cabinet-level blitz to press for congressional support of President Reagan’s $99 billion tax increase.  The proposed tax increase is needed to bring down interest rates and help the economy.  50 percent of the tax package is designed to close and tighten loopholes.  The bill would implement the budget resolution passed by Congress calling for $3 in federal spending reductions for every $1 in higher revenues in order to bring down the deficit.  Reagan’s proposal would reduce the federal budget deficit by $380 billion over the next three years.

headline: Penn State sets up special admissions
abstract: Pennsylvania State University has created a special program starting March 11 to admit high school seniors would lose Social Security benefits if they have not enrolled in full-time college by May 1.  This one time program covers all 19 Penn State campuses and will admit up to 2000 students, making it the largest such program in the country.

headline: Undamaged Reactor's Stability In Earthquake A New Concern
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has held up a vote on whether to rescind the orders shutting down Three Mile Island's (TMI) two reactors until details of a new report about TMI's ability to withstand an earthquake is released.

headline: Elderly shield; State senate passes stiff penalties for crimes against aged
abstract: For the first time, penalties with respect to crimes against the aged have been passed unanimously by the Senate. The legislation, sponsored by Sen. James J. Rhoades, R-Mahanoy City, now goes to the PA House of Representatives.

headline: State gives little help in crisis at Crucible plant
abstract: Although the Thornburgh administration made claims that its policies helped create thousands of new jobs for Pennsylvanians, they are unable to prove the creation of those jobs. However, the editorial states that the administration could do a lot more to save jobs by getting involved in the sale of Colt Industries unit in the Beaver County. By helping obtain a good purchaser, there is potential to save 4500 jobs.

headline: Sound Off: Legion, VFW
abstract: The American Legion has taken strong exception to the proposal by the National Academy of Sciences that there be a delay in starting a major study on the health effects of Agent Orange until preliminary results are available from an Air Force study of crews who sprayed the defoliant from planes over Vietnam.  Meanwhile, the Veterans of Foreign Wars is calling for legislation to be introduced in Congress which would authorize compensation for those Vietnam veterans exposed to Agent Orange and other herbicides who have service connected diseases and disabilities.

headline: House Votes to Return To $3,000 Deduction
abstract: The House of Representatives took a first step toward revoking its new business expense tax break.  Members voted 356-43 to return a $3,000 cap to their tax deduction on work-related expenses.

headline: What others say
abstract: Reprinted from the Standard-Speaker, Hazelton, PA:  If a reapportionment plan is not signed by February 16, Pennsylvania's Congressmen will be elected " at large", meaning there will be a statewide contest for all 23 districts.  The loss of districts reflects the fact that, even though Pennsylvania's population has increased, other portions of the country have increased considerably more.

headline: Heinz sees Wecht's SS cure a peril
abstract: Yesterday, U.S. Senator John Heinz labeled dangerous a suggestion by his Democratic opponent, Cyril Wecht, favoring taxing Social Security benefits for recipients with high incomes.  Senator Heinz says he strongly opposes taxing social security benefits at any income level.

headline: Lehrman Holds Early Lead
abstract: Republican Lewis Lehrman was edged out by Mario Cuomo in the New York gubernatorial race.  President Reagan's economic policies, particularly his supply-side approach to economics, figured prominently in the race.  Lehrman promised to bring the president's economic policies to the Empire State.

headline: Senate Oks Budget; Battle Over Taxes, Cuts Still Ahead
abstract: The Senate approved a $770-billion federal budget for 1983 that cut $12 billion in domestic spending cuts and $21 billion in tax increases and trims $7 million from Reagan’s requested increase in military spending.  The Congressional Budget Office estimates the budget is $116 billion in read—double the 1981 deficit.  Democrats approved the budget resolution.  Budget resolutions do not require the president’s signature.

headline: Penna. House passes bill to aid military recruitment
abstract: The PA House passed a bill sponsored by Representative Gregg Cunningham that would require all secondary schools to provide military recruiters with the addresses and home phone numbers of graduating high school seniors.  Previously, the state had no law compelling schools to aid military recruiters.

headline: US may dispose of damaged TMI reactor
abstract: The Federal Department of Energy is working on a plan to dispose of the entire damaged reactor core at Three Mile Island, dropping its earlier opposition to taking full responsibility. This was announced by Gov. Thornburgh.

headline: Elusive solutions in housing
abstract: The author of this letter to the editor is concerned about the housing situation in Montgomery County, and in particular Norristown.

headline: The city is gaining some jobs
abstract: Recently, 5 firms previously located in the suburbs have decided to relocate to the city with the help of some creative financial arrangements at the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation.  This is opposite the trend of jobs being moved to the suburbs and out of the area completely.

headline: Specter at Chester shipyard to aid campaign for the Iowa
abstract: Sen. Arlen Specter (R-Pa) visited the grounds of the Pennsylvania Shipbuilding Co., in order to obtain information for the campaign to bring the $300 million refurbishing of the battleship Iowa to Chester. Specter said that this contract would create a 1000 jobs and help preserve the nation's shipbuilding business.

headline: How GOP got egg on its face
abstract: The Republican State Committee was so certain that its Supreme Court candidate, Superior Court Judge, James Cavanaugh, would win, that it did nothing to support him. Finally, it was embarrassed when an obscure judge from Berks County, Forrest Schaeffer had one the seat.

headline: What others say
abstract: The mine fire in Centralia, PA has been going to 20 years, with very little being done about it.  Families took out ads in local papers reminding people to keep pressing the issue.  In the meantime, 27 families were relocated because of the noxious fumes from the fire under a project sponsored by the state and federal government.  Reprinted from the Bloomsburg Morning Press.

headline: Expressway may get federal OK
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has asked the Federal Highway Administration (FHA) to certify completion of the Allegheny Valley missing-link project as a saftey and air quality improvement for Allegheny County.  FHA certification is the first step in qualifying for an exemption from U.S. District Judge Louis Bechtle, who imposed a freeze on federal highway funds for Pennsylvania because of the state's failure to comply with a 1978 consent decree to implement an auto-emissions inspection program.

headline: Dougherty is fighting to keep seat
abstract: In a close race against three term state representative Robert A. Borski, U.S. Representative Charles F. Dougherty was fighting for his political life.  After early returns, it appeared that Borski's television commercials linking Representative Dougherty to the economic policies of the Reagan administration were working.

headline: So, What Spending Do You want to Cut?
abstract: President Ronald Reagan’s argument for the only way to balance the budget is to cut spending and that if Congress won’t do it, the public will have to, through Reagan’s proposed constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget.  Chairman James R. Jones of the House Budget Committee told the recent National Governors Conference that if the amendment sailed through Congress this year, and through 38 state legislatures next year, it would prevent new taxes to help balance the budget

headline: Pennsylvania's education funding needs
abstract: Photo:  Research DirectorBill Hughes of the Pennsylvania State Education Association outline the state's education funding needs for the next year.  The pitch for increased support comes 5 days before Governor Dick Thornburgh's funding address.

headline: This is a Test, and Only a Test: Hot Time at Three Mile Island
abstract: In an annual test of their ability to respond to a full-scale emergency, nuclear power-plant workers and state and federal officials ran through a stimulated accident at the nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island that ended with Unit 1 ostensibly being eased slowly toward a cold shutdown, its reactor core severely damaged by a loss of vital cooling water.

headline: Equal Justice for All
abstract: Perhaps we can take Governor Thornburgh's recent assurance the state will continue to contract for legal aid through Pennsylvania Legal Services Corporation to mean an end to the not-too-subtle effort to terminate the program by turning its funding over to a county option.

headline: Town Receives Federal Funds
abstract: The Borough of Pottstown, Montgomery County, received a $3 million federal grant to aid the expansion of Knoll International Inc., Governor Dick Thornburgh announced.  The federal grant is in addition to a $1 million loan for the firm by the Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority.  Thornburgh estimated the expansion would create more than 400 new skilled jobs in the Pottstown area over the next three years.

headline: State bill seeks a vote on freeze for N-weapons
abstract: Pennsylvania voters will be asked to vote yes or no in the November election on whether there should be a nuclear weapons freeze or not. This is present in the bill introduced by Rep. Robert W. O'Donnel, D-Philadelphia.

headline: How is Pennsylvania faring under Reagan's federalism?
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh claims that Pennsylvania is transitioning very well into the first phases of President Ronald Reagan's new federalism.  Thornburgh officials state the fast start made on last year's revamping of many federal-aid programs into the new block grant format.  Democrats insist that this is just a complicated budget-balancing act by the Thornburgh administration.

headline: Where the Democrats Clean Up
abstract: The pickup of seven governorships by Democrats should be cause for concern for Reagan in the upcoming presidential election. But for now, it simply means white house policies and attempts to campaign will be opposed by 34 of the 50 governors. In PA, Governor Richard Thornburgh won over opponent Representative Allen Ertel after a tougher than expected race.

headline: Better deals in vote buying
abstract: In this letter to the editor,  Sheik al-Fassi is criticized for asking Midland residents to sign a petition promising to vote against Ronald Reagan.  The writer calls this request bad form, but suggests al-Fassi's real error was not the petition; he simply picked the wrong town.

headline: Goode set to resign
abstract: Philadelphia city managing director Wilson Goode is resigning his post and plans to run for mayor.  A formal announcement of candidacy is expected after his resignation takes effect.  Goode says he would not have run had Mayor Greene decided to seek a second term.

headline: Sold out
abstract: The author states that Pennsylvania's Republican and Democratic politicians have once again helped the steel industry by providing import protection, and garnering a votes of these workers. However, the general public are the losers as they now have to pay higher for cars and other steel products.

headline: PFT is Urged to OK Pact: Union Committee Vote is Unanimous
abstract: The executive committee of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers (PFT) unanimously recommended approval of a three-year contract agreed to Saturday by Mayor Green and PFT president John P. Murray.  The recommendation cleared the way for ratification of the pact by the union’s 20,000 members tomorrow.  If ratified by the union and approved by the Board of Education the contract would allow schools to open on time.

headline: This week, a first clue to the fate of Limerick
abstract: Joseph J. Klovekorn, the administrative law judge for the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) has been presiding over the investigation on the need for Philadelphia Electric Co.'s controversial Limerick nuclear power plant. Sometime this week, Klovekorn is expected to issue his opinion after nearly a year.

headline: Example of Economies: Common Pleas Court is 'Mired in Politics'
abstract: Judges Edward J. Bradley and David N. Savitt claimed that the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas operates efficiently.  An audit report showed that 83% of the Common Pleas Court’s $48 million budget is spend on support services.  It was found that an estimated savings of $876,000 could have been made through staff reductions in custodial services.  Eighty-three court employees are responsible for cleaning 383,000 square feet of space.  This compares with 66 Department of Public Property employees who are responsible for cleaning 1,134,000 square feet of space.  The cost per square food is $4 for the courts, and $1.26 for the rest of the city government.  The courts are using 83 people to do the work of 29.   There are also other areas where controls are either weak or lacking in the courts.  Something needs to be done to change the direction that the courts seem to be headed towards.

headline: Treasury Lifts Cap on Housing Prices
abstract: Act 176 not only allows PHFA to issue single-family bonds but also allows cities with a population of 50,000 or more and Allegheny County to either participate in the bond issue or sell their ownbonds and run their own program.  In the first issue, only Harrisburg and Pittsburgh opted to run their own programs.  Harrisburg has indicated it will participate in the next issue.

headline: State's Top Legionnaire Heads War Veterans
abstract: At the recent state conventions of the various veterans’ organizations, Governor Dick Thornburgh listed a veterans’ home for the southeast area of the sate as an essential project.  The state now has two homes at Erie and Hollidaysburg, under the supervision of the Department of Military Affairs.

headline: How Philadelphia-Area Legislators Voted
abstract: This article tells how Philadelphia-area legislators voted last week on roll call votes in the PA House and Senate.

headline: Where the Press-release Watch Never Stops
abstract: null

headline: State House, West Shore
abstract: The Patriot News endorses incumbent state Representative John Kennedy for the 88th House District race.  Representative Kennedy, though displaying an unorthodox style, has an independent mind and a refreshing stance that is hard to find in either of his opponents.  Kennedy is running against Democrat Mary Weller and Consumer Party candidate David J. Leach.

headline: County Turnout Nearly 70%; Ticket Splitting Evident
abstract: In what experts are calling an "off-year presidential race," 70 percent of Dauphin County voters went to the polls yesterday.  The election was seen largely as a referendum on President Reagan's economic policies, and partial election totals showed considerable split-ticket voting.

headline: State budget plan; Modest 1.1 percent increase due from Washington
abstract: This article highlights the various aspects of the budget bill including issues with regard to education, health, social services, welfare, etc. The state is also in line for a 1.1 percent increase in federal funds from next year.

headline: Pitt students told to fight for US Aid
abstract: Legislators from Harrisburg and Washington have urged University of Pittsburgh students to write and shout their opposition to the proposed federal cutbacks in college aid. Under Reagan's proposals, student loan programs would eliminate aid to graduate students and limit the number of undergraduates who borrow money.

headline: Three mile reminders
abstract: Three years after the Three Mile Island (TMI) disaster, the lessons learned about issues relating to safety would be the positive outcome of this disaster. Along with the issue of cleanup-financing, the issues of prevention and limitation of future disasters needs to be looked into.

headline: Experts: Don’t' Alter Juvenile Law
abstract: The state and local experts are telling the state House Subcommittee on Crime and Corrections about proposed revisions of the state’s handling of juvenile delinquents.  The panel is considering legislation which would revise several aspects of the current Juvenile Act, but witnesses are saying the current law is working well and the proposed changes could do more harm than good.  One way legislation under consideration would alter the existing law is by lowering the age limit at which juvenile delinquents could be tried as adults.  Many feel as though this would increase the poor conditions in the state’s already overcrowded jails, and would increase costs.

headline: Two Schuylkill Firms Included in PIDA Loans: Governor Reveals Package to Spur Regional Businesses
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh announced the approval of more than $2.4 million in Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority loans, spurring six business development projects in Northeastern Pennsylvania.  Two Schuylkill County firms included in the program are Goulds Pumps Inc., of Ashland and C.M. Offray and Son, Inc., of Frackville.  Other firms are Secodyne, Inc. in Scranton, Linda’s pierogies in Mount Carmel and B.C. Manufacturing in Wilkes-Barre and Stroehman Brothers Company of West Hazleton.

headline: Sunk!
abstract: The refitting job on the battleship Iowa will go to shipyards in Mississippi and Louisiana, rather than to Pennsylvania Shipbuilding Corp. in Chester or Coastal Drydock at the old Brooklyn Navy Yard.  Chester may be the most depressed area in the country.  The area had 20 percent of its people on unemployment and 33 percent on welfare.  It would be hard to imagine an area more in need of the kind of massive infusion of jobs that a major defense contract would bring.  However, the United States Navy thought otherwise.  The argument for choosing the other locations was made purely on merit, on the greater ability of the Southern yards to do massive jobs.  Chester needs help as much as any city in the United States.

headline: How states rely on Washington
abstract: Chart shows US Treasury figures that show how much federal aid went to state and local governments in 1981 - both the total amount of grants and also the amount per capita.  PA falls slightly below average with $412 per capita.

headline: White House defends 'new federalism'
abstract: President Ronald Reagan and his staff began a campaign promoting the ''new federalism'' approach of transferring several federal programs to the states with no cost to the states.  The new push by the White House came in response to several governors and mayors' worries about funding.  Congress must approve the package first.

headline: Zimmerman: At&T tax pact is a legal one
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman announced yesterday that Pennsylvania's franchise-tax agreement with American Telephone and Telegraph Company (AT&T) was legal and no actions would be taken to challenge it.  AT&T's tax agreement first cam under scrutiny when George Ball, a former administrative assistant in the Revenue Department, complained that the agreement constituted a serious breach of ethics.

headline: Green's Last Hurrah: Can it Fly?
abstract: After announcing that he will not seek re-election, Philadelphia Mayor William Greene says he will not become a lame-duck mayor and promosied to turn the burners up during his last year in office.  Mayor Greene potentially faces two major crises during his last year in office--a SEPTA strike and dimished power in Harrisburg--both of which could stymie his efforts at avoiding lame-duck status.

headline: State in Black--or in Red
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh claimed that the state wound up the recent fiscal year with a $7.5 million surplus.  Democrats counterclaimed that that administration is dealing in illusions and that the Commonwealth actually is in the red.  Thornburgh said that in contrast to the budget deficits which preceded his taking office, “we have been able to achieve for consecutive years of budget surpluses, and have done so without a general tax increase.”

headline: Pitt tuitions increased as board OKs budget
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh Board of Trustees has approved a $319.3 million budget with tuition increases ranging from $240 to $1500. It depends upon the PA State Legislature approving a $78.2 million appropriation recommended by Gov. Dick Thornburgh.

headline: TMI Appeals on Underdamaged Reactor
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has been asked to lift a 1979 order that shut down the undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island.  GPU Nuclear Corp., said its request was not tantamount to proposing restart of the undamaged Unit 1 reactor, which is targeted for the first quarter of 1983.  The reactor’s steam generator tubes must be repaired and a challenge to court-ordered psychological stress studies must be settled before Unit 1 can be used again.  GPU Nuclear contended the commission said late last year that it would lift the shutdown order when the reason for suspension no longer existed.

headline: False Fire Alarms Troublesome at Prison
abstract: Borough Fire Chief in Carlisle, William Alwood, critical of lack of cooperation from Cumberland County Prison officials, has called for steps to combat frequent and troublesome false alarms at the prison.

headline: We're no. 4 in US Cities
abstract: Pittsburgh is the fourth best livable metropolis in the country according to the authors of the "Places Rated Almanac."  The authors weighed these factors in their judgments: climate and terrain, housing, health care and environment, crime, transportation, the arts and economics, transportation, and educational facilities.

headline: The looming nuclear issue
abstract: A strengthening movement, from town halls and state legislatures across the country, that calls for a freeze on nuclear weapons, moved into Congress. Seventeen senators and 142 House members endorsed a resolution calling on the United States and the Soviet Union to stop all testing, production and experimentation.

headline: How the Democrats gave us Reagan: The ten key moments of the 1980 campaign
abstract: Authors retrace the 1980 presidential campaign and pull out ten moments in the campaign where they feel the Democratic Party floundered, thus enabling President Reagan to pull ahead in the polls and eventually win the election.

headline: White House Endorses End to Forced Retirement at 70
abstract: The Reagan Administration urged Congress to pass legislation that would end the forced retirement of elderly workers.  Under the current law, people are required to retire at age 70 years.  The President believes this is the right thing to do and this is the right time to do it.

headline: Purge of Voters Stuns Democrats
abstract: State Democratic Party officials are shocked by massive purges of statewide voter rolls.  Democrats say they registered 195,000 new voters this year, but large purges--especially in Democratic strongholds like Philadelphia--all but eliminated new registration gains.

headline: Zappala Beats Schaeffer for High Court Seat
abstract: Allegheny County Judge Stephen Zappala defeated Berks County Judge Forrest Schaeffer and two minor party candidates for a seat on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court yesterday.

headline: State of the Union: Unsettling
abstract: Editorial: The newspaper believes that President Ronald Reagan is sincere that the state of the country is actually sound.  However, he skipped over the state of the economy, which has unemployment approaching 10%, and the shifting of several federal programs to the states means that these programs will most likely be sacrificed.  At least he has ideas, which are more than the Democrats seem to have right now.

headline: President of PSEA praises Ertel-Lloyd 'record of accomplishment'
abstract: The head of the Pennsylvania State Education Association said that its endorsement of the Democrats' Ertel-Lloyd gubernatorial ticket, would once again create  a team that will recognize the importance of funding education to the benefit of all Pennsylvanians.

headline: TMI Area Residents Showed More Stress
abstract: A recent Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) study showed that residents living in the area of Three Mile Island (TMI) exhibited moderate psychological stress factors more intensive than those found in a control group.  The findings may help the NRC determine what role peoples' mental condition should play in the possible reopening of TMI's Unit 1 reactor.

headline: Family praises outside probe of Bucks prison death
abstract: The family of a Bucks County Prison inmate, John P. Call Jr. who died last year after being injured in his cell, has hailed the decision to turn the case to an outside investigator. Bernard L. Siegel, a Deputy Philadelphia District Attorney, will conduct the third probe into the death.

headline: Wild Idea May Lift City's Downtown
abstract: The technology already exists for horizontal elevators that could move passengers across the rivers in Pittsburgh in less than a minute.  The system would be build along existing bridges to keep costs down.  Several firms would have to work together to create this since the elevators would be extremely expensive to build.  The consultants envisioned horizontal elevators linking Three Rivers Stadium with Gateway Center; Station Square with the Firstside area, South Shore with Stanwix Street; Allegheny Center on the North Side with Heinz Hall; and the Civic Arena with Grant Street and the Convention Center.  Although people-movers are used at many airports, no city has attempted to use horizontal elevators to link its fringe areas with the central business district.

headline: USS Iowa facelift eyed for Chester
abstract: A congressional committee that previously helped obtain contracts for the overhaul of two other aircraft carriers for the Philadelphia Navy Yard, is plotting strategies to win the renovation of the USS Iowa for Penn Shipyards in Chester. A number of other shipyards from across the country are vying for this lucrative contract.

headline: Icy grip
abstract: Winter is still with the Harrisburg area, but there are still lots of walks to be taken.

headline: Who should pay for traveling lawmakers?
abstract: Editorial concerned about lawmakers traveling on interest group money.  Gives the most recent list of local lawmakers doing so.

headline: Banks defer payment on TMI owner's debt
abstract: The consortium of banks that has kept the owner of Three Mile Island financially solvent since the March 1979 nuclear accident has waived a 41 million dollar short-term debt repayment.  Three Mile Isalnd owner General Public Utilities Corporation says the waiver represents an acknowledgment by the banks that the debt will not be repaid by the December 31 due date.

headline: Huge Democratic turnout gives Kostmayer the edge
abstract: High turnout among blue-collar Democrats in Lower Bucks County and redistricting combined to give Democrat Peter Kostymayer the margin of victory over incumbent Republican James Coyne in the Eigth Conressional District of Pennsylvania.  The race drew national attention and was interpreted by many to be a referndum on the Reagan administration's economic policies, which Coyne supported.

headline: State Owes $1.6 Billion For Unemployment Aid
abstract: Pennsylvania’s debt to the federal government for unemployment compensation is about $1.6 billion, the third highest in the nation.  Labor and Industry Department spokesman Michael Moyle said that the Dick Thornburgh administration had no plans to propose tax increases or tighten eligibility.

headline: Private Schools Receiving More Calls for Financial Aid
abstract: Parents of five children who were offered scholarships to attend the Baldwin School in the fall rejected the money because it just was not enough to pay the tuition.  The children’s parents decided to send them elsewhere according to the director of admissions for the Bryn Mawr girls school, a private institution where tuition for the 1982-83 school year ranges from $2,225 for kindergarten pupils to $4,750 for high school students.

headline: TMI Costs: Ratepayers Put on Notice
abstract: The ratepayers of Metropolitan Edison and Pennsylvania Electric, part-owners of the damaged reactor at Three Mile Island, will likely have to pay the brunt of the cost of decontamination.  PA's Consumer Advocate, the trial staff of the Public Utility Commission, the utilities and a few industrial ratepayers have reached an agreement on a rate increase that would charge Metropolitan Edison and Pennsylvania Electric customers for clean-up costs.  Editorial does not think that the ratepayer should be forced to pay for the mistakes made at Three Mile Island and that the corporations only should have to pay.

headline: Fed up
abstract: In a letter to the editor a father explains that he attempted to get an arrest warrant for his son from the Philadelphia Attorney General's office and was turned down since he did not see his son steal the radio.  The writer claims that the justice system is protecting his son by indifference, and asks that his son never enters his home again.

headline: A lot of irons in the fire helps Penna. Steel-maker cope
abstract: Carpenter Technology Corp. of Reading has been one of the few steel makers that was able to buck the industry trend of declining earnings. It is comparatively better placed, compared to its rivals. One of the reasons for this is that its products are diversified.

headline: Waste in the defense budget
abstract: Most members of Congress are calling for a cut in Reagan's proposed $258 billion defense budget for next year. However, despite a cut, politics will continue to produce costly "something for everyone" solutions.

headline: In favor of Limerick Unit 2
abstract: The author believes that the May 5th editorial calling the closure of Unit 2 at Limerick is nonsense and that it makes sense to not reject Unit 2. the author also feels that the editorial has got its facts wrong.

headline: Who's who in House race
abstract: Although Johnstown voters did not have much choice in the primary elections, the November elections would give them an opportunity to decide whether they want Republicans or Democrats to represent them in the General Assembly.

headline: A step ahead: The fast life of a political advance man
abstract: This article discusses the life of Andy Kind, a 22-year-old advance man for U.S. Senator John Heinz.  Andy and other advance men handle all of the seemingly minor details--like which traffic route to take--for Senator Heniz's campaign tour.  Kind has political ambitions of his own and hopes to be in Congress one day.

headline: Green tells of a stroll that prompted him not to run
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor William Greene tells reporters that a morning walk with his wife, Patricia, last Saturday made him sure of one thing: he would not seek re-election for another term as Mayor of Philadelphia.  He wishes to prioritize family over politics.

headline: State reduces debt by $67 million
abstract: The commonwealth has repaid its April loan from the Federal Unemployment Compensation Loan Fund by $67 million. This was announced by Labor and Industry Secretary Barry H. Stern

headline: Raiding the city treasury, while education withers
abstract: Philadelphia School Superintendent Michael Marcase and the rest of the school board are trying to get additional funding from the Philadelphia City treasury.  A previous attempt to obtain the money was thwarted.

headline: TMI Demineralization: Unit 2 Water Processed
abstract: General Public Utilities Nuclear officials announced that more than half of the radioactive water in the Unit 2 containment building at Three Mile Island Nuclear Station has been successfully processed by the Submerged Demineralizer System.

headline: First Amendment: Porno Ruling: Court Brought it On
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled unanimously that New York did not act unconstitutionally when it prohibited distribution of materials depicting children in “actual or simulated sexual intercourse, deviate sexual intercourse, sexual bestiality, masturbation, sado-masochistic abuse, or lewd exhibits of the genitals.”

headline: 1982 could be a $1 billion loser for Bethlehem Steel, analysts say
abstract: Bethlehem Steel Corporation will likely end this year with a loss of more than $1 billion largely as a result of its decision to discontinue operations in Johnstown, Pennsylvania and Lackawanna, New York. The group's anticipated fourth quarter loss, including a write-off of between $750 and $850 million will be the largest in the steel industry's history.

headline: With many a tug, carrier heads to sea
abstract: World War II aircraft carrier "Intrepid" was towed out of the Philadelphia shipyard enroute to New York where it will be converted into a museum.  The Intrepid Foundation raised $14.2 million to prevent the ship from being scrapped and paid for the refit.

headline: In Firemen's Speech: Commissioner Said Politicking
abstract: A Westmoreland County legislator has accused PA Fire Commissioner Charles A. Henry of politicking for Governor Dick Thornburgh when he addressed the Pennsylvania's Firemen's Association, but Henry says he was only making a progress report.

headline: Why punish Erie, Crawford?
abstract: The reapportionment struggle in the 24th district, has continuously tried to divide up the counties within the district.  However, the counties being considered actually grew in population compared to the rest of the state.  Also, USAir had a record profitable year in 1981, and the paper believes that feeder cities like Erie helped to contribute.

headline: PSEA Claims School Subsidies Fall Short
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Education Association claims that state school subsidies have fallen far short of required amounts for this fiscal year.

headline: Discontent in the region
abstract: Due to widespread ticket-splitting, both Democrats and Republicans saw victories in Tuesday's election.  Democrats made significant gains--regaining majorities in the Pennsylvania State House and congressional delegation, while Republican incumbent Governor Dick Thornburgh and Senator John Heinz were elected to second terms.

headline: State Repays U.S. UC Fund $39 million
abstract: The commonwealth has repaid $39,008,864 borrowed in July from the federal Unemployment Compensation Loan Fund.  The amount repaid, state Labor and Industry Secretary Barry Stern said was $21 million less than the $60 million July borrowing authority approved for Pennsylvania by the U.S. Labor Department.  The state will save approximately $500,000 in potential interest charges by making prompt repayment of the July loan.  However, this repayment will make it necessary to increase the estimated September borrowing by the same amount.

headline: Rat, Boondoggles Chased Through State 'Waste Line'
abstract: A "waste line" set up by PA Treasurer Budd Dwyer received a call about a visit of Rudy the Rat to the University of Pennsylvania.  Rudy is a character created by the state Department of Environmental Resources to educate elementary students, but the call was complaining about the waste of state funds on his visit to the college.  Other state hotlines have been in use since 1977.

headline: TMI Facts Distorted
abstract: A member of the Susquehanna Valley Alliance was quoted as saying that, if TMI had gone to a meltdown, the $560 million insurance fund provided under federal law would have had to be distributed to 800,000 people living within a 20-mile radius of TMI.  This would come out to just three cents per person while the average homeowner’s loss would be about $23,300.

headline: Flaherty Quits as Overseer: Assails Colleagues in Court Dispute
abstract: Supreme Court Justice John P. Flaherty submitted his resignation from his assignment as Deputy Chief Justice to administer the Philadelphia courts.  The resignation brings an end to a stormy five months in the courts that began when Chief Justice Henry X. O’Brien appointed Flaherty deputy chief justice on February 9th, with total authority to run Philadelphia’s Common Pleas, Municipal and Traffic Courts.

headline: A high-stakes high-pressure antitrust fight
abstract: Intense lobbying is underway in order to retroactively change the antitrust laws, as this is a matter of tens of millions of dollars for a handful of companies. Milliken Research Co., a South Carolina-based textile firm is leading this by appointing Republican Party boss William A. Meehan to lobby on its behalf. Millilken has the potential of reducing by two-thirds the damage judgment of $21 million, in a price-fixing law suit.

headline: $100,000 set to oppose Bell rate bid
abstract: The PA Office of Consumer Advocate filed a formal complaint against Bell of PA's $426 million rate increase, and said it is prepared to spend $100,000 on expert witnesses.

headline: In Jannotti case, ethics panel has no rules to enforce
abstract: Philadelphia Councilman Harry Jannotti will be the subject of resolutions introduced by John Street to authorize an investigation as to whether Jannotti's involvement in the Abscam case violated the city's ethics code.  Jannotti has been convicted of extortion and conspiracy changes, but has not yet been sentenced.

headline: Why we were bored
abstract: 75% of the registered voters did not vote in the recently held elections. However, they are not to blame as the elections itself were a mere formality and the incumbents merely needed a rubber-stamping to continue.

headline: PA Republicans again battling Demos edge in voters
abstract: Although the Democratic Party has the voter-registration advantage in Pennsylvania, during the past four years Republicans have enjoyed more electoral success than Democrats.  This trend will either reverse or continue as voters go to the polls on Tuesday.

headline: Blue Mountain water recalled by DER order
abstract: The Pennsylvania Environmental Resources Department announced that all Blue Mountain Spring Water bearing Permit No. 2 on its label and distributed before Monday is being recalled because sample analyses show low levels of coliform contamination.

headline: State revenue declines
abstract: The state Department of Revenue said that the non-tax revenue dropped significantly the previous month, deepening the hole in the state budget by almost $12 million. However, the tax revenue jumped above the estimates for that month. Officials attributed the drop to low miscellaneous tax collections and no profit transfers from the state liquor store system.

headline: Row over a college guide
abstract: A recent guide "The New York Times Selective Guide to Colleges" has debuted with a controversial "star" system that has left some notable schools, such as Harvard, in the back of the pack while others are brought forward because they have palm trees (Stanford) or a good basketball team (North Carolina).  Other schools were surprised to find themsevles in the guide since they never participated in it.

headline: TMI hearing wouldn't have heard much new
abstract: A snowstorm prevented a US Senate energy subcommittee from traveling to Harrisburg for a hearing on the financing of the Three Mile Island Unit 2 reactor.  The meeting has been rescheduled for February 2.  The PA Public Utilities Commission has previously said that customer rates are not allowed to pay for cleanup, but that may be changing as indicated by a recent price increase.  Other players are lining up with their own plans.  Opinion.

headline: Fooling with the Traffic Court
abstract: This letter states that the March 22 editorial "Major surgery is in order for city Traffic Court" was a bad idea, as it suggests an infusion of politics into Traffic Court. The author also believes that the proposal to use lawyers instead of judges, paid on a per diem basis, is an antiquated way of running the center.

headline: A hotel-room tax for Phila.
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a reader talks about the importance of revenues generated from tourists and conventions held in Philadelphia. The need to promote this, coupled with the levy of certain taxes, would be a great way to increase revenues.

headline: AT&T hauls out doomsday gear created after incident at TMI
abstract: Hundreds of reporters are landing up in White Sands Missile Range in order to cover the return of the space shuttle on March 29. However, due to the lack of telephones, AT&T decided to haul its doomsday equipment, created after the Three Mile Island nuclear disaster, to this area.

headline: In Pa. redistricting, they played the Republicans' song
abstract: A united Republican party prepared to go one up on their rivals, by coming out with a reapportionment plan. Last week, the Republican-controlled legislature finally passed a Republican drafted plan that reduced the state's congressional delegation from 25 to 23. This process altered the political landscape for the next ten years, till the next reapportionment, and clearly favored the Republicans.

headline: Will Bailey Enter Race as Republican?
abstract: The Democratic convention could not be complete without the usual assortment of party crashers, issue hawkers, publicity piggy backers, and other hangers-on.

headline: Senate Candidate Wants To Aid Economy's Victims
abstract: Cyril Wecht, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, argues that the most important issue in the upcoming elections is the economy.  Reaganomics has not helped those who are most vulnerable in society--the unemployed, the elderly, the working class--and Wecht vows to be a voice for these groups in Washington.

headline: Reading the returns
abstract: Tuesday's election results show that Reaganomics hurt the Republican Party and that the election of 1980 did not represent a major political realignment in American politics.  Democrats gained 20 plus seats in the House of Representatives, but Republicans held onto a 54-46 margain in the Senate.

headline: State Senate Kills '83 Tax Rollback
abstract: The latest Revenue Department report showed state tax revenues have fallen $80 million behind administration estimates for 1982 to date.  If the higher income tax rates are not made permanent before the end of the legislative session that Democrats might block an extension when they take control of the House in January.

headline: Scanlon confirms state funds for Vo-Tech
abstract: State Secretary of Education Dr. Robert Scanlon on Wednesday confirmed that the state will honor its commitment to sharing Bedford-Everett vo-tech school construction costs.

headline: TMI neighbors oppose restart of Unit 1 by 2-1 ratio
abstract: Residents of three counties close to the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear power plant near Middletown, Pa., voted in a non-binding referendum by a 2-1 margin against restarting the Unit 1 reactor there.

headline: Fooling with Traffic Court; Only now
abstract: The author believes that Controller Thomas Leonard claimed that the Traffic Court system is a den of political patronage only because it now under the administration of Judge Salvatore DeMeo, a Republican. When it was under Democratic administrations, no such allegations were put forward.

headline: A hotel-room tax for Phila.
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a reader talks about the danger of levying tax, in order to generate revenues based on tourism. On the contrary, the tax itself could be viewed as a rip-off by the tourists and could lead to a 10 percent decline in tourism

headline: Bell 'Bulletin' Deceptive, Coalition Says
abstract: A citizens coalition fighting Bell of Pennsylvania’s $426 million rate increase request plans to file a complaint with the State Public Utility Commission to determine the financing and targeted distribution of a Bell publication about the rate case.

headline: Interns Will Provide Senatorial Research
abstract: Senate Republican leaders recently launched an experimental intern program involving upper level college and graduate students.  The program aims to give students practical experience in state government and, equally important, to give the Senate the benefit of in-depth research on issues and problems facing Pennsylvania.  The pilot intern program has been under the supervision of Pennsylvania State University’s Capitol Campus.  The first five interns focused on five topics selected by Senate leaders: worker’s compensation, radioactive waste disposal, urban and rural enterprise zones, economic development policies for small businesses, and fiscal pressures on local governments.

headline: Will Bailey Enter Race as Republican?
abstract: U.S. Representative Don Bailey, a Democrat from Westmoreland and also the loser in the Democratic primary election, is considering running under the Republican banner in the 12th Congressional District.
