If he were to re-enter the race, he would retain his Democratic registration despite accepting the Republican endorsement.

headline: Senator Points To Record, Accessibility, Accountability
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz argues that his record of service demonstrates the accessibility and accountability needed to serve the interests of Pennsylvanians.  If elected to another term as U.S. Senator, Heinz will promote legislation providing more jobs for Pennsylvania; he will also protect the rights of seniors.

headline: Governorships Seen as Reagan Problem
abstract: After Democrats won 27 of the 36 governorships at stake in Tuesday's election, analysts say President Reagan's program of new federalism will not become a reality--at least in its present form.  New Federalism has already faced serious opposition from governors across the country, and now faces more obstacles to implementation.

headline: State Senator Charges GOP with budget 'gimmickry'
abstract: The Republican-led state Senate approved a bill which the top ranking Democrat on the Appropriations Committee assailed as a $51 million “gimmick” at the expense of the State Employees’ Retirement Fund to help balance Governor Dick Thornburgh’s already enacted no-new-tax budget for 1982-83.

headline: Scanlon defends PESEA data cut-off
abstract: Education Secretary Robert Scanlon has defended his decision to cut-off the flow of certain school statistical information to the state's largest teachers' union, saying that the 130000 member PSEA uses the data to distort the administration's proposal of a new method of allocating state subsidies to school districts.

headline: TMI Panel Says Cleanup Cost Won't Increase
abstract: Probes within the damaged reactor at Three Mile Island have indicated that the timetable and $1 billion price estimate for the cleanup will not need to be revised.

headline: For New State Prison
abstract: The design of a new proposed Ryan Township State Prison is anticipated to follow that of the State Regional Correctional Facility in Mercer County.  The state is expanding existing prisons, converting old structures into prisons, and building new facilities as part of its expansion of the correctional system.  3,600 additional cells will be added.  2,380 of these have already been funded by the General Assembly

headline: An Opportunity
abstract: KYW News has reported on many stories of businesses moving out of Delaware Valley and plants closing. KYW have examined solutions for this situation and one of them is in service industry. Now, we have a specific opportunity since big telephone company (AT&T) is splitting up into regional phone companies and one of them will include this area. Since, company is looking for new location and Delaware Valley is a strong possibility we hope that local business leaders will succeed to bring it here.

headline: Breaking up is hard to do: AT&T hangs up on the little guy
abstract: The author of this opinion piece is concerned that the divestiture of the AT&T companies will not mean increased competition and lower rates, but instead be bad news for consumers.

headline: Irate Democrats give Andrezeski buzz-off
abstract: PA Senator Anthony B. ''Buzz'' Andrezeski has learned the hard way that if he doesn't follow the party line, the party will cast him off.  The freshman Senator had to lay off 5 employees because he broke ranks with Democrats and supported the Republican redistricting plan.  Senate Majority Leader Edward Zemprelli also asked Andrezeski to step down from the Senate Democratic Election Committee.

headline: Will receive labor vote, Wecht says
abstract: Cyril Wecht, a candidate for the US Senate, says he is convinced he will receive the support of the labor movement in Pennsylvania, despite the state AFL-CIO's endorsement of incumbent Republican John Heinz.

headline: Rehabilitation A High Court Issue
abstract: Democratic Supreme Court candidate Stephen Zappala and his opponent, Berks County Judge Forrest Schaeffer, clashed over the issue of criminal rehabilitation.  Zapalla claims that attempts to rehabilitate criminals are illusory, while Forrest contends that rehabilitation can have a positive impact on the criminal justice system.

headline: Lame-Duck Bill Covets Post Denied to His Dad
abstract: As Philadelphia Mayor William Greene announced that he would not seek a second term as mayor on Tuesday, another campaign--his bid for Arlen Specter's Senate seat--began.  The U.S. Senate eluded Mayor Greene's father because of his association with machine-style politics, but Mayor Greene has no such connections to machine politics and has the kind of party loyalty that his father did not; this may make the Senate within his reach.

headline: State tax bill is pretty small; so is taxpayer
abstract: The state Department of Revenue imposes 2.2 percent income tax on the income of all persons, regardless of age or amount earned. Hence, Matthew Lenker, only 2 years old, has to pay a tax of $1.86 on $84.34 interest he earned on a local savings account.

headline: School block grants meet stiff opposition
abstract: Representatives on the PA House subcommittee on basic education were critical of Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposition to change education subsidies to a block grant program.  21 other state imposed mandates would also either be eliminated or reduced.

headline: TMI Probe Confirms Cleanup Cost Figures
abstract: GPU Nuclear Corp has said that no unexpected conditions were uncovered during three camera inspections of the Three Mile Island Unit 2 reactor that would revise earlier estimates on the duration and cost of the cleanup.

headline: Full house in America's prisons
abstract: America's prison population, swollen by tougher sentencing laws, soared by a record 12.1 percent in 1981. The details of the data in various states are displayed.

headline: Assigned risk plan's hike request berated
abstract: Representatives of consumers, an automobile association and three state lawyers' groups called on state insurance officials yesterday to reject a $51 million increase in insurance rates for drivers labeled "bad risks" by insurance companies. This would lead to an average increase of $165 per motorist.

headline: Cable TV Hearings: Policy Before Regulation
abstract: The government is proposing hightening regulations on cable television.  The House hearings on cable TV regulation were in reaction to a U.S. Supreme Court ruling affecting Boulder, Colorado, in which the court said that unless there is an articulated state policy on delegation of authority, municipalities could be subject to anti-trust suits where cable TV franchise contracts are awarded.  Because some businesses in the telecommunications industry are regulated and others are not, the need for a comprehensive state policy is essential if the public interest is to be served and protected.

headline: It's Freind over foe in Delco race
abstract: Joan Tarka lost the primary to Steven Freind by about 3000 votes, leading her to suggest that most of the Delaware County residents were obsessed with the candidates' positions on abortion.

headline: Will redistricting hand over part of county to a Democrat?
abstract: If the latest Congressional apportionment plan passes the legislature, putting Democrats in a district that has voted Republican representatives since 1858.  Other plans have kept Lancaster County intact, but they have been voted down as well.

headline: Voters approve loans for state boarding homes
abstract: Pennsylvania voters approved a ballot initiative that will allow personal care boarding homes to borrow money from the state for improvements and renovations.  The funding for loans will come from a 50 million dollar surplus left over from a nursing-home loan program, and the monies will go towards fire and saftey repairs.

headline: State waiting to take a tax bite out of Pac-Man
abstract: Rep. Karl Boyes is sponsoring legislation that would impose a $100 per machine state tax on owners of electronic games. The money generated would be used chiefly to help the physically handicapped. The Thornburgh administration is working with him on the bill.

headline: School board weighs TMI evacuation
abstract: A state-mandated plan for evacuating city school students, if at all an accident occurs at the Three Mile Island nuclear station, will be presented to the Harrisburg School Board for approval. The plan calls for the movement of students to "host schools" like Camp Curtin Early Childhood Center and the William Penn campus of Harrisburg High School.

headline: TMI status unnerving
abstract: Letter to the editor: Writer lives within close proximity to Three Mile Island and is worried that another accident looms, especially given the recent announced troubles with the undamaged reactor.  The author is getting continuously more concerned and thinks that it is justified.

headline: Fumo: Let Cops Give $$ to Pols
abstract: State Senator Vincent Fumo from Philadelphia says police officers and firefighters should be allowed to contribute money to political campaigns through political action committees like other public employees.  He plans on introducing a bill for consideration.  The legislation would lift the statewide ban that prohibits firefighters and police officers from forming or contributing to special political organizations that help fund political campaigns.  If the bill is passed, it is unclear how it would affect Philadelphia because it directly contradicts the city’s Home Rule Charter.  The Charter explicitly prohibits police and firefighters from contributing voluntarily or involuntarily for any political purpose.

headline: Bank change a good move
abstract: The battle over statewide banking is over, and it appears the winners will be the consumers of bank services.   The new law will allow banks to build braches anywhere in the Commonwealth by 1990.  Additionally, bank holding comapanies will also be allowed to hold as many banks as they want by 1990.  Opposition has come from small banks worried about being gobbled up by banks in the state's larger financial centers.

headline: Consumers need a voice
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania has 3.3 million customers in Pennsylvania and wants to raise charges between $3 and $5 per month.  Bell expects to spend $600,000 on legal fees from customer revenues to fight for the increase.  A new idea would require Bell to print and accept a $1 fee on its bills with funds directed to fighting the increase.

headline: Jacquin Labor Pact Should Reopen Flow to State
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh announced a tentative three-year contract with the Charles Jacquin distillery and Teamsters Local 500.  135 jobs would be saved as a result.  This would open the door for the PA Liquor Control Board to resume buying the Philadelphia distillery’s liquor.

headline: Witness: GOP leaders paid him to enter race
abstract: Richard T. Burke, a key prosecution witness in an election-fraud case against two Republican Party leaders, Nicholas F. Catania and Charles P. Sexton, testified that he had been offered anything he wanted for his agreement to enter the Democratic primary for county controller last March.

headline: Higher rates, lower interest  boost profits for GPU
abstract: The combination of favorable rate increases and declining interest expenses helped General Public Utilities Corporation, the owner of Three Mile Island, post a 6.4 percent gain in third-quarter earnings.

headline: State Windfall
abstract: The letter states that the revenue department is morally incorrect by rounding of the tax charge to the next highest number, even if it is closer to the lower number. The author also states that taxes are as it is high enough and this rule puts a higher burden on taxpayers.

headline: School Funds
abstract: Local school officials and property taxpayers have the right to know what the state’s legal funding responsibility is and that it is not meeting that responsibility.  For the past four years the PSEA has reminded Governor Thornburgh of his election year pledge to properly support local school districts.

headline: TMI Tests
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the Manager of Media Relations at the GPU Nuclear Corporation and the TMI Nuclear Station responds to inaccurate quotes that he said the newspaper printed.  The quotes were on the control rod tests at TMI Unit 2.

headline: Gekas critical of locating courts outside Harrisburg
abstract: Pennsylvania State Senator George W. Gekas does not approve that the appellate courts are not located in Pennsylvania's capital, Harrisburg.  The article continues to go into detail about Gekas's views on the courts' locations.

headline: Bar Group Urges Changes in State's Corporate Laws
abstract: Members of the Pennsylvania Bar Association warned a legislative panel that some major corporations will leave the state unless Legislative acts quickly to change Pennsylvania’s corporate laws.  Pennsylvania has fallen significantly behind other commercial states in the adequacy and acceptability of its business corporation laws, W. Edward Sell, chairman of the Bar Association’s revision committee, told the joint House-Senate Judiciary Committee.  The Association claims that Pennsylvania companies are over-regulated by outdated corporation laws.  The joint committee is considering revisions to the state’s corporation laws because a 10-year moratorium on them expires this year.

headline: Getting the jump on retail fraud
abstract: This editorial discusses the ways that Harrisburg area retailers can take action on bad checks received during the holiday season.  The editorial urges the creation of a telephone alert system so that retailers can be aware of fraudulent purchases in the area.

headline: Jim Ritter's Way--a Good Way
abstract: James P. Ritter said goodbye to his colleagues in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives.  He was the senior member of the Lehigh Valley legislative delegation.  The Allentown Democrat spent 18 years of his life serving his constituents, his district, the Lehigh Valley area and the state.  He was defeated in his bid for election to the 16th Senatorial District seat held by retiring Senator Henry M. Messinger by just 181 votes of about 65,000 cast losing to Republican Allentown Councilman Guy Kratzer.

headline: Woman's First Ticket Wins Lotto Millions
abstract: A suburban Pennsylvania bank employee who bought a $1 Pennsylvania Lottery ticket for the first time won $5.5 million, which made her the largest single lottery jackpot winner in the United States.  She will receive 21 yearly installments of $260,754.61 for a total of $5,475,847.  The lottery will withhold 20 percent of each payment for taxes, and the Thomases will have to report the remaining amount on their taxes each year.

headline: Road funds
abstract: U.S. District Court Judge Louis Bechtle froze more than 90 million dollars of Pennsylvania highway funds after the General Assembly failed to comply with a 1978 ageement that required the state to start measuring auto pollutants.  Judge Bechtle now is set to determine whether certain saftey-related projects should be exempted from the freeze.

headline: States fight excise tax rise
abstract: States urge President Ronald Reagan to reject proposals for an increase in Federal excise taxes.  These types of taxes have been considered a primary state revenue source, and even though the Reagan plan would return some of the money to states, it would undermine this source of revenue for states.

headline: School Panel Falls Behind on Closings
abstract: A Board of Education committee formed earlier in 1982 to identify under-utilized schools for closing is two months behind schedule and has yet to agree on any schools that can be closed in the coming school year.  The committee could not identify schools for closing primarily because the superintendents of the school district’s seven sub-districts have different interpretations of the committee’s criteria for recommending schools that could be shut down.

headline: TMI water issue tackled; Citizens group seeks data on disposal to offer to NRC
abstract: Although a decision on disposal of processed radioactive water at Three Mile Island Unit 2 may be a year away, a citizens panel has decided to gather information now before they make a recommendation to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

headline: Getting the Drunk Driver
abstract: By the estimate of Arnold Muller, State Health Secretary, drunken driving on Commonwealth roads is “epidemic.”  Health and police officers have been testifying before the House-Senate Judiciary Committee in Harrisburg.  Law and health officials are more aware than anyone of the tragedies connected with alcohol and drugs.  One of the provisions of the legislation would set minimum mandatory prison terms for those convicted of drunk driving.  One judge has the idea to for officials to confiscate vehicles of drunk drivers.

headline: Bed Firm to Change Advertising
abstract: Craftmatic Comfort Manufacturing Corp., based in Montgomery Country has misled consumers into believing they are receiving substantial savings in bed prices according to the Attorney General’s Bureau of Consumer Protection.

headline: Looking to 'High Tech'
abstract: Massachusetts and California have fended off much of the loss and strain of declines in manufacturing industries by attracting so called “high tech” industry, clusters of which have grown up around the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard, in the Boston area, and Stanford University.  Now Governor Thornburgh is talking of expanding a program to move Pennsylvania into the field of advanced technology, a move that would attract bright engineers, researchers, and others.

headline: Journalism, PR not same
abstract: Although it is common for journalism and public relations to be linked, they are not.  Journalists are to give a full accounting of facts in a palatable way.  Public relations are intended to influence public opinion.

headline: York County's Rep. Anderson to retire after current term
abstract: PA Representative John Anderson has announced that he will retire after 11 terms in the legislature.  Anderson will be 70 when he retires.  He is currently the Republican caucus secretary.  In his private life, he is a fruit farmer and president of Stewartstown Railroad Company.  Two other York County legislators have announced that they are seeking re-election.

headline: Women's Group Clash On Election Gains
abstract: Both anti-abortion and pro-choice activists in Pennsylvania claimed victories for their respective causes after Tuesday's elections.

headline: State's 'timely' budget
abstract: Governor Thornburgh takes pride that Pennsylvania, for the fourth time in a row, has a timely, balanced and fiscally responsible budget with no increase in state income or sales taxes. The governor further added that this sends an unmistakable signal that the state was capable of maintaining its fiscal house in order.

headline: School presidents to Reagan: Cuts would cripple us
abstract: President Ronald Reagan's proposed budget cuts for higher education represent a dramatic step backward, according to presidents of 13 Philadelphia-area colleges.  The cuts would affect funding for public schools as well as student grant funding for all schools.  Total cuts in the program are expected to be around $1.7 billion.

headline: TMI-2 Core disposal ok's; US Energy Department to remove it
abstract: The US Department of Energy agreed to dispose of the damaged fuel core at Three Mile Island Unit 2. The agreement calls for GPU Nuclear to reimburse the federal government for the estimated $10 million to $20 million cost of shipping, storing and finally disposing of the core.

headline: Graterford cellblock is locked and searched
abstract: Officials at Graterford State Prison continued a lockdown of a cellblock the day after a scuffle took place in which 9 guards were injured.  A search through each of the cellblocks for banned substances and potential weapons began, but it was not reported if anything was found.  The scuffle started when a prisoner tried to take his lunch back to his cellblock.  When officers went after the inmate, other inmates went after the officers.

headline: Bell customers subsidizing fight for rates, consumer leader says
abstract: Max Weiner, Director of Consumers Education and Protective Association, says that Bell of Pennsylvania customers are subsidizing the company's push to raise rates since money from bills is being used to assemble the petition.  He proposes a surcharge be levied to fund a case against Bell, but Public Utilities Commissioner Michael Johnson said that such a surcharge cannot be levied by the PUC.

headline: Protecting You from Yourself
abstract: There is a proposal to ban headphones in Philadelphia.  Councilman John Street introduced a bill that would make it illegal for pedestrians, drivers, and bicyclists to wear headphones on city streets.

headline: Judge Caldwell Certified Pension of $1,838 Month
abstract: Judge William W. Caldwell, who resigned from the Dauphin County Common Pleas Court to go on U.S. Middle District Court, has been certified by the State Employees Retirement Board to receive a monthly pension of $1,838.  Other pensions for other state employees were also mentioned.

headline: You cannot win if you do not pay: Here's your Chance!
abstract: The writer of this opinion piece discusses a plan from PA Senator Will Fleece to put some money from taxes into a lottery system to encourage taxpayers to give to the state more willingly.

headline: Philadelphia Nuclear Freeze
abstract: WCAU urges Philadelphians to vote YES to the nuclear-arms-freeze referendum on the November 2nd ballot.  A bi-lateral nuclear freeze would help alleviate fears and draw down the costly nuclear arms race.

headline: City Jobless Rate Rising, Expected to Stabilize
abstract: According to the latest U.S. Labor Department statistics, unemployment in Philadelphia is increasing; it rose from 8.3 percent in August to 9.2 percent in September.  These figures are lower than the national average, however, and are expected to stabilize.

headline: Super rich on welfare
abstract: The author states that the Democrats are right when they mention the need to cut out some of the phony tax shelters for the super rich and make them pay tax as well.

headline: School-aid update
abstract: While approving the state budget last week, the Legislature rejected Gov. Dick Thornburgh's idea of block grants for education. Surprisingly, the lawmakers re-wrote the formula for distributing state aid to the schools.

headline: Treen Measures Endorsed
abstract: Governor Dave Treen has convinced the National Governors Association convention in Afton, Oklahoma not to endorse changes in laws governing natural gas pricing.  The association also endorsed a Treen-backed statement that urges Congress to assure that the intrastate pipelines have equal access to gas produced in the Outer Continental Shelf, the governor’s office said.  The OCS gas is currently available to interstate lines and thus can be used only on a limited basis with Louisiana.

headline: Graterford hostages can't escape scars
abstract: 6 civilian hostages, now-former employees of Graterford Prison, have had a difficult time returning to life after an incident at the prison November 1981.  Most still see a psychiatrist weekly.  The state is continuing to pay their salaries while they are getting treatment.

headline: Booze Profit Drops 75%
abstract: Profits from state liquor sales dropped about 75 percent in the first four months of the fiscal year compared to the same period last year.  Statistics prepared by the Liquor Control Board Comptroller Hubert E. Simpson say that there was $2.6 million in profit relative to $10.2 million last year.  Mario Mele, the Republican on the three-member board, said that "poor management" was to blame for the decrease.

headline: PUC Rejects a Special $1 Bell Fee
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission denied the request of a Philadelphia consumers group to solicit a one-time $1 fee from the 3.3 million residential customers of Bell of Pennsylvania so the advocates could fight Bell’s proposed $426 million rate increase.  Five commissioners opposed the proposal by the Consumers Education and Protective Association, their reasons were different.  The result was a 3-2 vote to accept the motion to deny, offered by Commissioner Michael Johnson.

headline: Judicial center; Gaining legislative support
abstract: The Government of Pennsylvania has been indifferent to the need for having a centralized location for the state's higher courts. However, a new bill establishing such a center in Harrisburg has got some backing from well-regarded sources.

headline: You're right, Bill
abstract: Members of the Congress recently passed an amendment that allows each member to take a $75 per day tax deduction for expenses associated with his or her work in Washington. Since the Internal Revenue Service estimated that this estimated expenditure was reasonable, members of the Congress need not prove this. The author feels that if the expenses were at least shown, the tax deduction makes sense, but not in this case.

headline: DRUNK DRIVING
abstract: While we agree with the state Legislature that Pennsylvania needs tougher drunk-driving laws, we also think that any sensible law should balance the need for harsher punishments with rehabilitation and treatment programs.  Putting the emphasis solely on punishment will not allow us to get at the root causes of illicit behavior.

headline: Thumbs go up and down on a Goode run
abstract: Opinions among local politicians are mixed as to what kind of mayoral candidate Philadelphia managing director Wilson Goode will make.  Some see him as the first black candidate with a legitimate chance of getting enogh support among white voters to win; others think his personality and inability to raise enough campaign money will limit how serious a contender he will be.

headline: Taddonio's spending cap
abstract: Editorial:  US Representative Lee Taddonio's long drive for a spending cap tied to the Personal Income Index finally received approval from the House Finance Committee, an attempt to tie tax structure to ability to pay.  Democrats are expected to put up a strong fight against this measure, especially as they are attacking the new "Reagan Swap" federalism program.

headline: School-code bill amended, sent to Senate
abstract: The PA Senate Education Committee unanimously approved a bill designed to refurbish the state's 33 year old school code.  Senator Ralph Hess believes that the bill will be voted on in either March or April.  One of the most important changes to be implemented would require school districts to comply with rules set forth by the State Board of Education.

headline: Tribune-Review: Editorial Opinion Nuclear Puzzlement
abstract: This editorial looks at the endless, emotional drive to kill the remaining good power reactor at TMI. The move to shut down the other reactor befuddles and puzzles outsiders not caught up in the anti-nuke syndrome.  The communities near the GPU facility recently approved a non-binding referendum which said, in effect, let the entire project die just as it is.

headline: Graterford panel told of conditions
abstract: Witnesses have told a 7-member panel investigating the hostage crisis at Graterford Prison that officials were not prepared to handle the seige and may never learn how weapons were smuggled into the facility.  Officials said that they had been forwarned of an impending escape attempt, but not of the ensuing seige.  Witnesses claimed that the prison conditions were terrible, prompting the escape attempt.

headline: City Priest's Complaints Uncork Senate Probe of Liquor Stores
abstract: For two years, Reverend Donald McIlvan complained to the Liquor Control Board Chairman Daniel Pennick that state store clerks at the Larimer Avenue liquor outlet sold booze to teenagers.  The chairman ignored the allegations, so the Reverend went to a State Senate panel in Philadelphia examining LCB enforcement policies.  The panel investigated the allegations made by McIlvane and will continue to instigate any new allegations brought forth.

headline: The revolt in Big Run; Phone customers disconnect over high rates
abstract: Phone customers are disgusted with the Big Run Telephone Co. for poor service and for charging the highest rates in Pennsylvania. Hence they have gone ahead and voluntarily disconnected their service.

headline: Kauffman Appears Again at Larsen Probe
abstract: Former PA Supreme Court Justice Bruce Kauffman appeared for the second day in a row before an inquiry board probing charges of misconduct against Justice Rolf Larsen.  Larsen is accused of violating judicial ethnics because he engaged in political activity while on the bench.  Kauffman's testimony is believed to have sought in connection with a charge that Larsen lobbied on Kauffman's behalf for an appointment to a vacant seat on the high court in 1979.

headline: Zappala asks Democrat aid for high court
abstract: Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Stephen Zappala announced that he is seeking the Democratic endorsement for Chief Justice of the State Supreme Court.  The announcement came on the heels of current Chief Justice Henry O'Brien's retirement in January.  Republican James Cavanaugh, a superior court judge, has already announced his intention to run for the post.

headline: Panel approves drunken driving penalties
abstract: The state House Judiciary Committee approved legislation that imposes stricter penalties for drunken driving.  If the bill is passed by the full House, offenders would face mandatory jail time and longer license suspensions.

headline: Legislature's return: what to push or skip
abstract: In addition to voting on a measure that would decrease the confirmation requirements for gubernatorial appointments to six state agencies, the Pennsylvania General Assembly is expected to approve a measure to increase penalties for drunken drivers during this legislative session.  Legislative leaders do not expect to enact proposed reforms to the state's no-fault auto insurance or product liability laws, however.

headline: Tax hike rumors
abstract: Due to the sad state of Pennsylvania's economy, it will have more bills to pay than tax money to collect. As a result, there is a possibility of a tax hike after the November elections.

headline: Schools told to Teach Skills to Disabled
abstract: A federal judge approved a lawsuit settlement that requires the Philadelphia School District to provide severely handicapped children in public schools with an education that would help them become self-sufficient.  This ends an eight-year-old class-action suit against the school district and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania by the mother of two handicapped children and by two organizations concerned with the handicapped.

headline: Troubleshooter "Loved His Job"
abstract: As a troubleshooter with the Philadelphia Electric Co., Fred Worthington Jr. had a dangerous but important job: restoring power when failures occurred.  He lost his life rushing to aid 11-year-old Billy Miller, who fell off his bicycle into a 3 foot deep puddle crisscrossed by downed electrical wires.  Both were electrocuted.

headline: 'Guilty But Mentally Ill' Bill Awaits Governor's OK
abstract: The General Assembly has sent a bill to Governor Dick Thornburgh that would give Pennsylvania juries the option of returning a "guilty but mentally ill" verdict in criminal cases.  The measure gained attention following the public outcry over the June acquittal of John Hinckley Jr., who shot President Reagan.  Sponsored by PA State Senator D. Michael Fisher, the legislation would allow a defendant to be found guilty but mentally ill and then sentenced like any other person convicted of the same offense.  The bill would mandate that the mentally ill defendant receive the necessary treatment.  Should he be "cured" before serving his required sentence, however, he would then have to finish his time in either a correctional facility or probation or parole.

headline: Commercial Banks-Second Quarter
abstract: This article talks about different banks and how well they did the second quarter in 1982.

headline: WITF Accepts Contract
abstract: WITF-TV’s Finance Committee voted to accept a contract for the Governor’s Energy Council to provide facilities for the production of 10 and 30 second public service commercials.  The station must present its recently approved fiscal year 1983 budget to PPTN, the organization responsible for distributing state-allocated money to public television stations across Pennsylvania.

headline: Keep out of talks, mayor told
abstract: Commonwealth Court Judge James Crumlish told Philadelphia Mayor Green to stay out of teacher contract negotiations, as there is no basis for his involvement.  Mayor Green issued a statement indicating that he feels it is his duty to be involved and will not bow out.

headline: Zemprelli says: No governor race
abstract: Pennsylvania Democratic Leader Edward Zemprelli pulled out of the governor's race, but still believe that a Democrat can win.  The article continues to explain why Zemprelli pulled out of the race and his views on Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Reagan vows limit for imported textiles
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heniz said that the Reagan administration is willing to impose unilateral steps to limit textile imports if negotiations with foreign suppliers fail.  The president prefers to negotiate independent agreements with each supplier, but will limit imports to stem the increasing textile trade deficit if such ageements are beyond reach.

headline: Jobless rate still rising
abstract: According to U.S. Labor Department statistics, national unemployment increased three tenths of a percentage point to 10.4 percent in October--the highest U.S. unemployment rate since 1940.  Democrats used this as an opportunity to call for a public works program; President Reagan objects to such a program.

headline: Tax sweet talk
abstract: Although arguing against a balanced budget might not make sense, but doing so when taxes are raised to balance it does make sense. Raising taxes is not a solution to getting the state back to fiscal order.

headline: Senate Backs Off on School Bill
abstract: The recommendations of PA Secretary if Education John Pittenger's task force to update school legislation included expanding school board powers to those not listed in the school code. However, faced with only a few weeks left in its term, the PA Senate reinserted current authority limitations, known as Dillon's Rule, into the text of the PA House bill. Some changes are made to the school code however school districts are still required to uphold PA Department of Education standards.

headline: Udall will visit area, tour TMI
abstract: Congressman Morris Udall, chairman of the House Subcommittee on Energy and the Environment, will visit the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear facility in order to gain better insight into the problems faced by the reactor.  Mr. Udall will also receive an update on the cleanup and a status report on the problems with Unit One of TMI.

headline: Gypsy band jailed on Ohio charges
abstract: PA State police placed 9 gypsies in jail after finding that they were wanted in Ohio in connection with the theft of $6000 from a market.  This group was part of a larger group detained in connection with a separate shoplifting incident near Carlisle.

headline: Corporate Law Topic of Address by Davis
abstract: Secretary of the Commonwealth William H. Davis addressed the Westmoreland County Bar Association corporate section regarding Pennsylvania corporate law and the reorganization of the state corporation bureau.  The corporation bureau is the first state government agency a business encounters when registering their company in Pennsylvania.  Davis told the group that Department of State asked the government to sponsor a joint venture with the bar association to improve the corporation bureau and in turn help the economic revitalization of the state.  The result was that Governor Thornburgh’s forming of the Corporate Advisory Committee, consisting of members of the legal, business, and accounting fields.

headline: Pact is Rejected by Trade Group, U.S. Steel Corp.
abstract: Domestic steel makers have repeatedly alleged that steel imports were being sold at artificially low prices because of illegal subsidization by nations where the steel is made.  However, it now appears that the unfair-trade cases pending with the Commerce Department could result in permanent punitive duties being levied against European Steel products, intensifying a trade dispute.  The U.S. steel industry has been operating at slightly more than 40 percent of capacity, and one-third of U.S. steel workers ware on indefinite layoff.  All the major steel companies have reported huge losses on their steel operations for the second quarter of the year.

headline: Keep racial slurs out of this race
abstract: David Fatah of the organization House of Umoja urges the news media to keep race as an issue out of the upcoming mayoral election. Fattah argues for equal employment opportunities to be taken up by the incoming new mayor. He credits House of Umoja with helping to elect PA's first Jewish Governor, Irish-Catholic President, and Italian-American Mayor of Philadelphia. He hints that the best candidate for mayor on the horizon now is black.

headline: Zimmerman after 1 year: State's first elected attorney general quietly pursues top-level prosecutions
abstract: LeRoy Zimmerman, Pennsylvania's first elected Attorney General, has tended to be more cautious than his other state-level colleagues.  The PA General Assembly gave the elected office strong tools to root out public corruption, and of the 43 states with an elected Attorney General, PA is the only one to take civil authorities of electronic surveillance, grand jury investigation, and witness immunity to this office.

headline: Specter urges aid plan, Reagan-Begin meeting
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter said that the United States should withold all further aid to Lebanon until Arab and European nations joined in the creation of a comprehensive aid plan.  He also encouraged President Reagan to meet with Israeli Prime Minister Begin to clear up a misunderstanding that exists between them.

headline: Bid for high-tech centers
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature and Governor Thornburgh must make Technological Centers and technical training a high priority.  Technological fields, especially those of science and engineering, will provide the foundation for a new economy.

headline: Tax system will be the death of us
abstract: This letter stresses that until everybody can collect and spend it according to their choice, the entire national economic structure will deteriorate until it finally collapses. The collection of tax before the individual gets his earnings, not only will lead to a reduction in the standards of living, but also for everyone that supplies his needs too.

headline: Some Get fired, Some Get Pay Raises
abstract: The administration of York City Schools first proposed for the 1982-83 school district a budget based on a 20-million increase.  After citizens raised their concerns, the administration brought the increase down to 12-million, then 10-million.  Finally it was approved at 6.5 million by the York City School Board.  Twenty seven little people--24 janitors and three secretaries were laid off.  15 teachers and one principal will be let go also.

headline: US Panel wants TMI exam cheaters prosecuted
abstract: A special report to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has recommended that two former supervisors at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant should face criminal prosecution for cheating on examinations.

headline: Handgun Liability
abstract: When Californians go to the polls, they will vote on a proposal to require the registration of all concealable firearms within one year.  Other measures related to gun-control will also be voted on.  While legislative and ballot questions on gun control have received considerable public attention, a series of pending lawsuits across the nation may have farther reaching implications.  They assert that handgun manufacturers are strictly liable for criminal uses of the small, concealable guns they make.  The National Rifle Association dismisses the doctrine of handgun manufacturer liability as preposterous.

headline: Cyclops cools crucible talks
abstract: Cyclops' President and CEO, William H. Knoell, has said that the specter of imports, the troubled economy and Crucible's eroding customer base are making the decision to make a pitch for the Crucible Stainless and Alloy division of Colt Industries Inc., difficult.

headline: Pennsylvania's Bureau of International Commerce and Seven Pennsylvania Firms Receive Presidential "E" Award
abstract: During the recent Pennsylvania International Trade Conference held in Hershey, U.S. Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldridge presented Governor Dick Thornburgh and the Pennsylvania Department of Commerce with the President's "E" Award for "activities to increase awareness of international trade" of Pennsylvania products.

headline: Keep the heat on noble lords
abstract: The author of this letter states that he is happy a lot of pressure is being put on the Congressmen to repeal the tax breaks bill, they voted themselves. By putting such pressure would be the only way for them to repeal this Act.

headline: 10 Years After Agnes: The Lessons Still Unlearned
abstract: It was the 10th Anniversary of Hurricane Agnes, the greatest recorded natural disaster ever to strike Pennsylvania.  Memories of that catastrophe are sharp and poignant for its many victims.  They recall vividly the raw destructive force of the storm and the difficult problems of recovery in the aftermath.  There is no surprise that floods could occur in Pennsylvania in the future because it is built on flood plains.  U.S. Corps of Engineers spent $7 million on engineering projects and Johnstown was declared to be “flood-proof” after the 1936 Johnstown Flood hit.  The flood in 1977 proved otherwise.

headline: House Oks Thornburgh parole bill
abstract: The Pennsylvania House approved parole-reform legislation that significantly alters the state's parole system and allows judges to impose longer minimum prison sentences.  The purpose of the legislation is to prevent early releases from prison--effectively abolishing the current parole system.

headline: Scanlon says state won't pay for jail
abstract: State Democratic Whip Eugene Scanlon says it is unrealistic, given the recession, for Pennsylvania counties to expect the state to pay for the construction of new jails.  As unemployment continues to rise, the problem of revenue shortfalls will get worse and may require a state takeover of the entire criminal-justice system.

headline: Tax-collection outlook poor, Lewis claims
abstract: PA Senator H. Craig Lewis, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, drawing his projections on the latest revenue report worries that the bottom is falling out on tax collections and there is no turnaround in sight.  The shortfall in revenue estimates versus actual collections jumped another $20 million from $79.6 million at the end of December 1981 to $99.6 million as of January 30, 1982.

headline: State hikes tuition $75 at universities
abstract: Students at 14 state-run universities will pay an additional $75 this semester to pay for a $6.3 million salary settlement.  While it was billed as a means to pay off a one-time fee, the tuition increase will be permanent.

headline: Utility bill cuts goal of reforms
abstract: Opinion: Utilities are working to ease customers' utility bills by promoting tax reforms in the PA legislature.  The move is not one to help utilities, but rather to keep taxes added on to utility bills from getting out of control.  The primary culprit is the Gross Receipts Tax added to every utility bill in the state which is tied to energy production rates.  The writer believes the state is just as much to blame for high utility bills as are the utilities themselves.

headline: Hearing to being today
abstract: A 7-member panel to investigate the recent hostage situation at Graterford Prison will begin its work. Last November 7 inmates held other inmates and guards in an aborted escape attempt at the prison.

headline: Downtown building sales: Assessments lag
abstract: Beginning January 1, real estate value will be attributed according to its sale price. However this system is proving difficult to review, as Mellon Bank and Koppers Inc. bought real estate from U.S. Steel and the Equitable Life Assurance Society of the United States for prices below their value. County assessment director Charles T. Blocksidge said sales prices will be a much stronger focus than previously. In cases such as the two mentioned, other factors will also contribute to assessment.

headline: The Feast is Red: China Wins Mushroom
abstract: The U.S. mushroom industry wants the government to limit the amount of mushrooms the Chinese can ship to the United States.  However, a formidable lobby of mushroom importers is dissenting.  The dispute will be ruled on by members of the International Trade Commission.  The have until September 30 to issue a recommendation to President Reagan.  Of the 28 states that grow mushrooms, Pennsylvania is the most affected.

headline: Kennedy Leads Democratic Parade
abstract: Senator Ted Kennedy is a standout because he represents tradition at a time when the Democratic Party appears to be returning to its traditional values under pressure by the Reagan Administration.  He was scheduled to address the Democratic National Party Conference.

headline: A Watershed Ruling
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Nicholas Papadakos once again is approaching a complex problem by emulating Alexander the Great’s cutting of the Gordian Knot.  The judge is approaching the long-festering Saw Mill Run situation with a far-reaching ruling.  In a Saw Mill Run case brought by a developer partnership against Whitehall Borough, Judge Papadakos avoided the knots of immediate controversy by ruling that no municipality can impose any regulations under the Storm Water Management Law of 1978, Act 167, until there is an overall storm-water-management plan for its watershed.

headline: Perry County voters to decide on method of balloting
abstract: Voters in Perry County, Pennsylvania will decide on a November 2nd ballot question that asks them if they want to replace their current paper ballot voting system with a new, electronic punch-card voting system.

headline: Rizzo Says He'll Enter Philadelphia Mayoral Race
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo announced that he will run in the Democratic primary for mayor.   He will likely enter a three-way challenge for the Dmeocratic primary with Wilson Goode--Philadelphia managing director--and Thomas Leonard, the City Controller.

headline: Tax-refund filings in Pa. nearly triple
abstract: The number of Pennsylvanians seeking income-tax refunds from the state has nearly tripled this year, apparently because of a court decision allowing deductions of certain business-related expenses for the first time, according to preliminary Revenue Department estimates.

headline: State lags in education for adults
abstract: A lot more needs to be done to provide adult Pennsylvania citizens with education and training. The state is in the top 10 percent, in terms of number of people requiring help. However, in money allocated for education, it ranks near the bottom.

headline: Utility Charge Loses Again
abstract: Legislation approved by the Senate passed the PA House Consumer Affairs Committee after members struck down some amendments. Utility companies oppose the bill, which would prevent companies from charging for expansion of building costs until facilities under construction are in operation. Supporters argue ratepayers should not have to subsidize a facility until they reap benefits from it. It is up to the PA Public Utilities Commission to determine when a facility under construction is operational.

headline: High court hear Tony Boyle's appeal
abstract: After waiting three years, former United Mine Workers president W.A. "Tony" Boyle got another hearing yesterday before the PA Supreme Court on whether or not he received a fair second trial for allegedly ordering the assassination of a union rival.  In previous action on this case, the Supreme Court set aside the first murder conviction and three life sentences.

headline: Dread not dreadnought
abstract: Paper uses the example of Dreadnought Wines in dealing with the business of importing wines into PA and dealing with the Liquor Control Board (LCB).  By adapting to LCB rules, the company brought in several different types of wine previously unavailable, but the LCB has been working relentlessly to find reasons to fine the company.

headline: Trade War
abstract: Congressman Don Bailey made some good points about the need to boost capitalization in order to compete in the international marketplace. He also suggested a number of tax approaches in order to enhance investment money. However, if the government interferes in a negative option, it will only strengthen its international competitors.

headline: Labor Department gets new secretary
abstract: The Republican-controlled PA State Senate has confirmed Governor Dick Thornburgh's nomination of Barry Stern as secretary of the Department of Labor and Industry Development.  Stern was the Deputy Secretary and Acting Secretary for the past 8 months.

headline: Adams board weighs transit plan; Transportation for rural residents, elderly
abstract: The Adams County Commissioners accepted for consideration a 30-page proposal calling for a network of vehicles to form a rural transportation system serving residents and senior citizens.

headline: Gas, Oil Drillers' Surcharge Backed
abstract: State Representative William Wachob has proposed legislation that would establish a two percent surcharge on all natural gas and oil production.  Surcharge revenues would be used to enforce new environmental protections specifically related to the negative externalities of natural gas exploration and drilling.

headline: Postscript
abstract: Tuesday's election saw both Republican and Democratic victories across Pennsylvania.  Governor Thornburgh and Senator Heinz, both Republicans, were elected to second terms, while Democrats regained majorities in both the state House of Representatives and the congressional delegation.

headline: The Bill Nobody Wanted is Passed: $98.3 billion Tax Measure Goes to Reagan for Signature; Most Effective Jan. 1
abstract: The Republican controlled Senate approved a bill that raises taxes by $98.3 billion over the next three years.  It is now on its way to President Reagan.  The bill will double the federal cigarette tax to 16 cents a pack, tripe the 1 percent tax on telephone service, require that 10 percent of most dividends and interest be withheld for taxes; reduce deductions for medical expenses and casualty losses, raise the 5 percent tax on air fares to 8 percent.

headline: State panel's school tax talks heated
abstract: Tempers flared as the House Finance Committee attempted to move stalled school tax changes and to agree on a new approach for funding local education.  A PA Senate plan to allow school districts to use income taxes has stalled.

headline: Utility refund urged
abstract: The Pennsylvania Alliance for Jobs and Energy says that Duquesne Light should be ordered to refund at least $19.8 million to its customers for an extended outage in 1979 at the Beaver Valley nuclear power plant in Shippingport.  The company is expected to respond to the refund plea at a Public Utility Commission hearing.  The PUC's audit staff had recommended a refund of $13.3 million.

headline: Horizons Reach Beyond Walls of Confinement
abstract: 42 inmates at the Graterford Prison are taking college-level, college-credit courses in a variety of subjects that Villanova University offers several days a week inside the grim, gray walls of Graterford, in Montgomery County.  The courses are taught by Villanova faulty members, who go to Graterford once a week for the three hour classes.  The found and director of the Villanova-Graterford connection is James McKenna, a criminologist and sociology professor.

headline: Drunk drivers not only issue, panel told
abstract: The House Liquor Control Committee held a two-day session for guidance in drafting legislation to reduce the number of accidents caused by drunk drivers in Pennsylvania. The Committee was told that any effort to combat the danger from drunk drivers must consider the larger problem of alcohol use and how to reduce the consumption. This could be done by raising the taxes or by placing limitations on the number of roadhouses.

headline: null
abstract: A building complex has been named after Past Department Commander Thomas G. Douglas, one of Pennsylvania’s most patriotic and dedicated citizens.  Because of his efforts, many Pennsylvania veterans have gained the recognition they deserve for serving their country in times of war and displaying his spirit of freedom in times of peace.

headline: Larsen Hearings Recessed
abstract: A panel of the State Judiciary Board investigating charges of improper political activity by state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen has recessed its session, but will resume at the end of September, in Philadelphia.  Larsen is accused of improper political activity and making racist remarks about fellow Justice Robert N.C. Nix of Philadelphia.  He is also charged of campaigning against Nix’s retention of urging fellow Justice John P. Flaherty Jr. and District Attorney Bob Colville to run for the high court, and promoting by telephone calls to various political figures, including Governor Dick Thornburgh and the appointment of Bruce W. Kauffman of Philadelphia to the high court two years ago.

headline: Conserving The Future
abstract: A new book covers the history of the Western PA Conservancy and its efforts to return more land to public use by buying land and then reselling it to the state for development as park, forest, or game land. However, Reagan Administration cuts means the end of such programs and the Conservancy will have to come up with other ways to achieve its goals. The public should be thankful that so much land is now being made available for their use.

headline: A veto vetoed
abstract: Last week's congressional override of President Reagan's budget veto signals deep discontent in Congress and significant vulnerabilities in the Reagan administration.  Many in Congress were frustrated at what they saw as the president's portrayal of the legislation as "budget busting," as well as the fact that the administration's latest stopgap spending bill would have cut funding for important constituent groups, such as veterans and the elderly.

headline: Where Are We Going
abstract: Although Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh was elected to a second term, Democrats won control of the state House of Representatives, which will make it difficult for the governor to institute the reforms he started his first term.

headline: The higher education fiscal mess
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh is having a hard time getting the approval for the state budget in the Legislature, especially considering that this is an election year. A special concern is being placed on education, which forms the biggest portion of the budget.

headline: State students urge $75 tuition-boost boycott
abstract: Student lobbyists urged a boycott of a recently-imposed $75 tuition hike at state-owned colleges and universities.  The Commonwealth Association of Students told parents and students not to pay the additional fee until at least March 1.  The student association is considering legal and legislative action.  The fee was instituted after the state was ordered by a court to pay$6.3 million in back teacher pay.

headline: Valve's failure let a bubble build up in upstate reactor
abstract: The failure of a crucial valve during a nuclear accident in Ontario, NY, allowed a bubble to form in the reactor vessel.  Officials of Rochester Gas and Electric said the bubble briefly raised the possibility that the nuclear core might be uncovered and cause the kind of damage that occurred at the Three Mile Island plant in March 1979.  A backup valve kicked in and maintained plant pressure.

headline: House adopts bill clarifying custody
abstract: A bill sponsored by PA Representative Lois Hagarty that speeds the adoption process in Pennsylvania was voted unanimously in favor.  The bill was brought about by a recent court case in which the natural parents who gave up he child for adoption, decided that they wanted the child back after the child had been adopted again.  Also in the article, the PA Senate decides what to do with Lottery surplus.

headline: Editorial - KDKA Weirton
abstract: The National Steel Company is intent on selling its plant in Weirton, PA, due to tough industry conditions. The mill employs about 11,000 people and they need to take a decision to either shut it down or buy it from the company. Either way, they face some tough decisions, going forward.

headline: null
abstract: In three major campaign committees, Republicans have raised 146.3 million dollars over the last 18 months compared to 18.9 million for the Democrats.  The article also mentions some of the different elections taking place throughout the United States.

headline: Larsen, in Legal Papers, Admits Lobbying for Nominee
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen has filed legal papers admitting to a state inquiry board that he urged Governor Thornburgh to appoint Philadelphia lawyer Bruce W. Kauffman to the high court in 1980-but only after Kauffman sought his intervention.  The legal papers, signed by Larsen’s attorney, admitted that after Kauffman was appointed, Larsen lobbied "several members of the Pennsylvania Senate" to persuade them to vote in favor of Kauffman’s confirmation.  He also admitted to planting a question with a friendly senator during the confirmation hearing.

headline: Enjoy Lazy Summer Days
abstract: Enjoy lazy summer days in Northwestern Pennsylvania.  One can enjoy the summer sun at Presque Isle or Pymatuning State Park, at Chautauqua, or in the huge, and this summer, particularly, very green Allegheny National Forest.

headline: Reagan policies seen hurting Northeast
abstract: A recent study released by The Urban Institute found that Reagan administration policies are helping economically healthy states and adversely affecting troubled northeastern states such as Pennsylvania.  Specifically, cuts in domestic programs are disproportinately impacting those in the Northeast, as well as residents of some low-income southern states.

headline: Free the student hostages
abstract: Pennsylvania legislators must figure out a way to prevent or reduce annual teacher strikes.  The long, drawn-out strikes of school districts in the Johnstown area are evidence that something needs to be done.

headline: The phantom voter
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's budget of nearly $11 billion was approved in the Pennsylvania House by a margin of one vote. This was later traced to Republican George Kanuck. However, Kanuck wasn't even in the building and somebody else had pressed the button. Such slip-ups cast the law-makers in a bad light.

headline: State urges shots for all students
abstract: PA State health officials propose tightening regulations requiring school children to be immunized against certain diseases.  The new plans would extend the requirement to children entering all grades of school, rather than just those entering kindergarten.  At the time of the article, 38 other states follow the all-grades policy.

headline: Ventilation defect halts Unit 2 entry
abstract: Entry into the Three Mile Island Unit 2 containment building was halted when an electrical problem in the ventilation system was detected.  This week's assignments have been moved to next week for workers in the area.

headline: House approves adoption bill
abstract: The PA House unanimously approved a bill that would reduce the time natural parents have to rescind their decision to let their child be adopted from 6 months to 40 days.  The new bill would allow adoptive parents to go to court to get final approval for adoption 40 days after the natural parents have signed the consent form.

headline: Enact the hotel room tax
abstract: Legislators should give attention to the authorization of a hotel room tax in Philadelphia, designated for development of tourism and conventions. Last year alone, tourists and convention-goers spent about $1 billion and provided for an estimated 28,000 jobs in the city. This tax would only aid in the betterment of this industry.

headline: null
abstract: null

headline: Last change looms for reapportionment
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers will get their final shot at approving a reapportionment plan before a federal court takes over the process.  A ruling is expected soon, but PA Senate Republican leader Robert Jubelirer believes the week that it will take to assemble the three-judge panel to create the new plan will give them time to work finish their own.  Governor Dick Thornburgh will still have to sign the bill once approved by both houses.

headline: Flood Curb Bill For City Offered
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter introduced bills authorizing $418 million for flood and erosion control projects in the Wilkes-Barre, Harrisburg, Lock Haven and Presque Isle areas.  Specter said all of the projects have been recommended by the Army Corps of Engineers.

headline: A Search For Life-Saving Solutions
abstract: In an effort to reduce incidents of drunken driving in Pennsylvania, Governor Thornburgh has proposed mandatory jail terms for offenders.  Although mandatory sentencing for drunken driving has been criticized by those who see it as creating both practical and moral problems, many strongly believe that it is the first step towards getting drunken drivers off the streets and protecting the citizenry.

headline: Coordinated Attach Injured 21 Guards
abstract: Inmates at Holmesburg Prison were under lockdown yesterday after 21 guards and three prisoners were injured in a brawl.  The brawl appeared to be a coordinated attack.

headline: Thornburgh budget message: fiscal restraint
abstract: Despite rising unemployment and a cutback in federal funding, Governor Dick Thornburgh submitted a budget that called for no tax increases and fiscal restraint.  Recognizing unemployment as an issue, economic development gets top billing in his budget.  The rest is a summary of other new budget items.

headline: Student aid cuts: putting college out of reach
abstract: Editorial:  Hundreds of thousands of students could be denied access to college if the reductions in student aid proposed by President Ronald Reagan are passed by Congress.  Under the plan federal spending on financial aid would be cut by about one-third, and two programs which combined helped 893,000 students would be eliminated.  This is a bad idea.

headline: What will TMI's stress test prove?
abstract: US Court of Appeals ruled that Three Mile Island's nuclear reactor cannot be restarted pending a test of the neighbor's psychological health.  The editorial article talks about how the "psychological testing" rule may be applied to many other regulations and regulatory agencies.

headline: House Panel Delays Action on 'get tough' bills
abstract: Pennsylvania House Judiciary Committee has delayed action on bills that would lower the age at which youths who commit violent or drug-related crimes would be treated as adults by the state judicial and penal systems.  One of the reasons is because this would force youths into already over-crowded adult prisons.  The answer is to make the juvenile system workable.

headline: Erie Stadium Nearer Approval to Sell Beer
abstract: Legislation that could clear the way for new liquor licenses in the popular factory outlet area near Reading and sports and entertainment centers in other areas was approved yesterday by a House-Senate conference committee.  But the five-member panel refused to take up an amendment that would earmark two percent of state liquor profits for drug and alcohol abuse programs.  That would amount to about $1 million in this fiscal year.

headline: null
abstract: Philadelphia Councilman Harry Jannotti, whose conviction on Abscam-related charges was recently reinstated by a federal appeals court, will take a paid leave of absense at the request of Council President Joseph Coleman.  Under Pennsylvania law, Jannotti is not required to step down until he is sentenced.

headline: Late Sprint By Tuscano Trips Bailey
abstract: Prolonged efforts to award the Republican congressional nomination in the 12th District to Democratic U.S. Representative Don Bailey have been crushed by a dark-horse candidate who campaigned for only five hours.  William Tuscano, an insurance executive from Greensburg decided to run for the seat.  It must be regarded as one of the snappiest political campaigns in Pennsylvania history.

headline: Intact but decaying, Pennsylvania town resists preservation
abstract: West Middletown, PA residents resist having their town designated a historical district.  Article talks about the history of the town.

headline: Cheyney to Appear At Rally for Gekas
abstract: U.S. Representative Richard Cheyney will appear on behalf of state Senator George W. Gekas at a campaign rally next week.  State Senator Gekas is running for the 17th District Congressional seat.

headline: Good time to drop Watt
abstract: A year ago, Interior Secretary James Watt was extremely popular on the GOP fundraising circuit, but now--with increased awareness that President Reagan's laissez-faire environmental policies are not as popoular with the electorate as originally thought--Watt has become a political liability.  President Reagan must rethink his environmental policies and the best place to start would be by replacing James Watt.

headline: Thornburgh signs $11 billion budget
abstract: Gov. Dick Thornburgh signed a record $10.6 billion state budget package for the coming fiscal year. He also hailed the Republicans for their support and criticized the Democrats for engaging  in "political vendetta".

headline: Student Loan Bill Advances
abstract: A bill authorizing the Pennsylvania Higher Education Agency to issue tax-exempt bonds for student loans has passed the State Senate.  The legislation would fill a gap resulting from a cutback in federal loans to students.

headline: York Area Nuke Plant Plans Drills
abstract: Three nuclear power plants in Pennsylvania plan to hold full-scale accident drills over the next several months to demonstrate their ability to deal with actual emergencies.  Basic drills are required by law, but these drills will also include involve evacuations.  The Nuclear Regulatory Commission will be developing the accident scenario.

headline: House Passes State Court Bill
abstract: The PA House passed legislation to create 2 additional Justice positions on Commonwealth Court. The Justices would be required to run for election once the appointment expires rather than undergoing yes-no voter retention. Commonwealth Court President Judge James Crumlish has urged expansion of the Court to keep up with its caseload. Two seats on the Court are already vacant; Judge Glenn Miller took a seat on US District Court, while Judge Roy Wilkinson was elevated to PA Supreme Court.

headline: Firms Sells Plant, Pays Delinquent Taxes
abstract: The Atlas Concrete Co. Inc. was sold to the Allegheny County Sewer Authority.  The state was able to collect $189, 456 in delinquent sales and personal income taxes from the sale.  $185, 912 of the money was for the sales taxes owed by the corporation since 1974, with most of the rest coming from personal income taxes owed by the company’s three officers.

headline: null
abstract: The fourth floor of the Afro-American museum, which was to have included an archive, is still incomplete.  Given the city's current fiscal trouble, it seems unlikely that officials will supply the estimated $800,000 needed for completion.

headline: Laurie An Hixenbaugh Wins; Dallas Woman 2nd Runner-Up: New Miss Pennsylvania Crowned
abstract: Laurie Ann Hixenbaugh, was crowned Mss Pennsylvania 1982.  She defeated 22 other contestants in the state pageant for a chance at participating in the Miss America Pageant.  The new Miss Pennsylvania receives a $2,500 scholarship, the use of three cars during her one-year reign, a new wardrobe, a trophy, and a crown.

headline: New road repair chief discovers job's pitfalls
abstract: Carl Tosi had just accepted the position of Allegheny County maintenance manager for the PA Department of Transportation. He had some initial problems with regard to the challenging conditions of the job. However, he reiterated that he was looking forward to the challenge of maintaining the worst state road system for any Pennsylvania county.

headline: Special session a political ploy
abstract: Pennsylvania's unemployment compensation fund has one of the highest levels of federal debt in the nation, and fixing the indebted institution is a top priority of the state Legislature.  It is such a priority that House Minority Whip James Manderino wants Governor Thornburgh to convene a special legislative session to deal with reforming the unemployment compensation fund.  While we agree that fixing the fund should be a top priority, a speical session would not be productive--especially given the fact that Manderino himself has no substantive proposals to put forward.

headline: Home heat efficiency topic of state survey
abstract: The Governor's Energy Council is implementing a survey to better understand energy usage and attitudes toward energy conservation in Pennsylvania.  According to the council, roughly one third of residential energy use could be saved through conservation techniques--resulting in savings for consumers.

headline: Thornburgh signs new budget early
abstract: Gov. Dick Thornburgh today signed the 1982-83 General Fund budget and said that its early enactment, two months ahead of time, sends a strong signal to the business and financial communities that Pennsylvania is capable of managing its finances efficiently.

headline: Students take crash course in college aid cuts
abstract: Students across universities in the Allegheny county are worried about the proposed cut in federally-available funding for education. According to most college representatives, the situation will become disastrous if these cuts do occur in the coming year.

headline: Annual car test okayed
abstract: A bill that reduces most vehicle safety inspections in Pennsylvania from every six months to once a year, needs only Gov. Dick Thornburgh's signature to become law.

headline: How's that again?
abstract: Civil libertarians have attacked a bill introduced by Senator Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, which would make it a federal crime to be charged three times for certain offences.

headline: For healthy newspapers, look to the suburbs
abstract: A new trend in the newspaper industry shows that suburban-based newspapers are succeeding better than big-city newspapers. One of the main reasons for this is that people are reading suburban papers more than big-city dailies and major stores that followed these people, are stepping up advertising in these suburban papers to reach their customers.

headline: null
abstract: This cartoon depicts an employee at the Legislature Public Relations Department getting instructions about making sure that the new pay hike does not actually look like a pay hike.

headline: Lawmakers explain stand on No-Fault measure
abstract: Letter to the editor from State Legislators George Hasay, Frank Coslett, and Correale Stevens, defending their votes to refer the No-Fault bill to the Judiciary Committee.

headline: On the Trail in Pennsylvania
abstract: Pennsylvania Hikers are lucky.  More than 58 percent of the commonwealth is forest-covered, and walkers have their choice of hundreds of trails, from the civilized Wissakickon Gorge Trail in Philadelphia's Fairmount Park to the rugged and not-for-beginners Mid-State Trail between Huntingdon and Centre counties.

headline: Attorneys call plea bargaining indispensable
abstract: Pennsylvania attorneys say that plea bargaining is an indispensible and effective tool if used properly.  Attorneys also predict that Pennsylvania's new sentencing guidelines will not change the plea-bargaining process too much; they will simply change the terms of negotiation.

headline: Brandt May Lose Key Post
abstract: After last week's elections changed the party balance of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, sources say that state Representative Kenneth E. Brandt will lose his post as head of the House Republican Policy Committee, as well as his post as head of the House GOP Campaign Committee.

headline: Thornburgh's budget austere, optimistic, but possibly flawed
abstract: Opinion: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's new budget proposal for 1982-1983 seems to have something for everyone.  First, it is a balanced budget with no new taxes.  Second, it has welfare reform and mass transit increases.  But, the new budget does not include President Ronald Reagan's newest proposed cuts, and may not likely include enough allowance for inflation.

headline: Studies In Stress: Pressure Eating At College Students
abstract: null

headline: null
abstract: In this letter to the editor the author responds to a column in the June 20th issue of the newspaper.  Attempts are being made by the Pennsylvania Federation of Dog Clubs to revise a law that regulated and required specific licensing for laboratory dogs.  The law needs updating and also one important section has been eliminated in the proposed House Bill 2435: the provision that permits any "agent of any legally constituted law enforcement agency" to inspect dog dealers’ records.  This part must be put back in, because Pennsylvania has long been the center of interstate traffic in dogs for medical research.

headline: Humane Spirit Is Alive
abstract: The Supreme Court, far from following the election returns, has developed a new liberal majority.  Exchanges between the Democratic opposition and President Reagan convey the tenor of the political dialogue.  At the Midterm Conference in Philadelphia, the Democrats rallied around the slogan "Fairness to All." They heaped on the administration implicit charges of discrimination against women, minorities, and the poor.

headline: Girard Bank to Merge with Mellon, Penna's Largest
abstract: Girard Bank will merge with Mellon Bank.  This will provide advanced opportunities for both organizations.

headline: null
abstract: This cartoon depicts Governor Thornburgh with his state budget that includes no tax hikes. A reason for this is attributed to the upcoming elections.

headline: Lawmakers hoping voters are forgetful
abstract: With the state legislature elections only a short while away, incumbent candidates are hoping that the electorate is in a forgetful mood, especially of the recent back-door income tax bonanza handed them.

headline: Open house at historic sites
abstract: This page shows a series of photographs that depict various museums and historic sites operated by the Pennsylvania Museum and Historic Commission. The Commission is celebrating the state's 300th birthday by offering free admission to visitors at these places.

headline: State's Teacher-Strike Total Rises to 18
abstract: Currently there are 18 schoolteacher strikes in Pennsylvania.  The latest strike occurred on Wednesday when teachers from the Wilkinsburg School District walked off the job.  Statewide, the ongoing strikes involve roughly 2,860 teachers and 50,000 students.

headline: Second prison incident
abstract: Two guards at the Philadelphia Detention Center were assaulted yesterday by an inmate who had been transferred there because of his role in Saturday's brawl at Holmesburg Prison.

headline: Thornburgh's state budget
abstract: Cartoon depicts Democratic leaders Zemprelli and Manderino looking at a plate with Governor Dick Thornburgh's bare bones state budget and crying with dismay "No Fat!"

headline: Supporting schools with block grants
abstract: Although school districts seem to be in line for larger increases under the block-grant proposal, most school administrators are doubtful because they believe that the state is not paying 50 percent on average for all the districts, and that they may be using the block grants as a scheme to pay even less.

headline: $1.2 Billion OK'd for Pa. Bridges
abstract: The General Assembly enacted a $1.26 billion, eight-year program to rebuild bridges throughout the state. Another bill is headed for a possible vote on setting up a court-ordered automobile emissions inspection program.  As the Legislature headed into the final hours of its two year session, House Republicans also managed to push through a Thornburgh administration proposal to make the state’s current tax rates of 2.2 percent for personal income and 10.5 percent for corporate net income permanent.  In a consent decree signed by the US Environmental Protection Agency and the state in the waning days of the Shapp administration, the state agreed to establish auto emission inspections in those countries to curtail air pollution.

headline: In Bar Election, Jury to Deliver Verdict Dec. 9
abstract: Jerome R. Richter and David H. Marion are both running for vice chancellor for the Philadelphia Bar Association, a post that automatically leads to a one-year term as chancellor the 8,300 member group.  It is a job that involves money, power, and ego.

headline: Give Elders A Break on Bingo, County Urges
abstract: The PA State Assembly will introduce County Treasurer Jay Costa's measure calling for reduced license fees for senior citizens playing organized bingo. Legislation stipulates organizations wishing to operate games must be incorporated for 2 plus years, a standard Costa believes is unreasonable for seniors. Costa also argues against licensing fees for seniors on fixed incomes. Municipal police rarely enforce bingo laws. The County took in $56,000 in bingo fees last year.

headline: null
abstract: U.S. Representative Charlie Dougherty got wind that some California politicians were after Defense Secretary Caspar Weinberger to move the Army-Navy game from Philadelphia to the Rose Bowl, and he fired a blistering salvo listing all the reasons for keeping the game in PA.  In addition, Joe Certaine left the No. 2 job at Demo City Committee to kea a paying job with the Green Team’s Office of Housing and Community Development.

headline: Lawmakers: Are They Worth More?
abstract: Republican and Democratic leaders in the state House of Representatives introduced a bill that would raise legislative and judicial pay over the course of two years.  Has individual assembly members performed duties in a way that make them worth a certain amount of money now and more in two years is one of the key questions.

headline: Protect Valley Forge Park - II
