abstract: $4 million was recently appropriated by the US Congress to expand Valley Forge National Park, but $2 million is being held up the by US Park Service.  With federal budget cuts for national parks, the land may end up being developed by the private sector.

headline: Wilburn Wows D.C. Panel
abstract: Pennsylvania Budget Secretary Robert C. Wilburn explained to a U.S. House subcommittee how Governor Thornburgh's administration was able to revive the state's economy through debt reduction and a pay-as-you-go spending philosophy.

headline: Frank Rizzo Ponders Running Again
abstract: Although he was quoted in the New York Times as saying that he plans to enter the Democratic primary and win, former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo neither confirmed nor denied that statement and said he will have more to say in the coming weeks regarding his potential candidacy; Rizzo did confirm that 50 of his supporters met last week and each pledged 5,000 dollars to his campaign.

headline: U.S. Interest Increases Pressure on State's Jobless Fund
abstract: The state’s unemployment compensation system, created in 1936, was not supposed to run into debt.  Officials assumed that surpluses that would accumulate during times of low unemployment would provide the necessary funds when unemployment increased.  The total amount owed by all states to the federal government is about $8 billion, with Illinois, Michigan, and Ohio the biggest borrowers after Pennsylvania.  Until recently, states had little incentive to cut down on borrowing, assuming they would begin repaying their debts when the economy recovered.  But in 1981 federal officials, who have had to tap the treasury to allocate the funds, pushed through the harsh penalties on future borrowing.

headline: Tax credits for private school tuition
abstract: WTAE-TV4 editorial:  Few parents are more for tax credits for private school tuitons than those who have children trapped in school strikes.  In just this current academic year, there have been 25 teacher union strikes.  Strong public education is great, but there needs to be a counterbalancing system as well.

headline: $1.2 Billion Proposed For Bridges
abstract: PA House Majority Leader Samuel E. Hayes Jr. unveiled a proposal to finance the renovation of 745 state highway bridges with federal funds and fees charged to out of state truckers. Hayes noted fees for PA truckers will not increase. PA Secretary of Transportation Thomas Larson did not foresee any problem with the trucking industry. The construction work would create approximately 20,000 jobs, Hayes hopes. The article lists a number of counties in which projects will take place.

headline: In Jail And Crippled: Broken Bodies, Steel Bars Block Their Paths
abstract: Two inmates who are permanently bound to a wheel chair are examples of the lengths the Bureau of Corrections must go to in order to keep the inmates packed into the overcrowded prisons.  Article says that the inmates could be better treated at a state hospital but that is unable to happen with the current guidelines.

headline: Good Place for Steel
abstract: Bethlehem Steel Corp. is about to announce a decision on whether to suspend steelmaking at its modern new electric melt shop in Johnstown.  There is a glut of steel on the world market, and little incentive to build anything with it.  Bethlehem is one of the best places to make steel not only because of the modern facility and the capable management and the available work force but also because Johnstown labor has a natural aptitude for heavy industry.

headline: $1,075 to cut, deliver Yule trees
abstract: The state paid a Middletown tree firm $1,075 to deliver the Capitol's two 25-foot Christmas trees. Last year, the 35-foot tall outdoor tree donated by a West Shore family was never used for its intended purpose.

headline: Lazin to head crime unit
abstract: Malcolm Lazin, a former Assistant Federal Prosecutor who advocates joint crime-fighting efforts by state and local agencies, will become chairman of the Pennsylvania Crime Commission next week. He was appointed to the commission in 1979 by Governor Thornburgh.

headline: State buys parcel for fishing, boating
abstract: The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy has sold 7.6 acres of land along the Allegheny River in Harmar Township to the state for a fishing and boating base.

headline: House panel approves bill to alter state college system, trim costs
abstract: The House Education Committee approved legislation that would make state colleges independent of the state Education Department and rename them as universities.  Supporters of the bill claim it will save state colleges approximately 2 million dollars in administrative costs.  The bill will now be sent to the full House, where a vote may happen some time next week; the Senate has already approved the bill.

headline: Zimmerman argues case on prison transfer
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman told the U.S. Supreme Court that prison inmates have no legal right to automatically appeal transfer decisions.  Zimmerman appeared in the high court to challenge a U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that claimed officials at the State Correctional Institution at Huntingdon had improperly treated a prison inmate, Aaron Helms, when they transferred him in the wake of a prison disturbance.

headline: US steelmakers slim down for survival
abstract: As demand for steel reduces, US steelmakers are reacting with great speed to slim down their companies in order to help them survive the market collapse. Among the ones in Pennsylvania that are in the worst shape include Colt Industries Crucible division and US Steel based in Homestead, Pa.

headline: That's the Biggest Guitar I Ever Saw
abstract: State Education Secretary Robert Scanlon is pictured with Harrisburg Symphony Orchestra conductor Larry Newland and two toddlers at the "Tiny Tots Concert" held in the PA Education Building.

headline: $7.7M suit says pothole caused accident
abstract: John and Dianna Lozada filed a suit against the PA Department of Transportation claiming that PennDOT's failure to fix a pothole caused an accident that left a man in a coma.

headline: In Penna. Prisons, the Forsaken Mentally Ill
abstract: People with severe mental illnesses reside in each of Pennsylvania’s seven state prisons and two regional institutions.  Prison officials can only estimate their numbers as record keeping is poor, and treatment facilities non-existent.  The state prison population rose nearly 15 percent in 1981 and about 2,200 of Pennsylvania’s more than 10,000 inmates must sleep two to a cell.

headline: Governor Checks In To Sign Hotel Tax Bill
abstract: Governor Thornburgh will be in Pittsburgh to sign a bill allowing Allegheny County to raise its hotel tax from one to three percent. The money will go towards operating the David L. Lawrence Convention Center as well as to promote tourism in Allegheny County and  Monroeville.

headline: $15 Million Up for Grabs: With Lottery Money Prizes at Record Levels, Lines are Long and Visions are Lofty
abstract: In Pennsylvania the Lottery pot is at $6 million and is growing.  It is the biggest prize in the game’s 11 year history.  People were lining up to buy the tickets.  If anyone loses the drawing then about half of the funds will go to funds for the elderly, the disabled, veterans, and mentally ill.

headline: Legal Services Safe in State-This Year
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh spared the Pennsylvania Legal Services Center for 1982.  He renewed the non-profit agency’s $7 million contract.  There are concerns about what will happen if the Reagan Administration budget cutters and conservative state lawmakers will continue to attack the program.

headline: State obtains 500 acres for French Creek park
abstract: 500 acres of undisturbed forest land has been annexed into French Creek State Park and will be open for public use in the spring.  The PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) and the JN Pew Jr. Charitable Trust combined to pay $394,500 for the land from Benjamin Pupek.  The acquisition expands the park to 7,337 acres.

headline: Real obscenity
abstract: The most effective way for getting drunk drivers off the road would be the adoption of a federal law that revokes anyone's license for life after a drunk-driving conviction.  Such laws should also be coupled with steep fines and imprisonment--as these will have a deterrent effect.  Raising the driving age would also have a significant impact.

headline: Senate bill aims at oil companies
abstract: The Senate Environmental Resources and Energy Committee approved the oil divorcement bill, which will barr oil companies from the gasoline-station business.  Also, a subcomittee rejected a plan to triple coal-mining permit fees--warning that the increase could price Pennsylvania coal out of the competitive market.  Roughly 20 representatives of Parent-Teacher Associations rallied in the Capitol to urge the Senate to pass a new school code as well.

headline: Utilities Pass on State's Phantom Tax
abstract: Phantom taxes are a nightmare for consumers and a dream come true for utilities.  Phantom taxes have spawned a Senate investigation and sparked enough arguments to light up a small city.  Phantom taxes are revenues collected from customers, through utility rates to pay company income taxes.  However, by using business-tax incentives and credits, utilities are able to defer many tax payments and keep the difference; thus collecting a "phantom" tax from consumers.

headline: The Diary of a Narc
abstract: Excerpts from a diary kept by police officer Charles Albert Patton while posing as a student at Morrisville Junior Senior High School.

headline: $7.8 million set for Midstate winter
abstract: The State has authorized $7.8 million in funds for snow and ice removal on midstate roads this year. However, PA State Police urge motorists to use caution and common sense when driving. Trooper Robert Breen offered a list of safe driving tips for motorists. PA District Department of Transportation Engineer Bob Mueser outlined the supplies and equipment available to the Department for dealing with snow and ice.

headline: Individual calendar
abstract: KDKA TV2 editorial:  In Allegheny County's previous court system, cases were heard whenever a judge had free space.  Now, Judge Robert Dauer has set up a new system where, once a case is assigned to a judge, that judge stays with the case from beginning to end.  The new system has a major flaw in that if cases are not heard as quickly, there is a chance they could be thrown out after the 180 day window.  The new system is still the better system.  Give it time.

headline: Governor eyes jobs with $12 million bid
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has called on the state legislature to approve $12 million in spending to create jobs and attract high-technology business, in addition to continuing a previous $15 million program that provided low interest business loans.  The state jobless rate is at 11.2%.

headline: $5M Player No Eager Beaver
abstract: A winning ticket for the five and a half million dollar lottery jackpot was sold in Beaver County but remains unclaimed. The winner has up to a year to claim the winnings and it is not uncommon for other winning tickets to be claimed a year after the fact.

headline: Legislative Breaks
abstract: Republican leaders in the State Legislature decided to skip the idea of a five-month vacation after Democrats had claimed the Republicans wanted to avoid any more controversial issues that might jeopardize the re-election chances of Governor Dick Thornburgh and other GOP candidates.

headline: Waterway welfare
abstract: US Rep. Joseph Gaydos, along with Rep. Eugene Atkinson pointed out the plight of the region's navigable waterways. They pushed for the revitalization of Western Pennsylvania's worn-out locks and dams.

headline: Atkinson Heads List As Target
abstract: The congressional seat of Eugene Atkinson, the now Republican Congressman who switched parties in support of President Reagan's policies, has become of electoral significance for both the Republican and Democratic Parties.  Republicans are putting significant weight behind Atkinson--sending political lumanaries such as Vice President Bush to stump for him.  The Democratic Party is also spending a lot of time and energy on this race, sending former Vice President Walter F. Mondale to Atkinson's district to offer support to his opponent, Democratic state legislator Jospeh P. Kolter.

headline: Hearing begins on TMI's good unit
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is scheduled to hold a two-part hearing today regarding the issue of restarting Three Mile Island's Unit 1 nuclear reactor.  The NRC has set a December 10th deadline for deciding whether to lift its order that closed the unit-1 reactor, which was not damaged during the March 1979 incident.

headline: Vote on Tax Increase Was Nonpartisan and Joyless
abstract: Representative Bob Edgar cast his vote in favor of a $98.3 billion tax increase under the watchful eyes of his two young sons, who sat beside him on the House floor.  It was an issue that his family and staff were split against.  Soul-searching was the prevailing pass time last week as Pennsylvania legislators weighed the prospects of higher taxes and reduced social spending against lower deficits, tax reform and extended unemployment benefits.

headline: The making of an issue: school reform
abstract: The PA House Education Committee sent to the full House a bill that would give budgetary authority of the Philadelphia School District to City Council and Mayor Green.  It also reported out a bill to appease the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers that would create an elected school board with its own taxing authority.  After some debate, it looks like the first bill will pass the House.

headline: 1-a-year car check advances
abstract: Pennsylvania motorists would now have only one auto safety inspection each year, under legislation passed by Senate. The vote came despite criticism that this bill would increase the number of traffic fatalities in the state.

headline: Inside Rockview: The squeeze is being felt all over
abstract: The Rockview State Correctional Institution is currently facing a massive overcrowding problem. At current levels, it is the worst in the institutions 65-year history.

headline: Her suit heads fight for equal disability rates
abstract: Ellen Starer's complaint filed four years ago in the Commonwealth Court, was moved in 1980 to the Pennsylvania Insurance Department, which regulates premium rates. Hence, the insurance company has stopped selling insurance in Pennsylvania in order to escape from battling Starer.

headline: $600,000 visit by Reagan; Heinz, governor are benefactors
abstract: President Reagan came to Philadelphia yesterday and in a span of six hours made four appearances, gave two speeches and raised $600,000 for the re-election campaigns of Pennsylvania's Republican Governor, Dick Thornburgh and its Senior Republican US Senator, John Heinz.

headline: Legislator Tax Breaks: State Lawmakers Could Keep Deductions Federal Counterparts May Lose
abstract: State legislators may escape the attempt in Washington to cut down the tax shelter voted last year by Congress for itself and state lawmakers.  There is movement within the Congress to repeal the tax bonus of a $7 per day deduction during sessions.  Sources in the National Conference of State Legislatures said there is a distinct possibility that Congress, should it cut back on its own tax haven, will not touch the largesse which makes Pennsylvania legislators eligible for some $20,000 in retroactive tax deductions.

headline: Waterways Woes Focus of Regatta
abstract: Industries that rely on Pittsburgh’s rivers will be using this weekend’s Three Rivers Regatta to focus attention on the deterioration of locks and dams.  A giant petition will be on display at the Point and visitors to the Regatta will be asked to sign it showing support for efforts to obtain congressional funding to repair the locks.  William J. Lekse, president of Campbell Barge Line, said that waterway industries want to stress the importance of the rivers to jobs and the economy of the region.  The coal industry generates $1 million in the local economy in the production of coal transported by water.

headline: Heinz stays on sidelines in vote on tuition tax credits
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz did not vote on a bill that would allow tuition tax credits for parents of nonpublic school students.  Recently, Senator Heinz became disenchanted with the bill because it runs counter to recent deficit-reduction efforts and would occur in a climate where public education programs were saddled with funding cuts.

headline: State gets windfall from Sohio
abstract: As part of a consent order with the U.S. Department of Energy, Standard Oil has paid the state of Pennsylvania 1,416,686 dollars.  These payments resolve all issues of compliance with Department of Energy petroleum price allocation regulations from August, 19, 1973, through January 27, 1981, when President Reagan decontrolled refined petroleum products.

headline: Walgren, Atkinson oppose deduction
abstract: Rep. Doug Walgren, D-Mt. Lebanon, along with Rep. Eugene V. Atkinson, R-Aliquippa and Iowa Democrat Berkley Bedell, were the three members of Congress who asked a panel of Internal Revenue Service lawyers to remove the $75-a-day income tax deduction allowed them while working here on congressional business.

headline: The University System
abstract: Lock Haven State College has a new name-Lock Haven University of Pennsylvania.  The change is from one part of a bill signed by Governor Dick Thornburgh recently divorcing the state colleges from the PA Department of Education July 1, 1983.  The 14 state schools will establish an independent state university system.  By taking higher education out of the Education Department, this bill allows state universities to set up their own governing body.  It should help when the universities fight the big state-related schools, like Penn State and Pitt for state money.

headline: 2 Propose Auto-Exhaust Tests Anew
abstract: PA Representative Joseph A. Lashinger, alongside PA Senator Vincent Fumo, announced he was drafting a bill requiring annual auto emissions inspections in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia. The bill would limit what car owners have to spend on repairs and establish places where they can get second opinions. The announcement is in response to the previous PA Senate session's failure to lift a ban on spending state money for such a program. A federal court mandated the creation of such a program for the two cities in 1978 (a U.S. district judge found the state in contempt of the order this year); the PA Department of Transportation warned that without action they would be unable to proceed with federally funded highway projects, resulting in thousands of lost jobs because the money would be given to other states. Fumo and Lashinger claim the issue is tied up with a dispute among Western PA Senators over reducing the city wage tax suburban commuters pay.

headline: Judge Asked to End Eecrecy in Larsen Probe
abstract: Richard Sprague, Special Counsel to the PA Board of Judicial Inquiry and Review, said that the pane's secrecy rules open the possibility of a cover-up of judical wrongdoing.  It is believed that State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen was in ethical violations.

headline: Hershey-Keystone Link of Water Firms OK'd
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission authorized the merger of Hershey Water Company. with the Camp Hill-based Keystone Water Company.  The merger will help to hold down operating costs in the Hershey district.

headline: 1 Lost Life in Heroic Act: 2 State Rescuers Honored
abstract: President Reagan presented bravery medals yesterday to two Pennsylvania firefighters, one of whom died in the 1981 rescue of a small boy from a septic tank with poisonous gas.  Reagan also presented medals to youths from New Mexico and New York as well as community service medals to young men from Philadelphia and Altoona.

headline: Legislature Ending Session with Flurry of Bills
abstract: The State House was pushing through a long calendar of bills preparing for the summer recess.  Early approval was given for the 1982-83 state budget and passage of such major items as a revised congressional reapportionment plan, welfare reform, anti-abortion legislation, once-a-year car inspections, and stricter sentencing guidelines.

headline: . . . But Philadelphia deserves better
abstract: Senator James R. Lloyd does not support reducing the wage tax, H.B.1652, for those commuting in to Philadelphia for work, arguing that unless the $50 million loss in revenue could be offset with other taxes, the city cannot sustain it. Senator Lloyd recommends restructuring taxes in PA so that those who can afford to pay, do so. Lloyd would protect the suburban commuter by restructuring property taxes in particular.

headline: Commissioner on aging denies slashing funds
abstract: Lennie Marie Tolliver, the federal commissioner on aging, addressed a national conference on programs that provide meals to the elderly, and argued that the Reagan administration has been unfairly portrayed as insensitive to the needs of the elderly and aging.  She stressed that the administration is not cutting funding for programs that serve the elderly, and that funding for senior citizens has increased since President Reagan took office.

headline: New school code amended, sent to full Senate for consideration
abstract: The Senate Rules Committee approved a new school code on Monday after adding several amendments; the bill will now go to the full Senate for consideration.  Democrats have complained that the amendments are too broad and change the meaning of the bill.

headline: Wecht: Ditching assessments may be wise
abstract: County Commissioner Cyril H. Wecht has announced that throwing out the county's 1982 property tax assessments might be the right thing to do. However, this has received a lot of criticism from many sources.

headline: Thornburgh Signs Bill on Religious Instruction
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed legislation that would allow school districts to excuse students up to 36 hours per year for the purpose of religious instruction.  He also signed bills that would increase fish license fees, made a technical amendment to the state Municipalities Planning Code relating to the subdivision of land for agricultural purposes, provide for the renewal or transfer of a hotel liquor license if the establishment was destroyed by fire or natural disaster, revise the collection process for the motor vehicle sales tax, and permit Philadelphia County to pay up to $2,000 annually for membership expenses in the State District Attorney’s Association.

headline: 65 Bridges Due for Repairs
abstract: The massive $1.3 billion bridge repair program authorized by the General Assembly would affect 65 bridges in Allegheny and Beaver counties over the next six years.  Because federal funds are not available, however, it is not known when the repair program would advance beyond the talking stage.  A freeze on federal monies for bridge and road repairs was applied because the Legislature refused to comply with a consent decree in which the state agreed to institute emission-control inspection programs in the Pittsburgh, Philadelphia and Allentown Areas.

headline: Jail brawlers transferred
abstract: 15 Graterford prison inmates, identified as "aggressive participants" in a recent brawl that injured 8 guards will be transferred to other state prisons.  Prison officials say the transfers will allow them to investigate the incident, to make sure that potential inmate witnesses will not feel intimidated.

headline: Homeowners Take the Risk
abstract: Philadelphia was recently the host of an insurance convention.  The nation’s insurance regulators were there for the annual meeting of the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC).  One of the issues before the NAIC is how much it would cost homeowners to buy insurance against nuclear accidents.  Under the Price-Anderson Act, the public is guaranteed a total of $560 million compensation for all the damages caused by a nuclear accident, however, they are prohibited from suing anyone involved in a nuclear accident-regardless of negligence or fault.

headline: 10,500 Could Be Paid in Lotto Botch
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman said the state may pay 10,500 people whose winning lotto tickets were invalidated after a drawing error. The PA Revenue Departments awaits a review of Zimmerman's ruling before awarding prizes. PA Revenue Secretary and Lottery Director Lynn Nelson are hoping to pay winners of the invalidated drawing and a second drawing to replace the invalidated one, however the likelihood of paying winners of both drawings depends on the funds available.

headline: Legislature Runs on One House
abstract: It appears that Pennsylvania will have a unicameral Legislature this month, because only the House is returning from a three-month summer recess to conduct business.  The Senate will remain in recess indefinitely, probably until after the November 2 election.  The House is expected to meet for two or three weeks before recessing again to allow members to campaign for re-election.  Some of the top issues to be worked on are drunken driving and changing the law on insanity pleas.

headline: 6.3% tax boost Ok'd by Council
abstract: City Council has approved a $1.3 billion operating budget for the next fiscal year that calls for an increase in the mercantile tax and includes $27.5 million in cuts imposed by Council. Council also approved a $2.3 billion, six-year building program.

headline: Audit charges CCAC was overpaid by state
abstract: The Pennsylvania Auditor General released a report yesterday stating that the Community College of Allegheny County improperly received 603,021 in state reimbursements for continuing education credits.  Auditor General Al Benedict said that the overpayments, which appear to be the result of differing interpretations of state regulations, must be returned to the state.

headline: Underclass: Down and Out in Leftover City
abstract: Those who deal with the day-to-day reality of poverty and joblessness in Philadelphia say a permanent underclass is emerging in the city.

headline: When a plant is closed down
abstract: "Shutdown" is a recently published handbook of the congressionally connected Northeast-Midwest Institute and it documents the issue that plant closings are  a scourge in not only the country's older industrial heartland, but right across the nation. The underlying message of the book is that there are common strands in most of the plant shutdowns and that there are common solutions to most of these problems.

headline: Thornburgh's school aid plans draw pickets
abstract: The Allegheny Intermediate Unit Education Association believes that Gov. Thornburgh's proposed block grant budget program for education is disastrous for special needs students, especially if the school districts are given the power to spend as they wish. The unit believes that the governor is selling out quality education and going in for the cheapest possible education.

headline: A call for action on drunken driving
abstract: Patricia Neiman attended a preliminary hearing for the man charged in the death of her son, her second child to be hit in 7 months and killed by a drunk driver. Mrs. Neiman has joined MADD (Mothers Against Drunk Driving), and is promoting the impact of drunk driving as a percentage of the vehicular accidents.

headline: Jail population up 14%
abstract: PA prison population has raised by more than 14% in the last year, and the system is at capacity.  The legislature has approved a bond for the construction of additional cells.

headline: Hotel Tax Opens Doors of Economic Opportunity
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate approved a bill authorizing a hotel tax in Philadelphia.  The Senate vote completed legislative action in Harrisburg, sending the bill to Governor Dick Thornburgh for his signature, but enactment of the tax is the City Council’s responsibility.  Mayor Green supports the tax.  So does the city’s hotel industry.  The tax will bring in an estimated $2.4 million in the first year, to be used for promotion of tourism and convention business.  That in turn will generate more jobs and tax revenues for the city, the region, and state.

headline: 101,970 Register in County
abstract: With a little more than two months remaining until the fall election, Dauphin County already has 101,970 registered voters.  The article gives a breakdown of the number of women and men register and which how many people are registered in different parts of the county.

headline: Legislatures and Governors battle for control of US Block Grants
abstract: The legislatures in a number of states are struggling to take control of block grants from governors.  Previously, governors had been in control of Federal-to-state assistance, but state legislators are moving to establish a stronger voice in policy options.  This is of particular note because in most states, governors are more sensitive to the needs of minorities and the poor, the primary recipients of Federal aid, than are legislatures.

headline: 79,817 registered to vote in Cumberland County
abstract: A total of 79,817 Cumberland County residents are registered to vote in the upcoming primary election. This is only 981 more than were registered to vote in last year's primary election.

headline: Socialism, Says Mark Zola, Is the Answer
abstract: Mark Zola, the Socialist Workers Party candidate for PA governor, says that we need a government run by workers rather than one run by a few super-wealthy people.  Zola accuses his opponents, Governor Dick Thornburg and Cogressman Allen Ertel, of being anti women's rights, pro-war and pro big business.

headline: Supreme Court Bans the Bonds for Limerick 2
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled yesterday that the Philadelphia Electric Company cannot issue bonds to complete construction of the Limerick 2 nuclear unit until the Commonwealth Court decides if the state Public Utilities Commission has the authority to prevent or delay the construction of a nuclear reactor.  The Public Utilities Commission issued an order effectively halting construction of the unit on August 27th.

headline: Where States Are Headed
abstract: This article looks at which states are projected to have surpluses or deficits for 1983.  There have been measures taken by several states to help prevent deficits.  Higher taxes on alcoholic beverages, cigarettes, and motor-fuel are just some of the items being taxed.  Other sources of revenue will include lotteries, camping fees at parks, as well as other items.  On the opposite side of the budget ledger, virtually every state has taken steps to trim its expenses for the new fiscal year.

headline: Tuition Grants Still Available
abstract: College students whose families suffered a loss of income because of the recession may still be eligible for state higher education grants even though the deadline has passed.  State Representative Charles Laughlin, said the student’s families may apply for up to $1500 for an academic year by obtaining a reduction-in-income from the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency.  To qualify the family must have an adjusted income of less than $25,000 a year.  Higher income families may qualify for some aid, depending on the number of dependent children in the household and the number enrolled in post-secondary education.

headline: A yes vote for the Blue Route
abstract: The Editor believes voters in Radnor Township have revived the Blue Route, voting in favor of continuing construction by a majority. Opponents, including Delaware County commissioners, have attempted to block construction in the courts, however their arguments are wearing out. In response to environmental criticisms, PA Rep. Robert W. Edgar created a task force to redesign the Route to environmental specifications. The traffic jams have economically strangled the county, which has lost some of its population in the last decade.

headline: 'Jo Jo' Bowen leaves the courtroom after arraignment
abstract: This picture depicts 'Jo Jo' Bowen about to leave the court room, after his arraignment.

headline: In W. Va., Union Tries to Buy Mill
abstract: Weirton, Pennsylvania is threatened by the demise of the U.S. steel industry.  Instead of showing hopelessness and despair, the community is showing optimism and enthusiasm.  The employees of Weirton Steel Corp., a division of National Steel Corp., are trying to buy the billion dollar company.  The company said it would sell the mill if the employees could work out a deal.  If the employee purchase fails, the Weirton operation would be turned into a finishing mill with only about 1,200 employees.

headline: 12th District Republicans May Pick Bailey
abstract: Republican delegates from four counties will meet in Somerset to nominate a candidate for Congress in the new 12th District and there is a chance that the nod will go to a Democrat.  He is U.S. Representative Don Bailey of Greensburg.  He was defeated for nomination for another term by a Democratic colleague, U.S. Representative John Murtha of Johnstown.  Bailey is seeking the Republican nomination but has said he will not change his registration.

headline: Leonard says no to politicians
abstract: A meeting in which Philadelphia ward leaders were scheduled to request former City Controller Tom Leonard drop out of the race for Philadelphia Mayor was canceled by Leonard, who said the meeting would serve no purpose, since he did not plan to acquiesce. He then declared it was no longer the type of era in which ward leaders could steer an election. Leonard accused ward leaders of fearing him for his aggressive waste and corruption fighting tactics.

headline: A compromise for Philadelphia
abstract: The contracts that Philadelphia signs with its city employees affect Philadelphia's financial future by a substantial margin. Now these contracts are coming up again and the initial news coming out is heartening as leaders of the two major unions have tentatively approved the contracts with no raise in the first year and an 8 percent raise in the second.

headline: Puerto Rican week planned by Catholics
abstract: In observance of Puerto Rican week, the Spanish Apostolate of the Philadelphia Archdiocese will sponsor a Spanish Mass on Wednesday, September 22.  Cardinal John Krol, archbishop of Philadelphia, will celebrate 7:30 mass; Governor Thornburg and Mayor Green are expected to attend.

headline: Panel Bars Billing for Unfinished Power Units
abstract: A state Senate committee has approved legislation that would bar electric utilities from charging customers for construction work in progress.  The bill, which goes to the full Senate tomorrow, would bar electric utilities from including construction or expansion costs in customer charges until facilities are completed and producing power.

headline: A Cynical About-Face
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh vetoed a bill that would have severely limited abortions in Pennsylvania, however six months later he signed a revised anti-abortion bill.  There were some changes to the bill, but for the most part it was the same bill Thornburgh rejected previously.  Either he didn’t believe what he wrote in December when he stuck his neck out to veto the bill or he caved in under pressure from the so-called “pro-life” forces concerned about his prospects for reelection.

headline: Tuition increase
abstract: Due to rising education costs, Pennsylvanians are being given a choice to either pay for higher education trough taxes or through tuition increases. Education Secretary Robert Scanlon is seeking an 18% hike in tuition at state-owned colleges and the private schools will follow suit as well. However, many parents and students sat they cannot afford the new costs associated with education.

headline: Aid freeze threatens road work
abstract: A freeze on federal highway aid ordered by a federal court could affect 70 construction projects involving 25,000 jobs in the Pittsburgh and Philadelphia areas, according to PA Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson.  If the order is not reversed, it would cause an interruption in the largest highway and bridge-building schedule in Pennsylvania history.  The project-halt order came from a judge who found that the state failed to implement a previous court-ordered auto emissions inspection program.

headline: Jones denies getting $2,000, signing pledge of repayment
abstract: Former Harrisburg City Traffic Engineer Ronald Jones testified in a US Middle District Court trial that he did not receive a $2,000 bribe and did not sign a note promising to repay that amount to the briber.  But, in a taped conversation Jones acknowledged the the loan and there was a $2,000 deposit into his account.  William Miller, a former traffic products salesman, testified that he bribed over a dozen public officials and that he agreed to give Jones a 5% commission on every contract the city gave his companies until the loan was repaid.

headline: Insurance cuts urged for drivers
abstract: A bill proposed by PA Insurance Commissioner Michael Browne calling for an 8.9% cut in automobile insurance rates has been stalled in the House Judiciary Committee.  In September, Mr. Browne was unwilling to call for the cuts, but he says that he has studied further and is now willing to guarantee them if the legislature would pass them.

headline: 15 male OVR staffers remain fired
abstract: Commonwealth Court Judge Robert Williams Jr. today refused to order the Thornburgh administration to rehire 15 male staffers fired last week from the Office of Vocational Rehabilitation as demanded by the Pennsylvania Social Services Union.

headline: Leonard, a Dog and Mary Mason
abstract: A writer complains about no-show jobs for politicians.

headline: A super port agency won't work, task force says
abstract: A task force report recently concluded that the formation of a single, tri-state agency consolidating all government functions of Delaware River ports under one was politically infeasible.  Instead, the task force recommended that the Philadelphia Port expand its activities.

headline: PUC will probe Bell's new rates for business
abstract: Although the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission approved new rates for Bell of Pennsylvania yesterday, it also agreed to investigate business service charges disputed by the state consumer advocate.

headline: Schaffner wins panel's backing
abstract: The PA Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously recommended the confirmation of Governor Dick Thornburgh's nominee for a Dauphin County Common Pleas Court vacancy.  Dauphin County Solicitor Herbert A. Schaffner was approved by a 9-0 vote.

headline: Abortion Bill Ok'd by Senate
abstract: The Senate and House both approved a measure restricting abortions.  Now the legislation is waiting on the governor to decide whether to approve or disapprove it.  There are concerns from both sides of the debate over the issue.  Some feel as though it should be the choice of the woman to decide, others feel as though abortions should not be allowed.  The measure's fate will be decided by the governor.

headline: Tuition uproar linked to present system
abstract: Recent uproar over a proposed $75 tuition increase at PA state colleges may have been avoided if a proposed statewide university system had been implemented, according to Joyce Cheepudom, director of the Commonwealth Association of Students.  Had students been involved in such a panel, student protests could have been stemmed and input received.  Pennsylvania is the only state in the US where higher education is controlled by the Department of Education.  Senate bill 506 would change that if passed.

headline: All in Tizzy Over Auto Inspection
abstract: The safety inspection standards for automobiles and light trucks are expected to remain rigid, but a new program drops what many have considered "nuisance" rules requiring repairs of trunk lights, small cracks in side windows and minor rust spots.  Fred McCaffrey, Assistant Press Secretary for the PA Department of Transportation, said the change in inspection philosophy will require a different approach.  New regulations are designed to focus on the most critical safety features.

headline: Journalists Seek Open Hearings: Court Petitioned in Larsen Case
abstract: Sixty-five Pennsylvania newspapers and television stations petitioned the PA Supreme Court to open up closed hearings by the Judicial Inquiry and Review Board into alleged political misconduct by a justice of the high court, Rolf R. Larsen.  Larsen is accused of violating the judicial canon of ethnics by engaging in politics after his 1977 election to the bench.

headline: Jarring Decision
abstract: There are two letters to the editor for this particular article.  The first one is about Social Security being a business.  The business of operating pension plans.  Those that have paid into Social Security are stuck with the bad tree that bears bad fruit, but Social Security nevertheless should be phased out.  The second letter to the editor is about how male legislators chose to favor primarily male business lunchers at the expense of the primarily female waitresses who serve them.

headline: 2 double-talking birds of a feather
abstract: Republican Philip Price was supported for PA Assembly by the Democratic Party's conscience, Americans for Democratic Action, nearly fifteen years ago. Following an uproar over Democratic Sen. Joseph Clark's alleged support for a Republican, Price immediately denied this ever happened. Now, again, several reliable sources can quote a letter from Democratic Rep. William H. Gray III warmly endorsing Republican Price.

headline: Leonard: Dock Absent Court Employee's Pay
abstract: 22 Auditors began a head count, aimed at court reporters and the staffs of judges who were not conducting court.  Of 101 judicial aides, 61 were absent when the auditors arrived and did not return during the day.  Of 103 court reporters, 75 were not accounted for. The results are appalling.  Many of the employees were said to be on vacation or sick, but that no documentation existed to support such statements.

headline: A tax that won't hurt
abstract: In order to promote the David L. Lawrence Convention Center, state lawmakers have raised the tax of hotel rooms in Allegheny County by 3%. However, this move will not generate the required funds. Hence, instead of taxing other areas, it would be best to increase the hotel room tax, as it is fair to place the burden on the people who visit Pittsburgh, rather than the locals.

headline: States Get OK To Tighten Welfare Strings
abstract: The Reagan administration has published new rules that would allow states to require AFDC recipients to look for jobs.  The new rules are expected to save 181 million dollars next year and represent the implementation of program changes ordered by Congress last month.

headline: Zimmerman argues case on prison transfer
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman told the U.S. Supreme Court that prison inmates have no legal right to automatically appeal transfer decisions.  Zimmerman appeared in the high court to challenge a U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that claimed officials at the State Correctional Institution at Huntingdon had improperly treated a prison inmate, Aaron Helms, when they transferred him in the wake of a prison disturbance.

headline: Abortion Bill Under Study
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh will take his time deciding whether to sign or veto a law making it harder for women to have abortions in Pennsylvania.  He wants to look at what has been said on both sides before deciding.

headline: Turned off teachers
abstract: There is concern that fewer than half of the public school teachers like their jobs enough that they would re-enter their profession if given the chance to do it again. However, there could be other reasons that account for these disappointing results such as the age group of teachers responding to the survey or the agency carrying out the survey.

headline: Arrest the Drunks
abstract: Society will have to toughen up if it hopes to halt the slaughter of innocent bystanders by drunken drivers on our highways.  It’s less than encouraging to hear some policemen predict that drunken driving arrests would decrease if penalties for the offense were increased as proposed by an ad-hoc commission appointed by Governor Thornburgh.  Some people have branded as asinine the legislation proposed by state Senator Vincent Fumo of Philadelphia.  It would create drunken-driver license plates to “brand” such drivers.

headline: Judge Calls for Closing of Monitoring Office
abstract: A state official has applauded a ruling by a federal judge that could lead to the closing of an office overseeing the state’s compliance with rulings affecting the Pennhurst Center.  The state is under court order to transfer as many patients as possible from the Pennhurst Center to community facilities in Philadelphia, Bucks, Delaware, Chester and Montgomery counties.  The state has appealed that order to the U.S. Supreme Court.  Some 770 patients remain at Pennhurst awaiting transfer.

headline: Keep it Alive
abstract: U.S. Steel Corp is a viable part of the local economy in Johnstown.  The plant has 1,350 workers, the community makes $628,560 in weekly payroll which comes to $32.7 million per year.  The U.S. Chamber of Commerce estimates that for every 100 jobs at U.S. Steel, 68 additional jobs are generated in other manufacturing areas.

headline: 2 judges blast FBI for Abscam
abstract: Two federal appellate judges from Pittsburgh spoke out on Abscam and publically lambasted the FBI for what they termed an entrapment of politicians.  Philadelphia Councilmen George Schwartz and Harry Jannotti accepted bribes for a non-existent hotel project set up by the FBI.

headline: Let Lotto Winner Get Entire Amount
abstract: Mrs. Dorothy Thomas of Havertown won $5 1/2 million.  She won it fair and square and should be given a check for the entire amount.  Let her invest the money the way she sees fit.

headline: Atkinson challenged to debates
abstract: Jim Kunder of Beaver Falls has challenged US Rep. Eugene Atkinson of Aliquippa to a series of live debates as they are both contesting the Republican nomination for the 4th Congressional District. Also, Rep. Robert Edgar of Delaware County has endorsed Villanova University professor John Logue in his bid for the Senate seat held by John Heinz, R-Pa.

headline: City To Receive 500,000 In Rehab Money
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III visited with Pittstown officials on Friday to announce the anticipated 500,000 dollar grant to the city for community improvements and housing rehabilitation.

headline: Supreme Court Issues Rulings
abstract: This article discusses several cases that the U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to hear.  The court will decide whether the Reagan administration can override a sftey rule reuiring air bags or automatic seat belts in all new cars; the court will also decide if a South Dakota man should serve a life sentence for writing bad checks.

headline: Abortion bills
abstract: Letter to the editor: The writer believes there has been little newspaper coverage of meetings between aides to Governor Dick Thornburgh and backer of the anti-abortion bill, state Representative Stephen Freind (R-Delaware County).  The writer is worried this may represent an attempt to rush such a bill through the legislature before opposition mobilizes.

headline: Two Down And..
abstract: Wilkinsburg has lost two school board presidents in two weeks as a direct result of the teachers strike.  No one in his right mind would want to be a Wilkinsburg school director, especially the president of the board.  Directors face personal attacks from teachers.  Their homes have even been picketed.

headline: ASI shuts down, problems remain
abstract: The closing of the Alcoholic Services Inc. marks another loss in the fight against drunken driving. It had an estimated 70 percent success rate in the fight against this disease (based on the work it did with 12,000 patients since September, 1973). However, the author predicts that the Harrisburg region will regain another ASI in the next ten years, when people begin to realize the importance of this institution.

headline: Judge denies new lottery trial
abstract: Judge William Lipsitt denied pre-trial motions on behalf of Nick Perry and Edward Plevel refusing to overturn their convictions and grant a new trial.  Lipsitt wrote that "the court is satisfied a fair trial was held and defendants' rights were fully protected."  Lipsitt also presided over the trial of two stagehands who were also convicted in the lottery scam.

headline: Kennedy Urges Tax Cut Repeal
abstract: Senator Edward M. Kennedy called for a $700 tax cut ceiling and restructuring of the Federal Reserve Board to include representation of small business, labor and consumers.  The tax-cut ceiling proposal would realize $25 billion a year, which could be used to restore cuts in food stamps and Aid to Families with Dependent Children.

headline: 2 Men, 2 standards of justice
abstract: There are still several examples of high-profile crime that has occurred where race has played a role in either the determination of the sentence, or the life-after-punishment.  The editorial discusses two recent examples.

headline: Let the judges speak
abstract: Until now, due to strict rules set down by the PA Supreme Court, judicial candidates are forbidden to state their views on important legal issues. However, a new bill introduced by state Senator Stewart Greenleaf of Willow Grove, does away with this restriction, unless the Supreme Court decides that the bill erodes the authority of the court.

headline: Barr the Conciliator
abstract: Joseph M. Barr was the Mayor of Pittsburgh for 10 years.  He died at the age of 76.  Barr’s style was conciliatory rather than commanding when he was mayor.  His mode of operation was abetted by the fact that he made friends everywhere.  He was not considered an enemy even by those who disagreed with him. Some of the programs he worked on were the Three Rivers Stadium, the renovation of East Liberty and the retention of the U.S. Steel headquarters in Pittsburgh.  As a result of his efforts, Pittsburgh was among the first large cities in the country to obtain federal authorization and funding for what became the Community Action Program.  After leaving office, the former mayor was in failing health and unable to serve the community he once had.

headline: Dems Still Easy On Faltering Reagan
abstract: Democratic candidates continue to assert that President Reagan is personally popular--even though support for his policies has clearly declined.  Not only is this assertion inaccurate, but it is also self defeating, as Democratic candidates are reminding voters of the good qualities of the president and his party.

headline: Reopening of Three Mile Island Will be Aired at NRC Hearing Today
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is holding public hearings today to determine if they should reopen Three Mile Island's unit No. 1, which was not involved in the March 1979 accident.  The commission says that it will render a decision by December 10.

headline: Abortion Control: Yes
abstract: The proposal of the revised Abortion Control Act in the state legislature has rekindled the fires of debate about the subject.  There have been a lot of discussions about its political ramifications, and the means of moving it through legislature.

headline: Two Strikes Loom, Two More Begin in School Districts
abstract: Two more Western Pennsylvania school districts are expected to be hit by teacher strikes.  There are already two strikes happening in Pennsylvania schools.

headline: Auto inspections
abstract: Many people have mixed reactions to Pennsylvania's new law providing for once-a-year rather than twice-a-year inspection of motor vehicles. Service station operators, some safety authorities and others oppose the change on grounds of reduction in safety. Counter arguments include studies that show vehicle malfunctions constitute a small part for causes of accidents.

headline: Judge Gets a Rise out of Court
abstract: Judge Arthur Kafrissen rides a motorcycle.  He is a member of the Blue Knights motorcycle club.  The district attorney's office keeps memos on the performance on judges for the use of its staff.  The file on Judge Kafrissen mentions that he comes to court late and leaves early.

headline: Lancaster County's largest employers laying off 290
abstract: Armstrong World Industries Inc. and Sperry New Holland Inc., the two largest employers in Lancaster county, have announced layoffs totaling 290. Officials of the two companies, together, employ about 9000 people in plants and offices throughout the country. However, since the business has been hurt by poor sales of new housing, the need for layoffs has become apparent.

headline: 20 job counselor jobs spared from layoff plan
abstract: The Department of Labor and Industry agreed to delay and slightly reduce the size of a layoff of employees at the Office of Vocational Rehabilitation. This was done in exchange for the unions' agreement to drop a Commonwealth Court suit, challenging the proposed layoff.

headline: Letters to the Editor: Candidates Incite Lust for Tax Funds
abstract: Conservatives, liberals, Democrats and Republicans all based their campaigns on promises to get money from the federal or state government, usually to create jobs.

headline: Beefing up police
abstract: The concept of merging small police departments in order to better combat crime is not new and has been voiced before in Allegheny County. However, nothing seems to happen and, so, this latest rap is not likely to produce any results.

headline: Johnstown, PA, where crime is a scarce commodity
abstract: According to the FBI's 1981 Uniform Crime Report, Johnstown, Pennsylvania had the lowest crime rate in the country.  Johnstown represents a paradox, however; the crime rate is low, but unemployment rates are very high.  Also, despite chronic unemployment, the savings rate has increased.

headline: Savitt quits job in court
abstract: Philadelphia Common Pleas Court administrator David N. Savitt submitted his resignation yesterday.  Savitt will remain as a Common Pleas Court judge.  Savitt also called for an independent inquiry of the Philadelphia court system, but PA Supreme Court Justice John P. Flaherty said a study will not solve the problems of the Philadelphia courts.

headline: Abortion Curbs Draw Fight Funds
abstract: Republican dollars may find their way into Democratic campaign offers this fall via a political action committee formed to defeat supporters of the new abortion control law.  The Pennsylvanians for the Right to a Private Life received many small donations and “some large contributions from some very prominent Republican women.”  The group already said they would not support Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: With School District Peace at Hand, Some Ask: Was this War Necessary?
abstract: Mayor Green and the teachers union president, John Murray finally reached an agreement.  Now that it is over with many people are questioning whether or not the actions over both sides were necessary in the past.

headline: Auto-emission ruling denouced
abstract: This letter to the editor complains that state and federal judges are acting like dictators. In particular, the letter notes the recent ruling by Federal Judge Louis Bechtle of Philadelphia that cut off federal highway funding until the state implements a required auto-emissions inspection program in the Pittsburgh and Philadelphia areas.

headline: Judge Says FBI 'Grabbed' Suspects in Testa Shooting
abstract: Police said DeLuca, of the 6600 block of Dorel Street and Pedulla, of the 2700 block of Muhlfeld Street, were last seen by authorities late Monday afternoon, when county detectives served them with subpoenas to appear for a Tuesday hearing.  That hearing was requested by District Attorney Edward G. Rendell, who planned to ask that bail for the two be raised to $10 million apiece."  Judge Arthur Kafrissen believe the two are being held by the FBI, which they deny.

headline: LCB Chief:  Mob Ties to Bars 'Hard to Prove'
abstract: Liquor Control Board Chairman Daniel Pennick says that he knows of no ties between organized crime and any Pennsylvania bars or restaurants that have liqour licenses.  He also noted that LCB agents are not trained in sophisticated law enforcement techniques, and that the ties are just hard to prove.  So far, the PA Crime Commission has uncovered at least four examples of organized crime being involved in the liquor business.

headline: 40-Vessel Flotila Ships Out
abstract: Philadelphia bids goodbye to tall ships, small ships and baggy wrinkles.  There was a four day festival along the Delaware River with showcasing ships.  City officials proclaimed the Tall Ship celebration at Penn’s Landing a success.

headline: Letting ring the sound of freedom
abstract: Article recounts past Freedom Day celebrations in Philadelphia and throughout the country.  Also notes speeches given by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and Philadelphia Mayor William Green.

headline: Bill for 3% Hotel Tax Dies Quietly in Senate
abstract: The State Senate failed to pass a bill that would have brought a 3 percent hotel room tax to Allegheny County.  The failure to pass the bill is expected to cost Allegheny County taxpayers $1.25 million.  Some believe that the tax is unconstitutional.

headline: Industry: Immunity bill needed
abstract: Large oil and gas companies are lobbying the Pennsylvania General Assembly for legislation that would grant immunity from lawsuits to companies who assisted in the cleanup of another company's hazardous material spills.  Under the legislation supported by the oil, gas and chemical industry, assisting companies could be sued only if they were found to be grossly negligent.

headline: TMI operators' cheating is aired at NRC hearing
abstract: Officials from the General Public Utilities Corporation, the operators of Three Mile Island, say they did not condone cheating on any company wide or Nuclear Regulatory Commission exams.  The company fired and/or disciplined operators who were found to have cheated on licensing and qualifications exams.  The cheating scandal came to light in July and started a new series of hearings into whether General Public Utilities Corp could safely operate Three Mile Island unit 1.

headline: Abortion funding debated
abstract: A deputy attorney general said that a 1980 state law that would block funding for abortions for poor women "places no burden on anyone," but an opposing attorney said that law would limit women's civil rights.  A federal judge has already upheld the law as constitutional.

headline: Wrapup on Schools?
abstract: Pittsburgh’s oft-revised school desegregation plan is taking shape.  However, the Board of Education has yet to add its stamp of approval.  Superintendent Richard C. Wallace has expressed confidence that the latest proposed moves would bring an end to the dispute.  14 years ago the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission cited the Pittsburgh schools for racial imbalance and ordered the board to do something about it.  The board and the commission have been in and out of court over the many plans to rectify the racial imbalance.  In the most recent development, the Commonwealth Court ordered further changes in a 1980 plan which the board had implemented despite the commission’s unhappiness.  The changes involved the closing of three more elementary schools, shifts in attendance boundaries elsewhere, and academic enhancements at two mostly black high schools, Schenley and Westinghouse.

headline: Bad spot for bus depot
abstract: Bensalem township residents are protesting the purchase of 20 acres of land by Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority (SEPTA) for possible use as a bus depot.  SEPTA likes the location because its other North Philadelphia bus depot is overcrowded and this area is close to internstate-95.  Additionally, SEPTA would not pay property taxes on the area.

headline: Judge Trims Fee
abstract: Attorney Larry O’Toole says it isn’t worth defending twice-convicted killer Robert "the Codfish" Bricker in any more homicide trials.  O’Toole thought the $10,000 he submitted was cheap for representing Bricker in a four-day trial that ended in Bricker’s acquittal of criminal homicide in the June 1979 shooting death of Gary "Stretch" DeStefano of Monessen, Westmoreland County.

headline: LCB Cuts Ties with Jacquin: Cities Closed Plant, Late Deliveries
abstract: The Liquor Control Board (LCB) voted 3-0 to stop doing business with Charles Jacquin et Cie. Inc., the company that recently closed its Philadelphia distillery because of labor disputes.  LCB members said they were taking the action because the distillery closed and because the company had failed to deliver products on schedule for distribution in State Stores.

headline: 4th District
abstract: The liberals are attacking US Rep. Eugene Atkinson because he switched party affiliations to attack their spending. However, the Tribune-Review supports Atkinson because he has the foresight and determination needed to turn America around.

headline: Lewis shuns state race, will run again for Senate
abstract: PA Senator H. Craig Lewis said that he will not seek the Democratic nomination for Governor, but will seek re-election in his own district in Lower Bucks County.

headline: Bill giving mayor control of schools called legal
abstract: Philadelphia City Solicitor Alan Davis promotes the legality of a bill before the PA legislature that would give Philadelphia's mayor control of the city schools, and discusses how a similar bill giving power to the City Council would be illegal.

headline: Mr. Hype and the selling of Temple
abstract: Temple University's new president, Peter Liacouras, is hoping to change the university's image while remaining faithful to the original mission of the college, which was to provide a university education for the working class.  Liacouras wishes to add more student housing and tighten security to change the image of Temple as a commuter college that is unsafe.  Additionally, the president hopes to broaden Temple's student base and attract more high-achieving students.

headline: Bill Sets Method for Killing Pets
abstract: PA state Senator Doyle Corman introduced legislation which would prohibit animal shelters from using decompression chambers to kill unwanted domestic pets.  Senator Corman said decompression chambers are an unnecessarily cruel way of euthanizing domestic animals.

headline: Abortion Law Delay By Court Opposed
abstract: The Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals blocked the enactment of an abortion law that had been upheld by a lower court. PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman requested that the law be implemented while the appeals continued, but the court issued their ruling before the state motion could be filed. Opponents argue that the law would harm those seeking abortions while Zimmerman argues such harm had not been proven nor that the opponents could win on constitutional grounds.

headline: 21 More Toxic Waste Sites In State
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protetion Agency (EPA) has added twenty-one sites to a list of priorities for cleanup under the Superfund Program. This ranks Pennsylvania third in the nation with a total of thirty such sites. The Superfund Program authorizes the EPA to clean up the sites and then sue the dumpers to compensate for the cost. The article describes three Western PA sites in detail and then provides a list of all thirty.

headline: Baker Sees Gas-Tax Bill Passing In Senate
abstract: U.S. Senator Howard Baker predicted that a five cent per gallon increase in the federal gas tax, designed to raise money for highway projects, would pass in spite of a threatened filibuster. The U.S. House approved a similar measure yesterday. There are a number of opponents: the Teamsters and truckers, due to increased transportation costs; Friends of the Earth and the Sierra Club, because of increased highway construction; and the National Tax Limitation Committee and National Taxpayers Union, as a result of the increase in taxes. The article listed Western PA members of the U.S. House who voted for and against the increase.

headline: Judicial center gets Nix support
abstract: Editorial:  PA Supreme Court Justice Robert Nix became the first important Pennsylvania jurist to favor a judicial center in Harrisburg.  He expressed some reservations to PA Senator George Gekas, but also pointed out that 43 other states have a permanent location for their appellate courts, while 41 of those are in a state capital.  The newspaper believes that such a building should be constructed.

headline: LCB head denies lax enforcement
abstract: PA Liquor Control Board Chairman Daniel Pennick denied allegations the agency failed to enforce liquor laws in connection with a Philadelphia social club.  The PA Senate Law and Justice Committee will have a hearing to question Pennick on the accusations.  Pennick says that lack of enforcement personel and legal requirements prevented immediate results.

headline: 5 lawyers finalists for magistrate's post
abstract: Five attorneys have been chosen as finalists for the US magistrate's post, which will become vacant on May 1st, when incumbent John Havas returns to private practice.

headline: Lewis: Reaganomics until '89
abstract: U.S. Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis has promised the nation 7 more years of Reaganomics, a statement that could be interpreted as an early declaration for President Ronald Reagan's intentions to run for re-election.  Lewis, who also serves as Pennsylvania's Republican National Committee representative, said that the Reagan Administration sees signs that the national economy is turning for the better.

headline: Brother, it's no wonder
abstract: People have become cynical of their elected officials because of the way they play around with issues like Social Security to their advantage, focusing on gathering votes rather than doing what is right for the country.

headline: Attitudes on how to deal with drunk-drivers have changed
abstract: The Pennsylvania General Assembly is expected to take action on legislation that would require minimum jail terms for drunken drivers.  Currently no jail sentence is mandated by law.

headline: More humane killing of unwanted pets sought
abstract: PA state Senator Doyle Corman introduced legislation which would prohibit animal shelters from using decompression chambers to kill unwanted domestic pets.  Senator Corman said decompression chambers are an unnecessarily cruel way of euthanizing domestic animals.  The bill has the support of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.

headline: Abortion Law Valid Except for One Section U.S. Judge Says
abstract: U.S. District Court Judge Daniel H. Huyett upheld all but one provision of a Pennsylvania abortion control law passed in June 1981. He struck down a provision involving a 24-hour waiting period. Planned Parenthood was disappointed with the decision, and the Women's Law Project, which represented the plaintiffs, will appeal the decision because the law's constitutionality was not decided.

headline: $2.5 Million to Clean Up Bruin Lagoon
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protection has allocated $2.5 million to clean up Bruin Lagoon, an abandoned chemical waste dump in Butler County.  The allocation is a $900,000 increase over the amount originally estimated for the project.  When the cleanup was approved in July by EPA and state Department of Environmental Resources, it was estimated that it would cost about $1.6 million to stabilize the acid wastes and seal them with layers of clay, gravel, and soil.  The lagoon was cited last year by EPA as one of the 20 worst hazardous-waste sites in the country.  Ninety percent of the money for the cleanup project will come from a $1.6 billion federal fund established by Congress.

headline: Battling the Drunks
abstract: Five women from Mothers Against Drunk Drivers (MADD) met in Lancaster to start a chapter in their community.  These five women can make a difference to prevent drunk driving from happening, but so can present laws.  The law must be changed and the public must insist that our legislators change it.

headline: Judicial roadshow should settle here
abstract: PA appellate court judges have always been without a permanent base of operations since they were created, but now the American Judicature Society and the PA Bar Association have recommended that these judges should settle down in Harrisburg.

headline: LCB Seeks Tax Breaks for Bottlers: Wants to Keep Industry in State
abstract: The Liquor Control Board (LCB) called for tax breaks for bottlers and distillers based in the state.  If this is the case, one Philadelphia distiller will stay in Pennsylvania instead of moving to Florida like it had announced a few weeks prior to this announcement.  Pennsylvania only has three major bottlers or distilleries so maybe this announcement will attract more.

headline: 50 Groups Represented at Parley on Citizens' Interests
abstract: Organizers of a unique conference on citizens’ interest said they are gratified at the response to the weekend gathering in Boiling Springs, attended by representatives of 50 consumer and labor groups.  From Gray Panthers to members of a United Auto Workers local representing retire workers, about 160 participants attended seminars focusing primarily on energy and other utility-related topics.

headline: Lieberth returns to head new effort on municipalities
abstract: Charles J. Lieberth, former member of PA Governor Thornburgh's cabinet and executive director of the Governor's Human Resources Committee, is expected head a cooperative effort between participating Allegheny County municipalities. The Allegheny League of Municipalities and the Allegheny Conference on Community Development will work together to ensure funding and resource opportunities. Neither County Commission Chairman Tom Foerster nor Lieberth would confirm or deny his involvement.

headline: Campaign is rolling in Green
abstract: With the Democratic mayoral campaign a year away, Mayor Green already has a solid financial base - more than $250,000 - for his expected re-election campaign and is currently in a very comfortable position.

headline: Jobless pay woes mount
abstract: Democratic leadership in the PA state Legislature would like to hold a special session before the November election to deal with the deficit in the state's unemployment compensation fund.  Although the state has borrowed 1.8 million from the federal government to keep the unemployment fund solvent, it will need another 144 million by October to keep payments flowing to recipients.  Democrats are concerned with paying back this money to the federal government.

headline: Senate panel Oks judicial nominees
abstract: Yesterday, the state Senate Judiciary Committee approved several partisan Common Pleas court nominees--setting the stage for a showdown between Senate Democrats and the Thornburgh administration.

headline: Abortion Measure At A Glance
abstract: This article talks about the provisions of the abortion control law signed by Governor Dick Thornburgh.  It looks at the notice, information, consent, viability, reports, defects, public funds, and insurance issues raised by the bill

headline: $6 Million in Federal Aid Sought by DER to Control Centralia Fire
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources has asked the federal government for $6 million to help fund a project to control the Centralia mine fire.  The Department and the federal Office of Surface Mining have not yet selected a specific plan to put out or abate the 20-year-old underground fire, according to Robert Oberman of the Division of Abandoned Mine Reclamation.  Exploratory drilling to determine the extent of the mine fire will start in Centralia by early August.  The drilling will take six months, and a final report will follow four months later.

headline: Big Guys and Little Guys
abstract: The PA State legislature came very close to passing an oil divorcement bill during its post-election session.  It’s a break for Pennsylvania motorists that the House did not get around to it.  The divorcement bill would bar big oil companies from operating their own gas stations.  Portions of the Pennsylvania divorcement bill regulating station rent increases, wholesale prices and lease cancellations should be enacted to curb the worst oil company abuses

headline: Justice Nix Appears Before Larsen Probe
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. appeared before the PA Board of Judicial Injury and Review as the panel continued a secret hearing on charges of ethical violations against Nix’s colleague Justice Rolf Larsen.  It is believed that Larsen worked to defeat Nix in a retention election last year.  If so, this would be in violation of the Code of Judicial Ethnics.

headline: LCB to Sell Slow Movers At Wholesale
abstract: The Liquor Control Board slashed its standard 25 percent markup on 618 slow-moving items in a move to modernize its merchandizing and improve its cash flow.  The sale will continue until all the discounted items are sold.

headline: 90,075 GOP, 36496 Demos register here
abstract: About 138,546 Lancaster Countians are registered to vote in the May 18 primary election. This includes 90075 Republicans, 36496 Democrats and 11975 others. These figures are less than the 1980 general election registration.

headline: Ohio's Sen. John Glenn Seeks Out State Support For Presidency Bid
abstract: U.S. Senator John Glenn met with various PA Democrats, increasing speculation he will seek the Democratic nomination for President in 1984. In addition, PA Democrats, such as PA Senator Michael O'Pake and PA Auditor General Al Benedict, have also met with Walter Mondale to get their support for his possible quest for the Democratic nomination.

headline: Chester mayor's latest problem: The specter of man he succeeded
abstract: Mayor Joseph Battle of Chester has to deal with the returning of his predecessor, John H. Nacrelli, adding to the woes of the mayor. Chester has been facing numerous issues which has resulted in Nacrelly, Battle's predecessor, being remembered as a decision-maker who had a firm hand on city affairs.

headline: Most State Roads Not Built For the Traffic of the 80's
abstract: Several hundred miles of road built in Lancaster County are not capable of handling today's heavy trucks or traffic flows.  The roads, built over 50 years ago, are mostly rural--making it difficult for the state to justify spending money on major improvements.

headline: Judge stands firm on PA road money
abstract: U.S. District Court Judge Louis Bechtle froze more than 90 million dollars of Pennsylvania highway funds after the General Assembly failed to comply with a 1978 ageement that required the state to start measuring auto pollutants.  Judge Bechtle ruled yesterday that the state could have about 1.1 million dollars of the frozen funds, which are to be used only for saftey-related projects.

headline: Abortion Risks
abstract: A letter arguing that if doctors cannot counsel their patients about the risks and alternatives to abortions then they should not be allowed to perform them.

headline: 1000 are evacuated in I-80 chemical spill
abstract: A tractor trailor with aluminum chloride flipped on Interstate 80, forcing the evacuation of more than 1000 residents.  When mixed with water, the chemical produces poisonous hydrogen chloride gas.  The accident couldn't have happened on a worse day - it was raining.

headline: Bill Requiring Pike Board to Build New Super-roads up for Final Vote
abstract: A bill that would require the Turnpike Commission to build new turnpikes along routes of stalled highways in Western Pennsylvania is in position for final legislative vote.

headline: Juvenile court should not have to drop its 'veil of secrecy'
abstract: This opinion piece explains that an effort is being made to open juvenile court proceedings to the media, in particular with a recent case in Pittsburgh where 6 news organizations petitioned the Pennsylvania Supreme Court to allow media coverage.  The writers believe that this is simply a freedom of the press issue, but infringes on other 6th and 14th amendment rights.

headline: LCB trucking contract brings some boos
abstract: The Liquor Control Board has awarded a $11.7 million contract to Dennis Trucking Inc., of Philadelphia, to run the warehouse and deliver liquor and wine to about 200 State Stores in the five-county area. However, legal challenges with respect to the way the contract was given, should hold up the proposal for sometime.

headline: A Bad Beer Bill
abstract: If it could vote on it today, Congress would pass a bill that could raise the price of a can or bottle of beer by perhaps 20 percent.  Thanks to vigorous lobbying and courting of Congressmen by the National Beer Wholesalers Association through its SIXPAC committee, clear majorities in both the House and Senate would bend the antitrust laws to legalize the territorial monopolies in the beer industry and allow brewers to sell to a single distributor.  According to wholesalers, the bill would only codify existing arrangements between brewers and distributors.  They point out that Congress did the same thing for the soft-drink industry in 1980.

headline: 'Losers' in Ill-Fated Lottery Drawing Win Again
abstract: More than 10,600 Pennsylvania lottery players who won, and then immediately lost, a total of about $750,000 in October are winners once again.  The Bureau of State Lotteries will pay holders of tickets with numbers invalidated after a botched televised lottery drawing.  390 ticket holders who picked five of the six invalidated numbers are entitled to $792.50 each and that 10,268 players who picked four of the six numbers may collect $45 each.  There are no Jackpot tickets sold with all six numbers correct.

headline: City charter of 1951 sets out proper rules
abstract: Although Blacks and Hispanics account for 42% of Philadelphia's population, they make up only 18% of the police force. Hence, in order to obtain an effective police force, the representation of minorities must increase.

headline: Little mercy or charity in this state
abstract: In this article, letters to the editor address such topics as Pennsylvania's state employment fund deficit, Governor Thornburgh's relationship with the state Board of Pardons, and a proposed state-run auto-inspection system

headline: High Court Upholds Halt at Limerick-2
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that the Philadelphia Electric Company must temporarily halt construction of the Unit 2 reactor at the Limerick nuclear power plant.  The court sided with the Public Utility Commission and overturned a stay granted by the Commenwealth Court.

headline: Abortion veto ducks issue
