abstract: An opinion piece that is concerned with the rhetoric that has emerged from the Governor Dick Thornburgh administration regarding the governor's decision to veto the abortion bill.

headline: 11 Northeastern States Mull N-Waste Compact
abstract: Pennsylvania and 10 other northeastern states are delicately negotiating a compact to provide for disposal of low-level nuclear waste in the region after 1985.  None of the states has volunteered to "host" a low-level waste site, several of which will be needed because Congress two years ago ordered all states to handle disposal of the contaminated refuse on a regional basis by 1986.  To meet the federal requirement, the Coalition of Northeast Governors (CONEG) has attempted to orchestrate an agreement among the states on how, not necessarily where, the waste sites would be.

headline: Bill to separate oil companies from stations draws hard views
abstract: A Senate committee heard a testimony on whether gasoline prices will rise or fall under a bill barring oil companies from operating service stations. The local dealer association stressed on the issue that oil companies will be able to drive the dealers out of business by charging lower prices.

headline: Juvenile detention faces fiscal cuts; Efficient use of resources may prevent crisis
abstract: Warren Masters, deputy commissioner of the Administration on Children, Youth and Families of the Health and Human Services Department believes that efficient utilization of available resources may help prevent any crisis that may be caused due to the recent cutbacks in government spending.

headline: LCB Votes to Continue Boycott of Distillery
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board voted to appeal a Commonwealth Court contempt ruling, thus continuing its boycott of liquor products from Charles Jacquin et Cie Inc.  LCB Chairman Daniel Pennick said Jacquin has violated a consent agreement by failing to meet delivery schedules and disrupting the LCB's distribution system.  Forty-Five percent of Jacquin's $88 million in annual sales are to the LCB.  The board is also trying to force Jacquin to settle its labor dispute and remain in Pennsylvania.

headline: A Big Party: Capital Art Exhibit Opened
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and Mrs. Richard Thornburgh gave the biggest party of his career as head of state.  The event was held at the Executive Mansion, along the banks of the Susquehanna, brought together some 1,500 persons from all across the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.  The occasion marked the formal opening of a summer sculpture exhibit featuring the works of 'Pennsylvania Treasures," the 13th art presentation in the governor's Salute to Pennsylvania's Artistic Heritage series.

headline: Lottery sales exceed $13 million weekly
abstract: The Pennsylvania Lottery has set a weekly sales record at $13 million.  Michael Keyser, the Daily Number officer, believes the sales are due to the winter months, when participation is typically higher.  The previous record was $9.09 million.

headline: City Economic Development Unit Set Up; Director to be named soon
abstract: Mayor Stephen R. Reed announced Wednesday that he will establish a new economic development office within the city government. The primary purpose would be to attract new businesses and help existing companies to expand and prosper.

headline: More State Teachers Walk Out
abstract: In Pennsylvania, teachers in 20 school districts are on strike.  Roughly 3,300 teachers are on strike statewide.  With the anticipated walkout of teachers in the Woodland Hills School District, the number of PA teachers on strike is expected to increase to 3,700.

headline: Health Department abolishes 56 positions
abstract: The Pennsylvania Health Department has abolished 56 jobs as a result of federal and state funding cuts.  The department will also furlough 30 employees.

headline: Abortion-bill sponsors and governor meet on new bill
abstract: Sponsors of a stringent abortion bill already vetoed by PA Governor Thornburgh meet to try to work on a compromise on the bill.

headline: Air-Pollution Program Grossly Biased
abstract: PBS is accused of broadcasting a slanted and misleading examination of the Clean Air Act.  The author suggested that from the outset of the one-hour broadcast the program presented a bias of monolithic proportions.  The program portrayed Pittsburgh as a "Smoky City" however this is not the case.  From 1967 to 1980, according to the Allegheny County Bureau of Air Pollution Control, sulfur-dioxide emissions decreased in the county by nearly 225,000 tons, and particulate emissions declined from 145,000 tons to 27,300 tons.

headline: Boat Safety
abstract: This editorial talks about water safety and how there is a need for boat operator education since more and more people keep dying on waterways.

headline: Kafrissen's No Stranger to Controversy
abstract: Judge Arthur Kafrissen got a career break in 1977 when he was elected to Municipal Court.  Two years later, he ran unsuccessfully for a seat on Common Pleas Court.  He was rated unqualified by the Philadelphia Bar Association.  Later on Kafrissen was found as having owed $3,373 in delinquent real estate taxes.  His paycheck was deducted by the city to pay the bill.

headline: Liquid Asset Going Untapped
abstract: Industrial firms are moving to the Sun Belt, where warm weather reduces cost of both factory operation and home heating.  As more and more factories move to Arizona and its neighboring states, taking workers and their families along, it’s clear that agriculture in the southwest is running against a shortage of water.  By contrast, the region from Pennsylvania northwest through New England is rich in water.  This puts it in a good position to profit from the constantly increasing demands for food.  But to really capitalize on the adequate water supplies, they will have to use them more efficiently.

headline: A Childhood Lesson
abstract: Columnist Pete Dexter recalls Tom Leonard's campaign as City Comptroller of Philadelphia to root out waste, at one point promising to dock pay for workers missing when his officials visited Common Pleas Court offices. Leonard had no way of knowing why employees were absent when Judges were away for a convention. He is alienating friends of Frank Rizzo, also a candidate for mayor along with Wilson Goode, who helped Leonard get where he is today.

headline: Lotto Ticket Turns into Such a Deal
abstract: Joseph D. O’Leary was one of four people who will share more than $3 million a recent Pennsylvania State Lottery jackpot.  His wife, Anne, was the one that actually bought the ticket.  The first thing she did after winning was to call her boss and told him that she quit.

headline: City Wage-Tax Vote Likely
abstract: Slated for a vote is a city tax bill that has support not only from Philadelphia officials, but also from those who would pay the tax under the bill, which already has been approved by the House, Philadelphia would be allowed to impose a hotel tax of as much as 3 percent.  Other bills for consideration were also mentioned in the article.

headline: Drunken-Driving Leniency Must End
abstract: Pennsylvania could reduce the number of drunken-driving fatalities if it exacted harsher penalties on offenders.  Our current laws are too lenient.

headline: Design revealed for Capitol plaza
abstract: General Services Secretary Walter Baran dispayed architectural drawings of the 115,000-square foot addition to the state Capitol.

headline: Abortions Decline in State, City in '81
abstract: The Health Department reported that the number of abortions in Pennsylvania and in Philadelphia have dropped slightly from the previous year.  This was the first recorded decline in abortions since the Health Department started keeping statistics on abortions in 1975.

headline: Auto checks: defiance costs funds
abstract: US District Court Judge Louis Bechtle found the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania to be in contempt of court for not implementing a court-ordered auto emission inspection program.  No fines were imposed, but the judge ordered a cutoff of federal highway funds for the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh areas, two of the three urban regions where the inspection program was to begin.  Governor Richard Thornburgh has not yet posted a response.

headline: Borken-down PAT buses put riders in a jam
abstract: About 120 Port Authority (PAT) buses of the system's total fleet, are not on the road either because they are being repaired or are simply just falling apart.  Since mid-December, PAT has not had enough buses to operate all of its published routes.  Some drivers report for duty, then sit around until the day's patches are sufficient.

headline: Lab Wars
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners have created a new Department of Laboratories, combining the 5 separate labs into one department.  The County Coroner, Dr. Joshua Perper is in court trying to prevent the removal of the toxicology lab, and contends the move was part of County Commissioner Cyril Wecht to carry out a vendetta against him.

headline: Liquor Clerks OK Pact With Purchase Clause
abstract: The United Food and Commercial Workers, Local 1357, gave up an eight-year-old job-security provision guaranteeing that store clerks at the state’s 3,005 liquor-stores would hold their jobs, if they state turns over the stores to a private enterprise.  Last year, Governor Dick Thornburgh offered a bill to turn the liquor business over to private operators, but it was defeated by the state legislature after labor unions lobbied heavily against it, fearing that the change would result in job losses.  A similar bill is pending in legislature, but is not expected to come up for a vote until after the November gubernatorial election.  A new contract will give the employees an 8 percent pay increase for two years.

headline: A common strategy (inferred)
abstract: Photo: Kelly and Doyle on the roof of the DRPA'a Camden headquarters contemplating a single strategy for the tri-state area.

headline: Mandatory sentencing
abstract: The Senate Judiciary Committee has sent to the floor of the Senate a resolution that would approve the revised sentencing guidelines adopted by the Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing. The committee also approved a bill that would prohibit plea bargaining in criminal cases involving violent crime.

headline: Costs and cooperation
abstract: In a move that should be a relief to taxpayers, the Allegheny League of Municipalities, is encouraging Allegheny County's 130 incorporated communities to share services and cut costs. A study by the Consortium of Public Administration Field Services suggested that this job could be done through eight Councils of Government in Allegheny County.

headline: Midstate Rail Operations Still Unaffected by Strike
abstract: The nationwide locomotive engineers' strike is having almost no effect on midstate railroad operations.

headline: Problems await new Dem governors
abstract: Although Democrats won 34 of the nation's 50 governorships during the November 2nd elections, it is not clear that these victories will result in a leftward public-policy shift.  Most states face serious budget deficits, which will make a Great Society-type revolution among the states impossible; tight congressional budgets also signal less reliance on federal assistance to solve states' financial problems and fund programs.

headline: Aid Package: Blacks, an Undeveloped Nation
abstract: Jesse Jackson's idea is that black America's focus on government assistance and job creation has been shortsighted.  His goal is not full employment but full development for the black community.  The 7-Up agreement, for instance, includes commitments to use black bans, insurance companies and advertising agencies, as well as to increase the number of black executives, including an additional member of the board of directors.

headline: Auto emissions in Pennsylvania - I
abstract: KYW 1060 editorial: Pennsylvania is about to lose more than $300 million in federal highway funds.  A US District Court judge is witholding the money because three years ago, Pennsylvania agreed to start the program, and the state legislatue won't allocate the funds for it.  The auto emissions plan was originally agreed to by the state with the Clean Air Act.

headline: Break for motorists
abstract: The PA State Legislature is finally approving a switch to once-a-year auto-safety inspections thereby causing a lot of relief to motorists in Pennsylvania. Only six other states had the old twice-a-year auto-safety check-ups.

headline: Larsen formal probe would take months
abstract: Any formal probe by the Judicial Inquiry Review Board into alleged misconduct by Justice Rolf Larsen would probably last several months.  Additionally, board members refused to confirm reports that the panel has voted to charge Larsen with violating the state's rule against plilitcal campaigning by judges, a charge that would start the formal investigation.

headline: Liquor Licensees' Tax Delinquency Described as Within Norm
abstract: Tax delinquency among the state's 26,000 liquor stores following the norm for other industries, Revenue Secretary Robert k. Bloom told a state Senate committee.  Bloom's comments on tax delinquency came before the Committee on Law and Justice, headed by Senator Stewart Greenleaf, which is conducting a series of hearings on the operations of the Liquor Control Board.  Bloom said a study of sales tax history of some 200 licenses submitted by Greenleaf found that 54 had liabilities.

headline: A federal fix reaffirmed
abstract: US President Ronald Reagan's Justice Department, in washing its hands of an election fraud investigation in Delaware County, has sent a signal that the Reagan administration will look the other way when allegations of wrongdoing are made against local Republican officials.  This will eliminate work done by the US Attorney General in Philadelphia and a federal grand jury that was about to hand out indictments against influential Republicans.

headline: Many are unopposed in primary
abstract: The level of interest in the campaigns leading up to the 1982 Pennsylvania primary has been on the low side compared to previous times. Correspondingly, the number of interesting challenges between various opponents is considerably reduced.

headline: Council staff assails teacher pact benefits
abstract: Philadelphia City Council staff criticized the new teacher's union contract for failing to help ease the district's financial situation.

headline: Phila. Center Formed To Study the Elderly
abstract: Three institutions in Philadelphia have been awarded five-year, five million dollar research grants by the National Institute on Aging.  The grants will be used to create research centers where the physical and mental problems of the elderly can be studied.

headline: Bill Sets Method for Killing Pets
abstract: PA state Senator Doyle Corman introduced legislation which would prohibit animal shelters from using decompression chambers to kill unwanted domestic pets.  Senator Corman said decompression chambers are an unnecessarily cruel way of euthanizing domestic animals.

headline: Anti-Abortion Bill Ratified by House
abstract: The state House passed an anti-abortion bill that met objections raised by Governor Dick Thornburgh in vetoing similar legislation a few months prior.  The Senate was expected to also pass the legislation.

headline: Auto-emission program must now be implemented
abstract: Editorial: Pennsylvania will lose $400 million in federal highway funds unless it complies with a court order to begin an auto-emission inspection program.  Paper believes that this can be handled by the state legislature in the bill they are currently considering to change inspection requirements.  The cost-per-driver for the emissions program is only $.50.

headline: Bridge Repair Funding Axed
abstract: The PA State Senate defeated legislation which would have provided a funding mechanism for a proposed six-year, $1.2 billion bridge repair project.  The rejection was one of several actions taken by the Senate as it pushed toward adjournment of its 1981-82 legislative session.  The proposal targeted 745 bridges for repair or replacement.  It was also expected to generate 20,000 jobs and stimulate the state’s steel and concrete industries.

headline: Larsen's Lawyer in Inquiry has Links to Judge Leading the Hearings
abstract: The lawyer defending state Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen against misconduct charges served last year as an honorary campaign chairman for Common Pleas Court Judge Charles P. Mirarchi Jr., who heads the state panel now hearing testimony on the charges against Larsen.

headline: Loan company fined over debt collections
abstract: Avco Financial Services Consumer Discount Company, a consumer-loan company, has paid a fine of $15,000 and agreed to stop contacting consumers in ways that violated state law, after several complaints were received from consumers.

headline: A little joy for everyone
abstract: The congressional reappointment plan approved last week by the Legislature is a successful example of an agreement that allows each contending faction to proclaim a measure of victory. Hence, both sides end up being optimistic about the result.

headline: Mayor Barr Services Held
abstract: Former Mayor Joseph M. Barr was buried in St. Mary’s Cemetery in Lawrenceville after a Mass at St. Bede Church in Point Breeze.  Hundreds of political friends and former adversaries and those who simply liked Barr turned out for the service.

headline: Council's pay push
abstract: A plan by Pittsburgh City Councilman Tom Flaherty would push Council pay to over $55,000 in seven years.  However, yearly raises are prohibited by the City's home-rule charter for elected officials during their terms, meaning Councilman Flaherty's proposal would go to public referendum.

headline: City Court Reform: The Case Isn't Closed
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice John P. Flaherty, who resigned as court administrator last July, has been speaking with PA Supreme Court Justice Samuel Roberts--who is scheduled to take over the Chief Justice position in January.  Flaherty is asking Roberts to cancel his resignation so that he can implement sweeping reforms to the day-to-day operations of the Philadelphia court system.

headline: Plans for a Capitol addition
abstract: The PA Department of General Services revealed its plans for the Capitol-Plaza addition.  The article also contains an artist's depiction of the new plaza.

headline: At-Large Elections Face Legal Tests
abstract: A new Supreme Court opinion and an extension of the Voting Rights Act, the civil rights movement is expected to open a legal attack on at-large municipal voting systems in both the North and South.  The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People will try to force municipalities to establish voting systems that would reserve at least one city council seat for a black or other minority candidate.  The simplest method of achieving this is to carve up a municipality into separate city council districts, each with its own seat, and to assure that one district is dominated by black voters.

headline: Battle for Sewage Treatment Plant
abstract: The state ordered the expansion of Springettsbury Township’s sewage treatment plant, which serves 11 municipalities.  Now, $2.6 million later, the state is snubbing the project after the planning stage.  The state was expected to finance 75 percent of the $38 million cost of the project.  But on July 3 the state let it be known that funding for the project would be cut because of declining federal revenues.  The state argues that there are other projects around the state that are more urgent.  Springettsbury Township and the other 10 municipalities are preparing to fight back.  They are going to appeal the state's decision and will be given a hearing on August 16th.

headline: Bus Firm Picks Site in State
abstract: Bus manufacturer Neoplan U.S.A will occupy the Quality Coach Building in Montgomeryville, Montgomery Country, to fill a $157.8 million contract to produce 1,100 buses, Government Dick Thornburgh has announced.  600 buses are for the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) and 410 buses for the Port Authority of Allegheny County.

headline: Law curbs a growing Pa. industry that spurs abuse with pseudo-drugs
abstract: A new state law aims to curb growing production of fake amphetamines that are sold to teenagers for up to $1 per pill.  The bill was spurned into action by a recent US Food and Drug Administration crackdown and the realization that Pennsylvania was the leader producer of these types of drugs.  State officials say that there are more than 150 registered distributors around the state.

headline: Lottery fixers Perry, Plevel now behind bars
abstract: Nick Perry and Edward Plevel went to jail for rigging the Daily Lottery drawing in Pittsburgh. Perry worked as the announcer for the lottery drawing and Plevel was a security official. If the lottery officials had not investigated the drawing, Perry and Plevel could have made away with about $1.2 million.

headline: A Little Less Extravagance
abstract: Legislators ran up a $125,000 tab for wining and dining, and other “official business,” including a $460 beer and liquor bill for the office of retiring Senate Democratic Majority Leader, Martin Murray.  Flowers, soft drinks and snacks for office staffs, photographs of legislators and constituents, and reading material for Lt. Governor William Scranton III were all bought with public funds, apart from the $10,000 personal expense account each legislator receives annually.  The largest tab of $67, 278 was for meals and drinks associated with authorized business, often understandably after late evening legislative sessions.

headline: Mayor Griffith Vice President of Cities Unit
abstract: Mayor Donald Griffith has been elected vice president of the Pennsylvania League of Cities.  A resolution introduced by the City of Lebanon asking for the repeal of the Davis-Bacon Act was approved 15-7 by the general membership.  The Davis-Bacon Act calls for payment of prevailing wage rates in projects involving federal funds.

headline: Council's Perkins will head tax study panel
abstract: Jane Perkins will head the Harrisburg's 15-member Tax and Revenue Study Commission. The commission is empowered to examine and make recommendations on all matters concerning the raising of revenue for the City of Harrisburg.

headline: Duquesne Light criticized, praised
abstract: According to an audit released by the PA Public Utility Commission, Duquesne Light Company should improve operations of its Beaver Valley 1 nuclear power plant.  A consulting firm also recommended close monitoring of the plant, as well as improvements in management, training and budgeting.

headline: Viet vets get their due
abstract: The National Salute to Vietnam Veterans represents an attempt to bring an end to the indifferent and sometimes cold treatment that Americans have shown Vietnam Veterans.  Through Sunday, thousands of veterans will participate in parades; on Saturday, the dedication of the Vietnam Veterans memorial will occur.

headline: Ban on in-class prayer by teachers is upheld
abstract: Reaffirming earlier court decisions, the Commonwealth Court has ruled that no public school teacher has the right to pray aloud or read Bible stories as a religious activity in classrooms. The court upheld the Warren County School Board's firing of fourth-grade teacher Lloyd Fink in April 1978, for saying spontaneous prayers and reading the bible in class.

headline: Bill would keep strict air rules
abstract: US Representatives Henry Waxman and Toby Moffett are sponsoring a bill that is an alternative to an industry-backed bill that would seriously weaken a national effort to curb air pollution.  The Clean Air Act techinically expired on September 30, 1981, but its requirements are still in effect until it is renewed.

headline: Business booms for contractors
abstract: The Contractors Association of Western Pennsylvania hosted a lunch for city, county and state highway departments, the US Army Corps of Engineers and the Port Authority to thank the governmental agencies for their business and also get a sneak preview of 1982 projects.

headline: Law Reduces Waiting Time for Adoption
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has signed a bill that will streamline the state’s adoption procedures.  It eliminates the six-month waiting period before an adoption can be made final and will get adoptive children in to permanent homes as quickly as possible.  Once all legal requirements are met, the court can immediately make the adoption final.  Both the natural and adoptive parents are required to be informed of their rights in an adoption.

headline: Lotto topping $1.4 million
abstract: The Pennsylvania Lottery Bureau announced yesterday the jackpot in the next week's Lotto will be over $1.4 million since no player picked all six winning numbers in Friday's drawing.

headline: A matter of political integrity
abstract: The US Supreme Court has declined to overturn a ruling by a lower court holding that independent fundraising efforts are free to raise and spend unlimited funds in support of a candidate.  The effect of this is to leave in unenforceable limbo the Presidential Election Campaign Fund Act's provision that Political Action Committees (PACs) can spend more than $1000 in support of a candidate.

headline: Mele Seeks LCB Facts on Hiring
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's appointee to the Liquor Control Board has asked for a "dollar-by-dollar" account of expenses in connection with a new warehouse contract and the hiring of 40 extra employees.  Mario Mele asked the controller for accounting in what he called "a multimillion-dollar blunder" made during a seven week period.

headline: County dems meet to endorse
abstract: Members of the Allegheny County Democratic Committee who represent the 37th State Senatorial district, will meet in Bridgeville to endorse four candidates for the Democratic State Committee. This meeting became necessary when a vote last Saturday was voided due to an error in the voting machine.

headline: 777 is the lucky number and lottery payoff is rich
abstract: The daily number 777 produced a lottery payout of 4.2 million yesterday.  This is the second highest payout in the Daily Number Game's history.

headline: GOP, Democrats differ on job funding
abstract: Although there is growing bipartisan support in Congress for a new federal jobs program, Democrats and Republicans disagree on what shape the program should take and how to fund it.  Both parties appear anxious to reduce the nation's 10.4 percent unemployment rate, however.

headline: Blacks delay breakfast as governor fails to show
abstract: A breakfast held by a group of blacks Thursday was delayed an hour because of confusion over whether Governor Dick Thornburgh would address the assemblage in the William Penn hotel. The governor finally did not show up.

headline: 'Bottle bill' for state could test job claims
abstract: On one hand, people claim that the recently proposed deposit legislation will be costly and throw people put of work. On the other hand, a report from the New York state says this legislation will create 5000 new jobs and the costs to the beverage industry could be recovered through recycling. The only to find out which is correct is by trying out the deposit legislation in Pennsylvania.

headline: Camiel loses Pike panel post
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has ruled that former Philadelphia Democratic Chairman Peter Camiel cannot keep his post with the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission. Gov. Thornburgh suspended him after a federal grand jury him on charges of placing no-work employees on the state Senate payroll.

headline: Lawyer Hosts Judges
abstract: Cavanaugh was among the golfers at Sunnybrook.  He saw no problem with his attendance since many of the contributors to his campaign for the court were lawyers.  "Binns is an old and dear friend.  Most of the people I know in the world are lawyers," said Cavanaugh.  "I had lawyers contribute thousands of dollars to my campaign so I see nothing wrong with a golf game."

headline: Making exception
abstract: This reprint of a January 28 Wall Street Journal editorial discusses the recently push by Pennsylvania to catch people crossing the state line to get cheaper liquor.  Whenever a monopoly starts using strong-arm tactics to sell products, it becomes hard to ignore.

headline: A Plan to Raise Revenues, or to Create Patronage?
abstract: Mayor Green wants to raise more revenue to help balance the city budget.  He believes he can generate an additional $14 million by efficient collection of parking fines.  The mayor wants to transfer the collection function to the Philadelphia Parking Authority, which at the moment is responsible for operating city-owned parking lots and garages.  In order for the authority to assume new duties, under the mayor's plan unveiled Tuesday, it would be necessary to vastly expand its staff of 218 employees.

headline: 'Mellow' Rizzo Girds For Race In Philadelphia
abstract: Frank L. Rizzo who failed in his attempt to change the Philadelphia Charter so he could run for a third term as mayor, has begun making comments indicating he will run for the job in 1983. Noting that he had learned how to handle the press better, he criticized the outgoing mayor, William J. Green and his probable opponent W. Wilson Goode on the lack of projects leading to jobs. He also reminded people of things he did while in office that helped develop the city.

headline: County school districts get $4 million more
abstract: The Pittsburgh school district, with an additional $1.1 million, is one of 35 Allegheny County districts that will receive more state education aid under a new formula adopted by the state Legislature.

headline: extravagant irresponsible
abstract: Pennsylvania House Appropriations Committee Chairman Richard A. McClatchy Jr. argued that the recent contract demands of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) were irresponsible--especially given that the demands, if enacted, would cost taxpayers nearly 900 million dollars.

headline: Senate moving on auto emissions testing
abstract: In an effort to gain access to millions of dollars in federal highway funds, state Senate President Henry G. Hager has introduced legislation to establish an auto emissions inspection program in the Pittsburgh and Philadelphia areas.  In January, a federal judge froze the state's access to federal highway funds for failure to comply with an auto-emissions-inspection program.

headline: Challenge to a Legislature: Abortion Answer: A Law that May Not Last
abstract: One state representative from Philadelphia who was not identified voted for the abortion bill although he did not agree with it.  He said he voted for it because there are several churches in his district that pay very close attention to the abortion issue.  The House and Senate both passed the bill earlier in the week.  Governor Dick Thornburgh signed it to make it into law.

headline: Centralian plan rally to mark year of fear
abstract: Residents of Centralia, PA will rally at City Hall to protest government inaction in dealing with the underground mine fire that has raged for almost 20 years.  The fires have caused cave-ins, releasing lethal amounts of carbon monoxide into the air.

headline: Camiel ousted from turnpike panel - again
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has ruled that former Philadelphia Democratic Chairman Peter Camiel cannot keep his post with the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission. Gov. Thornburgh suspended him after a federal grand jury him on charges of placing no-work employees on the state Senate payroll.

headline: Lebanon Police drug use inquiry still under way
abstract: Lebanon City Police Chief George Gruber said an internal investigation into police drug use is continuing.  The PA Attorney General's office declined to take over the investigation because the city has already done much of the work.  The investigation began when two police officers were found to be using marijuana and hashish at least monthly.

headline: McKeesport Hopefuls Line Up
abstract: A television program was being filmed in Pittsburgh.  Many people lined up for a part in the production.  The program is being financed by a $160,000 grant from the National Endowment for the Humanities.

headline: A visitor from Pittsburgh
abstract: Columnist George Fattman notes that parking for 50 cents in Downtown Pittsburgh garages at night and during holidays is a bargain, but machines only take coins.

headline: Mondale: Don't Count Wecht Out
abstract: Current predictions to the contrary don’t cut Cyril Wecht out as a U.S. Senatorial candidate, says former Vice President Walter Mondale.  Mondale told a group of Wecht partisans that conditions are ripe for a Democratic victory on November 2nd.  He has an excellent chance of becoming the next U.S. senator from Pennsylvania.  Mondale has formed a political action organization called the Committee for the Future of America.  So far he has raised $1.2 million to finance his campaign for candidates other than for himself.

headline: Dig that courtesy
abstract: This editorial encourages Pittsburgh citizens and workers to be patient while downtown is excavated for the new subway tunnel.

headline: Sunshine action in 1983--Jubelirer
abstract: To make up for the shortcomings of Pennsylvania's current sunshine law, the state Legislature is expected to take action on a bill that would exact harsher penalties upon those conducting government business under the shroud of secrecy.  The bill under consideration would void any action taken in secret that should have been done in open session.

headline: Mayoral game: Rendell, GOP itching to play
abstract: Nine days after Philadelphia Mayor William Greene announced he would not seek a second term, only City Controller Thomas A. Leonard has actually declared his candidacy.  There are plenty of near-announcements of candidacy--including statements from former Mayor Frank Rizzo, Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell, and City Managing Director Wilson Goode.

headline: Church and state in court
abstract: Editorial discusses three recent cases that illustrate conflicts between church and state.  The first case involved an Amish business owner who had to pay Social Security taxes for his employees.  The second involved Bob Jones University's petition for tax-exempt status even though it engages in racial discrimination which University officials contend is part of religious faith.  Finally, Georgetown University has been sued by two homosexual student organizations over the witholding of student activity funds which would endorse the activity and thus be against the teachings of the Catholic Church.  Editorial advises the judges to strike a balance between First Amendment freedoms and the public policy of secular governments.

headline: Citizens' views sought on State's environmental master plan
abstract: Pennsylvanians are being asked for public comment on the new environmental master plan at hearing scheduled for this week and next in cities around the state.  There is not yet a state commitment to implement the plan.

headline: Car Inspection Fee Increase Denounced
abstract: State Representative Rudy Dininni is miffed that service stations and garages have responded to the new once-a year safety inspection law by raising their inspection fees.  Before August 1st, state motorists were required to have their cars inspected twice a year.  Under the new law safety checks are required annually.  Governor Dick Thornburgh said when he signed the legislation in May the owners of cars and small trucks would save at least $60 million a year in inspection fees.

headline: Legal Aid's Hard Times
abstract: These are not the best of times for legal aid.  The Thornburgh administration seems prepared to go ahead with its budgetary promise to defend the Pennsylvania Legal Services Center, principal provider and clearinghouse for legal aid in this state, and lump money for this purpose under the Adult Services Block Grant program, permitting counties to administer this program to whatever level they desire.

headline: Mellon will move to the east, but at its own pace
abstract: Due to the passing of the new banking law that allows for statewide acquisition and expansion, Mellon Bank will now be able to become a force in banking throughout the commonwealth. This will occur at a pace chosen by Mellon.

headline: Abscam defendant taking paid leave
abstract: null

headline: Monroe countian will bid for GOP post
abstract: Vice-chairman Robert F. Dick, a candidate for re-election, appears headed for a contest with Charles Krikwood, GOP chairman for Monroe County.

headline: Following in Dad's Footsteps
abstract: Nepotism is examined in PA with parents getting their teenage children enviable positions within various governmental agencies.

headline: Dininni asks House Ethics panel if his votes on banking legislation constitute a conflict
abstract: State Representative Rudy Dininni, stockholder and president of the board of Farmers Bank and Trust Co., has asked the state House Ethics Committee for an opinion regarding his votes on banking legislation.  Representative Dininni is not sure if his votes on such legislation are in conflict with his private banking interests.

headline: Governor signs bill on colleges
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed into law a bill that reorganizes Pennsylvania's system of higher education.  The new law changes the designation of Pennsylvania's 13 state-owned institutions from colleges to universities.

headline: Courting Abortion
abstract: The United States Supreme Court is responsible for continuing to decline every painful distinction between the rights of the individual woman, the state’s right to govern standards of medical practice and a community’s right to place obstacles in the path of the woman seeking to terminate a pregnancy legally.  The Court has agreed to hear five appeals stemming from three different suits.

headline: Clean air deadline looms for 44 states
abstract: If the Reagan administration stands by their commitments, 472 counties in 44 states could lose their federal highway money because of failure to comply with air pollution standards.  The standards in the Clean Air Act need to be met by December 31, and more states are coming forward with evidence that they are in compliance.

headline: Car inspections once a year
abstract: The recent legislation reducing the number of auto-inspections to once-a-year from two is commendable and makes sense on the face of information that said twice-a-year inspections were no longer a cost effective or logical solution to reducing accident rates.

headline: Legislation Toughens Child Abuse Law in State
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed legislation designed to strengthen laws against child abuse by making it easier for law enforcement officials to get access to confidential records.  Now police will not have to get court approval in cases that involve homicide, sexual abuse, serious injury or abuse by people who are not members of a child's family.

headline: Millionaires, Losers, Fixers and Fools; For a decade, the Pennsylvania Lottery has made big money on a bad bet
abstract: This article talks about the huge success of the Pennsylvania Lottery from the time it was introduced ten years back. Even after the first 50 millionaires are paid in full, the Lottery will continue to be around. It is considered as the most successful venture undertaken by the Pennsylvania state government.

headline: Activist Groups Provide Mini-Convention Sideshow
abstract: The Democratic Convention would not be complete without the usual assortment of party crashers, issue hawkers, publicity piggy backers, and other hangers-on.

headline: More hypocrisy
abstract: Rep. Eldon Rudd has decided to propose a resolution that calls for a 5% pay-cut for the members of the House of Representatives, in order to embark on a program of fiscal restraint. The ironic part about this is last December, Rep. Hudd was one of the 363 members of the House that voted for the special tax-break Congress authorized for itself and he has not supported any of the 41 bills introduced in the house, to repeal that law.

headline: For his involvement in primary, Frank Rizzo has paid heavy price
abstract: Although analyzing an election with only 20% voter turnout is not advisable, ignoring what those results will have on the fortunes of former Mayor Frank L. Rizzo would be a mistake. However the outlook for Rizzo continues to be grim, without a strong base of voters.

headline: Election '82: preliminary predictions
abstract: This article gives an overview of several top election-day contests across Pennsylvania, including the race between Governor Dick Thornburgh and his challenger,  Congressman Allen Ertel.

headline: HRA Allowed Extension
abstract: The commonwealth and the Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority (HRA) have reached a mutual agreement to allow the agency 15 more days to file objections to the state acquisition of HRA property in the 300 block of Market Street.

headline: Gay protection bill snagged
abstract: A bill designed to protect homosexuals from job and housing discrimination has been side-tracked in Pittsburgh City Council over who is actually going to introduce it.  The bill was drafted by the gay equality committee on the American Civil Liberties Union and the Political Club. The bill sat idle for lack of sponsorship.

headline: Cleanup Begins at Lackawanna PCB-Tainted Site
abstract: Removal of thousands of transformers and capacitors has started at a highly contaminated PCB site in Lackawanna Country, and federal officials expect to complete the project by the end of October.  U.S Environmental Protection Agency has identified the 5.4 acre storage area on the Lackawanna River as one of the most grossly contaminated polychlorinated biphenyl sites in the eastern United States.  The $1.4 million equipment removal is among the first projects in the nation involving monies from the federal government’s superfund program for disposal of hazardous wastes.

headline: Causes of potholes must be rectified
abstract: Potholes are a dangerous, costly and recurring problem. The two main factors for this are the use of salt during winter and the heavy truck traffic on the roads. By making use of sand instead of salt, some of the problems can be removed. The solution for the heavy trucks problem is to reconstruct and strengthen the highways in order to accommodate these trucks.

headline: Leonard errs on traffic court; A buffer needed
abstract: The author, president of the Pennsylvania Special Court Judges Association, believes that the Controller Thomas Leonard's criticism of Philadelphia's Traffic Court is unwarranted. The author also feels that by bringing in lawyers to act as administrators of the court, the primary objectives of the courts will cease to exist.

headline: Mob tied to liquor licenses
abstract: An unnamed witness testified that one-fourth of Pennsylvania's liquor licenses were controlled by organized crime.  The witness claimed the businesses with the licenses are used as fronts to launder money, prostitution, gambling, and narcotics trafficking.  PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) enforcement official John Pensiero heard the witness and believed that the statement was not close to accurate, and noted that the LCB would probably not have the resources to investigate mob influences.

headline: Aging Dept. Moves Soon to New HQ
abstract: The PA Department of Aging was scheduled to move to its new headquarters in the renovated Baro Building.  The department has 91 employees and two other with the Pennsylvania Council on Aging, has been in the Finance building since its creation in 1978.  The state will pay an annual rent of $408,344 for 37,360 square feet of space at a rate of $10.93, which includes all utilities, janitorial services and supplies under a 10-year lease.

headline: More School Strikes Are Possible, says Union's Leader
abstract: The number of Western Pennsylvania school districts facing strikes could double near the end of the month, said Francis Santicola, regional field director of the Pennsylvania State Education Association in Allegheny County.  He said an estimated 2,250 teachers in 12 districts continued strikes affecting about 29,000 students.

headline: Give Council Compacts
abstract: Philadelphia City Council members ordered new cars for job use and charged the city.  The editorial suggests that Council members should have designated cars from the city fleet, but not their own new cars.

headline: Thornburgh adviser might quit if the right thing comes along
abstract: Robert C. Wilburn, the State Secretary of Budget and Administration and Governor Thornburgh's top financial advisor, says he may leave the administration.  Wilburn has hopes of returning to an academic position, but says he will not leave before the November 2nd elections and will only leave if the right job comes along.

headline: Governor to Ink Legislation Altering State College System
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh plans to sign legislation that will transform the state college system into a Commonwealth System of Higher Education; the 13 state-owned colleges will be renamed universities, and state universities will sever their ties with the state Department of Education.  State universities will now be run by a 16-member board and a chancellor.

headline: GOP women laud governor for veto of abortion bill
abstract: The Pennsylvania Council of Republican Women has formally commended Governor Dick Thornburgh for his recent veto of the abortion control bill.

headline: Coal Needs Sensible Regulation
abstract: The intention of the Federal Service Mining Act was that prime regulatory authority would be picked up by individual states.  Should the states not opt for primacy, the Feds would be required to set up a permanent regulatory authority.  The act requires coal operators to pay 35 cents per ton of surface production and 15 cents per ton of deep production into a federal Abandoned Mine Reclamation Fund.  Pennsylvania coal producers have paid nearly $100 million into this fund and will continue to pay approximately $20 million or more each year.  The act also states that 50 percent of the Abandoned Mine Land funds collected in any state shall be allocated to that state once a permanent regulatory program is established.  Pennsylvania is now eligible for nearly $50 million.

headline: City misses the mark on tourism
abstract: Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce president Thacher Longstreth stated that the area was missing an opportunity to become a ''tourist mecca'' through inadequate promotion and financial support.  Longstreth also addresses the topics of the unfinished highway system, and a permanent source of funding for SEPTA (Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority).

headline: Letter from the Editor
abstract: The editor, Gil Spencer, had lunch with Chuck Stone, a fellow reporter who just recently helped to stem the hostage crisis at Graterford prison.  Mr. Stone thought about challenging Congressman William Gray for his seat, but decided not to.

headline: Mortgage Rates Woes
abstract: U.S. Supreme Court has said federally chartered savings and loan associations could stop homeowners from passing on low-interest mortgages to new buyers.  The long-run effects are less clear.  Richard Pratt, chairman of the Federal Home Loan Bank Board, the federal agency that regulates the 2,000 federal savings and loan associations, claims the decision eventually will benefit consumers.  By bolstering the financial position of the savings and loans, whose loan portfolios have been filled with mortgages paying interest far below today’s market rates.  The impact in Pennsylvania will be less dramatic than in the nearly 20 other states.

headline: Aiming High
abstract: AFSCME represents about 60 percent of the state’s 100,000 workers.  The union is demanding for a 20 percent pay raise, 35-hour work week, seven weeks of vacation, and much else.

headline: Mrs. Tucker is Latest Victim: State Sen. Fumo Making Career Out of Attacks on Black Women
abstract: Hardcore Black political critics have often contended that loyalty to either of the major parties-Democratic or Republican can be a curse especially for black Americans.  Mrs. C. Delores Tucker is one person that has been loyal to the Democratic Party.  The Tribune has learned that there is a serious attempt by a number of loyal party leaders to squeeze Mrs. Tucker out of the Democratic National Committee (DNC).  She was trying to get elected to the State Senate from the Fourth District.  She entered the race on the Consumer Party ticket against two incumbent Republican senators, Phil Price and Joe Rocks.

headline: Green closing in on school control
abstract: Mayor Green had said that the biggest frustration of his first two years in office was his inability to change the direction of the financially troubled School District. However, he is now on the verge of getting control over the district due to a bill that would allow him to replace the Board of Education with a handpicked commission.

headline: ARC outlook
abstract: Winifred Pizzano, President Reagan's nominee to the top federal post at the Appalachian Regional Commission (ARC), says the ARC will continue operating for another five years.  Pizzano said her top priority at the ARC would be improving the literacy and health status of the people in the Appalachian region.

headline: HRA Allowed Extension
abstract: The commonwealth and the Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority (HRA) have reached a mutual agreement to allow the agency 15 more days to file objections to the state acquisition of HRA property in the 300 block of Market Street.

headline: Governor Questioned Here On Abortion Bill Signing
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed an abortion bill that had already been passed in the State House and Senate.  At first he told reporters that the bill was still being studied but then later admitted to the fact that he signed it.

headline: Coal office probe done, DER reports
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources said that an investigation has been completed into alleged mismanagement of the state's surface coal mining enforcement office in Pottsville.

headline: Clarks Ferry at top of bridge plans
abstract: PA House Majority Leader Samuel E. Hayes Jr. introduced plans to renovate 750 bridges using a funding mechanism that includes federal, local government, and trucking fees. PA truckers would pay an increased cost per axle, offset by lower registration fees. The majority of the fees would be borne by out of state truckers. PA Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson attended a press conference announcing the plan. The PA Department of Transportation includes the Clarks Ferry Bridge among those to be renovated.

headline: Locked out by constable, she loses furniture
abstract: A constable locked Karen Lee out of her Point Breeze apartment and told her to call the landlord to get her furniture and clothing.  So, she tried to call the landlord for three days, and her calls were never returned.  On the fourth, she went to her apartment and found it empty.  The Saniel-Elkind Real Estate Company filed the first notice for the eviction, but not the second notice to take possession of her goods.

headline: New state grand jury begins term Monday
abstract: A new statewide investigating grand jury sought by PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman to probe alleged state job-selling and illegal sale of liquor store franchises will begin its 18-month assignment.  Zimmerman asked the PA Supreme Court to allow the panel to continue its probe into allegations of misconduct in the Auditor General's department and in sales of liquor store franchises which surfaced as a result of the Auditor General's actions.

headline: All Smoke, no Fire
abstract: The Democrats held a midterm pep rally in Philadelphia.  The conference seems to have accomplished very little.  The voters are confronted by the same tired, old faces.  Few fresh ideas emerged and there was no indication that the party might soon produce the inspired leadership that might serve as a credible rival to the politics of Reagan.

headline: Murray signals end to an era
abstract: Editorial says that the announced retirement of State Senator Martin Murray (D-Luzerne County) after his 6th term marks the end of an era dominated by political giants.  Murray is leaving with a clean slate, an achievement in itself considering the nature of politics.  Editorial notes that Murray leaves office with respect and gratitude.

headline: Green crosses his fingers; Much of budget hangs on if's and maybe's
abstract: Mayor Green is set to present a $1.3-billion operating budget this evening that is rumored to have no tax increases. However, with looming financial worries with regard to wage increases for city workers and other problems, the goal of not hiking taxes seems improbable. However, the Green administration has maintained since last fall that it is willing to ask for a 10% increase in the real estate tax rate, in order to raise $38-million towards a settlement with the school district.

headline: Fire Causes Emergency at N-Plant
abstract: An electrical fire caused a low-level emergency at the Susquehanna nuclear power plant.  The fire caused no serious damage or injuries and came 12 days after Pennsylvania Power and Light Company (PP&L), operators of the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station in Luzerne County, started low-power testing of the Unit 1 reactor under an operating license granted by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

headline: Panel eyes rules, bailouts for municipal pension plans
abstract: The Public Employee Retirement Study Commission has scheduled a meeting to adopt recommendations for the development of funding standards for municipal pension programs.  The panel will also consider a recovery system to bail out distressed pension systems.

headline: Hispanic coalition sues on redistricting
abstract: The local Hispanic Coailition has filed a suit in US District court to block a new legislative district created in North Philadelphia, contending the district was drawn for the purpose of diluting the minority strength of hispanics.  The suit requests that the lines be redrawn to guarantee a Hispanic population of 53% to 58% in the district.  The loss of seats reflects the loss of population in the City of Philadelphia.

headline: Conservation officers graduate
abstract: Saturday marked the fifty years of the Ross Leffler School of Conservation, with the graduation of the 18th class of wildlife conservation officers, from the Jefferson County facility. Various graduation exercises were held at the auditorium, as part of this event.

headline: Congress Oks $40 million in SEPTA aid
abstract: The US Congress has cleared a $40.2 million grant to help the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority (SEPTA), to be applied to operating expenses for the fiscal year that ends June 30.  US Representative Lawrence Coughlin said the grant is part of a deal between the US Department of Transportation and SEPTA, where SEPTA was already owed the money anyhow and had been held up in Congressional appropriations.

headline: Look At Costs
abstract: While many people may be happy with the new drunk driving law which sends violators to prison, no one ever looked into the costs of the law. Costs for actual enforcement were never brought up, nor for jailing those convicted, not to mention the cost of those who lose their jobs and become unemployable due to their convict status. Judges are unlikely to rigorously enforce the law, and eventually, the actual costs will be known.

headline: No-Fault Blamed for State Car Insurance Rise
abstract: Six auto insurers in the state are getting rate increases worth a total of $127.2 million, and Insurance Commissioner Michael Browne said flaws in Pennsylvania's no-fault auto insurance law are to blame.  The increases average 10.2 percent and will affect 3.7 million vehicles in the state.  Liability coverage has climbed because the Legislature has failed to pass pending nofault revisions.

headline: Altoona's founding fathers
abstract: Last fall, city finances were tight, and council members included themselves in wage freezes.  This fall, with elections finished, not all members of council are taking part in the wage freeze.

headline: Murtha emerges
abstract: Once again, US Rep. John P. Murtha has been voted to represent the 12th Congressional District. The runner-up Rep. Don Bailey fought a good fight and is loved by many in Western Pennsylvania.

headline: Green Lobbies Against Tax Bill
abstract: Mayor Green lobbied against a pending federal tax bill that would hurt Philadelphia.  The bill was already approved by the Senate; however, Green was planning on meeting with members of the House Ways and Means Committee to discuss the bill.  The bill includes a $1 billion reduction in the appropriation for operation bootstrap.  The program, which Green supported as a congressman in 1976, gives federal tax incentives to businesses for investing in Puerto Rico.

headline: Grand Jury Wants Agency's License
abstract: A grand jury has urged the Pennsylvania Department of Welfare to revoke the license of the Southern Home for Children--a 133 year old, non-profit private agency for troubled and dependent youth.  The grand jury accused the home of lax supervision and attempts to cover up attacks by residents and staff on one another.  The agency's executive director claims the report is a distortion of reality and amounts to a witch hunt by Philadelphia Distirct Attorney Ed Rendell.

headline: Study: TMI Easier Than Losing Jobs
abstract: A long-term study of the psychological impact of the Three Mile Island accident has found that a recession does more damage to the psyche than a major nuclear accident.

headline: Hospital managers: more blacks
abstract: According to the Urban League of Pittsburgh, more black Pittsburghers hold management-level jobs now than four years ago. Hospital staffs also have more black physicians than before.

headline: Dark Clouds of Prosperity
abstract: Dr. William Sharpe, water resources specialist for the Pennsylvania State University Cooperative Extension Service, was among speakers during a meeting in Hershey of the seven-state Northeast Association of State Department of Agriculture.  Agriculture in the Southwest is running short on water.  The region from Pennsylvania northwest through New England is “relatively water rich” in a good position to profit from the constantly increasing demands for food.

headline: Congress Unfair To Used-Car Buyers
abstract: The Federal Trade Commission tried to address the problem of fraudulent practices by used car dealers that would require dealers to disclose to customers major defects in used cars, however, both the House and Senate rejected the rule.  It is believed that the reason for the rejection is because of personal gains by members of Congress during elections from the National Automobile Dealers Association, which provided some members with campaign contributions.

headline: Lottery fix prosecutor discusses sentencing
abstract: This photograph shows Henry Barr, a Deputy State Attorney General and Chief Prosecutor in the Daily Number lottery scandal, while discussing the case with reporters on Tuesday, in the Dauphin County courthouse.

headline: Nyet to Soviet vodka
abstract: Pennsylvania has said no to Soviet vodka for the time being.  The PA Liquor Control Board voted not to purchase Soviet vodka until martial law is lifted in Poland.  This ban was in response to a state resolution that called for a boycott to demonstrate opposition to Soviet intervention in Poland.

headline: An army that fights crime
abstract: PA Representative James Williams has started a campaign in his district where he seeks youth to help lower crime in that area.  Additionally, PA Representative Hardy Williams worked on the Save Our Seniors campaign for the elderly.

headline: Murtha faces toughest primary challenge
abstract: The two incumbent members of US House, Rep. John P. Murtha of Johnstown and Rep. Donald Bailey of Greensburg, will be seeking the Democratic Nomination for new terms in the 12th Congressional District at the May 18 primary election. Both candidates have launched their campaign and this will mark Rep. Murtha's toughest challenge in a primary election to date.

headline: Green Plan for Cable is Delayed: Council Wants Public Hearing
abstract: City Council decided to delay action on Mayor Green’s administration’s proposal to redraw the boundaries for the city’s four cable-television franchises.  The council members sent the resolution to the Committee of Public Property and decided to hold a public hearing on the plan.

headline: Complaints about constables are aired
abstract: At a meeting in the office of the Allegheny County director of special courts, complaints about inefficiencies in the state's constable system were leveled.  Constable-system reform has been under consideration in the state legislature for the last three years, and the PA Supreme Court will not render a decision on reform until the General Assembly takes legislative action on the matter.

headline: Acid rain due action, not study
abstract: Pennsylvania must face the challenges posed by acid rain.  The state has for years tried to balance its coal and environmental interests--a strategy that has, for the most part, left environmental concerns unaddressed.  It is in everyone's interest--even the coal industry's--to address the environmental concerns posed by acid rain.

headline: Hospital's Abortion Policy Correct
abstract: York Hospital will continue to perform abortions.  The hospital didn't break under the pressure of anti-abortion pressure groups and withdraw from its patients a right embedded in national and sate laws. The hospital will not perform abortions on women who are more than 12 weeks pregnant or past their first trimester.

headline: Delaware River Panel Warns of a Drought Emergency
abstract: Unless there is heavy rainfall along the upper Delaware in the next few weeks, the Delaware River Basin Commission is prepared to issue a drought emergency in mid-December.  The commission controls the use of water resources in eastern Pennsylvania, western New Jersey, northern Delaware and lower New York State.

headline: Conrail line takeover plan offered
abstract: Three Warren-area companies have joined to take over a rail line marked for abandonment by Conrail.  The three companies would operate the line, while the state which own part of the line and would lease its portion to the companies for $1 per year, and add some additional monies to contribute towards maintainence costs.  The proposal is now before the Interstate Commerce Commission for review.

headline: Low-security jail dormitory eyed
abstract: Due to the crowding up of most lock-ups, officials in Dauphin County are leaning towards the construction of a minimum-security dormitory. The initial plan was to construct 60-120 maximum security cells at the current facility  but due to less demand and higher costs, that plan was scrapped.

headline: Odometers turned back, state says
abstract: An alleged unlicensed used car dealer in Lebanon has been sued by Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman's office on charges of rolling back odometer readings and "laundering" auto titles through North Carolina.  The state is seeking a permanent injunction, reimbursement for victims and financial penalties.

headline: An Offer He'll Refuse
abstract: A delegation of Philadelphia Ward Leaders, led by US Congressman Joseph Smith, will ask former city controller Tom Leonard to step out of a threeway Democratic primary. Ward leaders are concerned that with both presumably Frank Rizzo and Tom Leonard running, City Manager Wilson Goode has more of a chance to win. Some believe Goode would win outright. No black ward leaders will be participate in the delegation, whose request Leonard has promised to refuse.

headline: Murtha, Foglietta survive remapping
abstract: John Murtha and Thomas Foglietta are the survivors of hard-fought primary battles between two fellow Democratic incumbents in bids to retain their seats in the US House of Representatives.

headline: Green: Council an Overriding Failure
abstract: The Philadelphia lawmakers were attacked by the mayor.  He said they were "irresponsible" and "one of the worst legislative bodies in the Free World."  The mayor's statements came at a brief but unusually colorful news conference called by the major in wake of Council's 15-1 vote to override his veto of a bill requiring big companies to give workers at least 60 days' notice of plant closings.  This is part of a long series of mindless, irresponsible, economically foolish stands that the City Council has consistently taken, Mayor Green said.

headline: House Oks creation of state university system
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives voted yesterday to create a new state university system.  The new system would remove the state's 13 state-owned colleges and universities from the control of the Department of Education and would place them under the authority of a chancellor and a 16-member board.  Similar legislation has already passed in the Senate, and Governor Thornburgh said he will sign the bill.

headline: House Delays Debate, Vote on Abortion Bill
abstract: The electronic voting system in the House of Representatives had broken down, which delayed a debate and voting on an abortion-control bill.  There is concern that the bill will not be voted on until the fall session due to the delay.

headline: DER attacked as 'lax' on toxic-waste rules
abstract: In a testimony before a House fact-finding panel, environmentalists and manufacturers accused the Department of Environmental Resources of not enforcing the state's hazardous-waste regulations stringently enough.

headline: Despite Concerns Thornburgh Signs Drunken Driving Bill
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed a tough drunk driving bill into law to the applause of many backers including PA Mothers Against Drunk Drivers. Thornburgh believes that putting first time offenders in jail is counterproductive and creates a double standard with those committing crimes while driving getting harsher penalties than those who are not driving. He also believes that because there are not enough jail cells as it is judges would be able to use their own discretion when sentincing. Something which members of the legislature disagree with and may ultimately have to be decided by a court challenge.

headline: Lt. Gov: Clemency Usually Works
abstract: Lt. Governor William W. Scranton 3rd urges the public not to overreact to a recent study showing that more than one-fifth of the criminals who had been granted clemency in the last 14 years were rearrested.  Of 1,591 criminals whose sentences were reduced or whose offenses were forgiven by governors from 1968 to 1981, 346 were re-arrested, according to a study conducted by the Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency.

headline: Other Opinions: It's Time to Stabilize Auto Insurance Rates
abstract: Auto insurance rates are expected to increase.  The insurance industry appears to have little compassion for the high rates.  Something needs to be changed in order to stabilize auto insurance.  One is to change some of the current insurance regulations to help monitor and prevent padded claims.  Insurance companies should be monitored more closely and there should be a crackdown on highway safety laws that prevent unsafe drivers from being on the road.

headline: An Offer He'll Refuse
abstract: A delegation of Philadelphia ward leaders, led by US Congressman Joseph Smith, will ask former city controller Tom Leonard to step out of what is shaping up to be a threeway Democratic primary. Ward leaders are concerned with both presumably Frank Rizzo and Tom Leonard running, City Manager Wilson Goode has more of a chance to win. Some believe Goode would win outright. No black ward leaders will be participate in the delegation, whose request Leonard has promised to refuse.

headline: Murtha-Bailey race pits power versus power
abstract: The central issue of the Democratic nomination in the 12th Congressional District hits on power as the underlying theme. The election is contested by John P. Murtha, a member of the US House Appropriations Committee and US Rep. Don Bailey.

headline: Green's veto set aside… with a vengeance
abstract: City Council has unanimously voted to override Mayor Green's veto of a bill aimed at increasing the share of city contracts for businesses owned by minorities, but Green says he will not enforce its controversial provisions.

headline: PE appeals order to halt Limerick unit
abstract: The Philadelphia Electric Company (PE) has asked the Commonwealth Court to overturn a Public Utility Commission (PUC) ruling ordering PE to cancel or suspend work on Unit 2 of its Limerick nuclear generating station.  PE's appeal claims that the PUC made unsubstantiated judgments in its August 27th order regarding Limerick.

headline: How group shaped abortion bill
abstract: Americans United for Life, a Chicago-based anti-abortion organization, has designed the model for proposed state legislation to restrict abortions. It is considered likely to be passes into law, later this year.

headline: DER Seeks Funds to Reclaim Land
abstract: Pennsylvania may lose control of its coal industry if it doesn’t raise enough money to reclaim abandoned mine sites  The risk of further inaction is loss of primacy, Environmental Resources Secretary Pete Duncan told a Senate subcommittee.  Primacy, granted by the federal government, lets the Department of Environmental Resources write and enforce mine regulations designed to prevent scarring and pollution.  Under the arrangement, the state must reclaim mine sites abandoned by bankrupt or unscrupulous operators.  Duncan proposed last year tripling permit fees to $150 an acre to help raise the $45 million backlog that Pennsylvania runs a year.  Other ways to raise money would include a user fee paid by coal purchasers and a per-ton reclamation fee that could be passed on to the buyer.

headline: Cost of Car is Figured At .24 a mile
abstract: Gasoline may be a bargain in Pennsylvania compared to other states.  It costs nearly 24 cents a mile to own and operate a compact car, which is no different than anywhere else in the nation according to the American Automobile Association.  Gases prices in Pennsylvania are traditionally lower than other places because of the state’s proximity to refineries and cheap water transportation at ports on the Chesapeake Bay and Delaware River.

headline: Mafia Here Winning War for Youngstown
abstract: James Cononico of Mahoning County and Charles Frederick Grisham of Warren tried to muscle in on the gambling operations in Warren controlled by the Cleveland family.  The gambling operations were run by Joseph Perfette who answered to James Licavoli, the head of the Cleveland family.  Licavoli hired a hit man to kill Grisham and Cononico.  The FBI has launched a major investigative effort against organized crime in Youngstown now that seven other men believed to be affiliated with the Cleveland family have been charged with operating a drug ring

headline: Out-of-State Distillers Claim LCB Shows Bias
abstract: The group of out-of-state liquor companies angered by the state Liquor Control Board’s favoritism toward Pennsylvania firms has charged they were being discriminated against under the new policy.  Some 25 representatives of liquor firms that produce their spirits outside Pennsylvania appeared before the board to protest the new policy, designed to encourage manufacturers to locate plants inside the state.  The program adopted by the LCB last month gives the Pennsylvania firms favored shelf positions, prominent floor displays, and additional product listings and expedited payments.

headline: And the Southerners' Counterpoint
abstract: The Democrats left their mid-term national party conference in Philadelphia with a minimal goal.  They formed the firing squad in a straight line against the Reagan policies instead of a circle aimed at each other.  The Democratic Party needs to show the American people that it is a different party in 1982 than what they voted against in 1980.

headline: Murtha's GOP opponent to withdraw from race
abstract: 12th District Republican congressional nominee Clair Saylor has announced that he will withdraw from the race, leaving the choice of the replacement to district party leaders. Republican State Committee members from the 12th District must meet by Aug. 19 to select a new nominee to face Democratic incumbent John Murtha in the November general election.

headline: Hotel Tax Plan Advances In City Council
abstract: A Philadelphia City Council committee approved a tax on city hotel rooms in order to raise funds to promote tourism in the city. PA Governor Thornburgh signed legislation giving Philadelphia as well as Delaware and Montgomery counties the authority to levy the tax. He also signed bills giving parking authorities police powers, letting the Mayor, instead of Family Court, appoint a board of managers for the Philadelphia House of Detention for Juveniles, and permitting the Delaware River Basin Commission to set interest rates on bonds it issues.

headline: They're Off and Running
abstract: Last week, President Reagan began selling the Republican Party to the Amerrican people--stumping in Utah and Kansas, where he praised traditional values, a Constitutional Amendment for school prayer and anti-abortion legislation.  All of this was in anticipation of the 1982 mid-term elections.

headline: In the open; Abortion talks should be public
abstract: The author states that Marsha Woodall's April 30 article made a powerful statement on the state of Pennsylvania politics by publicizing Rep. Stephen Friend's (R- Delaware County) position on abortion and his morally incorrect political games.

headline: DER Tests 27 More Wells Near Letterkenny
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources announced that it has tested for volatile organic contaminants in 27 additional private wells near Letterkenny Army Depot.  The levels exceeded the risk levels established by the U.S Environmental Protection Agency.  Property owners whose wells tested beyond the EPA risk were advised to secure drinking water from another source or to boil or filter their water.  At the EPA risk level, it is estimated that a lifetime of water consumption in a large population would result in one additional cancer death among 100,000 people.

headline: Court lifts freeze on road funds
abstract: The 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals granted a state request to temporarily lift a freeze of federal highway funds for construction projects in the Pittsburgh and Philadelphia areas. The decision means that the decades-awaited start of construction on the East Street Valley Expressway would now become a reality. Earlier, US District Judge Louis Bechtle ordered that no more federal funds must be approved until the emissions program is setup in the state's top 10 counties.

headline: Mail order divorce may involve a 'danger'
abstract: Pittsburgh attorneys Michael Davis and Howard Singer have begun taking advantage of simplified procedures under the no-fault divorce law and have built up a mail order divorce business.  If clients can fall into the no-fault category, they are mailed a questionnaire, which is turned into a petition, and then filed with the court.  In most cases, the attorneys never even see the clients, and charge a flat-rate for the service.

headline: Penn National Sold to Lessee
abstract: Penn National Turf Club, financially crippled by the energy crisis and then soaring inflation, announced a pending sale of the race-track to its lessee, Mountainview Racing Association.  The price tag would be between $9-12.5 million.

headline: Appointment sought
abstract: Former mayor Frank Rizzo's top political strategist Martin Weinberg denied having anything to do with ward leaders recent plans to request former City Controller Tom Leonard drop out of the primary for mayor. US Congressman Joseph Smith had asked for an official appointment from Rizzo for his delegation to Leonard, however none was granted. Smith said as far as he is concerned, the matter is behind the ward leaders, who simply will not support Leonard. Smith warned support from ward leaders is crucial in a primary, while another Rizzo supporter said the delegation would make it difficult to raise funds now that he has been shown to be without political support.

headline: Nation's Needs Are Compatible with Job Needs
abstract: President Reagan’s response to the key domestic issue of the election is wise.  With Senate Republicans drafting a 200,000 job response and House Democrats pressing for a 600,000 job package, Reagan leans toward a 320,000 job program dedicated to the rebuilding of the highways and bridges.

headline: Job protection first with COG
abstract: The Lackawanna County Council of Governments (COG) has opposed a study of ways to implement local government through different means. The COG represents the first attempt to bring local officials together.

headline: In abuse cases, family gets benefit of doubt, York agency advises
abstract: Mary Ellen McMillen, executive director of the state House of Representatives' Committee on Health and Welfare, said that the amended Children Protective Services Act is designed to protect children.  Although prosecuting and punishing child abusers is of extreme importance, ensuring child protection comes first.

headline: Judges Open Remapping Suit to Black Plaintiffs
abstract: Philadelphia blacks should be given a chance to contest possible racial discrimination in the state’s remapping of voter districts, a panel of three federal judges decided.  The judges, hearing evidence in lawsuits challenging the constitutionality of Pennsylvania’s reapportionment plan, invited intervention by Philadelphia blacks.  And a lawyer battling the redistricting on behalf of a Chester woman said he expected to have three Philadelphia residents join suit.

headline: DER to close 20 offices in state
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources has announced the closing of 20 of its 46 local enforcement offices to save money. This move is being questioned by environmentalists.

headline: Coyne: Goodbye Managua
abstract: US Representative James Coyne arrived home February 22 after being stranded in Nicaragua by a bomb blast that killed 4 and closed the Managua airport.  He and fellow representatives Thomas Harkin (D-Iowa) and James Oberstar (D-Minnesota) were on a fact-finding mission to El Salvador for three days.  Their departure was delayed when officials closed the Managua airport because of the explosion and because Mexican President Jose Lopez Portillo was also visiting Nicaragua.  Coyne said the atmosphere in Nicaragua was very anti-American.

headline: Mandatory jail bill sent to governor
abstract: Mandatory jail terms for violent criminals, part of Governor Dick Thornburgh's anti-crime package, goes to the governor's desk for signing after House approval.
