The new law would mandate minimum 5-year jail terms for cimes involving firearms, second offenders, physical assault and crimes committed on public transportation.  The remianing unpassed portions of his package include reform of parole and elevation of the Bureau of Corrections to cabinet-level status.

headline: Pennsylvania banking enters new age
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed a legislation that will change the way banks do business, by allowing them to open branches statewide. The legislation also would permit banks to buy one bank per year for the next 8 years, after which all restrictions would be removed.

headline: Archdiocese questions candidates
abstract: For the first time, candidates in a spring primary are being asked to express themselves on Archdiocesan concerns, something usually reserved for November general election candidates.

headline: Native in Line for U.S. Post has Political Past
abstract: Richard T. McCormack, nominated for a high State Department position, was at the center of a political controversy a decade ago after it was discovered that he had used a fictitious name and posed as a newspaper report to get information about a Republican primary opponent.  McCormack is in line to head the Bureau of Economic Affairs, which has a staff of 228.  He was a protégé of Senator Jesse Helms.  As an assistant secretary of state at a salary of $58,500 a year.  McCormack, who had not been appointed to the post during Haig’s 16-month tenure despite reported pressure from Helms, is now awaiting a Senate Foreign Relations Committee confirmation hearing.  Helms is the third-ranking member in seniority on the committee.

headline: Judge delays hearing on Beaver surcharge
abstract: Clearfield County Judge John A. Cherry postponed a hearing on whether the years 1969 through 1977 should be re-instated in the Beaver County surcharge case. He also ordered attorneys and their clients not to talk about the case to the media.

headline: N. Strabane pension fund payment
abstract: PA Auditor General Al Benedict announced that the state will be witholding pension contributions to North Strabane Township.  Benedict said the funds were being withheld because the township used 103,000 dollars in previously disbursed pension contributions to pay other township bills.

headline: Keep Cool On Abortion
abstract: Both sides of the abortion debate shuold remain calm after a recent ruling by a U.S. district judge. With similar laws in other states now before the U.S. Supreme Court, their ruling could change the PA law. Consequently, flouting or pushing the law is unproductive at this point.

headline: Don't worry about acid rain
abstract: Opinion:  The problem of acid rain is being talked about a lot, while Congress is being urged by US citizens and the Canadian government alike to do something about it.  Any solution Congress would likely come up with now will be wrong.  More time and money should be given to study the problem.

headline: Del,'s Sobriety Checks Stop Traffic to Save Lives
abstract: The Delaware State Police are stopping drivers to see if the have been drinking and if they are drunk.

headline: Mandatory Sentencing--Your Responses
abstract: In this editorial, people responded to Pennsylvania's new mandatory sentencing law that would put most violent criminals in jail for at least five years.  There were some people that disagreed with the law, but for the most part everyone thought it was a good idea.

headline: Pittsburgh National directors OK merger with Provident
abstract: The merger of Pittsburgh National Bank and Provident National Bank into a $9.8 billion holding company, PNC Corp., was approved yesterday by the Directors of Pittsburgh National Corp.

headline: Area taxation on downswing
abstract: Harrisburg communities can look forward to 1983 being a down year in local government financing, while the previous year was an "up-year."

headline: Neal Peirce: 'Dead' in Washington, Liberalism's Hope in States?
abstract: President Ronald Reagan’s "new Federalism" and federal-aid cutbacks are forcing states to face issues they have ignored.  For better or worse, decisions will be made increasingly in our 50 state legislatures."  A new handbook designed for officeholders and candidates for office at the state and local.  It lists some 300 measures proposed, or already passed, in some of the more progressive states.

headline: Judicial dark horse quits GOP primary
abstract: Delaware County Judge Domenic Jerome withdrew today from the Republican Party primary for State Supreme Court. Jerome had drawn a poor ballot position last week in a lottery held by the state for the May 18 primary.

headline: Reinstate Camiel Thornburgh told
abstract: The Commonwealth Court ordered Governor Thornburgh to reinstate Peter Camiel to the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission.  Camile was suspended following his indictment for putting ghost employees on the state payroll; he was eventually acquitted in U.S. District Court.  If the governor follows the court order, the Turnpike Commission, which has not had enough members for a quorum since Camile's suspension, may be able to restore its regular activities.

headline: Leaders Say Blacks Need to Organize
abstract: Black leaders from six Northwestern states were warned repeatedly at a three-day conference this week that their lack of organization had caused them serious setbacks in recent years that could grow in this decade into racial polarization.

headline: Emissions-Test Proposal Dies with Legislature
abstract: The General Assembly has adjourned for the year inspite of a federal court order that Pennsylvania begin auto emissions inspections in the Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, and Allentown areas.  A bill that would have authorized PennDot to proceed with an emissions inspection program in a dozen counties died in the Senate as the 1981-82 legislative session ended.  The immediate loss of the bill not being approved is $83 million in highway funds for Pittsburgh and Philadelphia and the indefinite suspension of future road money.

headline: Don't Kid Yourself: You can't drink and drive safely
abstract: This editorial describes a New York Times article detailing the 54 deaths from drunk driving accidents last New Years Eve, and asks readers to prevent this from happening in Lancaster County by not drinking and driving on this New Years Eve.

headline: Mandatory-sentences bill signed
abstract: Legislation establishing mandatory minimum prison sentences for people convicted of using guns during crimes, was signed yesterday by Governor Thornburgh. The law will require judges to impose prison sentences of at least 5 years on persons convicted of using a gun in the commission of a rape, assault, kidnapping, aggravated assault, robbery or arson.

headline: Product Liability Bill Limits Are Tightened
abstract: The House Insurance Committee approved a product liability measure that would limit consumer’s ability to sue manufacturers over defective products.  The Senate approved the legislation but it was uncertain whether it would pass the House.  The bill would also prohibit any lawsuits against retailers.

headline: As Florida Grows, So Does Concern About Saving Sun-and- Sand Good
abstract: In Florida the thing that is noncontrollable is growth.  Governor Bob Graham has said that "as long as citizens of the United States have the right to live anywhere they want to, and as long as places like Florida are qualitatively superior, they will continue to receive an influx of migration."  "The challenge said the Governor "is to how to direct and accommodate that growth in ways that won’t degrade the very quality that generated that growth."  Some of the problems facing Florida are sewage, clogged highways, and water shortages.  There is concern over the impact of continued migrations of refugees from the Caribbean and Central and South America.

headline: Never give up: Numbers' players are a special breed of people
abstract: The author works as a lottery sales agent and discovers that the people who play are generally more fun because they are more loose with their money than others.  Article has different stories about others who routinely play the lottery.

headline: Keep the county's 911 system
abstract: A national report on the 911 emergency telephone system has criticized the use of this system because the number of criminals arrested has increased by only 0.3%. However, the benefits associated with this system, far outweigh this criticism.

headline: In Northeast, identity an issue for House races
abstract: John J. Swaim Jr., the state representative for Pennsylvania's 169th District, is facing off against Dennis O'Brien--the former Republican state representative who previously held the 169th District seat.  Representative Swaim has called the campaign tactics of O'Brien unethical; he claims that O'Brien is trying to give voters the impression that he is the incumbent.  O'Brien denies this and says that a lot of people simply assume he is still in office.

headline: Letters: on anti-abortionists
abstract: Letter to the editor: Pro-choicer writes in to explain advantages of being pro-choice, points out that most polls find that most Americans are pro-choice.

headline: Environmentalists form unit
abstract: A new Political Action Committee (PAC) has been formed to promote candidates with good track records for supporting pro-environment initiatives.  The committee will be comprised of members of the Pennsylvania Conservation Network.  It is the first of this type of PAC in Pennsylvania.  The group was formed in response to Reagan Administration cutbacks at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

headline: Drivers will find fewer inspections costly, mechanic says
abstract: Harrisburg-area mechanic Vance Conley comments on a new piece of legislation being considered that will cut the requirement for auto inspections from twice a year to once a year.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and the Pennsylvania AAA (American Automobile Association) Federation support the measure, and is expected to pass easily.

headline: Marital rape
abstract: Editorial: In Pennsylvania, a man who rapes his wife has a foolproof defense, he's married to her.  Under PA law, a man can rape his wife and get away with it since law defines the rape as forced intercourse with someone other than a spouse.  PA House member Allen Kukovich has a bill up for final passage that eliminates marriage as a defense against a rape charge and should be supported.

headline: Product liability measure creates split between top business groups
abstract: The Pennsylvania Manufacturers' Association and the Pennsylvania Chamber of Commerce have split over the enactment of a major product liability law which seeks to reduce law suits and attract jobs to the state.  Because neither group can agree on how far the bill should go, the bill has floundered in the PA House of Representatives.

headline: As the Editor Sees it: Out of Bounds
abstract: Pennsylvania has been borrowing money from the federal government to meet our unemployment which we cannot afford and cannot pay alone.  The state just received its second major loan this year to cover the cost of benefit payments.  The state is in hock to the federal government for a total $1.6 billion.  The state legislature should review the unemployment compensation annually and then revise it according to what we can pay.

headline: New bid to pass redistricting set
abstract: PA House Republican leaders scheduled a second effort to pass a congressional reapportionment bill, after the most recent plan failed to pass with 88 for and 111 opposed.  House Speaker Matthew Ryan was unable to rally enough Republican votes to pass the plan a second time.  Democratic Whip James Manderino's plan was also soundly rejected.  If a law is not signed by Governor Dick Thornburgh by February 16, a federal court will do the reapportionment instead.

headline: Lebanon County voter registrations down by 1000 for May primary
abstract: About 1000 fewer Lebanon Countians are registered to vote in the upcoming primary election as compared to those that were eligible to vote in last year's general election.

headline: For whom the sun shines
abstract: This opinion piece offers support for Senate Bill 1531, the state's Sunshine Bill.  The law would improve access to public documents and would require that votes be taken in public.  The legislation would also require that all other business of government be conducted within public view.  This is one of the most important pieces of legislation to come up for a vote in a long time.

headline: Making Money
abstract: Letter commenting on abortion providers having to raise their fees due to the Abortion Control Act, and observing that if they were truly concerned about poor women they would find a way to reduce other costs instead of taking advantage of women when they are most vulnerable.

headline: EPA eases threat to ban funds over air pollution
abstract: Despite threats, the United States Environmental Protection Agency said that it will be lenient in its enforcement of air pollution standards that hundreds of counties are not meeting.  Environmental Protection Agency officials said they will employ "maximum flexibility" in their use of the Clean Air Act when evaluating progress.

headline: Drunk Driving
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the person is responding to an article written by Hope Emerich, chairman of the Tri-County Chapter of Mothers Against Drunk Drivers (MADD).  MADD has unleashed an unprecedented savage, emotional vindictive attack against alcohol because of the comments made by Emerich.

headline: Marital Rape
abstract: The author applauds the newspaper for supporting the House Bill 1122 that would make rape in marriage a criminal offense and states that statistically, other states which legalized this, did not face any rush of women charging their husbands with rape.

headline: Resolved: That more US business go to small firms
abstract: According to federal government figures, small businesses provide for 55% of all non-government jobs and contribute 50% to the gross national product. Hence, a new bill sponsored by 9 senators, is being introduced that will would direct federal agencies to break large procurement packages into smaller components in order to give smaller companies a greater opportunity to submit bids.

headline: At large vs. district elections
abstract: In an exercise of futility, voters in the City of Pittsburgh had a choice of three separate and totally confusing issues in the last election to express their desires for either an election of Pittsburgh's City Council members by district or at large.  Despite the questions being intentionnally confusing, a judge would not take them off the ballot.

headline: 'New federalism' renews a debate on government
abstract: President Ronald Reagan's call for a ''new federalism'' with the shift of several programs to the state levels has rekindled the question of the role of government.  Some are worried that this will turn into the racism of the past.  Others are worried that this will mean less aid for transit programs.  Congress is not expected to pass the proposed legislation this year.

headline: Looking to November
abstract: After the preliminaries, the candidates have been selected for the November 1982 election. It is now up to the people of Bucks County to do their research and vote to get the best people in office. The focus of the 1982 election will be on Congress and state offices.

headline: Reorganization near for state higher-education system
abstract: Legislation that would reorganize Pennsylvania's system of higher education  is awaiting approval from Governor Thornburgh.  The bill would create an independent system of higher education--removing the state's 13 colleges from Department of Education control and administration.  The legislation would also redesignate PA colleges as universities.

headline: Mon clergy ask governor to name valley disaster area
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh promised yesterday that "appropriate" Cabinet members will discuss with clergymen what routes can be taken to help the economy of the Monongahela Valley, but he stopped short of declaring the valley a disaster area as the clergymen had asked.

headline: EPA reverses toxic waste policy
abstract: Editorial:  US Senator Robert Stafford, chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works committee, said that he did not believe that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) could not fulfill its mission with the agency's substantially reduced budget.  Given this, the EPA has been unable to complete its work on establishing regulations for the generation and disposal of hazardous wastes and it is stepping back from other previously imposed bans on chemical dumping in landfills.

headline: Drunk Driving Law is Toughened
abstract: The penalties for drunken driving will be increased and standardized under a bill recently approved by the General Assembly and sent to Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Marital-rape bill back in Judiciary
abstract: By a 102-87 margin, lawmakers returned a bill back to the Judiciary Committee that would have made it a crime for a man to rape his wife.

headline: Penna.'s Congressional Delegation, Despite its Size, is Seen as an Ineffective Voice for the State: 27 Congressmen who Lack Power and Recognition
abstract: Members of the Pennsylvania Railroads Association were in Washington to press their view on different issues.  One of the main issues they were there for was for pending legislation that would grant federal eminent domain powers to promoters of a coal slurry pipeline.

headline: At press time…
abstract: Quarterly summary of the activities of the Hospital Association of America.

headline: New legislative map deprives many areas
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a citizen is concerned about the redistribution of legislative districts and states reasons the districts should be redrawn.

headline: Mayor, Council may run Philly schools
abstract: The Mayor of Philadelphia and its City Council would take over the financial reins of the city's school system under a bill approved by the House. The measure would let the city control the school district budget and abolish the Board of Education.

headline: A quick message to Phila police
abstract: A message alterting Philadelphia Police of the mass slayings in Wilkes-Barre was sent to all districts throughout the city yesterday.  The Pennsylvania State Police first notified the Philadelphia Police of the incident and told them to be on the lookout for the suspect, George Banks.

headline: NAACP bid splits PSU workers, black community leaders
abstract: Black community leaders and Penn State University employees, divided over whether there is racial discrimination at the school, are struggling to overcome differences and restart an NAACP chapter. University officials who helped run the NAACP chapter that folded agreed that new leadership may be needed.

headline: EPA's plan for nuclear waste
abstract: Editorial: The Environmental Protection Agency has announced that it plans to permit resumption of ocean-disposal of nuclear waste.  This is a change from a 1972 policy that prohibited ocean-dumping, now allowing certain low-level wasted to be discarded in the ocean due to the short supply of land disposal sites.

headline: Drunk Law Enactment Postponed: Backers Wanted It in Force for Holiday
abstract: Pennsylvania’s new, tougher law on drunken driving will not be in effect during the upcoming holiday season.  Proponents of the law, which will take effect 30 days after the governor signs it, had urged Thornburgh to sign the bill in time for it to take effect by Christmas or New Year’s Eve.  The governor said he would not sign the bill for at least several days because his staff had not completed its review of the measure.

headline: Minimum term for crime against elderly approved
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh signed into law yesterday legislation establishing minimum jail sentences for certain crimes when they are committed against children or the elderly. The Governor stated that he felt this was necessary given the increased vulnerability of these two demographic groups. Governor Thornburgh also signed legislation barring utilities from charging customers for power plans under construction.

headline: Pennsylvania Voting Record
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a bill which would call for once-a-year inspections on passenger cars.  The State Senate adopted an amendment that would require all state officials to leave office 90 days after their terms expire.  Occupational therapists will have own State Board of Occupational Therapy and Licensure.  All landscape architects will need to get a license to practice landscape architecture.  The bill regarding rape within marriage was sent back to the Judiciary Committee for further study.

headline: Atkinson's switch key topic in 4th district primary
abstract: Five Democratic candidates are running in the 4th District primary for the right to represent their party in the November general election. The key topic in this primary would be US Rep. Eugene Atkinson's switch from the Democratic party and embracing the policies of the Republicans, lead by Reagan.

headline: New opportunities for Egan
abstract: Joseph Egan is the new executive vice president for the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation.  Editorial outlines Egan's previous work and explains why he is a good choice for this position.

headline: New castle joins in
abstract: New Castle has become the fifth city in Pennsylvania to adopt  a land tax which is higher for lands than for buildings. It is a strategy aimed at encouraging the development or re-development of urban areas.

headline: Prison Guard Kills 13 In Pennsylvania Spree
abstract: George Banks, a prison guard at the Camp Hill state correctional institute, went on a shooting spree in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania.  In all, the rampage left 13 people dead, five of whom were Banks' children.  After a six-hour standoff with police, Banks surrendered to PA state police.

headline: NAACP head protests warden's 'racial slur'
abstract: Harvey Adams, president of the local National Association for the Advancment of Colored Persons (NAACP), criticized Western Penitentiary warden George Petsock for a racial slur made in response to a comment that he runs the prison like a plantation.  Petsock said that his quote was not taken out of context but would not respond to the criticisms.  Petsock said that "if he thinks I run this place like a plantation, tell him to come on down and pick some watermelons."  Adams would not comment if the NAACP would ask for Petsock's resignation.

headline: EPA's toxic waste rules: Actions belie the words
abstract: Environmental Protection Agency administrator Anne M. Gorsuch announced the decision to reimpose controls on disposal of liquid hazardous wastes in landfills. However, the author believes that the administrator was not cautious while making this decision because she did not seek advice from state officials and other experts and that the EPA does not have a comprehensive reporting system in place to track hazardous materials.

headline: Drunke-Driver License Plate Foolish
abstract: PA State Senator Vincent Fumo of Philadelphia has come up with an asinine idea-a special license plate for drunk drivers.  His idea is to hold drunk drivers up to public ridicule by the issuance of this red tag, and it would also warn other motorists to stay out of their way.

headline: Misplaced priorities
abstract: The good news is that overburdened Bucks county courts will soon be getting some needed relief. In particular, the court is in need for tip staves and minute clerks.

headline: Pension Regulations Hit by State Panel
abstract: Dale D. Stone has faced mountains of costly paperwork in complying with the Federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974.  Specific items of reporting and disclosures would be required of every state and municipal pension plan.  There would be minimum detail and duration standards for plan record-keeping.  It also requires the establishment of a claims procedure for use in the event of a denial of benefits.

headline: Attorney Named To Head Group For Casey Funds
abstract: Robert J. Trace was named as Chairman, and John Durbin as Treasurer, of the Better Citizens Committee (BCC) a political action committee (PAC)  created to replace the one formed to raise funds for the late Robert E. Casey's PA State Treasurer reelection campaign. The BCC was formed on October 20, 1981, after Casey's reelection committee was disbanded (any remaining funds the reelection committee had were transferred to the BCC at the same time). Durbin stated that the goal of the BCC was to spend money as a PAC, although specific candidates, political parties, or political philosophies that would be funded were not specified.

headline: New remap suits filed; Democratic senators call plan unfair
abstract: Two new lawsuits have been filed in US Middle District Court, seeking to prevent the congressional reappointment plan which Governor Thornburgh signed on Wednesday, from going into force for the May 18 primary elections.

headline: No tax hikes seen in '83 city budget
abstract: Mayor Green will present a $1.3 billion budget for fiscal 1983 that calls for no new taxes, no layoffs and no pay raises for city workers. The increase from the previous budget of $1.2 billion will be met by a projected growth in real-estate assessments of 3 percent, an anticipated growth in revenues from the city's wage tax of 6 percent and the restoration of $46.3 million in state funding.

headline: Some anti-crime bills go too far
abstract: While mandatory sentencing and get-tough-on-crime approaches to deterrence are sometimes appropriate responses to violent crime, singling out crimes against certain classes of victims--as legislation currently under consideration in the state House and Senate does--represents a step in the wrong direction.  The legislation under consideration would require minimum jail sentences for those commiting certain violent crimes against persons over the age of 60 and under the age of 16.

headline: New responsibilities for blacks
abstract: Opinion: Black people must now work harder than ever to be in the American mainstream.  The writer is not sure how this will be accomplished given that voter registration figures in black neighborhoods are so low.  The writer believes that this has also allowed anti-black policies to occur since politicians perceive no political risk.

headline: Exhausted appeal
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency indicated that it will withhold more than $500,000 designated for other air-pollution control efforts in Pennsylvania, as a reprisal for the state's obstructionism on emission inspections. The state also lost $302 million in federal highway revenue due to differences between the state and the federal government.

headline: Editorial: The Long Run
abstract: This editorial talked about putting emphasis on the long term solutions to drunk driving.  Pennsylvania needs to adopt a similar program to that of Maine.  Maine levies a drunk driving tax on alocholic beverages.  In turn this money is used for an anti-drunk driving campaign that uses preventive, educational, treatment, and resarech programs to help prevent drunk driving.

headline: Montco Judge May Get Post as U.S. Attorney
abstract: The U.S. Justice Department is preparing to nominate Montgomery County Common Pleas Judge Anthony Scirica to be U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.  Philadelphia Family Court Judge Paul Dandridge was not being considered for the job as Chief Federal Prosecutor for Philadelphia and nine other southeastern Pennsylvania counties.  All appointments to the U.S. attorney positions are made by the President and must be approved by the Senate.  U.S. attorneys have more control over what types of crimes can be prosecuted.

headline: Perper Rips County Chiefs On Cutback at Morgue
abstract: Though it is true, that under Pennsylvania law, the elected coroner of Allegheny Court is not required to have any qualifications, it is a fact that speaks well of our voters that in the past 16 years they have consistently elected well qualified professionals to the office.  Judge Nicholas Papadakos has recognized that presently and in the recent past the office was run in all but name as a modern medical examiners office for the benefit of our citizens.

headline: Average '81 Salary $15,691
abstract: The Bureau of Labor Statistics announced that preliminary data indicated nationwide average annual pay was nine percent higher in nineteen eighty-one than in nineteen eighty. The figure for Pennsylvania was over eight percent however. The rest of the article lists rates of pay increases for all fifty states.

headline: No room at the Capitol
abstract: In this letter to the editor the author complained about the lack of parking around the Capitol building in Harrisburg, and the lines once he got into the Bureau of Motor Vehicles.

headline: One fight in Primary: Wecht-Logue; Little opposition for major candidates
abstract: The May 18 ballot has currently six candidates who are leading it. Of these candidates, only County Commissioner Cyril Wecht has an major opposition. Villanova political scientist John Logue is the most serious Democratic rival of Cyril Wecht.

headline: State Agencies' Public Meetings Listed
abstract: This article lists state agencies' public meetings for the week of September 26, 1982.  The article lists legislative meetings in the state House and Senate, as well as meetings for several executive agencies.

headline: Once A Fetus
abstract: Letter observing that in recent discussions of PA's new abortion law that no article, lawmaker, or health service spokesperson has taked about the rights of the unborn child. The author is glad that she never got pregnant when she was younger and pro-choice because she would have chosen an abortion.

headline: For $18,800 Flora and Fauna Board Needs an Aide with Flair
abstract: The state Wild Resources Management Board is looking for a person for publicity on making voluntary contributions to help preserve Pennsylvania’s endangered flora and fauna.  The job pays $18,800 annually, plus generous fringe benefits.  The Department of Environmental Resources is doing the recruiting.  The board was created under legislation for the management of the state’s endangered plants and non-game animals, with funding through a system of voluntary contributions by way of a check-off on refunds due on personal income tax returns.

headline: Emission-test ban may cost state $495 million
abstract: Time is running out to try lifting a ban on the federal auto inspection program before the PA Legislature expires its term. PA Department of Transportation spokesman James McCarron estimated federal funds lost for failure to implement mandatory auto inspections could exceed $459.4 million. The Legislature overrode PA Governor Thornburgh's veto of a bill to bar PennDOT from implementing the program last year. New federal funding loss estimates will be distributed to the Legislature prior to a vote.

headline: Murphy Welcomed
abstract: Erie’s Catholic community welcomes a new leader in Bishop Michael Murphy.  He took over reins from retiring Bishop Alfred M. Watson.  He inherits dioceses strong in religious faith and beset with economic problems familiar to both religious and lay areas alike.

headline: Phila. Exchange head puts stock in Reagan plan to shift controls
abstract: The Philadelphia business community gave President Ronald Reagan high marks with his plan to turn control of over 40 federal programs over to the states.  They also note that the President did not hide from the fact that there will be a high federal deficit, and was not sure how the stock market would react to that.  States could then choose which programs to fund and which ones to let go.

headline: Baker, in York, offers insight on White House
abstract: James Baker, White House Chief of Staff, said that he had urged President Ronald Reagan to propose limits on excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco, but was overruled because he didn't want to appear to be backtracking on his tax program.  Protesters were waiting outside the York Hotel for Baker, but there were no incidents.

headline: No-Fault
abstract: In this letter to the editor, Doug Arthur is responding to the editorial, "Gutting no-fault for profit."  He was a strong proponent for no-fault in the early 1970s knowing full well that the rising cost of bodily injury coverage could be blunted and more benefits in the form of lost wages, medical expense, etc., could be paid persons injured.  Unfortunately, the no-fault act passed bore little resemblance to that which was being advocated.

headline: Other cities tapping suburbanites
abstract: Pittsburgh does not have the ability to tap suburban revenues by the imposition of a sales tax or an income tax, resulting in higher-than-average real estate taxes for city residents.  Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri is asserting that because of this, Pittsburgh residents assume a disproportionate amount of the bill to provide safety and public services for the thousands of people who come to work in the City but live outside of it.

headline: Heinz Opposes Speedup of Natural Gas Decontrol
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz said he is opposed to attempts by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to speed up the decontrol of natural gas.  Senator Heinz claims that accelerating the process of decontrol could cost up to 1 million jobs across the country.

headline: Our Opinion: Veto Abortion Bill
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh would do the state a favor by vetoing the anti-abortion bill that was passed by the General Assembly.  He has until June 19th to sign it or veto it.  The bill automatically becomes law if he fails to do anything by that date.

headline: Fumes Hope
abstract: PA Representative Samuel Hayes said an emissions inspection program can be passed if it is separated from the reduction of commuter wage taxes. The PA Senate voted twice in its November lame-duck session against the program, putting almost three hundred million dollars in federal highway funding at risk.  Failure to pass it left the state in noncompliance of a 1978 consent decree signed by then Governor Milton Shapp with the U.S. government and a Philadelphia environmental group. Although Governor Thornburgh opposes the program, three Philadelphia lawmakers said they would support it. This is expected to be enough to ensure passage in the next session.

headline: Excess Land Could be Bonanza for Airport
abstract: Greater Pittsburgh International Airport is land-rich.  It has so much land it doesn’t need for present and proposed airport operations that the potential exists to make millions of dollars annually from acres that are fallow.  It will take the governor’s signature on a key piece of legislation before the airport can begin reaping its profit.  A number of other complex issues must be settled before the bonanza which may shape the future development of Western Allegheny County can begin.

headline: New Gun Law
abstract: The mandatory sentencing law for any criminal using a gun went into affect on June 6.  It will be an automatic 5 years in jail.  The first step toward deterrence is getting the word on the street.  Senator Mike O’Pake is taking care of that with a sweep across the state sponsored by the Pennsylvania Committee for Effective Justice.  He is trying to raise $100,000 by the end of the year to finance a public education program.  The second step is to get the word to the criminal underworld.  The third development will take place in court because more than likely the law will be challenged.  The final step is to provide enough jail space to handle the anticipated impact of the new law.

headline: Photo
abstract: A group photo of the six winners of a nine million dollar lottery jackpot with their first checks.

headline: Balancing Act; Reconciling concerns of environmentalists, industry is Penna. official's goal
abstract: This picture shows Peter S. Duncan, State Secretary of Environmental Resources, who has added support from the business community to his impeccable environmentalist credentials.

headline: Now Read This
abstract: Governor Thornburgh and Mayor Caliguiri have declared Wednesday as Literacy Day in both Pennsylvania and Pittsburgh.  The day is intended to call attention to the estimated 800 million people, 125,000 in Allegheny County, who have not mastered basic reading and writing skills.

headline: Oust-Atkinson drive uniting area democrats
abstract: State Rep. Joseph Kolter and attorney Peter Steege, both of Beaver County, have emerged as the leading contenders for consensus support in the Democratic effort to evict Republican convert Eugene Atkinson from Congress.

headline: Fox Chapel's 62,585 Leads County Income
abstract: With a median family income of 62,585, Fox Chapel has been reaffirmed as the blue-chip capital of Allegheny County.

headline: Pa. Senate Approves Abortion Bill
abstract: The PA State Senate approved a controversial abortion control bill.  The bill had already passed the House.  Now it goes to Governor Dick Thornburgh.  He vetoed a similar bill in December, but sponsors of the bill feel as though he will sign it.

headline: Gap Grow in Funds for Coal-Mine Reclamation
abstract: The first half of 1982 saw 939 acres of coal-mined land abandoned in Pennsylvania.  This left the state with a $5 million reclamation job and $1.4 million to get it done.  The figures came from the state Environmental Resources Secretary Peter Duncan, who testified before a Senate subcommittee looking into ways to close the growing gap between available and needed reclamation funds.  If Pennsylvania does not raise enough money to meet its reclamation commitments, it could lose control of the coal industry.  The Department of Environmental Resources could reduce costs by enforcing its concurrent backfilling requirement; making it easier and more profitable for reliable companies to mine and reclaim abandoned sites; and requiring small, new mine operators to put up higher bonds.

headline: Expensive, But Worth It
abstract: The renovations to Harrisburg's busiest bridge, the South Bridge, were completed well ahead of schedule. Unfortunately, as the second most expesive project of its kind in PA history it suggest that future renovation projects will have to be done more selectively and the construction of future highways will need to take future traffic flow and renovation into account.

headline: New Jail: Humane Treatment or Luxury
abstract: The proposed new County Jail would be a $116 million, 44-story skyscraper with all the modern conveniences.  One member of the prison board, Monsignor Charles Owen Rice, is against the stashing of offenders in spotless new high-rise quarters for the wrong reason entirely.  He contends it would be inhumane.  Putting prisoners in a jail that is sterile and automated would limit their association with human beings.  They would not have human contact with the guards.  A new jail is needed because the old is overcrowded now and will be still more overcrowded in years to come.

headline: Photo
abstract: A photo of death row inmate Charles Lee.

headline: Ballet Battle: Barbara Weisberger Tells Her Side of the Story
abstract: Barbara Weisberger, the Pennsylvania Ballet found and former director, said she kept quiet long enough about what happened to her at the Pennsylvania Ballet.  Her departure was a result of a power struggle complete with emotional confrontations and secret meetings.  At stake was control of Pennsylvania Ballet, which under Weisberger’s leadership reached artistic highs and financial lows.  Charles H. Rannells, who was the general manager and board president as well as board chairman David W. Brenner were all key players.

headline: Number of Jobs in State Continues to Drop
abstract: During the second quarter of 1982, Pennsylvania lost 91,000 jobs, the largest quarterly decline in the 13 years that the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has measured employment in the sate.  In Philadelphia alone 21,000 jobs were lost in the second quarter.

headline: Overcome partisanship
abstract: Mayor A.E. O'Block of Plum Borough has been vetoing every Republican-backed measure that he has been given, including a new police contract.  Are these actions really helping the community?  His actions seem to be polarizing the area.

headline: Sole survivor critical; stories on men differ
abstract: Neighbors of George Banks, the former Camp-Hill prison guard who killed 13 people, gave conflicting accounts of why Banks shot James Olsen and Raymond Hall.

headline: Pennsylvania Council of Republican Women
abstract: PA Council for Republican Women commends Governor Dick Thornburgh for vetoing the PA Abortion Control Act.

headline: Gypsy moth wings west, California braces for battle
abstract: The gypsy moth has already devoured more than 13 million acres of land from Maine to Michigan, and has now turned up in California.  The moths may attack California's fruit trees, which are a part of its $3 billion per year agricultural industry.  Aerial spraying of pesticides will be used.

headline: Fewer inspections, more problems
abstract: The author believes that there are more cars today with defective headlights than ever before. Hence, by cutting the number of inspections down from two to one, would only exacerbate the current situation.

headline: New Sentences for Crimes to Build Pressure
abstract: A 15-member panel of judges, legislators and lawyers, put together Pennsylvania’s new prison sentencing guidelines.  The guidelines were approved by the Legislature earlier in the year but just went into effect.  Some of the guidelines have already lost their punch because of Governor Dick Thornburgh’s tougher anticrime legislation that last month set mandatory sentences for criminals who use firearms.

headline: Photo
abstract: A photo of Governor Thornburgh delivering his Christmas message in the Capitol Rotunda.

headline: Beaver County judge named
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has nominated Beaver County attorney Robert E. Kunselman to fill a vacancy on the Beaver County Common Pleas Court.

headline: O'Brien's State House Victory is Certified
abstract: The City Commissioners certified Republican Dennis M. O’Brien as the winner in his tight bitter election battle with Democratic incumbent John J. Swaim in the 169th state House District.  The official margin was 61 votes.  The 169th District, located in Northeast Philadelphia, includes parts of the 57th and 66th Wards.  Other election results were also given.

headline: Paul J. Angstadt; Remember '80 run
abstract: Paul J. Angstadt, who unsuccessfully challenged Sen. Michael A. O'Pake for the 11th Senatorial District seat in 1980, is hoping that voters will remember his name and platform when they go to polls this time. Angstadt considers tax reform, education, jobs and farming to be the main campaign issues this time.

headline: Banks Talked of Suicide
abstract: A spokesperson for Governor Thornburgh said that George Banks, the man accused of killing 13 people in Wilkes-Barre, was placed on leave from the state correctional institution at Camp Hill after threatening to shoot himself while he was on duty.  After the incident, Banks received psychiatric treatment and expressed an interest in returning to work.  But before Banks could undergo analysis to determine if he was fit to return to work, he committed the mass murder.

headline: Philadelphia's 6 plantation wards
abstract: A US Department of Justice investigation into the voting practices in Philadelphia have found out that from the 10 previously elections, there has been a consistently lower black turnout that their registration.

headline: Gypsy-Moth Spraying in '83 to cost $30,000
abstract: Duayne A. Forsberg, a resource specialist with the conservation district, told county commissioners in Dauphin County that infested acreage is increasing in the country and an estimated 10,000 acres may need spraying next spring for gypsy-moths.  The state would pick up 75 percent of the tab but that will still mean the county and local municipalities will have to come up with $30,000.

headline: Fix the crossing, and bicker later
abstract: Editorial: Conrail's delaying in fixing a dangerous crossing in Pittston Township is unacceptable.  In 1979, the PA Public Utilities Commission ordered Conrail to install the safety equipment, with money to be provided by the PA Department of Transportation and Pottstown Township.  Conrail contends that the work must be put off to bring its other projects into conformity with the new Federal Highway Safety Act.

headline: Nix is Called to Testify at Justice Larsen Hearing
abstract: Supreme Court Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. was called as a prosecution witness to testify about his high-court colleague, Rolf R. Larsen.  Larsen is accused of violating the judicial code of ethnics by engaging in politics.  One of the key charges is that Larsen attempted to prevent Nix’ from being re-elected to a second 10-year term on the bench.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of U.S. Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis with U.S. Senators Dole and Long.

headline: Benefits for Felons, But Not Workers
abstract: Henry Cianfrani and Robert Bellomini, both former state officials who engaged in criminal acts while working for the State of Pennsylvania, were eligible for state pensions as a result of a Supreme Court decision.  They are also eligible for health insurance through the state.  This is interesting to several thousand retired state employees who do not receive such a benefit.

headline: O'Connell to offer third remap plan
abstract: The PA House of Representatives passed a completed reapportionment plan of its own on to the PA Senate, but it will wait there for a third plan to be introduced by PA Senator Frank O'Connell.  A conference committee will work out a final version of the senate plan.  Senator O'Connell has already tried to pass two earlier plans.

headline: Phila. Firing auditor who charged tax fix
abstract: A Philadelphia city auditor, Charles P. Elliot, who has made allegations of corruption in the City Revenue Department is being fired by Revenue Commissioner Eugene L. Cliett Jr.  Elliot has passed a lie detector test, but was fired on grounds of unauthorized release of confidential tax information to The Bulletin.

headline: He pulled the trigger before
abstract: This opinion piece questions public policies that allow ex-convicts, such as George Banks, to obtain firearms.  This is a policy that is in need of review and possibly reform.  Banks is accused of killing 13 people.

headline: Photo: Coretta Scott King and Atlanta Mayor Andrew Young march yesterday to mark the birthday of Martin Luther King Jr.
abstract: null

headline: Heinz bill to seek utility payments for TMI
abstract: Sen. John Heinz will introduce legislation to help finance the Three Mile Island (TMI) cleanup, hoping to gain more support than have proponents of other, similar bills in Congress, during the past two years. The measure would require the nation's largest electric utilities to pay fees totaling $192 million for the decontamination of the TMI Unit 2 nuclear plant.

headline: Forward on boating safety
abstract: A bill recently introduced by PA Senator Roy Wilt (R-Meadville), SB 82, calls for a study by the PA Senate Fish and Game Commmittee as to whether operators of motor boats should have formal training before being allowed to use them.  In light of the numerous accidents on the rivers, this bill should be passed.

headline: No charges in taping incident
abstract: District Attorney Edward G. Rendell yesterday said he would not prosecute anyone for December's Christmas Tree Bugging Case. He, however, criticized aides to Mayor Green, saying that they had lied about the incident to the news media.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photos of new U.S. Representatives from PA Tom Ridge and Joseph Kolter.

headline: Bid Denied for Election of 3 Judges
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has rejected a request by the president judge of Commonwealth Court to allow the election of three new judges on November 1st.  There are now two vacancies on the state’s third highest court, and a third will occur next June.  Justice Samuel Roberts said in a unanimous decision that Judge James Crumlish’s request be denied because he failed to pursue other available remedies such as asking for appointment of temporary extra judges.  Governor Thornburgh’s nominations to fill the current vacancies have not yet been confirmed by the state Senate.

headline: Other Opinions: Giving the Governor His Own Appointees
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has been thwarted in his efforts to name new members to fill openings on both the Turnpike Commission and Liquor Control Board since taking office.  The governor should have the opportunity to name his own appointees to these.  The Governor’s frustration results from the requirement that a 2/3 majority vote of the Senate is necessary in order to confirm members to the boards.  There is a bill pending in the Senate that would reduce the required 2/3 to a simple majority.

headline: Philadelphia's future - Your responses
abstract: In response to the bill that reduces the wage tax paid by suburbanites who work in Philadelphia, the responses obtained by this station were evenly divided between those who supported it and those who did not.

headline: State bankers' minuet
abstract: This editorial argues that statewide financial deregulation, signed into law seven months ago by Governor Thornburgh, has provided at least one positive result: Bankers have the ability to mobilize resources from disparate sources.  This newfound ability will make Pennsylvania Bankers competitive players in U.S. money markets.

headline: Planned parenthood vows to defy notification rule
abstract: Officials at Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania said yesterday that they would sacrifice an annual federal subsidy of $300,000 rather than comply with an impending federal rule requiring them to notify parents of teenagers who request birth-control prescriptions.

headline: House passes bill on toxic wastes
abstract: The PA House passed legislation to extend "good Samaritan" status to companies which voluntarily help clean up another company's hazardous waste. Good Samaritan status grants the company legal immunity. The legislation was backed by the PA Department of Environmental Resources and the PA Emergency Management Agency as well as a number of industry advocates. PA Rep. Robert O'Donnell did not support the legislation, claiming it excused all parties involved from responsibility.

headline: From Pa. to SEPTA, $4.5 million
abstract: The Southeast Pennsylvania Transit Authority (SEPTA) now has sufficient funding to keep the commuter trains running through the end of the year, according to a recent announcement by Governor Dick Thornburgh.  This money will allow the trains to continue running until January 1, 1983, when Conrail will no longer operate the trains.

headline: No Pay
abstract: Pittsburgh City Magistrate Joe James wants to arrest people who come before the city court, get fined and later forget to pay the fine. Although the amount to be collected is not large, ridiculing the law leads to the break down of respect for the law.

headline: Photo
abstract: Picture of U.S. Representatives Joseph Addabbo and Jack Edwards before a vote on MX missile funding.

headline: Bill gives final word on death
abstract: The State Senate passed legislation yesterday that for the first time would put a definition of death on Pennsylvania's law books. A person can now be declared legally dead if his blood flow and lungs were irreversibly stopped or all brain function ceased.

headline: Other parties should be considered
abstract: The impasses between Governor Thornburgh and the Legislature concerning appointments to the Turnpike Commission has a precedent in Kansas, where mutually acceptable appointees were selected. The same thing can be done in this situation as well.

headline: Pittsburgh City Council furnishings
abstract: Letter to the editor written in response to an earlier editorial by KDKA criticizing the lavish furnishings of Pittsburgh City Council:  Councilwoman Michelle Madoff would prefer that KDKA criticize her on the issues, not about the plants in her office.

headline: Experts differ on the election
abstract: As the 1982 midterm elections near, it is ultimately unclear how the November 2nd elections will impact President Reagan.  Many experts believe that traditional off-year congressional seat losses will be at historic lows; even if they are not at historic lows, some say that the president may not be blamed for the losses.

headline: Pro-lifers, Governor seek abortion accord
abstract: Pro-life members of the PA House came away from a meeting with the governor with a promise that Governor Dick Thornburgh will assist in their effort to draft new abortion-control legislation.

headline: In Pa., Rank Has no Privilege to Fish for Free
abstract: Most people wear their fishing licenses on their hats, but Ralph W. Abele, executive director of the Pennsylvania Fish Commission and one of the state’s foremost conservationists, wears his on his sleeve.  Abele traditionally issues the state’s fishing license No. 1 to the president of the United States.  But he has been somewhat irregular about passing out the free licenses to President Reagan.  Reagan was issued the special complimentary license in 1981, shortly after he took office, but has not been issued a 1982 Pennsylvania fishing license.  The licenses are valid for a year.  Abele, a lifelong Republican, has not explained why he has failed to send a license to Reagan.  But some close associates of Abele speculated that it probably had something to do with actions by Reagan appointees in some top environmental posts.

headline: Gas-station independents fighting to preserve role
abstract: The number of independent, full-service gas stations have decreased by 5000 in the last ten years. However, there has been an increase in company-owned, self-serviced stations due to the lesser number of overheads. Hence, it is becoming increasingly difficult for the former stations to continue in business, and hence, the owners association is currently fighting for a change in the legislation, that will prohibit oil companies from retail gasoline sales.

headline: One White Hill escapee caught
abstract: Victor Hare, who had escaped from Camp Hill State Correctional Institution, was captured on Gale Street in Mechanicsburg, PA.  Convicted murderer  Michael Lauver had also escaped and is still at large.  Story outlines Victor Hare's path to prison and the details of his escape.

headline: Picking up where the Bulletin left off
abstract: This article discusses the effects of the closing of The Bulletin newspaper on the Philadelphia area, with its primary focus on how advertisers will change and adapt their advertising patterns and an examination of the ways that other newspapers will try to fill the gap.

headline: Bill increases court judges
abstract: The PA House authorized an increase in the number of PA Commonwealth Court Justices from 9 to 11. The proposal awaits confirmation by the Senate before PA Governor Thornburgh can appoint two Justices to fill the newly created seats. Currently, only seven of nine seats are filled. The Commonwealth Court is responsible for civil suits and appeals involving state and local government agencies, including election law violations.

headline: Our ideas; The Economic revolt continues
abstract: Despite a majority of the people in the country responding negatively to several polls asking questions about the president's popularity, a recent survey indicated that four out of five Lancastrians still strongly favor President Reagan's economic program.

headline: Porn shop limit bill nears ok
abstract: A bill designed to limit the number of places where pornographic bookstores could be setup, is expected to receive tentative approval from City Council. The only major question was whether the council would set even stiffer standards for the location of suck bookstores than required by the bill.

headline: ROAD SIGN UPDATE
abstract: This editorial discusses the problem of confusing road signs in and around Philadelphia.  The author lists problem spots, which were determined with citizen input, and pledges to work with Philadelphians to find solutions to these problem spots.

headline: Public schools should not be vendors of contraceptives
abstract: Recently, Philadelphia's Health Commissioner, Dr. Stuart Shapiro, has said that the city's public schools ought to distribute birth control devices. However, by doing this, it would only insult young people and offend parents.

headline: Is Mother Nature going berserk?
abstract: A spat of unusual weather and natural disasters such as earthquakes and volcano eruptions have prompted scientists to wonder if this is part of a larger trend in the Earth's climate.  Article talks about potential causes for shifts in weather patters and geologica instability.

headline: Getting drunks off the highway
abstract: In this opinion piece, the author talks about the dramatization of certain topics by newspapers.  Article cites the little-heard 342 people who died in traffic accidents over the New Year's weekend, but that everyone knows about the 78 people that died in a recent plane crash.  To that end, the fact that there are 51,000 traffic deaths per year in the U.S. and that half are caused by drunk drivers has also become mundane news.  New state programs are finally starting to consider the impact of drunk driving more than they had before.

headline: Opposes immunity for state's judges
abstract: The author believes that the idea of "judicial immunity" in current Pennsylvania law is too broad and subject to abuse. Although judges need a certain amount of independence to act without fear or favor, some balance needs to be achieved by a new statue, that provides equal justice for all.

headline: Picture
abstract: This picture shows Governor Thornburgh and US Se. Arlen Specter outline the state's Gypsy Moth Battle Plan.

headline: Bit player standsto put districting back on express
abstract: A novel lawsuit filed by Wayne Long in Pittsburgh may be helping to do the most to push legislative redistricting along.  Mr. Long's suit claims that by not finishing redistricting sooner, his rights are being violated by the delay since he will not have adequate time to find out what his district will be and whom his representative will be.  A hearing is set for Monday, and if the judge finds in favor, reapportionment may be taken completely away from the Senate.

headline: Our Opinion: Now is Country's Time to Clean up Pittston
abstract: The Luzerne County commissioners cannot allow County Registration Director Thomas Pizano to slide out of his responsibility to clean up the county’s voting rolls.  The integrity of the Nov. 2 election must be assured, and it is the commissioners who must insist that Pizano begin a clean-up of the rolls immediately.

headline: Profiles in sleaze
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Senate is considering whether to go in for a bill that would give a tax break to Philadelphia commuters. However, as there is a tie in the number of votes, the decision lies in the hands of Senator Street, who believes this control shows his political acumen. However, the editorial believes that the Senator should do something constructive.

headline: MCKEESPORT BUS
abstract: Since Mckeesport High School students do not have transportation to school, we suggest that a compromise be struck between the school district and parents.  It is clear that the district cannot afford to pay the full costs of transportation, and it is also clear that busing is needed for some students; the parents and school district should share the cost.

headline: Second Domino
abstract: This letter states that in the 1970's, killing of life in the womb was legalized; in the 1980's killing of newborn kids who were not 'perfect' has been legalized. What will happen in the future?

headline: Killed
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate killed for this session a bill that would authorize a court-mandated auto emissions inspection system.

headline: Good News About Highways
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh made an announcement at the Pennsylvania AAA Federation in Hershey that the state plans to contract for more than $750 million worth of work this year.  It will involve more than 700 projects.  There will be more than 5,000 miles of roadway improvement, as well as road and bridge construction.  Pennsylvania taxpayers have had to endure driving on road surfaces which are an absolute disgrace, not to mention life-threatening.  The reforms at PennDOT during the present administration have helped straighten out the mess.  Management appears to be more efficient, patronage abuse in the filling of PennDOT jobs has been banned, and since the appointment of an inspector general, a policy of suspension and dismissal of wrongdoers has been implemented.

headline: Oral Hygienist Appeal Heard
abstract: The PA Commonwealth Courts heard arguments yesterday concerning Susan Edwards, an oral hygienist whose license was revoked for failure to practice under the supervision of a dentist. Edwards was found in contempt in November 1981 for failure to adhere to the law. Edwards appealed that the PA Dental Council and Examining Board violated her rights when it revoked her license.

headline: Picture
abstract: This picture shows the State Police Trooper Dick Giniewski, checking out new aircraft purchased for the state police. The planes will join the 7 helicopters to form the State Police Aviation Division.

headline: Biting the bullet at Sun Ship
abstract: The recent contract accepted by members of the Local 802 International Brotherhood of Boilermakers cleared the way for the purchase of Sun Ship and have given it a chance to be profitable again.  The loss in employment at the shipyard was due to a general decline in shipbuilding.

headline: Ousted by his Own, Schaeffer Seeks Shelter in GOP
abstract: Berks County Judge Forrest G. Schaeffer won the Republican nomination for Pennsylvania Supreme Court in May, but it’s still unclear whether or not the GOP organization will formally welcome him aboard the statewide ticket for the November campaign.  Schaeffer is a Democrat.  Several candidates in recent years have won both party nominations for a judgeship on the state appellate courts, in the cross-filed process permitted for judicial candidates.  This feat amounts to a sure election in November.  Schaeffer is the first to win the other party’s nomination without winning his own party.  However until Schaeffer is endorsed by the Republican State Committee, he isn’t part of the team and is not to be presented at full-ticket appearances of the candidates at GOP rallies or other campaign literature issued by the state committee.  It is difficult to say whether or not the state committee will welcome him.

headline: Progress on the hotel tax
abstract: The Philadelphia hotel tax is one of the few taxes that is actually vital for the tourism sector of the city. Revenues raised would directly go in promoting the city. Similar taxes at other cities have been very beneficial.

headline: Nursing Homes Need $$
abstract: President of the state commissioners' association, Ted Simon, has called for a moratorium on nursing-home reimbursements.  If the General Assembly answers the call of Simon, the state will have to raise taxes to subsidize nursing homes throughout the state.

headline: Rev vows to follow the straight and narrow
abstract: Philadelphia fundamentalist minister B. Samuel Hart says that his strong anti-homosexual feelings should not affect his nomination to the US Civil Rights Commission.  His nomination by President Ronald Reagan is being vigorously opposed by gay rights groups, feminists, and some civil rights activists.

headline: Last-minute bills doomed to die in state legislature
abstract: Several Philadelphia-area state legislators introduced legislation in the remaining weeks of Congress knowing it will not pass. Bills concerning public utilities and automobiles will raise public awareness and test the legislature's response, PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf admitted. Proposals included Senate Bill 1608 to establish a radioactive protection program in the PA Department of Resources, Senate Bill 1615 and 1617 concerning public utilities, and Senate bills 1695 and 1614 concerning "lemon" cars and false odometer reading.

headline: Governor fields varied questions by Arco workers
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has held out hope but made no promises that the unfinished 16-mile stretch of the Beaver Valley Expressway will be completed in this decade. He also said that the state relies on federal funding for over 50% of the construction costs, and that this would be very expensive at a time of high interest rates.

headline: Our Opinion: Stout Sentencing Seems to Lenient
abstract: Chester Stout, a convicted child abuser was sentenced last week to spend 2 ˝ to 5 years in jail for severely beating his son.  The sentence was given by Luzerne County Judge Patrick Toole.  It seems too lenient when one considers that he might be free on probation in six months.

headline: Political Storm Brewing Over Fed Policy
abstract: Jack Kemp and Ted Kennedy don’t agree on many things.  But when the conservative Republican from Buffalo and the liberal Democrat from Boston start to sound the same note, you can safely conclude that the whole political orchestra will soon be playing that tune.  Kemp voted against the Republican budget, which was backed by President Ronald Reagan.  He objects to the $20 billion in tax increases in the GOP budget-which he says will jeopardize the chances of an economic recovery and “hurt the working people who ought to be our constituents.”  He also believes there will be no real economic recovery unless and until the administration tackles the fundamental crisis in monetary policy.  Kennedy also lashed out at the Federal Reserve.

headline: Black Republican unit elects Woman of Area
abstract: LeGree Daniels of Susquehanna has been elected chairman of the National Black Republican Council.  In her new role, she will serve as an ex-officio member of the Republican National Committee's executive committee.  She has been deputy chairman of the Pennsylvania Republican Committee.

headline: Pa. Senators Don't Care?
abstract: Senators Heinz and Specter have voted for a budget that President Reagan favors.  The three of them want to cut into programs that eat into the very health and welfare of our lowest income people.

headline: Refused
abstract: The Philadelphia Council of Neighborhood Organizations (PCNO) wrote Mayor Green a letter, sent it by certified mail, and it was refused.  This group stumbled onto the little-known policy that certified mail can only be accepted by the person to whom it is addressed, meaning the mayor's staffers cannot take the mail.

headline: Not to Open Mine Exhibit Unthinkable
abstract: The model Anthracite mine at McDade Park is an excellent tourist attraction that could help increase tourism.  Questions over who will operate the mine, which is scheduled to open next spring, put the future of the mine in jeopardy, however.  This opinion piece suggests getting the Chamber of Commerce, industrial-development agencies, and federal and state legislators together to discuss the problem and to find a solution.

headline: Rights nominee yields: Under pressure, Hart withdraws
abstract: Reverend B. Samuel Hart and President Ronald Reagan agreed to withdraw Hart's nomination to the US Civil Rights Commission as pressure mounted on recent news that he had failed to repay more than $50,000 in state and federally-guaranteed loans.  Civil rights groups attacked his nomination originally, saying that he lacked a civil rights background and attacked his opposition to the Equal Rights Amendment, equality for homosexuals and strong federal enfocement of civil rights laws.

headline: Legislature Refuses to Yield in Opposing Auto-Emission Tests
abstract: The General Assembly has refused to back down on its opposition to annual auto-emission inspections, and GOP leaders say the state will now pay the price, which is a loss of at least $83 million in federal road aid.  The bill would have allowed the State Transportation Department to implement the anti-pollution emission tests in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and Allentown areas died along the 1981-82 legislative session.  Governor Dick Thornburgh and Republican legislative leaders said the bill was necessary to comply with federal court orders to set up the emission-inspection program in 12 urban counties.

headline: Had Pushed for Panel: Altoona Legislator Heads Rail Commission
abstract: High Speed Intercity Rail Commission named State Representative Richard A. Geist the chairman of a nine-member panel whose job is to study the feasibility of building a new cross-state passenger super-railroad which could operate at speeds of 150 mph or more, linking Pittsburgh and Philadelphia in two to 2 ˝ hours.  Act 144, was signed by Governor Dick Thornburgh that created the commission and gave it $850,000 to start with.

headline: Overcrowded Prisons II
abstract: This radio editorial discusses the effects of prison overcrowding on the general public.  Prosecutors contend that some judges are reluctant to sentence prisoners to jails that are overcrowded, meaning that the prisoners stay on the street instead of in jail.  Also, overcrowding taxes space in prisons used for rehabilitation, meaning if any is even offered, inmates are not getting the most and best instruction they could.

headline: Politics: Does Harold Stassen know about him?
abstract: Alvin Joseph Jacobson, for the third time, is seeking governorship of the State of Pennsylvania. In 1974, he came second behind Drew Lewis in the Republican primary. In the past races, he has supported strange laws including a requirement that all state doctors must have M.D degrees.

headline: Black Voices in Harrisburg..Speaker Vows to Open House to People
abstract: State Representative K. Leroy Irvis, after being elected Speaker of the House, vowed that the Democrats will keep the legislative process open and not resort to the Republican tactic of using the power of the majority to dictate.  He is the highest elected Black state legislator in Pennsylvania’s history and one of the highest ranking Blacks in the state government throughout the nation.

headline: Pa. Supreme Court's 3-way race
abstract: The upcoming Democratic primary to nominate a candidate for the PA Supreme Court is being contested by Common Pleas Judge Stephen A. Zappala of Allegheny County and Common Pleas Judge Forrest Schaeffer of Berks County.

headline: Remapping challenge renewed
abstract: US Representative Doug Walgren, D-Pittsburgh, renewed his effort to have the federal court take over drawing district lines for congressional races. This is because, the Democrats believe that the current plan, necessitated by the loss of population in the 1980 census, favors Republicans.

headline: Banks spoke of suicide before spree
abstract: George Banks, the man accused of killing 13 people in Wilkes-Barre, was placed on leave from the state correctional institution at Camp Hill after threatening to shoot himself while he was on duty.  After the incident, Banks received psychiatric treatment and expressed an interest in returning to work.  But before Banks could undergo analysis to determine if he was fit to return to work, he committed the mass murder.

headline: School Prayer: States, Local Districts Waiting for Congressional Action
abstract: As the battle over prayers in public schools shifts to Congress, which is considering a constitutional amendment to permit them, actions on state and local levels have largely subsided.  This doesn’t suggest any lessening of enthusiasm on the part of prayer advocates.  It’s just that efforts on those levels to institute prayer have consistently run into unfavorable court decisions, and the disposition lately has been to await the outcome of congressional debates.

headline: Lock Haven Seeks End to Cleanup
abstract: Lock Haven seeks end to cleanup of chemical waste.  35,000 gallons of chemical waste, 200 tons of sludge and several hundred pounds of toxic gases and explosive compounds were removed by the Environmental Protection Agency.  However, water and soil is still heavily contaminated.

headline: He won, Lost Some as SEPTA Head
abstract: Since Girard diCario arrived at SEPTA, service has greatly improved.  There are hundreds of new buses and trolleys, and more ordered.  The first train made up of new cars is expected to make its debut at the end of the next month.  When he came into office in 1979, SEPTA was spending less than $20 million in capital funds to improve its equipment and facilities, now it will spend $110 million.

headline: Overcrowding at Western Pennitentiary
abstract: Western Pennitentiary is at 123% capacity, and all of the prison's resources are being pushed to the limits.  Article goes through a day in the life of a prisoner and discusses how that life has changed as the prison population grows.

headline: Politics; O'Connell anticipates no major GOP backlash
abstract: Veteran Pennsylvania lawmaker, Senator Frank O'Connell believes that the media is a big part of the current problem and that it plays up the most extreme situations and never points out the positives already present. It also seems straightforward that O'Connell will survive any backlash from the GOP.

headline: Book to Record Year of Building Bridges of Understanding
abstract: In September 1982, a book called, "The Rainbow Connection"will be published.  The publishers are the Building Bridges of Understanding Committee C-Chairmen, Muriel Bezsylko and Karen Frank.  Three copies of the book will be printed.  One will be on display in the Fishing Creek Valley School Library, one will be given to the East Shore Library, and one will be given to Mr. Louis Sheparnias, executive director of the Governor’s Heritage Commission.

headline: Pageant remedy due, attorney general says
abstract: J. Morris Anderson, president of Fashionable Productions, was ordered to return contestant fees from the 1981 Miss Black America Pageant.  Contestants were paying for a trip to Jamaica, but ended up in the Poconos.  Contestants were also given a different scoring guide than the one given to judges.

headline: Rizzo Criticism 'inaccurate,' Green says
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor William Green refuted statements by former Mayor Frank Rizzo.  Mayor Green  identifies each of Rizzo's arguments and rebuts them.

headline: Wilkes-Barre Massacre
abstract: A photograph depicts a man standing in front of a funeral home.  The funeral was for one of the victims of the Wilkes-Barre massacre.

headline: Senate Tackling Abortions
abstract: The state Senate was prepared to take action on compromise legislation designed to discourage women from having abortions.  The House had already passed the measure by a wide margin.  Governor Dick Thornburgh in December vetoed similar legislation but it looks like he is favoring the revised measure.

headline: Mashing the moths
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources is employing an aerial spraying program to kill gypsy moths which have been ravaging trees in the region.

headline: Heavier Trucks isn't Answer
abstract: The final form of the administration’s gas tax, highway improvement proposal and the additional tinkering it has received in Congress are raising doubts in this quarter about the value of the final legislation that is likely to emerge.  The argument made by the trucking industry and its allies that raising truck limits will result in lower costs for consumers.

headline: Overcrowding in prisons grows worse
abstract: Prison officials says overcrowding in PA prisons is at its worst, with convicts being double-celled in record numbers.  The nine state prisons have a design capacity for 8,258 inmates and year-end statistics for 1981 showed 9,145 convicts behind bars - 10.7 percent over the rated capacity.

headline: Poor showing
abstract: The recent poor showing at the ballot boxes should not be attributed to the laziness and apathy of the voters. Instead, one of the causes could be little excitement from the Democratic party and little choice for the Republican voters.

headline: Borski Has Eye Surgery
abstract: State Representative Robert A. Borski Jr., a Democratic congressional candidate, was in good condition after having eye surgery to remove a nail from his right eye.  He was expected to make a full recovery for the fall campaign which was set to begin in September.

headline: Palladino to Fill Vacancy on Court
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh nominated Madaline Palladino to fill a vacancy on Commonwealth Court, a post she previously held until her defeat at the polls last year.  Palladino, a Republican, lost a bid to retain her seat on the state’s lowest appeals court when she was defeated in the November general election by Joseph Ted Doyle.

headline: Rizzo says he'll return to politics, but he won't say how or when
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo said yesterday that he will return to politics, but will not say how or when.  Among other reasons, Mr. Rizzo said that he has been frustrated at the first two years of Philadelphia Mayor Green, noting that the police force is demoralized and that there have been no development plans in Mayor Green's first two years.

headline: Wilkes-Barre Massacre
abstract: In the wake of George Banks' killing spree, Governor Dick Thornburgh expressed concern over a state policy that allows ex-convicts to have jobs that give them access to guns.  A state law forbids ex-convicts from carrying weapons.

headline: South Africa
abstract: South Africa was looking to setup a consulate in Pittsburgh. However, certain civil rights activists believe that South Africa should not be allowed to do so, as they are an openly racist government. However, by not letting South Africa open a consulate here, Pittsburgh will be adopting the same kinds of tactics used in South Africa.

headline: Mine watchdog's ouster stirs state agency fight
abstract: Bob Ging was a lawyer for the PA Department of Environmental Resources, but was fired by the Thornburgh administration because he was not respected or trusted by his superiors.  Ging believes the state thought that he was too strict an enforcer of the law.  As Democratic legislators begin an investigation of the Thornburgh administration's strip-mine control program, Ging's experience has proven valuable.

headline: High-speed rail link is eyed by Amtrak
abstract: Amtrak and a group of private investigators have announced the formation of a new corporation to develop high-speed rail passenger service in several urban corridors. This corporation will develop high-speed services between San Diego and Los Angeles and later, consider routes in Florida, Texas and the Chicago area.

headline: Overseer Named for City Courts: Flaherty gives White Control
