abstract: Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice John P. Flaherty has named James M. White special district administrator of Philadelphia’s court systems, a move that apparently wrests control of the courts, at least temporarily, from local judges.  The position gives White authority over the city’s Common Pleas, Municipal and Traffic Courts.

headline: Poor showing
abstract: Turnout was low in the recent election.

headline: Bucks Development Expert Hired for New Jobs Task Force
abstract: Democratic U.S. Representative elect Peter H. Kostmayer has hired a full-time industrial development expert to help lure jobs to Bucks County, but the idea is drawing skeptical yawns from Republicans already working to attract new companies.  Kostmayer announced the appointment of Alan J. Hedden to a $30,000 a year staff position as executive director of Kostmayer’s Eighth Congressional District Jobs Task Force.

headline: Panel to mull check offs on state tax-refund form
abstract: Supporters of a legislation that would add a check off box to the state personal income tax form (which allows taxpayers to decide how much of their tax refund would go to the new "Wild Resource Conservation Fund"), are trying to persuade Appropriations Chairman Richard Tilghman, to have his committee consider the bill in mid-April, although he still opposes the bill.

headline: Schools overruled on firings
abstract: Commonwealth Court has upheld an arbiter's decision that the Philadelphia school board violated a labor contract two years ago by firing more than 100 tax collectors, many of whom were patronage workers.

headline: Camiel Loses Pike Job--Again
abstract: The state Supreme Court ordered Peter Camiel off the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission.  The decision comes less than a week after the Commonwealth-Court ruled that Governor Thorburgh had to reinstate Camile.  Camile was suspended after he was indicted on charges of padding the state payroll with no-work employees.

headline: Special women's fund to aid 4 state candidates
abstract: Four female House challengers running in the May 18 primary, will be the first beneficiaries of the new Pennsylvania Women's Campaign Fund aimed at electing more women to public office. The group founders believe that of more women are elected to office, it would mean laws that are fairer to women.

headline: Moth assault begins
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources will begin the largest gypsy moth aerial spraying operation in the state's history.

headline: High-speed train idea advances
abstract: State Rep. Rick Geist, R-Altoona, says there is a strong possibility of having high speed trains zipping between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia. A High Speed Rail Commission has been appointed by Gov. Thornburgh to study the feasibility of such a project.

headline: Pa. constables work with little training
abstract: Across the state, there are numerous escapes from state constables, in Erie County alone there are 2-3 per year.  John Seib, President of the State Constables' Association, claims that constables receive no training in handling of prisoners and don't take a backup because they are only paid for one person.

headline: Pressure denounced
abstract: Philadelphia Democratic chairman David Glancey denounced ward leaders, led by outgoing US Congressman Joseph Smith, for planning to ask former City Controller Tom Leonard to step out of the race. The ward leaders on the plan are white, prompting Leonard to call the plan racially motivated and divisive. Ward leaders denied racial motivations, who say Leonard would cause City Managing Director Wilson Goode, who is black, to win. The ward leaders favor former mayor Frank Rizzo in the race.

headline: Budget problems may be much worse
abstract: A new idea gaining influence around the country is the drive to adopt a Constitutional Amendment requiring the federal budget to have a balanced budget.  In 1977, Harrisburg adopted a resolution calling for a Constitutional Convention on just that subject, in conjunction with 30 other states who have done so throughout the past five years.  If three more do so, Congress will be required to respond.

headline: Parkway
abstract: The Parkway East in Pittsburgh is up for reconstruction for the next 7 months and cannot be done smoothly without cooperation from citizens.

headline: She wants PHA seat. Not insults
abstract: Peggie Jones, president of the Mantua Scattered Sites Coalition, says she is insulted by a statement attributed to Mayor Green that appointing a tenant to the Philadelphia Housing Authority (PHA) board would be like appointing a student to the Board of Education. However, a source said that the mayor was looking for someone with housing, finance and management to fill the vacant position.

headline: Lewis Clears Road Funding
abstract: Despite a judicial freeze ordered by U.S. District Court Judge Lewis Bechtle, the U.S. Department of Transportation approved 82 million dollars in federal funds for two Pennsylvania highway projects.  Judge Bechtle froze the funds when the state Legislature refused to fund a federally-mandated auto-emissions inspection program.  Judge Bechtle must grant final approaval for release of the funds, however.

headline: State Aides Accused Of Randomly Moving Retarded 'Like Cattle
abstract: The Association for Retarded Citizens of Pennsylvania (ARC) accused the state of treating retarded citizens "like cattle" because of how they handling the movement of residents of a facility being renovated into a prison to other facilities. ARC argues that the facilities the residents were moved into are already overcrowded and of poor quality, moreover, it would be cheaper to place them in group homes. The group also wants more information on the closing of the original facility as well as future institutional closings or transfers.

headline: New N-Waste Plan Sought
abstract: The National Governors Association believes that a state should have the right to veto placement of a nuclear waste site unless both houses of Congress vote to overturn its decision.  Forcing the federal government to secure congressional support would promote safer site planning.

headline: Highway Robbery
abstract: Federal grand juries in seventeen states are investigating charges of bid rigging on highway projects.  Not everyone involved in public works construction is corrupt, but investigators have found collusion in virtually every aspect of the industry.  Nobody knows how much corruption adds to the cost of public construction, but estimates range from 10 to 50 percent of the total bill.

headline: Panel Oks bill that defines death
abstract: A bill that would legally define death was unanimously approved by the PA Senate Judiciary Committee.  The bill would also include brain death which may help solve several legal battles.

headline: Prexy's Firing Tied to 'Petty Poltiics'
abstract: The Commonwealth Association of Students charged that petty personal politics were behind the firing of West Chester State College President Charles Mayo.  They charged Governor Dick Thornburgh fired Mayo at the behest of Representative Elinor Taylor as part of a personal deal.  Democratic legislators last spring charged that Thornburgh made a deal with Mrs. Taylor in which he agreed to fire Mayo in exchange for her vote on his 1982-83 budget.  Thornburgh and Taylor have denied any kind of agreement.

headline: Bureaucracy
abstract: When the Pennsylvania Senate voted against funding an exhaust-emission testing program, the majority in the Senate voted for the majority of the people.  There cannot be anything "tragic" "rresponsible" or "perverse" about elected legislators voting the wishes of a majority of their constituents.

headline: Party United Against Reagan: Nation's Democrats Set For Philadelphia Session
abstract: The Democrats were planning on holding a party conference in Philadelphia that they hoped will be a showcase for alternative programs and candidates.  The state of the economy, the nuclear freeze movement and the Equal Rights Amendments are the key issues to be discussed.  5 candidates for the 1984 Democratic presidential nomination will address the opening session of the conference.  There will be issues workshops at which participants will work on party positions on various topics.

headline: Short memory
abstract: This letter question the playing up of the congressional redistricting. The author states that what is currently happening to the Democratic congressman today, happened with the Republicans 10 years back.

headline: Pass the drunk-driver bill
abstract: An editorial lends support to legislation that would increase punishments for individuals convicted of drunken driving.  This legislation has the potential to reduce the number of accidents, injuries and deaths caused by drunken driving in Pennsylvania.  The author argues that this is important legislation, and that no argument can be substantiated against the bill.

headline: State Anti-Abortion 'Zealots' Assailed
abstract: Abortion should not be a political issue.  It is the imposing of religious beliefs on all people.  Abortion has been going on since the beginning of time and will continue.

headline: Opportunity to comment
abstract: A citizens group thinks the PA Department of Environmental Resources should hold a public hearing to discuss the long-range effects of a water diversion project in the Delaware River before the department grants a construction permit.

headline: His Appeal Won, Camiel Regains Post-Maybe
abstract: Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission Chairman Jack Greenblatt said that he was reinstating Peter J. Camiel as a member of the Commission because Camiel had been acquitted in a fraud case, but aides to Governor Dick Thornburgh immediately indicated they would fight the action.  Greenbelt announced his order reinstating Camiel following a ruling issued by the Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.  That ruling upheld an earlier ruling by U.S. District Judge Clifford Scott Green, acquitting Camiel and two others on fraud charges.

headline: Pa. Trooper Charged in Payoff Ploy: Scheme Centered on Car Inspections
abstract: A Pennsylvania State Trooper was arrested for his alleged involvement in a payoff scheme that allowed the owners of nine state automobile inception stations in North Philadelphia to avoid the loss of their operating licenses, the State Police said.  Marcel N. Olevnik, an inspection station supervisor for the State Police has been charged with bribery, extortion, conspiracy, obstructing the administration of law and violating the public official ethnics act.

headline: Bush Stumps for Atkinson in Butler
abstract: Vice President George Bush attended a party for Eugene Atkinson and campaigned for him.  Atkinson is a Democrat-turned-Republican running for U.S. Representative.  Bush also defended Reaganomics.

headline: Passing politics
abstract: The May 18 primary election is provoking far more discussions and debates than most of the contests for nominations for the elective offices to be filled this year. The referendum, however, was certain to cause noisy stirrings among the people occupying public office.

headline: Successor to Marcase: Temporary
abstract: Charles A. Highsmith, who has worked for the Philadelphia School District in nearly every administrative capacity, is likely to become its next Superintendent. However, this only on an interim basis, as the Board of Education decided to continue its search for a successor to Superintendent Michael P. Marcase indefinitely, abandoning the March 31st deadline for applications.

headline: House choice: Keep mum or squeal about pork
abstract: Because it was submitted as a continuing resolution, recent pork-barrel legislation was approved without a vote.  This wasteful spending measure should anger American taxpayers in a time when fiscal restraint is needed; what should anger them more, however, is the fact that Congress has attempted to circumvent accountability by not having a vote or public discussion on the issue.  The measure can, and should, be called up for a debate and a recorded vote.

headline: State court upholds abortions for poor
abstract: Poor women in Pennsylvania may continue to obtain state-funded abortions until state courts determine the constitutionality of a 1980 law.  The funding was continued so that poor women may still be eligible for the funding in the instance of medically-necessary abortions.

headline: Pa. counties not in complained with Clean Air Act
abstract: This chart shows all Pennsylvania counties and indicates to what degree they are in compliance with the Clean Air Act.

headline: Inebriate at Wheel Ahead!
abstract: While Governor Dick Thornburgh checks out the new drunk driver legislation, it behooves all users of the public streets and roads to beware.  The reason for such defensive driving by sober motorists is that one out of every 10 drivers on the road on any given evening is drunk-not just drinking but legally intoxicated.  That’s the word of the National Highway Safety Council, issued as the tempo of the holiday season increases.

headline: Parole on Trial: 'Time for Crime' Cry Grows
abstract: The American parole system is on probation.  Legislation in Congress now would abolish the century old system.  Defenders of the system note that most paroled convicts steer clear of the law.  One prison official called parole "a valid and necessary release value for our bulging institutions".  Bureau of Justice figures show there are 223,800 convicts on parole and 509,308 in federal and state prisons.  A bill to end federal parole has passed the U.S. Senate and awaits House action.  The sentencing judge would set a minimum release date and guidelines.

headline: But an Image-Conscious Senate Cuts Down on Travel Expenses
abstract: State Senators have cut down on travel to seminars sponsored by two national legislative organizations in part because trips in previous years provoked charges of abuse.  House member spent $73, 339 in 1981 to attend meetings sponsored by the National Conference of State Legislatures and Council of State Governments, a United Press International review of expense records has shown.

headline: Passing politics
abstract: William W. Scranton, the present Lieutenant Governor, will be aspiring for re-election this year. As a candidate for statewide offices, he will help infuse a "local" flavor to this years politics. Also, State Sen. Bob Mellow has been guaranteed the Democratic nomination for another term as the county's representative in the Senate chamber.

headline: The challenge to the Center City Incumbents
abstract: Center City, for many years, has been a town divided in the state legislature. Broad Street ran through the middle, dividing the city. However, the recent legislative redistricting obliterated the Broad Street boundary and suddenly, there is no division in Center City.

headline: Ethics panel clears counsel to Thornburgh
abstract: The state ethics commission ruled that a senior Thornburgh administration official did not violate state law when he awarded a contract to a firm headed by former state Attorney General Harvey Bartle.

headline: Thanking columnist Flo Kain for views of the Abortion Control Act
abstract: Letter to the editor: The writer thanks a columnist for supporting the rights of women seeking a legal option of a safe abortion, and notes that had the bill been put before a public referendum, the bill would have been defeated anyhow.  Writer believes that the best way to prevent abortion is to improve access to family planning programs and sexual education.

headline: PCB spill fouls up day in Camden
abstract: After an exploding transformer sent a flood of PCB (polychlorinated biphenyls which are suspected of causing cancer), about 500 workers at the Camden County Administrative building were transferred to temporary quarters across the county.

headline: Inspect Thyself
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate and House both voted for annual auto inspections.  The inspections would be required when motorists get their yearly auto registration cards.  It is expected that Pennsylvania motorists can save around $61 million a year in mechanical service bills.

headline: Passed: Gulity But Mentally Ill: House Sends Bill to the Governor
abstract: The PA House of Representatives voted 138-51 yesterday to establish the verdict of guilty but mentally ill in the Pennsylvania criminal justice system.  The action came fewer than six months after a jury found John Hinkley not guilty by a reason of insanity in an attempt to assassinate President Reagan.  The state bill, which has been approved by the Senate, goes to Governor Dick Thornburgh for his signature.  Under provisions of the bill, a guilty but mentally ill defendant would receive treatment for the mental illness while incarcerated.  If the treatment were to end before the sentence, the prisoner would serve the remainder of the jail term.  Other legislation was passed.

headline: By attorney general's office: coal deal allegations reviewed
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman has referred to his Criminal Law Division, allegations that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh softened regulations for coal mining companies for campaign contributions.  Two of Zimmerman's top prosecutors, Henry Barr and James West, would not be prevented from contributing to the investigation despite prior associations with Thornburgh.

headline: Patronage power limited by court
abstract: This opinion piece suggests that PA Governor Thornburgh must rehire 8 Democrats that were saved by a US Supreme Court ruling that prohibits political firings, except top-level appointees.  Party credentials must be an "appropriate requirement" for the posting to warrant firing.

headline: The cost of justice in Philadelphia can and must be cut
abstract: The City Controller's Office has recently published a report on the administration of justice in Philadelphia, it found that it costs the court system 25% to 50% more for supplies and operations than it costs the city. This is something the city cannot afford.

headline: Clayton Leadeing for School Job
abstract: The Philadelphia Board of Education has expressed their unanimous support for Constance E. Clayton--a Philadelphia school-superintendent candidate.  The board will make a formal decision on Monday; if they approve Clayton, she will only require Mayor Greene's approval.  It is unlikely that Mayor Greene would block Clayton's appointment, as it would further strain his relations with the black community in Philadelphia.

headline: The Mayor's Lollygagging
abstract: Philadelphia African Americans protested Mayor William Green for allowing the number of African Americans on the city police force to diminish.  The Green administration counters by pointing out that they have a Black managing director and a Black housing chief.  However, the administration's inability to improve public schools and public housing are two issues that affect Black Philadelphia residents the most.

headline: Penna. Files plan with U.S. agency for regulation of its coal mines
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources asked the federal government for authority to regulate strip mining in PA.  It is a move that is intended to bring $40 million in federal funds for cleaning abandoned strip mine and deep mine sites.  Among other potential uses of the money would be to extinguish the underground mine fire that has forced residents of Centralia, PA to consider leaving their town.

headline: Is U.S. Catching Up To Big-Truck Safety?
abstract: It appears that the U.S. government may begin to start regulating the trucking industry. A study by the National Highway Safety Administration finds that highway medians and guardrails aren't designed for large trucks and that many drivers are inexperienced. It urges medians and barriers be redesigned and that states increase their inspection of trucks and drivers. Action is needed because as truck mileage increases so too will accidents.

headline: Penna. Poor in Limbo in Legal Help
abstract: The legislative opponents of Pennsylvania Legal Services (PLS), the main administrative agency for the 20 local legal-service agencies in Pennsylvania, wrote a change last month into the new state budget.  The change lumped the $7.7 million that Governor Dick Thornburgh had requested for legal services for the next budget year into an Adult Services Block Grant program designed to be run by county governments.

headline: By-District Question Ruled off Nov. Ballot
abstract: Civil Division Judge Stephen A. Zappala said that the question of whether or not to elect City Council members by district cannot be placed on the November ballot because it is flawed.  ACORN-The Association of Community Organizations for Reform Now had presented the Allegheny County Elections Department with a petition signed by about 25,000 citizens asking that citizens be allowed to vote on the proposed change council elections in a November referendum.  Despite Zappala’s ruling the referendum could possible still appear on the November ballot in the event that ACORN appeals and a higher court overturns Zappala.

headline: Pearlman and Rocks are engaged in bitter Senate primary campaign
abstract: Al Pearlman and M. Joseph Rocks are currently engaged in a bitter Senate primary campaign. Pearlman's huge white placards dotting front yards and store windows. However, Rocks posters are smaller and are on numerous utility poles across the region. There is also a lot of name-calling from both the sides, in this bitterly fought battle.

headline: The newest city politics; organize thy community
abstract: A growing number of community workers such as Michael DiBerardinis, a community organizer in Kensington for five years, are no loner content in protesting the traditional way. Once fiercely independent, they now believe that the best way to create change is to get on the inside and change it.

headline: Slay Suspect Shotgun Use Questioned
abstract: Corrections officials say that, even though a 1972 law barred ex-convicts from possessing firearms, George Banks--the ex-convict prison guard accused of killing 13 people--regularly carried a shotgun when he was on duty.  A spokesperson for Governor Thornburgh said the matter is being investigated.

headline: Thornburgh wrong on abortion veto
abstract: A letter to the editor takes offense to Governor Thornburgh's recent veto of an abortion bill.  The letter claims that the Governor's previous support stance was just meant to placate anti-abortion interests.

headline: Penna. weighing softening its new toxic-waste rules
abstract: The PA Environmental Quality Board is considering softening its seven-week-old regulation on the handling of toxic waste. This move seems to be triggered by effective lobbying by Western Pennsylvania industrialists.

headline: It worked
abstract: Once-a-year auto inspections have finally been passed, despite the threat of 27 senators to stall the bill three weeks ago. This was done in order to gain political mileage. However, it has now been passed with an overwhelming majority because the senators were put under pressure from the media and the public.

headline: Penna. Sits Tight on Confiscating Illegal Weapons
abstract: It is illegal for a civilian to own an automatic weapon in Pennsylvania.  1,575 useable automatic guns were registered in 1981 to individuals in the state.  This does not include the 858 registered to gun dealers and the 1,267 registered to government agencies.  Most of the guns are in clear violation of the law, but the state if not going to do anything about it.  Some people bought the guns when it was legal to own them.  The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms (ATF), the federal agency that registers the weapons, won’t tell the state who has them.  The state recommends that anyone who has automatic weapons to sell them to citizens of other states where it is legal to own them.

headline: Called 'alternative' party, Socialists reveal state races slate
abstract: Three labor union members announced their candidacies for governor, lieutenant governor, and US Senate, all in the Socialist party.  The PA Socialist party has about 500 members state-wide.  The party believes Governor Dick Thornburgh's programs have been disastrous.

headline: PEMA director guides agency to its niche
abstract: The Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency (PEMA) has earned its place as the leading arm for responding to natural and man-made disasters. DeWitt C. Smith Jr., head of PEMA, is acknowledged as one of the main reasons for the success of this organization.

headline: The story behind the story; Mayor's name cleared, but probe raises $10 million questions
abstract: Philadelphia, faced with a federal mandate to stop dumping its sewage in the Atlantic Ocean, would be forced to find another dumping spot. On the other hand, for Somerset County, this offered a golden opportunity to re-vegetate its hills. However, this has now become the focus of an investigation by the US Attorney's Office, into possible kickbacks in this deal.

headline: Heinz-Wecht debate excerpts
abstract: This article provides excerpts from the debate between U.S. Senator John Heinz and Allegheny County Commisioner Cyril Wecht.  Wecht is challenging Senator Heinz for his senate seat.  The debates cover such substantive areas as jobs and unemployment, school busing, the defense budget, personal wealth, Reaganomics and taxes.

headline: Voting rights act: no further delay
abstract: Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina is using obscure Senate rules to delay action on a measure extending key provisions of the 1965 Voting Rights Act and this is unfortunate because at the current juncture time is very important as critical provisions in the voting rights law will expire by end of August.

headline: Pennsylvania Tries Bacterial Attack in War Against Summertime Pests
abstract: Lee Cunningham, proprietor of the Riverview Campground near Duncannon, Pennsylvania, was assured that the dumping of 240 gallons of bacteria would assist in the killing of gnats.

headline: KQV14 NewsRadio Rebuttal Broadcast: Thursday, June 3, 1982
abstract: Lance F. James does not agree with KQV’s position that the Port Authority Transit purchase “local content” instead of merchandise at the lowest prices when it comes to manufacturing.  KQV wants them to purchase light rail vehicles with parts made by Westinghouse even though the same vehicles can be obtained for less cost elsewhere.

headline: Pennhurst Workers Disciplined in Wake of Abuse Probe
abstract: Disciplinary action was taken against 22 employees at Pennhurst, the Spring City, Chester County facility for the mentally retarded.  A five-month investigation concluded that workers were striking, hitting, kicking, and locking people in rooms alone.  Polly Spare, head of the Pennhurst Parent-Staff Association said that underemployment as the main reason behind the abuse.  Nine employees were suspended and a warrant for one of those nine was issued for simple assault and harassment of a Pennhurst resident.

headline: Camiel removed from Pike panel
abstract: A divided state Supreme Court today ordered former Philadelphia Democratic Chairman Peter Camiel removed from the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission. This ruling overturned a November 1981 Commonwealth Order to reinstate Camiel for this position.

headline: Primary Casualties Now Official as May 18 Vote is Verified
abstract: It’s all over but the pouting for the May 18 primary election in Philadelphia in which a congressman, a State Senator and four State House members were defeated for re-election.  The Board of Elections showed two turnarounds from the unofficial results available on election night and confirmed winners in several close races.

headline: The text of the mayor's fiscal 1983 budget
abstract: This article gives the text of Mayor Green's budget for fiscal 1983. The underlying idea behind this budget is that, although the city has been hit by a combination of the national recession and federal funding cutbacks, the budget does not propose to hike tax rates or layoff jobs.

headline: House passes tougher drunken-driving penalties
abstract: Yesterday, the state House approved legislation that requires mandatory imprisonment for repeat drunken-drivers and persons who kill someone while driving under the influence.

headline: Woman's voices heard faintly in state's legislative halls
abstract: Some prominent women have formed a Political Action Committee (PAC) that is intended to help in the election of women to the Pennsylvania Legislature. The group announced a new fund - Pennsylvania Women's Campaign Fund - that addresses the great need for more women representation, from the present 10 women out of 203 members.

headline: Reverse toxic waste plan
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency has scheduled a hearing in Washington on its plan to permit disposal of liquid hazardous waste in landfills after public outcry. The plan invites polluters to resume practices that have contaminated streams and groundwater supplies all over the US.

headline: Larson lifts road agency out of mismangement
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson responds to letters from citizens about the reduced level of corruption in the Commmission, the number of employees, and road standards throughout the state.

headline: Pennsylvania's Stiff New Prison Law is Part of Wider Anticrime Campaign
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has sent proposals to the State Legislature asking for abolition of the State Board of Probation and Parole and for elevation of the corrections board to a Cabinet-level department.  He also wants to raise the corrections budget for the next fiscal year by almost 15 percent.  The state has undertaken a $102 million prison expansion and construction program for 2,380 new cells.

headline: Can Democrats do better than GOP?
abstract: The prevailing view in Washington is that the Democrats will not make any substantial gains in the upcoming elections. This is also the view of some of the polls across the country. However, other polls state that there are chances, the Democrats might do better than the GOP. However, the author believes this will not be the case as relatively few Americans think the Democrats can do better.

headline: Primary Interest: What'll He Do?
abstract: The political speculation about the 1983 mayoral race was colored by one overwhelming unknown-whether Mayor Green was going to run for another term.  On November 2nd, Green announced that he was not going to run.  Since then, former City Controller Thomas A. Leonard has joined the fray, former City Managing Director W. Wilson Goode is to enter.  Former Mayor Frank F. Rizzo has been raising campaign funds at a furious pace.

headline: U.S. Steel Property Has Highest Tax Value
abstract: U.S. Steel Corp. is the largest holder of taxable property in Allegheny County.  The property was valued at more than half a billion dollars.  U.S. Steel Corp has provided the lifeblood of the economy in the county since the turn of the century.

headline: SCRANTON: Sees a state in profound transition
abstract: While campaigning for a second term as Lieutenant Governor, William Scranton III tells voters that Pennsylvania needs to forge a post-industrial economy--one built on high-technology industries.  The Pennsylvania economy of old, one that was built on coal and steel, is--and will be--no longer.

headline: Women employees shouldn't oust men
abstract: The author states that although there is a place for women in every profession, it is not at the expense of a man getting furloughed from his job because of a woman. This is in regard to the April 21 article, "Women Spared Rehab-Office Dismissals".

headline: Road Shut for 8 Hours at Norristown; Hundreds Flee: Chemical Tanker Spilts, Ignites on Turnpike
abstract: A truck carrying toxic chemicals split open and caught fire on the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  It closed the road for about eight hours and forcing the evacuation of hundreds of people, officials said.  The Rohm and Haas Co. tanker carried two chemicals, methyl methacrylate and butyl scrylate.  Philadelphia Water Department employees monitored the Schuylkill River downstream from the spill for any chemical contamination, but had found none by 6 p.m.

headline: Laxity over drunk driving is deadly
abstract: In this letter to the editor the author is concerned that drunk driving penalties are not strong enough.  In Norway the minimum penalty for driving while intoxicated is two weeks in jail.  Writer would like to see tougher penalties for drunken driving.

headline: Perry, Plevel denied bid for new trial
abstract: Dauphin County Superior Court Judge William Lipsitt denied post-trial motions on behalf of Nick Perry and Edward Plevel in connection with their attempt to fix the PA Daily Number Lottery drawing.  Other conspirators in the crime had already been sentenced to 1-to-5 years in prison.

headline: Candor in the court
abstract: The PA House of Representatives voted properly to reject a bid to exempt municipal officials and school directors from financial disclosure provisions of the state's 1978 Ethics Law.  It has been just 5 months since the PA Supreme Court ruled that people in public life place themsevles there voluntarily, the law constitutes no invasion of privacy.  Additionally, the House added judges and solicitors to the list of public officials who must disclose their finacnial interests.

headline: Promoters fined in mail scheme
abstract: Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman says that a mass mailing designed to draw business for Pocono resorts cost the promoters $10,000 because it misled the public.

headline: U.S. Steel, PPG Owe '82 Property Taxes
abstract: U.S. Steel Corp. and PPG Industries have not paid their 1982 property taxes on two unfinished Renaissance II skyscrapers, Allegheny County tax records show.  U.S. Steel said it did not pay the taxes because it was incorrectly billed by the city.  PPG did not own the land; therefore it was not going to pay the taxes.  Other businesses were delinquent on their taxes as well.

headline: Take over mills, Socialist candidate urges
abstract: The socialist candidate for governor, Mark Zola, argues that shut-down mills should be re-opened and taken over by the state.  At a sparsely-attended press conference, Zola said that neither of his opponents--Republican Governor Dick Thornburgh and Democratic Congressman Allen Ertel--are looking out for workers; they are both protecting the interests of business.

headline: Wrong number; Racial and religious bias on radio call-in programs
abstract: The study states that along with the popularity of call-in shows on radio stations, an increasing number of shows are airing controversial opinions dealing with racial, religious and ethnic groups.

headline: Sharp drop in TMI 2 radiation noted
abstract: Three Mile Island officials said radiation levels dropped significantly in the damaged nuclear plant's reactor. The success has been attributed to the clean-up experiment and removal of all contaminated water from a 1979 accident.

headline: Lewis mistaken on double-trailer plan
abstract: Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis wants to open the highways to double trailer trucks. Truck taxes would have to be increased to pay for the maintenance of roads and bridges. However, these trucks also pose safety problems and. hence, does not make sense.

headline: Phila. Men indicted in drug plot
abstract: Two Philadelphia men have been indicted by a federal grand jury in Newark, NJ., on charges of possession with intent to distribute illegal substance phenyl-2-propanone, an essential ingredient in the manufacture of methamphetamine or speed.

headline: Can't be any worse
abstract: It looks like federal courts will get the task of reducing the number of congressional districts in Pennsylvania from 25 to 23.  Whatever plan the courts impose could not be worse than any of the other proposed plans.  All of the plans proposed by the PA Congress have divided up Bucks County, and in some cases, have split municipal lines.

headline: Queen gets prosecutir nomination
abstract: David Dart Queen, formerly assistant U.S. attorney in Harrisburg, was  nominated by President Ronald Reagan to be U.S. attorney for the Middle District of Pennsylvania.  Queen will succeed Carlon O'Malley who served in the post through President Jimmy Carter's administration.  There is some question as to Queen's party alliances, he was once registered as a Democrat and an independent, as well as currently being a Republican.

headline: Vote on City Wage Tax Likely in Pre-Holiday Push
abstract: Legislators from Philadelphia suburbs will mount a drive to win approval of a measure that would reduce the city wage tax on Pennsylvania commuters when the state Senate convenes in an abbreviated pre-holiday session.  Under the bill, the city wage tax would be reduced from 4.31 percent to 2.9 percent for Pennsylvania residents who work in Philadelphia but live in its suburbs.  Commuters from out of state and city residents would continue to pay the 4.31 percent rate.

headline: George Banks charged with 8 more counts
abstract: Yesterday, George Banks was arraigned on eight counts of criminal homicide in the slaying of 13 people.

headline: Zimmerman Won't Fight on Abortion
abstract: State Attorney General Leroy Zimmerman would not appeal a ruling by a Chester County judge allowing doctors to perform an abortion if they deem it necessary to save the life of a comatose accident victim.  The case involves Patti Ann Wunsch, whose mother, Dorothy Pettite of Downingtown, last week won a ruling from Chester County Court Judge Lawrence E. Wood allowing doctors to abort her daughter’s fetus if necessary to save Ms. Wunsch’s life. State Representative Stephen Friend request last week that Zimmerman appeal the ruling on grounds that current state law says only the mother can give permission for an apportion.  Zimmerman declined to take the appeal.

headline: State and Strip Mining
abstract: The federal government’s decision to authorize PA to enforce environmental rules affecting the state’s strip-mining industry could be a good thing provided the PA Department of Environmental Resources and the Legislature maintain a proper balance between environmental and industrial needs and not confirm the fears of environmentalists that state responsibility means an inevitable weakening of enforcement.

headline: Montco and commuter rails
abstract: Montgomery County's participation is crucial to the success of SEPTA's (Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority) emergency funding plan to keep the commuter railroad operating.  About one-third of the 50,000 daily riders are residents of Montgomery County.  By March, SEPTA believes its commuter rail division will have serious cash problems, and is looking for a 15% increase in local funding to keep the trains moving.  Editorial.

headline: Phila. Mob Leader Ordered to Prison
abstract: A federal judge revoked bail for Nicodemo "Little Nicky" Scarfo and ordered the reputed Philadelphia area rackets boss to begin serving a two-year prison term for a handgun conviction.  Scarfo violated bail stipulations by associating with criminals.

headline: Capitol Newsroom Loses Dean: AP's Harrisburg Bureau Chief Leaving to Become PennDOT spokesman
abstract: Rich Kirkpatrick, the longtime leader of the Associate Press’ Harrisburg news bureau, is leaving the wire service to become the Press Secretary for the State Department of Transportation.  He led the AP’s Capitol newsroom for the past 16 years, reporting on everything from legislative initiatives to mine collapses as well as fostering the growth of dozens of young reporters under his tutelage.

headline: Reagan to help two candidates
abstract: President Ronald Reagan is planning to bolster the re-election campaigns of Sen. John Heinz and Gov. Dick Thornburgh by appearing at fund-raisers in their behalf on May 14 in Philadelphia. This is a sure sign that the Pennsylvania Republicans have survived the administration's election-year loyalty test.

headline: Wage-tax issue looms as threat to city-school bill
abstract: Suburban commuters who work in the city pay the same 4.31 percent wage tax that is paid by the city residents. However, suburban lawmakers intend to use the consolidation bill (reorganization of the Philadelphia School district) as a way to reduce this tax to 2.9 percent for commuting constituents.

headline: Ex-Rep. Goodling Is Satisfactory
abstract: Former U.S. Representative George Goodling was reported in satisfactory condition yesterday.  Goodling was admitted for observation after suffering from a lingering cold.

headline: 'Definitive' Ruling Sought In Trauma Center Court Case
abstract: Lancaster General Hospital Attorney Christopher Mattson says he expects definitive court action on the hospital's case against the Emergency Health Services Federation.  It would seek to halt all action on trauma center selection.  The federation, under contract to the state Health Department, has developed a regional trauma care plan which would establish trauma centers.  Lancaster General said it would suffer immediate and irreparable harm if the regional trauma center was established and is seeking to have it blocked.

headline: State DER airs reorganization plan
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources has proposed a reorganization plan affecting many of its offices around the state, and will discuss the plan at a meeting of its employees union in Harrisburg on February 23.  The plan would consolidate the environmental protection division and expand the waste management division.

headline: Neoplan gets bus pool pact
abstract: Governor Thornburgh inaugurated the nation's first statewide bus pool purchase with the award of a $157.8 million contract to Neoplan USA. He also allayed fears about the use of foreign steel in these buses.

headline: Phila. Prisons Separate Minorities
abstract: Puerto Rican and Cuban inmates in the Philadelphia prison system have been segregated after a stabbing incident earlier in this month in Holmesburg Prison, according to Prisons Superintendent David S. Owens Jr.  The stabbing incident began when a Puerto Rican changed the channel on a television that a Cuban inmate was watching according to officials.  State Representative James Williams, whom Owens called in to mediate the dispute, said there are 75 Puerto Rican inmates and nine Cuban inmates in the prison system.  Williams, whose district includes parts of West and Southwest Philadelphia, said Owens asked for his help because there are many foreign-born minorities, including Cubans, in Williams’ district.

headline: Casey ignores plea, will run
abstract: Former State Treasurer Robert E. Casey will run for the Lieutenant Governor position. Casey, who was an elected official in Cambria County, catapulted into statewide offices because voters thought he was Robert P. Casey, former auditor general and three-time candidate for the gubernatorial nomination.

headline: Second district: McElhatton
abstract: Democratic voters in Pennsylvania's Second State Senate District will have a choice of a veteran incumbent, Sen. Francis J. Lynch and a political newcomer, Daniel P. McElhatton, in the May 18 primary. On the Republican side, Samuel C. Stretton is unopposed.

headline: Wage-tax vote faces delay; Jubelirer warns budget is first
abstract: Senate Majority Leader Robert C. Jubelirer said yesterday that the bill that would cut the Philadelphia wage tax for Pennsylvania commuters might have to be delayed indefinitely if supporters are unable to get at least two more senators to support it.

headline: Pass drunk driving bill
abstract: The Patriot News supports House Bill 2533, which is intended to be a punitive deterrent for drunk drivers.  Although research shows that tougher penalities do not necessarily deter drunken driving, the bill also increases the discretion of the courts and allows judges to send offenders for additional drug and alcohol treatment; this feature may help reduce incidents among problem drinkers.

headline: Dental Board is Wrong
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Dental Council and Examining Board has issued citations for violations by state dentists. Those cited are practicing their profession in so-called retail store dental centers.  At issue is the enforcement by the board of a long-dormant regulation which prohibits licensed dentists from practicing in trade name facilities.  The dental board has no jurisdiction over dental centers or other types of group dentists working in trade name clinics.  By virtue of it disciplinary power, though, it can suspend or revoke the licenses of dentists practicing in such centers.

headline: State environmental plan draws little interest
abstract: A public hearing at Allegheny County Courthouse on the new state environmental "master plan" received very little public comment.  Work on the plan began in 1974, and is expected to be adopted by the Environmental Quality Board this summer.

headline: New Inspection Law
abstract: Governor Richard Thornburgh signed a bill that meant car owners in Pennsylvania only had to get their cars inspected once a year.  The bill will save state motorists $60-million a year without sacrificing safety.  However, many people feel that the bill is not good because it will prevent cars from being inspected more than once although some may need more inspections over the course of a year.  It is believed the new law is strictly political and comes in an election year.

headline: Phila. Task Force to Steer Traffic Court's Finances
abstract: State Supreme Court Chief Justice Henry X. O’Brien announced the appointment of a task force to improve the financial management of the Philadelphia Traffic Court.  Last year it was concluded that Philadelphia is losing between $7 million and $13 million a year in ticket fees and that more than half the tickets issued are disregarded by defendants.  An earlier announcement in the week about the court was to split the Common Pleas Court’s 57-judge trial division into civil and criminal sections in an effort to speed up disposition of cases.

headline: Caucuses and Cocktails: The Democrats Come to Phila.
abstract: The 1982 Democratic National Party Conference was scheduled to take place in Philadelphia.  Democrats would be there for three days of speeches, workshops, caucuses, cocktail parties and political gossip.  In recent years, the Democratic National Convention has been an occasion for bickering, back-stabbing, chaos, fratricidal warfare and blood in the streets, sometimes literally.  However, there have rules adopted for this meeting that will make it difficult for anything other than an appearance of unity to emerge.  There are seven people thinking of running for the presidential election in 1984.  Six of them will address the conference

headline: Ray D. Moyer
abstract: Ray D. Moyer, currently seeking the Republican nomination for the state House in the 187th district, believes that the PA General Assembly must bring cost efficiency into the government, for it to work successfully.

headline: Where were they?
abstract: Despite the Delaware County showing a remarkable degree of support to the Republican Party, the PA Republicans have gone ahead and chopped up the county's congressional district and, thereby, splintering the influence in Washington. Although there are some positives out of this, overall the county is losing a great deal ender this redistricting plan.

headline: Psychiatrist gave Banks a clean bill
abstract: A psychiatrist at the Luzerne County Mental Health-Mental Retardation Center gave accused mass-murderer George Banks a clean bill of health a week before he engaged in a shooting spree that left 13 people dead.  The phychiatrist, Dr. George Dreszer, no longer works at the Luzerne facility, and officials claim his leaving is unrelated to this particular case.

headline: Dr.: Tax Cigs to Keep Track of Cancer
abstract: Dr. H. Arnold Muller, PA Health Secretary, is urging doctors and hospitals to support legislation bogged down in the PA Senate Appropriations Committee which will increase cigarette taxes by half a percent. The tax will be used to fund a statewide cancer registry. The tobacco lobby and those concerned cigarette smuggling will increase oppose the legislation. William Kucenich, director of the PA Division of Chronic Diseases noted a PA cancer control program is well behind that of other states.

headline: State's Control of Strip Mining Hailed as Progress
abstract: The state will hire a number of additional inspectors as part of an agreement that gives the state more control over its strip-mining industry.  The state will also be responsible for issuing permits with funding provided for by the federal government.

headline: No good reason
abstract: Although both the State House had approved the once-a-year auto inspections bill, the Senate voted against it. There are many reasons for this including not giving Governor Thornburgh a popular victory just before elections.

headline: Philadelphia's prisons: A ticking time bomb
abstract: The number of inmates in state prisons has reached a breaking point that will be exacerbated if PA adopts mandatory sentencing.  This editorial argues that improving and expanding the prison system is vital to the well-being of the state.

headline: Cavanaugh receives top state Bar rating
abstract: The Pennsylvania Bar Association has rated Judge James R. Cavanaugh of Philadelphia "exceptionally well qualified" as a candidate for Republican nominations in the May 18 primary election for a seat on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.

headline: Reagan and Thornburgh hand-in-hand
abstract: Photo:  President Ronald Reagan shakes hands with Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: null
abstract: A 302 form was taken to Louis Levine to be signed because it appeared that he was a danger to not only himself but also to society.  The Levines were always reluctant to use 302s because they didn’t want to involve the police.  Larry was taken to the Fairmount Farm Hospital.  Since the 302 authorizes commitment for no more than five days, Larry was taken the following five Monday to a hearing before the mental health review officer, a magistrate of the Common Pleas Court.  Rita Levine, the public defender who represents most of the potential patients at these hearings, asked Larry if he felt he needed hospital care.  Larry said he didn’t.  He wasn’t particularly hostile this day and appeared competent during the hearing, so the master released him.

headline: Banks may be offered services by lawyer for Patty Hearst
abstract: J. Albert Johnson, a Boston attorney who helped defend Patty Hearst, may offer his services to accused mass murderer George Banks.  Johnson said he is assessing the situation, but no decision has been made yet.

headline: Elizabethtown Hospital Transfer Awaits Thornburgh's Signature
abstract: The Senate sent Governor Dick Thornburgh legislation transferring control of the Elizabethtown Hospital from the state to the Hershey Medical Center.

headline: Strip-Mine Replay
abstract: The Thornburgh administration eased bonding requirements for strip-mine operators while adding a $50-an-acre fee to finance the reclamation of abandoned coal sites.  Peter S. Duncan, Secretary of the PA Department of Environmental Resources confirmed the growing gap between revenues and the huge costs of restoring lands ravaged by strip mining.

headline: North Shore highway job OK'd
abstract: The Federal Highway Administration has approved the start of construction for the North Shore Expressway - one of four parts in the Interstate 279 system proposed though the Northside and North Hills.

headline: Piccola bill sets up training for prison guards
abstract: PA Representative Jeffrey Piccola has drafted a new bill requiring training for prison guards in a state-sponsored program.  The training program would be 120 hours in length and include psychological testing.

headline: Chamber Blamed in Tax-Shift Loss
abstract: Despite a strong bipartisan push, legislation that would substitute local income taxes for school property levies is dead for the session.  Supporters say the PA Chamber of Commerce is to blame.  They were able to exert enough influence to kill it.  The measure went right through the Senate, but then was stopped in the House.

headline: Reagan will seek governors' views on transfer plan
abstract: At a meeting at the White House with several state governors, President Ronald Reagan assured them that the "new federalism" program of transferring some programs between the states and federal government is a "two-way street".  The program and any guarantees made by the President to the governors still must be approved by Congress.

headline: A clarification
abstract: The reference to a cartoon in yesterday's Daily News was to State Sen. T. Milton Street and not to his brother, City Councilman John Street.

headline: null
abstract: This article discusses the genesis of the Newspaper in Education emergency curricula, which was started after the Three-Mile-Island incident.  The curriculum was developed by the Capital Area Intermediate Unit.

headline: Evening News: Mentually ill Suffer Effects of Change
abstract: The removal of mentally ill people from large institutions and their placement into community situations is not a new story, but it remains, even after a quarter-century of steady deinstitutionalization, a deeply troubling story.  Eleanor Owen, vice president of the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill testified that there were 750,000 mentally ill in nursing homes, 110,000 in short-term psychiatric hospitals, hundreds of thousands living in group homes and thousands in alleys and missions.  Despite efforts on behalf of the mentally ill, the trend since 1981 has been to reduce federal funding and relax federal standards for community programs.  The new policies reverse measures taken during the Carter presidency, when first lady Rosalynn Carter took a personal interest in mental health care issues.

headline: The garbage shift
abstract: Editorial: Some Pittsburgh residents are upset about a new policy requiring them to take their garbage to the curbs.  The editorial says that it would behoove city residents to pitch in and make the new program work.  The new policy is part of a cost-saving move to trim $1.2 million from the City's Environmental Services Department budget.

headline: Number of ships on the Delaware down for 3d year
abstract: Ship traffic on the Delaware River decreased for the third year in a row, accordint to recent statistics by the Philadelphia Maritime Exchange.  However, more expensive general cargo shipments have increased compared to bulk cargo.

headline: Piccola pushes anti-crime plan
abstract: State Rep. Jeffrey E. Piccola, R-Susquehanna Twp., told members of the Crime Clinic of Greater Harrisburg that elected officials have received a message from their constituents to crack down on crime.

headline: Chilling A 'Freeze' in Keystone State
abstract: The nuclear freeze issue will be fought again on many battlefields in November, but nowhere more sharply than in Pennsylvania, the state whose delegation killed the freeze in the ding-dong House battle last week.

headline: Reagan's changes on rights are starting to have impact
abstract: President Ronald Reagan is beginning his second year in office under a mounting barrage of assertions that he is undermining the civil rights of Americans in a broad range of areas.  Article gives a brief rundown of the ways the Reagan Administration has infringed on civil rights.  Some of these changes are due to be tested in courts, while the Reagan administration has contested that the President is committed to maintaining individual rights.

headline: null
abstract: This cartoon depicts President Reagan asking Gov. Thornburgh and Sen. Heinz how his economic policies were. The cartoon also shows Heinz with some doubts, and so, the President asks Thornburgh when he can come for the next fund raiser.

headline: Funds freeze may imperil road projects
abstract: Pennsylvania has been blocked by a federal judge from receiving additional federal highway monies until it implements an automobile emissions and inspection program.  The loss of funds would jeopardize transportation projects in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia over the next five years.  The state has appealed the judge's decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.

headline: Ex-LCB Boss Gets 'Stroke Pay'
abstract: An ex-Liquor Control Board boss suffered a stroke at a Harrisburg coffee shop where he had gone for lunch.  An ambulance was summoned, but Kaplan refused to go to the hospital.  He became sicker later in the day at work and was driving to the hospital by an aide.  He will receive stroke pay now because of the incident.

headline: U.S. court upholds auto-emission tests
abstract: A federal appeals court has upheld a judge's order that Pennsylvania establish an auto emission inspection program by May 1.  The ruling turned down a request by the administration of Governor Dick Thornburgh to allow the state a 20 month delay in implementing the program.  The program was agreed to by Governor Shapp in 1978 and was mandated by the Clean Air Act.

headline: Once-a-year auto inspection bill wins test
abstract: Legislation limiting Pennsylvania auto safety inspections to once a year overwhelmingly survived efforts to kill it in the Senate. Currently, Pennsylvania is one of only six states that require twice-a-year auto inspections.

headline: Plan to build 500 cells at Graterford is outlined
abstract: PA Bureau of Corrections Commissioner Ronald Marks outlined a plan to add 500 prison cells at the Graterford Prison.  Plan is part of a bigger plan to expand prison space state-wide due to expected influx from new mandatory sentencing policy.

headline: Choose, But Don't Look
abstract: The article discusses the problems surrounding electing judges. Merit selection is used in other states and is good in concept but deciding what merit is based on is difficult.  Inevitably the candidates are a member of the same party as the governor. Cross filing, in which the name of the candidate is listed on both major party ballots, is equally problematic as it results in confusion and has lead to most judges being from Philadelphia or Pittsburgh.

headline: Reagan's Lighting Rods
abstract: President Ronald Reagan’s name won’t appear on the Pennsylvania election ballot November 2nd, but it’s evident he will be very much an issue in the fall campaign, at both federal and state levels.  Two congressional elections for the seats of Republican incumbents Eugene V. Atkinson in western Pennsylvania and James K. Coyne in the southeast are bound to attract the national spotlight, probably as much as any others in the nation, for interpretation as a possible referendum on Reagan’s economic policies.  Five out of six counties in Atkinson’s district have an overall unemployment rate of 17 percent or better.

headline: 2 Dems, 1 Hallway: Fisticuffs
abstract: State Rep. James Williams and Harold Barksdale, Democratic leader of Southwest Philadelphia's 51st ward, engaged in a brief fistfight in the City Hall office of the City Commissioners. Barksdale and Williams are long-time political enemies.

headline: Why Heinz, Specter didn't back bill halting inspections
abstract: U.S. Senators Specter and Heinz did not support attempts to strip the Environmental Protection Agency of its authority to require states to implement auto pollution inspection programs.  Both senators said that pressures from leadership were partially responsible for their decisions.

headline: Fairview Has Weathered the Storm
abstract: Over a period of several years, Fairview has received a tremendous amount of bad publicity leading to the institution's closure.  Since then, the state was left with no other maximum security facility for the mentally ill and it was ludicrous to suggest Fairview’s closing and opening of new multimillion dollar facilities elsewhere.  That would have been an outrageous waste of public funds.  Now Fairview seems be getting along nicely.  It has a maximum security caseload of 203 patients, well below its limit of 225.  It is no longer overcrowded like it was before.

headline: U.S. Easing on Auto Tests
abstract: US Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis, announced he is going to reserve the state’s highway money at least a little longer before considering it forfeited.  Also, the Environmental Protection Agency endorsed a proposal that would substantially reduce the number of Western Pennsylvania motorists required to have pollution equipment on their cars impacted under the so-called I/M program.

headline: Once-a-year car inspections approved
abstract: The State Senate voted 41-6 to cut the number of required annual inspections from two a year to one. Gov. Thornburgh is expected to sign it into law.

headline: Police as politicians
abstract: Pittsburgh Councilman Jim O'Malley has proposed what could be the least urgently-needed change in city government that would allow policemen to become actively involved in politics.  Mr. O'Malley says that due to recent civil service reforms, the situation that prompted the 1950 law prohibiting police involvement in politics, no longer needs to remain in effect.  However, since police are currently policed by themselves, there may be discipline conflicts if an officer also holds political power.

headline: Cleaning Shift Darkens 'Great White Way'
abstract: Walter Baran, Secretary of the State Department of General Services is pulling the switch on nightly cleaning in state-owned buildings and expects to cut electricity consumption at 6 to 8 percent.  The Capitol dome will not be darkened.  There will be a pilot program of daylight office cleaning in the Transportation Building to eventually encompass all 250 custodial workers in various state office buildings in the city.

headline: Reagan's new brand of federalism
abstract: At first glance, the program proposed by President Ronald Reagan seems like vintage Reagan, cut everything out of the Washington government, and let the states deal with it.  But it is bigger than previous debates over block grants by shifting responsibility.  It seems to be a good deal for the states, because Medicaid costs are expected to grow by $9 billion by the end of the decade, while food stamps are only expected to grow by $2 billion, but the White House believes that centralized control of Medicaid will help to keep costs in line.

headline: A cabinet that travels in luxury
abstract: Although one of the first acts of President Reagan was to cutback on federal travel expenditure, almost 14 months later, many of the administration's top officials continue to travel in expensive private or government owned jets. Even on commercial flights, first-class is a standard among these officials.

headline: Dying Midland Awaits Miracle
abstract: Although the Midland plant of Crucible Steel is scheduled to close on October 15, many workers feel that their jobs will be saved by some miraculous occurrence.   The company is still awaiting a buyer; a deal was in place, but it fell through.

headline: Follow-up asked in private care for mentally ill
abstract: Senator Edward Howard, R-Bucks, chairman of a special Senate committee investigating the Office of Mental Retardation, says that Pennsylvania needs to spend more time making sure that minimum standards are followed in private-care facilities for the mentally-retarded.

headline: U.S., State open sump site probe
abstract: State and federal environmental authorities have begun inspecting an industrial waste dump in Allegheny County where U.S. Steel Corporation has allegedly been depositing waste illegally.  U.S. Steel had previously been cited by the PA Department of Environmental Resources for the illegal dumping.

headline: Opinion: As the Editor Sees it: Tough New Law!
abstract: Pennsylvania has enacted a new law intended to reduce drunken driving and the consequent loss of life and injuries caused by it.  The law requires a 48-hour jail term for convicted drunken drivers. The only option given the court is to waive the sentence to jail if the driver pleads guilty and agrees to participate in a rehabilitation program.  It requires breath tests if a driver is stopped.  It provides loss of a driver’s license for up to a year for anyone refusing to take the tests.

headline: Politics shown to influence Flaherty's aide
abstract: State Superior Court Justice John P. Flaherty selected James M. White, currently a lawyer in the Philadelphia Common House Pleas Court, to assist directly in the controversial efforts to investigate and improve the city's courts. However, the author has analyzed that there could be a political angle to this nomination.

headline: Cohen Asks Removal of Penrose Statue
abstract: Representative Mark Cohen has his own idea on how to beautify the Capitol: He wants to get rid of the statue of former Republican political boss Boies Penrose.  Penrose was the epitome of political corruption in Pennsylvania.  Penrose, a Philadelphia lawmaker and President Pro Tempore of the PA State Senate, was the last of the 19th-century Republican bosses.

headline: Reapportion now
abstract: This editorial suggests that it is time that the PA Legislature cracked down and passed an apportionment bill.   If one is not passed by February 16, all congressmen would have to run at large, which would be a ridiculous scenario.  The retirement of US Representative Marc Marks should make reapportionment easier because it no longer becomes a matter of saving that person, but that district has actually gained in population compared to others.

headline: A final vote that counted
abstract: Even after his death, M. Harvey Taylor was a factor in the recent primary election. Taylor sent in an absentee ballot in the GOP primary in his hometown of Susquehanna Township.

headline: Teachers Out In 16 Districts In 2nd Month
abstract: This article chronicles 16 teacher strikes in Western Pennsylvania and updates readers on the negotiation process and any progress that has been made.

headline: Giant blue cross rate hike studied
abstract: With regard to the proposal by Blue Cross of Western Pennsylvania that the rates for the elderly might increase by 57%, the Insurance Commissioner writes that he has the responsibility for final approval of rate hikes by Blue Cross and Blue Shield. As part of this process, the Insurance Department will conduct hearings throughout the state to solicit public input.

headline: US officials offer help in ending Centralia fire
abstract: State and federal officials have decided on a way to deal with the 20-year old Centralia mine fire.  They detail the way state and federal government are cooperating on this issue.

headline: Our Opinion: The Last Hurdle
abstract: The General Assembly approved construction for the missing link in the Beaver Valley Expressway.  It’s now waiting for Governor Dick Thornburgh to sign it.  The completion of the expressway which leads to the Greater Pittsburgh International Airport should boost the industrial attractiveness of Lawrence Country.

headline: Prison Cells too expensive
abstract: The author of the letter states that Governor Thornburgh's proposal of building 2705 prison cells at a cost of $112 million works to about $41,405 per cell, more than the four-bedroom house the author lives in. hence, the author believes that the government should take steps to prevent the drastic increase of prisoners.

headline: Coleman asks panel to study pay raises for top officials
abstract: Philadelphia Council President Joseph Coleman said he will appoint a committee to recommend pay raises to city officials, but raises would not apply to current office holders unless reelected.  If Council does approve pay raises, it will be the first salary increase for Philadelphia's elected officials since January 1974.

headline: Reapportioning shelved
abstract: The PA Senate adjourned last night until February 22 without approving a Congressional reapportionment plan, meaning that a plan will likely not be approved before the Tuesday deadline when a federal court will instead draft the plan or potential candidates will have to run at-large across the state.  Senate Majority Leader Robert Jubelirer claims that the time is necessary to let the issue rest with some people, and believes that as long as the Senate is still working on it, the courts will not step in.

headline: A new era
abstract: This letter states that symbol of America as an abode for the poor and weak was degraded by American courts which allowed the death of the mentally retarded child.

headline: CCP has found itself a home
abstract: The Community College of Philadelphia has a new, permanent home at 17th and Spring Garden Streets.  This gives the college an identifiable campus--something which it lacked until now.

headline: 'Good Samaritan' Bill Passes
abstract: A bill giving civil immunity to persons or companies assisting in hazardous waste cleanups is on the way to Governor Dick Thornburgh.  House-Senate conference report on the "Good Samaritan" bill was adopted by the State Senate.  The House approved it the week before.  The bill grants immunity against lawsuits similar to that provided to doctors when they offer care in emergency situations.

headline: Waste-Site Rules Receive State Nod
abstract: The PA Environmental Quality Board gave preliminary approval to regulations restricting where hazardous waste sites could be located. There will be at least one public hearing on the regulations. If given final approval almost seven hundred companies now storing such waste would have to abide by them.

headline: Over the long run, Commuter Rails: A political solution
abstract: Opinion says the potential for commuter rail service in Southeastern PA is dismal.  Demographic changes in the metropolitan region, historic collective bargaining agreements, and low levels of financial support and services from suburban governments have proved intractable problems during the 1970s and show no signs of easing.  Argues that abandoning rail service would save short-term subsidy costs, but would create irreparable damage to the regional economy in the long run.

headline: Prison jam prevention is upheld
abstract: PA Commonwealth Court affirmed 1981 court rulings that imposed population limits on Philadelphia prisons and permitted inmate releases  to relieve overcrowding.  In addition, the court ruled that three-person cells and total prison populations over 2190 were illegal in three Philadelphia prisons.

headline: Commentary: Bid-Rigging Probe
abstract: Allegations sparked that officials in the Dick Thornburgh Administration have undergone bid-rigging, when sealed bids at the offices of Westmoreland Human Opportunities (WHO), the county’s poverty agency were opened.  One of the bidders is cozy with the Republican Party and the Thornburgh Administration.  One of the proposals was mailed to WHO two days before Westmoreland authorities placed legal advertisements in a county newspaper asking for bids.

headline: Reapportionment passes in House
abstract: The PA House last night passed a reapportionment plan.  Republican leaders believe the plan will help them strengthen their hold on the state's congressional delegation.  The Senate earlier passed this new plan, with Governor Dick Thornburgh expected to sign it.  The plan will eliminate to districts currently controlled by Democrats in Philadelphia and Allegheny Counties.

headline: A new year brings a renewal of hopes
abstract: A history of the significance of New Year's traditions.

headline: They don't want to be liked they want to be feared
abstract: This article gives a first-hand account of the Pagan biker gang and its alleged illicit activities.  A reporter from the Philadelphia Inquierer interviews several key figures in the Delaware County affiliate of the gang.  Gang members say the police treat them unfairly and that the talk of illegal activity is patently false.

newspaper: z-Unidentified - Daily News (doesn't say which one)
headline: Greed Vs. Need
abstract: Editorial:  The health industry's voluntary effort to hold down the increase in hospital costs "certainly isn't working" claims Secretary of Health and Human Services Richard Schweicker.  19% increases just "blows our federal budget out of the water."  Now, he wants Congress to pass new cost containment legislation that will be proposed by US President Ronald Reagan.  Editorial says that a majority of the nation will not objected to a forced shift by the president to regulating the greedy to help the needy.

headline: Watchdog on Coal
abstract: Responsibility for the regulation of coal mining in Pennsylvania was recently passed from federal to state hands.  The transition marks the end of a four-year struggle by the Commonwealth to assume primacy for the regulation under provisions of the federal Surface Mining Act of 1977.  The state has demonstrated that its laws and regulations parallel or exceed those of the federal branch, and should be in force.  This will bring economic and administrative advantages for Pennsylvania.  It will eliminate the federal part of an expensive and redundant federal state mine inspection scenario necessitated by an injunction that delayed primacy for over a year.

headline: P. Gleason, 47; legislator led PennDOT probe
abstract: PA Legislator Patrick Gleason, who led a highly-publicized probe into the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT), died of cancer February 17, 1982.

headline: Prison Options Sought
abstract: Officials at the Dauphin County Prison are preparing to meet with the county’s district justices to discuss ways of reducing the number of prisoners since it has been overcrowded for more than a year.  Success could be important, since the start of a multimillion dollar expansion and renovation project at the prison still is at least two months away, and actual construction will consume even more time.  The prison’s inmate population was high as 338 just a week ago; its designed capacity is 222.  As a result, Bruce Beaudin, a representative of the National Association of Pre-Trial Services in Washington D.C. has been invited to address the county’s district justices Friday on the application of alternative and non-monetary bail procedures.

headline: Commissioners practice consistent inconsistency
abstract: This editorial complains that Luzerne County Commissioners are sending an inconsistent message by first saying that they need to control hiring and payroll expenditures, then they hire additional personnel and complain about individual salary increases.

headline: Recognized Fruits of Freedom: Captive Nations Week Proclaimed in Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh proclaimed the week of July 18-24 as “Captive Nations Week” in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.  In proclaiming “Captive Nations Week” the Governor said “we who enjoy the fruits of freedom must recognize that the right we hold to be self-evident do not exist in all countries.  We cannot and must not forget that some people are continually denied their most basic human rights in their homelands, they are forced to live in silence, hunger, and fear.”

headline: A struggling Pa. town climbs back, and gets a hand
abstract: Mayersdale, a small town southeast of Pittsburgh, was recently voted as one of only 10 "All-American Cities, 1981-82", by the National Municipal League. The jury were impressed by the town's work in developing new jobs, expanding rental housing and other similar achievements.

headline: Jailed and jeopardized
abstract: Although a 1970 state law requires police to make a dilligent effort to seek immediate treatment for diabetics, epileptics and persons with serious medical problems, an Inquirer investigation found that the Philadelphia Police regularly fail to provide adequate medical care for prisoners awaiting arraignment.  The article includes case studies of persons arrested by the Philadelphia Police.

headline: Handicapped Camper's Diet: No Sadness, Only Hope
abstract: Camp Susquehanna is operated by the Association for Retarded Citizens of Dauphin County with the cooperation of the county Mental Health/Mental Retardation Program.  It offers a wide variety of activities, including physical exercises, adaptive swimming, science and nature study, self-help skills and drills in manners and arts and crafts.  Open to all mentally and physically handicapped youngsters and young adults in the county, the camp meets in half-day sessions Monday through Thursday and for full-day field trips every Friday.  It is funded in part by the MH/MR program.  The field trips were financed by donations from businesses and individuals in the community.

headline: Water removal almost done at TMI
abstract: Technicians have almost finished removing 600,000 gallons of radioactive water from the basement of the containment building at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant.  Only 5 inches of water remain after the most recent round of pumping.  The 1979 nuclear accident at the plant left over 8 feet of water in the containment building.

headline: Pa. Loses Appeal on Funds: $90 Million for Highways
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court turned down Pennsylvania’s request for immediate action to rescue about $90 million in federal highway funds before a September 30th deadline.  The brief order from the high court meant that the state’s appeal of a lower court order would be considered on a normal court schedule.  Officials of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation said that they were disappointed by the court’s action but that they would make a last-ditch effort to save the money.  The state is asking the high court to overturn a decision by the U.S. District Court Judge Louis Bechtle that placed a free on the use of federal highway money in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  The order by Bechtle was a result of the state’s failure to establish an auto emissions inspection program in two metropolitan areas.  The state’s efforts to establish an auto emissions inspection program were blocked last year when the legislature overrode Governor Dick Thornburgh’s veto of a bill barring the use of any state money to set up the program.  The state had agreed to set up the program under a 1978 consent decree.

headline: Prison term guides: Will they work?
abstract: Guidelines regarding prison terms are not uniform across PA. Critics argue that this is not right and that there should be a uniform rule across the state. Two proposals dealing with the creation of uniform guidelines are currently being debated.

headline: Common Cause Can't Find Support Call for Senate to Convene in September Ignored
abstract: A call by Common Cause for the Senate to join the House in session during September and take up unfinished business is apparently falling on deaf ears among the Republican leadership.  Spokesman for the 11,000 member group appealed to Governor Dick Thornburgh, who told them he lacks influence over Senate President Pro Tempore Henry Hager, and the senator in a reply to a survey by Common Cause says he does not favor a September return.  When the legislature took its summer recess, the House adjourned until September 13th, but the Senate resolution leaves the time of convening up to Hager.

headline: Record Lotto's Lucky 6 Get First Of 'Millionaire' Checks
