abstract: The six winners of a nine million dollar lottery jackpot received their first of twenty-one annual checks today. The article explains what some of the winners plan on doing with the money, as well as the total amount each will receive annually.

headline: Affairs Chief; Decision a big 'must'
abstract: Shirley M. Dennis has traveled a long way from the days of a 23-year-old black divorcee with three young daughters and a practicing associate realtor. Today, at 44, she is the Secretary of the Department of Community Affairs that has an annual budget of $88 million and has over 300 employees.

headline: Help Prevent Arson
abstract: In honor of Fire-Prevention Week, this article offers readers tips to prevent arson.

headline: Health costs: Heinz boosts tax credit plan
abstract: The editorial notes despite new advances in health care, health care costs are continuing to soar.  US Senator John Heinz has a plan to give tax credits to families below a certain income level to care for chronically ill family members older than 65.

headline: Watt's modification?
abstract: The editorial complains that a recent letter released by Governor Dick Thornburgh's office does nothing to help the public understand  PA Interior Secretary James Watt's response to the Centralia Mine Fire. He suggested that the 20-year-old mine fire isn't dangerous and should be allowed to burn itself out.

headline: Pa. Truck-Inspection Law Upheld
abstract: The Supreme Court let stand an appeals court ruling that upheld Pennsylvania’s requirement that interstate trucks pass state inspection even if they already have federal safety stickers.  The justices refused to hear an appeal by trucking groups, noting that the state legislature had a legitimate goal-safety-when it passed the law.  In 1980, the General Assembly approved the sticker program, which requires that all trucks, truck-tractors and combinations be inspected twice a year in Pennsylvania or another state with a similar requirement.  All trucks must be inspected by the federal Bureau of Motor Carrier Safety from four to 12 times per year.

headline: Prisoner's Views on Criminal Justice
abstract: This letter to the editor comes from an inmate who has served 15 years of a 20 to 40 years sentence for burglaries in Pittsburgh in 1967.  They have been writing on corrections and the criminal justice system for the last five years.  The rest of the letter focuses on corrections and the criminal justice system.

headline: Common Cause: law on lobbyistts too weak
abstract: According to Scott Rubin, director of Common Cause's lobbying disclosure project, Pennsylvania's lobbyist reporting system needs to be revised to give voters a true picture of interest group spending.  He believes that current law allows most spending to go unrevealed.  A new bill supported by Senators Edward Howard and James Lloyd would transfer the reporting mechanism to the State Ethics Commission and allow the Attorney General to criminally prosecute.

headline: Redistricting delay prompts lawsuit
abstract: Wayne Long, a Carmichaels, PA businessman, went to a federal court to force the state to move ahead with a reapportionment plan, claiming that the longer the PA legislature delays, the more his constitutional voting rights are being violated.  The state has had since last April to come up with a new plan.  1980 Census figures show that the state lost population, and thus two House seats.  The election filing deadline of March 9 coming may restrict his voting options.

headline: Amid crane's din, Scranton talks of hope
abstract: A huge rescue attempt is in place for Gerald White, Sr., 32, an electrician who was trapped underground by a cave-in while he was working on a project to fill in an abandoned mine shaft here. This effort has been going on for the last 10 days.

headline: Democrats Make Economics Their Battle Cry
abstract: The Democrat's 1982 electoral strategy has been to attack Republicans on economic issues--especially as they relate to unemployment.  Gubernatorial candidate Allen Ertel, for example, has consistently tried to link Governor Thornburgh to the failed economic policies of President Reagan, arguing that Governor Thornburgh is partially to blame for Pennsylvania's high jobless rate.

headline: Health physicist at TMI to speak in Polyclinic
abstract: Paul E. Ruhter, a health physicist at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant, will speak at Polyclinic Medical Center's annual medication day on the 1st of April. His topic will be "Radiation Exposures Associated with TMI Unit II Recovery Operations".

headline: ZIPpity-DO-Dah
abstract: The idea of using postal ZIP codes to redraw the boundaries for auto-exhaust inspections in the Pittsburgh area has surfaced again.  It’s another gimmick aimed at undercutting public resistance to those dubious tests, ticketed for 12 counties in Pennsylvania, which for the time being remain in a legislative-legal limbo.  This plan, first hatched by the Thornburgh administration more than a year ago, and embraced last week by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, would exempt motorists in the outlying parts of those areas, as identified by their ZIP codes.

headline: Pa., W. Va Drivers Slow Down
abstract: The Federal Highway Administration’s latest speed summary listed Pennsylvania and West Virginia as the states where the fewest drivers are exceeding the 55 mile-an hour limit.  The biggest benefit of the slower speeds is the decline in highway fatalities, which has dropped at record levels the past two years.

headline: Questioning of Larsen is said to begin
abstract: The PA Judicial Inquiry and Review Board's Richard Sprague, formerly Philadelphia District Attorney, cross-examined PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen, accused of encouraging Allegheny County District Attorney Robert Colville to run for high court and attempting to defeat Justice Robert N. C. Nix Jr.'s reelection by alerting voters Nix is black. Sprague feels closed court proceedings are unfair. Executive Board Director Richard E. McDevitt says transcripts will be released.

headline: Common sense on redistricting
abstract: Editorial believing that the PA Supreme Court should not have upheld the final plan of the reapportionment commission.  Majority opinion writer Supreme Court Justice Samuel Roberts believes that the plan is closer to the 1 person, 1 vote principle than any previous plan.  Local reaction is described.

headline: Reed Takes Oath on Monday
abstract: Stephen R. Reed will take office as mayor of Harrisburg on January 4, 1982.  He will succeed Paul E. Doutrich Jr. as the city’s 36th mayor and will be sworn in with other city officials.

headline: Appearances by Rizzo keep Philadelphians abuzz
abstract: Although Representative Joseph F. Smith was the only major official at Palumbo's Café and Restaurant, the arrival of Frank L. Rizzo, former Mayor of Philadelphia, stole the spotlight.

headline: HIA Work May Jump 86,000
abstract: Because the Pennsylvania Bureau of Aviation drew up a work schedule which conflicts with several airlines' regular flights, the state may be stuck with a cost-overrun bill of as much as 86,000 dollars on a runway lighting improvement project.

headline: Hospital Strike is Called Off
abstract: Henry Nicholas, President of District Council 1199C, the hospital workers’ union, recommended that the union call off any plans to strike.  The action came in the wake of an announcement by Governor Richard Thornburgh of an increase in the state funding to Medicaid recipients.  The governor said he is directing that the cap on Medicaid hospital reimbursement be increased this year from 10 to 10.5 percent for urban and other hospitals which have a large Medicaid population.  $1.7 million will be made available to 36 hospitals across the state which have a high number o Medicaid patients or a high number of medical assistance recipients.  The governor was uncertain how much any of the 13 unionized hospitals in the city would receive.

headline: null
abstract: This picture shows Lt. Gov. William W. Scranton III inspecting a display of a power shovel for strip mining at McDade Park's Anthracite museum.

headline: Parkway East Lane Change Planned
abstract: A design error caused cracks to develop on the inbound lanes of the $58 million reconstruction project on 6.5 miles of the Parkway East in Pittsburgh.  PennDot is paying an estimated $1.5 million to repair the cracks and replace about 3 percent of the 8-inch thick concrete slabs poured the previous summer.  Another $200,000 is being spent to change construction methods so the same thing doesn’t happen again.  Traffic patterns are going to be changed in order to accommodate the repair.

headline: Rally opposes U.S. plan for subduing fire
abstract: Citizens and politicians rallied in Centralia, PA to protest a federal plan for extinguishing the 19-year old underground mine fire.  The plan calls for spending on exploratory drilling to find some boundaries of the fire, but the protestors believe that the fire should be completely outlined, which would better aid the fight.

headline: Compromise tried on reapportionment
abstract: PA Senators attempted a compromise on reapportionment, removing two plans that favored either Republican or Democratic territories, and set the stage for a conference committee to decide which two of the present 25 districts must be eliminated by voting down the Gallen amendments to Senate bill 805.  Both houses are in the process of choosing who will represent each on the committee.

headline: Reforms in no-fault a 'must' for state
abstract: The editorial states that Pennsylvania's no-fault insurance, now eight years old, needs some updating, particularly to take into account the inflation spiral since the law was passed in 1974. Some neighboring states have already started reforming the law, and the motorists seem to be pleased with the new arrangement.

headline: Asks restart issue be placed on ballot
abstract: The author is concerned that the question of whether to start TMI Unit 1 up again, has not yet been put on the ballot for the May primary election. The author believes that anybody interested in the future of Lancaster County, would want the issue of TMI to be placed on the ballot.

headline: Abortion restraints targeted
abstract: Planned Parenthood filed suit in U.S. Eastern District Court challenging the constitutionality of Pennsylvania's Abortion Control Act, which goes into effect on December 8th.  Representatives from Planned Parenthood say the law creates an atmosphere of deterrence and places multiple obstacles in the way of women who seek abortions.

headline: In some schools, asbestos remains a potential hazard
abstract: Two years after Congress declared that exposed asbestos in school buildings can pose a serious health hazard, the problem still exists in about one out of every five school districts in Pennsylvania.

headline: 22 Minutes Inside 'Sisi' Photographs 'hot' Unit 2 Sites
abstract: A 25-pound dynamo named "Sisi" made a foray into the Three Mile Island Unit 2 auxiliary building to survey cubicles considered too "hot" for its human counterparts.  The motorized, remote-controlled robot took photographs and made videotapes in two areas of the auxiliary building.  The two cubicles are inaccessible to humans because they contain highly radioactive ion-exchange filters contaminated during the March 1979 accident.  "Sisi," an acronym for System In-Service Inspection, is cable controlled and moves on treads.  It was supplied by the U.S. Department of Energy.  TMI technicians are able to guide "Sisi" using a television camera mounted between its treads.

headline: Pay now, or More Later
abstract: Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis pushed for an increase of 5 cents in the federal gas tax to pay for highways and public transit, but President Ronald Reagan put him off.  The rationale of the President and his top economic advisers was that a gas-tax hike would clutter the debate on the fiscal 1983 budget.  In reality, a gas-tax hike or some other kind of energy tax would have been a way of resolving some of the issues in the fiscal debate.

headline: Redistricting suit is rejected by U.S. judge
abstract: Saying that it was the legislature's responsibility to come up with a redistricting plan, a federal judge removed the lawsuit filed by Wayne Long.  The judge did, however, leave open the possibility of consideration by a federal court in Harrisburg.  Long was allowed to refile his suit after the deadline of February 16th had passed if there was not yet an approved redistricting plan.

headline: Computer voting; less fraud and lower cost
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioners are thinking of getting computer-run elections for the county. Although Dauphin has a history of not being an immediate adapter of new technology, using computers in elections makes a lot of sense as they reduce voter fraud as well as bring down the costs associated with running elections.

headline: Release of audit of local welfare termed 'unfair'
abstract: The PA Public Welfare Department has protested to Auditor General Al Benedict that his recent release of audit findings criticizing the Dauphin County Assistance Office unfairly depected current operating conditions.  John Cuddy, acting secretary for income maintainence, sent a letter noting that the office had not been sent the audit report or given chance to comment on it.

headline: Back on track in the Northeast; Millions at stake in efforts to create shortline
abstract: Due to changes in the 20th century, booming areas like Monroe County, Scranton region, etc. fell prey to an economic bust across the region. Consequently, rail service has deteriorated. However, currently there are negotiations taking place to create a shortline railroad tracks in both of these regions.

headline: Reactor walls in peril
abstract: According to a report issued by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the reactor walls of some nuclear power palnts are becoming brittle and may rupture if improvements are not made.  The report found no imminent danger, but suggested setting up a detailed system to examine each plant where the potential for rupture exists.

headline: Less Costly Telephones For Patient Use Backed
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission voted 4-1 that hospitals should use less costly residential phone service in patient rooms.  The vote endorsed a plea by the Hospital Association to have patient rooms slated for residential usage.

headline: 3 years after TMI
abstract: The expensive and dangerous accident that occurred three years ago at the Three Mile Island nuclear generator ended the idea of cheap nuclear power instantaneously. The author feels that it is now up to the federal government to take responsibility and show leadership, while taking future steps with regard to this reactor.

headline: PennDOT must pay in pothole injuries
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation has been ordered to pay $90,000 to a man who was impaled on a tree stump after his Jeep flipped on a pothole-filled road in Forward Township.

headline: Rendell Praises New System for Charging Suspects
abstract: District Attorney Edward G. Rendell mentioned that a new system of charging prisoners in Philadelphia will undoubtedly save the city money while helping to free people arrested in far less time.  During the first 10 days of the new system, Rendell’s office assumed the traditional police role of charging people with crimes, more than a quarter of the people arrested were freed without having to go through the formal arraignment before a judge.

headline: Concerns voices in Cabinet over 'New Federalism'
abstract: At least two of President Ronald Reagan's Cabinet, Secretary of Health Richard Schweiker and Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis, have raised questions about the proposal to shuffle federal and state programs.  They fear that complete federal control of Medicaid and Medicare may lay the groundwork for national healthcare under a future president.

headline: Remap Returns To Court
abstract: Pennsylvania’s controversial congressional reapportionment plan returned to the courtroom for a panel of three federal judges to consider arguments on its legality.  The redistricting plan, approved by the Republican-controlled Legislature, was challenged by U.S. Representative Doug Walgren, on grounds that it sapped minority voting strength and needlessly split municipalities.  Another reason the plan was attacked was because it used slightly erroneous population figures to pare the number of Pennsylvania members of the U.S. House from 25 to 23 to reflect national population shifts.

headline: Ballet: Pennsylvanians open season in Brooklyn
abstract: The Pennsylvania Ballet opened Tuesday night at the Brooklyn Academy of Music with a program entitled "In celebration of women choreographers" that consisted entirely of modern-dance works. Similarly, the other programs scheduled this season will follow the theme of modern-dance works.

headline: Deer On Demand; Espionage Target
abstract: Although the Communist Party has blamed air, noise and water pollution on the capitalist system, pollution is being recognized as a serious problem in many Soviet-bloc nations.  This article asks on whom the Soviet-block countires will spy for a solution to the problems posed by pollution.

headline: License Revocation of West Shore Dentist is Up
abstract: A Commonwealth Court Panel in a split decision upheld the license revocation of a West Shore dentist ordered by the State Dental Council and Examining Board for "gross malpractice and unprofessional conduct."  Judge Genevieve Blatt, said the decision to revoke the license of Dr. William Kundrat of Lower Allen Twp., was too harsh a penalty for a first offense in which the patient was "made whole" through an award of damages.

headline: 45 Bank group agrees to continue credit for Met-Ed
abstract: A 45-bank consortium agreed to extend short-term credit to Metropolitan Edison, part owner of Three Mile Island.  William Kuhns, chairman of the General Public Utilities Cooperation, explained Three Mile Island's positive financial outlook to the bank executives at the Ctibank offices in New York.  The banks will reconsider their involvement in April when a tax payment by Metropolitan Edison is due.

headline: PennDOT Oks Study of Route 42 Bridge
abstract: District 3 of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has authorized Gannett Fleming Transportation Engineers Inc.  of Camp Hill to proceed with a $210,000 preliminary engineering study of a new bridge over the North Branch of the Susquehanna River along Route 42.  The bridge would cost around $12 million, not including rights-of-way and engineering fees, and will be placed in PennDOT’s 12-year-plan update.

headline: Reporter at Large
abstract: Certainly there is too much crime these days, but the punitive backlash is getting extreme, too.  Pennsylvania is trying to outdo New Jersey in borrowing money to build more jail cells.  Defense attorneys eat sirloin on fees from the privileged, the Legislature raises minimum sentences to apply mainly to the underprivileged, and law and order is a growth industry.

headline: Confirmation Rule Queried
abstract: The General Assembly is considering a change in the way members of state agencies are chosen.  Under the present law, commissioners are nominated by the Governor, and confirmed by two-thirds of the Senate.

headline: Remedies sought for pension fund
abstract: This article talks about the various features of Bill 1141, that has been instituted as a remedy for the pension fund. It includes provisions like the 12-member investment advisory board and other requirements of the fund.

headline: Billy Joel Keeps His Promise
abstract: Bill Joel sang to victims of the steel industry's problems yesterday, fulfilling a promise to perform his latest hit, "Allentown" in the region.

headline: Foeign Aid That Never Makes Headlines
abstract: The Washington D.C.-based partners of the Americas has been helping Latin American countries in many critical, but often unnoticed, ways.  Recently, the group was responsible for delivering hand-operated water pumps to poor Nicaraguans, allowing them to bring up uncontaminated water 15 feet below ground level.  Partners is involved in many similar projects throughout Latin American.

headline: Medicare Supplement Program is Approved
abstract: The state Insurance Department approved a new Medicare supplemental insurance program for western Pennsylvania designed to offer the elderly services at a reduced rate.  Insurance Commissioner Michael Brownie said some 280,000 western Pennsylvania subscribers to the "65 Special" program would be eligible to buy the new program beginning on October 1st.  It would allow senior citizens to purchase additional insurance for medical expenses not covered by Medicare or "65 Special." The program calls for a yearly deductible of $250, with the insured paying 20 percent of all costs covered under the plan.

headline: 9 mile 2 plant consultants' fees cited
abstract: The utility companies building the Nine Mile Two nuclear plant paid 13 consultants $336,168 for testimony at a hearing to examine rising costs at the plant, according to the Public Service Commission.  The Commission is expected to vote to continue construction of the plant, whose costs are expected to exceed $5 billion.  It is expected that the consultant fees will be passed along to consumers in the form of a future rate hike.

headline: PennDOT Pothole Hotline cooling off in midstate in '82
abstract: The number of calls reporting potholes in the eight-county southcentral region have fallen in 1982 when compared to the previous year. Officials attribute this to the effective functioning of the pothole patching crews during February.

headline: Right Problem, Wrong Solution
abstract: Delaware County Judge Joseph Furia offers a commendable but inappropriate defense for the high cost of divorce in Delaware County.  He thinks that affordable divorce is not good for the country.  If it is to be the policy of the Commonwealth to discourage divorce, then that policy should be established as a law in all counties by the legislature.  It should not be the option of a local judge or band of lawyers.  If the Commonwealth should enact statutes making divorce difficult, the statutes should not merely make it expensive.  That would merely make divorces available to the rich and not the poor.  Finally, if the Commonwealth should ever find it necessary to impose a special tax on divorces, the tax funds should not be diverted to serve a special interest group.  As it is now, the Delaware County Bar Association collects $38 from each divorcing couple.

headline: Confusing districts
abstract: Editorial criticizes the way the state legislative districts were drawn because they did not take into regard municipal and county lines.  The districts were approved by the PA Supreme Court because they were equal in population.

headline: Rep. Dougherty threatens switch of party registration to Democrat
abstract: US Representative Charles Dougherty (R-Pa) is unhappy with the proposed reapportionment of his district and the urban policies of President Ronald Reagan.  Consequently, he may switch parties.

headline: Carnage on route 30
abstract: Treacherous Route 30, east of the City of Lancaster, has claimed two more lives - a mother and her daughter driving to a medical appointment. These days bring the total to 24 in the past five years. despite the concerns of the people in that area, the administration has not done anything to build a roadway adequate to the needs of that area.

headline: Groups Seek Injunction Against Abortion
abstract: Planned Parenthood filed suit in federal court challenging the constitutionality of Pennsylvania'a anti-abortion law.  The law requires a 24-hour waiting period before a woman can get an abortion, and also requires consent from at least one parent if the woman is younger than 18 years of age.

headline: Mental health month: Observance to focus on emotional fitness for everyone
abstract: May has been set aside by the Mental Health Association in Cumberland, Dauphin and Perry Counties Inc. for the theme "Mental health is for everybody". It also warns that mental fitness is an ongoing concern for the community at large.

headline: A happy face; GPU's annual report accentuates the positive
abstract: Although most analysts regard the situation faced by General Public Utilities Corp. (GPU), which owns the crippled Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear plant, to be dismal, the company in its latest annual report paints a rosy picture of 1981. it mentions that the groundwork has been prepared for improved finances and better prospects.

headline: PennDOT seeks funds to rebuild span in Lemoyne
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is seeking $1 million in federal funds to reconstruct the Third Street Bridge over the Harrisburg Expressway in Lemoyne as an additional part of the ongoing South Bridge - Interstate 83 widening and improvement project.

headline: Saturday court sessions a good idea
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell wants to keep the justice system moving at a faster pace by pushing courts to stay open on Saturday.  He has the support of President Judge Ed Bradley for this decision.  However, Phiadelphia Common Pleas Judge Ray Kremer believes this is just an attempt of Rendell to put the blame for the court backlog on the judges themselves.  Rendell's plan should be supported.

headline: Congressman Gray charges: Stone did not tell the truth about poll
abstract: In this letter to the editor PA Congressman Bill Gray responds to a Philadelphia Tribune article in which Chuck Stone slams his record.  Congressman Gray notes a poll used by Chuck Stone conducted by CABL (Committee for Accountable Black Leadership) that was supposed to be independent but actually had the cooperation of Stone, actually meeting at his house on a few occasions.

headline: Rep. Freind, Thornburgh to discuss abortion bill
abstract: PA Representative Stephen Freind is meeting with PA Governor Dick Thornburgh regarding a new, restrictive abortion bill.

headline: Caseworkers say layoffs hurt clients
abstract: According to two Office of Vocational Rehabilitation (OVR counselors), the Thornburgh administration is overlooking the needs of the handicapped community in its efforts to reduce the OVR staff by 25%.

headline: State to probe Rankin project
abstract: Due to projected increases in student enrollment, a Woodland Hills school director is asking the state Department of Education to examine the district's plan to build an addition to the Rankin Elementary School.

headline: 'Mismanagement' hit in nutrition program
abstract: A recent legislative report says the state's handling of a federal nutrition program WIC (Women Infants Children) had severe administrative problems, including at least $1 million in overspending for administrative costs to the state, but under spent federal program funds by $7.5 million.  PA Health Department Secretary H. Arnold Muller acknowledged the problem but said that they had been addressed.

headline: A Tax on Coal?
abstract: The disheartening increase in coal-mine sites abandoned by bankrupt or unscrupulous operators poses a problem that Pennsylvania must solve if it is not to forfeit regulatory control in this area to the federal government.  This is the warning Peter Duncan, Secretary of Environmental Resources had for the PA Senate Environmental Resources Committee.  A system of permit fees and bonding requirements geared to the sedate abandonment pace of the 1970s has fallen behind with 2,200 acres defaulted in 1979; 3,200 in 1980; and 1,800 in 1981.  Pennsylvania is the only major coal state without a severance tax.  This is due to worries that the tax would fall on Pennsylvanians because PA-mined coal is heavily used within the state and not exported.

headline: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation Notice of Project Initiation Final Design Studies
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has initiated the preparation of Final Design studies and plans for L.R. 1010 (Interstate 476), Sections 100 and 200, Delaware County.  The project is commonly referred to as the “Mid-County Expressway”, or the “Blue Route”  A series of Public Informational Meetings will be held throughout Final Design in order to provide the public with an opportunity to discuss the project with the Department and the Consultant; to be informed of the status of the project and the overall study approach; and to provide comments on issues related to the Final design construction activities.

headline: Schweiker replies; Parents' role must be included
abstract: This letter points out the importance in bringing the parents into the issue of teenage pregnancy through the proposed regulation directing federally funded clinics to notify parents when they have given prescription birth control drugs or devices to children under 18. The author feels that involving parents in this issue, is a vital step towards curtailing the rise in teenage pregnancy.

headline: Congressmen-elect Get Ready For New Jobs
abstract: The article details the orientation and adjustment process of several new U.S. representatives from PA, including Tom Ridge, Bob Borski, and Peter Kostmayer. This includes comments from the new representatives about adjusting to multiple meetings, committee assignments, and logistics, such as finding parking.

headline: Rep. Marks won't seek 4th term
abstract: US Representative Marc Marks will not seek a 4th term in Congress because of a chronic back ailment.  He said that he cannot undertake a re-election campaign because of frequent back pain which prevents him from walking or standing for any time.  He will return to a law practice when his term is over.

headline: Ch. 10 Punished enough; WCAU's name soiled, not mayor's
abstract: The recent accusation that Mayor Green was the target of a federal investigation over charges that he had received a $50,000 bribe from a sewage firm was first reported by WCAU-TV, citing unnamed sources. However, after finding out that this was false and that not enough research had been done, Channel 10 apologized for this mistake. Mayor Green is now threatening a lawsuit on the TV station.

headline: Centralia Fire Jumps Barriers
abstract: For the first time in 13 years, the Centralia mine fire has penetrated an underground barrier and left a 200-foot wide portion of burning coal under a section of the town.  Officials say evacuations are not yet necessary, but people will need to monitor closely levels of carbon monoxide and other gases in their homes.

headline: Misstatements on sickle cell
abstract: The author believes that the recent article in "Sickle-cell sufferers and narcotics" was extremely biased and demonstrated a lack of knowledge of the specific disease in question and treatment of patients with chronic diseases.

headline: A vote-no campaign under way on restart
abstract: Kathy McCaughlin says that an upcoming referendum on the restart of the Unit 1 reactor at Three Mile Island should not be viewed as a make-or-break opinion on nuclear power.  GPU Nuclear Corporation, which runs TMI, says that the proposed referendum is not binding, and was unable to comment on it.

headline: Perilous gap in railway safety
abstract: A train accident in Bucks County, PA raises question of responsibility for commuter train tracks in that area.  The track was previously operated by Conrail, but now that it is operated by Southeastern PA Transit Authority; the Federal Railroad Administration does not have jurisdiction since it is a regional line.  The PA Public Utility Commission is also investigating but its attorneys are not sure they have jurisdiction at places on the track other than railroad crossings.

headline: Secrecy Undermines Trust in Larsen Investigation
abstract: The secrecy surrounding the investigation into allegations of misconduct by Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen should gravely trouble every lawyer and judge in Pennsylvania who would like to persuade a justifiably skeptical public that the legal profession is committed to or capable of holding itself to a reasonable standard of integrity.

headline: Democrats' big names dropping out
abstract: Former Pittsburgh Mayor Pete Flaherty's decision not to run for governor removes the last of the early favorites of the Democrats to vie for that position.  Philadelphia Senator James Lloyd and PA Representative Allen Ertel are the next to be considered for the race.

headline: Rep. Rostenkowski covers his tracks
abstract: Rep. Doug Walgreen (D-Penn) charged House Way and Means Committee Chairman Dan Rostenkowski of altering his remarks in the Congressional Record to make it appear such that he had mentioned to his fellow representatives that the tax breaks were buried in the black lung bill, before they voted.

headline: Child of God
abstract: The author of this letter believes that the parents of the mentally retarded child who was put to death, will never know the joy of raising a truly special child of God, as these parents have.

headline: They Roasted Judge, Won in Court
abstract: Two lawyers who took part in and helped arrange a "roast" of Philadelphia Common Pleas Judge Stanley M. Greenberg won multi-million dollar settlements in his courtroom not long after the roast.  Judge Greenberg did not believe the roast constituted a breach of ethics, and argued that the code of Judicial Conduct does not prohibit a judge from being honored by lawyers who practice before him.

headline: New Cumberland woman appointed to health position
abstract: Luceille E. Fleming, a specialist in drug and alcohol abuse programs, has been appointed by Gov. Thornburgh as a deputy secretary for drug and alcohol programs in the Department of Health. She is currently the Executive Director of the Alcoholism and Addiction Association of Pennsylvania.

headline: A Wall Street view of TMI's problem
abstract: Uncertainty over the cause of a broken steam tube in the mostly functional Unit 1 Reactor of Three Mile Island is threatening a financial recovery plan by the plant's owner, the General Public Utilities Corporation.  As soon as the plant is restarted, the company would save $14 million per month in costs associated with obtaining replacement power.  A recently approved rate increase assumed that the plant would be operational again soon, however this may not be the case.  If so, rates for customers are expected to go up.

headline: PGW asks for $58 million rate hike
abstract: The Philadelphia Gas Works filed a request with the Philadelphia Gas Commission yesterday for a $58 million increase in gas rates, which the utility says it must have to finance operations, delinquent customer accounts and meet debt payments.

headline: Sees handgun ban as bad precedent
abstract: A court upholds the decision of a City Council to deny a community the right to own handguns in a high crime area.  In this letter to the editor, the author laments that this will hamper his ability to carry a handgun.

headline: Consumer Party Looks to Tucker
abstract: null

headline: Republicans uproot a struggling thorn
abstract: Alvin Joseph Jacobson has proved that anyone with $50 and time to spend can take part in the gubernatorial elections. Although he ran unsuccessfully during 1974 and 1978, he is back in the race again. However, this has raised doubts on whether it is too easy to get on the ballot.

headline: Concerned about funding
abstract: The authors state that their child, who was born with learning difficulties, has greatly benefited from the services of the Lancaster-Lebanon IU for over 4 years. However, with the Governor's plan for educational block grants, they are not sure of their child will continue to get the special that he needs.

headline: In Bucks, a test of Reaganomics
abstract: In Pennsylvania's 8th District Congressional race, Democratic candidate Kostmayer has tried to associate the incumbent, Coyne, with the policies of Reaganomics specifically, and the policies of the Reagan administration generally.  Coyne claims his voting record is squarely in the middle, however.

headline: Nurse shortage
abstract: Editorial notes a recent report by the National Commission on Nursing that reveals that the shortage of nurses is both wide-spread and growing.  He urges the health care establishment to do everything possible to seek to reduce the turn-over among registered nurses and to encourage more women and men to enter the nursing ranks.

headline: Another setback for TMI
abstract: Extensive cracking within steam generator tubes in Three Mile Island's (TMI) Unit 1 Reactor and uncertainty over the cause will potentially damage the financial recovery plan set forth by the owner of TMI, General Public Utilities Corporation.  There is no estimate as to the repair costs yet, but the plan will be shut down for a period of 6-12 months.

headline: Piccola defends PennDOT on ramp
abstract: PA Representative Piccola responds to a letter from Susquehanna Board president Jack Pincus to PA Department of Transportation complaining that PennDOT has not held up an agreement to finish work on Interstate 81 in the Susquehanna area.  Piccola states that PennDOT has done nothing to demonstrate that it does not intend to finish the proposed work.  PennDOT says that permanent work on the ramp is scheduled for Fall of 1983.

headline: Smoother Way for Adoptions
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh passed a new law that reduces the time required for the court to take approval of an adoption.  Under the new law, the natural parents may ask the court to terminate their rights within 30 days, the court hearing would be held in 10 days, and the entire process could be completed in 43 days.  If the natural parents don’t terminate their rights voluntarily within 40 days, the adoptive parents may seek involuntary termination, the court hearing would be held in 10 days, and the procedure could be completed in 53 days.

headline: Consumer Party Looks to Tucker
abstract: The Consumer Party offered C. DeLores Tucker, one of Pennsylvania’s leading black Democrats, the opportunity to run as the party’s candidate for State Senate in Philadelphia’s Fourth Senatorial District.  In recent days, Tucker has been under intense pressure from prominent black Democrats, to stay out of the race.  Her entry into the race would dramatically alter a contest that some politicians believe would determine which of the major parties will control the Senate in 1983.  The Republicans now have a 26-24 majority.

headline: Right-win leaders to push Hart nomination
abstract: Right wing leaders are convinced that they are being kept out of the administration of President Ronald Reagan, and have vowed to fight to place Reverend B. Samuel Hart on the US Civil Rights Commission.  The nomination has run into opposition from Democrats and some Republicans while Senators John Heinz and Arlen Spector look into Hart's past.

headline: Dems plan dinner
abstract: Around 700 people are expected to attend a Democratic Campaign Committee $75-a-plate fund-raiser that is happening tomorrow at the Pittsburgh Hilton.

headline: Cut out clipping
abstract: In order to avoid clipping at saftey-inspection garages, the state could either get rid of annual inspections or have the PA State Police conduct them.  Getting rid of inspections will not, as empirical data clearly shows, increase auto accidents.

headline: Nursing school stays open
abstract: The Central PA Nursing Education Consortium Incorporated worked with the state to succeed in keeping open the School of Nursing at Phillipsburg State General Hospital.  The state has agreed to lease the nursing school facilities to the consortium and provide certain services, including maintenance and utilities; other costs not met by tuition will be paid by the three consortium hospitals.  The Consortium says that it is necessary to keep open the school because local hosptials rely on its graduates.

headline: Anti-Nuke Nonsense
abstract: At a recent Three Mile Island rally, the writer of this editorial observed a spokesman for the group smoking his pipe while explaining his concern for his children.  If he knew that over 10,000 deaths have been documented as caused by pipe smoking, and at this writing, not so much as one pigeon has been reported lost due to TIM, his concern for the future generations would be directed toward abstinence from tobacco.

headline: Plan to save 'Burg-Warren railroad line is annouced
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and State Representative William Clinger announced a plan to save the railine between Johnsonburg and Warren.  A partnership would purchase the line from Conrail, which has marked the line for abandonment, and would then operate the line with Sloan Cornell which operates a similar line near Gettysburg.  The Warren County Industrial Development Authority will finance the plan with industrial revenue bonds based on the line's operating profit.

headline: Speeding devices: court clears way for local use
abstract: Dauphin County Judge William Lipsitt declared that police in Dauphin County may legally employ electronic timing devices to apprehend motorists who break speed laws.  A lower court agreed with the defendant, saying municipalities should adopt ordinances authorizing the use of such devices and post warnings for speed traps.  However, Judge Lipsitt's decision overturned the earlier ruling and hopefully paved the way for local law enforcement officials to catch up to law breakers.

headline: Consumer Party Wins Ballot Status
abstract: The Pennsylvania Consumer Party got enough votes in November's election to automatically get on the PA ballot in future elections. The article details the procedure for achieving such status as well as the party's previous attempts to do so.

headline: Rizzo loses two; Rocks, Foglietta beat Frank's friends
abstract: Former Mayor Frank Rizzo and former City Councilman Al Pearlman watch grim returns in the recent election.

headline: Examiner: Shooting death of Rep. Aden's daughter was a suicide
abstract: The Delaware County Medical Examiner ruled the shooting death of the teenage daughter of Rep. John Alden (R., Delaware) as a suicide.

headline: A New Superintendent
abstract: New Philadelphia school superintendent Dr. Constance Clayton has her work cut out for her; the district is facing spending cuts and budgetary problems, and the school system's top-level administration is fraught with politics and favoritism.  When dealing with all these challenges, she must remember: "The Children come first."

headline: O'Bannon Defends Welfare's Policy; State slow in paying health claims
abstract: Medicaid doctors wait twice as long to receive state reimbursements as do providers in other states according to a PA House legislative and budget committee report.

headline: Anti-nukes out of bounds
abstract: Judith M. Dykes, a proponent of nuclear energy writes to remind anti-nuclear proponents that if they want to be taken seriously, they should act more professionally. She resents the suggestion that nuclear power would endanger children and future generations.

headline: Public supports once-a-year inspections
abstract: A steady tide of public opinion is swamping organized opposition to a bill that cuts auto safety inspections to once a year.  Senate Majority Whip John Stauffer said that he and other senators have reservations about the legislation, but will bow to constituents' demands to pass it.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh believes that it will save consumers approximately $61 million per year.

headline: State High Court Undermining Ethics Law
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has not been kind to the Pennsylvania Ethics Law since its enactment in 1978.  The most recent ruling concerned the so-called "revolving door"section of the ethics law.  That section prohibits a former public official or public employee from representing persons on any matter before the governmental body with which the official or employee has been associated for one year after he leaves that body.  The Supreme Court ruled that the revolving door section is unconstitutional when applied to lawyers working at the State Public Utility Commission.  There was no written opinion to support the court’s decision, only an order finding the section unconstitutional.

headline: Cost Reduction Study Puts Shrink on State Government
abstract: In 1979, Governor Dick Thornburgh put a number of his Cabinet members on a new Cost Reduction Study Team and observers wondered if it would be just a another paper pushing effort.  It wasn't according to the statistics issued by Thornburgh's office.  In three years, the team cut enough fat from the bureaucracy and implemented enough improvements to come up with savings that now total about $200 million a year.

headline: Rizzo opens new office for 'talk'
abstract: Former Mayor Frank Rizzo has yet to officially declare his candidacy.  Officially running for Philadelphia Mayor is Former City Controller Thomas Leonard. City Managing Director W. Wilson Goode is also expected run, and it is said that District Attorney Ed Rendell is considering a run as well.

headline: Farm show upgrading ok'd
abstract: Facilities at the Farm Show Complex that is to be used by the Future Farmers of America and Future Homemakers of America has been approved by the Pennsylvania State Farm Products Show Commission. Officials will be spending around $10,000 to improve housing for youth participating in activities held at the complex.

headline: The Forum: Back to School
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the president of the Pennsylvania State Education Association responds to a Patriot News editorial that criticized gubernatorial candidate Allen Ertel's tax and education plans.  The author argues that the Patriot News fails to understand the school subsidy system in Pennsylvania.  Moreover, the Patriot News fails to provide a balanced assessment of the candidates' tax plans.

headline: Osteopathic support unit due by December
abstract: Community General Osteopathic Hospital's advanced life-support system will be functioning by the end of December, making Dauphin County the first Midstate county to be served by ALS units.

headline: A-plant mishap briefly releases nuclear steam
abstract: A tube burst in an upstate New York nuclear power plant causing small puffs of radioactive steam to spurt into the atmosphere and caused thousands of gallons of radioactive water to spill into a drainage area on the plant floor.  A series of precautionary measures were put into effect, and officials said the radiation poses no danger to health.  The plant shut down automatically, and will remain offline for repairs for 6-8 weeks.

headline: PUC Wants Local Firm To Resume Bus Service
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) wants bus service between Washington County and downtown Pittsburgh to be resumed by Suburban Lines Inc. instead of the company that bought it Short Way Lines Inc. The replacement of suburban drivers and mechanics by inexpereinced Short Way drivers and mechanics has resulted in several accidents and numerous late buses.

headline: State House Turns Down Prison, Parole Reforms
abstract: Prison and parole reforms were voted down by the PA House of Representatives.  The House rejected 47-140 compromise legislation that packed a Cabinet level Department of Corrections and a revision of the parole system into a bill originally dealing with prison visitors.  The governor will continue to push for the reforms.  The bill would have abolished the Board of Probation and Parole and replaced it with a Revocation Board.

headline: County breakdown of Dems' senate vote
abstract: This article gives the county-by-county vote in the Democratic primary for the US Senate.

headline: Rizzo Questioned at Larsen Hearing
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo testified before a panel called to review charges of ethnical misconduct by the PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen.  Larsen is accused of being in violation of the canons of judicial ethnics, unsuccessfully worked to defeat Nix in the Supreme Court justice’s re-election campaign last year. He may have also improperly aided the 1979 election campaign of Justice P. Flaherty.

headline: First ladies of the South
abstract: Extensive article detailing the contributions by each of the first ladies in the areas of mental health, education, the environment, and other projects in their states.

headline: Nuclear anxiety and expense
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) says Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor is seriously affected by an embrittlement problem.  The problem, which is caused by the bombardment of radiation, could lead to a core meltdown--the most serious type of accident a nuclear plant can sustain.  The NRC says the problem does not warrant immediate action, but simply additional study and review.

headline: PA measles program lacks only a method
abstract: Measles, one of the most preventable diseases, it continues to remain a problem for PA and about 10 other states. There have been about eight multi-case outbreaks of measles in PA in the last 2 years. However, the article suggests that this problem is more bureaucratic and political than it is medical.

headline: Arguments Against State Coal Use Do Not Hold Up
abstract: The Governor’s Energy Council says that Pennsylvania could be the OPEC of coal.  It’s true.  But before it happens, Pennsylvania must sincerely believe it themselves.  Federal regulations state that for every 100 tons of generic coal that is burned, about one ton of sulfur dioxide is released into the atmosphere.  Two things determine the amount of sulfur dioxide released: the amount of sulfur in the coal and the amount of energy in the coal.

headline: Rail Freight Service to Continue in Morrison's
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration and state Senator Robert C. Jubelirer announced a $130,000 cooperative venture by private industry and the Commonwealth to continue rail freight service on lines earmarked for abandonment by Conrail and save over 200 jobs in the Morrison's Cove-Martinsburg Blair Country area.

headline: State house vote may kill spousal rape bill
abstract: The House, by a 102-87 vote,  has shelved a bill which would make it a crime for a man to rape his wife in Pennsylvania. Opponents of the bill believe that it would be used as a tool to blackmail their husbands, rather than aiding abused women.

headline: County Job in Jeopardy? Wecht Faces Severe Test in Election
abstract: The U.S. senatorial election may be the most crucial on the ballot because both major candidates appear to be staking their careers on the results.  If U.S. Senator John Heinz loses to Cyril Wecht, the Republican incumbent can forget the White House.  On the other hand, if Dr. Wecht is defeated, his presidential ambitions will also be in limbo.

headline: Roldan Named to HRC post by Thornburgh
abstract: Harrisburg attorney Alberto Roldan was nominated by Governor Dick Thornburgh to serve on the PA Human Relations Commission.  He is a former director of Research Associates, a legal research firm in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and has served as counselor in the training and development branch of the New Cumberland Army Depot.  Thornburgh also nominated Rev. Carl E. Denson of Bethel Park, and Alvin E. Echols of Philadelphia.

headline: GOP's M. Harvey Taylor dies at 105, ending era
abstract: Former State Senator M. Harvey Taylor of Harrisburg died at his home in the Susquehanna Township at the age of 105. He is survived by his daughter and son.

headline: Council candidates face public hearing
abstract: Harrisburg City Council candidates are set to appear at a public hearing.

headline: Parents testify state's mental system harmful
abstract: Parents of retarded children testified before a state Senate committee that recent federal court decisions and bureaucratic red tape had endangered their children and society by removing them from institutions and placing them in community settings.

headline: Assembly Leaves with Work to Do: Taxes, PUC Funds Held Until Fall
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) lacks a budget for the fiscal year beginning July 1.  The fate of several other major legislative proposals remain uncertain as members of the Pennsylvania General Assembly head out for a summer recess of at least three months.

headline: Rail line fills a need
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority (SEPTA) took control of the Newtown-Fox Chase rail line from Conrail, and there has been a worker strike and two accidents.  However, riders are still confident in SEPTA's ability to run the trains efficiently, and believe that SEPTA acted responsibly and promptly after the two accidents.

headline: State Prison Chief: Relief in '85 for Bursting Jails
abstract: Ronald J. Marks is the Commissioner of the PA Bureau of Correction.  He oversees the state’s nine correctional institutions and their 10,200 inmates.  Last year, he watched Pennsylvania’s total prison population increase by 14 percent.  About 464 of the prison’s 1,608 inmates are double-celled.  The cage-like units measure by 6 feet by 8 feet; many prisoners have spread and tied long-sleeved shirts to the bottom halves of their cell doors in a meager attempt at privacy.  There is some sort of relief coming because a state Legislature appropriation will finance the building of 2,380 new cells.  There is a future concern that the prison population will continue to rise and people will stay longer mostly due to the baby-boom generation that has matured into the “crime prone” age, thereby partially causing an increase in violent crimes.

headline: Court asks redistricting panel: Many questions remain in impasse
abstract: US District Court Judge Sylvia Rambo took the first step in a process that would have the federal courts take over the redistricting process from the State Legislature.  The Court of Appeals for the Third District will create a 3-judge panel to create new districts while reducing the state from 25 congressional districts to 23.  The state legislature will still have more time to complete redistricting on its own, however.

headline: Ross Official Hired At Mall He Backed
abstract: Ross Commissioner Charles Earnest earned money from the architectural firm that helped design Ross Park Center. Earnest was later injured on a routine tour of the Ross Park Center site and eventually filed a claim through the architectural firm. Although he does not recall who he worked for at the time and denies ever filing a claim, Earnest does not believe he has a conflict of interest. Earnest voted twice to rezone land for the project.

headline: Great fishing, wild beauty
abstract: The author states that the stretch of the Clarion River between Coksburg in Cook forest and the Mill Creek Access area is one of the most beautiful streams in Pennsylvania. It also offers the finest smallmouth bass fishing in the state.

headline: Mondale, stumping in PA, criticizes Reaganomics
abstract: Former Vice President Walter Mondale was in Pennsylvania promoting the campaigns of several Democratic candidates.  He accused the Reagan administration of implementing radical economic policies that have brought the nation close to depression.

headline: Senate bill would OK disputed cancer therapy
abstract: A new but controversial therapy for cancer patients - immunoaugmentative - would become legal in Pennsylvania under a bill introduced on Wednesday by 23 state senators. However, the Federal Drug Administration has not approved this therapy yet.

headline: Beaver Valley N-Plant OK for Now, Firm Says
abstract: The Beaver Valley nuclear plant in Beaver County faces no immediate problems with the kind of radiation bombardment that is said to cause a reactor’s walls to become dangerously brittle.  The Shippingport reactor was one of eight in a Nuclear Regulatory Commission study saying reviews and repairs costing each plant as much as $20 million would be necessary to combat the problem.

headline: Rail Teamwork
abstract: There is a public-private effort to save a stretch of railroad in Export abandoned by Conrail.  Dura-Bond Protective Coating Co. and the state are investing more than $500,000 to keep the trains running and to save at least 700 jobs.  Governor Dick Thornburgh thought it symbolized his administration’s progressive drive toward teamwork with industry, but also typifies the Republican action plan for Pennsylvania and the nation.

headline: State Senate Approves Funding for Domestic Crisis, Rape Shelters
abstract: The House and Senate both approved legislation opening the door to direct state funding for rape crisis and domestic violence centers.  If the governor passes the law, the centers would be eligible for $1.5 million in state funds during the following fiscal year.

headline: Court gives pension to Cianfrani
abstract: The PA Supreme Court, in a 4-2 vote, yesterday ruled that state officials convicted of bribery and extortion are entitled to state pensions if they were vested before 1978. The decision means that former state officials like state Senator Henry "Buddy" Cianfrani, convicted of crimes, can receive lifetime pensions and health benefits.

headline: Saccone, Miller Are Given Key Posts
abstract: Dr. Nicholas D. Saccone has been named president-elect of the 6,3000 member Pennsylvania Dental Association.  Attorney David B. Miller has been named to a new National Motor Carrier Advisory Committee by U.S. Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis.

headline: Green denounces report he is target of US probe
abstract: Mayor Green, in a televised conference, said that he was outraged at a Channel 10 news report that said he was a target of a federal investigation on alleged kickbacks. US Attorney Peter Vaira issued a statement saying that Mayor Green was not subject to any investigation of this sort. However, there have been unconfirmed reports that an investigation is currently underway.

headline: In congress' 7th District: Re-elect Robert W. Edgar
abstract: In the 7th District congressional race, the Philadelphia Inquirer endorses the incumbent candidate, Robert W. Edgar.  Congressman Edgar is running against Steve Joachim, a Springfield Township Commissioner.  Congressman Edgar is a proven leader who stands up for the most vulnerable in society, and he has shown a commitment to garnering bipartisan support.

headline: Senate changes mind, passes bill that offers a definition of death
abstract: The state Senate reversed its earlier decision and passed the controversial "definition of death" bill. This bill is intended to provide physicians with a clear definition of death in cases in which a patient's brain has stopped functioning but the rest of the body is maintained by life-support systems.

headline: Bell leads off hearing, calls rate bid 'valid'
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania has proposed a $426 million rate increase and attributed this to cover the cost of inflation, competition, high interest rates and technological advances. Bell attorney Dan Whelan told Public Utility Commission Administrative law Judge Charles Hoffman that the company was in a very disturbing financial condition.

headline: Rail Unions Say They'll Stay On Job
abstract: Rail union leaders say that they will come to work on January first even if a contract with SEPTA has not been reached. SEPTA argues that it needs to reduce some wages and reform work rules in order to avoid deficits that would force commuter rail lines to shut down. The rail unions claim that they have gotten good pay and work rules over years of bargaining and that they should not have to give them up. If SEPTA needs more money, the unions observe, it should ask the government for it.

headline: State's Legal Aid For Poor Survives
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh said the commonwealth will continue to fund a statewide system of legal services for the poor.  The administration also warned the Pennsylvania Legal Services Center, which administers the statewide program, to curtail “activities in furtherance of political causes.”  The legal services office was also told to cut down their bureaucracy.

headline: Court Intervention Looms: Senate May Move on Reapportionment Plan
abstract: The threat of Federal court intervention may prompt state lawmakers to act on a congressional reapportionment plan stalled because of partisan bickering over how the new districts will be drawn.  All together, the PA Senate shot down 7 different plans before taking a one-week break on February 11.  The strategy now is to get the entire Republican vote, which by itself would be enough to pass the Senate.

headline: Sacred Relationships
abstract: A bill to remove Federal Trade Commission regulation of medical providers passed in the U.S. House. There is a correlation between those who voted for the removal and those who received large amounts of money from the medical industry. Advocates say the states can regulate these professions better, even though such agencies are controlled by the people they regulate. It's all about greed, that of the medical industry and of members of Congress. It is up to the U.S. Senate to keep this bill from going any further.

headline: Green: It's a lie; Mayor blasts channel 10 report of bribe
abstract: This photograph shows an angry Mayor Green arguing with Channel 10 reporter Bill Baldini, during a heated City Hall press conference.

headline: Senator Street says judge's ruling vindicates him
abstract: State Senator T. Milton Street, who plans to run for Congress, claims that he was vindicated when Common Pleas Judge Charles Lord ruled that the state must prove the exact amount of sales tax he owes on hot dogs he sold in the 1970s.  Street admitted that he did owe taxes, but claims the amount is much less than the state Department of Revenue suggests.

headline: Senate Panel Oks Bill to Allow Use of Experimental Cancer Treatment
abstract: The Senate Health and Welfare Committee approved a bill allowing Pennsylvania’s hospitals and doctors to practice immuno-augmentative therapy, known as IAT, without reprisals from authorities or state medical boards.  Senator Richard Snyder is the prime sponsor of the bill, which is also backed by 23 state senators.

headline: Breakthrough
abstract: Letter to the editor: The writer supports the decision of a US Appeals Court to halt the restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor.  The writer suggests that reactivating Unit 1 at TMI and the initiation of a new reactor at Limerick should be halted until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission can prove that they can solve the problem with the TMI Unit 2 reactor.

headline: Reconstructing the Schuylkill
abstract: The author believes that in response to the proposed reconstruction of the Schuylkill Expressway, it is important that there is a dialogue throughout the region concerning this significant undertaking by the PennDOT, before it is undertaken.

headline: State's Prison Population Rose by Record Rate
abstract: Pennsylvania’s prison population increased by 14 percent in 1981, this is resulting in the double-ceiling of inmates in every correctional facility for the first time, according to the PA Bureau of Correction’s 1981 Annual Statistical Report.  State Correction Commissioner Ronald J. Marks announced that the total population in the state’s nine prisons and 15 community service centers jumped from 8,243 in 1980 to 9,420 last year.  In an effort to cope with the expanding population, Marks said the state budget includes funding for the building of 2,380 new cells.  The design phase for the expansion project should be completed next summer.

headline: Court to Answer $100,000 Question
abstract: The question of who controls more than $100,000 in campaign contributions unspent by former State Treasurer Robert E. Casey has been sent to Dauphin County Common Pleas Court.  The Commonwealth Court said it had no jurisdiction to determine if the state Democratic Party can claim the money, left over from Casey’s unsuccessful 1980 re-election bid.  Commonwealth Secretary William Davis did not violate state election law by failing to report to authorities the alleged improper retention of Casey’s campaign funds.

headline: Scanlon's ship in trouble
abstract: This editorial talks about how the Education Secretary Robert Scanlon is making a tough job almost seem impossible. The Secretary has had a series of incidents which has brought a bad name to the Thornburgh administration and this article highlights some of them.

headline: Hardy works: That's the name of the game
abstract: Hardy Williams has run for a lot of elections including races for mayor, Congress and City Council, among others, in between winning five terms in the State Legislature. However, his up-again down-again career was seen once more when he narrowly won the 8th District State Senate seat from Southwest Philadelphia.

headline: Steelworkers Here React To Record
abstract: Pennsylvania steelworkers express frustration over current economic conditions and the policies of the Reagan administration.

headline: State All Smiles on Dentist Ads
abstract: State regulators have decided that dentists should be allowed and encouraged to advertise prices and special services.  The state board that licenses dentists, the State Dental Council and Examining Board, has proposed lifting a ban on dentist advertisements.

headline: Cabinet policy wastes energy
abstract: President Ronald Reagan proposed to dismantle the Department of Energy during the 1980 presidential campaign as a way to eliminate unnecessary bureaucratic waste and to save taxpayer money.  However, upon review it was discovered that the same amount of money would be spent on energy programs whether or not the DOE exists.  The editorial urges Reagan to keep the DOE and encourages the Reagan Adminstration to take an active part in defining energy policy.

headline: Renovated rail station is depicted in miniature
abstract: Local officials and inspected a model of the upcoming $8.9 million facelift for Harrisburg's Amtrak rail passenger station.

headline: State's Top Court Upholds Death Penalty
abstract: In a 4-3 decision the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld the state's four-year-old death penalty in its first constitutional challenge, concluding that it is not "cruel punishment" under the state's Constitution.  The case was brought over Keith W. Zettlemoyer's death sentence for a murder conviction, and the court also rejected other defense claims that the conviction should be overturned due to trial court errors.

headline: Coyne says he'll run, gets flak on districting
abstract: US Representative James Coyne announced his plans to seek re-election, while critics noted that he is doing very little to keep his district intact.  Coyne said that he did not pressure the state legislators on the issue because he believed that there is a seperation of federal and state powers.

headline: Schwartz Aide Re-Warded
abstract: City Council President George X. Schwartz stepped down from his position in the 34th Ward.  Robert A. Brady was elected to take over for Schwartz.  Other people were elected or re-elected at reorganization meetings across the city.

headline: Hitler is Alive
abstract: This letter states that Hitler is alive in America and may take the form of a lawyer, a doctor or even an ordinary parent. All this because America has legalized the death by starvation of the mentally retarded!

headline: PA majorette marches again, but weight rules called common
abstract: Drum majorette Peggy Ward, who was sidelined because she failed to meet a weight requirement, is taking her case to the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission.  Her parents say Peggy is being discriminated against because of her height and weight.  Apparently, such weight requirements are commonplace among high school drill-team and cheerleading squads in the United States.

headline: State Called Unfair to Retarded
abstract: The state, in its rush to convert a central Pennsylvania center for the mentally retarded into a prison, is reneging on its promise to place the center’s residents in small, homelike settings according to the Association for Retarded Citizens, Pennsylvania.  The conversion of the Cresson Center into a 500 cell prison is part of a 2,380 cell expansion of the state prison system approved by the Legislature last year to relieve overcrowding caused by the passage of mandatory sentencing laws.  The institution would be shut down in fifteen days.  The Association for Retarded Citizens said that moving the remaining 80 severely retarded clients in less than four weeks was unrealistic and unfair to the institution’s residents, some of whom have lived there since the institution opened 40 years ago.

headline: Camera tested
abstract: This picture shows technicians at Three Mile Island inserting a camera into Unit I of the reactor.

headline: Rise In Drinking Age To 21 Backed
abstract: The two Pennsylvanians in President Reagan's cabinet, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Richard S. Schweiker and U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis, are right to argue for the national drinking age to be raised to twenty-one. Teenage drinking is a growing problem, particularly in traffic accidents. Studies show that raising the drinking age reduces teen traffic deaths. Also while PA's drinking age is twenty-one, New York's is nineteen and many tragedies have happened as PA residents have driven north to drink and then gotten into accidents on the way back.

headline: The answer is not more prisoners
abstract: When serious social problems become politicized, slogans prevent rational solutions.  This is the case with "tough on crime" officials, who have done nothing but overcrowd the prisons.  Since new prisons are slow to be built, overcrowding has worsened prison conditions.  In the meantime, the Reagan Administration has cut funds for school lunches, sick, elderly but wants to build more prisons.  In the end, that just means that more of a cost burden will be shifted to state and local taxpayers.

headline: Cyril E. Sagan: A self-styled 'hound of hell'
abstract: Although Cyril E. Sagan, candidate for the Democratic US Senate nomination, has no campaign funds or staff, he offers himself as a candidate of contrast to the hard-nosed politics of Democratic frontrunner Cyril Wecht and to the high powered incumbency of Republican John Heinz.

headline: Scranton Pushing 'Own Identity'
abstract: After winning re-election, PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton is beginning to make plans to run for governor in 1986. While four years is a long time, Scranton said much of what he does now will be with that in mind. He also intends to be more vocal on a number of issues, but he does not believe it will conflict or undermine Governor Thornburgh's agenda.

headline: Idle steel workers live on hope
abstract: The 22,000 steel lay-offs in the Western Pennsylvania region since 1979 has an adverse impact on the people of that region. Some of it can be seen in huge unemployment lines, sold furniture and letters from bill collectors.

headline: Judge: 1 kidney no bar for football
abstract: U.S. District Judge Daniel Huyett III ruled that it is illegal and discriminatory to prevent a high school senior with only one functioning kidney from playing football.  The judge reasoned that keeping Richard William Grube from playing football denied him a right guaranteed by federal legislation.

headline: The Forsaken: Tomorrow
abstract: With the burden of care shifted to local communities, mental patients can live fairly independently--so much so that many fall out of the system entirely.  Those who need more time to adjust to the outside world may never get it, released prematurely because community hospitals can't wait that long.

headline: Campbelltown, Briar Get Nod on Water Rate Hikes
abstract: Two area water companies received authorization from the Public Utility Commission to increase rates.

headline: Road funds to the area ordered cut
abstract: Judge Louis Bechtle held the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in contempt for failing to begin auto-emissions inspections and ordered the federal government to suspend highway funds for the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh areas.  The ruling would hold $400 million of federal highway funding for Pennsylvania.  PA Governor Richard Thornburgh said that an appeal to the Third US Circuit Court of Appeals will be presented.

headline: The Forum: Fire Police Receive Benefits
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author is responding to a letter published in an earlier addition of the newspaper about the benefits afforded to volunteer firemen under Act 101, which was enacted by the General Assembly in 1976.  The act is administered by the PA Department of General Services.  The basis of the letter was to assert that volunteer firemen are not entitled to benefits under the act.

headline: Daily Tribune: Editorial Opinion Political Odor
abstract: This editorial talked about how two tax collectors in Plum Borough were fired by a new Democrat regime.  They were not fired because they did not do the job, but rather because they did not bow before the new regime.

headline: Scrantonian Readers Have A Say:
abstract: The PA Senate only works part of the time, but expects to get full-time pay.  It is unfair.  Pennsylvanians have a right to expect full time work for full time pay.  The PA House of Representatives continues to meet is obligations, even though the entire house is up for reelection whereas only half the Senate must face the voters in November.  It is wrong for the Senate not to meet before November.  At a time when public confidence in government is weak, it is startling to think that the Senate would contemplate drawing full pay for half a year’s work.  If the Senate leadership gets away with a stunt like this, it will encourage leaders of both parties to do more of the same in the future.  Common Cause urges all concerned citizens to urge their elected Republican officials to tell their Senate leadership to work this fall.

headline: Land of milk and no money
abstract: According to Jack Foflygen, when he was running milk, he never had the freedom as he was constantly badgered by the government and regulators. Now that he delivers newspapers, it is more closer to his reality of working for himself.

headline: Presenting the college on the hill
abstract: Philadelphia Community College's new 14-acre campus is located on Andrew Hamilton's Bush-Hill estate.

headline: Unemployment, Cutbacks Blamed For Sharp Upturn in Mental Health Crises
abstract: Unemployment and social service cutbacks contributed to a significant rise last year in mental health emergencies, according to a survey of crisis intervention centers.  The survey was conducted by the Crisis Intervention Association of Pennsylvania found 19 of the counties responding reported that emergencies in every category from homicidal to suicidal behavior to involuntary commitments to mental institutions increased dramatically compared to 1980.  Respondents to the survey generally agreed that a faltering economy, high unemployment and cutbacks in human services programs contributed to the rise in mental health emergencies.

headline: Caucus promotes Pa. coal
abstract: Due to persistent layoffs, curtailed work weeks and untapped underground wealth, about 80 legislators have formed a caucus aimed at revitalizing Pennsylvania's coal industry,

headline: Road Officials Try to Save Plans
abstract: The General Assembly’s failure to fund an auto emissions inspection program during the lame-duck session had state transportation officials busy trying to salvage the next construction season’s highway programs in the Pittsburgh and Philadelphia metropolitan areas.  Federal highway money has been cut off in 10 counties surrounding the two cities because of the Legislature’s continued defiance of a 1978 consent decree in which the state agreed to implement an emissions-inspection program in the two areas and comply with federal pollution standards.

headline: The Pennsylvania state police; Stopping rural crime
abstract: Rural crime is increasing all over Pennsylvania. Correspondingly, the Pennsylvania State Police face a crime rate that has quadrupled in the last fifteen years.

headline: Dawida expects battle for Dems' endorsement
abstract: PA Representative Michael Dawida expects a battle for the Democratic endorsement in the 36th district.  Robert Horgos is expected to get the party backing for that area.  Dawida lost his seat as a result of reapportionment.

headline: Se. Specter favors stiff gun sentences
abstract: Senator Specter says he voted against an amendment relating to a waiting period for a criminal-record check because he believes that existing safeguards are adequate. With regard to mandatory jail sentences, he intends to vote for the tougher, mandatory sentences.

headline: Less valuable than a 'normal' child?
abstract: This letter is written to protest the Indiana Supreme Court decision which allowed parents of an infant with Down's syndrome to withhold a surgical procedure which may have saved the child's life.

headline: Shoplifting a growth industry
abstract: Shoplifting hurts every consumer; we pay more at the register to make up for the losses that store owners sustain.  And although public awareness is one way to prevent shoplifting, the best defense against shoplifting begins in the home.

headline: Union: Guv Will Hike Aid to City Hospitals
abstract: Governor Thornburgh has told hospital union officials he will increase state funding to Philadelphia’s hospitals to assist in treatment of the city’s poor and avert a strike by workers at 12 area institutions, a union spokesman says.  Union workers at 12 area hospitals voted earlier this month to walk off their jobs to protest federal and state cutbacks that union leaders say have resulted in some hospitals turning away from poor people in need of treatment.  About 200 union workers have been laid off at area hospitals because of the cutbacks union officials said.  A spokesman for Thornburgh said that the governor will make a response on the hospital issue, but the aide, Jesse Lewis, would not confirm or deny the union’s clam that the governor intends to increase funding to cover hospital treatment for Philadelphia’s poor.

headline: Centralia 'decision' letter sent in error, U.S. says
abstract: An erroneous letter was sent to the Concerned Citizens of Centralia in Centralia, PA giving members of the group the mistaken impression they had won their fight for a drilling program to map the town's mine fire.  James Harris, director of the Office of Surface Mining said that no decision on the drilling was made.  The actual plans called for the drilling of 10-20 holes while the letter called for 85-109 holes.

headline: Road Study Estimate: $500,000
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation announced that it would take almost a year and cost $500,000 for a study to determine whether Pennsylvania needs or can afford additional toll roads.  The Governor’s Toll Road Task Force, is expected to hire a consultant to begin determining feasibility of certain highway projects.  The task force was formed by Governor Dick Thornburgh after he vetoed legislation that would have authorized construction of hundreds of miles of turnpike spurs.
