Thornburgh said the measure could have jeopardized federal highway funding.

headline: The 'principal's office', where police are policed
abstract: The Philadelphia Police Department has a division known as the Internal Affairs Bureau, which investigates officers accused of wrongdoing. Last year, about 19 officers and two civilian Police Department employees were fired from the Department.

headline: Deadline for Pa. voters is April 19
abstract: Registrations for the May 18 statewide primary elections in Pennsylvania can be done until April 19, 1982. This registration can be done by mail or in person at the Voter Registration Office.

headline: Seek political solution in El Salvador
abstract: Congressman Bob Edgar has come up with a political solution to the situation in El Salvador that require talks between the Duarte government and the rebels, an immediate cease-fire, and an international peace-keeping force.  President Reagan, on the  other hand, is pushing for more military aid to the government to stop the spread of Soviet influence.

headline: Low budget thrills; Nest of urchins in their hair
abstract: The article talks about a reporter's interaction with a group of school children who are being given a tour of the Capitol by Rep. Bradford McKean.

headline: Work to Begin to Replace
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources will replace a damaged portion of the Fabridam, which spans the Susquehanna River.  The Fabridam is a system of seven inflatable rubber bags that is used to back up water into the Lake Augusta impoundment.

headline: Urban League backs health systems panel
abstract: A bill designed to allow the abolition of the Health Systems Agency in Pennsylvania has drawn sharp criticism from the Urban League of Pittsburgh, and wants Governor Dick Thornburgh to veto it.  The bill, which defines home health care agencies, has a contingency rider that would abolish the "certificate of need" for health care construction if the federal government abolishes its HSA program.  The Urban League worries that this will drive up health care costs.

headline: Clements Urges Energy Department Be Retained
abstract: Texas Republican Governor William P. Clements Jr., calling energy as important as weapons to America’s defense, says President Reagan should not abolish the Energy Department.  Clements presented his proposed energy policy to the National Governors Association and invited input.  He said that the United States has no national energy plan and is on the brink of an energy crisis.

headline: Route 15; State should do its share
abstract: Maryland and Pennsylvania have shared responsibility for the improvements of Route 15 for many years. However, recently, Maryland has been doing some work on it, with Pennsylvania not chipping in.

headline: The Public Mandate
abstract: The state legislature is considering a bill that would mandate jail sentences for people convicted of driving under the influence of alcohol.  Members of the judiciary have strongly denounced the concept of mandatory sentencing, arguing that sentencing is a judicial function and as such cannot be legislated.  It violates the American system of check and balances.

headline: Dealers ask ban on new pill law
abstract: The makers and sellers of "look-alike" drugs contend that Pennsylvania's ban on the pill is unconstitutional and have asked a judge to halt enforcement of the law.

headline: Sen. Street files to run against Gray
abstract: Milton Street has filed as an independent candidate to run in November for the congressional seat now held by William H. Gray 3d.

headline: Lynch apologizes to Wecht
abstract: Former County Controller John P. Lynch admitted in a statement that he had no proof when on a 1979 radio talk show he said County Commissioner Cyril H. Wecht had used the county morgue for profit.

headline: Foglietta is looking over shoulder
abstract: Congressman Thomas Foglietta is embroiled in a ferocious electoral battle with his Republican opponent, Michael Marino.  Foglietta says that Marino is spreading lies and half-truths and distorting the complexities of the legislative process.  Interestingly, Marino and Foglietta do not differ much on key issues; both are liberals.

headline: Varied rates for workmen's coverage set
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh said that for the first time in 60 years, Pennsylvania insurance companies will be permitted to vary rates for worker's compensation insurance. He also said that this new initiative will encourage competition and reduce insurance rates.

headline: Companies Join in Fight Hikes in Natural Gas Costs
abstract: The Pennsylvania Manufacturers Coalition on Energy joined legislators in opposing the natural gas price increases proposed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

headline: Rusting Bridge
abstract: This letter calls for something to be done to the Highland Park Bridge as it is currently in bad shape, with rusting beams and disintegrating guardrails.

headline: The Pyromaniac: A Horror in the Community
abstract: This editorial supports the proposed Arson Murder Bill in the PA Legislature that would make anyone convicted of causing, or paying to cause, a fire in which a person is killed subject to life in prison without parole.  The editorial also urges more training for firefighters in arson investigation.

headline: Dear Mr. Pintea
abstract: Mrs. Marian Helminski wrote a letter to the newspaper in response to how Senator Heinz never responded or called in regards to an earlier letter she had written to the newspaper.

headline: Senate Action Urged on Drunk Driving Bills
abstract: As another round of legislative hearings gets underway on a bill that would crack down on drunken driving, a veteran Democratic Senator says it’s time for the Legislature to stop listening and start acting.  The hearings were held by a joint House-Senate committee.  The testimony was similar to that presented to legislative committees over the past two years on other drunken driving bills.  Senator Michael O’Pake, ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee encouraged both the House and Senate to act instead of just talking.

headline: M. Harvey Taylor dies at age 105
abstract: Former State Senator M. Harvey Taylor, the nation's senior state political leader, died at age 105. He had a life of 70 active years in politics and had been retired from elective office since 1964.

headline: 13 County Women Seek Election
abstract: Democrats attribute the disproportionate number of female Republican candidates in Allegheny County to a "sacrifical-lamb" strategy.  Corroborating this theory is the fact that many female Republican candidates are running in districts where they face overwhelming Democratic majorities.  The Allegheny Republican Committee denies that women are being used as "sacrificial lambs," and instead claims that they are the party of opportunity.

headline: Yes, extend immunization program
abstract: Scranton Times editorial: The paper strongly supports a new measure that would make it mandatory for school children to receive vaccinations against polio, measles, rubella, mumps, diptheria, and tetanus.  The original law requiring the immunizations was in 1974, but it was only for students just entering school, and found that older students were still getting the diseases.

headline: Consumer Advocate Loses PUC Vote in Bell Case
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission voted against State Consumer Advocate Walter Cohen’s motion to prevent Administrative Law Judge Morris Mindlin from issuing a rate hike.

headline: Say no to 'lemon aid'
abstract: The US Senate has hinted that it will allow America's automobile dealers to withhold information about defects in used cars. Consequently, it would go against the Federal Trade Commissions current stance of making dealers alert buyers to all known defects.

headline: The wheels of justice are following an uncharted path in Larsen probe
abstract: PA Supreme Court Justice Rold Larsen is being investigated for violating Canon 7 of the PA Code of Judicial Conduct - that he has engaged in political activity inappropriate to his judicial office.  The PA Judicial Inquiry and Review Board, chaired by William Cercone, is moving slowly and carefully because charging a PA Supreme Court justice with violating the PA Code of Judicial Conduct would be unprecedented.

headline: Death Benefits Listed By Retirement Board
abstract: The State Employees Retirement Board has approved a lump sum death benefit of $292, 429 to Helen E. Downs, as beneficiary of Donald E. Downs, an employee of the Public Welfare Department, who had 28 years of state service when he died.  Benefits were given to other people also that had state service.

headline: Senate defeats GOP's 3rd bid to reapportion
abstract: The PA Senate failed to pass for a third time a reapportionment plan.  7 Republican Senators and all of the Democrat Senators voted against the plan that would eliminate 2 Democratic seats.  Senator Robert Jubelirer warned that federal courts may step in to take over the process.

headline: Milk, Crown Vetch still in running for state beverage, plant
abstract: Pennsylvania currently does not have an official state beverage or a state plant. However, under a bill passed last June, milk would be the state beverage. Another bill passed in early December, designates crown vetch as the official state plant.

headline: Not a Very Good Record
abstract: According to ratings from the Pennsylvania Citizens Consumer Council (PCCC), Lancaster County's legislative delegation does not have a very impressive record on consumer issues.  The PCCC monitored six issues and found that the Lancaster County delegation voted with consumers only 54 percent of the time.

headline: A way to save farmland
abstract: Editorial: According to a recent report, Pennsylvania is losing 52,000 acres of farmland to commercial development and another 50,000 acres to erosion.  One way to reverse that trend is the "Clean and Green" amendment passed in 1973 that allows farmland to be taxed for use rather than commercial value, but the effect has been minimal.  A new bill proposed by PA Senator Edward Helfrick would set up a commission with the authority to place restrictions on the sale of land for anything but agricultural purposes.

headline: Council Drops TMI Proposal
abstract: Paxtang Borough Council has indefinitely tabled a proposal to support a Lower Swatara ordinance favoring full cleanup of the damaged Unit 2 nuclear reactor on Three Mile Island.

headline: Scanlon Wages War on Car Emissions Plan
abstract: Senate Minority Whip Eugene Scanlon, vowed to resume his fight to prohibit the PA Transportation Department from starting a court-ordered auto emissions inspection program.  H will push for an amendment on the Senate floor to ban PennDOT from implementing the program ordered by a U.S. District Court Judge.

headline: Tomorrow's Prison System: 2,880 New Cells for $134 Million, But No Quick Fix
abstract: Pennsylvania's prisons continue to grow more overcrowded.  New laws requiring mandatory sentencing, courts that are sentencing longer prison terms, and a governor with no executive clemency that wants to abolish parole are all contributing to this.  PA has unveiled a plan that calls for the contruction of 2,884 new prison cells at a cost of $134 million, but this will not be a quick fix.

headline: Dem Guvs Hostile to 'Federalism'
abstract: Top Reagan administration officials have agreed to compromise with the nation's governors on the president's plan to return federal programs to the states, but Democratic governors sharply attacked plans to cut aid to states by $10 billion next year.  They say that states must be financially strong in order for them to take over 40 programs from the federal level.  President Ronald Reagan's budget director David Stockman noted how few allies he had among the governors.

headline: Senate Democrats List Minority Appointments
abstract: PA Senate Democratic Floor Leader Edward P. Zemprelli announced the minority chairmanships of twenty standing committees for the coming year.  Senator H. Craig Lewis of Bucks County retained Chairmanship of the Appropriations Committee while Senator Patrick J. Stapleton was named Chairman of the Policy Committee.

headline: Milton Street acquitted
abstract: The picture shows State Senator Milton Street, R-Philadelphia after his trial in a charge of resisting arrest.

headline: GOP outspending Democrats
abstract: The Federal Election Commission reported that the national Republican Party outspent the Democratic Party by more than 5 to 1 during the first 18 months of the current election campaign.  Also, Republicans have 10 times more cash on hand than their Democratic counterparts.

headline: Boost state farm output
abstract: Pennsylvania imports 73% of its food at a cost of $8.4 billion, despite having some of the richest and most productive farms. In order to solve this, an overall state food policy to increase self-reliance and economic viability must be initiated as a step in solving this issue. The article also outlines how individuals can help with this problem.

headline: County movers get OK to hike rates Monday
abstract: Thirteen household good movers in Allegheny County and one in Indiana County are among the 37 across Pennsylvania that have been granted higher rates by the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Self service
abstract: In 1978, Pittsburgh had banned self-service stations due to worries about safety and customer convenience. However, the editorial says both these worries are unfounded and that customers must be given a choice about what they would prefer.

headline: Top aide to replace court administrator? Aide getting Savitt's job, sources say
abstract: The possibility is growing that the PA Supreme Court will give control of the city's court system to an independent administrator, a 28-year-old Chief of Operations for the courts. James White, under the current posting, works for the current court administrator, David N. Savitt.

headline: Democrat Lloyd Led Vote Getters
abstract: Official vote tallies released by the Bureau of Elections show Senator James Lloyd, Democratic candidate for Lieutenant Governor, garnered more votes than any other statewide candidate in the primary election.

headline: Senate non-race
abstract: The Democratic nomination for the US Senate is contested by Allegheny County Commissioner Cyril Wecht and two other relatively unknown contenders. The article stresses on Wecht's usage of shallow popularism and no strong opponents as an example of when voters are the losers in a political race.

headline: Miss Pa.'s Life a Constant Twirl on Road to Miss America Title
abstract: Laurie Ann Hixenbaugh from Belle Vernon, Fayette County is the new Miss Pennsylvania.  Look for her at garage and restaurant openings.  At county fairs and shopping malls.  Or, between appearances, at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Lou Maierhofer in Altoona.  He’s a state pageant official.  Altoona is the state headquarters of the Miss Pennsylvania segment of the Miss America Pageant, not to be confused with the Miss Pennsylvania segment of the Miss USA contest.  The difference is not just location, but that Miss America contestants compete for scholarships and not beauty titles.

headline: Woman IS Nominated
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh nominated Esther Good Holder as Lancaster County treasurer.  If confirmed by the Senate, Holder would replace the late Robert Fasnacht.

headline: Cream price to rise, some milk 'skimmed'
abstract: 2% milk and skim milk will drop in price by $0.02 while whole milk prices remain the same for western Pennsylvania residents as the Milk Marketing Board approved the new changes. Dissenting board member Marianne Olson said the move was just to "throw crumbs" to the City of Pittsburgh and to avoid another potential court appearance.

headline: Court Lifts Ban On Limerick 2
abstract: An August order by the PA Utility Commission (PUC) to Philadelphia Electric Company (PE) to stop work on Unit Two of its Limerick nuclear power plant has been overturned by the Commonwealth Court. In its order, the PUC declared that PE's financial situation made it unable to afford the simultaneous construction of both units and refused to allow the company to issue bonds in order to finance it. The company challenged the order arguing the PUC went beyond its authority and the Commonwealth Court agreed with that assessment.

headline: Senate Kills Exhaust Tests
abstract: Charges of blackmail and intimidation were hurled across the Senate floor as State Senators rejected an unpopular auto emissions bill and pushed toward final adjournment.  The vote against the bill was 28-20, with six Republicans joining solid Democratic opposition.  The legislation would have allowed PennDot to implement a federally mandated program requiring motorists in 12 Pennsylvania counties to have the anti-pollution equipment on their cars checked once year and repaired, if needed.  Before the vote, Senator James R. Lloyd said he and several of his Democratic colleagues were prepared to support the bill to prevent the loss of the road money.  But he was told by other members of his party that if he helped pass the emissions bill, they would contribute crucial votes to a measure damaging to Philadelphia.  The measure to which he referred was a Republican-backed proposal to cut the wage tax which Philadelphia levies against commuters, costing the city an estimated $60 million a year.

headline: Tough Ads Offer Message: Prison's a Rotten Place
abstract: The state’s new sentencing law, passed earlier in the year and effective for crimes committed after June 6, mandates five-year prison terms for people convicted of crimes involving a gun, for repeat violent offenders and for those who commit violent crimes on public transportation.  Philadelphia District Attorney Edward G. Rendell, co-chairman of a fund-raising group called the Pennsylvania Committee for Effective Justice, said the campaign was unabashedly using scare tactics to frighten potential offenders.  A second purpose is to educate the general public and raise morale.  Some people disagree on whether the new law will cut down on crime.  The new law, along with recently adopted sentencing guidelines for other crimes, will lengthen prison stays and further strain a correctional system already hard-pressed to house its inmates.

headline: Democratic Donkey Alive and Kicking
abstract: Now that the dust has settled, the November election and other events reveal the remarkable strength of the Democratic Party.  Democratic majorities were elected in 72 various legislative chambers, a gain of 10, while Republicans hold only 26.  Thirty-four states will have Democratic governors, a gain of seven.  Republicans only have 16.

headline: Senate Session is Just a Token: Hager Signs Bills for Governor
abstract: With the main body of Senators instructed not to return to Harrisburg, President Pro Tempore Henry G. Hager is convening the State Senate for a brief non-voting session to sign bills received from the House to sent them to Governor Dick Thornburgh’s desk for consideration.  Only a handful of area members attend such “token” sessions, which satisfies the constitutional requirement that the presiding officer sign all bills in the presence of the house over which he presides.  This completes what is known at the Enrolled Doctrine, which officially informs the Governor that all bills sent to him were properly enacted.

headline: Mistakes at the United Way
abstract: The United Way of Southeastern Pennsylvania adopted a system which allowed people to contribute to a charity through the United Way. However, some of the donations never reached the charities. United Way acknowledges this and plans to take important steps to make the plan work successfully.

headline: State Purchases 266-Acre Island
abstract: The state of Pennsylvania is purchasing the 266-acre Tinicum Island in the Delaware River.  The island will be used for a public environmental and recreation area

headline: Cumberland Seeks Federal Drought Relief
abstract: Cumberland Country Commissioners, citing a severe drought, which crippled crop production this year, asked Governor Dick Thornburgh to declare the country a disaster area.  Commissioners also asked the governor to request emergency loans from the federal Farmers Home Administration to help the estimated 600 Cumberland County farmers affected by the drought.  The commissioner’s request was prompted by the county U.S. Department of Agriculture Emergency Board.  According to the board, areas most affected by the dry spell are north of and immediately around the Conodoguinet Creek and south and east of Shippensburg.

headline: Cumberland adds ballot on restart
abstract: Cumberland County will add a ballot for citizens to voice their opinion on the restart of Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor in the May election.  The vote will serve as a non-binding referendum, but will serve as a frame of reference for future Nuclear Regulatory Commission decisions.  The specific question will be identical to the one approved by Dauphin County Commissioners for use in their May election.

headline: Senate Oks Funding
abstract: The Senate approved a one-year extension of funding for the Appalachian Regional Commission.  It would provide $100 million for highway projects and $50 million for non-highway projects to phase out ARC programs.

headline: Town Hails Mandatory Guns
abstract: The borough council of Franklintown, Pennsylvania is mandating gun ownership in order to prevent burglaries in the town.  The law exempts those who do not want to own weapons from being penalized up to $300 and 30 days in jail.

headline: Democratic Party Cuts McKinney's Staff in 'Reprisal'
abstract: Senator Anthony “Buzz” Andrezeski of Erie was punished for his vote in support of the Republicans’ version of statewide congressional reapportionment, which preserved his home district.  Andrezeski’s $90,000 account as minority chairman of the Senate and Military and Veterans Affairs Committee was reduced to $28,000, forcing him to terminate two top staffers and his secretary in his Capitol office and three part-time employees in his district office.

headline: Settle dispute, but run trains
abstract: After the Reagan Administration slashed federal transit funding, Conrail is struggling to establish profitability and served a notice of intent to terminate service, because SEPTA was unable to guarantee funding. Even after SEPTA approved further payments, Conrail countered that it was not sufficient and has taken the matter to the courts.

headline: New tactic to control publicity: Copyright the proxy statement
abstract: Allegheny International Inc. believes that it can influence the news coverage of its finances by copyrighting its proxy statement. Current laws are unclear if this is possible or not.

headline: Gray: Falling Short Of Expectations
abstract: Congressman William H. Gray is facing an electoral challenge form state Senator Milton Street.  Although most political observers agree that Gray is articulate and dilligent, some say he has fallen far short of expectations.  Gray has been criticized for not paying close enough attention to his work on the Appropriations Committee.

headline: Dead pets dumped into pits
abstract: Hundreds of Harrisburg area pets may have been dumped into pits on a Berks County farm after their owners paid for burial in a pet cemetery or for cremation. The pets would be among thousands of dead cats, dogs, rabbits and goats.

headline: Electric-bill control is lacking, according to some consumers
abstract: Residents across Pennsylvania are complaining about ever increasing utility costs in the state. Dr. Arnedt, of Pennsylvania, feels that Reagan's anti-inflation policies will never work if utility companies keep raising their rates. However, utility companies are not making their maximum allowed profits due to high costs related to transportation, environmental regulation, etc.

headline: Senate Rejects $1.3 Billion Bridge-Fix Bill
abstract: The State Senate rejected legislation that would have provided funding for a mammoth $1.3 billion plan to repair up to 930 bridges across the state. The action came at a marathon session, which lasted well after 2am.  They also approved legislation that would eliminate next year’s scheduled rollback in state’s income tax rates and enable the state to grab $80 million in unclaimed bank accounts for balancing the budget.  There was also other legislation that was passed.

headline: Trade-off questioned in no-fault proposal
abstract: PA Republican Representatives Lois Hagarty and Robert Reber worry about a new proposal before the House Judiciary Committee that would allow auto companies to lower insurance premiums for more restrictions on the right to sue for "pain and suffering."  Current law allows accident victims to sue for "pain and suffering" if medical costs would exceed $750.

headline: Democrats Facing Abortion Control Advocates May Get GOP Aid
abstract: The Political Action Committee (PAC) was formed to defeat supporters of the new abortion control law.  The group has received many contributions, which some have come from prominent Republican women.  PAC plans to finance campaigns against several key legislators in the gubernatorial election.

headline: Sgt. Jake Tokarski is the turnkey at Western Pen's main gate
abstract: Photo

headline: Not a boiling down but a blending together
abstract: Governor Thornburgh opened the cultural holiday festivity "Christmas .. An annual ethnic experience". He welcomed the visitors to the exhibit and stated that Pennsylvania is a combination of immigrants who came together to create this great Commonwealth.

headline: Teresa Heinz In a Dilly of a Pickle
abstract: Teresa Heinz is a member of Peace Links, an organization whose mission is to educate women's groups about the dangers of nuclear war.  Ever since U.S. Senator Jeremiah Denton called the organization subversive and others claimed the group is aiding the Soviets, the group has received national attention.  Teresa Heinz denied such allegations and said she "has no patience for communists."

headline: Farm Show History: Exposition Has Braved
abstract: Article details the growth of the PA farm show since its inception in 1917.

headline: Duquesne Light faces $10 million refund order
abstract: The PA Public Utilities Commission is expected to force Duquesne Light to grant rebates for briefly closing its nuclear power plant, Beaver Valley No. 1, in 1979. Duquesne disputes its fault, as it was ordered by the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission to close to respond to concerns over withstanding an earthquake. The PA Alliance for Jobs and Energy and PA Consumer Advocate Walter Cohen pushed for $3 per household. Duquesne could appeal to the PUC or Commonwealth Court.

headline: Senate Unit approves yearly car inspection
abstract: The Senate Transportation Committee has approved an amended bill requiring most motor vehicles to undergo safety inspection just once a year, rather than twice as under present law.

headline: Trial juror says he just couldn't let convicted child killer 'walk'
abstract: One of the 12 jurors who convicted 16-year-old Joseph Gerard Aulisio of first-degree murder, and then sentenced him to die on an electric chair, said that he just couldn't allow the child killer to walk away from such crimes.

headline: Democrats Pledge Cooperation But Remember Sessions Past
abstract: The Democratic caucus elected K. Leroy Irvis of Pittsburgh as house speaker and James Manderino of Westmoreland County as House majority leader.  Democrats won a 102-101 majority in the House but several close races are being recounted that could boost their margin of control.  Skyrocketing utility rates, support for public education and a state budget that gives priority to human services are some of the issues that will shape the Democrats’ legislative agenda.

headline: Shades of '78: Shapp's challenge goes unmet
abstract: Gov. Thornburgh may have made his first mistake last week, when he declined a challenge by former Governor Milton Shapp to debate the comparative merits of the Thornburgh and Shapp Administrations. This is a lost opportunity, especially with the upcoming elections, to showcase the Thornburgh Administration.

headline: Pa. Ballet May Kick Off Late
abstract: The Pennsylvania Ballet may delay its regular fall series for the first time in its 19-year history.  The plan involves cutting the company’s 38-week season to 30 weeks.  It’s the economic problems facing the company that is causing them to do this.  They already have a $2.4 million debt.  There was a major fund-raising effort that has raised about $1.1 million, with an additional million matching grant donated by Mabel Myrin Pew Trust.

headline: Promises, Promises!
abstract: Although Governor Thornburgh announced that the state will undertake a 200,000 dollar engineering study in Lancaster, local residents should not expect this to result in the construction of any new roads and/or bridges.  The governor has an important election coming up in a month, and this is his way of duping local residents; it is important we remember that you cannot drive a car on engineering studies.

headline: Farms Vital in Erie Economy
abstract: Farming is a vital part of Erie County’s economy.  Overall, Erie County farmers produce $64,000,000 worth of products and provide 5,300 jobs.  There is $275,000,000 invested in farm land, buildings, machinery and livestock.  The 200,000 acres of farmland in the county contribute $3 million in local tax revenue.  Still, farmers are having a particularly difficult time in the current recession.

headline: Duquesne Light wins $64 million rate rise
abstract: The Public Utility Commission accepted the $64 million rate hike filed by Duquesne Light Co. Although the company had initially asked for $100.4 million, in July it accepted a lesser and immediate increase.

headline: SEPTA Fares Go Up and Down
abstract: Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Agency is introducing the Trailpass, a combination monthly pass that would be good for unlimited trips on commuter trains, buses, subways, high-speed lines and trolleys.  Under the plan, a rider would be able to switch from rail to bus or subway in certain zones without paying additional fares.  Some people would pay less for public transportation then they are now but others would pay more, but with more benefits then before.  Elderly people wishing to use SEPTA commuter rail lines for free must meet certain qualifications in order to do so.

headline: Violent juvenile crime declining in state; County's figures double average
abstract: Violent crime is on the decline in Pennsylvania, according to statistics from the state's Uniform Crime Reports. There has been a 7.3% decline in the number of arrests from 1975-1980.

headline: Democrats ruin Pike Commission
abstract: The Senate Democrats' refusal to confirm any of Gov. Dick Thornburgh's appointees is causing an issue at the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission. As of today, there are only two active members in the five member commission conducting business.

headline: Short Fuse vs. Short Fuse: Heinz-Wecht Debate: A Clash of Egos
abstract: No event in the statewide campaign is likely to arouse more interest and suspense than The Great Debate between U.S. Senator John Heinz and Allegheny County Commissioner Cyril Wecht, assuming, of course, that it eventually occurs.  Because both of these gentlemen have short fuses, anything could happen, and it’s possible but not probably that either could below the election with a single goof.

headline: Party Blackmail
abstract: This letter questions the words like "Tyrannical" and "unwarranted" to describe Senator Anthony Andrezeski in the article "Irate Democrats give Andrezki Buzz-off" dated March 5th. The author says Andrezeski was elected to give his opinion only, irrespective of what other thought of it.

headline: Lives at Stake
abstract: Most neighborhood hospitals in Philadelphia are not equipped to handle serious injuries.  As a result, Philadelphia's Health Commissioner, Dr. Stuart Shapiro, wants to make sure that accident victims are brought to facilities where they can receive the care they need.  We agree with Dr. Shapiro that a plan needs to be in place to ensure that victims are brought to one of the 14 fully equipped trauma centers in Philadelphia.

headline: It’s the 66th Harvest for Pennsylvania Farm Show
abstract: PA's 66th annual Farm Show opens for 6 days at the state Farm Show Complex, bearing the theme "PA Agriculture - We're Growing Better."

headline: Early Warns of Canadian Coal Competition
abstract: West Virginia coal producers and state government leaders are going to have to devise new market strategies to offset an invasion into New England by Canadian power suppliers Governor Jay Rockefeller announced.

headline: SEPTA Head Takes Himself Off Fast Track
abstract: Lewis F. Gould Jr., a Philadelphia patent lawyer, is the frontrunner to succeed David F. Girard-diCarlo as SEPTA chairman, officials say.  Girard-diCarlo is giving up the post to devote more time to his private law practice.  He will keep his seat on the board.  Gould knows transportation and the system.  There are other people that have also shown interest in the position.  Girard-diCarlo was appointed by Governor Dick Thornburgh in 1979.  He has been a highly visible figure in both local and national transit circles.  The political and financial end is expected to grow even more complicated in coming months as Commuter Services Corp., a federally sanctioned agency, prepares to take over commuter rain operations from Con-rail, which now runs the 13 lines under contract with SEPTA.

headline: Women's Group Earmarks State Aid for Crisis Centers
abstract: The Pennsylvania Coalition Against Domestic Violence has named direct-service activities as its top spending priority, in determining how $1.5 million in state aid to crisis centers across the state will be spent.  Susan Kelly-Dreiss, Executive Director of the coalition said the range of funding available to each center will depend on the number of people served by the center, the scope of services offered and the size of the geographic area served.

headline: Democrats seek probe of strip mine 'deals'
abstract: House democrats will press for a vote authorizing the Committee on Mines and Energy Management to investigate an alleged relationship between the Thornburgh administration and some strip miners that may have resulted in a dilution of strip mine law enforcement.  PA Representative Thomas Michlovich said that he would seek subpoena powers for the committee so that it can demand testimony on strip miners contributions to the Republican party.

headline: Shortage seen in U.S. fund for states
abstract: A proposed federal fund that would finance dozens of programs which US President Ronald Reagan wants to shift to the states is almost $10 billion short of what those programs now cost, according to estimates by state officials.  However, a federal budget official says that the President intends to trim the programs further before turning them over to the states.  A nation-wide telephone poll shows that a slim margin of the public is in favor of the proposed program swap.

headline: Party's maverick attacks Fed policy
abstract: Maverick Democratic candidate Steve Douglas is demanding the removal of Paul Volcker from the Federal Reserve Board, in a bid to reduce the current interest rates.

headline: Tough territory for a Democrat: The race for Congress in the 16th
abstract: In Pennsylvania's 16th Congressional District, Republican voters outnumber registered Democrats by a 2-1 margin.  Even so, Jean Mowrey, a self-described liberal,  is challenging Bob Walker, an ardent conservative who has held the 16 District seat since 1976.  Mowrey contends that Congressman Walker is too extreme and out of touch with his constituents.

headline: Legendary aphrodisiac battles labor's lost love in Pennsylvania
abstract: Kennett Square, PA is the self-designated capital of the mushroom industry. However, this area is facing troubles that include a mushroom glut due to excessive supply, low-cost canned imports from the Far East, etc. The "mushroom men" are now pushing for legislation to help them survive.

headline: Elect PUC members
abstract: The author of the letter states that Met-Ed has a hidden charge of $6 in their bills. The chairman of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) says that these are merely operating expenses. The author believes that this will destroy confidence in the PUC.

headline: SEPTA Rails: Nobody's Foolin' about April 1
abstract: In this article, the author has analyzed the condition of SEPTA's troubled commuter train system. Due to huge financial burdens, the viability of the continued operations of SEPTA's train system, is doubted by the author, unless the Government comes out with concessions, to help the ailing organization.

headline: Wecht wins apology in suit against Lynch
abstract: County Commissioner Cyril H. Wecht today announced the settlement of his slander lawsuit against former controller John P. Lynch, marking Wecht's second victory in three major court battles stemming from accusations that he used the morgue for private gain while coroner.

headline: Democrats to convene Feb. 27
abstract: Democratic state leaders were called to convention on February 27 to endorse candidates for U.S. Senate, Governor, and Lieutenant Governor.  Additionally, the party warned former Pittsburgh mayor Pete Flaherty to decide if wants to seek party endorsement.

headline: Shuster panel challenges Duncan drive for petitions
abstract: The re-election committee for Rep. Bud Shuster, R-Pa., has filed suit in the Commonwealth Court on the ground that alleged improprieties occurred in Democratic congressional challenger Eugene Duncan's nominating petition drive.

headline: PennDOT installs new phone system
abstract: With the PA Department of Transportation installing a new telephone system, it should now be easier than ever to complain about potholes or get highway information.

headline: President of Firm Is Charged With Rigging State Work Bids
abstract: The president of Bituminous Emulsion Company was charged with violating federal antitrust laws in U.S. Middle District Court Yesterday.  The president, Vernon F. Dasey, allegedly rigged bids on work done for the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: Low fat, skim milk cut 2 cents a gallon
abstract: The state Milk Marketing Board approved a $0.02 reduction in gallons of reduced fat and skim milk in western Pennsylvania.  The price of whole milk will remain the same while the price of cream will rise.  Retailers are free to charge more as the board only set a minimum price.

headline: Electric Utilities Reconsider the Possibility of Deregulation
abstract: While some holding extreme views suggest that all electric service be freed from regulation, the opposing view suggests that things such as transmission and distribution should be left regulated.

headline: Servicing the independents
abstract: The editorial states that although these are not the best of times for service-station operators, legislation that would bar oil refiners from owning gas stations in Pennsylvania is not the answer to the problem.

headline: When 'gift offers' are scams
abstract: This editorial discusses Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman's response to hundreds of complaints about mail promotions by resort communities, primarily in the Poconos.  These gift offers are not illegal, but misleading or deceptive tactics violates fair trade practices.

headline: Democrats; A conflict at the top
abstract: The Democratic National Committee gave final approval to rules which will set aside about 550 seats in the 1984 convention for elected and party officials uncommitted to any presidential candidate. However, another commission began to work on how to make these elected officials accountable for the promises in the party platform. This illustrates the tension within the party.

headline: Signs of truce appear in battle over city courts
abstract: After nearly 10 weeks of "warfare", Edward J. Bradley, president judge of the Philadelphia Common Pleas Court, hinted that he was willing to make peace with John P. Flaherty, the PA Supreme Court justice assigned to investigate and improve the courts here. Flaherty also made similar hints of a truce.

headline: Philadelphians honoring one of their own, Princess Grace
abstract: Grace Kelly, daughter of a Philadelphia family, who later became a film actress and then Princess Grace of Monaco, returned today to a heroine's welcome. The occasion was "A Tribute to Grace Kelly, Actress", staged at the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg Center. This marks a key event of the city's yearlong celebration of its 300th anniversary.

headline: 7 Struck Schools Facing Average Earning
abstract: Teacher strikes are commonplace in Pennsylvania.  This year, 254 teachers' contracts were up for negotiation and there have been 33 strikes.  22 of those 33 strikes occurred in Western Pennsylvania, an area with a strong union history.

headline: Milk Surplus Seen Cutting Earnings
abstract: State dairy farmers have created a milk surplus in order to compensate for lower federal price supports.  The situation needs to be reversed.  Everyone from farmer to dealer, retailer, consumer, and ultimately the taxpayer are paying the price.  In the past farmers have been encouraged to produce more in when milk prices fall to the minimum level.  Congress is considering a bill that would give a minimum of 75 percent parity if farmers produce below their production goal.

headline: Engineers Plan Density Check at TMI today
abstract: Engineers at Three Mile Island hope to have a better profile of the Unit 2 core after back-to-back camera inspections and a density test. The July 21 inspection confirmed earlier studies which predicted the existence of the rubble bed.  They hope to learn through today’s experience whether predictions of less damage at the core’s periphery are correct.

headline: Similar plan for Pennsylvania
abstract: Editors suggest PA Budget Secretary Robert Wilburn's solution to funding a massive highway system renovation be considered in accord with US Transportation Secretary Drew Lewis' national highway renovation program. Both Secretaries are advocating a 5 cent tax on gas, however, editors recommend pushing PA's tax back a year should Lewis' tax not be incrementally introduced. Editors do not think a 10 cent gas tax will go over well with consumers.

headline: Who's Afraid of Virginia's Chair?
abstract: Frank Coppola had quit the Portsmouth police force in 1967 and had served time prior to a robbery for which he was convicted.  He was convicted of killing a woman while trying to obtain information as to the whereabouts of money during a robbery.  He was put to death by electrocution for his crime.

headline: Dems ask Flaherty to run for 4th District
abstract: Former Mayor Pete Flaherty said yesterday that he has been asked by some Democrats to consider seeking nomination in the 4th Congressional District, which is currently being represented by Eugene Atkinson of Aliquippa.

headline: Some county officials must return '76 raise
abstract: The Commonwealth Court yesterday ruled that county officials who accepted a pay hike in 1976, while in office, must now return the money to their counties. The Legislature adopted a wide range on pay increases for county officials in 1976. however, as Pennsylvania's constitution prohibits them from getting raises while in office, the Court ruled that these increases must be returned.

headline: Pleas for peace; At Independence Hall, Argentina's flag waves
abstract: Demonstrators gathered in front of the Independence Hall in order to portray that the Argentine government is not against the British government and that the most important thing is to gather together and pray for a peaceful solution.

headline: Intact ticket is sought for Lotto prize
abstract: State lottery officials are searching for the winner of a lottery drawing worth 4.6 million dollars.  Officials are concerned that the winner might have destroyed the ticket, as the initial drawing was fouled; the wrong numbers were broadcasted.

headline: 'New federalism' backed by Farm Bureau president
abstract: Robert Delano, president of the American Farm Bureau Federation, claims that many social programs would be better administered at the state level.  In 1981, farm exports from the United States totaled $47 billion.  The farm bureau claims that less government interference in the form of trade embargos and subsidies would help the industry.

headline: Evac plan not forced
abstract: The author wrote this letter in response to a letter from Virginia Southard who spoke out against nuclear power and removal of personal freedom with the development of evacuation plans. The author mentions that inflation and the economy were considered to be more important than what the anti-nuclear movement preached.

headline: Stalled on the turnpike
abstract: Political deadlock between the PA Turnpike Commission and Governor Dick Thornburgh drags on while stalling some needed safety projects.  In the meantime, state Democrats have blocked Thornburgh's attempts to install Republicans on the Turnpike Commission, and in response, Thornburgh has ordered Secretary of Transportation Thomas Larson, who sits on the Commission, to vote against any long-term projects.

headline: Wilburn's Graceless Letter
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has been trying to dismantle the Pennsylvania Legal Services Center, and turn the responsibility over to the counties.  Advocates of legal aid for the poor cried alarm, predicting this initiative would be the death of the system in many areas of the state, because many counties would not be able to pick up the burden.  Their estimate was an 85 percent reduction in legal services to Pennsylvania’s poor. State Budget Secretary Robert C. Wilburn wrote a warning letter that was half sour grapes, half blackmail.  He said that the legal service unit must avoid engaging in more class-action suits or political activities, but rather it should concentrate upon "providing actual and legitimate services to eligible clients."

newspaper: z-Unidentified Observer - Journal of the PA Liquor Industry
headline: Dems Hurt By Lack Of Cash
abstract: It’s the fear of lack of money and not the fear of the invincibility of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh that is keeping big-name Democrats from challenging the current governor in the 1984 election.  With the party still in debt, no Democrat can count on the party raising the kinds of money needed to mount an effective challenge to Thornburgh, or even to raise an amount equivalent to the governor's.  Article speculates that Thornburgh will have to overcome PA's 11.8% unemployment rate; minority unrest; and Reaganomics.

headline: Some Governors Defend Reagan Plan
abstract: President Reagan’s outnumbered defenders at the 74th annual conference of the National Governors Association say it’s not his fault that he failed to come up with a New Federalism plan for a swap of federal and state responsibilities.  Several governors said Reagan called them to relay his bad news right before the conference opened.

headline: Preparation; Constitution faces an anniversary, too
abstract: The author believes that the upcoming bi-centennial of the Constitution is a great time to re-examine the Constitution itself and to study the towering figures in American history who were involved in creating this work.

headline: Judge, Shouldn't the Punishment Be Tougher
abstract: The Luzerne County President Judge found Dolores Shaughnessy guilty of third degree murder in the starvation death of her two-year old daughter.  Although we agree with the guilty verdict, it is difficult, if not alarming, that the methodical starvation of one's child over a three-month period is not considered first-degree, pre-meditated murder.

headline: Organic Farming: One Answer to the Farm Crisis
abstract: American farmers face another bleak year of trying to survive a combination of low prices for their crops and steadily escalating costs of production.  One answer to this problem would be a basic transformation in the modern methods of farming, with its heavy reliance on energy and chemicals, to one based on organic principles of farming.  The Organic Farming Act of 1982 was introduced into Congress by U.S. Representative James Weaver, with the aim of providing farmers who want to make the jump with the research and information they would need to be successful.  The chemical industry and Department of Agriculture both oppose the bill.

headline: Experts Study Film of TMI Damage
abstract: A tiny video camera has given Three Mile Island officials their first look inside the reactor that some experts say was reduced to a “rubble bed” by the nation’s worst commercial nuclear accident.  Technicians lowered the $25,000 underwater camera into the reactor to help officials plan the next major step of the plant cleanup.  Experts are analyzing the videotape.

headline: State Fighting Bigger Trucks In Gas-Tax Bill
abstract: A U.S. House bill authorizing a five cent per gallon tax on gasoline has two provisions opposed by PA. One authorizes trucks to haul twin trailers, which PA state officials are concerned by for safety reasons, particularly in the hilly areas of western PA. The bill would also allow truckers to operate wider vehicles, something which would also force PA to change its laws. The changes are seen as a way to provide relief for truckers who will be bearing the brunt of other taxes in the bill. Money from the tax will be used for construction of roads and mass transit systems nationwide.

headline: Will Contestants Link Case with Larsen Probe
abstract: The latest skirmish in an eight-year battle over an $8 million will took place in federal court.  The challengers to the will of Paul C. Ciaffoni, his widow Concetta and his son, Robert, have argued that it is fraudulent.  The elder Ciaffoni died in Washington County in 1974, leaving a will prepared by former Superior Court Judge Richard DiSalle before his appointment to that bench.  Since then the intra-family battle over the estate has wended its way from Washington County Common Pleas Court up through the state’s appellate courts.

headline: Derry Twp.'s O'Connor Is Testing Track For State Senate Run
abstract: Democrat Joe O'Connor of Derry Township will begin going door to door to determine if he should run for the seat formerly held by Republican PA Senator George W. Gekas, who won election to the U.S. House of Representatives. O'Connor observes that if the people he canvases are satisfied with the way things are then he will not run as he will be unable to win. Yet, if they are unsatisfied with the way things are it may encourage him to run. Ultimately, however, it will be up to the state party to decide who will run for the seat.

headline: Specter pushing Information bill
abstract: Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pa., said the public's right to know will be strengthened under the new Freedom of Information reform bill currently before Congress.

headline: Pre-school children need handicap aid
abstract: The author states that although one of the speakers at the Allegheny High School auditorium had proposed block-grant funding would pit kids against kids, this is already occurring at various levels.

headline: Pull back from the brink: Yes for a nuclear freeze
abstract: Philadelphians should vote 'yes' to the November 2nd ballot question asking them if they support a   mutual United States-Soviet Unioin nuclear weapons freeze.  It is time we sent a message to Washington that the civilian population will not tolerate even a limited nuclear war; our leaders must take this message seriously and act accordingly.

headline: Pennsylvania farmers are holding their ground
abstract: Pennsylvania agriculture is bucking industry trends.  The amount of farmland being sold off to developers is lower in this state than any others, while corporate farming is at 3.4% in PA, compared to 12% nationally.

headline: False Economy in U.S. Coal Policy
abstract: Neither Congressman Joseph M. McDade nor Senator Arlen Specter seem to be making much progress in attempts to restore the policy by which the Department of Defense did its shopping for anthracite coal in Northeastern Pennsylvania.  Since the coal is used for American armed forces at bases in Europe, European suppliers are able to underbid U.S. firms for most of the anthracite needed.

headline: State finds 2 cases of price fixing in car inspections, suspects more
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman announced service station owners in at least two areas of PA have been given warnings after it was discovered the owners were engaging in price fixing schemes regarding state auto inspections. The American Automobile Association (AAA) estimated the average price of auto inspections in PA has risen to $14.23, similar to results of a PA Department of Transportation Survey. The significant increase from $10 last year leads Zimmerman to believe price fixing is widespread. State police investigating service stations are on the lookout for suspicious pricing.

headline: Women (not) behind bars
abstract: A recent proposal to move women from overcrowded jails in Allegheny County to outside locations such as unused convents seems like a good idea because it would relieve the afore-mentioned overcrowding problem somewhat and help to provide better services.  A survey of women convicts shows that most are in for non-violent crime such as petty theft.

headline: Desert Oasis
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the writer is writing about the unemployment problem in the United States.  There needs to be a solution found to the problem very quickly.

headline: State aide set as Reed assistant
abstract: O. Frank DeGarcia, a bureau director in the PA Auditor General's Department, has accepted an appointment as assistant to Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed.  In doing so, he will take a $10,000 per year pay cut.  Mayor Reed has yet to name most of the rest of his staff.

headline: Project David's Mission defined
abstract: In response to the article, "75 protestors quietly observe TMI anniversary", the author states that Project David participants are not anti-nuclear protestors, as the article called them. Instead, the author believes that Project David participants were merely asking fellow citizens not to pay up for the cleanup of Unit 2 and the maintenance and restart of Unit 1.

headline: Boarding Home Loans Up To State Voters
abstract: On November 2nd, Pennsylvania voters will decide whether the state's nursing home loan program should be expanded to include personal-care boarding homes.  The state Legislature unanimously approved the referendum, which will make licensed boarding homes eligible for low-interest loans that will be used to bring them into compliance with federal fire-saftey standards.

headline: PUC Orders Utilities to Aid Dairy Farmers
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission ordered West Penn Power Company to pay 75 percent of the cost for farmers Joel Wenger and Larry Mills to install systems to counteract stray voltage from the company's distribution system. Stray voltage traveled underground to pipes and milk parlor equipment, shocking cows and decreasing milk production. West Penn argued equipment owned by the farmers caused the problem, and that the systems purchased were a cost of operating a dairy farm.

headline: FDA Readies N-Plant Related Drug Plan
abstract: The President’s Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island concluded that an adequate supply of potassium iodide should be available on a regional basis for distribution to the general public and workers affected by a nuclear radiation emergency.  Potassium iodide’s effectiveness sharply drops if taken more than an hour after exposure to radiation.

headline: State Government in Review: Assembly Exercises 'No' Voting
abstract: The General Assembly decided to say no instead of yes on most of the important bills considered for passage.  They refused to give the green light to an automobile emission system inspection program for Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and Allentown areas, creating the possibility or likelihood that federal highway funds will be withheld from the state.  They also turned down a proposed out-of-state truck axle tax that would have provided the initial funding for a seven-year, $1.3 billion bridge repair and construction program. There were other issues that were rejected by the legislators.

headline: Yard ball: Graterford team must play outside walls or not at all
abstract: Opponents of the Graterford Buccaneers, a football team in the Delaware Valley Semi-Pro Conference, want the Buccaneers to be removed from the league because of a hostage drama at Graterford State Prison.  The other teams fear for their safety and will not play unless a football field is set up outside the prison walls.

headline: District vote at a glance
abstract: The article details all candidates for each office in the region's various districts.

headline: State Dems Given Major House Posts
abstract: With the Democrats regaining control of the PA House, seven of the twenty-one committees will be headed my members from Western PA. The article lists which members will be heading which committees.

headline: Protest day; Few turn to mark Woodland anniversary
abstract: Protests marked the first anniversary of US District Chief Judge Gerald J. Weber's order to merge five east-suburban school districts to form Woodland Hills School District. However, only about 50 people turned up for the marches and rallies.

headline: The Nastiest Political Fight In Town
abstract: Many black politicians are concerned that the heated and divisive election between state Senator Milton Street and Congressmen Bill Gray will weaken the political power of Philadelphia blacks.  The election is poised to tear asunder any political unity existing within the black community and threatens to diminish the power of a group that never has had political power in proportion to its size.

headline: Sitting on bales of hay
abstract: This picture shows President Reagan, Agricultural Secretary John R. Block and Reagan's host, Leon Wilkinson, surrounded by hundreds of farmers.

headline: For 2 Companies, Nuclear Insurance Sales a Disaster
abstract: Two Pennsylvania insurance companies started to offer nuclear insurance after the 1979 leak of radiation at the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant.  Although local homeowners were concerned over the damage done to their homes, the new sales coverage of nuclear insurance has been dismal.  One company has sold less than 100 nuclear endorsements to its 40,000 homeowner policyholders.

headline: State inspections argument
abstract: Cartoon:  Legislator tells a mechanic that only one inspection per year is what motorists want.

headline: 7 Charged in '1M-Plus' Food Stamp Scam
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman is expected to announce the arrest of seven more Philadelphians charged in a food stamp fraud investigators believe netted more than $1 million.  The fraud was cracked last fall when investigators discovered the headquarters of the alleged scam in the mail room of the State Office Building at Broad and Spring Garden streets.  There was massive theft of food stamp authorization forms that had been sent to food stamp recipients but had been returned when recipients could not be located.

headline: Dole's Plan Has Lame-Duck Drawbacks
abstract: In proposing that Congress wait until after the November election to consider the financial problems straining the Social Security program, Senator Bob Dole is asking a lot of the American people.  The accountability to their constituents that now disciplines members of the House and Senate would be weakened in a lame-duck sessions, particularly among those seeking new terms who had been defeated at the polls.  They would be accountable to no one but themselves.

headline: State Department driving a wedge
abstract: Columnist calls the State Department "Arabist" and says that it is isolating Israel from its European and other friends in order to give Arab states a free hand in the destruction of the country.  He says that the goal of the State Department is to drive a wedge between the United States and Israel.

headline: PUC Rapped at Session led by Past 60 club of York; Crime also a major topic of senior citizens
abstract: High utility rates, runaway inflation and crime prevention were major concerns expressed by about 40 senior citizens attending a meeting sponsored by the Past 60 club of York. The purpose of the club, which was founded about a year ago, is to consolidate senior citizen thinking on important issues and form a united front while attempting to solve the problems.

headline: PUC Chief Hits State On Hiring of Women
abstract: The chairperson of Pennsylvania's Public Utility Commission, Susan Shanaman, says the state government hires too few women, and that women occupying top governmental posts do not receive the same respect that is accorded to men in comparable positions.

headline: US Farm debt
abstract: This page shows three graphs that depicts various aspects of the US farm debt. The first graph plots 3 types of farm debt as a percentage through the years. The second graph shows who holds the real estate farm debt. The final graph shows who earns the non-real estate farm debt.

headline: Free Enterprise
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the writer was quite interested in the "Free enterprise, sort of" editorial in an earlier edition of the paper, particularly as relates to the objective interpretation of "private enterprise" and the subjective application to the GPU-Nuclear situation.

headline: State Oks annual car inspection bill
abstract: A bill that reduces most vehicle safety inspections in Pennsylvania from every six months to once a year, needs only Gov. Dick Thornburgh's signature to become law.

headline: Amish farmer must pay social security for employees
abstract: The US Supreme Court ruled unanimously that an Amish farmer must pay Social Security taxes for his employees even though it violates his religious beliefs.  Chief Justice Warren Burger's opinion said that the federal government's need to maintain the "fiscal vitality" of the Social Security system through mandatory participation outweighed the farmer's religious claim.  The decision was part of a continuing and troublesome attempt to determine when government must accommodate religion and when religion must accommodate government.

headline: Donations nail 'free congress' group
abstract: The Committee for the Survival of a Free Congress, charged with accepting as many as 5500 illegal corporate contributions, has paid a $9500 fine to the Federal Election Commission. The FEC determined that the committee accepted as much as $78,000 in illegal contributions.

headline: State employees may join tax-break
abstract: State employees would save millions in federal income taxes under legislation approved by the senate and now awaiting action by the House. The bill permits state employees to defer paying federal income tax on the portion of their salaries which they contribute to their pension fund. Employees would have to pay it only after retirement, by which time they would be in a lower tax bracket.

headline: Putting burden on children
abstract: The author first talks about people getting angry over government spending. They demand cutbacks and get it. However, they get angry when they see children beaten to death and blame agencies like the York County Children and Youth Services, which received cutbacks in its budget. Hence, the author says in order for agencies like this to function, it is going to cost the tax payers.

headline: Bucking the jobless tide
abstract: Although the Philadelphia region's jobless rate has been below national unemployment figures, experts say the city is likely to fall behind the rest of the nation when large-scale economic recovery occurs.  This has to do with the shift from manufacturing to service-oriented jobs in the city; service industries are slower to contract during recessions and slower to expand during economic recovery.

headline: Vineyard owners working hard to place Pa. on winegrowing map
abstract: Pennsylvania is the nation's fourth largest grape producer, and has 40 varieties of wine statewide.  Penn State's Dean of Agriculture believes that 15 of these wines have good profit potential.  Last year, the state ranked 15th among the 21 wine-producing states.

headline: Future looks no brighter to GPU shareholder
abstract: Most shareholders of the company that owns Three Mile Island have seen the cost of the shares drop from $20 to about $5. They also have not been paid any dividend since November 1979. Unfortunately, the future does not look bright for these shareholders.

headline: State, industries join to keep rail line
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh announced a cooperative venture of the state and private industry to continue freight service between Warren and Johnsonburg on lines that had been earmarked for abandonedd by Conrail.  The partnership will maintain 500 jobs in the area.

headline: Amish Taxes - No
abstract: Henry P. Yoder, General Secretary of the Franconia Mennonite Conference, disagrees with Channel 10's position that the Amish employers should be required to pay Social Security taxes. He believes that the Amish are a self-contained community and through their practice of mutual aid, they do not require Social Security.

headline: Don't apologize, fellas
abstract: Some Delaware County residents had received notices that they were going to be kicked out of their houses for not paying taxes, except that they really had paid them.  Not long after, the County realized that they had screwed up, but they didn't issue an apology.  Instead, they made the residents reprove that they had paid the taxes.

headline: State Government in Review: Political Feuding Occupies Time of Public Servants
abstract: Attorneys for Governor Dick Thornburgh told Commonwealth Court that Senator H. Craig Lewis already has access to the information on state lawyers and that his request overstepped the bounds of the usual relationship between the Legislature and the executive branch.  Lewis is trying to force Thornburgh to hand over information regarding salaries, dates of employment, addresses and other specifics regarding all lawyers working for the state.  The Senator has repeatedly charged Thornburgh rewarded political friends with lucrative state legal contracts.  Other news about Pennsylvania was given in the article.

headline: Questions Musto experience, qualifications
abstract: The author of the letter believes that Mr. Musto's claims about the issue being about experience is false due to a variety of reasons detailed in the letter. The author believes that Mr. Musto does not have the requisite experience in the legislature.

headline: Pork-Barrel Politics
abstract: This article provides a list of "balanced-budget-amendment phonies."  These are members of the U.S. Senate and Congress who say they support a balanced-budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution, but all the while cast votes for items that have contributed to the largest budget-deficit in the history of the United States.

headline: Wars and weather: trials and triumph
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh drives a utility tractor at the state Farm Show; opening day visitors to the Farm Show

headline: Game Commission members take part in a roll call vote on the nomination of Peter S. Duncan III as executive director
abstract: A photograph of the PA Game Commission depicts nine members of the Commission as they participate in a roll call vote on the nomination of Peter S. Duncan III for executive director of the Commission.

headline: State's annual loss put at $7 million
abstract: PA Senator Clarence Bell, chairman of the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee, found that the state was losing as much as $7 million per year through lax enforcement of the law requiring out-of-state trucks to carry a Pennsylvania identification tag.  The Department of Revenue issues the tags that produce and estimated $34 million of revenue for the state, but that estimate is about 20% short of what the Committee found that it should be producing.

headline: Cheese distribution complaint full of holes
abstract: This article talks about the confusion that resulted due to the flexible guidelines issued n the distribution of surplus government cheese. It also briefly talks about people's concerns that newspapers were not printing the information that people needed.

headline: Don't Strike, Teachers Urged
abstract: Philadelphia community groups urged city schoolteachers not to stage their third strike in as many years and the walkout by 755 Allegheny Intermediate Unit special education teachers, counselors, therapists and nurses entered its second day with no movement toward a settlement.  Even though no talks were scheduled, there is a need to find a solution.

headline: State joins lawsuit seeking aid based on 1980 census
abstract: Pennsylvania has joined nine other states in a lawsuit aimed at forcing the US Education Department to use the most recent census figures to distribute federal money for disadvantaged children. The suit was initiated by the US Education Department.

headline: Report says reactor part plagues industry
abstract: An internal federal report has stated that Three Mile Island Unit I is among 40 commercial nuclear units where weak steam generator tubes are practically impossible to fix and are causing higher operating costs and radiation exposure for plant personnel.

headline: Change for the better
abstract: Lower Southampton Township is changing the way it handles juveniles arrested for minor criminal offenses.  Instead of sending those arrested for minor offenses to the county juvenile court, which is where they now go, offenders will appear before a youth aid panel.  The panel will determine whether youths should provide restitution to victims or perform community service.

headline: 73,500 Jobs Lost In State During Quarter
abstract: The number of jobs lost in the third quarter of 1982 was an improvement over the same statistic in the second quarter. The majority of jobs lost were in the manufacturing sector.The article further details the number of jobs lost in Philadelphia.

headline: Gas company's shutoffs cited
abstract: The Public Utility Commission (PUC) has lodged a complaint against the National Fuel Gas Corp. of Erie for repeated violations of PUC service shutoff regulations. It is the first time that the PUC has taken formal action against a utility for such violations.

headline: State-Subsidized Altoona-Pittsburgh Train to be Discontinued
abstract: A daily Altoona-Pittsburgh state-subsidized Amtrak passenger train will be discontinued next month, state transportation officials said yesterday.  Poor ridership and a low cost-revenue ratio contributed to the demise of the line according to Don Bryan, deputy secretary for local and area transportation with the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: Cheese Giveaway: This Week, It's in North Philadelphia
abstract: Churches and community groups are expected to hand out 726,000 pounds of government surplus processed cheese in North Philadelphia in a 10-week giveaway.  Those eligible for the free 5 pound cheese blocks include disable veterans, the elderly, the unemployed and people receiving welfare.

headline: Drew Lewis to leave Reagan Cabinet
abstract: One of two Pennsylvanians will leave President Reagan's Cabinet when Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis resigns in February.  He had been rumored for months to be leaving for the private sector, and said that his decision was not based on policy differences with other administration members.

headline: State Lotto at $6 Million
abstract: The jackpot in the Pennsylvania Lotto will have a record value of at least $6 million, because nobody won it last week.  The prize will be the largest ever offered in the 10 1/2 year history of the State Lottery.

headline: Soccer, religion cross paths at bingo
abstract: In January 1979, Hopewell Township priest Anthony Cipolla, joined three fellow Pittsburghers to incorporate the Padre Pio Spiritual Refuge, a non-profit devoted to improving the moral and social condition of humanity. However, there is a striking similarity of this organization with Centre Area Soccer Inc., a non-profit, on many fronts.

headline: Not exactly true
abstract: Senator John Heinz's challenger, Dr. Cyril Wecht, seems incapable of offerring any constructive criticism of the Senator.  He has tried, rather unsuccessfully, to distance himself ideologically from Senator Heinz, and has resorted to criticizing Heniz and other Senators for how rich they are.  If Dr. Wecht does not have any constructive criticism of Senator Heinz's performance in Washington, it is best for him to drop out of the election and stay home this fall.

headline: 750 miners out in 2 strikes
abstract: About 750 coal miners in Washington and Armstrong counties remained off the job on Wednesday, as part of two separate strikes. One of the strikes was triggered by Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp.'s decision to fire three employees over violations of safety regulations. The other strike related to a dispute over allowable absenteeism at Rochester and Pittsburgh Coal Co.

headline: Gas decontrol may cost $454 a year here
abstract: Natural gas costs would increase between $373 and $949 a year by 1985 for a Pennsylvania family of four if federal decontrol is approved, according to a labor-citizen coalition. Although Reagan announced he would not pursue a congressional approval of a decontrol, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission is considering taking the administrative route to decontrol.

headline: Statewide pool purchase keeping PAT bus-poor
abstract: Editorial:  It will be another year before PAT gets relief from its shortage of busses due to its participation in a Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) venture to pool purchase 1000 busses.  Port Authority erroneously estimated the delivery dates for its 410 busses.

headline: Children on the auction block
abstract: Changes proposed by PA Welfare Secretary Helen O'Bannon will require child care centers to actually bid for slots for children.  The centers would have to develop a bid package stating that they can take care of 20 children for $3 per day.  If the state cannot find someone to underbid the package, then it will approve 20 children for the bidding center.  Opponents are worried that this will lower the quality of the child care centers.

headline: Easy answers only
abstract: Columnist James Kilpatrick is pleased that the State of New York sent Republican Barber Conable back to the US House of Representatives for his 10th term. However, he agrees with Conable's assessment that politicians are often unfairly labeled by the media. The answers to the questions from the concerned public are not so often a simple yes or no.

headline: State Native May Get U.S. Post
abstract: President Reagan has nominated 41-year old Richard T. McCormack, a native of Bradford, Pennsylvania and now a resident of Washington D.C., to be Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs.  If confirmed by the Senate, McCormack would move into a top policy job for the Reagan administration, handling arrangements for international economic summits, as well as for United States participation in airline, maritime and agricultural agreements.

headline: Speakes the Spokesman: A one year journey with the press
abstract: This collage shows White House Deputy Press Secretary Larry Speakes in different pictures. Two pictures show him in an office setting while one of them shows him attending a meeting.

headline: Firing of State College President Probed
abstract: The American Association of University Professors is investigating Governor Dick Thornburg's firing of West Chester State College President Charles Mayo.  Some believe that Mayo was fired in return for a vote the administration needed on the state budget.  Governor Thornburg claims Mayo was fired because he was not an effective leader or administrator.

headline: 950 layoffs set at 2 tube mills
abstract: Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corp. said that it will shut down the tube mill at its Allenport plant for two weeks starting Monday. About 800 steel workers will be affected, taking the plant layoff total to 1400.

headline: Gasoline Prices: Praise not decontrol for decline
abstract: Editorial: Recent gasoline prices have gone down, and some claim that it is a results of President Ronald Reagan's deregulation of oil.  However, the article believes that lowering interest rates and oil prices that occurred during the Reagan presidency were actually set in motion at the end of the Carter administration; the full effects were not seen until later.  Editorial blames Reagan for needlessly raising oil prices.

headline: Suburban aide blasts PennDOT closing
abstract: Susquehanna Board President Jack Pincus calls out the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation for reneging on its promise to provide an interim fix for Interstate 81 traffic problems along two roads.  The interim project was approved by PennDOT two years ago, but was put aside pending a consent decree, recently awarded by a Federal judge.

headline: Church group asks action for jobless
abstract: The Pennsylvania Council of Churches has urged state and federal governments to step up action against unemployment and provide more social services to those who need it.

headline: Ed Rendell's 2 Political Faces
abstract: At a recent Pennsylvania Judicial Selection Project conference, Ed Rendell spoke passionately about making the political system respond to the goals of more women and minority judges.  However, he did not follow through on this and in fact he became chairman of an all-white male board of directors.

headline: State Seeking Civil Engineers
abstract: The State Civil Service Commission is looking for experienced civil engineers for positions in the Department of Transportation's District 11 office, which covers Allegheny and Beaver counties.

headline: State AFL-CIO agenda full of politics
abstract: The Pennsylvania AFL-CIO convention where nearly 2000 delegates had gathered to select a new regime to head the federation, was characterized by the politics game over of which candidate gets to head the federation.

headline: Pay off on both numbers
abstract: After PA Lottery officials declared Friday night's drawing invalid--the product of either mechanical or human error--they held another drawing to determine the actual lottery winners.  This move damaged the credibilty of the game and will surely result in law suits on behalf of the original victors.  Instead of fighting these law suits, the state should pay off both series of numbers.

headline: Administrative Monies
