abstract: Since federal guidelines require that less than 20 percent of a program’s funds to be used for administration, it seemed odd that the Blair County Employment and Training Office had been targeted 28 percent for administration and that Bedford and Cambria counties were being targeted for 25 and 22 percent, respectively.  One explanation that we heard was that the guidelines amounts in the three counties would not be a problem because the federal government looks at the entire six-county Southern Alleghenies region when it authorizes administrative amounts.

headline: Gekas Jabs GPU Nuclear chief for reaction to 'no' on restart; Says vote on TMI-1 'shrugged off'
abstract: State Sen. George Gekas, R-Harrisburg, has rebuked the top corporate officer at TMI for not paying attention to the over-whelming three-county referendum condemning the restart of TMI Unit 1.

headline: Sun Ship takeover completed
abstract: Ownership of the ailing Sun Ship Incorporated shipyards formally changed hands to Levinston Industries, a privately-held shipbuilding and repair company based in Orange, Texas.  At the peak of the shipbuilding industry during World War II and the Korean War, the shipyards once employed over 10,000, but is now down to 1700.

headline: Community agency fears federal cuts
abstract: The Philadelphia Allied Action Commission (PAAC), started in 1965 as Philadelphia's anti-poverty agency, might not survive due to cut-backs in federal spending. Officials of PAAC believe that it will be a huge struggle to remain in operation for the rest of the year.

headline: Editorial: Protecting You From Yourself
abstract: null

headline: State Sen. Craig says he'll seek re-election, not the governorship
abstract: Pennsylvania Senator H. Craig Lewis, Democrat, announced that he would not run for governor and would seek re-election to the state Senate instead.  There is only one announced candidate, State Senator James R. Lloyd for Northeast Philadelphia, for the Democratic nomination to challenge Governor Thornburgh.

headline: State Miss Takes Crown In Altoona
abstract: Laurie Ann Hixenbaugh was named the 1982 Miss Pennsylvania.  She will receive a $5,000 college scholarship, a new automobile, clothes and other merchandise.  She will act as an official Keystone State hostess at hundreds of fairs, celebrations, and conventions.  She will model the latest fashions for merchants statewide; and will serve as an official hostess for some state governmental functions.

headline: Acid-rain damage to fish widespread
abstract: Richard Schneider, a state Fish Commission expert, says that Metallic compounds and acid rain are the cause of fish deaths in the headwaters of streams throughout Pennsylvania.  As a result, the state has removed from its fish stocking list several streams at higher elevations; the commission is also proposing amendments to the federal Clean Air Act to reduce sulphur dioxide in the eastern United States.

headline: All the king's men
abstract: Editorial:  Too many agencies are out there doing job hunting and placement, while there is not enough detailed data on who is actually jobless.  Harrisburg and Washington need to stop using meaningless unemployment figures to shunt money from the productive to the unproductive.

headline: Governor returns criticism
abstract: Paul Critchlow, Governor Dick Thornburgh's Press Secretary, fired back at Democratic allegations of impropriety in the Thornburgh Administration's handling of coal mine permits.  PA Representative Thomas Michlovic called for the House Mines and Energy Management Committee to investigate the allegations, and to look into the firing of Robert Ging, a PA Department of Energy attorney who attempted to bring regulatory action against Thornburgh-supporter Bradford Coal Company.

headline: Support mass transit
abstract: The mass transit system in Youngstown, OH shut down recently, making it the first such system to do so.  However, what happened to the Youngstown system may forecast the fate of Philadelphia's.  Local taxpayers have also said no to a transit tax and increased subsidies, as transit expenses are going up.

headline: County attacks state adult services shift
abstract: Representatives of the PA Department of Public Welfare got a disapproval to its proposed dumping of the Title 20 Adult Services Administration on the commonwealth's 67 counties and slashing of funds by 37 percent.

headline: Elected PUC sought
abstract: A house bill to elect members of the Public Utility Commission (PUC) to six-year terms, was introduced yesterday. Commissioners are currently are appointed by the governor to ten-year terms.

headline: State Senate Oks Gekas Bill as Work Shield
abstract: The State Senate has approved unanimously and sent to the House a bill providing that a state employee who serves as a municipal officer would not be deemed to have an adverse interest on any action taken by the municipal body if he or she abstained and submitted a disclosure.  Senator George W. Gekas is the bills sponsor.

headline: State to delay center payments
abstract: State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer has vowed to withhold $1.4 million in payments to contractors who built the David L. Lawrence Convention Center until a series of nagging problems are eliminated.

headline: State House Voting Record Made an Issue
abstract: Albert Branch, a Republican candidate for the 103rd District state Legislative seat, claims he will represent the will of the people--something which his opponents have not been able to do.  Branch says his opponenets vote the party line.

headline: An idle threat; Cuts mean fewer summer jobs
abstract: Philadelphia's Summer Youth Employment Program, which puts teens to work in public service agencies, has only enough money to hire 11,500 disadvantaged and poor teens for several weeks this summer. However, this is drastically below meeting the needs of some 65,000 unemployed youth.

headline: GPU Asks Approval of TMI cleanup Funding Proposal
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission has been asked to approve a re-negotiated settlement to expedite the use of customer revenues to finance the cleanup at Three Mile Island.  General Public Utilities Corp., owner of the damaged nuclear plant, announced that it had filed a plan with the state PUC to spend a total $21.7 million in customer funds for cleanup of the plant damaged in the nation’s worst commercial nuclear accident.  The action would not raise customer rates, but rather it would allow Metropolitan Edison Co., and Pennsylvania Electric Co. to make an accounting shift.

headline: The Forum: Males Dictate Political Rules
abstract: There are three different editorial responses in this article.  The first and second one has to do with women and how they are becoming more politically active.  The last one is on the recent crackdown on drunk driving.

headline: County rejects block grant plan, faces fund cutoff
abstract: Allegheny County has decided to reject an "all or nothing" offer from the state to take over a variety of adult social service programs, due to the reduction in funds offered by the state. The decision could leave as many as 11000 low-income residents without counseling or other help after July 1.

headline: Election dullness cuts votes
abstract: Nearly 75% of the voters did not turn up to vote in the recently held elections. One of the main reasons for this is due to the dullness of the elections and the impression that it was only a formality for the Republicans.

headline: State to drop 50-cent lottery games
abstract: Pennsylvania's Lottery Director Lynn Nelson said that $0.50 lottery games, the state's first lottery game, will be dropped in April due to declining sales.  A new weekly, computerize game with $1 tickets will take its place.

headline: State wants county to run adult services
abstract: Public Welfare Secretary Helen B. O'Bannon has asked the Allegheny County commissioners to reconsider their refusal to assumer responsibility for local adult services. Allegheny County has complained that the $1.06 million earmarked for adult services is 20 percent below current funding.

headline: Street censure up to voters
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a constituent of state Senator Milton Street praises Senator Eugene Scanlon for recommending a formal censure of Senator Street.  This constituent is alarmed by the Senate Ethics Committee Chairman's claim that the behavior of Milton Street does not warrant further investigation, however.

headline: As unemployment rises, so do benefit frauds
abstract: Unemployment benefit cheaters are draining untold millions of dollars from a system already strained by the swelling ranks of jobless Americans. These over payments amounted to $219 million last year, a 62% increase from 1980. Pennsylvania uses a hot-line system that encourages citizens to report fraud. It has also been using computers since 1969 to track fraud.

headline: GPU financial woes worsen as new snag at Three Mile Island prolongs closedown
abstract: General Public Utilities Corporation received yet another bit of bad news when it discovered that the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor would remain offline for at least another 6 months due to widespread damage.  Previously, GPU was intending to restart the Unit 1 reactor at the end of February.  The delay is projected cost its customers several million dollars in rate hikes.

headline: The Man Behind The Move To Hike Gasoline Taxes
abstract: A profile of the U.S. Secretary of Transportation, Drew Lewis, a former PA Republican chairman.  It describes his efforts to raise the tax on gasoline by five cents a gallon in order to repair the highway system and create jobs. Lewis also gained notoriety for his handling of the U.S. air traffic controllers walkout. It is assumed that he will eventually be promoted to a more prominent job within the Reagan Administration.

headline: Court Says State Owes Welfare Aid: Reimbursing of Counties Ordered
abstract: Commonwealth Court ruled that the PA Public Welfare Department (PWD) had failed to reimburse counties adequately for child-welfare programs two years ago and that the agency must seek additional funds from the legislature to make up the difference.  The court found that state reimbursement to the counties in fiscal 1980-81 was less than the 75 percent of total costs required as a minimum then.  Although it was unknown how much the department must seek, it could be as much as $26 million.  One-third would be for Philadelphia.

headline: Election-law defect
abstract: Commonwealth Court Judge Genevieve Blatt says that the provision in requiring candidates for statewide office to obtain signatures of 100 voters in each of the five counties, gives voters in sparsely populated counties a disproportionate influence in elections, and, so, has ruled this law as unconstitutional.

headline: State Veterans Open Meeting In Monroeville
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh was scheduled to be the keynote speaker at the 63rd annual state convention of the Veterans of Foreign Wars in Monroeville.  His democratic opponent in the November gubernatorial election, U.S. Representative Allen Ertel was also scheduled to appear.

headline: Teachers' union confirms Ertel-Lloyd endorsement; Parts company with Republican Gov. Thornburgh
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Education Association has endorsed Democrats Allen E. Ertel and James Lloyd for Governor and Lieutenant-Governor, formally parting company with Republican Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Heinz for Senate
abstract: In this article, the Philadelphia Daily news endorses incumbent U.S. Senator John Heinz.  Senator Heniz, who is running against Allegheny County Commissioner Cyril Wecht, has shown a good deal of independence from the policies of the Reagan administration and has been willing to put Pennsylvania first.  Cyril Wecht has offered nothing during his campaign--other than unsuccessful attempts to link Heinz to the policies of President Reagan.

headline: Bad News: Bethlehem Steel to Eliminate 10,000 Jobs
abstract: Bethlehem Steel Corporation says it will close some operation sin New York and Pennsylvania and eliminate about 10,000 jobs due to heavy losses and little hope of improvement.  Donald Trautlein, chairman and chief executive officer, said the future of the company relies on reducing employment costs.  Johnstown will retain nearly 3,000 more jobs than Lackawanna, New York will.

headline: GPU lost $15 million in '81; extraordinary items a factor
abstract: General Public Utilities Corporation (GPU), a part owner of Three Mile Island, reported a loss of $15 million for 1981.  The loss was not directly related to the continuing financial problems associated with the shutdown of the Three Mile Island reactors.  Both reactors have been offline since March 29, 1979.  GPU says that its maintainence costs have continued to mount while the facility continues to be unable to generate revenue.

headline: The New Schedule is Designed to Raise Revenue While Keeping Fares as Low as Possible for the Rider: Fare Compromise at SEPTA Brings Hardly a Squawk
abstract: Transit fares went up from 70 to 75 cents as part of Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority’s new fare package approved.  Civic and community groups representing riders did not immediately stage demonstrations or news conferences to protest.  Commuters will be paying considerably less beginning September 1st, when most passengers on the 13-line commuter rail network will enjoy substantially lower fares.  There are several new ideas offered as part of the restructuring of the commuter rail-fares that community leaders liked.

headline: Deadline May 14 to get aid with heating bills
abstract: Low-income families seeking help with paying winter heating bills must apply by May 14 at the county assistance offices in order to be eligible for the same.

headline: End registrar anomaly by abolishing registrars
abstract: The US Supreme Court has upheld the state's appeal of a ruling by US district judge Louis Pollack in the matter of 8 Democratic registrars of vital statistics in Delaware County.  The US Supreme Court found that it is unconstitutional to discharge public officials on the basis of political affiliation.

headline: State workers union admits illegal raffles
abstract: Pennsylvania's largest public employees union has been holding illegal raffles virtually under the nose of the state's law enforcement agencies to raise money for political candidates.

headline: Television: After all, life goes on
abstract: The author gives credit to Larry Kane for the professional and objective manner in which he handled the story about Mayor Green filing a $5.1 million libel suit against CBS, himself and four of his fellow WCAU-TV staffers.

headline: State rejects AFSCME proposal
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has rejected the latest AFSCME proposal.  Administration spokespersons say that AFSCME needs to revise its proposals to reflect the dire economic realities facing the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: City is falling short of its summer-job goal
abstract: Most of the 26,000 people from the ages of 14-21 who have applied for jobs through the city have not been lucky enough to secure one. One of the reasons for this include the drastic reductions in federal funding for jobs programs and the reduction in Philadelphia's Summer Youth Employment and Training Program.

headline: GPU's monitors can be trusted
abstract: A letter to the editor from William Gifford, Vice President of Communications for GPU Nuclear, disputes a recent editorial suggesting that Lancaster County should install its own radiation monitoring system rather than relying on the existing tie-in with GPU Nuclear's monitoring system.  Gilford says there is no need to spend additional monies on a redundant monitoring system.

headline: The Pennsylvania Department
abstract: Columnist George Fattman believes the PA Department of Transportation could have put money used for new signs along Route 219 to better use. After all, what was wrong with the old ones?

headline: Delay for Study Asked in State Day Care Plan
abstract: State Senator Jeanette Reibman asked the PA Welfare Secretary Helen O’Bannon for a three-month delay in plans that eventually would put state-supported day care on a voucher system.  The welfare department plans to centralize the process of determining eligibility for government-supported day care, which is now done on the local level.

headline: Ertel mum on governorship
abstract: US Representative says that he will make his official announcement about running for governor next week.  Ertel was last on the list of Democratic candidates to be considered when PA Senator Michael O'Pake withdrew.  The only other announced candidate at this time is freshman PA Senator James Lloyd.

headline: State Yule Tree Lighting Held
abstract: Governor Thornburgh helped light the State Christmas Tree in the State Capitol Rotunda. The Governor spoke of the world joining together in peace and the reminder to help those who are not as fortunate. The article relates stories of others who had attended previous ceremonies.

headline: Tell it to the publisher
abstract: Last week, the new format of the Sunday Patriot-News made it debut and it was generally well-received. Although there were certain negative criticisms, the positive ones outweighed the other.

headline: Odd Vote
abstract: It is difficult to comprehend why U.S. Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter favor a 227 million dollar appropriation for the Clinch River Breeder Reactor--especially during a period of huge government deficits.

headline: Congressmen Call on All Businesses to Support 'Hire the Youth' Program
abstract: A bipartisan group of congressmen have pledged their support of Rev. Leon H. Sullivan’s "Hire One Youth" jobs program.  The goal is to create one million jobs for unemployed young Americans.  Rev. Sullivan is the founder and chairman of the Opportunities Industrialization Centers of America, a job training organization headquartered in Philadelphia.

headline: Hazardous waste turned to fuel
abstract: Peter Kipin, owner of a Pittsburgh-based engineering firm, stated that his firm has developed a recycling process that can convert hazardous wastes such as oil residues and other harmful substances, into usable fuel.

headline: The vetoes that weren't
abstract: This editorial discusses PA Governor Thornburgh's decision to sign "two very flawed pieces of legislation".  One stiffened penalties for drunken driving and the other providing for a new verdict of "guilty but mentally ill."  Governor Thornburgh questioned both of these drafts but decided to sign them anyway.

headline: Disability Cuts Target of 2 Bills
abstract: Due to controversy over the cutoffs of thousands of Social Security disability payments, Senator John Heinz introduced two separate bills aimed at reforming the federal review process of such payments. “This legislation is urgently needed to protect the more than four million disabled workers and their families from the increasingly likely possibility that they will have their benefits terminated.”

headline: Ertel, armed with specifics, seldom bypasses a chance to argue
abstract: What US Congressman Allen Ertel seems to like most about his job is the chance to argue.  This reputation for quibbling would be something that would haunt him in a gubernatorial race.  Article discusses specific issues that Ertel has argued with others, including President Ronald Reagan, and its impact on the race.

headline: State-level public campaign funding
abstract: When Democratic gubernatorial candidate Allen Ertel proposed that he and Republican incumbent Gov. Thornburgh limit total spending in their election bids to $1.7 million, it was immediately rejected by Thornburgh. The author also states that spending limits generally hurt the challenger more than the incumbent.

headline: The Gala: Hope on Grace and hoagies
abstract: Bob Hope came up with some of the best lines during the Princess Grace gala on Wednesday night. His jokes spanned a lot of areas including Kelly, Annenberg and had political humor as well.

headline: County jail hearing reset amid charges of politics
abstract: A state Senate hearing on conditions at the Allegheny County jail has been moved from this Friday to November 5.  The hearing was moved because Allegheny County Commissioner Cyril Wecht, who is challenging incumbent U.S. Senator John Heinz, believed that the hearing would be used to discredit his U.S. Senate campaign.

headline: A look at events of the past week; Agent Orange victory
abstract: In a unanimous vote, the Senate passed a bill sponsored by Rep. John F. Cordisco of Bristol Borough that would create a 15-member Vietnam Herbicides Information Commission, in order to disseminate information about the suspected ill-effects of toxic herbicides and to determine the type of assistance needed.

headline: Day or night, night or day?; A shift from the normal work schedule, researchers
abstract: Researchers have concluded that shift work - where employees have other than a standard daytime shift - may be considered to be dangerous for both workers and the society. They also concluded that shift work was one of the causes for the Three Mile Island disaster.

headline: House says PUC can't OK billing for construction
abstract: The State House voted unanimously to strip the Public Utility Commission (PUC) of its authority to permit utilities to charge ratepayers for the construction costs of major generating facilities or other large projects before those facilities are placed into service.

headline: They're fighting back
abstract: Patricia and Richard Nieman have joined Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) and were out distributing petitions yesterday.  Their second child killed by a drunk driver was buried four days ago.

headline: Few Jobs Landed Through PEP Help
abstract: The Pennsylvania Employable Program found jobs for a fraction of those who asked for help this fall.  This program was expanded state wide with reforms in state welfare regulations, and the group placed just 5% of those who would have been removed from welfare rolls after receiving three months' benefits.

headline: Ertel's Sad Fate
abstract: If Allen Ertel beats Richard Thornburgh in the race for Governor he will have to raise taxes to the moon to gain the $400 million necessary to fulfill his pledge of 50 percent state subsidization of public education.  The Pennsylvania State Education Association abandoned Thornburgh because the governor refused to raise the taxes and left increases to the discretion of local school districts.

headline: States face hard times
abstract: Many state governments are facing difficult decisions as recession brings down state financial resources.  Article talks about the typical actions of state legislators faced with sagging state treasuries and potentially higher tax rates in an election year.

headline: The Irvis Report
abstract: House Democratic Leader K. Leroy Irvis lashed out against the Thornburgh Administration because of its efforts to suppress freedom of speech and subvert state laws on public access to information. This is in connection with Education Secretary Robert Scanlon's statement that Education Department employees giving information to or conferring directly with the Pennsylvania State Education Association would be fired.

headline: 4.6 Million Winner Fears for Saftey
abstract: After a lottery-drawing foul-up and subsequent re-drawing, state officials in Pennsylvania are withholding the name of the man who won 4.6 million dollars.  The foul-up, which involved the wrong numbers being called on a television broadcast, stripped several second and third-place winners of their prizes; some ticketholders are threatening to sue the state.

headline: null
abstract: Named after Section 302 of the state’s 1976 Mental Health Procedures Act, a 302 is the first step in getting psychiatric help for an unwilling person.  Without it police, hospitals, and even doctors can do nothing against the patient’s will.  Even after a 302 is signed, the patient cannot be moved until the county mental health and mental retardation administrator’s office is called, and someone there is convinced that the prospective patient satisfies the legal criteria to issue a warrant, entitling the police to bring him in against his will to a hospital or crisis center.

headline: Feds wage war on sweatshop eateries
abstract: The US Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division, which investigates employers accused of violating federal minimum wage and overtime laws, received more complaints in the last 18 months from Philadelphia restaurant workers than from any other single group of local employees.

headline: Idaho governor supports accepting wastes from TMI
abstract: Idaho Governor John Evans announced support of a federal plan to remove radioactive materials from the damaged nuclear plant at Three Mile Island and transport them to the Idaho National Engineering Laboratory. However, he opposed the federal proposal to require utilities throughout the country to share the costs of cleaning up the plant.

headline: Thornburgh fails on bridge problem
abstract: The author believes that the Governor does not care for the Coraopolis community as the government has not heeded the advice of the author to enlist the army to help build the Bailey bridge that could have acted as a substitute for the Groveton Bridge. Now, with the closing of the Groveton bridge, the community is cut-off from the rest of the region.

headline: Further challenges slated to ruling on welfare cuts
abstract: Douglas Dye, a lawyer representing two welfare groups, says he will challenge a ruling that allows Pennsylvania to implement Federally-mandated welfare cuts.  The 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the US Department of Health and Human Services had acted appropriately in implementing the cuts, overturning an earlier decision by a US District Judge that blocked the reduced payments.

headline: Ethics Code confusion
abstract: This editorial discusses the Ethics law passed by the state legislature requiring annual disclosure of sources of income over $500, to reveal conflicts of interest.  In Bucks County the filing of financial disclosure statements by public employees and elected officials has been confusing and problem causing and hopefully things will run more smoothly next time around.

headline: State's 'gag' ruling a ridiculous concept
abstract: The allegiance of a bureaucracy should be to the people and not to an administration. Hence, the Pennsylvania State Education Association (PSEA) has a right to information which the bureaucracy should purvey. However, this goes against PA Education Secretary Robert Scanlon's comments about ordering department employees to not pass on information to the PSEA.

headline: The Kitchen
abstract: A party will be held on Wednesday as a  show of gratitude to all those who made possible the operation of the St. Francis of Assisi Kitchen.

headline: Check 'em out at the deabtes
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the reader agrees with an editorial telling voters to evaluate the liberal voting record of U.S. Representative Robert Edgar before casting their vote.  In fact, at a recent debate Representative Edgar was much less impressive than his opponent, Steve Joachim.

headline: null
abstract: Public Relations and advertising executives between the ages of 45 and 64 years died from heart attacks, strokes, and other stress-related causes in a recent one-year period.  That conclusion was reached by two Trenton (N.J.) State College researchers, based on a comparison of insurance mortality statistics within 60 obituaries from Advertising Age, a trade publication.

headline: Hurting the Children
abstract: Pennsylvania has not found a way to avoid hurting its children when it comes to teacher strikes.  Objective studies have established beyond doubt that strikes are detrimental to youngsters.  As long as Act 195 continues to exist in its current form, students will continue to suffer.  The law will not change until the union lobbyists retreat in the legislature.  And this is not just about to take place in a commonwealth dominated by organized labor.

headline: In panel's decision, PE sees a ray of hope for Unit 2
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Company acknowledged that it will try to keep Unit 2 of the Limerick nuclear station alive merely by suspending construction rather than writing off its investment in the unit.

headline: Thornburgh gets Inspection bill
abstract: The Inspection bill that would set the number of auto safety inspections to once a year was passed by the Senate in a 41-6 vote.

headline: Geraldine Jones Case
abstract: Geraldine Jones was charged with the murder of a Philadelphia woman, but the police were not able to arrest her. Her contention was that she was never in hiding and mentions that she collected her welfare check three times, without being questioned. The article stresses on the need for the Welfare Department to not be an accessory to crimes like this.

headline: Even Differing, They're Alike
abstract: U.S. Representative Lawrence Coughlin, Republican and Democratic challenger Martin J. Cunningham Jr. are running for the 13th Congressional District, which includes Montgomery County and parts of Philadelphia.  Both believe that the other one should get out of the race.  Cunningham said that Coughlin used campaign money to pay rent and electric bills at a rented garage apartment.  Coughlin told reporters that he did use funds for rent and utilities but he said he had a written legal opinion from the Republican National Campaign Committee and a very specific advisory opinion from the Federal Election Commission said that such payments are legal.

headline: States try to assess the impact
abstract: Pennsylvania and New Jersey, still reeling from last year's $36 billion cuts in federal spending on domestic programs, reacted negatively to the new budget proposed by President Ronald Reagan for 1983 that included another $27 billion in spending cuts.  PA Welfare Secretary Helen O'Bannon expressed concern over the new proposal to count low-income energy assistance grants as income when calculating elidgibility for Medicaid.

headline: Thornburgh addresses Polish-American league
abstract: Gov. Thornburgh visited the annual convention of the Philadelphia-based Polish-American Citizens League, in the hope of winning their endorsement for his re-election.

headline: Williams for State Senate
abstract: The Philadelphia Daily News endorses state Representative Hardy Williams for state Senate.  Although Representative Williams has an uninspiring record, he has the experience and skill to get things done in Harrisburg--something which his his opponenet, clergyman Thomas M. Porter, lacks.

headline: null
abstract: The problem of placing mental hospital patients is a national one, which the federal government began to confront in 1977 when it established the Community Support Program.  This is an experimental effort to provide ex-hospital patients with comprehensive services- residential care, vocational training, counseling.  Since 1977 a total of $20 million in grants has been spent in 20 states including New Jersey but not Pennsylvania or Delaware.  Preliminary studies showed that patients did better if they received the extra CSP Services.  The program seemed to be working so well that last year Congress voted to double the annual appropriation to $15 million, to expand the program to more states.

headline: Increase In Average Weekly Wage To $306 Will Boost Jobless Benefits
abstract: Because PA's average weekly statewide wage increased in this fiscal year, unemployment compensation and workers' compensation benefits will go up as well.  The rest of the article details how much the benefits will increase for each category, when they will go into effect, and how much it will cost the state.

headline: Itkin Pushes Home Energy-Saving Standards
abstract: Representative Ivan Itkin from Squirrel Hill has accused the state Department of Community Affairs with "gross negligence" for allowing Pennsylvania’s residential energy conservation standards to be set to expire during the height of the home-building season. A Department of Community Affairs spokesperson said that the department had approved the updated regulations and sent them to the legislative reference bureau for publication in the Pennsylvania Bulletin.

headline: Thornburgh Here To Ink Axle Tax Bill
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh will visit the area today to sign a bill imposing a tax on truck axles. The revenue will finance a loan meant, along with funds from the U.S. government, to repair almost one thousand PA bridges, including seventy-five in Allegheny County. The same bill also reduces truck registration and annual marker fees.

headline: GOP-controlled Senate refuses to sweeten benefits for aging
abstract: The Republican-controlled PA Senate, concerned about the fiscal impact of a porposed one-time $200 anti-inflation check, has refused to approve a bill that would deviate from the previously-agreed $100 check.  The legislation would also increase property tax and rent rebate checks.  The benefits are financed with revenues from the state lottery fund.

headline: Ex-Area Man State's New Schools Aide
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh named William H. Isler as the acting commissioner for basic education.  He will receive a salary of $35,000.  Isler has served as executive assistant to the commissioner since August.  From 1972 to 1976, he was the director of children’s services for Monongahela Valley United Health Services in Monessen.

headline: Statewide banking
abstract: Although the Legislature finally approved state-wide banking, this would have existed despite the bill simply because of the vast array of new services being offered by non-banks.

headline: Toxic fumes overcome 20 Goodwill employees
abstract: Twenty employees of Goodwill Industries, many confined to wheelchairs, were overcome by toxic fumes on Thursday morning, when pressurized sulphur dioxide spread throughout the building, according to police and fire reports. Two city policemen were also overcome by the fumes. They were treated at the Harrisburg Hospital and later released.

headline: null
abstract: A picture shows incumbent U.S. Senator John Heinz and his opponent, Cyril Wecht, in their first debate.

headline: $70 Million Blue Shield Plan Gets "Close Look"
abstract: Frank K. Jones, president of the Citizens Committee for Ethnical Insurance, excoriated the insurance industry as “the greatest vultures feasting on illness that I can think of.”  He blistered the state Insurance Department as “an elaborate bill-collecting service for doctors by bureaucrats who have (elaborate medical) benefits without a concern for who has to pay the doctors’ bills.  People are paying through the nose for the lack of honesty by the Pennsylvania Insurance Department.

headline: 'Indomitable Spirit of Working People' Will Prevail: McBride
abstract: United Steelworkers of America President Lloyd McBride declared that there is "little to cheer for working America except for the indomitable spirit of working men and women."  This spirit is of far greater importance and benefit to the nation than the "continued optimistic promises" of the Reagan Administration, made in the face of economic depression and social despair that show no end in sight.

headline: Kill Clinch River Project Now
abstract: The time is at hand to eliminate the bottomless money pit that is the Clinch River Breeder Reactor project.  The House is expected to vote on Wednesday for additional funding for this outdated, outrageously expensive project that continues to drain the public treasury.  The project is designed to produce more nuclear fuel than it consumes while at the same time extracting plutonium from the fuel.  About $1.3 billion has been spent on the project, although no construction has begun.  The Energy Department says another $2.3 billion is needed to complete it.

headline: Thornburgh To Sign Bill On Drunken Driving
abstract: Although Governor Thornburgh will sign a tougher drunk driving bill today, because it won't go into effect for another thirty days it cannot be enforced during the New Year's holiday. While the bill was written by a Thornburgh appointed task-force, he insisted on a thorough review before signing it in order to identify areas he had concerns with.

headline: Governors Seek Reagan's Support for 'New Federalism'
abstract: Glossing over continuing differences with the White House, the nation’s governors voted to develop their own new federalism plan, but to actively seek President Reagan’s agreement in the process.  The governors contend that income maintenance programs should be a federal responsibility.  The White House agreed to make Medicaid a federal responsibility and maintain the food stamp program, if the states would take over the basic welfare program, Aid to Families with Dependent Children.

headline: Ex-judge now on ethics panel
abstract: Former Judge Roy Wilkinson has been appointed to the PA Ethics Commission by Governor Dick Thornburgh.  Wilkinson served for 10 years as a Commonwealth Court Judge before being named by Thornburgh to fill a one-year vacancy on the PA Supreme Court.

headline: Steelton man seeks vacated Gekas seat
abstract: Ernest Butler, active with the NAACP and a former member of the US Army and Air Force, submitted a letter to the Dauphin County GOP declaring a bid for the seat vacated by PA State Senator George W. Gekas. Gekas will leave his term early for US Congress. Butler is one of 5 Republicans vying for the seat, including PA Rep. Jeffrey Piccola, former Republican county chairman Robert F. Dick, John Shumaker, former president of City Council Miriam Menaker and possibly PA Rep. Joseph Manmiller.

headline: Welcome gun nuts!; The NRA put us to the test. Are we a great convention city - or not?
abstract: Philadelphia was recently the host city for the 111th anniversary of the NRA convention. This attracted hundreds of people all over the country and provided a great example to see whether Philadelphia was a great convention city or not.

headline: Health risks tied to large day-care centers
abstract: Two Pennsylvania doctors warn that large day-care centers can be hazardous to toddlers' health.  In Pittsburgh, outbreaks of hepatitus, meningitis and diarrhea have been linked to large day-care facilities.  Doctors say that outbreaks often result from parents not being able to take off from work to tend to sick children.

headline: 4 doctors, 2 others accused of Medicaid fraud
abstract: Four physicians and two businessmen were indicted by a federal grand jury on fraud charges and accused of collecting Medicaid payments for medical tests and services that were either unnecessary or not conducted.  The six men collected $300,000 in Medicaid payments, more than half was obtained through fraud.

headline: Iron Workers End Seven-Week Strike
abstract: Iron Workers went back to work after a seven-week strike.  Leo Puma, president of the organization declined to give details of the three-year contract, but said it included an "adequate" wage increase and resolution of other strike issues.  Under the local’s previous contract with the Ironworkers Employers Association of Western Pennsylvania, the top journeyman’s hourly wage was $14.24.

headline: Judge Denies Request to Dismiss Suit Against NRC
abstract: A federal judge has denied a government request to dismiss a $4 billion civil suit that accuses the Nuclear Regulatory Commission of negligence in the Three Mile Island accident.  U.S. District Judge E. Mac Troutman rejected government claims that the suit, brought by the owners of TMI, should be dismissed under laws that protect government agencies from liability.  Troutman delayed enforcement of his order to give the government an opportunity to appeal the decisions to the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

headline: Thornburgh Warns of Road Fund Freeze
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh says that Pennsylvania risks losing part of $1 billion in money from the federal gasoline tax increase due to the Legislature's failure to approve required automobile emissions tests. Governor Thornburgh commended Congress for passing the program but is pushing the State Legislature to work toward another solution.

headline: Guv Oks checks for elderly
abstract: About 420,000 low-income elderly Pennsylvanians will get a $100 'anti-inflation' check in April under legislation approved by Governor Thornburgh, as a measure of protection against the ravages of inflation. This law also has other new benefits for the elderly.

headline: Expense-ive
abstract: There are whole families in Philadelphia who live on $250 a week.  For Pennsylvania Court Administrator Alexander F. Barbierei, it isn’t enough to cover his lunch tabs.  It’s not that the judge is on his way to the poorhouse.  He’s paid $60,000 a year to oversee “prompt and proper disposition of the business” of the state’s courts.  The $12,000 a year on top of it is an unaccounted expense account.  That means it’s nobody’s business what the judge does with the money.  He doesn’t have to fill out an expense account like mere morals do.

headline: Steelworker Claiming $3.6 Million Lotto Win
abstract: A 31-year old bachelor is claiming more than a third of the record $9.2 million prize in the Pennsylvania Lottery.  His name is Nicholas Marianov.  He is planning on enjoying life with the approximately $3.6 million he is claiming.

headline: Winning on a shoestring
abstract: Nationally-ranked  Cheyney State has basketball Coach John Chaney whose team has won national NCAA Division II championships, but he still acts like the team equipment manager.  In his 9 years as coach, he has a record of 199 wins and 56 losses.  He's a good coach.

headline: 4.6 Million Winner Was Just Buying Time
abstract: The winner of a 4.6 million dollar lottery jackpot asked state lottery officials not to reveal his identitiy.  The winner, Nicholas Eisenhardt, wanted time to move from his Reading neighborhood to a safer location before his name was revealed to the public; Eisenhardt did not feel his neighborhood was safe and was worried about how his neighbors would react to the news.

headline: A Doctor Writes: Closing Pennhurst a Mistake
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the writer is responding to the article on Pennhurst on November 11th.  This person was a full-time physician at Pennhurst from 1981 to 1982.  He feels well-qualified to comment on the proposed Pennhurst closing.  He thinks the institution provides excellent quality care and provides a vital role in caring for the mentally retarded.

headline: Layoffs to continue at Cheseter Shipyard
abstract: Sun Ship Incorporated announced that it would continue the previous shipyard owner's layoff policy once it assumes control.  Employment at the complex has dropped from 4100 to below 1700 already.  A new labor contract that delays pay increases allowed the sale to go through.

headline: Lancaster 'Rate Rebels' Begin Hearings on PP&L
abstract: Two years after filling their complaint with the Public Utility Commission, some Lancaster County “rate rebels” had their day in court.  Barney and Evelyn Epstein have joined 200 other families who claim their electric rates are higher because of Pennsylvania Power and Light Co.’s unfinished Susquehanna nuclear power plant.  The couple filed the original complaint after PP&L threatened to shut off their service because they were withholding 10 percent of bill payments in protest of hidden costs of building the Susquehanna plant.  PP&L serves 29 counties in Central and Eastern Pennsylvania.

headline: Toll collection deading into computer age
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission has approved $27 million to computerize toll collection, the first major modernization project since 1940.  The new system will connect all of the toll plazas to each other and to the Turnpike headquarters, and speed services to motorists.

headline: Hearing scheduled on OVR furloughs
abstract: After the announcement that more than 100 job counselors and their supervisors are scheduled to be laid off along with 114 clerks and managers at branch offices, the Pennsylvania Social Services Union and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees each filed suit contending that the layoffs are illegal.

headline: Ex-Philadelphia Aide Moves to Grab Mayoral Contest Spotlight
abstract: The race for Philadelphia mayor appears to be a four-way primary for Democrats, with confirmed candidate Thomas A. Leonard, former City Comptroller, former Mayor Frank Rizzo, yet to "officially" declare his intent, possibly City Managing Director Wilson Goode, and potentially District Attorney Ed Rendell. Rizzo says he will win the primary, while Goode says he will win the election. Rendell is hesitant to run, not wanting to appear to be preventing Goode from being the first black mayor.

headline: Symbol of Kindness
abstract: The writer of this editorial discusses the view of Santa Claus  as a symbol of kindness (as named by a Pennsylvania judge) and encourages those who can to give to the New York Times Neediest Cases Fund.

headline: WITF's film at world's fairs
abstract: Excerpts from the WITF-TV, channel 33's production of "The National Nuclear Debate" have been selected for inclusion in the United States exhibit at the 1982 World's Fair.

headline: Suspected Rapist At Large
abstract: After escaping from a medium-security hospital in South Fayette, Kevin Cooper abducted, beat and raped a 17-year-old Upper St. Clair girl.  Pennsylvania Department of Welfare officials and state police are investigating the escape; Cooper is still at large.

headline: A great favor
abstract: This letter states that other letters which protest about the mentally retarded child whose parents allowed it to die, have not experienced what it is like to have a retarded child. The author understands the mental anguish undergone by parents of retarded children.

headline: More Jobless Face prospect of Exhausting Their Benefits
abstract: The number of Americans filing for their last few weeks of emergency benefits nationwide more than tripled in two months according to government figures.  Of 12 million Americans counted as jobless only 5 million are now collecting unemployment benefits.

headline: Leaky tubes at TMI plant a new strain
abstract: The problem of corroded and leaky tubes in the steam generators at the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor has proven to be unusually large and has taken a surprise turn, according to Robert Arnold, president of GPU Nuclear Energy Corporation.  Tests show that between 8,000-10,000 of the plants heat exchange tubes may be damaged. These problems will cause the plant to remain closed for up to one more year.

headline: Toll-road extension nears state study
abstract: The Senate Transportation Committee has approved a feasibility study for extension of the state's toll road system after rejecting PennDOT-backed amendments to the bill. The bill directs the Turnpike Commission to conduct the study limited to specific projects, mostly in Western Pennsylvania.

headline: Heinz: Isolate Social Security
abstract: As soon as Sen. John Heinz, R-Pa., made a proposal to take Social Security out of the budget, the bipartisan commission appointed to reform the system erupted into a partisan squabble.

headline: Far right hit list
abstract: The February edition of the Conservative Digest listed members of the President Reagan's cabinet who were not complete believers of extreme conservatism. The author believes that such kind of lists and criticism could be detrimental to the Reagan administration and might even return Congress to the one-party system of the 1960's and 70's.

headline: Stokes out of race
abstract: Robert F. Stokes, former Mayor of Clairton, yesterday withdrew as a candidate for the Republican nomination for Congress in the 18th District.

headline: More prisions are on the way
abstract: This article gives the details of prison construction and expansion plans in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware.  In Pennsylvania, the General Assembly has appropriated monies to build two 500-bed institutions at Graterford and Huntington Prisons.  The appropriation will also add cells to three institutions, and Governor Thornburgh's proposal to build a new prison in Schuykill County is under consideration.

headline: A Strike Threat Ends
abstract: A strike of hospital workers in Philadelphia would have imposed hardship on patients, making already difficult problems worse.  Thus it was a welcome development when Henry Nicholas, president of District Council 1199-C of the National Hospital and Health Care Employees, called off a strike he had threatened as a protest against inadequate health care for the poor.  Governor Thornburgh held a joint news conference with Mr. Nicholas to announce that the strike had been averted, supposedly because the governor promised to increase state reimbursement for Medicaid care to some hospitals in the city and other urban areas that serve large numbers of poor people.  Qualifying hospitals, those with more than 24 percent of their patients eligible for Medicaid, will receive an increase of one-half of 1 percent in reimbursement for care to those patients.  Other hospitals, with a lower percentage of Medicaid patients, will get a slight reduction in reimbursement.

headline: Non-Profit Co-op Urged for Worker Compensation
abstract: State House Democrats have proposed a restructure of the sale of worker's compensation insurance in Pennsylvania through the creation of a Pennsylvania Employers' Cooperative as the exclusive seller of the coverage.  It would not attempt to make a profit, nor would it require a sales force, but it would offer "a pure insurance service" to employers.

headline: Legal styles illuminate hearing
abstract: Two lawyers - one representing Duquesne Light Co. and the other representing a citizens' group - have emerged as key opponents in hearings on a five-month outage at the electric utility's Beaver Valley Nuclear Power Plant. The plant was shut down on worries about the safety of pipes and its ability to withstand an earthquake.

headline: Tolls on Interstates Not Uncommon
abstract: This editorial discusses the consideration to make portions of Interstate Roads 80 and 81 toll roads, and states that this is not as radical an idea as it seems.  Funds are needed to provide for maintenance of the road system but the writer also acknowledges that tolls slow the flow of traffic.

headline: Hoping for better use of our welfare fund
abstract: Governor Thornburgh recently signed House Bill 720 in order to facilitate his welfare reform program across the state.

headline: Far Short of Fair Return
abstract: The federal government is considering a “realignment” of the army at the Fort Indiantown Gap in Pennsylvania.  This is Pennsylvania’s only significant military base.  This would take jobs away from the state as well as placing the cost of maintaining the base on taxpayers.  Governor Dick Thornburgh and his Democratic opponent, Allen Ertel both agree that it would not be in the best interests of the state to have an Army realignment.

headline: Street Denied GOP Ballot Slot
abstract: A Commonwealth Court Judge has denied State Senator T. Milton Street, a second line on the November 2nd election ballot as a substituted Republican candidate for Congress from the city’s Second District.  This does not affect Street’s independent candidacy entered on May 25 under his own ballot label of “Milton Street Party.”  State Elections Commissioner Richard Anderson said at first it would be illegal for Street’s name to appear twice on the ballot, but later reversed himself after he consulted counsel.

headline: GOP, Democrats suffer failure of nerve
abstract: Republican supply-side economic theories are being challenged by Democratic investment-side approaches to the economy and recovery.  Just like supply-side theories rely on the implausible notion that tax cuts are self-financing, investment-side theories engage in the same sort of wishful thinking--arguing that government investment in infrastructure will pay for itself.  While neither vision is perfect, government intervention in the economy will only exacerbate economic woes.

headline: Are retarded entitled to treatment?
abstract: The US Supreme Court hears an appeal of the case Nicholas Romeo vs. the State of Pennsylvania to determine whether mentally-challenged individuals put in custody of the state are entitled to rehabilitation services or whether incarceration with care is sufficient.

headline: Our Opinion: It's time to Invest in Some Jobs
abstract: The amount of unemployment in the Philadelphia area stood at 9.1 percent.  It was 40 percent for black people.  A newly formed coalition of 40 community based organizations is requesting that corporations invest some of their profits in a program to create summer jobs for youths.

headline: Letters to the Editor: Election of PUC Would Breed Abuses
abstract: The Pennsylvania Electric Association fully agrees with The Press’s August 8 editorial objecting to the proposal to elect the Public Utility Commission.  The election of PUC commissioners would, indeed, politicize the PUC and lead to abuse that Pennsylvania is happily free of.  Electric rates rise and fall in response to economic forces over which neither the industry nor the PUC has control.

headline: Truckers fear backlash on proposed $36-an-axle truck fee
abstract: President of the PA Motor Truck Association, William Yocum, fears the bill introduced by House Majority Leader Samuel Hayes Jr., in conjunction with PA Governor Thornburgh's Administration, will create a backlash. Higher fees in one state lead to higher fees in another. Yocum says the Association will instead supporting a federal gas tax. Hayes' proposal combines federal and local government, and trucking fees to pay for bridge repairs. PA Department of Transportation spokesman James McCarron did not expect high costs of collect fees.

headline: Housing 'Tape' cut by Council
abstract: City Council has unanimously approved a bill aimed at eliminating illegal squatting by greatly reducing the time it takes for the city to turn abandoned houses over to needy families willing to rehabilitate them.

headline: Fascinating Exchange
abstract: Editorial discusses a recent exchange between Westmoreland Commissioners John Regoli and Robert Miller that had Regoli lamenting the loss of manna from state and federal heavens while Miller tried to face the realities of Reganomics with positivism. Editorial says that both commissioners now see the error of becoming too addicted to "outside" cash and both showed signs of a begrudging willingness to accept home rule.

headline: Swatara appoints 1st woman commissioner; Patricia Macut well-known in Enhaut
abstract: Patricia Macut, a 27-year-old state government employee, became Swatara Twp.'s first woman commissioner. She replaces Democrat Charles Kireta as representative from the township's 3rd Ward.

headline: Debatable format
abstract: Bucks County will have two congressional debates--one open to the public and another open only to evenly-divided contingents of the four candidates' supporters.  Ideally, debates should be open to the public at large, but the two distinct formats will provide useful lessons for future debates.  Regardless of format, all four cadidates--James Coyne, Peter Kostmayer, Al Reef, and Hans Schroeder--should be lauded for their willingness to participate in the debates.

headline: Astleford Suspected of Flexing 'muscle' in nursing-home rulings
abstract: There is evidence of political string-pulling to get a last-minute reprieve for three nursing-home projects by Astleford & Associates, Ltd.  The projects, proposed for sites in Cambria and Somerset counties, were saved when the State Secretary of Health rejected the recommendations of the Keystone Health Systems Agency and approved changes in the projects.  Astleford denies that they had that kind of influence to pull off a state-level decision.

headline: Potential Private Ownership Eyed in State Stores
abstract: The Commonwealth has reached agreement with the State Store Clerks union on a new contract which provides 8 percent wage increases effective July 1, 1981, and July 1, 1982.  Budget and Administration Secretary Robert C. Wilburn said that the contract is fair to the clerks and their employer-the commonwealth and its citizens.  "It provides for a ‘legitimate opportunity’ for interested and qualified State Store Clerks to acquire and operate private liquor stores if and when the General Assembly approves Governor Dick Thornburgh’s proposal for a private retail liquor system, and it provides a wage settlement consistent with that negotiated with the other major state employee unions last year."

headline: Letters: Test pro-nuclear voice
abstract: The writer of this letter is promoting the use of nuclear energy, and is concerned about the recent court decision delaying the re-start of the Three Mile Island nuclear reactor.

headline: Tunnel Vision
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the writer responds to the article the newspaper ran about the “Airport rail line: 13 years of delays.”  No one representing the city ever mentioned the airport line at all.  The focus was on the Center City Commuter Tunnel, so the city’s priorities were misplaced.

headline: How will America Care for Its Children?  One-Third of a Nation
abstract: This article looks at the 1970s and 1980s and examines changes in welfare population over that time frame.  The article mentions other federal programs such as Social Security.

headline: FFA To Attract About 1,700
abstract: 1,700 members representing Pennsylvania chapters of the Future Farmers of America will assemble at the Pennsylvania State University for their annual program.  There will be 24 categories of competition and the winners will be able to compete at regional contests in September at the Eastern States Exposition at Springfield, Massachusetts.

headline: Taddonio rules out 5th re-election bid
abstract: PA State Representative Lee Taddonio has decided not to seek re-election.  He has decided to spend more time with his family and get back into the computer business.  His strong pro-life stance drew Murrysville Councilwoman Dorothy Pack into the primary race potentially against him.

headline: null
abstract: A picture shows senatorial candidate Cyril Wecht speaking at a "Fair Budget Coalition" rally.  The caption states that Wecht became "ruffled" at the rally.

headline: Bill designates smoking areas
abstract: A new bill supported by the PA Health Department, would limit smoking in public places except in designated areas.

headline: PA Still in for Hard Times: Scranton
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton III urged Pennsylvanians to find their place in a new economic era.  The state, he said, must face head-on the post-industrial era,” when business is international and automated, and computer-oriented an era of mind rather than that of manual labor.  He sought to dispel some myths:  Pennsylvania is losing jobs faster than any other state, Pennsylvania is losing both population and employment; that companies are leaving Pennsylvania for the Sun Belt.  All states lose jobs at the same rate.  Pennsylvania’s problem is that it isn’t creating jobs fast enough.

headline: Limerick rulings have broader impact
abstract: The recent PUC decision to disallow the assessment of CWIP charges to the Philadelphia Electric Co. ratepayers to finance the Limerick completion has been hailed by the media. However, at a broader level, there are numerous negative impacts of this decision.

headline: Turnpike tolls; System loses human touch
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission is spending $27 million to modernize toll collections with the help of computers, in order to reduce costs. However, whether these savings would be past on to consumers is still unclear.

headline: Lebanon county agency on aging facing funds cutback of $58,090
abstract: Institution of block grant funding in the PA Department of Aging on July 1 will mean a reduction of $58,090 in service funds for the county's Area Agency on Aging, the commissioners learned on Thursday.

headline: Filipino to State Agency
abstract: Elias S. Dungca, a Filipino-American, has been named member of the Pennsylvania Heritage Affairs Commission.  Dungca, is the second Filipino-American named to a top state agency by Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Tale of two races: power politics, Philadelphia style
abstract: This article talks about political battles between Representative Charles F. Dougherty and Councilman Al Pearlman. Mr. Dougherty has decided to remain a Republican while Mr. Pearlman would seek a Democratic nomination. The races of these two contestants are intertwined in Philadelphia's Byzantine political machinations.

headline: Trailways Work to Start Soon
abstract: Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority officials say construction of a new Trailways bus facility could begin as early as December 1st.

headline: Blue Cross/Shield Get Boosts in '65+' Rates
abstract: State Insurance Commissioner Michael Browne approved major rate increases for the elderly in Blue Shield and all Blue Cross programs in Pennsylvania except Philadelphia’s.  The rates will go up in January for “65 Special” subscribers largely because of cutbacks in federal Medicare program, increasing health costs, and greater subscriber use of policies.  The increases also were necessary because providers of Medicare supplemental insurance now comply with new minimum standards recently developed by Congress for insurance policies marketed as Medicare supplements.

headline: PAT to give pay raises as agreed in contracts
abstract: Port Authority union employees who rejected the wage freeze proposed by PAT management in March will receive hourly pay increases of 30 and 25 cents next month, as provided by their contracts.

headline: May PP&L's hot line be a busy one
abstract: Editorial:  Pennsylvania Power and Light Company has had some bad experiences with the financing and construction of two nuclear power plants along the Susquehanna River.  It has announced a toll-free phone number for businesses seeking to contact plant locations in its service area.  The company has been a catalyst for economic growth in the Susquehanna region, and has been a good corporate citizen.

headline: Union Leader: SEPTA Provoking a Strike
abstract: Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority has taken another step to remove rail union members from its commuter train operations; provoking one labor leader to charge bitterly that SEPTA wants a strike.  The board voted to turn over ticket sales on the seven former Reading lines to a private contractor.  It will eliminate jobs for 111 people, but will save the authority between $700,000 and $1 million during the first year.  The Railway Labor Executives’ Association filed suit attempting to stop the transfer.  The authority would wait for the court ruling before actually awarding the $1.12 million contract to Blue Ribbon Services. Inc.  If the special federal court rules in SEPTA’s favor, the authority will transfer ticket sales on the Penn Central lines to a private contractor.  This would eliminate 500 Conrail jobs including all 240 ticket sellers and the accounting clerks who do related work.

headline: Letters to the Editor: Becoming Slaves to Welfare Monster
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author suggests that the newspaper has been misrepresenting the facts when it comes to welfare.  Only able bodied, single individuals, with no dependents between the ages of 18-45 will be cut off the welfare rolls a year from now, not families. Instead they will receive increased benefits.  Governor Dick Thornburgh is committed to economic development and the social well being of everyone.

headline: Fired attorney says aide to Governor muzzled him
abstract: Attorney Robert Ging claims that a top aide to Governor Dick Thornburgh tried to muzzle his efforts as a state mining enforcement attorney to avoid embarrassment to the governor's re-election bid.  Democratic legislators appeared with Ging to demonstrate that the Thornburgh administration has favored certain coal companies.

headline: Tall Ships, One They Left Behind
abstract: Century Four Director Fred Stein was glad to see the tall ships leave Philadelphia.  It wasn't that he wasn’t pleased with the successful visit of the international fleet of sailing vessels.  It’s just that he was responsible for anything that might have happened during their stay in Philadelphia.  That is why he was relieved as they pulled away, one by one, from the dock at Penn’s Landing.

headline: Bypass proposal scuttled
abstract: After the Camp Hill Borough Council refused to sign off on a PA Department of Transportation project to widen the Routes 11-15 Bypass, PennDOT officials say they may consider revising the plan.  Camp Hill officials rejected the plan because it would leave no room for pedestrians, bicyclists, and disabled vehicles, and would also prevent westbound motorists from making a left turn onto 21st Street.

headline: Changes in Mental Retardation Care
abstract: The number of retarded people in large residential facilities has declined since 1970 to less than 125,000 from about 200,000.  During the same decade, the number of community facilities for retarded people has grown by leaps and bounds.  Spending on programs for the mentally retarded has increased from $325 million in 1961 to roughly $11.7 billion.  In 1961, all the money went for institutional care, but of the $11.7 billion spent in 1981, just $3.7 billion did.

headline: Pitiful Situation
abstract: In April, the author of this opinion piece called Representative Eugene Atkinson and Senator John Heinz and all the other legislator officers and found out they were doing all they could about extending unemployment benefits.  In August, they still hadn’t done one thing about this pitiful situation of not having more than 39 weeks of checks.  They do not care one bit about the unemployed.  They are now making their campaign appearances and telling us of the things they will do for us. But all our calls where not returned.  This shows they do nothing.

headline: Met-Ed bill-payment boycott ends
abstract: South Middleton School District officials have ended their three-month boycott on payment of Metropolitan Edison Co. utility bills due to recently introduced legislative proposals on utility company regulation.

headline: US Aid for 410 PAT buses
abstract: The federal government gave Pennsylvania its latest installment of $15.9 million for the state's pooled purchase of nearly 1000 buses for 16 transit agencies. The grant brings the total federal funds to $84.9 million for this program.

headline: New Plan for Welfare is Starting: Cutoffs Seen at End of November
abstract: Pennsylvania welfare officials are sending out orders to county boards of assistance instructing them to put into effect many of the provisions of a new welfare law.  The new law will eventually trim 68,000 recipients from the rolls and will reduce state expenditures by $40.8 million in the current fiscal year.

headline: Flaherty and Casey again?  State Dems fail to form 1982 slate
abstract: PA Democrats have been slow in gathering opposition to Republicans Governor Dick Thornburgh, Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton, and US Senator John Heinz.  Former PA State Treasurer Robert Casey may run for Governor or Lieutenant Governor if Pete Flaherty decides to run for Governor.

headline: Tax Money Used to Buy Booze, Books
abstract: In 1981 the House and Senate leaders run up a $125,000 tab for wining and dining at the Capital’s finest restaurants and other "official" business, according to a review of legislative records by United Press International.  The funds come from accounts controlled by House and Senate officers and committee chairmen, and are in addition to annual expense accounts available to lawmakers.

headline: Scranton Weighs Run for Governor in '86
abstract: Luietenant Governor William Scranton III is not sure if he will run for governor in 1986, but says he is considering it.  Scranton believes in the economic policies of President Reagan and thinks supply-side economics and less, not more, government will lead to a healthy economy.

headline: Children's Hospital
abstract: KDKA runs a campaign for Children's Hospital Campaign. The campaign reflects the generosity of the three-state area people.

headline: Regan leaves Beaver County jobless in cold
abstract: US Treasury Secretary Donald Regan visited Ohioville, PA yesterday for a breakfast at the Seven Oaks County Club, just past a picket established by Pete Eritano, a local United Steelworkers Union president.  Mr. Eritano was hoping to ask Mr. Regan what is being done to protect and add manufacturing jobs.  Regan was campaigning on behalf of US Representative Eugene Atkinson (R-Aliquippa).

headline: Monitoring TMI
abstract: Editorial: Lancaster County Commissioners are congratulating themselves on having spent less than $2000 to install 13 gamma radiation monitors in the Three Mile Island (TMI) area.  A phone connection relays radiation levels to Lancaster County Emergency Management.  Paper contends that GPU has not been deemed trustworthy since the TMI incident, and that its monitors should not be trusted now.

headline: Yearly car inspection is tabled by Senate
abstract: After being passed in the House, legislation cutting Pennsylvania auto safety inspections to once a year failed yesterday to gain Senate approval that would have sent it to Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Many said 'Cheese', but few smiled about the giveaway
abstract: Although the distribution of surplus American cheese to people in extreme need, was successfully completed not may of the interest groups were happy about the idea of wholesale giveaways. Committee members believed that if a more "dignified" approach was adopted, like including the cheese in their regular food distribution program, it would have been much better. Also, the amount of cheese allocated this time was simply not enough to feed everybody in need.

headline: Flaherty suns governor's race
abstract: Former Pittsburgh Mayor Pete Flaherty has decided not to run in for Governor again, citing personal reasons.  He has run for three previous statewide offices and lost those elections.  With Flaherty out of the race, the next likely favorite would seem to be PA Congressman Allen Ertel.  The PA Democratic Party has agreed to support Ertel if he decides to run.

headline: Technology Aid Bill Adopted
abstract: The State Senate has given final approval to a bill creating a board for the Ben Franklin Partnership Fund, after rejecting more than a half-dozen Democratic amendments intended to initiate an economic recovery program.  The bill, goes to Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Look who's talking
abstract: Republican supply-side economic theories are being challenged by Democratic investment-side approaches to the economy and recovery.  Just like supply-side theories rely on the implausible notion that tax cuts are self-financing, investment-side theories engage in the same sort of wishful thinking--arguing that government investment in infrastructure will pay for itself.  While neither vision is perfect, government intervention in the economy will only exacerbate economic woes.

headline: Constitutional Guarantees Are Extended for Retarded
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled on the rights of mentally retarded people held in state institutions in the country, that the Constitution guaranteed them food, clothing, medical care, shelter, safety, training, and freedom of movement.  The case was brought to the Supreme Court after Nicholas Romeo, a profoundly retarded resident at Pennhurst, the state facility for the mentally and physically disabled, suffered dozens of injuries after he was committed in 1974.

headline: State aims for private jobs in workfare plan
abstract: The state has plans to place "able-bodied" welfare recipients in private industry jobs before getting them government jobs. This comes under the newly enacted welfare program as part of Gov. Thornburgh's welfare reform package.

headline: Monument to Fiasco: Northwest's Nuclear Mess
abstract: What started as a grand nuclear solution for the utilities of Washington, Oregon, and Idaho has become one giant cost-overrun, endless stream of rate increases.  Instead of getting five new nuclear plants as planned, there were just two under construction, even though residents will be billed for five.  Instead of $4.07 billion for all five plants, the projected total cost had reached an average of $4.8 billion for each plant by the time of the cancellations in January, $22.3 billion all told.

headline: Yearly inspections
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed into law the bill that would require only one auto-safety inspection a year instead of two, as expected. The biggest opposition for this bill has come from the auto-repair industry, which had been making huge profits of the twice-yearly inspections.

headline: Montco welfare unit audit sees $88,000 in errors
abstract: An audit by PA Auditor General Al Benedict of the Montgomery County Board of Assistance has revealed welfare fraud of more than $88,000.  The report stated that of the 526 welfare cases reviewed, 16% were determined to be fraudulent, with several clients who were inelidgible for welfare kicked off the books.  Most of the cases were due to welfare recipient's failure to report income.

headline: Foglietta wins in House race; Rocks gains nod for state Senate over Rizzo choice
abstract: US Rep. Thomas M. Foglietta won the reapportioned-forced battle for survival in Philadelphia's new First Congressional District, defeating US Rep. Joseph F. Smith for the Democratic nomination, by a narrow margin. Other results of the election are described.

headline: Tell it to the Publisher
abstract: A review of several of the comments about the Patriot-News itself that the Editor has received.  Paper reviews why it chooses the articles it does, and what its purpose is in publishing the editorials it does.

headline: Graterford Prison report: Responsible, constructive
abstract: A study of the takeover and seizure of hostages at Graterford Prison claims that a serious breach of security precautions and inadequate controls were responsible for the October crisis.  The study, commissioned by Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh, makes 45 recommendations for improving future incidents, and it is time for the governor to take action.

headline: County is Fearful of Cost in Nursing Home Changes
abstract: Dauphin Manor annually receives about $8.2 million in medical reimbursement for skilled care and $2.5 million for intermediate care.  In recent years because of improved cost accounting, the county has only had to spend about $400,000 a year out of general tax revenues to operate the home and hospital.  The remainder of the nearly $10 million comes from medical reimbursements and what non-assistance patients pay.  This makes up around 3 percent of the total revenues.  New regulation changes are designed to bring the state’s Medicaid program into line with the federal Medicare program.  The federal government found in 1977 that the state was not using the Medicare definition when making determinations on skilled care, but was using a more liberal definition.  The federal Social Security Act requires that Medicare and Medicaid definitions be identical.  Officials have said that with the new rules an estimated 16,000 Medicaid-funded nursing home patients will receive care at a reduced level to save the state and federal governments millions of dollars.

headline: State Jobless rate disputed by Democrats
abstract: The House Democratic Caucus released unemployment figures contending the state's jobless rate is 13.7 percent, compared to federal statistics of 10.6 percent. However, the Democrats believe that by including those people that left the state or stopped looking for jobs, could lead to a much higher rate of unemployment.

headline: Mr. Gekas Visits Washington
abstract: George Gekas has been in DC for two weeks preparing to take his seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. He seems unique in the city for acknowledging when he doesn't know something or has yet to make up his mind. He admitted he was unsure how he would have voted on MX missle funding and agreed that his stand on the Three Mile Island cleanup and reactor one restart is inconsistent.

headline: Boyle's Appeal Rejected by Pa. Court
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court rejected the appeal made by Untied Mine Workers president W.A. "Tony" Boyle in his murder trial.  Boyle did not take the stand in his second trial and his lawyer Clarence D. Bell argued that the introduction of previous testimony unfairly prejudiced the jury against Boyle.

headline: PA welfare secretary is cleared of contempt
abstract: A federal judge has purged the PA Welfare Secretary, Helen O'Bannon, of contempt after Secretary O'Bannon refused to finance a special master's office to oversee the transfer of patients from the Pennhurst Center to community living arrangements.

headline: For Responsible State Decision-Making
abstract: Senate Republican leaders recently launched an experimental intern program involving upper-level-college and graduate students.  The program aims to give students practical experience in state government and to give the Senate the benefit of in-depth research on issues and problems facing Pennsylvania.  The pilot intern program has been under the supervision of Pennsylvania State University’s Capitol Campus.  The first five interns focused on five topics chosen by Senate leaders: workers compensation insurance, radioactive waste disposal, urban and rural enterprise zones, economic development policies for small businesses and fiscal pressures on local governments.

headline: The Day Care Bonus
abstract: There is something extra in city employee's pay envelopes this week and that will pay off in long-term benefits. It is a questionnaire on day care that was developed by the Mayor's Commission for Women, and distributed to 31,000 workers. The WCAU-AM believes that gathered data should make an important contributions determining child care needs and preferences  since availability and costs of day care are primary employment issues.

headline: Running for the House
abstract: In this article, state Representative Rudy Dininni tells voters why he deserves re-election.  The 16-year veteran says he has acomplished a lot for the people of Dauphin County during his tenure.

headline: Cuts may lower emergency patient care
abstract: Pennsylvania Emergency Health Services Council director Joel Grottenthaler says federal and state cuts to Pennsylvania's emergency health services could reduce the quality of patient care.

headline: Strikes may halt work downtown
abstract: Threatened strikes by two Western Pennsylvania craft unions, Painters' Local 6 and the International Union of Operating Engineers Local 66, could hinder work on numerous construction projects, including at least four downtown.
