The unions confirmed that about 9,110 workers plan to stay off the job after their current contracts expire at mid-night tomorrow.

headline: 'Municipal Electrics' Aid Near
abstract: The PA House of Representatives passed legislation sponsored by state Senator George W. Gekas, enabling electric utilities owned by borough governments to join with other boroughs to achieve economies of scale and offer electricity at lower rates to their residents.

headline: null
abstract: Joseph Aulisio, 16-years old, was convicted of two murders and has been sentenced to die in the electric chair.  His victims were Cheryl Ziemba, 8, and her brother, Christopher, 4.  Joseph’s mother believes that he is innocent.  He was the youngest person on death row in America during that time.

headline: Pa. Office Conditions in Dispute
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare, its employees in the Boulevard District office in Philadelphia, the employees union, the welfare clients who use that office and the organization that represents the clients have all agreed on something.  They have agreed that the Boulevard District office on West Hunting Park Avenue is unsuitable in its current dilapidated and overstuffed condition.  That’s where the agreement begins, and that is where it ends.  The disagreement begins because the Pennsylvania Social Services Union (PSSU) recently informed the Department of General Services that it intends to press its eight-year-old demand that the welfare department either fix up or abandon the Boulevard District office immediately.  The Department says it will move as quickly as it can find a new site.

headline: For state Supreme Court: Cavanaugh and Schaeffer
abstract: The current Pennsylvania Supreme Court Chief Justice Henry X. O'Brien's term expires at the end of this year. This seat is being contested in the May 18 primary. The republican nomination for this primary is being sought by James R. Cavanaugh, Forrest G. Schaeffer and Stephen A. Zappala.

headline: The Dilemma Of Irvis: A Successful 'Failure'
abstract: K. Leroy Irvis, the ranking Democrat in the State House, discusses his 23-year career in the PA Legislature and whether or not he will consider running for Governor or Lieutenant Governor.  Irvis feels that he is a failure because civil rights are still not honored and respected.

headline: 106th District
abstract: Joseph O'Connor, a candidate for the 106th Legislative-District seat in the PA House of Representatives, says his opponent, Rudy Dininni, is too busy looking after all of his other ventures to be a full-time legislator; the 106th district has a lot of full-time problems, however, and deserves a full-time legislator.

headline: Danger: bureaucrat at work
abstract: An editorial about a recently introduced bill that prohibits smoking in certain public places. It suggests that the evidence of the danger of secondhand smoke is poor.

headline: Swelling The Rolls Of Jobless
abstract: A letter to the editor lamenting the almost seventy thousand people due to be taken off the public welfare rolls. The author also suggests that Governor Thornburgh be given updates on the living conditions of these individuals and that every candidate for public office be required to live for a month as an unemployed person looking for minimum wage work.

headline: N.Y. nuclear accident brings back old fears
abstract: Article concludes that things never really became bad at the Ginna nuclear power plant in Ontario, NY, and that the degree of apprehension that followed was out of proportion to the scope of the recent accident.  However, the decision by owners Rochester Gas and Electric to classify the accident as a "site emergency," which is only one emergency level shy of the highest, is called into question since the incident clearly did not meet the criteria.

headline: 2 begin prison terms for Lottery fix roles
abstract: Two men convicted of helping fix the April 24, 1980 drawing of the Pennsylvania Lottery have begun serving 1-to-5 year sentences at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill.  The pair will likely spend a month at Camp Hill undergoing psychological and educational testing before being permanently assigned to a state prison.

headline: Probation for food stamp cheater
abstract: Larry Caldwell pleaded guilty to theft and deception in the $300,000 rip-off of the food stamp program. Caldwell is one of 33 persons involved in the food stamp fraud. Judge Jackson has ordered that Caldwell repay $10000 to the State Department of Public Welfare.

headline: Franklin Democrat Claims Win
abstract: In a turnabout that will bolster the strength of Democrats in the PA House of Representatives if it stands, Democrat Jeffrey Coy said a recount shows he defeated GOP incumbent Harry Bittle in a Franklin County legislative race.

headline: The Election
abstract: Tuesday's primary election was ignored by majority of the voters. Consequently, analysis of this election wouldn't make too much sense. This has been further exacerbated by the fact that Republican nominees were basically unchallenged in this election, leaving not too much to motivate the voters.

headline: PAT shakeup rooted in move to avoid conflicts
abstract: After Allegheny Port Authority commissioners appointed 5 new members to its twelve-member board, several changes were made to break ties between the commissioners' offices and the Port-Authority board; these changes were designed to prevent staff members from serving on the board, as many felt such service would constitute a conflict of interest.

headline: Block grants for schools asked
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh announced drastic changes to the way state school districts are funded with the use of block grants.  School officials have to analyze the figures more to find out what the exact impact on districts will be.  Additionally, Thornburgh proposed easing some restrictions on how state money for schools is supposed to be spent, allowing local school districts to use the funds more efficiently.

headline: The jobless hear: 'Don't call us, we'll call you'
abstract: According to the US Labor Department, the unemployment rate has climbed to 9.4%, the highest level since World War II. Due to widespread layoffs witnessed in Pennsylvania, its employment is even bleaker, with unemployment at 10.7%

headline: N-Accident siren test due in Beaver County
abstract: Sirens are being installed around Beaver County that will be the first alert for area residents in the event of a nuclear accident at the Shippingport nuclear plant.  The installation of the sirens were a result of requirements put on companies after the Three Mile Island accident.  Smaller sirens are yet to be installed at more rural homes.

headline: 2 Charged with Scheme to Bilk State of $5,019
abstract: A PA Revenue Department clerk and another man were arrested in connection with an alleged forgery scheme to swindle $5,019 in state funds, according to Attorney General Leroy Zimmerman.  23 rent and property rebate checks allegedly were forged after being returned to the Revenue Department as undeliverable.  They had been issued under a program for the elderly funded by the Pennsylvania Lottery.

headline: Promoting a Euphemism
abstract: Pennsylvania Senator John Heinz, who has made the concerns of the aged a special project, was heard speaking about the effects of some program or other on "seniors."  Instead of using "Senior Citizens" people are using the word aging to refer to older people.

headline: Free haircuts for legislators 'clip' taxpayer
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers have exclusive barber shops where they can get their hair cut and shoe shined at taxpayers' expense. Sen. H. Craig Lewis calls it as "trappings from a by-gone era".

headline: The Forum: Tourist Inquiry Got Short Shrift
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the writer is talking about how he wrote to the Pennsylvania Bureau of Travel Department and the Commerce Department of Bureau of Travel in order to receive tourist information on the state.  All that he received was a four-page brochure extolling the virtues of Philadelphia.  There was nothing else on the rest of the sate.  The writer was extremely disappointed.

headline: County Dems' dinner beset with woes
abstract: The Kennedy-Lawrence fundraising dinner for Alleghency-County Democrats is in trouble for several reasons.  There is a controversy over the key-note speaker, U.S. Senator Gary Hart, and Mayor Caliguiri and County Commissioner Tom Foerster have reduced the number of tickets they are going to sell.  Also, tough economic times have left people with little or nothing to contribute financially.

headline: Block-grant plan will harm special ed, legislator says
abstract: PA Representative Edward Burns claims that Governor Dick Thornburgh's plan for block grants for education hurt special education programs and force school districts to raise taxes.  Mr. Burns believes that block grants will be defeated for categorical grants, but that these too may harm special education programs in school districts.

headline: Trumka I
abstract: Coal/miner lawyer Rich Trumka is the new president of the united mine workers of America. An editorial lists several suggestions to Trumka. For example he could start an ongoing dialogue between the operators and union, he should take into account stability and that is especially important for coal future, etc.

headline: New Agency To Give Energy Development Loans
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed a law today creating the PA Energy Development Authority (PEDA). PEDA will prepare an energy development plan, pay to issue bonds to finance research into renewable energy using PA resources as well as to build small-scale energy production facilities. It will also make small research grants. The law also lets the governor declare a state of emergency if there is a gas shortage. Details on the appointment of the nineteen member board of directors was also reported.

headline: 2 Face Jail, 25G Fine in Diner Skim
abstract: Two brothers have been sentenced to 366-day prison terms and fined $25,000 each for evading taxes by skimming nearly $500,000 from a diner they once owned in Cornwells Heights Bucks County.  Stelios Moschas and his brother Peter Moscholeas of Newtown, will remain free pending an appeal.  Another partner, Nicholas Katsiois, of Hightstown, N.J. was placed on three years’ probation and fined $20,000.  The Pennsylvania Crime Commission has alleged that the brothers are involved in counterfeiting and are linked to organized crime.  The three partners were convicted of conspiring to defraud the federal government through tax evasion and filing fraudulent tax returns for the Fountain Diner on Street Road in Cornwells Heights, which they sold in 1979 for $950,000.

headline: Prospects evaluated for workfare gains
abstract: Columnist Don Spatz is hopeful about the new welfare reform measure to be instituted under PA Governor Dick Thornburgh. With federal Comprehensive Employee Training Act funds drying up, the PA Department of Welfare will administer a program in which welfare recipients are required to work for their checks on local government projects. However, for the plan to succeed, it will require oversight. If the plan fails, it would be in this area.

headline: From the pulpit
abstract: Reverend B. Samuel Hart withdrew his nomination by President Ronald Reagan to serve on the US Civil Rights Commission.  He claims that he did not resign because of pressure, rather he was just happy to be back doing "God's work."  He claims that he realized he would not have the time to continue with his ministries.

headline: The Fox Talks
abstract: In this leader to the editor the writer is upset that his social security is not enough.  He says that the nation has gone to the dogs.  All the veterans and the dead have fought for what... So some political big wigs can make millions?

headline: TV debates: skin shows full of pitfalls
abstract: As an alternative to the staged, televised political debates that seem to dominate today's campaigns, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette has, for some time now, conducted editorial-board interviews with both candidates simultaneously, giving the public a chance to hear how each candidate responds to the same question.  Unfortunately, neither Senator Heinz nor Governor Thornburgh--as well as their respective opponents, Cyril Wecht and Allen Ertel--has agreed to this format.  We will therefore interview each separately and publish the transcripts for the public to read.

headline: Board votes school budget; would cut 1326 jobs
abstract: The Board of Education passed a $852.7 million Philadelphia School District Budget for fiscal 1983 that includes a $79.1 million deficit and the elimination of 1326 jobs. The budget was approved as a resolution that requires the local government authorities to authorize new taxes or yield the amount necessary to balance the budget.

headline: Unemployment Compensation
abstract: Six hundred thousand Pennsylvanians are out of work.  Unemployment compensation cushions the blow for many laid-off workers, however.  In Pennsylvania a person can collect up to $190 a week for thirty-nine weeks.  But after unemployment compensation runs out, the situation often gets desperate.  There is talk of having the federal government extend the unemployment compensation for an additional thirteen weeks.  This would cost $1 billion.

headline: New Coal Pier
abstract: The first phase of the new Philadelphia Coal Export Terminal will be operational in the third quarter of 1982 with an annual throughput capacity of three to four million tons of steam coal.  A second phase will follow which will provide a topping-off operation in the lower Delaware Bay area, employing 12,500 DWT self-unloading barges.  The terminal area offers strategic location for exporting coal from Pennsylvania, West Virginia and Ohio.  Also, excellent harbor and complete vessel support facilities exist.  The facility enjoys the shortest distance to European markets.

headline: 2 firms indicted in bid-rigging and price-fixing
abstract: A federal grand jury indicted two Harrisburg area firms, H&M Inc. and RSE Inc., for allegedly violating antitrust laws by rigging bids and fixing prices for highway projects in south central Pennsylvania.

headline: Senate fight likely on Pa. welfare plan
abstract: Legislation that would cause the stoppage of welfare cash grants to 68,000 able-bodied Pennsylvanians, appears headed for a floor fight in the PA State Senate. The Republican-backed bill, which also would require thousands of welfare recipients to do public-service work in order to receive payments, will need to be approved by the Senate, before going to Governor Thornburgh for his signature.

headline: Full-scale study of mine fire set
abstract: The US Department of Interior has agreed to conduct a full-scale study of the underground mine fire at Centralia, according to US Representative James L. Nelligan, R-Forty Fort. This is a reversal from the previous stand that the Interior Department had taken with regards to the scaling back of expenditure.

headline: The Last to Know
abstract: Sandy Starobin will be reporting from Harrisburg for KYW radio and KDKA, its sister station in Pittsburgh, but there’s a nasty divorce from the TV side for the veteran capital reporter.  Both sides have denied it, but there is a rumor that Starobin has been dumped from Westinghouse Broadcasting’s two Pennsylvania TV stations because of his refusal during the recent gubernatorial campaign to interview Governor Thornburgh’s barber and bootblack.

headline: City Acts to Forestall Massive Pension Debt
abstract: The Caliguiri administration is proposing legislation that calls for major changes in funding methods for police officer and fire-fighter pensions.  Current funding menthods would bankrupt the city of Pittsburgh by 2012.

headline: Board would hold tuition line
abstract: A State College Board and University Directors recommend tuition rates stay the same, drawing praise from student leaders. The Board is an advisory arm of the PA Department of Education. Last year's tuition increased for a court-ordered back pay settlement to faculty. Several student leaders said programs at their university will suffer. Department spokesman James Gallagher said quality can be maintained. PA Rep. Ronald Cowell said increasing the Legislature's match to universities is unlikely.

headline: Vo-Tech Has Rejected Fact-Finder's Contract Proposal, PLRB Rules
abstract: The Cumberland-Perry Area Vocational-Technical School rejected part of the PA Labor Relations Board (PLRB) report regarding teacher salary increases, leading to a rejection of the entire thing. The teacher's union agrees with the reports findings that teacher salary increases be based on weighted average "dollar increases" while the school believes it should be based on weighted average "percentage increases," which would be less money over the life of the contract.

headline: NRC Considers Appeal of Court Order Delaying Startup at Three Mile Island
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is trying to decide whether to appeal a court ruling that could considerably delay the start of the undamaged Three Mile Island reactor.   NRC has to consider the psychological health of the residents of the area.

headline: 2 Lottery Figures In Prison
abstract: Two men convicted of helping fix the April 24, 1980 drawing of the Pennsylvania Lottery arrived at the state prison in Camp Hill January 4, 1982 to begin serving one to five year sentences.  The two men plead guilty to weighting and switching ping-pong balls used in the live televised number drawing.

headline: Senate oks benefits for elderly
abstract: The PA Senate passed a bill 49-1 sponsored by PA Senator John Hopper that would use surplus lottery profits to fund a benefit package that includes a one-time $100 anti-inflation payment and property tax rebates.

headline: Fumo Loses Bid to Gain Senate Post
abstract: State Senator Vincent Fumo of South Philadelphia lost a bid for a leadership position among Senate Democrats when his party selected its 1983-84 legislative officers.  Fumo challenged Senator Craig Lewis, for the Democratic chairmanship of the Senate Appropriations Committee, which decides how to distribute state finances.  He lost, 12-11.

headline: The life and death of Senate bill 742
abstract: Article traces the entire life span of Senate bill 742 from its inception in the Cambria County War Memorial Arena on a Saturday night to its veto by Governor Dick Thornburgh.  There are two things one shouldn't watch being made - laws and sausages.  - Otto von Bismarck

headline: Cost of living found below average
abstract: According to a recent U.S. Labor Department study, the cost of living in Pittsburgh is slightly below the national average.

headline: Book Bans and Bankruptcy
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court, in a 5-4 vote, has condemned the practice by local school boards of arbitrarily banning books from school libraries and curricula because members of those boards do no like the ideas contained in those books.  In another decision, the Supreme Court ruled that portions of the bankruptcy law, passed by Congress in 1978, are unconstitutional.  The court is telling Congress that it must devise a new law which will give less jurisdictional power to bankruptcy judges.

headline: Worker docked for defying beard ban
abstract: A blast furnance worker was disciplined at US Steel's Duquesne Works for refusing to shave his beard.  The Steelworkers Union insists that a "neatly shaved" beard does not pose a safety threat with the equipment, but the company says that some gas-mask-type respirators may not fit properly.  Also includes a photo depicting US Senator John Heinz shown at his re-election speech.

headline: NRC Investigates Piping at N-Plant
abstract: The federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission is studying allegations that the small diameter piping at the Susquehanna Nuclear Power Plant was improperly designed and installed.  Pennsylvania Power & Light Co., operator of the $3.8 billion plant in Luzerne County’s Salem Twp., said it was conducting a separate investigation.

headline: 2 to a cell? Inmates divided
abstract: 20 cells are being converted to double occupancy in the Allegheny County Jail.  Article discusses inmates' reactions to the new additions to their jail block.  The double ceiling is needed because overcrowding in the jail has forced officials on occasion to house as many as 50 inmates in the jail's gymnasium, cutting down on inmates' exercised problem and creating dangerous situations.

headline: Social Security Issue Shows GOP Insecurity
abstract: Social Security may be one of the deciding factors in the upcoming fall elections.  Young voters may not benefit from Social Security by the time they are old enough so they might vote against it.

headline: Funds for disabled eaten up by wages
abstract: The author believes that although the Pennsylvania Department of Labor has solid financial reasons for the lay-offs in the Office of Vocational Rehabilitation, this has been obscured by the loud rhetoric by people who are more interested in preserving these jobs than in giving jobs to the handicapped.

headline: The Maps Are Wrong: There's no Such Place as Hershey, Penna.
abstract: Hershey, Pennsylvania is one of a myriad of small places in Pennsylvania that have no papers of incorporation, places that built up inside other larger, older rural tracts with histories all their own.  Legally, there is no place in Central Pennsylvania’s Lebanon Valley called Hershey.  People that live here pay their taxes to Derry Township.  There’s a quiet petition drive on to have the official name of this area that chocolate built legally changed to Hershey.

headline: The anti-Limerick resoultion may live again
abstract: Although Philadelphia Electric Company shareholders failed to pass a resolution forcing the company to abandon its plans to build the Limerick generating station, they did garner enough votes to bring a similar resolution to a vote next year.  The electric company is trying to avoid such a vote, however, claiming that it should be allowed to count abstentions in the vote tallies; if the SEC allows the counting of abstentions, which traditionally it has not, the resolution would fall short of the necessary 10 percent shareholder minimum and would not go to a vote.

headline: Booked: Five are Arrested in Bucks for Overdue Library Books
abstract: Five Bucks County residents, including a 10-year-old boy, were arrested on criminal charges of failing to return overdue library books, and they each face lines of more than $300.  The action followed formal complaints by officials of the Warminister Township Library to District Justice James M. Kelly.  After months of sending overdue notices and calling delinquents, library said they decided to take legal action.

headline: Youth group demands city add 1000 jobs
abstract: Although City Councilman Bill Robinson introduced a resolution supporting summer jobs for youths, he was criticized by a youth group which demanded that he increase the number of jobs available from 2300 to 3300.

headline: NRC overruled on TMI test
abstract: The Atomic Safety and Licensing Board has issued an order strongly disagreeing with a National Regulatory Commission report recommending criminal prosecution in a scandal by Three Mile Island employees.

headline: 2nd arrest in film sale
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman announced the arrest of a 2nd suspect in connection with the alleged theft of x-ray film sale proceeds totaling more than $28,000 from Polyclinic Medical Center.  The money was alledgedly paid by scrap film buyers, but never turned over to the hospital.  The arrest was made by the Medicaid Fraud Control Division.

headline: State conferences try to fix welfare reform bill
abstract: A committee of PA House and Senate members have set up the mechanics for overhauling the Republican welfare reform measures.  Senate Democrats presented their list of changes for their votes for the bill to pass.  Governor Dick Thornburgh has already endorsed the bill as well.

headline: Geka' Old Job Draws Interest
abstract: PA State Republican Representatives Jeffrey E. Piccola, Robert F. Dick, John Shumaker, Miriam Menaker and Joseph C. Manmiller have expressed interest in candidacy for the soon-to-be vacant seat of former PA Senator George W. Gekas, elected to US Congress. Dauphin County Democratic Chairman Larry Adler believes Joe O'Connor and Lawrence J. Hochendoner may also be contenders. Both parties will nominate a candidate for Gekas' seat in a special election or a May primary, which is more cost effective.

headline: The Pittsburgh School Board
abstract: The Pittsburgh Board of Public Schools is an example of a body whose members are pure political amateurs.  They put in very long hours of work without any direct monetary reward and the only benefit they might receive is a very occasional, expense-paid trip to exotic Harrisburg.  On the other hand, professional politicians who serve as members of Pittsburgh City Council or as legislators receive very ample full-time salaries for part-time work.  They attend expense-paid conventions, plus they get a limited amount of patronage with which to reward relatives or friends of their political supporters.

headline: For Mayview Neighbors, Crime Report Brings Fear
abstract: After a Mayview hospital escapee adducted, beat and raped a 17-year old nursing student, area residents began circulating petitions opposing a planned psychiatric hospital in Upper St. Clair township.  Residents have for years dealt with Mayview residents wondering off hospital grounds, but the latest incident has instilled a sense of fear and anger in the community.

headline: Cheyney State Inaugurates President
abstract: C.T. Enus Wright, the son of rural Georgia sharecroppers, was inaugurated as the fifth president of Cheyney State College in Delaware County-the oldest historically black college in America.  Wright, who has become widely known among black colleges and universities, was named to the presidency of Cheyney State by Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: null
abstract: Students in New Jersey are allowed to borrow less in Guaranteed Student Loans in the 1982 school year than in 1981.  In Pennsylvania, officials estimate that $130 million less will be borrowed.  Any student, regardless of income, can borrow up to $3,000 a year from the federal Parent Loan Program.  In its 1983 budget proposals, the Reagan administration has asked that the Guaranteed Student Loans no longer be made available to graduate students and has requested that the origination fee for a loan be raised from 5 to 10 percent.

headline: NRC predicts Limerick Plant N-Unit No.2 will be cancelled
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) gave Congress a list of 19 nuclear power plants under construction - including one unit of Philadelphia Electric Co.'s Limerick plant near Pottstown, which the NRC staff predicts will be cancelled.

headline: 6 indicted in Medicaid billing fraud
abstract: Officials at a North Philadelphia hospital were charged by a federal grand jury of collecting on more than $150,000 in fraudulent Medicaid charges.

headline: State's Right to Set Caseloads is Upheld
abstract: The Commonwealth Court ruled that the PA Department of Public Welfare has the authority to decide how many cases will be assigned to social workers and that the matter is not subject to collective bargaining.  Judge Joseph Doye, upheld the 1981 decision of the state Labor Relations Board, which had conclude that the interests of the state outweighed those of the Pennsylvania State Social Services Union.  However, the ruling applied only to the specific case of social workers in the State Welfare Department.

headline: Gekas draws top spot on ticket
abstract: State Senator George W. Gekas has drawn the top spot on the Republican primary ticket in the contest for nomination in the 17th Congressional District. The second spot went to Brian J. McCarthy and the third to Max Lampenfeld.

headline: The Politician's Handy Tool
abstract: Columnist criticizes public officials - at all levels of government - for writing letters to one another and to interest groups without actually taking action on anything.

headline: Altoona Switching As Railroad Throws a Curve
abstract: After the closing of A&P's Altoona division and two rounds of layoffs at Conrail, community leaders in Altoona are trying their best to market the city to businesses to help stimulate investment and reduce unemployment.  The city's underdevelopment, evinced by the lack of a major highway, has also served to exacerbate economic problems and lead to chronic unemployment in the region.

headline: Closing museum doors
abstract: State budgeting has forced the PA Historical and Museum Commission to close all of its museums for January and February.  Editorial notes that the actual cost-cutting involved is curious.

headline: $150 hike ok'd at Shippensburg State
abstract: The Board of Trustees at Shippensburg State College has approved a $150 increase in room and board charges for the following school year. The increase comes on the heals of a state-imposed $75 increase being rescinded.  The increases are a result of the college's contract with its food service provider which calls for annual increases in its fees.

headline: NRC Rates Beaver Plant in Safety
abstract: Beaver Valley 1 Nuclear Plant was among the least safe plant in the nation according to an internal memorandum for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.  The NRC memo was obtained by an anti-nuclear group, the Critical Mass Energy Project, through a Freedom of Information Act request.  NRC documents show more than 4,000 mishaps at nuclear plants in 1981.  Of that number, 140 were singled out as being particularly serious.

headline: 8 guards injured in fight with Graterford convicts
abstract: 8 corrections officers were injured yesterday after a lunchtime incident started a melee with inmates at Graterford State prison.  When officers tried to restrain an inmate, an undetermined number of cons jumped the guards.  The remaining prisoners not at lunch were kept confined to their cells until the incident was quelled.

headline: States would assume many federal aid programs
abstract: President Ronald Reagan's proposal to shrink the size of the federal government by turning over dozens of programs to the states consists of both a "swap" and a "turnover."  The primary component of the swap is to exchange Medicaid costs for Food Stamps and Aid to Families with Dependent Children.  The turnover would be partially financed by a trust fund created from federal excise taxes, but would mean these programs may face elimination after the trust fund has expired by 1988.

headline: Gekas in offer on redistricting
abstract: PA Senator George Gekas said that he is willing to renounce his congressional ambition if that should prove the major obstacle for the PA Legislature to reshape the 17th district.  He believes that the plan that was submitted would not be the best cultural division for the area.

headline: Thornburgh and Korean-American Community in Harrisburg
abstract: Photo of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh sitting with members of the Korean Congregation at the Market Square Presbyterian Church.  Text in Korean.

headline: SICKLE CELL ANEMIA
abstract: Although there is no cure for sickle cell anemia, advances in early detection, monitoring of patient care and education have led to longer life spans for victims.  As part of these advances, Pennsylvania has established a state Sickle Cell Anemia Program that provides comprhensive medical care and psycho-social services to roughly 1,100 patients in eastern and western PA.

headline: College President Censured by Board
abstract: The President of West Chester State College was given a unanimous vote of no confidence by the college’s board of trustees.  The vote was taken after Governor Thornburgh and State Education Secretary Robert Scanion requested an indication of the board’s support for the college president, Charles Mayo.  Board member James Unruh submitted a motion that the board show a lack of confidence in the total administration of the chief executive officer of the college.  The vote was taken before an audience of about 75, mostly faculty members and students who have supported Mayo in a series of disputes with the board.

headline: $5 million more for loans
abstract: An extra $15 million will be available in loans to fire, ambulance and rescue companies under a bill signed by Gov. Thornburgh. The bill also raises the maximum amounts that can be borrowed.

headline: 5 high school students to intern at TMI
abstract: GPU Nuclear Corp. plans to hire five high school students who will work at Three Mile Island this summer and could qualify for full-time employment after they graduate. The objective of the program is to provide concentrated exposure to the workings of a nuclear power plant and to give an experience similar to a college-level cooperative educational program.

headline: Nuclear plant in 'cold shutdown'
abstract: Technicians are expected to enter the shutdown Ginna Nuclear Plant this week, but it will be at least three weeks before the plant can resume power generation.  The plant was shutdown when a steam pipe broke, venting radioactive steam into the air and 11,000 gallons of radioactive water into the plant's concrete sump.  Before workers can fix the broken pump, the water must be removed and cleansed.

headline: A Bucks prison program begins - uneasily
abstract: A new program to improve the facilities for work-release inmates by providing accommodation different from jail settings. This has been the case with male work-release inmates for sometime now, but due to the minuscule number of females, a separate program was never in place. However, this program is facing opposition from local neighborhoods fearful of the influence of inmates in that area.

headline: Stymied Senate GOP puts welfare cutback on hold
abstract: PA Senators abandoned plans to pass legislation to purge state welfare rolls.  The measure, if passed by the Senate, would take 68,000 people off state welfare grants by December, instead qualifying them for only one check in a 12 month period.  In total, the state has almost 800,000 people on welfare.

headline: George Bush: GOP's Top Angel
abstract: In slightly more than 18 months in office, George Bush has visited 42 states, appeared at dozens of fund-raisers for conservative and moderate Republican candidates, and raised at least $12 million for GOP candidates.

headline: U.S. judge to hear redistricting suit
abstract: US District Court Judge Sylvia Rambo will hear a suit filed by US Representative Doug Walgren, asking that the entire state's primary election process be stopped until the state's congressional districts are redrawn.  An additional suit, filed by 11 Republican members of the PA Congress, asks that the state legislature be given until February 27 before the court steps in to redraw.

headline: Clean Air Gives No Comfort to Donora
abstract: Donora Pennsylvania, once a booming steel town, is one of the many cities affected by the decline of the U.S. steel industry.  The industry is operating at 40 percent capacity--a factor that contributes to chronic unemployment and tough economic conditions in Donora and other steel-producing regions of the country.

headline: College presidents assail fiscal 'freeze out'
abstract: Area college presidents lashed out at proposed slashes in the federal student aid, saying that this would shut out thousands of people who could not afford to pursue higher education on their own.

headline: 25 states raise taxes to offset recession loss
abstract: At least 25 states and many cities have raised taxes this year, trying to make up revenue losses caused by the recession and by federal budget cuts.

headline: 67,000 Students Affected: School Strikes Grow in State
abstract: Teachers in two more Pennsylvania school districts went on strike and a deadline was set in a third district as the number of students affected by walkouts throughout the state swelled to nearly 67,000.

headline: Nuclear Power Extracts Price
abstract: Since the revelation that nuclear power is not quite as pure and safe as the public had been led to believe, precaution or its appearance has become a belated virtue among nuclear utilities.  The public now has a much better understanding of nuclear power, its potential for harm and in our area, the public is kept dutifully informed about every development that takes place at the local reactor site, no matter how inconsequential.

headline: A collapse in law enforcement
abstract: A former Ukrainian-American Citizens Association Club in Philadelphia was transformed into a public-admission bar.  Because it was still classified as a "private club", under certain provisions it was allowed to sell alcohol until 3am under state law.  Several complains were sent to Philadelphia police, but neither the police nor the Liquor Control Board officials did anything.  As it turns out, the police new about it all along.

headline: The question in point: where do you get the cheese?
abstract: A memo from the PA Department of Agriculture has caused confusion about the location of centers in Philadelphia for the distribution next month of more than 500,000 pounds of surplus government cheese.  The list, which was written to provide members of the General Assembly with a county-by-county list of locations where poor families would be able to pick up the cheese, included only 12 distribution sites for Philadelphia compared to the more than 150 that will distribute the cheese.  Robert Dippre, director of the department's Bureau of Government-Donated Food said that it was not a complete list.

headline: Gerald Ford to speak at fund-raiser here
abstract: Former President Gerald Ford will address a gathering of Pittsburgh Republicans at a $250 per plate dinner at the Pittsburgh Hilton.  The dinner will be a formal fundraiser for Governor Dick Thornburgh's re-election bid.

headline: US judges study bid to halt primary
abstract: A panel of three federal judges appears to be giving serious consideration to ordering a halt to the state primary election process. The suits that have brought this case to court, contend that the congressional re-districting is unconstitutional because it disenfranchises minority voters and has too great  variance among a population of the districts.

headline: George Goodling Dies at Age 86
abstract: George A. Goodling, a six-term U.S. Representative from the 19th Congressional District, died yesterday at the age of 86.  During his years in Washington, Goodling advanced the interests of Pennsylvania farmers.

headline: College President's Job in Jeopardy
abstract: The job of the President of West Chester University is in jeopardy.  President Mayo was appointed by the Governor Milton Shapp in 1974.  By state law, the governor is the only official who can hire or fire the president of a state college or university.  After a no-confidence vote, Mayo denounced the trustees’ action as "another instance of the intrusion of Chester County politics into the affairs of the college community."  The Senate has passed Senate Bill 506, which would take control of the state college system out of the governor’s office.  It would establish a board of governors, headed by a chancellor, to head the system.

headline: 2-Barrel Democratic salvo; Block grants attacked
abstract: Democratic county commissioners from across the state denounced the Reagan and Thornburgh administrations for proposing social programs as a political ploy aimed at shifting the burden of fiscal problems from the federal and state to the local levels. The commissioners also added that they were not yet ready to endorse proposals like the abandoning of property tax in favor of more diversified revenues.

headline: A Conflict on Juice Standard
abstract: The PA State Education Department said it was looking into why one of its bureau directors endorsed a soft drink as meeting federal school lunch juice standards when another official said it doesn't.  He believes that the soft drink, Superjuice, can meet the 50 percent juice standard and be counted for credit in the school lunch program.

headline: Nuke plant spills radiation in N.Y.
abstract: A tube burst in an Upstate New York nuclear power plant yesterday, causing small puffs of radioactive steam to spurt into the atmosphere and thousands of gallons of radioactive water to spill onto drainage area on the plant floor.  After a series of precautionary measures were put into effect, officials said the released radiation posed no danger.  John Oberlies, a spokesperson for Rochester Gas and Electric, says that company officials believe the plant is now safe.

headline: A disservice to lawyer, merit process
abstract: Former chairman of the PA Bar Association, Joseph Foster, believes Editors should recommend PA Governor Thornburgh favor confirmation of Lowell A. Reed Jr. to PA Commonwealth Court. Reed was nominated twice before, however his nomination was withdrawn when the Senate did not have a 2/3 majority to confirm him. The Court in need of an appointee as Justice Madeline Palladino reelection. The PA Bar Association affirmed Reed's credentials, as did the PA Senate Judiciary Committee.

headline: Thornburgh, Elderly Disagree
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh exchanged hot words with a group of picketing senior citizens when they disputed claims that the state had not cut funds for programs for the elderly.  The Action Alliance of Senior Citizens claimed that the governor's budget for 1983 cuts funds for senior centers, meals, transportation and in-home services in Philadelphia by $1.6 million.  Thornburgh said this was not true.  Eventually Thornburgh acknowledged there might be less money provided overall because of federal cutbacks.

headline: German Day Proclamation
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh established June 28, 1982 as "German Day" Pennsylvania Germans are an important element of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.  Their contributions to American culture are prized and respected.

headline: The Single Vote
abstract: Official returns from the State Elections Bureau show that former Kutztown Mayor Forrest Schaeffer, now a Berks County judge, won the GOP nomination in the May 18 primary by 6,014 votes over Superior Court Judge James Cavanaugh of Philadelphia.

headline: Apples, Oranges and Mixed Fruits
abstract: This article describes the use of the word "lie" in several Pennsylvania political campaigns; the author notes that word has been thrown around with incredible ease, and more often than not its usage is the result of a semantic disagreement.  The article gives examples from the Thornburgh administration, the Wecht-Heinz campaigns and suburban-congressional races in Delaware County.

headline: Coming soon: the deficit that are Phila
abstract: Board of Education members will get a chance to see the School District's projected finances for fiscal 1982-1983. The picture does not appear to be very cheerful, with an estimated $100 million gap between the revenue and expenditure. Factors for this include an already huge gap to start with, higher operating costs and longevity increases on employee salary schedules.

headline: 2-Barrel Democratic salvo; Wecht: Fight 'Reaganomics' in Senate
abstract: Democratic Senate candidate Cyril Wecht believes that federal economic policies should be fought on the Senate battleground. He also believed that the President's proposed social service cutbacks will make it very difficult for counties to cope with.

headline: A Good Place to Start
abstract: Pennsylvania State Government has not lived up to commitments to fund its share of local basic education, training for the retarded, school lunches, child welfare, mass transit, community college tuition and many other programs.  One reason is because of tight budgets.  Full-funding couldn’t be achieved without an increase in state taxes.  The other reason is due to the breakdown in the "federalism" between state and local governments in the Commonwealth.  The pressure will be on for Pennsylvania’s next governor and Legislature to come to grips with its local government commitments.

headline: Nunzio Palladino, chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, says outside the damaged Three Mile Island nuclear plant that the cleanup is going too slowly.
abstract: Photo depicts Nunzio Palladino, chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, in front of the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant, claiming the cleanup was moving too slowly.

headline: About time
abstract: Editors are dissatisfied with the treatment of drunk drivers by the legislature and the courts. Recent legislation passed a tougher law against drunk driving, however it was clear legislators attempted to soften it with amendments and stall the legislation altogether. PA Governor Thornburgh is expected to sign the law, which is a step in the right direction. Now the courts must be educated to see drunk driving for what it is--a dangerous and irresponsible action that can result in the murder of innocents.

headline: Thornfare simplified
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh's welfare reform program will cut 64,000 to 68,000 recipients from general assistance rolls by classifying them as chronically or transitionally needy. The former group will receive checks through 1983. The latter, identified as able bodied, may receive checks in 1983 for any 3 consecutive months only, saving $35 million. The program will funnel workers through the PA Employables Program. A Philadelphia County Board of Assistance spokesman outlined 3 phases to identify transitionally needy recipients.

headline: Goode Finds Fence-Sitting a Little Uncomfortable
abstract: Goode believes he can do better than the current mayor.  They say he feels Green has been aloof from the city’s neighborhood and has failed to provide strong leadership on controversial issues.  Black politicians agree that an announcement of candidacy by Goode would immediately produce unified support from all elements of the city’s black leadership.

headline: The welcher
abstract: This editorial suggests that Governor Dick Thornburgh may look like the town banker, but he acts more like the Boss in those old western movies.  He has allowed the state legislature to widdle away at a $24 million package owed to the Philadelphia School District, and an additional $9.8 million package has also been jeopardized due to the governor's refusal to get behind it.

headline: Parkway to reopen ahead of schedule
abstract: Governor Thornburg said that all lanes of the Parkway East will open six days ahead of schedule.  He praised the state Department of Transportation for their efficiency.  For eight months, Traffic had been restriced on a 6.5-mile stretch of the parkway.

headline: Court backs woman's dismissal for an absence from school post
abstract: The Commonwealth Court reinstated a school board’s dismissal of a tenured professional employee for an unexcused absence, which the district considered immoral under Section 1122 of the Public School Code.

headline: 300 Confer on Federal Cutbacks: Pa. Officials Meet in Chesco
abstract: Officials from Pennsylvania’s 67 counties, disconcerted by federal budget cuts gathered in Chester County for three days of speeches and discussions on the regional effects of President Reagan’s “new federalism.”  People basically want to know if programs are going to be cut and if funding will be available.

headline: A lesson in living in the little town of Newmedia, PA
abstract: Claire Boyer, third-grade teacher at Media Elementary School wanted to take the study of local government beyond the textbook so for a midyear social-studies course, she asked her students to create a town for themselves and then run it.  The created town - Newmedia, PA - elected a mayor and built the town.

headline: Obstacles still exist in cleanup at TMI
abstract: There are still many hurdles that needs to be cleared before a citizen's group requests to provide immediate funds for the cleanup of Three Mile Island could be granted. This was announced by a Public Utility Commission lawyer.

headline: Accusations in tax evasion name house panel counsel; complaints list 13 counts
abstract: Morton A. Lutzker, a staff lawyer for the State House Insurance Committee, has been accused of under-reporting his income by $73,000 in a four-year period allegedly to evade paying state income tax. If convicted, he could face a maximum 26-year prison term and fines amounting to $145,000.

headline: United They Cope
abstract: The United Way of Southwestern Pennsylvania is in a classic bind.  On the one hand, layoffs and budget-trimming are making greater demands on charities on the other hand, the economy is making a cruel harvest of donors in the corporate world.  The United Way of Allegheny County authorized a 10 percent reduction in its charitable allocations.

headline: Goodling and Reagan's programs
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author is concerned about the actions of US Congressman Bill Goodling and his support of the Reagan Administration's programs.  The author explains why Reagan's programs are not what was promised.

headline: The welfare lion
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's welfare reform bill is in a PA Senate committee, and the editorial hopes that it will never be seen again.  Senate Majority Leader Robert Jubelirer realized that he could not get the votes he needed on the bill as it was.

headline: For the Supreme Court
abstract: The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette endorses Berks County Common Pleas Judge Forrest G. Schaeffer for the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.  Although his opponent, Judge Stephen Zappala, possesses the necessary credentials, we feel that Judge Schaeffer's greater length and diversity of experience, as well as his edorsement from the Pennsylvania Bar, makes him the more qualified candidate.

headline: DCA Chief Urges Young Blacks To Seek High-Tech Educations
abstract: Shirley M. Dennis, Secretary of the State Department of Community Affairs, addressed 200 members and guests of the York Branch of the NAACP at its fifth annual Freedom Fund dinner.  She encouraged young blacks to seek education in technology.  Education, employment, and economics go hand in hand.

headline: 4-county Jobless Rate Rises to 11.1% in May
abstract: The unemployment rate for the Pittsburgh area reached 11.1 percent in May of 1982.  It remained higher than the state rate of 10.4 percent for May and the national rate of 9.5 percent according to the State Office of Employment Security.  Employment declines in the steel industry and other manufacturing businesses continued to dominate the area’s unemployment.  Total manufacturing jobs dipped to 196,700 in May, a seven percent decline from April’s figure, and a 42 percent decline from the year-ago level of 239,200.

headline: A library amid change: The hope for survival
abstract: The Free Library of Philadelphia released an extensive self-study that details necessary cutbacks for its survival and community and city council reaction.

headline: Oil, gas leases under tight control, State says
abstract: Federal authorities have recently come under fire for mismanagement of oil and gas leases, prompting state officials to assure taxpayers that they are in more control.  At the federal level, a recent report states that sloppy oversight has led to losses of nearly $500 million per year in royalties.

headline: Adoption Process Needs Full Care
abstract: null

headline: US State Program 'swap' plan halted
abstract: The Reagan administration, after months of negotiations, has suspended its efforts to write legislation transferring welfare and food stamp programs to the states in exchange for federal assumption of all Medicaid costs. This was the main part of President Reagan's "new federalism" initiative.

headline: GOP Concentrates Aid: Targets 3 Vulnerable Congressmen
abstract: Five Pennsylvania Republican congressional candidates have been earmarked for the campaign help by ranking party strategists as part of a national election blueprint aimed at preventing Democratic gains in the House.  Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation could return to the Democratic column, reliable sources said.  A mid-summer prediction chart shows GOP strategists see the Democrats gaining three seats and a 13-10 majority of Keystone House seats, despite the district reapportionment efforts of the Republican-controlled Legislature.

headline: This Week's Lotto Prize: $1.5 Million
abstract: The Pennsylvania Lottery jackpot will be at least $1.5 million because there was no jackpot winner in Friday's drawing, the state lottery announced.

headline: A public role is vital in all nuclear decisions
abstract: A proposal establishing an Independent office of public advocate within the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) should be advanced vigorously through Congress.  Such a proposal would give citizens control over nuclear-power regulations--something which they desperately need given the NRC's passionate support of nuclear energy and its inability to make impartial decisions.

headline: Delay Seen on Changes in Curriculum
abstract: The State Board of Education was expected to delay action on any curriculum changes for Pennsylvania schools until at least September.  The Board would recommend public hearings be held in the Harrisburg, Pittsburgh and Philadelphia areas on any proposed modifications and that the effective date for implementation be delayed a year until July 1, 1984.

headline: A desperate tax
abstract: Opinion columnist writes against the Value-Added-Tax.  The author says that there is considerable support for the Value-added-tax in Washington and that it is already popular in the United Kingdom and other European nations.  The author suggests that the tax will adversely affect the middle-class and whose with low incomes.

headline: A new contellation at Buhl
abstract: Editorial: The renaming of the Buhl Planetarium to the Buhl Science Center and its new head of Josh Whetzel are signs that the Board of the Buhl holdings want to transform it into a major science center.  Mr. Whetzel has noticed that well-attended sciences centers have sprung up across the United States, and that Pittsburgh should have one too.

headline: Opposing Sides File Briefs on Bell's Rate Hike
abstract: The PA Consumer Advocate’s Office and the Public Utility Commission’s legal staff challenged an administrative law judge’s recommendation that Bell of Pennsylvania be given a $320 million rate increase.  In briefs to the PUC, which must rule on the rate increase by September 13th, the Consumer Advocate asked that the rate increase be held to $37 million.  The PUC’s legal division called for a $177.1 million revenue increase.  Bell had asked for a total rate increase of $402 million and it too filed a brief seeking the entire amount and warning that the judge’s recommendation seriously understates the company’s additional revenue needs.

headline: Aid plan for victims of lawyers revealed
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Henry X. O'Brien has said that the victims of legal malpractice will soon be able to receive compensation from the new Pennsylvania Client Security Fund established by the Supreme Court.

headline: Welfare bill ready for final ok
abstract: The new welfare bill, about to be signed into law by Governor Dick Thornburgh, will help to eliminate certain able-bodied applicants and create a new category called "chronically needy" to address those with physical or mental handicaps.  The bill was created by a predominantly Republican legislative committee.  Other able-bodied individuals who stay on the welfare roles will be put into the new Workfare program.

headline: GOP denies coal 'favorites'
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh's office issued a point-by-point denial of Democrat accusations of favoritism toward coal operators.  The governor's Press Secretary, Paul Critchlow, did acknowledge that one of the accusations were correct, that there were instances in which surface-mining permits were issued to companies that had violated mining laws, but that these instances had been promptly corrected.

headline: Thornburgh aided self, hurt state on taxes, Democrats charge
abstract: Democrats claim that Governor Dick Thornburgh may have helped his reelection bid by not raising taxes in his proposed budget, but hurt state and local government programs.  Democrats claim to be working to change his budget proposal, and are especially concerned with the $127 million block grant proposed for education funding.

headline: Benedict: Improve townships' fiscal controls
abstract: In an effort to improve fiscal controls, PA Auditor General Al Benedict proposed seven changes to the Second-Class Township Code.  The changes resulted from an audit of North Strabane Township, which revealed legal violations--such as using federal witholding taxes to pay township bills--and financial mismanagement.

headline: Dirty words
abstract: KDKA-TV2 editorial: Excerpts from a book called "Working"  by Studs Terkel about working life involves bad language where interviews with workers are reprinted.  These excerpts are required reading for a teacher at a voctional school in Gerrard, PA, and have come under fire by parents and students for their use.  The editorial believes that the teacher should be rewarded, not punished, for including this pertinent material.

headline: Allentown, Pa., takes pride in making do with less US Aid
abstract: Allentown, Pa., used to have a lot of things that made its people proud including a seemingly recession proof economy, 35 square blocks of housing rehabilitation projects, etc. Unfortunately, this town is now realizing certain problems that include high unemployment rate, budget cuts and layoffs of city workers. However, the mayor, Joseph Daddona, is confident that Allentown will be able to develop despite a reduction in federal aid.

headline: A state tax for schools
abstract: Opinion: Thomas Leonard, Philadelphia City Controller, believes that a long-term solution to the schools funding problem needs to be found.  PA House bill 2097, which is sets out to reorganize the school system, may be the best way to implement spending controls.

headline: Oregon's Hatfield to hold TMI hearings here
abstract: US Senator Mark Hatfield will hold hearings on the efficacy of the use of Federal funds for the Three Mile Island cleanup in Harrisburg.  He will question federal, state, and utility officials about the financial aspects of the slow-moving decontamination process.  US Senator Arlen Specter will also participate in the hearings.

headline: Allegheny Bomb Shelters Show Age
abstract: In Allegheny County many of the thousands of bomb shelters aimed at providing protection from a radioactive blast have been closed or abandoned.  At one point, about 1.4 million of the 1.6 million county residents could have been shielded from such a blast, but officials are saying that the number is far less because of the shelters which have been rendered inoperable.  Some people believe that the shelters have not helped in nuclear attack.

headline: Welfare Training Overbilled, HHS Says
abstract: The U.S. Health and Human Services Department has again found that the Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare claimed and accepted too much aid for a federally assisted state-run social program.  The state overcharged the federal government $592, 872 to train state welfare workers between July 1979 through June 1981.  Overcharges identified by HHS made up almost 10 percent of $6.6 million in federal training funds received by the state during the two-year period.  A similar situation in 1981, forced the state to repay $7.5 million in federal funds for expenses claimed during 1976-79 for state-run, federally assisted programs for the mentally retarded.

headline: GOP Governors Strongly Criticize Reagan's Policies
abstract: Republican governors, including PA Governor Richard Thornburgh, fired questions and criticisms of Reagan at pollsters, campaign consultants, and Reagan's assistant for intergovernmental affairs Richard Williamson during a post-election meeting. Attendees accused the hosts of making it difficult to capture women and black voters. Governor Janklow of South Dakota accused the Administration of allying with organizations like the National Conservative Political Action Committee (NAPAC).

headline: Thornburgh Proclaimed "Captive Nations Week"
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh proclaimed the week of July 18-24 as "Captive Nations Week" in the Commonwealth.  Proclaiming "Captive Nations Week" the third week in July began 23 years ago by a joint resolution approved by Congress which authorized and requested that the President of the United States issue a proclamation each year until freedom and independence are achieved for all captive nations.

headline: Welfare Workers Fight Changes
abstract: Allegheny County welfare caseworkers are opposing welfare-program changes that will drop 20,000 recipients from the rolls by next March.  The changes are designed to take able-bodied persons off the welfare rolls.

headline: Disappointed
abstract: Last week the Standard Observer called on area school officials to join with Lions Clubs in developing a curriculum to deal with drug abuse in schools.  The project has been given the full support of state education officials because they believe that an intoxicated mind is a horrible waste.  Several school districts have chosen to turn their backs on a worthy endeavor.  In Helping to inaugurate the project, Family Court Judge Charles Marker said the effort must start early in a child’s school career.  For many school officials, the effort has never started.  Hempfield School Director Betty Valerio criticized colleagues for ignoring the urgency of the problem, demonstrated by their failure to show up for the conference.

headline: Area Jobless Rate Rises to 14.1%; Job Loss Slows
abstract: The unemployment rate in Pittsburgh labor market area went up 0.3 percent to 14.1 percent in October, but there was a substantial drop in the number of job losses during the month, according to a report by the state Office of Employment and Security.  The manufacturing and non-manufacturing sectors lost 4,400 jobs in October, but this was considerably below the peak months of August and July, when the totals were 12,900 and 19,800 respectively.

headline: Acrimony Follows Integration Plans for Phila. Schools
abstract: There is talk of desegregating Philadelphia schools.  In Pittsburgh, every middle school in the city has been desegregated.  All but one high school in the city would be desegregated by 1986 as would half of the 38 city elementary schools that remain segregated.  The Philadelphia school district is more than 5 times the size of the Pittsburgh district.

headline: Our Opinion: GPU and the Facts of Life
abstract: GPU Nuclear Corporation has already had one large nuclear accident, so they should try to avoid anymore.  However, recently GPU has caught two control room operators cheating on licensing examinations.  In July 1981, it had discovered two other control room operators cheating on NRC tests.  They resigned.  The tests are part of the regular training for the operators, the people whose fingers are on proverbial "red" button.  The two only were suspended for two weeks without pay.  According to an Associated Press report, the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board recommended the suspension rather than have the Nuclear Regulatory Commission take action against the two, who work at the TMI Unit No. 1 reactor.

headline: Allegheny Coroner May Sue
abstract: New Allegheny County Coroner Joshua Perper threatened to file suit against the county commissioners after their shakeup of morgue operations and firing of four employees.  Perper accused the commissioners of destroying his office with budget cuts.

headline: Welfare-reform bill heavy with defects
abstract: PA Senator Mark Singel responds to an earlier editorial claiming that there is a lack of sentiment for welfare reform.  The Senator comments on the situation that Cambria County is in, and notes that the new welfare reform bill would eliminate 46% of the people receiving government assistance in his area.

newspaper: z-Unidentified Observer - journal of the PA Liquor Industry
headline: GOP Infighting Threatens Thornburgh Reapportionment Boast
abstract: A year ago, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh boasted to the Republican State Committee that the GOP-controlled Legislature would take care of the Democratic congressional majority through deft reapportionment of the districts.  The efforts have been thrawted, not only by solid Democratic opposition but also by a few Republicans who would not go the party line.

headline: Three months a county commissioner, Hochendoner enters 17th District race
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioner Lawrence J. Hochendoner has filed as a Democratic candidate for Congress from the 17th District. Hochendoner was appointed commissioner three months ago, to fill the unexpired term of Stephen R. Reed, who resigned after winning election as mayor of Harrisburg.

headline: Abortion benefits
abstract: The president of Planned Parenthood criticizes a letter to the editor and claims that 10 years of well-regulated, medically supervised abortion provisions have brough the United States lower death rates due to illegal abortions, reduced neonatal death rates, and an improvement in overall maternal and child health.

headline: Each school day, thousands don't have prepared teachers
abstract: The Philadelphia school district is having problems with finding substitute teachers for classes, when the regular teachers go absent. This problem, leading to thousands of school children not receiving prepared instruction, can ultimately lead to a drop in the quality of education.

headline: Big deficits draw fire
abstract: Critics of US President Ronald Reagan's "new federalism" plan that swaps state and federal programs see a budget with tax hikes and aid cuts.  The new budget proposed in Washington would mean that states will have to do a significant amount of new revenue generation to make up for federal budget cuts.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's new budget proposal, created before the federal announcement, does not include additional funds for the federal cuts.

headline: Advisers Help State Plan a More Modern Forum
abstract: In the winter 1980, with enthusiastic support of Governor Dick Thornburgh the Forum Advisory Committee was established.  It is composed of representatives of leading artistic groups in the community and others knowledgeable in performing arts.  Although the group is unofficial and unpaid, they have rendered tremendous assistance.  Meeting several times a year, they have advised on all aspects of theater management and they have provided an important link to the Central Pennsylvania community and its arts organizations.

headline: Pa. Advocate Appeals Part of PE Rate Hike
abstract: Nearly a fourth of the $221.7 million rate increase granted to PECO by the PA Public Utility Commission was appealed in Commonwealth Court by the PA Consumer Advocate’s office.  The office is challenging five areas in which it said the commission violated state rate-making policy in the Philadelphia Electric Co.  The City of Philadelphia also filed an appeal in Commonwealth Court of the PE rate decision.  The city based its appeal on grounds similar to those of the Consumer Advocate’s office.

headline: An explanation of the Pennsylvania Crime Commission's annual report
abstract: The author believes that the recent criticism on the Pennsylvania Crime Commission for issuing an annual report that contained old data and failing to depict organized crime's adverse economic impact is wrong for the reasons outlined in the letter.

headline: Workfare
abstract: The ancient adage about the road being paved with good intentions seems to apply as PA prepares to implement its workfare program. Under the plan, agencies of local, state and federal government, in addition to non-profit organizations, will have an opportunity to use these welfare recipients for public service work without paying for them.

headline: GOP Moves anew to Assist Nominees
abstract: Republicans have set in motion a third vehicle to try to make it easier for Governor Dick Thornburgh to install his nominees on six state regulatory agencies.  On a party-line vote of 4-2, a Senate-House conference committee used a non-related bill to insert amendments reducing the confirmation vote to a constitutional majority from the existing two-thirds requirement.

headline: Tide will turn in 1982, Wecht tells Democrats
abstract: According to Cyril H. Wecht, candidate for US Senate, 1982 is a turning point in for the history of the country as it would be the year the Democrats return to power and return the country to more prosperous days.

headline: Don't cross Blue Cross
abstract: The Pennsylvania state Senate is considering legislation that would require Blue Cross to pay hospitals at the same rate as commercial insurance carriers.  Blue Cross was established as a nonprofit corporation to provide low-cost medical coverage, however, and legislating an increase in their rates would seem to undermine the purpose for which the insurer was created.

headline: Early retirements for teachers proposed as way to lessen layoff
abstract: In order to reduce the impact of possible teacher layoffs across the state, Gov. Dick Thornburgh proposed a system of early retirements for veteran teachers that could save school districts $72 million and more annually. The plan has the immediate support of several education-related groups.

headline: Bi-partisan tricks
abstract: The "Economic Recovery Act" allows Congressmen to claim extra-ordinary exemptions from the payment of income tax, and this is an example of bipartisan chicanery. This is not right and must be cancelled with immediate effect. Otherwise, this must be remembered till next elections.

headline: Aliquippa School Bus Drivers go on Strike
abstract: Bus drivers and mechanics in the Aliquippa School District went on strike in an attempt to pressure the district for job security.  The strike affects almost 1,500 public and private school students.  85 percent of the school population reported to class.

headline: Panel Acts on Atomic Cleanup
abstract: The Senate Environment Committee voted to clear a bill for action that would require the customers of utilities using nuclear power throughout the country to pay part of the cost of cleaning up the crippled Three Mile Island nuclear power plant.  The committee passed the bill without a recommendation, and its senior member, Senator Jennings Randolph, Democrat of West Virginia, said it was the first time the Environment Committee had sent a bill to the floor in this manner.

headline: An Unusual Judge
abstract: Erie Court of Common Pleas Judge Richard L. Nygaard does not have the typical background of a judge.  He is a native of Thief River Falls, Minnesota.  Along with being a judge he is also a family man, farmer, and Sunday school teacher.  He has had some frustrations and failures as a judge.  This came from trying to get the Erie School Board and the Erie Education Association to sit down and settle on a contract.  However, he wasn’t able to do this.

headline: Workfare bill wins; 68,000 due off rolls
abstract: The Senate passed a legislation that would remove about 68,000 Pennsylvanians off state welfare rolls. It also imposes limited welfare for the first time in Pennsylvania. Governor Thornburgh has been pushing for welfare reform for the last three years.

headline: GOP National Committee to Air Controversial Postman TV Ads
abstract: The Republican National Committee is spending another $200,000 to air its controversial postman-Social Security ad in an additional 19 markets.  The ad condemned by Democrats, features a folksy mailman saying he is the most popular guy in town because he’s delivering Social Security checks with the 7 percent cost-of-living increase President Reagan promised and delivered.  Democrats are still shaping their advertising for the fall campaign and now are focusing on the theme of chaos in the nation’s economic program-including the largest tax increase in history one year after the largest tax cut in history.

headline: Time for Good Government
abstract: New Jersey State Senator Joseph Hirkala, a Democrat of Passaic County, wants to transform the state legislature from part-time governing body to full-time.  The press of business is just too great and the time is too short, he contends.

headline: TMI Unit 1 restart hearing Nov. 9 at CD High
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) announced final plans for the November 9th public hearing on the restart of Unit 1 at Three Mile Island.  The hearing will be the NRC's last opportunity to hear public opinion on the potential restart of operations at Unit 1.

headline: Education grants 'really a sham,' Sen. Lewis says
abstract: PA Senator H. Craig Lewis has called an education block grant program proposed by Governor Dick Thornburgh to be a screen for actually reducing funding of public schools.  To ease pressures on the school districts, the Governor proposed lifting 21 state-imposed mandates, 8 of which would require legislative approval.

headline: Buzzing Over Tax Reform
abstract: A new tax reform proposal that would eliminate virtually all deductions and require everyone to pay the same flat tax rate has Washington buzzing.  The tax rate would be no higher than 18 percent.  It is believed that economic growth would result from this, however, opponents argue that the rich would benefit at the expense of the poor.

headline: Angry about a $75 increase
abstract: Photo: 250 students protested a $75 tuition increase at the state capitol in Harrisburg.  Several other rallies were held around the state.  The tuition increase was a result of a court settlement that compelled the state to pay back salaries to state univeristy faculty.

headline: Paper Progress on Hydro
abstract: A survey by the PA Public Utility Commission found 66 small hydro sites in the application stage. - representing about 350 megawatts of capacity, but only one had cleared the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and would not be in operation until 1984.  A comparison with New York, which may have the most ambitious small hydro development plan in the nation, shows how far behind Pennsylvania lags in reaching its objectives.

headline: An Unusual Judge
abstract: This article discusses Common Pleas Judge Richard J. Nygaard and his sentencing patterns in the cases of career criminals and drunk drivers.  He has also taken a supportive role in working on creative ideas to deal with the problems of overcrowding at the prison.  One way is by "home release".  In this program, a minor offender who would qualify for structured probation would be sentenced to a certain amount of time in his home.  He would only be allowed to leave when he had to report to the jail.

headline: Working mother hit hard by welfare cut
abstract: Article describes how President Ronald Reagan's cuts in welfare benefits will affect a local woman.  The Reagan Omnibus Reconciliation Act will cut off 6,417 Aid to Families with Dependent Children recipients in Allegheny County, meaning that they will go without a monthly check and without medical benefits.

headline: GOP revives talk of carving up Ertel district
abstract: Acting on the rumors that US Representative Allen Ertel will declare his candidacy for Governor, PA Republican leaders are looking to his district to be carved up in a redistricting plan.  If this should happen, Ertel's district would be merged with another creating a new 17th district with no incumbent.

headline: Toll-free 'waste line' started by treasurer
abstract: State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer has installed a toll-free 'Waste Line' in his office to enlist citizen help in his efforts to crack down on wasteful, improper and illegal spending of state funds.

headline: Inside Erieland
abstract: An Erie-County Executive implores Governor Thornburgh to change the Medicaid reimbursement ceiling for the county.  If the ceiling is not changed, Erie will be unable to meet its state-mandated obligation to provide long-term care facilities for the indigent elderly and handicapped.  Medicaid ceilings are determined by a county's Standard Metropolitan Statistical Area, and for some reason Erie was lumped together with York and Adams Counties.  In Erie, the cost of living and demands for long-term care are far greater, however.

headline: Courthouse; County jobs crisis gets DC-area publicity
abstract: Luzerne County and Northeast Pennsylvania are besieged with unemployment problems and shrinking industrial base. This is getting a lot of publicity with Washington decision makers.

headline: Arbitrary
abstract: While it is important to make sure the Erie County Library can provide minimal services to its users, if it can be done with fewer people, why must the state mandate that the library have more?

headline: Peach Bottom Reactor Back in Operation
abstract: A reactor at the Peach Bottom Nuclear Power Plant in Lancaster County was put back in operation after a precautionary shutdown following the discovery of an open valve in a 1-inch air line.

headline: Anti-arson efforts urged
abstract: A PA arson task force recommended tougher criminal penalty, more training for fire and police personnel, and a package of legislation to combat arson in Pennsylvania.  After the results of the year-long study were released, the task force stressed the need for beefing up local efforts to fight arson and for more public awareness.  The State Legislature is considering three bills to promote anti-arson efforts.

headline: A "livable city"
abstract: The fact that Pittsburgh is a livable city has been a too well-guarded secret.  The AM radio station who authored this editorial hopes that the Allegheny Conference on Community Development can do a better job at getting that word out to the rest of the country.

headline: Retail Chain Sold by Miller
abstract: Retail chain is sold by Miller.  Miller has 17 stores, all in shopping centers or enclosed malls.  Four are in the immediate Harrisburg area and one each is in York, Hershey, Lancaster, Lebanon, Lewistown, Williamsport, State College, Altoona, Chambersburg, Waynesboro, Shamokin, Pottsville and Martinsburg, West Virginia.  The three year expansion plan would include stores in a 200-mile radius, with locations to be in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland.  The Miller’s stores have five primary product lines: tires, automotive accessories, replacement parts, lawn and garden materials and sporting goods.  Additionally, all have service bays and offer tire, muffler and shock absorber service and other services, including state inspection.

headline: GOP state Committee Elects Christopher Vice Chairman
abstract: David Christopher of Pittsburgh’s Mount Washington district, became the newly elected vice chairman of the Republican State Committee.  He has committed himself to work to build up the party’s minority auxiliaries as a means of broadening GOP influence and registration in Pennsylvania.
