The election of Christopher will move him into position to become State Chairman after the completion of a new two-year term by state Chairman Martha Bell Schoeninger, who was re-elected.

headline: Tom Leonard, Joe Smith
abstract: Ward leader Peter J. Camiel's comment, a caption under the photos of former City Controller Tom Leonard and Joe Smith, a US Congressman at the end of his term, claims Smith's delegation to Leonard was an attempt to remove all obstacles for former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo, another presumable candidate. However, the delegation failed.

headline: Cosmetic work on roads costly, Manderino says
abstract: House Democratic Whip James Manderino claims that Governor Thornburgh's surface-treatment program was an electoral ploy designed to give the impression of a large road-improvement project.  The governor, Manderino alleges, wasted 180 million of taxpayer money; Manderino claims to have videotape and photographic evidence corroborating the wastefulness of this project.

headline: Democrats oppose reducing deficit by excise taxes, congressman says
abstract: Democrats announce that they will oppose any efforts by President Ronald Reagan's administration to use new consumer taxes to reduce budget deficits.  Dan Rostenkowski, chairman of the House Ways and Means committee, additionally announced significant Democratic opposition to removal of natural gas price controls

headline: Area Schools Set to Reopen, 6 Without Pacts
abstract: Mechanicsburg teachers received $1,000 plus 2.5 percent of their previous salary in the first year of a two-year agreement and $1,100 plus 2.8 percent in the second year.  A three-year contract that last year was extended a year during a wage opener in Cumberland Vo-Tech School provided teachers with a $1,000 across-the-board increase in the first two years and $1,300 in the last two years.  In Dauphin County, Millersburg Area teachers came off a three-year contract that had been extended for the 1981-82 school year during a wage reopener.

headline: Pellets Leak Radiation at Coal Site
abstract: Consolidation Coal Co. has sealed off a coal exploration site in rural Southwestern Pennsylvania where two radioactive pellets the size of aspirin tablets leaked from broken equipment.  18 employees were exposed to the radiation from the synthetic element Americium.  Low levels were detected in articles of clothing and boots.  Another 10 workmen also may have been exposed.  Radiation experts for Consol and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission are monitoring the site.

headline: Arraignment, Low Bail In Mob Shooting Probed
abstract: Investigations into the speedy arraignment of two suspects in the shooting of Salvatore A. Testa may be completed this week, officials said Monday, while police looked for an assailant in the weekend assassination attempt on Harry "The Hunchback" Riccobene.  These are two key figures in the territorial dispute of organized crime.

headline: An economic strategy
abstract: Editors are hopeful in reviewing plans put forth for the region by the Allegheny Conference on Community Development. A Development Committee Taskforce outlined 5 strategic directions and 4 public policy areas as key to the success of the region. Included in the strategies are plans to focus on the arts and advanced technology. The editors also believe it is necessary for the region to partner with PA Governor Thornburgh's program, the Ben Franklin Partnership, to ensure success.

headline: Reverse-Mortgage Plan Reviewed
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter met with state government and financial officials to review legislation that would lead to a reverse mortgage program for elderly people in need of cash.  The measure is designed to attract more investors and banks into offering reverse mortgages in Pennsylvania and other areas of the country.  Through a reverse mortgage, elderly people who have paid off their original mortgage can convert the equity in their home to monthly income.  They sell their home to a bank or insurance company, which in turn gives the elderly person or couple a monthly income and a guarantee they can remain in the house for the rest of their lives.  When the person or couple dies, the bank or insurance company sells the house.

headline: GOP to remodel workfare legislation
abstract: PA Senate Republicans are going to rework the "workfare" portion of Governor Dick Thornburgh's welfare plan.  The original plan, passed by the House of Representatives, missed approval by one vote, and will be reworked by a Senate committee.  Republican Senators and Governor Thornburgh were unable to convince any of the detractors to change their votes.

headline: Top dems swing to pete-for-governor bid
abstract: Some Democratic Party leaders may be looking to Pete Flaherty for a gubernatorial candidate, but the official endorsement will not be announced for at least a month.  Other candidates such as Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell, and PA Representative Allen Ertel are also being considered.

headline: Lehigh qualifies for tech center
abstract: Lehigh University has qualified for the establishment of a state of Pennsylvania Ben Franklin Technology Center.  The General Assembly and Governor Thornburgh have approved a 1 million dollar appropriation for the Ben Franklin Partnership.  The goal of the program is to expand scientific development, education, and research and innovation in Pennsylvania.

headline: Don't demean the US Constitution
abstract: People who have followed the Pennsylvania government know that the law requiring balanced budgets is no guarantee against year-end deficits. Hence, it does not make sense to amend the US Constitution to require Congress to prepare a balanced budget.

headline: Better education: Students should also have contract demands
abstract: Opinion column written by the co-chairpersons for the Parents Union for Public Schools says that the children of the Philadelphia Public School system need and deserve a  genuine settlement of the current school crisis.  The Parents Union for Public Schools has created a list of miminum benefits which should be guaranteed to all students.  Most of the suggested changes deal with the way that the schools are funded, and with personnel evaluations.

headline: Philadelphia Electric disputes NRC report on nuclear facility
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Co. said that it does not plan to scrap or delay construction of its Limerick Unit 2 nuclear plant near Pottstown, Pa. This is in response to a Nuclear Regulatory Commission staff report predicting the unit will be staffed or delayed indefinitely.

headline: As the Editor Sees It: 'Dollar Justice'?
abstract: Two Altoona men charged with the cold-blooded murder of a State Police officer 10 years ago in Mifflin County were not prosecuted for murder in the first degree because the county objected to the high cost of such a trial.  The assistant district attorney, Arthur Shuman, said he thinks it is a "disgrace" that Mark R. Geddes and Charles H. Knisely have been paroled after what he called their "cold-blooded execution of Trooper John S. Valent."  The two were allowed to enter guilty pleas to second degree murder in 1972.

headline: An old state Capitol is getting a new look
abstract: The current Pennsylvania Capital Building does not have a fire exit or enough space for all of the legislators offices.  The cost of the new expansion project is projected to be above $66 million, of which $12 million will be spent to make the building conform to modern safety standards.  Other aspects of the project are more controversial, such as the $40 million Governor's quarters.

headline: Setback for Steel
abstract: American steelmakers are disappointed that the U.S. Commerce Department has softened somewhat a preliminary June ruling against foreign steel producers charged with receiving unfair subsidies.  The newest Commerce Department ruling cut back the findings overall of subsidy margins to 0-226 percent from the June rulings of 0-40 percent.  Subsidy margins reflect the subsidy violation as a percentage of value. But the department upheld previous charges that steelmakers in Britain, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium and Luxembourg have indeed received subsidies from their governments, enabling them to sell steel in the United States at unfairly low prices.

headline: GOP will rally forces for new redistricting try
abstract: PA Senate Republicans will try yet again to come up with a  new reapportionment plan.  This time, they will keep the Bucks County district intact, a fact which has sent Republican Senator Edward Howard voting against the plan.  A vote is expected soon.

headline: Tough ballot entry law studied by legislature
abstract: Fringe candidate Republican Alvin Joseph Jacobson has, until now, never found it difficult to get on the ballot. However, due to a bill tabled by the State Senate in February, the signature requirements and filing fees will be doubled.

headline: Economy Off In Dutch Country, But Not GOP
abstract: Even in York County, Pennsylvania, where the unemployment rate is higher than its ever been, voters believe that President Reagan's economic policies will bring the country out of recession and restore economic health.  Voters' support of Reagan's policies indicates that high jobless rates in York County will probably not hurt Governor Dick Thornburgh, an ardent supporter of Reaganomics, in the November 2 election.

headline: Early state budget looks likely
abstract: The approval for the new state budget can occur much earlier than the June 30 deadline. This change has happened since legislators took the responsibility of enacting budgets themselves.

headline: Beyond Name Calling
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Education Association placed Governor Dick Thornburgh on the same level as Adolf Hitler and Josef Goebbels.  Former Mayor Frank Rizzo filed a case against a Philadelphia weekly newspaper that did a similar thing to him.

headline: Plan spurs concern for shad
abstract: When Montgomery County developer Peter Cross unveiled plans to build a 6000-kilowatt power plant, it caused a lot of concern among anglers, who fear it might disrupt the annual shad migration.

headline: Barto Building Is Woman's 'Million Dollar Baby' She Supervised its Rehabilitation
abstract: Helen Wilhelm supervised the entire rehabilitation of the Barto Building, which is being leased to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Bureau of Real Estate, for the Department of Aging and the controller’s offices under Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman.

headline: Better boarding homes
abstract: Elderly boarding homes are so badly needed that code enforcement officials have been reluctant to crack down on poorly-maintained homes.  Allegheny County is making an effort to improve the situation.

headline: Sex bias in auto insurance rates ruled out
abstract: The Commonwealth Court upheld a decision by the PA Insurance Department that would have the effect of forbidding insurance companies to charge males more for automobile insurance than females. The judges stated that this was illegal as it violated the state Casualty and Rate Regulatory Act.

headline: Gorsuch: A Good Soldier In The Center Of A Constitutional Storm
abstract: Anne M. Gorsuch, administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), was held in contempt of Congress for withholding documents subpoenaed by the U.S. House. This was based on the advice of the U.S. Department of Justice, which has claimed executive privilege in the matter. She has, along with U.S. Secretary of the Interior, James G. Watt, been accussed of dismantling the EPA through budget cuts and reductions in research and enforcement actions. She responds that she is making the agency more streamlined and that EPA should be judged on its accomplishments instead. However, the controversy has secured her job, as being forced to resign would appear to be a political retreat, and made her appear more sympathetic in front of Congressional questioning.

headline: Tough Drunken-Driving Bill Among Pending Legislation
abstract: The issues wrapped up in pending legislation are SB171 Insanity Pleas; ; HB1652 Philadelphia Wage Tax; SB579 establishing a Department of Corrections; HB1300 School Code; SB1315 Park Rides Inspection; HB2530 Pay Raises for Lawmakers; SB784 Product Liability; SB86 Senate Confirmation; HB392 Abolishing State liquor retail; and HB1587 Home Ownership Taxes.

headline: Legal Moves Over Gag Order Delay Banks' Hearings
abstract: The Luzerne County Common Pleas Court will decide tomorrow if a gag order should be issued in the case of suspected mass murderer George Banks.  Banks' attorneys filed for the order after reporters from The Citizens' Voice and The Times Leader said Banks expressed a willingness to be interviewed.  The papers are expected to challenge the defense request for the order.

headline: Factory layoffs hurt jobs in other fields
abstract: More than 32,000 major manufacturing firm workers are either temporarily or permanently without jobs. As a consequence of this, there are thousands of other people in secondary metals and service industries who are also unemployed.

headline: Block grant pitfalls
abstract: Editorial: The plan to provide state money in the form of block grants to school districts is good for the proposed flexibility, but is bad because it is just less money.  The program also allows the state to get around a law that requires it to provide more money as costs of programs go up by not funding specific programs anymore.

headline: Plant Supervisor at 3 Mile Island Says All Safety Steps Were Taken
abstract: General Public Utilities Corporation of Parsippany, N.J. and its subsidiary Metropolitan Edison Company, owner and operator of Three Mile Island, are suing the manufacturer of some equipment used in their plants. Plaintiffs argue an accident related to these materials could have been prevented had revised safety procedures been issued after an accident in Toledo. Plant supervisor testified before Federal District Court Judge Richard Owen that a valve was stuck in accident. The defendant says plant workers were poorly trained.

headline: Battered children
abstract: A bill that would require case workers to transmit information of serious abuse to local police officials is pending in the state House. The Standard Observer believes that for the sake of children and humanity, this must be passed into law.

headline: Blackstone Building Demolition Work Contract Awarded
abstract: Demolition of the interior of the eight-story Blackstone Building was expected to start shortly.  J.E. Husic Wrecking and Excavation Co. from Dillsburg Firm was awarded the contract from the Dauphin County Commissioners.  It will cost $120,000 to complete the work.  Renovation of the building is part of the county’s multi-million capital improvement program.

headline: Small guys are sure of their tenure
abstract: With the new banking law that liberalizes the rules on bank expansions and acquisitions, small regional banks have a great chance to get acquired by larger ones. However, Jim Thorpe National Bank's chief, Harry Hintz, says his bank will not be interested in any merger or acquisition unless a high price is being offered.

headline: Governor barely meets election law deadline
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's re-election committee came close to violating state election laws when it filed its first campaign finance report an hour after the state Bureau of Elections had closed for the day.  If Richard Anderson, the state commissioner of elections and Thornburgh appointee, had not stayed late to work, the deadline would have been missed.  To date, Thornburgh's contributions of $580,121 dwarf any of his Democratic rivals.

headline: Toward a New Federalism
abstract: The latest setback for President Reagan’s New Federalism was not unexpected.  Republican and Democratic members of the National Governors’ Association rejected the plan at their annual summer meeting.  From the beginning, opposition to Mr. Reagan’s New Federalism has centered on the proposal that Aid to Families with Dependent Children be assumed entirely by the states at a cost of $8.1 billion.  The governors plan on drafting their own version of New Federalism and take it to congress.  Administration spokesman say the governors cannot expect approval of their program without White House support.

headline: 2 Against Dougherty
abstract: Two letters to the editor respond to a Philadelphia-Daily-News endorsement of Congressman Charles Dougherty.  Both readers are concerned with Dougherty's staunch support of President Reagan's policies--especially as they relate to nuclear-arms proliferation, defense spending, and U.S. policy towards Central America.

headline: 'Fed not to blame,' Heinz says
abstract: US Sen. John Heinz, R-Pa., believes that the Federal Reserve Board has made a number of mistakes, but should not be blamed for the present problems faced by the country. He also said that the rise of interest rates to above 20% three times in the last two years occurred only because of the Fed.

headline: Education no Ping Pong Ball
abstract: Taxpayer groups are springing up around the Commonwealth to make their voices heard on school and other issues.  One group is strongly opposed to a proposed new school in the Selingsgrove district, while another is vociferous in its opposition to a new school busing plan in the Danville District.  Too often, taxpayer groups may be well meaning, but don’t have all of the facts or all of the information at their disposal when deciding on issues.

headline: Plant Will Turn All of Solid Waste in State's Southeast Into Energy
abstract: A plant that will handle all the municipal solid waste from Southeastern Pennsylvania and turn it into energy should be in operation in Montgomery County by 1983.  The company announced that the pyrolysis plant will produce fuel by burning solid municipal waste.  When it is fully operational, it will be able to handle all the municipal solid waste from the southeastern part of the state.  It will employ about 400 workers.  Senator John Heinz was on hand for the announcement.  He said communities in Southeastern Pennsylvania are rapidly running out of landfill space.

headline: Bill Sent to Reagan: Specter Crime Curbs Pass
abstract: A bill sponsored by US Senator Arlen Specter containing two criminal justice measures was approved by the Senate yesterday and sent to the President.  One of the proposals would make a criminal with two or more previous robbery convictions subject to a sentence of 15 years to life in prison while the other would provide $100 million annually to form a Justice Assistance Administration to replace the controversial Law Enforcement Assistance Administration.

headline: Bond-Market Interest Rate Help Penna.'s Would-Be Homebuyers
abstract: Thanks to low interest rates in the bond market, the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency is offering an estimated 3,000 home buyers mortgages at an even greater discount than was originally anticipated.  PHFA officials announced that the agency had sold $115 million worth of tax-exempt bonds at a 12.74 percent interest rate, which will enable the PHFA to offer 30-year mortgages to qualified home buyers at a fixed 13.08 percent interest rate, or about 3 percentages points below the current market rate.  The family-income limit for those seeking the mortgages is $35,000 per year except for the Bethlehem-Allentown area, where the ceiling is $36,500 and the Pittsburgh area, where the income ceiling is $37,500.  A 5 percent minimum down payment toward the purchase price is required.

headline: State Backs Insurance Complaint
abstract: State Insurance Commissioner Michael Browne has refused a life insurance company’s request to dismiss a woman’s complaint that she was overcharged on her disability premium solely because of her sex.  Ellen Starer of Philadelphia sued the Massachusetts Indemnity and Life Insurance Company.  The law suit stated that the $325 which she pain in 1978 for her disability income insurance annual premium was 25 percent higher than what a man would have paid for the same policy.  She contended that there is no difference in the cost of insuring men and women.  The insurance company asked Browne to dismiss the complaint because the company is no longer marketing individual disability income policies in Pennsylvania.

headline: Governor Going Their Own Way on Federalism
abstract: After more than six months of negotiations with the White House, Chairman Richard Snelling of the National Governors Association told his colleagues that they should submit a plan of their own for a "New Federalism" to Congress.  As seen on the state level, the federalism proposal offered a major opportunity to accelerate a trend that has been unfolding for more than a decade-a rise in no strings federal aid to states and localities, and the grouping of individual federal programs into broad "block grants,”"which have greatly increased the authority and flexibility of governors.

headline: Traveling Man: Shuster covers a lot of ground
abstract: US Representative Bud Shuster (R-PA) has one of the largest districts in PA, covering parts of 10 counties, but spends more time traveling around Europe.

headline: Street Must Run As Independent, High Court Rules
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that state Senator Milton Street must run as an independent in the November general election.  Senator Street is trying to unseat U.S. Representative William Gray III.

headline: Federal Reserve official optimistic on area economy
abstract: According to Edward G. Boehne, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, the Harrisburg region is doing considerably better than the rest of the country. He also mentioned that the recession had "bottomed-out" but recovery was still no-where in sight. This will depend on the results of the budget deficit debate in the Congress.

headline: Educational needs; A dual responsibility
abstract: A Crawford County court decision last week concerning "educational malpractice" suit filed against a school district focuses on the issue of parental versus institutional roles. The concept of "in loco parents" (in the place of a parent) has always caused problems for those enforcing school regulations.

headline: Power Rationing: A Growing Social Dilemma
abstract: The Public Utility Commission is expected to rule on a request by Philadelphia Electric Company for permission to use a device that restricts the amount of electricity available to a household delinquent in paying its electric bill.  The number of delinquent utility customers is substantial and growing rapidly.

headline: Bradley Defends City Courts: Calls Criticism Undocumented
abstract: Edward J. Bradley, the president judge of Philadelphia’s Common Pleas Courts, dismissed criticisms of the local court system as "unsubstantiated evidence about alleged shortcomings" and said the courts were running better than ever.  He asserted during a news conference at City Hall that he had maintained control of the Common Pleas system here throughout the five months that Supreme Court Justice John P. Flaherty had been assigned as administrator pro tem with total authority over the local courts.  Flaherty resigned the administrator’s position.

headline: Boroughs Can Cash In on State Program
abstract: Small towns in the county have been alerted to the opportunity to obtain financial help from the state in establishing sites for industry.  The program offers funding for committees under a population of 50,000 for various improvement projects.  Among these is the acquisition of land for industrial parks.  Borough and township officials would well serve their constituents by looking into the program and taking advantage of it.  There is no guarantee that all applications will be successful.  While funds available total $42.6 million in the first year, $20 million of that amount was committed by the federal government before it transferred the program to the state government.  Nearly 2,000 towns across the state are eligible to apply even if only half of them do; competition for grants will be intense.

headline: State bonds for business growth in PA
abstract: PA industrial revenue bonds for business expansion are one of the principle components of economic development for the state.  But, the US Treasury realized that they are missing out on a chunk of tax revenue and are cutting back on all forms of these types of loans.  The Internal Revenue Service ruling is still on hold on this issue due to protests from PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and other state governors, but has already help up PA from starting a new $45 million bond pool.

headline: Governor probed in coal regulations
abstract: The State Attorney General's criminal law division is reviewing allegations that Governor Dick Thornburgh softened regulation of coal mining companies for campaign contributions.  However, two top directors of these divisions worked for Thornburgh while he was the US attorney in Pittsburgh between 1969 and 1975, and will be kept on the case.

headline: Tucker to Run for State Senate
abstract: C. DeLores Tucker, one of the more controversial figures in Philadelphia’s Democratic politics, yesterday took over the Consumer Party candidacy for the State Senate in Philadelphia’s 4th District.  She made it clear, however, that although she will be on the Consumer ballot she will be running as a Democrat and that if she wins she will sit with the Democratic caucus.  The state election code does not require her to change registration.  The Consumer Party is seeking to build its organization in Philadelphia.  Tucker was Commonwealth Secretary during the administration of former Governor Milton J. Shapp but failed to support the gubernational aspirations of former Lieutenant Governor Ernest P. Kline.

headline: Manderino: Repairs to roads cosmetic
abstract: House Minority Whip James Manderino claims that Governor Thornburgh's surface-treatment program was an electoral ploy designed to give the impression of a large road-improvement project.  The governor, Manderino alleges, wasted 180 million of taxpayer money.  A PA Department of Transportation officials says the surface-treatment program is a method used by highway engineers and contractors throughout the country for preventive maintenance.

headline: GOP hears diverse views of Reagan at state conclave
abstract: The recent Republican State Committee meeting drew differing views of federal economic policy. US Transport Secretary Drew Lewis endorsed the current practice of "Reaganomics". However, Sen. John Heinz did not think so as he believed the federal deficits proposed by the President are much bigger than required.

headline: Educators draw better teacher plans
abstract: The Coalition to Improve Teacher Education  has drawn up a list of recommendations aimed at upgrading teacher education in PA.  The report, while similar to one recently compiled by the Pennsylvania Department of Education (PDE), places more emphasis on local rather than statewide input into teacher training.

headline: Proposal by PE to Limit Delinquents' electric Use
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Co. (PE) is trying to have tiny electronic devices that automatically cut off power to delinquent households.  Some of the groups that are against it include the Action Alliance for Senior Citizens, the Tenant Action Group, the Consumers Education, and Protective Association.  They have contended that the device is merely an electronic tool designed to flout laws that prohibit “unsafe and unreasonable interruption of service.

headline: Bufalino asks hearing before Pa. crime panel
abstract: Reported crime boss Russell Bufalino is expected to testify before the PA Crime Commission in an attempt to clear himself from a contempt order. The order was issued by PA Commonwealth Court Judge David Craig for Bufalino's earlier failure to appear before the Commission. Bufalino, serving a 10 year sentence in federal prison for other crimes, was granted immunity from prosecution prior to the commission's request.

headline: Bring jobs to city, alliance urges council at hearing
abstract: City Council was urged to undertake a major effort to bring more jobs into the city. Legislation that would trade property tax exemption for new jobs has already been sponsored by Councilman Bill Robinson. The bill has not yet been out to vote, while the city solicitor's office tries to resolve questions about its legality.

headline: State Firms Told They Must Learn to Do Business with Government
abstract: Pennsylvania firms must learn how to do business with the government if they want to do their share of federal contracts.  A new federal-state pilot program aimed at increasing the percentage of federal purchases from small Pennsylvania companies was revealed at the conference of Small Business Operators.

headline: Governor Proclaims Friday POW-MIA Recognition Day
abstract: President Ronald Reagan proclaimed Friday July 9, 1982 as National Prisoner of War/ Missing in Action Day.  Governor Dick Thornburgh proclaimed the same thing in Pennsylvania.  Because there is belief that there are unaccounted for POWs in Southeast Asia, the day is set aside to honor these men that fought during the Vietnam War.

headline: Tuition at state colleges hiked; Board OKs $230 annual increase
abstract: The State College and University Directors voted to increase the tuition by 18% to $1480 a year. Board member felt that there was no choice in this decision and it will be implemented across all state colleges.

headline: GOP Accused of Fake-Photo Foul Play
abstract: State Representative John Showers has accused Republicans of dirty campaign tactics.  He alleges that the Republican State Committee doctored a photo showing Representative Showers standing with Representatives James Manderino and K. Leroy Irvis.  The photo was part of an attempt to link Showers, a Democratic representative in a Republican district, with big-city Democrats.  Showers says he never appeared at a function with Manderino and Irvis.

headline: GOP sends budget to Thornburgh; Fuming Democrats don skunk buttons
abstract: Despite opposition from the Democrats, state House Republicans have sent Gov. Thornburgh his new spending plan. This is the earliest budget approval in 20 years.

headline: Faculty pay measure 'untimely'
abstract: Despite the House approval for a $6.3 million cash infusion into the state college system, students will end up subsidizing the back pay for their professors. This is due to the fact that legislation to fund a retroactive faculty pay hike has failed several times in the last two or three years.

headline: Proposed Plan Would Cost UGI Customers $73 a Year
abstract: A proposed settlement submitted to a PA Public Utility Commission administrative law judge would boost the yearly average bills of UGI Corp. residential customers by $73.  If the plan is approved by the PUC, bills of average residential users would go from $671 annually to $744, instead of the $773 under the UGI request.

headline: Change the Law
abstract: D. Michael Fisher, State Senator,  is the primary sponsor of Senate Bill 171.  Under the provisions of the bill, juries would have the option of determining that a defendant was guilty but mentally ill.  The defendant would receive a prison sentence the same as anyone else who had committed the crime and if necessary would be hospitalized for treatment.  After the treatment he would be returned to prison to serve is sentence.

headline: City Tour Planned to Lobby for Port Aid Bill
abstract: Joseph O’Connor, a consultant who recently did a study on the port for Fumo, said the additional $5 million in state funds, if approved by the legislature and Governor Thornburgh would be used to continue the corporation’s international marketing efforts and to make further improvements in the port facilities.

headline: State gambling's a bad bet
abstract: A Philadelphia Democratic representative wants to introduce a bill that would legalize betting on football, baseball and other games. He states that the bill offers a legitimate way of doing something already being done. However, this is fallacious reasoning. The administration of this bill's requirements also would be overwhelming. Hence, introducing this bill would be a bad idea.

headline: Governor: Let me fill Pike Panel, or else
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has said that it will block major improvement projects along the PA Turnpike until two vacancies on  the Turnpike Commission are filled.  The current three-member panel has been slow.  PA Senate Democrats have refused to confirm Governor Thornburgh's appointments.

headline: Turning governors into mini-presidents
abstract: Under President Reagan's New Federalism the 50 governors will be almost as important as presidents. New arrangements will be made to signalize their new power. Steps like allowing each governor occupancy of the White House for one week every year have been taken in that direction. However, the author believes that there are dangers such as secret alliances that can occur after the transfer of so much power to the governors.

headline: Officials cleared in ethics ruling
abstract: The Ethics Commission ruled that Robert Audey--chair of the Johnstown Redevelopment Authority, did not violate the Ethics Act by being paid 3,000 dollars as a consultant to the authority.  The payments were deemed permissible because Audey is not considered a public official under the 1981 Ethics Act.

headline: GOP's raw power won on budget
abstract: Although six Democrats declared that Gov. Thornburgh's budget was a fraud and that they had all the Democrats backing them to vote against the budget. However, it turned out to be an empty threat and the GOP powered ahead with its budget.

headline: Faculty pay rise to come from college budgets
abstract: The State Department of Education is planning to take money from the general operating budgets of state-owned colleges and universities March 1 to being paying a court-ordered $6.3 million pay increase to faculty members, whether or not students pay a controversial $75 tuition increase.  The Department of Education will take 50% of what each institution owes its faculty in back pay from each one's operating budget in March, then the rest in April and June.

headline: Public Charged for TIM: PUC Approves Cleanup Deal
abstract: Pennsylvania electricity customers would for the first time be charged to help pay for the cleanup of the damaged Three Mile Island nuclear reactor under an arrangement approved by the PA Public Utility Commission.  The agreement will not directly affect rates now of Metropolitan Edison Co. and Pennsylvania Election Co. customers, two of the three utilities  that own TMI.  Instead, it calls for the utilities to make a bookkeeping shift to divert $21.7 million to cleanup from funds that would have been used to pay for the plant’s construction.  That bookkeeping shift is intended to convince Congress and the nuclear industry that TMI customers are paying some of the costs of cleaning up TIM, which has been estimated at $1 billion.  So far the federal government has committed only $68 million to the cleanup.

headline: Changes in Child Abuse Law Declared Valuable Tool
abstract: The passage of Senate Bill 348 amended the PA Child Abuse Act.  Among the new provisions is one that requires child welfare agencies to notify police of homicide, sexual abuse or exploitation, serious bodily injury to children.  Previously, the agencies were not permitted to notify police of abuse cases, although other persons, such as friends and relatives, could make the notifications.  Lebanon County child protective service workers predict that recent changes in the state’s child abuse law will be a valuable tool in forcing child abusers to receive the counseling they need.

headline: Commerce aide is in line to head city economic development agency
abstract: Joseph Egan Jr, Philadelphia's Deputy Director of Commerce, will be named January 6, 1982 by Mayor William Greene to head the city's major economic development agency, the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation (PIDC).

headline: State inaugurates 14% mortgage plan
abstract: Mortgage loans bearing below-market interest rates of 14.05% will now be available to first time buyers whose family income is under $35,000. The money for these mortgages has been collected through the sale of tax-free revenue bonds.

headline: Governor: Proclaim King Birthday US Holiday
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh asks US to make Martin Luther King's birthday a national holiday.  Several local governments already recognize the day, as well as the state of PA and 9 other states.

headline: TV Report on Philadelphia Mayor on ethics issue
abstract: The initial allegations that Mayor William J. Green was the target of a Federal investigation into kickbacks, have now been retracted by the local CBS affiliate, WCAU-TV. However, this has led to a dispute over journalistic ethics and hints of a libel suit.

headline: Dems Blast Reagan Here
abstract: At the annual Kennedy-Lawrence dinner, Democratic candidates Cyril Wecht and Allen Ertel criticized their respective Republican opponents, Senator John Heinz and Governor Dick Thornburgh, as well as the Reagan administration.

headline: Governor notes Surplus; Democrats say it Won't Last
abstract: The Democrats said that Governor Dick Thornburgh’s administration’s $13 billion budget for the 1982-83 fiscal year, which began on July 1, would lead to a crisis by December of 1983.  The 1982-83 budget failed to account for some $100 million in deficits which the administration rolled over from its 1981-82 spending plan.

headline: Failing grades for tuition increase
abstract: The recent $75 tuition hike at Pennsylvania state colleges comes at the wrong time.  Students have already been hit by years of consecutive increases, including $150 this previous year, for a total 32% increase over the past two years.  Pennsylvania now charges the highest tuition and fees among state colleges.  The Education Department, knowing that it may have to pay the extra money to faculty in back salaries, failed to plan for the cost.

headline: PUC Approves UGI, Met-Ed Rate Changes
abstract: Customers of Metropolitan Edison Co. will begin making a back-door contribution of $16.7 million annually to the Three Mile Island Unit 2 cleanup. The action is considered merely an interim measure until the undamaged Unit 1 reactor returns to service.

headline: Child protection law
abstract: The author describes a 1976 Pennsylvania legislature that declared child abuse to be a serious but treatable social problem. The author then states two cases that were, according to her, handled appropriately. However, in the Aleta Bailey's beating case on Jan. 12th, both Children's Services and the police were involved. Hence, the author wonders why the same, appropriate treatment not given in the Aleta Bailey case as well.

headline: Common Sense
abstract: James Stine, owner of the Dutch Haven Restaurant on East Bald Eagle Street has permission to keep his Pennsylvania Dutch “welcome” sign on the side of his building.  According to the city codes when the sign was first put up it was too big.  Sign codes have a purpose.  They can keep out an ugly sign that reflects poorly on a town’s image.  In the Dutch Haven case, however, the city’s actions are better described as "harassment" than "protection." The hexagonal sign is undeniably beautiful, and adds to the neighborhood.  The general intent of the sign ordinance says it is to "preserve" the wholesome and attractive character of the City of Lock Haven and to recognize that the general welfare includes a community plan that shall be beautiful as well as healthy, spacious as well as clean, and well balanced in its growth and development.  Rather than using a little common sense to work out an agreement, Stine had to get an attorney, pay $75 for a hearing and waste two hours he could have spent taking care of his business.   It is certainly no way to welcome a new member of the business community to a city that needs all the help it can get.

headline: State Senate oks bank bill
abstract: The PA Senate passed a bill that would lift branch restrictions on PA banks, and allow holding companies to purchase up to eight banks over eight years.  Currently, banks can only open branches in their home counties and those that border them.  Supporters believe that this will allow for better competition in the banking industry.

headline: Governors Back Away from Federalism Fight
abstract: The nation’s governors, backing away from confrontation with President Reagan agreed to un uneasy, facing truce with the White House on new federalism.  At the closing session of their annual summer meeting, the governors voted without dissent to draft their own federalism plan and then submit it to the president for his approval.  The clear threat behind the resolution was that if they can’t reach a compromise with the President, the governors will then take their plan to congress.

headline: Two Losers are Winners in Final Tally
abstract: A Computer mix-up left two candidates in the primary election in Philadelphia winners after having been declared losers.  The rest of the article talks more about the results from the primary election in May.

headline: State court rules Street can't run as Republican
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that state Senator T. Milton Street could not appear on the ballot as the Republican candidate in a race for a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives.  Senator Street is challenging U.S. Representative William H. Gray III.

headline: Grateful W. Germans Embarrassing Detroit U.S.
abstract: Many TV shows in West Germany motivated people in Western Germany to collect relief aid for Detroit. All this kindness has embarrassed and annoyed the U.S. Government and it has wounded the civic pride of Detroiters. Also, U.S. economic problems is key in Soviet propaganda efforts to persuade the world of Washington heartlessness in dealing with poverty and inevitable decline of capitalism.

headline: UC reform
abstract: This letter is a response a  letter written by Donald Patterson who criticized Gov. Thornburgh's proposal for reform of Pennsylvania Unemployment Compensation system because it did not address "pension-offsets provision". But, the Press Secretary of the PA Department of Labor and Industry is replying in his letter that Thornburgh did address that issue, and he is explaining how it was addressed.

headline: PE loan primed for vote
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Co. stands poised at a major turning point in its decade-long struggle to build the controversial Limerick 1 and 2 nuclear generating station in Western Montgomery County. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) is expected to decide whether to approve, modify or reject an ambitious plan to finance completion of the $5.8 billion project with the aid of a proposed $1.1 billion line credit form a consortium of 25 banks.

headline: Ex-Benedict aide cited as key figure in job-sale scheme
abstract: The statewide investigating grand jury named John Kerr, former executive deputy auditor general, as a key figure in a jobs-for-sale scheme that produced at least $200,000 in illegal payoffs over a periods of seven years. The article continues with a lot of details from the trial.

headline: State offers 4140,000 grant for Halifax- firm expansion
abstract: Dauphin County commissioners accepted a $140,000 state economic development grant to create 20 new jobs in Halifax Twp. The grant is for firms that manufacture plastic products for medical and electronic industries.

headline: Christopher Grabs GOP Reins
abstract: State Republican Vice Chairman David W. Christopher has declared himself acting chairman, setting up a confrontation with Chairman Martha Bell Schoeninger for possession pf the presiding gavel when the state committee meets June 18. The article continues with the description of the situation behind this confrontation.

headline: Thornburgh tight-lipped staff mirrors Reagan's media stance
abstract: Governor Thornburgh liked to have almost everything under control. That is especially true for his relationship with the media , because his administration has in each department one spoke person who is like a wall in front of the reporters. This protective attitude is very similar to the protective attitude of President Reagan in his relationship with the media.

headline: America's Union tradition faces a generation of doubt
abstract: As the American industrial economy crumbles the union tradition is following suit. Younger rank and file union members are questioning whether unions have outpriced themselves with high wage and benefit demands.Paul Bandish, president of Local 5134 of the United Mine Workers of America has seen his member drop from 3,400 to 90.

headline: Guv Faces Deadline On Budget
abstract: The state's budget drama neared a climax today, with Gov. Thornburgh facing a midnight deadline to act on a spending plan he has had on his desk for 10 days.  The article continues with the possible outcomes of the Governor's actions related to the budget.

headline: Unemployment
abstract: Recently WKBS Television dedicated a full week of Public Affairs programs to unemployment problem for all of its parts. TV representative said the t they found a major stumbling block in the unemployment problem and that is delay. Many who have paid taxes and helped charities during their working lives did that for services that they need now. So the advise is "do not avoid using them", although sometimes is hard to know where to go.

headline: PE Plans New Plea On Rates
abstract: Nine months after winning a $221.7 million rate increase, Philadelphia Electric Co. is preparing to ask the Public Utility Commission for another boost. Consumers and neighborhood organizations are already mobilizing to fight the request.

headline: Executions would Ease Budget Crisis
abstract: One small yet productive solution to help ease some of the budget crisis faces by PA and other states would be to execute all prisoners waiting Death Row. That is the way to save millions and to make a society more safe.

headline: State's Outside Legal Bill $272,589 - So Far
abstract: A $9 million lawsuit involving the Pittsburgh Convention Center has cost the state big money so far, and the cost is likely to go much higher. The state is suing contractors for what it contends was an inferior work and construction delays on the $37 million facility. The political controversy has arisen over hiring Philadelphia law firm to represent the Commonwealth (one of the most famous and most expenses attorneys). An attorney dismissed suggestions that he was hired because of his close political connections with Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Cianfrani asks for return of $30,232
abstract: A lawyer for former Senator Cianfrani told the Pennsylvania Supreme Court yesterday that the former Philadelphia legislator should not have been required to repay about $30,000 that he paid two "ghost" employees (employees who did little or no work) during his legislative career. Cianfrani was convicted of racketeering, mail fraud, obstruction of justice and income tax evasion.

headline: Thornburgh's Team Guards Environment
abstract: A letter is criticizing the editorial staff of the Pittsburgh Press for not mentioning all relevant facts about Thornburgh's choice for head of the state Department of Environmental Resources (DER). A writer claims that the current head of DER is more than qualified for that job since it had a significant experience in Carter and Reagan administration (while editorial staff only mentioned that he was once "public-relationship man"). Thus, writer of the letter claims, the Governor made an excellent choice.

headline: Who are to be electors of of federal representatives?
abstract: Total spending in federal elections has drastically increased over the years. And candidates who are not independently wealthy are obtaining more and more from political action committees. Anyone who thinks PAC give out of charity is wrong, they give only to get. The current election system needs reform.

headline: Heinz: Halt imports of steel for 5 years
abstract: Senator Heinz called for suspension for 5 years of steel imports in order to protest unemployed domestic workers. His proposal is supported by Senator Specter as well. Heinz thinks the federal foreign trade laws are unfair and he promises to launch an investigation into the effects of foreign steel purchases by American companies on the nation's unemployment rate.

headline: Union chiefs accept pact with AT&T
abstract: Leaders of three unions representing 675,000 striking American Telephone & Telegraph Co. workers voted yesterday to accept a tentative contract settlement that could return employees to their jobs later this week. The union leaders did not reveal the details but it is apparent that unions won employment security provisions that will set a pattern for workers in other industries.

headline: PE reported seeking $1 billion credit line for Limerick
abstract: In an apparent effort to obtain an alternative method for financing its controversial Limerick nuclear-generating facility, Philadelphia Electric Co. is negotiating a five-year $1 billion line of credit from consortium of 25 U.S. and foreign banks. Any agreement would require the approval of the Pennsylvania Utility Commission. It is still unclear for what purpose would money (if approved) be used.

headline: Ex-Fugitive Hanna Dies In Jail
abstract: Hanna, a key figure in Western Pennsylvania politics for two decades, died in jail under the shadow of corruption charges that turned his last year into a hide-and-seek game with authorities. He was pronounced dead from a heart attack and he was being held in lieu of $1 million bail, facing felony charges related to the sale of jobs and job promotions in the state auditor general's office.

headline: The Job Bidding Wars
abstract: An article talks about the recent race between Lancaster County and Westminster, Maryland for building a new cheese plant of Foods Co. Lancaster lost the bid, but local officials were more than generous in trying to attract the producer in Lancaster. At the end they lost, but the good this is that they had a sense to know when to stop with their offers.

headline: City advised to put lobbyist in Harrisburg
abstract: Two state representatives from Pittsburgh said yesterday that the city may be losing out on thousands of dollars annually because it does not have a full-time lobbyist in Harrisburg. They told they have called on Mayor of Pittsburgh a number of times to add a Harrisburg lobbyist to the city payroll or share the services of the lobbyist who now works for Allegheny County.

headline: Three will share $18 million pool
abstract: Although a record had been predicted, lottery officials said even they were surprised by the $18. 1 million jackpot in Friday's PA Lotto game. Holders of three winning tickets are expected to visit the lottery's office next week.

headline: Inmates break of hostage talks
abstract: The second day since two armed inmates, Richard henkel and Louis Coviello took hostages at a state prison, they have resumed talks with negotiators and have asked for nothing to end it. Negotiations are being handled by telephone.

headline: Help Promised
abstract: In his speech at a gathering of the newly formed Beaver Valley Conference for Economic Development, Gov. Thornburgh said that the state still has a goal of revitalizing the Pennsylvania 's traditional manufacturing industries. He discussed the steps his administration took in order to deal with this hard economic situation. He was also discussed the current negative trends in state traditional industries-high unemployment, for example.

headline: Union helps members find roads to success
abstract: An article starts with the story about the former hospital technician who became a doctor because union helped her financially. The article continues with a description of educational programs for workers that are sponsored by unions.

headline: Peach Bottom N-plant readies for annual accident alert
abstract: The 78 emergency warning sirens surrounding Peach Bottom Atomic Power Station will be sounded on Tuesday, and federal, state and local official will be placed on alert, just as they would be in the real nuclear accident. The alert will be part of the plant's second annual emergency exercise, which is required by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to test the ability of nuclear power plant operators to respond to a serious accident.

headline: Ex-justice: Larsen "Irrational" over Snub
abstract: Former Supreme Court Justice Kauffman told the state Judicial Inquiry and Review Board that fellow justice Larsen became "irrational" when he was not permitted to swear Kauffman in on the February 1980. The inquiry board cleared Larsen last week of 40 charges of misconduct. The board then voted to permanently withhold the 7,500 pages of testimony taken in 26 hearings. An article continues with a transcript of talk between Kauffman and board member.

headline: U.S. funds may create 600 jobs
abstract: The Caliguiri administration plans to apply for $7.1 million in additional federal funds that could spur as many as 600 temporary or permanent jobs for the local economy. Yesterday the Mayor released a "shopping list" of projects to be submitted to City Council for approval.

headline: Cleaning the record
abstract: The Philadelphia Inquirer incorrectly identified the fifth and sixth councilmanic districts in maps published few yesterday, and in this article Inquirer shows correct maps. The article also corrects the time and biographical information related to one candidate, since those were wrongly reported as well.

headline: Tinkering with political suicide
abstract: Gov. Thornburgh might have thought he had a gem with Hand Up, his idea for handing out the Lottery Fund profits to jobless people for mortgage refinancing loans. But he did not take into account the grip senior citizens have on lawmakers and what seems to be an iron-clad contract that reserves for the elderly the fruits of PA' lottery money. Senior citizens feel very strongly that lottery fund is their program and the money should be spent on their needs. The Governor thinks that some urgent situations (as high unemployment in this case) require spending in some other purposes.

headline: Standoff at Pa. Jail
abstract: Two armed inmates held a guard and prison employee hostage at Pennsylvania maximum security prison for a second day without making any demands.The hostages were reported as unhurt.

headline: Hidden tax on utility holdings
abstract: There is a hidden increase in the supplemental budget winding its way through the State Legislature that is going to raise the cost of electricity, natural gas and telephone service, which already are among fastest rising expenses being experienced by consumers, business and industry. The tax is based on a utility's real estate holdings and is passed on to consumers.

headline: USS Cuts Salaries By 5%
abstract: The US Steel Corporation has begun notifying about 28,000 employees that their paychecks will be cut 5 percent. The US Steel Chairman said that this is the result of depressed conditions in the industry. This is the second cut in the last 7 months.

headline: Pennsylvania's suspicious, shocked
abstract: Area residents, who already endured the 1970 Three Mile Island accident, generally found viewing TV movie "The Day After" a less than traumatic experience. The moves apparently deals with nuclear bombing issue, and it caused many reactions in the public.

headline: Ex-LCB agent to answer bribe charges before panel
abstract: A former Liquor Control Board agent Ford who refused this week to answer accusations that he accepted bribes will appear before a Senate committee. Law and Justice Chairman held ford in contempt after he ignored a subpoena requiring his appearance.

headline: USS closing 7 plants, ending 15,400 jobs
abstract: This article offers details about the plan and it anticipate impact of this decision. There are also some past statistics about closing plants. The pressing reason for this decision is the global economy trends and trials to stop losses.

headline: Cocktails at Dick's
abstract: Governor Thornburgh has scheduled a fundraising party at his mansion. The issue here is whether is proper to use executive mansion, or any other government building , for political fund-raising functions. The governor has set a bad precedent in more ways to come.

headline: To the 3 Candidates, It's All Business
abstract: Three candidates for Mayor of Philadelphia agreed that the business and economic development are most important issues. The article continues with their standings on this issue and with threir proposals to deal with the issue.

headline: Revenues Rise, Deficit Still Looms
abstract: Pennsylvania Revenue Secretary James Scheiner says despite an upturn in March revenue collections, the state's general fund deficit has grown to $133.7 million.

headline: House Leaders Draft Budget Compromise
abstract: The state budget crisis appears to be near the end, with an agreement from leaders of both parties. The House Speaker called the House back into session last night to restore more than half the $1.2 billion Gov. Thornburgh slashed from the budget. The  article further analyzes the new budget in detail (expenditures, cuts, new taxes, etc).

headline: USS seeks Johnstown contract freeze
abstract: The U.S Steel Corp. is again asking employees of its Johnstown Works for contract concessions beyond those the industry negotiated with the United Steel Workers of America. The Company claims it needs concessions in order to be competitive.

headline: Public Subsidy For TMI Opposed
abstract: The letter criticizes the management in Three Mile Island (TMI) for not being candid with people and that can only be a an indication that they have a desire for money or power. The main point here is that the wasting of money in the TMI should not be offfset by public money.

headline: Fatalities are down Down Under in 8 months of random breath tests
abstract: This story from Australia says that legions of police have been on the roads in last 8 months making random checks for drunken drivers. Statistics shows a decline in automobile fatalities ever since. The article reveals more details about this phenomena.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon carrys an ironical message about the cutbacks in U.S. Steel Corporation.

headline: Coleman, Green square off
abstract: City Council President Joseph E. Coleman contended yesterday that mayor Green was spreading "malicious and false accusation" about him and invited him to appear before the council to defend those statements. Green said he has no statements to defend before the council. The article continues with the description of cable TV issues in Philadelphia that were major reason for the dispute between them.

headline: Top court upholds 1982 redistricting
abstract: The Supreme Court yesterday upheld Pennsylvania's 1982 congressional redistricting plan without comment and without a full hearing of the case. The Westmoreland County Board of Commissioners had appealed the plan, which divided the county among three district.

headline: Judge refuses to halt dairy assessment
abstract: U.S. Middle District Court Judge William Caldwell refused to halt a deduction of 50 cents per 100 pounds of milk products sold. Pennsylvania Farmers Union and five farmers filed suit asking that the deduction not be allowed to take effect.

headline: House Sets A Vote on Budget Cuts
abstract: The House plans to vote today on a $600-million spending bill to restore about half the budget cuts made by Gov. Thornburgh. But it may wait for Senate action on the cuts before it considers a tax hike bill of more than $450 million.

headline: Violence escalates in truckers' strike
abstract: Violence attributed to the independent truckers escalated today with a report of a fatality, more windshields smashed and more shots fired. Acts of sabotage are reported in 16 states and the truckers' protest is in its second day and is directed against higher fuel taxes, highway user fees and excise taxes. The strike is opposed by the majority of the major regulated freight companies, represented by the American Trucking Association, and has not been supported by the Teamsters Union.

headline: PUC "failurism" deplored
abstract: State Public Utility Commissioner says consumers are frustrated and feel that protesting soaring utility rates is "an exercise in futility". Ratepayers were absent from hearing on UGI Corp.'s boost but the commissioner said he is not assuming people do not care because they did not attend the hearing. He said he received a lot of letters from customers.

headline: Firefighters fall under scrutiny as accused arsonists
abstract: In Dickson City, PA, eight volunteer firefighters and eight young firefighters were charged with starting 59 fires largely because of the thrill of fighting them. The fire department called an emergency meeting to suspend charged firefighters because they hurt the credibility of image of all the good firefighters. But it seems the phenomenon is the problem nationwide and most of the arsonists are either volunteers or young firefighters.

headline: A lopsided compromise
abstract: Members of the General Assembly should adamantly resist legislation proposed last week as a compromise among the factions warring over repeal of PA's current auto insurance system. The article argues against the new proposal as it blames Association of Trial Lawyers for this and gives reasons for that stance.

headline: Colville scored for stand on judge merit selection
abstract: District attorney Colville has been accused by his Republican opponent of a conflict of interest in testimony last week against the merit selection of judges. He ran for the state Supreme Court two years ago but he lost the election.

headline: Truce Ends State GOP Leadership Fight
abstract: A compromise over the leadership of the Republican Party in PA appears to have headed off an awkward confrontation when the GOP State Committee convenes tomorrow near Harrisburg. A truce between Martha Bell Schoeninger and state vice chairman Dave Christopher of Allegheny County was reached yesterday following a series of frenetic phone calls and conferences. Under the compromise, Montgomery County chairman Bob Asher will become state chairman, and Christopher will continue as vice chairman.

headline: Black Dems: Smith's win was racial
abstract: Philadelphia's Democratic Ward leaders voted 37-28 to select former U.S. Representative Joseph Smith over Edgar Campbell as the new party chairman. The vote was seen as a victory for mayoral candidate Frank Rizzo, but dashed the hopes of Black ward leaders that and supporters of mayoral candidate Wilson Goode. Several Black ward leaders charge that Smith won over Campbell soley because of his race.

headline: In anger and fear, jobless are uniting
abstract: From the auto sprawl of Michigan to the coal fields of Appalachia to the steel towns of Western Pennsylvania, hundreds of thousands blue-collar workers whose jobs were lost in the recession are about to run out of unemployment checks. Across the industrial heartland there is a fear and desperation, which have given birth to organizations that harbor an incipient militancy long foreign to blue-collar America. Many of them are going on welfare rolls and the article continues with the description of the new situation for them.

headline: Waiting for the ax to fall at VW
abstract: Volkswagen of America, which employs 4,400 workers at plant near New Stanton, said the lay-offs were the result of declining car sales. The lay-offs will be based on seniority and the proposed lay-offs are a major blow to the economy of the four-county Pittsburgh area.

headline: PUC friends
abstract: It is becoming apparent that the Gov. Thornburgh intends to apply the slogan "You have got a friend in Pennsylvania" to utility companies in this state. This is evidenced by the manner in which he has handled recent vacancies in the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Firefighter's Widow Appealing Decision Denying State Benefits
abstract: The widow of Perry County volunteer fireman has appealed a state Department of General Services decision denying her financial benefits entitled to survivors of firefighters killed in the line of duty. The victim died from heart attack but state officials say the heart attack and firefighting activity were unrelated.

headline: null
abstract: Paul Brown, WQLN's station support manager, says the advertising experiment has been lackluster in Erie. The station generated only $600 in ad revenue through December. He says the things should pick up with two major accounts but he acknowledges the amount of money wont be significant.

headline: Committee won't back candidate
abstract: After months of maneuvering, the deeply divided Democratic City Committee has decided not to endorse a mayoral candidate in the May 17 primary election, and not to endorse any candidate running for any local office. The reason is the City Committee's financial predicament (they have no money and without money they are powerless). Both candidates (Rizzo and Goode) did not decide yet whether they will have a slate.

headline: Two Pennsylvanians deserve recognition
abstract: An opinion talks about Frank Carluci and Drew Lewis - people from PA who were highly distinguished officials in Federal Government. They decided to continue career in private industry. An opinion concludes saying that they deserve special recognition.

headline: Black Vote, A.W.: Facts and Fantasies
abstract: America's Blacks finally have a national reason to strut. The National Urban League President John Jacob says that any national candidate that ignores the black vote does so at his peril. But, Blacks are not johny-come latelys. They've been instrumental in elections for years.

headline: Interest Withholding Should Be Withheld
abstract: An editorial agrees with the Congressman Walker's opposition of the Federal Government withholding 10% of all of people interests income. The Federal Government feels it is losing money, but the editorial lists several negative effects that this Federal Government's actions will cause.

headline: Welder tells of payoffs at Three Mile Island
abstract: Nine veteran welders told the Senate Labor Committee that many of the nation's welders had bought their way into jobs, including those at nuclear power plants, by paying off officials of the boilermakers union. They said unqualified welders had paid union officials as much as $1,000 for union memberships that routinely cost about $2,000.

headline: PUC haring attracts 60 opposed to UGI rate boost
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission held a hearing Tuesday night that differed from a session last month: Somebody attended. About 60 consumers showed up at the PUC hearing room in the North Office Building, and about a third of them took the stand to oppose the a rate increase request from the UGI Corp. that would boost residential natural gas rates by 16 percent.

headline: For Pa. state police, bias case adds a layer of tarnish
abstract: US District Judge in a favor of black lieutenant's contention that he was being harassed by a groundless, rationally motivated criminal prosecution and court - martial. This was the last case in a row of seven racial motivated discrimination cases that PA police lost. And once more, the entire department's reputation suffered once more, since from the very beginning of department things were not much different.

headline: "Dry" municipalities show slight net gain in state
abstract: A slight net gain of "dry" Pennsylvania municipalities was the result of local option elections held by 28 small communities in the May primary, according to the Liquor Control Board.  The article provides statistics related to the number of municipalities that took an action regarding liquor licenses, and other actions.

headline: Commonwealth Judicial Seats Are Sought by 5
abstract: Five diverse candidates are contenders in the Nov. 8 general election for three seats on Commonwealth Court, Pennsylvania Court, PA's most visible but perhaps least controversial statewide appellate panel. An article continues with the detail description of each candidate.

headline: U.S. representative from Penna. list personal finances
abstract: An article is a list of all U.S. representatives from PA and their personal finances (income, speaking fees, outside income, holdings, investment incomes and liabilities).

headline: Cameras, Recorders Ruled out by LCB
abstract: The Liquor Control Board members voted on a new policy to ban its members and news reporters from covering their meetings are using cameras or tape recorders.

headline: Job-Creation Plans: They're Costly Failures
abstract: Job creating bills should be looked at with caution since many of the bills in the past were expensive and did not get expected results. That message, however, is lost in the stampede to enact job bills, even though some law makers admit that the effort may be more symbolic than substantive. Many studies show that the previous projects were more expensive and slower at creating jobs than expected.

headline: Work Sharing May Aid Jobless
abstract: A plan to spread a burden on unemployment got a lukewarm endorsement yesterday from the PA MILRITE Council (state created group of business). Legislation is an alternative to full-time lay-offs (when faced with lay-offs, employers using work sharing would cut the work week equally for all affected employees, instead of laying off a few). Although some study concluded work sharing was slightly more expensive overall than full time lay-offs, proponents say that there is not enough track record to prove whether the work sharing would be uneconomical.

headline: PUC orders heat restored to disconnected
abstract: The Public Utility Commission today ordered utilities to restore heating service to disconnected customers who are able to pay either $200 or one third of the amount of overdue bills. Although the order only applies to the current heating season the PUC would study the problem further to come up the more comprehensive policy.

headline: Four Graterford guards will not face 2nd trial
abstract: Four Graterford prison guards accused on beating an inmate in the prison's restricted housing area in 1979 will not have to face a second trial, the Superior Court ruled. That means in fact the charges against them were dropped. Superior Court ruled that the mistrial was not required and that retrying the guards would constitute double jeopardy and that is being tried more than once for the same offense.

headline: 13.6% boost favored for Advocate's Office
abstract: House and Senate conferees struck a compromise today that would increase funding for the Consumer Advocate's Office 13.6 percent in the fiscal year starting July 1. The measure goes to House and Senate for approval. The measure allows the consumer advocate to intervene in cases at the federal level instead of only before state agencies.

headline: Commonwealth or Superior Court seats are goal of 13 candidates
abstract: An article lists detail description of all 13 candidates for the courts.

headline: Unemployed Bucks man wins $2.5 million in lottery
abstract: A Bucks County man who has been out of work for more than a year and who had lived part of that time on unemployment compensation has won $2.5 million in the state lottery. The article continues with some information about him and his win of the lottery.

headline: Pen quiet as standoff continues
abstract: The standoff between two hostage-taking convicts, Richard Henkel and Louis Coviello, and Western Penitentiary officials continued into its second day.

headline: Joblessness falls sharply, but too little for some
abstract: The nation's civilian unemployment rate plummeted from 10 percent to 9.5 in July, its sharpest one-month drop since 1959. The report surprised even the rosiest economic forecasts. While unemployment in PA remained significantly less than national rate, the unemployment of blacks is even worse - 19.5%.

headline: "Incompetence" is laid to McKeesport schools
abstract: The McKeesport Area School District is headed toward the state takeover unless school officials mend their ways, state Auditor General said. He found gross incompetence in the district related to the security, financial shape, settlement payment and many other things. There is also evidence about many thefts in the district.

headline: PUC Says It Will Retain Gas Cost Rates
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission said it will retain gas cost rates. But two members of the commission urged guidelines the utilities must follow when purchasing fuel. Gas cost rates account for about 80% of ratepayer's bill.

headline: Fullam's fair, firm sentences
abstract: Five former Philadelphia policemen were sentenced to federal jail for conspirating to extort money to protect prostitution, gambling and illegal liquor sales, and the federal prosecutor said the investigation of police corruption would continue. U.S. district judge Fullam said the evidence produced at the trial was just the tip of the iceberg.

headline: 2 bills ask repeal of Pa. no-fault law
abstract: Two bills calling for the repeal of Pennsylvania's no-fault auto insurance law were introduced in the PA Senate and are scheduled for consideration by the Senate baking and Insurance Committee. By repealing the current law the legislature could not continue to put off making  decision on reforming the current system.

headline: Complain to Harrisburg
abstract: A letter writer is criticizing a new state inspection system and is explaining few fallacies. He further urges general public to "do all complaining to Harrisburg on this one".

headline: Vacancy draws Democrats
abstract: No Democratic candidates are emerged as possible contenders to become the party's nominee against Republican incumbent for attorney general in Pennsylvania, and that race will take a place next year. The article continues with an analysis of possible candidates who could enter that race.

headline: Cons Denied Food During Talk Break
abstract: The Western Penitentiary negotiators awaited an agreed upon resumption of talks with two inmates, Richard Henkel and Louis Coviello, holding hostage a guard and prison employee. The negotiators are adamant against providing food or any other items that could prolong the hostage situation.

headline: Lawmakers Pushing Budget
abstract: Legislative leaders today continued their behind-the-scene attempts to fashion a state budget and get it passed by midnight Thursday. Amidst negotiations and legislative jockeying,  Pennsylvanians could face a record tax hike of almost $1 billion. Democrat and Republican leaders said, however, that there is still wide disagreement over how much new revenue is needed.

headline: "State, nation can run schools"
abstract: Veteran educator Magill thinks that state and federal governments should retain control of education and not give local boards any more power. He thinks that many local boards' members are not qualified enough and they are governed by self-interest. He urged for tougher academic standards for students, proposed individual education plan for each student and new way of financing education. He criticized President Reagan's proposal to return control of education to the states as well as local boards.

headline: PUC to Appeal Limerick Case
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission (PUC) voted unanimously yesterday to seek state Supreme Court review of whether it can halt construction of a second reactor at the Limerick nuclear plant in Montgomery County. An issue in the case is whether the PUC has the authority to indirectly control utilities' long range construction plans by indication ahead of time it will deny use of ratepayers' funds or borrowing to complete a project.

headline: Gave Up Nothing, Pen Officials Say
abstract: After 5 and half day hostage siege which the Superintendent said gained them nothing , two Western Penitentiary inmates were in federal custody today while prison officials were facing accusations of laxity for failing to prevent the hostage-taking despite advance warning. The two men held hostage were released yesterday unharmed, but emotionally drained. The article continues with detail description of an incident.

headline: 2 Hit Plan to Seize Bank Funds
abstract: Two Democrats charged yesterday the Thornburgh's administration is being deliberately vague in implementing a new law that allows the state to seize bank accounts that are inactive for seven years. Two Democrats said that the administration is failing to notify adequately about accounts it intends to confiscate.

headline: Confusion at the polls: Where are the reforms?
abstract: Little known candidate Lomento, during Philadelphia mayoral primary in Democratic Party received surprisingly large number of votes and that raised an issue about the clarity of ballot design and voting procedures. The article continues with shortcomings of electoral process and unclearness of ballot design and suggest that the reform should be made.

headline: variety of Bills Considered in Capitol
abstract: The status of major bills pending in the state legislature is listed in the article (for example, Work Sharing bill, Mortgages bill, Auto Emissions, etc). The article depicts each bill in few sentences.

headline: Layoffs Turn White-Collars Blue
abstract: Unemployment has become a new experience for thousands of white collar workers in the Pittsburgh area. Learning to cope with unemployment has become difficult for professional workers, technical and corporate managers. The article continues with a detailed analysis of the jobless problem that impacts not only blue but also white-collar workers.

headline: 1. US, state unit agree to cooperate on education-bias investigations  2. Teachers reject offer of amnesty
abstract: First: In "landmark agreement" the US Department of Education and Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission said that they would share investigative and enforcement action on civil-rights complaints in education. By reducing duplicative procedures, the agreement will save taxpayers money. Second: Teachers in PA longest public schools strike returned to the picket line after rejecting the school board's latest proposal for amnesty. The strikers said they feared that they still could have been punished after returning to work.

headline: Radiation Slows TMI Cleanup
abstract: With Congress poised to investigate alleged safety violations in the Three Mile Island cleanup, a federal report says the project is lagging due to recurring contamination and unanticipated levels of radiation. Three engineers involved in the cleaning have accused GPU of violating NRC regulations, and engineers are scheduled to testify today at congressional hearing whose chairman is Morris Udall.

headline: Intimidation by youths
abstract: The recent problem in Youngstown is the large number of youth that congregate at one area grocery story. The problem is more of social nature than of the criminal nature.
