abstract: The photograph depicts how PA first lady congratulates two new distinguished daughters of PA named by Governor Thornburgh at a luncheon.

headline: State May Gain 2 Billion From Gas
abstract: Pennsylvania will gain a total of 2.136 billion dollars in Highway funds over the next four years as a result of the new federal 5-cent gasoline tax increase; the new tax law goes into effect on Friday.

headline: Wage increase adds to tax burden
abstract: If PA's budget for state government in the fiscal year beginning July 1 were already established, it would now have to be changed. By agreeing last week to wage increases for 62,000 state workers, the Thornburgh administration has committed itself to additional payroll costs that must be extracted from taxpayers.

headline: Panel approves $2.7 billion for health care for jobless
abstract: A House committee yesterday recommended approval of a $2.7 billion package of health benefits for the unemployed and this was the first specific proposal of several considered by the House and Senate to move out of the committee. The proposal was supported by the bipartisan body of politicians.

headline: Hunting bill splits outdoors lobby
abstract: The outdoor community, although composed of varied groups, usually shares common goals, among which are clean air, clean water, etc. But sometimes the issue is not so clear and in  this case is easily to drive a wedge between preservationists and the user advocates, including those who hunt and fish. The case is the Alaska National Hunting Bill, which is proposed in the House and it produced a lot of debate among sportsmen, conservationists and developers.

headline: Span opens, Duquesne together again
abstract: The City of Duquesne celebrates the reopening of the Thompson Run Bridge that was closed more than a year. Governor Thornburgh reopened the bridge saying that the old bridge was a symbol of the deteriorated state of the nation's bridges, but the new one is a different, better symbol.

headline: Truck strike violence is no way to bargain
abstract: The independent truckers who have murdered, wounded, maimed and plundered as part of their strike have forfeited any claims for support in their protests against increased taxes and costs. As a result of their strike the normal flow of food and other supplies have decreased noticeably in the last week. Murdering, shooting, wounding and maiming in almost half of the nation are nothing more than anarchy. Governor Thornburgh has promised "every step possible to stop the violence".

headline: Hertel Amendment can Benefit Area
abstract: The author supports an amendment of representative Hertel, that would continue preferential treatment for labor surplus areas in the award of defense contracts. An amendment would establish a program for the purchase up to $3.3 billion worth of nonstrategic goods and services from business in parts of the nation with a high rate of joblessness.

headline: No Word on 2nd Term
abstract: President Reagan further delayed his decision on seeking the second term by declining, when pressed by aides this week, to agree to file an official declaration of candidacy when a reelection committee is formed for him on Oct.17, Republican sources said.

headline: Funds Sharing Would Help Governor Says
abstract: While testifying before a U.S. House sub-committee, Governor Dick Thornbugh said that a federal revenue-sharing program for state and local governments would help solve some of Pennsylvania's fiscal problems.

headline: Wage tax, cuts in unemployment benefits become law
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed into law a measure that creates a statewide wage tax. A wage tax will increase taxes on employers and reduce benefits for the unemployed. The sweeping changes are designed to rescue the state's deficit ridden fund for jobless Pennsylvanians. Those changes are expected to cost Pennsylvania employers about $1.4 billion over the next three years.

headline: Prescription Aid to Aged Is Approved
abstract: The Legislature approved and sent the Governor a bill that would create a co-pay prescription program for an estimated 700,000 eligible senior citizens. Under the bill, people age 65 and over would pay $4 for each prescription, with surplus state lottery funds picking up the rest.

headline: Joint panel OKs bill on emissions
abstract: A House-Senate conference committee yesterday reached unanimous agreement on an auto-emissions-inspection bill, apparently bringing to an end a long and bitter legislative battle. The agreement was approved by 6-0 vote after negotiations between Gov. Thornburgh and legislative leaders. The authorization for the inspection program would include a $24 million provision to reimburse some motorists for costs related to the emissions inspections over a two-year period.

headline: State Awarded Grant to Defray Cost of 200 Buses
abstract: PA has been awarded a $279 million federal grant to help buy 200 buses. The money will go to the state 's bus pool program, in which 16 local transit authorities are trying to save money by buying buses together.

headline: Two Conspiracies Alleged On State Road Contracts
abstract: In first indictment federal grand jury charged Hammaker Emulsions Inc. with one count of conspiracy and two counts of mail fraud in scheme that transpired from 1977 to 1982. in the second Windsor service Inc. of Reading and its vice president were accused of conspiring from 1974 to 1982 to violate antitrust laws in the state's engineering District 3.

headline: Hope is dashed with news from Beirut
abstract: The article talks about the families of Marines who were killed in the Beirut blast in Lebanon few days ago. The emphasis is on their feelings and dealing with the hard situation they are passing through.

headline: Northeast Wasn't the Key
abstract: W. Wilson Goode (a black candidate) scored a significant breakthrough among white voters in Northeast Philadelphia, but the balloting in that region did not determine the outcome of the primary election, as many experts had predicted it would. An article continues with detailed analysis of election results in certain regions of Philadelphia.

headline: Bell's rate plan rings in new era
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania asked the state Public Utility Commission to approve a 378.9 million dollar rate increase yesterday.  The proposed increase would mean that the average residential bill would increase by 25 percent.

headline: Waiting for Thornburgh, legislators are raring to go
abstract: Waiting for Gov. Thornburgh's budget has been given a lot of legislators an itch to do something on their own. The state's economy, particularly its 12.9 percent unemployment rate, has made legislators eager to try out new ideas. So far, Democrats have taken much of the initiative.

headline: Rights of the retarded
abstract: PA has come a long way in a dozen years or so to reshape its care for mentally retarded citizens - a problem that once was met by locking up the most severe victims in jail like institutions. How to strike a balance between placing the retarded in even the most humane institutions and in community living centers remains a vexing problem. There is also a controversial institutions Pennhurst that is now before the US Supreme Court and that case is also related to this issue.

headline: Kean to propose acid-rain fund at meeting of Northeast governors
abstract: Kean, the Governor of New Jersey, said he will propose at the coming meeting the fund of $35 billion to attack acid rain at its source - companies that pollute. The idea is that those companies should be taxed. An article talks about the formation of acid rain and the damage that it causes.

headline: State Cuts Back on Xway Project
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation plans to resurface, instead of rebuilding, the portion of the Schuylkill Expressway from Belmont Avenue to the Pennsylvania Turnpike during a $130 million project. PennDOT decided to resurface rather than rebuild the section of highway because of the success of a similar project on the other location.

headline: Uneasy presence
abstract: Female corrections officer are working in the cell blocks at the state prison in Grateford. Unlike the inmate shower who had come up with its own solution, more than a dozen states are finding that the answers to what became a thorny issue are not quite so simple. While inmate privacy is the most commonly cited reason for the restriction, some prison wardens say privately that posting officers of the opposite sex in cell blocks could lead to emotional entanglements between guards and inmates, and some fear guards could be more easily manipulated by an inmate of the opposite sex.

headline: Let Military Take Welfare Recipients
abstract: The writer of this letter supports Los Angeles proposal for dealing with welfare - sending applicants and recipients to a military recruiter. He argues that military tour would mature many able-bodied recipients very quickly.

headline: O'Bannon is dismissed at Welfare
abstract: Helen O'Bannon, one of two women in Gov. Thornburgh's cabinet, said yesterday that she had been fired as a secretary of public welfare. O'Bannon quoted Thornburgh as saying that he wanted a "new direction" and that it was time for "new people". O'Bannon reportedly angered Thornburgh by complaining month ago that cabinet members had been given no indication of their status in the second term.

headline: Sally can't add
abstract: Dr. David P. Gardner is chairperson of President Reagan's National Commission on Excellence in Education.  The Commission was given the task of formulating a response to what is seen as the continuing decline of the American educational system.  The commission is expected to report recommendations in the Spring; the recommendations will focus on five areas: time devoted to education, expectations of parents and schools, problems of the teaching profession, content of American schooling, and the role of government, community and parents in American schools.

headline: Welfare checks pile up in state
abstract: The Legislature reconvened on the fifth day of the new fiscal year with no evidence of progress toward a solution to the state's budget deadlock. As the lawmakers returned, approximately 52,000 welfare checks had already been held up by the expiration of the state's legal authority to spend money.

headline: Schweiker resigns Cabinet
abstract: Pennsylvanian Richard Schweiker resigns Health and Human Services Secretary. He quit to become president of the American Council of Life Insurance. Margaret M. Heckler, defeated for re-election after eight terms in Congress,  to become the new Secretary.

headline: Lawmakers Buckle Down On Car Bill
abstract: Legislative leaders of both parties, seeking the last-ditch compromise on auto emissions tests that has eluded them for weeks, prepared to square off in a conference committee. Until the Legislature implements the program , a federal judge is withholding the $419 million in federal highway funds for the state.

headline: State Senate Approves Auto Lemon-Aid Bill
abstract: A bill that would require automakers to give refunds or replacements to buyers of vehicles that turn out to be lemons approved unanimously by the state Senate. The bill was sent to the House that has passed the similar bill.

headline: Victims
abstract: An audit by a combined state House and Senate committee says the state's crime victims compensation program doesn't work too well. An article continues with the details about the program such as the application for the program, awareness of the victims for the program, money available of the program, etc. Finally, there are some recommendations for the program.

headline: Luck Was With Lower Paxton Marine Who Had to Sleep in a Tent in Beirut
abstract: A Lower Paxton Township Marine stationed in Beirut, Lebanon, wrote home earlier this fall that he had to sleep in a tent while some of the "luckier" Marines got to sleep in a building. But sleeping in a tent may have saved his life. He was unhurt in the Sunday's terrorist bombing of a Marine command post in Beirut that killed more than 200 U.S. service man and wounded many others.

headline: O'Connor to ask party certification as a Senate candidate
abstract: Joe O'Connor, Democrat, announced that he will ask Party to certify him  as a candidate, since there are not other candidates so far. There is a list of people who support him and possible opposing Republican candidates. Joe also explains his motives for this action.

headline: Crime-watch effort boosted by troopers
abstract: Pennsylvania State Police Commisioner Daniel F. Dunn announced the start of a statewide crime-prevention effort.  The prevention program will connect Neighborhood Crime-Watch programs with local state-police barracks, where officers will be trained and prepared to assist communities in organizing local crime-watch programs.

headline: What's rarer than a day in June? Action in July
abstract: An article depicts the unemployment issue in symbolical and ironical manner. It also  criticizes in the same manner government proposals to deal with this issue.

headline: Schweiler quits Cabinet job
abstract: Schweiker, Secretary of Health and Human Services, resigned and President Reagan accepted his quit. He is returning his business interests that had made him a millionaire.

headline: Leaving Centralia
abstract: Homeowners in Centralia voted on referendum 345-200 to leave the city that have been struggling for 21 years with underground fires from an abandoned mine. The Governor Thornburgh asked for a federal legislation that would sponsor the buy-out of he houses. An article continues with the story about this city and its problem with underground fires.

headline: State Senate approves gas-tax increase
abstract: The state Senate has passed and sent to the House a $513 million gasoline-tax increase package designed to restore the state Department of Transportation spending. Also approved was a companion bill to reauthorize the $141 million in PennDOT' budget cut because of expected lack of funds.

headline: Warden urges increased staff at Carlisle prison
abstract: The Cumberland County Prison warden is urging that prison staff be increased starting early next year in expectation of completion of the county's new prison and to improve security at the old facility. But the County Commission Chairman disagrees, saying such a move would be costly considering that the new prison probably will not be ready for the occupancy until 1985. The warden thinks there is a risk for the potential incidents in the prison.

headline: Mercy mission or media play?
abstract: There was an effort of Democratic presidental candidate to save the U.S. Navy aviator in captivity in Syria. President Reagan and some other are questioning whether this move is mercy act or the act of self promoting because of elections.

headline: Ohio woman wins Pa. Lotto
abstract: A housewife from Youngstown, Ohio, today claimed the $3 million Lotto jackpot from Friday's drawing. The winner is Ursula Schuller and she will receive 21 annual payments of $114,298.75.

headline: BALANCING THE GOLDEN EGG
abstract: Six states have lotto games and they are all doing well.  These games present a challenge to state lottery directors, as they require one to find the proper mix of payout sizes, frequencies and odds for big and small prize winnings.  Given the success of lotto games, Lottery directors are often eager to meet this challenge, however.

headline: Secretary Schweiker Leaves
abstract: Richard S. Schweiker has resigned from Department of Health and Human Services to join the life insurance industry. He is ending the long political career and will be succeeded by Margaret M. Heckler, an energetic and capable lawyer with 16 years of experience in Congress.

headline: Lube Tech Vows to Be Careful
abstract: Admitting that the public was not informed of equipment testing "as adequately as we should have" a Lube Tech Inc. spokesman pledged to air operation plans near here more fully as preparations are made to put the used motor oil reclamation facility on line next week. The plant's leakage about three weeks ago had some area residents upset about the potential for a smelly, and perhaps dangerous, neighbor in the Lube Tech plant.

headline: State to Issue Drivers "Friendly" Auto Plates
abstract: New license plates that say "You've Got a Friend in Pennsylvania" soon will be available to PA motorists, Governor said.

headline: Warning To Gangs: Back Off
abstract: City Officials and community leaders gathered yesterday on the front porch of a Southwest Philadelphia rowhouse that was firebombed early last month to deliver a stern warning to neighborhood youths whose violent acts have created a reign of terror on the community. The message was clear: the acts of violence will result in the future in the severe punishments. No one was hurt in the firebombing.

headline: National guardsman injured on duty sues state seeking workmen's comp
abstract: Commonwealth Court is deciding whether the National Guardsman called to active federal training duty by the Governor belongs exclusively to Federal rules or also to the state rules. He was injured in the duty recently and ever since has been seeking for the compensation for the four months he was unable to work.

headline: One has won Tuesday Lotto
abstract: One person correctly picked all six winning numbers in Tuesday night's PA Lotto drawing and will receive $1,372,161.45, the state lottery bureau said today. The winner will receive 11 annual payments of $124,741.95 less 20% of federal income tax.

headline: State's lobbying law is disgraceful sham
abstract: Although lobbying plays an integral and sometimes salutary role in the democratic process, we believe that lobbying activities should be part of the public record and open.  Currently, Pennsylvanians are not privy to vital information, such as how much money lobbying firms spend to influence state policy.  Lawmakers need to act swiftly to pass a law that effectively governs, and makes transparent, lobbying activities.

headline: Some Highlights of the Plan
abstract: An article lists the highlights of the plan approved by the Legislature to provide limited pharmaceutical assistance for PA's low-income elderly people. It discusses eligibility, funds for the program, etc.

headline: Mine Fire Affects About 140 Acres
abstract: The Federal Office of Surface Mining said yesterday that exploratory drilling at Centralia shows the mine fire affects about 140 acres, with two main areas of  isolated temperatures. The mining agency is expected to release the second report that suggests alternative plans for controlling or extinguishing the fire.

headline: States should decide legal drinking age
abstract: Legislation that would set a national drinking age of 21 in an effort to reduce drunken driving fatalities might produce the desired results. But the author of the article argues that setting of a drinking age should remain in the state power (as is now) and the reason is that each state has drinking statistics on which can base its decision.

headline: Widow of firefighter fighting to gain benefits
abstract: The widow of Perry County volunteer fireman has appealed a state Department of General Services decision denying her financial benefits entitled to survivors of firefighters killed in the line of duty. The victim died from a heart attack but state officials say the heart attack and firefighting activity were unrelated.

headline: State Court Rules Guardsman-Case Aid Entitlement
abstract: A man who was injured in National Guard military training mission is entitled to state compensation although he already received federal benefits, Commonwealth Court has ruled. He injured his back in August 1975 while unloading a truck during military exercise,

headline: One Issue's a Challenge; Ads Are Another
abstract: Last week's mayoral campaign began and ended with a discussion of issues. What changed during the course of the week was what was considered an "issues". Housing, jobs, crime and education may have been big hits on few days. But some other issues came across in some other days (public opinion pulls, negative advertising  and money from an Arab businessman).

headline: Critics Blast Broadening Of Sales Tax
abstract: Twelve people testified before the state House Finance Committee and addressed Governor Dick Thornburgh's 1983-4 budget proposal to extend the six percent sales tax to many other items.  Those who testified criticized the proposal and argued that it was regressive and potentially harmful to business owners.

headline: Some seniors lack aid
abstract: State's Legislature has given the senior citizens the sweet pill with a bitter coating. This is the new bill that would introduce co-pay prescription plan for an estimated 700,000 seniors. Under the plan they would pay $4 for each medical prescription and the state will pay the rest from the lottery funds. The article analyzes the quality of this solution by pointing out some good and some bad outcomes.

headline: Mine fire more serious, study finds
abstract: A long-awaited federal study showed that the coal-mine fire burning under Centralia is worse than anyone believed and that measures to control it could cost up to $660 million. The federal study strongly suggested relocating residents of Centralia in neighborhood village.

headline: State's slogan will be added to licenses
abstract: The slogan "You've Got a Friend in Pennsylvania" will be carried on new registrations or license plate replacements for passenger vehicles. The purpose of the action is the tourist promotion of PA.

headline: Witness says he sent rabbi to Larsen for counseling
abstract: A man under investigation by Judicial Inquiry and Review Board is Rolf R. Larsen because of political maneuvering, racial bias and personal animosities on the State Supreme Court. One of the witnesses said the Larsen met alone in his Pittsburgh office with the father (who is a rabbi) of the man whose murder conviction would later be appealed to the PA Supreme Court. The man who brought the rabbi and Larsen together said he introduced several of his friends and relatives to the justice, but not to try to fix the verdict, but for counseling on personal problems.

headline: Sunbury Marine Is Laid to Rest
abstract: A mother cried yesterday as her son, "a good Marine" was laid to rest after being brought home from Beirut, where he died in an bombing attack. The article describes in detail the burial and it has comments from the family.

headline: O'Pake bill would increase power of a auditor general
abstract: The auditor general would be given more power under a measure proposed by a lawmaker who said he probably will be a candidate for the office next year. He said auditor general needs more power to enforce audits that found money owed to the state and audit the state's public utilities.

headline: Steel Caucus to hear USS import plan
abstract: David Roderick, chairperson of U.S. Steel, agreed yesterday to appear before the Congressional Steel Caucus to discuss the company's plans to import semi-finished steel from Britain.  Several members of Congress hope to persuade the company to reconsider its plans to import steel, a plan analysts say could put some 3,000 persons out of work.

headline: Squelch the squeal rule
abstract: One of the Richard Schweiker's final acts as Secretary of Health and Human services was to approve a rule to require federally funded family planning clinics to notify parents whose daughters under 18 seek prescription contraceptives. This policy makes great conservative rhetoric but tends to ignore reality. Schweiker said the rule was designed to "encourage family participation" and "family involvement". However, the squeal rule is far more likely to have precisely opposite effect - more unwanted pregnancies and abortions instead of less.

headline: Mine fire report due tomorrow
abstract: Now, 21 years after a mine fire was discovered sizzling under Pennsylvania town of Centralia, congressional action may be taken to solve the Columbia County borough's problem. The Interior Department's Office of Surface Mining is scheduled tomorrow to release the findings of an extensive study.

headline: Taking a Toll Of Highways
abstract: The Governor's Toll Road Task Force recommends that Pennsylvania create a new system of toll roads and the estimated cost is $3.7 billion. Several important projects for PA may be founded by this proposal. The author is discussing these proposals and he approves the toll roads as a way to fund those projects but he opposes converting established highways into toll roads.

headline: woman charged; sales tax owed by restaurant
abstract: Attorney General announced the filling of charges against a woman whose Downtown Harrisburg sandwich shop allegedly has not paid sales taxes since 1979. The complaint lists seven counts of failure to remit sales tax, each carrying a maximum penalty of one year in jail and a $1,000 fine.

headline: Thornburgh Backs Agent Orange Aid
abstract: Gov. Thornburgh told 3,000 delegates at the state American Legion convention yesterday that Vietnam veterans exposed to Agent Orange should be compensated for their suffering. Veterans have filed claims saying agent has sickened and crippled them. They were exposed to an agent when the chemical was sprayed on enemy jungles in Southeast Asia.

headline: Opinion may bar Cohen in Cabinet
abstract: A staff lawyer with the legislative Reference Bureau has prepared a legal opinion which concludes that "political office" and "public office" are interchangeable. This definition if it stands would indicate that Consumer Advocate Cohen is ineligible to serve as Public Welfare Secretary in Gov. dick Thornburgh's cabinet.

headline: Goode denies he invited Jackson endorsement
abstract: Philadelphia mayoral candidate Wilson Goode tried to distance himself from Jesse Jackson's endorsement of his campaign, stating that he has not spoken with Jackson in seven years and that the two are not close.  The Rizzo campaign has accused Goode of lying about the endorsement and inviting Rev. Jackson to visit a West Philadelphia Church on Palm Sunday.

headline: State Medicaid Policy Rapped
abstract: The state's Medicaid policy is jeopardizing the elderly access to appropriate health care, nursing home officials told a state Senate. The state Department of Public Welfare official said that nursing home complaints about the new spending rules are expected.

headline: Must restore faith, EPA chief says
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) wreathed in controversy in recent months and must reestablish its credibility with the American people if it is to carry out its mission to "protect life", the EPA administrator said.  In his first major address before an environmental group since taking the helm of EPA, he pledged the agency will be forthright and open.

headline: Taking look at PennDOT's "accomplishments"
abstract: An author of the letter is reacting on previously published opinion from PennDOT engineers who was talking positively about PennDOT accomplishments. The author thinks opposite of that and he lists many examples where PennDOT proves its bad effectiveness.

headline: Yes for PACE
abstract: Senate bill 102would create the Pennsylvania Adoption Cooperative Exchange (PACE)  that would identify and place minors who are legally free for permanent adoption. Editor thinks that the bill is a good beginning to move children from faceless institutions to caring homes (although is not a reform for the foster care program).

headline: The shipyard let us down
abstract: USS Saratoga came to the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard and this was done by  putting a lot of efforts from politicians from this region. They claimed Philadelphia has necessary resources to maintain the shipyard. Thus, it is the embarrassment to the region that some work on Saratoga was not  done properly. The shipyard left Philadelphia in February and still did not come back.

headline: Ousted rep finds place in sun
abstract: After a year of surveying the possibilities and running into roadblocks, Eugene Atkinson has found the government job to his liking  - in the U.S. Travel and Tourism Administration. A year ago he lost his job as a representative, largely because of publicized switch to Republican Party.

headline: Judge on the spot
abstract: We recommend that Common Pleas Judge Silvestri recuse himself from Cyril H. Wecht's case.  In addition to Silvestri's daughter having worked for Wecht, the fact that Wecht, an Allegheny County commissioner, has control over the court's funding makes this case difficult for any Allegheny County judge to decide dispassionately.  As such, an out-of-county judge should handle the case.

headline: State plans to close Pennhurst
abstract: The state's most notorious (and maybe the nation's most notorious at the same time) institution for the mentally retarded persons would shut down according to the proposal to be filed soon in the federal court. The proposal will be funded by the state Department of Public Welfare and the reason is that the institution has been involved in many abuse stories.

headline: New Session - Auto Emissions
abstract: PA's new General Assembly has just been sworn in, and there is already urgent business that is overdue- auto emissions testing in greater Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. For four years now PA has been under a federal court order to start emissions test and since the state has not complied the penalty was almost half a billion dollars. Yet most of PA's lawmakers do not think those are serious losses (the bill failed last year because of political blackmail). There are no more excuses for delays.

headline: The Driver
abstract: Sara Liberati drove her car wearing contact lenses but PennDot still says that she is a danger to other drivers. She went to court to fight PennDot and two local judges agreed with her. Now, PennDot is trying to fight her by appealing to higher court. It is important that Sara keeps winning. All handicapped people need every chance they can get to prove they can make it on their own.

headline: Zimmerman: Judges too lax on drug cases
abstract: Attorney General Zimmerman blamed Pennsylvania judges for the fact that majority of people arrested by the state police for the drug offense and drug trafficking did not end up serving any time in prison. He said that the drug trafficking is rampant and that children can buy any drug they can afford. Despite his strong criticism he refused to name individuals.

headline: Thornburgh "Salutes" 23 Air Force Recruits at Capitol
abstract: Armed Forces Week was brought to the Capitol and Gov. Thornburgh participated in the swearing in of 23 young people into the Air Force. The 21 men and two women, came into the Air Force under the delayed enlistment program.

headline: P.T. Barnum said it best of all
abstract: PA's decision to increase the odds of winning the various lottery games makes the games less lottery and more tax. State officials think this will not reduce the ticket sales. The author thinks that the state is approaching a degree of honesty about the lottery. First, it was portrayed as fun and game, but now it becomes more obvious that the lottery is nothing but a tax with a chance that a taxpayer gets back some of his money.

headline: Legislators Plan Job Walk to D.C.
abstract: Two Pennsylvania state Representatives are planning to walk from the state capitol to the national capitol to hand-deliver a list of legislative proposals to President Reagan.  The representatives, Michael Gruitza and John Wozniak, say the proposals are designed to increase employment and security in economically depressed areas of the country.

headline: State pushes new welfare medical plan
abstract: State welfare officials are moving ahead with controversial plan to assign recipients in Philadelphia neighborhoods to a private company that would provide all of their medical needs for a fixes annual fee. One state official describes how that system works, but he rejected to disclose which parts of Philadelphia will be covered by this plan.

headline: New Water Tests Are a Step Closer
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources officials have given their approval to an Air Force plan for water testing at Sunset Golf Course in Londonderry Township to determine the extent of a pollution problem there. The Air Force initiated investigation because of the damping that is blamed for contamination of a dozen private wells in Londonderry.

headline: Too much to drink
abstract: The death of Pittsburgh Penguin's General Manager in an automobile accident underscored the tragedy of drunken driving. The author of the article thinks that the drunken driving is a serious problem and that the responsibility is not only on the drunk person. For example, if the person is already drunk, then the bartender and friends can carry responsibility for him (they can make sure he is not going alone in the car after that)..

headline: null
abstract: The photo depicts men gather to pass the time and wait for a meal outside the Drop-In Center in Philadelphia

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon depicts a man holding the newspaper with a title "Second Solar System Found". At the same time on the night sky stars formed a word "Hello".

headline: Push to oust Mezvinsky losing team
abstract: State Democratic Chairman Mezvinsky appears to be in a good position to survive the renewed attempt this weekend to oust him from his leadership post. He has been criticized for failures in communication and fund-raising. There should be a special session of the state committee for reviewing the issue but there are also some difficulties to reach the quorum.

headline: Police Urge Creation Of Crime Watch Programs
abstract: The Pennsylvania state police launched a statewide crime prevention campaign today and urged local communities to begin developing neighborhood crime watch programs.  Several local police departments, including the City of Pittsburgh, have instituted such programs.

headline: State Warns W. Chester Nursing Home
abstract: The state Health Department has ordered a Chester County nursing home to correct a long list of alleged abuses or  risk being shut down. 37 serious violations were uncovered at the facility and among allegations were a lack of nurses on some shifts and a shortage of other staff.

headline: No to Ridley Creek deer hunt
abstract: In the letter, an author is criticizing the Pennsylvania Game Commission's decision to allow killing of deer in the Ridley Creek State Park. He lists reasons explaining why deer do not represent the threat and why this decision is the wrong one.

headline: Those double-tractor rigs
abstract: An author of the opinion supports Gov. Thornburgh's saying to the nation's governors that federal government should reaffirm the right of states to say which highways will be open to double tractor-trailers. The states are in the best position to designate safe and coherent highway networks for large trucks. The issue is very important because large trucks are hurting the roads.

headline: "Moratorium" ordered on disability cuts
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has directed state Labor and Industry Secretary to place moratorium on the denial of Social Security disability benefits to all individuals who can show continuing disabilities "until the federal government establishes standards to evaluate medical improvement". Thornburgh said his directive is in the compliance with the U.S. Third Circuit Court of Appeals decision.

headline: null
abstract: The cartoon depicts a women inside the House who locked the phone in the hole on the wall with a sign " In a case of emergency break glass". At the floor is the newspaper saying the phone rates went up. This is the parody on minimum usage of phone because phone rates went up.

headline: Pa. Senate calls for new election date
abstract: The state Senate yesterday approved an amended bill changing the date of the forthcoming state primary elections to May 16, one day earlier than mandated under current law. The change was initiated by Rappaport because the regular primary election date conflicts with the Jewish holiday of Shavuoth.

headline: Inspections
abstract: After a day of casting aspersions at U.S. District Court Judge Louis Bechtle for holding that the state is in contempt of a consent decree it signed in 1977, the PA House of Representatives approved auto-emission inspections for the state, but only under the condition that vehicle owners are reimbursed for inspection and repair costs.  This should clear the way for the release of federal highway funds, which have been frozen since Judge Bechtle's initial ruling.

headline: Thornburgh gets co-pay bill
abstract: A bill that would establish a subsidized prescription drug program for 700,000 senior citizens, was approved 198-2 by the House, following the unanimous Senate approval earlier in the day. The program would be funded by the state Lottery fund ,and it is estimated to cost $86 million in its first full year of operation.

headline: Ocean toxic-burning plans require strengthened rules
abstract: The article talks about the hazardous waste from the Newark company, and different proposals for dealing with such a waste. There are some issues related to the rules that regulates this process and there is an interest of people, Philadelphians, that live close to areas where the waste was supposed to be placed.

headline: Transit, AAA conferences meet here
abstract: More than 800 transit officials representing agencies from across the United States and Canada and more than 50 American Automobile Association delegates will be visiting Pittsburgh this week. The event is Rapid Transit Conference at the William Penn Hotel.

headline: "Squatter" Eviction Vote Fails
abstract: A non-biding resolution asking the governor to remove about 30 demonstrators from the Capitol, in the 10th day of a live-in welfare protest, was defeated yesterday by a tie vote on the House of Representatives. The demonstrators, who have placed mattresses, clotheslines and tables inside the Capitol, are protesting last year's cut of at least 68,000 so called able-bodied people from the  state's welfare rolls.

headline: 2 Grants Awarded For Research Labs
abstract: The Ben Franklin Partnership approved its first grants yesterday of $250,000 each to establish two advanced technology centers that will work on everything from robotics to using microbes to desulfurize coal. Both centers are university partnerships involving matching contributions from corporations.

headline: Pa., union reach an agreement
abstract: Negotiators for the state and the largest union representing state employees have reached tentative agreement on a two-year contract boosting wages by 5.06 percent and providing most employees with one-time, 2 percent bonuses. The agreement came after several months of negotiations.

headline: Voting records of area legislators
abstract: This article lists the voting records of area legislators on various measures.  Legislation on Social Security and auto emissions, as well as an international treaty on damages paid to victims of airplane crashes were considered.  The article lists records for Congressmen Murtha, Clinger, Shuster, Heinz and Specter.  Records for state representatives Dietz, Geist, Hayes, Johnson and Haluska were also listed.

headline: Tipsy Walkers Cited In Deaths
abstract: Drinking and walking proved to be a fatal combination in about 40 percent of the pedestrian deaths in Pennsylvania last year, according to the state Department of Health. The statistics were compiled from blood samples submitted to the Department.

headline: Officials to monitor health effects of Londonderry pollution
abstract: Health Department officials were taking initial steps in trying to determine of contaminated water has had any ill effects on some Londonderry Twp. Residents whose wells are tainted. The questionnaires are designed to provide a health profile of the affected persons. The families have been without water since contaminants were found in private wells earlier this month.

headline: Trucker Replies To Criticism Of Rigs, Drivers
abstract: In response to a letter by one reader, the trucker replies in his letter that the reader is not familiar with the whole situation. The issue is whether the big truckers damage the roads. The trucker lists reasons he believes are important to allow truckers use the roads.

headline: "Thornfare" Foes Clash With Guv
abstract: They called the governor a "maniac" and a "murderer" and he in turn called them a "mob". The occasion was a demonstration by about 300 persons at the Capitol that accompanied the announcement of the introduction of a bill to repeal the state's welfare reform law. Critics claim that the law has deprived 78,000 people of an income. Many of the demonstrators brought the mattresses and food with them, vowing to stay in the Capitol until the bill becomes the law.

headline: An adversary on high: NASA tracks the gypsy month
abstract: A big-eyed NASA earth satellite will take pictures while it zips over eastern PA next week - not to spy on people, but to track gypsy months as they munch their way across the state, destroying millions of trees as they go. The NASA satellite is the key component of the project at Pennsylvania State University to monitor this summer's defoliation damage by the hungry gypsy moth caterpillars in the state.

headline: Panel Chilly to Guv's Plea on Jobless Aid
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh saw little evidence of the famous Southern hospitality when he asked  Southern-dominated congressional panel for help in pulling his state out of an unemployment compensation mess. Thornburgh and governors of other high-unemployment states want the federal government to defer interest payment until the economy improves but some committee members said they have little sympathy for states who did not help themselves.

headline: Budget Message to Put Green, Council at a Deficit
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor William Green will unveil his 1984 budget proposal tonight.  His budget is expected to call for tax increases and concessions from municipal employees.  The mayor has said that the city faces a budget deficit of 22-27 million--a deficit that will increase without spending cuts or revenue increases.

headline: Town and state at odds on study of local health
abstract: Disagreement persists over how best to determine whether this town's apparently high rate of bladder cancer is linked to carcinogens at two defunct chemical plants. Several residents of the town and officials of the state Health Department have agreed that there seems to be a high incidence of bladder cancer and urinary tract problems in the area. The Health Department recently developed a plan to determine the seriousness and cause of the problem. But the plan was criticized by  a citizens group that said proposal needed firmer guidelines.

headline: Ontological Concerns
abstract: An article talks about the Clinton County in PA that has state highest rates in deaths from leukemia and second highest from breast cancer and lymphatic cancer. Other types of cancer are also high in the state rank and the question is whether those things are linked to the chemical companies allegedly failing to protect workers and nearby residents from their waste. People are still not leaving this area and the answer to the previous question is not going to come very easily.

headline: Turnpike Chairman Vows Safety Actions
abstract: The PA Turnpike Commission will spend whatever it takes to crack down on unsafe drivers on the toll road, Turnpike Chairman said. The focus will be on the speeders, tailgaters, motorists with faulty equipment and truck drivers hauling hazardous loads without proper notice. The safety campaign was spurred in part by an increase in fatal accidents this summer.

headline: As Harrisburg dawdles, the poor suffer
abstract: When government fails, then the poor suffer the most, because the government could not pass the budget on time. More than 30,000 welfare checks were withheld and the were not sent to the welfare recipients. The article further continues with the analysis of this difficult situation for poor people.

headline: Computer Crime Measure Approved by Senate Panel
abstract: Unlawful use of a computer would become a new theft crime in PA under a bill approved by a state Senate Committee. Under the law, unlawful computer use could be either a felony or misdemeanor. The legislation is modeled on the proposed Federal Computer Protection Act of 1983.

headline: Papadakos gives county high court majority
abstract: Spurned by the Bar Association but embraced by voters, Judge Papadakos made official yesterday what was decided six month ago. He was unopposed in the election for a single seat that Supreme Court. Now, the four out of seven judges are from Allegheny County.

headline: Governor considering O'Bannon for post on PUC
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh is considering appointing Helen O'Bannon--the former Department of Welfare Secretary--to the state Public Utility Commission.  Thornburg's consideration of O'Bannon is surprising because the governor removed her from his cabinet two months ago--presumably for her independence from the administration's policies.

headline: Trench for Centralia believed hazardous
abstract: Health officials say residents here face the possibility of cancer, hearing loss and heart problems if a 450-foot-deep trench is dug to contain huge underground mine fire. But in issuing its study, the state Health Department could not say what the incidence of cancer would be from dust particles released in the air, nor what the chances were that a person might lose his hearing from the excavation noise.

headline: Pa.' radioactive waste plans lag
abstract: PA, the Northeast's largest generator of low-level radio active waste, is lagging behind its neighbors and most of the rest of the nation in deciding how to dispose of the toxic material into the 21st century. Congress set the deadlines for the states to decide what to do with a waste and in PA there are difficult questions laced with public apprehension about what course to take. PA officials must decide in the next 10 months.

headline: Two Common Pleas Court judges differ on drunken - driving law
abstract: The portion of Pennsylvania's new drunken driving law that requires motorists to be found guilty if they have a blood-alcohol content higher than 0.10 has been ruled both constitutional and unconstitutional by separate judges.

headline: Black says lottery can support medicines and mortgage aid
abstract: Secretary of Aging, Black says he is convinced that lottery surpluses can provide both a drug assistance program for the elderly and mortgage loans to unemployed home owners. Black had objected when Governor proposed in his budget address that lottery funds will be used to provide interest-free loans to unemployed homeowners and farmers facing foreclosures. Black said the money should be used instead for a prescription program for elderly.

headline: Computerized commonwealth
abstract: The Commonwealth initiated the nation's first state-used Data Processing Center. The article continues with the story about the computerization.

headline: Papadakos Race Cost $230,000
abstract: Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Nicholas Papadakos spent more than $230,000 in his bid for a state Supreme Court seat, campaign expense reports show. He unofficially won both the Republican and Democratic primaries for the high court. His campaign still has a debt of $50,000.

headline: Odds and Ends
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton seems poised for a gubernatorial run in 1986.  He is well aware of the important issues affecting Pennsylvania and is forthcoming with his opinions on those issues.

headline: Tylenol's consuming lessons
abstract: 7 people died from cyanide-laced Tylenol ( product of Johnson & Johnson), but Johnson & Johnson's dealing with crisis was quite different from what  American public used to see in similar situation. Johnson & Johnson immediately made protective public relations moves, putting its executives on television, providing free samples, quickly developed tamper-resistant package, etc. So, by voluntarily accepting responsibility and by looking beyond the bottom line they seem to have miraculously revived Tylenol's fortunes in marketplace.

headline: Pennsylvania Needs a Bottle Bill
abstract: A bill that would ban throwaway beverage containers in PA is a step in that direction. An article favors the bill because it would stop the litter and encourage recycling. The purpose of all that is to make PA cleaner.

headline: Violent acts escalate in truck strike
abstract: Reports of violence associated by independent truckers escalated yesterday as the protest against higher taxes for truck operations was carried into its second day. The most serious attack was the overnight shooting death of a North Carolina trucker. In PA 64 incidents were reported and the tax increase is the largest single one in the truck history.

headline: Budget office to study welfare cuts
abstract: State budget officials are planning a thorough study of the impact of recent cuts in welfare programs after the Thornburgh's administration rejected a proposal that a more costly study be done by  the welfare department. The study will be done by mailing questionnaires and some officials are worried that the study won't be objective and fair analysis because it is going to be done by state budget officials.

headline: Computers: Password to Christmas Giving
abstract: An article describes higher sales of computers in PA. There is an upward sales trend which is confirmed by many sellers and their quotes in the article. An article also has some details about the usage of computers and the advertisements at the national level for them.

headline: Papadakos Secures Supreme Court Seat
abstract: The final official results, certified more than three months after the primary election and obtained yesterday, shows the Allegheny County Judge Nicholas Papadakos secured a state Supreme Court seat by a margin of fewer 5,000 Republican votes. He will take the oath of office in January, replacing the retiring Chief of Justice Samuel Roberts.

headline: Governor Wants To Drop Hospital Business
abstract: Governor Thornburgh says he would like to see community-based organizations assume responsibility for the day-to-day operations of state-run hospital facilities.  He assured residents that no community would be left with inadequate care and that any trasfer of power from state to community groups would occur in an incremental fashion.

headline: Welcome Hospital Cost Change
abstract: With hospital and health care costs the fastest rising factors in the cost of living, most welcome is the news that PA hospitals are responding to government pressure to cut costs. The Hospital Association of PA will spend 8 percent more this year than it did last year and this is a good news because raise in the past was about 15  to19 percent in the year level.

headline: Polishing the DER image
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources (DER) is hiring six new people who will be working in public relations part. At the same time the DER is erasing jobs of some other persons (from other parts) and the question is why they are doing that? Perhaps they are aware of the bad picture they have in public and want to improve that picture.

headline: A look back at the turbulent Allen murder trial
abstract: An article depicts complicated situation in Common Pleas Court in Philadelphia during Richard Allen Homes murder trial. 83 witnesses are involved, many defense attorneys and jury, but the problem is that the jury, defense attorneys and judge are having difficulties finding the common ground. Defense attorneys accused jury for improper behavior. At the end one person was received the death penalty and two others got life sentences.

headline: But Jobs Don't Exist
abstract: How can people service with a welfare cuts (Gov. Thornburgh's welfare cuts) when they were unable to live on money before the cuts. There should be some type of alternate program for them to earn money while helping community. It seems that politicians are worried only about staying ahead in nuclear arms instead of being focused in well being of the people.

headline: Guy's Line: Hometown Superhero
abstract: Guion Bluford, appeared in his hometown in a meeting with a Mayor. He is the first African American to travel in space, and this time he is talking with many school students in Philadelphia, giving them advice and his thoughts. The article praises him, and talks about his place in history.

headline: Parties don '84 war point
abstract: The article talks about coming elections in 1984. There are many activities underway by representatives of both parties. Many of them are related to the primary elections  and selection of candidates. He also lists some rules from both parties that are related to the candidates selection.

headline: NO POLITICAL FOOTBALL
abstract: Philadelphia Gas Works (PGW), the main supplier of natural gas in Philadelphia, needs help from city government but is not getting it.  PGW is owed 50 million dollars by delinquent clients, and Mayor Green has refused to let the company shut off service to these delinquents.  PGW needs a system in place to help customers who really cannot pay, as well as a system to collect from deadbeats who can; it needs the help of city government.

headline: "Supermilk" touted, dairy farmers wary
abstract: State Agriculture Secretary is pushing for production of "supermilk", combination of powdered and lowfat milk. He says it will taste better and boost sales. Processors contend that the plan would force them to absorb the cost of a tremendous milk over supply that threatens to take money from farmers' pockets.

headline: Proposed Trench Shocks Some Centralia Residents
abstract: The prospect of having a 450-foot-trench gashed through a large part of Centralia town shocked some residents, but some owners are pleased (those who want to sell their houses but so far they could not find a buyer). The U.S. Office of Surface Mining prepared a report for the 21-year-old problem with underground mine fire. One part of report is proposal of trenching operation as a solution.

headline: null
abstract: Guardian Angels recently met with the local law enforcement officials. Two sides have agreed to use Dauphin County Chiefs Police Association as a liaison to coordinate their efforts. Editor thinks this is a first step toward a true working relationship between the Guardian Angles and  the police. Although one can argue whether Angles are needed, the editor thinks they are needed.

headline: Clergy does "arm-twisting" for jobless
abstract: Clergy and church members here have escalated a campaign to pressure banks and corporations into doing more to help the unemployed and other poor people , especially in the depressed Monongahela Valley. And if the banks do not respond , people may be asked to withdraw their savings from banks. The ministers do not expect all the clergy to support then since some might be skeptical or even hostile.

headline: 'Loose cannon" Drew Lewis sets them off
abstract: Drew Lewis, the sick-company doctor has just completed hid first six months as chairman and chief executive of money-losing Warner Amex Cable Communication Inc. He may be a tyro in a cable industry, but as a communicator he is not a slouch. He criticizes other people and outside facts for the failure of the company he is leading. This article about the management continues with a more detail about difficulties of his company.

headline: Party games
abstract: The most important thing in getting the party endorsement is the connection and appeal with rank-and-file committee members. Recent political party endorsement meetings in Pittsburgh were full of upsets. Two major Democrat leaders did not get the endorsement in part because their opponents outhustled them by appealing directly to high-ranked committee members. The situation is similar in the Republican party and the article continues with comments about that (impact on voters, etc.).

headline: Governor maintains silence on PUC choices
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh has kept silent on who he will select to the Public Utility Commission. This while two members are scheduled to leave their seats in a few days. William Green, the Governor's deputy press secretary says the Governor will make his announcements very soon.

headline: 3 Countries Don't  Want Pennsylvania's Chickens
abstract: PA's poultry has suffered one more blow because of epidemic of avian flu that was defected in some parts of the state. Three countries, Switzerland, Canada and Netherlands have banned the export from PA poultry companies. The Governor Thornburgh will meet with producers in order to find solution to help them.

headline: Radiation Mishap Disclosed by NRC
abstract: A well-drilling accident in a remote section of western Pennsylvania resulted in radioactive contamination requiring $1 million cleanup. The contamination level is low and poses no health threat to humans. NRC placed blame for the accident on the drill but federal regulatory agency also noted that there was inadequate use of survey instruments to detect contamination.

headline: null
abstract: The cartoon depicts prison and cemetery standing next to each other. Victims from the cemetery "say": "Speaking of overcrowding." The cartoon ironically talks about the claims that prisons are overcrowded but it is not fair toward victims to simply release prisoners.

headline: Community-based funding urged to reduce spending
abstract: In these days of spiraling inflation and tight budgets, the Department of Public Welfare can get more for its money by funding community based human service projects. The secretary of the department says that in that way a lot of money can be used more efficiently.

headline: Other subsidiaries offered more services
abstract: Times Mirror Cable Television, the only applicant for a franchise to provide cable service to South Philadelphia, may not be offering the city terms that are nearly as generous (lower rates, more channels and greater variety of a additional services) as it has proposed in the last two urban areas where the company sought franchises. The article describes in detail differences between the Philadelphia proposal and other areas proposals, but Wickwire (director of the Times Mirrors) said that this is economically realistic.

headline: Partying Shots - Thornburgh Throws a Bargain Bash…
abstract: Taste and dignity are what Gov. Thornburgh wanted for his second inauguration (with a modest cost to taxpayers). In the past it was a great opportunity to bring a parade, but with respect to today' s economic situation, Governor did not feel it should be that "parade" way. Thornburg's bash will cost taxpayers only about $5,000.

headline: Today drivers will pay 5 cent more for gasoline
abstract: Across the United States a nickel a gallon increase in the federal gasoline tax has taken effect. The tax is expected to raise $5.5 billion a year over the next four years.

headline: 4.2 million bird-flu toll is predicted
abstract: Daily reports of chicken flocks infected with deadly avian influenza are decreasing, but before the outbreak of the virus ends at least 4.2 million birds in PA will have died, the federal officials say. The text talks about the federal actions that were undertaken to prevent this disease, and the costs of these operations.

headline: Reagan criticized for ignoring Centralia mine fire in budget
abstract: A freshman representative castigated President Reagan for proposing a budget that completely ignores the 21-old mine fire burning beneath Centralia Pa. He said that it is not such a clever idea to spend $850,000 on investigating the fire, and then spend nothing on fixing the problem.

headline: null
abstract: The cartoon depicts the main building of the PA Supreme Court, but the title on the top of the building is " Pa. Supreme Disgrace". Furthermore, the two statues at the entrance say "Justice" and "Judicial Inquiry Board". The purpose of the picture is to show that then PA Supreme Court and Judicial Inquiry Board and Justice lost an honor and respect (especially in judge Larsen case).

headline: Court Airs Mixed Feelings
abstract: An article lists about 10 excerpts from the decision by the U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals upholding the Thornburgh administration's welfare - reform program.

headline: Phone increase sought; would raise local bills 93%
abstract: The last of a series of rate increase requests that would sharply increase the cost of basic residential telephone service across the nation was filed with the Federal Communication Commission. Taken together the increases would almost double the cost of the telephone services from $9.60 through $18.50.

headline: Pay Increase May Be Ticket
abstract: Whenever politicians start talking about increasing their salaries the immediate temptation is to holler "No". However, author of this article analyzes carefully pros and cons of the proposed salaries raise and concludes that there is even more reasons to support an increase this time.

headline: Area Man Given Post On Viet Herbicide Unit
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh appointed Terry Hertzler of Mechanicsburg as executive director of the Pennsylvania Vietnam Herbicide Information Commission. Hertzler is a Vietnam War veteran and former state adjutant for the Veteran of Foreign Wars.

headline: Avian flu spreads to 4 flocks
abstract: As teams of animal-health technicians visited Lancaster area farms yesterday to gather, gas and bury 250,000 chickens infected with a killer strain of avian influenza, federal agriculture officials reported the virus had been discovered in four more flocks. The federal authorities are involved in the case that caught several counties in PA.

headline: Recycling Trash on Upswing Across the State
abstract: Soaring dumping fees and dwindling space to bury garbage are prompting communities around the state to encourage, and in some cases to require, residents to separate recyclable materials from their trash. Those joining the trend are saving the on dumping costs, profiting by selling the materials and putting the people to work processing the collected paper, glass and metal. There are more than 250 recycling operations across the state.

headline: null
abstract: The photograph depicts three police officials (two from local municipalities and one state police commissioner). They laugh after the state police commissioner spoke on municipal police training.

headline: Court Stays Welfare Order
abstract: A federal court granted the state a stay yesterday on the ruling requiring resumption of payments to the 68,000 "able-bodied" residents cut from the welfare rolls last year. The Court said that a key portion of Thornburgh administration's Welfare Reform Act discriminated unconstitutionally on the basis of the age. The state officials told that this court measure would prevent some planned welfare benefits increases and enforce some benefit cuts.

headline: Space Center Official Shuttles Into City
abstract: The Space Center Official Page visited Gov. Thornburgh and his family in Harrisburg. Page is from Harrisburg and the Governor's son is a space enthusiast.

headline: Pay raise beckons
abstract: With the legislators off on an extended summer vacation and the state budget battle behind them, what better time than now for them to think seriously of raising their salaries. The idea is that they would not have to answer to constituents for it on the non-legislative elections in November nor the increase would be collected next year when their own seats will be up for election.

headline: Equitable Sales Tax Elusive
abstract: Pennsylvania Revenue Secretary James Scheiner told the House Finance Committee that the present sales tax is broken and in need of repair. The six percent sales tax has been accepted by the AFL CIO, Chamber of Commerce, 5 consecutive governors and 20 legislatures. It may be unfair and faulty but it works.

headline: Avian Flu Toll At 3.6 Million
abstract: Livestock workers are killing about 200,000 diseased chickens daily in the southeastern PA in efforts to stop a deadly poultry flu. In the last few weeks 3.6 million birds were killed in the 6 counties in this region. The birds were infected by a strain of avian influenza that does not harm humans.

headline: Report Due on Centralia Fire
abstract: For 21 years, a mine fire has been burning under the tiny central Pennsylvania town of Centralia while state and federal officials have played hot potato with responsibility of putting it out. Finally, the U.S. office of Surface Mining releases a long -awaited report that is supposed to detail the alternatives for extinguishing or controlling the fire. The report may be a spark that will force Congress to provide some money to solve Centralia's problem.

headline: "I...am insane"
abstract: In a note written 10 months before he was accused of killing 13 people in a shooting rampage. He said, in a note, he felt a compulsion to kill inmates at the state Correctional Institution at Camp Hill, where he was a guard. The article continues with more details about the pending trial.

headline: Disability purges are slowed
abstract: A bipartisan group of legislators passed a bill that ameliorates the suffering Social Security's unprecedented purge of the disabled. The bill is the best Christmas news for thousands of disabled people receiving Social Security insurance, and it provides disability insurance beneficiaries who appeal termination of benefits can have their benefits continued until administrative law judges decide the case. Unfortunately, the bill will not help all people like those who do not have the mental capacity nor access to legal representation to appeal. Eight of 10 applicants now being denied benefits.

headline: State, Industry Grants Could Create 8,000 New Jobs
abstract: A state grant of $35.5 million, matched by millions more from industry, will underwrite advanced technology projects that may create more than 75 small companies here and up to 8,000 new jobs the next four years. The state's Benjamin Franklin Partnership Board voted the grant to the Western Pennsylvania Advanced Technology Center. The Center was formed to promote regional research.

headline: Pay raise under the table
abstract: The opinion is the sharp criticism of the state lawmakers who approved the pay increase for themselves. The article continues to  criticizes the second-highest paid state legislators in the country.

headline: No end yet to strike by rail workers
abstract: SEPTA rail workers are striking until an acceptable contract agreement is reached. The strike has had little obvious effect on the region. Area residents see the strike as a temporary inconvenience, necessary for low fares. However, rail union leaders are disappointed in the silence of the public. They expect them to be upset with SEPTA.

headline: Bumper Crop
abstract: For most farmers in PA and New Jersey, the summer of 1983 will be remembered as a dry disappointment. It has meant stunted corn, withered hay and brown, dusty fields. But for those who grow grapes and make wine, the season's prolonged drought has been ideal. As the harvest begins this week, they anticipate a near-record crop of peak quality.

headline: Return on investment
abstract: This article is arguing for the new litter law in PA that would encourage a returnable beverage containers and would probably result in some kind of the deposit for those beverages. Some states already did that and this measure seems to be working for most.  The article continues with details about the litter and its negative impact on the environment.

headline: "Merit" selection of state judges is opposed
abstract: The president of the state trial lawyers association opposed a merit selection plan for state court judges, saying it is not less political, just less public. The House committee is considering bills to amend the constitution to take the filling of vacancies on the state Supreme, Superior and  Commonwealth courts out of the hands of voters and have the governor fill the them from lists submitted by nominating panels.

headline: FICA tax Exemption Proposed
abstract: Pennsylvania congressmen yesterday proposed expanded Social Security exemptions for the Amish religious sect and voluntary savings bond plan aimed at easing the retirement system's cash flow crunch. The program could reduce Social Security's cash flow requirements by $9.8 billion by 1989.

headline: Want telephone bills to carry request for funds to help fight Bell
abstract: A statewide consumers group has renewed its bid to set up a permanent mechanism to solicit funds from Bell of Pennsylvania residential customers so the advocates could fight Bell's current $378.9 million rate case. The same group has failed last year in the same attempt.

headline: Penna. Democrats schedule another straw poll
abstract: In an attempt to bolster the image of PA as a keystone in the 1984 presidential elections, the state's Democratic Party is will conduct a nonbinding presidential preference poll of about 400 party leaders on Oct. 1. However, because of the state's late entry into the "straw poll" sweepstakes, the national Democratic Party's opposition to such events and scheduling conflicts in the campaign of the six Democratic candidates, it appears unlikely that the seventh straw poll in the nation this year will attract much attention.

headline: Chicken Growers Fell Heat
abstract: Scorching temperatures during the weekend took a heavy toll in the nation's chicken population and will increase consumer prices within a  few weeks. Chicken houses are not air-conditioned and they suffered from the extreme temperatures.

headline: Senate's Emissions Bill Sidetracked
abstract: Parliamentary procedures sidetracked an auto emissions testing bill in Senate when the measure was unexpectedly returned to the appropriations committee. Senate rules require that every bill has to go to Appropriations Committee and have fiscal note attached before it can be passed. The bill is intended to get money back to state since US District Judge contempt an order that froze all federal highway funds for the Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Allentown-Bethlehem areas.

headline: "Operation Fence Buster" Noteworthy
abstract: An excellent example of law enforcement officers from a variety of agencies working in close cooperation was represented by last week's "Operation Fence Buster", an undercover fencing operation here that netted 34 suspects as well as narcotics, weapons, a car and other stolen property. This was the major boost for the often maligned criminal justice system.

headline: Former Welfare Recipients Take Fight Back to Court
abstract: Former welfare recipients are returning to court to continue their fight against PA's 1982 welfare law, which reduced benefits for at least 68,000 so-called "able-bodied" individuals. Attorney has asked the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia to overturn an earlier decision and strike down the law. The earlier decision said that the law is unconstitutional because it discriminated on the basis of age by cutting the benefits.

headline: "Buy American" auto proposal gets Senate OK
abstract: A "buy American" bill prohibiting public agencies from buying or leasing foreign motor vehicles in most cases has won Senate approval. Some voted against, saying that it would raise costs to taxpayers.

headline: Penna. Law on pensions overturned
abstract: Commonwealth Court President Judge declared unconstitutional a recently enacted 25 percent increase in the amount that 90,000 employees must contribute to their pensions. He  ruled against a statute that mandated an increase and he ordered the state to refund the amounts already collected.

headline: Synfuels Project Sparks Controversy
abstract: Pennsylvania is going ahead with plans to build a billion dollar synthetic fuels plant in Western Pennsylvania. The coal industry sees benefits for those that have struggling from the ailing economy. Opponents cite lack of rules. PA Governor Thornburgh supports the project.

headline: Congressmen find drought aid scarce
abstract: Four Central PA congressmen traveled a few blocks from Capitol Hill to the Agriculture Department to find out they were a long way from getting anything more than low-interest federal loans for drought-stricken farmers. One official said that the state did not filed the paper work properly in order to request a disaster  declaration.

headline: State Called Key in "Green Caucus" Campaign
abstract: After more than four years of organizing efforts, the Pennsylvania Conservation Network learned that the commonwealth has been targeted by the national League of Conservation Voters as a key state in its campaign to form a "green caucus" at the presidential conventions of both political parties next year.

headline: "Spousal Rape" Bill OK'd in Pa. House
abstract: The PA House approved the bill that would provide for the prosecution of spouses for sexual assault of theory marital partner rather than for a rape. The bill removed the language that would abolish marriage as a defense against rape.

headline: Governor Installs Deputy Secretaries At Public Welfare
abstract: Two new deputy secretaries have been installed in the Public Welfare Department, including an administration personnel chief and a former Philadelphia welfare commissioner. Governor Thornburg said they will bring "a great range of expertise and experience in providing effective social services".

headline: Cut imports - Carney
abstract: Job training grants are an aid to steel industry but steelmakers must have foreign import quotas to survive, the chairman of the Wheeling Pittsburgh Steel Corp. said. The occasion was the event where the Governor Thornburgh announces the grant program that was designed to help train 500 steel workers.

headline: Pennsylvania Society Hears Lehrman
abstract: Lewis Lehrman, chairman of Citizens for America, praised "Fourth American Revolution" that he said was symbolized by President Reagan's election in 1980. He praised Reagan's optimistic program in the future. The article offers more details from his speech at dinner meeting of PA Society.

headline: Probation, Not Jail, Ends most County Drug Cases
abstract: The Allegheny County Courthouse has a revolving door for drug offenders prosecuted there; turning first to let them in, then to let them out. Stephen Joyce, assistant supertindent of Pittsburgh police says they see few dealers going to jail, and hear judges complain of overcrowded prisons. 87% in drug cases get probation.

headline: Dairymen File Milk Fee Suit
abstract: Three York County dairy producers have filed suit in federal court to overturn a stop-gap federal milk marketing order that forces producers into sharing costs incurred by handlers in hauling surplus milk out of glutted markets. The independent producers ask the court to block the cost-sharing plan, claiming that it violates the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937 and that it was approved by USDA in an improper manner.

headline: State Court Ruling Opens Door For Asbestos Suits
abstract: Piercing the "corporate veil" of subsidiaries, Pennsylvania's Superior Court has opened the door to lawsuits against a British firm by scores of people claiming respiratory disease by exposure to asbestos. The unanimous decision handed down late last week said the Pennsylvania's courts have jurisdiction over Charter Consolidated Ltd., a London -base firm that mines asbestos in Africa.

headline: 2 charged in transfer of dynamite
abstract: Two men linked by the Pennsylvania Crime Commission to organized crime were charged with supplying dynamite for a former leader of a Teamsters Union local.

headline: Heinz Praises Social Security Bailout Plan
abstract: Sen. John Heinz yesterday called the compromise solvency proposal reached by the President's commission on Social Security Reform "a balanced one" he was confident Congress would act on promptly. He was the only member absent when the compromise was reached by commission. His staff told reporters that the Senator had been in contact with commission members and that he praise a proposal that would net Social Security trust $169 billion in raised taxes and reduced benefits over the next seven years.

headline: Governors to Meet On Employment And Trade Issues
abstract: Governors from seven Northeastern states will participate in a conference today on exporting trade, employment and economic development. The meeting will be held in Providence and is sponsored by Coalition of Northeastern Governors.

headline: Pension study group opposes service cut
abstract: Amid allegations of "chicanery" and "smoke and mirror tricks" concerning funding, a retirement study commission has opposed a bill that would reduce required years of service for normal retirement for members of the Public School Employees' Retirement system. The Study Commission voted to oppose a state House bill that would reduce from 35 years to 30 the service required for normal retirement at any age without reduced benefits.

headline: Getting Ready for Reagan Rerun
abstract: Most Pennsylvania Republicans are convinced that President Reagan intends to run again and are prepared to help help him in the campaign. Dave Christopher, Allegheny County Republican Chairman says he expects the president to announce his candidacy and would be surprised if he did not.

headline: Drought - Hit Farmers Can Buy Federal Corn
abstract: The worst drought in the last 20 years devastated PA's corn and hay crops this summer. The state government will help the farmers, and that are now allowed to buy the government owned corn feed at below market price.

headline: State Game Commission Seeks Big Bear Harvest
abstract: The State Game Commission is seeking a 1983 bear harvest of as many as 1,000 animals. This goal was presented when the agency met to establish license allocations for both bear and antlerless deer seasons this year.

headline: 2 other police majors angry
abstract: State police majors reacted with surprise and anger because of explained transfer of eight police officers. All commanders were ordered to new areas and state police officials did not comment the transfer.

headline: Hospital worker cheats welfare
abstract: An Allegheny County hospital worker collected almost $11,000 in welfare by not reporting her wages since 1979. Anonymous tip led investigators to the woman.

headline: Heinz, Specter, Vow Foreign Steel Probe
abstract: Senators Heinz and Specter promised more than 500 unemployed steel workers of the Crucible plant that they will seek an immediate investigation into American steel companies buying foreign steel. They will try to investigate how the purchase of foreign steel contributes to unemployment at home.

headline: People's Right Upheld by Court
abstract: The inquiry by a Democratic leader of the State Senate as to the identify of lawyers hired by the administration of Gov.
