Thornburgh has some obvious political overtones (the Democrats contend that favoritism was showed to those in the legal profession who were generous in financial support of the governor's campaign for office). Commonwealth Court judge has ordered governor to open the books on the names of in-house and outside attorneys employed by his administration. And the people's right to know is also involved, so the judge wrote "openness of information in government is to be encouraged, emphasized and if necessary required".

headline: Bigger Rigs role this week in Pa.
abstract: A new federal mandate took from states the power to regulate where trucks could travel. The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation will allow large trucks on all 1500 miles of interstate highway in the state and limited access highways.

headline: Drought Loans OK'd for State
abstract: Grain farmers in 17 Pennsylvania counties were allowed to apply for low-interest loans yesterday after Agriculture Secretary declared the drought area a natural disaster. In a letter to Governor Thornburgh, who asked for the declaration, Secretary confirmed substantial loses have been dealt to crops in a wide swath of central PA.

headline: State moves to start auto-emissions tests
abstract: The Thornburgh administration is taking steps to ensure that the state's auto-emission testing program begins as scheduled and that millions of federal highway dollars are not jeopardized, officials said. About $419 million in federal highway funds were frozen last year by a federal judge who ruled that the state had violated the legal agreement.

headline: 3 more county judges are approved by House
abstract: The House of Representatives voted on May 29, 1984 to give the Allegheny County three additional judgeships over the objection of the county commissioners.

headline: House Approves FICA Bailout
abstract: The House last night passed a bipartisan bill, which is a $165 billion plan to pull Social Security form the brink of bankruptcy. The retirement age is now 67 and the bill would make all American workers and retirees alike share the burden of bailing out of system. The rescue bill closely followed the blueprint prepared by the National Commission on Social Security reform.

headline: Nations at Summit To Target Inflation
abstract: President Reagan won "a very big gamble" on allied harmony as the leaders of major industrialized democracies pledged to seek lower inflation and interest rates while limiting government spending to reduce budget deficits. The heads of the states agreed during the two days summit that the joint course is needed to spread economic recovery to all countries.

headline: Phila. mayor candidates agree to poll to decide on Goode's foe
abstract: Mayoral candidates Leonard and Egan, in a political bombshell, have agreed to let a poll determine which of the two will drop out of race against front-runner Goode. Leonard is an independent and Egan is the Republican candidate. Goode is the favorite to become the first black mayor in Philadelphia.

headline: Emissions Hangover
abstract: The Pennsylvania legislature will continue to debate an unpopular subject--auto emissions inspections in 10 counties.

headline: 'Family of Year' Honored at Show
abstract: State Agriculture Secretary presented award to a 12-member mercer County family that has been participating in the annual agricultural exposition since 1936. Award went to George and Evelyn Hunter, their five sons, 4 daughters and George's father.

headline: State Nimrods Head for the Hills in Search of Bear
abstract: Keystone State hunters heading into the last remote areas of the Commonwealth tomorrow for the opening of a two-day black bear season will be seeking one of the premier trophy animals of the East. The article continues with recent and present hunting season, introducing many details as to licensing, hunting, etc.

headline: 33 Charged in $40 Million Drug Conspiracy
abstract: Thirty-three people have been charged with smuggling 100,000 pounds of marijuana and a half-million Quaaludes into Pennsylvania in a $40 million conspiracy which officials say is the largest drug case ever in PA. U.S. Attorney said that about 120 more people will be charged in additional indictments.

headline: House OKs Welfare Cuts to Unwed Cohabitants
abstract: Legislation designed to cut off or reduce welfare benefits to unmarried welfare recipients living with people who have incomes was approved by the state House yesterday. Many people will be affected but the department spokesman said that the hundreds of thousands is too much.

headline: Steel import tariffs, quotas draw fire
abstract: President Reagan's decision to impose a combination of tariffs and import quotas on foreign-produced specialty steel drew fire from virtually all quarters within hours if its announcement. Both steel worker unions and industry representatives are not satisfied with the proposed solution.

headline: Philadelphia Candidates Make Supreme Sacrifice
abstract: Two leading Philadelphia candidates for the state Supreme Court fell by the wayside yesterday as the Democratic Party leaders endorsed Allegheny County Common Pleas judge. With no clear leadership in the Philadelphia delegation, the two judges withdrew from consideration. The article continues with a situation regarding candidates in republican party as well and an atmosphere existing before elections for the state Supreme Court.

headline: Aid to People, State by State
abstract: The US government's direct payments to individuals averaged $1,228 for every man, woman and child in 1982.

headline: Farm Show Begins
abstract: In Harrisburg over half-million people are invited to the 67th Pennsylvania Farm Show. Agriculturalists will have their award winning food, clothing and animal exhibits on display. Members of the public will have an opportunity to see where milk, butter, meat and eggs actually come from.

headline: State to Take Water "Primacy"
abstract: The state is expected to announce this week that it is prepared to receive primacy - prime jurisdiction - from the federal government over administration of laws aimed at providing safe drinking water. The PA Department of Environmental Resources is close to an agreement on the state assumption of primacy with the federal government.

headline: 4 try to stop sheriff's sale, are arrested
abstract: Four people were arrested in Delaware county yesterday after they tried to unsuccessfully break up a sheriff's sale of homes owned by county residents. The arrested were among 15 protesters connected with the Mortgage Foreclosure Committee and their lawyer said he did not expect them to be arrested and that the point of protest was to call attention to the fact that this is part of national housing crisis.

headline: Hundreds "Celebrate Aging" At Festival in Pittsburgh
abstract: 350 people gathered in Allegheny County Courthouse yard decorated with balloons, clowns and booths, to "celebrate aging" during the county Senior Citizens Festival. The state Department of Aging provided vans to bring senior citizens from centers throughout the county and the idea was to get senior citizens out once a year.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon depicts Russian and Japanese fisherman chasing the powerful whale with a title "Whaling issue". Fishermen are on the boat that was broken by the whale. The name of the boat is "International Public Opinion".

headline: Plan devised to help solve municipal pension problems
abstract: The Public Employee Retirement Study Commission  adopted a plan yesterday that would revamp , and in some cases rescue, municipal pension funds throughout Pennsylvania. The crisis among state's 2,000 municipal pension funds, which have a combined unfunded liability of $2.5 billion, prompted a plan, which will be incorporated in legislation to be introduced in spring. The plan also calls for the state to establish a bail-out fund, starting with $35 million, to help distressed pension funds.

headline: U.S. jobless rate dips to 10.3 percent--In Pennsylvania it rises to 13.4 percent.
abstract: National unemployment fell slightly to 10.3 percent of the civilian labor force in March, bolstering hopes that the natinonal economy has stabilized and may be recovering. In Pennsylvania however, the March unemployment rate was 13.4 percent, up from February' 13.2 and reflecting the continued depressed condition of the states industries.

headline: Farmers Eligible For Emergency Loans May Apply
abstract: Farmers in 17 drought-stricken counties in Pennsylvania can now apply for emergency loans, the federal government announced. Only farmers who have lost at least 30 percent of their normal production are eligible for the loans. The application process will take about 60 days.

headline: States Agree To Work on Bay Clean-Up
abstract: Top officials from the three states (Maryland, Virginia and PA), district and federal government signed the historic contract to work together to clean up the Chesapeake Bay. However, many state officials who attended the conference, where the agreement took the place, were disappointed by the role of federal government (federal officials said the responsibility is mostly on the state end).

headline: 45 Men Face Execution In Jails Across State
abstract: In the first part article deals with number of people across state who are the facing death penalty. In the second part it gives a partial list of those people by listing names of offenders and short description of crimes that they committed.

headline: It lives
abstract: The Thornfare monster is wounded, but it is not dead. This is the point in the author's critics of the Gov. Thornburgh's welfare plan reform. The reform was rejected by a federal court as unconstitutional (it discriminated against certain age groups), but it seems the Thornburgh's administration does not intend to comply with a court order.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon depicts the incident when a Soviet military jet fired a missile into Korean passenger jet, killing 269 people and causing the anger and outrage of the President Reagan and other countries.

headline: Politics -  Marty and Frank Have Been Left Reeling
abstract: In the last two weeks many events resulted that Marty Murray (Democrat) and PA Senator Frank O'Connell are no longer the big club party politics. Democrats are talking about Murray in terms of his relinquishing his role as No. 1 in the Luzerne County Democratic Organization and at the same time Republicans are setting the stage to delude O'Connell's control over the county's GOP executive committee. The article continues with reasons for such actions.

headline: Egan to resign as PIDC head to join Fidelty
abstract: Joseph Egan Jr. executive vice president of the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation will resign to become a vice president of fidelty bank.

headline: Farmers fight U.S. surcharge on milk output
abstract: The Pennsylvania Farmers' Association, winding up a two-day congressional conference, criticized an impending federal surcharge on milk production as unfair and counterproductive. The dairy plan was designed to discourage milk production by charging farmers $1 per hundred weight.

headline: Strom Over the Environment
abstract: After denying one congressional subpoena and dodging the another head of Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) finally defended herself before Congress last week, denying under the oath that she was guilty of any impropriety in EPA in managing $1.6 billion toxic-wastes clean-up program. But her testimony was eclipsed by her own former employers in an effort to stop the spreading controversy over EPA. The clean-up was related to Times Beach, Mo. whose citizens are also interested in resolving this issue. The White House continued its internal investigation to determine whether the program had been manipulated for political purposes.

headline: 48 are arrested in protest at GE
abstract: Demonstrators were arrested on charges of trespassing when they entered the grounds of the General Electric Space Center in King of Prussia in protest over the company's work for the Pentagon. They were released afterwards with summary offenses on trespass.

headline: Last of the Big Spenders
abstract: An article analyzed briefly the successes of Nixon (as opposed to not so good service of his successor Carter). Nixon raised Social security by 20%, he proposed federally guaranteed income for all Americans, he linked state and local governments, set up an Environmental Protection Agency , etc. But these acts caused big spending in the budget and the Nixon's successors had to deal with debts of his "generous spending". Still he accomplished an admirable record of social accomplishments.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon depicts the relationship and power balance between U.S. and Western European nations and is mentioning sanctions on U.S. imposed by European nations. The U.S. is represented as much more powerful than European countries.

headline: Poll says 14th Ward committeemen back Wecht
abstract: The 14th Ward Democratic chairman says a poll indicates that county Commissioner Cyril Wecht will win the votes of most his ward's committeemen at Sunday's endorsement meetings. Several major party leaders including the Mayor Caliguiri have declared Wecht unelectable and have asked him not to run.

headline: Healthcare funding cuts must be fair and humane
abstract: Two years ago, Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh commissioned a 17-member task force on Health Care Cost Containment to come up with proposal to contain the skyrocketing costs of medical care in Pennsylvania. The commission have presented the first comprehensive study and it deserves some attention and debate.

headline: Farmers list major losses in drought
abstract: Lancaster County farmers estimate that the summer drought has cost them more than $42 million in crops stunted by the lack of rain and live-stock killed by the heat. Lancaster's Agricultural Emergency Management Board has asked the state to declare the county a disaster area and make farmers eligible for emergency loans.

headline: Surface Mine Sites Shorted In Funds For Reclamation
abstract: The federal government's district conservationist for Butler County is worried about dirt and gravel road that cuts through an abandoned coal mine about 16 miles north of Butler. He is worried because there is a high potential of ground going down on the road because of sharp slopes next to the road. However, there is no help on the way from the federal government because the money is mostly spent on underground mines where fires pose a serious hazard to the public.

headline: 5 ex-Phila. Policemen get prison terms for extortion
abstract: Five former Philadelphia policemen were sentenced to jail yesterday for conspirating to extort more than $125,000 to protect prostitution, gambling and illegal liquor sales, and the federal prosecutor said the investigation of police corruption would continue.  A U.S. district judge said the evidence produced at the trial was just the tip of the iceberg.

headline: Leave lottery alone
abstract: A letter's author says that today's society gives more importance to young people, and he also thinks that many of them pretend to believe the state lottery fund is designed only for elderly people. He suggests that the fund should be left alone.

headline: null
abstract: This cartoon depicts the start of negotiation between U.S. and Soviet Union (related to arms) in comical and ironical way.

headline: Poll: Goode First, Leonard Lagging
abstract: In the first independent survey taken since the May primary, WCAU-TV (Channel 10) - Teichner Poll last night showed Democratic mayoral candidate Goode leading his nearest competitor, Egan. Perhaps as important however, the poll placed Egan 11 percent ahead of independent Leonard, who has the choice of 12 percent.

headline: Accused Official in Revenue Unit Gives Resignation
abstract: Patrick Philbin, deputy secretary for enforcement in the Revenue Unit submitted his resignation. Philbin was accused of pressuring employees to contribute to Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburghs reelection campaing.

headline: Fatal avian flu virus spreads to turkey flock
abstract: Agriculture officials say they are not surprised that a deafly poultry virus has spread from chickens to turkeys. The virus doesn't harm people and the article continues with measures that will be undertaken to deal with this disease.

headline: Tax refunds sought for Pa. program
abstract: State officials hope to raise more than $200,000 through a new program under which residents are encouraged to donate a part of their income tax refunds to a conservation fund for the study and protection of wild plant and animal life. About half the states have some kind of fund for preserving non-game animals. Proponents of the program say money would be used to protect threatened and endangered species by preserving and enhancing their habitats.

headline: 5 indicted in probe of vice payoffs
abstract: A former Philadelphia Police inspector and four other current and former officers were charged yesterday with using the power of their badges and the threat of arrest to extort more than $115,000 from vice operations in Center City. Federal law enforcement sources said the indictments would be the first in a series of criminal charges against Philadelphia police officers during the next several months.  The article continues with an explanation of crimes and the careers of charged people.

headline: Legislation Affecting Senior Citizens Coming  Up in Fall
abstract: PA House Health and Welfare Committee approves a series of bills which represents one of the most comprehensive senior citizens benefits proposals to be founded by the Lottery and includes a cap of $100 million per year. The bills encompass a variety of important issues facing senior citizens today. The article describes further some of the most important isues.

headline: null
abstract: The cartoon depicts two men hiding (and standing out of the building)  from angry people inside the building who are throwing the chairs in front of the Arafat's office. One of those two is Yasser Arafat and he carries the big paper saying "negotiations".

headline: Population sag sends message
abstract: The population in PA is the same according to the Census Bureau and it will decrease slightly in the future. The point in this article is that this is the trend not only in PA, but in many other Northeast states. This will result in smaller power of Northeastern states on federal level while western and southern states will increase their power. And Thornburgh's administration will not help deal with this problem if they continue their partisan squabbling indefinitely.

headline: City signs pollution pact with state
abstract: After 2 and a half years of negotiations, the city of Philadelphia has signed an agreement with the state to curb air and water pollution at the Northwest Incinerator. Local residents and the Clean Air Council, an environmental group, are attacking the plan as inadequate.

headline: Fatal fly devours 150,000 Pa. fowl
abstract: A deadly strain of avian influenza is sweeping Lancaster County's poultry industry, threatening some farms with collapse and prompting calls to destroy possibly hundreds of thousands of the affected birds to contain the epidemic. There has not been a significant impact on industry yet.

headline: TCE Is Found In More Wells
abstract: Carcinogens and suspected carcinogens have been found in additional private wells in Londonderry Twp. Five more wells along the route 441 were taken out of service because results of water sampling last week showed the presence of trichloroethylene and other compounds above accepted levels.

headline: 9 released as jail seeks inmate cuts
abstract: Nine inmates from the Allegheny County Jail are on the street today because there is no room for them in the Ross Street lockup. The nine criminals were released on their own recognizance as part of the county's effort to meet a Monday deadline to reduce jail population. But even with these releases jail administrators are worried that that the population will still be over 600-inmate cap when the deadline arrives.

headline: Lottery Surplus Goals Are Listed
abstract: A group of key House Democrats proposed a package of measures yesterday that would spend three-fourths of a projected $340 million lottery surplus on expanded senior citizen and handicapped programs. The package would create a pharmaceutical assistance program, provide in-home and community-based services for those who otherwise might be in nursing homes, expand existing transportation, etc. They criticized Thornburgh 's administration for not actively supporting expanded programs for senior citizens and for sticking by its plan to use lottery funds.

headline: null
abstract: This comical cartoon has two parts. In the first one is the armed army with flayer saying "Libya bombs Pearl Harbor". It is crowdie and noisy outside, but from the window somebody is calling by: "Hey, keep it down! The President is trying to sleep". On the second part President Reagan is informed in his bed about the World War III six hours later and he seems to be pretty uninterested for the news.

headline: Power to the voters
abstract: Pennsylvania is not the among the close the half the states where the people have the powers of initiative and referendum. The chances of this state's joining the list are remote, although the implementing effort keeps recurring in the Legislature. The article continues with the pros and cons of referendum as a tool voters use to influence the Legislature, and it also analyzes the current political climate related to referendum proposals.

headline: Not a new tax or harassment
abstract: People are supposed to pay taxes on income derived from dividends and interest. Most do, but some don't.

headline: Lip service
abstract: Picture shows Gov. Richard Thornburgh making a movement with his tongue over the lips. He holds a jumbo glass with milk and the comment is that 'he seems to find this a good year for milk at the State Farm Show in Harrisburg."

headline: TCE May Be Buried at Airport
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources officials suspect that a former dumping site believed located under the main runway at Harrisburg International Airport is contaminating seven wills there. The seven wills have been out of the service since evidence of tricholoethylene (TCE), an industrial solvent used as a degreaser, was discovered in March. The article continues with the possible solutions of this problem.

headline: A better way of picking judges
abstract: Everyone knows that the Pennsylvania system of electing judges is a real mess. Too few voters know the qualifications of judges out of their home counties and sometimes even the political party support is not the determining factor. With this in mind, Gov. Thornburgh called on Republicans and Democrats to back one set of candidates for state appellate court judges. But the politicians, of course, did not accept his proposal.

headline: Mrs. Street Cleared in Welfare Case
abstract: Yvonne Hipp Street, wife of state Senator, was acquitted yesterday by a Common Pleas Jury of charges she fraudulently collected $4,134 in welfare payments. She is a community activist and a mother of three.

headline: "Let there be dark"
abstract: The cartoon depicts a creature that looks like a ghost, and that is throwing small missiles. The missiles have star mark which can be indication of Soviet Union.

headline: PS teachers on strike in 6 states
abstract: Public school teachers were on strike in six states yesterday, idling 200,000 students and other threatened walkouts clouded fall classes in school districts across the nation. The article continues with more detail from each of 6 states.

headline: null
abstract: The biggest unmet need of tri-state residents is housing. KDKA provided answers to residents with puzzling housing questions

headline: Panel Hears Decompression Chamber Foes
abstract: Opponents of decompression chambers used to kill surplus animals told a house Committee today that even when operated property, the machines cause excruciating deaths for dogs, cats and small animals. Witnesses before the Hose committee described the deaths in vivid terms hoping they will convince the House panel to approve legislation  banning the decompression chambers in Pennsylvania.

headline: The bottle bill on its way to state
abstract: The unofficial word out of Harrisburg is that the Legislature will pass some form of a bottle bill next year at this time. The reason is that conservation officials say the state's farmers are becoming very disgusted with the litter on their property and their lobbyists are getting stronger. The bill should encourage recycling and reduce litter.

headline: A personal touch in juvenile justice
abstract: The most interesting aspect of the 1982 report on dauphin County juvenile crime was not the 10% increase over the preceding year but the 5% decrease on the rate of recidivism that occurred between 1980 and last year. The decline is attributed to a new program in the county probation department which involved more close personal contact with offenders in the community in lieu of incarceration. The attraction of program has a practical as well as humane side in that the county realized a savings to the taxpayer by avoiding costly interment.

headline: New Report Deals with Needs of Rural Pennsylvanians
abstract: A policy committee in the House of Representatives has developed a report which thoroughly analyzed the quality of life in rural Pennsylvania, and makes recommendations for improvement in 25 areas that are severely decayed. The project is titled "Critical Issue for Rural Pennsylvanians" and is a part of the action to form a new subcommittee within the House called Rural Affairs Subcommittee.

headline: Bonn Leader Celebrates With Philadelphia
abstract: The German President visited Philadelphia and he gave an address on Conference on German-American history. The article gives a short history about German settlers and their beginnings in America compared with today's situation.

headline: PSEA Files Suit On Pension Law
abstract: The PA State education Association yesterday filed a class action suit in Commonwealth Court seeking to overturn a law increasing contribution rate of public school employees to their pension program. The increase was sought by Governor Thornburgh in order to reduce the state's contribution to the retirement fund. PSEA has charged in the suit that the rate increase violates contractual rights and that teachers and other school employees have been deprived of 1 percent of earned compensation.

headline: Officials Back Anti-Crime Bill
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman and Dauphin County District Attorney Richard Lewis endorsed legislation pending in the U.S. Senate that would permit a third time offender to be prosecuted under the federal system for armed robbery or armed burglary.

headline: Penna. Is assailed on food dole
abstract: The House Appropriations Committee yesterday heard criticism of the way the Pennsylvania Agriculture Department administers federal surplus food giveaway programs in the state, and Agriculture Secretary reported briefly that the his critics were "garbage business". Critics said the school lunch program was a victim of weak management and inertia.

headline: The deer killed on roads put food on tables of Pennsylvania needy
abstract: Not all the deer killed In Pennsylvania go to hunters. Some of the whitetails end up on the tables of non-hunters and the needy. That resulted form the new policy of permitting the person who hits a deer on the road with a vehicle to keep the animal. For some needy people, it is the first meal of meat in two or three weeks.

headline: A vote against corruption
abstract: A Republican Sheriff in Montgomery County was charged several times, but that was not enough for him to go out of the race for re-election. He was corrupt, and because of that, he was defeated in the election which is a right decision of voters.

headline: No friend
abstract: An article criticizes sharply the policy of President Reagan toward women who are considered poor and who are working. Many of them are single mothers and it seems that President Reagan thinks that it is their fault that they are poor and the government should not be involved in helping them to improve their lives. Therefore, the President is not a friend to women.

headline: Bush's message about nuclear parity prompts concern abut compromise
abstract: Vice president Bush visited  seven European countries and made a point that the surest mean of deterring nuclear war is to match the Soviet Union missile for missile. He tried to make the idea of missile deployment in Western Europe more palatable to Europeans. Many European leaders who have pledged support for missile deployment argued that as long as the United States appears inflexible, their public would remain suspicious of American motives.

headline: Public Employee Relations Act Is Not What Its Framers Had In Mind 13 Years Ago
abstract: The framers of this act (called Act 195) was supposed to give publiic employees rights similar to private sector employees, but the act included the right of strike and because of that things have not worked out as envisioned. There was a trial to change the law but without success, and it seems there will be repeated efforts to change the law.

headline: USW Protesters want import curbs, not retraining
abstract: Two local leaders of the United Steelworkers of America claim President Reagan's visit to Pittsburgh is an insult to the nation's steel workers. Andrew Palms, director of USW District 15, says steelworkers are appalled that Reagan came to Pittsburgh to brag about retraining displaced workers. Palm also says the workers want the president to do something about the nation's inept trade laws.

headline: Poultry farms quarantined in 4 counties
abstract: All poultry farms in a 1,500-sqare-mile area, including parts of Dauphin, Lebanon Berks and Lancaster counties are now under a quarantine to prevent a highly contagious chicken virus from spreading. An article lists more details about the virus and enforced measures.

headline: The slow pace of waste cleanup
abstract: Nine PA sites have been placed on a preliminary priority cleanup list of the U. S. Environmental Protection Agency and that caused mixed reaction. The good thing is that sites are placed on the list but the bad thing is that the cleanup process is every slow. The article continues with more details about some of the sites.

headline: A whistle-blower upheld
abstract: Clay Mankamyer, an 11-year state policeman, thought it "a duty" to speak out against district magistrates who went easy on drunken-drivers. His superiors punished him for that, but the arbiter who handled his formal complaint dismissed charges against Mankamyer, saying his acts served to increase public respect. The author thinks this was a good judgment.

headline: No plan to hike welfare benefits
abstract: PA Public Welfare Secretary said the welfare cutback law upheld by a federal court has worked as designed and the Thornburgh administration has no plans for additional aid to recipients. His staff will soon begin a study of the impact of the changes that reduced cash grant assistance to three months instead of a full year.

headline: Ceremonies, Luncheon Mark Pearl Harbor Day
abstract: The article talks about ceremonies that took place in Harrisburg. The event was anniversary of Pearl Harbor day. There were many survivors and politicians attending the event and the article offers more details about speakers.

headline: Put Raise in Fund for Needy, Lawmakers Suggests
abstract: A West Shore legislator is challenging his colleagues who, like himself, voted last week against a pay increase, to donate the after-taxes portion toward formation of a fund for Pennsylvania's needy citizens. He opposed the pay increase because he felt the legislators had not earned it.

headline: Concernd Mothers' tell NRC of fears on TMI-2 Cleanup
abstract: A group of concerned mothers living near Three Mile Island told the Nuclear Regulatory Commission that they are frightened by reports of mismanagement in the cleanup of the nuclear plant. GPU Nuclear Corporation, operator of the plant maintains that the cleanup program has safety as an ultimate concern.

headline: State to Post Rule Changes Covering Flu
abstract: State regulations governing 3,100 square-mile quarantine area have been upgraded to try to prevent the further spread of avian flu. The regulations require a halt to the movement of all live chickens and, nest-run eggs and, hatching eggs and day-old chicks from the quarantine area.

headline: Thornburgh gets bill to protect hunters legally taking game
abstract: A bill in Gov. Thornburgh's desk would make it a crime to interfere with hunters killing or wounding animals so long as the sportsmen are obeying game laws. The bill is aimed at groups as Greenpeace that engage in harassment of persons legally taking or attempting to take a game.

headline: A Women's Place?
abstract: An author of a letter is opposing the view that woman should be placed as guards in prisons. It is bad enough that woman are victims of rape and assaults and they should be peering in a man's prison cell and associating with rapists and women beaters.

headline: Nursing care rip-off
abstract: It seems strange that most objections to the Department of Public Welfare review of the type of care for patients come from nursing homes employees and administrators. An opinion continues with the critique of the nursing homes for choosing the costliest programs . Also, the nursing home industry has taken advantage of the program to make money for themselves by erecting new and additional buildings.

headline: Courtship - Phila. officials begin wooing a Saudi prince's investments
abstract: An article talks about the rich Prince from Saudi Arabia who is visiting Philadelphia and is planning to invest some of his money out there. Officials from Philadelphia are delighted with his intention and they are trying to make him invest more in Philadelphia.

headline: Quality, not quantity
abstract: The U.S. Census Bureau projections of a declining population in PA over the next two decades could prove to be dead wrong if they turn out to be correct, it may not be all that bad and, indeed, could be a blessing. The point is that states with rapid population growth have problems with water supply, housing, schools, employment, etc., and in PA all those problems could be managable if the population does not grow.

headline: The Pittsburgh Reagan Won't See
abstract: If it happens that President Ronald Reagan becomes bored with his itinerary in Pittsburgh, here are a few places he should visit to heighten his awareness of Pittsburgh's economic situation: J & L Mill in Hazelwood Southside, Monongabela River, and any local unemployment office.

headline: Sterilize your pets, PAWS is urging
abstract: Preservation of Animal Welfare Safety Inc. wants to dismantle the indifference many pet owners show about having their dogs and cats spayed or neutered. "Current dog and cat over population is a national tragedy" they say because there are no enough homes for litters. 20 million surplus dogs and cats are destroyed in shelters and pound annually because of that.

headline: Updating Refuse Plan
abstract: Lackawanna County recently was allocated $21,150 to bring up to date its 10-year old study on solid waste management. The 1973 recommendation was that each municipality continues to retain its responsibility to collect and dispose of refuse according to state sanitary standards. The author makes some recommendations as to how the study should be done.

headline: Above The Law
abstract: 28 volumes of secret testimony about the conduct of Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen were disclosed recently, but the Philadelphia Inquirer 18-month investigation shows far more questionable conduct than the actions of a single justice. It shows a court whose hallmarks are nepotism, politicking, misconduct and conflicts of interests. This article is the first of three that will highlight these issues by using a detailed analysis of certain court cases.

headline: Nursing home rules fought
abstract: Some 3,000 demonstrators are expected to converge on the Capitol tomorrow to protest Welfare Department regulations that critics say will harm the elderly and bankrupt nursing homes. The issue revolves around Welfare Department order changing standards for classifying the level of care nursing home patients receive Medicaid reimbursement. Director of the Welfare Bureau says that it is the federal government, and not the state, which is pressing for a mass reclassification to intermediate care. Representatives of for-profit nursing  homes, and hospitals that house nursing homes patients also are concerned.

headline: Gaffes by Philadelphia congressman stir ire in Belfast
abstract: Freshman U.S. representative went to private and unofficial visit to Ireland where he was meeting with Ireland officials. At the end he hold a news conference where he was giving some inappropriate foreign policy comments (related to "British Army terrorism" not approved by State Department), and that caused huge controversy in both U.S, and Ireland.

headline: Questions about state role in gaming
abstract: Two politicians are uncomfortable with Pennsylvania's lottery advertising. They think it is designed to pick the pockets of poor people and it is deceptive as private advertising can be. But few lawmakers would be willing to dismantle the little gold mine that the lottery has become for strained state resources. Although it is important to see state's role in legalized gambling, its adverse and advertising, the lottery success creates a strong dependency on it as a continuing source of revenues.

headline: Goodling, Gekas are split on bank withholding plan
abstract: U.S. Representatives George Gekas and William Goldling, sit on the same side of the aisle, but are split on the bank withholding plan. Gekas advocates repeal of the law requiring withholding of 10 percent of dividend and interest income. Goodling says he cannot understand opposition to the withholding concept.President Reagan has promised to veto any bill that would repeal the withholding plan.

headline: Study shows low-chemical farming effective
abstract: A new five year study shows that low-chemical farming can save money and increase the yields while reducing soil erosion and consumer's roles as "guinea pigs for the chemical industry", according to a PA organic farming research groups. The study comes as the federal government is de-emphasizing organic research.

headline: Waste burial problems mount
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources Secretary has urged local government officials to keep an open mind about hazardous-waste sites. He points out that if no area agrees to host these sites, it poses serious problems for industry and for the environment. The author agrees that PA must provide means for the safe and sound disposal of toxic chemicals, but the responsibility should not fall on the shoulders of local officials. The state should have a good system for the disposal of toxic materials and this is not the case now.

headline: Anti-crime cameras proposed by Leonard
abstract: Independent mayoral candidate Leonard, said that he would improve security for shoppers and would save money by reducing the number of police officers required on the scene. The money for cameras would come from the businesses in the targeted neighborhood and from the city.

headline: Nursing homes cuts protested
abstract: Demonstrators jammed into the Capitol Rotunda today to protest changes in welfare regulations affecting nursing home care of the elderly. "The administration is purely trying to save money and the result will be in a decrease in the quality and quantity in care for sick elderly people in Pennsylvania" - one of the demonstrators said. The cuts resulted from an executive order from Thornburgh and only could be revoked by him.

headline: German heritage enriches us all
abstract: More than 50 million United States citizens have ancestors who came here from the Germany. The 300th anniversary of the first German arrival is celebrated in Philadelphia. The article continues with the short story about Germans in the U.S..

headline: Reed asks state to halt DER move to East Pennsboro
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Reed, has urged the state legislators to block the Thornburgh administration's plan to buy the old Blue Shield Building in East Pennsboro Twp. for the  state Department of Environmental Resources. He offered another site and explained why that site is better.

headline: Thornburgh's hybrid news conference
abstract: Unlike past administrations, Pennsylvania Govenor Thornburgh created a hybrid of press conferences. Instead of standing infront of reporters and answering questions, Thornburgh would tell the Capitol Newsroom that Thornburgh was signing a bill or meeting dignitaries or making an important announcement. Thornburgh method allowed him to frame the discussion and avoid pesky reporters.

headline: $5 Billion Jobless Fund Debt: Who's To Pay?
abstract: The state Unemployment Compensation Fund (UCF) could be 45 billion in debt in three years and Gov. Thornburgh offered a plan that that would, according to him, make the UCF solvent in 1986 and debt free in 1992. Time is running out, and the business and union leaders criticized Thornburgh's plan. They will form a committee to start negotiation with Governor.

headline: Wetland rules make sense
abstract: After the flooding York County suffered last summer and this winter, who could blame local environmental activists for wringing their hands over a new state program that will make it easier to fill in wetlands? The article describes the new program and concludes in favor of it.

headline: Arbitration panel hears testimony
abstract: Binding arbitration hearings that will help a panel determine a new contract for 3,900 state police, working without a pact since June 30, are under way. State police are forbidden by law from striking, and the conclusions reached by the arbitration panel will be binding.

headline: Pa. in Checks Again & It's Assembly's Move
abstract: The state is churning out checks again for welfare recipients and commonwealth employees, now that Gov. Thornburgh has signed the 1983-84 state budget. But the fiscal year is only eased, not ended, because legislature will have to come up with a supplemental budget later this year with a tax program to finance it.

headline: Gray on Reds: They are Angry and Surprised
abstract: Representative Gray, returning from his meetings in Moscow, says Soviet officials say they do not think they are guilty of any wrongdoing in the destruction of Korean airliner carrying 269 people, and have expressed surprise at the worldwide condemnation. He said it is clear from conservation that they are paranoid about they security and they are not going to admit that they have made the mistake.

headline: Rating the Candidates
abstract: Judge Nicholas Papadakos is rated by Pennsylvania Bar Association as unqualified to be a justice, and she is very angry about that saying that the Bar's rating system is "riddled with politics". The article continues with the attitude that those ratings should be public and that criteria should be transparent.

headline: null
abstract: President Ronald Reagan shakes hand with Glenn Holmes of Mt. Oliver at Control Data

headline: 1. Except Women    2. Minus Number One
abstract: 1. It is widely recognized that there are more women in the labor force than ever before but it is less apparent that women are the exception to trends in employment. There were fewer employed in every population group of the labor force except women. Thus recession is having a greater impact on male workers.  Borrowing to pay jobless claims is tagging PA No. 1 in the nation but in a negative way - the unemployment debt is the largest of any state in the country. It amounts to $2.9 billion and it is difficult to put a good face on such a distinction unless reliance is on the commonwealth generosity to those who lose their jobs.

headline: Why we need "right to know" law
abstract: Pennsylvania is one of the most chemical hazardous exposed state in the US, and those chemicals can cause serious health problems. However, PA does not have "right to know" laws, unlike in many other states. The article describes what are the advantages of "right to know" laws and why it is important for PA to have them.

headline: Assault Charges Against Schuykill Coal Man Dropped
abstract: Charges were dropped yesterday against County coal executive charged with pushing a state mine inspector into a chemical containment pond. There was not enough evidence to hold a trial.

headline: Panel Approves Welfare Bill
abstract: A bill that would undo the part of last year's "Thornfare" welfare law and restore 20,000 people to the state's cash assistance tolls was approved yesterday by the state House Health and Welfare Committee. The measure could cost an estimated $ 12 million to $13 million this fiscal year. The article talks about present law and the parts that are going to be changed.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon depicts an oval cabinet in the White House together with the hole in the ground right below the White House. In the hole is an animal printing the papers saying "Reagan for president". The cartoon is probably trying to depicts atmosphere for presidential elections (1984) that are approaching.

headline: Rearrest of Montco sheriff assailed
abstract: Attorneys for Montgomery County Sheriff Hill and his former aide Reed, yesterday accused District Attorney Smyth of abusing his discretion in ordering their clients rearrested on election-code violation charges that had been dismissed last month. The attorneys made an "angry" statement on charges of violating the state election code and conspiracy.

headline: Bill introduced to rescue state's municipal pensions
abstract: Pennsylvania state Senator Edward Howard has introduced legislation to rescue the state's municipal pensions. According the Howard, PA has nearly two-thirds of the nation's municipal pension systems and half of them are in trouble. The proposed legislation would force municipalities to for the first time to set aside reserves for pension obligations. Identical legislation will be introduced in the House.

headline: 4 municipal unions decry mayor's plan for disbursing "jobs bill" funds
abstract: Leaders of four municipal labors unions yesterday denounced the Green administration' plan for spending $21.5 million allocated to the city in a federal "jobs bill". According to plan, the 40% of the money will be spent of housing. Unions think that the funds should be used to directly aid the city work force, which they said was being depleted through budget cuts and attrition.

headline: Woman's Ailment Caused by Dump?
abstract: A northeastern Pennsylvania woman is the second person to come to the attention of state investigators because of a rare respiratory ailment that may be linked to an illegal toxic waste storage site in the Pocono Mountains. The article continues mostly with her comments and reactions about this situation.

headline: Banks given death penalty
abstract: A jury sentenced former prison guard George Banks to death for his 12 first degree murder convictions (he killed 13 people). There was heavy tension in the court during the reading of the sentence.

headline: Panel passes repeal of benefit cut
abstract: The PA House Health and Welfare Committee approved a bill that restores full benefits to able-bodied welfare recipients, who now are limited to three months of benefits each year. Some members of the committee warned that the measure could jeopardize the entire program because it is not in the compliance with the federal law.

headline: null
abstract: An article is sharp criticism of the state General Assembly in a way it claims they do nothing - they only spend taxpayers money. The article lists their mistakes and costs they caused to taxpayers.

headline: Rebuttals come more quickly now
abstract: Opposing views are now coming more often on Capitol Hill with respect to different issues. One of them is a proposal to prohibit the oil companies from owning gasoline stations. The next example is discusses  marijuana use.

headline: Crafton's resignation is sought
abstract: Barry Jagoda, a spokesman for George Washington University, says the university wants Arthur Crafton to resign because of accusations he taught at two Pennsylvania colleges while on the staff. Crafton was sent a letter that expressed the university's concerns, it was the first of several steps in the formal termination process.

headline: 700 Will lose Jobs in Lebanon
abstract: Almost 700 people will be laid off when Bethlehem Steel Corp. begins a shutdown at its local plant for an "indefinite" period of time, due to non-competitive production costs and low demand. Local officials expressed deep concern regarding the impact of the shutdown. However, this is not the first shutdown-last year there were seven shutdowns.

headline: Work Has Begun On New Offices For GPU Nuclear
abstract: Construction started yesterday on a 14,200-square-foot for office building that will be leased to the operator of Three Miles Island for its environmental controls and off-site emergency operations. The new room will provide more room for the department which currently leases the building at the Harrisburg International Airport.

headline: Banks guilty of murders in 1st degree
abstract: George Banks was found guilty yesterday of 12 counts of first-degree murder and one count of third-degree murder in the massacre last fall of 13 people, including five of his own children. He sat impassively between two sheriff's deputies as the verdicts were read. The prosecution will seek a death sentence.

headline: Payments again may be delayed
abstract: State officials might be forced to delay issuing 33,073 more welfare checks today as the General Assembly and Governor Thornburgh remain deadlocked over a budget for the fiscal year that began last year. The state Treasurer said that checks would be processed but not sent out if an agreement on the budget were not reached.

headline: null
abstract: An author defends his proposal of the popular election of utility regulators that was criticized by KDKA. His idea is that the election of commissioners would place a burden of accountability of those elected.

headline: Reduce PUC To Three, Kury Urges
abstract: Former Democratic state senator, urged the Legislature to reduce Public Utility Commission to three members, noting that there are two vacancies and "no apparent replacement nominations in sight". He said the changes would benefit consumers and the public interest. He also points out that three commissioners can operate as effectively as five.

headline: The candidates do delicate dance on crime issue
abstract: The 1983 Philadelphia mayoral campaign provides examples of the various wonders politicians can come up with when given statistics. When questioned about crime, candidates Wilson Goode, Frank Rizzo, Dougherty, Egan and Gola each provide different answers and solutions relating to the city's crime issue.

headline: A criminal element emerges amid Soviet immigrants
abstract: Between 200 and 250 arrests involving Russian immigrants have occurred in Philadelphia over the last three years - one of the Philadelphia Police officers said. Also, every major investigation in Russian community seems to yield the same suspects, and those suspects seemed to move regularly between Philadelphia and New York. That is the trend across the nation and a lot of immigrants are coming from Odesa, the Ukrainian part of Soviet Union.

headline: 26 who ignored TMI subpoenas scheduled for court hearing
abstract: Former and current employees of Three Mile Island have been ordered to appear before federal court to show why they also should not be ordered to cooperate with Nuclear Regulatory Commission investigation. The commission is investigating alleged falsification of the test data prior to the 1979 accident.

headline: Banks reporting restrictions spark press-freedom battle
abstract: A judge's restrictions on reporters and photographers covering the murder trial of George Banks are the subject of a complaint now before the U.S. Supreme Court. The issue arose over rules imposed by Luzerne county Judge Patrick Toole "to protect and promote the privacy and security of the jury".

headline: Penna.'s budget impasse, and its human fallout, linger
abstract: Because of the budget impasse many people did not get their welfare checks on time and they are now waiting in the huge lines in order to pick their checks. Several of them have negative comments about the Governor and lawmakers that did not pass the budget on time.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Thornburgh is sending a letter to chairmen of Republican and Democratic Committees where he urges them to make every effort in choosing candidates for upcoming judicial elections next week. He says that if the parties will not come together to at least cross-endorse such judges (two mentioned judges were appointed by bipartisan merit), it will make it even more difficult to interest good people in seeking judgeships in the future.

headline: Reducing PUC to 3 members, reforms urged
abstract: Former Democratic state senator, urged the Legislature to reduce Public Utility Commission to three members, noting that there are two vacancies and "no apparent replacement nominations in sight". He said the changes would benefit consumers and the public interest. He also points out that three commissioners can operate as effectively as five.

headline: Let Judge Candidates Speak Out
abstract: Chairman of the Senate State Government Committee disagrees with some issues addressed in a former article regarding judges. The chairman believes not allowing judges to speak out on controversial topics is not a good element of the judicial election process.

headline: A formidable pair
abstract: An article talks about surprising deal between Pennsylvania Chamber of Commerce president and state AFL-CIO President. The deal may sound very strange, but the Unemployment Compensation reform is the direct result of their behaving civil toward one another and even ending to like each other. The article discusses whether such a constructive cooperation can go on?

headline: 5 reactors ordered shut down
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission's order to shut down five reactors for inspection and repair of possibility severe pipe cracks will carry a multimillion-dollar price tag for the utility industry. This was caused by growing evidence of dangerous corrosion and cracking in crucial reactor culling water.

headline: Banks: Cops Slew Some of 13
abstract: The defense rested its case in the trial of accused mass murderer George Banks, who testified he could see the slayings of 13 people taking place before his eyes but was helpless to stop them. Banks, described the shootings but charged authorities killed nine of the victims and mutilated their bodies to make the crimes appear more gruesome.

headline: Poor Penalized As Poverty
abstract: When Community Action Pittsburgh (CAP) was ordered shut down by the state seven weeks ago, it was promised to that no vital services to elderly and low-income city residents would be interrupted. But it has not worked that way, critics charge. CAP is forced to abandon certain activities, and they depend on state's promise.

headline: Board certifies pensions For Retired State Workers
abstract: An article lists "higher than normal annuities" certified by the board at recent meeting of the State Employees' Retirement Board. The Board certified payments to beneficiaries of seven deceased employees as well and payments are listed in the article.

headline: Refused debate
abstract: The letter to the editor says: "Now you see why Governor Thornburgh refused to debate. It is amazing what is said in election years and non-election years. I can hardly wait for the next election."

headline: Flaherty's Issues
abstract: Letter writer James Kent is misinformed when he attacks Councilman Tom Flaherty for not having passed any substantial legislation during his term.

headline: AFL-CIO to air problems of jobless
abstract: Health and housing finance programs for people who are out of the work will be high on the agenda at the 24th annual convention of Pennsylvania's major unions. Among the measures to be considered by the delegates, who will be attending the convention are recommendations that call for the state to fund emergency health insurance plans for the unemployed, and for some kind of help to prevent jobless from losing their homes because they cannot afford mortgage payments.

headline: A head rolls gently at TMI
abstract: Robert Arnold resigned as president of General Public Utilities that operates Three Mile Island nuclear power plant. The article talks about the management personnel in the General Public Utilities, skepticism of Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and all that in aspect of accident from 1979.

headline: Bar Ass. Stumbles In Rating Judges
abstract: An article is talking about how Pennsylvania Bar Association can asses some candidates as "well qualified", but many of them do not do well later in elections. An article lists a lot of example that support that, and it concludes that the current assessment of certain candidates for Supreme Court could have similar destiny.

headline: Protesters' ouster at Capitol sought
abstract: State representative Piccola asked Governor Thornburgh to order removal of welfare demonstrators form the Capitol Rotunda and provide them with more suitable space elsewhere if they continues the "sit-in". The demonstrators have been camping in the Rotunda for few days because of the Welfare Reform Act of 1982 (by law, able bodied people from 18 to 45 years old were reduced to three months of welfare benefits per year).

headline: null
abstract: Harrisburg lawyer Schwartz yesterday defeated Superior Court Judge Vincent A. Cirillo for the state Supreme Court endorsement. The article continues with detail analysis of votes received and comments of both candidates.

headline: Review of Court Puzzles Justice
abstract: Supreme Court's financial and personnel records are to be a subject to public scrutiny, according to resolution introduced by two state senators. Idea is that court should be subject to scrutiny as two other branches of government are, and the resolution proposes a committee that would review all courts in commonwealth. Proponents of the resolution say that this is not an answer to the Supreme Court's handling of investigation into the conduct of Justice Rolf Larsen, and it is not intended to be an inquiry into the Larsen matter.

headline: Thornfare Hurts
abstract: The Hunger Action Coaltion is helping community organizations, churches, labor unions, and politicans to repeal Act 75 also known asThornfare. The Act is resulting in 20,000 people in Allegheny County being cut off the welfare roles.

headline: AFSCME to seek agency shop as negotiable option
abstract: An attempt will be made next week to get the Legislature to authorize discussion of an agency shop in the future contract negotiations between commonwealth and its employee unions. The shop concept is not negotiable in current contract talks. Under an agency show, employees covered by a contract need not join the union involved, but must pay the union amount equal to dues charged.

headline: A misguided utility exemption
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate has before it bill which many legislators support but which none understands. The bill is undesirable on principle, unclear in intent and application and uncertain in impact. Our industry is obligated to ask whether the public interest is being served appropriately in such cases and to point out effects on other customers of preferential treatment to particular groups. (The bill would require a public utility to permit places of worship and fire companies, including volunteer fire companies, the option of having electricity measured by the method used for residential customers).

headline: Bar Wants Larsen Probe Details
abstract: The Pennsylvania Bar Association says it will sue, if necessary, to make public the findings of an investigation of state Supreme Court Justice Larsen. The investigation,  involving charges of misconduct, was due to end today. The board was expected to vote 6-3 to clear Larsen of alleged improper political activity.

headline: Protesters Push Fight On Welfare
abstract: Welfare demonstrators, insulted by their eviction for the state Capitol Rotunda, said that they plan to take their protest to the Capitol again today. They have been calling for repeal of a 1982 welfare-reform law that removed "able-bodied" people between the ages 18 and 45 from year-round cash assistance.

headline: null
abstract: The author of this letter sharply criticizes Governor Thornburgh and his distribution of lottery funds. The money should be only for the elderly people but it seems that the Governor does not think so.

headline: Rizzo nears decision on mayoral endorsement
abstract: Frank l. Rizzo, defeated in his quest for a third term as a mayor by W. Wilson Goode in the May 17 Democratic primary, is on the verge of deciding whom, if anyone, he will support in the general election and is likely to announce his decision next week. Some close to Rizzo say he will support Goode.

headline: Miracle Cure
abstract: After nine years of total disability Bill Jaehne received his termination of social security benefits.

headline: After years of feuding, AFL-CIO and chamber find accord
abstract: After a decades of fighting, a kind of peace has broken out in recent months between two old antagonists - PA Chamber of Commerce and the PA AFL-CIO, the major business and labor groups in the state. The new atmosphere has produced one landmark agreement, a multi-billion settlement in July on how to deal with PA's debt-ridden Unemployment Compensation Trust Fund.

headline: An assurance from the NRC
abstract: Director of Public Affairs office at Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is defending NRC against previously published criticism that investigative and inspection activities in NRC are poor. An author of the letter further lists arguments in support of his opinion.

headline: Bargain Justice
abstract: In Philadelphia, Private Civil Courts Will Compete with the Jammed Public System and that is going to be country's first private court system. The purpose of this system is to try to solve cases faster than the public system.

headline: Rally planned to support "Economic bill of Rights"
abstract: Representatives of labor, consumers and religious groups have called for legislative approval of a 10-point "Pennsylvania Economic Bill" to help the needy. Organizers of a June 15 " Jobs and Justice Day" rally at Capitol this week unveiled their plan to help the unemployed, senior citizens and low-income people.

headline: null
abstract: The comic cartoon depicts a person approaching ballot and he is making a comment related to candidate Goode (Philadelphia mayoral elections).

headline: Rizzo Plans To Endorse A Candidate
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo has scheduled a news conference Monday to endorse a mayoral candidate in the November general election. Wilson Goode, who defeated Rizzo for the Democratic nomination for Mayor in the city's May 17 primary, has said he expects Rizzo's endorsement because of Rizzo's loyalty to the party.

headline: '78 Brush Fire Sparked Career for Distaff Chief
abstract: A 1978 brush fire ignited a new career for Penny Haney, believed to be Pennsylvania's only female fire chief. Mrs. Haney says women firefighters make the the gang more efficient.

headline: Business, Labor Will Seek Joint Solution to UC Debt
abstract: Business and labor interests, setting aside traditional animosities, said they will seek a common solution to the state $ 3 million debt in unemployment compensation fund.

headline: Arnold leaves the post for good of TMI
abstract: Robert  C. Arnold, the president of the General Public Utility Nuclear Corp. (GPU) (operator of the Three Mile Island) has resigned two weeks ago, and he was one more among many others "sacrificial lambs". An article analyses that act, management crisis in the GPU, and all that in the light of possible restart of the undamaged (from 1979 accident)  Unit 1 reactor.

headline: Beating Death Conviction Appealed by Naylor
abstract: Jo Ellen Naylor yesterday appealed her conviction and sentencing in the beating death of her 5-year-old daughter to the state Superior Court. She raised 23 questions about handling of the case.

headline: Readied for Delivery
abstract: The picture shows workers in the Treasury Department's Bureau of Public Assistance Disbursements. Workers are loading sacks of welfare checks for delivery to recipients.

headline: null
abstract: This short article mentions with interest that Governor Thornburgh is maybe shooting for a spot in presidential 1984 elections. An article continues with sarcasm of current unemployment problems in PA and the idea of Governor running for president. Furthermore, an article mentions problems related to parking meters and to Bell Telephone credit cards.

headline: Rizzo's Aide Questions Goode's "Judgment" on Prison Registration
abstract: The right of prison inmates to participate in elections seems to have been a dead issue until former Mayor Rizzo briefly put former city Managing Director Goode on the defensive during the TV debate. Rizzo accused Goode campaign of signing up prisoners to vote in the May 17 Democratic mayoral primary. Goode denied claims saying that the Rizzo himself had signed the court-ordered consent decree, that gave inmates (1974) awaiting trial - the right to register and vote by absentee ballot.

headline: The Primary Problem is their Stony Silence
abstract: The May 17 primary is around the corner and all the candidates have officially filed, but they have hardly mentioned their approach to to solving many of the real problems that are of concern to voters.

headline: California teacher strike splits, embitters unionists
abstract: Although local steel and mine workers union leaders have pledged their support to teacher involved in the state's longest public school strike, those leaders do not have the backing of some of their members. The insistence by teachers that the contract retain a no-layoff clause has embittered many union employees.

headline: Arnold reassigned in TMI job shuffle
abstract: General Public Utilities Corp. today announced a revamp of its management structure at Three Mile Island, including the reassignment of Robert Arnold, who has headed the nuclear station since the 1979 accident. The article continues with managerial changes in Three Mile Island.

headline: Beyond power of legislation
abstract: There is a bill proposal in Pennsylvania General Assembly that would require a witness to a sexual assault to report it to the police immediately. The similar bill is already enacted in Rhode Island. The editor thinks that this is not the good bill since sometimes victims choose not to make public the pain and the humiliation of their victimization.

headline: Reagan policies are talking food out of the months of the poor
abstract: This article is a sharp criticism of President Reagan's policy toward poor people. It starts with statistics that reveal that the number of poor people increased in last year in U.S. and then continues with individual Reagan's acts that are not helping the poor people, but are in fact hurting poor people).

headline: "Ghost Voting:" a Legislative Trick or Treat
abstract: The issue of the article is the voting in behalf of the members who are not on the floor. Someone else pushes their voting switch and this is the violation of the House rules. However, legislators are not too much worried about that, and every time they look the "other way". The author argues that this practice should be abandoned.

headline: Running - Foerster still running, assails "plunking"…
abstract: Despite his previous pledges to support the endorsed Democratic slate, county Commissioner Foerster filed his nominating petitions yesterday for re-election. He lost endorsement in a dramatic upset to Commissioner Wrecht. Foerster accused the Democratic Committee members for plunk, or vote for one instead for two candidates. Wrecht denied charges.

headline: null
abstract: Daddy has to support a habit.

headline: Canada work-share plan could save U.S. jobs
abstract: Canada is developing fresh ideas on how to reduce its unemployment from 12 percent to 6 percent and the author of the article thinks these Canadian ideas deserve a study from the U.S. The basic idea of the proposal is that people who how have a job are willing to share work and income with the jobless. The article continues with analysis of this idea.

headline: Atom trial: New Doubts
abstract: The out-of-court settlement that brought an abrupt end to the trial over the responsibility for the Three Miles Island nuclear accident left many questions unanswered, especially the question of guilt. A statement accompanying the settlement said that "it would be counterproductive to incur the substantial costs of further litigation". But the trial could provide insights into shortcomings of both manufacturer and utility that were not available before. NRC is not commenting the trial.

headline: Bill creating legal fund for poor is approved in Senate committee
abstract: Despite oppositions from some lawyers groups, the Senate Judiciary Committee approved a bill creating the new voluntary system to fund legal services for the poor. The similar funds already exist in some other states and bill now goes to the full Senate.

headline: Rebate Proposed To Cut Property tax
abstract: State Senator edward M. Early unveiled a legislative proposal which would grant low and moderate- income families and the unemployed "long overdue relief from excessive property taxes". The measure would provide a state income tax credit up to $500 to any individual or family whose local real estate taxes in any given year exceeded 3.5 percent of total household income. The rebates would be financed by raising the income tax rate.

headline: "Green" Board Could End Thomas Tenure
abstract: Three potential candidates have emerged as possible challengers to the 10-year reign of school board President Thomas in board elections to be held Dec.6. The main behind-the-scene battle for the top spot on the nine-member panel is shaping up among appointees of outgoing mayor Green, according to board members.

headline: Sale of  free information by Senate staffers probed
abstract: Attorney general says he is investigating allegations that some Senate staff members responsible for "support services" used their work and state supplies and equipment for " personal purposes". There is a possibility that employees in the Senate bill room are providing the lobbyists and others with certain services in exchange for the money.

headline: State lottery is being probed
abstract: The administation of the Pennsylvania state lottery is under investigation by the Consumer Affairs Committee of the State House of Representatives.

headline: Ending Violence
abstract: The University of PA's Wharton School (which concentrates on teaching business) recently issued a report showing violence has become "a pervasive aspect of labor relations" and urged for the reform. They found the violence is directed at "third parties" who run competitive non-union operations. They charged that the change is needed the most on the part of those who are making the laws. The problem is that law's tacit approval of minor violence only serves to guarantee its recurrence.

headline: Buy cheaper gas, utilities urged
abstract: A consumer groups says four Pennsylvania utilities could save customers $41 million next year by shopping around for cheaper natural gas. But utilities insist they are locked into costly contracts they were forced to sigh with natural gas suppliers to ensure adequate reserves during the gas shortage of the late 1970s. PennPIC is calling on the state Legislature to pass a bill that would abolish the Gas Cost Rate and require utilities to purchase the cheapest gas on the market.

headline: Bill Pinpoints Fire-Unit Aid
abstract: State representative Foster intends to introduce a bill that would insure that the local fire companies get their due share of reimbursement from taxes collected on fire insurance premiums. He said the funds are frequently forwarded to the wrong municipalities when insurance agents list insured properties by post office addresses rather than by the municipalities where the properties are situated. The proposal, however, could adversely affect the communities that have large amounts of tax-exempt property, including Harrisburg and other areas with heavy concentration of states and charitable facilities.

headline: Schedule Announced For Welfare Checks
abstract: Public Welfare Department officials have announced the schedule for distribution of welfare checks that were withheld since July 1 while the state was without a budget and the power to spend the money. The Secretary of the Department said checks will be distributed in few days.

headline: "Hyping" the lottery
abstract: For two PA state senators the success of the state lottery program system, especially in attracting new bettors is a cause for alarm. They worry that "hard sell" advertising for the game amounts to exploitation of elderly people and other Pennsylvanians who would be better off husbanding their meager resources. Their reasoning is not a ridiculous argument (they claimed that some players would be profligate in their wagering), but the lottery is established anyway because such apprehensions were outweighed by the belief, which has been vindicated, that it would produce a windfall for senior citizens.

headline: Say cheese..
abstract: The House's month-long cheese hearings are over and they investigated the evidence of mismanagement or favoritism that supposedly plague the state's surplus food giveaway. Republicans and Democrats are thinking differently about results of the hearings and the article continues with more details of the investigation.

headline: The Record from Birth to Arrest
abstract: Paul Arthur Crafton's chronology from birth to his arrest

headline: Extension Welfare
abstract: Unemployment compensation was designed to help people during interim periods of joblessness. It was not designed as a welfare program for long term responses. Congress has repeatedly extended benefits, motivated by the economic adversity generated by the past recession.

headline: Chairman quits TMI citizens panel
abstract: The Chairman of the Three Mile Island (TMI) citizens advisory panel, said he is resigning because he can no longer remain neutral on issues dealing with the nuclear plant. He pointed out in his letter to the chairman of Nuclear Regulatory Commission, that the main reason he is resigning is the slowness of he TMI clean up. The reason for the slowness is the shortage of money.

headline: Bill to Ban Teflon Bullets Is Introduced
abstract: Teflon-coated bullets, known as "cop killers" for their ability rip through bulletproof vests, would be outlawed in the state under legislation unveiled yesterday. Although no police officer was killed so far. "we cannot wait until a police officer has been killed trying to protect innocent citizens", says the bill's sponsor.

headline: Second-Car Grant Denied York  Welfare mother turned down on appeal
abstract: Commonwealth Court has upheld the state Public Welfare Department denying a York County welfare mother's application for a special one-time grant to purchase an automobile. She already owned a car, state inspected and operable. She was receiving public assistance for the and her twins and was seeking a grant to buy a car under department regulations in order to transport her twins to a day care center and herself to work.

headline: "New Rizzo" plan was a bow to posterity
abstract: An article depicts a candidate for mayor of Philadelphia - Rizzo. He lost primary election, but an article depicts him in a positive light. It starts from the beginning of his political career, and it ends up with this election that he lost. The main point is that Rizzo has changed his image and his style (while younger he was energetic (as a tiger) and he could dismantle many political opponents) and that affected this election defeat.

headline: Scanlon's switcheroo
abstract: Robert G. Scanlon, former Education Secretary resigned abruptly from a state human resources position that he had held for less than a week. There are two possible interpretations of this act: "rank ingratitude' and "poetic justice". First one describes this act in negative manner and is especially criticized by Gov. Thornburgh staff, and the second describes  him as badly behaving in his former career and being often in on controversial  issues.

headline: State Defends 400G Legal Fee
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh's chief lawyer, Jay Waldman, defended a $400,000 contract with a politically connected Philadelphia law firm Dilworth, Paxson, Kalish, and Kauffman. The firm is handling a state suit against the builders of a Pittsburgh convention center. State Representative Max Pievsky, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee accused Thornburgh's administation of creating a pinstripe patronage system by hiring the Philadlephia firm.

headline: Fact-finding eyed in teacher strike
abstract: A special mediator appointed by the governor today was to consider a school board request for fact-finding in the California Area teachers strike. Teachers say they want a resumption of talks to end their bitter walkout. However, the Union had no comment on a board proposal that special state mediator order fact-finding the dispute.

headline: Change of coal rule probed again
abstract: Repeating previous allegations, Democratic lawmakers yesterday accused the Thornburgh administration of changing a coal regulation to please coal companies. An administration official denied the charge. The allegations were raised in the House Conservation Committee.

headline: Breaking prison drug links "hard"
abstract: This editorial describes a letter that was received from a prison inmate who is describing his drug addiction and the circumstances in the prison related to drugs. The point is that the  prisons are overcrowded and that many inmates are there because of drug charges. He describes several prison programs aimed to help drug addicted persons, and the families and personal life ties that are very important form quitting the addiction. However, the money is the main reason why quitting is very hard-many dealers make very easily $1,000 per week and they do not have enough incentives to do some other less paid job.

headline: Senate gets bill extending benefits of lottery to those who are excluded
