abstract: Governor Thornburgh's budget message to a joint session of legislature, and the details of accompanying budget proposals for the fiscal year beginning July 1, are flawed not so much by what he said and proposed but by what he failed to say and propose. He glossed over our fundamental realities: a current budget deficit, jobless Pennsylvanians and the fact that PA is among the hardest hit states in the national recession. These and other shortcomings in the governor's proposals do not prevent or excuse legislature from meeting its responsibilities.

headline: U.S. Steel to Close 3 Plants, Paper Says
abstract: The corporation, plagued by large losses in its steel business, plans to shut down three major plants and lay off as many as 10,000 workers, according to a weekly business publication.

headline: Outdated nuclear act needs thorough overhaul
abstract: The article talks about the necessity for changing the Price Anderson Act that is 26-year-old. The main issues are risks of catastrophic losses from utilities and the degree of liability. There are many reasons for the improvement of this bill and the article describes them.

headline: Enforce the Death Penalty
abstract: Since the 1978, the PA state has had a valid death penalty and under the law 20 people have been sentenced to die. But one has been executed, and none is likely to be put to death in the near future. The law is being locked endlessly by defense appeals and there is no sure punishment. We think it is the high priority to deal with this problem, since securing justice is the only part of the story.

headline: Quarterback Doran
abstract: City representative Dick Doran plays leads delegation to Washington for meetings the Secretaries of the Army and the Navy and his goal is to keep annual Army navy game in Philadelphia. But we are afraid that Philadelphia will drop the ball by taking the Army Navy Game for granted. That event could boost our economy since the Philadelphia will have 1500 hotel rooms ready for the game.

headline: Census Bureau Data Hard To Accept
abstract: PA, now the nation's fourth most populous state, will be passed by Florida by the year 2000 - just 17 years from now- according to U.S. Census Bureau projections. There are many reasons for that and one of them are high energy costs in the 1970 that caused many people from the northern states to move south and west. However, nobody knows what the impact of the energy costs will be in the future.

headline: They Came Not to Praise
abstract: Not only there was no one to offer an endorsement for Republican mayoral candidate John J. Egan, but there was not Egan himself to accept the endorsement. The event occurred at the Center City headquarters, and 20 minutes after the news conference was about to start, Egan's aide came and said something was wrong.

headline: Emissions Bill creates Warfare in Harrisburg
abstract: Pennsylvania state House Democrats and Senate Republicans current battle is more about political influence more than about saving $500 million in federal highway funds for Pennsylvania. Until the legislature lifts the ban on emissions inspections, highway projects in the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh regions will remain frozen under federal court order.

headline: Governors' group calls on Reagan to slash deficits
abstract: Leaders of the National Association called on the Federal Government to reduce  military spending, maintain the current level of social welfare spending and consider raising taxes to slash the Federal budget deficit over the next five years. It was the most comprehensive statement to date on federal fiscal policies. The proposal warned the Federal Government that large deficits could cause it to compete with large borrowers. Various governors described in detail why this is a necessary move.

headline: UC Plan May Go to Conferees Today
abstract: Legislation that would enact a solvency plan for the ailing jobless fund is expected to be introduced before a House-Senate conference committee today. The article continues with the description of the proposal in more details.

headline: Owner of TMI seeks a meeting on plant repairs
abstract: The owner of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant has asked that a public meeting be held in Harrisburg on the repairs that were made to Unit 1's steam generator tubes. The meeting would be part of three step process leading to the NRC approval of a license amendment for Unit 1, permitting it to operate with the repaired tubes.

headline: Error put Pa. escapee in low-security California prison
abstract: A Pennsylvanian sought on charges of slaying four people after escaping from a California prison had been placed in the low-security prison because California officials - who had been told of his previous escape from a Pennsylvania mental institution - had misfiled warnings about him.

headline: Science Center Helps Renewal in Philadelphia
abstract: Governor Thornburgh went to Philadelphia to pay tribute and give $250 thousand check to a research center that is also one the city's most successful urban renewal projects. The check is a matching grant to help pay for a project to be called Advanced Technology Center of Southern Pennsylvania Center.

headline: Chairmanship of Democratic Party is likely first battle for Rizzo, Goode
abstract: An initial confrontation between Democratic mayoral candidates Rizzo and Goode appeared to be taking shape yesterday as the candidates headed toward a battle over who will be the chairman of the Democratic City Committee. A new candidate will be chosen tomorrow evening. The article continues description of both candidates and their chances to win following elections for Philadelphia mayor.

headline: Thornburgh Lashed On Use Of Mansion
abstract: A letter writer depicts Jane Ellen Rosenberger's story on governor's usage of Executive mansion for private purposes (an act that was criticized by State Commission for Ethics). The Governor was strongly advocating creation of Ethics Commission and now he is calling its action partisan. Letter continues with a sharp critique of governor.

headline: Twin-trailer law unites 11 states
abstract: Pennsylvania united with 11 other eastern states to confront the Federal Highway Administration over its new law allowing twin-trailer trucks to ride along primary roads.

headline: Governors to Reagan: Slash arms spending
abstract: Governors across the nation said yesterday that Reagan must rein in federal deficits by slashing his defense buildup by at least half while eyeing tax increases that " do not unfairly burden already hard-pressed lower and middle classed Americans". A resolution was handed to Congress and the President met with governors. After the meeting Reagan was described as "angry and adamant".

headline: UC plan shares the load
abstract: The agreement reached on a bailout proposal of the state's Unemployment Compensation Fund is a painful but necessary compromise on one of the most serious and pressing problems facing PA. The compromise represents a breakthrough from the traditional dependence on business as the basic means of support for unemployment compensation. Employers will continues to pay heavily, but for the first time workers and unemployed will share the burden.

headline: Panel to vote today on PE's rate proposal
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission is scheduled to decide today whether Philadelphia Electric Co. (PE) should be granted 2 $228 million rate increase. PE filed for the increase because of the maintenance expenses. The plan would also raise the rate that consumers are paying.

headline: Ex-aide fired over tax checks sentenced
abstract: John S. Bell will be punished for his misdeeds. He cost Allegheny County $1.4 million in fines and interest from  1979 to 1981 - for some unexplained reasons - stuffing checks into his desk drawer that were supposed to be sent to Harrisburg to cover employee state income tax withholdings. He is sentenced to pay a fine, to serve in community halfway house and to be on probation for 4 years. Still remaining is the mystery of why Bell did it.

headline: State mortgage bill curtails aid program
abstract: The bill that is mortgage foreclosure prevention law is passed by lawmakers  and it would curtail sharply a program that has been giving tax breaks for 16 years to companies offering aid to impoverished neighborhoods. The bill is at the Governor's table. The article have more details about the bill and it has few quotes from lawmakers that address the bill.

headline: Choices narrowed down in appellate court races
abstract: While the most attention in the coming political season will be directed to local elections, voters also will be confronted with choices that will help shape the state's appellate courts for the next 10 years. Technically nine seats among the three courts will be on the ballot. The article continues further with more details about judicial elections and candidates.

headline: Thornburgh Taps Ryan
abstract: Merle H. Ryan of Camp Hill has been appointed Deputy Secretary of public works in the Department of General Services, Gov. Thornburgh announced yesterday. He will oversee all state-funded and bond-financed construction projects in excess of $25,000.

headline: Newcomers, Veterans Race for Appellate Seat
abstract: Pennsylvania Republicans and Democrats each will nominate one candidate for Supreme Court, five for Superior Court and two candidates for vacancies on Commonwealth Court. Some have run this race before, other are new to the game.

headline: State hospital cutbacks
abstract: The Pennsylvania Welfare Department plans to close the Dixmont State Hostpital and the Western Restoration Center, which are both mental hospitals.  This editorial is willing to support the cutbacks in the name of economic efficiency, but not if the former patients are put into the streets and left to wander.

headline: NRC rejects low-power start of Diablo Canyon
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission rejected a request for a low power operating license for the problem-plagued Diablo Canyon. Questions were raised regarding whether 14 miles of pipes where installed correctly and if the those operating the plants obtained appropriate level of experience.

headline: Justification through the law
abstract: This editorial suggests that if there is another trial in the case of the anti-nuclear advocates who broke into a General Electric plant in King of Prussia and damaged nuclear missiles, the Pennsylvania appellate court should not allow for a liberal interpretation of the PA law known as a "justification law."  The law says that certain actions normally defined as criminal in certain instances may be justified, but this editorial piece makes the argument that the activists' anti-war sentiment in this case, no matter how firmly it was held, does not justify their actions.

headline: Mortgage assistance program is keeping telephone lines busy
abstract: A Pennsylvania hot line that provides information about a new mortgage foreclosure relief lay has been expanded to handle the great number of calls.

headline: Ethics committee change disputed
abstract: The PA State ethics commission replaced its Democrat chairman Paul J. Smith with Republican appointee Herbert B. Conner but may have violated the 1974 Sunshine Law requiring agencies to conduct formal business.

headline: Sen. Specter backs use of artificial heart
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter says he will urge the federal government to approve Hershey Medical Center's request to use a short-term artificial heart in humans.

headline: Struggle to shut Pennhurst again hits snag
abstract: The federal Health Care Financing Administration said it has rejected the waivers for four Philadelphia-area counties to divert Medicare money from large institutions to community living arrangements because of irregularities in current CLAs in Philadelphia. Lawsuits such as Pennshurst case provided the public exposure and pressure to force the closings. The story of Pennhurst is the story of the nationwide struggle to shift retarded people to CLAs.

headline: NRC sets 'last' TMI restart hearing
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh plans to have a final public hearing on whether the Three Mile Island Unit I reactor should be restarted.  The article provides the details of the agenda for the public hearing and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's views on the issue.

headline: K-9 attacks off sharply since April report
abstract: Philadelphia Police Department K-9 dogs attacked six citizens in a four month period, which was an 88 percent decline from 1982.  This decrease is after the "Philadelphia Inquirer" reported that the police lost control of their dogs and allowed them to attack an unarmed man and woman.  The article goes further into detail about the four month period study and how the police department has changed its tactics.

headline: Movement to Legalize Casinos In More States Appears Stalled
abstract: After New Jersey legalized gambling, it was expected that several other states would follow.  The article discusses why other states have not followed New Jersey's Atlantic City, and what "Wall Street" analysts have to say about the gambling industry.

headline: Eyes, odds on Al Benedict
abstract: How candidate Al Benedict will fare in Southwest and the Southeast may tell at a glance whether he won or lost, even before the bulk of the statewide resutls are compiled.  Most believe that Benedict is the person to beat in the April 10 Democratic primary for the state treasurer nomination.

headline: Senate may OK PUC nominees
abstract: Two long-standing vacancies on the five-member Public Utilities Commission could be filled as early as this week, legislative sources say.  The nominees are William R. Shane of Indiana, a former PA state House Democrat who was chief administrative law judge for the PUC, and former Allentown mayor Frank Fischl.

headline: The press and cancer
abstract: The press should not to be blamed for public hysteria about all possible things leading to cancer. Instead, blame lies with alarmist scientists who either over or under state their findings. The press is only relying those findings. Furthermore, cancer is more likely to occur now because people are living to ages where they are more susceptible to the disease.

headline: NRC tied on TMI hazard issue
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission was unable to decide whether repairs on the Unit 1 steam generator tubes at Three Mile Island were potentially hazardous.

headline: Kerr is challenged on job applications
abstract: John Kerr, who testified on June 27, 1984 that he never took cash for jobs in the Auditor General's department, was challenged in the morning on June 28, 1984 in cross-examination. On June 27, 1984 John testified he received hand-delivered envelopes containg job applications from Michael Hanna, the Washington County Democratic Chairman who died shortly after being charged with job-selling. But Kerr said that he never received cash from Hanna.

headline: New Insurance law looks like bonanza for lawyers
abstract: Since the new insurance law became effective in Pennsylvania a lot of questions developed among policy makers. The most important ones concern the vehicle registration,  self-insurance, and medical benefits.

headline: Face-off
abstract: Both major party candidates running for PA state attorney general in 1984 - Ertel and Zimmerman - vowed on October 15 1984 to stay out of the race of governor in 1986. There is a photograph of ertel and Zimmerman who respond to question from the Post-Gazette. .

headline: Senate Oks bill to rescue municipal pension plans
abstract: The PA State Senate on November 29, 1984 passed a bill designed to rescue the 2,300 municipal pension plans in the state from underfunding problems and place them on sound actuarial footing. The final vote of 41-7 came in the dying hours of the current session.

headline: Va. firm gets contract on drug aid to elderly
abstract: The Computer Company, a subsidiary of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Virginia, won a $14.6 million contract to operate the prescription drug program for low-income, elderly Pennsylvanians. The contract is part of a $100 plan signed by PA Governor Thornburgh to help senior citizens purchase prescription drugs which will require senior citizens to pay $4 and the state to cover the balance. The average annual savings to seniors will be $180. Those who are eligible are single seniors with an income less than $9,000 and married couples with incomes below $12,000.

headline: NRC to disclose papers on TMI dispute
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission intends to release two documents that reveal an internal dispute over the significance of a September 1983 report on the Three Mile Island Unit 2 cleanup. The report found that the company tried to decontaminate Unit 2 and routinely violated atomic safety regulations.

headline: Kerr just a "fall guy", lawyer in job-selling trial
abstract: Former Deputy Auditor General John Kerr a "fall guy" in Pennsylvania political wars was framed by professional con men testifying for the prosecution. One of the prosecution witnesses pointed to Kerr as the "boss man" of a 200,000 job-selling operation in the Pittsburgh and Harrisburg offices of Auditor General Al Benedict.

headline: New levy taxes the imagination: No one wants to collect
abstract: The Thornburgh administration and the insurance industry both refused to take responsibility for the collection of a new $5 fee from motorists designed to pay the medical bills of injured motorists over $100,000.  The Governor's emergency regulations requiring the insurance industry to collect and the Court's order that that the state collect the fee are misaligned and many are confused about how the money will be collected.

headline: False PAC images
abstract: Those pundits who study Political Action Committees explode myths concerning their impact, but people keep on believing the PACs benefit the fat cats and keep the Republicans in office.

headline: Senate panel OK's Miller nomination
abstract: The PA Senate finance committee on May 22, 1984 reported favorably on the nomination of Stanley A. Miller to be a member of the state Board of Claims.

headline: Use of drug therapy rises-- as funds fall
abstract: Federal block grants for drug and alcohol programs in Pennsylvania are being cut by 18 percent, as record numbers of people are being referred for help. Part of the increase can be attributed to the state's new drunken driving law. PA Governor Thornburgh has asked state lawmakers for a 4 percent increase in drug and alcohol programs, yet most of the responsibility for making up for the lost funds will fall on the counties. PA state Representative Peter Wambach is pushing to raise by18 percent the tax on liquor and wine, one penny per 1.5 ounces or $10 million.

headline: NRC waiting game
abstract: This editorial argues that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has been exhaustive in its review and consideration of a restart at Three Mile Island, yet it has produced no results.

headline: Kerr to ask new trial in jobs-selling case
abstract: John Kerr's attorney will make an effort to win the former top aide to Auditor Al Benedict a new trial on charges he masterminded a job-selling scheme.

headline: Newspapers are eager to sell thir readers to liquor advertisers
abstract: On April 23, 1984 the Independent State Store union and other Pennsylvania state employees picketed the Post-Gazette. They are also going to picket Philadelphia Inquirer. They contend that newspapers' one-sided articles and editorials are inspired by the prospective revenues from liquor and wine advertisements.

headline: Family week
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh issued a proclamation, pointing out how family was recognized as the cornerstone of our society, in declaring on November 18, 1984 through November 24, 1984 as Family Week in Pennsylvania.

headline: Senate walks new ground to fight Street's opponent
abstract: The PA Senate rules committee is considering a historic resolution to have a Democratic candidate struck from the ballot in a Philadelphia senatorial district for allegedly not meeting the residency qualifications. The Senate has never before blocked a candidate from joining the Senate prior to an election. State Senate Democrats protested the action. However, Senate Republicans argue that the 4-2 state Supreme Court opinion, which Democrats formed the court's majority, says only the Senate itself has legal jurisdiction for testing the qualifications of its own members. Therefore, the Senate or House has the power to reject sitting members or even candidates when qualifications are not met. The race may determine who will control the state Senate after elections in November.

headline: Voices form across the USA/Do you think mental illness is a serious problem in America?
abstract: Mental illness is not as rare as it may seem at first. One in five can experience mental illness. Many people seek counseling - whether it is marital counseling, job-related, or interpersonal. As an illustration to the mental illness to which practically everyone can be subject to there are seven photographs of people from different professional spheres.

headline: Nuclear leaks worry commission
abstract: Members of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission agree that ruptures in steam generators at nuclear power plants were a problem but could not agree on how best to solve it.  More than 40 of the nation's 52 pressurized water reactors have suffered these leaks.  Staff members at the agency have urged the commission to survey utilities to find if they are taking appropriate safety measures.

headline: 'Know Who the Judges Are,' Blatt Tells Borough Officials
abstract: The senior judge on the Commonwealth Court, Judge Genevieve Blatt, told the PA State Association of Boroughs to know which judges are elected to appellate courts. These judges are important to local governments because they frequently have the last word when it comes to local problems.

headline: No special treatment
abstract: Lawmakers turn thousands of ideas, big and small, into bills that feed the legislative hopper. As an example, an amendment to the motor vehicle licensing code that would provide for a special license plate to be issued to the news reporters, struck the reporters who do not seek either favor from the government or teach them how to do their job.

headline: Ferraro in debate
abstract: Ferraro admitted that she has not debated since she graduated from high school and she express her concern that Bush could be a formidable debater than Reagan proved to be against Mondale on October 8, 1984.

headline: Senator authorizes audit of high court
abstract: A chairman of the PA Senate Appropriations Committee contracted a Philadelphia accounting firm to perform the first ever legislative audit of the state Supreme Court.  PA Senator Richard A. Tilghman said he awarded the contract to Ernst & Whinney at a cost of $45,000 on his own and not by action of the committee.

headline: $1.5 million plan would boost milk
abstract: Two years ago 83% of farmers rejected a 9-cent dairy assessment by 58-42 percent. However, a new proposal at 10-cent assessment  is gaining support from dairy producers. The tax will go towards a fund to promote PA dairy of all types. A 16 member board will oversee the promotion.

headline: Nuclear Plant Shutdowns
abstract: Shutdowns have occurred at Unit 1 at the Susquehanna nuclear electric power plant near Berwick. Once the bugs get worked out the public will be able to enjoy the benefits of the nuclear fuel economy.

headline: Kolter hails bullet train bill progress
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Judiciary administrative law and government relations subcommittee passed the bill granting a five-year study of bullet train service on May 9, 1984 with no debate. The measure's prime sponsor, representative Joseph Kolter said that he would not have expected the bill to pass at least for a few years.

headline: No state stores
abstract: The negative consequenses of the privatization of PA state liquor stores far outweigh the benefits that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh claims as he travels the state seeking support. It will be more difficult to curb corruption with 3,000 privately-owned stores compared to the 700 state-run ones now.  The letter pleads with fellow doubters to contact their state representatives.

headline: Ferraro says "Fritz has a plan"
abstract: The Democratic vice presidential candidate Geraldine Ferraro directed her criticism at the president. Ferraro gave a brief opening statement in Harrisburg area by saying that the inaccuracies of Reagan's media campaign would be exposed when he and Mondale would meet in the first of a series of televised debates.

headline: Senator pledges to recap lottery probe findings
abstract: The chairman of the PA Senate panel probing investment practices of the state lottery system said that he would issue a statement summarizing committee findings. PA state Senator Edward Howard, Republican, Bucks, Senate Finance Committee, said he was prepared to wrap up the inquiry.

headline: Avian Flu Seen Lasting for 5 Years
abstract: For 5 years Avian influenza has threatened Pennsylvania's $1 billion poultry business. State and federal officials have declared the PA's south-central and southeastern poultry producing counties a disaster area. All flocks with the infection are to be eradicated, however gaining compliance from framers in regards to quarantine rules remains a challenge for the federal-state Avian Flu Task Force. The federal government has authorized $82 million for poultrymen who lost birds in the eradication program. Pennsylvania has proposed $2 million to aid in cleaning farms. Vaccine development was recommended by the agricultural co-operative extension.

headline: Nuclear power dominos
abstract: The cancellation of the Midland nuclear power plant appeared to be another domino falling for a profoundly troubled nuclear power industry. The bad financial condition of the nuclear industry was underscored by the effort to rescue the Seabrook nuclear power unit 1 and public Service Company of new Hampshire from bankruptcy.

headline: Law offers trial costs payments
abstract: Dauphin County stands to be reimbursed for the costs of holding the William Bradfield murder trial and the trial of John Kerr, a man convicted of masterminding a jobs-sales scheme in the state Auditor General's Department.

headline: No-Fault Insurance Works -- Fears Federal Land Grab
abstract: No-fault insurance is a sound system and the passage of Senate Bill 942 would result in a return to a discredited insurance system.

headline: Ferraro: voters will defy polls
abstract: Democratic vice presidential candidate Geraldine Ferraro repeatedly scoffed at polls that show President Reagan Ronald with a wide margin support and predicted voters would defy the pollsters with a strong shift to Walter Mondale. There is a photograph of Geraldine Ferraro with Representative Bob Edgar.

headline: Senator Wants Mandatory Rain Dates
abstract: Pennsylvania state Senator James Lloyd plans to introduce legislation requiring entertainers to make up broken engagements.  The article goes into brief detail about Lloyd's proposed bill.

headline: Cow to visit Rotunda as dairy month opens
abstract: A cow will make a guest appearance in the Capitol Rotunda on June 1, 1984 and be milked as a feature of the opening festivities of Dairy month.

headline: Nuclear Power Wasn't on Trial
abstract: This editorial argues that despite the apparent criminal behavior of the former operator of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant, its guilty plea has nothing to do with whether the TMI Unit 1 should be restarted because  a different company is now in control of the plant.  Nuclear power and its benefits should be given another chance.

headline: Lawmakers making final pitches in job-selling trial
abstract: A Dauphin County Court jury heard seven days of testimony in the job-selling trial of John Kerr, but lawyers for the prosecution and defense agree the case may be decided based on which side presents the best closing argument. The defense concluded his case on June 28, 1984 in Kerr's defense.

headline: No-fault praised
abstract: Pennsylvania state legislators should work to keep no-fault auto insurance because it is a sound insurance system for the consumer and a blessing for the seriously injured.

headline: Filing date extended for nomination papers
abstract: Pennsylvania's deadline for independent and third party candidates to file nomination petitions for a place on the ballot in November 1984 was extended untill August 1, 1984.

headline: Senators blast Thornburgh's LCB plan: O'Connell says special interests wrote the bill
abstract: State senators from four districts in Northeastern PA met and denounced PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's plan to abolish the state's liquor monopoly.  The lawmakers argued that reform would mean lost jobs and lost money for the state.  They feel that the governor is supporting legislation drafted by special interests.

headline: Wall of silence surrounds firing of insurance chief
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh fired state Insurance Commissioner Anthony Geyelin. The reason for the firing is unknown and was not announced until rumors of the firing prompted reports to confirm the dismal. Mr. Geyelin said that he and the Governor's staff disagreed on some policies.

headline: Dairy faces loss of license on milk-price violations
abstract: The Pennsylvania Milk Marketing Board moved to revoke the license of a Pottsville dairy for breaking minimum price rules.  Executive secretary of the board Gene G. Veno said that the sanctions had been too small to force the dairy to adhere to rules previously, leading to the closing.

headline: Nuclear Power's Uphill Battle
abstract: For all of nuclear power's well-publicized troubles, a surprising number of industry experts contend that, on paper, nuclear power is still a good bet.  But others say that it needs to be not only cheaper but substantially cheaper than alternative energy sources in order to make the headaches it entails worth enduring.

headline: Lawsuits Against State Cost Taxpayers Plenty
abstract: Pennsylvania Legislators holding hearings on 1984-85 budget proposals are getting requests that they do something about the growing number of lawsuits against the state and the potential payout of tens of millions of tax dollars in claims.  "The exposure is the thing," said PA Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman, in explaining why he warned the House Appropriations Committee about the constantly mounting number of damage and negligence suits against the state.  Zimmerman recommended establishment of a permanent fund that could grow with time, ensuring, as more cases make it through the legal pipeline, money would be available to make the payments.

headline: No-fault repeal bill sent to governor
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate has sent PA Governor Dick Thornburgh a bill repealing the state's 1974 no-fault auto insurance law, but yet another battle lies ahead in the 10-year-old war over the no-fault system.  A compromise is yet to be made between the Senate leaders working on the repeal measure and the Thornburgh administration.

headline: Filings
abstract: U.S. Representative George W. Gekas, Republican-Harrisburg, will seek the Republican nomination for the 17th District congressional seat, Allen Ertel made his bid for the PA state attorney general's nomination, and U.S. Representative William F. Gooding, R-Jacobus, will seek another term on the Republican ticket as a member of the U.S. House of Representatives.

headline: Senators elect Dole; Heinz to head panel
abstract: Senator Bob Dole of Kansas was elected majority leader of the Senate on November 28, 1984 in a day of intraparty contests that also saw the return of Senator John Heinz to the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

headline: Wants 'unobstructed ' fight with Benedict: Quit race, Lewis asks Lotman
abstract: PA State Senator H. Craig Lewis has asked Arline J. Lotman to drop out of the race for PA state treasurer so that he can have a one-on-one fight with Al Benedict, the endorsed candidate.

headline: Dairymen, Hallowell hold talks
abstract: Milk dealers and farm and dairy organization leaders met with Penrose Hallowell, secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture, to discuss the state's proposed voluntary Milk Promotion and Marketing Program. The plan calls for 3,000 PA dairy farmers to be offered the opportunity to participate in promotional programs in PA.

headline: N-utilities give boost to cleanup
abstract: The nation's nuclear utilities took their first concrete step to meet thier pledge to help pay for the Three Mile Island cleanup. The Edison Electric Institute freed its members to start contributing toward the Three Mile Island unit 2 funding promised to Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh three years before. There are two photographs that depict Governor Dick Thornburgh and a Republican George Gekas.

headline: Nix takes over
abstract: If words follow actions, the swearing in of Robert N.C. Nix last Friday as chief justice of PA will mark a historic turning point for the state Supreme Court and for the entire state judicial system.  Nix promised in his installation speech at the Philadelphia Academy of Music to prevent "petty personality differences" from impairing the work of his court and to try to make the judicial system, and especially its disciplinary arm, more open and accountable to the public.

headline: Non-bank banks face problems Penna official doubts legality
abstract: A few dozens banks around the country applied to US Comptroller of the Currency for approval to open more than 200 so-called non-bank banks in more than 90 cities throughout the nation. Limited-purpose banks would either not make commercial loans or not take in checking accounts. Limited-purpose banks in Philadelphia appear to be illigal under PA law. Also, the loophole in federal law through which limited-purpose banks can squeeze does not exist in PA law.

headline: Firm's troubles may cost lottery
abstract: State officlials invested millions of lottery-fund dollars in annuities issued by Colorado company under increasing scrutiny across the country by insurance regulators concerned about its financial health. State records show that Pennsylvania purchased about 75 annuity policies during the last five years from Denver-based Capitol Life Insurance company to pay off the state lottery prizes worth more than $160 million. The concern is about the Capitol company's fiscal condition which holds the high volume of annuities. In case it is unable to make its payments to lottery prize winners, then the state woul lose $64.5 million.

headline: Sens. Lewis, Bodack quit state race for treasurer
abstract: PA State Senators Craig Lewis and Leonard Bodack have dropped out of the race for the Democratic nomination for PA state treasurer, leaving five candidates in the field.  The rest of the article is a roundup of PA primary election news.

headline: What happened in the legilature
abstract: There is a table of the key bills considered by the Pennsylvania Senate and House during the session in June 1984.

headline: Drain on dairymen's ranks seen raising prices
abstract: Pennsylvania's Grange master said on December 14, 1984, that the state's consumers will have to pay 10 cents more or a quart of milk if the drain on family farms continues at current rates.

headline: N-utilities give TMI cleanup plan a boost
abstract: The nation's nuclear utilities took their first concrete step on June 18, 1984 to meet their pledge to help pay for the Three Mile Island cleanup.

headline: Nix: Make Judge Probes Public
abstract: Pennsylvania Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. called for a constitutional amendment that would allow public proceedings against judges being investigated for allegations of substantive misconduct.  In front of the PA General Assembly, Nix also said that the state Supreme Court would adopt a rule requiring all state court judges to make full public disclosures of their personal finances.

headline: Not worth the gamble
abstract: County Treasurer Jay Costa resurrected the idea and proposed that a lottery, fashioned after one of the other games operated by the state, would yield $12 million a year.  This money would go towards Pittsburgh Port Authority's current operating deficit.  The article goes further into detail about the proposal.

headline: First step to election
abstract: This editorial argues that Pennsylvanians must put up and promote good candidates in order to see improvement in governmental performance, and it urges them to do so.

headline: Shanaman cites PUC role in bid for auditor general
abstract: Susan Shanaman, a republican who gained a statewide reputation while chairman of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, wants to be the first elected Republican auditor general since 1956. there is a photograph of Susan Shanaman.

headline: When a husband is the issue
abstract: Yvonne Street is running to represent the 197th District in the PA House of Representatives as a Democrat. Her husband is State Senator Milton Street who was elected as a Democrat but crossed over to the Republican Party. Philadelphia's elected Democrats and Democratic Party leaders oppose the Streets' in their bid for elective office( Milton's reelection, Yvonne's primary contest). The couple is running as a team which has sparked questions as to the independence of Yvonne Street and her loyalty to the Democratic Party.

headline: Egg industry battling for U.S. marketing protection
abstract: The troubled egg industry created a national task force on recommendation from a farm policy at odds with the Reagan administration. Poultry farmers want to protect their business through marketing orders that economists believe would add 15 cents to the price of a dozen eggs.

headline: Officials suggest ways to use TMI fund
abstract: One possible use for Dauphin County's Three Mile Island Emergency Preparedness Fund allocation might be to hire a consultant to study the evacuation plan, according to John E. Minnich, county commission chairman.  Commissioner Lawrence J. Hochendoner says the money might be sued to improve emergency drills or to get greater access on a more frequent basis to data on radioactive emissions from the nuclear plant.  The article provides different ways to use the Three Mile Island funding.

headline: Not many firm commitments
abstract: Employer-supported day care in the US is growing, jumping from 105 centers nation-wide in 1978 to 600 centers in 1984, but there is still a long way to go.There are two photographs, one depicts a toddler being tickled, another one depicts children playing with building blocks.

headline: NU-TEC losses booze license
abstract: The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board revoked the liquor license on October 24, 1984 held by financially troubled New Uptown Theatre and Entertainment Center in Northern Pennsylvania.

headline: Fischl, Shane given votes for PUC posts
abstract: The pair Mayor Frank Fischl, a Republican, and Democratic PUC Administrative Law Judge William Shane were nominated by PA Governor Thornburgh in January to fill the vacancies created in April 1983. However, they were withdrawn after failing to win sufficient Senate support. Senate Minority Leader Edward Zempelli said that everybody knew that Shane was running only because Fischl was approved.There are two photographs of Shane and Fischl.

headline: She finds votes elusive, like Jethro
abstract: About 500,000 people are spread out in 10 counties throughout the mountainous district and roughly 360,000 of them are eligible to vote. Most of them by a 2-1 ratio, vote Republican. 1984 is the year of House of Representatives election. There is a photograph of Bud Shuster, incumbent, Republican who spent 10 years in the House of Representatives who have short of 100 percent ratings.

headline: Who makes up the loss?
abstract: The Reagan administration drastically cut federal assistance to state and local governments, cutting bad programs along with good ones.  This editorial argues that the Reagan administration would have made many people better off had it not reduced funding to so many aid programs.

headline: Farm worker says he saw no inspectors in 32 years
abstract: Miquel Cabrerra, a man who has worked on 25 southeastern Pennsylvania mushroom farms in 32 years, testified to the state House Select Committee on Seasonal Farm Labor, that he has never seen a state inspector at the farms.  The article continues to provide details about farm wages, the status of farm working conditions, and testimony from the state Advisory Board of Pennsylvania Farm worker Opportunities Incorporated.

headline: Partial Cleanup at TMI Studied
abstract: Pennsylvania plans to ask the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to consider the environmental, safety and efficiency impact of stopping partway through the cleanup of Three Mile Island Unit 2 and sealing the plant.

headline: On watch; A stressful job takes its toll on prison guards
abstract: The article goes into full explanation about the prison guard job, its benefits and its cons.  It also discusses a recent study of prison guards' physical and mental health, along with divorce rates.  The article concludes with testimonies from guards and their thoughts on their job.

headline: Papers to show origin of steel
abstract: The 1978 Steel Products Procurement Act requires that only domestic steel be used in public construction. Emco Mechanical may have used foreign steel in the $13 million capitol addition project. The PA Department of General Services plans to ask the PA Attorney General to subpoena Emco's shipping and invoice records. General Services is withholding $158,000 from Emco until the steel can be proven to be of domestic origins.

headline: Flaherty aide defends rehiring of 7 auditors
abstract: An aide of City Controller Thomas Flaherty defended the firing of seven performance auditors and their rehiring at higher salaries.

headline: She is first lady's right-hand woman
abstract: The article talks about Louise Curl Adams, an aide to PA Governor Thornburgh's wife. She is responsible for arranging all scheduling, making contacts, planning lunches and gala dinners. Many details from her regular working day are presented in the article.

headline: Wilderness bill reaches new accord
abstract: According to a PA Senate aide, a Senate committee, the Pennsylvania congressional delegation and conservationists reached the final agreement on a bill to create an Allegheny National Forest wilderness area.

headline: Farm workers say '78 law did not halt abuse
abstract: Despite the 1978 Seasonal Farm Labor Act, farm workers are still living in unhealthly housing conditions, not getting appropriate state wages, working too many hours and experiencing unfair labor practices.  Legislators, members of the Select Committee on Farm Labor in Pennsylvania's Department of Environmental Resources and Labor and Industry listened to testimony from farm workers and have promised to ensure that the 1978 law was being enforced.  The article goes into further detail on the actions that are to take place to ensure that the law will be in place.

headline: PE pleads for point pleasant pump
abstract: On July 9 1984 the legal showdown on the fate of the Point Pleasant water diversion project opened in  Bucks County court with a Philadelphia Electric Company.

headline: Operation Penrose
abstract: There is a photograph that depicts John Hagan, special agent in charge of the Philadelphia FBI office and PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman at news conference at which results of "Operation Penrose" were announced by John Hagan.

headline: Parties prepare for liquor battle
abstract: The recent PA state Senate vote on PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's plan to sell 725 liquor stores to private enterprise has given strength to both caucases.  The Democrats were forced to use a procedural maneuver to avoid a direct vote on the issue, which gives both sides more time to buoy their criticisms or support, depending on their party.

headline: For Sen. Street, an Oak Lane house has generated a lot of controversey
abstract: By purchasing a home far outside of the state's Third Senatorial District, PA state Senator Milton Street invited controversey over the location of his legal residency.  His "home" inside of the district boundaries is owned by a non-profit and it is unclear whether Senator Street has ever paid rent there.

headline: She's Switching Party Hats to Seek Tayoun's Seat
abstract: Peg McCook has decided to run for the vacated 1st District City Council seat as an independent and buck the Democratic party after James J. Tayoun annouced he was vacating the seat to run for Congress against U.S. Representative Thomas Foglietta.

headline: Will Mill Run with GOP Against Jones?
abstract: The withdrawal of the Republican candidate for the third Senatorial District race on May 15, 1984 set the stage for a possible rematch between PA state Senator T. Milton Street and Roxanne Jones.

headline: Farmland bill aims to save it
abstract: A draft bill to provide added protection to the Pennsylvania's largest industry - agriculture - is pieced together slowly in the General Assembly's Legislative Reference Bureau. Walter Lamm,  executive director of the PA state House Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee, said the bipartisan draft was not complete, but work on the measure to protect farmland was continuing.

headline: Pe testimony on Limerick plan is distributed
abstract: A Wissahickon School District official said on November 20, 1984 that the district could not promise 20 buses for use in a emergency at the Limerick nuclear plant, contradicting testimony delivered earlier that day before a Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing panel.

headline: Opinion: The American's View; Reform for adoption
abstract: Due to recent legislation signed into law by Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh, Pennsylvania has adopted a statewide program to bring together families and adoptable children.  Adoption agencies will now be required to register information and a photograph of the child to be included in the Pennsylvania Adoption Cooperation Exchange  book.  This program is to make it easier for adoptive families and adoptable children to get together.  The article continues to explain how this new program is very beneficial to Pennsylvanians.

headline: PA's anti-takeover law one of the toughest
abstract: PA's new law is designed to deter hostile business takeovers. There are supporters and opponents to the statute. PA Chamber of Commerce spokesman Daniel Tunnel supports the the new law, while Senator Edward Zemperelli does not.

headline: For Treasurer, it's R. Budd Dwyer
abstract: The race for PA state Treasurer pits Republican incumbent R. Budd Dwyer against Democrat Al Benedict who completes his term as auditor general and will retire from his office.

headline: Shultz holds meeting: Gekas helps actor Quinn in try for diplomat role
abstract: Congressman George W. Gekas held a meeting between actor Anthony Quinn and Secretary of State George P. Shultz last week and Quinn offered to act as an ambassador-of-goodwill in Central America.  Secretary Schultz made no specific commitments but promised to respond to Quinn's offer.  Quinn says he is concerned that Latinos in the United States have a voice in issues involving Central American countries.  Additionally, Linda Lovelace testified at a sexual abuse-related hearing in Washington in which Arlen Specter was a participant.

headline: Winners Helms holds on. Losers Huddleston out
abstract: Jesse Helms, champion of the New Right, put down a challenge by North Carolina Governor Jim Hunt to hold onto his U.S. Senate seat. Two-term incumbent Senator Walter Huddleston of Kentucky lost in a major upset to county Judge Mitch McConnell. There are two photographs of Jesse Helms and Walter Huddleston.

headline: Farmland preservation furrows brows
abstract: According to Richard W. Newpher, administrative secretary of the Pennsylvania Farmers Association, the issue of farmland preservation would stop the two-year effort to provide for a purchase-of-development-rights program.

headline: PE to seek new boost in its rates: 'Less than 10%' will be sought
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Co. has requested an electric rate increase of less than 10 percent.  Part of the increase will go to recover higher operating costs. The public utility commission will rule on the decision in February 1985. Other rate increases for the company are still pending.

headline: Order in the courts
abstract: A modest yet earnest attempt to fix some of what's wrong with Pennsylvania's judicial system is in the works in the PA Senate.

headline: Penn National off-track betting plan OK
abstract: Penn National Race Course received approval for an off-track betting plan that involves placing wagering machines in selected locations statewide.

headline: Former aide to Solomon implicated
abstract: Bowie, who pleaded guilty to corruption charges at the beginning of November 1984, gave the same testimony on November 14, 1984. Bowie said protection payoffs were passed up the chain of command to the retired Lieutenant Walter McDermott and the commanding officer of the division, former Chief Inspector Eugene Sullivan.

headline: Shumaker stalling debate, Perkins says
abstract: PA Senate candidate Jane Perkins says that Senator John Shumaker is dragging his feet and will not agree to debate against her.  She has written him a letter stating that she is "extremely disappointed" and has also sent a letter to the League of Women Voters of the Harrisburg area asking them to set up a series of five debates.

headline: Witness hints of favors
abstract: The key witness in a federal investigation involving an alleged conspiracy by PA state Treasurer Budd Dwyer and others to obtain kickbacks in exchange for awarding a multimillion-dollar state contract hinted strongly in a sworn interview that sexual favors were performed to win the contract.

headline: Harvest Forecast: Corn-utopia
abstract: Farmers in the area are beginning to harvest what is expected to be the most bountiful feed-corn crop in history, according to Jay Irwin, director of the Pennsylvania State University agricultural extension service in Lancaster County.  Much of this is due to the weather being superb for growing and now farmers are trying to sell whatever they can as cheap as necessary simply to keep it from rotting in their fields.

headline: People's voice?
abstract: The author argues that the public's concerns over the handling of the Three Mile Island disaster are not being taken into consideration.

headline: Our Opinion: Citizens hold key to judicial reform
abstract: A judicial reform that is currently in front of the Pennsylvania House would replace the judge dominated disciplinary board with one including a number of laymen, eliminate secret disciplinary hearing and deliberations and it would require financial disclosure by judges.  Unless the PA House acts on the measure before August 5, 1984, it will not be considered again until 1987.  If Pennsylvanians wants confidence in their courts, then they should vote in favor of Senate Bill 846.  The piece goes further into detail about the flaws in the judiciary system in Pennsylvania.

headline: Pennsylvania official says firms should collect auto fee
abstract: Pennsylvania officials testified that having the state collect the new $5 per year insurance fee from each car owner in the state would be very difficult and argues that insurance companies should be responsible for collection.

headline: Four in GOP sue county committee
abstract: Four Dauphin County Republican Committee members have asked Dauphin County Court to order reconsideration of committee endorsements for state committee and national convention seats. The suit claims that nominations for endorsements were cut off without the proper motion and without affording any candidates other than those on the slate the chance to have their names placed before the committee. Moreover, the suit claims that committee bylaws were violated when a standing vote took place, instead of a secret ballot election.

headline: Sierra Club score card, only 2 Pa. representatives rank in the 90s
abstract: Sierra Club announced that their political education committee was endorsing two candidates for statewide office, Susan Shanaman, the Republican candidate for auditor general, and Allen Ertel, Democratic candidate for attorney general.

headline: Won't Face Jones, Milt Tells GOP
abstract: Pennsylvania state Senator T. Milton Street has turned down an offer by the Republican Party to run against Roxanne Jones in the next race.  Street lost to Jones in the Democratic primary.  The article goes further into detail about why Street will not accept the Republican Party offer.

headline: Hearing planned on farm labor act
abstract: The Pennsylvania state House Select Committee on Seasonal Farm Labor will hold a public hearing on the Seasonal Farm Labor Act and the migrant education program in Pennsylvania. PA State Representative James J.A. Gallagher, committee chairman, said the testimony will be limited to 20 minutes for each witness.  The article provides information on where and when the meeting will be held.

headline: Photograph
abstract: There is a photograph of a teenager swimming in his backyard during a drill at Three Mile Island. Cooling towers of limerick plant are located the background of his house.

headline: Owner faces theft charge
abstract: The owner of Scheps Cheese Company, Benedict Scheps, will face state charges in a scheme that bilked 321 Pennsylvania dairy farmers out of $3.6 million worth of milk, according to Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman.  The Bureau of Criminal Investigation will charge Scheps for agreeing to make  payments to the Farmers Home Administration.

headline: Plan on collection of $5 fee rejected
abstract: Proposed regulations to implement Pennsylvania's new auto insurance law to force insurance companies to collect a new five dollar fee from motorists was rejected by the Independent Regulatory Review Commission.  The article goes into further detail about the added fee, views from the insurance industry and the PA House and Senate committees.

headline: Franklintown Ex-Magistrate Investigated
abstract: A routine audit of District Justice Samuel A. Hill accounts found a shortage of $3,476. The shortages were made possible since financial duties were not sufficiently shared among employees, who serve as checks on one another, the audit report suggests. District Attorney J. Christian Ness has opened an investigation, noting he now has the criminal and supportive evidence to do so.

headline: Signs of the Debate Gone with the Wind
abstract: The Democratic Presidential debate, hosted by the League of Women Voters, was a success. The format allowed candidates to ask questions of each other and thereby allowed the public to learn more about each candidate. The league has received 60 calls thanking it for hosting the debate or asking about how to register to vote.

headline: Word of Mouth: Governors Are Just Nuts About Peanuts
abstract: A recent survey by Candy Industry Magazine tabulated the confectionary habits of the nation's governors and of the 20 who responded. Peanuts were the second most favored snack items.

headline: Milk-board functions create disagreement
abstract: A recommendation to eliminate minimum retail milk prices in Pennsylvania received a hostile reaction on May 23, 1984 from a committee dominated by PA state senators from rural districts.

headline: PP&L fined in incident at plan
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission staff on December 19, 1984 fined the Pennsylvania Power & Light co. $50,000 for an incident in which emergency power was cut off at its Susquehanna nuclear plant near Berwick, southwest of Wiles-Barre.

headline: Pa. amendment proposal prompts mixed reactions
abstract: A proposed amendment to the Pennsylvania Constitution which would permit prosecutors to use improperly obtained confessions to challenge testimony of criminal defendants is supported by district attorney Robert Colville and opposed by Pittsburgh trial lawyers and the American Civil Liberties Union.

headline: PLCB double-talk
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board (PLCB) should be abolished because it has established that it is willing to tolerate dishonesty among its employees.  There is evidence of this in the PLCB's recent decision to spare punishment for an employee who was in the middle of a job-selling scandal.

headline: Fundamentalist voters could aid Reagan in Pa.
abstract: U.S. President Reagan stands to gain from the voter-registration drives at the Worship Center and dozens of other fundamentalist Christian churches in central Pennsylvania.

headline: Silkwood Lawyers Offer County Help
abstract: Two attorneys who assisted in the nationally publicized Karen Silkwood have offered to defend for free Dauphin County's forthcoming clean-air ordinance if it is challenged.  The two lawyers believe that because of the social importance of the case they are willing to work for no charge.  The case would likely turn on the issue of federal preemption, which is how the Silkwood case was decided.

headline: Workers, managers urged to pull together; 'People count most on Labor Day'
abstract: Pennsylvania Chamber of Commerce President Clifford L. Jones, a former state Cabinet officer, gives a speech about how Labor Day is important because it is a time for candidates to kick off their campaigns, and discusses several other employment issues.

headline: Milking in Rotunda
abstract: There is a photograph of William Nichol, PA Holstein Association official giving a fourth-grader a quick lesson in milking a cow at the state Capitol Rotunda on June 1, 1984.

headline: Probe asked for Limerick
abstract: The Pennsylvania Consumer Advocate has called for an investigation by the Public Utility Commission to determine whether the Philadelphia Electric Company should ever resume construction on the Limerick 2 nuclear generating station in Montgomery County.

headline: Pa. appeals ruling on '80 abortion law
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman is appealing Commonwealth Court Judge John McPhail's ruling to strike down a 1980 law prohibiting the use of state Medicaid funds for abortions. The attorney general  has moved to speed up the appeals process by petitioning the state Supreme Court before the Commonwealth Court has finished with it. The attorney general argues that the case is urgent since it deals with state obligations and the expending of funds.

headline: Presents case in favor of state control of liquor
abstract: The best reason to oppose privitization of liquor stores in PA is to prevent harm to communities, particularly minority communities.

headline: Funds for Cameron St.
abstract: Since the flood in 1972, Cameron St. in Harrisburg has never recovered.  This editorial argues that its recovery is a crucial step not just for the vitality of Harrisburg, but also for PA.

headline: Simpler primary ballot would  eliminate election day confusion
abstract: In the primary election delegates are what candidates need to win. However, a vote for a candidate does not mean a for his delegates.  Currently, voters must cast a vote for a candidate's delegates, not the candidate him or herself. This should be changed to limit confusion and make a vote count.

headline: Worthy goals for state budget
abstract: This editorial argues that PA Governor Thornburgh's 1984-845 tentative budget goals are worthy ones and it is hoped that there is no repeat of the partisan confrontation last year and the years before, which delayed checks to countless welfare recipients and state employees.

headline: Move urged on container deposits
abstract: Farmers say they are finding metal, aluminum and glass in their crops. It is an expense to farmers' livelihood. A 5-cent deposit on containers was proposed in July of 1983 but has failed to move. Popular support is needed to ensure its passage. Pennsylvania state Representative Benjamin Wilson, a Republican, proposes that consumers return their bottles to the supermarket, who will in turn take the bottles back to the distributor. The model exists in several states.

headline: Public input on nuclear waste disposal planned
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration is planning to invite public groups to help decide the best technology for a potential low-level radioactive waste storage site in PA.  Much of the group's discussion will depend  on whether the state decides to join the rest of the Northeast in a regional compact to handle the low-level waste generated.

headline: Pa. lifers lose hopes for parole
abstract: In Pennsylvanaia there is no minimally set-term for a life sentence. The only means for prisoners to have their sentence shortened is by commutation by the Governor. PA Governor Thornburgh has been conservative in the number of commutations since entering office: 73 recommended by the Pardons Board, 4 granted. In 1976 there were 650 lifers in Pennsylvania prisons, in 1984 there are 1,211. 100 lifers enter prison each year compared with 25 a year in the 1960s, despite the fact that crimes such as murder are on the downturn. The rise is contributed to district attroneys that are less willing to plea bargin.

headline: Pressuring the LCB
abstract: The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board (LCB) should be dismantled, particularly in light the recent allegations that two of its employees paid bribes for jobs.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's plans to try and coerce the LCB into dismantling are needed.

headline: Gamble
abstract: The only states that had more votes to nominate Walter Mondale for the Democratic ticket for the presidential election are Florida, Georgia, Kentucky and New Jersey. They came before Pennsylvania in the balloting.

headline: Sinatra antics
abstract: In August of 1984, PA state Representative Corry Stevens, a fan of Sinatra, invited the singer to Pennsylvania in order to assure him that the state loves him.

headline: Young Bill Is 'Available': Eye on Senate, He'll Speak Anywhere in Pa.
abstract: This column discusses the moves being made by Bill Green as he considers a run for U.S. Senate against Arlen Specter in 1986.

headline: Pa. farmers cannot afford another harvest like 1983's
abstract: Drought cut corn production by 43 percent, alfalfa by 6 percent, soybean production by 15 percent and tobacco production by 12 percent. A mysterious virus killed nearly 11.5 million chickens, turkeys and other foul. And, changes in federal dairy supports cut 8 percent off the gross revenue of dairy farmers. These blows have forced farmers to move to cheaper land for higher profit returns and sell their homesteads to land developers. Government and private bankers have moved to restructure loans and advance additional short-term cash. Due to the drought, farmers had 40 to 80 percent of their crops lost.

headline: PUC has 5 memebers for 1st time in a year
abstract: The five-member Public Unitility Commission has been restored for the first time in a year. Democrats retain control of PUC, 3-2. There is also a photograph of three men: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh who is presenting the commissions of office to William Shane, left, and Frank Fischl, the two new members of the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Pa. senator testifies in inquiry; Computer deal is jury's focus
abstract: Pennsylvania Senator Eugene Scanlon appeared before a federal grand jury and denied afterward that he had any improper involvement with a California-based computing firm,  Computer Technology Associates Incorporated, under investigation.  The article continues to follow the grand jury's Computer Technology Associates Incorporated investigation.

headline: Private liquor system seen as revenue raisers
abstract: Pennsylvania  Revenue Secretary James Scheiner argues that under PA Governor Thornburgh's plan to transition from state monopoly of liquor sales to a private retail system would result in increased revenue for the state by $30 million per year. The argument is centered on the undocumented claim that 25 percent of liquor and wine consumption is from out-of-state sources, thus avoiding that PA's tax. Lower prices under a private system will lead people to buy from state sources and thus pay state taxes.

headline: Gary Would Bar New Investments in S. Africa
abstract: U.S. Congressman William Gary of Philadelphia has attached an amendment to the Export Administration Act to place restrictions on U.S. companies investing in South Africa because of South Africa's policy of apartheid repression of the black majority. The bill, now before the U.S. Senate, will go before a conference vote. U.S. Senator John Heinz, R-Pa., opposes the apartheid government but fears unfavorable business environment for U.S. firms.

headline: State extends a union-won raise to nonunion workers
abstract: Nonunion PA state employees, including some aides to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, have been granted 2 percent pay raises effective Jan. 1, a spokesman for the governor said.  The raises were equal to the increases granted to about 60,000 ununionized state employees.

headline: Zimmerman bash called unethical
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman violated the state's Ethics Act by allowing Liquor Control Board member Mario Mele to sponsor a fund-raiser for him at the same time that Zimmerman's staff was investigating the board's enforcement practices.  The article provides information from Liquor Control Board Chairman Daniel Pennick and further details about the allegations.

headline: Panel Opposes Milk-Price Rule
abstract: A legislative watchdog group released a report recommending that the Pennsylvania Milk Marketing Board stop setting minimum wholesale and retail milk prices.

headline: PUC must be changed, member says
abstract: Public Utility Commission Commissioner Michael Johnson argued that the state commission needs to be restructured, beginning with a shortening of commissioners' terms from 10 to 5 years.

headline: Pa. urged to build new prison: Unit would be in Phila. Area
abstract: A Pennsylvania House subcommittee said a 500-bed jail should be built in the greater Philadelphia area, and 322 new prison officers should be hired to help control extensive overcrowding of PA prisons.  The subcommittee generally rejected proposals to more quickly release more prisoners on parole as a way of dealing with overcrowding.  Instead, it supported plans for more trailer-like "modular" prison dormitories, and it urged that the planned construction of 3,030 cells be speeded up and that counties be given state loans to enlarge their own over-crowded jails.

headline: Senate debates bill to strip LCB of 2 functions
abstract: An effort to strip the Liquor Control Board of its licensing and enforcement functions reached the Pennsylvania state Senate floor and sparkled debate on two key elements of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's plan to dismantle the state liquor system.

headline: Gary's Guerrillas Invade State
abstract: A group of young high school students and college students have been dubbed Gary's Guerrillas for their fierce commitment to the presidential campaign of U.S. Senator Gary Hart. Hart has done well in attempting to steal away parts of Walter Mondale's labor base. Gary Hart suffered an overwhelming loss in the New York primary but his campaign is still trying to win Philadelphia.

headline: Snyder's unique newsletter filled with pungent thought
abstract: PA Senator Richard Snyder put out a newsletter differntly from other legislators - with philosophical reflection on a variety of topics ranging from television and news media criticism to historical notes to book reviews. There is a picture of a political writer for the Intelligencer Journal Gil Deloney.

headline: Zimmerman Tosses Hat Into Ring
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman announced that he is running for reelection.  He is expected to receive Republican backing.

headline: Dougherty's Out in 3rd
abstract: U.S. Representative Charles F. Dougherty was defeated in his bid for a third congressional term by state Representative Robert A. Borski.  Borski will now move from the Pennsylvania Legislature into a position as one of Philadelphia's leading politicians.

headline: Pay Policy Fixed For Sick Chickens
abstract: U.S. Department of Agriculture agreed to pay current market value for chickens destroyed to stop the avian flu. Until this policy change, the government paid market price for the date the chicken was destroyed. However, farmers who spent time cleaning up their farms found that they were priced out of the market because avian flu increased the wholesale cost of poultry. The agreement was produced after a bi-partisan, bi-cameral push for resolution.

headline: Reactor
abstract: After weeks of preparation the head-lift operation began on July 24, 1984 at 5.26 p.m. at the Three Mile Island Power plant.  According to GPU officials, the crane with the Unit 2 head would be moved faster than without it.

headline: Paid for jobs, 20 tell court
abstract: Jurors in the job-selling trial of John Kerr heard 20 witnesses testify on June 21, 1984 that they paid for jobs or promotions in that department.

headline: Ranking the states, but imperfect
abstract: Under Grant Accounting firm's "general manufacture climate", New York gets a gloomy ranking of 39th, but 4th by Inc. Magazine while South Carolina is the last dead - 50th and 15th under Grant's system. Ranking is very subjective. Governors and legislators seem not to care much about ranking while business and corporations take them seriously and try to improve the economic climate.

headline: Gekas files petitions for a second term
abstract: U.S. Representative George W. Gekas, Republican-Harrisburg, today filed nomination petitions with the PA state Elections Bureau for Republican renomination for the 17th District seat in the April 10 primary elections.

headline: Some state democrats feel woman should be on ticket
abstract: In a survey by the Associated Press, 28% of the 156 delegates contacted said they wanted a woman vice president candidate or could support the idea. Sixty four delgates to the Democratic National Convention said that they had no choice and did not indicate their thoughts on a woman candidate.

headline: City-owned land may net $3 million
abstract: The PA Game Commission offered to purchase more than 7100 acres of Harrisburgh-owned land surrounding the DeHart Dam in the Clarks Valley watershed for $3,053 million.

headline: He Took Political Legacy and Spent it His Way
abstract: This article chronicles the personal and political life of Philadelphia Mayor William J. Greene, who announced he will not seek a second term as Philadelphia mayor yesterday.

headline: Price war possible on low-fat, skim milk
abstract: The Pennsylvania Milk Marketing Board has decided to temporarily remove the minimum prices for low fat dairy. The Greater Pittsburgh Dairy Industry Association opposes this move saying that no public meeting was held, as the law requires. The Milk Market Board says its only following the lead of a court order. The deregulation may lead to lower prices for customers.

headline: Rickover briefing fails to sway Gekas
abstract: U.S. Representative George W. Gekas, R-Harrisburg, said retired Admiral Hyman G. Rickover did not change his mind about the primacy of cleaning up Three Mile Island (TMI) Unit 2 before a decision on the TMI Unit 1 restart is made. Gekas also wants the thorough radiation monitoring done by the Environmental Protection Agency to continue.

headline: Panel will seek outside review of K-9 teams
abstract: A Pennsylvania Senate committee will investigate allegations of unjustified attacks on civilians by a small group of Philadelphia K-9 teams. The testimony took place on June 29 of 1984 and was taken up by four experienced K-9 trainers: Anthony Taff, Randy Dill, Donald Laken and Anthony Taff, Jr. There is a photograph of Anthony Taff who held up the city's K-9 unit in 1962, speaking before the committee.

headline: Reform of LCB To Be Discussed
abstract: The pros and cons of proposals to reform the Pennsylvania's liquor system will be discussed by experts at Upper Dauphin High School. The forum is sponsored by PA state Rep. Jeffery E. Piccola, R-Susquehanna Twp.

headline: Giardiasis fight looms
abstract: A select committee, presided over by Senator Frank O'Connell of Luzerne County, held hearings on the problems posed by the outbreak of giardiasis in the northeastern and western Pennsylvania. Those hearings produced four legislative proposals.

headline: Sound Off: Van Zandt Earned VA Center Honor
abstract: The name of the Altoona Veterans Administration Medical Center is being changed to the "James E. Van Zandt Veterans Administration Medical Center" after the former US Congressman.  The author approves of this honor and wished to congratulate Zandt, as well as thank him.

headline: Flood Damage May Reach $25 Million
abstract: Flooding damage in the midstate last month could reach $25 million, according to preliminary estimates made by PA Emergency Management Agency officials in nine counties.

headline: Senate panel wants to keep milk board
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee approved continuing the Pennsylvania Milk Marketing Board with a few changes.  Additionally, the committee also approved a bill to create an Agricultural Product Development Commission and another bill to retain the PA Farm Products Show Commission.

headline: Scranton embarks on coal-selling trip
abstract: Lt. Governonr William W. Scranton III begins on May 16, 1984 a 10-day trip to Frans and Portugal to promote Pennsylvania coal. He is going to meet with government officials and with officers of national steel, coal and import companies in France and Portugal. There is a photograpgh of a coal car running to a dumping area so coal can be loaded onto a greek freighter at the port of Philadelphia.

headline: Parole officers half-police officers and half-counselors
abstract: For parole officers like Jim Robinson of Pittsburgh, tough-love is sometimes their best tool when helping criminals.  Playing both counselor and cop, trying to help and play Big Brother, parole officers are often fighting a losing battle because the chance of parolees holding a decent paying job is low.

headline: Retain state control over liquor in Pennsylvania
abstract: Control over liquor is best kept in the hands of the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: Glad it's over
abstract: The race for state treasurer is over in Pennsylvania. Republican R. Budd Dwyer was re-elected.

headline: Special aid for cities advocated by Coyne
abstract: Pittsburgh's Democratic congressman, William Coyne recommends the creation of a committee whose sole purpose is to help cities across America. His bill, introduced with 51 cosponsors June 29 would establish a temporary two-year panel called the House Select Committee on cities.

headline: Senate passes wilderness bill
abstract: On October 2, 1984 the Senate gave unanimous approval to a bill that would preserve vast areas of the Allegheny National Forest as wilderness and designate an even larger section of the forest as a national recreation area.

headline: Shelter for farmland
abstract: Act 43, passed in 1981, permitted farmers with 500 or more contiguous acres of land to form agricultural areas.  By becoming an agricultural area, farmers are protected from nuisance ordinances and the exercise of eminent domain.  The article continues to provide how the law intends to preserve the state's farmland.

headline: Secret transcripts show NRC's plight
abstract: Transcripts of nuclear regulatory commission meetings between October 1981 and January 1984 show an agency torn between getting tough on Three Mile Island nuclear plant owners and giving them the benefit of the doubt.

headline: Penna. Crime Commission urges a better-coordinated battle plan
abstract: The PA Crime Commission, in its annual report, departed from  its previous emphasis on organized crime and called for better coordination of the state's $1 billion resources  to fight crime. Crime in PA has been falling, but 94,000 serious crimes where committed in Philadelphia last year. PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman has made it clear that he would like to abolish most of the commission's functions and take over its $2.1 million budget. Under the Sunset Law, the question of the commission's existence is due to come up next year.

headline: Revenue, opinions key state stores issues
abstract: The state owned liquor store operation provides Pennsylvania with more revenue than free enterprise operations in other states. However, a majority of Whites, Republicans and men favor abolishing the state operated system. A majority of African Americans and women fear that teen-age drinking will increase under the private enterprise system.

headline: Goldwater's talk evokes shades of '64
abstract: Arizona Senator Barry Goldwater spoke at the Republican National Convention and gave blessings to Ronald Reagan running in the presidential race.  The article continues with a description on Goldwater's conservative views and his arguments against the Democrat party.

headline: Specter Wants Stiff Grain Dust Rules
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter has sent a letter to Occupational Safety and Health Administration Director Thorne Auchter expressing concern that the proposed rules to permit grain dust levels 1/8 inch is eight times too lenient. Specter notes that "pound for pound grain dust is more explosive than dynamite." The National Academy of Sciences' study, which was funded by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, recommended dust levels of 1/64 inch.  434 workers have died in the last seven years in grain elevator explosions.

headline: State is nation's most flood prone, ranks No. 1 in related losses
abstract: The state of Pennsylvania is the nation's most flash flood prone state and ranks number 1 in terms of flood related losses.  The article goes further into detail about the estimated damage caused by floods and possible reasons behind this weather pattern.

headline: State apple shipments destined for Kuwait
abstract: A Kuwaiti importer has agreed to buy $15,000 worth of Pennsylvania apples monthly.  The deal spawned from PA state Agriculture Secretary Penrose Hallowell's visit to the 1984 Middle East Food and Equipment Show.  According to Hallowell, expansion of PA's foreign agricultrual trade has been a top priority of the Thornburgh administration.

headline: Senate passes gas costs bill
abstract: The Senate passed the gas costs bill and sent it to the House on May 7, 1984. The House passed the measure by an overwhelming margin, but still has to consider a few changes the Senate made before adopting a new method for the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Pennsylvania's overcrowded jails
abstract: The inmate population in Pennsylvania county prisons and jails increased for the fourth consecutive year in 1982 and reached a record high year-end level, according to a report from the PA Bureau of Correction last November.
