This editorial argues that this is an enormous problem because overcrowded jails lead to larger problems, which is why legislators and PA Governor Thornburgh are working to solve it.

headline: Rise in sales feared,,,less control isn't the answer
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal to dismantle the state Liquor Control Board and turn liquor sales over to the private market will have negative consequences in PA because of the dramatic rise in alcohol consumption that will result.

headline: Good wilderness compromise
abstract: Two Pennsylvania Congressmen, Representatives  William Clinger and Peter Kostmayer, have introduced the Pennsylvania Wilderness Act of 1984, which would designate 9,400 acres in Allegheny National Forest in North-central Pennsylvania. The plan is a compromise which provides $ 2 million  to buy out mineral rights.

headline: Springsteen gets another fan
abstract: PA Representative Correale F. Stevens said he will introduce a resolution in the PA House to "unofficially proclaim" that Springsteen is the "Boss of rock 'n' roll."

headline: State parks beckoning nature buffs
abstract: Pennsylvania has 112 operating state parks almost all within an hour's drive of a large metropolitan area. All state parks have various facilities for hiking, fishing, boating and bycycling etc.

headline: State sheep industry stabilized, Penn State animal scientist says
abstract: After rising 14 percent in three years then declining slightly, the Pennsylvania's sheep industry has stabilized, a Pennsylvania State University animal scientist said Monday at the Farm Show here.

headline: Sign of the times
abstract: A Three Mile Island protester holds a homemade sign in a large crowd bearing one of the more popular messages of early TMI demonstrations: Hell No We Won't Glow.

headline: Pension boost, crime victims 'bill of rights"
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh on July 2, 1984 signed into law bills to create "a bill of rights" for crime victims and give state and school retirees a $20 million cost-of-living raise.

headline: Saving a steel plant
abstract: In Johnstown the steel plant closed by the US Steel Corporation in May was purchased by a group of local investors and will be reopened in the middle of July with a start-up crew of 20 to 25 members.

headline: Goode Urges Democratic Unity
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode urged Dauphin County Democrats to rally behind whoever is the Democratic presidential nominee after the April 10th primary and after the San Francisco convention. Mayor Goode has publicly endorsed former U.S. Vice President Walter Mondale.

headline: Stability of lottery fund debated
abstract: The Democratic lawmaker says that the state avoids a lottery fund investment while a top Thornburgh administration official says that the lottery's fund's investment portfolio is solid. The committee has to make a decision concerning the fate of the lottery fund. The findings will be reported in November 1984.

headline: 185 % rise in tax rate confirmed
abstract: Cumberland County residents face a record 185 percent increase in county property taxes next year under a proposed 13-mill increase.

headline: State to cover debt of firms to farmers
abstract: According to the Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman, the PA Milk Marketing Board will distribute state funds to farmers who were owed money by the bankrupt Scheps Cheese Company and three smaller firms.  The article provides further details on the reimbursement.

headline: Some will never pay utility bills, study says
abstract: According to a study released on June 20, 1984, some utility customers never pay their overdue bills. Therefore, the report, prepared for the state Public Utility Commission staff, recommended the creation of special programs to help these "chronic payment-troubled customers".

headline: Phila. K-9 dogs' attacks dip
abstract: According to figures released by the Philadelphia police department, attacks by city police K-9 dogs dropped sharply during the middle of 1984.

headline: Senate blocks LCB reforms
abstract: An attempt to end the PA Senate stalemate on liquor reform followed the path of its many predecessors by failing to gain sufficient support. Two different versions of legislation that would take the enforcement powers away from the Liquor Control Board lacked votes to clear the Republican-control number.

headline: Goode's for Fritz; Pols Forming Line
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Goode endorsed Walter F. Mondale for the Democratic presidential primaries.  Other black leaders in the city are supporting Reverend Jesse Jackson, but Goode feels that Mondale has the best chance to beat Reagan in the November election.

headline: Stakes are high in today's Penna. Primary
abstract: The race for the Democratic presidential nomination and its closeness has divided state politicians in their support for candidates. The Pennsylvania primary is the last of big state primaries until May 5th, when Texas holds party caucus. Pennsylvania will send 195 delegates to the convention and of those 117 will be selected by voters. 55 delegates will be selected by party officials. Pennsylvania could well determine the next Democratic nominee for president.

headline: Assesment reform needed
abstract: PA's counties, municipalities and schools raise more than $3 bln yearly through property taxes. But because of archaic assessments this system is loaded with non-uniformities and inequalities.County's Sen. William J. Moore says assessement is the most important issue to raise. However, it would take almost a miracle to pass Moore's package of reforms, which include state oversight on assessing and five-year renewals of tax-exempt certificates.

headline: Up Farm Show Exhibits
abstract: More exhibits are planed for the Pennsylvania Farm Show, which was recently named to the American Bus Association's list of top 100 tourist events in North America for 1984.

headline: State's coal industry, Conrail benefit from $15 million pact
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh announced a $15 million contract to ship state coal to utility plants in New England.  Under the one year contract involving Conrail, New England Electric and United States Steel Mining Incorporated, coal from Washington County's Maple Creek mines will be moved through Conrail's coal-exporting station to a ship, which will carry it to New England.  The article goes into further detail about mining.

headline: Plowshares Eight win moral victory with their 'greater evil' defense
abstract: The 1981 trial was marked by angry courtroom confrontations between the judge and the eight peace activists who were defending themselves against charges that they had broken into the General Electric plant in King of Prussia and damaged nose conses designed for nuclear missiles.  One of the causes of the disruption was the judge's decision to deny the defendants an opportunity to argue to the jury that their actions were justified because they believed the threat of nuclear war outweighed the seriousness for the break-in.  And that ruling by Montgomery County Judge Samuel W. Salus II was the primary reason that the PA state Superior Court decided to overturn the convictions and grant a new trial for the defendants, who called themselves the Plowhares Eight, a biblical reference to turning swords into plowahres.

headline: Senator says LCB counsel should quit
abstract: Liquor Control Board Chief Counsel Gary F. DiVito outlived his usefullness to commonwealth and has to resign, according to PA Senator Richard Tilgman who is unsatisfied with the employment performance of the borad.

headline: Goode's Performance Puzzles Local Polls
abstract: Philadelphia's Mayor Wilson Goode is busy getting his administration on line and his politics seem to be suffering as a result.  Many see the Democratic City Chairman Joseph F. Smith as a strong, independent leader, who seems to be guiding the party.  Goode disagrees.

headline: State announces certified vote tally
abstract: The Pennsylvania Electronics Bureau announced on December 20, 1984 Pennsylvania's certified vote totals in the November, 1984 presidential election.

headline: City-supported Tax Reform Bill Reaches Floor of House
abstract: A state tax reform bill supported by Meadville City Council, PA Chamber of Commerce, American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees and the PA School Board Association has reached the PA House of Representatives floor. The bill will raise the wage tax limit by .5 percent and an optional .25 percent municipal service fee. The bill would eliminate occupational privilege and per capita taxes. The bill help alleviate tax burden on property owners, unemployed workers and senior citizens.

headline: "Pa" doesn't end with "Y"
abstract: According to the Pennsylvania Labor Department, the average annual pay for workers in Pennsylvania's metropolitan areas declined by 3.1% in 1983 while it rose 5 percent nationwide. Average earnings increased to $18,183 in 1983 from $17,322 in 1982.

headline: The forum
abstract: This is the response to the letter by James Bogar and Richard Koenig in the Patriot June 1. The author discusses the Three Mile Island plant and he says that he talks on behalf of 4000 people who did not show up for restart, yet  he did not mean to be against the restart of Three Mile Island.

headline: Police have driven 2 Thornburgh sons to Mass. Schools
abstract: 800 mile round trips have become routine assignments for troopers in the executive protection detail. The exact number of trips could not be determined. Records show that troopers, in state vehicles, have provided transportation for two of Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh's four sons, age 17 and 25, to and from their campuses in Massachusetts. State troopers stayed in hotels in Massachusetts at PA tax payer's expense. The transportation was provided for security reasons, according to officials.

headline: Senators Propose Liquor Alternative
abstract: A bipartisan group of Pennsylvania state senators unveiled a plan to keep the state liquor system in business, with enforcement transferred to a new agency, and service improvements including the use of credit cards and personal checks.  A 15-page booklet, "A Plan to Retain State Stores in a Modernized System," outlines the proposed alternative to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's controversial plan to dismantle the existing system and sell the store franchises to private business.

headline: Goodling raps pay cut as another form of taxation
abstract: According to an aide, only 2 percent of Goodling's constituents are federal employees but the congressman was struck by the lack of fairness implicit in the pay cut.

headline: State black caucus elects chairman
abstract: According to an aide, Representative Peter Truman was elected chairman of the Pennsylvania Legislative Black Caucus on December 10, 1984.

headline: Council president rejects request that he step down
abstract: Robert Rade Stone refused to step down as City Counsel president on October 24 1984 in the wake of reports that he received money from one of five persons indicted in an alleged kickback scheme involving government contracts. There is a photograph of Councilwoman Michelle Madoff who calls on Robert Rade Stone to step down as president.

headline: 10,000 in Johnstown want to take jobs test
abstract: Due to steel plants closing in Johnstown, 10,000 people have signed up to take a test for job possibilities in the United States Postal Service.  There are no jobs currently available, but this will provide a new pool of applicants to draw from when any jobs become vacant.  The article goes into further detail about the examination, its process and types of postal jobs.

headline: Suit by gas station dealers settled
abstract: A federal judge granted preliminary approval to an antitrust settlement by 15 of the nation's largest oil companies on October 5, 1984. It would allow dealers who operate company-owned stations to buy gasoline from competitors.

headline: Prison crowding
abstract: The present overcrowding of the Philadelphia prison system is the result of an overabundant court system.

headline: Settling the CAT dispute
abstract: The Pennsylvania state Supreme Court resolved the troublesome dispute over who should collect the $5 fee for the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund. The Cat fund is to be funded through a yearly $5 assessment against each and every auto and truck owner in the state. The Thornburgh administration balked and the dispute went to Commonwealth Court.

headline: GOP Members, Chief Disagree
abstract: A group of county Republicans has accused the county committee chairman of undemocratic action in handling recent party office endorsements and has demanded that he allow the committee to reconsider them.  But Chairman William T. Smith said the endorsements were handled properly and he is "99.9 percent" decided against reconvening the committee.  He said the dissenters, who include county Commissioner Norman Hetrick, are "disgruntles candidates and their supporters."

headline: State budget accord seen
abstract: Even though predictions of an early settlement on the 1984-1985 state budget proved wrong, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and legislative leaders say no major obstacle stands in the way of a resolution by June 30, 1984.

headline: Delco doesn't buy city's tax reform
abstract: Delaware county officials torpedoed a proposal from Philadelphia to raise sales taxes throughout the region, sinking a yearlong bid to cut the city wage tax.

headline: 100 New Jobs at Lansdowne Co.
abstract: Lansdowne Steel & Iron Company has landed two U.S. Army contracts that will pump up employment at its Morton plant by as many as 100 workers.  The two contracts, worth a total of more than $10 million, call for sizable plant expansion and the production of 70,000 76mm artillery shells.  Lansdowne Steel manufacturers ammunition, textile equipment and tool joints for the oil-drilling industry.

headline: System that detects leaks early cited as TMI Unit 1 safeguard
abstract: General Public Utilities Incorporated detected and reported loose plugs in Unit 1 steam generators.  The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has yet to address the merits of General Public Utilities Incorporated's nuclear repair process or the safety of steam generators.  The article goes into further detail about how the early detections should be used as a safeguard.

headline: Prison overcrowding: stop laying blame and act
abstract: A three-judge Common Pleas Court panel held city officials in contempt and assessed fines that could amount to $3 million a year for failing to obey a court order to improve conditions at the city's three jails. The judges set a deadline of October 1 for compliance with an order placing a limit of 3,525 inmates.

headline: Sex-based auto rates debate still not over
abstract: Women's group hail it as a major victory while insurance industry spokesman assure female clients it will prove to be a disaster. The Pennsylvania state Supreme Court decision barring gender-based rates on automobile insurance policies is two months old, but debate is red-hot as the Insurance Department begins a series of hearings on how to implement the new system.

headline: GOP moves to reassure women
abstract: The confidential Government of the People polls indicate that women are judging the Democratic ticket on the issues, not on the sex of Walter Mondale's running mate (Ms. Ferraro, the Democrat's vice-presidential candidate).  The Republicans have laid plans to reassure women that their interest will not be ignored in a second Reagan administration.  The article continues to explain how the Republican's plan on running their campaign to counteract the Democrats.

headline: State cabinet members give financilal data
abstract: The article provides the information about the value of shares for PA Agriculture Secretary Penrose Halloween, Environment Resources Secretary Nicholas DeBenedictis and State General Service Secretary Walker Baran. The financial disclosure statements were filed with the governement's office.

headline: Despite apparent wage tax impasse, an agreement might be possible
abstract: The closed-door negotiations over the wage tax that began at the beginning of June among city legislators are aimed to reconcile two positions - of suburban legislators who insist on cutting the wage tax and of the suburbans who are unwilling to agree to shift the tax load.

headline: Business, Labor Ready for Capitol Clash
abstract: Pennsylvania's newly elected Legislature will be the battleground in 1985 for key economic and business issues, and the state's workers' compensation program is shaping up as the most controversial. There is a table of issues that business and labor would focus on in Harrisburg. They include bank deregulation, local tax reform, equal pay-comparable worth, health care cost, hazardous waste disposal and lower workers compensation.

headline: The Anti-Nukes Ignore Facts
abstract: This editorial argues that the nuclear industry is being hurt the worst by "rabid anti-nuclear" people who have stirred up problems where none existed.

headline: Progress in the K-9 Unit
abstract: This editorial reports that attacks by dogs in the Philadelphia Police Department's K-9 Unit have decreased dramatically, by 88 percent, in the last five months.  The department had been heavily scrutinized after the FBI and a federal grand jury investigated over reports that there were many attacks on unarmed men and women.  Previously there were 41 attacks per month. Attacks have now decreased to 1.5 per month.

headline: Shabby treatment of Sen. Zemprelli
abstract: Pennsylvania state Senator Eugene F. Scanlon, argues that the Pittsburgh Post Gazette is reporting unevenly about the PA Governor Thornburgh's plan to divest the state from operating the profitable state retail liquor stores. According to state Senator Scanlon, the Thornburgh proposal benefits "huge corporations," while the Gazette falsely accused state Senator Zemprelli of being beholden to special interests. Finally, the Gazette said in its editorial " Now He Wants to Talk" that before a debate takes place the senate debate must be held. Scanlon notes that an extended debate in the state Senate on the issue of public divesture from liquor sales has occurred.

headline: GOP needs woman candidate for auditor general: Shanaman gets a look
abstract: The PA state GOP has been searching for a woman candidate for the office of auditor general and Susan M. Shanaman of Mechanicsburg has been considered.  They seek a woman in order to help bridge the so-called Reagan gender gap, but also have other criteria that they seek to match.  The ideal candidate would have a recognizable political identity and preferably be from the southeastern part of the state, so as to complete a geographic balance for the statewide ticket in the April 10 primary elections.

headline: State delegation misses Mondale's visit to hotel
abstract: Walter Mondale was visiting political Caucases in their hotel on July 18 1984. He wanted to make a briefing before his return home. Mondale's wife, Joan told the media that she is proud of the fact that Pennsylvania has the largest number of delegates for Mondale and they would try to beat Reagan in November 1984.

headline: Enact business tax reforms
abstract: It is vital to Pennsylvania that the state legislature complete action on a bill that would enable Philadelphia Mayor Goode and the Philadelphia City Council to include business tax reform in the city budget for fiscal 1985.

headline: Contract combustion
abstract: Local 210 of the Steelworkers union has accepted contract concessions at the East Monongahela's foundry of Combustion Engineering, Inc., and this editorial states that it is a "painful but also hopeful choice."  After nearly half a year in bargaining, the plant nearly closed but the decision by Local 210 will keep the plant open and protect the jobs of the younger union members.

headline: The legacy of the Met Ed gand
abstract: Metropolitan Edison, the operators of Three Mile Island, misled Nuclear Regulatory Commission inspectors about the results of safety tests. The short-term consequence was a near meltdown at Three Mile Island. The long-term consequences are apparent in areas of international diplomacy, economic growth, environmental health and energy policy.

headline: Proposal for additional 17 judgeships advances
abstract: The Pennsylvania House approved the creation of new Common Pleas judgeships in 16 countries in order to help ease the caseloads on May 29, 1984

headline: SHIFT OF LCB ROLE URGE: Governor asks enforcement control by Revenue
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh, with his proposal to abolish the state liquor control system stalled in the state Senate, has called for swift legislative action to transfer liquor enforcement and licensing to the state Revenue Department. This transfer is one component of the governor's stalled plan. Thornburgh argued that at the least the Legislature should be able to agree that enforcement should be transfered and noted that he'll continue to fight for full public divesture from liquor retailing.

headline: GOP receives warm welcome in hot Dallas
abstract: U.S. Vice President Bush kicked off five days of Republican partying and politicking designed to launch President Reagan toward a second term.  The only controversy involved convention rules, specifically a proposal to increase the share of delegates from big states at the 1988 Government of the People convention was overwhelmingly rejected by the convention rules committee.  The article goes further into detail about Bush's meeting with the Republicans.

headline: State delegation's OK likely to be unanimous
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh said he was sure that the Pennsylvania delegation will unanimously adopt the 1984 Republican Platform.  The article goes into further detail about why Thornburgh feels that the delegation will be behind Reagan in the next election.

headline: Feud begins in mayor race
abstract: Mayor Richard Caliguiri presented a budget message hailed as a superb display of municipal wisdom, held the line on city taxes and he proposed a four-county economic development commission intended to assist this area in its transition from its heavy industrial base to a high-tech service center.

headline: Hazard areas of mines focus of safety study
abstract: A study conducted by the University of Pennsylvania's James Bennett and David Passmore, using data from 1977 to 1982, found that injuries are just as severe outside the mine's face, where coal is removed from the ground, as those away from the face. Duties away from the face include laying railroad track and checking for ventilation. Safety programs typically train for safety in the face, according to the U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration. The report also found no correlation with the worker's mining experience and the severity of injury.

headline: Thornburgh cites unresolved TMI safety issues; Restart-vote delay asked
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh asked the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to hold its decision on the restart of Three Mile Island Unit 1 until at least a half-dozen safety questions are resolved.  Thornburgh stated, “There should be no choice at all between resolving safety questions before cranking up a nuclear reactor, or simply putting off those questions and crossing our fingers.”  Among the questions Thornburgh said should be resolved was assured full funding for the Unit 2 cleanup. The full article goes into argument for the cleanup for safety concerns.

headline: Put Drug Bust Money to Good Use
abstract: A bill being considered before the Pennsylvania Senate would authorize money confiscated from suspected drug dealers to finance investigations into trafficking. Richard Weatherbee, director of the attorney general's Bureau of Narcotics Investigating and Drug Control, said that most local agencies don't have the resources to make good use of the funds. However, some argue that this legislation will motivate local law enforcement agencies to go after narcotic offenders.

headline: Some fear governmnet will lose at Philadelphia area racetracks
abstract: In exchange for Bo Brennan's promise to rebuild the fireravaged Garden State Park racetrack in Cherry Hill, New Jersy officials gave him twice as many racing dates, a reduction from 8% to .05 % in the betting handling tax, and 40 mln low-interest, and tax- free loan.

headline: GOP scans the action for its own
abstract: A dozen Republicans watch the Democratic convention and think that the way the Democrats make the news there will not be necessity in spying.

headline: State Democrat leaders want Benedict off ticket
abstract: Walter Mondale and Geraldine Ferraro, Democratic party's nominees saw any kind of difficulties within the state's 195-member delegation on the convention floor. Pennsylvania party leaders. However, look beyond the speeches at the nomination and try to decide to see what is best for the party in the sate come November 1984.

headline: First Black to Lead Philadelphia Emphasizes Voluntarism
abstract: W. Wilson Goode was sworn in today as the 126th Mayor of Philadelphia.  Goode is the first black Mayor of Philadelphia and he hopes to mend the rift that has grown between City Council and the mayor's office.

headline: Helping jobless too big a chore for the UC Law
abstract: The Pennsylvania Unemployment Compensation Law, hailed like others similar to it across the land as a safeguard against personal economic calamity, has weaknesses that must be addressed.  The editorial argues that the law was designed to serve as a short bridge between jobs or as a cushion after temporary layoffs, but instead it has become a crutch trying to support jobs that have vanished, particularly in communities like Beaver County where the steel industry collapsed recently.

headline: Three island cleanup effort receives boost
abstract: The electric utility industry finally opened its coffers to support the cleanup of General Public Utilities Corporation's Three Mile Island nuclear plant near Harrisburg.

headline: Senate confirms Scirica as federal court judge
abstract: Montgomery County Common Pleas Court Judge Anthony J. Scirica has been confirmed by the United States Senate to fill a vacancy in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.  He was approved unanimously for the post which comes with a salary of $76,000 per year.

headline: Thornburgh says he still opposes parts of the no-fault legislation
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh said that he still had substantial objections to a bill pending in the PA Senate that would create a new no-fault auto insurance system.  The governor said that he was dissatisfied with various sections of the bill, yet declined to say whether he would veto the bill.

headline: GOP sees slight gain in state
abstract: Republican strategists gave the party on October 16, 1984 a strong chance of picking up only one seat in the PA House delegation from Pennsylvania.

headline: State finances look good
abstract: Pennsylvania's government revenues run 6 percent above estimates at the 1984-85 General Fund reaches its half-way point with the turn of the calendar year.

headline: Goode leads a King memorial
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode hosted the largest mayor's prayer breakfast honoring the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in the city since former Mayor William J. Green initiated the observance in 1981.

headline: Job-hungry; Numbers of dislocated workers dwarf resources for retraining
abstract: Schools offer people courses and industry has trained workers.  The article discusses programs that are tailored to laid-off workers, college programs that intend to make students into acceptable workers, and goes further into detail about how the resources are becoming insufficient to fund these programs.

headline: TMI accident suit dismissed
abstract: Federal Judge Sylvia Rambo dismissed a York County man's suit on June 20, 1984 for damages as a result of the 1979 accident at Three Mile Island nuclear power plant because he refused to substantiate his personal injury claim.

headline: Rape
abstract: The new law would give spousal sexual assault the same penalty and reporting requirements as the crime of rape.

headline: Thornburgh to bide time on no-fault bill
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh says that he will wait for further legislative action before either signing or vetoing legislation to scrap the state's 10-year-old no-fault auto insurance law.

headline: GOP speakers ignore Ferraro
abstract: There was no mention of Geraldine Ferraro, Democrat vice president nominee, at the most recent Republican National Convention.  The article goes further into detail about how the Republicans have not mentioned Ferraro when discussing the election campaign.

headline: State funds for jobs must be spent fairly
abstract: In the April 10 balloting, Pennsylvania voters overwhelmingly approved the issuance of $190 million in bonds to expand employment. The funds should be dispersed based on need, rather than political power in the Legislature.

headline: Government still largest employer
abstract: Local government has remained the largest employer in Pittsburgh.  Attached to the article is a chart of the 50 largest employers in the Pittsburgh area and the article provides further details about the jobs in Pittsburgh.

headline: Officials back Crafton meat plant
abstract: Several elected officials pledged to support a group of former employees of the Armour Food Co. meatpacking plant in Crafton who want their jobs back.  Pittsburgh Mayor Caliguiri, county Commissioner Tom Foerster, City Controller Tom Flaherty, U.S. Representative William J. Coyne and U.S. Senator H. John Heinz are among the officials who were present at the conference and who were working to convince the plant's parent company Con Agra Incorporation to reopen.

headline: TMI and the NRC
abstract: This letter expresses gratitude to the Philadelphia Inquirer newspaper for "pressing for the public's right to know what goes on at meetings of the [Nuclear Regulatory Commission] whose sole legislative mandate is protection of the public health and safety in its responsibility to license and regulate nuclear power plants."

headline: Rape-by-spouse bill goes to governor
abstract: The PA General Assembly approved a bill that would remove marriage as a defense to a rape charge. The fate of the bill will be decided by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Two firms ask to lower rates
abstract: The state Insurance Department announced that Pennsylvania's largest automobile insurance company and another agency are reducing rates for coverage required under Pennsylvania's no-fault replacement law.

headline: Gov. Thornburgh yields, the special interests win
abstract: Instead of exercising his leadership to persuade the state General Assembly to make PA's 10-year-old no-fault automobile insurance law work the way no-fault is supposed to, the governor yielded to what his aides called the "political realities."  This editorial further argues that, when faced with the choice of defending the public interest against the special interests, the governor chose to give the special interests what they wanted.

headline: State incumbents have little time to savor
abstract: From Eastern to Erie, Bradford to Bedford, Pennsylvania voters opted for the status quo at the beginning of November, choosing to keep their president, congressmen, attorney general, state treasurer and assemblyman.

headline: Green rejoins law firm he left to become mayor
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor William J. Green has rejoined the law firm of Wolf, Block, Schorr & Solis-Cohen, a firm that earned more than $2 million in city-related legal fees during his four-year administration.  Green's close ties with the law firm were the source of some criticism during his administration, particularly from members of the Philadelphia City Council, who felt that the firm was receiving a disproportionate share of city-related legal work.

headline: Protests called harmful to the state
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh says that efforts to help the economy through development are being hurt by labor militants who disrupt church services and pour skunk oil on business firms to protest the loss of jobs.

headline: TMI blockade order is lifted
abstract: A temporary restraining order that was issued at the request of plant operator GPU Nuclear Corporation against demonstartors at Three Mile Island Friday was dissolved on May 23, 1984 in Dauphin County Court. Judge Herbert A. Schaffner lifted the order he imposed after protesters blocked TMI's North Gate.

headline: Resignations halve jail's nursing staff
abstract: Two of four nurses employed at Dauphin County Prison quit. One of the nurses found a job closer to her home and another cited the death of a 23-year old inmate as the reason of her resignation.

headline: Upstaters assail tax-paid insurance plan
abstract: Local government proposed to include elected and appointed officials under tax-paid health insurance.  The proposal is contained in a bill that was approved by the PA senate.  The article goes further into detail about the proposal and the fears of smaller municipalities.

headline: In 7th District: Bob Edgar
abstract: We endorse Bob Edgar in the Democratic primary. He has championed the cause of veterans  and has worked against pork barrel spending. Across the board-- forgein affairs, domestic issues, constituent services-- Represenative Edgar has an outstanding record.

headline: State legislators put tax reform at top of priority list
abstract: (Editor's Note: This is the last of a five-part series detailing the PA Legislature's response to an Associated Press questionnaire.)  PA Legislators prioritized 36 issues and chose tax reform as number one overall.  Second on the list was the improvement of the state's economy.

headline: Guidelines suggested for city contracts
abstract: A task force appointed by Pittsburgh Mayor Caliguiri recommended on November 7, 1984 a standardized procedure for all city departments to use in awarding no bid personal service contracts.

headline: Right-to-know
abstract: In Chicago a man working in a factory died from the fumes he inhaled. No one had told the worker that the substance he was working with was poisonous. It is hoped that nothing like this would happen in Pennsylvania due to the right-to-know bill which would ensure that workers are informed about the substances they are required to work with.

headline: TMI Cleanup Forecast Was Way Off the Mark
abstract: J.C. Devine Jr. GPU Nuclear Corp.'s technical planning director for Unit 2, maps out the TMI cleanup plan.

headline: Right-to-die issue for comatose man splits the family
abstract: In their court petition, family members argue Tweed's constitutional right of privacy is broad enough to encompass his decision to decline medical treatment under certain circumstances.

headline: USS sees future for Mon Valley Works
abstract: Even though Pittsburgh was hit hard by U.S. Steel Corporation's year-end job cuts, the company's chief financial officer maintains there is a future for steelmaking here, including the possibility of modernization.

headline: Interviewing is not a picnic
abstract: The author of the article describes in dialogues the way the interview is performed in the light of presidential race. It shows that people who are called to talk about their political preferences do not even know their candidates and easily confuse them with others.

headline: State Meetings
abstract: Article is a list of PA legislative committee and state agency public meetings of general interest scheduled for this week in the Harrisburg area.

headline: Krajewski questions 'mini-City Hall' in Northeast
abstract: Nearly 400,000 residents live in Philadelphia's Northeast end, enough to be the second largest city in PA. Therefore, Mayor Goode and community leaders support the idea of a mini-City Hall to support the area's resident s and enable better access to city services. However, City Council Majority Leader Joan L. Krajewsk, who represents part of the Northeast end,  is hostile to the idea because she says it will add another layer of government to an already constrained budget. However, some argue that she is hostile to the idea because she is protecting her political turf because she wants constituents to bring their problems to her satellite office instead.

headline: Right-To-Know Abuse
abstract: Pennsylvania state Representative Jim Manderino and Representative Allen Kukovich are proposing a law which could create more unemployment throughout Pennsylvania.  They want businessmen and industrialists to invest more than $200 million into labeling hazardous and non-hazardous chemicals, known as House Bill 1236.  The article goes further into detail about the reasoning behind the proposed bill and how the Senate Labor and Industry Committee will respond.

headline: TMI emergency plan is rejected
abstract: The staff of the Nuclear Regulatory Committee decided that the emergency plan for the communities around the nuclear station  at Tree Mile Island is inadequate.

headline: Rizzo files a libel suit over editorial cartoon in the Daily News
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank L. Rizzo filed a suit in Philadelphia against the Daily News, three editors and its editorial cartoonist contending that the cartoon caused him severe emotional distress and forced him to quit the job. The cartoon depicted Rizzo as a gas man with wads of dollars bulging from his pockets, seeking a handout from a homeowner identified as "John Taxpayer". There is a photograph of Frank L. Rizzo.

headline: Welcome Johnstown corporation
abstract: July 6, 1984 was a red-day for the Johnstown community, the official launching of the Johnstown corporation, which took over the Johnstown Works of US Steel Corporation.

headline: Government does not police itself well
abstract: Editorial argues that the PA Senate and House have not done a very good job of policing themselves.  Reports in the Philadelphia Inquirer note that some legislators have collected daily expense payments when they are, in fact, not in Harrisburg and not performing state-related work.  The editors feel that lawmakers should me more trustworthy.

headline: State members of Congress split on deficit fight
abstract: Pennsylvania members of Congress see mixed signals from voters and sharply differing views among themselves on federal taxes and spending.

headline: Mayor is criticized in the Pernsley case
abstract: Philadelphia's Mayor Goode was sharply criticized by two city council members for his recent statements suggesting that city Welfare Commissioner Irene Pernsley would be fired if progress is not made soon in stabilizing her troubled department.

headline: State shorted when US gave out funds to help jobless
abstract: The $5 billion emergency jobs bill approved by congress in 1983 was blind to the high unemployment emergency in many states like Pennsylvania.

headline: TMI has week of big news, most of which is favorable
abstract: On July 25 1984 Three Mile Island workers lifted the top off the crippled Unit 2 Reactor for the first time since the accident at the plant on March 28, 1979.

headline: Scepticism about Crime Commision
abstract: When the PA Crime Commission gave its annual report to the state Legislature hardly anyone came. The reason is that state attorney Zimmerman urged the elimination of the Crime Commission. The state attorney's office is underfunded and he assumes that free money (from Crime Commission's budget) would help him to find extra money to fill up the gaps in his resources.

headline: What about State Store profits?
abstract: This editorial argues that the privatization of liquor sales in PA would benefit both state coffers and consumers.

headline: Governor asked to save area jobs
abstract: Six Allegheny County senators have asked PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to join in an effort to save 950 Pittsburgh area jobs marked for elimination by Westinghouse Electric Corporation.  They hope that the governor will meet with executives and local officials to see if it is possible to get Westinghouse to reverse its recent decision.  There was no immediate response from Thornburgh.

headline: State needs legislation to limit election spending
abstract: The editorial discusses how the dilemma of how to finance election campaigns can be solved. The solution is that PA needs law to stop high cost of running for office.

headline: New law allows property tax rise
abstract: The PA House approved a bill on June 26, 1984 that could open the door for the future Allegheny County property tax increases. The bill would allow the county to levy up to 5 additional mills of taxes to cover its annual contribution to the operation of the Community College of Allegheny County.

headline: State, Philadelphia Gain Jobs in 4th Quarter '83
abstract: Pennsylvania gained 41,900 jobs in the fourth quarter of 1983, when adjusted for seasonal factors, and the Philadelphia area also registered an increase in employment, according to the U.S. Labor Department .

headline: TMI N-DOSE TOTALS RISING: Prolonged cleanup blamed for new work force radiation estimates
abstract: Dr. Bernard J. Snyder, director of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Three Mile Island Program Office, said delays in the cleanup have contributed to the increased risk of workers.  The Nuclear Regulatory Commission's revised radiation dose estimates for workers in the Three Mile Island Unit 2 cleanup are six times higher than projected in 1981.

headline: Screen child-care staff
abstract: Legislation proposed by Pennsylvania state Senator Michael O'Pake is intended to make background checks mandatory for those that work in the child care field.  The article continues to provide reasons why the legislation is a good idea.

headline: What will the new insurance law do? For now, at least, nobody knows
abstract: On October 1, the new law written largely by the Insurance Association of PA and the PA Trial Lawyers Association, will replace the state's nine-year-old no-fault system with a system that eliminates restrictions on lawsuits.  The state Insurance Department has no estimate of how the new law will affect insurance rates.

headline: Governor denominates 4 judges
abstract: On July 16, 1984 PA governor Dick Thornburgh accused the Senate of putting politics before merit in thwarting his efforts to fill four vacancies on Allegheny County Common Pleas Court

headline: State pacts prober alleges stonewalling
abstract: Pennsylvania Representative Gordon Linton, chairman of the House special committee on minority contracts,  accused the governor's office of directing state agencies to stonewall in a House probe of the number of state contracts awarded to business owned by minority members and women.  The article goes into brief detail about Linton and his beliefs of Thornburgh's office.

headline: Occupation Tax Dilemma
abstract: Ending the hated occupation assessment tax will not bring tax relief to taxpayers because the money will need to come from somewhere.  Likely, the loss of the substantial sums raised by the occupational levies would be replaced by other taxes.

headline: Steel workers expect jobs back, study says
abstract: A study of Pittsburgh's displaced steel workers indicated that many are unwilling to admit that their jobs might to gone for good. About 100 steel workers were interviewed by the Appalachian Regional Commission. Most of the displaced workers are between 22 and 40 years old  and lack mobility because of economic commitments like mortgages. As a result of the mass job loss the survey shows that these workers mistrust government, business and even their own unions. The commission also found that nearly 100 programs exist in the Pittsburgh area to aid displaced workers.

headline: TMI needs no boosters; it needs strong regulators
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission was created in 1974 because its predecessor, the Atomic Energy Commission, acted as a booster of nuclear energy instead of regulator.

headline: Senate clears bill to strip pusher profits
abstract: The PA senate unanimously approved a bill designed to strip drug traffickers of their profits.  However, many Democrats object that it is being used to boost Republican campaign efforts.  The bill is sponsored by state senator Michael Fisher, and it will set a maximum life sentence for large-scale operations and a $100,000 fine.

headline: Why not let people vote
abstract: Dauphin County chair of the Libertarian Party, Richard D. Prescott, argues in favor of a public referendum on the issue of public divestiture of state liquor stores. He argues that United Food and Commerical Workers of Pennsylvania's opposition to any such referendum is rooted in their ability to control politicans better than they could the entire population.

headline: Governor does some shuffling of top officials
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Richard Thornburgh appointed a new press secretary and two cabinet secretaries, and moved another cabinet secretary to a top advisory position.  The reshuffling was prompted by the departure of a number of top aides.  The article continues to provide details about the changes and the people that were newly appointed to their positions.

headline: State program lags
abstract: Since the nation's first weights and measures law signed by President John Adams on March 2, 1799, there was a consent between the law and merchants to make sure that consumers get full value for their money.  According to the PA Legislative Budget and Finance Committee, Pennsylvania is not doing a good job in that area.

headline: Occupation tax has got to go
abstract: Occupation tax reform and changes in other nuisance taxes were long needed in Pennsylvania. It may be the time when unfair, inequitable tax levied by some area school districts and municipalities will be abolished.

headline: Sun's New Layoffs Will Hit Hard Here
abstract: Sun Oil Co., which last month announced plans to lay off 800 workers, including 500 at its Marcus Hool refinery, will cut 1,400 more workers from its nationwide operations, the company said yesterday.  The new dismissal will affect primarily white-collar, professional employees.  Although the company officials did not specify where the cuts will fall, they did agree the brunt of the layoffs will be in Philadelphia, where many of the company's corporate operations are concentrated.

headline: TMI restart decision is postponed
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission voted to postpone the decision to restart the undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island, which has been called a victory by anti-restart activists.  Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh urged the vote be postponed until funding was made certain to fix the other reactor and hearings on the integrity and competence of the plant's operator are completed.

headline: Senate Vote Oks Govt. Executions
abstract: Death-penalty supporters won their biggest victory in 10 years on Capitol Hill as the Senate passed legislation to reinstate capital punishment for federal crimes.  The victory may only be symbolic because of staunch opposition stifling the chances for passage of any death penalty bill in the House.  On a 63-32 vote, U.S. senators passed and sent the House a bill backed by the Reagan administration providing execution as punishment for treason, espionage, terrorism, murder on federal property and attempted assasination of the president.

headline: Wine sales in food stores
abstract: This editorial argues in favor of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal to divest liquor stores, but, more specifically, it argues that PA should at the very least permit the privatization of wine sales in the format commonly known as "Wine in Food Stores."  According to a national study, liquor control states (18 out of 50) that permit wine in private food stores generate significantly more revenue without the negative consequences.  The modification would also boost the economy due to increased jobs and businesses, the reversal of the trend where Pennsylvanians go out-of-state to by wine, and with the increased production of wine in grape belts like Erie County.

headline: Governor in ad criticized
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh irked a senior citizens' group and several lawmakers by starring in an ad for a lottery-funded drug program he initially did not support.

headline: State Sets Up Meeting With Capital Contractor
abstract: Allegations that steel used in the $12 million PA State Capitol Addition project is foreign-made began to surface five months ago after State Representative Thomas Caltagirone, D-Reading, received a "tip" from a caller whom he refuses to name.  The 1978 Steel Products Procurement Act requires that all public bodies use only domestic steel in construction, which is why state officials will meet with the general contractor, Emico Mechanical, on Wednesday in hope of some answers.

headline: Phila. offices being the search for budget cuts
abstract: Philadelphia fears facing a $104 million deficit in the next fiscal year, so all Philadelphia government offices are attempting to find places to cut their spending.  The article goes into further detail about where the different offices will cut their budget and predictions on the next fiscal year's spending and savings.

headline: Unions Forever
abstract: The decline of major American industries is due to myopic management and under investment. Tax policy also encourages factories to close. Unions benefit America. Unions are what differentiate the American worker from the Polish worker.

headline: TMI Worker Exposure Discussion Slated Here
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission will hold a session  to discuss possible revisions to the Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement.

headline: Seventh judge for Berks courts
abstract: If the PA General Assembly approves a bill there will be seven judges at Berks court. This may exceed absolute requirements, but current popular conceptions are challenged by the proposal.

headline: Work-Rest Bill Stalled In House
abstract: Business community protests have stalled PA House legislation requiring one day of rest for workers after six days on the job, and may result in public hearings, the measure's chief sponsor says.  Tim Holt, the director of employee relations and insurance for the PA Chamber of Commerce, said that the intent of the legislation is commendable, but it fails to address the real problems that would be faced by businesses operation on a continuous basis.

headline: Governor says state judiciary reform needed
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh urged on may 23, 1984 that judges be subjected to the same public scrutinity required of other state officials. Governor Thornburgh called on the PA House to pass a constitutional amendment that would be accessible and accountable to the public.

headline: State to appeal ruling against 2-tier wage tax
abstract: PA officials said on June 11, 1984 that they would appeal to the State Supreme Court a Commonwelth decision that struck down Philadelphia's two-tier wage tax.

headline: Philadelphia's wage tax must be part of reform
abstract: Last year the city of Philadelphia raised the wage tax rate to 4.96 percent for city residents but left it unchanged at 4.3125 percent for non-residents which could not be changed because of a cap imposed by legislature in 1977. The Independent candidate for Mayor petitioned the Commonwealth Court to invalidate the two-tier wage tax on grounds that it violates the uniformity clause of the Pennsylvania Constitution. The city's position is that it is unconstitutional, but opposes any change that would significantly alter the city's budget.  The editorial board believes that the city and suburbs can work together for comprehensive regional tax reform.

headline: Workers, Firms Taxed More
abstract: Pennsylvania state taxes are now higher for workers and employers as part of a law enacted last year to bail out the unemployment compensation fund.  The reform law also contains other measures that will reduce benefits in an effort to make the jobless fund solvent by 1986.

headline: TMI-1 comments on tube repairs
abstract: Repairs at Three Mile Island's Unit 1 were claimed to be unsafe at the hearing before the Nuclear regulatory Commission on July 16, 1984. GPU officers testified that the firm's plans are to adequately meet both the Nuclear Regulatory Commission conditions and to ensure the plant's safe operation.

headline: Sex-offender treatment units pushed
abstract: PA State Representative James G. Greenwood prepared to introduce legislation that would create diagnostic and treatment centers for convicted sex offenders. The bill would also prohibit parole for the sexually dangerous offenders.

headline: CARTOON
abstract: Cartoon depicting Uncle Sam sitting in a chair and getting his shoes polished.  The small boy polishing his shoes has gotten polish all over the ground around Uncle Sam's feet and the words "cost overruns" is written in the polish.  The small boy holds out his hand for his pay and behind him is his shoe shine kit that has "Defense contractors" written on it.

headline: Governor selects nominee for post
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh said on November 14, 1984 that he would nominate Alma Jacobs, chairman of the state Commission for Women, to be secretary of the state Department of Aging.

headline: State workers' salary, benefits slip
abstract: The 1984 Governor's Annual Work Force Report, made available on May 8, 1984, showed pay and benefits decreased slightly because of cuts in retiremnet and workers' compenstation costs.

headline: Pittsburgh is healthy
abstract: Without denying the very painful problems of industrial dislocation resulting from the severe slump in steel-related activities, the authors of this onion piece believe that Pittsburgh's economic condition is, in fact, beginning to show some very significant signs of improvement.

headline: ...'Basics' ordered by acting city superintendent
abstract: The new temporary superintendent, Donald M. Carroll, Jr., has stated that he intends on making permanent changes in the school district and has a "back-to basics" approach on education.  The article provides a brief biography on Carroll, his ideas on how to transform the education system, and how much money and time it will cost for the changes.

headline: Transcripts reveal new information
abstract: The transcripts of 28 closed door meetings held by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission during the past two and a half years revealed new information about investigations of alleged improprieties at Three Mile island.

headline: Shumaker Revives Effort to Move State Courts Here
abstract: PA State Senator John J. Shumaker has revived a proposal to unite under one roof the Pennsylvania Supreme, Superior and Commonwealth courts as well as the Judicial Inquiry and Review Board and Pennsylvania  Sentencing Commission. The original proposal died because of objections to the $200,000 cost of a General Services Department Study. Shumaker argues that the fragmentation of the facilities leads to delays in administration of the appellate system and carrying out justice and that the centralization follows the recommendations of the 1982 Pomeroy Commission Report.

headline: Confidence in the shipyard
abstract: The announcement that a third aircraft carrier will be coming to the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard for overhaul was great news for the region's economy, as it will be a $630 million job.  It is essential that shipyard workers continue the good work in hopes of obtaining future contracts with the Navy.

headline: Governor takes risk on television rating
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh plans do to a once a month cable television program and the state will pay production costs.  Since popularity is very important to a politicians career, the article voices its worries towards the television ratings.

headline: State, Libertarians Nearing Settlement
abstract: PA Libertarians have filed suit in regards to filing deadlines, which are among the earliest in the nation, and thus make it harder to get independent candidates on the ballot. Currently,  third party candidates are requried to obtain fifty times the signatures needed by the two major parties candidates.

headline: Pittsburgh's 1985 budget
abstract: Mayor Caliguiri revealed a document that is not only robust in its fiscal dimensions but also challenging in its political content. Its broad outlines contain a payoff to the residents of Pittsburgh and the Caliguiri administration for sustained confidence and careful city management.

headline: A blueprint for disruption
abstract: The 1982 Pennsylvania state bill that states school officials, "shall excuse any student from school attendance for a total of not more than thirty-six hours per school year in order to attend classes of religious instruction," has disrupted the public school system.  The Pennsylvania law appears designed to circumvent the United States Supreme Court ruling that prohibits religious practices in public schools by using school hours.  The article provides more explanation on why religion in public schools is unacceptable.

headline: Trial of nine here looms as N-Forum
abstract: Dauphin County Court trial set for August 6 1984 has the makings on the hazards of nuclear power. The defendants are nine people charged with obstructing a public passage in 1983, when they demonstrated against the proposed part of Three Mile Island. The State Superior Court ruling in April 1984 cleared the way for them to argue that their action was justified on the basis that the obstruction of public passage is less harmful than the prevention of the harm.

headline: Southside arson ring is probed by police
abstract: Pittsburgh police believe that an arson-for-profit ring was formed on the south-side after a series of minor fires began to be reported in October 1983.

headline: Democrats on "the day after"
abstract: The recent Democratic National Convention talked about controlling nuclear weapons, outlawing nuclear weapons and/or putting into effect a freeze on nuclear weapons.

headline: Governor's priorities please legislators
abstract: The supportive words of a Democratic state senator from Johnstown, a long-time critic of Thornburgh administration economic policies, may be the most telling sign of a generally positive reaction yesterday to Governor Dick Thornburgh's 1984-85 budget proposal.  The only major reservations from lawmakers dealt with Thornburgh's plans to fund some programs from lottery revenues -- a source rejected soundly by lawmakers last year, except for senior citizens' programs -- and for selling state liquor stores.

headline: State: a mixed bag
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman was an aggressive prosecutor. Zimmerman's campaign accepted $10,000 in contributions from 28 members of Kidder-Peabody and Co., a New York brokerage firm. It is not an illegal donation but questionable since the attorney general's office was engaged in an unsettled dispute.

headline: Stop the budget chaos
abstract: Cambria County commissioners adopted a 1984 budget without following the budget process stipulated in the PA County Code, which this editorial argues is an unacceptable practice.

headline: A software opportunity
abstract: Pittsburgh got a boost in the second week of November when the Defense Department announced award of a $103 million, five-year contract to Carnegie-Mellon University to establish a computer software research center on the university's campus.

headline: U.S. Is Against Dismissal of Met-Ed Charges
abstract: Federal prosecutors filed papers opposing each request by the former operator of Three Mile Island to dismiss criminal charges stemming from the 1979 accident at the nuclear plant in Londonderry Township.

headline: Sprague sues judge Snyder $278,389 said due in judicial -misconduct defense
abstract: Lawyer Richard Sprague sued Judge Bernard Snyder who he represented earlier in misconduct investigations. The reason for his claim is that the judge did not meet his obligations - to pay $75,000 under a retainer agreement. There are also two photographs of Richard Sprague and Bernard Snyder on both sides of the article.

headline: Freedom
abstract: There is a cartoon depicting demonstration with the pacifist signs such as "Disarm now" and "Better red than dead". Also, there is a crowd of merry people dancing around enjoying freedom. The people who participated in the demonstration say that they should probably have demonstrated some other time.

headline: Grist of Benedict-Dwyer campaign mill
abstract: The comment came during the initial comments of a face-to-face meeting between state Treasurer Budd Dwyer and Auditor Al Benedict who have been fighting a nasty campaign for state Treasurer. They both are punctuated by barrage of charges and counter charges directed at alleged improprieties on the part of both candidates.

headline: State's home investment
abstract: At the beginning of July, the Public School Employees' Retirement System announced that it would invest $50 million in mortgage certificates offered by the Pennsylvania Mortgage Corporation.

headline: Stronger Sunshine
abstract: This editorial advocates the approval of Senate Bill 932, the so-called Sunshine Bill, which is designed to make it more difficult for school boards, borough councils, township supervisors or county boards and agencies to hold closed-door meetings or "executive sessions" from which the public is excluded.

headline: A success after 20 years
abstract: There is a photograph that depicts the University Science Center president standing in a parking lot where a new $3 million building is scheduled to be located by 1985.

headline: Unusual Event' Declared at TMI
abstract: An "unusual event" was declared at Three Mile Island's Unit 2 reactor when neither of two backup power generators was working, the plant's operator said.  An "unusual event" is the lowest of four emergency categories at a nuclear plant defined by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

headline: State by state, marital-rape statutes are being set
abstract: In the 1970s prosecutions for raping a spouse were nonexistent. In the 1980s 22 states permitted spouses living together to be prosecuted for rape. Pennsylvania would become the 23d state if PA Governor Thornburgh signs the bill.

headline: Memories and losses bind war's survivors
abstract: Survivors of Correidor, Stalag 17, Korea and Vietnam gathered for POW/MIA Recognition Day. 2,484 Americans are listed as missing in action in Vietnam.

headline: Guardsmen sample ready-to-eat rations on summer
abstract: Soldiers in the US Army started eating differently: they eat meal ready to eat which includes pork, spiced beef, hot dogs and beans and sausages, turkey, ham loaf, dried fruits and crackers with peanut butter or jelly.

headline: State's hungry must not settle for red tape
abstract: The Governor and Penrose Hallowell, secretary of agriculture, should not have given their personal attention to a program as important as feeding hungry people. For the second year running, the PA Legislature authorized that $8 million be used to purchase food for the state's needy.

headline: Tax Bill OK'd By State Panel
abstract: The Urban Affairs Committee approved by 13-4 vote a bill  to shift the tax burden away from property towards an ability-to-pay tax model centered on wages.  Cities will be able to eliminate the $10 occupational privilege tax in favor of a $50 flat tax or 1 quarter of 1 percent tax on earned income. PA Rep. Marvin Miller, R- Lancaster argues that this bill frees absentee landlords and downtown businesses, who use a bulk of city services, from paying their fair share.

headline: A Textbook Example of Conservation
abstract: A program announced in Augus offers any school that reduces energy bills more than 4 percent, a 40 percent rebate on the money saved. Pennsylvania Lt. Governor William Scranton, who is chairman of PA Governor Thornburgh's Energy Council, visited George Washington High School which has saved over $32,000 and has saved the district $1.3 million.

headline: Without reforms, nuclear's no choice
abstract: In light of the recent bad news surrounding nuclear power, nuclear power, in order to survive, must be safe and cost-competitive, and plants must be well-built and well-managed, argues this editorial.

headline: State court ruling favors Bell in employee firing
abstract: PA Commonwealth Court ruled on May 24, 1984 that Bell of Pennsylvania acted reasonably in telling an employee who had been on extended leave because of anxiety to be examined by a psychaitrist before returing to work.

headline: Navy veteran fills nuclear panel vacancy
abstract: Lando Zech, a retired veteran of the Navy nuclear submarine fleet was sworn in on July 5, 1984 as a member of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. At the public meeting, Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman Nunzio Palladino welcomed Zech to the $71,000-a-year-job. There is a photograph of Lando Zech and Nunzio Palladino.

headline: Guv Controls a 167G Political Bankroll
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, who has repeatedly denied any aspirations for higher office, amassed a $167,000 political nest egg last year, state records show.  Senior aides to the governor said that he plans to use the bulk of the money to underwrite campaigns of Republican candidates for statewide offices and legislative seats.  Some state party leaders and GOP leaders criticized the means by which Thornburgh acquired the funds, but most of this has been resolved after the disclosure of fund records.

headline: State's primary race begins
abstract: In Pittsburgh the three Democratic presidential contenders--Jesse Jackson, Gary Hart and Walter Mondale-- will meet for the third nationally televised League of Women Voters debate. Hart is presenting himself as a forward thinking Democrat and casting Mondale as representing the politics of the past.

headline: Tax bill reviewd for Lebanon unit
abstract: Even though the tax reform bill in the PA House would provide needed relief for the revenue-poor Lebanon, the package does not go for school districts.

headline: Aligning the alumni
abstract: The South Philadelphia High School alumni association raises thousands of dollars a year for student awards and scholarships. It uses prominent alumni for fundraising.

headline: York Commissioner Hovis opposes restart at TMI
abstract: York Country Commissioner Loraine Hovis, the Commission's lone Democrat, would favor a resolution requesting that Nuclear Regulatory Commission deny the restart of Three Miles Island Unit 1. The Republicans on the commission have opposed any such proposal stating that the matter lies with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. A delegation from Fairview Township has requested the adoption of such resolution and notes that 14 other counties and communities have already done so. Also, the commissioners approved a proposal to add a referendum to the ballot on whether the board may increase its membership by two.

headline: State hunts bookie mole in troopers
abstract: The PA state police barracks in Washigton County became the focus of a state grand jury probe into how numbers baron Anthony Graso and other gambling boses keep abreast of investigations into their operations.

headline: Still a big problem for Vietnam vets: Joblessness chronic
abstract: Unemployment is as chronic among Vietnam veterans as it was two years ago in spite of the lower percentage of unemployed people in PA.  Vietnam Veterans Outreach Center in Harrisburg is working against this trend, but is hindered by negative stereotypes against veterans and the competitive job market.

headline: Hager foe reports visit from investigations
abstract: State investigators recently visited Victor Carone, chairman of the Williamsport Municipal Authority and a member of the city Planning Commission, to discuss  his allegations that Senate President Pro Tem Henry Hager has a conflict of interest.  The attorney general's office is investigating the relationship that Hager has with the Insurance Federation of PA.

headline: State's role in Harrisburg project is probed
abstract: The PA attorney general's office is investigating  the role of the PA Department of General Services, which oversees all state construction, in a $45 million dollar project behind the Capitol. Emco, the project contractor, has failed to furnish the invoices to prove that pipes and fitting in the project did not violate the state's 1978 "buy American" steel act.

headline: Tax freeze on November ballot
abstract: Property tax increased so much that the senior citizens and working class people get forced out. The referendum would permit a freeze on property taxes for longtime neighborhood residents in two counties - Philadelphia and Allegheny.

headline: An Agenda For La Salle University
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh made an official announcement of the decision of the Department of Education to confer University status on La Salle.  The article continues to provide details now how La Salle University is planning on living up to their new status.

headline: Zimmer aide tries to keep plant nuclear
abstract: A high-level executive of Cincinnati Gas & Electric Company has been attempting to resurrect the William H. Zimmer nuclear plant despite the utility's announcement that it will try to convert the plant to a coal-fired facility.

headline: State police 'chauffeuring' Thornburgh sons
abstract: The Philadelphia Inquirer has reported that 800 mile round trips have become routine assignments for troopers in the executive protection detail. Records show that troopers, in state vehicles, have provided transportation for two of PA Governor Thornburgh's four sons, age 17 and 25, to and from their campuses in Massachusetts. The transportation was provided for security reasons, according to officials.

headline: PUC moves to help confused phone customers with their bills
abstract: The Bureau of Consumer Services in the state Public Utility Commission has been trying to work with telephone companies to simplify bills.  According to Joseph W. Farrell, director of the bureau, they have steadily received increasing number of complaints from customers who cannot understand their phone  bills.

headline: Handling of Ginny's Voucher Leaves Thornburgh Fuming
abstract: A recent dispute between the PA governor's office and state treasurer R. Budd Dwyer apparently has left Governor Dick Thornburgh fuming.  Instead of contacting the governor and his wife directly when seeking remimbursement for state-paid travel expenses, Dwyer leaked the matter to the press.  Thornburgh was offended because of Dwyer's handling of the situation and also because his wife agreed to pay the expenses prior to the trip.

headline: State's 'scoreboard' in Congress
abstract: PA's US senators and US House members introduced 346 bills and resolutions in 1983, addressing issues ranging from nuclear arms control to National Pretzel Month.  The state's 23 US House members were responsible for 212 of the 5,642 pieces of legislation introduced in that body, which is an average of nine measures each, compared to an average of 13 for all members of the House.  On the other hand, the state's US senators, John Heinz and Arlen Specter,  introduced more than double the average of bills per senator.

headline: Tax reform proposal merits action
abstract: For Altoona and other third-class cities, long-needed tax reforms mean the difference between life and death.  Existing PA state law concerning their powers to tax prohibits them from solving the problems and legislation to update this inefficiency may now be in the works.

headline: Better sunshine law would assure access
abstract: The board of trustees of the Bucks County Community College voted to renew a food service contract worth half a million dollars with the same local firm which has held it for the first 11 years.

headline: null
abstract: Harrisburg as the capital of Pennsylvania is badly in need of a new airport. That was apparent on November 20, 1984 both early in the morning on arrival and later in the afternoon before leaving. The airport is run by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: State policeman will appeal ruling that forces retirement
abstract: A 34-year old veteran of the state police served notice in federal court that he would appeal a ruling that upholds forced retirements of PA state police officers. Lt. Oto J. Binker of New Cumberland requested in an injunction barring forced retirement at age 60 until appellate court decides the appeal.

headline: Scare marketing from Bell
abstract: The Public Utility Commission has approved Pennsylvania Bell's request to charge for repairs to inside-the-house telephone wiring. Letter to the editor complains about Bell's wiring maintenance contract that he says uses scare tactics.  Phone users are billed for this repair service $.50 each month and the coverage does not cover likely causes of wiring problems like nature, fire, vandalism and/or improper installment.  The take it-or leave it approach by Bell is non-consumer friendly and amounts to deplorable scare tactics.

headline: Hard times and tight budgets
abstract: The city of Chester's largest remaining industry is $389,000 in arrears on its local real estate taxes. The $14.3 million budget includes no pay raises for the city's 164 noninformed employees and threatens layoffs or early retirement in the police and fire departments. There is a photograph of a Councilman Timothy Gorby.

headline: Statewide candidates list sources of outside income
abstract: A PA state department spokesman said that PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman received more than $22, 000 in income in 1983 from his former law firm.

headline: null
abstract: There is a cartoon that depicts a bar attendant standing behind the bar stand and wiping a glass with a wipe.  Above him are two signs. One says Five to seven p.m. Happy Hour 2 for 1 and another one says 3 for 1 if you promise not to mention politics.

headline: Beyond Bankruptcy
abstract: Pennsylvania has no straightforward legal method for dealing with bankrupt manucipalities. The conference held at the University of Pittsburgh called for the governor and the general Assembly to shape legislation for municipal bankruptcies based on a school-district model.

headline: null
abstract: There is a cartoon that depicts the subway in Pittsburgh. There are two skeletons waiting for the subway to open. One of them says to another one not to give up hope and wait for the train to come. There is a grand opening sign with a lot of crossed out deadlines such as Thanksgiving 84, spring 85, July 85, 12th or never.

headline: Strip search
abstract: Women inmates at the state prison in Muncy plan to file suit in federal court to stop a new policy requiring a daily quota of strip searches there.

headline: Senators in phone probe advised to use caution
abstract: A Pennsylvania Senate panel exploring confusion over new telephone services was asked to proceed with caution and deliberation.  Pennsylvania state Senator Clarence D. Bell, chairman of the Senate Consumer Protection Committee, mentioned that several people are confused and angry over changes in the way their services are obtained.  The article continues to provide details about the public hearing, the committee's thoughts, and the Public Utility Commission's thoughts on the change.

headline: Hart mounts Pa. Campaign
abstract: U.S. Senator Gary Hart holds a basket of Pennsylvania apples in Harrisburg, as he opens his bid for the Democratic nomination for president in Pennsylvania before the April 10th primary.

headline: Suburban Reps KO City's Biz -Tax Plan
abstract: Suburban Philadelphia republicans demanding a sharp cut in the city's wage tax on commuters blocked enactment of a major busniess-tax proposal. The proposal was defeated on May 22, 1984 despite intensive lobbying by its supporters.

headline: [Cartoon]
abstract: null

headline: Bill on school-closings hearings is passed
abstract: The Pennsylvania House sent the governor a bill to require local school boards to hold public hearings at least three months before a board's decision to close a school. Current law only requires a school district to hold a hearing before building a new school.

headline: "Buy American" forces may be losing battle over bridge
abstract: Port interests opposing "buy American" requirements appear to be winning the latest skirmish over where new steel decking for the Benjamin Franklin Bridge will be manufactured.

headline: Superior Court rejects slaying verdict appeal
abstract: The PA state Superior Court rejected on October 15, 1984 the appeal of a man convicted of killing an 11-year old Cumberland County boy. John Vincent was convicted of first-degree murder and involuntary deviate sexual intercourse and was sentenced to a 4-to 10-year term concurrent with his life term. .

headline: State is facing phone rate hikes, too
abstract: Telephone company Bell of Pennsylvania is excised from AT&T by court order, which will result in PA paying one amount to Bell for its network and another to AT&T for long-distance calls.  The increased competition in telecommunications services could result in savings or higher rates.

headline: Hart tries old techniques
abstract: The Gary Hart Campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination has had a disconnect with its message and its campaign techniques. U.S. Senator Hart, of Colorado, is the candidate. Hart is young and upwardly mobile and touts a new era for politics. However, he uses old tactics such as meeting with steel makers in Pittsburgh, attending black churches and traveling via whistle stop. Hart has been hard at work to court the elderly and union vote as they make up the critical mass of voters in PA. Hart's appeal however is in that he brings new ideas.

headline: Syria paid some bills for Jackson
abstract: The Syrian government paid some hotel bills for the delegation that Reverend Jesse Jackson led to Damascus in his successful effort to gain the release of captured Navy Lieutenant Robert O. Goodman, said Jackson's aides.

headline: [photo]
abstract: Depicts PA Governor Thornburgh congratulating Bishop William Keeler after his installation as the 7th bishop of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Harrisburg.

headline: Bill would aid preservation efforts
abstract: The Philadelphia Historical Commission's power to preserve historic buildings would be increased under a bill introduced in the Philadelphia city coucil on June 21, 1984.

headline: $4 billion ticketed for pike
abstract: A bill authorizing a $4 billion expansion of the Pennsylvania Turnpike including several proposed spurs in Western Pennsylvania won the overwhelming approval of the House.

headline: Supplement legal services
abstract: The current funding level for legal services in Pennsylvania allows only the providsion of some basic survival services, such as aid when a family is about to lose its home. The PA House included $2 million supplemental increase for legal services.

headline: 7 nations to curb steel to U.S.
