abstract: A federal grand jury indicted a physician at Delaware County Memorial Hospital in Drexel Hill, charging that the physician paid more than $10,000 for a medical degree from schools that he never attended.

headline: Group plans appeal on N-plant tests
abstract: Charles Elliot, attorney for Limerick Ecology Action, said that the Pottstown-based organization opposed to Philadelphia Electric Company's nuclear plant under construction in Limerick would appeal a ruling that authorized a license for low-power testing at the plant.  The article continues to provide details about the appeal and how the plant intends to fight the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's plans.

headline: Helping crim victims
abstract: The Crime Victims Compensation Board faces extinction as it is put up for review this year under the Pennsylvania Sunset Law.  The PA state House has passed three bills that are designed to improve the efficiency of the board.  This editorial argues that the state Senate should pass these bills and that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration should focus on easing the lot of victims of crime.

headline: Hazardous waste proposal aimed at small businesses
abstract: Thousands of small businesses in Pennsylvania would be required to track the disposal of their hazardous waste under proposed federal legislation.

headline: Dirty business
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and the other members of the Senate Judiciary subcommittee should not be misled by the false arguments of pornography publisher Al Goldstein and the involved actresses.

headline: Reforming the Turnpike Commission
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh vowed to reform that discredited, patronage-riddled agency and did so by installing professional managers and hiring on the basis of merit.

headline: Plain language bill is good
abstract: PA State Representative Allen Kuckovich, Greensburgh Democrat, was one of the chief sponsors of the plain language bill. The author supports the idea to make the language of the bills plain and understandable to anyone.

headline: Doctors Back Freeze on Fees, Poll Shows
abstract: After conducting an informal poll it was found that a majority of the York County Medical Society members favor a one-year voluntary freeze on medical fees. The idea is the brainchild of the American Medical Association. Medical fees charged by doctors represent 15 to 20 percent of the cost of medical care.

headline: Half-Built Indiana Nuclear Plant Abandoned at a $2.5 Billion Cost
abstract: The Public Service Company of Indiana announced that it was abandoning a half-finished nuclear power plant on which $2.5 billion has already been spent.  This is the most expensive nuclear project ever to be abandoned and is a serious setback for the nuclear power industry, which has been plagued by a wave of plant cancellations in recent years, since the accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.

headline: High court suspends title change
abstract: Responding to pressures from the legislature and an organization of lower court judges, the Pennsylvania state Supreme Court backed down on June 19, 1984 from an order to change the titles of municipal judges.

headline: Hiring Outlook Bright--Poll
abstract: 33 percent of Harrisburg area employers will add jobs to the local economy in the next three months which outperforms the national average of 30 percent, according to a recent national polling firm. Employers indicating the strongest tendency for new hires are in manufacturing and construction.

headline: Disaster area status granted in flood areas
abstract: U.S. President Reagan has declared a major disaster area in seven western Pennsylvania counties that suffered flash floods.  Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh had previously declared a disaster emergency in the region, directing state agencies to assist local and county governments with recovery efforts and placing units of the Pennsylvania National Guard on active duty.  The article goes into brief detail about the federal aid will encompass.

headline: Reforms, "gender gap" key to auditor general contest
abstract: Both major party candidates for PA Auditor General - Republican Susan Shanaman and Democrat Don Bailey - believe that significant reforms are needed in the scandal-ridden department. Gender issue could have captured public attention early in the campaign, but according to Bailey, it would no longer have any influence in the contest. Also, during the campaign Bailey raised more money than Shanaman. It is believed that it would happen due to some political pressures that Bailey would impose on his workers. However, Shanaman received gifts of her own from state workers.

headline: Plan debates now
abstract: Presidential and vice presidential debates should be scheduled for the fall now, so that the competitive antipathy will not be a factor in the scheduling process.  The article gives further detail to past debates where Reagan and Thornburgh were successful in television forums and an instance that Thornburgh opposed a debate with the negative repercussions.

headline: Elderly Sick of Partial Medicare
abstract: The Dauphin Council of Senior Citizens notes that only 25 percent of Dauphin County doctors who file claims for Medicare reimbursement accept the assignment as full payment. The council has informed area doctors that those who refuse to accept a Medicare assignment will not be included in its 'target list' of doctors, which goes out to 41,000 seniors.

headline: Heinz questions a TMI cleanup pact
abstract: Senator John Heinz and nuclear industry officials called for the government to look into a company hired to spend nuclear fuel from the disabled Unit 2 reactor.

headline: House Oks "wrongful birth" measure
abstract: The Pennsylvania State House approved legislation that would outlaw lawsuits that seek damages because a child was born instead of aborted. The wrongful birth ammendment was added to an unrelated bill by 124-73 vote and the bill itself was approved and sent to the Senate on June 20, 1984.

headline: House Committee Oks small games of chance
abstract: The PA House State Government Committee approved legislation on June 27, 1984 to allow non-profit groups to operate small games of chance in countries where voters approve.

headline: Disclose finances, Nix says: Lawmakers like plan for judges
abstract: Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. of the PA state Supreme Court has made a series of recommendations -- including mandatory financial disclosure for the state's judges -- aimed at making the courts more accountable to the public.  Legislators, after an unprecedented appearance before a joint session, responded favorably to Nix's call for judicial reform.

headline: Remember Those Whistle Stops?: Hart Paused Here Briefly
abstract: U.S. Senator Hart stopped in Harrisburg to stump for his candidacy as president. The candidates (U.S. Senator Gary Hart and former Vice President Walter Mondale) disagree on domestic content legislation. Tony Schertler, Hart's deputy planner, was dispatched to Pennsylvania to help set-up the 18 minute speech given by Hart.

headline: PLCB member Mario Mele to address GOP women
abstract: Mario Mele, a member of the PA Liquor Control Board will speak to the New Cumberland Council of Republican Women January 24 in New Cumberland.

headline: Fifth vets' home planned for state
abstract: The federal government is ready to fund a fifth soldiers' and sailors' home in Pennsylvania. According to chairman of the House Subcommittee on Veterans Hospitals and Health Care Bob Edgar, the facility will be situated in the Philadelphia, Pennsylvania area. The federal government will provide 65% of construction costs and 30% of day-to-day operating costs.

headline: Hope to sock us to clean up TMI
abstract: Utilities in New York state have requested permission from the New York Public Service Commission to spend $7.1 million from their Research and Development Fund on the Three Mile Island cleanup efforts. Several New York state officials as well as New York City officials were angered by the request which would spend money on an out of state effort. The New York utilities want to join 118 other utilities that belong to the Edison Electric Institute in contributing $150 million to the cleanup  effort.

headline: House Oks 3 new judges for county
abstract: The Pennsylvania House approved the bill which would add three new judges to the Allegheny County's Court of Common Pleas and a total of 22 judges in 18 counties.

headline: How they voted
abstract: The PA Senate passed the bill to allow bettors at Commodore downs racing track in Erie to wager on races televised from the Meadows race Track in Washington County.

headline: Disparity in benefits noted
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Local Government Committee was asked to approve legislation that would give to township supervisors the right to tax paid health insurance benefits.  Legislators benefit from tax-paid health care benefits and so do all other state payrollers.  The article provides different sides of the debate over the benefit issue.

headline: Rendell may run for governor
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell said on November 8, 1984 he expects to be a candidate for governor in 1986.

headline: Plight of jobless; House panel pledges to help displaced workers
abstract: The special Pennsylvania state House committee has pledged to make the General Assembly more sensitive to the problems of laid-off workers of folded factories.  Pennsylvania Representative Peter J. Daley, chairman of the committee, said the committee would continue to hold hearings.  The article provides details on specific testimonies of people from unions and public officials, and it provides information on why the matter of high unemployment is harmful to the state economy.

headline: Grant will help Phila. Homeless
abstract: A Philadelphia group plans to help 6,000 homeless people a year receive medical care under a $25 million nationwide program unveiled on December 19, 1984.

headline: How can NRC vote on TMI restart?
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is ready to vote on June 27, 1984 on the restart of the undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island, but it has to take into consideration the questions of safety and health of people.

headline: House Oks no-fault divorce bill
abstract: The Pennsylvania House approved on June 5, 1984 a bill that would make it easier to obtain a unilateral no-fault divorce in PA. According to the current bill, a spouse can obtain a divorce if he/she lived apart from the other spouse for two years.

headline: Improved liquor stores proposed
abstract: Opponents of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's private liquor store bill unveiled an alternative proposal that they said would "modernize" the existing state store system.  A bipartisan group of four senators called for legislation that would: permit state stores to accept credit cards and personal checks, establish several "super stores" to give customers a wider selection, and institute modern marketing techniques and give state store clerks additional training.

headline: Document Room Probe Absolves Senate Employees
abstract: An investigation into alleged document selling in the PA state Senate Bill Room failed to uncover any wrongdoing, according to Robert L. Keuch, executive deputy attorney general.  The probe began about a year ago when the PA Attorney General's office began looking into allegations that out-of-town firms may have been charged a fee for requested bills and other documents -- services that are intended to be free to the public.

headline: Reporter at large
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh marked his 39 birthday on July 16, 1984. there is a photograph of the reporter Paul Beers.

headline: Political Switch
abstract: PA State Representative Fred Belardi, recently switched from Republican to Democrat, is roommates with one of each.

headline: Health costs climb
abstract: Despite the lower inflation and major efforts at controlling costs undertaken by government and providers, the cost of health care in Pennsylvania continues to increase at a dangerously high rate.  Pennsylvania's health-care bill is being paid in part by employer-paid health insurance plans and in part by the government-operated Medicare and Medicaid programs.  The article goes into further detail about health care costs.

headline: Legislature at a glance
abstract: Pending legislation before the Legislature include proposals that would: 1) require companies to list toxic substances they use and their health effects; 2) bar gas utilities from using automatic gas cost rate to increase rates and require utilities to purchase the cheapest gas available;  and 3) require high school students to pass a competency test before graduating. This is not a unabridged listing.

headline: House opposes "wrongful life" suits
abstract: Lawsuits for "wrongful birth" would be barred in Pennsylvania courts under a bill approved by the House of Representatives. The measure would restrict suits against physicians for failing either to recommend or to perform an abortion, or failing to inform parents of a likely birth defect that would have led to a decision to abort the pregnancy.

headline: Insurance companies often burned by arson
abstract: Due to the increase of fraud-arson cases nationwide, there are Insurance Claims Services Incorporation and Insurance Crime Prevention Institute which provide fraud investigative services to any property and causality.

headline: Don't clutter ballot with useless questions
abstract: PA Senator Mark Singel of Johnstown and three of his collegues signed  bill introduced by Senator Edward Howard, to ask Pennsylvania voters if the federal government should reduce spending on nuclear weapons aid and use money for domestic social programs.

headline: Reporter's Notebook: Star Tracking
abstract: Mrs. Jeanette Oswald predicted that Vice President Walter Mondale would win the Democratic nomination. She also predicts that Ronald Reagan would be re-elected president.

headline: Power play
abstract: Republican senators were inundated by heavy lobbying by five colleagues seeking to become Senate majority leader, amid signs that no clear front-runner had emerged. There are photographs of five Senators for majority leader's job.

headline: Hospital's expenses rise at slower rate
abstract: Hospital expenses do not rise any more because of new government policies and lower inflation rates. Hospital rates went up at an annual rate of 7.4% during the last six months of 1983, about half the 15 percent average annual jump since the early 1980s.

headline: Japan's $18 million to aid TMI
abstract: Seventeen Japanese companies agreed to pay the U.S. government $18 million over 5 years for research and development on Three Mile Island's damaged core. Thus, individual nations need not bear the full cost of research and development for benefits that are shared. The Japanese also agreed to provide 100 man-years of engineering assistance over the next five years. The U.S. Department of Energy has committed $159 million in research and development.

headline: House panel approves 13 more judgements
abstract: A bill that would add 13 more common pleas court judgeships in counties across Pennsylvania, including Adams, Cumberland and Yor was appoved by the PA House Judicial Committee on May 1, 1984.

headline: Insurance inequities
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh kept his promise that the Insurance Department would represent the public.

headline: Don't lift ban on politicking
abstract: PA Representative Jeffrey Coy and 20 other representatives are attempting to force Pennsylvania into a great leap backward to the 19th Century. Coy is a co-sponsor of the bill to lift the state ban on certain political activity by state service employees.

headline: Representative Clinger listed as wealthiest in state delegation
abstract: According to financial reports released on May 16, 1984 representative William Clinger was the wealthiest member of the Pennsylvania delegation in 1983 with stocks and other holdings worth $1.1 million to $1.9 million. There is also a photograph of Representative George W. Gekas who made only $250 in honoraria.

headline: Pre-eminent issue
abstract: PA state Senator Mike Fisher, the Post-Gazette and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh feel that the price of a bottle of liquor is the pre-eminent issue.

headline: Hospital's release of mental patients is strapping Norristown, panel told
abstract: Norristown Borough officials and community leaders told the Pennsylvania state House Health and Welfare Committee at a hearing on the Norristown State Hospital that slumlords are profiting and legitimate business people are being hurt due to the release of psychiatric patients unable to fend for themselves.  The hearing was requested by PA state Representative Joseph Lashinger who wanted to show the suffering of the borough due to what he termed as "the failures of the state's current mental health policies."

headline: Keep TMI Down, Guv Urges NRC
abstract: Pennsylvania’s Governor Thornburgh has urged the Nuclear Regulatory Commission not to allow Three Mile Island to resume operation. The Governor questioned the wisdom of restarting Unit 1 when it could be halted because of lack of funds and potential for unexpected release of radioactive material from Unit 2 among other concerns. The entire article also discusses safety concerns and management at Three Mile Island.

headline: House panel Oks drug law revision
abstract: A bill that would provide a comprehensive revision to the state's 1972 drug law was approved by a state House Committee on November 26, 1984.

headline: Insurance lobby asks that Hager delay job reply
abstract: The chief lobbying organization for the insurance industry in PA has asked PA state Senate President Henry G. Hager not to accept its offer of its top job until questions are resolved concerning two investigations into his relationship with the group.  Frank Tarbox, chariman of the Insurance Federation of PA, said the federation board agreed earlier to suggest to Hager that he consider not responding immediately to a job offer made to him by the group late last year.

headline: Dwyer refuses to pay witnesses for Kerr from Benedict's office
abstract: According to PA state Treasury officials, the auditor general's office wrongly sought taxpayer reimbursement for expenses incurred by six of its employees when they were character witnesses for the man convicted of masterminding an office job-selling scheme.

headline: Republican governors get advice
abstract: The nation's Republican governors were urged on December 1, 1984 to seek help from congressional Republicans in an effort to win more statehouses in 1986, a crucial factor in their hopes of achieving political realignment over the next several years and becoming the nation's majority party.

headline: President quotes her wise words
abstract: U.S. President Reagan quoted an 8-year old Chambersburg girl, Leah Kline, in his acceptance speech at the Republican National Convention.  The article provides a brief background on Kline and provides part of Reagan's speech he had given.

headline: Licensing needed in home care field
abstract: The writer of this letter asserts that the rapid growth of home health care agencies in Luzerne County and throughout Pennsylvania should make implementing a state licensing law passed in 1980, but which has never been enforced. a priority.  Four years after the law was passed, the writer urges the state to make it actionable.

headline: Key cleanup step planned for a 3 Mile Island Reactor
abstract: On July 19 1984 the owners of the Three Mile Island Reactor announced that they were preparing a major step in the decontamination of the plant's damaged reactor. The officials plan to remove the top pf the plant's Unit 2 reactor vessel to provide access to the radioactive debris inside. There is a photograph of an engineer C. Hultman who explains the process of removing top of the reactor vessel.

headline: House panel studies revamp of Hill security
abstract: The Pennsylvania House special subcommittee panel, headed by PA state Representative Victor Lescovitz, is discussing techniques to improve protection on Capital Hill. The techniques range from possible terrorist attacks or bomb threats to security from theft.  Louis A Mayo, a former PA House sergeant-at-arms and member of the National Legislative Services and Security Association, told the panel the House must decide how much it would spend for security purposes before becoming involved in improving the protection on Capital Hill.  The article goes further into detail on how security measures are taken in other states.

headline: Insure; 50 companies late in bids for new auto premium rates; Some answers on key points
abstract: Companies that have not yet submitted proposals will probably not receive approval for the new rates by the date the law takes effect, stated acting Insurance Commissioner William R. Muir Jr.  Since these proposals have not been submitted in time, motorists may not be notified about the new rates.

headline: Dwyer releases copies of his last 5 income-tax returns
abstract: PA State Treasurer Budd Dwyer released copies of his federal and state tax returns since 1979. Dwyer, Republican runs for re-election against Auditor Al Benedict, the Democratic candidate.

headline: Republicans here quietly accept re-election
abstract: In Allegheny County when Reagan lost by fewer than 100,000 votes, not many people had strong reactions, a few smiled, some applauded, in general no cheers, no banners waving. There is a photograph of a GOP volunteer Ron Cumming  of Ross who cheered speakers at a rally Downtown with the post that says 'Sold Reagan'.

headline: President's race shows a toss-up
abstract: Despite national polls that showed that Ronald Reagan ahead by 23 percentage points in his race for a second term,  the president was running close to his challenger Walter Mondale in the northwestern Pennsylvania.

headline: Long delays are choking awards of black-lung program benefits
abstract: Officials at the Department of Labor acknowledge that those who are involved in black lung cases must wait too long before a final decision is reached.

headline: Legislation will help limit ease of gas rate hikes
abstract: The Pennsylvania state Senate is expected to vote on a compromise bill that will bring to an end the system that allows gas companies to automatically pass along higher fuel costs to their customers. Under the compromise measure, the Public Utility Commission would have six months to consider proposed rate changes sought by gas companies as the result of higher gas costs.

headline: How they voted
abstract: Western Pennsylvania legislators in the PA General Assembly voted in the following ways: the Senate defeated 30-19 amendments to the Constitution; passed 27-22 the law that allows statewide judicial candidates to cross-fire; rejected 29-19 a resolution calling on Senate to give immediate barring wage; passed 124-70 the law that would require state insurances to cover treatment for alcoholism; adopted an amendment to prevent a woman who gives birth to a deformed child from suing her physisian on grounds that he should have counseled her to have an abortion; defeated the bill that would provide public financing for candidates running for Supreme, Superior and Commonwealth Courts; and passed 178-19 the law that would require employers to inform their workers when they are exposed to toxic chemicals.

headline: Insurer with PA lottery contracts voluntarily suspends sales in Mass.
abstract: Capitol Life Insurance Company responsible for paying about $160 million in Pennsylvania lottery prizes voluntarily suspended sales in Massachusetts after questions were raised about its financial condition

headline: Dwyer: Benedict harassing my employee
abstract: Pennsylvania state Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer accused Auditor General Al Benedict of harassing one of Dwyer's employees.  Benedict's office denied the charge.  The article provides further information on the alleged harassment.

headline: Right-to-know act represents a compromise
abstract: The Worker and Community Right-to-Know Act, passed by the PA General Assembly on October 2, 1984 and signed into law by PA Governor Thornburgh on October 5, 1984, represents a compromise between business concerns and labor groups which addresses the health and safety of workers in the commonwealth. There is a photograph of Dr, Frank Wright, Secretary for policy and planning Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

headline: Pressure from benedict revises Dwyer's memory
abstract: PA State Treasurer Bud Dwyer held a news conference July 23 1984 to dispute allegations revealed by Al Benedict that the treasurer was supposed to receive a $300,000 campaign contribution in exchange for awarding a state contract to Computer Technology Associates.

headline: Looking at a county health agency
abstract: In 1957 York county voters rejected the formation of a county health department. Some people tried for 10 more years to get a county health department created. And now the proposal has resurfaced. City offcials asked the state Health Department for information about starting a local health department.

headline: Lewisberry family sues TMI, cites health woes
abstract: A York county family sued the owners of the Three Mile Island nuclear power station, claiming the March 28, 1979, accident caused them physical and emotional harm.

headline: How to cut a murder rate
abstract: Under the direction of Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh and a state legislature willing to get tough with hardened criminals, Pennsylvania incarcerated more murderers than ever before. As a result, the murder rate dropped.

headline: Insures asked to help sell child seat
abstract: Insurance Commissioner William Muir wants insurance companies to help Pennsylvania drivers buckle up their babies.

headline: Editorial was too kind to Dwyer
abstract: Al Benedict thinks that the fact that editorial did not mention that Benedict's name was indicted by grand jury shows how much in favor of Benedict the editorial is.

headline: Ron's Cuts Hurt City, Foes Say
abstract: U.S. President Reagan's proposed election-year budget was attacked as potentially dangerous to Philadelphia.  Philadelphia City Councilman David Cohen and other speakers at a news conference said that the budget's proposed cuts in human services pose a particular threat in urban areas.

headline: Prize could be forfeited
abstract: A $1.1 million Lottery prize will be forfeited if not claimed by 4:30 p.m. on May 21, 1984.

headline: Lost in transition
abstract: The entire mental health system undergoes a massive change, the consequences of which begin to come into focus and thousands of mentally ill people are turned out of mental hospitals. The trouble is that the change occurs at the same time large-scale budgetary constrictions are imposed on the system at all levels.

headline: Limerick start-up postponed
abstract: The Philadelphia Electric Company said that the start-up of the Limerick nuclear generating station would be delayed from April 15 until at least July and each month delay would add $30 million to the price of the $3.7 billion project.

headline: Inform juveniles' parents
abstract: Current Pennsylvania law does not require authorities to notify parents when their juvenile child is arrested and charged with summary criminal offenses, nor are parents required to attend their child's arraignments.  Despite being told by the court administrator that it was improper, York County District Justice Roy Lam has made it a practice to notify parents when their child has been charged with a summary offense. PA State Representative Bruce Smith, Republican-Newberry Twp., has taken it from there and introduced legislation to commit to law what Lam has done in practice and this editorial supports such a law.

headline: Keep watch on insurance
abstract: During a decade of no-fault, rates rose steadily. Pennsylvania's average annual auto insurance premiums are the highest in the nation. Some insurance companies and agents responded to the problem with seminars, mailings and other methods of informing their clients.

headline: Efforts continuing to register voters among state's poor
abstract: "Freedom Summer '84" is a national campaign to register voters who are in lower economic situations, and has made it their goal to register one million voters.  The article goes further into detail on about the campaign.

headline: Ruling Frees Judges From Financial Disclosure
abstract: The PA Supreme Court held as unconstitutional a section of the state's ethic law that required judges to disclose their personal finances.

headline: Probe hears Sen. Scanlon on CTA pact
abstract: Pennsylvania Senator Eugene Scanlon appeared before a federal grand jury and denied afterward that he had any improper involvement with a California-based computing firm,  Computer Technology Associates Incorporated, under investigation.  The article continues to follow Scanlon's supposed ties to the company and the investigation.

headline: Medicaid Reimbursement Cut Opposed
abstract: Regulations that would reduce state reimbursements for Medicaid patients in nursing homes by $5.1 million were rejected by a Pennsylvania state Senate committee in an effort to make up for the loss incurred by nursing homes as a result of a downgrade of about 16,000 patients from "skilled care" to "intermediate care" a year ago.  The unanimous vote is only advisory though.

headline: Local TMI group sees Reagan letter as start
abstract: President Reagan has expressed his commitment to a resolution of the problems at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in a letter to the Concerned Mothers and Women.  The article goes further into detail about the previous letters that the Concerned Mothers and Women's group had sent to Reagan and the estimated amount the Department of Energy intends to spend.

headline: Innocent error, Hallowell says
abstract: Pennsylvania Agriculture Secretary Penrose Hallowell will plead innocent to a citation charging that he pocketed a $4.99 cassette tape at a Montgomery County store without paying for it.  PA officials described the incident as a mistake on Hallowell's part.  The article goes into detail about what Hallowell says about the case.

headline: Keystone Track Eyed in Race Fix Probe
abstract: The office of PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman is investigating allegations of attempts to fix horse races at Keystone Race Track in Cornwells Heights. 8 jockeys, 2 trainers and an outrider have been subpoenaed. As a result of the investigation a law enforcement officer has been arrested for taking $400 in bribes. Prior allegations of race fixing at Keystone Race Track have been made but never resulted in convictions.

headline: Elected PUC is no panacea
abstract: Two legislators from northeastern Pennsylvania, Representative Gaynor Cawley and Representative Thomas Tigue announced that they plan to go all out in the new session to gain an elected PUC.

headline: Rumors say Thornburgh may join Reagan's staff
abstract: There is a speculation in Harrisburg that 'PA Governor Dick Thornburgh may resign to take a position in U.S. President Reagan's administration. A spokesman for Thornburgh denied the rumors but would not rule out the possibility of Thornburgh going to Washington, DC. There is a photograph of Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Probers of Campaign Funding Frustrated By Inadequate State Laws on Disclosure
abstract: Common Cause, a citizens' lobby group,  has come out saying that Pennsylvania has inadequate financial disclosure laws.  They attempted to determine how much money was given to PA Governor Thornburgh's 1982 campaign and found that less than half of his major contributors had been named.  This problem is prevalent in many states across the country, not just in Pennsylvania.

headline: Medical coverage for alcoholism supported
abstract: Pennsylvania State Health Secretary Arnold Muller on May 10, 1984 supported a measure requiring health insurers to cover the costs of treatment for alcoholism on the same basis as other diseases.

headline: Lone TMI defendant seeks grand jury, NRC files
abstract: James R. Floyd was the only person charged with criminal acts as an employee at the Three Mile Island nuclear power station.  William J. Fulton, Floyd's Defense counsel, stated that Floyd may have been singled out for prosecution.  Fulton levels the charge in seeking federal court approval to open the record of grand jury and Nuclear Regulatory Commission probes into criminal misconduct at Three Mile Island.  The article goes into further detail about Fulton's statements to the courts.

headline: Irvis asks more study on court bill
abstract: Pennsylvania House Speaker K. Leroy Irvis will consider creating a committee to study a judicial reform bill.  The bill would open certain judicial disciplinary hearings to the public and require legislative review of judicial rules and regulations.  The article goes further into detail about Irvis' fears of the bill being instituted and the existing system.

headline: LCB breakup will spur alcohol abuse
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh's divestiture bill will stop the liquor stores from being under control of the state and promises to increase revenues.  By taking the state out of the liquor store equation, prices will go down for alcohol and make consumers more apt to purchasing it.

headline: Election 84
abstract: There is a cartoon that depicts an elephant.

headline: Scandal Skirmishing Snarls State Candidate Activities
abstract: Recent campaign announcements from Democrat PA Auditor General Al Benedict were overshadowed by the severe political damage Benedict suffered when court testimony linked him to a job-selling scandal in his office.

headline: PUC salaries deserve review
abstract: In 1983 PA state legislators were busy raising their own salaries and the salaries of Cabinet officers and judges that they neglected to improve the salaries of five officials who have one of the toughest jobs in government working for the Public Utility Commission. Their salaries have not been raised since 1978.

headline: Mentally ill prisoners' facility sought
abstract: The Board of the Mental Health Association in Cumberland, Dauphin and Perry counties unanimously supported a statement calling for a facility in central Pennsylvania designed specially for mentally ill prisoners and for appropriate treatment of mental health clients in prisons.

headline: Met-Ed Airs Guilty Plea, 6 No Contest
abstract: Metropolitan Edison Company agreed in federal court to plead guilty to one count of criminal misconduct in operating the Three Mile Island nuclear power station and no contest to six other charges.  In making the agreement, Met-Ed exposed itself to fines of up to $45,000, plus costs of prosecution, and agreed to pay $1 million to the PA Emergency Management Agency for emergency preparedness planning in the 20-mile area around the Londonderry Township facility.

headline: Kill greyhound-racing bill
abstract: Letter to the editor urges Pennsylvania state representatives to vote against House Bill 1456 that proposes to legalize greyhound racing in PA. The cruelty of dog racing is evident in the starvation and abuse techniques associated with training that begins at 8-months old. Furthermore, the legalization of gambling provides undesirable consequences and the potential for drug abuse.

headline: LCB Code Compromise Negotiations at Impasse
abstract: Bipartisan negotiations on reforming the liquor code have failed. Republicans want to turn over enforcement to the Pennsylvania Revenue Department and Democrats want to create a new agency for enforcement. Negotiations started after PA Governor Thornburgh's proposal to end the state monopoly of liquor died in the state Senate.

headline: Elections director steps aside over CTA
abstract: Allegheny County Elections Director James Scanlon was relieved of his supervisory responsibilities by the county commissioners on October 25 1984 because he was named in the CTA scandal. There is a photograph of James Scanlon and county Solicitor James McLean at a commissioners meeting.

headline: Scandal suspect enters guilty plea, cooperates
abstract: One of five people accused of being involved in a large-scale scheme to bribe state officials pleaded guilty on November 9, 1984 to one count before U.S. Senior District Judge Malcoln Muir.

headline: Nearing the end of chicken pox
abstract: Among childhood infections such as diphteria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, measles, mumps and rubella, only chicken pox remains to torment 3 million children a year. However, a recently developed vaccine in Japan can effectively prevent the spread of the disease.

headline: Metropolitan news in brief
abstract: On July 5, 1984 officials at Three Mile Island said that they would begin removing damaged nuclear fuel from the crippled Unit 2 reactor in July 1985.

headline: Law Takes Homes Off Auction Block
abstract: A new moratorium under a state foreclosure-prevention law signed by Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh, has replaced a yearlong local moratorium ordered by Common Pleas President Judge Edward Bradley.  As a result, about three-fourths of the 310 properties scheduled for foreclosure were knocked off the docket.  Only commercial property, or those vacated by the owner went up for sale.

headline: LCB manager fired after arrest in fraud
abstract: Robert E. Hockenberry, a Liquor Control Board manager, has been charged with one count each of forgery, false swearing, tampering with public records and theft.

headline: Employees hostage to political gamesmanship
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh is offering a bipartisan slate again for the Public Utilities Commission, and if the offer succeeds Democrats will hold a majority of the five commissioners.  Typically the entire process of appointing someone to office is a matter of partisan politics.

headline: School retirement system plans to invest in housing
abstract: The Public School Employees' Retirement System plans to invest $50 million in mortgage certificates to aid PA's housing industry.

headline: Needy to receive free medicine for giardiasis
abstract: The Allegheny County Health Department announced that 3 suppliers of medicine--Thrift Drug and 2 other private sources which were not named, financial screenings will take place. Also, Pennsylvania Lt. Governor William Scranton has said the outbreak is urgent but does not warrant a declaration of state of emergency

headline: More heat on NRC
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh told the Nuclear Regulatory Commission that a vote to restart the undamaged Unit 1 nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island was not appropriate due to safety issue concerns.

headline: Judge blocks transfer of the retarded
abstract: Pennsylvania Common Pleas Court Judge Alfred J. DiBona blocked the state rom transferring 92 mentally challenged residents from a center operated by Temple University to the Embreeville Center in Chester County. The state Department of Public Welfare said the move was necessary because of the poor conditions of the building. Parents complained about the planned transfers, citing the progress of their offspring and the 45 mile distance they would have to travel to visit.

headline: LCB votes to let bars sell T-shirts
abstract: After turning its back on the practice for years, the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board has decided to sanction the sale of promotional T-shirts in bars.

headline: End bewilderment over sludge issue
abstract: There is a public mistrust that sludge could possibly be safe when applied in the proper manner and the editorial feels that there might come a day when it is available for purchase.

headline: Schoolboy's letter opposed prayer
abstract: The proposed constitutional amendment to authorize organized, spoken school prayer was voted down in the U.S. Senate  56-44 with Pennsylvania Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter in the majority. Senator Heinz read on the Senator floor a letter by a Pittsburgh 2nd grader who is Jewish. In the letter Justin Ross said he used to attended schools in Canada where children had to recite a prayer. Those who did not pray were mocked by fellow classmates.  Senator Specter said he had 100,000 contacts on the amendment, which was backed by President Reagan, and 91 percent favored school prayer.

headline: Nursing home sales tied to care, payment shifts
abstract: The downgrading of many nursing home patients from skilled to intermediate care is blamed by a large home operator for the recent sale of four nursing-care facilities in Pennsylvania.

headline: Nader calls Midstaters nuclear industry's 'first victims'
abstract: Consumer protection advocate Ralph Nader was the keynote speaker at a rally opposing reopening TMI. Nader suggested that corporations who make massive blunders that endanged public health should lose their charters. Nader also suggested that President Reagan allowed international trafficking of plutonium to become part of his platform for free trade. Present at the event were Pennsylvania state Senator John Shumaker, R-Harrisburg, Harrisburg City Councilwoman Jane Perkins and Dauphin County Commissoner Lawerence J. Hochendoner.

headline: Judge denies request to give up Larsen suit
abstract: A Pennsylvania Common Pleas Court judge denied a motion to disqualify himself from presiding over a suit filed by Justice Rolf Larsen against two newspapers, ruling that the motion filed by Larsen was without basis or merit.

headline: LCB will slash 1,000 prices
abstract: The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board on June 27, 1984 is going to put 1,000 discounted liquor and wine items on sale at half the list prices.

headline: Endorsements Walter F. Mondale for President
abstract: The Philadelphia Inquirer endorsed Mondale for President, it states that Mondale would make a good and responsible president. The Inquirer urges that Mr. Mondale be elected.

headline: Scranton names woman to new assistant position
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton announced the appointment of Diane Kiddy to a new position of special assistant for human services.  She will be responsible for coordinating policy planning for Scranton who is directing a two-year study of PA's human services system.

headline: Officials here hit Hershey Hosp. for avoiding Pa. rules
abstract: Local hospital administrators launched an eleventh hour effort to stop Hershey Medical Center from avoiding a law that requires all Pennsylvania hospitals to obtain state approval before making large capital expenditures for building equipment or new beds.

headline: Need questioned for 2nd reactor
abstract: A majority of the Public Utility Commission wants the Philadelphia Electric Company to show why it should be allowed to build its Limerick Unit 2 nuclear reactor.

headline: Judge in prison to hear inmates
abstract: Federal Judge R. Dixon Herman put himself behind bars at the state prison for a one-day trial on charges that the prison's conditions amount to cruel and unusual punishment.  A dozen inmates testified that overcrowding has increased the incident of violence, heightened the potential for rebellion and caused a cut in services and programs.  The article continues to describe the case and the inmates' testimonies.

headline: LCB's 10% holiday sale is a cheap trick, guv says
abstract: The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board announced it would cut prices on all wines and spirits before the Christmas holidays.

headline: Ertel
abstract: null

headline: Scranton starts early in race for GOP's gubernatorial nomination
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton 3d is working quietly to lock up the 1986 Republican nomination for governor.  He has raised about $400,000 and enlisted support of some of the wealthiest business leaders.

headline: Panel: Delco Doc bought degree
abstract: Brian March, 26, employed as a physician at Delaware County Memorial Hospital was indicted on July 12, 1984 for applying for a Pennsylvania license with phony medical credentials obtained through a broker who sold about 100 falsified degree across the country.

headline: New TMI crane defect "disturbs" NRC
abstract: A key federal official claims the new Three Mile Island crane brake system is a real safety consideration.

headline: Judge puts his work on the line
abstract: Philadelphia Common Pleas Judge Richard Klein conducted a hearing by telephone hookup from his chambers in 1 East Penn Square to a courthouse in Bradford County in northern Pennsylvania.

headline: LCB's 2 roles conflict
abstract: When Pennsylvania official's created the Liquor Control Board they gave the agency dual roles as both liquor retailer and enforcer of state laws governing liquor sales.  The board is thus in the paradoxical position of selling liquor to the very establishment it regulates.

headline: Ertel condemns foreign-steel use
abstract: Allen Ertel on October 19, 1984 entered the controversy surrounding charges that foreign-made steel was used in the Capitol addiction in violation of the law.

headline: Scranton stumps Delaware for gubernatorial candidate
abstract: PA Lt. Governor William W. Scranton stumped for Lt. Governor Michael N. Castle in Delaware's gubernatorial contest. Scranton came to know Castle through the National Lieutenant Governor's Association. He praised Castle  for improving public education and promoting though anti-drunken driving laws.

headline: Pennhurst Foes: Ruling Won't Stop Closing
abstract: Advocates for the mentally retarded say the U.S. Supreme Court reversal of a court-ordered shutdown of the Pennhurst Center should not affect Pennsyvania's plans to close the institution by 1986.  According to Thomas Gilhool, an attorney for the PA Association for Retarded Citizens, the Court's decision deals only with the state law question, offering an opinion on federal jurisdiction and saying hardly anything about the rights of the retarded.

headline: No Bulletproof Shields Required for Taxicabs
abstract: The Public Utility Commission said will not require bulletproof shields to protect cabdrivers, but suggested that taxi companies consider using them voluntarily.  The PUC rejected the proposed requirement because of raised costs and inhibited communication.

headline: Judge threatens action to move inmate
abstract: Pennsylvania Common Pleas Judge Samuel Strauss ordered county jail inmate Lenny Moore be committed, but two state mental hospitals have refused to take him.  Common Pleas Judge Robert Dauer has threatened contempt proceedings against a state official if Moore is not committed.  Barbara Hafer, chairman of the county Prison Board plans on speaking to Secretary of Welfare Walter Cohen and other commissioners about the commitment.  The article provides further detail about the reasons why the two state mental hospitals, Farview and Mayview, refused to admit Moore.

headline: Legislator: city is poised to win business-tax fight
abstract: The wage-tax fight between city and suburb legislators that held up passage of the Goode administration's business-tax plan would be settled in a week according to a senior suburban legislator.

headline: Ertel Form Taxless in '80 and '81
abstract: Allen Ertel, a democratic candidate for PA attorney general, avoided paying any federal income taxes in 1980 and 1981 as a result of heavy losses in a business venture.  His opponent in the campaign, Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman said that this news is particularly shocking because he was a member of Congress during the years in question - implying that he was earning a sufficient and steady paycheck.  Despite this, Pennsylvania has no law requiring candidates to disclose their tax returns when they run for public office.

headline: Scranton urges applying new technology to old
abstract: An interview with Pennsylvania Republican Lieutenant Governor William Scranton, III, where the "Pittsburgh Business Times" asks a series of questions from reconstructing the Pennsylvania government to the Philadelphia-Pittsburgh passenger train.

headline: Plan bared by dentists to cut bills
abstract: Nearly 700,000 low-income senior citizens would save money on dental bills through a plan unveiled by the Pennsylvania Dental Association.  Dr. W. Arthur George, Chairman of the association's Dental Health and Planning Committee said that those eligible will receive a discount of 15 percent on all dental work done by participating dentists and specialists.

headline: No vacation without taxation
abstract: Pennsylvania appears to have one of the highest gasoline and admission taxes that prevent tourists from visiting the state.

headline: Judges can sue, but can't be sued
abstract: Several judges of Pennsylvania's Supreme Court sued Times Observer for libel.

headline: Let the public decide the fate of state stores
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh already failed twice in his quest to dismantle the state's antiquated liquor monopoly, that but did not deter him. The approach is different this time - the voters will be asked whether or not the present state store system should be replaced by privately-owned stores.

headline: Ertel leads Zimmerman early, but close finish seen
abstract: Democrat Ertel held a slight lead in the race for attorney general over incumbent Republican LeRoy Zimmerman.

headline: Sears workers get GOP election pitch
abstract: Three Republican candidates for PA state legislative seats made their election pitch to about 100 employees of Sears Roebuck and Co. during a session in the furniture department of the Berkshire Mall store on October 13, 1984.

headline: Quality of Nursing Care Is at Stake
abstract: As a result of a change in rules authorized in a new Pennsylvania nursing home law that was adopted to comply with federal standards, about 16,000 nursing home patients will be reclassified as no longer requiring "skilled" care and instead will only require "intermediate" care.  This editorial argues that the subsequent reduced care resulting from this change gives cause to finding a more permanent solution.

headline: NRC assails nuclear-waste rules: But it tentatively approves administration's plans
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission said it would go along with the government's guidelines for selecting the nation's first high-level radioactive waste dump only if there were major improvements in the plan, including more specific information and further environmental studies.  The commission's proposed changes in the guidelines would effecitvely enable the administration to postpone until after the November elections the politically sensitive task of narrowing the list of possible sites.

headline: Judging the judges
abstract: Even though the court system had been significantly improved since the 1970s, it has failed to change the two-level funding arrangements for the courts.

headline: Letters Pa. Insurance law poor
abstract: Consumers are enraged over the increases the new law brings to their auto insurance policies.

headline: Ertel raps attorney general's environmental protection role
abstract: Democratic attorney general candidate Allen Ertel proposed greater involvement by that office in policy-making and enforcement of the state's environmental protection laws on October 1, 1984. In case Ertel were elected, he would take the reins over litigation and prosecution which was delegated by Zimmerman to the Office of General Counsel under the governor.

headline: Self-Destructing with Al Benedict
abstract: A vote for Al Benedict for PA state treasurer is a vote for destruction of the PA Democratic Party.  Instead, votes in the April primary should go to Arline Lotman in order to include a woman as part of the state ticket and restore geographical parity to the state ticket.

headline: Red cross unit to hear state official
abstract: Arnold Muller, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health, will be the guest speaker at the annual luncheon meeting of the Harrisburgh Area Chapter of the American Red Cross at noon on June 14, 1984 at the Harrisburgh Mariott Inn. There is a photograph of Arnold Muller.

headline: NRC beseiged on 2 fronts on TMI
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh said that a Nuclear Regulatory Commission decision on the restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 1 nuclear reactor was not currently appropriate because cleanup of Unit 2 must take place first.

headline: Jury indicted Pagans in drug empire probe
abstract: A federal grand jury indicted 22 members of the Pagan motorcycle club, including four of its top officers, on charges of racketeering in the manufacture and distribution of millions of dollars worth of methamphetamine and similar drugs.

headline: Liquor compromise
abstract: The political battle between Pennsylvania Democrats and PA Governor Thornburgh's Republicans over turning control of the state's 723 state liquor retail stores may not soon be settled. However, both sides can agree that enforcement should be improved and may be better off transferring such powers from the Liquor Control Board to another entity.

headline: Ertel Unit Reports
abstract: The campaign of Allen E. Ertel, Democratic candidate for PA attroney general, has a balance of $14, 111 two weeks before the April 10 primary. All contributions were $2,000 or less.

headline: Selling is 'war' for man who won Dwyer contract
abstract: John Torquato, well known salesman and writer, was hired by Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer to recover Social Security tax overpayments, but the contract was cancelled because of allegations that Torquato promised kickbacks and payoffs to get it.  The vice president of Computer Technology Associates Limited, Janice Kincaid, was the one that reported the allegations.  The article continues to explain the relationship between Kincaid and Torquato, a brief biography of Torquato, and the reasons behind the allegations.

headline: Schweiker named to company board
abstract: Richard Schweiker, former U.S. secretary of health and human services and a former U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania, was named to the board of directors of National Medical Enterprises Inc. There is a photograph of Richard Schweiker.

headline: NRC calls TMI lift's risk light
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission staff announced its approval of a GPU Nuclear safety evaluation report at the Three Mile Island media center where officials would describe the procedure.

headline: Jury to resume deliberations today in case against suspected job-seller
abstract: The jury in the John Kerr trial appeared to have problems reaching a verdict, but attorneys in the case said they remain hopeful one will be returned on June 30, 1984.

headline: Many Smuggle Liquor From Maryland
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh estimates that 25 percent of all wine and liquor consumed in the state is purchased illegally in other states. However, no official state estimate exist. Consumers of wine and liquor may be driven to purchase out of state beverages due to lower prices. For example, Windsor Canadian, the best selling beverage in Pennsylvania sells at $14.62 for 1.75 liter compared to Piper's in Maryland it sells for $9.99.

headline: Ertel's tax returns filed with ethics unit
abstract: Allen Ertel refused to make his public federal tax returns for the previous five years and on June 4, 1984 he was asked during a news conference in the Capital Rrotunda if he expected the tax return issue would be brought up again. Ertel surprised anyone by filing copies of federal returns for 1983 and 1982, but not for previous years.

headline: Sen. Fumo helped to break the ice
abstract: For PA state Senator Vincent Fumo, the fight to save the Philadelphia Eagles began at the beginning of November, 1984 with a chance encounter in a Miami restaurant and an invitation to see a football game. This would draw Fumo in negotiations of his professional career.

headline: Specter studies black baby death rate
abstract: Pennsylvania Senator Arlen Specter may sponsor legislation that would establish satellite health centers in areas like the Hill District and Northview in Pittsburgh, because the city has the highest black infant mortality rate in the nation.  The article provides further details about the studies into the infant mortality rate, the legislation proposed, and how other cities approach this problem.

headline: NRC orders action
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is increasingly concerned and dismayed that funding for cleanup, which is ample for 1984 would be considerably less than adequate in 1985. NRC Chairman Nuzio Palladino directed staff attorneys to determine the agency's authority to order Three Mile Island-owner GPU Nuclear Corporation to adhere to a shedule for the cleanup.

headline: Justice be any other name
abstract: Doolittle Daley shares his thoughts about the judicial system in general and the Supreme Court in particular, with the writer Carmen Brutto.

headline: More On Liquor-Law Enforcement System
abstract: Pennsylvania state Senator Stewart J. Greenleaf's effort to remove liquor-law enforcement from the PA Liquor Control Board and give it instead to the Department of Revenue needs to be taken one step further: permitting liquor-code violations cases to be heard in the area where the offense occurs to ensure that police are not traveling too far for hearings.

headline: Ethics
abstract: This editorial argues that the PA Supreme Court judges, by ruling unconstitutional certain portions of the Ethics Act of 1978, were wrong and that they should impose rules on themselves instead of exempting themselves from filing reports on their personal finances.

headline: Sen. Lewis Unveils Data on State Spending for Legal Services
abstract: PA State Senator H. Craig Lewis and the Thornburgh administration are still at odds over state spending for legal services.  While the governor's administration contends that payroll costs for lawyers increasing at a slower rate than other workers, Senator Lewis argues that those figures do not reflect what state agencies pay to outside law firms for specialized legal services.

headline: Garment workers tell of woes
abstract: Garment and textile workers complain of losing jobs due to an increasing number of imports.

headline: OK for hot-waste dump
abstract: This editorial looks at the process of setting up a multi-state compact for locating a radioactive-waste dump in PA.   With the PA House giving its approval to set up a joint operation with West Virginia, Delaware, and Maryland, an important step has been taken.  The PA Senate has passed a similar bill, and now all that remains is ironing out the differences.  This process is necessary under a federal law requiring all states to develop plans for getting rid of low-level toxic waste.  The editiorial states that this problem will not disappear, and the fact that it continues to grow means the process may need to speed up.

headline: House passes moratorium on private prisons in Pa.
abstract: A bill that would impose a one-year moratorium on the operation of private prisons in PA was overwhelmingly approved by the state House of Representatives.  The bill also requires the PA Commission on Crime and Delinquency to conduct an investigation into the use of private prisons.  The bill is expected to get buried in a Senate committee.

headline: 'Veterans are the winners' in site for nursing home: Battle for facility started decade ago
abstract: After working for more than a decade, PA veterans were finally awarded a new nursing care home at the New Horizons Building in Pennhurst.  This new building will be used to house 150 veterans.

headline: A primary creeps up on Phila.: Low turnout expected in Tuesday's election
abstract: Voters in Philadelphia will select party nominees for judgeships, district attorney and city controller at the May 21st primary election, but there is not much interest in the event.  The campaign was quiet, but became inaudible after the city was traumatized by the fire and death that ended the MOVE siege.  Mindful of the MOVE aftershock, most politicians said they expected voter turnout to be even lower than they had previously predicted; experts predict turnout around 27% for a nice day and as low as 10-15% if it rains.

headline: Turnpike bill returned: Senate pulls blinds on Sunshine Law
abstract: This article includes a round-up of action that occurred in the state Senate.  Discussed are two amendments to the Sunshine Law--one that eliminates penalties for public officials who intentionally violate the law, and the other to give greater leeway for administrative actions by local government.  The state Senate also made another stab at finding a solution to the turnpike construction impasse.  They also approved a bill that would permit the staging of contests of skill in taverns and clubs.

headline: GM picked site for labor peace, analysts say
abstract: Auto industry experts speculate that General Motors Coporation (GM) chose Spring Hill, Tennessee as the site for its new Saturn automible plant in an effort to find a labor climate that was stripped of traditional union rules.  GM was eager to break away from states such as PA, Michigan, and Ohio, where worker attitudes have been shaped by years of labor-management friction, analysts say.  Although laid-off United Auto Workers members will be given first priority for jobs in the new facility, most of these employees are likely to be younger and not bound by traditional work rules.  In an effort to reduce the $1,500 to $2,000 per-car cost advantage that the Japanese manufacturers have over their US counterparts, the new Saturn plant will also implement new auto industry ideas from Sweden and Japan.

headline: Pa. House bill paves way for waste dump
abstract: With a federal deadline fast approaching, the PA House unanimously approved legislation that paves the way for the state to host a regional, low-level radioactive waste dump.  Procedures for selecting the actual site for the disposal facility will be contained in separate legislation that has not yet been introduced.  Under the proposed "Appalachian" states compact, PA would manage a site within its borders and accept shipments of low-level wastes from neighboring states such as West Virginia, Maryland, and Delaware.  In response to a Congressional mandate for states to develop compact plans, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh proposed last January that PA be the host state for its three small neighbors.

headline: House votes to regulate "stun guns"
abstract: The PA House voted yesterday to have "stun guns" regulated as handguns.  The House passed the bill, which would bring "stun guns" under the Uniform Firearms Act, onto the Senate.  The initial bill proposed would have placed a six month moratorium on the use of stun guns, with the exception of police, but it was changed after State Representative Fred Noye argued the moratorium was unnecessary.

headline: Veterans' home battle ties up building funds
abstract: A battle between the state House Appropriations Committee and Governor Dick Thornburgh over the location of a veterans' home in the Philadelphia area has delayed $800 million in statewide construction money.

headline: A streamliner at Energy: Herrington may aid merger
abstract: John S. Herrington was named by President Reagan as the Secretary of Energy.  Reagan hopes that Herrington can work with Donald Hodel, Secretary of the Interior, to create a merger of the two agencies.

headline: Two key Reagan aides switch jobs
abstract: President Ronald Reagan announced that his chief of staff, James Baker, and his Treasury secretary, Donald Regan, will trade jobs for Reagan's second term.  The job change would involve expanded responsibilities for both men, giving Cabinet rank and membership on the National Security Council to both.

headline: Harvest time
abstract: Each year, roughly 4,000 seasonal and migrant farmworkers harvest the majority of PA's $350 million fruit and vegetable crop.  PA spends about $3 million a year, mainly in federal money, on services for these migrant workers and their families.  State departments are regularly criticized by farmworker support groups and political adversaries for failing to meet fully their responsibilities.  The PA Department of Environmental Resources is responsible for inspecting housing and sanitary facilities that growers provide for their seasonal workers.  The PA Farmers Association contends that the state's growers have generally treated their workers well and are undeserving of criticism.  The ethnic make-up of migrant populations has changed over the past few decades as well.  Farmworker advocacy groups believe that the state's Seasonal Farm Labor Act is adequate for protecting workers, but enforcement by the PA Labor and Industry Department falls woefully short.  The PA Department of Education also enrolls about 4,600 students from 52 countries in it migrant education programs and will spend $1.9 million in 1985-86.

headline: Panel OKs Graterford evacuation: Way cleared for Limerick license
abstract: The federal Atomic Safety and Licensing Board approved nuclear-evacuation plans for Graterford state prison, clearing the way for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue the Philadelphia Electric Company a full-power operating license for the Limerick Generating Station.  The Board said the state's emergency plans for the prison, which is eight miles from the plant, addressed inmates' concerns that they would be evacuated quickly and adequately in the event of a serious nuclear accident.

headline: How the bomb decision was made: Although the bombing of a radical strongpoint by Philadelphia police caught the citizenry by surprise, contingency plans for it had been made weeks, even months before.
abstract: This article provides a reconstruction of the events and decisions that led to the bombing of the MOVE house in West Philadelphia.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts people standing in line at the "Ohio Bank Cash Machine"; a lady in line receives the message "You have reached a non-working number."

headline: A win for Pittsburgh
abstract: This editorial applauds members of Pittsburgh City Council for unanimously approving four pieces of legislation that will make possible a complex deal for the takeover of the Pittsburgh Pirates; the deal also binds the Pirates to Three Rivers Stadium for at least five more years.  The editorial also praises Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri for forming a public-private partnership to negotiate for the rescue of the Pirates.

headline: Unfinished business:  House will be the deciding factor
abstract: When the PA Legislature returns from its holiday recess in 1986, it will be taking up 1985's unfinished business.  They will do so with a PA House that is split by the narrowest margin since 1981; Democrats hold a one-seat advantage.  The business the PA Legislature will have to deal with includes reforms to the PA Liquor Control Board and PA Public Utility Commission, legislation governing seat belts, cable TV pornography, and privatization of prisons.  The article includes a review of battles over these issues in 1985, as well as a look ahead to future battles in 1986.

headline: Imports lid is rally cry at Capitol
abstract: About 4,000 textile and garment workers gathered on the steps of the state Capitol to rally for restrictions on imports.  Labor leaders say that PA has lost more than 11,000 jobs in the textile and garment industry and that restricting the market will protect jobs.

headline: PE expected to seek higher return on equity
abstract: Joseph Brennan, a New Jersey consultant specializing in utility finances, is expected to tell the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) that Philadelphia Electric Company's (PE) profits need to be bigger than average because the utility is seen as a risky investment on Wall Street.  The hearing, the first in a series on PE's request for a $670.7 million annual rate increase, will focus on the company's claim that it needs to earn a profit equal to 15.75% of its stockholders' equity to keep its standing in the financial markets.  Under PE's plan, electricity prices would rise nearly 30% by mid-1988 for most users in Philadelphia and its suburbs.  The PUC could reduce PE's rate increases by as much as two-thirds, or more than $400 million by adjusting PE's rate of return.

headline: How the fire spread past MOVE
abstract: The philadelphia Inquirer reconstructs the events that lead to the bombing of the MOVE house in West Philadelphia and the subsequent fire that burned 61 homes and left 250 people homeless.  The article says that firefighters had to wait too long to fight the fire, and that they faced a lack of water pressure; moreover, police and fire commissioners did not know what to expect when they dropped the bomb.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: Cartoon depicts two mechanics gleefully watching an older lady enter the shop as one mechanic says, "Oh boy, here comes one of those 'I'm leaving everything up to you' gold mines."

headline: Adviser to Williams on DA Campaign:  Don't
abstract: According to an internal campaign memo prepared by Robert Williams's pollster, Paul Maslin, Williams was essentially told that the less the public knew about him the better off he would be.  Maslin even suggested that Williams should not debate Ron Castille, who eventually won the campaign for Philadlephia District Attorney.  The poll also concluded that the more that people learned about William's background as a judge, the more vulnerable he was to defeat.  The article also gives a brief look at the different campaign styles of the two candidates.

headline: Unions form coalition
abstract: The American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees and five other unions said they are forming a coalition called State Workers United for Fairness to publicize their case and lobby legislators.  The unions have threatened to go on strike when their contract expires if a new pact is not in place.  The Thornburgh administration has proposed a 2% wage increase over the next three years, but union leaders have rejected that as "totally unacceptable."

headline: Jail union revocation confirmed
abstract: The state Labor Relations Board has decertified the Pennsylvania Social Services Union Local that represented workers at the Cumberland County Prison.  The county salary board voted to give those workers retroactive pay raises and return them to the mainstream of the county employment system.

headline: PE files reply to review: Faults law judge over Limerick
abstract: A Philadelphia Electric Company (PECO) spokesperson said an administrative judge's recommendation to the Public Utility Commission represented an unlawful intrusion into the management of the utility.  The judge's recommendation prevented PECO from borrowing money to complete its second nuclear reactor at the Limerick power plant.   Judge Allison Turner, after a year-long investigation, said that the second reactor was "not in the public interest" and that it could lead to an increase in electric rates for PECO's customers.  PECO disputes the finding of Judge Turner, and in its response attacks the fact that Turner used evidence provided by consumer and anti-nuclear groups.

headline: In Our Opinion: Marital Rape Illegal
abstract: A new law in PA has made spousal sexual assault a crime.  The editorial argues that this legislation was needed, but courts will have to work hard to ensure that it does not become a weapon of vengeance in marital battles.

headline: "Premature" LCB Measure Rejected
abstract: The PA Senate narrowly rejected a surprise motion to continue the life of PA's Liquor Control Board for another 10 years.  Moreover, the PA Senate's Committee on Law and Justice approved a measure that would allow grocery stores and specialty shops to sell table wine, though this measure is expected to be defeated when it is taken up by the PA House.  Leaders in the PA Legislature expressed doubt that the issue of LCB "Sunset Review" can be resolved by the December 31, 1985 deadline.  They also predicted that the debate over the future of state liquor operations would be long and heated.

headline: Afflerbach won't seek re-election
abstract: PA State Representative Roy Afflerbach has announced that he will not seek re-election next year.  Afflerbach, a Democrat, is considering possible runs for lieutenant governor, PA Senate, or US Congress.

headline: Unusual chain of events fuels Democrats' declining numbers
abstract: Cumberland County Democrats have faced difficulties since the 1960s as the minority party; at one point they cut the Republican registration advantage down to 10,000.  Recently Democrats trail Republicans by more than 18,000.  The article discusses possible reasons for the Republican advantage, including the death of two incumbent commissioners and the implication of a former Commissioner in thefts at the county home, as well as a real estate tax increase.

headline: 'Jobs, not hot air' is slogan of those seeking US aid
abstract: More than 500 people, many of them unemployed persons from PA, traveled to Washington DC for a demonstration on the steps of the Department of Labor.  Demonstrators were trying to urge Congress to extend the Federal Supplemental Compensation program for long-term unemployment.

headline: Philadelphia Electric wants 28% rate hike to finance Limerick plant
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Company (PECO) said yesterday that it will ask the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) to raise its electric rates by 28.2% for all customers over the next three years.  PECO is raising rates to pay for the Limerick Nuclear Generating Station.  Philadelphia Electic says that it needs to recover $671 million in operating costs incurred from Unit 1 at its Limerick Plant.  PECO provides electric, gas, and steam service to 1.3 million customers throughout southeastern PA.  The rate increase would raise the bill for the average residential PECO customer from $58.35 to $75.86 per month.  Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode and state Consumer Advocate David Barasch said that they plan to file formal protests of the proposed rate increases.  Barasch's complaint will focus on whether the economy of southeastern PA can continue to subsidize the high costs of the Limerick plant and whether the area needs the plant at all.

headline: Inmate Describes 'Muncy Monopoly'
abstract: A female inmate at Muncy State Correctional Institution complains that the inmates are used as pawns in a power struggle between the male and female guards at the prison.

headline: 18% credit ceiling sent to Thornburgh
abstract: A bill to allow retailers, bankers and other providers of consumer credit to continue to charge as much as 18% interest on credit cards and charge account balances was approved by the state Senate and House and will be sent to Governor Dick Thornburgh.  It is expected that the Governor will sign the bill.  If he does not, the maximum interest rate will fall to 15% on March 25.

headline: AFSCME, state haggle to the end
abstract: Efforts to reach a contract settlement and avert a strike by tens of thousands of state workers went down to the wire.  Chief negotiators for the Thornburgh administration and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees met privately and engaged in "meaningful talks" about wages and fringe-benefit concessions.

headline: US Attorney General
abstract: US Attorney General Edwin Meese and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh received honorary doctor of laws degrees from Spring Garden College in northwest Philadelphia today.  There was talk that Governor Thornburgh may be headed to a cabinet position in President Ronald Reagan's administration.  Thornburgh praised Spring Garden and its new 33 acre campus, which he believes will train more young people to take their place in the economy of the future.

headline: Keep spending on job retraining?
abstract: A columnist argues that spending money on job retraining does not work unless there is a strong business climate; without a strong business climate, re-trained workers will not get hired.  The columnist also says that the government should pay close attention to what methods work best for retraining.

headline: Politicizing the PUC
abstract: This editorial worries about two provisions in the recently-passed bill that reauthorizes the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC).  The bill would allow an incoming governor to pick the chairman of the PUC and would reduce the terms of future commissioners from 10 to 4 years.  The editorial believes that both of these changes would subject the PUC to political pressures from which it is currently insulated.  This would move away from the "good government" idea of independent, poltically-insulated regulatory commissions.  The editorial believes that this, along with calls for public election of PUC commissioners, is undesirable, as it will inject politics into what should be an independent process.  Publicly elected commissioners will either take funds from the utilities they are supposed to regulate, or campaign on an anti-utility platform, giving the consumers the worst of both worlds.  The bill that is about to enter the PA Senate should be given a long look.

headline: Inmates break into canteen at Graterford
abstract: Inmates at Graterford state prison broke into the commissary, a prison canteen where prisoners can purchase snacks and personal items.  Prison officials said the inmates would receive disciplinary hearings at the prison.

headline: A fight to keep rates up: Credit-card firms face Pa. deadline
abstract: Bankers and retailers in PA are lobbying the General Assembly to renew the 18 percent ceiling on interest rates for retail purchases.  The law is set to expire in March and the rate will return to 15 percent. Lobbyists for the retailers say that companies will lose money at the 15% rate; others say that a lower rate is better for consumers.

headline: Alaska's governor, facing impeachment, denies lying to grand jury
abstract: Alaska Governor William Sheffield is facing impeachment on the grounds that he manipulated specifications for a $9.1 million state office lease; the building is owned partly by Lenny Arsenault, a campaign contributor to Sheffield.  Governor Sheddield is also accused of lying about his connections to Arsenault.  However, several state senators have said that the required rules committee votes for impeachment are not there.  Under tough questioning from members of the Alaska State Senate, Sheffield denied showing any favortism to Arsenault, even though he knew that Arsenault had a financial interest in the building; Sheffield said the building was chosen because he felt it was the best location and deal for the state.

headline: US: GOP chief tried to control computer bribe
abstract: US Attorney James West told jurors that, in return for his awarding a multi-million dollar contract to a California computer firm, a $300,000 bribe was offered to State Treasurer Budd Dwyer's 1984 re-election campaign.  West also testified that State Republican Party Chairman Robert Asher threatened to notify authorities unless that money was given to the State Republican Committee.  West made his remarks to jurors at the opening of the bribery trial of William Smith and Alan Stoneman--two lawyers for  Computer Technology Associates (CTA), the California firm.
