headline: More aid is sought for jobless
abstract: Despite President Reagan's opposition, US Senators John Heinz and Carl Levin have launched a bipartisan effort to extend federal supplemental jobless pay for 321,000 workers whose benefits are due to run out in two weeks.  Senators Heinz and Levin want to extend the program for three months at a cost of about $500 million.  Reagan does not support the extension of the program and says that the unemployed should rely instead on job-training programs.

headline: PUC begins to pare Bell rate hike request
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania may end up taking a significantly smaller amount than it originally sought in its current rate case before the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC).  The PUC began discussing the case based on a non-binding poll of 38 issues and is believed to be close to entitling Bell to an annual increase between $28 and $35 million.  The commissioner of the PUC often sided with the ruling by PUC Administrative Law Judge Robert Christianson.  When the commissioners did differ from Christianson, they often sided in favor of consumers.  PUC commissioners did break with Christianson and side with Bell on the rate of return that Bell's investors should be allowed to earn.

headline: Inquiry board stands up in censuring Judge Snyder
abstract: This editorial urges the state Supreme Court to remove Common Pleas Court Judge Bernard Snyder from the bench as the Judicial Inquiry and Review Board has recommended.  Snyder held repeated private conversations with the plaintiff's attorney in a 1982-83 libel suit against Philadelphia Magazine.  Also, at a post-trial hearing the judge testified as a witness while continuing to preside over the hearing.

headline: A steel mill is reborn in Johnstown
abstract: One year after its shutdown by the US Steel Corporation, the steel mill in Johnstown, now known as Johnstown Corporation, is humming with activity under new owners.  The enterprise embodies a growing trend as entrepreneurs across the country take over the aged mills that Big Steel has abandoned.  The company faces many obstacles, but its owners are optimistic that the mill can be profitable.

headline: All Lobbyists Are Asking Is A Litter Access
abstract: An opinion-section piece examines the role of being a lobbyist.  The piece focuses on how they lobby legislators to support certain legilsation, how they are paid, and how they become lobbists.  A list of former PA politicians who have become lobbyists is provided.  Special attention is also paid early in the piece to the important concept of "access" to politicians.  The Opinion piece concludes that all lobbyists want is access.

headline: Vendetta?
abstract: Delaware County lawyer Robert Surrick, a former member of the PA Judicial Inquiry and Review Board, has charged that PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen sought his help in 1980 to oust Justice Robert Nix Jr. from the state's highest court.  Surrick said that Larsen considered a television advertising campaign to emphasize the fact that Nix is black; this represented an effort to defeat Nix's bid for retention to a 10-year court term in 1981.  Had Nix been defeated, Larsen would have become the chief justice of the PA Supreme Court by virtue of his seniority on the court.  Surrick made this disclosure in papers filed yesterday with the PA Supreme Court; he filed papers asking the court to dismiss a complaint filed against Surrick by Larsen.  Larsen could not be reached for comment.

headline: Morton Bahr
abstract: The article profiles Morton Bahr, the newly elected president of the Communications Workers Association.  Bahr, who is characterized as down-to-earth, inherited a union that is facing increased foreign competition, rapidly changing technology, and the court-ordered break up of the American Telephone and Telegraph Corporation.  Bahr's rise through the union is dicussed, as well as his efforts to reach out to non-union workers, such as those high tech workers in Silicon Valley.  Bahr believes that unions must stop reacting to changes and get a voice in how new technology is introduced.

headline: PUC Nominee Defeats Self: Brucker Withdraws
abstract: This editorial examines the withdrawal of John Brucker, Governor Thornburgh's nominee to head the state Public Utility Commission (PUC),  from senatorial consideration.  Two colleges that Brucker attended are now under FBI investigation.  The editorial poses the question of why PA Governor Dick Thornburgh did not care to investigate further the background of Brucker.  The editorial also recommends that Susan Shanaman, who served excellently as chairman of PUC, be renominated by the Governor.

headline: Jesse Probing Or Politicking
abstract: The Reverend Jesse Jackson visited the MOVE disaster in Philadelphia.  This prompted political observers to say that Jackson's visit was intended as a political poke at Mayor Wilson Goode by local black political leaders who have seen their own influence eclipsed by Goode's emergence as the city's most powerful and respected African-American.

headline: A step toward casino gambling
abstract: An amendment to a PA law allows taverns to hold tournaments in cards; this amendment has upset many people.  An editorial argues that people should be concerned about the effects of the amendment, which could be considered a first step in encouraging legalized gambling.

headline: Angry Democrats on the Senate
abstract: PA State Senator Craig Lewis, his party's leader on the PA Senate Local Government Committee, complained that Chairman Frank Pecora, a Republican, lied to committee Democrats and cost the chamber its voice in regulating how federal money is distributed to communities.  Lewis said he was concerned the new regulations did not carry out a 1984 law aimed at de-politicizing the distribution process.

headline: Viewpoint from Harrisburg: General Assembly Resolves More Than It Legislates
abstract: A columnist discusses the proclivity of lawmakers to make proclamations and adopt resolutions, as opposed to passing bills or making laws.  He says that resolutions are often used to grab headlines, allowing legislators to avoid passing bills.

headline: Newpaper chief warns strikes
abstract: Sam McKeel, Philadelphia Newspapers Incorporated (PNI) President, warned striking employees yesterday that they are too far apart on new contracts.  Saturday, 4,774 employees of PNI's morning Philadelphia Inquirer and afternoon Philadelphia Daily News went on strike.  McKeel said he expects the strike to be very long and very costly and cannot believe that issues that could not be settled for months will now be settled in a few days.  Federal mediator Robert Kyler said he was waiting for something fresh to develop before trying to bring negotiators back to the table.  PNI's spokesperson as well as the major union representing the workers said that they are waiting for the mediator to make the call and bring them back to the table.

headline: PUC plan
abstract: According to a report released by the PA House Consumer Affairs Committee, the PA Public Utility Commission will be revamped and given additional power to try and control utility operating costs.  The committee concluded that the PUC had failed in its efforts to pursue the public interest; the committee also concluded that the PUC is responsible for the four-fold increase in fixed utility rates since 1970.  Under the new plan, the PUC would assign its own inspectors to electric plant construction sites and its own aditors to major utility company officers.

headline: Joy, resignation greet ruling on drunken driving law
abstract: The state Superior Court upheld the state's new drunken driving law in a case last week.  The District Attorney who tried the case said the decision was a precedent-setter with state and national implications.  The defense attorney, however, claims that it is a bad law because of its mandatory minimum sentences.  He says that the law is unconstitutional because the mandatory minimum sentences violate the separation of powers doctrine.

headline: A tale of two mills: 'Experiment' at Weirton profitable in its first year
abstract: Steel industry analysts are closely watching Weirton Steel Corporation because it was purchased one year ago by employees.  The employee-owners took a 20% pay cut and were able to turn around the company and create a profit.  Analysts are concerned if the future will also be as profitable, but employees of Weirton Steel remain optimistic.

headline: Angry words on solemn day
abstract: As part of the first day of the American Gathering of Jewish Holocaust Survivors, a crowd of about 12,000 Holocaust survivors paraded through Center City and honored their dead at the Monument to the Six Million Jewish Martyrs; the monument is located on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway.  The parade was solemn, but there were many speeches of outrage against President Ronald Reagan's planned visit to a military cemetery in Bitburg, West Germany, where Nazi SS troopers are buried.

headline: Vote "Yes" on Questions
abstract: The editorial urges PA constituents to support two resolutions that will be on the ballot in Tuesday's election.  Joint Resolution 1 would extend absentee balloting privileges to people who cannot get to the polls because of their religion or because they are election bureau employees required to work during polling hours at a location far from their designated polling places.  The editorial believes this amendment will be fair to poll workers and would avoid conflicts with religious holidays during elections.  Joint Resolution 2 would extend property tax exemptions on residencies for disabled or severly handicapped veterans to unmarried living spouses.  The editorial believes these are fair and sensible reforms.  The editorial also urges residents in nine municipalities in Lancaster County to vote "Yes" on a question that will ask if they want to begin using voting machines instead of paper ballots.

headline: Newspaper Strike Nears End
abstract: The 39 day Philadelphia newspaper stike appears to be nearing its end, as negotiators move towards a settlement.  Although reports say the two sides are close to a tenative agreement, the announcement of a settlement has been labeled premature by both union leaders and management.  The Philadelphia Inquirer and Daily News have not been published since the strike began on September 7.  The nine unions that are stiking represent 4,700 employees, including reporters, mailers, and truck drivers.  A major noneconomic issue--manning levels for new automated newspaper-stuffing equipment--was settled earlier.  The latest settlement proposal from Philadelphia Newspapers Incorporated  offers the unions a weekly increase of $150 over four years, as well as other benefits.

headline: PUC To Investigate West Penn Rate Request
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) will look into an $84.6 million annual rate increase proposed by West Penn Power Company.  The PUC suspended the request for investigation a few days ago, a normal action for large proposed rate increases.  The PA Consumer Advocate, the US Department of Defense, and some of West Penn's industrial customers have filed complaints against the boost.

headline: Judge backs state funds for courts
abstract: PA State Supreme Court Associate Justice Stephen Zappala, in addressing the annual meeting of the PA State Association of County Commissioners, said that PA would best be served if the costs of running courts were taken off the backs of county commissioners and paid directly by the Commonwealth.  Currently, the state reimburses each county for court-related salaries and other expenses.  The county must make up the shortfall if its expenses exceed this, however.  This is a problem for counties with limited tax bases, and Zappala says this can lead commissioners to make political decisions on funding, which could result in inequity or injustice.

headline: A Thornburgh Administration Decision
abstract: A decision by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration to stop payment on a contract with Xpress Truck Lines Incorporated, which hauls the state's liquor products in Southeastern PA, will likely end up in court.  The order to stop payment of the contract was the latest volley in an ongoing battle between the Republican governor and the Democrat-controlled Liquor Control Board (LCB) over the shipping pact.  LCB Chief Counsel Gary DiVitto accused Governor Thornburgh of grandstanding.

headline: Appeal filed in CTA case transcript ruling
abstract: Transcripts of May 22nd and 23rd sidebar conferences at the trial of Computer Technology Associates (CTA) are scheduled to be unsealed on Tuesday.  Attorneys for the defendants asked the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the ruling that calls for the transcripts to be unsealed.  The bench conferences took place during and after testimony by state Republican Party Chairman Robert Asher, a defense witness.

headline: Zimmerman denies hearing CTA bribe remark
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman, testifying at a federal criminal trial against Computer Technology Associates (CTA) attorneys William T. Smith and Alan R. Stoneman, denied overhearing a remark about a bribe at a Republican Party fund-raiser last year.  John Torquato Jr, head of CTA, testified previously that Zimmerman had heard the remark but merely walked away.

headline: Over $1 million set to train 2,200 laid off by Bethlehem Steel
abstract: According to the PS Department of Labor and Industry, more than $1 million has been set aside to retrain 2,200 steelworkers who lost their jobs with Bethlehem Steel Corporation.  The program is one of five across the state that will utilize federal, state, and local funds to help displaced workers find jobs.  Employment opportunities for displaced workers are slim unless their skills can be upgraded or they can be retrained to enter new fields.  Having secured the money in June 1985, the PA Department of Labor and Industry solicited project proposals from affected companies, service delivery areas and the United Steelworkers of America.  A breakdown of funding and the counties it will go to is included in the article.

headline: Radioactive Waste
abstract: This editorial talks about radioactive waste disposal sites appearing in PA.  Federal law dictates proper disposal of radioactive waste, and the PA State Senate approved a deal for waste disposal.  PA, which is the largest creator of waste in this part of the nation, will establish a contract with Maryland and Delaware; West Virginia has already signed on to work with PA.

headline: Judge funding spat hurts victims
abstract: This editorial examines a problem facing PA's courts: the lack of senior judges to hear cases.  The budget for senior judges, retired judges who do day work to augment the ranks of regular judges, has been underfunded by about $300,000.  There is currently a battle brewing between the PA Supreme Court and the PA Legislature over the fact that the PA Supreme Court refused to allow the PA Senate to fully examine how it spends tax dollars.  PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert Nix curtailed the working hours of senior judges in order to pressure the legislators to cough up extra money.  The editorial believes this battle between the Legislature and the State Supreme Court is a joke that is hurting victims and their families who are waiting for their cases to be heard.

headline: A VIOLENT WIND: THE TORNADO AFTERMATH
abstract: A photo depicts Chris Bradley carrying a basket of artificial flowers as he picks his way through the wreckage of his uncle's house in Atlantic, PA.  The wood-frame building was knocked on its side when a tornado hit.

headline: Audit urges raise, more rate-case time for PUC
abstract: The state Legislative Budget and Finance Committee conducted a performance audit of the state Public Utility Commission, and said that the commissioners should spend less time on administrative duties and concentrate primarily on rate cases and policy decisions.  The audit also recommended a pay raise for the commissioners, and urged that they develop a uniform system of holding public comment hearings in rate cases.  Commissioners agreed that there is room for improvement in the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Zimmerman press aide gets new title
abstract: Patrick Boyle, press secretary for PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman, will assume the new title of special assistant to the Attorney General, in which he will work to improve communications among all divisions of the office.  Zimmerman said that the change of duties was motivated by trying to do what is best for Boyle's health, as he is currently suffering from lymphoma.  Robert Gentzel, an assistant press secretary, will take over for Boyle.  Boyle had previoulsy testified in the Computer Technology Associates bribery trial.  Zimmerman said the duty change has nothing to do with Boyle's involvement in the case.

headline: Philadelphia Newspaper Strike Over
abstract: A 46-day newspaper strike, the longest in Philadelphia's history, ended today as the last of the nine unions striking approved new contracts.  Teamsters drivers and three other unions approved the settlement with Philadelphia Newspapers Incorporated.  The Teamsters had rejected the proposed contract settlement on Friday, but union leaders rescheduled a new vote today because they claimed that members misunderstood the proposal.  The contracts call for an average increase of $37.50 per week over four years.  The mailers union said they won assurances about staffing levels relating to the company's proposed installation of new equipment.

headline: Restart foes to block TMI's north gate next Wednesday
abstract: Convinced that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission will vote next week to allow Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor to restart, a group of activists is planning to block TMI's north gate next Wednesday.  Brian Hunt, spokesman for the group which plans to block the gate entrance, says "The people of central PA have both a right and a responsibility to protect themselves from TMI, the criminal management that owns it and the federal bureaucracy that would unleash it upon us a second time."  A vote by the NRC to allow the restart of Unit 1, would end six years of hearings and consideration of the unit's fate by the commission.

headline: Judge in rape-case dismissal ousted
abstract: Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. relieved Judge J. Quint Salmon of his assignment in Allegheny County after he dismissed a rape case brought by a 14-year-old girl because she was late for trial.  Salmon dismissed the case against Geoffrey Adams because the accuser and her mother were between 15 and 30 minutes late for the trial.

headline: Accused in odometer case, dealer agrees to close
abstract: Rather than face charges of rolling back odometers on his used cars, Samuel Marino, a used car dealer in Montgomery County, agreed to close his business and pay $10,000 in consumer refunds and fines .  This was one of four odometer-tampering lawsuits brought about statewide by the PA Bureau of Consumer Protection.  A 1983 study by the PA Attorney General's Office showed evidence of odometer tampering in at least 20% of all automobiles sold at auction, and the National Transportation Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that odometer tampering represents $1.5 billion in fraud each year.

headline: Bailey and Casey Get Early Nod From Pro-Life Federation PAC
abstract: The PA Pro-Life Federation Political Action Committee has unanimously endorsed the candidacy of Bob Casey for PA Governor and Don Bailey for US Senator.  Both have strong pro-life records, and both gave speeches at recent convention for the group supporting the pro-life movement.  The article also examines the 1986 elections and where candidates stand on the issue of abortion.

headline: Voters show distaste for moving levers, go for electronics
abstract: Dauphin County voters approved electronic voting machines for the county.  William E. Barnes, director of the county Bureau of Registration and Election, said that the electronic machines could be in place as early as November.  County voters also approved a 2-mill proposal for the county library system and voted for judges.

headline: Philly newspaper unions give leader confidence vote
abstract: The Coucil of Newspaper Unions, which represents all nine unions that are striking, gave a vote of confidence in its leader yesterday, Teamsters' President William Gullifer.  The action came one day after the Teamsters Union rejected a tenative contract agreement by a 175-163 vote, crushing hopes of ending the 6-week-old strike.  Gullifer had actually recommended that the Teamsters accept the tenative pact.  After the Teamsters rejection, other unions quickly cancelled their ratification meetings for the Philadelphia-Newspapers-Incorporated proposal.  Union officials know the reaction to the Teamsters rejection was mixed but said the unions' solidarity remained intact.

headline: Review declined by Supreme Court
abstract: The US Supreme Court cleared the way yesterday for restarting Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor.  In doing so, the high court voted not to consider reviewing an appeal by the citizens group Three Mile Island Alert, who sought hearings on the integrity of TMI operator GPU Nuclear Corporation.  The Supreme Court also lifted a court-ordered June restart stay that gave TMIA time to appeal the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's May 29 approval of the restart.  GPU Nuclear was preparing last night to begin the three-month start-up process.  TMIA and PA State Senator John Shumaker will request a stay of the restart in the US 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals in Phialdelphia.  The suit seeks to force the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to hold license revocation hearings on GPU Nuclear.  TMIA also wants PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to ask the PA Public Utility Commission to hold hearings on GPU Nulcear's corporate character, but Thornburgh spoke of no such action yesterday.  TMIA would like GPU Nuclear to hold public hearings to discover the extent to which utility officials were involved with or condoned leak-rate falsifications.

headline: Judge polls committee on Democrat endorsement
abstract: Judge John Feeny has polled all 2,500 Democratic county committee members to determine the qualities they consider most important for judges.  He is among 25 Democrats seeking the committee's support for Common Please Court at its endorsement convention.

headline: Aces High on Blackjack Tables: Rental firm takes advantage of gambling loophole
abstract: A Feasterville man took advantage of a controversial law that allows restaurants and bars to hold blackjack and poker tournaments with cash prizes.  The Feasterville man began a firm called "Aces" that rents blackjack and poker tables, gambling chips, cards and personnel.  The firm is doing good business in the Philadelphia area and has increased its business each week--despite disapproval by law-enforcement officials.

headline: Barton, Ruth, Horn, Roe lead York judgeship voting
abstract: Democrats Jack H. Barton and Gerald E. Ruth apparently will face Republicans Richard H. Horn and Gordon A. Roe in the November general election for two York County judgeships.  With 115 of 143 precincts reporting unofficial returns from the May 21 primary, Horn, Roe, Barton and Ruth had the most votes.

headline: Ways, means of getting a seat: Coyne found a guardian angel in Murtha
abstract: US Representative William Coyne was given a seat on the Ways and Means Committee, mostly due to the negotiations of US Representative John Murtha, who sits on the Steering and Policy Committee.  There were three Pennsylvanians on the Steering and Policy Committee; this allowed for favorable assignments for most PA representatives.

headline: PSSU study says job stress 'killing' welfare workers
abstract: A study released by the PA Social Services Union shows that abnormally high rates of stress, burnout, hypertension and disease among welfare workers are nearly twice that of the general population.  The 10,000 member union is in contract negotiations with the Thornburgh administration and job stress is one of the issues.  Anna Burger Price, PSSU president, said the health problems of welfare workers result primarily from cutbacks in personnel, the introduction of automation, and the crushing workloads created by the administration.

headline: Ruling to boost in-state long-distance competition
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) approved a judicial recommendation that allows customers to choose a long-distance carrier for toll calls within the state's calling regions; currently, this service is provided only by Bell of PA and other local companies.  The PUC also rejected, for the time being, a judge's recommendation that Bell of PA cut $80 million in access charges to independent long-distance companies, who argue that the access charges subsidize local service and should be reduced.  The PUC approved a plan for 11 phone companies to begin providing customer-owned, coin operated phone service, and approved a decrease in the energy cost rate charged by Columbia Gas of PA.

headline: Judge Says He Erred on Cops and 5th
abstract: Attorneys representing several Philadelphia news organizations have persuaded US District Judge James McGirr Kelly to admit that he was wrong when he let police officers refusing to testify before the MOVE commission invoke their Fifth Amendment rights against self-incrimination.  However, with the MOVE hearings expected to end today, it is doubtful that the commission will recall the six officers who already have asserted the Fifth Amendment privately.  Judge Kelly initially sided with lawyers representing several police officers, saying that the Fifth Amendment would prevent harming the officers' reputations.

headline: Aid centers opening for tornado victims
abstract: Nearly 800 survivors of several tornaodes that ripped through western PA signed up for disaster aid, but Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Officials caution that it may take several weeks before any money is handed out.  Rhonda Brooks, a FEMA public affairs officer said that federal officials must review the application, visit the disaster site and verify the need before they can free federal money.  The series of tornadoes claimed 64 lives and damaged or destroyed over 2400 homes and businesses in PA.

headline: Bill Gray: A man to watch in '88?
abstract: A columnist discusses the possibility of William Gray III, who is currently the US House Budget Committee chairman, being selected by the Democrats to run for Vice President.  The columnist feels that Gray would be a good candidate because of his record in Congress and his work to increase the numbers of minority and women officers in the Foreign Service.

headline: What happened in the legislature
abstract: This is a box that has "A look at the key bills considered by the PA Senate and House during this session."  The article lists key bills with a description and comments.

headline: Representatives of the Turnpike
abstract: Representatives of the PA Turnpike Commission and three Teamsters Unions continued contract negotiations in the hopes of averting a strike.  The Teamsters Unions, which represents more than 1,500 workers, rejected the commission's latest offer Monday, and will strike on Thursday at midnight if a contract is not reached.  Among other demands, the unions are seeking a $1.65 per hour salary increase over three years, though the Turnpike Commission is currently offering a $1.38 increase.

headline: Safety panel backs license for Limerick
abstract: The Atomic Safety and Licensing Board recommended that the Philadelphia Electric Company (PECO) be granted a full-power license for the Limerick 1 Nuclear power plant--despite a continuing dispute over emergency evacuation plans for Graterford Prison. The state Public Utility Commission also gave PE permission to build four pumps at a man-made reservoir in Bucks County.  The pumps will be used to supply cooling water for the plant.  PECO spokesperson Ron Harper said that the company welcomed both actions, and that PE hoped the Nuclear Regulatory Commission would grant the license for the Montgomery County plant by the end of the month.

headline: Judge Spaeth's retirement
abstract: PA Superior Court Judge Edmund Spaeth Jr. decided not to seek retention at the conclusion of his term this year because he felt that there were problems in the current method of electing judges to appellate courts in PA.  This editorial urges Spaeth to continue to speak out on the need for change in the justice system in PA; the author also urges Spaeth to work toward that goal.

headline: An ugly LCB battle
abstract: A columnist says that the battle between Governor Dick Thornburgh and the Liquor Control Board will be vocal and contentious--much like a political campaign.

headline: Blair County Democrat is making a "businesslike" bid for governor
abstract: Jules Pratt, a wealthy Blair County businessman, jumped into his first campaign for public office.  Blair is running for the PA governorship.  Pratt pumped large amounts of his own money into his campaign, hired prominent political operatives, and opened a Philadelphia headquarters.  Pratt has since reshaped his campaign, but his resolve and message remain the same.  Pratt believes that PA's state government needs the same entrepeneurial business skills that enabled him to start from nothing and earn $150 million in real estate projects over 13 years.  Though Pratt is far behind in many polls, he says that he has not yet come out of the gate, and many believe that his money could make him a factor in the race.

headline: Why GOP is split on help for needy
abstract: PA House Republicans have rejected the compromise efforts of the Senate GOP, and they invited Governor Dick Thornburgh to veto social welfare legislation.  This article examines the theories on why there is a split between House and Senate Republicans.  House Republicans tend to be more split and not move as a group because there are more of them.  House Republican leaders also tend to side more with Governor Dick Thornburgh and urge fiscal conservatism, while Senate Republicans are more liberal.

headline: Saturn pact calls for salaries, job security
abstract: The United Auto Workers (UAW) and Saturn reached a landmark agreement yesterday that will be applied to a new Saturn facility.  The facility will be built in Spring Hill, Tennessee.  General Motors, the makers of Saturn, refused to comment on the announcement.  Some major points of the agreement are:  Payment for employees will be by salary rather than hourly, a labor-management partnership in reaching decisions, and permanent job security for no less than 80% of the 6,000 workers.  UAW President Owen Bieber said that the agreement established the UAW as a "full partner" in decisions from the shop floor to executive levels.

headline: Senate approval of ex-Navy official to NRC expected
abstract: President Ronald Reagan's nomination of former Vice Admiral Lando W. Zech to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) sailed through a Senate confirmation hearing.  Zech is an advocate of expediting NRC decision-making to spur commercial nuclear power development.

headline: Judge won't as funds for election bid, quits
abstract: Judge Edmund Spaeth Jr, the resident of PA's Superior Court, has elected to retire rather than seek funds to campaign for a retention election.  Superior Court justices must be elected then face a yes-no retention election every 10 years.  Electing judges is a politically divisive issue in the state.

headline: Auto insurance rates increasing in spite of changes, official says
abstract: Acting state Insurance Commissioner William Muir said changes in the no-fault auto insurance law may have slowed premium increases, but they have not reduced them.  A law that went into effect October 1, 1984 was designed to help stop rate increases.  Muir said there were a variety of reasons for the increases in premiums.

headline: Boards lack staff, panel told
abstract: A series of witnesses complained about lack of staffing and attorneys for the state's professional boards during the confirmation hearing of Richard Anderson, who was nominated to be commissioner of the Bureau of Professional and Occupational Affairs.  Anderson told the state Senate Consumer Protection and Licensure Committee that he was conducting an in-depth review of the bureau and would have to wait for the results to determine if more staffing or attorneys are needed.

headline: Wilburn rejected for turnpike panel
abstract: The state Senate rejected the nomination of former Thornburgh Cabinet member Robert Wilburn for the PA Turnpike Commission.  The vote ignited accusations from both Senate Democrats and Governor Thornburgh's administration that politics is blocking a $4.5 billion toll-road expansion that could boost the state's economy.  The Senate has rejected Thornburgh's nominees for the Turnpike Commission 11 times, and Thornburgh has said that he will block the $4.5 billion until one of his nominees is approved.

headline: State whistle-blower law gets support
abstract: Witnesses testified at a state House Labor Relations Committee hearing on a proposed "whistle blowers' protection act," including Auditor General and State Representative Peter Wambach.  The legislation passed the house unanimously last session, but the Senate failed to act on it.  The witnesses say a law is necessary to protect employees who disclose waste and mismanagement.

headline: SHOREHAM IS GIVEN PERMIT TO START LOW-LEVEL TESTS…SUFFOLK APPEALING MOVE…Decision Called Major Setback for Efforts by County and State to Bar Reactor
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission voted to allow the Shoreham Nuclear Power Station to begin testing at up to 5% of full power.  The order would not take effect until 5pm Feb 13 and would give Suffolk County and New York State officials time to block the decision through legal action.  Suffolk County and New York State are opposed to the power plant operating at an output above 5% because evacuation of the surrounding area would be impossible in an emergency.

headline: Judges Are Surveyed
abstract: A survey by researchers of 570 judges in PA, Wisconsin, Georgia, Colorado, California and Maryland indicates that judges favor harsher penalties for drunken driving laws, especially for repeat offenders.  This editorial argues that judges should be given more discretion on how to penalize drunken-driving offenders.

headline: Auto insurers push legislation allowing gender factor
abstract: The Insurance Federation of PA and several individual insurance companies sponsored a press conference to praise state Senate legislation that allows insurers to continue using gender as a factor in determining auto insurance rates.  The legislation would address a 1984 PA Supreme Court ruling that deemed sex-based auto insurance rates unfairly discriminatory.  Mavis A. Walters, senior vice president of the Insurance Services Offices Incorporated, said that women benefit if rates are not unisex because they pay lower rates for auto insurance.

headline: Bucks official, sayig he's not a 'public slave,' seeks raise
abstract: Bucks County Commissioner Andrew L. Warren has called for the commissioners to schedule a public hearing to discuss raising salaries for commissioners and elected row officers.  Warren hopes to schedule the hearing before the November 5 election so that raises would be effective for row officers on January 1, 1986.

headline: Williams' Defeat Wasn't a Pretty Sight
abstract: An opinion piece looks at the failed candidacy of Robert Williams for Philadelphia District Attorney.  The author believes that Williams' horrible concession speech is a prime example of why he lost the election.  The author also examines Williams' ties with Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, his largest political supporter.  Though many other factors may have come into play in this election, the author believes that Williams had a lot to do with his own defeat.  The author also admits that she worried about Williams becoming District Attorney for several reasons, among them that someone so close to Goode would be in charge of any investigation of the mayor.

headline: State's unemployed join in battle for extension of US financial aid
abstract: More than 500 people, many of them unemployed persons from PA, traveled to Washington DC for a demonstration on the steps of the Department of Labor.  Demonstrators were trying to urge Congress to extend the Federal Supplemental Compensation program for long-term unemployment.

headline: Sparked Nuclear Plant Ready To Start Up
abstract: A photograph shows an elderly woman protesting a Federal court decision that affirmed the granting of a license to Three Mile Island's (TMI) Unit 1 Reactor.  Since the Unit 2 Reactor was crippled on March 28, 1979, TMI has remained in cold shutdown; that will change once the Nuclear Regulatory Commission gives final clearance to turn on Unit 1.  The protestor is holding a sign that claims the Governor and the Health Department are withholding a TMI-Cancer Study.

headline: Judging the judges
abstract: A columnist says that those who wish to be a federal judge must prove themselves to the far-right and prove themselves to be ultra-conservative.  The author says that "as far as the White House is concerned, when it comes to selecting judges, the right-wing-zealot's word is law."

headline: Back and forth: House passes, retracts games-of-chance bill
abstract: The state House of Representatives narrowly approved a bill to allow small games of chance in private clubs; the House immediately retracted the action and decided to reconsider the bill, or one similar to it, however.  This action was likely due to the fact that they had inadvertently legalized bar-room gambling the previous year.  Opponents to the bill said that it is full of loopholes that enable enterprising promoters to turn the small games into large-scale gambling operations.

headline: Burdened legislators see slowness as asset
abstract: The 1985-86 General Assembly appears to have gotten off to the slowest start of any PA Legislature in recent history, but many legislative leaders say that the slow pace is a public service because the assembly makes too many laws.  Senate Majority Leader John Stauffer says that the Legislature has before it some complex issues this year, such as the sunset review of the Liquor Control Board; this review requires careful study and research before any public votes can be taken

headline: Word to GOP leaders:  Hold off on '88 for now
abstract: Max Hugel, a long-time backer of US President Ronald Reagan, has announced plans to form a group called Project '88.  The group is designed to keep top Republicans neutral and focused on Reagan's programs instead of posturing for the 1988 GOP Presidential nomination.  Hugel, who played a crucial role in Reagan's victory in the 1980 New Hampshire primary, rejected the notion that this new venture would be an effort to stop Vice President George Bush, who has been actively courting top Reagan supporters.

headline: Steel Operations Split Into Three by LTV Corp.: Company Will Close Aliquippa Plant
abstract: Staggering losses caused by a surge in imports have forced LTV Steel Corporation to split up its steel group, shut down most of its giant Aliquippa, PA, steel mill, and lay off 1,300 workers there.  The three-point restructuring is designed to strengthen LTV, the nation's second-largest steel maker, and improve its financial position.  Under the new plan, LTV would fashion three separate and new companies out of Cleveland-based LTV Steel; each is expected to have its own management and marketing staffs, and each is expected to cut costs and increase efficiency.

headline: State aide:  PUC nominee to ask withdrawal
abstract: John Brucker, PA Governor Thornburgh's recent nominee to the Public Utility Commission, will be asking the governor to withdraw his name from consideration.  Brucker's resume lists three advanced degrees from schools under investigation by the FBI for being diploma mills.  Brucker obtained two business degrees from Southwestern University, in Tuscon, Ariz., which was recently closed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.  There was also confusion over where Brucker got an undergraduate degree.

headline: Justice delayed: Civil court clogged by loss of judges to criminal trials
abstract: The Allegheny County Common Pleas Court released its annual report which indicated that a record number of criminal cases were handled in Allegheny County during 1984; the record was broken at the expense of the court's civil division, however.  President Judge Michael J. O'Malley pointed out that the civil division suffered because more judges had to be assigned to handle criminal cases due to a state law that requires that criminal defendants come up for trial within 180 days after their arrests.  Both judges and lawyers are concerned about the decrease in civil cases, but neither side has a solution because the number of courtrooms and staff are limited.

headline: Ban Is Considered: Happy Hours Endangered
abstract: This editorial thinks that a ban on happy hours would not change the drinking patterns of people.  The author argues that it would be an infringement on the business to ban discount prices.

headline: Business Climate In Pennsylvania Good, Davis Says
abstract: Before a business luncheon in Oil City yesterday, PA Secretary of State William Davis said that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has fulfilled his campaign pledge to run PA like an efficient business, and that PA citizens are profitting from his performance.  Davis pointed to a nationwide survey conducted in 1984 that measured manufacturing climates across the United States; the study rated PA's government debt 29th nationally and said that labor costs in PA were competitive.  Davis also credited Thornburgh with improving the efficiency of state agencies.

headline: Youth vs. experience:  Which is the better lawmaker?
abstract: An opinion piece looks at whether today's younger, better-educated and better-paid legislator is also a better lawmaker than his counterpart of a generation ago.  Veteran lawmakers, such as PA State Representatives James Gallen and Lester Fryer, believe that younger legislators who are staight out of college, with no work experience, and without even the experience of raising a family, cannot match up to the old-timers.  Freshman PA House members David Levdansky and Michael Veon believe there is a greater degree of independence among the younger legislators, and that a mix of young and old in the Legislature is good for PA.  The trend in the PA Legislature is definitely towards youth, from 1963 to 1983 the average age of PA legislators dropped from 51 to 45, mainly due to the good pay and benefits of the position.

headline: Strikers ask state to probe contractor
abstract: Local 29 of the Service Employees International Union, which is locked in a bitter labor dispute at 18 Downtown Pittsburgh buildings, has asked the PA Attorney General to investigate a Homestead-based contractor.  The union's critiques of the firm are included in the article.  In addition to its charges, the union also called attention to a federal court case dealing with the Commonwealth Building Maintenance Company (CBM), which allegedly failed to pay $40,597 in contributions to the Pittsburgh Building Owners Welfare Fund and the Pittsburgh Building Employees Pension Fund.  CBM President Fred Montgomery refuted the charges and offered several clarifications.

headline: State is saving $1,000 a day
abstract: The state is saving about $1,000 a day because of an energy conservation program and could save much more, according to Robert Shinn, executive director of the Governor's Energy Council.  According to Shinn, the state could save $20 million a year by making its buildings more energy efficient.

headline: Justice Nix searching for ways to stop lawyers' thefts
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Robert Nix Jr. is looking for ways to stop lawyers from robbing their clients, even though the rate of lawyer thefts in the state is relatively low.  Nix has asked the Pennsylvania Bar Association to recommend procedures to discourage lawyers from depositing trust fund, estate or lawsuit settlement checks into their personal accounts.

headline: Ban on beer price ads lifted
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) voted unanimously yesterday to lift the 33 year-old ban on advertising beer prices.  The members of the LCB concurred with the PA attorney general's office that consumer benefits from price advertising far outweigh the objections of small distributors that could be driven out of business.  This issue was brought before the LCB after the Beer and Pop Warehouse, a supermarket style beer distributor, was accused of undercutting competitors prices by advertising beer prices.  The warehouse is also the subject of another lawsuit by 75 other local distributors; they claim it has engaged in unfair, monopolistic trade practices.  These smaller distributors believe consumers will be hurt if they go out of business.

headline: Caliguiri, two others seek Democratic endorsement
abstract: In Pittsburgh, three mayoral candidates, 25 judicial candidates and 17 City Council candidates have filed for endorsement by the City Democratic Committee for the primary election.

headline: Zeo seeks GOP nomination for Wilson's seat in House
abstract: George Zeo, a Republican from Chalfront, is the first Republican candidate to emerge in the 1986 race to fill the 144th District PA House seat vacated by Benjamin Wilson.  Zeo is active in Citizens For America, an organization supporting the policies of US President Ronald Reagan.  Zeo pointed out several campaign positions he would take on state liquor sales, education, and the economy.

headline: Temple employees threaten strike
abstract: More than 2,400 workers at Temple University and Temple University Hospital are threatening to walk off their jobs at 6am Monday, July 1 unless they reach tentative agreement on new contracts.  At issue are four contracts between the university and its hospital workers, who are represented by District 1199C of the National Union of Hospital and Health Care Employees.  Union spokesperson David Fair said the contract dispute centers on a union proposal to encrease the employer's contribution to the union's health plan.

headline: State's mine death legacy is long, sad
abstract: Northeastern PA's anthracite coal industry, once the bustling economic base of the region, has a sad and lengthy legacy of death beneath the earth's surface.  In 1985, five people have died while mining the coal, and thousands have died since 1870, the first year the PA Department of Environmental Resources began keeping records.  Hard coal production has fallen steadily and rapidly since the introduction of oil as a heating fuel source.  Unemployment has also fallen off greatly.  A history of some of the men killed in Northeastern PA is included in the article.

headline: Kafrissen has court officer suspended
abstract: A Municipal Court administrative officer was suspended for improperly allowing a television news crew into Judge Arthur Kafrissen's chambers.  Kafrissen also contends that three files were taken from his office.  These files supposedly would exculpate Kafrissen from charges that he had violated a judicial canon by acting as a private attorney for abortion clinics.

headline: Ban on specials easy for Bay State bars to swallow
abstract: Massachusetts became the first state to ban taverns and nightclubs from holding happy hours in any form, including ladies' nights, multiple drink specials, drinking contests and all-you-can-drink promotions.  This ban has been accepted favorably by bar and tavern owners.  The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board is considering a similar ban; the ban is opposed by lobbyists for bars and taverns.

headline: Campaign costs: Money shouldn't be key to political success
abstract: This editorial argues for campaign-finance reform.  The author also supports altering the political structure to reduce the number of state primaries and caucuses through the creation of regional primaries.  The editorial says that money should not be a crucial factor in political success because it excludes people from the political process.

headline: Zimmerman, agency differ on fate of SS tax funds
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman says that school employees are entitled to recover Social Security tax payments that led to the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery scandal, but the federal Social Security Administration has questioned whether the school employees are entitled to the refunds of the taxes.  A Social Security Administration official in Philadelphia said Zimmerman's opinion will be reviewed before a final decision is reached.

headline: The Philadelphia newspaper
abstract: The Philadelphia newpaper strike is dragging into day number 34 and is taking a toll on both the city and state economies.  Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode entered the dispute and talked to both sides.  Meanwhile, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh is making a personal appeal to end the strike.  Thornburgh claims that retailers are losing business because they cannot advertise; the governor also claims that the state is losing tax revenue.

headline: State's PUC To Undergo Legislative Form of Change
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) is currently being subjected to the state's Sunset Review Act, which stipulates that the effectiveness of each state agency must be assessed every 10 years by the state Legislature; such review means that legislative reform of the PUC is a viable option.  Consumer advocacy groups are pushing for reform--citing a state audit of the PUC that shows how PA's commission does allow utility companies to charge more in comparison with other states.  State Representative Allen Kukovich introduced a bill last month which would reduce the current term for PUC commissioners and completely abolish the current slate of commissioners.  No one is sure exaclty how the PUC will be reformed, however.

headline: Keep delinquency office
abstract: The Reagan administration is recommending that Congress cease funding the Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention.  This editorial argues that Congress should not do this because the agency has been a bargain in terms of cost effectiveness.  It funds juvenile delinquency prevention programs through grants to local governments and privately run community-based organizations.  Most of the programs have had success in rehabilitating young offenders.

headline: Banking chief pledges to protect state system
abstract: PA Banking Secretary Ben McEnteer championed a bill that would provide strict examination and approval for mergers between PA banks and those from seven other states and the District of Columbia.  Examination and approval of mergers will be conducted by the PA Department of Banking.  McEnteer wants to ensure that outside interests do not take over the banking business in PA.  McEnteer cited the importance of community banks in relation to small business, but also added that there is a place for big banks.

headline: Campaign fund curbs overruled: High court frees PACs on spending
abstract: The US Supreme Court held unconstitutional a provision in federal election law that bars political action committees from spending more than $1,000 to help elect presidential nominees.  Justice William Rehnquist, writing for the majority, concluded that the $1,000 limitation that had been imposed on PACs violated First Amendment guarantees of free speech and association, without noticeably protecting the public against political corruption or the appearance of corruption.

headline: Despite May's rainfall, drought continues in the area, officials say
abstract: Despite a wetter-than-expected May, drought conditions prevail, the Delaware River Basin Commission said.  The Delaware River and the Schuylkill remain about one-third their normal flow levels, the commission reported.  The commission's experts warned that the most trying months lie just ahead and that conditions will not improve over the summer.

headline: Tracing the course of the city's newspaper strike
abstract: This article deeply examines the 46-day Philadelphia Newspapers Incorporated strike.  Included are the events that led up to the strike, the strike itself, and the events leading up to a contract settlement.  The article is very in-depth and gives special attention to the unions and negotiations within them.

headline: State's utility fees must be fair to all
abstract: An editorial complains about legislative proposals that seek to grant special utility rates to favored groups.  The editorial says that while the legislative proposals are well-meaning, they will lead to a chaotic rate structure that will benefit no one.  Rate strucutres should only reflect the cost of providing service.

headline: Keep Roadblocks To a Minimum
abstract: This editorial applauds a decision by the PA Superior Court determining that police roadblocks designed to catch drunk drivers are unconstitutional.  The editorial believes that freedom of movement is a fundamental hallmark of a free society.  The editorial acknowledges that drunk driving is a major problem in PA, and states that it will continue to support all reasonable efforts to curtail the toll in lives and property damage wreaked by drunk drivers.  However, the editorial does not feel that the problem is so serious that the right to move from one place to another should be curtailed.

headline: Beer price advertising pits 2 types of outlets
abstract: The Liquor Control Board is holding hearings on permanently lifting the ban on beer price advertising.  At least 75 Western PA beer distributors would like the ban to remain in effect because they believe it will stop the growth of large supermarket-style beverage stores.

headline: Cancelling Lifelong Memberships
abstract: This opinion piece examines the phenomenon of Democrats celebrating the recent success of Republican candidates.  The author takes an especially strong look at the members of labor unions.  Union members have been showing up to Republican campaign headquarters more and more since President Reagan was elected.  On this night, several Democrats showed up to support Republican Ron Castille for Philadelphia District Attorney.  The author also examines how these disaffected party members still strongly identify with the Democratic Party.

headline: States agree to conserve Great Lakes
abstract: Leaders of eight states and a Canadian province all pledged to protect the Great Lakes region's supplies of fresh water from diversion to other parts of the continent.  They all signed the Great Lakes Charter to protect the region's water supply.  Pennsylvania is one of the states belonging to the charter.

headline: Transit meter running
abstract: This editorial looks at an impending strike between Allegheny County Port Authority and Local 85 of the Amalgamated Transit Union.  At no time in the 21 year history of the Port Authority has there been such disparity between what management is offering and what the union wants.  The editorial is unhappy with the fact that the PA Legislature has ducked this issue.  The editorial believes that steps need to be taken to make the Port Authority's management stronger; certain over-extended powers of union members must be taken away, however.  The editorial worries about the implications of a strike on the economic health of Pittsburgh.

headline: Support governor
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) plans to have a vote on whether or not to restart Three Mile Island's undamaged reactor before June--even though there are still several unanswered questions regarding safety and management integrity.  Governor Dick Thornburgh has brought up his opposition to the vote by asking a federal appeals court to block the vote and order further hearings.  This editorial urges the public to support Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Kerr denied new trial in job selling
abstract: John Kerr, the chief deputy to former Auditor General Al Benedict, was convicted of 139 counts of bribery and related charges nine months ago; yesterday, Kerr was denied a new trial by a panel of judges.  Kerr was convicted of selling government jobs and promotions in exchange for cash.

headline: Beer pricing ads should be allowed
abstract: This editorial argues that the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) should allow beer price advertising because it is a major part of the free market.  Those who argue against beer price advertising are asking the LCB to protect those charging higher prices, which is misstating the purpose of government.  The LCB's vote on beer advertising will send the message of whether its agenda is one for the 1980's or the 1930's; the decision also comes at a crucial time, as the PA Legislature is deciding whether to retain or scrap the agency.

headline: Candidate for Lt. Gov. Stops in Clearfield
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton, considered the front-runner for the Republican gubernatorial nomination in 1986, is keeping quiet about who he would like to share the ticket with.  One hopeful, Republican Earl Baker, stopped by Clearfield on Thursday; Baker is campaigning across the state.  Baker claimed that his experience and support-base would make him a strong candidate for Lt. Governor.  He has also begun fundraising for the race.  Baker believes in minimal government, and he favors increased cooperation between the private and public sectors to achieve state goals.  He would also like to turn more power over to county and municipal governments.

headline: Willdlife and timber loss heavy
abstract: State Game Commission officials, after viewing the destruction to western PA's forests, say they fear that tornadoes caused extensive damage to wildlife and destroyed at least $10 million worth of timber.  Officials say that the greatest loss to wildlife occurred at a great blue heron rookery in Mercer County; the rookery was destroyed.

headline: Turnpike expansion means jobs
abstract: In this letter to the editor, Jack Anderson, President of the International Union of Operating Engineers Local 66, urges Governor Dick Thornburgh to pursue the extension of the state toll-road system.  Such an extension will create many short-term jobs for construction workers and will help to bring new industry to the state.

headline: TMI: Six years later. TMI may radiate court cases for years to come
abstract: Although six years have passed since the accident at Three Mile Island's Unit 2 nuclear reactor, the court cases against General Public Utilities Nuclear Corporation have not slowed and could continue for another 20 years.  Governor Dick Thornburgh brought suit in federal appeals court to derail the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's go-ahead order on Unit 1's restart; other suits may follow.  This article gives a list of the suits that were filed in the previous six years.

headline: Kerr to stay out on bail
abstract: John Kerr, the former deputy auditor general convicted of job selling, was granted his request for bail pending appeal by the state Superior Court.  William Costopoulos, Kerr's attorney, said that Kerr will be free on his own recognizance during the appeal to Superior Court, which could take from nine months to a year.  Kerr was convicted of running a scheme in which job applicants paid between $1,000 and $10,000 for jobs in the auditor general's department.

headline: Big winner at poker table
abstract: A 60-year-old businessman from St. Louis raked in $63,500 in the first event of the World Series of Poker, which will award more than $4 million in prize money during its three-week run.

headline: Candidates assembling for '86 statewide election
abstract: A columnist outlines the likely candidates for the 1986 gubernatorial election.  He says that Lieutenant Governor William Scranton will likely run as the Republican candidate, and that Robert Casey--former Auditor General--has expressed interest in being the Democratic candidate.  K. Leroy Irvis, Speaker of the House, has said that he would run as Lieutenant Governor if Casey asked.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts a man, wearing a shirt that says "Cities."  The man is standing on his porch looking at his yard; the yard is covered with tree trunks.  While he is standing on his porch,  a man in a truck filled with logs labeled "Budget Tree Trimming" tells the man, "Remember, tell all your friends!"

headline: Turnpike workers ratify contract
abstract: According to the PA Turnpike Commission, unionized turnpike workers have ratified a three-year contract that calls for a 15% salary increase.  The contract calls for an average $1.38 per hour wage increase over the life of the contract.  The union represents toll collectors, maintenance workers, and clerical employees in the turnpike system.

headline: TMI's effects still debated 6 years later
abstract: Six years after the Three Mile Island nuclear accident, questions still persist about the adverse health effects caused by radiation releases.  The state Health Department is conducting four studies to determine if the midstate suffered more health problems after the accident.  The Department is studying cancer incidence and cancer mortality rates of residents living within five, 10 and 20 miles of TMI; these rates will be compared to cancer rates across the state and the nation.

headline: Key decisions are the issues in MOVE probe
abstract: This article discusses the developments in the MOVE disaster investigation and discusses the fundamental questions before the MOVE commission; the commission will open its public hearings October 8, 1985.  The article says that, in order to determine if the city's response was irresponsible, the commission will have to take a hard look at the actions of Philadelphia Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor, Philadelphia Fire Commissioner William Richmond, former City Managing Director Leo Brooks and Philadlephia Mayor W. Wilson Goode.

headline: Bill seeks visible pricing of groceries' scanner items
abstract: State Senator Francis Lynch, who says he has been inundated with consumer complaints, has filed a bill requiring grocery stores to place individual price tags on most items in grocery stores; the legislation also requires the utilization of electronic scanners at checkout counters.  Lynch said that without price tags on each item, it was impossible for consumers to determine whether the prices had changed when they were scanned electronically.

headline: Candidates Take Stands, but DA Debate Was Sedate
abstract: The three men campaigning to be Philadelphia District Attorney--Ronald Castille, Robert Williams, and John Scott--met in a debate at LaSalle University.  The three candidates tended to take the same stands on the issues, and they were very polite to one another.

headline: "Broke" MOVE Panel Double-Busts Budget
abstract: According to figures released by the Philadelphia Controller's Office, by the end of 1985, the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission will have spent almost $715,000 more than double its original budget of $259,000.  The commission was formed to investigate the clash between Philadelphia police and the radical group MOVE.  The fees for expert witnesses and the length of the investigation, which extended beyond the Labor Day deadline, contributed to the cost escalation.  A breakdown of other costs is included in the article.

headline: Union says PAT's concessions would drive workers to strike
abstract: The Port Authority Transit (PAT) and Local 58 of the Amalgamated Transit Union are divided financially, ideologically, and emotionally over contract negotiations.  The PAT has requested far-reaching concessions by the union; this has caused union officials to say that the PAT is posturing for a strike.  The union has asked for several things for the first time:  longevity pay, pay adjustments, a pension program, and a leave of absence.

headline: TMI's Unit 1 generates power
abstract: Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor reached 15% power yesterday and began generating electricity for the first time since the accident at Unit 2 in 1979.  According to GPU Nuclear Corporation, Unit 1 was producing enough power for 50,000 to 60,000 households.  Unit 1 was restarted last Thursday and completed testing at 3% power Monday.  GPU Nuclear said there were minor "glitches" experienced during the startup process, but that they were expected.  Three Mile Island Alert, an opponent of the restart, was concerned that TMI operators had not made all the appropriate steps to ensure Unit 1's safe operation.  Customers of the utilities that own TMI will be able to take advantage of lower rates when TMI Unit 1 operates for 100 hours at 35% power or more.

headline: Kids' 'Bill of Rights' clears Senate
abstract: A five-bill package known as the "Kids' Bill of Rights"--legislation that would protect children against sexual abuse and courtroom pressures--quickly passed the PA Senate and is expected to receive quick action in the House.

headline: Blackjack status left hanging: Bewildered panel tables gaming bill
abstract: Due to a number of amendments that left state lawmakers confused about whether they were voting to permit or prohibit blackjack games, the state House Liquor Control Committee tabled a bill that was written to repeal a controversial law allowing drinking establishments to hold blackjack tournaments with cash prizes.

headline: Cappy bows out of court race
abstract: According to the state elections bureau, Allegheny County Judge Ralph Cappy has withdrawn as a candidate for Superior Court.  That leaves three Republicans and five Democrats in contention for three appellate court seats.

headline: 2 Dem rival groups pitted in takeover try
abstract: The 14th Ward Democratic Committee, the largest in Pittsburgh, will be the target of a takeover attempt by the 14th Ward Independent Democrats Club; they are currently battling regular party Democrats.  The Democratic Club may face an obstacle.  Last April they gave their endorsement to James Ferlo for City Council; Ferlo eventually lost, but now has a job with City of Pittsburgh Controller Tom Flaherty--a political opponent of Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri.

headline: Union Switch plant sold to developer
abstract: Union Switch & Signal Corporation yesterday told union and management employees that it has agreed to sell its 40-acre manufacturing complex in Swissvale to the Radice Corporation, a Florida-based developer of suburban office parks.  The announcement ends the hopes of United Electrical Workers Local 610 to persuade the company to continue producing railroad products at the plant.  The union was frustrated by management's refusal to say what concessions were needed to keep the plant operating.  Financial details of the sale were not disclosed by either party, and Radice declined to detail its intentions for the property.  Swissvale Mayor Charles Martoni said that the sale was a low-blow, as Union Switch never gave the local government an opportunity to sit down and try to keep the plant open.  United Electrical Workers Local 610 is also faced with a similar situation at the Westinghouse Air Brake Company plant in Wilmerding.  At Westinghouse, management has served notice to the union that it plans to relocate most of the work done at the plant to other sites.

headline: Too many rate hikes
abstract: This editorial looks at how much has changed since the days when nuclear power was touted as the answer to America's growing appetite for cheap and clean energy.  The accident at Three Mile Island showed the world that nuclear energy is not clean and safe, while recent requests for rate hikes by Philadelphia Electric Company have shown that nuclear energy is no longer as inexpensive as people were once told.  In all fairness to Philadelphia Electric, delays in construction have increased estimated costs, causing Philadelphia Electric to now ask for a 28% rate increase. Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode is concerned about the impact of the rate increase on businesses and homes, and is joining with the state consumer advocate to block the rate increase before the PA Public Utility Commission.  The editorial believes that the consumer must be protected.

headline: Law abiding must be protected
abstract: A letter to the editor questions how anyone can be against the death penalty for those who have committed cold-blooded murder.  The author does not believe that these individuals should be allowed to live in prison at the expense of law abiding citizens.  These "animals" robbed children of the opportunity to know their mom and dad.  The author wants to know how a person who represents the civil liberties groups that argue for the lives of these "animals" could look in the eyes of the people who lost loved ones to these murders.  The author also congratulates PA Governor Dick Thornburgh for his decision to sign the death warrants for three inmantes on death row.

headline: Bush, Guv Tour Devastated Area
abstract: President Ronald Reagan sent Vice President George Bush to Wheatland, Mercer County, for a first-hand report on one of the 12 tornado-devastated PA counties that Reagan has declared federal disaster areas.  Bush, accompanied by Governor Dick Thornburgh, visited Wheatland, a town that lost virtually all its industry in the storm.  The twisters swept through parts of PA, Ohio, New York and Ontario, killing at least 87 people and caused at least $250 million in damage.

headline: Carnegie update: A fresh look at Institute's stodgy image
abstract: Robert C. Wilburn, president of Carnegie Institute, is investigating ways to improve the Institute.  To this end, he has created the Carnegie One Hundred--100 citizens from the professions invited to take a look behind the institute's seemingly stodgy façade.  Wilburn has been nominated by Governor Thornburgh for the PA Turnpike Commission, and he is awaiting a legislative decision on his appointment.

headline: 3 River tax break will pass, school board head predicts
abstract: The Pittsburgh City School Board is expected to approve a tax break for Three Rivers Stadium, an agreement that several Pittsburgh city officials believe is crucial to save the Pittsburgh Pirates.  Some school board members question whether private investors will benefit at taxpayers' expense, and whether the agreement to give up real estate taxes on the stadium for 26 years is too long.

headline: Union, W-P ink contract
abstract: Yesterday, officials at the Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corporation and the United Steelworkers of America signed a labor agreement which ended a historic 98-day strike.  The signing ceremonies took place amid optimism that the bankrupt steelmaker would survive.  Wheeling-Pittsburgh has also restored management salaries which were cut by 10% nearly two months ago.  The plant has also withdrawn its membership in various Chambers of Commerce and economic development organizations.

headline: U.S. Panel Votes to End Shutdown Of a Reactor at Three Mile Island
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission voted 4 to 1 to lift the order that has kept the undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island shut down since 1979.  A barrage of challenging lawsuits began within minutes of the vote.

headline: Law(yer) suit
abstract: Typical malpractice suits against attorneys stem from a missed deadline, an error that could cost a client a day in court and possibly hundreds of thousands of dollars.  According to the PA Bar Association, attorneys who file personal injury suits are among the most vulnerable to malpractice claims, with attorneys dealing in securities also being particularly vulnerable.  Malpractice suits against attorneys can claim outright fraud or failure to follow a client's instructions, but often these suits stem from administrative errors.  According to Thomas Caldwell, whose firm makes its livelihood off of defending lawyers, the client still must prove that the negligence cost him something.  According to Caldwell, malpractice suits are very rare against criminal lawyers and represent almost zero payout in damages.

headline: Card-game repeal sent to the House
abstract: Legislation to repeal a controversial card-game bill passed through the state Senate in just 8 days and passed with a vote of 40-9; senators tried to avoid being identified as among those favoring gambling.  The bill's prospects in the House are uncertain because house leaders have said they are undecided about what changes might be made to the controversial law.

headline: Casey eyes 4th run for governor: Irvis mentioned for No. 2 spot
abstract: Robert Casey has said he is considering making a fourth race for governor, and there are speculations that state House Speaker Leroy Irvis would be his running mate for lieutenant governor.  The article also mentions other politicians who might run for governor and discusses Casey's background.

headline: 90% of state localities say taxes may rise if revenue sharing goes
abstract: A survey conducted by the PA League of Cities and the PA Intergovernmental Council shows that ninety percent of PA's boroughs, first-class townships, cities and counties would very likely increase taxes if the federal revenue-sharing program is eliminated as proposed by President Ronald Reagan.

headline: Unions assail high-court ruling that bars disciplining of strikers
abstract: American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations Secretary-Treasurer Thomas R. Donahue addressed the 52nd annual convention of The Newspaper Guild.  During his address, Donahue said that a Supreme Court decision barring unions from taking disciplinary action against members who quit the union and return to work during a strike weakens worker solidarity.  The Supreme Court decision upheld a National Labor Relations Board decision on a case that stemmed from a strike by the Pattern Makers' League of North America.  In the case, the NLRB ruled the union violated federal laws preventing unions from coercing members to take part in collective bargaining activities.

headline: Unit 1 help on bills could be offset fast
abstract: It may take only a few weeks for customers of Metropolitan Edison Company to realize decreased electric bills from the restart of Unit 1 at Three Mile Island.  Those decreases could be short-lived, however, if the state Public Utility Commission grants the rate increase that Met-Ed is seeking.  Residential customers would not see a large change on their electric bills, but large companies would likely see a significant decrease after the start of Unit 1, even if Met-Ed is granted the rate increase.

headline: Lawmaker says panel spurred troopers' arrests
abstract: According to PA State Representative Alphonso Deal, a pending government probe by the PA House Select Committee to investigate the PA state police is helping to spur arrests of state troopers.  Recently, two veteran troopers were arrested; one was charged with bribery and two violations of the PA Ethics Act, as well as theft by extortion.  PA State Police spokesman Tom Lyons has denied that the arrests are in conjunction with the PA House committee's probe.  The PA House select committee will look into alleged crimes committed by state police troopers, as well as political favoritism within the deparment.

headline: Cards and sausages
abstract: The State House took many confusing votes aimed at straightening out a controversial tavern-gambling law.  The editorial urges the state House and Senate to start over in order to create a better bill.

headline: Castille Warming Up DA Campaign
abstract: The Republican candidate for Philadelphia District Attorney is trying to gain attention by going to the campaign headquarters of his Democratic opponent, former Commonwealth Judge Robert W. Williams.  Castille accuses Williams of ducking his attempts to arrange debates between them.

headline: Amusement taxes come under fire
abstract: A survey of the 20 largest metropolitan areas in the US found that Pittsburgh has the highest city amusement tax, at 10%, a fact that has drawn the ire of local sports teams, movie theater owners, and convention planners.  Nationally, New Orleans, Boston, and St. Louis are all taking steps to lower their amusement taxes, especially after sports team owners threatened to leave.  Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri refuses to reduce the amusement tax until the PA Legislature allows the city to impose a levy that would fall primarily on suburbanites.  The most vocal critics of the tax have been officials of the Pittsburgh Pirates, who had to pay $600,000 in amusement taxes last year.

headline: US urged to end jobless benefits
abstract: Representatives of business groups told Congress that continuing to fund the Federal Supplemental Compensation (FSC) system would create a bigger problem--one that the system is not equipped to handle.  The FSC will end on March 31, 1985 without Congressional action.  Under the FSC system, the federal government takes over the cost of jobless payments after an unemployed worker exhausts the 26 weeks of payments funded by the state.  Business owners say that these benefits are inappropriate and that the long-term unemployed should seek other forms of financial assistance.

headline: Unit 1 reactor due to be fired up Tuesday: N-chain reaction would be TMI's first in 6 years
abstract: Barring equipment malfunctions or a court order, control rods will be raised in the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor core Tuesday June 11.  This will permit the first controlled nuclear chain reaction on the island in six years.  Officials of General Public Utilities Nuclear Corporation, which operates TMI, unveiled the steps they plan to take to bring the undamaged reactor from inactivity to full operating capacity.  Officials said the company could begin selling electricity when the reactor exceeds 12% of operating capacity, which could come five days after the restart.

headline: Lawyer's injury halts bribery trial
abstract: Testimony in the Computer Technology Associates bribery trial was postponed abruptly because of a back injury suffered by defense attorney John Rogers Carroll.  Carroll represents William T Smith, who is on trial on 16 counts of mail fraud, conspiracy and interstate transportation in aid of racketeering.

headline: CAT collection plan change a sensible move
abstract: This editorial argues that the reason for the initial unpopularity of the auto insurance CAT fund was due mainly to the confusion surrounding the annual $5 fee.  The enactment of the legislation creating the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund was met with great opposition, resulting mainly from a lack of understanding.  Under the new state insurance law, insurance companies may pay as much as $100,000 for an accident victim's medical expenses.  If the motorist pays the annual $5 CAT fee, the CAT fund will pay additional expenses up to $1 million .  The editorial believes that the CAT program is an excellent idea that was handled horribly by the Thornburgh administration and the State Legislature.  It would have been less confusing to put the information about CAT on the auto registration application.
