headline: Changing times help Thornburgh win allies on balancing U.S. budget
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has been fighting for three years to gain support from the National Governors Association for a resolution calling for a balanced-budget amendment to the Constitution.  Thornburgh says that he finally gained support because Democratic governors are moving more to the middle-of-the-road.

headline: Bill would create Penna. 'bank' to help infrastructure projects
abstract: State Representative Joseph Lashinger has proposed a bill that would create the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Development Bank, a revolving state fund that would lend local governments money for infrastructure projects at little or no interest.

headline: Why state lost Saturn
abstract: A letter to the editor from Blaine E. Knupp, a member of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Union (AFSCME), argues against PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's notion that there is an improved business climate in Pennsylvania.  Knupp argues that the Thornburgh's administration is part of the bad labor-management climate.  Knup also states that during recent negotitiations between the Commonwealth and AFSCME, the Thornburgh administration took a very anti-union and adversarial stance.  Knupp says that this attitude needs to change before PA loses more commercial ventures.

headline: Valve error laid to GPU
abstract: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) cited GPU Nuclear Corporation with a minor safety violation during the Three Mile Island Unit 1 start-up program.  The violation occurred on the same day (June 7, 1985) that the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals blocked an NRC order that would have allowed GPU Nuclear Corp. to restart Unit 1, a decision which is currently being reviewed.  The minor violation, which does not carry a fine, occurred when a maintenance employee left a valve on one of the reactor coolant pumps at Three Mile Island Unit 1; this could have caused damage to the pump seals during normal operations.

headline: Leaders of five N.Y. crime families indicted
abstract: The five reputed leaders of New York's Mafia families--Paul Castellano, Anthony Salerno, Gennaro Langella, Philip Rastelli, and Antonio Corallo--were rounded up and charged in a federal court with being the "ruling body" of a criminal enterprise that deals in murder, labor racketeering and extortion.  US Attorney General Rudolph Giuliani predicted that there would be a struggle for control and that victims of the Mafia would likely come forward.

headline: CAT Fund not cat quick
abstract: This editorial bemoans the billing process of PA's Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund (CAT).  State legislators are beginning to get complaints that that billing process is too slow.  State Representative Richard Geist is urging his constituents to send their vehicle registration forms and $5 CAT Fund fees to his office, and he has promised that an office worker will walk each renewal form through the necessary paces at the PA Department of Transportation.  The editorial also likes Geist's enthusiasm for helping his constituents, but believes that it should be directed at improving the CAT Fund.

headline: Chicago consultant cites "serious" fraud in Philadelphia voting
abstract: Richard Anderson, executive director of the Committee for Honest Elections, a nonprofit group that specializes in investigating election fraud, has spent the last four months investigating Philadelphia's voter rolls and believes there may be as many as 25,000 fraudulent votes cast in recent elections.  This estimate was disputed by the Philadelphia City Commissioners and the Committee of Seventy, an independent group that monitors Philadelphia elections.  Anderson was asked to come to Philadelphia by the PA Republican State Committee.  Anderson's critics claim he erred in taking 44 and in projecting a citywide figure of 25,000, but they do acknowledge that Philadelphia has to do a better job keeping voter rolls up to date.  Budgetary constraints and court rulings have hampered the ability of City Commissioners to purge bad registrations.

headline: Citizens try to keep Centralia on map
abstract: A die-hard band of residents in Centralia have formed a group called Save the Borough and are drawing up survival plans in an effort to keep the fire-beleaguered borough on the map.  Centralia has suffered from an underground mine fire for over 25 years, and government leaders estimate that by 1990 less than 30 households will remain of the 500 that were there before the fire.  Save the Borough has hired an attorney and is drawing up plans to provide services in the hopes of preventing the borough from being dissolved into surrounding Conyngham Township.

headline: Why strikes won't sove steel's problems
abstract: Editorial:  Steel worker labor unions currently face the daunting task of sacrificing jobs and collective bargaining agreements so that the steel industry, in the face of pressures from an international market, may have a chance at survival.  The tension and stress that unions must face when they deal with management is none the more evident than when looking at the current Wheeling-Pittsburgh stoppage, the first major strike at an American steel company since 1959.  There are no easy answers, but it might be helpful if management and employees share information and  both parties address the full scope of the business issues at hand.

headline: Warnings on radon ignored
abstract: Four years before radon contamination forced the Watras family to leave their home, the PA Deparment of Environmental Resources (DER) knew that radiation levels were abnormal in their neighborhood.  The PA DER had been warned that the potential for radiation contamination existed in the Reading Prong, a geologic formation rich in uranium.  In the PA portion of the prong, the DER estimates that 20,000 homes need to be checked for radon.  DER officials say that they were sidetracked by the massive volume of work created by the Three Mile Island nuclear accident of March 1979.  Radon gas has been linked to lung cancer, and as many as 20,000 people will die from radon-induced lung cancer this year.  An in-depth examination of the reporting process for the Reading Prong from 1979-1983 is in the article.

headline: Legislator raps judge, urges at least 5 years for pair
abstract: PA State Representative Jeffrey Piccola is upset that a Dauphin County judge refused to give two 19-year olds a five year minimum prison sentence for armed robbery.  The state law calls for a mandatory 5-year minimum sentence for those convicted of crimes committed with a firearm, but the judge cited the 1953 Youthful Offenders Act that provides indeterminate sentences for people 15 to 21 years old.  Piccola is urging the District Attorney to appeal to the judge to modify the sentence.

headline: Charge-card interest of 18% passes House
abstract: A bill that allows the interest ceiling on retail charge accounts and bank cards to continue at 18% was passed by the state House of Representatives; the bill is expected to pass the Senate later this month.

headline: City seeks state OK on refinancing
abstract: Philadelphia is racing to beat a January 1, 1986 deadline for the approval of two bills that would allow Philadelphia to replace construction-project bonds with new bonds at lower interest rates.  Other local governments in PA can simply decide to retire older, more costly bonds.  However, a 1972 state law that prohibits the city from deciding on its own to refinance construction bonds is holding Philadelphia back from doing the same.  The city therefore must get state approval to refinance.  There is some urgency to get this process done, as the US Congress and President Ronald Reagan are likely to rewrite the tax laws to remove cities' ability to refund bond debts by the end of the year.

headline: Consolidation's cowards
abstract: Johnstown Mayor Herb Pfuhl criticized state lawmakers for not adopting enabling legislation that would clear the way for annexation, consolidation and municipal boundary changes.  The editorial agrees with Pfuhl and says that consolidation can be for the betterment of the state's cities.

headline: Workers Comp proposal includes inflation factor
abstract: PA legislators and union leaders announced legislation that would overhaul PA's Workers Compensation system, including a proposal that would adjust benefit rates according to inflation.  The proposal would also expedite hearings in Workers Compensation cases and provide medical insurance for injured workers.  The package is called the BASEC program, as it addresses benefits, administration, safety, eligibility, and cost issues.

headline: Waste makers should provide
abstract: This editorial argues that Vermont Governor Madeleine Kunin was on very loose footing when she tried to lobby other Northeastern governors to oppose the location of a nuclear waste depository in the region.  Vermont is more dependent on nuclear power than any other state.  The editorial believes that states which have nuclear power plants and generate high amounts of nuclear waste have no moral or ethical ground to demand that nuclear waste be deposited somewhere else.  The editorial does side with Governor Kunin in her assessment that unpleasant features of modern society, like nuclear waste dumps, tend to be put in the countryside, where there are often fewer people to offend.

headline: Leo's Subordinates Lionized Him
abstract: Philadelphia Managing Director Leo Brooks' staff expresses sadness at his resignation.  Brooks was involved in planning the disastrous siege of the MOVE house in West Philadelphia in which 61 houses were burned.  Brooks said that he was planning his resignation before the disaster.

headline: Coaches, Umpires and other
abstract: Under bills recently introduced in the PA House and PA Senate, coaches, umpires, and other volunteers for sports teams would be immune from certain negligence lawsuits.  Sponsors say the legislation will cut high liability insurance rates paid by little league and similar groups, and could also attract volunteers now scared away by the threat of "frivolous" lawsuits.

headline: City voters can improve Court of Common Pleas
abstract: This editorial says that the most important votes in Philadelphia's May 21 primary election are those for judges of the Common Pleas Court.  The editorial says that voters can improve the quality of the Common Pleas Court and, eventually, its administration and operation by electing the best available candidates for judgeships.  The Inquirer endorses seven judges: Mary Rose Fante Cunningham, Frank M. Jackson, Bill Knauer, Steven E. Levin, G. Craig Lord, Thomas L. McGill Jr. and Esther R. Sylvester.

headline: County faces $30 million deficit
abstract: Allegheny County faces a $30 million deficit next year, mainly due to the fact that it has lived on reserves and has not raised taxes for four years.  As the county prepares to adopt a new spending plan, the gap between revenues and anticipated spending is larger than ever.  The only real solution is to raise taxes or make drastic service reductions.  The anticipated revenues and spending for next year's Allegheny County budget are further examined in the article.  The views of several elected officials on dealing with this deficit are also included in the article.

headline: Workman's fund needs fine tuning
abstract: This letter to the editor talks about problems facing the PA Workman's Compensation Fund and the PA business environment.  One of the reasons that PA lost out on the General Motors Saturn plant was the heavy tax burden that PA places on business and industry.  The jobless fund, health care, Social Security, and Workmen's Compensation are very costly for PA's industry to shoulder.  In addition to reforming the Workman's Compensation Fund, the Legislature will also consider proposals to cut employee health care costs without reducing the quality of care.  The author believes that as necessary as it is to put PA industry on a competitive level, it is just as necessary to obeserve safeguards.  If some of the heavy burdens on industry can be reduced, PA's economy will benefit.

headline: Waste site
abstract: This editorial looks at the process of establishing a nuclear waste repository in PA.  PA had previously joined a compact with Maryland, Delware, and West Virginia.  Under this compact, PA agreed to provide a nuclear dump site.  However, due to the snail's pace at which PA has implemented the plan, Maryland and Deleware have decided to pull out and forge agreements with other states.  In 1980, Congress gave the 47 states without nuclear repositories five years to provide for their own waste storage.  Though Congress may grant a grace period, the cost of dumping will most certainly be increased.  The editorial argues that there is no good reason for this legislation to be held up in the state Legislature any longer.

headline: Little new information arises on decisions about fire
abstract: The four men who directly presided over a fire at the MOVE compound testified yesterday before the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission, but gave no new answers as to why the fire was allowed to burn down 61 row houses.  The four city officials gave long and detailed reponses, but all held firmly to their earlier testimony in the face of blatant contradictions from fellow officials.  The article gives further examination of the testimony by Philadelphia Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor, Fire Commissioner William Richmond, and former Managing Director Leo Brooks.

headline: Conference committee gets gaming repeal bill
abstract: Because of opposition to amendments that had been inserted in a House version of the bill, legislation that would eliminate casino-type gambling in PA bars was sent to a House-Senate conference committee.  Tavern owners are lobbying at the Capitol to urge lawmakers to keep blackjack games in the legislation.  Tavern owners say that gambling in New Jersey has hurt their business.

headline: Clayton deserves support in her plans for the schools
abstract: This editorial applauds the work of Constance Clayton, superintendent of the Philadelphia Public schools, for averting a teachers' strike and managing to open the schools on time.  However, the editorial fears that Clayton may have lost power in the negotiation process, and that teachers now may be less responsive to her initiative.  The editorial believes that the people of Philadelphia are behind Clayton, and believes that the union should get behind her and do what is constructive for the city.

headline: County raises pushed
abstract: The PA House is expected to vote again today on a bill designed to almost double the paychecks for four Allegheny County row officers; the officers will be elected next week.  The same bill was rejected by the House yesterday, but supporters said after the vote they would move to have the bill reconsidered today.  Under current law, the county commissioners may only approve across-the-board percentage increases for the 13 row offices.  An amendment to the bill would allow the Legislature to apporve salary boosts for the four row offices without granting equal increases to other officeholders.  The measure was defeated largely because Republican lawmakers saw the bill as a possible way to reward political favors in the Democratic-dominated county.

headline: $15 Mil Training Appropriation
abstract: At an Urban-League press conference in Pittsburgh, US Senator Arlen Specter announced a $15 million appropriation for pre-vocational and vocational training programs for economically and educationally-disadvantaged youths.  The appropriation will go to community-based organizations such as the National Urban League, the national Opportunities Industrialization Centers and local educational agencies; the purpose of the grant is to improve and intensify existing vocational education programs by providing pre-vocational, self-help, and motivational training.

headline: Wasteland: State swamped on coal min sites
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources has acknowledged the problem of reclaiming coal lands.  The number of ravaged mine sites is increasing rapidly and there is a shortage of funds.  The DER is taking steps to remedy these problems.

headline: Little-known chapter: The bombs were bursting in air over the US
abstract: When Philadelphia police dropped a bomb on the MOVE house in an attempt to open up the house and evict the occupants, many people said that this was the first time a bomb has dropped on American soil.  A columnist says that the bombing of the MOVE house marked the first time that a city government dropped a bomb on a house within its jurisdiction, but not the first time that a bomb was dropped on American soil.  The first bomb dropped on American soil was by the Japanese in World War II.  The columnist urges the panel investigating the MOVE incident not to keep details hidden from the public.

headline: Congratulations on Upholding Underage Drinking Laws
abstract: A sarcastic editorial discusses a case in Luzerne County Court--a case in which Judge Bernard Brominski let the Station, a famous bar in downtown Wilkes-Barre, off the hook on four alleged incidents of serving alcoholic beverages to minors.  The judge let the bar off the hook because Liquor Control Board officials did not move swiftly enough in prosecuting the case.  The editorial also features a cartoon depicting Judge Brominski holding an LCB official in one hand saying,"Can't you even be on time!"; the judge is patting the owners of the Station on the head with the other hand.

headline: Coalition backs retention elections for PUC members
abstract: Passage of a bill that would make members of the state Public Utilities Commission (PUC) subject to voter approval was supported by the PA Public Interest Coalition (PennPIC) during publich hearings held by the state House Consumer Affairs Committee.  PennPIC representatives urged the panel to approve a House bill that would reduce commissioners' terms from 10 years to four and would require a retention election--similar to those required for state judges.  Commissioners currently are nominated by the governor and must be confirmed by a two-thirds majority of the state Senate, a procedure that the bill would keep intact.

headline: Democrats' record 'distorted'
abstract: A columnist defends the Cumberland County Democratic Party and says that remarks by the former chairman, Bill Feuchtenberger, are false.

headline: 7.1% boost eyed in school unit budget
abstract: Harrisburg area school districts will be asked to approve a 7.1% increase in the 1985-86 general operating budget of the Capital Area Intermediate Unit.  This unit provides professional and technical services to school districts in Cumberland, Perry, northern York and Dauphin counties.

headline: 'We Don't Want to Live With TMI'
abstract: At a Nuclear Regulatory Commission hearing, several concerned citizens were joined by several PA politicians who oppose the restart of the Three Mile Island Unit-1 Reactor.  The list of politicians included Governor Dick Thornburgh, US Senators Arlen Specter and John Heinz, and US Representatives George Gekas and Don Ritter.  Thornburgh and the other PA politicians told the NRC that two key issues--safety and management integrity--have not been resolved to their satisfaction.

headline: MADD and meddling
abstract: This editorial notes that Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) went too far when they attend court hearings and passively tried to influence the jury.  MADD members attended the hearing of a West Virginia man who was convicted of the felony of "driving under the influence of alcohol, resulting in death." The Supreme Court of West Virginia ordered a new trial for him because the MADD members constituted a "formidable, albeit passive, influence on the jury."  The editorial says that the West Virginia Supreme Court decision is a reminder that righteous anger cannot be allowed to give way to fanaticism, especially in a court of law.

headline: Consumer Activist Ralph
abstract: Consumer activist Ralph Nader claims that the growing liability insurance crisis is being manufactured by "price-gouging" insurance companies who are attempting to reduce victims' rights to sue.  Nader's comments came in testimony before the US House Insurance Committee's investigation into the problems of high liability insurance premiums and cancelled policies.  Insurance industry representatives have blamed the premium increases on larger and more frequent judgments in civil suits.  The insurance industry and Nader battled over industry recommendations.

headline: Coalition fails its promise for industrial states
abstract: This editorial attacks the Northeast-Midwest US Congressional Coalition as ineffective.  A recent study showed the area that this group represents as having lost more manufacturing jobs than any other area in the country--with the auto and steel industries being hit the hardest.  The Northeast-Midwest Coalition has done little about this situation, aside from releasing reports, holding press conferences, and speaking at public functions about the dire state of the local economy.  The editorial wants the Northeast-Midwest Coalition to become more than a study group, especially given the fact that the Northeast and Midwest remain important sections of the country.  The coalition should have significant political clout to exert influence in government and on business leaders.

headline: Did not cheat Stone, Torquato testifies
abstract: John Torquato Jr. has testified that he did not cheat Robert Stone, president of Pittsburgh City Council, by giving him $6,374 and 25,000 "worthless" stock options in a California holding company.  He said he initially agreed to split profits on a city contract with Stone, but he instead gave the city official $6,374.86 and stock options in COMMAX.  This was because both men agreed that there was a potential for the money to be traced.

headline: 82% of students pass state's 1st competency test
abstract: More than 80% of Harrisburg area public school students passed the first state-mandated competency tests.  These tests are part of Governor Dick Thornburgh's education reform package: "Turning the Tide: An Agenda for Excellence in Pennsylvania Public Schools."  State funds will be provided to fund remedial programs for students who did not make the necessary grades.

headline: Why even hesitate?
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh will appear before the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to make a final appeal against the restart of the undamaged Unit 1 nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island.  This editorial questions why Thornburgh took a day to confirm that he would testify in front of the commission.

headline: Man with jail record tied to Pa. card games
abstract: A Northeast Philadelphia man who pleaded guilty in federal court to mail fraud and embezzlement charges was involved in the operation of blackjack tournaments at a Philadelphia hotel and at least three taverns.  This has lead to concerns that there are no regulations for these tournaments, and that they will bring organized crime into the state.

headline: Consumers Winners
abstract: This editorial praises the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) for coming down on the side of consumers in ending the ban on beer-price advertising.  The issue pitted large beer warehouses against smaller distributors, who claimed that advertising of prices would drive them out of business.  However, the editorial states that every other business enterprise, except regulated monopolies, must deal with competitive pricing.  The LCB ban on advertising served as an artificial shield against competition for customers.  The board made the right decision in favoring customers.

headline: Commonwealth secretary to quit early
abstract: Secretary of the Commonwealth William R. Davis has told top aides that he plans to resign later this year or at the beginning of 1986; he plans to return to Westmoreland County to run his family's business, Davis Paint and Wallpaper Incorporated.

headline: Early warns of "commuter bandit" Caliguiri
abstract: Calling Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri "the latest commuter bandit," PA State Senator Edward Early is urging his fellow legislators to be wary of a possible attempt by the Caliguiri to have the PA General Assemby enact a wage tax on suburb residents who work in the city.  Caliguiri, in his budget message to Pittsburgh City Council, said any Democratic gubernatorial candidate who expects his support must endorse some form of tax relief for the city.

headline: Advances in vocational education
abstract: A guest columnist comments on a recent Patriot-News editorial and a study on public education by the Committee for Economic Development (CED).  The columnist says the editorial failed to mention that the study found that schooling contributes greatly to the economy, and the author urges the state and federal governments to pick up their financial support for public education, which has wained recently.  The author also likes the CED's recommendation for raising entry-level teacher salaries to attract better teaching prospects.  The author also believes the CED report overstates the discipline problem in most schools and points to a survey done by Pennsylvania State University on PA's teachers and their thoughts about discipline in their classrooms.

headline: Workers to begin heating up Unit 1 at TMI tomorrow
abstract: Doug Bedell, a spokesman for General Public Utilities Nuclear Corporation, said the Unit 1 reactor will begin heating up tomorrow evening in preparation for restart next week.  Attorneys for the Commonwealth of PA and two citizens' groups have asked the Third US Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia to block the restart until the court reviews whether the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission acted correctly in authorizing the restart.

headline: McSlammers
abstract: This editorial calls for the PA State Senate to follow the PA House in passing a bill that would keep private enterprise out of PA prisons.  It's too bad that politicians would consider putting prisons in the hands of private business instead of convincing voters of the need for better facilities and serious rehabilitiation programs.  The editorial believes that the administration of justice cannot be left to private businesses, as they may go bankrupt, be sold, or cut corners to make profits for stockholders.

headline: Crime panel
abstract: A letter to the editor from Gary F. DiVito, Chief Counsel for the PA Liquor Control Board, accuses Governor Dick Thornburgh of trying to politicize the Liquor Control Board; the author claims that the governor is politicizing the board in an attempt to discourage the Legislature from renewing the board.

headline: Communities assured of state pension aid
abstract: State Auditor General Don Bailey said the Municipal Pension Reform Law enacted in December won't affect aid given to fiscally sound communities.  Bailey admitted that the complex piece of legislation is confusing, and that it will take $1.1 million to implement the new measure.  He also said that his department has not received any funds.

headline: Goode says he is politically stronger than ever
abstract: Despite the May 13, 1985 MOVE confrontation, 85% of Philadelphia residents think that Mayor Goode and his administration are doing a "fine job."  Though numerous leaders inside and outside city government disagree with this assessment, Stephen J. Teichner--a Philadelphia pollster--found, from a survey of 300 Philadelphia residents, that 97% of residents felt some action against MOVE was needed, and 71% approved of how Mayor Goode handled the incident.  Mayor Goode also believes the MOVE incident has not hurt Philadelphia's image, as he points to the fact that $3 billion in construction will be going on in the next five years.  Also, there were a million people on the Parkway over the Fourth of July weekend, and 101,000 people attended Live Aid.

headline: Agriculture in the classroom? Yes!
abstract: After a 20-month study, Education Secretary Margaret Smith and Agriculture Secretary Penrose Hallowell have recommended agribusiness-education partnerships to promote awareness of the state's Number 1 business.  This editorial argues that this is a good idea and that agriculture should be taught in elementary and secondary schools so that students can be up-to-date on technology.

headline: York Hospital staffer speaks out: Area cancers can't be tied to TMI, doctor concludes
abstract: Dr. David M. Shearer, chief of York Hospital's nuclear medicine division, has monitored hundreds of cases coming into his department annually since the Three Mile Island accident.  Dr. Shearer says he cannot attribute any of the cases to the accident.  Shearer attributes higher incidences of cancer to smoking cigarettes, rather than from any exposure caused by TMI.

headline: More police refuse public testimony
abstract: Five more Philadelphia bomb squad police officers refused to testify before the Philadelphia Special Investigations Commission, which is holding hearings on the MOVE incident; the bomb-dquad members cited their Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution.  There were several confrontations between commission chairman William Brown and the attorney representing the police, Patrick Artur, yesterday.  On Wednesday, US District Judge James McGirr Kelly ruled that the commission had the right to read aloud from notes taken during the private questioning of witnesses who have since invoked their Fifth Amendment rights for public testimony.  Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell and US Attorney Edward S.G. Dennis Jr. both said that their offices are investigating the MOVE incident.

headline: Criticizing the LCB
abstract: Under PA's "Sunset Law," the Liquor Control Board will cease to exist at the end of 1985, unless it is renewed by the state General Assembly.  A columnist says that Governor Dick Thornburgh wishes to see the end of the agency and is doing everything possible to point out its mistakes so that it will not be renewed.

headline: Congressional delegation's votes
abstract: This article looks at the votes of area members of US Congress on key issues during the week that ended on Friday, September 13.  Among the issues considered are the US House rejecting additional cuts in Amtrack's federal subsidy, and the US House blocking landfill funds for New York's Westway.  Other issues include the US Senate refusing to vote on South Africa sanctions, and the US Senate voting to allow federal judicial review of school prayer cases.

headline: Goode, Caliguiri urge congressmen to oppose parts of Reagan tax plan
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode and Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri traveled to the US Capitol to try and persuade PA's congressional delegation to fight against parts of the Reagan administration's tax-overhaul plan; the mayors say the plan will hurt cities.  The mayors objected to three provisions of the proposed tax revision: the elimination of state and local taxes as deductible items; the elimination of tax-exempt financing for some public works projects, such as pollution control and airport construction, and the end of tax credits for historic rehabilitation.

headline: Black Student Enrollment At
abstract: According to a school spokesperson, enrollment of black students at Penn State University has increased by more than 15% in the last year.  At all 22 Penn State campuses this fall, 2,308 black students are enrolled; this figure comprises 3.7% of the total Penn State student body.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts a car crashed into a light post at a cemetery.  In the cemetery, a thought bubble is coming from one of the graves and the person is saying "Who wants a law telling me to wear seat belts?! I say GIVE ME LIVERTY OR, uh..."

headline: MOVE battle: Phila. Police bomb radicals in siege
abstract: An attempt to bring a peaceful end to a confrontation between police and a radical back-to-nature cult called MOVE collapsed late yesterday--turning a West Philadelphia neighborhood into a battle zone.  Police had attempted to negotiate with the MOVE members to get them to leave the house peacefully after complaints from neighbors, but MOVE members refused to leave.  Police and MOVE members traded fire and the siege ended with two blocks of houses on fire.

headline: Debate on enforcement focuses on LCB measure
abstract: After yesterday's failed attempt to give the state police responsibility over enforcing PA's liquor laws, the state Attorney General is the prime candidate to take over liquor-law enforcement.  The debate came up during an attempt to amend a Senate bill that would make comprehensive changes in the PA Liquor Control Board.  Amendment foes contended that the police do not want the job.  Supporters of the police measure say that giving powers to the Attorney General would create a conflict of interest.  However, State Senator John Shumaker said the Attorney General has already agreed to take on the added enforcement powers.

headline: CTA official: Smith talked of bribes
abstract: A former Computer Technology Associates (CTA) official, Judy Ellis, testified for the prosecution in the CTA bribery trial against William Smith.  Ellis testified that Smith had talked seriously and joked about bribe offers to state officials to get a $4.8 million Treasury Department contract.  Smith is on trial for 16 counts of conspiracy, mail fraud and interstate racketeering in connection with the contracts CTA obtained from the Treasury, the city of Pittsburgh, and Allegheny County.

headline: He wants you to know
abstract: An editorial commends state Senator Raphael J. Musto for voting against an amendment to Senate Bill 303 that would allow local governments and school boards to conduct meetings behind closed doors.  The editorial says that the amendment would have crippled the state's Sunshine Law and that local government business should be conducted under the public eye.

headline: Board spares day-care program
abstract: The Pittsburgh School Board announced that it will not end its day-care program.  School Superintendent Richard Wallace said that pay concessions granted by the city teachers union will allow the day-care center to operate for another year.  The school district originally said it would have to close all 12 day-care centers because the state Welfare Department wouldn't provide enough funding to keep them operating.

headline: $1.2 billion offer set to buy 85% of Conrail
abstract: An investment consortium assembled by Morgan Stanley & Company will unveil a $1.2 billion offer at a news conference today.  The offer is to buy the government's interest in Conrail, and will certainly challenge the administration's plan to sell the railroad to Norfolk Southern Corporation.

headline: MOVE Bomb Contained C-4: City denied use of the explosive
abstract: The bomb that triggered a fire in which 11 MOVE members were killed was recently discovered to be made of the explosive C-4, something that had previously been denied by city officials and Philadelphia Police Commissioner James S. White.  This revelation came on the same day that the police officer who built the bomb, along with the one who dropped it on the roof, were set to be interviewed by the special commission that Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode formed to investigate the incident.  The article also talks at length about the events on the day of the MOVE confrontation through the eyes of Police Lieutenant Frank Powell, the officer who dropped the bomb.

headline: Disasters Differ, Thornburgh Says
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh said that comparisons can't be made between the state's decision to help tornado-ravaged communities and its decision not to offer immediate aid to a Philadelphia neighborhood destroyed in the police-MOVE confrontation.  Referring to the destruction of the tornadoes, Thornburgh said that there are many differences in the two disasters, primarily that the areas damaged by the tornadoes have very little in the way of assets and would be unable to meet the immediate needs of the people.  In sharp contrast, Philadelphia is America's fourth-largest city and has the resources to deal with the disaster.

headline: CTA trial shows legislative process schemes
abstract: Four days of testimony in the trial of two attorneys for Computer Technology Associates (CTA) depicted PA's legislative process as a system rooted in clandestine meetings, questionable favors and outright bribes.  William Smith and Alan Stoneman are accused of actively participating in an elaborate scheme to secure a lucrative state contract for CTA.  This scheme included attempts to influence and bribe public officials; John Torquato, the scheme's alleged mastermind, has already pleaded guilty.

headline: Judge Checks In, Pays His Dues
abstract: Philadelphia Chief Assistant City Solicitor Andrew Bralow said that Municipal Judge Arthur Kafrissen paid more than $4700 in delinquent taxes on his Chestnut Hill home by delivering a check in person to the city solicitor's office.  The Philadelphia Daily News had reported that he owed back taxes in 1984.

headline: Cheyney gets new life with extension
abstract: The Commission on Higher Education of the Middle States Association has granted Cheyney University 18 months to improve its curriculum and administration problems before the Commission will remove accreditation from Cheyney.  Had the school lost its accreditation, any degrees or course credits it awarded would have had little merit in the rest of the academic community, and the school would have lost any federal funding.

headline: $5 auto-insurance fee unfair
abstract: A letter to the editor complains about the $5 auto-insurance fee required from all vehicle owners in the state.  The money will go into the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund to pay medical bills for persons severely injured in traffic accidents.  The author says that "this is another way our government can once again rob us, legally."

headline: MOVE commission and Senate panel get into a row
abstract: State Senator Frank A. Salvatore, chairman of the Senate's Urban Affairs and Housing Committee, announced that he would defer his own investigation of the May 13 MOVE incident until after the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission had finished its work, on the assumption that the Commission would allow his adies to attend its meetings and give the aides access to every piece of raw material in its possession.  However, Commission chairman William H. Brown III said that Salvatore's assumption was incorrect and that the aides would not be permitted to sit in.  The Senate committee's newly appointed special counsel, Philadelphia lawyer Richard A. Sprague, said that the committee would use its subpoena power if the commission did not cooperate.

headline: Disasters in '85 cost insurers $2 billion
abstract: In 1985, disasters such as Hurricane Gloria, the tornadoes of May, and the block-long destruction that followed the bombing of MOVE's headquarters have cost the insurance industry a record $2.45 billion.  The question now is when will people begin to see a rise in premiums to cover this loss.  In PA, underwriters must get rate hikes approved by insurance departments.  The nation's 3,500 property-insurance underwriters have paid out $21 billion more in claims than they have collected in premiums. Most insurance companies try to consider the likelhood of natural disasters occurring when setting homeowner premiums.  How much premiums rise depends on several factors, including the insurance company's financial stability and the amount of insurance it carries on itself.

headline: CTA trial to proceed, judge rules
abstract: US District Judge Malcolm Muir denied a defense motion for a mistrial in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery trial and ordered the jury to proceed with 11 members after one of the jurors was seriously injured in an auto accident.  Muir sided with acting US Attorney James West and used an untested 1983 Supreme Court rule that allows a judge to continue a trial with 11 jurors if certain unforeseen circumstances arise.  Muir said that a mistrial should be avoided because of the trial's extreme length.

headline: Local borrowing: Debt should not be incurred without public consent
abstract: An editorial says that the state should implement a referendum requirement for a local governments and school districts so they are able to incur debt.

headline: Cheyney to lose accreditation unless its appeal is successful
abstract: The Commission of Higher Education of the Middle States Association of Colleges and Schools has decided to remove its accreditation of Cheyney University of Pennsylvania, the nation's oldest black public college.  Cheyney plans to work with other state universities to develop a plan to get the commission to reconsider its decision.

headline: $5.7 quadrillion suit dismissed
abstract: After his license was suspended, Frank A. Messina sought damages from PA Department of Transportation Secretary Thomas A. Larson in the amount of $5,764,609,563,143,700.48.  Messina alleged that the suspension was illegal and that it cost him his job and subjected him to public ridicule.  William E. Breene, president judge of the Venango County Court, dismissed the suit and agreed with the state's contention that the case was groundless.

headline: MOVE commission sets no dates for hearings
abstract: The Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission met yesterday, but has yet to set a date for its public hearing on the May 13, 1985 siege and fire at a MOVE compound.  Commission Chairman William Brown III said through a spokesman that a formal announcement of the schedule and format of the public hearing will take place at the commission's next meeting on August 15, 1985.  An unidentified member of the commission acknowledged heightened public concern about the investigatory process--especially given Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode's recent statement that he will not discuss unanswered questions about the incident with his subordinates, as well as the discovery of an unspent bullet in the remains of one of the 11 MOVE members who died in the confrontation.

headline: Gambling movement has swung from Poconos to state's taverns
abstract: Gambling, specifically the type that involves slot machines, blackjack and high-stakes poker games, has been a perennial Pocono issue for the past decade.  Currently, lawmakers are considering legalizing video-game machines and games of chance for all the state's liquor-license establishments.  This new development affects those pushing for gambling in the Poconos, as they will no longer be able to bill gambling as the main attraction for coming to the Poconos.

headline: Converting New Republicans
abstract: An editorial approves of Republican Party plans to court blue-collar Democrats in PA, Florida, Louisiana and North Carolina; the author expects that many people will switch to the Republican Party.

headline: MOVE Fallout
abstract: Columnist Pete Dexter wrote a previous column criticizing the way Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode handled the MOVE siege.  In this column, he presents letters that he received from angry readers defending Goode.  Dexter defends his criticism of Goode and says that Goode is responsible for the tragedy and that opinion polls would not support him if the tragedy had occurred in a white neighborhood.

headline: Church-state law reinforced by high court
abstract: The US Supreme Court, in two decisions that upheld the separation of church and state, condemned the spending of millions of tax dollars in Michigan and New York to send public-school teachers into religious-school classrooms.  By a 5-4 vote, the justices invalidated a "shared-time" program in Grand Rapids, Michigan, that for six years had sent 470 public-school teacheers into religious schools to conduct remedial, enrichment and other special classes.  In a second case, the justices found constitutional flaws in a New York City public-school program that spent federal monies on remedial and special education programs for low income, religious-school students.

headline: 14 States Adopt Seat-Belt Laws But Not Pennsylvania
abstract: This editorial states that PA lawmakers should join the dozen or more states that have passed laws requiring drivers and passengers in motor vehicles to use seat belts or be subject to penalty.  More than ten bills on this subject have failed to win support in the PA General Assembly.  Trips to New York and New Jersey, the first two states to adopt laws requiring seat belt use, have helped to get PA residents into the selt belt habit.  It is time that the PA General Assembly adopt a seat belt requirement law.

headline: MOVE hearings:  Quietly momentous
abstract: This article provides an in-depth examination of the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission, which investigated the MOVE incident of May 13, 1985.  Although the commission did not find any new blockbuster information or smoking guns regarding the events of May 13, it did come up with some interesting pieces of information and left the public with a series of strong images.  Each of these is elaborated on in the article.

headline: Drought fears hurt business: Fewer are taking trips on Delaware
abstract: Owners of businesses that rely on tourism and recreation on the Delaware River--such as canoe- and tube-rental operations--are using advertising to lure people back to the river--even though the state is facing a drought.  The drought has hurt the $50 million Delaware River recreation industry.

headline: Council ballot includes Stone
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council President Robert Stone filed his candidacy for City Council, but was not endorsed by the Democratic City Committee.  Stone was named, but not charged, in a federal grand jury indictment issued in connection with a bribery investigation; this lead to his not receiving a Democratic endorsement.  The article names other local politicians seeking office.

headline: MOVE: The Aftermath…After worst day of his career, Goode moves aggressively
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode defends the way he handled removing the back-to-nature cult, MOVE, from a West Philadelphia neighborhood.  Goode said that his decision was right and criticized the media for sensationalizing the event.  He also said that he planned to rebuild the entire West Philadelphia neighborhood by Christmas.

headline: CMU trustees raise 1986-87 tuition 9 percent
abstract: The Carnegie-Mellon University (CMU) trustees raised tuition to $10,250 for the 1986-87 school year.  CMU President Richard Cyert said that the 9% increase should not be a problem because CMU's tuition is a bargain when compared with other highly selective schools that CMU considers its competition.  CMU officials said they will increase their financial aid budget in proportion to tuition.

headline: 3 oppose aiding Altemose center
abstract: A Philadelphia union leader and two legislators said they would fight efforts by suburban lawmakers to secure $44 million in state funds for road improvements to the Valley Forge Convention Center.  They denounced the proposal because it involved the use of nonunion labor.

headline: MOVE Inquiry Harming Reputation of Mayor
abstract: For months, Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode had avoided any political fallout from his handling of a confrontation with the radical group MOVE.  However, that has changed dramatically in the three weeks since the Philadelphia Special Investigations Commission began its hearings into the city's confrontation with MOVE.  Polls have show that the mayor's popularity is down and even his staunchest allies concede that the inquiry has hurt him.  Goode faces re-election in two years, and must deal not only with the final report by the special commission investigating the MOVE incident, but also with the cost of rebuilding the area damaged by the confrontation, and a police-corruption scandal.  The article also looks at Goode's initial policy towards MOVE and the events that occurred during the assualt on MOVE headquarters.

headline: Drunk on patronage
abstract: This editorial urges Governor Dick Thornburgh to continue his fight to abolish the state-store liquor system.

headline: County GOP to mark inauguration in area: Others go to Washington
abstract: This article discusses the plans of local Republican committees for President Reagan's inauguration.  It outlines the inaugural events that will take place in Washington DC, as well as the Dauphin County inaugural celebration that will take place locally.

headline: New Sunshine Bill
abstract: The open-meeting law passed in 1974 specified that decision-making, not just voting, must be done in public at municipal, city, or other official unit meetings.  This editorial argues that the meetings do not need to be made public, but that members of official agencies must publicly state the reason for voting as they do.

headline: College financing: State Master Plan to prescribe austerity, efficiency
abstract: A report from the Governor's Commission for the Financing of Higher Education--the "Kirby report"--provides ideas for ways to finance higher education in PA.  This editorial suggests that the real problem with higher education is the poor economy in the state.

headline: 35 percent of state bridges called 'deficient' or 'obsolete'
abstract: A federal Department of Transportation report on the state of the nation's bridges shows that almost one-quarter of PA's 21,719 bridges are structurally deficient, which means they are unable to carry the weight they were designed to handle; another 10 percent were not intended to accommodate current vehicle sizes and are considered "functionally obsolete."  Federal Highway Administrator Ray Burnhart said that classifying a bridge as deficient--either structurally or functionally--does not mean that the bridge is unsafe; with proper load postings and enforcement, many structurally deficient bridges can continue to serve most traffic.

headline: MOVE member to testify before Philly commission
abstract: Gerald Ford Africa, a spokesman for MOVE, has become the first move member to say that he will testify before the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission.  The commission is investigating a May 13, 1985 confrontation, which ended in a fire killing 11 people and destroying 61 row houses.  Gerald Africa also claimed that MOVE founder John Africa was not killed in the fire, as was claimed by John Africa's sister, and that the police bomb weighed twice as much as city officials had previously said.  Philadelphia's fire marshal reported yesterday that the "entry device" dropped on the MOVE house caused the fire.

headline: Federal Aid Necessary
abstract: This editorial looks at the effects of Hurricane Gloria on Lackawanna, Luzerne, and Wayne counties.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh asked US President Ronald Reagan to declare all three counties federal disaster areas so they could qualify for federal aid.  The Governor did not see the damage first-hand and relied instead on teams of inspectors who visited stricken neighborhoods in the counties.  The editorial believes that this situation warrants the release of federal funding to these areas.

headline: Crossover Clout: Meehan Pitches Smith
abstract: Joseph Smith, Democratic Chairman of Philadelphia, has confused many political insiders by enlisting the help of William Meehan, the Republican Chairman.  Smith is seeking an appointment to the Board of City Trusts and has asked for Meehan's support and assistance.

headline: No funds budgeted by county for Bucs
abstract: In presenting his annual budget proposal yesterady, Allegheny County Controller Frank Lucchino said that alarming deficits and decreasing revenues make it difficult for the county to justify lending $426,000 per year to help Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri buy the Pirates.  Lucchino also criticized city officials for seeking county funds without offering the county any say in how that money will be spent.

headline: Denver U. Dean Is Appointed Interim President at Cheyney
abstract: LeVerne McCummings, a dean from Denver University, was named and approved unanimously by the board of governors of the State System of Higher Education as interim president at Cheyney University.  Cheyney is appealing a decision by the Middle States Association of Colleges and Schools that withdrew the university's accredidation; McCummings is expected to help with that appeal.

headline: A confident voice in high-speed debate
abstract: A columnist discusses the PA High-Speed Rail Commission's plans to connect Philadelphia and Pittsburgh with a new high speed line that would cut the seven-hour trip to between two and four hours.  The Rail Commission's executive director, Robert Casey, said that the cost of the proposed railroad would be $10 billion--a sum which could be paid off in 10 years.  The columnist says that the real test will come at the end of 1986 when lawmakers will have to decide whether or not to fund the proposal.

headline: MOVE panel to be given subpoena power
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said that he would issue an executive order giving "administrative subpoena" power to the commission set up to investigate the MOVE confrontation.  Administrative subpoena power would give the commission the right to demand the testimony of private citizens as well as city officials.  Eleven people died and 61 homes were gutted or destroyed in the confrontation and fire in West Philadelphia on May 13.

headline: Few face sky-high "unisex" boosts, officials say
abstract: Insurance industry officials claim that only a handful of the more than 200,000 female drivers in PA would see tremendous increases for car insurance under proposed unisex car insurance rates.  Officials made this claim at a hearing of the PA Insurance Department.  These ratings are scheduled to take effect March 1, 1986, and would bar insurance companies from setting different rates for male and female drivers.  Under the proposed rates, the costs would be averaged.  This would mean large increases for young women and decreases for male drivers under age 25.  Acting Insurance Commissioner George Grode said he planned to stand by the unisex order, despite a pair of bills in the PA Legislature that would change insurance regulations to allow sex-based ratings.

headline: CTA and the price of power
abstract: This editorial follows the events that transpired in the investigation of the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery scandal.  At issue is the awarding of a no-bid $4.8 million contract for state computer services to CTA; CTA was to help recover overpayments in Social Security taxes made by school districts.  The scandal shows how campaign fundraising can be confused at times with out-right bribery.  CTA founder John Torquato Jr. bought influence for passage of legislation that he wrote; later on he had CTA's legal adviser offer a bride to PA State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman for CTA's exclusive rights to the recovery process.  The editorial notes that the CTA case should lead to renewed dedication to ethics in state government, something which is long overdue.

headline: On the MOVE: Officials blew it; get homeless quick help
abstract: This editorial questions the actions of Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode and the Philadelphia police in evicting the radical group MOVE from their West Philadelphia home.  The actions resulted in over 50 homes being burnt and left over 250 people homeless.  The editorial approves of Goode taking responsibility for the disaster and urges the city to provide quick help to those left homeless.

headline: Educating the Handicapped
abstract: A letter to the editor argues against a statement made by Eileen Gardner, an aide to the US Education Secretary, in which she said that a handicapped person is in some way responsible for his or her disability.  Author argues that Gardner's resignation was for the betterment of the Department of Education; Gardner would have been involved in setting the tone for the department and would have thus kept handicapped people out of public schools.

headline: A Regulatory Agency Has
abstract: A regulatory agency has approved PA Department of Transportation regulations for a lottery-funded transportation program that will benefit senior citizens.  The Thornburgh administration had modified the regulations to eliminate some controversial restrictions; this helped them win the support of senior citizen groups and lawmakers.  A group of Philadelphia transit operators said they will try to block the new rules in PA Commonwealth Court--complaining that the new regulations place limits on the amount they can be reimbursed for providing rides to the elderly.

headline: MOVE panel wins challenge: Judge speedily drops FOP suit
abstract: After the May 13 MOVE tragedy, Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode appointed the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission to investigate the tragedy and discover what happened.  The Fraternal Order of Police filed suit and asked the court to dismantle the Commission on the grounds that Goode exceeded his authority in creating it; the suit was dismissed by Common Please Court Judge Alfred J. DiBona Jr.  In dismissing the suit, DiBona said that Philadelphians were entitled to know the full story of the MOVE confrontation and that the commission, made up of 11 individuals of "impeccable reputations," was an appropriate vehicle for telling the story.

headline: Firms told to file gender-neutral auto-insurance rates
abstract: The state Insurance Department has ordered insurance companies to submit "gender-neutral" auto-insurance rates for state approval by October 1, 1985.  Insurance Commissioner William Muir said that all companies writing auto insurance in PA would be given until January 1, 1986 to implement the new rates.

headline: CTA bribe scandal brings no call for reform
abstract: A columnist discusses the fact that the Computer Techonolgy Associates bribery conspiracy has not prompted cries for reform of state government.   Since the public is not crying for reform, legislators will be unlikely to do it on their own.

headline: Paying the Bills
abstract: The residents of Philadelphia have already paid for the surveillance of MOVE, as well as the cost of police actions and firefighting efforts that followed the city's actions against MOVE.  Now, residents will begin paying to rebuild the 61 houses that were destroyed.  They will also pay for city officials' legal representation and any lawsuits that come against the city and its leadership.  It is also interesting that some city officials have different stories as to why the fire was allowed to burn, which means that we'll never now the real story behind the events of that day.  We'll have to pay for them, however.

headline: Education agency will borrow $31 million
abstract: The State System of Higher Education will issue $31 million in bonds to finance construction of an energy co-generation plant at Indiana University of PA.  The bond issue will mark the first time the unit, which oversees 14 state-owned universities, will have gone into debt since it was separated from the state Education Department in July of 1983.  Co-generation is the simultaneous production of electricity and heat; the heat will be converted to steam to heat campus buildings at IUP.

headline: A Seat Belt Law?
abstract: This editorial supports a seat belt law because it will reduce fatalities.

headline: MOVE threatened to burn neighborhood if attacked
abstract: In a letter police received two days before bombing the radical group's fortress, MOVE threatened to burn its neighborhood.  Mayor Goode released copies of the letter, signed by Ramona Africa--the only adult known to survive the police raid--on a day declared by Goode as a citywide day of prayer for the 11 people killed in the assault and the 270 people left homeless as a result of the conflagration.  Political leaders around the nation are now questioning Goode's decision-making process when evicting the group.

headline: Fix the system
abstract: PA Representative Joseph Battisto explained to the Monroe County League of Women Voters how a controversial gambling provision was inserted into a liquor bill; as a reslut, the provision went unnoticed by virtually all legislators.  The editorial describes the tactics legislators use to get controversial bills passed, and says that the system should be tightened so that amendments are fully revealed.

headline: CTA chief: Suspects bragged of payoffs
abstract: Judy Ellis, president of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), admitted to taking part in a scheme to bribe PA officials.  She says her fellow conspirators often joked and boasted about making payoffs to win a $4.8 million state computer contract.  Ellis implicated both defendants, William Smith of Harrisburg and Alan Stoneman of Orange California.

headline: Pittsburgh Mayor Says No Tax Hikes
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri unveiled his proposed $284.4 million city budget for 1986 on Tuesday.  Caliguiri also said there will be no tax increases during the next two years, but that he anticipated a reduction in some city services in 1987.  The mayor expects a $20 million gap in 1987 between anticipated revenues and the amount of money the city actually receives.

headline: Emphasis on teaching should improve schools
abstract: This editorial states that greater effort needs to be placed on teachers as the key to reforming and improving public schools.  The National Education Association and the National Association of Secondary School Principals recently began a joint project aimed at establishing conditions necessary for successful teaching, and the NEA recently adopted resolutions on teaching certification to improve the level of classroom excellence.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has put forth a plan to require graduating teachers to pass tests before receiving state certification; the plan also requires teachers and administrators to take continuing-education courses.  The editorial believes that this revitilization of the public school system will benefit students.

headline: Airport expressway gaining new ground
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh announced yesterday that the state would provide $8 million for design and engineering work of the Southern Expressway.  The grant was hailed by Allegheny county officials and gave them hope that construction of a new airport terminal is closer to reality.  The county commissioners hope the Southern Expressway will speedu up the flow of traffic and open up 1,000 acres around the airport  for development.  Commissioner Barbara Hafer believes that the county should proceed with the construction of the $400 million terminal without waiting for private airline financing.  Governor Thornburgh would like private financing, but believes that the new terminal is a linchpin for economic development in the region.  The new terminal is the centerpiece of Strategy 21, a $1.9 billion economic development plan for Western PA.

headline: MOVE was city target, panel told: Supporter relates plan to surrender
abstract: MOVE supporter Jerry Africa, testifying before the Philadelphia Investigation Committee, said that the May 13 shootout and fire that claimed 11 lives followed years of conspiratorial behavior on the part of city officials determined to eliminate the radical organization.  Africa contended that MOVE had intended to surrender at the time of Ramon Africa's arrest during the May 13 fire.  Panel members did not challenge Africa's version of events and one member, Michael Tosta, who is associated with the National Memorial Foundation of African American Historical and Patriot Society's Symbol for a New Direction, said his organization would demand the arrest of Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode for premeditated murder, involuntary manslaughter, arson, conspiracy, suffering, pain and injury, and public trauma.

headline: Gekas helped
abstract: A letter to the editor thanks Congressman George Gekas for playing a pivotal role in getting funding to the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC).  The CCC, due to lack of funds, was about to suspend price support payments to farmers when Gekas offered a compromise that allowed the bill to pass and be signed into law.  The CCC resumed price support payment to farmers the next day.  The letter was written by a Congressman from Minnesota.

headline: CTA figure defended in seeking state GOP chief's aid
abstract: State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer testified that Republican State Chairman Robert Asher told him that William T. Smith, defendant in the Computer Technology Associates bribery trial, pressured him to recommend CTA to Dwyer.  The defense, however, maintained that there was nothing illegal about this.

headline: Pittsburgh trails state in economic growth
abstract: Joseph W. Duncan, corporate economist and chief statistician of Dun & Bradstreet Corporation, told a group of Philadelphia business leaders that Philadelphia is leading the state to moderate economic growth this year, while Pittsburgh--hobbled by heavy industry--brings up the rear.  Duncan said that overall the state's economy is poised for moderate improvement in 1985, as growing service-based industries compensate for the ailing manufacturing sector.

headline: Faculty group is said to rip Cheyney leaders
abstract: A key Cheyney University faculty group voted "no confidence" in the university's administration, including President CT Enus Wright and James McCormick, the chancellor of the PA system of higher education.  The faculty group was convened after the announcement that the Middle States Association of Colleges and Schools, a regional accreditation agency, had voted to withdraw accreditation for Cheyney.

headline: Airport hotel proposed
abstract: According to the PA Department of Transportation, four national hotel chains have made unsolicited offers to build a "quality" hotel and convention center at Harrisburg International Airport.  The interest was sparked by a new terminal at the Lower Swatara Township Airport, and construction could begin as early as the fall of 1986.  Some local hotel operators are afraid that the airport hotel, along with a string of other hotel plans mentioned in the article, would saturate the lodging market of Harrisburg.  A survey found that airport hotels usually do better than center city hotels; they also charge cheaper rates.

headline: MOVEr Is Sentenced For Threatening Cop
abstract: Alfonso Robbins Africa was sentenced to serve 15 months to five years in prison for threatening a police officer in 1984.  Africa wrote a letter to Common Pleas Judge Samuel Lehrer in which he told Lehrer that he and other judges were being watched on how they handled MOVE.  Africa also said that Lehrer should remove himself from the proceeding because he obvioulsy hated Africa and MOVE.  Lehrer, before sentencing, told Africa that he was following "a pathological and mentally ill source" who preaches "hate, contempt, and confrontation"

headline: Genuine liquor reform needed
abstract: The author of this editorial is encouraged by proposed reforms to the PA Liquor Control Board.  Since the PA Legislature has returned from its recess, it has become clear that the votes for complete elimination of the LCB are not there.  However, there are several bills with worthwhile provisions--principally the legalization of wine sales in specialty stores and food markets and the transfer of the LCB's enforcement powers to the PA Attorney General.  The editorial believes that a meaningful beginning of genuine reform is within reach.

headline: D.A. hopefuls run on tight budgets
abstract: The two Democrats running for Philadelphia District Attorney are both facing difficulties with campaign funds.  John Scott raised about $70,000 for his campaign, and he had $915 left as of May 6.  Robert W. Williams Jr., the endorsed Democrat, raised $142, 754 for his campaign, and he had $43,693 as of May 10.  Both candidates were able to raise significantly less money than Edward Rendell and Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode--both of whom will not campaign until 1986 and 1987 respectively.

headline: Private Sector Can Help City Avert Tax Rise
abstract: In an opinion piece, W. Thacher Longstreth--a Philadelphia City Councilman at large--gives his recommendations for reducing the mayor's proposed capital program by $50 million.  Longstreth feels that each department in the city should look for ways to reduce spending; departments should also consider contracting out to the private sector in order to reduce spending and increase tax dollars.

headline: Flaw seen in M.D. licensing: state's rules not as strict
abstract: Two medical schools in the Dominican Republic closed last year amid revelations that officials there had sold as many as 2,000 degrees.  A review of these schools revealed that PA's laws on granting medical licenses were lax and should be tightened to protect patients.  PA regulations require only one year of residency for applicants and there is no oral examination or any review of the educational facilities.

headline: An I-95 intersection has become infamous - and costly
abstract: A dangerous intersection in Tinicum Township, PA has caused many accidents over the years.  This will soon be remedied by I-95 being extended around the airport and keeping the highway traffic off of local roads.

headline: Murderer asks for stay on Dec. 2 execution
abstract: Convicted murderer Keith Zettlemoyer and his lawyer have appealed to the PA State Superior Court asking for a stay on his December 2nd execution.  Zettlemoyer was convicted in 1980 for the murder of former Patriot-News correspondent and Sunbury radio reporter Charles DeVetsco; DeVetsco was going to testify against Zettlemoyer in a robery trial.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed Zettlemoyer's death warrant earlier this month.  In his appeal, Zettlemoyer attacked the jury selection process and deemed his lawyer ineffective in representing him.  Dauphin County Court Judge John Dowling accused Zettlemoyer of trying to delay his execution by filing an extensive petition.

headline: Group wants liquor out of state's control
abstract: Herbert Engelbert formed Pennsylvanians for a Responsible End to the State Store System  (PRESSS) to lobby PA legislators to eliminate the PA Liquor Control Board.  PRESSS wants the free market--not a government agency--to determine the prices and products that liquor stores provide to consumers.  PRESSS estimates that as much as 25% of PA's liquor sales are made out of state, as PA residents are sick of dealing with the state-store system.  The United Food and Commercial Workers Union, the union for state liquor store clerks, disputes the statistics that PRESSS released to the public; the union also questions whether having alcohol available in more businesses at longer hours will have an effect on drunk driving in PA.

headline: Dawida gives Bailey apology
abstract: PA State Representative Michael Dawida wrote a letter of public apology to PA Auditor General Don Bailey for inappropriate, intemperate, and downgrading remarks made by PA State Representative H. William DeWeese.  DeWeese made these remarks after he and 25 other members of the PA State House announced their support US Representative Bob Edgar as a nominee for the Senate.  Dawida, who was one of the 25 at the meeting, said in his letter that he will continue to support Edgar and believes that Bailey would be best served by remaining the Auditor General.  Dawida will support Bailey if he wins the Democratic nomination for US Senate, however.

headline: Race for Spirko's seat splits GOP
abstract: James Spirko has announced that he will not seek a fourth term as the minority member of the three-member Allegheny County Jury Commission.  This announcement has set off in-fighting among Republicans, as at least nine people have expressed interest in the position.  The Republican County Committee will meet March 21 to endorse candidates.

headline: Gimmicks no substitutes for salaries
abstract: Editorial argues that recent cuts in aid to the nation's schools, particularly by President Ronald Reagan, have led to decreased salaries for teachers and have hurt the education of children.  The editorial gives some credit to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's PA Teacher of the Year program, though it criticizes it for substituting--as opposed to complimenting--a living wage for elementary and secondary school teachers.  The number of teachers in the Commonwealth decreased by 11% over the past decade, and there also was a significant decline of people entering the teaching profession during that time.  The editorial argues that until teachers start to see a decent salary, the numbers can be expected to stay the same.

headline: An old trick
abstract: A letter to the editor discusses an article in the Post-Gazette.  In the article, US Senator Arlen Specter complained that he was not given a chance participate in the federal announcement that $19.7 million was being granted to Pittsburgh for the completion of its subway system.  Because of this omission, Specter did not get credit for securing the financing for the project.  The author says that no one but the taxpayers should get credit for projects completed with taxpayer money.

headline: No Choice in Gartner Case
abstract: A letter to the editor from Fred Jacobs, chairman of the Board of Probation and Parole, clears up confusion over how long the Board has to supervise someone on parole.  He says that the Parole Act of 1941 requires the Board to supervise those persons released on parole for the remainder of their sentence.

headline: House, Senate diverge on LCB bills
abstract: Yesterday, the PA Senate and House of Representatives headed in different directions in their efforts to decide on what to do with the state's 51 year-old state-run system of liquor stores.  The PA Senate voted in favor of legislation that would transfer responsibility for liquor-law enforcement to the offices of the PA Attorney General.  In the PA House, members of the Liquor Control Committee continued rewriting an earlier liquor-law-enforcement bill that the PA Senate had sent them.  The two chambers are struggling with the controversial Liquor-Control-Board issue because of a state Sunset-Law deadline.

headline: Defeated judge favors selection by merit
abstract: PA Common Pleas Judge Don Lee, one of two incumbent judges who lost his seat in Tueday's election, said yesterday that he believes a change is needed in the way judges are selected--particularly in large counties like Allgheny and Philadelphia.  Lee has long advocated a merit selection system, in which judges would be appointed for initial two-year terms and then would have to run for retention.  However, Judge Charles Scarlata, who also lost his seat, is not certain whether merit selection is the answer.  The results of the race for Common Pleas Court are also included in the article.

headline: the FORUM: Board 'bought' big tax hike
abstract: A letter to the editor argues that the tax increase in Cumberland County could have been prevented by proper budgeting and setting aside monies for capital expansion.  The author argues that a new budget director should be hired and county commissioners should be allowed to retire.

headline: Governor announces grants for 60 schools
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has announced the awarding of 60 grants to schools, intermediate units, colleges and universites, and individual educators for a variety of special projects; the projects are aimed at finding the most effective ways to use computers in schools.  The funds, which are part of PA's $23.1 million federal block grant allocation, will be used to develop and evaluate computer-based instruction for students in kindergarten through 12th grade, and will also be used to train teachers in the most effective use of computers.  Practices deemed highly successful will be shared among school districts that want to incorporate similar practices into their own programs.

headline: And in Harrisburg
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and Democratic state lawmakers have reached a compromise in the long-running dispute over control of the PA Turnpike Commission.  Under the agreement, three Republicans and three Democrats will be appointed to the commission, and the governor will get to appoint the chairman.  The agreement will clear the way for a four billion dollar toll-road expansion project.

headline: No jail time: Grosso to name state police tipster
abstract: Anthony M. Grosso admitted to 13 criminal counts associated with his gambling operation and agreed to reveal the name of a state police officer who was on his payroll; Grosso gave this information in return for not getting a prison sentence.  Grosso paid at least one law enforcement officer more than $100,000 to leak information about the police investigations of Grosso's gambling operation.

headline: Governor Dick Thornburgh was
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh was dealt another setback in his push to reform the PA Liquor Control Board when the PA Senate rejected a proposal that would have drastically improved his chances of placing nominees on the LCB.  The amendment, which was rejected by the PA Senate, would have allowed Senate confirmation of Thornburgh's LCB nominees by a majority vote in 1986, instead of after Thornburgh leaves office in 1987.  The PA Legislature still must renew the LCB under the Sunset Law by December 31, 1985 or it will cease operations.  Thornburgh's views on the PA LCB served as the focus of debate in the PA Senate.

headline: Defendant Denies Campaign $ Linked to CTA Contract
abstract: William T. Smith, a defendant in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery trial, told a federal court jury about a discussion he had with Patrick T. Boyle, state Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman's press secretary.  The conversation was about campaign finances and was unrelated to his pursuit of a legal opinion from Zimmerman that would be favorable to CTA.  Boyle claimed that Smith offered the attorney general's reelection campaign $100,000 in return for the favorable legal opinion.  Smith and Alan R. Stoneman are former CTA lawyers charged with 16 counts of conspiracy, racketeering and mail fraud in connection with a state contract awarded to CTA.

headline: West Hanover gets OK on legal expenses
abstract: The state Ethics Commission has ruled that the West Hanover Township supervisors may use township funds to pay for outside legal counsel in its defense.  Allegedly, the board erred in not advertising for bids on two 1983 construction contracts.

headline: Inquiry Tests PAA…School Board Links To South Africa Under Scrutiny
abstract: Pittsburgh Public School officials have begun an investigation into the district's investments and bank deposits to try and ensure that the school district is not doing business with any banking institutions that do business in South Africa.  These measures are due, in part, to the Pittsburghers Against Apartheid (PAA) and the anti-apartheid sentiment in the state.

headline: Auto and insurance firms, safety activists push seat belts
