abstract: This article examines the well-financed and intense lobbying push for a seat belt law in the PA Legislature.  The lobbying effort is being lead by an alliance of insurance firms, automakers, and safety activists.

headline: Officer Refuses to Testify at Bombing Inquiry
abstract: Philadelphia Police Lieutenant Frank Powell, who dropped the bomb on the MOVE house on May 13, refused to testify before a commission investigating the incident, invoking his Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution.  Lawyers for the police union objected several times to questions from commission chairman William Brown.  Lieutenant Powell also told the commission that Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode vetoed a plan to allow a crane to destroy the bunker on top of the MOVE house because he thought it cost too much.  Lieutenant Powell chose to exercise his constitutional rights just hours after a Federal District Court ruled that witnesses called to testify before the MOVE panel could invoke Fifth Amendment rights.

headline: Governor mum as Senate dismantles unisex insurance
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, after waging a successful court fight for unisex auto insurance rates, has taken no public position on legislation that would allow insurance companies to continue using gender as a rate-making factor in auto coverage.  On Septemeber 19th, the PA Senate voted in favor of two bills that would maintain gender-based auto insurance rates.  Many lawmakers are concerned about the impact that switching to unisex rates will have on PA drivers, particularly women and those under 30.  A year ago, the PA Supreme Court voted to uphold an order by the PA Insurance Department that auto rates based on gender were unfairly discriminatory.  The insurance industry maintains that females are safer drivers than males, especially between the ages of 16 and 30, though it cannot determine exactly why.  If the PA Senate succeeds in changing the law, the next court case could be based on the PA Constitution's Equal Rights Amendment.

headline: Democratic governors get apology
abstract: A fund-raising letter singed by US President Ronald Reagan urged Republican gubernatorial take-overs in 27 states and portrayed Democrats as free spending liberals who had undermined Reagan's tax cuts.  The letter has been withdrawn, however.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, at a meeting of the National Governors' Association, said that the letter would no longer be sent out and that the remaining ones would be destroyed.  Democratic governors Dukakis and William Clinton said that the letter threatened the bipartisan makeup of the National Governors' Associations and went beyond the bounds of political rhetoric.

headline: Would this help Erie?
abstract: An editorial discusses the two-rate property tax that allows cities to tax land at a higher rate than buildings.  The result of this is that it costs speculators a great deal to hold onto vacant or under-utilized properties.  The editorial questions whether this two-rate tax would help Erie and mentions a study by the PA Economy League to discover if it would work.

headline: Learning a lesson
abstract: New PA laws allow the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency to have more power to pursue student borrowers who have defaulted on their student loans.  This editorial approves of these measures to get money from "deadbeat" students.

headline: Axle tax on trucks is ruled out by court
abstract: The Commonwealth Court declared an axle tax on trucks of 26,000 pounds or more violates the US Constitution by discriminating against out-of-state trucks.  PA will have to refund more than $140 million to more than 15,000 trucking companies.  PA will appeal the decision to the state Supreme Court.

headline: 'Operation Gallstones' recovers millions: Two ex-legislators indicted in FBI sting
abstract: A five-year Federal Bureau of Investigation sting dubbed Operation Gallstone has lead to the recovery of $500 million in phony securities and the indictment of 29 "international con men," including two former PA state representatives.  Federal officials said the investigation, which extended to Europe, the Far East, Canada and the Caribbean, uncovered trafficking in counterfeit securities, drugs, stolen travelers checks, fraudulent tax shelters, and criminal case-fixing.

headline: Governor signs gambling law repeal
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a bill to repeal a law that allowed blackjack and other tournaments in state bars and clubs.  The Liquor Control Board, in a break with the administration, has said that the agency will not enforce the law for 30 days because they feel that the repeal is a blow to the industry.

headline: Democrats To Examine $5,000 Filing Fees
abstract: PA's Democratic leaders will review a controversial plan to charge statewide candidates $5,000 to appear in five forums.  The purpose of the forums is to provide candidates exposure, to test their demeanor under fire, and to give local Democrats a more active role in the party's endorsement process.  The first forum is scheduled to take place in Pittsburgh on December 7, 1985, and the other four forums will take place around the state.  Robert Casey, who is expected to run for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, called the filing fee a "price tag" on free speech.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts the "Mona Lisa" with spiked hair and long earrings holding a can of Coke while saying, "If Coke can change..."

headline: Merit pay, testing should be supported
abstract: This editorial criticizes teachers for not supporting merit pay or certification tests.  The author urges teachers to support merit pay and a testing-certificate program because it would reflect positively on the profession and would help good teachers move forward.

headline: Blue Route appeal may go to top court
abstract: The legal battle against the creation of the Blue Route may be heard before the highest court in the US.  The Nether Providence-Swathmore Alliance of Civic Associations will make a decision within the next two weeks on whether to appeal the case to the US Supreme Court.  The 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed an opinion by a US District Judge on October 4, 1985, approving construction of the expressway.  A meeting to decide whether to appeal will come sometime next week.

headline: Osage builder accused of hitting photographer
abstract: Ernest Edwards Jr., the developer rebuilding the West Philadelphia homes destroyed in the MOVE confrontation, was accused of punching a New York Times photographer, who was taking pictures yesterday at the construction site; he is also accused of having his workmen confiscate the photographer's cameras.  The Philadelphia district attorney's office last night charged Edwards with two counts each of robbery, simple assault, conspiracy, theft, receiving stolen property and disorderly conduct, and one count each of making terroristic threats, riot, and criminal mischief.  The photographer, Dan Miller, gives his entire account of the events detailed in the article.

headline: Governor still seeks LCB's end
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh yesterday quarreled with a report issued by the Senate Law and Justice Committee.  The report argued that the Liquor Control Board should not be scrapped, and that it only needs to improve its marketing techniques.  Senate Law and Justice Chairman John Shumaker's position reduces hopes for Thornburgh and other Republicans to eliminate the LCB and sell liquor in private stores.  Shumaker said that increasing public concern about alcohol-related problems is what convinced him that liquor should not be made available in the private market.  The LCB is currently being reviewed under the PA Sunset Law, which means that the LCB will expire at the end of this year unless legislation is approved to continue it in some form.  Shumaker said he could find no substantiation to claims by Thornburgh that a quarter of alcohol consumed illegally in PA is smuggled in from out of state, or that there is overwhelming public support for a private-liquor system.

headline: Dems' Judgments Unsupported?
abstract: The Philadelphia Democratic City Committee voted to endorse a controversial group of judicial candidates for the May 21 primary.  The slate includes no women, a candidate Mayor Wilson Goode said he opposes, and three Republicans.  Analysts believe it will trigger numerous rival slates supported by groups and ward leaders who believe they have been left out.  The judicial candidates eventually nominated by the party will be those able to work their way onto the most ballots.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: A photo depicts a girl eating a cheeseburger with the caption: "At Henderson High, a cheeseburger appeals to Michele Dennis."

headline: Military junk calls
abstract: This editorial argues against proposed legislation in the state legislature that would require public schools to give military recruiters the names and telephone numbers of graduating seniors.

headline: Cab company's request
abstract: The Public Utility Commission ordered a hearing on Yellow Cab of Philadelphia's request for an $11.1 million increase in annual fares.  Under the company's proposal, the fares would go from $2.10 to $2.70 for the first mile and from $1.32 to $1.40 for each subsequent mile.  The company also asked to charge an extra 50 cents for each ride between 7pm and 5am.

headline: Other MOVE Houses: What the City's Doing
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode says the city will move in the near future to shut off water service at the two remaining MOVE houses where the occupants have run up unpaid bills totalling more than $2,100.  Goode was asked if the city will treat these properties the same as the MOVE compound destroyed at 6221 Osage Avenue where the MOVE members were permitted to break civil and criminal laws with impunity and obtain gas and water from city-owned facilities without paying.  Goode says the city is planning to take a different tack because officials do not believe the MOVE members at these locations have weapons.

headline: Governor's LCB plans suffer setback in Legislature
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's goal of abolishing the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) suffered more setbacks on December 10, 1985; the PA Senate killed a proposal for private wine sales and the PA House approved a bill to keep liquor-code enforcement with the LCB.  If the PA Legislature fails to renew the LCB by December 31, 1985, the board will have to close down in 1986.  Governor Thornburgh is hopeful that a legislative agreement can be worked out by week's end, though he has said that he will veto any bill on the LCB that does not meet a few of his conditions.  The history of the LCB and liquor legislation in the PA Legislature is spelled out in the article.

headline: Dentists seek lottery funds for the poor
abstract: Pennsylvania dentists unveiled a campaign to urge the state legislature to approve spending $100,000 in lottery funds to provide free dental care for elderly residents with an annual income of less than $9,000.  Dr. Benedict Kimmelman, chairman of the PA Council of Dental Care, said an estimated 600,000 elderly residents of PA need dental care and cannot afford it.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: A photo depicts Governor Dick Thornburgh and his wife, Ginny, sitting on a couch in the governor's mansion.  They are admiring Sidney Goodman's painting, "The Matriarchs."  Goodman has received the Hazlett award.

headline: Much-used libraries struggle in unemployment areas
abstract: Libraries across the state are discovering that many unemployed people depend on libraries.  As a result, library circulation has increased as unemployment in the state has increased.  Dozens of libraries across the state are in danger of closing because they do not have the necessary funding.  The poor economy has hurt library funding.

headline: Calls for 'Pike study
abstract: PA Turnpike Commissioner James J. Dodaro has called for the commission to hire a professional management consultant to study operations of the commission.  Dodaro expressed hope that the administration would move forward on the $4 billion toll road system expansion and improvement.

headline: Pa. agriculture secretary quits; will appeal conviction
abstract: PA Agriculture Secretary Penrose Hallowell, who was convicted of shoplifting a $4.99 Boston Pops cassette tape last September, resigned his Cabinet post.  Hallowell denied he was guilty of shoplifting and added he plans to appeal the case to Superior Court.

headline: Guess Who Profits
abstract: An opinion piece argues that the $5 CAT-fund fee is unfair because it only benefits the auto insurance industry.

headline: Does voter turnout really matter?
abstract: A columnist discusses low voter turnout in the primary and says that such apathy is a great threat to democracy.  The author says that if people don't take voting more seriously, they could well lose the opportunity altogether and he urges people to vote.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: A photo depicts workers using special screens to sift through what is left of the MOVE house at 6221 Osage Avenue in Philadelphia.

headline: Penn State's recruitment of black students is attacked
abstract: Legislators criticized the Pennsylvania State University for unfair competition with the 14 state-owned universities in the recruitment of black students.  They said that black enrollment at the state-owned universities was declining because of Penn State's attempts to comply with a federal court order mandating increased minority enrollment.  Penn State has more money to recruit students away from other schools in the state.  Bryce Jordan, Penn State President, said that the problem was the low numbers of blacks graduating from high school and that they would continue to recruit blacks aggressively because of the federal order requiring Penn State to raise its black enrollment.

headline: Car Seizure OK'd
abstract: This editorial praises a new law in New York.  The law grants police the authority to impound the car of a motorist  who is found to be driving under the influence, if that motorist's license is already suspended for drunk driving.  The editorial asks PA lawmakers to monitor the application of this law in New York and see if it is possible to apply it in the Keystone State.

headline: Pa. bill would force support by financially able parents
abstract: State Representative Richard McClatchy (R, Montgomery) introduced a bill that would require financially qualified divorced parents to pay more for child support; the legislation would also set uniform standards for the awarding of a minimum amount of child support in divorce actions.  McClatchy said such a requirement could save the state $25 to $30 million annually in welfare payments.  The article also discusses other legislation introduced by Philadelphia-area legislators.

headline: 'Happy Hour' Ban No Rx for Alcohol Abuse
abstract: An opinion piece discusses the possible ban on happy hours in bars and taverns in Pennsylvania.  The author does not think that a ban on happy hours will end excessive drinking and alcoholism.  The editorial states that a wholesale review of the Liquor Code and the PA Liquor Control Board is needed.  The author argues that a better educated and informed public is the answer to ending alcoholism and alcohol abuse--not a ban on happy hours.

headline: Duquesne Light lobbies for Rep. Laughlin
abstract: Duquesne Light Company, through its Harrisburg lobbyist, is helping PA State Representative Charles Laughlin sell tickets to a political fundraiser in Harrisburg on Tuesday.  Laughlin, chairman of the House Consumer Affairs Committee, has projected an image as a battler for consumer rights against utilities.  Dupac is Duquesne Light's political action committee and is responsible for sending out the letters.  Laughlin said that Ernest Varhola, a Dupac lobbyist who helped send out the letters, agreed to send them because they are casual friends; he did not send the letters because of an association with Duquesne Light.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: A photo depicts jazz pianist Walt Harper,  Allegheny County Commissioner Pete Flaherty, and TV personality Bill Cardille.  The second photo depicts Governor Dick Thornburgh performing "Brush Up Your Shakespeare."  Both photos were taken at a benefit for the Three Rivers Shakespeare Festival.

headline: Perry districts target kids who failed test: Schools plan remedial courses
abstract: School districts in Perry County are planning remedial programs for pupils in the third, fifth and eighth grades.  Remedial programs are for students in these grades who failed the state's Testing for Essential Learning and Literacy Skills (TELLS) exam.

headline: Child safety seat law is toothless, cops claim
abstract: With a year of enforcement gone by, only $4,200 in fines has been collected in PA for violations of the state's child safety seat law.  Some police officers in the state believe this is because the law has no teeth.  To get out of a ticket, all one needs to do is present notice to a judge or district justice that a child safety seat has been obtained.  This goes hand-in-hand with a fundamental fact of police work:  Officers are less inclined to enforce a law when they know there is no penalty.  Police estimate that some 9,000 children under the age of 5 are involved in traffic accidents in PA every year.  Studies show that safety seats, if used properly, reduce child automobile fatalities by 90%.

headline: Panel Oks bill to ban private jails for 1 year
abstract: The state House Judiciary Committee approved a measure calling for a one-year ban on the operation of privately owned prisons.  Controversy over private prisons has escalated with the development of a plan to open a 760-bed facility in Beaver County and another one in Armstrong County.  The American Civil Liberties Union has threatened to sue the owners of the facilities if privately operated prisons are allowed to lock up people in the state.

headline: Happy hours at Penna. Taverns are scrutinized by liquor board
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board is holding hearings around the state to help determine whether it should pass regulations limiting or eliminating the practice of happy hours.  Legislation has been introduced in the PA General Assembly to ban happy hours.

headline: Dwyer event passes panel's scrutiny
abstract: The PA Commission on Charitable Organizations has said that friends and employees of PA Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer who helped pay his legal bills do not have to register with the state as a charitable organization.  This means that Dwyer will not have to report who organized a fund-raising party on August 21.  Dwyer has declined to reveal publicly how much money was raised, but he will comply with a law requiring that all gifts worth $200 or more be reported in his ethics statement.  Dwyer requested an opinion from the Commission on Charitable Organizations following publicity about his party, which raised money for his legal battle.  Dwyer is currently under federal investigation for a multimillion dollar contract he awarded to Computer Technology Associates.  Acting US Attorney James West said the grand jury now is turning its attention to the public officials who were offered bribes.

headline: A day of prayer for fire victims
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode called for a citywide day of prayer in the wake of the MOVE tragedy.  St. Carthage Catholic Church, just three blocks from the devastation on Osage Avenue, and other churches around the city held special masses to pray for the people who lost their homes in the disaster.  250 people were left homeless after a fire was started when police were trying to evict the radical group MOVE from their Osage Avenue home.

headline: PSU main, branch salaries differ
abstract: A Pennsylvania State University Senate study concluded that the salaries of Penn State faculty members are generally lower at branch campuses than at the main campus.  The study also concluded that the school should concentrate on raising all salaries, not necessarily creating parity among campuses.  The report said the salary differences result in part from the greater percentage of main campus teachers and researchers who hold doctoral degrees and greater seniority.

headline: Compromise on the turnpike
abstract: This editorial examines the compromise made between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and Democrats in the state Legislature over control of the PA Turnpike Commission.  The most significant part of the deal includes a genuine reform that will take effect in June 1987, after a new governor is elected.  Gubernatorial appointees to the Commission will require two-thirds confirmation by the PA Senate and will have their terms reduced from 10 to 4 years.  The editorial states that these changes are welcome, but offer no guarantee of more efficient management of the turnpike system or less reliance on political patronage in the dispensation of jobs and contracts.  Under the interim arrangement, it remains to be seen whether a politically-divided commission can work together.

headline: Pa. Official Guilty: Tape Shows Shoplifting, Judge Rules
abstract: PA Agriculture Secretary Penrose Hallowell was convicted of shoplifting a cheap cassette tape from a Montgomery County department store.  His attorney said the conviction could ruin his career.  Governor Dick Thornburgh's press secretary said the matter is under careful review.

headline: Hearings on gambling ideas continue: 'Skill' may be trump card for bars
abstract: Several groups testified before the state House Liquor Control Committee that skill games should be allowed in bars and taverns in throughout the state.  Bar owners testified that not allowing games such as darts, billiards and bowling, hurts their business.

headline: Dwyer, agency trade accusations
abstract: State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer and the Department of Labor and Industry are blaming each other for the recent voiding of a state contract that might have helped local school districts recover $40 million in Social Security tax overpayments.  The contract was voided after the Federal Bureau of Investigation began probing Computer Technology Associate's possible bribery of state officials in the awarding of the recovery contracts.

headline: Ballet Finds Its Footing: Pa. troupe ready to cash in on critical acclaim
abstract: The Pennsylvania Ballet has consistently received critical acclaim, yet was struggling with a debt crisis for many years.  Today the ballet is on firmer grounds with less debt and more sponsorship.

headline: Rally supports home schooling
abstract: A group of parents, organized by Parent-Educators of PA, rallied at the PA Capitol yesterday to urge changes that would make it easier to teach their children at home instead of sending them to public or private schools.  The demonstration showed its support for legislation defining specific statewide requirements for in-home schooling.

headline: Conrail decision expected to leave officials steaming
abstract: The US Transportation Department is considering three buyers for the Conrail freight railroad.  This has lead to nasty fights between Dole and opponents, primarily L. Stanley Crane, Conrails chief executive.  Lobbyists for both sides are concerned about the future of Conrail.  Crane says the buyers are only out to make a quick profit and are not concerned about the railroad and its workers.  Dole is opposed to a public stock sale that Crane proposes.  Labor leaders are investigating all possible solutions to ensure that workers will keep their jobs.

headline: Pa. Officials "Harvest" 891 Marijuana Plants
abstract: The nationwide crackdown on marijuana growing, code-named Delta 9, netted PA law enforcement 981 marijuana plants as of August 5, 1985.  The US Drug Enforcement Administration said that local, state, and federal officials found marijuana growing in Chester County and surrounding areas.

headline: Help's here: 12 counties to get US disaster aid...
abstract: President Ronald Reagan, who said the storms that hit Western PA were among the worst in decades, declared 12 counties a federal disaster area and asked Vice President George Bush to inspect the tornado-ravaged region.  The federal declaration is expected to speed federal disaster relief to Beaver, Butler, Crawford, Erie, Forest, Lycoming, McKean, Mercer, Northumberland, Venango, Union and Warren counties.  The federal aid will include subsidies covering up to 75% of the cost of repairing public facilities; grants of up to $5,000 per family for losses not covered by insurance; temporary housing; debris removal assistance; and low-interest loans from the Small Business Administration to rebuild homes and businesses.

headline: Dwyer, Zimmerman, Manderino expected to testify at CTA trial
abstract: Defense attorney John Rogers Carroll told the federal court jury that many public officials, including state Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer, Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman, House Majority Leader James Manderino, and Republican Party Chairman Robert Asher, will testify for the defendants in the Computer-Technology-Associates bribery trial.  All of those officials have been linked by prosecution witnesses to the case, but none have been charged; all have denied giving any favorable treatment to CTA in return for offers of political contributions.

headline: Capitol Hill Budget Plumbers
abstract: There are four cartoon pictures on the page.  The first shows the Capitol Hill Budget Plumbers trying to fix a series of pipes leaking red ink, to symobolize the national budget deficit.  Another picture shows an astronaut being asked by ground control whether he preferred Coke or Pepsi, as he is drinking Pepto-Bismol.  A third picture shows a farmer stading at an abandoned train station waiting to board the US Economy train; he then notices that the tracks have long since been abandoned.  The fourth shows a large black chess piece with a flag that says "South Africa"; the black chess piece is facing a small white chess piece; the caption says "white's move."

headline: Recruiting lists
abstract: This letter to the editor urges members of the General Assembly to oppose PA House Bill 370, which would require public schools to provide the names, addresses and telephone numbers of graduating seniors to military recruiters.  The author says that military recruiters do not need the assistance because the Pentagon is already spending more than $1 billion for recruiting.

headline: Cost of expressway construction 10% less than expected so far
abstract: According to the state Department of Transportation, construction of the East Street Valley Expressway is about $20 million below budget.  If that savings trend continues with the remaining seven contracts for the 13-mile expressway, the final cost of the highway could drop from $400 to $360 million.  Rudolph Melani, PennDOT's design liaison engineer for the East Street project, says design changes and close bidding among contractors are the reasons for the savings.

headline: Panel chairman: Probe of MOVE siege to be 'open.' Group has first meeting; Goode asks for truth
abstract: The 11-member commission appointed by Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode to investigate the May 13 MOVE confrontation will hold public hearings and request testimony from the mayor and other city officials.  The commission will attempt to investigate the incident in a manner that will give the people of Philadelphia as complete and full a report as possible.  Mayor Goode urged the commission to tell the public the truth about what happened.

headline: Here's one view on "CAT Fund"
abstract: A letter to the editor raises a question about the PA CAT Fund's operation.  The author says that she continues to hear about what the CAT Fund will do after the $100,000 mark.  However, the author asks what people will do who carry less than $100,000 in insurance.  How can a person on a limited income carry the difference between what they an afford and the $100,000 they have to have?  The author concludes that people are being forced to carry insurane that most cannot afford.

headline: Dwyer: GOP chief made call on pact
abstract: State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer testified at the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery trial.  He said that the chairman of the Republican State Committee, Robert Asher, called him to ask about the progress of negotiations for a computer contract.  Dwyer said that Asher told him that defendant William T. Smith had been "bugging him" to lobby on behalf of CTA.  Smith and Alan R. Stoneman, both CTA attorneys, have been charged with conspiring to bribe state officials in connection with a no-bid contract that Dwyer awarded CTA to recover Social Security tax overpayments by school districts.

headline: Career put Stone in seat of controversy
abstract: This article looks mainly at the professional history of former President of Pittsburgh City Council Robert Stone.  Stone was named to fill the empty City Council seat of Thomas Fagan in 1972, and controversy immediately followed him.  Mayor Pete Flaherty claimed that Stone did not live in the city, a requirement to fill the council seat.  Friends say that Stone possesses a well-honed sense of the city's finances and understanding of ethnic tradition.  Critics, meanwhile, point to Stone's personal finances, which have gotten him in trouble for failing to pay taxes and non-disclosure of assets.

headline: School board solution hinted
abstract: State Supreme Court justices hinted at the fact that they favor placing the entire Pittsburgh school board on the ballot this year.  The school board does not agree with this plan because it puts the homes of six incumbents in only three districts.  Justices have indicated that the only fair solution is to have all nine members elected in the same year.

headline: Cuts would be costly to SEPTA: Drops in service, fare hikes seen
abstract: President Ronald Reagan's budget cuts would hurt the Southeastern PA Transit Authority (SEPTA) and other regional transit authorities.  The federal government has recommended that transit agencies should be funded more from state and local governments than the federal government.

headline: Panel seeks answers on MOVE fire
abstract: The Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission, dogged by controversy, opens hearings today into May's police bombing of the headquarters of MOVE; the bombing destroyed 61 row houses and killed 11 people.  The commission hopes to find out why the bomb was dropped, who ordered firefighters not to control the blaze, and when Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode knew about the decisions made at the scene.  Many Philadelphia police officers believe they are being made scapegoats for the events of that day, while Mayor Goode's popularity has dropped in the months following the May confrontation.  The PA Supreme Court recently denied a request by the police union to delay the meetings.  Critics of the commission say that three commission members gave money to Goode's campaign, while others work for firms doing business with the city.

headline: House Approves Auto Insurance Measure
abstract: The PA House of Representatives approved legislation that would allow insurance companies to use gender-based premiums for 18 more months.  The legislation was in response to court-ordered implementation of unisex rates, which do not allow gender to be used in setting premiums.  Backers of the new unisex rate plan argue that the new insurance plan would eliminate discrimination in rate-making.  Opponents of the plan argue that gender is a legitimate basis for determining risk, and unisex rates would cause young women's insurance rates to increase drastically.

headline: Dwyer: No CTA gift accepted. Says he refused aid from firm
abstract: State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer testified in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery trial.  Dwyer claimed that, shortly after he had awarded CTA a multi-million dollar state contract, he spurned a fund-raising offer made by CTA attorney William T. Smith.  Dwyer also characterized the offer by Smith as "generic," not the "substantial campaign contribution" that federal prosecutors contend was a bribe for the contract.

headline: Defeating the purpose
abstract: Illinois Governor James Thompson has ordered officials to destroy about 1,000 buttons bearing the slogan "Build Illinois."  Thompson ordered the destruction because the buttons were made in Indiana.

headline: Schools ask for funds to save day care
abstract: Pittsburgh Public Schools Superintendent Richard Wallace said that Pittsburgh Public Schools will stop running day-care centers after June 30 if the state Welfare Department does not provide more money.  Department of Welfare Secretary Walter Cohen said that the Pittsburgh schools are running the "highest cost day-care operation in the state," and that the department would not provide more money.

headline: Dole, Norfolk So. Defend Conrail bid
abstract: Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole appeared before the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation and defended her plan to sell Conrail, the government owned railroad, to Norfolk Southern Corp.  Senators did not firmly commit to the sale.

headline: Parents have right to know
abstract: This editorial praises legislation that will require district justices to notify a parent when a juvenile is arrested for offenses that include public drunkenness, retail theft, and criminal misconduct.  Current law provides that a teen who breaks the law can simply plead guilty and pay a fine, without his parents ever having to know of the incident, possibly leading the teen to believe that minor infractions are just alright; this leads to repeat offenses.  A district judge who already has taken it upon himself to notify parents when he deals with juvenile offenders has seen great success in lowering repeat offenses.  There is some concern that this may put an excessive work load on police and judges.  The editorial believes that in order for youths to adhere to the rules, parents and the legal system must do their part.

headline: House fails to bar cards in taverns
abstract: In an effort to repeal legislation that allowed gambling in taverns, the PA House passed a bill that both expands and reduces gambling.  It is expected to be at least two more weeks before the bill will be sent to a House-Senate conference committee; in committee, a final version of the legislation will be drafted.

headline: Edgar:  It's time to rebuild Pa.
abstract: Bob Edgar, saying that PA is "crying out for new leadership," yesterday became the first candidate to throw his hat in the ring for what is expected to be a hotly contested Democratic primary for the US Senate.  Edgar also immediately began his attacks on incumbent US Senator Arlen Specter.

headline: Fern Hetrick: Mixing politics, peacocks
abstract: This article provides a profile of Fern Hetrick, a peacock farmer who also is interested in politics.  Hetrick served as chairman of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission.

headline: Some area pupils to enter special programs
abstract: As a result of the first round of PA state literacy tests, school officials will be using state funds to design remedial programs for those students who missed the cutoff mark on the tests.  The local remedial programs cause some school districts to be penalized for excellence since the funding was distributed on the basis of the number of children who fell below the state cutoff mark.  School administrators say that many children qualify to leave the program after post-remediation tests are conducted.  Conflicts in the remedial course system can occur because those remedial courses which are funded federally have stringent regulations placed on them; also,  students cannot enroll in both state and federal programs full-time.  The article goes on to discuss how local schools in the Harrisburg and Dauphin County areas are forming their remedial programs.

headline: Don't Raise Speed Limits, Trucker Pleads
abstract: A bill that would permit states to raise the current speed limit on interstate highways is before the US Senate and House.  Gerard Trippiletti, president and chief operating officer of Matlack Incorporated, writes that raising the speed limit is not a good idea.  He says that raising the speed limit would increase the severtiy of accidents and would result in a loss of fuel efficiency for all vehicles.  It would also increase the heavy cost burdens for the trucking industry.

headline: Philadelphia Action Called 'Last Resort' Against MOVE's Threats
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode said that he had allowed the police action to evict the radical group MOVE from its West Philadelphia headquarters as a last resort.  He said the action was the only way to end the nearly four years of psychological warfare by MOVE members against their neighborhood.  Goode also cited a letter from MOVE received by city police two days before the action; in the letter, MOVE threatened to destroy its neighborhood with gas, fire and bullets.

headline: How About Customers
abstract: This editorial states that the talk around Harrisburg on changing the authority of--or eliminating--the PA Liquor Control Board has not changed since former PA Governor Milton Shapp came up with the idea 10 years ago.  However, no one has taken the customer into consideration during this whole process.  Customers in PA must pay more for liquor and wine in this state than those surrounding our borders, and they cannot go to supermarkets to get beer.  The editorial concludes that it is still the customer who is left out in the cold and not even taken into consideration.

headline: Ely blames composite photo for lost votes in '82 race
abstract: Donald Ely, a midstate Republican who ran for state representative in 1982, is seeking damages in a civil trial from the Republican State Committee, the Republican Legislative Campaign Committee, and two House Republican Cacus staff members who helped him with his campaign.  Ely says that he was in striking distance of a campaign victory until a composite photo appeared in his campaign literature.  Ely was behind in the polls 43% to 30% just before the photo was published, but his opponent won with almost 70% of the vote.

headline: Harrison Ford takes aim
abstract: A photo depicts Harrison Ford taking aim at a killer in the movie "Witness," which features Philadelphia's 30th St. Amtrak station.

headline: State simplifies child care law
abstract: A 1984 law that requires the operators of child care institutions and school administrators to review the criminal history of each applicant before offering employment has been simplified; its effective date has also been  postponed.  The new law, which was passed by the PA State Legislature, requires that a person seeking work in child care or school teaching obtain the required records and make them available to prospective employers.  This is a great benefit to public schools, considering that the majority of hiring is done in August and the old law would have made it difficult for some schools to fill employment openings by September.  The PA State Senate is also considering legislation to open teacher contract negotiations earlier than current laws allow.

headline: Expressway commuters get warning
abstract: State Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson warned commuters of the Schuylkill Expressway reconstruction and said there would be serious commuting snarls unless 250,000 drivers a day abandon their use of the Schuylkill.  He outlined the measures that PennDOT has taken to alleviate the problems and urged drivers to take public transit or alternative routes.

headline: Philadelphia Officials Accused of Delay: Crescendo of Complaints Preceded Police Action Against Radical Group
abstract: Neighborhood groups and newspaper editorials are complaining that it took Philadelphia city officials too long to try to evict members of the radical group MOVE from their West Philadelphia home.  Many people feel that the reason the mayor and the police waited so long was that they did not want a violent confrontation.

headline: In response, state swings crisis unit into operation
abstract: For the fourth time in six years, the PA Emergency Management Agency (PEMA) swung into full operation, helping residents deal with the tragedy of the Friday night storm in western PA that killed 61 and injured more than 300 people.  Working with the American Red Cross, PEMA workers coordinated the opening of 11 schools and gymnasiums equipped with bedding and bathrooms.  PEMA also sent state employees from various agencies across the state to start assessing damage.

headline: Empire and Keystone States
abstract: This Editorial looks at the differences between state government in PA and New York.  It also looks at the differences between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and New York Governor Mario Cuomo.  US Census figures show that New York hires 563 people for every 10,000 residents, while PA hires 380 people for every 10,000 residents.  Both Governors Cuomo and Thornburgh have national political aspirations, but they espose different views.  Thornburgh sides with President Ronald Reagan's tax policies, while Cuomo would like to maintain local and state deductions on federal income taxes.  The editorial concludes that PA is the much more frugal state, but it may change as state employees try to negotiate contracts similar to their New York counterparts.

headline: HI, Uncle Sonnyboy
abstract: A cartoon shows a little boy asking to get a hair cut just like his dad's.  The barber cuts off most of his hair, making him look quite bald; the boy says it looks perfect.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: The cartoon depicts a man in a suit speaking to an unknown audience.  He says, "I'm 'Rosty' Rostenkowski, and I'm going to help the president pass tax reform. We need a tax system that's simple and fair...and I’m the guy that can close up all those loopholes in the code.  Who do you think they put them there?"

headline: State's curriculum changes hit vo-tech, business students
abstract: Students enrolled in vocational and business education courses will feel the greatest impact as the new PA state curriculum regulations are phased in over the next four years.  The new graduation requirements will force these students to add mathematics and science courses to their programs at the expense of electives that might be better suited to their courses of study.  Some in vocational schools believe that the new requirements do not necessarily constitute a better educational program.  School officials in Cumberland, Perry and Dauphin Counties have also upped some of their graduation requirements by requiring additional courses.

headline: Fares up, with state surplus
abstract: This editorial complains that, in a year with a budget surplus in excess of $200 million, appropriations for mass transit fell below requests and expectations.  This has led to necessary fare increases and the possibility of service cuts.  The editorial suggests that the state Legislature ought to enact a permanent funding mechanism for mass transit.  The editorial also encourages Governor Dick Thornburgh and the state Legislature to use a portion of state tax revenues as a reliable funding base for the 22 mass transit authorities across PA.

headline: Plight of 'lifers'
abstract: In PA cases where those sentenced to life in prison are unlikely to become repeat offenders, we need legislation that allows for alternative programs.  The author says that inmates serving life sentences who are not likely to repeat their crimes should be eligible for programs such as furloughs, educational release, work release, community service centers or automatic parole review.

headline: Insurance firm granted 9.8% increase
abstract: More than a million PA motorists will pay 9.8% more for car insurance next year under a rate increase granted to Insurance Services Office Incorporated.  The increase, approved by the PA Insurance Department, will cost motorists about $88 million next year.  The PA Insurance Department also approved a 5% increase for Keystone Insurance Corporation.

headline: Enthusiasts are trying to get Caliguiri to run for governor
abstract: Democratic Party officials say they consider Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri to be a frontrunner for the party's nomination for PA governor in 1986.  Caliguiri's strong showing in the mayoral primary--a primary in which he took 75% of the vote against three opponents--demonstrates his political strength.  Other strong Democratic candidates for governor are Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell and former state Auditor General Robert Casey.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article highlights significant events that happened on April 1 throughout history.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: The cartoon depicts a man standing on the sidewalk in patched clothing.  He is trying to sell an apple for 5 cents to a smartly-dressed businessman.  The cartoon is making a statement about the status of the economy in the 1980s and is obviously comparing it to the Great Depression.

headline: Students as 'bargaining chips' in dispute?
abstract: Students in the PA System of Higher Education have been placed in the middle of a labor dispute between administrators and faculty.  The faculty's 4,600 member union has voted overwhelmingly to strike, claiming that faculty salaries must be competitive if the system hopes to keep its best and brightest faculty.  The state system and its chancellor say that, unless tuition is raised by $300, there will be no more money to meet faculty demands; such a tuition increase would make the 14-university chain among the most expensive in the nation.  Some students feel as if they are being used as a bargaining chip by both sides.

headline: Generic road signs get specific
abstract: The generic blue and white signs that currently inform motorists of lodging, food, and gas are being replaced by new signs that will feature the logos of businesses that provide travel services to motorists.  Companies will have to pay an average of $6,000 for two coporate logos at each exit and up to $200 annually for maintenance.

headline: Police chief:  Goode knew of explosive
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor, testifying yesterday to the special commission investigating the MOVE tragedy, said that he had informed Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode about a plan to use explosives to drive members of MOVE out of their barricaded headquarters.  Sambor's testimony contradicts Goode's, who claims he had no prior knowledge of police intent to use explosives in the confrontation.  Sambor reiterated this point at least a half-dozen times.  Similar testimony of Goode's prior knowledge came from former Managing Director Leo Brooks.  Sambor told the 11-member commission that he had advised Goode in October 1984 to take action against MOVE, but was rejected.

headline: Insurance Rates Woes
abstract: Efforts by the PA Legislature to resolve the insurance industry's gender-based car insurance rates are currently on hold until January 1986.  Insurance companies have traditionally set different rates for different segments of the population.  The PA Supreme Court has ruled that the state insurance commissioner has the authority to decide if certain insurance rates are discriminatory, and the commissioner came to the conclusion that gender-based rates are discriminatory.  The PA House adopted a bill allowing for gender-based rates to continue for 18 months, but the PA Senate failed to take action on the bill.

headline: Ethics rules posed convention-center
abstract: The tenative agreement reached between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode on the proposed convention center in Philadelphia includes tight ethics provisions that bar close relatives of elected officials from getting contracts or otherwise benefitting from the project.  The accord also would give either the state budget secretary or Philadelphia's finance director the power to disapprove any line item in the authority's capital budget.  Another controversial section of the accord would exempt the authority from the city's rules requiring participation of minorities and women in contracts.  The accord will be drafted into bill form, as it has only been approved in concept by the city and state legislators.  PA Senate Republicans refused to take up the bill before the PA Legislature recessed for the year.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article looks at significant historical events that occurred on August 27 throughout history.  Included is the birth of President Lyndon Johnson in 1908, the signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact in 1928, and President Ronald Reagan announcing that Christa McAuliffe would be the first "citizen astronaut" to fly aboard a space shuttle in 1984.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: The cartoon shows President Ronald Reagan stealing from the refrigerator of a middle-class family.  While the president is stealing from the refrigerator,  the family's father reads a newspaper with the headline: "Budget hurts middle class."

headline: Survey says asbestos found in 80 percent of state schools
abstract: According to a statewide survey, 80% of PA school districts have reported that materials containing asbestos are in one or more of their buildings.  More than $100 million has been spent by local school boards in asbestos abatement efforts.  In many cases, local tax revenue has been the only source of funding for asbestos-related work; in some cases, however, costs have been reimbursed by federal and/or state funds.  The most serious problems encountered in eliminating asbestos were in determining the scope of asbestos conditions in buildings, the cost of performing necessary corrections, and complying with appropriate standards for asbestos work.

headline: Gov. Dick Thornburgh
abstract: A photo depicts Governor Dick Thornburgh getting a free ride on some of the equipment that will be used for construction of the Route 15 Mansfield bypass.  Another photo depicts Robert Bartlett, president of the PA Highway Information Association, commenting on the accomplishment of bringing the Mansfield bypass project to the construction stage.

headline: Police Firebomb House in Philadelphia Siege
abstract: An attempt to bring a peaceful end to a confrontation between police and a radical back-to-nature cult called MOVE collapsed late yesterday, turning a West Philadelphia neighborhood into a battle zone.  Police had attempted to negotiate with the MOVE members to get them to leave the house peacefully after complaints from neighbors, but MOVE members refused to leave.  Police and MOVE members traded fire and the siege ended with two blocks of houses on fire.

headline: It's the State Store bureaucracy they hate
abstract: An opinion piece examines the frustration that restaurant owners endure when dealing with PA's State Store liquor sale system.  The author, who claims to have talked to several owners of restaurants in PA, says that most of their problems come on the wholesale end, when they are trying to get large amounts of wine delivered.  Another major issue for the owners is the fact that they must place 25% of the cost of their purchase down as soon as they place an order.  The nature of the bureaucracy surrounding the State Store system also seems to create some headaches for owners.

headline: Eyeing Thornburgh Bid, Specter Starts Running
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter has begun campaigning furiously in Lancaster, PA, as PA Governor Dick Thornburgh continues to send messages that he is considering running for Specter's US Senate seat.  Specter said that he does not believe Thornburgh will run for the seat, as a divisive primary between the two Republicans could make it easier for the Democrats to take Specter's Senate seat in the general election.  Specter, a moderate Republican, has been criticized by some conservatives because of his opposition to President Ronald Reagan on certain issues, though Specter says that Reagan will campaign for him in the general election.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article looks at the significant historical events that occurred on October 10th throughout history.  Included in this list is the opening of the US Naval Academy in 1845, Chaing Kai-shek taking the oath of office as president of China in 1943, and the resignation of US Vice President Spiro Agnew in 1973.

headline: $9.3 billion state budget gets tentative OK
abstract: Less than 48 hours before the General Assembly's scheduled recess, legislative leaders agreed on a tentative compromise $9.3 billion dollar budget.  The tentative budget includes a tax cut from the present 2.35% to 2.2% and goes into effect on January 1, 1986.

headline: Tech students excel
abstract: A letter to the editor responds to an recent editorial that appeared in the Patriot-News.   The editorial cited a survey that was critical of vocational education at the national level.  The author, who works at Dauphin County Technical School, disputes these findings and says that the school in which he works offers an array of fourteen programs--including language and computational skills.  The author also cites the high scores that students achieved on the recent Educational Quality Assessment.  The letter also looks at the success of graduates from the technical school.  The author also believes that narrowing each student's vocational education would be a mistake--especially given the way technology is changing the workforce.

headline: How to win friends and influence public works
abstract: A columnist tells a funny story that illustrates the problems between the state Legislature and the governor regarding the PA Turnpike Commission.

headline: Praise for a juvenile-crime initiative
abstract: A letter to the editor praises Governor Thornburgh's initiative to create legislation to deal with serious juvenile offenders but cautions against overly rigid legislation that will be harmful to youth.

headline: It's time to let the LCB fade into the 'Sunset'
abstract: An editorial supports letting the Liquor Control Board die at the end of year because it is a corrupt, inefficient agency.  The editorial also says that before anything is decided with the LCB, partisan politics need to be worked out so that both sides can have a broader perspective on the issue.

headline: Failure to debate Castille apparently hurt Williams
abstract: This article provides an analysis of Republican Ronald Castille's victory over Democrat Robert Williams in the election for Philadelphia's District Attorney.  In the end, Williams and the Democrats did as much to lose the election as Castille did to win it.  Williams had banked on the ability of the Democratic ward organization to turn out the party faithful.  However, Williams refusal to debate Castille cost him greatly, especially among the white, liberal vote that was crucial to Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode's 1983 election.  Williams had support of the top Democrats and labor unions in the city, but could not get support at the grassroots level.  Goode gave his heavy support, personally, politically, and financially, to Williams, but it was not enough to win him the election.  Goode's popularity has been sliding since the MOVE hearing commenced, and this was the first election Philadelphians had to voice their opinion of Goode's handling of the MOVE incident.  Last night's results could be a sign of trouble ahead for Democrats in the city.

headline: Highlights in History
abstract: This article looks at the significant historical events that occurred on September 11th.  Significant moments include the appointing of Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury in 1789, the American victory over the British at the Battle of Lake Champlain in 1814, and the death of Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev in 1971.

headline: 1040 EZ Listening: IRS says no to tax deductions for Live Aid tix
abstract: The Internal Revenue Service said it will not allow people to treat monies spent on Live Aid concert tickets as charitable contributions--even though most of the money will be used to help Ethiopian famine victims.  The IRS said that the price of Live Aid T-shirts will be deductible, however, and that direct payments to the famine releif fund are clearly charitable contributions.

headline: Test results released: Student scores mixed in county
abstract: The state Education Department released a district-by-district list of TELLS (Testing for Essential Learning and Literacy Skills) exam results.  This list provided a statewide comparison of third, fifth, and eighth-grade students.  The list allows viewers to compare results in math and reading by school district.

headline: I-95 Open After Just 25 Years
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode were together yesterday to celebrate the formal opening of the last piece of Interstate 95 in PA.  The north-south interstate highway is now complete from Florida to Maine, with the exception of sections near West Palm Beach and Boston.  Thornburgh and Goode spent much time answering questions about the unsuccessful process of building Philadelphia's long-planned convention center.

headline: Private Prisons
abstract: This editorial believes that several issues must be resolved before privately-operated jails are allowed to do business in the commonwealth.  The editorial believes that taxpayers will still have to shell out just as much money to cover costs at correctional facilities.  What will happen when management at the private facility is pressured to generate a greater return on investor dollars?  If studies show that non-public facilities operate at a cost which is comparable to the government's, then a proposal for privately-operated prisons should move ahead, but only after legislation is enacted to appropriately regulate these institutions.

headline: Join Ohio to win GM plant, Erie lawmaker urges state
abstract: PA state Representative Tom Ridge said that PA could double its chances of winning General Motors' Saturn plan by teaming up with Ohio.  Ridge proposes that the plant be built on the border of the two states.  PA Commerce Secretary Jim Pickard is putting together a proposal to be delivered to GM by Governor Dick Thornburgh.  Almost every state in the nation is seeking to be the host of the new GM plan.

headline: Fairness?
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh and leaders of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, which represents more than 50,000 of 75,000 unionized state workers in PA, are holding fast to sharply disparate positions on wages and fringe benefits concessions.  State worker union leaders, who initially sought a 15% pay raise in a one-year contract, have cut their demand in half and say the salary issue is negotiable, while the administration has offered a maximum of 6% over three years and will not compromise on efforts to cut employees' sick leave, holidays and vacations.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article looks at the significant historical events that occurred on September 27th.  Among them are the US recognizing the Nationalist Chinese government in 1928, the surrender of Warsaw, Poland to the Germans in 1939, and the final report of the Warren Commission in 1964.

headline: A surplus in Harrisburg:  Use it for local tax relief
abstract: This editorial calls for reform of the PA tax structure at all levels of government.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh yesterday announced his budget would include tax cuts for both businesses and individuals, as the state was projected to have a surplus of $110 million dollars.  In contrast to these surplus conditions, many local governments in PA are experiencing severe financial harships.  Local property taxes and wage taxes are placing a heavy burden on PA taxpayers, while regional and local transportation systems are raising their rates due to financial distress.  This editorial argues that the state surplus of $100 million dollars should be used to enact constructive reforms of state tax policy.

headline: Test results: TELLS pinpoints scholastic trouble spots
abstract: Results from the Testing for Essential Learning and Literacy Skills (TELLS) exam indicates that about one in five Pennsylvania students are in need of remedial assistance.  This editorial notes that more funding will be needed to give the necessary remedial assistance to students; the article also notes that testing can be used in a positive way to help students.

headline: Infringements
abstract: A letter to the editor complains that mandatory seat-belt laws are an infringement of rights and should not be enacted.

headline: Private prisons held risky
abstract: David R. Wright, the Democratic policy chairman of the state House of Representatives, responds to an editorial in the Pittsburgh Press.  The editorial opposed legislation to prevent the operation of private prisons in PA until the PA Council on Crime and Delinquency could study the concept and its legal implications.  Wright says the legislation is needed in order to protect the neighbors of private prisons, the rights of the prisoners and the rights of the guards.

headline: Keep State Liquor Stores
abstract: A letter to the editor, written by a member of the United Food and Commerical Workers Union, states that PRESSS, a coalition to rid PA of its state liquor store system, is made up of big business types who want the big profits the state stores generate from the sales of wine and liquor.  The recent Sunset Review Audit is now being overlooked because the findings conflicted with Governor Thornburgh's views.  It found that the stores carry an adequate selection and that prices within the stores are very competitive compared to other states.  The author hopes that people realize that the state will lose the revenue generated by these stores if they are privatized.

headline: Federal jury convicts CTA lawyers of plotting to bribe state officials
abstract: A federal court jury found William T. Smith guilty of conspiracy and eight other counts.  The jury found Alan R. Stoneman guilty of conspiracy, but not guilty of six counts of mail fraud and nine counts of interstate transportation in aid of racketeering in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery trial.  The two defendants were lawyers for CTA, which received no-bid contracts from the state, Allegheny County and Pittsburgh in 1983 and 1984 to recover Social Security tax overpayments.  Both Smith and Stoneman said they would appeal the verdicts.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article looks at the significant historical events that occurred on October 22nd throughout history.  Among the events included are Princeton University receiving its charter in 1746, Sam Houston being inaugurated as the first president of Texas in 1836, and West Germany joining the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in 1954.

headline: Amusement park makes payment on back taxes to avert shutdown
abstract: The Williams Grove Amusement Park in Monroe Township came within minutes of being shut down by police and PA Revenue Department tax agents for not paying $37,000 in back taxes.  Officials at the park were able to avert a shutdown by making an $8,600 payment and will meet with representatives from the PA Attorney General's Office to work out a payment plan.  The management at Williams Grove claims not to have paid taxes for several years due to low revenues and bookkeeping errors.

headline: Threats to higher education
abstract: The board of trustees for the Carnegie Foundation went on public record to encourage federal support for aid to higher education.  The Foundation says that higher education will be increasingly necessary for Americans to get a good job, and says that it is worried about proposed curtailments in the Guaranteed Student Loan Program.  The editorial says that the Carnegie Foundation's warning against too great a slashing of the federal role in higher education needs to be heeded.

headline: Lead content in gasoline to be cut: Drivers could face fuel shortages, rising prices
abstract: American motorists could face spot shortages and rising pump prices in the aftermath of the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) decision to reduce the lead content in gasoline by more than 50%.  Alarmed by substantially higher lead levels in the air than just three years ago, the EPA announced new regulations in March 1985 that will lower the limit on lead in gasoline to 0.5 gram per gallon.  The EPA estimates it will cost refiners 2 cents more a gallon to produce the new low-lead fuel.

headline: Privately owned prisons need controls, report says
abstract: A report by the PA Legislative Budget and Finance Committee says that laws should be drafted to regulate private prisons to ensure that they are run properly.  According to the report, there are currently no state regulations to protect the interest of the public or the rights of the inmates in privately run prisons.  Private facilities can give local government officials more flexibility in handling prison populations, and private owners can construct these facilities faster and for less money than governments.  A federal judge recently determined that the 268 Center in Armstrong County, a private jail, is adequate for housing prisoners, but the judge also imposed guidelines on the jail's operation.

headline: Law against blackjack enforced immediately
abstract: The state Legislature passed legialtion repealing a 1984 law that enabled taverns to hold cash prize tournaments involving card games, billiards, darts, bowling and other activities.  Gary DiVito, chief counsel for the Liquor Control Board (LCB), said that the LCB would allow a 30-day grace period before citing taverns.  LCB chairman Daniel Pennick, however, contradicted DiVito and said that the LCB would begin enforcing the law immediately.

headline: Feds Probe Rep, Seek Bad Cop's Link to Club Deal
abstract: Federal authorities are inquiring into the circumstances surrounding PA State Representative David Richardson's alleged receipt of $15,000 from two vice figures, Lester Barry and Francis Patrick O'Rourke; authorities are also investigating the role played in that transaction by former Deputy Police Commissioner James Martin.  Barry and O'Rourke told the Federal Bureau of Investigation that they lent $15,000 to Richardson in 1983 to help him finance the purchase of a club.  Martin also played a role in the purchase of the club.  In 1984, Martin was convicted of extortion and racketeering as the leader of a ring that squeezed more than $350,000 from vice operators.  Barry introduced Martin to Richardson in 1983; at the time, Martin was trying to get support for an appointment as Philadelphia Deputy Police Commissioner.  The remainder of the article describes the exact nature of how Martin and Richardson met and Richardson's purchase of the club.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article looks at the significant historical events that occurred on September 23rd throughout history.  Among the significant events is the birth of Augustus Caesar in 63 B.C., the Lewis and Clark expedition returning to Saint Louis in 1806, and former Argentine President Juan Peron returning to power in 1973.

headline: Bill filed to cap wage tax at 4.31%
abstract: State Representatives Stephen Freind and Matthew Ryan have developed a wage-tax proposal that would legally cap the current Philadelphia wage-tax rate at 4.31%.

headline: Thornburgh says top teacher, finalist should get cash
abstract: Speaking at the National Forum and annual meeting of the Education Commission of the States, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh proposed that "Teacher of the Year" finalists be given cash awards for the first time.  In 1983, Governor Thornburgh proposed a statewide Excellence in Teaching Award program that would provide grants for up to 5% of each school district's teachers; the PA State Legislature has not funded the awards program in its proposed form, however.  The Education Commission of the States is a nationwide organization formed to help state governments and education officials develop policies to improve the quality of education.

headline: Lawmakers leave issue unresolved
abstract: This editorial urges Monangahela Valley residents to confront their local state representatives and put pressure on them to resolve the PA Turnpike Commission issue.  The editorial discusses the dispute over the turnpike commission and the $4.5 billion toll-road construction money that will not be released until Governor Dick Thornburgh is able to have one of his nominees approved for the Turnpike Commission.  The editorial says that the money is needed for the Mon-Valley Expressway in order to improve the area's economic future.

headline: Probation, rehabilitation to be asked for state official
abstract: Leonard LeMelle Jr., the director of the PA State Bureau of Police and Safety, was arrested for driving while intoxicated on January 31, 1985.  LeMelle will be recommended for probation under the Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition program (ARD).  The ARD is a program for first-time offenders, and those who refuse the program face a mandatory prison sentence of two days.  A dely in processing LeMelle's application was due to a backlog of requests to the PA Department of Transportation.  LeMelle was suspended without pay for a week as a result of the charge.  If LeMelle completes the ARD requirements, the charge will be dismissed and removed from his record.

headline: LCB Dems Seek Fines Against Guv
abstract: Democrats on the PA Liquor Control Board want Governor Dick Thornburgh and two of his top aides held in contempt for trying to trim the LCB's complement of enforcement agents.  LCB Chairman Daniel Pennick claims that Thornburgh slashed the addition of 25 liquor enforcement agents and nixed several other proposed supervisory posts.  The LCB says that this violates a February 1984 court order that overturned Thornburgh's effort to freeze all LCB hirings and pay raises.

headline: Finally, a blow to nepotism
abstract: The state Department of Public Welfare said that state departments are not allowed to hire relatives.  The editorial says that practicing nepotism was rampant in PA, and that it will take more than a directive to eliminate the nepotism.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article offers a list of significant events that happened on May 15 throughout history.

headline: Budget fight rages; funds running out
abstract: The US Senate yesterday refused to close debate on a proposal to require a balanced budget by 1991--leaving in doubt legislation that would continue the government's borrowing authority.  The failure to end debate has prolonged efforts to increase the national-debt limit, which, according to US Treasury officials, must be increased to avoid disruptions of government financial operations.  US Senator Robert Byrd has offered support for a small increase in the debt limit to allow more time for consideration of the controversial balanced-budget amendment.  Opponents of the balanced-budget plan say it would disproportionately hit domestic spending programs and give the president too much power to cut spending.

headline: Tuition up 1.9% at Pa. universities
abstract: The board of governors of the state system of higher education, which oversees the 14 PA state universities, approved a 1.9% tuition increase.  James H. McCormick, chancellor of the state system of higher education, acknowledged that tuition in PA state owned colleges and universities was higher than in most other states, and that the "very modest increase" for the coming year would help reverse the expensive tuition trend in PA.  The tuition increase was necessary because higher education officials received a 5.5% budget increase from the legislature beginning July 1, 1985.

headline: Legislators vow to fight rail fees
abstract: Two members of the US House of Representatives from the Philadelphia area have vowed to fight a US Senate proposal that would raise fares for Philadelphia and New Jersey rail commuters by forcing PA and New Jersey transit authorities to pay more for their use of Amtrak's rail lines.  SEPTA spokesman Dave Murdoch said the amendment "would double our costs for Amtrak service."  The proposal, an amendment to the budget reconciliation bill, was not opposed by either US Senator Arlen Specter or US Senator John Heinz.

headline: Program helps inmates visit more with families
abstract: In Muncy, Parents and Children Together is making it possible for family members and prisoners to spend more time together.  A play area for children has been constructed outside the visitor's building, and there is also a mobile home nearby where children and parents can talk privately.  Prisoners have also formed a child-care detail to watch youngsters.

headline: LCB gives $183 million to state treasury for year
abstract: Despite a decrease in state-store profits, the PA Liquor Control Board turned over $183 million to the state treasury during fiscal year 1984-85.  In addition to other deposits, the LCB turned over $41.5 million in sales taxes and $106.9 million generated from the emergency tax.  Reasons for the smaller profit by state stores include a general pay increase for state employees and a change in accounting systems.  The sales figures for last year, according to the LCB, also show a leveling off of alcohol purchases in PA.

headline: For Singel's vote, a better deal on 219
abstract: A columnist supports state Senator Mark Singel in voting against Governor Dick Thornburgh's nominees for the state Turnpike Commission.  The columnist says that Singel is holding out because Route 219 in Johnstown is not a high priority, and that he is holding out for a better deal.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article provides a list of significant events that happened on April 25 throughout history.  It also provides a "Thought for the day" and the city trash-collection schedule.

headline: Catch cheats with LCB data
abstract: Since LeRoy S. Zimmerman became the PA Attorney General and Jim Scheiner became the PA Revenue Secretary, officials say it has become increasingly difficult and risky for Pennsylvanians to cheat on their taxes.  Additionally, new legislation proposed by state Senator Stewart Greenleaf will help the PA Revenue Department further prevent tax deliquencies and cheating.  Greenleaf's proposal would make the annual renewal and issuing of taproom and beer-distribution licenses contengent upon the applicant's furnishing his or her personal income tax identification and sales-tax numbers.

headline: University President Resigns After Threat to Accreditation
abstract: CT Enus Wrigt, president of Cheyney University, has announced his resignation, effective April 20, 1985.  Wright has been under fire since the Commission of Higher Education of the Middle States Association of Colleges and Schools voted to withhold the college's accreditation.

headline: Legislature to tackle unisex, CAT insurance
abstract: Two major issues ranking high on the PA General Assembly's fall agenda are the CAT fund and unisex auto rates.  As a result of protests from motorists, there will be a move in both chambers to abolish or at least simplify the collection procedures for the new Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund.  In the PA state Senate, there will be a bipartisan effort to preserve gender-based auto insurance rates.  The insurance industry contends that there is justification for charging higher rates to males under 30 because they have more accidents than women.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will be handed a setback when the PA Senate Law and Justice Committee issues a report calling for retention of the state liquor stores.  Thornburgh has campaigned for four years to abolish the state-store system.

headline: Protesters' Chant: 'Goode Is a Murderer'
abstract: About 100 people marched on City Hall under the banner of a coordinating group calling itself Citizens' Committee for Humanity and Justice.  The group demands an independent investigation of the MOVE confrontation and the city officials in charge of the operation.  The rally did not include MOVE members or a statement of support for MOVE itself.  The May 13 confrontation began with a dawn shootout between MOVE members and police trying to arrest them and ended with a fire that destroyed 61 homes and killed 11 MOVE members.

headline: LCB gives beer price ads an OK
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) approved Wednesday regulations that will allow beer distributors to advertise prices.  The Board voted unanimously, 3-0, despite the objection of smaller distributors.  Mario Mele, the lone appointee of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, said the ban denied customers the right to know the price of what they buy before they buy it.  LCB Chairman Daniel Pennick said the board could find no evidence that price advertising would in itself pose any adverse effect on the beer industry.

headline: For the first time
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has finally set a timetable for deciding whether to challenge US Senator Arlen Specter for the Republican nomination for US Senate.  Thornburgh says that he is grateful for the support that many across the state have given him and that he expects to make an announcement after election day 1985.  Specter said that he does not fear running against Thornburgh, and Specter believes he would be a better candidate against Democrats.  A Republican party loyalist told a reporter that he believes that Thornburgh will not run unless he believes he can bet Specter in the primary and then win the general election.

headline: Highlights in History
abstract: This article provides a list of significant events that happened on March 29th throughout history.

headline: Crusade for lower taxes to be organized
abstract: A Carlisle man has created and organized the Pennsylvania Tax Crusade for Lower Taxes--a group whose mission is to limit state and local government spending.  The group is lobbying to end "outrageous" salaries for government officials, as well as the cessation of tax increases.   The group also supports legislation that would allow for the recall of elected officials.

headline: What TELLS says about students
abstract: The Testing for Essential Learning and Literacy Skills (TELLS) exam was designed as a statewide measure of students' performance in the third, fifth and eighth grades.  The exam claims to measure for basic competence in math and reading skills.  A guest columnist argues that parents must work with their children and the school district  to ensure that their child is receiving the necessary remediation.

headline: Major tri-county road jobs to start
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation Officials are about to start major road construction in Dauphin, Cumberland, and Perry counties and warn of slowed traffic on at least two major commuter arteries that serve Harrisburg.  This article gives a list of streets and intersections that will be closed or detoured.

headline: Questions still lingering about the siege and blaze
abstract: Six days after the police battle with MOVE, several questions about what happened at 6221 Osage Avenue remain unresolved.
