For example, why did no one know how many people were in the MOVE house? Can top-level officials confirm that there was a firefight between MOVE members and police shortly after the bomb was dropped? Why did the fire department not know what kind of fire might follow from the use of powerful explosives?

headline: LCB No Good At Image Game
abstract: Under PA's "Sunset Law," the state Liquor Control Board will legally cease to exist on December 31, 1985 unless the General Assembly votes to extend it.  A columnist discusses the woes of the agency and its image problems.  The author says that the LCB needs to project a different image if it wants to survive the sunset review.

headline: Gerhard opens bid
abstract: Robert Gerhard, a Cheltenham commissioner for six years, announced Monday that he will seek the PA state House seat in the 154th district.  Gerhard, a Republican, will face opposition from incumbent Republican Charles Nahil Jr., who has yet to announce he intention to seek re-election, and Democrat Phyllis Magerman.  An outline of issues that Gerhard is concerned about is also included in the article.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article outlines important events that happened on February 21 throughout history.  It also provides celebrity birthdays for February 21st and a "thought for the day."

headline: Cutting the Top off Taxes
abstract: This editorial supports Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal to reduce the state income tax from 2.35% to 2.15%.  The governor's proposed tax cut would be an effective use of the current budget surplus.

headline: WPIAL: A house divided
abstract: This article shows a map of the Western PA Interscholastic Athletic League--the body that governs the athletic prgorams for 146 high schools in a nine-county area.  It also provides a district breakdown of the number of schools in the district along with its operating budget.

headline: Mandatory Seat Belts:  Saving Us from Ourselves
abstract: An opinion piece argues that sometimes the government must pass a law that protects us from ourselves, such as the law that has been proposed in PA to require people to wear seat belts when they drive their cars.  The author believes that arguments made by civil libertarians that it is a constitutionally protected right to choose whether we should wear seat belts in our automobiles are silly.  The author then points to laws which outlaw suicide, limit the age at which we can drink alcohol, and restrict the use of certain drugs, as being in the same vein as the seatbelt law.  Once the law is passed in PA, the author believes that arguments against it will die down.

headline: Radical Group's Homes Under Watch
abstract: Philadelphia police are watching two MOVE homes in West Philadelphia because they expect more violence from the group.  Eleven MOVE members were killed and over 50 homes were destroyed when police tried to evict MOVE from their home on Osage Avenue in West Philadelphia.  MOVE spokesmen say that they will not give up in their struggle to have 9 MOVE members released from prison.

headline: LCB, PUC Reform Delayed Until New Year, IRRC Dead
abstract: Decisions on changing the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) and the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) will be delayed until 1986.  The PA Legislature began leaving for the holidays without agreements to renew both agencies.  The PA Senate narrowly rejected a bill required to renew the PA Independent Regulatory Review Commission (IRRC), which means the IRRC will have to cease operations December 31.  A committee of the PA House and PA Senate will meet today to extend the deadlines for the PA Legislature to reauthorize the LCB and PUC under the Sunset Law.  The newswire story talks about the long-standing battle between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and the PA Legislature on the future of the LCB.

headline: Givens to ask backers: Stay in mayoral race?
abstract: Councilman Richard Givens said he will decide, after talking to his supporters, whether to drop out of the Democratic mayoral primary.  Givens is running against Mayor Richard Caliguiri for mayor of Pittsburgh.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article outlines important events that happened February 25 throughout history.  It also provides celebrity birthdays for February 25th and a "thought for the day."

headline: Everyone Knows Where To Cut The Budget
abstract: This cartoon shows various interest groups pointing at each other and indicating that that the budget cuts should come from somewhere else.  The cartoon also depicts various constituent groups: students, the elderly, the poor, farmers, and the military.

headline: null
abstract: A Pennsylvania Conservation-Corps project will put 32 disadvantaged youths to work improving recreational facilities at Luzerne County Community College.  According to officials from the state Department of Environmental Resources, Luzerne County projects will receive about 15% of the total statewide Conservation-Corps budget.

headline: Merger disaster
abstract: A letter to the editor, written by US Senator Arlen Specter, argues that the proposed merger of Norfolk Southern and Conrail would be disastrous to the future economic vitality of PA and the Northeast-Midwest region.  Specter claims this has been proven through the seven hearings he conducted on this issue in PA and Washington, D.C., as well as by numerous independent studies.  The merger would threaten PA's 15,000 Conrail employees, 2,300 shippers, and 12 million customers.  Specter's alternative is to return Conrail to the private sector through a public offering of stock.

headline: Ramona in Hospital; Searchers Hit Bottom
abstract: Ramona Johnson Africa, the only adult survivor of the destroyed MOVE compound, was taken from the House of Correction to Guiffre Medical Center when the condition of the second-degree burns covering 40% of her body worsened.  Investigators also reached the bottom of MOVE's compound at 6221 Osage Ave in West Philadelphia and found no more bodies and no evidence of tunnels or heavy weapons.

headline: LCB, PUC, 7 other agencies receive one-year reprieves
abstract: A unanimous action by a six-member leadership committee of the PA Legislature has granted a one-year reprieve to the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB), Public Utility Commission (PUC), and seven other agencies.  The action prevented the agencies from being forced to phase out their operations by June 30, 1986.  The group was unable, however, to prevent the scheduled extinction of the PA Independent Regulatory Review Commission, which will go out of business on December 31, 1985.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh lashed out at legislative leaders, particularly Republicans, for postponing by one year a decision on the LCB's future, something he has made a top priority.

headline: Goode Hits 'Unfair' $200M Budget Cuts
abstract: According to Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, if Congress enacts the budget cuts that Reagan is proposing, Philadelphia will lose more than $200 million in federal funds for its 1986-87 operating and capital budgets .  Good says that SEPTA (South Eastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority) will be hit the hardest and would have to cut routes and charge higher fares.  Philadelphia would have to make cuts in reconstruction projects and assistance to the poor.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article outlines important events that happened on March 11th throughout history.

headline: For my next trick...
abstract: A cartoon shows US President Ronald Reagan trying to get an elephant, which has the word "Budget" written around its neck, to balance on a stool.  Reagan then pulls the rug out from under the stool and the elephant falls flat.  The final slide shows a moster with "Deficit" written around its neck; the monster is about to pull the rug out from under President Reagan as he stands on the stool.

headline: 42 hurt as chemical cloud spews from Arco plant in West Chester
abstract: Fourty-two people were hurt yesterday when a 1,500-gallon brew of chemicals overheated and blew out a release valve.  This caused a white cloud of chemicals to blow east towards Philadelphia.  At the peak of the crisis, Chester County officials declared a state of emergency and readied themselves to evacuate the roughly 30,000 residents whose homes were in the clouds path.  The leak was declared under control at 2:30 a.m., and the state of emergency ended an hour and 15 minutes later.  The 42 residents who required medical attention complained of skin, eye, and throat burns, and one man needed to be hospitalized due to asthmatic complications.  It will be several days before Arco Chemical Company officials know whether human or mechanical error caused the leak.  The Environmental Protection Agency characterized the gases that leaked as irritating but not toxic.

headline: Michigan Legislature Passes Seat-Belt Bill
abstract: The Michigan Senate sent legislation to Michigan Governor James Blanchard that requires automobile drivers and front-seat passengers to wear seat belts.  The bill will take effect in July 1985 and imposes fines of $10 for drivers.

headline: Rape data targets victims: Assaults often go unreported
abstract: The US Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Statistics released a report based on findings from the National Crime Survey, which furnishes information on both reported and unreported crimes.  The report showed that only about half of rapes or attempted rapes are reported to authorities.  They estimated 1.5 million rapes or attempted rapes took place between 1973-82.

headline: Legal gambling's foes, fans ante up for next hand
abstract: Special interest groups and legislators met head-on to discuss the future of legalized gambling in taverns.  A bill to repeal a law permitting card games in bars and taverns is expected to be sent from the state House to the Senate soon.  The Senate will then have to decided whether to approve it or send it to a conference committee.  Legislators give their thoughts on legalized gambling in the state.

headline: GOP adopts non-endorsement stance: Decision may hurt judicial candidate
abstract: Republican leaders have ruled against judicial endorsements in Superior Court races, a decision that may hurt the candidacy of the party's nominee, Jon LaFaver of New Cumberland.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article outlines important events that happened on March 12th throughout history.

headline: For taxes: AFL-CIO head asks delay of proposed income tax cut
abstract: Julius Uehlein, president of the PA American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations, said that Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposed personal income tax cut should be delayed or be phased in over two years.  Uehlein believes that an incremental process is needed given the state's financial health.

headline: Another Bond Issue Proposed: Asbestos in Schools
abstract: This editorial expresses concerns about a proposed $300 million bond issue to pay for the removal of asbestos from schools.  The editorial is concerned that school districts will not be able to pursue lawsuits against those who supplied asbestos.

headline: More on Seat Belts
abstract: A letter to the editor argues in favor of legislation that recently passed the PA Senate.  The legislation requires seat belts to be worn by all PA drivers and their front-seat passengers.  The author dismisses the argument that the state would be infringing on drivers rights by forcing them to wear seat belts.  The author also does not buy the argument that legislation requiring seat belts to be worn is akin to legislation banning smoking, drinking, or overeating.

headline: Rendell plans criminal probe over MOVE bomb
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell announced that his office will conduct a criminal investigation into how Philadelphia's top police officials were misinformed about the composition of the bomb that ignited a May 13, 1985 fire.  11 people died as a result of the fire, which was started in an attempt to evict MOVE members from their West Philadelphia home.  A focus of the investigation is likely to be police officer William Klein, who constructed the explosive device dropped on the roof of the MOVE compound; Klein neglected to inform anyone that it was made of C-4, a powerful explosive.  An official in Rendell's office stated that this revelation is inconsistent with official accounts of the incident.

headline: Legislators face long final week
abstract: Before its holiday break, the PA Legislature faces another long week of work.  In particular, the Legislature must decide what to do about the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB).  Legislators in the PA House appear ready to take up a measure that would re-establish the LCB with a separate enforcement division for policing the liquor code.  Both the PA Senate and the House are examining the entire liquor system as part of their review of the LCB, which will cease operations in 1986 unless renewed by the Legislature.  The Legislature also must deal with legislation authorizing PA to host a regional low-level radioactive waste disposal site.

headline: GOP caucus stays of Thorny-Specter fight
abstract: The caucus controlling the largest block of Republicans in PA is split, and will not endorse incumbent Republican US Senator Arlen Specter in his bid for re-election, according to party sources.  The caucus wants to remain neutral in the possible battle between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and US Senator Arlen Specter.  There have been reports that Specter may attempt to force Thornburgh's hand by calling for an endorsement at a meeting of the Republican State Committee.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article outlines important events that happened on March 21st throughout history.  It also provides celebrity birthdays for March 21st and a "thought for the day."

headline: Going for tax reform
abstract: This editorial supports President Ronald Reagan's proposed tax reform.

headline: Asbestos removal aid
abstract: This editorial lauds a proposal of state Representative James Gallagher.  The proposal calls for a $300 million bond issue to pay for the removal of asbestos from PA schools.  Such legislation would provide state funding for the removal of asbestos and would help to relieve local governments' financial burdens.

headline: More Politics as Usual
abstract: An editorial looks at how the new members of the PA Turnpike Commission got their jobs.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh appointed James Malone, a former finance chairman of the PA Republican Party, and James Goodman, a Democrat who was recommended by PA House Democratic Floor Leader James Manderino.  Goodman has a political reputation, as he was manager of several campaigns for US Congressman Allen Ertel.  The editorial already has praised the efforts of those involved for breaking the political deadlock.  However, it should be noted that politics and patronage will still play a significant part in running the Turnpike Commission.

headline: Rendell, Greenleaf propose minimum drug sentences
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell and state Senator Stewart Greenleaf have called for the passage of legislation requiring minimum prison sentences for crimes involving large quantities of dangerous drugs.

headline: Like other agencies: Game panel warrants review
abstract: A letter to the editor from state Representative Max Pievsky says that the PA Game Commission should not be exempt from a fiscal review or from the sunset review process.

headline: GOP chief denies CTA bribe
abstract: PA Republican Party Chairman Robert Asher, while recalling no discussions of campaign contributions with officials of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), testified at the CTA bribery trial of attorneys William Smith and Alan Stoneman.  Asher testified that he placed several calls to the state Treasury Department at their request.  John Torquato, head of CTA, has said that he and Smith offered Asher a $500,000 campaign contribution for the Republican State Committee in connection with the state contract CTA was seeking.  Asher acknowledged using his political contacts to help Smith and Torquato, but he denied there was talk of campaign contributions related to either contract.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article outlines important events that happened on March 4th throughout history.  It also provides a "thought for the day."

headline: Governor OKs state spending of $9.3 billion
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed the state's $9.3 billion budget bill on June 30th and related tax bills on July 1st.  Thornburgh proposed a $9 billion budget in February and asked legislators to cut the personal income tax rate from 2.35% to 2.15%.  The Legislature, in a budget compromise worked out by leaders from both chambers, set the rate at 2.2% and the budget at $9.3 billion.

headline: Back-to-nature plan for suburban rabbits
abstract: The PA Game Commission has proposed to catch 60,000 cottontail rabbits in urban and suburban areas; the commission will transport them to state game lands and other rural areas. If the state Legislature approves higher hunting license fees, this proposal will be undertaken as one of six new projects.  Only about 5% of the rabbits are expected to survive, but the agency considers it a good will public-relations gesture for the hunters.

headline: More transportation rights in bill
abstract: The PA House of Representatives gave unanimous approval yesterday to a bill that would enable local governments in Allegheny County to combine private and public funds for transportation projects.  A law was enacted in July permitting the formation of transportation partnerships in all of the state's counties except Allegheny.  State Representative Ron Gamble removed Allegheny County from the earlier law because of his concern that it might lead to the passage of a transit tax, but he is now the sponsor of legislation that would make Allegheny County eligible for the program.

headline: Rendell: Halt MOVE Suit
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Edward G. Rendell and Medical Examiner Marvin Aronson filed objections in court to an effort by lawyer William Kunstler to force a grand jury investigation and a coroner's inquest into the May 13 MOVE confrontation.  Kunstler, a prominent civil rights lawyer, filed suit on behalf of Louise James--the mother of one of the MOVE members who died in the disaster and owner of the Osage Avenue house occupied by MOVE members--and Stnaley Branche, a businessman and former civil rights leader.  In preliminary objections to the suit, Rendell and Aronson claimed that those filing the suit did not have "a clear legal right to relief."

headline: Liquor board chief says governor is in comtempt of court
abstract: PA Liquor Control Board Chairman Daniel Pennick has filed a petition in Commonwealth Court saying that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and a two of his top aides should be held in contempt of court for violating a 1984 Commonwealth Court ruling that prohibits them from cutting jobs at the Liquor Control Board (LCB).  At issue is whether Thornburgh and his two aides violated the court order by telling the LCB that 190 positions were being eliminated.  Thornburgh's spokesman admitted that the 1984 ruling prohibited the administration from acting, but he said the current reductions are part of an overall workforce slash.

headline: GOP likely to take shot at Gallagher
abstract: An opinion piece examines the race for the 141st PA Legislative District between incumbent State Representative James Gallagher and Republican Ralph McClellan Jr.  The author believes that the race will tell a lot about whether Briston Township Republicans can parlay their election victories this year into a string of glorious campaigns.  Bristol Township means a lot to Democrats because of its huge majority in Democratic voter registration.  Republicans finally have a candidate in McClellan who may be able to generate interest among voters.  Given the upcoming Democratic battle between incumbent PA Senator Craig Lewis and challenger John Cordisco for the 6th District Senate seat, the race will be even more appealing.

headline: Highlights in History
abstract: This article reviews significant events that occurred on July 25 throughout history.  Among the highlights are King Henry IV of France converting to Roman Catholicism in 1593, Benito Mussolini being dismissed as Italy's premier during WWII in 1943, and the signing of a treaty prohibiting nuclear weapons testing in the atmosphere, space or underwater in 1963.  The article also looks at significant events that occurred on July 25 ten years ago, five years ago, and one year ago.  Finally, it gives a thought for the day, by James Russell Lowell, an American poet.

headline: Governor pledges to reduce 2 taxes
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will include personal and corporate tax cuts in his 1986-1987 budget proposal.  Thornburgh stated that Pennsylvania is currently projected to have a surplus of $110 million in 1986.  PA House Majority Leader James Manderino, a Democrat, said that the tax cuts could have been larger for 1986.

headline: Bad water in Third World killing millions every year
abstract: The lack of clean, ample water is a matter of daily terror in Third World countries.  According to the World Health Organization, about 80 percent of all sickness and disease in the world arises from inadequate water or poor sanitation.

headline: Motorist loses battle over drunkenness test
abstract: If motorists arrested for suspected drunken driving refuse to take a breath test, the Commenwealth Court has ruled that they can have their driver's license suspended.  The court cited time as the main reason for its ruling.

headline: Replace chair with needle?
abstract: PA State Representative James Barber plans to reintroduce a bill that would replace the electric chair with lethal injection.  Barber, who opposes the death penalty in any form, believes that this method of capital punishment is far more humane and leads to less suffering.  Barber had introduced this bill in 1983, but it was not acted upon.  With Governor Dick Thornburgh's signing of three death warrants two weeks ago, the death-penalty issue has returned to prominence.

headline: Liquor board's enforcement power
abstract: This editorial supports a bill before the state Senate that would transfer the PA Liquor Control Board's law enforcement power to the state Attorney General, but wants any action to be delayed until the Senate Law and Justice Committee makes its recommendations about the fate of the LCB.  The editorial urges the state Senate to not renew the LCB; the author also suggests giving enforcement power to the Attorney General.

headline: GOP split feared by Heinz
abstract: US Senator John Heinz said yesterday that a primary race between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and US Senator Arlen Specter could deal a severe blow to the PA Republican Party and could lead to the defeat of Lieutenant Governor William Scranton in his bid to become governor.  Heinz also said that the Republicans have their work cut out for them to retain their majority in the US Senate; Heinz also spoke on President Ronald Reagan's tax policy and international relations.

headline: History highlights
abstract: An article reviews the major historical events that have occurred on August 29th.  Among the highlights are the death of Brigham Young in 1877, US Senator Strom Thurmond ending a record filibuster of more than 24 hours, and the Beatles giving their last concert in 1966.

headline: Governor: Cut tax rates. Swelling surplus key item
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh, citing a stronger than expected economic recovery, announced that Pennsylvania is running a budget surplus of $297 million.  The governor argued that the surplus should be used to cut the personal-income tax rate and unemployment-fund contributions.  Democratic lawmakers are exploring other options for the surplus.

headline: Bill unfair to trappers
abstract: This letter to the editor argues that PA sportsmen are under attack because of a new bill that would ban leghold traps.  The author believes that the PA Game Commission is doing an excellent job with trapper education, but argues they could use more support.  The author does not like proposed alternatives to leghold traps, and he is concerned that the Legislature will come after hunter's guns next.

headline: Not save bridge? Incomprehensible!
abstract: An opinion piece argues that the bridge in Luzerne County connecting Nanticoke and West Nanticoke is vital to the area and needs to be repaired.  Luzerne County only has $4.6 million in federal, state and county money available for much-needed repairs to four of its bridges; it needs an additional $4.5 million to do the job right on all of them.  Columnist says that more than 4,000 people signed a petition to save the Nanticoke bridge, and that some of the money from the state's $1.3 billion bridge repair program should go to repair that bridge.

headline: Reply to the Judge
abstract: A letter to the editor chastises Judge Louis Hill's sentence of William Chestnut.  The letter writer is Chestnut's brother, who was tried by Hill previously.

headline: Little Banks Bought Time
abstract: PA's big banks had been pushing hard for an interstate banking law, but it was the little banks that got their way.  Big banks wanted  to expand across state lines; they also wanted protection from an onslaught of large New York City banks.  Small banks are going after the same protection from big banks within the state.  Those who want limitations on interstate banking say jobs would be threatened if a few big banks drew most of the state's deposits.  Senate lawmakers, beleaguered by debate over the Philadelphia Convention Center and other isses, decided to put off their decision until later.

headline: Gov. Edwards Offers No Indictment Odds: Louisianan Says He Would Stay in Office
abstract: Louisiana Governor Edwin Edwards said he did not know if he was about to be indicted on charges of misusing his office to benefit former business associations.  He says that if he is indicted, he will remain in office and possibly run for Senate.

headline: Like a father: Harrisburg's kindly bishop remembered
abstract: A columnist fondly remembers the Reverend George L. Leech, the bishop of Harrisburg for more than 36 years, who died in March 1985.  He discusses Leech's past and his friendship with state Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman.

headline: Governors split as Reagan pushes his tax overhaul
abstract: A group of eight governors, all of whom were handpicked by the White House, gave mixed reviews of President Reagan's tax-revision package.  The governors were picked to help the president offset mounting objections to his tax proposal.  The five Republican governors, including PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, wholeheartedly endorsed the president's plan, while the three Democratic governors objected to several features of Reagan's plan.

headline: Bills seek EPA probe of radon gas in "Reading Prong"
abstract: Legislation introduced in the US House and Senate yesterday called on the Environmental Protection Agency to explore ways to eliminate problems posed by radon gas in eastern Pennsylvania.  Of specific concern is a granite formation that contains a seam of uranium from which radioactive radon gas is escaping.  Inspections of homes in the area found that scores of them had radon present at unacceptable levels.  Exposure to radon can increase the risk on cancer.

headline: Officials Hope to Drive You Away
abstract: State Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson had a press conference with local officials to discuss the Schuylkill Expressway Improvement Project; he also  warned motorists that there would be considerable delays.  The PA Department of Transportation is urging commuters to find alternative routes and to leave the expressway only to trucks.

headline: Reports of crime show new decline: Rape, assaults increase in same period
abstract: The Federal Bureau of Investigation's Uniform Crime Report, released April 20, 1985, showed that reported crime decreased 3% in 1984, including a 4% drop in murders, but rapes and aggravated assaults rose at the fastest pace since 1980.  These figures are based on a compilation of crimes reported by nearly 13,000 state and local police agencies around the country.

headline: Local group assures Bucs proposal to buy is on deck
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri, Allegheny County Commission Chairman Tom Foerster, Westinghouse Electric Chairman Douglas Danforth, and US Steel Chairman David Roderick met to discuss the future of the Pittsburgh Pirates baseball team.  After the meeting, Caliguiri met with Pirate President Dan Galbreath and assured him that the city would do everything possible to keep the Pirates in Pittsburgh.  Galbreath wants to sell the team after a $6 million loss in 1984 and has been courted by buyers who would move the Pirates out of town.

headline: Gov. Thornburgh Versus Specter?
abstract: This editorial argues that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh would not beat US Senator Arlen Specter for his US Senate seat.  Though Arlen Specter is a bit too liberal for some more conservative voters in PA, he does have strong support in Philadelphia.  With his unpopular labor contracts, Governor Thornburgh has angered many of the most politically powerful unions in PA, such as the PA State Education Association and state-employee unions.  The editorial argues that Governor Thornburgh is just doing some political manuevering to keep his name in the news, as he would be a strong candidate for becoming a US Vice Presidential nominee on the on the Republican Presidential ticket in 1988.

headline: Pa. excels in new rating of cities
abstract: Robert M. Pierce, an associate professor of geography at the State University of New York at Cortland, analyzed cities in the US to determine the "most liveable city"; his results were published in the July issue of American Demographics Magazine.  Five of PA's metropolitan areas were in the top 25--including Pittsburgh at number six, the Harrisburg-Lebanon-Carlisle area at 21, the Scranton-Wilkes-Barre area at 22, Philadelphia at number 11, and Reading at number 14.  Pierce's analysis was based on a statistical method that ranked such factors as economic health, weather and crime as being more important than the presence of a symphony orchestra or a museum.

headline: Gray rejects tax hike: Supports freeze to reduce deficit
abstract: US Rep William Gray III (D-Philadelphia), the new chairman of the House Budget Committee, says he opposes a tax increase but favors deficit reduction through an across-the-board spending freeze in all government agencies.  Senate Republicans have also included a freeze in their plan to reduce the deficit--a plan that differs from President Reagan's.

headline: Bottle Bill
abstract: A letter to the editor argues against the proposed "bottle bill"--legislation that would require a $.05 deposit on all beer, mineral water and soft drink containers made of glass, metal, or plastic sold in Pennsylvania.  The author urges enforcement of the littering fine, rather than the enactment of this new bill.  He also says that enacting the bottle bill could cause the closing of several glass plants throughout the state.

headline: P&LE agrees to buy parts of Conrail
abstract: Norfolk Southern Corporation was required to sell portions of the rail system that it would acquire in its proposed acquisition of Conrail.  These measures were required by the anti-trust section of the Justice Department in its review of the Norfolk Southern bid to purchase Conrail.  Pittsburgh & Lake Erie Railroad will acquire the rights to some 480 miles of track.

headline: Reps. William Gray III, Robert Borski, Thomas Foglietta visit fire scene
abstract: A photo depicts US Representatives William Gray III, Thomas Foglietta, and state Representative Robert Borski visiting the fire scene in West Philadelphia.  Over 50 houses were destroyed in West Philadelphia when Philadelphia police tried to evict the radical group MOVE from their Osage-Avenue fortress.

headline: LTV coke battery shuts down today
abstract: Despite an 11th-hour appeal from the United Steelworkers union to keep the battery running while the union studies whether the Works could be independently operated, LTV Steel Corporation plans to bank the fire at its last operating coke battery at Aliquippa Works .  LTV blamed high import levels for its decision to indefinitely idle the coke-making facility at its Aliquippa plant.

headline: Governor absent from Holtzman bash
abstract: A VIP list that included some of the top members of President Ronald Reagan's administration and the Republican Party showed up to a fundraiser for Marc Holtzman, who is considering running for the GOP nomination for PA's 11th Congressional district.  Holtzman is quite popular within the Republican Party, having been the executive director of the PA Reagan-Bush campaign in 1980.  Holtzman says that he did not invite PA Governor Dick Thornburgh because Holtzman supports US Senator Arlen Specter and thinks that the Thornburgh's consideration of running against Specter is inappropriate.  Thornburgh's Press Secretary, David Runkel, claims that the Governor did have an invitation, but that he does not go to pre-primary activities.  Holtzman has already raised $360,000, which is more than any other Republican challenger; he said that he expects to raise about $950,000 to finance his campaign through the general election.  Holtzman also plans to bring in some of the rising stars in the GOP to campaign for him.

headline: Reagan cancer is called "confined"
abstract: Yesterday, July 15, 1985, US President Ronald Reagan had a cancerous tumor removed from his colon.  However, there was no evidence that the cancer had spread beyond the inner wall of President Reagan's colon.  Doctor Steven Rosenberg of the National Cancer Institute said that the chances of the President's five-year survival are greater than 50%.

headline: Inappropriate 'reform': Don't tax employee benefits
abstract: This letter to the editor says that President Ronald Reagan's tax plan is a bad idea because it would tax Americans on almost all of their employee benefits.  The author, a member of the United Auto Workers, argues that tax simplification and reform must not be used as a guise for shifting even more of the tax burden onto the backs of overtaxed Americans.

headline: Bottle law: Deposit-return key to clean countryside
abstract: This editorial urges legislators to pass a "bottle bill" that would require a deposit on beverage bottles and cans.  The author says that states with bottle laws are experiencing a 90% return rate for deposit containers; such legilsation will also help with landfill space.

headline: Panel: Who will run Amtrak?
abstract: US Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole fielded questions posed by House Transportation subcommittee members.  She fielded questions about Amtrak and who will run the company if the government pulls its $648 million annual subsidy.  Dole said that at least part of Amtrak should be preserved, but she had no alternative to the federal funds that have kept Amtrak running for 14 years.

headline: Rev Forms 2nd Panel On MOVE
abstract: The Reverend C. Hamilton Robinson, pastor of the Christian Fellowship Church in Philadelphia, has organized a community panel to hold a "fair and impartial" hearing on the city's handling of the May 13 MOVE confrontation.  The 11-member Philadelphia Investigative Committee will hear testimony from eyewitnesses to the MOVE siege and will release their results.  Three of the panel members, including Robinson, have been vocal critics of Mayor Wilson Goode, but claim that their results will be as impartial as the investigative commission appointed by the mayor.

headline: Luzerne tavern owner leads charge against tourney ban
abstract: Members of the Luzerne County Restaurant and Hotel Owners Association traveled to Harrisburg to lobby against a possible ban on holding cash card tournaments in bars and restaurants in the state.  They received a favorable greeting from some legislators, but were told by others that voters do not support gambling.

headline: Governor and Democratic leader clash over state political scandals
abstract: Democratic State Committee Chairman Edward Mezvinsky and Governor Dick Thornburgh exchanged barbs after Mezvinsky accused Republican Party leaders of failing to curb corruption and of allowing a shadow of scandal to darken PA's political landscape.  Mezvinsky singled out Republican involvement in two scandals that have been the focus of recent trials--one involving the Computer Technology Associates bribery trial and the other involving a doctored photograph being used in a Republican campaign.  Thornburgh accused Mezvinsky of making "political hay" and of engaging in a "character assassination."

headline: Reagan Cancer Was 'Confined': Chance of recovery 'excellent'
abstract: President Ronald Reagan was told by his doctors that the tumor removed from his colon was cancerous, but that there was no indication the cancer had spread beyond his bowel.  Dr. Steven Rosenberg of the National Cancer Institute said that the President has an "excellent" chance of living a normal life.

headline: Investing Surplus
abstract: This editorial is critical of state politicians and their proposals to spend the state's budget surplus.  And  although some have proposed a tax cut, the author questions why a surplus was generated in the first place, and concludes that the only thing worse than a deficit is a surplus, as it brings out the worst in givers and takers.

headline: Bowley Hails Committee Approval Of Bottle Bill
abstract: State Representative Curt Bowley gave a speech at the Pennsylvania Grange convention.  Representative Bowley touted the approval of a bill that requires stores to refund customers five cents for each beer and soft drink container returned; the bill also bans pull tabs and metal cans.  This "bottle bill" was the first of its kind to pass committee in 15 years.  The Conservation Committee also approved legislation that allows for a low-level radioactive waste disposal site in the state.  Bowely urged everyone in attendance to become aware of issues and use letters and telephone calls to make him aware of their importance.

headline: Parking spaces get Walker's attention
abstract: US Congressman Robert Walker was one of 38 members of the US House of Representatives who complained last week to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that US Supreme Court officials and diplomats should not be using Congress' parking lot at the National Airport.  A formal letter complaining about the situation was sent to the FAA and was signed by both liberals and conservatives in the House.  Legislation is currently pending to turn the National Airport over to a regional authority.  US Senator John Heinz is undecided on President Ronald Reagan's farm bill because of a provision to lower the support price of government purchased surplus milk.  Heinz and US Senator Arlen Specter also backed a Senate amendment last week that restored $570 million to the General Revenue Sharing program.  Some PA local governments depend on this federal revenue sharing program for 15% to 20% of their revenues.

headline: Revenue agents sue agency official
abstract: Two agents of the PA State Department of Revenue claim that William Bucher, head of the department's Bureau of Motor License Funds, violated the state's Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Control Act by tape-recording a two-hour discussion without their knowledge.  The agents have filed suit.  The suit names as defendants, among others, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.  The two agents claim that during the two-hour discussion, which they believed was confidential, they aired complaints about other agents and their immediate supervisor.  The next week at a meeting, Bucher revealed that the discussion had been taped and disclosed contents of the discussion.  The two agents claim the disclosure has done great harm to their relationships with their supervisor and coworkers.

headline: More falling behind on mortgage payments
abstract: Despite a decline in the state's unemployment rate late last year, the number of Pennsylvanians who were behind in their mortgage payments grew to record levels--9.45%--by the end of 1984.  Experts say changes in delinquency rates generally lag behind changes in unemployment.

headline: Governor eyes race for Senate
abstract: An opinion section looks at future of some of PA's politicians.  In regards to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh challenging US Senator Arlen Specter, the author says that, although Specter has "straddled the fence" on a number of social issues, his record with the African-American community is far better than Thornburgh's.  The opinion section praises Specter for voting against William Bradford Reynolds' nomination for associate attorney general, and blasts Thornburgh for being a shadow of US President Ronald Reagan.  The editorial also criticizes Thornburgh for not divesting PA's pension funds from South Africa.  In other news, there is mounting speculation that former US Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis may run for the Republican nomination for Governor next year; Democratic PA State Representative Dwight Evans is continuing to make strong moves to become a candidate for Lieutenant Governor.  Jimmie Smith has announced that he will be a Democratic candidate for the 181st Legislative District in 1986; he will run against State Representative Alfonso Deal.

headline: Seeing Ourselves as Others See Us: How MOVE Tragedy Looked Abroad
abstract: Columnist discusses how the British media viewed the MOVE tragedy.  He says that the British media viewed the situation as a small but harmless group of back-to-nature wackos destroyed by the typical American macho overkill.  Columnist says that the US should do something to change its "international outlaw" image.

headline: IRS cutting down interest on overdue refund checks
abstract: The Internal Reveune Service (IRS) has been following a policy that reduces the amount of interest paid on backloged tax refunds.  This policy has lowered the effective interest rate on most late refunds to 9 or 11 percent--rather than the 13 percent owed.  The IRS policy has angered both taxpayers and lawmakers, but has reduced the IRS' overall interest expense by millions.

headline: Brandt Poll:  Yes to Bottle Bill, Higher Hunting Fees
abstract: PA State Representative Kenneth Brandt recently sent out questionaires to his constituents in Lancaster County.  Of the 22,000 questionnaires sent out, just under 2,000 responses were received.  Among the responses, 72% of respondents supported the PA Game Commission's decision to raise hunting-license fees, and 71% supported a "bottle bill" that requires mandatory deposits on bottles, cans, and other containers.  A large majority also favored laws to ban or restrict smoking in public.

headline: PAT cuts defended
abstract: This editorial labels a letter written by State Representative Fred Trello as extremely irresponsible.  The letter deals with Port Authority Transit cuts.

headline: Richmond Decides to Stay Despite MOVE Criticism
abstract: Philadelphia Fire Commissioner William Richmond, citing support from firefighters and Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, said he will not resign in the face of criticism over his handling of the MOVE incident.  Richmond has become the only top official directed involved in last May's tragedy to stay in Goode's administration.  Richmond noted that the final report of the MOVE commission had not been issued, and that he may change his mind later.

headline: N.J. officials criticize Pa. card law
abstract: New Jersey gaming regulators are criticizing the PA legislature for passing a liquor law with a loophole that allows blackjack and poker games in bars and restaurants.  NJ is concerned that it will affect their Atlantic City casinos, and also that organized crime will become a factor in the unregulated games.

headline: Governor hails 6 state women
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has chosen six women as 1985 Distinguished Daughters of PA.  Since 1948, the governor has named between two and ten Distinguished Daughters annually.  The women selected are nominated by organizations within the sate in recognition of their accomplishments.  The names and a brief bio of the women are included in the article.

headline: Shapp to take part in agency's events
abstract: Former Governor Milton J. Shapp will speak Monday, May 20th as part of the Dauphin County Area Agency on Aging's "Anniversaries Celebration."  Dr. Arthur S. Flemming, former secretary of the Department of Health, Education and Welfare, will also speak at the event.

headline: Jobless rate in district averaged 12.1% last year
abstract: According to the US Department of Labor, civilian unemployment in the Pittsburgh district averaged 12.1% during 1984, a decrease of 2.9% from the 1983 average of 15%..  The report defines the Pittsburgh district as Allegheny, Beaver, Washington and Westmoreland Counties.

headline: Cause for concern at DER Advisory Council
abstract: This letter to the Editor expresses concern about the status of the Citizens Advisory Council (CAC) to the state Department of Environmental Resources (DER).  The CAC reviews the work of the DER and makes appropriate suggestions regarding PA environmental laws.  Recent changes in the council, such as the appointment of five individuals with an industry orientation, mean a lack of membership continuity in the CAC; this is a cause for concern.  The council's membership is especially of concern given recent Environmental-Protection-Agency proposals that would make individual states responsible for setting certain environmental standards.  Such proposals make it imperative that the Citizens Advisory Council be composed of qualified people who have an interest in protecting the environmental health of PA.

headline: PAT gets grant to complete subway line: $19.7 million freed by US covers cost
abstract: The US Urban Mass Transportation Administration (UMTA) released $19.7 million to the Port Authority Transit.  The money will cover cost escalations in the 10 and 1/2 mile Light Rail Transit line being constructed between Downtown Pittsburgh and South Hills Village.  The grant from UMTA's Rail Modernization Discretionary Account assures completion of the entire subway line by fall 1986.

headline: Richmond Was Ready To Testify
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor and Fire Commissioner William Richmond took opposite approaches to their testimony before the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission.  Sambor testified without having read the testimony of Mayor Wilson Goode, and without having followed the proceedings at all.  Richmond and his lawyers spent hours with him watching video tapes of the hearings and reviewing his notes from May 13, the day of the MOVE incident.  Richmond was the first public official to break down on the stand, but he quickly recovered, and at times it seemed as if he was directing the proceedings.  Richmond also questioned his subordinates about the events of May 13, something that Goode and Sambor did not do.  Sambor's strategy, according to some lawyers, may have made him appear passive, but it also limited some lines of questioning the commission could pursue with him.  Richmond, on the other hand, chose a more active role.

headline: Naked cities
abstract: This editorial examines the effect of PA's "sovereign-immunity" principle, which granted governmental bodies immunity from lawsuits.  As this doctrine has been struck down by states throughout the country, juries have handed down large monetary rewards against states, municipalities and school districts.  A hearing of the PA House Insurance Committee this week looked at one of the side effects of these lawsuits; insurance companies are increasing their premiums and in some cases dropping their insurance of governmental units.  Some of the suggested solutions to this problem at the hearing were creating self-insurance limits, limits on judgments, and forming a massive self-insurance pool.  The PA Supreme Court has invalidated the principle of sovereign immunity.

headline: Governor hints at Senate race if poll shows it would help party
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, while continuing to deny any present intention of running against US Senator Arlen Specter for his Senate seat, hinted that he may run against Specter if poll results show Thornburgh's candidacy would help the Republicans and President Ronald Reagan.  Thornburgh also called premature reports that Ed Rollins would run his campaign against Specter.  Rollins, who is a good frend of Thornburgh's, is leaving his White House post and would like to run Thornburgh's campaign against Specter.  Specter maintains that Thornburgh will not run and will end up supporting him in the GOP primary.

headline: The Governor's Home Is Everybody's House
abstract: A columnist discusses the history of the Governor's mansion.

headline: Legislators' Panel Backs Tax Revision: Policy Shifts After White House Push
abstract: The National Conference of State Legislators (NCSL) is concerned with President Ronald Reagan's tax revision plan--specifically its restrictions on tax-exempt bonds and its elimination of deductions for state and local taxes.  However, the NCSL did formally endorse tax simplification, which President Reagan will try to push through Congress in the fall.

headline: Centralia loses its bid for $2.4 million: US agency denies 'last-resort' money
abstract: The US Office of Surface Mining denied a request by the State Department of Environmental Resources for $2.4 million in "last-resort" federal housing money to relocate residents of Centralia.  Borough residents are choosing to move because the area is on top of an underground mine fire.

headline: PAT Justice
abstract: This editorial is critical of Jim Manderino and other PA House Democrats for klling Bill 1505, legislation which would have allowed the Port Authority Transit to keep rolling along at a reasonable cost.  The bill would have encouraged collective bargaining as the best way to achieve agreements and would have eliminated the current binding arbitration which has created high and uncontrollable labor costs.  These labor costs have hit riders and resulted in service reductions.  The editorial calls on Democrats who sponsored the bill to stand up and fight James Manderino over his dictatorial procedure.

headline: Richmond:  Sambor was in command
abstract: Philadelphia Fire Commissioner William Richmond told the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission yesterday that he considered himself a subordinate of Philadelphia Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor during the MOVE confrontation of May 13.  Sambor and his deputy fire commissioner both indicated that they did not support Sambor's characterization of them as equals able to challenge or disobey police directives.  Richmond told the commission that he learned of plans to assault MOVE's compound only 72 hours before they went into action.  Commission members also heard from a few police involved in process of detonating the bomb on MOVE's roof.  However, the commission is still working with the Fraternal Order of Police to get testimony from other members of the Philadelphia Bomb Squad who have refused to testify.  The commission also heard testimony police officer Lawrence D'Ulisse about the detonation of the bomb on MOVE's roof.

headline: New director begins job with a Lotto activities
abstract: Blair Gettig recently took over as executive director of the PA Lottery Bureau.  Gettig replaces Lynn Nelson.  Since 1974, Nelson served as director of the PA Lottery Bureau; he recently left the state to become a lottery consultant.

headline: Governor Kukovich?
abstract: An editorial discusses state Representative Allen Kukovich's gubernatorial campaign.  It criticizes him as too far left and urges voters not to support him.

headline: The Scene: In Philadelphia and its suburbs
abstract: This article shows side-by-side pictures of comedian Ed Wynn and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.  The picture is one in a series of celebrity look-alikes.

headline: Legislature nears vote on budget
abstract: With a legal deadline only two days away, the state Legislature moved towards final approval of a $9.26 billion state budget and a tax reduction package of nearly $300 million.  Although a tentative agreement on the tax and budget bills was reached among legislative leaders, final action was delayed several hours by last-minute negotiations.  Unless a formal budget is approved, the state will be unable to pay its bills or its employees after June 30, the end of the current fiscal year.

headline: Changes in EPA PA Role Suggested
abstract: PA has applied for final authorization to operate its hazardous waste management program without the US Environmental Protection Agency, which would make the agency more of an overseer than a regulator.  If the request is approved, the PA Department of Environmental Resources will be able to issue permits for treatment, storage, and disposal of hazardous wastes.  To receive final authorization, state programs must be equivalent to the federal program.

headline: PAT looks to Mellon for loan approval
abstract: Port Authority Transit (PAT) officials believe that the PAT can stay in operation beyond June, 1985 if Mellon Bank renews a 90-day, $14 million line of credit.  The PAT's 1985-86 fiscal year begins in July, when PAT will get more county, state and federal government loans; this should enhance the chances of Mellon renewing its line of credit.  Without the money, the PAT could be forced to shut down services in June.

headline: Salmon awaiting word he's off bench
abstract: Senior Common Please Judge J. Quint Salmon says he has not been formally notified of a state Supreme Court order relieving him of his assignment as a visiting judge in Allegheny County.  The order will stay in place pending an investigation into Judge Salmon's dismissal of a rape case.  Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix released a statement announcing that he was relieving Salmon of his judicial responsibilities in Allegheny County.

headline: New Insurance Fund Billing: It's Two Fins Per Car
abstract: Under PA's new auto insurance law, insurance companies pay only up to $100,000 for an accident victim's medical expenses, and the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund will pay up to $1 million for medical expenses over that amount.  Motorists are billed $5 for each car and truck to set up the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund; the $5 is to be paid each year when renewing the vehicle's registration.

headline: Governor says he'll push to the end: Thornburgh outlines his 'unfinished agenda'
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh outlines his agenda for the rest of his second term.  This includes: Continuing his six year battle to get the state out of the liquor business and dismantling the Liquor Control Board; dissolving the impasse that leaves the PA Turnpike Commission adrift without direction; pushing for a judcial reform package that includes replacing judicial elections with a merit-selection process, and reforming the local tax system.

headline: What happened in the legislature?
abstract: This article looks at key bills considered by the PA Legislature during its current session.  Among the issues are:  radioactive-waste disposal, seat bealts, interest rates, judicial selection, anti-apartheid legislation, and the PA Liquor Control Board.

headline: Local jobless rate falls to 3-year low
abstract: Unemployment in the Pittsburgh area fell in December to its lowest level in three years.  The reasons cited for the drop were a sharp decline in both the size of the civilian labor force and the number of people counted as unemployed, as well as a slight increase in total employment.

headline: Chesapeake Bay finds friends in state landowners
abstract: In order to help clean up the Chesapeake Bay, more than 120 landowners along the lower Susquehanna River basin have applied for aid from the state Department of Environmental Resources (DER).  The DER is implementing a new cost-sharing program that will help control erosion and nutrient runoff for farmers in the area.

headline: PAT plans closure, scraps cuts in service
abstract: Port Authority Transit's (PAT) board of directors has elected to keep trolley, bus, train and incline service at current levels in the Pittsburgh area; the services will be kept until the agency runs out of money.  If the county or state governments do not come to the PAT's financial rescue, it promises to cripple Pittsburgh and restrict the mobility of 300,000 daily riders, including thousands with no other means of transportation.  PAT officials have been warning of an impending shutdown for months.

headline: Sambor out; Armstrong replaces him
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor formally tendered his resignation yesterday following an emotional farewell speech to his fellow police commanders.  Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, hours later, announced the appointment of Deputy Commissioner Robert Armstrong to serve as interim commissioner, and said that a formal search for a replacement for Sambor will begin.  In Goode's official statement on Sambor's resignation, he made no mention of the MOVE controversy, police corruption, or other issues that have plagued the police department under Sambor's command.

headline: No more lives for this CAT
abstract: This editorial praises the PA State Senate for restructuring the mechanism by which the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund is operated.  Unfortunately, the original exercise in collecting the CAT's fees will cost taxpayers hours of frustration and millions of dollars.  The editorial believes that the theory behind the CAT Fund, providing PA motorists coverage for massive medical bills, was sound.  However, the collection process, which the editorial examines closely, was anything but sound; it was more like a massive bureaucratic blunder.  The editorial does wonder why this blunder was not eliminated immediately.

headline: Governor, Goodling to challenge Specter?
abstract: US Congressman Bill Goodling is considering running for the Republican nomination for US Senate against incumbent Arlen Specter.  Representative Goodling believes that a Republican primary that involves Specter--and possibly Governor Thornburgh--could turn ugly, but says he would be the perfect candidate to "bring the party back together for November."  One thing that could stand in his way of getting the nomination could be fundraising, as he does not have the prowess of Specter or Thornburgh in the fundraising arena.

headline: What makes your state special?
abstract: This article contains the answers to several questions sent to the governors of all 50 states.  Some of the questions were:  "what's the one thing you wish your state had; what is your favorite weekend getaway; and what is the most romantic spot in your state?"

headline: Making the case for income-tax revision: In Malvern, President asks people to speak out for plan
abstract: In a speech to more than 10,000 people in Malvern, PA, President Reagan campaigned for a revisions to the federal income-tax code.  The visit to Malvern marked the end of the first week of President Reagan's public-opinion campaign for tax revision.  The president hopes that a tax-overhaul plan, and lower tax rates, will be the prime domestic legacy of his second term.

headline: Citing Need for Disposal
abstract: This photo depicts Raymond E. Hein, manager of Armco's Butler-Zanesville works, and Robert L. Clouse, supervising engineer, discussing the need for waste-disposal sites with state Environmental Resources Secretary Nicholas DeBenedictis.  Looking on are state Representatives Howard Fargo and protestors from Citizens Against Toxic Sites.

headline: PennDOT fix-it bill:  $1 billion
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT) spent just over $1 billion to rebuild, repair, and restore highways and bridges last year.  The department's construction program was centered during the year ending June 30 on finishing sections of the interstate highway system.  The $1 billion maintenance and construction bill is more than half the department's $1.9 billion annual budget and represents the largest amount that PennDOT has spent during any single year in its history.  The highlights of the $1 billion spent are examined in the last part of the article.

headline: Scranton targets crime on streets, in office: Measure would force authorities under indictment to step down
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton has proposed an anti-crime program that would require high-ranking state officials indicted on criminal charges to leave office.  The package also calls for strengthening state laws against drug traffickers and violent, repeat offenders, and would mandate minimum sentences for those convicted of rape or selling illegal drugs.  Scranton, who is running for governor on the Republican ticket, will unveil details of his proposed anti-crime package at four locations across the state.  His running mate, State Senator D. Michael Fisher, will explain the program at three locations around the state.  Scranton's proposed Code of Conduct Law would expand an executive order issued nearly six years ago by Governor Dick Thornburgh; the order requires employees under the governor's jurisdiction either to resign or be suspended until the charges against them are resolved.

headline: No problem seen in Pennsylvania
abstract: State-charted savings and loans in Ohio have been facing problems, but members of the PA Savings Association Insurance Corporation (PSAIC) say that they will not face the same problems because the laws in PA are more conservative.  After PA required deposit insurance for all state-chartered thrift institutions, PSAIC was set up for the state's smallest savings and loans .  The institutions covered by PSAIC generally don't qualify to be insured by the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation.

headline: Governor: No more concessions to end strike
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh said that the state would not make any changes in a tentative contract offer reached with the largest state employees' union.  The contract offer, which was accepted by leaders of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, calls for employees to get a 3% increase in each of the next three years; Thornburgh also won reductions or concessions on sick leave and vacation time.  The PA Social Services Union and the PA Employment Security Employees Association went on strike after being left out of negotiations that AFSCME and the United Food and Commerical Workers Union had with Administration Secretary Murray G. Dickman.

headline: Making the case for income-tax revision: Proposal is a major retreat from the progressive tax rate
abstract: The administration's tax proposal, promoted as a populist measure by President Ronald Reagan, represents a retreat from our progressive tax-rate system--a system originally designed to place a heavy burden on the rich.  The wealthiest Americans will benefit enormously from the administration's proposal.  The tax code, altered by inflation and legislative tinkering, has been placing a growing burden on working and middle-class Americans.

headline: Cleaning up abandoned coal mines in the state
abstract: In 1984 PA received $44.3 million in federal grant money to help clean up hazardous mines.  This year, the state is applying for $60 million to be used on projects considered  "life threatening."  This editorial urges the federal government to give more money and to clean up these sites as quickly as possible.

headline: PennDOT hears protests on Perry intersection
abstract: A group of 40 Perry County elected officials, area residents, and school bus drivers met with PA Department of Transportation District 8 engineer Robert Mueser yesterday to demand safety improvements on US Routes 11-15.  Residents voiced their concerns about the intersection of Limekiln Road--a heavily traveled highway where 8 people have died and 60 have been injured.  Several protesters had their own ideas about how to improve safety, including establishing a no-passing zone and reserving the middle lane for left-hand turns by northbound motorists.

headline: Shifting to private jails
abstract: This editorial examines the transition from public to private jails that is currently going on in Allegheny and Butler Counties.  The decision to turn over the operation of jails to private industry is experimental and precedent-setting for both counties.  Allegheny County intially resorted to allowing private jails because of overcrowding in several county prisons, while Butler County's move was more economic, allowing the county to save $200,000 a year.  The shifts to private industry are opposed strongly by prison-guard unions, as well as the PA State House, which voted last April to bar for-profit prisons from PA for a year.  The PA Senate, however, did not pick up the issue, allowing Allegheny and Butler Counties to pursue private jails; this issue will be under close scrutiny over the next few years.

headline: North Carolina Bustles With People and Money
abstract: Amid good news about the economy of the state, James Martin was sworn in as Governor of North Carolina.   Reports are indicating that NC is able to attract new residents and businesses and transfer to a modern and diversified economy.

headline: Governor's office studies clerk of courts controversy
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's office is examining Lebanon County's decades-old practice of electing two people to control the clerk of courts office.  In December 1984, the county commissioners of Lebanon announced plans to merge the clerk of courts office under the prothonotary, as the duties are currently split between the prothonotary and recorder of deeds.  The change was prompted by the discovery that $74,000 was missing from the office, as well as an internal audit that criticized the dual control system as ineffective and sloppy.  State Senator David Brightbill did raise some legal questions with Thornburgh's staff on this matter.

headline: More of us working, but the pay isn't going as far
abstract: Employment among the civilian population is the highest it has been since the government started keeping employment statistics.  This trend is obscured by an official unemployment rate that has remained stubbornly high, however.  Changes in workforce composition, as well the types of jobs available explain this trend.  In the last decade, almost half of the new jobs created were service-sector jobs; during this time manufacturing employment declined.

headline: Cloud of smoke may bear fruit
abstract: State Senator James Ross has asked that his constituents be exempted from annual auto-emissions inspections.  Senator Ross claims that industrial-plant shutdowns and high unemployment have combined to improve air quality in Beaver county.  Ross wants the Environmental Protection Agency to re-monitor various areas of the county.  He argues that thousands of unemployed people in the county are finding it hard to pay for car inspections and the corrective work that the EPA requires.

headline: PennDOT rescinds order forcing transit fare cuts
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT) rescinded an order requiring county and private transit systems to subsidize senior citizen fares or lose all lottery support.  Officials of many local transit systems around the state had threatened to reduce services or close up shop if PennDOT enforced the directive.  PennDOT officials, citing abuse by local systems, said the cuts were needed because the department does not have enough money in its Reduced Fare Program to cover the senior citizen subsidies.

headline: Should you not be able
abstract: A cartoon shows a cop sitting down and reading a long list of "rights" to a criminal he just caught.  The cartoon insinuates that there is little chance of the theif actually going to jail.  If he does go to jail, the state will finance his attorneys through the appeals process until the criminal is released or the state goes bankrupt.

headline: 'Nuisances' and nuances
abstract: This editorial looks at the issue of nuisance bars in Pennsylvania, an issue which the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) has long ignored, but is now getting attention as the LCB is under its "sunset" review.  The Pittsburgh Department of City Planning and the Pittsburgh Neighborhood Alliance have joined forces against nuisance bars and have pushed the PA Legislature to adopt Senate Bill 964.  The editorial supports SB 964, up until the point where the proposal takes away the LCB's enforcement power and cedes it to the state Attorney General's Office.  The editorial believes that no convincing explanation has been given for this shifting jurisdiction, and that placing that power in the hands of an elected official is no guarantee of better enforcement.  The LCB, as the editorial sees it, does not have a conflict of interest in selling and enforcing liquor licenses.

headline: Gray vows to oppose domestic cuts
abstract: US Representative William H Gray, chairman of the House Budget Committee, was the keynote speaker at the 78th anniversary dinner of the Urban League of Philadelphia.  He repeated his promise to fight further cuts in federal social programs and create efficient, lean government.  Other prominent African American leaders also spoke at the event.

headline: More People Working Than Ever: State Sets Record
abstract: According to the US Department of Labor, 5,168,000 of PA's citizens were employed in June of 1985--a record for the state.  High employment is positive news and shows that PA is on the path toward economic recovery and sustained employment.  The editorial cautions against being overly enthusiastic, however, as pockets of severe unemployment still exist in the state.

headline: Compromise sought on Montco trash
abstract: Montgomery County legislators are working with county commissioners to reach a compromise plan for county control of municipal trash disposal.  Legislators promised to return within two weeks with compromise language for Senate Bill 305, which would give Montgomery and Delaware Counties the authority to require municipalities to contract with them for trash disposal.  Montgomery County needs the legislation to ensure that enough trash is generated to make county processing facilities feasible.

headline: Pike bill signed, 2 named to panel
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh yesterday signed a $4 billion turnpike expansion bill into law and appointed prominent Pittsburgh lawyer James Malone III and former Democratic lawmaker James Goodman as new members of the PA Turnpike Commission.  The appointments were part of an agreement reached between the Thornburgh administration and PA House Democratic Leader James Manderino.  As part of the agreement, Goodman and Malone will not require PA Senate confirmation.  Goodman is considered the key to the new commission's framework because of a pledge from Manderino to Thornburgh that Goodman will work closely with the three Republicans on the commission.  The commission has been hamstrung by partisan deadlock for a long time.

headline: Shrouded justice
abstract: This editorial comments on the fact that PA's new capital-punishment executioner must remain anonymous.  The editorial says that when the state executes someone, the executioner must be anonymous and the electric chair must be hidden away in a chamber.  Such procedure forces the state to stoop to a cruel level of dispensing justice that does not show its face.

headline: Numbers game
abstract: The House Finance Committee yesterday voted 12-2 to recommend that the Independent Regulatory Review Commission (IRRC) reject the PA Revenue Department's plan to hold an additional Daily Number and Big Four drawing the same day as a regularly scheduled drawing.  Committee members feared that the plan would reduce lottery fund revenues that pay for senior citizens programs.  The PA Revenue Department said, however, that the special drawings would increase consumer interest and stabilize sales, which are now about $9.1 million a week for the Daily Number.  Based on current figures, the special Daily Number and Big Four drawings would cost the state an average of $700,000 and $270,000 respectively.  Department officials believe that increased interest would make up for these costs.

headline: Hail Shapp
abstract: A letter to the editor criticizes Governor Dick Thornburgh's behavior in regards to the portrait hanging in the Capitol of former Governor Milton Shapp.  Thornburgh delayed the portrait hanging and was not present at the ceremony.

headline: Nation's joblessness holds at 7.3%: State's rate rises to 8.3%
abstract: According to the US Department of Labor, civilian unemployment in April was stuck at 7.3% for the third straight month.  Also, jobs in manufacturing continued to decrease during this time.  Unemployment in Pennsylvania hovered near the 8% level, which a government economist attributed to a slowdown in the national economy.

headline: Conservation lobby gives 2 from Phila. High grades
abstract: After ranking them among the most pro-environmental representatives in the country, the League of Conservation Voters awarded tulips to Philadelphia Democrats Bob Edgar and Peter Kostmayer .

headline: Police idea wrong one
abstract: This editorial argues against the PA State Police's recent decision to reinstate the random sobriety check point program.  The editorial is in favor of any effort to get drunk drivers off the road--though it objects to random checkpoints on the grounds that police can also fine people at these checkpoints for other things.  Having to wait in line at these checkpoints also generates ill will on the part of the public towards the police; the editorial says that these random checkpoints are reminiscent of a totalitarian state.

headline: Socking it to the "soo-m" crowd
abstract: An opinion piece lauds the US Supreme Court for fining John Hyde for pursuing a frivolous lawsuit.  Hyde brought a lawsuit against the federal government for using paper money as legal tender; his suit was promptly thrown out by the US Supreme Court, and Hyde found himself slapped with a fine.  The author goes on to cite several other frivolous lawsuits across the US.  The author believes that when grievances are real and substantial, and cannot be settled by negotiation, an injured party has every right to seek redress in court.  The US has more lawyers per capita than any country, and if they choose to burden the courts with trivial pursuits, then they do a disservice to their profession.

headline: Ohio S&Ls may get temporary coverage
abstract: Ohio state officials have been working with the insurance industry to create a plan to provide $1 billion worth of temporary insurance for Ohio's privately insured savings and loan associations.  The plan will be presented to a group of major insurance companies   The policy would only last until the institutions are covered by federal deposit insurance or are merged with companies that already are federally insured.

headline: Hands off
abstract: An editorial criticizes the Pennsylvania State Education Association's proposal to spend the state's projected $201 million surplus for teacher raises.  The author says that there is no reason for any special interest group to use the money, but that it should be returned to all Pennsylvanians; the author also argues that the teachers' union is harmful to the state because of strikes over money.

headline: No buget monkey business, please
abstract: The state Legislature should be able to pass a formal budget without last-minute scrambling to prevent unnecessary spending.

headline: Counties await word on nuke-waste site
abstract: After Governor Dick Thornburgh agreed to a four-state compact for radioactive-waste disposal, counties in the northeastern part of the state anxiously wait to hear where the disposal sites will be placed.  Citizens of the counties are opposed to these sites, as are county officials.

headline: Political paving for Thornburgh
abstract: The opinion section looks at the recent compromise over expanding the PA Turnpike system.  Governor Thornburgh, known as a hard-line negotiator, finally decided to compromise with Democrats and gave up his demands that the PA Turnpike Commission be turned over to Republicans.  Given how heated the controversy over the Turnpike Commission was, the compromise took most lawmakers by surprise.  Though Thornburgh and the Republicans will essentially have control over the commission, it will not be the overwhelming majority for which Thornburgh had initially argued.  The author believes that Thornburgh decided to compromise for the sake of his political career.  Thornburgh has neutralized an issue that could have been used against him politically, and he can now take personal credit for ending a bitter partisan dispute.  Thornburgh is politically shrewd, and if he campaigns for the US Senate, people will remember him for breaking the turnpike impasse.

headline: Specter, N.Y. official clash on Goetz
abstract: Although Bernhard Hugo Goetz was charged with shooting four teenagers at a New York subway, he will not be indicted on assault or attempted murder charges.  Senator Arlen Specter has asked the attorney general of New York to take the case away from the Manhattan district attorney who tried it, and to resubmit assault charges against Goetz to a grand jury.  Specter feels that the case has national significance, and that the district attorney should have sought an indictment.  The district attorney, Robert Morgenthau, replied angrily to Specter that he did not understand the case.

headline: Only 1 tornado-aid center open
abstract: Yesterday, state and federal disaster officials closed all but one emergency center to aid the victims of the May 31 tornadoes.  Officials set up special county telelphone numbers for late aid applications.  Barry Ernest, spokesman for the PA Emergency Management Agency, said 1,798 Pennsylvanians had registered for state and federal aid programs at assistance centers so far.  According to authorities, the torandoes killed 64 and injured about 700 people in PA.

headline: Hands off local pensions
abstract: An editorial discusses pending legislation that would provide increases for retirees.  The editorial also urges the state Legislature to reject proposals to usurp local-government authority to determine the size of benefits paid out of pension plans that, in many cases, already are more generous than they can afford.

headline: Officials say tax plan may help Pa.
abstract: According to the state Revenue Department, President Reagan's proposal to eliminate deductions for state and local taxes would save Pennsylvanians millions of dollars.  Revenue Secretary James Scheiner has said the combined effect of lower federal tax rates and the elimination of deductibility could pump as much as $217 million a year into the state.

headline: County unveils plan to curb asbestos risks
