abstract: Responding to what experts see as a flawed federal program, the Allegheny County Health Department has proposed its own program to curb the risks of exposure to cancer-causing asbestos.  The proposal would virtually replace the Environmental Protection Agency's approach to asbestos hazards in schools, and would create a tougher, locally-run program.  Details of the program are spelled out in the article.

headline: Poor image plagues high-speed rail plan
abstract: Preliminary results from a survey of travelers riding intrastate trains, turnpike interchanges, and airports in Philladelphia, Harrisburg, and Pittsburgh, found that an effort is needed to dispel the stereotype of rail service as "dirty, old, and poor."  The PA High Speed Inner City Rail Passenger Commission yesterday heard the initial opinion from marketing and utility assesment surveys, and PA State Representative Richard Geist, the commission's chairman, said that the "numbers are smashing".  While high-speed rail services are incredibly popular in Europe and Japan, Amtrack's problems in the US seemed to have soured many on rail travel.  A magnetic levitation train currently under study would be able to traverse the state from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh in about 2.5 hours.

headline: Sprague: Lawmen Should Probe MOVE Disaster
abstract: Philadelphia lawyer Richard Sprague, selected by the state Senate Urban Affairs and Housing Committee to investigate the MOVE confrontation and fire, called the city's actions May 13 a "reckless step" that merits an investigation by law-enforcement agencies.  State Senator Frank Salvatore, a Republican who represents Northeast Philadelphia, will head the Senate's MOVE investigation as chairman of the committee.  Salvatore's committee plans to wait to begin its investigation until the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission completes its hearings and announces its findings.

headline: Open Gambling
abstract: This editorial chastises the PA General Assembly for allowing a bill to pass with an amendment that legalizes cash-prize card tournaments in bars.  The author argues that this will pave the way for wide-open gambling in PA.

headline: Hart left 'bleeding by defeat in state
abstract: Gary Hart's defeat in the PA Democratic presidential primary has dealt Hart a significant delegate deficit that will be hard to overcome. Former Vice President Walter Mondale leads Hart with 1, 060 delegates to Hart's 577 delegates. 1,967 delegates are needed to win the nomination.

headline: Our opinion: A tax cut ahead?
abstract: When the state General Assembly convenes to consider the Commonwealth's 1985-86 budget, Governor Dick Thornburgh will announce that he wants to spend the state's projected budget surplus on income-tax cuts.  This editorial considers other uses for the budget surplus.

headline: Covering lifted at TMI
abstract: Crews at Three Mile Island lifted a 55-ton covering off the damaged Unit 2 reactor--completely clearing the way for removal of radioactive fuel later this year.  Cleanup at the site is expected to be completed by 1988.

headline: PUC chief urges city to regulate its own taxicabs
abstract: The chairman of the Public Utility Commission (PUC) recommended that Philadelphia consider a licensing program for cab drivers.  The PUC says that it would be beneficial for the city to have local regulations of the industry, rather than state regulations that are inefficient and difficult to enforce.

headline: State court will hear trucking official's case
abstract: The Commonwealth Court will hear arguments on Anthony Cerone's complaint that the state Crime Commission's annual report may include false and defamatory information about him.  Cerone's complaint alleges that a summary report prepared by the Crime Commission incorrectly said he and another officer of his firm were convicted in the case.  Cerone says that the charges against him were dropped.

headline: Pa. Businesses Must Provide Child Care, Scranton Urges
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton told PA businesses to emphasize human-resource issues so that they can stay current and not lose a valuable talent pool.  He spoke at a conference called "Employees' Child Care: Is It Any Business of Business?" The conference was held at Montgomery County Community College; Scranton said that Montgomery County provides a model for the rest of the state.

headline: Having top officials means top pay
abstract: A letter to the editor supports high pay for public officials so that they can attract top people.

headline: Panel Oks state income tax decrease
abstract: The state Senate Finance Committee voted to approve a bill that would lower the personal income tax rate from 2.35 percent to 2.2 percent.  The bill also includes a provision that would allow some businesses, chiefly steelmakers, to receive a $1 tax credit for each $5 they invest in capitalization.  Governor Dick Thornburgh proposed both the tax cut and the tax-credit plan.

headline: Debate set on beverage deposit bill
abstract: The Reusable Container Act, a bill that would require nickel deposits on nearly all beverage containers, will be debated in the state House May 9.  There is strong opposition to the proposal, which is aimed at reducing road-side litter.  The Keystone Solid Waste Council Incorporated, which counts the AFL-CIO, US Steel Corporation, Bethlehem Steel, Kaiser Aluminum and dozens of other companies among its members, issued a position paper that outlined the council's opposition to the bill; the council opposes the bill because it would create higher prices and hurt  manufacturers and consumers.

headline: Rail panel splits on type of high-speed equipment
abstract: The PA High Speed Intercity Rail Passenger Commission split 3-3 over what type of train equipment to recommend for high-speed rail service in PA.  Three of the commissioners preferred the magnetic levitation train that floats above a roadbed and is propelled by electromagnets, while three others preferred a steel-wheel-on-steel-rail train.  The high-speed rail system would run from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh, with stops at Paoli, Lancaster, Harrisburg, State College, Altoona, Johnstown and Greensburg.

headline: State is listed as No. 1 in use of amphetamines, secobarbital
abstract: According to a report prepared by the federal Drug Enforcement Agency, more amphetamines, stimulants, and more secobarbital, a depressant, were consumed per person in PA than anywhere else in the nation in 1983.

headline: Pa. Death Toll Climbs to 62
abstract: PA Emergency Management Agency (PEMA) reported that PA was hardest hit by the May 13 tornadoes; the state reported 62 deaths in the storm; Ohio reported 12 deaths and Ontario had at least 13.  The Red Cross and PEMA were unable to estimate the number of homeless, but PEMA officials said that 1,520 homes were damaged.  Insurance agents arrived in many towns yesterday morning and many wrote checks on the spot for those who lost their homes.

headline: He who has gold rules politics, business, according to Torquato.
abstract: John Torquato Jr, head of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), testified for the government in the CTA bribery trial.  He said that, "He who has the gold rules."  Torquato pleaded guilty to federal charges that he and four others attempted to bribe and influence public officials to secure a lucrative state contract for CTA.  Torquato has offered much insight into "how the political game is played" in PA.

headline: Pennsylvania income tax: To cut or not to cut
abstract: Columnist supports Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposal for a cut in the tax rate from 2.35% to 2.2%.

headline: Decision date set in lawsuit against DER
abstract: Almost three years after he filed a discrimination suit against the PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER), James Leber may get his day in court.  Part of his suit is scheduled to be decided on November 22nd by the US 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.  Leber claims that DER officials discriminated against him because he was a whistle-blower.  Leber was a former DER mining inspector in PA's anthracite region.  State attorneys have attempted several times to have the case dismissed.  Although federal law prohibits the type of discrimination that Leber claims was directed at him, DER attorneys argued the law does not apply to them because the department does not engage in surface mining, while Leber contends otherwise.  The DER's challenge to this law has gone through several state and federal legal hurdles.  The US Interior Board of Land Appeals ruled that proof of surface mining did not bring the DER under the law's jurisdiction, though Leber has appealed this decision.

headline: Railroad town has the jitters
abstract: Residents of Conway, PA are concerned about the proposed sale of Conrail, the government-supported railroad.  The railroad employs a large amount of people in the town and local residents are concerned that a new owner would move operations from the town.  The loss of Conrail from the town would not only cause a loss in jobs, but also tax revenues needed to run the borough.

headline: State law is required to protect the elderly
abstract: This editorial says that a bill combating abuse of the elderly is laudable yet frightening.  This is because a group as vulnerable as the elderly must be protected from physical and mental abuse by state legislation.  The bill currently under consideration would require health care, social service and law enforcement officials to tell the state if they suspect that a patient or client, aged 60 and older, needs protective services.  The editorial says that legislators should make sure that the abuse-reporting law has enough teeth in it to be enforced.

headline: Pa. law turns into a bad bet: Legislature tries to repeal inadvertent sanction of gambling in bars
abstract: PA legislators created a law that allows breweries to sponsor and pay cash prizes in bowling, darts, and card tournaments.  Many legislators are now trying to repeal the law.  Tavern owners are pleased with the law because it increases their business.  Legislators worry the law encourages drinking and could attract organized crime.  They are trying to repeal or revise it, but are facing difficulties.

headline: Head of subcommittee questions IRS report on its processing rate
abstract: US Representative J.J. Pickle accused Internal Revunue Commissioner Roscoe L. Egger Jr of manipulating figures to show the agency was processing tax returns at a pace ahead of last year.  This accusation came at the end of a heated hearing on the IRS by the House Ways and Means subcommittee on oversight.  Egger denied that millions of tax returns had been lost or destroyed by IRS employees, but he also said that as many as 1.5 million taxpayers who have waited more than 12 weeks for their refunds should refile.

headline: Picture of Governor Thornburgh
abstract: Picture of Governor Thornburgh leafing through data on the fiscal needs of various state departments for the 1985-86 fiscal year.

headline: Delaware River basin in drought emergency
abstract: The Delaware River Basin Commission declared a drought emergency and urged the governors of New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware to immediately impose restrictions on water use in the portions of their states located in the river basin.

headline: Red Tape in Congress: $7 Billion in Highway Funds Tied Up
abstract: This editorial urges US Congress to act quickly to pass two pieces of technical legislation that would free up more than $7 billion in already appropriated highway funds; this would allow highway projects across the nation to be undertaken.

headline: State troopers to vote by mail on new contract
abstract: PA's nearly 4,000 state police officers will be mailed ballots today to vote on a new two-year contract; the contract would provide across-the-board pay raises of $1,100.  Under the terms of the new contract, longevity pay would increase slightly, as would accrual of sick leave and medical insurance.  Also, a committee would be established to discuss revisions to the existing promotion policy.  The tenative agreement was only the second reached outside of binding arbitration, which is required by state law when negotiations reach an impasse.

headline: Panel Oks a tough bill on alcohol
abstract: A special state House subcommittee on underage drinking approved legislation that will suspend the driver's licenses of minors who are caught with alcoholic beverages; the bill also creates other harsher penalties for minors caught with alcohol.

headline: Heat's On: Politicos Get Break on Bills
abstract: Documents obtained by the Philadelphia Daily News indicated that city-owned Philadelphia Gas Works is secretly giving preferential treatment to several local politicians by reducing their personal gas bills or allowing them to run up thousands of dollars in unpaid bills without loosing service.  The article gives examples of politicians receiving special treatment.

headline: Proposals in Congress threaten housing finance agency
abstract: The Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency (PHFA), which sells tax-exempt bonds for the construction of apartments and provides mortgages for single-family homes, could be hurt by any of the three income-tax proposals before Congress.  Each of the tax proposals would eliminate tax-exempt bonds for housing.  PHFA is continuing its work, however, while keeping a close watch on developments in Congress.

headline: DER graft probe tied to toxic waste industry
abstract: An investigation into corruption within the state Department of Environmental Resources has lead to a probe into the toxic waste industry in western PA.  Vincent Luci, a former Department of Environmental Resources official, admitted in court to taking bribes from a landfill operator and has agreed to cooperate in an investigation of the waste-disposal industry in western PA.

headline: Rep. Shuster's criticism illogical
abstract: This opinion piece criticizes US Representative Bud Shuster's comments on selling Conrail to Norfolk Southern Corporation.  Shuster has criticized anyone who would speak against a Norfolk Southern sale, and the author thinks that speaking against the sale would guarantee additional commitments from Norfolk Southern.  The author questions if Shuster is working for Norfolk Southern.

headline: State's high court names ethics board chairman
abstract: Philadelphia lawyer John M. Elliot has been chosen by the state Supreme Court to chair its disciplinary board, which supervises the ethics of the state's 37,000 lawyers.

headline: Panel agrees to hold antitrust hearing: Conrail sale foes win another round
abstract: The US Senate Judiciary Committee agreed to hold another hearing on the antitrust aspects of the sale of Conrail to Norfolk Southern Corporation.  This represents a victory for opponents to the sale, many of whom feel that the government could get more money by a public offering of Conrail stock.

headline: Heinz fights curbs on PAC funds
abstract: PA Senator John Heinz is leading the fight against a bill in the US Senate that would limit campaign spending by political action committees.  Heinz called the proposal "flawed" and said it would lead to the very kind of influence-buying the bill attempts to control.  The bill would put limits on individual contributions to candidates and political action committees' contributions to candidates.  Heinz plans to introduce a counter-measure that would lift the spending cap currently imposed on political parties.

headline: Reagan seeks huge tax system overhaul
abstract: In remarks prepared for a nationally televised Oval-Office address, President Ronald Reagan proposed an overhaul of the nation's tax code, denouncing the current system as so complicated and unjust that it is "un-American" and offering a "revolutionary" plan to cut most individual tax rates and close loopholes.  A fact sheet distributed by the White House said that overall taxes paid by individuals would be reduced by 7%, while total taxes paid by corporations would be increased by 9%.  Democratic spokespersons feel "optimistic" that the Republican president is bucking his party's tradition as protector of big business and the wealthy, but say they will not rubber-stamp Reagan's proposals.

headline: DER sets up nutrient management fund
abstract: As much as $30,000 will be available to farmers who take part in a nutrient management program initiated by the state Department of Environmental Resources.  As part of the state's $2 million effort to help clean up the Chesapeake Bay, the nutrient program is geared towards keeping animal waste and fertilizers out of the Susquehanna River.

headline: Road repairs get PennDot priority in billboard fight
abstract: State Department of Transportation officials say that Pennsylvania has fallen short of the goals set forth in the 1965 National Highway Beautification Act because repairing bridges and roads is more important than getting rid of billboards.

headline: State's new marital rape law to have first court test
abstract: In February 1985, PA became the 23rd state in which husbands who rape their wives can be prosecuted for sexual assault.  A man who was accused by his common-law wife of rape is set to go on trial July 22 in Philadelphia Common Pleas Court; this is the first case involving the new law.

headline: Panel approves bill on LCB enforcement
abstract: The state Senate Law and Justice Committee approved a bill to transfer liquor law enforcement from the Liquor Control Board to the attorney general's office.

headline: Heinz predicts GOP gain in Senate despite polls
abstract: At a general session of the Republican National Committee, Senator John Heinz said that he expects the GOP to gain form more seats in 1986.  Heinz has been selected to lead the campaign efforts of 22 Republican incumbents.  Governor Dick Thornburgh also gave similar assurances for Republican successes in 35 gubernatorial races in the next 2 years.

headline: Reagan TV plea brings calls, many negative
abstract: President Ronald Reagan, in an address to the nation Wednesday evening, urged his viewers to telephone or write their members of Congress to urge the passage of the 1986 budget compromise.  An unscientific random sampling of the PA delegation indicated that congressional offices did receive additional calls, but that many of them were negative--expressing opposition to the President's budget.

headline: Drought Getting Worse: PG&W Supply Ample
abstract: Even though we are in the beginnings of a drought, the PA Gas & Water Company's reservoirs are 90% full.  The editorial urges readers to conserve water to ensure that reservoirs have enough water to last through a dry summer.

headline: Road study urged
abstract: This editorial looks at the unity that has developed among regional development groups in Southwestern PA; these groups are working together to ensure completion of the entire PA Turnpike extenstion from Pittsburgh to West Virginia.  The Turnpike extension legislation currently places the Mon Valley Expressway in the second phase of construction and the Fayette Expressway in the third phase of construction.  The PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT) has made no provision in its advance planning for the work allong this corridor because it is part of the PA Turnpike plan.  Two regional development bodies in Fayette County have asked PennDOT to come up with $200,000 for a feasibility and needs study of that route.  The editorial believes this is a reasonable request for the good of all concerned.

headline: Stays of execution cover 3 inmates
abstract: The executions of three death-row inmates--John Lesko, Keith Zettlemoyer, and Michael Travaglia--have been delayed by the PA State Supreme Court.  Zettlemoyer and Travaglia argued that the PA Superior Court should hear their appeals under the Post Conviction Hearing Act before the PA Supreme Court reviews their cases; the PA Supreme Court agreed.  Lesko has been granted a 14-day stay of execution in order to file a motion for reargument with the PA Supreme Court.

headline: Panel for private wine sales
abstract: The PA Senate's Law and Justice Committee approved a bill on December 3, 1985, that would allow food stores to sell wine in addition to state stores, and would also allow wine sales in specialty wine shops.  The committee also discussed some related issues that will be sure to induce a lengthy debate when the full Senate takes up the PA Liquor Control Board's fate.  The Senate must, under PA's Sunset Law, renew the board or it will cease to exist.

headline: Heinz supporting Specter if Thornburgh enters race
abstract: US Senator John Heinz, who serves as chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, has said that he will support US Senator Arlen Specter in his bid for re-election--even if PA Governor Dick Thornburgh enters the race.  Governor Thornburgh has not ruled out running against Specter in the Republican primary for US Senate; Thornburgh has recently gained the support of many conservative groups who have been critical of Specter.  Senator Heinz's decision to support Specter highlights both the close working relationship that the two have and the divide between Heinz and Thornburgh.

headline: Rainy day is here
abstract: This editorial approves of Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposed budget for 1985-86, but disagrees with setting aside a "rainy day" fund.  The editorial also says that the money should be spent now to further boost the economy.

headline: Drought measures necessary
abstract: In the face of a possible drought, this editorial urges the public to conserve water.  The editorial commends Governor Dick Thornburgh and New Jersey Governor Kean for taking precautionary actions to restrict the use of water; the article also urges the public to follow these restrictions before the situation gets critical.

headline: Road-repair aid sought for Altemose center
abstract: State legislators from Montgomery, Chester, and Delaware Counties say that they would seek $44 million for road improvements to benefit the new Valley Forge Convention and Exhibit Center in King of Prussia.

headline: Stewart says Pinamonti's mismanagement cost $500,000
abstract: District Justice Michael Stewart said that nearly $500,000 in 1982 traffic and parking violations are uncollectible because Joseph Pinnamonti's district-justice office never processed the tickets.  Pinamonti and Stewart are both seeking nomination for the district justice post in the May 21st primary.  Pinamonti disputed the claims and said that Stewart was "throwing mud."

headline: Panel OKs tavern-games bill: Senate measure would continue gambling ban
abstract: The state Senate Law and Justice Committee approved legislation that would permit taverns to hold contests of skill; the bill also allow them to offer cash prizes to the winners, but does not permit gambling.  At the same time, several hundred bar owners gathered in the Capitol rotunda to rally for legalized video poker and small games of chance.  The bill would allow a bar to conduct games of "skill, speed, strength or endurance," but specifically prohibits card games, dice and any other games of chance.

headline: Hello, PGW? Add My Name to That VIP List
abstract: Philadelphia residents complain about Philadelphia Gas Works' practice of designating local politicians, business leaders and other customers as "VIPs."

headline: Reagan cuts called 'war' on region
abstract: President Ronald Reagan's 1986 budget cuts for US cities have been criticized by state and local government officials.  Governor Dick Thornburgh, however, praised the proposal as "a good step in the right direction on balancing the federal budget."  The budget will make cuts in many programs that assist cities, as well as many public assistance programs.

headline: Edgar vows to seek waste-site funds
abstract: US Representative Bob Edgar, the Democratic candidate for US Senate, pledged to work to make sure the federal government provides adequate money to clean up toxic waste sites in PA.  Edgar, who is running against Republican Senator Arlen Specter, made his remarks after visiting Tysons Dump in Upper Marion Township, which has been identified by the US Environmental Protection Agency as one of the most dangerous toxic waste sites in the nation.  Edgar called toxic waste a domestic crisis and criticized Specter and Congress for failing to act to ensure that sites such as Tysons Dump are cleaned up quickly.

headline: Ruling hinders efforts to catch speeders
abstract: This editorial deals with a ruling by the PA State Supreme Court regarding a device called an Excessive Speed Preventer (ESP).  The court ruled that ESP could not be used by police departments in Pennsylvania.  The ruling also means that speeders already caught by police using ESP will have their tickets legally torn up.  ESP is classified as an electronic device, a category of equipment only state police can use under state law.  The reason for this law was to prevent communities across the state from setting up speed traps to raise revenue through ticket fines.  The editorial believes that the state law should spell out devices that local police can use and not leave the matter so open to court interpretation.

headline: Stolen Cars
abstract: This editorial exmaines the problem of car theft in Western PA and what politicians are doing about it.  PA State Represenetative Joe Markosek's is holding hearings for the newly formed PA House Special Committee to Investigate Auto Theft and Chop Shops.  The hearings have found that more money will need to be spent on training police and protecting parking lots.  Some politicians also believe that licensing salvage yards and auto body repair shops would help.  The editorial believes that the chief deterrent, beyond increasing police converage, lies with the owners and drivers of vehicles--especially in regards to locking their cars.

headline: Panel votes to abolish catastrophic loss fund
abstract: The state House Transportation Committee voted to abolish the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund (CAT) and its $5-per-vehicle fee created under the state's new auto-insurance law.  The CAT Fund is used to pay for accident victims' medical bills that exceed $100,000, with a maximum of $1 million.

headline: Hoeffel Says He's Ready For 2nd Battle for Congress
abstract: Former PA State Representative Joseph Hoeffel, a Democrat, will likely step into the ring again to battle US Representative Lawrence Coughlin over who can best represent the constituents of PA's 13th Congressional District.  Hoeffel says he anticipates making a formal announcement of his candidacy in February.  Coughlin's district, which had been overwhelmingly Republican, has been reapportioned to include more registered Democrats, though Republicans still maintain 56% of the voting electorate.

headline: Reagan hits tax reform trail today
abstract: President Ronald Reagan will attempt to revive public support for his tax-reform plan by giving weekly speeches across the US and having several administration members, such as Vice President Bush and Treasury Secretary Baker, tour the nation in support of the plan.  According to a recent survey, 63% of respondents want a new tax system, but fewer than half endorse Reagan's plan.  Speaker of the House Tip O'Neill says he hasn't found much support for the plan, but will make sure it gets to the House floor for a vote to avoid accusations that Democrats killed the chance for tax reform.

headline: Efforts deserve legislative support
abstract: This editorial writes of the need for county governments to coordinate solid waste management with municipalities.  The editorial says that Blair County Commissioner William Stouffer is on the right track by seeking a coordinated effort among the six counties of the Southern Alleghenies Planning and Development Commission; Stouffer deserves the support of state legislators and the public.

headline: Running Scared? That's PennDOT's Plan
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT) is trying to get motorists off the Schuylkill Expressway so they can complete construction projects.  They are encouraging motorists to take alternate routes and/or public transportation.  They are also trying to scare away as many drivers as possible.  PennDOT wants the Expressway to be used by out-of-towners and trucks only.

headline: Stone's indictment
abstract: This editorial examines the role of Pittsburgh City Council President Robert Rade Stone in the Computer Technology Associates Incorporated (CTA) bribery scandal.  A federal investigation formally accused Stone of playing a role in the scandal.  Last October, Pittsburgh Councilwoman Michelle Madoff called for Stone to step down because of his link to CTA, but no other members were willing to endorse the idea.  The editorial claims that a proposal calling for Stone to step down should be fully supported by City Council.  The editorial believes that Stone has engaged in questionable, and perhaps unethical, conduct and should be removed from his post as Council President.

headline: Pennsylvania in business
abstract: A letter to the editor from James O. Pickard, secretary of the PA Department of Commerce, discusses a survey by Alexander Grant and Company of the 48 continental states.  The survey seeks to evaluate the 1984 manufacturing climate and ranks each state accordingly.  Pickard says that the Department questions the subjective methodology, but also points out high points in the conclusions made by the study.  Pickard says that the study shows that there is a positive trend in PA's business climate.

headline: I'm Tough Enough, Candidate Says
abstract: This article takes a deep look at the candidacy of US Congressman Bob Edgar for the US Senate.  The article examines Edgar's background as a Congressman and issues such as fundraising for his US Senate campaign, which will be a major issue for Edgar.  Edgar has already scheduled more fundraisers early in the campaign than any other candidate.  Edgar's personal history is also glossed over as well.

headline: Record number working, but jobless rate edges up
abstract: According to the US Labor Department, the nation's unemployment rate rose in 1984, but so did new job creation.  Given the growth in new jobs, labor experts remain cautiously optimistic about the unemployment picture from 1984.

headline: 'Extremely minor fraction'
abstract: This editorial thanks the Wilderness Society for fighting for and protecting forest lands across the US.

headline: Safety
abstract: A letter to the Editor applauds PA for passing a law that requires children under age 5 to be in child restraints while in a car.  The author also criticizes the fact that there are not safety belts in school buses.

headline: Talks: Settlement hopes foundered on issue of future arrests
abstract: Prior to police going to MOVE headquarters with search and arrest warrants, Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode had sent in three negotiators to try and negotiate with the cult members so that they would leave peacefully.  The negotiations ended when Goode could not promise that the city would not arrest the cult members in the future, and that they would not release 9 cult members imprisoned for the 1978 murder of police officer James Ramp.  The police tried to evict the cult peacefully with search and arrest warrants, but the day ended in gunfire as MOVE member fired on the police.

headline: Pittsburgh-area unit's cost soars to $27,760: LCB to pay more than 300% hike in store's rent
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) approved several store rental-hike contracts, but the one that caught the eye of the LCB was a store in Miracle Mile Shopping Center.  At Miracle Mile, the rental rate increased from nearly $7,000 to $29,760.  The major increase at the Monroeville store was due to the completion of a renovation of the shopping center.

headline: In and out for Drew Lewis
abstract: This editorial examines the curious non-campaign of Drew Lewis for governor.  A few weeks ago, Lewis said that he might seek the Republican gubernatorial nomination next year, putting him in opposition to Lieutenant Governor William Scranton, the presumed front-runner.  This ended earlier this week when Lewis made it clear that he would not be a candidate next year and gave his support to Scranton.  While this does end the possibility of a divisive Republican primary, the editorial believes that it also will foreclose any debate or choice for Republican voters.

headline: Record straight: Thornburgh-Cuomo debate puts taxes in perspective
abstract: This  editorial supports Governor Thornburgh's endorsement of Reagan-administration tax proposals, which would eliminate state and local tax deductions.  The editorial also argues that New York Governor Mario Cuomo's arguments against the Reagan tax proposals were unfounded.

headline: Fast state train gets environmental OK
abstract: A study submitted to the state High-Speed Intercity Rail Passenger Commission proposed argued that a 180-mile per hour Philadelphia-Pittsburgh railroad would have "no overriding potentially adverse environmental effects." The sparse population in the middle of the state will minimize displacement and could improve overall air quality. Of the 22-county corridor, 40 percent is forested and 33 percent is agricultural.

headline: Safety Belt Paranoia
abstract: This editorial argues against PA and other states making mandatory seat belt laws.  Seat belts are looked on by many as a panacea, and may give some drivers a false sense of security.  In reality, according to the editorial, seat belts are the last source of hope for survival.  The editorial believes that fining people for not wearing seat belts may get them to wear them for a while, but eventually people will fall back into their old habits.  The editorial also states that police cannot enforce this new law without being discriminatory and invading drivers' privacy.  Paranoid protectionists currently hold sway in government and they are trying to invade your privacy and control your every action.

headline: Task force offers 8 points to cut prisons' overcrowding
abstract: A state task force on prison overcrowding proposed an eight-point plan to help relieve prison overcrowding.  The plan includes giving inmates time off for good behavior, raising the number of parole agents, and building a 500-bed prison in southeastern PA.  These proposals require either legislation or funding by the Legislature before they can be adopted.

headline: PLCB depends on duplicity to stay alive
abstract: This editorial is distressed at the notion at the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) will remain intact, most likely only losing its power of liquor-law enforcement.  The editorial derides the "unholy alliance" of support for the agency, which includes the blue-nosed Bible-belt constituency, the tavern industry, the liquor industry, the beer-distributor industry, the Democratic Party, and enough Republicans to ensure that no changes will take place at the LCB.  Given the rampant corruption at the LCB and its callous disregard for consumer preferences, there was hope that 1985 was the year it would be reformed, but that will not be the case.

headline: In judiciary races, the Democratic leadership faces a test
abstract: Under Chairman Joseph Smith, Philadelphia's Democratic City Committee will face a difficult test in the May 21 primary; the committee hopes to have its entire slate of endorsed candidates win.  The Committee is currently hurting financially and being ignored by many of its ward leaders.  Smith remains confident that the endorsed slate will win.

headline: Return surplus
abstract: This editorial argues that the state's budget surplus of $297 million should be returned to the people who created it: the taxpayers.

headline: Fee for emissions test to rise in Sept.
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a bill increasing the amount that service station dealers may charge for auto emissions tests in the five-county Philadelphia area and the Pittsburgh and Allentown regions.  The increase, for which participating garage owners had lobbied vigorously, takes effect September 1, 1985.

headline: Save bridge for future use
abstract: A letter to the editor urges Dauphin County commissioners to take action to preserve the Conrail-owned Susquehanna River bridge; it also encourages them to try and obtain state and federal funding for a commuter rail system.

headline: Testimony ends in Hill's macing trial
abstract: Testimony in the macing trial of former Montgomery County Sheriff Frederick B. Hill ended; the judge is expected to render his judgment today.  Hill had been charged with 55 counts of macing and official oppression, as well as six counts of conspiracy.  The prosecution contended that Hill had pressured his subordinates into buying tickets to county Republican fund-raising events and making contributions for a Hill reelection billboard.  This pressure is considered macing.

headline: Puritans and pols together
abstract: This editorial argues against the findings of the PA Senate's Law and Justice Committee, which defeated major reform of the state's liquor monopoly.  The committee argued that state revenues would decline or liquor consumption would increase if the government lost control of liquor sales.  The editorial believes that the state store monopoly is attempting to fulfill two contradictory roles: selling alcohol while discouraging the use of alcohol.  The neo-Puritans, who wish to impose Prohibition on PA, rejoice in the state store's low sales figures.  However, this fails to take into account that many PA residents buy their liquor out of state or simply go to a bar.  The editorial praises PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's condemnation of the state store system, and knocks the politicians who use the system to provide jobs for their pals.

headline: Inauguration Photos
abstract: A photo depicts PA Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman taking an oath from PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr.; Zimmerman's son and wife look on.  A second photo depicts PA Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer discussing plans for his second term.

headline: Revolving charge interest should be brought into line
abstract: This editorial argues that the state General Assembly should create legislation tying the revolving-charge rate to the economic climate.  The editorial proposes that the revolving charge rate should increase and decrease with the ebbs and flows of inflation and interest rates.

headline: Firm asked to stop transit of chemical on state roads
abstract: US Congressmen Doug Walgren, Joseph Kolter, Austin Murphy, and Thomas Ridge, all of whom represent Western PA, have written a letter to FMC Corporation asking them to stop using the state's roads to transport deadly methyl isocyanate, the chemical that killed more than 2,000 people in Bhopal, India.  FMC transports the chemical through all four congressmen's districts on its way to a plant in Middleport, NY, where it is used to make pesticide.  FMC has its trucks escorted by police and followed by vans carrying experts at handling chemical spills.  The congressmen all admit that the government has little regulatory control over the shipments.

headline: Schuylkill Expressway work set
abstract: The second phase of the reconstruction of the Schuylkill Expressway will begin in 1986, but work needed to prepare for the project will start on Monday, June 17.  The PA Department of Transportation said six miles of shoulder of the westbound portion of the heavily traveled highway in  Montgomery County will be improved as part of a $7 million contract.

headline: The credibility fallout as MOVE probe deepens
abstract: This editorial argues that despite what Philadelphia city officials would have citizens believe, there was no official plan for dealing with MOVE.  The operation against the group on May 13th was simply a shoot-from-the-hip action.  The events of that day cannot be characterized as a "mistake" as Mayor Wilson Goode and others like to call them, as the case can be made that there is cause to investigate official wrongdoing in the incident.  The Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission's findings may determine if Philadelphia residents can repair their trust of the city's officials--a trust that was shattered by the MOVE bombing.

headline: Quick repeal effort promised by legislative leaders
abstract: PA General Assembly leaders have said that repealing the state law that has allowed card tournaments in bars and taverns will be a top priority this legislative session.  They expect that there will be much arguing and bargaining in both the House and the Senate between proponents of gambling and those who want to keep it out of the state.

headline: Incumbency key to city hall contests: Council presidency up for grabs in '86
abstract: Pittsburgh Democrats chose nominees for four seats on City Council; the nominees are favorites to be elected in the November election.  Because City Council President Robert Rade Stone did not seek re-election, at least one new council member will be seated.  Three incumbents sought re-election, Ben Woods, Sophie Masloff and William R. Robinson.  Woods and Masloff are the favorites.

headline: Ron Outlines 'Simple, Fair' Tax Proposal
abstract: In launching his plan to re-write the tax code, President Ronald Reagan called for a tax system that is clear, simple and fair for all.   Under President Reagan's plan, most people would pay about the same or less in taxes as they do now, and the tax burden would shift slightly from individuals to corporations.  Democrats have said that they welcome President Reagan's proposal, but will measure it against their own traditional standards of reform.

headline: Firm Hopes to Sell Philadelphians on PCBs
abstract: Chemical Waste Management, an Illinois firm, is conducting a public relations blitz aimed at making Philadelphians willing to accept the presence of PCB--a carcinogenic chemical--at marine terminals in the city.  Chemical Waste Management is trying to sell the idea to city and state politicians, as well as to local community groups.  Chemical Waste Management would like to make Philadelphia its terminal for regular at-sea incineration of PCBs, but needs approval from the  US Environmental Protection Agency to do so.  US Senator Arlen Specter is concerned about the proposal and has addressed a letter to the EPA.

headline: Seat belt laws do save lives, Sen. Corman
abstract: This editorial urges Senator J. Doyle Corman, head of the state Senate Transportation Committee, to act on a bill introduced by Senator Edward Early that would create a mandatory seat belt law.  The editorial demonstrates the effectiveness of a seat belt law and urges Corman to act on the bill, rather than let it die in his committee.

headline: The 'Dump-Down' Theory
abstract: An opinion-section piece agrees with ex-Philadelphia Mayor Bill Green, who described the MOVE commission hearings as pursuing a "reverse Nuremberg" line of inquiry to fix responsibility.  The author gives the description another name, the "dump-down" principle, meaning that Philadelphia Mayor Goode and other high officials plead that their executive decisions were governed by directions from below.  This cop-out might have been seen to exonerate those high in the chain of command, but it smeared policeman and firefighters on the scene.  However, the MOVE hearings have been made a lot fairer since US District Judge James McGirr Kelly correctly ruled that policemen are entitled to the same constitutional rights as the citizens they risk their lives to protect.

headline: Second $5 Auto Fee Due Only Weeks After First
abstract: Under PA's new auto insurance law, insurance companies pay only up to $100,000 for an accident victim's medical expenses; the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund will pay up to $1 million for medical expenses over that amount.  Motorists are billed $5 for each car and truck to set up the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund, and that is to be paid each year when renewing the vehicle's registration.  Motorists were billed in May and June, but those whose registrations are due in October will be billed again in July.

headline: Incumbency key to city hall contests: Mayoral primary lacked excitement
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Richard S. Caliguiri easily beat three challengers in the Democratic mayoral primary.  Caliguiri has maintained that his eight-year record of putting new office-building skyscrapers Downtown and renovating housing in city neighborhoods, which he calls Renaissance II, has earned him a third term.  Caliguiri will face Henry Sneath, a 26-year-old Republican lawyer, in the general election in November.

headline: Running it like a business
abstract: This editorial praises PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and his handling of the PA State Budget, and argues that he would be a welcome addition to either the US Senate or the administration of President Reagan.  Governor Thornburgh has met his pledge to run the commonwealth in a business-like manner--something evinced by multiple budget surpluses.  Governor Thornburgh could give those in the US Congress a real lesson on fiscal responsibility.

headline: Game Commission bill splits sportsmen
abstract: Groups clashed over a bill that would increase hunting and fishing license fees and would require legislative approval of the state Game Commission budget.  Philip Kloss, president of United Sportsmen of PA, said his group supports the legislation because it would make the Game Commission accountable to hunters; he also said that the fee increases were excessive.  Michael Protz Jr., president of the PA Federation of Sportsmen's Clubs, said his group opposes the legislation because it would give the Legislature control of the commission and politicize it.

headline: Seat belt measure divides residents of 92nd District
abstract: State Representative Bruce Smith released the results of a spring poll taken in his 92nd district on current legislative issues and said that his constituents were almost evenly divided on the issue of mandatory seat belt use.  District residents favored Governor Dick Thornburgh's proposed reduction of the personal income tax and supported legislation to increase penalties and fines for game-law violations.

headline: The Family Court crisis:  A case study of injustice
abstract: This editorial examines the problems facing the Philadelphia Family Court, which had to postpone many of its hearings recently.  The Family Court has always been severely underfunded and understaffed, especially since no other court in Philadelphia is as critical in dispensing swift and effective justice.  Political squabbling between the PA Senate and the PA Supreme Court has made the problems facing the Family Court more acute in recent months.  There is some hope that conditions might improve, as persistent lobbying by Family Court Administrative Judge Nicholas Cipriani has gotten additional full-time judges to be assigned to the court.  The editorial concludes that it is the duty of the PA Legislature, the PA Supreme Court, and Philadelphia court officials to ensure that this problem at Family Court never evloves again.

headline: Rental Car Insurance
abstract: An opinion-section piece argues that a loophole in PA rental insurance policies--one that allows insurance companies not to cover a person renting a car who is found to have his/her driving ability impaired by alcohol--should be reviewed by the PA State Senate.  The argument is not for the protection of the drunk drivers, but their victims--who would be denied compensation because the driver was under the influence of alcohol.  This favors insurers of rental cars, and the PA Insurance Commission should re-examine this policy so that it adheres to the standards required of other vehicles.

headline: John R. Torquato Sr., 77, a longtime political power
abstract: John R. Torquato Sr., 77, who served for 36 years as Cambria County Democratic chairman before his 1978 conviction on charges of extortion and conspiracy, died yesterday at Conemaugh Valley Memorial Hospital in Johnstown Pa.  Torquato Sr.'s son, is the key witness in the Computer Technology Associates bribery case.

headline: Sales tax: Feds should leave this revenue source to states
abstract: This editorial argues against a national sales tax, and contends that sales tax should be determined and enacted by state and local governments.

headline: Game Commission in Jeopardy: Senate Can Save It
abstract: This editorial opposes state House Bill 585, legislation that would require the state General Assembly to review the state Game Commission's budget each year.  The editorial feels that this would allow the legislature to set the policies of the Commission; such a policy would not be sound wildlife management.

headline: Seat belt statistics
abstract: A letter to the editor recounts the PA State Senate Transportation Committee Public hearing of July 24, 1985; the hearing dealt with impending seat-belt legislation.  The author opposes mandatory seat belt laws in PA because it violates peoples freedom of choice, but believes that the bill will be railroaded through the Legislature.

headline: The House is not guilty of haste
abstract: A letter to the Editor from state Representative David W. Sweet discusses a past Post-Gazette editorial that criticized the General Assembly for acting too quickly and for grandstanding when it passed child-abuse legislation.  Sweet says that the House Judiciary Committee, which he chairs, is studying the issues carefully, hoping to avoid further postruing, grandstanding and self-congratulation.

headline: Replace Penna. Banks
abstract: A letter to the editor expresses disgust with a new bill put forth by the PA Bankers Association.  The bill would take the 18% ceiling on loans off because they believe that most consumers don't ask the rate when they apply for a loan.  The author finds the notion that consumers don't shop around for loan rates laughable.  If the banking lobby is allowed to support this bill, which the author deems a "rape of the consumer," than a consumer group should submit a bill that would give residents a break, and a statewide vote should be held on the issue.  The author hopes that "money-hungry" banks move to Delaware and more consumer-oriented banks move to  PA.

headline: Judge candidates trade jabs for TV
abstract: The three Dauphin County judge candidates met at WITF-TV's studio in Susquehanna Township to film a talk show that will air before the May 21 primary election.  The candidates, Norman P. Hetrick, Joseph Kleinfelter, and Sebastian D. Natale, discussed their experience and ideas on judges.

headline: Saturn site selection process like a three-ring circus
abstract: A columnist discusses the site selection process for General Motor's new Saturn plant; 36 states competed for the plant.  The columnist speculates that GM had a site in mind long before the states spent time and money submitting sophisticated proposals to the company; the proposals were a publicity stunt designed to generate interest in the car manufacturer's new brand.

headline: Game of misguided politics
abstract: PA's Game and Fish Commissions receives no general revenue funds; they primarily are financed by licenses and fees and need not seek legislative approval of their budgets.  The legislature must approve changes in license fees, however.  This editorial argues that legislation requiring the General Assembly to review the Game Commission's budget would force the commission to alter its management programs so they suit legislators' whims.  Such a policy would end an era of sound wildlife management.

headline: Seat belts right way to go
abstract: A letter supports the proposal by the PA General Assembly to make mandatory the wearing of seat-belts in cars.  The letter also attempts to refute several arguments made by those who view wearing seat-belts as infringing on their rights.  The author also points to the fact that similar mandatory seat-belt laws have been enacted in New York, New Jersey, and nearly a dozen other states.

headline: The News Was There First: Our Joe O'Dowd Beat a TV 'Exclusive' by 38 Hours
abstract: A columnist notes that an "exclusive" newscast by Channel 10 reporting that a police stakeout team had engaged the radical group MOVE in an underground gun battle for several hours was actually first reported by Daily News veteran police reporter Joe O'Dowd; O'Dowd's story ran in the Daily News 38 hours before Channel 10 claimed the story.  The columnist asks why no one at the news channels reads the papers.

headline: Sanfus in the CAT fund
abstract: An editorial looks at the further confusion caused by the annual $5 fee to the PA Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund (CAT).  It is obvious that the kinks in this new system have not been fully worked out.  In the second year of the program, when the $5 fee is paid, a green sticker is issued, which must be affixed to a motorist's application for a registration renewal.  However, the stickers were not issued when the $5 fees were collected earlier this summer.  While the concept of the CAT Fund is attractive, setting up the funding for it has been filled with headaches and misundersandings.  The auto insurance companies passed off the responsibility to collect the $5 fees to the PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT); PennDOT in-turn passed them off to a separate non-profit.  The Editorial believes that the PA Legislature may have to get involved to cure the CAT Fund's problems.

headline: Judge for yourself: Name recognition looms large in race for 8 seats on county bench
abstract: This article discusses the campaigns for eight seats on Allegheny County's Common Pleas Court and gives pictures and profiles of all of the candidates for the May 21 primary.

headline: Something for Everyone: Tax Cuts Proposed
abstract: This editorial approves of Governor Dick Thornburgh's budget proposal because it cuts taxes and provides more money for many social programs.  The editorial expresses reservations in setting up a rainy day fund, however.

headline: Grange seeks views on license plan
abstract: The PA State Grange would like to hear from subordinate Granges on the PA Game Commission regarding the proposal to increase hunting license fees.  The Grangers were urged to take a careful look at several Game Commission proposals, including a seed packet program, border cuttings, conservation easements, and payments to farmers for delaying alfalfa cutting.

headline: Seat-belt laws
abstract: A letter to the editor opposes a mandatory seat-belt law in Pennsylvania.  Although the author believes this law is utilitarian, he believes that the law is taking away an individual's rights to do what he or she wants, especially if it does not harm anyone else.  The author believes that the insurance lobby is behind this proposed law because they believe they can save millions of dollars.

headline: The Resignation
abstract: This editorial is very critical of the record of former Philadelphia Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor; the author believes that Sambor is completely incompetent.  The MOVE commission revealed several layers of incompetence within the administration of Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode.  The editorial calls on Mayor Goode to appoint a commission to find a new police commissioner.

headline: Savers, investors face diverse worries, choices
abstract: Thanks to the federal deregulation of the banking industry, investors have many more opportunities.  This means they face a large variety of worries as well.  Federal regulators have been warning for months that the structure is fragile; they are particularly concerned about increasing strains on insurance funds that are supposed to protect depositors' money.

headline: Judgeship's lure more than money
abstract: Several Pittsburgh area lawyers and judges are seeking to fill three vacancies on the federal bench.  Though it is a cut in pay for many of the lawyers, they believe that the chance to make a difference in the field of law is an opportunity that cannot be passed up.  Nine candidates have been deemed qualified to fill the vacancies.  The article looks at the qualifications and legal histories of the candidates.

headline: State tax plan praised; fight likely on surplus
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's 1985-86 budget proposal uses a 201 million dollar surplus to fund income tax cuts.  The possibility of federal spending cuts has made some Pennsylvania lawmakers wary of the proposed tax cuts.  In general, lawmakers disagree on how to spend the budget surplus.

headline: Groups push Superfund law
abstract: PA environmentalists and national lobbyists have joined together to petition the Congess to pass a tougher Superfund law.  The groups joined forces as a truck collecting petitions and soil samples suspected of contamination rolled into Harrisburg yesterday.  In all, four trucks with petitions and soil samples are scheduled to arrive in Washington D.C. on Thursday, as Congress considers a new Superfund law.  According to the Sierra Club of PA, Congress is backing away from the stronger Superfund legislation that it considered last year.

headline: Seat-belt laws are Big Brotherism
abstract: A letter to the editor laments that mandatory seat-belt laws represent "Big Brotherism" and that state intervention is not necessary.

headline: US judge upholds state's conduct law
abstract: US Middle District Judge Richard Conaboy said that a recently-challeneged portion of PA's disorderly conduct statute passes constitutional muster.  Paula Pringle, a Chambersburg woman, had challenged the statute's constitutionality in an attempt to overturn her conviction on a disorderly conduct charge.

headline: Securities group fights tax proposal on bonds
abstract: The Public Securities Association (PSA) is lobbying furiously to defeat a proposal from the Reagan administration that would severely limit the use of tax-exempt bonds.  The Reagan plan would deny the current tax exemption for interest on some bonds that finance public-interest projects.  The PSA estimates that 80% of bonds would lose tax-exempt status.  In Pennsylvania, the loss of tax-exempt status would cost state and local governments $2.1 billion in added interest by 1990.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, in a somewhat surprising move, testified a month ago that industrial development bonds, which he has described in the past as a major economic development tool in PA, should be on the table for tax reform.

headline: Justices Enhance Federal Powers Over the States
abstract: In a rare move, the US Supreme Court overruled one of its own recent precedents and significantly enhanced the power of the Federal Government to regulate state activities that had been considered immune from Federal control.  The Court ruled that Federal minimum wage and hour standards cover employees of publicly owned mass transit systems.  By extension, the decision also restores most other state employees to protected status under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

headline: State's bite bigger: Reagan revolution burdens revenue mechanism
abstract: This editorial notes that President Ronald Reagan's philosophy of shifting the responsibility for funding social programs from the federal government to state and local governments has resulted in lower federal taxes but higher local and school-district taxes.  The editorial questions if the total tax bill for an individual has changed at all, and wonders how high local governments will have to raise taxes to pay for services previously provided by the federal government.

headline: How state can cut trash
abstract: This letter to the editor supports legislation that requires a deposit on beverage containers.  When they return the container, their deposit is refunded; the only cost is separating the trash at home and brining the bottles or containers back to the store or a recycling center.  Taxpayers will save millions in waste collection and millions in landfill or other disposal costs with such a program.  The author says that nine states have already adopted similar legislation and that PA should join them.

headline: Seat-belt lobby making progress in effort to deflate air-bag rule
abstract: An intense lobbying effort, characterized by the auto companies as the "Battle of the Belt," is currently underway.  The auto industry is currently making an intense lobbying effort to get states to adopt tough, mandatory seat belt laws, so that it will not be forced, under federal law, to equip cars with air bags by April 1, 1989.  Insurance companies, however, say that new laws are not strong enough to measure up to federal standards.  Some states have also watered down their seat-belt laws.  Michigan is beginning to see a decline in fatalities due to its mandatory seat-belt law.

headline: The View from those Closest to the Fire
abstract: A columnist discusses Father Charles Diamond's role in the West Philadelphia neighborhood that was destroyed when police tried to evict the radical group MOVE from its home on Osage Avenue.  Diamond has been active in the neighborhood his entire life and helped many of the residents who are now homeless.  Diamond says that no one who lived on the 6200 block of Osage Avenue has complained about how police handled the situation, but that complaints have been coming from people who did not know the situation.

headline: Selling the Pennsylvania lottery
abstract: The glory days of the PA Lottery--when the only sure bet was that ticket sales would increase dramatically--may be over.  Though the PA Lottery remains the nation's largest, revenues have leveled off recently.  The PA Revenue Department says that it is not planning to develop gimmicks to make the hard sell.  However, PA Senator Mark Singel already thinks the state has gone too far in selling games.

headline: Kean and Shapiro Clash on Toxic-Waste Cleanup
abstract: New Jersey Governor Kean and Peter Shapiro, the Democratic candidate for Governor, clashed over several issues during a debate yesterday.  Governor Kean said that New Jersey is pursuing a vigorous toxic-waste cleanup, and said that the US Congress's failure to reauthorize the Federal Superfund for toxic cleanup has hurt these programs across the country.  Shapiro countered that the state had yet to clean up the 97 worst sites on the Superfund list, and said that if elected, he would establish a single state agency to deal with the cleanup program.  Shapiro also blamed the Kean administration for politicizing the State Motor Vehicle Division through appointments and contracts awarded to major Republican campaign contributors.  Governor Kean charged that Essex County, where Shapiro is the County Executive, had given contracts to major Democratic contributors.  The two candidates also sparred over the location of a military base that would, most likely, house nuclear weapons.

headline: Sweet says caucus on coal is "ready"
abstract: PA State Representative David Sweet, chairman of the House Coal Caucus, says the reorganzied caucus is ready to address the coal industry's problems.  Included in the article is a list of problems that Sweet cited as hurting the coal industry; the article also lists the new agenda for the Coal Caucus.

headline: Steel unemployment reports may be low
abstract: According to a recent study, unemployment and related problems such as depression and anxiety are more serious in Pittsburgh than US government statistics indicate.  The survey also found a correlation between unemployment and certain crimes--such as assault, disorderly conduct, and alcohol-related crimes.

headline: Hunters And Private Property
abstract: Greene County landowners have demanded an amendment to state game laws that would require a person hunting on private property to receive written permission from the property owner to do so.  The editorial says that such an amendment is unlikely because it is not supported by the state Game Commission.  The editorial also says that the Game Commission should schedule a public hearing in Greene County to consider the complaints of the property owners.

headline: Seniors in transit: Subsidy cut hurts rural elderly, efficient operators
abstract: Facing the prospect of a major shortfall in funds, the state Department of Transportation has ordered local transportation agencies receiving senior-citizen fare subsidies to cut fares by 20% or lose their subsidies.  This editorial argues that this plan hurts agencies that are efficiently run, such as that in Cumberland County; the plan is also unfair to elderly people.

headline: Thornburgh's new sentencing initiative
abstract: This editorial believes that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh is on the right track in trying to find sentencing guidelines that would adequately cover every person who is convicted of a crime.  In particular, the editorial lauds the governor's proposal of legislation that ensures people convicted of serious crimes get longer sentences.  The governor's proposed law would allow judges to set a prisoner's minimum jail term.  Judges also would have to be consulted before prisoners are released.  The governor also proposes allowing prisoners to earn time off for good behavior, a concept already used in the federal prison system.  The editorial believes this proposal will allow PA to stay at the forefront on the fight to get tougher on criminals.

headline: Senate Law and Justice Committee votes to continue LCB
abstract: The PA Senate Law and Justice Committee has endorsed a bill that proposes the continuation of the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB).  The bill, authored by State Senator John Shumaker, contains more than 30 proposed changes, among them stripping the LCB of its enforcement powers and turning them over to the PA Attorney General's office.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh opposes the Shumaker bill, and said that it shortchanges the free enterprise system and the public generally.  The hottest issue up for debate yesterday was whether wine should be sold in privately owned stores, a proposal that was eventually turned down.  A call for a public referendum on state-store divestiture was also turned down.  Approval was given for the sale of wine coolers by beer distributors.  A separate article on the page lists other proposals contained in the Shumaker bill.

headline: Kerr suspended from practicing law
abstract: The state Supreme Court has suspended John M. Kerr, the former deputy auditor general who was convicted last year of selling state jobs, from practicing law in PA.  Edwin Frese, counsel to the court's disciplinary board, said the suspension was ordered because of Kerr's conviction on 139 counts of bribery, conflict of interest and obstruction of justice.  The convictions stemmed from a $200,000 job-selling scheme in the auditor general's office; job applicants paid $1,000 to $10,000 each for jobs and promotions.

headline: The chronology
abstract: This article provides a chronology of significant events relating to the Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart.

headline: Stockman quits Cabinet amid budget talks
abstract: President Ronald Reagan's budget director, David A. Stockman, announced his resignation.  Stockman, a constantly outspoken cabinet member, has recently been warning that tax increases would be necessary to cut the $200-billion-plus deficit unless Congress adopted the program cuts proposed by the Republican-controlled Senate.  These cuts include a freeze of Social Security cost-of-living allowances.  Stockman will become a managing director with the New York investment firm of Salomon Brothers Incorporated.

headline: In No-Doubt Drought, City Flows with Gallon-t Conservation
abstract: The Delaware River Basin Commission is expected to call a region wide declaration of drought emergency today.  The decree would be the third time a drought emergency has been called in the basin.  All states and municipalities would immediately face a ban on non-essential water use.

headline: Some see plan to sell Conrail as giveaway
abstract: Many US Congressmen are criticizing the proposed sail of the government's railroad, Conrail, to Norfolk Southern Corporation.  They are arguing that the Transportation Department did not press a hard-enough bargain in its rush to get the government out of the railroad business.  Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole rejects that criticism and contends that the price is fair and stood the test of competitive bidding.  The sale must be approved by Congress before it is completed.

headline: Three on Death Row: All-Time Record Set
abstract: There are currently three Lackawanna County residents under the sentence of death, an all time record for the county.  This editorial laments the state of "civilized" society because there are so many murders taking place in the county and throughout the state.

headline: Senate panel modifies liquor-code bill, reducing local powers
abstract: The state Senate Law and Justice Committee voted yesterday to revise a liquor-code bill; the bill would have given local police departments and residents certain powers in combating the presence of nuisance bars.  The PA Tavern Association requested the changes, as it was concerned that if local police deparments were given authority over liquor-code violations, police might use the power to shut down bars they don't like.  The bill will not be voted on until after the State House and Senate return from their summer session recess on Sept. 18.

headline: Kukovich Launches Grass-Roots Campaign
abstract: PA State Representative Allen Kukovich is attempting to form a grass-roots, populist support base that will be strong enough to win the gubernatorial race in Pennsylvania.  Kukovich claims that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has been more concerned with following President Ronald Reagan's line than with doing what is best for PA.  Kukovich also acknowledges that he will need to do well among African-American voters if he hopes to win the governorship.

headline: The FORUM: Nuclear still best power
abstract: This letter to the editor defends nuclear power and says that any complaints about nuclear energy are unfounded.

headline: Survey says state construction employment is at 5-year high
abstract: According to the PA Business Survey, Employment in the state's service and construction industries increased significantly in March; employment fell to a record low in non-durable goods, however, because of a flood of imports.

headline: It'll soon come to pass that state will not have hazardous waste sites
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) announced its plans to close Sechan Limestone Industries, one of four commercial hazardous waste sites in the state.  The DER also intends to close three more sites in the near future.   A DER spokesman said that new sites will not be available for three to five years because of a lengthy permitting and public-hearing process.

headline: Specter amendment gives Amtrak subsidy new life
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter steered a budget amendment salvaging funding for Amtrak through the Senate, but the rail passenger service's future remains uncertain.  The funding was included in a last-minute substitute budget resolution.  Specter said the vote in favor of his amendment should be a signal to the Reagan administration and the Senate leadership that subsidizing Amtrak is important.

headline: Thumbs Down for Ex-Benedict Aide
abstract: Dauphin County Common Pleas Judge William Lipsitt rejected arguments by John Kerr, former chief aide to Auditor General Al Benedict, for a reversal of his July 1984 jury conviction on 139 counts of conspiracy, bribery, obstructing justice and violations of state ethics laws.

headline: Senator John Heinz Thursday
abstract: US Senator John Heinz used a helicopter to tour flood-ravaged parts of Western PA.  He then met with local officials, homeowners, and businessmen to determine their needs.  The Federal Emergency Management Agency and PA state officials are conducting damage assessments and expect to submit a formal request for federal disaster assistance Sunday.  As a result of severe flooding, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh already has declared an emergency disaster in several Western PA counties.  Federal aid will be needed to rebuild infrastructure, public services, and locks and dams.  The article also examines issues of water purification, tetanus immunizations, and runaway barges along the river.

headline: Kukovich to sit this one out
abstract: An opinion piece talks about the withdrawal of PA State Representative Allen Kukovich from the race for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination in PA.  The author states that, although Kukovich spent a lot of time talking about serious issues, he may have been the only candidate to do so; he also did not spend the same amount of time trying to fund his campaign, which in the end led to his withdrawal.  Kukovich said that he expects the party that raises the most money to win the governorship.  The author states that talking about the issues may not be a wise move politically.  He said that instead politicians should concern themselves with getting elected.  By withdrawing, Kukovich can introduce legislation next year designed to gain the goals he espoused as a gubernatorial hopeful.

headline: The undamaged reactor
abstract: The undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island will be starting up tomorrow.  Angry anti-nuclear activists are stunned by the Supreme Court's decision allowing the restart, and they are making their anger known.  They promise one more court appeal, but it may be too late as GPU Nuclear Corporation wants to bring the plant on line by noon tomorrow.  GPU Nuclear is very confident at this hour, especially considering that a key opponent of the restart, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, has decided to go along with the Supreme Court decision.

headline: Tax cut too small
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh recommended that the $297 million budget surplus be used for a personal income tax cut.  This editorial says that, in addition to returning all of the budget surplus to the citizens, the state should reduce personal income tax rates.

headline: Keep an eye on Capitol
abstract: A columnist writes of bills that could possibly have an effect on outdoor activities.  Bills considered are the legalization of rattlesnake sacking contests;  increases in hunting license fees; and bringing the Game and Fish Commissions under "sunset" legislation.  The author feels that these agencies should not be subject to review by the Legislature, and that they should be able to set their own policies.

headline: Specter bemoans rail sale
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter said that it would be "cataclysmic" for PA if Conrail is sold to Norfolk Southern Corporation.  Citing the loss of jobs in PA and the elimination of competition, Specter said that he and US Senator John Heinz are fighting US Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole's recommendation that the federal government's 85% interest in Conrail be sold to Norfolk Southern.

headline: Time to crack down on young offenders
abstract: On the day after the PA Senate Law and Justice Committee rejected his plan to abolish state liquor stores, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh was pushing hard for the passage of two more bills that will close the loopholes through which juvenile criminals often escape prosecution.  Speaking to members of the PA Juvenille Officers Association, Thornburgh said that the "dangerous juvenile offender" legislation he has already signed into law did not provide all the tools needed by law enforcement officers in the fight against crimes committed by juveniles.  Thornburgh would like to establish a statewide registry of photographs, fingerprints, and criminal histories of chronic juvenile offenders; the database would be maintained by the state police.

headline: Show Car Insurance Industry the ERA of Their Ways
abstract: An opinion piece rails against the passage of PA Senate bills 743, 744, 745, which will now go to the PA House of Representatives for a vote.  These bills, according to the author, will unfairly overcharge women, low mileage drivers, and senior citizens on auto-insurance premiums.  The intent of these bills is to overturn the PA State Supreme Court's decision by legalizing sex discrimination in auto insurance rates.  Auto discrimination hurts everyone, and the author calls on everyone to write their state representative and urge him or her to vote against these bills.

headline: Lacking votes, Justice panel delays action on Reynolds
abstract: The Republican-controlled US Senate Judiciary Committee, unable to muster enough votes to approve William Bradford Reynolds as associate attorney general in the Justice Department, unanimously agreed to postpone a decision for a week.  The delay was a sharp, though not necessarily fatal, setback for President Ronald Reagan, who has been lobbying wavering senators in an effort to rescue his faltering nominee.  Reagan and Attorney General Edwin Meese III now have an extra week to try to persuade three key senators--Charles McC. Mathias, Howell Heflin, and Arlen Specter--to back Reynolds or to send the nomination to the Senate without a committee recommendation.

headline: They're moving but still fight TMI restart
abstract: Norman and Marjorie Aamodt have been fighting against the restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor for six years.  They used to live only 45 miles away from the nuclear plant, but recently they sold their farm and moved to New York.  The couple still feels it is necessary to fight against the restart of the plant.

headline: Tax cuts top a Pa. budget crafted with little rancor
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a record $9.3 billion budget for the 1986 fiscal year.  The budget featured a 6.38% reduction in the personal income tax rate, a $189 million reduction in business unemployment tax, and a $25 million tax-credit program for depressed industries.

headline: Legal bottleneck
abstract: This editorial supports legislation limiting the sale of beverage bottles and cans to those for which a deposit is paid.  The editorial says that this legislation will alleviate the overfilled landfills and will also help to clean up the highways.

headline: Specter urges further Conrail study
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter said he would urge the Senate Republican leadership to delay action on the proposed sale of Conrail until a full divestiture study is completed.  The divestitures were ordered by the Department of Transportation to meet possible anti-trust objections to the combination of the two railroads.

headline: Torquato attorney testifies
abstract: This article outlines pretrial motions of defendants in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) alleged bribery case.  The defendants are charged with being involved in attempts to bribe public officials to help CTA win Social Security tax recovery contracts.  The defendants had planned a joint defense, but that fell apart when two defendants entered a guilty plea.

headline: Skinned by the CAT
abstract: This editorial discusses the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund (CAT) and says that the state Department of Transportation should collect CAT fees in order to avoid confusion.

headline: Lancaster Lawmakers and Their Committees
abstract: An opinion piece takes a closer look at the committee assignments of Lancaster County lesgislators.
