The article looks at the assignments of US Congressman Robert Walker and PA State Senator Noah Wenger.  The opinion piece praises both men for improving Lancaster County's positions--something that was facilitated by their placements on strong and important committees.

headline: Three Mile Island Suits Involving 19 Settled by Insurers
abstract: Dauphin County Court approved $3.9 million in settlements involving 19 people who were allegedly injured during the 1979 Three-Mile-Island accident.  The settlements were approved out of court.

headline: Tax lobbying push begins
abstract: President Ronald Reagan declared that an overhaul of the nation's tax code is all but inevitable and that under his plan, "making ends meet is going to be a lot easier for a lot of people."  In general, the biggest winners in Reagan's proposal would be the wealthy, as well as low-income families who claim few deductions.

headline: Limit on mud bugs lifted by commission
abstract: The state Fish Commission decided to eliminate the daily limit on catching dragonfly nymphs--more commonly known as mud bugs.  Because dragonfly nymphs are considered fish bait, they were subject to the 50-per-day creel limit, like other fish bait.  But a staff review of nymphs and their lifestyles led to the conclusion that regulating the habitat of nymphs is more important than the imposition of general daily limits.

headline: Spend it on transit: No to downtown ramps on I-95
abstract: A letter to the editor argues against the building of five ramps along Interstate 95 to connect it to Center City and Market Street.  The author believes this will simply lead to more traffic jams and cars polluting the air of this historic district in Philadelphia.  The author also believes that this expansion will undermine public transportation and lead to more rate hikes.

headline: Torquato's 4-year term upheld
abstract: A US District Judge has refused to reduce a four-year prison term imposed on the alleged mastermind of a scheme to bribe state and local officials in return for government contracts.  John Torquato Jr., whom federal prosecutors called the "prime mover" in the Computer Technology Associates scam, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy.

headline: Small Banks Put Delay on Interstate Bill
abstract: Backers of an interstate banking bill, legislation which is supported by bigger banks, were told to work out a compromise with smaller banks on the proposed bill.  PA Banking Secretary Ben McEnteer endorsed the interstate banking bill, which is a modified version of a proposal put forth by the PA Bankers Association, which was also supported by the state's larger banks.  However, legislators indicated they were concerned about the future of small banks and the depersonalization of services that might result from interstate banking.

headline: Lawmakers rebuff Thornburgh, back more heating aid
abstract: PA lawmakers approved a compromise bill that would provide $11 million in state money to a program that provides home heating aid to low-income residents.  Governor Dick Thornburgh has expressed opposition to providing state funds for this program and has said that sufficient federal funds are available.  Legislators disagree however, and said that it is necessary to put additional money in the program.

headline: Three Mile Island: Accident without an end.  The lethal legacy inside TMI
abstract: This article discusses the history of Three Mile Island (TMI) and gives a timeline of the accident and the costs of the cleanup.  The author notes that the costs of cleanup extend beyond the healthcare costs of the cleanup workers.  The TMI cleanup is never-ending.

headline: Taxpayers may get $160 million break
abstract: It is expected that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will include a tax cut in his proposed budget that would lower the tax rate from 2.35% to 2.2%.  This tax cut is due to the $188 million surplus expected at the end of the fiscal year.

headline: Litter Lifters
abstract: A photo depicts Boy Scout Troop 98 picking up litter along the road in front of the Tri-County Market in Londonderry Township.  The cleanup project was undertaken as part of the PA Department of Transportation's "Keep PA Beautiful" program.

headline: State goes slow in trend toward mandatory seat belts
abstract: State Senator Edward Early has introduced two mandatory seat belt bills and has received some support, but most legislators appear either apathetic or downright hostile to the idea of a mandatory seat belt requirement.  Many legislators feel that requiring people to wear seatbelts is too much government interference.  Governor Dick Thornburgh has no position on the bill.

headline: Tough on criminals
abstract: This editorial states that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's signing of three execution warrants this month ended a policy followed by his predecessor, Governor Milton Shapp, of commuting sentences so inmates could be eligible for parole.  Thornburgh's approach is that the sentence imposed by the judge should be imposed.  The editorial says that Thornburgh's tightening of standards for commutation is one way that the state can fight against the increasing crime rate.

headline: Sputters: New rules for used car dealers rejected by regulatory panel
abstract: The State Board of Vehicle Manufacturers, Dealers and Salespersons proposed regulations to set minimum standards for used car dealerships.  However, the Independent Regulatory Review Commission, established to keep bureaucracy from overstepping its bounds, voted unanimously against the proposed rules.  The Comission said that the provisions did not appear to be in the public interest because they may go beyond legislative intent.

headline: Legislature gets down to business: Area frosh lawmakers settle in
abstract: The first day of legislative work consisted of reorganizing committees; no important votes were taken.  The article discusses the first day of Allentown-area freshmen legislators.

headline: TMI 'chorus'
abstract: This letter to the editor says that Met Ed, owners of the Three Mile Island (TMI) nuclear power plant, is seeking Public Utility Commission approval for a $47.3 million rate increase.   If the increase is granted, it will offset any savings that would come from restarting TMI's Unit-1 Reactor.  The author says that Met Ed should not be granted a rate increase, and they should not be allowed to restart the Unit 1 reactor.

headline: The cities are in line for another whack
abstract: A columnist criticizes Reagan's tax simplification plan and domestic spending cuts because the spending cuts will be devastating to social programs for Philadelphia's poor, and the tax proposal will hurt most of the city's physical development programs.

headline: Local incident emphasizes need for steel trap ban
abstract: This letter to the editor argues that steel-jaw traps should be outlawed because they are cruel and often harm animals that are not targeted.  The author references a recent accident involving a dog.  The author urges concerned citizens to write to their congressman to ban the steel-jaw-leg-hold trap throughout the US.

headline: State needs seat-belt law
abstract: This editorial supports a mandatory seat-belt law in PA, citing evidence that such a law saved lives in New York.  The editorial believes that the law should be passed as soon as possible.

headline: Trooper siezed, linked to Grosso
abstract: State trooper Corporal Donald Hughes was arrested after a grand jury charged him with taking bribes, compromising police raids, and accepting vacations and other favors from numbers boss Anthony Grosso.  The investigation began 18 months ago when members of the state police and Pittsburgh Police Department told the PA Attorney General's Office that they believed their investigations centering on illegal numbers operations were being compromised.  In April 1985, Grosso was fined and put on 10 years' probation after pleading guilty to 14 gambling-related charges.

headline: State catastrophic fund collections begin: That $5 auto insurance bill is for real
abstract: PA switched from a no-fault insurance system, and the state Legislature decided to create a pool of funds to be used by any Pennsylvanian who incurred more than $100,000 in accident-related medical expenses.  To finance the pool, all PA vehicle owners will pay an annual $5 fee to the PA Motor Vehicle Insurance Collection Services, a nonprofit agency set up by the Legislature to collect the fees.

headline: Lengthy CTA-jury deliberations likely
abstract: It appears that jurors in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery-conspiracy trial intend to take their time in returning a verdict.  Within 20 minutes of beginning deliberations, they had asked the court for permission to review the testimony of 22 of the 103 witnesses.  CTA attorneys William T. Smith and Alan R. Stoneman are each charged with one count of conspiracy, six counts of mail fraud and nine counts of interstate transportation in aid of racketeering.  The case alleges that Smith and Stoneman conspired with others to bribe public officials in return for obtaining government contracts for CTA.

headline: TMI critics qualified
abstract: In response to a series of Philadelphia-Inquirer ads criticizing General Public Utilities (GPU), GPU placed an ad in the Patriot-News.  This letter to the editor gives the credentials of the experts that were quoted in the Inquirer ads.

headline: US gets more in tax than it spends in Pa.
abstract: According to a recent study, Pennsylvania sent an average of $201 more per resident to the US Treasury in 1984 than it received in federal spending.  PA's net loss in federal taxes versus spending came largely because it fares relatively poorly in defense spending.

headline: Low bear harvest this year makes 5-day season likely
abstract: Gary Alt, a PA Game Commission biologist and nationally recognized authority on black bears, believes that the reported two-day kill of 1,025 animals last week was insufficient to stabilize PA's black bear population.  This means that there may be a five-day bear season in PA hunters' future.  Alt believes that at least 1,500 bears need to be killed in order to stabilize the population.  In other news, field personnel of the PA Game and Fish Commission voted 68 to 43 last week to accept a new contract with the agencies as a separate bargaining unt within the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees.  Another successful firearms antlered deer season seems likely after a reported opening-day harvest of 29,000 animals.

headline: State panel to consider exotic 'levitation' train
abstract: Members of the state High Speed Intercity Rail Passenger Commission voted narrowly to consider linking Pittsburgh and Philadelphia with a $10 billion high speed magnetic-levitation train.  The panel also decided unanimously to study the possibility of advanced high-speed trains with steel wheels that would cost $7 billion.

headline: Trooper's son quizzed in shooting
abstract: Investigators probing a drug arrest that led to the death of an undercover officer and the arrest of two men have questioned the son of a state trooper; the trooper's son was seen at the crime scene shortly before the incident; he is not considered a suspect, however.  Undercover officers made a drug purchase that lead to the death of one of the officers.  Two men were arrested.

headline: State Debates Liquor Control
abstract: Under a state law that calls for the periodic review of government agencies, the PA Liquor Control Board will go out of business at the end of the year unless the General Assembly extends it.  Governor Dick Thornburgh is an opponent to the state liquor system and has proposed ending it over a five-year period.  Retailers and wholesalers are following developments closely.

headline: Lewis declines to run for governor in '86 primary
abstract: Drew Lewis said yesterday that he will not challenge PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton for the Republican nomination for Governor of PA in 1986.  Lewis cited his loyalty to Scranton as the main reason for his refusal to run.  The attempt to draft Lewis was the first public sign of doubt in Scranton by some Republicans, who think he is too liberal.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has said that he will announce his decision on whether or not to run against US Senator Arlen Specter for his seat after the November 5 elections.  Lewis ran unsuccessfully for governor in 1974, but then went on to serve a key roll in US President Ronald Reagan's 1980 campaign; he later became Secretary of Transportation.  Scranton is now prepared to run a well-financed campaign and is considered a formidible opponent to most Democrats.

headline: TMI critics who paid a price
abstract: Engineers and workers who complained about safety problems in the cleanup of Three Mile Island were forced into silence, suspended or fired.  Federal investigators are researching these allegations, as well as saftey problems, at the plant.

headline: Thornburgh and Cuomo clash on White House tax plan
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh and New York Governor Mario Cuomo testified byefore the House Ways and Means Committee on the most controversial part of President Reagan's tax plan: the repeal of deductions for state and local taxes.  Thornburgh, a Republican, supported the plan and said that the state-and-local deduction, which totals about $34 billion per year nationwide, forced many states to subsidze such high-tax states as New York.  Cuomo, a leading Democratic critic of the tax plan, argued that those benefiting form the break "aren't the wealthy elite, they're the backbone of middle America."

headline: Making an Opposing Point
abstract: Photo depicts Phil Martello, president of the New Castle-based Citizens Against Toxic Sites group, explaining his opposition to a proposed landfill in North Beaver Township; Martello is expressing his opposition to Environmental Resources Secretary Nicolas DeBenedictis.

headline: Strict enforcement of turnpike laws planned
abstract: A million vehicles are expected to travel the PA Turnpike over the Labor Day weekend; the Turnpike Commission and PA state police intend to strictly enforce the speed limit and other traffic laws, such as hitchhiking and parking regulations.  The commission said that turnpike service stations have enough fuel to handle the holiday traffic.  They also said that tow trucks and other emergency vehicles will be available to help motorists where needed.  Oversize and overweight vehicles will be banned during the holiday, however.

headline: Troubled times for the state police
abstract: An editorial believes that the recent arrest of three Greensburg-based state policemen on drug charges should serve as the impetus for a review of the state police department's hiring and personnel rules.  Between 1981 and 1984, 12 to 16 state policemen were arrested each year on various criminal charges.  The editorial highlights the many instances of criminal acts within the state police this year.  The editorial also believes that the state police may be in danger of losing their reputation as a model of integrity.

headline: State drops CAT stickers
abstract: Responding to widespread public criticism, Insurance Commissioner George Gorde announced yesterday that the state is abandoning a proof-of-payment green sticker system for the state's Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund for motorists.  Grode said that motorists will no longer have to attach the green sticker to their vehicle registration renewals, but instead will certify on the form that they have paid the $5 insurance fee.  The PA Department of Transportation will be able to verify payment through a computer check.  When a collection agency set up by the state and the insurance industry began sending bills for the $5 fee earlier this year, state lawmakers began getting complaints--many of which centered around the requirement that a motorist secure proof-of-payment before being allowed to renew his vehicle registration.  A new application form for use starting in December will spell out the revised certification process.

headline: Lewis-Scranton fight near
abstract: An opinion piece examines the possible candidacy of Drew Lewis for Governor of PA.  Lewis has strong support with US President Ronald Reagan; he is the former US Secretary of Transportation and could run with Reagan's tacit support or full backing.  Lewis's candidacy, taken in context with PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's hints that he may challenge US Senator Arlen Specter for his seat, means that both of these Reagan candidates could run as a team.  It could also complicate Thornburgh's relationship with Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton, who will be running for the governorship as well.  Lewis may have trouble in heavily unionized southwestern PA, due his handling of air traffic controllers' strike in 1981.  Lewis has been pushed to run for governor by several Republican representatives who view Scranton as too young, liberal, and laid back.

headline: TMI feedwater rated low in reliability
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has classified Three Mile Island's (TMI) Unit 1 emergency feedwater system as having low reliability--meaning that the feedwater system, which removes heat from the plant's primary system, could be expected to fail once in 1,000 times.  GPU Nuclear, which runs TMI, plans to make improvements to the feedwater system; these improvements will raise it to medium reliability.  This report comes at a time when the US Third Circuit Court of Appeals is reviewing the NRC's decision to allow GPU Nuclear to restart Unit 1.  The Union of Concerned Scientists has long held TMI Unit 1's feedwater system and backup systems were highly susceptible to failure.

headline: Thornburgh criticizes steel companies: Governor raps lack of investment
abstract: While testifying before the US House Ways and Means Committee, Governor Dick Thornburgh criticized PA's steel companies for thier use of tax incentives.  Thornburgh argued that steel companies are not using the capital gained from tax incentives to invest in equipment and infrastructure.

headline: Municipal officials stress need for sewage treatment fund
abstract: Representatives from six municipalities journeyed to Harrisburg to re-emphasize their needs for government funds to construct sewage treatment plants.

headline: Stuck with CAT fund
abstract: A letter to the editor accuses the state CAT Fund of bamboozling money from motorists.  In October, the author paid $10 to the fund for his family's two cars, expecting the money to pay for a year's coverage.  Now, the author has received a second bill.  The author claims that he calculated a pro-rated premiums and sent in the balance due with a letter of explanation.  When the check was returned, the author was told that the law was retroactive.  The author doubts that he would have been paid by the CAT Fund had he filed a claim in December of 1985; now residents are stuck with the fund.

headline: Tucker Named to Top Police Job
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode yesterday named Kevin Tucker, former head of the Secret Service in Philadelphia, to head the 7,000 member Philadelphia Police Department.  Tucker is the first person named commissioner to come from outside the department since 1924.  The decision to select an "outsider" triggered an angry reaction from some officers in the department and officials of Lodge 5 of the Fraternal Order of Police.  Goode appealed to police officers and the public to support Tucker on the job.  Tucker will have to confront a corruption scandal which has severely damaged the credibility of the department.

headline: State plans insurance program
abstract: A program to help local governments, day-care centers, and taverns find liability insurance coverage in PA will begin January 6, 1986.  Acting Insurance Commissioner George Grode, joined by insurance industry representatives, said that program will ease the liability insurance crisis in PA, even though it will not address high coverage costs.  Under the Market Assistance Program, three committees appointed by Grode will help find coverage for local governments, day-care centers, and establishments that sell alcoholic beverages.  A further description of the process is contained in the article.

headline: Local GOP Using a New Weapon
abstract: Lancaster County Republicans recently bought a new computer system that will enable them to do amazing things in tailoring their appeals to specific segments of the electorate.  In the last few years, the Republicans have bought over $13,000 worth of computer equipment and software.  County Democrats simply do not have the funding to do what the Republicans are doing.  The Republicans just started a database on county voters that will allow them to conduct random polling of all voters; it will also allow them to target specific neighborhoods to focus on issues of importance to the voters in that area.  Republicans are just beginning to think of other uses for their new computers.

headline: TMI letter was not accurate
abstract: A letter to the editor, written by a Manager of GPU Nuclear's Communication Services Division, refutes several claims made by Gail Bradford, who wrote a previous letter objecting to a Post-Gazette editorial.  The author contends that Ms. Bradford's charges are baseless; Ms. Bradford alledges that senior GPU management lied to Congress and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission about the severity of the Three-Mile-Island accident.  Also, The management of GPU Nuclear Corporation did not, according to the author, condone cheating by reactor operators on licensing examinations in 1981.  The author also refutes Ms. Bradford's points regarding  TMI's steam generators and the issue of disposal of high-level radioactive wastes.

headline: Thornburgh enjoys that big surplus
abstract: A columnist discusses Governor Dick Thornburgh's fiscal policies and the fact that he has been able to create a surplus in the budget during tough economic times.  The columnist also says that Thornburgh is concerned about his political future and wonders if he is eying higher office.

headline: Municipalities will vie for sewer funds at hearing
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources (DER) will hold a public hearing to determine which municipalities will receive federal money to help pay for sewage treatment plant construction.  Nearly 100 municipalities have filed plans with the DER for construction of new plants or improvements to old plants.  According to a DER spokesperson, projects with a higher priority rating are first on the list to receive federal money.

headline: Study links seat belt use, laws
abstract: A Lafayette College researcher has found that drivers in New Jersey, where there is a law requiring seat belt use, buckle up more often than their PA counterparts.  The researcher also believes that, although seat belt legislation seems to increase seat belt use, continued publicity is needed to sustain the initial use rate.  New Jersey's law is somewhat weak, in that police cannot pull over a car simply because the occupants are not wearing restraints.  Seat belt legislation is currently pending in the PA Legislature.

headline: Tucker's challenge is a department challenge, too
abstract: This editorial looks at the daunting tasks facing new Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Tucker as he takes over as head of the Philadelphia Police Department.  Though some in the police department are disappointed that Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode went outside the department for the hiring, the editorial believes that such a move was necessary to distance the new commissioner from the department's past.  An ongoing graft scandal, the MOVE confrontation, and other questionable police actions have exposed a glaring failure of command.  The editorial believes that Tucker has a lot of qualifications to turn the situation around and gives him a 50-50 chance of doing so.  Although Tucker cannot do it alone, Mayor Goode and the Philadelphia Police Department need Tucker far more than he needs them.

headline: State should change name
abstract: An opinion piece argues that PA's laws about gambling are hypocritical.  The author notes that bingo is legal but casino gambling is illegal, and that the state operates a lottery system and says that the state should either outlaw gambling entirely or remove all the barriers and let it flourish or stagnate on its own.

headline: Local Republicans advise Thornburgh to set out senate race
abstract: While Democrats have begun jockeying for position for next year's gubernatorial race, the question of whether PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will run against US Senator Arlen Specter for his Senate seat still remains unanswered.  Several PA Republicans said this week that Thornburgh should stay away from the Senate race.  US Senator John Heinz says that a Thornburgh-Specter primary would benefit a Democratic candidate and would hurt the Republican Party.  Marlene Carrier, state director for the PA Council of Republican Women, believes that Specter's governing philosophy better represents PA as a whole.

headline: TMI observance
abstract: A letter to the editor criticizes Three Mile Island (TMI) spokesperson Lisa Robinson for saying that speaking out against the company was "fear mongering."  The author criticizes the company and says that it cannot be expected to safely operate Unit 1 at TMI.

headline: Thornburgh's budget
abstract: Editorial complains about the yearly arguments and political bickering that is caused by state legislators trying to adopt a budget.  Lawmakers have promised that there should be no problem this year, and that the PA state budget should pass easily.  This editorial hopes that lawmakers are right and that the budget passes easily.

headline: N.J. radioactive-waste plan may shift
abstract: The plan to store low-level radioactive waste in PA could complicate a similar effort in New Jersey.  All states are moving to join regional groups in planning for waste storage.  New Jersey is involved in the Northeast Compact with Connecticut, Maryland, and Delaware.  PA announced the Appalachian Compact with Maryland, Delaware, and West Virginia.  If Maryland and Delaware join the Appalachian Compact it will affect New Jersey.

headline: Taxi services for elderly spurn rate cut
abstract: In April, the state Department of Transportation ordered all cab services for the elderly to accept a 20 percent fare cut by May 17 or lose their state subsidies.  Only two of the 19 Philadelphia-area taxi services have accepted the fare cut, raising fears that many of the region's senior citizens might lose their low-cost transportation.  The state pays for 90 percent of the cost of the rides, and senior citizens pay for 10 percent; the program is popular and has cost more than anticipated.

headline: Turnpike hiring draws suit
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has asked the state Supreme Court to find the Turnpike Commission's vice chairman, Peter Camiel, and its executive director, James Wilson, in contempt of court for violating Supreme Court orders issued September 12 and April 8.  These orders permit Camiel to fill job vacancies in only those posts previously approved by a majority of the panel's members.  The suit, filed by Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson, says Camiel approved the hiring of a regional assistant executive director, a job not approved by the commission.

headline: State, county officials deny Shapp's claims about Limerick plan
abstract: Former PA Governor Milton Shapp charged that confusion existed between Montgomery County and the state over who had the responsibility to provide uncontaminated food and water for evacuees in case of a nuclear accident at Limerick nuclear power plant.  However, Dorothy Charney, a spokesman for the PA Emergency Management Agency, and H. Lindley Bigelow, coordinator of Montgomery County's office of emergency preparedness, both denied that there was any basic disagreement between the state and the county.

headline: Local Tax Reform
abstract: This editorial calls for the state to give local governments broader taxing powers.  The editorial feels that there should be more balance between property and income taxation for local governments.

headline: TMI restart is OKd
abstract: The US Supreme Court yesterday lifted a lower-court order barring the restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 1, which has been idle since Unit 2 was damaged in March 1979.  Barring a last minute legal hitch, the reactor could be cleared by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for restart today.  Three Mile Island Alert, an anti-nuclear group, filed the request asking the Supreme Court to prohibit the restart pending the outcome of appeals challenging Unit 1's operation.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, Harrisburgh Mayor Stephen Reed and the Union of Concerned Scientists filed supporting documents.  TMIA will ask the US 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals to block the restart on a separate legal action challenging the integrity of GPU Nuclear.

headline: Thornburgh's budget short $450 million, Fumo says
abstract: State Senator Vincent Fumo said that Governor Dick Thornburgh's 1985 budget falls at least 450 million dollars short of meeting the state's needs.  Senator Fumo says there may not be enough political courage in the Legislature to stand up to the governor.

headline: N.Y. Drained '65 Drought
abstract: As a result of the 1954 landmark Supreme Court ruling on Delaware-River water rights, New York City turned off the spigots in 1965 and ceased to spill water into the Delaware river.  President Johnson summoned all parties of the Delaware River Basin Commission to the White House and declared the region a disaster area.  The current drought conditions are not expected to bring about the "Water war" that occurred in 1965.

headline: The bridge problem
abstract: A federal Department of Transportation report shows that almost a quarter of PA's 21,719 bridges are "structurally deficient." This means they are unable to carry the weight they were designed to handle.  Another 10 percent are of PA's birdges are "functionally obsolete," which means they are not intended to accommodate current vehicle sizes.  This editorial urges the state to fund a program to rebuild or replace bridges that are deficient or obsolete.

headline: U.S. Attorney MOVEd to Investigate
abstract: The US Justice Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation are launching an investigation into the Philadelphia siege of a MOVE house in West Philadelphia that led to the death of 11 people.  The FBI and Justice Department will cooperate with Philadelphia's own investigation of the MOVE siege, which is being conducted by the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission--an 11-member panel appointed by Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode.  The PA State Senate's Committee on Urban Affairs and Housing also will be launching an investigation into the matter.

headline: State's beer distributors get OK to advertise prices
abstract: Daniel Pennick, chairman of the state Liquor Control Board, announced that the board has imposed a moratorium on enforcing a regulation that barred advertising of price information by members of the malt- liquor industry.  The ruling, which will affect the state's 1,580 wholesale beer distributors, came at the recommendation of LCB staff counsel Gary DiVito, who researched legal aspects of the code provision.

headline: Looking for Doughnut Holes?
abstract: In this Opinion piece, the columnist looks at how his view of last month's Young Republican roast of County Commissioner James Huber may have been overly pessimistic.  In a story he had written earlier, the author noted that there were seven empty tables and numerous absentees among GOP leadership for the event.  Ernie Schreiber, a fellow journalist who covered the dinner for the Lancaser New Era, said that "GOP insiders" blamed the lack of attendance on displeasure with Huber's administration.  Also, when taken into the context of two other GOP fundraisers held during during that week, the Huber roast was the most highly attended; it even beat out a 1982 roast of US Congressman Robert Walker, which had several high profile names attend.  Two lessons are learned from this event.  First, empty seats are a lot less noticeable when people are spread out.  Second, always hold your event in a hall smaller than the crowd you expect to draw.

headline: TMI restart stopped by high court
abstract: US Supreme Court Justice William Brennan yesterday halted the scheduled restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 2 Reactor.  Responding to an appeal from TMI Alert Incorporated, an anti-nuclear group, Brennan continued a court order that was due to expire at 4 p.m. today; the order gives the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the owners of TMI time to respond while the case is appealed to the US Supreme Court.  The 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals lifted the stay last week, which prevented the restart of the undamaged Unit 2.

headline: Three Plans To Choose From: Cutting State Taxes
abstract: The $297 million budget surplus is a blessing for Pennsylvanians that will likely mean lower taxes and more state aid to local school districts.  Legislators must exercise caution, however, so that state government can remain financially secure in lean years as well.

headline: New themes point way to solutions
abstract: This opinion piece urges cooperation in tackling the problems faced by the Southern Alleghenies Planning and Development Commission.  The six counties in the Commission are facing problems with solid waste disposal.  The author urges the Commission to work with Advanced Technology Centers at Pennsylvania State University, the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University to develop a solution to the problem.

headline: The Expressway Crunch
abstract: Two photos depict West River Drive before and after construction began.

headline: U.S. attorney seeks to end CTA conspirator Smith's bail
abstract: US Attorney James West wants a federal appeals court to revoke bail for William Smith, a former Dauphin County Republican Committee chairman who was convicted on five counts of interstate transportation in aid of racketeering.  The charges against Smith stem from a federal grand jury investigation of contracts between Computer Technology Associates and the City of Pittsburgh, as well as between Allegheny County and the PA State Treasury Department.  Smith was allowed to remain free pending the outcome of the appeals process because US Judge Malcolm Muir argued that unique aspects of the case--specifically the fact that only 11 jurors decided Smith's fate--made it especially likely that an appeals court would overturn the lower court's ruling in the case.

headline: States complying
abstract: Currently, 37 states in the US have laws that comply with the Uniform Minimum Drinking Age Act, which raises the minimum drinking age to 21.  States that do not comply with this law by October 1, 1985, face a loss of their fderal highway funds.  The act, however, is set to expire in 1988, but US Senators Frank Lautenberg and Jack Danforth have introduced and passed amendments to make the federal penalty permanent.  The bill is still to be considered by the US House of Representatives.

headline: Lottery play grows at 3% a year, revenue chief says
abstract: In a status report on the Lottery to the Committee on Aging and Youth, PA Revenue Secretary James Scheiner said lottery play is experiencing 3 percent annual growth and is expected to plateau at that rate.  He said that there may need to be changes in the method of funding senior citizen programs.

headline: TMI settlements: Down's syndrome child born after accident gets $1 million
abstract: A Dauphin County judge has approved $3.9 million in settlements for injury claims resulting from the 1979 Three Mile Island accident.  An attorney for the insurance companies said that "These settlements represent an economic decision arrived at by the insurance companies and do not constitute an admission of liability by any of the companies involved.

headline: Three-state area lags in the race for federal dollars
abstract: Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware all receive less in federal spending than the national average, with both NJ and Delaware receiving less than they pay in federal taxes.  Economists, however, point out that one of the goals of the progressive federal income tax is to redistribute income from relatively wealthy states, such as New Jersey and Delaware, to poorer states.  Thus, wealthier states should not expect the system to give them back as much as they put in.

headline: Officials strive to outslick spill in the Delaware
abstract: The US Coast Guard and PA state environmental officials worked yesterday to contain 400,000 gallons of crude oil that spilled from a Panamanian tanker into the Delaware River.  The incident is believed to be the worst in the Delaware Valley.  The Panamanian tanker, carrying 22 million gallons of crude oil, ran aground off the Delaware coast in Claymont on Saturday.  The oil slick stretched 15 miles from where the 761 foot Grand Eagle ran aground, and was expected to spread another two miles to the Chesapeake and Delaware canal.  The spill is expected to move about eight miles a day--causing concern for wildlife in the area.

headline: The Great Train Robbery
abstract: A letter to the editor from James Scahill, executive vice-president of the PA Coal Mining Association (PCMA), supports a Senate bill calling for a public stock offering to accomplish the sale of Conrail to Norfolk Southern Railroad.  PCMA feels that a public stock offering will create competition and will allow for competitive rates to shippers.

headline: Use of fake IDs rampant among teen-age drinkers
abstract: This article examines the problem of fake driver licenses among teenagers in Bucks County.  A PA state trooper estimated that three-quarters of the 667 seniors at William Tennet High School have fake or altered forms of identification.  The problem is not confined to high schools; Corporal Victor Hillaert, who recently investigated a counterfeit driver's license ring, estimated that 500 students at Bucks County Community College carry phony driver's licenses.  Several personal stories are included in the article.

headline: Steel firm files for bankruptcy: Union rejects loans for Wheeling-Pittsburgh
abstract: Hours after union leaders rejected a restructuring proposal, Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corporation filed for bankruptcy; Wheeling is attempting to eliminate a $514 million debt.  The company said it filed for protection under Chapter 11 of the US Bankruptcy Code less than 24 hours after the United Steelworkers union rejected a proposal to restructure the debt and mortgage the firm's assets.

headline: Luzerne attorney wins GOP Senate nod
abstract: Charles Lemmond, a Luzerne County attorney, will be the Republican candidate in a special election to replace former PA State Senator Frank O'Connell.  O'Connell resigned on August 31 for personal reasons.  Lemmond was chosen at a GOP convention on Sept. 9.  Democrats were expected to choose their candidate last night.  The special election will be held on November 5.

headline: TMI teams to remove fuel soon
abstract: In one to two weeks, workers at Three Mile Island nuclear power plant will begin removing 150 tons of intensely radioactive uranium  fuel and fuel debris from the Unit 2 reactor.  The work is considered the heart of a $1 billion cleanup operation and will take 18 months to complete.  The debris will be loaded into special containers and shipped to a US Energy Department laboratory in Idaho for research.  The employees performing the cleanup will use special tools to cut apart the core debris; workers will stand on an 18 foot-diameter rotating platform that is six inches thick and made of stainless steel.

headline: Unemployment dipped in Feb., but not for blacks
abstract: The US Labor Department reported that overall unemployment dipped from 7.4 to 7.3 percent in February, but the jobless rate for blacks jumped sharply to 16.3 percent.  Also, the total number of civilian jobs rose by 300,000.  Joblessness among factory and mining workers also worsened.  Labor Department analysts said that they had no explanation for the rise in black unemployment.

headline: Opposes Bottle Bill
abstract: An opinion piece by Asa L. Day Jr., President of Keystone Coca-Cola Bottling Company and Secretary of the PA Soft Drink Association, opposes the bill in the PA General Assembly that would require a 5-cent deposit on all non-refillable beer and soft drink containers.  He says that the soft drink industry opposes the bill because it will raise consumer prices, increase business costs and cause a loss of skilled jobs in the packaging industry.  Moreover, the bill will not make a significant contribution to solving the litter problem.

headline: The major test for PennDOT
abstract: This editorial notes that the PA Department of Transportation was ranked as the best-run state agency in an AP poll of state legislators, but says that the agency's major test will come in the reconstruction of the Schuylkill Expressway.

headline: Victim of political persecution, ex-DA claims
abstract: Herman Bigi, the former Washington County District attorney, was charged with 10 felony counts and 13 misdemeanors.  Bigi claims that he was a victim of political persecution and that he was set up.  State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman described a pattern of corruption during Bigi's term as district attorney.

headline: Steel industry going through some changes: No silicon in the Mon Valley
abstract: A columnist discusses how the collapse of the US steel industry has hurt rust belt cities such as Braddock, PA.  The author says that President Ronald Reagan's proposed tax reforms would hurt steel plants struggling to survive and modernize.

headline: Manderino denies knowing of any alleged wrongdoing
abstract: State House Majority Leader James J. Manderino, testifying in the federal bribery-conspiracy trial of two Computer Technology Associates (CTA) lawyers, denied knowing of any alleged wrongdoing involving efforts by officials of CTA to win state contracts.  He admitted that the mastermind of the scheme, John Torquato Jr. sought his help after then Auditor General Al Benedict started investigating a CTA contract; Manderino said that there was nothing criminal about his actions.

headline: TMI turmoil not over
abstract: An editorial questions whether the problems caused by the Three Mile Island (TMI) accident will ever be solved.  The author urges GPU Nuclear Corporation, the owner of TMI, to find the necessary funds to clean up the damaged reactor.

headline: A special day for celebrating black history
abstract: William C. Longstreth Elementary School in Southwest Philadelphia celebrates an "African Culture Day" program with traditional African dances and art.

headline: Outdoors Today with Charlie Burchfield: Hunting Licenses Increased
abstract: Columnist discusses the increased fees that will be charged by the state Game Commission and other changes in hunting.  Columnist says that new legislation subjecting the Game Commission to an annual legislative review and audit of the Commission's operating budget will allow the General Assembly to be aware of the activities of the Commission.

headline: Time to End Impasse on Turnpike
abstract: A House-passed bill that would authorize about $4.5 billion in improvements and additions to the PA turnpike is now in the Senate chamber.  Governor Dick Thornburgh has said that he will veto the bill unless the Senate approves his nomination for the vacant seat on the turnpike commission.  Democratic senators are now lobbying to have Thornburgh's nominee, Robert Wilburn, approved so that the Turnpike Commission can begin to make improvements.

headline: Victim's Bill of Rights
abstract: A photo depicts state Representative Jon D. Fox displaying his proposed "bill of rights' for crime victims as he speaks during a news conference in Harrisburg.  Fox said that he intended to incorporate the 10-point proposal in legislation that will be introduced in the state House.

headline: Stevens backs listing grocery prices
abstract: PA State Representative Corry Stevens is supporting legislation that would require grocery stores to mark costs on items before they get to the checkout counter.  Stevens says that the new scanner systems used in stores have caused problems for some customers.  In addition to using the scanner system, Steven's bill would require grocers to post the cost on the merchandise.  John Gould, owner of Gould's IGA in Conyngham, PA, has used electronic scanners for five years, and says that he has had very few complaints.  Gould also says the 60% of the items in the store are priced, and that the scanners will be very important to the future of the grocery industry.

headline: Many state workers unhappy with new pact
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh is happy with the new state employees contract.  Many state employees are not happy with the contract--even though they narrowly accepted it.  The contract calls for an average 3.5 percent pay increase in each of the next three years, but fewer days off.  The American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, representing 57,000 of 100,000 state workers, announced that they had narrowly ratified the contract after 11 days of voting.

headline: TMI: Six years later. Cleanup is costing more than plant's construction
abstract: General Public Utilities Nuclear Corporation will spend a total of $1 billion for the cleanup of the accident at Three Mile Island Unit 2.  One reason for the high cost is that the reactor was in a unique situation and much of the tools and equipment had to be made from scratch.

headline: 'Abortion-neutral'
abstract: A letter to the editor from F. James Sensenbrenner Jr., the ranking Republican member of the US House Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, says that he will sponsor amendments to make HR 700, the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1985, "abortion-neutral."  Sensenbrenner says that HR 700, combined with Title IX regulations, would require any college or university accepting students who receive Federal Guaranteed Student Loans to permit abortions in their student health programs; the amendment would also require schools to offer insurance plans that cover abortions for employees.  Sensenbrenner says that his amendments will preserve the rights of the unborn and of people to practice their religion as they see fit.

headline: PennDOT pushes emissions test record-keeping
abstract: Since PA emissions inspections began in June 1984, about 100 of 3,000 service station owners authorized to conduct the tests have been cited for improper record-keeping.  Many, like Rock Ferrone, have found that simply having a computerized auto emissions testing machine is not enough, as they must keep manual records of the weekly calibration of the machine.  Four station owners have lost their licenses over failing to keep manual records of the machine's calibration, according to the PA Department of Transportation.  Many station owners do not understand why they had to pay extra money for computerized equipment when they have to duplicate the information on manual forms.  PennDOT says that it uses the computer information to double check records turned in by service station owners.  The information is then turned over to the US Environmental Protection Agency to show that the state is in compliance with the emissions program.  Emissions tests began last year in the Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, and Allentown areas under a federal court order.

headline: Too drunk to drive? Device can help you decide
abstract: The "No Drive Meter" can give an accurate reading on whether a drinker is too drunk to drive.  Police and anti-drunk-driving groups have made favorable comments about this device.

headline: Victim's board ordered to pay benefits
abstract: The Commonwealth Court ordered the state Crime Victim's Compensation Board to provide survivors' benefits to a Clairton woman--even though her estranged husband had stopped support payments long before he was murdered in 1980.

headline: Stop delaying on unisex insurance
abstract: The PA Supreme Court ruled in 1984 that, under the PA Equal Rights Amendment, sex-based auto insurance rates were illegal.  A letter to the editor complains that acting Insurance Commissioner William Muir is delaying the enforcement of unisex rates.  He is wasting taxpayer dollars and time as he conducts hearings on unisex auto insurance.

headline: Mayor backs some council-by-district voting
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri and Republican mayoral nominee Henry Sneath both agree that some members of the Pittsburgh City Council should be elected from districts; this would better assure minority representation.  However, both would also like some of the council members to be elected at large, to retain the big-picture perspective to some degree.  Sneath also said that he would like to see specific information about the sale of the Pittsburgh Pirates and the city's role in it.  Caliguiri claimed that his administration was still putting together a very complicated financial package, and that it is not best to do that in public.  Sneath also said he believes city costs are too high; he proposed to reduce the city payroll if elected.  The two also sparred over taxes and development plans for the city.

headline: Return to Interior Dept.: Hodel's views tied to Watt's
abstract: Donald Hodel was nominated by President Reagan as secretary of the interior.  If approved by the Senate, Hodel will replace James Watt, a man with whom he shares similar views.

headline: Anti-black protests die down in Phila.
abstract: City officials hope the worst is over in a predominantly white neighborhood where residents protested outside the home of a black family and an interracial couple.  After the protests, Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode delcared a state of emergency .  Clergymen in southwest Philadelphia issued a statement calling for an end to public demonstrations, while a black civil rights group called off a march after an appeal by Goode.

headline: Phila. Sludge making W.Pa. a wasteland?
abstract: Residents in Somerset, Cambira, Indiana and Clarion counties don't like being the receptacle for Philadelphia sewage sludge and have mobilized against the program with public meetings, legislative hearings and door-to-door petition drives.  Their central argument is that the sludge, used as a nitrogen-rich fertilizer to quickly revegetate former strip mines, contains known hazardous materials with unknown long-term effects and the residents fear that the contaminants could seep into water supplies and the food chain--potentially posing potential health problems.  Scientific studies are inconclusive on whether or not the sludge poses health problems, but the state Department of Environmental Resources allows the sludge to be spread.

headline: Train station looking up
abstract: The $13.4 million renovation of the Harrisburg train station has made the building almost unrecognizable.  New floors, new paneling, new light fixtures, new ticket counters, and restoration of the two granite PA signature fireplaces have made the train station a city showpiece.  The only concern is that the Amtrak system may be totally defunded, as the Reagan adminstration hopes, thus leaving Harrisburg without passenger rail service.

headline: Vote likely on private prisons bill
abstract: The PA State Senate is expected to vote this week on a bill that would impose a moratoriumon the operation of private prisons in PA.  The bill has already passed the PA House.  The PA Senate is also expected to send back to committee a bill that would extend the life of the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) for four years.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has campaigned unsuccessfully for years to abolish the Democratic-controlled LCB and turn the State Stores over to private enterprise.  The governor has tried to use the Sunset Law as leverage to achieve this goal.  Thornburgh has been unable to get much support in the PA Legislature, however.

headline: Storms strike again: Tornadoes hit Great Lakes
abstract: At least three people were killed and 24 injured by tornadoes and severe thunderstorms that swept through northern Wisconsin and Michigan.  Authorities were trying to account for campers and tourists in the Wisconsin Northwoods area hit by the twisters.

headline: Mayor's successful primary race had $236,000 price tag
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri's final primary campiagn report filed with the county Elections Department shows that Caliguir outspent City Councilman Richard Givens--his major opponent in the Democratic primary--by almost 30 to 1.  Caliguiri spent $236,000, while Givens' expenditures totaled $8,000.

headline: Review of medical board may bring boost in power
abstract: A sunset review of the Board of Medical Education and Licensure will most likely lead to an increase in the powers of the agency.  Two state Senate bills have been drafted to broaden the agency's powers and the board has published a set of proposed regulations that would add detail to some requirements.  These bills would give the board the power to suspend doctors who are under review and also to penalize unlicensed doctors.

headline: Civil Rights Commission repudiates comparable worth
abstract: The US Civil Rights Commission repudiated the concept of comparable worth - equal pay for jobs of similar value - and urged federal agencies and Congress to do likewise.  The panel voted 5-2 to adopt a draft report recommending rejection of comparable worth and reliance instead on "the principle of equal pay for equal work."  The report recommends that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and other federal civil rights enforcement agencies reject comparable worth, and that the Justice Department oppose the concept when it arises in court.

headline: Plan for Pennsylvania Toxic Dump Gains Support
abstract: Legislative leaders in PA are leaning towards support of Governor Dick Thornburgh's strategy to create an Appalachian States Low Level Radioactive Waste Commission with West Virginia, Delaware and Maryland; Pennsylvania would host the site.

headline: Transit actions reversed
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh gave transit agencies an additional $4.6 million in state lottery money to subsidize transportation fares for senior citizens.  PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT) officials are to channel the additional money to transit systems they believe will need more cash to make it to the end of the 1984-85 fiscal year.

headline: Walker:  Execute Spies
abstract: A columnist discusses US Representative Robert Walker's crusade to win passage of a new law providing for the death penalty in espionage cases.  Walker has also been pressing for the death penalty for spies in the legal arena, joining the Washington Legal Foundation in filing amicus curiae briefs in three highly-publicized spy trials connected with the John A. Walker Jr. family.  Washington Legal Foundation, which has argued in front of lower federal courts and the US Supreme Court in favor of capital punishment, is arguing that the 1972 US Supreme Court decision of Furman v. Georgia, which voided death penalty laws in all 50 states as they were written, did not void the death penalty provisions for the federal espionage law.

headline: S-U-C-K-E-R-S!!!
abstract: An editorial attacks the PA Lottery, as well as lotteries as a whole, saying that it victimizes bettors, erodes social values, and provides questionable economic benefits.  The editorial cites experts who say that lotteries promulgate the "culture of poverty" by randomly producing millionaires who do not have to develop any skills or values.  Lotteries, which are played by a high proportion of poor people, vicitimize their players in subtle ways, including the fact that the amount of money bet is often not returned in prizes.  The editorial concludes that lottery revenues frequently find their way into general state budgets rather than being used to aid special programs.

headline: Mine violations allegedly ignored: Dismissal of DER accuser upheld
abstract: The state Civil Service Commission upheld the firing of a state inspector who accused the Department of Environmental Resources (DER) of ignoring mining-regulation violations.  The man was fired for continued absences, insubordination and continued disregard for supervisory authority.  The man said he lost his job because he went to the US Department of Interior to complain that the DER focused its attention on small mine operators and ignored violations by bigger companies with more political clout.

headline: Ripe setting for frequent vetoes
abstract: Experts expect that Governor Thornburgh will veto more bills in the 1985-86 session than he previously has.  The major reason for this is that lawmakers generally try to get along with a newly-elected or re-elected governor, but now that he is a lame duck members of the General Assembly are more likely to pursue their own interests.

headline: Club votes to let women be members
abstract: The National Exchange Club, during its annual convention in Philadelphia, voted to amend its constitution and allow women to join the organization.  This ends an all-male tradition that began when the exchange club, a business and professional organization, was founded 74 years ago.  The Exchange Club is involved in a variety of community activites and has established 19 child-abuse centers around the country.

headline: Plan to mine toxic site renews scrutiny of businessman
abstract: This article looks at the possible purchase of an 111-acre quarry site, that has been used as a toxic waste dump for years.  The possible mining of this site has area residents, the US Environmental Protection Agency, and the state environmental agency concerned.  The state has spent $407,000 to clean up the quarry, and the EPA has declared it one of the most polluted areas in the US.  Peter Parker, who is trying to purchase the land, is drawing questions from many residents due to the fact that he is a disbarred lawyer who has served time in federal prison.  The article reviews Parker's run-ins wth the law, his professional history, and the current state of his attempt to buy the 111-acre quarry site.

headline: Transit cuts hurt elderly
abstract: A letter to the editor from the Harrisburg League of Women Voters discusses the benefits of public transportation and urges citizens to write their US senators and representatives; citizens should urge them to support federal funding for public transportation.

headline: Water lines to MOVE to be shut
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said yesterday that city officials plan to shut down water service to two Philadelphia houses occuppied by MOVE members.  The residents are delinquent on their water bills and real estate taxes; they are also in violation of city building standards.  Before the annual convention of the National Association of Black Journalists, Goode fielded numerous questions on the his handling of the May 13 incident involving city police and MOVE members.  The confrontation bewteen MOVE and Philadelphia authorities led to 11 deaths and 61 houses being destroyed.

headline: Sunday and St. Patrick
abstract: This editorial disagrees with a Pittsburgh Press editorial that called a Sunday-sales-exemption law anti-Irish.  The law, which is currently under consideration in the state House, would make an exemption to current liquor laws and would allow for Sunday alcohol sales on Saint Patrick's Day.  The editorial urges people to leave ethnicity out of the discussion.

headline: Misues of government funds charged to Walters
abstract: George Walters, the suspended president of Allied Services for the Handicapped, and three of his top executives were charged with alleged misuse of federal and state funds; a proposal to fire them from the company has been postponed so that they may have a chance to respond to the charges.  An internal audit committee recently made the accusations against the three company executives.  The PA State Department of Public Welfare will also be looking into the alleged misues of public funds at Allied Services.  The findings of the internal audit are included in the article.

headline: Rizzo Poised to MOVE Against Goode?
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo has given hints recently--especially since the May 13, 1985 MOVE debacle--that he wants another shot at Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, the man who defeated him for the Democratic mayoral primary in 1983.  Two other possibilities to battle Goode include PA State Senator Vincent Fumo and former Republican mayoral nominee John Egan, both are already planning fundraisers with a mayoral race in mind.  Although potential rivals to Goode have existed all along, they have been emboldened by a perception shared by many city politicians that Goode has been seriously hurt by the MOVE debacle and that he could become its final victim.

headline: Coretta King: Overlook Jackson's 'Hymie' Quote
abstract: Coretta Scott King accepted the Jules Cohen Memorial Award. King is the first women to win the award presented by the Jewish Relations Community Council. Mrs. King was asked about Jesse Jackson's controversial use of the term 'hymie' to refer to Jews. Mrs. King said that sometimes we make a bigger deal of things then they really are, and sometimes things are said without understanding what is being said. Jackson is running for the Democratic presidential nomination.

headline: Protecting Water Supplies
abstract: This editorial examines the coal industry's opposition to a proposed regulation that would require the replacement of water supplies damaged by underground mining.  The editorial does not buy the argument put forth by John Shirvinsky, president of the Keystone Bituminous Coal Association, that the passage of the bill would mean a loss of jobs.  This argument states that additional mining regulations would lead to additional expenses, which would increase the price of coal and make it less competitive.  The editorial believes that Shrivinsky contradicts this argument when he says that most companies do water replacement already.  If they do, the editorial reasons, then what is the harm in making the practice mandatory?  The editorial concludes that requiring coal operators to protect water resources is the fairest way to assure the public will not be cut off from traditional water supplies.

headline: Turnpike tail-chasing
abstract: An editorial chastises both Republicans and Democrats in the state legislature for the political bickering surrounding the confirmation of a Thornburgh nominee to the Turnpike Commission.

headline: We've Had It, Neighbors Warn
abstract: People living on the 6200 block of Osage Avenue in Philadelphia complain that they are suffering from profanity, threats and unsanitary conditions as a result of MOVE, a back-to-nature cult, having a house in the neighborhood.  The residents organized themselves into a group called the United Residents of the 6200 block of Osage Avenue and held a press conference to notify city and state officials that they are disgusted with the threats and profanity from MOVE.  Residents say they will take matters into their own hands if the elected officials cannot do anything about it.

headline: Tainted Riunite recalled
abstract: PA state stores have stopped selling some Riunite wines because of a nationwide warning issued yesterday that they may contain traces of diethylene glycol (DEG), a solvent used in antifreeze and cosmetics.  The PA Liquor Control Board said that DEG is used to sweeten some low-grade wines so they can be sold for higher prices, though ingesting large amounts of DEG can cause liver or kidney damage.  The US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms has been testing wines since July, when traces of DEG were found in Austrian brands.  Though the amount of DEG per liter in Riunite is not enough to be harmful, the importer has agreed to a recall.  Riunite has suspended purchases from the Italian wineries where traces of DEG were found.  Further information about the types of bottles and what to do is contained in the article.

headline: Montour Oks teacher raises; strike may end
abstract: The Montour School Board last night approved 8.4% raises for striking teachers, leaving the teacher's union to vote on the pact later last night.  The school board began classes last Wednesday and used substitute teachers to replace the strikers.  When union teachers were turned away in an effort to return to work, the union claimed they were "locked out."  A labor lawyer advised school officials that the union had a very good chance at winning a lock-out lawsuit, and the board ended the substitute program.  The 8.4% wages are roughly average for teacher contracts in Western PA over the last two years.  Peters Township teachers ratified their new agreement Saturday, and school is set to start there today.  The teachers won new wage increases, changes in the way they are evaluated by superiors, and an increase in life insurance.  Southwest Butler School District and its teachers union have reported no progress in weekend bargaining.

headline: Row officer pay hike stymied
abstract: State legislators introduced a bill that would raise the salaries of the Allegheny County sheriff, coroner, and juy commissioners.  Yesterday, the legislators asked the PA House to wipe out that proposal and substitute in its place a measure that would allow Allegheny County commissioners to raise the salaries for the four row offices without affecting all other major county officeholders.  The PA House agreed to revamp the legislation, but did not agree to pass it and send it to the PA Senate.  The measure will be reconsidered today.

headline: Dr. King's dream lives on in many ways, Gray says
abstract: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr's birthday was celebrated at Haverford College with many prominent leaders present, including US Congressman William Gray III.  Gray was recently elected chairman of the House Budget Committee.

headline: Public has right to know how game commission works
abstract: This editorial supports a state House bill that would restrain hunting-license fee increases by the state Game Commission, but does not support an amendment to that bill that would give power over the Commission's budget to the state Legislature.  THe editorial urges the Game Commission to do a better job of keeping the Legislature and public informed of its activities and needs.

headline: Turnpike workers to vote on pact
abstract: About 1,800 employees of the PA Turnpike Commission will vote next week on a contract offer that Teamsters Union leaders say falls short of what they want.  The toll collectors, maintenance workers, and clerical workers were covered by a contract that expired on September 30.   If the workers reject the contract offer, negotiations will continue.  Earlier offers have been rejected at the bargaining table.

headline: When it's federal courts vs. the state courts
abstract: This article is an exerpt from a speech by PA Chief Justice Robert Nix Jr.  Justice Nix talks about the relationship between US federal courts and state courts.  Justice Nix says that the role for each should be clearly defined.  Justice Nix says that the judicial activism of the Warren Court did not bother him as much as some others in the country.  However, Justice Nix does believe that the state judiciary should shoulder the responsibility for defining fundamental rights.  The federal system can, at best, only serve to supply the minimal guarantees afforded by the evolving concepts of due process and equal protection.  The state, being smaller, usally more homogenous, and sharing the same customs and traditions, is better suited for determining when added protections are appropriate.

headline: Task Force Can't Hurt
abstract: This editorial looks at the proposal to form a special task force in the PA House to study the problems municipalities are having in obtaining adequate liability insurance.  The task force would be headed by the Local Government Commission.  The editorial agrees there is a growing insurance crisis in municipalities, mainly because of the loss of immunity for municipalities from lawsuits; this has caused insurance companies to raise their premiums or get out of the business of insuring municipalities.  Studying the problem is great, but action needs to be taken as well.  A public campaign should be undertaken to inform the public that excessive jury verdicts can come back to haunt the public in higher taxes.  Communities should also seek the best legal talent, and the courts should be less liberal in permitting unrealistic awards to stand.

headline: Municipalities staring at big cost increases
abstract: An editorial looks at how liability insurance and overtime pay for municipal employees are creating skyrocketing costs for local governments; these costs may break their budgets.  Representatives of local governments testified before the House Insurance Committee; they said that the cost of liability insurance has become so high that some municipalities are operating without it.  This is due to the fact that recent court decisions have applied broader definitions as to what constitutes liability.  A Supreme Court ruling that the Fair Labor Standards Act applies to state and local governments; this will now force local governments to apply overtime and minimum wage provisions to their employees and volunteers.  The editorial believes that none of the decisions by the courts is wrong, but that their unintended fallout will have serious effects on communities.  In repealing or revising some of these guidelines, however, the US Congress must be careful to respect the rights of employees and those hurt by government negligence.

headline: Run by Tom Flaherty enlivens mayor's race
abstract: Pittsburgh city Controller Thomas Flaherty announced his bid for the Democratic Party endorsement for the mayor's race, attacking incumbent mayor Richard Caliguiri with criticisms.  Other Democrats also declared their candidacy for the four open City Council seats and are seeking endorsements.

headline: Held 28 years without cause, she'll join society
abstract: US District Judge Daniel H. Huyett III said that inept, parsimonious and unconstitutional pracitices deprived Carolyn Clark, a mentally-retarded women, of her freedom for 28 and a half years.  Clark has been institutionalized against her will since 1956--despite public-policy reforms, professional recommendations, and court rulings that expanded the rights of the institutionalized.  The judge ordered the state of Pennsylvania to pay for Clark's treatment in a community-living arrangementy and ordered her release from her current insitution.

headline: Ravaged land, poisoned water: How the energy scramble fouled Pa. The 1974 oil crisis caused a frenzied hunt across Western Pennsylvania for coal, oil and gas. Prospectors took $2 billion worth of fuel and left a poisoned legacy.
abstract: The 1974 energy crisis brought energy prospectors to Western Pennsylvania in search of oil, gas and coal.  Since then, prospectors have extracted $2 billion worth of energy, but have destroyed land and water in the process.  Pollution from drilling and mining has fouled more than 100 miles of streams and water supplies.  Strip miners have left more than 23,000 acres of abandoned mines.  It will take about $110 million to reclaim those acres.  Officials say that the problem came from a failure of enforcement by the state Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: We Question Trial Lawyers' Problems
abstract: This editorial blasts PA's trial lawyers for not supporting a bill that would make it mandatory for all motor vehicle occupants to wear seat belts.  Trial lawyers want an amendment excluding seat belts as a mitigating factor in awarding damages.  The editorial believes this to be "hogwash" and feels that present civil and criminal laws already deprive jurors of too much vital information they need when considering the degree of negligence and consequent financial responsibility of a party in a civil suit.  If PA passes the mandatory seat-belt legislation, compliance with that law should be permitted to be part of the record in civil lawsuits arising from auto accidents.

headline: When kids are crooks
abstract: An editorial compliments Governor Dick Thornburgh's call for a crackdown on juvenile crime and agrees that creating a new category of "dangerous juvenile offender" is a good idea.  The editorial says that it is necessary to crack down on young criminals.

headline: Tavern video-poker merits quick defeat
abstract: Philadelphia's City Council has asked the state Legislature for permission to legalize video-poker in taverns.  Columnist urges the Legislature to move carefully on this issue, rather than make another mistake and legalize gambling again.

headline: Musto Reports on Harrisburg
abstract: A columnist discusses the adverse effects that domestic budget cuts would have on PA.  President Reagan's proposed 1985-86 budget calls for significant domestic budget cuts.  He criticizes Governor Dick Thornburgh for not taking a more thorough look at Reagan's budget.

headline: Running off from a contest
abstract: This editorial examines the issue of runoff elections.  The issue of runoff elections was first brought up by Democratic presidential candidate Jesse Jackson last year; recently, a federal judge struck down New York City's runoff primary and said that it violated the Voting Rights Act and the US Constitution.  US District Judge Charles Brieant Jr. argued that runoff elections contribute to "racial polarization" and "racially slanted campaign tactics."  He recommended that NYC's threshold for avoiding a second primary be lowered from 40% to 30%.  The editorial believes that this issue may be a political dead-end for blacks and other minorities.  In campaigning to lower the plurality for runoffs, opponents are simply saying that whites will not vote for minority candidates.  Finally, given the reality that whites are the majority, any minority politician must attract white support for their candidacy to be a success.

headline: Medicaid and abortions
abstract: This editorial urges the PA Supreme Court to quickly hear an appeal on Medicaid-funded abortions and whether the state Department of Welfare should stop funding for abortion procedures.  A funding cutoff is required by a 1980 law which was upheld by the Commonwealth Court.

headline: Resistance seen on acid-rain bills
abstract: PA's Acid Rain Caucus said that the US Congress is likely to drag its feet when it comes to dealing with acid- rain legislation.  The Caucus, whose members are state House and Senate members, is pushing for federal legislation on acid rain to avoid a "hodgepodge" of different state laws.

headline: Well, tonight it's
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh was on hand to mark the end of the main construction work on a four and a half-mile stretch of the Schuylkill Expressway.  Thanks to good weather and excellent contract work, the PA Department of Transportation said the $27 million project was able to finish six weeks ahead of schedule.  The early completion will give contractors more than a million dollars extra in incentives.  Governor Thornburgh thanked drivers for their patience in the completion.

headline: Wid chips fall in the judicial forest
abstract: Wid Schonek, a Westmont businessman who is very involved in Cambria County's politics, has said he will back District Attorney Gerard Long for judge.  Schnoek has often helped candidates over the years and the columnist speculates that he can "call in his 'wid' chips" to get support for Long.

headline: Taverns must protect themselves from drunken drivers
abstract: Under the PA Liquor Code, a bar owner, manager, bartender or waiter who serves alcohol to a person who is "visibly intoxicated" can be held liable for damages that that person may inflict on a third party.  The editorial argues that bar owners should make bartenders and waiters aware of the law so that they will be more watchful of patrons.  The editorial also argues that bars should hire a person whose only job would be to spot drunks and stop them before they hurt themselves or somebody else.

headline: No Contest:  Guv's Exit Is Applauded
abstract: Although Philadelphia Republican City Committee Chairman D. Donald Jamieson did not issue a sigh of relief as he talked about PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's decision not to run against US Senator Arlen Specter, it was clear he was relieved.  Jamieson was afraid that a GOP primary between the two would have put Philadelphia Republicans in an awkward position.  US Senator John Heinz applauded Thornburgh's decision, and said that the Republican Party could not afford a bitter primary.  The two leading Democrats running against Specter--PA Auditor General Don Bailey and US Representative Robert Edgar--are ready to zero in on Specter's record.

headline: Rural vote key to center funds
abstract: Philadelphia will likely depend on votes from rural legislators in order to get funding for its $441 million Center City convention center.  This is because suburban representatives have threatened to vote to try and block state funding for the center because they were angry about Mayor Wilson Goode's failure to resolve the long-running fight over the city's wage tax.  Urban, rural and suburban legislators all agree that this issue will be a battle in the legislature.

headline: Messrs. Kunstler, Conyers: No to your preconceptions
abstract: This editorial criticizes William M. Kunstler and US Representative John Conyers Jr for accusing Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode and the Philadelphia police of racism.  Kunstler and Conyer's accusations came in wake of Goode's decision to evict the radical group MOVE from their west Philadelphia home.  The editorial says that Goode's decision to appoint an investigative commission is the good idea.  The author also argues that it is best for the city if people like Kunstler and Conyers do not intervene because they do not know the facts.

headline: Senate approves raise in fumes testing fee
abstract: Legislation to increase the fee for performing auto-emissions inspection tests was put on the fast track; the legislation passed the state Senate easily and was sent to the state House.  Some 3.1 million motorists in the Pittsburgh, Philadelphia and Allentown areas are required to pay the fee during annual anti-pollution inspections of their vehicles.  An analysis done by the PA Department of Transportation suggests that the increase is justified because the cost to service stations is usually higher than $5.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts a masked man running out of a liquor store carrying a bag.  A startled police officer says, "Halt, or I'll... I'll...Say, are you considered armed and dangerous?"

headline: Wild Card in the Morgue
abstract: A columnist tries to piece together the events that happened in the Phialdelphia morgue when the bullet was discovered in MOVE member Frank Africa's remains.
