The author criticizes Philadelphia Health Commissioner Stuart Shapiro for trying to take over the process of examining the remains and performing autopsies, and for not allowing the chief medical examiner, Dr. Marvin Aronson, to do the job.  Aronson is now being asked to come back and review vital findings from the autopsies and to bail Shapiro out of the embarrasment of misjudging and mishandling vital evidence.

headline: The FORUM: Who's behind blackjack law?
abstract: A letter to the editor wants to know which lawmakers added the amendment to the liquor law that allowed card games for money in bars and taverns.  The author says that citizens should know who it was so that they can be voted out of office.

headline: No surprises in petitions for primary
abstract: March 12th at 5pm was the deadline for filing May 21st primary-ballot petitions.  Most candidates have already been campaigning.  In Philadelphia, 10 judgeships and the positions of district attorney and city controller will be filled; there is only one contested primary for district attorney, however.

headline: San Diego mayor's retrial in conspiracy set to begin
abstract: San Diego Mayor Roger Hedgecock will be going on trial a second time this week; he is being tried on charges of criminal conspiracy and perjury.   For his alleged involvement in a plot to illegally finance his 1983 campaign, a jury voted 11 to 1 to convict Hedgecock; however, without all 12 votes to convict, a mistrial was declared.  Though Hedgecock admits making mistakes on state-mandated disclosure forms, he alleges that San Diego County District Attorney Edwin Miller has a personal vendetta against him.

headline: Our Hands Tied, Officials Say
abstract: In response to citizen complaints, Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode says he wants to evict the radical MOVE group, a back-to-nature cult, from its fortified house in West Philadelphia.  The mayor says he has no legal solution or any immediate hope of one, however.  Mayor Goode and other city officials have been advised that arresting MOVE members or trying to evict them would result in the city being accused of violating the MOVE members' civil rights.

headline: Sides shaping up on state N-waste
abstract: State legislators are planning to introduce legislation that will delay the storing, processing, and disposing of radioactive waste in the state.  Governor Dick Thornburgh is urging that it is necessary to find a place in the state to dispose of low-level radioactive waste, and he is beginning to discuss site possibilities with the Legislature.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts Ariel Sharon wiping his hands of a libel-suit verdict.   Sharon filed a libel suit against against TIME magazine.

headline: Witness: Pair Joked About Bribing Dwyer
abstract: Judy Ellis, former president of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), testified at the CTA bribery trial that two officials of CTA boasted that they had bribed state Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer to win a multimillion-dollar, no-bid state contract last May.  Ellis said the jocularity quickly gave way to panic last July when the FBI began asking questions about the firm's $4.8 million contract to recover Social Security taxes wrongly paid by PA school districts and employees.

headline: The great interest rate debate: lawmakers vote for the creditor
abstract: An editorial criticizes the state Legislature for approving a bill that would allow credit card companies to continue to charge 18% for another three years.  The author says that legislators should have fought harder to get a lower rate for consumers.

headline: O'Donnell, Scanlons testify on Torquato
abstract: Allegheny County Director of Administration Scott O'Donnell testified in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery trail that he threw away a letter from CTA officials offering him stock in a related firm.  Scott appeared as a defense witness for two CTA attorneys; he appeared along with Allegheny County Election Director James Scanlon, Robert Scanlon, and Barbara Scanlon.  All were asked to recall their dealings with John Torquato Jr, the admitted mastermind of a conspiracy to win government contracts from the city of Pittsburgh, Allegheny County and the state Treasury Department.

headline: Scanlon and lobbying
abstract: This editorial discusses state Senator Eugene Scanlon's role in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery trial and questions where the line should be drawn on gifts that legislators receive from lobbyists and lobbying groups.  The editorial suggests that wider public scrutiny on spending by lobbyists would be a deterrent to high-powered influence-peddling.

headline: Pa. abortions on Medicaid end Feb. 15
abstract: The state Department of Public Welfare announced that pubic funding of most abortions will end on February 15th.  The funding cutoff results from the implementation of a 1980 Pennsylvania law which has been the subject of a court battle for the last four years.  Under the new law, public funds will still be available for abortions, but only under certain circumstances.

headline: Soil in yard radioactive, cleanup cost $800,000
abstract: A federally-funded study estimates that it will cost at least $800,000 to remove about 20 tons of radioactive soil from a yard in Delaware County.  The Environmental Protection Agency reported gamma radiation 10 times higher than acceptable under federal guidelines, though they said there was no danger to the public.  The sewers in the area will also have to be removed for fear of contamination.

headline: null
abstract: A photo depicts a Pennsylvania state trooper standing on a busy highway.

headline: 2 legislators vow to probe cheese gaffe
abstract: PA State Representatives Allen Kukovich and Italo Cappabianca warned yesterday that they will seek the subpoena power of the PA House Appropriations Committee if PA Governor Dick Thornburgh does not name and fire the official who rejected two months' worth of free federal food for the poor,

headline: The Harrisburg gamblers
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh and the State Legislature passed a bill extending the hours of Sunday liquor sales in restaurants and taverns, but they failed to realize that the legislation had an amendment legalizing some forms of gambling.  The amendment will likely be reversed by a new bill, but the editorial urges the Governor and General Assembly to carefully read the bill this time.

headline: Official hits buy-American-car law
abstract: A 1984 state law requiring state and local governments to buy American-built cars has instead made it "virtually impossible" for public agencies to purchase any vehicles, a state official said yesterday.  Stephen Gardner, spokesman for the state Department of General Services, said that "no manufacturer or dealer has certified that their cars comply with the law's guidelines."  The law was designed to help ailing US industries, particularly the steel companies important to PA's economy.

headline: Schools get 'can of worms' on SS refunds from Dwyer
abstract: State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer told officials of school districts, intermediate units and other school entities across the state that they will have to submit individual applications for the Social Security tax overpayments for school employees, which are estimated at $40 million.  This move is yet another bizarre twist in the tax recovery story, in which three people have pleaded guilty to involvement in a bribery scheme; two others are on trial in federal court in Williamsport and a slew of prominent politicians have been implicated in court testimony.  Dwyer made the statement even though a law enacted in 1984 authorizes the treasure to recover the tax overpayments; he also sent a letter to districts in 1984 advising them "school districts and entities are to have no discretion in the matter."

headline: Reagan's plans opposed on affirmative action
abstract: A proposal by the Reagan administration that would forbid the use of quotas or ratios in the hiring of women and/or minorities has drawn criticism from black and women's leaders.  Critics of the Reagan plan say it would slam the door on minority hiring.  Harvey Adams, president of the Pittsburgh NAACP, said that affirmative action, despite its flaws, is still the only way that minorities and women can be considered for hiring in America's white, male-dominated society.  The Young Women's Christian Association, the National Organization for Women, the Mayor's Task Force on Women, and the Pittsburgh Coalition of Labor Union Women also oppose the plan.

headline: State cautions on picking up wildlife
abstract: Wildlife conservation officers from the state Game Commission are making their annual plea that fawns, baby birds and other young wildlife be left in their natural habitat.  The commission said that few people have the training or expertise to raise wildlife, noting that young birds and animals handled by humans usually die, despite the best of intentions.

headline: $2 million back pay won by secretaries
abstract: The state Supreme Court let stand a 1983 Commonwealth Court decision that awarded an estimated $2 million in back pay to secretaries of Allegheny County district justices.  The Commonwealth Court decision ordered the county courts to award back pay to between 80 and 100 women.  The women worked as secretaries for district justices beginning April 1973.  Back then, women were paid much less than their male counterparts.

headline: 2 sides of care home regulations shown
abstract: Deputy Welfare Secretary Scott Nelson yesterday sat before a hearing of the PA House Health and Welfare Committee and cited his department's achievements in regulating PA's personal care home industry.  Nelson assured the committee that his office will continue to review its licensing efforts to esnure consistent application of regulations, as well as to maximize the health and safety of personal care home residents.  However, he had no firm answers for legislators who wanted to know how some homes had escaped the licensing process, or have been closed for not complying with the Welfare Deparment's minimum state standards.  State Representative Elinor Taylor would like the Department to adopt surprise inspections, while others cited personal care regulations that allowed too much room for abuse.

headline: The Liquor Control Board:  Has it outlived its usefulness?
abstract: An editorial reviews the argument for and against the elimination of the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB).  The editorial does not believe the argument that the LCB prevents widespread alcoholic consumption within PA.  Last year, the LCB had $750 million in sales, so it cannot be thought of as a curtailing alcoholic consumption.  Liquor is big business in PA, and the editorial believes that experience tells us that in matters of business, the private sector can do it better.

headline: Once more, Sunshine Bill reform faces a test
abstract: This editorial supports state Senate Bill 303.  The legislation rewrites PA's Sunshine Law and requires that discussions and deliberations about government-agency business be open to the public.  The editorial urges members of the General Assembly to approve the bill because it will allow the public to attend meetings; it will not allow public business to be conducted in private.

headline: Scott Nibbles at Williams Fund-Raiser
abstract: Former Municipal Judge John Scott tried to bait his opponent, Bobby Williams, in the Democratic race for Philadelphia district attorney; Scott took a few political shots at Williams' $1,000-a-person fund raiser.  Williams did not respond and said that the campaign should stick to the issues.

headline: Reporter At Large
abstract: In this section, a book about Ginny Foat, California's first woman president of the National Organization for Women, is reveiwed.  The Opinion section also looks at events happening in the Harrisburg area, including the return of Halley's Comet and the Second Annual Greater Bear Jamboree.

headline: State may help city obtain cleanup loan: Metals in water to be removed
abstract: The state's Water Facilities Loan Board has offered technical assistance to Harrisburg City Council in applying for a loan to help the city rid its water of heavy metals.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: A photo depicts Philadelphia Managing Director Leo A. Brooks, coordinator of the city's assault on the MOVE compound, answering a question during a news conference with Police Commissioner Gregore J. Sambor in April.

headline: A Congressional audit
abstract: An audit by the US General Accounting Office, the auditing arm of the US Congress, is fueling criticism of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's program to distribute free federal food to the poor.  The audit showed that the PA Agriculture Deparment lost a significant amount of cheese and butter that could have been distributed to the poor.  The audit says that the PA Agriculture Department failed to keep accurate records of food distribution and inventories.  In responding to the audit, John Nikoloff, a spokesman for the PA Agriculture Department said the administration of the food program has improved immensely in the last two years and is now considered a model program by federal officials.

headline: The Senate in its first ever
abstract: The PA Senate has overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to allow wine to be sold in specialty shops and by private wholesalers.  The issue surfaced as the Senate debated a bill to extend the life of the PA Liquor Control Board (LCB).  The PA House is also working on an LCB extension plan, but the proposals are so different that it is unlikely the two chambers will be able to agree on a compromise plan by the end of the week.  In the PA House, a proposal to shift liquor-law enforcement powers from the LCB to the PA Attorney General was defeated.  The PA Senate also adopted a proposal that requires 36% of the electorate to sign a petition in order to have a local-option election on liquor sales.

headline: One very canny player of the political game
abstract: This article discusses the background and political career of US Representative William Gray III, a minister from North Philadelphia.  With his recent election as chairman of the Budget Committee, Gray has risen from a freshman representative with no political portfolio to one of the most powerful leaders in Congress.

headline: Scranton Dynasty - 3 Strong Generations
abstract: This article examines the Scranton family's involvement in PA politics, from Mrs. Worthington Scranton, a Republican National Committee woman, to William Scranton--a popular governor.  The article also looks at William Scranton III, who is coming on strong in the state political scene.

headline: Rosa Parks honored as 'catalyst' for blacks
abstract: Rosa Parks was honored on Martin Luther King Jr. Day at a luncheon in Philadelphia.  Philadelphia School Superintendent Constance Clayton was a speaker.

headline: State waste plan
abstract: This editorial examines a proposal by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to deal with a looming garbage-disposal crisis.  Over the last 15 years, 800 dumps and landfills have been closed; currently only 127 operating landfills handle the nine million tons of trash generated every year in PA.  Thornburgh plans to place incinerators around the state, utilizing their waste-to-energy design.  The Thornburgh plan calls for a modest tonnage fee to be imposed on landfill operators; the revenue generated from the tonnage fee will be used to pay the cost of designing incinerators and recycling centers.  The editorial also likes the fact that the Thornburgh plan would transfer the responsibility for waste disposal from the municipal level to the county level.  The editorial does find it disappointing that the Thornburgh plan lacks a beverage-container deposit bill, which has been successful in other states.  Overall, the editorial believes that the Thornburgh proposal is the correct way to go.

headline: (Photos)
abstract: One photo depicts officials in the MOVE house in West Philadelphia examining the upstairs front room.  Another photo depicts a hole dug in the backyard of the Chester MOVE house.

headline: Awaiting federal approval, state again delays medical plan for poor
abstract: The start of a new healthcare program for welfare recipients in South and West Philadelphia has been delayed once again; state officials are confident that it will win federal approval by December 5 and go into effect by March 1, 1986.  Under the program, the state will pay a fixed monthly fee to a private firm, HealthAmerica of Tennessee, for each covered patient, and then that firm will contract with doctors, hopitals, and other health providers to deliver the medical services.  Federal approval is necessary because the program will serve as a substitute for the existing Medicaid program, which is more than 50% funded by the federal government.  Community Legal Services of Philadelphia, an opponent of the new program, said they remained concerned about the program, but they are glad that the PA Welfare Department had agreed to seek assistance from the PA Health Department in setting quality-of-care standards for the program.

headline: The States Enter the Venture Capital Game
abstract: Many states across the nation, including Pennsylvania, are investing in new and risky high-tech companies as venture capitalists.  These states feel it is worthwhile because the returns are often high, and it allows them to invest in job creation in the state.  Pennsylvania's Ben Franklin Partnership offers seed money to help start private venture-capital partnerships.

headline: Pa. declines to call Osage disaster area
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh announced that he had decided, at least for the moment, not to declare the fire-ravaged blocks around the MOVE house in West Philadelphia a disaster area.  The governor said that such a declaration was not appropriate and could prove to be counterproductive.  Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode had asked Thornburgh to declare the area a state disaster area because the designation would have given the governor emergency powers to deal with the disaster; it would have allowed him to allocate up to $5 million in disaster aid without legislative approval.  Thornburgh said that such a designation would tarnish the image of Philadelphia and deter tourism to the city.

headline: Scranton incumbent is one of the few who lost
abstract: Scranton Mayor James McNulty, in seeking re-election as mayor, adopted the unusual strategy of refusing to campaign up until one week before the election.  McNulty's strategy did not pay off, as he lost one of the closest races in PA to Republican David Wenzel.  A Lackawanna County judge has ordered a recount and McNulty has refused to concede.  The article also examines the re-election of incumbent mayors in PA's other cities, as well as the vote for members of the PA state Superior Court.

headline: Rosa Parks: Movement's Still Alive
abstract: Rosa Parks was given the "Drum Major For Social Justice" award from the Philadelphia Martin Luther King Jr. Association for Nonviolence.  The award was presented by Philadelphia Schools Superintendent Constance Clayton.

headline: State's northeast fears nuclear dump
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh announced that he had formed a compact with Maryland, West Virginia, and Delaware that would allow those states to ship their low-level nuclear wastes to an unspecified site in Pennsylvania.  This announcement worried residents in the northeastern part of the state because of a Pennsylvania State University study that found seven northeastern counties to be suitable sites for a low-level radioactive waste disposal facility.

headline: 11 appointed for probe of MOVE siege
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode appointed an 11-member commission to investigate and publicly report on all aspects of the confrontation and fire that left 11 MOVE members dead and destroyed or gutted 61 West Philadelphia row houses.  The panel will be headed by Philadelphia lawyer William H. Brown III, former chairman of the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and includes three other prominent Philadelphia lawyers.  The commission also includes a former FBI special agent, three clerics, a bank executive, a community activist and a law professor.  Former Philadelphia Mayor William Green criticized the appointments  saying that they are allies, supporters and recipients of city business; they will not be unbiased.

headline: Bill seeks system to check on elderly who live alone
abstract: A Montgomery County legislator is trying to expand a small program that monitors the health and safety of senior citizens in Abington Township and Rockledge Borough.  The program, called Operation Reassurance, provides daily telephone contact for senior citizens who live alone.  There is legislation to establish a similar program statewide at a cost of $1 million; the money would be provided from the lottery fund.

headline: This gambling didn't pay off
abstract: An editorial discusses the mess created by a bill that created a loophole allowing gambling in state bars and taverns.  The author says that everyone involved in the mess showed a callous disregard for the public interest and an alarming contempt for the law.

headline: Pa. dossier: Thornburgh may cast his eye on politics in 2nd term, but says he won't shirk state
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh discusses his administration's plans for the next two years.  He says he will continue to work on his current proposals and will devote more time to his duties as chairman of the Republican Governors Association.

headline: Scranton seizing GOP reins
abstract: A columnist discusses the many ways in which Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton is preparing for his gubernatorial campaign.  The article also discusses how he has made a name for himself without relying on his father or Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Schenley desegegation delayed 2 years
abstract: The PA Human Relations Commission granted a two-year delay on plans to desegregate Schenley High School in Pittsburgh, but warned that reluctant white students must be forced to attend Schenley if enough whites do not volunteer by September 1987.  The Pittsburgh School Board had committed itself to integrating Schenly, which is 70% black, by the end of the year, but couldn't entice enough whites to volunteer.  Pittsburgh Schools Superintendent Richard Wallace promised to meet the new 1987 deadline by moving a mostly-black health careers magnet program to another high school and increasing the attractiveness of Shenley's high technology and international studies magnet programs.

headline: The acid rain controversy
abstract: For the third straight year, Pennsylvania received the most acidic rain of any state in the nation.  While acid rain continues to pelt down on the country, President Ronald Reagan continues to call for more study of the problem.  PA would like to see the federal government start an abatement program and has recommended that a national tax be placed on electricity to fund it.  This editorial believes it is highly doubtful that Reagan will shoulder the responsibility for a new costly tax.  However, according to a federal study, acid rain causes $5 billion of damage a year in the US.  The editorial asks if the nation can afford not to start such an abatement program.

headline: 15 abortion protestors guilty of defying court
abstract: A Montgomery County jury convicted 15 anti-abortion activists of violating a court order that limited the number of picketers at a Bridgeport abortion clinic.  The medical center, which since has closed, had been the site of numerous anti-abortion demonstrations.

headline: Cab trips for elderly spared
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, under pressure from senior citizens groups and lawmakers, backed away from imposing harsh new restrictions on the lottery-supported taxi program for the elderly.  Thornburgh administration officials yanked a provision to the elderly's use of the shared-ride program that would have denied service to many of those living within a quarter-mile of mass transit service.  The PA Transportation Department also reversed itself on a proposal that would have prevented many non-profit agencies from paying a senior citizen's 10% cost of door-to-door transportation.  Transportation providers and advocates for senior citizens contended that the proposal would have denied service to almost all residents of the densely populated Philadelphia and Allegheny Counties.

headline: Tighten The Rules On Legislature
abstract: After a law allowing card tournaments in bars was passed surreptitiously, an editorial calls for tightening the rules of the PA Legislature.  The amendments that allowed card tournaments were added in conference committee and then returned to the House and Senate chambers on a busy day when supporters knew that few lawmakers would take the time to read the bill; lawmakers were also told that the new language was virtually identical to the previous language.

headline: Panel Oks new rules for candidates
abstract: The state Senate Rules Committee unanimously approved a bill setting new residency requirements for candidates for the state General Assembly.  The bill is the result of a compromise between Senate Republicans and Democrats.  Senate Republicans agreed not to challenge the seating of Philadelphia Democrat Roxanne Jones in return for Democratic support of election-law changes.

headline: Second vote on Wilburn postponed
abstract: The Republican-controlled state Senate delayed until Tuesday a controversial second vote on the confirmation of Robert Wilburn to a post on the Turnpike Commission.  The issue has become a test of wills between Republicans and Democrats, as the GOP has tied Wilburn's confirmation to passage of a long-pending bill that calls for some $4 billion in extensions and improvements to the state's toll-road system.  The Democrats have refused to confirm Wilburn, a former Cabinet member in the Thornburgh administration, because it would cause them to lose their narrow control of the commission.

headline: Sniping at affirmative action
abstract: This editorial argues against a proposed executive order by President Ronald Reagan that would abolish affirmative action rules for government contractors.  Administration officials argue that current rules for affirmative action amount to a "simple euphemism for quotas".  However, the editorial states that it is the government's obligation to see that contractors being paid with funds from all taxpayers do not discriminate against some taxpayers for reasons of race, sex, ethnic origin, or religion.

headline: Terrain vehicles roll on
abstract: All-terrain vehicles moved a little closer to state forest lands yesterday as the PA Environmental Quality Board approved regulations on the vehicles.  The regulations would establish a licensing and registration program for the vehicles and set criteria for selecting trails for them on state land.  A law was passed in July authorizing the PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) to add all-terrain vehicles to the snowmobile law.  The rules have certain stipulations for operators younger than 16 and 10 years old.  Before state lands are selected for all-terrain vehicle trails, the areas will be studied to see the environmental impact of such decisions.  The DER estimates that there are about 70,000 all-terrain vehicles in use throughout Pennsylvania.

headline: 18 Months of Neglect: How MOVE Neighbors Became the Victims
abstract: A Daily News investigation reveals that in the 18 months prior to the May 13 MOVE shootout and fire, city government adopted a "hands off" attitude toward the occupants of the MOVE house at 6221 Osage Avenue in West Philadelphia.  Article provides a timeline of key events preceeding and during that period and the city's role in them.

headline: Charity gave a nod to MOVE: Group eligible for United Way plan
abstract: The Community Action Movement (CAM)--a branch of the MOVE organization that is self-described as an education and training group for future MOVE members--was admitted in January 1985 into the United Way of Southeastern PA's "donor-option program."  This allowed the group to receive tax-free contributions.  John Waggy, United Way campaign director and senior manager for the donor-option program, said the criteria the United Way uses to approve such groups is that they have to have a tax-exempt status from the Internal Revenue Service; they also have to be providing human health and social services, and they have to provide those services in the Delaware Valley.  Waggy said that he did not believe that the group had received any money through the United Way donor-option program.

headline: TMI-area communities have evacuation plans
abstract: Guided by plans from federal and state emergency management agencies, Dauphin, Cumberland, York and Lebanon counties have developed ways to move people out of the emergency zone if the restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 1 nuclear reactor results in another accident.  In addition, municipalities and school districts within the emergency zone have developed their own specific plans in conjunction with the county plans.

headline: Pa. pension money invested
abstract: The board of the Public School Employees Retirement System authorized the investment of $20 million with a partnership to be formed by Century Four, a Philadelphia-based firm.  Representative Thomas Murphy said he was disappointed that the money did not go to venture-capital firms in Pittsburgh.  The state employees' fund announced the investment last week.

headline: Sen. Reibman voted conscience
abstract: An editorial applauds state Senator Jeanette Reibman for breaking ranks with the Democratic party and voting to approve Governor Dick Thornburgh's nomination of Robert Wilburn for the PA Turnpike Commission.  Senate Democrats have thwarted Thornburgh's nominees 11 times and want to keep the 2-2 deadlock on the Turnpike Commission.

headline: State facing 45-day limit on bias plan
abstract: The US Office of Civil Rights (OCR) has given state officials 45 days to respond to deficiencies found in efforts to eliminate racial discrimination in colleges and universities receiving state funds.  The OCR review was conducted to determine whether the state was meeting its commitments under a two-year-old compliance plan to eliminate desegregation in state-supported colleges and universities.  State schools could lose all federal funding if the OCR were to determine that they failed to meet commitments to eliminate desegregation.

headline: The reclamation issue
abstract: This editorial examines a PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) solution for finding funding to reclaim 15,000 acres of abandoned strip mines in Pennsylvania.  The editorial claims that the DER's preferred solution, which would have the PA Legislature take up the matter, is wishful thinking if PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and the Secretary of the DER do not provide the push.  A bill that would increase the minimum reclamation bond has already languished in the PA House.  The coal industry is opposed to higher bonds, permit fees, or a direct tax on the product, but the editorial believes that it would also be unfair to have taxpayers pay for reclaimation.  The editorial concludes that the best method of fnding funding is through the imposition of higher bonds, and the author urges state legislators to pass bond-increase legislation.

headline: 2 charged in weapons
abstract: Two people described as "remnants" of the Weather Underground have been indicted by a federal grand jury on weapons charges.  Dr. Alan Berkman and Elizabeth Ann Duke were indicted on Thursday, June 20.  This was nearly a month after their arrest by Federal Burea of Investigation agents in Doylestown.

headline: Court stalls new rules put on ride-sharing
abstract: A PA Commonwealth Court injunction has put on hold controversial changes to a program that provides subsidized taxi and van rides for senior citizens.  The rules would prohibit able-bodied senior citizens from participating in the program if they live within a quarter mile of public transportation and would prevent senior citizens' groups from paying the 10% portion of the costs not funded by the program.  Taxi drivers and senior citizen's groups have challenged the new rules in court, saying they will endanger senior citizens' safety and cut taxi cab profits.  The PA Department of Transportation says the changes are necessary to overcome program abuses and bring costs in line with the budget, however.

headline: TORNADO COVERAGE
abstract: A photo depicts a man sitting in a chair in the middle of a tornado-ravaged shopping plaza.  The caption says, "The horrors of the destruction caught up with one rescue worker as the search for bodies continued at the Big Beaver Shopping Plaza."

headline: Pa. workers OK contract, end strike
abstract: Members of the PA Social Services Union (PSSU) and the PA Employment Security Employees Association (PESEA) went back to work July 3 after voting by a narrow margin to end a two-day strike.  The striking workers gained little and voted to accept the same contract offer that the leaders of the state's largest union, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), accepted from the Thornburgh administration.  The administration's three-year offer calls for state employees to get a 3% increase in each year, and the unions agreed to concessions on holiday time, sick leave and vacation time.

headline: Sen. Scanlon's testimony
abstract: State Senator Eugene Scanlon testified at the trial of officials of Computer Technology Associates (CTA) that he supported CTA's initiative and assisted CTA head John Torquato in his attempt to gain a contract with the state.  Scanlon's family received many favors from Torquato.  The editorial criticizes Scanlon and says that his behavior reveals a particularly flawed sense of the public interest.

headline: State law official to argue before Supreme Court
abstract: PA's Senior Deputy Attorney General, Andrew Gordon, will argue before the US Supreme Court on November 5, attmepting to persuade the court that the US Third Circuit Court of Appeals acted improperly when it struck down several provisions of PA's Abortion Control Act.  PA's appeal to the US Supreme Court claims that the Third Circuit Court exceeded its jurisdiction by not limiting itself to the 24-hour waiting period provision.

headline: The unhappy hunters' bill
abstract: A bill that would give the state Legislature expanded control over the state Game Commission is currently under consideration in the Senate Game and Fisheries Committee.  This editorial opposes passing the bill because it would take the state away from a sound program of game management.  If the legislature must approve the Game Commission's budget, it would be impossible for the commission to run properly.

headline: 28 to rise in ranks of police
abstract: Acting State Police Commissioner Jay Cochran Jr. has announced the promotion of 28 officers and the transfer of 10 others.  The article lists the troopers who were promoted or transferred.

headline: Food for error
abstract: This editorial examines the PA Department of Agriculture's rejection of 203 truckloads of free federal food for the poor.  This rejection occurred because some unnamed bureaucrat was concerned that federal money to transport and store the food would be unavailable.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has tried to right this wrong, he wrote to the US Agriculture Department to override the original rejection and request that the food be sent.  This is, however, a mistake that should never have happened.  Finanical considerations should not take priority over the poor and needy when it comes to foodstuffs.

headline: Tornado Workers Find 6 More Bodies
abstract: Relief workers and volunteers searched for victims and sought to restore power and telephone lines in tornado-ravaged communities in Ohio, PA and Ontario.  Workers found six more bodies, bringing the death toll to 93.  The town hit hardest economically was Wheatland, PA, where tornadoes destroyed 95% of the industries that provide jobs for the towns 1,122 residents.

headline: PAC, individual aid of $23 million given
abstract: According to the Federal Election Commission, Political action committees and individuals spent nearly $23 million on the 1984 election--much of which was dispersed by conservative groups.   The biggest individual spender was California businessman Michael Goland; he spent $419,573 to help unseat former US Senator Charles Percy.  The National Conservative Political Action Committee shelled out $9.8 million for President Ronald Reagan, and conservative PAC's as a whole spent $15.8 million to promote Reagan.  Liberal PAC's spent only $803,923 trying to elect Walter Mondale.  Campaign expenditures are considered independent if the activity they finance is not organized by a candidate's campaign.

headline: Senate expenses
abstract: A letter to the editor, written by the chief clerk of the PA Senate, corrects several points made in a December 2, 1985 letter to the editor written by PA State Representative Anthony May.  The author states that May miscasts the procedures for review of PA Senate expense records, which the Senate makes available to the Legislative Audit and Advisory Commission.  The commission, which audits the PA General Assembly at least once a year, is supposed to protect the public interest.  The PA Senate also makes all its expense reports available to the press.

headline: The Senate has approved
abstract: The PA Senate approved legislation moving Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday commemoration from January 15 to the third Monday in January; this new date conforms with the US federal observance.

headline: 'Things weren't right'
abstract: This article discusses the health problems of men who were hired to help with the cleanup of Three Mile Island.  These men fear that they were exposed to too much radiation and will face worse health problems further down the road.  They took the job because it was a high-paying job for a laborer.

headline: 3 on death row plan appeals
abstract: Three men who were scheduled to be executed are expected to appeal their decisions; this means that their executions might not happen for months or years.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed execution warrants for the three men yesterday.  These are the first executions to take place in PA in 23 years.  Under the state's Post-Conviction Hearing Act, appeals after the conviction can be filed at the PA State Supreme Court and then at the US Supreme Court to try to overturn the state decision.  A brief history of the moratorium on the death penalty in the state, as well as a history of the cases of the three men, is also given in the article.

headline: Free food rejection questioned in House
abstract: The truckloads of free federal government food turned away by the administration of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh could have helped feed 500,000 needy PA residents, according to figures released Monday by Democrats in the PA House.  PA State Representatives Allen Kukovich and Italo Cappabianca lashed out at the Thornburgh administration for its decision not to accept the 203 truckloads of surplus and called for the bureaucrat's firing or the transfer of responsibility for the food program to another agency.

headline: Tornadoes accompany storms
abstract: Tornadoes touched down in Philadelphia, Cumberland, and Sussex County yesterday, as heavy storms battered the Southeastern PA, Deleware, and South Jersey.  Rains caused heavy flooding throughout the region, most severely in Cumberland Country, NJ.  At the height of the storm, 20,000 electricity customers lost power for varying times of the afternoon and evening.  Several deaths and multiple injuries were reported in conjunction with the storm throughout the region, which left trees uprooted, power lines down, and homes damaged.

headline: Paper work buries state ethics panel
abstract: The PA State Ethics Commission, while managing to snare a few culprits of government corruption, has missed many other scandals, including jobs being sold in the PA Auditor General's department and the bribery scandal involving Computer Technology Associates (CTA).  A study of the ethics commission and court records found several reasons why the reform process has fallen short, among them is the fact that the Ethics Commission is buried under an avalanche of paperwork.  A lot of the the Ethics Commission's power was reduced by a 1983 court decision declaring that public employees and public officials don't have to report on the financial holdings or income of immediate family members.  Some disclosure advocates question whether officials or governmental bodies at any level ought to be responsible for evaluating their own behavior.  PA State Representative Allen Kukovich believes that public financing of major state campaigns is the next major step to thrwart "big money".

headline: Senate votes to alter setup on pike panel
abstract: Due to a great deal of political maneuvering between Governor Dick Thornburgh and state Senate Democrats over who will control the Turnpike Commission, Senate Republicans attached to a toll-road construction bill provisions for confirming commissioners with a simple majority.  The provisions also called for shortening commissioners' terms from 10 to 4 years and requiring commissioners to leave office within 90 days of the expiration of their terms--even if successors haven't been chosen.  This would give power over the Turnpike Commission to whichever party holds the governorship when a commissioner's term ends.

headline: THE WAGE GAP
abstract: According to the US Labor Department, women are concetrated in just 20 of the 441 jobs listed in the Census Occupational Classification System.  All of these jobs, which are traditionally related to homemaking, nurturing, or supporting others, pay less than predominantly male jobs.  As a result, women, as a group, earn about 40% less than men.  To bridge this pay gap, many groups have begun to argue for the concept of comparable worth.  Advocates of comparable worth argue that women earn less than men because jobs held by women are paid less regardless of the value to the employer.  Opponents of the principle claim that the marketplace sets rates of compensation, not individual employers.  All the states surrounding PA have begun pay equity studies, and a bill explaining pay equity and appropriating funds for a study was introduced in the PA House last year, but did not pass.  In Pittsburgh, an ad hoc committee is preparing to make some recommendations regarding comparable worth.

headline: Trash ban:  Lebanon agency puzzled by DER's letter
abstract: Greater Lebanon Refuse Authority officials would like the PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) to clarify a three-page letter it sent out to all major PA landfills.  The letter forbids the dumping of pathological and infectious wastes, such as waste from hospitals and other medical facilities.  The law is meant to prevent disease from spreading to water and is also designed to protect landfill employees.  The DER wants landfills to secure its permission before accepting pathological and infectious waste.

headline: 3 sought in $78,000 student-loan fraud case
abstract: Arrest warrants have been issued for three people charged with forging the names of bank and univeristy officials to swindle $78,000 from the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency.  This is the largest single student loan faud scheme in state history.  Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell said the three suspects, who have not been apprehended at the current time, had a very sophisticated scheme which involved forging the names of applicants and officials of higher education institutions; they used this process to apply for $188,000 in loans from 1980 to 1982.  The charges against the three could bring a maximum of 398 years of imprisonment.

headline: Fuel Aid Effort Runs Out of Gas
abstract: House Republicans ended efforts by Democrats to override Governor Dick Thornburgh's veto of an $11 million state allocation.  The allocation would have helped poor homeowners pay fuel bills.  The House was eight votes short of the two-thirds needed to override the veto.  Governor Thornburgh vetoed the bill because he said that federal funding was enough to cover the need.

headline: Tornadoes' legacy: Fear, guilt
abstract: Counseling programs are under way in all 13 PA counties that were declared federal disaster areas after the May 31 tornadoes that killed 64 people in PA and 26 in Ohio and Ontario.  Psychiatrists say that those who survived the tornadoes will likely feel emotionally numb, have feelings of anger, helplessness, and disbelief and/or guilt.

headline: Party Dispute With Punch
abstract: Punches were thrown at a Democratic City Committee meeting in Philadelphia.  At the meeting, party officials endorsed a slate of candidates for the upcoming May primary.  The fighting was between leaders of the Northern and Southern Wards; they were fighting because the Northeastern wards are not high performing.

headline: 'They took my job away,' steelworker says
abstract: Yesterday, the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Aging heard testimony from a number of older workers facing age discrimination.  Last year, the Bureau of Labor Statistics found that of the total 940,000 laid-off workers over age 55, 25% were seeking jobs but still unemployed, while 15% had left the workforce entirely.  Members of the House committee urged stricter enforcement of federal regulations against age discrimination.

headline: Waste not, want not
abstract: This photo depicts State Department of Environmental Resources Secretary Nicholas DeBenedictis as he takes a box of his household trash to the Derry Township Recycling Center.  This was immediately before Secretary DeBenedictis presented a $28,000 check to township Supervisor Kathryn Taylor for a study on the feasibility of a curbside recycling program.

headline: 4 Inmates Injured In Graterford Scuffle
abstract: Four inmates were treated for minor injuries last night after a melee broke out in Graterford Prison.  The fight started when two inmates started chasing a third; others joined in and a fight ensued.  Prison guards quickly broke up the fight.

headline: Funds set up for those left homeless by fire
abstract: The outpouring of contributions for fire victims in West Philadelphia was overwhelming.  Several funds were set up for the victims of the MOVE evacuation on Osage Avenue.  Financial gifts should get sent to the Fund for Philadelphia.

headline: Tornado's aftermath: Some start to rebuild, others plan to move on
abstract: Crawford County Deputy Sheriff Morris Wain says that Atlantic, PA was always a fairly poor community, and he does not expect many people, except the Amish, to stay in the city. This is because almost all of the 100 structures in the city were damaged or destroyed Friday after a tornado hit the area.  The PA Emergency management Agency reported that at least 61 people died, 600 were injured, and 1,520 structures were damaged or destroyed by tornadoes.  Many residents of the areas that were hit say that they plan to move, rather than rebuild.

headline: Party Government
abstract: The movement to increase membership of the Republican Party by encouraging Democrats to switch party afiiliations is destroying the two-party system; it is making the US more like Russia or Cuba.  The plan could also create a bigger divide between those who have what they need and those who do not.

headline: Too many blacks in prison
abstract: This editorial looks at the racial disparities of the prison popoulation in Pennsylvania.  In 1980, blacks represented 5% of the population of the 24 counties in Western PA, while making up 55% of the prison population at the Western Pennitentiary.  The editorial also criticizes the bias sentencing practices, pointing to the fact that blacks serve 25% longer sentences in federal prison than whites.  The editorial argues that a "Get Tough" approach on sentencing, favored by the some in the black community as well as conservative lawmakers, would just perpetuate the already racially biased sentencing that leads to black-on-black crime being punished less harshly than black-on-white crime.

headline: Waste storm coming
abstract: The state Legislature is expected to approve Governor Dick Thornburgh's negotiated four-state agreement for the disposal of low-level radioactive waste; there is sure to be controversy over the sites chosen for waste disposal.  The editorial argues that a site must be chosen and notes that the key to resolving the issue is communication and education.

headline: 5 BODIES IN ASHES OF RADICALS' HOME; ASSAULT DEFENDED…Philadelphians Stunned…Fire, After Police Drop Bomb Burns Down 50 Houses - City Vows to Rebuild
abstract: Firefighters recovered five bodies from the charred rubble of a radical group's house (MOVE) in West Philadelphia.  The house was leveled in a police assault that set fire to the surrounding neighborhood and destroyed more than 50 homes.  Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said the city would rebuild the houses gutted by the blaze; he also defended the action against the back-to-nature group MOVE.  The police action was part of an attempt to evict fewer than 20 MOVE members from the row house in a middle-class West Philadelphia neighborhood.  According to neighbors, MOVE members accumulated an arsenal, built two rooftop bunkers, kept dozens of cats, refused to pay utility bills and harangued the neighborhood at all hours.

headline: Funds to help prevent homelessness nearer
abstract: PA legislative leaders and administration officials yesterday made public a compromise plan for starting state-funded programs to prevent homelessness.  The $5.5 million plan was immediately hailed by leaders of a coalition of religious and social service organizations.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh had previously proposed one-time-only spending improvements for shelters, boarding homes, and domestic violence centers, but expressed support for the compromise plan.  Under the revised bill, about $3.5 million in state money would be distributed for renovation of vacant buildings and the creation of about 400 low-rent, long-term, single-room occupancy housing units.  Another $2 million would be distributed for the establishment of about 250 units of so-called bridge housing.

headline: Towns rallies in support of victims
abstract: Residents of northwestern Pennsylvania communities have come out in droves with donations of clothing, food and money for their neighbors who were hit the hardest by Friday's tornado.  Ben Evans, eastern regional director of disaster services for the American Red Cross, said that the concern of the Red Cross was mass care.  Evans said it appears as if each community is taking care of its own, however.

headline: PAT gets grant to complete subway line: Dole's selection irritates Specter
abstract: The announcement of the Port Authority Transit's $19.7 million grant from the US Department of Transportation irritated US Senator Arlen Specter.  This was because the announcement of the funding was released through Governor Dick Thornburgh's office, rather than through Specter's.  Normally, such good tidings would be funneled through a congressional office, allowing a lawmaker sharing the party label of the administration to bask in a little reflected credit for the federal largesse.  A Specter aide speculated that the perceived snub came because Specter has emerged as a vocal opponent of Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole; Specter has objected to the proposed sale of Conrail to the Norfolk Southern Corporation.

headline: Value of life in perspective
abstract: This letter to the editor puts abortion in perspective by comparing it to farmers and food suppliers who destroy their crops to create a food shortage.  The author says that only when our lives are threatened do we decide that it is wrong to destroy life.

headline: Water quality: State standards take a step backward
abstract: The PA Environmental Quality Board (EQB) adopted revised water-quality standards that could undo progress that has been made since the 1970s.  The National Audubon Society, the PA Federation of Sportsmen's Clubs, the Sierra Club, and the National Wildlife Federation formally petitioned the EQB to reverse its recent decision on water quality.  This editorial urges the EQB to reverse its decision and to remember its role as the guardian of the environment.

headline: 5 More Bodies Found; 2 Were Kids
abstract: Police, firefighters and federal agents uncovered the bodies of three more adults and two children, raising the death count at the MOVE compound in West Philadelphia to 11.  Police investigators plan to begin questioning more than 40 stakeout officers in order to help clear up questions that have arisen concerning events at the rear of the compound; these events occurred in the early stages of a six-alarm fire that eventually devastated the neighborhood.

headline: Ginny Thornburgh: presence without pretense
abstract: This article discusses Ginny Thornburgh, wife of Governor Dick Thornburgh, and how she is an advocate for the handicapped throughout the state.

headline: Visitors say city's image will survive
abstract: Out-of-town visitors to Philadelphia's tourist attractions predict that the city's image will not suffer terribly as a result of the standoff between Philadelphia Police and the radical group MOVE.  The standoff resulted in the destruction of the entire Osage-Avenue neighborhood in West Philadelphia.

headline: Pat Stapleton is ready to run
abstract: This article examines the prospects of PA State Senator Patrick Stapleton's run for PA Lieutenant Governor.  Stapleton has made no secret of wanting to be Bob Casey's running mate, he has already told Casey that he is available, and Stapleton believes that he can add something to Casey's campaign: broad-based support among traditional Republican groups.  Stapleton has already established his own political committee, and he also believes that his support among the state's farm community will give him a big boost.  Stapleton believes that a possible fight between PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and US Senator Arlen Specter could actually hurt the gubernatorial campaign of PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton; such an electoral contest would benefit the Democrats.

headline: Williamsport case tests separation of chuch, state
abstract: The US Supreme Court is set to begin hearing the case of Bender v. Williamsport Area High School--a case that centers on a group of students who wanted to meet for prayer at Williamsport High School during morning activity period; their request was denied by the school board.  The case will also decide on the constitutionality of the Equal Access Act, which was passed by Congress in 1984; the act gives religious clubs the right to meet in public schools.

headline: Water rate hike action delayed
abstract: A proposed settlement to Mechanicsburg Water Company's request for a $214,400 annual rate increase is heading back to the drawing board.  The state Public Utility Commission postponed action on a $133,500 settlement--reached by the company and the PUC staff--on grounds that the borough was not given ample opportunity to state its case.

headline: 9 wardens taken on tour of private jail
abstract: Nine Western PA jail wardens and several reporters toured the 268 Center in Armstrong County, a private jail for non-violent offenders.  As soon as the Center can get the proper sewage permits, Allegheny County hopes to send 57 inmates to the center, .

headline: Groups ask state funds for food aid
abstract: A rally sponsored by the PA Coalition on Food and Nutrition and the Association of Food Banks drew about 500 supporters to the Capitol Rotunda.  The rally was in support of a $12 million emergency food program

headline: 'We All Go to Work': Amish, Uninsured, Are Ready to Rebuild
abstract: The Amish do not carry insurance against disasters, such as the tornadoes that splintered homes across northwestern PA.  However, with the help of their brethren throughout this rural region, Atlantic, PA's 26 Amish families plan to begin rebuilding immediately.  In the non-mechanized, self-help world of the Amish, insurance comes not in the form of written agreements, but in a spiritual covenant among friends.  The Amish predict that their homes and barns will be rebuilt by the end of the summer.

headline: Perjury hinted in Alaska hearing
abstract: Special prosecutor Sam Dash, in his closing statements before the Alaska State Senate's impeachment proceeding against Alaska Governor Bill Sheffield, argued that Sheffied's failure to remember meetings and facts surrounding the sale of a state office building could constitute perjury.  At the heart of the matter is the award of a $9.1 million state contract for a Fairbanks, Alaska office building owned by Sheffield's political ally Joseph "Lenny" Arsenault.  Phillip Lacovara, Sheffield's attorney, said that the grand jury had only received half of the story, and there is no convincing evidence to show that the governor had a motive to lie.

headline: (Picture)
abstract: A photo depicts Dr. Richard Lyons, the former chairperson of the Pennsylvania Board of Medical Education and Licensure, sitting with Dr. Barbra Shore, the current chairperson of the medical board.

headline: Water restrictions eased after rainfall soaks state
abstract: Three inches of rain fell in the Lycoming Valley during the last two weeks, enough for officials in Williamsport, PA to postpone a water-rationing plan that was set to begin November 25.  In southern Schuylkill County, a 1.7 inch rainfal was enough to convince the Pine Grove Council to lift a water emergency that has been in effect since July 29.  The PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) says that drought conditions in eastern PA have improved substantially since August, and the DER has even lifted its drought emergency for the Delaware River Basin.

headline: A Day of Anguish
abstract: This editorial calls for straight answers from local officials to help the public understand the decision-making process that led police to drop an explosive device on the MOVE house in West Philadelphia; the police were trying to evict the residents.

headline: Groups seek override of heating fund veto
abstract: At a Capitol news conference, labor and religious groups asked the state House to override Governor Dick Thornburgh's veto of a proposed $11 million state allocation for a program that helps low-income households pay for heat.

headline: What the LCB audit really said
abstract: A letter to the editor from state Representative David Wright says that the Post-Gazette published an untrue editorial; Representative Wright seeks to clear up misstatements about the Liquor-Control-Board audit by the state.

headline: Pete Flaherty alive and well, even if he's out of sight
abstract: A columnist discusses ex-Pittsburgh mayor and current Allegheny County Commissioner Pete Flaherty's political career and possible political future.  Flaherty was a very popular mayor; he ran in three different statewide campaigns, all of which he lost by narrow margins.  Flaherty said he enjoys being commissioner but will consider another statewide race--either for US Senate or for governor.

headline: 67 Complaints: A Ringing endorsement for Toll-Free Line
abstract: The Bureau of Occupational and Professional Affairs has created a toll-free hot line for consumers to register complaints about doctors, nurses, dentists and other professionals.  During the four-day period after the number was made public, the state received 67 complaints and 80 additional calls.  The Bureau urges other media outlets to publicize the number, but has no plans to pay for advertising.

headline: Water shortage
abstract: This letter to the editor says that the current water shortage or drought is not the real problem, but only a symptom of the problem.  He says the real problem is the lack of water storage capacity and that new and expanded reservoirs would fix the problem.  He urges the Governor to mobilize forces and to solve the problem permanently.

headline: A force divided
abstract: An investigative report looks at the many problems facing the Pittsburgh Bureau of Police.  Police Superintendent Robert Coll said that problems of supervision and discipline have made the police less than diligent.  According to Federal Bureau of Investigation figures, the Pittsburgh Police solved a smaller percentage of major crimes last year than police in six cities of comparable size.  Interviews with women and minority officers have also found that sexual and racial divisions still deeply affect the bureau.  Older officers tend to view the problems with the bureau as a lack in the quality of recruits.  Younger officers, as a whole, said their performance has suffered because they are poorly guided by their supervisors and shunned by seasoned officers.  The bureau is also very lax in its discipline, especially for officers who abuse the absentee system.

headline: Harrisburg is hindering food aid
abstract: A letter to the editor describes the ways in which she feels that Governor Dick Thornburgh tries to handicap the food stamp program.  The author says that those eligible for emergency food stamps must get them through Harrisburg; this results in a delay of two weeks to a month.  This is in violation of the federal law that says that emergency food stamps must be received within five days.

headline: Why CAT?
abstract: A letter to the editor from State Representative William Rybak, chairman of the PA House Insurance Committee, disputes the accusations of a previous letter that stated that PA's CAT (Catastrophic) Fund was only benefitting the insurance companies.  Rybak states that the beneficiaries of the CAT Fund are those who are so severely injured in motor vehicle accidents that their medical and rehab expenses exceed $100,000.

headline: Petitions for vote recount filed by Balph
abstract: William Balph, who lost a bid for Lawrence County Common Pleas Judge in the November 5, 1985 election, filed petitions with President Judge Glen McCracken Jr. to have votes recounted in 54 of the county's 105 precincts.  The official results, certified by the Lawrence County Return Board on November 22, showed Balph losing to PA State Representative Ralph Pratt by 95 votes.  Balph wants 14 precincts recounted in New Castle and 40 in the boroughs and townships of Lawrence County.

headline: Adequacy of state funding for medical fees is doubted
abstract: Aides to Governor Dick Thornburgh are reviewing the state budget to determine if the state Legislature provided sufficient monies to fund $40 million in fee increases for medical-care providers.  At issue are provisions in the $3 billion Medical-Assistance portion of the budget--a portion that mandates fee hikes for services provided to the indigent by doctors, hospitals and nursing homes.  Top legislative aides and representatives of health-care providers say the administration does have sufficient money and should follow the legislative mandate.

headline: Well water faces more contaminants
abstract: Contamination of ground water is being discovered with growing frequency in PA.  The sources range from chemical spills and hazardous-waste dumps to fertilizer spreading and sewage disposal.  Half of the state's 12 million people drink ground water, either from private wells or from public systems using wells.  There is no explicit national legislative mandate to protect ground water.  It is difficult and expensive to detect and clean up ground water contamination.

headline: A judicial oversimplification
abstract: PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert Nix blamed prison overcrowding on the poor quality of public education and a lack of parental responsibility.  This editorial defends the public school system and says that overcrowded prisons are the result of various societal, environmental, physical and emotional causes.

headline: Hearings to study handicapped's needs
abstract: A special state House committee, created by a House resolution and directed to determine whether handicapped people over age 21 are being educated sufficiently for independent living, voted to hold statewide public hearings to study the availability of services for handicapped adults.  The two greatest difficulties facing the committee are determining the number of handicapped people in the state and estimating the cost of providing services.

headline: Why give N.J. all gambling taxes?
abstract: A letter to the editor complains that the Philadelphia area loses around $250 to 300 million each year to Atlantic City casinos.  The author suggests that PA officials should not repeal the law that allowed blackjack games in the state; the law will keep money in PA.

headline: PGW's Reply: No Discounting Of VIP Charges
abstract: James McKee, chairman of the Philadelphia Facilities Management Corporation, which operates Philadelphia Gas Works, said that hundreds of elected officials, prominent business people and others have been designated as "VIPs" by the city-owned gas company.  He said they only get special handling, not special rates.  These comments came following an article in the Philadelphia Daily News; the article alleged that PGW was giving preferential treatment to local politicians.

headline: AIDS Test Set For City Pupil
abstract: According to Schools Superintendent Constance Claytonan, an unidentified Philadelphia public school student suspected of having AIDS has been removed from school for medical examination.  School officials hope to receive the results of the exam by the child's doctor at the end of the week.  If the child is found to have AIDS, the school board will decide whether the student will be allowed to go to school and whether parents of the child's classmates will be informed.  An AIDS Task Force formed by Clayton is currently trying to form a school district policy on the disease.

headline: Where to get help for water problems
abstract: This article offers advice on where to get help for water problems--regardless of whether you are served by a public water system or a household well, spring, or cistern.

headline: A town meeting would have handled MOVE situation better
abstract: An opinion piece says that a town meeting would have been the better solution to the MOVE problem in West Philadelphia.  Author says that the way the police handled the situation--spraying the house with a water cannon for hours then dropping a bomb on it to remove the people --was wrong and that it could have been better handled if the neighbors would have had a meeting with MOVE.  The author defends MOVE and says something about racism.

headline: Heinz picnic nets $21,773 for food bank
abstract: A picnic hosted by US Senator John Heinz netted $21,773 for the Greater Pittsburgh Food Bank.  David Kerr, president of the food bank's board, said the money will be used for the shelter's capital fund drive, which has a goal of $1,660,000 and ends this month.  Part of the capital fund money was used to purchase the former Potter-McCune warehouse at 32nd and Walnut streets in McKeesport.  Earlier yesterday, Senator Heinz visited Action-Housing headquarters to honor 14 VISTA volunteers who will help the homeless in Pittsburgh shelters.

headline: Wine-sale hearings "informational"
abstract: PA State Senator John Shumaker, chairman of the Law and Justice Committee, said that the daylong hearing on expanding wine sales to private outlets was "informational" and not necessarily for the purpose of developing legislation.  The hearings were held because of an agreement Shumaker made when the committee was considering Sunset legislation for the PA Liquor Control Board.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, through his press secretary, reiterated his position that the state should not attempt to duplicate free enterprise.

headline: Pike hiring injunction sought
abstract: State Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson and Turnpike Commissioner Rank Ursomarso filed suit asking the state Supreme Court for an injuntion to block Democrats from hiring people for the Turnpike Commission.  The suit says that at least 129 people were hired for turnpike jobs in violation of two state Supreme Court orders.  Larson and Ursomarso said that people were hired without the necessary finding that they were critically needed to maintain turnpike operations, as well as without the action being placed on the commission's agenda.

headline: Ambulance services face new state regulations
abstract: For the first time, ambulance crews in New Jersey and Pennsylvania will be subject to new rules and regulations that require ambulances have working equipment and a well-trained crews.  Until recently, the only government checks on ambulance services in the two states were non-mandatory inspection programs.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: This photo depicts Harold Stoner hoeing in his garden before a demonstration by 250 people at the entrance of the Three Mile Island Nuclear Plant.  Demonstrators were protesting the possible restart of the Unit 1 reactor.

headline: Abuse Charges Close Berks Co. Child Home
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman said his office is investigating Ruff Edge Farms Incorporated, a facility that provides housing and schooling for children and mentally retarded young adults.  Zimmerman alleged that residents of Ruff Edge were subjected to indecent contact, deviate sexual intercourse and attempted sodomy by staff members.  The farm operators denied the abuse allegations.  The residents of the home were removed.

headline: High error rate cited in welfare
abstract: A report on PA's state-funded General Assistance program for the needy shows that errors were made in 20.3% of the 1984 cases that were audited.  The error rate was detailed in a report filed last week by the PA Department of Public Welfare.  State legislators worried about the error rate, but were also angry at the Department of Public Welfare for not releasing the report until the Legislature threatened a funding cutoff.

headline: Zimmerman warns of pitfalls in Conrail's sale
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman warns that a merger of Conrail with the Norfolk Southern Corporation is likely to affect adversely the ability of PA industries to compete with those in other states.  The report says that the plan would pose the greatest threats to the coal and steel industries in PA because those industries would face higher shipping rates; this would harm their competitive position relative to firms in other states.

headline: Pittsburgh mayor decides to sit out '86 governor's race
abstract: At a press conference in Pittsburgh yesterday, Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri said that he will not be a candidate for governor next year.  Supporters had urged Caliguiri to run, citing favorable poll numbers, while other Democrats pressured him to make an early decision to avoid in-fighting.  Former PA Auditor General Robert Casey believes that Caliguiri's absence from the race will make him the front-runner to win the Democratic nomination for governor.  PA State Representative Allen Kukovich also believes that Caliguiri's decision will help him gain support in Western PA.  PA State Democratic chairman Edward Mezvinsky said that he is uncertain whether Kukovich will benefit or whether Pete Flaherty, a former Pittsburgh Mayor, will consider running.

headline: An entire nation struggles to cope with dreaded killer
abstract: This article looks at the hysteria surrounding the AIDS virus.  The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) estimates that 500,000 to 1 million Americans have been exposed to the virus, but that 90-95% will not develop AIDS.  A Gallup poll recently showed that 66% of people believe AIDS will soon spread to all kinds of people in the US.  The CDC does not believe that AIDS will ever become an epidemic among the heterosexual population.

headline: 2 PUC nominees "placekeeping"
abstract: A spokesperson for PA Governor Dick Thornburgh said that, until the state Legislature resolves issues with board-member terms, he will not offer serious candidates to fill two PA Public Utility Commission vacancies.  Although Thornburgh sent the names of two aides to the PA Senate yesterday, this was done only to meet a constitutional requirement; the two aides sent to the Senate have no intention of joining the PUC, which is currently being reviewed under the state's Sunset Law.  The PA Legislature has until December 31, 1986 to decide whether to change and renew the PUC.

headline: Academy's safety worries state official
abstract: The PA State Fire Academy in Lewistown, particularly the "burn building" where live exercises are conducted, is currently in a major state of disrepair due to overuse.  As of September 1, just resident classes are allowed to train in the fire academy.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh proposed a $300,000 renovation last summer when he visited the academy; the governor signed a capital budget bill authorizing $125,000 to repair parts of the academy.  However, the the fire academy is still waiting on the $125,000, which is still going through General Services; it is also waiting on the $300,000, which is still in the Senate Appropriations Committee.

headline: House Calls for Investigation Into Food Program
abstract: The PA House today ordered a legislative committee to investigate the PA Department of Agriculture's handling of the federally funded Temporary Emergency Food Assistance Program, which provides free food to the needy.  State management of the program has come under attack since November 1985, when it was revealed that the PA Department of Agriculture turned down about 200 truckloads of free food that was to be distributed to the state's most impoverished residents.  The US General Accounting Office released a report on the incident that criticized the state's inventory management systems, though it said they have improved since the study was conducted.

headline: Defense Aide Tells Why Phila. Yard's on 'List'
abstract: An assistant secretary of defense said that the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard was put on a list of military bases that could be closed.  This is because the Navy determined that other shipyards could handle the work now done there.  A list of facilities that could possibly be closed was created by the Navy, but they do not recommend closing any bases this year because of high costs and restrictive legislation.

headline: Plummer opens mayoral bid, challenges Reed to debates
abstract: During a press conference, former Harrisburg City Councilman Wesley Plummer yesterday challenged Mayor Stephen Reed to a series of five debates.  Plummer will announce a list of his supporters on Thursday, a list which includes Democrats and Republicans.  He said he is runnign because Harrisburg needs an "alternative" to Reed.

headline: Be somebody's friend for life. Give blood.
abstract: An advertisement for the American Red Cross depicts Governor Thornburgh standing with  Lt. Governor Scranton.  The advertisement reads: No matter how many times a year you elect to give blood, there's nothing like the winning feeling that giving blood gies you.  It's easier than running for office. It's safe. And it takes less time than a press conference.  Blood donations have also never been more needed.  All blood used to save lives in the Delaware Valley comes from volunteers like you.  Won't you join the campaign to save lives? Give blood with a friend through the American Red Cross.  Be somebody's friend for life.

headline: 3 Mile Island plant back in operation
abstract: At 1:30 p.m. yesterday, GPU Nuclear Corporation announced that Three Mile Island's (TMI) Unit 1 Reactor reached the restart threshold known as "criticality", signalling the return of power to TMI.  Despite a two-to-one vote against the restart in a non-binding referendum by residents of the area a year ago, there was little visible public opposition to the restart.  The US Supreme Court laid the debate over restarting Unit 1 to rest when it refused to consider a request by Three Mile Island Alert and the Union of Concerned Scientists that the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission be ordered to hold more hearings on safety and management integrity issues.  GPU Nuclear officials plan a steady build-up to 100% power capacity within three months, and plan to produce electric power for GPU's customers in PA and New Jersey at 12% of capacity in two weeks.  The NRC has deployed 10 inspectors on round-the-clock shifts to monitor the restart.

headline: After the fire, smoldering emotions: Residents criticize city's decision to resort to a bomb
abstract: Philadelphia citizens from the 6100 block of Pine Street and the 6200 block of Osage Street complain about the way police and Mayor Wilson Goode handled the situation with the back-to-nature cult MOVE.  Citizens wanted MOVE out of the neighborhood, but half of the neighborhood was burnt down in the process; residents feel that the situation was handled in the wrong way.

headline: Insulation agencies may be cut
abstract: The PA Department of Community Affairs is considering a plan to eliminate 26 local and regional agencies from the federally funded weatherization program.  The program is designed to help low-income people reduce their heating costs.  The cutting of these agencies would make the program more manageable, according to state officials.  All seven weatherization agencies in Philadelphia are expected to be cut, and the city will get a contract instead.

headline: Extradition of hijackers analyzed, Specter critical of Egypt's role
abstract: According to Harrisburg-area scholars, there really is not a clear precedent for extraditing the four Palestinian hijackers of the cruise ship Achille Lauro to the United States.  According to international law, the hijackers could not be tried for murder, given that it happened in international waters.  They could be tried for piracy or hijacking, which extends beyond a country's borders, however.  US Senator Arlen Specter also criticized Egypt for its part in releasing the terrorists who hijacked the Achille Lauro.  Specter said he was shocked at Egypt's decision to release them and urged the US to cut foreign aid to Egypt in half.  Specter also urged extradition for the four terrorists being held by the Italian government.  Ever since American warplanes forced an Egyptian plane carrying the terrorists to land in Sicily, the Italian government has been holding the terrorists.

headline: Politics si, public no
abstract: This editorial complains about Governor Dick Thornburgh's nomination of Robert Wilburn to a post on the state Turnpike Commission, and says that Thornburgh is playing partisan politics.  The author also refernces the Senate Democrats refusal to confirm any of Thornburgh's nominees.  The editorial says that the public is the one who has to pay the price for partisan politics.

headline: Bills allow health license suspension
abstract: A package of bills calling for the immediate suspension of any doctor, nurse, osteopath or pharmacist convicted of a drug-related felony, either in- or out-of-state, was approved unanimously by the state House.
