The licensing boards that oversee the health-care professions do not, under current law, have the power to refuse to issue licenses or immediately suspend the certification of members who have been convicted on drug charges.

headline: 50-50 meltdown: NRC findings press nuclear insurance reform
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission testified at the request of the US House Subcommittee on Energy Conservation and Power that there is a 50-50 chance of a "severer core melt accident" occurring over the next 20 years.  This editorial argues that if they allow a 50% chance of a meltdown, then the NRC should require nuclear power plants to have insurance to cover all possible costs; insurance would be used to cover all clean-up costs and would prevent the public from having to foot the bill.

headline: AIDS threat at state prison
abstract: The PA State House held a subcommittee hearing yesterday on the problems of dealing with prisoners who have AIDS.  The PA Deparment of Corrections says that precautions have been taken to protect health care workers and others who deal with inmates who have AIDS.  The American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees, says that the state's policy is not specific enough.  Paul Detrick, a prison guard who testified, said that the Department of Corrections should test all inmates for AIDS and should isolate those that test positive.  State Representative Corry Stevens supports this plan.

headline: Joan Specter proposes volunteer plan for elderly
abstract: Philadelphia City Councilwoman Joan Specter proposed that the PA Department of Aging develop a program that would allow senior citizens to earn credits toward their own care when they volunteer to help other senior citizens.  Specter said she would introduce a resolution in Philadelphia City Council after Thanksgiving to urge the state to set up an Older Volunteer Service Bank.

headline: Guv, Rep Vie over Vets Center
abstract: The Thornburgh administration will not abandon its efforts to convert the Pennhurst Center into a veterans nursing home--even though a legislator has threatened its funding.  Representative John Cordisco has said that he would seek to restore $6.17 million in the 1985-86 budget for the necessary renovations to the Pennhurst facility, but only if Thornburgh goes along with spending $12.4 million more to establish a separate veterans nursing center in Northeast Philadelphia.

headline: Politics was on the Waldorf menu
abstract: An opinion piece talks about the 87th Annal PA Society Dinner and weekend soiree at the Waldorf in New York City.  The event is steeped in Republican tradition, though a few Democrats were invited this year.  Much of the conversation centered around the upcoming elections, with Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell talking about his upcoming Democratic gubernatorial primary with Bob Casey.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh was asked by several why he chose not run against US Sentaor Arlen Specter in the Republican US Senate primary.

headline: Cancer study
abstract: This editorial argues that the findings of a PA Health Department study should quell the concerns of local citizens who believe that radiation released during the Three-Mile-Island accident caused an increase in cancer among local residents.

headline: 67 claims filed in most recent suits against TMI
abstract: Yesterday, 67 people and one estate filed suit against the owners and designers of Three Mile Island (TMI) in Dauphin County Court.  Since February 1985, more than 600 claims have been filed against TMI in Dauphin County Court by people with cancer, anxiety, and other ailments or by estates of people who died; all claim that the 1979 accident at TMI caused them emotional distress and exposed the area to radiation.  TMI and government scientists who investigated the accident claim that not enough radiation escaped to harm anyone.  The article lists the 67 persons who filed suit and their ailments.

headline: All should resign
abstract: A letter to the editor urges the citizens of Philadelphia to call for the resignations of Mayor W. Wilson Goode, Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor, Fire Commissioner William C. Richmond, and Managing Director Leo Brooks.  The writer is calling for resignations because of their handling of the MOVE crisis.

headline: Kicks off state program at Three Springs site
abstract: Dubbed the "unofficial kickoff" of a new $10 million program of state assistance to older Pennsylvanian's, Governor Dick Thornburgh presented a $22,286 check to officials of the Three Spring Senior Citizens Center.  The Three Springs senior center will utilize the monies to upgrade its facility, which serves an estimated 77 members.  The program will use state Lottery monies to upgrade some 541 senior centers in the state, and will be used to ensure that all senior centers meet safety standards and are handicapped accessible.

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: This article provides a review of the major historical events that occurred on August 7th throughout history.  Among them are the establishing of the US War Department in 1789, the dedication of the Peace Bridge between the US and Canada in 1927, and the passing of the Gulf of Tonkin resolution by Congress in 1964.

headline: Poor manners
abstract: A letter to the editor comments on a picture showing several people holding a banner that says, "Thornburgh Is Gutless."  As a senior citizen, the author believes the attitude reflected in this banner shows the underlying lack of respect that young people nowadays show towards law and order.  The article under the picture, written about Three Mile Island Unit 1, is biased in favor of good manners and respect for PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Cancer study debunks link to TMI mishap
abstract: According to a study by the PA Department of Health, the cancer rate in the four communities directly downwind of Three Mile Island is 10% higher than should be expected of a population of that size.  However, the 10% difference is not statistically significant to link the cancer rate to the 1979 accident at Unit 2.  The study also found that cancer deaths in both a 10 and 20 mile radius of TMI was lower than expected for similar populations.  The department's study countered a survey done by a Lancaster couple who identified a big increase in cancer deaths tied to the TMI accident.  State Health Secretary Dr. H. Arnold Muller said that survey was biased and had no statistical basis.

headline: A good bill
abstract: This editorial supports a bill that would require the Public Utility Commission to approve the restart of any nuclear power plan that was shut down.  Once the PUC approves or disapproves a restart, the Legislature would have to OK or reject the PUC decision, giving the General Assembly the final authority over any restart.

headline: Although indigent defendants
abstract: The PA Superior Court has ruled that, although indigent defendants have the right to a "spirited defense," their attorneys may not be considered ineffective if they decide not to pursue meritless appeals.  The decision arose from the appeal of Sherman McGeth of Philadelphia.  McGeth sought a re-hearing of his 1978 rape and robbery conviction.  In his appeal, McGeth had contended that his court-appointed defense lawyer was ineffective because he failed to challenge the verdict at a post-conviction hearing.  The PA Superior Court said that McGeth did deserve a spirited defense, but recognized that his defense attorney was correct in his assessment that the appeal would have been frivolous.

headline: More funds for day care
abstract: This editorial says that the state Welfare Department and Governor Dick Thornburgh are being extremely short-sighted in the state's plan to raise subsidies for day-care programs by just 2%.  The editorial argues that day-care centers help to keep people off welfare and that they need more money to continue running.

headline: I Dunno...I Guess
abstract: A cartoon shows US President Ronald Reagan as Superman banging on the outside of a plane window.  Inside the plane are what appear to be Middle Eastern terrorists, one of whom says "I dunno...I guess I always pictured him as a younger fellow..."

headline: Portrait of a snub: Thornburgh won't show up for Shapp
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will not attend the ceremonial unveiling of former Governor Milton Shapp's official portrait.  It is speculated that Thornburgh does not think highly of his Democratic predecessor and the entire process has been fraught with politics.

headline: Curbing malpractice
abstract: Editorial complains that the state Board of Medical Education and Licensure does not have enough power to prevent doctors from practicing while they are being investigated for malpractice or other charges.  Editorial suggests that the Board should be given more authority.

headline: A monkey wrench may
abstract: PA's efforts to establish an Appalachian states low-level radioactive waste compact may be in danger.  There have been indications that Maryland and Delaware, which had expressed interest in joining with West Virginia and PA, may have lost their interest.  Both Maryland and Delaware are also part of the Northeast Compact, which includes Connecticut and New Jersey, and neither state has enacted legislation designating their choice for a nuclear waste compact.  State Representative Camille George syas that if the two states decide against the Appalachian Compact, Governor Dick Thornburgh has no one to blame but himself because he took so long to tell the PA Legislature what he wanted.

headline: Amendment Likely For Private Prisons
abstract: A proposal by PA State Senator Stewart Greenleaf would give the PA Department of Corrections the power to regulate and license privately operated prisons.  Though many believe private prisons are an idea whose time has come, lawmakers say that, without proper regulation, the facilities could pose a threat to public safety.  The article closely examines how the amemdment would lead to greater oversight in private prisons.

headline: More hungry families
abstract: An editorial discusses a recent increase in the number of people going to food distribution agencies in the Pittsburgh area.  The editorial reminds citizens of the need for financial and volunteer support for organizations dealing with the hunger problem.

headline: Navy Yard Had Inkling
abstract: This article gives a chronology of events leading to the Navy's announcement that jobs must be cut at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard.

headline: Power
abstract: According to unofficial results from the Allegheny County Bureau of Elections, women captured nearly 70% of the east suburb governmental offices they sought in last week's municipal elections.  Women ran for 39 of the 160 major available offices, and won 27 of them, or 16.8% of the total slots available.  Women won positions such as town council members, tax collectors, auditors, and mayors.  This counters the old notion that a woman's political place is on school boards.

headline: Deputy appointed for welfare post
abstract: Joseph J. Scartelli, director of the Selinsgrove Center for Mental Retardation for the past 13 years, has been apointed acting deputy secretary of public welfare for mental retardation.  Named to the post by Governor Dick Thornburgh, Scartelli will be in charge of the Office of Mental Retardation, which regulates and sets standards for 43 county-level programs, operates 11 mental retardation centers and administers an annual budget of more than $525 million.

headline: A sunset decision
abstract: This editorial examines possible reforms that would make the PA Public Utility Commission more responsive to the needs of ordinary citizens.  The PUC may have made a crucial mistake when it ignored the request of Lieutenant Governor William Scranton to derail construction of the Limerick 2 power station.  Scranton, who may very well be the next governor of PA, has fought for years to reform the PUC and may make it a key issue in his campaign.  The editorial believes that the PUC is moving quickly to the forefront as a campaign issue in 1986.

headline: Appeals court upholds limits at county jail
abstract: The 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals has upheld US District Judge Maurice Cohill's decision to limit the population of the Allegheny County Jail.  An Allegheny County Commissioner said that the county will urge Cohill to raise the population limit by at least 20 males to limit the release of inmates.  The County is currently in the process of building a new auxiliary jail downtown.

headline: Officials say a computerized
abstract: In an effort to cut costs and fraud, PA state officials may expand to other communities a computerized food-stamp program the federal government started in Reading, PA.  The computerized system replaces traditional coupons with plastic cards that users insert into computer terminals at grocery counters.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh announced that the state will take over the pilot program in April, as it was scheduled to end December 31 under the US Department of Agriculture.  The new system cuts down on food stamp thefts and counterfeiting and eliminates paper work at banks.

headline: Navy Yard Meeting Set
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode plans to meet with elected officials and business leaders from the tri-state area to discuss strategies for retaining jobs at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard.  The shipyard employs about 12,000 workers and is a major force in the area's economy.

headline: Preserving political lore
abstract: The Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission has started an oral history project to collect the recollections of retired legislators and legislative staff members.  The commission said the project would focus on legislators who played a major role in the state.  This project was funded by the state legislature.

headline: Doctor issues alert on rabies and children
abstract: Dr. Jerome Boscia, a physician at the Medical College of PA's division of infectious diseases, said that animals with rabies can spread the disease to humans by licking around a person's eyes, mouth or open sores, not just by biting.  Boscia warned parents to keep children from handling wild animals.  The warning came as the state Health Department released the latest figures on rabies cases for the portion of the year ending May 31.

headline: And back here in Pennsylvania
abstract: A reporter talks to anti-nucler activists, who, despite a federal appeals court giving Three Mile Island (TMI) officials the OK to restart Unit 1, say their fight is far from over.  The activists are protesting outside of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's mansion.  Eric Epstein, an anti-nuclear activist, says that the protest is friendly and that most of the activists are happy with the way the governor has handled the situation.  The anti-nuclear groups would like the commonwealth to appeal yesterday's federal court decision.

headline: Assault Planned in 1984
abstract: As early as the summer of 1984, the Philadelphia police had planned to evict MOVE members from a safehouse in Philadelphia; police had planned to use explosives to blast a hole in the roof.  This plan was modified for the assualt on the safehouse that happened on May 13, 1985.  The plan was modified because MOVE had fortified the walls, windows, and roof of the house.  Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode has said that he had no knowledge of the 1984 plan.  The mayor says he learned that the police planned to use explosives only 17 minutes before the bomb was dropped.  Former Managing Director Leo Brooks also denied knowledge of the plan, and former police Sergeant Herbert Kirk, architect of the 1984 plan, said he did not know whether Brooks or Goode knew of the plan.

headline: Pa. delays cutbacks in taxi aid to elderly
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT), under pressure from lawsuits and PA legislators, is going to postpone its plan to place some restrictions on senior-citizen use of the Shared Ride, or ACCESS, program.  PennDOT hopes to implement the restrictions eventually to cut down on what it sees as abuses of the program.  Port Authority Transit, along with some groups representing the elderly and transportation providers, argue that the new restrictions will place a severe burden on the elderly.  The Independent Regulatory Review Commission will eventually rule on the guidelines using advice from legislative committees and interest groups.

headline: Nuclear anxiety
abstract: A letter to the editor says that the most terrible legacy of the arms race is the fear that it has brought to children.  Thanks to the arms race, children now must fear a nuclear war.

headline: President Reagan addressing governors at White House
abstract: A photo depicts President Ronald Reagan addressing governors at the White House.

headline: Drug Course Backed
abstract: This editiorial examines addiction to drugs and alcohol among underage children.  The editorial argues that education courses, like the ones advocated by Representative Stanley Jarolin, should  be taught in elementary and secondary schools across Pennsylvania.  Representative Jarolin believes that accurate information, if presented on a consistent basis throughout a youngster's formative years, could provide a valuable key to breaking the cycle of underage drug and alcohol addiction.

headline: Another blow to the
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has signed legislation to tear dow the incompleted reactor number two of the Limerick Plant in Montgomery County.  There have been questions about the state's rights in cases where it feels that the public interest is not being served by a reactor.  The Public Utility Commission has already said the reactor should not be built.  Philadelphia Electric, which owns the reactor, says that tearing it down could cost a lot of money.

headline: At last, high risk
abstract: This editorial supports a new law that will allow the state to seize the assets of drug dealers; the money will be used to finance the investigation and prosecution of drug traffickers.

headline: Pennhurst case seen aiding community care
abstract: Thomas K. Gilhool, chief counsel of the Public Interest Law Center, a Washington-based organization for the handicapped, said that the decision to close the Pennhurst state center for the mentally retarded should help push the case for community-based care.  Gilhool said that closing Pennhurst means that PA has turned the corner in the trend toward deinstitutionalization and that roughly half of the 12,000 mentally retarded people in the state's social-service system are now in group homes or apartments.

headline: POW-MIAs get recognition
abstract: A Delaware County man walked from his home to the Capitol in order to present a special POW-MIA (Prisoner of War - Missing in Action) flag to Governor Dick Thornburgh.  Charles Langley, a veteran, left Upper Darby Township on July 8 and was joined by two others who took part in the trip honoring prisoners of war and Americans missing in action.  The black-and-white flag, which says "POW-MIA You Are Not Forgotten," was presented to Thornburgh at the Capitol after he signed a proclamation declaring the week "POW-MIA Recognition Week."

headline: Pressure mounts, but Caliguiri still refusing to declare for '86
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri is facing mounting pressure to announce whether or not he will run for the Democratic nomination for Governor of PA.  Caliguiri has resisted the pressure on him and statewide overtures on his behalf; he has done nothing to stop Pittsburgh area Democrats from committing to others in the governor's race.  It was widely believed that Caliguiri would run for governor after securing his third term as mayor, simply because he had nothing to lose by running.  Some of his close personal friends have indicated that he really enjoys being mayor.  Former State Auditor General Robert Casey may benefit the most if Caliguiri chooses not to run, as he is very popular in Western PA.  Casey is leaning towards picking a popular Allegheny County Democrat as his lieutenant-governor running mate.

headline: Each of us has his own preferred risks
abstract: This opinion piece looks at how various people deal with risk in their lives.  Some refuse to fly planes, but are chain smokers, while others may eat very healthily, but go hand-gliding.  Each of us assesses risk differently.  The most recent and emotional scenes of public risk-assessment are related to HIV and AIDS, with parents demonstrating outside of schools that have allowed AIDS victims to enter.  This is a prime example of how we handle and mishandle risk.  Part of the problem comes from scientists and other officials, who instead of giving promises and garuantees as some parents would like, give qualifications.  This argument will continue in two different languages, numbers and emotions, odds, and anxieties.

headline: Better do without
abstract: This letter to the editor supports Governor Dick Thornburgh's motion to ask the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to delay putting into effect the order to restart the Unit 1 reactor at Three Mile Island.  The governor wants to delay the restrat until the US Court of Appeals completes hearings on the integrity of the plant's management.  The author says that it is better to forgo the beneifts of nuclear development for the supply of electricity than to tamper with the health and life of the unborn and others.

headline: At news conference...
abstract: A picture shows Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell holding an object found in the body of MOVE member Frank James Africa.  The object was originally thought to be a bullet; the object has since been proven to be a pressure valve piece.

headline: PP&L wins OK on aiding poor
abstract: Pennsylvania Power & Light's (PP&L) $2 million Winter Relief Assistance Program--a program that helps low-income customers weatherproof their homes--was approved by the state Public Utility Commission (PUC).  This program was ordered by the PUC after PP&L's last rate increase.

headline: Reagan aides show interest in 'Star Wars' deal
abstract: Many of US President Ronald Reagan's top arms control advisers would support a trade-off with the Soviet Union that would greatly cut its nuclear missile program.  The tradeoff would mean that the US would abandon its "Star Wars" space defense system, or the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI).  However, no one knows whether Reagan would be willing to agree to such a deal, as he has been pushing for the SDI from the start and many consider it to be his baby.  Soviet premier Mikhail Gorbachev, in meeting with US Senator Robert Byrd, has indicated that he would be prepared to make radical proposals to stop the US militarization of space.  Reagan and Gorbachev are set to meet in Geneva, Switzerland in November.

headline: Primary "wide open" for Democratic rivals
abstract: A Democratic candidates' forum signaled the start of a full-scale primary battle for next spring.  After speaking to the PA Democratic Committee, four gubernatorial and two Senate candidates all said they intend to stay in the race through the May 20th Democratic primary--even if they do not receive the committee's endorsement.  Several candidates pushed for an open primary, while others pushed for an early endorsement by the party.  Candidates also began to take shots at their Republican opposition in both races.

headline: Ex-con doctor
abstract: This letter to the editor finds it deplorable that Dr. McCormick, an ex-con who spent years after his release studying to be a doctor, will be denied a state license to practice medicine because of a recent law passed by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.   The author concludes that if Dr. McCormick is qualified as a medical doctor, he should be permitted to work as one.

headline: Bill seeks new power for PUC: Could halt work on nuclear power plants
abstract: A bill was filed in the state House that would grant the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) the authority to halt construction of nuclear power facilities.  The article also does a roundup of other bills proposed by Philadelphia-area congressmen.

headline: Automation for courts part of plan
abstract: The state Supreme Court, through a steering committee appointed by Chief Justice Robert C. Nix Jr., has requested a study that would automate the courts and bring them into the 21st century.  Funds for the initial phase of the long-range program have been appropriated in the Legislature's 1985-86 budget.

headline: Reprieve for elderly transit
abstract: An editorial states that PA Transportation Secretary Thomas Larson acted prudently in postponing the implementation of proposed rule changes to door-to-door transit service for elderly Pennsylvanians.  Under the current proposal, the state pays 90% of the fare, with elderly users and sometimes third parties paying the remaining 10%.  The editorial also argues against some of the changes, such as denying service to elderly who aren't handicapped and live within a quarter mile of public transportation.

headline: Reagan Presses Hill On MX Production: GOP Senators Seek Spending Compromise
abstract: President Ronald Reagan is putting pressure on US Congress to approve continued production of MX missiles so that the US can have more negotiating power with the Soviet Union on arms reductions.  US House Democrats and Republicans are split on defense spending and are seeking a compromise with domestic spending cuts.

headline: Primary importance: Crossed judicial races, library tax make vote vital
abstract: This editorial urges readers to vote, as there are a number of significant contests in the May 21st primary election.  Voters will select three candidates for judge of the Superior Court.  Voters in Dauphin County also will vote on a special two-mill tax to help support the county library system.

headline: General Hospitals
abstract: This editorial looks at the divestiture of PA's state-owned, community general hospitals to local governments--a transition that should have occurred a long time ago.  Coal-region communities have often fought attempts at state divestiture, in part because of patronage jobs that the hospitals provided in areas of chronic high unemployment.  If these hospitals are to survive, they will need imaginative and aggressive leadership at the local level.

headline: Bit of radioactive steam released at TMI
abstract: A "minute" amount of radioactivity was released on December 1, 1985, when the Unit 1 reactor at Three Mile Island shut down automatically after a malfunction in its electrical generator.  Officials of GPU Nuclear Corporation, which operates TMI, determined that a relay device malfunctioned and shut down the generator.  This event triggered the automatic shutdown of the reactor, resulting in a brief release of steam from the plant's main steam safety valve.  The steam contained around 0.033% of the limit of 10 millirems, according to GPU Nuclear.

headline: Better deal than CTA's was offered, court told
abstract: Charles E. Collins, a former Pittsburgh Arthur Young and Company official, testified before a federal jury in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery-conspiracy trial.  Collins testified that he persistently and unsuccessfully tried to win a data-processing contract from the state Treasury Department.  CTA won the contract to recover Social Security tax refunds for public school employees for $4.8 million.

headline: Scranton urges changes in human services system
abstract: Lieutenant Governor William Scranton, speaking yesterday at the Women's Agenda statewide conference in Hershey, said that PA's human-services systems has to undergo compelling changes in the years ahead.  Scranton emphasized that the human services system must not only care for people, but empower them to deal with their own problems.  Scranton pointed out several economic and demographic trends in the state that will have a significant impact on the future of PA's human services-system.

headline: Service in Vietnam linked to cancer for the first time.
abstract: An inconclusive study, which traced the medical histories of veterans longer than any previous study, suggests for the first time that there is a link between increased risk of cancer and service in Vietnam.  The study found a disproportionate number of deaths from rare soft-tissue cancers among Vietnam veterans.  The study seems to corroborate suspicions that cancer may have been caused by dioxin, a residue of Agent Orange, which was used extensively in Vietnam.

headline: Public campaign financing backed
abstract: Sponsors of legislation to revamp campaign finance laws believe that a long federal investigation into the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) scandal will erode Republican opposition to campaig-finance reforms.  State Representative Tom Michlovic presented a bill to establish a voluntary program of partial public funding for statewide, non-judicial campaigns; he also encouraged candidates to seek smaller contributions.  A similar bill for judicial campaigns was introduced by State Representative Allen Kukovich.  Though both bills face an uncertain future, they are getting support from several interest groups.

headline: Give Shamokin same deal
abstract: Editorial argues that Shamokin State General Hospital should receive the same up-front money from the state that Connellsville did when they transitioned their hospital from the state hospital system to a private hospital.  Why should Shamokin State General Hospital settle for $500,000 when Connellsville received $4 million?  The editorial questions what leverage or political clout that Connellsville holds over the Commonwealth to get such a lucrative grant, especially when circumstances at the two hospitals are similar.  The trustees of the Shamokin hospital should meet with PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to ask for a similar financial arrangement.

headline: Boosting the salaries of Public
abstract: PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) member Bill Shane believes that boosting the salaries of PUC members to attract better qualified commissioners is the most needed reform of the agency.  Shane also believes it would be "absurd" to reduce commissioners' terms from ten years to four years, a reform which is supported by consumer groups and endorsed by the PA House.  Shane opposes the election of PUC commissioners, who are currently appointed by the PA Governor.  He believes that elections would be "a field day for the wet-fingered politicians".

headline: Bill would mandate foster-care reviews
abstract: Senator Stewart Greenleaf and Representative David Sweet are introducing legislation that would mandate periodic court reviews of cases that involve children placed in foster homes or institutional care.  The ultimate goal of the legislation is to find a permanent home for each of the state's 11,500 dependent children, Greenleaf said.

headline: State turns down food for needy
abstract: The PA  Agriculture Department declined a federal program that would offer free federal cheese and butter to local agencies for distribution.  A spokesman for the Agriculture Department said the state declined the food because of doubt about federal funding to pay administrative, transportation, and storage costs of the program.  The PA Coalition on Food and Nutrition says that PA was too cautious and failed to seek alternatives o the federal funds.  The Temporary Emergency Food Assistance Program was begun in February 1982 and set to expire September 30 of this year.  The program provides surplus commodities to people who qualify for other assistance programs.  A number of states have reacted cautiously about the lack of federal money for the program, while others are more optimistic.

headline: State VFW, Legion to convene: Vets' groups to discuss proposed VA medical cutback
abstract: The state departments of the American Legion and the Veterans of Foreign Wars are holding their annual meetings and will discuss proposed cuts in Veterans Administration medical services.  Leaders of both organizations feel that a crisis point is being reached on medical benefits, and the groups are seeking to take action.  Article also discusses other veterans issues from around the state.

headline: Ready to Walk, State Workers Say
abstract: State workers in the PA Social Services Union, the American Federation of State, County, and Municpal Employees, and other unions have formed a coalition called the State Workers United for Fairness; they have threatened to go on strike if their demands are not met by the state.  The state wants to reduce sick pay and vacation leave and has offered a series of raises totaling 6 percent over three years.  The workers have asked for a one-year contract providing for a 7.5 percent in pay increases.

headline: Governor offers proposal to curb health-care costs
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh yesterday proposed a four-point program to control escalating health care costs, including a temporary cap on capital expenditures for hospitals.  Though health care increases have slowed recently, Thornburgh said action was necessary because those increases still were more than double the rate of inflation.  Thornburgh called on the PA General Assembly to give swift approval to all four proposals.  Thornburgh acknowledged that his proposals did not include more stringent cost-control proposals that had been recommended in a task force report presented to him more than two years ago.  Thornburgh rejected the report, which called for the creation of a state board to regulate hospital costs and expenditures and establish a uniform payment system similar to the one in New Jersey.

headline: Chairman Palladino writes: NRC is not rushing TMI issue
abstract: Nunzio Palladino, Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, writes a letter to the editor defending the activities of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in its efforts to protect the safety of the public and the workers at Three Mile Island.  He says that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is committed to safety and will not allow Unit 1 to be restarted if it compromises public saftey.

headline: Bills deserve passage
abstract: This editorial argues for the passage of two bills that currently confront the PA General Assembly.  The first is a PA State House bill that would improve enforcement of child support orders.  The second bill, which would amend the state constitution, would provide the state with the right to demand a jury trial in criminal cases; the law is designed to lower the number of compromise verdicts and sentences.

headline: State action cuts food for needy, groups say
abstract: Community group leaders meeting in Homestead say that the PA Department of Agriculture has short-changed the needy by refusing to accept foodstuffs under the federal cheese and butter program.  The result is a severe cut in supplies across PA that began to be felt last month and will continue into December.  The state declined more than 7.5 million pounds of free dairy products under the federal program because state officials worried they would have no assurance that it would be reimbursed for warehousing expenses.  State officials argued that food agencies should direct their lobbying efforts toward the Allegheny County commissioners, not the PA Department of Agriculture.

headline: State's veterans deserve more help
abstract: An editorial believes that PA State Representative Richard Kasunic's proposal to create a cabinet-level agency that would be responsible for providing PA's 1.75 million veterans with services and information could be a reasonable answer to better serving PA's veterans.  Kasunic believes that federal offices for veterans in the state are overworked and understaffed.

headline: Reagan no magic for GOP senators up for re-election
abstract: The 19 Republican US Senators up for re-election next year are putting some distance between themselves and US President Ronald Reagan.  In contrast to Republican Senators whose terms will run longer, they have voted contrary to Reagan's wishes twice as often in this session of Congress.  While Reagan himself is very popular, his policies are not, and a loss of only four seats in the Senate would give Democrats complete control of Congress.  Opposing Reagan can have both its risks and benefits, as US Senator Arlen Specter, who has become a target of both Democrats and conservative Republicans, has discovered.

headline: Head-injury research halt at Penn appears warranted
abstract: US Health and Human Services Secretary Margaret M. Heckler suspended an annual $1 million federal grant for head-injury experiments on baboons at the University of Pennsylvania, citing "serious concerns" about procedures and personnel training and supervision in Penn's labs.  Heckler's concerns were based on a four-month review by the National Institutes of Health that found favor with the scientific merits of the Penn research, but did not approve of the care and use of laboratory animals.  This editorial supports the suspension of the grants and hopes that it will encourage Penn to review its research methods and make the necessary changes.

headline: Clean-up worker is contaminated
abstract: A clean-up worker at Three Mile Island (TMI) was contaminated Friday, March 22, 1984, with low levels of radiation.  The worker accidentally brushed his face with his protective hood after working in the auxiliary building.  The worker was not harmed and alarms signaled that low-levels of radiation had been released in the building.  Friday's incident was the 45th time a TMI employee had suffered minor skin contamination.

headline: Boston lawyer aids Dwyer employees
abstract: PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer has hired Maurice Flynn, a Boston-based former federal prosecutor, to advise his aides in their dealings with the grand jury investigating the Computer Technology Associates bribery scheme.  Flynn is being flown in from Boston and paid at the taxypayers' expense; Dwyer feels this is justified because state Treasury officials are entilted to legal counsel on Treasury matters.  Dwyer, however, has his own legal counsel, as he is believed to be the focus of the continuing grand jury investigation.  There is no state law which restricts the hiring of legal counsel so long as their advice is related to official duties of government personnel; it is unclear whether there is precedent for Flynn's hiring

headline: State must pay for food stamps
abstract: Federal Judge Sylvia H. Rambo ruled that PA must reimburse the US government for more than $500,000 worth of improperly issued food stamps.

headline: Veterans' Caucus Rejects Arlen
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter was recently denied access to a congressional caucus of Vietnam-era veterans, due to the fact that he never served in the Vietnam War.  Specter said there is nothing unusual about him trying to join the group, which meets periodically to discuss legislation relating to Vietnam veterans.

headline: Record is Deceiving
abstract: An editorial attacks the process of "ghost voting"--a process in which a member of the PA Legislature jams a paper clip to their electronic voting device to cast a vote when they are not in the PA House chamber.  The electronic voting system in the General Assembly continues to be abused because neither branch is inclined to enforce the rules against "ghost voting."  This practice hurts politicians' credibility with constituents, who cannot be certain now if their representative was actually present for a vote.  A recorded vote also entitles the member to $75 for staying in Harrisburg to vote.  The editorial concludes that a legislative body that relies on deceit does not easily gain the confidence of the public.

headline: Health program gets U.S. approval
abstract: The US Department of Health and Human Services gave its conditional approval to an experimental prepaid health-care program that will serve about 100,000 needy people in South and West Philadelphia.  Federal approval was necessary because the program will serve as a subsitute for the Medicaid program, which is partially funded by the federal government.  The program will involve a two-year contract with HealthAmerica, which will subcontract with doctors, hospitals, and other health providers who will deliver the health services.

headline: Conrail President Stuart
abstract: In a speech Thursday to members of the Cincinnati Coal Exchange, Conrail President Stuart Reed said that selling Conrail to Norfolk Southern Corporation would inhibit competition in the railroad industry--competition made possible by the regulatory freedoms of the Staggers Act of 1980. Reed also said that Conrail's competitive pricing programs, made possible by the Staggers Act, help coal producers market their products here and abroad.

headline: Bradley re-elected president judge
abstract: Common Please Court Judge Edward Bradley was re-elected to a third term as president judge.  Bradley has been a Common Please Court judge since 1965 and president judge since 1975.  Bradley received significant support from Philadelphia's political leaders.

headline: State seeks US approval of new emergency-room fee
abstract: Officials of the state Department of Public Welfare are seeking federal approval for a unique and controversial fee system designed to keep welfare patients from going to emergency rooms for routine medical care.  Under the proposal, a welfare recipient who went to a hospital emergency room in a non-emergency situation would have to pay a $2 fee, double the normal $1 charge.  The higher fees, which are supported by the Hospital Association of PA, are designed to discourage welfare recipients from using emergency rooms and to encourage the use of less costly services, such as outpatient clinics.

headline: Yard gets a 'well done' for Forrestal work
abstract: The aircraft carrier Forrestal, having undergone a massive overhaul at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, passed its Navy sea trials.  The success of the Forrestal work--which had been considered the key to the yard's retaining overhaul work through the end of this century--was announced by Captain Pack Willimon, acting commander of the yard.

headline: Reeher is given $84,900 salary
abstract: After the PHEAA board of directors sidestepped legal obstacles to give him a $10,000 raise, Kenneth Reeher, the head of the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency, became the highest-paid official in state government.  Governor Dick Thornburgh criticized the move, but the board defended it, and said it was necessary to keep Reeher from moving to the private sector.

headline: Heinz:  Many patients released prematurely
abstract: US Senator John Heinz claims that thousands of elderly patients have been discharged prematurely from US hospitals because of revised Medicare regulations.  The US Department of Health and Human Services revised Medicare rules in October 1983 to give hospitals and other medical facilites a financial incentive to discharge patients early, though the department retained the authority to deny payments to hospitals that abused the system by sending patients home before they were well.

headline: Consumer champion Johnson leaving PUC
abstract: Michael Johnson is retiring from the Public Utility Commission but does not plan on staying quiet about utility companies.  Many feel that Johnson was the best voice for consumers that the state had on the commission.

headline: Bribe case hearing set
abstract: A hearing on motions to unseal a list of unindicted co-conspirators in an alleged state contract bribery scheme was postponed.  The Patriot-News Company and Philadelphia Newspapers Incorporated have petitioned to have the list of names unsealed.

headline: State should help poor with heating assistance
abstract: This editorial argues that state funds are needed for heating assistance.  Governor Dick Thornburgh used a line item veto to eliminate an $11 million appropriation in the 1985 budget; some of this money would have been used to help the poor with heating assistance.  PA relies overwhelmingly on federal money for heating and utility assistance.  The editorial urges Governor Thornburgh to use some of the surplus funds to help the poor with heating.

headline: Yard Hopes To Cut Loss To 512 Jobs
abstract: Philadelphia Naval Shipyard officials hope that no more than 512 full-time workers will be laid off because of a Pentagon-ordered 9.8% reduction in the yard's work force.  A spokesperson for the Philadelphia yard said resignations, retirements and the layoffs of temporary workers will produce the bulk of the cutbacks, and that the worst-case scenario would be losing 512 full-time employees through involuntary RIF's (reductions in force).

headline: Regressive State Lotteries
abstract: This editorial says that the state lottery should be considered a regressive tax because lotteries are supported overwhelmingly by the poor.  The editorial argues against creating a national lottery.

headline: Homeless react with shock, disbelief
abstract: Velma Carter, a mental health clinician and supervisor for The Consortium, a mental health services agency, set up shop in a converted recreation center in Philadelphia.  Carter says that her agency is working with people who lost their homes in the Osage-Avenue fire.  Osage Avenue burned after a police standoff with the back-to-nature cult MOVE.

headline: Countdown
abstract: This letter to the editor looks at the exact dates of the accident at Three Mile Island (TMI) Unit 2 and the restart of TMI Unit 1; it also looks at the signifcance of those dates and the numbers associated with them.  The author believes that it is important to think about these numbers.

headline: Buckingham prepares for retirement: Judge says York County still needs family court
abstract: York County Judge James C. Buckingham must retire on October 19, 1985 because he will reach the mandatory retirment age of 70 for judges.  Buckingham campaigned on the need for a family court in York County.  Buckingham thinks that York County should continue to have a family court after he leaves.  The article describes the highlights of Buckingham's career.

headline: State to get food aid
abstract: Federal agriculture officials said yesterday that they would make some additional food available to Pennsylvania, which last summer quietly turned down 203 truckloads of free cheese, butter, and other items that would have been given to the needy around Christmas.  A source in US Senator Arlen Specter's offices said that the US Department of Agriculture might be able to send 50 truckloads of cheese to Pennsylvania--half the amount to which the state was entitled.  Governor Thornburgh yesterday requested additional food, and said the decision to turn down deliveries for October and November was made by an unnamed official, who the governor said acted without prior consultation from his office.  Further information is given about the federal food program and other states that have also rejected it.

headline: null
abstract: A photo depicts a tornado funnel cloud touching down near Wheatland, Mercer County, on Friday May 31.  Vice President George Bush toured Wheatland yesterday to inspect damage.  Wheatland is one of the towns hit hardest by the tornadoes.

headline: Rendell says it's no secret he'll run for governor
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell, at a fund-raising dinner sponsored by the Northampton County Democratic Society, said that it's only a matter of time until he formally announces his candidacy for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination.  Rendell has not officially announced his candidacy because Philadelphia's charter prohibits him from doing so while he is still the city's district attorney.

headline: Hospital aid may result in other cuts
abstract: PA Health Department officials say a special $750,000 allocation to St. Christopher's Hospital for Children will force cuts in some maternal and child-care programs.  Due to the fact that a $13 million federal block grant for prenatal medical programs has not been increased, other programs funded through the block grant had to be cut.  The possibility of cuts in the maternal and child-care programs has Philadelphia health officials concerned, as the programs serve roughly 10,000 women a year.

headline: Court halts TMI start-up pending June 27 hearing
abstract: Just hours after workers began heating up the plant in preparation for resuming operations, a federal appeals court blocked the start-up of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor.  The three-judge panel in Philadelphia unanimously ordered that the reactor remain dormant until the court decides whether the Nuclear Regulatory Commission was correct when it authorized the restart.  Attorneys for the Commonwealth of PA, two citizens' groups and a Coatesville couple had petitioned the Third US Circuit Court of Appeals to prohibit Unit 1 from starting up, saying there was no guarantee that the reactor could be operated safely.

headline: Cap on State's Liability Upheld
abstract: The Commonwealth Court upheld the constitutionality of a state law that places a $250,000 cap on the damages a person can collect in negligence suits against the state.

headline: Surplus Food Mixups
abstract: This editorial calls the handling of surplus food by the Thornburgh administration reflective of a disturbing lack of concern for the needs of the poor in Pennsylvania.  The PA Department of Agriculture recently refused 86 truckloads of surplus food from the federal government, despite the fact that the unemployment rate in PA is far above the national average in several parts of the state.  This rejection is compounded by the callous decision during the summer to refuse 200 truck loads of surplus food for October or November; Governor Thornburgh did request a shipment and received a few dozen truckloads, however.  The US General Accounting Office has also found widespread mismanagement of the surplus food in PA.  The editorial concludes that the Thornburgh administration is supposed to serve as a conduit between bulging warehouses of surplus food and the poor who need it, and the administration has been failing at that job.

headline: 5 people die, more than 50 hurt: Upstate areas reel from killer storm
abstract: A vicious tornado that struck the upstate area killed five people and left more than 50 injured in Lycoming County, Union County, and Northumberland County.  Emergency service officials estimated damage in the millions of dollars.

headline: Rendell stepped in: How the Democrats almost had a 'delegate-gate'
abstract: A bizarre episode in the 1984 Democratic nomination fight conceivably could have cost Walter Mondale the Democratic nomination.  Days before the PA primary in 1984, a volunteer lawyer for Mondale surreptitiously seized records being kept of activities of the PA At-Large Delegate Committee for Mondale; the records were returned only when the head of the at-large committee, District Attorney Ed Rendell, demanded the records be sent back.  Rendell says that if the incident had ever come out in the media, it could have crushed Mondale's chances of getting the nomination.

headline: House Approves Sunset Bills
abstract: Legislation approved by the PA House will maintain the five boards that oversee health care professionals in the state.  The legislation contains new provisions for dealing with osteopaths, podiatrists, and nurses with drug or alcohol problems, and gives discretion to boards overseeing osteopaths and nurses to license applicants who have been convicted of a drug-related felony.

headline: Court lifts its stay on Limerick 1
abstract: The Third US Circuit Court of Appeals yesterday lifted its temporary stay against full-power testing at Unit 1 of the Limerick nuclear power plant.  The court also denied the request for a longer stay by Limerick Ecology Action and the inmates of Graterford Prison.  Both groups were concerned with the safety of the plant and the potential consequences of radiation leaks and/or core meltdowns.  The two groups now await a Nuclear Regulatory Commission appeals board meeting on the groups safety concerns.  Philadelphia Electric Company told the court that a prolonged shutdown could cost the company money and force it to lay off employees.  Now, Philadelphia Electric Co. must focus on finding enough cooling water to complete its testing.

headline: Charges multiply for MOVE man
abstract: Mo Africa, a MOVE member, appeared in court July 3.  Prosecuters allege that he assaulted a police officer and threatened the same officer at a hearing nine days after the alleged assualt.  Prosecutors also allege that he threated a Common Pleas Court jury on May 7.  If convicted of all charges, Africa could face up to 22 years in prison.

headline: The poor need state help to pay their heating bills
abstract: A bill was introduced in the state House of Representatives that would commit state funds to assisting the poor who are unable to pay their heating bills.  This editorial believes this is necessary but cautions using the surplus for this.  Instead it should be part of the regular budget and surplus funds should be used as seed money for tax reform.

headline: Bell of Pa. says time has come to meter local calls
abstract: Bell Telephone Company of PA is seeking permission from the PA Public Utility Commission to  adopt a plan that would charge callers for how long they stay on the telephone; the plan would also increase by 60% the cost of flat-rate service.  The PA office of the state consumer advocate opposes the plan and believes it will hurt the elderly and handicapped.  Bell also would like to make its per-call charges more sensitive to distance within regional calling areas.  Business Users Group, which represents Scott Paper Company, Bethlehem Steel Corp., and the PA Retailers Association, also opposes the plan.

headline: Rep. Edgar Starting War Chest
abstract: US Representative Bob Edgar has begun fundraising to amass the $5 million he thinks is needed for a 1986 Senate race against Republican Senator Arlen Specter.  Edgar already has about $60,000, while Specter has already raised $600,000.

headline: House Oks Crackdown On Bad Drs.
abstract: The state House approved a bill that enables the state Board of Medical Education and Licensure to suspend immediately the medical license of a doctor it considers dangerous to the public.  The bill is expected to pass the Senate without opposition and will be sent to Governor Thornburgh for his signature.  The state medical board must currently go through a lengthy hearing process to discipline doctors.

headline: Court stays license for Limerick 1: Would halt testing at full power
abstract: The US Court of Appeals in Philadelphia ordered a temporary stay of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's decision to grant a full-power operating license to Unit 1 of the Limerick nuclear power plant.  The stay was granted in response to a pair of appeals filed after the NRC voted to approve full-power licensing.  The appeals were filed by Limerick Ecology Action and inmates at Graterford Prison.  Both lawsuits argued that full power operation creates an enormous public health and safety risk.  However, the stay could be lifted soon if the judges decide that operation of the plant is not causing irreparable harm to the public.

headline: Chester Balks on MOVE Info
abstract: Chester city officials yesterday refused to turn over their records to Philadelphia Authorities. Also, Chester City Solicitor Edward Zetusky questioned whether the Philadelphia Special Investigations Commission, formed by Philadelphia Mayor Goode to investigate the May 13, 1985 MOVE incident, had the authority to subpeonea witnesses or documents outside Philadelphia County.  The commission would like to obtain records from a Chester police raid on a MOVE "safe-house," which occurred on the same day that 11 people died and 61 homes were destroyed or damaged in a MOVE confrontation with the Philadelphia police.  Chester police have joined the Philadelphia Fraternal Order of Police in refusing to testify "voluntarily" before the MOVE commission.  The police fear legal action.

headline: The state has bungled the food program
abstract: A letter to the editor, written by PA State Representative Allen Kukovich, criticizes the adminstration of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and the state Department of Agriculture for their mishandling of a federal program that gives surplus food to the poor.  The author is particularly unhappy that the PA House has been unable to pinpoint who is responsible for rejecting 289 truckloads of food slated for Pennsylvania.  Kukovich cites an investigation by the US General Accounting Office into PA's mismanagement of the surplus-food program as evidence that the current program is deficient.  Kukovich concludes that the most reasonable way to make sure the hungry are fed is to take the operation of the program away from the PA Department of Agriculture and give it to a special commission whose sole function would be to oversee the surplus-food distribution.

headline: Bell rates should be cut, advocate contends
abstract: PA Office of the Consumer Advocate Secretary David M. Barasch said that Bell of Pennsylvania should be denied all of its recent request to raise its rates by $325 million a year; hea also said that the company should be required to cut its rates by $36 million.  In filing with the state Public Utility Commission, Barasch accused Bell of including in its request millions of dollars in charges that other government agencies have ruled cannot be included in its rates.

headline: Rep. Friend Defends Position on MOVE
abstract: A letter to the editor from state Representative Stephen F. Freind defends his position that the state should not help to pay for the victims of the MOVE tragedy.  Freind believes that the City of Philadelphia was responsible for the tragedy, so the city should pay, not taxpayers from the rest of the state.

headline: Labor attacking health costs
abstract: The American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO) launched an effort to control medical costs through disease prevention and early detection of illnesses.  THis editorial is encouraged by the actions of the AFL-CIO and argues that something needs to be done to reign in rising healthcare costs.

headline: Court Upholds Conviction of Former TMI Supervisor
abstract: The conviction of former Three Mile Island (TMI) supervisor James Floyd--who was convicted of making false statements to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission--has been upheld by the US 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.  Floyd was the Operations Supervisor at TMI when the Unit 2 nuclear reactor was crippled in March 1979.  Floyd was convicted in November of 1984 for cheating on a federally required re-licensing exam.

headline: Child bill awaits pen of governor
abstract: Legislation that would require immediate police investigations of missing-children reports was approved unanimously by the state Senate.  The legislation was sent to Governor Dick Thornburgh.  This legislation stems from reports that as many as 150,000 children disappear each year without a trace.

headline: Unwilling guest of Pa. looks to freedom
abstract: This article describes how Carolyn Clark, a mildly retarded woman who was institutionalized at Laurelton Center for 28 years, fell through the cracks of the state system.  The Laurelton Center staff recommended her release, and several laws were passed that should have granted her case a review.  Due to bickering between the state and county, she never received a review.  In 1981, Clark got a lawyer and her case is currently being reviewed. The article says that Carolyn Clark is just one of the many people who were institutionalized and fell through the cracks.

headline: Bell to ask $325 million hike
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania is planning to ask the state Public Utility Commission (PUC) for a $325 million rate increase.  Company leaders say the increase is necessary because of increased operating costs, a shortfall between the amount the PUC has authorized Bell to earn and what it is actually earning, and changes in Federal Communications Commission rules that have cut depreciation allowances.  Most of the increases will come from increases in the cost of basic local service.

headline: Rep. Letterman Plans To Seek Re-Election In 1986
abstract: PA State Representative Russell P. Letterman of Milesburg plans to seek re-election next year to the post he has held since 1970, but said he is not sure he can support Bill Wachob, a fellow Democrat, if he chooses to run against US Congressman Bill Clinger in 1986.  Although Letterman and Wachob are in the same party, Letterman is more conservative, and said that Wachob would have to change some of his views before Letterman will support him.  Clinger has been very helpful to Letterman's district, recently getting $1 million in Economic Development Administration money and assisting in getting money to rebuild and renovate the branch line from Mill Hall to Energy Industries.

headline: Legislation Would Extend Medical Licensure Board
abstract: A measure that would keep the PA Board of Medical Education and Licensure in operation also makes changes to how doctors are regulated.  The bill, which passed the PA House, requires medical residents to complete two-year residencies before they are allowed to take their licensing exams.  The bill also deals with the licensure of doctors.

headline: Customers must pay for shut reactors
abstract: A divided state Commonwealth Court ruled 4-3 that two Western PA electric utilities can charge customers for $45 million in costs incurred by canceled nuclear power plants.  The ruling upheld a 1983 Public Utility Commission order allowing Duquesne Light Company and PA Power Company to recover over 10 years their $45 million investment in four Ohio atomic facilities that were canceled following the 1979 Three Mile Island accident.  The state consumer advocate challenged the PUC decision--arguing that a 1982 state law forbids including power plant construction costs in rates until the plant provides power.

headline: Child-abuse politics
abstract: This editorial discusses problems with a child-abuse bill pased by the state Legislature.  The author urges the state Senate to consider a new bill that fixes those problems and repeals the earlier bill.  The editorial says that Legislators need to fix the problems in child-abuse bills; they need to concentrate on the main problem of prosecuting child abusers.

headline: Victims still burning from MOVE flames
abstract: A May 13 fire destroyed 61 housees around Osage Avenue during a confrontation between Philadelphia police and the radical group MOVE.  Clifford Bond, a former resident of the block, is a community organizer who wants the residents to be able to control the $1.8 million collected for them.  The money, donated city-wide, is supposed to be combined into one fund today, and the American Red Cross has been overseeing the collection.

headline: Better alert needed for killer tornadoes
abstract: This editorial says that there should be a better warning system in place for tornadoes.  Such a warning system would give people a chance to protect themselves from tornadoes, such as the ones that killed 62 people in Pennsylvania on May 31.

headline: Republicans walk out in vote recount dispute
abstract: Bitter Republicans walked out as the US House Administration Committee recommended that the Democratic candidate, Frank McCLoskey, be seated in a disputed Indiana congressional election on the basis of a four-vote recount win.  The Republicans failed to have the 8th District seat declared vacant so Republican Governor Robert Orr could call a special election.

headline: Licensing of homes a paper tiger
abstract: A review by The Pittsburgh Press found that state licensing for personal-care homes may be falling short of its original goal of protecting residents.  The article describes state licensing as a "paper tiger" and provides examples of where it does not work.

headline: Debate focuses on bill putting PUC over N-power firms
abstract: Opponents and supporters of state House Bill 838, legislation that would require approval by the state Public Utility Commission for the construction or restart of nuclear power plants, testified before a House Consumer Affairs Subcommittee on Public Utilities.  Supporters of the bill argue that the state must have more control over its own destiny.  Opponents say the bill would be in violation of the 14th Amendment and the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution.

headline: Children and the courts
abstract: This editorial praises PA Senate Bill 176, which protects children by allowing them to testify on video tape in sexual abuse cases.  THe author also complains that the bill permits the use of hearsay evidence in child sexual-abuse cases.  The author argues that the use of hearsay evidence is best left to the discretion of the judge.

headline: Welfare board gets criticism during review
abstract: A study by the PA Legislative Budget and Finance Committee yesterday gave poor performance grades to the PA Board of Public Welfare, saying that the board was not effectively carrying out its duties, and that its abolition would not endanger public heath or safety.  However, Richard Dario, the committee chairman, added that termination of the board would remove "a potentially valuable source of public input" on Department of Public Welfare policies.

headline: Censoring cable
abstract: This editorial looks at the recent wave of censorship that has been aimed at pornography on cable television.  The editorial is disheartened by the fact that PA State Senator Mike Fisher, who is usually level-headed, is inclined to lead this attack by sponsoring legislation that would use criminal penalties to restrict the showing of sexually explicit material on cable television.  The editorial points to the fact that subscription to cable television is voluntary, and that subscribers are free to cancel specific channels they find offensive.  Though it is likely that the Fisher bill, if enacted, will eventually be declared unconstitutional by a court, the editorial believes that state legislators should defeat this mischevious legislation before it reaches the courts.

headline: Senate-printed Salvatore newsletter scrapped because of donation appeal
abstract: A four-page newsletter from state Senator Frank A Salvatore to 60,000 of his constituents had to be scrapped and reprinted because of a request for a small contribution to help pay for the newsletter.  The state pays for each senator to mail up to 100,000 newsletters each year and this was not mentioned in the request.  Salvatore apologized for the misunderstanding and printed a revised copy of the newsletter.

headline: Mail Order Drugs: A Logical Extension
abstract: This editorial supports a bill in the state legislature that would enable low-income senior citizens to buy state-stubsidized prescription drugs over the counter and through the mail.  Eligible individuals will pay only the first $4 for a prescription, and the rest of the cost will be met by the State Lottery Fund.  The editorial urges Governor Dick Thornburgh to sign the legislation into law.

headline: Decline of coal in state has industry digging for answers
abstract: PA's coal indsutry, which played a major role in shaping the state's history and economic development, is in horrible shape.  The past decade shows production and employment at their lowest levels in a century.  Coal executives and industry analysts say the decline in PA coal production stems from a variety of factors, including the recent worldwide recession, reduced steelmaking, decreased demand for PA's medium and high-sulfur coal, growing competition from Western and foreign coal suppliers, and government red tape.

headline: Clergy backs Goode
abstract: The Black Clergy of Philadelphia called the outcome of the city's efforts to oust the radical group MOVE "tragic," but said it unanimously supported Mayor Wilson Goode's handling of the situation.  The clergy have fixed the next two Sundays as Cobbs Creek Community Emergency Fund Days to raise money for those left homeless by the events.  The attack on MOVE occurred Monday, May 13, in a predominantly black, middle-class, West Philadelphia neighborhood.

headline: Workfare Must Replace Welfare
abstract: This editorial agrees with a recent column in the New York Times arguing against a plan by US President Ronald Reagan to cut back federal welfare work funding.  The editorial believes that the primary purpose of workfare is not to save money, but to encourage people on the riverbottom of American society to move into the mainstream.  Given the huge amounts of money that the federal government has spent on welfare, it seems logical to spend more modest amounts on workfare.

headline: Funding sought for improved flood forecasting system
abstract: US Representative George Gekas has reviewed the $5 million Flood Forecasting System Improvement Program proposal by the Susquehanna River Basin Commission; Gekas has agreed to pursue funding and implementation of the program.  If implemented, the program would enhance the ability of the National Weather Service to give more timely and accurate flood warnings to communities in the river basin.

headline: Senators gathering record war chests
abstract: According to a study released by Common Cause, thirty one senators up for re-election in 1986 gathered $20 million in campaign funds in the first half of 1985.  Common Cause believes the campaign funding system is out of control.  On average, according to the study, 31 incumbents raised $645,442 during the first half of the year.  US Senator Robert Packwood, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, raised more than $2.65 million.

headline: Medical ethics
abstract: The Pennsylvania Chiropractic Society (PCS) endorses Senate Bill 541--The Health Care Professional Reporting Act--because the legislation will give professional organizations a way to prove their responsiveness to consumer demand.

headline: Delaying tactic
abstract: This editorial looks at the actions of those who oppose a restart of the Three Mile Island Unit-1 Reactor.  Anti-nuclear groups are asking PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to order the PA Emergency Management Agency to withdrawal plans to evacuate people in the event of an accident; opponents have also asked Dauphin County commissioners to withdraw similar plans.  Nuclear plants are required to have an approved emergency plan in order to operate, and the anti-nuclear groups are following the path of New York State and Suffolk County officials who refused to participate in emergency planning for the Shoreham Nuclear Plant.  The editorial believes that the two situations in New York and PA are totally different and that substantial sums of money and manpower have been put into the PA emergency planning effort.  In a desperate rush to find a new defensive line against the restart, nuclear opponents should resist this strategy, as it can be a public danger in its own right.

headline: Commission pathologist cites a litany of errors by city
abstract: Nationally renowned forensic expert Ali Hameli testified yesterday before the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission.  Hameli testified that he was very disappointed in several lapses by the Philadelphia medical examiner's office.  The medical examiner had failed to maintain proper refrigeration of the bodies of MOVE members, causing them to deteriorate faster than they had to.  The medical examiner also did not properly identify the 11 MOVE victims; Hameli also said that his team found metal fragments in three bodies that were consistent with shotgun buckshot, which goes against the city's claim of having found no evidence of bullets.  A list of failures that Hameli found in the medical examiner's office is also included in the article.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: A photo depicts residents of the 6200 blocks of Osage Avenue and Pine Street in West Philadelphia taking turns breaking ground for their new homes.  The residents' homes were destroyed in the MOVE seige and the ensuing fire.  The ceremonies, over which Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode presided, began the city's $5 million-plus program to rebuild the 61 houses as quickly as possible.

headline: Growing piracy prompts new state law: TV is new 'love object'
abstract: A new law went into effect that regulates illegal cable and gives cable operators more muscle to get court action.  This law can be confusing unless the cable operator directly lays out what a cable customer can and cannot do.  This opinion piece is in favor of the law, and notes that as long as there is pirating of cable TV signals, the honest customer is going to be paying for the service he or she receives and for the service that is being stolen.

headline: Shuster wealthiest of district's congressmen
abstract: According to state House financial disclosure records, Representative Bud Shuster appears to be the wealthiest of Western PA's congressmen.  Shuster has personal holdings worth at least between $355,000 and $1.3 million.  The article also details the financials of other Western PA members of Congress.

headline: Melnick Gets Stay Of Probe by Board
abstract: A Commonwealth Court judge has temporarily halted state medical board proceedings against Dr. Joseph Melnick, who the board alleges violated state medical standards while treating a 13-year-old abortion patient and her child.  The petition by Melnick contends that medical board proceedings against him should be halted until criminal charges are resolved.  The judge agreed that allowing medial board proceedings to continue concurrently with criminal proceedings unconstitutionally forces Melnick to choose to forgo either his right to remain silent or his obligation to respond to the medical board's citation.

headline: Earnings of PE dip in quarter
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Company (PE) reported lower third quarter earnings yesterday--citing a one-time charge of 20 cents a share that stemmed from an order of the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC).  The charge resulted from a PUC order last week that forced PE to absorb $73.3 million in replacement power costs during 1983 and 1984.  The PUC ruled that PE could not recover the $73.3 million in replacement power costs incurred when the company's Salem 1 nuclear power plant was out of service.  This was the largest disallowance in the state's history, and it forced PE to charge the money lost against earnings.  PE plans to appeal the ruling in Commonwealth Court.  The PUC is still studying a PE request to recover $45 million spent for replacement power bought during outages at its Salem 1 and Peach Bottom 2 nuclear power plants in 1984 and 1985.

headline: CTA ringleader admits burning data
abstract: John Torquato Jr., head of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), said on cross-examination that he, not defendant Alan Stoneman, burned some incriminating evidence that had been overlooked by FBI agents last July.  Torquato also said that Stoneman may not have been in the room when the evidence was burned.  He also said that he signed Stoneman's name to a contract that allowed CTA to recover Social Security tax overpayments for Allegheny County government workers.  This weakens the government's case.

headline: 35 cities in the state are newly eligible to compete for US grants
abstract: The US Department of Housing and Urban Development has named 35 cities in PA as eligible to compete for an estimated $330 million in urban grants next year.  The additions brng to 726 the number of PA cities that may apply for US Urban Development Action Grants.  The grants are used to build stadiums, industrial parks, housing developments, and other urban projects.

headline: Here we go again
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania has filed a $325 million rate increase request with the state Public Utility Commission (PUC).  Seventy-five percent of the increase would be raised through residential service charges.  The editorial complains that the phone company continues to rob consumers and is allowed to do so by the PUC.

headline: Smith handed 12-year term, fined $63,000
abstract: A US Middle District Judge Malcolm Muir sentenced lawyer William T. Smith to 12 years in prison and fined him $63,000 for his role in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery-conspiracy scandal.  Smith was convicted in June on one count of conspiracy, three counts of mail fraud and five counts of interstate transportatio in aid of racketeering.  Another defendant, Alan R. Stoneman, will be sentenced by Muir on July 25.

headline: Mental-health system deplorable
abstract: The failure of Pennsylvania's mental health system has been a problem and will remain a problem until several basic issues are addressed.  First, there is great inefficiency in the process required for involuntary hospitalization of dangerous mentally ill people.  After mentally ill people are committed, there is often poor communication from one facility to the next.  Second, after discharge there is no duty to report to local authorities that a dangerous patient has been discharged.  A very important part of this problem is the state's determination to reduce the availability of treatment facilities, which results in the elimination of state hospital beds.  The author believes this problem will not be solved until elected officials endorse the establishment of inpatient treatment programs that will fully accept the responsibility to provide good care and to make competent discharge decisions.

headline: Electrical fire leaves TMI-1 inoperable
abstract: The owners of Three Mile Island will have to investigate the cause of an electrical fire which occurred at 3:58 a.m. Saturday; the fire left Unit 1 inoperable for at least the next few days.  The fire damaged electrical switches used to operate the nuclear reactor control rods.  The reactor itself was not damaged, and an emergency was not declared.  Unit 1 has been shut down since March 1979, and although the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has authorized restart, the unit remains shut down pending the outcome of appeals filed in the US 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.

headline: County sues state over court funding
abstract: The Allegheny County Law Department filed a petition for declaratory judgment in Commonwealth Court to resolve the question of which governmental body must fund the county court system.  Thomas Rutter, first assistant solicitor for the county, said a declaratory judgment--simply a statement of what the law means--would address the issue of court funding most effectively.

headline: 7 governors ride airwaves in Saturn quest
abstract: Governors from seven states, including PA Governor Thornburgh, appeared on the "Donahue Show," a nationally syndicated talk show, to explain what advantages their states had to offer the proposed General Motors Saturn plant.  General Motors Chief Executive Officer Roger Smith said they hope to choose a site by April.

headline: Major tornado losses recalled
abstract: This article provides a list of some of the deadliest tornado outbreaks in the US.

headline: Sneath set to refute Caliguiri's strategy
