abstract: Henry Sneath, a Republican candidate for Pittsburgh mayor, has said that he will use Pittsburgh's Number 1 position in the Rand McNally Places-Rated Almanac against Mayor Richard Caliguiri in his campaign.  Sneath contends that the almanac doesn't address genuinely important issues about the city's infrastructure.

headline: Mrs. Thornburgh to be run's starter
abstract: Ginny Thornburgh, the first lady of Pennsylvania, will be the honrary starter for the "Reservoir to River Run '85"--a 3.1 mile race that benefits the Association for Retarded Citizens of PA.  PA's first lady has long been a supporter of programs to benefit the retarded.

headline: Equitable pushes for gas shutoffs
abstract: Equitable Gas Company is seeking permission from the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) to shut off heat to hundreds of its customers for failure to pay their bills.  The information on these proposed terminations came out the same day as a PUC survey that shows Equitable Gas leads gas utilities in the state in disconnected service.  Groups representing low-income ratepayers are accusing Equitable of using a collection service that tries to intimidate hard-pressed customers into paying their bills.  Equitable denied any misconduct and defended its new hard-line stance in dealing with customers.

headline: Court upholds MOVE hearings
abstract: The PA Supreme Court denied a Philadelphia Fraternal Order of Police petition to block hearings of the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission.  The commission is probing the police battle with MOVE.  The Fraternal Order of Police believed the hearings could violate the constitutional rights of officers who were called to testify about the events of May 13, 1985.  They also said that the city was looking for a scapegoat in the confrontation.  The Commission argued that they could only advise Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode on the events of the conflict and could not accuse anyone of wrongdoing.  The police wanted the hearings to be delayed until October 16th, when a Commonwealth Court judge is scheduled to hold hearings on two suits which challenge the commission's authority.

headline: A convention hall, the hard way
abstract: The problems that have plagued the David L. Lawrence Convention Center in Pittsburgh set an example of how not to go about the convention-center building process.  Philadelphia wants to build a convention center twice as large as Pittsburgh's, and the city should learn from Pittsburgh's mistakes.  Awful weather and strikes by several skilled tradesmen combined to delay the construction of the David L. Lawrence Convention Center by over two years; these factors also caused the project to go over budget considerably.

headline: New state bill to reduce sex on cable TV
abstract: A bill that would make cable companies liable for transmitting sexually explicit material is going to be taken up by the PA State Senate this week.  The bill already was given unaminous support from the PA Senate Judiciary Committee, and many expect it to pass the PA Senate.  Several church and anti-pornography groups joined forces to back the measure.  Cable companies and other critics of the measure say that it is too far-reaching and that it will never pass the courts.  There is no certain answer as for what the PA House will do when it takes up the bill.

headline: Sneath strategy to assail Caliguiri as more interested in governor race
abstract: Republican Henry Sneath, a candidate for Pittsburgh mayor, says that his strategy for the general election is to contend that Caliguiri is really running for governor and will spend the first year of his third term running for governor.  Caliguiri's executive secretary, David Matter, said Caliguiri has consistently disavowed allegations that he is conducting a dual campaign, or that he has decided to run for governor.

headline: Nursing home's licensing fought by Thornburgh
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh ordered state attorneys to appeal the decision to issue a new operating license to the owner of the 68-bed Golden Age skilled-care home in Brownsville, PA.  Governor Thornburgh said the home has operated in an aura of indifference to the physical, medical, mental and social needs of its patients.

headline: Facts support TMI safety
abstract: This letter to the editor criticizes The Patriot-News for not being objective about the restart of Three Mile Island (TMI).  He says that not all of the area residents are against the TMI restart and that the Patriot-News should not give the impression that the area is opposed to nuclear energy.

headline: Court upholds wiretap statute
abstract: A PA appeals court yesterday upheld the state's wiretap statute and rejected arguments that the wiretap violated the US Constitution.  Judge Donald Wieland said that the PA state constitution serves only to prohibit a non-consenual electronic interception without warrant or court order.

headline: A naďve effort to attract GM-Saturn
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh is trying to encourage General Motors (GM) to locate their new Saturn plant in PA and has rejected the idea of state Representative Joseph Kolter to offer a $25 million package to entice GM.  This letter writer supports Thornburgh's efforts and notes that to a large company like GM, $25 million is small change.  The author also urges Legislators to work with Thornburgh in a united front to help entice General Motors to locate in PA.

headline: Phone rate hearings
abstract: The Public Utility Commission ordered hearings on requests by Quaker State Telephone Company and Continental Telephone Company for a total of $3.2 million more in annual revenue.  The Hershey-based sister companies both serve parts of central and eastern PA.

headline: Some Lotto players are cool to idea of third drawing
abstract: The Bureau of State Lotteries is expected to add a third weekly Lotto drawing and a third weekly Big Four drawing after a state regulatory board approves the plan.  Several Lotto players were interviewed and were not overly excited about the idea.  The move is intended to sustain sales, rather than increase them.

headline: Official chided about delay in response on TMI
abstract: A PA Department of Health study found that, after the 1979 Unit 2 accident, cancer rates within five and ten miles of Three Mile Island were no higher than normal.  The state study has come under fire since reports surfaced that the state may have diluted its results by including residents from outside its study area--a move which the Health Department says was necessary because remaining inside the boundaries would have been impossible.  The state's study critiqued an earlier study conducted by Marjorie Aamodt that found high cancer rates near TMI.

headline: Fear of TMI
abstract: This letter to the editor urges officials not to restart Three-Mile-Island Unit-1 until safety issues are resolved to the public's satisfaction.

headline: Courts Silent as 4 Pa. Killers See Sands Run Low
abstract: Although nobody expects Michael Travaglia and John Lesko to die in PA's electric chair on November 19, the courts have yet to back the scheduled executions.  Lesko and Travaglia were convicted of four brutal slayings, and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed their death warrants in July.  Both men have filed appeals that most legal experts believe will take a year to exhaust.  Travaglia's appeal hinges on the selection of jurors who sentenced him to die.  The execution draws closer and closer as defense attorneys are awaiting the court to block the sentences.

headline: Albany fields baseball while Harrisburg strikes out
abstract: This article discusses the reasons why Albany was able to get a minor-league baseball team and Harrisburg was not.  The main reason is that the Albany area's $1.2 million Heritage Park was publicly funded, while Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed was dependent upon private donations to build a park on City Island.

headline: PUC says hello to quarters-only pay phones
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) agreed yesterday to drop a provision in its pay-phone rules that required that all pay phones accept nickels, dimes, and quarters.  The decision came from a request by Gladwin Incorporated, a phone equipment maker that manufactures quarters-only phones.  The US Federal Communications Commission recently decided that states can ban quarters-only phones for interstate calls only if such phones are found to pose "legitimate public health, safety, and welfare concerns," but that states should feel free to require three-coin phones for intrastate calls if the states so choose.  PUC Commissioner William Shane said that allowing a disparity between in-state and out-of-state regulations would only cause confusion.

headline: Some who use state-owned vehicles will pay extra taxes
abstract: Adhering to new federal tax regulations, PA will deduct up to $45.76 in additional Social Security taxes from the checks issued to employees who drive state vehicles home and earn less than $39,006 a year.  According to a spokesman for PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, the deduction covers all of 1985.   In 1986, portions of the Social Security deduction and a new federal income tax deduction will be taken from each paycheck.

headline: Order to close Pennhurst ends landmark case
abstract: A historic, decade-old legal battle over abuse and neglect at the Pennhurst Center for the mentally retarded was brought to a close by US District Judge Raymond Broderick; Judge Broderick formally approved a negotiated settlement and ordered the facility closed.  The landmark class-action lawsuit, originally filed in 1974 to correct a number of dangerous living conditions at the Chester County facility, evolved over the years into litigation that challenged the manner in which the mentally retarded receive treatment and theories regarding their care.

headline: Firm gets state cogeneration permit: Boilers will produce power from culm in West Mahanoy
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh announced that Electrodyne Research Corporation has been given a state permit to construct two fluidized-bed boilers that will generage electricty and steam by burning anthracite coal refuse.  The plant will use modern technology to eliminate unsightly coal refuse banks by turning them into efficient, low-cost energy.

headline: Crime panel wins subpoena rights
abstract: The Pennsylvania Crime Commission won a battle in the state Supreme Court, allowing it to subpoena corporations and individuals, but it will need action from the state Legislature if it wishes to continue as an investigative agency with the power to get witnesses to talk.

headline: Apartments lined up for homeless families
abstract: While the city seeks to fulfill its pledge to rebuild destroyed neighborhoods by Christmas, thirty-nine families who lost their homes in the MOVE inferno will be given temporary apartments .  Their homes were destroyed by a fire that arose after the police dropped a satchel of explosives onto the roof of the MOVE house.  Robert G. Hazen, executive director of the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority announced that seven builders had been invited to submit bids of the reconstruction of the burned houses on Osage Avenue and Pine Street in West Philadelphia.

headline: PUC should concentrate on phone changes, panel told
abstract: Patricia White, staff member of the state Legislative Budget and Finance Committee, said that the Public Utility Commission (PUC) needs to devote more staff time to deal with the breakup of American Telephone & Telegraph Company (AT&T), as well as to initiate a study that projects how anticipated rate increases will affect households that have telephones.  The Committee is auditing the PUC as part of a sunset review of the agency.

headline: Specter backs off bid for early endorsement
abstract: Republicans who fear that their party will be fractured by a Specter-Thornburgh fight for the party's 1986 US Senate nomination have had those fears alleviated for the moment.  Specter, speaking at a meeting of the Republican State Committee, called off his bid for a vote of endorsement from the committee, which would have been aimed at discouraging Thornburgh from challenging Specter.  The article also takes a brief look at potential Republican nominees for Lieutenant Governor.

headline: Pharmacists wage a private battle against illegal Rx's
abstract: Pharmacists across PA regularly receive forged or medically unsound drug prescriptions, but many say that they avoid reporting suspicious perscriptions to authorities and have resorted instead to their own policing efforts to control the problem.  Druggists, interviewed individually, as well as officials of professional pharmacists' organizations, say costly court appearances, lenient judges, ineffective law enforcement and inadequate drug restrictions discourage them from working closely with police and prosecutors.  As a result, many pharmacists wage a private battle against the drug problem, using telephone networks and written communications to alert fellow druggists to what they call "bad scripts."

headline: Fuel of inflation
abstract: This editorial examines the relationship between oil prices and inflation.  The editorial begins by looking at the rise of inflation from 1968 onward.  When the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) cut off the flow of oil from the Middle East in 1973, not only did that make the price of oil the barometer of America's fortunes, it also represented a major transfer of wealth from industrialized countries to oil-producing countries; the effect of this transfer was charted in the surge of inflation.  Oil-price increases were relatively moderate from 1974-1978 and inflation was as well.  During the second oil crisis in 1979, the inflation rate surged.  The editorial concludes that there is no question that energy is a key component in the ups and downs of inflation, but many often do not appreciate this fact.

headline: Crime victims get no respect
abstract: A letter to the editor responds to comments made by US Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall, who made a speech opposing the death penalty on September 6.  The author believes that too often the rights of the criminal who committed a violent crime are put above the rights of the victims of that crime.  The author also is incensed that a Justice of the Supreme Court would support a criminal being given such special treatment.  The author's daughter was a victim of a violent crime, and he asks for his dignity and rights as a law-abiding US citizen.  Mention is also given to a bill presently in the PA Legislature that would provide for victim's rights.  The author wants everyone to write to their legislators supporting the bill.

headline: As McKeesport goes…
abstract: McKeesport's corporate and community leaders developed the McKeesport Enterprise Development Strategy to help develop the area.  This editorial supports the development plan and says that development of McKeesport will improve the entire Pittsburgh region.

headline: Sidetracked jet stream to blame for East's drought
abstract: During the last nine months, a major jet stream has passed over the East Coast.  The result of this is that storm systems, which are steered by the jet stream, have not passed over the area and have caused the worst Eastern drought in more than 20 years.  Meteorologists do not know why the jet stream has changed its normal course.

headline: Specter Calls Cuts 'Unacceptable'
abstract: Pennsylvania's US Senators--Arlen Specter and John Heinz--both agreed that President Reagan's budget cutting fell too heavily on programs important to PA.  Neither Senator thinks that the budget will pass through Congress.  The congressmen take note of the budget-cut programs that are vital to the Northeast.

headline: Plan to save Lemington pondered
abstract: Allegheny County and PA state officials said yesterday that they have reached an understanding on saving the struggling Lemington Home--a nursing home in East Liberty.  The two sides are at a tenative position to have the nursing home declared a public facility for funding purposes.  The state would like the county to contract the home for operation, while the county would like the state to appoint it as "master" of the home.  Both proposals would qualify the home for the higher Medical Assistance reimbursements that public facilities receive over private ones.  The difference would be whether the state or county would be responsible if costs exceed reimbursement levels.

headline: Fuel removed at TMI
abstract: More than 6.5 years after the Three Mile Island nuclear accident, the most important part of the $1 billion cleanup is under way at the TMI nuclear power plant near Harrisburg.  Highly trained technicians have begun the process of removing the severely damaged, highly-radioactive fuel from the Unit 2 reactor core.  GPU Nuclear Corporation estimates that it will take 18 months to load the core's contents into steel canisters; the core's contents include 100 tons of fuel and 50 tons of steel and other metal components.  The article goes into an in-depth examination of the clean-up process at TMI Unit 2.

headline: Crime watchers honored for extending long arm of the law
abstract: Alfred Miles and Louis Searles were among 25 state residents yesterday who received the 1985 Governor's Volunteer Recognition Award for Community Crime Prevention.  The two did surveillance and gumshoe work that led to the apprehension last year of a burglar who had robbed four or five neighborhood homes in Fox Ridge.  Anthony Galloro received his award for his leadership in creating and coordinating North Middletown Township's Crime Watch.

headline: Business "catastrophe" feared
abstract: Philadelphia's failure to gain state support for a new convention center could kill several city hotels, freeze development along East Market Street, and seriously cripple future tourist and convention business.  Without a center, rival cities like New York and Boston will continue to entice conventioners and their dollars away from Philadelphia.  Philadelphia's Commerce Director, David Brenner, said a new convention center would "pump dollars and new blood into the city."

headline: Storms force 100 from W. Pa. homes
abstract: On July 9th, nightlong rainstorms--accompanied by spectacular lightning, thunder and hail--caused scattered flooding in western PA; the flooding forced more than 100 people from their homes in Westmoreland County.  The National Weather Service said 5 inches of rain fell on portions of the county.

headline: Specter in the spotlight
abstract: This editorial urges US Senator Arlen Specter to vote against confirming William Bradford Reynolds as associate attorney general, the third-ranking power in the Justice Department.  The editorial says that as head of the Justice Department's civil rights division, Reynolds perversely mocked civil rights laws, systematically using them against blacks to elevate whites.

headline: Public smoking bill an issue among Berks lawmakers
abstract: Legislation in the PA House of Representatives that would restrict smoking in public places is making some area lawmakers uncomfortable.  The bill would require the proprietors of all public buildings to set aside an area for smokers.  PA State Representative Paul Angstadt sees the proposal as an infringement on inidividual rights.  PA State Representative James Gallen believes that encouraging businesses to set up non-smoking areas voluntarily is better than doing it by legislation.  PA State Representative John Davies agrees that something should be done to curtail smoking in public places, but he does not want to see businesses hurt by the legislation.

headline: Gas going up: Prices may rise through summer - and beyond
abstract: Experts predict that gasoline prices will likely climb through summer and could continue after the summer ends.  A host of factors--tighter US standards on leaded gasoline, decreased competition, and the end of the British coal strike--are cited to explain higher fuel prices.

headline: Criminals Seeing More of Jail: Sentences Tougher
abstract: The PA Commission on Sentencing said that judges handed out stiffer prison terms for aggravated assault, burglary, rape and robbery in 1984 than before mid-1982--when mandatory sentencing and sentencing guidelines went into effect across the state.  This editorial applauds this fact and says that mandatory sentencing leads to fairer sentences.

headline: Business groups back Pirate's plan
abstract: Appearing at a press conference, leaders of a half dozen influential organizations have come out in support of Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri's plan to keep the Pittsburgh Pirates in town.  In a statement, the organizations said that the team generated $36 million for the local economy last year, despite record-low attendance at Three Rivers Stadium.

headline: The cable censors
abstract: This editorial attacks a bill in the PA Legislature that would ban "pornography," obscene, or sexually- explicit materials, from cable television.  The editorial believes that the bill's version of sexual explicitness goes well beyond a reasonable definition of pornography.  The bill amounts to, in the editorials words, making children the standard for what adults may watch on cable television in PA.  This is topsy-turvy, in that in most healthy families, parents tell the children what is suitable to watch on television.  The bill also goes out of its way to ban several types of scenes that have become commonplace on cable television.

headline: Specter says he's confident of Reagan's support
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter said yesterday that he was confident he would soon receive a letter from US President Ronald Reagan endorsing his candidacy for the US Senate.  However, David Runkel, press secretary to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, doubts that the President will want to get involved in a potential fight between Specter and Thornburgh.  Specter has recently been criticized by several conservative groups, and has made an effort to reach out to the White House and other Republicans in PA for support.

headline: Rabies Cases Reach 39-Year High
abstract: With six weeks left in 1985, the PA Department of Health has already recorded 387 rabies cases and expects to record 400 by year's end.  All of this year's cases involve animals, although hundreds of people have been forced to receive rabies immunizations after being exposed to the bite or saliva of rabid animals.

headline: Generating surplus beats shortage
abstract: An opinion piece, written by the president of the PA Electric Association (PEA), looks at recent events in PA's electrical utilities and how the Patriot-News has responded to these events in its editorials.  The PEA shares the Patriot-News' view that it is desirable to have in place a procedure to determine the need for new electric generation facilities.  The author does point to a PA Utility Commission (PUC) investigation that found that reserve generating capacity was not sufficient, and the author also contends that all electric plant construction currently being undertaken is warranted.  The PUC clearly had knowledge of the situation, and nothing was planned without their involvement.  The author also says that the major reasons for cost overruns in plants have been mandate design changes, construction delays, and unprecedented inflation.

headline: CTA bribe trial begins tomorrow
abstract: Testimony is expected to begin tomorrow in the trial of two men accused of participating in a political bribery network designed to ensure state and local contract work for Computer Technology Associates (CTA).  US Attorney James West is expected to present evidence to the jury that CTA offered jobs, cash and favors to elected officials and public employees to steer work to the company.

headline: City Halts Firm's 273G For Osage Repair Work
abstract: Payment of more than $273,000 to a contractor for repairs on homes damaged during the May 13 MOVE disaster has been halted by the Philadelphia City Controller, who has termed Ronix Corporation's administrative charges exhorbitant.  Joseph Vignola, the city controller, has ordered paymet to Ronix Corporation stopped until it gives him sufficient documentation of the billings.  Vignola questions several of the amounts that Ronix has charged the city, and Philadelphia Deputy Controller Thurman Bullock said that Ronix has refused to be audited.  Ronix Corporation's history with the Philadlephia city government is also examined in the article.

headline: Toll call competition?
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission (PUC) voted that, under the terms of the 18-month-old breakup of American Telephone & Telegraph Incorporated, Bell of PA cannot have a monopoly on toll calls that do not cross the boundaries of PA's five regional calling areas.  The PUC decided that the long-distance companies should compete with Bell within each region.

headline: Specter sees no challenge from Thornburgh
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter yesterday expressed doubts that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh would challenge him for his US Senate seat in 1986.  A spokesman for Thornburgh, however, said that he has not made a decision one way or the other on whether he will run.  Specter said he believes that if Thornburgh decides to run, it could hurt the Republicans ticket in both the Senate and PA gubernatorial race.  Specter believes that if Thornburgh runs, it will make his administration's record an issue and hurt PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton in his bid for the PA Governorship.

headline: Record numbers seek help for alcohol abuse
abstract: Deputy Health Secretary Luceille Fleming said that record numbers of Pennsylvanians are seeking medical treatment for alcoholism.  Fleming says that the increases are the result of a growing acceptance of alcoholism as a disease, not a jump in the number of alcoholics.

headline: Glut vanishing: US policy leaning once again on others' oil
abstract: The United States should be wary of making decisions about oil based on its current availability and inexpensiveness.  Also, the US should start thinking about ways to conserve oil use.

headline: CTA defendant gets OK to subpoena Zimmerman data
abstract: A federal judge has granted a request by a defendant in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) case to subpoena records from PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman.  The federal grand jury said that CTA officials attempted to bribe local and state officials to win contracts.

headline: City sees no conflict for convention-center firm
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has indicated that it would be inappropriate for the city of Philadelphia to work with the Reading Company to develop the convention center because of ties between city officials and Reading Company executives.  Thornburgh has also questioned the appropriateness of using a private developer--as opposed to developing the convention center with public funds.  Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode will meet with Governor Thornburgh to discuss the project.

headline: Tornado victims begin to rebuild lives: Fatalities in state rise to 62
abstract: National Weather Service meteorologists have confirmed that at least seven tornadoes touched down in Western PA and Eastern Ohio on Friday, March 31.  The latest tally of the death and destruction caused by the twisters in PA includes 62 dead; 600 injured; and 1,520 buildings destroyed.  The Red Cross and the PA Emergency Management Agency are in the area assisting people and searching for missing persons.

headline: Specter the Key Vote on Rynolds Nod
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter may hold the key vote that determines whether William Bradford Reynolds, the controversial chieftan of the Justice Department's civil rights division, ascends to the associate-attorney- general position.  Specter refused to comment on his vote, saying he would make his intentions public only at the committee hearing.  Specter, who is up for re-election next year, is under pressure not only from President Ronald Reagan--who wants him to vote along party lines--but also from major civil rights groups who oppose Reynolds.

headline: Reservoir Park race will benefit association for retarded
abstract: Ginny Thornburgh, PA's first lady, will be the honorary starter of the Reservoir to River Run '85, a run to benefit the Association for Retarded Citizens of PA.  Mrs. Thornburgh will be presenting awards at the end of the event.  The Association for Retarded Citizens of PA will receive proceeds from the entry fees.

headline: GPU can't salvage much from self-serving study
abstract: This opinion piece examines a report for GPU Nuclear about the Three Mile Island (TMI) Unit 2 accident.  The Steir report looks closely at leak testing at TMI Unit 2, and comes to the conclusion that the leak test employed was defective; the report also states that employees viewed the test results as unreliable and often discarded them--a situation management was unaware of.  The author believes that GPU did know about the leak-rate falsifications.  This is simply an attempt by GPU to manipulate public perception by purchasing an investigation of corporate conduct it did not want exposed by the publuc sector.

headline: Curbing Abuse of Elderly: Bill Being Considered
abstract: This editorial supports a bill that would protect the elderly by requiring the reporting of possible abuses to the Department of Aging.  Such a bill would be similar to a law that deals with child abuse.

headline: City vs. state: A philosophical feud over convention center
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode and Governor Dick Thornburgh agreed that the rift between city and state officials over the Center City convention center was a matter of philosophy.  Thornburgh said that it wasn't right for the city to develop the $441 million public-works project in a partnership with a group of private investors who were expected to make a profit.  Goode and city officials responded that the public-private partnership they had labored for years to form was perfectly legal and expressly designed to save taxpayers' money.  Goode has called for a city-state summit meeting on April 24th to discuss the differences in opinion.

headline: Tornado warnings provide little time for preparation
abstract: National Weather Service policy often gives the first communities in a twister's path little time to prepare for the blow.  This is because the weather service does not issue a warning until a twister has been sighted, said Chuck Heckler, director of the weather service's Pittsburgh office.  The weather service issued a tornado watch at 5pm on Friday, May 31; this signaled that conditions were ripe for a twister.  A tornado warning for Erie County was released at 5:13pm, two minutes before official reports said the twister hit, but a minute after some residents' clocks stopped due to downed power lines.

headline: Specter vulnerable in '86, White House memo says
abstract: An internal White House memo assessing the political strength of the 22 Republican US senators running for re-election in 1986, labeled US Senator Arlen Specter as one of the eight "most vulnerable."  Specter is considered vulnerable because of the demographics of PA, with Democrats holding an 800,000 voter-registration edge in the state.

headline: Sanctions imposed on doctors, dentists
abstract: The state Dental Council and Examining Board put Dr. Ira Schwartz of Pittsburgh on five years porbation after he pleaded guilty to a drug law violation.  Also, Dr. George Wehrle was reprimanded after he pleaded no contest to a welfare fraud charge in Allegheny County Court.  Additionally, the Medical Education and Licensure Board summarily suspended the PA doctor's license of Russell Manfredi, who is charged with murdering his wife in Connecticut; the board has also reached an agreement with Dr. Donald McMillan of Pittsburgh, who has agreed to relinquish his right to practice medicine because of his age.  The state Medical Education and Licensure Board was able to revoke or suspend these licenses under a new law that allows it to suspend the license of a doctor without normal legal proceedings if he or she is believed to be a threat to his or her patients.

headline: GPU denial of alleged harassment raises old question
abstract: The article examines a $64,000 fine against GPU Nuclear Corporation for the company's alleged harrasment of Richard Parks, once a senior engineer on the Three Mile Island Unit 2 cleanup project.  The fine was announced in August, almost two and a half years after Parks held a news conference to say that GPU Nuclear was bypassing safety procedures in their cleanup operation.  A US Labor Department review found that Parks was subject to harrasment, in violation of the NRC's non-discrimination regulations.  After being granted more than a month's delay to respond, the utility denies that the manner in which Parks was handled was anything less than professional.  Parks is currently unemployed and living in California.  GPU Nulcear's point-by-point rebuttal of the US Labor Department's finding is included in the article.

headline: D.A. candidates miss confrontation
abstract: Republican candidate for Philadelphia district attorney Ronald Castille, a Commonwealth Court judge, was hoping to confront his Democratic counterpart, Robert Williams, outside of the MOVE hearing room.  The confrontation never happened because Williams left the hearing room out a side door.  With the election two weeks away, Williams holds a 14 point lead and has the endorsement of Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode and Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell.  Castille, however, has been the more active campaigner and has been trying to bait Williams into having a televised debate with him.  The Citizens Crime Commission, a nonpartisan group, has offered to sponsor the debate, but Williams is reluctant to agree to the debate unless the commission spells out how it will be conducted.

headline: City: Free convention hall funds
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode asked Governor Thornburgh to lay to rest his deep concerns over the planned Center City convention center project; Mayor Goode has asked the governor to release $43.9 million to buy land for the project.  Governor Thornburgh is preparing a reply restating his postion that the money will be withheld for now because there is legislative opposition to funds for convention center construction.

headline: Why tornadoes struck district
abstract: According to meteorologists at the National Weather Service in Pittsburgh, a combination of violent thunderstorms, warm temperatures, high humidity and an impending cold front managed to crack the shield of hills and mountains that generally protect Western PA.  This caused the violent tornadoes that struck the area.

headline: Stand, don't crouch, sir
abstract: This editorial urges US Senator Arlen Specter to vote against confirming William Bradford Reynolds as associate attorney general.

headline: State AFL-CIO urges legislation to control health costs
abstract: The PA American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations is lobbying for legislation that would help to reduce the costs of health care.  The group is urging for laws reducing the length of hospital stays and urging more outpatient care.

headline: GPU wants generator rules eased
abstract: General Public Utilities Corporation has requested that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission let it test and operate steam generators at Three Mile Island Unit 1 without plugging hundreds of worn generator tubes as plant technical specifications require.  The GPU plan suggests that the two Unit 1 generators still pose thorny safety problems for the restart of Unit 1 at the nuclear plant.

headline: DA Names 4 Judges He Says Are Too Lenient
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Edward G. Rendell, lobbying for a state constitutional amendment that would allow his office to demand trials by jury, accused a group of judges of being lenient, and named four of them--Common Pleas Judges Victor DiNubile Jr., William J. Mazzola, Michael E. Wallace, and Thomas N. Shiomos.  Rendell said that those judges are most inclined toward compromise verdicts; a compromise verdict is when a judge, in a non-jury trial, reduces serious charges in a gesture aimed at compromise or avoiding tougher mandatory sentencing requirements.  Rendell says that juries are less inclined toward compromise verdicts than judges.

headline: City: Osage houses won't sap funds
abstract: Philadelphia's plan to rebuild 61 West Philadelphia row houses destroyed in the May 13 MOVE siege will not jeopardize state funding for numerous nonprofit community-development corporations.  Jill Michaels, executive director of the Community Development Coalition, said that numerous community development corporations (CDCs) would face serious financial difficulties if the city used state funds designated for housing rehabilitation to help rebuild the MOVE neighborhood.  State officials have responded by claiming that no state funds designated for housing rehabilitation would go to the reconstruction project.

headline: Apparel, shoe industries move up on trade deficit list: both once provided major employment in state
abstract: PA continues to suffer the erosion in jobs and profits that the US trade deficit has caused.  Apparel and shoes--two industries that were once major employers in the state--have risen to third and seventh on the trade deficit list.  Most of the other domestic industries, or their suppliers suffering trade deficits, contribute to a major portion to the PA economy.  These include petroleum, automobiles, iron and steal, electronics, and non-ferrous metals.

headline: State car parts law in need of change
abstract: A state law that requires state agencies to purchase cars with three-fourths of the parts made in the USA has kept most agencies from being able to purchase cars.  A letter to the editor urges the Legislature to adopt an amendment that would permit the purchase of cars with most of their parts made in North America; the author says that this would be a realistic response to the problem.

headline: State aid for nursing home sought
abstract: A coalition of public officials and charity leaders have asked Governor Dick Thornburgh if the state will run Lemington Home until a plan for its future can be devised.  Lemington home is a nursing home in Pittsburgh that is scheduled to close June 27 because of financial difficulties.  Speaker of the state House K. Leroy Irvis predicted that indigent elderly patients would die on the streets if the nursing home closes.  Irvis and the others believe that if the state takes over and runs the home for six months, a community-based plan to keep it open can be put in place.

headline: Groups sue to halt start of reactor
abstract: Two lawsuits were filed yesterday against the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), one by Limerick Ecology Action and the other by inmates at Graterford Prison.  The groups are seeking a stay of the NRC's decision to allow Unit 1 at the Limerick nuclear power plant to begin full-power testing.  The suit contends that the decision to allow power testing poses a severe risk to public safety.  Philadelphia Electric Company, which owns the Limerick plant, contends that power testing has been studied thoroughly and their is no need for additional review.

headline: DA Taking City To the Cleaner?
abstract: Two city cars driven by Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell and some members of his staff have accumulated 96 parking tickets over a two-year period.  The tickets were dismissed through an administrative procedure requiring no formal Traffic Court hearing.  According to Traffic Court records, the 96 tickets totaled about $3,200.  Some of the tickets were given while the cars were being used for what appear to be personal errands.  Rendell acknowledged that he received the tickets, but insisted any trips on which he received them were official business.  The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office was already the subject of an internal ticket-fixing investigation this summer; that investigation led to a resignation, a firing, and several suspensions.  Rendell has vigorously defended his record as a public servant.

headline: Clairton may not meet U.S. guidelines for aid
abstract: Clairton, a Pittsburgh area community on the verge of bankruptcy, may not meet a federal agency's guidelines to qualify for the $1 million in emergency aid that US Senator Arlen Specter is seeking.  Specter asked the Senate Appropriations Committee to put the money into the Sudden and Severe Economic Dislocation Program of the Economic Development Administration (EDA), which is designed to aid cities that have lost a major employer.  The shutdown of US Steel's Clairton Works has devastated the city and crippled its tax base.  The EDA, however, uses a formula that takes into account the rate of unemployment and impact of the plant shutdown in an entire region.  A town in an isolated rural area, therefore, would be more likely to qualify for SSED funds than a municipality near a major city.

headline: Damn Foreigners
abstract: A cartoon shows a massive dump truck with slogans on the side showing the problems currently facing the US in regards to budgetary, fiscal, and trade policies.  The front of the truck is the "Record Federal Deficit," followed by the "Overvalued Dollar," and "Trade Deficit."  The truck is filled with imports from other countries.  Behind the dump truck is a small car with "Protection" written on the back and an angry driver waving his fist.

headline: State Democrats to woo labor unions
abstract: Democratic leaders have agreed to revive efforts to increase organized labor's representation on the Democratic State Committee.  At a meeting in Camp Hill Saturday, the state committee shot down a proposal to add 25 at-large members, of whom approximately 10 would have been labor leaders.  Opponents of the proposal did not like the fact that at-large members would be appointed, whereas rank and file committee members would be elected by Democratic voters.

headline: State revises plan to curb drug costs
abstract: PA Deputy Welfare Secretary Gerald Radke said yesterday that state welfare officials were revising a proposal to limit state payments to pharmacists because they are being reimbursed for medications at an inflated rate.  Under the current State Medical Assistance Program, pharmacists are paid the average wholesale price for each drug given out, as well as a $2.75 dispensing fee.  Federal audits have showed that pharmacists are buying medication for substantially less than wholesale prices and are being reimbursed at rates that are 16% higher than their actual costs.  Radke said the new proposal plans to limit payments for many brand-name drugs to 90% of the average wholesale price.  Some representatives of the pharmacy agency criticize the new proposal and say that the discounts were common knowledge.

headline: High court keeps TMI closed as state argues against restart
abstract: Three Mile Island's (TMI) Unit 1 Reactor remains shut down while the US Supreme Court considers an appeal to keep it that way.  The Commonwealth of PA became the last party to file comments before the noon deadline yesterday.  Three Mile Island Alert (TMIA) asked the court to maintain an order blocking the restart until a decision on the appeal is rendered.  The federal government and GPU Nuclear argued yesterday that the court cannot keep blocking the restart simply because TMIA thinks that Three Mile Island is a controversial nuclear power plant.  The federal government also argued that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's decision to allow a Unit 1 restart was, given the commission's expert judgment, well-informed.

headline: Davis should step down
abstract: Somerset Judge Charles Coffroth has refused a request by the state attorney general to suspend Sheriff Guy Davis as warden at the Somerset County Jail.  Davis has been charged with forcing inmates to engage in homosexual activities and for making pornographic pictures.  This editorial asks Davis to step down from his office; if he will not step down, Judge Coffroth should suspend him.

headline: Confirming Stereotypes
abstract: A letter to the editor complains about the process in the PA Legislature of finding funding for a convention center in Philadelphia.  The delicate deals to get funding together are continuously shaping up and then falling apart.  The author is particularly annoyed with elected representatives who are fighting over control of covention center construction.  The author is also annoyed by a provision in the plan that would prohibit political figures or their relatives from contracts and employment on the project.

headline: Issue is fair trade, not "free trade"
abstract: A letter to editor agrees with recent editorials by the Erie Daily Times.  The editorials argue that free trade is essential for jobs in our community.  The article does, however, acknowledge the downsides of free trade, which is apparent in the rows of empty factories in Erie.  The author believes that this country needs "fair trade," which will allow domestic industries the same advantages and government support that is given to foreign industries who dump their products on US shores.  The decline of the American steel industry is used as an example.  The author is annoyed with the lack of response to these foreign practices by the federal government, which has simply offered verbal admonishments.  The author also bemoans the "good-old-boy" system in Washington D.C., where former federal employees have become lobbyists for foreign businesses.  The letter would like to see US trade representatives be more realistic in addressing American access to foreign markets.

headline: State election law would stop Lincoln, candidate says
abstract: Gene Basalyga, a 68-year-old Lackawanna county man who has ran for public office and failed 14 times, is suing the commonwealth in US Middle District Court.  He contends that the increased filing fees and number of signatures needed on nominating petitions constitutes discrimination.  He challenges the new Election Code provisions as violations of his constitutional right to equal protection under the law.

headline: State revokes license of Germantown nursing home
abstract: The state Department of Health has revoked the license of Cedars nursing home in Philadelphia, citing poor living conditions and serious violations of state and federal laws governing health-care facilities.  Jay Laff, administrator of the Cedars nursing home, said he would appeal the revocation.

headline: History of the Limerick project
abstract: This article reviews the history of the Limerick nuclear-reactor project.  Included in the key points are the PA Public Utility Commission ordering the suspension of construction for Unit 2, the second nuclear reactor, in May 1982, as well as the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issuing a full-power license for Unit 1 on August 8, 1985.

headline: Dealing with shoplifting
abstract: Pittsburgh District Attorney Robert Colville has agreed to set up a retail-theft diversion program, a copy of a program that has had successes in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  The program allows a first-time shoplifting suspect the chance to avoid a trail and a criminal record by attending a special five-hour class conducted by a private agency.  The editorial supports this program because it could help to curb retail theft, unclutter the courts, and help first-time petty thieves avoid becoming repeaters.

headline: Consortium consolation
abstract: An editorial notes that the Pittsburgh region learned a lot in its unsuccessful bid for the Software Productivity Consortium.  The editorial says that the effort to attract the defense contractors' cooperative research venture reflected substantial flexibility and maturity in the region's ability to court major new entrepreneurial ventures.

headline: Mushrooms: Butler County farm losing 250 jobs to cheaper foreign imports
abstract: Butler County Mushroom Farm Incorporated plans to shut down its West Winfield operations by July 1985, idling at least 250 workers.  Cheap mushroom imports from Taiwan, China, Korea and Europe are a major factor in the state, since PA grows 52% of the commercial mushrooms cultivated in the US.

headline: State GOP chief intends to resign 4 months early
abstract: State Republican Party Chairman Robert Asher said yesterday that he will resign in February, four months before his term expires.  Asher, who was handpicked by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to head the party, said that he was resigning so that Lieutenant Governor William Scranton, who will be the likely Republican nominee for governor, would have the chance to pick his own party leader.  Party officials say that Asher was among those urging former US Secretary of Transportation Drew Lewis to run against Scranton for the Republican nomination for governor.  Asher says that he and his county support Scranton 100%, but would not say whether he would support Thornburgh if he runs against US Senator Arlen Specter for his Senate seat.  Asher came under fire earlier this year over allegations that he was involved in the Computer Technology Associates bribery-conspiracy scandal.

headline: State signs pact on health care for Phila. poor
abstract: PA state Welfare Secretary Walter Cohen yesterday announced the approval of a $185 million contract with HealthAmerica to implement a health-care proposal for 100,000 needy individuals in South and West Philadelphia.  The proposal still has to be approved by the US Health Care Financing Administration (HCFA), which has raised some questions about the state proposal.  Due to provisions that allow HealthAmerica to be reimbursed for start-up costs if the HCFA should reject the plan, the propoal is somewhat controversial.

headline: House Panel to Scrutinize Nuclear Safety Rulings
abstract: The Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy Conservation and Power will hold public hearings on charges by a member of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission that the agency's safety decisions have been hasty and overly favorable to the nuclear power industry.  Similar charges of procedural shortcuts have been made by others who say the commission has been rushing headlong to relieve the nuclear industry of the huge financial burden incurred when nominally operable plants were shut down.

headline: Death Penalty for Children in N.J.?
abstract: Lawmakers in New Jersey are considering an amendment to the state's capital punishment law that would exempt those under the age of 18 from the death penalty.  The amendment has the support of Governor Thomas Kean and State Senator John Russo.  However, strong doubts about the amendment surfaced during a meeting of the General Assembly's Judiciary Committee, with some legislators saying that the change could kill the entire death penalty law.

headline: Dented dreams
abstract: The article recounts the day in 1978 when New Stanton, PA was projected to be the next boomtown.  This was because Volkswagen built its first American auto plant here.  Everyone was very optimistic--including PA Governor Milton Shapp--that New Stanton would see a population and economic boom.  However, the boom never materialized, as economic pressures led to layoffs at the plant, which in turn led many to leave the small town for good; this hurt local businesses.  Many in New Stanton believe this is a lesson that people in Spring Hill, TN, which will be getting a new Saturn plant, should not ignore.

headline: Nixon arrives in China to "see my old friends"
abstract: Former US President Richard Nixon arrived in China yesterday to evaluate China's progress under a package of sweeping economic reforms; the reforms were instituted by leader Deng Xiaoping.  Nixon, who made a historic trip to China in 1972 that signaled the end of 23 years of hostility between the US and China, is making his fifth visit to the country in 13 years.  Nixon remains highly respected in China, despite the Watergate Scandal.

headline: State government's payroll shrinks; costs keep growing
abstract: State government in PA is getting both bigger and smaller.  The Commonwealth of PA is the biggest employer in the state at 100,000 employees working in various branches, down from 110,000 in 1975.  The state's spending has increased, however, from $8.1 billion in 1975 to $16.8 bilion for 1985.  PA is still 49th in the nation in the ratio of state employees to the general population.  The article contains a description of PA taxes and the institutions that make up the state government.  Legislative pay in PA, at $35,000 per year, is among the highest in the nation.

headline: Stress: Tornado survivors face hidden wounds
abstract: Mental health experts say that those affected by the May 31 tornadoes that swept across western PA are experiencing "hidden" injuries,  such as tremors, choking sensations, and panic attacks.  Dr. Gordon Foster, director of psychiatry at Butler Memorial Hospital, says that they have teams of workers in the community trying to assess problems and help people through the coming weeks.

headline: In TMI shadow
abstract: Letter to the editor defends the Patriot-News' ongoing coverage of the Three Mile Island (TMI) accident and subsequent arguments over its restart.  The author also praises US Senator John Heinz (R-PA), US Senator Arlen Specter (R-PA), Governor Dick Thornburgh, and US Representative Gekas for asking the Nuclear Regulatory Commission not to allow a restart of TMI.  The author criticizes the NRC for voting for a restart.

headline: Death Row Inmate Gives First Interview
abstract: Michael Travaglia, who was sentenced to death for four murders in Western PA, told Pittsburgh radio station KDKA that he regretted the killings but did not fear his fate.  Travaglia also said that death would mean closeness to God, and that life in prison would allow him to spread the word of God.

headline: Divide and be conquered
abstract: This editorial begins by talking about the traditional political divisions of Pennsylvania.  Dividing the state is not the way to conquer its problems, however, and the editorial points to a speech by Joseph Egan Jr., president of the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, who called on the various regions of the state to unite for mutual benefit.  The editorial believes that it is time for PA residents to consider uniting.

headline: Rush to protect
abstract: Editorial looks at how the US Congress is dealing with the nation's trade deficit, which is approaching $160 million annually.  Democrats, Republicans, and President Ronald Reagan are all proposing new protectionist policies; the editorial views these protectionist policies as wrong.  Protectionism is the most costly and least effective of all trade policies because there is no barrier that can protect and preserve an economic process that is inefficient, inferior, and replacable.  American workers and business need to be made more efficient, and new products, improved quality and production techniques, and new marketing strategies all can help companies survive competitive pressures posed by imports.  In cases where American firms cannot compete, prudence and common sense demand that we discontinue efforts in these fields.  The US must do a better job of helping firms move to more fertile grounds of business, and must help retrain and secure new jobs for workers in firms that cannot be saved.  Change is an intrinsic element of society that leads to its advancement; if given unfettered freedom, change can also be a devastating and heartless force.

headline: State hikes its offer to six unions: Offers 3 percent each year of pact
abstract: As contract talks continue, the Thornburgh administration improved its financial offer by offering a 3 percent wage increase in each year of a three year contract to six state employees' unions.  The lead union in the negotiations, the American Federation of State, Count, and Municipal Employees Council 13, has requested a one-year contract with a 7.5% pay increase.  Still on the negotiating table are administration demands that unions give up some sick leave, holidays and vacation time.

headline: The cases of two mentally ill
abstract: At a news conference, the state employees unit of the PA Nurses Association and the PA Association of State Mental Hospital Physicians urged the state Legislature to approve a resolution calling for a government task force study of the mental health system.  The resolution has passed the PA Senate and is awaiting action in the PA House.  Physicians and nurses cited the cases of two mentally ill women as reasons for reform. One mental-health patient went on a shooting rampage in a mall; the other was wrongfully hospitalized for nearly 30 years.

headline: Incinerator power idea catches on
abstract: A letter to the editor examines the idea of placing more energy-producing incinerators in Pennsylvania.  The author includes several advantages of incinerators and addresses the concerns associated with increased incinerators, among them pollution.

headline: Debate on prisons is lively
abstract: A columnist discusses the many different opinions on whether or not the state should allow private prisons to help deal with the overcrowding in public jails.

headline: Goode Cools Flap with Guv Over Center
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode released a letter he sent to Governor Thornburgh last week in which he assured the governor that he in no way intended to question the sincerity of his commitment to the convention center.  Goode and Thornburgh have been arguing over state support of the Center City convention center, and the $43.9 million that Governor Thornburgh has not yet released to the city.  Mayor Goode offered to clarify any questions or confusion that the governor had about the center.

headline: Soviet Union buys additional US corn
abstract: According to the US Department of Agriculture, the Soviet Union has bought an additional 200,000 metric tons of US corn for delivery through September 30.

headline: State lottery rejects US securities
abstract: Pat Wood, a spokeswoman for state Revenue Secretary Secretary James I. Scheiner, said that the agency had shelved a proposal to use federal securities to pay winners of large cash prizes in the state lottery.  The proposal was shelved because of concerns about the safety of such investments.  Wood said the agency would continue to purchase annuities from life insurance firms to pay large lottery prizes.  A special state House commmittee had recommended the use of federal government-backed securities.

headline: The Health Department plans
abstract: Officials at the PA Health Department say that the department plans to establish the state's 12th screening center for AIDS in Scranton; the Health Department is also considering four additional sites.  The state-operated screening program was established by the PA Health Department in June 1985 to ease the pressure on blood collection centers that already test for the disease.  At last count, PA had 341 confirmed cases of AIDS.

headline: Industrialists want Unit 1 restarted
abstract: A group of state industrial leaders has asked Governor Dick Thornburgh to soften his opposition to restarting the undamaged Unit 1 reactor at Three Mile Island.  These industrialists told the governor's top aids that further delay in returning the nuclear reactor to service could force some companies to close or leave the state because of the high cost of replacement electricity.

headline: Dennis MOVEs Over for D.C. Probers
abstract: US Justice Department attorneys are set to determine whether the events of May 13, 1985--the MOVE confrontation--warrant criminal prosecution.  The investigation will be headed by Linda Davis, the chief of the criminal section of the US Justice Department's Civil Rights Division.

headline: Families left homeless get $2,500 each: Rep. Conyers tours site with Goode
abstract: The people left homeless by the fire that devoured the MOVE house and 60 surrounding houses in West Philadelphia received $200 in cash and a $2,300 check from the city to help them find places to live.  The money was donated to the city from private sources.  US Representative John Conyers Jr., chairman of the House subcommittee on criminal justice, toured the area.  After touring the area, Conyers conferred with Mayor Goode and confirmed his intentions to hold a congressional investigation of the MOVE siege.

headline: Specter imports bill hits snag
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter ran into administration objections to a bill he is pushing that allows American firms damaged by unfair imports to seek direct court action.  The bill, which allows federal court judges to issue injunctions and impose penalties for unfairly priced imports, was unanimously approved by the Senate Judiciary Committee.  Specter heard strong opposition from the administration before the Senate Finance subcommittee and the panel chairman, Senator John Danforth.  Gilbert B. Kaplan, deputy assistant secretary for import administration, said the Specter bill violates international trade agreements and provides no guarantee that domestic industry complaints would be more quickly addressed.

headline: State payroll facts
abstract: A letter to the editor from a state employee defends state employees in PA.  The author says that state employees are not overpaid and there are not too many state employees, as the media often claims.

headline: They'd Pledge Hospitals To Poor's Right to Care
abstract: Robert McKeown, acting president of the Delaware Valley Hospital Council, agreed to try to get representatives of Philadelphia's 42 hospitals to sign the "hospital pledge of responsibility," which calls on hospitals in the city to stop requiring large deposits before treating non-insured, low-income patients.  The pledge of responsibility also requires them to begin treating low-income people who qualify for--but do not have--state medical assistance cards.  The pledge was written by the Philadelphia Unemployment Project, an advocate group for the jobless and poor.

headline: Industry loss linked to TMI
abstract: The price for power will be unstable until the Three Mile Island Unit 1 issue is resolved, said Clifford Jones, president of the PA Chamber of Commerce. The president of the York Chamber of Commerce, Carl Neu, said unemployment remains high because of the Three Mile Island issue and its impact on the willingness of businesses to invest in the region.

headline: Distinction
abstract: Several letters to the editor appear on this page about the MOVE confrontation and the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission's hearings on this issue.  The first letter praises two Philadelphia police officers who were on the scene of the MOVE incident on May 13.  The second letter calls for the formation of a police review board to hear complaints about police actions; the author does not believe that the police force can be counted on to police itself.  The third letter states that certain members of the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission are not impartial and have implied prejudices that hurt the commission's accountability.  The final letter states that the group MOVE is not in fact a terrorist group if you actually follow the definition of a terrorist group.

headline: Fearing neighborhood is lost, despite funds
abstract: Residents of the West Philadelphia neighborhood that was largely destroyed by a fire after a standoff between police and the radical group MOVE question whether city and federal money will be able to rebuild the neighborhood.  Residents question if the new houses will be of the same quality as the old ones, and whether the displaced will move back to their old homes.

headline: States Turn On to Exporting, But Their Timing May Be Off
abstract: A roundup article discusses exporting hopes for states around the nation, but says that the strength of the dollar relative to other currencies has ruined the foreign market for a lot of American goods.  US Senator John Heinz of PA was the prime sponsor of the export trading act.

headline: State police figure in state's political battles
abstract: The article investigates how deeply the PA state police are involved in the political process, and how they have been used for political purposes.  Major charges come from Allen Ertel, who unsuccessfully campaigned for PA Governor three years ago, who mentions that someone cancelled a rendezvous he was supposed to have with state police officers; the rendezvous was supposed to notify him of an alleged threat on his life.  Democrats also charge that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh is using the state police to conduct a polictically-motivated investigation into Democratic management of the Turnpike Commission.  Politics was also visible in shaping the fortunes of the state police during the parliamentary burial.

headline: Transfer Forecast
abstract: This editorial sympathizes with personnel at Scranton State General Hospital who have been furloughed because of a continuing decline in the number of patients served by the hospital.  The author recognizes that the PA Department of Public Welfare would be remiss in its stewardship of taxpayer dollars to allow the hospital to retain unneeded medical workers, however.  The 176-bed hospital is averaging 60 patients, and its annual deficit is projected at almost $4 million.  The editorial believes that the state is correct to try to get out of the hospital business.

headline: Integrity Issue Still Vital: TMI Restart OK'd
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission voted 4-1 to allow the reopening of Unit 1 at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant.  This editorial says that everyone would feel more secure about restarting Unit 1 if the NRC had addressed the issue of  management integrity as Governor Dick Thornburgh had requested.  The editorial hopes that the integrity issue will be addressed when the case is heard by the US 3rd District Circuit Court of Appeals.

headline: Doctor's note brings delay of Ramona Africa hearing
abstract: Ramona Johnson Africa, who is still recovering from burns suffered in the MOVE confrontation on May 13, was unable to appear in court yesterday to face the criminal charges.  Municipal Court Judge Earl Simmons postponed a preliminary hearing after Assistant District Attorney Joseph McGill read a letter certifying that Africa was still in detention at Giuffre Hospital recuperating from skin burns.  Africa was taken into custody by police after she escaped from the flames engulfing the MOVE compound in West Philadelphia.

headline: Federal agency still mum on $2.4 million for Centralia
abstract: A letter from Nicholas DeBenedictis, secretary of the PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER), has been ignored by the US Office of Surface Mining (OSM).  DeBenedictis was requesting 2.4 million dollars for displaced residents of Centralia.  The federal agency on January 25 rejected the DER's request for $2.4 million in last-resort housing money, even though US Congress had allocated $3.5 million for that purpose.  The borough of Centralia has been plagued by an underground mine fire that has caused all but 35 families to abandon the area.  The DER and the Office of Surface Mining disagree on how far the families should have to move from their old neighborhoods, as well as how much money each family should get.

headline: The foreign steel scam
abstract: This editorial examines a new wrinkle that foreign steel makers have found to bedevil the American steel industry:  steel exports from countries that lack steel-making facilities.  In an effort to limit foreign steel to 18.5% of the domestic market, US President Ronald Reagan has negotiated import restraints with 15 nations already; some of those states are exceeding their quotas by using countries not covered by restraints, however.  The editorial worries that when this is combined with subsidized exports and goods sold here at artificially low prices, these practices could incite Congress to protectionism that would damage world trade.  The editorial also attacks the Reagan administration as a semi-paralyzed group that preaches trade fairness but is unwilling to take steps to implement it.

headline: State Senate moving to end expense abuse
abstract: The PA Senate is close to implementing a series of rules changes aimed at reducing abuse of the Senate expense-account.  However, the PA House continues to bar the public from access to documents--such as receipts and leases--used to justify House members' individual expense reimbursements.  In the Senate, one major cause of abuse of the expense-account was automobiles.

headline: Trying a different route to get Medicaid on track
abstract: PA is trying to change the way in which people receive Medicaid services by enrolling people in a system that assigns them a primary-care doctor.   The primary-care doctor will be given the task of practicing preventive medicine and directing patients to specialists.  There will be a demonstration of this new system, called Health-PASS, run in South and West Philadelphia by a for-profit company.  This editorial urges state officials and welfare rights organizations to allow the demonstration to take place and to carefully consider its results--especially since the new system could provide better health care in the state.

headline: It's back to work
abstract: The PA Legislature returns from its summer break with lots of work on the table.  Several issues that must be dealt with include laws governing the state's Liquor Control Board and Public Utility Commission, as well as developing a plan to safely get rid of PA's radioactive waste.  A special committee of the State House also released its sunset review of the Public Utility Commission, which indicates that the commission has failed to vigorously pursue the public interest in regulating utilities; the review recommends changes in PUC policies.

headline: Don't rush into profit prisons
abstract: The state House of Representatives passed a bill that would delay the certification of privately operated prisons for a year; this will allow the PA Crime Commission to take a thorough look at them.  The editorial commends the House on its action and urges the state Senate to continue the moratorium until the full costs and responsibilities of prisons-for-profit can be examined by the people of PA.

headline: Funds gain for MOVE rebuilding
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode's funding package for the MOVE neighborhood began to solidify as City Council's Appropriations Committee sent the full Council two ordinances that were worth $1.5 million.  City officials have yet to determine how much money the state will contribute to the package, which now includes $5.5 million in city funds and $1 million in federal funds.  Under a redevelopment plan approved by both the Planning Commission and the Redevelopment Authority, a total of $3.26 million would have to be spent in the West Philadelphia neighborhood to repair streets, utility lines and to aid dislocated homeowners and tenants.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts a couple leaving the "Le'vart Travel Agency."  The agency has signs that say, "See the Mideast" and "Visit Places."  The travel agent says, "When you get there, don't drink the water... It's been poisoned!"

headline: State taxes low
abstract: A letter to the editor from David Runkel, press secretary for Governor Thornburgh, says that the US Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Regulations (ACIR) identified PA as 26th in the country in per capita state and local taxes in 1983;  Runkel said that PA is a low-tax state.  He says that President Ronald Reagan's proposed tax reform plan would help the state because the ACIR identified PA as one of 36 states that are net losers under the current taxation system.

headline: Way open for MD to get license
abstract: Legislation opening the door for ex-convicts like Timothy McCormick to get a PA medical license was signed yesterday by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.  The legislation, which is primarily designed to re-establish the PA Medical Education and Licensure Board, also contains a provision enabling the board to, under certain conditions, license people with drug-related felony records.  McCormick could not be reached for comment but indicated earlier that he was not satisfied that this bill would benefit him.

headline: Judge Bars Restart of TMI Reactor: Hearing Set June 27 On Undamaged Unit
abstract: Judge Collins J. Seitz of the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ordered that the Unit 1 reactor at Three Mile Island remain in cold shutdown pending a Nuclear Regulatory Commission hearing on June 27th.  The order was requested by the state of PA, the Union of Concerned Scientists and a central PA public interest group--Three Mile Island Alert.

headline: Event draws all 3 D.A. candidates
abstract: The three candidates for Philadelphia District Attorney made an unusual joint appearance.  Each had 30 minutes to present his views on the best ways to prosecute crime.  Republican Ronald Castille and Democrats John Scott and Robert W. Williams Jr. spoke at a forum sponsored by the community safety program of the Northwest Interfaith Movement at La Salle University.

headline: Goode Meets Guv's Terms on Convention Center
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode abandoned plans for a public-private construction venture for Philadelphia's proposed convention center.  In doing so, Mayor Goode won a renewed commitment from Governor Dick Thornburgh to provide $185 million for the project.  Goode acceded to Thornburgh's demand that the $441 million center be publicly owned and constructed by a firm selected through a public bidding process.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts President Ronald Reagan giving a speech at Bitburg, Germany.  The president says, "I come to Bitburg to honor Germany's fallen soldiers...Except for that one, that one, those two in the corner...

headline: State workers' demands reasonable
abstract: A letter to the editor from Karen Donaldson, Assistant Shop Steward of the PA Social Services Union (PSSU), discusses the union's demands in its contract negotiations with the state.  Donaldson says that the main concern for the union was the benefits package; Donaldson said that the state does not want to offer good benefits to the union.

headline: What To Do About Mental-Health System
abstract: This editorial restates its previous position that PA's policy of de-institutionalizing mentally ill, mentally handicapped, and mentally retarded persons has gone too far.  The editorial now asks what can be done to change this situation.  Although public disclosure of deliberate or unintentional abuse of patients is good for a newspaper, in the long run such publicity may pose serious problems.  There is also a danger of overreaction from continuing to publish these stories and a fear that the current system of de-institutionalizing will be replaced with a worse system.  There is also a concern about the credibility of the stories about abuse, since many come from mentally ill patients.  The editorial concludes that, although the newspaper will continue to publish stories, the only way to get real change is by working within the current system and reporting problems to the appropriate officials.

headline: Last Stand of the Anti-Nukes
abstract: This editorial believes that Three Mile Island's Unit 1 should be allowed to restart, and that the only thing holding it back is a stubborn group of anti-nuke activists.  The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has compiled more than 100,000 pages on TMI and has concluded it is safe; the PA State Health Department, along with the vast majority of responsible scientists, has concluded that the TMI accident caused no health damage to people in the area.  Given all of those who believe that TMI Unit 1 can be run without danger, it is time for the anti-nuke activists to stop playing martyr to a dead cause.

headline: Ex-coroner ordered to pay $250,000
abstract: Former Allegheny County Coroner Cyril Wecht must pay the county more than $250,000 for private pathology work his office did without the county's authorization.  Wecht was charged with using his staff and county facilities to perform work for other counties and for Wecht's private laboratory.

headline: Goode pleased but cautious on convention-center progress
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said he was pleased that state and city officials had made progress this week in breaking the deadlock over control of Philadelphia's proposed convention center.  Mayor Goode cautioned that a final agreement had not been reached, however.  The PA House voted in the spring of 1985 to appropriate $141 million to the construction of the convention center.  Key legislators in the PA Senate, however, have blocked a vote on that appropriation, pending resolution of the question of whether the city or the state would control the convention center.  Under the terms of the proposal to resolve the impasse, two boards will be created--one to govern construction of the center and another to govern the operations of the center.  The city of Philadelphia would have a greater voice over opreations--but not construction--of the center.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon depicts the "Khomeini Travel Agency."  The agency has posters around it such as "Summer Special: Visit 5 Terrorist Targets in 6 days." "See Europe while it's still here." "Beirut." and "Fly TWA."

headline: State yields on salary issue
abstract: An official at a session between Thornburgh administration negotiators and representatives of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) said that the governor has moved away from an offer of a 2% pay increase in a three-year contract.  The new offer from the administration involves 2% pay increases in each of the first two years of the contract and another 2% in the third year to be distributed on a "merit basis."  AFSCME is asking for a 7.5% pay increase and has threatened to call a strike unless a contract agreement is reached by July 1.

headline: Who's Watching the Doctors?
abstract: A Philadelphia Daily News investigation found out that The Pennsylvania Board of Medical Education and Licensure rarely finds out about incompetent doctors, and when it does, takes an average of three years to investigate and take action.

headline: Legislative panel Oks coal bills
abstract: Legislation designed to stimulate the use of PA coal was unanimously endorsed by the House Mines and Energy Management Committee.

headline: Executions routinely allowed, Marshall says
abstract: US Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall yesterday charged that the US court system is allowing murder and other capital defendants to be executed even though they have had incompetent, inexperienced defense attorneys.  Marshall, who opposes the death penalty, said that at their trials, defendants facing the death penalty "frequently suffer the consequences of having trial counsel who are ill-equipped to handle capital cases".  Marshall added that the defendant's chances of succeeding on appeal are further diminished by the US Supreme Court's view that a criminal lawyer meeting only a minimal standard of competence may represent clients in capital cases.
