In recent years, the US Supreme Court has streamlined that appeals process due to what it sees as stalling tactics by defense laywers in capital appeals, something Marshall calls a "rush to judgment."

headline: Goode Shifts Attention To Rebuilding: Philadelphia to Get $1 Million US Aid
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode focused his attention on rebuilding the west Philadelphia community shattered May 13 when a police assault against a militant radical group's headquarters left 11 persons dead and 53 homes destroyed.  Goode led US Housing and Urban Development Secretary Samuel R. Pierce and US Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter on a walking tour of the neighborhood.  This was prior to Pierce announcing a $1 million federal grant to assist in the rebuilding program.  Pierce also said that rent and mortgage subsidies and federally-owned temporary homes would be made available to those whose homes had been destroyed.

headline: 2 Germanys, 2 recollections
abstract: The ceremonies marking the 40th anniversary of the liberations of the Berge-Belsen concentration camp and the Ravensbruck concentration camp contrasted dramatically the different paths that West and East Germany have taken as each nation seeks to explain and reconcile the horrors of the concentration camps.  In West Germany, the path has been agonizing and awkward; the ceremony at Bergen-Belsen was sponsored by the Central Jewish Council, not by the government, and is the only ceremony of its kind in West Germany.  The East Germans have not experienced such difficulties and the anniversary of the liberation of the camps provides them an opportunity to reinforce their ties with the Soviet Union.  They do this by honoring those who suffered and died in what they consider a victorious struggle against fascism.

headline: State's 'sunshine'law a continuing disgrace
abstract: According to a recent report prepared at the University of Minnesota and released by the public interest group Common Cause, PA has the least-open sunshine law of all 50 states.  This editorial supports state Senate Bill 303, which would require all state and local government agencies to hold their deliberations of public business in open session if a quorum is present.

headline: Ailing poultry industry on the comeback trail
abstract: After battling the Avian flu in 1984, the poultry industry in PA is making a comeback.  This comeback is evidenced by the return of poultry to the Farm Show.  More than $50 million in state tax money was spent battling the Avian flu; this involved killing birds that could possibly be infected.  The industry is on the rise again, but there is still cause for concern.

headline: Limerick points
abstract: Letter to the Editor:  The July 22nd editorial "PUC law judge says 'No' to completing Limerick 2" was incorrect in its assesment that Administrative Law Judge Allison Turner recommended that Philadelphia Electric Company be allowed to recover its $897 million investment.  Judge Turner ruled that Philadelphia Electric Company only be allowed to recover those portions that it can show to be prudent, and a careful reading of her decision also shows that there may be a portion of their investment that is imprudent.  Furthermore, the editorial, in its mention of those who opposed completion of Limerick 2, forgot to mention the Public Utility Commission trial staff.

headline: Expert:  Police Erred on Bomb
abstract: James Phelan, a consulant who used to be one of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's principal bombing specialists, testified before the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission yesterday that the bomb dropped on the MOVE house May 13 could not possibly have knocked off the fortified bunker from the roof.  Phelan was also critical of the bomb's creators saying they were wrong in their choice of explosives and wrong to deliver the device from a helicopter.  Phelan also concluded that the bomb was more powerful than the one described by Officer William Klein, who assembled it.  Most of the commission's morning session yesterday was devoted to accounts from police officers who either witnessed or participated in the escape of two MOVE members from the flaming house.  The most dramatic testimony was from Officer James Berghaier who told the commission how he rescued Birdie Africa.

headline: Goode, Guv Sparring Over Funds for Center
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode asked Governor Dick Thornburgh to reaffirm his support fot the city's proposed convention center by releasing $43.9 million in state funds earmarked for the project; the governor has frozen the funds.  The governor responded with a stinging letter chiding Goode for the city's inability to line up legislative support for the full $185-million state portion of the $441 million convention-center package.

headline: 2 sick hostages may go free: Hijackers cheered by Shiites
abstract: One week after two young Shiite gunment seized a TWA Boeing 727 on an Athens-Rome flight, hundreds of Shiite Moslem radicals demonstrated and showed their support at the airport near the TWA jet.  Meanwhile Shiite leaders were considering releasing two  hostages who have health problems.  Both the US and Israel have refused to negotiate with those holding the hostages.

headline: Stevens wants seat belt referendum
abstract: PA State Representative Corry Stevens will introduce a bill Monday calling for controversial mandatory seat belt legislation to be placed on the May primary ballot as a public question.  Stevens only wants the question added to the ballot if no action has been taken on it before the election.  Many other representatives support this idea, and Stevens may ask that it be a binding vote.  This would mean that the government would have to abide by the wishes of the electorate.

headline: Amusement rules long overdue
abstract: This editiorial argues that the PA Department of Agriculture, which is charged with regulation of amusement park rides, should produce an official set of safety standards to help enforce the Amusement Ride Inspection Act.  The current safety standards being used are a weaker substitute for the type of comprehensive regulations that are required.  The editorial wants PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to step in and see that this deficiency is corrected.

headline: Message same as in '82 vote: Keep TMI shut
abstract: Dauphin, Cumberland and Lebanon county residents commemorated the third anniversary of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart referendum by gathering in Riverfront Park to say their message remains the same: Keep the reactor shut tight.  The demonstration was sponsored by Three Mile Island Alert because they fear that the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission will vote in favor of GPU Nuclear Corporation's request to restart the Unit 1 reactor.  The group wants the NRC to know how the public feels about restarting the reactor.

headline: Ex-state police commander testifies in trial of trooper
abstract: A state police probe of allegations against PA State Trooper James Drenning showed that none of the allegations could be substantiated.

headline: Groups Say Growth Plan Slights Neighborhoods
abstract: About a dozen speakers representing a variety of neighborhood and civic groups told Philadelphia City Council's Advisory Committee on Economic Development that a plan catering to big-business economic development projects downtown, proposed by Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, gives short shrift to neighborhood projects.  Goode's development plans are designed to help Philadelphia recover from economic troubles over the last 20 years.  Other concerns raised at the committee meeting are also included in the article.

headline: Byrons en route to base
abstract: Colonial Park, PA resident Carolyn Byron boarded a jet bound for West Germany last night to be reunited with her husband, who was taken hostage the last time the Byrons traveled overseas.  Byron will greet her husband, Leo C. Byron, one of the 39 Americans freed yesterday by Shiite terrorists.

headline: Sticky issues awaiting Legislature's return in January
abstract: Much of the PA General Assembly's energy in 1985 was spent on liquor, gambling, toll roads, and car insurance.  And although major progress was made in some areas, most of these issues remain unresolved.  The article is a review of major work that the PA General Assemby did in this legislative session.  The issues discussed are the PA Liquor Control Board, the licensing of health-care professionals, the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund, state taxes and budgeting, hunting license fees, and the PA Turnpike Commission.

headline: Apple Growers Slice Promotion Program
abstract: Earlier this summer, PA apple growers voted to disband an 18-year-old apple marketing program.  Instead, the PA Department of Agriculture has decided to fork over $75,000 for a pared-down fall program.  Though no one is quite sure how the money will be spent, radio promotions and point-of-purchase advertising will probably factor into the equation.  Apple growers may reinstate their own advertising program in the next spring.  In other news, the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers, the city's largest teachers union, is using advertising to get the public to better understand their demands in a new round of contract negotiations.

headline: Met-Ed bills will fall at the end of a roller-coaster ride
abstract: Customers of Metropolitan Edison Company are about to be in for a wild ride with their electric bills.  The company's electric bills will decrease when Three Mile Island Unit 1 is operating at 35% of full output for 100 consecutive hours.  Bills will also decrease further due to the fact that the electricity Metropolitan Edison is purchasing is significantly less expensive than estimated.  However, a separate case involving a request for $47.3 million more a year in earnings may increase Met-Ed electric bills.  PUC Administrative Law Judge Harry Cohen recommended that Met-Ed may be entitled to $19.9 million of its request, and it appears that the PUC's total is going to come close to the judge's decision.  A rate boost of $19 million would cancel out the decrease in energy cost, allowing the restart of TMI Unit 1 to slightly lower electric bills.  PUC commissioners agreed yesterday with Cohen's recommendations for trimming Met-Ed's request for $47.3 million.

headline: Ex-state worker tells of influence on contract
abstract: David Herbert, a former state employee, described to a jury how a California businessman courted him with company stock and free trips to the West Coast in exchange for ensuring that Computer Technology Associates (CTA) won a $4.8 million state contract.  Herbert also said he was induced by the hope that CTA lawyer William Smith would pull political strings and get him a better state job.  Smith and Alan Stoneman, CTA's California lawyer, are on trial here on charges of conspiracy; this is all part of a bribery scheme behind a state computer contract that Treasurer Budd Dwyer awarded CTA.

headline: Heat aid cutoff gets cold shoulder
abstract: At a public hearing, dozens of speakers and interest groups attacked a plan by the PA State Department of Public Welfare to make it more difficult for poor people to qualify for federal heating-assistance aid.  The federally funded home energy program dispersed $113 million last winter to 356,474 households across the state, with 70% going to homes with income below $7,000.  Faced with the prospect of getting $6 million less this winter, the PA Department of Public Welfare would like to cut off some people whose income made them eligible last year.  Senior-citizen groups said that the new guidelines will particularly hurt the elderly, most of whom are on fixed incomes.

headline: Ex-hostage Byron weighs TWA settlement, lawsuit
abstract: Leo Byron, a former hostage from TWA Flight 847, said that he and his lawyer have recenlty been discussing a possible settlement offer with Trans-World Airlines (TWA) regarding the airline's handling of the incident.  TWA Flight 847 was hijacked by Lebanese Shiite Muslims as the plane left Athens, Greece.  TWA has made initial offers to the hostages of the flight, though some have decided to sue TWA in court for negligence and failing to take appropriate safety precautions.  Byron would not comment on the merits of these lawsuits, but did say that the incident has left a strong mark on the lives of the hostages.

headline: The advertising for Robert Casey, which talks about the real Bob Casey, might be confusing for those people who were not in PA at the time of the elections
abstract: The Casey-family  phenomenon has played a large part in PA state politics; it has also played a part in Casey's other political defeats.

headline: Blackflies on the run: Pest war expensive; other counties should help
abstract: The blackfly has been plaguing the midstate area since 1979.  However, thanks to "Neighbors Against Gnats," work by State Representative Jeffrey Piccola, and the state Department of Environmental Resources (DER), more than $1 million was allocated to fight the problem and scientists were able to develop "Bti" spray to kill the bugs safely.  This editorial commends the community, the DER, and Piccola, but says that all 26 midstate counties should have helped to pay for the program--rather than just Dauphin and Cumberland Counties.

headline: Met-Ed deserves $19.9 million rate boost, PUC judge says
abstract: PA Public Utility Commission Judge Herbert Cohen said yesterday that Metropolitan Edison Company is entitled to $19.9 million of a requested $47.3 million annual rate increase.  Cohen also disallowed a requested $9 million in depreciation expenses for the undamaged Unit 1 reactor at Three Mile Island.  PUC officials could not immediately determine what effect Cohen's decision would have on average cusomter rates.  Met-Ed filed for the rate increase in January 1985, claiming the extra revenue was needed to meet increasing operating expenses.  The return of TMI Unit 1 will automatically trigger rate adjustments that already have been approved.  Cohen also recommended approval of Met-Ed's request for an accounting move that would transfer an extra $8.3 million to the cleanup at TMI Unit 2.

headline: Ex-TMI manager gets fine, community-service sentence
abstract: US District Judge Sylvia Rambo fined James Floyd, the former supervisor of operations at Three Mile Island's Unit 2 reactor, $2000 and sentenced him to perform 400 hours of community service; he was also placed on probation for two years.  Floyd was convicted on two counts of cheating on a federal licensing exam.

headline: Helping the homeless
abstract: This editorial defends Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode's actions.  Mayor Goode had police officers force all homeless people in from the sub-zero cold to shelters.  The editorial describes one of Philadelphia's drop-in homeless shelters and the work that is done there to help the homeless.

headline: Harrisburg greets 'tired' ex-hostage
abstract: After 17 days as a captive of Shiite Moslems in Beirut, former hostage Leo C. Byron has come home to PA feeling "very thankful" but also "very, very tired" .  Governor Dick Thornburgh and his wife, Ginny, were at Capitol City Airport to greet Byron, an executive assistant in the state Department of Public Welfare.

headline: Still in race: GOP coroner hopeful off ballot, will seek write-in
abstract: Republican Sandford Edberg, whose nominating petition was judged one signature shy of the 500 required, is expected to launch a write-in campaign for Allegheny County coroner in the May 21 primary.  Coroner Joshua Perper had challenged Edberg's petition, which contained 526 signatures; Perper said that some of the signatures either were illegible, cross-signed, or belonged to people not registered to vote.

headline: Farm workers told to define impact on state's economy
abstract: Mark Voulavka, a research analyst for the state House majority leader, spoke during the annual PA Farmworkers Opportunities conference and told farm workers that, in order to get positive legislation from the state General Assembly, they must demonstrate specifically how they are impacted as a group by government action or inaction.  Voulavka said there is a conflict between what farm workers want from the government and what the government sees as the needs of the farm-business community.

headline: Met-Ed files for $26.7 million more in yearly revenue
abstract: Metropolitan Edison Company filed rate requests with the state Public Utility Commission that would generate $26.7 million more a year in revenues.  State Consumer Advocate David Barash said that he would fight the case because the rate increases were unreasonably high.

headline: FBI Retrieves C-4 Explosive from Police
abstract: The US Federal Bureau of Investigation removed their stock of the military explosive C-4 from the Philadelphia Police Academy yesterday, less than a week after federal authorities acknowledged having supplied the police with the material.  The existence of C-4 came to light on Friday during a hearing of the Philadelphia Special Investigation Commission.  There is some speculation that C-4 was used in the bomb that was dropped on the MOVE house, however police sources deny that charge, saying that the officer who constructed the bomb did not know it was available.  A letter from the FBI said that the C-4 was given to the Philadelphia Police because of a specific request.  Officer William Klein, who constructed the bomb, has refused to testify before the commission, but has said in police interviews that C-4 was used in the bomb he made.  Prior to this point, the police had maintained that they only had a small quantity of C-4.  There is still some question about inventory records at the Philadelphia Police Academy, where the C-4 was stored.

headline: Housing the homeless
abstract: This editorial discusses the plight of the homeless in the winter months and notes that eight Pittsburgh companies and corporate foundations have contributed $60,000 to fund three new emergency shelters for the homeless in Pittsburgh.

headline: Heinz Under Pressure From Apartheid Foes
abstract: US Senator John Heinz III is being pressured by Pittsburghers Against Apartheid (PAA) and the Pittsburgh National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) African and Foreign Affairs Committee to vote for tough economic sanctions against the Repulic of South Africa.  Heinz sits on the Senate Banking Committee, which is now considering legislation that would ban certain types of US-South Africa business.  Referred to as the Anti-Apartheid Act of 1985, the bill is intended to use American moral and economic influence to end South Africa's racist apartheid system.

headline: Stone denies charges in CTA case
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council President Robert Rade Stone strongly denied wrongdoing in connection with the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery scandal.  Stone's statement came in response to a lawsuit filed by city Controller Thomas Flaherty, who accused Stone and five others of illegally using their influence to gain a $150,000 city contract for CTA.  The suit charges that after recommending CTA to city officials, stoned received a check for $6,374 and an option to buy 35,000 shares in a company that John Torquato, head of CTA, planned to establish.

headline: Farmers Testify Before House Committee
abstract: Bradford County farmers affected by the financial collapse of their milk hauler, Northeast Dairy Cooperative Federation Incorporated (NEDCO), testified before the PA Legislature Friday, and said that they favor legislation which would require dairy cooperatives to contribute to a milk security fund.  NEDCO, which is in financial trouble, has missed payments to several of its milk suppliers.  This follows the bankruptcy of Scheps Cheese Company, which owed $3.2 million in payments to its milk suppliers.  Donald Hamilton, a former NEDCO member, said that co-ops must shorten the length of time between milk shipments and when payment on the milk is received.

headline: More motions filed against research chief
abstract: Motions have been filed with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission urging that Ivan Smith be ousted from the panel considering the Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart.  Motions were filed by the Union of Concerned Scientists, Three Mile Island Alert, and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania; all cite similar charges.

headline: Federal officials are pressing forward with child porn crackdown in midstate
abstract: Federal officials continue a rigorous crackdown, working 50 hours a week, on child pornography in central PA.  There have been seven arrests and one conviction in the first two months of the investigation.  Part of this stems from a 1984 change in federal law that now makes it illegal for a person to receive child pornography.

headline: Hundreds line up to seek homes
abstract: Over 2,000 people waited in line to fill out applications to receive a home for rehabilitation in Philadelphia.  Philadelphia has a program through the Office of Housing called a "special acquisition effort" that allows city residents who own no property and who are within certain income limits to apply to receive a home for rehabilitation; they must live in the home for at least five years.  The city will acquire 1,600 properties that are vacant or tax delinquent and allow those who qualify to live in them and rehabilitate them.

headline: Home is where the ex-hostages are, at last: Ex-captive says name Ali is out
abstract: Dr. Arthur Toga of St. Louis, a man who was held hostage by Shiite Moslems on TWA Flight 847, promised his captors that he would name his unborn child Hussein Ali in order to facilitate his release.  Upon his return to the US, Toga announced that he will not live up to that promise, and that his child will not receive either name.

headline: Study it: Special legislative panels stir debate on their worth
abstract: The excessive number of special committees formed by the State legislature, particularly the House of Representatives, is being criticized by the Thornburgh administration and Republican lawmakers.  Critics say that too many times these committees are designed for political purpose and are a waste of taxpayer money.

headline: Food plan position clarified
abstract: State Agriculture Secretary Penrose Hallowell said he had "no objections or major comments" about a proposal to move an emergency food program to the Department of Health.  However, Department of Agriculture officials are now saying that they want to administer the emergency food program if the Legislature decides to budget money for the program.

headline: New deluge of health lawsuits filed against TMI firms
abstract: More than six years after the accident at Three Mile Island nuclear facility, roughly 1,300 Dauphin County area residents are filing lawsuits against General Public Utilities Corporation and other TMI-related corporations.  The plaintiffs claim they were exposed to radiation because of the March 1979 accident and that it increased their risks of cancer, birth defects, vertigo, and other medical ailments.  According to TMI, studies show that the mishap was not a health concern to local residents, and lawyers representing TMI have vowed a rigorous defense.

headline: Fewer convicts avoided jail in '84, study says
abstract: A report issued by the PA Commission on Sentencing showed that, in 1984, a larger proportion of convicted criminals were sent to state prison and county jails; the report also showed that those criminals will likely stay in jail longer.  The commision indicated that the increases were the result of guidelines and mandatory-sentencing rules imposed for crimes committed after mid-1982.

headline: K-4 could add spark to area
abstract: This editorial talks with pride about the return of K-4, a historic locomotive, to Altoona.  The locomotive has rusted, but is about to undergo a $250,000 makeover.  The editorial believes that K-4 is an example of what happens when a community works together; the repaired engine may eventually haul more economic developments to the area.

headline: Home is where the ex-hostages are, at last: President pledges to try to free remaining captives
abstract: Thirty former hostages of TWA Flight 847 returned home and were welcomed by President Ronald Reagan.  The president said there will be no forgetting that one of their fellow captives was killed, and that seven other Americans remain imprisoned in Lebanon.  The freed Americans, who had been held hostage in Beirut with nine others for 17 days, arrived at Andrews Air Force Base aboard a special TWA flight from Frankfurt, West Germany.

headline: 'Sunshine law' revision needed
abstract: This editorial urges state legislators to pass legislation that would amend the Sunshine Law and require preliminary meetings of local government to be open to the public--rather than just meetings in which a vote takes place.

headline: Grand champion bull selected
abstract: The Grand Champion, Polled Hereford bull, was selected at the state Farm Show in Harrisburg.

headline: New Light Shed on 1979 Reactor Accident
abstract: A new report released by scientists at the Idaho National Engineering Laboratory, a contractor for the US Department of Energy, shows that some nuclear fuel melted twice before cooling and resolidifying at the base of the reactor during the 1970 Three-Mile-Island accident.  The report offers new evidence of how close the TMI Unit-2 reactor came to a meltdown.

headline: 'First ladies' summit' slated at White House
abstract: Nancy Reagan is bringing together the wives of prime ministers and presidents from around the world for the White House's first "first ladies' summit" on drug abuse.

headline: Norfolk Southern seeks to reassure civic leaders on Conrail takeover
abstract: Executives from Norfolk Southern Corporation came to Philadelphia in an attempt to calm the fears of Mayor Wilson Goode and business leaders about the effect that the company's acquisition of Conrail would have on the region's economy.  They did not promise that they would not cut jobs at Conrail's corporate headquarters in Center City; 4500 persons are employed at the Center-City location.

headline: Home is where the ex-hostages are, at last: VIP hello served up for Byron
abstract: Former TWA Flight 847 hostage Leo C. Byron, a supervisor with the state Department of Public Welfare Office of Client Rights at the Harrisburg State Hospital, got a VIP reception at Capital City Airport as he was welcomed by Governor Dick Thornburgh and his wife Ginny, as well as 15 co-workers and friends.  The Byrons were on their way from Athens to Rome when terrorists commandeeered the TWA jet they were aboard and held the passengers hostage.  Carolyn and Pamela, Byron's wife and daughter, were released in Algiers, Algeria, after 33 hours aboard the plane.

headline: Taxing City's Resources: Cliett Wary of Deduction Reduction
abstract: Philadelphia City Revenue Commissioner Eugene L. Cliett Jr. said that some of the changes in the federal income tax law proposed by President Ronald Reagan would have a negative effect on Philadelphia's ability to generate tax revenue.  Cliett said the proposal to abolish deductions for state and local taxes would lead to increased pressure to lower city and state taxes.  All of this would come at a time when the city is under serious financial strain.

headline: Growing U.S. Taste for Mushrooms
abstract: This article looks at the increasing popularity and diversity of mushrooms in America.  In Reading, PA, a strong growing interest in regional and natural products, coupled with the back-to-the-land movement of the 1970's, gave a strong push to wild mushrooms in the area.  Mushroom culitivation has also progressed, with mushrooms that were orginally harvested in other countries now being harvested in America.  The remainder of the aritcle looks at various types of mushrooms and the types of food with which they go best.

headline: N-industry funds help communities prepare for crises
abstract: Counties and municipalities near the five nuclear power plants are now eligible to receive annual allotments from a nuclear-emergency fund.  Act 147, passed last year, created the two funds, which will be made up of annual contributions from nuclear utilities and companies that ship nuclear fuel.  Act 147 requires owners of nuclear power plants to pay $100,000 a year into an emergency response fund.  Each at-risk county is then alloted $3,000 for itself and$1,000 for each at-risk community within it.

headline: Former candidate awarded $10,000
abstract: A Dauphin County Court jury has awarded $10,000 to Donald Ely, a midstate Republican who sued his party's campaign committee and two campaign workers after he lost a state legislative race in 1982.  The jury awarded Ely $2,000 from the Republican Legislative Campaign Committee and $4,000 each from Stephen Pancoe and Stephen Dull; these men selected a "doctored" photograph for use in Ely's campaign literature.  Ely charged that his reputation, his chances in the campaign and his political future were damaged by the negative publicity surrounding this photograph.

headline: MOVE neighbors say contractor cut corners in rebuilding work
abstract: Homeowners who lost their houses when the Philadelphia Police confronted MOVE on May 19th are unhappy with the current effort to rebuild their neighborhood.  Almost all of the 270 residents, who were displaced when a fire started by a police bomb destroyed 61 row houses, now live temporarily at International City, an apartment complex near Philadelphia International Airport.  United Survivors of the Cobbs Creek Disaster, which represents the displaced residents, filed a preliminary objection in Common Pleas Court, as an insurance policy.  If the residents are displeased with the work, they may refuse to accept the houses and then sue the city for their losses.  The developer hired by the city has become a cause for concern, as he failed to report two earlier bankruptcies and has been charged with forgery by his former partner.  Some residents are also dismayed that the price of their new houses has soared to 35% over the original estimates.

headline: Hostages Are Moved, Amal Says: Shiites issue warning against a US strike
abstract: The American hostages in Beirut were moved to new hideouts. Shiite Amal leaders warned that any US military activity would cause serious harm to their captives.  Shiite leaders threatened to return the hostages to the hijackers of TWA Flight 847 in a couple of days if no progress was made in negotiations for the release of 766 Lebanese prisoners held by Israel.  The US is holding Amal militia leader Nabih Berri responsible for what happens to the hostages.

headline: Testimony implicates state aide
abstract: Janice Kincaid, a former Computer Technology Associates (CTA) employee, said that a Thornburgh administration aide helped CTA work with the Treasury Department without Governor Thornburgh finding out.  CTA did not think that Thornburgh would sign legislation because of his feud with state Treasurer Budd Dwyer; to circumvent this problem, the legislation was attached as an amendment to a bill that dealt with school closings.  Kincaid said that John Pierce, special assistant to Administration Secretary Murray Dickman, said Thornburgh "had to sign this bill."  Pierce has denied his involvement.

headline: Here's the beef! Casey hightails it to Farm Show title, trailed by Chester
abstract: The state Farm Show's grand champion and reserve champion baby beef award was announced.

headline: No democracy
abstract: A letter to the editor cites the US Supreme Court's refusal to stop the restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor as proof that we do not live in a democracy.  The author contends that power is vested in the dominant class; we live in an oligarchy.

headline: Former district justice wants his old job again: King of Hill Pinamonti is ready for comeback
abstract: Joseph Pinamonti, the former district justice who was suspended by the state Supreme Court because of allegations that he sexually harassed female employees, is planning a comeback.

headline: New companies taking up jobs slack, group says
abstract: Penn Southwest Association believes that too much attention is being paid to Pittsburgh's economic problems and not enough attention is being paid to its successes.  Since 1980, 45,000 jobs in traditional metalworking industries have left the area, but 270 companies have moved to southwestern PA during that time.  According to Penn Southwest, the new firms have generated 40,000 new jobs, and foreign firms, which represent 142 of the 270 new firms, have brought in roughly $4 billion in investment.  Penn Southwest officials believe that Pittsburgh has a bright future as a major growth area for financial institutions, health centers, foreign firms, and high-tech industries.

headline: Keeler reports on famine in Africa
abstract: Bishop William Keeler, speaking at a press conference yesterday at the Diocese of Harrisburgh, said that the lives of thousands of starving Africans have been saved through the actions of Catholic Relief Services, which has given $20 to $30 million to help pay for digging wells and providing medical services.  Bishop Keeler had just returned from the 43rd International Eucharistic Congress in Nairobi, Kenya, where he was struck by the devotion and expressions of faith by Catholics there.  Pope John Paul II, who attended the Congress, expressed support for the African church as it faced various challenges such as tribalism, racism, famine, a refugee problem, and serious problems affecting family life.

headline: Testimony in the CTA case raises questions about the contract award
abstract: Testimony in the bribery trial of Computer Technology Associates (CTA) demonstrates that the state Treasury Department contract was handled poorly.  Testimony clearly shows that no company other than CTA ever got a chance to negotiate for the state contract to handle the recovery of $25 million to $40 million in overpaid Social-Security taxes.  State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer insists that he was a victim in the bribery scandal.

headline: Lower Allen Twp. Man named acting secretary of agriculture
abstract: George F. Grode, a Lower Allen Township man, was appointed acting state Secretary of Agriculture.  He will take over for Penrose Hallowell, who resigned because of a shoplifting conviction.  Governor Thornburgh stressed that Grode was not a candidate to become the new secretary.

headline: Non-nuclear utility costs customers less
abstract: This editorial examines electrical utility rates in PA.  PA's cost of electricity is somewhat above the national average.  PA's cost of electricity is also higher than that of its neighbors.  The editorial believes that in PA, nuclear power has probably done more to increase rates than it has to restrain them.  West Penn Power Company, which has the lowest rates in the state, is the only utility among the seven largest in the commonwealth that has not invested in nuclear power for its customers.

headline: Free enterprise?
abstract: Buckingham Security Ltd. has had to scrap its plans to construct a private prison in Beaver County.  Citing a state moratorium on the operation of privately run prisons, Buckingham Security is seeking to sell 68 acres it bought in North Sewickley last year.  The proposed sale has angered some Beaver County officials, but they admit there is little they can do about it.  Butler County officials, on the other hand, are pleased with the cost-worthiness of their deal with Buckingham.  However, Butler Prison Warden Glen Bargerstock and other employees of the Bulter County Prison are displeased with the privatization of the prison, which will lead to Bargerstock's dismissal as warden; they are threatening legal action.  Butler County officials believe there is no clause in their current contract with prison employees that prohibits subcontracting.

headline: No bailouts likely, state tells Clairton
abstract: Clairton, a Pittsburgh area community teetering on the brink of bankruptcy, will receive little more than technical help from the state in its battle against an avalanche of unpaid bills.  Clairton, though not alone in its problems, will have to do without state assistance because the PA Legislature has never addressed this issue.  Tony May, a spokesman for the House Democratic Caucus, says that 1983 legislation that would have aided financiall ailing cities was eliminated during a budget compromise.  The most the state will do for Clairton is have state police patrol the city, as the city's police force has been laid off.  If Clairton does file for bankruptcy, a court will appoint a judge to work out debt payments and reorganize its finances.  Pittsburgh-area lawmakers continue to press for legislation to help cities caught in the region's continuing economic cruch.  Some lawmakers oppose state assistance because they believe that cities should tighten their financial belts rather than receive handouts, while others see too many small communities around Pittsburgh that have duplicate social services.

headline: President to nominate Honduras ambassador
abstract: President Ronald Reagan said he will nominate John Arthur Ferch, a Foreign Service officer who has served in Cuba for the past three years, to be US ambassador to Honduras.

headline: The Forum: State Library not open to all
abstract: A letter to the editor complains about the hours of the State Library and notes that anyone working 9-5 is only able to use the library for 3 hours on Tuesday nights.  The State Library was forced to close on Saturdays due to budgeting issues.

headline: Milk panel hears plea for price cut
abstract: The PA Milk Marketing Board heard testimony from an advocate of the Hunger Action Coalition who testified that low-fat and skim milk will become more available to poor and hungry persons if minimum prices are reduced.  The hearing is expected to determine if there should be a change in minimum milk prices in the Pittsburgh area.

headline: Not Enough Consumers
abstract: This editorial discusses a bill sponsored by state Representative George Hasay that would prohibit lawyers from serving as members of the state's Public Utility Commission.  The editorial says that there should be a bill to prohibit lawyers from serving in the state Legislature because there are too many of them there.

headline: Fugitive of 12 1/2 years nabbed
abstract: A man who walked away from his prison assignment and regained his life for 12 years was recently caught in the web of the Fugitive Investigative Strike Team.  The strike team is an operation of federal, state and local police that has captured 3300 fugitives in the northeastern US.

headline: No despair over our industry
abstract: This editorial looks at the reasons for General Motors (GM) choosing to locate its new Saturn plant in Tennessee instead of other states that offered GM short-term financial assistance packages.  GM chose Tennessee because it has no personal income tax, a low corporate income tax, and it is a "right-to-work" state.  The editorial says that not getting the plant located in PA is disappointing, but it is not the end of the world.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will continue to push hard to get businesses to come to PA.

headline: Shiite leader insists hostages were moved
abstract: Shiite hijackers commandeered the Athens-to-Rome TWA flight and demanded that Israel free hundreds of Shiite Moslems captured during its withdrawal from southern Lebanon; they also demanded that Spain release two Shiites held there.  Shiite militia leader Nabih Berri said that he told the hijakcers to move the hostages off the plane, but the US State Department said it believed a total of 43 people were still being held hostage.

headline: The lure of politics
abstract: This editorial looks sinically upon the political practices of PA Auditor General Don Bailey, one of the many politicians who is already looking for another job; Bailey was just elected, however.  Just last year, the Westmoreland County Democrat was elected to serve in one of the Commonwealth's most important positions, which requires him to keep an eye on how taxpayer money is spent.  Once Bailey took office, he immediately began preparing to challenge Republican US Senator Arlen Specter.  Bailey's press operation has already cranked out 225 press releases, and he recently signed a $36,000 state contract with National Media Consultants of Philadelphia.  During all this, Bailey is not minding taxpayer money.

headline: Milk-pricing charade
abstract: This editorial argues that the Milk Marketing Board, which sets minimum retail prices for milk, has outlived its usefulness and no longer serves the best interests of PA residents.  The Board is still strongly supported by dairy interests, however.  The dairy interests say that without the Board, dealers would be forced out of business.  The dairy interests neglect to realize that PA has already witnessed the demise of many dairies even with the protections of the Board.  The editorial also believes that many dairy farmers are mistaken in their assumption that milk-price fixing, a haven from the competitive forces of other markets, is good for the residents of PA.

headline: Not 'facts'
abstract: This letter to the editor complains that ads by GPU Nuclear Corporation do not present the facts about nuclear power; the letter urges the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to vote against restarting Three Mile Island.

headline: Full court press: Superior Court at full tilt to cut backlog
abstract: The state Superior Court has nearly doubled the number of legal arguments it will hear this year and has become much less lenient in granting delays to lawyers preparing legal briefs on their appeals.  The change has left lawyers in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh scrambling to complete far more cases than they normally do.  Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert Nix is responsible for the high number of cases; he has appointed 11 retired Common Please judges to help the 15 Superior Court judges hear arguments.

headline: Opinion: Altoona beginning to move forward
abstract: James Pickard, Secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Commerce, announced that Altoona was selected to get $50,000 to put together an application for enterprise-zone designation.  This designation could bring millions of dollars to the city.  This opinion piece praises local and state legislators for their work in bringing about this designation.

headline: Shiites free ailing hostage, propose moving 39 others
abstract: Shiite militia leader Nabih Berri freed hostage Jimmy Dell Palmer and proposed that 39 other Americans captured by hijackers of a TWA jet be placed in a Western embassy in Beruit until Israel releases 735 Arab prisoners.  If no Western nation will hold them at an embassy until the hijackers' demand for freedom of the prisoners in Israel is met, Berri said the remaining American hostages might be sent to Syria.  The Americans--who were passengers on a TWA Boeing 727 that was hijacked June 14--are thought to be held in separate groups in and around Beirut.

headline: The showman-mayor of Scranton acts to get city back on the map
abstract: Scranton Mayor James McNulty, a Democrat seeking a second term, says he uses prominent promotions to cure the city of its spiritual and economic malaise.  Scranton, once a center of the anthracite coal business, has seen its population dip over the last 50 years from about 143,000 to 88,000 as mining slumped.

headline: Minimum retail milk price to fall
abstract: The state Milk Marketing Board cut minimum prices by 2 cents a gallon on February 1 and will do so again March 1.  The decrease is based on a federal government announcement of a cut in prices paid to dairy producers.

headline: N-power production safer, many industry leaders say
abstract: Although the accident at Three Mile Island's Unit 2 Reactor nearly killed the US nuclear-power industry, lessons learned from that accident are making nuclear power production safer than ever before.  This was the consensus of nuclear industry leaders speaking at a conference sponsored by the American Nuclear Society.  Henry Stone, Vice President of General Electric Company, said that it is time to tell the public that nuclear power is a safe energy option.  R.A. Langley, Vice President of Bechtel National Incorporated, believes the ultimate impact of TMI will be a new generation of nuclear plants that are more reliable and easier to maintain.  Since the accident at TMI, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has required 6,400 separate changes for nuclear reactors.

headline: Gekas bill diverts profit from insanity-case books
abstract: US Representative George Gekas introduced a bill that would divert literary profits from people who have been found not guilty by reason of insanity.  This measure is an add-on to the Comprehensive Crime Control Act, which put literary rights sales of those found guilty of crimes causing personal injury into a special victims' compensation fund.  Specifically, this provision would apply to John Hinckley, who attempted to assassinate President Ronald Reagan in 1981.  Hinckley is reportedly collaborating on a book about his life.

headline: Osage area's rebuilders have links to Goode
abstract: The newly created firm of Edwards & Harper Incorporated was selected to rebuild the homes destroyed in the MOVE confrontation.  In announcing the selection, officials at the Redevelopment Authority said Edwards & Harper Inc. won the job as developers of the West Philadelphia neighborhood largely because its $4.96 million bid was the lowest, and because the firm met all the bid specifications.  Beverly A. Haper, one of the owners of the firm, served as a paid consultant to Wilson Goode's 1983 mayoral campaign.

headline: Ted Koppel of Nightline will interview Libya's Moammar Khadafy
abstract: Ted Koppel of Nightline will interview Libya's Moammar Khadafy. Some protesters have gathered in opposition of the interview.

headline: Thornburgh amendment advances
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh has a proposed a constitutional amendment that calls for a balanced budget.  The goal of the amendment would be the elimination of the national deficit by 1990.  His proposal received unanimous support from the executive committee of the National Governors Association, and he hopes to get support from the rest of the governors association.  This amendment puts Thornburgh at odds with President Reagan--who has called for substantial military spending.

headline: Pride of Pennsylvania: 69th annual tribute to agriculture opens Monday
abstract: The Pennsylvania Farm Show Week will be held in Harrisburg and will cheer the $35 billion farming industry and the 59,000 PA farming families.  This editorial applauds the farming industry and shows pride in the event.

headline: NRC benefits US
abstract: This letter to the editor refutes several assertions made in a recent editorial about the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and its decision to allow Three Mile Island's Unit 1 Reactor to restart.  The letter, written by the chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), states that the editorial's assertion that the NRC is insulated from accountability and public scrutiny is wrong.  The NRC is very accountable to the US Congress as well as to numerous public groups; the NRC has also made a strong effort to get the public involved in its proceedings on the restart.  The letter also says that the safety record of the nuclear power industry is proof that the NRC is benefitting the American people.

headline: Generation gap splits police
abstract: Under the cost-cutting policies of former Pittsburgh Mayor Pete Flaherty, the Pittsburgh Bureau of Police did not make any hires from 1970 to 1976.  This has created a distinct gap between the age groups of the police officers in Pittsburgh and has hindered communication between young police and their superviosrs.  A newly initiated seniority system by the Fraternal Order of Police also hinders the development of younger police officers.  This is because officers with seniority can choose their working shifts, leaving most younger officers to pair with supervisors with considerably less experience.  The police trial board, formed to allow officers to appeal the suspensions of their superiors, also has created a problem; most superior officers believe their decisions will be overturned by the board, so they fail to discipline officers in the way they would like.  All of this has led to inexperienced officers making serious mistakes.

headline: Out of Ashes, Stronger Phila. Might Emerge
abstract: A guest columnist discusses his thoughts on the MOVE disaster.  The author urges readers to help those left homeless by the disaster and to have compassion for the MOVE family.  The author says that the deeper meaning is that a healthy, vibrant city requires healthy and vibrant neighborhoods, as well as a rededication to the sharing of resources.

headline: The five in Reagan's 'confederation of terrorist states'
abstract: President Ronald Reagan denounced five countries as members of a "confederation of terrorist states": Cuba, Iran, Libya, Nicaragua, and North Korea.  The article gives brief descriptions of each of the countries and Reagan's reasons for including them in his list.

headline: Thornburgh drops lawyer as nominee
abstract: Due to a lack of support from State Senate Democrats, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh yesterday withdrew the nomination of Carrol Purdy Jr. for a judgeship on Commonwealth Court.  Purdy said he needed seven Democratic votes and had expected Thornburgh to withdraw his name.  Purdy does believe that Thornburgh will renominate him later this year.

headline: Protecting pet and owner alike
abstract: This editorial supports legislation proposed by state Senator Edward Helfrick that would require all dogs in PA to be vaccinated against rabies; the law would also require proof of vaccination as a condition for obtaining a dog license.  The author says that this legislation would protect both pets and pet owners.

headline: NRC Delays Decision on TMI Unit: Citizens Claim Victory as Hearings on Operators Proceed
abstract: Under heavy pressure from opponents of nuclear power, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission postponed a decision on reopening an undamaged reactor at the Three Mile Island power plant until hearings are completed on the plant operators' competence and integrity.

headline: Good intentions...but there's a moral in the MOVE confrontation
abstract: A columnist examines the disaster that occurred as police tried to remove MOVE members from their West Philadelphia home.  The columnist says that it should teach lessons of broad significance about the dangers of pursuing good intentions with the wrong means.  The author says that using a bomb on the house was the wrong way to try and remove the MOVE members from their home.

headline: Philadelphia Prays for Fire Victims, and for Itself
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode asked the city to pray for itself, the  11 people killed, and the 250 people left homeless by the police siege and bombing at the fortified house of the radical group MOVE on Osage Avenue.  Goode wants the destroyed and damaged homes to be rebuilt by Christmas.

headline: Windows changed
abstract: A letter to the editor takes a look at recent events that have occurred to PA State Senator Edward Early.  Senator Early recently went to China with the hope of opening a window for Pennsylvania in the communist nation.  In an ironic twist of fate, Early returned home from trying to open this window only to find that the Harrisburg Architectural Review Board had ruled that he had to remove 16 new windows that he had installed on his apartment.  The board ordered Early to remove the windows because they violate a historic district ordinance.  The author sides with Early, who must remove the single pane, heat-saving windows he installed and replace them with the original sash; the author says that the whole situations seems like a pane in the sash.

headline: Thornburgh not interested in Mrs. Heckler's HHS job
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh said yesterday that he is not a candidate to become secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).  Embattled HHS Secretary Margaret Heckler resigned the Cabinet position last week, after being at odds with White House Chief of Staff Donald Regan.  Thornburgh did not, however, close the door to an appointment to the position.  Thornburgh also reiterated that he is not currently a candidate for the US Senate seat held by Arlen Specter.  The governor addressed a number of issues as well, ranging from possible sanctions against South Africa and formulating a state policy for handling prison inmantes diagnosed with AIDS.  He also discussed legislation that would strip the PA Liquor Control Board of its enforcement powers.

headline: State drug use ranks first
abstract: A report by the federal Drug Enforcement Agency ranks PA first among all states in per capita consumption of prescribed stimulants and depressants.  This editorial urges the state Health Department to conduct its own study to determine the reasons behind such high use of legal drugs.

headline: NRC hearing 'cruel hoax'
abstract: A letter to the editor complains that GPU Nuclear Corporation has an unfair advantage in the Nuclear Regulatory Commission hearings, and that the hearings are a "cruel hoax" because the commission has not given enough consideration to the community and to organizations such as Three Mile Island Alert.  The author says that GPU should not be given back its license to operate TMI.

headline: Goode testifies he opposed MOVE bombing
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said that, after being told that the group was prepared to use explosives and guns, he ordered the police to evict MOVE members from their barricaded house.  Mayor Goode said that he did not authorize an aerial attack, however.  Goode also denied prior knowledge of police plans to blow holes in the walls of the MOVE house and then pump it full of tear gas; he was also unaware that police were armed with automatic weapons.  Goode told the commission he had delayed police action for a year, despite threats of MOVE violence, in an effort to resolve the situation peacefully.  Goode said he decided to act when he was told that MOVE had explosives and was ready to use them.  The mayor said he was unhappy with the managing director and police commissioner because they did not follow his directives, and that he would deal with them after the commission was finished with its work.

headline: Pittsburgh needs to get its political act together
abstract: A columnist discusses Strategy 21, which is an amalgam of regional economic-development projects put together by Pittsburgh city and Allegheny county governments, the University of Pittsburgh, Carnegie-Mellon University and the Allegheny Conference.  The columnist says that community leaders from the Greater Pittsburgh area need to bring Strategy 21 to the attention of the governor and the state Legislature by setting up a meeting with them.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon depicts a reporter interviewing a politician about unlimited political spending.  The reporter says, "The Supreme Court says unlimited political spending is constitutional, but opponents say unlimited political spending is wrong. As a Candidate, what do you accept?"  The politician responds with a big grin, "Visa or MasterCard!"

headline: Thornburgh ponders his future, talks of challenges facing GOP
abstract: An opinion piece examines PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's political future as well as a current trip he took to Yale University.  At Yale, he talked about spreading President Ronald Reagan's policies beyond the Washington D.C. beltway.  At the same time as he gave this speech, Republicans won races in Philadelphia and Scranton against heavily favored Democratic candidates.  The author considers how Thornburgh would run his campaign against US Senator Arlen Specter and how Specter might respond; the implications of Thornbrugh running for Senate are also discussed.

headline: State's Yule tree sales grow
abstract: At the PA Farm Show, the Pennsylvania State University School of Forest Resources said that PA Christmas tree growers are selling their trees throughout the state and throughout the East Coast.  PA growers are increasing their sales.

headline: NRC hearings
abstract: Letter to the editor criticizes the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for its decision to end the hearings on opening Unit 1 at Three Mile Island.  He says that the investigation was focused on concealment of the truth and saving the nuclear industry.

headline: Goode:  Never Asked Why Firemen Delayed
abstract: Questioned by a panel of reporters at the National Association of Black Journalists yesterday, Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said yesterday that he did not ask former Managing Director Leo Brooks, Police Commissioner Gregore Sambor, or Fire Commissioner William Richmond about their actions during a May 13th confrontation with MOVE; the mayor said he did not believe it was his place to do so.  Goode says he still does not know why firefighters delayed in trying to put out the blaze that started when police dropped a bomb on the roof.  Goode also said that city officials plan to shut off water service and enforce code violations at two remaining MOVE homes in the city.  Mayor Goode defended the motives of city officials on the scene of the MOVE confrontation.

headline: Post office won't flee downtown completely
abstract: Ron Hamen, a US Postal Service spokesman, said that USPS may keep its Harrisburg mail carriers working from a downtown office even if it moves its regional sorting center to the suburbs.  Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed worries that moving the post office will hurt other local business due to the loss of postal employees--many of whom spend money eating and shopping downtown.

headline: (Cartoon)
abstract: A cartoon spoofs President Ronald Reagan's policies and accuses him of budgetary mismanagement, militant rhetoric, and an ideologue who politicizes all issues.

headline: Thornburgh Says He Has Washington Options, But Won't Seek Senate Seat
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh says he expects to have career options in Washington after his term is completed, but after "considerable soul-searching" has decided not to run for US Senate next year.  This puts an end to nearly six months of speculation that he might run against incumbent Republican Senator Arlen Specter.  Thornburgh complimented the work done by Specter in representing PA and called him a "friend."  Thornburgh felt that if he ran for the US Senate, he would be unable to work effectively for the gubernatorial campaign of Lieutenant Governor William Scranton.

headline: Thumbs up for tractor
abstract: A photo depicts PA Governor Dick Thornburgh giving the thumbs up sign as he tries out a blue tractor at the Farm Show in Harrisburg.

headline: NRC members issue order explaining views on restart
abstract: Nuclear Regulatory Commission members issued an order explaining why a 3-2 majority believes the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor should be restarted without prolonging the proceedings.  The majority said that they had received enough information to make a decision, and that "holding trial when none are required is not a responsible regulatory action."

headline: Goode: Aide Reported Rapid Fire. Mayor's source: Brooks
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said that he had been told by Managing Director Leo A. Brooks that MOVE members were firing automatic weapons at police during a siege of their compound on Monday, May 14th.  Goode was responding to the fact that the four-day search through the rubble of MOVE's compound ended with officials having reported the discovery of two shotguns, one rifle and three pistols--but no automatic weapons.

headline: Salvatore's Position On Convention Center
abstract: A letter to the editor, written by PA State Senator Frank Salvatore, disputes a recent editorial written by the paper.  The editorial argued that Philadelphia should control construction of the proposed PA Convention Center, while PA Senator Salvatore argues that a regional authority should be responsible for its construction.  PA Senator Salvatore refutes the argument that Philadelphia will contribute 60% towards construction of the convention center, and says that the city currently lacks the means to raise such an amount of money.  Salvatore concludes that the convention center is a regional issue, and that the current administration in Philadelphia has done a poor job of building any confidence so it can raise money.

headline: "Sunshine" bill promising
abstract: An opinion piece states that PA legislators are soon going to be asked to improve the state's Sunshine Law, as the current one is not worth the paper it is written on.  The current Sunshine Law has several holes that allow politicians to conduct their business in private, away from the public eye.  The author believes the best solution is for school boards, councils, and commissions to give people their assurance that their business will be conducted in the light of public opinion.  The author also comments on a recent article by Louis Banks.  The article appeared in the October 1985 issue of "Fortune."  Banks believes that businesses should select journalists to whom they can dispense information; they should then monitor the supply of this information, as controlling information gives them power in dealing with the press.  The author of the article believes that withholding this information does not necessarily mean that it will not be obtained through other means.

headline: Thornburgh says he's considering "urgings" to challenge Specter
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh yesterday continued to send signals that he may consider running against US Senator Arlen Specter for Specter's US Senate seat in next year's Republican primary.  Sources have said that some in the administration of US President Ronald Reagan would like someone to challenge Specter, as they are angered over his opposition to the White House nomination of William Bradford Reynolds as associate US Attorney General.  After discovering that he got three degrees from two mail-order enterprises currently under federal invetigation for being diploma mills, Governor Thornburgh also accepted the withdrawal of John Brucker as a nominee to the PA Public Utility Commission .

headline: 115 to lose jobs in Trafford sale
abstract: Blaming a continuing decline in the electrical equpiment market, Westinghouse Electric Corporation announced further layoffs at its Trafford plant and new ownership for its Westmoreland County facility.  About 115 union and salaried workers at the Trafford plant will lose their jobs by the end of the year; all of this coming as the result of Westinghouse's merger with Siemens-Allis Incoroporated.  Westinghouse also agreed to sell its industrial ceramics plant in Derry to P.W. Porcelain Corporation.

headline: NRC orders halt at test lab: Pittsburgh firm's Cleveland plant affected
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission ordered a halt to all licensed operations at Pittsburgh Testing Laboratory's Cleveland facility, and stripped the plant manager of his supervisory duties.  The NRC order is based on an August 1984 inspection of industrial radiography operations.  Several safety and training violations are charged against the plant.

headline: Goode's plan for police:  A precious second chance
abstract: An editorial welcomes Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode's announcement of a plan to combat the systemic corruption that has stained and subverted the Philadelphia Police Department.  Though the plan is incomplete and offers only the barest of outlines, several modest steps in the right direction are included, such as long-term appointments to an Ethics Unit, and tougher screening and probationary periods for promoted officers.  Even with these new standards, reform in the police department will be difficult for the new commissioner and will require strong support from the mayor.

headline: Sleight of hand
abstract: A letter to the editor from state Senator Vincent J. Fumo says that Governor Dick Thornburgh is deceiving and defrauding the most needy of PA's citizens by announcing that $3.8 million from the Department of Community Affairs was available for housing assistance to victims of the MOVE tragedy.  Fumo says that no "new" funds have been made available to the people made homeless by the MOVE fire, but instead that Thornburgh is proposing to abandon existing plans for providing housing assistance to the poor and homeless people of the city.

headline: (Photo)
abstract: A photo depicts President Reagan and Nancy.  First lady Nancy Reagan shows her disappointment at forgetting to introduce President Reagan before she sat down with him at an inaugural party in Landover, Maryland; the party was held for those who couldn't march in the canceled inaugural parade.

headline: Thornburgh vows push for Wilburn in turnpike post
abstract: In an attempt to get his nominee for the PA Turnpike Commission, Robert Wilburn, confirmed by the state Senate, Governor Dick Thornburgh said he will take his fight to the people through a media campaign and a tour of the state.  The Commission is currently deadlocked with two Republicans and two Democrats, and Senate Democrats have refused to confirm any of Thornburgh's nominees for the fifth spot.

headline: 50 who lost jobs picket Shadyside nursing homes
abstract: About 130 employees of the Shadyside Manor and Negley House nursing homes lost their jobs on July 2.  These loses were the result of  an ownership change.  About 50 employees picketed outside their former work places July 8.  The former employees are members of Distric 1199p National Union of Hospital and Health Care employees, and they charge that the long-standing employees were fired for new workers who would make less money.  Pittsburgh City Controller Thomas Flaherty, State Representative Joe Preston, and others supported the picketers and pledged to try and help the employees win their jobs back.

headline: NRC postpones full-power vote on Limerick
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commissionboard (NRC) voted unanimously to postpone a vote on whether to grant Philadelphia Electric Company permission to operate its Limerick plant at full power.  The vote means that a final decision on the controversial plant near Pottstown has been indefinitely put off pending an examination of details regarding a lawsuit filed by 19 Graterford Prison inmates.  The lawsuit charges that evacuation plans in the event of a nuclear accident are inadequate for the prison.  Critics of a full-power start-up of Limerick have focused on emergency planning and evacuation for people living nearby; critics have also focused on the use of the Schuykill River for cooling water.

headline: Governor signs bills to fight child abuse
abstract: Legislation to revise a controversial law designed to fight child abuse was signed by Governor Dick Thornburgh.  The law, which will take effect January 1, 1986, requires schools and day care centers to check with the state police and the PA Department of Public Welfare to determine if reports of child abuse are on file for a prospective employee.  The changes amend the procedure by limiting the background checks to employees who would actually work with children.

headline: State may not use all economic aid OK'd by voters
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh says it may not be necessary or even possible for PA to spend the entire $190 million authorized by state voters last year for 11 new economic development programs.  Thornburgh said that improvements in the state's economy may have lessened demand for programs that require private matching money for loans and grants from the PA Economic Revitalization Fund (PERF).  Some Democrats in the PA Legislature have charged the Thornburgh administration with "dragging its heels" in implementing PERF programs, citing an adminstration estimate that $45 million out of the $190 million has been spent or committed on PERF programs.

headline: 1986 governor's race is off to an early start
abstract: Following the trend toward ever-longer political campaigns, each of five gubernatorial hopefuls tried this weekend to show Democratic Party leaders and workers that he should be the one supported in 1986.  Former Auditor General Robert P. Casey, state Representative Allen Kukovich, Blair County businessman P. Jules Patt, Montgomery County businessman Buck Scott, and Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell all are seeking the Democratic nomination for the 1986 gubernatorial race.

headline: Thornburgh, GOP not buying: House 'solves' turnpike impasse
abstract: The state House approved overwhilemingly a $4.5 billion turnpike expansion bill containing a provision that Democrats say could break the impasse over appointments to the toll-road commission.  The bill calls for the four sitting members of the Turnpike Commission--two Democrats and two Republicans--to select a fifth member; the appointment would require 34 Senate votes for approval.  Senate Majority Leader John Stauffer called the proposal "totally unacceptable" and said that Senate Repbulicans won't support the expansion project unless Governor Dick Thornburgh gets the person he chooses to fill the commission vacancy.

headline: 70 at Steelton face layoffs
abstract: Bethlehem Steel Corporation will lay off 70 to 75 salaried employees at its Steelton plant by April 1, 1985.  Since 1981, the company has laid off 35% of its salaried employees.  Bethlehem Steel says the downsizing is necessary in order to be competitive with foreign steel.

headline: NRC rejects citizens' request to look at TMI effects
abstract: The Advisory Panel for the Decontamination of Three Mile Island Unit 2 wants to examine, at the request of many residents living near the damaged reactor, potential adverse health effects from radiation released during the nuclear accident.  The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has voted against this idea because NRC technical staff members have concluded that accident health effects lack direct relevance to the advisory panel's charter.

headline: Grandparents get wider rights to visit grandchildren in divorce
abstract: A new PA law will expand the rights of grandparents to visit a grandchild whose parents are divorced or separated.  PA Governor Dick Thorburgh approved the measure yesterday as part of an omnibus bill dealing with child custody and support.  An amendment to this bill authorizes judges to grant grandparents the right to spend time visiting with a grandchild away from the child's legal parent or guardian.

headline: State must attract more industry
abstract: A letter to the editor asks the question of why PA was not chosen by General Motors to build its new Saturn plant, which went to Tennessee.  While the author states that much has been done in PA to make it more attractive for business, he believes that something must be done to attack the fastest growing cost in PA: runaway medical expenses.  Last year, PA racked up $13 billion in medical bills, and a fourth of the Commonwealth's general fund budget goes to pay for medical bills.  The author believes the solution to this problem is a package of four bills being reviewed by the PA Legislature; the package of bills would curb increases in the cost of medical care without reducing the quality of care.  The author is the CEO of Alcoa.

headline: 3 lawmakers demand quick action by IRS
abstract: Three members of Congress from PA--Senator Arlen Specter, Senator John Heinz, and Representative Peter Kostmayer--demanded that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) take prompt action to locate missing tax-return information at the Philadelphia Center.  They also demanded that the IRS issue refunds to an estimated 500,000 mid-Atlantic tax-payers, some of whom have been waiting for as long as five months for money owed to them by the IRS.  The Philadelphia center lost tax-return data when a computer malfunctioned and did not record the data that was filed.

headline: Thornburgh's farewell?
abstract: A columnist says that Governor Dick Thornburgh, speaking at a "Distinguished Leader breakfast" in New York, summarized what he perceives to be his most important acheivements.  Thornburgh said he defied conventional wisdom by cutting taxes, reducing waste, slicing 13,000 from the payroll, paring $1 billion from state-funded health-care costs, and removing 300,000 from the welfare rolls by phasing some former recipients into the private sector and enrolling others in "workfare" programs.  The columnist says that Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton--who is planning a run for governor--will emphasize his part in these successes, but will not campaign often with Thornburgh because it would be awkward to suggest that he could do it even better in the presence of the man he hopes to succeed.

headline: Clerical employment to drop, studies say
abstract: According to the US Labor Department, clerical workers will represent a declining share of the labor force in the next decade.  Clerical workers as a percentage of the workforce peaked several years ago; at thei peak, clearical workers represented the largest occupational job in the economy.  Recently, however, the clerical work force as a percentage of employment has been falling; it fell from 16.3% in 1983 to 15.9% last year.  More professionals and managers are getting desktop computers, which are performing operations that used to be done by clerks.  Changes in staffing paterns can also account for the decline in clerical workers.

headline: NRC to vote on TMI-1 restart
abstract: After six years of hearings, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is preparing to decide whether power may again be produced at the Three Mile Island Unit 1 Reactor.  The Unit-1 reactor was not damaged in the 1979 accident.  Governor Dick Thornburgh and anti-nuclear activists are vowing a long court fight if the commission votes to remove orders keeping the undamaged Unit 1 reactor dormant.

headline: Graterford inmates vs. Limerick: So far, the prisoners hold the power
abstract: Thomas W. Martin, an inmate at Graterford Prison, and 17 other inmates filed suit on behalf of the 2,500 prisoners at Graterford prison.  The prisoners argue that Philadelphia Electric Company (PE) should not be allowed to obtain a full-power license for the Limerick 1 nuclear reactor because the emergency plans for the Graterford prison do not ensure either their safety or that of prison staff.  The Nuclear Regulatory Commission requires reasonable assurance that adequate protective measures can and will be taken to protect everyone within 10 miles of a nuclear plant in case of an emergency.  The NRC licensing board granted a provisional license to PE--pending approval of Graterford's plan, but the NRC appeals panel ordered the lower panel to reconsider PE's request.

headline: State to Offer G.M. 2 Sites for a New Auto Factory
abstract: New York Governor Mario Cuomo will offer two sites--one in western New York and one in the Hudson Valley--to General Motors for its new $1.5 billion Saturn car plant.  Governors and mayors from across the nation have been attempting to woo General Motors into locating the plant in their area.

headline: 34 Governors Strut as Democrats' Future
abstract: Along with their Republican counterparts, 34 Democratic governors gathered in Washington DC for the National Governors' Association's winter conference.  Democratic party strategists are concerned about how well and how soon these individuals can transform the party's national prospects.

headline: Thornburgh's Got a Secret
abstract: An opinion piece examines the suspense and "guessing orgy" over whether PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will challenge US Senator Arlen Specter for his Senate seat in the Republican primary.  The author believes the odds are 55-45 that Thornburgh will choose to run against Specter.  If Thornburgh believes he can raise the money to run a campaign, the author believes he will run.  A Specter-Thornburgh primary may challenge the independence of US President Ronald Reagan and his political supporters, who have not liked several of Specter's more liberal positions.  The author comments that Thornburgh genuinely seems undecided as to whether he will run or not, even to the point that his own wife does not know what he will do.

headline: Businesses face disclosure requirements on hazardous substances
abstract: Under the state Worker and Community Right-to-Know Act, thousands of PA businesses will be required to inform their employees and state officials of hazardous substances used or stored in the workplace.  The PA Department of Labor and Industry will make this information available to the public beginning on October 5.

headline: Nuclear Agency Estimates Probability of a Meltdown
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission estimates that, over the next 20 years, the chance of a severe core-meltdown accident at a nuclear reactor in the United States is 45%.

headline: Guards, state split on AIDS testing for prison inmates
abstract: State prison guards are urging the PA Legislature to require mass testing of inmates to determine the extent of the AIDS problem in state prisons.  The PA Department of Corrections, however, is opposed to these tests--arguing that current tests are inconclusive in their early stages.  The Department of Corrections says that there are currently two confirmed AIDS patients among 14,000 state prison inmates.  The department has circulated a brochure among inmates and staff to correct what they believe is "misinformation" about AIDS and how it is spread.

headline: States have competed since January: GM Saturn site pick is still up in air
abstract: A little more than half a year has passed since General Motors Corporation (GM) announced the formation of a company to produce subcompact cars.  The company would compete in cost and quality with the lowest-priced Japanese models.  Since then, at leat 36 states have submitted proposals for the plant to be located there.  GM is still remaining silent about their final selection.

headline: 50% pay hike in works for county officials
abstract: Before the November 5th election, some Allegheny County legislators are making an attempt to have pay raises enacted for the sheriff, coroner, and jury commissioners.  The bill, which will go before the PA Legislature next week, would also undo part of a 1979 statute that turned county salary-setting responsibility over to county commissioners--a power that used to reside with the PA Legislature and governor.  The raises would be in addition to pay boosts of 15.6% for the four row officers; this legislation has already been approved.  Because the terms of all county row officers do not coincide, the sheriff, coroner, and jury commissioners have collected fewer pay raises than the other row officers.  There was concern among some officials that, without this bill, these three officers would not see a raise until 1990.

headline: Thornburgh's Record After 6 Years on Job
