abstract: A columnist evaluates Governor Dick Thornburgh's record after six years on the job and says he is doing pretty well.  Highlights include cutting 11,000 jobs off the state payroll, reducing corporate taxes and the personal income tax, and promoting the PA economy.

headline: Conrail and union agree on pay hike
abstract: Negotiators for Conrail and its largest labor union signed an agreement giving 12% raises to 8700 Conrail clerks.  This move was made in the hopes of selling the railroad through a public stock offering.  The move will give management support from the unions when bargaining.

headline: Nuclear comeback at TMI
abstract: This Eeditorial looks at the restart of Three Mile Island's Unit 1 nuclear reactor.  Opponents to the restart, have lost a major ally in PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, who said the state would drop its resistance to the restart following a decision by the US Supreme Court.  While safety has been a major concern to those opposed to the restart, some are just opposed to nuclear power anywhere in the country; such opposition should be taken into account.  Since the accident at Unit 2 in March 1979, many questions have surfaced about nuclear power in general.  These questions have been examined exhaustively, and major steps toward improving safety have been taken.

headline: Gunfire forced retreat back into MOVE house, Birdie Africa has said: The 13-year-old's account contradicts police on events in the alley
abstract: Birdie Africa, a 13-year-old boy who escaped from the MOVE house during the fire, provided a tape-recorded statement to two Philadelphia Fire Department investigators.  Africa's said that the MOVE members tried to escape from the burning house but were unable to because police fired at them.  Africa's statement contradicts the police account of what happened at the house.

headline: Suburbs Lead City in Economic Growth
abstract: The suburbs of Philadelphia are outpacing the city in economic growth, according to economists and development experts.  Boeing Vertol, a helicopter manufacturer, is used as an example of the growth of companies in the Philadelphia's suburbs.  Although economic growth in the suburbs has been more robust, it is taking place within Philadelphia as well.  The regional shift from manufacturing to service industries also has increased employment opportunities in the city.  Unemployment in the Philadelphia region is lower now than in the 1970's, and growth in the "suburban ring" continues to exceed the national average.

headline: 6 charged in toxic landfill scheme
abstract: State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman charged six people--two of them public officials--with bribery and racketeering to support large-scale illegal dumping of toxic wastes.  The central figure in the presentment, landfill owner William Fiore, was charged with 168 criminal counts, including illegal dumping, bribery and perjury.  A state grand jury reported that Fiore's firm carried out four major types of illegal dumping between 1979 and 1984.

headline: To color a caucus
abstract: State Representative Babette Josephs, a rookie lawmaker who represents Center City in Philadelphia, asked to be admitted to the Black Caucus because she said she shares the concerns of the Caucus and her district is one-sixth black.  Josephs is white, however.  This has caused a great deal of controversy in the Black Caucus about what exactly they represent and whether or not to allow Josephs into their group.

headline: Cuts or no jobs: Would modernize, B&W tells workers
abstract: If each union worker takes an average cut in wages and fringe benefits of about $7,000 a year, Babcock and Wilcox says it is willing to spend $185 million to modernize its three Beaver County tubular-steel products plants.  If workers do not agree to the cuts,  the company says that it may have to close the plants that employ 2,400 in Beaver County, PA.

headline: Nuclear Reactor Near Toledo Closed in Accident
abstract: A nuclear reactor near Toledo, Ohio suffered an accident similar to the early stages of the one at Three Mile Island six years ago, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).  The accident was similar in the early stages, but was quickly resolved and there was no release of radiation; there was also no major damaged at the plant.  The NRC is investigating the incident.

headline: Had Others Agreed to Surrender?
abstract: The only adult survivor of the police siege on the radical group MOVE, Ramona Johnson Africa, told a lawyer that MOVE members decided to surrender to police but she and Birdie Ward Africa, 13, were the only ones who fled the house.  Africa said that the eight adult MOVE members and five children were inside the basement of their fortified house, which had filled with dense smoke, when they decided to surrender.  She said they did not realize the house was on fire, and thought that the smoke had been caused by tear gas.

headline: Tax loophole lost chance to give - and receive
abstract: Major corporations could take advantage of a tax loophole in the PA Homeowners' Emergency Assistance Act by contributing to a program that provides financial assistance to homeowners who are unable to make mortgage payments.  Corporations can receive a credit towards PA taxes equal to 70 percent of the gift if they take advantage of this.  No corporation has taken advantage of the program yet in PA.

headline: A candidate of the eloquent gesture
abstract: This article looks at the Scranton mayoral election.  The election is between incumbent Democrat James McNulty and Republican Dave Wenzel.  McNulty is a self-described, flamboyant figure, who hands out roses and has traveled around the world.  Wenzel is a soft-spoken Vietnam veteran who has been serving as a local tax collector.  McNulty has done little campaigning for this election and has rarely even mentioned Wenzel's name.  Wenzel, meanwhile, has campaigned hard and tried to portray McNulty as a terrible administrator who refuses to delegate authority; Wenzel says that McNulty is more interested in flying around the globe than tending to business in City Hall.  McNulty believes that Scranton can become a major destination for tourists, given its geographic position.  Many believe that McNulty has benefitted politically from Hurricane Gloria, as he personally directed clean-up efforts, held hands, and dried tears.

headline: Tomorrow, the Senate probe of the missing IRS records comes to Phila.
abstract: A congressional investigation into the loss of $300 million in corporate tax records by the Philadelphia regional office of the Internal Revenue Services will arrive in Philadelphia on March 18, 1985.  Senator John Heinz will conduct a hearing focusing primarily on an incident in October of 1984; that incident involved the disappearance of tax-withholding payment records made by companies in the Middle Atlantic region.

headline: Day care frees workers
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton urged business to take a more active role in providing child day-care service.  PA Auditor General Don Bailey has proposed the establishment of a day-care program for state employees.  This editorial notes that these services are necessary and applauds the state for taking the lead in this area; the author also notes that there is a need to improve the quality of services beyond mere babysitting, however.

headline: Nuclear waste dump in Pa. gets backing
abstract: Under a proposal from PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, the state would accept and process radioactive waste from West Virginia, Maryland, and Delaware.  This proposal has already passed the PA Senate and is up for consideration by the PA House.  Several Reading-area legislators think that it actually might be a good idea, especially consdering the alternative of the federal government drawing up its own plan, which could be more unacceptable to the states.

headline: HANDS OFF OSAGE
abstract: A Philadelphia Daily News investigation of the MOVE tragedy shows that there was a "concious policy" not to enforce the law, and that city agencies and police adhered to what amounted to a hands-off policy toward MOVE.  Both Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode and District Attorney Edward Rendell said they hoped the MOVE compound residents would quietly go away.  Neighbors say that city agencies treated the MOVE house differently; the Water Department did not shut off their water even after their bill was unpaid for a long time, and housing codes were not enforced at the MOVE compound.  The events will be investigated by the commission set up by Goode to review the MOVE tragedy.

headline: Tennessee's gain is our loss
abstract: This editorial points out the significant victory Tennessee has won by being selected to have General Motors (GM) build its new Saturn plant in Spring Hill (TN) instead of PA, Michigan, or Illinois.  GM believes that Saturn will be the answer it needs to combat the waves of Japanese imports flooding the US auto market.  Though PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's efforts to get the plant built in PA were unsuccessful, the experience may help the state the next time an opportunity occurs for a major industry.

headline: A giant publicity mill grinds in Harrisburg
abstract: The bill for state elected officials and bureaucrats to tell the public about themselves is expected to come to at least $6 million in 1985; this publicity is paid for with tax dollars.  Most politicians strongly defend the cost, and say that it is worth paying to communicate with constituents; this is because some of the information distributed tends to be helpful and informative.  The article cites numerous examples of elected officials using the media to put out information about themselves.

headline: Torquato: Dwyer made threat to scuttle deal
abstract: John Torquato Jr, head of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), testified that State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer threatened to back out of a bribe arrangement because he feared bad publicity if he awarded a contract to CTA.  Torquato said he tried to bribe Dwyer with an offer of a $300,000 campaign contribution.  A competitor for the contract had offered to do the job, which involved the recovery of Social Security tax overpayments made by school districts, for about half the fee CTA would have charged.  Because of this, Dwyer backed out of the deal.

headline: Dislocated workers may get aid
abstract: The Reagan administration appears to have softened its opposition to the Trade Adjustment Assistance Program (TAA), which offers supplementary unemployment benefits to thousands of workers idled because of foreign-competition-induced industry downturns.  The TAA program is set to expire on October 1st unless Congressional action is taken.  Since its creation, the TAA has provided up to 52 weeks of extra unemployment compensation to more than 130,000 recipients.  Pennsylvania has seen a large portion of benefits from the TAA, as its industries have been especially vulnerable to foreign competition.  Opponents criticize TAA as a welfare program, while supporters say that it has not gone far enough.  TAA is one of the last remaining supplemental aid programs that provide extra financial support to the unemployed.

headline: Nuclear's problem: It isn't safe enough
abstract: This editorial discusses the averted accident at the nuclear power plant, Davis-Besse, in Ohio and its similarities to the Three Mile Island nuclear accident.  The editorial says that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the nuclear industry need to make plants more cost-effective to ensure that reactors are absolutely safe before they are brought on line.

headline: Hard-core delinquency
abstract: This editorial notes that after a 25-year epidemic of juvenile delinquency, Pennsylvanians are beginning to respond forcefully and intelligently.  In order to deter future criminals, Dauphin County, for example, is about to release to the public the names of youngsters involved in 14 serious crimes.  In vital programs such as probation, the editorial believes that the fight against delinquency must be stepped up.  Probation offers face troublesome kids and a national drug problem, but make minimal salary; this leads to high turnover.  The editorial sides with federal Judge R. Dixon Herman, who noted that children raised in good homes by parents with strong morals rarely get into trouble.

headline: Thornburgh holds the key to city's convention center
abstract: This editorial comments on the impasse in the PA Legislature over the Philadelphia Convention Center project.  The editor believes that the convention center project has stalled because the political powers could not decide how to divide the spoils.  The editorial blames PA Governor Dick Thornburgh for his insistance that there be public bidding for the construction projects; this has forced the city to abandon its plan to have a private developer build and operate the center.  The current impasse in the PA Legislature is mainly over the ethics language of the bill and the matter of affirmative action.  Again the editorial blames Thornburgh for the impasse, as he has the greatest power to end the impasse.

headline: A House Committee approved
abstract: The PA House State Government Committee approved two measures that would provide for partial public funding of statewide election campaigns, exluding US-Senate campaigns.  State Representative Thomas Michlovic, who sponsored one of the financing bills, said the measures would limit the impact of political action committees, who make large contributions to campaigns.  Opponents of the bill expect Republican members to gut the bill by amending the legislation.

headline: Torquato: political spat a factor
abstract: John Torquato Jr., head of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), testified that an aide to Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman rejected, for political reasons, an offer of a "substantial" campaign contribution in exchange for a favorable legal opinion.  Zimmerman's press secretary backed away from the offer for fear of involving the attorney general in a dispute between two other Republicans--Governor Dick Thornburgh and Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer.

headline: Exemptions ordered in labeling law
abstract: US District Judge William Caldwell said PA's 16,000 manufacturers do not have to comply with provisions in the PA Worker and Community Right to Know Law, which requires the identification and labeling of chemicals in the workplace for the benefit of employees.  Caldwell did rule that manufacturers still have to disclose information about potential environmental hazards to emergency officials.  The PA Right to Know Law has been the focus of a turf battle between the state and federal government over who has the authority to govern information about workplace chemicals.  Caldwell ruled that the state could step in where the federal government left off.

headline: Official vows to fight utility's rate hike bid
abstract: State Representative Allen Kukovich announced that he has formed a coalition to fight West Penn Power Company's request for a $96.6 million rate increase.  The rate increase is now the subject of a state Public Utility Commission hearing.  West Penn serves 591,000 residential, commercial, and industrial customers in 23 counties in western and central PA.

headline: Hours before MOVE bomb, blasts may have killed 2
abstract: According to Philadelphia Police Sergeant Edward Connor, one or two MOVE members may have been killed by a series of explosions on the porch of the group's West Philadelphia row house.  Connor's group, dubbed "Team B," was supposed to blow a few holes in the porch and then pump tear gas into the house.  The plan changed when the police dropped an explosive device on the roof, which started a fire killing 11 MOVE members and destroying 61 row houses.  A very detailed explanation of the actions of Connor's group is given in the article.

headline: Union will oppose Lebanon steel plant purchase
abstract: Officials of Local 1374 of the United Steel Workers are opposing the awarding of a $3.1 million grant to an investment group led by Lawrence W. Poe.  The grant will be used to purchase Bethlehem Steel Corporation's Lebanon plant.  Union officials oppose Poe buying the plant because he has said that imported steel would be used at the plant; the union also fears possible wage and benefit concessions.  Lebannon City Council and Mayor Martin Schneider have agreed to seek the federal grant, which if received would be loaned by the city to the investment group.  Poe's group is also seeking $6.5 million from the PA State Industrial Development Authority for capital improvements.

headline: A law against reality
abstract: This editorial complains about the 1984 buy-American law that required state agencies to buy cars assembled in the US.  This law has prevented state agencies from being able to buy new cars.  The editorial says that the state legislature should cope with reality and find a way to work with the way things are, not the way they wish things could be.

headline: Torquato: Zimmerman overheard bribe talk
abstract: John Torquato Jr, head of Computer Technology Associates (CTA), testified that state Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman overheard and walked away from a discussion concerning the attempted bribery of state Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer.  Torquato also suggested that Zimmerman was directly offered a bribe by CTA attorney William Smith; this was denied in a statement issued from Zimmerman's office.

headline: B&W protesters defy court order
abstract: In Western Pennsylvania, as many as 250 members of United Steelworkers Local 1082 defied a court order limiting the number of pickets to six when they held a mass demonstration outside the Babcock and Wilcox (B&W) steel plant.  There is a 4pm deadline today set by B&W for the workers to return to their jobs under terms of the company's last offer, or they will be replaced by the 2,500 job applicants B&W says it has.

headline: Montco Asks State Aid For SEPTA
abstract: Montgomery County Board of Commissioners Chairman Paul B. Bartle released a letter asking the state to help SEPTA cover a twenty-five million dollar deficit in order to avoid regional commuter chaos if proposed cuts had to be made instead. Noting that SEPTA had the highest fare in the country Battle disagreed with the formula that lowered state subsidies when fares are raised. He also noted that Montgomery County is a leading contributor to the state treasury and PA Governor Thornburgh's notion that the state had given enough money to SEPTA and was not planning to give more was disingenuous. Bartle said he supported a plan allotting a percentage of the state sales tax to the counties for whatever use they saw fit.

headline: State plans new housing help for unemployed, elderly
abstract: The PA House is examining a bill providing for the continuation of the Home Mortgage Foreclosure Prevention Program, proposed by House Speaker K. Leroy Irvis, which loans funds to families who cannot afford mortgage payments. The bill also accounts for preserving the life of the PA Housing Finance Agency, which has helped 4,500 Pennsylvanians retain housing. The PA Department of Aging used a $49,000 federal grant to ask the PA Builders Association and the PA Society of Architects to design three model houses geared towards helping the elderly.

headline: Computer 'glitch' delays the vote on Philly Convention Center bill
abstract: While voting for the third time on a bill to oversee construction of the Philadelphia Convention Center, votes on scoreboard in the PA House chamber disappeared. PA Representative Stephen Freind, who opposes the bill and favors a reduction in the city's wage tax for suburbanites, accused House Majority Leader James Manderino of causing the malfunction. The convention center project, a product of negotiations between legislative leaders, Philadelphia city government, and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, has been in the House since it was passed by the Senate on march 10.

headline: Political magic
abstract: Taxpayers of Pennsylvania are paying $120 million for expansion of government facilities in Harrisburg. The Pittsburgh -Post Gazette says the  plans to expand should be scrapped and jokingly says that the new granite buildings should be turned into the world's largest house of prostitution.

headline: Bill aimed to aid PAT OK'd by House again
abstract: The PA House passed legislation proposed by Representative Frank Pistella allowing Pittsburgh's Port Authority Transit to have more control over its finances. The bill also removes PAT's bus drivers' union of its right to binding arbitration. The union and the AFL-CIO deemed the bill anti-labor.

headline: Muscle For The Mid-Mon
abstract: Anyone who has driven the traffic-clogged and stoplight-laden Highways 51 or 88 to the Mid-Monongahela Valley understand the need for a Mon Valley  Expressway. Not only is it a matter of congestion, but the cities of the region need better access to Pittsburgh if they ever hope to replace the still declining steel industry. That is why the feasibility study recently approved by the PA Turnpike Coimmission is so welcome, however, because tolls will be insufficient to cover the cost of construction, there is still a question of whether or not it will be built, but the study is a step in the right direction.

headline: Taking a cheap shot at Philadelphia
abstract: Joseph M. Egan, Jr., president of the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, writes about an ad that appeared in Allegheny County newspapers that opposed a bill in the PA General Assembly for Philadelphia's convention center. The ad was funded by Philadelphia suburbanites who commute into the city to work, and it claims that the convention center will act as an economic drain on Allegheny County, when the suburbanites are in actuality concerned with the Philadelphia wage tax increase likely to accompany the convention center. Egan writes about the benefits of the convention center, which include many new jobs and increased revenue from trade shows, and a no-strike clause in contracts with the city's building trades unions.

headline: Congressional hopeful raises over $368,000
abstract: Marc Holtzman, a 25-year-old  Republican seeking to become the youngest member of Congress, financially topped PA House challengers and incumbents by raising more than $368,000 in campaign contributions.

headline: Political Pep Talks And Potshots
abstract: With the fall campaign in full swing both parties held rallies to mend fences, laud candidates, and take potshots at the opponents. In Pittsburgh, Democrats claimed party fences had been mended after a tough primary fight and U.S. Senate candidate Bob Edgar noted his support for "jobs, justice, and human rights," while gubernatorial candidate Robert P. Casey argued that his record shows he could effectively bring change to the state. In Harrisburg, Republicans were doing the same thing, with U.S. Senate incumbent, Arlen Specter, lambasting Edgar as being out of the mainstream on numerous issues, and gubernatorial candidate, and current Lieutenant Governor, William W. Scranton III said he had a positive plan for growth education, crime, and the environment.

headline: Coal firms: Union hurts local trade
abstract: Coal shippers in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania are battling a Longshoreman's union over work rules that the shippers say are threatening the future of Philadelphia as a center for coal exports.  The shippers say that the rules have significantly increased the cost of loading ships with coal and have caused the diversion of coal cargoes from Philadelphia to other ports.

headline: New Bridge Bill Will Help Defuse More "Subtle Time Bombs"
abstract: PA has spent the last three years trying to defuse a "subtle time bomb" as thousands of bridges in the state risk collapse due to much needed maintenance. As traffic increased and the weight of trucks went up bridges, which were not designed for the huge expansion of either, began wearing out. However, as cars became more fuel efficient and inflation increased during the nineteen seventies, PA chose to build more bridges rather than repair the ones already built. This changed in 1982 when the first billion dollar birdge program was approved. At that time almost 7,000 bridges needed some form of repair. The program was funded by a federal gas tax as well as a PA tax on truck axles. However, the trucking industry is calling the tax unconstitutional and has sued PA. the state argues that it is trucks which have done most of the damage, and they note that without additional funding weight restrictions will have to be placed on more bridges, forcing trucks to take expensive detours. If the trucking industry wins, PA's second bridge rebuilding program will be put at risk.

headline: Tool-and-die flourishes in Meadville
abstract: The 100 tool-and-die firms in the Meadville, Pennsylvania area employ 2,000 and are a legacy of Talon, Incorporated, once the city's biggest employer but now a shadow of itself, partly because of foreign competition.  The City of Meadville is looking to diversify its employment, with an unemployment rate of 12.6% in February.

headline: Congressman from Scranton is third on most-traveled list
abstract: In a survey of taxpayer-financed foreign trips compiled by Public Citizen Incorporated for the period January 1984 through September 1985, U.S. Representative Joseph McDade turned up as the third most traveled member of the U.S. House.

headline: POLITICS NOTEBOOK
abstract: A listing of the candidates running in Pennsylvania and in Allegheny County in the upcoming May 20 primary.  State Democratic Chairman Edward Mezvinsky has called for all Democratic candidates to agree to attend a May 22nd news conference for show of political unity.

headline: Commends Scheetz Bill
abstract: Albin W. Simokat, President of Pennsylvanians for the Right to Work, supports PA Representative Terry Scheetz's bill prohibiting jobless benefits for union strikers.  Simokat added that Pennsylvania's ratings in terms of business climate are already poor, and paying striking union members only compounds Pennsylvania's problem.

headline: New rating system could affect about 1.2 million young drivers
abstract: Unisex auto insurance rates are set to take effect in Pennsylvania effective June 1, which could affect as much as 1.2 million young drivers.  600,000 young females could be paying as much as $150 more per year for car insurance, with the same amount of young males paying as much as $150 less per year.

headline: Thornburgh ties 2 terms in office to Pa. progress
abstract: At a meeting with the editors of the Reading Times and Reading Eagle newspapers after a fundraiser for PA Senator David J. Brightbill, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh discussed the successes of his two terms in office, citing economic development and decreased crime as prime examples. He also discussed plans for the 1986-1987 budget, which include increased funding for education, bridge building and programs for the homeless, as well as proposed income tax cuts, despite anticipated federal funding cuts. He also plans to disband the PA Liquor Control Board.

headline: CTA Jury Requests Review of Testimony
abstract: Court jurors hinted they remain far behind from reaching a verdict in the federal bribery-conspiracy trial of PA Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer and former state Republican chairman Robert Asher.  A brief history of the case is included in the article.  Dwyer and Asher face up to 55 years in jail if convicted, though they maintain their innocence.  The jurors have asked to review the transcripts of testimony by John Wellington, the PA Treasury Department's chief counsel.  The question of retrieving the transcripts for the jury remained unresolved, as of December 17, 1986.

headline: Politics Scuttled Nomination
abstract: Governor Thornburgh's nomination of Republican Carroll F. Purdy to the Commonwealth Court failed for the second time for partisan reasons. While he got all of the Republican votes, seventeen Democrats voted against him. As a result the nomination will have to be filled through an election next year. The governor has the right to appoint whoever he wants and this should not be held up for partisan purposes. The confirmation process should rest solely on qualifications not on politics, if Democrats cannot find a better reason to vote against the nomination other than politics, then they should not have done so.

headline: Deadline looms on Mack Truck concessions
abstract: Union members looked for ways to save 1,800 local jobs as Allentown's Mayor held little hope of keeping Mack Trucks, Inc. from building a factory outside PA. As a condition for building the $80 million plant in the Lehigh Valley, Mack demanded union members accept a $2.04 cut in hourly wage. Instead, United Auto Workers officials proposed employees invest up to 6% of their wages in Mack securities.

headline: On The Schuylkill, The Worst Yet Is Just Ahead
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation is urging motorists not to use the Schuylkill Expressway from tomorrow through Tuesday as the number of lanes will be reduced due to ongoing construction. Drivers are urged to plan ahead if they must use it.

headline: Time to Join In
abstract: Writer overviews a problem in Pennsylvania of prospective homeowners receiving mortgages at one rate only to find out later that the rate was never locked in or even available.  This is a result of high demand for housing and lenders who are not certified or licensed.  In response the state Senate passed a bill that would give the state increased powers to regulate mortagage firms.  The writer advocates passage of the bill in the House.

headline: Contempt of Court
abstract: Almost a year ago, an article was published that told of how Republican U.S. Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter had chosen three would-be judges for the U.S. District Court in Pennsylvania from a list of nine candidates recommended by a merit-screening panel.  The Reagan administration had not acted and then, recently demanded that senators submit at least three names per vacancy.  This author believes that this is not a bad idea but that the vacancies need to filled as soon as possible.

headline: Politics tops agenda at labor meeting
abstract: At the annual meeting of the PA AFL-CIO, president Julius Uehlein said that the state's 38 labor lobbyists are not coordinated, which results in ineffectiveness when lobbying the state Legislature. The AFL-CIO executive council endorsed US Representative Bob Edgar, while some local unions back Don Bailey, the auditor general. The delegates to the meeting will also discuss resolutions regarding federal legislative measures.

headline: Dems do a job on Guv's claims
abstract: Just hours after PA Governor Dick Thornburgh provided a rather optimistic view of the Pennsylvania job market, House Democrats released a study to the contrary.  The study showed that many Pennsylvanians are being pushed out of manufacturing jobs and forced into lower paying jobs.  While Thornburgh does not deny that manufacturing jobs are disappaearing, he thinks the situation isn't as bad as the study shows.

headline: Pa. Panel Cuts Deal on Seat Belts
abstract: A Pennsylvania House-Senate conference committee negotiated a proposed compromise that would require the use of seat belts in Pennsylvania, allowing a fine to be levied only if a driver is convicted of another violation committed at the same time as the seat-belt offense.

headline: Vow on convention center hiring challenged
abstract: The pledge last week by the Building and Construction Trading Council to abide by city affirmative-action laws during construction of the proposed Center City convention center has been hailed by some, while others question the enforceability of it.  GOP leadership in Harrisburg earlier won an agreement with Philadelphia Mayor Goode which would have construction of the center governed by state affirmative-action laws, which led to criticism by City Council members which want stricter requirements.

headline: Council chief was active with state, too
abstract: It has been a high-profile year for Reizda Moore, first as Harrisburg City Council President and then as counsel for a special PA House of Representatives committee investigating kickback and payoff allegations in the $212 million Capitol expansion project.  Moore, who worked for PA House Democrats, became the subject of several investigations himself.  Moore spoke a lot about his role on Harrisburg City Council and the initiatives and projects undertaken during the year, and what is planned for the future.

headline: Politics, And he thinks Beirut was a home run hitter
abstract: When PA gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey heard of the Casey-Singel combination for the election, he immediately thought of the losing manger of the 1964 Mets.

headline: End benefits for union strikers
abstract: Albin W. Simokat, President of the Pennsylvanians for the Right to Work, writes that he approves of PA Representative Terry Scheetz's legislation to banning jobless benefits for union strikers.  Simokat adds that PA ranks near the bottom in every business survey taken in terms of business climate, and commends the effort by Scheetz to improve business climate.

headline: Pa. Town Has A Ticket For Amtrak
abstract: An Amtrak train was cited by the borough of Marysville for sppeding within the town limits. The ordinance was passed after Conrail increased the allowable speed from twenty to forty miles per hour due to improved track conditions in the area. Local residents complained that the increased speed caused too much noise and was unsafe. Amtrak was still studying the citation but believes that communities lack the authority to regulate rail speed.

headline: WANTED: LEADERSHIP - Mayor Refused Business' Help After MOVE
abstract: In the second part of an expose on leadership in Philadelphia, the author discusses the effect of the MOVE scandal, in which an entire neighborhood was destroyed.  The city has bungled the effort to rebuild the neighborhood, showing a serious lack of leadership.

headline: Council hikes pay for itself, Caliguiri
abstract: In a five to four vote, the Pittsburgh City Council approved to raise its own pay by two percent, and the pay for Mayor Richard Caliguiri.

headline: Politics: GOP is it
abstract: An answer to a question by a Pennsylvanian who was confused over recent elections that listed members of the Republican Party and the New Republican Party.  The answer suggests that the questioner should switch to the Diet Republican party as well as the Caffeine Free Republican party.

headline: Give DLI a nudge
abstract: Approximately 400 permanently laid-off Johnstown steelworkers will be included in a federally funded job retraining program if the PA Department of Labor and Industry approves the program. The Tribune Democrat says that there is a delay and the quicker laid-off workers can be retrained, the quicker they may be able to pursue some new line of work.

headline: Panel Sells Bonds For Turnpike Work
abstract: The PA Turnpike Commission issued over eight hundred million dollars in bonds yesterday as part of a four billion dollar expansion program approved by the legislature and governor last year. Toll increases of thirty percent this year and another thirty percent in five years are expectred to be necessary in order to pay for the bonds.

headline: We're Building A Center For Philadelphia
abstract: While Governor Thornburgh vetoed over one and a half million dollars for Johnstown's Inclined Plane, he committed the state and its taxpayers to larger and more long-term costs when he approved over one hundred forty million dollars for Philadelphia's convention center. Not only is there the interest on the bonds to keep in mind, but given Philadelphia's well known corruption, witness the recent accusations of extorion around the city's Penn's Landing project, and the potential for delays or costs overruns, do not be surprised if Philadelphia area legislators return to Harrisburg seeking more money.

headline: Court crisis seen in removal of judges and vacancies
abstract: Philadelphia courts are facing a crisis due to a shortage of judges.  This comes from 5 vacancies and 5 other vacancies due to removal of judges accused of misconduct.  Some blame PA Senate Democrats for not approving PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's appointees, but Democrats respond that Thornburgh has been refusing to consult with them about the appointees.  The crisis is weighing heavy on the remaining judges who have had to accept heavier case loads.

headline: Polling Problem? Check This Out
abstract: If you feel someone is interfering with your right to vote or tampering with the electoral process, you don't need to feel helpless.  Advice and help are as close as your telephone, if you know who to call.  This article lists the laws and helpless in the Philadelphia region of Pennsylvania.

headline: Governor due at ceremony in Lycoming
abstract: PA Govenor Dick Thornburgh will take part in a ground-breaking ceremony at the Grumman plant in Lycoming, which has received a $1.1 billion U.S. Postal Service contract to make nearly 100,000 delivery trucks over the next eight years and will add 350 jobs to the present work force of 225 at Grumman.

headline: Pass the mandatory seat-belt law
abstract: The author advocates that the Pennsylvania Senate pass Senate Bill 483 without amendment. The bill calls for the mandatory safety belt use for drivers and front-seat passengers

headline: W-P To Move Headquarters To Wheeling
abstract: Bankrupt Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corporation announced that it will move its headquarters from Pittsburgh to Wheeling. The statement came as a surprise to PA, which had lobbied aggressively, including a five million dollar assistance package, to stay. The company noted that West Virginia not only gave it a better deal, including helping to pay for building renovations and moving expenses, but that company executives needed to be closer to the majority of its workers if it had any chance of survival.

headline: CTA case lawyers jockey
abstract: The trial of PA Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former Republican State Chairman Robert Asher started today.  They are charged with conspiracy, mail fraud, interstate transportation in aid of racketeering, and perjury in connection with a no-bid contract that Pennsylvania awarded to Computer Technology Associates, a California-based computing firm.

headline: Polls give Specter an easy lead
abstract: Polls show that incumbent Senator Arlen Specter has a significant lead over opponent Bob Edgar.  The two are continuing to campaign, both making stops to talk about the steel industry.

headline: Guidelines Offered On Workers Problems
abstract: There is a productivity problem in the U.S. and some of it is attributed to substance abuse and personal problems employess bring with them to work. A recently held conference is trying to cope with those issues by advising employers on how to develop Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs). Such programs are designed to give employees low or no-cost help for their difficulties. The conference was designed to help employers identify employees who could benefit from EAPs, how to promote the programs and make them credible, and establishing guidelines for what will happen if problems persist.

headline: PAT chief asks keeping of transit aid
abstract: Allegheny County Port Authority executive director William Millar appeared before the PA Senate Housing and Urban Affairs Committee to say that the administration's budget proposals might force the authority to raise fares, cut service and lay off workers. He also asked the senators to oppose cuts in federal assistance for transit, which would prevent PAT from performing several expansion projects.

headline: "YOUR CHICKEN KIEV, SIR!"
abstract: Cartoon depicting a restaurant with a waiter bringing a customer chicken kiev while the customer measures it with a geiger counter.

headline: CTA Conspirator Aids Prosecution Of Dwyer, Asher
abstract: William T. Smith, already convicted in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) scandal, is cooperating with prosecuters in the case against PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer and former state Republican Chairman Robert Asher. Lawyers for Dwyer and Asher are trying to have the indictment dropped because the grand jury was improperly extended. Smith and former Dauphin County Republican Chairman Alan R. Stoneman were convicted of conspiring to bribe Dwyer and Asher in order to win a contract for CTA.

headline: Pollster: Voter sentiment was shifting at campaign end
abstract: A Republican pollster, in an effort to illustrate how the gap between Republican William Scranton and Democrat Robert Casey kept changing in Pennsylvania's gubernatorial race, claimed that if the campaign had lasted several more days there could easily have been a Governor-elect Scranton rather than Governor-elect Casey.  The remark also serves as a partial defense for some seemingly erratic and conflicting poll results that were made public prior to the elections last week.

headline: Idled steel workers win again in jobless pay
abstract: A federal district court ruled that Pennsylvania steel workers could continue to collect unemployment benefits.  The ruling went against USX Corporation who had filed a suit to stop the state from paying benefits to the workers who have been idle for the past two months due to labor disputes.  While USX claims that the work stoppage is due to a strike, the Office of Employment Security ruled the stoppage as a lockout by the company.  USX plans to appeal the decision.

headline: PAT Official Resigns As Shakeup Starts
abstract: One of the architects of the Port Authority's internal management shakeup is leaving the day those changes are to take place. Joseph Mundo is leaving to join DeLeuw Cather, which is desigining a new rail transit system for Dallas. The reorganization is meant to improve efficiency by having decisions made at lower management levels.

headline: 116-Day Strike at USX A Sharp Contrast to '52
abstract: For 116 days, the steel operations of the USX Corporation have been idled by a strike, however, despite the closing of the nation's largest producer of steel, there has been little effect on the nation's economy.  The ready availability of steel amid the absense of USX, which commands nearly 1/5 of the market, displays the dramatic overcapacity of steel in this country.

headline: CTA contract-fixing scheme results in 7 convictions
abstract: Seven people have been convicted in the Computer Technology Associates contract-fixing scandal.  Guilty verdicts have been returned on PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer, former PA State Republican Chairman Robert Asher, CTA owner John Torquato, and David Herbert, former PA director of Social Security for Public Employees, among others.  William Smith, the former Dauphin County Republican Committee co-chairman, agreed to accept a lesser sentence in return for his testimony in Dwyer and Asher's trial.  Two appeals by those convicted were denied by the US Supreme Court.

headline: Possible rainy day expected to dampen voter turnout
abstract: Rainy weather throughout much of Pennsylvania is expected to depress voter turnout for today's primary election, despite lively contests among Democrats for nominations for governor, lieutenant governor and U.S. Senator.  Voters of both parties are also making decisions on candidates for the state's 23 congressional seats, all 203 positions in the state House of Representatives and half of the 50 state senatorial districts - plus electing hundreds of members of their respective party state committees.

headline: It's An Unfortunate Strike But Stout Seeks Too Much
abstract: The current strike by local uniformed Philadelphia city workers is largely due to union leader Earl Stout, and Mayor Wilson Goode is right to resist his demands. Rather than striking over wages, Stout wants to keep the city from privatizing jobs done by union workers, but this is something the city has done in the past and if used effectively can be a good way to increase efficiency and reduce costs; it is an option the city should fight to keep. Stout also wants back payments on health and welfare benefits along with an increase in future layouts, while the back payment issue can be negotiated, the city needs to make sure it has a strong voice in controlling future costs.

headline: PAT, union meet again today in 'new spirit' of negotiations
abstract: Port Authority management and union officials are to meet with Allegheny County lawmakers about legislation to change their collective bargaining process.  The legislation would not affect currently-stalled negotiations to replace an expired contract between the Port Authority and the union of 2,600 bus drivers, trolley operators, mechanics, and maintenance workers.

headline: A feeding frenzy among area bankers
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives is scheduled to begin debate, and possibly to vote, on legislation enabling Pennsylvania bank-holding companies to acquire banks across geographic borders in a mid-Atlantic region of six states and the District of Columbia.  Many local banks are seriously discussing mergers these days.  Expanding across state lines could make them big enough to compete when New York's giants enter the game.

headline: Cumberland GOP spurns legislator
abstract: Three-term PA Representative John Kennedy failed to get the backing of the Cumberland County Republican Committee, which endorsed a full slate of candidates for the May primary election. Despite the setback, however, Kennedy says he will remain in the race.

headline: Praise Mammon!
abstract: In Pennsylvania, state public official Foster Pinwheedle praises the Republican Party, free enterprise, and President Reagan's former budget secretary Mammon.

headline: 'Jobs Aid' Draws 600 To Aliquippa
abstract: A rally designed to draw attention to the loss of industrial jobs due to US President Ronald Reagan Administration's trade policies was held at LTV Steel Corporation's idled facility in Aliquippa yesterday. The rally, which had a lower turnout than expected, was also beamed to fifty other sites around the nation and sought to create pressure on US Congress to override Reagan's veto of the Textile and Apparel Trade Enforcement Act, which limits the importation of certain goods. Politicians such as U.S. Representative Bob Edgar, who is running for the Senate, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey, and U.S. Representatives Joseph Gaydos and Jospeh Kolter also attended. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter is trying to help by introducing legislation to increase highway spending by seven billion dollars and requiring that all steel used in those projects come from domestic sources.

headline: PAT's Legislative Victory
abstract: When PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signs a bill eliminating the union's ability to unilaterally invoke arbitration against Port Authority Transit (PAT) and requiring both sides to agree instead, PAT will finally have the power it claims it needs in order to reduce costs. While the paper supports the move PAT will have to use its power judiciously so that labor costs can be reduced while still providing service to those who need it. Ultimately it is up to PAT to establish its own viability.

headline: Agency needed here
abstract: The editorial board hopes that the firing of the manager of the Scranton-based State Workmen's Insurance Fund won't result in moving the agency back to Harrisburg.  The board adds that the agency provides 110 jobs in the area and operates cooperatively with Harrisburg because of computers.

headline: Days (and weeks) of our lives
abstract: Recent mailings from PA Governor Dick Thornburgh declare certain days and weeks to be for good causes, such as Teacher Appreciation Week and Keep PA Beautiful Day. The article pokes fun at the fact that Secretaries Week is also Victims' Rights Week.

headline: Presidents and prejudice
abstract: New York Governor Mario Cuomo was questioned as to whether he could carry his region, and the nation, in a presidential race.  The Pittsburgh Post Gazette says that one of the problems Mario Cuomo may face in running for president is being an Italian, citing that race and ethnicity are major factors when people vote.

headline: Labor wins victory as House votes to limit use of polygraph test
abstract: The U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill limiting lie detector tests.  Organized labor achieved a major victory with passage of a bill to bar most employers from forcing employees to take lie-detector or polygraph tests to get or keep a job.

headline: PAT's new contract
abstract: A new contract was announced for the Port Authority Transit.  The contract was put together under looser arbitration rules than those approved by the PA General Assembly.  While the union did not completely feel the contract was to their advantage, it did reflect some of their interests.  The writer feels that it should help to point to the common interests shared by both labor and management.

headline: Alcohol trouble in workplace costs $110 billion annually
abstract: Members of the Greater Harrisburg Area Chamber of Commerce were told that the cost nationally of alcoholism in the workplace is $110 billion annually. There has been a greater effort to partner the business industry with drug and alcohol abuse programs.

headline: Debates will air hot rhetoric
abstract: A debate will occur between the candidates for Pennsylvania's 8th legislative district.  The debate is expected to be quite heated as the candidates, incumbent Democrat Peter Kostmayer and Republican David A Christian, have a history of doing so with each other.  The two have been going at each other since they first ran against each other in 1984.

headline: Price of CTA
abstract: Two articles appear on this page.  The first is a biography of the political career of PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer, who was recently convicted in the Computer Technology Associates bribery case.  Dwyer became the highest-ranking PA official convicted in office this century.  Dwyer's career, from an assistant high school football coach to PA State Treasurer is documented in the article, ending with the CTA scandal.  The second article is a biography of the career of Robert Asher, who was convicted in the same case as Dwyer.  Asher, a longtime chairman of the Montgomery County Republican Committee, aided PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's re-election in 1982.  Thornburgh later appointed Asher as head of the PA Republican State Committee.

headline: Labor's image has worked against expansion
abstract: The poor perception of labor in PA has hurt state efforts to expand the state's economy, an image that has resisted actual changes. The problems include an outgrowth of work stoppages, highly publicized labor conflicts, and a perception of work-role inflexibility.

headline: Penn Dot
abstract: Clair Kuncelman wrote a letter to the Tribune-Democrat regarding the bad job the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation did clearing snow from roads stating that the snow started at 3 a.m and Penn DOT got its road crews out approximately nine hours later. Kuncelman also states that Penn DOT goofed on the January 20 snow storm and should do better next time.

headline: Bank executive says state banking laws are in dire need of updating
abstract: Richard F. Laux, chairman of the board and chief executive officer of the United Penn Bank, writes in favor of the PA state Legislature providing for the state to join an interstate banking system. Such measures have recently been approved by West Virginia and New Jersey, which joined a banking region consisting of Ohio, Kentucky, Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. He believes PA will be left behind if it does not join the region.

headline: Debts mount for Casey and Rendell
abstract: Advertising expenses in the Democratic Gubernatorial primary are adding up for candidates Robert Casey and Edward Rendell.  Meanwhile, in the Democratic US Senatorial primary, Bob Edgar has aired ads in four of the state's six television markets, skipping Philadelphia and Harrisburg, while opponent Don Bailey has also been running ads for over a week and did not run ads in Philadelphia.

headline: Primaries Show Women Emerging As Seasoned Political Contenders
abstract: The results of Tuesday's primaries show a number of interesting results. First, they mark the increasing prominence of women. Both parties are nominating women in their fifties and sixties who are professional candidates chosen because of their ability to get votes and their focus on local issues. The importance of ideology was difficult to assess as some candidates who emphasized their ideological leanings were successful and others were not. However, the lack of national themes may make it difficult for Democrats to defeat incumbents as there is no "wave" that candidates can ride on to victory. Riding the coattails of popular candidates was also a mixed bag as some candidates with little popular support defeated heavily favored candidates who had the backing of notable party members.

headline: Labor's protest parade
abstract: There was an unexpectedly large turnout for the union protest parade in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania yesterday.  45,000 union members protested the use of non-union labor by the Tom Mistick and Sons construction company in a $20 million renovation of the Penn Central Station.

headline: PennDOT blamed for blocking firm's expansion
abstract: Due to a dispute with the state, Stambaugh's Air Service Incorporated is adding 50 jobs in Georgia instead of PA.  An additional 150 to 250 jobs could also be moved to Georgia if the firm, located at Harrisburg International Airport, does not get the additional space it claims it has under lease.  Stambaugh's recently won a legal battle in Dauphin County Court over fees owed to the PA Department of Transportation.  PennDOT maintains that Stambaugh's owes the state back rent for use of the airport.  The issues is further clouded by plans for an industrial area at the airport.

headline: Beer Distributors Win Senate Panel's Support For Sale Of Wine Coolers
abstract: The PA Senate Law and Justice Committee approved  legislation sponsored by PA Senator John Shumaker allowing beer distributors to sell wine coolers (currently only state liquor stores have been allowed to sell them). The measure is opposed by the Liquor Control Board and the State Store managers union over fear of lost revenue and because it goes a against a policy that allows only State Stores to sell wine products as well as state grocery operators who want the bill expanded to include them.

headline: Democrat favors limit on PAC contributions
abstract: PA State Representative John Cordisco wants to limit the amount of money candidates for state office can receive from political action committees (PACs). Cordisco wants to limit PAC contributions to $5,000 per candidate and prohibit one PAC from donating money to another.

headline: Primary '86
abstract: PA Representative Michael Dawida introduced a resolution calling a regional primary election for the 1988 presidential race. The region would include PA, New Jersey and New York. Dawida claims such a primary would boost the region's influence on the selection of presidential nominees.

headline: Mack: The first bill for taxpayers
abstract: The PA Secretary of Labor’s offer to get the state involved as a disinterested mediator between the United Automotive Workers union and Mack Trucks is too late. The selection of a South Carolina site on which to build Mack's new $80-million plant has been announced by the company. The Morning Call says that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration should have spent more time in the outcome of the Mack and United Auto Workers negotiations instead of losing jobs to South Carolina.

headline: PennDOT Earns Praise
abstract: Writer gives praise to Pennsylvania Department of Transportation for fixing driving conditions on Route 502.

headline: Bucking the trends
abstract: This author finds that Pennsylvania is lagging behind national trends on both liquor control and safety belts.

headline: Democrat pulls out of primary field
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioner Larry Hochendoner has withdrawn from the PA Democratic primary race for lieutenant governor stating that the party should be united behind its endorsed ticket.

headline: Primary '86
abstract: Polls show that US Representative Bob Edgar is ahead of PA Auditor General Don Bailey in the Democratic primary race for US Senate. The poll was conducted by WCAU-TV. Bailey dismissed the results as "silly."

headline: Mine-death probe ends with 23 citations
abstract: The on-site investigation into a Schuylkill County coal mine accident that killed one miner has ended with another citation issued for a safety violation. The operator of the mine was cited for not having an escape ladder leading from the mine shaft. It was the 23rd violation uncovered by PA state and federal investigators since the January 7, 1985 accident.

headline: PennDOT Plan Must Maintain Priorities
abstract: Residents of Lycoming County frustrated with the PA Department of Transportation's (PennDOT) continued failure to repair a dangerous stretch of road is pinning its hopes on a public private partnership. The idea has been used successfully in Houston and California, and PennDot argues that with declining federal help seeking private assistance is a way to get much needed work done. However, PennDOT must reassure citizens that priorities will not change simply because private partners insist that other projects be completed first.

headline: 'Can you top this?'
abstract: The PA Senate Banking and Insurance Committee approved a bill sponsored by Senator Stewart Greenleaf imposing a $3,000 fine on drunk drivers to be sent to the PA's Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund, which pays medical bills for vehicle accident victims. The board, however, does not believe the fine will have any desirable effect on the incidence of drunk driving, or the solvency of the CAT Fund.

headline: Democratic D.A.'s endorse Rendell gubernatorial bid
abstract: Democratic PA gubernatorial candidate and former Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell has organized a political base with the help of his professional connections, useful for fund-raising and other activities. Rendell entered politics with a boost from U.S. Senator Edward Kennedy and has acquired a reputation as a tough prosecutor and is respected amongst most Democrats.

headline: Primary '86
abstract: Some Democratic candidates attended the party's Jefferson-Jackson reception. Ed Rendell showed up late, while Robert Casey didn't show up but sent two of his sons and his lieutenant gubernatorial candidate, PA Senator Mark Singel, on his behalf.

headline: Not enough money to go around
abstract: The chart depicts information regarding Job Training Placement Act programs by area in western PA. The information consists of total expenditures, total amount not spent, number of eligible for JTPA programs, number of those who completed JTPA programs, and number of job placements. The Erie area was number one, which had 28,800 eligible, 1,213 completions, and only 436 placements. The chart's source are internal reports from the PA Department of Labor and Industry.

headline: Phila. Expressway work to drag on until late 1989
abstract: PA Department of Transportation officials said that reconstruction of the Schuylkill Expressway, a main artery to and from Philadelphia, will drag on unil Thanksgiving 1989, more than two years past its original deadline.  A delay has occurred with the firing of one construction company and the hiring of another.

headline: Caught In The Insurance Crunch
abstract: The crisis of spiraling insurance premiums and limited coverage has hurt small businesses the most. Because of their size they lack the ability to band together and form their own insurance companies and they can raise prices only so much, in response to rising premiums, and still stay competitive. An increasing number of lawsuits and an inability to recoup losses through investments due to interest rate changes has made insurance companies unwilling to take on new business. The state has responded to the flurry of complaints by preventing insurers from dropping coverage except for nonpayment or significant change in risk. PA now also requires sixty days notice of non-renewal and of any rate increases. But the options for small businesses are still limited.

headline: Democrats face critical choice
abstract: The assumption is that Democratic PA gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey will settle on someone from the southeast or southwest of Pennsylvania to fill the lieutenant governor's spot. The Patriot News says that the state must have within its borders an experienced industrialist willing to become lieutenant governor.

headline: Primary '86: Rendell discloses personal finances
abstract: Gubernatorial candidate Edward Rendell released his family's personal finances. An aide to Rendell's rival for the Democratic nomination, former PA Auditor General Robert P. Casey said that Casey would disclose the same information later this week. The presumptive Republican candidate, Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III, also committed to disclosing family finances.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of a client at The Consortium being escorted past strikers

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of the PA Turnpike

headline: Clearer Language For Contracts Urged
abstract: The PA Senate Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure Committee held a hearing yesterday on adding a plain language requirement to all contracts. James Dayananda, a Lock Haven University professor, said that it would help people understand complex legal and financial agreements that are a part of everyday life. Opponents say using plain English eliminates the specificity and accuracy necessary for such documents. Under proposed legislation if a court or state agency determined that a contract or policy was not written in plain English it would be voided.

headline: Democrats fear Casey-Rendell race is party's loss
abstract: A profile of the two PA Democratic gubernatorial candidates, Robert Casey and Edward Rendell, in preparation for the May 20 primary.  They differ more in style than substance, with Casey the image of stately reserve and seriousness, while Rendell is extroverted, witty and can appear aggressive and even arrogant.  Many feel that too much time, money, and mud was spent in the primary race, with November's election still months in the future.

headline: Primary Results
abstract: A listing of all Pennsylvania primary race results, including the U.S. Senate primary, the gubernatorial primary, and all the State House and Senate races by County.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of United Steel Workers member Craig Negley at the rally

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of a worker walking on a ramp leading from the Spring Garden Street Bridge to the Schuylkill Expressway

headline: Court orders that Senate act on LCB bill
abstract: The three-judge panel in Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court directed state Senate Republican leaders to place on the calender a resolution for keeping the state Liquor Control Board.  The Republican leaders said they would appeal the ruling to the state Supreme Court.

headline: Democrats go West in governor, Senate races
abstract: While the Pennsylvania primary is being held all across the state, the Democratic candidates for governor and for the U.S. Senate are spending much of their time in the western part of the state, particularly the Pittsburgh area.  Critical issues that are important in the region include jobs and economic development. The west has higher voter turnout rates than the east, and western Democrats are traditionally more absorbed into state politics than those in the eastern part of Pennsylvania.

headline: PSEA Asks Split Ticket, Hails Scranton Education Stand
abstract: The PA State Education Association (PSEA) announced a split ticket, endorsing Republican William Scranton for governor and Democrat Bob Edgar for U.S. Senate. Scranton had been snubbed by the organization when he ran as Governor Thornburgh's running mate, but the PSEA acknowledged that Scranton's stances were different from Thornburgh's and that Scranton was willing to make tough choices regarding education.

headline: Social Work Bill Discussed
abstract: The PA legislature is working on bills to protect consumers from incompetent social workers. Currently there is nothing preventing a social worker fired from one job from getting a job elsewhere. A bill in the PA Senate would create a licensing board, and those who do not meet the licensing requirement would face a fine and jail time if they claim they are licensed. Paul Krissel, secretary-treasurer of the PA Services Union Local 668, said he would oppose the PA Senate bill and support a measure in the PA House which does not have a licensing requirement. There is concern that social workers are already regulated and a license is unnecessary and that it would also make it more difficult for crisis centers and hotlines to get volunteers.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of SEPTA board Chairman Lewis F. Gould Jr. with fellow board members Thomas M. Hayward and Robert J. Thompson

headline: Court to rule on LCB by Dec. 29
abstract: PA Commonwealth Court President Judge James Crumlish said he would issue a decision on the future of the PA Liquor Control Board by December 29, 1986.  Crumlish chose the date to prevent any disruption in state liquor sales on January 1, when the LCB is scheduled to begin being phased out of existence.  Crumlish made the statement at a hearing to decide if outgoing PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's plans to dismantle the Democrat-controlled LCB should be halted temporarily until the court can decide whether the governor's actions are legal.  Thornburgh signed an executive order that would dismantle the LCB.  The order has been challenged in court by the LCB, among other groups.  The LCB wants the court to order Thornburgh's Alcoholic Beverage Control Coordinating Council to stop meeting.  Crumlish did criticize the LCB for publicly stating that it would close all PA State Stores as of January 1, 1987, unless otherwise directed by the court.

headline: Democrats identify 31 LaRouchians on ballot
abstract: PA Democratic State Committee Chairman Edward Mezvinsky has identified 31 candidates on the Democratic ballot for the May 20 primary as followers of Lyndon LaRouche, who heads the National Democratic Policy Committee, and is not a mainstream Democrat, despite the name of his committee.  The 31 candidates fall short of the 130 candidates the LaRouche campaign claimed it would field.

headline: Public Official Given OK-Hiring of Son Ethical?
abstract: The PA State Ethics Commission are sharply divided on whether there is a conflict of interest when a public official participates in a vote to hire a family member for a public post.  A majority of members did rule that Luzerne County Commissioner James Phillips was justified in participating in the action of hiring his son for office.

headline: State offers unemployment aid to those left jobless by flood
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Labor and Industry will begin taking disaster unemployment assistance applications tomorrow from those whose jobs were washed away in the flash floods that occurred in western Pennsylvania at the end of May.  State officials believe that about 100 businesses were affected by the floods, with preliminary estimates of workers eligible for unemployment compensation at between 700 and 1,000.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of the Schuylkill Expressway looking east from the Spring Garden Street bridge

headline: Dislikes Banking Bill
abstract: The President of the Bank of Hanover and Trust, Co. urges amendment of the Pennsylvania State Senate Bill 1075, regarding Interstate Banking, to ensure consumer protection and safety.  He believes that questions remain that Pennsylvania representatives need to address.

headline: Democrats keep edge in county
abstract: The number of Allegheny County residents who are registered to vote in the May 20 primary has dropped about 3 percent since last fall's general election, with the ratio between the number of Democrats and Republicans countywide - about 2.5 to 1 - has not changed.  35% of countywide Democrats live in  Pittsburgh, with less than 15% of countywide Republicans living in the city.

headline: Public pension cost impact heavy on government
abstract: Figures suggest that the apparent explosion of pension costs are a growing budgetary concern in Pennsylvania.  As PA Senator Edward Howard pointed out, the pension costs are the second highest component in the commonwealth budget.

headline: State Workers Seek Day Care
abstract: A recent proposal seeking on-site day care got as much bad publicity as good. Another ruckus was raised by parents using a stae logo to generate more donations. Both situations are ironic given all the solicitations made in state offices by businesses. Business owners need to understand that the only way some people have money to spend is by getting paid at places that also take care of their children. Taxing businesses for day care would free up spending for many state residents, which would be plugged back into the economy and boosting state businesses.

headline: Photograph
abstract: An American Automobile Association worker inspects a car in front of the Capitol building.

headline: End To Liquor Board Pushed By Governor As Term Wanes
abstract: With only five months left in his term, Governor Thornburgh is trying to reconcile those things he knows he will be unable to accomplish with those that he believes still have a chance. Because taxes are below the national average, the momentum for local tax reform is absent. Efforts to establish merit selection of judges has run out of steam as measures passed in the PA Senate have been allowed to die in the PA House. The governor remains confident that a measure mandating counties prepare plans for garbage disposal now in the PA Senate can, given enough pressure, also be passed in the PA House. He also believes that his efforts to end PA's monoply on liquor will succeed because the sunset provision giving the Liquor Control Board its authority is set to expire and there has been little effort in either chamber to come up with a compromise plan.

headline: Democrats map attack on LaRouche candidates
abstract: Democratic State Chairman Edward Mezvinsky will attempt to expose the names of all Lyndon LaRouche supporters running in PA. LaRouche supporters, whose platform includes quarantining AIDS victims and spending $10 billion on laser weapons, gained Democratic nominations in Illinois for the posts of lieutenant governor and secretary of state. Mezvinsky wants LaRouche's organization, the National Democratic Policy Committee, to release the names of its PA candidates so that they can be published before the May 20 primary.

headline: Race for Gov Transcends Plain Politics
abstract: After a long campaign of negative ads, the Pennsylvania gubernatorial race between Democrat Robert Casey and Republican William Scranton will be decided tomorrow.  This article outlines their stances on the issues, including budget deficit, the Iran-Contra affair, control of handguns, and abortion.

headline: Strikes Not Hurting Local Economy, Experts Say
abstract: While Pittsburgh at one time had a reputation as a "strike-happy" town, the current strike at USX Corporation is the first strike in the industry in almost thirty years. Moreover, even though almost four thousand people are on strike in the area, the local economy has barely noticed. This is not only due to the fact that the number of other jobs that depend on steelworker jobs has declined significantly, but service jobs have continued to grow even as manufacturing jobs have declined. Many of those on strike have also not lost a large portion of their incomes; steel workers were ruled eligible for unemployment benefits and are receiving support from union strike funds while teachers will recoup all of their pay as long as they teach the state-mandated 180 days.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Picture of a Greenville, Pennsylvania  resident walking across an empty railyard.

headline: Equality is primary issue
abstract: Babette Josephs, PA House Representative for the 182nd District, writes in response to a previous editorial regarding unisex insurance rates. Josephs points out that the board even questions its own conclusion. She also agrees with another editorial statement that insurance companies act for nothing but profit. She states that PA Department of Transportation statistics show that women have fewer accidents than men, and question why women pay the same or often greater amounts for insurance than men.

headline: Democrats map strategy to regain state, D.C. control
abstract: PA Democrats held a state committee meeting to discuss a battle plan to maintain control of the PA General Assembly. At stake in the 251 races is the future of the Democrats' legislative plan, the political clout of southwestern PA, and the effects on congressional seats following the 1990 census.

headline: Singel takes early lead over Flaherty and Evans
abstract: Pennsylvania State Senator Mark Singel emerged as the early front-runner in the three was Democratic primary for lieutenant governor.  With only 37% of the vote counted, Singel was leading with 47% to opponent Thomas Flaherty's 39% and opponent Dwight Evans' 13%.

headline: The Right To Work Is A Basic Right
abstract: The author feels that the right to work is a basic right and should not be limited to those willing or forced to join a union. It should also be noted that only twenty percent of U.S. workers are in a union. If they are so wonderful, why aren't more people members? Unions only help the small number of people who are members and hurt everyone else by driving up prices and forcing employers to move to places with lower labor costs, such as GM's Saturn plant which is being built in Tennessee instead of here. Ultimately, freedom is based on choice, and if you cannot work unless you join a union then the right to work is lost because choice is lost.

headline: Pittsburgh-Phila. High-speed rail line touted
abstract: Advocates of a high-speed rail connection between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia contended that the trains would have a number of benefits including, cutting travel time between the cities to two hours, revitalizing rail-related industries, and turning Philadelphia into a national crossroads.

headline: Flood Relief Bills Stalled State Senate at Fault
abstract: The Republican Majority in the PA Senate has refused to vote for $20 million for the relief of flood and tornado victims in eight counties of PA. The Scranton Times says the biggest loser from the flood in Northeastern PA is the city of Scranton which paid more than $3.7 million for cleanup work and still has nearly $300,000 in unpaid flood relief bills to meet and the Senate should have brought relief.

headline: Democrats' Process Called Undemocratic
abstract: The process for electing Pittsburgh's Democratic Party Chairman is being called undemocratic. Kevin Forsythe, argues that instead of nintey-six ward officers voting, all eight hundred sixty committee members should participate. County Democratic Chairman, Edward E. Stevens, is willing to make such a change as part of a larger package of reforms that won't come into effect for two more years. The other reforms include each person casting their secret ballot in public and allowing voting in the suburbs rather than forcing everyone to vote in a single location in Pittsburgh.

headline: RANDOM NOTES
abstract: Opinion begins by noting that former PA Governor Milton Shapp must be rubbing his hands in glee at the convictions of PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer and former PA Republican Chairman Robert Asher.  The author also notes that the conviction of Dwyer and Asher on the heels of the Republican's defeat in the race for PA Governor is somewhat of a catastrophe for the party.  The other random notes in the article include:  Charles Luger criticizing the 1987 Lackawanna County budget put forward by several Democratic County Commissioners, an extraordinary political gathering at the Hilton at the Lackawanna Station, the status of two openings on the Lackawanna County Court, and the significance of the PA Society dinner in New York City every December.

headline: Too few jobless get help
abstract: One of every three jobless workers was receiving unemployment benefits last year. The Tribune-Democrat says that a when Americans think of their society and the benefits provided, they perceive unemployment compensation as something the jobless deserve. The Tribune also notes that a person who lost his job through no fault of his own should not be forced to lose everything he has gained.

headline: Pothole loophole gives woman a sinking feeling
abstract: Allean Stanton of Harrisburg struck a pothole which damaged her car.  Stanton called the PA Department of Transportation to file a complaint for repair costs, but PennDOT never informed Stanton that due to a loophole in the system she had no chance of receiving money.

headline: Flood water is down, but victims still need support - emotional
abstract: After flash floods in the Pittsburgh area, flood victims are likely to need emotional support and perhaps even professional counseling.

headline: Democrats say GOP stymies granite probe
abstract: Democrats on a legislative committee charged with investigating a state Capitol expansion project have accused the PA Attorney General Leroy Zimmerman's office and the administration of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh of colluding to block the probe.  The investigation is looking into payoffs and kickbacks as well as tipoffs to administration officials.

headline: Rare tome back to the stacks
abstract: The PA State Library's recovery of a volume entitled "Townsend's Collection" is being celebrated.  The book was published in 1657 and has been missing from the library for at least 85 years. It showed up inside a blank manila envelope in the return bin over the Christmas and New Year's weekend.

headline: Unfinished expansion gritted with probes
abstract: An inspection by the PA Department of Labor and Industry found 52 violations of fire and safety regulations in 1978 in the PA state capitol building. Many unfinished costs and overruns have raised questions about the PA Sate Capitol expansion.

headline: 'Privatization' Not the Issue Conrail Plan Blurred
abstract: In approving U.S. President Ronald Reagan's plan for the sale of Conrail, the U.S. Senate has succumbed to a public relations gimmick. The Scranton Times says Reagan did not point out the disadvantages of the Norfolk Southern Corporation’s purchase offer when compared to two more substantial proposals, citing that he skipped the merits of the various proposals and insisted on getting the government out of the rail business. Privatization was the overwhelming consideration.

headline: For Bellevue employees. 'family' is breaking up
