abstract: The article includes vote totals in the Pennsylvania gubernatorial race between Democrat Robert Casey and Republican William Scranton by county.  Casey is leading with about half the precincts finished.

headline: Scranton, Specter are top fund-raisers
abstract: Republican gubernatorial aspirant William W. Scranton III has started the year with more campaign cash on hand than all of the Democratic contenders combined. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter led all statewide candidates with almost $2.2 million in the bank on January 1. Neither Scranton nor Specter is expecting serious primary election opposition.

headline: Vo-Tech Suffering Enrollment Is Cut
abstract: The Scranton School District has decided to send only juniors and seniors to the Lackawanna County Area Vocational-Technical Schools in September, while current policy allows sophomores to attend.  The change is due to a new state regulation on the number of electives that may be included in the curriculum. The Scranton Times supports state mandates to upgrade school education, but also hates to see a new initiative damage vocational education.

headline: 11 judges could be suspended
abstract: The PA Judicial Inquiry and Review Board has taken steps that could lead to the suspension of as many as 11 Philadelphia judges who US federal prosecutors say took cash gifts from Roofers Union Local 30-30B.  If the 11 are suspended, it would bring to 16 the number of judges who have been removed from the Philadelphia Common Pleas and Municipal Court benches after allegations of misconduct.  The 11 judges were informed on December 19, 1986 that they had 10 days to respond to the review board's petition asking the PA State Supreme Court to suspend them temporarily or to reassign them prior to a final decision by the state's high court. PA State Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. talked to members of Philadelphia's criminal justice system about ways to deal with the decrease in judicial manpower.

headline: Senate veto kills unisex insurance
abstract: On a 43-6 vote the PA Senate joined the House in overriding PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's veto of legislation permitting gender-based car insurance rates.  It marked the first time since October 1981 that a PA legislature was able to override Thornburgh's veto.

headline: Election-day watchdogs get little to bite into
abstract: Although officials in Philadelphia said the volume of voting day complaints was running higher than in the last primary election, no widespread or flagrant irregularities were reported.  Voter registration administrators said that voters encountered the usual problems of a few late-opening polling places and lost registrations, but that the complaints had been minimal.

headline: Search for the missing
abstract: Three days after flash floods hit the Pittsburgh area of Pennsylvania, rescuers are still searching for missing persons.  There were reports that up to 30 people could still be missing.

headline: A view from the Chesapeake
abstract: Karen Helm, the manager of the Cumberland County Convervation District, and 15 other Pennsylvania county, state and federal officials traveled 200 miles to study the Chesapeake Bay and learn how Pennsylvania has become its leading polluter.

headline: A better way to protect public
abstract: This editorial looks at legislation proposed by PA State Representative Paul Clymer that would have allowed background checks on those applying to be police officers.  The legislation, however, expired with the end of the 1986 legislative session.  Clymer's effort was motivated by the case of a former state police officer who molested a 10 year-old boy, was fired from his job, but then managed to find work with other police departments.  During his employment, he would continue to molest more children.  The editorial concludes that the mandatory background check on people applying for positions in PA police departments would correct an oversight that exists in the manner in which some municipalities screen candidates.

headline: Several Penna. Cities are pushing their pasts
abstract: Communities all over Pennsylvania are endorsing tourism as a means to ensure their economic future, with cities like Johnstown pushing its flood history as an attraction, having faced the reality that traditional industrial production is gone and not coming back.

headline: 'Embarrassing Scenarion' Ends By Freeing Grants
abstract: The PA Senate voted to approve a bill eliminating language from the PA state budget prohibiting the release of human services money until after the November election. However, the controversy refuses to die, with PA Lieutenant Governor, and gubenatorial candidate, William W. Scranton III charging the Democrats with playing politics and Democrats responding that Scranton "can't act as an effective advocate for human services." Scranton's insistence that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh use his line-item veto to remove an additional seven million dollars in human services spending has reinforced that charge.

headline: Second string mud slinger
abstract: Letter stating that writer believes Bob Casey's reliance on mud slinging may be why he has already lost two runs for governor.

headline: Aimed at hazardous waste bills merit passage
abstract: Democrats in the PA House of Representatives have proposed legislation that would revamp how the PA Department of Environmental Resources deals with toxic waste.  The Scranton Times says that is refreshing news and wants to bring the fight against those who pollute the environment up a notch or two.

headline: A drug out affair
abstract: A group of politicians including US Senator Arlen Specter, Philadelphia City Councilman Angel Ortiz and US Representative William J. Hughes of New Jersey visited a cocaine infested section of North Philadelphia, where local grocer Marcial Cintron testified about the drug problem. Local resident Henry James is angered by the fact that the politicians' visit was most likely motivated by publicity. Local drug dealers state that if their operations are shut down in this section, they will simply move to another one.

headline: Sex based insurance could stay
abstract: The insurance industry's chief lobbyist in PA predicts that the industry will win its legislative campaign to retain gender-based auto insurance rates. Opponents, however, still hope that they can scrape together enough votes to defeat the insurance companies.

headline: Emotions run high as Israel welcomes freed Shcharansky
abstract: Anatoly Shcharansky, an imprisoned Soviet human rights activist, was freed and flown to Israel.  The 38 year-old Jewish dissident, locked up in the Soviet union for nine years as a spy, had become known as the "prisoner of Zion."

headline: Senate Candidate's Firm Under Scrutiny By URA
abstract: The company run by PA Senate candidate William Pendleton will be examined by the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) to determine if the company, BP Associates Incorporated, is performing a "commercially useful function" for the Liberty Center construction project. Pendleton states that his company acts as a middleman, buying custom hardware products directly for delivery to other contractors. He notes that hardware manufacturers refuse to deal directly with contractors, which is where his firm comes in. The fact that Pendleton is black and his company is a minority-owned business is also useful to contractors because it can go towards their minority business set-aside goals. While the URA lacks guidelines of its own for what is considered a "commercially useful function," those it has used from other agencies, such as the PA Department of Transportation, have disallowed similar practices.

headline: Any U.S. rain likely to carry radioactivity
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency said yesterday that airborne radioactivity from the Chernobyl nuclear accident is now so widespread that it is likely to fall to the ground wherever it rains in the U.S.

headline: A little cheer for inmates in a crowded holiday season
abstract: On Christmas Eve 1986, corrections officers in Graterford Prison went cell-to-cell handing each inmate a stocking stuffed with presents and a cup of eggnog.  It was an attempt by staff and volunteers to bring some cheer to inmates during their most depressing, and crowded, time of year.  Earlier this month, Graterford had more inmates than cells.  The article looks at how the Christmas season generally sees a rise in the prison population throughout the eastern part of PA.  State corrections officials actually report that, statewide, October and November bring the greatest number of inmates to the system.  Several other prisons, including Graterford, had additional activities for the inmates on Christmas.

headline: Sex the policy in this House
abstract: The PA House voted to allow gender to be used as a factor in car insurance rates.  The vote overriding PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's veto of gender-based rates was 144-50.

headline: Endorsements
abstract: The editors of the Times Leader endorse Republicans William Scranton for PA Governor, Michael Fisher for Lieutenant Governor, and Arlen Spector for U.S. Senate, among others.

headline: Senate Oks Agency Shop
abstract: The PA Senate voted again to approve agency shop legislation for school and state employees (it had to be revoted on because absences last week led to a tie vote). The law lets state and public school employees negotiate contracts while requiring non-union members of the bargaining unit to pay fees equal to members dues minus a percentage based on non-contract negotiation related union expenditures.

headline: At tax time, Pa. plant life finds support
abstract: Thirty-three states have taxpayer check off programs to conserve wild resources, but Pennsylvania is considered to be the first state to preserve and manage wild plants as well as non-game animals.  The PA Wildlife Resources Conservation Fund receives virtually all of its money from taxpayer contributions checked off on income-tax returns.

headline: A Thornburgh issue
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has declared the discrimination that Lieutenant Russell Clanagan experienced with the PA State Police as a state police problem. Since the PA State Police Commissioner was appointed by Thornburgh, the issue may come back to haunt his administration and plague Lieutenant Governor William Scranton chances to be the next governor.

headline: Shearson, 6 Men Charged With Laundering Scheme
abstract: Shearson Lehman Brothers Incorporated, one of its employees, and five members of an illegal gambling ring were all indicted with laundering money from the illegal gambling ring through Shearson accounts. Over one million dollars in profits from the gambling ring, which operated from 1982 to 1985, were deposited in local banks (under ten thousand dollars in order to avoid federal reporting requirements) and then exhanged for bank checks and money orders that were then deposited in Shearson accounts, in the names of individuals who did not control them, and then used to buy municipal bonds and other securities. The names of those charged along with the full list of charges was also listed in the article.

headline: Endorsing Scranton
abstract: The Democrats have been trying to link PA gubernatorial candidate and Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III to unpopular policies implemented by his boss Governor Dick Thornburgh. However, that hasn't prevented the state teacher's union from endorsing him in the upcoming election. While this came as no shock to Democrats, there is still doubt as to whether or not it will send any votes Scranton's way.

headline: Senate races marked by divergent styles, philosophies
abstract: The Pennsylvania U.S. Senate race primaries will be held on May 20.  The Democratic candidates, Auditor General Don Bailey is seen as an athletic warrior, while democratic opponent U.S. Representative Bob Edgar is seen as peace loving.  U.S. Senator Arlen Spector is seen as the favorite in the Republican primary, though he is still campaigning throughout the state.

headline: Auditor general study very critical of DER
abstract: PA Auditor General Donald Bailey released a report criticizing the PA Department of Enviornomental Resources (DER) for failing to deal with Pennsylvania's trash problems.  The report accused the department of failing to establish a comprehensive plan and being lax on cracking down on illegal landfills.  The department issued a response denying the allegations and claiming that the auditor general's report contained numerous factual errors.

headline: A win for drunk-testing
abstract: In a ruling this week in Pennsylvania's Commonwealth Court, the Judge upheld the use of the Smith and Wesson Breathalyzer 1000, once the most prevalent breath-testing machine, but which the defendant is seeking to permanently ban.

headline: State cuts estimate, asks U.S. flood aid to towns
abstract: Pennsylvania has dropped its estimate of public works damage from the May 30 flash flood from $13.2 million to $5.8 million, which is still higher than federal estimates of $3.5 million.  The state has asked federal authorities to reassess their estimate, with the state's revised estimate putting total damage at $22.8 million, including the $5.8 to public works and $17 million to individuals and businesses.

headline: Eric Shuster
abstract: Donald Pasquale, a former Republican candidate for lieutenant governor, complemented the Philadelphia Inquirer on an article reporting political consultants in the Philadelphia area.  Pasquale added that he was surprised that his own consultant, Eric Shuster, was not mentioned.

headline: Senate rejects cigarette bill
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate rejected a cigarette-tax bill that would have helped fund the mass transit system, mostly in Philadelphia.  Lawmakers without discussion and with no dissenting votes returned the legislation to the Senate Appropriations Committee, with many believing the bill to be dead.

headline: Blast kills worker at chemical plant
abstract: An explosion at a chemical processing plant killed one worker and seriously injured another, released fumes that sickened firefighters and rescue workers, and forced the evacuation of 100 nearby residents.  The explosion occurred inside a 200-gallon vessel that contained sulfuric acid, vinyl cianide, and iospropyl alcohol, which were being mixed to create a compound used in paint.  The blast was reported at the Savage Industries Incorporated plant in Bath, PA.  The US Environmental Protection Agency said the operators of the plant have been cited several times and fined twice in recent months for violations of environmental regulations.  Fire officials called the explosion "extremely forceful."

headline: ACLU criticizes drug bill hysteria
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union criticized a new bill that has been introduced into the Pennsylvania legislature as fanning "drug hysteria".  The bill would require hospitals to report all drug related cases to police.  The police, however, would not be required to act unless the patient worked for an airline, in which case the employer would have to be notified.  The bill brings up issues of both legal and medical confidentiality.

headline: State helps Cumberland win insurance extension
abstract: Cumberland County secured a renewal on its liability insurance coverage, which was canceled on April 1. The extension was given thanks to help from the PA Department of Insurance in negotiating with the county's insurer, Forum Insurance Company of Chicago. County Commission chairman Marcia Myers says that the two-month extension will allow the county to be covered while it finds a new insurer.

headline: Errant recruiting
abstract: The National Republican Senatorial Committee accidentally mailed letters to two U.S. Senate Democrats, inviting them to join an elite group of Republican contributors called the Republican Senatorial Inner Circle. There is no sign that the Democrats will join.

headline: Senate, 78 to 21, Overrides Reagan's Veto and Imposes Sanctions on South Africa
abstract: The Senate joined the House in voting to override a presidential veto of a bill that will impose economic sanctions on South Africa.  The law will go into effect immediately, although some of the provisions will be phased in over 45-90 days.  Article includes complete roll call list of Senate votes on the veto.

headline: Bottle Bill
abstract: A proposed law imposing a five cent deposit on soft drink and beer bottles and establishing centers to handle the returns appears likely to die in committee, where it has not move since January of last year. The editorial board at the Reading Eagle hope it dies there as a comprehensive solution to the litter problem requires more than piecemeal efforts like a bottle deposit law.

headline: Animal-fight events are now felonies
abstract: A new PA law makes it a felony to operate or wager on animal fights, which PA Governor Dick Thornburgh called a "cruel blood-sport" that will not be tolerated in PA.  The bill, signed by Thornburgh, stipulates maximum penalties of seven years in jail and fines of up to $15,000 for running, attending, or wagering on animal fighting events.  Previously, animal fighting was punishable as a summary offense.  Supporters of the bill say the stricter sanctions are intended to reduce a surge in dogfighting and cockfighting contests in PA.  The law also increases the penalty for killing or disfiguring zoo animals and adds a mandatory fine for killing or disfiguring domestic animals.

headline: State Lends Its Name To New Specialty Beer
abstract: After lending its services to Jim Koch and his Samuel Adams Boston Lager, Lawrenceville-based Pittsburgh Brewing Company is helping Pittsburgh-native Tom Pastorius with his own brew, Pennsylvania Pilsner. Pastorius developed a love for German beer after spending twelve years in West Germany, however he could not find a similar beer on the market in the U.S. and his home brewing was also unsatisfactory. So he contracted with Pittsburgh Brewing Company, and using a recipe developed by Thomas Owades, who also created the Sam Adams recipe, to make a beer of his own. It will initally be marketed in Philadelphia, where Pastorius's ancestor Francis Daniel Pastorius originally settled, but there are hopes it can be marketed throughout the rest of the state.

headline: Ertel Opens Farm To Sow Seeds Of Support
abstract: Former PA Democratic gubernatorial candidate Allen Ertel held a rally at his farm yesterday to help generate statewide grassroots support for current gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey, and U.S. Senate candidate Bob Edgar. Ertel believes that the slow start to his campaign ultimately cost him the election and he wants to prevent that from happening in 1986.

headline: State Senate Oks job-claims help
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate voted unanimously to boost the number of Bureau of Workers' Compensation referees from 39 to 49 and increase the complement of clerical helpers from 91 to 98.

headline: Bureaucracy grinds on as Pa. toxic sites fester
abstract: Two years ago PA Governor Dick Thornburgh announced that the state would take over the Havertown PCP site and seven other toxic waste sites from the federal government to accelerate the cleanup process. None of the sites, however, are close to being cleaned up.

headline: Area prisons deal with problem of overcrowding
abstract: In the fall of 1986 there will be a $330,000 expansion and renovation project at the Centre County Prison.  The increase in the crime rate of the late 1970’s is what is causing the overcrowding conditions and the need for expansion in Centre County.

headline: State Stores
abstract: A letter where the author supports privatization of the Liquor Control Board in Pennsylvania.

headline: Ethics probe OK with O'Malley
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman James O'Malley says he will welcome a PA State Ethics Commission probe into his actions as a part-time real estate agent.  O'Malley criticized Pittsburgh City Controller Thomas Flaherty for calling on him to resign from council.  Flaherty has vowed to request an ethics Commission probe if City Council ignores O'Malley's recent behavior as an agent for Oliver Realty, a job O'Malley quit recently quit.

headline: Statelines
abstract: Three small articles on news in PA are included on this page.  The first article notes a study by the PA Commission for Women that says the number of women in local elective office has increased slightly over a two-year period.  The second article says that William Smith, the federal government's key witness in the Computer Technology Associates bribery-conspiracy trial, has been discharged from Harrisburg Hospital.  Smith underwent emergency surgery hours after testifying against PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer.  The third article says that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh appointed Judge George Twardy as president judge of the Philadelphia Traffic Court.

headline: Casey Unveils Proposal For Water, Waste
abstract: Gubenatorial candidates Republican William W. Scranton and Democrat Robert Casey discussed economic initiatives at the annual convention of the Pennsylvania Association of County Commissioners yesterday. Scranton advocated revamping the local government tax system and expanding the state Enterprise Zone Program with additional tax credits and investment incentives. Casey announced the creation of a PENNVEST program which would leverage over five hundred million dollars in unused state money into two billion dollars that could go into upgrading the state's infrastructure, all without raising taxes.

headline: Attorney general to refile tax case dismissed after defendant paid up
abstract: Last month, a District judge dismissed a tax case against defendant Anthony Arriviello, Jr., a Phildelphia print-shop owner accused of failing to file sales tax returns, who then paid over $4,000 in back taxes.  The PA Attorney General's office said it would refile the case, saying the judge had no authority to dismiss the case unless the prosecution and the PA Department of Revenue agree.

headline: State To Issue CAT Fund Bills
abstract: Vehicle owners whose registrations expire in November will soon be receiving bills from the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund (CAT). The fund is meant to help residents who have suffered serious injuries in car accidents by helping to pay their medical bills.

headline: Ethnic nepotism
abstract: This letter decries the recent announcement by Governor-elect Casey of two Cabinet appointments as ethnic nepotism.

headline: State's delegation in House can almost bet on job security
abstract: A post-election analysis of Pennsylvania's delegation in the U.S. House of Representatives shows that most of the 23 politicians are steeped in job security, with 15 of them winning with 61% or more of the vote and four others had no opposition in the general election.  Fourteen of them have served five terms or more, while another two won their third and fourth terms respectively.

headline: Cleanup fund a step nearer
abstract: The PA House of Representatives gave preliminary approval to a measure that would set up a $10 million cleanup fund for hazardous waste sites that do not get U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Superfund money. The measure which passed unanimously, was an amendment to a conservation bill and sets up a program for the cleanup of spills and waste sites.

headline: Bar chief, Select judges on merit
abstract: The chancellor of the Philadelphia Bar Association has called for sweeping changes in the way judges are selected, and for improving methods of policing judges once they are in office.

headline: States And Fortune 500
abstract: A Duke University research project included all fifty state governments in Fortune's annual list of the United State's five hundred largest companies. It crystalizes the fact that governors and CEOs have much in common, states are businesses striving to develop a "corporate" culture, and businesses seek ways to better speak with the outside world.

headline: Evans for Lt. Governor
abstract: The editors endorse PA Representative Dwight Evans (D) for Lieutenant Governor over Pittsburgh Controller Tom Flaherty and PA Senator Mark Singel of Johnstown.

headline: State's top watchdogs vow to be impartial
abstract: When Robert Casey takes the governor's oath in Pennsylvania on January 20, Auditor General Don Bailey and Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman will be positions to watch him.  Bailey is a friend and supporter of Casey but claims that nothing will deter him from doing his job, while Zimmerman is a Republican, making this the first time Pennsylvania has an independent attorney general of a different party than the governor.

headline: DER cites work against giardiasis
abstract: PA Department of Environmental Resources Secretary Nicholas DeBenedictis told a PA House of Representatives committee that the agency is continuing its efforts to stop further outbreaks of giardiasis, an intestinal virus. PA Department of Environmental Resources say 21 sources of water are contaminated.

headline: Beyond Duty
abstract: This letter to the editor praises the paper's article on the life of a Philadelphia cop during a recent strike. City residents should be proud of the fact that officers worked twelve-hour shifts with no days off in order to protect them. While the overtime was nice, it does not make up for what the time lost.

headline: Stepping Aside: Pickets To Permit Razing Of Dorothy For Industrial Park
abstract: Members of the United Steel Workers (USW) in a work stoppage against USX Corporation since the first of August, have agreed to allow workers to cross picket lines at the company's idled Dorthy Six blast furnace in order to begin demolishing it. The facility has been idle for over two years and previous efforts to begin demolition work were delayed by union efforts to restart the plant independently, which proved to be uneconomical. USX has agreed to turn one hundred fifty-five acres of the site into an industrial park.

headline: Ex-teacher seeks time to repay
abstract: A former Pittsburgh city teacher who eluded prison by promising to repay all the money he stole from unwitting investors asked a judge for more time to accumulate the necessary funds.  In a plea bargain, he had agreed to repay the $60,000 he stole from investors and not sell any securities for five years.

headline: Statute of limitations shouldn't apply to fugitive hit and run drivers
abstract: This author believes that the Pennsylvania House Bill 1763, which would eliminate the two-year statute of limitations on homicide by vehicle prosecutions, deserves unqualified support.

headline: DER probe of tainting to continue
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) will continue its investigation of well contamination in the area of the Silver Spring Industrial Park, after discovering the presence of a suspected carcinogen was identified in four of five wells in the most recent round of testing.  The DER has idenfied that the company Flight Systems Incorporated is the source for the contamination, but probably not the only one.

headline: Bill fails to resolve judicial election dilemma
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a bill that eliminates cross filing for PA Superior and Supreme Court judges. The Times Leader reports that a bill singed into law by Thornburgh creates another imperative for a decision on what PA is going to do with its judiciary.  If nothing else, the Leader says that the new law demands that PA prepare now to make the decision: do we want to free our courts, or do we want to hand them over the control of the political parties?

headline: Tavern to fight LCB order
abstract: The operators of a Lower Paxton Township tavern that has go-go girls as entertainment plan to fight an order to hand in their liquor license.  Among the citations issued by the PA Liquor Control Board against the establishment are claims that it allowed lewd, immoral, and/or improper entertainment and allowed entertainers to have contact with patrons.

headline: Ex-turnpike officer waits for ruling
abstract: Former Chief Financial officer of the PA Turnpike Commission should know in two weeks if he can have another preliminary hearing or if bribery and racketeering charges against him will be dismissed.  He has been charged by the PA Attorney General's office with funnelling more than $1.3 billion in turnpike investments to Florida brokeage firms where his daughter worked.

headline: Strikes Are A Common Resort In Pa. Districts
abstract: In nineteen seventy PA allowed public employees, including teachers, to strike. In the first ten years there were six hundred teacher strikes, more than in every other state combined; currently there are fifteen school districts on strike, six in the Philadelphia area. School officials say that part of the reason is because there is no penalty for striking, as long as one hundred eighty days are taught teachers don't lose pay, however in New York, teachers lose two days pay for every day on strike. Donald F. Morabito, assistant executive director of the PA State Education Association notes that only ten states allow strikes and given the over six hundred districts in PA many strikes wouldn't be unusual - in fact less than ten percent of districts are on strike. In Philadelphia there is frustration that many strikes are happening in wealthy districts where school boards can afford to pay higher salaries but refuse to do so. The school boards argue they are trying to hold the line on property taxes by limiting costs and using subsidies to pay for things instead of tax revenue. Because strikes tend to happen in clusters there is also the perception of not wanting to be seen giving in to the other side and having to raise or lower demands accordingly. Trying to avoid accusations of collusion is also a concern.

headline: Environment-Public attention dims but problems remain
abstract: According to the 17th annual Environmental Quality Index compiled by the National Wildlife Federation, the nation's overall environmental problems are more extensive than previously estimated.  The National Wildlife Federation wants to encourage people to focus more on the environment.

headline: Bill on underage drinking bounced
abstract: The PA Senate shifted a bill back to committee that will try to curb underage drinking, with license suspensions even in cases not involving automobiles, and fines for parents furnishing underage drinkers costing as much as $1000.  Critics of the bill said that the penalties are too harsh, and license suspensions for actions not involving automobiles are unjustified.

headline: Taverns' happy hours cut
abstract: In regulations published by the PA State Liquor Control Board, happy hour at PA bars and restaurants can last only two hours and must come to a close by midnight.

headline: Ex-URA Officer Accused Of Misusing Office
abstract: The PA Ethics Commission recommended that ex-PA Urban Redevelopment Authoirty (URA) employee David Panza be criminally prosecuted for funneling over $900,000 of URA money into projects and companies that he had an interest in. The Ethics Commission also lambasted the URA for failing to have any oversight which would have prevented Panza's illegal activities. Panza responded that there were many other people involved in corrupt activities that he would be willing to divulge.

headline: Subpoenas for 2 in granite probe quashed
abstract: The PA State Supreme Court quashed subpoenas ordering two businessman whose company supplied granite in the controversial $122 million expansion of the PA Capitol to reveal financial records from 1981 through 1985.  A special committee of the PA House of Representatives had subpoenaed records of Carl Lunderstadt and John Scott, owners of North American Industries in Elizabeth, PA.  The PA House committee was looking into allegations that the $30 million cost of granite for the Capitol's addition was inflated by questionable business practices and kickbacks to contractors.  The PA State Supreme Court's decision said the subpoenas should have specified the types of transactions and approximate times they occurred.  Scott and Lunderstadt claim to have voluntarily given financial information to US Attorney J. Alan Johnson and PA State Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman.

headline: EPA targets new effort to stem radon exposure
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency has launched a five-year national program to minimize exposure to radon. The program will ultimately include a nationwide survey to determine the extent of the problem, programs to minimize radon exposure in both new and existing homes, and a voluntary program to test the accuracy of radon-measuring devices used by private contractors.

headline: Blueprint For Traffic Court
abstract: Philadelphia's Traffic Court has a long record of corruption and corruptability. PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert N.S. Nix Jr. has prepared a plan that would help solve the problem. It includes: decriminalizing minor traffic offenses, establishing an agency separate from the court to collect fines, and Traffic Court judges would hear only the most serious cases. For this to happen the PA State Legislature must decriminalize traffic offenses, reorganize the Traffic Court, and establish an agency to collect the fines. Philadelphia City Council must also not allow the Traffic Court to be used as a Republican fiefdom. This is not a matter of preserving patronage jobs, it is a matter of good and efficient government for all Philadelphians.

headline: Taverns put damper on happy hour
abstract: The PA State Liquor Control Board has reduced bar and restaurant happy hours to last only two hours. The new guidelines have caused some bars and restaurants to change, and in some cases cancel, happy hour deals.

headline: Fathers Recalled With Affection
abstract: Various politcally prominent Pennsylvanian's are asked to recall their fathers, including PA Governor Dick  Thornburgh, Attorney William C. Costopoulous, Dauphin County District Attorney Richard A. Lewis, Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton III, PA Public Utilities Commission Chairwoman Linda C. Taliaferro, Harristown Development Corporation Board Chairman Barton A. Fields Sr., and retired PA Commonwealth Court Judge Genevieve Blatt.

headline: Sunshine, At Last
abstract: A thank you is due the PA House, especially PA Senate President Pro Tem Robert C. Jubelirer, for passing a new Sunshine law that fixes the hole created by a Commonwealth Court decision nine years ago. Now if a state or local government has a quorum when it meets, the meeting must also be open to the public.

headline: Firm stops hauling toxin across Pa.
abstract: The FMC Corporation has stopped shipping deadly methyl isocyanate, the chemical that killed about 2,000 in India, across PA. Instead, the company has built a $20 million plant in West Virginia that transforms methyl isocyanate into a relatively safe and stable powder called carbofuran where it is then driven to Buffalo, New York.

headline: Burger Quits High Court
abstract: President Reagan announced yesterday the retirement of U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice Warren Burger and his replacement with Justice William Rehnquist. He also announced the nomination of Antonin Scalia to be a judge on the court. Not only do the nominations preserve a conservative majority on the court, but with Scalia's youth, also reduces its average age from seventy-four to seventy-one. Scalia is a proponent of "judicial restraint," the belief that courts shouldn't exercise their authority to change laws written by Congress or executed by the president unless the Constitution specifically requires it to do so.

headline: the FORUM: WCTU says no to liquor candy
abstract: The membership of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union on Pennsylvania is opposed to the pending legislation in the PA Senate, namely Senate Bill 251, which would change the Pure Food Laws to permit the manufacture and sale of candy containing alcohol.

headline: FBI launches probe of Capitol expansion
abstract: The Federal Bureau of Investigation is looking into allegations of wrong doings in the PA Capitol expansion project. Two agents from the FBI spent about two hours interviewing the chairman and chief counsel of a special PA House committee that uncovered evidence of alleged kickbacks and other improprieties linked to construction of the $117 million capital addition.

headline: Support 'Sunshine' Law
abstract: The Pennsylvania League of Women's Voters in Lancaster County supports the 'Sunshine' bill, which will be considered by the State Legislature when it reconvenes, calling it an important step toward improving the open meeting law of Pennsylvania.

headline: Forester defends Casey on water ads in campaign
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Tom Forester defended Democratic gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey against a campaign commercial that implies Casey may be responsible for water pollution in Pennsylvania.  Forester crticized the commercial, sponsored by Casey's Democratic rival Ed Rendell.

headline: Camp Hill Escapee Still On The Run
abstract: Of the thrity-seven inmates who escaped from the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill between 1982 and 1983, four are still on the loose. Gregory Tarkentos was serving a life sentence for first degree murder, Mark Edward Young was serving a life sentence for second degree murder, Wendell Cherry was serving a four to ten year sentence for robbery, and Keith Robinson was serving a five and a half to seventeen year term.

headline: The insurance system can work
abstract: Ellen Klimon writes to the Philadelphia Inquirer about the problems confronting the liability insurance industry saying that much has been discussed but in a nonproductive way.  Kilmon says a discussion of effects involves little more than a competitive waving in the air of premium bills and insurance-carrier financial statements.  It is time to go back to some basics in order to come up with a workable solution.

headline: Federal probe of granite deal asked by state
abstract: PA General Services Secretary Walter Baran has asked federal officials to investigate alleged payoffs in the purchase of granite for the $117 million Capitol extension project.  The payoff allegations surfaced during a PA state House of Representatives committee hearing into the construction project.

headline: Supreme Court's supreme folly
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has upheld the rule that prohibits certain employees of the judiciary from running for political office without first resigning their jobs and then denying such persons the right to collect unemployment benefits. The Morning Call says that the Supreme Court's edict is nothing less than selective discrimination in the judiciary by the judiciary.

headline: Hazardous waste is commonwealth time bomb
abstract: Paul C. Nickalls, president of Heritage Metal Finishing Incorporated writes about the hazardous waste regulations placed in industries by the state and federal governments. He states that these institutions play up public fears of haphazard dumping, when new landfills under the jurisdiction of the PA Department of Environmental Resources are currently being considered. He states that members of the PA  House and Senate must convince their constituents that the options are to either construct hazardous waste landfills, or pay high costs to ship the waste to other states, mostly at the expense of small businesses.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon of two children watching TV. One child asks the other if he wants to "See stories about sex, drugs, and violence." The TV announces the beginning of the six o'clock news.

headline: Uncorked
abstract: Checkout lines were thirty people deep and there was little room to move in most state liquor stores as the PA Liquor Control Board (PLCB) cut prices by twenty percent yesterday. A similar two-day sale in June resulted in sales of nineteen million dollars, totals on today's sales are not expected until Wednesday. The Independent State Store Union crticized holding the sale on Labor Day weekend, when driving is particularly heavy and contending the PLCB is undermining its mandate by promoting liquor instead of controlling it. LCB officials observed that most people were stocking up for later use rather than drinking everything immediately.

headline: Final juror selected for Dwyer trial
abstract: The final juror was selected in the conspiracy trial of Pennsylvania state Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former state Republican Chairman Robert Asher.  They were indicted in May on charges of conspiracy, perjury, mail fraud, and interstate transportation in aid of racketeering.  Opening statements are scheduled to begin today.

headline: Sweet says he'll run for 2 posts
abstract: PA State Representative David Sweet has officially announced his candidacy for the Democratic nomination for PA lieutenant governor. He has also confirmed a plan to file nomination petitions for both the lieutenant governor's office and for re-election to his seat in the PA House.

headline: Hearing slated on radioactive waste disposal
abstract: The first of six public hearings scheduled to explain state plans to develop a low-level radioactive waste-disposal site will be held today in Harrisburg.  Pennsylvania is one of the largest sources of slightly radioactive waste in the United States and as such the PA Department of Environmental Resources has come up with plans for its disposal.

headline: City's senior judges asked to skip pay
abstract: Philadelphia court officials have asked that Philadelphia's 23 senior judges alternate between working one month for pay and working the next month without pay. The new compensation plan was ordered by PA Chief Justice Robert Nix Jr., who has the power to assign work to senior judges.

headline: Thornburgh gets bill to modernize insurance firms' investment rules
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate unanimously approved and sent to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh an investment-law bill that rewrites the 1921 Insurance Company Act as it applies to Pennsylvania-based-life insurance companies.  The bill would permit life insurance companies to enjoy investment opportunities, including investments in repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements.

headline: Fined $10,000, CTA 'mastermind' has paid up
abstract: The admitted mastermind in the Pennsylvania Computer Technology Associates bribery-conspiracy scheme, John Torquato, Jr., has paid his $10,000 fine in full.   Pennsylvania State Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former state Republican Chairman Robert Asher were indicted in May in the same case, with jury selection for their trial set for next month.

headline: Tally: Walgren Leading Buckman In Campaign Funds On Hand
abstract: While Ernest Buckman has promised U.S. Representative Doug Walgren a tough race, he has yet to raise the money to do it. Walgren has almost twice as much money on hand as Buckman. In the race between Bill Wachob and U.S. Representative Bill Clinger, Clinger has raised only slightly more money than Wachob. Meanwhile U.S. Representative Joe Kolter has a substantial fundraising lead over Alexander H. Lindsay Jr., and three U.S. Representatives up for reelection, William Coyne, Austin Murphy, and Joe Gaydos are running unopposed.

headline: Hearings on low-level radioactive waste site scheduled by DER
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources scheduled a public hearing regarding legislation to construct a low-level radioactive waste site in Pennsylvania.  Waste would come from West Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, and Pennsylvania.  Due to an agreement by the Appalachian States Low-Level Radioactive Waste Compact, Pennsylvania would be the site for waste, since it is the greatest producer of it of the four member states.  Pennsylvania would have executive control over the waste site, however, all four states would share the construction costs.

headline: CTA lawyer appeals, says Torquato testimony inconsistent
abstract: A lawyer convicted of participating in a scheme to bribe public officials has filed an appeal, claiming the chief witness against him gave inconsistent statements at his trial and at the trial of former Pittsburgh City Council President, who was given a four-month jail sentence and a fine.  The chief witness was the alleged mastermind of the bribery scheme that involved attempts to win government contracts for his data processing company.

headline: Thornburgh veto allows unisex rates
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh vetoed a bill that would have allowed insurance companies to continue using gender as a factor in determining PA auto insurance rates.  The veto means that annual insurance premiums will rise by an average of about $150 for women ages 16 to 24 and drop by a similar amount for men in the same age group, according to the PA State Insurance Department.

headline: Flaherty demands Schmeiser resign for choosing CTA
abstract: Pittsburgh City Controller Thomas Flaherty has demanded that finance director Ronald Schmeiser resign because of the Computer Technology Associates scandal.  Flaherty accused Schmeiser of gross negligence and incompetence in picking the Computer Technology Associates for a $150,000 tax-recovery contract with the Pittsburgh.

headline: Tearfully, Goode tells radio listeners of his pain over MOVE
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode expressed regret over the botched MOVE house confrontation and said he hopes to recover his momentum in the rest of his term.  The mayor said he still loved being mayor and will seek a second term.

headline: Hunters told to spare the deer
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) rejected a report filed by the Pennsylvania Game Commission and has decided to ban deer hunting in Ridley Creek State Park this season.  The DER does not agree with the Game Commission's assessments of what the deer population will be this year or on how many deer the park can support.  Many residents near the park praised the decision.

headline: Dangerous Backlog In Courts?
abstract: A study by the Citizen's Crime Commission in Philadelphia concluded that by the end of 1985, the number of judicial cases still awaiting trial in Common Pleas Court was more than 6,000, a record for the past decade.

headline: Thornburgh was right
abstract: Murray Howden of Allentown praises PA Governor Dick Thornburgh for vetoing an insurance bill that "promised discrimination." He encourages maximum public participation in automobile and health insurance.

headline: Fleece and friends braced for TV
abstract: This columnist discusses televising the U.S. Senate, saying how dull and uninteresting it is for viewers, as an argument against doing the same with the Pennsylvania State Senate.

headline: Televised debates planned
abstract: The League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania have planned to sponsor a statewide televised debate this year between candidates for PA Governor and U.S. Senator.

headline: Lake Arthur compromise
abstract: The appointment of a task force to study the potential for water pollution in Moraine State Park's Lake Arthur is a fair compromise move on the part of the PA State Department of Environmental Resources.  Nicholas DeBenedictis, PA Department of Environment Resources secretary, formed the task force after his department turned down a state legislator's request for a ban on strip mining near the lake.

headline: Counseling Abused Children: Gentle Approach Needed
abstract: Betty Burston, caseworker at the Dauphin County Social Services for Children and Youth, has thirty days to complete each case she works on.  Just last week, one of her half-dozen new cases included a four-year old girl with a venereal disease, and Burston has to determine if there was abuse or if the case is "unfounded."

headline: Thornburgh's going-away present: goodbye to LCB
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh wants the PA Liquor Control Board out of business and turned over to private companies as a going-away present as he retires from office at the end of the year.  He believes that governoment has no place in business and that Utah and Pennsylvania are the only two states with this monopoloy.

headline: For Better or Worse?
abstract: Writer expresses skepticism over benefits of new revised tax code legislation.  He/She doubts that the legislation will make filing individual taxes any easier.  Additionally, the writer thinks the new legislation will only grant more loopholes for special interest groups.

headline: That's Entertainment!
abstract: Instead of having an electoral contest between two legislators we are having a contest between two actors. In the PA Congressional race between Bill Clinger and Bill Wachob, the candidates have brought in Ed Asner and Charlton Heston to speak for them. Now it appears that candidates are more about the company they keep, with people voting on which actor they prefer. So much so that actors should be brought in based on the issue the candidate is running on, i.e. crime - Don Johnson, taxes - The Equalizer, etc.

headline: Legislator seeks funds for stream improvements
abstract: PA Representative Gaynor Cawley has asked the PA Department of Environmental Resources to create a $20 million stream improvement program.  Cawley said the money would be allocated over a 20-year period.

headline: Counties may get funds to begin '911' systems
abstract: Counties throughout PA could receive state help in establishing 911 emergency telephone number systems under legislation approved by the PA State House of Representatives. The measure would provide $1.5 million to counties that want to develop the emergency calling systems or upgrade existing operations.

headline: Thornburgh's order on LCB called 'joke'
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh's executive order to begin dismantling the PA Liquor Control Board went virtually unnoticed as state stores continued to do a brisk holiday business and PA Liquor Control Board enforcement agents went about their normal tasks. PA Governor-elect Robert Casey, who is set to take office in January, opposes the order.

headline: For governor: Casey, Rendell disagree on cutting income tax and on judge selection, but not on Thornburgh
abstract: A article that features a debate between Pennsylvania gubernatorial democratic candidates Robert Casey and Ed Rendell, who discuss income tax reduction, judicial reform, education, abortion, environmental regulation, current governor Thornburgh, and the Pennsylvanian economy.

headline: The Constitution party grows ever grander
abstract: The plans and costs for the celebration of the Constitution's bicentennial in Philadelphia have become more and more ambitious over the past few months.  The city is now hoping to raise $45 million for the event.

headline: Let the SUNSHINE in!
abstract: A staff member writes to urge the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources to disclose its activities to community members, arguing that the agency should come under the provisions of the PA Sunshine Law.

headline: County police report may clear firm of mob tie
abstract: Police in Allegheny County investigated a firm that had been negotiating a contract to build a $3 million cargo facility at Greater Pittsburgh International Airport, after county officials discovered that a New York publication had identified an executive of the company as having organized crime connections.  The background check found no organized crime ties.

headline: Tighter Disaster Aid Criticized At Hearing
abstract: U.S. Representative George Gekas and U.S. Senator John Heinz voiced opposition at a public hearing today over new regulations that would tighten restrictions on Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) funding to states after emergencies. No state could request aid for damage to uninsured public facilities that exceeds one dollar per capita, for local governments the total would be two dollars fifty cents per capita. If total damage exceeded that amount, federal aid would decline from seventy-five percent of eligible aid to fifty percent. Moreover, because each disaster is considered separately it is possible for an area to be damaged several times and still not receive aid. According to the PA Emergency Management Agency's director, John L. Patten, this would force the state to pay over eleven million dollars more before it could get aid. Gekas and Heinz have introduced bills in their respective chambers to change FEMA should the new aid proposal pass.

headline: For Lynch
abstract: A letter that supports Pennsylvania state senator candidate Francis Lynch over candidate Carol Coady, who the author says is a tax scofflaw.

headline: The costs of guarding the governor
abstract: PA taxpayers paid about $9,000 in salaries, overtime, and expenses to provide security for PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and his family during a vacation in New England. Overall, the records show that salaries, overtime, fringe benefits, and expenses paid by the state for the security detail are about $1.1 million a year.

headline: Mayors Reprove Congress About Costly New Mandates
abstract: A National League of Cities panel, made up of top officials from scores of major cities, passed two resolutions to warn the US Congress that before they impose new federal environmental, employment or other mandates on cities they had better provide the money to pay for them.  Officials estimate that it will cost the nation's cities $250 million over the next three years to comply with the Medicare requirements and $8.5 billion simply to submit applications for storm water permits.

headline: Court Backlog's Downright Criminal
abstract: The Philadelphia city court system has 9.418 open criminal cases, which continued to pile up while investigations of judicial misconduct sidelined six Common Pleas and Municipal Court judges, and the PA General Assembly waiting for PA Governor-elect Robert Casey to take office have left five judgeships vacant until at least next spring.

headline: Tighter Rules On Mortgage Deals Asked By Zimmerman
abstract: After a flurry of complaints in recent weeks from Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, and Harrisburg residents, PA Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman has proposed emergency regulations requireing mortgage brokers to return fees if they are unable to deliver a mortage on time and at the agreed upon interest or who increase the interest rates after the fact.  Currently such brokerages are not regulated by PA leaving officials unable to do anything.

headline: For US Senate
abstract: Editorial board criticizes Arlen Specter's record on issues affecting blacks.  Say while he originally supported issues important for blacks, he had stopped doing so in recent years.  They do not endorse his opponent, but they do make clear that they do not support Specter.

headline: the FORUM: Pay-raise plot will resurface
abstract: This letter opposes the proposed pay-raise of Pennsylvania legislators of $10,000 as the epitome of unmitigated gall, particularly given that Governor Thornburgh has restricted state employees to 3% raises.

headline: McKeesport agency rejects water sale
abstract: The McKeesport Muncipal Water Authority has turned down an offer from the Western Pennsylvania Water Company to buy its water system.  The President of the  McKeesport Muncipal Water Authority said it would sue any municipality that tries to sell its part of the system.

headline: Court upholds Pa. 'shield law" for reporters
abstract: The U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals has unanimously affirmed the constitutionality of the PA shield law which allows reporters to protect the confidentiality of their sources. The shield law states that no news person "shall be required to disclose the source of any information procured or obtained by such person, in any legal proceeding, trial, or investigation before any governmental unit."

headline: Topless bar Mr. G's string running out, Liquor Control Board pledges
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board ordered Mr. G's bar to turn in the liquor license that allows them to operate the bar which features topless female dancers. The order has been appealed and under PA law, a bar is granted an automatic stay when it appeals Liquor Control Board actions, and allows the bar to remain open until the appeal is decided.

headline: Fourth time's a charm
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor-elect Robert Casey (D) called his victory a victory for all those who were knocked down and got back up, winning after three unsuccessful runs for the governorship, the first one two decades ago.

headline: The gubernatorial battle is going down to the wire
abstract: In Pennsylvania's gubernatorial race, after spending $10 million and campaigning virtually non-stop the last 60 days, Democrat Robert Casey and Republican William Scranton remain locked in a tight race.  Both camps are unsure what Election day will bring.

headline: Milk shows iodine increase
abstract: Spokesman for the PA Department of Environmental Resources said that increased levels of radioactive iodine-131 from the Chernobyl accident continue to be detected in Pennsylvania milk, but the agency does not consider it to be hazardous to consumers.

headline: Crime panel's renewal voted
abstract: The PA Senate voted in favor of legislation renewing the PA Crime Commission, and will send the bill to PA Governor Dick Thornburgh. The legislation was a result of a "sunset" law requiring periodic reviews of state agencies. PA Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman told the PA Senate last year that the Crime Commission should abandon its investigative operations and become an advisory panel to the General Assembly.

headline: U.S. Steel Planning Further Staff Cuts
abstract: The United States Steel Corporation, the nation's larged steel producer and located in Pittsburgh, annouced that it will reduce its management staff by 10-15% this year, meaning a loss of 1,200 to 1,800 jobs.

headline: From Poconos to Penn, Edgar urges turnout
abstract: Senatorial candidate Bob Edgar traveled from the Poconos to Philadelphia seeking large voter turnout to overcome his standing in the polls.  He believes that he will end up getting strong support from environmental groups and labor unions.

headline: The Healer
abstract: Arnold Decker, has been classified as 100% disabled from a wound in Vietnam and had applied for a city disability position until Philadelphia District Attorney Ron Castille mentioned a possible political appointment job for Decker. Decker's lawyer says his back has been improving and a decision has been made not to pursue the disability application. The Philadelphia Daily News says maybe Ron Castille is a faith healer.

headline: Mine coverage OK'd without inspections
abstract: A two-month influx of applications for mine subsistence insurance in Western Pennsylvania has created such a backlog for the PA Department of Environmental Resources that it is approving some homes for coverage sight unseen.  Though risky, homes not checked before they are insured under the state-sponsored plan will be inspected by an agent afterward and changes may be made to the policy.

headline: D.A. to ask court ban at J&G bar
abstract: The Philadelphia district attorney's office said it would file a civil complaint in Common Pleas Court asking a judge to grant a preliminary injunction ordering the closure of J&G tavern in South Philadelphia.  The tavern features go-go girls and has remained open despite repeated complaints by neighbors and numerous citations by the PA Liqour Control Board.

headline: Unisex insurance seems doomed
abstract: The PA House voted 144-50 to override PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's veto of legislation that would allow insurance companies to base car insurance rates on gender.  This included 92 of 98 Republican house members voting against fellow Republican Thornburgh's veto.

headline: Full text of Thornburgh's State of the State address
abstract: The fiscal Year 1986-87 Budget Address of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh before A Joint Session of the Pennsylvania General Assembly House Chamber 11a.m. February 4, 1896, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania is transcribed.

headline: The lottery craze
abstract: A report by Francis Flaherty of The Progressive argues the negative social effects of the lottery, and that no more than half, and often less, of lottery revenues end up going to the state.

headline: No dearth of deer
abstract: Due to the plentiful deer population, the Pennsylvania Game Commission is considering opening a second deer hunting season in certain areas of the state, including Allegheny County.  The writer then goes into detail about population numbers and the details of the current hunting season rules.  The author concludes by saying that the high population demonstrates that humans and deer can coexist, however, the population must still be controlled and thus a second season should be supported.

headline: Day 1: City Goes On Amid Disruption
abstract: Most essential city services in Philadelphia were being maintained during the first day of a strike by nonuniformed municpal employees. Other than trash, which has begun piling up in areas across the city despite pleas by Mayor Wilson Goode to keep it inside until more specific instructions are issued, services such as police, fire, and water continue to be provided. However, there have been sporadic reports of vandalism and violence among the strikers. At the request of the city, Common Pleas Court Judge Alfred J. DiBona Jr. issued a temporary restraining order limiting mass picketing and clearing all doorways to buildings by lunchtime.

headline: 'Unisex' plan was not so bad, readers indicate.  Here's what our poll found.
abstract: Results of a Sunday newspaper referendum in Harrisburg indicate only lukewarm support for the auto insurance rating system that allows insurers to base rates on gender.  There were 281 respondents who said they believed insurance companies should use gender regardless of age while 172 disagreed.

headline: Fumo-Thornburgh dispute prevents filling city court
abstract: At least five vacancies on the Philadelphia Common Pleas Court will remain unfilled until at least February because Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh is frustrated by the refusal of Democratic state senators to approve his selections, with Governor-elect Bob Casey (D) to be confirmed January 20.

headline: Unconventional Wisdom form the Real Savvy Reader
abstract: Linda Paustian writes to the Philadelphia Daily News wondering why taxpayers have to pay a half of a billion dollars to build the Philadelphia convention center.  She writes that there are other ways to spend that amount of money that could really help the community.

headline: Ordered to stop polluting, plant continues operating
abstract: In Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, Quality Container Corporation, a Port Richmond firm ordered to shut down by a judge until it reduces smoke and other emisions to city-approved levels, continued to operate yesterday morning and produce smoke until neighbors complained.

headline: Death Penalty
abstract: In response to the reinstatement of the death penalty in PA, Enola resident Stacy Baker writes a letter to the Patriot News saying that she feels the death penalty means justice is finally done, with death.  If people are aware of the punishment for a crime, Baker thinks they will think twice before taking another person's life.

headline: Vintage bureaucracy: Uncork state's winemaking potential
abstract: Pennsylvania ranks as the fourth largest grower of grapes in the country, but the state's 46 wineries are limited in how much they can make by oppressive and unwarranted restrictions.  A bill approved by the PA Senate Law and Justice Committee would expand production quotas, the number of retail outlets, and would allow the production of wine coolers, the fastest growing segment of the wine industry.  This bill deserves the Legislature's approval.

headline: G.O.P. Governors' Post Gives Kean New Stage
abstract: New Jersey Governor Kean was installed as chairman of the nation's 24 Republican governors, a post that will enable him to play a role in shaping the party's national platform in the year leading up to the 1988 Presidential election.

headline: The Scene: In Philadelphia and its suburbs
abstract: A column where the author discusses upcoming gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races in Pennsylvania, using a play on words (such as masticate and pedagogy).

headline: Our opinion: Leisure trail
abstract: The author believes that the PA Department of Environmental Resources is right to fight the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' plan to alter a trail through Presque Isle, claiming that the trail poses a threat to wetlands.  However, the author remains unconvinced, and believes this is all bureaucratic nonsense.

headline: Death Penalty Covers More Killers
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh signed the first expansion of the state's death penalty since it was reintroduced almost ten years ago. Individuals previously convicted of third-degree murder or voluntary manslaughter are now eligible for the death penalty if convicted of a second murder. The expansion was requested by PA district attorneys who argued there were some cases they believed warranted the death penalty which they were unable to pursue. Two separate PA Supreme Court decisions overturning death penalty sentences for those previously convicted of third-degree murder and voluntary manslaughter were also cited. The American Civil Liberties Union argued that the death penalty was only to be used for the most heinous crimes and this expansion goes against that intention.

headline: Why bank law is needed
abstract: The author argues that with state legislatures in New Jersey and West Virginia enacting regional, reciprocal, interstate banking laws, the PA General Assembly needs to enact similar laws to ensure its rightful place as a leader in the national banking scene.

headline: GAP picking Walgren opponent; Sneath, Buckman confident of nod
abstract: Republican Allegheny County committee members in the U.S. 18th congressional district are casting endorsement votes in a lively battle between Henry Sneath and Ernest Buckman for party support in the May 20 primary.

headline: The Thornburgh legacy
abstract: The editors are impressed with Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh's record, particularly saving the state taxpayers $6.1 billion.  This has been done with many programs, such as reducing the state vehicle fleet by 20% of the last eight years, as well as converting the fleet to compact and subcompact cars, improving fuel economy.

headline: PA. fire officials on the lookout for rain
abstract: PA state officials said yesterday they were counting on rain to give firefighters a break after a rash of brushfires have blackened 8,886 acres this year.  There have been 591 brush fires around the state this year, up from 50 this time last year according to a spokesman from the PA Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Decision On AIDS Program A Good One
abstract: Erie County Executive Judy Lynch has signed a contract with the state to continue an AIDS counseling and testing program. Many people don't like dealing with AIDS and respond with moral condemnation, the editorial board is glad that officials of Erie County are not among that group.

headline: With job losses, Pa. Town slips into hard times
abstract: Article details the hardships of Greenville, a small Western Pennsylvania steel town, since the collapse of the steel industry.  The article goes in depth in examing the town and showing the devastating impact that the exit of steel has had, while also trying to point to signs of hope for the town's residents.

headline: Gekas aides say old time advice of 'let George do it" won't work
abstract: According to Ed Uravic, administrative assistant to PA US Representative George Gekas, 90 percent of a congressional member's staff time is devoted to constituent services, with 10 percent administrative-legislative.  More often than not, staffers are called on to be "ambassadors of good will" says Uravic.

headline: The Various Ploys Of Conniving Politicians
abstract: With the legislative session over, it is worthwhile to review various legislative customs. For instance, most work gets done in conference committees. In the PA General Assembly they are made up of six members two from the majority party in each chamber and one from each chamber's minority party. Compromise is crucial in these committees. For example, Erie wanted two new judges, however, its population did not justify the increase, but PA Representative Samuel Rappaport noted that without the two judges he would not sign the conference report and no one, including those desperately in need of them, would get any judges. Past statements are also becoming a tool. There are an increasing number of staffers with long memories who regularly remind members from opposing parties about things they said previously which contradict their current statements.

headline: Park reservoir called 'feasible' based on study
abstract: Consultants studying the water quality in Swatara, PA State Park say that construction of a reservoir there would be feasible.  PA Senator David J. Brightbill cautions that feasible does not mean economically possible. The PA Department of Environmental Resources had the water studied to determine the cost of meeting federal water-quality standards required for a permit to construct a 6-mile-long reservoir in the park.

headline: Deflecting NRA's Warped Aim
abstract: The National Rifle Association has prepared a media blitz against Bob Edgar in his race to unseat U.S. Senator Arlen Specter over his vote against a bill easing restrictions on guns enacted after the Robert F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King assassinations. Only one thing needs to be said though, no one is proposing taking away hunter's guns, and while gun rights is an important issue hunters would be better off evaluating candates on environment, taxes, 'Star Wars,' and a host of other issues that affect their lives more directly.

headline: Air Service Firm Gets Navy Contract
abstract: The U.S. Navy awarded a contract to Stambaugh's Air Service Incorporated to refurbish airframes on the A-4 Skyhawk aircraft. This is in addition to the extension of a contract for similar work on T-2 jet trainers. The company expects hire up to one hundred people for the A-4 contracts and two hundred for the T-2 contract. The company would also like to expand on its Harrisburg International Airport Property but is in a dispute with the PA Department of Transportation over whether the land on which it wants to expand is part of its lease.

headline: GOP Aim: 100,000 New Voters
abstract: Earl M. Baker, chairman of the PA Republican Party established a goal of one hundred thousand new registered Republicans before the registration deadline in October. Noting that most Republicans are under forty, the national Republican Party chairman, Frank J. Fahrenkopf, said that it was the party of the future that could turn out large numbers of new voters through calls and canvassing. While he acknowledge there was a perception issue with minorities and blue collar workers, Fahrenkopf argued the party had a great deal to offer them.

headline: These lobbyists go door to door, selling their point
abstract: The success of citizen action groups has piqued the interest politicians and party officials, who see door to door canvassing by these groups as effective ways to get messages out.  US Representative Bob Edgar has hired 10 canvassers from the League of Conservation Voters to raise money and contact supporters for his US Senate nomination.

headline: Plan To Hike Mining Fees Is Dropped
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration dropped plans to raise by fifty dollars permit fees for surface coal mines. The extra money was to go into a fund to pay for land reclamation of areas strip mined between 1977 and 1982. However, a compromise was reached after $3.3 million dollars was made available through the state budget and and another seven hundred thousand dollars from industry penalties was added for a twenty-five year long program. The coal industry was happy that it would not have to pay for problems other companies caused while environmental groups were disappointed the industry did not have to share in the extra cost for land reclamation. The change was sought due to concerns that the higher fee would be too difficult for the industy to bear.

headline: Delaware's sieve-like jail
abstract: This author believes that the people of Delaware have reason to be both alarmed and outraged by the escape of four prisoners from a Delaware Correctional Center near Smyrna last week and subsequent disclosures that prison officials had advance warning of a possible escape attempt

headline: Chesco site for veterans is dedicated
abstract: The Southeastern PA Veterans' Center was officially dedicated by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and a host of state officials and dignitaries in an outdoor ceremony.  The veterans' home was established on the grounds of the Pennhurst Center, a former state institution for the mentally retarded.  Thornburgh first proposed turning Pennhurst into a veterans' center two years ago, in order to provide both nursing-home care and independent living for up to 600 aging veterans in the Philadelphia area.  Further renovations to the complex are planned for the future.  The PA Department of Military Affairs said that some of the future renovations could cost $6.7 million, though the money has already been appropriated by the PA General Assembly.

headline: GOP enjoys foes' brawl
abstract: The author discusses the Pennsylvania Republican campaign strategy for upcoming state-wide elections, which includes letting Democrats cut themselves up in a hotly contested primary race, occurring on May 20.  Over the past few decades, Pennsylvania voters have been inclined to change their state administrations every eight years, and with a Republican as Governor, it is no wonder that Democrats are fighting in a primary that may yield the next Pennsylvania governor.

headline: Thornburgh boosts Scranton as his successor
abstract: Current Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh endorses Republican gubernatorial candidate William Scranton, who is the current Lieutenant Governor of Pennsylvania.

headline: Pop The Lid Off Bottle Committee Snag
abstract: Prospects for a bottle deposit bill remain grim. A bill proposed in the PA Senate hasn't moved in over eighteen months, and one in the PA House has been stuck in committee for nine months. A bill is necessary not only because of the litter that builds up, but because such litter damages farm equipment and hurts livestock. While oppoents argue that costs will rise and jobs will be lost, those states who have deposit laws have seen jobs created in recycling industries, while retailers are able to keep the deposits if cans aren't returned. All four of Centre County's representatives are behind the bill, but they need to spend more energy on it if there is any hope of it passing.

headline: Detentions Upheld in S Africa
abstract: The highest appellate court in South Africa handed down a ruling that upheld indefinate emergency detentions of critics of the government.  The decision overturned a lower court's decision that the emergency detentions law was invalid.  Human rights advocates viewed the new decision as a major setback.  They had hoped that the decisions by several provincial courts was helping to undermine the regime, but this new ruling negates such progress.  The detention law allows any member of the security forces to detain a person indefinately and without charges if they are seen to be a danger to the public order.

headline: Governors are up in arms over Guard overseas role
abstract: The U.S. Defense Department plans to send nearly 5,000 Army and Air National Guardsman over the next few months to train in Honduras. The guardsmen are being sent for the first time in large numbers into a country that is the staging area for the U.S. backed troops battling the Sandinista government in Nicaragua. Concern for the safety of the guardsman is an issue.

headline: GOP Governors Predict Gains In Fall Elections
abstract: Although Democratic governors outnumber Republicans thirty-four to sixteen, Republicans are optimistic that they will be able to significantly narrow the gap if not overcome it. PA Governor Richard Thornburgh, chairman of the Republican Governors Association, predicted a best-case scenario of eight to ten seats and at worst six seats picked up. He argues that it will be a chance for the Reagan revolution to be spread beyond Washington. Democrats note that they appear vulnerable because they have the most seats up for reelection, and they point out that their stronger organization at the state level, coupled with problems such as the farm crisis and the trade deficit should help them.

headline: Thornburgh doesn't rule out running again
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, a Republican, said it was "highly unlikely" a year ago that he would seek a third-term as governor in 1990 if a Democrat won this year.  Now, he seems to have developed a politician's proverbial never-say-never mentality.  Thornburgh, who would be running against PA Governor-elect Robert Casey, says that it is much too early to make any assessment of what is going to happen in 1990.  Thornburgh had pondered a US Senate campaign, but backed off in 1985.  Thornburgh has remained adamantly tight-lipped about his intentions once he leaves office.

headline: Bridge feasibility study suggested
abstract: Pennsylvania Transportation Secretary Thomas D. Larson has suggested an economic feasibility study as the first step toward building a bridge across the Susquehanna to improve York County's access to the Harrisburg International Airport.

headline: $200,000 In Budget For Subsidence In City
abstract: Although not specifically mentioned in the new state budget signed by Governor Thornburgh,  $200,000 has been included to compensate Schenley Heights homeowners for mine subsidence. According to PA House parliamentarian and aide to PA House Speaker K. Leroy Irvis, the PA Department of Community Affairs, in whose budget the money was placed, has been advised that the PA Legislature intends for the money to be used for the subsidence damage. While putting money for a specific purpose in a department's operating budget is not unheard of, it happens infrequently. Irvis placed it there because he thought the money would be available sooner.

headline: Port Authority Can't Get the Drop on Pigeons
abstract: Thanks to impassioned pleas of a bird lover on the board and an animal-welfare spokeswoman, the Delaware River Port Authority rejected a plan to poison the pigeons that have converted the Philadelphia Ben Franklin and Walt Whitman bridges into bird bathrooms causing health and safety problems..

headline: District judge blasts Senate on bill
abstract: A York County district justice says the PA Senate is short-sighted in refusing to consider a bill that would require parents to appeal in magistrate’s court when their children are charged with summary offenses.  Some PA Senators believe that the law would be to costly to implement.

headline: Our Opinion-The Strike
