abstract: The nurses at the Soldiers and Sailors Home are back on the job after recently walking off.  The Erie Morning News says that a walk out at a state facility is more serious then a strike at an ordinary hospital and that everyone should be glad that the walk out was settled quickly.

headline: GOP plans selection of candidate
abstract: Philadelphia's Republican party is looking for a candidate for the mayoral election in the city, scheduled for next year.  They are screening candidates who want to challenge current Democratic Mayor Goode, including former Mayor Frank Rizzo, former Republican mayoral candidate John Egan Jr., and Councilman Thacher Longstreet.

headline: Thornburgh flood aid cut stuns lawmakers
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh slashed nearly $8 million from the $15 million fund the PA Legislature voted to give to victims of the Monongahela River flood and other natural disasters last year.  PA Representative Fred E. Taylor and Senator J. William Lincoln were opposed to Governor Thornburgh's action and said the House and Senate would likely pursue an override to Thornburgh's veto and restore the money.

headline: Aspiring federal judge is called anti-black before Senate panel
abstract: Jefferson Beauregard Sessions, a controversial nominee for a federal judgeship, appeared before a Senate committee yesterday.  Testimony against him included assertions by several civil-rights activists that he was prejudiced against blacks.  Sessions is accused of ignoring civil rights law suits and claiming that the Klu Klux Klan is an "OK" organization.

headline: $229.5 million Pa. surplus forecast
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh boosted estimates for surplus for the current year and revenue for the next fiscal year, citing statewide economic growth.  There are calls for reduction in taxes.  In response, legislators in the PA General Assembly criticized Thornburgh for underestimating revenue by a substantial margin.

headline: Progress, And Work, On Chesapeake
abstract: The Chesapeake Bay is a national treasure not only because of its natural beauty, but also because it serves as a source of a variety of animals and provides jobs for tens of thousands of people. That is why the federal government, Virginia, Maryland, the District of Colombia, and PA are working together to try and save it. These efforts involve striking a balance between the number of people wanting to live there and the Bay itself, enforcing discharge permits, especially those who are regularly in violation, and controlling runoff. While it is easy to be critical of the effort, it is in its early stages and with continued work and cooperation, the situation will improve.

headline: Dog-Fighting Bill
abstract: The PA legislature should be commended for making dog fighting a felony, but it must also be noted that kittens and other innocent animals are often used to whet the dogs' appetites for blood and children are often brought to the events. PA Representative Gordon Litton is right to introduce the bill but it is still a slap on the wrist given the barbaric nature of the activity.

headline: Political Cartoon
abstract: Political Cartoon depicts Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan in a diner booth in Iceland with the press peeking around the booth.  The cartoon is titled "Suddenly, Gorby swept his unsuspecting date into his arms!…" In the cartoon, Gorbachev is reaching for Reagan and pulling him closer saying "Oh Ronnie! I can't bear it any longer!  Abandon these silly star wars dreams! Let's sign an arms agreement, now!"  Reagan, dressed as a woman, is saying "Oh! Oh, my! Gorby! On only our second date? Um..I..can't!"  The press looking on is saying "Have you ever seen Gorby so passionate?" "Ooh! How could Reagan resist such an offer?"

headline: GOP's No. 2 candidate releases list of clients
abstract: Republican candidate for Lieutenant Governor D. Michael Fisher released his list of legal clients he has had during his tenure as a state legislator.  This came not long after releasing his tax information as well.  The release is the latest in a round of public disclosures of tax and client lists by the gubernatorial and lieutenant gubernatorial candidates, each of whom is trying to make a political issue out of the others' information.

headline: Thornburgh gives Casey economy-sized blast
abstract: Governor Dick Thornburgh jumped into the race for his successor by harshly criticizing Democratic candidate Robert Casey for distorting the state of the Pennsylvania economy.  Thornburgh claimed that Casey used outdated figures in criticizing the state's economic development progress.  The Governor denied charges that his attack was a result of polls that show republican candidate William Scranton either behind or in a dead heat with Casey.

headline: Businesses are coping, and many are hurting
abstract: The Transport Workers Union strike against the Southeastern Transportation Authority (SEPTA)--now three dyas old--is beginning to hurt local businesses.  The effect is two-fold; rates of employee absenteeism have increased and store foot traffic has decreased--especially in retail outlets.  Gas stations seem to be the only businesses benefitting from the strike.

headline: 1986 Income Tax Guide
abstract: Filing income taxes in Pennsylvania can be difficult to understand. To help avoid making mistakes, the income tax guide provides advice and pointers to state taxpayers.

headline: Public Loses Crucial Forum
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh promised that the public would have a say in the rules that regulate a regional nuclear waste disposal site designated for PA. However, as deadlines approach the public review is being eliminated. Instead of writing the rules and sending them out for review, the rules will be written by the Thornburgh Administration and the public will simply be told what they are. Moreover, they are no longer rules, but merely guidelines. The sixteen member advisory board could conceivably speak for the public, but because nuclear waste generators are also participating the public's voice will likely be drowned out. The governor has broken his promise, it is up to the legilslature to make sure that he keeps it.

headline: Don't Halt Probe In Midstream
abstract: The Patriot's insistence that the committee investigating mismanagement and misconduct in the PA State Police be ended is both misguided and inflammatory. It is ironic that the paper orignially supported the committee's work and is now insisting that it stop after only four days of hearings, perhaps because of its own political reasons. The resolution creating the committee made it clear that an in depth approach was needed. Moreover, the Republican effort to stop the committee's funding was due to their belief that PA House staff should be used instead of an outside counsel. The committee has already discovered a lack of psychological screening as well as weapons familiarization, race relations, and alcoholism prevention programs; along with cases of drug use, sexual harrasment and disciplinary problems. The work of the committee is just getting started, much more needs to be done.

headline: VFW unit pushes for state agency
abstract: The PA Department of Veterans of Foreign Wars is considering creating a PA Department of Veterans' Affairs. Joseph L. Vicites, former Veterans of Foreign Wars national commander in chief spoke to members of the PA General Assembly about the importance of such a department, currently being considered by the PA Senate Military and Veterans Affairs Committee. He said that veterans' affairs are handled by a number of state and federal agencies, but no one agency to coordinate it all.

headline: Gov.-elect Casey to start building team
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor-elect Robert Casey this week begins the task of creating the team of public-private officials he promised would direct Pennsylvania's economic revitalization.  Casey refused to comment on the controversial issue of the state Liquor Control Board, a state monopoly on the sale of liquor.

headline: Thornburgh sets goals for last year in office.
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has begun his last year of eight years in office. In the year, Thornburgh is seeking to build on the foundation of past policy victories but also hoping to lay a few more cornerstones for state government.

headline: Job in Pennsylvania
abstract: Although February statistics showed that Pennsylvania's unemployment rate was lower than the nation's, this statistic does not necessarily indicate full economic recovery; the state employment climate must continue to improve before we start bragging about such figures.

headline: After 6 Mos., A Boost In Factory Jobs
abstract: Data shows that the unemployment rate dropped slightly this month - ending six straight months of manufacturing job losses. In addition to the widespread nature of the emplyment increases, the length of the average workweek and the amount of overtime worked also increased. While all of the numbers are good signs, there is no indication that things have improved in the long-term as a single month of data does not constitute a trend.

headline: Radiations levels up but not dangerous
abstract: Background radiation levels were roughly four times higher than normal yesterday in the air in Pittsburgh, far below dangerous levels, but high enough to warrant examination.  The samples will be sent to the University of Pittsburgh, School of Public Health for further analysis.

headline: Edgar Facing Hunters' Ire Over Gun Control
abstract: Richard S. Schweiker's defeat of incumbent Joseph S. Clark for the U.S. Senate almost twenty years ago was credited by Schweiker to his opposition to gun control and the support of gun rights groups. That election changed the influence of gun rights groups statewide, and with 220,000 dues paying members in the state, the National Rifle Association (NRA), along with the PA Sportsman Coalition, are a force to be reckoned with in state politics. Numerous politicians when running for statewide office have had to contend with their stance on gun control, some like PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and U.S. Senator John Heinz have even changed earlier pro-gun control stances. In this year's election for U.S. Senate, Bob Edgar has gone against the grain and the NRA has vowed to do whatever possible to keep him from winning, even giving him a grade of "F" because of his opposition to a bill overturning gun control measures passed after the Martin Luther King and Robert F. Kennedy assassinations. However, gun control is a non-issue with most state voters.

headline: A month's rain in an hour
abstract: Almost a month's rain fell in an hour yesterday afternoon in several areas of Allegheny County, spawning flash floods that killed at least four people.  Meteorologists believe that the storm was actually several storms that were slow-moving, resulting in an overabundance of rain.

headline: Governor backs chief clerk's authority at Traffic Court
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh took sides in the dispute over who runs Traffic Court, siding against the man he appointed, President Judge Salvatore DeMeo. The panel named Chief Clerk Royal D. Hart to administer the court after it had become enmeshed in a ticket-fixing scandal that resulted in the convictions of 13 people.

headline: Thornburgh Signs Budget Patch-Up, Vetoes Added Funds
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed a bill, passed in a rare summer legislative session, which freed up money for various social programs that had been frozen by language inserted by Democrats. The language said the  funds could not be distributed until after the November elections in order to prevent gubernatorial candidate and Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton III from getting political support out of distributing the money. Republicans and PA counties objected and a special session was held to repeal the wording. Democrats also used the special session as a chance to approve additional funds for various social programs. Governor Thornburgh used his line-item veto to remove the money arguing that it was more than was available.

headline: 1 million state grant to extend Clemente Park, develop shore
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh awarded a 1 million dollar grant to the Pittsburgh Urban Redevelopment Authority.  The grant will be used to extend the Roberto Clemente Park and Allegheny Landing on the North Shore.  The project is part of the North Shore Redevelopment Plan, and the most recent grant will be used for public access areas, walkways, benches and lighting.

headline: Another Thornburgh tax cut
abstract: In his latest budget proposal, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has recommended that the personal income tax, which was cut from 2.35% last month to 2.2%, be reduced again to a 2.1%.  He also suggested that the corporate net income tax be reduced again from 9.5% to 8.5% which would follow a reduction from 10.5% that went into effect last year.

headline: Radon: House sends bill to governor
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives averted a last-minute attempt to sidetrack legislation that would help people rid their homes of radioactive radon gas, sending the PA Senate amendment to PA Governor Thornburgh.  The bill provides money for the PA Department of Environmental Resources to develop and improve low-cost techniques for removing the gas from homes.

headline: Drug penalties created unequal in federal and state courts
abstract: Article looks at the differences between state and federal penalties for drug offenders.  Federal sentencing guidelines are strict and require significantly harsher penalties than state guidelines.  The disparities have left police and prosecutors frustrated.

headline: House panel to investigate explosion aboard Challenger
abstract: A U.S. House of Representatives Science and Technology Committee has vowed to investigate the causes of the explosion of the shuttle Challenger. Most members of the panel that authorize National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) programs said the Challenger flights should continue once the cause of the accident is found and remedied.

headline: Governor sees no administration stain in bribe case
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Thornburgh said that allegations of corruptions in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) case in which two top Republicans were indicated, will not stain his administration's record of integrity.  The two top Republicans were indicted for their alleged role in the case involving CTA's efforts to win a multimillion dollar contract from the State Treasury Department in 1984.

headline: Thornburgh Torpedoes 6 Myths About Gov't
abstract: In a recent New York City speech Governor Thornburgh proved wrong six myths about government, namely: the size of government cannot be reduced, taxes cannot be cut, taxes cannot be simplified, the welfare system cannot be reformed, tough anti-crime measures do not work, and the PA industrial economy will always be weak. He also listed the five principles of the Republican party: the importance of the individual, free enterprise, fiscal responsibility, government decentralization, and balancing compassion with toughness, which helped guide him and could also attract votes. So, what does he do now? Unless a post opens in the federal government, certainly a possibility, he can always go to a law practice in Philadelphia, which keeps him close enough to Boston, New York, and Washington to have an influence, or he could consider running for a more prestigious office in a couple of years.

headline: Bill would scrap tax cut
abstract: State Representative paul Wass wants to cancel Governor Thornburgh's proposed income-tax cut and use the revenue increase for education spending.  Cancelling the income-tax cut would obviate the need for local tax increases and reduce planned tuition increases for state universities.  A bill that would make this change and set up an Educational Supplement Account was introduced in the state House with more than 30 co-sponsors.

headline: Area's lawmakers split on budget cuts
abstract: In a move that may well foreshadow the rest of the legislative year, PA House Republicans tried unsuccessfully to force the Democratic-controlled PA House of Representatives to accept proposed cuts of $11.7 billion to state spending in this year's budget.

headline: Reckless of waste: Casey at bat against nuclear pact
abstract: Pennsylvania Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey said that he might not honor a previous agreement with Maryland, Delaware, and West Virginia for Pennsylvania to host a waste site for all four states.  The editorial board feels that the fact of the matter is that Pennsylvania, as the nation's largest generator of low-level radioactive wastes, cannot avoid hosting a repository for them.

headline: Drug Testing: State workers' unions denounce it
abstract: Union officials representing thousands of PA state employees say they would oppose any plan to test workers for drug use. Union officials say that such testing would violate constitutional and civil rights. The U.S. President’s commission on organized crime wrote a report that stated the use of random drug testing could help prevent the drug epidemic.

headline: PUC: Bell Confuses Callers In 412 Area
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) charged Bell of PA with failing to tell customers in the 412 area code that they no longer need to dial one for long distance calls in their region. This violates a PUC policy by creating a situation in which people may make long distance calls without knowing it. Bell of PA spokesman Noah Halper said that the changeover was well publicized two years ago and that there have been no complaints. The move is part of a plan to create additional phone numbers by including area codes as part of the number. When completed nationally, 1 will have to be dialed for all long distance calls.

headline: Governor wants state lawyers to file disclosures
abstract: The Dick Thornburgh administration said that it wants the state Supreme Court to overturn a lower court ruling that would exempt government attorneys from financial disclosures.  The state Ethics Commission is appealing the ruling.  Thornburgh says that the exemption could damage credibility and public confidence of the government.

headline: Thornburgh would consider cabinet post
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh said he would consider a cabinet post with U.S. President Ronald Reagan's Administration, but has stressed that his major concern is improving Pennsylvania’s economy

headline: State funds OK'd for parole by panel
abstract: The PA House Judiciary Committee approved legislation that would require the state to pay 90 percent of the cost of parole and probation services in the state's 67 counties.  Although several county governments support the bill, legislators say it could face serious opposition in the Senate because of its cost.

headline: Brief prosperity
abstract: Except for two one-month aberrations in 1982 and 1981, PA’s unemployment rate has not been below the national rate for a significant period of time since the mid-1970's. PA Governor Dick Thornburgh said that the unemployment rates are a symbolic breakthrough for the state's economic development strategy. The Patriot News says that this breakthrough may be short lived, but only time will tell.

headline: Recycling has bright future
abstract: Nicholas DeBenedictis, secretary of the PA Department of Environmental Resources, writes to call for support for PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's solid waste plan. The plan calls for curbside recycling programs, in which citizens sort out recyclables from non-recyclables. DeBenedictis points out that many citizens have testified before the PA Senate hearings on the legislation, which aims to reduce dependency on landfills.

headline: Electing Judges
abstract: The editorial board supports an amendment to the PA state constitution that would allow for electing appellate court judges.  The board adds that it is rare that any judges are from central PA, and currently all of the appellate court judges are from Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, or Schuylkill County.

headline: State panel to air phone deregulation
abstract: The PA Senate Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure Committee will hear testimony from representatives from eight phone companies and industry groups as they try to look at whether the state's telephone companies should be freed from regulation of all but local calling services.

headline: Granite Firm Boss: Aides Asked 20G for Payoff
abstract: A Pittsburgh area businessman told a special PA House of Representatives committee that he gave $20,000 in cash to two associates who claimed they needed the money for a "payoff" in connection with a massive PA state construction project last year.

headline: Thornburgh-Eye View
abstract: Writer notes that Governor Dick Thornburgh has switched from wearing glasses to contact lenses.  He then opines that he does not think it will help Thornburgh "to see the plight of the poor".

headline: Household toxic wastes pose disposal woes
abstract: Since there are no laws governing household disposal of toxic waste in Pennsylvania, experts worry that toxic materials will be disposed of with regular trash items and eventually contaminate groundwater.  Currently, the only organized statewide effort aimed at safe disposal of hazardous household waste involves the collection of used motor oil.  As such, state Senator John Schumaker has introduced legislation that would pay a professional hazardous-waste disposal company to collect materials regularly throughout the state.

headline: Budget politics
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has announced tax cuts for PA residents.  A letter to the editor at the Patriot News says that the income tax reduction for individuals is so small it is meaningless.

headline: 'Resource recovery' disposal plants being planned, built
abstract: Resource recovery plants are being planned, designed and built across Pennsylvania, with the first county-operated facility in the state to go on line this summer.  Construction of others is expected before the end of the year, regardless of whether the waste disposal plan proposed by the PA Department of Environmental Resources is accepted by the PA General Assembly.

headline: Emergency number will stir debate
abstract: The PA General Assembly seeks to establish a statewide emergency 911 telephone system.  The Times Leader says that if the bill is approved the 911 system would not be established in cites or counties unless residents approve it by a referendum vote.

headline: Storms impossible to pinpoint
abstract: The National Weather Service said that they were ill equipped to predict or measure the intense concentration of small storms that caused flash flooding in the Pittsburgh area on Friday, resulting in at least five inches of rain in three hours in one area.  It is the type of storm to normally occur in the midwest and caused massive damage in western Pennsylvania.

headline: Granite-deal probers give House hearing records to prosecutors
abstract: A PA State House committee, under pressure to cooperate with state and federal probes of alleged wrong-doing on the Capitol addition, gave transcripts of its hearings to prosecutors.  During the hearings, committee members were told that two officers of stone companies paid $65,000 in kickbacks to two former owners of one of the companies. Those allegations and General Services Secretary Walter Baron's call for a probe by prosecutors prompted an investigation into the matter.

headline: Thornburghs prepare to enter the next phase of their lives
abstract: Article focuses on Governor Dick Thornburgh's wife Ginny and her experience as a governor's wife and what her plans are after he leaves office.  Article goes into detail about her.

headline: The People's Law
abstract: The PA House of Representatives should approve the new Sunshine Bill, which was approved by the state Senate last week.  The new law will increase government transparency--something desperately needed in Pennsylvania.

headline: Budget Struggle Expected
abstract: Going into next week's deadline for passing the ten billion dollar state budget, members of the PA General Assembly can expect a full work week along with late night legislative sessions. There are a host of issues waiting to be dealt with, including the distribution of over two billion dollars in aid to schools. Democrats want all the money to go to basic education programs while Republicans want some of the funds to go towards local tax relief, student testing, and remedial education programs. Tax cuts are also an issue with House Democrats seeking to create a twenty-five million dollar program to help create jobs. Republicans believe the program will cost more. Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton III is also at odds with Governor Thornburgh, seeking more money for emergency food aid and nutrition programs. Fixing a loophole in the state Sunshine Law is also on the agenda.

headline: Ridley deer get no rest
abstract: The PA Game Commission, in response to numerous requests, met with residents in the vicinity of Ridley Creek State Park and Tyler Arboretum. Many people in the area do not like deer hunting at the park and residents were promised that illegal hunting would be curtailed. The PA Game Commission promised to step up enforcement with deputy game protectors on patrol.

headline: End problem image of state police
abstract: The editorial board is pleased that the special PA House committee investigating the state police had found no widespread corruption in the department, but also worried that they found that state police officials do not aggressively puruse wrongdoing within the department's ranks, that internal discipline is uneven and unfair and that the agency's efforts to bring minorities into the force have been inadequate.

headline: Trade-Secret Law Urged
abstract: Speaking at the annual Pittsburgh High Technology conference yesterday, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh issued a call for a new law that would provide civil remedies for the misappropriation of trade secrets. The law would be in addition to rather than a replacement of the Theft of Trade Secrets Law, which provides criminal penalties for industrial espionage.

headline: Gray in the 2d District
abstract: The Philadelphia Inquirer endorses Democratic candidate William Gray for representative of the Second District, which encompasses part of West Philadelphia, Center City and North Philadelphia wards.  The democratic primary basically will decide the winner of the election, as there is not Republican candidate running.

headline: Those High Growth Cities
abstract: The editorial board mentions how Harrisburg was mentioned in a survey to be just behind Boston as the Northeast city most likely to experience dramatic economic growth in the next decade.  The editorial board argues that Erie could be a prime candidate for growth as well, and the perception of Erie has to improve nationally.

headline: Goode sets tough goals in no-tax-hike budget
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode proposed a 1.7 billion dollar budget to City Council that avoids a tax increase for municipal purposes.  This objective, while difficult, is achievable and worthy of taxpayers' support.  There are, however, significant variables built into the mayor's budget.

headline: Budget's In, Checks Out
abstract: Yesterday, PA Governor Richard Thornburgh signed a general fund budget that fell just under ten billion dollars. The general fund budget is the core of the over eighteen billion dollar state budget and provides the money and authority to run state agencies and pay state public employees. This year’s budget also contains personal and business tax cuts, and additional money for a variety of social programs including several that provide food aid to the poor. However, because the budget was not signed by 12:01 AM, the state temporarily lost the authority to fund certain programs and forcing thousands of welfare checks to be delayed.

headline: Rules on chemical hazards rejected
abstract: The PA Independent Regulatory Review Commission voted against a PA Department of Labor and Industry regulation to implement the 1984 chemical hazard law, the Worker and Community Right to Know Law, which was sponsored by PA Representative Mark Cohen. However, IRRC may approve the regulation if the DLI makes the law more practical for non-manufacturing businesses to be effected by it. A federal court decision exempts 17,000 manufacturers, who will instead follow guidelines laid out by the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration. The PA AFL-CIO finds delaying the law anymore to be unjust.

headline: Ex-court employee alleges judges had tickets fixed
abstract: A former employee of the Philadelphia Common Pleas Court contended that he routinely had parking tickets fixed for 25 different judges and that the district attorney's office took no action when told about it.

headline: Warm up can have cruel twist
abstract: Killer storms in the last 2 years have struck far from the usual 'tornado alley.’ Tornados are the offspring of warming weather. Government statistics show tornadoes begin increasing sharply in March, with fatalities peaking in April and the total number of storms reaching its maximum in May.

headline: Gray Just Another Joe?
abstract: A letter to the editor that criticizes Pennsylvania politician Bill Gray, who is running for re-election, for wasting money earmarked for social problems.

headline: Time running short for political races
abstract: Article addresses a variety of issues such as the closeness of the gubernatorial race, the World Series, and the problems with the Erie water delivery system.

headline: Thornburgh doesn't share Kean's concern on Gramm-Rudman
abstract: Governors Dick Thornburg and Thomas Kean, though both Republicans, exhibit different responses to the federal deficit-reduction act.  Governor Kean, who is sometimes critical of President Reagan's economic policies, has been quick to state, in rather concrete terms, the impact that deficit reduction will have on New Jersey, while Governor Thornburgh--an ardent supporter of President Reagan's economic policies--has been more vague in his statements about deficit reduction and its impacts on Pennsylvania.

headline: Buisnesses owe $100 million in jobless-pay taxes
abstract: Democrats in the PA General Assembly have accused PA Governor Richard Thornburgh’s administration of mismanagement based on recent revelations that state businesses have failed to pay over $100 million in unemployment compensation taxes.  The administration has denied the charges.

headline: Soviets admit N-release
abstract: A nuclear accident in Chernobyl is likely to have killed and injured many, and sent a radioactive cloud 1,000 miles west to Scandinavia. The US Environmental Protection Agency said the cloud could reach the US West Coast in 5-6 days. Charlie Porter of the EPA's Radiation Alert Network said there is no way of knowing if Americans will be affected until the agency gets a radiation level reading. It is also unknown what effect the accident will have on residents of nearby Kiev.

headline: Faceless men perform
abstract: Death penalty executions require executioners who must either  throw the switch, fire the rifles, and/or inject lethal fluid. Society has long been ambivalent about them, and the executioners are seldom left untouched by the ritual they perform. Anonymity shrouds the executioners.

headline: S. Africans Listen When Boesak Speaks
abstract: Reverend Allan Boesak, leader of the United Democratic Front, a South African political movement, spoke before a National Association of Black Journalists luncheion last week to talk about apartheid. As a 'colored,' those designated by the South African government as neither white nor black, but in between, life is made a little easier. However, he noted that they still cannot vote or own property, and are therefore, not free. His movement has spread throughout the country, encompassing not just coloreds, but Zulus, Indians, and whites too. Boesak predicts that apartheid will soon end, and points to the anointment, by the South African government, of Mangosuthu Buthelezi, leader of the Zulus, as head of the country's blacks. Designating someone who would otherwise be considered a thug as a leader highlights the systems weakness.

headline: Group from state told damage tops Watergate
abstract: More than 200 Pennsylvanians, including business executives, professors, ministers and others from the commonwealth, each paid $60 for a public full-day seminar on national security issues sponsored by U.S. Senator John Heinz, where Admiral Stansfield Turner, CIA director during the Carter administration, called the Iranian arms deal more damaging than Watergate.  Heinz has sponsored similar seminars, with this topic chosen long before the Iran-Contra scandal was revealed.

headline: Today's sports shorts
abstract: Carlisle's Michael Owens will be recognized as one of Parade Magazine's All-American high school football team members during a Rotary Club luncheon at The Embers Convention Center.

headline: Private prisons barred, 268 Center is curbed
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed legislation that temporarily bars any new private prisons from opening in the state and places restrictions on a prison facility in Armstrong County.  The legislation was motivated by controversy over the transfer of 55 prisoners to Armstrong County from Washington D.C.

headline: Bullish: Economy seen growing through end of 1987
abstract: The National Association of Business Economists said its latest survey of 330 of its members found that the U.S. economy, which has endured an extended period of sluggish activity, is about to rebound with substantially higher growth – expected to last through 1987. The report attributes part of the turnaround to the dramatic plunge in oil prices and interest rates.

headline: Sportsmen Back Spector
abstract: A member of the Unified Sportsmen of Pennsylvania writes a letter describing why his organization believes that incumbant US Senate Candidate Arlen Spector should be supported.  He feels that gun control and the rights of hunters is one of the most important issues.  Spector is pro-gun ownership, while his opponent Bob Edgar favors tougher gun control laws.  He also approves of Spector's record on environmental issues.

headline: Families, Too, Are Prisoners Of Love
abstract: A number of inmates, and family and friends of inmates in PA's prisons talk about the lack of conjugal visits. Some are concerned not with conjugal visits but just having general private time to talk about things that should not be discussed in an open prison atmosphere. Others express dismay at the collapse of families because of the policy.

headline: An Invitation For The President
abstract: The six black front-line states bordering South Africa have issued an invitation to US President Ronald Reagan urging him to attend a summit so that he better understands the nature of the problem represented by South Africa's destabilizing policies in the region. The author spoke with Angolan President Jose Eduaro Dos Santos who also invited President Reagan to come and see the effects U.S. support of UNITA rebels is having in the country. Both of these overtures represent unique opportunites for the president, who has never vistied Africa, to meet face-to-face with national leaders in order to better understand their problems and further the cause of peace in the region. Failing to respond to this will mean a failure to achieve the highest values of the American people.

headline: Gubernatorial race put at $12.7 million
abstract: The cost of the campaign for Pennsylvania governor was at least $12.7 million, more than double that of the 1982 election, according to expense reports filed in the state capital of Harrisburg yesterday.  Common Cause, a citizens lobbying group criticized both candidates for spending so much on the election.

headline: Toxic-labeling law not effective, official says
abstract: PA Secretary of Labor and Industry James Knepper said that PA's 1984 Worker and Community Right-to-Know Law, intended to get employers to label and identify hazardous chemicals, is fragmented and unenforceable. A US District Court ruling removed manufacturers from the law's jurisdiction. Knepper's office was given some time to revise the law, which was rejected by the PA Independent Regulatory Review Commission. Aides of PA House Majority Leader James Manderino said that the law could play a role in the House's decision whether or not to extend the IRRC's life at the end of the year.

headline: Attorneys decry viewed erosion of clients' trust
abstract: Roughly 100 Pennsylvania attorneys took part in a panel discussion on attorney-client privilege.  Attorneys criticized the somewhat common practice of calling attorneys to testify before grand juries as an erosion of attorney-client privilege and the right against self-incrimination.

headline: Close budget-watch needed
abstract: PA Governor Richard Thornburgh is not expected to pull money from the state’s rainy day fund when he makes his budget proposal to the PA General Assembly in February.  However, the PA State Treasury’s emergency may yet come into play as the federal government contemplates cutting funds to the states.

headline: State To Provide Money For 7 Superfund Sites
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) said it would provide one million dollars to continue cleaning seven Superfund sites that would otherwise be slowed down by the failure of Congress to pass additional funding.While the total amount is still unknown the DER is almost certain that it will receive federal money.

headline: FBI agent, Dwyer aide differ in testimony
abstract: In the case against PA Treasurer Budd Dwyer, on trial in federal court on bribery-related charges, a top aide said that Dwyer would have given a multimillion dollar contract to a firm other than Computer Technology Associates (CTA) if his staff had recommended it.  This is in direct contrast to a federal agent, who said that two years ago Dwyer heavily influenced the selection of CTA.

headline: At naturalization ceremony, talk of Old World disaster
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh addressed one of the largest naturalization ceremonies ever held in Montgomery County, using the time to discuss the Chernobyl disaster and saying that it might never have occurred if people in the USSR were free to question governmental authority.  The ceremony was presided over by the Montgomery County Court President.

headline: Gov Vetoes Extra $7M Funding
abstract: Governor Thornburgh signed a bill yesterday removing language prohibiting the distribution of human services money until after the November election. The language was added by PA House Majority Leader James Manderino in order to prevent Lieutenant Governor and gubernatorial candidate William Scranton III from gaining political support from distributing the funds. Scranton promised not to make the announcements and with the urging of the counties the legislature met in special session to remove the language. Democrats in the PA House also used it as a chance to approve additional money for a variety of social programs, but Thornburgh removed it with his line-item veto.

headline: Training in fairness Parking employees are qualified
abstract: A letter to the editor written by William Rasky, the executive director of the Philadelphia Parking Authority, says that there have been erroneous impressions about the quality of employees and efficiency of management in the parking authority.  Rasky wants residents to rest assured that a competent group of employees is serving the citizens of Philadelphia.

headline: Bush Welcomed
abstract: Vice President George Bush received a warm welcome at a fundraiser for gubernatorial candidate William W. Scranton III.

headline: Discouraged workers missed
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author states that a drop in the unemployment rate in the Harrisburg area is not necessarily a sign of vigor in economic activity, and may well be bad news.  The author looks at how the unemployment rate is tabulated, and focuses on the fact that the unemployment rate does not take into account "discourgaed workers", or those who give up looking for a job.  The author concludes by noting that if the regional unemployment rates fell because many central PA residents gave up looking for work, then that is not news to celebrate. The letter was written in response to a December 9, 1985 editorial in the Patriot-News.

headline: State Toxic Waste Superfund Sought
abstract: One Old Forge Toxic Waste Removal Committee member favors establishing a Pennsylvania Superfund provided the PA Department of Environmental Resources is expanded.  The PA state Superfund legislation, which has been sent to the PA Senate, has been proposed by legislators who believe the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Superfund is not adequately cleaning up state toxic waste sites.

headline: Figures On Missing Children Disputed
abstract: The number of stranger kidnappings in PA is in dispute. The state police says of all the state's missing children only two were stranger kidnappings, the remainder being runaways or taken by parents in a custody dispute. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children disagrees arguing the definition of kidnapping is too narrow and when examing cases in Florida found that cases classified as sexual assault and murder also involved kidnapping. Ultimately definitions are not as important as prevention  and PA Senate Judiciary Chairman Stewart Greenleaf says that a new law requiring immediate investigations of missing children will benefit everyone.

headline: Carter talk gains enthusiastic reception
abstract: Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter gave a speech on "Religion and Foreign Policy" to an enthusiastic group at Messiah College.  The enthusiasm continued after Carter's address.

headline: HACC board raises president's salary to $73,100
abstract: Dr. Kenneth B. Woodbury, president of Harrisburg Area Community College will earn a $73,100 salary effective July 1.  With the raise Woodbury will rank amongst the highest paid state officials.  Governor Dick Thornburgh has a salary of $75,000, although the new governor will earn $85,000.

headline: Trip limit tightened by panel
abstract: The Pennsylvania state Ethics Commission has set tighter limits on privately financed trips for public officials, with a half-dozen guidelines written to be used by public officials in determining whether it would be proper to accept payment for travel.

headline: TMI defendants ask September trial
abstract: Defendants in the Three Mile Island trial are requesting a September trial that would deal exclusively with the question of how much radiation escaped and where it went; questions of injuries sustained would be answered in ensuing trials only if a jury decides that radioactive emissions were at high enough levels to cause human harm.  The defendants claim is that the complexity surrounding radioactive emissions warrants separate consideration.

headline: Employment: New Hampshire's workers do a job on US record
abstract: The unemployment rate in New Hampshire dropped below 3 percent, making it the first time since 1979 that any state in the U.S. has achieved such a feat.  The article also contains various other unemployment figures and trends for selected states.

headline: State's No. 1 Spot In Acid Rain Causes Worry
abstract: PA's rainwater now has the highest acidity of any state in the nation. The change is a result of emissions from power plants and cars which is absorbed by rainwater, thereby changing its acidity. Acid rain is already starting to cause problems, it leaches aluminum from the soil and other metals from pipes, these metals as well as the acidic nature of the water itself is absorbed by fish and plants making them more vulnerable to disase. The PA Fish Commission has already started replacing fish in  thousands of miles of PA waterways with those more resistant to the acidity. However, the long-term solution involves reducing power plant and car emissions, which the Reagan Administration is unwilling to do because of cost and other considerations. PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's support of Reagan makes him equally unsupportive of such measures.

headline: Final agony:  Is electric chair death quick or is it 'cruel and unusual'?
abstract: It has been 24 years since anyone has been electrocuted on death row in PA, but it may change soon.  Experts have been arguing over the details of the method of death to prisoners, deciding whether its quick justice or cruel and unusual punishment.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon of President Reagan talking to a lawn ornament, asking if it wants to be the U.S. Ambassador to South Africa

headline: Handicapped voter access in Pa.
abstract: Writer accuses state of dragging its feet on complying with a federal law requiring polling places to be handicapped accessible.  She says that the polling places should have been in compliance by the primaries.  She outlines the various provisions of the federal law.

headline: Tullio's Pet Peeves
abstract: Editorial discusses a comment by Erie Mayor Louis Tullio to democratic gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey.  Tullio expressed frustration over unfunded mandates from the state to the local governments.  Casey agreed that they are unfair.  Article also includes information about other Erie politicians and public figures.

headline: Heinz pushes bill to boost medical benefits for ex-POWs
abstract: Senator John Heinz has sponsored legislation that would ensure better access to health care for prisoners of war--many of whom do not have the ability to prove that their injuries are service-related.

headline: Excerpts from Thornburgh's budget address to the General Assembly
abstract: Excerpts from PA Governor Thornburgh's budget message to the PA General Assembly are given, including growth projections and tax proposals.

headline: States urged to form coalition to fight acid rain
abstract: A PA environmental defense fund scientist has said that Pennsylvania must work with other states to combat the corrosive hazard of acid rain.  Such joint efforts may spur the federal government into long overdue action on the problem.

headline: For Juvenile Offenders, No More Games
abstract: Prosecutors say legislation signed yesterday by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh refomring state juvenile laws will expand their ability to identify and punish serious juvenile offenders, ending an eight-year battle between the state's prosecutors and Democratic legislators who opposed toughening juvenile laws.

headline: Distressed by charges, U.S. says
abstract: The Reagan administration said it was distressed by Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's charges that the U.S. and its allies tried to take political advantage of the Chernobyl nuclear accident.

headline: 'Hands' Didn't Fall
abstract: A letter that disputes another's opinion that Hands Across America was a failure.

headline: Two misspent vetoes
abstract: This author writes that with the flurry of interest in the latest election, President Reagan vetoed two important pieces of legislation that had the unanimous support of Congress, the Clean Water Act and a bill that would have established nationwide energy efficiency standards for major household appliances.

headline: Government operated best in the sunshine
abstract: Sunshine laws in Pennsylvania have increased the accessibility of the people to their governments.  This access is crucial in a representative democracy; citizens need to be a party to the arguments leading up to the final vote on an issue.

headline: Government reports job rise
abstract: Statistics show that employment in Pennsylvania rose by 58,000 jobs in January 1986, to 5.16 million. Residents reporting unemployment fell in Pennsylvania by 11,000 to 421,000. The rise in employment in the state follows a national trend spurred by increased hiring in construction and retail jobs.

headline: Trash plan is assailed at hearing
abstract: About 300 South Philadelpia residents denounced the proposed trash-to-stream plant at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, including PA Senator Vicent Fumo, who said they did not want the facility there.  Politicians and residents both criticized the Navy for not highly publicizing the rally, with a notice appearing in the Federal Register only in recent days.

headline: For Prisoners, Love Is Out Of Reach
abstract: People both in and out of PA's prisons have begun a campaign to allow conjugal visits for married inmates. Proponents note that such visits improve prison security by instilling respect for the institution and creating disincentives for inmates to cause problems, while also improving inmate security by reducting violent homosexual acts. Prison officials note the additional costs of building facilities for the visits, especially within an already overcrowded prison, as well as the issue of deciding who gets the privilege and when. Officials in New York expressed similar concerns but found granting the privilege to be a great success.

headline: Groups Decry South Africa Detainee List
abstract: According to the Detainees Parents' Support Committee (DPSC), a list released by the South African Ministry of Law and Order containing the number of people detained since a state of emergency was declared in June has only half as many names as it should. The group claims the list should have as many as fifteen thousand names, instead of the over eight thousand claimed by the government, because it should include those who were released after lengthy detentions and those held for fewer than thirty days. The DPSC argues that according to its analysis most of the people arrested were members of student groups, political parties, or trade unions.

headline: Hands in the cookie jar
abstract: William Dietz Jr. of Allentown writes to the Morning Call thanking PA State Representative Greenwood for his fight to allow the public to see records that PA House of Representative members submit in order to draw expense account funding.

headline: U.S. Senate: Pennsylvania vote
abstract: Vote totals in the Pennsylvania U.S. race between Democrat Bob Edgar and incumbent Republican Arlen Specter by county.  Edgar is leading with about half the precincts reporting, though the central counties, traditionally Republican, have yet to report.

headline: Circumcision has medical merit
abstract: A local physician argues that Pennsylvania Blue Shield or other health-insurance companies should not refuse to pay for routine circumcision.  Even though circumcision is the product of parental choice, it is as procedure with medical merit.

headline: Governor plans cut in tax rates
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will call for a reduction in the personal income tax from 2.2% to 2.1% in his last state budget address.  He will also ask for a cut in the corporate income tax rate from 9.5% to 8.5%.

headline: Water Goes Off At Homes,Hospitals
abstract: Water was cut off to over twenty thousand Philadelphia homes and several hospitals for almost five hours yesterday. Some areas began to notice a decline in water pressure around twelve thirty in the afternoon, but most service had been restored by six in the evening. Philadelphia Water Commissioner William J. Marrazzo said the cause of the problem was still undetermined and that while city strikers had attempted to disrupt water service previously, there was no evidence that they were responsible.

headline: Forget It-Dial-it callers unaware of $2 fee won't have to pay
abstract: The PA Attorney General's office is investigating a company that had programmed a "dial-it" telephone number and charged customers $2 for each call without disclosing that there would be a fee.

headline: Legislator raps South Africa link
abstract: PA State Representative Alphonso Deal has criticized the state's retirement system for investing in companies with South African ties.  Deal says PA should not support racist regimes.

headline: Heinz, Specter: We Need Roads
abstract: As one of the largest and most industrialized states, PA is a vital commercial link, which means adequate roads are crucial. However, look at federal funding for work in the central part of the state. It is included in a U.S. House bill but is nonexistent in the U.S. Senate version, although programs are included in the home states of every U.S. Senator on the Environment and Public Works Committee. Where are U.S. Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter? As long serving Republicans they should be able to get the necessary funding. Perhaps it is because neither one of them is from Central PA. This is something to think about come election time, which for Specter is now.

headline: U.S. subpoena of Colafella stalls
abstract: A PA judge has temporarily delayed enforcement of a federal grand jury subpoena seeking documents collected by a PA House of Representatives committee investigating the $117 million dollar Capitol expansion project. The committee uncovered allegations of kickbacks and a payoff in the project.  The subpoena requires Colafella to appear before the grand jury along with a host of documents and records gathered by the committee during its year-long investigation.

headline: Flaherty panics Democrats
abstract: State Democratic leaders are alarmed by Tom Flaherty's informal candidacy announcement for Liuetenant Governor.  Flaherty, the Pittsburgh City Controller, has strong name recognition throughout the state, giving him a large advantage over his rivals.

headline: Governors Get Reagan Sympathy
abstract: The nation's governors came away from a meeting with US President Ronald Reagan without assurances that the president intends to do anything to help ease cutbacks in domestic spending - hampering states trying to balance their budgets. The governors had better luck trying to influence the pending tax bill in the US Congress, which would ease the financial burden on their constituents.

headline: Water Is A Western Pennsylvania Asset
abstract: Two editorials earlier this month involving an impending PA labor shortage and water shortages in the South go hand in hand. The authors note that high-tech industries are beginning to offset heavy industry and that there may be too few people in the region to support such growth in the future. They also point out the limited water supplies that are available in the South. Western PA is blessed with ample rain-based water supplies. The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) has made a concerted effort to take care of the land and make sure that this water remains clean and available. If the PUC continues to do this it will lay the foundation for people to come streaming back in the future.

headline: Former councilman to get a new trail
abstract: Former Philadelphia City Councilman William Cottrell was granted a new trial by a federal judge in a case involving alleged illegal use of funds.  Even though Cottrell was convicted, he was granted a new trial since the judge had failed to fully instruct the jury on the law governing the case.  Cottrell was convicted of 6 total charges that dealt with conversion of money from employee benefit plans.

headline: Mob in Harare Attacks South African Offices
abstract: A mob in the Zimbabwean capital of Harare attacked the South African trade mission and airline offices.  The mob was vowing revenge for the death of Mozambican president Samora Machel, whose plane crashed outside of South Africa.  African National Congress leaders have accused South Africa of assasinating Machel.

headline: Heston Joins Clinger Campaign Against Wachob, Asner
abstract: Charlton Heston has donated his celebrity status to help U.S. Representative Bill Clinger campaign for reelection. Heston's support comes in response to the assistance given to Bill Wachob, Clinger's opponent, by Ed Asner. Both actors are known for their opposing political views. Heston attacked Asner for participating in events which he said raised money for a pro-Soviet newspaper and Communist rebels in El Salvador.

headline: Unisex Battle-It Makes for Some Strange Bedfellows
abstract: After the PA House voted to override Governor Dick Thornburgh's veto of a ban on unisex auto insurance in Pennsylvania, Democrat House Majority Leader James Manderino has moved to have the chamber to reconsider the issue.  It marks the only time ever that Democrat Manderino and Republican Thornburgh have been aligned against the Republicans in the PA House and Senate.

headline: USA strikes back: Full report, 4,5A
abstract: This article gives a detailed description and pictorial representation of United States air-to-surface missile attacks in Libya.

headline: House bloats budget plan by millions
abstract: The PA House added an estimated $547 million in spending to the $9.7 billion state budget proposal for 1986-87, with lawmakers attaching more than 100 amendments, influenced by special interests, to the budget bill.

headline: What U.S. giveth, Penna. town would give back
abstract: A $12 million federally financed sewage treatment plant may have PA residents paying hookup costs as high as $2,500 per house, having monthly sewer bills of $32 and up, and seeing the potential loss of one-fifth of the township's half-mile long business district. Robert Scott, township supervisor, is campaigning to have the government scrap the $12 million plant in favor of a less ambitious system that would cost about $2 million.

headline: Former trooper used pot, coke, he tells panel
abstract: In Pennsylvania, ex-trooper Alvin Wilson told a legislative committee he smoked marijuana and was high on cocaine while on duty and knew of other troopers at his barracks who used illicit drugs.  He said that  cocaine addiction led him to commit 11 robberies while a member of the force.

headline: NICARAGUA CONTRAS
abstract: A cartoon depicting a sled pulling up to a building marked Nicaragua Contras, carrying President Reagn and pulled by reindeer.  The reindeer say 'WE"RE HERE BOSS!' and Reagan replies "GOOD (YAWN) ... NOW WHICH GUY'S THE AYATOLLAH?'

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: Historical events on April 29 include Joan of Arc's entering the city of Orleans in 1429, New Orleans' fall to Union forces in the Civil War in 1862, and the liberation of Dachau concentration camp by American soldiers in 1945. It is also the birthday of Japanese Emperor Hirohito.

headline: University honors senior judge
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh awarded Commonwealth Court Senior Judge Genevieve Blatt the Bicentennial Medallion of Distinction.  Blatt received three degrees from Pitt and also taught political science there.  She was also the first female elected to state office as well as the first female elected to state judicial office.  Pitt also gave medals to four other alumni.

headline: Why Miller Opposes the Governor's Tax Cut
abstract: Representative Marvin Miller, a Republican, opposes a tax cut proposed by Governor Thornburgh.  Miller wants the revenue that would fund a tax cut to be used for secondary and post-secondary education.  Miller is one of 40 state representatives co-sponsoring legislation to give money to education instead of cutting the income tax.

headline: House firmly rejects Reagan's budget as Republican stage protest.
abstract: The Democrat-controlled US House of Representatives rejected US President Ronald Reagan’s budget for the 1987 fiscal year, causing seventy-seven angry Republicans to refuse to vote for it.

headline: $90 million could go to Pa. in oil case
abstract: Pennsylvania could receive at least $90 million over three years for energy related programs under a proposed settlement of an oil-overcharge case, involving more than 100 crude-oil producers between 1973 and 1981.

headline: Freshie's Role Is Debated As Racketeering Trial Opens
abstract: The federal prosecutor in the trial of Freshie Company argued today that the company had a corrupt relationship with the Philadelphia School District for eight years, while the attorney for the company contended that Freshie was the victim of an extortion attempt by corrupt school district officials. The company is charged with paying over forty thousand dollars in bribes to get a lunch contract with the school district that ran between 1978 and 1981. The company's president along with four school district officials have already pleaded guilty to mail fraud and other charges in the scandal. Officials decided to approach Freshie because it was already bidding on a contract with the Philadelphia Recreation Department and was also a big contributor to then-Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo's campaign.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of Princess Grace with George Hauptfuhrer and his wife

headline: Highlights in history
abstract: Historical events on April 29 include Joan of Arc's entering the city of Orleans in 1429, New Orleans' fall to Union forces in the Civil War in 1862, and the liberation of Dachau concentration camp by American soldiers in 1945. It is also the birthday of Japanese Emperor Hirohito.

headline: Unknowns are uneasy elements in elections
abstract: If minor political party candidates get good ballot positions or have familiar sounding names, they can get anywhere from 3% to 6% of the vote and sometimes more. Sometimes that percent margin can make or break candidates favored in the election.

headline: Court upholds NRC rulings on TMI restart
abstract: Yesterday, the U.S. Supreme Court voted 8-1 that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission properly allowed last year's restart of the Unit-1 reactor at the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant.

headline: House proposes $500 million in state budget additions
abstract: The PA House proposed to add more than $500 million to the Democratic leadership budget package for the 1986 fiscal year.  Among the major added spending programs approved were $20 million for various aid programs to non-public schools and $50 million for mass transit.

headline: 20,000 more flee Chernobyl
abstract: Soviet officials said that 20,000 people are being moved out of areas found to be contaminated by the Chernobyl disaster.  They also said that the cleanup should be completed by the end of the year and those evacuated were taken to villages and towns up to 25 miles away.

headline: Going to far on lawyer discipline
abstract: The writer, who is a lawyer familiar with the PA Code of Professional Responsibility, says that he takes strong exceptions to comments reported in the Inquirer made by Chief Justice Robert Nix Jr. about discipline of criminal attorneys.  The writer adds that Justice Nix's comments add confusion to an issue already misunderstood by the public.

headline: S Africa Accussed of Raid Plot
abstract: South African forces were accused of preparing a raid on the Mozambican capital of Maputo by the Mozambican government.  The accusation was made at a summit between the six front-line nations bordering South Africa.  Mozambique says that South Africa is planning the raid due toe a land mine explosion near the nations' border, which South Africa contends was committed by the African National Congress with the approval of the Mozambican government.  The two nations have had a non-aggression pact since 1984, although both accuse the other of supporting rebel groups in one anothers nation.

headline: Hospital transfer bill voted down in Senate
abstract: In Pennsylvania, the Thornburgh administration's campaign to transfer state general hospitals to local controlled suffered a setback when it failed to pass in the state Senate.  Nearly all Senate Democrats vetoed against the bill and the transfer was opposed by the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees.

headline: Unopposed, but campaigning
abstract: Pennsylvania Republican gubernatorial candidate Bill Scranton is campaigning throughout the state, waiting for the Democratic primary between Bob Casey and Ed Rendell at the end of the month to see who his opponent will be in the elections in the Fall.

headline: State to honor area agencies
abstract: Three area organizations will be honored today for their volunteer community-service programs: the Dauphin County Area Agency on Aging, the Migration and Refugee Services of the Catholic Social Services and the Retired Senior Volunteer Program.

headline: Illogical To Reject A Tax Cut
abstract: In this editorial, the Inquirer contends that taxes should be cut during both economic growth and stagnation, even if it means a reduction in government services during growth. It is arrogant to assume that in good times the government is better able to spend money than the taxpayers. Moreover, Philadelphia's wage tax, which the paper supports, is a main stumbling block toward local tax reform that the paper also advocates. Until such contradictions are resolved, this paper's opinion is that Harrisburg will continue to be viewed with skepticism.

headline: 25 generator tubes fail test, TMI finds
abstract: Tests found that 25 steam generator tubes in the Three Mile Island nuclear plant's Unit 1 were cracked. Tests required by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission were performed on the unit as part of a restart program following Unit 2's near-meltdown in 1979. Joanne Doroshow, a lawyer for the citizen group TMI Alert Incorporated said the failure to test all steam tubes was unacceptable.

headline: In A Program For Juveniles, Treatment And Tragedy
abstract: The deaths of ten VisionQuest youths in six years has prompted a number of investigations. While the company has been cleared of criminal wrongdoing, that does not mean it is free of problems. The deaths from a staph infection could have been prevented had staff members allowed the youth to see a doctor; they refused because it is normal for new participants to fake their way through the program by feigning illness. The company was also involved in a boating accident that took the lives of 7 people. The Coast Guard found that no person on the boat at fault, but because no one on the boat had a license or certificate the company was not necessarily free of guilt.  It later paid a fine to the Coast Guard for a lack of boat inspection certificates. Prompted by the deaths, PA set up a committee to look at VisionQuest and its juvenile rehabilitation services.

headline: South Africa Is Not Clinging to Apartheid
abstract: In this opinion piece, the author believes that no other nation has as much influence on the nations of Southern Africa than South Africa does. We base our relations with our neighbors on mutual respect. We seek friendship with the nations bordering us as long as their territory is not used for violence against us. The economies of many of the poorest nations in Sub-Saharan Africa are closely linked with South Africa's and they want to prevent the rest of the continent from sliding further into despair. They are not clinging to apartheid, it is this constant attack that keeps the countries of the region separated from one another and undermines further prosperity.

headline: House Approves Aid To Contras
abstract: The U.S. House approved one hundred million dollars in lethal (seventy million dollars) and non-lethal (thirty million dollars) aid to the Contras last evening, which was a reversal from a similar vote in March. This marks the first time the U.S. government would openly give help to the group. The heated debate centered around needing to provide aid in order to limit the growth of communism in Central America while opponents noted that much of the aid previously given ended up in numbered bank accounts or with the Honduran military. There is speculation the bill passed this time because three hundred million dollars in economic aid to Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, and El Salvador was also included, giving opponents a reason to change their vote. This bill now goes to the U.S. Senate for final passage. A list of how the PA House delegation voted was also included in the article

headline: Vote bill a blow to Consumer Party
abstract: Under the rules of the PA state election code, a candidate of the Consumer Party would only need to collect signatures from other party members to be placed on the ballot. A new proposed bill by the PA General Assembly bill would make the Consumer Party collect a percentage of signatures. Until PA governor Dick Thornburgh signs the bill, or if he vetoes it, the Consumer Party is in the unique position of being the only party that can set its own rules for nominating candidates.

headline: Every man a connoisseur
abstract: In California, winemakers are experimenting with a device that provides a detailed map of a given wine's molecular structure.  Winemakers will use this map to recreate classic wines, such as a 1961 Chateau Latour.

headline: Keeping Low: Area Unemployment Steady In July
abstract: The Philadelphia-area unemployment rate remained at just above five percent in July, its lowest level in over a decade. Job growth was broad-based encompassing many of the regions firms, but the greatest growth was in non-agriculture sector. For the state as a whole, unemployment fell to 6.7 percent in July compared with 7.3 percent in June. Nationally, unemployment was just under 7 percent for July.

headline: 500 evacuated near Philly, gas leak being mopped up
abstract: Emergency services workers continue to clean up a gas leak in the northern Philadelphia suburbs which led to the evacuation of some 500 residents and the closure of a 22 mile section of the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  The cause of the gas leak has not been identified.

headline: GPU's Drug-Test Plan Is In Court
abstract: A grievance by the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers union at Three Mile Island have filed a petition in court requesting a halt to random drug testing until the issue has been dealt with in arbitration. The union not only objected to the unilateral way the policy was carried out but also the unreliability of the tests. The American Civil Liberties Union argued that the tests presume people are guilty and that it unreasonably allows the search and seizure of a person's bodily fluids. General Public Utilities argues that the tests are for worker and community safety and that only when both halves of a sample test positive will a person face disciplinary action.

headline: Thornburgh And Backbone
abstract: The authors are skeptical of Governor Dick Thornburgh's reasoning behind his sudden review of PA's ties to South Africa. Arguing that he did not want black leaders from the opposing political party to make up his mind for him, he travelled to Africa to see for himself, however, he failed to go to South Africa and instead met with leaders of other African nations who are concerned and confused by U.S. policy. We are disappointed with the decision as well as the "reasoning" behind it, just as we are disappointed with his refusal to fight to keep Conrail independent, especially given its economic importance to the state.

headline: House Democrats look to Casey for better communication
abstract: In Pennsylvania, the State House Democrats are hoping for improved lines of communications between the Legislature and the governor's office under newly elected Democrat Robert Casey.  The House majority leader James Manderino, said that Democrats, despite having control of the House, had no link with Republican Governor Dick Thornburgh on major legislation, which suffered as a consequence.

headline: Vote for Arlen Specter
abstract: After discussing the negative campaigining which has been rampant in elections in Pennsylvania this year, the author supports Republican incumbent for U.S. Senate Arlen Specter, saying he alone remains unscathed in purpose and character.

headline: Why insurance situation is a crisis
abstract: Governor Thornburgh is calling for tougher regulations on insurance companies that would limit their ability to cancel commercial policies.  He is also forcing companies to provide at least 60 days notice of cancellation.  These steps will help end the insurance crisis in Pennsylvania.

headline: Local jobless rate jumps
abstract: Data shows that the adjusted unemployment rate increased by a half percent in the Pittsburgh area, hitting the 8 percent mark. This figure is one percentage point above the national average.  Causes for the increase include: seasonal downturns, the completion of summer programs, and a work stoppage at the USX Corporation.

headline: 55-mph limit under attack
abstract: Abundant supplies of oil and falling gasoline prices are fueling a move to increase the national 55-mph speed limit.  This person argues that the 55-mph is supported by 70% of Americans, it saves lives and fuel, so why change it.

headline: Grand jury probe vowed in Philly MOVE bombing
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Ron Castille called for a grand jury to investigate the siege and bombing last May in Philadelphia that killed 11 people.  The probe could result in criminal charges against Mayor Wilson Goode and other top city officials for the bombing of MOVE's fortified row house in West Philadelphia that killed five children and six adults.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon shows a plane designated "N289VA", which is most likely trying to fly around the world without landing.  In the background of the plane, flying into the distance, is the Wright Brother's plane that first flew at Kittyhawk, North Carolina.

headline: House Gets South Africa Bill With 'Real Bite'
abstract: The U.S. House has adopted rules allowing it to consider a U.S. Senate bill banning new U.S. investment in South Africa, even though it is weaker than the total embargo outlined in a U.S. House bill. The decision was made in order to ensure that the bill would land on President Reagan's desk prior to a congressional recess. This would force Reagan, an opponent of South Africa sanctions, to veto the bill instead of letting it die during the recess.

headline: VOTERS GUIDE: Pa. primary: The choices on May 20
abstract: Pennsylania primary voters guide title page.  It covers race-by-race listings compiled by the League of Women Voters.

headline: Sunshine?
abstract: Although the PA Senate approved a new Sunshine law last week, the bill is insufficient and needs to be reconfigured by the state House of Representatives.  The first iteration of the bill was perfect, but Senate amendments have placed serious limitations on requirements of governmental transparency and allow for too much secrecy.

headline: Losing money
abstract: The directions for PA's Personal Income Tax stipulate that income in excess of $45 necessitates filing a tax return, even if it's a child with $45 in bank account interests. This amount yields $1 in taxes, despite the fact that it presumably costs the state and taxpayers more than $1 to process the tax return. The author contends that she was the first person to bring the issue of the cost of processing an income tax return to the attention of PA Senator Mark Singel.

headline: Area around plant varies widely
abstract: The area around the Chernobyl nuclear facility is highly varied, ranging from thinly populated wooded steppe to the third largest Soviet city, Kiev. The population most affected is located in the town of Pripyat, which was built for employees of the Chernobyl facility. The Soviet Union reported that three other towns near the site had been evacuated.

headline: Groll Killer May Face Execution
abstract: Two men were convicted of murdering Dr. Michael Groll on New Year's Eve. Christopher Briggman was found guilty of second degree murder, which carries an automatic life sentence, and David Steward was found guilty of first-degree murder, making him eligible for the death penalty. Steward's lawyer, Arthur James, trying to spare his client's life told the jury Steward was guilty but that it wasn't premeditated. He also said he would bring in numerous character witnesses during the penalty phase, which began yesterday afternoon, to show he was a decent person. Montgomery County District Attorney Thomas Waters was frustrated that both were not found guilty of first-degree murder, but accepted the jury's ruling and is now focused on securing the death penalty for Steward.

headline: "CALL SCRANTON AND SPECTER AND TELL 'EM DON'T OVERTRAIN "
abstract: A Cartoon depicting the Pennsylvania Democratic candidates for governor and for U.S. Senate running towards the 'Dem. Marathon' while people watch from the windows of the GOP headquarters.  Mud is being slung over the Democratic gubernatorial candidates Robert Casey and Edward Rendell.

headline: House gets Sunshine Law
abstract: The PA State Senate gave unanimous approval to a bill aimed at reinvigorating the state's Sunshine Law.  Described as a compromise, the measure was sent to the PA House of Representatives. The new measure would require that discussions by a quorum of members of an agency be open to the public.

headline: Zimmerman discussed donation, Smith says
abstract: A former Republican official, Smith, testified in the Computer Technologies Associates (CTA) case, where Pennsylvania state Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former state Republican Party chairman Robert Asher are accused of an array of bribery charges in granting a state contract to CTA.  Smith accused Zimmerman, the Pennsylvania attorney general, of being complicit in the scandal.

headline: Governor cites effort to promote exports
abstract: At the annual conference of the United States Export-Import Bank, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh argued that other states can follow Pennsylvania's lead in fighting the nation's massive trade deficit.  He lauded a 10 million dollar program designed to help PA industries increase their shares of foreign markets.

headline: New U.S. Tax Proposal To Have Little Effect On State Collections
abstract: Pennsylvania, which does not couple its income tax to the federal definition of taxable income, will feel little impact from proposed changes in federal income tax regulations. Surrounding states such as Ohio, New York, and Maryland expect large windfalls and are already preparing changes in their state tax laws in order to return most of it to the taxpayer. In West Virginia, because so few people itemize deductions, changes in revenue will be minimal. States without any income tax will be hurt the most. Part of this is due to the fact that they will miss the federal windfall, but also because their residents will pay higher federal taxes with the loss of sales tax exemptions.

headline: At Shippingport, nation's first nuclear reactor is being dismantled
abstract: Turned on in 1957 and dedicated by US President Dwight Eisenhower, the Shippingport Atomic Power Station was the nation's first commerical nuclear power plant.  It is now becoming the first nuclear power plant to be dismantled.  The decommissioning of the Shippingport reactor has come to be regarded by the US Energy Department and some in the US Congress, as a model for how a dismantling can be done.  However, the methods at Shippingport may not be used, elsewhere, given that the conditions there differ from those at the large commercial plants.  The article looks at ways that nuclear power plants can be decommissioned.  Shippingport's decommissioning will cost an estimated $98.3 million and take five full years to complete.
