A detailed account of the dismantling of Shippingport is included in the article.

headline: Gun Control Advocates: Leave Dream World--No Place is Safe
abstract: The writer responds to a previous letter that advocated gun control and criticizes it.  The writer believes that gun control won't make people any safer and that the cities are so dangerous that people need guns to protect themselves.  Gun control advocates live in a dream world.

headline: 1986 legislative calendar familiar
abstract: The PA General Assembly starts its 1986 session. The Patriot News says the tentative calendar for the PA House of Representatives shows important issues hanging on the agenda and says they are unresolved because they are controversial and are not likely to get addressed this year.

headline: House opposition gathered force quickly
abstract: PA Republican House members were resigned to voting for a bill creating a nine-member Philadelphia Center City Convention Center Authority.

headline: Voters In Nine States Select Candidates For Nov. 4
abstract: Voters in nine states had the chance to determine their party's candidate for a variety of offices, including U.S. House and Senate seats and governorships. The rest of the article details specific races, none of them in PA.

headline: Casey calls on Scranton to demand state police chief's firing
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert P. Casey accused Lt. Governor William W. Scranton, his Republican opponent, of tolerating racial discrimination in the Pennsylvania State Police.  Casey's accusations stem from the PA State Police's refusal to give command of the York barracks to Russel Clanagan, a black lieutenant who filed racial discrimination cases against state police.  Casey was specifically critical of Scranton for saying that the state police chief handled the situation well--even after a U.S. District Court ordered the state police to give Clanagan the post.

headline: Reed submits bigger budget, no extra tax
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed unveiled his proposed 1987 budget and urged Harrisburg City Council to approve the plan that would increase general city spending by over 12% without raising taxes.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: A cartoon showing U.S. Department of Energy officials walking through piles of nuclear waste with one commenting that they should have snuck it into Philadelphia and Detroit when they had the chance.

headline: Gun Control Needed
abstract: The author believes it is ironic that people talk about needing guns to protect ourselves from criminals when it's the nice guy who wipes out his family or the insane person who shoots a cop. Will society ever learn?

headline: 2 Heavies Seek to Lead Demo Ticket
abstract: The Democratic primary in Pennsylvania is held on May 20, when two Democratic gubernatorial candidates will face one another with many believing the winner virtually a shoe-in for governor. Robert Casey is endorsed by the state's Democratic leaders, while Ed Rendell has raised more money and is thought to be the more energetic candidate.

headline: House Plan Tough On Bond Issues
abstract: Restrictions on the use of state and municipal bonds in a recently passed U.S. House bill could hit PA hard warns the Public Securities Association (PSA). The bill would limit to just under three hundred million dollars the total value of bonds PA could issue for various non-profit activities. In nineteen eighty-four alone PA issued almost six hundred million dollars in bonds just for hospitals and another almost two hundred million dollars for private higher education. The bill also limits the number and type of bonds that could be tax exempt, thereby increasing borrowing costs which are then paid by the public in higher taxes and user fees. The PSA is advocating a less restrictive U.S. Senate version of the bill. Both will have to be reconciled in a mid-July U.S. House-U.S. Senate conference.

headline: Voters Reward Past Performance: Specter, McDade Win
abstract: As expected, in Pennsylvanian elections yesterday U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and U.S. Representative Joseph McDade won decisive victories.  The editors did not support either candidate in the U.S. Senate race, though they admired them both, and unanimously supported McDade.

headline: Hoeffel gears to fight La Rouche candidate
abstract: Democratic congressional candidate Joe Hoeffel says he takes the campaign of his Democratic primary challenger, Jack Sheetz, seriously and will wage a vigorous campaign against him.  Sheetz was formerly the mayor of Landsdale and is a supporter of Lyndon H. La Rouche's platform.  Hoeffel is surprised by Sheetz's embrace of LaRouche's radical views.

headline: Sales tax deduction ended
abstract: In this editorial, the authors believe that Pennsylvania is a loser in the recent change to federal tax law. The change will do away with deductions for state sales taxes, while retaining deductions for state income taxes.  They note that PA depends heavily on the sales tax for state spending.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon of Uncle Sam sitting on a pile of nuclear waste and calling Texas to see if they would be interested in "a big government giveaway".

headline: Hazards Alleged For PA. Inmates Kept On Death Row
abstract: Additional testimony was heard in the lawsuit by PA death row inmates against the state regarding the conditions they are held in. An outside consultant stated that inmates were being kept in hazardous conditions such as poor air circulation, falling plaster, and various fire hazards. A former corrections official from Maryland testified that inmates complained to him of limitations on visits and the long number of hours they are restricted to their cells. The official also noted that while most states with the death penalty isolate those inmates from the rest of the population almost all are less restrictive than PA.

headline: 2 in CTA case lose appeals
abstract: The 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals refused to give new trials to attorneys William T. Smith and Alan Stoneman, who conspired to bribe PA public officials to obtain no-bid contracts for Computer Technology Associates, a data processing company. Smith and Stoneman argued that US District Judge Malcom Muir was in error for not granting each defendant a separate trial.

headline: House Votes To Free Grants, Adds To Spending
abstract: The PA House of Representatives approved a bill that would remove language from the newly passed state budget prohibiting the release of human services money until after the November elections. The language was added by PA House Majority Leader James Manderino, who claimed gubernatorial candidate and current Lieutenant Governor, William W. Scranton III would make public check presentations in order to win votes. A new wrinkle has been added, however, as the PA House also included an additional seven million dollars for other social services programs. While Governor Thornburgh will likely use his line-item veto power to eliminate the funding he will have to publicly explain why.

headline: Wachob Votes
abstract: I have to respond to a letter recently written by a reader regarding Bill Wachob. While the reader argues that his voting record is too clean, I consider it a nightmare. He voted for a bill to weaken state efforts against illegal drugs and opposed Governor Thornburgh's welfare reform bill. Wachob is ultra-liberal, the question is, are the voters?

headline: I-95 Access Proposal Splites City Civic Groups
abstract: Members of several neighborhood groups say that the Queen Village plan to improve access to and from Penn's Landing violates an agreement entered into with the Queen Village Neighbor's Association.  The plan calls for the construction of an underpass beneath I-95 and is being opposed by a coalition of communitites.

headline: Send Us Mail-Order Taxes, Pa. Says
abstract: PA's Department of Revenue is suing mail-order companies L.L. Bean and Bloomingdale-by-Mail Limited in order to force them to collect sales tax on products bought by PA residents, or provide sales records so that the state can bill residents directly. The state argues it lost $77 million dollars last year alone in uncollected mail-order sales tax. The lawsuit is part of a larger effort to get companies to start collecting and reporting sales tax to the state. Pennsylvania is already sharing tax information with Ohio and New York and is beginning to pressure Delaware to do the same, in order to collect taxes on interstate purchases. Both companies contend that expecting them to collect sales tax for PA would force them to do so for other states and cities, which would become an administrative nightmare. More significantly, they argue that because they have no physical presence in the state, they are not obligated to do so, according to a U.S. Supreme Court decision almost twenty years ago. A panel of PA Commonwealth Court judges recently heard the case and is expected to rule on the matter in the next couple months.

headline: Charges of mismanagement, possible job loss confront PE rate plan
abstract: PE may have to change its rate plan in order to remain productive. Under PE's plan, if the nuclear plant is forced off line by malfunctions or a lack of cooling water in the summer, ratepayers could be charged more-costly replacement power from other sources. Under the OCA-sponsored proposal, the one-time rate increase of $133.7 million dollars of about 5.3%.

headline: Hidden Behind Veil
abstract: A law recently passed by the PA legislature and too widely interpreted by local judges has thrown a veil on the crime of child abuse. While protecting the identity of innocent victims is something that should be promoted, judges are closing whole files, denying the public access to information on the crime itself or the person responsible. In so doing all the effort at throwing light on a problem that has for too long been in the dark is being undermined.

headline: 2 In Thornburgh's Cabinet To Testify In Probe Of State Capitol Expansion
abstract: PA Budget Secretary Robert A. Bittenbender and PA Administration Secretary Murray G. Dickman will be asked to appear before a PA House committee investigating alleged kickbacks and price inflation in the project to expand the state capitol, a project whose cost expanded from $56 million to $117 million. The continuation of the hearings has been controversial PA Attorney General Leroy Zimmerman failed to find evidence of wrongdoing after a two-year investigation and two federal grand juries have yet to hand down any indictments. At issue is a thirty million dollar no-bid contract for granite. Accusations of election-period posturing have been traded by both sides.

headline: How About Young People?
abstract: Pennsylvania lottery funds go to provide a wide array of senior citizen benefits while young people are leaving the commonwealth in droves.  These editors question the wisdom of ignoring the young in favor of the old.

headline: Waiting for Casey
abstract: The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette holds meetings with candidates in races where it determines that there is a contest of significance.  However, in Pennsylvania's gubernatorial race it has been impossible to get both Democrat Robert Casey and Republican William Scranton together.  Casey failed to show up in a scheduled meeting, citing Scranton's negative campaigning, which he had said he would stop doing but continued anyway.

headline: Incumbents having a good year
abstract: In this year's general election, incumbents in Pennsylvania find themselves at an extreme advantage.  Roughly one third of current state House members seeking re-election will run unopposed, and approximately one fourth of those seeking re-election in the state Senate will run unopposed.

headline: Spending Up, Taxes Cut
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh hailed the state’s budget for the upcoming fiscal year. Not only does it provide increases in a wide variety of social services, with total spending up more than 3% from last year, but it also includes over $160 million in tax cuts. The PA Legislature and Governor Thornburgh should be commended for passing a budget that both increases crucial state spending while lowering taxes at the same time.

headline: Chernobyl Contamination Is Worst Ever, Experts Fear; 5,300 May Die
abstract: A report prepared by the Soviet government for the International Atomic Energy Association concerning the nuclear accident at Chernobyl indicates that over five thousand people may die from radiation-induced cancer as a result of the accident; an amount higher than from the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The report also raises questions about why it took over a day to begin evacuating the nearby city of Pripyat and even longer for a number of local villages. U.S. scientists reading the report also believe it seeks to minimize casualties in some areas; they believe cancer deaths could be even high than the report predicts.

headline: House Approves Gun Law Change
abstract: A bill approved in the PA House by a 186-0 vote, and with the agreement of the National Rifle Association, will allow for local gun permits to be valid for five years.

headline: 2 More Legislatures
abstract: The writer agrees that a Constitutional amendment eliminating two terms for a US president is a bad idea, but it takes thirty-eight state legislatures, not thirty-six, as your editorial states, to ratify an amendment.

headline: How 'guru ad' carried Casey to win
abstract: In Pennsylvania, the race for governor had ups and downs, with Democratic winner Casey falling in the polls after revealing his anti-abortion stance, then Republican opponent William Scranton faltering after sending a negative mailing, after promising to end all negative campaigning.  The final nail in Scranton's coffin occurred when Casey aired a guru ad that painted Scranton as flighty.

headline: Walker, Ritter Labeled As Most Conservative Voters
abstract: The American Conservative Union (ACU) labeled PA U.S. Representatives Robert Walker and Don Ritter as the most conservative among PA's delegation. Based on their support for the MX missile, Gramm-Rudman legislation, Star Wars funding, and against South Africa sanctions, both were credited with supporting conservative issues eighty-six percent of the time. PA U.S. Senator Arlen Specter was only given a score of thirty-six percent due to his opposition to Nicaraguan Contra funding and the Gramm-Rudman bill. ACU Chairman David Keene argues that such scores show an increasing gap between Republicans and Democrats with Democrats becoming increasingly liberal and out of touch with mainstream conservative American values.

headline: Consumer Party Wins Ballot Slot
abstract: Although Governor Thornbugh signed legislation barring the Consumer Party from registering primary candidates in upcoming elections, U.S. District Judge Norma Shapiro has ruled that Pennsylvania must place Consumer Party candidates on the May primary ballot.

headline: State Budget A Good Package
abstract: Democrats in the PA General Assembly beat Republicans at their own game by passing a business tax credit linked to corporate payments in order to pay mounting debts of the Unemployment Compensation Fund. Democrats like it because the money goes to job creation, while Republicans approve of measures designed to improve the state’s business climate. The rest of the Democrat's budget plan matches PA Governor Richard Thornburgh’s proposal, but both show the spirit of bipartisanship now evident in Harrisburg.

headline: Chernobyl couldn't have happened here
abstract: The author claims that the disaster at Chernobyl could not have happened in the United States given the industry stress on safety, the differences between the reactors in the accident and those in the U.S. and because of the establishment of the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations, which today plays an important role in maintaining the utmost safety standards.

headline: House panel approves a court-discipline bill
abstract: The PA House Judiciary Committee approved a bill for revamping the state's system of disciplining judges.  The primary target of the bill is the replacement of the PA Judicial Inquiry and Review Board, which many claim in too secretive and not impartial. The bill, in the form a Constitutional Amendment,  would create a new Judicial Conduct Board, tightening financial disclosure requirements for judges.

headline: 2 on Capitol panel want governor to testify
abstract: Some PA House of Representatives have called for PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to testify regarding the Capitol expansion project currently being reviewed, following testimony by a former legislative liaison that claimed specific dollar figures were never discussed while former deputy secretary for public works claimed that costs and contract specifics were discussed in detail.

headline: How The Legislature Got The Job Done
abstract: The last two weeks of this year's legislative session were surprisingly productive. Much of the credit for such smooth operations can be given to House Majority Leader James Manderino. This is surprising because he maintains good relations with Governor Thornburgh even though he refused to budge on issues important to the governor. For instance, Manderino refused to bring up a state constitutional amendment reforming the state judiciary's disciplinary practices because he is an ally of the Democratic-dominated Supreme Court. PA Republicans have also been impressed with his willingness to reach across the aisle and work with them. The session also showed the lack of influence area representatives such as PA House Speaker K. Leroy Irvis and PA Senate Minority Leader Edward Zemprelli have. Both were absent from the governor's signing of the budget, and Zemprelli was unable to get an Allegheny County judge confirmed to Commonwealth Court while Irvis has become more of a figurehead, contenting himself with getting extra money for nutritional aid to low income families in the budget.

headline: Wallace stunned area in '72
abstract: Sherley Uhl writes that George Wallace's success in the 1972 Democratic Primary in Allegheny County should have predicted the conditions today, with a new conservative tide electing Reagan president, and the underrepresentation of blacks in the Pittsburgh area.

headline: Three Candidates Campaign in City
abstract: Three of the four candidates for the Democratic nomination for lieutenant governor--state Representative Dwight Evans, Pittsburgh City Controller Tom Flaherty, and state Senator Mark Singel--were in Scranton today seeking support for their May 20 primary election bid.

headline: State jobless rate falls to 7-year low of 6.4%
abstract: The unemployment rate in Pennsylvania fell to 6.4%, the lowest rate for the state since July 1979, with the US rate slightly above at 7%.  However, the unemployment rate for the four-county Pittsburgh area rose to 7.9% in September.

headline: Chernobyl takes back seat at engineers' meeting
abstract: The most interesting thing about the convention of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers' is the lack of discussion about the disaster at Chernobyl.  The reasons for this include the lack of comparison between American and Soviet industry standards, the lack of information being released by the Soviets, and the feeling of those at the convention that they have to keep the nuclear option.  When more information becomes available, more discussion will emerge.

headline: How 'Just' Is Death Sentencing
abstract: The PA House Judiciary Committee, led by PA Representative H. William DeWeese, held a hearing yesterday to better understand why almost half of the inmates on PA's death row are from Philadelphia while only five are from Pittsburgh. Many allege that it is a result of poor representation of local defendants. Stuart H. Schuman of the PA Council to Abolish the Death Penalty notes that public defenders trained in death penalty defenses are rarely appointed to such cases. Others noted that the appointment of public defenders is political with little focus on attorney competence, and that attorneys are paid so little they lack the resources to conduct proper investigations. PA Representative Andrew Carn stated his belief that racism was involved and indicated legislation may be necessary to ensure fair and equitable justice.

headline: 2 seek CTA case material
abstract: Lawyers for Pennsylvania State Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former state Republican Chairman Robert Asher filed a motion in Federal court asking for details of allegations made against their clients in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) bribery-conspiracy case.  Both men have been charged in connection with the award of a state contract to CTA to recover overpayments of Social Security taxes by school districts in the state.

headline: Hundley, Paterno grew up together
abstract: William Hundley and Paul Killion, who both defend Budd Dwyer and former Pennsylvania Republican chairman Robert Asher, and James West, who is trying to convict them, all launched careers as tough prosecutors.  Their biographies are detailed here.

headline: WANTED: LEADERSHIP
abstract: The first of three parts that discusses Philadelphia's dirth of leadership, both in business and government.  The author details many local politicians, businesses, and even religious leaders with a critical eye on their contributions and drawbacks in helping the city.

headline: Legislators to introduce product-tampering bills
abstract: State Representative Charles Nahill announced that he will introduce a two-bill package that would make product tampering a second-degree felony; currently product tampering is considered an unclassified misdemeanor.

headline: State tax reform needed
abstract: The author believes that the tax-reform proposal from the US Senate that will lower the tax rate to it's lowest in 50 years is long overdue, however, the number of different taxes in Pennsylvania is ridiculous and must be eliminated or consolidated.

headline: Coal waste become entrepreneur's gold
abstract: Energy entrepreneurs are scrambling to stake their claim to millions of tons of coal-mining waste that has accumulated in mountainous piles over two centuries.  Fluidized bed combustion permits the coal screenings to be burned efficiently to produce steam. This new technology has the opportunity to create cheap fuel and a nice profit.

headline: In our opinion: Dismissal should be automatic
abstract: These authors support the Pennsylvania State Police Commissoner who announced that the illegal use of drugs will not be tolerated in the police force and that anyone caught wil be removed from the force immediately.

headline: 3 Democratic hopefuls in state seek unity here
abstract: PA Auditor General Don Bailey, who has been endorsed in the race for the US Senate, fears apathy playing a role in upcoming statewide and congressional elections. Allegheny County Commissioner Tom Foerster also said that a low turnout may hurt Democrats' chances of electoral success. Robert Casey, the gubernatorial hopeful and his running mate, lieutenant gubernatorial hopeful Mark Singel, discussed their plans for the state at a breakfast rally along with Bailey in Penn Hills.

headline: If Rendell Beat Goode … Black Leaders Might Prefer Even Frank Rizzo
abstract: In the Philadelphia mayoral race, scheduled for next fall, local politician Wilson Goode, a democrat, said that if Ed Rendell runs and wins the democratic primary than Goode would run as a third-party candidate.  With Frank Rizzo including to a Republican candidacy, it could mean a three way race for mayor in the fall.

headline: Warning from the GOP
abstract: Letter to the editor, written by PA State Senator Clarence Bell, is a response to a Scranton-Times article of December 6, 1986 called "Random Notes", which says that PA Governor-elect Robert Casey could obtain confirmation of PA Public Utility Commission and PA Turnpike Commission members.  The author advises The Scranton Times that there are 26 Republicans in the PA Senate, and that when PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel is sworn in, there will be 23 Democrats.  The author concludes by noting that the Republican majority in the PA Senate will not give Casey a wide-open door for his appointments.

headline: D.C. admits error on prisoners
abstract: While testifying before the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee, a District of Columbia corrections official admitted that his department made a mistake in sending two busloads of inmantes to a prison in Armstrong County, PA.  Governor Thornburgh protested the transfer, and his adminsitration was unsuccessful at obtaining a restraining order that would have effectively barred the transfer.

headline: States Get Mixed Budget Preview
abstract: The chairman of the US Senate Budget Committee told the nation's governors they cannot expect to be spared from major domestic cutbacks either by slashes in defense spending or by federal tax increases. The governors got better news, however, concerning the prospects for federal tax deductions of state and local taxes and the handling of tax-exempt bonds.

headline: Copter Pilot's Suit Blames TMI Radiation For Cancer
abstract: A helicopter pilot hired by CBS News to carry reporters over the damaged Three Mile Island reactor during the accident has claimed that radiation from the reactor caused his colon cancer. He is joining in a suit with almost two thousand other plaintiffs seeking damages from the plant's owner, General Public Utilities Company and others.

headline: Irate Neighbors Hope Judge Bars the J&G
abstract: A Common Pleas judge in Philadelphia is expected to decide this week whether a South Philadelphia go-go bar will be temporarily padlocked while the district attorneys's office pursues closing it for a year under the state's nuisance bar law.  This comes after persistant neighbor complaints, police action, and disciplinary actions by the PA Liquor Control Board.

headline: 3d District candidates report $361,500 in costs
abstract: Candidates for the 3d congressaional district, including Democratic incumbent Robert Borski, reported that so far they have spent approximately $361,500 together on their campaigns.  They plan to spend much more in the closing weeks to the election, especially on television commercials.

headline: In Republican suburbs, issues outweigh labels
abstract: A liberal by inclination, a Democrat by registration, Don Williams seemed a long-shot candidate for the Board of Supervisors in Republican-dominated Newtown Township, a Philadelphia suburb, yet he worked on the growing community's leading issue, traffic.  He believes that global politics don't become part of local elections, otherwise, he could not have won.

headline: Was There Influence Peddling In Airport Project
abstract: County Commissioners' Chairman Tom Foerster and Repulican minority Commissioner Barbara Hafer have requested an investigation by the U.S. attorney of all county staff regarding the awarding of contracts for expansion projects at the Pittsburgh International Airport. The request is a result of allegations made against a Hafer appointee, Frederick Armstrong, in a letter by local developers Richard and Robert Evanko. The letter claims that Armstrong, who oversees federal Urban Development Action Grants (UDAG) in the Department of Development and is also chairman of Hafer's campaign committee for lieutenant governor, could influence Hafer's decision on who was awarded contracts in exchange for help in her political campaign. All three of the UDAG projects processed by Armstrong last year had principles who contributed to Hafer's campaign. The Evankos held a variety of social events meant to improve their political connections, Armstrong, along with other local political appointees, attended some of them.

headline: The incompetence defense
abstract: Some Philadelphia lawyers have been intentionally depriving clients of adequate representation so that there would be adequate grounds for appeal if one's client is found guilty.  In response to this trend, Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Edward Bradley has decided to refer attorneys using this defense to the state Disciplinary Board.  We believe this is the best way to end such abuses.

headline: Surplus for services
abstract: The authors of this editorial wonder if PA Governor-elect Robert Casey will be able to match current PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's record for finding surpluses at the end of each fiscal year.  Thornburgh has projected a $207 million surplus by June 30, 1987, an estimate based on revenues running ahead of schedule.  Thornburgh has suggested that the surplus be used to cut business taxes and help local governments, though he will leave office in a month.  The editorial also looks at PA House of Representatives Speaker James Manderino's budget plans.  Though tax cuts are popular, there is only so much that can be trimmed before services are curtailed to the point where they no longer meet the need.  The editorial looks at areas that can be improved in the state, and concludes by saying that it is not too early to plan how to use a potential surplus.

headline: Court denies TMI foes access to state data on pregnancies
abstract: A PA Commonwealth Court denied two opponents of Three Mile Island access to PA Department of Health data on the effects on pregnancies since the 1979 nuclear accident. In a unanimous decision, the three-judge panel ruled that the department may withhold the information to protect confidentiality of participants in the study.

headline: Judge advises of probe
abstract: In Philadelphia, Common Please Court Judge Kennenth Harris notifiied court officials that he was the target of a federal investigation and was promptly removed from deciding any court matters, the sixth Philadelphia judge to be removed from hearing cases this year as a result of allegations of wrongdoing. Little could be learned about the nature of the investigation, other than that it involved both local and federal law enforcement agencies and touched on Harris' conduct as a judge.

headline: 4 Jurors Picked in Conspiracy Trial
abstract: Four jurors were picked for the trial of Pennsylvania Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former state GOP chairman Robert Asher, who face charges of conspiracy, perjury, interstate transportation in aid of racketeering, and mail fraud.

headline: In the 18th District..
abstract: Editors endorse incumbent US Representative Doug Walgren over his opponent Ernest Buckman.  They believe that Walgren has had a good record as a representative and think that Buckman just wants to make money and represent the extreme right wing.

headline: Who 'Won' Party Vote?
abstract: Mayor Goode's victory with the election for the Democratic City Committee chairmanship of Bob Brady may be a hollow one, especially as it comes after the defeat of his budget and the party's support of Ed Rendell instead of Bob Casey in the gubernatorial primary. The Democratic Party in the city is fractured, particularly along racial lines. In the two votes, black members, Mayor Goode's base, voted against him. The surprise challenge against Brady was a result of Goode's failure to provide patronage jobs to his base, while support for Brady came largely from Goode's political enemies. The weakness of the party may provide an opening for Rebulicans in the future.

headline: TMI plus 7
abstract: After six years of debate, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission finally decided to restart the undamaged Unit-1 reactor at Three Mile Island.  Even though the plant has operated without serious incident since October, it is important that the plant's operators remain vigilant and avoid returning to the lax attitude that contributed to the 1979 accident.

headline: Tax-refund interception helps state collect loans
abstract: In Pennsylvania collections of defaulted student loans have increased, partly because the US Internal Revenue Service intercepted tax refunds of Pennsylvania violators, keeping $5.6 million in tax refunds from people who had defaulted.

headline: Don't Silence PGW's Only True Voice
abstract: The Philadelphia city-owned Philadelphia Gas Works asked the five-member Gas Commission to approve rate increases which would result in $59 million more in revenue, with the Commission indicating it would approve increases of 40% of the initial request.  This author urges the Gas Commission to base their decision on rate increases on sound data rather than emotion or political expedience.

headline: Law Upheld On Crimes With A Gun
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court upheld a PA law requiring a minimum sentence if there is minimal proof that the defendant has a gun when committing the crime. The decision was a result of four PA judges refusing to issue the sentances because of their belief it was unconstitutional and a subsequent overturning of those decisions by the PA Supreme Court. The law was challeneged because it allows a judge and not a jury to determine the sentence and the standard of proof. The court noted there is no Sixth Amentmdnet right to jury sentencing and that the level of proof was sufficient.  Dissenters are concerned that the standard will be used to make conviction easier in other cases. Two other states have such a law and proponents including PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and the PA Attorney General Leroy Zimmerman argue it has helped reduce gun crime.

headline: '85 Council Election Expenses Don't Add Up
abstract: A review by the Pittsburgh Press of the nine Pittsburgh city council members' 1985 campaign spending shows several different instances of questionable spending and reporting, and apparent violations of state law.  The Allegheny County election officials said they will review the council members' campaign expenditures.

headline: Independent will run in 94th District
abstract: Charles T Johnson has decided to run against incumbent republican state representative Gregory Snyder as an independent.  Johnson criticized Snyder for not being a full time representative since he also maintains a law firm.

headline: Who'll Succeed Edgar?
abstract: Pennsylvania Representative Bob Edgar, who represents what he calls America's most Republican district represented by a Democrat, will not run for reelection, so the editors are endorsing former Delaware County Commissioner Bill Springler.

headline: Casey attacks Rendell over his record as D.A.
abstract: Robert P. Casey, who is seeking the Democratic primary nomination for PA governor, attacked his opponent, Ed Rendell, for his record as Philadelphia district attorney, as well as a dispute involving Rendell over 96 unpaid parking tickets.

headline: Thornburgh expected to propose $100 million in tax cuts
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh is expected to propose a record state budget of nearly $9.6 billion and a tax-cut package that would reduce levies for personal and business taxes by more than $100 million.  Thornburgh is scheduled to deliver his final annual budget message to a joint session of the PA General Assembly.

headline: Electrician gets TMI radiation dose
abstract: An electrician at Three Mile Island's Unit 2 reactor was contaminated with a slight radiation dose when a fellow worker touched the back of his head with a gloved hand.  It was unclear if the worker, employed by Catalytic Incorporated, suffered internal contamination.

headline: Judge's job has lost it's appeal
abstract: PA Common Pleas Judge William Martutani is disgusted with the political system and has decided to resign his judgeship.

headline: 9 judges took Roofers' gifts; 2 others take Fifth on query
abstract: Nine current or former Philadelphia judges acknowledged accepting cash gifts from leaders of the Roofers Union in documents they filed with the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, while two other judges invoked their fifth amendment right against self-incrimination.  The FBI labor squad is currently investigating allegation that top officials of the Roofers Union received kickbacks from fees paid to a Philadelphia Center City law firm, using those funds to then make cash payments to numerous public officials, including Philadelphia Common Pleas Court and Municipal Court judges.

headline: Indictment thrusts 'mystery woman' into spotlight
abstract: An indictment has pushed Deborah Scullin into the public eye.  She has had a long time relationship with city councilman Leland Beloff.  The indictment is looking into whether Beloff made a developer give Scullin an apartment for free.

headline: Why the negative commercials?
abstract: Writer questions why politicians spend so much money on negative commercials. Suggests they spend the money to talk about the positive plans they have if elected.

headline: State reforms in sheriff sales
abstract: A bill currently under consideration in the PA House of Representatives would reform the state's Sheriff sale process in ways that would give more protection to homeowners without reducing the rights of tax collectors and creditors.  We believe that this bill should receive bipartisan support; the state needs to provide whatever protections it can to ensure that those losing their homes are not exploited for profit.

headline: Thornburgh to seek budget of $9.5 billion, cuts in taxes
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh will propose a record PA state budget of nearly $9.5 billion and a tax-cutting package reducing levies on individuals and businesses by $141.5 million a year.  He is scheduled to deliver his budget message during a joint session of the PA House of Representatives and PA Senate.

headline: Electric utilities defended
abstract: The author calls the Pittsburgh Press editorial about the reform of the Public Utility Commission inaccurate and misleading.  This writer, from the Pennsylvania Electric Association, says that PA Senate action on the Public Utility Commisison Sunset bill can not be termed a windfall for electric firms.

headline: Judicial Revision Blocked
abstract: PA House Majority Leader James J. Manderino refused to bring to the floor a state constitutional amendment dealing with judicial reform. The amendment would change the Judicial Inquiry and Review Board (JIRB), which some complain is dominated by judges. Heading off criticism by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, Manderino stated that his priority was getting the state budget passed before the legislature's summer recess. If the constitutional amendment is not brought up before the recess it could not be brought before the voters again for two more years. PA Representative Allen G. Kukovich, a sponsor of a similar measure in the PA House speculates that it has more to do with PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen who's JIRB investigation three years ago led to the calls for change. If the amendment were approved before the recess it would go to the voters at the same time that Larsen was up for a retention vote, and Manderino may not want that extra attention. Governor Thornburgh's effort to get around the PA House by calling for a limited constitional convention was undermined by the PA Bar Association which opposed the call for the convention over fears that it would do more than deal with the JIRB issue.

headline: A Better Way
abstract: The Commonwealth of PA wants to direct control over construction of Philadelphia's convention center. The Philadelphia Daily News says it's hard to understand why Philadelphians cannot be trusted with their own projects when the state does not do much better, as shown by the recent extension of the state Capitol building.

headline: Initial Casey, Scranton debate is fiery
abstract: In Hershey, Pennsylvania, Gubernatorial Democratic candidate Robert Casey and opponent Republican William Scranton debated for the first time since the May 20 primary.  Casey's central issue was corruption in government and tried to link Scranton, the reining Lieutenant General, to recent scandals.

headline: Will room be gym or shrine?
abstract: In the state Capitol expansion project in Pennsylvania, scheduled to be finished next spring, a plan for a gym and locker rooms was erased from plans in 1984, but many legislators believe that it will be slipped in at the last moment.  Many feel it is a waste of taxpayer dollars.

headline: null
abstract: This cartoon depicts Jesus being nailed to the cross.  A Roman soldier observing the crucifixtion states: "I expect that'll be about the last we'll hear from Mr. Christ!"

headline: Thornburgh's Surplus
abstract: Tom Carr of Philadelphia writes to say that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh creation of a state financial surplus is built on a pretense.  Thornburgh has added 6 cents-a gallon tax on top of an already high tax on gas, six cents on a pack of cigarettes which is already highly taxed, alcoholic beverages have more than doubled in prices, and the state income tax goes on. Carr says that these items should create a surplus but also a personal cost as well to taxpayers.

headline: Evaluation Finds TMI To Be Safe
abstract: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) gave the operations at Unit 1 of Three Mile Island high marks. While it noted that some problems were caused by a hurried pace and that some areas needed additional focus, overall the NRC found that the plant was operated in a safe and competent way. General Public Utilities, which operates the plant said it would adress those areas listed as deficient in the NRC evaluation.

headline: Jury being chosen for CTA bribe trial
abstract: Jury selection continues in the federal court trial of former Pittsburgh City Councilman Robert Stone on a charge of extorting a bribe from the head of a California computer firm in exchange for helping the company land a contract with the city to recover Social Security overpayments.

headline: A Borderline Decision
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court's ruling last week allowing gerrymandered districts to be challenged in court even if it does not violate the "one man, one vote" rule will open the floodgates for litigation. US Justice Byron White wrote that a court reversal would be appropriate if the redistricting was done in a way that a voter or a group of voter's influence on the political process was consistently degraded. Yet that logic is so vague that it encourages the loser in every redistricting battle to file a lawsuit.

headline: Innocent, say Dwyer, Asher
abstract: Pennsylvania State Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former state Republican Party Chairman Robert Asher pleaded innocent to charges that they were prepared to take bribes in the Computer Technology Associates contract scheme.  Both men were charged by a grand jury on May 13 with one count of conspiracy, one count of perjury, four counts of interstate transportation in aid of racketeering and six counts of mail fraud.

headline: Williamsport Is Site For Dwyer-Asher Trial
abstract: U.S. District Judge Malcom Muir denied a motion by lawyers for R. Budd Dwyer and Robert Asher to move their bribery trial to Harrisburg or Carlisle to make it less expensive for witnesses to travel. Muir instead  decided that the trial would still be held in a federal court in Williamsport.

headline: Squabble
abstract: Some employees of the State Correctional Facility at Greensburg have resigned or been suspended following two separate investigations into the facility's purchasing practices.  Investigations were carried out by both the state Department of Corrections and the state Auditor General, Don Bailey.  Auditor General Bailey has yet to issue his investigative report, however, and there is specualtion that he may be delaying its release because the audit implicates the daughter of one of his top aides.

headline: Tightening
abstract: The mandates of the Gramm-Rudman Act, passed by the US Congress and  designed to impose greater discipline on the federal budget process, are likely to introduce uncertainty to the fiscal planning of state and local governments across the nation. The law dictates that the annual federal deficit be reduced to zero by 1991. If the U.S. Congress fails to do so, spending cuts would go into effect on all federal spending programs, with the exception of Social Security.

headline: Experts say reactor had 'meltdown and vaporization'
abstract: Nuclear experts from a local electrical utility in western Michigan said that the reactor core of the Soviet nuclear plant at Chernobyl suffered a complete meltdown and vaporization after physically examining six of 15 students from a tour group who spent two days in Kiev after the accident.

headline: Justice Nix scheduled for questioning in case
abstract: PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. is scheduled to come to Williamsport for questioning by the lawyer for suspended Potter County Judge Harold Fink.  US Middle District Senior Judge Malcolm Muir denied a motion that would have prevented the questioning of Nix.  The motion also sought to prevent the questioning of James Rowley, chairman of the PA Judicial Inquiry and Review Board, and Robert Potter, the board's special prosecutor.  Fink claims his rights were violated when he was suspended without a hearing.  Fink was reassigned by the PA Supreme Court to duties that do not involve decision-making pending the outcome of an investigation by the review board into alleged misconduct.

headline: A choice for governor
abstract: Editorial board endorses William W Scranton III for PA governor.  Mostly they hope that he will continue the economic policies of current PA Governor Dick Thornburgh.

headline: Irvis announces run for 15th term; Robinson to stay in primary race
abstract: PA House of Representative Speaker K. Leroy Irvis has requested the Democratic endorsement for a 15th term in his position. The Democratic primary challenger for Irvis’s seat is Former Pittsburgh City Councilman Bill Robinson, who says he will remain in the 19th District race.

headline: Win came almost too soon to savor
abstract: Television networks called Arlen Specter the victor in the U.S. Senate race in Pennsylvania less than a half hour after the polls had closed.  His opponent was Democrat Bob Edgar.

headline: Candidates' nomination petitions are challenged
abstract: In Pennsylvania's Fourth Congressional District, challenging the nomination petitions of opponents has become commonplace.  For example, the nomination petition of Alexander Lindsay Jr. was challened by a supporter of U.S. Representative Joseph Kolter--Lindsay's Democratic opponent.  Additionally, Lindsay has filed a challenge to the nomination petition of John Loth--another Republican candidate.

headline: Transformation Of A State
abstract: PA Democrats and their gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey Sr. have a problem running against William Scranton III, the successor to a governor who has clearly made the state better off than it was eight years ago when state debt was at an all time high, its credit rating was the lowest in the country while unemployment was among the highest. Now corporate and personal income taxes are at new lows, balanced budgets are passed in a timely manner, and the climate for small and high tech businesses is among the best in the country.

headline: Fair share vital to PUC reform
abstract: PA Consumer Advocate David Barasch writes to correct certain misconceptions contained in another editorial concering the present public utility law in Pennsylvania.  He supports examining economic considerations when asssessing public utilities.

headline: Justice sought for judge's suit
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has been asked to assign a Justice to hear a civil suit brought by three Lycoming County Judge's against the Lycoming County Commissioners. County judges filed the suit to force the commissioners to approve a new clerk position in the domestic relations office.

headline: A cop-out on revenue sharing
abstract: The PA General Assembly is busy going through some 5,000 bills and resolutions as it attempts to wrap up its 1985-86 session by Thanksgiving, though it seems unlikely that important legislation will emerge during this wind-down.  This is illustrated by the PA House's decision to table a proposal for $132 million in state revenue sharing to help offset the end of federal revenue sharing for local governments, which these authors believe is a mistake.

headline: Issue Still Could Be Special-Session Item
abstract: A dispute involving the delay in the release of human services money until after the November gubernatorial election could be resolved in a special session of the PA House and Senate. The provision was inserted into the PA state budget by PA House Speaker James J. Manderino to prevent gubernatorial candidate, Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton from getting political benefit from giving out the money. PA Senate President Pro Tem Robert Jubelirer has asked PA House Speaker K. Leroy Irvis to consider a special session to resolve the issue. Jack Reed, a spokesman for PA Senate Democrats, said that if a special session were held then Democrats would ask that other issues be taken up too. Negotiations to remove the language without a special session are underway.

headline: Winner of Traffic Court showdown still faces a tough task
abstract: Chief Clerk Royal D. Hart has a tough road ahead in trying to run Philadelphia's traffic court, after the court has been enmeshed in a ticket-fixing scandal resulting in the convictions of 13 people.

headline: Big business grows from the selling of candidates
abstract: For Philadelphia political consultants, the business of packaging politicians has become a new growth industry, comprised of strategy, media and marketing.

headline: Two Pennsylvanias: Economically, a state divided
abstract: Article examines the economic stratification occurring in Pennsylvania.  A shift has occurred in the economic base making southeast Pennsylvania prosperous and the rest of the state, especially the areas that had relied on heavy industry, increasingly destitute. Note, the article includes bar graph with unemployment figures for each county.

headline: Fewer face cold without heat
abstract: A PA Public Utility Commission report claims that the state's electric utilities shut off 15% fewer customers for non-payment of bills this year while the state's gas companies shut off 26% fewer.  The number of customers still without their primary source of heat heading into winter is down 78% for electric utilities and down 56% for gas companies.  The PUC attributed the improvements to recent PUC efforts to persuade utilities to seek other means of dealing with payment-troubled customers instead of terminations.  Several Harrisburg-area utilities are documented in the article.

headline: Kerr's Sentence For Job Selling Is Upheld
abstract: Former Deputy Auditor General John Kerr, who was convicted two years ago for selling public jobs, had his two year prison sentence upheld despite claims of inadequate legal representation. While one of the members of the three judge panel questioned some the evidence that was allowed, it was still a two to one ruling.

headline: A disastrous year for GOP
abstract: This opinion piece begins by noting that it has been a bad year for Republicans, both in PA and nationwide.  After eight years in power in Harrisburg, Republicans, particularly the well-respected administration of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, are deserting the city in advance of a Democratic invasion on January 20, 1987.  US President Ronald Reagan has lost popularity, Democrats have regained control of the US Senate, and the Republicans are battling the Iran-Contra scandal in the US Congress and the Computer Technology Associates scandal in PA.  The opinion piece looks at the fall of the Republican Party, starting from a year ago.  The piece concludes by noting that Democrats are probably out in front in the early 1988 presidential race, at least in PA.

headline: Issues, tactics are debated by Senate hopefuls
abstract: US Senate candidates Arlen Spector and Bob Edgar exchanged heated words and accusations in a face-to-face meeting in Pittsburgh.  The two met at the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.  The two levied accusations attacking each other's voting records and campaign tactics.

headline: Winners In The Primaries
abstract: Chart outlining the winners of races in all nine states that held primaries

headline: Driking-age law could trim road funds
abstract: A new federal law requires states to raise the minimum drinking age to 21 or lose some federal highway funds.  While this law does not affect Pennsylvania--which has had its drinking age at 21 since 1933--four states have refused to comply with the law, and one state--North Dakota--has filed suit questioning the constitutionality of the new federal law.

headline: Two Pennsylvanias: Pockets of unemployment amid prosperity
abstract: The Harrisburg area's low unemployment rate is one manifestation of a robust regional economy that includes most of southeastern Pennsylvania, while other parts of the state, particularly the western part of the state, have an bleak employment picture.

headline: For evacuees, a day to remember
abstract: Residents were allowed to return to their homes after police had cleared an area of North Philadelphia due to a gas leak. Beyond an evacuation, the leak also caused street closures.  Police searched the area to ensure that no gas remained and to ensure that looting had not occurred.  Article goes on to detail stories of specific residents who returned.

headline: Lesko closer to execution after ruling
abstract: John Lesko is one step closer to being executed, but there are still legal appeals left that stand in the way.  Lesko was sentenced to die for killing an Apollo police officer after a six-day killing rampage.

headline: A frantic finish looms in race for governor
abstract: This article details what campaign efforts the leading gubernatorial candidates will be making in the last weeks before the election.  The election remains very close and opinion polls show a dead heat between the two leading candidates, Republican William W Scraton III and Democrat Robert P Casey.

headline: It's Candidate-Swarming Time
abstract: All four gubernatorial and U.S. Senate candidates were in the area yesterday campaigning for votes. Republican gubernatorial candidate, and current lieutenant governor, William W. Scranton III, was at a small factory to talk about an economic development plan he would initiate if elected. His Democratic opponent, Bob Casey, was at a senior citizens center discussing how the state is like a family in which everyone needs to work together in order to move ahead. Incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter was at a local Conrail Yard where he was lauded by union workers for fighting the company's sale to Norfolk Southern. His opponent, Democratic U.S. Representative Bob Edgar was at an idle steel mill speaking with locked out workers about his plan to increase highway funding to generate enough demand for steel to get workers back on the job.

headline: Won't budge, Goode tells center foes
abstract: At a private meeting, Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode told black politicians who oppose his convention center proposal that he will not back down, amid worries of minority hiring in the center's construction project. The meeting's attendees include US Representative William H. Gray III, City Council President Joseph E. Coleman and Councilman Lucien Blackwell and John Street, and state Representatives David P. Richardson Jr. and Dwight Evans. Critics of the project state that it does not guarantee minority participation, while Goode says that the project as it stands is better than no project at all.

headline: For once, he doesn't want a company to turn around
abstract: Drew Lewis, President Reagan's first secretary of transportation, has accepted a five-year post as chairman and chief executive of Union Pacific Railroad Corporation.  Although Lewis plans to serve for the duration of his contract, he says he will continue to take an active role in politics--citing the recent sale of Conrail as largely a political decision.

headline: U.S. cuts looming for county
abstract: Allegheny County will lose nearly $32 million in federal money next year under U.S. President Ronald Reagan's proposed budget.  Although the total cuts would amount to $32 million, the real effect will not be known until the U.S. Congress begins deliberation on the federal budget.

headline: Gorbachev urges N-plant safeguards
abstract: Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, in a message to the U.N. General Secretary, urged the world to create an international system of safeguards against such nuclear disasters as the Chernobyl incident.  He also urged agreement among governments on measures against nuclear terrorism.

headline: Letters to the Editor - Capital Punishment Guarantee That Killer Will Never Kill Again
abstract: In this letters to the editor, the author writes in response to Philadelphia Daily News columnist' Chuck Stone's discussion about the death penalty.  Stone talked about the death penalty in regards to a poor, black convict who was put to death while John Hinckley, a white, wealthy man who shot President Reagan was not.

headline: A Friend in Harrisburg?
abstract: Most Philadelphia Democrats feel that the election of Robert Casey (D) as the next Governor of Pennsylvania bodes well for the city, feeling it will mean more money for the city and usher in an era of more cooperation and collaboration between the levels of government.

headline: It's Ringgold over Schulze
abstract: Editors endorse Tim Ringgold over incumbent Richard Schulze for a seat in the Pennsylvania House.  While they recognize the value of Schulze's seniority, they do not feel that he is an effective leader in regional cooperation.

headline: Woodland in state ravaged by flames
abstract: PA state officials said that rising temperatures, low humidity and high winds fanned flames that charred as much land in the past week as fires did in all of 1985.  Since March 24, more than 400 wildfires blackened more than 6,500 acres of land statewide.

headline: Gettysburg schools prepare to repay state 350,000
abstract: The state auditor general's office has found that the Gettysburg Area School District was overpaid in state subsidies between July 1, 1980 and June 30, 1984.  The school board has accepted the auditor general's findings and is prepared to repay the Pennsylvania Department of Education approximately 350,000 dollars.

headline: Unanimous House Vote Passes Cuts In State Tax
abstract: The PA House unanimously voted to cut state taxes for workers and businesses. A similar measure is moving through the PA Senate, and because Governor Thornburgh has proposed a similar move, little opposition is expected. However, the proposed bill by the PA House also includes a provision giving businesses tax credits in the hopes of fixing the Unemployment Compensation Fund escalating debt. Businesses filling newly created jobs would get credit for the per-employee tax paid for each worker. PA House Majority Leader James Manderino says it encourages the creation of jobs while PA House Minority Leader Matthew Ryan noted that it may cost more than Democrats believe.

headline: Handy Surplus Power
abstract: A recent heat wave resulted in additional strain on power generators as people tried to keep cool. The strain was so great that some utilities bought power from companies with excess capacity in order to meet the demand. This serves as a reminder that excess capacity, which has been receiving so much criticism recently, is a good thing. In this case, having too much power serves everyone. Without it we would all be sweltering.

headline: Life On Death Row: Can It Be Unconstitutional?
abstract: U.S. District Judge Joseph L. McGlynn Jr. is scheduled to hear testimony today on the constitutionality of the conditions in which death row inmates are held. The prisoners argue that being isolated from the rest of the prison population, going outside for one hour a day, and having limited access to legal materials is unconstitutional. PA contends that every other state isolates its death row inmates, and that it is done for security reasons, as the prisoners have been convicted of violent crimes and have nothing to lose.

headline: A hall for quiet heroes
abstract: This editorial discusses the opening of a Pennsylvania Voter Hall of Fame.  It would include people that had voted in every election for at least 50 years.  Writer approves of the idea and likens it to halls of fame for baseball and football.

headline: Jackson rips Reagan, Specter in impassioned speech at church
abstract: The Reverend Jesse Jackson voiced his support for Democratic candidates in Pennsylvania during his speech at a Harrisburg church yesterday.  He discussed how Reagan, he believes, has given tax cuts to the 'haves' and given 'have-nots' a wage cut.

headline: Wrap-up weekend for Democrats
abstract: The Pennsylvania U.S. Senate primary on May 20 had the two candidates doing some last minute campaigning, with democrats Auditor General Don Bailey in downtown Philadelphia and opponent Bob Edgar in Pittsburgh.  Both candidates are tired and looking forward to the primary tomorrow.

headline: Tight ship at White Hill
abstract: Pennsylvania's 1.1 million dollar improvement plan, designed to enhance security at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill, has proven successful.  Camp Hill, once considered an easy prison from which one could escape, has not had a single escape incident since July 1984.  This shows us that a modest allocation, coupled with realistic administrtative policy, can go a long way in reducing prison escapes.

headline: Unemployment Dip Masks Loss Of Jobs
abstract: The national unemployment rate fell to just over 7% in June. While hailed as a sign of continued progress by US President Ronald Reagan’s administration, economists contend that because the manufacturing sector continues to lose jobs, the true rate of unemployment has remained unchanged. Meanwhile a separate private survey of businesses showed that the number of Americans with jobs actually fell, although this is due to differences in how striking workers are counted. In PA, the unemployment rate dropped almost 1.5% to 6.5%. This still puts the state in fifth place, among the eleven largest states, with the highest unemployment rates.

headline: If there's a nuclear disaster, who pays?
abstract: Currently the liability insurance of nuclear plants is governed by a special law.  The New York Times says that the U.S. Congress should renew that law, the Price-Anderson Act, which expires next year, saying that the alternative would be a lot worse.

headline: Lightning-Sparked Fires Hit 3 Western States
abstract: A line of thunderstorms passing through the West last week sparked almost four hundred wildfires due to lightning strikes. U.S. Forest Service tankers have dropped chemical retardants and firefighters scheduled for relief after working in Oregon are now waiting to be used in nearby states. Hundreds of fires in Montana and Idaho are being left unattended, burning thousands of acres; while in Utah firefighters were able to contain five small blazes and are continuing to fight two others.

headline: A Little More Sunshine
abstract: The PA General Assembly deserves only limited praise for closing the loophole created in the Sunshine Act by a PA Commonwealth Court decision. It is certainly beneficial that official policymaking meetings now require advance notice and must be open to the public, and that when there are closed sessions, for personnel, collective bargaining, or real estate matters, the reason must be disclosed. However, the job is only half done. The PA Legislature has still seen fit to exempt itself from the same requirements it imposed on the executive branch. Erie-area legislators could perform a needed public service by taking the lead on changing that.

headline: Jury Selection For Dwyer, Asher Trial Delayed
abstract: Senior U.S. Middle District Judge Malcolm Muir postponed jury selection in the trial of PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer and PA Republican Chairman Robert B. Asher due to the volume of pretrial motions, which make Muir's July fifteenth deadline impossible to meet. Dwyer and Asher are charged  for their involvement in the Computer Technology Associates (CTA) scandal. Both are charged with perjury, for lying during the separate conspiracy trial of lawyers involved in the affair, and conspiracy, for their involvement in accepting bribes for awarding CTA the state contract to recover overpayments of Social Security taxes by state schools.

headline: York Countians Lose Avian Flu Case
abstract: A York County farm couple lost its bid to get reimbursement from the federal government for business lost during an avian flu outbreak two years ago. U.S. District Judge William W. Caldwell ruled that state and federal officials acted within their authority, nor were the couple's due process rights violated, because it could be reasonably concluded that the government was acting to promote a legitimate purpose.

headline: Heavywieght clashes
abstract: The battle for the Pennsylvania Democratic gubernatorial nomination is turning into a real brawl, with Robert P. Casey leveling aggressive attacks against his challenger, Philadelphia District Attorney Ed Rendell.  Casey, the former PA Auditor General, has recasted his Mr.-Nice-Guy image--appearing blunt and hard-charging in his latest television commercials.

headline: Western Pennsylvania is preparing for economic prosperity
abstract: With the structure of the western Pennsylvania economy changing, the author looks to the strengths that this area possesses, including university complexes with unique skills, high tech equipment, strong leadership, and a remarkable track record. He urges government funds to be channeled into areas like these, rather than in large federal programs.

headline: Is nuclear power really worth it?
abstract: This author believes that the Chernobyl disaster is a result of the Soviet plan to rapidly develop and modernize, often at the expense of safety regulations.  This disaster should remind us that there is a price to pay for the reliance on exotic technologies and that we should look for alternative technologies.

headline: Pa. high court lifts Zettlemoyer's stay of execution
abstract: The PA State Supreme Court lifted a stay of execution for convicted killer Keith Zettlemoyer, clearing the way for PA Governor Dick Thornburgh to set a new execution date and sending lawyers scurrying for their law books.  However, whether or not Thornburgh, who has less than a month remaining in his term, can issue a warrant for an execution that would take place under PA Governor-elect Robert Casey, is an issue.  A spokesman for the PA Corrections Department agreed that the legal issue would need to be addressed before any new warrant could be issued.  Casey said that he favors the death penalty in limited circumstances spelled out by the state's death-penalty statute.  A history of Zettlemoyer's case and appeal process is documented in the article.

headline: A mad race for 2nd banana
abstract: The race for PA Lieutenant Governor has seen a surge in interest, there are 6 republicans and 12 democrats running. The Pittsburgh Press says that state government has become so complicated that the lieutenant governor now actually performs useful services, in addition to presiding over the PA Senate.

headline: Just what do those guys do?
abstract: Writer recounts a conversation he overheard between two people discussing the gubernatorial race between William Scranton and Robert Casey.  The recounted conversation mostly focuses the position of lieutenant governor and the responsibilities of the job.

headline: Your Opinion: TM 'Immensely Effective'
abstract: This letter refutes the letter Governor elect Bob Casey sent in the Pennsylvania election, that tried to discredit opponent Bill Scranton by alluding to the latter's assocation with Transcendental Meditation, which this author says is not a cult nor is it a religion.  It is a technique that has proved effective in reducing stress and enhancing mental and physical health.

headline: TMI Still Concern
abstract: When the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) granted GPU, the owner/operator of Three Mile Island, permission to restart its Unit-1 reactor, its decision was based largely on "hardware issues"--or the physical capabilities of the plant.  The NRC makes most of its regulatory decisions on such "harware issues" and concedes that it is not well equipped to assess questions of management integrity.  This is problematic, as management integrity was specifically what was at issue in the case of Unit-1 and GPU; it is clear that another authority is needed to monitor factors related to management integrity.

headline: Your Opinion
abstract: In a recent editorial, the Scranton Times called proposed tax cuts by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh negligible. However, James Scheiner writes to the Times to say that ignoring the significant impact of the cumulative effect of those taxes and past tax reductions would be ignorant. Scheiner also says that PA has its fiscal house in order and its taxes are headed down.

headline: Join the Forces Opposing TMI
abstract: A letter to the editor that calls for an end to the threat of a nuclear meltdown at Three Mile Island.

headline: Make it mandatory: Settle divorces by mediation
abstract: This author is arguing for Pennsylvania to follow other states in making it mandatory for divorcing couples to have divorce mediation in place of the present adversary system of courts and lawyers.

headline: A policy designed to ward off endorsements
abstract: Although it has not officially declared endorsements for upcoming congressional and gubernatorial elections, the Democratic City Committee is unofficially supporting Robert Casey for governor and Don Bailey, the current PA Auditor General, for US Senate, snubbing US Representative Bob Edgar and PA Representative Dwight Evans, respectively. Casey is supported by City Chairman Joseph F. Smith, while Ed Rendell has the support of Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode. The vast difference in candidate preferences among ward leaders led the DCC not to make any endorsements.

headline: Kickbacks, profiteering cited in Capitol work
abstract: Millions of dollars in kickback and exorbitant profits being used in the construction of an addition to the PA state capitol are being reviewed by PA officials. In the first three days of testimony, attention was focused on the 190,000 cubic feet of granite that the state spent $27 million to purchase, paying $11 a cubic foot to middle men when it could have been purchased directly from Vermont for $8.

headline: 8 die; cleanup continues
abstract: In Western Pennsylania at least 8 people died following flash flooding that battered several of the Pittsburgh north suburban communities.  There is also massive economic damage as the cleanup continues and people try to rebuild their lives.

headline: Sweet Withdraws from Race
abstract: State Representative David W. Sweet withdrew from the Pennsylvania lieutenant governor race.  Sweet ended his campaign because he could not compete with the name recognition of Pittsburgh Controller Tom Flaherty.

headline: A challenge to bias
abstract: The author believes that the US Supreme Court ruling against the use of the peremptory challenge, which allowed lawyers to exclude a prospective juror without stipulating a reason, has in effect defeated two forms of racism.  One which allowed lawyers to eliminate black jurors from juries and the other which sought to place black jurors on juries in the belief that black jurors would be more sympathetic to a black defendant.  This ruling will hopefully allow for the trial process to be healthier, and fairer, as a result.

headline: Leak-rate tests violated rules NRC tells GPU
abstract: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued the operator of Three Mile Island a notice of violation for events that took place at Unit 1 more than seven years ago. The violation cited the company for lacking adequate testing procedures, failing to maintain proper records, and failing to correct deficiencies once identified.

headline: Male officers at Muncy charge bias
abstract: 14 male correctional officers have filed a suit claiming discrimination in duty and promotion practices at the Muncy State Correctional Institution.  They claim that the institution conspired to create job classifications based on gender.  They claim that men were barred from jobs due to gender and not because of security or privacy issues at the mostly female prison.  Prison officials deny the charges.

headline: A Rare Battle Brewing In Bucks County Race
abstract: In Pennsylvania's 6th District in lower Bucks County, the PA Senate primary is hotly contested, with one candidate being accused of only living in his district part-time while the other is criticized for a trip to Europe billed to taxpayers.  Other PA Senate races are also discussed.

headline: Kostmayer and Christian debate for first time
abstract: Candidates for the 8th Congressional district, incumbent democrat Peter Kostmayer and republican David Christian, held a heated debate that will be broadcast on television.  The two attacked each other throughout the debate calling into question each other's integrity in both personal and professional matters.

headline: A rising threat from Lake Erie
abstract: In Pennsylvania, Lake Erie is rising, with state officials expecting it to hit a record high in the next two weeks.  The historic level is a result of years of above-average rainfall and below-average temperatures, combining to increase the water in all the Great Lakes by as much as 14%.  There is little to be done, though the rising waters threaten all who live around the Great Lakes.

headline: State should change the way judges are elected
abstract: Hopefully, Pennsylvania voters will learn from Illinois--where voters recently elected two LaRouchites to state office--and adopt a merit system for judges of statewide courts.

headline: Abortion issue casts its shadow on this year's gubernatorial race
abstract: This article details the impact of the abortion issue on the 1986 PA gubernatorial race.  Oddly, the race finds the two main candidates on the opposite of where their parties normally stand on the issue. The Republican candidate, William Scranton III, is the more pro-choice candidate, while the Democratic candidate, Robert Casey Sr. is seen as Pro-Life.  The issue has become so important for this race because anti-abortion activists are confident that the US Supreme Court will overturn the Roe v. Wade case soon allowing each individual state to decide whether to outlaw it or not.

headline: Limerick rate increase could cost 19,000 jobs, economist says
abstract: The Philadelphia region could lose 19,000 jobs by 1989 if the Philadelphia Electric Company gets the electric rate increase it has requested to in order to pay for Limerick 1 nuclear power plant. A dozen government agencies and consumer groups are challenging Philadelphia Electric's plan to raise electric rates.

headline: MOVE panel airs its finding
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Ronald Castille has assembled a team of prosecutors to decide whether to pursue the MOVE commission’s recommendation that a grand jury be empanelled to determine whether Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode and other city officials should be charged with crimes for their role in the MOVE disaster.  Goode announced that he would make his formal response to the commission's 31 findings and 38 recommendations.

headline: A revenue sharing contingency plan
abstract: Officials from local governments are urging the Pennsylvania General Assembly to approve a state-run revenue-sharing program.  This author believes that, with the new Gramm-Rudman law, which forces cuts in federal spending, local and statet governments should have contingency plans to pay for uses such as maintaining water and sewer systems and streets.

headline: Krajewski, Beloff Tally Top Council Accounts
abstract: With the 1987 Philadelphia City Council primary elections more than a year away, Leland Beloff and Joan Krajewski have each amassed a campaign war chest almost equal to all other council members combined.  At the end of 1985 Krajewski had a total of $33,697 in her campaign treasury. Beloff claimed a campaign bank account of $30,455.  Neither reported any outstanding debts.

headline: Adams County Gets Drought Aid
abstract: The U.S. Department of Agriculture declared Adams County a disaster area yesterday and was asked to make similar designations for Montgomery (because of drought) and Lancaster (because of storm damage) Counties. With the declaration, low-interest loans will be available to farmers and businesses in the area.

headline: State House foregoes action on unisex to mark holiday
abstract: State Representative David W. Sweet is preparing new legislation that would delay the implementation of gender-neutral insurance rates in Pennsylvania.  Sweet's legislation would delay implementation by one year so a joint commission could study the issue.

headline: Abortion Stand
abstract: Leaders of the Pro-Life Federation have asked their members to vote for US Senator and Republican Arlen Specter, who is Pro-Choice. The author wonders what impact this will have on the Republican Party’s stand on the abortion debate, and fears that the party will move to the left on allowing abortions.

headline: Look Harder At Utility Rates
abstract: The laymen's ability to understand requests for utility rate increases is very difficult, however, the fact that utilities ask for such increase regularly creates a need for those requests to be examined carefully. Peoples Natural Gas seeks a ten percent increase while at the same time reducing the rate for industrial customers by seventeen percent. They argue that industrial customers will stop using gas without the reductions and everyone will be paying more. Penelec's request is equally problematic. Not only is it higher than the rate of inflation but it comes at time when energy prices and interest rates for utility borrowing are falling. For the sake of consumers the PA Public Utility Commission needs to look at these requests thoroughly.

headline: No Stranger To Controversy
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Judith L.A. Friedman continues to defend her decision last week to reverse a jury's guilty verdict in the murder case of Donald Ciaccia. Arguing that the prosecutors had failed to prove Ciaccia's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt." While this is the first use of a procedural rule passed three years ago giving judges such authority, this is not the first time Friedman has made controversial decisions. Over three years ago, as a deputy coroner, she ruled that defendants acted in self-defense when they killed a man. Five weeks later, one of those defendants, Abdullah Ibn-Sadiika, killed another person during a robbery; over five years ago she ruled that there was not enough eveidence to hold a man, later convicted, of killing his wife. In the current case, not only was the decision itself controversial, but others are also upset that she waited until after the jury had ruled instead of ruling early in the trial.

headline: A Step Beyond Sanctions
abstract: The writer discusses the recently passed economic sanctions against South Africa's apartheid regime.
