He claims that while the action was good, it still lags behind what the US public really wants.  He then outlines a plan by US Representative William Gray III from PA's 2nd Congressional District.  Gray's plan would give aid to 'frontline' states which may face economic reprisals from South Africa.  The writer supports Gray's plan.

headline: Lancaster firm seeks to avoid campaign law headache
abstract: Armstrong World Industries Incorporated wants to encourage and coordinate political contributions by its senior management, but does not want to report them publicly to the Federal Election Commission.  The company has proposed to the FEC a "Program to Broaden Participation of Senior Management in the Political Contribution Process"  hoping to avoid triggering federally required record keeping and disclosure.

headline: City Gets 2.55-Inch Rainfall
abstract: Severe thunderstomrs with high winds and large size hail struck Dauphin, Perry, and Cumberland counties last night. There were widespread reports of downed trees and flash flooding, and hundreds of people were still without power.

headline: House adds 304,000 to pay senior judges
abstract: A measure allocating an additional 304,000 dollars for payments to senior judges assigned to help various counties with caseloads was sent to the state House yesterday.  Governor Thornburgh has not yet agreed that the judges, most of whom have been working without pay, need additional money, however.

headline: Another Sneaky Anti-Abortion Amendment
abstract: The PA House continues to try and undermine the US Supreme Court's abortion ruling by including anti-abortion amendments into every bill possible. The most recent example is PA House Bill 843 which now has an amendment requiring abortion providers to get a certificate of need (CON). Originally meant to control costs by limiting the number and size of hospitals – the House is using it as a stealth measure aimed at closing abortion providers. Moreover, it sets the stage for anti-abortion groups to challenge every CON issued in PA and forcing the state to spend money and time defending them in court. The PA House should quite wasting time and defeat this bill.

headline: Man injured as rack falls in Unit 2
abstract: A man working inside the reactor building of Three Mile Island's damaged Unit 2 reactor was knocked to the floor and sustained skin contamination when a rack holding a lead-filled curtain toppled over on him.  The man was taken to Hershey Medical Center by a General Public Utilities Corporation ambulance and crew.  The man sustained low levels of contamination that can be cleaned with soap and water.  The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission was notified of the incident and an NRC inspector has been present during an internal review of the incident.

headline: No Such Thing As A Right To Be Left Alone
abstract: If adultery were a crime then almost half of adult Americans would be in jail. Pennsylvanians should consider themselves lucky that the legislature's view is not as backwards as that of Georgia's or the U.S. Supreme Court. We must all be on guard to protect our rights to privacy and consensual private behavior.

headline: A subplot ripe for TV
abstract: Malinda Beckley, a 55-year-old Berks County teachers aide, has won $1,000 a week for life in lottery winnings.  Ironically, the Commonwealth National Bank's Strawberry Square Branch was being robbed at the same time as Beckley victory. Robert Judge was arrested by city police minutes after the 12:30 p.m. robbery at the bank's Strawberry Square branch.

headline: LaRouchians Found Few Friends in Pa.
abstract: Pennsylvania voters generally rejected candidates of political extremist Lyndon LaRouche in the Democratic primary yesterday.  Steven Douglas ran a distant third to winner Robert Casey and opponent Edward Rendell in the gubernatorial race, and lost all other races in the state.

headline: Creek surges past home on Saxonburg Boulevard
abstract: Photograph showing an overflowing creek that resulted in flash flood warnings in western Pennsylvania on Friday, May 30.

headline: Treatment admissions hit high
abstract: According to the state Department of Health, the number of admissions to Pennsylvania drug and alcohol treatment centers hit an all-time high during the 12-month period ending June 30, 1985.

headline: Black and White in Pittsburgh
abstract: Provided is a chart using US Census Bureau data illustrating socioeconomic differences between black and white residents in Pittsburgh.  Figures include statistics on college degrees, infant mortality rates, median income, and poverty levels.

headline: Meltdown possible at second reactor
abstract: Reagan administration sources believe that a second of the four reactors at the Chernobyl complex has already experienced, or is experiencing, a meltdown of its core, according to U.S. intelligence agencies, though other administration officials believe it is too early to reach a conclusion about a second meltdown.  Intelligence officials stress that they had no independent assessment of how much radiation had been released into the air.  A newly created Interagency Task Force on the accident could only speculate on the causes of this accident.

headline: No Such Thing As A Right To Be Left Alone
abstract: The paper's previous editorial regarding the U.S. Supreme Court's decision upholding a Georgia sodomy law creates a right of every American to be left alone whenever it suits their deviant sexual purposes. What about on April 15 when the state takes my property, the state does not ignore me then. As the paper admits, in cases of abuse the state needs to intervene so the fabric of society  does not necessarily stop at the bedroom door. Moreover, twnety-six states agree that sodomy is a crime that undermines the social fabric. The decision declares that if states want to have such laws they should be allowed to do so, this is reasonable given the health hazards from engaging in sodomy. The right of privacy is a convenient justification for modern liberalism. There is no right to be left alone and the only people concerned about it are those with something to hide.

headline: Accentuating the negative
abstract: Despite furor about negative political campaigns, it appears they are here to stay, as evidenced by the victory of Democrat Robert Casey in Pennsylvania's gubernatorial race, which many feel may be attributed to a last-minuate 'guru ad' on television.  The ad featured sitar music, a picture of the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi and 15-year-old pictures of Republican candidate William Scranton with long hair and a beard, geared to remind voters of his experimentation with drugs and involvement with the Transcendenal Meditation movement.

headline: Leadership a key in race between Scranton, Casey
abstract: Writer asserts that leadership will be the central issue in gubernatorial election.  Writer outlines a leadership model that he feels could serve as an effective rubric for judging leadership qualities.  Some of the points included in the model are a vision for the future, courage, and pragmatism.

headline: Flood Answers Finally On The Way
abstract: The devastating flood in the Monongahela Valley last year left many questions unanswered. The committee formed to look into those issues is expected to finish its report soon. We believe that the committee chairman, PA Representative Peter J. Daley, and the other members have done a thorough job finding answers to many of the flood victims' questions.

headline: Proposes putting off wage issue
abstract: The president of Transport Workers Union Local 234, Roger Tauss, proposed temporarily setting aside wage issues and returning to the bargaining table to negotiate with SEPTA about the alleged harassment of union workers.  A spokesperson for SEPTA said the transit agency had already negotiated on the harassment issue.  The SEPTA strike has left 440,000 commuters in search of alternative modes of transportation and icaused massive congestion on major roadways and impacted retail businesses throughout the city.

headline: Black leasers' suit challenges at-large voting
abstract: Vowing to end "political white supremacy" in Pittsburgh, a group of black community activists called the Metropolitan Pittsburgh Crusade for Voters, filed a suit in US District Court challenging the city's at-large election process.  The MPCV contends that at-large elections deny Pittsburgh's 101,813 black voters their constitutional right to equal representation by making it difficult for a black person to be elected to City Council.

headline: Met-Ed seeks rate cute based on tax savings
abstract: Pennsylvania utility company Metropolitan Edison Company has proposed cutting its rates by about $8.2 million on January 1 because of changes in the federal tax law, pending approval by the PA Public Utility Commission.  The company had considered the impact of the new tax law, which allows rates to rise, when it agreed to settle a pending rate case.  The increase could be nearly wiped out by the newly proposed reductions.

headline: Not forthcoming
abstract: PA State Police Commissioner Jay Cochran, citing security reasons, refused to make public how much money is spent to protect PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and his family.  Cochran refused to tell the PA Senate appropriations committee how much the department's budget was earmarked to protect the governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general, because he said the information could aid an assailant in planning an attack.  PA Democratic senators are willing to go to court to find out.

headline: Access to the Polls
abstract: The editorial board supports Pennsylvania election officials who say they will make Pennsylvania's voting precincts more accessible to elderly and disabled citizens prior to the 10 year federal deadline.  As of now, 40% of Pennsylvania's precincts have physical barriers and inaccessible polling places.

headline: Legislative leaders urge changes in Sunset Review Law
abstract: All four PA legislative floor leaders are not completely satisfied with how the PA Sunset Review Law is working. Options to fix it are being discussed.

headline: Flood woes
abstract: A concerned citizen commends all who speak out about Scranton's flood problems, which occur with every heavy rainfall. They state that the only way Scrantonians might get their problems fixed is to sue the PA Department of Environmental Resources. The author also commends President Reagan for standing strong against Russia.

headline: Keep politics out of the PUC
abstract: Changes to the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) proposed by interest groups like the PA Public Interest Coalition are undesirable and will, in the long run, increase the cost of electricity.  Also, enacting reforms designed to increase public accountability--reforms such as reducing commisioner terms from 10 to four years--will open the commission up to politics and destroy the independence an appointed body like the PUC needs to serve the public interest.

headline: Black state trooper's promotion is upheld
abstract: A federal appellate court in Philadelphia upheld a lower court's decision ordering that a black police lieutenant be assigned to a PA State Police barracks as station commander.  Russell Clangan had risen through the ranks with the help of affirmative action policies.  The judge presiding over the proceedings at the district level had found that Clanagan's appointment to the barracks had been blocked due to discrimination by the state police.  PA Governor Dick Thornburgh also had sided with state police in opposing his appointment, opening Thornburgh up to charges of racism.

headline: Method Used To Try TMI Cases Will Be Determined Today
abstract: Dauphin County Senior Judge William W. Lipsitt will hold a conference today to decide how to handle lawsuits filed by people claiming injury from radiation released during the Three Mile Island accident. The plant's owner, General Public Utilities Co., former plant operator Metropolitan Edison Company, and other related firms want a trial that focuses on only two issues: how much radiation escaped and where it went. Lawyers for those claiming injury are seeking several test cases which will be used as a basis for determining if an out of court settlement or a complete withdrawal should be pursued.

headline: On judges: House panel approves its bill to alter judicial review board
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Judiciary Committee yesterday approved a Democrat-sponsored alternative to a Senate Republican bill for revamping the state's system of disciplining judges.  Both bills seek to replace the PA Judiciary Inquiry and Review Board, with the House bill differing in its appointment process for selecting members for a new Judicial Conduct Board and tightens some other language, but essentially contains equivalent provisions.

headline: Accountability-bill lobbying grows
abstract: Opponents and supporters of a bill that would ease accountability standards for state corporate directors and officers stepped up lobbying efforts.  The American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO) headed efforts to urge PA House members to oppose the legislation.  The bill was authored by lawyers for some of the state's largest corporations.

headline: Legislative Surprise
abstract: A rare mid-summer session for the PA House and Senate had to be held to correct political maneuverings that never should have made it this far. PA House Majority Leader James Manderino wanted to keep gubernatorial candidate, and Lieutenant Governor William Scranton from gaining political points by handing out social services checks to counties, so Manderino prohibited the checks from being distributed until after the elections. However, the uproar created by the counties, who discovered that money they had been counting on would be delayed, forced both chambers to reverse themselves. While the dispute appears to be going away at little cost to anyone, it never should have happened to begin with.

headline: Lawmaker Denied Information On State Flood Aid
abstract: PA Representative Peter Daley was denied access to the names and addresses of individuals in the Monongahela Valley applying for flood aid. He wants to survey the recipients in order to determine if aid already issued and more set aside for them in this year's budget will be adequate for their needs and to see if it is getting there quickly enough. Surveys done by staff members on Daley's committee investigating the issue indicate that there are significant unmet needs. The PA Public Welfare Department refused the request on confidentiality grounds and instead offered to inform recipients of Daley's survey.

headline: Highlights in History
abstract: This article lists several events of historic significance that occurred on this date, March 3rd.  Events cover science, politics, and general human interest.

headline: Blacks fcing more challenges, NAACP is told
abstract: The president of the Pioneer Community College in Kansas City, Missouri and president of the city's National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) spoke to the Harrisburg chapter of the organization.  In her speech, Dr. Zelema Harris claimed that the dismantling of America’s industrial economy is greatly affecting the black community as the former social structure has disappeared.  She blames this for the rise in drug use and unwed pregnancy for inner city blacks.  She pointed out the need for action through the community to curb these trends.

headline: New PUC Law Could Topple PE Rate Hike
abstract: A new law signed by PA Governor Thornburgh may result in reductions in a Philadelphia Electric Company (PE) rate increase recently approved by the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC). PA Consumer Advocate David M. Barasch said he plans to amend his request for reconsideration of the increase based on provisions of the law restricting a utilitiy's ability to recover costs from taxpayers for plants that generate excess capacity and let the PUC reject rate proposals from utilities with substandard service. PE's rate increase was for its Limerick I nuclear reactor, which Barasch claims will never generate economic benefits. Utility representatives claim the provision will limit their ability to plan for future needs and Governor Thornburgh in signing the bill called on state legislators to have remedies ready should that happen.

headline: Our Opinion-State Police probe will restore honor
abstract: In recent years, charges of racial discrimination, bribery, and other crimes have been leveled at the PA State Police. The Times Leader says that there are problems in the force which are evident and that these charges and others should be the main focus in a legislative hearing by a PA State House of Representative Committee.

headline: Action will speak louder than mayor's mea culpa
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode held a press conference to introduce a new executive management group that could help prevent another MOVE disaster. The Philadelphia Inquire says that the Mayor needs to lead like he promised and prevent things from getting out of hand.  The Inquirer notes that another bureaucracy will not help situation, only good leadership will.

headline: Legislators close session with a trail of loose ends
abstract: Pennsylvania legislators close their session with many bills not passed, including a package of bills that called for the state to sever financial connections with South Africa.  Also, because the House and Senate failed to either kill off or renew the Liquor Control Board in the waning days of the session, Governor Thornburgh will be able to begin shifting the sale of liquor to the private sector, a move that will be opposed by Governor-elect Casey.

headline: Local officials hail release of flood-protection funds
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh received praise for his decision to provide $6 million for flood-control work in the Scranton area. According to state Representative Frank Belardi, the Northeast Delegation took a hard-line stance on the administration-backed bill to provide $185 million to the Philadelphia convention center project. Seconds before the House was to vote on the convention center bill, the governor's office issued a press release stating that Thornburgh had ordered the Office of Budget to release the flood funds. Belardi commended the move, but stated that the $6 million had already been allocated in the 1984 capital budget. Scranton Mayor David Wenzel approved of the funds being released.

headline: Specter denies suggesting D.C. send prisoners to state
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter denied claims made by the District of Columbia Government that it had been encouraged by Specter's office to consider placing inmates at a private prison in Pennsylvania.  Senator Specter has called the D.C. government's statement false and astonishing.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon of people lining up for at a Public Access TV station, including a woman claiming to be God, an ex-Nazi, a Klansman, and an alien.

headline: New questions on TMI
abstract: This Editorial recalls that it has been almost seven years since the Unit 2 reactor at Three Mile Island was shut down because of a partial meltdown, there are still big decisions to be made.  The billion-dollar cleanup has focused largely on water decontamination, waste shipment, and removal of fuel from the damaged core.  The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission is due to start an environmental impact study shortly.  The editorial believes that this study is a step into the unknown, given that there is no history to draw upon.  The editorial is particularly annoyed that General Public Utilities has brushed off questions about the cleanup as premature.  The editorial believes that it is not premature for the company to announce what it wants to do at the end of 1988.  The editorial looks at several other issues stemming from the cleanup, including the possibility of Unit 2 being reactivated.  The editorial concludes that TMI should be cleaned up, and then shut down, as a reminder of the danger of nuclear power.

headline: Pa. State police needs watchdog, committee says
abstract: Pennsylvania House Democrats produced a report calling for the creation of a legislative oversight capacity for the state police.  The authors cited evidence of unchecked criminal behavior, discrimination, and abuses of the court martial and promotion system as reasons for the need of such a capacity.

headline: Ad critical of record angers Casey
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey has expressed anger over a television ad his opponent Republican William Scranton III has aired.  The ad attacks Casey's record as PA auditor general.  Casey said he would send a note to Scranton asking him to pull it, however, Scranton's campaign manager gave little hope that it would be honored.  The ad attacks Casey for missing a majority of meetings for two governmental boards that he served on during his time as auditor general in the 1960s and 1970s.  Scranton's campaign manager said the ad was a response to a similar ad by the Casey campaign that criticized Scranton's attendance record as PA lieutenant governor in presiding over PA Senate sessions.

headline: Legislators' dining room takes shape in $117 million new state Capitol annex.
abstract: Photograph of construction of the legislators' dining room in Pennsylvania's new state Capitol annex.

headline: Many helping with cleanup including former victims
abstract: After flash floods in the Pittsburgh area last week, many residents are assisting with the cleanup.  People have offered their homes to any people without places to stay and at the Salvation Army's main post there are lists of people willing to help in any capacity needed.

headline: Social Security refunds lost in high-stakes game
abstract: State and local governments throughout the U.S. claim that the Social Security Administration (SSA) is erroneously interpreting a 1979 Social Security guideline so it can avoid paying out millions in refunds to states and localities.  At issue is a guideline stating that pay earned during sick days is not necessarily subject to Social Security tax.  In several states, the SSA has turned down refund claims based on a narrow interpretation of this guideline--thus denying many refund claims that states and localities thought were settled.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Drawing of a Native American slumped on a horse carrying a U.S. Mail satchel with a U.S. Post Office in Edmond, Oklahoma in the background. The caption reads: Trail of Tears 1986.

headline: No Danger From TMI 'Boil'
abstract: It is frustrating to read a letter calling for scientific information in order to better understand the effects of radiation which then fails to provide any information on the minimal amount of radiation involved in the evaporation of processed radioactive water. In fact the amount emitted is equivalent to an additional hour of exposure to background radiation.

headline: Panel Asked for help in dealing
abstract: Interest groups met with state representatives to look into ways to curb teen pregnancy.  Opinions varied widely on what types of approaches should be taken ranging from abstinance only programs to in-depth sex education programs focusing on contraceptives.  Most everyone involved agreed that one goal must be to ensure the pregnant teens graduate high school rather than drop out.

headline: Agency denies blame
abstract: The PA Department of General Services has denied negligence in the 1985 accident that resulted in the loss of a window washer's forearms.  The window washer, Nathan Stewart, filed suit in Dauphin County Court.  The state also said that Stewart was contributorily negilgent.  A detailed description of the event that led to Stewart's accident is included in the article.  Stewart was working on a state-owned building in Harrisburg.  Stewart is also suing PA Power and Light Company.  Stewart has denied any negligence in the matter.

headline: Legislature may try to resurrect agency
abstract: PA Legislative leaders will try to resurrect the Independent Regulatory Review Commission as the PA state legislature returns to its normal schedule.  The commission created to review proposed regulations by state agencies, died last month when senate opponents blocked a bill that would have reauthorized it.  The agency irritated many legislators by ignoring their concerns.

headline: Our opinion: Presque Isle
abstract: The author urges the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources to invest its limited resources in supplying lifeguards to Presque Isle in Erie, claiming that this is a major tourist attraction.

headline: Disaster aid bill advances
abstract: Under a bill unanimously approved by the state House of Representatives, Pennsylvania homeowners living in counties that were declared federal disaster areas during last year's floods and tornadoes would be eligible for maximum grants of 12,500.  The legislation awaits Governor Thornburgh's signature.

headline: Coretta King Meets, Praises Winnie Mandela
abstract: Coretta Scott King and Winnie Mandela met for ninety minutes yesterday. King described the meeting as one of the most meaningful moments of her life and compared the struggle of Mandela's husband, Nelson - in jail for plotting sabotage in South Africa, with that of the American Civil Rights struggle in which numerous people were jailed for civil disobedience.

headline: Notification About TMI Train Debated
abstract: A train carrying fuel from the damaged Three Mile Island reactor was stopped briefly in Nebraska over a dispute about the state being notified of the shipment. Nebraska Governor Bob Kerrey insisted that the state was never notified exactly when the shipment would be arriving and that unless such information was forthcoming, future shipments would not be allowed. A spokesman for the contractor handling the shipments claimed that a Nebraska state trooper was told twice that shipments were coming, but noted that no request was ever received about specific dates and times as happened in other states where the train travelled.

headline: Panel chairman says Richmond should resign
abstract: A PA state commission has considered whether it should make recommendations relative to the retention or termination of elected or appointed senior Philadelphia city officials who had grave responsibilities before and during the May 13, 1985 MOVE bombing incident.

headline: Allegheny County official in lieutenant governor race
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Barbara Hafer has announced her candidacy for PA lieutenant governor on the Republican ticket in the May 20 primary.

headline: Legislative races in the suburbs center on Bucks
abstract: This article discusses the hotly contested Pennsylvanian State Senate races in Bucks County, where are all but one of the suburban contests are being fought this primary season.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of people rafting in Ohiopyle State Park

headline: SEPTA and union agree to resume direct talks today in transit strike
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) and the Transport Workers Union Local 234 have agreed to resume direct talks in the transit strike.  The agreement was reached today.

headline: Court Nullifies State's Abortion Curb
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court reaffirmed its 1973 Roe v. Wade decision legalizing abortion and struck down a Pennsylvania law that it said attempted to intimidate women seeking abortions.

headline: N-plant watched in drill
abstract: A nuclear emergency drill at the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station of Pennsylvania Power & Light Co. is expected to get good marks.  An observation by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission will be known in a few weeks.

headline: Philly Mayor says he should not be indicted
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode said he does not expect to be indicted if a grand jury is convened to investigate the May 13 MOVE battle which left 11 people dead and 61 homes destroyed. Goode also said changes are under way in the Philadelphia Police Department and in the city's crisis management centers.

headline: An early line on the '87 mayoral race
abstract: In Philadelphia, a year before the 1987 primary, 17 months before the general election, the scramble for mayor is already underway.  Democrats dream of defeating current Mayor Wilson Goode in the party's primary election while Republicans feel that at long last, the GOP's tme to return to City Hall has arrived.

headline: Let Pittsburghers Decide
abstract: The fact that a quarter of Pittsburgh is black and yet no blacks are on the city council shows that the at-large system of electing city council members is a failure. A ward system should be created, but a bill introduced in the state legislature by PA Representative Tom Murphy and  another by PA Senator James Romanelli allowing by-district elections has been stalled in the PA Senate Local Government Committee by PA Republican Senator Frank Pecora. This is ironic since in addition to helping blacks by-district elections would also help Republicans.

headline: Reagan rejects pleas of aid for flood victims
abstract: The Reagan administration rejected a plea by twelve Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania area municipalities to be included in a public disaster declaration, with Federal Emergency Management Agency Officials saying that the request was turned down because of questions concerning the accuracy of damage estimates.  The area was hit hard by floods at the end of May and the municipalities are seeking $13 million in aid for cleanup costs as well as repairs to roads, bridges and waterworks.

headline: Greater and Greater Pitt
abstract: Because of the actions taken by its dominant carrier, US Air, and its abundance of land,  the Federal Aviation Administration estimates that Greater Pitt will be the nation's fastest-growing airport over the next decade.  The lingering question is how comfortably and efficiently the growth at Greater Pitt will be accommodated.

headline: Defends Pro-Life Slates
abstract: The author argues that pro-life supporters do not mix morality with politics since this group of voters often lends political support to candidates on both sides of the debate. The issue is really about the high priority people place on politics rather than morality. However, voters and pro-life groups should stick to their beliefs if they think that abortion is murder.  The author questions how deep the country's moral fiber goes.

headline: NRC goes in reverse on radiation standards
abstract: A proposal offered by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission will change radiation exposure standards for workers, ultimately affecting over 1.5 million workers. The Philadelphia Inquirer says that the standards are not high enough and that many people from around the world are affected by radiation from nuclear energy.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of firefighters boarding a plane in Harrisburg to travel West and help fight forest fires there

headline: An Ethnic Mixed Bag
abstract: This year's "Congressional District Fact Book," written by the Joint Center for Political Studies, broke down all four hundred thirty-five congressional districts. A number of the twenty-three districts in PA ranked in the top ten in a variety of categories involving ethnicity, level of education, and level of income.

headline: Let sun set on review panel
abstract: This author believes that the Pennsylvania legislature should close the Independent Regulatory Review Commission, an agency on the state government that is due to end this year unless a bill to extend its life is passed.  It was created three years ago to prevent state departments and agencies from implementing regulations.

headline: Reagan authorizes funds for city flood-control project
abstract: President Reagan signed a bill yesterday authorizing nearly 400 water projects worth $16 billion around the country, including the $133 million Harrisburg flood-control project.  The signing of the first comprehensive public works bill in 16 years significantly changes how harbor and waterway projects are selected and financed by boosting the share paid by state and local authorities.

headline: For the Convention Center
abstract: It is time for the city of Philadelphia to follow through with the convention-center project.  The project means thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue for the city.

headline: Falwell support
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author criticizes Jerry Falwell for saying he is staying out of Pennsylvania politics, but then pledging support for US Senator Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, who is pro-choice.  He believes that Falwell‘s support of a pro-choice candidate contradicts the mission of the Moral Majority.

headline: NRC rates Unit 1 'good', will cut inspector staff
abstract: Satisfied with the results of a three-month power increase program at Three Mile Island Unit 1, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission will reduce its number of inspectors on the island.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of PA State Trooper Robert Buser preparing to testify before a PA House committee. He testified that he was an alcoholic and urged more aid be given to a program that helps troopers like him.

headline: An Important Election
abstract: The editors hope that there will be high voter turnout for the gubernatorial election.  They provide 5 endorsements for the upcoming elections--3 democrats and two republicans.  They endorse Democrat Robert Casey for governor, Joseph McDade, Robert Mellow, Fred Belardi, and Robert Davis.  They could not make a decision on who to endorse in the US Senate race between Arlen Spector and Bob Edgar.

headline: Letter: Gov Saw No Saving in Rebid
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has decided to proceed with the $177 million PA state capitol expansion after being advised that rebidding would not save him any money on the project. The only way forecasted to save money on the project would be to make cuts in quality, but Thornburgh wanted the job done right so no changes will be made.

headline: Relocate "Gate" to Sunken Garden
abstract: This author believes that Harrisburg, Pennsylvania's newest outdoor public sculpture, "Egyptian Gate", which has appeared in a riverfront park, is not located in the best possible place.

headline: Candidate Will Need Court OK
abstract: An official from the PA Election Bureau said that Robert Castellani, who is seeking the Republican nomination for the state Senate in the 22d Senatorial District, will need to get the Commonwealth Court's approval  to amend his nomination petitions; he mistakenly listed the wrong senatorial district on the petitions.  Castellani wishes to oppose Democratic state Senator Robert J. Mellow in the general election this fall.

headline: GOP Team Position On Family Masks Abortion Disagreement
abstract: PA Republican gubernatorial candidate William Scranton III, and his running mate for lieutenant governor, D. Michael Fisher, announced their position on a number of family issues except abortion. Scranton supports abortion rights while Fisher opposes abortion. The issue where both agree, however, involves teen pregnancy, not only in terms of ways to reduce it, through better access to family planning services, but also supporting teen mothers with information on adoptions, referrals to a new Family Resources program, and an "Adopt-a-Teens-Parent" program through the Department of Aging's volunteer program.

headline: Nuclear accident
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author cautions the United State from believing that what happened at Chernobyl could not happen here.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of U.S. Supreme Court Justice Warren Burger before he was sworn in as chief justice

headline: An Irresponsible Bill Vetoed
abstract: The authors of this piece argue that union leaders across the state seem to assume that there is wide support for the "agency shop" bill recently vetoed by PA Governor Dick Thornburgh. However, given the slim majority by which it was passed and the fact that there is no effort to override it should prove that there is minimal support for such a bill. In fact, Democrats are biding their time, hoping Bob Casey wins so that when the bill is reintroduced they will not have to worry about a veto. Republican Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton would veto the bill, which is another reason to vote for him. Forcing people to pay dues to a union they do not want to belong to is unprincipled and unamerican.

headline: Non-voting is suicide
abstract: The board strongly speaks out against the idea of non-voting, which it believes harms the black community more so than any politician could. It commends the election of Philadelphia's black mayor Wilson Goode, but cites the defeat of Robert Williams in the race for district attorney as a product of black non-voting. It encourages blacks to vote in all elections, whether federal, state or local.

headline: Rescue methods at park studied
abstract: Criticisms over a failed rescue attempt of a 10 year old child at McConnells Mill State Park have led to a review of emergency rescue procedures.  Most talks centered around improving communications at the park and in general, as this was seen as the root cause of the failed rescue attempt.

headline: Inmates here refuse to eat
abstract: Some inmates at the State Correctional Institution at Pittsburgh sent a list of 32 demands to Governor Thornburgh, the warden and the state commissioner of corrections and have threatened to remain on a hunger strike until their demands are resolved.

headline: In ruling, majority cites privacy
abstract: The article includes excerpts from the US Supreme Court ruling that Pennsylvania's abortion law is unconstitutional. The Court cited rules and reporting requirements for doctors as violating the privacy rights of their patients.

headline: Nuclear research needed
abstract: In light of the recent accidents at Three Mile Island and at the Chernobyl plant, this author finds it disburbing that the Reagan administration is proposing funding cuts for civilian nuclear resarch by 60%. This author argues that more research needs to occur, not less, to explore such things as accident-proof reactor designs.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Picture of Judge Genevieve Blatt.

headline: Anger explodes in capital
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter got into a snarling rumble with U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz.  Many outbursts and displays of anger have erupted in the U.S. Capitol over the last several months.

headline: Lobbyist Season In Harrisburg
abstract: Because the PA Constitution requires a new budget on July first, the last week of June is traditionally the most hectic as lobbyists come out in force vying with each other for a few minutes of a legislator's time in order to get a few more dollars for a particular program from money that has yet to be committed to anything. It is also an unofficial deadline for other pieces of legislation, which the lobbyists also try to influence. While some lawmakers lament the strain and fear it can lead to unintentional consequences through poorly worded bills, others believe that if it works why worry about it. Because so many lobbyists are present it also becomes a time for many politicians, especially those seeking reelection, to hold fundraising events, thereby representing the flip side of the legislator-lobbyist relationship.

headline: Restoration At Gettysburg
abstract: While most of the attention this weekend is on the restoration of the Statue of Liberty, another restoration closer to home deserves equal attention. The PA Memorial at Gettysburg was rededicated by Governor Thornburgh after a seven month restoration and a cost of over one hundred thousand dollars. It is the duty of future generations to remember and honor those who fought and died and one way to do it is by taking proper care of their cemeteries and the places where they fought. Restoration of other monuments are underway, largely through private funds. This is something which must be expanded and accelerated.

headline: South African sanctions
abstract: We believe that it would be a political, diplomatic and moral mistake for President Reagan to veto a recently-passed bill that would impose new economic sanctions on South Africa.  This veto effort would be fruitless, as the legislation passed with large enough majorities in both chambers to override any veto attempt.  Moreover, it is time for the United States to take a clear moral stance and send a message to South Africa that it refuses to be complicit in apartheid.

headline: Job rights for pregnant argued before high court
abstract: The US Supreme Court heard a case concerning the treatment of pregnant women in the work force. The case examines what kind of job benefits should be afforded to women temporarily unable to work due to pregnancy.

headline: Nuke cloud heads west; Soviet deaths feared
abstract: The Soviet Union admitted that there were casualties in the nuclear accident at its Chernobyl nuclear facility, the first instance in which the Soviet Union acknowledged an accident at a nuclear plant. The Reagan Administration stated that it would be willing to respond to calls for aid. The accident sent a radioactive cloud towards Scandinavia, and the cloud may reach the United States' West Coast in six days.

headline: Police powers increased in cases of domestic violence
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has signed a new law that gives police more power in domestic violence cases. The new law allows police to make an arrest if they have probable cause such as physical injury or other evidence that a person has been abused.

headline: Another side of medical liability
abstract: Donald Harrop writes to the Inquirer about a recent argument posted in the paper stating that there is no medical liability problem in PA. Harrop says the argument flies in the face of the evidence acknowledged by all involved in the recent negotiating processes. The real problem is that both sides stalemated leaving further attempts for negotiations fruitless.

headline: Lobbyists unwanted
abstract: Pennsylvania Republican State Senators, and members of the Senate Rules and Executive Nominations Committee, objected when Governor Thornburgh submitted the name of a petroleum industry lobbyist for a position on the State Board of Education, causing his name to be withdrawn.

headline: Save Fairmount Park
abstract: Samuel L. Evans' crusade to seize 40 acres of Fairmont Park and turn it into a garden of sculptures honoring black Americans has come under fire. The Philadelphia Inquirer says that if the park commission is going to be steamrolled by Evans' political bandwagon, there should be no hesitancy in asking the courts to preserve Fairmount Park.

headline: Insurance Monopoly
abstract: Some critics object to my proposal for state-provided auto insurance because they feel it will decrease competitive rates and services.  What these critics fail to realize is that private insurance companies operating in Pennsylvania already set unifrom, non-competitive rates through the Insurance Services Organization.  My plan for state-provided auto insurance will lower administrative costs and premiums, and it will reduce the number of uninsured motorists on Pennsylvania roadways.

headline: Killing Babies Not 'Just'
abstract: This letter is in response to Planned Parenthood of PA Executive Director Morgan Plant's praise for the U.S. Supreme Court's recent decisions on abortion. The author argues that abortion should be illegal under all circumstances, and is outrage that the PA General Assembly is considering raising the fine for dog fighting to $15,000 when abortions cost much less.

headline: Oversupply of coal seen as lasting 2-3 more years
abstract: The mining congress, made up of representatives of the nation's coal-mining companies, met in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania to discuss the problem of oversupply in the industry, which has caused prices of coal to remain low.  This is predicted to continue for at least 2-3 more years, with predictions of nuclear power shrinking coal's utility market share by the 1990s.

headline: Politics Enters Police Probe
abstract: The editorial board states that it supports the PA House of Representatives probe into the problems with the state police initiated by PA Representative Alfonso Deal, but urges that it be done jointly  with the PA Senate.  The board also asks that politics remain out of the investigation, and that the investigation could potentially clean up the image of the state police.

headline: Anti-abortionist for Casey
abstract: A letter from a Republican who feels confident that many other Republicans will cross party lines to vote for Democrat Robert Casey for Pennsylvania governor, since he is anti-abortion, and since Republican opponent William Scranton urged the current governor, Dick Thornburgh, to veto a bill that included a strong amendment against teenage drinking.

headline: Local Services: Government Units Join For Efficiency
abstract: The PA Economy League predicts that with the loss of federal revenue sharing many local governments will face difficult times. However, this may not be a bad thing as it will force the numerous governments and local authorities to consolidate their duplicate services in order to reduce costs and increase efficiency. This may be easier said than done, as school consolidation was championed for the same reasons, yet they failed to occur. A good middle ground might be local councils of government in which certain functions are handled at a multi-governmental level. Where they have been tried they have been quiet successful. But the challenge remains to find a type of local government that is efficient, but which doesn't alienate citizens.

headline: Senate To Cut Flood Victim Aid
abstract: Legislation approved in the PA House meant to give relief to areas of the state hit by flooding and severe weather last May will be significantly reduced by the PA Senate. PA Senate Majority Leader John Stauffer said that only seven to eight million dollars is needed in addition to the money already released by Governor Thornburgh. The over twenty million dollars approved by the House is "way more" than necessary.

headline: Political zeal threatens real anti-drug legislation
abstract: It appears as if neither the House nor the Senate will be able to agree on new anti-drug legislation before adjourning by mid-October to campaign for the November 4th general election.  There are two bills under consideration--one bill has spending levels that will be too high for many fiscal conservatives and the other has several questionable amendments that represent a stumbling block to final passage.

headline: Heating aid to rise due to surplus
abstract: With a $14 million budget surplus of home-heating aid program money for the poor, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh announced a retroactive 20% increase to aid recipients.

headline: Legislators would stop clinic move
abstract: The expected relocation of the Northeast Women's Center to a new site has prompted anti-abortion lawmakers in the PA General Assembly such as PA Senator Joseph Rocks and PA Rep. Stephen Freind to draft legislation which could block the center's relocation by placing the center under the jurisdiction of the state's Certificate of Need Law (CON). The Philadelphia Zoning Board of Adjustments granted the building a new permit, but rescinded the permit after protest by local residents. The NWC took the city to federal court, where US District Judge Louis C. Bechtle found the zoning laws to interfere with a woman's constitutional right to an abortion.

headline: PE gains in bid for rate increase
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Utility turned down a plea from PA Consumer Advocate David Barasch to reduce the rate request of Philadelphia Electric Company on the ground that Limerick 1, the company's nuclear plant, is an uneconomical source of power.

headline: Powder keg
abstract: PA Auditor General Don Bailey said that the state is sitting on a powder keg because of understaffing in the Pittsburgh city's prison system and inadequate fitness requirements for guards.

headline: Apologize, Casey
abstract: The author of this letter wants Governor-elect Robert Casey to apologize to Pennsylvania voters for the use of a negative piece of campaign literature sent to thousands of voters the weekend before the election.

headline: Local Tax Plan Falls Short
abstract: The PA House Finance Committee is considering legislation that would allow municipalities to raise property taxes by three mills for trash collection and two mills for liability insurance. However, this only creates an even larger mosaic of exceptions that local areas are able to choose from and does not get at the hart of the issue of genuine local tax reform. Because the needs and priorities of local areas are different, cash strapped towns seek exceptions each time they reach the state limit. It would be better if towns were able to raise property taxes a certain number of mills subject to the approval of local voters, so they have a chance to decide how much government they want.

headline: Setback For Lake Arthur
abstract: An advisory panel established to review strip mining around Lake Arthur in Moraine State Park came up with the wrong answer in approving the project because it puts too much faith in the restrictions currently in place as well as the state's ability to detect violations. Given that there is no need for additional coal mining and the large numbers of people attracted to the area why risk damaging it? Private areas near the park, such as mine seeps and a malfunctioning sewage disposal facility, are already damaging the lake,so why court additional problems?

headline: Candidate agrees to name former law firm clients
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert P. Casey will disclose the names of former legal clients by the end of the month.  Casey has been acused of engaging in old-style politics by his opponent, Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III, and has been pressured by Scranton's campaign to disclose former clients.

headline: Human-services crunch
abstract: New evidence of how hard the Gramm-Rudman budget law will hit human services in PA has been found in a report from The Urban Institute. The study, done in conjunction with the Health and Welfare Planning Association of Pittsburgh, covered health care, social services, housing and community development, employment and training, arts and culture, and income maintenance.

headline: Minority Contractors: Pa., City Differ
abstract: Philadelphia's efforts to award contracts to minority-owned firms have been unsuccessful because many white contractors establish fronts with a minority at the head to win contracts.  The actual money and work are then funneled to white controlled companies. A Philadelphia Inquirer investigation reported that over forty percent of city construction contracts in the last two years were awarded in this manner. However, the wording of the actual ordinance is so loose that it has been difficult for the city to prosecute violations and has had to rely on state prosecutions instead.

headline: Peach Bottom violations draw $200,000 NRC fine
abstract: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), citing inattention to detail, has fined the Peach Bottom nuclear power plant in York County, Pennsylvania $200,000.  Initially the NRC issued a $100,000 fine but doubled it in light of the plant's poor history of its staff following procedures.  Since 1983, the plant has been issued five violation notices that have cost the company $170,000.

headline: Precious Life
abstract: A letter that expresses remorse that the MOVE disaster, when Philadelphia officials burned down the household of John Africa and his organization, and with it, a neighborhood.  The author feels that the MOVE members are the ones responsible for the deaths of innocent children burned in the fire.

headline: Apology accepted, Casey says
abstract: Accepting an apology his opponent never said was offered, Robert Casey removed his objections to debating Ed Rendell , his main opponent in the Democratic Gubernatorial Primary.  Last week, Casey said he would not debate Rendell until he apologized after Rendell compared Casey to several right-wing politicians.

headline: 'Lou Grant' Battles 'Moses' In Upstate House Race
abstract: Although PA's twenty-third U.S. congressional district is one of the most sparsely populated and rural in the state, it is now home to a new political theater. In the race between incumbent William F. Clinger Jr. and Bill Wachob, both candidates have asked for the assistance of Hollywood actors, Charlton Heston and Ed Asner. It began with Wachob asking Asner to come and help him raise funds. In response Clinger asked Heston for his support. Heston agreed and did a radio ad claiming that among Asner's previous works was helping to raise funds for communist-backed rebels in El Salvador. How effective either effort was is unknown, polls done by Wachob show that only twenty-two percent of people were even aware of the Heston ads, and seventy-one percent of them said it did not affect their view of Clinger.

headline: State parks ill-equipped for crises
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources operates the 113 parks around the state, and provides limited emergency services in 75 of them.  It has ambulance service in only one and the other 74 parks with manned first-aid stations can treat no more than cuts and bruises and are not equipped to handle water rescues, heart attacks, or drowning incidents.  264 people have died in state parks since 1975, 165 of them in accidents such as drownings and car crashes.

headline: Drug Issue Injected into Congressional Debate
abstract: At their first public debate, Third Congressional District candidate Robert A. Rovner took a hard-line stance on illegal drugs and attacked his Democratic opponent, Robert A. Borski, as being ultra liberal and a pet of special interests.

headline: Jones Home Sale Coming By Oct. 29
abstract: The Kay B. Jones Nursing Home in Wilkinsburg is in the process of being sold to a new owner. The PA Welfare Department took over the home after a large part of the staff was fired and others quit. The home has been cited in the past for rodent infestations and poor handling of medication. The state was reluctant to close the home due to the trauma it would have placed on the residents, and with its sale it will not be forced to do so.

headline: Minority group says Caliguiri plan 'ploy'
abstract: A group of black contractors attacked Pittsburgh Mayor Richard S. Caliguiri's recent proposal to give minority-owned firms a larger share of city contracts by calling for a referendum to change the city charter. The charter change would allow for set aside programs for minority-owned companies.  The group believes that a referendum is not enough in a city that has no black city council members, yet 25% of the population is black.  They want the City Council to approve a new ordinance setting aside a certain percentage of city contracts for minorities.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photo of two evacuees covering their faces after a gas leak in Philadelphia.

headline: Prisons Abuse Child Offenders
abstract: As an inmate in a PA correctional institution I have seen with my own eyes the consequences of the Youthful Offenders Act. It is nothing more than legalized child abuse, as children who could have led productive lives are irrevocably altered due to the physical and sexual abuse they undergo at the hands of other inmates. The public needs to know what happens to the children they send here and stop it at once.

headline: Appointment Of A County Judge
abstract: The death of PA  Judge Gordon A. Roe has been exacerbated by the illnesses of two other judges. A backlog is threatening to reappear and a new judge needs to be appointed soon. PA Governor Thornburgh must nominate someone who then needs to be approved by the PA Senate. However, because the PA Senate is in recess until late September it will be almost five months after Roe's death for his replacement to be named. Because it is an election year it could take even longer, perhaps not even until the first of the year. A backlog in cases could reappear in York County because of unnecessary political delays.

headline: Lucchino backs off race for No. 2 state job
abstract: PA Democrats have shown no determination to forge a consensus ticket for the 1986 gubernatorial race. Due to the lack of consensus, Pittsburgh County Controller Frank Lucchino has withdrawn as a prospective candidate for lieutenant governor.

headline: Stopgap action sought to control flooding
abstract: Initial efforts to establish a flood control project for the Lackawanna River and streams took place Thursday at the request of Scranton Mayor David Wenzel.  An array of federal, state, city, and county officials met and were told that it could be five years before the project can begin, after a $1.2 million study is completed by the US Army Corps of Engineers.

headline: USX seeks ways to boost its value
abstract: In response to significant trading by speculators, USX corporation has asked investment bankers to study and recommend ways of restructuring the the oil and steel company to increase shareholder value.

headline: Just a ploy?
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has proposed putting more mentally retarded citizens into community group homes over the next five years. Union workers at Polk Center are skeptical about Thornburgh’s budget.  The Morning News says PA residents want the handicapped helped, but no one wants residents of Polk dumped anywhere so the move will take serious budget funds.

headline: No Title - Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon depicts four years, 1770, 1870, 1960, and 1986.  In 1770 it says 5 1/2 million blacks brought to America as slaves and depicts a slave market, and in 1870, it depicts the Ku Klux Klan lynching a black man.  1960 depicts colored and white water fountains side by side, and 1986 shows a white man saying 'they can't lay me off before some black with less seniority!  That's discrimination!'.

headline: Plummeting oil prices force layoffs in state
abstract: The drop in oil prices has had a resounding impact on PA's oil industry, especially the drop in price on Pennsylvania-grade crude used for lubrication purposes. According to the Independent Petroleum Association of America, there are 17 drilling rigs producing Pennsylvania-grade crude, compared with 49 a year ago. Layoffs in PA include 500 employees at Halliburton Service's Pittsburgh division since the beginning of 1986, and Pennzoil Exploration and Production Company's termination of 26 jobs in the Bradford district, which covers western PA and southern New York.

headline: Probe clears ex-state official of cocaine use
abstract: An in-house investigation at the PA Attorney General's office has cleared Richard Guida of allegations from a reporter that he used cocaine, two months after he resigned as the state's top criminal prosecutor.  The reporter had refused to reveal his sources, inhibiting the investigation and Guida's ability to defend himself.

headline: As Democrats look to '88, Jackson is feared as a barrier to unity
abstract: As the leaders of the Democratic Party gathered to celebrate recent wins in the November elections and look toward the 1988 Presidential election, the Reverend Jesse Jackson is seen as one of the party's biggest potential problems.  Based on his 1984 campaign, he is widely viewed as an obstacle to party unity and a threat to the party's painstaking attempts to fasion a mainstream image.

headline: Many GOP governors believe Reagan on arms scandal
abstract: The nation's 24 Republican governors are meeting at a three day conference in New Jersey, where they said they believe President Reagan is telling the truth about what he knew about the Iran-Contra arms scandal.  They also are meeting to discuss the party's future and ways to build grass-roots support.

headline: Timothy Cricks and his mother, Delores, comforted each other as they stood near the bank of Little Pine Creek off Beiger Drive in Indiana Township
abstract: Photograph showing Timothy Cricks and his mother, Delores, as they comforted each other as they stood near the bank of Little Pine Creek off Beiger Drive in Indiana Township after flash flooding in the Pittsburgh area of Pennsylvania occurred this week.

headline: Consumer unit chief resigns
abstract: The director of the Pennsylvania Bureau of Consumer Protection, Michael J. Pekula, is stepping down as of October 3rd to become the director of consumer affairs for Aamco Transmission in Philadelphia.

headline: One black man's welfare reform
abstract: Columnist Chuck Stone commends Michael A. Mond, a taxicab dispatcher, for submitting his idea for welfare reform. Stone references the US Supreme Court case Gitlow v. N.Y. for the importance of ideas. Stone states that if more people took the time to think out the matter, as Mond did, solutions would be provided to the black community's "pathologies."

headline: Parents do care
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author notes that PA Rep. Stephen Freind is not the only Pennsylvanian looking to challenge abortion providers. Many others in the state also support a recently introduced statute that would require a minor seeking an abortion to get permission from a parent or judge.  Despite the existence of cases where family relationships have broken down, parents are ultimately responsible for their daughters, according to the author.  The author is particularly critical of an article written by Post-Gazette reporter Sally Kalson on December 27, 1986, and calls for her to do another article with interviews from groups who care for women after they have had abortions.

headline: PUC grants boost in water rate over staff objections
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) granted Dauphin Cosolidated Water Supply an annual rate increase, despite petitions filed by its own trial staff and state Consumer Advocate David Barasch.  The increase will raise the average residential customer's bill by about $13 a year, with higher rates effective immediately.

headline: Records seized at 2 cemeteries in N.E. Penna.
abstract: The PA Attorney General's Office has seized the records of two Lackawanna County cemeteries in an investigation of reports of trust fund violations.  Kevin Colgan, a special agent with the PA Attorney General, said records were taken from Hyde Park Cemetery in Scranton, PA and Abington Hills Cemetery in Clarks Summit.  Both cemeteries are owned by John Rogan.  Under PA law, cemeteries must deposit 15% of all proceeds from the sale of burial lots into a perpetual-care trust fund for care of the cemetery.  A search warrant affidavit claims that Rogan deposited no money in the trust fund for either cemetery for at least three years.

headline: As Polls Close, Race for Mayor Begins
abstract: In Pennsylvania, the polls had barely closed yesterday, with the race too close to call Democrat Robert Casey governor-elect, when former Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell worked the crowd, looking and sounding like a man who might like to be Philadelphia mayor.  The mayoral race is scheduled for next year.

headline: Map
abstract: Blowup map of the U.S. highlighting contested congressional seats in each region

headline: What To Do When The Flash Floods Come
abstract: Flash floods occur with only a few seconds warning, and no two are alike. Instead of trying to outdrive a flash flood a better course of action is to wait in the upper floor of a house or other building.

headline: The war against drugs
abstract: We do not endorse fully the drug-control measures passed by the U.S. House last week, as they represent a foolhardy and unconstitutional response to a serious problem.  We need thoughtful war on drugs--one that is grounded in well financed and researched methods of eradication and prevention.

headline: Rent Rebate
abstract: The PA state lottery fund provides a rent rebate for persons retired at age 65, or for widows or widowers at age 50 with limited income. Ruth E. Starner of York writes to the Patriot News saying she feels that there is discrimination against persons who are divorced, never married, have a limited income, and who are 50 or older since the state lottery fund program provides a rent or a tax rebate only to some.

headline: Probe urged in the firing of Singley
abstract: Nine organizations with ties to Philadelphia's black community called on local, state, and national agencies to investigate the circumstances surrounding the removal of Carl E. Singley as dean of Temple's School of Law.  They argue that Singley has been an outspoken leader and role model for black and minority youth and given the lack of explanation or justification for his removal as Dean, there is reason to believe that race may have played a role.

headline: PUC prices time of day at 55 cents
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) gave telephone companies the right to charge for a variety of customer-requested operator services within local calling areas, including the right to charge 55 cents for telling customers the time of day.

headline: Reopen the McCracken case
abstract: The editorial board believes Delaware County Common Pleas Court Judge Robert A. Wright should reopen the case of Terence McCracken Jr., who was convicted of second-degree murder. An eyewitness was questioned by Delaware County law enforcement officials and had three different stories for the three days he was questioned, while a State Police forensic test on gunshot residue on McCracken's hand was indecisive.

headline: Back Room Blockage
abstract: PA House Republicans and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh have refused to hand over nearly $180 million in funding for the convention center unless their demands are met. The Philadelphia Daily News says that Thornburgh and PA Senate Republicans should release the Philadelphia convention center from Harrisburg if they genuinely care about the future of this region.

headline: Media group hears Edgar, Spector spar
abstract: Senatorial candidates Bob Edgar and Arlen Spector spoke separately to an assembly of the Pennsylvania Association of Broadcasters.  While the content of the speeches was quite controversial as the candidates ripped into each other relentlessly, the format was equally controversial.  Rather than appear together and debate, the candidates appeared separately, one after the other.

headline: A new tack on track
abstract: Although Pittsburgh City Council voted down a proposal aimed at putting a dog track in the city, McKeesport Mayor Louis Washowich has a new initiative aimed at getting support for a dog track in his town. Washowich claims that dog racing tax revenue could help his struggling city.

headline: Hike state store pay
abstract: The Pennsylvania state store 20-percent-off sale creates total chaos in stores as well as headaches for state-store employees.  If the state is going to continue these 20-percent-off sales, it needs to compensate employees for their extra troubles by sharing some of the sale's pofits with them.

headline: Scranton And Fisher Have Taken On A Tough Issue
abstract: Republican candidates for governor and lietuenant governor, Bill Scranton and Mike Fisher, respectively, have come out with a position paper on families that is unusual for its making sense. It argues that PA's future lies in its families but that many families are not being helped when they most need it. Not only have many programs been cut, but of those that remain there are duplications and restrictions that can force families to be split up. The paper outlines a plan to increase low income housing, expand programs that support working mothers, increase state aid for nutrition programs and other things. It's encouraging to know that some candidates have the courage to deal with this issue.

headline: Racially Motivated Ciolence Increasing
abstract: Since July of last year racially motivated violence in PA has risen 85%. Much of this is occurring as minorities move into all-white neighborhoods, and as whites and minorities compete for increasingly scarce jobs. The reporting of incidents is also an issue, not only because there is a split among advocacy groups about whether it does any good, but many also argue that it is not worth the effort due to fears of reprisals and a lack of prosecutions – records show that only a dozen have been prosecuted under the anti-intimidation law, but less than half resulted in convictions. In order to increase reporting of incidents, a tension task force has been created to coordinate activities between the PA Human Relations Commission and minority groups. The PA HRC is holding seminars, publications on intimidation are being printed in lesser known languages, and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) has set up a hotline to report racial incidents.

headline: PUC Suspends Met-Ed Rate Increase Pending Investigation
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission yesterday suspended a request by Metropolitan Edison Company to increase rates by almost ten percent until it has time to investgate it. The company cited increased operating and maintenance costs as well as spending more on customer service programs and improving its transmission and distribution systems as the reason for the request.

headline: Report offers panel's verdict on who was telling the truth
abstract: A PA state commission has rejected Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode’s testimony that he had no knowledge of the explosive material that was used in the MOVE disaster. The former Philadelphia police commissioner and other witnesses contradicted Goode’s testimony.

headline: Bailey campaign trail leads down fun path
abstract: PA Democrat Don Bailey, the current PA auditor general and candidate for the US Senate against Republican Arlen Specter, says he is having fun on the campaign trail.  Bailey says that his opponent in the Democratic primary, US Representative Bob Edgar, is too liberal for the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: Membership in unions fluctuates among state workers
abstract: There was a flurry of union resignations among state employees last June when negotiations stalled for a new contract. The American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees, the largest of unions, has always suffered resignations just before contracts expired, the only point at which members may pull out.

headline: A register of wills, Democrats are welcome.
abstract: The Philadelphia Register of Wills Office is the only city office not bound by the city charter. The city charter's ban on city employees engaging in political activity or doing business directly or indirectly with city government does not apply to those at the register of wills.

headline: Scranton pledges aid for higher education
abstract: Yesterday, the Republican candidate for governor, William Scranton III, promised increased state funding for higher education as part of a plan to help foster an intelligence-based economy.  Scranton also said that he would make efforts to stabilize tuition in the State System of Higher Education if elected governor.

headline: Scrap new welfare office, protestors say
abstract: East Poplar residents in Philadelphia marched on the PA state office building threatening to block bulldozers and prevent construction of welfare offices in their neighborhood. PA State Department of Welfare spokesman Joe Kintz said the new offices are part of the statewide effort to upgrade welfare offices and make them more accessible to clients.

headline: Reluctant Reed To Let King Blvd. Name Become Law
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed said he would neither sign nor veto a City Council bill renaming Market Street the Reverend Doctor Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard. Reed opposes the measure noting that the renaming will not serve as a lasting tribute and that a statue or a series of plaques, which could act as a rallying point and place for commemorations would be of greater service to Harrisburg City Council's goals. Various council members cited the public's support for the measure as the reason to go forward and dismissed the idea of reconsidering it.

headline: PUC told: give PECO $358 million rate hike
abstract: A Public Utility Commission judge recommended that Philadelphia Electric Company receive more than half its proposed $681.8 million rate increase, the largest request the commission has ever considered.  The increase would cover costs associated with the Limerick, Pennsylvania nuclear power plant in Montgomery County and facilities common to Limerick 1 and Limerick 2, which is not complete.

headline: Scranton says CLANAGAN case handled well
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor William Scranton voiced support for PA State Police Commissioner Jay Cochran for his actions involving a black PA state trooper's bid to assume command of the PA State Police York barracks. Some PA state legislators are calling for Cochran’s resignation.

headline: Bailey greets a potential voter in Pittsburgh, where he spent much of the last day of the campaign
abstract: Photograph showing U.S. Senate candidate for Pennsylvania Don Bailey.

headline: Mezvinsky To Step Down As State Democratic Chief
abstract: Pennsylvania State Democratic Chairman Edward Mezvinsky said today that he won't seek re-election as head of the Pennsylvania Democratic Committee, but will serve until a new chairman is picked at a committee meeting following the May 20 primary election.  Mezvinsky survived attempted coups in 1983 and 1984 when western county party members tried to oust him, arguing that he poorly managed the state committee and did little for committee-endorsed candidates.

headline: Advisers hope Goode, on TV, can turn tide
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode will give a televised speech which should answer all questions about the MOVE bombing. Mayor Goode’s advisors hope that the speech will bring the mayor back into good terms with some residents.

headline: Edgar Has A Real Fund Time
abstract: At the biggest fundraiser of Congressman Bob Edgar's senatorial campaign, the theme was miracles.  Attendees, many of whom were members of Congress, praised Edgar and were hopeful that he would overcome a large deficit and beat incumbent Pennsylvania Senator Arlen Specter.  If Edgar wins, he will be Pennsylvania's first Democratic Senator in 25 years.

headline: Senator pushes for file on state's food-for-the-needy role
abstract: PA Senate Democrats have asked PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's administration for the complete file on the state's decision-making process in the shipment of free federal food to PA.  Senators have also asked for any minutes, orders, or decisions which may have been made by the PA Department of Agriculture concerning this program in an effort to figure out who is responsible for the state's failure in July and August to apply for the food.

headline: Ron's Popularity Best Ever Among Women, Blacks
abstract: According to a New York Times Poll, a record number of women and African-Americans say they support U.S. President Ronald Reagan. The poll found that 68% of the American people now approve of the way Reagan is handling his job.

headline: PUC urged to cut rate for water
abstract: PA Consumer Advocate David Barasch's office has asked the PA Public Utility Commission to order the Dauphin Consolidated Water Supply Company to cut its rates by more than $400,000, which would reduce the average residential customer's water bill by about $12 a year.

headline: Senate gets bill to alter judge voting
abstract: The PA Senate Judiciary Committee approved a measure that would have appellate court judges elected from judicial districts rather then elected statewide. Currently the judiciary is heavily influenced by Pittsburgh and Philadelphia. The new method would allow a more representative judiciary.

headline: Bailey has 'no complaints': Defeated Senate hopeful to support winner, Edgar
abstract: PA Auditor General Don Bailey wants to get back to business, after losing in the U.S. Senate democratic primary to U.S. Representative Bob Edgar on May 20.  He lost by just over 20,000 votes out of more than 880,000 cast.  Bob Edgar will face Republican incumbent Arlen Spector in the November general election for the U.S. Senate seat in Pennsylvania.

headline: Money From Nothing
abstract: The Dauphin County General Authority was established two years ago to run the county parking garage, but now it has decided to float almost six hundred million dollars in tax-free bonds and lend it out to other agencies and communities statewide. This is an abuse of the privilege of issuing such bonds as well as the intent of the Dauphin County General Authority. It seems perverse that local government entities are borrowing large amounts of money and reinvesting it at high interest rates with the U.S. government and taxpayers footing the bill. The authority should stick to running a parking garage.

headline: Assessment Unfairness
abstract: John M. Kelly, a Realtor from Scranton, writes to say that injustice is rampant in Philadelphia, citing that the failure of local authorities to adjust assessments to reflect changing market value; the lack of equity that many times brings on court appeals that collectively wreak havoc with the tax base; injudicious granting of exemption privileges that erode the tax base; and the lack of statewide uniform ratios comprise the litany of very justifiable complaints that have been heard for decades.

headline: Panel Oks extending review process
abstract: The state Senate Government Committee approved a bill extending the life of the Pennsylvania Independent Regulatory Review Commission until 1991.  The five-member panel reviews proposed state rules and regulations.

headline: Specter Would Expand Job Training For Welfare Recipients
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter said he would introduce a bill in the U.S. Senate designed to get more welfare recipients into federal job training programs. Working with the National Urban League and the Opportunities Industrialization Centers the proposal would end obstacles to welfare recipients seeking job training by adding support services such as child care and remedial education. There would be no additional cost to the program, rather it would reallocate money already set aside under the Job Training Partnership Act but being poorly used. In a separate bill Specter wants to let welfare recipients continue to receive Social Security benefits during their first year of employment in order to eliminate a disincentive to seeking work.

headline: Seeks pro-life victory
abstract: Writer outlines her belief in the importance of pro-life issues in politics and tries to convice people to vote for pro-life candidates.

headline: Questions Rasied On Limerick 2
abstract: The dispute over Philadelphia Electric Company's (PE) construction of the Limerick Two nuclear reactor continued at a PA Commonwealth Court hearing yesterday.
