Lawyers from the PA Consumer Advocate's Office and the Governor's Energy Council argued that alternative's to the reactor, such as coal or oil-fired plants were not considered adequately, and that a cost cap implemented in December would not sufficiently protect consumers from cost overruns or make the facility economically efficient. Officials from PE and the PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) contended that the cost difference between Limerick Two and other alternatives were insignificantly small and that once completed it would be economical and efficient for consumers.

headline: Senator files bill to raise speed limit in Pa. To 65
abstract: Article outlines several bills introduced into the state legislature including: a bill to increase the speed limit to 65, a bill requiring doctors to report to police patients who came in due to reactions for overdoses from illegal drugs, an auctioneer recovery fund, specialized hearing-impaired smoke detectors for hotels, and a bill to create a system for reporting individuals with serious burns.

headline: Bailey says he and Casey leading foes 2-1
abstract: PA Auditor General Don Bailey stated that his own polls show that the Democratic Party's ticket is leading 2-to-1 throughout the state.  At a Democratic County Committee fundraiser, support for Bailey and Casey was so fierce that Allegheny County Commissioner Tom Foerster could not be heard. There is a potential typo in the article, as it states that the Democratic State Committee endorsed Bailey for governor and Robert P. Casey for US Senate. Casey is actually running for governor, and Bailey is running for US Senate.

headline: Mortgage Note
abstract: Former Cumberland County Democratic Chairman Willis Kocher distorts the record when he says that Bill Feuchtenberger left the party in debt. The figure is the result of the mortgage on Democratic headquarters. Kocher had no desire to become a trustee on the building when he discovered he'd have to sign a note to do it.

headline: Bottom line is the vital point
abstract: The Allentown County Administration has paid two lawyers a sum of $40,000 in tax monies to pool expertise in liability insurance costs by local municipal governments. The Morning Call says it looks like an act of patronage. On one hand is the concern over the possibility that the county administration was involved in patronage peddling; on the other hand, however, one must wonder about the timing of the attack.

headline: Ex-state official attacks letter alleging he's gay
abstract: Robert P. Kane, the former Pennsylvania Attorney General and Secretary of Revenue, held a press conference yesterday and asked federal and state officials to help him discover who circulated a letter saying that he and his son, Timothy Kane, organized a gay lawyers' referral service.  Robert Kane says the letter, which alleges his homosexuality, was neither drafted nor signed by him, and that the substance of the letter is patently false; neither he nor his son are homosexuals.

headline: State recovers duplicated checks worth $200,000 in welfare aid
abstract: The PA State Treasury Department has recovered more than $200,000 in duplicate welfare payments, including more than $29,000 from five counties in the Pittsburgh region.  The collections were made as part of the PA's Act 75, which authorizes the Treasury Department's Bureau of Investigations to collect restitution from welfare recipients who received duplicate checks.

headline: South Africans Divided in Reaction to Senate Vote
abstract: South Africans offered different opinions about the imposition of economic sanctions on the nation by the United States government.  Many black South Africans praised the legislation and feel that it will help their fight against apartheid.  White South Africans said the legislation would only deepen divisions and promote apartheid.

headline: Radiation deaths to grow
abstract: American and Soviet doctors trying to save victims of the the Chernobyl accident said that more deaths are inevitable and the human cost of the accident will not be known for years to come.  The official death toll so far is nine, with 299 hospitalized victims with various degrees of radiation exposure, though that number could increase.

headline: Senators revive a bill on judicial discipline
abstract: PA Senators who support a proposed constitutional amendment that would change the way state court judges are disciplined, have decided to try passing the bill again. The PA Senate Judiciary Committee voted unanimously on Senate Bill Number 1, a measure that would effectively remove much of the power state court judges now enjoy over their own disciplinary procedures and in deciding how to spend state money.

headline: Ban on cross-filing goes to Thornburgh
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh must decide whether to sign or veto a proposed end to ballot cross-filing by candidates for statewide judicial offices.

headline: Municipal officials seek state help, tax reforms
abstract: U.S. President Ronald Reagan's administration is ending the federal government's traditional partnership with local government requiring PA to step in with tax reform and other measures to help fill the breech. The proposed elimination of general revenue sharing and cuts in community service and development grants may be difficult for local PA governments.

headline: City of Chester swears in its first black mayor
abstract: The city of Chester, PA has sworn in its first black mayor in 362 years.  Councilwoman Willie Mae James Leake was appointed to mayor by her fellow council members to complete the unexpired term of Mayor Joseph F. Battle, who was being sworn in simultaneously as the new sheriff of Delaware County, PA.

headline: Good news expected on par proposal
abstract: At a press conference today, state officials from the Department of Environmental Resources (DEP) are expected to announce good news regarding the proposed Swarta State Park.  The DEP is expected to announce the feasibility of the project, as well as what measures, if any, can be taken to reduce the high levels of acidity in the waters of Swarta Creek.

headline: The Forum Benefits should be fair for all
abstract: Letters were written to the Patriot News showing disgust for taxes levied on senior citizens who make more then $25,000. David J. Leach of Lemoyne writes to the Patriot News saying he has nothing against senior citizens but states that if someone makes over $25,000, then they should not complain since there are people who suffer making a lot less money. Leach says there should be more legislative action for poor people not just the elderly.

headline: The Savvy Reader
abstract: Some people are questioning the idea of putting a black sculpture garden in Fairmont Park, which is owned by all the people of Philadelphia.  The garden would be called the African American Hall of Fame and Sculpture Garden.  It would cost about $ 23 million to build and the money would be raised by the American Foundation of Negro Affairs.

headline: Radon: New household worry was detected by alarms
abstract: Stanley Watras, a nuclear power plant worker, kept setting off radiation alarms where he worked.  His managers sent a team of health specialists to Watras's home where they found levels of radon gas equal to those found in uranium mines. The U.S. Environment Protection Agency has created guidelines for citizens on radon.

headline: Serious Crime Increases
abstract: Although state statistics indicated that crime had decreased in PA last year, early data from this year shows that crime, particularly serious crime, is increasing. The number of prostitution arrests have jumped along with reports of thefts, burglaries, and vandalism.

headline: Beloff: Not Over Till It's Over
abstract: Although Philadelphia City Councilman Leland M. Beloff acts as if nothing has changed since his federal complaint was withdrawn, nothing could be further from the truth. Not only did the federal prosecutor acknowledge moving prematurely in order to ensure the Penn's Landing project was fairly evaluated, but the fact that detailed evidence links Beloff, his aide, and an organized crime figure with extortion is not something that can be easily dismissed; especially as the council continues to recover from the effects of Abscam six years ago. While Philadelphians seem to have a high tolerance for the outside activities of its councilmen, every seat is up for election next year and if the City Council does not clean up its act, voters will have a chance to do it for them.

headline: Municipals left out of bond rally
abstract: When the state of PA sold $100 million worth of bonds last week, it got the best deal any state has received since the beginning of the decade. The issue was sold at interest rates that were more than 1.5 percentage points below those demanded by the market for the state's last bond issue, in May 1985.

headline: Flaherty ready to repay Norton
abstract: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania city Controller Thomas Flaherty said he is now willing to pay former Pittsburgh public safety director John Norton only about $4 less than he asked for last year to reimburse him for job-hunting expenses in 1985.  This dispute over Norton's expenses led to charges that he double-billed the city for the same expenses.

headline: AFNA leader says program still strong
abstract: In response to reports that the city of Philadelphia is freezing 100,000 in job-training funds from the American Foundation for Negro Affairs (AFNA), some 700 students, alumni and friends attended a rally at Tindley Temple United Methodist Church.  The funds are being withheld pending an investigation by the U.S. Labor Department.  Amid rumors that the AFNA is dissolving, the group's chairman, Samuel Evans, said that the Labor Department's investigation is politically motivated and represents an attempt to destroy the AFNA's credibility.

headline: Upstate senior centers asked to help pay their rent, bills
abstract: Faced with the loss of $25,000 in federal funding for the fiscal year beginning July 1, the Snyder Area Agency on Aging has asked members of six senior centers to help make up the shortfall.

headline: Vacancy on Supreme Court awaited: Abortion foes see victor a vote away
abstract: The US Supreme Court’s recent ruling in Thornburgh v. American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists upheld Roe v. Wade. The 5-4 decision, however, gives abortion opponents hope that a vacancy on the court could shift the balance in their favor.  In recent years the anti-abortion movement has failed to gather the support for a constitutional amendment to ban abortion, but has used the abortion issue to defeat political candidates as well as tie up many issues in Congress.

headline: Rate hike opposed
abstract: In this Letter to the editor, the author opposes the PA Public Utility Commission action granting a $439,422 annual rate increase ot the Dauphin Consolidated Water Supply Company.  The author believes this is inconceivable  in view of the PUC's own recommendation that the company be ordered to reduce its rates by $200,000 a year.  The author, a member of Paxtang Borough Council, says he has received numerous complaints regarding the inadequate service furnished by Dauphin Consolidated.  The author ends by attacking PUC Chairman Linda Tailaferro, who said that Dauphin Consolidated is doing a good job.  The author suggests she drink some of the water that Dauphin Consolidated provides.

headline: Sodomy Decision Doesn't Affect Pa.
abstract: Yesterday's US Supreme Court decision upholding a Georgia law prohibiting deviant sexual acts will have no impact on the state due to the fact that the PA Supreme Court struck down a similar law based on the PA Constitution six years ago. University of Pittsburgh law professor John M. Burkoff notes that state constitutions can give more rights to citizens than the U.S. constitution does. The PA decision was based on the arrest of a group of individuals seven years ago for performing sex acts at a local adult theater. The arrests were challenged and a Common Pleas Court judge agreed. The PA Supreme Court agreed, with Justice John P. Flaherty arguing that police enforcement should not extend to the private acts of consenting adults and that an inconsistent distinction was created between acts which were legal if done by a married couple but illegal if done by an unmarried couple. Justice Rolf Larsen joined in the decision but explained that all public sex acts should be illegal. Robert N.C. Nix Jr., now chief justice, dissented, stating that it was not a private intimate act between consenting adults but sexual acts done in exchange for money.

headline: Big Firms Benefited From Specter Tax Vote, Edgar Says
abstract: Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, Bob Edgar, blasted his opponent, incumbent Arlen Specter, for "giving away the store" on a tax bill he voted for five years which enabled numerous companies to avoid paying any taxes or receive a refund. A dozen of those companies, according to Edgar, have now contributed to Specter's campaign. Edgar contrasted this with his pledge to make sure that corporations pay their fair share. Specter's press secretary, Dan McKenna, observed that it was those tax cuts which helped to stimulate the economy and that Edgar represents the party which brought high inflation and unemployment.

headline: New Cumberland's Murray to seek post
abstract: John R. Murray, New Cumberland Borough Council President, has announced his candidacy for the 88th district PA State House of Representative seat now held by John Kennedy. A primary election is expected.

headline: Letters to the Editor: Thornburgh Surplus Eyed Hungrily by Mismanaged Phila.
abstract: This author believes that the assertion of the Philadelphia Daily News that the budget surplus in Pennsylvania should be given to help Philadelphia with its financial woes will be misused and Philadelphia needs good management, not handouts.

headline: Let Project VOTE do its job
abstract: The Thornburgh administration has prevented Project VOTE from registering people to vote in public buildings--even going as far as having Project VOTE workers arrested for declining to cease their registration efforts at the State Bureau of Employment Security.  While we do not know the motivations of the Thornburgh administration in this case, we are hopeful that he changes his mind on registration policy.

headline: Welfare needed
abstract: Ruth Mimms of Philadelphia wrote a letter to the Philadelphia Inquirer stating that she is living through the welfare crisis of a one-parent household.  Mimms says welfare is not the answer but it reaches out to those who have lost their way in education, wisdom, and understanding. Mimms wants other readers to know that everyone on welfare is not a bum, but a human being who has gone wrong in life and needs help.

headline: Why GOP blacks face test
abstract: In this opinion piece, the writer analyzes the impact that former Democrat-turned-Republican, and current Michigan gubernatorial candidate, William Lucas will have on African American voters and their lack of support for the Republican Party.  He dismisses the claim that his candidacy could alleviate past alienation between the black community and the GOP.  The author examines a variety of reasons while African Americans overwhelmingly support Democrats, including: misperceptions that blacks will always vote for black candidates, and perceptions that the Republican Party does not support minority interests.  He concludes that American politics is not color blind.

headline: REMEMBER CHERNOBYL
abstract: A cartoon that depicts two men in a nuclear plant with a sign on the wall that says "remember chernobyl".  One man says to the other, "I think it means if we have an accident don't say anything for three days".

headline: Sportsmen Lend Support To State Firearm Bills
abstract: A hearing of the PA House Judiciary Committee heard testimony on a wide range of proposed firarms laws. The most controversial involved making shooting ranges immune to prosecution for noise violations if they meet the restrictions that were in place at the time the facilities were built. PA Representative Terrence McVerry charged that it would allow ranges to fire cannons twenty-four hours a day because there were few noise ordinances in place when they were built. Alan S. Krug, spokesman for the for the PA Sportsmen's Coalition, said his group wanted to be good neighbors and would not oppose reasonable restrictions.  Other items included changing the definition of shotgun by reducing barrel length to eighteen inches, standardizing the gun license application and only allowing the county sherrif to issue them, and preventing addicts and the mentally disabled from owning firearms.

headline: Big Question from the Scranton Fissure-Why is Casey-Singel?
abstract: Some polling has shown that people are not very familiar with the names of candidates running for public offices.

headline: Newly registered voters urged to go to polls
abstract: In Pennsylvania, members of the Black Political Empowerment Project are urging the nearly 6,000 recently registered black voters to show up at the polls today.  They are providing transportation to and from polling places for senior citizens all day.

headline: Mayor vetoes wrong electrical-codes measure
abstract: Mayor Stephen R. Reed vetoed the wrong bill regarding changing the city's electrical code.  The city council realized that they had sent Reed the wrong version of the bill and not the final one that had been passed by the council.  Officials are currently looking into the law to determine how to correct the mistake and send the correct version of the bill to the mayor's desk.

headline: Gentlemen, start your advertising: They have, and some of it stings
abstract: U.S. Representative Bob Edgar, Senator Arlen Specter's Democratic challenger, has launched a series of negative campaign ads.  Specter claims the ads are a misrepresentation and distortion of his record.

headline: Welfare Reform - Governors Seek Preventive Approach
abstract: The National Governor's Association has acknowledged that the best way to reform welfare is to prevent people from needing it. Welfare creates a cycle of dependency and an underclass that lacks education and spirit. To achieve these goals the task force will review ways to get people into good jobs and increase the role of families. While resolving any one aspect of these two goals is a task unto itself, resolving all of them is nothing less than resolving poverty itself. But this is a task that needs doing not only because it is right but because it is the only way that our society can be called civilized.

headline: Why Single Out South Africa?
abstract: While bills in the PA House and Philadelphia City Council prohibiting both chambers from depositing money in banks doing business with South Africa are commendable, such policies need to be applied to other regimes or else it becomes hypocritical. For instance, countries such as Saudi Arabia, Liberia, and Angola have human rights records that are equally as bad, yet receive large amounts of U.S. aid. To continue giving aid to these and similar regimes makes a mockery of the effort the PA House and Philadelphia City Council are trying to make.

headline: Rickover
abstract: An editorial by the paper asserted that the late Admiral Hyman G. Rickover both approved and abhorred nuclear power. When he was on the verge of senility, General Public Utilities paid Rickoverfor comments urging the restart of the company's Unit I reactor at Three Mile Island. However, his opinion on the subject  also was noteworthy for his disappointment and fear about nuclear power.

headline: State House overrides drinking-bill veto
abstract: In Pennsylvania, tough penalities for underage drinking and a new hurdle for abortion clinics passed the PA House a second time, after PA Governor Dick Thornburgh had vetoed it, but now faces Senate opposition, funding cuts and a possible court challenge.  This bill calls for a 90-day driver's license suspension for the first conviction of underage drinking and public hearings before abortion clinics can be built, moved or expanded.

headline: Big winner: Kukovich takes 45 of 46 precincts in 56th Legislative District battle
abstract: In Pennsylvania's Westmoreland County's Democratic primary, PA Representative Allen Kukovich won in all but one of 46 precincts, with opponent John Abraham winning in only his home precinct.  In the November general election, Kukovich will run against Republican Leonard Santimyer.

headline: News articles trigger Edgar-Bailey fight
abstract: A series of stories in a western PA newspaper are triggering the latest battle between Democratic US Senate hopefuls Don Bailey and Robert Edgar.  The series of articles say that Auditor General Bailey has been sitting on a state prison audit for 10 months which has a daughter of an associate on it.  Bailey says the reports are incorrect and potentially libelous, while Edgar asked voters in a press conference if Bailey "is really our kind of Democrat."

headline: Panel gives plan to end school tax uniformity the cold shoulder
abstract: A proposal to change the PA State Constitution to permit school districts to tax residential and commercial properties at different rates has  not been well received by a PA House committee. The proposal by Representative Fred Trello would end the tax uniformity clause for school purposes, and allow districts to replace the residential with another form of taxation.

headline: Specter blamed in slow cleanup
abstract: The Clean Water Action Project, a Washington-based environmental organization, claims that U.S. Senator Arlen Specter should be blamed for a slowdown in Pennsylvania's Superfund-cleanup program.  Senator Specter voted against a bill that would have reauthorized Superfund-site cleanups.

headline: $2 billion state revitalization plan unveiled by Casey
abstract: Democrat gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey unveiled a $2 billion revitalization plan for Pennsylvania that he says will slow job loss, keep plants open, and keep the state's youth from leaving the state for education.  The candidate is pushing this 50-point plan in an 18 city tour throughout the state.

headline: Women's 'Rights,' 'Wrongs'
abstract: In this opinion piece, the author condemns the recent decision by the US Supreme Court in Thornburgh v. American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and is outraged by Planned Parenthood of PA Executive Director Morgan Plant’s praise on the ruling. To the writer, the US Supreme Court's decision to let stand the Roe v. Wade decision was inexcusable.  The courts and legislatures need to listen to the millions of Americans who want to end legalized abortion.

headline: Rickover Foundation Got TMI Study Funds
abstract: General Public Utilities Corporation (GPU) contributed three hundred eighty thousand dollars to a foundation established by the late Admiral Hyman G. Rickover in return for a report, prepared by him, declaring that Unit 1 at GPU's Three Mile Island plant should be restarted. The report, issued three years ago, was the centerpriece of GPU's successful effort to get the unit restarted. GPU's Chairman William G. Kuhns requested the report and Rickover suggested money be donated to the Rickover Foundation. GPU gave twenty-five thousand dollars a month from September 1983 until March 1985.

headline: State Police Biased In Discipline Action?
abstract: Statistics reviewed by a PA House committee investigating problems in the PA State Police showed that a larger percentage of minority troopers were disciplined than white troopers. Numbers for 1980 showed that almost 12% of minority troopers had disciplinary action taken against them as compared to almost 3% of white troopers. Numbers for the years 1980 to 1985 showed similar percentages. Deputy State Police Commissioner Richard Weatherbee argued that the figures were misleading because some troopers were disciplined multiple times. A. Roy DeCaro, the committee's lawyer, responded that such numbers would have a minimal impact on the final percentages and that some white troopers had also been disciplined multiple times. The committee also reviewed cases where troopers were stopped for drunk driving but only given a minimal punishment.

headline: Bill Requiring Union Dues Vetoed By Governor
abstract: As expected, PA Governor Dick Thornburgh vetoed an "agency shop" measure requiring non-union members to pay fees based on union dues minus costs for unrelated collective bargaining activities; failure to pay the fees would cost the employee their job. Thornburgh claimed the fee violated the worker's ability to choose whether or not to join a union while proponents noted that non-union members were party to the same collective bargaining agreement negotiated by the union and by not paying fees were acting as free riders. The veto is unlikely to be overturned given the time of year and the limited support for it in the PA Senate, however, unions insist that the measure be taken up again next year.

headline: No Crimes Found Yet In Granite Pact Probe
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman said at a press conference yesterday that there was no evidence of wrongdoing involving delays and cost overruns for the expansion of the state capitol. Zimmerman and federal prosecutors started looking into allegations of bribery after testimony by a contractor at a PA House committee hearing stating he had to give money to the owners of a stone company in order to get in on the project. While Democrat Nick Colafella, of the PA House, never believed Zimmerman was capable of running a serious investigation he also admits that his committee has yet to uncover evidence of criminal wrongdoing. Because businesses often deal with each other through fees and commissions, it is possible that the payment testified to could have been misrepresented as something improper.

headline: Pittsburgh blacks' paucity of political clout stirs struggle over the city's at-large electoral system
abstract: Pittsburgh is one of the last major cities with a large black population using an at-large election system, controversial because of its tendency to dilute political power from minorities.  Pittsburgh is currently the only major city with a large black population to not have a black on city council.

headline: State Senate rebuffs anti-apartheid issue
abstract: Senate Republicans in Pennsylvania rejected an attempt by Democrats to vote on anti-apartheid legislation.  Republicans have kept a House-passed divestment bill, which would ban state holdings in banks that lend money to South Africa, bottled up in committee for almost one year.  Senate Majority Leader John Stauffer said many GOP senators feel the issue of apartheid is a foreign policy concern best handled by the federal, not state, government.

headline: 3 STATES IN REGION SHOW JOB GROWTH
abstract: A new study of employment in the 1980s commissioned by the National Academy of Science and conducted at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill found that although the West and South are still leading the rest of the nation in job gains, some other industrial states (like Ohio and Pennsylvania) are moving far ahead of others in their regions.  California has the highest number of jobs gained, followed by New York, Florida, Ohio, Texas, Virginia and Pennsylvania.

headline: A Better Way To Beat Rabies
abstract: PA needs a better way to combat the rabies problem sweeping the state this summer. The author believes the proposal to have dog owners provide proof of their dog's rabies vaccination before getting a license is counterproductive. Responsible dog owners already vaccinate their animals, to expect them to pay for a certificate proving it before they can get a dog license only discourages from doing both. Moreover, there are large numbers of unlicensed dogs in the state, not only does the bill not address that issue, it also fails to address the real problem, rabid wildlife. A better idea is allowing the PA Department of Health to establish risk areas where all dog and cat owners must show proof of rabies vaccination upon request. The PA Game Commission also needs funding to establish a multiyear wildlife vaccine research program. Rather than forcing legitimate owners to get another piece of paper, the state should focus on the latter, which will go much further towards stopping the rabies problem.

headline: Rickover Report: GPU Paid $385,000 For Admiral's TMI Restart Recommendation
abstract: The late Admiral Hyman G. Rickover, founder of the "nuclear Navy," was nearing senility when he was approached three years ago by General Public Utilities Corporation (GPU) to prepare a report recommending that Unit I at itsThree Mile Island (TMI) plant be restarted. GPU paid twenty-five thousand dollars a month into the Hyman G. Rickover Foundation (now the Center for Excellence in Education) between 1983 and 1985. The report was cited by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) in its restart decision last year. GPU Chairman William G. Kuhns decided to approach Rickover and it was Rickover who suggested money be donated to the foundation. Because Rickover's senility was known by many, opponents of the TMI restart have demanded that the NRC rescind its decision and a thorough investigation be conducted. The NRC contends that the report was one piece among a large pile of data leading to their decision while PA Governor Dick Thornborgh insisted that Rickover's report had no influence on his office.

headline: State police probers ask more funds
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Rules Committee approved spending $150,000 in additional state money to fuel a special legislative committee's investigation of the state police.  The investigation is concentrating on allegations of drug violations and other crimes, racial discrimination, sexual harrassment and uneven disciplinary measures.

headline: Bill Scranton's Initiative
abstract: This article supports William W Scranton III for PA governor and focuses on his idea to try and start an initiative and referendum program for Pennsylvania.  The program would allow voters to bypass the PA General Assembly and get bills placed on the ballot after getting a specified number of signatures.

headline: No heroes
abstract: A letter discusses the MOVE disaster in Philadelphia where officials burned down a cult household and with it, a neighborhood. The author believes all parties involved have much to be ashamed about - the city officials, the MOVE members, and even the neighbors.

headline: Region Still Has Outgo Of People
abstract: According to the U.S. Department of Commerce, the Pittsburgh metropolitan area continues to lose population. Since nineteen eighty, the area's population has dropped by three and half percent. Such continued losses will result in less money from federal government allocations and revenue sharing programs. The area is also likely to lose a congressional seat after the 1990 census when district lines are redrawn. Beaver County suffered an even steeper loss, almost five percent, and because it is now under two hundred thousand people is no longer eligible for federal block grants.

headline: House approves magic act budget
abstract: Because of the Gramm-Rudman deficit-reduction law, the U.S. House yesterday approved a budget that relies on accounting tricks, asset sales and user fees.  Representatives admitted to using "every somke-and-mirror tactic available," and that the budget does not solve the real structural problems of the deficit.  The Reagan administration has warned that policy changes in the budget bill, such as defense spending cuts, could lead to a presidential veto.

headline: Airport Terminal Backed
abstract: Governor Thornburgh announced yesterday that he supported money allocated in the capital budget for a new terminal at the airport, a new Buhl Center of Science and Technology, and a high-technology center that Carnegie Mellon University wants to build. The governor noted that all three still required additional local money before the projects could proceed. However, Mayor Caliguiri and County Commissioner Foerster praised the announcement. The money became available after the legislature created a fund supported by real estate tax money which will act as a back-up that will allow the state to borrow almost three hundred million dollars for capital improvements.

headline: A Blossoming Legacy Of Princess Grace
abstract: Shortly before her death four years ago, Philadelphia’s Princess Grace, nee Kelly, was nearly complete in establishing a foundation in her name to provide grants to the performing arts. Starting with donations as small as five dollars and two lavish galas, the foundation has been able to provide $400,000 in grants to students and artists at crucial points in their careers, as well as to other schools and foundations that target specific artists for support. The foundation is due to have a third gala next month and it is hoped that it will be able to give out a million dollars a year once a significant endowment is established.

headline: Senate makes disputed changes to PUC bill
abstract: The PA Senate made a number of amendments to a bill preserving the life of the PA Public Utilities Commission. PA Senator Clarence Bell and the PA Public Interest Coalition deemed the change to one particular amendment, which would have limited the costs that utilities could charge to consumers for new generating facilities, as anti-consumer. Supporters of the amendment contend that it is needed to allow utilities to gain returns on their investments.

headline: State police reinvestigate sex-harrassment complaint
abstract: A two-year old case involving a sexual-harrassment charge against a senior Pennsylvania state police official was recently reopened by state police, shortly after a special Pennsylvania House committee asked for records of the case.  One likely effect of the renewed investigation would be to preclude a separate inquiry by the House committee, which has said it will not take up cases in which there are ongoing internal investigations.

headline: Bitter Blasts For Ron's South Africa Speech
abstract: US President Ronald Reagan outlined in a speech yesterday a number of steps the South African government should take to end apartheid but once again refused to call for economic sanctions. Members of US Congress from both parties commented that regardless of the speech, sanctions were almost certain to pass. Bishop Desmond Tutu blasted the speech, declaring that the West could "go to hell," and another anti-apartheid clergyman commented that as long as Reagan backed South Africa the regime would never negotiate with black activists.

headline: No law school for legislators
abstract: Writer opposes use of taxpayer funds to pay for state legislators to obtain their law degree.  Although she recognizes the importance of lawmakers to understand the law, she does not feel the taxpayers should fund it.

headline: Rizzo Lets His Goode Side Show
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo, speaking to the men's club of a Jewish congregation in Northeast Philadelphia, blasted current Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode for the MOVE disaster, and dropped references to the upcoming mayoral campaign.  Rizzo, however, stopped short of officially declaring his candidacy.  Rizzo did note that the city was mired in chaos, and lauded his leadership when he was Philadelphia's mayor from 1972-1980.  Rizzo gave a detailed account of his opinion of Goode's handling of the MOVE disaster.

headline: Hospitals would face task of organ donation queries
abstract: A bill that would require hospitals to set up procedures for approaching families about the donation of dead relatives' organs passed unanimously in both the state House and Senate.  The bill now goes to Governor Dick Thornburgh.  The bill is designed to increase organ donations.

headline: Audit Finds More Funds To ICON
abstract: The Inner City Organizing Network (ICON) got over eight hundred thousand dollars from the city over a two and a half year period. ICON, and its president, Charles L. "Boo" Burrus are under criminal investigation due to alleged mismanagement of the money, including payments made to members of MOVE before their confrontation with the city last year. The program was established to help low-income families rehabilitate abandoned homes, but Burrus was one of the most vocal critics of the housing program he was now receiving money from. How the city handled the contracts also raises questions as Burrus admitted he had no experience managing a housing program and that he needed accounting help. While not directly related, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) has prohibited the city from giving federal block grant money to nonprofit groups until fiscal controls are implemented and U.S. Senator John Heinz has said he wants the city to give a thorough accounting to HUD.

headline: Among black people, AIDS is taking a heavier toll
abstract: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) has stricken more than 17,800 Americans. Figures show that the African American community in the US has been stricken with the disease at a higher proportion then the national rate at large.

headline: Soviet attitude on disaster chills area émigrés trying to reach kin
abstract: Russian immigrants in Harrisburg, numbering in the thousands of families, anxiously try to reach family and friends near Kiev, where the disaster at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant recently occurred.

headline: State police study panel to get funds
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Rules Committee approved spending $150,000 in additional state money to fuel a special legislative committee's investigation of the state police.  The investigation is concentrating on allegations of drug violations and other crimes, racial discrimination, sexual harrassment and uneven disciplinary measures.

headline: Blacks may comprise a third of city voters
abstract: Registered black voters in Pittsburgh number between 55,000 and 60,000 or about 25 percent higher than the official figure, which means that blacks account for nearly 30% of the Democratic total and 25% of all voters in Pittsburgh.

headline: No Mention of GOP
abstract: John T. Martino, the Republican County Chairman, writes to express his dismay to see the Intelligencer headline "Why is the GOP against the people." Martino says that nowhere in the letter is the word Republican or GOP mentioned by the author. Martino states that the Intelligencer Journal needs to keep political bias in the editorial section and not in letters written to the newspaper.

headline: Senate Oks Commuter Wage Tax Cut
abstract: The Pennsylvania Republican-controlled State Senate voted to amend the wage tax cut bill already passed by the state House that would slash the wage tax paid Philadelphia by suburban commuters by about 20%, setting the stage for a final vote on the bill today.  The cut in wage tax rates would cost the City of Philadelphia $68 million in 1991, the first full year of the reduction.

headline: Veto this abortion bill
abstract: Governor Thornburgh should veto the latest back-door anti-abortion bill that passed the state Legislature this week.  The latest bill, which was tacked on an underage drinking bill, requires abortion clinics to obtain certificates of need from health planning agencies, and represents an attempt to restrict further the rights of women and doctors in Pennsylvania.

headline: Mercantile tax on beer distributors barred
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has ruled that PA cities cannot impose a mercantile business tax on beer distributors.  The court said that the state already controls beer distributors through fees, regulations, and taxes, and that cities cannot do likewise.  The case involved an appeal by Wilsbach Distributors Incorportated against lower court rulings that it had to pay over $1,500 a year in business privilege mercantile taxes to the city of Harrisburg.  Pittsburgh's finance director, Ronald Schmeiser, said the city has not collected such a tax from beer distributors since the case went to court several years ago.

headline: Another side of medical liability
abstract: Carol Shepherd writes to the Philadelphia Inquirer that malpractice fees are not that high.  Shepherd says requiring physicians in less risky fields of medicine to help underwrite the costs of insuring their colleagues in higher-risk specialty areas will not solve the existing crisis and is totally unacceptable.  The present crisis in malpractice costs is largely due to trial lawyers and runaway tort claims in the court system.

headline: Soviet media offers little data on accident; Kiev effectively put off limits
abstract: The Soviet media agency Tass issued a brief report on the nuclear accident at Chernobyl, offering very little details on the event. They neglected to mentioned that Chernobyl is only 60 miles away from Kiev, the capital city of the Ukraine and home to 2.4 million people. Foreign correspondents in Moscow were told that Kiev was off limits, and that they must write letters to the government if they wish to go to Kiev.

headline: State police team to handle terrorist, hostage situations
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Police has formed a new SWAT-type team designed to handle high-risk situations involving hostages or terrorist groups.  The first Special Emergency Response Team, which will cover eastern Pennsylvania including Harrisburg, completed training last month.

headline: Blocked in state Senate, Purdy is likely to run for judgeship
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh was unable to convince PA Senate Democrats to come up with the minimum seven additional votes with 27 Republicans needed to confirm appointees to the PA Commonwealth Court.  Carroll Purdy said he is about 90% sure he will place his name before voters in 1987 for PA Commonwealth Court as judge after failing to receive support from state Senate Democrats.

headline: NO TITLE
abstract: The last time a democratic candidate won a Pennsylvania seat in the U.S. Senate was Joe Clark's victory in 1962.  Democratic candidate Bob Edgar hopes to defeat that streak, though Republican incumbent Arlen Specter is leading by at least a dozen points in the polls.

headline: State mayor to take oath in California
abstract: Lanesboro Mayor Taylor Swoop is expected to be sworn into office in California.  The swearing-in ceremony for Taylor Swoop will be held at Santee City Hall California, allowing him to continue his California vacation without disruption. The action is legal.

headline: Partial divestiture urged by governor on aprtheid
abstract: In order to send an unequivocal message of opposition to South African apartheid policies, Governor Thornburgh announced a proposal that would restrict state fund investments with businesses having connections to South Africa.  This partial divestiture was criticized by House Majority Leader James Manderino, who called the effort a "halway step" and much less extensive than legislation that has been under consideration for the last four years in the General Assembly.

headline: Minority fronts easily gain city certification
abstract: In contrast to many other regional and local government's, the certification process in Philadelphia as a minority or female-owned business is comparatively easy.  There is little oversight by the city, with city investigators saying they conduct on-site inspections in only about one of every 10 cases.

headline: Audit completed at Johnstown center
abstract: A Pennsylvania state vocational rehabilitation center, providing services to handicapped persons, amassed a huge deficit over the past seven years because of poor accounting and budgetary procedures, according to a recent audit.  The PA Department of Labor and Industry operates the Johnstown center through its Office of Vocational Rehabilitation.

headline: Soviets admit to delay in pullout
abstract: Soviet officials said that the Chernobyl disaster was probably caused by a chemical explosion and that evacuation was delayed 36 hours because the plant staff did not realize how serious the accident was.  Western officials have criticized the Soviets for failing to provide timely and sufficient information about the disaster to the rest of the world.

headline: State Senate panel approves underage drinking bill
abstract: A PA State Senate committee voted 8-1 in favor of a bill that would change the penalties for underage drinking. The Law and Justice Committee amended the original PA House of Representative bill to drop the maximum penalty for a first offense from a third-degree misdemeanor carrying a $500 fine to a summary offense with no fine.  The measure goes to the floor for full PA Senate consideration.

headline: Bob Edgar: He will make a superb Senator
abstract: Article endorses Bob Edgar for US Senate.  It refutes charges by incumbent Republican Arlen Specter that Edgar is a fringe liberal.  Goes through various accusations and provides evidence to the contrary about Edgar's stance on the issues.

headline: NRA Defeated Edgar
abstract: This author believes that in Pennsylvania U.S. Senator Arlen Specter won re-election because most of the National Rifle Association voted for him rather than for opponent, and anti-gun advocate, Bob Edgar.

headline: Sunshine violation
abstract: Phyllis T. Kernick of Penn Hills states that PA's "sunshine" open-meeting law requires amendment. When she was the mayor of Penn Hills, 3 council members held meetings prior to regular council meetings but denied that any decisions were made at these meetings. She insists that the PA House adopts Senate Bill 303 to protect the public's right to know.

headline: Hazardous litter
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is planning to remove illegally posted political signs--regardless of their party affiliation--from state roads.  Department of Transportation officials say the signs are a saftey hazzard--creating a visual distraction--and pose a litter problem.

headline: Mr. G's gets once-over by visitor
abstract: Michael Sullivan visited Mr. G’s topless bar to inspect the atmosphere. He found it fairly peaceful and fairly profitable for a small local tavern.

headline: Beaver County Urged To Shut Boarding Home
abstract: PA Attorney General Leroy Zimmerman has asked a Beaver County court to immediately close a personal care boarding home to avoid further risk to patient safety. The facility was ordered to close last year because it had no license, but the owner Sylvia Hastings, appealed the decision. Zimmerman now wants to close it because of a series of incidents of neglect which led to the deaths of two patients, the amputation of another's limb, and two with untreated broken hips.

headline: Soviets cite gain at plant - Say main danger over at Chernobyl
abstract: Top Soviet officials supervising the Chernobyl cleanup said that they had reached a turning point in their endeavors and said a nuclear meltdown was no longer possible.  The emphasis has now shifted to sealing off the destroyed reactor, decontaminating the surrounding areas, and getting the three remaining reactors into a condition to resume generating electricity.

headline: State's Fire Crews Head West
abstract: Forty specially trained PA firefighters left Harrisburg today with firefighters from other Northeastern states to travel West and help fight forest fires started by lightning strikes last week. After landing in Boise, Idaho the firefighters will be sent to various states to help control the blazes.

headline: Bolus put on 10th District ballot
abstract: Robert Bolus was placed on the Democratic primary ballot for the race for PA's 10th Congressional District. Lackawanna County officials were notified after Bolus was approved by Commonwealth Court President Judge James Crumlish. The PA Bureau of Elections had initially prevented Bolus from running due to a discrepancy in the number of valid signatures needed to be placed on the ballot.

headline: NRA to gun for Edgar, plug Spector in commercials
abstract: The National Rifle Association (NRA) is running radio ads throughout Pennsylvania in support of Senator Arlen Spector.  The NRA opposes Democratic candidate Bob Edgar due to his support of handgun control legislation.  Because Spector is not working directly with the NRA on their support campaign, the group is not subject to campaign contribution limits and thus can spend as much as they want on advertisements.

headline: Tax break for new buildings is pushed
abstract: A bill that would allow school districts, municipalities, and counties to give property tax exemptions for up to two years to new residential construction was approved by the PA House Finance Committee.  The bill was sent to the PA House of Representatives for consideration.

headline: Group blasts funding cuts
abstract: According to the National Association of State Alcohol and Drug Abuse, federal funding for state drug treatment programs has dropped 46 percent under the Reagan administration, and President Reagan's proposed new funding will not come close to restoring the money already cut.

headline: New law limits liability of Pa. corporate boards
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a bill yesterday that allows shareholders to amend corporate bylaws to limit the liability of individual members of a board of directors, which should make Pennsylvania an even more attractive home to business, and bring more jobs to our state.

headline: Beware the welfare version of HMO
abstract: In a  letter written to the Philadelphia Inquirer,  PA Representative Babette Josephs  warns that across Philadelphia people who do not have access to comprehensive health insurance plans are signing up for health insuring organizations, or HIOs. Babette says it is a poor person’s version of a HMO or health managing organization. Unfortunately, HIO’s often underinsure treatments for the state’s working poor.

headline: Soviets report 18 in serious condition after accident
abstract: According to Soviet officials, 18 victims of the Chernobyl nuclear accident are in serious condition, though radiation levels continue to drop.  The brief statement from the Soviet Council of Ministers was in keeping with their insistence that they main danger from the explosion had passed.

headline: 'Sue Me, Sue you'
abstract: The widow of a mass murderer is suing the McDonald's chain where he committed his crime as well as his workplace for contaminating him with chemicals that led to his rampage. While the lawsuit appears frivolous it highlights the doctrine in which juries award damages on the slimmest evidence simply because the defendant can probably pay. Yet, this does have a cost, the more insurance companies have to pay the more expensive insurance becomes and the more expensive things become for consumers. The PA legislature needs to bring these types of deep pockets lawsuits back down to Earth.

headline: Boosts Too Drastic
abstract: This editorial notes that the US Commission on Executive, Legislative, and Judicial Salaries has recommended whopping salary increases for 3,000 top US officials.  The main argument for the increases is that the cost of living in the US has risen 226% in the last 17 years.  The editorial does not object to some corrections but strenuously objects to the boosts the commission proposes.  The editorial also does not buy the claim that the federal system will not attract good people if salaries are not equal to those in private industry.  Government positions carry with them an aura that cannot be measured in money.  The editorial points to PA Governor-elect Robert Casey as an example.  The editorial concludes by noting that it would be unconscionable to grant raises on the scale the commission suggests.

headline: NRA urges its Penna. Members to vote for Bailey over Edgar
abstract: The National Rifle Association sent nearly 200,000 members throughout Pennsylvania a letter urging them to vote for state Auditor General Don Bailey over U.S. Representative Bob Edgar in the Democratic race for the U.S. Senate.

headline: Tax-reform alternatives offered
abstract: The Patriot News published an editorial about fair alternatives to the property tax. Thomas J. Gentzel writes that if the Patriot News is concerned with local tax reform, it should spend less time jumping on bandwagons and devote more effort to understanding and explaining this complex issue.

headline: Publicity's value argued
abstract: President Reagan has called on Americans to join a national crusade against illegal drugs.  In response to the president's message, state Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman argued for mandatory prison terms for anyone caught selling drugs in proximty to schools.

headline: One Source Of New Jobs
abstract: While it is easy to think of only large businesses, it is important to remember that small businesses represent half of all jobs and are responsible for eighty percent of all job creation. However, in order for small businesses to remain an important component of the economy more needs to be done to solve the federal budget deficit and the liability insurance crisis. It is also good to note that the state's banks are strong as an industry and are more than able to withstand the competition that newly approved interstate banking will bring.

headline: Beware the welfare version of HMO
abstract: In a letter to the Philadelphia Inquirer, Barbara Barren argues that health maintenance organizations, or HMO’s, are being used to contain the cost of costly healthcare treatments. The jury is still out on whether HMO’s are effective in maintaining costs and providing a sufficient level of care.

headline: Soviets say danger zone has shrunk
abstract: A top Soviet official said that 49,000 people were evacuated from areas around the Chernobyl disaster, and livestock within a 12 mile radius were destroyed.  The danger zone, an area around Chernobyl where exposure might prove fatal, has shrunk from an initial 18-mile radius to a 12-mile radius.

headline: Tax Power Proposed For Trash Collection
abstract: PA Representative Charles Nahill, at a PA House Finance Committee hearing yesterday, proposed a separate tax be implemented to help municipalities pay for trash collection. Trash collection and other services are draining local budgets forcing towns to eliminate police and fire protection and rely on the state instead. Nahill argues that the tax would help cover some of those municipal costs and allow them to resume police and fire service again.

headline: Breaking faith with the voter
abstract: The Morning Call says that the incumbents who wish to climb higher on the political ladder should resign in their current political office so that their contract with the voters is voided honorably. The Call says that to do otherwise is to hedge political bets on themselves at the expense of the voters.

headline: Odds and Ends
abstract: Article notes that the conviction of PA State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer surprised many who had been following the trial.  One surprise was that Dwyer himself never took the stand.  The author notes that this is probably the end of Dwyer's political career.  Both Dwyer and Robert Asher will make their appeals.  In the cases involved with the Computer Technology Associates scandal, the federal government has been very successful in winning convictions.

headline: Very bad bill
abstract: Robert Robinson writes that the Pittsburgh Post Gazette has demonstrated a biased opinion in it's writings regarding the issues of the Pittsburgh Port Authority. If PA House bill 1505 is passed in its current form, Robinson says it will have a devastating effect on the people of Allegheny County.

headline: Cost-cutting steps OK'd in state workers' fund
abstract: Governor Thornburgh and union officials agreed yesterday to cost-cutting provisions designed to prevent the bankruptcy of the Pennsylvania Public Employees Health and Welfare Fund. The fund handles the health and welfare program for 54,000 members of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees.

headline: Only two states left
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved a resolution that would maintain the state's current liquor monopoly, a clear rebuff to the governor and, for that matter, a number of newspapers around the state.  Pennsylvania and Utah are the only two states left in the United States that do not have private liquor sales.

headline: Bill aiding disabled to be signed
abstract: PA Governor Richard Thornburgh is expected to sign into law the Attendant Care Services Act, which provides attendants to individuals with physical disabilities so that they may perform everyday activities. The act will expand 10 existing programs to provide services in 41 counties in the state.  New programs will be set up to cover the state's remaining 26 counties.

headline: Soviets seeking help in handling 'hot molten mass'
abstract: Soviet officials have asked West German scientists for help in dealing with a hot molten mass that may have burned through the concrete floor of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, endangering the region's underground water supplies with radioactive contamination.

headline: The Death Penalty
abstract: The writer seeks to correct an article on the dealth penalty which cited the percentage of capital cases in Philadelphia County as fourteen point four percent. However, if the number of cases where the death penalty was overturned, and the number of times the state sought the death penalty but did not get it, the percentage is really eighty-four point four or eighty-six point four percent.

headline: Breaking The Rules In Pennsylvania
abstract: PA Democrats have developed a unique political tradition over the last 25 years. The state has voted more Democratic in presidential elections than any othe state, despite voting more Republican for state and local offices. This trend is the reverse of many of states. Republicans hope that this will change during the upcoming election, but it won't be easy. Republican candidates for governor, current Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton III, and U.S. Senate, incumbent Arlen Specter, exemplify moderate Republicans. Scranton argues in support of affirmative action and divestment from South Africa while Specter lauds his frequent votes in opposition to President Reagan. However, Democrats are fielding their strongest ticket in years. Gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey, well known in PA politics, plans, rather than highlighting Scranton's history of drug use and affiliation with Transcendental Meditation, will argue that Scranton frequently jumps from one job to another. Edgar has a different strategy built largely around the politics of causes, and he plans to go after Specter's "disputes" with Reagan by highlighting the numerous shifts in his votes on issues. While both Democratic candidates are being outspent, another trend the party has not been able to overcome, both intend to finish strong and their fundraising efforts have improved.

headline: Off-budget expenses
abstract: Pennsylvania House Democrats believe that they can improve on Governor Thornburgh's budge proposal, while still giving businesses and individuals a reduction in taxes.  They seek to provide employers with a subsidy for employees, believing that would spur job creation, as well as minimum wage level for teachers in the hopes of attracting new people to the profession.

headline: "WHY, WHEN I WAS A BOY WE WERE SO BAD OFF WE DIDN'T HAVE A SINGLE CELEBRITY INTERESTED IN OUR PLIGHT!"
abstract: Cartoon depicting a old man in a rocking chair with a child on his knee in a rural setting, with the caption, "Why, when I was a boy, we were so bad off we didn't have a single celebrity interested in our plight!"

headline: Whistles, songs, skits assail chief justice in Burger Roast
abstract: Outside of the building where Chief Justice Warren E. Burger gave a speech on the value of the U.S. Constitution, gay and lesbian demonstrators protested the Supreme Court's sodomy decision and demanded recognition of gay human rights.

headline: Options on liability insurance
abstract: The editorial board describes how everyone is at loss with high liability insurance rates, whether it’s citizens or businesses. Arthur J. Glatfelter will head the PA Civil Justice Coalition, a group which seeks to halt the rising costs of insurance rates. Some possibilities include "limiting the percentages of winnings an attorney can claim [and] limiting punitive damages."

headline: Bill Seeks $250,000 For Poison Center
abstract: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia could receive a quarter of a million dollars in state aid according to a bill pending in the PA House. Much of the money would go to the hospital's Poison Center, which by eliminating unnecessary hospital trips and reducing the length of hospital stays has provided significant cost savings. However, the center could close in the future because of financial constraints. The bill has been stuck in the PA House Appropriations Committee since May and still has yet to go to the PA Senate. And because it is a non-preferred appropriation, since Children's is a private hospital, a two-thirds majority is needed for passage. Further complicating matters is the fact that two other Children's hospitals in Philadelphia already receive this aid, raising some concern in PA over the lack of support for children’s hospitals in Pittsburgh.

headline: Soviets tll of Chernobyl heroes
abstract: The official Soviet news agency reported that three workers at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant dived voluntarily into a pool of radiation-contaminated water under the reactor to drain the water and prevent a steam explosion.  The report did not mention if the men suffered any ill effects.

headline: The mayor's message on MOVE: I'm sorry
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode apologized for the bombing of the MOVE house which killed six adults and five children. The mayor has not yet answered whether he will seek another term, but vows to work hard for the city until the time comes.

headline: Broker Testifies On Turnpike Deals
abstract: Testimony was heard yesterday in a hearing before a district judge who must decide if a bribery case against Arthur Delinko should go to trial. Delinko, Comptroller and Chief Financial Officer of the PA Turnpike Commission until last October, has been accused of accepting bribes from Florida stockbroker Alvin Dern. Delinko's daughter Frances worked for Dern, and in exchange for bribes, in the form of commissions to his daughter, Delinko agreed to give business, in the form of securities swaps, to Dern. Dern, who was given immunity for his testimony, argued that splitting commissions from the sales with Delinko's daughter was a common practice.

headline: Old campaigners
abstract: Four photographs in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, one of U.S. Senate Democratic candidate Bob Edgar, one of his opponent Republican Arlen Specter, and one each of Pennsylvania gubernatorial candidates Republican Bill Scranton and Democrat Bob Casey.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Drawing of the Statue of Liberty covered in merchandise, with the statue saying: "Give me your tired, your poor. . .give me a break!"

headline: Viewing Harrisburg
abstract: A group of Pennsylvania Common Pleas Court judges argues that a 1974 change in the state pension law improperly put a stop to benefits for new judges--benefits that had been granted to those already serving on the bench.  The judges' suit claims that it is illegal to discriminate between judges holding equivalent positions solely on the basis of their date of entry into service.  Critics of the suit say a win for the judges would be disastrous for the state pension fund and would cost taxpayers an exorbitant amount of money.

headline: Pa. Coalition Starts A Campaign For Insurance-Industry Reforms
abstract: Now that PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has signed a bill reforming the PA Public Utility Commission, the PA Public Interest Coalition (PennPIC), is targeting the insurance industry. The group says it will work to strengthen the PA Insurance Department's ability to regulate the industry, insist on disclosure of profit and loss statements, and establish a consumer advocate's office for insurance rate requests. The group also wants to lower costs by capping rate increases and allow more joint underwriting. The insurance industry's lobbying group, the PA Insurance Federation, says the proposals are not new and would only make the bureaucracy larger.

headline: Cancer study team: Balky TMI-area hospitals drive up cost
abstract: Due to delays by some hospitals, a study of cancer cases near Three Mile Island will nearly double in cost.  Some of the hospitals that agreed to the study have not released patient records due to confidentiality concerns.  The study seeks to determine if cancer rates were significantly affected by the accident at the nuclear plant.

headline: Specter to help with power plant
abstract: Alleghany County planning officials met with U.S. Senator Arlen Specter to urge him to expedite approval of a study to determine the feasibility of building a co-generation plant near the Greater Pittsburgh International airport.  The plant would be able to produce electricity and steam from coal and solid waste, and the study would be funded by the U.S. Department of Energy.  Specter believed there was a good chance for approval.

headline: The problems of coed prisons
abstract: In Pennsylvania at the Muncy prison, recent integration of men into a women's prison has brought problem, including stricter regulations and punishments for women who became pregnant.  However, the whole notion of co-corrections has worked in some ways, but only with  very conservative implementation.

headline: Buckman: Walgren soft on terrorism
abstract: US Congressional candidate Ernie Buckman has made a campaign commercial accusing Democratic incumbent Doug Walgren of being soft on terrorism.  Walgren's campaign manager responded by saying that Buckman is just resorting to desperate measures to gain votes.

headline: 'Old-time' politics in disfavor
abstract: This author discusses County chairmen,, Republican and Democrat, in Pennsylvania who are still looked to as the primary dispensers of political patronage.  Most citizens are turned off by this and those who still practice it will soon lose their offices.

headline: Cartoon: Didn't I tell you this would happen?
abstract: A cartoon of a wife talking to a football sitting in a recliner, insinuating that her husband has turned into a football due to all the football games he has watched.

headline: Black Ministers Line Up: Edgar, Yes; Specter, No
abstract: The Black Clergy of Philadelphia offered their endorsement of Bob Edgar for U.S. Senate.  They also expressed disapprobation for the voting record of incument Senator Arlen Specter, who voted with Jesse Helms and Strom Thurmond against a tough sanctions bill opposing apartheid in South Africa.

headline: Pa. Dept. Of Agric. Leaves Its Mark All Over The World
abstract: Because PA law requires bakers to be licensed if they want to sell their goods in the state, the PA Department of Agriculture has issued licenses to six thousand companies around the world. Rather than making a product for PA and a product for the rest of the world, foreign companies simply stamp that their goods are registered with the PA Department of Agriculture. The law originated over fifty years ago as more people began using regional bakeries and were unable to know what went into the product or the cleanliness of the facility. The law required that those facilities be inspected annually for cleanliness and the employees have medical exams. The state has established agreements with inspectors in foreign countries, but  the stamp must be included to sell those goods in PA.

headline: Chernobyl death toll hits 25
abstract: The nuclear disaster at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, (part of the Soviet Union) has claimed two more lives, bringing the death toll up to 25, with 18,000 people initially hospitalized after the accident.  Residents were hospitalized for up to three days but all were in perfect health.

headline: State oil industry's skids greased
abstract: Falling prices in the oil industry have boosted the stock market and saved consumers lots of money, but have hurt producers, such as Ray Stiglitz of Stiglitz's Allegheny Well Service Company.  According to the PA Department of Labor and Industry, less than 1% of the state's work force is employed in the oil industry, but the state supplies about 40% of canned or bottle motor oil. The low oil prices have made the biggest impact on drilling and exploration, according to the Independent Petroleum Association of America.

headline: The real special interest court reform would serve
abstract: PA Senate Bill 1, which calls for a constitutional amendment to change the makeup of the PA Judicial Inquiry and Review Board, the body that investigates complaints about judicial misconduct, has been reintroduced into the senate a second time..

headline: Casey, Rendell stress economy as top issue
abstract: The two major Democratic candidates for Pennsylvania governor, Robert Casey and Ed Rendell, say plans for reviving the state's economy will be the pivotal issue as the primary race enters its final two weeks.

headline: Open the door to judicial reform
abstract: Author Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh expresses his concern for the delay in judicial reform in the state, calling for a state constitutional convention to consider reform in these areas.

headline: Champs: Herd paws 'magic' carpet
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh met with the Carlisle High Thundering Herd Quad-A championship basketball team, and the team captain Michael Owens gave the governor a #1 button, poster, and t-shirt referring to the team's back-to-back state titles.  The Governor handed out "classy, glossy" certificates to all 12 members of the team.

headline: Hoffman heads PUC trial unit
abstract: Charles F. Hoffman has been named director of the Public Utility Commission's new office of Trial Staff.  Hoffman will supervise a team of lawyers and rate experts who are given the task of representinng the public interest at Public Utility Commission hearings.

headline: Pa. levying 'use tax' on furs and jewels
abstract: The PA State Department of Revenue says that tax bills are being sent to Pennsylvanians who purchased furs and jewelry in New York without paying levies on the items.  Customers are responsible for paying the 'use tax' because New York firms were not authorized to collect PA's sales tax.

headline: Diagnosis: State Mental Health Law Heading For An Overhaul
abstract: Ten years after it was passed, the PA Mental Health Procedures Act is undergoing a review. PA Senator F. Joseph Loeper said that the law is inadequate, especially in regards to treating violent and non-violent patients. Issues covered in a hearing in Pittsburgh yesterday included: involuntary commitment of non-violent patients (something which the law currently does not provide for), procedures and qualifications of those conducting discharges, costs to the state and insurance coverage, patient rights, and homeless patients. The issue of commitment was heated; some complained that patients had to become violent before being committed, while those who were committed complained of ineffective treatment. Civil rights groups are also expected to oppose easing commitment standards.

headline: Stockholm, Bonn seek details of Chernobyl mishap
abstract: Officials in Sweden and West Germany expressed anger over the Soviet Union's neglect to inform them of the nuclear accident at the Chernobyl nuclear facility, while the Soviet government asked West Germany and Sweden for advice on how to stop a continuing fire at the Chernobyl site. Swedish officials pressed the Soviets for precise details regarding the accident, and based on the fallout, predicted that a meltdown of the fuel core of one of Cherobyl's 4 reactors had occurred. The Swedes are highly critical of the Soviet Union's refusal to allow international atomic inspectors into their plants, and of the lack of safety features such as containment buildings.

headline: The Time is Right For Judicial Reform
abstract: This author believes that Pennsylvanians deserve an election system in which the most qualified candidates become judges, courtroom autonomy is assured, and which provides for a critical but fair review of the judiciary.  Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh has a plan for judicial reform in the state, which calls for the changes in the nine-member Judicial Inquiry and Review board, which wields little power, conducts its sessions in secrecy and has little incentive to reform.

headline: Bucks legislator defends tab for '84 trip to Europe
abstract: PA Representative John Cordisco has been accused by a political opponent of taking a 10-day junket to Europe in 1984. Cordisco acknowledged that the trip was for legitimate purposes mainly to visit solid waste disposal sites. Cordisco was accompanied by an unidentified woman on the trip and wrote no report of the events which occurred.

headline: Opinion: Legislators: It's time to work
abstract: Given the upcoming November elections in Pennsylvania, this author believes that there is little time left for Pennsylvania legislators to pass important bills and should work hard to do so now.  The author believes that though there are important issues, the lawmakers will put many things on the back burner until after the election.

headline: David Eisenhower fills 'Ike' fans in on book about his grandfather
abstract: David Eisenhower, grandson of the former U.S. President and husband to the daughter of former U.S. President Richard Nixon, spoke to 150 people at the Pennsylvania State Museum in Harrisburg about his book, "Eisenhower At War: 1943-45" and his lack of political ambition.

headline: City rejects 2.4 million
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council rejected a 2.4 million dollar housing grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.  The grant would have subsidized apartment rentals for the handicapped in a 101-unit apartment building that was to be constructed on the North Side of the city.  The Allegheny West Civic Council opposed construction of the apartment because the building was too high and did not blend in with the neighborhood.  The council's decision is only preliminary, and a final decision will be rendered on Monday.

headline: Panel OKs insurance nomination
abstract: The PA Senate Banking and Insurance Committee approved PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's nomination of George F. Grode as the state's new insurance commissioner. At the same time, a House panel approved a bill setting a $3,000 penalty on people convicted of drunk driving, and having those funds be placed into the state's Catastrophic Trust Fund. The House Insurance Committee also reviewed insurance company investment bills, which have recently come under scrutiny by the Insurance Federation of Pennsylvania.

headline: Dick Thornburgh, Governor of Pennsylvania - "Take the simple, free test - it could save your life"
abstract: An advertisement for a early detection of cancer test endorsed by Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh.  The test is free at a local drug store.

headline: The Chernobyl Syndrome
abstract: While the U.S. nuclear power industry has gone to great lengths to convince people that the disaster at Chernobyl could never happen here, the fact that human error was considered to be the main cause there, as well as at Three Mile Island, means that it can happen here. Lulled into a sense of overconfidence that nothing could go wrong, operators in both incidents did not react until it was too late. Because the possibilty of human error cannot be mitigated, nuclear power will always be dangerous.

headline: This bill should get quick approval
abstract: This article advocates swift passage of a bill before the PA General Assembly that would freeze assests of convicted criminals awaiting sentencing to life in prison.

headline: Bush leads '88 race in state
abstract: This columnist discusses current US Vice President George Bush, complimenting him for his poise during the Iran-Contra scandal, a scandal that many feel may inhibit his presidential ambitions.

headline: Order to shut down LCB faces fight
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh's order to dismantle the Liquor Control Board before he leaves office in January will be challenged in court, according to the agency's chairman and union representatives for more than 2,500 employees.

headline: Early Ukranian Man
abstract: Cartoon that depcits two cavemen, entitled Early Ukranian Man, and one of them says to the other, "Really…It's nothing.  A couple of people got bit by a dog, that's all, don't worry about it".  In the background a dinosaur is eating people and bones are everywhere.

headline: Group to make Route 34 pleas
abstract: The Route 34 Action Committee is lobbying the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation for improvements to an accident-prone segment of Route 34.  The group is planning to present recommendations for improvement to Robert Muesser, the District 8 engineer for the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation District.

headline: Pa. Tourist Attractions Attendance
abstract: Chart showing attendance at a number of PA attractions in between July of 1985 and 1986 along with a notation of the percentage change between the two

headline: Doctors' insurance deadly
abstract: Lynne J. Haubelt, D.P.M. writes that she is alarmed by the Pittsburgh Press' articles highlighting the skyrocketing costs of medical liability insurance. As a doctor, Haubelts has paid malpractice premiums for years, and is in jeopardy of financial ruin if proposed increases take effect.  Those increases would triple her yearly rate. She urges the PA General Assembly to take action on the matter.

headline: The Nuclear Appetite
abstract: A letter that is concerned about nuclear garbage generated to date.

headline: Top court to monitor common pleas courts' work
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has asked that reports be done on judges in three county court systems because of potentially unethical activities.  The order applies to the Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and Delaware counties.

headline: Bush, Jackson to stump in midstate
abstract: US Vice President George Bush will appear in Lancaster to campaign for Republican gubernatorial candidate William W Scranton.  Reverand Jesse Jackson will appear in Harrisburg to campaign for Democrat and US Senatorial candidate Bob Edgar.

headline: Our Ideas: $6.1 Billion in State Cuts
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh, following his initial election as governor in 1979, appointed a six-member "cost reduction study team" which has reported that the state had projected savings over the eight-year term of Thornburgh of $6.1 billion.  These cost reductions have allowed for tax cuts and Standard and Poors have upgraded Pennsylvania's bond credit ratings, the first upgrade since 1970.

headline: Highlights In History
abstract: A list of events that happened in history on January 23, 1986 is given.
