Some historical events include,  the establishment of  Georgetown College, the U.S. Congressional decision to make all national elections on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, and Dr. Elizabeth Blackwell became the first woman to receive a Medical Doctor degree.

headline: Highlights in Histroy
abstract: This article details several events throughout history that occurred on this date, Thursday, September 18th.

headline: Panel Approves Plan For Savings Banks
abstract: The PA House Banking and Commerce Committee approved legislation allowing savings banks and associations to participate in regional interstate banking if reciprocal laws exist in the respecitve states where the business will be conducted.

headline: Doctors make senseless attack on Sen. Stauffer
abstract: At a hearing between physicians and members of the PA Senate, doctors attacked the General Assembly for failing to deal with the rising number of malpractice suits and the rising cost of insurance.  The author believes that the doctors were out of line.

headline: The TMI Accident Reports
abstract: General Public Utility's report on the health effects from the Three Mile Island accident support what the utility has long argued, a minimal amount of radiation leaked from the damaged reactor and the health effects from the accident are minimal. There have been numerous other reports and a large volume of evidence made public to support this claim. The various groups which have sponsored the studies rule out any possibility of conspiracy by the utility, and the only reports that claim there would be health consequences have been dismissed by the state and the U.S. Supreme Court. The obvious conclusion to reach is that no serious health problems will occur in the area of the reactor.

headline: Trial Delays Cause Overcrowding
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Ronald Castille's letter arguing for a new 250-bed youth detention facility is unnecessary. If attorneys on both sides were better prepared then hearings would not have to be constantly delayed forcing defendants to remain in holding for unacceptably long periods of time. Moreover, the proposed facility would lack the security needed to hold the 8% of juvenile offenders responsible for 75% of the offenses. A new facility places an unacceptable cost on Philadelphia residents especially when the money could be better spent on juvenile support programs and probation systems.

headline: Butler judge nominee named
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has nominated Lee Montgomery to fill a vacancy on the Butler County Common Pleas Court. If confirmed by the PA Senate, Montgomery would replace former Judge John Dillon who died in October.  Montgomery would hold the post through 1987, when he would have to win election in order to stay on the bench.

headline: Our Ideas-Let's See Expense Accounts
abstract: The Lancaster, PA New Era newspaper asked PA democrat and republican lawmakers if PA taxpayers should have the right to examine expense accounts of members of the PA State House of Representatives. The democratic leadership of the PA House responded no, while Republican leaders said yes. Under current rules, the public knows how much a representative spends, but not how it is spent.

headline: Highlights In History
abstract: A list of events that previously happened on this day.

headline: GOP role disrupts granite probe
abstract: Democratic members of a bipartisan legislative committee investigating the construction of a 122 million dollar state Capitol addition project alledge that Republicans have compromised the investigation and obstructed justice.  These charges came after Republican panel members announced they met privately with top Thornburgh administration officials to discuss the project.  The bipartisan committee is investigating evidence of kickbacks and payoffs among contractors on the project.

headline: Panel would ban insurance cutoffs
abstract: A PA House committee recommended approval of regulations that would allow the PA Insurance Department to permanently bar insurers from indiscriminately cancelling or refusing to renew liability insurance policies.  The regulations originally implemented under a Thornburgh administration emergency order lasting 120 days are being considered today by the PA Independent Regulatory Review Commission.

headline: Drug-card holders get a reminder
abstract: The PA Department of Aging is reminding cardholders to submit renewal applications for the state's prescription drug benefit program.  More than 150,000 cardholders still have to do this as of March, according to Secretary of Aging Alma Jacobs.

headline: There's No Accounting for PGW's Steak in Million
abstract: Former PA Senator Milton Street received gas service at his North Philadelphia steak shop last year without ever receiving a bill from the Philadelphia Gas Works.  Despite widespread publicly for the opening of Street's Steak Shoppe and a long-running controversy over Philadelphia Gas Works treatment of political VIP's, the business operated for more than four months and then closed without the city-owned gas company having any formal record of its existence. Philadelphia Gas Works does not disclose information about customers to the media.

headline: Troopers Escaped Prosecution, State Committee Is Told
abstract: A PA House committee investigating the state police discussed in a hearing yesterday lenient disciplinary action against officers. In almost twenty cases troopers were involved in crimes yet were often only given paid suspension. The committee's counsel, A. Roy DeCaro was unimpressed with the testimony of Deputy State Police Commissioner Richard C. Weatherbee, who was unable to comment on the appropriateness of discipline in a variety of cases even though, according to DeCaro, he had been given information on the cases to be discussed a month ago. There was also bickering between Democrats, who want to continue the hearings, and Republicans, who have been trying to end them.

headline: BUZZ
abstract: A Philadelphia political gossip column, where the author talks about public relations firms and the restaurant of a former Philadelphia Mayor.

headline: Our Opinion: Much is at stake in Tuesday's election
abstract: In Pennsylvania, the editors urge voters to get out to vote in tomorrow's election.

headline: Highlights In History
abstract: A list of significant events that previously happened on this day.

headline: Governor's S. Africa divestment call included much that is already policy
abstract: Top administration officials admit that many of Governor Thornburgh's South African divestment proposals have already been in place for up to four years.  State Treasurer R. Budd Dwyer, for example, has restricted investments in South-African related companies and followed the Sullivan Principles.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of the checkout line at a PA state liquor store on Saturday

headline: Governor Signs Bill To Establish Health-Cost Panel
abstract: Yesterday, Governor Richard Thornburgh signed Act 89 of 1986 creating a state panel to collect and publicize data on health care costs. The Health Care Cost Containment Council will collect data statewide on the cost and quality of care at hospitals, ambulatory clinics, and health insurance companies. Supporters believe that making such data public will encourage competition and force providers to lower their costs. Thornburgh, however, still believes that putting a temporary cap on how much a hospital can spend on expansion would better achieve that goal. He also believes that the PA Health Department should be gathering the data. The law also mandates that the council collect information on and make recommendations regarding indigent care.

headline: TMI advisory unit to discuss cleanup
abstract: The Advisory Panel for the Decontamination of Three Mile Island Unit 2 is meeting 7 p.m. Thursday at the Holiday Inn Center City.

headline: Truck axle tax, coal mining law aired before U.S. Supreme Court
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court yesterday took preliminary steps toward rulings in two major Pennsylvania cases involving regulation of coal mining and taxation of the trucking industry.  The Keystone Bituminous Coal Association claims that the state's regulations governing deep mining violate the Constitution since they take private property without compensation, since the law requires operators to leave as much as 50% of their coal in the ground.  The American Trucking Association contends that two successive Pennsylvania levies on out-of-state trucks violate the constutional ban on restrictions on interstate commerce.

headline: BUZZ
abstract: For the first time ever, all 80 PA State legislators from the Delaware Valley have been invited to meet in the same room to discuss regional issues. The Philadelphia Daily News says that they did not know there was a room big enough to hold their collective egos.

headline: Pa. Democrats failed to develop new group
abstract: PA Democratic leaders have announced plans for the creation of the Democratic Institute, a new political arm to help the party develop modern campaign tools and techniques. The goal is to raise $1 million a year and use it for public opinion polls, advertising, voter registration, candidate assistance, and issue development.  The institute would not exist as a distinct political organization and there would be no public record of funds raised and money spent under its name.

headline: Highlights In History
abstract: A list of things that happened in history on January 3, 1986. Some events included, Martin Luther King's excommunicated from the Roman Catholic Church, General George Washington's army was routed by the British in the Battle of Princeton, NJ and Britain seized control of the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic.

headline: Cyanide found in Rite Aid aspirin
abstract: After a Massachusetts woman found three cyanide-tainted tablets in a bottle of Rite-Aid aspirin, Rite-Aid Corporation pulled some of its own brand aspirin tablets from its drugstores yesterday.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Picture of the now closed Greenville Steel Car Company building in Greenville, Pennsylvania.

headline: hospital group attacks House bill that seeks to curb health-care costs
abstract: The Hospital Association of Pennsylvania contends that a cost-containment bill being discussed in the PA House of Representatives would drastically increase rather than control or reduce health-care costs in the state.  John A. Russell, HAP President, has vowed to fight the bill, which was approved by the PA House Health and Welfare Committee.

headline: TMI calls Unit 1 test OK
abstract: Three Mile Island's Unit 1 reactor automatically shut down on 1-3-1986 in a test marking the final phase of a three-month restart sequence. The test released a burst of steam and caused a loud noise. Three Mile Island operators planned the test to check the reactor's ability to shut down automatically when other plant components stop operating.

headline: Upstate Diabetic's Suit Ruled A Class Action
abstract: U.S. Middle District Senior Judge Malcom Muir approved a class-action status for a Williamsport girl whose diabetes requires supportive health services. The suit aginst PA Education Secretary, Dr. Margaret Smith; Commissioiner of Basic Education, Dr. D. Kay Wright; Director of the Bureau of Special Education, Dr. Gary Makuch; and others is based on the state's failure to provide placement and evaluation procedures for handicapped students who do not require special education. Over one and a half million PA students require such support.

headline: CAMPAIGN '86
abstract: Cartoon depicting a dirty voter, who sighs, as he looks at a voting booth, which is a shower.

headline: Pa. Review Commission Proposes Rules For Itself
abstract: The Independent Regulatory Review Commission (IRRC), a five member panel created to review and possibly block proposed rules and regulations by all PA agencies, has for the first time issued rules for itself. If the rules are finalized, which is expected within sixty days, those wishing to appeal an IRRC decision would have thirty days in which to file and the commission would have another thirty days in which to rule. Another change would require any revisions in proposed rules be submitted at least five days before the IRRC hearing.

headline: Highlights In History
abstract: A list of things that happened previously on this date.

headline: Prompt decision needed on Penn's Landing ramps
abstract: Although arrangements have been made for private financing to cover the cost of a retail and entertainment complex on the Philadelphia waterfront, celebration should be restrained until construction of new I-95 exit and entrance ramps are built in the Penn's Landing area.  Mixed-use development of Penn's Landing, which is designed to attrack large numbers of visitors like the Baltimore inner-harbor area, is dependent upon access to and from I-95.

headline: Pickets block USX's Clairton chemical plant
abstract: Motivated by worries that USX might sell its Chemical Division in order to avert a hostile Wall Street takeover, members of a local chapter of United Steelworkers blocked railroad tracks outside USX's plant in Clairton to prevent shipment of chemicals.  Union members stood watch throughout the night.  The Union president said they'd allow traffic in to maintain the plant, but they would thwart shipping.

headline: Hospitals say budget proposal would cost them millions
abstract: PA Hospital officials say program cuts and a price freeze proposed in PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's $9.48 billion budget would reduce the payments they receive under the PA Medical Assistance program by nearly $60 million a year.

headline: TMI cleanup utilizes robot
abstract: Workers at the Three Mile Island Unit 2 nuclear plant are using a newly modified six-wheeled robot in the latest attempt to cut intense radiation levels in the plant's basement.  General Public Utilities Nuclear Corporation said the remotely controlled vehicle began using a new high-pressure water spray to strip cement off the basement walls in the containment building.  In 1979, the Unit 2 basement was flooded with highly contaminated reactor coolant water, a result of the nation's worst commercial nuclear accident.  GPU officials hope to gain limited manned access to the basement by the end of the cleanup, which is scheduled for late 1988.

headline: VisionQuest: A Last Resort
abstract: Although ten juveniles have died in its care, and its sometimes confrontational style have been a source of controversy, VisionQuest is a popular alternative to actual jail for many PA juvenile delinquents. The company was founded thirteen years ago as a way to teach youths that the keys to adulthood came through hard work, responsibility and commitment. Investigations into the company and its program have been equally mixed; judges, probation officers, and parents and family members of many VisionQuest participants have lauded it while child advocates and others have lambasted it. The ten deaths that have occurred at different Vision Quest facilities prompted an investigation by PA, but the task force was impressed overall by the program and recommended that it continue to be used.

headline: Campaign focuses on Flaherty name issue
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial and lieutenant-gubernatorial candidates Robert Casey and Mark Singel have launched a media campaign against Pittsburgh City Controller Tom Flaherty, Singel's opponent in the race for lieutenant governor. The campaign makes use of the confusion of Tom Flaherty for Pete Flaherty, a controversial PA politician. Meanwhile, Casey's opponent for the Democratic nomination Ed Rendell said that either Singel, Flaherty, or PA Representative Dwight Evans would be acceptable runnings mates. PA Auditor General Don Bailey, lashed out against US Representative Bob Edgar, his rival in the race for US Senate, for having actors pose as veterans in a recent TV ad, when he does not actually enjoy the support of the American Legion.

headline: Pa. to Phila.: drop dead
abstract: The editorial board writes about a bill for Philadelphia's convention center, which would have failed in the state house for a third time had the voting machines not mysteriously malfunctioned. Even legislators from Philadelphia, along with upstate legislators and US Representative William Gray opposed the bill. Philadelphia will have to reconsider provisions for building a convention center, and might have to do so without the state's help.

headline: Highlights in History
abstract: Article listing events that occurred in history on October 21.  Events included the invention of the light bulb, women's suffrage in France, and the opening of the Guggenheim Museum.

headline: Creehan's inside track
abstract: James Creehan, the executive director of the Allegheny County Sanitation Authority, has for years kept the details of his personal and professional background from public view.

headline: Poultry firm rebounds from blaze
abstract: Twelve weeks after a fire damaged the Empire Kosher Poultry Co. plant in Walker Township, production resumes and a new facility is planned.

headline: Lawsuit Rx sought by doctors
abstract: Pennsylvania doctors want limits on jury awards in medical malpractice suits.  After months of negotiations between doctors and lawyers failed to produce an agreement on the issue, the Pennsylvania Medical Society is moving ahead with its own legislative package on medical malpractice.

headline: TMI fund wasted
abstract: In a letter to the editor, the author agrees with the organization Three Mile Island Alert, which has expressed concern that the Three Mile Island Public Health Fund has not and will not be appropriated with the community's best interest in mind.

headline: What About The State's Responsibility For MOVE?
abstract: Even with all of the controversy surrounding the tragedy of the MOVE assault, Governor Thonrburgh and Lieutenant Governor William Scranton still have not been held accountable for their role. Just like the city of Philadelphia, the state of PA allowed a violent organization to terrorize local residents and violate various laws for two years without doing anything; neither Thornborgh nor Scranton is on record as having contacted Mayor Goode to find out what was going on. Even worse was the fact that neither local nor state authorities made any effort to rescue the children inside the MOVE headquarters prior to the assault even though it was well known that they played alone in a nearby park for over twelve hours a day. Finally, the use of a PA State Police helicopter to drop the bomb which destroyed the MOVE headquarters would not have been done without the permission of the PA State Police who would not have gone forward without permission from the political higher ups. Just as a grand jury was held to examine the city's role, so too must one be held to examine the state's role. This is necessary to ensure justice is done, because of Thornburgh's poor record in this state, and because his deputy, Scranton, is running to replace him, and he has ads with Thornburgh detailing how valuable Scranton is to his work, implying that Scranton would have a good idea of the state's role in this situation. What must ultimately be answered is would Thornburgh have acted differently if MOVE had been terrorizing a neighborhood of white Republicans?

headline: Campaign Issues Gearing Up, But Issues Stay Murky
abstract: This year's election is unusual in that there are no national issues driving the campaign, instead the U.S. House, U.S. Senate, and governor races are largely revolving around local issues. Both Republicans and Democrats concede that while President Reagan is extremely popular, his economic policies, particularly in the middle part of the country, are not. Because of the large number of contested seats and lack of defnining issues, both parties are running primarily defensive campaigns. Republicans are not declaring a political realignment to the right while Democrats are avoiding talk of new spending or criticism of Reagan. Both parties are playing to the middle, looking similar to one another in order to avoid the labels of the party of privilege  (Republicans) or the party of the past (Democrats). Instead both sides are running local contests, with Republicans comfortable with their candidates running against Reagan's record if it helps them and Democrats playing up economic problems in specific districts to gather votes. The article also examines key races in each region of the country.

headline: Panel approves plan for judicial reforms
abstract: The PA Senate Judiciary Committee approved legislation that could lead to a state constitutional convention considering judicial reform. Some provisions include reshaping the Judicial Inquiry and Review Board and replace judicial elections with an appointment process.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: Article looks at the significant historical events that have occurred on December 22.  Among those events included are:  The US Congress passing the Embargo Act in 1807, French Army Officer Alfred Dreyfus being convicted of treason in 1894, and 82 crew members of the US intelligence ship Pueblo being let go by North Korea after 11 months.  Significant birthdays on this date are also included in the article.

headline: Candiate Scranton comes to grips with his use of drugs in the past
abstract: The previous drug use of William Scranton III, the current Lieutenant Governor of Pennsylvania and Republican gubernatorial candidate, has become a serious campaign issue.  His drug use has become public knowledge at a time when drugs are the focal point of the Regan administration's national agenda.

headline: Profit motive
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Dick Thornburgh's move to transfer the PA liquor stores to private retailers has this author worried, feeling that private companies may not have the same incentive to avoid selling to minors.

headline: Medicaid, like Medicare, has changed to control costs
abstract: Across the country, many state governments have recently undergone changes to their Medicaid programs in order to curb rising costs. This follows a similar effort to control Medicare costs. In PA, those changes have included a crackdown on abuse by providers and recipients.  Also implemented are changes to hospitalization copayments, prescription drug coverage, charges for doctors' office visits, and a prospective payment system for hospitals.  PA spends more than $2 billion annually to provide medical services to more than 1.1 million recipients. To make the transition for state residents easier, the PA Department of Public Welfare increased aid when the copayment plan started.

headline: TMI operator fined for violations in cleanup of the damaged reactor
abstract: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued a fine to the operator of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in reaction to a "serious" violation of procedures during the cleanup following the partial meltdown at the plant in 1979.  The violation was related to a polar crane used in the damaged Unit 2 reactor.

headline: Why do I have to come down here and give my fingerprints when they're all over the refrigerator?
abstract: Cartoon of a child giving fingerprints while being overlooked by his parents.  The child says "Why do I have to come down here and give my fingerprints when they're all over the refrigerator?"

headline: Campaign spending will set a record
abstract: The article goes over rising cost of campaigns in congressional races.  It is expected that they will reach an all time high.  This is attributed to rising costs of advertising and political action committees (PACs).  It shows that while there is talk about trying to reduce special interest money in elections, nothing has changed.

headline: Passing Politics
abstract: In what is unusual for primary campaigns, Republican gubernatorial candidate William Scranton III and congressional candidate Mark Holtzman are using TV ads in the area to build their image. There is also a fight brewing for Republican County Chairman between John Roberts and Peg Cole. For the local Democrats a unified party is necessary so Casey can get every vote possible. However, the county chairman fight is also expected to be divisive between Pat Mellody and Bill Gerrity or John Szymanski.

headline: Highlights in History
abstract: Brief article listing events and birthdays that occurred throughout history on October 17th.  Some of the events listed include British surrender at Saratoga, the creation of the Radio Corporation of America, and the arrival of Albert Einstein in the US as a refugee.

headline: Specter wrong on court
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter's support of Justice William Rehnquist as chief justice is problematic.  Specter's opponent, Bob Edgar, has openly denounced Rehnquist's appointment; Edgar is a better candidate and could better represent Pennsylvanians.

headline: Singel in lt. governor's race
abstract: There are three candidates for the Democratic nominee for Pennsylvania lieutenant governor, a primary which will take place on May 20th.  This paper endorses Pennsylvania State Senator Mark Singel, believing he is the best qualified of the three democrats to fill this office.

headline: Meeting On Malpractice Slated
abstract: Six hundred fifty doctors and twenty members of the PA General Assembly will meet Tuesday to discuss medical malpractice and tort law in Pennsylvania. This is one of nine such meetings, sponsored by the PA Medical Society, taking place throughout the state that day. The goal is to show the state legislators that doctors are serious about working with them on liability and tort reform. One doctor argues that obstetrical services are being lost in the south-central part of the state because of liability costs, and the PA Medical Society observes that diagnostic tests done to avoid lawsuits add thirty-five million dollars to medical costs, while all liability insurance carriers in the state have announced rate increases.

headline: TMI to shut Unit 1 in test
abstract: The operator of Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Plant in PA plan to shut down the Unit 1 reactor for several days. The test will mark the final phase of a three month start-up program and will cause a release of steam. Unit 1 will return to maximum power with the approval of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

headline: Witness' perjury ends LCB cases
abstract: A key witness in the trials of two officials of the PA Liquor Control Board pleaded guilty to perjury, causing prosecutors to drop corruption charges against the officials.  The witness, Edward Fataicher, admitted that he lied under oath as a prosecution witness in the trial of James H. Henmon, currently supervisor of the Philadelphia regional enforcement office.

headline: Candidate busy in Pa., Congress
abstract: The article talks about busy schedules of US Senatorial candidates Republican Arlen Spector and Democrat Bob Edgar.  Both men are busy travelling between Washington, D.C. and various parts of the state to campaign. The campaign is reaching the point where both men are expected to take part in television debates.

headline: Passing Politics
abstract: While it is unusual for someone like the chairman of the Republican National Committee, Frank J. Fahrenkopf Jr. to visit Scranton, he is doing so to help one of our local boys beat another local boy for the governorship. He is here to help raise funds for the state party and can be expected to discuss not only how many conservatives there have always been in America, but how popular it is to be one now. The anniversary of the Women's Suffrage Amendment is approaching, and it seems quaint to note that the fear at the time of its passage was that women would take over politics, when in fact, approximately five percent of PA's legislators are women. Common Cause also recently released a report detailing the top thirty poetical action committees in the country. Finally a local fundraiser for Bob Casey's gubernatorial campaign will be held soon.

headline: Highlights in History
abstract: Highlights from things that happened on the date February 26, throughout history. Some historical events included, Victor Hugo's birth, Napoleon Bonaparte's escape from the Island of Elba, and the establishment of the Grand Canyon National Park in Arizona.

headline: Death penalty finds favor in House
abstract: U.S. Representative George Gekas drafted an amendment to the omnibus anti-drug bill that was heavily supported by the Reagan administration.  The amendment, which calls for capital punishment for "kingpin" drug dealers who commit murder, passed by an overwhelming majority in the House last week.

headline: Singel rips Flaherty
abstract: Pennsylvania candidate for Lieutenant Governor, Pittsburgh city controller Thomas Flaherty, accused opponent Pennsylvania State Senator Mark Singel of voting against interests of consumers on public utility matters, causing Singel to accuse Flaherty of having his facts backwards.  Singel is the hand-picked choice of gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey on the Pennsylvania Democratic ticket.

headline: Mental Health Programs Get Boost In Funds
abstract: PA has increased the amount of money given to counties to support mental patients discharged into the community. The program has been controversial because union officials charge it is an effort to reduce employee numbers, while communities where group homes are located claim that their presence lowers the value of surrounding properties. The PA Office of Mental Health argues that placing people in the community who can care for themselves provides a sense of dignity and speeds their recovery process.

headline: TMI Unit 1 runs at full power
abstract: Three Mile Island Unit 1 has reached 100% of its potential power. It is the first time the reactor has operated at full capacity since February 1979, when it was shut down.

headline: York command ruling appealed by state police
abstract: The PA State Police have challenged a federal judge's order that a black lieutenant be given immediate command of the York barracks. U.S. District Judge Green ruled that state police improperly handled Lieutenant Russell Clanagan's request to become commander of the York barracks and ordered that he be given the post.  The PA House of Representatives has empanelled a select committee to look into alleged wrongdoing, misconduct, and accusations of racism in the state police.

headline: Candidate loses spot on ballot
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Buck Scott was scratched from the ballot after a judge's ruling.  PA Commonwealth Court Judge James Crumlish Jr. ruled that a petition in York County had 98 signatures, two short of the requirement.  A gubernatorial candidate needs at least 100 signatures from 10 different counties to appear on the ballot.

headline: Patient politician
abstract: Robert Casey, a former state senator, former auditor general, and 3-time gubernatorial candidate, is once again running for the office of PA governor. He enjoys the support of the PA AFL-CIO in his bid for the Democratic candidacy in the gubernatorial, the winner of which will face Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III. PA Senator Robert J. Mellow has described Casey as a "no-nonsense worker."

headline: Highlights In History
abstract: Listing of notable events that happened previously on this day

headline: State House to study seat-belt legislation
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representative is set to begin studying seat-belt legislation.

headline: Sliver in Lebanon County has vested interest in race
abstract: In Lebanon County, Pennsylvania voters will pick a state legislator, with six-term Republican John Davies running against immigrant Zia Mahmood a Democrat who holds a doctorate in education administration.  The election is this week.

headline: Most Hospital Pacts Ratified; Talks Continue At 2
abstract: Almost as soon as a strike was called at Philadelphia area hospitals, it was called off. Union officials authorized the strike after management failed to respond to a new wage proposal, reducing their pay increase demand from seven percent a year to five percent. Shortly thereafter, one of the hospitals responded with a proposal of their own and the strike authorization was called off. The new three-year contract has a five percent wage increase the first year, a four percent increase, the second, and a three percent increase the third. The hospitals also agreed to raise their contribution to the pension system from 12% to 12.2% (the union had originally requested a fifteen percent increase). Two hospitals, Hahnemann and Consortium are still threatening strikes. Hahnemann wants to raise wages only two percent a year for each year of the contract and cut pension contributions, while Consortium wants a ten percent pay cut along with ending benefits to family members and freezing pension contributions.

headline: TMI Unit 1 shut down for repairs to leaky line
abstract: The Unit 1 reactor at Three Mile Island nuclear power plant will be out of service for at least a week as plant workers repair a leaky steam line.  The U.S Nuclear Regulatory Commission was notified.

headline: York County judge remains hospitalized
abstract: York County judge Richard H Horn was admitted to the coronary intensive care unit.  Horn had previously been hospitalized for fatigue.  A spokesman for the judiciary said they are waiting to determine whether Horn's case load will need to be redistributed to other judges or not.

headline: Candidate's polling stroll leads to violation charges
abstract: PA House Candidate Vincent Hughes, who faces PA Representative James D. Barber, was charged with violating state election code by visiting polling sites last November. His case will be held in a Philadelphia Municipal Court. The code prohibits those who are not voters nor election officials from entering polling places.

headline: Pay grab decried
abstract: Writer derisively wonders whether state Senator and lieutenant governor candidate D. Michael Fisher will be able to live on the lieutenant governor's salary.  He says that as senator Fisher voted to give himself a raise.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: On this date in history in 1483 Martin Luther was born, in 1954 the Iwo Jima Memorial was dedicated in Arlington, VA, and in 1982 Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev died.

headline: Probe Me? Probe You, Evans Tells Federal Agency
abstract: A spokesperson for the Labor Department says that the FBI and the U.S. Department of Labor are investigating the use of federal funds by the American Foundation of Negro Affairs (AFNA).  The AFNA and its leader, Samuel Evans, are accused of using federal funds to provide youth scholarships to children who were ineligible for assistance.  Evans claims the investigation is politically motivated.

headline: Smith Acts To Delay CTA Jail Term
abstract: William T. Smith has filed an appeal with the U.S. Supreme Court seeking a review of his, as well as Alan R. Stoneman's, conviction for conspiring to bribe public officials in the Computer Technology Associates scandal. An appeal to the U.S. Third Circuit Court affirmed the convictions.

headline: Nicholas Orders Picketing
abstract: Strike preparations began in at least eight Philadelphia hospitals and six health-care institutions after six months of contract negotiations broke down. Sit-down strikes have already begun at four hospitals while negotiations continue at two others. Union leader Henry Nicholas says the hospitals have failed to respond to its demand for a five percent wage increase over each of the next three years (revised from seven percent), and other demands include job security and greater health care coverage. Negotiations have continued at a third hospital even though Nicholas ordered union negotiators to leave. The federal mediator there was optimistic that a settlement could be reached.

headline: TMI Waste-Train Route Opposed
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council passed a resolution yesterday requesting the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) reroute nuclear waste from the damaged Three Mile Island reactor away from the city, citing health concerns and the risk of derailment. The DOE said no routes will be changed nor will information on the shipment be provided. The department also insisted that the containers the waste is stored in have already been throoughly tested for leakage. It is estimated that it will take over two years and thirty-five to forty shipments to transport all of the waste.

headline: Zimmerman asks extra $2.7 million for drug war
abstract: PA Attorney General LeRoy S. Zimmerman wants $2.7 million more for his office than is earmarked in the governor's 1986-87 budget proposal.  Zimmerman told the PA House of Representatives Appropriations Committee that a portion of the extra money would be used to provide 29 additional drug enforcement agents and a prosecutor who would concentrate on drug cases.

headline: Candidates stump east, west: the 'real' Bob Casey keeps bouncing back
abstract: Democrat Robert Casey attended the annual PA AFL-CIO convention in Pittsburgh, attempting to sell his candidacy for PA governor. After several unsuccessful gubernatorial bids and confusion amid other candidates named "Bob Casey," the former auditor general and former PA senator Casey is once again running for PA governor. His running mate, PA Senator Mark Singel, are developing an economic recovery plan to be the centerpiece of their campaign.

headline: Pay raises
abstract: This letter is from an irate reader who is upset that Pennsylvania state legislators are seeking a $10,000 pay raise.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: On this date in history, in 1758, in the French and Indian War, the British captured Fort Duquesne at what is now Pittsburgh and in 1920, radio station WTAW of College Station, Texas broadcast the first play-by-play description of a football game, between the University of Texas and Texas A&M.

headline: S. African Farmers Face Land Dilemma
abstract: Due to apartheid policies, South-African farmers face a serious dilemma.

headline: Smith quite race in hope of helping Spector win
abstract: Independent US Senate candidate Robert Smith dropped out of the race saying he did not want to risk losing republican control of the Senate.  Although Smith had painted himself as the true conservative candidate and had branded Arlen Spector as a liberal, he claimed that he was dropping out after conversations with the White House.  He said he withdrew out of loyalty to the republican party.

headline: No AIDS being spread in state workplaces, expert says
abstract: A study shows that AIDS does not spread with daily interaction with victims, just through blood interactions and sexual contact, and that those stricken with AIDS are unlikely to pass it to coworkers.

headline: TMI Workers Criticize GPU Plan To Test For Drugs
abstract: A grievance will be filed by members of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers union after General Public Utilities (GPU) announced that random drug tests of all employees, including those at Three Mile Island, would begin in September. The union argues that the unreliablity of the tests as well as the unilateral way in which the policy was created promted the grievance. GPU says the policy is a way to enforce its prohibition on drugs and alcohol and notes that workers will be transferred while they receive drug treatment. Those refusing the tests could be dismissed.

headline: $6 Million In Heat Aid Not Used Last Season
abstract: Six million dollars left over in a state fund to help the poor pay their heating bills will be rolled over into next fiscal year's fund. Advocates argue that the surplus shows that the benefits being paid out by the fund are too low.

headline: Candidates stump east, west: to chagrin of staffers, Rendell talks up issues
abstract: Former Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell often disregards advice from his advisers, most recently claiming that he would never raise taxes as governor. He faces former PA Auditor General Robert Casey and Lyndon LaRouche disciple Steve Douglas in the Democratic primary for the gubernatorial election against Republican Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III. Rendell has been trading blows with Casey, who enjoys the endorsement of the Democratic State Committee and the PA AFL-CIO.

headline: Penna. Voters return incumbents to House
abstract: Incumbents appeared headed for easy victories in most of Pennsylvania's congressional elections in unofficial results last night.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: On this date in history, in 1863 President Lincoln announced his plan for Reconstruction on the South, in 1941 the United States declared war on Japan, one day after Pearl Harbor, in 1949 the Chinese Nationalist government moved from the Chinese mainland to Formosa, and in 1980 rock star John Lennon was shot to death in New York.

headline: A victim of the anti-drug war
abstract: With his advocation of harsher penalties for drug pushers who sell to children, Pennsylvania Attorney General LeRoy Zimmerman has jumped on the anti-drug bandwagon.  As a result of this move, one of Zimmerman's staff members, Richard L. Guida, was forced to resign his position after rumors circulated that he had used drugs.

headline: State eyes moving up primary
abstract: Members of both political parties in the PA Legislature have shown interest in moving up the April 26, 1988, PA US Presidential primary by three weeks to coincide with the New York primary on April 5, 1988.  The move would bring more candidates to PA earlier and force presidential hopefuls to raise issues important to the mid-Atlantic region and intensify news coverage of those issues.  Other states are considering moving up their primaries as well.  Critics of the move say that it would force candidates to start even earlier on the already exhausting and expensive process of campaigning for president.  The bill was passed overwhelmingly in the PA House of Representatives, but languished in the PA Senate before the legislative session ended.

headline: Nurse Response
abstract: Deborah B. Raygor writes to the Tribune-Review that she has decided to continue working at the Correctional Facility in Greensburg during the Pennsylvania Nurses Association strike. Raygor believes that the PNA is poorly run and rarely stands up for its members.

headline: TMI workers use drill to cut up damaged core
abstract: Cleanup workers at Three Mile Island are using a large drill to break up the parts of the core that were damaged by the nuclear accident there.  Officials have said the the drill has been working well in breaking up the core into more manageable pieces.

headline: 33% fewer seniors riding PAT for free
abstract: In Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania the number of senior citizens taking advantage of free Port Authority Transit rides has dropped 33% since 1979 because of service cuts, a perception of crime downtown, a shift in where the elderly live and other reasons.

headline: Candidates urge voters to the polls
abstract: With the May 20 primary on the horizon, local Pennsylvania candidates are spending one last weekend trying to convince Philadelphia voters to go to the polls on Tuesday.  Turnout in Philadelphia is expected to be around 30-35% of those registered, with experts blaming the low turnout on negative advertisements that that turned voters off.

headline: PENNSYLVANIA
abstract: An overview of upcoming gubernatorial and U.S. Senate elections in Pennsylvania, discussing Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey's announcement to stop all negative ads and his anti-abortion stance, while Republican opponent William Scranton had to explain an anti-Casey mailing that was mailed from his camp.  For U.S. Senate Republican incumbent Arlen Specter is facing little opposition from Democrat Bob Edgar.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: On this date in history, in 1872 America's first black governor took office as Pinchney Benton Stewart Pinchback become acting governor of Louisiana, in 1936, Britain's King Edward VII abdicated in order to marry American divorcee Wallis Simpson, in 1941 Germany and Italy declared war on the United States, and in 1946 John Rockefeller, Jr. offered to donate a six-block piece of Manhattan real estate as the site for a United Nations headquarters.

headline: PA Prisons at 133% Capacity
abstract: According to a report released by the PA Department of Corrections, the state prison population grew by 73 percent between 1980 and 1985.  The growth was caused, in part, by tougher sentencing policies.

headline: Some election ideas
abstract: A letter to the editor that bemoans recent elections in Pennsylvania for negative ads, believing we are not governed by voters but by interest groups.

headline: Nurses to Strike Pa. Institutions
abstract: Mental hospitals, prisons, and other institutions are ready to strike by a union representing nurses, pharmacists, and other state health care employees whose contract expired June 30, 1986. The union wants members shifted to higher levels on the state's salary scale.

headline: Trains to start hauling TMI fuel in May
abstract: Trains will begin hauling damaged nuclear fuel from Three Mile Island to an Idaho research site in May, but there are no plans to tell residents along the route exactly when the trains will travel.

headline: A Bad Welfare Program, A Good Welfare Program
abstract: A two-framed comic strip; the first is of people waiting in line at the welfare office with a caption saying "a bad welfare program;" the second is with people busy at work with a caption saying "a good welfare program."

headline: Capitol annex a real palace
abstract: A PA House committee, led by PA Representative Nicholas Colafella, is examining the indulgent construction of the PA Capitol annex, which includes mahogany desks for General Assembly members, the $750,000 relocation of an air condition so as not to disturb the office of PA Representative James Burd, and the role PA Governor Dick Thornburgh played in awarding construction contracts. The article alleges that everyone from first-term legislators to bureaucrats at the PA Department of General Services has some authority over aspects of the construction of the annex.

headline: Pennsylvania Rep. Edgar In Tight Senate Primary: Packwood, Spector Likely to Be Renominated
abstract: Rep. Bob Edgar and Auditor General Don Bailey appeared to be in a tight race for the Democratic Senate nomination in Pennsylvania, while Robert Casey took an early lead over Edward Rendell for the party's gubernatorial nomination.  Republican Sens. Bob Packwood of Oregon and Arley Spector of Pennsylvania are expected to win renomination easily.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: On this date, in 1788 South Carolina became a state, in 1934 Bonnie and Clyde were shot to death, and in 1960 Israel annouced it had captured former Nazi official Adolf Eichmann in Argentina.

headline: Repairs to Route 15 reportedly promised
abstract: According to state Senator Roger A. Madigan, the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) is intensifying efforts to obtain funding for improvements to Route 15.  Senator Madigan also called for the establishment of a route 15 coalition to ensure that PennDOTcompletes the improvement project.

headline: Some pro-lifers lost
abstract: A letter in which the author discusses Pennsylvania politicians who are pro-life, of which Governor-elect, a democrat, numbers.

headline: Officials form 'health-fraud team'
abstract: State and federal officials are joining forces in effort to combat the growing health-fraud industry.  Officials from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and seven eastern states, including Pennsylvania, have joined together in a task force in Philadelphia to work as a unified front against health-fraud violators.

headline: U.S. satellite gave close look at burning plant
abstract: Less than 24 hours after the Soviet news agency announced the Chernobyl nuclear power plant accident, U.S. officials had satellite photographs of the damaged plant.  This photographs enabled U.S. Department of Defense and Central Intelligence Agency officials to see that the plant was still burning, that the fire threatened a second reactor, and that the initial Soviet casualty repot of two dead was absurd.

headline: 'Cashing Out' On Welfare
abstract: PA is being sounded out as a testbed for a Reagan Administration welfare reform program. Under the 'cash out' proposal various welfare benefit programs would be replaced with a direct cash handout to welfare recipients. The goal is not only to reduce costs by eliminating bureaucracy but also to increase the independence of the recipients. Some advocates are concerned that simply giving money to welfare recipients will create even more problems because many do not know how to budget money.

headline: Capitol Calm Shattered By Summer Session
abstract: A 'crisis' that started in June was finally resolved this week. In order to prevent Republican gubenatorial candidate and Lieutenant Governor William Scranton III from gaining political accolades, PA House Majoirty Leader James Manderino inserted language prohibiting distribution of the money until December. When the counties objected the legislature was forced into special session to remove the language. While both sides continue to blame the other for causing the crisis it may ultimately be a non-issue as Democratic gubenatorial candidate Robert P. Casey says he will not bring it up and Scranton saying he would only do so if the Democrats did.

headline: Philly Convention Center wins final Senate approval
abstract: Long delayed legislation to get the stalled Philadelphia Convention Center moving finally received PA Senate passage. The PA House of Representatives could vote on the bill immediately, leaving only PA Governor Dick Thornburgh left to sign off on it. The bill creates a nine member authority to oversee the project.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: One this date in history Henry VIII married Catherine of Aragon in 1509, the Continental Congress formed a committee to draft a Declaration of Independence from Britain in 1776, and in 1979 actor John Wayne died.

headline: For some, transition rules smooth adverse effects of bill
abstract: Transition rules are designed to help certain construction projects by exempting them from current tax laws.

headline: Some see
abstract: In Chester County, Pennsylvania, Democratic party officials are beginning to complain that Patricia Baldwin, the county's only democratic county commissioner, is too soft-spoken and not aggressive enough to hold a seat in Republican county.

headline: Pa. acts to simplify review of health plans
abstract: The PA Health Department, faced with a growing workload and the near-collapse of regional planning units, has proposed rules designed to strengthen and streamline its review of major health care projects across the state.  Under the proposal, the Health Department would establish periodic deadlines for submission of plans for major health care projects.

headline: U.S., Pennsylvania-grade crude oil prices
abstract: The graph depicts falling prices for US crude oil and PA-grade crude oil. US crude fell from $32.51 in 1983 to $11.86 in April 1986. PA-grade crude fell from $28.50 in 1983 to $13.50 in April 1986. The source is the US Department of Energy.

headline: Council Rejects Probe of ICON, Other Programs
abstract: The City Council rejected a proposal by W. Thacher Longstreth to investigate city housing service programs including the Inner City Organizing Network (ICON). While Longstreth acknowledged the current criminal investigation into ICON he argued that a broader investigation was needed due to the high administrative costs of various housing programs; he noted that forty percent of housing funds are spent on administration.

headline: Capitol Crimes?  Probe Is Welcome
abstract: The Scranton Times welcomes the news that the PA State Attorney General and the Federal Bureau of Investigations have launched investigations into the $117 million Capitol expansion project. The Times says that the PA House has done a good job giving it public exposure and thinks there is enough information to warrant federal and state criminal probes.

headline: Philly's Daily News endorses Casey
abstract: The Philadelphia Daily News, the second largest newspaper in Pennsylvania, endorses Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey's campaign rather than former Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell.  Casey has also been endorsed by the Pennsylvania Democratic State Committee and the Pennsylvania AFL-CIO, whereas Rendell has been endorsed by the Pennsylvania United Auto Workers.

headline: HIGHLIGHTS IN HISTORY
abstract: This article highlights important events on this day in history, including the wounding of General Stonewall Jackson in 1863 and the announcement of the fall of Berlin and the surrender of Nazi troops in Italy and parts of Austria in 1945.

headline: Limerick security firm hit
abstract: A federal indictment was issued yesterday charging Yoh Security, the firm hired to protect the Limerick nuclear power plant, with conspiracy and making false statements.  The firm apparently defrauded the federal government by claiming that its untrained guards knew how to handle situations ranging from nuclear emergencies to terrorism.

headline: Special Council Session Set For Bills On Penn's Landing Stalled By Beloff
abstract: Philadelphia City Council President Joseph E. Coleman announced yesterday that he would hold a special session to consider two Penn's Landing development bills being held up by Councilman Leland M. Beloff. Beloff, his chief aid and a reputed organized crime soldier were recently arrested and changed with trying to extort one million dollars from the developer of the project in exchange for favorable action on the two bills. In an unusual move Mayor Goode called Coleman three times on Thursday asking about the status of the bills. The tradition of allowing councilmen to hold up specific bills for whatever reason has not been questioned and Coleman sees no reason to do so now.

headline: Pa. readies hospitals for strike
abstract: Nurses and other health care employees at PA state hospitals and health facilities were poised to go on strike, and some patients were being transferred to community hospitals or sent home.  The strike has been called for today, but local units have been given the option of selecting what time to begin the strike.  Negotiations between the state and union broke off January 10, 1986.

headline: Unit 1 reactor at TMI reaches power output of 91%
abstract: Unit 1 at Three Mile Island will be held at 91% power until 1-6-1986 while a full power balance is achieved throughout the reactor's fuel core.  The plant will then continue escalating to its maximum achievable power level.

headline: Emergency Aid Pried From DPW
abstract: Facing the loss of almost thirty-seven million dollars in federal fees, the PA Department of Public Welfare (DPW) agreed to abide by a court decree ordering it to implement a food stamp program for the destitute. In a suit filed against the DPW and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, it was determined that PA's program was virtually non-existent with the state arguing it complied with regulations as it interpreted them, and county officials claiming a lack of staff or knowledge, and the state's centralized administration system.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: A cartoon of President Reagan talking about using the carrot and stick approach to convince countries to change their policies. One frame has Reagan feeding carrots to a reclining South Africa and the next frame shows Reagan beating Nicaragua with a large stick.

headline: Phony
abstract: Writer opposes a mandatory seat belt law.  He especially opposes the way the  bill has been written so that it is lenient before elections, but will be strict after elections.

headline: Line of Death
abstract: Cartoon depicting a shot fired by a Libyan boat in the Gulf of Sidra being deflected by a dotted line labeled the "Line of Death," in reference to the US naval presence in the Gulf of Sidra.

headline: Shameful records
abstract: This editorial endorses Bob Edgar and criticizes U.S. Senators Arlen Specter and John Heinz for their votes on aid to Latin American Contras and weapons spending.

headline: Specter announces his candidacy here
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter officially announced his candidacy for a second term in the Senate.

headline: Panel kills cutback in drug fees: Welfare Dept. plan voted down
abstract: Rules proposed by the PA Public Welfare Department to cut payments to pharmacists providing prescription drugs to the poor were unanimously rejected by the PA Independent Regulatory Review Commission.  Last week in response to intensive lobbying by druggists, PA House and Senate committees voted unanimously to urge rejection of the proposed rules.

headline: Utilities Must Consider The Long Term
abstract: Joseph Martin of the PA Public Interest Coalition (PennPIC) portrays the recent passage of the PA Utility Commission sunset legislation as a great victory. However, he fails to take into account the short and long-term nature of our industry. Utilities must plan for plants fifteen to twenty years in the future as well as the forty to fifty years that they are expected to operate. Fifteen years ago it appeared that increased demand for energy would require additional plants and now, through uncontrollable circumstances, there is more capacity than need. Instead of having additional capacity in the future, our customers may have to pay higher prices for short-term energy.

headline: Foundations Try To Compensate For Lost Federal Aid: Self-Help Stressed
abstract: The Community Technical Assistance Center has paired ten local non-profit agencies with mentors to help them more effectively raise funds. The mentor will work with the board and staff of their respective agency to develop a fundraising plan as well as a specific grass-roots fundraising project.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon of President Reagan running into the Constitutional Convention and demanding the framers to line up for a drug test

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of West Homestead Mayor John Dindak with some of the town's lotto winnings.

headline: Matters Of Opinion
abstract: A letter expressing witty comments on a variety of issues including: nurses addicted to drugs, Congressional franking privilege, unfit doctors, and alimony.

headline: There are uses for that surplus
abstract: In all likelihood, Pennsylvania will have another budget surplus.  We believe that the surplus should be used to provide tax relief for local governments and school districts, as well as financial aid to distressed transit authorities.

headline: Specter Erred, Kolter Says
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph Kolter was angered by U.S. Senator Arlen Specter's visit to the Veteran's Administration (VA) Medical Center in Butler Township expressing his support for an expansion of the facility. Kolter noted that the Gramm-Rudman budget legislation, which Specter supported, ended plans for the expansion and the VA noted that no major construction was planned at the facility through the end of the decade. Specter indicated, however, that he believed his membership on the U.S. Senate Armed Services and Appropriations Committees would allow him to provide the needed funding.

headline: Patient rights-Strengthen discharge appeal process
abstract: The Patriot-News says that they were wrong when they wrote that a Medicare patient can appeal his discharge from a hospital without becoming liable for the cost of the additional stay even if the decision goes against him. Instead, the paper found that a patient can ask for a Peer Review Organization evaluation even without a written notice, if he or she believes discharge would jeopardize their health. Without written notice, however, the PRO is under no legal obligation to consider the appeal nor is the patient protected from payment for any additional days he or she may stay in the hospital.

headline: Westinghouse celebrates centennial
abstract: PA’s largest private employer, George Westinghouse has received a plaque at company head-quarters. The company pioneered the use of alternating electrical current, the air brake, automated washing machines, the first commercial radio station, the first commercial nuclear reactor, and the engine in the nation's first nuclear submarine.

headline: Funds For Day Care Go To Few
abstract: Allegheny County's system of subsidizing day care has been a continuing source of controversy. Although there are an estimated seven hundred day care providers in the area, only a handful get contracts to offer subsidized slots. Critcs call it an "old boy's network" that denies choice, while proponents point out that spreading already limited aid even further could deny even more people help. They also argue that many of the day care centers are unlicensed and subjected to limited oversight by PA unlike the licensed centers which get the subsidies. Some also point out that choice is a fallacy because many who receive subsidies lack the transportation options that would enable them to use a center outside of their neighborhood. The county did try to revamp the system by contracting with the Health and Welfare Planning Agency (HWPA) to develop a new model. However, the effort ran into problems and was shelved early, with the remaining funds being distributed in the traditional manner. HWPA contends that not enough money was provided up front to handle the administrative costs associated with implementing a new program and working out its problems. They believe that had more money been spent on the front end, more money would have been saved on the back end. Public Welfare Secretary Walter Cohen believes that changes to the system will eventually happen; he has commissioned a Philadelphia consulting firm to study day care in Allegheny County. PA House Welfare Subcommittee Chairman Michael Dawida agrees. The Legislative Budget and Finance Committee has also agreed to study the day care system and produce results by March of next year.

headline: Casey Advantage over Rendell Doesn't Extend to Fundraising
abstract: In the Democratic Gubernatorial primary, Robert Casey leads in the polls, but does not have a money advantage over opponent Ed Rendell.  Each candidate has a little over $1 million, which means they both lag behind Republican candidate William W. Scranton, who is unopposed in his primary and has over $2 million on hand.

headline: Casey, Scranton agree on clean environment, not how to get it
abstract: Although gubernatorial candidates William W. Scranton III and Robert P. Casey both believe that environmental concerns are exxtremenly important, they differ significantly on their solutions to environmental problems and their proposals for funding environmental improvements.  They also offer conflicting ideas on how to manage the state Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Specter Has Large Lead In Election Cash On Hand
abstract: While U.S. Senator Arlen Spector and his Democratic opponent U.S. Representative Bob Edgar raised almost the same amount of money during May and June, Specter was able to rely on larger cash reserves, giving him almost two million dollars while Edgar has over one hundred thousand dollars. Edgar notes that he had a primary election to pay for while Specter did not. Between May and June, Specter spent over eight hundred thousand dollars campaigning while Edgar spent over three hundred fifty thousand dollars. The article also details individual and corporate contributors to both campaigns.

headline: Pennsylvania's Helath-Care Rx
abstract: A bold step has been taken in gaining control of health care costs with the creation of a state panel to collect data on the costs and quality of patient care statewide. There have been attempts to do this locally but they were too indirect to be effective. For consumers to truly have a choice and for competition to be effective people need to know how good the care is and how much it will cost. This panel will answer both of those questions.

headline: What about TMI?
abstract: Writer discusses his concerns about fallout from the Three Mile Island accident in light of the recent Chernobyl nuclear accident.  While acknowledging that the Chernobyl accident was much worse, she still feels that officials have downplayed the actual effects of Three Mile Island.  She expresses concern for the victims of Three Mile Island and the need for the community to support them.

headline: Ceremony Is Set For Center Funding
abstract: A ceremony is to be held today to celebrate Governor Thornburgh handing to Mayor Goode over thirty million dollars in state funding for the convention center. It was originally withheld because Thornburgh was unsure that the legislature would approve the money; now that that has been given the transfer can proceed. The money is part of the almost two hundred million dollars approved as the state's contribution to the center, the rest will be held until needed.

headline: Casey agrees to debate Rendell
abstract: Democrat gubernatorial candidates Edward Rendell and Robert Casey agree to another debate before the Democratic primary.  The Casey campaign accepted Rendell's words that the letter attacking Casey was a "mistake" as an apology, while the Rendell campaign insists that no apology was made.

abstract: Photo of a Pitt student moving in.

abstract: Photo of a shopper at the L.L. Bean store in Maine

headline: Specter pressed to retract aide's attack on challenger Edgar
abstract: Democratic state Chairperson Harris Wofford has asked U.S. Senator Arlen Specter to retract a staff member's personal attacks on his challenger, U.S. Representative Bob Edgar.  Senator Specter's press secretary, Dan McKenna, is accused of using harsh and profane language to describe Representative Edgar and his campaign tactics.

headline: Specter support
abstract: A letter to the paper in which the author is surprised by the paper's endorsement of Democrat Bob Edgar for U.S. Senate in Pennsylvania rather than Republican Arlen Specter, who this author believes has been a strong and independent voice for Pennsylvania.

abstract: Photo of a medical clinic run by a doctor convicted of Medicaid fraud and now under new management

headline: Winds shift radioactivity east, south
abstract: Winds have shifted radioactive clouds caused by a nuclear accident at Chernobyl in the Soviet Union away from Scandinavia, and back towards Soviet bloc countries, where Poland is most affected. Polish state television recorded increased levels of radioactive iodine, and banned the sale of milk from cows that feed on fresh grass. The article is accompanied by photographs from Soviet Life's February issue of the Chernobyl reactor's facilities.

headline: City convention business checking out
abstract: The future of a $455 million Philadelphia convention center is uncertain.  The PA House voted down funding over a month ago, but the issue could reemerge as early as this week.  Proponents of a new center mention how the city continues to lose potential conventions business for the city.

headline: Casey backs lawyer to chair state Democrats
abstract: Pennsylvania Democratic gubernatorial nominee Robert Casey has written members of the Democratic State Committee asking them to support Philadelphia attorney Harris Wofford to chair the party through the November election.  The 400-member committee is expected to comply with Casey's request at its reorganization convention June 28 in Philadelphia.

abstract: Photo of a staffer and youths cutting firewood at a PA VisionQuest camp

headline: Disaster aid sought for Logan
abstract: Yesterday, Governor Dick Thornburgh asked the federal government to declare the Logan section of Philadelphia a disaster area.  In Logan, underground settlement is causing structural damage to homes and has forced the relocation of an entire block of 11 homes.  Governor Thornburgh's actions were criticized by Democratic state legislators--most of whom accused Thornburgh and other Republicans of delaying a bill in the state legislature that would provide 200,000 dollars in state funds to relocate families forced from their homes.

headline: Specter views role as bridge to Democrats
abstract: After a contentious and often bitter U.S. Senate race in Pennsylvania, Republican Arlen Specter, who had defied a nationwide Democratic tide in Senate races in rolling to an easy victory over Rep. Bob Edgar, described a new role for himself in his second term as a bridge builder between the Reagan administration and the Senate's new Democratic majority.

headline: Polyclinic makes changes after study on death rates
abstract: Polyclinic Medical Center’s participation in a comparison of death rates in hospital's intensive-care units has brought changes to its critical care program.  Polyclinic was one of 13 hospitals in the country that voluntarily participated in the study.

abstract: A cartoon depicting a New York City street with people yelling, getting beat up, and total chaos, while inside a cab the driver asks,"SO, ARE YOU STILL GOING TO LONDON FOR YOUR VACATION THIS SUMMER?" and the passenger answers "ARE YOU KIDDING? AND RISK GETTING BLOWN UP BY SOME DERANGED TERRORIST?"

headline: Convention Center Back on Track
abstract: Fred DiBona, President of the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce, says that the Philadelphia Convention Center will soon be a reality, however, another issue has surfaced; the naming of a chairman to run an as-yet-to-be appointed authority to supervise the construction and operation of the $455 million facility.

headline: Casey backs Philadelphia lawyer for state chairman of Democrats
abstract: Pennsylvania Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey endorsed Philadelphia lawyer Harris Wofford, Jr. for chairman of the Democratic State Committee. Nominations for the position will take place at its June 28 meeting, with the chairman succeeding Edward Mezvinsky, who annouced earlier this year that he would step down from the post and give the Democratic gubernatorial nominee the traditional freedom to hand-pick his choice to head the state committee.

headline: The potential dangers of hazardous cargo
abstract: Every day, roughly 500,000 trucks carry hazardous materials across the United States.  And while industry cite the small number of hazardous-materials accidents as evidence that there is no cause for concern about the dangers of transporting these materials, emergency officals say that the relatively low number of accidents is as much a function of luck as it is a function of existing saftey standards; the trucking industry could do much more to help firefighters and police handle accidents.

headline: Specter, Edgar Follow Same Road On Billboard Industry Matter
abstract: As opponents, Bob Edgar and incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter disagree on many issues, but billboards is one that both seem to agree on. Specter recently put a hold on a U.S. Senate transportation bill until his concerns about preserving a 'just compensation' requirement to owners of billboards that are torn down were addressed. His opponent, U.S. Representative Bob Edgar, voted for a compromise  measure in the U.S. House version of the bill that also puts a freeze on new billboards, which is ironic since someone as environmentally conscious as Edgar would normally want to cut back on billboards not just freeze them.

headline: Rabies cases exceed 500
abstract: For the first time in four decades, Pennsylvania has recorded more than 500 cases of rabies in a year. The last time this occurred was 1945, before a rabies vaccine was used.

headline: 55 Okay Even If Violated
abstract: Surveys reveal that most motorists drive faster than fifty-five but don't want the speed limit raised. However, it is important to note that speed does kill, and in addition to the energy that was conserved, numerous lives were also saved when the new limit was implemented. For that reason alone, it is not worth raising it.

headline: Convention center dealt 2nd setback
abstract: The PA Senate Appropriations Committee removed $141 million for the Philadelphia Center City Convention Center project from a $1.2 billion capitol budget bill. This setback has left many wondering if the convention center will ever get underway.

headline: Casey Carries A Debt Into Race For Governor
abstract: Going into his gubernatorial election fight against Republican William W. Scranton III, Democrat Robert P. Casey has almost half a million dollars of debt due to his primary campaign against Edward G. Rendell. The article provides a list of major contributors to both the Casey and Rendell campaigns.

headline: State given high marks for initial efforts on bay
abstract: One year after Pennsylvania joining the Chesapeake Bay Commission, more industries are complying with the federal Clean Water Act, more farmers are controlling erosion, more fisheries are conserving endangered species of fish, and more citizens are joining efforts to save the bay.  In all, more Pennsylvanians are cognizant of the problems affecting the Chesapeake Bay, and more citizens want to help resolve those problems.

headline: State AFL-CIO Endorses Edgar In Senate Contest
abstract: The AFL-CIO endorsed U.S. Representative Bob Edgar in his campaign to unseat U.S. Senator Arlen Specter. The union noted that both candidates were favorable to labor, but that Edgar had a higher percentage of votes supporting labor issues than Specter. In addition, Specter's efforts to block Edgar's endorsement by the union, including calling every member on the executive committee and subtly threatening to  vote against the union on future issues backfired by generating resentment and appearing to try too hard. Specter is not without union support though, The Teamsters, International Ladies Garment Workers Union, Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union, and an number of building and construction unions support him. The endorsement is important to Edgar not only because it provides campaign volunteers, but it is also an additional source of money.

headline: Rendell supports health benefits for jobless
abstract: Edward Rendell, Democratic gubernatorial candidate and former district attorney for Philadelphia, said he supports a bill currently in the PA General Assembly that would provide health insurance to the jobless for up to one year. Legislation is also being examined in PA and in three other states to provide health insurance to those below the federal poverty line. Rendell said that no new taxes would be needed to fund the bill, but that the state's estimated $180 million surplus would cover the costs.

headline: A Bad Connection
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornrbugh's veto of a bill providing thirty-six million dollars to SEPTA was a serious mistake, especially at a time of a state budget surplus. He argued that many agencies ask for more money than they need, but in SEPTA's case it is necessary. Ten million dollars was supposed to go towards replacing cars that were new at the time of President Harding. PA Senator Joe Rocks is pushing a bipartisan effort to override the veto and examine ways to readjust state funding of mass transit. Such changes are necessary in order to ensure the long-term survival of mass transit in all parts of the state, not just in Philadelphia.

headline: Convention Center Design Firms Sued
abstract: The state and the general contractor for the David L. Lawrence Convention Center are suing the designers and engineers of the building over design flaws and poor planning that resulted in the building being finished a year-and-a-half late and eight million dollars over budget. The PA Department of General Services and the contractor had originally sued each other but eventually settled out of court.

headline: Casey 'deplores' posters attacking Scranton
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey has asked that his supporters stop distributing posters that have offended his Republican opponent William W Scranton III.  The posters ridiculed aspects of Scranton's past including his drug abuse, military deferments during Vietnam, and his wealthy background.  The fliers were circulated by the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), a large union that has endorsed Casey.

headline: State commerce chief resigning Dec. 31
abstract: PA State Commerce Secretary James Pickard will resign effective December 31, 1986, three weeks before other members remaining in PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's Cabinet.  Thornburgh praised Pickard as a "constant champion" of policies to broaden the state economy.  Pickard had considered leaving Thornburgh's Cabinet to enter the May 1986 Republican primary for Lieutenant Governor, but decided against it.  A short description of the major initiatives that Pickard undertook as PA Commerce Secretary, a position he began at in January 1983, is included in the article.

headline: Senate Panel Fails To Back Drug Plan
abstract: The PA Senate Public Health and Welfare committee, following a similar recommendation in the PA House, rejected the latest cost-cutting measure by the PA Welfare Department's prescription drug program. The revisions, which regulate the types, costs, and distribution of the program's drugs, will be voted on later by the Independent Regulatory Review Commission (IRRC). However, it is likely that the IRRC will be asked to vote against the changes in order to give the program time to make additional alterations. Robert Williams, who has tried to coordinate the changes, notes that given next year's budget seven million dollars in savings will have to come from somewhere.

headline: A consumers' eye view of PAT
abstract: Peter Floyd, President of the citizens action group Allegheny County Transit Council, says certain steps need to be taken to prevent public transit in the Allegheny area form falling to financial ruin.  Floyd adds that a better method of negotiation between labor and management needs to be implemented, and the operator's code of conduct needs to be enforced.

headline: Convention center gets support
abstract: For the second time in 18 months, Philadelphia City Council approved a resolution for a convention center in Center City.  Mayor Goode said that the action sent a "clear signal" to officials and legislators in Harrisburg to approve funding of the long delayed $455 million facility.

headline: Casey emphasizes jobs; Rendell takes aim at utilities
abstract: Both Pennsylvania Democratic gubernatorial candidates Robert Casey and Ed Rendell traveled through western Pennsylvania yesterday, with Casey pushing a platform of jobs and family values while Rendell called for tougher regulation of utilities to reduce costs and promote Pennsylvania gas and coal.  The Democratic primary takes place on May 20th.
