headline: Reagan years cost state 6.5 billion, study figures
abstract: A new study has found that the first five years of the Reagan administration cost Pennsylvania 6.5 billion dollars in federal grants to social programs and state and local government.  Across the United States, roughly 50 major grant programs received 114.8 billion dollars less than they would have if 1981 service and federal-funding levels remained intact.

headline: State Senate may block governor's court nominees
abstract: Pennsylvania State Senate Democrats are likely to block Governor Thornburgh's nomination of two men to fill vacancies on Commonwealth Court, because they would prefer that Democrat governor-elect Bob Casey fill the vacancies after he is sworn in on January 20.

headline: 'Sick tax"
abstract: PA State House Bill 1971 would establish the Health Care Cost Reform Act. The Patriot News says there is little in the legislation that could be expected to control health care costs in any direct or significant way, citing that it seeks to create a large and cumbersome new bureaucracy by imposing a tax on medical and physician care. The Patriot News also says that meeting the needs of the sick is a responsibility that all of society should share, not just those who provide the care.

headline: A decision coming soon on rise in bridge tolls
abstract: The Delaware River Port Authority, consisting of eight members from Pennsylvania and New Jersey, is approaching an important decision on bridge tolls.  Public hearings have been held on a staff proposal for an increase from 75 cents to 90 cents, with relatively little opposition voiced on either side of the river.  Tolls have not been increased since 1981.

headline: Convention hall cost up $24 million, city says
abstract: The cost of the proposed Center City Convention Center in Philadelphia has increased to nearly $455 million, a jump of nearly $24 million. The increase comes at a time when the city is trying to win approval of legislation to free up nearly $180 million in state funding for the project. City officials are hoping their approval will come within the next two weeks.

headline: Casey fundraiser held
abstract: 25 year-old Bob Casey Jr. runs a fundraiser for his father, Bob Casey, who is running in the PA Democratic gubernatorial primary. About 150 people attended.

headline: Teen drinking
abstract: This editorial urges Governor Thornburgh to veto HB 843, legislation that suspends the driver's licenses of underage drinkers.  The bill, which suspends driving privileges anywhere from 90 days to one year, is excessive and will actually reduce responsible alcohol consumption in the state.  The zero-tolerance nature of this bill--something evinced by a fine of up to 1,000 dollars for a parent who shares a beer with a child--makes alcohol a forbidden fruit and is likely to induce abuse.

headline: State Senate moves to resurrect agency
abstract: Resurrection of the Independent Regulatory Review Commission began when the PA Senate agreed unanimously to revitalize the agency, which had died at the end of 1985.  Should the PA House of Representatives go along with the Senate, the Independent Regulatory Review Commission would once again be the agency through which all governmental regulations must flow before they may be given final approval.

headline: Smoking drug mix seen as coming threat
abstract: Luceille Fleming, Deputy Secretary of PA Health for Drug and Alcohol Programs, said a practice called space basing is growing among West Coast addicts and can be expected in Pittsburgh in less than two years.  Space basing involves smoking a mixture of crack cocaine, phencyclidine, and either marijuana or tobacco.  Fleming expects Philadelphia to see space basing sooner due to the fact that it is in "the corridor" between Boston and Washington.  Fleming got a glimpse of PA's future drug habits at a meeting of the National Association of State Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program Directors.  PA residents can look for abuses of a substance called "black tar heroin" in the near future as well.  Charles Winek, toxicologist for the Allegheny County Coroner’s Office, agreed with Fleming's forecast.

headline: Alcohol tied to 704 state road deaths
abstract: According to the PA Department of Health, drunk drivers were involved in 625 traffic accidents that killed 704 people in Pennsylvania in 1984.

headline: Convention vote: setback but not defeat
abstract: The planned Philadelphia convention center has seen many setbacks, and the editorial board writes that supports should not let up now.  Just within a month, the vote against the convention center went from 128-68 to 108-90, so there is reason to be positive and for supporters to keep pushing for funding for the new convention center.

headline: Casey hopes campaign lands safely this time
abstract: Pennsylvania gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey believes he will win the Democratic primary today, despite losing in gubernatorial primaries in 1966, 1970, and 1978.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of Governor Thornburgh meeting with third-graders

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photograph depicts Carnegie Mellon President Richard Cyert speaking at the opening of the Pittsburgh Technology Park.  Also pictured on the state are Paul Brophy, Frank Brooks Robinson, Governor Dick Thornburgh, Wesley Posvar, John P Robin, Mayor Caliguiri, Tom Foerster, and K Leroy Irvis.

headline: Camp investors need protection
abstract: This editorial urges state legislators to pass a recession law that protects consumers who purchase campsite contracts.  These consumers are often mislead and are pressured into lifetime contracts that cannot be vacated; this leaves unsuspecting consumers with a contract they cannot get out of and a camp site that is virtually impossible to sell.  A recession law would provide much-needed regulation to this industry.

headline: Smoking issue set for airing
abstract: PA Representative Michael Dawida has introduced the Clean Indoor Air Act, or House Bill 259, in order to create smoking sections in restaurants. A similar bill died in committee last year but support for this bill is strong. A vote on the PA House of Representatives floor is expected.

headline: Arlen on Conrail Sale: 'It's an Uphill Fight…'
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter is trying to rally public support to have the sale of Philadelphia-based Conrail to a Virginia company derailed. Spector has been fighting the proposed acquisition of Conrail, fearing the new owners would move some of Conrail's 15,000 jobs out of state and shift company headquarters from Philadelphia.

headline: County, USAir Start Terminal Finance Negotiations
abstract: Allegheny County has begun negotiations with USAir and others over leases for a proposed terminal. The fees are important because they will guarantee funds the county wants to issue for the project. Although the state has agreed to help fund the project along with the county the exact amount has yet to be decided. Also at issue is where in the state budget the funding will be. Governor Thornburgh wants to put the money in the general operating budget where it would have to be approved every year, while Democratic legislative leaders want it in the capital budget where the money would need to be authorized only once. The project is considered vital to Allegheny County's development not only because of the immediate jobs created by the additional flights, but also because of the jobs from businesses that are expected to move onto the land developed for the terminal.

headline: Casey literature annoys Scranton
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate William W Scranton III called on democratic candidate Bob Casey to stop using controversial posters that focus on Scranton's past.  The posters depict Scranton's admitted drug use during the 1960s and 1970s.  Casey responded that he had not approved the posters.  The posters were made by the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), a large union that has endorsed Casey.

abstract: Photograph depicts the raising of a flag for the Pittsburgh Technology Center in Hazelwood.

headline: State Catholics oppose legislation to aid the poor by taxing hospitals
abstract: The Pennsylvania Catholic Conference opposes a PA House of Representative's bill that would establish a new PA state tax on hospitals to help pay the medical bills of indigent patients. The proposed legislation, House Bill 1971, would create a Health Care Cost Containment Commission and impose a 1% tax on the gross operating revenues of the hospitals.  The commission would also gather data on health care costs.  The Hospital Association of Pennsylvania opposes the bill as well.

headline: Bill aims to hit teen drinkers where it hurts: driving
abstract: In Pennsylvania, a bill that would require a three-month driving license suspension for first-time convictions of minors for any alcohol-related offense has already been overwhelmingly approved by the PA House. The bill is supported by a number of citizens' groups, tavern assocations, and law enforcement agencies. It could be considered as early as next week by the PA Senate.

headline: Effectiveness of economic development in Pa. disputed
abstract: Pennsylvania offers a wide range of economic development programs, but critics argue that the programs work least in areas where they're needed most.  Specifically they charge that the programs merely subsidize development that will occur anyway and that the programs are of very limited use to the mill towns of west and north-central Pennsylvania.

headline: Casey mindful of '78 loss
abstract: Robert P. Casey, a lawyer from Scranton and gubernatorial hopeful, is mindful of his 1978 loss in the gubernatorial election which was won by Dick Thornburgh. Casey says he is most proud of his work as PA Auditor General, although he was also a member of the PA Senate. He has tried three previous times to run for governor, but lost primaries to eventual winner PA Governor Milton Shapp and Pittsburgh Mayor Peter Flaherty.

abstract: Picture of Ginny Thornburgh.

headline: PA House debating seat belts
abstract: Yesterday, the PA House of Representatives debated controversial seat-belt legislation that would require front-seat passengers to buckle up or face a fine of five dollars.  The deabte is expected to continue today; a similar measure has already passed in the state Senate.

headline: State panel will study health costs
abstract: The newly established PA Health Care Cost Containment Council, under Act 89, has a timeline of 180 days to three years to develop a plan for the containment of costs and quality of service provisions.  The council has a budget of $1.8 million and will have temporary headquarters in the PA Health Department offices.

headline: Buckle up, urges judge who sees crash results
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the writer mentions that automobile accidents are the leading killer of young people in Pennsylvania.  The writer, a traffic court judge, asks for a law mandating the wearing of seatbelt use in cars.

headline: Elections, organs, mortgages
abstract: Editorial outlines three brief legislative actions that the editorial board feels deserves praise.  First, the state senate passed a bill that would allow Pittsburgh voters to decide whether to change how the Pittsburgh City Council members are elected; whether they will continue to be elected at large or change to be elected by district.  Secondly, the legislature approved a bill requiring hospitals to ask family members of dead or dying patients to donate the patient's organs for transplant.  Lastly, the state house passed a compromise bill guaranteeing homeowners will be able to recover some equity from their foreclosed property if it is auctioned at sheriff's sales.

headline: Casey pick has hidden consequence
abstract: PA gubernatorial Democratic candidate Bob Casey officially introduced Mark Singel as his choice for lieutenant governor.

abstract: Photo of gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey at a senior citizens center

headline: Political Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon showing one soldier insisting that another soldier put out a cigarette because they're harmful while explosions go off in the background.

headline: 59 million cut in rates advocated for Duquense Light
abstract: As a result of savings the company will see from federal tax-overhaul legislation, Pennsylvania's consumer advocate argued that Duquense Light Company should have its rates cut by 59 million dollars a year.  In contrast to the consumer advocate's position, the company has requested a rate increase of 48 million dollars.

headline: State setting up AIDS program
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh’s administration has offered state money for education programs on HIV/AIDS.  Alarmed at the explosion of new cases of Acquired Immune Deficiency or AIDS syndrome, many states are rushing money and resources into HIV/AIDS education.  In his budget message, Thornburgh proposed that $250,000 be spent on a program in Pennsylvania.

headline: Bumpity-Bump
abstract: In this letter to the editor, the author feels that since they  have had a chance to drive on Market Street, they believe it is no honor to have the street named after them. Instead it should be identified as the pothole-filled, alignment-damaging road that it is.

headline: Escalating costs
abstract: The graph depicts the rise in cost estimates for finishing the PA Capitol Building since 1980. In 1980, the cost was $15 million, while in 1984 the estimates were $117.8 million. The source is a testimony submitted in 1984 to the PA House Select Committee to Investigate Compliance with the Steel Procurement Act.

headline: Casey set to launch gubernatorial bid
abstract: Former PA Auditor General Robert P. Casey will announce his candidacy for governor today.  The Harrisburg portion of the campaign is scheduled to kick-off at noon in the Capitol Rotunda.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of gubernatorial candidate William W. Scranton III

headline: The Movie We'd Really Like to See: Best Picture Out of Africa
abstract: Political cartoon portraying a movie poster for "Out of Africa," with a hunter bearing a resemblance to President Ronald Reagan kicking a monkey bearing the resemblance of Libyan head of state Muamar Quadaffi, with a caption on the bottom saying "A Gulf of Sidra Production."

headline: Will push for changes at Alcosan, state lawmakers says
abstract: A state legislator has proposed changes to how the Allegheny County Sanitary Authority's board members are chosen.  State Representative Tom Murphy criticized the Pittsburgh City Council for its oversight of the authority, and he introduced a plan that would require one of the board members to be a Brighton-Heights resident--the neighborhood where the authority's waste-treatment plant is located.

headline: State, nursing union to resume negotiations; strikers plan rally
abstract: More than 800 striking members of the Pennsylvania Nurses Association are expected to rally at the Capitol Building in Harrisburg shortly before talks between the union and the state resume.  The union represents 3,800 nurses, pharmacists, and medical technicians who work at state-owned institutions.  About 75% of its members have been on strike to protest a four-month contract dispute with the state.

headline: By feet, bike or car, we'll get there somehow, SEPTA patrons say
abstract: SEPTA patrons say the will get to wherever they are going by biking, walking, or taxi if Philadelphia mass transit employees go on strike. Philadelphia officials are expecting and preparing for the worse.

headline: Funds sought to start Carlisle shelter
abstract: A local PA coalition applied for a $180,677 state grant to establish a shelter for the homeless in a downtown hotel.  The grant, sought from the PA State Department of Public Welfare, would allow the Cumberland County Coalition Shelter to buy and refurbish the James Wilson Hotel.   As planned by the coalition, the shelter would be available for families, single parents, domestic and public violence victims, disaster victims, needy senior citizens, the unemployed, and "prisoners released to nowhere."

headline: Casey stressing government experience
abstract: Former PA Auditor General Robert P. Casey is trying to make another run for governor of Pennsylvania. Casey has lined up support among key political leaders around the state.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of idle garbage trucks

headline: Today's sports shorts
abstract: Daniel and Jeanne Schmedlin have advanced to the regional competition in the Equitable family ski challenge, with a combined time of 56.94 at Ski Roundtop.

headline: Judges who took union money heard roofers' cases
abstract: A Philadelphia Inquirer investigation found that many of the same judges receiving gifts and campaign contributions from the Roofers Union were also deciding cases involving union workers--sometimes only days after receving contributions.  The decisions usually benefitted the union workers and often resulted in the dispensation of less severe penalties than state sentencing guidelines require.  Currently, the FBI is investigating cash gifts from the Roofers Union to public officials in 1984 and 1985.

headline: Tenfold increase seen in AIDS cases
abstract: A new report by the US Center for Disease Control for the city of Philadelphia found that by 1991 nearly 3,800 people in the city will either be suffering from AIDS or have died from it over the preceding decade, a tenfold increase from the current number of reported AIDS cases in the city.

headline: Cancel SEPTA service cuts
abstract: Independent examiners who conducted public hearings on the Philadelphia area's public transit system, SEPTA, concluded that the proposal for massive service cuts would be devasting and recommended that they be rescinded.  This author supports this as well as saying that the cuts are unnecessary, given PA Governor-elect Casey's commitment to solving the financial problems of SEPTA.

headline: GAO urged to expand Phila. Housing probe
abstract: Pennsylvania Senators John Heinz and Arlen Spector have asked the General Accounting Office to investigate the use of federal housing monies by Philadelphia.  They want the Office to look into why the city tended to exceed the cap on administrative costs for projects as well as to examine the oversight by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development to ensure that the city is in code with their regulations and that the Department is treating the city fairly.

headline: Casey takes funds lead
abstract: Party-endorsed Pennsylvania Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey led opponent Ed Rendell in fund-raising in in the most recent period.  The democratic primary takes place on May 20.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of Jeffrey Blum outlining the PA Public Interest Coalition's new agenda

headline: State United Way executive named
abstract: Juliet C. Rowland was named president and chief executive officer of the United Way of Pennsylvania.

headline: The agenda: The states focus on children ...
abstract: Dozens of state legislatures throughout the United States are enacting educational initiatives for children, including state-subsidized day care, new  pre-kindergarten programs, increased aid for dependent children benefits, along with expanded maternal and child-health and nutrition efforts.  The impetus for these measures came from a rash of alarming statistics concerning the wellbeing of children in the US.

headline: CAT Fund collection system makes work, not sense
abstract: Columnist Tom Bigler writes about the Catastrophic Trust Fund, which he believes is a good program despite PA's law requiring motorists to be insured. However, the CAT Fund is a government fund collected and administered by private firms. He states that the CAT Fund could just as easily be administered by the PA Department of Transportation, but suggests the state Legislature made the CAT Fund privately handled to avoid outrage at likely increased license renewal fees, should the CAT Fund be placed in the hands of PennDOT.

headline: Goode Would Aim State $ at Logan
abstract: Mayor Goode has said that the city would pay to purchase properties owned by the federal government in order to relocate residents of the Logan neighborhood, which is becoming dangerous due to sinking ground in the area.  He would use state funds that he is hoping to receive.  Already some residents have been relocated by Human Services in order to protect children that live in the homes.

headline: Casey to give speech as officials sworn in
abstract: Former PA State Auditor General Robert P. Casey, who is expected to seek the Democratic nomination for PA governor this year, will be the guest speaker on 1-6-1986 as city and county officials take the oath of office.

abstract: Photo of a VisionQuest camp resident with an animal

headline: Saftey Belt Proposal
abstract: The mandatory seat-belt law before the state House is insufficient and needs to be strengthened; the bill needs to resemble the Senate version of the bill, which is much stronger.  The penalty of five dollars needs to be increased to twenty, and the secondary-offense provision--a provision that allows for the fine to be imposed only if someone is stopped for another violation--needs to be removed.

headline: Still Practicing Medicine On An Unwitting Public
abstract: With tighter regulations and improved oversight the PA Department of Public Welfare (DPW) is citing and dismissing an increasing number of doctors for Medicaid fraud. Yet the state medical boards rarely follow-up, and many continue to practice on unwitting patients. According to state records: thirty-four doctors are currently barred from Medicaid and also convicted on criminal charges and another group of physicians have been dropped because their methods violate Medicaid practices. Of the 142 medical professionals barred from Medicaid, state licensing boards have failed to take action on 88 of them, enabling them to continue seeing patients. Various licensing boards in the state rarely discipline professionals convicted of fraud or found to have committed unprofessional practices, generally responding only to those who have harmed their patients. Even when boards do act it often takes years to investigate, with professionals allowed to practice in the interim period. The system itself is ripe for fraud. The large volume of bills that are received daily by the state, 100,000 on average, are impossible to review adequately. Working almost as an honor system, DPW has been trying to fix its review method by using computers to flag unusual billings and establishing a Bureau of Utilization Review to ensure that patient care is up to standards. Since the effort began six years ago, 600 medical professionals have been expelled from the program, most lasting from three to five years.

headline: Compliance figures 'fudged'
abstract: The formula that determines whether enough drivers obey the speed limit for states to collect millions of federal highway money is confusing and states that may have figures showing they are out of compliance, by the time the figures are reconfigured, are in compliance.  If not for the fudge factor, nearly all states - including Pennsylvania- would face federal sanctions.  When diluted, the number of Pennsylvania drivers ignoring the speed limit in 1985 drops from 50.8% to 36.8%.

headline: GOP drops Phila. as site in '88
abstract: The Republican National Committee has removed Philadelphia from the list of possible sites for the 1988 Republican National Convention because it failed to meet the hotel and media workspace requirements.  The list is down to three possible sites: New Orleans, Kansas City and Atlanta.

headline: Casey undecided on running mate
abstract: Democratic PA gubernatorial candidate Robert P. Casey says he will select his running mate before the March 11 filing deadline. As of now the PA lieutenant governor's race remains uncertain.

abstract: Photo of Laurey Coover eating ice cream on the statehouse steps as part of an ice cream manufacturers promotion

headline: Writers to discuss ex-Gov. Lawrence: Seminar set at Wilson College
abstract: Three authors of former Pennsylvania Governor David L. Lawrence biographies and men and women who knew most about his public life will meet June 14 at the 16th Rose Hill Seminar at Wilson College, Chambersburg, Pennsylvania.

headline: Study Asks Tougher Restrictions On Prescription Drugs In Penna.
abstract: PA Health Secretary H. Arthur Miller released a study yesterday recommending restrictions on the prescription of amphetamines. The report notes that PA, and Philadelphia especially, ranks among the top ten in the nation in abuse of the drug.  Many of the prescriptions for it can be traced back to a handful of doctors. The report suggested that if state medical licensing boards did not start issuing regulations then state-level action would have to be taken. It also urged that the state and licensing boards communicate better, particularly when notifying the other side about doctors punished for questionable prescriptions.

headline: Compromise on bridge tolls
abstract: The Delaware River Bridge Authority reached a compromise on raising tolls on several bridges connecting PA and New Jersey. The toll increase will maintain fares on the Port Authority Transit Corporation's High Speed Line. The DRBA also postponed committing to a bond issue, whose proceeds might presumably fund redecking the Benjamin Franklin Bridge.

headline: Greater Pitt aid grounded
abstract: The state House has rejected a $1.2 billion capital projects bill that includes $97 million for the restoration of the Greater Pittsburgh International Airport.  The bill now goes to a joint House-Senate conference committee where lawmakers will attempt compromise.

headline: Casey, Bailey endorsed at Democratic convention
abstract: Scranton attorney Robert P. Casey and PA State Auditor General Don Bailey were endorsed for PA Governor and U.S. Senator nominations at a Democratic State Committee convention. Other democratic candidates vowed to run in the primary.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of lobbyists waiting outside the Senate majority caucus room

headline: Teen birth control backed
abstract: The author would like to support the May 21 article by Joyce White supporting the concept of school-based clinics whose function, among other health-care services, would be the provision of contraceptive services to adolescents.

headline: Conflict Follows TMI Train
abstract: Controversy continues to follow the Three Mile Island (TMI) accident. For the next eighteen months material from the accident will be shipped by train to a facility in Idaho for storage and study. However, opposition over the route, through a number of Pittsburgh neighborhoods, and various other cities further West as well as a variety of concerns about the security of the rail cars themselves continue to generate complaints. The hands of General Public Utilities (GPU), TMI's operator, are tied in terms of the route as federal regulations require the fastest and highest quality route be used. As for the rail cars themselves, there is concern that the decision not to dry the material (in order to save millions of dollars and prevent months of delays) risks an explosion. GPU argues that it will force out as much moisture as possibel prior to shipment and that the materials packed inside will prevent any remaining moisture from causing an explosion. There are also arguments about the ability of the container car to withstand a crash. Finally, Marvin Resnikoff, a staff scientist for the Sierra Club argues that the material could easily catch fire while in transit.

headline: Group gets federal housing loan
abstract: The US Department of Housing and Urban Development granted a contract to Volunteers of America to construct a housing complex intended for elderly and disabled persons in Harrisburg.

headline: Casey, Scranton And Patronage
abstract: Patronage has been on the decline in PA over the last several years, especially under PA Governor Dick Thornburgh who refused to fire people for political reasons. Both Robert P. Casey and William W. Scranton III should express their views on patronage, especially since there is specualtion that Scranton may revive it.

abstract: Photo of national Republican Party chairman Frank J. Fahrenkopf

headline: Thornburgh signs anti-rabies bill affecting dogs, cats
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed legislation mandating anti-rabies vaccines for dogs and some cats.  Taking effect in 60 days, the law mandates vaccination once every three years for all dogs and those cats that spend part of any day outside.  Rabies among wildlife has become an increasingly serious problem in PA, with 561 confirmed cases of rabies in animals in 1986, as opposed to 450 in 1985.  The PA Department of Health says the outbreak covers 28 counties and involves 10 animal species.  The PA Department of Agriculture will continue to assist in establishing low-cost anti-rabies clinics, and it may contract with the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia for a comprehensive multi-year wildlife vaccine research program.

headline: Critical Needs In Transit
abstract: There are growing signs of a bipartisan effort to increase funding for the state's twenty-two mass transportation authorities, including SEPTA. PA Senator M. Joseph Rocks pushed last week for more money to meet the capital and operating needs of transit systems statewide. PA Representatives Charles F. Nahill Jr., Jon D. Fox, and Richard A. McClatchey Jr. have started writing a bill to provide additional money to every PA transit authority. Neither gubernatorial candidate has talked about transportation funding in their campaigns. If they don't talk about it now, then how much effort will they spend advocating it in the future?

headline: Group submits priority list for federal funds
abstract: Leaders of 46 public and non-profit agencies in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania called on the community to help set funding priorities for city and county services following projected budget cuts resulting from the Gramm-Rudman balanced budget law.  This law would especially hurt housing and neighborhood improvement projects, and the group of leaders released recommendations on how to address the budget cuts, including urging the state to remove restrictions on the Lottery funds, encouraging state grants, and encouraging religious institutions to invest in local communities.

headline: Casey, Scranton To Debate Spurs For Economy
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert P. Casey accepted the challenge of his opponent Republican Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton to debate how each would improve PA's economy. In his response, Casey noted that Scranton rather than contemplating an overhaul of the PA Department of Commerce was merely adding one bureaucracy on top of another by creating a Department for Employment and Training. He also alleged that Scranton's proposals came without a price tag, although Scranton's campaign responded that an estimated cost of $100 million had been provided previously. Casey has proposed spending $229 million over four years for economic development.

abstract: Photo of PA Representative Correale F. Stevens displaying a t-shirt supporting the state police, which he later gave to PA House committee chairman Alphonso Deal.

headline: Too many babies dying in state
abstract: Pennsylvania has a higher rate of infant mortality than even poverty stricken Third World countries such as Costa Rice and Cuba.  Even worse, the infant mortality rate for non-whites is double the state average. The Women's Agenda, a statewide organization lobbying for women and children, urge adoption of a comprehensive maternity care program.

headline: Drinking penalty
abstract: The writer refutes a previous letter that said that they agreed with the veto of a anti-underage drinking bill that would have suspended driving privledges for offenders even if they were not driving at the time of the infraction.  The author disagrees that it would be discriminatory to do so and recounts the trial of his stepson when he refused to take a DUI test and subsequently lost his license.

headline: 'Hands' expects 150,000: Local link ready for today's event
abstract: 150,000 people were expected to join hands at 3pm today in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania as part of Hands Across America, the huge effort to fight homelessness and hunger in the United States.  Nationwide about 6 million people are needed and at last count organizers were a couple of million short.  It is estimated that between $5-7 million was raised in the state.

headline: Casey, Scranton to vie for governor
abstract: Scranton lawyer Robert Casey defeated former Philadelphia District Attorney Edward Rendell in the Democratic primary yesterday, which means he will face Republican Lt. Gov. William Scranton in the gubernatorial election in November.  According to unofficial returns from half the state's 9.539 precincts, Casey led Rendell 53 percent to 45 percent.

abstract: Photo of PA Senate Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer

headline: 255 farmers selected to join state land conservation program
abstract: 255 Pennsylvania farmers have joined the Conservation Reserve Program, which takes erodible land out of farming for 10 years.   It is a good deal for farmers, who make money on their erodible land while gaining control over the environmental impact of erosion.

headline: Drivers urged to turn on headlights for seat-belt bill
abstract: The Pennsylvania Association of the National Head Injury Foundation is urging drivers to turn on their headlights on Wednesday in a statewide show of support for the seat-belt legislation that is in the PA House Consumer Affairs Committee, having been passed by the PA Senate last year.

headline: High-Tech Center On J&L Site Funded
abstract: Carnegie-Mellon University (CMU) is slated to receive thirty million dollars for a new high technology center on the site of an old steel mill on Second Avenue. The center would house firms working with the school's Robotics Institute and Software Engineering Institute to design and build robots. The state capital budget also includes money for roadwork and site preparation work at the former steel mill site as well as money for a new science center near Three Rivers Stadium.

headline: Casey, Thornburgh meet over lunch
abstract: Pennsylvania Democratic Governor-elect Robert Casey met current Republican Governor Dick Thornburgh for lunch in the first meeting between the two since Casey defeated Thornburgh's lieutenant governor, William Scranton, in a bitter campaign.

headline: Avian flu scare brings order to kill chickens
abstract: PA Department of Agriculture is moving to head off a return of the avian flu epidemic having ordered the destruction of 7,200 chickens.  The Agriculture Department has urged farmers to maintain strict sanitation of birds to prevent the disease’s spread.

headline: Drunk-driving law's costs nag enforcement officers
abstract: Financing stricter enforcement of the state's tough drunken-driving law has been a concern to law enforcement officials since the legislation was proposed in 1981.  Enforcement of the drunken driving law has tightened, according to statistics compiled by the PA Department of Transportation.

headline: High-tech firms lead job growth, study says
abstract: A study released by the Pittsburgh High Technology Council in Pennsylvania said that advanced technology companies accounted for a quarter of the employment growth in the past two years, though still a relatively small part of the region's economy.

headline: Casey's Cabinet appointees
abstract: By the time Robert Casey becomes Pennsylvania's 107th governor on January 20 he will have formed most of his Cabinet, with the makeup of the Cabinet going a long way in determining how well the state can deliver its services to the people.  This author urges Casey to remember the makeup of the Cabinet is vital to political success.

abstract: Photo of Philadelphia City Councilman Leland M. Beloff being sworn in by Judge J. Sydney Hoffman

headline: Breeder Predicts Hefty, Red Cattle Will Win Favor With Beed Farmers
abstract: PA's first full-blooded Salers bull attracted much attention at Ag Progress Days. Breeders predict the breed will soon gain favor with other farms because they produce more beef, are higher in protein, and have less fat, cholesterol, and calories than other beef on the market. The breed originated in France and is descended from Egyptian Red cattle.

headline: Early morning light yesterday revealed scene of devastation
abstract: Photograph showing scene of devastation along Saxonburg Road on the North Side (Pittsburgh), including these twisted vehicles not far rom intersection of Brown Hill Road in O'Hara that followed from flash flooding this week.

headline: Hillas is an excellent choice
abstract: PA Governor Thornburgh's announcement that Roger S. Hillas has agreed to chair the Philadelphia Convention Center Authority should expedite construction of the new facility in the city.  Many think it is welcomed assurance that the project will move forward under capable leadership.

headline: Casey's candidacy bolstered in west
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Richard Caliguiri and Allegheny County Commissioner Pete Flaherty have put their support behind Robert P. Casey, for the Democratic Party's gubernatorial nomination.  Caliguiri also announced that Erie Mayor Louis Tullio and Allegheny county Commissioner Thomas Forester have backed Casey.

headline: Canada requested to reconsider ban
abstract: Both of PA’s U.S. Senators have asked the Canadian government to withdraw its ban on unprocessed PA poultry products, saying the avian influenza outbreak is under control.  The senators say the ban was unfair because the avian flu affected only four of state's 67 counties.

headline: Enforce belt law
abstract: A letter that urges enforcment of the seltbelt for children under four law in Pennsylvania.

headline: Hope for the other Philadelphia
abstract: The post-industrial wasteland surrounding Philadelphia's thriving inner core has lost more than 140,000 manufacturing jobs in the last two decades and has high crime rates, unemployment, drug use, mental illness, broken families, and school dropouts. Now city officials are focusing on so-called enterprise zones, three slices of this area created to spur economic development, in a state-funded program that is designed to assist areas such as these.

headline: Casey's choices: Round 1
abstract: This author sees Pennsylvania Governor-elect Bob Casey's initial choices for his cabinet and executive staff as revealing a preference for both competence and personal familiarilty - as well as a flair for surprise in the selection process.  The author also sees the slow pace of selection as displaying needed caution in the selection process.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of President Harding

headline: Disagreement Spills Out Over Federal Milk Plan
abstract: A program by the federal government to reduce dairy production and raise milk prices by buying up dairy herds has met with mixed reviews. The PA Agriculture Stabilization and Conservation Service, which is administering the program, estimates the buyout will reduce PA dairy production by three percent. However, beef producers argue that it has also resulted in beef prices dropping between five and eight dollars as many of the dairy herds were sent off to slaughter. Whether the buyout will end production surpluses over the long-term is unknown, with several people noting it is still too early. Milk surpluses are a result of increases in U.S. government price supports in the previous decade which resulted in increased production.

headline: Expressway plans grind to a halt
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) announced yesterday that it would stop the work on the Schuykill Expressway in the Philadelphia area because the contractor hired to complete the last segment of the $175 million project were unable to finish the work.  In turn, the two contractors filed a complaint with the Pennsylvania Claims Board seeking $48 million in damages from PennDOT.

headline: Housing here too old, builders say
abstract: Builders say that Pittsburgh housing is in dire need of renovation if the area hopes to become a high technology and service center.  Low home prices will not make up for the fact many of the houses are almost 50 years old.  The builders say a rebirth of the housing industry would be impossible unless the federal government reduces interest rates and long approval procedures.

headline: Casey's promise
abstract: Editorial praises PA Governor-elect Robert Casey for appointing William Keisling, a registered Republican, to be his chief of staff.  Democrats have claimed to be "shocked" by the move.  The ediorial believes that many PA residents needed to be shocked like this.  The editorial hopes that Casey continues to buck tradition this way, and notes that appointments such as this should be based on merit, not party.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of President Reagan, U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice Warren Burger, Justice William Rehnquist, and nominee Antonin Scalia at a press conference

headline: Dogs star
abstract: A three-hour hearing was held in regards to legislation proposed by Pittsburgh Councilman Jack Wagner, who supports construction of a dog track somewhere in the city of Pittsburgh.  Wagner's bill would not legalize dog tracks but would ask the Allegheny County Board of Elections to place a nonbinding question about dog racing on the May primary ballot.

headline: cartoon
abstract: A newspaper cartoon showing a tractor trailer driver holding a bicycle horn in his hand. The caption reads, " Forget about the brakes and tires take a look at my brand-new horn."

headline: In City Council, The Reaction Is Shock And Anger
abstract: The leader of the City Council's Democratic majority, Joan L. Krajewski, believed she was taking routine action when she held up consideration of two measures involving the development at Penn's Landing at the request of Councilman Leland M. Beloff (in whose district the redevelopment would take place). However, after Beloff's arrest for trying to extort a million dollars from the project's developer in exchange for favorable treatment of the project, it appears that the City Council was duped. The arrests remind some of when Council President George X. Schwartz and Councilmen Harry P. Jannotti and Louis P. Johanson were indicted six years ago for accepting money in an FBI sting. Council members interviewed expressed the hope that a special session would be held soon in order to move the project forward.

headline: Cawley Bill Defeated
abstract: The writer expresses no surprise that a bill intruduced by PA Representative Gaynor Cawley that would permit communities to refuse trash from other municipalities was defeated.  The author says that the government needs to devise alternate methods for cities to dispose of their garbage.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of Robert Redford and associate conductor of the Utah Symphony, Charles Ketcham

headline: Midstate Drought Fails To  Put Bite On Potato-Chip Makers
abstract: While York County potatoes have been one of the hardest hit crops in this year's drought, it has little impact on local potato-chip manufacturers. Because most get their potatoes from other parts of PA and even as far away as Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina. The drought has produced only a limited reduction in supplies, although some note that the quality and size of some loads of potatoes has been lower than normal.

headline: Frightening safety defects
abstract: One out of every three trucks checked in Pennsylvania is being ordered off the road because of safety defects, causing the editorial board to say that the crackdown by state inspectors against trucks with safety defects is long overdue.

headline: Lawmakers Set Aside Convention Center Differences
abstract: PA state legislators have agreed to a compromise on the bill that will allow construction of the proposed $455 million Center City Convention Center in Philadelphia. Philadelphia officials have been trying to get approval and the final agreement was the language of an affirmative-action clause governing the award of construction contracts and employment on the project.

headline: Center set for key vote
abstract: The PA Senate is scheduled to vote on a bill to create an authority to oversee the $55 million Philadelphia Convention Center. Objections raised by Philadelphia City Council President Joseph Coleman may delay the venture once again.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of the Dorthy Six blast furnace from the Fairview Cemetery in McKeesport

headline: Photo
abstract: A photo of John S. Thompson Jr. showing stunted corn and dry soil

headline: Gamble Township claims road work state's job
abstract: Gamble Township residents will ask the state to help maintain dirt roads around Rose Valley Lake, a PA Fish Commission facility.  With the aid of PA Representative Alvin C. Bush, the town has petitioned the state in effort to persuade that it cannot support the upkeep of the roads around the 400-acre lake.

headline: Legislators to push for disabled again
abstract: Bills to expand the Pennsylvania state handicapped accessibility law were introduced in both the State House and Senate and were embraced by organizations representing disabled Pennsylvanians.  Changes would require many renovated public buildings to be made wheelchair accessible and would give the State Department of Labor and Industry power to enforce regulations.

headline: Challenger Backs Out Of Debate
abstract: David A. Christian, who is challenging incumbent U.S. Representative Peter Kostmayer, backed out of a televised debate on defense and foreign policy issues he agreed to last May citing a desire to debate only on one of the three TV networks in order to get greater exposure to the community. Kostmayer quickly pounced noting that a failure to keep this commitment indicated an inability to keep political commitments. He also noted that while he had accepted invitaitons to six other debate forums Christian had failed to accept any of them. Producers for the debate still hope that Christian will reconsider.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of the PA House Judiciary Committee, including members Kevin Blaum and H. William DeWeese, as well as chief counsel Michael P. Edmiston at a hearing in Philadelphia on the death penalty

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of dairy farmers Eugene and Dee Graham

headline: Gasoline Tax increase backed
abstract: Article details PA Senator Roger Madigan's support of an increase in the state gas tax.  Madigan has been concerned with ways to raise revenue for the PA Department of Transportation for various road and highway projects.  However, with cuts in federal highway funding, he feels that an increase in the gas tax may be necessary.

headline: Manderino says growth funds stall
abstract: PA House Speaker Manderino is attempting to get more funding for democratic initiatives.  Many of the initiatives provide money for minority business and small business loans. Bipartisan research in the PA General Assembly have produced a report providing some support for Democrats' proposals.

headline: Changeable Skies Forecast Under New 'Sunshine Law'
abstract: Before PA Governor Dick Thornburgh signed the amendment to the Sunshine Law, the public was only able to attend government meetings when votes were taken. However, the amendment changes little, not only because issues involving personnel, litigation, labor relations, and real estate transactions (all of which play a large role in determining tax rates) are still exempt. Moreover, informational and working sessions are also exempt; establishing a distinction between just sharing information and actually deliberating has not been made. Because this was a compromise amendment which had the backing of many municipal officials it can be assumed that they are satisfied with having to divulge no more information to the public than is absolutley necessary.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of U.S. Senate candidate Bob Edgar talking to locked out steel workers

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of Delaware farmers unloading hay donated by Allentown farmers

headline: Goode: Penn's Landing future depends on I-95 ramps
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode vied yesterday to continue to push for a state highway bill that would provide funding to build additional ramps off of I-95, which Goode and other city leaders say are crucial to ensure development of the Penn's Landing project.  The issue arose again after PA Senator Vince Fumo from Philadelphia inserted an amendment into the highway bill blocking the funding.  Fumo claims that the city and developers did not meet with communities to see how they would be affected by the construction.  Goode denies these charges and claims that he held numerous meetings with the affected communities.

headline: Market Square: Soured Deals, Delays Hurt Revival
abstract: Difficulties in a variety of Market Square renovation projects has stymied efforts to revive the area. Plans to renovate the USF&G [No definition given] building fell through because the developers could not get enough people to prelease space. The sale and subsequent rennovation of the Dauphin Building fell through. Plans to beautify the square itself have been met with snags from the PA Department of Transportation and the U.S. Urban Mass Transit Administration. In addition to these problems, numerous buildings remain fully or partially empty as tenants have gone out of business or moved. There are some signs of progress though with several small shops still open, MetroArts concerts drawing crowds, and plans for a parking garage still moving forward.

headline: Chicago Election Watchdog Is Back To Investigate Philadelphia Voting
abstract: Richard H. Anderson, the Chicago-based investigator of fair elections, who charged last year that 25,000 votes were routinely stolen in city elections is returning to investigate the primary held in May. Based on investigations last year he concluded that there were 120,000 voters on city roles that shouldn't be there, and he felt vindicated when the city announced a purge of over 134,000 names. However, his contention that 25,000 votes are routinely stolen is widely disputed. The independent Committee of Seventy which oversees local elections acknowledges voter fraud but says Anderson's figures are overblown. Committee members note that he took a sample of 150,000 suspected cases and extrapolated from there, with one person noting that of 31 confirmed cases only 9 had sufficient evidence to warrant criminal investigations. Anderson says that with more accurate data his work this time around will be more accurate, and he expects to make a lot more people in Philadelphia angry.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of U.S. Senator Arlen Specter

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Richard E. Lyng, U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, and U.S. Representative William F. Goodling surveying a farm.

headline: Governor: Airport funding adequate
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh has strongly rejected Alleghany County Official’s claims that a $50 million state commitment toward a new midfield terminal at Greater Pittsburgh International Airport is inadequate. Thornburgh said county officials sought from him a 30-year state loan for the $293 million project with the county making no interest payments for the first 10 years.

headline: Mortgage Welfare
abstract: PA using tax exempt bonds to allow those making less than forty thousand dollars annually to buy one hundred thousand dollar houses is obscene. What about all of those people who made that much and bought their homes by scrimping and saving, or who were never able to buy a home? What happens when the homeowners can no longer afford to pay ever increasing property taxes? Why is PA even involved in banking like this? Do building contractors need the help? A person making less than forty thousand dollars a year does not need state help to buy a home.

headline: Chief proposed for Philly project
abstract: PA Governor Dick Thornburgh and others involved in drafting legislation for the Philadelphia Convention Center have agreed on a chairman for the authority that would oversee the project.  The governor identified the proposed chairman as Roger Hillas, who is the chief executive officer of Provident National Bank.

headline: Photo
abstract: Photo of U.S. Senator Arlen Specter

headline: Political Mileage From The Drought
abstract: The visit by the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture, Richard E. Lyng, and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter to northern York County yesterday is a rather cheap trick. While farmers heard that aid will be sped quickly to them once the county is declared a disaster area, which is what the law already requires the U.S. Department of Agriculture to do. Instead, it was supposed to show how Specter, who is running for reelection, can get things done for his constituents in Washington.

headline: Heinz To Seek More Funds From U.S. To Fix Bridges
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz said yesterday he will seek to get half a billion dollars removed from a bridge repair bill put back in. A Heinz aide claimed that the funds were removed from the bill by senators from Western states who are more interested in highway construction than bridge repair.

headline: Out of rubble, robotics
abstract: State, city, and university officials came together to announce the start of the Pittsburgh Technology Center in Hazelwood.  The technology park will be built in the spot of a former steel mill and will hopefully serve as a symbol of a new direction for the Pittsburgh economy.  The project is a joint venture between the city, county, and state governments as well as with the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University.

headline: CHUCK STONE: A Few Endorsements for May 20
abstract: In Pennsylvania, Columnist Chuck Stone endorses US Rep. Thomas Foglietta for 1st Congressional District, Carol Coady for the 2nd PA Senate District, John Cordisco for the 6th PA Senate District, and PA Rep. James Barber for the 190th PA House District in preparation for the May 20 primary.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photo of Maryland House candidate Stewart Bainum meeting with Walk Plosila, Weldon Latham, and Harvey Kushner at a fund-raiser.

headline: Rep. Walker Plans Farm Visits
abstract: US Representative Robert Walker of Lancaster is planning visits to three area farms to speak with farmers about the state of farming, last year's farm bill, and trade problems. Lynwood Heagy plans to tell Walker about how programs that pay farmers not to produce milk or grow grain are costing him money through additional fees and increased competition.

headline: Heinz wants to get PAT's subsidies back on track
abstract: US Senator John Heinz says that he is proposing legislation to retain the capital and operating subsidies for public transit the Reagan Administration is threatening to eliminate.  If Congress does not act by September 30, close to all the federal money for public transit nationwide will be eliminated because of the combination of US President Reagan's budget proposal and the expiration of the Surface Transportation Assistance Act of 1982.

headline: Pa. Steel Community Working On Its Resume
abstract: Counties and communities that once relied on mining and manufacturing for prosperity and are now realizing that most of the jobs lost over the last few years will never come back. Communities like Aliquippa are having to rely on service industries: retail, medical, financial, etc. and attract businesses with fifteen or twenty new jobs instead of large plants with hundreds of jobs as in the past. PA is trying to refocus its growth around the concentration of universities and medical centers. Philadelphia has been the strongest part of the PA economy with its new concentration in financial services, pharmaceuticals, and biomedical technology. However, many workers who spent most of their adult lives working in steel mills and mines are struggling to find jobs that can use the skills they have, often for much less than they were making, or retrain themselves. It will take years for these areas to regain what they lost.

headline: City contract bargaining should focus on benefits
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode has denied abandoning his goal of freezing wages for city employees for two years beginning on July 1, when new negotiated contracts with municipal union workers go into effect. The Philadelphia Inquirer says the a more important question is what the mayor will do about bringing excessive costs of fringe benefits including, sick pay, pensions, and health care under control.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Photo of state representative Peter H Kostmayer

headline: Reservoirs Drop As Hay Lifts Spirits
abstract: Parts of the Southeastern US got hay from fellow farmers in the rest of the country. The hay will be used to feed cattle herds and prevent a flooding of the beef market due to farmers selling the animals early because of a lack of feed. Georgia has seen eight months of below normal rainfall, and throughout the region tens of millions of dollars in damage has been caused from damaged crops, reservoirs are also dropping, and barge traffic has been slowed in some areas due to low water levels.

headline: House delays vote on plan to limit PAT union rights
abstract: For the second straight day, the PA House of Representatives has failed to act on legislation designed to alter Port Authority Transit workers' rights during contract negotiations. PA House members voted to postpone consideration of a bill dealing with Port Authority Transit workers' rights.

headline: Pennsylvania Lacks A Housing Policy
abstract: PA's housing problem is exacerbated by the fact that the state's housing policies have been created over a series of administrations based on their own priorities and economic viewpoints. To better deal with the issue of homelessness, the state's housing policies should be better coordinated. Moreover, such a policy should be constantly adapting to the needs of the population and the economic conditions of the time. Ultimately, priorities should focus on responding to short-term crises and preventing future crises by establishing long-term solutions, such as using subsidies to encourage developers to build more affordable housing.

headline: City Payments To Union Health Fund Arise As Key Issue
abstract: Earl Stout has been trying to improve medical benefits for the city of Philadelphia workers since he became head of their union twelve years ago. He was able to lift the ban on members going anywhere other than the union hosptial and negotiated a contract with then-Philadelphia Mayor Rizzo nine years ago that got the city to pay 100% of union employee medical costs. It is that agreement which has become a major issue in the current strike. Mayor Wilson Goode insists that the contract requires the city to pay less than 100% (although a number of courts have ruled otherwise) while Stout contends the city has failed to live up to the deal and owes the union millions of dollars in back payments. The city, as it has done twice before, is also trying to get joint control over the medical fund, with Goode insisting that he will not turn over any money without some sort of oversight

headline: photograph
abstract: Photograph of Senator Edward Kennedy speaking after vote to override veto regarding sanctions against South Africa.  Also pictured are Coretta Scott King and Representatives Howard Wolpe and Mickey Leland.

headline: State Bill Tabs $250 An Acre To Keep Builders Off Farms
abstract: Because PA's most productive farmland borders it's most populous areas, it's also the most attractive for developers. In fact, the state loses fifty-two thousand acres of farmland every year. To combat this problem, PA Senator Noah Wenger has proposed amending Act 43 by allowing one-time lump-sum payments to farmers who agree to change their deeds to prevent their land from ever being redeveloped. It would give teeth to an act which created agricultural districts, which are designed to prevent local governments from green lighting farmland for redevelopment. At a time when many farmers are walking off the land because of an inability to make money, such a bill is considered especially timely. However, Wenger concedes that it will be difficult to convince urban legislators to vote for money (almost fifty million dollars) to preserve farms.

headline: cartoon
abstract: A cartoon strip of a huge tractor trailer plowing through traffic with a caption that reads "I'll be glad when they raise the speed limit to 65 so I can go 75."

headline: PHEAA ends bid to buy Towne House
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) board of directors agreed yesterday to drop plans to buy the 20-story Towne House Apartments building amid litigation in the city of Harrisburg by the Harrisburg School District and the Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority to stop the sale to PHEAA since the sale would take the building off the tax rolls, costing them thousands of dollars in tax revenues.  PHEAA is tax-exempt.

headline: Civic Unit: enforce ban on politicking
abstract: A civic watchdog group called on Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode to enforce a city charter ban on political activity by municipal employees.  The group points to two specific instances where city employees on leave have been working on campaign teams for politicians running in the upcoming election.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Picture of Robert F Smith, former independent US Senate candidate.

headline: State's farmers say ag secretary faced tough job
abstract: PA farmers have mixed feelings about the resignation of U.S. Agriculture Secretary John R. Block. Both supporters and opponents of Block expressed their view in interviews at the opening of the 70th annual PA Farm Show, however, all have agree that Block presided over some of agriculture's toughest times since the Depression.

headline: Is the House serous about saving lives?
abstract: The editorial board criticizes the Pennsylvania House version of a seat belt bill as too lenient and shows that lawmakers are not serious about saving lives.  He disagrees that a stricter bill would lead to road blocks or check pionts by police, which would tie up traffic.  Addtionally, the editorial explains the board's decision regarding publication of a cartoon about Pat Robertson, while objecting to a Doonesbury cartoon.

headline: Philadelphia Councilman Charged With Extortion In Development
abstract: Philadelphia City Councilman Leland M. Beloff, his aide Robert Rego, and an alleged member of organized crime, Nicholas Caramandi were arrested on charges of extorting the developer of a project on the city's waterfront in exchange for passage of the required bills. The City Council had to approve two bills before its summer recess in order for the developer to meet the deadline for an Urban Redevelopment grant and city-backed loan guarantees crucial for attracting private investors. In an affidavit, the FBI explained how Rego introduced an employee of the developer to Caramandi who insisted on a payment. An initial payment was made, at which point Beloff, in whose district the redevelpment would occur, introduced the bill in the City Council. When the developer refused to pay any more money until the bills were approved, Beloff, on Thursday, asked that the bills be withdrawn. City Council President Joseph E. Coleman announced that a special session would be held to move the bills forward.

headline: Clark can vote
abstract: Marion S. Damick, a chairwoman for the Advisory Committee for Probation and Parole in Pittsburgh says that a December editorial relating to former Congressmen Frank Clark was confused about an ex-offender's right to vote.  In PA, if you have had a felony conviction or a misdemeanor, once you are no longer incarcerated you have a right to vote. Damick says since Clark is not incarcerated, he has a right to vote.

headline: Photograph
abstract: Picture of US Representative and Senatorial candidate Bob Edgar.

headline: Swift Aid Promised To Farms
abstract: U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Richard E. Lyng, along with U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and U.S. Representative William F. Goodling toured a farm in northern York County yesterday to survey the damage caused by the recent drought. Normally at the top of PA's agricultural production, many farmers are seeing half of there output lost with others losing as much as three-quarters or almost one hundred percent of their crops. Lyng said that the county's request for aid would be processed as quickly as possible and once approved farmers would become eligible for low interest loans and emergency feed programs.

headline: Just A Start On Port Problems
abstract: The Philadelphia Port Corporation took an important first step in fixing its problems when it accepted Executive Director Oliver Leggett Jr.'s resignation. Leggett's lack of port experience and inability to gain the confidence of terminal operators made it necessary for him to go. His replacement needs to be someone with significant port operations experience who is guaranteed not to have political interference in his work. The port also needs to be more aggressive in attracting business to its facilities, conslidate its fragmented organizational structure, and reduce rents.

headline: PIDA Choice Confirmed
abstract: The PA Senate unanimously confirmed Governor Thornburgh's nominee to head the PA Industrial Development Authority (PIDA). PIDA provides low interest, long-term loans to PA businesses.

headline: Closing arguments given in Dwyer-Asher bribe case
abstract: Attorneys for the prosecutive and the defense offered contrasting portraits of PA Treasurer Budd Dwyer and former state Republican Chairman Robert Asher during closing arguments in the Computer Technologies Associates (CTA) bribery trial in federal court.

headline: Pickard Wants to Run with Scranton
abstract: PA State Department of Commerce Secretary James O. Pickard is in the running for Lieutenant Governor.  He acknowledged that he is interested in serving as a running mate on the ticket with undeclared Republican gubernatorial candidate William Scranton III.

headline: The dog racing dispute
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council debated a bill that would bring dog racing to the city. Pittsburgh Councilman Jack Wagner is offering legislation that would put a dog racetrack in the city despite the fact that dog racing is not legal in PA.

headline: Keep The Sign
abstract: The author regrets the unwillingness of the PA Department of Transportation to warn drivers of the hazards of Route 15. Having recently driven on the road, the writer can attest to the perils involved in travelling on it, and found the sign to be a valuable reminder of that fact. They hope that in spite of the Outdoor Advertising Act, the sign is allowed to remain.

headline: Poor Town Has A Lotto Faith
abstract: The town of West Homestead has fallen on hard times with the collapse of the steel industry. In an effort to improve its finances, the mayor and almost three dozen borough employees have, for almost two years, put two dollars into a fund to buy lottery tickets. If the city hits the jackpot it will use the money for civic improvements.

headline: Coast-to-coast conscience
abstract: Sunday's human chain of Hands Across America invoked a sense of being involved in something special, but whether it will have any real impact on the nation's hungry and homeless remains to be seen.  These authors hope that it is not just another 'feel-good' exercise and a substitute for real action.

headline: Plays Catch-Up Politics
abstract: The author believes that the comments of an aide to U.S. Senator Arlen Specter are shocking. The aide said that crying defeat was premature when funds for Route 220 were not included in a U.S. Senate transportation bill. If it were not for the efforts of U.S. Representatives Bob Edgar and Bud Shuster, who serve on the U.S. House Transportation Committee, the funds would have never been made available and Route 220 would have been unfinished. Senator Specter made a serious mistake and now he's trying to play catch-up, the voters deserve better.

headline: Too Late: Rain Fails To Resurrect Crops In York County
abstract: Although the rain that fell over the weekend was a welcome relief, it was too little too late for most farmers. Many crops, particularly corn and potatoes have already grown past the point where they need the most water. Consequently, the dry conditions over the past several weeks have left many crops permanently stunted. York County Commissioners have already started completing paperwork for the U.S. Department of Agriculture to get the area declared a drought disaster area. If the paperwork is accepted, farmers in the area would be eligible for low-cost loans.

headline: LARRY McMULLEN: New Fares, Old Grudges
abstract: Columnist Larry McMullen discusses fiscal irresponsibility in recent Pennsylvania elections.  Also, he talks about the proposed raise in SEPTA's fares.

headline: Providing a push for change
abstract: The Advanced Technology Center of Southeastern Pennsylvania has distributed $13.4 million to local companies in four years. The money, which comes from Pennsylvania’s Ben Franklin Partnership, has attracted $53.4 million worth of cash and business sources and has been parceled out to more than 100 projects.  Most of the ATC's projects are in the early stages so the effect on the region’s economy cannot yet be gauged.

headline: Comic
abstract: A comic strip showing a large elephant with the Philadelphia Convention Center on its side with a person holding a sign that says "tax payer" and a group of people labeled as "Philly State House Reps" looking in fear with a caption saying "if only it was a black and white elephant."

headline: Political battle for state begins
abstract: The battle for PA governor gathered momentum when PA Lieutenant Governor William W. Scranton announced his candidacy for governor. Scranton called for party unity at the Republican endorsement convention. The Republican strategy is to avoid a primary fight and gain an advantage over the Democrats.

headline: U.S. Farmers Vs European Farmers
abstract: Through the recently passed farm bill, the U.S. government is directly challenging the subsidy and tariff policies of the European Community (EC). Through the EC, fourteen West European nations coordinate their agricultural policies to guarantee a market for all agricultural production, by keeping internal prices high, placing tariffs on imports, and dumping any surplus on the world market. Consequently, U.S. agricultural goods are unable to compete. The farm bill responds by threatening retaliatory tariffs on a variety of EC goods. While the EC has backed down for now, the larger issue of eliminating subsidies and tariffs on agricultural production worldwide has yet to be addressed.

headline: Let's aid steel, not airport
abstract: A locked out steelworker writes in to criticize US Senator Arlen Spector for soliciting funds to be used for Greater Pittsburgh International Airport.  The writer feels that money should have instead been solicited to revitalize the steel industry in the Monongahela Valley.  He suggests that perhaps Democratic candidate Bob Edgar would better serve the interestes of the steelworkers.

headline: River areas to receive state aid
abstract: One of PA Governor Dick Thornburgh's programs calls for $15.3 million to be allocated for economic development in Monongahela and Beaver Valleys.  Of that money, $3 million is earmarked for economic planning grants for the Upper and Mid Monongahela valley and the Beaver Valley, enabling local industrial development organizations to develop strategies to attract new investors.

headline: Comic
abstract: A comic strip with Lee Iacocca dressed as the Statue of Liberty holding his autobiography with a caption that says "Fired??? And just when the renovation was coming along so nicely."

headline: Political Cartoon
abstract: A political cartoon showing U.S. President Ronald Regan spraying a can of Raid on a General who is wearing RITZ on his hat.

headline: Audits charge job program mismanagement
abstract: The federal government's Job Training Partnership Act, intended to help the unemployed find jobs, has been riddled by charges of mismanagement in western PA. Washington County Controller Patricia Beharry revealed information about fund mismanagement in Washington and Greene Counties. Most recently the issue was brought to light by a study performed by the Pittsburgh Press on JTPA documents from federal agencies, the PA Department of Labor and Industry, and various national associations.

headline: Mass Transit Seeks Dedicated Tax
abstract: While the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority (SEPTA) needs an emergency infusion of state money in order to avoid eliminating services, the real solution to the probem involves a tax that will underwrite all mass transit in the state. This in not a Pittsburgh or Philadelphia issue as all but six of the state's mass transit systems will be operating losses by the middle of the next decade. Moreover, mass transit is too important to regional economies and future regional economic growth for them to cut back service. However, with an election around the corner imposing a new tax is unreasonable and Thornburgh's insistence that local areas should contribute more money is equally unrealistic given the severe restictions on taxation that they have, it also highlights the urgent need for local tax reform too. PA is one of the few states that lacks a tax for mass transit, this is something that needs to change.

headline: Something Worth Keeping
abstract: This author urges Pennsylvania Senators to continue the Homeowners Emergency Management Assistance Program, which provides loans to help homeowners who are unemployed or mired in financial problems meet their mortgage payments.  The program is faced with foreclosure unless the General Assembly votes to reauthorize it.

headline: Committee clears funds for Kodak
abstract: The PA Senate Appropriations Committee approved legislation that would appropriate $14.7 million to help Eastman Kodak Company open its new Pharmaceutical Division in Chester County.  The bill, already approved by the PA House, will now move the the full Senate, where it is expected to pass.

headline: Political Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon depicts Mikhail Gorbachev bowing to Ronald Reagan and saying "May I have this pre-dance? A chance to, shall we say, get a little better acquainted before we actually dance?"  Reagan, dressed in a ball gown, bowing back, responds "Why that would be delightful.  We can pre-talk while we pre-dance…"

headline: Innovative budget expected of Casey
abstract: Gov. Casey is set to unveil his first budget, which is said to focus on economic development, education, and the environment.

headline: Agency to Appeal Towne House Ruling
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency plans to appeal a court decision that prevented it from buying the Towne House Apartments and annex.

headline: Plymouth disputing DER findings in hearings on planned trash plant
abstract: The fate of Montgomery County's trash-to-steam plant was the issue today in Harrisburg during the second round of hearings on Plymouth Township's appeal of the permits for the facility.

headline: Licenses Revoked
abstract: State Transporation Secretary Howard Yerusalim announced the state was discontinuing the "You've Got a Friend in Pennsyvlania" liscense plates and to leave them uncluttered to help ease the workload of the courts.

headline: Misdirected praise
abstract: Letter to the editor requesting clarification from Judge Robert Dauer, who praised Gov. Casey for his quick response to a request for a courtroom at "Western Penitentiary." The writer claims that neither Casey nor his administration was involved in that decision.

headline: Insurance cheaters beware!
abstract: Insurance issues continue to plague the state although there has been a slight easing in the availability of liability insusrance, but costs are still so high they cause some drivers to drive without insurance.

headline: Casey names 42 to economic board
abstract: Gov. Casey revealed the list of those who he will have lead the new Economic Development Partnership. Casey has yet to propose the legislation to create the agency and have it replace the Dept. of Commerce.

headline: Legislature called 'most greedy'; support of part-time unit urged
abstract: State Rep. John Kennedy announced that PA's legislature is the most expensive to run in the country.

headline: South Africa reacts angrily to Sullivan call
abstract: Rev. Leon Sullivan's remarks (that all U.S. companies doing business in S. Africa should withdrawl within 9 months) were met with hostility by the South African government, saying they were "neither in the interests of the workers nor of the United States itself."

headline: Jobless rate rises here; dips in state
abstract: Pittsburgh region's monthly unemployment rate for January rises to 7.5% while the state rate held at 5.5%.

headline: Aid for chronically ill in classrooms blocked
abstract: A Commonwealth Court judge blocked a state Department of Education effort to ensure that schools accommodate the needs of the physically disabled and chronically ill students.

headline: Policy Clarified
abstract: Man from the Environmental Protection Agency writes to the newspaper to clear up a mistake the newspaper made regarding the Clean Water Act.

headline: Norristown calls SEPTA project vital
abstract: Ground was broke at the site of a new SEPTA terminal in Norristown, which will hopefully provide the revitalization that the struggling borough needs.

headline: Molinaro's name should be submitted
abstract: The Trial Court Nominating Commission named to suggest up to five persons worthy of filing the vacancy on the Fayette County Common Pleas Court has a weeks to complete deliberations.

headline: Insurance firm comes up $83M short
abstract: Mutual Fire, Marine, and Inland Insurance Co. is $83 million in the hole for claims, making it the largest insurance failure in PA and the second largest in the country.

headline: Casey names 7 to court vacancies panel
abstract: Gov. Casey named 7 people, including 2 Pittsburgh residents, to a commission that will recommend nominees to fill vacancies on state appellate courts.

headline: It's off to the races
abstract: Today is the day when the voters get to respond to all the campaigning that has been done on behalf of various candidates, as the primary elections for a number of local Philadelphia offices are held.

headline: Southern Democrats get super primary but not a candidate
abstract: Michael Dukakis of Massachusetts is the early favorite in the Democratic primary.  He won the New Hampshire primary but will need the support of AFL-CIO and New York Governor Mario Cuomo to succeed as the Democratic candidate.

headline: Lancaster Co. economic roundup
