abstract: Lone Star Technologies Inc. of Dallas will not complete a deal to purchase and operate five Babock & Wilcox Co. steel plants in Beaver County, but the United Steelworkers of America may make a new offer in the future.

headline: Lotteries aren't just a bad idea - they're a bad investment
abstract: Points out that those participating in the lottery are often those who can least afford it, because they're hoping to strike it rich and see it as one of their only hopes.

headline: City Looks For Ways to Trim Cost fof New Justice Center
abstract: The city's downtown Criminal Justice Center project has been put on hold by Mayor Goode while officials sit down with the contractors in an attempt to reduce the project's costs.  Public Property Commissioner Benjamin Ellis Jr. will try to shave costs by 20 percent, due to the fact that bids were $25 million over the $170 million budgeted cost of the center.

headline: Sharon Steel
abstract: The CEO of Sharon Steel Corporation says that employees are interested in buying the company.  Sharon Steel has not said whether or not the financially troubled company is for sale.

headline: League issues background on health department
abstract: Rochelle Sonnenfeld of the League of Women Voters of Montgomery County prepared this article to inform the citizens of Montgomery County on the debate as to whether or not a county department of health should be created. Creation of county departments of health became permissible due to a bill which passed in the Legislature in 1951, although Montgomery County as well as all other second class counties are currently provided with public health services by the PA Department of Health. Creation of a county department of health would allow the county to receive state and federal funds, although higher taxes might result from such a measure.

headline: Senate Oks increase in higher ed grants
abstract: Legislation that would allow the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) to provide some college and university students with up to $500 more money each year for tuition under a bill has passed unanimously by the PA Senate and now must be passed in the PA House of Representatives. PA Senator Ralph Hess, Education Chairman and a PHEAA board member, said there may actually be enough money to award $100 more this fall semester to each student recipient of the agency's grants, making the bill effective immediately.

headline: Judge won't block radioactive water evaporation
abstract: Anti-nuclear groups are speaking out against a decision by the PA Department of Environmental Resources to exempt the Three Mile Island power plant from a clean air permit for the evaporation of radioactive water. Frances Skolnick, coordinator for the Susquehanna Valley Alliance, said it is the responsibility of those who feel strongly against the decision to speak out. Administrative Law Judge Terrance J. Fitzpatrick ruled that TMI had not shown they would be irreparably injured by radioactivity.

headline: Camp Hill prisoners tell of being beaten
abstract: Michael Hackman of the Pennsylvania Prison Society toured the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill and was told by prison inmates that they were beaten after the recent riot was quelled. Stefan Presser of the American Civil Liberties Union, who recently won a federal court lawsuit to remove the prisoners' shackles, contends that unfair treatment includes refusal to provide some inmates with soap and blankets. Kenneth Robinson of the PA Department of Corrections contends that there have been no "substantiated allegations" of beatings, while members of the state House Judiciary Committee who toured the prison described it as a "war zone."

headline: U.S. cocaine seizures up a third in 1 year
abstract: The U.S. Customs Service reported that in the three month period ending on Dec. 31, the agency had confiscated 45,530 lbs of cocaine, an increase of more than a thrid of the amount seized in the three month period a year before.

headline: USX chief expects strong year for steel
abstract: Thanks to low unemployment numbers, a stong economy, and increased capital spending, USX chairman David Roderick believes it will be a good year for steel, as well as USX.

headline: Lt. Gov. Mark S. Singel
abstract: Lt. Gov. Singel to visit Levittown for two days.  Background given on his issues: tax reform, recycling effort, and the evironment-- and his plan to be more accessible to the people of Bucks.

headline: City mulls property tax hike
abstract: Scranton city Treasurer William Baker and Mayor David Wenzel believe that the city will have to increase property taxes by as much as 43%. The tax increase is needed to offset a $3 million income shortfall the city projects in the 1990 municipal budget. Wenzel states that the $3 million could be cut in half if the city negotiates a garbage contract with the Keystone Landfill in Dunmore, and that the city's mercantile and business taxes might be reduced.

headline: Meat fraud
abstract: A Pennsauken, NJ meat processing company and three of its officers pleaded guilty to bribing meat inspectors.  They were trying to watered down and mislabeled ham.  The company agreed to pay a $1,000,000 fine.  Authorities say that is the largest such penalty ever given in such a case.

headline: New pact ends hospital strike at Lewistown
abstract: Lewistown Hospital service employees returned to work yesterday after approving a new contract, ending a 2-month strike.

headline: Small classes better, some officials say
abstract: When it comes to class size, some school officials believe smaller is better while others say the quality of the teaching is more important.

headline: Lawmaker proposes delay on gas requirements
abstract: The threat of long gasoline lines and soaring pump prices in his region promted western Pennsylvania lawmaker, D. Michael Fisher, to propose a bill delaying adoption of reduced gasoline volatility requirements.

headline: Capital Offers Unlimited Turf To Drug Dealers
abstract: The explosion of drug- related killing that has made D.C. the nation's murder capital was triggered, experts say, by the popularity of crack.

headline: U.S. prisons are ill-equipped to deal with arrested users
abstract: Larry Jackson has served four prison sentences on account of drug use and drug-related crimes. His case is an example of how initiatives to halt drug use both in and out of prison are failing. Officials have a difficult enough time dealing with prisons, as evidenced by the recent riot at Camp Hill state prison facility. A survey by the American Jail Association showed that two-thirds of the 3,400 city and county jails in the US have no drug treatment programs.

headline: USX- Korean venture dedicated amid protest
abstract: Amid protests, USX Corp.'s steel division and a South Korean partner, Pohang Iron & Steel Co., dedicated a new $400 million steel finishing line that officials said reflects a trend toward increased foreign investment in domestic production.

headline: Lyons doesn't know when to go
abstract: City Councilman Otis Lyons is refusing to leave his post, councilman-at-large, despite the fact that it will no longer exist come next January as a result of a reorganizing of the makeup of couuncil.

headline: Clayton cuts budget request, seeks tax hikes
abstract: Philadelphia School District Superintendent Constance Clayton reduced the district's budget request by $11 million but proposed an increase in property and other taxes to compensate for the $33 million she needs.

headline: Crazy Eddie
abstract: Crazy Eddie, a regional electronics chain has been sent into liquidation by vendors who refuse to extend the store credit any longer.  The business will close its remaining 18 stores after a year of bad sales, and collapsing credit.

headline: Local pregnant women await decision on rides
abstract: The Red Cross in Butler County arranged for a van to be used to take pregnant women insured by Medicaid from Butler County to West Penn Hospital in Pittsburgh, when the women couldn't get prenatal care in Butler County. As numbers grew, the Red Cross van wasn't enough, so a local car dealership loaned a car to the service. Now that that deal has expired, a meeting of social service agencies, doctors and Butler Memorial Hospital will be held to discuss the future of the transportation service.

headline: Spepcial education children hurt by proposed funding cut
abstract: A concerned foster parent writes in about Gov. Casey's plan to cut some support from special education programs, saying that all children, not just kids with special needs, would be hurt by the cuts. It would force special needs children into regular classrooms, which are unequipped to deal with the extra attention needed by these kids.

headline: Lawsuit against PUC to end if accord on meetings OK'd
abstract: The state consumer advocate will drop a lawsuit against the Public Utilities Commission in exchange for a pledge that closed meetings will not be held, such as the PUC discussion with Bell of Pennsylvania.  That discussion resulted in a $500,000 penalty against Bell regarding an investigation of a whistleblower within the company.

headline: Capital punishment: an overview
abstract: The article consists of two charts regarding executions and death row populations. The number of executions in the US has dropped considerably since 1935, but increased around 1983. The 10 states with the largest death row populations are Florida, Texas, California, Illinois, Pennsylvania, George, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Arizona.

headline: U.S. should not execute children
abstract: The US Supreme Court has ruled in two 5-4 decisions that it is legal for criminals ags 16 and up (at the time of the crime) and the mentally retarded to be executed, prompting opposition from the editors, who say that it is "cruel and unusual punishment" under the 8th amendment.

headline: USX, Kobe of Japan Join Hands At Lorain
abstract: In a agreement which brings together the two top steel producers in the U.S and Japan, USX and Kobe entered into a joint venture which will operate USX's bar and tubular products plant in Lorrain, Ohio.

headline: Making a farce of state ethics law
abstract: The writer criticizes the state legislature for failing to produce an effective new ethics law, explaining that in the legislation being considered now, lawmakers have an escape clause which essentially exuses them of all guilt in ethics violations.

headline: Commission OKs 7-Mill Property Tax
abstract: The Butler Renaissance Commission approved a budget that will require property owners in the business district to pay a 7-mill property tax to finance it.  A mandatory reassessment is included in the budget, though the program can be defeated by property owners.

headline: House panel again backs merit selection of judges
abstract: By a vote of 12-9, the House Judiciary Committee passed a bill that would end the controversial practice of electing judges in PA.  It is the second time they've voted on the issue.  The issue is expected to be held up by House Speaker James Manderino who disagrees with the provision that would allow the bill to pass the chamber with a simple majority vote.

headline: Long-term elderly care still getting lip service
abstract: This letter to the editor addresses the issue of long-term care for the ill elderly. The author believes the issue is not about adequate funding, but rather it is about the quality of care available in long-term nursing homes. The US Senate Special Committee on Aging found that the problem with these homes are the inefficient and neglectful manner in which they are run, rather than the funding.

headline: Someone pays
abstract: The Montgomery Area School District does not comply with federal guidelines for handicapped access.  The editorial board argues standardization of federal and state guidelines, or for the feds to provide funds for change.

headline: Letters:  TMI article 'shabby'
abstract: The opinion letter states unhappiness with an article about Three Mile Island and the lasting effects.  The reader was dissapointed that the author neglected to report that Pennsylvania declared that there were no health risks from the accident.  The reader felt that the author used the people's fears to sell more papers.

headline: Cascio's action correct
abstract: The editorial board supports Somerset County Judge John M. Casio's decision to end the trial of Marlene Joan Nagle. Nagle was charged with endangering the welfare of children at the United Cerebral Palsy Daycare and Development Center, where she teachers. The case was ended because the prosecution did not provide factual evidence against Nagle.

headline: Unified trouble?
abstract: The author of an Opinion piece believes that the establishment of a "unified judicial system" with a single source of funding in Pennyslvania may take longer than expected.

headline: Voters to decide if raffles, small games will be legal
abstract: Voters in municipalities throughout the midstate will be asked next week to decide whether local fire and ambulance companies and social clubs should be allowed to hold raffles and small games of chance.

headline: Manderino to introduce new tax option
abstract: State House Speaker James Manderino has proposed putting tax reform up for voter approval in simpler stages in order to gain support.

headline: Commissioners Expected To Support Proposed Tax Reform Legislation
abstract: Crawford County Commissioners are expected to act on a resolution in support of the proposed tax reform legislation at a meeting this morning.

headline: Archbishop meets with abortion opponents
abstract: Roman Catholic Archbishop Anthony J. Bevilacqua said that the church could not provide financial assistance to keep women from getting abortions.  He was speaking to a group of 60 abortion opponents.  The archbishop also made more general comments as to the direction of legislation in Harrisburg.

headline: Lung cancer deaths in Pittsburgh
abstract: Neighborhoods in the City of Pittsburgh are listed in order of most to least lung cancer-related deaths. North Side, Woods Run and South Manchester top the list with 162 deaths per 100,000 people in 1987. The sources are the Allegheny County Health Department and the University of Pittsburgh's Epidemiology Data Center.

headline: Souderton calls for tax hike
abstract: Souderton Area School District homeowners face a 32-mill increase in their tax bills for 1989-90 if the school board adopts a proposed $28.8 million budget.

headline: Letters:  What leaf photo nuked?
abstract: This opinion from a reader describes the author's exaggerated analysis of the Three Mile Island accident.  The reader clearly felt that the photograph of a mutated maple leaf was distorted with a picture editing program.

headline: Casey calls for drug bills support
abstract: Gov. Robert Casey wrote several bills regarding the war on drugs and urges their support.  The bills would help drug enforcement efforts and give the police and the courts all of the tools that they need.  An example is the death penalty for drug related murders.

headline: Urban League targets youths
abstract: The Urban League of Philadelphia targets youth and youth development in light of poverty, child abuse, and drug abuse in the city.

headline: Voters will have final say on small games of chance
abstract: A statute legalizing small games of chance for non-profit organizations will become effective Friday, although voters in local boroughs and municipalities will have to approve of their use through referenda during a municipal primary election.

headline: Masloff struggles with campaign to project her real self in public
abstract: In preparation for the mayoral electon in Pittsburgh, Mayor Sophie Masloff struggles to appear strong and capable in her seat.

headline: Communities balance taxes, services
abstract: Midland used to be a larger community because of its steel plants.  Since the 70s, the community's population has dropped, as well as their employees for the basic necessities such as garbage removal, policing, and street repairs.  Their real estate tax is one of the highest rates in Beaver county.  The article also summarizes the happenings in other communities including: Shippingport, Aliquippa, Ambridge, Hanover, Franklin township, and Brighton township.

headline: Philly man convicted in ax murders
abstract: A South Philadelphia man was convicted of killing three people with an ax in a drug house.  The report says that the man did so because he was out of cash and in need of a cocaine fix.  Harold Wilson, 31 killed the victims in the morning of April 10, 1988.  Police found the as a block and a half from the Philadelphia rowhome where the victims were found. The case now moves on to sentencing where the jury is expected to decide whether Wilson should be put to death.

headline: Lyme brochure available
abstract: State Sen. Edwin Holl has prepared a brochure on Lyme disease which can be obtained by contacting his office.  It is designed to help people prevent, detect, treat, and become educated about the disease.

headline: South Butler Parents Ask for New Negotiators
abstract: Parents groups in the South Butler area are asking that new negotiation teams be appointed by the school board and education association in hopes of avoiding a potential stike come time for classes.

headline: Local group to fight gas rate hike
abstract: Pennsylvania Gas & Water Co. is planning a gas rate hike, but the leader of a local group (Citizens Conocerned About Taxes) has vowed to fight the increase.

headline: Casey Is Racist In Commutations
abstract: The writer accuses Gov. Casey of racism in his dealings with commutation requests for three prisoners who have "turned over a new leaf."  Casey commuted the two white prisoners and not the black man.

headline: Victim's Family Opposes Clemency for Former Philadelphia Psychiatrist
abstract: The family of a murdered psychiatrist Leon Weingrad is opposing clemency for the former colleague Lois Farquharson who inspiried her lover and former patient to murder Weingrad.  Farquharson has reportedly been an "exemplary inmate" for 15 years and is now "a danger to no one."

headline: We don't need all of this help
abstract: The editorial claims that the PA Senate's proposal for auto insurance reform is unreasonable and is just a P.R. ploy, and the reforms will have to be fought between the House and Senate for even longer now that the two bodies have such different plans.

headline: Mayoral hopefuls air differing views
abstract: Nine candidates presented their platforms to the people in an attempt to become mayor of Scranton, Pa.  Major issues concerned police and fire protection, garbage and landfills, and wage taxes.  All candidate's platforms are summarized.

headline: Controller fails to inform public, challenger says
abstract: Republican challenger Rosemary Berry has accused Harrisburg's Democrat Controller of allowing Mayor Stephen D. Reed's administration to spend money freely. McCarthy replied by stating that he challenged budget transfers by Reed's administration. Berry stated that the controller must tell the public periodically how the city's administration is spending their tax money.

headline: Homeless group travels to capital
abstract: Homeless activists are descending on Washington DC in pursuit of more federal funding for affordable housing.  The story follows a number of people making the journey across the country to participate in the march.

headline: Medicare fee to stay till computer switch
abstract: The US Congress repealed a Medicare program that charges participants $5.30 a month for inadequate care, but people will still be required to pay for the first five months of the year. The money will be refunded by the Treasury Department at some point after June. Social Security Commissioner Gwendolyn S. King said it would take five months to reprogram the agency's computers to drop the charge. Senate Aging Committee Chairman David Pryor of Arkansas deemed the situation unacceptable.

headline: Special ed officials fight to keep state from decreasing funds, reducing staff
abstract: Special ed officials fight to keep state from decreasing funds and reducing staff.  The budget crisis has pitted the state against the 29 regional intermediate units that provide special education services.

headline: Meadowcrest Water Company tells PUC it will make improvements, raise rates
abstract: The Meadowcrest Water Company, in compliance with a court order, will be improving its facilities and operation, though it will be raising its rates in order to pay for the improvements.

headline: Casey to revisit Danskin facility
abstract: Danskin Inc., an industrial facility, will receive the governor next week for his tour of the company's new child day-care center which can accommodate up to 30 young children.  The center was begun with the help of the Casey administration and is one of the first examples of on-site child day-care.

headline: Volunteer at prison honored
abstract: A Lebanon County man was named "volunteer of the year" last night at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill.

headline: Whistle blower: House approval sends new bill on protecting workers to Bush
abstract: Ten years ago a Treasury Department financial analyst, Elaine Mittleman spoke up when Crysler Corp. failed to deliver reports to the government in exchange for a federal bailout loan to keep them out of bankruptcy. A new bill was sent to Bush to protect whistle blowers in the future.

headline: Mayoral Poll Shows Lucchino Ahead
abstract: According to a Pittsburgh Post- Gazette poll, incumbent Mayor Sophie Masloff trails Allegheny County Controller Frank Lucchino in the race for the Democratic nomination for mayor.

headline: Daniel Boone school face 14.1-mill land tax increase
abstract: According to a new budget proposal by the Daniel Boone School District, residents would face a 14.1-mill increase in property taxes.

headline: After 4 years, authority returned to Traffic Court president judge
abstract: Four years after the state stepped in to control the scandal ridden system, the Philadelphia Traffic Court is back under the control of its President Judge George Twardy.  Twardy was not president at the time of the takeover.  He says he is "gratified by the high court's confidence in him."

headline: Medicare Surtax to Be Subject of Hearing
abstract: The Senate Finance Committee is arranging a hearing this month to examine the new catastrophic illness insurance program and the surtax imposed on Medicare recipients.

headline: Special ed reorganization urge
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Education Secretary Donald M. Carroll said yesterday that proposed regulations for special education are similar to the need for restructuring one might find in a Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganization. Carroll said regulations would require school districts to evaluate students more carefully before placing them in a special education classes as well as cause the state to give more scrutiny to special ed budgets submitted by school districts. Previously, the result of the state approving special ed budgets was a $99 million deficit in the state's special ed budget.

headline: NRC chairman noncommittal on Limerick license
abstract: The new chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Committee expressed his approval of Philadelphia Electric Co.'s Limerick 2 nuclear plant, though warned that official approval must wait until legal questions have been answered.

headline: Child- abuse cases up 30 percent in city
abstract: Child- abuse cases shot up nearly 30 percent in Philadelphia last year, a rate that towered over a statewide increase of 8.6 percent and was attributable in large part to cocaine, officals said.

headline: Wagner cruises toward victory over Molinaro
abstract: With about 75% of precincts reporting, John Wagner seems to have bested Carmine Molinaro in the race for a 10-year judgeship on the Fayette County Court of Common Pleas.

headline: Windfall
abstract: After the Bevill, Bresler and Schulman Asset Management Corporation declared bankruptcy, Dauphin County received checks totaling $440,000 after a lawsuit to recover lost interest. The editorial board suggests that the money could be used to offset the expected failure of another investment firm, ESM Government Securities, or that the county could give its citizens a tax break.

headline: Mayor's husband in hospital
abstract: Mayor Sophie Masloff's husband, Jack Masloff, was admitted into Shadyside Hospital upon complaining dizziness and weakness.

headline: Council counts on sewer fee to balance budget
abstract: Counting on an expected fee of $480,800 from Cornwall borough as payment for sewerage treatment plant capacity for a planned project, Lebanon City Council members have balanced the 1990 general fund budget and expect to pass the budget on December 26. Public works director Ed Keener said the Lebanon Sewer Authority has permitted Cornwall to purchase sewerage capacity, paid in full by September 1, 1990. The expected revenue from Cornwall has allowed the city county to balance the budget without an increase in property tax, although it does adopt a new $10 residence tax.

headline: Better tools
abstract: The editorial lists the recent changes to state criminal law and the benefits they will have for PA.  Specific policy changes they are in favor of include laws to keep drug dealers from dealing around schools, a broadening of the state's aggrevated assault law, and stiffer penalties for children caught with drugs.

headline: Mental health funding: 'A lot to be desired'
abstract: Mental health personnel and political leaders call for more mental health funding to help keep many programs afloat.

headline: Special ed transfers anger parents
abstract: Parents of learning disabled students are threatening to take the Spring-Ford Area School District to court if is transfers their children as it has planned.  8 learning disabled children were scheduled for transfer, but their parents are willing to file suit to keep them at their current school and avoid the trauma caused to the students.

headline: NRC Decision Expected In March
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission will decide by March 20 on a proposal by GPU Nuclear Corp., which operates Three Mile Island, to evaporate 2.3 million gallons of treated water from the March 1979 accident.

headline: Child advocates urge city to speed adoption process
abstract: A coalition of child advocates, including representatives from the Juvenile Law Center, the Support Center for Child Advocates, and the Defender Association, have criticized the city of Philadelphia for taking too long to decide a child should be put up for adoption. After reviewing 79 cases, the coalition said the city should be doing more for those children who have no hope of returning to their parents, which encompasses most of the 5,400 Philadelphia children living in foster care. The coalition found frequent delays in the Department of Human Services and the City Solicitor's Office. Guy Vilim, Deputy City Solicitor, said that his office, which represents the department in adoption cases, is "overworked and underfunded".

headline: Human services workers deserve better pay
abstract: It is time that individuals with careers in the realm of human service receive a minimum salary for their work.  One out of every two American households benefit from some form of assistance provided by human service, and its hardworking professionals should not be forgotten.

headline: Army will transfer 536 from Kentucky to Letterkenny
abstract: As the Department of Defense readies to move 536 jobs from Lexington to Letterkenny, studies into the potential environmental and sociological effects go into action.

headline: Mayor's Race: Jim Connors
abstract: James P. Connors, director of community development in the Mayor David Wenzel administration, is running for Mayor of Scranton.  The article discusses Connors' persona and views.

headline: Council drops electrical-permit requirement
abstract: Philadelphia City Council has dropped the requirement that an electrical permit be obtained when factory-wired partitions are installed in office building to create cubicles.  The bill was hotly contested between carpenters and electricians, as the carpenters were forced to subcontract to electricians under the previous requirement.

headline: Hugo Relief
abstract: Governor Casey is waiving special fees charged to those hauling oversized loads through the state in hopes that it will help the relief effort in SC.  Large equipment is needed in the region to help residents clean up after Hurricane Hugo.

headline: Montco voters say 'yes' to health department
abstract: In a binding referendum, voters of Montgomery County voted in favor of establishing a county health department. The question appeared on the ballot thanks to the efforts of the Public Health Planning Group. County Commissioners Chairman Paul B. Bartle said that the health department will be implemented "in a prompt time frame," while the PHPG's vice chairman Neil Goldstein said that the next step is to notify the PA Department of Health.

headline: Special education change could save state millions
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Education hopes that changing regulations and standards governing special education will reduce its $83 million deficit and help aid the escalating cost of serving gifted and handicapped students. Donald M. Carroll Jr., the acting secretary of the Department of Ed, said that the state is in a Chapter 11 bankruptcy "as far as special education is concerned." Robert E. Feir, executive director of the State Board of Education, said the state currently pays districts' excess costs, which is the difference between the cost to educate a student in a regular classroom versus the cost to educate a student in special education. The Board of Education is considering changes to the regulations to control the increase in cost.

headline: NRC experts divide on Peach Bottom plant's safety
abstract: Half of a 6-person panel from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission believes that in the event of a meltdown, the containment facilities at the Peach Bottom nuclear reactor would fail, while the other half believes it would be effective.  The plant, however, was rated as having a "one event in 220,000 years" probability of a meltdown, making the containment issue somewhat less urgent.

headline: Children Armed for Drug Trade?
abstract: 18-year-old Detra J. of D.C. said that "everyone knows how to get a gun if they want one," and also that she knows children as young as 12 who are armed because they're involved in drug trafficking.  Detra works with her local Recreation Dept. to help keep kids off the streets, and says that most government regulations about gun control aren't working.

headline: Indigent-funeral bill backed
abstract: A bill to make the state pay more than twice what it used to in burial assistance for poor adults was approved by a House committee.  The state aid would increase from $350 to $900.

headline: Congressman remembers the area's veterans
abstract: Congressman George Gekas pays honor to veterans in a speech at the Riverview Cemetery in Northumberland.

headline: Mayor's Race: Ted Rosencrans
abstract: The fourth in a series of articles on the candidates in the race for Mayor of Scranton, Ted Rosencrans is presented as a "working man's candidate" for mayor.

headline: Councilmen Defend $50 Dollar Garbage Fee
abstract: Scranton city councilmen Michael Melnick and Thomas Comerford defend the $50 garbage fee saying the council did its best with the budget and worked to avoid higher taxes.

headline: Officials: New Jersey Air Cleanest in Decade
abstract: Environmental officials in NJ credit new petrol controls in the dramatic increase in air quality observed recently.  The controls implimented include vapor recovery systems and gas volatility reductions.  Officials say that motorists paid 1.5 to 3.5 cents more per gallon of gas because of these regulations.

headline: More in area may have AIDS that state statistics indicate
abstract: State statistics of the number of AIDS-infected people in Erie County are considerably lower than the real number because of the counting system used.  Another reason for the lower numbers is that many people do not get tested for the disease out of privacy concerns.

headline: Special education draft presented
abstract: Acting state secretary of education Donald M. Carroll Jr. delivered a "semi-final" proposal on special education to county superintendents. This draft will be presented to the PA Board of Education next week. The proposal includes measures regarding funding for special education programs, intelligence quotient ranges, and services available to students currently enrolled in special education programs.

headline: NRC finds Limerick slipping
abstract: The Philadelphia Electric Co. received yesterday the lowest possible passing grade for its emergency preparedness capabilities at the Limerick Nuclear Power Plant from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. PECO received a rating of 3 from the NRC for the period from May 1, 1988, to August 31, 1989. The NRC cited "ineffective corporate oversight and support" and weaknesses in training programs as the biggest factors in the low rating. Executive Vice President-Nuclear of PECO, Corbin A. McNeill Jr., said he believed major changes instituted later in the assessment period will improve performance in the lower rated areas.

headline: Chippewa permits teen rehab center despite opposition
abstract: Chippewa Township supervisors have unanimously agreed to grant a conditional use permit to the Gateway Rehabilitation Center to open a teenage drug and alcohol treatment facility amidst concerns from township residents regarding security and privacy. The conditions include giving treatment priority to Beaver County youth, discharging teens caught leaving the facility unchaperoned, and improving the grounds, among other things. Township Supervisor  Dale Laughner attempted to push the issue to a later meeting, but Supervisor Kathleen Krecek and board Chairman Tom Roberts chose to vote immediately.

headline: Job funds for Bux- Mont
abstract: Montgomery and Bucks counties were given a share of $58 million in federal funds to provide job training to low- income Pennsylvanians.

headline: Diver wins round in bid to view 'Monitor' shipwreck
abstract: Undersea photographer Gary Gentile might be able to get close enough to photograph the "Monitor," one of the first ironclad warships. The "Monitor" sits 220 feet below sea level, a depth which the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration deemed dangerous to divers lives. Commerce Department administrative law judge Hugh J. Dolan said that given Gentile's experienced record, he should be allowed to dive to the "Monitor."

headline: McDade sponsors mortgage bill
abstract: U.S. Congressman Joseph McDade introduced a bill that would establish better support for rural low and middle-income families to finance a house.

headline: County budget proposes tax hike for 1990
abstract: Montgomery County Commissioners proposed a $180 million budget for 1990 that includes a 3.75 mill real estate tax increase, causing an approximate $30 increase to homeowners. Commissioner Chairman Paul B. Bartle said the 13.6 percent tax increase was necessary because of higher costs and added personnel. The budget includes a 5.5 percent salary increase for county employees, a 4 percent pay raise for row officers, 59 new jobs, and increases for the county's health services.

headline: Bill targets work at home firms
abstract: A bill to protect workers from potentially unsafe working conditions is taking aim at an unexpected workplace: the home.  State Rep Mark Cohen (D-Phila) has put forth a bill that will ban at-home garment production and provide a telephone hotline to report abuses among other things.  The bill mainly targets the garment industry but would also affect other businesses and tasks including envelope stuffing.

headline: More on health agency
abstract: Three members of the Ambler Borough Board of Health express their support for the creation of a county board of health by the Ambler Borough Council. The Montgomery County Medical Society voted in favor of creating a county health department.

headline: 'Special' Interests
abstract: The state has decided to give school boards funding for special education spread out over the next six years, which has school officials riled up, as they won't be receiving as much money on time.

headline: Outgoing GPU chief looks ahead
abstract: William G. Kuhns, retiring chairman of General Public Utilities Corps., declared yesterday that he believes nuclear power still has a future, though it will take time for the industry to regain public confidence.

headline: Cities on the front lines fight grassroots war on drugs
abstract: A number of cities with major drug problems have anti-drug initiatives, ranging from help from local police to citizens holding all-night vigils to keep drug dealers and pushers off the streets. President Bush declared war on drugs in September, but cities are complaining that they are left to finance the war themselves. Randy Arndt, a spokesman for the League of Cities, said that drugs are the number one problem for cities.

headline: Labor's Dole says veto awaits child-care bill
abstract: US Secretary of Labor Elizabeth Dole warned that President Bush will veto the child-care bill that Democrats are pushing through Congress because of conflicting philosophies on how the government should give child-care aid to poor families.

headline: Gov. Casey Visits Fort Indiantown Gap
abstract: Gov. Casey visited Fort Indiantown Gap yesterday, watching training drills and combat simulations.  He was presented with a Franklin flag, which is a replica of the first flag ever flown from a navy ship during the Revolutionary War.

headline: McHale gets Democrats' backing for court race
abstract: Among four persons who received the Democratic Party's endorsements for the May 16 primary election, state Rep. Paul McHale was backed by the Democratic State Committee for a nomination to fill a vacancy on the Commonwealth Court.  McHale's support for a though ethics bill was a factor in the nomination bids.

headline: County budget vote due, tax increase in question
abstract: The Allegheny County Commissioners are expected to adopt their 1990 budget today but officials are unsure as to whether it will include a property tax increase. County Controller Frank Lucchino had proposed a $508.3 million budget without a property tax increase, but commissioners do not have to follow Lucchino's proposal. Board Chairman Tom Forester said a tax increase depends on whether the commonwealth of Pennsylvania provides all of the funds it has pledged to the county to pay for the operation of Common Pleas Court., for other parts of the criminal justice system, and for human services programs. The commissioners are also expected to consider a gentrification bill that would provide some tax relief to elderly and long-time homeowners.

headline: Former officer says Five Squad members stole from drug dealers
abstract: Philadelphia Police Officer Leo Ryan testified against his former co-workers on the Five Squad for the second time this year.  He accused them of using their job to steal from their suspects.  Ryan said he learned how the Squad worked soon after becoming a member.  He became a witness for the government after being caught stealing from drug dealers himself.

headline: Mother, proud of sons' victories, worries others may face defeats
abstract: A mother of two heavily mentally handicapped sons spoke out against Gov. Casey's plan to cut special education funds, which could destroy programs that helped her children become the functioning adults they are today.  She hopes other families will be able to make use of the programs.

headline: Special-education costs could increase
abstract: Members of the PA House of Representatives are worried that an overhaul of the state's special-education system going into effect next year will drive up the costs of a program that already has serious financial problems. The House Education Committee yesterday sent a letter to the State Board of Education voicing concern over the absence of any financial figures with the overhaul, as mentioned by PA Representative Ronald R. Cowell, chairman of the Education Committee. Executive Director of the State Board, Robert E. Feir, said the figures will be available within the next few weeks.

headline: Pa. urged to move ahead on cutting gas vapor to reduce ozone pollution
abstract: The Northeast States for Coordinated Air Use Management wants Pennsylvania to cut gasoline volatility even though the oil industry is pushing for it to help with higher prices and supply shortages.  The cut in gasoline volatility would aid the state in decreasing ozone pollution.

headline: City Awards $75,000 To Victim's Family
abstract: Pittsburgh has awarded a victim's family $75,000 in an out-of-court settlement for the death of Peerce Platt.  Platt jumped off a bridge into the Allegheny River, where rescue workers, thinking he was already dead, towed him through the water to the shore, only to discover vital signs.  Platt died three hours later.

headline: Lottery Fund deficit could affect elderly
abstract: According to PA Secretary of Aging Linda M. Rhodes, senior citizens might have to pay a higher cost for the services offered to them by the state on account of the state Lottery Fund's expected deficit next year. Under federal law, the state must have a plan on aging. Deputy director for the Dauphin County Area Agency on Aging Jeremy Pollack said that his group does not want to have to make a waiting list or prioritize senior citizens.

headline: Mo Valley Official Responds To COG Opinion on Guard
abstract: An official from The Moshannon Valley Economic Development Partnership has responded to the Centre Region COG's requests concerning an Army National Guard helicopter unit.  The official says that the choppers aren't under jurisdiction of the COG because they fly in at over 1000 feet, national airspace.

headline: McNulty, Scacchitti Cleared of Serious Counts
abstract: James McNulty, former Democratic mayor of Scranton, and Edmund Scacchitti, former city solicitor, were cleared of criminal charges that they violated the state Ethics Code and the Election Code.  They were also cleared of charges associated with failing to file reports for various Political Action Committees.

headline: County endorses tax bill
abstract: As the decision on tax reform looms nearer, the Monroe County commissioners Tuesday voted 2 to 1 to support the bill and to urge county residents to vote "yes."

headline: Senate balks at repealing health plan
abstract: The Senate voted down a proposal sent by the House to repeal universal health coverage for senior citizens.  While passing the bill to repeal much of Medicare, they also rejected a Senate proposal to expand Medicare by the largest percentage since its inception in 1965.  Sen John McCain (R-AZ) has put forth a proposal in the Senate which would end coverage of expensive prescription drugs and high doctor expenses.

headline: MR/ MH strains
abstract: The co-chairman of the Parents Action Committee for mentally retarded and mentally ill (MR/MH) Adults opposes the transfer of MR/MH funds from Allegheny County to Philadelphia.

headline: Spring Grove searching for answers; hires consultant
abstract: School directors of Spring Grove, such as superintendent Alan K. Lindquist, voted to hire a consultant to solve the district's problems, which include contract disputes with teachers and administrators leaving the district. Officials say that the teachers' average pay doesn't reflect revenue from the school tax. The article also lists the names of administrators who have left the school district.

headline: Patrylo quits as president of facticious PGW
abstract: Robert Patrylo quit his position as President of the Philadelphia Gas Works yesterday, succumbing to pressure from the board of directors and politicians who didn't like his "adversarial style."

headline: City cellblocks simmer
abstract: There has been a recent increase of violence and attacks on officers in the City of Philadelphia's four adult jails.  Reasons such as overcrowding, poor conditions, staff shortages, and improper recreation facilities are often cited.  The drug dependencies of many inmates is also a significant problem.

headline: Lottery fund woes
abstract: The editorial addresses the fact that the Pennsylvania Lottery Fund is inadequate to cover the $54.3 million deficit of its welfare demands. Former PA Governor Richard Thornburgh saw that the lottery program was not sufficient to meet the welfare demands and tried to shift lottery program obligations to the general fund, but currently Democrats have reversed the procedure so that programs are back under the Lottery Fund. The editorial board believes that the PACE prescription drug program, for which Democrats have proposed to reduce support, and other programs should be included in the regular welfare program.

headline: More Recruits Released, Recruitors Punished
abstract: In addition to 30 recruits for the Marine Corps who were disqualified, it was discovered that an additional 135 recruits were also sent home for similar reasons.  Marine Corps investigators have reported that 25 of the 47 recruitors at the Pittsburgh station have been reprimanded after reports that the recruitors fabricated high school diplomas and overlooked criminal records of recruits, among other violations.

headline: Meeting today will try to settle sewer issue
abstract: A meeting will be held today to make decisions on the sewer issue between Snake Spring Township and Memorial Hospital .  The piece outlines some of the predicted terms of the agreement.

headline: County salaries: first, let's reform the system
abstract: The editorial board calls for reform of the government for Dauphin County. This call comes as a result of county commissioners' decision to raise their salaries by 5%. The board also believes commissioners are too wrapped up in issues more appropriate for smaller districts, such as the likely increase in property tax, which would help balance the county budget in the coming year.

headline: Four-day nuclear power plant drill at TMI will test emergency preparedness
abstract: An emergency drill is set to take place at Three Mile Island.  Sirens will wail for several minutes on Oct 17 followed by a message on the Emergency Broadcasting System.

headline: Neshaminy Manor billing change raises questions
abstract: Physicians who administer to patients of the Neshaminy Manor Home will now bill insurance companies directly, as opposed to requesting payments from the county.  The move, although it will not reduce the quality of care to the patients, could save the county as much as $700,000.

headline: State board to begin work on special education rules
abstract: A committee of the State Board of Education will revise special education standards and regulations, in keeping with a bill passed as part of budget negotiations.  After public hearings, the revisions are scheduled to be completed by January.

headline: PE needs to shape up
abstract: The writer criticizes the PUC for giving Philadelphia Electric some slack, i.e. allowing a rate increase after a the Peach Bottom "fiasco."  PE was rated one of the worst  utilities in handling customer complaints in a recent PUC survey.

headline: City fingerprint network announced; funding lags
abstract: There could be a delay in Pittsburgh's entry into a statewide computerized fingerprint network-- the state has yet to approve money to fund the high- tech crime- fighting apparatus.

headline: Lt. Gov. Singel Speaks to AARP Groups On Tax Reform
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark S. Singel spoke before a large group of American Association of Retired Persons (AARP) on Tax Reform, Friday.  Singel spoke of the need to stop unfair poperty taxes for seniors.

headline: National Guard Moving Along in Efforts to Relocate in This Area
abstract: U.S. Army Company G and the 104th Aviation Facility's Support Unit of the PA National Guard are continuing the process of moving into their new accomodations, both at the former General Cigar Building and the Mid-State Airport.

headline: Members of Gov. Casey's Cabinet
abstract: Members of Gov. Casey's Cabinet, as part of the York "Capital for a day" program, answered questions at York Hospital's Campbell Auditorium.

headline: Filing deadline extended for state rebate program
abstract: The filing deadline of June 30 has been extended to Dec. 31 for the state property tax/rent rebate program, giving those eligible more time to apply for the rebate.

headline: Health official blocks publication of AIDS pamphlet on condom use
abstract: Assistant Secretary for Public Health Kay James has come under fire for blocking the publication of a pamphlet that explains how to use a condom.  The pamphlet's main mission is to help stop the transmission of AIDS through education.  A discussion of the benefits of condom use continues with doctors and other experts weighing in.

headline: Ohio AIDS workers dismayed over lack of spending
abstract: Despite being given $3.1 million in federal funds to fight AIDS, Ohio spent only half that amount on AIDS prevention programs. Directors of AIDS programs such as the Health Issues Taskforce and the Columbus AIDS Task Force. Congress appropriated $121.7 million for community-based programs in 1988.

headline: State budget could save $40 a year for average taxpayer
abstract: As a result of increased special education funding in the state budget, Erie School District officials say that property taxes could be reduced by 4 to 6.5 mills.  The state budget contains between $2 and $3.2 million for special education in Erie.

headline: Peach Bottom put on group's 10 worst list
abstract: An anti-nuclear group put the Peach Bottom Atomic Power station on its list of the 10 worst-run commercial reactors in the country.

headline: Clairton's ambulance crisis
abstract: The city of Clairton faces the loss of its city wide ambulance service.  Lifestar will leave the city due to threats made to the Lifestar vice- president's wife, allegedly by the head of another ambulance service.

headline: New center will assist retired federal workers
abstract: A new center in Philadelphia will assist retired federal workers with benefits information, as federal workers are not covered by Social Security.

headline: State agency loses dispute with veterans
abstract: The state Dept. of Agriculture has lost a legal dispute with a veterans' group which could cost the dept. $284,000.  The dispute was over payment to the group for work they did about 6 years ago.

headline: Morel of the story: It's a fungus
abstract: Although singing its praises, the House yesterday voted 107-89 against making the mushroom the offical Pennsylvania vegetable.

headline: For more state aid, the city needs success stories
abstract: A review of the Philadelphia city budget, which has looked to the state government to provide funding for help for the homeless and AIDS.

headline: Four Superior Court Candidates Cite Experience
abstract: Democrats Kate Ford Elliott of Allegheny County and Judge Joseph Hudock of Westmoreland County and Republicans Walter Cohen of Dauphin County and incumbent Superior Court Judge Joseph Melison of Philadelphia are vying for two available seats on the Superior Court.  The 15 member court hears all criminal appeals and many civil appeals.  A brief explaination of each candidate's experience follows.

headline: One of the best bargains around
abstract: The editorial board commends the legislature of New Jersey for their plan, called Maternity Outreach and Managed Services (MOMS) on providing prenatal care to all pregnant women in the state. Lack of prenatal care has devastating consequences for children, and each dollar spent on prenatal care saves about three dollars in the cost of taking care of a baby who doesn't have it. The editorial said the state of New Jersey will save $1.9 million a year and profit from the productive citizens that will result from the program's services.

headline: State budget increase means smaller PSU tuition hike
abstract: As part of Gov. Casey's plan to give more money to universities that keep tuition increases low, PSU will be receiving its largest appropriations increase since 1971, 9.2% over last year.

headline: PECO Lineman Electrocuted In Bewildering Accident
abstract: A Philadelphia Electric Co. lineman was killed on the ground when his crew's crane touched a 13,000 volt electrical line while he was touching the metal crane, which was against standard safety code.

headline: Closing statement given as corruptions trial ends
abstract: Closing statements to a jury from defense attorney James Yelovich said accused Cambria County Judge Joseph O'Kicki was "an activist judge who sought to make reforms to his court." O'Kicki is on trial for alleged violations spanning more than a decade, including bribery, extortion, coercion, and open lewdness. Deputy Attorney General Lawrence Claus maintained that O'Kicki is guilty of the ten charges of corruption filed against him. In related news, O'Kicki's wife Sylvia was noted for threatening a newspaper reporter who had testified during the eight-week trial.

headline: Pa. welfare agency might get new title
abstract: In accordance with legislation introduced in the state House yesterday, the state Dept. of Public Welfare might get its name changed to the state Dept. of Human Services.

headline: Supreme Court clears way for veterans' home
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has dismissed a request for an injunction against the destruction of the unused Scranton State General Hospital in order to pave the way for a new veterans' home to be built on the site.

headline: Mr. Jubelirer, it's too late now
abstract: Sen. Robert Jubelirer is a leading public spokesman against the proposed tax reform.  The Editorial Board believes that a sensational letter sent by his committee about the tax reform discredits his name.

headline: Franklin gets $25,000 grant
abstract: Franklin Borough will receive a $25,000 grant under the Financially Distressed Municipalities Act, which will be used to help facilitate a state-suggested merger with Conemaugh Twp.

headline: Lawmakers want to add, schools ask what to subtract
abstract: Educators are beginning to worry that increased attention provided to the minutae of school curriculum by state legislators is going to come at the cost of the basics of public school education.  State mandates such as ones that require sign language, the dangers of alcohol and tobacco, and parenting, educators argue must eventually come at a cost to the basics.

headline: Other rising costs aggravate nursing home staffing shortages
abstract: The vice president of the Pennsylvania Health Care Association writes about the difficulties in staffing nursing homes, in an effort to attact attention to the issue.

headline: State forming plan to keep pupils from dropping out
abstract: The state Department of Education and the state Board of Education are holding hearings across the state in an effort to develop programs for students at risk.

headline: Pellet- plant decision postponed in Palmer
abstract: The Palmer Township Planning Commission postponed a vote Tuesday night on plans to build a 400- ton- per- day plant that would convert trash into fuel pellets to be burned for electricity.

headline: Cocaine gangs are rich and ruthless
abstract: A report released by the federal Drug Enforcement Administration discusses the nature of gangs involved in dealing crack cocaine. The drug trade involves violence among gangs in competition for turf to sell the drug. Pittsburgh's Assistant Police Chief Earl Buford said that Pittsburgh has not been afflicted by the drug trade because his department worked early on to convey the message that Pittsburgh will not tolerate drug dealing.

headline: Pa. welfare secretart focuses on homeless
abstract: Secretary John F. White Jr. of the State Department of Public Welfare wants to find permanent solutions to the issue of homelessness.  Focusing less on temporary shelters, the Department of Public Welfare is providing money for mortgages and job traning and employment for low-income families.  Money for housing for the mentally ill and child care costs are also part of the focus.

headline: Volunteer military puts pressure on recruiters
abstract: In the wake of the Marine Corps scandal where 25 recruiters were reprimanded for apparent recruiting improprieties, officials have admitted that such a scandal is not the first and probably will not be the last.  U.S. Rep. Tom Ridge cited pressures recruiters face due to the all-volunteer military as a reason for increases in recruiting violations.

headline: Mrs. Casey's trip to area noted
abstract: A list of Gov. Casey's wife's itinerary of travel for the "Capitol for a Day" program.

headline: Governor, Use The $90 Million To Give Us Tax Rebates
abstract: The editorial opposes Gov. Casey's plan to provide $90 million in funding for anti-drug efforts, saying that it will only result in catching more "little guys", not actually helping solve the problem.  They suggest using the money for tax rebates instead.

headline: Area's legislators still more solidly against abortion
abstract: The PA state legislature is regarded currently as the most anti-abortion legislature in the country.  The most anti-abortion of the legislators come from the southwestern part of the state.  A chart is included that shows all legislators from this part of the state and scores them based on their vote for six different abortion proposals that have come before the legislature.

headline: pa-children
abstract: In response to the growing need of single parents for day-care, state Senate Democrats today proposed a 10-part bill which would encourage businesses to implement day-care facilities.  One part of the bill would create an Office of Child Care in the governor's office.

headline: State Funding Deficit Tops CIU Board Meeting
abstract: Concern for the special education program was expressed last night at the monthly Central Intermediate Unit No. 10 Board meeting at the Clearfield High School.

headline: Penelec Plans Rate Reduction
abstract: Penelec has asked the state Public Utility Commission for a rate reduction because the company's customers have met their share of the cost of cleanup for the nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island.

headline: Cocaine: Bucks' favorite?
abstract: Bucks County District Attorney Alan M. Rubenstein addressed a meeting of the Pennridge Community Action Team, and stated that cocaine is the most commonly-used drug in Bucks County. He said that cocaine's popularity was attributed to the fact that the county has many affluent people who can afford the drug. Rubenstein also stated that drugs are the main source of crime in the county, and that the best way to halt drug use is to educate children early.

headline: Public welfare secretary is slated to speak
abstract: John F. White Jr., state Secretary of Public Welfare, will be the key- note speaker for today's annual meeting of the Mental Health Association of Luzerne County.

headline: 2 bills target case handling by PUC, Bell
abstract: In response to an investigation concerning Bell of Pennsylvania's treatement of a whistleblower and its use of an internal probe, the PA House passed a bill which would protect utility company employees who may speak out against their companies.  In addition, the House also passed a bill which will force the Public Utility Commission to issue a report outlining Bell's response to the whistleblowing incident.  The Senate is expected to pass similar legislation.

headline: Murphy withdraws
abstract: State Rep. Tom Murphy (D) has decided not to run for Pittsburgh Mayor against Democratic incumbent Sophie Masloff as a Republican, though he had the choice because of write-in votes.  He was likely hesitant to put himself under that Republican banner, and will surely resurface again in politics.

headline: Grucela says human services may be altered
abstract: Northampton County Council President Richard Grucela said the county's experimental system for human services clients may have to be dismantled because of its high costs. Grucela said the program has a projected 1989 deficit of at least $1.5 million for children and youth programs and for placing children in institutions. County Executive-elect Gerald Seyfried said he would like to see the program adjusted rather than dismantled. The program began in 1987 with a goal of centralizing services at no additional cost, but it has failed to improve services and has overburdened caseworkers. The council also may not approve a possible reappointment of Dennis Stewart, director of the human services department.

headline: Abortion session may not hurt Martinez
abstract: Experts expect that although abortion will be taking a big role in an upcoming special session of the Florida State Legislature, it will play only a marginal role in the upcoming 1990 election.  The current governor, Bob Martinez will be up for election.  His approval ratings have increased on a year-to-year basis.

headline: pa-inspect
abstract: In an effort unparalleled in the country, the state Dept. of Health will review the quality of health care provided by health-maintenance organizations, or HMOs.

headline: State gets extension in lawsuit
abstract: Plaintiffs in a special education case against the state Dept. of Education have allowed a third extension for the state to submimt a plan to provide fair treatment for special education students, though the plaintiffs say they will not be so compromising if the next deadline is not met.

headline: PSU, Italy to study coal burning
abstract: PSU is participating in a study developed by the US Dept of Energy and the Italian government, in which coal will be used in boilers instead of oil, which is more expensive.  If the experiment is successful, the technology could boost US coal sales and reduce dependence on foreign oil for both the US and other nations like Italy.

headline: Come together
abstract: Residents of Swatara Twp. were thrown off by the vandalization of a family's home with racist graffiti in an area with little history of such acts.  Residents came together to support the family, and the editorial stresses the importance of standing strong in the face of potential change.

headline: Report questions rules for $19 billion-a-year disability program
abstract: A study conducted by the US Census Bureau showed that citizens who are not receiving benefits under the Social Security Disability Program were in similar health status to those who do receive benefits. The study was requested by Senator John Heinz of Pennsylvania. The Social Security Administration has stated that it considered conducting personal disability interviews.

headline: 330 twisters hit state in 38 years
abstract: Tornados aren't very common in PA when compared with the Midwestern states, but can sometimes be just as destructive.  PA ranks 25th nationwide in the number of confirmed tornados from 1950-1988.

headline: Mustacchio: Experience pre-requisite for DA post
abstract: A profile of C.J. Mustacchio, a Democratic candidate for district attorney.  He assails David Rinaldi (who got the Democratic endorsement) as having no criminal justice experience.

headline: Hard Decisions Ahead
abstract: With the city of Scranton facing an election for mayor and three members of City Council, the decisions ahead promise to be imporant ones.  Among the issues which new city officials will have to confront are trimming city personnel and the city's variety of taxes.

headline: Classical addition enriches state capitol
abstract: For $13,000,000 the state of Pennsylvania got a great deal on their Italian Renaissance capitol building with its 272-foot high dome modeled after the dome of St. Peter's in Rome.  The accessible benefits of the building are also lauded.

headline: Paper: Social Security screening faulty
abstract: A study by congressional investigators showed arbitrary screening for the 1 million people who apply annually for disability benefits. The investigation was conducted by the General Accounting Office and the Senate Special Committee on Aging. Last week US Senator John Heinz released a report that found little difference between applicants who received benefits and those who didn't.

headline: State Mediator Named
abstract: A state mediator has been named to assist contract talks between the Clarion Area School Board and the Clarion Area Education Association (CAEA).

headline: PUC deadlocked over NFG rate hike
abstract: Public Utility Commissioner (PUC) members are deadlocked over how much National Fuel Gas Distribution Corp. (NFG) will get from its $23.6 million rate increase request. The administrative law judge conducting the hearings of PUC members on issues surrounding the rate increase has recommended that NFG be given a $17.4 million of the proposed increase. The most important difference brought out in the PUC member polling was over take-or-pay expenses. Many commissioners want to reduce the amount of take-or-pay expenses NFG could pass onto customers.

headline: Complaints about judges should be open, task force says
abstract: According to a task force appointed by the Twentieth Century Fund, the public should be given further ability to file complaints against federal judges. The task force's study was prompted by the indictment of three federal judges, one of whom was convicted of income tax evasion. The task force recommended the creation of a special committee of scholars, judges, and members of the public to oversee complaints against judges.

headline: Senior citizens help hand Sunday lottery drawings a defeat
abstract: Persuaded by a group of senior citizens who came to watch the political process, a House panel yesterday unanimously approved a measure to prohibit state lottery drawings on Sundays.

headline: A crack in the shield
abstract: Editors oppose House Bill 1052, which provides exceptions to PA's "shield law," which protects the media from disclosing anonymous sources.  Those in power dislike the shield law, as it makes it more likely that negative stories concerning their activities can leak out through confidential sources.

headline: N/A
abstract: Upon review of campaign expense reports, it was shown that the freshman members of the state Senate spent an average of $135,000 on their campaigns, while the freshmen members of the state House spent an average of $39,000.

headline: Johnstown gears up for centennial of its darkest day
abstract: The city of Johnstown is marking 100-year anniversary of the great Johnstown Flood (May 31, 1889), which nearly destroyed the town.

headline: Fallout clouds school board appointments
abstract: Mayor Goode of Philadelphia has alienated a number of key constitutencies with his recent appointments to the Board of Education.  Asians had hoped for a seat on the board with their ever-rising numbers throughout the district.  Mayor Goode has also not gained any friends with the Hispanic community.

headline: Partner Says Hospital Management Pays Doctors To Refer Clients
abstract: A group holding a partnership in a Florida hospital has filed a federal lawsuit accusing a King of Prussia company of paying doctors to refer patients to its hospitals.

headline: State's logic out of whack
abstract: South Eastern School District is caught in a catch-22 of sorts, as they do not receive reimbursements for students they bus close to the school, because the district has deemed a road too dangerous to walk.  PennDOT will not reimburse the school because it is unable to deem a road dangerous unless students walk on it, but they don't because the school buses them because it's too dangerous.

headline: PUC Deadlocks On UGI Discount
abstract: The PUC deadlocked today on a proposal by UGI Corp. gas division to offer a temporarily discounted rate to consumers who switch to natural gas instead of oil or other fuels.  The PUC deadlocked with a 2-2 vote.

headline: Computer- enhanced police
abstract: Legislation being promoted by state Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. would make way for the creation of a computerized, statewide, central repository of intelligence information.

headline: Social Security field worker hits the street to find homeless
abstract: Patricia Betch is a Social Security field representative who along with Kathy Lorenzo, a psychiatric outreach worker for Health Care for the Homeless, seeks to help homeless people in Baltimore by getting them to accept Social Security benefits. However, many of the homeless with whom they work refuse the benefits for fear of being committed to a mental institution. Baltimore Mayor Kurt Schmoke wants a state worker to accompany Betch and Lorenzo.

headline: Bell Atlantic's Caller ID Program Sparks Controversial
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union is claiming that Bell Atlantic's caller ID program is an invasion of privacy.  Bell Atlantic will soon be offering the service to Maryland callers, and it is already available in New Jersey and will soon be unveiled in Pennsylvania.

headline: New leadership
abstract: US Congressmen Dick Gephardt and Bill Gray have been elected majority leader and whip, respectively.  The two hope to revitalize the Congress in order to restore its effectiveness improve its reputation with Americans.

headline: Legislators, experts debate aspects of tax revision plan
abstract: A meeting last night in Allentown drew about 60 people to hear what local legislators and a panel of experts had to say about the Local Tax Reform Act, up for vote in referendum May 16.

headline: Difference remain over drug signs
abstract: Some residents are skeptical of a program to put up signs in neighborhoods that say "Drug Watch."  Police support these measures as a deterrent to criminals, but some residents interviewed say that drug dealers aren't afraid of signs.  They wonder why they signs aren't everywhere.  One resident suggests that they should put the signs everywhere or just take them down.

headline: Penn nursing school gets part of $10.8 million grant
abstract: The Independence Foundation, a private non-profit organization based in Philadelphia, announced a $10.8 million grant to be given to nursing schools at nine private universities, including the University of Pennsylvania. The Independence Foundation's chairman Robert A. Maes hopes the grant will help solve the country's nursing shortage. Claire M. Fagin, dean of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Nursing lauded the grant.

headline: Strife feared as teachers cross strikers
abstract: Teachers represented by the PA State Education Association crossed the picket line of striking teachers represented by the PA Federation of Teachers so that they could teach the 1,034 students at Belle Vernon High School.  The school board says the strike is illegal because the union did not notify the district of the strike at least 150 days before July1.

headline: PUC Suspends Media Water Request
abstract: The PUC suspended for investigation a requested rate hike by Media Borough Water Works for consumers outside the borough.  The investigation could take up to 7 months.

headline: Court permits RICO to fight porn
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled yesterday that the states may use their versions of the Racketeer Influencedand Corrupt Organizations Act to crack down on adult bookstores.  The court found that the use of the law did not violate the First Amendment right to free speech.  In addition, the court ruled on various cases concerning abortion, religion, and summary jury trials.

headline: Social services boosted by revival
abstract: Social services information and recruiting booths set up near the city-wide religious revival site are enjoying the extra exposure they receive from having so many people visit their stands and learn about their cause.

headline: Call-blocking option should be available
abstract: Joseph Rhodes Jr. of the PA Public Utilities Commission believes that Bell Telephone's allowing the use of Caller I.D. services violates Pennsylvanians' rights. He argued against the service in a PUC public hearing, describing Caller I.D. as "illegal, unconstitutional and simply bad public policy," but approved services such as call-blocking. He reiterates the suggestion of legislative action from an editorial article written November 12.

headline: New Sandycreek Supervisor Named
abstract: Denton E. Lake was unanimously appointed last night to the Sandycreek Township Supervisors board.  In other news, the board began work on plans for a township sewage system which would include new sewage lines and tanks.  Adams, Graney and Associates and Pantech Engineers Inc. were hired to develop the system.

headline: Let's no rush to judgement on Pennsylvania's 'tax reform'
abstract: James Broussard, chairman of the Dept. of History and Political Science at Lebanon Valley College, argues that although Gov.Casey's tax reform proposal would provide municipalities with greater flexibility in setting local income and property taxes, the legislation is full of loopholes.  The proposed law could hurt small businesses, and it also allows for increases in property taxes after a mandated decrease.

headline: Orange: Lemoyne police join seat-belt program
abstract: Lemoyne's police department will be the first in the country to install orange seatbelts in their police cruisers in order to show people that police wear their seatbelts too.  This comes months after a police officer was killed in a crash while not wearing his seatbelt.  The move will show residents that police are serious about following the law themselves.

headline: PennFree troubles D&A official
abstract: JoEllen Steinbrunner, a Blair County drug & alcohol program specialist, voiced her disappointment that Gov. Casey's PennFree anti-drug fund will likely focus more on law enforcement than on treatment and prevention.  She said that the testimonies presented during the short public hearing period were weighted toward enforcement.

headline: Student Hung By Ankles In Cold In Fraternity 'Tradition'
abstract: The attention of Penn State officials has been drawn to Delta Theta Sigma after an incident where a fraternity member was hung half-nude by his ankles and other members threw water, vomit, and food at him.  Hazing is against school policy and state law.

headline: PUC suspends proposed rate increase for American Water
abstract: The state Public Utilities Commission, in compliance with recommendations, halted a proposed $15.2 million rate increase which was pursued by Pennsylvania American Water Co.

headline: Court removes last major hurdle to Dalkon Shield settlement
abstract: The US Supreme Court rejected a challenge by women likely to share in a trust fund set up by A.H. Robins Company. A.H. Robins Co. manufactured the Dalkon Shield, a birth control device which was found to be faulty and was recalled in 1984. Justice Byron R. White voted to hear arguments against the lawsuit, which involves a $2.5 billion settlement for victims of the product.

headline: Tax Day Walk
abstract: An official of the United Steelworkers union is asking people to participate in the Tax Day Walk and Rally that supports social and economic justice.  The president of the USW union feels that federal government involvement in social and economic justice is 'shameful' and feels that they need to put people before brokers and corporations.

headline: Cap proposed on charges for some pay phone calls
abstract: A bill passed the House on Tuesday which which puts a cap on the cost of using pay phone and hotel phones for in-state calls.

headline: New tack for Casey after the tax vote
abstract: After his tax reform referendum was defeated by voters, Gov. Casey moves on to new issues to avoid dwelling on the loss, thereby minimizing political damage.  Republicans ponder how they could potentially use Casey's defeat in the next gubernatorial election.

headline: Local tax reform is a good idea, but...
abstract: The editorial staff at the Evening Phoenix  make their suggestion to voters about the tax reform proposal.

headline: House scheduled to resume efforts on bills expanding anti-drug laws
abstract: The state House will be working on a number of small anti-drug measures in the upcoming days.  As many as nine bills are expected to be looked at which have policy implications ranging from suspension of drivers licenses for drug offenders to underage drinkers.  The measure could cause as many as 15,000 new suspensions per year.

headline: Pharmacists lobby for 'freedom of choice' bill
abstract: More than 300 pharmacists lobbied Tuesday for a bill designed to save independent pharmacies from contracts between insurance companies and chain- pharmacy operations.

headline: Students call BU officials 'hypocrites of the arts'
abstract: A handful of Bloomsburg University theater students protested twice Wednesday to let visiting state executives know they're fed up with BU's "hypocritical" attitude toward the arts.

headline: Singel seeks to hasten research in alternative fuels
abstract: Lt. Gov. Singel announced a $1 million plan to "jump start" PA's interest in alternative fuels by providing money to convert some state and public vehicles to natural gas and promoting research into other alternative fuels.

headline: Darby blues
abstract: The editorial board criticizes Delaware County District Attorney William H. Ryan Jr. for not acting quicker in response to allegations of police brutality and ticket fixing against the Darby Police Department. The board also criticizes Borough Police Chief Robert Smythe and Darby mayor Louis Saraullo for not responding to complaints. In addition to several reports of brutality, the police department acknowledged a practice of giving out more parking tickets during election times to benefit Republican officials who could get the tickets repealed.

headline: The sad dance of child abuses and government
abstract: The city of Philadelphia, including the mayor and the city Dept. of Human Services, has had an incredibly poor record concerning the protection of children from abuse.  In the end, the state Dept. of Public Welfare Secretary John White removed the city DHS's license, refusing to relax the state's standards.

headline: Court sets a hearing in Bell case
abstract: President Judge Paul J. Crumlish requested the attendance of top Bell executives and two members of the Public Utility Commission in a court case: a consumer advocate versus the PUC.  David Barasch's lawsuit claims that PUC violated the state's Open Meetings Act when it reached a closed-door settlement with Bell involving the misuse of utility resources.  Barasch and the PUC agreed to a new policy to avoid the secrecy.

headline: Nicholas rebuffed in union vote
abstract: A recent vote to determine where members of a Philadelpihia health-care union would affiliate left the president of the union with only a third of his former constituents following his advice and allying with AFSCME rather than SEIU.

headline: Manor Pact Is Ratified
