abstract: Venango County commissioners signed a contract with the union at Venango Manor, providing a 2% pay raise for each person.  Commissioners are also discussing designs for a new county jail.

headline: The graying of the campuses
abstract: The first of a three part series on the growing population of older Americans at college campuses taking classes and graduating.  The sight of older students was highly uncommon as few as 20 years before the publication of the article.  In 1974 the average age of a student was 20.9.  In 1987 it was 22.4.

headline: Phila. Mayor hospitalized again
abstract: Philadelphia mayor Wilson Goode was hospitalized for a rapid heart beat. This is the mayor's second trip to the hospital for irregular heart activity. Goode's physician, Dr. Edward Cooper, said that the mayor was recovering.

headline: Study: Changes won't end special education deficits
abstract: According to a fiscal analysis by the staff of the Senate Education Committee, new special education programs proposed by the Pennsylvania Board of Education would wipe out any initial savings from cost-cutting measures in the regulations after three years. The article addresses five of the key points of the analysis.

headline: Report: Pennsylvania ranks fourth in coal production
abstract: Details which states are producing the most coal and provides some information about why coal production has improved.

headline: Convictions urged in drug killings
abstract: In the trial of two killings over drug money, Assistant District Attorney Michael McGettigan asked the jury to convict all four men charged with the death of two young men. McGettigan said the defendants, Miguel "Mike Martinez, Mark "R.P." Christian, Kelly "Raheem" Robinson, and John "Ronnie" Garrett, are linked together in their actions in the murders of Anthony, 13, and Cornell Williams, 15, who had apparently lost or squandered drugs and drug money belonging to the defendants. The death penalty could be sought for two of the defendants who were over the age of 18 at the time of the killings.

headline: Welfare benefits backed
abstract: A new study says that low-income single parents trying to get off welfare by getting a job should be extended welfare benefits during the transition phase, otherwise it's much more likely that they'll end up returning to welfare.

headline: New evidence, adding Bell's response
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania today announced that it is reopening its investigation into the misuse of company resources by employees in its Pittsburgh office.

headline: Nitpicking on ethics
abstract: In order to maintain the state ethics commission, the Legislature must pass a new law before June 30.  The current bill is much stronger than one proposed last year, containing provisions such as the banning of honoraria or speaking fees for public officials and disallowing the hiring of immediate family as well.

headline: Manor To Appeal
abstract: Cornwall Manor is appealing to the state Supreme Court to review a ruling by the Commonwealth Court upholding property taxation of parts of the manor's 85-acre campus.

headline: Casey honors manufacturer' new products
abstract: Governor Casey honored a number of new products produced by companies in PA.  They included a cloth pig, a crane and landfill foam.  Those were some of the honorees at the 7th Annual New Products Awards.  The state uses this to show its commitment to the manufacturing and industrial community in PA.

headline: Tires roll in while residents' anger mounts
abstract: Residents of a block in Philadelphia are becoming increasingly frustrated with city government for failing to remove the massive mountain of discarded tires which has been growing for 6 years on an empty lot, and now sometimes spills into the street.

headline: Philadelphia AIDS czar criticizes governor on funding
abstract: Davd Fair, the head of Philadelphia's AIDS program, said that no new money to fight the AIDS epidemic was in Gov. Casey's 1989-1990 buget.  Although the administration has increased monies allotted for AIDS treatement to $28.9, Mr. Fair said there is no AIDS-specific program or staff provided for by the state.

headline: Teachers critical of special education cuts
abstract: PA director of special education James Tucker spoke at the local PSEA, where many teachers are unhappy with the proposed special education funding cuts.

headline: Settlement in '86 PECO rate case
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission approved a settlement to disputes stemming from a 1986 rate increase from the Philadelphia Electric Company. The decision will leave intact the $351 million rate increase the company awarded last year, while PECO will have to drop its appeals against rate cases stemming from its 1986 increase. Court appeals will also be dropped by the PUC, the Office of Consumer Advocate, the University of Pennsylvania, and the Utility Users Committee, according to the decision.

headline: County erects holiday displays despite ruling
abstract: The photograph depicts workers in Luzerne County constructing a nativity scene outside the county courthouse despite a ruling against the construction. Luzerne County commissioner Frank J. Trinisewski Jr. approved. A Jewish menorah and other secular symbols were also placed on the ground.

headline: Welfare Dept. wins in lottery
abstract: The writer notes that the Welfare Dept. is benefitted by the PA lottery, sometimes at the expense of older Pennsylvanians, since the Welfare Dept. recently decided to reduce a patient's medical assistance by the amount of the lottery rebate they receive.

headline: Projects for needy to benefit from $500,000 Bell penalty
abstract: In an agreement reaached with the state Public Utilities Commission, Bell of Pennsylvania will donate $500,000 to charities and projects.  The donations are a penalty for the company misleading the commission regarding its investigation into certain employee actions.

headline: No Business is show business
abstract: A citizen from State College writes in opposition to an official state song, saying that politicians lack music taste and state pride is out of vogue.

headline: Mayor ponders law on private clubs
abstract: York Mayor William J. Althaus said Wednesday he plans to meet with the city Human Relations Commission to discuss possible legislation forbidding discrimination at private clubs.

headline: Profit in disposal
abstract: A local resident questions whether local dumps have done enough to assure residents that the out-of-town trash they house is safe and won't be a burden to their communities.

headline: A first step to alter taxes
abstract: The editorial supports a standardization of the statewide local taxing system so that it's less confusing for taxpayers, saying that it would be the first step in a long journey to tax reform.

headline: Philadelphia and Pittsburgh hospitals discuss merger
abstract: Officials from Philadelphia's Hahnemann University Hospital and Pittsburgh-based Allegheny Health Services Inc. were discussing a merger that could create a medical, research, and teaching institution controlling about 1,900 beds. Hahnemann University spokeswoman Phyllis Fisher said both parties have committed to exploring all possibilities, while Allegheny Health Services spokesman Thomas Chakurda declined to add any additional information. Any deal would involved the Medical College of Pennsylvania as well as the Allegheny General Hospital, both of which are affiliated with Allegheny Health Services.

headline: Teens 'Standing Tall' against drugs
abstract: Brought to the Elco School District by John Wiley, football coach and teacher at Danville High School, the Stand Tall program challenges young people to abstain from drugs and alcohol and submit to voluntary random testing to prove it. Gimmicks to entice students include receiving a Stand Tall identification card and a t-shirt after testing clean. The program is attempting to use positive peer pressure to make students abstain from drugs and alcohol. When presented to Danville schools, Wiley found that about 61 percent of the student body grades 6 through 12 signed up for the program.

headline: Shutdown costs soar for N-plant
abstract: After the Nuclear Regulatory Commission shut down the Peach Bottom plant in 1987, the Philadelphia Electric Co. and its three partners have been forced to comply with regulations by repairing equipment and replacing electricity.  The costs are likely to reach at least $735 million.

headline: County jail can't move prisoners out
abstract: York County Prison is almost full of inmates. In response to the rioting at Camp Hill state prison, the PA Department of Corrections stopped accepting prisoners from York County Prison, among other county prisons. Warden Richard Hahn says that he will figure out what to do once the prison reaches its capacity.

headline: What Senate day-care bill really means
abstract: The writer opposes the US Senate day-care bill because she says it doesn't provide real relief for families who need affordable day care, since in order to get a tax refund for day-care, families need to buy expensive health insurance for their child or other restrictions.

headline: PUC-Bell case windup
abstract: Judge James Crumlish approved a settlement between the Public Utility Commission and Bell of Pennsylvania and the consumer advocate. The case related to illegal activity at the telephone company and Bell gave $500,000 to charities so that PUC would brush the problems under the table.  Every meeting is to be public, which is why the consumer advocate  took it to court.

headline: No plans for city training center, Casey office says
abstract: A spokesman for Gov. Casey's budget office indicated today that there are no plans to build a regional training center for emergency personnel in Altoona.

headline: Mayor targets trial board
abstract: Mayor Masloff of Pittsburgh and Public Safety Direction Glenn Cannon held a meeting with Philadelphia lawmakers concerning suggested changes to the trial board system.  The legislators said they would likely be in support of letting Pittsburgh determine its own trial board reglations.

headline: Homeless start early to crowd city shelters
abstract: An influx of homeless are stressing the already burdened homeless care systems throughout the country an in Harrisburg.  Shelters report that once-generally spracely used facilities are filling to the brim.  Some shelters are allowing some people to sleep on floor mattresses.

headline: An analysis of tax reform
abstract: An in-depth analysis of various facets of the upcoming tax reform referendum.

headline: Philly mayor back in hospital for tests
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode was hospitalized for the third time in two weeks on account of rapid heart action. Drs. Edward S. Cooper and Arthur Whereat said that the mayor was recovering. While in the hospital, Goode was able to talk with city officials via telephone from the University of Pennsylvania Hospital.

headline: Tests Suggest Unhealthy Levels in Nation's Schools
abstract: Preliminary tests suggest unhealthy levels of radon exist in schools across the country, the Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday in urging every school to test for the gas.

headline: Singel announces close watch on fuel
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel reported that numerous state agencies and all county emergency management agencies will closely monitor the availability of heating fuels in Pennsylvania. Singel, who chairs the PA Emergency Management Council and the PA Energy Office, directed the PA Emergency Management Agency and the PEO to monitor the fuel supply situation and its impact on communities. Jim Siracuse, executive director of Luzerne County's Emergency Management Agency, said there is a shortage of propane fuel in Luzerne County, but there is no real emergency.

headline: County sells 'drug cars,' with message
abstract: A first-of-its-kind auction happened Friday when Bedford County auctioned off two cars confiscated as part of drug cases.  The money garnered from these types of auctions goes to help fight drug marketing and use.

headline: null
abstract: According to a report in the Philadelphia Inquirer, negotiators for the City of Philadelphia promised a cap on city real estate taxes for a new sports arena which will be built in an effort to keep the 76ers basketball and Flyers hockey teams in the city. The arena would cost $100 million, and would have to be approved by the City Council and the PA State Legislature. A spokesman for Spectacor, the company which owns the current arena as well as the Flyers, stated that no deal had been reached, while the Casey administration proposed that the state would fund the demolition of an older stadium to make room for the new arena.

headline: Talks open over a new phone pact
abstract: Coming off a successful contract negotiation with AT&T, the Communications Workers or America now sets its sights on Bell Atlantic.  Bell contends that it will not use the AT&T contract as a model, though the CWA will try to replicate many of the provisions in that contract.

headline: Norristown stunned as Democrats mull majority vote
abstract: William DeAngelis, John McGuigan and Stanley Darden, all Democrats, won elections in a surprise upset for the Republican candidates. DeAngelis defeated Samuel Vallone in the mayoral race, while McGuigan and Darden will become councilmen. State Representative Joseph A. Lashinger, a Republican, attributed the Democrats' success to infighting among Republicans.

headline: New York revolt joins property tax fight
abstract: Suffolk County residents are protesting the massive property tax increases in the County, saying that they taxes are excessive for the amount of government services they receive.  Many people point to government patronage and corruption when looking at the county's billion-dollar budget.

headline: Coatesville today seeks an order ending strike
abstract: School officials in Coatesville say that they will head to court to seek a court order demanding that striking teachers go back to work.  The 450-strong force of striking workers have been off the job since the beginning of the school year.  The district warns that if they want to let children finish the year before the end of June, they must be back at school by Oct 19.

headline: An endorsement for state tax reform plan
abstract: State Rep. Art Hershey argues that the proposed statewide tax reform legislation is important because it is fair and egalitarian, but also because fair taxation is an issue which was formative for this nation.  The proposed reform is needed because it takes into account those with lower incomes; has a farmland provision initiative; and will affect taxes at the county, municipality, and school district levels.

headline: Picketers Urge State Not to Cut Funds for Mentally Ill
abstract: 35 family members and mental patients protested outside of the State Office Building yesterday, asking the Casey administration to continue to fund treatment of patients of Philadelphia State Hospital, also known as Byberry, after the state shuts it down.  The picketers said that the cut in the governor's budget of $39.5 million for patient care in the community  in 1988 to $19 million in 1989 was unacceptable.

headline: They don't believe new regs will help
abstract: Pennsylvania is attempting to change its special education regulations and standards, amidst the opposition of some special education parents. The PA State Board of Education maintains the changes will improve the program by offering better ways of identifying students' needs and encouraging parental involvement. Richard Campbell, director of special education for Lincoln Intermediate Unit 12, which serves York, Adams, and Franklin counties, said he does not yet understand how the new initiative will affect the special education programs. Robert E. Feir, executive director of the PA Board of Education, said the regulations would not apply to students currently enrolled in the program, only those that join after it has been enacted.

headline: SmithKline sues county for methane gas problem
abstract: Leading research and development firm SmithKline is suing Montgomery Co. for neglecting contractual obligations to monitor the migration of gases from a nearby former landfill.  The suit claims that the gases were the cause of an explosion of a SmithKline utility conduit.

headline: Court orders evidence hearing in Reinert case
abstract: The state Supreme Court yesterday ordered an expedited hearing to determine the validity of newly discovered evidence in connection with the murder trial of Jay C. Smith.  Smith, a school principal, is own death row for the murders of a Montgomery County schoolteacher and her two children.

headline: $6 million in bonds to fund city town houses
abstract: The Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority agreed to sell $6 million in bonds to build 100 town houses in the city's midtown section between the Broad Street Market and Reily Street, on land half-owned by the authority and the City of Harrisburg. The town houses would sell for approximately $70,000 each and are aimed to appeal to working people who cannot afford the closing costs of purchasing a house, Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed said. City authorities said Commonwealth National Bank has shown interest in assuming the risk in the project. Reed said the city would not lose much money even if none of the town houses can be sold.

headline: Carlisle coup: Firm to make roofing in U.S.S.R.
abstract: A Carlisle-based roofing company has reached an agreement to produce roofing materials in the Soviet Union, an impressive deal for a small Pennsylvania company.

headline: Not a Casey defeat
abstract: The piece state that the defeat of the tax reform proposal was not a political defeat for Gov. Casey or the Democratic party, but instead was a result of the public's wariness of changing the taxing structure when they were unsure of how it would affect them.

headline: No positions on tax reform
abstract: None of the Bucks County commissioners have come out in favor of or against the Legislature's tax reform proposal which will be placed before voters on May 16.

headline: Implantation of Frozen Embroyos Produces Twin Boys
abstract: The first multiple birth in the Philadelphia area by the implantation of frozen embryos occurred recently.  The babies were born at Thomas Jefferson University Hospital in Philadelphia.

headline: Area official responds to tax reform questions
abstract: In the second part of a series of articles on tax reform, Representative Merle Philips's arguments are outlined against the proposed tax plan.

headline: Plan gives free health care to children of working poor
abstract: Justin Coles, a 7-year-old suffering from recurring ear infections, is one of many children who now qualifies for the Caring Program for Children, sponsored by Blue Cross of Western PA and PA Blue Shield. According to the Children's Defense Fund, the number of children living in poverty from by 1.2 million from 1980 to 1988. The program, whose funding was augmented by a grant from the American Academy of Pediatrics and the federal Office of Maternal and Child Health, is intended to help families above the state Medicaid level, but below the federal poverty level.

headline: U. Merion police probe Norristown gridiron fight
abstract: Upper Merion Township police are investigating a fight that erupted between players and fans from Norristown Area and Upper Merion Area High Schools after a football game on Thanksgiving. Upper Merion police Captain Frank Ferlick, who is heading the investigation with Lieutenant Thomas Lawler, said a decision will be made based on interviews with school officials. Both Upper Merion schools superintendent Charles Scott and Norristown schools superintendent Dr. James Holton said they had viewed the tape of the brawl and were trying to figure out the best way to deal with the situation.

headline: State Pushes Natural Gas Car Conversions
abstract: As part of an effort by Lt. Gov. Singel, the state will be converting 125 vehicles to natural gas fuel, and is providing money for an additional 125 conversions in both Philadelphia and Pittsburgh areas.  The rest of the $1 million initiative will go towards alternative fuel research.

headline: Court ruling doesn't end political battle over judgeship
abstract: After the recent state Supreme Court decision concluded that the voter-approved constitutional amendment which forces state judges to retire at age 70 was valid, state Rep. Michael Bortner said GOP senators had a "moral obligation" to approve Thompson J. McCullough as the new county judge.

headline: 3 decades of big plans gone awry
abstract: Willard G. Rouse's abandonement of plans to develop the 37-acre plot of land along the Delware River known as Penn's Landing is only the latest in a long line of failed attempts at development.

headline: Steel importers say fair-trade laws are being abused to protect steel companies in this country from foreign competition
abstract: Steel importers are urging an international trading body to examine the issue of fair-trade laws being abused to protect steel companies from foreign competition. Officials of the American Institute for Imported Steel said foreign producers can run afoul of anti-dumping laws because of the drop in the value of the dollar while a consultant for the group said that US Department of Commerce officials admitted to selectively prosecuting foreign companies as a warning to others.

headline: Numbers in State Workforce Hit 20 Year Low
abstract: While the state payroll peaked in 1976 with 109,000 employees, it has now reached at 20 year low with 79,537 employees.  The area most affected can be found in the Dept. of Public Welfare.

headline: Once a rising star, Philadelphia Mayor faces big problems
abstract: Mayor Wilson Goode is being blamed for all the city's problems.  Many people feel that he is not doing a good job as mayor.

headline: Jury Convicts Three Charged in Atlantic City Cocaine Ring
abstract: Prosecutors won the conviction of three people charged with running a $1,000,000 a month drug ring in the housing projects of Atlantic City, NJ.  The jury worked on the case for 14 hours before deciding.  Some of the defendents plan to appeal the verdict.

headline: Bank wants court to invalidate newly enacted tax
abstract: The First National Bank of Fredericksburg has asked the Commonwealth Court to invalidate the revised bank tax that was approved five months ago. Sherill T. Moyer, a lawyer representing the bank, said the revised tax was flawed and suffers constitutional and legal infirmities. The administration of PA Governor Robert P. Casey maintains that the tax is constitutional.

headline: Powerful Medical Lobby May Be the Big Loser As Congress Attempts to Rein In Medicare Costs
abstract: Trying to avoiid budget cuts in their specific field, the doctors of the medical lobbies jockey for position against one another.  This internal strife is weakening the cohesiveness and strength of medical lobbies.

headline: Union School Talks Break Off
abstract: Contract talks broke off last night in the Union District, where teachers went on strike earlier in the school year.  No further negotiations have been scheduled.

headline: State sets alternative-fuels goal
abstract: Lt. Gov. Singel has announced a plan to help make PA somewhat less dependent on foreign oil by emphasizing the use of compressed natural gas for fuel and granting more money for alternative fuel research.

headline: Courthouse security awaits federal study
abstract: Changes such as expansion and increase in the number of cells in the prisoner holding facilities in the York County Courthouse must await a study by the Courthouse Security Division of the United States Marshals' Services, part of the US Department of Justice. The study was prompted by the escape of Marion Brooks, a convict, from the courthouse's facilities after being sentenced by Judge John H. Chronister. In 1988, York County President Commissioner Lorraine B. Hovis said funds were being set aside in the 1989 budget to finance improvement of prison facilities in the sheriff's office.

headline: 600-acre development proposed near quarry
abstract: Richard Woodfin, vice president of Eastern Land and Resources Company presented a proposal to construct a 600-acre housing development to municipal and county officials. The proposal also included a golf course and some condominiums. Donald Umberger, a South Annville Township supervisor, said that the townships will have to look at zoning before anything can happen.

headline: The Russians are buying! The Russians are buying!
abstract: Three York businesses are working with the Soviets, just a few of the U.S. firms that stand to benefit from perestroika- the Soviet's Plan for sweeping internal economic reform.

headline: Obstructionism still runs rampant
abstract: In the divided PA legislature (Dem. House, Rep. Senate), Democrats are upset over a new "roadblock" to House legislation.  The Editorial Board believes that Republicans would be just as upset if the tables were turned.

headline: Pennsylvania-financial news in brief
abstract: Marie Haley of Uniontown has been sentenced in a federal court after she pleaded guilty to participating in a rebate scheme. The Edward DeBartolo Corporation has submitted plans to build a shopping mall in Washington County to South Strabane Township officials and the PA Department  of Transportation. The Pittsburgh City Council is investigating alternatives, such as increasing property taxes, to Mayor Sophie Masloff's plan to lower the wage tax. Senior citizens are critical of the tax swap. Cyclops Industries of Pittsburgh will not sell its Cytemp Specialty Steel unit to a new company formed by an Employee Stock Ownership Plan.

headline: Steroids
abstract: House members approved legislation to restrict the use of steroids in PA.  The bill moves on to the Senate.

headline: Bartle: Tax Plan Too Vague
abstract: Montgomery County's two Republican commissioners are urging residents to vote against the tax reform because they feel it is too vague.

headline: Prison AIDS-care unit urged
abstract: State prison officials would like to open dialogue with health-care firms regarding the construction of a health facility for state inmates with AIDS.  Gov. Casey's budget has outlined funding, totalling $1.9 million in two years and more than $2 million a year after that, for such a facility.  It is estimated that more than 60 inmates have tested positive for HIV-AIDS.

headline: Universities seek more funding
abstract: Representatives from state-related universities as well as those universities in the state system went to Harrisburg yesterday to lobby for state funding.  University officials threatened tuition hikes of between 5 and 10 percent if no additional state funding was awarded.  PA ranks 47th in the country in state aid to higher education.

headline: State to probe accusations of fuel-oil price gouging
abstract: The Pennsylvania Attorney General's office said it is investigating charges of price gouging by heating-oil suppliers who some believe are taking advantage of the cold weather. PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. said he is concerned that price increases are "the result of illegal activity rather than natural economic forces." PA Governor Robert P. Casey also requested a federal investigation. John Zinkand, executive vice president of the petroleum association, said heating-oil distributors cannot accept that the skyrocketing increases in the cost of fuel are due entirely to subzero temperatures. Zinkand added that the final price is not the fault of the distributor who has had to pay the same increases as homeowners.

headline: Courthouse shuffle
abstract: The planned $170 million criminal justice center project, which was stopped two weeks ago by Mayor Goode, must be compromised upon if it is to come to fruition.  A start is Judge Edward J. Bradley's proposal concerning judicial chambers; he agreed to no new chambers being built, but maintained the need for 70 new courtrooms and 440 new holding cells.

headline: A graceful out for Pietragallo
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman Michael Coyne has recommended that public-housing residents be penalized for the failure of Daniel Pietragallo, the executive director of the Pittsburgh Housing Authority, to leave his position. Mr. Coyne has asked Mayor Masloff of Pittsburgh to delete from the budget a more than million-dollar request for funds to renovate low- and moderate-income housing to encourage Pietragallo's resignation. The editors request that Mr. Pietragallo announce his resignation so that recipients of public-housing funds do not suffer.

headline: No business on Sunday for Polish Solidarity leader
abstract: Lech Walesa, the leader of Poland's Solidarity movement, visited Philadelphia as part of a goodwill tour of the United States. While in the country, he met with the president, Congress, and former US Supreme Court Justice Warren Burger. A ceremony at the National Shrine of our Lady of Czestochowa was arranged by the Copernicus Society with help from the Polish Scouting Organization.

headline: Officials' calls multiply for help with red tape
abstract: Profiles the importance of constituent work in state politics, and discusses the ammendment of the small games of chance referendum to now include political parties as a group allowed to conduct such games.

headline: Pennsylvania-Financial News In Brief
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Council has approved a $320.9 million budget for 1990, an increase of $17.8 million from 1989. National Intergroup Incorporated of Pittsburgh wants to repurchase the 85 percent of an oil distribution business it sold in 1987. A county judge in Ohio has ruled that Rite Aid Corporation of Shiremanstown, PA, and its president, Martin Grass, will stand trial for allegedly bribing an Ohio Board of Pharmacy member. The British defense contractor Ferranti International Signal, which faced problems when it acquired International Signal and Control Group of Lancaster in Lancaster County in 1987, has changed its name to Ferranti International P-L-C. United Water Resources, which has acquired Pennsylvania Gas and Water Company's water assets for $220 million, says residential water customers may have to pay one dollar a day more for service within the next three years.

headline: No alcohol ads for college paper
abstract: The staff of the Aquinas college newspaper at the University of Scranton have been told that they can no longer accept ads for alcoholic beverages.  The ban will mean a loss of $2,000 in revenue that comes from local taverns and bars that advertised in the paper.  The unviersity says that allowing such ads would contravene the university's alcohol policy.

headline: Battle lines are drawn in tax reform debate
abstract: Battle lines are drawn in the tax reform debate over how each side is portrayed and what each side argues would be the effects of the tax reform.

headline: Program Called Feasible in New York
abstract: If rules regarding the treatment of methadone addicts were liberalized, administrators of would-be affected programs believe that New York City's 200,000 heroin addicts could begin taking daily doses of the drug in only a few weeks.  New York State is home to roughly half of the nation's opiate-addicted population.

headline: University officials say growing problem must be faced
abstract: The Anti-Defamation League of B'nai B'rith sponsored a conference on bigotry and racism on college campuses at the University of Pennsylvania. The US Department of Justice's Community Relations Office has reported an increase in the number of incidents involving racial tension. Temple University President Pete J. Liacouras, the conference's keynote speaker, and ADL Director Abraham H. Foxman emphasized the need to end racism on college campuses.

headline: Ten years after Three Mile Island
abstract: Ten years after the the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island, people in the industry and citizens in the town pause to reflect.

headline: Courthouse: Youth Forum Will Have Center- Stage This Week
abstract: The Editorial Board hails a day- long seminar for 62 area high school seniors at the Courthouse to discuss county government and the criminal justice system as a tremendous opportunity.

headline: A great plan offered for the waterfront
abstract: Praises the plan for Penn's Landing and the city's handling of the selection process.

headline: null
abstract: During the Senate confirmation hearings over Pres. Bush's nominee for the position of Secretary of Defense, John G. Tower, the former senator acknowledged that he had lobbied directly on behalf of one major defense contractor which paid him nearly $250,000.  In 1984, upon his retirement from the Senate, Mr. Tower pledged, "The one thing I'm not going to be is a lobbyist."

headline: Old Forge Board and Teachers Disagree on Tentative Contract
abstract: There is disagreement over a settlement between the Old Forge School Board and the teachers' union which ended four months of labor strife.  The disagreement surrounds the interpretation of teachers' first-year salaries of the five-year contract.

headline: Pennsylvania-Financial News In Brief
abstract: Unisys Corporation of Blue Bell reported that it has received a $47 million dollar computer order from the West German Air Traffic Control organization. Timothy Thyreen has been appointed as the 14th president of Waynesburg College, effective this upcoming academic year. Authorities have seized 148 video poker machines in raids at 31 businesses, two tractor-trailers, and 14 motor vehicles in Allegheny County. Pittsburgh city officials are appealing the ruling by US District Judge Barron McCune that the Jewish organization Chabad is permitted to set up a menorah outside the City-County Building for Hanukkah. In Westmoreland County, state police have arrested at least 29 suspects in a burglary ring that has operated in six counties.

headline: Lewis Popper appointed
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh named university counsel Lewis Popper to be general counsel and secretary of the board of trustees and the corporation.

headline: Both sides agree tax vote means big changes
abstract: The author of this piece creates a metaphoric "tax tower" to illustrate the breakdown of taxes under the present and proposed tax plans.

headline: Public should understand limitations of no-fault
abstract: No-fault insurance has severe limitations, one of which is the fact that under its guidelines drunk drivers would be let off the hook.  However, no-fault does not address the true causes of increasing auto insurance rates: namely, the high cost of automobile parts and repairs on the property side, and increasing health care costs on the personal-injury side.

headline: Unofficial School Board Results
abstract: Listing of preliminary results for the school board elections two days ago.

headline: Sudy: Glatfelter plant poses high cancer risk
abstract: A federal study indicates that there are considerably higher cancer rates near eight industrial plants in PA, including the P.H. Glatfelter Co. in Spring Grove.  The study was immediately refuted as inaccurate by the plants.

headline: Criminals would pay a user's fee under bill
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman Mark H. Pollock introduced a bill which would require criminals to pay a "user's fee" to the Bureau of Police when arrested. He acknowledged that after attorney fees, most criminals wouldn't be able to afford the fee, so the city should target criminals known to have significant resources. Assistant chief of police Donald Aubrecht described the ordinance as "unenforceable."

headline: Addition to hotel possible
abstract: Abraham Lincoln Associates, a development group, is seeking to purchase the Abraham Lincoln Hotel for $4 million from owner Grace Charleston.  The group is appealing to the PA Housing Finance Administration for up to $18 million in reconstruction costs, as it looks to make the hotel into a retirement home.

headline: $83 million- and it could climb higher
abstract: Although the jackpot for Wednesday's Super 7 drawing soared to a record $83 million on Monday, state officials said it won't change the fact that Pennsylvania's lottery is going broke.

headline: On car insurance agenda: Meetings
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey and PA Senator F. Joseph Loeper Jr., Senate Majority Leader, met to discuss the urgency of car insurance legislation and announced in a news conference that more meetings will be held to discuss the topic. Casey and Loeper said they hope to produce legislation that can be voted on by the General Assembly when it returns from winter recess on January 22. Recently both sides of the auto insurance debate have accused the other of purposely delaying passage of legislation, but the meeting of Casey and Loeper was noteworthy because it marked the first sign of a truce.

headline: Putting the brakes on billboards
abstract: The City of Philadelphia's Planning Commission will examine a proposal brought forth by staff member Thomas Chapman on reducing the number of billboards in Philadelphia. Provisions include freezing the number of billboards in the city, then gradually reducing the number, in addition to restricting their proximity to schools, parks and major roadways. The anti-billboard group Scenic America lauds Philadelphia for this proposal on billboard removal, which is a trend in cities throughout the country.

headline: Stock exchange merger
abstract: The Philadelphia and American Stock Exchanges say they have ended talks of a possible merger of the two stock exchanges.  They say that no new talks have been scheduled.

headline: Casey gives last-minute tax-plan pitch
abstract: Governor Casey voices his support for the tax reform on election day, also saying tax reform won't come back up for a long time after this vote, so it's one of very few chances to make some changes.

headline: Punt questions Casey drug program
abstract: State Sen. Terry Punt said that he won't support Gov. Casey's $140 million anti-drug program until he sees real details about how the money will be used, contending that at the moment, the program doesn't have specifics and is more of a P.R. ploy.

headline: Valania resigns as NW principal
abstract: NW Area High School Principal Peter Valania said he will remain acting principal until the board decides on a replacement.  Valania is also a guidance counselor at the school, a post he will keep, and resigned from being the principal because he was "tired of having two jobs."

headline: The psychological half life of TMI accident
abstract: Residents of Middletown prepare to reflect on the ten year anniversary of the accident at Three Mile Island.  Uncertainty and fear still remain for many townspeople.

headline: Crowded Bucks jail inmate likely to be woman
abstract: The article is a feature on women in the Bucks County Prison system, which is not extensive enough to accommodate for the increasing population of women entering the prison system according to Warden Arthur M. Wallenstein. Eloise Andrews is an example of one of these women, as she is in her mid-20s, have children, and can trade legal troubles to drug use. A major reason women are filling prisons is because of recent laws requiring mandatory sentencing for drug-related crimes.

headline: Area mayors to lobby for federal urban grant program
abstract: The mayors of Johnstown and Altoona will lobby for the revival of a threatened federal program which gave grants to cities for economic development.  Johnstown has used the grants effectively through the years, and Altoona hopes to receive some if the program is continued.

headline: 1,000 Cheer Casey at Peckville 'Salute'
abstract: In stops at both Peckville and Wilkes-Barre, Gov. Casey met with roughly 1,400 supporters, thanking them for their political, moral, and financial backing.  Numerous local government officials and candidates were also on hand.

headline: On the fringe of better benefits
abstract: Townsend Engineering of Des Moines, Iowa has cutting-edge employee benefits, such as a fitness center, weeklong all-expenses paid vacations, and free financial counseling. Modern companies are coming up with new types of benefits for their employees, such as AT&T revamping its union contracts to allow for 6-month unpaid maternity leave for its employees. According to the US Census Bureau, more than half of American women with infants work.

headline: Reassessing Berks real estate at 100% ratio is a good idea
abstract: The Editorial Board believes that reassessing Berks County real estate at a 100% ratio is a good idea.

headline: In three way city controller's race, debate is largely a 2-man brawl
abstract: The city controller race in Philadelphia pits Republican M. Joseph Rocks against the incumbent Democrat Jonathan A. Saidel.  The candidates are being pelted by attacks from a third party challenger, Consumer Party candidate Max Weiner.  The candidates squared off at a 1 hour debate at the WCAU-TV studios.   The candidates showcased their experience relevant to the job and discussed other issues.

headline: Budget deadline nearing
abstract: Legislative leaders are cautiously optimistic about the prospect of getting the state budget passed by tomorrow's deadline, saying that the legislator and the Casey administration are only $10 million apart.

headline: Rabies cases rivaling '45 epidemic, Pa. warns
abstract: With 255 confirmed rabies cases through May, 1989 is on track for a huge year total of cases.  The legislature has approved $300,000 to help fight the diease.

headline: Where can you find help
abstract: The article is a directory of groups offering help with addiction, from crisis intervention to public education programs. The non-all-inclusive directory is provided by the United Way HelpLine, also including groups that are not affiliated with United Way such as Alcoholics Anonymous. The directory included group names, telephone numbers, and a description of the purpose of each group.

headline: Utility Ups and Downs- Energy Bills Headed In Opposite Directions
abstract: Electric bills may be going down, but natural gas charges are heading up.  Pennsylvania Electirc Co. has asked for a rate reduction, while National Fuel has filed to boost bills.

headline: Crudup saw beyond juvenile crime symptoms
abstract: The insightful coverage on the part of the local media regarding overcrowding at prisons has shown that such cramped conditions endanger both staff and inmates.  Mr. Crudup, the retiring director of the Youth Study Center, has also discussed the importance of treating and rehabilitating children rather than simply locking them up.

headline: Authority reviews Pun'xy, county projects
abstract: The Jefferson County Redevelopment Authority reviewed 5 projects in the county applying for a block grant from the PA Department of Community Affairs, all of which were rejected. One of the proposals was a sewer-extension project put forth by the borough of Punxsutawney. Barb Hopkins of the county Department of Development said that the sewer project has since been redesigned.

headline: An odd little sign of corruption
abstract: Common Cause of PA placed a sign labeled "countdown to corruption" in the state Capitol to remind people of the June 30 deadline to vote for a new Ethics Act.  Unfortunately, the sign was stolen.

headline: 'One more try, Bob… and if we still don't move, we'll try pulling up the anchor…"
abstract: This political cartoon features PA Governor Robert P. Casey and a member of the Pennsylvania Senate. It addresses the issue of automobile insurance reform that has been argued between the PA Legislature and the Executive for a long time.

headline: Seniors hear debate on tax reform
abstract: Senior citizens attending a tax reform forum at Montgomery County Community College Wed. night heard the merits of property tax relief, while being warned to think twice before voting for the plan.

headline: Steps to a bright, clean City Hall
abstract: Mayor Goode described his new efforts to take pride in Philadelphia City Hall.  He is shown standing under a banner that says "Philadelphians Care About City Hall."   Things like cleaner windows and corridors and hiring more janitors will be among the priorities.  Other larger projects including the renovation of heating and cooling systems are discussed.

headline: Budget Message
abstract: State Senators Anthony Andrezeski, John Peterson, and Roy Wilt each acknowledged that Gov. Casey's 1989-1990 budget request would mean more money for northwestern Pennsylvania.  Better educational programs, increased funding for the Erie Soldiers and Sailors Home, and a statewide attendant care program for the physically handicapped were all mentioned a signficant benefits to the plan.

headline: Rabies epidemic moves closer to Philadelphia
abstract: A woman from Roxborough was attacked by a rabid raccoon, the 22nd such incident confirmed this year. Robert Sharrar, assistant health commissioner for medical affairs for the Philadelphia Department of Health stated that the rabies epidemic is becoming a great cause for concern in the city, and encourages pet-owners to have their pets vaccinated.

headline: WACC to be Penn State branch
abstract: The Williamsport Area Community College will become a PSU branch campus, thanks to legislation signed into law yesterday.  Enrollment is expected to increase, though an official says that there will be no noticable changes on campus.

headline: TMI owner to boost non-nuclear power supply
abstract: The owner of Three Mile Island nuclear power plant plans to significantly increase its power production from non-nuclear sources.

headline: Cruiser may aid drug war
abstract: Sen. Arlen Specter of Philadelphia called for the Navy and Dept. of Defense to aid in anti-drug efforts involving other nations and drug trafficking.  He wants to create a multi-national force against drug traffickers and terrorists.

headline: Banking on Pittsburgh
abstract: According to Stanley Lowe, founder of the Pittsburgh Community Reinvestment Group, some banks have not made a loan to Pittsburgh's black community for more than a decade. Mayor Sophie Masloff proposed that the city rate its banks on a 100-point scale for quality of service and for progress in meeting goals set by the federal Community Reinvestment Act. The act requires all financial institutions to help meet the needs of the community.

headline: Another GOP tantrum
abstract: Charlie Sexton and Tom Jugde of the Delaware County Republican Committee reject the appointment of one of their committee members to a high state post for control reasons.

headline: One Ticket Remains Out In Super 7
abstract: Pennsylvania lottery officials have received calls from five people who claim to have the final Super 7 ticket from last week's $115.5 million jackpot.  Only one winner is left to be named.

headline: Set-aside policy is rejected
abstract: US District Judge Charles R. Weiner struck down a Philadelphia School District program giving preference to minority contractors. His ruling was based on a ruling by the US Supreme Court in a case involving a similar program in Richmond, Virginia. The City of Philadelphia also has a minority "set-aside" program for businesses which is under court challenge. Charles Bowser, the attorney hired by the city, believes the city's plan will withstand court challenges because there are "profound differences" between the city plan and the school district plan.

headline: A boost for steel heritage
abstract: The US House has approved money to be used in the Monongahela Valley to preserve historical steel manufacturing sites.  The appropriation comes to $525,000.  The editorial lauds the approach and the legislators that made it happen.

headline: Budget process
abstract: There have been arguments and conflicts stemming from the method of passing the state budget over the years, as things have ranged from all legislators having a crack at the budget to a very few people controlling the whole thing.  Lawmakers are searching for an equitable compromise between the two methods.

headline: Rash of area rabies cases could prompt state action
abstract: With large numbers of cases of rabies in PA mounting, the state legislature is working on a bill that will provide funding for rabies education and prevention.

headline: Watch those holiday meals, says author
abstract: Nancy Locher, dean emeritus of advisement at Gettysburg College and an author, says that students returning home for the first time after leaving to attend college are likely to instigate discussions with their family. She says they might go so far as to challenge parental authority, and recommends that parents leap the discussions rational.

headline: TMI reactor to restart today
abstract: Three Mile Island operators planned to restart the nuclear power plant's Unit 1 reactor. Doug Bedell, spokesperson for GPU Nuclear, the plant's operator, said the workers discovered a probable cause for the cause of a recent automatic shutdown.

headline: Cuomo's embattled drug-treatment czar wants to stay
abstract: Julio Martinez, leader of the New York state Division of Substance Abuse Services, has been under fire for an alleged string of abuses. New York Governor Mario Cuomo's embattled drug treatment czar was being investigated by a state Commission on Government Integrity, led by Fordham Law School Dean John Feerick. The commission found that the agency suffered from a web of favoritism and infighting. Douglas Rosenberry, a spokesman for Martinez, said he has no plans to resign and intends to continue to function in his present role.

headline: Basile to offer land
abstract: A local developer is considering donating a strip of land to the township to be used for a ramp between routes 100 and 724.  He is using the donation to gain leverage in his own plans to build a motel complex near the intersection.

headline: AP-PA-Inauguration
abstract: Some 500 Pennsylvania Republicans could be found in attendance at the President's inaugural ball at the Washington Hilton Hotel.  They celebrated gains in PA Republican voter registration, the election of Sen. John Heinz to his third term of office, as well as the elections of Barbara Hafer and Ernie Preate to the positions of auditor general and attorney general respectfully.

headline: One-liners keep coming from Quinlan
abstract: Waverly Mayor Andy Quinlan, who is up for reelection this month, still kept the one-liners coming even after the court proceedings for that day.

headline: State, federal program responsibilities
abstract: This article addresses the responsibilities of the Adams County Commissioners, discussed during a meeting of the Commissioners over the 1990 county budget, which is scheduled to be adopted at the regular public meeting on December 27. The responsibilities include the following: adopting federally-mandated programs without federal funds; funding the county's solid waste plan; funding administration and monitoring of the Agricultural Preservation Act; increasing the prison budget to account for the number of inmates that have increased from new laws against drunk drivers; funding formerly state-matched moneys for emergency equipment; and continuing to fund the Adams County Economic Development Commission.

headline: Stiffer penalties proposed for seat belt law
abstract: A Washington County lawmaker is putting forth a proposal to suspend the licenses of drivers who fail to properly secure their child in their car.  Democratic Rep Leo Trich says that it was spurred on by the recent two deaths of children in auto accidents that could have been preventable.  The current penalty comes only with a $25 fine.  Trich expects to have as many as 40 cosponsors for this bill.

headline: Bush Quotes Pa. mother Hearbroken Over Addicted Son
abstract: In his budget address to the legislature, President Bush cited a letter he received from a Pennsylvania mother who had just recently found out that her son was addicted to cocaine.  President Bush used the story while asking for a $1 billion budget increase for the war on drugs.

headline: Recovering addict influx response working, project director tells City Council in report
abstract: Charles Haun, project director of the Comprehensive Community Response initiative, says that the program has made significant progress in its first 6 months in a report given to Williamsport City Council. The program is meant to help Williamsport deal with the recent influx of recovering drug and alcohol addicts. Haun also appealed to the US Council of Mayors to help develop an HIV/AIDS education program. Doctor Michael Gross of the Pennsylvania Public Health Association says that the city's immigrant population is the main source of the AIDS virus.

headline: What business can do for schools
abstract: This opinion article addresses what businesses can do to Philadelphia schools. The author, Donald M. Levinson, executive vice president for human resources and services at Cigna Corp., presents five lessons that public-private partnerships between businesses and schools have learned.

headline: U.S. to aid Beth. Steel project
abstract: The United States government will provide $31 million in federal funds to Bethlehem Steel to develop a new way to fire blast furnaces at its Burns Harbor, Indiana, plant. US Energy Department Secretary James Watkins said Bethlehem Steel is one of 13 selected for $1.3 billion total in federal funding to promote clean coal technology. Marshall R. Mazer, Bethlehem Steel's manager of government programs, said the new technology will be installed in 1994. The plan calls for injecting granulated coal, rather than typically used coke, into the furnace as a means of lowering energy costs and reducing pollution, government officials and company spokesmen have said.

headline: DA says local law agencies should get the monies for striking down drug traffic
abstract: Westmoreland County District Attorney John Driscoll told county legislators that money proposed by Gov. Casey for a state strike force on drugs is misdirected and could be used more effectively by local law enforcement.

headline: Bill names developer of hotel
abstract: Philadelphia City Council will vote on legislation that would name the Marriott Corporation as developer of the city's convention center hotel. Labor unions such as Local 274 of the Hotel and Restaurant Employees International Union opposed the choice of Marriott because of its strictly nonunion policies. The convention center construction project cannot get underway without a hotel developer.

headline: Approaching recess, legislators vie for attention
abstract: As the summer recess draws near, there is always a flurry of legislation, and state Sen. Greenleaf wrote this column to report on which bills he supports and their status in the legislature.

headline: Only 3 from state publicly back boost
abstract: If no vote is held by Congress on the proposed $40,000 salary increase for memebers, the increase will be made law; despite the fact that members of Congress received a 15.6 percent increase two years ago, three PA lawmakers have publicly stated that they are for the salary increase.

headline: Tax forum attracts large attendance
abstract: Dozens of citizens attended a community meeting Tuesday on tax reform at courtroom one of the Northumberland County Courthouse.

headline: Mental Health Chief Resigns Amid Controversy
abstract: The state's top mental health official Martha B Knisley has resigned to take on a new job in Ohio.  The resignation comes after a number of months of uneasy relations with the administration and local mental health officials in Philadelphia.  They say she resigned voluntarily, but it came after recent controversy at the Philadelphia State Hospital, Byberry.  Three former patients were found in the Schuylkill.  Two of them drowned.

headline: Casey backs tax reform plan at meeting in Lower Bucks
abstract: Governor Robert Casey backs his tax reform plan in a meeting in Lower Bucks.  The crowd is divided on the issue, with opponents worried that tax reform would be a burden to monitor and carry out.

headline: Repeal of health law opposed
abstract: Negotiators in the US House and Senate are attempting to repeal the 1988 Catastrophic Coverage Act and to approve a deal which would cut the federal budget deficit. Senator John McCain of Arizona and Senator Robert Dole of Kansas argued against repealing the law, which provides Medicare for hospital bills for the elderly. The law also accounts for the financing of health insurance by income taxes on middle- and upper-income citizens.

headline: What Others Say
abstract: A new movement supported by some educators and by Pres. Bush is for students to choose which school they attend and if they go to magnet school.  The author calls for further idea development.

headline: U-S-X says it has corrected safety problems at two Pennsylvania plants
abstract: USX Corporation of Pittsburgh it corrected safety problems following a federal government proposal to fine the firm $7.3 million dollars after the Occupational Safety and Health Administration cited the company for unsafe working conditions. The PA Public Utility Commission approved a $2 million natural gas rate increase for Pennsylvania Gas and Water Company. NUI Corporation of Bedminster, New Jersey, plans to merge with Pennsylvania Enterprises Incorporated, the parent company of Pennsylvania Gas and Water Company.

headline: Dauphin County budget strained by juvenile crime
abstract: Due to an unexpected increase in juvenile crime, Dauphin County will likely have to raise taxes in the next fiscal year.

headline: Bond Request: Owner asks another $2.8 million to finish High Pointe apartments
abstract: RHA Inv. Inc., the owner of a controversial apartment complex in Susquehanna Township, has requested that the Dauphin County Redevelopment Authority float an additional $2.8 million in low-interest loans.  The authority has already floated nearly $9 million in tax-free bonds for the project.

headline: Area representatives report gifts, extra income
abstract: According to the most recent release from the state Ethics Commission, only two lawmakers in the region reported receiving gifts or honoraria in 1987: Sen. Robert Mellow and Rep. Frank Yandrisevits.

headline: Only 5 of Pa. S&Ls considered troubled
abstract: During his release of a review he undertook to assess the health of the state's savings and loans, U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski said only 5 of Pennsylvania's 169 S&L institutions were troubled.  A strong economy and sound management were credited with the success.

headline: Tax forum important
abstract: A tax forum will be held tonight in Stroudsburg with a panel of state- level experts on taxes and tax reform to educate citizens leading up to the May 16 primary.

headline: Kaye Rafko
abstract: Former Miss America Kaye Rafko will stand up for the nation's nurses publicly this year.  As a former registered nurse, she believes that her experience will help further the cause while she still has celebrity left.

headline: Casey sees support for tax issue
abstract: Governor Casey has been  focusing on the  upcoming vote on state tax reform, attempting to build support through greater understanding of the proposal.

headline: Retarded returning to institutions
abstract: Due to a lack of funding, many mentally retarded people will be sent to institutions instead of normal environments.  County administrators put it on Casey and the state legistature to help fund mental-retardation services to keep mentally retarded people out of institutions.

headline: When change is not for the better
abstract: Steven Wills comments on the idea of giving parents and students the choice of attending any public school in their state. The concept behind this plan is to increase competition among schools, with the better-performing ones winning federal funding. The plan was implemented in Minnesota, where many families chose to change schools for reasons of convenience. Wills is highly critical of the plan saying that convenience has nothing to do with the quality of education.

headline: Utility gets approval to increase gas base rates
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission approved a settlement allowing the Pennsylvania Gas & Water Company's gas division to raise its base rates, a move PG&W said was needed to cover operating costs. In a separate case, the company asked for a reduction of rates to reflect lower prices it paid to pipeline suppliers. PG&W serves 9 counties in PA.

headline: Delays hurt prosecution of state environment cases, Preate says
abstract: State Attorney General spoke about the difficulty in prosecuting environmental crimes and levied for extra money in order to add offices to the environmental crimes section, which Gov. Casey endorsed.

headline: Bucks County cited as top HUD performer
abstract: The U.S. Dept. of Housing and Urban Development has afforded the Bucks County Housing Authority the designation of "Recognized Performer," which means that it will be relieved from regular HUD reviews and requirements.

headline: Area votes in Congress
abstract: The article lists US Senators and Representatives from PA, New Jersey and Delaware present at roll-call votes in a recent Congressional session. The House voted on pay and ethics, the US Civil Rights Commission, and funding population control. The Senate voted on the US' contribution to the UN Population Fund, and endorsed President Bush's cuts in the capital-gains tax rate for individuals and corporations.

headline: Outlet sells out-of-state lotto tickets
abstract: A new company, Lotto Fever Inc., has been established to make out-of-state lottery tickets available in the area.  These "lottery courier service" companies tread very thin ropes, as there are many laws and regulations to follow.

headline: Tax Reform- Cities
abstract: The Pennsylvania League of Cities, at a meeting in Easton today, urged voters across the state to adopt local tax reform so that municipalities won't be forced to cut services.

headline: Philadelphia Flyers to South Jersey
abstract: The owners of the Philadelphia Flyers are considering a move to Camden, NJ.  They are still in negotiations with city officials to keep the team playing in Philadelphia.  If the move to Camden happens, one suggests that the arena could be called the "Campbell's Soup Bowl" after the soup company headquartered in the NJ city across the river from Central Philadelphia.

headline: Casey set to reveal budget plan
abstract: Gov. Casey is set to unveil his budget proposal tomorrow, in which he is expected to focuses predominantly on the war on drugs, child abuse, and maintain or reduce specific taxes.  State legislators, both Republicans and Democrats, are looking forward to a conciliatory tone in Harrisburg between the two parties.

headline: Reversing the drug trend
abstract: Based on a survey conducted by the University of Michigan, it has become apparent that drug use by teens has gone down, although world-wide availability of illegal drugs is skyrocketing.

headline: Wilson teachers return to jobs
abstract: The 110 striking teachers of the Wilson Area School District returned to work after a one-day strike because of the failure of negotiations between the teachers and the school board over a pay increase. The negotiating team for the Wilson Area Education Association decided to end the one-day strike because nothing was being accomplished, according to local president Robert Creveling. Albert Zarbatany, superintendent of the Wilson Area School District, said the negotiators notified him before the deadline of 2 pm on Sunday that they would return to school on Monday.

headline: WE seeking higher fees for risks at nuclear plants
abstract: Westinghouse Electric Corporation proposed increases in the fees it receives from the US Department of Energy, in order to manage three nuclear weapons facilities in South Carolina, Ohio, and Washington, along with three other DOE units. Westinghouse, however, might incur liability for managing government facilities. Energy Secretary James D. Watkins believes contractors should receive greater incentives.

headline: Despite the local cast, Washington deserves Bennett's anti- drug effort
abstract: Washington D.C. has been picked by drug czar William J. Bennett for an anti- drug campaign.  The Editorial Board believes that an increased police force will help the drug problem.

headline: City panel targets housing for poor
abstract: While the city of Harrisburg is witnessing economic developmen and the opportunity for job creation in many areas, individuals representing community and religious organizations recognize that the need for low-income is increasing as well.

headline: Area votes in Congress
abstract: The article records senators and representatives present for vote in sessions of the US Congress. The House voted on foreign aid, policy towards El Salvador, and catastrophic care. The Senate voted on pay and ethics and aid to El Salvador.

headline: PA House and Senate taking different roads toward judicial reform
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives passed legislation calling for regional elections of appellate judges, brought to the table as an amendment to a bill that would change the state's judicial discipline system by PA Representative Robert L. Freeman. At the same time, the Senate moved toward approval of a system in which the judges would be appointed, where Senate Majority Leader F. Joseph Loeper believes the merit-selection process will pass.

headline: Tax reform seminar planned at CCBC
abstract: A tax seminar on local tax reform will be held for local officials. The seminar will educate the officials about the tax reform proposal to lower real estate taxes and ensure thtat businesses pay their 'fair share' of taxes.

headline: Tennesseans Can Play Lotto by Telephone
abstract: A PA gaming company and a Kentucky telemarketing company are teaming up to device a way to allow people from states without a state lottery such as Tennessee to play the lottery by telephone.  The TN Attorney General says that such a plan should be legal as TN residents are allowed to play other state's lotteries as long as such lotteries are legal.

headline: Casey Spending Requests Concern Legislators
abstract: New spending requests from Gov. Casey's office have slowed budget talks, though legislators had agreed on nearly all the provisions of the existing spending plan.  The new introduction has worried some lawmakers that the budget won't be completed by the June 30 deadline.

headline: Ritter says health-care tax is a burden to elderly
abstract: US Rep. Don Ritter called for the repeal of a health care law that he says poses an unfair tax burden on the elderly, forcing them to spend money instead of save or invest it since doing so would cause them to pay more taxes.

headline: null
abstract: The PA Game Commission commented on a number of issues regarding the current hunting season. Counties have reported several injury cases, in which hunters were shot while not wearing the state-recommended fluorescent orange vests. Additionally, 22 citations were given to hunters who were using lead shot, which violates state and federal laws prohibiting toxic shot, as well as some for shooting protected species.

headline: Why price caps can't be applied to utilities
abstract: The Public Utility Commissioner writes a letter in response to an editorial which raised questions about utility regulation with response to a "price cap" regulation adoped for AT&T.

headline: District Attorney Hopefuls Congenial
abstract: In a fast- paced but congenial exchange, the Republican candidates for Venango County district attorney outlined their priorities and qualifications during a League of Women Voters forum.

headline: Canton seeks grant for Main Street plan
abstract: Canton Borough Council is seeking $35,000 in grant funds for its downtown revitalization program.

headline: Area votes in Congress, What happened in the legislature
abstract: Key bills considered in the Philadelphia City Council include legislation that names Marriott Corporation as developer of the convention center hotel despite opposition from the Local 274 of the Hotel and Restaurant Employees International Union, as well as the establishment of height controls for buildings in Center City. Key bills considered in the Pennsylvania General Assembly include a constitutional amendment to replace the Judicial Inquiry and Review Board with a two-tier discipline system; a bill that places restrictions on abortion; as well as one that includes first-degree murders involving drug trade or the slaying of certain government officials or informants to the list that may be considered by juries in death-penalty cases.

headline: Pa. Bell's new boss sets out to correct the 'blemishes'
abstract: The new top official at Pa. Bell, Bob Valentini, is focusing on integrity and customer satisfaction to try and regain the company's repuation in the wake of scandals and failed business ventures before his tenure.

headline: Taxes Keep Rising
abstract: This resident does not believe Mayor Goode when he says that if he's allowed to raise taxes this year he won't raise them again for another 5 years.  In 1987, Mayor Goode also said that he wouldn't raise taxes until 1991, but this resident's taxes have gone up each year for the past 6 years.

headline: Council President Charged
abstract: The PA attorney general's office says that it charged the president of the Sharon City Council with illegally collecting in excess of $5,000 of fraudulent travel expenses.  Vito Manilla, 78, is accused of sending in duplicate vouchers to different offices to collect double the money in reimbursements.

headline: Casey trims budget proposal
abstract: Gov. Casey has proposed spending cuts in appropriations for state agencies in order to combat the declining state surplus.  There are also winds of a potential compromise on the future of the $140 million Casey wants to use to fight drugs.

headline: Routine restraint of nursing home residents causes growing concern
abstract: The article addresses the accusation that some nursing homes using restraint mechanisms on their residents do more harm than good. Critics say restraints are often used for convenience and seldom reduce the risk of injury, sometimes increasing problems and injuries. Federal surveys show that 41 percent of nursing home residents were restrained in 1988, a 16 percent increase from 1977. Jill Blakeslee, director of health services for The Kendal Corporation, a non-profit Pennsylvania corporation governed by Quakers that pioneered the concept of restraint-free nursing homes, has joined with the US Senate Committee on Aging to increase awareness about restraint in nursing homes.

headline: $19 million for water, sewer jobs
abstract: Six area water and sewer projects will receive $19 million in PennVest loans and grants.  $1.2 million of that will be used by Altoona City Authority to expand and improve their sewage-treatment plant. Other loan and grant recipients include the Nanty Glo Water Authority, the Windber Area Authority and the Central Pennsylvania Water Supply Co.

headline: $400 million train proposed
abstract: A $400 million high-speed train has been proposed as a link between Pittsburgh and the Greater Pittsburgh International Airport's new terminal, scheduled to open in 1992. Some Japanese companies have agreed to provide $250,000 for a feasibility study of the project, and the administration of PA Governor Robert P. Casey is considering a request for $300,000 for additional study funding. Casey is very interested in the "applicability" of magnetic levitation trains in Pittsburgh, according to Mary Ellen Keating, spokeswoman for PA Secretary of Commerce, Raymond Christman. The proposal was developed by Carnegie Mellon University's high-speed ground transportation center.

headline: Document calls O'Kicki testimony into question
abstract: The testimony of Judge Joseph F. O'Kicki was called into question yesterday when the prosecution revealed a document that contradicted some of O'Kicki's testimony. O'Kicki had testified that he had excused himself from a court case involving Black Cadillac-Pontiac because he was having problems with the car dealer, but the document, produced by chief prosecutor Lawrence Claus, revealed that O'Kicki had not removed himself from the case. Other contradictions began to arise under cross-examination by Claus that occurred on the second day of O'Kicki's 12 hours of testimony.

headline: Carlisle approves plans for business center
abstract: The Carlisle Borough Council voted unanimously in favor of subdividing the Watts Business Center. The council also attached a schedule of public utility and highway improvements to be completed with state funds given to Watts developer Donald H. Mowery. The PA Department of Commerce awarded the borough a grant to improve and extend sewer and water lines.

headline: Ask first and tax later
abstract: The Bucks County Republican commissioners' authorization of $43 million in county borrowing, without a public forum or discussiono of the issue, was wrong.  Because taxpayers will eventually be forced to pay for the bond issue, they should have had a say in the matter.

headline: Push on for 'stiff' ethics code
abstract: If the legislature does not produce a bill reauthorizing the State Ethics Commission by June, it will cease to exist.  Gov. Casey vetoed legislation last year which would have extended the life of the commission for four years, but the bill also would have severely weakened ethical requirements of state legislators.

headline: Two-county agency is organized
abstract: An organizational meeting and election of officers was held for the new Northumberland-Montour Training Services, Inc., which broke from the Central Regional Training Services.  The new agency will provide services under the Job Training Partnership Act to area residents.

headline: Drugs
abstract: Law enforcement arrested 26 today in a round up triggered by a grand jury probe into a marijuana and cocaine drug ring.  Authorities will not release the names of the suspects at this point.  The raids end a 2 year investigation between the FBI, state Attorney General's office, and local law enforcement.

headline: Casey: Say yes to tax reform
abstract: Casey urges people to vote 'yes' for tax- reform which will benefit average homeowners, wage-earners, and retirees.

headline: Santa's health worries doctors - but he has lived 1,700 years
abstract: The article discusses the health of "Santa Claus." Included are quotes about the proposed health problems a 1,700-year-old man would have from officials from Pittsburgh's St. Margaret Memorial Hospital, Allegheny General Hospital, and the Allegheny County Health Department

headline: 2 companies get hazardous-sites contracts
abstract: Two Allegheny Co. companies have received $2 million contracts from the DER to participate in the Hazardous Sites Cleanup Program.

headline: $472 million plan proposed to improve access to airport
abstract: Pittsburgh regional planners have proposed a plan that would improve access to the airport, at a cost of $472.  There is currently no funding for the plan, and the city is looking to the state and federal government for funds.

headline: Dog finds jail drug-free
abstract: A drug-sniffing dog found no contraband in the Fayette County Prison on a recent raid.

headline: Casey attends to Penn's work force
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey announced the creation of a committee of the Pennsylvania Economic Development Partnership (EDP) to establish a work force development policy for the commonwealth. The announcement was made at the quarterly meeting of the EDP Board. The new Committee on Workforce Development will give businesses a voice in developing policies to deal with labor supply issues. Casey also announced the date of the upcoming Pennsylvania Technology Conference, which is sponsored by the EDP.

headline: Assembly will have its hands full in fall
abstract: As much of the first half of this year's session of the state legislature was spent determining what issues needed to be addressed rather than actually addressing the issues, this fall should be a busy one for PA legislators.

headline: Pa.'s Baker lauds new party chief
abstract: Pennsylvania Republican Chairman and state senator Earl Baker praised the new Republican National Chairman Lee Atwater yesterday.  Atwater siad that the party face great opportunity, especially among women, blacks, and blue-collar Democrats.

headline: Watsontown budget given tentative OK
abstract: The Watsontown Borough Council gave preliminary approval to a budget that would make residents pay $1 more per month for refuse collection and the same increase for sewer rates to help fund an 8.6 percent increase in the proposed 1990 budget. In a report read in part by Council President Walter Guthrie, the council blamed the increased cost of sludge disposal and major repairs and equipment purchases for the increased sewer rates and increased costs of using the landfill for refuse collection. The council in its report also addressed the improvements made to the borough this past year to justify the increase in spending.

headline: CAT Fund fees may be killed
abstract: Legislators are trying to figure what to do with the fees associated with the recently killed CAT Fund.  The fees have been used to pay for medical expense of car crash victims.  Locla governments are mandated to pass on these huge fees to people ticketed.  Rep Jeffrey Piccola (R-Dauphin) and Stewart Greenleaf (R-Montgomery) have introduced a bill to repeal the fees.

headline: Casey's budget proposal wins Republican support
abstract: Republicans were largely accepting of Gov. Casey's budget proposal for the 1989-1990 fiscal year, in which the governor did not raise taxes and outlined an $11.7 billion general fund to fight child abuse, drug abuse, and improve higher education.  A few county officials, however, criticized discrepancies in what Casey pledged for human services and what is outlined in the actual budget.

headline: Schools bill doesn't pass
abstract: The editorial from The York Daily Record addresses the drug-free schools bill sent from Congress to be signed into law by the President that grants emergency money from the US Department of Health and Human Services to schools in high drug-use areas. The editorial board believes a provision by US Representative Bill Goodling of Pennsylvania that says schools and universities must write anti-drug policies or lose federal funds is the wrong way to approach the initiative. A better approach, the board believes, would be to offer local schools incentives for implementing anti-drug classes.

headline: 210-pound bear killed in Lewistown Narrows
abstract: A male black bear was killed by a vehicle in the Lewistown Narrows and is now frozen at the PA Game Commission's regional office in Huntingdon.

headline: A tax hike in view for SEPTA?
abstract: Louis J. Gambaccini, general manager of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority and a member of the American Public Transit Association, admitted that the transit authority might need to increase taxes to pay for maintenance, new buses and new railroad cars.
