abstract: According to a public opinion poll, many people are dissatisfied with the state legislature and its members, saying that they feel individual taxpayers don't have enough influence, legislators should have a limit to the number of terms, and that the legislature needs new blood.

headline: Potty Parity
abstract: Rep Bruce Smith (R-York) has put forth a proposal in the House that would require that public buildings create more bathrooms for women than men.  It will only apply to newly constructed buildings.  This should end some of the systemic inequities that come with separate restrooms.

headline: Legislature-Outlook
abstract: While behind-the-scences work is being done in preparation for the 1990-1991 state budget, few bills are expected to come before the House and Senate this week.  However, each house is expected to vote on a proposed constitutional amendment which would reduce residential property taxes.  If passed by both houses, the public must approve the amendment via a referendum.

headline: Wife- killer not allowed travel rights
abstract: Richard Greist, who brutally stabbed his pregnant wife to death and injured his daugher and grandmother in 1978, has been denied the opportunity to leave the grounds of a state mental hospital with other patients.

headline: County Solid Waste Authority Updates Status of Two Projects
abstract: Contract proposals for long- term waste disposal service and the status of both a county solid waste management plan and a multi- county feasibility study were reviewed Tuesday by Crawford County Solid Waste Authority.

headline: County, state officials discuss viaduct funding
abstract: State and county officials met to discuss funding issues concerning the replacement of the Oakland Avenue viaduct in Sharon and other bridges.

headline: Federal Judge Sets New Prison Population Cap
abstract: US Judge Norma Shapira said she wants Philadelphia's prison population decreased to 4200  from its current total of 4700 by the end of September.  Prison officials will employ an anaggressive building plan and programs for jail alternatives.

headline: House approves package to benefit Philadelphia sports teams
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved a plan to help keep Philadelphia's professional basketball and hockey teams from leaving the city and moving to New Jersey. The legislation was part of a plan presented by PA Governor Robert P. Casey last week to keep the Flyers and the 76ers in Pennsylvania, which was a counteroffer to the teams against a financial package from New Jersey. Some suburban Philadelphia lawmakers, including PA Representative Joseph Lashinger, questioned the measure for an hour before voting.

headline: Casey gets ethics, civil service bills
abstract: The House passed bills that would renew the State Civil Service and Ethics commissions, saving them from destruction on June 30 by the Sunset Law.  They are now up to Gov. Casey to approve.

headline: Portrait in statehouse was of wrong patriot
abstract: An error dating to 1823 caused a mix-up in the Rhode Island Statehouse. A portrait labeled as former Rhode Island Governor Stephen Hopkins was actually a portrait of PA statesman John Dickinson. The error was discovered in 1972 by Irma B. Jaffe, a former professor at Fordham University and a scholar on John Trumbull, who painted the portraits.

headline: Disunity: Some political battles are fought at the church pulpits
abstract: An article about the state of the hispanic community and their historical political tendencies.

headline: Local tax reform issue will be decided at ballot box
abstract: On May 16, state residents will vote on a proposed overhaul of their local tax structure, a plan alternately described as a break for homeowners or an omen of higher taxes.

headline: Wistar Vaccine
abstract: Philadelphia's Wistar Institute is hoping that Virginia will say that an island off its coast can be used for the field testing of a wildlife rabies vaccine.  One state has already turned down the project.

headline: County wants to rake in leaves, grass
abstract: Bucks County commissioners voted to apply for a $182,400 grant from the state Dept. of Environmental Resources to begin a program of large-scale composting.  Based on Gov. Casey's signing of the mandatory recycling law last year, counties are required to make plans to move leaves and grass from landfills and turn them into "fertilizer" or "soil supplements."

headline: Couty to examine $1 billion highway 'wish list'
abstract: A $1 billion dollar 'wish list' will be proposed to the Chester County Commissioners Highway Task Force.  If it is approved it can be presented to the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: Federal Strategy Is Planned in Drive on Capital Drugs
abstract: The Bush administration's plans to combat drug- related crime in NYC include Federal construction of a prison and the use of National Guard troops for clerical jobs to free up police officers.

headline: Housing chief pledges 'new era'
abstract: Housing and Urban Development Secretary Jack Kemp said his priorities were enforcement of the new fair-housing law, revitalization of the economies of inner cities, and making significant strides in ending homelessness.  However, several members of the U.S. House committee before which Secretary Kemp testified urged him to provide housing programs with more funding.

headline: Casey gets Piper off ground
abstract: This photograph depicts PA Governor Robert P. Casey evaluating a Piper aircraft with Bill Piper, the grandson of Piper founder William T. Piper and an executive of Piper North.

headline: Potty parity bill moves through House
abstract: The PA House State Government Committee approved a measure requiring more women's restrooms in public places built or majorly renovated after January 1. The State Department of Labor and Industry will determine how many restrooms are needed. The bill was sponsored by Representative Ruth Rudy.

headline: Parents are key to education
abstract: The opinion encourages people to stop allowing children to get away with bullying teachers with false accusations of improper conduct.  Parents are needed to back the teachers and help maintain the needed environment for learning to effectively occur.

headline: Local tax reform worth another try
abstract: States the importance of some form of tax reform, despite the recent defeat of Casey's tax reform referendum.

headline: York refuses day-care zoning bid
abstract: Council members voted 5-0 against an amendment which would have allowed day-care homes in York's RS-1 zones, areas which are limited to single-family homes.

headline: Cuomo can offer only little help to dump opponents
abstract: New York Governor Mario Cuomo said he could review complaints of opponents of a low-level radioactive waste dump but was powerless to stop the selection process. Cuomo rejected calls of the group of opponents from Allegany and Cortland Counties for the resignation of the members of the New York Low-Level Radioactive Waste Siting Commission. The Commission is under federal mandate to designate and develop a site to store low-level radioactive waste generated annually by New York facilities. Cindy Monaco, a consultant hired by Cortland County to fight the waste site, and Jim Lucey, a spokesman for dump opponents in Allegany County, both said the meeting with Governor Cuomo was fruitless.

headline: Crack in bridge force 50-mile detour on I-70
abstract: Due to cracks found in bridge supports, a portion of I-70 was closed for repairs, forcing a 50-mile detour for motorists.

headline: Firm hired to oversee Cumberland courthouse renovation
abstract: Cumberland County commissioners hired Harrisburg architectural firm Crabtree, Rohrbaugh & Associates to oversee a $1.7 million renovation of the county's courthouse. Robert Moore, commission chairman, said the architect's fee will be 7.5 percent of the final construction cost. The purpose of the project is to restore the courthouse to its original condition and make the building handicap accessible, Moore said. Crabtree, Rohrbaugh is also the architect for an almost $700,000 project to convert the old county prison to a center for Cumberland's archives, transportation department, and election offices.

headline: Kemp targets drugs in public housing
abstract: Jack F. Kemp, U.S. secretary of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, has created a massive "sweep- up" plan aimed at eliminating drug traffic in public housing.

headline: Committee approves minimum wage boost
abstract: A House committee approved a bill that would raise the state's minimum wage by $0.95 in two years.  Congress is considering raising the national minimum wage as well.

headline: Power plays
abstract: Ben Woods is the acting president of the City Council of Pittsburgh. Many have lauded his rise to power, and he has enjoyed the support of former Pittsburgh Mayor Richard S. Caliguiri and current City Controller Tom Flaherty. Woods was taught by Charles Lieberth, the secretary of licenses and inspections under former PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, and spent time as a business agent for Sheet Metal Workers Local 12. Woods join the City Council in 1981 after winning a race for a spot vacated by US Representative William J. Coyne.

headline: Drawing Attention to City Problems
abstract: President Bush's new anti-drug overhaul is leaving some impressed and others unimpressed.  Many mayors are lauding the increase in funding to help stem the flow of illicit drugs.  Houston Mayor Kathryn Whitmire says the funding is inadequate, however.  She says that her city will receive only a fraction of what is needed.

headline: Localized Pain: States Increase Taxes And Curtail Services As Revenues Dwindle
abstract: Many of the nation's 82,000 state and local governments are facing debilitating defecits and are looking toward raising taxes and reducing spending.  One example of such an effort to reduce spending is the closing on Tuesdays of the Philadelphia Museum of Art.  Part of the problem is the curtailing of federal grants to state and local governments.  Local governments in Pennsylvania may get the opportunity to impose income taxes or cut property taxes with a state referendum.

headline: Adams apple growers to get state money
abstract: Apple growers in Adams Co. and throughout PA will benefit from the new state budget, which gives $100,000 to the PA Apple Marketing Board.

headline: Cuomo gives bottle commission more time
abstract: New York Governor Mario Cuomo gave an extension to a special commission investigating whether the state should confiscate bottle deposits being held by the beer and soda industry. Cuomo appointed the commission after the NY state Legislature rejected his proposal to have the state unclaimed bottle deposits and use the money for the state budget. The commission's chairman, Robert Amdursky, said he might use the commission's subpoena power to have the industry reveal records about funds generated by the bottle return law.

headline: Crash victim tries to save CAT Fund
abstract: A crash victim of Lancaster works to preserve the availability of catastrophic- medical coverage for motorists in Pennsylvania.  The current fund will expire on May 1, and a replacement is needed.

headline: Five Pennsylvanians are among the 47 killed in this week's gun turret explosion aboard the U-S-S Iowa.
abstract: Five Pennsylvanians are among the 47 killed in this week's gun turret explosion aboard the U-S-S Iowa.

headline: Kemp's priorities
abstract: During his confirmation hearings last week, designated Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Jack Kemp made a strong pledge to fight homelessness in America's cities.  Such an energetic commitment contrasts sharply with the falling federal subsidies deemed for urban housing under the Reagan administration.

headline: Bush nominates Buckwalter to US District Court
abstract: Ronald L. Buckwalter, a Lancaster County Common Pleas Court judge, was nominated by both President Bush and US Senators Arlen Specter and John Heinz for a seat on the US District Court for the Eastern District of PA. Before he was a judge, Buckwalter was the district attorney for Lancaster County.

headline: Power shift will one day lift Mellow to Senate control
abstract: As Republicans back measures to increase their influence in the Senate, the author of this piece states that as power shifts, the Democrats will be back in control.

headline: Charges Dropped
abstract: DUI charges were dropped for a man charged with causing a series of car crashes on the Pennsylvania Turnpike Northeast Extension.  The second of the two crashes caused five people to be killed when a tractor trailer crashed into a long line of vehicles waiting for the first crash to be cleared.  The evidence that was obtained had to be thrown out on a technicality.  Authorities are having trouble finding anything substantive to charge the suspect with.

headline: Look for bottom line on tax reform, both sides say
abstract: Supporters and opponents of the local tax reform educate on the bill leading up to voting on May 16.  Both sides say that voters should look at the bottom line of whether there will be a large increase.

headline: Concept fairly new to state, expert says
abstract: Stuart Perkins of Mifflintown, a retired Army colonel, is a farmer and a pioneer of LISA, low-input sustainable agriculture, in Pennsylvania. LSIA is a new concept for PA, according to John Haberern, president of Rodale Institute that operates an agricultural research center near Kutztown. Sustainable-agriculture proponents say that the soil is in bad shape from being overloaded with fertilizers and toxic pesticides and herbicides. Dr. Robert D. Hart, director of the Rodale Research Center, said that sustainable agriculture is different from conventional agriculture because it keeps in mind the future of the soil.

headline: Dam proposals in Delaware basin
abstract: The author of this piece believes that the dam in the Delaware water basin should be expanded based on supply- side solutions to the area's water problem.

headline: Drunken drivers missing the point
abstract: The editorial claims that the main problem with drunk drivers are those that don't understand the gravity of the situation and the severity of the crime.  It suggests tougher penalties and possibly a required special license plate to show others that the driver has been convicted of a DUI.

headline: Five young teenagers arrested; seven others being sought in the brutal bludgeoning and rape of Wall Street investment banker in New York's Central Park.
abstract: Five young teenagers arrested; seven others being sought in the brutal bludgeoning and rape of Wall Street investment banker in New York's Central Park.

headline: Loans offered for improving multiunit homes
abstract: The Multi-County Home Improvement Loan Program, operated by the Redevelopment Authority of the City of Butler and local banks will allow owners of multiunit homes to improve their homes. The program was also made available in part by a grant from the PA Department of Community Affairs.

headline: Butler Chamber Board Opposes Tax Reform Bill
abstract: The Butler County Chamber of Commerce board voted yesterday to oppose the state tax- reform proposal appearing as a referendum on the Primary election ballot.

headline: Preate asks court to ban alleged fund-raising scam
abstract: State Attorney General Ernie Preate has filed a lawsuit against Watson and Hughey Co. of Virginia, asking the Commonwealth Court to ban the company from distributing further sweepstakes solicitations through the mail.  The attorney general has labeled such solicitations deceptive.

headline: Bill Would Bar Sludge
abstract: PA Rep Camille "Bud" George (D-Houtzdale) has put forth a proposal to bar out-of-state sludge from being dumped in PA.  He says that the state has limited landfill space left and is warning that NJ wants to dump 129,000 tons of it soon in the state.

headline: Lower surplus forecast by GOP
abstract: With only a month left in the fiscal year, the state surplus is projected to be considerably lower than the $275 million estimated by Gov. Casey.

headline: 'Dangerous dogs' measure sponsored by Rep. Brandt
abstract: A local state lawmaker, Rep. Kenneth Brandt, introduced a bill allowing dog officers to label dogs a 'dangerous' forcing the owner to confine the dog and get insurance for it.  The bill also allows for putting down an animal that attacks a person or another animal.

headline: Delay rises cost of Lebanon County dam, officials say
abstract: The projected costs for the Christian E. Siegrist Dam in Schuylkill County will be higher than the initial $1.7 million, because the Lebanon Water Authority cannot meet a deadline to issue a notice of construction. Schuylkill County filed an appeal against the dam to the Environmental Hearing Board, since the dam construction might cause the county to lose coal-mining permits. Samuel G. Weiss, LWA's solicitor, will amend the authority's contract with ASI RCC Construction Company.

headline: Eased traffic would be costly in job, businessman claims
abstract: A businessman operating companies along a stretch of Rt. 11 near the PA Turnpike claims that building new roads to help decrease congestion and dangerous situations would put hundreds, if not thousands, of people out of work.  State Sen. Michael Dawida supports the new roads, saying they will save lives.

headline: Ford City police study
abstract: The Ford City Council should be commended for requesting the Garman state study of its police force, which recommended that the city add training and two additional police officers to its force.  These recommendations do not mean that the Ford City police force is underperforming or is being criticized.

headline: Main Street program to get 4th-year grant
abstract: Thanks to verbal approval from a Dept. of Community Affairs official, Main Street Manager Agnes Connolley said that the program was approved for a fourth-year grant of $10,000.  The money will go to design expenses and façade refurbishment in the downtown Danville area.

headline: Byberry's reprieve
abstract: Public Welfare Dept. Secretary John F. White Jr. made the correct decision when he announced that the total phaseout of Philadelphia State Hospital, also known as Byberry, would be postponed until Sept. 30.  Although this paper is still for the eventual closing of Byberry, postponing some of the patients' release makes sense.

headline: Preate Now State's Chief Law Officer
abstract: Former Lackawanna County District Attorney Ernest D. Preate Jr. was sworn in as the state Attorney General.  He promised that his highest priority would be curbing the drug epidemic.  Also on hand to be sworn in were auditor general-elect Barbara Hafer and treasurer-elect Catherine Baker Knoll.

headline: Hugo stirs humility
abstract: Survivors recount their experiences during Hurricane Hugo and describe things that they take for granted.  Other disruptions of the disaster are described.  Governor Casey urges PA residents to help out where they can.

headline: Mellon Index Rises For Pennsylvania And Drops For Pittsburgh
abstract: The Mellon Index of Economic Performance for Pennsylvania has climbed .1 percent since November, while for the Pittsburgh area the rate declined by .5 percent over the past month.

headline: Eggs With Less Cholesterol: Industry's Salvation or Sham?
abstract: With eggs sales dropping due to heart disease concerns, some egg producers are marketing lower cholesterol eggs.  This article goes into whether or not these eggs are actually better for you or not.

headline: Delco official under fire as EPA nominee
abstract: A state lawmaker has called for an investigation into the recommended appointment of a Delaware County administrator as regional head of the Environmental Protection Agency.

headline: East Brady bridge nears opening after two years
abstract: The Hard Scrabble Bridge will link two sections of East Brady after two years of construction. Steve Jadlocki of the Clarion County Planning Commission stated that much of the concrete work had been completed. The bridge was condemned by the PA Department of Transportation 2 years ago.

headline: Former Mayor Under Subpoena
abstract: Jack Narcelli, the former mayor of Chester who has been in prison since 1979 for accepting bribes related to illegal gambling, will reportedly testify before the PA Crime Comission.  Nacrellie is believed to have been associated with mob figure Santo "Chester Sam" Idone.

headline: March on Washington planned for homeless
abstract: Homeless activists held news conferences in cities across the nation, announcing a planned "March for Housing" in Washington on Oct. 7.  Advocates want increased funding for housing initiatives and to increase awareness about the scope of the problem.

headline: Cabinet-level discussions productive
abstract: Lycoming County officials considered PA Governor Robert Casey's Capital for a Day program to be an encouragement for the area. Peter A. Loedding, president of the Williamsport-Lycoming Chamber of Commerce, commended the governor and his cabinet, stating that private meetings with the various secretaries were the most beneficial. Local commissioners commended the governor and his cabinet for their work on local projects such as Route 15 and the Pine Creek Valley recreation trail.

headline: Preate urges businessman Pickard to give up candidacy
abstract: PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. yesterday urged Lancaster businessman James O. Pickard to give up his candidacy for the Republican gubernatorial nomination for the sake of party unity. Preate said Pickard's divisive candidacy could be a hindrance to the party's chances of stopping the reelection of current PA Governor Robert P. Casey. Preate now endorses Auditor General Barbara Hafer and instead Pickard should be chosen for a leadership position within the party.

headline: Medicine tainted by AIDS, hemophiliacs say in lawsuit
abstract: Armour Pharmaceutical Co of Blue Bell, PA is accused of marketing drugs tainted with AIDS.  6 hemophiliacs from Canada have filed suit against the company under this cloud of suspicion.  The suit alleges that the company failed to properly handle, test, and treat the product to ensure that it was disease free.

headline: Now we need statesmanship to produce true tax reform
abstract: The editorial staff of the New Era emphasizes that the Governor and legislature must now work for better tax reform instead of letting the issue rest for years, since the tax reform referendum was defeated.

headline: Farm Show enriches area economy
abstract: Business leaders agreed that the 73rd Pennyslvania Farm Show boosted the capital region's economy during the six day exhibition.

headline: DER a no-show; 4 free of charges
abstract: Four people arrested during a peaceful protest were acquitted of charges because no representatives from the state Department of Environmental Resources were present at the court hearing.  The protest group plans to continue protesting a hazardous waste dump in Yukon.

headline: Economy League Elects Six; PennDOT Secretary Speaks
abstract: Six people were elected to the Butler County committee of the PA Economy League, and Howard Yerusalim (secretary of PennDOT) spoke on the effects of transportation on the economy.

headline: Four children returned to mother in custody case
abstract: Montgomery County Common Pleas Court Judge William T. Nicholas Jr. ordered four children who had been abducted by their father to return to their mother's custody. The boys' father, Louis Behr, was arrested on October 16 after abducting his sons and claiming that their mother and her boyfriend subjected the boys to sexual abuse and forced them to take part in satanic rituals. Nicholas also ordered Mr. Behr to seek psychological counseling.

headline: Metropolitan business report
abstract: The article and charts discuss the various statistics in citing in which city is located the largest metro market in the United States. One measure finds Los Angeles as the number one largest metro market, which is exemplified in the "Ten largest metro areas" chart, while another measure finds New York City to be No. 1. Another part of the article addresses the income gains of Philadelphia-area residents in the 1980s, accompanied by a photograph that cites "Growth in per-capita income" in the Philadelphia area from 1980 to 1987.

headline: Campaign Bank Accounts Getting Bigger
abstract: 18 of Pennsylvania's 23 United States congressmen increased their campaign reserve funds from 1987 to 1989.  Public Citizen, a Washington-based public interest group, found that U.S. congressmen in general had an average of $154,334 in campaign reserves; all 23 of Pennsylvania's congressmen won reelection in 1988.

headline: Preate's aim is aggressive drug effort
abstract: The new attorney general, auditor general, and state treasurer all pledged to fight corruption and uphold integrity within their respective offices.  State Attorney General Ernie Preate said he would prosecute environmental polluters and would focus attention on enforcing civil rights legislation.

headline: Our state's budget appears encouraging
abstract: The editorial commends legislators and Gov. Casey for what is deemed as a successful state budget, which appropriated money to a variety of areas, including education, parks, human service, and anti-drug.

headline: Farmers Want 9-Cent Boost Left In Place
abstract: The PA Farmers Association and the PA Farmers Union asked the state Milk Marketing Board to maintain a 9-cent per gallon increase in the price of milk to offset costs related to the recent drought.

headline: DER asks for probe in Salisbury
abstract: Amid allegations that a home's septic system did not comply with state law, a Dept. of Environmental Resources official asked the township to investigate.  The local sewage enforcement officer, upon investigation, found that the home did in fact comply.

headline: Engineers release plans for central Pa. toll road
abstract: Plans for a toll road connecting the PA Turnpike and I-80 were released, allowing the next step, an environmental impact study, to be undertaken.  Potential financial sources for the road are being considered.

headline: Freeman's rise was steady
abstract: Robert M. Freeman, the superintendent of the Camp Hill prison, had a steady career in the PA Department of Corrections. He was suspended by state Corrections Commissioner David S. Owens Jr. after Camp Hill prison experienced two riots in one week, largely due to negligence of the leadership to fix broken lock controls. Investigations are being carried out by the Department of Corrections and by a commission appointed by PA Governor Robert Casey.

headline: Montgomery to seek $150,000 FmHA grant
abstract: The borough is seeking a housing preservation grant from the Farm Home Administration of $150,000 to begin a housing development program aimed at low-income families.  Because the borough was turned down for Community Development Block Grant Competitive Funds totally $218,000, officials are now seeking a grant with the FmHA.

headline: Capital idea
abstract: PA's decision to change its slogan from "You've got a friend in PA" to "America starts here" was unpopular. The decision to change the slogan was made by the Casey administration. The board thinks the state needs a more profitable slogan.

headline: Primary ballot's top spots go to McNulty, Bolus
abstract: James Barret McNulty was in the lead slot for Democratic nomination for mayor.  Robert Bolus was the top Republican nominee.

headline: PA taxes
abstract: Citizens will vote on whether the state constituion should be amended so local taxing authorities can cut residential property taxes.  The vote is key to Gov. Casey's plan to overhaul local taxes.

headline: Farmland protection planned
abstract: York County plans to spend more than $1 million to help protect farmlands from development.

headline: DER called negligent on sewage
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources' regional office in Wilkes-Barre has been called negligent for ignoring the dumping of sewage sludge into the Lackawanna River for eight years.

headline: Exxon and the oil spill
abstract: The Exxon Valdez oil tanker unleashes the worst oil spill in United States history, while its captain is legally drunk.  The author believes random drug tests of those in transportation are the solution.

headline: Garbage suit
abstract: Helen Swercheck of North Catasauqua has filed for a court order to restrain the borough from enforcing part of a garbage ordinance that she believes is being misapplied to the compost pile to which she attends. Swercheck filed the lawsuit in a Northampton County Court against the borough and its health officer, Evelyn Byrne.

headline: N. Britain zoners reject premise of rehab center
abstract: The New Britain Twp. Zoning Hearing Board rejected a proposal to establish a teen drug rehab center in the municipality, stating that the plan was not in accordance with the best interests of the twp., nor was it "consistent with the spirit, purpose and intent of the zoning ordinance."

headline: Carbon voters soundly defeat tax reform proposal
abstract: A review of the results of the primary election the day before.

headline: Professional legislators too costly
abstract: This letter to the editor addresses the large salaries of members of the US Congress and the PA Assembly, who defend their salaries by saying that their public service is a 24-hour per day, year-round job. The author of the letter says that the pace of accomplishing anything in Washington, DC, or Harrisburg speaks to the inefficiency of the legislatures. The author suggests that we return to the idea of "citizen representatives" that take time from their own occupations to transact public business a few weeks or months out of the year.

headline: Pennsylvanians split on question of tax reform
abstract: The opposing opinions about tax reform are presented, with the notion that most people want lower property taxes: some favor the proposed method of change, while some hold out for something else.

headline: Keeping open space requires action
abstract: US Rep. Richard Schulze (R-5th )writes to agree with his colleague, Peter Kostmayer (D-Bucks), and to promote his Family Farmland Preservation Act, which would help protect family farms from "enormous federal estate tax burdens."

headline: DER Considers 2 Applications for Buffalo Landfill
abstract: Applications for Phases I and II of a proposed demolition landfill in Buffalo Township have been sent to the state Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Five international gates planned
abstract: Three international gates may be added to the two already planned for a terminal being built at the Greater Pittsburgh International Airport. The two already planned were established to provide for aggregating traffic due to airlines USAir and British Airways increasing their services. Aviation Director Scott O'Donnell said the two international gates would already be claimed by the time they open, leaving no room for growth.

headline: Gays lose suit against retail chain
abstract: After two hours of deliberation by the US District Court, a jury decided the Caldor Inc. retail chain did not engage in "gay bashing" against two former employees who alleged they were victims. Philadelphia residents Jeff Slavin and John DiDonato said that, while working at the Caldor retail outlet in Willingboro, NJ, four Caldor workers verbally and physically harassed them because they were gay. Caldor attorney Thomas Wagner and jury foreman Michael Koals agreed that there was no sufficient evidence to support the charges. The jury did not believe that the men had been victimized by "extreme or outrageous conduct," one of the key legal yardsticks provided by US District Judge Charles R. Weiner.

headline: Officials can live with new code
abstract: With the new revisions to the state Municipalities Planning Code becoming effective today, many public officials have conceted that the true impact of the legislation will not be known for at least several months.  The law provides significant loopholes and advantages to developers, including an elimination of a provision which would have allowed municipalities to impose development impact fees to cover the cost of off-site improvements due to development.

headline: Carlisle OKs study of other forms of government
abstract: Carlisle Borough Council President William Duncan is considering attempting to change the system of government of Carlisle from borough to city or home-rule.  He will begin looking into possible benefits of the other systems.

headline: Proponents outspending opponents in last-minute advertising
abstract: In the last couple weeks before the election, proponents of the tax reform proposition hold a significant fund-raising advantage over their opponents, though both sides claim that the money difference doesn't tell the whole story.

headline: Pennsylvania's Economy Should Mirror Nation's In '89
abstract: William D. Anderson, a Penn State economist, wrote in the February issue of the Pennsylvania Business Survey that employment in 1989 should continue to set new records, with the unemployment rate falling below five percent.  Last year, PA's unemployment rate was 5.1 percent, while the nation's was 5.5 percent.

headline: Montco farmers shield lands from suburban sprawl
abstract: Farmers in Montgomery Co. municipalities are attempting to protect their farms from development by placing more that 3,000 acres in special preservation districts.  The county is moving forward with the idea, and they are expected to have the program ready by next year.

headline: DER files law suit against Centerville
abstract: The DER has filed suit against Centerville borough and the sanitary authority for failing to meet deadlines on a sewage project mandated by the state.  The sanitary authority had no comment on the suit.

headline: Flawed work on the Blue Route
abstract: It has become evident that poor-quality work has been accepted or overlooked by officials involved in the construction of I-476, "the Blue Route." According to the PA Department of Transportation and the Federal Highway Administration, weak concrete and mottled columns were observed on the highway. Joseph J. Bondi, a former Blue Route supervisor, filed a lawsuit in federal court against PennDOT, claiming that he was told to accept and cover up poor work on the highway.

headline: Godshall leads charge against gun ban
abstract: The PA House of Representatives recently failed twice to pass a ban on assault weapons. The ban was spearheaded by Representative Tom Michlovic, who cited automatic and semi-automatic weapons as accounting for two-thirds of the weapons seized by the US Drug Enforcement Agency. Representative Robert Godshall, a prominent member of the National Rifle Association in the state Legislature, claimed that Michlovic's bills would interfere with the rights of law-abiding citizens. The article is accompanied by a cartoon of a drive-thru assault weapon store.

headline: Open Line gets grant
abstract: The Open Line Inc. of Pennsburg, a program helping solve problems in unemployment, underemployment, and welare dependency, has been awarded a $10,000 grant by the PA Dept. of Community Affairs.

headline: Casey adds battle plan to drug war
abstract: Gov. Casey gives his State of the Commonwealth address before a joint session of the General Assembly.

headline: Proponents see success for judge-selection bill
abstract: Supporters of legislation that calls for appellate judges to be appointed rather than elected said they were "cautiously optimistic" that the bill would pass on its second try this week. PA Senators Vincent J. Fumo and Robert C. Jubelirer, who is Senate President Pro Tempore, said they were working to change votes to support the bill. The bill calls to end popular election of judges and instead have justices of the Supreme Court and judges of the Commonwealth and Superior Courts appointed by the governor with a two-thirds confirmation from the Senate. Some dissenting Senators said they would vote for the bill as long as it gives counties the option of adopting a merit-selection system if approved by voters in a local referendum.

headline: Personal Income Up In Pa.
abstract: Pennsylvanians' personal income was an average of 6.4% more than last year according to a PSU economist.  Earning accounted for a smaller percentage of the average personal income, pointing to the aging of PA's population, as the elderly garner more income from investments than earnings.

headline: Rabies cases growing at record rate
abstract: Rabies cases in PA animals are growing at a rate of about 2 cases per day, which would make this a record-setting year if it continues.

headline: DER finds spill in Mon River near Charleroi
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources said "hundreds of gallons" of diesel fuel or a similar substance have spilled into the Monongahela River in a 9-mile stretch in Washington County.

headline: Four killed, seven injured in I- 83 crash
abstract: Court records show that the truck driver charged Tuesday in causing the collision on I- 83, which killed four and injured seven, was on probation for a previous durnk- driving convition.

headline: Good police work deserves our praise
abstract: The editorial praises the PA Police for a successful investigation into a planned kidnapping and murder.

headline: Open space around cities is shrinking
abstract: The writer, a US rep, testifies that open space near and in cities is crucial to the American mindset and has invaluable historical and aesthetic value.  He also emphasizes that if we do not save open space now, it will be impossible to recreate later.

headline: Casey aide gets new job
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey named Thomas Patrick Foley as the new special assistant to the governor, a position vacated by the late James R. Lloyd, a former state senator. Foley is currently the executive deputy secretary in the state Department of Labor and Industry. Foley has also worked as chief speech writer and foreign policy researcher for US Senator Joseph R. Biden of Delaware.

headline: Proposed raise would make Florio one of two highest-paid governors
abstract: In a new proposal endorsed by New Jersey Governor-elect James J. Florio and current NJ Governor Kean, Florio would receive a $45,000 raise in his first gubernatorial term and become one of the two highest-paid governors in the country, along with Governor Mario Cuomo of New York. A three-member salary commission made the proposal and recommended that the raises take effect when Florio takes office in January, meaning it needs to be approved by the New Jersey legislature beforehand. The governor's pay raise is controversial because of the state's worsening budget climate and the Kean administration's contract stalemate with the Communications Workers of America, noted salary commission member Bruce Coe.

headline: Peters proposes shaving $1 million from reserve
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioner Carol A. Peters, a Democrat, yesterday said the county could reduce a planned $1.4 million tax increase by putting less money into a reserve fund next year. The reserve fund acts as a savings account to be used in the cases of emergency. Last year the county used about $3 million from reserves to support operations at the overcrowded Dauphin County prison. The commissioners last month approved a tentative $38.7 million budget that increases real estate taxes by $1.4 million; Peters voted against both the budget and the tax increase.

headline: Tainted Hot Dog Recall Expanded; Pennsylvania Now Included
abstract: The government's recall of Plantation Foods brand turkey franks has been expanded and Pennsylvania is now one of the 22 states being alerted.

headline: DER grant aids DuBois recycling program
abstract: A grant of nearly $225,000 will help DuBois' recycling program begin operations as early as next spring.  The program will still be voluntary for the city, but would eventually be required by law.

headline: Gambaccini's gambit
abstract: SEPTA's general manager Louis J. Gambaccini's declaration that the transit authority can only continue with increases in passenger fares may seem imprudent; however, it is difficult to argue against his reasoning.

headline: Goode to press for beer ban at Eagles' games
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, in conjunction with the Philadelphia Eagles, is seeking a ban on the sale of beer at Eagles' home games and attempting to eliminate drinking during tailgating in Veterans Stadium parking lots. Eagles owner Norman Barman said he requested the ban in light of rowdiness at recent games and hopes it will go into effect for the Eagles' next and last home game of the season on December 24. Goode said he would direct the Philadelphia city solicitor to examine the city's contract with Ogden Allied Services, which provides the stadium with concessions, to begin negotiations about eliminating beer sales.

headline: PA House OK's Casey plan for city arena
abstract: The PA House of Representatives passed a plan proposed by PA Governor Robert P. Casey to help keep the 76ers and the Flyers in Philadelphia, rather than moving to Camden, New Jersey. The plan gives the city a $2 million annual fee in lieu of property taxes on a planned sports arena in South Philadelphia, which is part of a package that includes $8.5 million in state aid over the next three years to help with site preparation. Mayor John Goode of Philadelphia commended the actions of the House. The Pennsylvania Senate is expected to pass the proposal tomorrow.

headline: Casey asked to appoint Lyter to job
abstract: Gov. Casey resubmitted Barbara Lyter's name to the Senate for interim district justice, based somewhat on her impressive showing in the recent primary election.

headline: Protesters to attend North talk
abstract: Protesters against U.S. escalation of intervention in Central America plan to attend a speech made by Oliver North in Lancaster County.

headline: Plan could slow suburban jobs
abstract: The change in income tax proposed under the state's tax reform could cause a slow movement of jobs to the suburbs.

headline: Two-year-old program planted seed to preserve farmland
abstract: Two years after Pennsylvania voters approved a $100 million bond to preserve farmland, only one farm has been saved from the program. The PA Agricultural Land Preservation Board authorized in November the purchase of development rights to the land of a 173-acre poultry and dairy farm in Lancaster County. PA Governor Robert P. Casey supports the program as a means to save farmland to produce food for future generations, rather than develop farmland into highway, housing, or commercial space.

headline: DER lifts ban on Oaks sewer hookups
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources has lifted a ban on new sewer hookups to the Oaks treatment plant, allowing for increased development in Montgomery County.

headline: Getting tougher with drunk drivers
abstract: Two PA lawmakers are looking at other states' laws on DUIs, and are considering using some of those tactics to get tougher on drunk drivers.

headline: Governor signs counseling bill
abstract: Gov. Casey signed a bill, proposed by Sen. James Greenwood, that will provide intensive family counseling as a possible alternative to foster homes for children.

headline: Pa. grant to help center provide affordable housing in Reading
abstract: The Hispanic Center in Reading received a $110,000 grantwhich it will use to help provide affordable housing for low-income families in Reading.

headline: Casey asks a new use for funds
abstract: Gov. Casey called for the $140 million meant for his failed tax reform plan to be used to combat drug abuse, though members of both parties protested, saying that not all the money should go to one place.

headline: Public should participate in decisions
abstract: The Editorial Board believes that citizens should educate themselves on issues such as tax reform, instead of saying after the fact, "This isn't fair!" or "I didn't know!"

headline: Problems with local tax reform
abstract: Robert C. Jubelirer, Republican in the Senate, states that Gov. Casey's local tax plan constitutes less than the reform Pennsylvanians were looking to achieve.

headline: $4.2 million in job training funds announced
abstract: Gov. Casey has announced grants totaling $4.2 million through the federal Job Training Partnership Act to retrain unemployed workers throughout PA.

headline: DER lifts its ban on new sludge dump sites here
abstract: The DER lifted a 2-year ban on new sludge disposal sites in Lancaster Co., because the say that the moratorium is no longer needed due to other new sludge regulations.

headline: Group Vows To Continue Fight To Propose Rt. 119 Improvements
abstract: A group advocating improvements to Rt. 119 will continue fighting for the projects it supports, although PennDOT has moved four of the six into its high-priority, first four years of its 12-year plan.  The projects may still need community support to get farther than the feasibility study.

headline: Governor targets abuse
abstract: In his address to the joint session of the Legislature on Tuesday, Gov. Casey focused on a renewed effort in the war on drugs, as well as new steps to target child abuse.  The governor cited the state's expected $275 million surplus as the reason for having such new initiatives with no new taxes.

headline: Parkers in downtown to be 'crunch bunch'
abstract: With the beginning of excavation for the Berks County services center, the 138-space parking lot at Reed and Court streets will be closed.  This closing represents the start of a series of parking lot closings which will complicate the city's already tenuous parking situation.

headline: Casey begins busiest 'Capital' program in, around Uniontown
abstract: Gov. Casey continues his "Capital for a Day" program in Uniontown, with a busy schedule for the two days spent in the city.

headline: Questions and Answers On State Tax Reform:
abstract: The article gives an analysis of the state's local tax- shifting proposal arranged in a question- answer format.  The information is derived in part from the state Dept. of Community Affairs.

headline: Reed sees self as aggressive leader
abstract: Mayor Stephen R. Reed of Harrisburg sees himself as an aggressive CEO, a superior manager of a city whose $24 million general fund budget rivals the budgets of many smaller corporations.

headline: $7 million fine urged for USX
abstract: The US Occupational Safety and Health Administration proposed a $7.3 million fine on USX Corporation. Three workers at USX's Fairless Works died in the past two years, and the company's facilities were found to be deficient, such as rusted and deteriorating walkways. The company's Clairton Works were inspected following complaints from the United Steelworkers of America. Secretary of Labor Elizabeth Hanford Dole said that the corporation was indifferent to worker safety and health.

headline: DER to probe prison system's sewage pumping
abstract: The DER will investigate the Philadelphia prison system's pumping of raw sewage into storm drains which filter into streams, a practice they were ordered to stop two years ago.  The pumping only occurs when there are heavy rains and the sewage lines are in danger of backing up.

headline: Groups File Suit Challenging SEPTA Fare Increase
abstract: Three consumer groups in Philadelphia filed suit to stop the regional transit authority from increasing fares.

headline: Grandma cuddles addicted baby-and prays
abstract: Vera Duke sued for custody of her newborn granddaughter, JaLeesa ChaLie. JaLeesa's mother is a drug user, who tested positive for cocaine use at the time of birth. Erie County Judge Jess Jiuliante granted Duke temporary custody of the baby.

headline: Path to the Vet led through N.J.
abstract: When the owner of the Philadelphia 76ers basketball team was considering NJ for a new stadium not long ago, he probably didn't realize he was "following in the footsteps" of the Phillies owner in the 60's, Bob Carpenter Jr., who nearly built a stadium on the very land the the 76ers were considering before Philadelphia officials helped build Veterans Stadium.

headline: Casey challenged on accuracy of tax revision TV ad
abstract: Reporters questioned the accuracy of 29-second TV commercial touting the tax revision question in a news conference with Governor Casey yesterday.

headline: Quinlan: 'I didn't say it'
abstract: The street commissoner, Margaret Aronstam was refused her request for $1000 for renovations to the street department office.  Mayor Andy Quinlan refused her request, but was asked to make a public apology to the street dept. for stating that they should get their furnishings from the 'dump'

headline: Rebound coming, state official says
abstract: Andrew T. Greenberg, executive deputy secretary of commerce, predicted that Beaver County and much of southwestern Pennsylvania will improve economically in the 1990s due to expanded financial assistance from Harrisburg. Greenberg spoke at the second quarterly session of The Times Economic Forecast Panel. Beaver County exceeds the average unemployment rate in PA, but Greenberg said the number of manufacturing jobs in the county has increased in some areas. Greenberg, who also serves as the associate director of the Pennsylvania Economic Development Partnership, admitted that leading economic indicators nation-wide led to an economic slowdown in 1989, but that he believes the PA economy is on an upturn.

headline: 3-county group to receive $85,664 to train jobless
abstract: The Carbon-Monroe-Pike Wayne counties' area of the Job Training Partnership Act will receive $85,664 to retrain jobless workers in the area.

headline: Disapproves of Landfill Site
abstract: Citizen disapproves of the landfill dump site in the Cooper Township area.  Citizen says that voters should reexamine their views on local and couty political officials.

headline: Hauling garbage in food trucks
abstract: Recently drivers of trucks that transport food have had to haul loads of garbage in the same trucks, which is a dilemma but not illegal. Curtis Coker, chief of food and cosmetic safety for the US Food and Drug Administration said that federal officials have not linked a case of food poisoning to the dual-use trucks, but intestinal disorders that would be caused by garbage-contaminated food are so general that they are difficult to trace. In Pennsylvania, Interstate 80 has become a garbage connection extending through PA to Illinois.

headline: Gray Panthers fill a void at Graterford
abstract: The Gray Panthers, the national organization that fights for the rights of senior citizens, has established a chapter at the Eastern State Correctional Institution at Graterford in central Montgomery County. Maggie Kuhn, the group's founder, said the chapter, granted to 40 inmates, is the first established at a prison. The Gray Panthers got involved at Graterford at the urging of Julia Hall, a professor of gerontology at Drexel University, who said there are more than 1,100  prisoners over age 50 in Pennsylvania. Kuhn said older prisoners face difficulty with the health system, problems with housing and overcrowding, and sometimes do not have anywhere to go once they are released from prison.

headline: Penelec Is Helping To Attract New Firms
abstract: Pennsylvania Electric Co. is working bring new businesses to the area and, thus, more local economic growth.  The company has just distributed $100,000 to economic development groups and project from the 1988 budget, and has also begun other programs as well.

headline: Casey endorsement
abstract: Ron Brown, a former aide to Sen. Edward Kennedy and presidential candidate Jesse Jackson, has received the endorsement of Gov. Casey for chairman of the national Democratic Party.

headline: Singel seeks 'yes' vote on tax reform
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark S. Singel Thursday night called on people attending the Somerset Veterans of Foreign Wars banquet to support the local tax reform referendum on the May 16 primary ballot.

headline: Reform really tax grab
abstract: A citizen writes to say that the proposed tax plan is not a reform, but an effort to take citizens' money.

headline: American Electric to close, cut jobs
abstract: American Electric announced that it will close its Pittsburgh facilities.  About 200 people in the company's factory and warehouse will lose jobs.

headline: Domnick nixes incinerator
abstract: Mayor Joseph J. Domnick issued his opinion Monday against the Bechtel Corp. waste- to- energy incinerator proposed for the Dunmore borough.

headline: Heavy holiday traffic expected
abstract: The PA State Police are conducting an awareness campaign about the importance of seat belts for car safety.

headline: Guard calls prison management 'mentally gridlocked'
abstract: The Adams Commission report cites corrections officers as noting "mental gridlock" as a reason for the October 25-27 riots at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill. Prison guard John Caffas said he was told by an inmate that a riot was going to occur. The lack of communication between the staff of the prison and the management was what led to the second night of rioting, said prison guard Sgt. Anthony W. Russ. Caffas said the prison's deputy for treatment, Terry W. Henry, did not give the orders to enter the prison during the riots while two guard were being tortured. Caffas blamed the "unbounded arrogance" of Henry, state Corrections Commissioner David S. Owens Jr., prison Superintendent Robert M. Freeman, prison deputy for operations Richard C. Smith, and Major John Stover as the reason for the siege.

headline: Pennsburg mulls permit fee hike
abstract: The Pennsburg Borough Council is considering a change in the process of building permit fees, from a fee based on projected construction costs to one based on square footage.  The change would likely bring more money into the borough.

headline: Casey evaluation plays to mixed reviews
abstract: Gov. Casey's state of the commonwealth address brought measured criticism from York County Republican lawmakers, who saw the governor's speech as an attempt to begin his reelection campaign and take advantage of many of the commonwealth's successes, even if those were initiated by the legislature.  Democrats praised the speech

headline: Reeher blames politics
abstract: Kenneth R. Reeher, executive director of the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency, yesterday called his recent indictment on charges of accepting a kickback a "political persecution."

headline: Resolutions aim to resolve interstate dispute on income taxes
abstract: PA Representative Keith McCall reports on resolutions he introduced to end the dispute over New York's income tax on the spouses of commuters. One resolution requests that New York repeal or revise part of its tax code on non-resident taxpayers, while the other urges the PA Attorney General to assist Pennsylvanians wishing to bring a lawsuit against New York. The law is opposed by PA Governor Robert Casey and US Senators, and McCall believes that commuting Pennsylvanians should not have to pay for New York's budget deficit.

headline: Area takes Economic Blows on Chin
abstract: GTE Corp. announced yesterday that it will shut down a plant located in Montoursville by August, a move which would affect 100 workers.  The GTE plant closing comes after a rash of other shutdowns in the area which total 850 lost jobs.  However, local analysts say the effects will not be permanent.

headline: Don't ban plastic and foam packaging
abstract: Donald B. Shea, executive VP of the Council for Solid Waste Solutions, believes that plastic and foam packaging should not be banned as non- eco- friendly.  Their products should be recylced.

headline: High-speed train deserves study
abstract: Despite the potential for excessive costs, the prospect of a high-speed cross-state train system deserves to be looked into, as it shouldn't be ruled out without enough information.

headline: Guards bemoan lack of riot training
abstract: Prison guards testified that they did not have adequate riot training or equipment to fight an October 23 inmate uprising at the PA State Correctional Institution in Huntingdon. Sergeant John Moyer told the Senate Judiciary Committee that he was "prepared but not ready" for an uprising because of the lack of equipment. Prison superintendent Thomas Fulcomer insisted under questioning by PA Senator John Shumaker that correctional officer training was adequate to handle the riots. Another issue the riot brought up was the problem of overcrowding in prisons, as Huntingdon has a capacity of 1,327 but was housing 1,990 inmates.

headline: Philadelphia plans yearlong celebration of Ben Franklin
abstract: The City of Philadelphia will have events planned for each month starting in January 1990 to celebrate the 200th anniversary of Benjamin Franklin's death. The celebration will begin with a luncheon sponsored by the city's Convention and Visitor's Bureau. Franklin lived in Philadelphia, and contributed to many important establishments such as the University of Pennsylvania.

headline: Casey is asked to bar Sunday lottery drawings
abstract: A large majority of state legislators are opposing Gov. Casey and the Revenue Dept.'s decision to begin 7-day-a-week lottery drawings.  The Senate approved a resolution (40-10) to ask Casey to bar the Sunday drawings, and the House is now discussing one.

headline: Reform is worth the price
abstract: The editorial addresses the issue of a pay raise bill that included other reforms as well. The editorial board supports the proposed limits on outside income for members of Congress that would decrease the money they collect from special interest groups for "speaking fees," saying the system was eroding public trust and tainting the image of Congress. The board commends US Senators Tom Ridge and Bill Clinger from Pennsylvania as voting against the pay raise, but speaks out against the entirety of the US Congress for not being able to make a solidified decision in relation to the nation's finances.

headline: S&L Negotiators On a Tight Deadline
abstract: Members of the US Congress are under a deadline for action on the savings and loan legislation, as all parties want to finish it before the month-long recess beginning Aug. 5.  Many pivotal, yet tentative bills still need to be addressed, however.

headline: AT&T pact expeceted within 2 weeks, union told
abstract: Contract talks between AT&T and the Communication Workers of America union are expected to end before the the May 31 expiration of the current contract.

headline: Drought shows need for pump
abstract: Although opponents of the Point Pleasant water supply project may gloat that a drought is expected which will affect consumption of water from the Delaware River, they might consider two things.  In addition to the fact that the pump would help diversify how 100,000 customers in the region obtain their water, there is no current legitmate alternative to drawing water out of the Delaware River.

headline: Highway turning lane set
abstract: Gregory L. Brown, district planning and programming manager for the PA Department of Transportation stated that PennDOT has committed itself to a project establishing a fifth lane to Route 309 in Quakertown. The project, which is meant to accommodate vehicles turning left off the road, is estimated at $1.6 million, and will be completed under a cost-sharing arrangement with the federal government.

headline: Guards criticize response to Camp Hill riot
abstract: Guards at the Camp Hill prison criticized the prison's officials. Lock boxes and control panels which controlled prison cell doors were reported broken by several guards, but requests to fix the problems were not handled properly. This allowed prison inmates to reach out of their cells and open the doors. PA State Corrections Commissioner David S. Owens Jr. suspended Camp Hill's superintendant Robert M. Freeman, a decision which PA Governor Robert Casey agreed with.

headline: Projects in peril
abstract: Willard G. Rouse III, the developer who pulled out of the planned Penn's Landing project, should considering moving the convention project at Atlantic City to Penn's Landing.  Costs may even be lower than plans for the Reading Terminal location.

headline: Casey nominees, 100
abstract: The PA Senate unanimously approved two of PA Governor Robert P. Casey's nominees. Donald M. Carroll Jr. was endorsed as Secretary of Education and David Rolka was confirmed as a member of the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Rehnquist would widen gap
abstract: Author feels that Judge Rehnquist's plea for a pay increase for federal judges is ridiculous because they are asking for 30 percent.  Author fels that it would widen the gap more between the poor and the wealthy.

headline: Sales taxes and teir clever disappearing act
abstract: Details how some states aren't garnering as much revenue from sales tax as predicted, and the causes of this discrepancy.

headline: Boroughs face retrenchment after jobs loss
abstract: Middletown and Steelton boroughs were shocked this week when Fruehauf Trailers announced it would be laying off 370 workers, and Bethlehem Steel Corp will lay off 800, leaving almost 1,200 local workers jobless.

headline: Drought Warning Lifted Today
abstract: A drought warning issued in January for 7 million people in four states ended this morning, but officials are stressing continued water conservation to get throught the summer.

headline: Holl touts plan to cut auto rates
abstract: Senate leaders Tuesday touted an auto insurance plan, introduced by Sen. Edwin Holl, which would greatly reduce insurance rates across the state.  The plan addresses issues of insurance fraud, high medical costs, uninsured motorists, and unnecessary mandatory coverages.  However, the plan did not address limiting bodily injury lawsuits, which the Casey administration supports.

headline: Guards told a state Senate committee today that cell keys are missing in the wake of two riots in the Camp Hill state prison in October.
abstract: Guards from the Camp Hill state prison testified before the PA Senate Judiciary Committee that the situation at the prison is still volatile and it has been suggested that there may be another riot in the future. The Committee is investigating insurrections at the prison that occurred between October 25 and 27, 1989. Officer John Caffas said he received a letter that there is another riot being planned. PA Corrections Department spokesman Ken Robinson said officials have been aware that keys have been missing since the riots.

headline: Reading Terminal merchants in Philadelphia have sued the Pennsylvania Convention Center Authority
abstract: The Reading Terminal Market Merchants Association filed a lawsuit against the Pennsylvania Convention Center Authority because the merchants contend the agency is trying to run them out of business by reneging on a 1988 agreement to provide assistance.

headline: CASEY PICKS SOLICITOR
abstract: County Solicitor Thompson McCullough was nominated by Gov. Casey for recommendation to the state Senate to be placed on the York County Common Pleas Court.  The nomination may be complicated by the retiring Judge John F. Rauhauser Jr., who is challenging the mandatory retirement age for judges in the PA Supreme Court.

headline: Representatives introduce plan to change judicial selection
abstract: A bipartisan group of House members yesterday proposed legislation which would make judges for the Supreme, Superior, and Commonwealth courts appointed by the governor and not popularly elected.  Under the proposal, a yes-no retention election would be held for judges four years after being appointed.  Senate Democrats have proposed similar legislation.

headline: Same, old budget exercise
abstract: True to tradition, it seems as though the budget negotiations will extend beyond the "deadline" of June 30.  The editors believe that there should be some other mechanism in place to force legislators to get the budget done on time.

headline: Casey Opens Steel Valley Job Training
abstract: Gov. Casey and county commissioners gathered yesterday to initiate an innovative job training program at the Steel Valley Council of Governments building in Homestead.

headline: Dumping fine is $195,000
abstract: A businessman will pay $195,000 in fines for dumping hazardous industrial wastes into abandoned underground coal mines a decade ago, the state Dept. of Environmental Resources said yesterday.

headline: House approves 65 mph limit for turnpike
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved a measure that would give the state Turnpike Commission to raise the speed limit to 65 mph on the main east-west portion of the highway. The northeast extension of the turnpike will be not effected and only passenger cars will be allowed to drive 65 mph; trucks will still remain at 55 mph. PA Representative Eugene Saloom of Mount Pleasant sponsored the measure, while PA Governor Robert P. Casey and PA Transportation Secretary Howard Yerusalim both have said they oppose raising the speed limit.

headline: Guards want action on their needs, ideas
abstract: Corrections officers from the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill rallied in the Capitol Rotunda in Harrisburg, claiming that nobody listens to their needs. In response to the riot at Camp Hill on October 25-27, the guards are calling for better representation, since the inmates have the American Civil Liberties Union on their side and the union, the American Federation of County, State and Municipal Employees, is not aggressive enough. The corrections officers want action from PA Governor Robert Casey and the General Assembly.

headline: Report: Convention center agreement near
abstract: Philadelphia City Council is close to approving a lease agreement for a convention center that has been in the works for a long time.  There are still some concerns about the cost and the effects of the center in its proposed neighborhood.

headline: Casey says senior citizens are real winners in lottery
abstract: Gov. Casey praises the PA Lottery system , as it gives all profits to programs that benefit older Pennsylvanians.  He also noted that PA needs to work on new guardianship laws to help protect older people.

headline: Request for 659 new court workers angers state panel
abstract: In reacting to a request by the administrator of the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts for 659 new staff jobs in the statewide court system, members of the state Senate Appropriations Committee said she lacked credibility.

headline: School budget hikes taxes by 10 mills
abstract: The Hazleton Area School Board approved a budget which includes a 10-mill property tax increase, though everyone involved seems to be content with it, as the board is expecting tangible results from this year's actions.

headline: Coal strike
abstract: Negotiations to settle the nearly nine-month-old Pittston coal strike resume this afternoon, according to a spokesman for the federal mediator. Seventeen hundred Pittston Company miners from Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky went on strike in April of 1989 over retirement and health benefits.

headline: E. Pikeland to initiate recycling
abstract: Citizens of East Pikeland Township will begin its recycling program with a two-day initiative run by the township's Environmental Advisory Council. According to resident Robert Sharp, Browning-Ferris Industries of West Chester will donate collection bins and arrangements will be made with BFI. Part of the initiative entails setting up posters at the township's two polling places during the November 7 election.

headline: House Approves Bill That Would Require Headlights In Inclement Weather
abstract: The House overwhelmingly approved a measure on Monday that would require motorists to turn their headlights on during bad weather.

headline: Gun control is public health issue
abstract: At an annual convention of the American Academy of Pediatrics, gun-control advocates and gun enthusiasts debated on how young people could be protected from death by firearms. Physician Katherine Christoffel and Chief Judge William Bauer of the 7th US Circuit Court of Appeals cited recent deaths as reasons for increased gun control, while Linda Farmer, a gun dealer from Georgia, said that greater education efforts are the solution, not limiting gun accessibility.

headline: Residents briefed on relocation timetable
abstract: Officials from the PA Department of Community Affairs and Columbia County Redevelopment Authority met with residents affected by the Centralia Relocation Project, a project being implemented in Conyngham Township for residents who will potentially affected by a mine fire. Jack Carling, of the DCA said that the US Office of Surface Mining will provide the mine fire relocation funds to 16 property owners. Ten property owners not receiving federal funds received the support of PA Senator Edward Helfrick and PA Representative Robert E. Belfanti Jr.

headline: Casey sees sunny day for Piper
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey will ask the PA General Assembly for $10 million in Sunny Day funds to bring Piper Aircraft Corporation to Lock Haven. The bill will be introduced into the House by Representative Russ Letterman. The PA Department of Community Affairs will also contribute $2.4 million to the corporation.

headline: Restoring Airline Competition
abstract: Declining competition in the airline industry, an issue to which the Reagan administration turned a deaf ear, should get far more serious attention from President Bush.

headline: State excise tax ruled unconstitutional
abstract: The PA Supreme Court ruled that the state's excise tax was unconstitutional, a decision which could cost the state from $100 million to $423 million.  The decision was brought about from a challenge by the First National Bank of Fredericksburg, which argued that federal law disallowed state and local taxes on securities.

headline: Commemorating the Homestead Strike
abstract: The piece mentions some of the bloody history of the labor movement and strike-breaking, and makes a few criticisms of current worker exploitation.

headline: Empire seeks permit to accept ash, contaminated soil
abstract: Empire Landfill in Taylor, PA, wants to import ash from a mass-burn incinerator in Warren County, NJ, and contaminated soil from the Plymouth Transport Co. in Plymouth Meeting, PA. Alan Stephens, operations manager for Empire, said the materials are non-hazardous and will be tested by the PA Department of Environmental Resources. But environmentalists in Taylor are angry at the idea, as communicated by Alison Skaluba, a member of Citizens' Alert Regarding the Environment, who said she will oppose importation of the ash and other contaminants. The people of Lackawanna County have already opposed the construction of a mass-burn incinerator from Bechtel Corporation in Dunmore.

headline: House committee approves 65 mph. rural speed limit
abstract: The state House Transportation Committee approved a measure that would increase the speed limit on some rural PA interstates from 55 to 65 mph, despite strong warnings that it would promote unsafe driving and raise insurance rates.

headline: Hafer featured/ Alice Paul House event
abstract: Pennsylvania Auditor General, Barbara Hafer, complimented the Alice Paul House for their aiding of victims of domestic violence and sexual assault.  She founded the first funding for victims of violent crime in Pa because she felt that the previous funding was inadequate.

headline: 'Robin HUD' indicted in scandal
abstract: Marilyn Louise Harrell, nicknamed "Robin HUD" by federal investigators, was indicted for embezzling $5.6 million from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development. As an escrow agent, she took funds given to her by HUD and used it to buy properties for charities and homeless families. She was also charged with making false statements to the federal government.

headline: Casey signs bill to extend Civil Service Commission life
abstract: A bill has been passed that extends the life of the Civil Service Commission, which was in danger under the state's Sunset Law, ensuring that the state will continue to receive over $4 billion in federal funds.  The committee will continue with increased restrictions on political activities of workers it covers.

headline: Reverse the Lottery Raid to Help Penna.'s Elderly
abstract: The author of this opinion piece believes that the funding base for programs for the elderly should be shifted from the Lottery fund to the general fund to guarantee support for the aging population.

headline: So far, panel is averse to a tax increase, chairman says
abstract: The head of Mayor Goode's Tax Policy and Budget Advisory Committee, William V. Donaldson, said that the committee was reluctant to sign on to the mayor's proposed $70 million tax increase next year.  Members of the committee, however, stated that no final decisions had been made.

headline: Commissioners extend contract with job training program
abstract: County commissioners Tuesday extended the contract for a job training program which places citizens in for- profit businesses and non- profit organizations.

headline: End spills, guv tells feds
abstract: Gov. Casey demanded stronger federal legislation to prevent oil spills like the one in the Delaware River two days ago.

headline: House panel OKs bill to raise speed limit
abstract: A state House panel approved legislation that would increase the speed limit on rural areas of the PA Turnpike from 55 to 65 mph.  The bill is opposed by PennDOT, some insurance companies, and Gov. Casey.

headline: Hearing Draws Angry Comments
abstract: Home and business owners attended a public hearing last night to air their complaints regarding a law being considered by City Council.  The law would levy charges for those with a burglar or fire alarm system wired into the police department's alarm system and would set charges for false alarms.

headline: Rough weather sending homeless to shelters earlier
abstract: After one homeless woman has died from exposure to the cold, outreach workers are attempting to encourage homeless people of Philadelphia to take shelter from the cold. Jane Malone, director of the city's Office of Services to the Homeless and Adults, said the low temperatures were forcing even the chronically homeless to seek shelter. Philadelphia's Outreach Coordination Center sent out teams over the weekend and placed 56 of 58 people in shelters. City shelters have felt the pain of city budget cuts by losing 1,600 beds this year.

headline: Casey sounds and looks like candidate in visit here
abstract: In a recent visit to the Pittsburgh area, Gov. Casey noted that he "doesn't have a timetable" for if or when he will announce his candidacy for governor in the elections next year, though some of his actions suggest that he is gearing up for another race.

headline: Review requested of legislative landlord decision
abstract: Attorneys for the PA General Assembly are asking the PA Ethics Commission to review its ruling against a representative. Representative Italo S. Cappabianca is reimbursed by the state for his law office, which is located in a building in which he has financial interest. The commission's ruling could affect other senators and representatives who have law offices in buildings they either own or have interest in.

headline: State budget snags on drug-war funds
abstract: One of the final unresolved issues in the state budget is the future of the $140 million that Gov. Casey plans to use for anti-drug efforts, and Republicans want to use for special education and highway maintenance.

headline: Concerns: Paper workers seek role in changes at firm
abstract: Union workers at Appleton Paper Co. said yesterday they are worried about the separation of their company from its British parent, B.A.T. Industries. John Smith, president of the United Paperworkers International Union Local 1098 at Appleton's Lower Allen Township plant, said the union should be included in the process that will make the company independent from B.A.T. The plan is for Appleton and Wiggins Teape Ltd., B.A.T.'s British paper business, to be combined as Wiggins Teape Appleton. The move is part of a defense strategy announced by B.A.T. in response to a hostile takeover attempt last summer by corporate raider Sir James Goldsmith.

headline: Engineering a new era in recycling
abstract: Day & Zimmermann Inc. is opening up a new plant in NJ that will handle large amounts of plastics recycling.  The recycled plastic will be used to make carpets and car parts.

headline: I-70 bridge is closed until further notice
abstract: Additional cracks were found in a bridge already closed for repairs on I-70, meaning the bridge will be down for at least another week, causing an almost 50-mile detour.

headline: Hearing provides little insight into prison riot
abstract: PA Corrections Commissioner David S. Owens appeared before the PA Senate Judiciary Committee to address a 2-day riot at the Camp Hill corrections facility. PA Governor Robert Casey appointed a 3-member commission to investigate the riots, while state police conduct a criminal probe. State Senators question why the National Guard was not used, while local police and fire departments were brought in to quell the riots. Inmates have been transferred to other state correction facilities and federal prisons.

headline: Slowdown in Permits For New Housing
abstract: New housing permits issued so far this year are down 20% from this time last year, and construction values have declined as well.  This is the first significant decline in PA since 1982, though last year there was a slight decrease in permits from 1987.

headline: Casey to deliver keynote speech at economic development meeting
abstract: Gov. Casey will be the keynote speaker at the May 19 Fayette Economic Development Conference.

headline: Ridge Announcing Whether He'll Run For Governor
abstract: US Rep. Tom Ridge will soon announce whether he will run against Gov. Casey in the 1990 gubernatorial race.  He is possibly the GOP's best hope to unseat Gov. Casey, though Ridge has been unsure whether he wants to run.

headline: State moves close to budget accord as deadline nears
abstract: As tomorrow's deadline draws closer, it seems as though legislators and the governor's office are nearing an agreement on the state budget.  Legislative leaders and the administration say that they are "less than $10 million apart."

headline: District 2 coalfields still in upheaval
abstract: United Mine Workers of America's District 2 coalfields have continued their walkouts, protesting against the federal courts, government policies, and corporations attempting to destroy unions.  About 27,000 mine workers are still engaged in walkouts in 9 states.

headline: Environmental chief: ground balloon launches
abstract: State Environmental Resources Secretary Arthur Davis requested that groups stop mass launching helium-filled party balloons, since they eventually come back to earth, often in the ocean, where they can be mistaken for food by turtles, whales, and other sea life.
