The balloon insudtry is opposing the suggestion.

headline: Impact of Rt. 422 expressway studied
abstract: A federally funded study is looking at the impact that Route 422 Expressway from King of Prussia to Pottstown has had on the 13 municipalities along the route. Rhonda Urkowitz, senior analyst with the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission (DVRPC), told the Montgomery County Planning Commission that the study will look at the changes that have taken place since 1985. Richard Bickel of the DVRPC said the Pottstown corridor was basically a rural area before the expressway was built, and this study may be able to indicate dramatic population changes in the area.

headline: Heed the Constitution and remove Stout
abstract: PA Attorney General Ernest Preate Jr. told the state Supreme Court Wednesday that it should heed the will of the people and remove Justice Juanita Kidd Stout from the high court.

headline: State grant to aid N. Broad business
abstract: A state grant of $50,000 will be used to "encourage economic and cultural development" on the North Broad Street corridor in Philadelphia.

headline: Casey to visit York Monday
abstract: Casey to campaign for his local tax reform in York days before the general election.

headline: Ridge to give decision on governor candidacy
abstract: US Rep Tom Ridge is scheduled to announce whether he will run in next year's gubernatorial race, most likely against Gov. Casey.  Insiders doubt that he will run, and GOP leaders are already searching for other potential candidates.

headline: State slashes funding for Ben Franklin
abstract: The new state budget includes a $4.3 million funding cut for the acclaimed Ben Franklin Partnership, which provides support for economic development.  Two board members argued over who was responsible for the cuts.

headline: Fairview Du Pont continues phase-out
abstract: The Du Pont Electronics plant, which manufactures connectors, in Fairview Township is still on schedule for closing.  Most of the plants remaining 400 employees will move to either the Emigsville or Valley Green plants by the end of March.

headline: EPA chief pushes school radon tests
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said yesterday that every classroom in America should be tested for radon, after preliminary tests found scattered unsafe levels in schools across the nation.

headline: Improvements to Route 413 back on state's plans
abstract: Improvements to Rt. 413 seem as though they may actually take place after being delayed many times.  Several steps must be taken before actual construction starts, which means that it could be a few years before any improvements are actually made.

headline: Heroin teen dies alone and helpless
abstract: Earl T. Parsley Jr., a 19-year-old from Gettysburg, died of an accidental overdose of a morphine-based substance, according to Gettysburg Borough Police. He had a history of heroin use, and had been arrested in Baltimore, Maryland for possession with intent to distribute. Earl's mother, Nannie E. Bosley, attempted to get him placed into a methadone clinic, but he was denied and merely recommended for counseling.

headline: Task force hoping for land use guide
abstract: The Bedford County Economic Revitalization Task Force has accepted a new guidebook for economic development, particularly for land use.

headline: Casey vetoes renewal of review commission
abstract: Gov. Casey vetoed a bill which would renew the  existence of the Independent Regulatory Review Commission, which handles oversight of state regulations.

headline: Robbins enters Senate race
abstract: PA Representative Robert D. Robbins has announced his candidacy for a State Senate post vacated by Roy W. Wilt, who is retiring. Robbins is opposed by Charles W. Flynn, a Meadville councilman, and has established goals such as economic growth, creating jobs, and securing infrastructural funds. Robbins is a veteran of the US Army, serves on the joint House-Senate legislative budget and finance committee, and is a member of the Center for Rural Pennsylvania.

headline: State taxes will go up
abstract: Now that the tax reform proposal has been defeated, voters can't expect any new tax reforms to surface for many years.

headline: Federal court rules against Fayette company
abstract: Williamhouse-Regency in Fayette County lost a lawsuit against the union over Williamhouse's deletion of two clauses from the union's contract without approval.

headline: EPA cites risk, urges end to fungicide use on 45 crops
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed to cancel the use of EBDC fungicides on 45 crops to reduce the risk of cancer to consumers. The proposal would end 90 percent of the fungicides' use. The four major manufacturers of the chemicals had already decided to withdraw EBDC fungicides for 42 crops effective January 1, but EPA administrator William K. Reilly extended the withdrawal to three more crops that account for 40 percent of consumers' exposure to EBDCs. The program will cost consumers $90 to $300 million in higher fruit and vegetable prices.

headline: Inspections: More than meets the eye
abstract: Bridge inspections all over the state executed by PennDOT never go more than 2 years without a comprehensive inspection, and the inspections are partly funded by the state.  This spotlight on bridge inspections comes after a few local bridges were marked for repair.

headline: High-profile inmates place strain on prisons
abstract: Wardens, officials, and officers face strains on prison life when high-profile inmates enter their prisons. For example, Jim Bakker is now housed at a federal institution in Rochester, Minnesota. US Bureau of Prisons senior executive Joseph Bogan says that these high-profile inmates are not to be given special treatment.

headline: Tax hike likely in Hummelstown, official says
abstract: Hummelstown Borough Manager Michael O'Keefe said the Borough Council will probably have to recommend an increase of three-tenths of a mill in the 1990 tax rate at the council's recent workshop meeting. Three-tenths of a mill is equal to $12 on a $40,000 home. O'Keefe said the increase will be necessary so that the borough will not have to make a larger increase in the tax rate in the future. The council also discussed renovations at Hummelstown High School, renovations at the Nye elementary building, and approval of the Downtown Improvement Plan.

headline: Casey vows to make use of Pa. 'tools'
abstract: In the first state of the state address delivered to the General Assembly since 1975, Gov. Casey outlined the state's significant increase in jobs and the opportunity available to PA to make further progress, while many Republicans labeled the speech as simply the beginning of a reelection PR campaign

headline: Roddey quits authority post
abstract: James Roddey resigned from his post as chairman of the Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority because he is considering becoming involved in next year's gubernatorial campaign. He will serve as Western Pennsylvania campaign manager for PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer if she formally declares her candidacy. Roddey is also former chairman of the Port Authority Transit, and is believed to have fallen out of favor with Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff when he supported PA Representative Tom Murphy's bid for mayor.

headline: States not saving: Weak budgets would make a recession rough riding
abstract: Viewed as a whole, the nation's economy is booming with healthy job growth and low unemployment. States, however, are overspending at a rate that their revenue growth cannot match.

headline: Grinnell workers vote to continue walkout
abstract: Defying their international union, striking Grinnell Corp. workers voted Sunday to continue their 18- month strike.

headline: EPA signs clean up agreement for Revere site
abstract: The EPA has signed an agreement with four companies - AT&T of Berkeley Heights, Carpenter Technology Corp., IBM Corp. of Armonk, NY., and Yates Industries - for a comprehensive pre-cleanup study for a Superfund site located off of Route 611.  It is believed that the companies are each responsible for the etching solution waste, heavy metals, and acids found in lagoons at the Nockamixon Township location.

headline: Insuring no progress
abstract: The editorial criticizes PA Senate Republicans of playing politics with the auto insurance legislation, causing it to be delayed until after the summer recess, meaning drivers statewide must continue to pay high rates or drive uninsured.

headline: Highspire calls halt to purchase of weapons
abstract: Highspire Borough Manager Robert Sabatini Jr. said requests from the borough police association for $4,751 in weapons were rejected. The police requested money for more weapons because they feel underarmed in the wake of the riots at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill. Borough Councilwoman Joanne Kern said the police association should not be using borough funds for such requests because of the discrepancy in the number of weapons requested, 18 handguns, when there are only 12 police officers.

headline: Team members
abstract: This photograph depicts Bob Leonardi and Lawrence Kluger of Kingston, who are two members of PA Governor Robert P. Casey's economic development response team. The group acts to help businesses grow, prosper and relocate in the state.

headline: Casey, senators talk amendment at VFW meeting
abstract: Gov. Casey and US sens. Specter and Heinz (both R-PA) spoke at a VFW meeting in support of an amendment that would make burning the US flag a federal crime, unprotected by First Amendment freedom of expression.

headline: Ron Brown, The Practical Politician
abstract: Ron Brown became the new chairman of the Democratic National Committee.  It is controversial because he is a black man and has worked closely with Jesse Jackson.  Some Democratic senators are uncomfortable with his appointment, yet are denying that it is because of his race.

headline: State's surplus to be $83 million less
abstract: The state's surplus carrying over to the next fiscal year will be $83 million less that originally predicted by the Casey administration.  Lawmakers are optimistic that the new budget will be completed by the deadline.

headline: House approves bill to ease child labor law
abstract: The state House passed a bill that would allow 14 and 15-year-olds to work until 10pm on school nights, a three hour extension of the previous restriction.  The bill was supported by farm groups, which said that some farm chores can't be performed until sundown.

headline: EPA: too soon to tell if auto pollution still a problem
abstract: The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency state that recent air quality warnings were more so a result of seasonal leaf burning and stagnant air than auto pollution. Cincinnati's air quality index reached 101, which prompted the Southwest Ohio Air Pollution Control Agency to issue a health advisory warning. Cincinnati's assistant health commissioner Malcolm Adcock stated that the health advisory warnings may help people to focus on air pollution as an everyday problem.

headline: Interchange, 110
abstract: The administration of PA Governor Robert P. Casey announced that the state and private developer Western Development Corp. will jointly fund improvements to a busy interchange on Interstate 95 in northeast Philadelphia. Improvements include realignment or relocation of several ramps, the widening of other ramps, and the widening of a local road.

headline: Hitting the brakes
abstract: The PA House easily passed legislation which was opposed by trial lawyers, doctors, and insurers in order to decrease auto insurance costs and premiums, though one of the measures will likely not stand up to judicial scrutiny.

headline: The Convention Center; It's a Cruel Hoax Being Played on Phila. Taxpayers
abstract: The writer opposes the proposed convention center being considered by Philadelphia City Council.  The center will cost $500,000 at a time when the city is already having financial troubles, forcing the city to decrease spending on other services and tourist attractions.

headline: Casey: drug war's vital
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey inaugurated a public affairs forum in honor of Charles J. Volpe, a former state Representative and former deputy mayor of Scranton. Casey cited Volpe and former US President Harry Truman as examples of administrators committed to transferring power from the public. He also spoke extensively about drugs as being one of the greatest challenges to modern society, and of the need to fight against drugs.

headline: Ross, Ertel, Cappy in tight Supreme Court Race
abstract: Each of the candidates vying for the Democratic nomination for a seat on the state Supreme Court have strong points going for them.

headline: Tax Reform
abstract: Comments on the difficulty in selling the tax reform proposal to the public, and notes at how tax reform could have been implemented more effectively.

headline: House approves higher minimum wage
abstract: The US House of Representatives approved a bill to raise the national minimum wage to $4.25 by April 1991. President Bush supports the bill, and the Senate will take a vote on the bill next month. Robert Shapiro, an economic analyst at the Progressive Policy Institute, says that families will pay $135 a year to compensate for the higher prices caused by the wage increase.

headline: Erie industrial site to become game preserve
abstract: Most of a 5,000 acre tract bordering Lake Erie that was originally earmarked for a huge steel mill will be transformed into a wildlife reserve and open to the public for hiking, hunting, and other recreation.

headline: Interstate-78 between Phillipsburg, N.J. and Fogelsville opens
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey stated that the opening of Interstate Route 78, which connects the Lehigh Valley to New Jersey, will open up new opportunities for businesses and commuters. A lawsuit was brought against the PA Department of Transportation by Edward Weiner, a developer who owns a business park in Salisbury Township and who claims that sound barriers should be constructed near his land. Commonwealth Court Senior Judge William Lipsett ruled that the sound barriers were not necessary.

headline: Holiday postal recruits fail drug tests
abstract: According to Thomas Mansmann, director of operations at Pittsburgh's General Mail Facility for the U.S. Postal Service, seven out of every eight job applicants for temporary postal workers failed a newly mandatory drug test or background check or refused to participate. Mansmann said 798 prospective employees were screened and only 100 were hired for the holiday rush, in comparison to the 200 hired last year before the drug tests were required. The Pittsburgh general office sees up to 10 million pieces of mail daily during the holiday season, which is double the normal amount.

headline: The EDZ failure
abstract: The editorial board expresses its hope that Scranton's next mayor will examine the city's Enterprise Development Zone, which they claims has been nothing but a program appealing to political cronies and interest groups. The program has been unproductive, and most recently spent $19,000 on materials which count have been furnished to businesses in the EDZ, or city officials, state officials, or federal officials.

headline: Casey's bankroll keeps foes away
abstract: It is expected that an opponent, to make a competitive bid against Gov. Casey in the 1990 gubernatorial race, would have to raise approximately $12 million.  Possible Republican candidates include U.S. Sen. John Heinz, state Sen. Robert Jubelirer, and U.S. Rep. Thomas Ridge.

headline: Rudy's restroom bill flies
abstract: PA Representative Ruth Rudy from Mifflin County proposed a bill that calls for restroom equity for women, which passed unanimously in the House State Government Committee. The measure calls for additional women's restroom facilities in public places that are built or undergo renovations after January 1. Rudy said she got the idea when speaking with female legislators from other states where similar measures were passed.

headline: Surplus helps ease budget woes
abstract: The budget surplus left over from the last fiscal year helped ease some of this year's budget proceedings by providing a little leeway for legislators.

headline: Job Center gains praise during visit
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark Singel and state Labor and Industry Secretary Harris Wofford helped open a new job center in York.  The York County Job Center is on of 22 accredited centers throughout the state which help people find employment and access job information agencies across PA.

headline: Farmers, couples affected along with big developers
abstract: Increased efforts to preserve wetlands have had a huge impact on large developers, family farmers, and people looking to build vacation or retirement homes. Legislation proposed by PA Senator Roger A. Madigan of Lycoming would require the state to compensate landowners who aren't allowed to use their land as they choose. However, the PA Department of Environmental Resources said providing compensation to landowners could have serious legal ramifications affecting their other regulatory programs. Roger Flickes, chief of DER's division of rivers and wetlands conservation, said compensation could set a precedent of people requesting compensation for not being able to use the land as they would like. On the other hand, landowners are demanding compensation be paid if they are denied the use of their land.

headline: John blasts shoddy work
abstract: Schuylkill Township Supervisor Chairman Herman John attacked the Philadelphia Suburban Water Company for failing to conform to PA Department of Transportation standards on a road surfacing project on Country Club Road. John accused the company of poor workmanship and instigating accidents by not providing flagmen.

headline: Holmesburg inmates say guards beat them after riot
abstract: Inmates at the Holmseburg prison state that they were beaten by prison guards during and after the riot on October 28.  Prison Warden Willie Gray said that the riot was started by only a core group of inmates, yet even prisoners not wanting to be involved in the riot were beaten by guards. Inmates are set to testify before a 3-member Common Please Court Panel on prison conditions.

headline: The Steep Price of No New City Taxes
abstract: Mayor Goode's Finance Department, for the first time, has released alternatives to his proposed $70 million tax increase.  The alternatives include cuts in homeless programs, the elimination of Class 500 grants to community groups, and the closing of possibly one-half of the city's branch libraries.

headline: Casey's Capital for a Day: Good publicity, and it works
abstract: Gov. Casey's "Capital for a Day" program is great publicity for him, but it also seems to be a sincere effort to hear about the public's concens and make them more involved in the governing process.  Casey holds a town meeting at each temporary "Capital" and will listen to and answer questions for hours, making sure that everyone has had their chance to speak.

headline: Rural-affairs post given ex-legislator
abstract: Gov. Casey appointed former state Rep. John Showers to head the new Office of Rural Affairs.

headline: Tax apprehension hits home
abstract: Compilation of several responses from readers concerning the proposed tax reform.

headline: Job center grand opening is Friday
abstract: PA Department of Labor and Industry secretary Harris Wofford will be present at the grand opening of the St. Mary's Job Center, along with the center's manager Millie Huff. The center will offer job-search services to local jobseekers. The Department of Labor and Industry has more than 70 such centers operating in the state.

headline: Faster Than a Speeding Bullet?  Not Quite, but It's a New DER
abstract: Although the Department of Environmental Resourcse has always responded to toxic spills and moved against violators of the state's environmental laws, the agency's regional headquarters now has the personnel and means to do so more quickly than ever.

headline: Keep speed limit at 55
abstract: The editorial opposes the current proposed increase of the speed limit along parts of the PA Turnpike, saying it would lead to more accidents and increase insurance rates.

headline: House Oks $822 million for anti-drug effort
abstract: The U.S. House approved a $3.7 billion spending bill which includes $822 million to be added to the federal government's efforts against drug trafficking.

headline: UDAG funds not available for Indiana
abstract: A federal grant is unavailable for a renovation project in downtown Indiana, PA.  However, an Indiana developer is still seeking some sort of grant.

headline: Caterpillar, Superior companies at top of York RITC's appreciation award list
abstract: Caterpillar and Superior were each honored for their commitment to either hiring clients of the Rehabilitation and Industrial Training Center or subtracting out their work to the RITC.  Secretary of the Commonwealth James Haggerty was on hand to present the awards.

headline: Say what they want, KKK spells hatred
abstract: Despite the Klan's attempts to seem non-racist, few believe that the KKK has really turned away from its old ways of hatred.

headline: Tax filing deadline- a time to 'live dangerously'
abstract: By April 7, the IRS had received only about 65 million of the 109 million individual tax returns expected for the year. The U.S. Postal Service and companies like H&R Block feel the last- minute rush.

headline: Job Security a Mirage for Unions Despite Wage Concessions of 80's
abstract: Since 1979, labor unions have used wage concessions as a way to prevent companies from laying off workers or closing plants.  On the whole, this strategy of emphasizing job security over wage increases has seen little success: only 75 of 1,060 labor contracts signed in 1988 had any job security provisions at all.

headline: Federal and state officials from Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey are meeting later this month about the future of the Delaware Estuary
abstract: Federal and state officials from Pennyslvania, Delaware, and New Jersey are meeting later this month about the future of the Delaware Estuary.

headline: Landlocked seniors hope for reprieve
abstract: For the past year, clients of the Dillsburg Senior Center and the Redlands center in Lewisberry have been stuck with limited transportation after the Public Utility Commission ruled against cross- county transport by the York Transportation Club.

headline: 'I wasn't ready to help myself'
abstract: A woman only identified as "Patricia" is a client and a counselor at the Community House in Erie, PA. She had her first child at age 16, and fell under the influence of alcohol, marijuana and cocaine. She joined the Community House after a friend was murdered for drugs and on the recommendation of a counselor at the Greater Erie Community Action Committee.

headline: Ufberg, Boscov cut deal
abstract: Negotiations concerning the building of a proposed $85 million mall on Lackawanna ave. too a significant step forward on Thursday after a draft agreement was committed to between co-mall developer Al Boscov and Ufberg Home Furnishing owner Howard Ufberg.  The agreement states that the city will pay Ufberg $1,975,000 for the properties.

headline: Chadwick to send newsletter to registered county voters
abstract: Rep. J. Scot Chadwick announced he is mailing a newsletter with important information about local tax reform to all registered voters in the 110 Legislative District.

headline: School officials endorse fifth star for general
abstract: Fox Chapel school board members have encouraged members of the Fox Chapel Area Student Council to urge President Bush and Congress members to elevate retired Army General Matthew B. Ridgway to the rank of five-star general. US Senator John Heinz last month wrote to Defense Secretary Richard Cheney to ask that Ridgway be awarded a fifth star because of his devotion to the service of the United States.

headline: Tax hikes loom in 23 states
abstract: Taxpayers in at least 23 states could face tax increases in fiscal year 1990 as governors strain to make ends meet.

headline: Job security top union priority, survey shows
abstract: According to the labor research and publishing group called the Bureau of National Affairs, it is likely that unions will place as their top priority in collective bargaining agreements job security.  Following that issue in importance will be curtailing the use of strike replacements and pay increases.

headline: Firm had been warned about waste, DER says
abstract: A York County firm had been warned of problems before the DER shut down the firm's hazardous waste operations indefinitely, according to a DER spokesperson.  The DER is concerned that a fire could result in damage to the environment or the public.

headline: Laughlintown group calls for a truck ban
abstract: A group in Laughlintown is calling for a ban on heavy trucks on a stretch of road where 5 people were recently killed when a truck went out of control.  Other crashes have occurred on the same strip of road.

headline: Indicted Cambria County judge faces day in court
abstract: Cambria County Judge Joseph O'Kicki faces trial on accusations of official oppression. Supporters of O'Kicki have published an insert into a weekly shopper portraying him as the victim of a "witch-hunt" by state police. O'Kicki was first elected as a jurist in 1971 and was voted president of the Pennsylvania Conference of State Trial Judges in 1983.

headline: United Way honors local man
abstract: The PA United Way honored Harold Rosenn as the 1989 Golden Key Volunteer of the Year for years of outstanding community service.  Gov. Casey presented the plaque to Rosenn in Hershey.

headline: Chambers of commerce remain neutral on reform
abstract: Local chambers of commerce have chosen to remain neutral on the proposed tax reform.  They are unanimous in saying that the legislation is too complex and they are not sure how it will affect them.

headline: Second From Lancaster County To Head Minty
abstract: John Martino, a former Lancaster County Republican chairman, is being recommended by Pres. Bush for the superintendent position of the US Mint in Philadelphia.  If confirmed, he will be the second Lancaster County resident to hold the post.

headline: Tax plan backers answer critics' questions
abstract: There are many questions surrounding the tax reform referendum which will be placed before the public on May 16, including whether the reform is optional, whether real estate taxes will actually drop by 25 percent, how senior citizens and businesses will be affected, and whether the tax reform will actually be a tax increase.

headline: Judge says coal strikes violate law
abstract: US District Judge Dennis Knapp has ruled that the "wildcat strikes" of about 43,000 coal miners are violating federal labor law, and that the workers must cease strike-related activities.  The United Mine Workers union is not sanctioning the strikes, but said it will attempt to comply with the court injunction.

headline: Firm seeks DER permits for Cambria power plant
abstract: Interpower of Pennsylvania, Incorporated are awaiting two permits from the PA Department of Environmental Resources to build an 80 megawatt plant. The DER is reviewing Interpower's applications for a water discharge permit and an air quality permit. Two other cogeneration plants are being built in Cambria Township.

headline: Law enforcement officials trying to fight the worst drug problem in the state's history are focusing more on their efforts to snare street- corner dealers who know customers by name.
abstract: Law enforcement officials trying to fight the worst drug problem in the state's history are focusing more on their efforts to snare street- corner dealers who know customers by name.

headline: Ingenious drug users vex police searches
abstract: Sargeant John McMahon of the Pittsburgh Office of Organized Crime, Narcotics and Intelligence stated that drug users and dealers frequently come up with new ways to store and transport drugs. Recent examples include double-compartmented containers for everyday products such as motor oil, which hold drugs on the bottom and the product on top.

headline: Vartan plan OK assailed as 'not legal'
abstract: Vartan Parc, which was named in December to build a $19 million 10-story office building in downtown Harrisburg, had its plans approved last week by the city's Affirmative Action Review Committee.  However, the action may be challenged by City Council, where some members have called Vartan' plans illegal due to a resolution council passed in July 1987.  That resolution required that any waivers associated with affirmative action provisions must be approved by City Council, not the Affirmative Action Review Committee.

headline: Chester County unlikely to receive increases in human servicese funds
abstract: Human services are unlikely to receive significantly increased funding in the upcoming state budget, and state Sen. Earl Baker says that rather than increased money in human services, the need is for increased efficiency.

headline: Selection needed now on district justice post
abstract: The West Shore has a vacant position for district justice since Robert Failor retired in June and, while Gov. Casey has twice appointed Charles Clement Jr., the process is likely being held up by West Shore Republican Sen. John Hopper.

headline: Tax reform facts
abstract: David Davare, Regional Manager of the PA Economy League, writes that he was misquoted about tax reform and that the Economy League presents facts not bias.

headline: Laid-off Fruehauf workers tell of hopes, fears
abstract: Workers laid off from Fruehauf Trailers are now searching for new livelihoods after abruptly seeing their seemingly secure job disappear.

headline: Firms discuss radioactive waste dump
abstract: Two firms, courting citizen support for Pennsylvania's first low-level radioactive waste disposal facility, talked to 250 people at a meeting in Meadville Tuesday.  The $50 million facility will either be constructed by Chem-Nuclear or U.S. Ecology, pending a selection by Deparment of Environmental Resources Secretary Arthur Davis.

headline: Lawmaker Prods Casey to Act on New York Commuter Tax
abstract: State House Rep. Chadwick has criticized Gov. Casey for remaining inactive on a new commuter tax levied by NY on non-resident workers.  The tax is costing commuting workers between $100 and $200 more a year.

headline: Inmate cap at jail is often exceeded
abstract: The maximum occupancy of the Allegheny County Jail is often exceeded, despite a recent increase in capacity.  Plans for a new jail are being considered.

headline: Washington's Landing development pact near
abstract: The Urban Redevelopment Authority and Buncher Corp. have indicated that they are close to an agreement concerning the URA's purchasing of 10 acres of land on Herrs Island in the Allegheny River.  Plans have been at a standstill since last year, when it was discovered that hazardous wastes were on the property.

headline: Choice of Vanston for Judgeship Draws Opposition
abstract: Gov. Casey nominated District Attorney Brendan Vanston to become the President Judge of Wyoming and Sullivan counties.  There is strong oppostion to this nomination by Democrats and Rebulicans alike.  Much of the opposition is due to Vanston's handling of the Joyce Ann Harding murder case.  Gov. Casey had Vanston investigated by the state Inspector General's Office before the nomination and it turned up with nothing.

headline: Senate Approves IRRC Bill; Senator Predicts Casey Veto
abstract: The Senate, discounting objections raised by the Casey administration, approved legislation that would re-establish an agency that reviews state regulations.

headline: Tax reform gets reserved push
abstract: The paper's editorial board casts a cautious vote for the tax reform ammendment while acknowledging its inherent complexities.  They highly suggest that each individual voter look into it and form their own  opinion.

headline: Lawmaker Proposes Minimum Wage Boost
abstract: House Labor Relations Chairman Mark Cohen proposed increasing the hourly minimum wage from $3.35 an hour to $4.65 by Jan. 1, 1991.

headline: Fishing Limits
abstract: In a letter to the editor, a citizen asks why the Pennsylvania Fish Commission put restrictions on fishing near an easy- access area of Petroleum Center Park.

headline: Legislators say editorial about school bus safety treated them unfairly
abstract: Legislators George C. Hasay and Stanley J. Jarolin respond to a Jan. 7 editorial which referred to them as "jellyfish" for their attempt to abolish certain aspects of a school bus safety proposal.

headline: Inmate in critical condition after attack
abstract: According to the PA State Police, a man serving a life sentence at the State Correctional Institution at Pittsburgh was attacked by three other inmates. He was taken to Allegheny General Hospital.

headline: Wasting our tax money in Philadelphia
abstract: This editorial addresses PA Governor Robert P. Casey's proposal to spend more than $8 million to prepare a site in Philadelphia to build a new sports arena and improve parking. The object of the proposal is to keep the Philadelphia Flyers and the 76ers from moving to New Jersey, as both team owners have been given generous offers from New Jersey's Sports and Exposition Authority to relocate there. The editorial board thinks it is ludicrous for the PA government to spend taxpayers' money on the sports teams in Philadelphia, suggesting that Philadelphia figure out how to deal with the problem on their own, as Pittsburgh had to do to keep the Pittsburgh Pirates from moving to another city.

headline: City Controller challenges union results
abstract: Pittsburgh City Controller Thomas Flaherty along with the PA Labor Relations Board challenged the outcome of a union election which chose the United Steelworkers as the bargaining representative for Flaherty's professional employees. Flaherty and two controller's office officials were sued by Philip Retenauer, an employee of the office, who accused them of threats and harassment. Retenauer's claim, filed with the Allegheny County Common Please Court, said that the threats were in response for his talking to a PA Ethics Commission investigator.

headline: Senate Approves Tax Amendment, Clears Way For Ballot Vote
abstract: With a vote of 36-13, the state Senate joined the House in passing a constitutional amendment tax reform bill which would give greater power to municipalities and school districts in raising revenue from new sources.  For the amendment to become law, voters must approve the bill in a referendum expected on the May 16 primary.

headline: Tax reform issue has last debate here
abstract: Lancaster houses a debate about the upcoming tax reform referendum.  Five people presented their views on the proposal.

headline: Lock Haven is designated as a new 'Job Center'
abstract: Pennsylvania's Labor and Industry accredited the Clinton County Job Center.  The job center helps workers find new or better jobs, as well as helping employers find qualified workers, by creating a network of services.

headline: Food trucks that haul garbage may be seized
abstract: If a new bill passes the state House and Senate, trucks hauling food after garbage would be seized upon discovery by the DER.

headline: Legislators start slowly after election recess
abstract: Legislators are preparing for major bills in the future, including auto-insurance proposals and next year's budget.  However, for now lawmakers are in start-up mode after a break.

headline: Inmate Treatment Facility Opens At Rockview Prison
abstract: The $6.8 million treatment facility, part of the state Correctional Institution at Rockview, was dedicated yesterday.  It is designed to rehabilitate criminals and make them productive contributers to society.

headline: Who's among the homeless?
abstract: Points out that helping the "homeless" is becoming more difficult as the lines between homeless and ne'er-do-wells become more blurred, and that there needs to be a way to separate the two so that the homeless can be properly supported.

headline: City's campaign has undermined giving
abstract: The 1989 City of Philadelphia Employees' Combined Campaign, representing only a narrow set of specialized interests, risks dividing the community and further penalizing the United Way for past deficiencies.  The campaign allowed nine separately funded organizations to appeal for contributions a the same time, which risks homogenizing the city's diverse array of civic groups.

headline: Senate Democrats Propose Eliminating Judicial Elections
abstract: A constitutional amendment has been proposed by Senate Democrats which would alter the selection of judges for the state Supreme, Superior, and Commonwealth Courts.  Instead of popular elections, judges would be appointed by the governor.  The process was begun, tangentially, when Gov. Casey formed a commission to study the idea in 1987.

headline: Tax reform on the ballot: Opinion split on what it would mean, how it would work, what it would cost
abstract: Citizens and lawmakers remain split on the proposed tax reform with reference to what it would mean, how it would work, and what it would cost taxpayers.

headline: Low- wage earners on the increase in Penna., Senate study indicates
abstract: The number of Pennsylvania workers earning low wages grew significantly between 1979 and 1987, while the state's middle- income segment shrank considerably, according to a U.S. Senate study.

headline: Forest fire in Carbon County contained after two days
abstract: A Carbon County forest fire that destroyed more than 1,500 acres was placed under control early Monday after a two- day fight by fire crews.

headline: 'Maglev' trains would link most U.S. cities, report says
abstract: An industry panel issued a report yesterday about the posibility of linking many American cities with maglev trains, though skepticism as to the technology's potentials continues in many levels of government.

headline: Inmate's treatment came too late
abstract: The article is a human interest piece about the lack of adequate health care and diagnosis for prison inmates. The main example was Albert "Bear" Viall, an inmate at the State Correctional Institution at Graterford, who visited the prison infirmary on numerous occasions complaining of a back ache. Two hundred of his fellow prisoners refused to return to their cells one night until he was taken to the county hospital, but he was still not treated for the cancer that would soon take his life without anyone knowing. According to the Criminal Justice Institute, Inc., a national crime statistics clearinghouse in New York, 82 percent of all prison deaths in the state and federal systems in 1988 were due to AIDS or other medical causes.

headline: A choice in auto insurance
abstract: Stephen Friend, Republican chairman of the House Insurance Committee, writes in support of his new Insurance  bill, attempting to gain support from the public in order to combat lobbyists which are against it.

headline: Coal Bill
abstract: The House State Government Committee unanimously approved a measure introduced by Rep. William Lloyd which would force state buildings to burn PA coal.

headline: Senate panel votes to strengthen ethics law and save its enforcer
abstract: A state Senate committee voted unanimously to strengthen the state's ethics law.  The vote saves the Ethics Commission from dissolution, as it would have been allowed to die if the ethics legislation was not renewed by June 30.

headline: Tax Reform Plan Supporters Outpace Opponents
abstract: Despite raising about $127,000 less than their rivals, the most vocal opponents of the local tax restructuring plan downplayed the difference by saying they received more contributions from individual tax payers.

headline: Man who was homeless gets job teaching
abstract: Allen Delano Johnson lost his wife, family, house, and job, and has managed to get back on his feet and earn a job teaching commercial and residential electrical installation at the Triangle Tech School in Pittsburgh. Johnson, a trained electrician, had lost his electrical contracting business in Lorain, Ohio, and moved to Pittsburgh but had trouble breaking into the skilled electrician's field. With the help of the Adkins Life Skills Program, a part of the Jubilee Soup Kitchen's Career Development Program, Johnson earned his current position. Johnson did so well that he was honored as one of seven program graduates from three states to earn the Life Skills Achievement plaque of the year.

headline: Franklin proves recycling does pay
abstract: The town of Franklin, which has already begun its recycling program, despite the fact that it's not required for another 14 months, is reaping the benefits of the system, as it provides a small amount of profit and decreases the amount of trash taken to landfills.

headline: Magnetic-levitation trains zoom on air
abstract: Suggested plans for a high-speed maglev train through parts of PA hit a stumbling block in the legislature and other administration.

headline: It happened in Harrisburg
abstract: PA Representative Paul W. Semmel writes about the issue of prison overcrowding, and how it can be dealt with. Citing the recent riots at Camp Hill and Huntingdon state prisons, Semmel discusses legislation to solve prison overcrowding, including building more prisons, creative punishment, and alternative sentencing. He also discusses Mothers Against Drunk Driving's opinion that drunk drivers will be among the first left off the hook, and a US Department of Justice report on prisoners serving multiple sentences.

headline: A measure of prosperity
abstract: Galleria is a location where retailers are selling their high-priced goods to see how the tastes have changed in Pittsburgh.  Here the affluent, who are purchasing  evening wear and sportswear, are examples of how the market has expanded and illustrate what life is like in 'the most livable city'.

headline: Comedian Jackie Mason hosting lunch for Specter
abstract: Comedian Jackie Mason, the former honorary campaign chairman for New York mayoral candidate Rudy Giuliani, is hosting a lunch in honor of his friend, US Senator Arlen Specter. Mason resigned from Giuliani's campaign after he made comments against Giuliani's opponent, black Democratic candidate David Dinkins. Mason insists the lunch is not about politics.

headline: Senate rejects Martin, 1 other judge nominee
abstract: The state Senate rejects Gov. Casey's nominees for seats on Allegheny and Berks county courts.  Negative votes were cast by Democrats in what some see as a message to Republicans rather than a vote against the nominees.

headline: Tax Reform- Pro: It gives a break to those who deserve it
abstract: The author of the opinion piece believes that the proposed tax reform gives relief to those who need it most, middle income families.

headline: Minimum wage battle continues
abstract: The battle over minimum wage continues to rage in Washington after President Bush vetoed a raise to $4.55 but would support a smaller increase.  PA recently raised its minimum wage and is considering further increases, though many lawmakers would rather see nationwide increases rather than state-by-state.

headline: Fumes Overcome Lifeguard; Swimmer Evacuated
abstract: Chlorine fumes overcame a lifeguard at a city swimming pool, forcing the evacuation of 100 to 125 children from the pool building.  A leak causing the gas to seep into the room was closed quickly after its detection.

headline: Make Harrisburg accountable for SEPTA funding
abstract: This editorial discusses how the state of Pennsylvania has not provided adequate funds for public transit agencies, including the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA). US Representative Bill Gray has proposed an idea to tie Pennsylvania's public transit agencies directly to the state's receipt of federal highway funds. The editorial board believes the proposal would force Pennsylvania to develop a plan to provide stable funding for public transit agencies or risk losing millions of federal highway dollars.

headline: Judge Addresses citizen group
abstract: Judge Albert Stallone, in speaking to the West Side Concerned Citizens, said that a solution to the drug epidemic must focus on education, enforcement, the court system, and rehabilitation.  Stallone handles all of the drug cases in the 6th Ward.

headline: Aliquippa Works topples into history
abstract: LTV Steel Company is closing its Aliquippa Works, once the country's largest fully integrated steel mill. According to Rich Vallecorsa, president of United Steelworkers Local 1211, only 20% of the plant remains in operation. The company had to close down to the facility on account of high costs of maintaining environmental standards set by the PA Department of Environmental Resources. PA Governor Robert Casey remains committed to creating jobs in the Beaver Valley.

headline: Commissioner Klein would spend next life as an editorial writer
abstract: Chairman of the Dauphin County Board of Commissioners Sally Klein wrote a heavily sarcastic letter criticizing the Patriot-News editors of a lack of complete knowledge about the actions of the county, particularly with respect to the Dauphin Manor, for praising or criticizing contradictory sides of issues, and for proposing bland, meaningless solutions to the problems.

headline: Senator John Heinz of Pennsylvania has introduced legislation calling for President Bush to develop a plan to better deal with oil spills.
abstract: Senator John Heinz of Pennsylvania has introduced legislation calling for President Bush to develop a plan to better deal with oil spills.

headline: Tax reform: some cases defy explanation
abstract: An analysis of the proposed tax reforms in relation to individual people.  Points out some of the odd technicalities and confusing aspects of the reforms.

headline: Minimum wage bill to have little effect here because of labor shortage
abstract: The federal government passed a bill supported by President George Bush increasing the national minimum wage to $4.25 per hour by April 1, 1991. The bill is likely to have little effect in York County, where the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate is about 4%. PA Secretary of Labor and Industry Harris Wofford lauds the bill, whole York Area Chamber of Commerce President Thomas F. Donley considers the bill moot in the local area.

headline: Gains claimed in combating research peril
abstract: The state will soon finish its investigation into whether or not to impose increased regulations on research involving biological agents.  There is some concern that agents used in research could pose a threat to the surrounding area.

headline: Make it 65 and enforce it!
abstract: The editors support raising the speed limit on rural sections of the PA Turnpike because the speed limit of 55 mph is largely ignored and stats show that there are not considerably more deaths in 65 mph zones.  They do stress that strictly enforcing the 65 mph limit would be very important, however.

headline: Judge allows schools to award contract in set- aside case
abstract: A U.S. District Court judge has given the Philadelphia Board of Education permission to award a contract being challenged by a white businessman contesting the board's minority set- aside rule.

headline: Area businesses turn to vo-tech for trained help
abstract: David Carver, president of the York County Industrial Development Corp. and the new chairman of York County Area Vo-Tech's general advisory committee, said that due to low unemployment vo-tech is a great educational resource.  With 34 percent of the county's workforce in industry but only five percent of this year's graduating class having studied welding or metal machinery, vot-tech fills an important economic niche.

headline: Commissioners Conference
abstract: The PA State Associaton of County Commissioners opens its two- day spring conference in Harrisburg today.  Financial matters, such as budgets and agricultural issues, are on today's agenda.

headline: Shaffer helped ethics
abstract: The writer applauds state Sen. Tim Shaffer for helping push the new ethics law through the legislature and making it substantial instead of including a myriad of loopholes.

headline: Taxpayers have say in reform
abstract: A staff researcher with the PA Economy League, a non-partisan state and local government interest group, spoke with business representatives about a new personal income tax that could be utilized by school boards and municipal governments.  If a statewides referendum approves the tax in the upcoming primary election, the new law could broaden the tax base by an estimated 20 percent.

headline: Montoursville firm to lay off 72 employees
abstract: Schnadig Corp. will lay off 25 percent of its workforce, or 72 union and non-union workers, due to a lack of business and a shifting of business priorities.

headline: Game Commission Studies Ideas For Bear Licenses
abstract: The PA Game Commission has a new recommendation under advisement concerning bear licenses.  The new proposal would eliminate annual license deadlines and would allow hunters to buy licenses anytime after the season begins in June.  The Commission has also suspended a five year study of alternatives to the county deer management system.

headline: McCall seeks aid in push for new I-80 interchange
abstract: PA Representative Keith R. McCall encouraged all parties interested in an interchange on Interstate Route 80 that was not included in the PA Transportation System's Twelve-Year Plan to push for the project to be included in the upcoming biennial update. McCall's suggestion was read at a meeting of the Carbon County Planning Commission, which also welcomed Jack Miller, who replaced Albert Castagnola on the board after Castagnola was sent to federal prison on drug charges. Secretary of Transportation Howard Yerusalim stated that testimony was presented to his department.

headline: Kill drug traffickers
abstract: The writer supportsa plan to authorize increased covert action against drug kingpins abroad, including possible assassinations, which will come to President Bush for his signature soon.  If several leaders of a drug cartel were eliminated at once, it would disrupt operations for a long period of time.

headline: Area counties included in Pa. drought watch
abstract: The Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency, or PEMA, declared a drought warning which included the counties of Carbon, Lehigh, Monroe, and Northampton.  Eastern Pennsylvanians are encouraged to cut water consumption by 10 percent.

headline: Common Pleas reform judges winning terms
abstract: A slate of judges appointed by Gov. Casey are now up for election, and only received campaign money from what the Philadelphia Bar Association could raise.  This reformed practice was used to avoid receiving money from lawyers who could eventually come before the judges in court.

headline: Singel glows; you pay
abstract: The editorial accuses Lt. Gov. Singel of excessive self-promotion in his 20-page "Office of the Lieutenant Governor Annual Report" which features updates on his actions throughout the past year, including 15 pictures of Singel himself.  Singel sends the brochures to those who have helped him or could help in the future.

headline: The big decision on tax reform
abstract: It is important that people who go to the polls on May 16 understand the issue of tax reform and what it is the bill actually seeks to do.  Although the bill could cut real-estate taxes by as much as 25 percent, it also allows for municipalities and school boards to institute sales and personal income taxes.  In this way, the so-called tax reform is neither an across the board tax cut, nor tax simplification.

headline: New Rockwell plant owners eliminate 40 positions
abstract: The former Rockwell International Plant in Uniontown has eliminated 40 jobs though layoffs and normal attrition, about a month after becoming part of BTR Dunlop Inc.

headline: Game Commission, Trout Chapter OK Guard's Move to Mid- State
abstract: The PA Game Commission and the Woodduck Chapter of Trout Unlimited are among the groups to approve the proposed relocation of U.S. Army National Guard Company G to the Mid- State Airport at Philipsburg.

headline: Meeting pleases bypass backers
abstract: Lebanon County commissioners and members from the local Chamber of Commerce met with state Transportation Secretary Howard Yerusalim regarding the building of the Route 72 bypass.

headline: Jails sell
abstract: A new prison-building method of pre-molding cells such that they can be lifted by a crane and placed in their spot is giving a boost in business to a once-small concrete firm, and provides a fast way for jails to increase their capacitancy.

headline: Artist begins facelift on Towanda fence
abstract: Local artist Bonnie Bell Baker began painting a mural yesterday on a fence that surrounds Towanda Iron and Metal.  She intends to depict the Susquehana River and its surrounding towns from the 1600s to today.

headline: Commonwealth Court Hopefuls Say Experience Counts
abstract: Four Democrats and one Republican seeking nominations to a Commonwealth Court seat claim that experience is their best qualifier.

headline: Six towns down on label of population losers
abstract: The United States Census Bureau has estimated population changes between 1980 and 1988 in 36,000 communities across the nation. Six Philadelphia suburbs have lost more than 10 percent of the populations by 1988. The Census Bureau used birth and death certificates and federal income tax returns instead of a head count, said Donald Starsinic, chief of the population-estimates branch of the population division of the Census Bureau.

headline: The public's opinion:
abstract: The Wyalusing Area School Board proposed the building of a new administrative building because of poor storage and working conditions.  The article explains the opinions of a few choice taxpayers that will be affected by the project.  Residents are concerned with higher taxes but some are willing to let their taxes be used to improve the administration's working conditions.

headline: No- strike pact a good start
abstract: The no- strike agreement between Allegheny County and local labor unions insures that work at Greater Pittsburgh International Airport will proceed with little or no labor troubles.

headline: Glass recycling increases in state
abstract: The PA Glass Recycling Corp. reported that glass recycling in 1988 was up 12.9% from 1987.  Mandatory recycling programs will be in effect for many municipalities starting in 1990.

headline: Mid-State Airport Authority Receives Visit from DROP
abstract: The Airport Authority received a visit from members of the environmental group Don't Ruin Out Park, who are opposed to the relocation of an Army National Guard to the Mid-State Airport.  Other news concerning the Airport Authority is included in the piece.

headline: Judge Dalessandro indicted
abstract: The U.S. Third Circuit Court in Phila. has been asked to appoint a special judge from outside PA to preside at the trial of Arthur D. Dalessandro, a Luzerne County jurist indicted on income tax fraud.

headline: Auto makers would ante up under "lemon-aid"
abstract: State Sen. Stewart J. Greenleaf recommends revising the current lemon law in order to crack down on the ability of auto manufacturers to resell lemons without consumers being made aware of the car's history.  Greenleaf's Senate Bill 528 would expand the law and provide greater protection for consumers.  In addition, a consumer not happy with a settlement under a manufacturer's arbitration process could use the state arbitration process instead of undertaking further expensive legal action.

headline: Company relies on computer to invest
abstract: Intelligent Investment Management, the money management subsidiary of Intelligent Technology Group that uses a computer program to pick stocks, experienced the sixth-best investment performance among management funds over the past year. The information was released by Pensions and Investment Age, which also rated Intelligent Investment's five-year returns as the highest among money management companies surveyed. Intelligence Investment uses a sophisticated artificial intelligence system to choose the stock portfolio based on historical trends.

headline: Small Games of Chance Receive Heavy Support
abstract: A short review of the voting results from the ballot questions on May 16th's election.  Focuses mainly on the passing of the small games of chance question.

headline: The tax plan made its mark in the state's history
abstract: The tax reform proposal was defeated by over a million votes, making it the worst rejection of a proposed PA constitutional amendment in history.

headline: OSHA sets new standards for hazardous materials
abstract: Yesterday the Reagan administration overhaled the Occupational Safety and Health Act, issuing new exposure standards for almost 400 hazardous materials.  The regulations go into effect March 1, and were greeted with care by both manufacturing and worker safety groups.

headline: Group seeks ban on other states' waste
abstract: A solid waste task force is searching for a way to prohibit or regulate out-of-state trash from being brought into local landfills, among other initiatives.

headline: Milroy bypass will soon become reality
abstract: PennDOT has moved a Route 322 bypass of Milroy into its high-priority four-year section of its 12-year plan, pleasing local residents who are waiting for a bypass to ease traffic volume.

headline: Judge fines Phila. over failure to finish prison security measures
abstract: A federal judge fined Philadelphia for failure to complete a perimeter fence at Laurel Hall medium security prison.  The prison faces over- crowding and asks to restrict bench- warrant jailings.

headline: Auto plan readied by Casey
abstract: Details about Gov. Casey's auto insurance proposal will soon be released.  The plan hinges on the consumer's choice of lower rates but restricted rights to sue, or higher rates and more rights to sue.

headline: Congress reforms family aid program and forgives $92 owed by Pa.
abstract: The US Congress forgave a $92 million debt owed by the state of Pennsylvania, a debt which Jerry Friedman, deputy secretary for income maintenance at the PA Department of Public Welfare, says would have been disastrous for the state if it were forced to pay up. The debt was owed under the federal Aid to Families with Dependent Children program, but amnesty was given to states in a budget bill passed by Congress. Under the program, states are given federal funding for the AFDC program, but are also monitored for overpayments. Alicia Pelrine of the National Governors Association criticized the system.

headline: Some May Consider Work Boring, But Hudock Wants Superior Court Job
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Joseph A. Hudock says that despite voters' apparent disinterest in the Superior Court race and the perception that the judges' work is boring, he wants the job.

headline: The tax reduction can be increase in disguise
abstract: A citizen writes that Gov. Casey's recent visit to Bucks County was made to push his state tax reform package, which she sees as an increase in disguise.

headline: OSHA: USX plant decaying
abstract: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration has cited USX Corporation on numerous counts of unsafe working conditions in several of its facilities, including the Clairton Works near Pittsburgh and the Fairless Works near Philadelphia. The US Department of Labor has stated that the company cut back on maintenance and repairs that were necessary for worker safety. The National Wildlife Federation cited USX as being one of the country's biggest toxic polluters, while George Cafasso, chairman of the United Steelworkers' safety and health committee stated that "the company kept stalling."

headline: Gypsy Moth Spray May Begin Friday
abstract: Spraying for gypsy moths will begin on Friday in Crawford and Venango counties, barring bad weather conditions or some other preventative situation.

headline: Montgomery circles town center
abstract: Montgomery Township is considering heavily developing four tracks of land, but would need to depend on PennDOT to improve the roads in order to handle increased traffic density.

headline: Judge fines state over Western Pen conditions
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Corrections has until January 1 to pay a $1,000 fine after Chief US District Court Judge Maurice B. Cohill Jr. ruled the department had ignored his order to hire an environmentalist to improve conditions at Western Penitentiary. Cohill ruled in August that conditions at the prison were unconstitutional and had given the department until December 1 to submit proposals on the issue. On November 28 prison officials requested a time extension because of a number of setbacks and have been given until March 15 to submit plans and hire the environmentalist. Kenneth Robinson, press secretary for the Department of Corrections, issued a statement that thanked Cohill for the extension and reinforced the commitment the department has made to improve Western Penitentiary.

headline: Bankruptcy judge denies trustee for AI
abstract: US Bankruptcy Judge Joseph Cosetti has denied a motion to appoint a trustee to oversee Allegheny International Inc., a company that makes small appliances. Allegheny International Inc. filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in February 1988.

headline: Coroner requests dismissal of residency challenge
abstract: Former Attorney General LeRoy  S. Zimmerman filed an action last month against Dauphin County Coroner Dr. William Bush, alleging that he did not fit the residency requirements necessary to hold office.  Dr. Bush subsequently filed a preliminary objection stating the attorney general's complaint was comprised of "scandalous and impertinent matter."

headline: Source: FBI asked Gray about Phila. accountant
abstract: The FBI has questioned state Rep. William Gray III about the Philadelphia accountant Neil Godick of Godick & Co., who is under investigation of embezzlement.  Sources say that Gray is not under investigation, and is simply giving the FBI his cooperation.

headline: Well! Whaddaya know? State budget talks stall
abstract: With stories in the past few days of optimistic outlooks on the prospect of passing a state budget by the deadline, people must have been expecting some sort of roadblock, as no budget proposal goes without a hitch.  Right on cue, Gov. Casey requested more spending on anti-drug efforts.

headline: P&LE workers lose Supreme Court case
abstract: Railroad workers unions took a blow yesterday when the US Supreme Court ruled for Pittsburgh & Lake Erie Railroad, saying that it was not obligated to bargain with its union workers over the impact of a proposed sale of its track and equipment.

headline: Handling of trash is changing throughout Bucks
abstract: If all goes as according to plan, 21 of the 54 Bucks Count townships and boroughs will have working trash disposal plans for the next 5 to 10 years.  Many are also now implementing centralized curbside recycling programs, whereby the state will pay for 90 percent of the cost.

headline: Montgomery cool to transit tax
abstract: Montgomery County commissioners stated that a mass transit tax currently being considered by the state Legislature to aid the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority should not be restricted to regional taxpayers. Montgomery County commissioners' chairman Paul B. Bartle stated that the burden should be shared by the entire state, since southeastern PA is the "economic engine for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania." He stated that areas without mass transit could use the tax money in other ways, perhaps to develop a paratransit system.

headline: Judges foster change
abstract: 11 Philadelphia Common Pleas Court judges are working to try to improve the Philadelphia courts system, which is sufferring from massive caseloads and long backlogs.

headline: bc-cashdollar
abstract: Paul Cashdollar ageed to pay $1,000 in restitution, penalties, and costs in a settlement with the attorney general's Bureau of Consumer Protection.  Cashdollar was alleged to, among other violations, have run a financial loan business without properly registering with the Pennsylvania Dept. of State.

headline: Council proposes pay-boost package
abstract: City Council has introduced an overall pay raise package of 5.5 percent for 81 management-level employees for the 1989 year.  The total pay package will cost $2.07 million with a formal vote expected on Monday.

headline: South Butler Mediator Awaits Official Notice
abstract: Joseph Kadilak, a former state mediator appointed to help settle the teacher contract negotiations in the South Butler County School District, said he has not received the court order from the judge.

headline: Will loss of tax plan affect Casey's future?
abstract: GOP Chairman of the Republican State Committee says that the defeat of Casey's tax reform plan exposes the weakness of his administration, while others say that this defeat will ultimately benefit the Governor.

headline: pa-foodstrike
abstract: Amid contract talks, 30 cafeteria workers in the Blairsville-Saltsburg School District went on strike today.  The workers are employed by Nutrition Incorporated.

headline: Hauling food -- and garbage too
abstract: The piece expresses concern over the fact that growing numbers of trucks are transporting waste and food in consecutive trips, establishing a potential for food contamination.

headline: More people buckling up, federal agency reports
abstract: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports that 47 percent of people in the United States are buckling their seatbelts, Pittsburgh, Pa is at 43.9 percent.  The increase could be due to the prevalence of new automatic belts, yet seatbelts are saving an increasing number of lives.  The Harrisburg International Airport has also been given a $750,000 grant for improvement.

headline: Judicial-commission chair replies
abstract: The chairwoman of the Governor's Judicial Reform Commission responds to an article by a former Common Pleas Court Judge which made some incorrect claims about the commission.

headline: Blacks disadvantaged in steel crisis aftermath
abstract: Workers of all races were laid off during the steel industry's collapse, but a historian says that in the aftermath, Blacks are finding it much harder to find new jobs.  He blames the racial segregation between 1900 and 1960 in steel companies.

headline: Council rejects bill on ethics
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Council rejected an ethics proposal by Councilman Mark H. Pollock that would have instituted a new code of conduct for elected officials and city employees. The Council defeated the legislation after receiving a legal opinion from city Solicitor Dan Pellegrini who called some sections of the bill "unworkable" or "illegal". Pollock said he would attempt to write new ethics legislation, but he remains in office for only three weeks so is pressed for time.

headline: State archives to be closed
abstract: The PA State Archives in Harrisburg will be closed to the public for over 5 months for renovations including repairs, asbestos removal, and waterproofing.  Emergency access will still be possible for certain types of documents and situations.

headline: Wilmington Democrat Offers Alternate Tax Cut Proposal
abstract: Senate Majority Whip Robert Marshall has introduced a measure to give all Delaware residents a $64 tax cut while exempting a greater number of poor residents from taxes than would benefit under Gov. Michael N. Castle's tax cut proposal.

headline: Painting a grim picture of danger at Fairless Works
abstract: Earl B. Rhinehold, who had his leg severed while working at the Fairless Works plant of USX Corporation, is one of the many cases being cited by the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration for poor worker treatment. USX has been cited and fined for its refusal to improve its unsafe working conditions, and is currently being sued by Fairless's union local for the presence of asbestos. The lawsuit is being handled in Bucks County Court.

headline: Hazardous waste disposal funded
abstract: Montgomery County Commissioners agreed to a household waste survey in 20 municipalities and is to be done by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources.  Household wastes include paint thinner, oil cleaners, paint, and cleaning agents.

headline: New Ellwood bridge possible in two years
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has announced that it recommends a replacement for an Ellwood City bridge to be constructed by 1992. Joel Bowman, PennDOT assistant design liaison engineer, said the proposal is to move the southern end of the bridge 32 feet east. The announcement was made at a public meeting in Ellwood City. The final recommendation from PennDOT has not yet been made as feedback is still being taken about the plan.

headline: Juniata County Courthouse firming work almost done
abstract: Geo-Con of Monroeville said it expects to complete firming up the Juniata County Courthouse foundation and basement floor within the next few days. A Geo-Con official made this announcement at a job conference involving the Juniata County commissioners. The commissioners also addressed a problem with the basement sewer line, now agreed to be worked on by Manbeck Construction Co. The improvement projects are being funded by a $1.5 million bond, although the commissioners are unsure if the repairs will end up saving them money.

headline: Boro takes chance with new legislation
abstract: The Montgomery Board of Commissioners approved a resolution which will place a referendum concerning small games of chance on the May 16 ballot.  If the referendum is approved by voters, non-profit groups which own property within the borough would be eligible to run such games as punch boards, beans-in-a-jar, and lotteries.

headline: Council to vote on Pollock ethics bill
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council will hold a vote on an ethics bill proposed by City Councilman Mark H. Pollock. City Councilman Jack Wagner, the only dissenter among the 4 councilmen president, argued against the bill, saying that ethics is already governed by state legislation. Pollock believes that city council should "lead the way on ethics," and cited the conviction of former Acting Council President Ben Woods on charges of racketeering and extortion.

headline: State bureaucrat paid to push tax reform
abstract: In a letter to the editor, a citizen protests against a recent letter on tax reform written by Ed Geiger, saying that Mr. Geiger is a bureaucrat in the Casey Administration being paid to endorse the bill.

headline: You'll Be Asked a Very Taxing Question on Tuesday
abstract: Points out many of the intricacies of the tax reform proposal that supporters and opponents glaze over concerning their side of the debate.

headline: Palmerton's ZCA plant hit with $2 million fine: OSHA says employees exposed to hazardous concentrations of lead
abstract: The Zinc Corporatiton of America was fined close to $2 million for exposing employees to dangerous amounts of lead.  This was the highest fine given out in the state by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

headline: Help to state in plan viewed as 'inadequate'
abstract: Environmental groups are complaining that Pres. Bush's new clean-air proposal will reduce PA's acid rain too slowly, causing continued damage to streams and forests.  The plan calls for a 50% reduction of sulfur-dioxide emissions nationally by the year 2000, but also considers some past reductions as part of that 50%.

headline: New times for SEPTA
abstract: SEPTA schedules are changing for the summer for all routes of the SEPTA City and Suburban Transit Divisions.

headline: Jurors were split from the start
abstract: There was a split in the jury when they could not reach a unanimous decision in the Five Squad police corruption case. Senior U.S. District Judge John Hannum declared a mistrial. There was concern about defendants speaking with some of the jurors and the 3-month long trial coverage in the media may have affected juror decisions.

headline: British firm named likely Harsco suitor
abstract: A British-American holding company, Hanson PLC, is likely to take over Harsco Corporation, which is based in Camp Hill. Karen Levy, Hanson's director of investor relations would not comment on the takeover speculation, while Donald A. Patterson of C.J. Lawrence, Morgan Greenfell Incorporated called the takeover "informed speculation."

headline: County- executive hopefuls tangle at Dem Q&A session
abstract: After a string of somewhat cordial candidates nights, the three Democrats running for Northampton County executive, Jim Mazza, Ladd Siftar Jr., and Gerald Seyfried, mixed it up at a Dem. Q&A session.

headline: State contests include mayor races aplenty
abstract: Philadelphia's upcoming elections pit Republican incumbent Ronald Castille against Democrat Walter Phillips Jr. in the race for District Attorney, while there is a three-way contest for city controller between Consumer Party candidate Bessie Weiner (who replaced her husband Max Weiner after his sudden death), Democrat Jonathan Saidel, and Republican State Senator M. Joseph Rocks. Pittsburgh's mayor Sophie Masloff is running unopposed, while Lancaster's mayoral election pits Republican Mary Lou Brought against Democrat Janice Stork.

headline: null
abstract: A rally at Princeton was held by the New Jersey chapter of the American Association of ex-Prisoners of War against flag-burning. Members of the association honored a Princeton student who stopped a flag-burning just as it began, and also said they "wanted to show students what Old Glory meant to them and other POWs."

headline: Pennsylvania-financial news in brief
abstract: City workers in Erie, members of Teamsters Local 397, will be given a contract proposal expected to raise their salaries to levels comparable with Erie police and fire departments. Super Fresh grocery workers of Local 1776 United Food and Commercial Workers are on strike on Philadelphia. The Pittsburgh Symphony Society will use the orchestra's endowment fund to retire a $3 million operating deficit. The PA Department of Environmental Resources will meet with a firm from Massachusetts to develop PA's first licensed hazardous waste landfill.

headline: Holl sponsors bill to ban cancer- causing chemicals
abstract: Contaminated water supplies have become such a widespread problem, state Sen. Edwin Holl, R- 24th, is sponsoring a bill to ban many cancer- related chemicals.

headline: NO TIME TO BACK OFF
abstract: Philadelphia police officers should abide by a recent law in Pennsylvania which allows police to confiscate a driver's license plate who is operating a vehicle illegally.  This will curb the violent accidents and fatalities which continue to occur on the city's streets.

headline: Jury won't be quizzed on contacts
abstract: In the federal racketeering trial of the Five Squad, an elite group designed to fight drug trafficking in Philadelphia, a federal judge refused a request by the prosecution that jurors be questioned about their contacts with defendants in the case.  Closing arguments were held yesterday.

headline: Casey, lawmakers lock horns on auto insurance reforms
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey and state lawmakers are locked in a feud surrounding auto insurance reform that will prevent Pennsylvania motorists from getting relief from rising insurance bills. The PA Senate defeated Casey's plan on a complicated procedural move that results in approval of the proposal drafted by PA Senator Joseph Loeper and PA Representative Robert W. O'Donnell. Loeper said his bill would guarantee an immediate 10 percent cut in premiums for all motorists and freeze rates at reduced levels through the end of May 1991. Casey called this plan a "cruel hoax" that will keep insurance companies from instituting the rate rollbacks. Casey says his proposal, on the other hand, would reduce by 21 to 40 percent the premiums of motorists who agree not to sue over accident injuries except in cases of severe injuries, disfigurement or death.

headline: County nears end of 9-year salary rift
abstract: Settling a 9-year arbitration dispute, Allegheny County has agreed to pay increases of between $400 and $4,000 for court-related employees represented by the Allegheny Court Association of Professional Employees.

headline: State delays on 2 Vartan leases
abstract: The state has delayed approval for two leases for buildings owned by Harrisburg developer John Vartan.  Treasurer Catherine Knoll says that the delay is needed because they were unfamiliar with the details of the settlement of a lawsuit between Vartan and the Casey administration.

headline: null
abstract: The PA Senate voted in favor of a new bill restricting abortions, requiring women to notify their husbands if they plan to get an abortion and banning abortions after the 24th week of pregnancy. States near PA might see similar legislation. Linda Bowker of the New Jersey Chapter of the National Organization for Women criticized the law, while John Tomicki of the New Jersey chapter of the Right-to-Life Organization says his group will push for similar legislation in New Jersey.

headline: Pennsylvania-financial news in brief
abstract: City workers in Erie, members of Teamsters Local 397, will be given a contract proposal expected to raise their salaries to levels comparable with Erie police and fire departments. Super Fresh grocery workers of Local 1776 United Food and Commercial Workers are on strike on Philadelphia. The Pittsburgh Symphony Society will use the orchestra's endowment fund to retire a $3 million operating deficit. The PA Department of Environmental Resources will meet with a firm from Massachusetts to develop PA's first licensed hazardous waste landfill.

headline: Hot stuff
abstract: A federal law decrees that states must provide a dump for low-level nuclear waste, such as uranium, thorium, cesium, protective clothing used by workers, and any other contaminated equipment. States can either form compacts with other states in which one state hosts all the other states in the compact's nuclear waste, or create dumps for their own waste. PA is slated to host the Appalachian compact.

headline: no title
abstract: The Transport Workers Union is making progress concerning their contract with the Philadelphia transit authority.  There are 5,600 possible members planning to strike unless a new contract can be reached.  Roger Tauss met with a SEPTA manager and made progress, however no agreement was reached.

headline: Justice Stout's status
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court must decide whether Supreme Court Justice Juanita Kidd Stout should continue to serve after surpassing the mandatory retirement age.

headline: Business in brief: committee supports bill for citizens' council
