abstract: The PA House Insurance Committee approved a bill that would allow a citizens' council to represent consumers in insurance matters and to advise and oversee the state Insurance Department. Representative Stephen Freind stated that the bill would only set up more bureaucracy.

headline: County workers begin to get the bad news
abstract: Chief County Clerk/Administrator Eugene Klein of Luzerne County informed 24 employees that under the proposed budget for the upcoming year, they will be dismissed as of January 1, 1990. Maria Romanelli and Colleen Swartwood, two per-diem employees in the recorder of deeds office, were both informed that they were to be dismissed, although they said that Klein offered to write letters of recommendation for each dismissed employee. A total of 101 county employees will be laid off if the proposed 1990 county budget passes as it currently stands.

headline: State GOP backs Hafer
abstract: The Republican State Committee yesterday endorsed PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer as its gubernatorial candidate for the 1990 elections. PA Senator John Peterson, who had been slated to nominate Lancaster businessman James Pickard for candidacy, said Pickard withdrew from the race very near the time of the committee voting because he did not want to be the cause of a "fight over endorsement." A committee roll call vote on delaying the endorsement until February met with heavy opposition, as a majority of members supported Hafer.

headline: null
abstract: The US Supreme Court rejected a challenge by 650 women to a $2.5 billion lawsuit against A.H. Robins Company, maker of the Dalkon Shield birth control device. The women are thought to share in a trust fund set up by A.H. Robins Co. after lawsuits in 1985 led the company to reorganize in 1985 under federal bankruptcy law. Women involved in the lawsuit against the company contend that the trust fund settlement bars future lawsuits against the company.

headline: Philadelphia Gets Federal Grant to Train Youths for Jobs
abstract: Philadelphia is among the 12 cities to receive grants from the US Dept. of Labor for development of job-training programs for poor youths.  The grants, totalling $1.05 million must be used in poor areas, and if they are successful, the cities may be eligible for further grants.

headline: House Panel Approves Landfill Prohibition
abstract: The House Conservation Committee on Tuesday approved a bill which would restrict the number of landfills in the state.  They are now sending it to the House floor for consideration.

headline: Official: New airport no threat to Martinsburg
abstract: Altoona Intown Airport Manager Robert Russell said that new plans for the airrport would not put it in competition with the Altoona-Blair County Airport in Martinsburg.  Renovations to the Altoona Intown Airport include lengthening the runway and constructing hangers, as well as implementing charter and private flights.

headline: Killer Ted Bundy executed
abstract: Theodore Robert Bundy was executed via the electric chair in Florida State Prison yesterday.  He was suspected of killing at least 20 women in Florida, Colorado, Idaho, Utah, and Washington.  Bundy was the 20th man to be put to death in FL, and the 106th in the U.S., since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976

headline: Business News From Pennsylvania
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Council has approved a tax-swap plan to cut Pittsburgh's wage tax and increase land taxes, which city officials say is needed to keep younger wage earners from moving to the suburbs. The US Air Force and the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh have renewed their $165 million five-year contract that will fund research and development in computer software technology for the Defense Department. Allied Services in Scranton is opening a treatment facility to specialize in computer-controlled exercise programs for victims of paralysis. AT&T  Bell Laboratories in Lehigh Counties said it has developed a new integrated circuit that is the highest information processing chip of its kind. CIGNA Corporation of Philadelphia has signed a five-year contract with AT&T to provide communications services to more than 900 CIGNA company locations worldwide.

headline: Court says Hafer may not sit on state leasing board
abstract: The PA Commonwealth Court ruled that Auditor General Barbara Hafer may not be a member of the Board of Commissioners of Public Grounds and Buildings. PA Attorney General Ernie Preate delivered the opinion at the request of PA General Services secretary David Jannetta. Hafer stated that she wants a higher court to resolve the matter.

headline: State officials lobby for positions on board to oversee Phila. ports
abstract: Auditor General Barbara Hafer and Treasurer Catherine Knoll are attempting to have themselves put on the new board in the planned takeover of Philadelphia's ports.  A bill allowing the state to assume control of the Philadelphia port system as the city finances for it dwindle has already been agreed upon by the legislature.

headline: 300,000 march in capital
abstract: A crowd of at least 300,000 people marched on the Capitol in Washington D.C. to show their support for abortion rights and the Equal Rights Amendment.

headline: Philipsburg Job Center To Present Open House
abstract: Open house ceremonies will be held at the new Philipsburg Job Center at the Philipsburg Job Service Office on Jan. 23, and will attended by state Secretary of Labor and Indiustry Harris Wofford and Executive Deputy Secretary of Labor and Industry Tom Foley.  The Job Center is one of the first in the state as part of Gov. Casey's goal to organize a centralized location for job services in communities across the state.

headline: House Panel Chairman Says Acid Rain Bill Would Unfairly Burden Nine States
abstract: A House panel chairman says proposed legislation to cut sulfur dioxide emissions would place an unfair burden on nine states.

headline: One more drill before I-78 opens
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has announced that Interstate Route 78 will soon be completed. However, the editorial board recommends that one more safety drill be conducted before the route is to be opened. A.J. Heightman, executive director of the Eastern PA Emergency Medical Service agrees that one more safety drill is in order.

headline: Killing of suspect new drug horror
abstract: Douglas Nelson Plautz was high on cocaine and heroin when he took a hostage at knifepoint in the Muhlenberg Shopping Plaza. Laureldale Sargeant David L. Reichlein was force to make a decision, and killed Plautz. Heather Cunningham, Plautz's mother, said that she was sorry her son was gone but realized that the officer was only doing his job.

headline: BYOB under fire
abstract: This editorial addresses a new initiative within the Pennsylvania Senate to outlaw the practice of allowing diners to bring their own bottles of alcohol to a restaurant that does not hold a liquor license. The editorial board believes this issue is miniscule compared to the other issues, such as funding public transportation and lowering auto insurance rates, on which the Legislature has failed to pass bills. The board also questions the motive for this bill, accusing the Senate of catering to tavern owners and licensed hotels and restaurants whose trade associations back the bill.

headline: Courtesy Call
abstract: Iceland's President Vigdis Finnbogadottir visited Gov. Casey and was given a book about PA.

headline: State pension fund plan draws fire
abstract: PA State Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll proposed that the state uses its $25 billion public pension fund to encourage the economy and bring young people to Pennsylvania. Knoll wants fund managers to invest millions of dollars in local real estate, state highways and bridges, and new businesses. Many pension managers, consultants, and pensioners, including Richard C. Rowland, executive director of the Pennsylvania Association of School Retirees, oppose the plan because of the risks involved with investing pension money.

headline: Abortion bill is victory for neither side
abstract: The editorial board believes neither pro-life nor pro-choice camps can claim victory with the passing of an anti-abortion bill in the PA State House of Representatives sponsored by Representative Stephen Freind. The bill, the board states, neither eliminates abortions nor severely restricts a woman from obtaining one. The bill must pass before the Senate before it can be submitted to PA Governor Robert Casey.

headline: Pickets Mass, Judge Reacts
abstract: UMW picketers have continued their protests, and stood outside a non-union mine in an attempt to get workers to join the union and to gain support for their ongoing walkouts.  A Washington County judge ordered that no more than 8 pickets be at the mine at a time, though there were 30-50 there in the afternoon.

headline: In the region
abstract: First, Mifflin and Juniata counties are slated for an extensive dog license check beginning today.  Second, the state has agreed to pay most of the costs for a solid waste plan for Juniata County.

headline: Overloaded Trucks
abstract: Part of a garbage truck's load was ripped off while going under an underpass.  It was assumed that the truck was illegally overweight and trying to avoid a weight check on I-79.  This could become an issue of public safety and a legal matter.

headline: Law officers pay last respects to trooper
abstract: Law officers gathered to pay respects to PA State Police Trooper, Wayne D. Bilheimer, who perished Wed. when the helicopter he was passenger in struck a power line in Lower Chanceford Twnshp.

headline: Casey makes pitch for insurance plan
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey appealed to the PA Senate to reconsider a car insurance reform plan that would, most controversially, give drivers the option to forgo their right to sue in all except severe accidents for commensurate cuts in premiums. Six months earlier the Senate rejected the proposal, while the House passed the plan earlier this year. Opposing senators, such as PA Senator Roy Afflerbach, believe the bill is a short-term financial fix that would take away people's rights to access the court system. PA Senator Robert Mellow said he predicted Casey would receive more votes than he received in the previous vote, but did not predict passage of the bill.

headline: Courts union rejects offer from county
abstract: Units of the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees union voted last week to reject a final contract offer from the county.  The group represents approximately 300 court and court-related employees.

headline: State Revenue Chief Quits Post, Cites Stress
abstract: State Revenue Secretary Barton A. Fields resigned from the Casey administration citing stress and the "rigorous schedule" of the job.  Although Fields was part of a number of controversies and failings within the Renue Dept., the governor's office said that none of these issues factored into Fields' decision to leave.

headline: Abortion camps look to 1990 elections
abstract: Members of pro-choice camps are rallying to oust lawmakers and PA Governor Robert Casey in the upcoming 1990 elections for their pro-life stances, evidenced by the successful passing of a bill restricting abortions in PA. Frances Sheehan of Pennsylvanians for Justice and Freedom of Choice is forming a political action committee with other pro-choice groups. Barbara Hafer, the state Auditor General and a pro-choice Republican, is slated to win the Republican nomination for gubernatorial candidate.

headline: Prices Were Up And So Were Wages
abstract: The price index and Philadelphia area urban workers wage index have both increased about the same amount since 1982-84 according to a recent announcement by the US Dept. of Labor.

headline: In-state disposal unit urged
abstract: Experts hired by the PA Department of Environmental Resources have resolved to blow up a wastewater storage pond thought to contain nitroglycerine in McKean County. Business in PA produced more than 700,000 tons of hazardous waste per year, yet PA has no commercial hazardous waste disposal facilities. The US Congress has twice enacted a "Superfund" to help clean up toxic waste.

headline: Paxtang and Dauphin? No comparison!
abstract: A citizen writes to say that Dauphin County is very different from Paxtang, with respect to the need for highway improvements.

headline: Lawsuit possible over bill for stadium
abstract: Lackawanna County officials are considering filing a lawsuit against GSGSB, the Clark's Summit architectural firm that designed Lackawanna County Stadium. The suit would attempt to recover damages caused by the firm's delay in construction estimates, which were nearly 100 percent higher than the budget. Lackawanna County Commissioners Joseph Corcoran and Ray Alberigi, as well as county solicitor Joseph O'Brien, said filing the lawsuit is a possibility but not confirmed as the county wants to make sure it is doing the right thing.

headline: Casey needs a win in auto insurance race
abstract: The writer claims that Gov. Casey needs a political win in the auto-insurance reforms to help his re-election bid next year after the sound defeat of his tax reform plan in May.  His insurance proposal has potential, though the leading House Democrat opposes one of the main facets of Casey's plan.

headline: Creative thinking wave of future
abstract: Thomas P. Foley, a special assistant on eastern PA to PA Governor Robert Casey, addressed the Greater Willow Grove Chamber of Commerce. Foley stated that employers will have to abandon traditional methods to accommodate workers' needs, such as day care, flexible time and flexible locations. He also spoke of the need to accommodate older workers, women, minorities, and non-native English speakers.

headline: State seeks change on disaster plans
abstract: The Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency (PEMA) mandated that counties make preparations to be able to respond to a range of emergencies, including nuclear attacks, oil spills, and hostage situations. The document updates a 1977 state disaster plan and is a result of more than 10 years of planning. PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, PEMA's council chairman, said that he and PA Governor Robert P. Casey directed that all state agencies review their emergency responsibilities also. York County's Emergency Management director, Robert Straw, said York is basically up-to-date with state guidelines.

headline: Abortion camps reflect new state legislation
abstract: The PA Senate and House of Representatives passed a bill to enact new limits on abortion, much to the dismay of some legislators and pro-choice advocacy groups. The bill makes Pennsylvania the most restricted state in the country in which to receive an abortion, with such stipulations as banning gender abortions; requiring a 24-hour waiting period between the time a doctor sees a patient and when the abortion is performed; requiring underage girls to obtain parental permission or judicial bypass if seeking an abortion; requiring a woman to notify her husband or give reasons for not doing so; among other stipulations. PA Representative Lois S. Hagarty voted against the bill because she did not believe it is in the best interest of the women of PA. PA Senator Richard A. Tilghman voted agreed, saying the bill is an "unwarranted interference by state government" into PA women's lives.

headline: R&P calls on UMWA to end strike
abstract: Rochester & Pittsburgh Coal Company officials are calling on leaders of the United Mine Workers union to put a stop to walkouts that they say are severely hurting local economies, many of which are already depressed and somewhat precarious.

headline: It's DER obligation to monitor landfill
abstract: The Editorial Board believes that it is the responsibility of the Department of Environmental Resources to monitor changes planned by the Tri- County Industries Inc.'s landfill.

headline: Pothole complaints were minimal this spring
abstract: The state Department of Transportation got fewer calls this year than last from motorists reporting potholes in the Philadelphia region.  This parallels a state-wide trend for the year.

headline: Lawyer, prosecutor vying for judgeship
abstract: Republican candidate Robert J. Shenkin faces Democratic candidate Jacqueline M. Carroll in the election to be a judge in the Chester County Court. Shenkin is a member of the American Bar Association, and has served on the boards of the Pennsylvania and Chester County Bar Associations, while Carroll is Chester County's Deputy District Attorney. The spot on the Chester County Court was vacated by Robert S. Gawthrop III who became a federal judge.

headline: Casey offers plan on auto insurance
abstract: Gov. Casey outlines his new auto insurance plan, designed to decrease insurance premiums and lawsuit quantities.

headline: Critics' choice: Masloff acts boldly,  but does she lead?
abstract: Review of Mayor Masloff's accomplishments and priorities after 8 months on the job, while discussing the possibility of her running for reelection.

headline: State still needs tax reform
abstract: PA voters rejected local tax reform, but should not be satisfied with the current system plagued by high real estate taxes and nuisance levies. The state Legislature is not likely to move for tax reform any time soon. The constitutional amendment was defeated in May's primary election.

headline: Abortion facilities picketed
abstract: More than 350 individuals were arrested in five states as anti-abortion protests were staged across the country.

headline: Retain the ban
abstract: The U.S. Department of Labor has proposed a repeal on the ban of manufacturing women's apparel in the home.  The editorial board believes such bans should remain to prevent worker exploitation.

headline: Judge Accepts No Contest Plea
abstract: Ashland Oil Inc. entered a no contest plea to two misdemeanor counts of violating the Clean Water Act and the Refuse Act.  A federal grand jury issued the indictments in response to the company's 713,000 gallon diesel fuel spill in January, 1988.  18 civil damage suits are still pendin in federal court.

headline: Pa. shorted in U.S. road fund formula
abstract: Pennsylvania gets short-changed under the formula the federal government uses to distribute highway funds, PennDOT Secretary Howard Yerusalem told lawmakers Thursday.

headline: League Urges Judicial Reform Action
abstract: A bipartisan group of lawmakers joined the League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania today in calling for a new system of judical discipline.

headline: Casey plan flawed
abstract: This letter to the editor discusses a supposed error in a December 10 editorial about PA Governor Robert P. Casey's auto insurance plan that stated that insurance companies do not want lower premiums. The author, President and Chief Executive Officer of the Insurance Federation of Pennsylvania, Henry G. Hager, states that affordable auto insurance and improved availability are goals of both insurers and PA residents. Hager says the federation will back a proposal that recognizes controlling claims costs as essential to breaking the rise in auto premiums, rather than support Casey's proposal because of its numerous flaws.

headline: Crowded ballot for the primary
abstract: With 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans registered to run for Mayor of Scranton, 10 Democrats and 6 Republicans registered to run for City Council, and 10 Democrats registered to run for Scranton School Board, the primary ballot promises to be crowded.  County races will further complicate the picture.

headline: State told of housing crunch here
abstract: Local officials met with Karen A. Miller, Secretary of the PA Department of Community Affairs, to discuss housing for low- and middle-income people. Miller stated that PA Governor Robert Casey made affordable housing the number one priority of her department, and suggested that locals write to their congressmen for federal funding. She also said that her department is not in agreement with the General Assembly on the content of some bills regarding housing legislation.

headline: Abortion foes broke anti-racketeering law, court in Philly rules
abstract: The U.S. Court of Appeals in Philadelphia ruled that 27 protestors violated the federal law known as RICO, or the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act.  The decision marked a significant victory for abortion-rights supporters and will likely spur more organizations that are the focus of protests to file charges under the act.

headline: Ruling extends jobless benefits
abstract: A state unemployment compensation referee made the workers of a now-closed Volkswagon assembly plant eligible once again for their benefits, but the decision will likely  be decided in a state or federal court.

headline: Legislature asked to outlaw use of plastic foam
abstract: The North Penn Area Regional Waste Management Comission called for the state legislature to look at banning the use of plastic foam, also known as styrofoam.  The commission faces pressure to increase its use of recylcing as it also looks at the idea of building a trash incinerator in Franconia Township.

headline: Pa. will build one of 17 wood 'test' bridges here
abstract: A wooden bridge is planned for Lancaster County as part of an effort build more cost and time-efficient bridges from PA materials.  Wood bridges are planned for several small spans, and cost considerably less than concrete or other materials, and also take less time to build.

headline: Left off at the border, courtesy of Bucks police
abstract: A police officer from Lower Southampton Township in Bucks County dropped a mentally-ill woman at a bus stop in Philadelphia's Northeast section. Police Chief Edward Donnelly said that his officer was simply helping the women get back to her home in Philadelphia. However, Jeanne Smith, an observer stated that the officer did not do enough to help the woman, and that incidents like this frequently occur with police departments from other townships in Bucks County.

headline: CAT Fund alternative passes, goes to Casey
abstract: The Legislature yesterday approved a compromise bill that would require private insurers to make  catastrophic- medical insurance available to the owners of 7.5 million automobiles licensed in the state.

headline: Cuomo Considering Drug Testing For Top State Workers
abstract: ALBANY, N.Y. - The Cuomo administration is considering the possibility of drug testing for the governor and other top state government bureaucrats.

headline: State treasurer off to bad start
abstract: State-Treasurer-elect Katherine Baker Knoll is planning a $1,000-a-head plate dinner before her inauguration, one which features bankers and brokers and has the appearances of a conflict of interest.

headline: Abortion rights backers say they'll renew fight next year
abstract: Members of Congress who support expanded abortion rights, such as Representative Les AuCoin of Oregon, are conceding defeat this year, but claim that their fight for abortion rights will be aided by political pressure building up as a result of President Bush's veto of a bill with liberal policies towards abortion. Last summer the US Supreme Court gave states more power to regulate abortions. The Senate also voted for a provision in a foreign aid spending bill to send $15 million to the United Nations Population Fund.

headline: Slippery Rock workers want to unionize
abstract: The 12 employees of Slippery Rock Borough have asked the state Labor Relations board to form a union. The decision was unanimous, and was spurred on by the fact that Slippery Rock Council's 1990 budget did not include wage increases. Paul Dickey, superintendent of the water department, said that communications with the council have been problematic in recent times.

headline: Janesville Dam Restoration High Priority, DER Reports
abstract: The DER has reported that the restoration of the Janesville Dam, which was polluted by a local coal company, is high on its list of priorities.  The coal company is currently required to pursue the clean-up, though the DER may take over if the company doesn't follow through.

headline: Painter Falls Off Ben Franklin Bridge, Missing in River
abstract: A painter working on the Benjamin Franklin Bridge fell into the Delaware River and is still missing, as he was wearing heavy work gear, preventing him from floating.

headline: Less than half of Pennsylvania counties have 911 emergency service
abstract: Only 31 out of PA's 67 counties have 911 emergency service, most of which is concentrated around Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. Bills are now before the PA Legislature to appropriate funds for establishing the service. Edward Truitt, Delaware County's director of emergency services, said that even if the funds are provided, it could take a year to set up computer equipment necessary for the emergency service.

headline: CAT Fund and choice
abstract: The author of this opinion piece states that while some consider the CAT Fund replacement a victory for consumer choice, it may be a costly victory and not just in higher automobile insurance.

headline: Cuomo Finds All Work and No Play Lacks Efficiency
abstract: NY Gov. Mario Cuomo instructed his staff that it was important to take an occasional vacation or weekend off, amid concerns that his staff was feeling overworked.  In addition, the governor proposed various taxes as part of his recently-presented $46.6 billion budget.

headline: State Treasurer would employ pension funds for social aims
abstract: PA Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll wants the managers of PA's public pension fund to invest in local real estate, highways, bridges and new businesses. She wants to help PA's elderly after retirement and help young people secure jobs. Federal law mandates that pension fund managers must consider only the financial merit of an investment. Richard C. Rowland, executive director of the PA Association of School Retirees questions pension fund investment, saying that it might sacrifice benefits and jeopardize earnings.

headline: Abortion rights pulls activist up front
abstract: Kate Michelman, a former executive director of a Planned Parenthood office and current executive director of the National Abortion Rights Action League, spoke out fiercely against an anti-abortion bill passed in the Pennsylvania State House of Representatives. Michelman is praised by abortion-rights activists for her intellect and personality. The bill, sponsored by Representative Stephen Friend, comes after a majority in the US House of Representatives voted to expand Medicaid coverage to abortions.

headline: State Approves Training Funds
abstract: A grant application for customized job training written by the Venango County vo-tech school received verbal approval from the state Customized Job Training Board yesterday.  The grant will go toward training 40 Oil City Tube workers in the production of quality-welded steel tubing.

headline: Judge weighing case against Avtex
abstract: The Commonwealth of Virginia insists that Avtex Fibers Incorporated, a firm based in Berwyn, PA, should pay fines for and clean up the polychlorinated biphenyls it dumped into the Shenandoah River. Deputy Attorney General R. Claire Guthrie contends that Avtex should be used as an example to other companies for its disregard for state environmental policies, while Avtex's attorney William L. Gardner argued that the company could not afford the fines since Virginia forced the company to close its plant in Front Royal. The US Environmental Protection Agency as well as other state agencies are supervising the cleanup of toxic substances.

headline: Panel studies I-80 tolls to fund local expressway
abstract: The state Turnpike Commission is studying the possibility of turning Interstate-80 into a toll road to help raise money for the proposed $1 billion Mon-Fayette Expressway.

headline: Let electronic media in state courtrooms, Senate panel urged
abstract: A Senate panel has suggested that electronic media, including television, radio, and photo, be allowed to cover state courtroom proceedings, claiming that the equipment has no negative effect on proceedings and allows the public to be more connected with the workings of the judicial system.

headline: CAT FUND REPLACED?
abstract: Under a proposal submitted by state Rep. Bill Lloyd, private insurance companies would be compelled to provide catastrophic insurance for auto-related medical costs from between $100,000 and  $1.1 million.  Insurance companies would have to create a pool, which would enable them to keep premiums between $24 and $30.

headline: dc-aliens
abstract: With his appointment as ranking Republican on the Census and Population Committee of the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee, Rep. Tom Ridge is expected to push that illegal aliens be counted in the census but not for reapportionment or represenation reasons.  Ridge has already filed suit in federal district court in Pittsburgh challenging the constitutionality of using illegal aliens for reaportionment figures.

headline: State wn't deal with firm for 6 months in ethics case
abstract: Henry Associates Inc. has been suspended from doing business with the state for 6 months as part of the reprimand for ethics violations.

headline: Abortion view inaccurate
abstract: This is a response from the editor of the New Era to a reader who recently sent in a letter to the editor.  The reader's letter grossly exaggerated the negative aspects of abortions, stating that many tax dollars are being spent on abortions and advertisements.  The editor chose to educate the public by responding that Pennsylvania's tax dollars are not being spent on abortions, or Planned Parenthood ads.

headline: Testing makes it difficult to fill holiday jobs
abstract: Thomas Mansmann, director of Pittsburgh city operations for the U.S. Postal Service, said they are having trouble recruiting temporary workers to process the increased amount of holiday mail because of newly required drug tests and a declining labor pool. Because of the improving economy in the city, there are fewer applicants for temporary work at the post office, said Postal Service spokesman William Zaken. Zaken also said that since August 1989, all post office applicants have been required to take a urinalysis test, which are necessary because postal workers taking drugs face an increased risk of injury on equipment.

headline: Justice and an oil spill
abstract: Ashland Oil Inc. was fined $2.5 million for an oil spill that occurred in 1988.  The oil spill resulted from a freak accident and was dealt with as effectively as possible by Ashland.  Still Judge Gustave Diamond ruled for the company to be fined because of the "seriousness of the event".

headline: PATrain ends service today
abstract: Today was the last day to ride a commuter train through the Mon Valley.  The PATrain has discontinued service due to high costs and low ridership.

headline: Lethal shot leads lawmaker survey
abstract: A bill to replace the electric chair with lethal injection as a more humane way to putting inmates to death has support in the PA legislature, though some lawmakers are against the death penalty altogether.

headline: CAT fund replacement approved
abstract: The Senate has approved legislation that would replace the state's CAT Fund, but lawmakers predict that the General Assemly will miss a May 1 deadline for having a new program in place.

headline: Dear Mr. Thornburgh: About this newspaper monopoly…
abstract: The advertisement calls on the people of York to write to Dick Thornburgh, the Attorney General, to contest the proposed Joint Operating Arrangement between the York daily newspapers.

headline: State-coal-only bill passes House committee
abstract: The House State Government Committee unanimously approved a measure introduced by Rep. William Lloyd which would force state buildings to burn PA coal.

headline: Abortion, parents' rights and no threat to Roe
abstract: This editorial addresses the newly raised issue in the US Supreme Court of requiring parental notification when a minor seeks an abortion. Nearly 85 percent of Americans approve of some form of parental notification. The issue arises from two cases in Ohio and Minnesota in which the states are arguing against judicial bypass when it is not a parent's consent that is required, but notification. There are two sides to the issue, one presented by the American Civil Liberties Union and one by the administration of US President George Bush.

headline: They Rally Around The Station
abstract: Amtrak workers Philadephia, Altoona, and Pittsburgh rallied against efforts to cut wages and charge working conditions in a contract dispute, which could lead to a strike.  Union leaders are calling on Amtrak to provide a better contract for workers or face the threat of a strike in the coming year.

headline: Keep PA Beautiful Day is a community project April 22
abstract: April 22 is Keep Pennsylvania Beautiful Day, and municipalities in the Upper Bucks area are banding residents together to pick up trash from township and state roads, parks, and recreation areas.

headline: PennDOT opens talks with property owners
abstract: PennDOT officials will begin talks with property owners along Route 601, which is scheduled to be widened and improved.

headline: Life is shorter in the capital of crime, crack, and cancer
abstract: With 372 slayings last year and a homicide rate of 59.5 per 100,000, Washington is the nation's murder capitol. Drug czar William J. Bennett will target the drugs and violence in the city.

headline: Catastrophic insurance options available
abstract: The state's Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund (CAT) expired June 1, and now in order to get catasrophic medical insurance, motorists must go to private insurance companies.

headline: Defender of Clymer
abstract: Opinion of Rep. Paul Clymer's publicized apology for saying 'people earning minimum wage are minorities, slow learners, students, and part-time employees'.  The author felt that the statement was fact and deserved no apology.  The author supports Clymer in all endeavours.

headline: State's overtime pay up 15%, Casey reports
abstract: Due to an insufficient workforce, higher salaries, and inflation the state paid $71.5 million in overtime pay to state workers during the 1987-1988 fiscal year.  The Dept. of Corrections recorded the highest number of overtime hours.

headline: Abortion-finance backers give up on Bush veto
abstract: Congressmen such as Senator Tom Harkin of Iowa who support expanded federal financing of abortions gave up their struggled to override President Bush's veto of a bill that would have permitted federal money for Medicaid abortions for victims of rape and incest. Bush had vetoed a similar appropriations bill last month. The AFL-CIO debated, but eventually backed away from, taking a position on abortion at its annual convention.

headline: Turmoil in coal fields bodes ill for UMW, industry
abstract: Wildcat strikes of coal miners in 9 states could have far-reaching effects, including lost revenue for the companies, decreased tax revenue from workers, lost jobs, rising utilities costs, and non-union companies could gain a market share.

headline: Key differences between proposed wetlands regulations and wetlands legislation
abstract: This article is a list of the differences between wetlands regulations and wetlands legislation that are being proposed as solutions to the problem of landowners not being able to use their own land because of increased environmental regulations on it. The subjects that the regulations and legislation address include agricultural waivers, mitigation, compensation to landowners, designation of exceptional value wetlands, municipal authority, and "buffer zones."

headline: PennDOT outlines county road work
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation officials urged representatives of Jefferson County government agencies, businesses and school districts to notify PennDOT when they see problems on state roads. At an annual Transportation Outreach program, PennDOT District 10 Community Relations Coordinator Ken Rich asked the group of attendees to be PennDOT's "eyes" out on the roads when problems may arise. PennDOT has already provided some improvements in Jefferson County, such as new flexible reflective road markers designed to bend and snap back in collisions.

headline: Local state police boss to step down
abstract: Sgt. Joseph Donnelly will step down from his post as commander of the Bloomsburg barracks of the state police in order to become vice president in charge of security for United Penn Bank.  Sgt. James Cockler has been tentatively named as his successor.

headline: Catastrophic Loss Fund proves difficult to replace
abstract: Gov. Casey feels that abolishing the Catastropic Loss Fund (CAT) was an irresponsible idea in that there is no medical coverage for motorists.  However, Casey has had to enforce CAT coverage using tax payer money.  New proposals are being considered to replace the CAT; one proposes that auto insurance companies offer catastropic loss coverage at rates approved by the state Insurance Department.  It appears that private coverage will be more expensive that the CAT coverage was.

headline: Deficit is forecast for state's lottery fund
abstract: A Senate Appropriations Committee listened to the Department of Revenue's secretary, Barton Fields, as he explained that the lottery may experience even more of a deficit.  The fund is losing money because of the expenses for prescription programs, long-term care, and rent/rebate programs for the eldery as well as a decrease in ticket sales.

headline: Statewide judges on Tuesday's local ballot
abstract: Democrat Ralph Cappy is running against Anita Brody in the race for PA State Supreme Court. Cappy cites his high rating with the PA Bar Association as qualification for the job, while Brody hopes to become the first woman on PA's Supreme Court. In addition to elections to the PA Superior Court, Commonwealth Court and appellate courts, there are a number of local elections, such as mayoral races in Lancaster, Erie and Pittsburgh and races for Philadelphia District Attorney and Philadelphia City Controller.

headline: AIDS among top 5 killers of Black women
abstract: According to a recent study by the Center for Disease Control, AIDS has become the fifth leading killer of African-American women. Health and AIDS outreach officials say the AIDS explosion has a great deal to do with the crack epidemic, fear, and a general lack of communication by male partners. Rashidah L. Hassan, executive director of Blacks Educating Blacks about Sexual Health Issues (BEBASHI), said crack-addicted women are creating a domino effect within the African-American community of spreading AIDS among partners. Hassan said BEBASHI officials have begun a street outreach program to women in Philadelphia.

headline: Two employers will observe Workers' Memorial Day
abstract: Two York County union locals and two major employers will today observe Workers' Memorial Day, an observance of American workers killed, injured or made ill on the job.

headline: Kunin's ambitious plan ignites Vermont critics
abstract: Vermont Governor Madeleine M. Kunin has proposed numerous environmental programs in her state. Most recently, she developed a $350 million plan, or a little more than half of the state budget, for a decade-long environmental plan that might necessitate a tax increase.

headline: PennDOT pushes anti- litter program
abstract: PennDOT pushes the "Keep Pennsylvania Beautiful" anti- litter campaign to cleanup the roads of the commonwealth with the help of volunteers.

headline: Lockdown in Graterford cellblock after fight
abstract: Officials at Graterford State Prison decided to stop taking prisoners from county jails after an altercation in one of its cellblocks. Prison spokesman Alan Lefebvre said that the altercation was a result of prison overcrowding. There have been 4 disturbances at prisons in PA since October 23: 2 at Camp Hill state prison, 1 at Huntingdon state prison, and 1 at Philadelphia's Holmesburg county prison.

headline: Centaur Presses Ahead With Meeting Plans; Pennwalt Mum
abstract: Centaur has raised its offer for Pennwalt Corp., a chemical company based in Philadelphia, from $100 to $110 per share.  Pennwalt has refused to discuss the company's position on the increased offer.

headline: Delco Democrats confront long odds in judicial contest
abstract: Democrat Elizabeth K. Ainslie, a former US Attorney, is up against incumbent Edward S. Lawhorne and lawyer Hal F. Doig as well as three Republican contenders in the race for Common Pleas Court of Delaware County. Lawhorne cites his high rating by the Delaware County Bar Association and was appointed to the Common Pleas Court by PA Governor Robert Casey in 1987, while Ainslie hopes her gender will have a factor in voting patterns. The Republican candidates include a former mayor of Chester, Pennsylvania and a former member of the Upper Darby Council.

headline: Symbol of the city
abstract: An editorial about City Hall and its (accurate) symbolization of Philadelphia as "a dump."

headline: Allentown council did right by flag
abstract: The editorial praises 3 Allentown City Council members for blocking a resolution asking to overturn the Supreme Court's flag-burning decision.  It says that "public officials have more important things to do than try to prove who is the most patriotic."

headline: U.S. settles union suit
abstract: In an attempt to curb the 1.6 million member Teamsters union of organized crime, the Justice Dept. reached an agreement with the union which will institute secret ballot elections of officers and court-appointed supervision.

headline: Landfill dispute targeted
abstract: At a meeting Thursday night, the owner of the Colebrookdale landfill - the Delaware County Solid Waste Authority - and township residents moved closer toward reconciling some of their more pronounced differences.  The DCSWA said it would work toward reducing trash blowing off of trucks driving to the landfill and would also study whether Shenkel Road was build over buried trash, which could lead to water contamination.

headline: PennDOT Schedules Work
abstract: Listing of PennDOT's planned road work for June 5-9 in Lebanon County.

headline: Long ride: calm CAT drivers haul inmates
abstract: Jeanine Napper and John Whooley are drivers for Capitol Area Transit. They helped to transport inmates from the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill, which had been in a state of riot for 2 days, to other correctional facilities in the state. The Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency ordered the CAT buses, escorted by state police, to help move inmates. Napper believes her tax money should not go to rebuilding the Camp Hill facility.

headline: Chamber, Governor Deny Deal On Tax Referendum
abstract: The president of the PA Chamber of Business and Industry denied a deal was cut with the administration of Gov. Casey for the organization to remain neutral on a referendum on local tax reform.

headline: Delco native in post
abstract: Delaware County native Terry Dellmuth has been chosen by Gov. Casey to fill the director's spot in the Dept. of Education while a successor for Thomas Gilhool is found.  Dellmuth has served in the Dept. of Public Welfare, as a director of the Greater Chester Movement and chief of staff in the Dept. of Education.

headline: Student loan agency hits snags on bonds
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency is facing technical problems in relation to setting up a new bond issue for 16,000 students to pay $20 million in tuition bills next semester,  spokesman John Ebersole said. The issue is the first the agency is trying to pass since the completion of a contract-kickback trial of Kenneth R. Reeher, its executive director who was acquitted, and Harry P. Casoni, a former top aide convicted of conspiracy, bribery, mail fraud, and interstate transportation in aid of racketeering. Ebersole said PHEAA had similar problems setting up bond issues in the past, although he could not go into detail about the nature of the problem.

headline: Area state senators vote in favor of abortion bill
abstract: Area PA Senators Pat Stapleton, William J. Stewart and Gene Porterfield, all voted in favor of PA's new bill restricting abortions. Provision in the bill include requiring women to notify their husbands if they plan to get an abortion, and requiring them to wait 24 hours after consulting a physician before the abortion is performed. Senator Stapleton does not believe the legislation will set up a test case for the 1973 Roe vs. Wade decision.

headline: USX failings start at top, groups say
abstract: The upper-level management of USX Corporation is blamed by plant-level management and joint plant-union committees for failure to respond to worker-safety complaints. The US Occupational Safety and Health Administration proposed fines totaling $7.1 million against the corporation for worker safety violations at its Irvin and Edgar Thomson steel mills in the Mon Valley, as well as at the Clairton Coke Works near Pittsburgh and the Fairless Works near Philadelphia. Plant safety officials as well as members of the United Steelworkers union have been filing complaints for years against USX.

headline: Landfill Fine
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources has fined the owner of the Colebrookdale Landfill in Berks County over $71,000.  The penalties are for illegally dumping 40,000 tons of trash at the site.

headline: PennDOT told Fayette needs roads done now
abstract: Fayette county is suffering economically, and as an effect the highways are in dire need of repair. Many feel that the repairs will foster tourism, attract employers, and make the roads safer for travel.

headline: Make users drug war targets
abstract: Larry Goodwin, a developer in Washington, believes drug users should be targeted in the drug war. Goodwin thinks that the threat of arrest and exposure would be a deterrent for non- addict users.

headline: Citicorp dropped Centaur deal, ex-partners say
abstract: Citicorp, a banking company which originally planned to finance the takeover of Pennwalt Corp. by Centaur Partners, backed out of the deal after it learned about actions by the takeover company's partners.  Some investors were the focus of enforcement actions by the SEC, or the National Association of Securities Dealers.  Pennwalt Corp. is fighting the takeover in and out of court.

headline: Democrats make Ohio a 1990 Statehouse target
abstract: The Democratic National Committee is preparing to send money and advice to Ohio to try to take control of the state Senate away from Republicans in 1990, as part of an initiative called Project 500 that is aimed at controlling statewide offices that will remap congressional districts after the 1990 census, Tim Dickson, director of the project, said. Ohio is one of 18 states targeted by Project 500 that gives block grants to state legislative chambers, which then distribute funds for key campaigns.

headline: Student- loan agency puts Reeher on leave
abstract: The executive director, Kenneth R. Reeher, of the state student- loan agency was placed on leave of absence without pay yesterday, after being indicted by a federal grand jury for accepting bribes.

headline: Arrested anti-abortion marchers should get chance to justify acts, judge says
abstract: In upholding their convictions, one judge said that though 11 anti-abortion protesters were engaging in illegal activity, they should be allowed to defend themselves by arguing that their actions were justifiable.

headline: Victory for labor
abstract: The president of the PA AFL-CIO writes in support and praise of the Solidarity Union in Poland, and says that is a victory for labor everywhere, that US laborers can take some small pride in.  He also notes the efforts of Pennsylvanians for Right to Work to "suppress organized labor" and compares them to the communist regime in Poland.

headline: Landfill officials find DER backwards
abstract: The Bedford-Fulton-Huntington Solid Waste Authority's landfill committee is being asked by their Bureau of Water Quality to make decisions without enough information.  A leachate treatment system is to be built and will handle the landfill's contaminated water.  The authority is not ready to answer that question before Phase 1, the new landfill, is approved.  However, the Department of Environmental Resources wants to be sure that the drainage from the new landfill can be treated with the leachate system before they approve the new landfill permits.

headline: PennDOT unveils Crows Run idea
abstract: PennDOT has announced a proposal for building the Crows Run Corridor, calling for a 4-lane road though seeking significant support from the counties and towns that currently own the right-of-way.

headline: Man Sentenced in Death Plot
abstract: The former operator of a Westmoreland County landfill was sentenced to up to 10 years in prison for his role in an unsuccessful plot to murder a state DER official.

headline: Companies File CAT Proposals
abstract: The Erie Insurance Group and State Farm Mutual Insurance Co. have each submitted proposals to provide coverage for medical bills from between $100,000 and $1 million for auto accident victims.  Such proposals have occurred in light of the imminent termination of the state's CAT Fund, and will be reviewed by the Insurance Dept.  Other firms are likely to submit proposals.

headline: Democrats may benefit in the long run
abstract: The Democratic party may unexpectedly benefit eventually from the current turmoil in the party caused by scandals forcing two prominent Dems to leave office.

headline: Surveillance gets attention of legislators
abstract: State legislatures across the nation are becoming more involved in the regulation of electronic surveillance of individuals in the workplace.  Computer and telephone monitoring are becoming more present, and such monitoring techniques have even been sanctioned by workers groups.

headline: 'Best, brightest' women in Cabinet
abstract: Gov. Casey and his five female Cabinet-level secretaries met with York women leaders today in a celebration of the strides women have made in state and local affairs.  There are more women in the Casey Cabinet than in any previous administration.

headline: West Shore school contract dispute lands in hands of state labor board
abstract: The West Shore school board recently filed unfair labor practices against the West Shore Education Association; now a decision must be made by the state Labor Relations Board.  The dispute revolves around teacher pay and alterations which would have to be made to the agreed upon fact-finding report.

headline: Landfill to accept only country trash
abstract: According to Supervisor Joseph B. Warner of the Mount Carmel Township Board of Supervisors, no more trash from outside Northumberland County will be allowed into the Mount Carmel Landfill. He said that regulations from the PA Department of Environmental Resources prompted the move, in addition to a plan to close the landfill altogether. The landfill may reopen, pending review of reports from the DER and the township's landfill engineer.

headline: PennDOT works to get edge on winter storms
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has been preparing since May for the upcoming winter season by readying trucks, plows, spreaders, other equipment and drivers, said Robert Boyer, PennDOT's Northumbreland County maintenance manager. William Hutchison, assistant district engineer at PennDOT's Montoursville office, said a single storm in a single county can cost upwards of $100,000. Hutchison said he is hoping for a mild winter, as in previous years, which helps keep costs down.

headline: Marathon Blue Mountain fire officially extinguished
abstract: The final forest fire crews left the scene of the marathon Blue Mountain Fire in lower Carbon County this morning.  A district inspector said the fire was officially declared under control yesterday afternoon.

headline: company corrects its 1987 yearly earnings
abstract: Union Pacific Corp. of Bethlehem states that its fourth quarter earnings increased 34 percent, with its revenues for the year having increased from $5.4 billion in 1987 to $6.1 billion in 1988.

headline: Democrats praise governor's speech
abstract: In the wake of Gov. Casey's state of the Commonwealth address, Democrats largely praised the govenor for being the initiator on such issues as tax reform and auto insurance reform.  Republicans were more hesitant and skeptical in their compliments.

headline: Survey: Lawmakers Rate Their Relationship With Casey
abstract: Of 106 state lawmakers who responded to the Associated Press poll, opinions on Gov. Casey ranged from calling him "the fineset governor this state has ever had" to "a jerk."  Casey's toughness was viewed as both an asset and a hindrance among respondents.

headline: Bishops, Catholic politicians lock horns over abortion
abstract: Roman Catholic politicians are facing ecclesiastical sanctions in a special appeal by the nation's bishops to restrict legalized abortion. Catholic legislators that dissent from the Church on the issue of abortion rights are facing ex-communication for their pro-choice stances. Bishops believe Catholic legislators have a moral responsibility to work to curtail abortion, but many legislators believe the Church should remain separate from political life.

headline: 12 teachers to receive bonanzas in back pay
abstract: The Mechanicsburg Area School District approved salary adjustments last week to provide $102,000 in back pay to 12 teachers who were not being paid in accordance with steps on the salary scale.

headline: Large Participation Overwhelms Recycling Program
abstract: Recycling officials in the Philadelphia area were overwhelmed by the rate of participation in an area to which they recently expanded services.  The participation rate was about 90%, consdierably above the predicted 30%, causing the plant to shut down in order to ease the backlog of materials.

headline: Pennies are still good for piggy banks, or tossing in a well.
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission officials said pennies are requested to not be used at Pennsylvania tolls. John Hook of the Turnpike Commission's Fare Collection Department said pennies slow traffic down at toll booths. Drivers are asked not to use pennies at tolls, though they will still be accepted.

headline: Mayors agree on tax boosts, tougher gun laws
abstract: Member of the US Conference of Mayors voted with near-unanimity on a few issues, including calling for higher federal taxes and tougher gun laws.  There was, however, contention over a vote held to decide on the 3rd-in-command of the group, which is usually decided by a private panel, which was deadlocked this year.

headline: Compromise sought on car insurance
abstract: Gov. Casey and Senate Majority Leader F. Joseph Loeper on Tuesday agreed to work on a compromise car insurance plan that might be ready for consideration.The two met in private for two hours and afterwards would not discuss with the press the specifics of their conversation.

headline: Democrats request independent probe of Pierce
abstract: A group of Democrats including in the US House of Representatives requested investigation by an independent counsel of Samuel R. Pierce Jr., the former head of the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Attorney General DickThornburgh accused the Congressmen of partisan politics, but promised to report back to the House Judiciary Committee. The request for the investigation was announced by Representative Charles Schumer.

headline: Tame that monster
abstract: The Editorial Board believes that granting teachers the right to strike created a monster that needs to be tamed.

headline: Casey expects to sign abortion bill Friday
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey stated that he may sign what would be the country's most restrictive anti-abortion bill. Pro-life state senators, such as Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer, were outraged at Casey's attempt to have a motion to suspend the Senate rules rejected. The bill must be signed by House Speaker James Manderino before it is sent to Casey.

headline: 8 schools here high on loan default list
abstract: 7 local trade schools and one community college in the Allegheny Co. area have high student loan default rates, according to the US Education Dept.  One school official said it's not the schools' responsibility, it’s the lenders'.

headline: Larksville council intends to sue DER
abstract: The Larksville Borough Council instructed solicitor John O'Connor to file a suit against the PA Department of Environmental Resources to attempt to close the portion of the West Side Landfill located in the borough. The landfill authority had submitted a closure plan to DER in 1987 but the site was never officially closed, according to borough council members. O'Connor said the suit would be the way to get the DER to actually move on the closure plan.

headline: Pennsylvania men among Marine crash victims
abstract: A list of the 18 Marines killed in the helicopter crash in South Korea. It also lists the 15 men that were injured.

headline: Menorah case back with 3rd circuit
abstract: The decision of whether to place a menorah outside the Pittsburgh City-County building has moved into the hands of a panel of judges from the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals. The Jewish organization Chabad that is trying to display the menorah sued the city last week saying the city was violating their civil rights and freedom of expression. Judge Joseph F. Weis Jr. stopped the order of US District Judge Barron P. McCune that would not delay the decision about placing the menorah on the bottom step in front of the building because he wanted three members of his court to review the matter. Weis said the issue is not religion, but rather if the step is a "public forum." The US Supreme Court ruled last summer that the menorah was permitted on the steps because it was accompanied by secular symbols of a Christmas tree and a sign promoting liberty.

headline: Consumer advocates push for return of price tags
abstract: The PA Consumers Citizen Council is petitioning the state Legislature to enact a bill which would require supermarkets to individually price items. Louis S. Meyer of the PACCC claims that shelf tags are often outdated or confusing to read. Philadelphia City Council is enacting similar legislation.

headline: Democrats to select new chief
abstract: Cumberland County Democratic committee people will elect a new chairperson after current Chairman David Ferris resigns after serving for 18 months. Ferris said he is resigning to avoid any appearance of conflict of interest concerning a new job he has taken with the Pennsylvania State Education Association's government relations unit, a job that will require him to lobby state government and deal with party caucuses.

headline: Tax- reform campaigns suffer- Both sides find voters reluctant to contribute cash
abstract: Fund-raisers on both sides of the tax issue say they have generated only a fraction of the money needed to run modest campaigns.

headline: Chipping away at legalized abortion
abstract: Although the Webster case currently before the Supreme Court may not imminently endanger the precedent set by Roe v. Wade, it does threaten to chip away at that decision's legacy of practical availability of abortions to women.

headline: Adult literacy- Rural areas getting shortchanged?
abstract: Rural residents are getting short- changed under the state's adult literacy program, claims the Center for Rural Pennsylvania, a legislative agency of the PA General Assembly.

headline: Lehigh Valley, follow Perkasie
abstract: The town of Perkasie has implemented an effective recycling program which garners a lot of community participation by making it economically beneficial for residents to recycle.  The editors believe that other Lehigh Valley communities should follow Perkasie's lead.

headline: Petroleum Street Bridge Repairs Set Next Month
abstract: Extensive repairs on part of the Petroleum Street Bridge will begin next month, causing a detour for trucks but still allowing cars across the bridge.  The repairs should only take a few days.

headline: Missing keys reported at Camp Hill state prison
abstract: Keys that unlock many buildings and cell blocks within the Camp Hill prison are missing, according to both prison guards and officials. Officials said two of the missing key rings belonged to two top administrators, Deputy Superintendent of Operations Richard C. Smith and Deputy for Treatment Terry W. Henry. Officer Daniel J. Murdock said another set of missing keys belonged to maintenance supervisor Stanley T. Smith. PA Department of Corrections spokesman Kenneth Robinson said one of keys are not missing while others are not confirmed. Prison guards say they feel unsafe in the concern that prisoners are considering another siege similar to that which occurred in October 1989.

headline: Consumer Group Calls For Renewal Of No-Fault Auto Insurance
abstract: The New Start Consumer Insurance Project would like PA to reinstate no-fault insurance coverage, which would stop lawsuits for minor injuries and damages.  The group contends that true no-fault insurance could save an average of $90 per insured car.

headline: Democrats, GOP dispute tax vote effect
abstract: Members of both partiese are trying to sort out what the fallout will be from the defeat of Gov. Casey's tax reform proposal.  While the governor is moving his attention to lowering auto insurance costs, he says he is still making tax reform a goal.

headline: Tax reform is issue with Adams commissioners
abstract: Educating voters on tax reform will be one of the top issues on the agenda when the Adams County Commissioners attend a statewide conference today and Tuesday.

headline: Christmas controversy
abstract: Commissioners in Allen County in Indiana have voted to not erect a Nativity scene outside the local courthouse in order to avoid a controversy over state-sponsored religion, according to commissioner Edwin Rousseau. The decision was made after evaluating two US Supreme Court decisions earlier this year about religion in Pittsburgh, PA. In one case, the court rule that a Nativity scene at the Allegheny County courthouse was an endorsement of religion, but in the other justices allowed a menorah and Christmas tree to remain in Pittsburgh City Hall as cultural symbols.

headline: After fight, Senate Oks $191 million for bill
abstract: The Senate passed  a $191 million spending bill, which included money for special education, mental retardation, and highway maintenance.  The bill will likely be edited in the Democrat-controlled House.

headline: Let's stop the landfill madness
abstract: This editorial article addresses the proposal to build a landfill in southwestern Schuylkill County next to Broad Mountain. Both plans require special permission from the Schuylkill County Zoning Hearing Board and permits from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources. The editor expresses anger that the two corporations proposing the landfills would do so against all efforts by Schuylkill County residents to improve environmental standards and reduce pollution in natural areas. The editor encourages all county residents opposed to the proposal to voice their concerns to the zoning hearing board and the county commissioners.

headline: Pittsburgh seeks high-speed trains
abstract: This editorial voices support for a proposal that would build a 20-mile-long high-speed train between downtown Pittsburgh and Greater Pittsburgh International Airport. According to a Pennsylvania Department of Commerce spokesperson, the administration of PA Governor Robert P. Casey is "very much interested" in the project. The $400 million project is seen as a means to bring new business to economically hard-pressed Western Pennsylvania. The possible sources of funding for the project are seen as making it financially feasible, and the editorial board supports it as an investment in a technology that is to become a major mode of transportation in Europe in the 1990s.

headline: Model Antidrug Measure Is Being Drafted for States
abstract: The director of federal drug policy said he is drafting model legislation for the states that would increase civil and criminal penalties for narcotics users.

headline: Corrosive Issue: Dow chemical product is assailed as causing brickwork to collapse
abstract: The stel bolts holding building exteriors in place are deteriorating and mortar is loosening. The Dow Chemical Co. could be held responsible for millions in damages if the pattern continues. The Dow introduced Sarabond, a cement additive said to strengthen the mortar, however, it may be the cause of weakening hundreds of brick structures.

headline: Deputy disagrees with sheriff
abstract: In the controversy surrounding Somerset County Deputy Sheriff John Mastillo's resignation, Sheriff Ronald DeLano made statements that were disputed by Mastillo, causing another response by DeLano.  DeLano claims that Mastillo is resigning because of the overtime pay policy, but Mastillo has declined to specify his reasons.

headline: 'Tax reform' not as bad- or as good- as opponents, proponents claim
abstract: The author of this piece believes the local tax change will be "neither the panacea the proponents say, nor the draconian smash pictured by the opponents."  Exaggeration exists on both sides.

headline: City lags in award of minority contracts
abstract: Pittsburgh doesn't come close to its stated goal of giving contracts to minority and women-owned firms, awarding just 2 and 1.1%, respectively, of total contracts instead of the goal of 15 and 5%.  Officials are looking into possible ways of encouraging development by such firms.

headline: ALEM offers help
abstract: ALEM, a program in the Jim Thorpe school district, offers extra help for students in elementary schools.  It is focused in classes with students with slight educational handicaps, but is not limited to those children, as it also helps regular students.

headline: Letters:  What about the pump?
abstract: Author was surprised to read that the Point Pleasant Pumping Station was not included in an article about the drought and the Delaware River.

headline: Poetic justice
abstract: In an effort to garner more money for the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund, PA officials molded a plan that will employ a surcharge for safety violations (DUI, overweight truck, etc.) that would go directly to the fund.

headline: Monroe County seeks new probation officer to assist in juvenile drug cases
abstract: Monroe County is applying to the PA Juvenile Court Judge's Commission for an extra county probation officer to deal with drug and alcohol problems of clients. Chief Probation Officer Steve Houloose requested the application, saying the county has needed the extra officer for years. Houloose said the number of drug and alcohol caseloads is rapidly increasing, with about 50 percent of all adult criminal cases requiring drug or alcohol treatment, and the new person would work with 16 to 20 juvenile cases at one time. At the same meeting, the county commissioners deferred a decision about participating in the state gypsy moth program run by the PA Department of Environmental Resources, among other items on the agenda.

headline: Cost-cutting insurance plan unveiled
abstract: Gov. Casey introduced his auto insurance plan yesterday, which would rolll back insurance rates about 21%.  Its fate in the Senate is uncertain, though it will likely pass the House.

headline: DER is worst-run agency in state, many legislators feel
abstract: According to an Associated Press survey which garnered responses from 106 lawmakers, 40 percent believed that the Dept. of Environmental Resources was the worst-run state agency.  Reasons cited for this classification were the difficult decisions the agency must make, its large size, and its overburdened bureaucracy.

headline: Tax reform spurs high voter turnout
abstract: Attributes the high voter turnout on the recent post-presidential, off-year election to the ballot questions concerning tax reform and small games of chance.  Goes on to mention some of the results of the various candidates for the party nominations.

headline: Committee considers new anti-discrimination bill for local government
abstract: The State Government Committee of the PA House of Representatives is considering a new measure which would allow the state Human Relations Commission to cut off state funds to any agency found discriminating against individuals on the basis of race, sex, religion, etc. The bill, similar to federal anti-discrimination laws, was criticized by Elam Herr, director of legislation for the PA State Association of Township Supervisors, for being too strict. Homer Floyd, executive director of the HRC, said he supports language requiring the commission to receive approval by Commonwealth Court before cutting off funds.

headline: Arguments on apple-chemical issue increase fury: Harrisburg schools join boycott
abstract: The Harrisburg School district removed apples from the menu because of parental concerns about the chemical in some apples causing cancer.  Local apple growers felt that the move was an inappropriate overreaction.  Harrisburg schools were following in suit with other school distrcts across the country, including Los Angeles and Chicago.  Pennsylvania apple growers deny the use of the chemical, Alar, since 1987 but are still concerned about a possible economic loss.

headline: Limestone a concern at Barner Landfill
abstract: Limestone was brought up at a board meeting as an issue for the Mifflin County Solid Waste Authority in improving the Barner 2 waste site. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resource is reluctant to approve the proposal without proof that two layers of limestone under the site will remain stable. Steve Tucker, program director at the Barner 3 landfill, said construction should begin soon on the improvements to the Barner 2 site.

headline: Police train efforts on safety along Lebanon-area rail lines
abstract: Lebanon City Policemen were out yesteday in support of railway safety, as they noticed that many children had been playing near the lines, and even adults didn't follow appropriate safety procedures.

headline: More cells not enough
abstract: The editorial expresses support for an initiative proposed by PA Governor Robert P. Casey to add 1,440 prison cells within six months and to increase the rate of prison construction. The editorial board believes that this would be a timely response to the current emergency situation in which the state's prison system is operating at about 50 percent over capacity. However, the board also suggests that Casey and the PA Legislature look at alternatives to incarceration, such as providing incentives for prisoners to enroll in rehabilitation, educational or vocational programs, and intensive parole supervision programs. The board suggests the Legislature approve a package of bills by PA Senator D. Michael Fisher that discusses some of these alternatives.

headline: County lawmaker wants small businesses to receive better answers to tax questions
abstract: PA Representative Gregory M. Snyder proposed a bill that would increase the 1 percent discount small vendors receive on the sales taxes they collect to 5 percent. The bill would also allow more businesses to file quarterly, rather than monthly, sales-tax returns. The bills have been referred to the House Finance Committee for consideration.

headline: Dirty business of raising lawmakers' pay
abstract: United States lawmakers voted to give themselves a pay raise of nearly 40 percent over the next two years, amidst mixed feelings and comments by lawmakers. Some legislators such as US Democratic Representative Harold Volkmer of Missouri voted for the pay raise, while other such as US Republican Representative Jim Hansen of Utah did not vote for the pay raise but will still reap the benefits of it.

headline: Tax Reform, Judges Top May 16 Ballot
abstract: Tax reform and statewide judges top the May 16 primary ballot, giving people extra choices to go with local races.

headline: Effects of racism remain obvious
abstract: The editorial board speaks out against racism in New Castle, and in the United States in general. Effects such as the economic gap between whites and blacks are evidence that racism still exists.

headline: Award-Winning Teacher Reprimanded For Criticizing Science Teaching
abstract: Walt Tremer, a Southern Lehigh High School science teacher who was named one of the top five teachers in the country last week, was reprimanded by his superintendent for saying that science teachers need to move into the real world, and out of the textbook.

headline: Limits on non-Pa. trash scrutinized
abstract: At first glance, PA Governor Robert Casey's executive order halting the flow of out-of-state trash to PA and restricting landfill establishment permits issued by the PA Department of Environmental Resources might seem like a good idea. The order was praised by State Senator Barry Stout, who sponsored a similar bill which was passed in the Senate but failed in the House. However, the executive order might clash with a law passed over a year beforehand, mandating that the DER must review all landfill permit applications within 60 days of submittal and must make a decision within a year.

headline: Political patronage still drives hiring for entry-level Turnpike jobs
abstract: Many people who apply for jobs at the Pennsylvania Turnpike are not considered unless they have a cover letter or a recommendation from a politician for jobs such as toll collector and maintenance staff.  Political patronage has been questioned many times, yet the Turnpike officials defend its use in their hiring practices.  Organizations like PennDot and Port Authority Transit have removed these practices and it improved the productivity and public opinion.

headline: More defendants serving time in community service
abstract: While most criminal sentences are still served in terms of months and years, an increasing number of defendants in Bucks County are doing time by the hour in the form of community service.

headline: Court Allows States Wide Antitrust Law To Shield Consumers
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled today that states may pass laws permitting consumers to bring antitrust suits that would be barred under Federal law.

headline: Does Manderino have his sights set on judgeship?
abstract: "Big" Jim Manderino, state legislator for Monessen, might retire from the state Legislature only to obtain an $80,000 per year judgeship on the Westmoreland County Common Pleas Court. If Joe Hudock wins the election to Superior Court, there will be two judgeships, since attorney Al Gaudio was removed as a judicial candidate following his appointment as solicitor of the Westmoreland Municipal Authority. Manderino may have to deal with PA Governor Robert Casey for support in the appointment to the court.

headline: Tax Reform, Landfills Top Grange Legislative Dinner
abstract: Tax reform and the state solid waste management bill were top issues discussed at the annual legislative dinner sponsored by Pomona Grange No.33.

headline: Equal Opportunity
abstract: In the recent election, Walter Phillips Jr. (who is white) easily won the Democratic primary for DA, carrying almost have of Philadelphia's predominantly black wards against his opponent, who was black.  The author wonders if whites would similarly vote in large numbers for a better qualified black candidate.

headline: Barbs, insults mark injunctive hearing
abstract: A heated exchange between the Old Forge School District Superintendent and the striking Old Forge teachers' solicitor took place during a hearing concerning selective strikes by the teachers.  At issue in the case is the interpretation of "selective strike" and its effect on students education.

headline: Local man honored by agency
abstract: Wilbur F. Lynam was recognized as outstanding deputy wildlife conservation officer of the year by the PA Game Commission. Regional Director Lorraine Yocum cited his investigative skills and public speaking ability as reasons for his recognition.

headline: Proposed Route 202 bypass gets a new life
abstract: A proposed Route 202 bypass between Doylestown Twp. and Montgomery Co. has gotten another chance, as PennDOT has included a preliminary engineering study on its list of high-priority projects.  There is a chance that the study, if performed, would discourage PennDOT from spending further money on the project.

headline: Most aides respected
abstract: The writer, the vice president of the Western Center Parents Group, argues that the Western Center is not a barbaric institution, as one might believe after reading excerpts from a Welfare Dept. report not yet released to the public.

headline: Deep-discount drugstore chain gains area foothold
abstract: Phar-Mor, the drugstore industry's second largest discounter, is opening a new store at the Union Square shopping center in Lower Paxton Township.  According to the National Association of Chain Drug Stores, the deep discounting business has grown considerably in the past five years.

headline: Don Quixote on Capitol Hill
abstract: Renegade former state rep. John Kennedy states that he is considering running for governor.  Kennedy goes "against the grain" of most politicians.

headline: Tax revision foe ready to form citizens' group
abstract: A chief opponent of Gov. Casey's tax reform plan in May is looking to form a permanent statewide taxpayer rights group, which would lobby for meaningful tax reform and to elect officials who share its views.

headline: Farview Gets Seminary Chaplain
abstract: St. Tikhon's Seminary will begin a chaplaincy program at Farview Hospital in Wayne County, which will help the Seminary to continue its mission of scholastic and theological learning of pastors.

headline: Bedford eyes education expansion
abstract: Bedford County Commissioner Kim Coon will meet with officials from Shippensburg University to discuss establishing post-secondary education opportunities in the county. The university has expressed interest in opening a branch campus in Bedford County, but does not know that it can afford building a branch campus.

headline: Oil hits the shore at an island preserve
abstract: Oil from the spill of a Uruguayan tanker in the Delaware River has reached Pea Patch Island, a nature preserve, and threatens some of th 13,000 birds nesting and mating there.  Booms set up to prevent the spill from spreading are dealing mixed results.

headline: PUC Sets New Deadline For Pocono Turnpike Permit
abstract: The PUC is requiring a vacation resort operating a private toll road to apply for a turnpike permit or face fines of $250 a day.

headline: N. Britain Township: In search of a post office
abstract: Township manager Robert C. Bender will ask the U.S. Postal Service to put a post office in New Britain.  Such an act would aid fire departments, police, and ambulance squads.

headline: Drought status improves, but floods feared
