abstract: After a month of drought worries, drought restrictions may soon be lifted from much of PA, as rainfall has greatly increased recently.

headline: Down for the count?
abstract: U.S. Congressmen from PA and other states are angered that illegal aliens will be counted in the next census and factored into House seat appropriations for states.  This would mean that states with more illegal aliens, i.e. Texas & California, would gain seats at the expense of states without illegal aliens like PA.

headline: Tax revision supporters outspent foes
abstract: Supporters of the ill-fated tax reform ballot question in May out spent their opponents by about 5 to 1, with much of their money coming from large groups like unions, companies, and political groups.  Opponents of the plan raised a substantial amount of their money in donations of $50 or less.

headline: Find middle ground
abstract: The editorial board believes that PA's new anti-abortion law is too restrictive. The state Senate approved the legislation, which came after the US Supreme Court gave states more rights to regulate abortions in July 1989. The board believes the law erodes a woman's right to control her own body.

headline: Boeing Gives Penn State $750,000 For New Laboratory
abstract: Boeing Co. has given $750,000 to Penn State University, which will be used for a new laboratory in the College of Engineering, the university announced.

headline: Loans approved for water system projects in Slatington, Walnutport
abstract: Two Northern Lehigh municipalities, Slatington Borough and Walnutport, will share more than $1-million in low-interest loans from the state's Penn-VEST funding to improve their municipal water systems. PennVEST spokesman Tom Kelchner announced the 20-year financial arrangements. The Slatington project includes replacing and cleaning water mains, repairing a leaking reservoir, and constructing a 250,000-gallon reservoir to eliminate an unfiltered water sources. The Walnutport project consists of constructing a one-million gallon covered water reservoir and installing a new 12-inch diameter transmission main.

headline: Reed gives boost to light railroad commuter plans
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed said yesterday at a Capital Region Economic Development Corporation (CREDC) meeting that the city is willing to help establish a light rail commuter system for the region. Reed said the Capital Area Transit or a new transit authority could be used to obtain low-interest financing for light rail as an alternative to increasing highway congestion. Reed and CREDC officials called for regional approaches to economic development, rather than local government approaches.

headline: New Hope Woman Charged In School District Theft
abstract: The FBI filed a 54- count indictment against a Bucks County woman for the theft of over $2 million from the New Hope- Solebury School District.

headline: Ferlo wants small games referendum
abstract: Councilman Jim Ferlo said yesterday that city residents should decide, through a referendum placed on May's ballot, whether they favor games of chance.  The referendum would be in compliance with a new law enacted by the state Legislature, which permits small games of chance by non-profits groups if a munipality through referendum concurs.

headline: Former health official charged in bribery case
abstract: John B. LaFrance, a former high- ranking official in the Phila. based regional office of the U.S. Public Health Service, has been indicted by a federal grand jury on charges of bribary and conspiracy.

headline: Taxpayers ill served by silence
abstract: Explains the benefits of the proposed tax reform, and questions the intents of various groups that have come out against the reform.

headline: A sludge disposal solution takes root in Royersford
abstract: A potential solution to the problem of sewage sludge disposal comes in the form reeds to be planted along the waterways carrying the sludge, so that less must be taken to a landfill.

headline: Flag stand
abstract: Gov. Casey has just announced his plans to propose a bill banning the desecration of the US flag, though PA already has such a law.  A spokesman for the state attorney general said that PA needs a new law since the old one is of questionable validity with the Supreme Court.

headline: Boiling down to 'up or out'
abstract: Fred Croop, a business professor, is employed at College Misericordia. He was recently employed by Wilkes College, where he was denied tenure and forced to leave the college, and believes that his dismissal was unfair. The tenure system varies at each establishment, but the basic idea was developed with the founding of the American Association of University Professors.

headline: M.B. Research files an appeal
abstract: M.B. Research Laboratories has filed an appeal with the Environmental Hearing Board in order to attempt to get permission to continue operating its incinerator after the DER ordered it shut down until a permit was acquired.

headline: Singel Tells IDC Members Project On Front Burner
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark Singel promised the Lebanon County Industrial Authority that a decision regarding the proposed Route 72 bypass was imminent.  He said that PennDOT would be making a determination as to the feasibility project within 2 to 3 weeks.

headline: New prison planned for N. Camden
abstract: Plans are underway for a new state prison to be built in North Camden in an attempt to lighten the burden of an overload of inmates at other prisons.

headline: Fiures for Recovering Steel Industry
abstract: The American Iron and Steel Institute, which is composed of 25 companies representing 80 percent of the industry, state that the steel industry is expected to post profits of of approx. $2 billion in 1988.  PA represents 13 percent of the nations production in steel.

headline: Drew Lewis asks for delay of GOP endorsement
abstract: Drew Lewis, an influential member of the Republican party, wrote a letter to party state chairman state Senator Earl Baker requesting a postponement of the party's vote on a gubernatorial candidate. State Auditor General Barbara Hafer was slated to win the nomination. Baker shot down the idea of a postponement, saying that it will only start rumors that PA Governor Robert Casey is not running for re-election and that Drew Lewis aspires to the Republican nomination.

headline: TELL IT to Gov. Casey
abstract: A opportunity to ask Gov. Casey questions or share concerns but cuting it out and mailing it in to the newspaper. On March 30, 1989 the Times will publish a sample of responses.

headline: Acid Rain Hit List Includes Utilities In Pennsylvania
abstract: Two plants in PA appear on President Bush's "acid rain hit list," a list of the top-20 polluting utilities contributing to acid rain.  Sulfur dioxide emissions cuts will be ordered as part of the President's new clear air legislation.

headline: Flag-burning shouldn't be a problem
abstract: James L. Newton, a veteran of the Vietnam war, states that he believes "legislation banning flag-burning does not address the problem." He says that he will defend the US Constitution and the rights it bestows upon citizens, but will not stand idly by while the flag is burned. He states that more Americans need respect for what the flag stands for.

headline: Boos and Bravos
abstract: This article provides "bravos" for three items of interest: 55 workers are to be trained for new jobs at Laminations, Inc., under a grant to Luzerne county Community College announced by PA Governor Robert P. Casey; former secretary of education under Casey Thomas K. Gilhool is teaching at a Philadelphia public school; many PA farmers are participating in the Chesapeake Bay cleanup program to reduce fertilizer pollution runoff. The article cites "boos" for the following: the FBI continues after 7 years to collect information on a New Jersey teen who attracted FBI attention by contacting foreign countries for a world encyclopedia; the number of Philadelphia homicides is increasing; nearly half of all child care teachers are leaving their jobs each year because of low salaries.

headline: Man-made  wetland serves as hamlet's sewage system
abstract: A man-made wetland in Mount Pleasant, a development of 43 homes, has  been installed to undertake the treatment of sanitary waste which an antiquated septic system was unable to handle.  Wetlands are increasingly looked toward by environmentalists as a cheaper and safer alternative for waste disposal.

headline: Rainbow Riders to pony express from Troy to Wellsboro
abstract: A pony express for charity is happening on June 17 along the route from Troy to Wellsboro.  Proceeds from the special envelopes, which can be bought specifically for the event, go to the Rainbow Riders Riding Program for the Handicapped.

headline: New York's Drug Lesson for America
abstract: New York's plan to send special police teams (Tactical Narcotics Teams) to reclaim neighborhoods overwhelmed by drug violence has caused overcrowding in prisons and heavy costs to taxpayers.

headline: French firm purchases two local plants
abstract: A Paris corporation has finalized a takeover of Burndy, a Connecticut-based manufacturer which has two plants in York County that employ 200 workers.

headline: Elderly Growing in Number and Influence
abstract: Elderly people comprise a larger percentage of the population than ever before, as life expectancy increases due to modern medicine.  A larger percentage of the elderly vote than in other groups, giving the demographic a slight political advantage.

headline: Testimony about proposed phone service is mixed
abstract: Caller*ID received mixed responses yesterday in a public forum, as there are benefits and detriments to the feature.

headline: Across the state, ozone pollution worsens, study says
abstract: A study released yesterday by Pennsylvania Public Interest Group found that ozone pollution is becoming an increasingly dangerous problem, with the number of days in PA where federal ozone pollution standards were violated incresed from 12 in 1986 to 36 in 1988.  A spokesperson from the state Dept. of Environmental Resources agreed that the issue is a statewide problem.

headline: For senator, state's pro-choice fight not over
abstract: PA Senator James Greenwood, the Senate's "point person" for the pro-choice movement, stated that even though the state's abortion bill was signed into law, the pro-choice fight is not over. He stated that the 1990 gubernatorial election will be critical, since a pro-choice governor could veto anti-abortion legislation. The state's abortion bill has provisions to overturn the US Supreme Court's Roe v. Wade ruling, if the Supreme Court affirms it.

headline: Butler schools reinstate last of furloughed aides
abstract: The final two of five teachers' aides furloughed earlier in the year because of budget cuts were reinstated to their jobs in the Butler Area School District. All of the aides worked in special education classes. The board also approved the "Fair Share Plan for Special Education" to ensure that every school district in the Midwestern Intermediate Unit is reimbursed for special education services.

headline: Massive Program Assures New Wells, Dams, Safe Water
abstract: A new well, with upgraded storage and distribution capabilities, will be built in Kratzerville, PA, thanks to a grant and a Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority (Pennvest) loan.  Pennvest has granted loans toward 66 drinking water projects, including the Kratzerville project, and will assist in the state's 25 year commitment to rehabilitating PA's water supply infrastructure.

headline: Raise pike speed limit
abstract: The editorial board believes that the speed limit on the PA Turnpike should be raised to 65. Representative Eugene G. Saloom plans to attach an amendment to a transportation bill soon to appear before the House. The proposal would allow the PA Turnpike Commission to restrict the raised speed limit to certain areas of the turnpike.

headline: Notes from the cocaine front
abstract: This article is a special interest piece where reporter Clark Hallas documented experiences of men and women involved in the struggle of the Pittsburgh community's drug industry. The story explores the federal view of the cocaine business in Pittsburgh.

headline: Gambling Decision Appealed
abstract: Assistant DA Marie Veon is asking a judge to reconsider his choice to disallow evidence in an illegal gambling case against the Oil City VFW club.

headline: Endorsements
abstract: The editorial board announces its endorsements for upcoming elections to local and state posts, as well as for the New Jersey gubernatorial race. The board endorses Ron Castille for Philadelphia District Attorney, Jonathan Saidel for Philadelphia City Controller, Ralph Cappy for State Supreme Court, and Dan Pellegrini for Commonwealth Court, among others.

headline: Thank Minor for a major victory
abstract: Citizens' efforts, led by Mary Minor, to block Keystone Landfill's request to expand were successful yesterday in what the editors view as the right decision.  However, the decision leaves unanswered the question of where the garbage will go.

headline: Act now to reduce acid rain damage
abstract: Although more studies on the effects and causes of acid rain are important and in order, action is needed now to begin to curb the problem of acid rain.  With new bills addressing this issue coming before the PA General Assembly and the U.S. Congress, the opportunities for action will emerge.

headline: Going to the dogs
abstract: Bob Steinbacher of Rutherford expresses his discontent with the American Civil Liberties Union's support of prisoners involved in riots. He uses a metaphor of neighborhood dogs rioting against their owners and being protected by the "Animal Civil Liberties Union" to show his disapproval.

headline: Casey offers more funds for special education
abstract: Gov. Casey is pledging "transitional" money for special education, as the administration is being sued to stop the $40 million in special ed cuts.  Others are wondering where this money will come from, "when there are holes in his budget right now."

headline: May rainfall good news for Boyertown
abstract: The heavy rains in May spelled good news for Boyertown residents, as the Trout Run Resevoir has dramatically increased its water supply.  Fears of a drought were abound before the heavy rains began.

headline: Regional officials eye state to boost funding for SEPTA
abstract: Bucks County Commissioner Andrew L. Warren, joined by Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode and Montgomery County Commissioners Chairman Paul B. Bartle, held a press conference on a study conducted on public transportation in Southeastern PA. The report favored increased federal funding for the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, which currently accounts for less than 5% of the authority's operating budget. State Secretary of Transportation Howard Yerusalim expressed support for the plan. Warren and other officials will ask the state Legislature to help find a way to raise money for SEPTA. Warren, Goode and Bartle favor a tax for SEPTA, although Bartle opposes a regional sales tax.

headline: Number of executions drops despite forecast
abstract: The number of executions in the US dropped from 25 in 1987 to 11 in 1988, despite the US Supreme Court's rejection of challenges to the death penalty in 1986 and 1987. Chief Justice William H. Rehnquist endorses a proposal in Congress which limits inmates' federal appeal rights. For the past 13 years, the Supreme Court has decided that capital punishment is constitutional if states ensure legal safeguards against error and unfairness.

headline: Gambling Lawyer Loses Clients' Millions On Stocks
abstract: A Pittsburgh attorney with a gambling addiction was suspended from his practice after losing $2.9 million of his clients' money.

headline: Ertel back on campaign
abstract: After winning the Democatric primary last year, but losing out on the final vote, Allen Ertel is again running for PA Supreme Court.

headline: The consummate politician he isn't, but Phillips pushes his credentials
abstract: Walter M. Phillips Jr. is the Democratic candidate pitted against Republican incumbent Ronald D. Castille in the election for Philadelphia Attorney General. Phillips' individualistic persona has garnered both praise and criticism as he worked as an assistant US district attorney in New York and as a state prosecutor under PA Attorney General Robert Kane. Former PA Governor Milton J. Shapp created his federal job, a move which was criticized by the state court system and then-Philadelphia mayor Frank L. Rizzo.

headline: Allentown is ready to begin 'new era' in recycling
abstract: The Health Bureau of Allentown has formulated a plan to recycle newspapers and three types of waste. Betsy Levin, Allentown's recycling coordinator, said the recyclables will be collected once per week from the city's 35,000 households by the city's trash hauler, J.P. Mascaro Inc. Allentown Mayor Joseph Daddone, recently returning from a meeting of the National League of Cities in Atlanta, said that recycling is on the agenda of many cities throughout the country. Larry Grim, Mascaro's operations manager, said the recyclables will be transported to an interim dealer who will separate them and sell them to manufacturers to prepare them for recycling.

headline: High court again tests abortion law
abstract: A case of a pregnant Minnesota teenager has been brought before the US Supreme Court, following the court's recent decision to give states more authority on regulating abortions. A law in Minnesota requires pregnant teens to notify their parents or a court judge if they plan to get an abortion, which the girl's lawyers say violate her right-to-privacy. The case was taken to the Supreme Court with the help of the American Civil Liberties Union.

headline: Casey Pushes Plan to Hold Line on College Tuition Costs
abstract: In his 1989-1990 budget proposal, Gov. Casey called for a 7 percent increase in state funding for the 14 state-owned colleges in the PA System for Higher Education, Pennsylvania State University, the University of Pittsburgh, Temple University, and Lincoln University.  The increase could rise to 10 percent if the schools pledge to not raise tuition by more than $100 each year.

headline: MC Twp. board approves sewage proposal for plant
abstract: The Mount Carmel Twp. Board of Supervisors voted to approved a PennDOT sewage project proposal which would bring sewage service to a Foster Wheeler congeneration plant going into operation this fall.

headline: Rep Looking For Ride to Budget Fight
abstract: State Rep. David Richardson will have to find a ride to the annual budget battle, as his driver's license has been revoked due to a DUI incident.  His petition to get his license reinstated was not granted.

headline: Officer suspended
abstract: Police Officer Anthony O'Donnell was suspended by the Allentown City Council for attacking a prisoner in the police holding cell on October 3. O'Donnell's attorney, Wallace Eldridge, said plans for an appeal will be discussed with John Waldron, who is representing O'Donnell on two aggravated assault charges in connection with the incident. O'Donnell did not deny that he hit detainee Dennis McPherson during the testimony.

headline: Games bill expansion indicates legislatorrs had hidden intentions
abstract: Expresses the opinion that now that the small games of chance referendum has been passed, legislators are changing it to their advantage and adding things that would have prevented the people from voting for it in the first place.

headline: Ethics bill is sent to full House
abstract: The state House Appropriations Committee voted unanimously yesterday to send an ethics bill to the full House which would restrict legistors from accepting honoraria but would do little to stop such legislators from hiring their own family.

headline: The franking privilege
abstract: The editorial criticizes the the "franking privilege" given to US senators and congressmen, which allows them to send mass mail to every address in the US for free.  The mail is nearly always used for self-promoting pamphlets, and costs taxpayers over $113 million a year.

headline: And then there were some...
abstract: The article discusses a number of prominent figures involved in Centralia, PA, a town disrupted by a mine fire which started in 1962 and was never fully extinguished, according to the US Bureau of Mines. Centralia Mayor Ann Marie Devine criticized the PA Department of Environmental Resources for its indifference towards Centralia's situation, as well as the Columbia County Redevelopment Authority for treating the residents of Centralia who stayed as "second-class citizens." Devine also states that the DER was more active under former governor Dick Thornburgh than it is under current governor Robert Casey.

headline: High court limits scope of bias law
abstract: The US Supreme Court ruled that the 1866 law mandating fair treatment for blacks and minorities in job hiring does not protect them from racial harassment in the workplace, angering civil rights lawers and activists.

headline: Cheyney shows growth by 20%, tops in state
abstract: According to figures released by the Pennsylvania System of Higher Education, enrollment at Cheyney University in Thornbury increased by 20.6 percent from 1987 to 1989, after nearly losing accreditation in 1985. Cheyney University, a predominantly and historically black university, experienced a higher increase than the 4.3 percent of the 14 universities in the system. Vernon Clark, vice president of Cheyney, said the increase was partially due to an improvement in the university's marketing and support services for students. James H. McCormick, chancellor of the state system, commended Cheyney for its work in recruitment.

headline: Monroe experiencing 'positive' reaction to recycling efforts
abstract: Among townships and municipalities, members of the board of the Monroe County General Authority have found a "generally positive" response at attempts to institute a voluntary recycling program and facility.  The Authority is also planning on developing an incinerator in the East Stroudsburg area.

headline: Road painting suspended
abstract: Planned road painting Route 100 is suspended due to ongoing construction.  The painting will begin once the contruction is complete.

headline: Officers stretched ever thinner
abstract: A shortage of police officers in Philadelphia makes it difficult to respond to calls.  Vital community duties such as patrolling alleys and parks are dropped.

headline: Gov. Casey delivers bag of good economic news
abstract: Gov. Casey's announcement that $1 million in state money will be allocated to finishing a four-lane highway from Allegheny Township to the Freeport Bridge was good news to southwestern PA.  He also gave a check for $250,000 to the Alle-Kiski Valley Revitalization Corp., which will help the region attract new business.  The governor's attention to this area was a result of pressure from local and state government officials, as well as the Ludlum and Strongland Chambers of Commerce.

headline: Europe chain reaction unpredictable
abstract: At a recent visit to the Presque Isle State Park in Erie, US Senator Arlen Specter said that recent events in Eastern Europe have signaled a solid victory for Western-style Democracy. Specter, a member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the 1989 social changes in the Communist bloc could not have been predicted by the American intelligence community. Specter commended the US Congress and President George Bush for the accolades they have been giving Lech Walesa, Poland's Solidarity leader, and other Eastern European leaders.

headline: The IDA needs help
abstract: The editorial discusses the vacancy in the Executive Director position of the Delaware County Industrial Development Authority, which has been vacant for three months. The board believes that most qualified candidates are not interested in the position, while Thomas C. Rapone of Upper Darby, former Delco prison warden and currently a US marshal, has already all but filled the position. Rapone has a positive relationship with US Representative Curt Weldon, who is chairman of the Partnership for Economic Development. The editorial board expresses its belief that the IDA should not choose Rapone and should rather find a better-qualified candidate.

headline: Anglers Ready For Opening Trout Season
abstract: On Saturday morning, the trout fishing season will begin.  The PA Fish Commission has stocked more than 2.6 million trout in anticipation of opening- day.

headline: House Judiciary chief to back abortion curbs
abstract: The new chairman of the House Judiciary Committee says that he will make a point to hold hearings and bring forth measures which will be concerned with restricting the use of abortions.  This position stands in contrast to predecessor H. William DeWeese, who refused to consider anti-abortion legislation.

headline: Child- intervention program threatened
abstract: Early Intervention Programs Inc. may lose funding on June 1 because of changes by the state Education and Public Welfare departments.

headline: Municipal Waste To Be Tested
abstract: Special rail cars would be used in a proposal to bring several "test loads" of municipal waste to the Greentree Landfill in Elk County.  A permit must be obtained from the rail line.

headline: Route 30 site to get new warning sign
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) is placing another warning sign near the North Hills Road and Route 30 intersection in York. PA Representative Greg Snyder of York, along with Springettsbury Township officials, has urged PennDOT to place another sign there. Springettsbury Township officials reported that there had been 36 traffic accidents with two fatalities and 41 injuries at the intersection in the past two years.

headline: Official wants jailed MOVE members released
abstract: Philadelphia city managing director James S. White wants the PA Parole Board to rethink releasing imprisoned MOVE members to settle a feud between the city and the radical group. White requested this at a weekend symposium on the 1985 clash between police and MOVE members where 11 MOVE members died. White's comments followed a speech in which Alberta Africa of the group said that at least six of the 14 imprisoned members of the group are eligible for parole but will not receive it unless they are willing to leave MOVE.

headline: Group: Seven auto insurers redlining
abstract: The Pennsylvania Citizen Action group filed a complaint with the PA Insurance Department accusing seven of the state's biggest insurance companies of redlining by failing to offer automobile insurance in certain geographical locations, according to a study the group conducted in 1988. Jeffrey Blum, executive director of the group, said the city of Philadelphia is a location where redlining occurs, and he named insurance companies of Nationwide, Aetna Life and Casualty, Harleysville, Erie, Allstate, State Farm and Keystone. In the complaint, the group requested that state insurance commissioner Constance Foster investigate the charges.

headline: Ex- official lambastes Cabinet member
abstract: A former aide to Gov. Robert P. Casey has questioned the competence of General Services Secretary David Jannetta, saying he's in "over his head" and impedes the future of the administration.

headline: The mayor's malady
abstract: The editorial board suggests that Philadelphia mayor Wilson Goode take a vacation, in response to his second hospitalization in less than two weeks for an irregular heartbeat. The board cites his 14-hour work days as a possible cause for the mayor's condition, and lists his most recent Saturday schedule which included a reception for the American Red Cross.

headline: Area Landfill Proposal Draws Opposition
abstract: Opposition is mounting against a proposal to sell a private landfill to the 4-county Solid Waste Advisory Council.  The council is expecting to solicit proposals from private firms offerring disposal services to manage the Clarion County site.

headline: House limits abortion
abstract: The PA House of Representatives approved an anti-abortion bill sponsored by Representative Stephen Friend. The bill may provide a legal challenge for the US Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v. Wade ruling, and has caused outcry from state Representatives such as Vincent Hughes and Babette Josephs. The bill has been attacked by groups such as the American Civil Liberties Union and the National Abortion Rights Action League, while supported by other groups such as the National Right to Life Committee.

headline: City school officials get jump on metrics
abstract: Dr. Jerry Underwood, the director of the metrics programs office of the federal Dept. of Commerce, told a representative of the Reading School Board that by 1992 all federal agencies will be required to begin utilizing the metric system of measurement.

headline: Murphy updates Anchor on proposed bottle bill
abstract: US Congressman Austin Murphy plans to update Anchor Glass Container Corp. on a federal bill that would make beverage container deposits mandatory nationwide.  Anchor Glass and other glass companies oppose the bill, as recycling is preferable to the companies.

headline: School bus drivers to face re-licensing under new law
abstract: In compliance with the Commercial Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1986, bus drivers in PA will have to take classes and undergo examination to renew their licenses, according to a spokesman for state Representative Charles F. Nahill, Jr. Upper Dublin School District transportation director Norma Withsosky, along with others, have already begun preparations for testing their drivers. Springfield School District transportation director Wayne Johnson said the law would be expensive in the long run.

headline: Officials laud free- needle programs
abstract: Directors of AIDS prevention programs told a congressional panel yesterday that providing clean hypodermic needles to drug addicts has not increased drug abuse but has reduced needle sharing.

headline: Growing seen for wine stores
abstract: A state law which requires five percent of the Liquor Control Board's stores be devoted to premium wines could be financially risky, said LCB Chairman James A. Goodman.  Only two premium wine stores are currently open, and four more are in the planning stages.

headline: Excellence Awards
abstract: Governor Casey poses with the recipients of the Governor's Awards for Excellence, Riccardo Muti, Jerre Mangione, and Baruch Blumberg.

headline: The new Lee Atwater lies low
abstract: Harvey LeRoy "Lee" Atwater is the chairman of the Republican National Committee who came into politics as an intern in the office of Senator Strom Thurmond. He formerly was the campaign manager for President Bush. He is described as being a workaholic, and having a "single-minded pursuit of his calling." He was once involved in a scandal surrounding a race for the US House, in which a negative campaign was launched against candidate Tom Turnipseed for being a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People.

headline: Area ready for new water standards
abstract: Several Erie area communities governed by new water regulations will have little to no problems complying with new restrictions, as many communities aleady have good water treatment facilities.

headline: Human Relations Commission Targets AIDS Bias
abstract: The Philadelphia Commission of Human Relations will apportion part of its staff in the area of AIDS bias complaints.  It will review complaints in such areas as discrimination in housing, employment, and public accomodations, while also raising awareness about the disease.

headline: City schools do well in poll
abstract: According to a survey of elementary school parents, Harrisburg schools have a positive reaction from parents, despite the inability of the schools to score well on "pencil-and-paper" tests.

headline: Nesquehoning engineer 'urged' to turn over sewage project data
abstract: The Nesquehoning Borough Authority urged its engineer to provide aerial photos of the borough's sewage project. Authority solicitor William McDonald drafted a letter to John Krisa, attorney for the engineering firm R.P. Bielinski. Additionally, the Panther Valley School District is faced with creating a sewage system under pressure from the Department of Education.

headline: Schuylkill backs highway project
abstract: The Schuylkill County commissioners began to implement a highway project which will focus on pedestrian safety, enforcing the use of child restraints in cars, and edcuation against drunk driving.  Authorization was also given to Schuylkill County Sheriff Timothy Holden to reorganize his staff and an Assessment Board of Appeals was created to deal with new construction assesments for 1989 taxes.

headline: Officials piece together what happened
abstract: With the support of the Casey administration, officials from the PA Department of Corrections investigated the cause and escalation of the riot at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill. Ken Robinson, a spokesman for the department, said the cause is unknown. The riot, which lasted two days, necessitated the appearance of state and local police forces.

headline: Highlights of auto insurance plans
abstract: An overview of the various aspects of Gov. Casey's, the Republicans', and the Democrats' plans for auto insurance.

headline: Ex-official admits fund theft
abstract: Robert M. James pleaded guilty to stealing funds from the Northwest Strawberry Mension Neighborhood Advisory Council, for which he formerly served as an official. He was ordered to repay the funds to the council by Common Pleas Court Judge Charles Klein. The advisory council, which was shut down for failing to pay federal wage taxes, had two bank accounts; one for funds from United Way and private contributors and another for federal funds.

headline: The race for a seat on Pa.'s high court
abstract: A three- way contest for the Democratic nomination for the PA Supreme Court is marked by quiet intrigue, as judicial candidates must remain above the fray.

headline: Asbestos cleanup work continues
abstract: The cleanup of an asbestos contamination in the Blair County PennDOT building which started on April 17 is still underway.  The project is expected to cost about $2 million.

headline: Inflicting, prolonging pain
abstract: Melanie Long of Millersburg states that after having two miscarriages, she was informed that there is no legal or medical difference between "miscarriage" and "abortion." She states that the Abortion Control Act will have abominable implications.

headline: C-L eyes 'at-risk' program
abstract: The Cornwall-Lebanon School District has implemented a number of programs for students at risk of drug and alcohol abuse, as well as dropouts and teen suicide. Robert Mauer, assistant district administrator is a member of a team developing a "Student Assistance Program," Cornwall-Lebanon's newest. The school district is very active in preventative and education programs, such as active chapters of Students Against Drunk Driving and Mothers Against Drunk Driving at Cedar Crest High School.

headline: New grumblings on deer herd are sounded
abstract: The high concentration of deer in Bedford County is frustrating farmers, who lose crops to the animals, and motorists, with about 1500 deer killed on the roads last year.

headline: Senators Want Tougher DUI Standards
abstract: Three Republican senators on Tuesday introduced legislation designed to toughen penalties for driving under the influence of alcohol.

headline: O'Kicki subpoenaed in courtroom
abstract: A subpoena was issued to Cambria County Judge Joseph F. O'Kicki in his trial on 11 counts of public corruption. Judge Richard Grifo of Northampton County had a sheriff's deputy hand the subpoena to O'Kicki, whose defense attorney, Richard Galloway, had to reveal an "unfavorable" letter written to O'Kicki by one of his former secretaries. The secretary, Brenda Nasser, had been contacted by the PA Attorney General's Office about O'Kicki's behavior.

headline: Hiring: A problem for big and small business- Applicants' lack of skills decried
abstract: Two of every three Philadelphia area companies see a trend toward lower- quality job applicants, a problem that extends from entry- level jobs to the professional and management ranks, according to a survey.

headline: Extension co-op valuable resource for all
abstract: The Penn State Cooperative Extension, whose agents answer questions concerning topics from water quality to financing, has grown to influence each of the state's 67 counties.  In addition, through Penn State's Dept. of Agriculture, extension agents can consult with nearly any expert in any field.  Some issues the extension works on include nutrition, building human capital, and revitalizing rural America.

headline: The Reeher indictment
abstract: Kenneth Reeher, executive director of the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA), and a former top aide have been indicted on allegations they participated in a contract- kickback scheme.  The editorial board believes a resolution of the case will be bad either way.

headline: At least outhouses were cheap
abstract: Due to overbearing mandates by the federal government and the PA Dept. of Environmental Resources, the Lehighton Sewer Authority must either build a totally new sewer system or halt construction altogether.

headline: Justice O'Connor probes limits in abortion laws
abstract: US Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O'Connor stated that a Minnesota law on teenage pregnancy may unconstitutionally restrict the teens from getting abortions. O'Connor's remarks are especially significant, because the other court justices are divided 4-4 on issues of abortion. Janet Benshoof of the American Civil Liberties Union argued that the Minnesota law did place unconstitutional restrictions on minors, but does not think the justices want to use the case to "dismantle" the 1973 ruling in Roe v. Wade which legalized abortion.

headline: Classes set for Governor's School
abstract: Classes in the PA Governor's School for the Agricultural Sciences with begin in July at PSU for 64 of the state's finest students, who will attend the specialized school for free during the summer.  There are several Gov. Schools in the state for various fields.

headline: New study to delay Swatara Creek dam in Lebanon County
abstract: Construction of a dam in Lebanon County were suspended because of the Army Corps of Engineers' mandate of another environmental study.  The piece also explores the various other troubles the county has gone through during the planned building of the dam.

headline: Separate, not state, toll roads sought
abstract: Frustrated with delays in state highway projects, Republican Senators Earl Baker and D. Michael Fisher proposed legislation to allow local officials to build regional toll roads.

headline: O'Kicki, defense team angered by judge's rulings on testimony
abstract: Judge Richard Grifo, who is presiding over the corruption trial of Judge Joseph F. O'Kicki, angered the defense team by making different rulings when the defense tried on two occasions to attack the credibility of a prosecution witness, Brenda Nasser. O'Kicki faces 10 counts of corruption, including four counts of bribery, two of criminal coercion, one of open lewdness, and one charge of official oppression.

headline: Hiring: A problem for big and small business- Firms get tips on luring workers
abstract: Last week, a group of Philadelphia- area small- business owners gathered at a seminar sponsored by the Wharton Small Business Development Center to learn tips for recruiting and hiring workers.

headline: Ex-workers sue auditor general
abstract: Six ex-employees of state Auditor General Barbara Hafer are sueing her based on allegations that she fired them solely to fulfill campaign promises.2

headline: Three candidates drop out of Supreme Court race
abstract: Three candidates pulled out of the running for state Supreme Court. No one dropped out for the Superior or Commonwealth courts.

headline: Authority, DER See Eye-To-Eye
abstract: The state DER and the Warren County Solid Waste Authority are in agreement over the drilling of 5 test wells for a new waste disposal site.  This marks a change in relations between the two agencies, as the authority has  been frustrated with the DER of late.

headline: Justices Back Abortion Limits
abstract: In the wake of a Supreme Court decision lending its support to abortion-restricting laws, lawmakers in PA, NJ, and Delaware are preparing for battle over such laws, which will likely be proposed this fall after the summer recess.

headline: Classroom no place for ad campaigns
abstract: This editorial by York Daily Record executive editor Berl Schwartz addresses advertising in schools through Channel One, a daily news broadcast for secondary schools. Whittle Communications, an advertising firm, will provide video equipment for schools in exchange for broadcasting the show to students. Schwartz maintains that advertising to students in the school environment takes away from the classroom setting and provides an unspoken endorsement of the school towards the products being marketed.

headline: New-school ruling expected Monday
abstract: A ruling is expected on a group's attempt to halt the construction of a new elementary school wing.  They are contesting that building the wing would cause "irreparable damage" to the environment, though they have been accused as having environmental concerns seconrdary to their ideological opposition to the consolidation project.

headline: SEPTA Board to Hold Closed Session on Fare Litigation
abstract: Fare increases blocked by a judge's ruling may be imposed anyway by the Philadelphia- area mass transit agency.

headline: On the Front Lines Against Drugs
abstract: Charles R. Schuster, director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, said that although his job is to seek medical solutions to the drug problem, one must recognize that drug abuse has both individual and societal causes.  Dr. Schuster was reluctant to say that a cure for drug addiction could be found; instead, he said the real issue is getting a former drug addict into a position whereby they can contribute productively to society.

headline: House approves CAT Fund from insurers
abstract: Governor Csey supports the bill for motorists to be insured by private insurers instead of from the state's CAT Fund.  The CAT Fund is also known as the Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund for severely injured motorists.  Bills were also approved to lower Pennsylvania car insurance rates, especially for motorists in Philadelphia.

headline: Eye on state Senate
abstract: The state Senate Rules Committee approved a resolution last week to allow televised coverage of sessions.  The Ed. Board believes this is an improvement, but there should be fewer filming restrictions.

headline: The slimming surplus
abstract: While it's good that PA doesn't need to worry as much about its finances as other states, which are taking huge measures to compensate for huge debt, it's important to keep in mind that spending still needs to be controlled so that the state can remain at that threshhold.

headline: Balloons can kill marine lie, DER warns
abstract: The DER announced that launching helium-filled party ballons can endaged marine life, as the balloons often return to earth over the ocean, where they are sometimes mistaken for food.  The DER has called for voluntary cessation of such launches.

headline: Klan Members Upset About Jobs
abstract: Members of the Ku Klux Klan held a recruitment rally in Huntingdon, featuring two hours of speeches and a ceremonial cross-burning.  Many of the estimated 100 to 150 PA Klansmen have joined the Klan because minorities have been hired to their jobs.

headline: Clayton overruled in Gilhool case
abstract: A plan by Constance E. Clayton, Superintendent of the Philadelphia School District, to discipline 6 employees involved in a teacher's exam scandal has been overruled by the Philadelphia Board of Education. The scandal involves the teacher's exam taken by former state Education Secretary Thomas K. Gilhool, who applied for a teaching job in the school district and took his exam in a private office, not a standard test-taking auditorium. After his application was frozen, Gilhool filed a complaint with the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers and hired a lawyer.

headline: Newspapers trying to boost recycling effort
abstract: Although The Patriot-News has not been allocated any recylcing newspaper from its parent company Newhouse Newspapers, the industry does plan four trees for each tree it cuts down, and it is environmentallly-concious - the compnay removed all of the asbestos from its plant in the 1950s.  The Patriot-News takes readers concerns regarding recylcing seriously.

headline: SEPTA can't impose hikes during appeal, judge rules
abstract: SEPTA's attempts to raises transit fares were once again blocked, though the organization is desparate for extra revenue to compensate for its continuing losses.

headline: Only half of felons go to jail, study shows
abstract: A recent study, undertaken by the Justice Dept., found that 46% of the nation's 583,000 felons convicted in state courts were given prison sentences, and 67% of those were actually locked up: 46% in state prisons and 21% in local jails.  The study also found that 75 of the largest counties, although only comprising 37% of the nation's population, accounted for nearly one-half of crimes reported to the police.

headline: House Committee Approves Package of Insurance Bills
abstract: The state House Insurance Committee approved a package of bills which will, among other things, raise penalties for uninsured drivers, expand insurance options available to drivers, and increase penalties for fraudulant insurance claims.  One bill would also create the Philadelphia Automobile Insurance Authority.

headline: Faulty machines could spew out bonus lottery tickets
abstract: A sarcastic attack against State Rep. Thomas Petrone's idea of legalizing video poker games and having them dispense lottery ticket certificates intead of cash.  The writer sarcastically suggests many other times to give out lottery tickets, i.e. MAC machines, skeeball, and vending machines.

headline: The state House today approved legislation that would reauthorize the state Civil Service Commission for another 10 years.
abstract: The state House today approved legislation that would reauthorize the state Civil Service Commission for another 10 years.

headline: Bethlehem officials request water conservation
abstract: Bethlehem officials announced a drought warning in hopes of avoiding mandatory water restrictions.  This would call for residents to voluntarily monitor their water use.  Another problem arose in which there was a foul taste and odor in the water due to an algae buildup.  However, the water is safe to drink.

headline: Koop's decision on abortion study was right
abstract: Surgeon General C. Everett Koop's refusal to manufacture negative data on women who decide to have an abortion is remarkable, especially considering what must have been significant pressure from the Reagan administration to do so.  This action stands in contrast to Dick Thornburgh's "prostitution of himself" concerning abortion.

headline: Close 5 city schools, study says
abstract: The Pennsylvania Economy League released a report which recommends that two city high schools, two elementary schools, and the North Scranton Intermediate School should be closed.  The recommended closings are a result of demographic changes, reduced enrollments, and a decrease in birthrates.  The closings could also positively affect taxes.

headline: NJ says Philadelphia debris going to river shoreline
abstract: The results of an investigation by the New Jersey Division of Criminal Justice concluded that antiquated sewer systems, slopping trash hauling, and poor street cleaning in Philadelphia were sending trash that washed ashore along the Delaware River in New Jersey last summer. NJ Attorney General Peter N. Perretti Jr. did not criticize the cities of Philadelphia or Camden, and instead blamed today's "disposable society." Commissioner Christopher J. Daggett of the New Jersey  Department of Environmental Protection said public education is the key to reducing the waste. Philadelphia officials have not yet seen the report and are wary of its results, but Streets Commissioner Alexander L. Hoskins said he and other city officials are willing to meet with New Jersey authorities.

headline: SEPTA order releases tokens
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) passed an emergency order to purchase 500,000 additional tokens because of complaints by SEPTA riders and community groups that the agency was hoarding tokens to make passengers pay the straight fare. The Committee for a Better North Philadelphia, the Association of Community Organizations for Reform Now, and the Consumer Education and Protective Association are suing SEPTA over its proposed fare hike. SEPTA general manager Louis J. Gambaccini said that passengers, not the authority, are the ones hoarding the tokens. Steps are going to be taken to deal with the problem.

headline: Open Drug Market Draws Shoppers From Suburbs
abstract: Labeled by police as the most dangerous neighborhood in Philadelphia, West Kensington is an open-air market for cocaine, heroin, crack, and marijuana.  Within the 25th Police District, there were 5,804 major crimes reported according to the FBI and 3,144 drug-related arrests.

headline: House Panel Approves Protection Proposal for Used Car Buyers
abstract: A state House panel approved legislation to protect consumers who unknowingly buy faulty used cars.

headline: Feeding the voters junk
abstract: The editorial board is disgusted with "dirty politics," such as negative campaigning and mudslinging. They cite the recent gubernatorial elections in New Jersey and Virginia, as well as the 1988 presidential election, as examples of elections plagued by dirty politics. They cite Gannon University professor Dr. David Kozak's talk at a local Young Men's Christian Association meeting, who said that negative campaigning can lead to alienating voters and deterring good candidates.

headline: The state Senate is poised to approve a resolution allowing television coverage of its sessions, but it is not the bold step forward that some senators pretend it is.
abstract: The state Senate is poised to approve a resolution allowing television coverage of its sessions, but tight camera angles and a prohibition against panning the Senate floor will cause much to go unseen.

headline: Bill would target cleanup of bay
abstract: PA Representative Samuel Morris, chairman of the House Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee, said efforts are underway to help bring Pennsylvania into compliance with the tri-state Chesapeake Bay Agreement. The bay cleanup campaign aims to reduce harmful nutrient runoff into the bay by 40 percent by 2000. Efforts are being made to control industry and the committee is reviewing potential bills to affect farmers.

headline: Labels for lyrics? Parents should be aware of what their children are listening to
abstract: PA Representative Ron Gamble of Allegheny County is the author of this opinion piece addressing the House Bill he proposed that addresses the problem of graphically violent musical recordings that are aimed at young people. Gamble argues that the proposed bill, requiring warning labels be placed on offensive recordings, is an efficient way of solving the problem, but he also maintains that it may not be the only solution.

headline: CMU, Penn State receive $1.2 million for science
abstract: Carnegie Mellon and Penn State universities were both awarded with $1.2 million grants by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.  The money is to be used undergrad education in biology and related sciences.

headline: Officials: Drought emergency near
abstract: The Delaware River Basin Commission said it would declare a drought emergency and ban nonessential uses of water unless it rains in the next few days.  Commission oficial fear that it may be the most severe drought in the history of the basin.

headline: SEPTA sets hearing as step to reimposing increase
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority announced it would hold public hearings on January 3 about its planned to once again increase in fares. In a lawsuit brought on by 3 community groups including the Consumer Education and Protective Association, the PA Supreme Court ordered SEPTA to roll back its fare increases earlier in the month, which SEPTA general manager Louis J. Gambaccini has said could create a $4 million deficit by the end of the year. Arlin M. Adams, a retired judge from the Third US Circuit Court of Appeals will preside over the hearings.

headline: Opponents set for fight over prison
abstract: A meeting was held in Mont Alto to discuss PA Governor Robert Casey's plan to build a maximum-security prison on a 137-acre site in South Mountain. Local residents complained that the prison would prevent people from enjoying the area for activities such as wilderness recreation and hunting. Furthermore, they argued that the prison would bring unwanted parties into the area, namely families of inmate who might supply drugs.

headline: House passes bills on auto insurance targeting fraud
abstract: The state House approved more bills concerning auto insurance yesterday, adding to those passed on to the Senate last week as well.  Most of the components of Gov. Casey's insurance reform package have been accepted.

headline: Flaherty challenges union vote
abstract: Pittsburgh City Controller Thomas Flaherty challenged the results of an election which resulted in the United Steelworkers being designated the bargaining representative for Flaherty's professional employees. Flaherty and his attorney Thomas May petitioned along with the PA Labor Relations Board, since he claims that the election was based on 20 professional auditors in his office, when he had 19 professional auditors at the time of the vote. Anabell Kinney, a union organizer, called Flaherty a hypocrite since he promoted himself as a labor-friendly candidate.

headline: The wishy-washy political machine
abstract: Rita McMillan, a committeewoman for Wilkes-Barre, criticized a smear campaign against Dolores Seacrist, who was running for Director of the Wilkes-Barre Area School Board. However, McMillan herself conducted a smear campaign against Seacrist's opponent, Sally Jervis. Seacrist lost to Jervis in the Democratic primaries, then cross-filed and appeared on the Republican ballot.

headline: Builders unleashed by state
abstract: The state has lifted a ban on new sewage hookups to the Oaks treatment plant, spurring a lot of new development in the area.

headline: Lebanon City Council turns down idea for anti-obscenity ordinance
abstract: The Lebanon County chapter of the American Family Association requested that City Council enact a local anti-obscenity ordinance which would give police greater flexibility in investigating alleged violations.  However, members of council argued that, by following state law rather than local ordinances, penalties would be stiffer.

headline: College approves free birth control
abstract: A committee of the Gettysburg College Board of Trustees has approved a proposal to provide complimentary contraceptives to students through the college health center. The school, which is affiliated with the Evangelical Lutheran Church of America, has faced some opposition in the new proposal that must be approved by interim college President Charles E. Anderson before going into effect. The students interviewed about the program approve of the program.

headline: Oil spill fouls Delaware River
abstract: Oil leaking from a tanker that ran aground in the Delaware River is posing a potential threat to fish and other wildlife in the area, though environmentalists say there will likely be very little long-term effects of the spill.  The cause of the accident is under investigation.

headline: SEPTA Slowed by Judge: Increase Denied & Refunds Owed
abstract: The fare increase for SEPTA has been denied by a Commonwealth Court judge.  Refunds will be given to commuters.

headline: Our readers insist: no taxes to uncrowd state prisons
abstract: The article outlines the opinions of readers of The Reporter that responded to a telephone survey about whether or not they are willing to pay more taxes to alleviate overcrowding in prisons. The majority stated that they are not willing to pay more and provided other solutions instead. Harry Wood of Lansdale suggested that criminals be placed into extra military installations. Marian Kreider of Colmar said she would like to see only violent criminals sent to prison, while white-collar criminals and those that commit non-violent crimes should pay full restitution plus court costs and punitive damages. Other readers made suggestions as well.

headline: House proposal to replace CAT slated for vote
abstract: State Rep. William Lloyd Jr. is confident that his proposal to replace the CAT Fund will pass the state House easily with bipartisan support.  House Republicans and Democrats appeared to finally reach a compromise, agreeing on a voluntary non-pooled catastrophic insurance system which would cost approximately twice as much as the $24 state-run CAT Fund.

headline: Flood of damage at Capitol
abstract: A window left open over the weekend in PA Senator Vincent J. Fumo's office resulted in a frozen pipe bursting into a flood in the Capitol building. The flood most affected the Senate Republicans' data processing headquarters, in a basement two floors below Fumo's office. The flood caused a water shutoff that put out of order 19 bathrooms in the main Capitol building. Dean Roth, a computer consultant to the Senate Republicans, said numerous computers, printers, and disk drives were damaged in the flood. Computers and a printer in the office of PA Senator Eugene F. Scanlon were also damaged.

headline: The Young Turks' Crusade
abstract: Former state senator Richard Snyder writes on the state of the GOP leaders in the US House, and details some of the obstacles they will have to overcome.

headline: Burning question: How far will mine fire go?
abstract: A mine fire that has been burning for 25 years will soon force more families to relocate, some for the second time.  There is some debate as to whether more should be done to try to put it out.

headline: Legislature given new latitude
abstract: Some legislators are looking forward to the fall session, when the legislature will again consider abortion restrictions now that the Supreme Court has allowed states more freedom to restrict the practice.  PA will likely enact significant restrictions, as the lawmakers have traditionally been pro-life.

headline: College help on the way
abstract: Within Gov. Casey's proposed budget for the 1989-1990 fiscal year was a measure which would help families purchase reduced PA general obligation bonds which will mature by the time tution bills need to be paid.  A similar proposal will be promoted by Senate President Pro Tem Robert Jubelirer.

headline: One small step toward cleaning up the bay
abstract: A bill in the state House would prohibit discharging phosphate detergents into the Susquehana River, which is not the main cause of pollution in the river and the Chesapeake Bay, but at least it provides a small help.  Agricultural runoff is the main cause of phosphate pollution in the waterway.

headline: Single- Engine Plane Runs Out of Fuel, Crashes
abstract: A Vermont pilot was in satisfactory condition after his plane ran out of fuel and crashed in Adams County, state police and hospital officials said.

headline: Outrunning drugs
abstract: Melvin Wingate, a former radio show host and current social service agent, holds track meets for inner-city youths who are susceptible to the influence of drugs. He believes that the best way to keep children away from drugs is to give them something else to do. Wingate's efforts have garnered praise from many, including Harrisburg City Councilwoman Sherri D. Levin.

headline: House rejects conference committee insurance promise
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey praised the House's rejection of a compromise that would have cut car insurance rates in Pennsylvania by at least 10 percent but had other negative effects on Pennsylvanians. The House voted against the bill that had been worked out by a conference committee earlier in the day on Tuesday that would have cute rates by 10 percent by cutting the amount of mandatory coverage motorists carry. The legislators were trying to push a bill to Governor Casey before their winter recess, which will no longer be possible now that the House has rejected the proposal.

headline: For a long-embattled lawyer, vindication
abstract: Robert B. Surrick, who as a member of the state's Judicial Inquiry and Review Board fought for reopening an investigation against state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen, was vindicated in the Supreme Court's ruling that he had not breached the review board's confidentiality rules.

headline: Thomas Nolan, former leader in state Senate
abstract: Thomas M. Nolan, the former majority leader of the state Senate, died of emphysema in Bradock General Hospital.

headline: Car Show move stirs Butler Twp. Concern
abstract: The proposed movement of the Carlisle Car Show to Butler Township has garnered opposition from residents, who have environmental and logistical concerns.  Township Supervisor Jay Thomas comments on the fact that localgovernment has no power over the state agencies involved in the move.

headline: Local activists on both sides say issue will end up in court
abstract: Kathy Morris, president of the Lebanon County chapter of Pennsylvanians for Human Life, believes that PA's new bill restricting abortions will be challenged, perhaps even taken to the Supreme Court.  Doctor Julie Ann Allender of the National Organization for Women and Planned Parenthood agrees. The bill passed in state House and is expected to be signed by PA Governor Robert Casey.

headline: Community: College Senior spurs Annville-area recycling
abstract: Thanks to a Lebanon College senior, community leaders through an ad hoc committee are seeking ways to begin a volunteer recylcing program.

headline: Over due
abstract: The editorial board expresses its approval with the Scranton City Council's ordinance restricting landfills and garbage transfer stations, but its disapproval with the fact that the council took so long to pass such an ordinance. They believe the current ordinance needs refinement, but will suffice for the time being.

headline: Some Share-A-Riders to end up on buses
abstract: Senior citizens may have to take a bus now as it was decided that those living within three blocks of a bus stop must take the bus.

headline: Owens: More prisons needed when drug war cranks up
abstract: According to PA Corrections Commissioner David S. Owens Jr., Pennsylvania's prison population is growing by 10 percent per year. Owens said more prisons and other facilities, such as regional Driving While Under the Influence centers, are needed. Owens cited the administration of PA Governor Robert Casey as moving in a positive direction of more facilities. Another attendee at the meeting with the Times Publishing Co. editorial board, Secretary of Labor and Industry Harris Wofford, mentioned alternative punishments for different people, such as restitution, community service, welfare-to-work programs, and other such programs.

headline: House Takes Up Insurance; Senate Looks At Export Bills
abstract: This week the state House will debate auto insurance proposals, while the Senate will look at bills designed to increase state exports.  Discussions on the state budget will be ongoing as well.

headline: For Supreme Court- Eunice Ross in the Democratic Party
abstract: The Inquirer endorses Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Eunice Ross for a seat on the Supreme Court.

headline: Thornburgh & FBI Chief Have Their Differences
abstract: Amid reports of tensions with Attorney General Dick Thornburgh, FBI Director William Sessions has stopped get-to-know-you breakfasts with congressmen.  Some speculate that Thornburgh would like to replace the FBI director.

headline: Carbon planners support stand against tire pyrolysis plant
abstract: The Carbon County Planning Commission reiterated its stance that it was opposed to the reapplication of the Keystone Carbon and Oil to build a tire reclamation facility in the Packer Township.  The Commission is concerned that the facility would contaminate the Hudsondale Reservoir System, from which 40 percent of the Hazelton community receives its potable water.

headline: Local, national lawmakers predict easy passage of flag-burning ban
abstract: Legislative leaders predict that if a flag-burning ban amendment came to the states to ratify, PA would be one of the first to approve it.  Very few politicians oppose the amendment, as they say it would be a restriction of the First Amendment right to freedom of expression.

headline: CREDITORS NOT PLEASED
abstract: Financial news concerning creditors of Allegheny International of Pittsburgh and Youngwood Electronic Metals of Greensburg was reported.  It was noted that researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University are conducting new reseach into steel making process.

headline: PA firm charged with burying toxic waste
abstract: The PA Attorney General's Office charged Bear Automotive Service Equipment Co., a local auto parts firm, and two former employees with illegally burying about 1,650 gallons of hazardous waste on the company's property from January 1984 through December 1985, according to Jack Lewis, spokesperson for the Attorney General's Office. Charles Sampson, former maintenance supervisor for the company, and Clay Gregory, former company vice president, have been charged with illegal management of hazardous waste, unlawful use of land as a waste-disposal area, and illegal dumping. The investigation was prompted by a PA Department of Environmental Resources referral.

headline: Springetts residents fighting to keep road open
abstract: Residents are opposing the closing of a short stretch of road which allows access to East Market Street, as it would increase congestion on other already congested roads.

headline: PA prison rules ignored, deaf prisoner says
abstract: Larry Hockenberry, a deaf prison at the State Correctional Institution at Pittsburgh, has been requesting from the PA Department of Corrections a number of special services he says he needs, and has been granted none. Hockenberry, who is deaf, mute, and has spinal bifida, began asking for a sign-language interpreter to help him in counseling, disciplinary hearings, and training and educational sessions, and was turned down. After writing to the National Center for Law and the Deaf in Washington, DC, lawyer E. Elaine Gardner filed a federal civil rights complaint on Hockenberry's behalf to the US Department of Health and Human Services. Pittsburgh lawyer Jere Krakoff is now working on Hockenberry's behalf against the PA Corrections Department, which has failed to follow its equality policies.

headline: House turns focus on bills to revamp car insurance laws
abstract: The state House is now focusing on auto insurance bills, including Gov. Casey's proposal and Robert O'Donnell's bill.  Auto insurance reform is attempting to decrease premiums while finding an acceptable equilibrium for coverage and personal rights.

headline: Fourteen Congressmen On Fact-Finding Mission Meet Mubarak
abstract: 14 US congressmen led by William Gray III on a "fact-finding mission" met with President hosni Mubarak of Egypt to discuss the International Monetary Fund and the US' continued support to Egypt both militarily and economically.

headline: Thornburgh nominee may face trouble
abstract: US Attorney General Richard Thornburgh's nominee for assistant attorney general for civil rights will face scrutiny during his confirmation hearings due to some potential ethics violations.  Thornburgh also surprised the Bush administration by announcing the nomination on his own, while Bush was touring the Far East.

headline: War on Drugs: More funds needed, Specter told
abstract: Local and state law officials told U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter that they need more resources to fight the war on drugs.

headline: Mandatory retirement for Pa. judges upheld
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled, 5-1, that a mandatory age retirement provision for judges which was approved by voters as an amendment to the state constitution was constitutional.  Lawyers arguing against the provision said that it violated the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment and that it was tantamount to age discrimination.

headline: Curtin School proves appropriate
abstract: The choice of Curtin Middle School for the town meeting with PA Governor Robert Casey was deemed appropriate, since the school is named for former governor Andrew G. Curtin. The school's sports teams are nicknamed "The Governors."

headline: PA gets tough on W.S. dump
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources has set a 90-day deadline for an acceptable closure plan for the West Side Landfill, said DER spokesman Mark Carmon. The DER also made demands in a letter to the landfill authority for a permanent plan for liquid runoff within 30 days, leachate pumped out of an on-site lagoon within 30 days, and a permit modification application should the authority choose to reopen its transfer station. The Plymouth Township dump has been shut down since mid-1987, and the DER was not satisfied with a closure plan submitted by the landfill authority in March 1987. Authority board chairman Bill Evans said he was frustrated with the demands of the DER's letter and criticized its timing.

headline: State to fund computerized weather system for private pilots
abstract: Thanks to the Pennsylvania Dept. of Transportation, PA will become the first state to fund a computerized system which will give pilots the latest up-to-date weather conditions available.  The new $440,000 system will be maintained via a state tax on jet fuel.

headline: Pa. bill seeks suspension of licenses in drug cases
abstract: A bill that passed the House Judiciary Committee would allow judges to suspend the driver's licesnse of anyone convicted of a drug offense.  It would also make it illegal to sell drug-free urine, which could be used to dodge a positive drug test.

headline: House votes to cut car insurance rates
abstract: Surprisingly, the House passed legislation to decrease insurance rates by 25% for every person in PA, in addition to accepting much of Gov. Casey's proposal yesterday.  The rollback and Casey's plan passed overwhelmingly, with only a few proposals failing to pass, as some lawmakers are counting on the Senate to edit the bills.

headline: Fourth draft of Casey trip to Uniontown is released
abstract: A fourth draft tentative schedule of Gov. Robert Casey's upcoming visit to Uniontown for his "Capital for a Day" program was released Monday at a planning meeting.

headline: Time may be right for changing tort laws
abstract: After 5 failures in 10 years, the PA Legislature might be able to pass legislation reforming tort laws, those which deal with court-written liability by writing guidelines into its statutes. Michael C. McLaughlin of the PA Task Force on Product Liability says that there is a lot of pressure on the Legislature this session. If passed by the House Labor Relations and Judiciary Committee, it will face the PA Senate, which recently shot down PA Governor Robert Casey's plan to limit rising auto rates by limiting court action.

headline: Warden suspended in Wake of Prison Guards' charges about riots
abstract: PA Corrections Commissioner David S. Owens Jr. suspended Robert Freeman, superintendent of the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill. This decision came as a result of the prison administration's ignorance of guards' requests to fix broken lockboxes and control panels, which allowed the inmates to escape during the second day of rioting. Additionally, the prison administration ignored guards' reports that inmates were telling them of a planned riot.

headline: Mayview refuses to accept any more abortion protesters
abstract: Allegheny Co. will no longer be allowed to house arrested abortion protesters in Mayview Hospital, as the hospital had originally agreed to house them temporarily, not permanently.  The county doesn't have room for the 48 protesters in county jailhouses.

headline: Cuts may threaten jobs of IU teachers
abstract: Planned cuts for special education in the state budget are threatening both the education of many special needs children and the jobs of some of their teachers.  Efforts by several groups are underway to convince the state to continue funding special education at an appropriate level.

headline: PA probes water woes
abstract: During a routine, quarterly water quality test by the PA Department of Environmental Resources, a coli form level 23 times the maximum allowed was discovered at Concord Elementary School in the Garnet Valley School District. Dan Norin, sanitarian for DER, said the lapse in time between the test and when the school district was notified of the problem may have violated the Safe Drinking Water Act that says that a water-testing company must notify its client of an elevated coliform level within an hour of receiving the test results. Thomas Czop, manager of operations for the district's well testing company, C.E. Moore Environmental Consultants of Exton, said the notification of the heightened coliform level could have occurred more quickly.

headline: Strongly worded study calls for better trolleys
abstract: A yearlong SEPTA and city study recommended spending $80 million to $200 million to upgrade trolley Route15, Route 23, and Route 56.  A "Transit First" policy was advocated by the study's authors.

headline: Packed prisons a powderkeg
abstract: Montgomery County Prison and Bucks County Prison are overcrowded by about 70% over capacity. Montgomery County assistant warden Dennis Molyneaux and Bucks County warden Arthur Wallenstein stated that prison overcrowding is not the cause of disturbances, but overcrowding does exacerbate tensions in prisons. Neither prison experienced disturbances as a result of the recent riots at the Camp Hill state prison.

headline: Icahn filing fuels speculation
abstract: Investor Carl Icahn, who owns Trans World Airlines, Inc., is seeking federal approval to increase his stake in USX Corp., but it is doubtful that he will attempt to takeover the energy and steel company, according to analyst Gregory Drahuschak of Butcher & Singer in Pittsburgh. USX Chairman Charles Corry said that he was given no indication from Icahn about Icahn's plans for the stocks, but speculation is that the purpose of the increased shareholding is to encourage Corry to speed up restructuring or sell major assets of the company.

headline: Freind 'a real statesman'
abstract: Carolyn Bergey of Harleysville expresses her support for PA State Representative Stephen Freind, describing him as 'a real statesman of great moral fortitude.'

headline: To Run or Not to Run?  Nunn Maintains He's Not Interested
abstract: As chairman of the DNC and the leading Democrat who helped kill President Bush's first nominee for the posittion of Secretary of Defense, the Georgian Senator Sam Nunn has been at the center of many partisan attacks.  He contends that he is not interested in a presidential bid in 1992.

headline: We fight drug use, too
abstract: The writer is responding to comments by state Rep. Raymond Bunt, who said that giving anti-drug funds to social service agencies "is like throwing money down a rat hole."  The writer contends that money given to the agency she directs is well-used, and a minimal amount is spent on administration, contrary to the rep.'s allegations.

headline: Memo to Legislature: they vote
abstract: The editorial board states that PA's new Abortion Control Act violates women's rights, echoing state Senator Vincent Fumo's description of the bill as a "national disgrace." The board describes the act as "a many-sided attempt to legally coerce women and their doctors." The board implies that women voters will retaliate in future elections.

headline: Dallas museum filling void for Kennedy mourners
abstract: The Sixth Floor Exhibit, a museum in the Texas School Book Depository, depicts events surround the assassination of President John F. Kennedy. The public approves of the exhibit, but Senator Edward Kennedy opposed it, preferring that the public remember JFK's life, not his death. The exhibit includes information on the Warren Commission's report and hundreds of photographs.

headline: pa-earn-chambers
abstract: Chambers Development Company of Pittsburgh, which collects solid waste and recycling, reported earnings for 1988 of $20.7 million.

headline: Study: highways aid local growth
abstract: According to a report released by the PA Highway Information Association, the newly-constructed Route 220 has brought economic growth to Blair and Bedford counties. Examples include increased retail sales and more companies investing. The PHIA suggested the construction of an "economic generator highway system" in the state.

headline: PA-Five Squad Trial
abstract: The federal racketeering trial of the Five Squad, an elite group designed to fight drug trafficking in Philadelphia, is coming to a close.  The five narcotics officers are charged with stealing more than $400,000 from drug dealers.

headline: Impact of Proposition 103 Goes Beyond Rate Rollback
abstract: A court decision last week upholding most of Proposition 103 is turning California into a laboratory for overhauling the nation's insurance laws.

headline: From Harrisburg: Women Still Languishing
abstract: After the 1988 elections, women held only 6.7% of the seats in the General Assembly: 15 out of the 202 members in the House and 2 of the 50 members in the Senate.  Such numbers place PA, in terms of female legislator representation, ahead of only Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi, and Kentucky.

headline: Top commissioner pay to be $52,269 in 1995
abstract: The salary for the chairman of the county commissioners for Dauphin County will increase to $52,269 as a result of a public hearing on county officials' pay scale. Chief County Clerk Jeffret T. Haste stated that some row officers requested initial pay increases, while Commissioner Russell L. Sheaffer said that the salary increases were necessary to account for inflation. The highest paid official is the district attorney, whose salary of $79,000 is set by the PA Legislature.

headline: Why wait for guns? Ask the Bear
