abstract: This editorial compares the amount of time that the Justice Department said it will take to study methods through which convicted felons might be identified when they try to purchase handguns, three years according to US Attorney General Dick Thornburgh, with the one month that Thornburgh says is too long for current technology to investigate a gun customer's criminal record before he or she can purchase a gun. The editors cite Jim Brady, the security guard who took a bullet for President Ronald Reagan in 1981, who supported a waiting period for the purchase of a handgun.

headline: National black caucus of state legislators set to discuss state of affairs
abstract: Among the attendees of the upcoming meeting of the National Black Caucus of State Legislators is PA Representative David P. Richardson. The meeting will include discussions on drugs, abortion, and the recent US Supreme Court rulings on affirmative action. The number of black state legislators has increased from 168 in 1970 to a current 408.

headline: Delaware has lowest student loan default rate
abstract: Delaware has the lowest default rate for fiscal year 1988 student loans at 2.7%, compared to PA's 8.6% rate and the national average of 10.4%, according to the US Department of Education. Maria Taylor, program administrator for the Delaware Postsecondary Education Commission, said that Delaware ranked fourth for the lowest default rate in fiscal year 1987. Leo Salazar, spokesman for US Department of Education's Office of Postsecondary Education praised the schools, lenders and state for working together.

headline: Pass acid rain law, state aide tells Congress
abstract: James K. Hambright, director of PA's Bureau of Air Quality Control, testified before a House subcommittee in Washington that Congress must pass a law to curb acid rain.

headline: Superhighways are made for 65 miles an hour
abstract: The writer contends that raising the speed limit on the PA Turnpike would be beneficial, saying the roads and cars are made for those speeds, and going faster would force people to pay more attention, which is a major factor in many accidents.

headline: Panel asks changes in appointing attorneys
abstract: A judicial committee has recommended changes in the system used by Allegheny County to appoint private defense attorneys for poor criminal defendants. The committee recommended limiting cases assigned to any individual lawyer to 20 a year so as to equalize the number of cases these lawyers receive. Common Please Judge Robert E. Dauer said he expects the 16 judges in that division to adopt the plan. The judicial committee said that over $760,000 was spent in 1988 on court appointments in the criminal division with a large disparity in the amount of money received by a small number of attorneys.

headline: Industry reports weekly production
abstract: According to the American Iron and Steel Institute, domestic steel production totaled 1,664,000 net tons during the week ending December 16, 1989, down 3.5 percent from the previous week. The weeks' production represented 74.8 percent of the industry's domestic capacity. Domestic steel production is 1.2 percent below last year's production at this time, AISI said.

headline: Fumo backs appointment of state appeals judges
abstract: Sen. Vincent J. Fumo proposed a constitutional amendment yesterday which would implement a merit system of selection of Supreme, Superior, and Commonwealth Court judges.  Merit selection, or selection through appointment, would replace the current method of popular election of judges.

headline: Top- paid state official to be indicted
abstract: The state's highest paid official and one of his former top aides at the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency will be charged with corruption- related offenses in a federal grand jury indictment.

headline: Woman sentenced in drug sale
abstract: A Pittsburgh woman who pleaded guilty to selling heroin to former suburban Wilkinsburg Councilman Patrick O'Leary has been sentenced to three to six years in prison and two years' probation.

headline: 'Neanderthals' in the legislature?
abstract: This opinion by Brad Bumstead, Harrisburg bureau chief for Gannett News Service, cites the "Neanderthal" label that some pro-choice leaders call the Pennsylvania Legislature since it approved the Abortion Control Act of 1969. Because of limits placed on abortion in PA in a recent law signed by PA Governor Robert P. Casey, such as spousal notification, the banning of sex-selection abortions, and a 24-hour waiting period, some pro-choice leaders have called PA a "Neanderthal state" in its position towards women and abortion.

headline: Delay cuts at schools, group asks
abstract: The Coalition for Quality in Special Education is asking Gov. Casey to delay his funding cuts for special education for a year while creating a task force to help resolve special ed concerns in that year.

headline: Paying the price
abstract: Stephen E. Artman refutes a claim made in a previous letter that most beer and soda that produces trash along highways is consumed by lower-income families. He also commends PA Governor Robert Casey on reducing the amount of out-of-state solid waste that is disposed in PA.

headline: Surplus money could be used for potholes
abstract: The writer supports using some of the $140 million surplus for highway maintenance, namely filling in potholes and paving roads.

headline: Panel OKs subpoenas of prison riot guards
abstract: The PA Senate Judiciary Committee voted in favor of giving's its chairman, Senator Stewart Greenleaf, the power to subpoena prison guards at the Camp Hill state prison. PA Governor Robert Casey named a 3-member panel to investigate the riots alongside Senate and House investigations. Greenleaf denied allegations that the committee had treated Corrections Commissioner David S. Owens unfairly.

headline: Insurance Commissioner Sees Annual Increases
abstract: Insurance Commissioner Constance Foster said that comprehensive automobile insurance reform is needed for customers to see a real reduction of insurance rates.  The governor will propose an insurance package which will call for a $10,000 liability threshold for lawsuits, the pooling of insurance to reduce costs, and changes in the filing of rates with the Insurance Dept.

headline: Fumo Is Master of the Game of Politics
abstract: State Sen. Vincent J. Fumo is often labeled as an insider and powerhouse, using the weight of his state staff of 30 and stature as the minority chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee to influence how much state money the city of Philadelphia receives in each annual state budget.

headline: Top spot on Democratic ballot for Supreme Court goes to Ertel
abstract: Allen E. Ertel has the first spot on the ballot for the Supreme Court primaries.  However, he is not the endorsed candidate by the Democratic party since last year's election cancellation when he felt that Gov. Casey should have been sued for scheduling last year's elections on an even nymbered year, which goes against the constitution.  Other candidates for the Supreme Court, the Superior Court, and the Commonwealth Court were listed as well.

headline: York County Prison crowding seen despite new units
abstract: Although 118 inmates will be moved into minimum-security modular units tomorrow, the main prison building will still be forced to house 400 inmates - nearly twice its designed capacity.  According to early estimates, a permanent expansion would cost approximately $15.5 million.

headline: Not enough minorities get good jobs, some say
abstract: The article describes the employment situations of several members of minorities. According to the US Department of Labor, people between the ages of 16 and 19 in 1988 faced a 13.7 percent unemployment rate in Dauphin County. Reamus Jones of the Central PA Minority Business Association says there is inherent discrimination in the job selection process against black and Hispanic men. Minority women supposedly have an easier time finding good jobs.

headline: District suspends set-asides
abstract: The Pennsylvania Board of Education has suspended its programs that set aside a portion of school district contracts for minority and female-owned businesses. The Board ordered that a new plan be devised to meet standards set by federal courts of US District Judge Charles R. Weiner last month, and it directed school officials to complete a report in 60 days on race and sex-neutral means by which to increase minority and female participation in school district contracting. School district spokesman William C. Thompson said contracts and bids have been put on hold while the new reports are being filed.

headline: Pennsylvania financial news in brief
abstract: The Scranton Sewer Authority found that the Collins Supply and Equipment Company was dumping cyanide into the city's sewers, prompting the city government to place a cease-and-desist order on the company. Elderly couples will be able to keep more of their income and still be eligible for Medicare thanks to a new federal law, said PA Department of Public Welfare Secretary John White. Pittsburgh's National Steel company reported third-quarter earnings of $12.6 million.

headline: Survey Released On Gas Tax Increase, Highway Issues
abstract: The state Transportation Secretary has criticized a survey that indicates Pennsylvanians support an increase in the state gasoline tax, calling the poll findings ''inconclusive and contradictory.''

headline: Passage of anti-drug bills by House hailed
abstract: PA Representative Richard J. Cessar of Allegheny County said that passage of 16 bills to combat drug sales and use in Pennsylvania was one of the most important actions the House took before the holiday recess. PA Governor Robert P. Casey is expected to sign the bills into law this weekend. The bills will crack down on steroid use by high school athletes, toughen penalties for drug crimes, revoke licenses of drivers convicted of drug crimes, and provide more protection for law officials working on drug cases, among the measures. Cessar noted that the General Assembly failed to approve any auto insurance reform, which was also an important issue this year.

headline: Insurance Commissioner: Constance B. Foster
abstract: Insurance Commissioner Constance B. Foster to visit Middletown for the day.  Background given on her issues and her plan to offer Bucks the help of the Consumer Services Bureau.

headline: Gilhooley Enters Democratic Fray On Pledge To Reform Government
abstract: Councilman Thomas Gilhooley, who is also the director of clinical services at the Lackawanna County Prison, announced his candidacy for mayor of Scranton Saturday afternoon.  He will join one of Democratic candidate, although others are expected to enter the race.  Gilhooley pledged to not raise taxes, as well as support the redevelopment of Lackawanna Ave. and implement a citywide recycling program.

headline: Traditional garb
abstract: Patricia Stringer (an Administrative Officer with the Governor's Scheduling Office) and other women who are dressed in traditional clothing prepare to leave for Centre County for the annual Women of Color Day and the first day of National Women's History Month.

headline: Youth-shelter proposal stirs panel's doubts
abstract: There are several concerns about the effectiveness and location of a proposed youth shelter.

headline: On abortion, Bush stands his ground
abstract: The US Senate passed a version of social-services bill, stripped of provisions opposed by President Bush that permitted Medicaid funding for abortions in the case of rape and incest. Molly Yard of the National Organization for Women criticized pro-choice Congressmen for backing down from the fight. Proof of the debate over abortion includes pro-life candidates' recent loss in gubernatorial elections in New Jersey and Virginia and President Bush's expected veto of a District of Columbia spending bill that would permit city tax money to be used for abortions.

headline: Districts waiting for special education money
abstract: School districts are waiting for the state to approve legislation that would pay them the special education subsidies they are owed.  Several distrcits are owed considerable amounts of money for special education, like Souderton, which is owed $600,000.

headline: PennVEST program loan sought by Lansford-Coaldale authority
abstract: The Lansford-Coaldale Joint Water Authority, in beginning its plans for removing and renovating water lines, has begun to move forward on a application for a low-interest loan through the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority program.

headline: Survivors credit seat belts
abstract: Car crash survivors, such as Barry E. Miller, Leonard W. Przydzial and Brian Youngerman, attest to the importance of wearing seatbelts. Each was involved in an accident which could have been fatal had they not been wearing seatbelts. A law requiring wearing seatbelts was passed in November 1987.

headline: pa-starvation
abstract: A Luzerne County judge has found that Larry and Leona Cottam will face third-degree murder charges for the starvation death of Eric, their 14 year-old son.  The two also face two charges of recklessly endangering another person and endangering the welfare of children.

headline: Insurance consumers best served by preserving legal options
abstract: This opinion is written by James R. Ronca, who is affiliated with the Harrisburg law firm of Schmidt and Ronca. Ronca writes about automotive insurance as a subject in the Legislature and the media. He provides four points that he believes the public should be aware of before they support a no-fault legislative solution to the auto insurance problem in Pennsylvania.

headline: Giuliani continues assault on Dinkins
abstract: Republican candidate in the New York City mayoral race Rudolph Giuliani has described the race as "a referendum on integrity" as part of a series of attacks on Democratic candidate David Dinkins. Dinkins' campaign has been plagued by accusations, including allegations of failure to pay taxes and accepting cruises for unions. Dinkins vowed that he would not let New York City become a "Republican beachhead," as the city was described by President George Bush.

headline: Trench says pump paments a political ploy
abstract: Bucks County Democratic Commissioner Lucille Trench is accusing two Republican commissioners of paying over $400,000 to speed up construction on a water diviersion project in order to help their own re-election campaigns.  They have denied the allegations.

headline: Aging agency finds its funding going up
abstract: Despite falling funding for most human resources, funding for agencies on aging has increased recently.

headline: Opposing forces picket at Bucks courthouse
abstract: Picketers from both the pro-chioce and pro-life camps met today outside the Bucks County Courthouse, where shouting matches developed in the "tense peace."

headline: Drug-education spending plan passes House
abstract: The PA House of Representatives passed a bill that would require all 501 districts a share in $6 million set aside for anti-drug programs. The original bill proposed by PA Governor Robert P. Casey said 118 districts had been chosen to receive half of the funding based on the percentage of students from welfare families, dropout and absenteeism rates, and standardized testing results. Some lawmakers, such as PA Representative Jeffrey Piccola, were angered by the plan because it ignored the need of more prosperous school districts with drug problems. Piccola said the amendment added to the bill is a more equitable distribution of the PennFREE money.

headline: Pine Grove's landfill sets example
abstract: Despite opposition from residents of Schuylkill and Lebanon counties, the PA Department of Environmental Resources granted a landfill permit to Pine Grove Landfill Incorporated. The article describes the state-of-the-art landfill's construction, as well as how the landfill functions.

headline: Survivors sue sailor, U.S. over fatal accident
abstract: Carole M. Altieri and Thomas Fogel of Allentown brought a lawsuit against the enlisted men's club at the Philadelphia Naval Station, after a drunk underage sailor hit their daughter Tracey Lynn Fogel with a car in South Philadelphia. The navy made an out-of-court offer which was rejected. The sailor, Roby C. Warden, was 20 years old at the time.

headline: Pennsylvania Financial News In Brief
abstract: Allegheny County resident Wayne Alton was sentenced by US District Judge Gustave Diamond to eight years and nine months in prison for his armed bank robbery conviction. US District Judge Maurice Cohill sentenced California resident John Keffalas, convicted of mail fraud, to three years in prison and to pay $5,000 in damages. US District Judge Gustave Diamond also will sentence Westmoreland County resident David Waldman for bank fraud on December 28. A Jewish group has argued in Pittsburgh federal court that it should be allowed to set up a menorah outside a city building to celebrate Hanukkah; a judge did not rule on the case. Donald Kovach of Indiana County died in an industrial accident in O'Hara as he was surveying a ditch that caved in on him at the Con-Travis-Gurz construction site.

headline: Insurance Deparment Approves One CAT Coverage, Rejects Another
abstract: State Insurance Commissioner Constance Foster approved Erie Insurance Co.'s proposal for a uniform $45 a year catastrophic auto insurance premium across the state which would be put into effect on March 1.  Mrs. Fost rejected a proposal by State Farm Mutual Insurance Co.

headline: Glenn's career fading, Republicans say
abstract: Ohio Republicans state that Senator John Glenn's political fortunes "are in a tailspin." Glenn, along with 4 other US Senators are being investigated by an outside counsel hired by the Senate Ethics Committee for their involvement in a campaign contribution scandal with Charles H. Keating Jr. of Lincoln Savings and Loan. The investigation was brought on by Ohio GOP Chairman Robert T. Bennett and Common Cause.

headline: Tucker: 'Everyone should be treated fairly'
abstract: A profile of Common Pleas Court Judge Petrese Tucker, who is running for her first full 10-year term after being appointed by Gov. Casey.

headline: Concerned About Heating Bills
abstract: The Director of the Philadelphia Corp. for Aging writes to express concern about cutbacks to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the effect of cutbacks on senior citizens.

headline: Pa. passes toughest U.S. abortion law
abstract: The PA Senate voted in favor of a bill restricting abortions, and PA Governor Robert Casey said he would sign the bill. The bill came as a result of the US Supreme Court's decision to give states more authority on regulating abortions, and two weeks after New Jersey and Virginia elected pro-choice governors. Some state senators joined groups such as the National Abortion Rights Action League in criticizing the bill.

headline: Education chief says Delco will get special education fund boost
abstract: The Casey Administration disputed the charge that special education in Delaware County and other parts of the state will be short-changed by millions of dollars in the coming school year.

headline: Pins drawn by makers of diapers
abstract: Representatives of the National Association of Diaper Services will begin a yearlong campaign to convince parents to cease using disposable plastic baby diapers.  It is estimated that 18 billion such diapers were purchased last year, with 90 percent of those going directly into landfills.

headline: Tentative budget okayed for borough of Turbotville
abstract: The Turbotville Borough Council approved its budget of $337,737 for 1990, which will be divided into areas covering sewers, general fund, water and special highway. Council President Jean Shively said there was no planned increase in taxes, despite this year's budget being higher than last year's. The council also reviewed a letter received from the PA Department of Transportation regarding traffic problems at the intersection of Routes 44 and 54, as well as set prices for building permits.

headline: Pennsylvania's largest public employees union says it totally opposes any attempt by state prison officials to close South Mountain Restoration Center
abstract: The American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) urged state prison officials to not close South Mountain Restoration Center near Chambersburg, but rather to increase state prison cells and state correction officers. State AFSCME leader Edward Keller says Pennsylvania's prisons will be read to explode if more cells are not built and more officers are not hired.

headline: Insurance firm failures were similar
abstract: Some insurance company transactions were of questionable nature, possibly leading to the collapse of the industry. One example investigated by the US House Commerce oversight and investigations subcommittee examined Transit Casualty Company of Los Angeles, which boosted its business by allowing agents to write policies and set their own rates.

headline: Glossary of Terms
abstract: This piece presents a glossary of terms often used in the debate over local tax reform.

headline: Tuition Plan
abstract: Pennsylvania Senate Democrats estimate that a bill designed to help families pay for the cost of college could run up a $21 million deficit in 10 years.

headline: Congress targets community service
abstract: Five major bills have been introduced to make the government promote community service by young Americans. The article summarizes each bill.

headline: Penn State, Protesters Plans To Keep Racism In Public Eye
abstract: 30 politicans and local leaders helped unfurl a banner Friday which read "United Against Racism" as part of a continued push to raise consciousness regarding racism on campus and in the community.  The efforts come in the wake of offensive fliers and attacks on several black students.

headline: Education Program Aimed At Reducing Fires Set By Children
abstract: According to State Fire Commissioner Charles A Henry, about 40 percent of arsons are caused by children and teenagers.  Because of this statistic, the state has announced a new education program called "Curious Kids Set Fires," which will educate children about the dangers of fire.

headline: Plymouth rejects county trash plan
abstract: Plymouth Township Council has remained opposed to Montgomery County's proposed trash- to- steam plant in Plymouth Township.

headline: The next airport
abstract: A compromise agreement between Atlantic City officials and Atlantic County officials regarding control over the Atlantic County Transportation Authority and the airport outside Atlantic City was finally reached.  Improvements will be made to parking facilities and a new terminal will be built.

headline: Pennsylvania's prisons: No place to get sick
abstract: The photograph depicts Jay Clark, an inmate at the Pittsburgh penitentiary who is partially paralyzed. His comment of "I'm an inmate. To them I'm scum. I doubt anything will ever happen." is a criticism of the state of treatment in Pennsylvania prisons.

headline: Insurance firms ask rate rises
abstract: Four of PA's largest auto insurance companies are asking the state Insurance Department for rate increases. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company is the largest in the state, and is asking for a rate increase of 2.3%, while Aetna Casualty & Surety Company, the fifth-largest in PA, seeks a rate increase request of 25.6%. Amy Dugan of the PA Insurance Department said that more rate increase request are expected in the next 2 months.

headline: GOP candidates write themselves onto Democratic ticket in Chester
abstract: Two Republicans organized write-in campaigns in order to fill the two vacant Democratic spot in the primaries for the Chester City Council.  Also, more reports on a few other candidates in the area.

headline: Tullio supports top aide, not nephew, for mayor
abstract: Retiring six-term Erie Mayor Louis J. Tullio will back his longtime office administrator, Patricia Lieibel, over his nephew, city Treasurer Carl "Skip" Cannavino.  Liebel will be the first woman to run for Erie mayor.

headline: County takes state to court over funding for geriatric center
abstract: Beaver County officials are suing the PA Department of Public Welfare over $5 million in lost Medicaid funding for the Beaver Valley Geriatric Center. With the help of local PA Representatives, the county hopes to gain the funds which were lost on account of Beaver County's reclassification as a Primary Metropolitan Statistical Area, which helped the county gain federal funds but also made it lose state funds. Beaver County Commission Chairman Gerald LaValle met with DPW Secretary John White to discuss the lawsuit while White was visiting the county for the opening of the Beaver County Court House Annex.

headline: Pro-choice legislators discuss abortion votes
abstract: Pro-choice Catholics in the Pennsylvania Legislature are coming under scrutiny by Catholic church officials, who have released a statement saying Catholic legislators have a moral responsibility to oppose abortions. PA Representative Peter Wambach and PA Senator Vincent Fumo both are pro-choice Catholic legislators that believe in the right of a woman to make the decision about abortions. They have both argued for the separation of secular politics from the private matter of religion.

headline: Education Spending is Investment in Future
abstract: A state House Republican leader is praising the Legislature for overriding Gov. Casey's plan to slightly scale back education spending for public schools.  The budget provides $4.5 billion for education this year and $1 billion for higher education

headline: Project to raise Center sewer rates
abstract: A multi-million dollar sewer improvement project will raise sewer rates for Center Township residents in the next few years as the township sewer authority plans to send funds to an $11.7 million bond issue for a new project to upgrade the township sewer system. There are two phases of the project that will take about two years to complete; the first expands the Elkhorn Run plant while the second expands sewerage to the entire township. Rates for residents will increase from $15 to $25 within 3 years and then drop in 1994.

headline: The one that got away
abstract: Sears decided not to move a 6,000-employee Merchandise Group to Pittsburgh after months of consideration because Illinois provided a slightly better incentive package, though it is encouraging that the new Midfield Terminal at the Greater Pitt. Airport was so attractive to the company, as it bodes well for future investment by other companies.

headline: Penologist assails overcrowding in prison
abstract: Overcrowding of the State Correctional Institution at Pittsburgh has contributed to numerous other problems there, including fatal assaults by inmates on other prisoners, a high level of tension and shortages of basic supplies, a penologist said yesterday.

headline: Insurance industry: driver surcharges not our doing
abstract: Insurance lobbyists are denying any involvement in legislation adding $30 to $200 surcharges on motor-code violation fines.

headline: GOP is off to a slow start in '90 gubernatorial race
abstract: As the state GOP gropes for a candidate to challenge Democratic Gov. Casey next year, the clock is running on the length of time the eventual nominee has to raise money.

headline: TV Guide: Marie Shriver nevers stops running
abstract: NBC achorwoman Marie Shriver, profiled in TV Guide magazine, has a hectic schedule but manages to keep everything more or less together, between 7-day workweeks, homes on both coasts, and an expected child.

headline: Delco praised
abstract: State Welfare Secretary John White praised Delaware County as "the most progressive state in the commonwealth" in the area of human services, though he stressed that not all is well in the County, and more needs to be done.  He heard suggestions from a group of human resources workers and toured facilities in the county.

headline: Put back on the defensive, pro-choice groups mobilize
abstract: Now that abortion rights are being threatened again due to the ruling in a recent Supreme Court case, pro-choice groups are gaining more support from individuals who until recently hadn't seen a need to fight for the issue since abortion was legal.

headline: Effects of state tax reform outlined
abstract: According to a study undertaken by the Pennsylvania School Board Association, the Shikellamy School Board would have to raise the personal income tax to 1.36 percent in order to conform to the state's proposed tax reform law.

headline: Public access is problem for sportsmen
abstract: Private land use access is becoming a problem, according to the PA Game Comission's Bureau of Land Management.  As of today, there are 4.5 million acres of private land which is available for hunting, although there has been an increase in property owners posing against access.

headline: Too many uninsured motorists
abstract: The largest bloc of uninsured motorists in PA are in the Philadelphia area, but pose a problem for the entire state. The board believes that part of the problem lies in the high cost of insurance, which families must account for in their budgets. The board does not think higher rates alone will solve the problem, and suggests strict enforcement and tougher penalties for uninsured drivers.

headline: Phila. Shower Posse Trial Opens
abstract: The trial begins for members of a Philadelphia drug-dealing posse which used children as dealers.  Some members are also facing murder charges.

headline: Insurance overcharge alleged in Pa., N.J.
abstract: A PA consumer group is supporting a lawsuit that is attempting to force State Farm Insurance Co. to pay back $6.8 billion of surplus funds to its policyholders nationwide, as they allegedly have been overcharging on premiums.

headline: GOP lacks strong contender to challenge Caasey in 1990
abstract: With hopes for U.S. Senator John Heinz or U.S. Attorney General Dick Thornburgh to run against Gov. Bob Casey in 1990 waning, Republicans in Harrisburg must look to other alternatives.  Among the possible candidates are Philadelphia District Attorney Ronald Castille and state Sen. D. Michael Fisher.

headline: Uniontown officials prepare for governor's visit
abstract: Uniontown officials get ready for Gov. Casey's visit to the city as part of his "Capital for a Day" program.

headline: Demonstrators rally at Capitol to press for aid for disabled kids
abstract: Hundreds of citizens gathered  Wednesday at the Capitol rotunda in Harrisburg, where they rallied for more state funding of programs for preschool children with mental and physical disabilities.

headline: Questions for Catholics
abstract: Lucy Killea, a California Assemblywoman, was barred from receiving communion by the Roman Catholic Church for her staunchly pro-choice position. She is a Democrat running against a pro-life Republican. Bishop Leo T. Maher of San Diego might force the members of the church to clarify their message.

headline: Erie school board cuts $2M in budget
abstract: The Erie School Board cut about $2 million from its budget proposal, but still needs to cut more, as the current figures would require a 10-mill tax increase, which board members refuse to approve.

headline: Public lists concerns for Lackawanna River
abstract: Nearly 30 residents of Lackawanna County attended a brainstorming session held by the Lackawanna River Corridor Association (LRCA) about the environmentally beleaguered waterway. The residents addressed issues such as pollution, flooding, over-development, the public's perception of the river, and lack of aquatic life, among other things. The attendees also suggested solutions, such as public and private partnerships to rejuvenate the river and reclaim it from polluters and developers. LRCA president Bernie McGurl said the decisions made at the meeting are vital to the county, as he believes a boom in economic growth is approaching.

headline: Three key road projects move ahead
abstract: In a letter prepared by Blair County Planner Richard T. Haines, the PA Department of Transportation has stated that is requesting federal funds for three major projects around Altoona. The projects are engineering the Hollidaysburg bypass, construction of a bridge over a railroad in Altoona, and construction of a bridge over Sugar Run in Allegheny Township. PennDOT secretary Howard Yerusalim said that the reconstruction of Route 22 from Cuba Mills to Pittsburgh is of high importance as well.

headline: Philly killings hit record
abstract: After a murder-suicide in Northeast Philadelphia and a shooting in West Philadelphia, the city reached a new record of 445 homicides in a year. The previous record of 444 was set in 1974 on account of increased gang violence. Philadelphia police believe crack cocaine was involved in the West Philadelphia shooting.

headline: Insurance plan facing battle
abstract: The editorial emphasizes the importance of auto insurance reform, despite objections from the insurance industry and other lobbyists.

headline: Gov. Casey blasts tax reform opponents
abstract: Gov. Robert P. Casey on the road to drum up support for a local tax reform reform, said opponents of the plan were guilty of using scare tactics against the elderly.

headline: Vartan suit against state reported near settlement
abstract: A lawsuit against the Casey administration filed by John Vartan will likely reach an agreeable settlement in the next few days, after both parties spent time in closed-door negotiations.  Vartan's suit had to do with the state's disqualifying him for leases.

headline: Goode budget unveiled- Social cuts exceed $100 million
abstract: Mayor W. Wilson Goode of Phila. called for more than $100 million in budget cuts, including massive reductions in human services, health and welfare benefits, and AIDS eduction programs.

headline: Religions take differing views on issue
abstract: Religions take differing views on the issue of abortion.  Catholic leaders say natural law dictates abortion is evil.  Jewish and Protestant teaching is generally more lenient and pro- choice.

headline: Exeter Oks 100-student day care site
abstract: Township supervisors have approved land development plans for a 100-student day care center to be operated by a Pottstown-headquartered firm.

headline: Putting lid on imported garbage
abstract: The Patriot-News of Harrisburg expresses its support for PA Governor Robert Casey's decision to restrict the flow of trash from other states into PA's landfills. Casey put a moratorium on the approval of expanded landfill capacity, which will affect the roughly 60 applications to the state Department of Environmental Resources for landfill use. Although Casey's decision does not eliminate the flow of out-of-state trash, it sets reasonable limits.

headline: Three Latrobe Plans Advance
abstract: Three projects in the Latrobe area received support from PennDOT, and will therefore be acted upon sooner than initially expected.

headline: Pittsburgh turns over records to Feds
abstract: Pittsburgh's city controller Tom Flaherty has turned over subpoenaed records to federal investigators of the U.S. Justice Department looking into bid-rigging in demolition contracts. Paul Imhoff, former head of Pittsburgh's Building Inspections Bureau, resigned two weeks before after he received a subpoena from a federal grand jury.

headline: Insurancemania I: The House Wrestles with Auto Rates
abstract: The state House will soon discuss auto insurance legislation, despite predicted opposition from lobbying groups, because of high public interest in decreasing premiums.

headline: Gov. Rizzo? It's unlikely; he has a job
abstract: It's unlikely that former Philadelphia mayor Frank Rizzo will run against Gov. Casey next year.  Rizzo would rather stay out of the campaign circuit and stick with his successful radio show.

headline: Vicki Bumbarger rides rail to announce 76th candidacy
abstract: From the steps of the Bellefonte Railroad Historical Society's train, Centre County Commissioner Vicki Bumbarger announced her candidacy for the Republican nomination for the 76th district House seat. Bumbarger is the second person to announce candidacy for the seat, after aide for PA Senator J. Doyle Corman, Jim Eckert. Bumbarger said she will focus her campaign on economics, education and the environment. Bumbarger said she feels confident she can win the position and represent her district in Harrisburg.

headline: Evicted woman becomes symbol
abstract: An elderly woman evicted from her home became something of a martyr for a bill to get more support for elderly citizens having trouble paying real estate taxes.  The US bill requires states to provide social workers with the name of seniors facing eviction, though some say that the extra service will overburden social workers, nor does it address the problem of limited income for the elderly.

headline: Session on women's rights enlivens US-Soviet conference
abstract: At the Chautauqua Conference on US-Soviet Relations, one of the most active sessions was the one on women's rights. Former congresswoman and former vice presidential candidate Geraldine Ferraro chided President Bush for vetoing a bill which would allow Medicaid payments for abortions involving rape and incest, saying that women voters will retaliate in the 1992 elections. Speakers at the sessions also included Alvetina Fedulova, first deputy chairwoman of the Committee of Soviet Women, and Marlo Thomas, an actress who spoke about the portrayal of women on TV.

headline: Exeter school board approves 8-mill tax hike
abstract: The Exeter Twp. School Board approved its $14.2 million budget, including an 8-mill tax hike.  The hike is 2 mills higher than initial expected, due to an expected decrease in state funding for special and gifted education.

headline: Questions are flowing again on Farming Ridge water supply
abstract: Questions are again being asked about the water supply reliability on Farming Ridge Blvd. after 1,500 gallons of water were removed from the hydrant system by Stonersville Fire Co., causing residents to lose water pressure.

headline: Too many toll roads a bad idea
abstract: There is a proposal in Harrisburg concerning funding for highways that will use the money from toll roads to meet road building needs.  The Editorial Board believes that too many toll roads is a bad idea.

headline: Police adding CAT charge to traffic violation fines
abstract: Fines for traffic violations will be increasing due to surcharges added to supplement funding for the indebted state CAT fund.

headline: Investment risky when subject to fluctuating political moods
abstract: Many U.S. firms are cautious about doing business in the Communist bloc because U.S.S.R. business decisions are strongly influenced by political agencies.

headline: Gov. Roemer Struggles After Tax-Issue Defeat
abstract: Explains some plans and difficulties that Louisiana Governor Buddy Roemer is faced with.

headline: Vote turned on turnout and power
abstract: Analyzes the important factors in the recent election, including turnout, campaign funds, and gender.

headline: Farmers Coupons
abstract: Pennsylvania is one of 10 states that will receive federal funding to give coupons for fresh produce to low- income pregnant women and women with small children.

headline: State Senate OKs abortion bill
abstract: The PA Senate voted 33-17 in favor of a new bill restricting abortion. The bill came as a result of a US Supreme Court decision to give states more authority on regulating abortions, and PA Governor Robert Casey has said that he will sign the bill. Pro-choice members of the Senate attempted to attach amendments, but all 9 were rejected.

headline: Expelled student claims racial bias
abstract: Joseph Ferguson, a black student expelled from the Dickinson School of Law in Carlisle, has filed a federal complaint against the school, prompting an investigation by the US Department of Education. John A. Maher, the school's dean, and other administrators stated that the student's allegations were unfounded. If the school is found to have violated the Civil Rights Act, it will lose federal funding.

headline: Raccoon Creek beach closed
abstract: The beach at Raccoon Creek State Park has been closed due to high levels of bacteria found in the lake.  Sampling is underway to determine if the bacteria will be a continuing problem.

headline: Town's longtime fears realized with horrific crash
abstract: A truck crash killing 5 hastens plans for a project making a section of road near Laughlintown safer.

headline: Police call for calm in Daily death
abstract: Philadelphia police appealed to the community to stop the rumors and violence after the killing of Sean Daily, the son of a police officer.  Spokemen say that the killing was not racially motivated and should not be viewed as such by the community.

headline: It's SmithKline Beecham now
abstract: The SmithKline Beckman Corp. has merged with the Beecham Group of Great Britain to create the world's second largest maker of both prescription and OTC drugs.

headline: Harrisburg businessman sued by state for supposedly taking wrong granite
abstract: John Vartan, a Harrisburg businessman, is being sued by the state for taking granite that was meant for the Capitol addition.  It appears that there was much confusion as Vartan thought he was taking used granite which was in a different location than the new granite.  Officials rebuff saying that Vartan new of the different locations and should have been able to see an obvious difference between the old and new granite.

headline: Vote: Maybe they'll give lollipops
abstract: A list of reasons to vote in the election the next day, most of them comical.

headline: Food-Distribution Center Project Begun in Harmony
abstract: Gov. Casey spoke at the groundbreaking of a new food-distribution center in Harmony.  The center will provide new jobs and opportunities for Butler County workers.

headline: States Are New Battlegrounds For Anti-Abortion Movement
abstract: Anti-abortion advocates nationwide are preparing state legislation to restrict abortions as allowed by a recent Supreme Court decision.  States now have the right to impose restrictions on abortions, though they still may not be outright banned.

headline: Fairfield school board eyes 27-mill tax increase
abstract: The Fairfield school district has requested a tax increase, which would be used almost exclusively to pay teachers.

headline: Recycling grant eyed in Blair
abstract: Blair County commissioners agreed to apply for a state grant to begin a curbside recycling program in Altoona and Logan Twp.  The grant of $27,000 would be used in conjuction with a previous grant of $43,000 and $3,000 in county-raised funds to "get it [the program] up and running."

headline: Tracks near stubborn fire declared safe by PennDOT
abstract: A PennDOT inspector has declared the tracks above the site of a 28-year-old ongoing underground fire to be safe for trains.  Local officials are becoming frustrated with the EPA and the DER because of their inaction on the fire.

headline: Police examining notebook, field in bus shooting case
abstract: Authorities are investigating why 16-year-old student Robert Butler shot a 16-year-old classmate, Adam Ferrence, on a school bus and then killed himself. Police Chief Thomas Brletic said Butler had obtained the gun from his father, a former policeman. State police Cpl. Robert Griffin, an expert on satanic rituals and the occult, said symbols used in satanic rituals were found in Butler's notebook and religion textbook, although Griffin did not connect the drawings to the shooting. Allegheny County Coroner Joshua Perper said Butler had undergone brain surgery, although he did not believe this was connected to Butler's death either.

headline: Judge extends pensions for W-P retirees
abstract: US Judge Paul Simmons approved an emegency request to extend pension payments that expired last month to nearly 1,000 retirees of Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corp.  W-P is in the middle of bankruptcy reorganization efforts, and argued that if the request had been denied, there would have been major setbacks.

headline: Governor brands tactics 'scurrilous'
abstract: Gov. Robert P. Casey denied Wednesday that any deal was made with any group opposing local tax reform and called the tactics of his opponents "scurrilous."

headline: Voter cynicism beat tax reform, say Casey's aides
abstract: Some of Gov. Casey's aides are saying that his tax reform proposal on the ballot in May's primary election was defeated because votes didn't have enough faith in their local governments.  The sound defeat of his tax plan will likely have little effect on Casey's political future, and nor will the reult of the current auto-insurance reform proposals in the legislature.

headline: Foster mother to 213 gives love
abstract: Mary Romano of Upper St. Clair, Pennsylvania, has been a foster mother to 213 children over the last 27 years. Romano works with Family Services of Western Pennsylvania, a private, non-profit agency funded mostly by the United Way. Sue Collins, director of Family Services' foster care program, praised Romano for the help she has given so many children. At the age of 77, Romano currently has two children in her care, a 14-year-old girl and a 3-month-old boy.

headline: The sensible approach to abortion dilemma
abstract: The editorial claims that the Supreme Court shouldn't have left abortion restrictions up to the states, as women from more restrictive states will just go to another state to have the abortion if they're determined to have one, unless they resort to more unconventional methods.

headline: First lady takes, leaves behind fond memories
abstract: In Gov. Casey's "Captial for a Day" prograrm, Mrs. Casey visited Uniontown with the rest of the Casey administration.  She spent her time reading to children to promote literacy and visiting various places, including the Touchstone Center for Crafts, where she reflected upon her days as an art major.

headline: Recycling need for Boro outline
abstract: Recycling was discussed at a meeting of the Borough Council of Punxsutawney. Herman Hetager, a VISTA volunteer with Community Action, said the purpose of the discussion was to talk about initial planning to implement Act 101, which encourages recycling. William Shuffstall of the Penn State Cooperative Extension office gave an overview of the requirements of the act, saying that the county's role is to plan for solid waste disposal for ten years. The PA Department of Environmental Resources has determined the quantity of waste per person in Pennsylvania and has instituted actions throughout the state to being recycling all of this waste.

headline: Transit panel clears way for more raod projects
abstract: The state Transportation Commission adopted its latest two-year update to the 12-year highway plan, clearing the way for the next stage of developments to continue.  Various projects have been moved up in priority or added to the list of projects that are part of the plan.

headline: Police Log: Inmate arraigned
abstract: A Graterford prison inmate, Haddrick Byrd, was arraigned for kidnapping the prison's school principle, Irwin Schmuckler, and holding him for seven hours.  Byrd was already serving a life sentence for second degree murder and robbery.  His new charges include simple assault, kidnapping, reckless endangerment, false imprisonment, and possessing a weapon.

headline: LCB plans evaluation on staffing
abstract: The state Liquor Control Board has formed an independent six-member committee which will investigate ways to make its use of employees more efficient.

headline: Governor Casey is being challenged to a debate on his plan to restructure local taxes.
abstract: Governor Casey is being challenged to a debate on his plan to restructure local taxes.  Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer, a leading opponent of the plan, made the challenge today.

headline: Voters Are Saying, 'No More Taxes'
abstract: The editorial claims that, for better or for worse, citizens are more willing to let the governent make spending and program cuts rather than raising taxes.

headline: Handicapped Helping Others Like Themselves
abstract: Karl Fuls, a former steel worker, has created a non-profit organization known as The Broken Wing, which helps match those with recent disabilities to individiuals who have overcome similar disadvantages.  Fuls lost his legs to circulatory problems.

headline: They are accessories
abstract: The writer posits that pro-lifers could stand as accessories to some of the atrocities committed by women against their newborn children.  It is argued that such pro-lifers do not understand the difficulties many indigent new mothers face.

headline: Franklin Directors Hold Tax Line, OK Pay Hikes
abstract: The Franklin School Board approved $13.8 million budget with administrative pay hikes, a half-million deficit and no tax increase.  According to the superintendent, by next year the decifit should be decreased to $163,000, though they must still be careful with their finances.

headline: Recycling not as difficult nor as time-consuming as you may fear
abstract: Monthly columnist Bernadette Swartley reflects on the changes for local recycling service consumers and provides a few helpful tips. She recommends contacting the PA Department of Environmental Resources for more information. The Environmental Resources Department sometimes provides grants to local communities to start recycling programs.

headline: Transport for elderly gets a lift
abstract: A shared-ride program in Montgomery County is applying for additional funds for expansion of its services.

headline: Police: Drug arrests message to dealers
abstract: A series of arrests of suspected drug dealers in Lycoming County is being conveyed by authorities as a message that illegal narcotics dealing in the county will not be tolerated. PA State Police Lieutenant Robert Brobson said the emphasis is on cleaning up the area. According to county District Attorney Brett O. Feese, 20 suspects are city residents targeted by the Lycoming County Drug Task Force, 22 anticipated arrests stem from a county investigative grand jury, and 11 others were targeted by investigations by the state police Region Four Strike Force of State College. Williamsport City Police Chief William F. Miller said a total of 27 city residents are to arrested for what is considered street level crack and cocaine dealing and dealers of larger quantities of illegal drugs.

headline: Legislative panel endorses off-track betting but not implementation
abstract: A special panel in the Maryland Legislature has endorsed the concept of off-track betting but has indefinitely avoided any plan to implement a proposal that is supported by racing industry interests but opposed by Maryland Governor William Donald Schaefer. Maryland Senator Thomas L. Bromwell said the legislature needs to send a bill to the governor, while Senator Edward J. Kasemeyer said he does not believe off-track betting will be acted upon in the upcoming 90-day General Assembly session. The panel did vote to propose legislation that gives the Maryland Racing Commission the power to impose $5,000-a-day fines on track owners who do not comply with state rules and regulations.

headline: Governor pitches for Pesci on the streets of Ford City
abstract: Gov. Casey campaigned with county Controller Tim Pesci in Ford City, a highly competetive district in the upcoming election.  Casey outlined the importance of instilling a Democrat in this seat of the state House.

headline: Voters bury tax reform
abstract: The Casey-supported tax reform proposal was soundly defeated in the previous day's election.

headline: Hughes seeks funding
abstract: State Rep. Vincent Hughes is seeking funding for his proposed Human Development Action Fund, which would target state money toward fighting substance abuse, AIDS, and homelessness. He seeks  to garner money from the state's "Rainy Day Fund."

headline: Totally female process
abstract: Judy Seltzer of Lock Haven attacks PA Representative Stephen Friend and pro-life lawmakers for their attempts to control a woman's body. She states they will never know anything about a "totally female process."

headline: From GHS to TV to the Capitol, Rita Frealing is going first class
abstract: Rita Frealing, a Gettysburg High School graduate, is currenlty working for the Commonwealth News Bureau as a Deputy Secretary for Public Information.  She is a also a graduate of Penn State and the Dickinson School of Law.

headline: Recycling plant due for Phila.
abstract: A joint venture between Du Pont Co. and Waste Management Inc. will locate a $5 million plant to recycle plastics in the Harrowgate section of Philadelphia, which will bring about 70 new jobs to the city, according to an announcement from the two companies. The plant is scheduled to open next year and will serve as the first site for the joint venture, called the Plastic Recycling Alliance. Du Pont executive vice president Nicholas Pappas said Philadelphia will provide a site and a steady flow of items for recycling. Philadelphia recycling coordinator Alfred Dezzi said the venture will create markets for recycled products because it will give material a place to go.

headline: Transportation secretary rips gasoline- tax study
abstract: The state Transportation Secretary has criticized a survey that indicates Pennsylvanians support an increase in the state gasoline tax, calling the poll findings "inconclusive and condtradictory."

headline: Posthumous honor
abstract: PA Police Commissioner Ronald Sharpe presents the State Police Cross to the mothers of two state policemen who died in a helicopter crash. The policemen who died were Corporal Paul Almer and Trooper Wayne Bilheimer.

headline: Legislators getting a free ride
abstract: This editorial discusses how taxpayers in Pennsylvania are not only footing the bill for legislators to drive expensive cars, but also helping subsidize their auto insurance premiums. The editorial board cites PA Senator Edward W. Helfrick as the example of this, as in 1988 he paid only $69 for insurance for his state-sponsored Mercedes-Benz. The editorial board cites the irony in the fact that legislators have state-subsidized auto insurance while they are also considering an auto insurance reform bill that would take away either rights or coverage for lower premiums for Pennsylvania taxpayers.

headline: Governor Robert Casey has nominated lawyer James Maza, a Democrat, to fill the Montgomery County treasurer's post vacated by Republican Floriana Bloss
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey nominated James Maza, a lawyer and a Democrat, to take the place of Republican Floriana Bloss as Montgomery County treasurer. Bloss was appointed a Montgomery County Commissioner.

headline: Voters turnout varied across state
abstract: On the day after an election, the article reports of how the candidates for various offices spent their last-minute campaigning time and how the election worked out on the ground.  Doesn't provide information about reulsts.

headline: 1,400 fans turn out for Trini
abstract: 1,400 people gathered to pay tribute to County Commissioner Frank J. Trinisewski.  Governor Casey praised Trinisewski, who a year before had been a registered Republican, for public service.

headline: U.S. abortion by age
abstract: The graph shows the percentage of Americans who got abortions by age in 1983. The largest portion were age 20-24 with 34.8%, followed by age 25-29 with 20.8% and age 18-19 with 15.5%.

headline: Gilhool's resignation bring mixed reactions from educators
abstract: Educators are split on whether Gilhool should have resigned, but most agree that his resignation will have few noticable impacts.

headline: Rep. Kanjorski wins approval for water allocation to Northeastern Pennsylvania
abstract: US Rep Paul Kanjorski (D-PA) fought for and won the rights for Northeastern PA to use some of the water to be stored in a reservoir being expanded in the area.

headline: Troy concerned about downtown traffic problems
abstract: Pedestrian crossing and traffic blockage was an item discussed by members of the Troy Borough Council at their meeting last night.  Councilmen debated the value of a crosswalk.

headline: Preate urges laws to help kids
abstract: Speaking at a conference on child homicide, PA Attorney General Ernest Preate criticized PA's child welfare agencies, citing the case of Beatrice Bird who died while under the protection of Columbia County Children and Youth as an example of the agencies' failures. Preate had earlier been criticized in House hearings on a new child abuse bill for trying to give police more power in solving child abuse crimes. The conference was also attended by Deborah Daro, director of research of the National Committee for the Prevention of Child Abuse.

headline: Let voters decide gambling issue
abstract: 28 municipalities in Mercer County have placed the "small- games of chance" issue on their primary ballot.  The editorial board believes it is right to give the people the decision to allow gambling.

headline: Governors Talk Funding Prospects with Administration
abstract: The Democratic chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, Sen. James Sasser, told the nation's governors at the midwinter meeting of the National Governors' Association that "we're fresh out of cash here in Washington."  He predicted that more financial problems could plague the governors' states.  However, some governors believe that President Bush will be more attuned to the states' problems than his predecessor.

headline: Votes counting set today in health-care union election
abstract: Ballots are to be counted today for a referendum to split the nations largest health-care union between two larger unions.  Debates on which union workers will join has been fierce.

headline: 18 who bought jobs are fired by Hafer
abstract: Barbara Hafer, the first Republican auditor general in 28 years, made good on her promise to fire individuals who bought their jobs during previous administrations.  Of the 18 workers who were fired, one was hired by former Auditor General Don Bailey and the rest were hired by Al Benedict, Mr. Bailey's predecessor.

headline: Voters changing candidates' ideals
abstract: The editorial criticizes public official hopefuls who formerly held anti-abortion stances but have since become defenders of the woman's right to choose in order to become elected into office. After surveys have been released that reveal a pro-choice majority in some states, many men and women running for office have changed their stances on the issue. The article cites Ohio Attorney General Anthony Celebrezze, who is expected to be the Democratic gubernatorial candidate in 1990, has recently said he would veto anti-abortion legislation, whereas three years before he said he would support any bill outlawing abortion. The editorial board encourages Pennsylvania voters to elect candidates in 1990 that are firm in their platforms and do not always change according to the always-changing public sentiment.

headline: Good higher education news
abstract: The integration of Villa Maria College and Gannon University, as well as Penn State's commitment to increase graduate work at its Behrend campus, has ensured that the education field will continue to provide strong growth for the local economy and area.

headline: Rohm & Haas chemical storage plans defended before Gwynedd planners
abstract: Concerns about the chemical storage facility proposed by Rohm & Haas were discussed by company and township officials.

headline: Trump loses lawsuit in crash investigation
abstract: US District Judge Joseph Lord III refused to allow a representative from Donald Trump to investigate a helicopter crash which killed three of Trump's officials. Lord did allow officials from the helicopter's manufacturer to participate in the investigation being carried out by the National Transportation Safety Board, stating that the company could provide technical expertise.

headline: Preate: Pa. skimps on child services
abstract: Pennsylvania spends far less to protect children from abuse and neglect than the national average, state Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. told a panel of legislators yesterday.

headline: Let's rewrite the no-fault insurance law
abstract: Looking at the PA no-fault insurance law, it would seem as though no-fault doesn't work, while in fact, PA and many other state just didn't employ the strategy properly.  A few states that effectively legislated no-fault auto insurance have reaped its benefits.

headline: Governors Warning of an Ignorant U.S.
abstract: A panel of governors at the winter meeting of the National Governors' Association warned that the United States is not prepared for international trade and must stress second language study in college.  Also, members of the NGA said that governors would have to be the prime movers in domestic policy reform, citing governors' influence in welfare reform from the previous year.

headline: Voting rights
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature has proposed to allow voters in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia to go four years without voting before re-registration is required as well as to allow homeless people to vote if they can establish addresses. The editorial board believes the former encourages apathy and the latter requires safeguards. The board maintains that a more open voting registration system would bring more citizens into the democratic process.

headline: 2 utility overseers take campaign funds from them
abstract: Two Bucks County Republicans seem to be embroiled in corruption involving fundraising from the sectors they are meant to be overseeing.

headline: Wilt leaves debate, votes 'no' by proxy
abstract: PA Senator Roy Wilt left a debate session on legalized abortion for a meeting of the Great Lakes Commission in Detroit, Michigan. He voted by proxy against the anti-abortion bill which the Senate eventually passed. The bill challenges some of the aspects of the US Supreme Court's 1973 decision to legalize abortion.

headline: Gov. Casey's education plan leaves district's budget short
abstract: Dallastown School District officials say that Gov. Casey's education plan will leave the district short more than $115,000, because the plan would only guarantee the district 97.5% of funding it should receive.  Taxpayers will most likely make up the difference, although the district's taxes may not necessarily be raised.

headline: Royersford exploring options for trash recycling
abstract: Borough Council officials have stated their intentions to begin a recylcing program, even though such an evdeavor would be more expensive than a typical waste removal plan.

headline: Turnpike collection hasn't taken its toll on this man
abstract: Chester Detweiler is a toll collector on the Pennsyslvania Turnpike.  He summarizes life in the toll booth: people are generally nice, he ignores the rude people, and he has tried to keep drunk drivers off of the turnpike.

headline: Pressure on jail warden is 'all part of the turf'
abstract: Charles J. Kozakiewicz, warden of the Allegheny County Jail, is known for his strict but fair treatment of inmates. Kozakiewicz has had to release inmates in the past under rulings from US District judges, and in some cases he has been fined for defying these rulings. Kozakiewicz commands the respect of his guards and inmates, and has been praised by John Pastor, president of the jail guards union.

headline: License limitation the law
abstract: The letter-to-the-editor is written by a former beer distributor owner, who wrote to counter a recent editorial about a November 30 hearing held by the Pennsylvania House Liquor Control Committee. The author accuses the editorial of misleading the reading public by not being clear about the most important point discussed at the hearing, which was the law that forbids a person from owning "more than one distributor or importing distributor license." The limitation on license ownership was agreed upon by the members of the committee as meaning that any one person is precluded from having financial interest in more than one beer distributor license. The author says he supports the distributors who testified at the hearing as objecting to multiple locations by the same owner.

headline: Gray Is Elected Majority Whip
abstract: US Rep. William Gray III (D-PA) of Philadelphia was voted majority whip of the US House.

headline: Wage increase vetoed
abstract: President Bush vetoed a bill that would have raised the minimum wage from $3.35 to $4.55.  A compromise will soon be underway between the President and Congress over a reasonable solution to the problem.

headline: 30 laid off at ex-Rockwell plant
abstract: BTR Dunlop Inc. bought the Pittsburgh division of the former Rockwell International Measurement and Flow Control.  With that, thirty employees were laid off, leaving only 170 workers at the headquarters.

headline: X-rated lyric legislation
abstract: The opinion article discusses the recent passage through the Pennsylvania House of Representatives that requires retailers in PA to label albums and tapes with "offensive" lyrics, or face up to 90 days in jail. The author expresses the belief that the manufacturer should be the group labeling some albums with sexually explicit lyrics on a voluntary basis. Another problem with the bill that the author addresses is the House's definition of offensive language, which includes songs that "advocate or encourage suicide" or the excessive use of alcohol. The article expresses the hope that, because the Senate has not had the chance to vote on the legislation yet, that their better judgment will keep it from being passed as is.

headline: Governor Proposes Acquiring Theater
abstract: Gov. Casey is asking Legislature for $4 million to renovate a black performing arts theatre in N. Philadelphia, building a 350-seat auditorium, new light system, classrooms, offices and apartments.  The theater was established in 1966 and has been cited as one of the outstanding black theaters in the country.

headline: Secretary of Environmental Resources: Arthur A. Davis
abstract: Secretary of Environmental Resources to visit Bucks county.  Background given on waste site, recycling, and state park issues.  Davis plans to visit GROWS landfill and listen to Bucks residents.

headline: Turnpike speed limit remains 55
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives has killed an amendment to a highway bill that would have given the Turnpike Commission the option to raise the speed limit to 65 mph. PA Representatives James Burd and Eugene Saloom, who sponsored the bill, lamented the failure of the bill to pass, while PA Representative William Lloyd said fatalities would increase with a higher speed limit.

headline: Prison board leaves many matters unresolved
abstract: The Bradford County Prison Board left several matters unresolved in their special meeting yesterday, including staffing, food service, lockers, radio equipment, and uniforms.  Several members of the board voiced the opinion that they should meet more often so as to resolve the outstanding matters.

headline: Liquor price cuts are still a long way off
abstract: As a result of a US Supreme Court ruling, PA may now be able to negotiate with liquor suppliers over prices, allowing possible savings for the state and hopefully for the consumer.

headline: Gregg Twp.: Good news on sewer rates
abstract: Gregg Township supervisors were pleased to hear that they would actually have to pay less per household per year for sewer services because of faulty data from a federal government-issued report. Bob Garrett of the Union County Planning Office brought the good news to the supervisors who are concerned about prices for the new sewage system in the township. Garrett showed the supervisors the federal government's error, which concerned the inclusion of the Allenwood Federal Prison Camp. Garrett said the actual price per household will be $179, rather than the $529 then government report estimated.

headline: Walker named deputy whip by Gingrich
abstract: Republican Robert S. Walker was named a deputy whip in the House by Minority Whip Newt Gingrich.  Walker was a co-founder of the Conservative Opportunity Society.

headline: 4 names surface for job of URA executive director
abstract: Four candidates for the Urban Redevelopment Authority director position have been named, and talks with the candidates will begin soon.

headline: null
abstract: A study conducted by the American Academy of Pediatrics has shown that most common medicines can be taken by a nursing mother without harming her child. Coffee was found not to be harmful, but 10 prescription drugs and 6 commonly-abused drugs such as cocaine can be dangerous to nursing infants.

headline: Grants to Assist Teacher Training
abstract: Gov. Casey announced $2 in grants for Lead Tecaher training centers and other teacher-learning programs.

headline: Serafini, Belardi introduce leachate disposal legislation
abstract: PA Representative Frank Serafini and PA Representative Fred Belardi, both of Lackawanna County, proposed a bill to control the disposal of leachate from landfills. The package of proposals would require the transportation of leachate from a landfill to a disposal facility by a double-lined pipe or tractor trailer. Serafini said the subsidence problem in Northeastern Pennsylvania has allowed leachate to leak into mines and rivers of PA, while Belardi said that transporting leachate by truck will allow the testing of the liquid waste by controlled volume and eliminate the problems created by uncontrolled release of leachate through sewer lines.

headline: Typical day for PennDOT chief not a typical day at all
abstract: The article charts a typical day for the secretary of the PA Department of Transportation, Howard Yerusalim. He flew from Harrisburg to Pittsburgh, met with Mayor Sophie Masloff and Port Authority Transit executive director William W. Millar to discuss the city's needs from PennDOT, and met with police about a federally-funded program to help police monitor drunk drivers. Yerusalim also traveled to regions outside Pittsburgh before returning to Harrisburg at night.

headline: Prison crowding and the D.A.
abstract: The writer accuses the Philadelphia DA of engaging in a public relations battle over the prison overcrowding instead of trying to hasten criminal prosecutions in order to lighten the load on jails.

headline: Little risk in games of chance
abstract: Montgomery Co. DA Michael Marino said that violations of the small games of chance law will be at the bottom of his priorities, which may encourage organizations to abuse the law.

headline: Groups hunting votes for small games of chance
abstract: The legality of small games of chance (ie. Lotteries and raffles) will be voted on during the May 16 primary elections.  Groups that benefit from the fundraisers hope the referendum will be approved.

headline: We ain't just whistlin' Dixie here
abstract: In the state House, 135 members got very worked up about PA's lack of a state song.  The author of the opinion piece believes that there are more important things for which legislators should worry.

headline: 6 Penna. counties sue officials for state funds
abstract: Six counties are suing the state because, in compliance with a court ruling, the state paid Philadelphia $4.9 million for services for the retarded, but in order to pay the city, funding for retarded citizens in 66 other PA counties was cut back.

headline: $140 million to Pa. drug fight
abstract: Gov. Casey's plan to create a $140 trust fund for anti-drug efforts is being discussed around the state to determine if it's the best way to use the money.  Casey stressed that drugs are a major cause in many other problems, so the drug problem must be dealt with before others can be attacked.

headline: Group Fights Rockland Plan
abstract: Concerned parents and other residents of the Cranberry Area School District have organized to fight the elimination of 3rd and 4th grades from Rockland Elementary School.

headline: Sewage Is Spilled Into Creek: Third Incident Near Refuge
abstract: As many as 3 million gallons of untreated waste spilled into a nearby creek at the Tinicum National Environmental Center, the third spill within the past year.  The Executive Director of the Delaware County Regional Water Quality Control Authority said a preventative back-up pumping station is forthcoming.

headline: U.S. orders rear-seat lap, shoulder belts
abstract: The US government yesterday ordered that most new US-made cars built after mid-December are required to have back seat lap-and-shoulder belts and front seat airbags or automatic shoulder restratints.

headline: Prison miscarriage probed: Warden doubts truth of allegations
abstract: The warden of the Montgomery County Prison has said reports that inmate Delores Raby had a miscarriage due to prison staff treatment are untrue.  The warden is still undertaking an investigation and Raby has filed suit in a federal district court seeking $75,000 in damages.

headline: Lloyd's 'cat' bill a strong beginning
abstract: Rep. William Lloyd's proposal, which would create a pooled risk plan for auto insurance companies, would keep voluntary annual premiums for catastrophic auto insurance between $24 and $30.  Also, the bill has provisions for raising money to pay off the state's hundreds of millions of dollars in unfunded liability from the CAT Fund.

headline: Gus Yatron recuperating after receiving new hip
abstract: U.S. Rep. Gus Yatron, the 61 year-old Reading Democrat, was recuperating after having surgery on his hip.  There were no complications from the surgery.

headline: We should all keep an eye on new bill
abstract: State Sen. Frank A. Pecora has introduced a bill which seeks to close a loophole allowing county authorities and municipal governments to use their powers of eminent domain to take over land outside of their respective boundaries.  The bill could have real implications regarding a landfill dispute in Berks County.

headline: 60 and older group grows 8%
abstract: Between 1980 and 1987, the population of people in PA age 60 and older has increased 8%, while the population of those under 60 has decreased 1%.  PA now ranks second to Florida in percentage of population over 60.

headline: 10,000 elderly to lose insurance in Blue Cross dispute
abstract: About 10,000 senior citizens, who are I.D. Craig Services Co. group subscribers, will have their health insurance policies terminated at the end of the month due to a decision rendered by a Commonwealth Court.  The termination comes as a result of disagreements between Blue Cross and Craig, an organization which offers its members reduced group insurance rates purchased through Blue Cross.

headline: Group: Special ed programs might be trimmed
abstract: The Council for Exceptional Children is trying to drum up support and awareness for special education programs, which will likely see funding cuts.

headline: Sewage upgrading projects starting to flow
abstract: Many of the municipalities of the Poconos are still undergoing the transformation of building sewage systems in response to the years of population increase.  Questions remain regarding wether the explosion at the First Church of Christ Scientist was related to a sewage project.

headline: Union Township delays OK of developer's road plan
abstract: Township officials have declined to approve a developer's drainage and road plans, saying they need more time to review proposals.

headline: Prison planning gets go-ahead in York County
abstract: The York county Prison Board approved a proposal to enlarge the York county prison.  The expansion would increase the capacity to accommodate 668 prisoners, 796 if the second phase is approved.  The prison's population is constantly rising and it is becoming difficult to house all of the prisoners.

headline: Loan lands Piper back in Lock Haven
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey signed a $10 million state loan on Wednesday to help Piper Aircraft Corporation return to Clinton County after a five-year absence. Casey signed the Sunny Day Fund loan in a courtroom surrounded by local dignitaries, Piper officials, and speculators including a sixth grade class from Lock Haven Catholic School. Casey hailed PA Senator J. Doyle Corman and PA Representative Russell P. Letterman for their work on the loan. M. Stuart Miller, owner of Romeo Charlie Inc., owns Piper, which is the last company in the world to manufacture a full line of small aircraft. Piper North, Inc., will create 670 jobs in Lock Haven over the next five years.

headline: Hafer files leasing board appeal
abstract: PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer filed a case to the PA Supreme Court to overturn the Commonwealth Court's ruling preventing her from sitting on the Board of Commissioners of Public Grounds and Buildings. The last auditor general to serve on the board was current governor Robert Casey, who thought it would be a conflict of interest to approve financial cases he might later have to audit.

headline: Weiner question hovers over Philly election
abstract: The death of Consumer Party candidate Max Weiner in the Philadelphia City Controller race has led to his wife, Bessie Weiner, being placed on the ballot. Weiner's death led the Democratic candidate Jonathan Saidel and Republican candidate Joseph Rocks to speculate where Weiner's support base will shift. Politicians speculate that Weiner's death will also affect the race for Philadelphia district attorney.

headline: 88- Year- Old Congressman Checked In To Johns Hopkins Hospital
abstract: BALTIMORE- Rep. Claude Pepper, the oldest member of the U.S. Congress, has been admitted to Johns Hopkins Hospital for a digestive disturbance.

headline: 11 hospitals and union for 8,000 talk on, facing contract deadline
abstract: Contract talks continue for a health-care workers union and hospital representatives, and are expected to continue until the midnight deadline tomorrow.  There is a chance for a strike, though both parties are attempting to avoid one.

headline: HACC trustees approve branches
abstract: Harrisburg Area Community College officials plan to open a new branch campus in Lebanon County and expand one in Lancaster County..

headline: Sewage, Garbage Hikes Proposed
abstract: Oil City Council approved rate hikes for both sewage and garbage services last night.  The sewage hike is to fund unforseen repair projects caused by storm damage, and the sewage hike is part of a new three-year contract with a collection firm.

headline: User fees
abstract: The Editorial Board believes that user fees should be raised on highways to provide the funds to complete road repairs.  Otherwise, industries that rely on the roads will move elsewhere.

headline: Prison problems
abstract: Nelson Charles Mikesell of the State Correctional Institution in Pittsburgh suggests solutions to PA's prison overcrowding problem. He commends the General Assembly for conducting investigations of the riot at Camp Hill state prison, since leaving the task to the state Department of Corrections alone would not solve the problem.
