abstract: The Delaware County Department of Solid Waste suggests methods of cutting down trash produced by year-end holiday celebrations. The advice was given in a press release written by Edward Peabody, who called recycling "a very successful approach to life."

headline: ABC seeks sealed documents
abstract: ABC News is seeking information from US District Court Judge Sylvia Rambo regarding "sidebar" conferences she had with US Attorney James West and lawyers for the defendants in a case against the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency. Harry Casoni, top aid to PHEAA's executive director Kenneth Reeher, was convicted of steering a state contract to an Illinois firm for personal gain. Reeher had been acquitted in the trial.

headline: Spring City police slow to use Vascar anti-speeding device
abstract: The Spring City police are selling a recently-purchased computerized Vascar anti-speeding device that has been gathering dust due to a lack of personnel certified to use it.  Officials say that  the force will continue using traditional methods of speed-detection.

headline: PSFS's name is sold off
abstract: Meritor Savings Bank said it would sell the PSFS name and 54 of its 83 branches to Mellon Bank Corp. of Pittsburgh for $335 million. The sale would break up financially owed Meritor and allow it remain alive while nearly tripling Mellon's market share. Mellon will keep alive the name of the nation's oldest savings bank, which was the Philadelphia Savings Fund Society, by using "Mellon PSFS" on its newly acquired branches. Mellon outbid at least two other banks for the PSFS name.

headline: If you're alive, you vote
abstract: The author of this opinion piece believes that black people and all minorities have a duty to make their voices heard by voting in the coming mayoral election.

headline: Log cabin resident opposes dam
abstract: Armar Border, the only remaining resident in Swatara State Park, opposes the state builiding a dam in the park.  He says that mine acids in the water and the threat of flooding make building a dam a bad idea.

headline: City programs for retarded targeted
abstract: An investigation will be made into Philadelphia's spending on programs for the mentally retarded.  State welfare officials say the spending is too high on services that are run poorly.

headline: Other business at NEB
abstract: The Northeast Bradford school board addressed several issues, including letters to state rep. J. Chadwick about extra reimbursement to bus contractors, the hiring of a new business office secretary, and the rejection of a couple's request that their child attend kindergarten at NEB unless they could pay tuition costs.

headline: Use of phosphate detergent being banned
abstract: Gov. Casey signed the Phosphate Detergent Act, banning the use of phosphate detergents beginning in 18 months.  The act is intended to cut down on pollution in groundwater and streams.

headline: About those injured in Camp Hill riots
abstract: The article lists the names of those injured during the riots of October 25-26 at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill. Those injured are a mix of corrections officers, firefighters and inmates. The injured were taken to a number of facilities such as Harrisburg Hospital, Holy Spirit Hospital, Polyclinic Medical Center and Community General Osteopathic.

headline: State attorney general files suit over Supreme Court judge's age
abstract: Attorney General Ernie Peate Jr. files suit in Commonwealth Court questioning whether state Supreme Court Judge Juanita Kidd Stout should continue to serve after passing the mandatory retirement age.

headline: Public hearings on tourism to be held in November
abstract: PA Representative Keith McCall states that the PA House Business and Commerce Committee will hold a two-day hearing to discuss PA's tourism industry. Tourism is the state's second-largest industry, and he is working with the committee's chairman, Representative Fred Taylor, to promote participation in the event. McCall encourages citizens involved in the tourism industry to present testimony.

headline: In fight against fare hikes, a voice for 'people power'
abstract: Tyrone Reed, president of the Committee for a Better North Philadelphia, along with other leaders in low- income areas challenged and temporarily stopped the SEPTA fare increase.

headline: Making money with state parks
abstract: The editorial board approves of the idea of increasing development at some of PA's state parks. PA Senator Tim Shaffer was one of the first to advocate development of state parks, and now a House-Senate committee is working to increase development. Examples of development include cabins for rent, which have proven successful at Moraine State Park in Butler County.

headline: City Sees Higher Costs After Byberry
abstract: PA would have to provide at least $6.2 million this year for services to replace those lost because of the closing of the Philadelphia State Hospital, which will affect five times the number of mentally ill people as initially expected.

headline: Pa. salaries rank 14th
abstract: PA ranks 14th nationally in teacher salaries, though it's lower than most of the surrounding states, such as NJ, which is 9th.  Officials note that it's good that PA is improving, but that it should rank higher and should continue providing more money for teachers.

headline: Valdez Tragedy
abstract: In a letter to the editor, a citizen asks, why in a time of increased concern for ecological treasures was more attention not given to the Exxon Valdez oil spill.

headline: Accounting of drug money sought
abstract: Walter M. Phillips Jr., the Democratic candidate for Philadelphia District Attorney, stated that if elected he would use assets confiscated by drug dealers to fund anti-drug groups. He also attacked the Republican incumbent district attorney Ronald D. Castille for failing to provide accounts of how money from drug dealers had been spent in the past. A state law places limits on the information district attorneys can disclose about the use of confiscated drug money, and Phillips believes Castille should have lobbied the state attorney general to set guidelines on what information can be made available to the public.

headline: State fined over prison
abstract: US District Judge Maurice Cohill has fined the PA Department of Corrections $1,000 for failing to name a person to cure environmental hazards at the PA State Correctional Institution in Pittsburgh. The state was under an order by Cohill in August to hire an environmentalist and submit a plan to fix problems by December 1.

headline: Publisher Says Lengthy JOA Hearing Threatens Paper
abstract: The publisher of the York Daily Record says the newspaper could be forced to shut down if federal authorities drag out their review of a proposed partial merger with the paper's primary competitor.

headline: In Pennsylvania, incumbents' seats are very safe
abstract: The unchallenged incumbent seats in elections for the PA House are compared to the unchallenged seats in Soviet elections where seats are saved for loyal party members.

headline: Mt. Pisgah dedicates nature center
abstract: DER officials and a state senator and about 25 others attended the dedication of a new nature center at Mt. Pisgah State Park.  A program celebrating the 10th anniversary of the park was held, focusing on the Pennsylvania Conservation Corps, which built many of the parks facilities.

headline: A time when the 'average voter' really has some clout
abstract: Recent redistricting will give voters a new chance to make their mark upon our democracy.  Voters will elect the majority of governors and state legislatures this coming election.  Republicans are tasked with the challenge of using their ability to win presidential elections to win other smaller races that impact that broader national scene.  Their inability to move into pivotal state legislatures where redistricting decisions are made is seen as a disadvantage.

headline: City warns state of cuts in service to the retarded
abstract: Philadelphia warned the state yesterday that they city would have to make cuts in services to the 4,500 mentally retarded Philadelphians unless the state added more than $7.5 million to the city's appropriation.

headline: Palmyra Board Approves 12-Mill Tax Increase, Record Budget
abstract: The Palmyra Area School Board approved a record budget of over $12 million, including a tax hike of 12 mills, the largest hike in 15 years.  One board member dissented, saying the budget and hike were "a little larger than is really necessary."

headline: Valley municipalities sign sewer agreement
abstract: Four municipalities signed an agreement to share the sewer facilities in Athens township.  They are now looking for a loan from the state to get installations underway.

headline: Agents raid reputed "head shops"
abstract: Agents from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, US Drug Enforcement Administration, US Customs Service and the Pittsburgh police raided 8 businesses in Pittsburgh. The businesses sold paraphernalia used with illicit drugs. Postal Inspector William Scott described the raids as a success.

headline: State officials and the union representing police troopers will sign a new two-year contract today
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey and officials of the Fraternal Order of Police State Police Lodges will sign a new contract today. It is only the third time in 20 years that state officials and the union have negotiated a labor agreement without resorting to binding arbitration.

headline: PUC study shows UGI rates high in consumer complaints
abstract: UGI Corp. received an high rate of complaints from customers, though the company attributes the complaints to their credit collection philosophy.

headline: In Phila., chambers are forming for commerce with other nations
abstract: Chambers are forming for commerce between the Philadelphia region and France, Israel, Chile and Australia.  The foreign visitors traveled to Dallas and Atlanta before arriving in Phila. on Friday morning.

headline: Olyphant plans to sue DER if flooding occurs
abstract: Olyphant Council President John Gilgallon was warned the DER that the borough is prepared to sue if flooding occurs as an effect of the proposed Keystone Landfill.  The DER assured the borough that flooding would not occur, but PennDOT warned that flooding would be possible.

headline: Stork tries to refocus campaign on city's economic needs
abstract: Democratic mayoral candidate Janice C Stork is attempting to shift the focus of the campaign to economic development.  While she says other candidates have focused on crime and drugs, she wants to take a more comprehensive approach and include ways to grow the city's economy.  Stork wants to ensure that the city has the ability to pay for the improvements to public safety that the other candidates promise.

headline: Columbia adopts drug-free zones
abstract: Drug-free zones were established within 1,000 feet of parochial and public schools. Charles Coombs, principal of Columbia High School, has worked with the borough to obtain "drug free zone" signs from the PA Department of Corrections.

headline: pa-racism
abstract: At a news conference in Harrisburg attended by Penn State President Bryce Jordan, state Attorney General Ernest Preate said that he will launch an investigation into at least three racially motivated attacks on black students at Penn State.

headline: Waste Plan Will Clear Up County's Cloudy Future, Consultant Says
abstract: In the face of a seemingly bleak future when it comes to waste disposal, Clearfield County officials announced details of a waste management plan that should alleviate some of the county's worries about future waste problems.

headline: AIDS cases: 100,000 and still climbing
abstract: With AIDS cases on the rise and having just hit the 100,000 milestone, there is little hope for a slowing of the epidemic.  AIDS is actually expected to spread faster than ever before in the coming years.

headline: State ordered to house juvenile offenders
abstract: Commonwealth Court Judge James G. Colins has ordered the Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare to provide new housing for Philadelphia juvenile offenders or face fines of $5,000 per day per youth within 10 days. The order came in a suit filed by District Attorney Ronald D. Castille to relieve overcrowding at the Philadelphia Youth Study Center. Castille had argued that PA law requires the state to place youths judged delinquent, which is the requirement for sending youths to development centers, in a state-run facility. Officials said 40 youths have been judged delinquent. DPW spokesman LeRoy Hedgepeth said the department has not yet decided what to do because it does not have a place to put the individuals.

headline: Resolution honors Carbon County Conservation Unit
abstract: PA Representative Keith McCall discusses a resolution he introduced into the PA House which recognizes the Carbon County Unit of the PA Conservation Corps. The unit received the Exemplary Project Award from the National Association of Service and Conservation Corps for its work on behalf of Carbon County. The House will vote on the legislation following its election recess.

headline: It's costly to be a candidate
abstract: The Editorial Board states that the 1990 gubernatorial election is likely to cost over $20 million.  The Editorial Board believes that the strength of money should not overpower the strength of ideas.

headline: One-room schoolhouse approved
abstract: The Maxatawny Township Zoning Hearing Board approved a proposal to build a one-room schoolhouse by a group of Old Order Mennonites as part of the Kutztown Parochial Schools.  The schoolhouse will have no electricity, running water, or bathrooms.

headline: Area school dropout rates
abstract: Chart listing the dropout rates of area schools.  They include Trop, Wyalusing, Towanda and Sullivan.  Towanda has the fifth lowest dropout rate of those listed.  They have a rate of 2.88%.  The state average is 3.1%

headline: Complaints key to state smoking law
abstract: On Sunday the state's new smoking law will go into effect and will ban smoking in public stores, offices, auditoriums, and other public spaces unless designated otherwise.  Larger restaurants also must provide for a non-smoking section.  Sen. Michael Dawida was the law's sponsor in the House.

headline: pa-susquehanna
abstract: A new two-tiered tuition structure at Susquehanna University in Selinsgrove has been instituted for the 1989-1990 school year, with freshmen and upperclassmen witnessing hikes of about 17 percent and 9 percent respectively.

headline: Water plan is 'fast shuffle'
abstract: The writer opposes a bill going through Congress which would amend a 1961 compact for the Delaware River Basin which would allow officials to charge more users of the basin.

headline: Alabama law capping damages is tested
abstract: Insurance companies are closely watching a challenge to an Alabama constitutional law restricting punitive damages to $250,000 in a lawsuit. The law is being tested in a case in which a wounded hunter suing a gun swivel company was awarded $1 million in punitive damages by a federal jury, damages which were reduced in accordance with the state law. Insurance companies claim that the law caused a surge in litigation which in turn caused premiums to rise.

headline: State police seek to add nearly 500
abstract: The PA State Police commissioner made a pitch to the state Senate for a large increase in manpower to be able to deal with the current stresses on the force.

headline: Resort plan criticized at hearing
abstract: A proposal by the US Forest Service to increase development near the Allegheny Reservoir has garnered the criticism of both environmentalists and elected officials, such as PA Representatives Curtis S. Bowley and Peter Kostmayer. Development of the area is favored by the Warren County Commissioners and the Warren County Chamber of Commerce, who argue that development will bring tourism and jobs to the area. Groups such as the Coalition for No Kinzua Resort oppose the development.

headline: Lawmakers see need for fitness suite
abstract: State lawmakers are attempting to garner state funds to help build a fitness center in a wing of the Capitol Building so that they can more easily stay in shape.  Critics accuse them of wanting to use taxpayer money for their own benefit, when they could just go to a different health club or gym.

headline: River basin panel approves project, water allocation
abstract: The Delaware River Basin Commission approved a plan to allocated 20 million gallons of water a day for dry times, and met with some criticism from environmentalists.

headline: Homeless Hit Road
abstract: 300 homeless from Chester's East Side Ministries will set out on a 1125-mile walk to Washington DC where they will participate in the "New Exodus March."  It is part of the "Housing Now!" effort to increase awareness of homeless issues.  They are looking for the federal government to restore $25 billion to the housing budget to help homeless get into housing.  Organizers are expecting anywhere between 100,000 and 500,000 to attend.

headline: Conestoga View does need problem-solving
abstract: The editorial board discusses an inspection by the PA Department of Health of Conestoga View nursing home. The public has praised the institution, but the department inspection found many shortcomings at the institution. The board questions the use of the contracted company which runs Conestoga View, Diversified Health Services, as well as county health standards.

headline: Pay old debts before new ones
abstract: The editors believe that instead of following Gov. Casey's plan to use $147 million for anti-drug efforts, most of that money should be used to pay the state's debt to school districts, totalling $96 million, for special education.  The money has been withheld from districts because of various other spending plans in which they were shortchanged.

headline: We must ban plastic, foam packaging
abstract: Bob Long, member of the St. Paul City Council, believes that plastic and foam packaging should be banned because they are harmful to the environment.

headline: Albany panel says $2 million in anti-drug funds is wasted
abstract: According to a report by the New York State Commission on Government Integrity, most of the $2 million dollars supposedly directed towards New York's drug abuse agency is unaccounted for and has not gone towards the treatment of drug addicts. The four programs cited were created to receive financing to combat crack addictions through residential treatment programs, although three out of four never treated anyone. The report criticizes Julio A. Martinez, director of the Division of Substance Abuse Services as well as the administration of NYC Governor Mario Cuomo. Cuomo had realized an urgent need for drug-treatment programs but did not accurately oversee the use of the state funds given to the Martinez-led division.

headline: State running out of time for prison reform
abstract: The editorial board expresses its belief that prison reform should be one of the top priorities for PA Governor Robert Casey and the state General Assembly. The board cites two incidents of riot, one at Camp Hill and one in Huntingdon, and a federal judge's ruling of the need to overhaul Western Penitentiary as evidence for the need to reform the state prison system. The board agrees with William Reznor, Mercer County Commissioner and Chairman of the PA State Association of County Commissioners' Jail Overcrowding Task Force, who stated that the state needs to re-examine its prison system.

headline: RIDC will spend $20 million to revamp Westinghouse plant
abstract: The Regional Industrial Development Corp., a non-profit company which purchased the old Westinghouse Electric Corp.'s East Pittsburgh works, has decided to spend $20 million in renovation costs.

headline: It's time for former City Council members to fade away
abstract: This opinion article addresses the end of the political terms of four Harrisburg City Council members, who had lost their bids for Democratic nominations in May. The author, Connie McNamara, ridicules the City Council members for how they exited their positions, by taking shots at Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed and the media. McNamara comments on the parting comments of Council President Reizdan B. Moore and Council members Harriet Braxton and Calvin E. Gilchrist. The author notes at the end the positive accomplishments of the City Council.

headline: Saving space
abstract: Suggests a way to try and save scenic and historic space from development and heralds the importance of having open space.

headline: Interviews Explore A-C Valley's Needs
abstract: Quality roads and infrastructure in northern Butler and Clarion Counties are seen as a driving force for local students moving away after they graduate.  The bad roads make it hard for the area to attract industry, in turn making it hard for jobs to settle in the region to supply the residents of the area.

headline: County home gains on troubles
abstract: A recently released report said that the Dauphin Manor nursing home, where problems had been found previously, could regain its full operating license before the end of the year says December Dauphin Manor administrator James H. Hetrick, because of improvements that have been made to the home. Health inspectors from the PA Department of Health say only three problems remain, including physicians' standing orders for patients, infection control in laundry areas, and staffing.

headline: Penn State opens center in hub of city professional community
abstract: Penn State President, Bryce Jordan, announced the opening of the Penn State Downtown Center at the Penn State-Harrisburg campus.  The building offers three classrooms and is hoped to offer closer connections to government officials and state agencies.

headline: Westinghouse eyes PCB drum disposal
abstract: Westinghouse is in one of the last stages of a cleanup process along a Gettysburg road, which involves moving and disposing of 41 drums containing the toxic chemical PCB.

headline: Allentown Activist Pushes for 'Children's Bill of Rights'
abstract: Allentown Activist, Tom Watts, pushes for a 'Children's Bill of Rights' amendment to the Constitution.  He has approached U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter and children's rights agencies with his proposal.

headline: Staving off the agony follows drug-induced ecstasy
abstract: The article discusses how crack, a purified form of cocaine, works to give the user brief euphoria and then depression which leads to recurring use of the drug. A manual published by the American Psychiatric Association states that cocaine abuse is a psychological problem while cocaine dependency is physical.

headline: RJR Nabisco signs American Express' chief
abstract: Louis V. Gerstner Jr., the president of the American Express Co., was named as the chairman and CEO of RJR Nabisco Inc.  Gerstner faces a challenge after Nabisco was the recipient of a hostile takeover by the firm Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co.  The company also faces anti-trust allegations by the federal government.

headline: It's who you know...officials hope "Capital" contacts pay off for city
abstract: Williamsport Mayor Jessie L. Bloom called PA Governor Robert Casey's Capital for a Day initiative "very productive." PA Department of Labor and Industry Secretary Harris Wofford said it was good for cabinet members to get to know their local offices, while PA Representative Alvin C. Bush encouraged future governors to continue the Capital for a Day program. Casey discussed several local issues, including a $2 million grant to Williamsport Wirerope Works to help purchase a former Bethlehem Steel Corporation facility, and the PA Department of Transportation's contract to pave Route 15, north of Williamsport.

headline: Show may not go on
abstract: Moosic Mayor John Segilia has announced that an Independence Day concert and party today at a local park may not be held there, as the park has been closed for two years and would need to be inspected for health and fire safety.

headline: Fire the Handicapped: Losing more than their jobs
abstract: A lengthy feature in the Philadelphia Inquirer Magazine about the plight of the employed handicapped during times where budgets are slashed for social-services.  The stories of a number of such workers are shared.

headline: County seeks drug prevention aid
abstract: York County is waiting to see how much, if any, money it will receive from Gov. Casey's plan to create a $140 million fund for the fight against drugs.

headline: Philadelphia schools undergo complicated asbestos removal
abstract: PA school districts are faced with the costly and time consuming task of removing asbestos from various parts of school buildings, but are sometimes procedurablly impeded by the DER, as schools aren't supposed to begin the process without authorization, but the DER is behind in reviewing plans.

headline: Weston receives $46 million EPA contract
abstract: Roy F. Weston Inc. was awarded a $46 million contract by the EPA to support cleanup efforts at Superfund sites throughout the northeast.  The West Chester-headquartered company is expected to obtain net revenues of $20 million over the life of the 10 year contract.

headline: Amish say Bush wasting his time with drug talk
abstract: The Amish are concerned about President Bush's real reason for visiting their community.  They do not feel that many of their teenagers are using drugs, and many are apprehensive of government involvement

headline: Steps proposed for Berks prison
abstract: A task force formed in October to analyze the inmate overcrowding problem at Berks County Prison came up with several short- and long-term solutions.  These solutions were presented to members of the prison board, which will undertake a review and and then respond to the recommendation at a February meeting

headline: Seeking reforms
abstract: This letter to the editor, written by PA Senator Michael M. Dawida, is meant to clarify the auto insurance legislation that was voted on the week before. Dawida says that two philosophies emerged; the first was a package by PA Governor Robert P. Casey that included as its main element a limited no-fault system which lessened the right to sue and tied in specific rate reductions to the savings generated in the legislation. The second option reduces mandatory health care benefits. Dawida discusses the two flaws he sees in the compromise that emerged from legislative discussion. He pleads with readers to continue to demand car insurance reform and pressure the legislature to find the best solution in the coming year.

headline: Jubelirer admits, in duplicate, his tax letter erred
abstract: State Senate President, Robert C. Jubelirer yesterday admitted that a fund- raising letter bearing his name contained wrong information about a tax- revision proposal.

headline: State wants input on parks
abstract: The DER wants input from citizens about the state parks, and is putting questionaires at parks that can be filled out by parkgoers.

headline: Rally says 'no' to city drug dealers
abstract: 2000 people marched against drugs in Harrisburg yesterday.  Organizers say they want to take back their communities from the drug dealers.  Most of the supporters were black and wanted to participate because they say drugs have ruined their communities too.

headline: DA hopes nursing home abuse conviction sends a message
abstract: Timothy S. Berrena, a nurse's aide at State College Manor nursing home, was convicted on charges of abusing elderly residents. Centre County District Attorney Ray Gricar said he hopes that Berrena's conviction will send a message to others to stop abusing the elderly. State College Manor was closed under the order of the PA Department of Health. Jury foreman Wesley Wagner is an engineer for State College borough.

headline: Pitt classroom reflects African culture
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh says its $250,000 African Heritage Classroom - the 22nd nationality classroom built at the school's Cathedral of Learning - is the only room built to reflect African culture. Nancy H. Lee has been raising money for the project since 1972 because of a lack of wealthy people to ask for money. The room duplicates the courtyard of an 18th century Asante village, typical of those in Ghana, West Africa. The design was created by Pitt history professor Laurence Glasco, who spent three years researching African culture for the project.

headline: What Do You Know Can Hurt You?
abstract: A state law requiring businesses and others handling hazardous materials to notify the public of this fact and how to deal with the materials in the event of problem is now being implemented more and more.

headline: Another Band-Aid for the drug problem?
abstract: Editorial stating that in order to win the "war on drugs", anti-drug efforts would require massive amount of money, which they're not currently receiving.  It says that sometimes an issue gets talked about too much and the rhetoric looses its meaning.

headline: Stevens, other Das join Preate in war on drugs
abstract: Luzerne County District Attorney Corry Stevens announced that he was in full support of state Attorney General Ernie Preate's recommendations concerning the prosecution of drug dealers.  Stevens is currently evaluating the possibility of setting up a county anti-drug task force.

headline: Senate in gear for insurance reform
abstract: Senate Republican leaders and pushing ahead with auto insurance legislation, saying they want to reach a compromise before the end of the session on June 30.  Democrats and Republicans have somewhat different strategies to the reform, but a compromise should be workable.

headline: Judges order talks on Old Forge pact
abstract: Four judges of the Lackawanna County Court, sitting en banc, denied a temporary restraining order which the Old Forge School District sought against its striking unionized teachers.  A hearing will be conducted next week on a preliminary injunction against the job actions.

headline: Swatara dam project faces another logjam
abstract: Additional delays in the Swatara dam project are possible, as the Army Corps of Engineers has suggested that a full environmental-impact study may be required before a permit is issued.  The project has been under consideration and planning for 21 years.

headline: Centre County looks to Maryland firm as a recycling outlet
abstract: Centre County is looking for an outfit to take delivery of the proceeds of its new recycling program.  Although the nation is experiencing a glut of newsprint, Centre County officials are looking to arrange a deal with a company to reprocess the paper that is recycled in the county.  A description of the success of the new recycling program in Centre County continues.

headline: Danger Of Lyme Disease At Presque Isle Minimal
abstract: As a result of recent increased efforts to provide awareness and treatment for Lyme disease, some people have avoided visiting certain areas because of the fear of the disease.  Officials say that visitors to Preque Isle have very little chance of encountering the ticks, as they live in underbrush, of which there is little on the island.

headline: Pitt's affirmative inaction
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh has seen a major decrease in the number of black faculty joining the school in recent years. Pitt lost 12 black faculty members from 1983 until 1988, a disturbing decline that parallels other colleges attracting more diverse faculty. The editorial says this declining trend presents a problem for Pitt. Dr. Barbara K. Shore, chairman of the Pitt Faculty Senate's committee on affirmative action, said the school put into place a program to improve the numbers of diverse faculty at the University and thought it was working, but declined to pay attention to the proof of its success, or lack thereof.

headline: Windsor's water woes approaching resolution
abstract: Windsor borough's struggle to resolve its water woes is near an end, as the DER has granted a water allocation permit to the Windsor Borough Water Authority to draw 150,000 gallons of water a day from the Red Lion Municipal Water Authority.

headline: Anti-drug message in Berks schools: 'Don’t Be A Dope'
abstract: State Senator Michael O'Pake distributed "Don't Be A Dope" pamphlets to Berks County high school students as part of "Say No To Drugs Week."

headline: Syphilis testing is ordered in Chester arrests
abstract: A Delaware County judge- in cooperation with the state Dept. of Health- has ordered all district justices in Chester to deny bail to defendents in drug cases unless they submitt blood tests for syphilis.

headline: Senate opts for compromise insurance plan
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate approved an amendment compromise to the auto insurance issue that is highly opposed by PA Governor Robert P. Casey. Casey said he would veto the measure if it passes the Legislature and comes to his desk. Supporters of the amendment said it could cut premiums from 10 percent to 50 percent for drivers statewide, while some Democratic opponents such as PA Senator Michael O'Pake said they do not understand where the numbers came from. The compromise omits a reform package proposed by Governor Casey. PA Senator Joseph Loeper, Senate Majority Leader, said the compromise would reduce rates for all Pennsylvanians.

headline: Judicial process based on politics
abstract: Thompson J. McCullough, who was nominated by Gov. Casey to be the county's next judge, awaits Senate confirmation of his appointment.  The Senate confirmation process stagnates on party lines.

headline: The Delawarer estuary
abstract: A look at the Delaware estuary and some of its history and current ecological needs.

headline: Interest free energy loans available to all
abstract: All New Yorkers, regardless of income are eligible for low-interest loans for energy or energy efficiency.  Everything from new furnaces to storm windows will be covered.  The loans will be available between $2500 and $4500.  Part of the idea is to reduce the impact of foreign oil on the economy by increasing energy efficiency.

headline: 'Down with dope, up with hope'
abstract: By wielding hammers to seal a drug house in Northwest Philadelphia, PA Governor Robert P. Casey and Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode announced through the symbolic gesture the donation of grants to community organizers in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and Reading as part of a statewide comprehensive anti-drug education and prevention campaign. Governor Casey said the approximately $156,000 in PENNFREE funds would go to Mantua Against Drugs and Team Fight Against Drugs to finance prevention programs in Philadelphia school districts. Other grants were awarded to anti-drug programs in Pittsburgh and Reading.

headline: Pleasant Valley administrators reveal budget
abstract: Pleasant Valley School District's administrators recommended the '89-'90 budget to the school board, which will then move to public inspection before it becomes final.  Also, scores from a standardized test suggest that Pleasant Valley 5th graders are slightly below average.

headline: With Air Quality Bit
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency listed the areas across the United States that violated a federal air quality standard for one of six air pollutants including: ozone, carbon monoxide, lead, smoke (dust and soot), nitrogen oxide, and sulfer dioxide.

headline: As a way to relieve prison overcrowding a group of state lawmakers are proposing so-called motivational boot camps for first-time non-violent offenders.
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers propose boot camps to help rehabilitate first-time offenders and ease prison overcrowding, according to PA Representative Dwight Evans. Evans said the same system practiced in other states has shown promising results for inmates. The boot camps require inmates to follow a rigorous schedule of physical activity and drug and alcoholism treatment. Inmates aged 30 or under who are convicted of minor drug charges or first-time non-violent offenses would be selected for the voluntary six-month camp by the corrections commissioner.

headline: Street Corner Drug Sales
abstract: Despite increasing efforts by law enforcement, drug abuse and trafficking is ever-increasing, and reports say that drugs are being sold for the lowest prices ever, meaning that there's an abundant supply.  Clearly, the solution is not in enforcement, it's in education and prevention.

headline: Senate passes its plan to cut car insurance
abstract: State Senate Republicans unveiled their version of the auto insurance bills passed by the House in the past two weeks, leading Democrats to criticize the Republicans, saying that they were moving closer to confrontation than compromise.  Hopes of finishing the legislation before the summer recess are now dimming.

headline: Judicial reform
abstract: Comments on and condemns the legislature's clever comination of a judicial reform bill and the incentives for the legislature in it.

headline: Trail may cost up to $5 million
abstract: A proposed hicking and biking trail to be converted from an unused railway between Confluence and Cumberland, MD.  The estimated cost is between $2 and $5 million.

headline: Fogel: I Could Legally Drive
abstract: Former federal judge Herbert A. Fogel is serving 22 consecutive suspensions on his driver's license.  He was first suspended in 1986 and will get his privledges back in 2000.  In spite of this, a month ago Fogel told reporters that he was allowed to drive.

headline: Drug package submitted
abstract: The Senate Republicans received a proposal for a very comprehensive drug package for Pennsylvania concerning the illegal drug market. The proposed drug package calss for education , treatment, and punitive measures to combat the illicit drug problem.

headline: Poor Marks- 'Education deficit' requires action
abstract: With PA test scores fallen for the third year in a row, the author of this opinion piece calls for an increased focus on education.

headline: WMI backs from plan to take NY ash
abstract: Waste Management Inc. has backed away from a plan to dispose of as much as 1,000 tons of NYC incinerator ash each day at its planned Falls Township landfill.

headline: Assault- NRA stifles attempts to ban them
abstract: Three state representatives have introduced legislation to either ban or ease the buying of so- called assault rifles.  The NRA and its 200,000 state members oppose the measures.

headline: Street prices
abstract: This is a chart of current drug prices during stages of the distribution chain in the City of Pittsburgh. The prices for the different sizes of heroin, cocaine, crack, and marijuana are provided.

headline: Small games need chance to work
abstract: This opinion piece addresses how Pennsylvania state legislators want to revise the small games of chance law before Revenue Department regulations have been put into action. PA Representative Fred Trello of Allegheny County, who is chairman of the House Finance Committee, said the Revenue Department has erected too many obstacles for some smaller groups, discouraging them from offering games. Trello opposes some requirements that exclude organizations from participating. The writer of the opinion suggests that committee members allow the law to take effect before attempting to revise it.

headline: Jury commissioner bids for 2nd term
abstract: Republican Marianne R. Sutton, the current Berks County jury commissioner, has said that she will seek reelection in the May 16 primary election.

headline: Views on state parks weighed: Most oppose development, results of survey show
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources distributed a questionnaire answered by approximately 14,000 people about their feelings on the state park system. The majority of people believe that more modern cabins should be built in the parks but no more development should occur, said DER Deputy Secretary James R. Grace. A report released by DER officials recommended this same suggestion and the department will hold public meetings to gather additional information and comments from the public about how the parks should be operated. Other results from the survey are mentioned as well.

headline: High Court Lets PA Require Judges Retire at Age 70
abstract: The US Supreme Court turned away suggestions that its law requiring judges to retire at age 70 is unconstitutional.  Since 1968, PA has required all state judges to step down at age 70.  Federal judges have lifetime tenure.  The court upheld the law on the grounds that it was a reasonable way to advance the state's goals.  This includes promoting younger judges and preventing harm caused by senile judges.

headline: Drug plan is praised in suburbs
abstract: Gov. Casey's plan to create a $140 million fund for anti-drug efforts was praised by suburban officials, while Republicans have their own plan for the $140 million, including special education , highway maintenance and some anti-drug efforts.

headline: Possible $83 million deficit has lawmakers squirming
abstract: An $83 million deficit is expected in June of 1990 in relation to special education debt, and regulations proposed by the Pennsylvania Board of Education do not seem to address the problem. Legislators in both the House of Representatives and the Senate are struggling to encourage the board back on track, as they had just committed $99 million to cover special-education debt accumulated over six years, during the June before. Hearings on the proposed regulations from the Board of Education will take place before the board submits the final version  to the Independent Regulatory Review Commission in January.

headline: Yorks angles to stay on Fish Commission
abstract: Columbia County Commissioner J. Wayne Yorks, who has been on the PA Fish Commission since 1980, is seeking another eight-term.  Members of the commission must be appointed by the governor and confirmed by a two-thirds vote in the Senate.

headline: At first, mom didn't believe stories about confinement
abstract: Patricia Bonner was shocked to find that her son's teachers at the Lincoln Center in Camp Hill punished him by placing him in a "box," which turned out to be a 6-foot-4-inch by 6-foot-8 inch enclosure with 3 locks on the door. Her son has emotional problems, but does not believe the solution to the problem is placing him inside the structure which she likened to solitary confinement. Her son has since been suspended from the school, and a panel of experts from the Capital Area Intermediate Unit and from Central Dauphin School District have remanded him to in-home instruction.

headline: 'Suicide' bills cause concern
abstract: The writer opposes the "Suicide" bills in the House, which would mandate classroom time allocated for teen suicide prevention, among other issues like drugs, alcohol, and sex.  It would also require "peer-sharing" or "affective education," which would involve kids talking with each other about such issues, which has sometimes been shown to actually increase involvement in those activities.

headline: Small games of chance applications now available
abstract: Applications for licenses to conduct small games of chance are now available for qualitfying organizations and clubs.

headline: Keep exposing legislators' greed
abstract: The writer requests that the Inquirer run more stories exposing how self-serving legislators and other elected officials can be and routinely are, so that citizens will be moved to do something about it.

headline: Wild, scenic river bill could slow Bucks growth
abstract: US Representative Peter H. Kostmayer will propose a bill to designate a 32-mile stretch of the Delaware River as part of the federal Wild and Scenic River System. Doing so would prohibit the construction of structures and prohibit development along the river. Kostmayer stated that the bill would limit growth along the river, thus preserving the area's rural character.

headline: Researchers Say Underground AIDS Drug Ineffective Against Virus
abstract: Researchers found that a popular underground drug being consumed by many AIDS patients is ineffective against the dangerous virus.  The government is suggested to take a stronger role in encouraging people to take only proven, tested drugs.

headline: FDA finds most generics are safe
abstract: The US Food and Drug Administration deemed most generic drugs safe for use, but continues its investigation. FDA Commissioner Frank E. Young was removed from his post and given a new job in the government's health bureaucracy a week before the FDA made its announcement. The Congressional probe into generic drugs was prompted by Pittsburgh's Mylan Laboratories, which claimed that the FDA routinely delayed approving its drugs for use.

headline: Pottsgrove to spend $4.8 million for school projects
abstract: The Pottsgrove School Board approved the spending of $4.8 million for two construction projects.  The plans were nearly abandoned due to high construction costs.

headline: Yule trees face the grind
abstract: Allentown's 30,000 Christmas trees will be recycled as part of the city's effort to cut down on landfill wastes. The trees will be collected by J.P. Mascaro and Sons, the city's trash haulers, and will be transported to a city Parks Department facility where they will ground into mulch. Betsy Levin, the city's recycling coordinator, said the city may use the mulch in its parks or make it available to citizens next spring.

headline: Attorney sentenced for stealing
abstract: Allegheny County attorney Thomas Macurdy was sentenced by Common Pleas Judge Jeffrey Manning for taking $28,000 from a client's estate. Macurdy was ordered to pay back the $28,000 plus interest, and to serve 3-7 years in prison. He is concurrently serving a 23-46 month sentence for stealing $100,000 from another client's estate.

headline: Suit to protest funding for pump is thrown out
abstract: Bucks County President Judge Issac S. Garb dismissed a lawsuit brought by a group of more than 100 county taxpayers regarding a then-$14 million dollar loan sought by Bucks County Commissioners Andrew Warren and Mark Schweiker.

headline: SmithKline chairman's pay cut by half during struggling year
abstract: Pharmeaceutical company, SmithKline, has lost profits and employees.  Corporate restructuring allowed for many former employees to receive hundreds of thousands of dollars each in severance pay.

headline: Keller nominated
abstract: Gov. Casey nominated Berks County Solicitor and former GOP County Committee chairman, Scott D. Keller, to fill a vacancy on the Berks court of common pleas.  The state Senate will now proceed with confirmation hearings.

headline: Williamhouse groundbreaking set Thursday
abstract: Supervisors will attend groundbreaking ceremonies for the Williamhouse Regency addition Thursday, a ceremony that will also be attended by Gov. Robert P. Casey.

headline: Abortion Foes Freed After Protest
abstract: Police released 176 anti-abortion protesters after refusing to identify themselves when confronted by police under the orders to disperse.  A number of protesters used tar to vandalize the clinic and otherwise made it difficult for law enforcement to get control of the situation.

headline: Firms rethinking Medigap rates, coverage
abstract: In response to increased costs associated with the repeal of the Medicare Catastrophic Coverage Act, many insurance companies will be changing prices and coverage in the near future. Therefore, insurance officials are saying it is not the time for subscribers to shop for new insurance policies. The Coverage Act had limited the amount older patients needed to pay for hospital stays to $560 a year, but now elderly patients must pay deductibles of $592 for hospital stays each quarter. Insurance companies providing insurance to supplement Medicare coverage, called "Medigap" policies, will pick up extra fees.

headline: Priorities for special education
abstract: Mother of a mentally retarded child expresses her concerns about the quality of special-needs education.

headline: 200 to be hired from local union for pipeline work
abstract: About 200 workers from a local laborers' union will be hired from out-of-state firms for the replacement of pipeline for natural gas.

headline: Battle over product liability brewing in Harrisburg
abstract: The fight over product liability began with the opening of the legislative session last month, largely between the Trial Lawyers Association and a group called the Pennsylvania Task Force on Product Liability.  The task force is comprised of such companies as Phillip Morris and General Electric, and it would like to focus on the issues of timeliness with lawsuits, punitive damages, assumption of known risk, and making manufacturers of products that are state of the art immune from lawsuits.

headline: Support Cases Settled, Collections Hit Record
abstract: Venango County is being more strict with fathers who have neglected to pay child-support, even threatening jail time until payment arrangements are made.

headline: Some see bailout of S&L proportions looming for insurers
abstract: Michael R. Levin, an industry analyst at the Towers Perrin Consulting Firm, foresees a government bailout of the insurance industry similar to that of the savings and loan industry. According to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, its watch list of trouble companies contains 570 liability underwriters, up from 132 in 1979. A report by the Congressional Research Service showed that the public questions the industry's stability.

headline: Key provision of bills on judges' appointment draws fire from Casey
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey suggested that he could not support legislation that would replace the election of judges with an appointive system and a two-thirds vote of confirmation rather than a simple majority. Governor Casey said he believed the new system would reintroduce politics into the appointment of justices. There are two divergent groups in the Legislature, one that believes a majority is preferable but is not opposed to the two-thirds confirmation, and another that believes the two-thirds confirmation is necessary to protect the party not in power.

headline: 2-Tier taxation unfair
abstract: The writer opposes the tax system in Butler County, where commercial and residential property owners pay significantly different percentages on the assessed market value.

headline: Abortion on agenda at capitol
abstract: PA is considered a key battleground in the abortion battle after the US Supreme Court moved to give states new rights in regulating abortion.  One legislator called the legislation before the PA legislature "the strongest pro-life act … in the nation."  Gov Robert Casey annouced his support for the legislation predicting that it would pass constitutional challenges.

headline: Free health care for children of working poor
abstract: The parents of Justin Coles, a 7-year-old with recurring ear infections, make more than the state cutoff for Medicaid, but less than the federal poverty cutoff. As a result, they qualify for the Caring Program for Children, a health care initiative sponsored by Blue Cross of Western PA and PA Blue Shield which inspired similar programs in other states. The initiative is working on a $341,000 grant awarded by the American Academy of Pediatrics and the federal Office of maternal and Child Health.

headline: Protection imperative at museum
abstract: In light of the recent disappearance of a display at the Reading Public Museum, new measures must be taken to increase protection of the museum's priceless artifacts, even if those measures mean higher spending

headline: A coalition of Philadelphia- area consumer groups has been granted an emergency court hearing for today to present their case for blocking recent mass- transit fare hikes.
abstract: A coalition of Philadelphia- area consumer groups has been granted an emergency court hearing to present their case for blocking recent mass- transit fare hikes.

headline: Bell puts security officer on leave
abstract: Bell of Pennsylvania has suspended with pay its former security chief, Robert Meinert, a day after he admitted he gave law enforcement authorities confidential information on phone calls.

headline: Supreme Court finds government not liable in cases of child abuse
abstract: The Supreme Court held yesterday that governments and their agencies are not obligated by the Constitution, under the due process clause found in the 14th Amendment, to protect citizens not within their custody.

headline: State House rejects timeshare industry's concellation proposal
abstract: The PA state House rejected an amendment, favored by the timeshare industry, which would provide consumers only 5 days to cancel a timeshare vacation contract.  The House ended up passing an amendment which provided for a 7 day grace period.

headline: KKK Rallies In Easton
abstract: A KKK rally held on Independence Day attempted to appeal to young potential members in a convergence of national and state Klan leaders.

headline: A New Twist For Tax Reform... Little- known fact would override 4-year cap on property tax hikes
abstract: A little known fact about the tax revision plan is beginning to emerge, and could reshape the debate: Local governments wouldn't have to wait until a four- year revenue cap expires to raise property taxes.

headline: Poll: Drugs a problem, not in our back yard
abstract: 60% of adults say drugs are not a problem in their community while 1/3 of people say they know someone who uses cocaine.  Citizens were polled on President Bush's drug plan as well.

headline: From 'warehouse' to hospital: Danville State evolves through 100-year history
abstract: The article summarizes the 100 year history of the Danville hopital.  It includes a long-term care building for the mentally ill. Many of the residents have lived there for multiple decades and communities are concerned about the push to close state hospitals, which could leave the mentally ill to survive on their own.

headline: Public schools foresee deficit of $22 million
abstract: The Board of Education was presented with a $1.1 billion budget, with a $22 million deficit, and a challenge to its affirmative action program.

headline: Any radiation has potential to alter human cells
abstract: The author of the opinion piece believes that radiation at any level has the potential to alter human cells, so GPU's on- site evaporation proposal is a bad idea.

headline: Bennett weighing forced treatment in cases of pregnant cocaine addicts
abstract: Drug czar William Bennett is considering calling for forced treatment of cocaine-addicted pregnant women in order to avoid negative effects in their babies.  Babies born to cocaine users often have physical, educational, or mental disabilities or impairments.

headline: Supreme Court Upholds Reversal In Pa. Drunk- Driving Case
abstract: The Supreme Court today let stand the reversal of a PA man's drunken- driving conviction because the jury was played a video tape recording of the man's sobriety test.

headline: State investigating squeeze on small beer distributors
abstract: The PA House Liquor Control Committee will investigate reports that large beer distributors are receiving "unwarranted" discounts from breweries and that small distributors are being driven out of business because of the rise in the purchase amounts needed for bulk discounts. An unidentified industry expert stated that small distributors will testify before the committee to prove that large distributors are getting unfair discounts. They allege that these discounts allow the distributors to charge less to consumers, which violates PA liquor law by encouraging greater consumption.

headline: Knoll's plan
abstract: The editorial highlights the innovative plans of PA State Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll. It covers her plan called Reciprocal Investment Commitment of Conscience, a plan to make state pension funds aware of investment opportunities in other states in exchange for those states' investments. The editorial board praises Knoll for her efforts in saving the state of Pennsylvania money.

headline: Adams County levies 5-mill increase in tax
abstract: Adams County taxpayers will pay 25 percent more in real estate taxes in the coming year as voted yesterday by county commissioners. The tax increase is meant to cover estimated expenditures of $8.4 million. Minority commissioner Catherine W. Cowan said the county has now reached the maximum levy on real estate allowed by Pennsylvania state law. Cowan said increasing the budget of Children and Youth Services and judicial services in past years has caused the tax increase. The commissioners said that they hope a countywide tax reassessment under way will ultimately reduce real estate taxes.

headline: Industry reports weekly production
abstract: Domestic steel production totaled 1,793,000 net tons during the week ending Sept 30, 1989.  That is up 2.2% over the last week.  Domestic steel production is slightly down over the entire year though.

headline: Goode hospitalized
abstract: Philadelphia mayor Wilson Goode was admitted to the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania due to rapid heart activity, his second trip to the hospital in two weeks. Goode's doctor, Edward Cooper, stated that the mayor was recovering. Press spokeswoman Karen Warrington expects that Goode will remain in the hospital for several days.

headline: Rep. posing anti-strike legislation
abstract: PA State Representative Peter R. Vroon has proposed anti-strike legislation in the House which would financially penalize teachers and school districts while striking. Vroon has been attempting to pass this bill ever since he was elected, and most recently his proposal came as a result of a strike by teachers who have not accepted an offer from the Phoenixville Area Board of School Directors. Vroon called the situation a "contest head to head with the Pennsylvania State Education Association."

headline: Bedford REC has 50th anniversary
abstract: The Bedford Rural Electric Cooperative celebrated its 50th anniversary of bringing electricity to rural areas.

headline: Bill advocates lethal injection
abstract: Lethal injection would replace electrocution as PA's method for executing convicted murderers under a bill passed unanimously yesterday by the Senate Judiciary Committee.

headline: Surcharge reducing traffic citations
abstract: A surcharge of $30 on traffic violations has caused a decrease in the number of citations given out by police officers in Somerset County. Conemaugh Township Police Chief Larry Kush, a member of the state Chiefs of Police Association, has said that his officers are complaining about giving out citations. Kush also sent a letter to the governor's office asking to repeal the surcharge.

headline: State officials hoping tourists flock to slogan
abstract: PA adopts a new state tourism slogan, "America Starts Here."

headline: Kostmayer tackles new post
abstract: New House Interior subcommittee chairman Peter Kostmayer of Philadelphia focuses a lot of his attention on environmental issues.

headline: Altoona: No new giant billboards
abstract: A new legislation in Altoona has determined that no new huge billboard may be built, though existing ones are allowed to stay.  Size limitations on other sign were also included in the legislation.

headline: Standoff in Pike County Coalfields Ends Peacefully
abstract: A picketing miner was hit by a non-union truck trying to cross the picket line, workers say.  350 coal miners walked off the job in two states.  While tensions were high after the worker was hit by the truck, a standoff was averted when 38 state troopers were sent to the scene.  The worker says he will press charges against the driver.

headline: Goode hospitalized
abstract: Philadelphia mayor Wilson Goode was hospitalized for rapid heart activity. The Associated Press expects more news to come.

headline: Restore grants: Aid key to black enrollment
abstract: One reason for decreased numbers of blacks entering college is the Reagan administration's reduction in federal grants for low-income college students.

headline: Caller ID approved, Consumer Advocate files suit
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) approved a request by Bell of Pennsylvania for customers to be able to apply for caller identification services. State Consumer Advocate David Barasch said the device in an invasion of privacy and filed suit against Commonwealth Court to overturn the PUC's decision. Administration law judge Michael C. Schnierle had recommended approval of the service if Bell offered a free blocking device to people who want to protect their phone number and location.

headline: Bird team can't 'see the forest' in death probe
abstract: State-appointed investigators who are looking into the death of Beatrice Bird and Children and Youth will return to Columbia County within 2 weeks to finish their work.  The group will then report its findings to state Dept. of Public Welfare Secretary John White, as well as county commissioners.  A county case report has alleged that Children and Youth staff were negligent concerning the death of Bird.

headline: Task force deservese full commitment
abstract: The editors hope that Chambersburg Borough officials give serious consideration to supporting the Franklin County drug task force, saying that the only way the force can work is if it has significant support from many municipalities.

headline: State panel approves first OTB permit
abstract: The PA Horse Racing Commission has given the go-ahead for the first application for an off-track betting (OTB) facility in Reading. Kenneth Kirchner, executive director of the commission, said the approval of the application from Penn National race course near Harrisburg came less than a week after a public hearing on the track's plans. Kirchner said a hearing has been scheduled for Tuesday on Philadelphia Park's proposal for an OTB parlor near City Hall. The PA Harness Racing Commission also approved its first application for Pocono Downs to open an OTB outlet in Erie. Under legislation passed in 1988, Pennsylvania's four racetracks are permitted to open a total of 23 OTB parlors throughout the state.

headline: Lawmaker sings some measures to save a measure
abstract: State Rep. James J. Gallen broke into song on the floor of the state House to keep the bill for a state song alive.  His efforts worked, as the song was approved 135- 59.

headline: Area legislators not keen on local tax reform
abstract: Profiles various state lawmakers' positions on the tax reform referendum.

headline: Mandatory Retirement for State Judges Upheld by US Supreme Court
abstract: The US Supreme Court upheld a law requiring that PA judges step down at age 70.  The court is stocked with four members over 70.  They did not comment on their decision.

headline: GOP bill asks stricter monitoring of mentally ill
abstract: A battle is revived over mental instituitions.  State Senator F. Joseph Loeper advocates for broadened commitment laws and stricter monitoring of the mentally ill. Some in the field say it's not the answer.

headline: Rossi retires from Penna. state police
abstract: Ronald W. Rossi, a 29-year veteran of the PA State Police and former member of the US Marine Corps, has retired. He is known through the Lehigh Valley for his work as a safety education officer in kindergarten, elementary, and secondary schools. His work has been acknowledged in many ways, such as recognition by the Bethlehem Area School District.

headline: Casey asks for review of oil prices
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey wrote a letter to US Secretary of Energy James D. Watkins and Commissioner Janet D. Steiger of the Federal Trade Commission asking them to investigate the price increase of home heating oil and to determine the cause of supply shortages within the state of Pennsylvania. Casey's actions follow suit with requests from officials in Massachusetts, New York, new Hampshire, and Rhode Island, all of which have experienced similar price jumps. PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. said he would be investigating suppliers for possible violations of antitrust and consumer protection laws. PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel also released a statement saying the state was involved in negotiations with suppliers to secure full allocations for state oil distributors.

headline: Boot camp proposed for teen-age drug offenders
abstract: Terry Spence, speaker of Delaware's House, has proposed a "boot camp" for first time juvenile offenders. He stated that the program would last 6 months, with an additional 6 months of counseling, and would be run by Delaware's Department of Services for Children, Youth, and Their Families. That department's chairman, Charles E. Hayward, has not seen the proposal yet.

headline: Under cross-examination, Hund admits addiction to drugs, alcohol
abstract: Former Philadelphia narcotics officer Charles A. Hund III admitted, during cross-examination as part of a racketeering trial of six ex-officers, that he was addicted to drugs and alcohol while in the department.

headline: State pays legislators' car insurance as others foot own bills
abstract: This opinion piece by Nancy Eshelman is written about how Pennsylvania taxpayers pay almost 100% of car insurance for their legislators while PA citizens sometimes cannot even purchase car insurance at an affordable rate. Eshelman quotes Pennsylvania Representative Frank L. Oliver of Philadelphia as asking "What's the big deal?" about the car insurance situation, while taxpayers pay over $2000 a year for insurance on his car. Eshelman says Pennsylvania and California are the only states that reimburse their legislators for the lease and insurance of their cars.

headline: Lawmakers' Views
abstract: Rep. Tom Ridge voices his support for an increase in the minimum wage, as the puchasing power of that wage has decreased by 30% since it was last raised, and his disappointment in President Bush for vetoing the legislation that would have raised minimum wage.

headline: Basketball team extends Philly's deadline on proposal
abstract: Harold Katz, owner of the Philadelphia 76ers basketball team, has extended the deadline for the City of Philadelphia to make a proposal for a new arena. Katz and officials from the Philadelphia Flyers hockey team are considering moving the teams to New Jersey, where a gubernatorial election will soon be held. Katz's decision to extend the deadline was affected by PA Governor Robert Casey's efforts to keep the 76ers in PA, as well as the recent hospitalization of Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode.

headline: Eye-opening experience likely
abstract: The editorial suggests that state education bureaucrat Donna D. Wall's decision to spend more time in the classroom will prove to be beneficial to the future of the state's education policy.  Tearing down bureaucratic walls are discussed as important challenges in the current environment.

headline: Government must assure health care
abstract: The author of an opinion piece believes that minimum health care should be assured so low- income families are protected.

headline: Ruling gives handicapped wider rights
abstract: The US Supreme Court refused to review a case brought forth by school boards (and the National School Boards Association), administrators, and organizations of local government officials regarding public funding for special education. The case dealt with the refusal of a New Hampshire school district with a $15.6 million budget to provide education for a severely disabled young man. Additionally, the court let stand a ruling that strip-searching people accused of minor traffic violations violates their rights.

headline: Cawley, Tigue Would Support Anthracite Industry Study
abstract: State Reps. Thomas Tigue and Gaynor Cawley both stated their support for a new study which would assess anthracite mining laws and fund coal and geological surveys.  However, each was skeptical as to the social, environmental, and health effects renewed coal mining would have.  Representatives of the Legislative Coal Caucus also endorsed an 11-bill package which would revitalize the state's coal industry.

headline: Brady's appeal
abstract: James Brady, crippled and forced to sit in a wheelchair after being shot by John Hinckley during his assassination attempt on Ronald Reagan, appeared before a US Senate subcommittee. He asked the Senate to initiate legislation on a 7-day waiting period when purchasing guns. The National Rifle Association disagreed with Brady's appeal.

headline: The system doesn't intimidate the intimidators
abstract: The victim of an attempted assassination by the Junior Black Mafia was forced to recant his previous identification of the two men that shot him, as there was a mafia "enforcer" in the courtroom with a gun at his hip, thus setting the suspects free.  This shows that many mafia and drug groups are unafraid of the justice system.

headline: Suit accuses dealers of odometer rollbacks
abstract: A lawsuit filed by the state attorney general's Bureau of Consumer Protection against three used car dealers accuses them of rolling back the cars' odometers to make them more attractive to buyers.  The bureau wants the dealers to pay $1,500 to each of at least 60 consumers who bought such cars.

headline: Let the voters choose gubernatorial candidates in primaries
abstract: The message of this letter to the editor is that the media needs to provide better coverage of all of the candidates running for gubernatorial positions, rather than focusing all of their energy on only two candidates. The writer of the letter encourages Republicans to not settle for one of the options for the Republican candidate, Barbara Hafer, and instead evaluate other options such as businessman James Pickard and former PA Representative John Kennedy. The writer also encourages the media to be more honest about Hafer's record and expose the credentials of the opposing candidates as well.

headline: Beaver looking to raise property tax by 1 mil
abstract: Beaver Council adopted a preliminary budget of $1,321,900. This would necessitate an increase in property taxes for homeowners. The tax money will most likely be used to remodel and repair the roof of the municipal building, purchase a new pumper truck, and fund new housing for the fire department.

headline: Sobriety checkpoint legality to be decided
abstract: The US Supreme Court has agreed to take on a case to determine the legality of sobriety checkpoints.  The decision is expected to be the first challenge for the now solidly-conservative body.  Michigan courts recently struck down such checkpoints saying they were an unwarranted breach of privacy.

headline: Health plan resumes payments to doctors
abstract: Maxicare Health Plans Inc. is in bankruptcy court but has resumed payments to doctors that were suspended last week.  Many Maxicare members have been refused care since the bankruptcy filing, but the judge is now ordering doctors and others to honor existing agreements with the company. The company executive vice president and chief financial oficer resigned the day before.

headline: SAHS maintenance worker appeals disciplinary action
abstract: A maintenance supervisor at Souderton Area High School is appealing the disciplinary measures taken against him by the school district for his report that a custodian was told to dumb hazardous substances down the drain.  The custodian denied the report, and the district reprimanded the supervisor for passing on faulty information.

headline: Costlier living
abstract: Pittsburgh's inflation rate over the last 2 months was slightly greater than the national rate for the first time since 1984, partly due to plant closings and increased gas prices.

headline: Braig gets 3 years on probation
abstract: Former Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Joseph Braig was sentences to 3 years on probation, 300 hours of community service, and a $3000 fine as a result of his conviction of mail fraud.

headline: The U.S. attorney's office in Philadelphia has called a morning news conference.
abstract: The U.S. attorney's office in Philadelphia has called a morning news conference.  Authorities say they'll announce indictments, raids, arrests and seizures involving a major drug ring in the Del. Valley.

headline: Sunday Pa. lottery sales getting off to a slow start
abstract: In the first Sunday lottery drawing in PA, sales were relatively low, but that doesn't worry lottery officials.  They expect sales to increase and for the extra day of drawings to produce about $50 million in sales a year.

headline: Let's move on DER building
abstract: The postponements regarding the constuction of the new Dept. of Environmental Resources building have gone on long enough, and Harrisburgers are tired of seeing a large fenced in hole where the building should be.  The Dept. of General Services now says that the building might be occupied by 1992.

headline: Borough misses deadline to replace Mont Clare mains
abstract: The Phoenixville borough has missed the deadline set by the PUC for the replacement of two water mains in the Mont Clare section of Upper Providence.  The projects will take about 8 more weeks to finish, and the borough is seeking funding from PennVEST for the construction.

headline: Rite Aid reports rise in sales, earnings
abstract: Rite Aid said its sales and earnings have increased for the second quarter which ended Sept 2.

headline: HEALTH-CARE COST containment draws boos from many unions
abstract: In upcoming contract bargaining, labor leaders are expecting a tough fight in resisting attempts to roll back or cut health care benefits for their members.

headline: Salaries, enrollments force school tax hike
abstract: The Boyertown Area School District administrators approved a budget calling for a 3.7-mill tax hike because of increased teachers' salaries and increasing enrollments.  The average homeowner will pay an extra $70 because of the hike.

headline: Fall Start Seen For New Plant
abstract: Construction plans for a new electrical generating plant have been delayed until fall, as financing for the project was not yet finished.

headline: Commissioners tighten security
abstract: Dauphin County officials tightened security at the weekly commissioners meeting yesterday after an anonymous caller threatened Chairperson Sally S. Klein. Officials in the commissioners' office said they took action as a precaution because they believe the same female caller has threatened Klein twice before. The caller has complained about the county budget process, proposed changes in the tax rates, and then makes descriptive threats. District Attorney Richard A. Lewis is investigating the matter, and said the calls were interpreted as a threat.

headline: These terms of endearment needed in war against drugs
abstract: With both Gov. Casey and Attorney General Ernie Preate pronouncing their determination to fight the war against drugs, Pennsylvania should be able to make some strides in curbing the drug trade epidemic.

headline: Surcharges no way to finance insurance fund
abstract: The editorial criticizes the state's imposed surcharges on traffic violation fines to help pay for the CAT Fund, saying that raising fines is an inappropriate method to gain more money for the fund.

headline: Lettieri confirmed for state arts council
abstract: Gov. Casey's nominee Robert Llettieri has been confirmed to the PA Council on the Arts.

headline: Borough's Mayor Latz dies at 71
abstract: George Latz, 16-year Shiremanstown Mayor, died at the age of 71 two days ago.  He was praised by his colleagues as being "a good man.  He was a good mayor to work for."

headline: Letters: Garbage Problem
abstract: Local resident complains that only Gaynor Cawley seems to be interested in stemming the flow of out-of-state garbage being dumped in the region.

headline: Heinz battles to get disabled girl benefits
abstract: US Senator John Heinz spoke at a news conference as he backed the fight for adequate benefits for mentally disabled minors. To be eligible for disability benefits from the United States government, children are at a disadvantage because they are limited to a list of specific impairments. Senator Heinz has introduced legislation that would standardize eligibility requirements for children and adults.

headline: School Budget Cuts
abstract: This cartoon shows an executioner (marked "City Council") yelling "Next!" and leading schoolchildren (many of whom are black) up to a guillotine marked "School Budget Cuts."  It's representing the view City Council is hanging children out to dry with cuts in funding.

headline: Feud may threaten state oil industry
abstract: Despite being the home state of the petroleum industry, PA might drive its oil producers out of business due to recent directives by the PA Department of Environmental Resources. Well owners, most of whom are independent and own only one well, must pay a $2,500 bond for each well owned and must also account for well-drilling waste such as rock and salt, measures which might be cost-prohibitive. Steve Rhoades, executive vice president of the PA Oil and Gas Association and George Parsells of the PA Independent Petroleum Producers say that producers are already struggling due to well and real estate taxes, and this DER directive coupled with new federal rules would strangle PA's petroleum industry.

headline: Bucks trying to improve security in holding cells
abstract: Taxpayer's money has gone to renovations on the first floor of the Bucks County Courthouse where new holding cells will be built. The renovations are supposed to improve security as well.

headline: They Rally to Force Cop Issue
abstract: 100 local residents rallied at a Kensington church to voice their complaints to memebers of City Council regarding a lack of police protection.

headline: The CAT Is Out of The Bag
abstract: Two insurance companies, Erie Insurance Exchange and State Farm Insurance Co., submitted catastrophic auto insurance proposals yesterday which would replace CAT after its termination on March 1.  The proposals, ranging in costs of $45 to $80, will be reviewed by the state Insurance Department.

headline: Lewis to Jenkins: The party's over
abstract: Powerful Republican Drew Lewis has suggested to Montgomery County GOP leader Frank Jenkins that he consider resignation.  Speculation as to whether or not he will resign and if so, who his successor would be is running wild.

headline: Bucks officials feud over port board choice
abstract: Contention between two Bucks County Commissioners is increasing over the county's upcoming choice of its representative on the new Philadelphia Port Authority.  One commissioner claims that she doesn't have any input and that Bucks Co. GOP Chairman is really the one choosing.

headline: Clinics launch campaign against abortion control bill
abstract: Representatives of 13 abortion clinics in the state have asked the state to reconsider the proposals put forth that would curtail abortion rights in PA.  They are planning education campaigns, and voter registration services.

headline: Highlights of Speech
