abstract: Among the highlights of Gov. Casey's State of the Commonwealth address were plans for $10.8 million in funds to fight the drug epidemic, a renewed focus on child abuse, and a commitment to reduce auto insurance rates for Pennsylvanians.

headline: School districts cope with loss of special ed funds
abstract: School districts statewide are lamenting the lack of funds for special education departments, as the state has withheld payment to many districts, though some are optimistic that the new payment date of June 30 will be met.

headline: Fire aboard tug slows movement of nuclear reactor
abstract: An electrical fire aboard a tugboat delayed the movement Tuesday of an old nuclear reactor up the Columbia River for burial at Washington's Hanford Nuclear Reservation.

headline: Building prisons isn't the answer
abstract: The editorial board believes that PA's corrections officials should be doing more to solve the problem of prison overcrowding. Law-abiding citizens should not have to pay more taxes to build expensive prisons. They suggest other correctional means, such as house arrest and counseling programs, as a remedy to prison overcrowding.

headline: Thornburgh weighing end to organized-crime task forces
abstract: Attorney General Dick Thornburgh  is considering removing the organized-crime task force programs and to have U.S. attorneys handle the cases, or rather merge with the strike forces.  The strike force lawyers are against the merging of the two, but a majority of U.S. attorneys are interested in joining forces.

headline: The self-insurance trend
abstract: The graph predicts a rise in the number of governments and private organizations setting up "captive insurers." Self-insurance "captured 35% of the property/casualty market," and the graph estimates they will have 52% of the market by 1995.

headline: Likely GOP gubernatorial candidate is bottom line pro-choice
abstract: US Rep. Tom Ridge is considering giving up his seat to run for governor against Gov. Casey in 1990, and commented that despite the fact that the two have several differences of opinion, he believes that the most devisive would be abortion.

headline: Budget cut keeps Greenville taxes at 1989 level
abstract: Greenville Borough Manager Marie H. Julian delivered a budget proposal to the Greenville Borough Council that totals about $1.7 million, 11 percent more than the budget in 1989 even though it carries no increase in real estate taxes. If the budget is adopted, borough residents will pay the same rate on real estate of 49 mills they paid in 1989. The lack of real estate tax increases allows the borough to hold down expenditure increases but has caused the elimination of community programs such as codification of local ordinances, street improvements, equipment purchases, and, most significantly, does not provide for the funding of increasing the borough's police department.

headline: Union and Vocational Service Reach Tenative Agreement
abstract: A tentative agreement between members of District Council 47 of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees and the Jewish Employment Cocation Service was reached Wednesday night avoiding a strike.  A walkout would have affected thousands of Philadelphians who use job training centers.

headline: Honestly, There's no Best Policy
abstract: Many drivers in the Philadelphia area have resorted to dishonesty, claiming to live in neighborhoods far removed from the high insurance rate areas of Philadelphia and New Jersey.  Philadelphia competets with Los Angeles for the city with the highest rates, while New Jersey has the highest state average rates in the country.

headline: School Official to Undergo Psychiatric Test
abstract: Former junior high principal Malachi Robinson was arrested twice last week for threats against the Philadelphia Area Superintendent Clayton.  Robinson has been ordered to undergo a psychiatric examination.

headline: Gas rate increase unpredictable until PUC members vote Dec. 21
abstract: Even after polling members of the Public Utility Commission (PUC), it is difficult to predict how much National Fuel Gas Distribution Corp. will get from its $24.6 million rate hike when the PUC votes on December 21. Based on the poll, customers would see an increase in the basic service charge of $2.66 for residential customers and $16.88 for commercial customers. The poll also found that a majority of the PUC commissioners want to reduce the amount of take-or-pay expenses NFG can pass onto customers. NFG spokesman David Waples said the utility believes all the take-or-pay costs should be paid for by the consumer.

headline: Cambria firm gets prison job
abstract: According to PA Department of General Services Secretary David L. Jannetta, the state named a Cambria County architectural-engineering firm to do the design work for reconstruction of buildings damaged at the October riots at the State Correctional Institution in Camp Hill. L. Robert Kimball & Associates of Ebensburg will begin the design project immediately. The reconstruction will involve the prison's support facilities, including the education building, auditorium, gymnasium, food-services area, and main control area.

headline: Three Jurors Chosen In Murder Trial
abstract: Three jurors have been chosen in the trial of David Copenhefer, a man who is charged with kidnapping and killing a banker's wife last summer.  Jurors are being selected in Pittsburgh, even though Erie County is the jurisdiction in which the crime took place.

headline: The to legalize 'small games'
abstract: The newspaper is suggesting a "yes" vote for legalizing 'small games' for non-profit organizations such as volunteer fire departments, which have recently been suffering from a lack of funding.

headline: New PHEAA building to be on 7th street
abstract: The Capital Commercial Corporation of Harrisburg will build a new headquarters for the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) to keep the agency in the city of Harrisburg. According to Kenneth R. Reeher, executive director of PHEAA, PA Governor Robert Casey as well as Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed wanted to keep PHEAA in the city to contribute to city taxes and keep the approximately 1,000 jobs the agency provides in the city.

headline: Carbon-Lehigh IU members hear budget offering
abstract: The 1990 budget for the Carbon-Lehigh Intermediate Unit was presented to members of the board of directors as well as the resignation of Weatherly representative Joseph E. D'Andrea, who has accepted a seat on Weatherly Borough Council. The $1.25 million balanced budget reflects an approximate 11 percent increase from the 1989 budget and a 7.9 percent increase in local school district funding for the institution. Over half of the IU's expenditures will go towards salaries and employee benefits, while other beneficiaries include professional services, supplies, property, other services, and the budget reservary. Executive Director Jerry B. Stout said the budget cannot be approved until the IU receives its state funds for the year.

headline: Abortion foes herald unveiling of new PA bill
abstract: Abortion foes are looking forward to the new abortion bill unveiled by the legislature recently.  They hope to move it through the legislature quickly through huge rallies planned around the Capitol.  Among other things, the bill would ban abortion after 24 weeks of pregnancy.

headline: Hospital union leader threatens July 1 strike
abstract: Union leader Henry Nicholas pledges to lead a strike of up to 10,000 hospital and nursing home workers if health care aid does not increase and hospitals do not promise to care for uninsured poor.

headline: School tax picture comes into view
abstract: In Bedford County, depending on which school district one lives in, the school taxes can be drastically different for property assessed at the same value.

headline: General Public Utilities Corp., from financial meltdown to industry leader
abstract: Ten years after the Three Mile Island accident, General Public Utilities Corp. has regained strength financially. In the years following the accident, GPU handled financial disaster, personal injury suits, and shareholder suits, but they are once again thriving.

headline: Camp Hill action eases Blair jail crunch
abstract: The State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill is once again accepting inmates, after entering a lockdown state in response to a two-day riot at the prison. Some inmates from Camp Hill being held at Blair County Prison will return to Camp Hill, and Blair County Commissioner William C. Stouffer hopes that the state will reimburse Blair County for maintenance of the prisoners. The question of prison overcrowding now stands before the PA Legislature.

headline: Top court refuses to block Roderick Frey execution
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court refused to block the execution of Roderick Frey, of Lancaster, for the arrangement of his wife's murder.  There is currently a review of the constitutionality of PA's death penalty law.

headline: Traffic fine surcharges pay CAT fund debt
abstract: Due to a lack of funding for the state's Catastrophic Loss Trust Fund, the state will add surcharges to traffic fines in order to help supplement the CAT's funds.

headline: Lobbyists' freebies slip through Pa. ethics law
abstract: Because of a large loophole in PA's new ethics law "small gifts" from lobbyists, such as free admission to football games, ski-lift passes, etc., need not be reported, allowing such gifts to add up considerably.

headline: CCAT votes to withhold real estate taxes
abstract: A meeting of the Citizens Concerned About Taxes (CCAT), a grassroots group aimed at curbing Scranton city taxes, met to discuss withholding real estate taxes as a message to those who handle the city's budget. CCAT president Myron Wolkoff urged the approximately 500 people attending to use the tax-withholding strategy against the wishes of Mayor-Elect Jimmy Connors. Connors pleaded with the crowd to allow him to work on the city's budget or suffer the consequences of the city having to borrow money if people do not pay their taxes. CCAT vice president Elaine Dougherty circulated a petition to send to PA Governor Robert P. Casey requesting the passage of legislation that would enable the PA Consumer Advocate to represent the state with insurance rate increase issues.

headline: AIDS cases among women in Philadelphia rising rapidly
abstract: M. Louis van de Beek, medical director of the Philadelphia city AIDS office is warning that the plight of women is being overlooked in the city's AIDS battle.  The statistics cited show that women with AIDS were more likely to be black, latino and heterosexual than male AIDS patients.  The highest percentage group was women between 20-39.

headline: Jail dispute resolved
abstract: County and city officials appeared to be on a collision course concerning a solution to the federal court mandate to deal with prison overcrowding. However, a deal was reached shortly before a City Council meeting, placating city officials concerned about the height of a new facility and its effect on the city skyline with changes in design and location. The facility is estimated to be complete within 6 months after the deadline. Until then, the holding facility will be moved to the original downtown prison.

headline: Hafer returns to abortion issue
abstract: After down-playing the abortion issue somewhat during the summer, Hafer has returned to emphasizing her pro-choice stance, appearing in front of the National Organization for Women and making it her main point in press conferences. She hopes to win some Democrats over with the issue.

headline: 20-year-old teacher-strike law draws criticism
abstract: The state law giving teachers the strike to strike marked its 20th anniversary this year, but it is drawing criticism. Supporters see the right to strike as needed and helpful to overall productivity. Opponents see strikes as taking away valuable teaching time. They believe that the act has only worsened problems from wildcat strikes. Amendments to the act are being debated in the legislature right now.

headline: Voices. Should your tax money pay for local schools or schools statewide?
abstract: The article lists national responses to the question "Should your tax money pay for local schools or schools statewide?" The responses are varied.

headline: Saving water is an issue, too
abstract: Editors remind readers that issues pertaining to environmental stewardship are not as simple as they same. For example, proposals to install low flush toilets in PA, New Jersey, Delaware, and New York Communities have resulted in arguments over the long term cost of the toilets versus their short term environmental efficiency.

headline: SEPTA may let firms run some routes
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority is considering contracting out a few of its bus routes to private firms, which it has not done in nearly a decade. SEPTA may choose to use another firm because it may cost less to allow a private firm to do it. The Transport Workers Union Local 234 has yet to take a position on the action.

headline: Mifflin-Juniata-Snyder MADD chapter gets charter
abstract: The photos of officers elected to the recently chartered Mifflin/Juniata/Snyder MADD chapter are pictured, including: Lori Cottrill, President; Karen Goss, First Vice President; Sarah Drayer, Second Vice President; Marlene Swartz, Secretary; and Sue Reigle, treasurer.

headline: State Farm to cut auto policy rates
abstract: PA Governor Casey announced State Farm Insurance Co. agreed to reduce rates in accord with a new state law mandating a 10 and 22 cuts, which will be instituted when the PA Insurance Department hears a request for a 2.3 percent rate increase. Vice President of the Insurance Federation of PA Paul Laskow says cuts won't save drivers money. State Farm and the State have agreed to abide by a Commonwealth Court ruling on whether the company may increase rates, whether or not it is denied by the PA Insurance Department.

headline: Committee Approves Midwives Bill
abstract: The PA Senate Consumer Protection Committee approved a revised bill that recognizes lay midwives; it draws a distinction between nurse midwives and lay midwives. There are about 120 licensed midwives in PA and about 50 who do not have their licenses according to the PA Health Department. The bill was drafted following the state Board of Medicine tried to ban a lay midwife in Mercer County from practicing and this case is pending in Commonwealth Court.

headline: Adams turnout rates among lowest ever
abstract: Adams County experienced one of its lowest voter turnouts in yesterday's primary election, in which fewer than 1/4 of the county's registered voters showed up at the polls. Tom Collins, chairman of the Adams County board of commissioners said that apathy wasn't the source, but rather predictable election results. In November, Democratic incumbent Kenneth Cole will face Republican John Wolfe in the race for 91st district in the PA House, while Auditor General Barbara Hafer sealed the Republican gubernatorial election in the statewide primary.

headline: GOP area leaders line up behind Nahill and Bartle
abstract: GOP leaders in Montgomery County are split between the two Republicans running to lead their party. Frank Bartle has been criticized because he was a registered Democrat until 1980.

headline: NJ candidates try to tie opponents to Florio's tax hike
abstract: Many Republican candidates in New Jersey are attempting to link their opponents with Democratic NJ Governor Jim Florio's recent $2.8 billion tax package, which has some residents angry at increased taxes.  Democrats have been trying to distance themselves from Florio's tax hike.

headline: Voters of California sent wrong message
abstract: Most of the results from California's elections are negative  but there is one ray of hope from the election. Proposition 111 includes a 9 cent tax increase on every gallon of gas, a substantial increase in state truck tax, and a large increase in the "Gann spending limit" removing constitutional curb on the legislature and allowing it to vote tax and spending increases. All the propositions that would increase the state's bonded indebtedness passed overwhelming. The voters literally voted in favor of every possible tax increase. Voters rejected the two propositions that would have neutralized or reduced the ability of politicians in the legislature to redistrict after the 1990 census.

headline: Jail Foes Rebuked
abstract: An editorial urging citizens to be aware of the economic benefits of having a maximum security prison in Greene County.

headline: Hafer strengthens pro-choice stand
abstract: Hafer further entrenched herself in her pro-choice stance in a press conference at the Liberty Bell, referring to herself as "the pro-choice candidate."

headline: Army layoffs affect third of work force
abstract: Layoffs at the New Cumberland Army Depot affect around a third of the workers there, with 870 transfers, demotions, separations, and eliminations.  There have been few complaints, but workers still aren't happy with the situation.

headline: Vo-Tech Program Chaos Looming
abstract: The defection of some school districts from the Pennsylvania College of Technology vo-tech program is causing financial turmoil as other districts try to find a replacement program.

headline: Scientists say part of burner site may be termed wetlands
abstract: Two scientists with expertise in Soil Sciences and Geotechnology found hydric soils, an indicator of a wetland classification, in the area that USPCI Corporation plans to site a hazardous waste incinerator. The siting manual of the PA Department of Environmental Resources forbids the siting of hazardous waste treatment facilities on wetland areas. Though studies of the area were completed by Baker Engineers, the firm hired by USPCI to evaluate the site, no site-specific mapping was done of surface soils.

headline: SEPTA resumes trains on Sundays
abstract: With the completion of a recent 4-month track construction, SEPTA is once again offering train service between Fox Chase and Center City Philadelphia. To reduce confusion, buses will remain operable though shuttle bus service will be discontinued starting Sunday. The train service on Sundays will continue until all schedules change in the spring.

headline: Mile by mile, police on foot patrol earn public's trust
abstract: York city police officers involved in the foot patrol through the hispanic neighborhood say that their patrols are slowly paying off, as more and more citizens are calling them with tips.

headline: State Farm won't issue auto policies in Pa.
abstract: State Farm has stopped writing new auto insurance policies in PA because of the new auto-insurance laws, which make it economically unsound for the insurance company to continue writing new policies.

headline: Bull Run watershed study awaits final OK from county
abstract: A study of the Bull Run Watershed is scheduled to start within the next few weeks, once it's approved by Union County Commissioners.  It will examine the effects of storm water runoff patterns created by developments.

headline: Administration to aid ozone fund
abstract: In a policy reversal, White House spokesman Peter Hart announced the Bush Administration has decided to join other First World countries in contributing to a fund to phase out CFC use by developing countries. The US will contribute $25 million to a fund totaling $100 million. The US' previous stance threatened to disrupt an international conference in London next week to strengthen a 1987 treaty designed to phase out the use of CFCs by the turn of the century.

headline: GOP Chairman Wants Six Casey-Hafer Debates
abstract: The leader of the state Republican party believes that PA Governor Casey and opposer Barbara Hafer should hold six regional debates leading up to the November election, while the Casey camp has only just agreed to go into talks about one.

headline: No cause to celebrate this 20th anniversary
abstract: Editors celebrate the 20th anniversary of Act 195, which granted PA teachers the right to strike, while hoping the Legislature revises the law before next year. While the law certainly has its benefits, the most recent strike in Morrisville is an example of the need for revision. The editors suggest final best offer binding arbitration as well as a condensed negotiating period so as not to interfere with the school year, and equitable economic losses for both sides for each day of the strike.

headline: Voters Return Steighner, Fargo to State House
abstract: Butler county voters re-elected incumbent Joseph Steighner against challenger William Neel Jr. and incumbent Howard Fargo against opponent Don Megnin to PA House seats. Megnin, a full-time professor at Slippery Rock University, said he planned to run for public office again.

headline: Jail Inmates
abstract: US District Judge Maurice Cohill scheduled a hearing to addresss mentally ill inmates of the Allegheny County Jail, who claim they are unconstitutionally denied visitation, the right to smoke, recreation, and library privileges. In the meantime, Cohill ordered conditions at the 20-bed facility be improved.

headline: Hafer stumps on abortion stance
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer spoke at the state conference of the National Organization for Women, emphasizing her pro-choice stance.

headline: Baker wants home- work ban repeal
abstract: PA state Senator Earl Baker wants to repeal an archaic state law that keeps manufacturers from having their employees work home. He introduced legislation to repeal the Independent Homework Act, which was originally created 53 years ago to affect child labor, minimum wage, and worker safety. He claims its purpose when it was enacted has gone. Now it discriminates again women who can do seamstress work from home and not have to hire babysitters.

headline: What the districts will receive
abstract: A list of what local school districts will get in the new budget.

headline: Sen. Heinz takes part in environmental talks
abstract: U.S. Senator  John Heinz and other U.S. lawmakers met for the second international conference of Leaders of Global Legislators Organization for a Balanced Environment (GLOBE). The legislators discussed tropical and temperate forests, global climate change, hazardous waste exports and the lack of environmental protection in the current General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade talks. Director of the Environmental Protection Agency, William Reilly addressed the conference and fielded questions.

headline: SEPTA routes studied
abstract: Montgomery County Commissioner Floriana M. Bloss said the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority is considering trimming their annual budget by $414,000 by canceling seven bus lines with ridership levels below 50 percent of capacity, including two in Montgomery County. The two bus lines provide transportation to Montgomery County Correctional Facility, the State Correction Institution at Graterford, Bishop McDevitt High School and Beaver College. Around 50 travelers are inmates of the county jail enrolled in work-release programs.

headline: Missed opportunity
abstract: Rural communities enter 1991 with rising crime rates because Governor Casey vetoed a bill that would have created a resident state trooper program within the PA State Police.  The proposal passed in both chambers of the state legislautre and would have given state troopers the assignment of patroling rural areas that do not have police forces.  Governor Casey stated that such an assignment would negatively affect the image of the state police as the elite law enforcement body of the state.  The authors of the article disagree and provide arguments to support their position, ultimately calling for the reintroduction of the bill or a compromise to suit the governor.

headline: State loses auto insurance round: Companies' plans to pull out upheld; Casey vows to fight
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey was criticized by insurance agents at a campaign stop in Pittsburgh when asked about a recent ruling permitting Harleysville Insurance to continue informing its customers that it was quitting the auto insurance business in PA.  Casey has disapproved of the insurance company's decision and promises to bring down insurance rates in PA.

headline: Business on the horizon
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey shakes hands and speaks with Ralph Hutchinson, president of Metalized Paper Corp., the first major business to locate in the Industrial Center of McKeesport.

headline: Ads give a boost to Hearn
abstract: Peter Hearn is reaping dividends from his early television campaign leapfrogging from last to second place in a new poll on the 1991 Democratic mayoral primary. He only trails former District Attorney Ed Rendell. His TV ads have portrayed him as an outsider who will shake up local government.

headline: GOP chief: Pa. going broke under Casey's leadership
abstract: PA chairman of the Republican Party, Anne B. Anstine claimed that PA has become a bankrupt state under PA Governor Robert P. Casey. She charged Casey with mismanaging the state's finances and creating a $1 billion debt. Despite Hafer's lack of popular support, Anstine supported Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer in addition to PA legislature candidates Michael Oser and Bob Nyce.

headline: No cause to celebrate this 20th anniversary
abstract: The author is talking about the 20th anniversary of the state law, Act 195, that granted teachers the right to strike and believes that it has produced some benefits but needs to be modified. The author believes that the law provided an orderly bargaining process, but the problem is that in disputes where it cannot be settled there is no incentive for compromise. The best solution the author can find is the final-best-offer- binding arbitration  that makes both sides eliminate unrealistic demands.

headline: Voting dilemma
abstract: The author supports neither Representative Donald Dorr nor Representative Michael E. Bortner in the upcoming PA Senate race as he disapproves of their negative campaigns. The author disapproves of Dorr's vote to legalize small games of chance and his vote against an anti-abortion bill.

headline: Jail records show workers committed racial crimes
abstract: The prison worker and two inmates at Camp Hill in 1986  had at least one thing in common: they were white. They held down a black inmate and tightened a rope around his neck in a mock hanging. The worker also said the Klu Klux Klan is on the move again. The prison is wrecked with racial discrimination that lead to the October riots.

headline: Hafer visits L.V., shares views
abstract: Speaking a abortion, PA Gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer, said the time has come for a leader to tell the government to get out of our bedrooms. She spoke to about 75 at a National Abortion rights Action League meeting about abortion, gas tax increase, and PA Governor Robert Casey. In the primary she beat out an abortion foe for the nomination.

headline: Bakery walkout averted
abstract: A tentative agreement was reached on a contract for about 1,100 employees of Stroehmann Brothers Inc, averting a strike that had been planned for midnight. The Bakery, Confectionery and Tobacco Union Local 464 was seeking better health coverage and pensions. Details of the agreement were not available, but a union official said that they were somewhat short on some of their demands.

headline: Why doesn't Gettysburg stand up?
abstract: A senior citizen wants to know why Gettysburg residents cannot muster the courage of Littlestown School District residents and demand a tax reduction by the local school board. Senior citizens cannot afford steadily increasing taxes.

headline: Senate Delays Vote on Clean Air Bill Over Coal Miner Amendment
abstract: The Senate is delaying debate over the Clean Air act so legislators and the White House can negotiate how to help coal miners now unemployed from stricter pollution control.

headline: Should Fort Pitt work be done all at once?
abstract: PA Department of Transportation Secretary Howard Yerusalim said it may be possible to renovate the Fort Pitt Bridge and Tunnels in one construction season instead of two, if that’s what the public wants. PennDot originally planned to disrupt traffic on Western PA's busiest stretch of highway as little as possible by extending work over a two-year period. Douglas P. Dick, an official for Dick Corp., the largest heavy construction firm in the area, suggested the department do the work all at once.

headline: Money for Emergency Crews, Prison Work Up to Voters
abstract: A referendum will be on the upcoming gubernatorial ballot to allow the state to lend up to $25 million to volunteer fire, ambulance and rescue companies to update and purchase equipment and up to $200 million to expand and renovate county prisons. Passage of the referendum would also allow for "retroactive" grants of up to $1 million each for counties that have built or revamped prisons in the past five years.

headline: State protects purchasers of credit life insurance
abstract: On June, the National Insurance consumer Organization and the Consumer Federation of America charged that the sale of credit life insurance is inappropriate, expensive and poorly regulated by state insurance departments. The charges contained inaccuracies and could be potentially misleading to consumers who may have a legitimate need to purchase credit life insurance, which is usually bought to pay off a loan in case of death. Not everyone needs credit life insurance. The PA Insurance Department has been a leader in the regulation of credit life insurance for 30 years.

headline: Busy Beaver
abstract: Busy Beaver Building Centers, Inc., the leading retailer of lumber, building materials, and hardware for the "do-it-yourself" market, filed in US Bankruptcy Court for Chapter 11 bankrupcty. President and CEO Charles C. Bender says the company hopes to emerge from protection stronger. Total assets are listed at $22.2 million, with total liabilities at $20.6 million. The filing comes as the company was unable to secure a cash infusion from lenders in the slow winter months.

headline: Advertising barrage by Casey to start today
abstract: A million-dollar, two-week TV advertising campaign starts today for Gov. Casey's camp, despite the fact that it's still early in election season and Casey has a 40-point advantage in the polls.  His opponent, Barbara Hafer, will wait until later in the campaign to go on TV, she said.

headline: GOP is offering a positive future
abstract: USA Today's editorial board interviewed U.S. Representative Newt Gingrich about various topics, including his upcoming televised workshop showing ways of replacing the bureaucratic welfare state.

headline: no headline
abstract: PA Representative George Hasay has urged state police to be on the lookout for illegal dumpers using a one-month trial program in Luzerne, Sullivan, Bradford, and Lackawanna counties.  Representative Hasay sent a letter to Captain Francis Anzelmi asking them to step up prosecutions for littering and to increase patrols of areas where illegal dumping is evident.

headline: Wagner critical of Gigliotti mailings
abstract: Pete Wagner 19th Ward Chairman criticized PA Representative Frank Gigliotti (Democrat-Brookline) on his decision to send out a mailing to constituents in his district.  Wagner claims that Representative Gigliotti violated a House rule on state-paid mailings.  Wagner challenges Gigliotti in the May 15th Democratic primary in the 22nd district.

headline: Jails Crowd 'State of Emergency'
abstract: The Philadelphia prison system may be declared in a "state of emergency" and restrict the number of new inmates.  Yesterday the inmate population was at an all time high of 5387, 1600 over a court-mandated 3750 cap.

headline: Health Club Ordered to Lift Ban on Males
abstract: The PA Human Relations Commission said 10 LivingWell Lady fitness centers in the Philadelphia area were unlawfully discriminating against men and ordered it to accept both genders. Senior vice president of LivingWell, Robert L. Waters said the company would appeal the decision to the Commonwealth Court. The question of discrimination arose in 1984, when a man complained to the commission that he had been excluded from applying for a job at the Langhorne gym because of his sex. A commission spokesman said that the Human Relations Act does not recognize exceptions based on customer preferences.

headline: Blind man fights to get ESU job back
abstract: Kevin Parton, who worked as a silverware sorter and East Stroudsburg University, is now in limbo because of health regulations concerning his guide dog in the workplace.  He will not return to the job until the DER hands down a ruling.

headline: York districts to offer opportunity
abstract: The editor believes one of the major problems leading to high dropout rates is the inability of the system to indentify students with difficulties and give them attention. Five York County School Districts are pooling resources to provide the opportunity to area dropouts. The proposed York County High School is designed to deal with dropouts of all ages and provide curriculum and encouragement to complete education.

headline: Senate Kills Tax-Credit Proposal for Clean Air Bill
abstract: The Senate defeated Arlen Specter's amendment to the Clear Air bill that provided tax credits to utility companies that install expensive air pollution equipment on coal-powered plants.

headline: Specter, Heinz Prevail. Victory for Democracy.
abstract: The editorial board believes that U.S. Senators Arlen Specter and John Heinz were right to water down a transportation bill authored by Representative William Gray III of Philadelphia in the closing moments of the 101st congress. The legislation would have required PA to establish a dedicated funding source for mass transit and the Southeast Pennsylvania Transit Authority or lose $150 million in federal highway aid. The board believes that establishment of a dedicated source should be decided in Harrisburg, not in a national forum.

headline: Montco police mount united anti-drug push
abstract: Representatives from 37 of the 49 police departments in Montgomery County signed an agreement creating an inter-municipal drug task force, established through PA Attorney General Ernest D. Preate's office and approved by Montgomery County District Attorney Michael D. Marino and the county Police Chiefs' Association. The state will provide money for drug pays and to pay confidential informants. The PA Legislature enacted the "Hold Harmless" bill, which says the state will pay if a task force case ends in a lawsuit in which judgment is rendered against the municipality.

headline: State provides technical help to smaller firms
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey established the Industrial Resource Center network to assist companies in meeting industry trends. The program is administered by the PA Department of Commerce but each center is run by nonprofit companies. Del Val IRC operators include the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce. DVIRC primarily assists in industrial plant design. The Consortium for Supplying Technology Applications Regionally, or COSTAR, in Philadlephia offers services unique to its location.

headline: Busy Beaver
abstract: Busy Beaver Home Centers Inc. has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Pittsburgh US Bankruptcy Court. President Charles Bender, who came on board in 1985, cited a seasonal cash shortage for the 13-store chain, which mainly operates in western PA. Bender says the company fully expects to recover and emerge from Chapter 11.

headline: Advertising barrage by Casey to start today
abstract: A million-dollar, two-week TV advertising campaign starts today for PA Governor Casey's camp, despite the fact that it's still early in election season and Casey has a 40-point advantage in the polls.  His opponent, Barbara Hafer, will wait until later in the campaign to go on TV, she said.

headline: GOP leader has had it with current campaigning, but precious few heed his call
abstract: David S. Broder believes US House Minority Leader Bob Michel is not the only one who should be angry about the way his campaign finance reform proposal was received by Democrats. Speaker Thomas Foley has delayed bringing it to the floor and hinted at prohibiting Republicans from offering amendments. Foley seems determined to pass a partisan bill that will most likely be vetoed. Democrats are benefiting from finances via special interest groups, and they don't want to give it up.

headline: No legislative raises
abstract: The editorial criticizes the PA legislature, particularly Senate Majority Leader F. Joseph Loeper and Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer, for suggesting that the legislature may give itself a raise after the election this November.  The editorial points out that the country seems to be sliding into a recession, and that Pennsylvania's are the second highest-paid legislators already. Loeper said that judges' salaries will likely be increased, and that usually legislators' salaries are increased when that issue comes to the table, but the editors urge the legislature to take on the issues separately.

headline: Warden-elect appointed for Perry County prison
abstract: Perry County Commissioners approved the appointment of Robert Shull of New Bloomfield RD 1 as warden-elect of the new Perry County prison, according to Commissioner Elwood Mohler. Shull said that Perry County will have an institution that will be recognized.

headline: Jersey's bursting jails
abstract: The Camden County Jail has been hopelessly overcrowded a little over two years after it was opened. It is operating at 3 times its intended capacity. It is not entirely untypical of jails in the state. The opinion believes the state has to take greater responsibility off the counties.

headline: Hispanics Protest Chain of Events
abstract: Thirty Hispanics protested the alleged closing of the Philadelphia's Commission on Human Relations field office.

headline: Business group predicts job losses would result
abstract: The Partnership on Health Care & Employment, a business coalition, predicted in a study that about 3.5 million Americans would lose their jobs if the US Congress forced employers to provide health insurance for workers.  Supporters of national health-care reform criticized the study, saying that such predictions were made before many other reforms, such as the 8-hour work day, minimum wage, and child-care, but they never played out.

headline: null
abstract: A contractor discusses the potential for wetland development, involving planting to change the landscape. If the plants soaked up enough water so that the wetlands were not as wet as they currently are, the contractor might be able to continue with construction plans in the area.

headline: Sewer Bills Likely to Be Top Local Utility Cost in Future
abstract: Environmental officials say Williamsport residents will see increased sewage bill costs, as those not served by proposed million-dollar sewer lines could be forced to spend thousands to repair or replace neglected septic systems. William P. Parsons, assistant regional director for the PA Department of Environmental Resources said that the department will focus on on-lot septic systems. The state's top local priority is to take care of sewage issues in Loyalsock Township.

headline: Speed limit not only issue
abstract: The writer worries that the gubernatorial election will be characterized by a fervent abortion debate with a few frivolous issues, such as the PA Turnpike speed limit, thrown in for a little variety, while other important  issues are not being addressed.

headline: Morales receives execution stay
abstract: Death row inmate Salvador Morales has received a stay on his execution, allowing him more time for appeals.  The stay leaves three inmates still under death warrants by the state.

headline: State residents' S&L bill: $11.1 billion
abstract: PA has avoided the widespread savings and loans failures, but state residents will help pay the bailout costs just the same. Taxpayers will pick up 70% of the $325 billion tab and the companies will cover the other 30%. Only six out of 149 thrifts in PA have gone bad. Nationally 440 banks have failed.

headline: Can rates be driven down?
abstract: The Pennsylvania auto insurance reform issue involves a number of different actors. The Insurance companies say they are actually losing money and would like to increase raters, whereas citizens are demanding that something be down about the already high rates. Meanwhile the trial lawyers speak of victims rights, while at the same time the public is weary over lawyers profits. Legislators are planning action early this year.

headline: AFL-CIO endorses Casey-Singel ticket
abstract: Gov. Casey and his running mate, Lt. Gov. Singel received the endorsement of the PA AFL-CIO, the largest labor organization in PA.

headline: GOP official claims Casey will deliver state deeper into debt
abstract: Ann Anstine, state Republican committee chairwoman, projected at the Fayette County Republican Committee banquet that PA will be $1 billion in debt if PA Governor Robert Casey is re-elected. She urged voters to vote for Republican candidate Barbara Hafer.

headline: No love lost between candidates for 4th District seat in state House
abstract: The race for the 4th District seat in the PA House of Representatives has been something of a personal grudge match between freshman Dem. Representative Tom Scrimenti and former Republican Representative Harry Bowser, but they expressed differing views on various issues in interviews yesterday.  The article sums up the candidates positions on the issues of a budget deficit, auto insurance, road repairs, local taxes, and their top priorities.

headline: Washington D.C. Or Bust
abstract: The cartoon displays PA Democratic PA Governor Robert P. Casey as a hitch-hiking donkey. The figure is wearing a pin that says "Casey '92" and is holding a sign that says "Washington D.C. or Bust".

headline: John Wolfe bill would repeal Pa. Widow's Tax
abstract: Republican legislative candidate John Wolfe has already drafted a bill to repeal the Widow's Tax. PA Governor Robert P. Casey said a law to repeal the tax would have little effect on low and middle income families and would give a $30 million tax break to wealthy families, though he pledges to work for the reform of guardianship laws. The American Association of Retired Persons disapproves of the tax.

headline: Honors for a pioneer of integrated housing
abstract: Long-time civil rights activist Morris Milgram was among several honored with the Clarence Farmer Service Award by the Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations. Milgram and his long-time friend James Farmer fought hard for years to promote integrated housing in the days of segregation, and have continued to battle for improved civil rights and integration.

headline: Center Open
abstract: PA Secretary of Labor and Industry presented a federal grant for jobs skills training and other services for United Mine Workers of America, districts 2, 4 and 5. In another ceremony, Harris Wofford opened the Punxsutawney Area Job Center, the 89th opened under PA Governor Robert Casey. In attendance were State Reps. Same Smith, Paul Wass, a representative from State Rep. Pat Stapleton, Mike Lawrence of North Central Planning and Development, and Punxsutawney Groundhog Club President James Means.

headline: 3 sites in Somerset County considered for waste facility
abstract: Commissioner Chairman Brad Cober is disturbed that Concord Resources Group Inc. is considering Somerset County for the location of a $100 million hazardous waste disposal facility. A law passed by the Legislature calls for construction of two hazardous waste facilities in the state. The company expects to submit an application for a site to the PA Department of Resources by early 1991. Former PA Speaker of the House K. Leroy Irvis leads the company's public participation committee.

headline: Sharon will begin its recycling program Sept. 24
abstract: Outlines the recycling rules as defined by Sharon city officials.

headline: Spot Sobriety Checks Net Several Arrests
abstract: State Police in Butler conducted their Selective Traffic Enforcement Against Drunk Driving detail along Route 8 garnering six driving under the influence arrests.

headline: More Crime in the Streets
abstract: Pittsburgh Police Chief Ralph Pampena is right that citizens should not be surprising at increasing rates of crime, but his reasoning behind it might be faulty.

headline: State Senate clears compromise 911 Bill
abstract: Dialing 911 for emergency assistance may soon be a reality throughout PA. A joint Senate/House conference committee has approved a plan that will allow counties to impose a charge on residents through their telephone bills pay for 911 installation and maintenance. The monthly charge to telephone customers should be relatively small.

headline: Cap on accident victims' prescription charges hit
abstract: Some pharmacies have stopped filling perscriptions for auto accident victims because of restrictions in the state's new auto-insurance law which force pharmacists to only charge 80% of the normal fee to accident victims.  The restriction on pharmacies may soon be lifted.

headline: AFL-CIO endorses Casey-Singel ticket
abstract: PA Governor Casey and his running mate, Lieutenant Governor Singel received the endorsement of the PA AFL-CIO, the largest labor organization in PA.

headline: GOP party chairman's race could hinge on fund raising
abstract: Montgomery County Republican Party faces fundraising issues as it heads into this years election. Oppostion has formed to current GOP chairman because lackluster fundraising efforts.

headline: No Politics? That’s a joke, right?
abstract: President George Bush has said that the flag burning amendment that is being discussed is not a political one. The author though thinks that it is a “30-second spot” for the minority Republicans in the House and Senate before an election.

headline: Watchdog group endorses Sunshine Law bills
abstract: PA Reps. Jon Fox and David Heckler have sponsored a bill which they are attempting to pass out of the PA House Committee on Local Government which grants more authority to the state's Sunshine Laws. The bill was prompted by what Representatives say was an illegal closed meeting of the Abington Township/School Liaison Committee. Common Cause of PA has endorsed the legislation.

headline: Judge Blake's mission
abstract: The PA Supreme Court is breathing down his neck is a familiar for Judge Edward Blake, the newly elected president of Philadelphia's troubled Common Pleas Court. State and city officials are feeling pressure to trim court costs as much as $16 million. Judge Blake isn't sold on these ideas yet. He says he's generally committed to implementing a broad range of changes put forward by a panel of judges who studied the city court system.

headline: How voters view abortion.
abstract: This chart shows how voters nationwide on Election Day responded to the question: "Which of these statements comes closest to your view about abortion? 1) It should be legal in all circumstances; 2) It should be legal only in some circumstances; or 3) It should not be legal in any circumstances."

headline: Coal Strike
abstract: The National Labor Relations Board said that the United Mine Workers and Pittston Coal Group have reached a settlement of pendinig litigation involving pickets.

headline: 500 Protest Against Hazardous-Waste Burner
abstract: Concord Resources Group is proceeding with applications for a state permit to build and operate a hazardous waste incinerator and dump in Clarion County. Concord official had planned to tour the proposed site but retreated after facing more than 500 protesters at the location. Michael W. Smith, coordinator of the PA Department of Environmental Resources' hazardous waste siting team, said the DER cannot use adverse public opinion as a reason for denying a permit.

headline: Signs to warn river boaters of dam threat
abstract: On account of the second fatal boating incident near Cumberland County's Dock Street Dam, the PA Fish Commission will install warning signs. The Commission concluded in conjunction with city representatives, members of the Harrisburg River Rescue, the PA Department of Environmental Resources and the PA Department of Transportation that buoys and dam modifications may be delayed until it is clear whether the sign will be enough of a preventative measure.

headline: State College Repaving Approved
abstract: Centre region planners approved major repavement projects for areas of South Atherton Street and College Avenue.

headline: More money needed for drug fight, Preate says
abstract: PA State Attorney General Ernie Preate has said that the state needs more money if it is to win the war on drugs. He called the amount allocated for law enforcement in the Governor's proposed budget inadequate

headline: State takes over health insurer to small businesses
abstract: The PA Department of Insurance has begun liquidating a Wayne company that sold health insurance to small businesses, a s step the firm's found said should help protect roughly 6,000 policyholders wo are owed money for their medical costs.

headline: Car Insurance
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey sent a letter to Aetna Casualty and Surety Company denouncing its decision to stop selling car insurance in the state.  The decision would leave thousands of PA motorists without car insurance in the following year.

headline: AFSCME Ruling
abstract: In a six-to-one ruling, the PA Commonwealth Court upheld the reinstatement of two employees, both members of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, that Auditor General Barbara Hafer had fired. Hafer alleged the employee's jobs were bought during former Auditor General Al Benedict's administration. Benedict and two top aides were convicted in a job selling scheme in 1988 and sentenced to prison. The ruling came a day after Hafer's loss in the gubernatorial election.

headline: GOP rival rips Freeman plan for county sales tax
abstract: Brian Leidy and PA Representative Robert Freeman have exchanged blows in what could be a hostile general election fight for Freeman's seat in the PA State House.  Leidy ripped Freeman's proposal to establish an optional 1-percent sales tax for Pennsylvania's counties.  Freeman is a co-sponsor of the b ill which would allow counties to add 1 percent to the 6 percent sales tax.

headline: No, You Can't See My License Photo!
abstract: An opinion expressing annoyance and embarassment at the whole process of getting your driver's license photo taken.

headline: Wecht was acquitted
abstract: Dr. Cyril H. Wecht is writing a letter about a previous article that references a case that he was involved in. The article was written about what was set forth in a document file by Justice Rolf Larsen where he leveled accusations against Chief Justice Robert N. C. Nix Jr. He believes that the paper should have stated that the person was completely exonerated in a formal legal procedure if they are going to refer to a criminal case against someone.

headline: Judge considered jail for abortion protestors
abstract: 12 demonstrators received parole, fines, and orders to pay court costs. Four of the defendants were placed under house arrest, though PA Common Pleas Court Judge Robert Dauer considered prison terms for their part in an abortion protest. Dauer estimated the costs of the trials at $72,000, but some lawyers have not yet submitted bills. The defendants must pay juror fees and fines. Assistant District Attorney Micahel Pawk was pleased with the sentences.

headline: Idaho Gov 'Agonizing'
abstract: Idaho Governor Cecil Andrus is torn over whether to sign the state's strict new bill banning abortion.  If he does, the Supreme Court could get involved.

headline: Depot work force to be cut
abstract: About 4% of civilian employees at the Tobyhanna Army Depot will lose their jobs as part of a nationwide move to cut federal jobs.  Orders to cut the work force came from Army Materiel Command in Alexandria, VA.  The cuts are a result of an expected shortfall of $116 million for the entire command.

headline: 700 North Lebanon residents oppose composting-plant plan
abstract: 700 residents have signed a petition opposing a composting plant to be built at the municipal landfill in North Lebanon.  The residents believe the plant is a good idea, but don't want the facility in a residential area.

headline: Six-year sewer battle has man crying foul
abstract: Larksville resident Fred Roberts has had had a six-year battle with local officials about installing a new sewage treatment plant due to sewage flowing through his property and contaminating Brown's Creek. U.S. District Judge Edwin Kosik ordered Eugene Bartoli, Valley View Estates owner, to submit an application to the Department of Environmental Resources for a new sewage treatment facility, or else face jail time. Bartoli faces fines for violating the Federal Water Pollution Control Act and Clean Steams Law, and has not yet filed an application.

headline: State drivers paying more in tax due to '83 law, rising gas prices
abstract: Due to the combination of state law about taxes on gasoline and the rising fuel prices, motorists could soon be paying slightly higher state gas taxes. The state's "oil franchise tax," a tax on oil companies that gets passed on to consumers, fluctuates depending on the wholesale price of gasoline, and if it reaches $1.20, then the tax would hit its 7.2 cent/gallon "ceiling." The tax was created to give the PA Department of Transportation a steady source of revenue.

headline: Mother Killed Editor
abstract: A special report of a firsthand recounting by Kevin Flynn of the Bethlehem Globe Times of a murder suspect's surrender to a Bethlehem newspaper office.

headline: State tourists find spirit of Christmas in Bethlehem
abstract: The City of Bethlehem was named after the biblical town on Christmas Eve in 1741. The decorations and celebrations highlight the Christmas spirit in ways that very few town can. Tourists travel from far and wide to witness the magical star that was originally built in the 1930's.

headline: Car-insurance agent: Business is hurting
abstract: Two of the three auto-insurance companies the Rummell Insurance Agency handles are not allowing new policies and the third is canceling policies if payments are a day late. Insurers are claiming that they are all being hurt by the new car insurance law that goes into effect July 1. The effort to bring down runaway car insurance rates has sparked an uproar in the insurance industry has led to 27 legal challenges. They are challenging the constitutionally of the law.

headline: Aide Vows Full Review. Casey Open-Minded Over Judgeship Bill.
abstract: The PA General Assembly passed a bill creating new judgeships for Lycoming, Clinton and 16 other counties and sent it to PA PA Governor Robert P. Casey before the end of the legislative session. Casey said he would make an individual review of counties' needs before any decision is made on a veto. Assemblyman Thomas W. Dempsey said some legislators were concerned that the bill, adding five judicial seats to Philadelphia, would represent a state bailout of the bankrupt city.

headline: GOP says Casey ads exaggerate the positive
abstract: Some Republicans are criticizing incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey of exaggerating his achievements in his recent TV ads, saying that he is taking credit where it's not due, though there are no "glaring mistruths, according to Patrick Killian, Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer's campaign manager.

headline: Nothing 'fascist' about facts
abstract: Michael Sturla, Democratic candidate for Lancaster's seat in the PA state House, has called recent polling tactics by Republicans "fascist tactic."  The House Republican Campaign Committee executed a telephone poll and asked if the resident would be voting for Sturla, and if they received a "yes" answer, they would ask if that would be changed by the fact that federal tax liens had been placed on Sturla's business.  The editorial supports the right of the pollsters to remind residents of such facts and says that such tactics are not "fascist" or dirty.

headline: We'll figure it out.
abstract: The author disapproves of Attorney Daniel M. Fennick's recent letter supporting Bortner. The author of the letter criticizes PA Senate candidate Michael Bortner's attempt to remove popular election of judges and his support for last year's tax reform, both measures that failed in the PA Senate.

headline: Judge drops charges against 29 of 34 in mass drug trial
abstract: Philadelphia Municipal Court Judge Michael J. Conroy dismissed charges against 29 of 34 defendants charged by the District Attorney's Office with distributing cocaine, methamphetamine and marijuana, saying many were simply purchasing drugs. The cases of those ordered to stand trial were the only ones in which drugs were seized by the prosecution. Assistant District Attorney Frank Keaney said the District Attorney's Office would re-examine the cases and likely would rearrest some of them. County Detective Mike Reynolds testified that he was able to identify defendants from taped telephone calls.

headline: In Boise, Idaho
abstract: A photo captures pro-choice supporters celebrating Idaho Governor Cecil Andrus' veto of a bill to restrict abortions.

headline: Dog food plant shuts down; 54 left jobless
abstract: Faced with a plant closing that will leave 54 employees jobless, Everson Mayor Tim Shoemaker hopes another plant will take over Royal Canin's operations. The plant accounted for almost all of the borough's wage tax collection. A union meeting for workers who are members of American Federation of Grain Millers-Local 240 will be held at the Everson Veterans of Foreign Wars. The borough depends largely on grants like those awarded by PA Rep. Jess Stairs and PA Sen. J. William Lincoln.

headline: 8 communities to get state loans
abstract: The PA Infrastructure Investment Authority, known as Pennvest, will grant $10 million in loans to 8 counties for sewer and water main renovations. Chairman of the board, PA Governor Casey, said a top priority of residents in PA is clean drinking water. The loan recipients include Franklin Township, Lower Burrell, four Allegheny County communities, North Fayette Township, Harmar, Beaver Falls and Economy Burough.

headline: Sludge fight
abstract: East Hopewell Residents, led by Mary Sennet of the East Hopewell Concerned Citizens Group, plan to question township solicitor D. Reed Anderson on the availability of a sludge permit submitted by PA Representative John Barley for public review. The group is also calling for a town meeting on the proposal and extension of the application review from the PA Department of Environmental Resources. Sludge spreading is common in the county and said to be safe by officials.

headline: State House rejects gas-tax amendment
abstract: The PA House failed to pass a bill to fund mass transit through a gas tax. The tax would have provided funds for capital projects rather than general operating expenses. Opposition focused on the fact that the Southeastern PA Transit Authority would benefit more so than other areas. Others said the project would divert funds from bridge and road work. PA Rep. Gordon Linton was disappointed. The Senate thwarted attempts to attach a similar proposal as an amendment to another bill.

headline: Murder conviction upheld
abstract: The PA Superior Court ruled 2-3 to uphold the murder conviction of Bernard Williams for the death of PA Rep. William Telek. The court merged two theft sentences into Telek's life-sentence, saying it was unnecessary to treat them as separate counts since there is no parole on life-sentence. Williams alleged his trial should have been moved to another county. Dissenting Justice Patrick Tamilia said the court used race to bar certain jury members from service and should grant Williams a new trial.

headline: State vinters plan to fight 'sin tax'
abstract: A proposed federal tax could devastate the state's wineries and amount to a sin tax on beverage the has long been accepted. Wine has not had the same sin tax, because it is considered a food as well as a beverage. The wine community is gathering together to at least get the bill modified. Every winery regardless of size would pay $19,000 a year, which wine makers consider unfair and could put them out of business.

headline: Casey address insurance, budget issues
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey is concerned about whether motorists will realize lower rates slated for July 1 under the state's new auto insurance law that calls for cutbacks of 10 percent for all drivers. Motorists who give up their right to sue will get a 22 percent reduction. Insurers have filed 37 lawsuits in an effort to dodge mandated rollbacks and Commonwealth Court issued three conflicting decisions. Two backed up company objections and one upheld the policy. He also said the administration is slashing year-end spending to avoid a deficit.

headline: An AP News Analysis
abstract: In the wake of the 1990 election, observers are hypothesizing that: PA Governor Robert P. Casey will run on the national ticket in 1992; PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel will run for U.S. Senate against incumbent Arlen Specter; the GOP will nominate someone to run against Specter; the GOP will nominate someone to run against Auditor General Barbara Hafer; Hafer will run again for governor. The article suggests that the possibilities lead to the conclusions that the Republican party will see in-fighting and that the Democrats have many strong candidates.

headline: GOP Seeks To Gain Enough Senate Strength To Bid for Control in 1992
abstract: Republicans have begun political strategizing and are hopeful for the approaching elections to gain a majority in the Senate for Congressional control.

headline: Nothing Raises One's Profile Like a President's Ire
abstract: A presidential rebuke can bolster political merit for a congressional figure in the opposing party.

headline: West Shore School District seeks early settlement on teacher pact
abstract: The West Shore School District offered teachers $10,600 in pay raises over three years in hopes of settling contract negotiations two months in advance of the deadline to avoid contention over the contract. Union officials declined to comment, as many union members have yet to see the official contract offer, but several teachers were hopeful that they could avoid a strike, which happened during the 1988 contract negotiations.

headline: Judge expected to approve sale to Vartan
abstract: A federal bankruptcy judge is expected to approve a deal today allowing up to 448 city properties to be sold to John Vartan for $10,000. Similar deals are being worked out as well with other properties.

headline: In Chesco, dismay at Klan plan to march
abstract: Groups are calling for their members to stay away from a scheduled march by the Ku Klux Klan on January 12, 1991. They don't want the group to get the attention they desires.

headline: Expanded Job Center is Opened
abstract: The new, recently opened Meadville Job Center offers a vast array of career services and opportunities for unemployed residents of Crawford County.

headline: 80 confront Clarion County toxic dump developer
abstract: Clarion County residents and local elected officials met with representatives of Concord Resources Group and Concord's public participation committee, led by former PA House Speaker K. Leroy Irvis, to voice disapproval of a plan to develop a hazardous waste complex in the county. It is not certain that Concord will seek the required environmental permits from the PA Department of Environmental resources in the case that neither of the two proposed sites is acceptable. Chairman of the Clarion County commissioners David Black said Concord's plan would destroy the nature of the county, with its emphasis on tourism and outdoor sports.

headline: Somerset resort drops plan to dam area stream
abstract: The head of Seven Springs Mountain Resort was withdrawn his plans to dam a stream in Somerset County.

headline: State police plan crackdown on drunk drivers
abstract: Police in three states plan a crackdown on drunk driving starting Labor Day weekend.  They plan to use sobriety checkpoints and additional policemen stationed along roads, including more unmarked cars.

headline: N.J. court rules trash is private
abstract: A New Jersey Supreme Court ruling is in direct contradiction to the US Supreme Court, which ruled trash left outside on the curb is no longer considered private property and does not require a warrant to be searched. However, the New Jersey Supreme Court ruled that since trash reveals much that is personal, it is indeed private property and should be free of meddling by the state. PA is one of several states which does not have a privacy right regarding trash.

headline: State Will Have to Help Pay CAT Fund Benefits
abstract: Constance Foster, state Insurance Commissioner informed senators that Pennsylvania must most likely help pay medical bills of CAT Fund benefit recipients in the current fiscal year.

headline: Casey calls Aetna 'callous' on car insurance pullout
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey sent a strong-worded letter to Aetna Casualty and Surety Co. calling its decision to stop selling car insurance in the state "arrogant and callous".  Aetna is the state's fifth-largest insurer and claims that they will lose $20 million during the next year due to PA's new car-insurance law.

headline: An AP News Analysis
abstract: This article lists hypothetical situations that might occur due to the 1990 general election results.

headline: Gov. Casey awards work of three
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey awarded August Wilson, Houston A. Baker Jr., and Herbert A. Simon with the 1990 Governor's award for excellence in arts, humanities, and science.  The winners were chosen on recommendations of three five-member panels of leaders in each field and the awards were established in 1988 to honor Pennsylvanians for their cultural contributions to society.

headline: Notice who Okd dubious pensions
abstract: A concerned citizen suggests the Inquirer cover every meeting of the Board of Pensions and Retirement, and the author of last week's article do more research to uncover just who was present and how they voted in a 4-2 decision to award a pension to Jack Dautrich. Only Deputy Personnel Director Linda Seyda seemed concerned with protecting the public's money, 1 of 5 public officials among 4 employee organizations representatives of the 9 member board.

headline: Wetlands:  More than just Swamps
abstract: First story in a series on wetlands and their relationship to other kinds of land usage and agriculture, and their control.

headline: Judge O’Kicki given 2 to 5 years
abstract: Joseph O’Kicki, a suspended Cambria County judge, argued his case of public-corruption to the Senior Common Pleas Judge Richard Griffo before his sentence of two to five years in prison was passed. O’Kicki was convicted on six charges of public corruption and official opposition.

headline: Interfaith group, lawmaker at odds over poker machines
abstract: A group representing churches in PA opposes State Rep. Fred Trello's proposal to legalize video poker machines for liquor licensees. Trello says revenue will assist local governments and school districts . PA Rep. Jerry Mirmelin warned this is only the first step in a path to legalize casinos. Video poker has been successful despite police raids. Watching a rally by protestors, director of the PA Taverns Association Dennis Nicholson said the bill is important to keep taverns in business.

headline: Fact-finding a good tool official says
abstract: Patricia Crawford examines the criticism against the PA Labor Relations Board on fact-finding in public employee union contract disputes and concludes that the critics may not understand the facts. She concedes that fact-finding is a controversial area, but very successful when used. Both sides have discussed using it with differing opinions on when it should be allowed.

headline: Acid rain squeezing life from Pa. lakes
abstract: According to researchers from Lehigh University, acid rain falling in PA has turned PA lakes such as Bruce Lake in Promised Land State Park acidic. This in turn affects diversity, so that species living in the lakes are starting to disappear. According to the Environmental Defense Fund, 4,000 lakes in the US have been affected by acid rain, while studies at the Pennsylvania State University show that the rain falling in the Poconos is among the most acidic in the country.

headline: Spill Poses No Apparent Danger
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources says that the undetermined amount of fuel that spilled into the Allegheny River in Amrstrong County has not affected drinking water supplies.  Heavy rains likely caused the fuel to seep from the soil that was saturated in the rupture of an interstate fuel pipeline further upstream.

headline: State Police to Set Up Checkpoints for Drunken Drivers
abstract: In an effort to deter drunk driving, the state police are setting up checkpoints at sixty areas across the state with high rates of drunk driving accidents, but the ACLU claims these violate motorist rights.

headline: N.M. governor, staff pass first drug tests
abstract: New Mexico Governor Garrey Carruthers and two dozen of his top staffers passed drug tests they took earlier in the week.  The tests marked the beginning of a policy that will subject applicants and employees in safety-sensitive jobs to random urine tests to check for illegal drugs.

headline: State's ailing S&Ls total six
abstract: A list of the failing Savings and Loans in PA.

headline: Casey hopes others follow State Farm’s lead
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey is looking for an agreement with the State Farm Insurance Agency to bring the other two large insurers in like on PA’s rate-slashing care insurance law that was signed. Casey announced the truce between the PA Insurance Department and the state’s largest car insurer that agreed to comply with the law that will bring every insurance consumer reductions. Allstate and Erie Insurance Group have argued that the Insurance Department should hear their reasons for being exempt of the law, the dispute is being heard in the PA state Supreme Court.

headline: Another Ouster
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Masloff vacated the seat of Michael Gardner on the Housing Authority board. He is accused of violating residency requirements.

headline: Gov. Casey tabs Kingston lawyer as Luzerne judge
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey chose Kingston lawyer Hugh Mundy as the next judge in Luzerne County Court. The final decision to appoint Mundy as senior Judge Bernard Podcasy's replacement rests with the PA Senate, which has 25 legislative days to confirm Casey's nomination. Mundy was selected from a list of five candidates recommended by a local nominating commission.

headline: NOW Democrats to vote for Hafer
abstract: Members of the Democratic National Organization for Women (NOW) have voted to vote for Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer instead of Democrat Casey.  The decision hinged on Hafer's pro-choice stance, while Casey is pro-life.

headline: What do you think of Hafer's "Redneck Irishman" remark?
abstract: Mount Carmel resident, John Miller (pictured) condemns mudslinging and believes Hafer was wrong and that candidates should refrain from personal attacks.

headline: Judge Oks County's Move to Recover $65,387 Shortfall
abstract: Gifford Cappellini, Luzerne County Judge, approved county Controller Joseph Tirpak's petitition to amend his 1987 report thus allowing the county to try and recover $65,387 in supposedly missept funds by Bernard Olsen, former county human services director.

headline: Judge gives abortion foes warning on protests near physician's home
abstract: U.S. District Judge Lowell A. Reed Jr. issued a warning to abortion protesters picketing near the home of physician Kenneth Lakoff, who performs abortions at the Northeast Women's Center.  In a previous injunction, Reed stated that protesters were barred from demonstrating at the residences of employees or staff of the Center.

headline: Few Problems Founds with Plant-Closing Law
abstract: Though opponents feared economic havoc as a consequence, officials found that companies had little problem with the law requiring employers to give 60 days notice to workers of plant closings or big layoffs in its first year.

headline: Action taken after fatalities
abstract: Despite a recommendation by some PA Fish Commission officials to restrict water travel under the South Bridge, workers began hanging pier signs warning Susquehanna River boaters to stay away from the Dock Street Dam. A dispute within the Fish Commission over how to prevent more drowning at the 87-year-old dam intensified after the June 19 deaths of three fisherman. Eleven people have been killed there in the past 20 years. People believe they are trading fish for human lives.

headline: Solid waste disposal question looms
abstract: PA Representative David Argall writes on progress in PA in municpal solid waste disposal. With the enactment of Act 101, PA is moving towards alternatives to landfulls, statistics from the Department of Environmental Resources of PA showing a drop from 72 to to 48 percent of waste landfilled and the American Legislative Exchange Council supporting declining statistics. Nationwide the US Environmental Protection Agency  estimated 28 percent of solid waste will be combusted by 1992.

headline: State says bridges can be torn down
abstract: Two railroad bridges scheduled for demolition have been approved, as they have been determined as having no significant historical value.  This allows work on a new bridge project to continue.

headline: Nearly half-million are on parole in USA
abstract: A list of the number of paroles in every state.

headline: State's proposed anti-takeover law blasted, lauded
abstract: The top financial adviser for the $10 billion state employees pension fund said he would lobby against buying stock in state owned companies if a proposed anti-takeover bill is passed. Proponents say the bill would give companies badly needed protection from corporate takeovers. Opponents say it discourages competition.

headline: Casey lauds Ford’s idea
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey commends Ford Motor Company for deciding to build a $117 million state-of-the-art electronics plant near Montgomery County. Casey said that this decision is the highest compliment a company could pay the state.

headline: Anti-incumbent or not, just vote.
abstract: The editorial board encourages readers to vote in the upcoming election despite an alleged anti-incumbent sentiment in the state. The board suspects that though many residents disapprove of Congress as a whole, they approve of their own local representatives. The board reminds readers that actions that representatives may take to serve the constituents also represents unpopular government spending and may lead to increased taxes.

headline: Gov. Casey to open headquarters
abstract: PA Governor Casey is scheduled to open the Bortner/Beeler campaign headquarters in Hanover on Tuesday.  Bortner is running for state Senate and Beeler for the House.

headline: Now, the voters get their say; Local and state contests energize county electorate
abstract: York City voters are turning out in large numbers to vote in the gubernatorial, PA House and PA Senate elections. While some are turned off by negative campaigning in the heated race for the 28th District senate seat between Donald Dorr and Michael Bortner, it has energized others.

headline: What do you think of Hafer's "Redneck Irishman" remark?
abstract: Mount Carmel resident, Kerri Kondisko (pictured) believes that a comment such as Hafer's would hurt a campaign and because of close media scrutiny candidates should consider their words carefully.

headline: Judge says O'Kicki showed no remorse
abstract: Until Senior Judge Richard Grifo of Northampton County informed former Cambria County Judge Joseph O'Kicki Jr. his sentence is harsher for his sentiment during his hearing, O'Kicki showed no remorse. O'Kicki said after leaving the hearing, he was not sorry for anything, including 3 counts of bribery, official oppression, coercion and demanding money for a promotion. The defendant and his lawyers predicted O'Kicki would win an appeal because Grifo refused to move the trial elsewhere.

headline: Judge strikes down Pa. abortion law, appeal certain
abstract: A federal judge declared PA's abortion law unconstitutional, the state will certainly appeal to the Supreme Court.  Supporters hope that the law will be upheld, effectively overturning the Roe vs. Wade decision from 1973.

headline: Greyhound chief claims victory in drivers' strike
abstract: Fred Currey, chief executive of Greyhound bus lines, announced victory over a 2 month old strike by a union representing 6,300 bus drivers and 3,000 maintenance and office workers.  Ed O'Neil, vice president of Local 1043, and the AFL-CIO disagree with Currey's statement that the company can operate efficiently despite the strike.

headline: Ammonia leak stirs Biglerville
abstract: An ammonia leak at a fruit processing plant in Biglerville yesterday disrupted classes and forced neighborhood residents indoors, but was later dubbed "a minor incident."

headline: Solid Waste Hearing Scheduled In County
abstract: A public hearing to give Venango County residents a voice on a proposed solid waste management plan has been scheduled.  Residents are encouraged to attend and voice their opinions and suggestions.

headline: State to rebid welcome center in early 1991
abstract: According to Pam DiSalvo, spokeswoman for the PA Department of General Services, a welcome center planned for Antrim Township will be re-bid early next year. Initial bids were rejected when they came in $70,000 higher than the planned budget. PA Governor Robert P. Casey released $1.6 million to build the center, which will be run by the PA Department of Transportation.

headline: Neighborhood held hostage.
abstract: A payphone placed in a Norristown neighborhood used for drug deals has increased crime rates in the area. Officials at Bell of PA say that they could curb incoming calls on the phone, but that the process is so complicated that it takes months to complete and must be done on a case-by-case basis from the Public Utilities Commission. Even when the process is approved, the restrictions only last for six months.

headline: States regulate storage, disposal of old tires
abstract: Twenty-two states have passed regulations about the storage, processing and stockpiling of the used tires that are discarded annually. The states support theses programs by using disposable fees, retail sales charges, titles fees or sales taxes.

headline: Casey lauds Ford's idea
