abstract: PA's tight financial situation has forced officials to postpone addressing the $100 million question facing the state park system. Where will the state find the money to pay for an estimated $100 million in needed repairs to the marinas, roads, and campgrounds and other facilities at the 114 parks? No answer is apparent. In the new state budget the parks will get $900,000 more than last year.

headline: Voices
abstract: The article lists the responses of citizens to the question: "Should doctors be allowed to counsel patients on the option of abortion?" The responses are varied.

headline: Assembly must retain authority
abstract: the PA Board of Education has been criticized for several mandates in which it added new state special education programs. Sen Ralph Hess, R-Spring Grove, chairman of the Senate Education Committee, accused the board of usurping legislative authority. Rep. Ronald Cowell, D-Allegheny, chairman of the House Education Committee, shares Hess's concerns. This editorial agrees, saying that legislators are ultimately held accountable by the voters for these programs and who must find ways to fund them. They are the ones therefore, who should create them-not the Board of Education.

headline: Company Plans Recycling Center in Beaver County
abstract: Piccirilli Disposal Service, a local division of Waste Management Inc., has a major recycling center opening in the Pittsburgh area

headline: Yukon group wants DER off case
abstract: Ten families from Yukon, Westmoreland County, filed a lawsuit against the PA Department of Environmental Resources in Westmoreland County Common Pleas Court, asking that the agency relinquish its responsibility for protecting natural resources in the town. Lawyer Robert Ging will also ask in the injunction that Mill Services Incorporated stop putting hazardous waste, such as carcinogens, arsenic and lead, into the groundwater. Ging and the families assert that the DER's tests of the soil, air and water in the area have not been extensive enough

headline: A Use for the Wall
abstract: An editorial opposing the building of a prison in Greene County.

headline: Product liability falls to tobacco fears
abstract: The PA Senate tabled a bill aimed at limiting frivolous lawsuits over unsafe products over suspicions that it contained protections for the tobacco industry. Senate Minority Leader Robert Mellow said the issue is too complex to resolve in the lame-duck session and that PA Governor Robert P. Casey won't support the bill because of its ambiguity. The bill was opposed by consumers' groups and the PA State Trial Lawyers Association but supported by the PA Product Liability Task Force.

headline: Change in School District Real Estate Tax Levies
abstract: This chart details the change in several PA school district real estate tax levies from 1985 to 1990.

headline: Insurance industry challenges Delaware law allowing banks to underwrite
abstract: Delaware Governor Michael N. Castle signed a new law allowing banks with operations in the state to sell and underwrite insurance nationwide, and it was promptly challenged by members of the insurance industry. According to William R. Anders, associate general counsel of the National Association of Life Underwriters, a petition was filed with the Federal Reserve Board to block Citicorp from taking advantage of the law. Citicorp is the largest banking company in the US.

headline: Bush cuts go beyond HHS fat
abstract: The editors advise caution in the federal government's attempts to balance the budget. Plans to cut the budget of the US Health and Human Services Department drew complaints from Secretary Dr. Louis Sullivan against Budget Director Richard Darman. While the editors acknowledge serious corrective steps are necessary, the miniscule amount of money that cuts will save and the great affect there will be on consumers does not seem worth the trouble.

headline: Hafer ordered to rehire seven more fired workers
abstract: PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer has been ordered to rehire seven workers she fired last year after alleging that they bought their jobs under a previous administration.  The rehiring of these workers could cost the state  $716,000 in pack pay and benefits.

headline: Population Declines In City and County
abstract: According to the preliminary 1990 census data, several cities in Crawford County and the county itself experienced population declines.

headline: State tourists find spirit of Christmas in Bethlehem
abstract: Historic Bethlehem, PA offers bus tours of its lighted city as well as walking tours to tourists. The city's historic five pointed star, representing music, education, religion, recreation, and industry, is a focal point of the tours.

headline: Women, minorities need civil rights law
abstract: Editors implore US House Representatives to amend the Civil Rights Act of 1990to attack discrimination in the workplace. The act attempts to strengthen Civil Rights Legislation some say was weakened by US Supreme Court rulings. Some, including President Bush, say the amendment is more discriminatory, forcing companies to hire with regard to quotas rather than merit. Editors want a law that gives women and minorities tools to fight unfair practices and for everyone to get an even break.

headline: Baltimore Mayor Recommends School Chief Not Be Rehired
abstract: Baltimore Mayor Kurt Schmoke brought the dispute between city hall and the school administration to a climax when he publicly condemned Baltimore public school Superintendent Richard Hunter. Schmoke's displeasure with Hunter has been known for several months, as the two have disagreed on the pace, extent, and the nature of change necessary to improve public schools. Hunter has been criticized for appearing to be aloof from community members and school personnel.

headline: Conflicting nitrate reports have Seven Valleys puzzled
abstract: Conflicting numbers in nitrate tests performed by different groups in Seven Valleys have residents and officials confused as to who is doing the tests incorrectly and if the drinking water is safe.

headline: Zerbe board hears proposal for recycling facility
abstract: Plans for a significant recycling facility were disclosed yesterday, and the proposal will now be up for review and approval by the PA Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: A victory over the mob
abstract: The editorial board believes the successful prosecution of nine men in the federal court in Pittsburgh was one of the most significant victories of U.S. Attorney Thomas W. Corbett Jr. and the U.S. Department of Justice in the war on organized crime. The Michael Genovese family has been a key factor in narcotics and other illegal activities in Western PA. Lawyers are now looking to undercover financial resources to satisfy the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act demand that all illegally obtained profits be forfeited.

headline: Product liability laws produce lawyer fees
abstract: President of Hickok Manufacturing Peter Hickok disagrees with local trial attorney James Ronca who accused the proposed product liability reform bill of being a smokescreen for tobacco companies. In Hickok's opinion, the reform would have provided a more equitable product liability law as well as rights for consumers to sue over injuries caused by genuinely defective products.

headline: City asks state for $50 million short-term loan
abstract: Philadelphia officials asked the state to buy up to $50 million in short-term notes. Mayor Goode seeks a plan that will include a city sales tax, the sale of some city assets and state oversight of city finances. PA officials responded noncommittally to the oral request, asking for a formal proposal. The city was thrown into a cash crisis after its failure in September to sell $375 million in short-term notes and will run out of cash around December 1st without help from the state and Wall Street.

headline: Insurance politics
abstract: PA's recent law mandating lower insurance premiums is falling apart, as insurance firms are refusing to write new businesses in the state, while lawyers stand to profit from lawsuits from auto accidents. The state has also encountered problems with the Trial Lawyers Association as a result of the state's pursuit of a policy allowing citizens to sign away their rights to sue. The editorial board calls for legislation which will solve all parties involved in the insurance crisis.

headline: Bush hints quick, 'surprise' choice
abstract: President Bush is looking for one good conservative to appoint to the US Supreme Court preferably a kinder, gentler version of Robert Bork without a track record on abortion. Bush is in the middle and has to please voters and conservatives. His only hints were that the appointment would be quick and a surprise. A minority pick will not entirely satisfy the conservatives.

headline: Hafer predicts GOP team will be household word by Nov.
abstract: PA Auditor-General predicted that the names "Hafer-Mowery" will be household words by the time the state votes for Governor in November. Hafer named Rep. Harold Mowery Jr, R-Cumberland, as her choice for Lt. Governor. The pair will likely face incumbent Governor Casey and Lt. Gov. Singel in November.

headline: Possible Casey-Hafer debate still doubtful
abstract: A meeting of PA Governor Casey's campaign manager with the League of Women Voters produced no agreements or commitments as far as a debate, and despite the numerous groups calling for one, it looks unlikely that Casey will accept a debate.

headline: That land is our land
abstract: The editors commend the Richard King Mellon Foundation, which has donated 93,000 acres across several states, including a 266-acre tract in PA to the national park system. They only wish the federal government's priorities were the same. Foundation president, Seward Prosser Mellon, hopes to acquire additional acreage to donate.

headline: Mehrabian surprised by CMU's $50 million debt
abstract: Robert Mehrabian, new President of CMU, was somewhat surprised when he found out the magnitude of the university's $50 million debt, and is working on a plan to pay it off without using funds meant for other programs.

headline: Women's Day Observance Brims with Ideas, Honors
abstract: The empowering International Women's Day event was held early in Harrisburg and celebrated women and their achievements.

headline: Bill would give grads vote forms
abstract: 60 students, members of the Pennsylvania Association of Student Councils, went to the state capital in Harrisburg to lobby the PA Senate for passage of House Bill 656, which would amend the Public School Code to make schools give voter registration forms to eligible high school graduates.  House Bill 656 is currently being reviewed by the Senate Government Committee after being passed in the House.

headline: Conservation Groups to Buy Wetlands in Poconos, Let State Preserve Them
abstract: Three private conservation groups will acquire about 4,000 acres of wetlands in the Poconos which will eventually be sold to the Pennsylvania Game Commission for preservation.

headline: 60 families evacuated near blast sites
abstract: Allegheny Fire Marshall John Kaus believes a loose natural gas valve in a private natural gas well selling to Equitable Gas is responsible for the explosion and evacuation of 60 families in South Park. Neighbors who complained of a natural gas smell were quieted when the PA Department of Environmental Resources repaired a loose valve. However, an explosion leveled a home and sent the Vitodian family to the hospital after they tried to escape from burning rubble.

headline: A young police hero lived his dream- all too briefly
abstract: A commentary about the last day of Philadelphia police officer Joaquin "Jack" Montijo. He was killed in the line of duty when he missed his mark and was shot by a suspect. The author says that he will be attending the funeral to show respect for the newest cop to die while trying to protect the city.

headline: Promise of Sex Voids Conviction
abstract: The police's promise of conjugal visits to a suspect who confessed to a shooting voided his manslaughter charge.

headline: City fee increases
abstract: The article details fee increases in certain Pittsburgh sectors, such as the zoo, the pool, Schenley Park Golf Course, residential parking permits and vehicle store fees.

headline: Insurance reforms lauded
abstract: PA Motorists are satisfied with the rate cuts. PA Insurance Commissioner Constance Foster announced the state will begin citing companies not in compliance, with lawsuits and court orders pending. President of the Insurance Federation of Pennsylvania, Henry Hager, says reforms do not allow companies to profit. The reforms call for stricter penalties for uninsured drivers. Some thought this provision would mean little more than increased paperwork for the PA Department of Transportation, while others were more optimistic.

headline: Bush starts search for new justice
abstract: President Bush met with top advisers to consider who should be nominated to replace liberal Justice William J Brennan Jr. on the Supreme Court. The administration would like to appoint a justice who is anti-abortion. Senators who like to see a Moderate conservative be nominated and confirmed.

headline: Hafer ready to barnstorm state as GOP endorses running mate.
abstract: The Republican state committee has unanimously endorsed gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer's running mate against Gov. Casey. State Rep. Harold Mowery and Hafer are to begin a barnstorming tour of the state. President Bush has promised personal appearences.

headline: Potty Parity
abstract: The PA House approved a bill that would require more restrooms for women in buildings owned or leased by the state and local governments and certain other public entertainment facilities, and sent it to PA Governor Robert P. Casey for approval. The bill would only apply to new buildings or those undergoing extensive renovations. Representative Ruth Rudy said that women's issues have been long overlooked.

headline: City tax plan greeted cooly. Legislators lukewarm to raising occupation levy.
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masleff's proposal to raise the occupational privilege tax was not well received by county legislators, though she hopes to push it through during the Legislature's lame-duck session. The city would also reduce the amusement tax, a move supported by the entertainment and sports communities. Opponents argue that the entertainment tax decrease would only serve to subsidize professional athletes' "million-dollar salaries" and that the occupational privilege tax is regressive.

headline: null
abstract: The cartoon depicts a librarian; with a nametag of Michael Hershock, PA Budget Secretary and angry elephants reading books title PA Budget.

headline: Webster: The Abortion Debate Renewed
abstract: A photo captures participants protesting the 17th anniversary of the Roe v. Wade ruling in an annual March for Life in Washington.

headline: Board slices tax hike to 6.5 mills
abstract: The Waynesboro Area School board reduced a budget proposal which raised funds by 14 mills, to 6.5 mills, after increasing the budget by 10 mills in the year prior. The Board will use funds from the sale of East Junior High to pay for an air quality project at Summit View Elementary School. Leading the faction to reduce the budget were Nelson Rock and Duane Thomas. President Douglas Harbaugh and directors Valerie Dick and Thomas Singer favored using the sale to create a surplus for the District instead.

headline: Contaminant Levels
abstract: List of contaminant levels compared with federal standards.

headline: Mill foes: Opposition is growing
abstract: Members of a local citizens' group, Committee to Save New Germany, opposed to a proposed Japanese steel mill/ cogeneration plant complex here told a crowd of more than 100 people last night that support for their cause is growing. Plans for the $500 million development, projected to create 250 new jobs, call for a 380-megawatt coal/natural gas fired cogeneration plant, a small steel rolling mill and a brine treatment plant.

headline: Abuse probed at Fayette youth camp
abstract: The PA Department of Welfare is investigating the Pressley Ridge School in Fayette County amid allegations of nine incidents of physical abuse. About 60 boys, mostly coming from troubled homes, live at the wilderness camp. Allegheny County Judge Eugene Strassburger has set a closed-door hearing to learn the results of the investigation.

headline: Proposal scrapped for prison at WSH
abstract: PA Senator David J. Brightbill amended a House bill which authorized $20 million for conversion of buildings on the grounds of Wernersville State Hospital into a drug-and-alcohol treatment-based prison. After opposition from residents, mental health officials, the PA Welfare Department, and the PA Board of Probation and Parole, a $5.5 million facility will be erected in Forest County under the PA Bureau of Corrections. PA State Senators Michael O'Pake and Rep. Thomas Caltagirone supported the changes.

headline: City Hall Going Broke? Tourists Don't Care.
abstract: Tourist bookings have nearly doubled at the Philadelphia Convention and Visitors Bureau, despite the city government's current fiscal crisis. Workers at the city's tourism agencies show optimism in the government's ability to resolve the budget deficit. Eight historic buildings at Independence National Historical Park remain closed because the National Park Service didn't budget enough money.

headline: Insurance Suit
abstract: The Keystone Insurance Company has challenged in court PA's new auto-insurance reform bill because it mandates a cut in rates.

headline: Bush urged to sign family bill
abstract: White House Spokesman Marlin Fitzwater announced President Bush intends to veto the Family and Medical Leave Act passed by the Senate. Bush is said to support the concept, however he opposes making it mandatory. Republican sponsor of the bill, Rep. Marge Routhema, is urging the President to sign it, saying failure to support it could backfire on GOP. Senate Leader George Mitchell read from a Bush campaign speech to remind Bush he supported the concept before becoming President. Neither House has the votes to override a veto.

headline: Hafer rebuffed on TANs proposal
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Auditor General Barbara Hafer has refused to sign PA Governor Robert P. Casey's tax anticipation note documents, saying they misrepresent the state's fiscal condition. Hafer's attempt to sign the notes 'by addendum', a move that has been declared legally invalid, has resulted in delayed payments to school districts. Budget Secretary Michael Hershock made payments of $146 million to the 231 poorest school districts, but delayed payment to the remaining 270 districts.

headline: Power grip. The incumbents' advantage in congressional elections.
abstract: The chart shows that since 1970, PA House members seeking re-election have won at an average rate of more than 90 percent. Serving larger, statewide constituencies, U.S. Senate incumbents have been somewhat less successful in their re-election bids.

headline: City unveils $9.36 million 'frail' budget
abstract: Johnstown Mayor Herb Pfuhl Jr.'s department directors unveiled a $9.36 million budget proposal for 1991. Cost increases through Blue Cross/Blue Shield premiums and union contracts with the Fraternal Order of Police, the International Association of Firefighters and American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, which still must be settled, could reduce it. The budget allows for no wage or benefit increases and would require union workers to pay for any premium increase in Blue Cross/Blue Shield.

headline: null
abstract: "There's no free lunch. If you take ($62 million in revenues) out of our budget, somebody's got to pay for it. And guess who will pay for it: Working men and women, OK?" -- PA Governor Robert Casey, on his opposition to attempts to repeal the "widow's tax" on inheritance.

headline: Why not a Klan Scholarship for Blacks?
abstract: An opinion expressing interest that the Ku Klux Klan fund a scholarship for deserving black students rather than attempting to reform by helping adjudicate morality in regards to pornography.

headline: Book learning may become year-round for U.S. students
abstract: Some educators are viewing the idea of year-round school in the U.S. with increasing favor. The move would be made in order to make American school more competitive with those abroad.  Of the 775-800 American schools currently on a year-round schedule, most have chosen it because of overcrowding, and some have switched back to the traditional schedule. Extending the school year or making it year-round (usually on a 9-week school, 3-week "vacation" schedule) is an expensive venture.

headline: Corps' Lake Raystown plan to get input from Casey first
abstract: The Army Corps of Engineers are attempting to use Lake Raystown as a source of fresh water to try and balance the mix of salt and fresh water in the Chesapeake Bay.  Both PA Governor Casey and Congress would have to approve the use of the Lake's reserves.

headline: NRC removes Peach Bottom from list of troubled nuclear plant
abstract: Federal Officials have removed the Peach Bottom nuclear power plant from a list of troubled nuclear power plants. It is operated by the Philadelphia Electric Co.

headline: Abused Children, 150
abstract: Gov. Robert P. Casey said $1.8 million in state funding will go to helping families of abused children,

headline: Proposed law to target city skateboarding
abstract: The statue in front of Harrisburg's city hall is moving because skateboards are being lean against it. Now skateboarding is being banned through out the city. Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed says he'll refuse to sign the bill if it bans skateboarding completely though.

headline: City is late mailing tax forms
abstract: A mix up at the Board of Revision of Taxes means that the financially strapped city government of Philadelphia will not receive personal-property tax payments on time.

headline: Insurance talks continue
abstract: Talks between the financially strapped Blue Cross & Blue Shield of West Virginia Inc. and Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Ohio of a possible merger are continuing.  The Ohio insurance company may be seeking to unite with the WV company and another BC&BS company in West Virginia.

headline: Bush visit will not raise cash for Hafer
abstract: PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer will be at the head of the table when President Bush comes to Philadelphia to raise money next week, but her campaign committee will be farther back in line when the event's proceeds are distributed. The bulk of the $500,000 that Republicans hope to collect will be funneled through the Republican State Committee.

headline: Hafer responds to Casey under equal-time ruling
abstract: Hafer made her first statewide radio address this weekend, as PA Governor Casey has done for two years.  The time was given to her as a result of the equal time rule of the FCC.

headline: Practicing before the big game
abstract: The latest issue of a state-government magazine bears a painting on its cover of a woodchuck standing on his hind legs. There is also a hunter in the background about to shoot him. The author believes this is bad for children to see, because the woodchuck is so cute.

headline: Controller Warns on Philadelphia Funds
abstract: The city of Philadelphia will likely run out of cash within 9 months, and is looking for new investments and perhaps new taxes and state money.  The investment future could be grim, as Philly's current state of debt won't attract many investors.

headline: $19.6 million school budget in Gettysburg
abstract: The Gettysburg school directors passed a $19,636,382 budget with a $1.6 million capital reserve account, but only raising taxes 6 mills instead of the proposed 10 mills. Some were upset at the increase in taxes because there was a surplus last year.

headline: Will the GOP keep its stand on abortion?
abstract: The decision by leading Republican strategists, such as Lee Atwater, to welcome pro-choice Republicans into the party is creating a rift, with pro-life Republicans claiming that pro-choice goes against the parties ideas.

headline: Brain Busters
abstract: The Boys Club tutoring program Brain Busters helped Abey Salaam get off the streets and improve academically.

headline: County designates official landfill
abstract: Northumberland County commissioners designated the Pine Grove Landfill as the county's official landfill. The announcement is part of the county solid waste advisory committee's plan for the next 10 years. Commissioners also adopted a resolution urging support for the county prison facilities improvement referendum on the ballot this November.

headline: pa financial news
abstract: The Public Utility Commission is investigating whether Equitable Gas Company followed proper procedure in shutting off gas to the Pittsburgh home of a doctor who died of exposure.

headline: ACLU files suit over tree's decorations…
abstract: The ACLU has charged the state with violating the US Constitution for displaying crosses on the Christmas tree in the Capital rotunda. They have also asked the court for a temporary restraining order to remove the crosses. The state said the crosses did not show endorsement of one religion over another. There are only a few crosses among a thousand ornaments.

headline: Prosecutor: Guida Sentencing May Be Delayed
abstract: The sentencing of former deputy OA Attorney General Richard Guida has been delayed until it is seen whether or not he can be of any help in the case against former Justice Dept. aide Henry Barr for drug charges.  Guida pled guilty to cocaine distribution charges and could face up to 20 years in jail and a $1 million fine.

headline: City proposes state oversight authority
abstract: The Philadelphia Mayor Goode administration has proposed giving the state some control over city spending in a plan to erase large budget deficits forecast for this and next fiscal year. It calls for a creation of an oversight authority that would borrow money to cover a $229.5 million shortfall in the fiscal year. The city would be required to assure that means are in hand to prevent deficits in the future. Details will go to the PA legislature. Banks are in negotiations with the city and they want the city to have an independent board with veto power over city spending.

headline: Insurers Act to Meet Auto Law Deadline
abstract: As PA prepares to institute a new auto insurance law which mandates premium cuts of 10 percent and 22 percent for those who surrender their tort options, the PA Department of Insurance is experiencing resistance. Though State Farm has agreed to comply, it will institute the new rates based on a 2.3 percent increase approved by the Department as "extraordinary rate relief." The company has agreed to abide by a Commonwealth Court ruling regarding whether or not the 2.3 percent increase may serve as a base for cuts. Other companies have taken to the courts as well, with Judge Alexander Barbieri allowing Erie Insurance Group to continue its current rates until the Department agrees to a rate relief hearing. Whether the Legislature has the right to mandate rate cuts below profitable margins is questionable.

headline: Busy Itinerary Established for Capital Day Visit by Gov. Casey
abstract: Governor Casey has a packed schedule of events in his Capital for a Day program from Thursday to Friday as he tours Lancaster County.

headline: Hafer Restates Her View that Casey's a Redneck
abstract: Auditor General and Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer stood by her view that Governor Casey is a "redneck" but claimed she never meant to offend the Irish.

headline: Preate Plays Down 'Redneck' Remark
abstract: The Republican State Committee endorsed Rep. Harold Mowery for the Lt. Gov. nomination, and Attorney General Preate said that Gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer's reference to Gov. Casey as a 'redneck irishman from Scranton' wouldn't hurt their campaign there.

headline: Council not quite ready to push sales tax
abstract: Proponents of raising Philadelphia's sales tax by 1% delayed action until next week in order to give themselves more time to win support for the action.  The measure is hoped to alleviate some of the stress on Philadelphia's coffers, which are expected to be empty in about two months, though officials say that more will need to be done to ward of insolvency.

headline: $200 million in Pa. notes sold
abstract: The state's plans to borrow $495 million took a large step toward completion as Gov. Casey and Barbara Hafer made a compromise on the wording in the sale of the short-term notes, leading Hafer to sign for their distribution.

headline: Wisconsin Abortion
abstract: State lawmakers decided Tuesday not to vote on a measure to repeal unenforceable criminal penalties for doctors who perform abortions, but they continued debate on a bill to require minors to get permission for abortions.

headline: BU trustee faces a new sex charge
abstract: James Gross, a Bloomsburg University trustee, Pottsville city controller, and middle school teacher, is accused of making improper sexual advances to two teenaged boys and indecently assaulting a 16-year-old boy.  He intends to plead not guilty.

headline: County landfill may have longer life
abstract: Grunderville Landfill could remain open for an additional year as a result of action taken in the PA House of Representatives. The bill passed the House carrying an amendment that included municipal transfer stations as well as municipal landfills.

headline: PE declares unusual event at Limerick
abstract: The Philadelphia Electric Co. declared an "unusual event" at the Limerick nuclear power plant in Montgomery County, since a worker who suffered a heart attack while on the job was transported to the hospital while still in his contamination clothing. Hospital officials checked for contamination and found none. Regulations require the reporting of an unusual event when a worker leaves in his/her contamination clothing.

headline: ACLU Joins Caller ID Opposition
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union has joined the Ohio Association of Chiefs of Police, the Ohio State Highway Patrol, and the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms in a motion to block caller-ID services proposed by Ohio Bell telephone company.  The motion was filed with Ohio's Public Utilities Commission and expresses concerns over caller's privacy.

headline: Protecting our children
abstract: Editors urge people with suspicions of child abuse to report their suspicions. In order to keep child abusers from working with children again, they must be successfully convicted, which can only result from reporting one's suspicions. The editors also suggest parents with children enrolled in extracurricular programs make sure their children are in the care of multiple adults.

headline: City says county hasn't paid $76,000 in rent
abstract: Pittsburgh is investigating claims that Allegheny County has not paid over $76,000 in rent for a joint city-county building where county operates its Family Court. Councilman Jim Ferlo noted the county paid $25,746 for use of the facility last year. That is only a quarter of the amount stipulated in a 10 year lease contract between the two parties. Newly appointed city General Services Director Louis DiNardo could not explain the lack of a new lease agreement or enforcement of the old agreement.

headline: Item Pricing
abstract: The Pennsylvania Food Merchants Association's efforts to allow consumers to verify prices before checking out comes at the heels of a city item pricing bill.

headline: CAHT tale
abstract: This letter to the editor agrees with PA Senator Robert Mellow's concerns with a group known as the Citizens Against Higher Taxes. The author believes the group is partisan and it can be seen through their funding of only Republicans, thus not a citizen's group.

headline: Hafer Says Buget Would be her Top Priority
abstract: At a press conference, auditor general and Republican gubernatorial candidate, Barbara Hafer said she would target the budget first as governor, criticizing Governor Casey's current management.

headline: Predictably, they're after the pension fund
abstract: Philadelphia's present attempts to avoid insolvency are not different from efforts of big corporations that have found themselves in eleventh-hour negotiations, daily crises and a bunker mentality. Using employees' pension funds have been discussed and caused heated debate. Employees are not happy with the idea of the city spending their money set aside for their future, but other plans have failed or not approved.

headline: Council aims to put unused $45,000 to use
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Council indicated that it will give each of its members $5000 to spend on the community project of their choosing. The money was originally budgeted for the establishment of district offices for the council members, but Mayor Masloff vetoed the appropriations after overwhelming public opposition to the expense.

headline: $330.7 million school budget holds tax hike
abstract: A 1991 budget of $330.7 million with no tax increase, school board members warned that austerity must begin now to avoid a tax hike in 1992. They voted down expensive additions like computer labs.

headline: Workforce Distribution
abstract: This chart shows the distribution of women and minorities in the workforce in 1988 and projected figures for 2000 according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

headline: Buckle up on school buses
abstract: Some parents of Pittsburgh public-school students want the school board to install seat belts in all the district's buses. District officials say that, they don't have to put seat belts in the large buses. It might save them money on injury costs. Federal law already requires vehivles smaller than 10,000 tons have seat belts.

headline: County nixes zoning vote, trash bids
abstract: The Adams County Commissioners voted to delay action on expanding interchange zoning in the county and also voted to begin anew the search for a site to dump the county's solid waste. Common planning practice calls for such areas to be zoned for commercial and light industrial uses. But residents of the resort community of Lake Heritage, with roughly 500 homes and up to 350 more expected in coming years say the area is already overwhelming residential.

headline: PECO Chief Vows to Appeal Cut in Proposed Rate Boost
abstract: Joseph F. Paquette, chairman and CEO of Philadelphia Electric Co. declared he would appeal the proposed eighty percent cut in a rate increase requested to defray the cost of building a nuclear power plant as it would ruin PECO's ability to raise money to continue plant expansion.

headline: ACLU may sue over jail crowding
abstract: After PA Governor Robert Casey and PA Department of Corrections Commissioner Joseph Lehman announced a plan to put another 1,179 beds in a state prison system already overcrowded, the American Civil Liberties Union threatened to sue. The changes were described as temporary emergency measures. An 11 percent budget increase was approved and new facilities will be constructed. The ACLU argued emergency measures may cause more rioting and violence within the prisons.

headline: Protest Scenes
abstract: The photograph shows people looking at an area where a wetlands violation was reported. The recent disclosure has sparked considerable outcry.

headline: Kill video poker bill
abstract: The editorial board criticized the PA House vote to legalize video poker machines in bars, clubs and restaurants as an act of political cowardice and opportunism. The board rejects poker advocates' claims that revenues from the machines would go to make up tax revenue shortfalls for local governments. The board urges the Senate to reject the legislation and if it fails to do so, urges PA Governor Casey to veto it.

headline: Call for change in 53rd District
abstract: The editorial board endorses Democrat Cliessa Nagle for the 53rd PA Legislative seat, citing her emphasis on family-related matters important to the changing demographic of Montgomery County and her campaign reliance on "the issues". The board praises four-term incumbent Republican Robert Godshall's action on issues such as the impact fees charged to developers, but believes Nagle is a more accessible candidate.

headline: Hafer Says Calling Governor "Redneck Irishman" was a Joke
abstract: Despite strong criticism Republican Gubernatorial candidate did not apologize for calling Gov. Bob Casey a "redneck Irishman from Scranton", saying "They're going to try to shake me up and I'm going to go after them".

headline: Preparing for the Governor: Streets Cleaned, Cars Moved, Food Readied
abstract: Lancaster city is busy with preparations to welcome Governor Casey as he visits as part of the Capital for a Day program.

headline: Council cautious on plan for fees.
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff's proposed widespread increase in the city's permits, licensing and fees was met with mixed reviews by City Council members. The members, including Council President Jack Wagner, who said they would approve most of the increases, were concerned about the proposed doubling of summer swimming pool fees. Increases proposed for the Pittsburgh Zoo and the Schenley Golf Course are intended to make those operations self-sufficient.

headline: A crucial year
abstract: Editors wonder how effective a part-time legislature is. They, along with PA Senate Majority Leader Joseph Loeper, question whether the budget for the upcoming year can sustain the state as the Casey administration maintains. A tax increase may indeed be necessary, although not if politicians are diligent in making sensible decisions. Casey and Legislators must be more flexible in adapting to changes in the economy if they are going to pass the test of keeping the state economically viable.

headline: York Hispanics use survey to sound off on language barriers encountered daily.
abstract: A new survey addressing the concerns of York Hispanics finds that the lack of information available in Spanish is the biggest challenge they face linguistically.

headline: Butler Schools' TELLS Score Down
abstract: State mandated tests in reading and math for third, fifth, and eighth graders have fell 2 percent since last year.

headline: County non-reusable cups to be non-usable by staff
abstract: In Dauphin County, the county commissioners have voted 2-1 to halt the use of Styrofoam cups in their offices in an effort to contribute to the recycling effort in the area.  Commission Chairman Sally S. Klein plans to meet with officials from other agencies to see if ways can be found to cut back further on waste.

headline: Power Plant Takes Giant Step
abstract: Mid-Atlantic Energy's proposed development of a 30-megawatt power plant in Clarion County has been approved by the Public Utility Commission in Harrisburg.

headline: ACLU sues state over woes at prisons
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union has filed a class-action lawsuit in U.S. District Court against the PA Department of Corrections, alleging that it violates the constitutional rights of inmates by subjecting them to cruel and unusual punishment. Stefan Presser, legal director for the ACLU in PA, said the organization is seeking to change corrections policy to alleviate overcrowding and the consequential internal violence. Corrections Commissioner Joseph D. Lehman said the lawsuit fails to recognize significant steps the state has taken toward expanding and reforming the system.

headline: Public attitudes about Camp Hill prison riots
abstract: Poll on how the public feels about the Camp Hill prison riots and public officials.

headline: It's 'put-up' time. The city's knights of the fiscal roundtable had better have a plan- or else.
abstract: The editorial board calls for officials state-wide and city workers unions to announce a concrete plan to save Philadelphia from its fiscal crisis. The board wants the "numbers" in the plan to add up, and to know which city facilities might be sold, where cuts might be made and what revenues could be used to pay off bond sales. The board says it will allow for some ambiguity, but wants officials to fight for the program.

headline: Call poll gives Casey 2-1 lead
abstract: With the election nearing, PA Governor Robert P. Casey holds a 2-1 lead over opponent Republican Barbara Hafer among voters in Lehigh and Northampton counties, winning support from 48 percent of respondents with a 4.5 percent margin of error. Hafer's television ads only began in late October, a move that have been inaccurately reflected in the polls. The article goes on to detail poll responses to specific issues and questions.

headline: Hafer says Casey would cut aid to Temple, Penn State and Pitt
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate said the PA Governor Robert Casey would cut aid to state universities in order to balance the state budget if he is reelected. Casey denied the claim. Hafer said that Casey would not be able to solve PA's economic troubles, saying that "We're looking at a $1 billion deficit."

headline: Preservations still available to hear Barbara Hafer speak
abstract: The Bradford County Council of Republican Women is sponsoring a luncheon with special guest PA Auditor General and gubernatorial challenger to PA Governor Robert Casey, Barbara Hafer. Hafer has cited education, corrections, and transportation as her top priorities if elected. Hafer has been active in politics for nearly 20 years, serving in various levels of government, including Allegheny County Commissioner.

headline: Council checks off no-tax-hike budget plan
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Council left Mayor Sophie Masloff's 1991 budget proposal largely intact, adding $518,000. In an informal agreement, each member of the council was allotted $40,000 to distribute in grants to charitable institutions. Some changes were made to reinstate positions cut by the mayor, however Masloff may choose not to appoint persons to those positions. The mayor has the power of line item veto, however the council may override vetos with a 2/3 majority.

headline: Administration asks for smaller budget
abstract: PA Governor Casey has asked legislative leaders to carve as much as $100 million from the pending state budget, because of sagging corporate taxes. Some legislators are skeptical about reaching the $100 million mark for cuts, because the current budget only asks for 2.3% increase in spending. The possibility of a reduced budget has been discussed for months though.

headline: YWCA's pro-choice stance explained
abstract: Kathy Taylor of Hershey, a YWCA member, writes to explain the YWCA's pro-choice stance despite its religious affiliations. She said that the protection of individual freedoms and privacy rights were a primary reason, and stressed the importance of helping the victims of sexual assault, rape, and incest, and not forcing them to bear their assailants' child.

headline: Candidates' battle over school funds comes to an end
abstract: The two gubernatorial candidates finally resolved a dispute over a footnote in the application for tax-anticipation loans for the state so it can pay for education and other programs.

headline: county Official Defends Gypsy Moth spray Effort
abstract: Clarion County Commissioner David Black says a news release from PA Representative David Wright unfairly blames county officials for failing to take advantage of additional state monies to alleviate tree damage done by gypsy moths. He claims the county made an educated choice to not take the money because of the limitations attached to the money like no PA Department of Environmental Resources expertise relative to proper execution of second round spraying and lack of administrative and technical ability to properly conduct Option II on their own.

headline: Prince of oil plunges; will gas follow?
abstract: Despite the fall in crude oil prices, the article warns consumers not to expect a similar drop in gas prices, as the trend in the industry suggests that the price of gas will remain high, or maybe even increase.

headline: Across U.S., states ring in the new laws
abstract: Across the United States, the New Year sees new laws, as California has instituted a waiting period and background check before customers purchase rifles and shotguns. In Florida, the state is barring legislators and approximately 30,000 other public officials from soliciting or accepting any gift over $100 from lobbyists. Maryland and New Hampshire are instituting laws to curb drug possession. The federal government is raising the national gas tax by a nickel.

headline: Punt opposes prison
abstract: State Sen. Terry Punt asked Gov. Robert Casey to withdraw plans to construct an $86 million state prison at South Mountain.

headline: Key Florio aide to step down, head casino panel
abstract: New Jersey Governor Florio's chief of staff, Steven Perskie, is stepping down and will become the chairman of the Casino Control Commission.  Perskie, who helped legalize gambling, will now be faced with attempting to help revitalize the casinos in Atlantic City.

headline: Campaign money; Casey leads
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey has a huge lead in campaign funds over the Republican challenger Barbara Hafer. From May 1st to June 4th Hafer has taken in $118,331 and Casey has raised $402,469, according to the PA State Bureau of Elections. Since the beginning of the race Casey has raised $2,089,818 and Hafer has raised $515,730.

headline: Hafer Stays Upbeat But Long Odds Don't Go Away
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer faces a 40-point deficit in public opinion polls and a $3.7 million deficit to incumbent Robert P. Casey's bankroll to television commercials. Despite these obstacles, Hafer continues her extensive grassroots campaigning.

headline: Professors clash over proposal
abstract: A PA Senate Committee headed by PA Sen. Steward Greenleaf spent much of the day debating legislation introduced by Rep. Jeffrey Coy and passed by the House in march. The product liability legislation would protect the tobacco industry from liability costs which have risen by more than $5 billion in the past three years. The three legal scholars and four layer-members of the Senate Judiciary Committee were accused of turning the matter into an intellectual classroom debate on civil suits.

headline: Council lifts cap on tax abatements
abstract: Councilwoman Joan Specter and Councilman David Cohen were the only two council members who opposed the Council's plan to introduce three years of tax abatements for new homeowners with property values over $70,000. Mayor Goode's administration favored the proposal, as did Councilman John Street, saying the tax abatements were a way to draw people back to Philadelphia. Specter and Cohen, however, said the tax abatements only helped the rich and did nothing to help the poor and middle classes.

headline: Another budget crisis
abstract: The editorial comments on the "budget crisis" in Harrisburg, noting that more than $250 million in payments to human services agencies are being held back, including payments to nursing homes, mental health/retardation programs, children and youth services, and homeless programs. It also criticizes PA Auditor General (and Republican gubernatorial candidate) Barbara Hafer for holding back tax anticipation notes, which would have allowed the state to borrow money against its future collections as it usually does around this time of year.

headline: null
abstract: A federal jury has decided that Armour Pharmaceutical Company of Blue Bell, PA cannot be blamed for infecting a former Bradenton, Florida, boy with AIDS. The lawsuit charged that the boy contracted the disease from blood products manufactured by Armour that were given to him to treat his hemophilia. It's the second time in two months that parents of children with AIDS have lost legal battles against companies that make blood products.

headline: Carnegie closing downtown Pgh. Library
abstract: Despite a $220,000 cash infusion approved by the Pittsburgh city council above the amount recommended by Mayor Sophie Masloff, the Carnegie Library announced it will close its downtown branch until 1993. The library's business branch and reading rooms will be relocated to different facilities for the time being. City and county officials plan to lobby for more money from the state above the $2.5 million for the past fiscal year.

headline: County officials voice frustrations over landfill laws
abstract: Lycoming County commissioners are complaining about costly state solid waste management regulations, which are requiring the construction of a leachate treatment plant at the Lycoming County Landfill, even though the facility is expected to be needed only sporadically.

headline: PUC Approves $18.8 Million Rate Hike For Equitable
abstract: The Public Utility Commission approved a $18.8 million rate increase for Equitable Gas Company that an administrative law judge said may be illegal in part. As part of the agreement, the commission agreed to an $1.8 million energy assistance problem paid for by residential customers that will bill needy customers on their ability to say. Administrative Law Judge Michael Schnierle said such a program would require legislative power of taxation.

headline: Across US, states ring in new laws
abstract: New years day brings into effect many new laws like keeping criminals from buying guns in California, lobbyists from lavishing gifts in Florida, and the federal government raising taxes on cigarettes and alcohol. Indiana is going to cut taxes. Many states are making it harder to get and keep licenses. Maryland is suspending drug user's profession and business licenses. New Hampshire is allowing judges to take drivers licenses away for up to life for people convicted of intent to sell drugs. Many other states are doing similar programs. Other states laws form balloon maintenance to divorce are discussed.

headline: Put the Blame on Owens
abstract: An opinion piece rebuking the proposal of Camp Hill Corrections Commissioner David Owens to recompense inmates for lost property due to the riots at Camp Hill.

headline: Laid off Union Switch Workers get settlement money
abstract: Members of Local 610 of the United Electrical, Radio, and Machine Workers claimed Union Switch & Signal failed to follow proper seniority rules in laying off 77 employees. The claim was upheld by an arbitrator and in a court of federal appeals. To aviod prolonging the appeal process, both sides agreed the company would pay workers 75 percent of the pay they missed and 100 of medical expenses incurred.

headline: Campaign politics add partisan spice to lunch for League of Cities
abstract: A photo depicts PA Community Affairs Secretary Karen Miller and Easton Mayor Sal Panto listening to Barbara Hafer, the state's GOP Candidate for gubernatorial elections.

headline: Hafer sticks to secret plan claim
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer is sticking by her assertion that incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey has a "secret deal" to financially bail out Philadelphia, although she recently appeared to retract her claim. Hafer is using this assertion as an explanation of her refusal, as PA Auditor General, to authorize Casey to borrow $495 million in tax anticipation notes until he assures her in writing that the money would not be used to help Philadelphia. Hafer claims that Casey is hiding millions of dollars in state deficits from the last fiscal year and the current one.

headline: Progress is Challenge
abstract: The editorial board believes that PA Governor Robert P. Casey and local legislators should address environmental, mass transit, budget, tax reform, tourism development and teachers union issues and resolve the Philadelphia fiscal crisis in the next four years. The board supports a hotel occupancy tax in Lackawanna County, recycling and environmental programs to reduce out-of-state garbage, highway construction and a system of arbitration for collective bargaining for teachers.

headline: County must keep ECC goal in focus
abstract: The editorial comments on the decision of Burnham Borough and Derry Township to leave the agreement to establish a county-wide emergency communications center in Mifflin County.  It says that communities in the county need to find a solution to the current emergency dispatching crisis while keeping in mind the goal of a county-wide system.

headline: Area Budget Reflect Excesses Of 'Go-Go' 80s'
abstract: The suburbs around DC, including Montgomery and Fairfax counties, can no longer afford the level of service of during the 1980s. As a reflection of an economic downturn, bloated budgets must be cut. Walter Sheiber, executive director of the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments admitted municipal officials overlooked the longterm picture when budgeting. Education, decreases in federal aid, and costs of public safety and corrections are resulting in budget cuts.

headline: null
abstract: Photograph of an unused building at Wernerville State Hospital which will be reopened as a Berks County home for terminally ill AIDs patients.

headline: Casey announces $14.5 million in higher ed capital projects
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey approved $14.5 million of capital projects at state-owned universities. The projects include funding renovations at West Chester University, overhaul of Cheyney University's electrical system, and improving handicapped access at Bloomsburg University.

headline: Deer Dilemma
abstract: The editors are talking about the excessive deer problem in Crawford County and rural areas of PA. The commonwealth's deer population is about 38% over Game Commission targets and they agree with the PA House passed resolution asking the Game Commission to develop plans to deal with the overpopulation of deer.

headline: PUC Approves 4 Percent Boost for PG&W
abstract: The Public Utility Commission approved a settlement that will allow PA Gas & Water Co. of Wilkes-Barre to add about 4 percent to the typical annual bill. The settlement was signed by the company, the PUC's Office of Trial Staff, and the PA Office of Consumer Advocate. Administrative Law Judge Richard M. Lovenwirth recommended approval of the settlement. Gas utilities are required to filed projected fuel costs six months in advance for PUC review and approval and must show that they are taking steps to keep fuel costs as low as possible.

headline: Activists Say Journalist on Death Row was Framed
abstract: The Partisan Defense Committee, a labor-socialist organization in New York, is saying that Mumia Abu-Jamal’s former membership in the Black Panthers Part was used to convict him in the killing of a Philadelphia police officer. The PA Supreme Court has rejected Jamal’s appeals of his 1982 conviction.

headline: Radio Trial
abstract: A jury has awarded $650,000 to the former news director who sued a Pittsburgh radio station and two disc jockeys who made sexual jokes on the air. Liz Randolph said she suffered from panic attacks because of the jokes.

headline: Law keeps toy ducks afloat. Legislation contains loophole that should cover local race.
abstract: PA legislators passed a bill that may provide a legal loophole to allow betting on the Shenango Valley Chamber of Commerce toy duck race. The bill, sent to PA Governor Robert P. Casey for approval, allows for lotteries or drawings that have passive selection devices. The toy duck race was canceled after Hermitage Police Chief John A. Marriott said it constituted illegal gambling. Several legislators criticized the bill for expanding the gambling industry and giving a "green light" to organized crime.

headline: Campaign politics add partisan spice to lunch for League of Cities
abstract: Unable to attend the PA League of Cities convention in Allentown due to budget negotiations, PA Governor Robert Casey sent State Department of Community Affairs Secretary Karen Miller to plug him for the gubernatorial election. Casey faces PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer, a former Allegheny County Commissioner who favors a tax on gas to cover transportation improvements a separate state budget for education. The convention focused on such issues as recycling and sewage programs.

headline: Hafer sticks to secret plan claim
abstract: Republican gubernatorial challenger Barbara Hafer is sticking by her claim that PA Governor Robert Casey has a "secret deal" bail out the financially floundering Philadelphia government after the general election in November. Hafer made this claim in a letter to school superintendents, school board presidents and university heads explaining why she is preventing Casey from borrowing $475 in tax anticipation notes. As Auditor General, her signature is required in order to borrow the money, but she wants Casey to promise that the money will not be used to help Philadelphia.  Casey's Press Secretary, Vince Carocci said that the idea of a "secret plan" is ridiculous and untrue.

headline: Prosecutors Outline Case They Plan Against Ex-Union Boss Earl Stout
abstract: Federal prosecutors outline their case with multiple charges against influential and controversial former Philadelphia union boss Earl Stout.

headline: County sees 1991 budget as austere
abstract: Northhampton County in PA has $1 million in federal funds that allowed the County Executive Gerald Seyfried to lift the hiring freeze in departments of government. Several jobs in the county's processing center for drunken drivers, 4 counseling jobs in the county prison, and 3 child support secretaries can now be hired. There is a halt on creation of new positions and purchases of new equipment for 1991, which will affect the 1992 budget.

headline: Barbara Hafer proposes separate budget for education
abstract: Barbara Hafer, Republican gubernatorial candidate, proposed creating a special budget for education. She has said she would not rule out raising taxes because she thinks education should be a priority. Hafer criticized PA Governor Robert P. Casey for not providing enough money  for education and forcing property owners to make up the difference.

headline: null
abstract: The director of Godspeed House, a charity for AIDS patients, said she will move two tenants from a West View duplex to a new shelter home at an undisclosed location. The decision came after the Borough Council denied Director Kathleen Coyne a permit to operate an institutional home in a residential neighborhood.

headline: Casey praises Vann excellence
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey visited the all-black Robert L. Vann Elementary School where students routinely outperform pupils district wide in reading and math exams, even though they are mostly poor and many from split families. Casey said it was one of the best public schools in the nation. The success is credited to the practice of only letting students advance after they have mastered lower-level material.

headline: DER assailed on wetlands program
abstract: State Rep. George Hasay will try introducing an amendment to an unrelated bill to transfer the regulation of wetlands from the PA Department of Environmental Resources to the Department of Agriculture. An official from the State College US Fish and Wildlife Service's office, Edward Perry, says the transfer will cause the US Environmental Protection Agency to step in. Debbi Tingley of the PA Builders Association is unhappy with the DER, as is John Bell of the PA Farmers Association.

headline: PUC Awaiting Expiration Of PG&W Sale Agreement
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission decided to keep its hands off the deal between Pennsylvania Gas & Water Co. and United Water Resources. PG&W originally planned to sell its water company to UWR and its gas company to NUI, however UWR backed out of the deal when Goldman Sachs failed to find the deal in the best interest of stockholders. NUI has agreed to buy both PG&W's gas and water companies, however all parties involved must wait for the original agreement to expire on Saturday.

headline: Agents Posing as Car Dealers Nab Theft Suspects
abstract: Undercover agents pose das car dealers and recovered stolen cars worth about 41.3 million in what Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. Called the largest stolen-vehicle sting operation in PA history. Preate said that several vehicle sales led to undercover drug sales to agents of the Bureau of Narcotics Investigation. Arrest warrants, most of them charging auto theft and receiving stolen property, were issued for 34 people.

headline: Receives check
abstract: A photo shows Dr. Cataldo F. Corrado of the Fayette County Emergency Management Services Council accepting a check presented by PA Reps. Richard Kasuni, Fred Taylor and William DeWeese. The funds will be use for the purchase of equipment and training seminars for county ambulance and firefighting personnel as well as rescue technicians and law enforcement officials.

headline: Lawmakers move against rebellious insurance firms
abstract: PA Senate and House Democrats introduced bills to fight insurance companies currently threatening to leave the state as a result of the new insurance law. The Senate bill is sponsored by Eugene F. Scanlon and Robert Mellow, while the House bill is sponsored by Mike Veon, who stated that the House and Senate are determining which version will best deal with the problem. Under the proposals, companies currently selling insurance in PA would have to submit an application to the state insurance commissioner, complete with a timetable for withdrawal. Although many insurance companies are complying with the law, seven have refused and are being taken to Commonwealth Court by the state.

headline: Campaign-reform dawdling
abstract: Now that Charles Keating Jr. is no longer a daily news item so is talk of a US Senate compromise on campaign finance reform. Keating made large donations and then asked for intercession with federal regulators n behalf of his failing savings and loan company. Now that the public upset over this died down the parties have returned to their polarized positions. The editorial board outlines what they would like to see in campaign reform.

headline: Hafer struggles to overcome rocky start; convinced of win
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer got off to a difficult start in her campaign, and now lies 40 points statewide behind incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey.  However, Hafer is convinced that she will be able to close the gap and perhaps even win the election.

headline: Public defender vies for Gates' seat
abstract: PA Assistant Public Defender Joseph Mesics is a new attorney considering a candidacy for the vacant seat left by retiring Lebanon County Thomas Gates. He is considered an acceptable choice to both parties. He worked in the district attorney's office from 1968 to 1969 and was the county's public defender from 1970 to 1982. In 1988 he returned to Lebanon County to serve as assistant public defender.

headline: Cranberry: No tax hike but sewage rate to rise
abstract: There will be no property tax increase for Cranberry Township residents in 1991.The budget maintains all of the township's current programs and calls for anticipated increases in expenditures for oil, gasoline, and tires. There are decreases in highway construction and rebuilding.

headline: Casey gets tough on budget surplus
abstract: Editorial agrees with PA Governor Casey's demand that the PA General Assembly return its $80 million surplus to the state treasury and justify future budget requests. The governor is completely in line to keep spending in line with incoming revenue. Until this year the judiciary justified their budgets, but this year it asked for a lump sum just like congress. The editorial believes this should stop.

headline: 5 state mental patients sue over confinement
abstract: Five mental health patients who are confined to a maximum-security building at Norristown State Hospital filed a suit in federal court, contending that the state is keeping them in a prison-like setting unnecessarily. They ask to either be moved to a less restrictive unit in the same hospital or released into he community and treated from there. Three of the five were initially assigned to the unit after being charged for a crime, but their status has changed since but not their placement.

headline: Casey signs Boot-Camp Bill, Others
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey signed bills inlcuding legislative alternatives to prison sentencing, specifically military-style boot camp. Other legislation includes allowances for municipalities to pass on impact fees to developers and for families caring for elderly to receive state assistance. In addition, the state Department of Education must ensure high school students receive drug and alcohol education.

headline: DER falls down on the job in Berwick
abstract: Editorial blames PA Department of Environmental Resources for Berwick's sewage. They issued a permit that allowed Berwick to construct a plant using an unproven design, even though DER as it admits doubted it would work. It has now become expensive. The design cost itself $2 million and it has drawn a fine from the US Environmental Protection Agency for $98,000. Now the DER is point fingers all around, but issued a permit.

headline: PUC chief confirms he's stepping down
abstract: Bill Shane confirmed yesterday that he will resign as chairman of the PA Public Utility Commission. Speculation on where he will go from here will be settled when he gives details tomorrow at a news conference. It is likely he will go into private practice as a lawyer.

headline: Aid to counties coming
abstract: Michael H. Hershock, budget secretary for PA Governor Robert Casey, writes about a May 24 article which he states left an "inaccurate impression about the governor's position on reimbursements for county prosecution" of inmates at the recent disturbances at Camp Hill and Huntingdon state prisons. Casey will in fact provide reimbursements once the costs have actually been set. Hershock also asserts that the article's author included an unfair criticism from the Senate Republicans' general counsel about the reimbursements.

headline: Recording industry unveils new warning-label system
abstract: The recording industry has unveiled new warning labels that will be on the lower right hand corner of albums dealing with sex, violence, suicide, drug abuse, bigotry or satanic worship.   As a result of this decision, PA Representative Ron Gamble D-Allegheny will withdraw his proposal to require warning labels on objectionable record albums.

headline: Lawmakers move against rebellious insurance firms
abstract: PA Senate and House Democrats introduced bills to fight insurance companies currently threatening to leave the state as a result of the new insurance law. The Senate bill is sponsored by Eugene F. Scanlon and Robert Mellow, while the House bill is sponsored by Mike Veon, who stated that the House and Senate are determining which version will best deal with the problem. Under the proposals, companies currently selling insurance in PA would have to submit an application to the state insurance commissioner, complete with a timetable for withdrawal. Although many insurance companies are complying with the law, seven have refused and are being taken to Commonwealth Court by the state.

headline: Campaigns ignoring finance law requirement
abstract: Both of PA's two gubernatorial candidates, PA Governor Robert Casey and Republican challenger Barbara Hafer, have not been fully complying with the state's campaign finance laws by not collecting the occupational information of donors giving more than $250.  Each campaign lacks the information for about a third of such donors, and each says that they are in progress of getting the information.

headline: Hafer talks about area incinerator, hopes
abstract: Hafer spoke about the proposed incinerator for Union County, and other concerns, while at a Union County Republican Committee picnic.

headline: Putting on the squeeze
abstract: With costs piling up for Persian Gulf military actions, the US government is looking to get other nations to support the actions.  Japan is one of the chief targets for involvement, though its long-standing isolationist tendencies will have to be broken through.

headline: Credit rating plunges
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode cites City Council's refusal to approve taxes to counteract a budget deficit as the reason for Standard & Poor's reduction of the city's credit rating. Hyman C. Grossman, S&P managing director, cites the city's $2.1 billion budget, which does not account for ongoing arbitration with police and firefighting forces, nor a possible refund of the real estate transfer tax, nor the consideration of the city's proposed .5 sales tax increase by the PA Legislature until after the gubernatorial election, as reasons for the decrease in ratings.

headline: Budget accord is nearer
abstract: PA Governor Casey is expected to continue refusing to use Rainy Day Funds to balance the budget. If Budget Secretary Michael Hershock and leaders of the party caucuses cannot come to an agreement by midnight tomorrow, the state technically loses its ability to spend. A major obstacle in negotiations has been the issue of education spending. PA Governor Casey has proposed withholding money for special education programs until the end of the fiscal year, when districts would be reimbursed. Casey has made budget cuts during the past few days of negotiations.

headline: A painful wait. State lags in head-injury funding promised 6 years ago.
abstract: Though Governor Dick Thornburgh signed a law creating the Commonwealth Head Injury Program in 1985, more than $7 million in funding still remains unspent in state bank accounts. The Health Department recently completed regulations to guide the program, but they still must go through a potentially lengthy review process. Executive Director of the House and Welfare Committee Mary Ellen McMillen says numerous senator and House member have been pushing PA Governor Robert P. Casey to spend the money that has been allocated in accordance with the law.

headline: Casey Still Strong on Schools
abstract: Governor Casey assured teachers of increased education spending and the high priority of education in his second term in office, stating the progress he wants made in Pennsylvania schools.

headline: DER hands area firm a setback in bid to open 59-acre landfill
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources denied an application by the New Hanover Corporation to build a landfill in New Hanover Township. Township manager Anita Jogn expressed her approval of the DER's decision. Township residents had been fighting the proposed landfill for 3 years, and formed an activist group in the process, the Paradise Watchdogs.

headline: PUC To Analyze Peoples Gas Rate Hike Request
abstract: Faced with numerous complaints, the Public Utility Commission rejected a proposal by Peoples Natural Gas Company to increase gas rates for residential ustomers to meet higher operating costs.

headline: An Adoption Awareness
abstract: Mandates for adoption instruction, along with fostering awareness of unplanned pregnancy prevention, in public schools is Representative Thomas Tangretti's new concept in the abortion debate.

headline: Reform of state judicial system urged
abstract: Three citizens groups; Common Cause, the League of Women Voters and the Young Attorneys Association of the PA Bar Association; urged certain constitutional amendments be made to reform the PA’s judicial system. The bills they support call for the adoption of the merit system to appoint judges and the installation of a strong judicial disciplinary system. The bills are on the current PA House calendar.

headline: Lawyers, Doctors Argue Auto Insurance Law Unfairly Targets Them
abstract: Under a new auto insurance reform law, New Jersey lawyers, medical professionals and auto body shops are charged a $100-a-year fee, and motorists are charged increased registration fees to help pay state debt. The state says that these professions were ordered to pay because they benefit from auto accidents. Attorneys for the New Jersey Bar Association, the Medical Society of New Jersey and the Osteopathic Society of New Jersey charged in court that the law constitutes an unfair tax.

headline: Canceled lease
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has rejected a 29-year, $60 million lease on a new home for Commonwealth Court proposed to be built at Fifth and Walnut streets, across from the Forum. They gave no reason for the rejection. The editorial demands they give an explanation.

headline: Hafer threatens to hold up funds
abstract: PA Auditor General and Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer is refusing to sign off on $475 million in bonds that incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey wants to sell in order to make payments to school districts next week. Hafer wants Casey to provide written assurance that the money will not be used to help bail out the financially strapped Philadelphia, and for him to admit to creating a $190 million deficit in the state, which Casey denies exists.

headline: Putting on the squeeze
abstract: With costs piling up for Persian Gulf military actions, the US government is looking to get other nations to support the actions.  Japan is one of the chief targets for involvement, though its long-standing isolationist tendencies will have to be broken through.

headline: Cumberland official alleges favoritism
abstract: County Controller Alfred Whitcomb alleged yesterday that recent promotions were made based on favoritism rather than merit, and that Cumberland County Commissioners failed to adopt a payroll and wage system which would save the county money in the long run. Commissioner Chairman Robert Moore dismissed Whitcomb's allegations, saying the promotions were made based on recommendations by department heads and the late nature of Whitcomb's payroll system proposal.

headline: Court System Still Flawed
abstract: In response to the resignation of Edmund Spaeth, chairman of Pennsylvania's Judicial Inquiry and Review Board, Governor Robert P. Casey urged the General Assembly to reform the system for disciplining judges.  Casey's support comes as bills to overhaul the process of investigating and punishing judicial misconduct have stalled in the state House.  Although Casey supports general reforms, he is noncommital on one of the important issues stalling reform legislation--a proposal to replace the election of appellate judges with gubenatorial appointments.

headline: Budget and Population Growth
abstract: A table of bar graphs shows the operating budgets for area jurisdictions in 1981 and then in 1991 in millions, for counties around the DC area. Bar graphs also show the populations for each area of jurisdiction in the years 1980 and 1990. Population figures are according to US Census Bureau statistics.

headline: A reorganized system for paying asbestos victims
abstract: The Manville trust fund will make staggered payments to victims of asbestos diseases based on severity of illness under a tentative settlement of tens of thousands of claims, lawyers said yesterday. The deal would have to be approved by U.S. District Judge Jack B. Weinstein, who earlier this year ordered the Manville trust overhauled after it ran out of cash to pay new claims. The plan replaces a highly criticized system under which claims were processed based on time of filling, not severity of illness.

headline: Chesapeake Region School Bosses Leaving
abstract: Montgomery County School Superintendent Harry Pitt rejected an offer by the PA Board of Education to remain for another 4 year term. Instead, Pitt plans to retire after presideing over one of the nation's biggest, best-regarded and most diverse school systems. Over the next five years, the district is expected to see a 25 percent increase in enrollment.

headline: DER heads to court in effort to force dump authority to get its act together
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources filed a petition with Commonwealth Court to force the West Side Landfill Authority to meet with the DER. Ed Shoener, director for environmental protection, stated that the petition was not meant to be punitive, but to get all parties involved to negotiate. The DER mentioned a number of municipalities in its action which are clients of the landfill, including Courtdale, Edwardsville, Forty Fort and Luzerne. The DER brought about the court action to have the authority stabilize its landfill facility by removing leachate from a local landfill nicknamed "Mount Trashmore."

headline: Rep. George: Energy for the '90s and beyond
abstract: PA State Rep. Camille George, of the join PA House-Senate Committee on Air, Water and Pollution Control, has an important message--don't forget the oil crisis of the seventies! Though the Federal government could be doing more to promote and mandate the use of renewable energy, PA has a lot to gain by promoting clean coal technology and revitalizing the coal industry. At the same time, more should also be done to promote such technologies as solar power and wind power.

headline: Appeals Court Affirms NJ Businessman's Conviction
abstract: The 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals denied a convicted New Jersey businessman his appeal.

headline: Relatives of Police Say System of Hiring is Stacked Against Them
abstract: Ten applicants sued the Philadelphia Police Department claiming rejection due to discrimination against relatives of current or former officers.

headline: Legislators want to keep off-track betting out of county
abstract: Local legislators spoke out against the idea of an off-track betting parlor proposed for Lancaster County.  There are no rules or laws against such an establishment.

headline: Candidate gets little attention
abstract: Chuck and Cindy Gough of Somerset lament the little media attention being given to Republican gubernatorial candidate Peg Luksik. Luksik has established an international network of facilities to help single mothers, and is the co-founder of the statewide Parents Commission. The Goughs feel that Luksik is the best candidate for governor of PA.

headline: Hafer to begin TV ads next week
abstract: Republican candidate for PA governor, Barbara Hafer, expects to begin running television ads next week, and will buy as much air time as her money will allow in all six media markets, including the expensive Philadelphia market, where she expects to fare well with her economy-focused ads due to the fiscal crisis in the city. Incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey has already been running ads throughout the state, spending $500,000 a week. Hafer will run 2 ads focusing on the state's fiscal problems and 1 on abortion.

headline: Quotelines
abstract: Quotes from the Mayor of Martinsburg, West Virginia, Tony Senecal, and Mayor Sue Myrick of Charlotte, North Carolina, are listed along with a quote from Tony Reinis of the California Homeless Coalition, and Nancy Nagler, an advocate for the homeless.

headline: Democrats Left Off Tax Debt List
abstract: The Democratic City Committee was not on the initial list of Philadelphia's top twenty tax-delinquent properties and owners.
