headline: Workers at group homes strike; some clients moved
abstract: Group Home workers from the Institute of Human Resources and Services went on strike Saturday, forcing 13 of the institutes' handicapped patients to move home with their families or to other facilities.  The strike affects roughly 39 mentally or physically-handicapped patients in 12 group homes throughout Luzerne County.  Luzerne County human service officials say they will assist the institute if it cannot provide care during the strike.

headline: Budget bills to raise taxes, reform tax system introduced in Legislature
abstract: New Jersey governor Jim Florio's budget plan is being examined in the PA Legislature in a series of 15 bills. Florio hopes his plan will raise over $2 billion in new taxes and reduce the state's reliance on property taxes. The bills include provisions to increase the sales and income taxes, as well as provisions for public school funding.

headline: A setback in battle against TB
abstract: Tuberculosis cases are on the rise, especially among the nation’s homeless population. PA health officials researched the disease after a school custodian died of TB in Marple Township and the PA Health Department has stated that the disease can develop anywhere. However, in PA the disease has decreased from 738 to 710 cases, but the state is not exempt from the national trend of the disease being on the rise.

headline: City district mulls year-round school
abstract: The York City School District is considering year-round education as an alternative to deal with enrollment projection. A team of 30 teachers, non-instructional staff and school board members is studying the possibility of staggering students' education in order that more students may use the school building during the calender year. The school board will vote tomorrow night on sending representatives to the National Association for Year Round School annual conference in San Diego.

headline: DER investigating Penn State fish kill
abstract: About 150 have died as a result of an accident at Penn State University, where chlorinated water from a pool drained into stream waters instead of the treatment facility.  Both the PA Department of Environmental Resources and the state Fish Commission are looking into the incident.

headline: Report on Heating Oil Notes Low Inventories
abstract: The considerable increase in home heating oil prices in December is likely to have been caused by low inventories and speculative trading.

headline: Arkansas to be the 14th State to Execute an Inmate
abstract: John Edward Swindler will be the first inmate to be put to death in Arkansas sine 1964 and joins thirteen other states in carrying out the death penalty. Swindler is being put to death for the killing of Randy Basnett, a Fort Smith police officer, in September of 1976.

headline: Rent-a-trooper bill meets opposition from state police
abstract: A bill that would authorizing the hiring and training of up to 50 new state troopers for contractual assignment to municipalities awaits PA Governor Robert P. Casey's approval. While legislators and some local officials approve, state police press secretary Thomas C. Lyon said the PA State Police do not support the bill as written. John G. Brown of the PA State Association of Township Supervisors said it would allow municipalities better police coverage without administrative hassle.

headline: Legislature Ends Two-year Session This Week
abstract: The PA legislative session will end this week, leaving lawmakers scrambling to pass bills and send them to PA Governor Robert P. Casey. Legislation not approved before the end of the session must be introduced again next year. The Senate will consider legislation allowing municipalities to impose fees on developers, allowing video-poker gambling, adding 24 judges to county courts and providing $290,000 for a study of high-speed trains.

headline: Candidate Hafer Visits Franklin
abstract: Gubernatorial Candidate PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer criticizes PA Governor Casey for a budget deficit, compared to the surplus left by Governor Dick Thornburgh and accuses him of misleading voters about the budget. Hafer spoke at a luncheon sponsored by the Franklin Area Chamber of Commerce. Hafer won the Republican primary against Margueite Luksik. Her pro-choice stand has proved troubling in the campaign. Hafer favors a several cent gas tax for road improvements.

headline: Hafer Undeterred By Polls
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer said she was undeterred by results showing PA Governor Robert P. Casey held a 40 percent lead in popular support polls. Hafer believes the polls aren't representative because they were taken only shortly after her recent television ads appeared. On the campaign trail, Hafer continued to attack the Casey administrations' fiscal mismanagement and his pro-life stance.

headline: Quotients
abstract: A list of quotes about taxes in California

headline: Don't blame Mayor Goode
abstract: The letters emphasizes that Philadelphia's current troubles aren't Mayor Goode's fault, and that in fact, Goode has done fairly well for the city during his term.

headline: Arrive Alive
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Police announced that they will set up mobile sobriety checkpoints at 105 drunk-driving hot spots across the state.  The sobriety checkpoints catch drunk drivers and also provide a deterrent effect.  In 1987, the PA Supreme Court affirmed a 1985 law that created checkpoints.

headline: Budget blues
abstract: PA state tax revenues for the fiscal year are running $47 million below estimates, and the collection from September was $4 million less the estimate, according to the Casey administration.  Some Republicans say that the state will eventually face a $1 billion deficit.

headline: ACLU Charges Discrimination; Some Deny It
abstract: AIDS activists say that dentists are continuing to refuse treatment to AIDS-infected patients despite guidelines against such discrimination.  Several dentists under scrutiny for such practices are denying that the infection was the reason for their rejection of the patient.

headline: City school budget rises, but not taxes
abstract: The city school district's budget is $500,000 higher than last month's proposal, but taxes remain at the status quo. Executive director of business affairs for the school board, Aldo Colautti detailed the additional expenditures raising the budget, among them an expanded Head Start program, dues to the Alliance for School Restructuring, and insurance. The funds were earmarked for students who failed the Testing for Essential Learning and Literacy, however the Legislature failed to mandate spending to raise scores.

headline: DER looks into Newberry Township chemical dump site
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources is about to begin inspection of a supposed hazardous waste site in Newberry Township. The site is owned by Industrial Solvents and Chemical Company is charged with violating the state's solid waste management law. Industrial Solvents' owner, Andrew Rawicz, a former chairman of the York Area Chamber of Commerce, is being charged with storing hazardous waste at sites in Newberry Township and Emigsville.

headline: Residents return to homes as coal mine fire sealed off
abstract: Crews have finished sealing off a Washington County coal mine fire, cutting off its air supply so that it will eventually burn itself out, so that hundreds of residents were able to return to their homes. Residents were evacuated because of high carbon monoxide levels and the danger of being too close to the mine while the status of the fire was still unknown. A mine official said that the fire could take 6 to 9 months to burn out, leaving 400 miners out of work for its duration.

headline: Audit finds some problems with crime victims' fund
abstract: An audit by the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee reported that the Crime Victims Compensation Board faces a financial crisis and will likely run out of operating funds before the fiscal year ends. The report urged the board to seek supplemental funds and to improve its budget-request procedure. Members of PA Governor Robert P. Casey's budget office said the office was unaware of any problems. At a recent hearing, the board's counsel, Judith Schimmel, said officials were having trouble collecting a fee from criminal defendants in Philadelphia, where routine cases often are settled out of court.

headline: Replanting the seeds of disorder
abstract: The editorial points out that now, a year after violent riots at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill, the situation looks like one that could breed another such event. Because of overcrowding and vicious treatment of the prisoners by guards, whether the prisoners were involved in the riots or not, could threaten to incite prisoners again.

headline: Let's fine insurers defying law
abstract: After nearly two weeks, there are still a number of insurance companies that have not filed reduced automobile insurance rates with the state. Some are awaiting court decisions on appeals of the new law, which mandates that each company file 10 percent rate reductions for each policyholder and 22 percent reductions for those who would waive their right to sue for pain and suffering. The editorial says that the companies should stop pouting and comply.

headline: Capital rumor mill grinds on about raise for lawmakers
abstract: Columnist Larry Hicks comments on the prospect of legislators in PA giving themselves a pay raise after the November 6th elections, saying that it's inappropriate, since only a few years ago the salary went up, and that the current $47,000 plus benefits is more than enough, particularly for a part-time job, as most legislators are not always in Harrisburg and the General Assembly has several recesses.

headline: Hafer uses air time she fought for to blast Gov. Casey
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer used her first radio address to malign PA Governor Casey for "fiscal gimmickry."  Casey used this week's address to talk about the "New Directions" program which provides social services.

headline: Race Features Rematch
abstract: In a rematch, Democrat Dai Williams will be challenging incumbent Republican Senator Joe Loeper in the election this November.

headline: Ex-Eagle Delinquent on Property Tax
abstract: Former Philadelphia Eagle Wilbert Montgomery owes the city $16,823 in property taxes.

headline: How serious is the drug problem in the Poconos?
abstract: This article gets the opinions of 3 students, one local resident, and one teacher on the issue of drug abuse in Pocono schools.  Most of the students and teachers agree that drugs are a serious problem in Pocono schools.  In fact, an elementary school teacher says her third graders tell her they're hearing about drugs on the school bus.

headline: Budget deadline closing in
abstract: PA lawmakers are getting ready to work on the state budget that is usually controversial and will continue their closed-door budget meetings. The legislature has to reconcile over the $12.3 billion spending plan that PA Governor Robert P. Casey proposed. The major stumbling blocks are whether to dip into the $126 million Rainy Day Fun and what to do about the $84 million debt owed to public schools. Casey maintains, despite a $226 million shortfall in revenue collection, that the state will end the fiscal year with a balanced budget.

headline: Administrator, nursing director get probation in Manor case
abstract: The administrator and director of nursing of the defunct State College Manor Nursing Home were sentenced to probation after pleading no contest to the charges they ignored reports of elderly abuse at the home. John Fabrizio and Eleanor Kraft were each sentenced in centre county Court to four years probation, $1,000 in fines and 400 hours of community service.

headline: City schools could lose aid if audit is upheld
abstract: Pittsburgh city schools discounted a report by PA Audit General Barbara Hafer and the PA Department of Education alleging the schools employed teachers without proper certification and assigned them to cover material for which they were not certified. The schools maintain the audit reveals paperwork errors. Superintendent Richard Wallace found it distasteful that results were released before the district could reply. Board President Barbara Burns and President of the Pittsburgh Federation of Teachers Al Fondy say teachers are certified.

headline: DER Not Happy With Groundwater Monitoring System at Pl. Valley
abstract: The State Department of Environmental Resources wants another well dug at the new Pleasant Valley Middle Shool because it disapproves of the current spray irrigation groundwater-monitoring system.  However, the school is reluctant to oblige due to the permit the DER mistakenly issued them.

headline: Simulated accident to test preparedness at Peach Bottom
abstract: A simulated accident is scheduled for the Peach Bottom Atomic Power Station in southern York County in order to test the readiness of Philadelphia Electric Co. and local and state agencies.

headline: Bankrupt criminals relieve of restitution
abstract: The US Supreme Court upheld a decision by the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals which would allowed convicted criminals to avoid making restitutions to their victims. The provision, known as Chapter 13 bankruptcy, was the basis for the Circuit Court's ruling in the case of Edward and Debora Davenport of Bucks County, who pleaded guilty to welfare fraud. The National Association of Attorneys General is considering drafting legislation to amend the bankruptcy law.

headline: Report: Drug Arrests Don't Tell Full Story
abstract: Funds earmarked for the war on drugs and drug education programs run out at the end of June. The programs are funded under Pennfree, designated by the PA Legislative Budget and Finance Committee. The Committee called for Governor Casey and Attorney General Ernie Preateto adopt an agreement for forml cooperation between Attorney General and state police drug probes. Plans are underway to persuade Philadelphia authorities to sign a cooperative agreement with the state as well.

headline: Local patron of arts held in NY scam
abstract: A Montgomery County man, Richard Scholl, who emerged as a patron of the arts in the Philadelphia area over the last four years was arrested at his Wyndmoor home  on charges that he helped orchestrate a $15.2 million insurance scam while working for a New York insurance company.

headline: Carefully taught for what?
abstract: The collection of individuals who got the Three Rivers Art Festival  hunky sanded off the hemline of the steelworker statue in Point State Park was a lynch mob. The opinion piece disapproves of the actions of Tom Flaherty, the Pittsburgh city controller, who has a nose for the trivial and divisive. The union members add to the drama when they made it clear they were upset with he festival committee.

headline: Hafer wants audit on Philadelphia aid
abstract: PA Auditor General and Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer said that she will do a "compliance audit" of the PA Department of Community Affairs to find out why the Casey administration refuses to declare Philadelphia, which is in a severe financial crisis, a "financially distressed municipality."  The law establishing this designation was passed primarily to aid western PA municipalities, and it excludes Pittsburgh and Philadelphia from receiving any financial help.

headline: Rainbow Kitchen director has quit
abstract: Rainbow Kitchen director Bob Anderson has resigned from the organization, saying the he achieved his goals with the Kitchen and wanted to move on and write, study, travel, and continue his political activism elsewhere.

headline: Give state something to do
abstract: Lawrence County commissioners are crying the blues like most other county commissioners over increased spending. One third of the state's counties were at their legal tax limit when they began working on their 1991 budgets. Lawrence County is having to focus on whether or not to raise property taxes. The author believes they should to reflect today's market values and generate more revenue. He also suggests the state should take over some of the county's burden.

headline: Casey Announces Allocation for Summer Job Programs
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Robert P. Casey announced the allocation of more than 27 million dollars in federal funds for summer job programs for economically disadvantaged children.  The summer-job program helps get youths involved in public-service projects and provides an opportunity for service, work and remedial learning for approximately 25,000 Pennsylvanians.

headline: Budget Gap Grows Larger in New Jersey. $600 Million Shortfall Prompts Hiring Freeze.
abstract: Five months after enacting the largest tax increase in New Jersey history, Governor Jim Florio announced a budget shortfall of more than $600 million. PA Treasurer Douglas C. Berman said the state was ordering an immediate freeze on hiring and major building projects while it develops plans for likely layoffs and the possible dismantling of 19 government departments. Berman said the state would not raise taxes.

headline: AFL-CIO pushes for socialized medicine
abstract: William George, president of the Pennsylvania AFL-CIO, PA's largest labor union, said that a national health-care program should be established to guarantee coverage for all Americans.  Some critics of the system argue that such a program would cut back on the availability of health-care.

headline: City schools may solicit private financial help
abstract: The Pittsburgh Public Schools System is conducting a confidential survey of corporate leaders and wealthy individuals to determine whether $15 million could be raised be raised from the private sector to fund programs designed for at-risk and disadvantaged students.

headline: DER orders Pine Grove to correct water problems
abstract: The PA state Department of Environmental Resources has ordered that the Pine Grove borough develop a plan to rectify its drinking water system deficiencies within 60 days. James Resslet, the sanitation supervisor for DER’s Pottsville office, issued the order and that the order comes from a problem the agency uncovered in the borough’s drinking water system. The plan has to rectify the contamination and should provide for continuous filtration and disinfection of water. If the borough does not do this then the reservoirs must be disconnected from the system by August 1993.

headline: Singel Praises Wayne County Energy-Efficiency Program
abstract: PA Liutenant Governor Mark Singel praised a $250,000 state grant to Wayne County for its energy-efficiency plan, one of the first in the state.  The ambitious plan could lead other counties to follow suit and make government buildings more energy efficient.

headline: Battered Woman Ohio
abstract: A woman arrested in Dayton, Ohio for killing her husband will use the newly approved 'battered-woman-syndrome' as her defense in court. Though given the chance to plead guilty to voluntary manslaughter, Joyce and her lawyer, Bobby Joe Cox will take their chances in a trial by jury. Ohio Governor Richard Celeste recently granted clemency to 25 women convicted of killing their husbands.

headline: Road Checks: Where the Police Put Drunken Drivers to the Test
abstract: A photo depicts two police officers conducting a sobriety checkpoint after the US Supreme Court upheld their constitutionality.

headline: Looking to the RTC for work
abstract: The federal government's sale of billions of dollars of property once owned by now defunct savings and loans is the world's biggest land sale: 36,000 properties are listed. It basically the only game in town for realty with the current slump. Some properties will be sold at auctions and others will be first come first serve.

headline: Carter is honored for his activism
abstract: Former President Jimmy Carter received the Philadelphia Liberty Medal as the world citizen who has contributed the most to those values of freedom celebrated on the Fourth of July. He said Americans should be proud of their record on human rights, but they should be more compassionate to the homeless. The Carter Center in Atlanta is where he bases his work and specializes in conflict resolution. He has donated the $100,000 prize that comes with the medal to the center.

headline: Hafer wants to abolish 13 LCB jobs
abstract: Auditor General Barbara Hafer called on her election opponent PA Governor Casey to support a bill to abolish 13 unneeded positions on the Liquor Control Board that cost the state considerable amount of money.  A Casey spokesman seemed supportive of the idea.

headline: Ranks of lobbyists growing; most states lack oversight
abstract: A report on lobbying reveals loopholes in PA laws. PA registered lobbyists reported spending only $362,000. Smaller states had higher reports, and in California, the figure was $90 million. PA Rep. Allen Kukovich believes lobbyists have too much money. Florida Senator Tom Brown referred to campaign contributions as bribes. The growth in the number of lobbyists comes as the US Congress is shifting more responsibility to state and local governments.

headline: Give state something to do
abstract: The editorial board suggests PA run programs it mandated for counties, as its tax base is larger. Lawrence County Commissioners are complaining about their budget, forced to raise property taxes to only one mill below the legal limit of six. The board notes if the commissioners conducted a property reassessment they would not be in a bind for revenue. Commissioner Chairman Elizabeth Verterano estimated PA mandated children's services programs cost the county a 2.5 mills increase in 2 years.

headline: Exodus Continues
abstract: Fanny Farmer Candy Shop will close its South Main Street Store in Wilkes Barre by the end of April--maikng it one of seven stores that has closed in downtown Wilkes Barre since January.  In an effort to save downtown merchants, a group of store owners is putting together a new merchant's association to coordinate promotions and organize activities downtown.

headline: Budget reveals new priories
abstract: PA Governor Casey's strategy for the three E's economy, education and environment are reflected in his budget. It was increased, but with the recession it has been scaled back. New priorities has arisen and taken their place like juvenile crime and prison overcrowding.

headline: AIDS spread rises in some groups
abstract: Des Jarlais, a collaborator with the National Research Council of the National Academy of Science which recently released "AIDS: The Second Decade," notes AIDS is slowing among older gay men, but soaring among teens, women, crack addicts and heavy drinkers. President of the International AIDS Society which picks the site for the annual International Conference on AIDS, announced neither the US nor any country which bars persons with AIDS from entering, will be host to future International Conferences on AIDS.

headline: City schools off to solid start
abstract: School in Harrisburg began on schedule yesterday despite talks of teacher strikes, which were in part headed off by new superintendent Randolph Outen.

headline: DER says Falcon Oil Co. responsible for gasoline spill cleanup
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources has decided that the Falcon Oil Co. will be totally responsible for the environmental cleanup following the crash of a gasoline tanker in Pittston Twp. which dumped about 8,000 gallons of gas into nearby Collins Creek.

headline: Singel: Wean Pennsylvania From Foreign Oil
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel says the state Energy Office will use nearly $12 million to reduce PA's dependence on foreign oil by researching alternative fuels, converting state-owned buildings from oil use,  recycling motor oil, and ensuring that hospitals, colleges, and schools are energy efficient.

headline: Bear Brigade
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey's wife, Ellen Casey, is photographed with Hug-a-Bears made by members of Telephone Pioneers of America. The bears were given to state police to use to calm down child victims in traffic accidents and crimes.

headline: Routine Flyover Yields Marijuana Crop
abstract: The PA State Police on a routine drug hunt found 1,000 marijuana plants from a helicopter in northern Centre County woods. Police say that the remoteness of the area makes tracking down the growers difficult, so they have made no arrests.

headline: Ludlum advances schedule for step-saving steel caster
abstract: Allegheny Ludlum Corporation and an Austrian partner have speeded up their timetable to install a newly developed technology that will revolutionize the steelmaking process. The technology eliminates the need to make semi-finished steel products and turns molten steel directly into strips and sheets.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Cartoon of PA Attorney General Barbara Hafer woken up in bed by Peg Luksik saying "How'd ya do in Lancaster County?"

headline: Hafer, other GOP candidates meet with Bush, answer tax questions
abstract: Fourteen Republican gubernatorial candidates from across the country, including PA’s Barbara Hafer, met with President George Bush during the same week that Bush took back his “no-new-taxes” pledge. Hafer maintained that she and Bush talked about PA’s problems (in education and transportation), and not federal taxes. The PA Governor Robert P. Casey’s re-election committee took Hafer to task for saying the trip was about meeting with Bush to discuss her education plan.

headline: Reapportionment Guided by Fairness Mechanism
abstract: A new feature of the reapportionment of election districts for the federal Census includes information on each block, allowing precise mathematics to help with the redistricting.

headline: Goode: Ads Got City $3M In Back Taxes
abstract: Philadelphia has gotten over $3 million in back taxes by publishing the names of people who owe taxes in the newspaper as part of the larger Special Tax Enforcement Program.  The majority of top offenders are major local businesses.

headline: Hafer faults Bush's wife on PA visit
abstract: Barbara Hafer, a Republican gubernatorial candidate, expressed concern that Barbara Bush's appearance at a literacy conference hosted by Governor Casey gave the impression that Bush supports Casey.  She claims that Bush's appearance sends the wrong message.  A spokesperson for Barbara Bush said that this was a major literacy conference and the First Lady, who has long worked on the issue of literacy, was there to show her encouragement--not to endorse a political candidate.

headline: Budget Shortfall: The Problem...
abstract: One chart shows the current revenue shortfall projections and unexpected new costs for the New Jersey budget. Another chart shows Governor Jim Florio's new budget plan, including layoffs of city workers, reduction of travel and consulting, and freezing of building projects.

headline: AIDS vaccine possible in 1990s
abstract: Dr. Jay Berzofsky of the National Cancer Institute predicts a vaccine for AIDS in the near future. The vaccine is not intended to prevent infection with AIDS, but to help those already infected. Wayne Koff of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases agreed with Berzofsky. The US Food and Drug Administration is expected to approve human trials. At the Sixth International Conference on Aids, the AIDS Coalition to Increase Power protested discrimination against women, children and minorities in access to clinical trials.

headline: City teachers ratify pact day before start of school
abstract: A Harrisburg teachers union ratified a new three-year contract yesterday, allowing school to begin today on schedule.  The contract gives paid tuition for 6 college credits and an increased starting salary.

headline: DER Starts Inspecting Storage Tanks to Ensure Registration
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources began canvassing facilities to make sure that their above and underground storage tanks are registered to comply with the state's new Storage Tank Spill and Prevention Act.

headline: State may join suit to block radioactive waste dumping
abstract: PA will likely join a lawsuit against the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in order to stop the NRC from dumping low-level radioactive waste into landfills.  The NRC contends that the waste doesn't carry enough radioactivity to harm anyone.

headline: Beaver Countian's execution ordered
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey has ordered the execution of a Beaver County man who was sentenced to die for the brutal slayings of a co-worker's wife and two children, Charles Eugene Cross. He will be executed on Oct. 1.

headline: Ruling spurs inquiries into living wills
abstract: Chairman of the medical/legal committee of the PA Bar Association, James Ronca, noted PA's Proxy Directive is more suited to situations in which decisions must be made for comatose patients than living wills. PA does not recognizes living wills, but some hospitals do. Nancy Coleman, director of the American Bar Association's Commission on the Legal Problems of the Elderly, said a living will provides protective measures for a person's will, but it does not grant decision making power to another person.

headline: Many businesses still in the dark on recycling
abstract: Many businesses will likely be in violation of a law requiring recycling programs by September 26, though it's not their fault.  A large percentage of businesses either don't know about the legislation or don’t know when it takes effect.

headline: Casey accused of arrogance: Lehigh Demo chairman writes to party officials statewide
abstract: Lehigh County Democratic Party Chairman Glenn Moyer wrote a stinging letter to Democratic officials throughout PA accusing Governor Robert P. Casey of "arrogance in action" and urged party member to support opposition democrats.  James Carville, spokesman for Casey's re-election committee, dismissed Moyer's actions.  In his letter, Moyer criticizes the actions of Casey and his administration while in office.

headline: Hafer, too, gets radio spot after invoking FCC rule
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer will soon have her own radio address to accompany Democrat Gov. Casey's under the equal-time rule.  The addresses won't necessarily make it to the air waves, since radio stations can use them at their own choosing, and rarely do.

headline: Redistricting should aid GOP, but Democrats hold the keys
abstract: A photo of former US Senator Chiles from Florida is printed alongside a photo of the state's Governor Martinez, whom Chiles is expected to challenge in the upcoming elections. Republicans in the state are attempting to gain the Florida Senate.

headline: Goode's authority sustained
abstract: In a ruling that Philadelphia Mayor Goode said clearly establishes the authority of the mayor to make critical budget decision, a Common Pleas Court judge has thrown out a City Council lawsuit challenging Goode's right to close two fire stations. Goode was pleased with the ruling.

headline: Senate revives bill from veto
abstract: The PA state Senate voted to override Governor Robert P. Casey's veto of a commercial drivers bill that grants limited licenses to drivers who have had their privileges revoked for breaking traffic laws. Governor Casey vetoed the measure because the bill will allow dangerous drivers on the road.  Several Senate members responded by arguing that the bill affords the secretary of transportation the discretion to deny dangerous individuals licenses.  The bill now moves to the state House for consideration.

headline: Budgetary baloney
abstract: The editorial criticizes the new federal budget plan, as it allows spending to exceed revenues by $250 billion.  It says that new taxes have hardly made a dent in that figure, and that defense spending, thanks in large part to the ongoing Persian Gult crisis is about $303 billion.  Most domestic programs will keep up with inflation, except for Medicare, which could see $5 billion in cuts.

headline: Alcohol-binge death leaves puzzle, shock
abstract: City police and PA Bureau of Liquor Enforcement officials are investigating the death of John Yoffee, who was found dead with a blood alcohol content of .741, almost unheard of, on his 21st birthday. The diseased visited only 3 bars, the last of which is the Brooklyn Alley Depot, where bartender Oran Eberhart remembers him. Eberhart says bartenders flag patrons who have had too much to drink, which was not apparent in Yoffee's case.

headline: Closing door on campus crime
abstract: Princeton officials have taken measures to secure its largest residence hall with an electronic card reading lock system, however students are up in arms. Concerns among university officials echo those of universities nationwide, as suburbia continues to be encroached upon by urban sprawl. Jerrod Witsil, Princeton's director of security, cites the stabbing of a woman in a Princeton library as the incident alerting the university to the need for increased security measures.

headline: DER to get bills for recycling
abstract: Monessen and North Belle Vernon can start to bill the PA State Department of Environmental Resources for their recycling programs, which will amount to $134,923. The funds are to be used for curbside recycling programs to collect aluminum, steel cans and glass.

headline: The meltdown in uranium prices
abstract: A graph depicts the downward slide of the price of domestic uranium since the Three Mile Island incident.

headline: Beaver orders manger removed
abstract: Beaver County commissioners ordered the removal of a nativity scene from the courthouse lobby after the threat of lawsuit from the ACLU. It was removed yesterday by its owner, Holy Name Society. The commissioners said a legal fight would be fruitless and expensive.

headline: Schmelzlen work includes varied functional instruction
abstract: A photo depicts an inmate enrolled in Cambria County Prison Warden William Wolford's pre-release program receiving instruction from administrative assistant Paulette Schmelzen.

headline: Mellon's condition improving. Losses mount at other banks.
abstract: Despite previous internal fiscal problems and widespread downturns at other major banks, Mellon Bank expects record profits and growing returns on capital and assets. Mellon plans to continue its program of acquisitions and divestitures aimed at fine-tuning its business units.

headline: Casey Addresses Legislature; Republicans Criticize Speech
abstract: Republicans called Casey's optimistic assessment of PA misleading. In his annual address Gov. Casey highlighted the past three years accomplishments and alluded to plans to toughen auto emissions.

headline: Hafer, too, gets radio spot after invoking FCC rule
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer will soon have her own radio address to accompany Democrat PA Governor Casey's under the equal-time rule.  The addresses won't necessarily make it to the air waves, since radio stations can use them at their own choosing, and rarely do.

headline: Redistricting should aid GOP, but Democrats hold the keys
abstract: Redistricting after the US Census should aid Republicans, with 50 percent of the districts supporting George Bush having grown by a majority in the last election. In many of those states, Democrats hold governorships and/or key positions in the legislature. In PA, Governor Bob Casey appears to be very strong in terms of his power to redistrict. The state as a whole will most likely lose 2 or 3 of its 23 seats in the US House. The state legislature, under control of different parties, will be a battleground.

headline: Grant Tax
abstract: Pittsburgh has abandoned the concept of taxing University research grants.

headline: Unsafe proposal
abstract: A bill under consideration by the state House heavily favors manufacturer, rather than consumer,  interests.  The bill contains an amendment that protects tobacco companies against suits from people whose health injuries stem from smoking before Washington required warning labels on cigarette packs; also, the legislation forbids product-liability suits resulting from products purchased at least 15 years before a claim is made.  These changes heavily favor corporate interests.

headline: Campaigning for a loan
abstract: The editorial laments that Gov. Casey and Barbara Hafer have turned the $495 million in tax-anticipation notes needed to pay for various education programs into a political issue, and suggests they forward the loans and take their political squabbles elsewhere.

headline: As Many as 15,000 could be exposted to Hepatitis
abstract: The PA state Health Department says that clinics will be available for as many as 15,000 people who may have been exposed to Hepatitis Type A virus when they ate at an Allentown restaurant.

headline: CMU to buy estate for president
abstract: Carnegie Mellon University is planning to purchase a home for its new president, at $1.9 million. Chairman and past presidents of the university say the practice of a university owning the home in which its president resides is common. Current President Robert Mehrabian and his wife Victoria, president of the California Cattlewomen's Association, currently live in California.

headline: DER to hold workshops about lead levels
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources will hold 34 workshops around PA in October and November to teach school and day care center administrators and maintenance personnel how to identify and correct problems with lead in drinking water, which can be dangerous to children.

headline: U.S. laws on energy proposed
abstract: An investigation into the oil industry's recent price hikes since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait is underway to check for evidence of price-fixing.  Some groups are calling for a more effective national energy policy.

headline: Bedford 'riot,' 2 Camp Hill inmates linked
abstract: Two inmates arrested for taking part in the Camp Hill prison riot allegedly participated in an earlier revolt at Bedford County Prison.

headline: Schuylkill drug force seizes pair
abstract: After a high-speed chase, a task force arrested a pair of men transporting cocaine from Philadelphia to the Tamaqua-Hazleton area.  An investigation into the men is ongoing.

headline: Mellow Says New Law Restricts Northeast Truck Center
abstract: The Northeast Truck Center on Keyser Avenue will remain closed until its owners secure a state permit to operate as a trash transfer station. PA Governor Robert Casey has signed into law a bill that guarantees the controversial center cannot reopen without a permit.

headline: Casey adds four new commercials to arsenal
abstract: Incumbent PA Governor Robert P. Casey (Democrat) has released four new TV commercials touting his positions and achievements on the issues of drugs, employment clean water, and the environment in a $4 million "media blitz."  Casey's opponent, Barbara Hafer, has not yet amassed enough money to run television ads, but will need to if she hopes to content in the election.

headline: Hafer: anti-takeover law is bad for state
abstract: Barbara Hafer, a Republican candidate for governor, said she opposes an anti-takeover bill signed by current PA Governor Robert P. Casey.  PA State Senator Noah W. Wenger, a Republican from Lancaster County, was the author of the anti-takeover legislation.

headline: Reform the budget process
abstract: Editorial would like PA Governor Robert Casey and the PA Legislature to agree to a new state spending plan. Right now when budget are passed it is with no debate, no coverage, and no guts. The secrecy is troubling, because it is sponsored by younger leadership. The paper would like to see to see an end to backroom dealing.

headline: Guess who's resurrecting tax reform in the legislature
abstract: This editorial explores property tax reform. Republicans had previously disapproved of tax reform, but now they are calling for it. There is very little difference from the one from last year and this year's. The main difference is towns are allowed to formulate their own tax systems.

headline: State facing another redistricting battle
abstract: Pennsylvania congressional districts will be reshaped by the 1990 Census and elections for the state General Assembly.  The state is is poised to lose 2 of its seats in Congress, and each party will try to make redistricting work to its advantage.

headline: Casey '91 budget expected today
abstract: Gov. Casey is expected to propose a $12.3 billion budget today.

headline: Asbestos compensation claims could soar, new studies suggest
abstract: Asbestos liability claims appear to be receding which could gradually reduce the size of settlements to victims, according to statistics compiled by the US Office of Administrative Courts in Washington. At the same time though a study by the American Cancer Society showed that wives and children of asbestos workers are dying of cancer at 1 1/2 times the rate of the general population.

headline: CMU to get $15 million for data research
abstract: Carnegie Mellon University is targeted to receive up to $14.6 million over the next five years to fund research on the technology used to store data in computer systems.

headline: DER to Sewer Authority: Stop Composting or We'll Order It
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources is requesting that the Scranton Sewer Authority shut down its outdoors composting activities, as they are the alleged source of offensive odors in South Scranton and Minooka.

headline: TMI Shutdown
abstract: An unusual noise in the process to evaporate 2.3 million gallons of slightly radioactive water from the Unit 2 reactor accident in March 1979 caused workers to shut down the operation. The noise has since been identified as a wobbly compression shaft, which sheared off 14 bolts attaching it to a compressor. Spokesperson Mary Wells said a vendor is on-site to replace the shaft, however operations will not resume until after Christmas.

headline: Bennett: On the state of the nation's war on drugs
abstract: An interview with Federal Drug Czar William J. Bennett is conducted by Philadelphia Inquirer editor Henry Bryan. Bennett is scheduled to address the PA state Legislature tomorrow. He identifies PA as on of the few states which has done a good job of addressing the drug problem. Herman Wrice, a local Philadelphia activist, is cited as a success in his work against drugs. Bennett notes federal agency budgets for dealing with education and treatment have been increased. Bennet quotes John Jacobs, President of the Urban League to rate the drug problem.

headline: Second O'Kicki trial to start soon
abstract: A second trial of former Cambria County judge O'Kicki is scheduled to start Nov. 30, though O'Kicki contends that it should be suspended until his appeal of his first trial is heard, as it could affect the second trial.

headline: Mixed response to anti-takeover law
abstract: When the PA Legislature passed anti-takeover legislation, among the toughest in the nation, it allowed publicly held companies to opt out by a deadline. Approximately 60 of 300 have. President of the PA AFL-CIO William George says he sees the laws bringing corporations to the state in the future to product jobs and ensure growth. The legislation forces investors who unsuccessfully direct a takeover attempt to cede their profit from the sale of their shares within 18 months of the action.

headline: Casey aide to speak to local Democrats
abstract: Robert Grotevant, former press secretary to PA Governor Robert Casey and now a senior special assistant, will speak at the annual Jefferson-Jackson dinner sponsored by the Lebanon County Democratic committee.

headline: Hafer: anti-takeover law is bad for state
abstract: Barbara Hafer, a Republican candidate for governor, said she opposes an anti-takeover bill signed by current PA Governor Robert P. Casey.  PA State Senator Noah W. Wenger, a Republican from Lancaster County, was the author of the anti-takeover legislation.

headline: Regan violated State Ethics Law
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman Bernard Regan violated State Ethics Law in 1989 when he failed to list his ownership of rental properties on campaign financial disclosure statement. The commission will take no further action against Regan, because there is no evidence he intended to concealed the financial interests he had in numerous rental properties.

headline: Hike in occupation tax called unlikely
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff wants to raise the city's occupation privilege tax and reduce the amusement tax. PA legislators said it was unlikely that the General Assembly would approve the plan before the legislative session ends in four voting days. Some said there is an unwillingness among the county delegation to consider a tax bill at a time when voters seemed to send a strong anti-tax signal in the Nov. 6 election.

headline: null
abstract: An estimated 200,000 gallons of diesel fuel, gas and oil spilled into the Allegheny River after a landslide broke a 10-inch pipeline.  Federal and Pennsylvania environmental agents continue to investigate the cause and possible delays in reporting the spill.  The operator of the pipeline--Buckeye Pipe Line Company--apparently failed to give the Department of Environmental Protection propmt notice when they realized the leak started; this prevented early efforts of containment.

headline: Casey admits possible deficit of $1 million
abstract: The Casey administration admitted that a $1billion deficit is possible this year, but PA Budget Secretary Michael Hershock and some legislators dismissed a tax increase as unnecessary. They say the deficit predicted is a worst case scenario. Republicans do believe this deficit will be the truth. The costs of running he state will be higher next year because of underestimations in things like the needy and school costs.

headline: Baby Boom: 1988 Births hit 17-year record
abstract: According to the PA Department of Health, older women who had delayed starting families gave birth to a small baby boom in 1988.

headline: Collecting last cent repudiates good sense. Computer threatens student borrowers.
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency sent a letter to several hundred student loan recipients bills for pennies after a computer error that rounded up parts of a cent and tried to collect. PHEAA public information officer John Ebersole said that though the problem was solved, new federal regulations may force agencies to go after borrowers for every cent.

headline: DER wants to know what's killing Roaring Brook
abstract: A study by the PA Department of Environmental Resources revealed acid mining pollutants in Roaring Brook.  The study did not implicate DeNaples Auto Salvage as a cause of the pollution. However, the yard is making many improvements and the DER will return when the water levels are lower to see if the pollution is less concentrated. DeNaples also plans to propose purchase of a car shredder to the Dunmore Planning Commission as well as the Lackawanna County Regional Planning Commission.

headline: Township's water rates cut for now
abstract: Water rates for Susquehanna Township residents may decrease by 32 percent next month, but the rate is only temporary. Harrisburg will increase rates to pay off approximately $50 million in bonds it must sell to finance water system improvements. The authority agreed to roll back rates for 3,300 customers to the amounts it charged before it imposed a 32 percent increase last May.

headline: Better laws needed to protect children
abstract: An 11 week old Lancaster County, PA child was believed to have died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, until prosecutors ordered an autopsy which revealed 35 small fractures--the baby had been shaken to death. In order to prevent child abuse, the editors urge mandatory autopsies in all SIDS caes, supported by the SIDS Foundation. In addition, they request more assistance for social workers, better training for coroners, more funding, and more thorough investigations.

headline: Secrecy and settlements
abstract: A bill designed to protect businesses from certain product liability lawsuits is under debate and revision, but the writer points out one amendment that should survive.  The amendment prohibits settlements of liability cases that allow manufacturers to conceal information about unsafe of defective products.

headline: National Intergroup Earnings Rise
abstract: National Intergroup Inc. has announced a 27 percent increase in earnings in the fiscal third quarter due to gains in operating income posted by its Foxmeyer Drug and Ben Franklin Stores.

headline: Casey and Hafer on the campaign issues
abstract: The article summarizes the positions of incumbent Democrat PA Governor Robert P. Casey and his Republican challenger Barbara Hafer on various issues.  The issues covered are abortion, car insurance, drugs, economic development, education, the environment, family leave, merit selection, Philadelphia's financial situation, and taxes.

headline: Hafer's Lopsided Loss Tilts Legislative Races
abstract: Analysts said Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer's unpopularity and poor election results, in which she won 32-percent of the vote against PA Governor Robert P. Casey, played a part in the failures of GOP candidates in the PA Legislature. Eight Republican incumbents were unseated in the House along with seven Democrats. In the Senate, Republicans lost control of the 4th and 28th Districts. Republican House Minority Leader Matthew Ryan said that a half-dozen victories were decided by a total of less than 1,000 votes.

headline: Rendell is '90% sure' he will run for mayor
abstract: Former District Attorney Edward G. Rendell said that he is "90 percent sure" he would be a candidate for the Democratic mayoral nomination in 1991. A city-wide poll showing him beating either City Councilman George R. Burrell or Councilman Lucien E. Blackwell. These men are not happy with the results of the poll.

headline: Holdout by Council complicates rescue plans
abstract: The Republican-controlled Philadelphia City Council refused to sign on to the recently-announced city fiscal recovery plan and budget supported by House Speaker Robert W. O'Donnell, Mayor Wilson Goode and other key Democratic officeholders. Council members were wary of embracing a timetable and unpopular tax increases in light of the upcoming election in which all 17 Council seats are up for grabs. The plan envisions a sale of loan notes, borrowing money, selling assets and raising a city sales tax.

headline: Spill Moves Toward Ohio, West Virginia
abstract: Federal state and local agencies are investigating the cause of a fuel spill that leaked at least 75,000 gallons on diesel, gasoline and kerosine into the Allegheny River.  Although the spill did not represent a threat to the Beaver County water system, some residents of Harrison Township were asked to boil water to kill bacteria.

headline: Casey Budget Snubs A-K Revitalization
abstract: Governor Casey's $22 billion budget proposal, though a balanced budget without requiring tax hikes for the fourth consecutive year, received dismal reactions from lawmakers on Capitol Hill.

headline: Be thankful
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey, in cooperation with the PA Association for the Blind, proclaimed the upcoming week "Thanks for Sight Week". The editorial board urges readers to become aware of the health complications of glaucoma and to schedule regular eye examinations.

headline: College cost inaccurately calculated
abstract: A new study shows that parents and students often know very little about the costs of college and potential aid sources.

headline: DER wants wetland developers to be locked up
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources has petitioned for weekend jail sentences for William Ramagosa and his two sons, William Jr. and Robert, for ignoring orders to restore 60 acres of wetlands they destroyed in Dingman Twp. The DER's petition charges that the Ramagosas violated a DER order and a Commonwealth Court order to restore the wetlands at Sunrise Lake development.

headline: Trucking firms add surcharges to cover fuel-cost rise
abstract: Trucking companies are implementing surcharges to their loads in order to cover increases in diesel fuel cost.  If and when fuel costs drop, the companies say that the charges will be dropped.

headline: Biden Calls For More Judges To Fight Drugs
abstract: Delaware Senator Joseph Biden Jr. says that the federal court system needs additional judges to deal with the nation's drug problems.  Biden appeared with Senator Arlen Specter at a joint news conference to recommend the strategy that Philadelphia is using allowing state drug cases to be tried in federal courts.

headline: Senate approves broad crime bill
abstract: The US Senate approved a broad crime bill that stiffens prison terms for savings and loan fraud, bans nine semiautomatic weapons and makes three dozen federal offenses punishable by death. The election-year measure sailed through the Senate. It is the toughest anti-crime bill in US history.

headline: National Steel Earnings Drop
abstract: National Steel Corp. has reported a 14 percent drop in earnings in the final three months of 1989, due in part to reduced sales in the automotive industry.

headline: Casey beating Hafer
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey is ahead of Republican opponent PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer in fundraising for the current gubernatorial campaign.  Both Casey and Hafer are raising more money than their opponents in the upcoming primary.

headline: Hafer's running mate vows to better election campaign
abstract: Harold Mowery Jr., Barbara Hafer's running mate in the gubernatorial race, promised that their camp was not a "one-issue" team, but that they just hadn't done as good a job getting their views out as they would've liked.  He expects the fall election to be close between Hafer and PA Governor Casey.

headline: Rep. Friend is this season's MVP
abstract: PA Representative Stephen Friend is the Legislature's anti-abortion leader, but is one of the most effective member so far in this session. He has lead legislation in a variety of areas. Both sides of the aisle listen to him. He is not afraid of failure or rejection and speaks his mind.

headline: How the city's financial crisis might affect tax rates
abstract: In an attempt to raise money for the city's empty pocketbooks, Philadelphia Mayor Goode has proposed local sales tax and  wage tax increases.

headline: Cavazos Bristles at Democrats' Education Bill
abstract: U.S. Education Secretary Lauro Cavazos claims that some House Democrats are playing politics with President Bush's bill to improve U.S. schools.  He argues that the administration's legislation has been treated in a partisan fashion, and that Democrats refuse to give the president credit for his efforts and leadership in educational reform.  Many Democrats and education leaders support Augustus Hawkins' bill, which is more comprehensive than President Bush's.

headline: Casey claims budget meets essential needs
abstract: PA Governor Casey signed budgets in the past which did not increase taxes, but in approving the most recent budget, which Republicans say is underfunded, Casey implied it might be necessary. A few PA Democrats raised concerns, but increases are unlikely during elections. The budget, constructed without Rainy Day Funds, gives more aid to schools, county and local governments, and state and county prisons. The budget is funded by a combination of state and federal funds

headline: Blue Cross rate plan called 'robbery'
abstract: A crowd of senior citizens protested the PA Insurance Department's hearing of Blue Cross of Western PA's proposal to raise premiums for the 65-Special policy, a supplemental Medicare program. It is the second year in a row that Blue Cross has increased premiums for the 65-Special program, citing increases in the Medicare in-patient deductible. Officials say the company has lost many subscribers age 65 to 69 to commercial insurance companies.

headline: Coming up short on education
abstract: The editorial claims that PA Governor Robert P. Casey's defense of the status quo as far as education in Pennsylvania is unacceptable, and is challenging Casey to stand up for PA's students, even if it means enacting new taxes to provide more funding for poor schools.  Casey has danced around questions about education, as he is loathe to "ruffle the political feathers" so close to an election.

headline: DER:  No Problem With Water Company's Source
abstract: Shelf samples of Pocono Pure Mountain Spring Water contained traces of phenol and phthalate, suspected carcinogens found in plastics and detergents, but officials from the Department of Environmental Resources found the company's source to be chemical-free.

headline: Unit 2 Susquehanna plant shuts down
abstract: A glitch in the electricity distribution system triggered an automatic shutdown of the Unit 2 reactor at the Susquehanna nuclear power plant Tuesday. The plants operator, the PA Power and Light Co., said that it was the first unscheduled shutdown of the unit 2 reactor in more than 1,000 days.

headline: Bids To Be Opened For State Prison Addition
abstract: Chief U.S. District Judge Maurice B. Cohill Jr. agreed with prisoners' class-action lawsuit seeking better medical care, ruling conditions at the Pittsburgh prison were inhumane and unconstitutional. Cohill ordered the state to develop a plan for resolving the problems, which also included overcrowding. The state plans to build a new infirmary and open it for bids. After bids on the health building are opened, the PA Department of Corrections will have 49 days to award a contract for construction.

headline: Senate Panel Issues Prison Report
abstract: Though Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee Senator Stewart Greenleaf said that abuse occurred, the panel did not recommend any disciplinary action against guards and state police officers who allegedly beat inmates during prison riots. The panel's investigative report made recommendations to prevent future problems, though it did not address inmate abuse. Commissioner of the Department of Corrections Joseph D. Lehman said that there have been no instances of abuse, though the department would take action if there were.

headline: New challenges facing Lashinger
abstract: PA Representative Joseph Lashinger, who was defeated two weeks ago in his bid for re-election, is being sued by a former partner in an auto dealership for $184,000 he was given in a loan. He claims it is purely a legal dispute, and not reflection on the business.

headline: Casey camp: Hafer comment a fabrication
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey's spokesman, Vince Carocci, said that Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer has consistently gotten her facts wrong and "has fabricated political charges" against Casey. This comment was in response to Hafer's accusation that Casey has "a secret deal" to bail out Philadelphia, which is in financial crisis. Deputy Auditor General said that a state plan to funnel $200 million to Philadelphia in order to assure investors that the city could pay its debts was nothing more than a "bailout."

headline: Handler staff competent
abstract: Letter to the editor writes that contrary to the media Rosalie G Handler Center is innovative, accessible, and knowledgeable. The letter points out that the things the affect of this upheaval is having a negative affect of the lives of clients. The future is uncertain for the Handler Center despite its good deeds.

headline: Rep. McDade now 'dean' of state delegation
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph McDade will become the "dean" of the PA House delegation in the next Congress, giving him the responsibility to organize gatherings of the delegation. The position is awarded to the most senior member of the party which molds a majority in the delegation. The upset of Representative Doug Walgren by Rick Santorum gave Republicans the majority. Administration officials said that the delegation has been responsive to PA Governor Robert P. Casey's requests.

headline: Huber defends record on Ag Preserve budget
abstract: Lancaster County Commissioner Jim Huber defends himself in a letter to the editor. He does admit to being on the Agricultural Preserve Board until this year and twice voted as commissioner to budget less than what they requested. He claims to have been fiscally conservative and budget realistically. He says if he wasn’t so the county would be bankrupt.

headline: Bill to curb corporate raiders passes House, goes to Senate
abstract: The PA state House approved legislation that protects Pennsylvania companies from corporate raiders.  Those seeking to take over a company would be denied short-term profits resulting from takeover attempts, as well as immediate voting rights.  Although the legislation is designed to protect Pennsylvania companies, some critics argue that it protects incompetent management and stifles investment.

headline: Casey is not a liar
abstract: Letter to the editor protests the false and irresponsible assertion that Gov. Casey lied about PA's fiscal affairs during the gubernatorial campaign. It's a baseless charge that has no foundation in fact. PA Governor Casey cut the growth in his 1990-1991 budget request from 2.3 percent to 1.7 percent and lowered the revenue estimate by $100 million.

headline: Blue Cross, affiliated hospitals to open community health centers
abstract: Blue Cross of Western PA will link two suburban Pittsburgh hospitals to open community health centers in mid-1991 in order to increase the agency's visibility in growing areas and give subscribers access to primary care physicians. Some doctors believe that, as an insurance provider, it is inappropriate for the agency to compete directly with private-practice physicians. Head of Alliance Ventures, David O'Brien said a number of doctors who will work at the centers will not be employed by Blue Cross.

headline: Crowded colleges: State must tend to its universities
abstract: Comments on the rising costs and overcrowding problems in Pennsylvania's 14 state universities in the State System of Higher Education.  The PA state universities have been receiving limited financial support from the state despite increasing demand for higher education.

headline: Derailment Cleanup Continues
abstract: Crews in Craigsville began retracking cars of a Pittsburgh & Buffalo Railroad train after 28 or 29 cars derailed in a sparely populated rural community near the Butler and Armstrong County border.  There were some fires as a result of the derailment and local fire crews have been working to get them under control.  The PA Department of Environmental Resources did not think that oil spilled into the Buffalo Creek posed a threat to drinking water in the area.

headline: Utilities reject public-dump use for mildly radioactive waste
abstract: Three eastern PA utilities have decided not to risk public backlash by sending slightly radioactive waste to public dumps, despite its legality.

headline: Bill addresses prison overcrowding
abstract: A bill has been introduced in the PA Senate that would implement Montgomery County District Attorney Mike Marino's plan for solving some prison overcrowding issues.  His plan involves allowing non-violent prisoners to lessen their sentence by performing community service.

headline: Senate Stalls Lawsuit Legislation
abstract: The PA Senate tabled a bill aimed at limiting frivolous lawsuits over unsafe products over suspicions that it contained protections for the tobacco industry. Senate Minority Leader Robert Mellow said the issue is too substantive to resolve in the lame-duck session. The bill was opposed by consumers' groups and the PA State Trial Lawyers Association, saying the bill would restrict the ability of residents to sue manufacturers when injured by products.

headline: New law raises fees for services
abstract: License fees on such businesses as making frozen desserts and selling sacramental wine have increased under a new state law aimed at covering the state's costs in processing various applications. PA Legislation signed raised a variety of fees by a total of about $12 million. Some of the fees haven't been raised since the 1930's.

headline: Casey Campaign Hits The Airwaves
abstract: Gov. Casey began his $4 million TV campaign with ads across the state, which will continue until election day.  Casey has refrained from using his infamous negative ad strategy so far, though it hasn't been ruled out for the future.

headline: Hard times ahead for elected officials
abstract: Falling revenues and widening budget gaps and causing the state and local governments to lay off workers, trim services, and limit aid to the old and poor. It is going to be very difficult to the a politician in these times. State colleges tuitions are being raised and hospitals are being closed in response.

headline: Rep. Pesci's latest win was tougher
abstract: Democratic incumbent Tim Pesci's victory over Republican Jim Scahill in the 60th PA Legislative District was achieved by a larger margin than his previous win over Scahill 17 months ago. Pesci had to struggle against the national anti-incumbency movement and a fragmented Democratic organization. Though mentioned as a potential candidate, Scahill rejected a run for county commissioner and said he had no plans to run again for the legislative seat.

headline: Leaks
abstract: An architectural firm claims the Westmoreland County Courthouse dome is falling down because of poor quality terra cotta used during restoration.

headline: From Burma's jungles, a brutal warlord rules a growing heroin trade
abstract: The fugitive running the world's largest opium operation, Khun Sa, has offerred to end heroin production and trade if the United States would buy his crop for 300 million dollars.  Sa's operation is responsible for nearly 85 percent of the heroin entering New York City, and two weeks ago the U.S. Justice Department unsealed an indictment charging Khun Sa with exporting heroin to New York.

headline: Casey moves to offset loss in tax income
abstract: PA Budget Secretary Michael Hershock declared a recession as PA Governor Casey continues to try cutting costs. Most recently, Casey considered tapping into the state's Rainy Day Emergency Funds. Plans are also under negotiation with the Hospital Association of Pennsylvania to pool funds to receive more federal grant matching. As of yet, the state has not examined how to comply with a PA Supreme Court order mandating a unified judicial system. Casey hopes to refrain from raising taxes.

headline: Blue Shield wants $1.2 million back
abstract: PA Blue Shield's Medical Review Committee has requested a record $1,241,551 from 19 medical practices for procedures that were misreported, upgraded, or not medically necessary. Jon Dubs, secretary for the Medical Review Committee at Blue Shield, said that it's critical that the company safeguard fund for health-care claims that are truly necessary, and said that just because Blue Shield is requesting refunds from providers does not mean that fraud is occurring.

headline: CV board hears ire of parents
abstract: Parents packed a Cumberland Valley School Board meeting yesterday to voice their displeasure at the ongoing teacher strike in the district.

headline: Derry citizens protest mandatory recycling
abstract: The Derry Township municipal building continue to receive calls and letters protesting the mandatory recycling fees. The recycling advisory board said that they will investigate means of providing relief for those who cannot afford the $133 annual fee for recycling and waste pick-up but the board is standing by the fee.

headline: Utility Ready To Resume Routine Operation Of Nine Mile 1
abstract: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Restart Assessment Panel authorized the restart of the Niagara Mohawk Power Corporations Unit 1 Nuclear Reactor after a 2.5 year shutdown. 2 forced outages, a 3,000 gallon water spill, 2 rapid shutdowns, and a power outage due to a windstorm have not caused the NRC any major concerns. The company must wait several more weeks in order to determine whether the NRC is satisfied with changes the company has made to restart the Unit.

headline: Bill addresses prison overcrowding
abstract: A bill has been introduced in the state Senate that would implement Montgomery County DA Mike Marino's plan for solving some prison overcrowding issues.  His plan involves allowing non-violent prisoners to lessen their sentence by performing community service.

headline: Senate, House approve injection, Casey reviews
abstract: The PA House voted to replace the electric chair with lethal injection as the means of state executions. The bill, sponsored by PA Senator Stewart J. Greenleaf, which already passed the PA Senate, will go to PA Governor Robert P. Casey for approval. Some representatives opposed the bill, citing arguments that injections are no less painful, that the sudden change may give death-row inmates more avenues for appeals and that inmates don't deserve more humane treatment.

headline: No wonder it's chaos
abstract: Norman W. Rickert Jr. of West Chester writes to point out what he calls a reason for Philadelphia's financial troubles and high insurance rates. He sarcastically suggests that Steven Testan should lend Philadelphia some of his $170,000 settlement with an insurance company. Evidently, Testan won a settlement against an insurer on questionable terms, though Rickert doesn't explain anything about it.

headline: Casey can blast Hafer without appearing sexist
abstract: Incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey has not had to deal with the trouble of appearing sexist in criticizing his challenger, Barbara Hafer, since his press secretary, Karen Chandler, does most of the criticizing.  Also, the traditional style of an incumbent is to run on one's record, and to disregard the other candidate as much as possible.

headline: Harrisburg in Northern Tier
abstract: A caption describes two pictures which demonstrate the state government's interest and involvement in the northern part of the state. State Agricultural Secretary Boyd Wolf, who will accompany PA Governor Casey on his visit through the area, talks with Troy Borough Fair President Lonnie Thomas at Mount Pisgah State Park. In the second picture, Tioga County Commissioners Brian Edgcomb and Marie Cooper hang a banner.

headline: Rep. Ridge opens 'war chest' to aid Republican teammates
abstract: Faced with no Democratic opponent, U.S. Representative Tom Ridge used $7,000 of his campaign money to fund Republican PA Legislature candidates and gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer. The party that gains control of the PA General Assembly will have a large say in redrawing congressional districts next year. Half of Ridge's funding came from special-interest political action committees.

headline: Lebanon voters face study-panel question
abstract: Lebanon voters will be asked to approve a government study commission and to select its members. The Pennsylvania Economic League recommends eliminating the current commission form and restructuring city government. Problems with current form arise from residents voting for council members based on general qualifications, without knowing what department they will go to. Council members thus may lack the expertise needed to run a specific department. Any changes in city government operation would have to be approved by voters in a future election

headline: Clean-air bill gets Senate OK
abstract: Yesterday, the U.S. Senate approved an overhaul of the Clean Air Act that tightens controls on the major sources of smog, acid rain and toxic air pollution.  Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell credited President Bush with breaking the political gridlock when he proposed a clean-air bill last year.  Mitchell and Bush worked together and drafted the compromise plan that was approved yesterday.

headline: Casey Offers Lean Budget
abstract: Gov. Casey has released his proposed state budget that does not raise taxes, but provides increases in funding for education, economic development, environmental protection and other major programs.

headline: Bogus Health Survey Reported in Decatur
abstract: A man and a woman posing as Hershey Medical Center representatives conducted a false health survey in Decature Township.

headline: Demand better education, NAACP urged
abstract: William Lucy, a well-known labor leader, urged the Harrisburg-area branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People to more aggressively demand better education halt the widening of the gap between rich and poor.  He criticized the federal government, saying it is to blame for Americans losing their competitive edge over other countries by being a government of the "rich dealing for the rich."

headline: Devious waste plans stink!
abstract: The editorial criticizes "devious" plans to illegally transport waste from other states into PA in order to avoid using up their landfills and to avoid restrictions.  It was also an attempt to avoid rules set in place by PA Governor Casey on out-of-state trash.

headline: Water Firm Abandons Role in PG&W Purchase
abstract: With its Goldman Sachs financial advisor unable to determine if the deal was fair, United Water Resources withdrew its offer to acquire the water and real estate assets of PA Gas & Water Co., the principal subsidiary of PA Enterprises Inc. NUI Corporation of New Jersey said it would continue merger discussion with PEI despite the withdrawal. PG&W said it will now pursue settlement discussions with the PA Public Utility Commission regarding a rate hike for its customers in the  Scranton area.

headline: Bill battle expected over new judges
abstract: A battle is expected over two pieces of legislation moving through the PA Senate that would give Lancaster County two new judges next year. The Republican controlled Senate Appropriations Committee has stripped one bill of five new judgeships earmarked for Philadelphia. Democratic Senator Vincent Fumo said Republicans blocked the Philadelphia judges in an attempt to gain political leverage to get more Republicans on the Philadelphia bench.

headline: Senator Says U.S. Should Have First Shot at Thrift Assets
abstract: U.S. Senator John Heinz criticized the PA House of Representatives for refusing to pass his proposal giving precedence to government lawsuits against S&L criminals over claims of thrift owners. Heinz's proposal was adopted by the Senate previously as part of the Financial Institutions Reform Recovery and Enforcement Act, but was stripped from the final bill by the House. Heinz said that lobbying by association lawyers and the bankruptcy bar has prevented the measure from passing.

headline: Nobody really understands the rules in this convoluted game, so here are some options to try
abstract: The editor is commenting on the PA state’s auto insurance reform law that is about to be implemented. The editor says that the one problem is that the law is understand because the law does not clearly assess the blame for “bad driving.”

headline: Casey confident despite expected long, tough race
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey addressed a crowd in Erie and Crawford County on his re-election campaign.  Casey's challenger in the primary, Phillip Berg, has joined the race to give voters a choice on abortion as Casey is pro-life.  The Republican favorite for the gubernatorial nomination is Auditor General Barbara Hafer.

headline: Harrisburg scene
abstract: PA House Republicans are trying to pass a discharge resolution to free from committee a bill eliminating a 6 percent inheritance tax for widows. In an election year, those favoring it will gain the votes of seniors. Democrats, led by PA Governor Casey, trump the tax as an important source of revenue in a tight budget. The Republican charge is led by House Leader Matthew Ryan. Rep. Michael Gruitza, who sponsored the legislation, said he will break ranks to vote for the discharge.

headline: Report: City out of cash in a month without loans
abstract: In an attempt to raise money for Philadelphia, which will run out of cash in about a month, Mayor Goode is looking for buyers of $450 worth of short-term notes and searching for ways to save money.

headline: Legalize Tax Rebates
abstract: An editorial urging the reform and legalization of tax rebates so the elderly are not unjustly burdened and so school taxes are fairer.

headline: Spill not reached Pittsburgh intake valve yet
abstract: Because of a fuel-pipeline leak, communities in Allegheny and Westmoreland counties banned all non-essential use of water.  The spill also induced towns north of Pittsburgh to close water-inlet valves--restricting water supplies for nearly 1 million people.  Water rationing is not anticipated in Pittsburgh because of the large storage capacity of the city's water treatment plant, but state and county emergency agencies have set up potable tanks to provide drinking and cooking water in case they are needed.

headline: Casey or Hafer, taxes may be on the way up
abstract: The two candidates for governor, in separate visits to the area, suggested Pennsylvanians might be paying more in taxes soon. PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer would like a 6 percent per gallon tax increase on gasoline. Also PA Governor Robert Casey cited a sluggish economy and increased demands on state revenue as reasons why he would not rule out an increase in taxes.

headline: Cabinet Profile - Health
abstract: Brief career history of N. Mark Richards, pictured right. Before becoming the secretary of health under Casey's administration, he was the department director of medical services in the Allegheny County Health Department.

headline: Directors approve bond issue
abstract: Franklin School Directors approved a $1.5 million bond issue to pay for renovations to the high school auditorium. Details of the loan are given.

headline: Districts go to school on recycling
abstract: A law requiring state-funding institutions to recycle various materials has school districts readying to employ recycling programs.  Many districts are realizing that recycling is cost-effective, since it will reduce garbage and some carriers even pay for recyclable materials.

headline: Westinghouse buys into Michigan nuclear plant
abstract: Westinghouse Electric Corporation long known as a designer and builder of nuclear power plants, has agreed for the first time to be an owner of one. The company said it will join Consumers Power Company and Bechtel Power Company as stockholders in Palisades Generating Company a venture formed to purchase the Palisades nuclear power plant on the Lake Michigan shore.

headline: Bill permits computerization only of what's already on paper
abstract: Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr., with the support of representatives of the PA District Attorneys Association and the PA Chiefs of Police Association, wrote that a recent editorial "Data bank threatens privacy" was factually incorrect. Preate says current laws prohibit police from computerizing information on criminal activities and using computers to organize their notes and supports a proposed bill that would allow these activities.
