Because of a court case, the budget allocates money for new prison guards at Graterford prison. It also commits $650 million to schools for state education.

headline: Debate over reporting AIDS-related diseases
abstract: A new law passed by the Philadelphia Health Department has sparked controversy, as it required laboratories to file detailed reports on all patients that have any of about 20 diseases commonly contracted by AIDS patients.  The law is an effort to uncover the estimated 30% of AIDS cases that are unreported, but critics say that the law will create huge volumes of data about patients without their knowledge.

headline: Faculty at Temple set to go on strike
abstract: Faculty at Temple University are ready to go on strike, as classes were scheduled to begin today.  The administration vowed to continue classes and events, but it will be made difficult with over a thousand faculty members on strike.

headline: EPA to watch Superfund
abstract: An announcement by the US Environmental Protection Agency that it will now oversee Superfund hazardous waste sites is designed to boost public confidence and protect Americans from harmful chemical contamination. The announcement was made in response to an analysis of cleanups ordered by the Senate Superfund subcommittee, chaired by Sen. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey.

headline: Bartle still sees no tax for SEPTA
abstract: Montgomery County Commissioner Chairman Paul Bartle is disappointed the PA House failed to pass an amendment allowing PA Motor Vehicle Fund funds to be used by the South Eastern PA Transit Authority. The Commission opposes a regional sales tax to help SEPTA, but there is no backup plan. Rep. Geroge Saurman voted against the measure, fearing funds for road and bridge projects would dry up. Bartle says the amendment might have passed last week, but stalled when Republicans tried to force PA Governor Casey to use Rainy Day Funds for special education.

headline: Casey signs death warrant
abstract: Though courts have blocked previous death warrants signed by PA Governor Casey, the Governor signed his fifth since becoming Governor yesterday. The execution warrant of Leslie Beasley, convicted of murdering a city police officer, has been set for September, according to the PA Department of Corrections. Beasley is being held in a state prison in Huntingdon.

headline: State Police Seize $68 Million Worth of Cocaine at Bedford
abstract: In the biggest ever drug seizure, the Pennsylvania state police confiscated over $68 million worth of cocaine from a truck along the turnpike in Bedford County.

headline: Pittsburgh threatens bank with fund withdrawal
abstract: Pittsburgh will withdraw $2 million from a local bank unless the bank improves its record making loans to low and middle-income neighborhoods.  Bank officials claim that they are making enough loans to the targeted income range.

headline: Casey signs cap on doctor's fees under Medicare
abstract: Mae McHugh, president of a group of retired union employees, was thrilled with legislation sponsored by PA Rep. Allen Kukovich and approved by PA Governor Casey which protects the elderly from overcharges by doctors where Medicare is concerned.

headline: House Approves Living Wills Bill; Future Uncertain
abstract: The PA House passed a bill to recognize living wills, documents allowing residents to end artificial life support if they become terminally ill. The bill must go back to the PA Senate for agreement on House changes. Some legislators said amendments added to the House could mean it won't get to PA Governor Robert P. Casey for his signature before the two-year legislative session ends.

headline: Russell P. Letterman, 56, lawmaker nearly 20 years.
abstract: State Rep. Russell P. Letterman, 56, a Democrat who represented the 76th District for nearly 20 years, died yesterday at Centre Community Hospital.

headline: Real Help for a Reeling City
abstract: The editorial praises some of Philadelphia's largest employers, as many of them collectively agreed to prepay about $30 million in 1991 corporate real estate and wage taxes to help with the city's financial problems. It stresses that this is not the end-all solution and that a long-term solution is still needed from city and state officials, and urges citizens to voice their opinions about the use of their money.

headline: Clean Air Bill Heading to House Floor
abstract: Clean air legislation was approved by the House Energy and Commerce Committee and will now go to the House floor for a vote.  The measure passed committee after a compromise designed to help Midwest states pay for pollution cleanup was reached; a similar compromise was reached in the Senate earlier this week.

headline: Governor calls district's bluff
abstract: Editors thank the Altoona Area School District for managing its budget well enough to enter a fifth consecutive year in without a tax increase. The Board attempted to bluff the state into increasing subsidies, saying it would have to raise taxes, but it backed down when PA Governor Casey pointed out the school's $6 million surplus. Editors hope the school is also looking to the future to avoid a sudden disproportional tax increase for residents.

headline: Delco given grant to improve care for mentally disturbed children
abstract: Delaware County has been given a $2.4 million grant from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation in order to improve its mental health care for severely mentally disturbed children.

headline: Fire destroys HACC-Lebanon. Classes move to other sites.
abstract: The Harrisburg Area Community College Lebanon Campus was destroyed due to a fire three months after it opened. Classes will resume at Lebanon County Vocational-Technical School, Lebanon High School and Lebanon Valley College. The fire was a setback to the HACC administration's goal of expanding its offerings in the midstate region.

headline: EPA, lung group mark radon week
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency and the American Lung Association are sponsoring Radon Action Week, which is aimed at informing people about the dangers of radon and how to detect and eliminate it.  Radon is a colorless, odorless, tasteless gas that is a byproduct of uranium which seeps into homes through cracks, sump pumps and crawl spaces.

headline: Beneath the street, a deadly train ride
abstract: The deadliest train crash in the history of the South Eastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority ocurred when a bolt designed to hold the train's engine in place came loose, causing the engine to dangle until it became caught in a switch, throwing 3 passenger cars off track.The crash occurred on the Market-Frankford line in an underground tunnel west of 30th Street Station.

headline: Casey signs referee assault bill
abstract: Gov. Casey signed a bill that would stiffen penalties for those who assault sports officials.

headline: State Prisons: Dark to Dawn?
abstract: Problems in the PA Prison System have gone from bad to worse. The state's 15 prisons are 60 percent overcrowded. A temporary solution is to cram 1,179 beds into the system. Ideally inmates should have the opportunity to rehabilitate themselves through programs.

headline: PPG Will Close Missouri Glass Plant
abstract: PPG Industries plans to close its Crystal City, Missouri glass plant by 1991, saying that they couldn't justify the cost of replacing equipment in the 100-year-old plant.  The 273 workers at the plant will be laid off.

headline: Casey spokesman says Hafer's 'secret deal' comment based on speculation
abstract: Spokesman Vince Carocci for PA Governor Robert Casey said that Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer has consistently gotten her facts wrong and "has fabricated political charges." He said that her allegation that Casey is planning a "secret deal" to help Philadelphia is untrue.

headline: House Candidate's Residency Doubted
abstract: Jefferson County chairman of the Republican Committee, John B. Brandon, requested an election probe into the residency of Democratic candidate Daniel J. Shannon. Brandon also wrote Secretary of the PA Commonwealth James J. Haggerty, requesting Shannon's name be removed from election ballots for US Congress should it be determined he does not meet requirements. Brandon contests the Jefferson County Courthouse has no real estate records for Brandon.

headline: Safest time to pass legislative pay hike
abstract: Rumors of legislative pay increases have peaked since the General Assembly is in the lame-duck period of the 1989-90 session. This period is normally the safest time politically for state lawmakers to pass offensive legislation, as pay raises approved now will not be as easily remember in elections two years later. PA legislators make on average $47,000 per year and PA Governor Robert P. Casey will earn $105,000 per year in 1991.

headline: Redistricting battle expected to pit city against suburbs
abstract: Early census figures show that Allegheny County may lose a seat or two in the PA state House, which will require redistricting in the state, which in Allegheny County may pit the city of Pittsburgh against its suburbs. There will likely be contention over which legislators' seats will be eliminated as well.

headline: Clean Air
abstract: This article lists the Pennsylvania cities that exceeded federal air quality standards for smog pollution in 1988.  The numbers were reported by the federal Environmental Protection Agency.

headline: Groups express anxiety on cutbacks if Casey's budget is penny-pinching
abstract: Officials representing local agencies in Pittsburgh expressed concern that Gov. Casey's proposed 1990-91 budget would force service cutbacks. State revenue collections have dropped $108 million below estimates in the current year, prompting legislative aides, lobbyists and others to predict that Casey will be forced to make budget cuts.

headline: Director of Carlisle shelter quits
abstract: The Executive Director of James Wilson Safe Harbour has resigned, citing mounting on the job frustrations. He called the support services inadequate.

headline: Flex better way to teach
abstract: The editorial board supports the Flex pilot program in the York City School District, saying it allows educators to be flexible and get to know their students better. Both teachers and parents had to sign contracts to support the program, and increases in students' grades reflect this commitment. By allowing teachers to interact with students in situations away from the school, the program shows students the relevance of education.

headline: Fair Hearing Needed
abstract: Editors urge the Throop Property Owners Association to study the positive and negative affects of accepting an offer from Keystone Landfill for a sewer line which will facilitate leachate drainage. The US Environmental Protection Agency and the PA Department of Environmental Resources sanction leachate drainage through sewer pipes. As Keystone offered to pay he Lackawanna River Basin Sewer Authority for installation of the system, the association should not pass it up without research.

headline: Blanket Hill highway work on schedule
abstract: PA Department of Transportation community relations coordinator Ken Rich announced the joint federal and state funded project to add a passing lane to Route 422 is on schedule. The project will cost $1.7 million. It was contracted with Bracken Construction Co. Upon its completion, two more projects will be undertaken.

headline: Casey tells judicial conference of PENNFREE program's success
abstract: PA Governor Casey attended a national judicial conference to speak about the PENNFREE anti-drug program.  Also speaking at the conference were NY Governor Mario Cuomo and Soviet Justice Minister Veniamin Yakovlev.

headline: State reviewing changes proposed in Concern case
abstract: The PA Department of Public Welfare (DPW) are reviewing policy changes a local foster care agency has proposed following charges that a staff member sexually abused teenagers during admissions interviews.  The agency's Concern board granted agency director Paul Ernst's request for a paid leave of absence and will operate with a provisional license until it meets state demands for a policy outline.

headline: Preate urges enactment of antitrust legislation
abstract: PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. urged the enactment of antitrust legislation in Pennsylvania while appearing before the PA state Senate Judiciary Committee.  Preate pointed out that PA is the only state without an antitrust law and that it is necessary to protect consumers from unfair business practices.

headline: Casey takes in campaign money, hands out praise
abstract: The Casey camp held a fundraiser yesterday for supporters, some of whom were looking to advance their personal interests by attending.  Gov. Casey voiced his support for several Democratic incumbents and candidates in the upcoming election.

headline: House hopeful opposes filing tax returns, he says at hearing
abstract: Max Lampenfeld, a Republican candidate for the 106th District state House seat, say he does not believe in filing tax returns.  His position has gotten him into trouble with the IRS, as they claim that Lampenfeld owes more than $100,000.  Lampenfeld has to comply with the IRS request to produce documents and records to determine how much he owes or he will be held in contempt of the court.

headline: Saidel accuses administration of ignoring problems
abstract: Philadelphia's chief auditor and City Controller, Jonathan Saidel, released several audits, claiming that the Goode administration has ignored administrative problems that have been costing the city money, though they could easily be fixed.

headline: Residents complain of ATV driving
abstract: Township supervisors of West Cornwall heard residents complaints concerning All Terrain Vehicles being driven through township alleys. Supervisors encouraged residents to notify police of such incidents, which are illegal, but specified police cannot pursue ATVs through fields, as they are not designed for such purposes. Supervisors also conducted other business, including the reading of a proposed ordinance to form a municipal authority. A hearing date was set for its consideration.

headline: Clinger Testifies at Hearing on Earthquake Legislation
abstract: A congressional panel held hearings to strengthen federal earthquake legislation  Congressman Bill Clinger explained to the panel that the eastern United States is in danger of a major earthquake and is not prepared for such a disaster.  He urged the committee to help local governments with developing cost-effective means of educating their populations and updating building codes.

headline: Hafer agrees to sign documents for state borrowing
abstract: Auditor General Barbara Hafer said that she would sign documents allowing the state to borrow $905 million, ending a three week quarrel with PA Governor Robert P. Casey's administration. Hafer previously refused to sign the tax-anticipation notes because she contended that Casey did not accurately describe the state's fiscal health to potential investors. Hafer has said that the state is headed for a $1 billion deficit and that Casey pushed payments back to make the budget appear balanced. The disagreement delayed payments of state money to some school districts.

headline: Doctors fight limits on fees they charge senior citizens
abstract: Medical societies and other doctors' groups are fighting a law that would set a cap on the fees they charge for senior citizens under Medicare.  They claim that the state does not have the authority to make legislations concerning Medicare, which is a federal program.

headline: Fre ind: Use reserves for education
abstract: PA Rep. Stephen F. Friend proposed to use Rainy Day Funds for special education. The idea is supported by some Democrats. PA Governor Casey proposes to pay for special education through a reimbursement system. A spokesman for PA Budget Secretary Michael H. Hershock, Rod says the General Assembly should put control of Rainy Day Funds in the hands of the Governor. Bond ratings in PA continue to hold steady, partly because the Governor has yet to spend the state's reserves.

headline: Farmer: Pump project all wet
abstract: Jerry Harris' property in East Rockhill Twp, Bucks Co., has been massively eroded due to the increased water flow in a creek now fed with water from the Point Pleasant pump, which directs water to the Limerick nuclear plant.  Harris' experience, however, is an exception, not the norm.  The new water flow has not produced such extensive erosion in other areas.

headline: Blue Route delay is expected Completion now seen by late 1991
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation has said that the long-awaited Blue Route interchange will be completed in late 1992. Parts of the highway are already built but there are still parts that are unpaved and behind schedule, so PennDOT has decided not to open the highway in sections.

headline: Casey vetoes widow's tax bill
abstract: PA Governor Casey vetoed a bill that would have phased out the state's 6% widow's tax, saying that it would primarily benefitted the rich.  The move could be risky, with an election less than a month away. Casey has vowed to sign a law that would target the "truly needy" for relief from the tax.

headline: State strengthens fight against drugs
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey and PA Attorney General Ernest Preate Jr signed an agreement strengthening the cooperative efforts of State Police and the Attorney General's Office in fighting illegal drug trafficking in PA. It covers office location, staffing, equipment, expenses, asset sharing, duties, and dispute resolution.

headline: Prescription for change
abstract: As the system of state insurance regulation comes under fire nationwide, many expect House chairman of the Oversight and Investigations subcommittee John Dingell to introduce legislation that would set federal guidelines for insurance regulation. Joseph Belth, editor of the Insurance Forum agreesE there needs to be better coordination between the efforts of the National Association of Insurance Commissioners.

headline: Casey to picnic at Selinsgrove cottage
abstract: PA Governor Casey will hold a fundraiser picnic for supporters on the Isle of Que.

headline: House Leader Facing Scathing Attacks at Home
abstract: William DeWeese has become the majority leader of the PA House of Representatives and is being challenged by Farley Toothman in the upcoming primary. Toothman charges DeWeese with having too many loyalties in Harrisburg and losing touch with the constituents in the 50th District.

headline: Saidel sccuses administration of ignoring problems
abstract: Philadelphia's chief auditor and City Controller, Johnathan Saidel, released several audits, claiming that the Goode administration has ignored administrative problems that have been costing the city money, though they could easily be fixed.

headline: Residents Turn Red Over Pastel City Hall
abstract: New Kensington Mayor John Monaco's idea to paint the recently moved and renovated city hall bright shades of color elicited a strong negative response from residents. Architect Dave Vargo expects the color scheme to become a campaign issue in the next election, but welcomes the controversy that has gotten people involved in political processes. A poll is being conducted by the local Arnold Feed and Garden Center in the form of ballots, with proceeds going to the Salvation Army.

headline: Steps to stop oil price gouging
abstract: Three state attorneys general--including Attorney General Ernie Preate of Pennsylvania--are on a task force that is preparing a report of the heating oil and propane crisis of last year.  The crisis, brought on by an unprecedented cold wave, led to an unconscionable increase in heating oil and propane prices.  The task force is expected to release its findings and recommendations this summer, and the article lists 12 steps that should be followed to ensure consumer protection.

headline: Hafer hammers Casey on finances; says deficit will hit $1 billion
abstract: PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer accused PA Governor Robert P. Casey's administration of fiscal mismanagement that will cause the budget to be $1 billion in deficit by the end of the fiscal year. Hafer said she would support increases in the personal income and gasoline taxes and opposes a state bailout for debt-ridden Philadelphia.

headline: Donor organs needed locally as well as nationally
abstract: Hazel Pursel, nursing manager of Lewistown Hospital's dialysis unit, doesn't have to look far to see that donor organs are needed locally. She just has to open her office door. When kidneys fail to properly cleanse impurities from the blood, dialysis is necessary. While patients can live indefinitely on dialysis to allows for little flexibility in their daily lives. Only 9 of her patients have received a kidney in 9 years.

headline: Gettysburg school board eyes 10-mill hike
abstract: Gettysburg school board directors expressed interest in a 10-mill tax increase for an estimated budget of $18.5 million, up from their current budget of $17.8 million.  The new costs faced by the school board include three elementary school staff positions, refunding an elementary home-school visitor, and permanent program funding for the Gettysburg Adolescent Parenting Program.  The directors will have another meeting to discuss the budget.

headline: Farmers mail cans to legislators to protest roadside-trash dangers
abstract: Farmers mailed discarded empty beverage cans to lawmakers yesterday to lobby for a law providing refundable beverage containers, which would make littering less common and make trash-cleanup slightly profitable.

headline: BPU Acts for Trash Truck Safety After Pennsy Sues, Cites Crashes
abstract: New Jersey state regulators ordered safety inspections of all interstate trucks hauling trash.

headline: Chancery-court plan questions answered
abstract: William H. Clark, a lawyer from Pittsburgh, writes to answer a few questions posed by the Patriot about his proposal to create a chancery court system in PA.

headline: State to automatically deduct wages for child support
abstract: The Federal government instituted laws for employers to deduct child support from pay, said Judge Gene Strassburger, head of the Family Division of Allegheny County Common Pleas Court. President of Fathers United for Equal Rights Jim Clonan says the law is unconstitutional. Gary Stout, manager of the Family Division says it will alert organizations like the Pittsburgh Chamber of Commerce. Director of the PA Welfare Department's bureau of child support enforcement Jack Stuff predicted most employers would not attempt to recoup administrative fees.

headline: Prescriptions for change
abstract: Box inside an article that gives suggestions on how the state regulation of insurance companies. They include minimum standards and more federal involvement.

headline: Casey To Tap Lottery Reserve, Paper Says
abstract: Losses to the state Lottery Fund will force PA Governor Robert Casey to take $120 million in a reserve account for prescription drug discounts for senior citizens. The Lottery Fund is expected to go broke without the reserve, though budget secretary Michael Hershock believes altering Lottery procedures may provide the fund with a surplus instead. House Republican budget analyst Michael Rosenstein called the plan illegal and dangerous. Senior Citizens may sue to prevent Casey's action.

headline: House Leaders Boost Office Expense Account by $350
abstract: PA House leaders voted to raise the amount members get for district office expenses from $450 to $800 per month to go toward rent, utilities, and equipment and furniture rentals. Executive director of the Bipartisan Management Committee Robert Hendershot said the change would enable lawmakers to pay for office costs out of one account. The increase was approved during an informal meeting of the House Rule Committee and was made by consensus.

headline: Sample was too small
abstract: Frank P. Lalley of Upper Gwynedd writes to criticize The Reporter for publish the results of a survey rating the local state legislators, for which 85 people were polled. He also says that most of those polled didn't respond, and that some were lobbyists, another possible reason for the inaccuracy of the survey.

headline: Senate panel votes to permit wage-tax hike
abstract: Legislation to allow local governments to raise their wage tax by 1% was approved by a PA Senate committee. The measure now moves to the Senate floor. The increased wage tax would keep local governments from increasing property tax. None of the changes would take place without approval by voters in local referendums.

headline: Tests sought to see if oil seeped into ground water
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection is trying to determine if the Allegheny-River oil spill contaminated ground water.  So far, there is no evidence that ground water or wells have been contaminated.  The agency is also asking the company responsible for the spill, Buckeye Pipe Line Co., to conduct tests.

headline: House GOP task force urges new direction for state economy
abstract: A PA House Republican task force is recommending a new direction for the state's economy to try and avoid the fate of other Northeastern states, which have had to increase taxes and reduce services.

headline: Donor organs needed locally as well as nationally
abstract: Nursing manager of Lewistown Hospital's dialysis unit explains the need for organ donors, especially kidney donors as she describes the life of a kidney dialysis patient. The article includes information on organ donation via the United Network of Organ Sharing and the Delaware Valley Transplant Program as well as the procedure through which hospitals must register as transplant institutitions.

headline: Gov. Casey finds a friend in Pennsylvania teachers
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Education Association endorsed Governor Casey in the gubernatorial campaign, citing his efforts to improve teachers' starting salaries, reducing dropout rates, and encouraging schools to improve college enrollment rates.

headline: Fast-food packages should be recycled
abstract: Pa. Sen. Michael Fisher proposed legislation to require restaurants in communities required to participate in the state's curb-side recycling program to recycle 30 percent of their food and drink packaging. The law would apply to all communities, but those outside the curb-side requirement would be given a longer to comply. Senate Bill 1219 requires environmentally friendly packaging to bear a biodegradable symbol and contain no chemical toxins. The Senator encourages the House to pass the legislation.

headline: 'Bread and butter' driver license law signed
abstract: PA Governor Casey signed a law allowing drivers to regain driving privileges if their license is suspended in a minor infraction. Those wishing to qualify must prove their license is necessary to continue working or schooling. Truckers and heavy machinery operators must take a written test to renew their licenses by April 1992. The PA law does not supersede the Federal law which suspends licenses of drivers speeding in excess of 15 mph 3 or more times.

headline: Charges Refiled Against Former Newspaper Editor
abstract: Charges filed against Tribune-Democrat editor-in-chief Theodore Beitchman by Bucks County Chief Assistant District Attorney Ted Fritsch alleged the editor posed as a state deputy attorney general to make threatening phone calls to a couple whose son was involved in a traffic accident with Beitchman's brother. The charges were dismissed for insufficient evidence at a preliminary hearing by District Justice Susan McEwen. Fritsch has refiled, citing more evidence has been found.

headline: State troopers are honored
abstract: Eight state police officers were awarded PA Commissioner's Letters of Commendation for their contributions to the department's Operation Whiteline drug interdiction program. Two of those troopers had previously received awards at the PA State Police Academy, presented by PA Governor Robert Casey.

headline: Proposed anti-takeover bill could lead to loss jobs
abstract: Criticising PA's anti-takeover bill which is pending because it will lead to job loss. Making it nearly impossible to takeover a company, firms will have little incentive to become competitive, thereby eventually going under.

headline: Casey touts own record to Democratic women
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey is confident that he is in tune with PA voters and it is rattling off his accomplishments to the state's most influential women. While they agreed with most of his views, they did not agree with his pro-life stance.

headline: House provides some races
abstract: Two of the three people running to represent the 81st legislative district in the PA state house aren't talking much about the upcoming election.  State House Minority Whip Samuel E. Hayes Jr. has represented the district for over two decades and is running for reelection.  Huntingdon County Register and Recorder John P. Mills and three-term Huntingdon County Commissioner Larry O. Sather are challenging Representative Hayes for his seat.

headline: Sanitation Authority Overspending
abstract: As conditions worsen, the Lower Lackawanna Valley Sanitary Authority made a report of its overspending for January and February

headline: Senate panel votes to permit wage-tax hike
abstract: The Local Government Committee voted on and approved the Republican local tax-reform plan, sponsored by the Senate President Pro tem Robert Jubelirer. The plan calls for counties, municipalities, and school districts to impose or increase wage taxes as an alternative to the heavily used property tax.

headline: Smoking by aid recipients targeted
abstract: State Senator John E. Peterson, chairman of the Senate Health and Welfare Committee, introduced legislation that would provide 133,000 to the Department of Public Welfare for people who use prescriptions or enter programs designed to help them quit smoking.  Studies have shown that providing funds for cessation programs and medications may in fact be less expensive than providng outlays for the long-term health problems associated with smoking.

headline: How lawmakers voted on budget
abstract: An article describes lawmakers from both parties reactions to the $12.2 billion budget passed by the legislature. Supporters call the tight budget necessary to survive the economic downturn. However critics say the budget, which does not call for a tax increase to raise revenue, inappropriately garners revenue from programs not meant to be used as sources and will invariably need revenue from a tax increase. PA Governor Casey approved the budget.

headline: Don't cut MH-HR
abstract: Anne Kline, a York/Adams County Mental Health and Mental Retardation program board member, is outraged by PA Department of Welfare John White's order that all MH-MR administrators cut their budgets by 6 percent. When Kline first wrote Governor Casey in March, she received promises of a 7.3 percent budget increase for programs. When the Governor and other high-level employees are ready to take a pay cut of six percent, then they can try to reduce the budget for MH-MR programs.

headline: Gov. Casey has boosted education
abstract: Deputy chief of staff and secretary to PA Governor Robert P. Casey's Cabinet, Helen D. Wise responds to the editorial board's endorsement of Republican Barbara Hafer and an editorial on education. Wise criticizes Hafer's contradictory statements regarding Philadelphia's fiscal crisis and refusal to sign tax anticipation notes despite Wall Street bond counsel approval of them. Wise claims that the editorial quoted 1987 education figures that don't accurately reflect Casey's increase of the minimum starting teacher salary, and loan forgiveness, "Lead Teacher" and school performance incentive programs.

headline: Fat, waste in state government recycled into cash
abstract: Despite claims that the commonwealth of PA has tightened its belt and is a lean operation, the truth is that there are tons of fat to be found every year in the state government. State waste is outlined and estimated at 15 tons. The state has started saving this and turning it into money. Sale of debris last year was $1.25 million.

headline: Buckle up: Troopers plan belt-use drive
abstract: PA Turnpike officials and the PA police are planning a seat belt-use drive over Labor Day weekend.

headline: Child Abuse Program Gets Cheers, Boos
abstract: In a letter, a Lewistown parent both praised and criticized The Mifflin County School District's pilot program on child abuse prevention.

headline: State, counties reach accord
abstract: The Casey administration and PA's 67 counties agreed to settle a suit over child protection funding with a promise of an additional $17.5 million next year plus a promise not to underfund programs in the future.  The counties have persistently complained that the state requires the counties to carry out programs but does not provide funding.  The announcement was made by PA Governor Casey and Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode.

headline: PUC rejects 9-1-1 funding, Officials mulling new plans
abstract: Bucks County Commissioners Chairman Andrew L. Warren says the county plans to implement 911 service, with or without a state funding mechanism. After the PA Public Utilities Commission denied a request to earmark a settlement between the PA Consumer Advocate and Bell of Pennsylvania for a statewide 911 system, legislators are seeking other ways to fund 91.PA Rep. Raymond Blunt Jr. favors a local surcharge but Rep. Robert Godshall favors low cost loans. However the state budget is tight, and loans are unlikely.

headline: Casey TV ads begin re-election campaign
abstract: PA Governor Casey's TV ad campaign kicks off today, as his first four commercials begin airing.  His overall TV campaign is expected to cost between $3.5 and $4 million.

headline: House Race Very Tight
abstract: At press time, the 6th Legislative District race in Crawford County between Republican incumbent Connie G. Maine and Democrat Teresa E. Brown was too close to call. With 43 of 44 districts tallied, Maine had 7,881 votes to Brown's 7,890. Maine is seeking her third term as representative.

headline: Santorum dissects upset win, vows never to accept pay raise
abstract: U.S. Representative-elect Rick Santorum's victory shifts the PA delegation in the U.S. House to a 12-11 majority in the GOP's favor. Santorum attributed his win to large grassroots organization and his anti-abortion position. He vowed to never accept a pay raise while in office and said he would seek seats on House committees that deal with transportation and veterans' issues, as both represent the needs of the region.

headline: 'Sick' -- and proud of it
abstract: In response to David Lynch's searing comments about the city of Philadelphia, the Inquirer staff reminds him that he would not be who he is today had he not lived in the city for years.

headline: Ideal versus Reality
abstract: Although Philadelphia District Attorney Ronald Castille has the moral highground in his dispute with the Goode administration over city prison overcrowding, the Goode administration's plan is more realistic.  Mr. Castile's plan would allow city jail inmates to earn time off their sentences through doing community work, enrolling in education programs or entering substance abuse treatment programs.  Since the city does not have the finances to support such programs, the Goode administration's plan, which reduces an inmate's sentence by two days for every week he/she is well behaved, is more realistc and practical.

headline: In Harrisburg: State facing budget deficit
abstract: PA Representative Jim Distler comments on the impending budget deficit that could be in excess of $100 million.  This deficit is hard to understand in light of the surpluses that the state had last year.

headline: Drug foundation set up, Preate says
abstract: PA Attorney Gen. Preate announced the creation of the Foundation for a Drug-Free Pennsylvania, a non-profit group that will use private donations to fight drug abuse in the workplace.  It is made up of corporate, legal, medical, and labor leaders.

headline: Gov. Wilder's Cuts: How Deep?
abstract: Virginia Governor Wilder has announced a $1.4 billion government spending cut, leaving many agencies and programs with sharp decreases in funding.  48% of his cuts are headed for the education budget, hurting public schools, colleges, and universities.

headline: Fight bigger landfill
abstract: The writer is asking for people to come out to the Department of Environmental Resources public hearing concerning the presenting of the public testimony about the proposed expansion of the Modern Landfill. The writer does not want this expansion because they believe it will add to pollution and contaminating the ground and water for many miles around it.

headline: Building Ship Wasn't Without Problems
abstract: The restoration of the US Brig Niagara in Erie ran into a few roadblocks during the project, but the final product was well worth the effort, says PA Historical and Museum Commission director Brent Glass.

headline: Child Sex-abuse case workers listed
abstract: A Dauphin County conference led to creation of a manual entitled "Child Sexual Abuse Task Force Document," which serves as a "who's who" of health professionals, and lists resources and suggestions officials hope will inspire caseworkers to become more trained and knowledgeable. Copies are being distributed to area school districts, police, district justice offices, hospitals and human services. Kathy Wingert, county assistant district attorney, estimated abuse cases rises 10 percent annually.

headline: State: Police mobile station rounds the bureaucratic bend
abstract: The purchase of a mobile police station, made possible by a $200,000 federal grant from the Federal Bureau of Justice, was proposed for use in Germantown and other high-crime areas in  Philadelphia.  Despite U.S. Senator John Heinz and District Attorney Ronald D. Castille's promise, the mobile station has yet to be opened.  Captain Chris Braun hopes the station will arrive soon but approval is still needed from Philadelphia Mayor Goode, among other city bureaucrats.

headline: Racing panel says no to Paradise betting parlor
abstract: The PA Horse Racing Commission denied an application from Penn National Race Course to convert a restaurant in Paradise Twp., Lancaster County, into an off-track better parlor. Local residents and politicians opposed the prospective parlor, saying that it would hurt the area's family-oriented tourism and attract crime and misery, though the racing commission said that it rejected the parlor because of traffic, sewage, and classiness, not morality, which is says has already been decided by the state legislature.

headline: Casey Unwraps Plans for High Tech in State
abstract: Governor Casey declared outlined a new state technology policy in Philadelphia emphasizing his determination to make Pennsylvania the leader in high technology for the coming decade.

headline: Housing chief for a day
abstract: Pittsburgh's Mayor Masloff blocked the city Housing Authority's appointment of its new Executive Director. Masloff and other officials were angered that the board made the decision behind closed doors and failed to interview other candidates.

headline: Saurman paints gloomy picture of state finances
abstract: PA Representative George Saurman says state government faces an unprecedented financial challenge next year, but don't look for the PA Legislature to cut lawmakers salaries, perks or benefits. He hopes to capture some common sense ideas in his suggestion box. He believes everyone should be looking for places to cut government spending.

headline: State examining legality of plan to loan city $50 million
abstract: State officials are uncertain whether they can legally loan Philadelphia $50 million to help the city out of its financial bind. Unless the city sells $375 million in short-term loan notes, Mayor Wilson Goode warned the city will run out of cash by December 1 without help from the state and Wall Street. PA Treasurer Katherine Baker Knoll is restricted by law to investments with a solid credit rating. Philadelphia's bonds were downgraded to junk-bond status by Wall Street rating firms.

headline: Singel is slated to speak at annual Democrat dinner
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel is slated to be the keynote speaker at the annual Berks County Democratic Spring Fling dinner.  As Lieutenant Governor, Singel presides over the state Senate and is chairman of the state Board of Pardons.

headline: Jobless
abstract: Pennsylvania's unemployment rate increase half a percentage point last month even though the state recorded a record-high labor force.

headline: Dull ache of paper work driving dentists from welfare program
abstract: The article reports on one dentist who has alerted Secretary of the PA Department of Welfare John F. White that she will no longer see patients covered by Medicaid. For this dentist, it is because of the paperwork, however President of the PA Dental Association Dr. Herman Aqua says for most, it is because the state's reimbursement rate has dropped from 75 percent of the fee charged to privately insured patients to less than 50 percent, barely enough to cover overhead.

headline: Governors Outline Specific Education Goals by Year 2000
abstract: The National Governors Association approved six education objectives:  Readiness, School Completion, Student Achievement and Citizenship, Mathematics and Science, Adult Literacy and Lifetime Learning, and Safe, Disciplined, and Drug-Free Schools.

headline: Fines studied against USX for emissions at Clairton
abstract: A power failure at USX Corporation's Clairton Coke Works caused the emission of raw coke oven gas for three hours last Friday. According to Guillermo Cole, the county Health Department, PA Department of Environmental Resources, and federal Environmental Protection Agency are collaborating to investigate the emission, with the possibility of penalizing USX. Groups such as Group Against Smog and Pollution, the Sierra Club and Residents Against Chemical Environment protested for fines and increased regulations on the part of USX during a news conference at the county courthouse.

headline: Building Ship Wasn't Without Problems
abstract: The restoration of the US Brig Niagra in Erie ran into a few roadblocks during the project, but the final product was well worth the effort, says PA Historical and Museum Commission director Brent Glass.

headline: Children's Agency Expects License
abstract: Officials of Butler County's Children and Youth Agency expect the agency's license to be fully reinstated based on corrections made to practices violating state laws. Case loads were depleted to the max cases allowed, and an additional supervisor hired to manage the ratio of caseworker to supervisor. The agency is accepting cases on a priority basis, encouraging caseworkers to work through problems more quickly and efficiently, said executive director Joseph McCloskey.

headline: State's case against fund-raiser crippled by ruling
abstract: A professional fund-raiser, Events International, charged with cheating non-profit groups and the public may continue operating for now a judge has ruled. The attorney general's office is seeking a permanent injunction to bar Events from PA. Judge Silvestri said the state failed to prove Events engaged in fraudulent or deceptive solicitation practices. Events ran fundraising for the Bucks County Police Association, Central Bucks Ambulance and Recue Unit, and the American Handicapped Association.

headline: Raising the hotel-room tax
abstract: The editorial supports the idea of raising the hotel-room tax in Pittsburgh, which would add significant amounts of out-of-town dollars to the Convention and Visitors Bureau's budget, providing funding for convention centers and promotion of tourism and travel in the city.  The editorial suggests that the PA legislature take up the issue.

headline: Casey visit, check help a candidate
abstract: Democratic PA Representative Ralph Kaiser visited Castle Shannon, a Philadelphia suburb that is part of the district whose seat he is fighting to retain this election cycle, and was joined by PA Governor Robert Casey, who voiced support for Kaiser. Kaiser also presented a $10,000 check to a Castle Shannon senior citizens group.

headline: How much is that one right there?
abstract: The cartoon shows a cash-laden incumbent pointing to a Congressional district map and asking "How much is that one right there?"

headline: Saurman paints gloomy picture of state's finances
abstract: PA Representative George Saurman suggested constituents use a "comments box" to energize the state government's perspective in a year when up to a billion dollar deficit is projected. Nevertheless, Saurman said he does not see the Legislature changing its operating procedures, which include travel provisions for conferences in exotic, out of state locations.

headline: Ten Ways to Turn DC Around
abstract: David Osbourne, who has studied the way governments may be modified by adopting principles of market economics and competition, shares ten suggestions with new Washington, D.C. Mayor Sharon Pratt Dixon. His most important principles involve pointing outing the bureaucratic monopoly of government. Osbourne cites numerous examples of improved government in areas where government was forced to compete with private enterprise and nonprofit agencies.

headline: Repeated delays of PEI's merger draws stockholders' ire
abstract: Although the merger between PEI and NUI corporations has been delayed three times, stockholders say the delays will not change their feelings or final votes on the merger.  Last year, PEI, the parent company of Pennsylvania Gas and Water Company, agreed to merge with the NUI corporation of New Jersey.

headline: Jobless jump: Blip or bellwether?
abstract: State labor analysts believe PA's jump in the unemployment rate in October to 6.1 percent, up from 5.5 percent in September, as reported by the U.S. Labor Department, is probably an aberration. The editorial board suggests that the state's economy has indeed become "sluggish and that the overall trend is toward higher unemployment, despite relative economic stability in Central PA.

headline: Employers, insurers wrangle over who pays for drug rehabilitation
abstract: A "hidden front" in the war on drugs is in the fights over who pays for rehabilitation of drug addicts, their employers or the insurance companies.  Many addicts do not undergo the suggested treatments for their addictions because their insurance companies will not pay for them.

headline: Grads' job prospects little changed
abstract: Mimi Collins of the College Placement Council said recruitment of recent college graduations is about the same this year as in the year previous. Companies are enthusiastically hiring entry-level employees in the face of a possible labor shortage on the down the road. Students in environmental engineering and the math and sciences fields in general are in high demand. Students on the east coast appear to have been negatively affected by recent scandals on Wall Street while West Coast students are faring well with foreign firms.

headline: Fire victims still skeptical
abstract: Skeptical residents with houses around the burned St .Jude Polymer Corp. plant say they will wait for soot and soil sample results before they stop questioning the safety of their houses. As two PA Department of Environmental Resources representatives took samples in and around the most severely damaged home, residents waited on their porches for DER's word on specially what would be sampled from which houses. The samples are mostly soot and being scraped off mainly windows and mirrors.

headline: Butler Area Transit System Changes Hands
abstract: The Butller Township Joint Municipal Transit Authority is the new owner of the Butler Area Transportation system after voting Wednesday to accept responsibility for the system.

headline: Childwatch.
abstract: The editorial board notes that there is only one city-funded residential treatment program for Philadelphia adolescents with substance abuse problems. It holds 54.

headline: State's law a model for the rest of the nation
abstract: The Protection from Abuse Act passed in 1976 was the first of its kind in the nation to be adopted and has since been viewed as a model for other state legislative acts.  The legislation arose from the need to expand public awareness about domestic violence.  Article discusses provisions under the law.

headline: Regulator's Failure to Halt Insurer's Slide Shows Flaws in System
abstract: Life Assurance Company of Pennsylvania has been on a national watch list of shaky insurers. It was supposed to sell its policies to another insurer and get out of the business and so officials decided to give them more time even though they were over drawn by $2.8 million. They slowly stopped paying most claims and angry phone calls came pouring in. It represents the flaws in the regulation of insurance companies across the country. Overall the article hopes that the government will learn from this failure and will regulate the insurance companies more with check ins and other measures.

headline: Casey Will Debate Hafer Next Month
abstract: The League of Women Voters announced a televised debate on Oct. 9 between PA Governor Casey and Barbara Hafer, the gubernatorial candidates.  The candidates will answer questions posed by a panel of journalists, who will be selected from across the state.

headline: How They Voted
abstract: A list of how area Congressmen voted on a few key issues.

headline: Saving Philadelphia
abstract: The city of Philadelphia has appealed to state officials in Harrisburg for a bail-out action from the state that would allow the city to continue providing basic services as the city is facing severe financial crises.  With Philadelphia verging on bankruptcy, many state politicians don't want to commit to anything so close to elections.  If PA Governor Casey helped bail out Philadelphia, he'd lose many rural votes.

headline: Susquehanna finds money to keep going
abstract: Susquehanna Township is receiving a payback from a  $247,000 loan given to the sewer authority 20 years ago, a move that will relieve its $200,000 deficit. Commissioners will review a budget-proposal expected to include a tax increase to alleviate financial problems caused by a plunge in fees from new developments in the past year. Commission President Jack S. Pincus discussed the possibility of bringing the authority under direct control of the commission as one possible way to cut future township costs.

headline: In the Halls
abstract: This article asks four Wilkes University students why kids take illegal drugs.  Most of the students interviewed felt that peer pressure played an important role in illegal drug use.

headline: Jubelirer Disagrees
abstract: PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer takes issue with an editorial criticizing his tax restructuring proposals, noting PA Governor Casey's unsuccessful proposal excludes homestead exemption or local referendum. Jubelirer believes allowing voters control over the tax structure that gives local governments, counties, school district options is key, saying criticisms are based on Sen. Robert Mellows faulty views. Taxpayers should not have to wait til Casey or his supporters are gone to obtain tax reform.

headline: Enforce vending law, city urged
abstract: PA Health Secretary N. Mark Richards has urged Pittsburgh officials to vigorously enforce new restrictions on cigarette vending machines, which now require machines in public places to accept tokens rather than coins or bills, which will help restrict abuses of the machines by minors.

headline: Gubernatorial candidate visits her Lower Gwynedd alma mater
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Marguerite "Peg" Luksik visited her old school, Gwynedd-Mercy Academy. At the school, she spoke about her life after she graduate, and how she came to be a pro-life candidate. Luksik founded Mom's House, a group of privately-funded day care facilities for single mothers returning to high school or college.

headline: Firm hears Clarion protests, to proceed with waste plant
abstract: Despite protests from the community, Concord Resources Group will continue with its plans to build a hazardous waste plant in Clarion County if the sites meet all the technical requirements.  The company says it regrets that the plant must be built, but it's unfortunately unavoidable.

headline: Butler mayor charged with DUI: Stopped hours before MADD tree-planting ceremony
abstract: Butler Mayor Marian Taylor was charged by state police with drunk driving and speeding hours before she attended a Mothers Against Drunk Driving tree planting ceremony.  Most Butler council members were reluctant to comment on the incident.

headline: Church divorces sought. Legislator outlines plan.
abstract: PA Representative George E. Saurman of Montgomery unveiled a proposal that would allow couples to obtain a legal divorce from their church without court approval. Saurman believes that many divorces that could otherwise be resolved quickly instead result in protracted litigation because the process requires lawyers and judges. The PA Catholic Conference will likely oppose the measure and the PA Trial Lawyers Association expects the proposal to move slowly.

headline: Students, Police face Off
abstract: Police officers raided Halloween parties at Bucknell University and faced a disturbance from several hundred students. About 70 state police, 50 officers from Lewisburg and nearby communities and 60 to 70 guards from the federal prison responded. Afterwards, about 200 students met with university president Gary Sojka to protest Bucknell's alcohol policies.

headline: Relief in sight. No big issue, perhaps, unless you're in line.
abstract: The PA Legislature passed the so-called "potty parity" bill requiring a like number of toilets for men and women in public buildings, parks and other entertainment facilities. The bill will only affect new buildings and those undergoing large structural renovations, and exempts restaurants, hotels, malls and small parks. The editorial board supports the legislation and urges readers to show more respect for "the facilities we all need".

headline: Casey will not rest with Hafer in pursuit
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey holds an advantage over opponent Barbara Hafer in four fields: incumbency, money, organization and registration. Casey holds a 60 percent-plus rating in polls. The article gives analyses of the candidates' stances on car insurance, drugs, economic development, education, environment and family leave.

headline: How They Voted
abstract: The article lists how Pittsburgh area members of the PA Legislature voted on: an amendment to prohibit withholding artificial life support from a comatose pregnant woman unless there was medical determination that her unborn child could not survive; a bill giving young non-violent prisoners a chance to participate in motivational boot camps; a bill legalizing and licensing video poker machines. All but the life support amendment, which returned to the Senate, were sent to PA Governor Robert P. Casey.

headline: School Goals in Hand, Governors Face Reality
abstract: The National Governors Association began to confront the details of their education reform plan by deciding how to put the lofty goals in place and how to finance them.

headline: Tax-rate rebate deadline nears
abstract: PA Rep. Nicholas Moehlmann reminds constituents that the state's deadline to apply for property tax-rent rebates is June 30. The rebate is based on income, which cannot exceed $15,000, property tax, and rent. Eligible are those 65 and older, widows and widowers 50 and older, and disabled persons 18 and older. In the past, the PA Department of Revenue has extended the deadline, however there is no guarantee it will do so this year as well.

headline: Preate puts off session on drug unit
abstract: PA State Attorney General Ernie Preate delayed his trip to Cambria County for the formation meeting of the county drug task force.  Attorney General Preate is postponing his trip until local authorities determine whether they want one task force or two; currently there are two task forces.

headline: Jubelirer plan irresponsible
abstract: While a few parts of PA Senator Robert Jubelirer's local tax legislation cleared the Senate in in bipartisan fashion prior to the PA Legislature's adjournment for the summer, key elements of his plan hit a brick wall. It is not comprehensive or responsible. He is just trying to save face after property tax increases. He does not believe in fairness in the tax system. It includes doubling local wage tax and promises real tax cuts for the wealthy. It does not include anti-windfall provisions to guard against excessive revenue growth.

headline: Ex-Byberry patients' families vent anger over closing
abstract: The families of former Philadelphia State Hospital patients got their day in court voicing anger and frustration over the hospital closing in an emotional hearing before a federal judge. At the same time several said their relatives were doing better than expected living in the community with the support of newly created programs.

headline: HACC gives contracts for automotive center
abstract: Officials of Harrisburg Area Community College have awarded contracts totaling $3.2 million for the construction of a new automotive technology center, which will have 13 automobile bays some of which will be incorporated into classrooms.

headline: Fish stamp becomes law Jan. 1
abstract: PA's trout/salmon stamp will become effective Jan. 1, 1991. Anglers will need a $5 stamp to take, kill or possess trout or salmon starting next year. The stamps can be bought from the same dealers and offices that sell fishing licenses for the PA Fish Commission. Money from the stamps will be used for fish propagation, renovation of hatcheries, fisheries habitat and other cold-water programs.

headline: By George, Go for It, Gekas!
abstract: The editorial board supports US Congressman George Gekas' plans to introduce legislation to stop the nationwide recession and spur completion of the Route 15 improvement project. Gekas will push for the release of monies from the federal Hughway Trust Fund, meritting, in the board's opinion, exemption from congressional term limitations should an amendment to that end be passed. Gekas outlined his Persian Gulf and energy policies in an address to the Harrisburg Lions Club.

headline: City crime rise twice state rate
abstract: The PA State Police Uniform Crime Report revealed an overall rise of crime in Philadelphia at twice the rate of the rest of the state and surrounding suburbia. The largest percentage crime increase in the city was for homicide. Serious and Part II crimes in the state rose by 4.6 percent. Arrests concerning drug violations increased by 17 percent. Only the percent of rape cases showed a decline in the state, and by a slight percentage.

headline: Supports fire volunteers
abstract: Charles J. Testa, a past president of a local volunteer fire department in Lansdale, writes to support PA state Senator Edwin Holl, whose performance he says has been questioned lately. Testa says that Holl always supported volunteer fire departments with his votes and with genuine concern.

headline: Restaurant allowed to keep liquor permit during court fight
abstract: Cumberland County Judge Edgar B. Bayley ruled against the PA Liquor Control Board, saying a former Mechanicsburg bar that has reopened as a family restaurant can keep its liquor license while the LCB challenges in Commonwealth Court an earlier Bayley decision involving the bar. Francis X. O'Brien Jr., chief counsel for the LCB, said his agency is considering appealing the most recent ruling to Commonwealth Court as well.

headline: Casey Wins, but 17 Incumbents Lose
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey captured 66 of Pennsylvania's 67 counties to win his re-election bid against opponent Auditor General Barbara Hafer. Democrats increased their presence in the PA House and two ballot questions allowing the state to loan money to fund volunteer fire and rescue companies, and county prison renovations were also passed. Hafer said she would continue to monitor Casey's state finances and said he would likely have to raise taxes in the next year.

headline: How they voted
abstract: The article reviews recent action in the US Congress and lists how legislators from the area voted on the various issues.

headline: School salaries in Allegheny County compare well
abstract: Among PA's 501 districts, the gap between the average salary of the best- and worst-paid teachers in 1989-90 was more than $30,000 a year. In Allegheny County, that gap was less than half as much. Robert Baldis, director of Allegheny County/Pittsburgh for the PA State Education Association said despite success in raising salaries, inequalities still exist. Teachers in West Mifflin have the highest salaries due to consolidation operations and layoffs that ensured that the vast majority of teachers have 16 or more years of experience.

headline: The downhill ride of a municipal rattletrap
abstract: An article traces a history of corruption and mismanagement in Philadelphia extending back even to 1875, resulting today in the city's financial crisis. Public trust in the city has waned, even in the Legislature there is racial discrimination preventing the city from receiving necessary funds. Federal aid to the city has declined, taxes are soaring, and the election campaigns of numerous mayors promising balanced budgets have proven untrue.

headline: null
abstract: Because they made material misrepresentations to the U.S. Treasury Department, Bell Atlantic has been temporarily barred from doing business with the federal government.  One of Bell Atlantic's subsidiaries is accused of including misleading information in a bid for a 100 million dollar contract, and a contract will not be awarded until the Treasury Department completes an investigation of the alleged misrepresentation.

headline: Jubelirer warns state is $1 billion short
abstract: PA Senator Robert Jubelirer (R-Blair) warned on Monday that PA may face a $1 billion shortfall in revenues, despite PA Governor Robert Casey's assurances that the state is in good financial shape. Though the budget is technically balanced, Jubelirer says that it's not an honest budget, and that there were several efforts to cover up deficits and that the state will pay for it in the next year.

headline: Father drops abortion request for mentally incompetent daughter
abstract: The father of a 33-year-old mentally incompetent woman dropped his request in court  that she have an abortion after hearing of the dangers of having an abortion so late in pregnancy.  The woman is in her 23rd week of pregnancy, and was apparently raped while in the care of the Daughters of Miriam Nursing Home.

headline: Hafer proposes separate educational budget for state
abstract: PA Auditor General and Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer, speaking to officials of the Altoona Area School District, proposed a separate state education budget and restructuring taxes away from a reliance on the property tax. Hafer noted education funded by the state dropped since PA Governor Robert Casey took office. Hafer claimed school districts were forced to raise property taxes. She supports PA State Sen. Robert Jubelirer's proposal to use Rainy Day Funds for education.

headline: Fish tumors baffle scientists
abstract: Public awareness of cancerous tumors plaguing catfish has been growing over the past few years. Federal and State officials of the PA Fish Commission say they don't have the money to investigate the cause. Reading, PA Mayor Warren Haggerty Jr. is concerned because tumors have appeared on fish in the water which supplies the city, prompting public outcry and a study to see if the tumors appear seasonally. Studies have not shown results and therefore have not been publicly released.

headline: Cabinet Profile - Transportation
abstract: Brief career history of Howard Yerusalim, pictured right.  Before joining Casey's cabinet in 1987 as transportation secretary, Yerusalim was the PennDOT deputy secretary for administration since 1983.

headline: City's former ban leads to suit over clubs' losses
abstract: The owners of two Harrisburg clubs are suing the city for losses suffered when the city banned their businesses for a year before the law was overturned by a state court. Commonwealth Court found the law, which closed BYOB clubs located within 500 feet of a residence or church, was an improperly enacted zoning change. Both owners are now facing either bankruptcy or outstanding bills.

headline: Supreme Court reverses death penalty for 25th straight time
abstract: The New Jersey State Supreme Court struck down the death sentence of 40-year-old Nathaniel Harvey in its 25th-straight overturning of a death penalty sentence. State Attorney General Robert Del Tufo blasted the ruling, saying that the court should simply outlaw capital punishment in the state if it is going to strike down any capital sentence that comes before it. The case will return to Superior Court in Middlesex County for retrial.

headline: Crown fights to keep reign over mall industry
abstract: Frank Pasquerilla, owner of Crown American, a development company heavily invested in building and leasing commercial properties, is bracing for the real estate market depression. Pasquerilla is slowing plans for new development, and using innovative marketing to draw in unusual leases including municipal office space in malls. Pasquerilla formerly worked for the Pennsylvania Department of Highways, the precurser to the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: S&Ls seek solace of 'savings bank' label
abstract: Several Pittsburgh-area savings institutions have changed their names to "savings banks" to distance themselves from the negative association of the label "savings and loan" with a $300 billion federal bailout and fraud. By appealing to the Banking Department, these institutions can avoid a level of federal bailout law regulation by amending their by-laws or converting their charter.

headline: Casey withdraws choice for district justice post
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey withdrew his nomination of Antonio Deraco to fill the Lebanon district justice post that was vacated with the retirement of Catherine Coyle. The nomination withdrawal reportedly came at the request of PA Senator David J. Brightbill.

headline: HUD abuses cost $2 billion, congressional report says
abstract: Congressional investigators concluded that taxpayers lost $2 billion as a result of fraud and favoritism during the administration of former Housing and Urban Development Secretary Samuel R. Pierce Jr. The report leaves to an independent counsel the question of whether to bring perjury charges against him after his denials of participation in the abuses. Also charged were Pierce's executive assistant, Deborah Gore Dean and Maryland real estate agent Marilyn Harrell.

headline: Schools, Hospitals 'Hostages,' Casey Says
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey said  Auditor General Barbara Hafer's refusal to sign $475 million in short-term loans to prevent possible funding problems, "routine business for the state," is a political maneuver. Hafer, the Republican gubernatorial candidate says that Casey is hiding a deficit that will require a sizeable tax increase and program cuts. Casey is running on a campaign of support for job creation, environmental legislation and state park funding.

headline: The unsettled tax-exempts
abstract: The editorial board argues that the Pittsburgh and Allegheny County governments and the local school district, under the pretense of tax-fairness, have been looking towards tax-exempt nonprofit institutions for payments without any apparent organization. The local taxing bodies forced the University of Pittsburgh to pay a total of $80,000 a year, in exchange for ending attempts to try to tax Pitt Stadium and the university-owned home of its president. Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff said she will seek state legislation to levy a realty tax on non-profit hospitals.

headline: Expert urges better day care
abstract: Dr. Jay Belsky, a professor in the department of human development and family studies at Penn State, argues that the quality of care in a majority of the nation's day care centers is not conducive to the emotional development of young children.  Belsky cited ratios between caregivers and children as an important metric for the quality of care, and also argued that extensive care--20-30 hours per week--during a child's first year could be detrimental to his/her development.

headline: Legislators speed up work on spending plan
abstract: Though the state's budget talks among Legislators are going smoothly for now, delays are expected over issues such as funds for school districts to pay for special education. PA House Minority Leader Matthew Ryan noted there are still two weeks left in which to pass the budget, which is why Legislators are not squabbling yet. Despite the state's gloomy revenue shortfall, the budget has increased 2.3 percent over last year's and PA Governor Casey expects that it can be balanced.

headline: Fiscally, Medicare Cuts Called a Success
abstract: While cuts in Medicare spending work well to save money for the government with few political repercussions, continued decreases in funding may start to deteriorate the quality of healthcare.

headline: Halloween party turns ugly
abstract: More than 100 police officers raided Halloween parties at Bucknell University and faced a disturbance from several hundred students. Afterwards, about 200 students met with university president Gary Sojka to protest Bucknell's alcohol policies and the 'overzealous enforcement' by campus police.

headline: Flooding Frustrates Marion Residents
abstract: Residents from near Slippery Rock Creek are plagued by flooding during rainstorms and seek help from the Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Cameron Bridge should go
abstract: The editorial board discusses Cameron Bridge, which has served Shamokin and Coal Townships through many eras, all the while being repaired and maintained. However, they assert that the bridge is now acting as a bottleneck on traffic patterns. Coal Township commissioners proposed a study into improving municipal transportation facilities, which was received favorably by Howard Yerusalim, secretary of the PA Department of Transportation. The matter must now find its way into the PA Department of Transportation's 12-year plan.

headline: Civil lawsuit filed in death of area PennDOT flagman
abstract: The wife of a PennDOT flagman killed while directing traffic is suing the construction firm for wrongful death and negligence.

headline: Supreme Court used state cases on several key issues to shape law of the land
abstract: The US Supreme Court several PA cases to help shape the laws of the land during its just completed 1989-1990 term. It did so by ruling on cases involving the death penalty, drunken drivers, pensions, and Allegheny County's overcrowded jail.

headline: Crown fights to keep reign over mall industry
abstract: Somebody comes up with a better way to cluster retail business than shopping malls. Frank Pasquerilla runs the third fastest growing mall developer. He is worried if his company doesn't take steps to hold on to tenants, they slip away and he'll be the victim. They will not be building new projects for a while, but instead taking care of what they have.

headline: Saidel's miscalculation. Never bet that things can't get worse.
abstract: Philadelphia City Controller Jonathan A. Saidel defied Mayor Wilson Goode's directive to place $52 million in an escrow account to reassure city bondholders, reasoning that the city's credit ratings couldn't get worse. However, Moody's Investors Service Inc. lowered to junk-bond level its rating on two more categories of city bonds last week. This move weakens the city's chances at finding lenders willing to provide around $300 million in short-term needs and reducing the $230 million budget deficit.

headline: Casey, Hafer agree to a televised debate
abstract: PA Governor Casey and challenger Barbara Hafer will participate in one televised debate during the campaign for the governor's office.  Hafer initially wanted to have six debates, though the Casey camp was deciding whether to debate at all, though eventually caved to pressure from the media and allowed one debate.

headline: 'I need my counselor,' he pleads
abstract: Because of Philadelphia's financial crisis, the Congreso de Latinos Unidos, Philadelphia's largest Latino social service agency, was not able to keep paying salaries and had to lay off 38 of its 100 staffers, one of whom was Valentino Burgos' drug counselor. Burgos has been hooked on heroin for 4 years but has been clean for 3 months, but says that he won't be able to stay clean very long without the support of his counselor.

headline: Schulze proposes campaign reforms
abstract: US Rep. Richard Schulze of PA supports campaign finance reform. A co-sponsor is House Republican Leader Bob Michel. Schulze's Democratic opponent Sam Streton accused him of accepting vacation offers from special interests. The bill limits PAC contributions to $1000. Schulze is ranked 7th among the state's 23 US Reps.  in the amount of money contributed to his campaigns by PACs. Schulze aids said the Congressman's announcement is not a response to Stretton's comments.

headline: Tour de 'Toona rides into sunset
abstract: The final leg of the Tour de 'Toona bicycle race was completed today without a hitch and only minor crowd problems.  Organizers are looking for next year's race to be even bigger and better.

headline: Governor boosts Philly transit
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey has proposed increasing financial support for Philadelphia's ailing mass-transit system.  Even with the proposed support, the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority's general manager says a fare increase will be needed.

headline: Legislators: Budget 'phony'
abstract: All area Republican lawmakers voted against the $12.2 billion PA budget signed into law, saying it's phony and crafted with smoke and mirrors. They believe it doesn't honestly address the state's fiscal problems and that tit puts off a likely state tax increase until after the November election.

headline: Glenolden man with AIDS sues hospital, three doctors
abstract: Glenolden resident John McKnight has sued three doctors, Episcopal Hospital and the American Red Cross, saying that doctors failed to notify him that he had been given blood contaminated with HIV, even though the doctors knew it 18 months before he was diagnosed with the disease. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court, contends that McKnight requested an AIDS test that doctors indicated was unnecessary despite their knowledge of the contamination.

headline: He Missed Law School
abstract: A man missed his first day of law school yesterday because he fell out of an airplane on a skydiving run.  His gear got caught on the plane soon after takeoff, and he landed using a tattered parachute and a convenient tree.

headline: Forest patrol commendable
abstract: Editors commend the use of forest patrol officers to maintain the integrity of lands under the care of the PA Bureau of Forestry. The Bureau's tight budget and limited resources have led to the establishment of a trial program in Lycoming and Tioga counties which has already resulted in 120 arrests for infractions. Citations include everything from littering, to cutting firewood without a permit, to all-terrain vehicle trespassing. The editors recommend the program be expanded across all state forest lands in PA.

headline: Casey approves SEPTA funds
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey signed legislation to provide $35 million to Southeastern PA Transportation Authority and almost $19 million for other transit systems. The funds will be used to overhaul trains and buses.

headline: Claims against Drexel may hit $20 billion
abstract: Lawyers for investors and companies that bought junk bonds from the investment firm Drexel Burnham Lambert Inc. filed claims for over $10 billion in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court, in addition to $6.8 billion sought by two federal thrift bailout agencies. More than 100 civil lawsuits have been filed against Drexel, who has only about $3 billion in assets. Most claims are related to Drexel's 1989 guilty plea to six felony counts including illegal trading.

headline: Suspect walks out of hearing
abstract: A prison inmate, Anthony Rivera, charged with operating a telephone fraud scheme from inside the State Correctional Institution at Pittsburgh cursed at a city magistrate and walked out of his hearing saying he did not have time to prepare his defense. He is one of about two dozen inmates at the Pittsburgh facility who have used fraudulently obtained credit card numbers to order merchandise by telephone.

headline: Cumberland approves $5.46 million refinancing
abstract: Cumberland County Commissioners approved a $5.46 million bond refinancing the a Pittsburgh firm claims will save the county more than $278,000. Under the plan the county will issued $5.46 million in bonds to be bought for $5.35 million. The bond proceeds will be used to pay off $4.95 in current interest bonds from the $14.8 million 1985 issue on Sept. 1.

headline: Saved from the abyss?
abstract: Philadelphia city officials plan to raise $300 million to head off a cash crisis by allowing short-term loans from local banks, private investors, the city's pension funds and the state teacher's retirement system. While teachers and municipal workers support the program, as do the editors, police and firefighter's unions are attempting to block a pension loan in court. The editors feel the city has tried to make loans safe; if the arrangement fails to convince investors, nothing can.

headline: Casey, Hafer argue over universities
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer has accused incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey of considering cutting the budgets of Penn State, Pitt, and Temple, which would cause tuitions to increase. Casey's aides claimed that Hafer was misrepresenting his statements. Casey did say that he would consider cutting some funds from the state's non-preferred appropriations, most of which go to the aforementioned universities, in order to help avoid a tax increase next year.

headline: In 2 days, GOP will map out its trenches
abstract: 14 Republican area leaders will sit down Thursday with county GOP chairman Charles Nahill, Jr., to decide on the two candidates they will recommend for the 1990 commissioners race in Montgomery County. The session is expected to be heated, as commissioners chairman Paul Bartle seeks his fourth term. Amidst controversy surrounding Bartle's leadership, two party factions have formed. A number of candidates, including PA Representative Jon D. Fox, are expected to challenge Bartle.
