headline: Schulze way ahead of Stretton in piling up campaign funding
abstract: US Representative Richard Schulze raised over 160 times as much money during April as Sam Stretton a Democratic challenger. Schulze received 72% of his money from political actions committees.

headline: Voters get chance to expand township boards. Supervisors in Tobyhanna and Barrett question wisdom of change from three to five person body.
abstract: Voters in Tobyhanna and Barrett Townships will vote on a referendum determining the expansion of their township board of supervisors from three to five people. Barrett Township supervisors originally refused to place the resolution on the ballot. It was added when a group of citizens presented a petition to the Monroe County Board of Election. Most board members believe the expansion is unnecessary and would cause undue complications.

headline: Northeast's woes mount as agency downgrades Conn.
abstract: Standard and Poor's has downgraded Connecticut's rating on 2.8 billion dollars of general obligation debt.  The state now jjoins Massachusetts in the ranks of recently downgraded states in the economically troubled Northeastern Unites States.  The downgrade was the result of increased budget problems.

headline: Local jobless rate up for 2nd month in a row
abstract: According to the PA Office of Employment Security, Lancaster County's unemployment rate increased slightly in August, after increasing in the previous month as well.  It now stands at 3.9%, which is still the lowest among PA's metropolitan areas.

headline: Government distributes $60 million in drug treatment grants
abstract: The US Department of Health and Human Services awarded $60 million in drug treatment grants to eight large cities and almost 100 programs aimed at youth, minorities, public housing residents and criminals. The grants are intended to increase services and develop more effective treatment methods.

headline: Higher education in the Harrisburg area
abstract: The image shows the locations of colleges and universities in the Harrisburg area and details on their funding and type.

headline: Fowl Play; Borough might ban bird feeding.
abstract: New Cumberland Borough Council is expected to vote on an ordinance that would prohibit feeding wildlife in the Front Street and Reno Avenue park. Council president John Murray says the goose and duck waste poses a health hazard to the public. PA Game Commission and U.S. Wildlife Service officials say that although the ban might not keep wildlife out of the park, it is the first step toward eliminating the problem.

headline: Casey comes to town
abstract: A picture of PA Governor Robert P. Casey attending a ground-breaking ceremony in Chippewa Township for the Beaver Valley Expressway extension project.

headline: Clarion Court Using Home Monitoring Unit
abstract: Clarion county has begun using monitored ankle bracelets on criminals as a way to track them. Two men in Clarion County have been fitted with the device.

headline: Task force agents catch drug fugitives
abstract: The Greater Pittsburgh Fugitive Task Force arrested three fugitives Tuesday. A woman who overdosed on heroin spent the night in Central Medical Center after being pulled over for a traffic violation. The woman, who had served time in the Federal Correctional Institution for women in W. VA. was wanted for violating her parole. She was picked up the next morning by a man in a car reported stolen to police. Police stopped the pair after a traffic violation. The woman is being held in Allegheny County Jail. A third man was arrested in connection with cocaine distribution.

headline: Curmudgeons find a home in Mifflintown
abstract: The editorial bemoans the state of Mifflintown, saying that "it seems that an attack of old-fogyism has struck," as the borough council has attempted to ban trick-or-treating this Halloween, citing the waves of complaints usually received on the night. The editorial says that there aren't enough young people in the area.

headline: Seyfried files union grievance
abstract: Northhampton County Executive Gerald E. Seyfried filed a union grievance against Bethlehem Steel Corp. over denial of his leave of absence. Seyfried worked as a union machinist at the plant for 25.5 years before being elected last fall. Bethlehem steel denied the request saying a leave of absence relationship with the county's top elected official might raise questions of conflict of interest.

headline: Casey, Hafer duel in race's lone debate
abstract: In last night's gubernatorial debate between incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey and Republican challenger Barbara Hafer, Casey praised PA as a "state of opportunity" making strides under his administration, but Hafer contended that the state needs "fundamental change."  The debate will likely be the only one in this year's governor's race.  The candidates attacked many of each others' stances on various issues, and also criticized comments made by the other at various times.

headline: In debate, Bradley mum on tax issue
abstract: US Senator Bill Bradley (D-NJ) and Republican challenger Christine Todd Whitman argued about federal taxes last night in their first televised debate, but Bradley once again refused to reveal his position on Governor Fflorio's unpopular $2.8 billion tax increase plan, saying that he would not "exploit" anger over state taxes "for political purposes" in an attack on the GOP.

headline: Schwartz for Senate
abstract: The editorial explains that the Inquirer is endorsing Allyson Schwartz's bid for Philadelphia's Fourth Senate District against incumbent Republican PA Senator M. Joseph Rocks. The editorial board says that Schwatz has been attacked illegitimately by Rocks as being a Philadelphia "outsider," though she has spent her entire adult life in the city, and has impressive credentials. It also explains that it is difficult to tell what Rocks stands for, as he has changed his position on several issues through his political career.

headline: What Md. official told township about TDR's
abstract: Manheim Township officials visited Buckingham Township and spoke with Dennis Canavan, a Montgomery County, Md., planner to learn about adopting a transferrable development rights program that would save local farm lands. The Montgomery County program is considered the most successful of its type in the country. Canavan said that though Montgomery County is much larger than Manheim Township in both size and population, growth pressure is more important than the size of the community.

headline: Ryan White loses struggle against AIDS
abstract: Ryan White lost his 5-and-a-half-year battle with the AIDS virus yeaterday.  White, who won a court battle to attend public school and faced almost insurmountable prejudice, was a national spokesperson for children with AIDS.  He appeared at numerous congressional hearings and was even on the cover of People Magazine.

headline: Local tax payment causes pain if not penury
abstract: The opinion piece comments on the high local taxes due to the school tax, and wishes that they were paid in installments instead of a lump sum.

headline: Government will cover experimental surgery costs
abstract: The US Department of Veterans Affairs, faced with a lawsuit by Marjorie Moore in US District Court, agreed to cover the $150,000 procedure for the cancer patient. Moore, a veteran's widow, receives medical coverage from the Department under a program for families of veterans. The Department had previously refused to cover the procedure, classifying it as "experimental." However, testimony from two doctors recommending the treatment caused the Department to offer full coverage.

headline: Higher Education’s lower standards
abstract: The article discusses how higher education has become a subsidized entitlement in an effort to give more and more Americans more education. There are lax college and high school standards, since now almost anyone can go to college and earn a degree (mostly in the fields of business and communications). The author believes that there is a casual attitude towards learning which leads to less serious students and dedicated teachers.

headline: Get the lead out: schools lag on water testing
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency warned parents of Philadelphia public school students against allowing their children to drink from school water coolers until the coolers have been tested for lead, since the Philadelphia School District has only tested 73 of its 1195 coolers in the 2 years since a federal law required the tests. Of the 73 tested so far, 47 were found to have hazardous levels of lead, and 32 of those were high enough to lead EPA estimators to believe that there is lead in the plumbing system.

headline: Casey considers Hanover truck bypass
abstract: PA Governor Casey acknowledged the needs for improved road systems in the Hanover area on a visit to the groundbreaking of the campaign headquarters of candidates Bortner and Beeler for the state Senate and House, respectively.

headline: Clinton County Likely to Be Included. PA Approval Pending for Fourth Local Judge.
abstract: PA Senator Roger A. Madigan said a bill that would create a fourth judgeship for Lycoming County and a second judgeship for Clinton County would likely be approved before the Legislature closes its session. Proposed judgeships for Philadelphia were erased from the bill to reflect the Senate's unhappiness with the city's fiscal crisis, but will be approved later in a House bill. If the new judgeship is created, the election winner will take office in January 1992.

headline: Task force explores local AIDS shelter
abstract: There has been a positive response toward the AIDS Task Force which has a committee that is looking to see how shelters were founded. The committee is trying to stress the need for shelters exist and are trying to figure out where the shelter would be located and what kind of services the shelter should provide. At the moment the members of the committee are learning all they can about existing shelters.

headline: Dem wants records on 44 loans
abstract: Democratic congressional candidate John Innelli has requested access to records concerning 44 businesses that received federal loans through the Partnership for Economic Development, now defunct.  County officials denied the request, citing confidentiality requirements.

headline: Shareholders' group targets 2 firms based in midstate
abstract: A shareholders' group is attempting to force six PA companies to incorporate elsewhere because of their support for a new anti-takeover law.

headline: Casey, Hafer prepare for gubernatorial debate
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey and Republican challenger Barbara Hafer will face each other tonight in what will likely be the only debate in the 1990 gubernatorial race.  According to Penn State University political science professor Michael Young, Casey needs to come across as a sincere, experienced leader and make no big mistakes, and Hafer needs to offer rational solutions to issues and to provide a more stable image of herself.

headline: In election year, Casey speech is big on the good news
abstract: Gov. Casey's annual "State of the Commonwealth" speech focused on the good news in Pennsylvania, highlight achievements of his term in office, while ignoring unpleasant realities. The Republicans were quick to point this out in their response. Such a speech was to be expected, as Casey is almost certain to run for reelection.

headline: Schwartz-Rocks hostility flares in high-stakes Senate campaign
abstract: PA Republican Senator M. Joseph Rocks and Democratic challenger Allyson Schwartz clashed in their second debate yesterday over abortion, Philadelphia's financial situation, and negative campaign tactics.  The result of the race could help determine control of the state legislature.

headline: Why city banks rethought loan for Phila.
abstract: Bankers had made it clear that they would not take cash for the city without fundamental changes in handling municipal finances. The realization that banks can force politicians to do only so much and that they themselves can only handle so much public pressure helped change their minds. Bankers are backing down from their high demands, but still would like to see some long term solutions.

headline: Adams was recommended for Supreme Court by Nixon and Ford
abstract: Retired federal judge Arlin Adams has been appointed as a special prosecutor to investigate claims against top officials of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.  There has been testimony before Congress that several HUD officials conspired to defraud a government program by steering rent subsidies to politically connected developers.

headline: Local unemployment rate increased slightly in July
abstract: Unemployment in the Johnstown area rose in July according to a report from the PA Department of Labor & Industry.  An analyst says that this rise is fairly typical in July, because of the seasonal nature of some jobs.

headline: Governor signs senior citizens' health-costs bill
abstract: Surrounded by dozens of delighted senior citizens, PA Governor Robert Casey signed a bill designed to make health care more affordable for the state's older residents. The new law, which takes effect in 60 days, requires doctors and other health-care providers to accept fees set by Medicare as payment in full for services provided to PA's 2.5 million senior citizens.

headline: House approves costly measure to help school improve education
abstract: The US House of Representatives gave overwhelming approval to a billion-dollar-a-year bill aimed at helping schools reach the educational goals set by the nation's governors and President Bush. It's a feel good bill that educational groups are not embracing. Budgets groups believe it spends too much for the current fiscal environment.

headline: Goals for the State, Casey seeks tougher vehicle emissions controls
abstract: In his annual State of the Commonwealth address Gov. Casey called for tougher contols on vehicle emissions and for the resolution of the debate on auto insurance reform. His administration has been working on a compromise with legislative leaders.

headline: Casey dedicates first stretch of Mon-Fayette Expressway
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey hailed the first completed section of the Mon-Fayette Expressway as a "road to better jobs." The road will eventually reach from Interstate 70 and US 40 to US 48 in West Virginia.

headline: Coalition Asks Washington Governor to Free Jailed Battered Women
abstract: The King County Coalition Against Domestic Violence is asking Washington state Governor Booth Gardner to follow the lead of Ohio's Governor by freeing 65 women jailed for assaulting or killing their husbands to protect themselves. Since taking office, the Governor used his clemency power only to commute the sentence of a woman who said she had been battered. The Governor will take into consideration the Clemency and Pardons Board review and recommendations.

headline: The Free Drug Question
abstract: Politicians and legislators debate contrasting views on how to help fight the country's war on drugs.  Some advocate harsher penalties and stricter laws while others advocate radical changes such as decriminalization of illegal substances.

headline: Economic Development Group Faces Financial Trouble, Cuts Jobs
abstract: The Economic Development Council of Northeastern Pennsylvania faced a $130,000 deficit for months and fired 30 workers.

headline: Size of cuts startles USAir workers
abstract: USAir's decision to fire 1500 workers somewhat surprised baggage handlers yesterday, not because there were going to be layoffs, but because of the number of layoffs.  It remains to be seen what jobs will be eiliminated and at what locations.

headline: Casey, Hafer spar a bit, but offer little that's new
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey and Republican challenger Barbara Hafer held what will likely be the only televised debate of the 1990 gubernatorial campaign.  The candidates disagreed on nearly all issues discussed, though neither brought anything particularly new to the debate.  Hafer scored a few points when Casey admitted that he does not drive, and so would seem "out of touch" with the state's auto insurance problem.

headline: In New Jersey, the '91 election season has already begun
abstract: The biggest income-tax increase in state history was passed last night under intense politics. Marlene Lynch Ford voted for the increase even though she ran as a anti-tax candidate. Now she will be attacked in her next election for being a taxer. Republicans need four seats to recapture the majority, o they will be fighting for every seat they can get.

headline: Scolding of Peters was premature
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioner Carol Peters was scolded by Joshua Lock, the county's MH/MR attorney, for publicly seeking information on an apparent suicide of an individual who sought treatment at a former MH/MR center which had been taken over by the county.  Peters claims she only publicly sought the information after other efforts failed.

headline: Wishes taxes were reduced
abstract: A resident does not understand why property and school taxes in Adams County are being increased. In the Monroe County Stroudsburg school system, tax millage was reduced. It should be reduced in Gettysburg also.

headline: Osprey gets lift
abstract: A study showing that the V-22 Osprey is more economical than possible alternatives may convince Congress to retain the aircraft.  Defense Secretary Richard Cheney did not include funding for V-22's in the defense budget, as he felt that the V-22 should be dropped in favor of coventional helicopters.  The V-22 program has the support of Senator Arlen Specter and Representative Curt Weldon.

headline: Maryland Won't Be Able To Escape This Recession, Experts say
abstract: Maryland officials, including Robert Rader, director of the Bureau of Revenue Estimates for the state comptroller, are seeing changes in the state's service economy. It appears Maryland is being dragged into the national recession despite federal government spending over the past years which has been a safety net. As the federal government begins to experience budget cuts, the work force in Maryland will be depleted, as the federal government is the largest state employer, employing $140,000.

headline: Grant to boost poor women's prenatal care
abstract: A $2.6 million grant over four years from the Pew Charitable Trusts will go to four hospitals for offering prenatal care to eligible pregnant women.

headline: Incentive pushed for school mergers
abstract: PA Representative Victor John Lescovitz, who sponsored an unsuccessful merger initiative bill this session, met with state Education Secretary Donald Carroll in hopes of persuading him to include incentive funding in his 1991-92 budget request to the governor. Carroll is expected to research feasibility and local desire before budgeting funds as a financial incentive to merge certain school districts. Lescovitz believed this funding would improve the bill's chances when reintroduced next year.

headline: Gov. Casey pays visit to Maxwell facility
abstract: Gov. Casey visited the Maxwell Lock and Dam, saying he was concerned about the economic, social and environmental problems created by the 30 runaway barges jammed there. "I have a serious concern about the continuing navigation problem" Casey said.

headline: Casey passes railroad line bill
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey signed a rail-to-trails bill that clears the way for the state to acquire abandoned railroad rights-of-way for development as recreational trails. It creates the Rails-to-Trails Program under the PA Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Cocaine use falls out of favor, experts say
abstract: According to defense lawyer William Costopoulos, cocaine has fallen out of favor as the popular drug it was in the last generation, as baby boomers start seeing more of the negative effects of the drug in society, such as in Hollywood and through the prosecutions of white-collar professionals.

headline: The Problem of Child Abuse: What Can We Do?
abstract: Bret Yarczower M.D. Pediatrics discusses child abuse statistics in the United States generally and offers possible reasons why this behavior occurs in parents.  He also lists contact information for agencies in the Luzerne County area that help victims of child abuse.

headline: Employment outlook
abstract: This chart shows the percent change in employment of certain Pittsburgh industries in 1989-90 and the expected percent change in 1990-91, according to the University of Pittsburgh Center for Social & Urban Research.

headline: Small Games
abstract: The PA Senate agreed to House-proposed revisions of PA's 1988 small games of chance law and sent the bill to PA Governor Robert P. Casey for approval. Senator Gibson Armstrong of Lancaster County said that the Legislature has set the stage for further expansions of gambling. Casey said he opposes expanded gambling.

headline: Casey, Singel supported
abstract: Bill George, president of the PA AFL-CIO announced that the group will endorse PA Governor Robert P. Casey and PA Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel for re-election, along with Congressional and state legislative candidates. The endorsements, which required a two-thirds approval of members of the group's Executive Council, were based on an examination of the candidates' backgrounds, voting records on labor issues, responses to surveys and the recommendations of local central labor bodies from the candidates' districts.

headline: In other races...Waleff, Arnold and Sheetz merit voters' support.
abstract: The editorial board endorses Democrats Louis Waleff and Ed Arnold and Republican Terry Scheetz for seats in the 98th, 99th and 102nd Legislative Districts respectively. The newspaper is not endorsing either candidate in the 100th Legislative District and believes that Jere Strittmatter of the 97th District should act like the tax-supported representative he is and not the lobbyist that he used to be.

headline: Scramble
abstract: After 20 years in office, state House Minority Whip Samuel E. Hayes Jr. unexpectedly announced that he will not run again, and Huntingdon County Commissioner Larry O. Sather will seek a Republican nominated for the recently vacated seat.

headline: null
abstract: During a block party, children jump rope. The photo captures a celebration held in honor of a drug-free Beaver Street.

headline: PennDOT addresses Wesley water situation
abstract: In response to resident complaints, Tim Hazlett, assistant construction engineer for the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation in Franklin, said the state has agreed to move a cross pipe further south along the Route 8 counstruction site.  Village of Wesley residents were complaining of water runoff from the construction site, and PennDOT is moving the pipe to alleviate the runoff situation.

headline: Masloff budget holds tax line, raises fees
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff is expected to generally avoid tax increases when she introduces the 1991 budget containing cuts in the work force and increases in licensing, permits and fees. Masloff will continue layoffs, will seek region tax relief in Harrisburg and favors an increase of the occupation privilege tax. Representatives from local sports and entertainment organizations will lobby legislators for a reduction of the city's 10 percent amusement tax.

headline: Granting the right to die
abstract: The editorial board joins with the PA Bar Association and the PA Medical Society in endorsing a bill in the PA House that would allow adults to execute "living wills". Living wills allow people to outline in advance what type of medical services they would accept in terminal illness cases. The bill, which grants a right already held by residents of 43 other states, would protect medical personnel from civil or criminal liability for following living will instructions.

headline: Investiture set today for new dean of law school
abstract: John Maher will be invested as the new dean of the Dickinson School of Law.  Maher has a passion for education and Dickinson and has been on the Dickinson faculty since 1973.  He said that he does not plan to make any attempts to increase the size of the school, which currently enrolls about 560 students.

headline: If Contract Won DER To Keep Tabs On Trash Tonnage
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources will be closely monitoring the volume of waste accepted by the Empire Landfill if the facility receives a 1000-ton-a-day contract.  The scrutiny would be to ensure that the out-of-state waste does not exceed 30% of total accepted.

headline: Casey Say He'd Veto 65 MPH Speed Limit
abstract: PA Governor Casey said he would veto legislation that would allow a 65 mph speed limit on the PA Turnpike and criticized election opponent Barbara Hafer for backing such legislation.  The increase is unlikely to be pursued because of Casey's promised veto.

headline: Cohill Considering Delay in Prison Single-Cell Order
abstract: U.S. District Judge Maurice B. Cohill, Jr. stated that he would oblige the state's request for a 90-day delay in an order that bans double-bunking inmates at the Pittsburgh State Correctional Institution.

headline: Three recommended for federal judgeships
abstract: Montgomery County Common Pleas Court Judge William Yohn Jr., Philadelphia lawyer Harvey Bartle III, and assistant US Attorney Timothy Lewis were all nominated for federal judgeships in PA, Yohn and Bartle for Philadelphia District Courts, and Lewis for Pittsburgh District Court.

headline: Fayette CAA programs extended
abstract: The Fayette County Community Action Agency will continue to offer 50 percent state tax credits to businesses which donate private homes for renovation and donation to needy families. Funding for the program partly comes from the PA Department of Community Affairs. The County will also continue its participation in the PA Employment and Community Conservation program. The program helps provides housing assistance, life skills training and referral services.

headline: Sony Interested in Old VW Plant, CMU's Cyert Says
abstract: Sony Corp. chairman Akio Morita told Carnegie Mellon University President that it was likely that Sony would build a Pittsburgh plant.

headline: Casey, with caution
abstract: The editorial board reluctantly endorses PA Governor Robert P. Casey for election against opponent Republican Auditor General Barbara Hafer, despite his unpopular tax and auto insurance reform attempts, veto of a bill to end the "widow's tax", and manipulation of budget figures to hide the state's financial condition. They charge that Hafer's inability to address these issues, her confrontational style and her lack of demonstrable competence as Auditor General and minority commissioner in Allegheny County makes her unelectable.

headline: In Passing: With friends like this…
abstract: Joe McHugh, Republican candidate for Northeast Philadelphia's 173rd legislative district in the PA House, accused Democrat Michael McGeehan of having been now-Philadelphia-Mayor Wilson Goode's "Northeast coordinator," though McGeehan worked to defeat Goode in the primary election and did nothing to help Goode in the general election.

headline: Secretary of General Services returns with Mideast postcard
abstract: PA General Services Secretary David L. Jannetta, a major in the Air National Guard back from a tour of duty in the Persian Gulf, delivered PA Governor Robert P. Casey's Saturday radio address. Jannetta said heat, crude living conditions, bad food, culture shock and fear of chemical warfare make life difficult for soldiers stationed in Saudi Arabia as part of Operation Desert Shield. The cabinet official urged Pennsylvanians to write to friends and family members stationed in the gulf.

headline: Baseball Update
abstract: A summary of baseball standings.

headline: Pro-balloon protest launched
abstract: Phil Levin, president of Harrisburg-based Balloon City U.S.A., is protesting a bill that would make it illegal to launch more than 10 helium-filled latex ballons at a time.  The bill is designed to prevent pollution and protect wildlife.  Levin is vowing to launch 30 ballons every weekday in protest of the legislation, and claims that such legislation will kill the balloon industry.  Levin argues that groups exaggerrate the dangers balloons cause to animals.

headline: Midwest heartbeat still heard in the steady hum of factories
abstract: In 1982 and 1983, unemployment rates in the Midwest city of Rockford, Illinois were near 25% due to the collapse of steel companies.  The city, among many others, has made a slow recovery but there are signs of revitalization, and the economies of Midwestern states, though still vulnerable, are climbing back to prominence.

headline: Group goes to court over hospital funds
abstract: The Hospital Association of Pennsylvania is going into Commonwealth Court with the PA Welfare Department, which, according to Welfare Secretary John F. White Jr., would stop state payments to cover medical assistance to the poor. The state Legislature failed to pass a bill to supplement the fund, while PA Governor Robert Casey asked the Legislature to approve a spending bill which included over $61 billion to reimburse hospitals for services for Medicaid patients. The hearing is scheduled for May 23.

headline: It Happened in Harrisburg
abstract: An opinion by Representative Merle Phillips about the special education crisis, criticizing the Casey Administration's special education program revisions and ignoring of the deficit.

headline: Grant will buy recycling equipment
abstract: A grant has been approved for Bradford County, which will be used to buy recycling equiment so that the county will be able to comply with the mandatory recycling required by 1991.  The article also reviews other business covered at the recent business meeting.

headline: Casey to open highway section
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey will participate in the ribbon-cutting ceremony for two new sections of the Mon Valley/Fayette Expressway in Washington County, PA.

headline: Commissioners Close Fire Department
abstract: Harrison Township commissioners voted to freeze financial support and remove township-owned gear from a Harrison Township fire company after it failed to respond to an eight-alarm blaze. The firefighters claimed they were unable to answer the alarm because locks at the hall had been unexpectedly changed. The commissioners are considering either starting a new fire company or reorganizing the old company under the township's supervision, commissioners board chairman George Conroy said.

headline: Three SEPTA Officers Charged In Beating
abstract: According to prosecutors, three Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority police officers beat and kicked a restaurant worker because he was making too much noise. The district attorney's office announced that the officers, Sergeant Richard Sanders and Sergeant Otto Yarbrough, were jailed on charges of aggravated assault, simple assault and conspiracy.

headline: Firm is hired to study collapse
abstract: An investigation is underway as to the cause of the collapse of part of an airport building under construction which killed one man and injured another.

headline: Soon, Pa. mechanics will have a new role as insurance police
abstract: Spokeswoman for the PA Department of Insurance Amy Dugan noted the regulation requiring mechanics to check a car's insurance and registration policies is an added layer of protection to ensure drivers have insurance. Local mechanics feel the measure is unfair and only proves the PA Bureau of Motor Vehicles is unable to perform efficiently. PA Department of Transportation Spokesman Rick Schoen said the PA will increase random checks for insurance when registering vehicles.

headline: Casey: State must project new image
abstract: This year's recipient of the David Glick Award, given by the World Affairs Council of Pittsburgh, formerly the Foreign Policy Association, is John C. Marous Jr., chairman and CEO of Westinghouse Electric Corporation. As a speaker, PA Governor Robert Casey talked of the uniqueness offered in the PA economy through intellectual infrastructure and the Industrial Resources Center Network, a government funded privately-run system of centers which trains workers to relate globally.

headline: In Richmond, Romance Rumors Fly
abstract: Virginia Governor L. Douglas Wilder may be romancing Patricia Kluge, estranged wife of the nation's richest man. Reports says Wilder has been using state-owned aircraft to socialize with Kluge. They claim to be just friends and he claims he has not misused state equipment.

headline: Selection of Souter sets the stage for heavy-duty choices for next vacancies
abstract: David S. Broder can see why President Bush appointed David H. Souter to the US Supreme Court. The politically non-controversial appointment allows Bush  to negotiate with Democrats on the budget after abandoning his "no new taxes" attitude. And, it does not mean a fight over controversial issues he would like to keep out of the midterm election. However, it does amount to political capital for the next judicial appointment.

headline: Baseball update
abstract: The Philadelphia Phillies suffered a 9-5 defeat at the hands of the San Diego Padres, bringing their losing streak to 3 games in a row. The Phillies are in second place in the National League East Divison, behind the Pittsburgh Pirates. Phillies center fielder Lenny Dkystra is approaching a .400 batting average. The article features box scores of the game against San Diego, as well as league standings.

headline: Linton's pick in 4th Senate District spells further split for Democrats
abstract: State Representative Gordon J. Linton endorsed Democratic Senate candidate Jeff Blum yesterday, marking a setback for Allyson Schwartz--one of his primary rivals--and signaling further divisions among Democratic leaders over potential challengers to Republican Senator Jospeh Rocks in the fall.  This split in support between Blum and Schwartz may help Robert Blasi, the state Democratic Party's endorsed candidate, win the nomination.  The split in support between Schwartz and Blum also amounts to a proxy war between Philadelphia's major political forces, with several political lumanaries of city politics throwing their support behind each of the three candidates.

headline: Monroe's jobless rate lowest of '90
abstract: Monroe County's unemployment rate fell to a year-low 5.2% in August, down from 5.8% in July.  The rate has been decreasing since February, when it was 7.7%, though it expected to rise again until February 1991.

headline: Group sues state over medical aid
abstract: The Hospital Association of PA has gone into court to prevent the PA Welfare Department from stopping medical-assistance payments to hospitals across the state that are treating the poor. PA Welfare Secretary John F. White said state payments to help cover the cost of out-patient treatment would stop next week because the fund has run out of money and the PA Legislature has failed to pass a supplemental appropriations bill, which PA Governor Robert Casey has called for.

headline: Japan Seeks CMU Help in Computer Software
abstract: If Carnegie Mellon University establishes a software engineering program near Tokyo, a Japanese businessman has agreed to raise $35 million.

headline: 'Greenscam' seeps into Pennsylvania
abstract: Wyona S. Coleman, Conservation Chair of the PA chapter of the Sierra Club, writes to warn voters about "Greenscam," which is when legislators pose as pro-environment for public relations purposes, but actually vote and act in ways against those principles.  She uses the example of PA Senator Michael Fisher on the issue of amendments to PA's Oil and Gas Act.

headline: Casey won't knuckle under
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey plans to hold steady in the face of a US bill, which will probably pass, that would deny PA about $142 million in federal highway funding unless the state comes up with a permanent funding base for mass transit by June. Casey said that the state has done well funding mass transit, and called on the federal government to offer more aid to the state's mass transit before threatening PA with requiring more state funding.

headline: Commissioners debate future of Pine Street jail
abstract: Bradford County Commissioner Chairman William McNett attempted to mediate between Commissioners Richard Eaton, who supports renovating the former County prison, and Robert Horton, who favors a sale. Eaton maintains high renovation costs will be offset by decrease in rent the County pays for office space, but Horton claims moving costs would wipe out savings and hurt taxpayers. McNett awaits the completion of studies to examine all options concerning renovating costs before a decision is made.

headline: Time in a different prison
abstract: Probation and parole officers were made to feel like old people with popcorn in their shoes, rubber gloves to reduce touch, cotton in their ears, eyeglasses with Vaseline covering them. It was a sensitivity training to get professionals ready for an expected avalanche of aging prisoners, parolees and people on probation. The aging are one of the largest growing groups in the nation's prison population, but professionals do not know how to deal with the elderly.

headline: Fiscal crunch forces job freeze, PHA chief says
abstract: Philadelphia Housing Authority executive director John Paone has initiated a freeze on hiring and promotions, due to underfunding for this fiscal year's budget by the US Office of Housing and Urban Development. Poane said he was also considering asking the PA Department of Public Welfare to reinstate a mandatory overdue rent payment for tenants of public housing. There is a backlog of uncollected rents totaling $9 million.

headline: Soviet industrialists promote 'glasnost' while visiting Erie
abstract: Soviet industrialists are visiting Erie to get aquainted with the business methods at Erie's Kaiser Aluminum and Chemical Corp.

headline: Casey-Hafer debate tackles major state issues
abstract: The article summarizes the positions taken by PA Governor Casey and Republican challenger Barbara Hafer in the gubernatorial debate last night.  Issues covered in the article are: Education, abortion, taxes, auto insurance, the widow's tax, legislative terms, and the Philadelphia financial crisis.

headline: In Texas, the governor's race is down 'n' dirty
abstract: The Texas gubernatorial race between Democratic PA Treasurer Ann Richards and businessman Clayton Williams has been characterized by negative campaigning, name-calling and "fiery" politics. The article suggests that PA could use this passion in its own gubernatorial election between PA Governor Robert P. Casey and PA Auditor Barbara Hafer, in which a 50-percent turnout is expected. A 75 percent turnout is predicted in Texas.

headline: Sen. Nunn Cautiously Exploring Possibility of a White House Run in 1992
abstract: In recent Senate hearings concerning the question of Persian Gulf policy, US Senator Nunn appears to be his party's shadow commander in Chief. Republicans are suggesting Nunn's contention with the issue is in preparation for a presidential bid. Nunn maintains he has always challenged presidential judgement regardless of party affiliation, and that despite exploring the possibility of running, he is doing so cautiously and not by challenging the federal Persian Gulf policy.

headline: Carlisle band to march in Tournament of Roses
abstract: The Carlisle Senior High School Band has been invited to march in 1992 Tournament of Roses Parade. The band director, Dave Rohrer, called it the most prestigious event a band can be in.

headline: Judge eulogized as brilliant legal mind, modest man
abstract: This article eulogizes Judge R. Dixon Herman, U.S. Middle District Senior Judge, who died of a heart attack on Thursday.  Judge Herman presided over the 1971 trial of seven people charged with conspiring to kidnap former presidential advisor Henry Kissinger.  Judge Herman was well liked and respected as a jurist with a brilliant legal mind.

headline: Nonagriculture jobs in PA at record high in November
abstract: The number of nonagriculture jobs increased by 8,800 in November to reach a record high of 5.18 million according to the PA state Department of Labor and Industry.

headline: Growth spurt for schools of nursing
abstract: There's been a recent spurt in admissions to nursing schools, as the profession fell on hard times in the '80s as the female-dominated field saw many prospects opting for other jobs.  Barbara Barnum, editor of Nursing & Health Care, said that any time there's an economic slump, nursing schools pick up.

headline: Jogging around; Rivalry going
abstract: Editors suggest the University of Pittsburgh look into protecting its interests, particularly when it comes to its athletic football schedule. Since Penn State University has announced it will join the Big 10, the school has already hinted it may not be able to continue attending games with Pitt.

headline: Ground Water Protection is Problem
abstract: William Parsons of the state Department of Environmental Resources expressed concerns about efforts to protect ground water.

headline: Casey: I'll veto 65 mph
abstract: PA Governor Casey said he would veto legislation to raise the speed limit on the PA Turnpike to 65 mph, saying that he wants to keep drivers safe, and driving faster would also use more fuel, which would be unwise considering the current  crisis in the Middle East.

headline: Community organization clowns around to help drive AIDS, drug measures home
abstract: The Central Allison Hill Community has started a program called "Children We Care" program which is a unique program. The children are able to come and enjoy entertainment while social workers give other guest lectures about the dangers and warning signs of AIDS, drug addictions, and child abuse. The organization depends on community support for funds.

headline: Time to kill widow's tax
abstract: The editorial urges PA Governor Robert Casey to add his support the repealing the "widow's tax," which levies a tax on anyone taking control of a deceased spouse's holdings that were under only one name.  The PA Senate and House have both already voted overwhelmingly to repeal the tax.

headline: Funding jeopardy, Pa. tells Montco agency
abstract: The PA Deptartment of Community Affairs has warned the head of Montgomery County's Opportunity Board that the agency could lose federal funding due to the possibility of a conflict of interest involving her ascension to the leadership role.

headline: Steel puts kink in recycling
abstract: Though residents have not noticed a problem, scrap dealers who collect aluminum cans have had to make adjustments as some manufacturers have resorted to using steel. It is hard to distinguish visually between aluminum and steel cans, which are not as profitable for recyclers. Executive Vice President of the Mid-Atlantic Canners Association, John Manske, said Coca-Cola is using only aluminum in the Mid-Atlantic region.

headline: Casey's camp now says he may debate Hafer after all
abstract: After pressure from the media, and a "communication misunderstanding," the Gov. Casey's campaign manager says he's willing to consider a debate Casey's opponent, Barbara Hafer.

headline: In wake of GOP loss, Miller calls for Showers' resignation
abstract: In light of recent poor election results for PA Republicans, GOP leaders are assigning blame to gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer and the leadership of the PA committee. Former PA Representative Marvin E. Miller Jr. of Lancaster County called for the resignation of Republican Lancaster County Chairman Byron Showers, saying he has consistently lost seats on council, the mayoral council and two of seven House seats in the county.

headline: Sen. Nunn: Democrats' Shadow Commander
abstract: US Senator Sam Nunn learned of President Bush's Nov. 8 decision to nearly double the size of American forces in the Persian Gulf when Secretary of Defense Richard Cheney called him two hours before the announcement was made. The White House may not give him credit but his colleagues in Congress say his vote counts the most.

headline: Cartoon
abstract: Woman holding shampoo saying "I'm gonna wash man right out of my hair…"

headline: Political grandstanding
abstract: State Representative Jeffrey E. Piccola's suggestion that Governor Casey is playing politics with the operation of the Department of Corrections is nothing more than political grandstanding during an election cycle.  Governor Casey has a panoply of issues to deal with, ranging from senior citizens, unemployment and the health and welfare of all Pennsylvanians.  Prison overcrowding, which is Piccola's main concern, has been a problem for years, and was an issue during the Thornburgh administration, but Piccola apparently had no problem with it then.

headline: Nonagriculture jobs in Pa. at record high in November
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry reported an increase of 3500 jobs in the number of nonagricultural positions in the state since the 5.18 million reported last month. Service-industry jobs have reached a high of 3.89 million, an increase of 18,400 since last month's figure. The largest increase was reported in the Allentown-Bethlehem area. Johnstown and Beaver County reported declines.

headline: Handler Center being mishandled
abstract: The author of this letter is upset at how the mental health/mental retardation administration, Stan Mrozowski, has made a political parade of the case worker contract with the Handler Center. He claims Republican commissioners do not care about the lives of the mentally ill and the mentally retarded. Rosemary Madi inherited a mess when she took over as director of the Handler Center a little over a year ago. Losing her because of politics would be a shame.

headline: Jordan reflects on PSU presidency
abstract: Penn State president Bryce Jordan will soon retire, and the article looks back on his achievements, effects, and troubles during his tenure.

headline: Group Gets State Grant to Recycle
abstract: The state awarded a $62,000 grant to several upper Dauphin County communities to help finance an effort to establish recycling programs.

headline: Cheats abound, but SEPTA is fighting back
abstract: More than four months after the deadliest accident in Southeastern PA Transportation Authority history, it has received 274 claims for compensation of injuries stemming from the derailment of a Market-Frankford subway train. Officials believe more people have filed claims than were on the train, which has happened before. They are currently trying to ferret out fakes, so they can give money to the people who really do need the compensation.

headline: Confirmation process
abstract: A box inserted outlines the steps in confirming a US Supreme Court justice.

headline: Tired of wait: County commissioner sues clerk
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioner Carol A. Peters filed suit for $10,000 against the county's chief clerk, Jeffrey T. Haste, for defamation after a commissioner's meeting in July.  Peters said that she regrets that it had to come to her filing suit, but that she had to clear her reputation. She also said that if Haste publicly apologizes for his remarks, she would drop the charges.

headline: Funds sought for deepening river
abstract: US Sens. Arlen Specter and John Heinz, US Representative James Saxton of New Jersey want to deepen the Delaware River to keep the city of Philadelphia's ports competitive and create new jobs. Port officials were present for a press conference. In the past, the condition and use of the city's ports has declined. Efforts are being made to unify public and private agencies managing area ports. Heinz and Specter have requested $1 million from the Senate Appropriations Committee.

headline: Stockholder interests not #1
abstract: An editorial supporting PA's anti-takeover law and urging its passage, saying that it will "look to the future" and protect "communities from profiteering corporate raiders"

headline: Casey's chances don't shake Hafer
abstract: Republican candidate Barbara Hafer continues to predict a $1 billion PA deficit though some argue that this will cause her to lose in both the upcoming gubernatorial and auditor general elections. PA Governor Robert P. Casey's administration says there will be no debt and characterize her actions as political posturing. Republicans are considering coming up with someone to run against Hafer in the GOP primary for auditor general in light of her divisive behavior.

headline: In York County, more than a state Senate seat is at stake
abstract: Democrat PA state Representative Michael Bortner and Republican Representative Donald Dorr are campaigning for a PA state Senate seat that is viewed as a crucial seat by both parties. The outcome of this election could decide the control of the state Senate, and perhaps the entire legislature, especially as the General Assembly will redraw boundaries of the state's congressional districts. The campaigning has turned dirty, with each candidate airing attack ads about the other.

headline: Sen. Wilt reflects on 22-year legislative career, offers advice
abstract: Voluntarily ending his 22-year legislative career, PA Senator Roy W. Wilt reflected in an interview about the lawmaker's job, the impact of state government on local affairs and his personal plans. PA Representative Robert D. Robbins was elected as Wilt's successor in the 50th District.

headline: Christopher Herman
abstract: Christopher Herman from Milton Junior High School is Milton's Lions Club's Student of the Month.

headline: Abortion Protest Trial for 72 Opens in Makeshift Courtroom
abstract: The largest trial in Allegheny County history is being held in a makeshift convention center courtroom.  The trial for 72 pro-life protesters opened on Monday with prosecutors and defense attorneys questioning potential jurors.  Eighty six people were arrested on October 28th after protesters charged through police barricades outside the Allegheny County Reproductive Health Center.

headline: Old Lycoming facing deficit, property tax increase in 1991
abstract: Raising taxes in a possibility to cover a $138,000 deficit in the town's proposed budget. While spending is down the township also expects less revenues next year. Also the township received a $30,000 PA Community Development Block Grant last year that it did not receive this year.

headline: Haverford Township ends legal battle against group home
abstract: Two weeks after a federal judge ruled against Schuylkill Township in a similar dispute, Haverford Township ended its legal fight against a group home for five former residents of the Pennhurst State School and Hospital. Independent Support Systems Inc. sued the Delaware County township in U.S. District Court, saying its civil rights and federal fair-housing laws were violated when township officials prevented five retarded adults from moving into a new group home.

headline: Judge orders strikers back to classrooms
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Samuel Lehrer ordered the striking Temple Association of University Professionals back to work, saying that the strike had damaged the education of Temple students and harmed the public. Union leaders immediately asked PA's Commonwealth Court to vacate the injunction and let the strike continue.

headline: Group Opposing Dump Seeks State's Support
abstract: During PA Governor Casey's "Capital for A Day", PA Secretary of the Department of Environmental Resources Arthur Davis met with the Pine Creek Headwaters Protection Group. Robert Ross, with the US Fish and Wildlife research center, is concerned by a facility sought by Phoenix Resources Inc. The National Guard will build neutralizing systems, but the facility needs a DER permit. The group said PA legislators will propose to designate the creek a scenic river. Shippen Township began land preservation efforts in light of higher taxes which make subdivision attractive.

headline: Checks of route 1 trucks bar 60% from the road
abstract: Sixty percent of the trucks inspected by the state police on Route 1 are ordered off the road because of safety violations. Cpl. John Frantz aid on May 15 and 16 his five member team conducted a spot check of seven trucks and ordered them not to operate. The public are speaking out against unsafe truck drivers who tailgate and speed. When they began spot checks three years ago they had an 80% shutdown rate.

headline: Convicted judge O'Kicki to seek another 10-year term
abstract: Convicted Judge Joseph O'Kicki, former president judge of Cambria County, notified the PA Board of Elections he intends to seek re-election for another 10-year term, a move not unusual in his position said deputy legal counsel for the state's Judicial Inquiry and Review Board William Arbuckle. The board has asked the PA Supreme Court to remove O'Kicki from office. He faces trial on March 16 for 16 counts of corruption.

headline: Top secret -- Congress kept in dark about weapon thefts
abstract: After a 1987 report by the US General Accounting Office about soldiers stealing weapons and explosives from Fort Bragg, NC, the US Department of Defense has stopped keeping careful records of such thefts, and keeps very few statistics about missing weapons or about contraband weapons found in communities nationwide. Warren Nelson, of the House Armed Services subcommittee on investigations, sees this as very suspicious and as an effort to avoid embarrassment rather than fix the problem.

headline: Gehl firm breaks ground for plant to employ 200
abstract: Gehl Company broke ground for a $10 million manufacturing plant in South Lebanon Township that will employ an estimated 200 workers. PA Commerce Secretary Raymond R. Christman said the PA Department of Commerce approved an $8.4 million low-interest loan through the PA Economic Development Financing Authority to encourage the company to stay in the state. Another grant through the state's Business Infrastructure Development program was awarded to the Lebanon Valley Economic Development Corporation to build an access road to Gehl's property and to extend water and sewer lines.

headline: Study links loss by Pa. stocks to the takeover law
abstract: A recent study by two finance professors at Drexel University suggests that PA's anti-takeover law, the strongest in the nation, is a chief reason that shareholders in the state's major corporations lost about $4 billion.

headline: Casey's feel-good ads abound
abstract: Incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey, in contrast to his advertisements four years ago, has run only "feel-good" ads in this year's election, proclaiming his accomplishments and saying that PA is "the rising star of America."  The article also explains Casey's positions and the situation on taxes, the budget, and abortion.

headline: Incentive to vote: stake in outcome
abstract: The piece stresses the importance of maing voting boards more accessible so that it's easier for people to register to vote, so that hopefully the trend towards apathy will be reversed.

headline: Sen.: Why I am voting for Judge Souter
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter (R-PA) explains why he plans to vote for the confirmation of Judge David H. Souter for the US Supreme Court. He says that Souter has the academic background, experience as a lawyer and attorney general, and has demonstrated judicial excellence. Specter also respects that Souter has not made any comments on his position on abortion and other hot issues on which he will likely need to eventually make rulings.

headline: Coal industry leader R&P's Charles Potter, dies
abstract: Dr. Charles J. Potter, a past president of Rochester & Pittsburgh Coal Company, died Sunday. His life is reviewed in detail from his beginnings to his retirement in 1988.

headline: Group home closings disrupt lives of clients
abstract: A strike by group-home workers resulted in the Institute for Human Resources and Services closing four of its 12 group homes for the mentally disabled and relocating 13 clients.  This has uprooted residents and forced some to move back in with families or into other facilities, thus disrupting the day-to-day lives of residents and impacting their functioning.

headline: PA breaks economic slump
abstract: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) has reported that the per capita income and employment opportunities will surpass the national trends for the first time in thirty years. Economists warn that PA still has a lot of improvement ahead of it but there is an end to the bad economy in PA.

headline: Health Care Cost Containment Council Releases Survey
abstract: Industry officials warned consumers not to base their decision on where to obtain health care solely on a new Hospital Effectiveness Report.  Consumers are encouraged to learn as much as they can before making their decision.

headline: Judge to rule on injunction
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Samuel Lehrer promised a ruling by this morning on an injunction ordering striking Temple University professors back to work.  The university was planning on cancelling many classes that have yet to meet if professors weren't back by this morning, but Lehrer told them to wait until his decision was announced.

headline: Group to fight waste burner at Allenwood
abstract: A local group opposed to the proposed incinerator at Allenwood held a meeting yesterday to recruit new members and make its views heard.

headline: Child auto safety drive is helping
abstract: Child deaths in vehicle accidents are slowly decreasing, thanks in part to a mandatory car seat law now in place.

headline: Convicted judge O'Kicki to seek another 10-year term
abstract: Joseph K. O'Kicki, the former President  Judge of Cambria County who was convicted of corruption and sentenced to two to five years in prison, has notified the PA Board of Elections he intends to seek re-election to another 10 year term.

headline: Top state court to debate lawyer-fee seizures in drug cases
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has agreed to hear a Cumberland County case that will determine whether PA prosecutors may seize fees paid to lawyers in drug cases. Joseph Hess had his lawyer's retainer fee seized and claims that violated his right to an attorney and due process of law. The Supreme Court has previously held that this is acceptable, but may change its course with this case.

headline: Grant for Jay supervisors
abstract: PA Rep. Jim Distler announced a $15,000 grant to Jay Township from the PA Department of Community Affairs. The grant will be used for construction of a pavilion and restroom and a park, engineering studies, and a bridge. Distler noted the importance of grants in smaller communities, which do not have the tax base of larger communities.

headline: Survey shows continued slowdown for area manufacturers
abstract: According to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, manufacturers in the Philadelphia region reported a slowdown in business activity for the 18th month in a row. 59% of the firms surveyed said their operations were slowing down in Oct., and only 4% saw an increase in activity.

headline: Casey's support firm as Milko pays back taxes
abstract: Gov. Casey is standing by his nominee for country treasurer even though she herself had fallen behind in property taxes by more than $17,500 dating as far back as 1957.

headline: Incumbent Mellow running on record...
abstract: PA Senator Bob Mellow, representing Barrett, Price, Coolbaugh and Paradise townships, says he is running his re-election campaign for his sixth term on the economy, the environment and education. Mellow supports legislation protecting wetlands. Mellow received the endorsement of the PA State Educational Association.

headline: Senate chief wields reapportionment threat
abstract: Senate President Pro Tempore Robert C. Jubelirer showed local newspapers a map of a hypothetical congressional district that could be drawn by Democrats to pit U.S. Representative Bill Goodling against two other Republican incumbents in a primary. Jubelirer used the map to advocate support for Representative Donald W. Dorr in the PA Senate race. However, no reapportionment plan can be drawn until the U.S. Census Bureau releases official data next year.

headline: Ethnicity conference emphasizes understanding others' cultures
abstract: Cultural traditions are being lost with more working mothers and increasingly blended families. The Governor's Conference on Ethnicity is exploring these issues and bringing policy makers together to learn how people from different cultures can work together and be more sensitive to each other. Apparently people are still doing the things their ancestors did without even knowing it, like a German farmer farming the same way his ancestors did 200 years ago.

headline: Striking group home workers to meet with state official
abstract: Striking workers from the Institute of Human Resources and Services are planning to meet with state Public Welfare Secretary John F. White on Friday.  Workers will attempt to get more money from the state to solve the funding crisis that prompted the strike.  A decrease in state funding for wages led to the strike and caused the institute to close four of its homes.

headline: PA Budget
abstract: David Donahoe, state Secretary of Revenue stated that revenue growth is not as quick as previously expected.

headline: Health care spending pace quickens
abstract: Health and Human Services Secretary Louis Sullivan said growth in healthcare spending, putting the cost at $2400 per person, is alarming, cutting some off from medical care, and placing a heavy burden on other users, including nursing home patients. Sullivan is leading a Domestic Policy Review of the health-care system which favors continuattion the public-private system rather than government healthcare. Statistics were most recently released by the Health Care Financing Administration.

headline: Lack of funds forced protestors to settle dispute
abstract: Children In Distressful Situations had to settle because they could not afford two weeks of witnesses. They were tiring to keep mine blasting from occurring near an elementary school. They estimate it would have cost $20,000 to $30,000 not to settle. Blasting will be forbidden during school hours, blasting will not be allowed within 800 feet from the school, along with some other mine regulations.

headline: Grouse, squirrel season promising
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission and other officials are predicting good hunting for ruffed grouse and squirrels this season, as small game season begins Saturday. According to biologist Bill Palmer, PA's ruffed grouse population has increased since last year, and Game Commission field officers are reporting squirrel levels that are the same or higher than last year.

headline: City May Give Helicopters a Whirl
abstract: A feasability study is underway concerning a potential heliport at the site of an old incinerator in Philadelphia.  The heliport could be open for passenger service in addition to regular uses.

headline: Convicted murderer Miller dead in Camp Hill prison
abstract: Death row inmate J.R. Miller was found unconscious in his cell this morning and later died at the hospital.  He had appeals pending.

headline: Tough N.J. laws mean jammed jails
abstract: New Jersey's continued policy of "tough on crime" is resulting in massive overcrowding of prisons at both the state and county level. Neither the courts nor the state budget can keep up with federal court orders to address prison overcrowding.Timothy Roche of the National Center on Institutions and Alternatives notes the response to crime in New Jersey resulted in increased crime rates. Some aides to New Jersey Governor Florio are advocating alternative sentencing.

headline: Grant would help moderate-income families buy homes
abstract: An application for state funding for a new housing construction program to help moderate-income families buy homes was approved by the Lebanon county commissioners. The application for $350,000 will provide the authority with funds to offer a second mortgage to owners of newly constructed homes. Lebanon Valley National Bank has agreed to participate in the demonstration program by offering 80 percent of the costs of a new home at an interest rate about 2 percentage points below current mortgage rates. The remaining 20 percent will be covered by the authority's deferred mortgage. The estimated cost of a new home is $75,000.

headline: Take it
abstract: The editorial board recommends Philadelphia Mayor Goode's administration take the deal offered by banks to advance money for operating expenses with the rest of the funds conditionally distributed if the city presents a long-term reform plan for raising revenues. However, the editors caution against banks demanding too much and the city accepting too early, with some officials warning the city will not receive as much state aid if the crisis is ameliorated by loans through banking institutions.

headline: Casey's wife announces library conference delegates
abstract: PA Governor Casey's wife, Ellen Casey announced the names of 292 delegates who will attend the Governor's Conference on Libraries and Information Services, which she will chair.

headline: Incumbents look safe despite voters' ire
abstract: The article is analysis of the upcoming mid-term election in which voters will pick a new Congress and 36 gubernatorial seats. An estimated $1 million has been spent by two candidates for a PA Senate seat in PA, where Democrats look to take control and monopolize the state reapportionment process.

headline: Senate confirms district justice
abstract: The PA Senate has approved Hazel Swisher as a replacement for District Justice Lucy A. Pietsch in Lebanon County, who retired in June.

headline: Honors bestowed on heroes. City commends 6 citizens for rescue efforts.
abstract: Several people were honored with the civilian Award for Valor, Harrisburg's highest award for citizens, for their heroic actions. David Decima and Robert Martin both rescue a person trapped in a burning home. Harry Felkner rescued a woman attempting suicide. Michael Peterson rescued Blue Swan Jazz club patrons from a fire. James Segrist rescued a wind surfer whose craft had flipped above a dam. Robert Strieweg Jr. saved three people from the Susquehanna River.

headline: Keep funding for TELLS program
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey did not include any funding for the Test for Essential Learning and Literacy Skills remediation in next year's budget.  The General Assembly should restore funding for the TELLS program for two reasons.  First, even though the state is not funding the program, it still will require school districts to give the tests to students; this is unfair.  Second, poorer districts in the state will not be able to fund their own remediation programs.  A lack of state funding will mean that children in need of math and reading remediation will be underserved.

headline: pa financial news
abstract: PA has lost 17,100 non-agricultural jobs last month, but the Department of Labor and Industry says the state's remaining 5.15 million job toal is the third highest on record.

headline: Health Chief's goals: Staff, survey
abstract: New health chief outlines immediate goals for the time that he will be in office.  Montgomery County's new health department has been allocated $1 million for its first-year needs.  The county may be able to receive state reimbursement for up to 50 percent of the health department's first-year costs.

headline: Latchkey programs give safety, care for children
abstract: The article promotes the use of latchkey programs for kids who get home from school before their parents are home.  The programs provide a safe, enjoyable atmosphere for kids, and peace of mind for parents.

headline: Gypsy Moth Requests Due Friday
abstract: Applications from property owners for aerial gypsy moth spraying are due Friday.

headline: City to revamp red lights by '92
abstract: The city of Harrisburg received a federal grant to install a system of traffic light controls, allowing motorists to move quickly through the city by timing lights more efficiently. Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed says the system will aid businesses transporting goods through the city. PA Department of Transportation engineer Barry Hoffman said it should help frustrated motorists. The Tri-County Association for the Blind gave money to the project for street-crossing aids for the blind.

headline: Cooperation the key to skateboard woes
abstract: The writer believes that the Lewistown Borough should restrict the use of skateboards on the streets and sidewalks and provide a proper place for the youth oriented activity. The writer believes that the skateboarders pose a problem and that little can be done by the law enforcement.

headline: Transferred inmates miss their families
abstract: Prisoners transferred into the federal prison system after riots at the PA State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill last Oct. have been scattered into federal prisons throughout the country, and therefore have received very few visits from their families and have been less able to talk to them via telephone because of high long-distance costs. The situation was supposed to be temporary, but due to the federal budget impasse, the prisoners have stayed at their temporary prisons longer than planned.

headline: Ground Broken for Tules Run Development
abstract: Construction began on the Tules Run housing development project in Fairfield Township after six years of attempts to gain state and local approval. U.S. Congressman George W. Gekas and PA Senator Roger A. Madigan said the project will provide a boost for local real estate companies, relieve housing pressure, and hopefully spread through Lycoming County in light of the current economic downturn. Chairman of the Fairfield Township supervisors said Tules Run is a good example why municipalities need to assess impact fees on developers.

headline: Takeover Attempt Stalled as Company Wins Ruling
abstract: The Delaware Chancery Court ruled in favor of National Intergroup, Inc. in their struggle over control of its board of directors with an investment group.

headline: Caught in the Middle of a Family Feud.
abstract: PA Senator Vincent Fumo and House Speaker Robert O'Donnell spoke in the Philadelphia City Hall alongside Mayor Wilson Goode and City Controller Jonathan Saidel to deliver the Financial Recovery Plan intended to save the city from fiscal crisis. The legislators criticized the City Council for being irresponsible and unhelpful in the planning process. Two PA Supreme Court justices promised to reduce court spending in the city. U.S. Representative William H. Gray III promised to get $33 million in federal dollars for the city.

headline: Incumbents winning in war chests
abstract: Many incumbents in the U.S. Congress running in PA have built up large campaign war chests, whereas their challengers commonly have much less money at their disposal.

headline: Senate group supports Attorney D. Michael Stine as judge in Schuylkill
abstract: The unanimous confirmation by the PA Senate Judiciary Committee of Tamaqua attorney D. Michael Stine to serve on the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas bodes well for confirmation of PA Governor Casey's nominee by the full senate. Stine was chosen by Casey from a list of three candidates recommended by the Schuylkill County Bar Association. Formerly, Stine served as an assistant district attorney. Rep. Edward Lucyk accompanied Stine to the hearing, while Sen. James Rhoades recounted Stine's achievements to the Committee.

headline: In Passing: Buddy Ryan for mayor
abstract: The article sarcastically suggests that the coach of the Philadelphia Eagles football team should run for mayor next year, as it seems that he won't be coaching the Eagles and Mayor Wilson Goode will be out of office.

headline: Jobs: We Need A Lot More of Them In Area
abstract: This article discusses employment statistics in Oil City, Pennsylvania.  Specifically, the article discusses the shift from a manufacturing to a service-oriented economy.

headline: Pa. candidate Hafer spends taxing day at White House
abstract: It was a taxing Thursday for PA GOP gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer, who came to the White House hoping to talk about education but was pelted with questions about President Bush's tax stance. The president just announced that there will be tax revenue increases despite his campaign promise of no new taxes. Reporters hounded Hafer about her thoughts on the tax increase.

headline: Health club rises where disco fell
abstract: A plan to establish a health club on the site of a former disco joint is praised in this editorial.  The Strawberry Square Fitness and Aerobic Center is scheduled to open by the end of the year and will offer aerobics, weight-training, massage, sauna, and even a juice bar and lounge.

headline: Law Schools
abstract: The Univeristy of Pennsylvania Law School is the only Pennsylvania institution in the U.S. News and World Report's rank of best law schools in the nation.

headline: Hafer: Double recycling goal
abstract: Gubernatorial Candidate and PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer called on PA to raise its recycling goal to 50 percent rather than 25 percent. Bethlehem, Allentown, Easton and other communities have already begun recycling programs in advance of the law taking effect. Hafer favors a gas tax to help fund mass transit, criticizing PA Governor Bob Casey for expecting residents to pay half the bill for transit renovations. She also noted the PA Department of Environmental Resources needs better leadership.

headline: Coalition Launches Drive to Obtain Osprey Funding
abstract: An organization of legislators and businesses are seeking federal funding and support for the Osprey to advance American aircraft and defense technology while reducing long-run operation and maintenance costs.

headline: Cop Sentence
abstract: Charles Hund, a corrupt ex-Philadelphia cop, was sentenced to eighteen months in federal prison for cocaine trafficking.

headline: Troubled prisons earmarked for funds
abstract: The budget approved by PA Governor Casey increased for the PA Department of Corrections, allowing Graterford State Prison to hire more employees to comply with a court ruling and presenting a referendum issuing bonds for county prisons to voters. PA Rep. Raymond Blunt said the budget increase will be used for Cost Of Living Adjustments in salaries. An amendment introduced by Sen. Stewart Greenleaf to place non-violent offenders in community prisons was deleted by the House.

headline: Guru Plans 'Heaven on Earth' in Pittsburgh, Philadelphia
abstract: A company owned by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi wants to build self-contained houses in pollution-free communities in the 50 largest metropolitan areas in North America, including Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.  Some developers in Pittsburgh were skeptical that the plans would work in the area.

headline: The failings of Fellheimer
abstract: Alan Fellheimer, CEO of Equimark, will be stepping down as a result of his failings in providing for the success of the company.  Equimark has declined since the beginning of his leadership, and the company board is now looking for a successor who will be able to return the bank to its former credibility.

headline: Census Bureau Aims to Count as Many of Homeless As it Can Today
abstract: The Census Bureau plans to count as many homeless people as it can today.

headline: Indicted Zemprelli Jokes at PSU Meeting
abstract: Retired state Senator Edward P. Zemprelli, facing conspiracy and fraud charges, attended a PSU board of trustees meeting with wit and eloquence, claiming innocence.

headline: Senate has control over speed of confirmation
abstract: President Bush says he wants the new member of the US Supreme Court confirmed and sitting on the bench by the time the court's term begins in October. But that will be up to the Democratic majority in the Senate may have its own ideas. A lot depends on whom Bush nominates.

headline: Jogging around; Kudos
abstract: The editors commend the Leetsdale Council for its purchase of two large movie screens for the community park. Boy Scout Troop 108 will sponsor the events.

headline: County to take manager role from Handler
abstract: As an alternative to competitive bidding for its case management, Dauphin County is immediately taking over management of services for the 4,000 mentally ill and retarded persons now being treated at the Rosalie G. Handler Center.  The takeover was approved by a majority of county commissioners yesterday and calls for the county to install its own manager to oversee Handler's case management; the current staff and facilities will continue to be used, however.

headline: Pa. lawmaker drafts letter denouncing higher taxes
abstract: PA Representative Robert Walker gathered signatures of 90 House Republicans to a letter expressing opposition to higher taxes, within hours after President Bush said tax revenues are needed to offset the federal deficit. Bush emerged from budget negotiations and said tax revenues increases are needed.

headline: HealthPass audit firm has ties to industry
abstract: The privately owned firm, Medical Services Agency Inc., hired by officials of Healthcare Management Alternatives, a firm which provides health care to low-income residents of South and West Philadelphia as a publicly-funded pilot project, appears to have questionable conflicts of interest among them an auditor, Thomas Trite, who is affiliated with the PA Pharmaceutical Association, an organizations that lobbies state officials on behalf of independent drug store owners.

headline: Lawmaker seeks Rainy Day Funds to pay for special education deficit
abstract: A lawmaker has proposed that PA dip into a reserve fund to get rid of a $84 million special-education debt. PA Representative Stephen Friend said that the state is short-changing school districts by not giving them enough money to cover the mandated special education; he wants to introduce legislation that enables the General Assembly to use the Tax Stabilization Fund or the Rainy Day Fund. Under the current law only the governor can use the reserve fund, which holds $124 million.

headline: Handling waste
abstract: PA regulations employing mandatory recycling begin later this month, are predicted to be a success, as the public greatly supports the initiative.  It is hoped that with a PA success in recycling, other states will begin to mandate recycling programs as well.

headline: Conrail Exceeds Buyback Objective
abstract: Conrail Corp. said it would buy back about 22.34 million shares of its stock at $49 per share.

headline: Corrections officials: No more room come July
abstract: Testifying before the House Judiciary Committee, acting PA Corrections Commissioner Joseph Lehman declared PA prisons will run out of room by July. The Department of Corrections is overcrowded by 58 percent, testified Robin Lubitz of the PA Commission on Sentencing.
