Lehman, appointed by PA Governor Robert Casey, said the Department has considered housing prisoners in office space, hospitals, or even Fort Indiantown Gap. PA houses some prisoners in Federal prisons at a cost of $1 million per month.

headline: Trying To Find Extra Cells Risks Lives and Wastes Money
abstract: Due to massive overcrowding in jails across the country, prisoners often have to be transported for miles between the jail they're held at and the courthouse they're tried at, providing more chances for traffic accidents and escapes, and adding costs to police and attorneys.

headline: Guru plans pollution-free communities
abstract: Representatives of the Maharishi Heaven on Earth Corp. of Malibu, CA, owned by Maharishi Mehest Yogi, are visiting Pittsburgh this week to explain their plans and find a local developer to buy hundreds of acres of land to build 100 to 200 solar-powered houses.  PA Builders Association President Murray Rust was not supportive of the idea.

headline: The Uranium shuffle
abstract: With the downward slide in the price of uranium, many uranium companies are realizing it is cheaper to buy overstock from other companies and sell it at marked up rates to other companies rather than mining uranium themselves.

headline: Census counts for blacks
abstract: Claude Lewis examines the US Census Bureau from a minority point of view, saying there is suspicion in against giving information out. Many suspect information is given directly to federal agencies, rather than stored "non-publicly" in a database. One representative from the black community says the government purposely under represents census data for minorities. Census Bureau employees hope organizations like the Complete Count Committee will help earn the trust of minority communities.

headline: Intersection news is good; more needed
abstract: Word came from the office of PA Senator Edwin Hool recently that about $2 million in state funds have been secured to improve 10 intersections in the North Penn area over the next three years. This is welcome news. These only represent 25 of the 40 that were designated as needing major improvements.

headline: Senate OKs Swisher for magistrate
abstract: The PA Senate unanimously confirmed Lebanon County deputy sheriff Hazel Swisher to fill a vacant district justice post.  Swisher will likely assume the post within a few weeks.

headline: Knight Commission, 840
abstract: Eight of the nation's leading college football coaches presented a unified front when they appeared before the Knight Commission that is ruling on new NCAA legislation.  The panel will also hear from basketball coaches during the two-day session they are holding to discuss potential changes with coaches.

headline: U.S. may freeze assets of fraud-linked S&Ls
abstract: The U.S. Justice Department announced that it may freeze the assets of thrifts and Savings and Loan officers accused of fraud.  Congress authorized such asset freezes in last year's Savings-and-Loan bailout bill.  Although the Justice Department has not frozen any assets to date, there are currently several cases under investigation.

headline: Pennsylvania unemployment at 6.1 percent for October
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry reported that the state's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 6.1 percent in October, up from the 5.5 percent in September. The U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the nation's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 5.7 percent, unchanged from the September figure. Analysts said the labor force has grown by 120,000 while employment has remained constant.

headline: Heinz wants smokers to pay health care
abstract: US Senator John Heinz proposed a 16 cent tax on packs of cigarettes to pay for health insurance for poor children and pregnant women.

headline: Lawmakers pass Florio's school plan
abstract: New Jersey Governor Florio campaigned on a platform not to raise taxes, however in order to pass and education spending overhaul, that is exactly what Florio championed. The budget plans will redistribute school funds so that even the poorest schools receive funding equal to the wealthiest. The plan raises taxes on the wealthy as well as the sales tax, extending it to cover new products, sin taxes and the income tax in general. Republicans accuse Florio of instituting a plan to establish mediocrity. The New Jersey Education Association denounced Florio as well.

headline: Hauler quits; recycling halts
abstract: Ralph Nestor, owner of Nestor Sanitation, has stopped hauling for the Schuylkill Communities Awareness Recycling Program, halting recycling in 10 municipalities, causing large pileups of recyclables. Nestor quit hauling because SCRAP was not paying him, hoping that the revenue from the recycling would be enough to cover costs, but Nestor said that he'd need $200 a week more to cover his costs. This development is due mainly to the depreciation of recyclable materials now that many communities are recycling.

headline: Conrail Narrows Search For Center, Officials Say
abstract: Pittsburgh is being considered for a new national Conrail customer service center which would employ about 900 people.

headline: Council Reaches 'Unbelievable' Drug War Draw
abstract: In a final budget review session, City Councilman Carl Curchoe failed to achieve support necessary to appropriate funds for an additional undercover agent in the war on drugs. The result was that funds for code enforcement were depleted as the money was moved into a general appropriations fund. Curchoe enlisted the District Attorney's Office, however against testimony from the chief of police and the mayor, it was not enough. The Mayor hopes to gain support to reinstate the money for codes enforcement.

headline: TV show to focus on Adams girl
abstract: NBC, in doing a spotlight on the life of children of migrant workers on the "Today" show, will focus on Minouche Laurent, an 11-year-old fifth-grade girl whose parents, Haitian émigrés, work in Adams County picking fruit in the fall and in Florida in the winter.  Laurent attends a school that has the Migrant Child Development Program designed for children like her.

headline: Helping hand. Loans aid low-income home buyers.
abstract: Neighborhood Housing Services, a Pittsburgh arm of the national non-profit organization Neighbor-Works, teamed with Dollar Bank to provide up to $500,000 in mortgage funding and free home ownership training programs to low-income residents as a part of the Home-Help Lending program. Participant buyers don't have to pay a down payment or closing costs, as the fees are figured into the mortgage.

headline: Thornburgh's Report on Partial Merger of Record, Dispatch
abstract: Attorney General Dick Thornburgh's thorough report on the York Daily Record's and the York Dispatch's application for approval of a proposed joint operation arrangement.

headline: Census success
abstract: A chart lists the percentage of the population counted by the census in counties and cities across PA as well as the US national average. In every area listed save that of Philadelphia, the percentage counted is higher than the national average, which stands at 84 percent.

headline: Is Act 195 feeling the winds of change?
abstract: For 20 years a state law that allows teachers the right to strike has been cloaked in an aura of invincibility. Political winds have been changing and even supporters of Act 195 are wondering if some changes to the law may occur. Still most say it is not likely that the law would ever be repealed. Some proposed changes would be secret ballots for teacher strike and limits to strikes.

headline: Senate race pits riches against rags
abstract: Altoona City Councilman Alan Mikula, in his race for PA Senate against Senate President Pro Tem Robert Jubelirer, is struggling to raise funds. Jubelirer has received contributions to the Friends of Senator Jubelirer Committee, including some from the Committee for Advancement of State and Local Government, a GOP national Committee member and a PA Securities and Exchange Commissioner. Donations to other incumbents from PACs are also noted.

headline: Larry King Apologizes for Remarks About Miss Pennsylvania
abstract: Talk show host Larry King apologized for televised comments saying the Miss PA was the ugliest contestant in last week's Miss America Pageant, saying that he made the comments "in jest with no intention to offend."  King is a judge in the pageant and made the comments on The Joan Rivers Show.

headline: Now It's Claytie and the Lady
abstract: Texas State Treasurer Ann Richards emerged victorious from a mudslinging Democratic gubernatorial runoff, setting up a November election battle between her and oilman-rancher Clayton Williams.

headline: Pennsylvania’s Casey tells State Legislators His Spending Plan Has to be Reduced
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey told PA legislators that the $12.2 billion budget proposal for 1991 will need to be reduced due to lower-than-expected corporate tax collections. According to the administration corporate tax collections would have to increase 15% in 1991 to balance the budget that was originally proposed by Casey. Overall for the year tax revenues have been about 2% short of the expectations but the state is still expected to end the year with a small surplus.

headline: High price of delivering health insurance
abstract: According to a study released by Citizen Action, an advocacy group for national health insurance, commercial insurance firms have an administrative cost of 33.5 cents for every dollar paid in benefits.  This figure is vastly higher than government insurance overhead rates, with 2.3 cents per dollar for US Medicare for the elderly, and 3 cents per dollar spent by Canada's national health program.

headline: LCB to set hearing on pizza shop license
abstract: A petition filed by the Palmyra school district, originally rejected by the PA Liquor Control Board was refiled after district officials remeasured the distance of the school from Roma Pizza Restaurant. The new figure calculated puts the school within the distance in which it is allowed to comment on the Restaurant's request. In addition, the district filed a petition to intervene in proceedings on behalf of the drug and alcohol principles espoused by the school, said Superintendent Clarence Fox.

headline: Hazmat site plan spurs more action
abstract: The Concord Resources proposal to build a hazardous waste facility in Clarion County has spurred action on many fronts, including mass opposition from Clarion residents, Auditor General Barbara Hafer will be in Clarion County to take comments on the plan today, and Concord said it has sent out 9000 letters to residents explaining the program and their commitment to public health and the environment.

headline: Consultants like Millard
abstract: State agencies indicated Millard airport in South Annville Township, one of four sites considered by Lebanon County Commissioners for an airport, would have the least impact on area farmland. Commissioner William Carpenter was concerned a county airport might put small private airports out of business, however Fritsche says the trend of privately owned planes is decreasing and small private airports are unreliable. They also do not qualify for federal funding grants. Lebanon County has been named by the Federal Aviation Administration as an area that needs a public airport.

headline: Councilman Wants Study of Free Drugs for Addicts
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council has authorized officials to determine whether or not handing out free drugs to addicts and users would reduce crime.

headline: Two city businesses seized as drug fronts
abstract: Federal marshals seized two city businesses alleged to have been fronts for a pair of large scale Dominican-run drug distribution rings that were dismantled last week during a massive narcotics sweep. The properties will remain under federal jurisdiction until the court decides whether they will forfeited and sold. Thus far 56 reputed cocaine and heroin traffickers have been jailed.

headline: Hilton Hotel ready to help revitalize city
abstract: Following an aggressive advertising campaign, the Harrisburg Hilton and Towers opening is expected to secure convention and meeting business and stimulate the local economy. General manager of the hotels, William D. Kohl said the Hilton will have spin-off benefits for other downtown businesses. Kohl reported that many state associations will increase conventions held in the capital.

headline: Thriving: Maker of truck cranes adds employees, space
abstract: A local truck-crane manufacturer is growing. Company officials also expect that US Truck Cranes will gain a larger share of the market as new dealers are signed to distribute its products. It will be adding more employees and moving production lines to York

headline: Census Takers Count People in Subway Passageways, on Steam Vents
abstract: In the country's most ambitious attempt ever to count homeless people, Census takers scoured cities today.

headline: It'll happen, but nobody knows when
abstract: PA State Legislators take guesses at when the budget will be passed as the deadline approaches. PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel predicts it will be passed early. Others, like Reps. Gaynor Cawley and Gerard Kosinski predicted an on time passage, while Reps. Dwight Evans and Gordon Linton were less optimistic.

headline: Senators oppose foreign aid cuts
abstract: Efforts by U.S. Senator Bob Dole to reduce American aid to Isreal and Egypt in order to send more aid to Eastern Europe have been rebuffed in a letter signed by Seventy-three Senators including PA's Arlen Specter and John Heinz.

headline: Little League treats fan to world-series honors
abstract: Skipper Carillo, a mildly mentally retarded man of Laguna Beach, was treated to a trip to the Little League World Series by his friends and family as a way to thank him for his volunteer work.

headline: Medical Report Fails to Boost Centocor Stock
abstract: After a medical study of Centocor's new infection treatment drug did not work as well as anticipated, the company's stock dropped.  The study showed that the infection-treatment drug, Centoxin, only reduced the death rate of patients suffering from septic shock from 49 to 30 percent.  Analysts were hoping for a 50 percent reduction in deaths.

headline: Pittsburgh job gains
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry reported job growth in Pittsburgh at a rate of 1 percent for the month. Statewide, the number of jobs on record is the 4th highest recorded.

headline: High-Tech Care in a Club Setting
abstract: The high-tech design of the  Pennsylvania Hospital Adult Day Health Center has been carefully planned to accommodate many health needs and serves as a model for other adult day-care centers.

headline: LCB to set hearing on pizza shop license
abstract: Roma Pizza will not be allowed to sell beer if residents get their way. The PA state Liquor Control Board has received 35 protests and a hearing will be set to on the proposed transfer. Both the school district and Palmyra council have opposed Roma's request that malt liquor license to the restaurant at 19 Railroad St. The school district opposes it because of the closeness to the middle school. The school district is within the 300 feet rule by just three feet, so they can object to the placement.

headline: Hegins brawl: Shared insanity
abstract: The writer comments on the improprieties of both sides of the Hegins Pigeon Shoot, saying that the protesters are insane for protesting it so adamantly, as there are more important, human issues that could use attention, and the "sportsmen" are insane for considering it sporting to shoot 6000 captive pigeons in the first place.

headline: Contractor paints eastbound I-78 drivers into a corner
abstract: A construction problem on I-78 caused major traffic backups and several car accidents during morning rush hour.

headline: Counties to confront state on child-support collection rules
abstract: The cost of collecting child-support could drastically increase for counties as a result of a new contract with the state on the matter to be drafted soon.

headline: Two plead guilty in drug case
abstract: Two former state officials pleaded guilty to cocaine use or distribution while in office.  One of them is attempting to reinstate a previous plea agreement.

headline: Holl hopes to have an impact
abstract: PA Senator Edwin Holl has introduced a bill to legalize the practice of levying impact fees on developers.  The bill has gained much more support than a House bill addressing the same issue.

headline: Top ten insurance state and their regulators
abstract: Top ten insurance states tabled.

headline: Centre referendum on DA removed
abstract: The Centre County district attorney's long quest to become a full time hit another snag when the county's elections board revoked an advisory referendum question on his status. His salary would double to $79,000 if it went to full time. Sixteen of the state's 67 county prosecutors earn full-time salaries.

headline: It's Budget Attack Time
abstract: Governor Casey's budget has faced much criticism especially with the upcoming gubernatorial election.

headline: Sensible Souter
abstract: The editorial supports David Souter in his nomination for Supreme Court Justice, and explains that he's stood up against some of the beliefs of the party that nominated him, and supports the "legal status quo."

headline: Masloff, Shore- Distinguished Daughters of Pa.
abstract: Among five other women, Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff and Barbara Shore, the director of the University of Pittsburgh's doctoral program in social work, were honored as "Distinguished Daughters of PA" due to their outstanding contributions in law, education, business, arts, culture, sports, science or government. Masloff's nomination was backed by the Pittsburgh Conference on Soviet Jewry and the Catholic Youth Association.

headline: Mellon Acquiring Tellers From Cleveland Bank
abstract: Mellon Bank has acquired the automated teller machine business of the InstaNet regional network from Ameritrust Corporation, one of Cleveland's largest banks.  The deal is Mellon's second automatic teller acquisition in the last five weeks.

headline: Politicians criticized at area rallies
abstract: There were several rallies held today around the nation, organized by the Council for Citizens Against Waste, protesting against federal lawmakers because of their recent passage of a budget plan that will increase taxes. The rallies were also against the general perceived wasteful spending by lawmakers on pet projects and other areas "while Social Security and Medicare are being cut."

headline: Home will halt misuse of restraints
abstract: York County Hospital & Home officials have promised the PA Department of Health that they will no longer allow patients to be held in restraints for longer than the legal 2-hour limit, after which the patient is supposed to be released to get exercise and go to the bathroom. The problem was unearthed in a surprise visit by PA Department of Health officials, during which they found that half of the 26 patients held in restraints had not been freed every 2 hours.

headline: Lenker to head group
abstract: Gary Lenker, Vice President of Donco Construction, has been elected president of the PA Builders Association. He will head the 160-member board of directors and be responsible for overseeing the trade association's activities on the state and national levels.

headline: Heinz boasts of dolphin-safe StarKist tuna
abstract: The Heinz Company is now on of three US tuna canners who now refuse to buy or sell tuna caught in nets that also kill dolphins.  The company is attempting to employ more environmental efforts where possible.

headline: County should support airport
abstract: Opinion urging New Castle area business groups and related organizations to acknowledge the problems at the New Castle Airport, and to exert pressure on city and county officials to address the facilities needs. The airport is vital to the local economy.

headline: County 911 cost will be less
abstract: An update to the 911 service is now estimated at costing $400,000 less that the original cost.  It expected to be functional in about two years.

headline: U. Bucks man sentenced to die
abstract: Kenneth J. Williams is the first man sentenced to death in Lehigh County in decades. His attorney and a group of nine supporters say they will appeal to the PA Supreme Court. Williams was arrested using stolen credit cards of a murdered truck driver with whom he had hitched a ride. Williams will be transferred from the County prison to Graterford State prison. Supporters say they will employ Centurion Ministries to establish Williams innocence.

headline: Homeless shelter benefitting from local generosity
abstract: The financial outlook for Lewistown Shelter Services is brighter. Director Lucinda Eby was pleased by the local community support the shelter is receiving. Some companies asking employees to donate to the shelter rather than spend money to exchange presents with coworkers, and one local business is even donating a day of profits to the shelter.

headline: Top Ten Insurance States-And Their Regulators
abstract: A chart lists the top ten insurance states; PA is not on the list. The chart also contains the costs of premiums statewide for each state, the insurance department budget of each state, the number of staff employed by the department, and regulatory spending asa percent of the total premium for each state. Data was obtained from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners.

headline: Chamber's Goal 200 Members As 1991 Campaign Set to Go
abstract: The Williamsport-Lycoming Chamber of Commerce will begin its 1991 membership drive, seeking to top its position as the sixth-largest chamber in PA. Drive chairman and president of marketing for Commonwealth Bank and Trust Co. James Briggs said the chamber's goal is to add 200 companies to its existing 980 members.

headline: It's Election Day in the U.S.A.
abstract: This election day, PA voters will elect the governor, U.S. Congress members and PA House and Senate members. Elections take on added importance, as PA legislatures will be a factor in redrawing congressional districts. The article goes on to list information about voter registration, typical turnout, poll locations, transportation arrangements, the predicted weather, closings, and candidates and questions on the ballot.

headline: Service is set for R.W. Abele
abstract: A memorial service is set for Ralph W. Abele who was the executive director of the PA Fish Commission. He died due to complications associated with an open-heart surgery.

headline: Move ex-president's grave, man says
abstract: Tim Buchanan, of the Harrisburg area, has mounted a campaign to move former President James Buchanan Jr.'s grave to the president's Wheatland estate.  Tim Buchanan fears that the late president is drifting farther into obscurity, and his gravesite at the unkempt Woodward Hill Cemetery is not helping.

headline: Post-Gazette reporter to be mayor's press secretary
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff named Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reporter Albert J. Neri as her press secretary.  Neri will become the city's first communications director with the expanded duties of coordinating the city's promotional efforts.

headline: Poll: Pennsylvanians would support some taxes to offset deficit
abstract: According to a poll, a majority of Pennsylvanians would support higher taxes on alcohol and cigarettes in order to reduce the federal budget, though they would not support additional income or gasoline taxes or an increase in Medicare premiums and other Medicare costs.

headline: Hospital
abstract: Philadelphia's Girard Medical Center filed for federal bakruptcy protection which would allow a merger with St. Joseph's Hospital and continued medical services for North Philadelphia's poor.

headline: Libraries to get $400,000 in aid
abstract: The Dauphin County Library System's East Shore and Elizabethville branches will receive $400,000 from a federal grant through the state Department of Education.  Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel will announce the grant at the East Shore Area Branch.  The money will go toward expansion of the East Shore library branch.

headline: Hope seen for death of burner
abstract: USPCI of Pennsylvania, Inc, will be subject to examination when it formally submits its incinerator proposal to the Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Court Oks drunk-driver checkpoints
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled that police seeking to curb drunken driving not violating motorists' privacy rights by stopping them at sobriety checkpoints. The 6-3 decision upheld Michigan's checkpoint program and similar operations in most states.

headline: County end voluntary placement of children
abstract: Northhampton County will stop admitting children to placement centers, including foster and group homes, on a voluntary basis. A court order will not be required in order for the Department of Human Services to place a child. Lack of funds is being cited as the reason for the change.

headline: U.S. Attorney Backs Drug Case Handling
abstract: US attorney for central and NE PA James West has been accused of covering up some aspects of a drug case against former co-workers.  West took himself off the case last year so that there would be no suspicions about his loyalties.

headline: Homeless Union Seizes Homes in Philadelphia
abstract: Demanding that the government provide more available houses and rent subsidies, homeless people moved into federally-owned vacant homes in three cities.

headline: Trump deal a losing hand
abstract: Donald Trump is trying to stay one step ahead of creditors who are threatening to force him into bankruptcy. Late in the year Trump and the bondholders reached an agreement in which Trump and the bondholders reached an agreement in which Trump got reduced interest payments but gave up half-ownership in the Taj Mahal Casino Resort and will lose control entirely if profit goals are not met.

headline: City Attorney Protests Dismissal; Announces Plans to File Suit
abstract: Camden city attorney, Patricia Darden, believes her removal by Mayor  Aaron Thompson was the result of an alleged conspiracy with influential Democratic leaders, though he denies all accusations.

headline: It's not my fault
abstract: PA Representative Joseph F. Markosek of Monroeville writes to attempt to clear his name from the effects of a letter published recently from his opponent in the upcoming election, which suggested that Markosek's voting record had in come way helped cause the current savings-and-loan crisis in the US.  Markosek claims that as a state legislator, he made no votes and had no authority to have an effect on a national problem such as this.

headline: Singel hits a high note at home for senior citizens
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel went to nursing home to entertain a few of the old folks and, no doubt, score some political points. He didn't know they'd make him sing for his supper. He was a good sport and strummer several tunes from a song book. One man heckled him and told him he better not quit his day job.

headline: Retailers' markdowns coaxing shoppers
abstract: Many stores desperate to boost cash flow have announced clearance sales and deep discounts in the past 10 days which analysts said rival post-Christmas promotion in previous years. Stores are worried that by after Christmas people will be spent out.

headline: null
abstract: This article discusses a proposal to turn sludge resulting from coal power generation into compost fertilizer.  This proposal is the cheapest and most environmentally sound method of sludge disposal.

headline: President's Retreat from tax pledge causes problems for both parties
abstract: US Republican congressman are angry with President Bush for not preparing for the statement he recently issued, changing his "no new taxes" position to one that will consider taxes in order to address the federal budget deficit. Possible solutions being posed to the deficit are cutting domestic spending, raising taxes, and cutting entitlements. Republicans oppose raising taxes, while Democrats are opposed to cutting funds for existing programs.

headline: Hospital accountant charged with stealing $260,000
abstract: A former accountant for Hahnemann University Hospital was indicted for authorizing payments worth $260,000 to "workers" who never actually were on the payroll or provided any services.

headline: Library to receive $10,000 state check
abstract: PA Representative Don Dorr will present a $10,000 check to Collinsille Library officials tomorrow. The library will be built at the Clearview Elementary School. The Philadelphia Electric Co. donated three modular units, which will make the library three times larger than it is now.

headline: House approves major overhaul of clean-air laws
abstract: The US House passed the Clean Air Act, the first such legislation since 1977, which will be sent to the Senate, where it is expected to pass. The bill's provisions could cause price increases in cars, gasoline, and even dry-cleaning in some cities. The plan covers five areas: acid rain, smog, cars, toxics, and the ozone layer.

headline: Crashes Spur New Turnpike Policies
abstract: A Senate investigation of two fatal crashes on the Pennsylvania Turnpike last year resulted in the adoption of several new emergency policies.

headline: County jail population now at 252
abstract: Lackawanna County Prison is presently housing an all-time high of inmates at 252. Extra office supplies have been given to help ease the excess. Bills that may affect prisons are listed.

headline: Underage drinking sentences defended
abstract: Downtown District Justice Jacob Williams said he is not concerned about a request from two state legislators for an inquiry into handling of underage drinking cases. They want to examine if Williams ignored state requirements that youths convicted of underage drinking have their licenses suspended for 90 days. He gave some youths community service instead of 90 days.

headline: House Calls on Pro Baseball Teams to Postpone Good Friday Games
abstract: The state House of Representatives requested that the Pittsburgh Pirates and the Philadelphia Phillies postpone their game on Good Friday as a sign of respect.

headline: Trump deals a losing hand
abstract: Donald Trump's Taj Mahal Casino Resort failed to perform as expected, even after Trump opened his $800 million showplace. Contractors and creditors waited for their money as Trump struggled to make interest payments. In November, failing to make a payment of $47 million, Trump and bondholders met to negotiate an agreement in which interest payments were reduced, however Trump lost half-ownership of the casino and stands to lose control entirely if profits are not met.

headline: City computer chief full-time again
abstract: Philadelphia's computer chief Eugene L. Cliett Jr. is returning to full-time work in Philadelphia after spending part of his time working for the New Jersey state government for the past six weeks.  Cliett has faced some criticism that the Philadelphia computering center is too slow in processing taxes and city payroll.

headline: Lawmakers seldom write or understand bills
abstract: Article on how bills get written in the PA state legislature. The elected members of the House and Senate do not write many of the major pieces of legislation they consider. Some don't even understand the bills they vote on. Lobbyists are big helpers in the writing process.

headline: Singel living in a dream
abstract: Letter to the editor about state servants and a speech PA  Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel. The author encourages people to go to work for the state government, but is critical of Singel's dream.

headline: Safety of carnival rides checked
abstract: Charlie Brewbaker is an Inspector for the PA Bureau of Amusement Rides and Attractions. An estimated 300 million people ride amusement park and carnival rides per year, estimates the Outdoor Amusement Business Association. PA employs five full-time licensed inspectors in its bureau, with each carnival operation charged with the responsibility of checking its own equipment and employing its own state-licensed inspector.

headline: To balance city budget, take on the unions
abstract: Philadelphia's budget problems are not, as Mayor Goode contends, caused by a lack of revenue.  Much of the city's budgetary problems can be solved by curbing the monopolistic power that the city's labor unions have over the provision of vital services.  Recently, Waste Management offered to provide city garbage collection for 40 million less than unionized sanitation workers charge; unions should be allowed a bid on annual contracts--not a monopoly over them.

headline: Read his lips: more taxes
abstract: Jim Florio, the newly-elected governor of New Jersey, took initiatives to serve New Jersey as soon as he took office. For example, facing an increasing budget deficit, Florio announced a plan to raise over $2.6 billion in taxes, including doubling income taxes for the state's upper-incomes citizens. Policymakers in Washington are carefully observing Florio's tactics, especially since President Bush's declaration in 1988 to not raise taxes.

headline: Hospital must seek financial answer
abstract: Abington Memorial Hospital is one of the most fiscally healthy hospitals in the area, according to an industry finding. According to the study, 22 hospitals reported an opening loss for the year, 28 reported an operating surplus, and 18 either did not report or did not authorize a release of financial information. The report measured only the operating margin of each hospital.

headline: Library was mute on assets
abstract: The writer is against the Cumberland County library tax that they feel is taking money on the homeowners, especially senior citizens on limited fixed income. The New Cumberland Borough library system is taking most of the money from the taxpayers to keep the library running.

headline: House Panel Gives Nod to Waste Bills
abstract: A package of three bills designed to protect Northeast Pennsylvania from becoming a waste dump for New Jersey and New York was given unanimous approval by the PA House Conservation Committee. The bills would impose strict safety inspections on out-of-state trucks entering PA and violators of these standards would have to pass an inspection within six hours of entering the state. PA Governor Robert P. Casey proposed the measures after two accidents earlier in the year.

headline: Cumberland begins drunk-driving 'blitz'
abstract: Cumberland County police boosted their efforts to combat drunk driving last night. Officers in six municipalities kicked off a four-night "DUI blitz" watching area roads for drunk driving. The main purpose is to make roads safer for the holiday weekend.

headline: County legal fees: Prices of politics or prudence?
abstract: Montgomery County has paid to one Philadelphia law firm $3.47 million to represent it since 1988. Accusations and defenses have swirled around this figure, but the first question should be whether the county truly received $3.47 million worth of work out of the attorneys. Unfortunately the lawyers can probably justify have fee down to the last post it note. The county defends the costs by saying it has to defend itself in lawsuits.

headline: Unger's escape record grows
abstract: The escape of Franklin County resident Merle Winfield Unger, convicted of the murder of an off-duty Maryland policeman, from DeSoto Correctional Institute in Florida adds to his extensive escape record. Police in PA, Maryland and Florida are on the lookout for him and are confident he will be caught. Unger's escape partner, Richard Frazier, was captured by DeSoto County sheriff's deputies shortly after the escape.

headline: Housing affordability
abstract: This chart shows the median price, minimum income, affordability gap and affordability index for selected communities within the Delaware Valley region of PA and New Jersey, according to a study conducted by the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission.

headline: T-Shirt Saying Angers Anti-Rape Group
abstract: When the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust picked a Dorothy Parker pun to print on t-shirts to benefit the Trust and the Benedum Center, it did not intend to anger the Pittsburgh Action Against Rape group which recently acquired signatures and presented the Trust's President Carol Brown with a letter of protest. The slogan read, "you can lead a horticulture but you cannot make her think." Marketing director Holly Van Dine said the slogan may be dropped from the next printing but should not be taken literally.

headline: City eases forecast on cash position
abstract: Philadelphia can avoid running out of cash for a couple months by shifting money between accounts and deferring payments, but the city is still desperately in need of outside help.  A few foreign and local institutions are considering letters of credit.

headline: Lead in polls gives Casey luxury of ignoring Hafer
abstract: Gov. Casey's significant lead over opponent Barbara Hafer in opinion polls allows him to avoid confrontation, and even allows him to avoid traditional campaigning for the time being.  Hafer is searching for ways to close the gap between Casey and herself.

headline: Singel see tax reform defeat
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel predicted the demise of a tax plan proposed by the PA Senate Pro Temp Robert C. Jubelirer when the package hits the state House. Jubelirer says his plan fixes problems the governor's proposal didn't address for counties to reassess properties. He says it also gives people a bigger voice in local government taxation by including local referenda measures on tax increases. Singel doesn't believe it has a chance of passing.

headline: Special Olympians mix with Big 33 gang
abstract: It was a light workout for the Hershey High School football team. The teammates are "buddied" with Special Olympic competitors, who were on hand to see the team practice.

headline: Shell Unveils New Gas Officials Say is Better for Environment
abstract: Shell Oil Company is introducing a new gasoline that reduces hydrocarbon and carbon monoxide emissions.

headline: Real tax reform
abstract: The editorial stresses the importance of listening to normal citizens, citing some letters to newspapers, on the issue of tax reform.  It also claims that tax reform is still vital to PA, and that Casey and the legislature need to work together to implement it.

headline: Hospital to help pay tuition for nurses-to-be
abstract: As part of a new recruitment plan for the Graduate Hospital in Philadelphia, the hospital will pay up to 60% of the tuition of qualified students at the University of Pennsylvania in the nursing department if the student agrees to work for at least two years at the Center City hospital after graduation.  The plan is known as the Hospital Nurse Scholars Program.

headline: Ligonier Valley schools to open with substitutes; other talks started
abstract: With sweetened deals for substitutes teaching during teacher strike, classes will begin tomorrow for seniors in the Ligonier Valley school district.  Contract talks are making headway, but administrators wanted to start classes as soon as possible for students.

headline: Household Hazardous Waste Ignored, Senator Says
abstract: State legislators believe Governor Casey's administration is wrong to refuse to provide funding to municipalities to implement household hazardous waste collection programs.

headline: Cumberland begins drunk-driving 'blitz'
abstract: Officers in six municipalities in Cumberland County kicked off a four-night Driving Under the Influence blitz during New Year's. Chief driving under the influence agent John Rich is one of a number of officers recommended for service in the effort. Overtime pay will be covered by a $152,000 grant from the PA Department of Transportation. The funds will also be used to establish the first county-run, county-wide sobriety checkpoint program in PA beginning next month.

headline: County surpassed inmate all of July
abstract: The Allegheny County Jail exceeded its capacity for the entire month of July, something of a record for the jail.  Many efforts are underway to help reduce overcrowding at the prison.

headline: Unrest Flares Locally in Bus Strike
abstract: Police arrested a Greyhound picket who was supposedly preventing bus departures while passengers waited for hours.  The strike began over job security and wage rates when contract agreements collapsed.

headline: Housing Authority Closes Its Doors
abstract: The Williamsport Housing Authority voted to stop accepting applications for its low-income housing project, saying there already are 600 waiting and more on the way. U.S. Housing and Urban Development guidelines permit such action if there is no likelihood of placing applicants within the next 12 months.

headline: Turning Up the Heat on the Top
abstract: A bill signed by PA Governor Robert Casey establishes PA's anti-takeover legislation as some of the toughest in the nation. It is opposed by many corporations, and PA Senator Vincent Fumo.  Wall Street, lobbyists, and legal experts condemn it as an infringement on property rights. The law redefines obligations of a CEO-appointed board directors, allowing them to act in the interests of consumers. The law mandates time periods in which takeovers must occur, along with penalties for unsuccessful attempts.

headline: City Hall Needs A New Attitude
abstract: The writer stresses that just by focusing on the big loans and issues facing the city, Philadelphia will likely never turn the corner on its financial situation.  He claims that more attention needs to be paid to the smaller details that are costing the city money bit by bit.

headline: It's official: Pa., N.J. losing clout
abstract: PA is one of 13 states losing clout in the US House of Representatives according to the US Census Bureau. William P. O'Hare of the private, nonprofit Population Reference Bureau found redistribution of seats ironic given the increase of power in California is attributed to the growth of the immigrant, non-voting population. PA has dropped to fifth place as the most populous state. Some experts have said the redistricting bodes well for Republicans, as seats were mostly gained in Republican states.

headline: Singel weighs run at U.S. Senate seat
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, who just won re-election with PA Governor Robert P. Casey, is weighing a bid for the U.S. Senate in 1992 against Republican Senator Arlen Specter and a run for governor in 1994. A victory against Specter would mean PA's first bipartisan representation in the U.S. Senate since 1968. Though Singel would be the apparent candidate for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, the last three lieutenant governors to run have lost their bids.

headline: Stapleton subs for Bob Casey
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey asked state Senator Pat Stapleton to officiate in his place during festivities at the Divisions II Championship Event of the Pennsylvania State Athletic Conference. Casey was away attending a Pennsylvania Society Dinner, so Stapleton participated with North Dakota Governor George Sinner in the coin toss prior to the game. Stapleton commented on the significance of the event to the PA State System of Higher Education.

headline: Lawmaker Abortion
abstract: The PA House of Representatives asked Blue Cross to change an abortion caluse in its health contract.  The change ensures that abortions for members, staffers and their families are not financed with taxpayer dollars.

headline: 'Recession is here,' most economists believe
abstract: Three out of four of the nation's top business economists, including members of the National Association of Business Economists, believe that the United States economy is in a recession. Association president Richard D. Rippe said the Persian Gulf oil-price shock played a role in causing the recession. The U.S. Commerce Department announced that the national trade deficit reached its highest imbalance in a year. The Consumer Confidence Index continued to decline.

headline: Hospitals sue state for medical payments
abstract: The Hospital Association of PA has asked Commonwealth Court to force the PA Welfare Department to continue medical assistance payments, claiming that 30 of the association's members might have to stop treating poor patients. State funding is caught up in a dispute between PA Governor Robert Casey and the Republican-controlled state Senate.

headline: Pa. high school to be represented at Moscow environmental conference
abstract: Four representatives from Abraham Lincoln High School in Philadelphia will be a part of a week-long environmental symposium in Moscow.  The high school is the only American school that will be represented at the conference.  Teacher Joe Bartlett said that it's important that "they [the Russians] realize the environment has no geographical boundaries."

headline: Hundreds think landfill idea stinks
abstract: 200 or so Dorrance Twp. Residents voiced their anger over a proposed landfill to the Luzerne County Landfill Sitting Committee.

headline: Delays, disagreements imperil building of Crows Run Corridor; Highway project imperiled
abstract: Controversy over an expansion of Freedom-Crider Road that connects Beaver County with Cranberry Township continues.  The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation ultimately decides whether or not to repair and expand the road, and risk losing federal funding if a decision is not reached soon.

headline: County to give youths a peek at inmates' lot
abstract: Commission Chairman Sally S. Klein proposed "Tough Talk", a program that would take juvenile delinquents under the care of the county's probation and parole office and bring them to the county jail to experience the adult criminal justice system. Klein and Commissioner Russell L. Sheaffer, who chairs the prison board, created the program in hopes of deterring future delinquency. Judge Sebastian D. Natale, who oversees the county's juvenile court, said getting approval from the courts is likely.

headline: Violent Crimes Rise 18% in Pittsburgh
abstract: In every category excluding homicide, violent crimes and crimes against property in Pittsburgh rose eighteen percent.

headline: Housing Funds Sought
abstract: A housing rehabilitation program in Sugarcreek Borough will receive a financial boost if the borough receives a $70,000 state grant. The grant from the PA Department of Community Affairs would provide funds for low to moderate income residents in the Village of Rocky Grove. Each house would be grant up to $5,000 in repairs.

headline: Uninsured mayhem
abstract: The writer feels that the laws and penalties for not having auto insurance are too lax, and that if a driver doesn't have insurance, they shouldn't have a license.

headline: City native confirmed for marshal post
abstract: Native Philadelphian Gary Shovlin was confirmed by the US Senate as US Marshall for the 33-county Middle District of PA. The White House as well as US Senators from PA Arlen Specter and John Heinz had recommended Shovlin, who previously served in the White House secret service.

headline: It's official: Pa., NJ losing clout, census shows both states will lose House seats
abstract: The 1990 census figures increased the political clout of CA and the Southland carried good news to Republican president candidates for at least the rest of this century. They diminished the political strength of PA and NJ. California, Florida and Texas will control nearly one-quarter of the votes in the US House of Representatives.

headline: Slatington food bank volunteer receives award from Gov. Casey
abstract: Ruthann Mantz, volunteer/coordinator of the Northern Lehigh Food Bank in Slatington, was among 13 volunteers throughout PA who were honored for outstanding service to their community. They were presented with certificates of commendation by PA Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel and Secretary of Agriculture Boyd E. Wolfe.

headline: The Trumps in happier times
abstract: A photo captures Donald and Ivana Trump in happier times, before a judge granted Ivana a divorce this December.

headline: NOW Targets Oregon, Nevada for Next Abortion Fights
abstract: The National Organization for Women is holding rallies and fundraising drives in Oregon and Nevada to support abortion rights.  In Oregon, the group is protesting a ballot initiative that would severely limit abortion rights, and in Nevada the group is rallying to support a pro-choice referendum.

headline: Recession is here, PNB economist says.
abstract: Pittsburgh National Bank chief economist Stuart Hoffman said the U.S. economy has entered a recession, but the Pittsburgh area will suffer less and recover more quickly than most of the country. It takes two consecutive quarterly declines in Gross National Product for a recession to be declared. Hoffman said the recession was due to higher taxes, a weak job market, falling home and stock prices and the Persian Gulf crisis.

headline: Hospitals suing over missing payments
abstract: The Hospital Association of PA plans to file suit against the state to force the resumption of a weekly $20 million Medicaid reimbursement, which the state is late in sending and does not know when more payments will be sent due to cash flow problems. Association spokesman Lou Gable said that the funds go to 300 hospitals and support about 1.2 million poor patients, and that "they [the state] cannot simply stop paying us," saying that it was illegal. The problem is being further aggravated by PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer's refusal to sign $475 worth in tax anticipation notes, since she claims that PA Governor Casey plans to use the money to bail Philadelphia out of its financial crisis.

headline: Local school directors invite USPCI officials
abstract: The Milton Area School Board voted to invite representatives of a proposed waste incinerator in the area to speak to the board, because the school board is considering taking a public position on the matter, as many other government bodies have opposed the incinerator. The board members decided that in order to take a stance, they should hear from the representative of the incinerator before making their decision.

headline: Hydro plants here fuel debate on fish kills and water quality
abstract: The Pennsylvania Fish Commission has found that hydroelectric dams can lead to fish kills. The Youghiogheny Resevoir Dam is the cause for a fish kill the Commission reported, and it fears that it could happen again. In the late '80s the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission licensed 21 hydrolectric plants in the upper Ohio River basin-13 in southwester Pennsylvania.

headline: Differences remain over impact-fee bill
abstract: The PA legislature could not decide how to restructure impact fees, so legislators will consider the bill in September. Townships and municipalities depend on the fees to fund transportation, parks, recreation, sewer and water lines. Now that local governments not get state and federal aid for these projects, a new funding structure must be developed to assess fees. Lou Biacchi of the PA Builders Association would like for transportation improvements not to be eligible for coverage by the fees.

headline: County, prison guards given deadline on promotions pact
abstract: Dauphin County prison and the union representing the guards have until January to develop a way to promote its prison guards to now-vacant corporal and sergeant slots. The deadline is a result of a decision made after binding arbitration that stemmed from a complaint filed by the union representing the Swatara Township prison's guards. The union is proposing a promotion process that would include a written test, interview, review of the personnel file and notice of seniority.

headline: Voices. Do we need a drug czar?
abstract: The article details citizen responses to the question "Do we need a drug czar?". Conducted nationwide, the responses are varied.

headline: Housing grant pursued in Gallitzin, Patton
abstract: Residents of Gallitzin and Patton boroughs are hoping that the PA state Department of Community Affairs gives a grant totaling $640,000 for housing rehabilitation in the communities. If the grant funds are approved the homeowners would be entitled to grants of up to $6000 for housing rehabilitation and the remainder of the funds would cover administrative costs.

headline: UPI Pennsylvania Business News
abstract: National Steel Corp. of Pittsburgh says fourth quarter earnings were $28.4 million or down 14 percent for the period one year ago.

headline: County Democrats predict victory
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, speaking in Lionville, Chester County, predicted Democratic victories in elections across the state, including a "impressive victories" in Chester Co. Chester County is a traditionally Republican county, but many Democrats are predicting that it will finally go Democrat in the upcoming election.

headline: It's OK; it's our pork
abstract: People don't like the idea of pork barrel spending but they like it when it benefits their districts. Districts want their congressman to bring home the bacon, but don't like government spending overall. The editorial wants people to understand and not be upset when they see the bill.

headline: Smith replaces Shane as chairman of PUC
abstract: PA Governor Casey appointed William Smith as Public Utility Commission chairman. He has been a PUC member since July 1987. He is now the commission's vice chairman. He is also an old friend of the governor.

headline: Some schemes to be wary of
abstract: List of schemes and scams people should watch out for by the Better Business Bureau.

headline: Footing the bill
abstract: The state of Pennsylvania has agreed to pay for the construction of pedestrian ramps and a widened walkway on the Fort Duquense Bridge.  This will improve access from Downtown to Three-Rivers Stadium, and will eliminate bottlenecks that occur on the bridge's stairways before and after Pirate and Steeler's games.  City officials hope to begin the project this summer.

headline: Record tax hike on board agenda
abstract: The South Easton School Board meets to vote on a proposed $12.58 million budget that includes a 32% hike in property taxes. Superintendent Luther C. Natter blames the increase on the state's failure to reimburse PA school districts to fullest amount.

headline: How parents joy turned to anguish
abstract: Digna "Carmen" Rodriguez and her husband Joseph were shocked to hear their premature son, George Albert, was never going to come home. After two months in the hospital, George's death was sudden and unexpected for the couple, whose son was receiving care at Albert Einstein Medical Center.

headline: Location and size are key factors in choosing a college
abstract: In the college application and selection process, most students base their decisions primarily on the size and location of the school.  Narrowing down the plethera of colleges in the country can be a daunting task, but with a good system, it can be made easier.

headline: In flight
abstract: The Raystown Shooting Preserve offers hunters the option of bringing their own hunting dogs or using dogs provided by the Preserve. The Preserve is a 240 acre farm owned by Jeff Hollingshead, which gives members of the public the chance to hunt quail, ringnecks, or chukars for a fee.

headline: District justices base DUI decisions on evidence presented at hearings
abstract: David Judy, on behalf of the eight other members of the Dauphin County District Justices Association, disagrees with statements made in a recent column inferring the presence of Mothers Against Drunk Driving volunteers helped send drunk driving cases to court at preliminary hearings. Judy argued that as public servants, justices are not to be swayed by public opinion, and that the fate of drunk driving cases is decided by the preparation of the prosecution and the presentation of proper evidence.

headline: County's new jail may not meet the need
abstract: Prison overcrowding issues still plague Allegheny County, which recently added more beds, which were quickly filled.  The county is searching for other places to put criminals and is working on plans for a new jail.

headline: Voters to decide on fund for volunteer-service units
abstract: Voters will be asked to decide in November whether to create a $25 million loan fund for volunteer fire, ambulance and rescue services. PA Governor Robert Casey signed legislation authorizing the referendum. Casey nixed provisions that would have given two state agencies a total of $500,000 to contract with volunteer groups to provide emergency services for state buildings and roadways.

headline: Housing ministry still on shaky fiscal footing
abstract: Two years ago Jimmy Carter started Philadelphia's Habitat for Humanity two years ago, but is still struggling for funding. Their pleas are being ignored even though the city is being given unprecedented funding from the private sector rehabilitating low-income housing. Developers are falling all over themselves for tax credits, but Habitat cannot get the money. Habitat has the workers but not the money to create housing.

headline: USAir deal in Philadelphia delayed by Justice request
abstract: The U.S. Justice Department has asked for more time to consider USAir Group Inc.'s proposed acquisition of 11 Midway Airline gates in Philadelphia in light of antitrust regulation. The deal would give USAir, already the largest operator in Philadelphia, more landing slots, authority for routes to Toronto and Montreal, 11 gates and other facilities. PA attorney general Ernie Preate raised objections to USAir's first attempt to purchase the gates, but has not filed any formal complaints about the current bid.

headline: County finds new revenue
abstract: Facing a deficit in its Department of Human Services, Northampton County officials found reimbursements owed by the Federal Government in reviewing records with the PA Department of Public Welfare. But fiscal affairs director Pete Houck said the real problem is that the demand for services is outpacing the amount of state funds. The county identified key areas in which the budget could be cut, but it alone cannot correct the problem, noted County Executive Director Gerald Seyfried.

headline: It's the election of voters' discontent, but still most incumbents fear not
abstract: The article describes a nation-wide sentiment of discontent with federal and PA representatives and the efforts of certain individuals to mobilize to overthrow incumbents. Despite this discontent, long-standing incumbents are unlikely to lose upcoming elections due to political clout. Incumbent PA Governor Robert P. Casey is expected to easily win the upcoming gubernatorial election against Barbara Hafer.

headline: Socialist party fields candidates
abstract: The Socialist Workers Party is fielding candidates in the November election, though it doesn't expect to garner many votes.  The main goal of the party is to spread the word that workers of the world have to stand up for themselves and unite.

headline: Drug Violators Face Property Seizure
abstract: According to a Federal Bureau of Investigation drug agent, individuals possessing even small amounts of drugs could have their car or house seized.  Selling the property of drug dealers is one of the ways that law enforcement officials are cracking down on illegal drug use.  Money from the sale of seized property is funneled back into the war on drugs.

headline: Red Lion budget proposal increases property tax rate
abstract: The board of education for the Red Lion Area Schools agreed to increase the 1990-1991 budget to $19.3 million and raise property estate taxes to 11.5 mills.  The proposed budget is a 15% increase over the current budget.

headline: Insurance problem sets back asbestos-removal program
abstract: Asbestos-removal work at the Dauphin County nursing home will be delayed at least two days because the contractor failed to provide the necessary proof of insurance. The county commissioners had planned to approve a contract with Bristol-based Falcon Associates for asbestos removal and insulation replacement at Dauphin Manor, but they decided to hold a special meeting to reconsider the contact if the insurance documents are received. Work is expected to take three weeks.

headline: March by arts students protests repeated attacks
abstract: Students at Philadelphia's elite High School for the Creative and Performing Arts marched near the school to protest the lack of security for students, who have been the frequent victims of muggings, assaults, and other abuses on their commute to and from school in South Philadelphia. Their demand that the school do more to protect them comes after two students were mugged yesterday, one of who's nose was broken.

headline: Incinerator foe questions land acquisition
abstract: Members of Organizations United for the Environment claim that the land USPCI wants to develop into the Susquehanna Industrial Park, which includes a hazardous and industrial waste incinerator, was acquired through deceit by Pennswood Development Corp., a Philadelphia real estate firm. The group contends that Pennswood President Walter N. Norley IV was involved with USPCI President Anthony J. Donatoni. Donatoni claims that the land acquisition is irrelevant and that the incinerator will be safe.

headline: Ex-SEPTA manager is back in Pa.
abstract: The ex-general manager of the South Eastern PA Transit Authority, who left after just five dramatic weeks, is back in the area working as a civil engineer. Stead had claimed he was misled by Chairman Lewis Gould concerning undisclosed bonuses for top SEPTA managers. Coming back to the area as a resident, William Stead says he can understand more the actions of local legislators. Stead's father was the Chambersburg borough engineer.

headline: Court action shows need for change
abstract: The editorial claims that the PA Supreme Court was wrong in reinstating a judge who allegedly accepted services for free from a defendant, but by doing so, the court strengthened the campaign for judicial reform by displaying how faulty the system is now.

headline: War zone: Everywhere troopers looked, there was fire
abstract: The wall of state troopers outside the fence awaited the order to storm the prison, impatiently watching inmates building impromptu barricades on the gates, lighting fires and pelting police with debris. The image was imprinted in the minds of some troopers who stormed the compound. They are ordered not to talk about October's uprising at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill, but agreed to speak about it as long as their names were not used.

headline: Housing program gets grant
abstract: A $448,000 federal housing grant will help 32 area families become first-time homeowners through the United Way of York County's Housing Initiatives Program.  The money will be used to provide low- to middle-income families that buy the 32 townhouses to be built on East King Street with a $14,000 second mortgage that doesn't have to be paid and doesn't gain interest until the family sells the property or uses it as rental property.

headline: Vartan agrees to purchase 5 percent of Homestead
abstract: Businessman John Vartan agreed to purchase $60,000 worth of Homestead Holding Corp. to strengthen the company's capital position. Last year, Homestead was named one of the top 200 small businesses by Forbes Magazine. However it faces increasing regulations, announcing it will allocate $12 million for loan-loss reserves, making Homestead unable to comply with federal requirements. The association now must file future compliance guidelines with the US Office of Thrift Supervision.

headline: County GOP Unit Wants Dunio to Run Against Mellow
abstract: The Lackawanna County and state Republican Committees want Donna Dunio, a former Republican candidate for Scranton City Council, to run for Democrat Robert Mellow's state Senate seat.

headline: It's time to correct regressive taxation in Pa.
abstract: Ted Keller of Wilmington writes in to discuss how Pennsylvania unfairly taxes its lower and middle income citizens for the benefit  of pension incomes for wealthier individuals.  Keller calls for an "ability to pay" principle for taxation.

headline: Some smaller unions pay officers top dollar here
abstract: A list of the 50 best paid union officers, using records annually submitted to the US Department of Labor, revealed salaries do not always correspond to duties, rank, dues, or membership. Topping the list was Jospeh Laquatra, president of the Laborers District Council and business manager of Laborers Local 1058. Following were Thoedore Cozza, president of Teamster Local 211 and International General Executive Board member, and president of Labors Local 211, Dennis Martire.

headline: State officials must get message of prison problems
abstract: State-mandated sentences for DUI's have caused two serious problems.  They have led to overcrowding at county prisons and have caused the jailing of persons who probably would have been better served by rehabilitative, rather than purely punative, dispositions.  As County Commissioner William Reznor has argued, judges should be given the discretion to determine if placement in a jail or a treatment center is the best sentence for a DUI conviction.  If jail time is chosen, the state should pay for it--not the counties.

headline: Report by Hafer shows big deficit
abstract: As the Casey administration announced that the state is facing a $1 billion budget deficit, PA Auditor General was finishing her review of last year's budget which shows the state had a $421 million deficit. She predicts a $1.4 billion deficit instead and the state will have the cut spending by 12% to balance it by June.

headline: It's a hit for Senior Citizens!
abstract: Nancy Keenan looks back on her membership in the Regional Council of the Pennsylvania Council on Aging and is pleased with the result--the "Health Care Practitioners Medicare Fee Control Act", a victory for senior citizens on Medicare, signed by PA Governor Casey. Secretary of Aging Linda Rhodes was also present. Those with Medigap and Medicare will get 100 percent coverage of doctors bills. Those without Medigap will get 80 percent coverage. Government and special interests were present to see law signed.

headline: Mediation Coming In Jersey Shore Teacher Talks
abstract: At Jersey Shore, the only county school district without a teachers' contract, Jersey Shore Area School Board solicitor Paul W. Reeder said that he plans to meet with the state mediator for the first time since negotiation began last week. Three school board members and three teachers were negotiating until they reached an impasse.

headline: Incinerator foes vow to fight on
abstract: Developers of a proposed Glendon incinerator won the last legal battle, but opponents are making sure it won't be the last the incinerator must face.  Whichever side loses ground in the upcoming Environmental Hearing Board is likely to appeal the issue to Commonwealth Court.

headline: Fast and Furious
abstract: With more than 80 percent of people refusing to follow the speedlimit, it may be time to re-examine speed limit laws. Such a high percentage indicates that the problem may not be with the people, but with the current speed limit.

headline: Court changes supported
abstract: The PA Legislature has taken the first step toward a constitutional amendment the would change the way errant judges are disciplined and repeal a PA state Supreme Court ruling that made the state responsible for county-court costs. It must be approved by the Legislature elected in November and approved by voters in a referendum which cannot happen before next May's primary. The bill would give the PA Legislature the right set judicial budgets and to determine the source of the revenues for them.

headline: Welfare officials cleared in death
abstract: In a federal ruling, Westmoreland County welfare officials are not being held liable for the beating death of a 3-year-old girl by her mother's boyfriend.  The death occurred two months after welfare officials investigated a separate abuse report, and the girl's father claims that the officials did not do enough to ensure her safety after the first incident.

headline: HUD Audit Blasts Delaware County Spending, Wants Repayment
abstract: Federal authorities with the Department of Housing and Urban Development found that Delaware County officials may have misspent up to $5.6 million in federal funds. The auditors are recommending termination of HUD funding .

headline: Veto video gambling
abstract: The editorial board urges PA Governor Robert P. Casey to veto a video gambling bill recently passed in the Legislature. The board disapproves of the fact that only 32% of the income from the machines would go to state and local governments and school districts, the rest going to the owners and operators. The board believes that taxes are too high and that the government must be more efficient, but that these issues cannot be resolved on the wallets of gamblers.

headline: County is Casey country
abstract: Luzerne County, a traditional Democratic strong-hold, formed a strong percentage of Democratic PA Governor Robert P. Casey's supporters and helped him to win his re-election campaign. County voters disapproved of opponent Barbara Hafer's pro-choice position, her accusations that Casey reduced state contributions to local school districts and forced them to raise property taxes, and her negative remarks regarding Casey's ethnic background.

headline: It's time to debate, governor
abstract: The editorial states that it is important for Gov. Casey to engage in a televised debate with his opponent Barbara Hafer.

headline: Some suggestions when Casey visits
abstract: Reading is to become the "Capital for a Day" program in which Gov. Casey, his cabinet members, and their staff visit Reading. This editorial criticizes Casey's agenda for his day in Reading which includes mostly meeting and dining with local business leaders, saying "If the governor is going to be directed only to those people and to those facilities which politically and aesthetically are pleasing, we doubt he is goingn to get a true picture of Reading and its people".

headline: Water runoff problem addressed
abstract: Several residents in Franklin, PA have complained that a contractor used diesel fuel to keep brush piles burning during the winter months.  Some of that fuel mixed with water runoff and contaminated the water local supply.  Complaints have been filed with the state Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Report by Hafer Shows Big Deficit
abstract: It appears PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer was right in budget calculations pinpointing the deficit at $1 billion with an addition $400 million deficit from the prior fiscial year. PA Governor Casey was optimistic about the budget during his re-election campaign, ignoring Hafer's warnings. Budget Secretary Michael Hershock said the adminstration will attempt to trim the budget as much as possible before the fiscal year ends, looking first to the Department of Public Welfare.

headline: North Side losing only hospital detox unit
abstract: St. John's Mercy Health Center plans to close its drug and alcohol detoxification unit by July 6. It will eliminate a fourth of the hospital detox beds in the Pittsburgh area. The county had a $200,000 annual contract that the hospital would accept all patients, with or without medical coverage, for detox. The shutdown stems from a licensing change at the North Side hospital that merged with Mercy Hospital in July 1989.

headline: Mifflin County school budget calls for no tax hike; School district budget calls for no hike in taxes
abstract: The Mifflin County School District should be able to implement the 1990-1991 school year budget without having to raise taxes.  The tentative budget was proposed by Superintendent Dr. Robert Bohn before a special session of the school board.

headline: Incinerator Proves Burning Issue. Backers Claim Sincerity.
abstract: The United States Pollution Control of Pennsylvania Inc. plans to build and operate a hazardous waste incinerator in Gregg Township, Union County. President of USPCI Anthony Donatoni defended the incinerator against opponents, including the Gregg Township Board of Supervisors and Organizations United for the Environment. Donatoni rebutted allegations that USPCI will prove a lasting threat to the safety and reputation of the area.

headline: First section of expressway opened
abstract: PA Governor Casey and other officials took part in a dedication ceremony for the first completed section of the Mon-Fayette Expressway, which is 8 miles long and will be operated by the PA Turnpike Commission as Route 43.

headline: Court hails new judgeships, candidates abound
abstract: President Judge John E Erb of the York County Common Pleas Court said he remembers when staying lattés and burning the midnight oil was the exception than the rule. The ever-increasing number of cases has judges begging for relief. In 1992 the number of county judges goes from 7 to 9 and the 7 current judges are anxiously awaiting that time. Many lawyers are eyeing hose two judgeships.

headline: West End Fair set to start on July 29
abstract: Union County's 65th Annual West End Fair will feature the dedication of a new concessions and office building decorated with "Say No To Drugs" posters. The displays are part of the West End Fair Association's participation in PA Governor Casey's PENNFREE Anti-drug Abuse Campaign. The PA Office of Attorney General and the PA Association of County Fairs are also program initiators. Awards for the best poster will be given by a consortium including the PA Department of Agriculture.

headline: Impact fee issue keeps builders, officials apart
abstract: PA land developers and local government officials are getting ready to go to "all-out war" in the General Assembly in Harrisburg over the issue of impact fees on developers.  The groups have differing views on the bill which will soon be debated in the state House, which many see as a "builder's bill."

headline: Video Poker - Gambling With the Law
abstract: The Pennsylvania Attorney General's office are devising solutions to video poker gambling so bar owners are getting rid of the machines even though patrons like them.

headline: County pays Haste legal bill. Peters says suit is just between the 2 of them.
abstract: Dauphin County's liability insurance carrier is paying for County Chief Clerk Jeffrey T. Haste's legal defense costs related to County Commissioner Carol A. Peters' suit against him for comments he made in a television interview. County officials defended the payments, saying Haste's comments were made as part of his job. After saying he found no problem with Peters' financial interest forms, Haste told a reporter that Peters had incorrectly dated her statement. Haste also criticized Peters for going into financial asset files without authorization.

headline: Jackson, Beazley vie for GOP 101st spot
abstract: The primary on Tuesday will decide which Republican will be the nominee for the PA House seat in the 101st legislative district.  The two opponents are incumbent PA Representative George W. Jackson and school teacher Thomas Beazley.  They differ on the issues of abortion and a proposed Route 72 bypass around the city of Lebanon.

headline: Some Winners and Losers
abstract: The article details the election results of the 1990 race in several states. PA Governor Robert P. Casey defeated PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer with 68-percent of the vote, a victory that failed to shake the Republican's hold on the PA Senate. The party controlling the PA legislature will reapportion the Congressional districts in 1991.

headline: Legislators, keep hands off rebate
abstract: State lawmakers are trying to use a Bell-Atlantic settlement to finance a statewide 911 network.  While a statewide 911 system is a worthy goal, all of the 35.2 million dollar settlement should be returned to Bell-Atlantic cutomers; it was they who were duped into buying unnecessary services because of Bell-Atlantic's shady sales tactics, and it is they who should be compensated.  The victims--Bell-Atlantic customers--should not be penalized and forced to pay for the 911 system.

headline: Report shows where budget ax falls
abstract: The House Appropriations Committee released a report giving a better picture of who might be hurt in the budget cuts proposed by Governor Robert P. Casey.  The departments of Education and Public Welfare will receive the bulk- 84 percent- of all the budget cuts proposed.  The Black Caucus is concerned that the state's budget will most negatively affect African Americans and Latinos, who are typically on the bottom rung of the economic ladder.

headline: Nurses Accept Hospital's Offer
abstract: After winning a $1.20/hour raise, nurses of McKeesport Hospital ended their strike with concessions for both parties.

headline: Mount Union School Board Oks budget
abstract: The Mount Union School Board approved a budget which increased over initial projections. Superintendent Dr. Jerry Dunkle said the increase was due to a notice that the school would receive funds not included in initial projections. Property taxes were increased in Mifflin and Huntingdon Counties. Board members had a difficult time but finally were able to approve a new $49, position of director of education, appointing Richard Botteicher to the position.

headline: Incinerator Proves Burning Issue. Mistrust Fuels Opponents.
abstract: Clyde Peeling, a spokesman for Organizations United for the Environment, spoke out against the United State Pollution Control of Pennsylvania Inc. plan to build and operate a hazardous waste incinerator in Union County, saying it would prove a health and safety threat to the area. The group advocates laws restricting  the amount of waste industries can produce and says industries themselves should dispose of their waste.

headline: Four county groups help with highways
abstract: Four Lawrence County groups, including the Eagles' Lodge 455,  are participating in the PA Department of Transportation's "Adopt-A-Highway" program. When participating in the program, groups enter into a 2-year agreement with PennDOT to pick up litter along their designated stretch of highway four times a year. PennDOT then posts signs recognizing the group's commitment along the highway and provides safety training for the members.

headline: Court keeps woman alive
abstract: The US Supreme Court reached a divided decision of 5-4 that states may insist that food and water be given to a patient in a coma even if the relatives want treatment stopped to allow the patient to die. Chief Justice William Rehnquist wrote that the Constitution does not allow the establishment of this procedure. The case involves Nancy Cruzan who was critically injured and there have been court battles to decide whether she will continue to live.

headline: Westmoreland County Approve Jail Expansion
