abstract: Westmoreland County authorities have approved plans for a new 386-bed jail that could cost up to $28 million.  The county prison board voted Wednesday to replace the current 108-bed facility which has had problems with crowding.

headline: Impact fees
abstract: The article supports the municipalities in their fight for impact fees for developers.  It discusses the benefits and attempts to quell fears about the fees.

headline: Video poker at stake in House
abstract: Members of the PA House Finance Committee held a hearing on legalizing video poker, machines of which can be found illicitly in some taverns despite crackdown efforts by state police. The representatives, who assert that legalizing video poker will allow more regulation, heard the arguments of the PA Conference on Interchurch Cooperation, which claimed that legalizing video poker will bring about more social ills. Del Guerrini of the PA Amusement and Music Machine Association stated that video poker would boost the tavern industry and generate money for local government.

headline: Court likely to move to the right
abstract: No matter who takes former Justice William Brennan Jr's place on the bench, the US Supreme Court is certain to move further to the right. President Bush is guaranteed to at least nominate a Moderate Conservative for the old liberal stalwart's seat.

headline: James L. Wright Jr., veteran state legislator
abstract: PA state Representative James L. Wright Jr. died of cancer yesterday, at 65 years old. Wright represented Bucks County in the General Assembly for 25 years, and was House Business and Commerce Committee, the senior member of the PA Historical and Museum Commission, the co-founder of the Bucks County Mental Health/Retardation Board, and he served on the boards of the American Red Cross and Valley Day School.

headline: Souter backs privacy right
abstract: President Bush's nominee for the Supreme Court, David Souter, refused to comment about his views on abortion, saying that he didn't think he should reveal his views about such a divisive topic, which would further politicize the nomination.

headline: Modest Tuition Hike Expected
abstract: The board of governors of the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education has requested a 9.74 percent increase over last year's budget.  If the new budget is approved, tuition per student will only increase 100 dollars.  James H. McCormick, chancellor of the state system, argued that the budget increase will allow for only a modest tuition increase, thus keeping college education within the reach of our citizens.

headline: Republicans warn of $1 billion budget problem
abstract: Republicans in the PA State Legislature say PA faces "billion-dollar budget problem." PA Governor Robert Casey's administration denies that there is a budget crisis and the rumor that this will lead to tax increases in the near-future.

headline: Nurses Ratify Contract with  McKeesport Hospital
abstract: Nurses on strike at McKeesport Hospital have ratified a new contract and will come back to work based on the demand of patient load.

headline: Nanticoke is Ordered to re-hire Teacher
abstract: A Luzerne County judge ruled that the Greater Nanticoke Area School District reinstate a social studies teacher that was improperly furloughed due to alleged declining enrollment.

headline: Indiana County spills roust hundreds
abstract: A mix of chemicals in a garbage truck created toxic fumes yesterday, causing a four-block section of Blairsville to be evacuated until it could be contained.  A stretch of Route 85 was closed due to the crash of a truck carrying potential blast agents.

headline: Gambaccini gets blunt on SEPTA
abstract: Louis Gambaccini, general manager of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, is beginning to take a hard-line stance on the problems facing the mass transit firm. SEPTA is plagued by many problems, such as the need for maintenance on a number of facilities including railroads and bridges, while also facing public outcry against proposed fare increases, which would generate about $30 million in the authority's proposed operating budget. PA Governor Robert Casey stated that he would not support a regional sales tax to benefit SEPTA.

headline: Court orders new sentence in failed plot
abstract: PA State Superior Court has ordered a lower court to resentence former landfill operator William Fiore, who was convicted in a failed plot to kill a PA Department of Environmental Resources official. Fiore's 5 to10-year prison sentence was recently modified to be consecutive with his sentence to 9 to 18-year prison sentence for environmental crimes, and the Superior Court determined that although the increase was proper, the modification should not have happened without Fiore's presence and without a hearing.

headline: What happened in the legislature
abstract: A list of events in the PA Legislature including judicial reform where judges are appointed not elected, encouraging, recycling packaging, product liability reform, and a bill allowing prisoner to earn time off their sentences with good behavior or earning educational diplomas.

headline: Impact fees would help communities
abstract: The editorial supports the idea of impact fees on developers, but also is suggesting changes to the current bill in the PA House on the subject.  Levying impact fees on developers would help pay for improvements to infrastructure required for the new development.

headline: Video Poker bad idea
abstract: The writer believes that there is a pro-gambling faction in PA and is trying to push a bill in the House Finance Committee to legalize video poker machines. The justification is that poker machines will raise millions for the Treasury without raising taxes. The writer believes this will lead to more legalized gambling and substituting gambling for taxes is bad.

headline: Court nominee called workaholic, intellectual
abstract: David Souter, President Bush's choice for the Supreme Court, is a shy intellectual who lives in a tiny New Hampshire town where he is admired but considered something of a hermit. He has shunned partisan politics. He is described as both a workaholic and a perfectionist.

headline: Jersey Exodus; Florio places blame for flight of firms
abstract: New Jersey Governor Jim Florio cited high property taxes, traffic gridlock and an insufficient supply of educated workers as the reason why many firms are leaving the state, many heading for PA. Florio has been under intense criticism since raising taxes during his term.

headline: Souter prepares for senators' questions
abstract: President Bush's Supreme Court nominee David H. Souter faces Senate confirmation hearings in the near future which will undoubtedly press him for his views on controversial issues, including abortion. However, many on Capitol Hill declared Souter a good choice as he is not seen as a controversial figure, although he is known to be conservative. Neither the American Way nor the Heritage Foundation had much to say regarding Souter, saying his track record is unknown.

headline: New court unit helps victims of domestic abuse
abstract: A new domestic-abuse unit of the Philadelphia Family Court will allow abuse victims to get free and efficient assistance in obtaining cout orders against abusive partners.  With the new unit, abuse victims can file for protective court orders 24 hours a day, and will not have to contend with the long waits previously experienced.

headline: Revenue collections still laggins, administration reports
abstract: Revenue officials reported that PA tax collections were $13.8 million below projections for the month of January, bringing revenues $107.7 million below estimates for the fiscal year thus far.

headline: Officials:Rabid Raccoons Heading Toward New York State
abstract: New York state officials have issued a rabies warning after rabid racoons were found entering the state.

headline: Negotiations Continue in 79 School Districts; Two Strike
abstract: Contract talks continued in many school districts statewide, as two teachers unions went on strike yesterday and one today, stranding about 7900 students.

headline: Ingenuity Puts Beaver Falls in Driver's Seat with Recycling
abstract: Beaver Falls Street Department workers built a homemade recycling collection vehicle.

headline: Gasoline tax hike coming?
abstract: The transportation committee of the Central Susquehanna Valley Chamber of Commerce was informed that there will be no increase in the state's gasoline tax until at least November. According to committee chairman Todd Roup, who is also a representative for PA State Senator Edward Helfrick the increase may be approved by a lame duck session of the legislature in November. In the past, discussion has been held on increasing the tax on gasoline to finance repairs to roads and bridges throughout the state.

headline: Court turns down appeal of Pennsylvania man in environment case
abstract: The US Supreme Court turned down John Pozsgai's appeal; Pozsgai had been given the longest prison sentence, 3 years, and the biggest fine, $200,000, for anyone convicted of an environmental crime.  Pozsgai was found guilty of dumping waste from his truck-repair business on a protected "wetlands" area that he did not own, though he was in the process of attempting to acquire a permit.

headline: What happened in the legislature
abstract: Reviews some of the bills considered by the PA General Assembly recently, including judicial reform, recyclable packaging, product liability, and prison sentences.

headline: Impact fees: ignored again
abstract: The editors assume PA Legislators were too busy hammering out the state's budget to pay attention to impact fees before their summer recess. Nonetheless, there is still no answer to the future of development impact fees municipalities may leverage against developers. When the Legislature reconvenes in September the editors hope sheer laziness and political gamesmanship will not prevent legislators from doing their job.

headline: Video poker gambling is a real loser
abstract: Editors do not think PA State Rep. Fred Trello and Rep. Paul Clymer's revenue estimates from video poker machines for participating municipalities are realistic. Municipalities could only participate if residents agreed by local referendum. Editors point out that legalizing games of small chance so far have yielded little for private interests. Most revenue goes to senior citizens, veterans, and fraternal organizations. If the Legislature does not do away with the idea of video poker, PA Governor Casey should.

headline: Critics trying to close loopholes used by lobbyists
abstract: Lobbyists can buy breakfast for lawmakers completely legally in Harrisburg. A PA senator can receive $15,000 from one political action committee. These are just two examples of problems with lobbyists funding PA politicians. Many would like to be stricter rules about how much they can receive. Some say the laws are already restrictive enough and point out it is better than it was 20 years ago when cash was given for votes.

headline: Jogging around; Bandwagon
abstract: Editors note the rush of politicians to urge an amendment to ban flag burning now that the US Supreme Court has struck down a national law banning flag desecration. Along with President Bush, the list now includes gubernatorial candidate and PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer.

headline: Special tax proposed for senior citizens' programs
abstract: Dauphin County Commission Chairman Sally Klein said she will ask her fellow commissioners to approve placing a referendum on the November ballot asking voters to support a special tax to fund only senior citizen programs.  There is a rising demand for service for seniors in the area.

headline: Walking over the water
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Robert P. Casey called a project to widen a walkway and provide new access ramps along Fort Duquense Bridge a good investment in Pittsburgh's future.  The Pirates and Steelers make a major economic contribution to the city, and the widened walkway and new access ramps will also benefit other city events.  The governor presented a 4.2 million dollar state check for the construction efforts.

headline: Revenue dip fails to sway Casey's policy
abstract: Despite the fact that in September, state revenue collections lagged behind predictions for the third month in a row, PA Governor Casey said the dip in revenue would have little effect on the budget.  He also said that he is looking for ways to avoid a tax increase next year, but can't guarantee another 4-year stint of no new taxes (if he is reelected) as in his first 4 years.

headline: PA bill seeks tax to give care to the uninsured
abstract: A bill to extend health services to 1 million people who have no insurance by taxing hospitals was introduced to the PA House yesterday. It calls for hospitals, insurers, and businesses to share in the cost of providing care to the uninsured. A PA Blue Shield executive attacked a requirement that their plans statewide pay for free primary care for uninsured children as part of their tax-exempt social mission. Details of the plan are very complicated and hospitals are not supporting the bill.

headline: New Castle teachers ready strike vote
abstract: Teachers in the New Castle Area School District will vote on Wednesday morning on whether to begin a strike on the first day of classes.  The district wants teachers to accept a wage freeze as a result of the district's $1 deficit.

headline: Joint Effort Seeks Site For Leaves
abstract: Butler County, Butler Township, and the city have agreed to join forces to find a suitable site for leaf composting. The county commissioners said they would be willing to find a composting site after the city and township offered to assume all financial and administrative responsibilities at the site. A new state recycling law prohibits leaves being taken to a landfill.

headline: Get moving on turnpike link
abstract: This editorial board wants building to begin on new roads. No major road has been built through the region since the 1950's. The pending problem was discussed more than 25 years ago but nothing has been done about the limited access highways. Two weeks ago the possibility of an express highway to connect Route 309 and the PA Turnpike with state and county officials. The editorial just would like actual action to come from all the talk.

headline: Court: O'Kicki 1985 jailing of board wrong
abstract: A PA Commonwealth Court found former Cambria County Court Judge Joseph O'Kicki did not follow the law when he cited and cited members of the Penn Cambria School Board. O'Kicki responded to a suit by students against the board and the Penn Cambria Education Association by ending a strike and ordering classes to resume, amending meeting times for the two sides several times. The Judge gave defendants insufficient time to prepare a defense and favored those who withdrew their appeal, vacating their sentences.

headline: What will they do for an encore?
abstract: Columnist Dan Geringer comments on what he calls the "theatrical" antics of the Philadelphia City Council, which this week "performed" in front of an audience of firefighters who attended the meeting because Philadelphia Mayor Goode included four fire companies on his "hit list" of possible cuts because of the city's financial crisis.

headline: Impact-fee bills closer to reality. Law would force developers to pay some improvement costs.
abstract: The PA Senate passed a two-bill package that would force developers to help pay for municipal improvements triggered by development, sending one of the bills to PA Governor Robert P. Casey and the other back to the PA House. The legislation was written in large part by Lehigh County PA Representative Donald Snyder. The PA State Association of Township Supervisors opposes the bill, as it would require townships to set up impact-fee advisory boards, a costly and complicated process.

headline: Video Poker Machines Draw Fire from Casey
abstract: The Casey Administration declared a massive effort to stop illegal video poker businesses in Pennsylvania.

headline: Crowded Republican Field, Three from Montgomery mentioned as possible Hafer running mates
abstract: State Rep. Joseph Lashinger of Norristown, State Rep. Jon Fox of Jenkintown and Mario Mele of Fort Washington, a fromer member of the LCB are on Barbara Hafer's list of potential running mates as she will run for Governor in the fall as the Republican endoresed candidate to challege Gov. Casey.

headline: Jogging around; Tax reform
abstract: Editors don't understand why the PA Legislature expects voters to respond any different now to property tax reform than they did last time when the issue was voted down in a state referendum.

headline: Specter to fight for Jobs
abstract: On tour of the Scranton Army Ammunition Plant, US Senator Arlen Specter said he, US Senator Heinz, and Representative McDade will do their best to fight for jobs at the plant. Specter is a member of the Senate Defense Appropriations Committee. The PA delegation faces Democrats from a Louisiana plant competing with the Scranton plant. Specter supports maintaining trade restrictions against South Africa, and voiced support for an amendment banning flag desecration.

headline: Restoration ends in a nightmare for family in Bucks
abstract: A Doylestown family suffers from lead poisoning, but has a difficult time getting properly diagnosed.  The family's pediatrician dismissed their requests to test for lead poisoning, and when the family was finally tested, all members had elevated levels of led.  The extent of permanent damage is still unknown.

headline: Revenue drop clouds state's fiscal outlook
abstract: PA state tax collections fell $70 million below expectations in May, further worsening PA's financial outlook. With May's tax collections ballooning the shortfall for the 1990-91 fiscal year to $226 million, Budget Secretary Michael Hershock promised to curtail spending but maintained the state would end the year with a balanced budget. The state started the year projecting a $1.4 million surplus at the end of June. Collections have fallen off 2.1 percent.

headline: Pa. boosts funds for AIDS patients at Betak
abstract: The PA Department of Public Welfare said that it will pay for medical care for AIDS patients at an unoccupied Mount Airy nursing home that was taken over by an AIDS activist group.  DPW spokesman John Harwood said that the state is willing to pay $140 a day ($64 more than normal) in Medicaid reimbursements for AIDS patients if the home, which has been named Betak, becomes an AIDS hospice.

headline: New law requires clarity in English of college teachers
abstract: Although some Pittsburgh college students have had trouble understanding their teachers, local campus officials say a new A law requiring all universities and colleges to certify that their instructors are proficient in English will cause few changes. The English Fluency in Higher Education Act effective September 7. He had received several complaints that professors were hard to understand in the classroom. It does not apply to professors already hired.

headline: Landfill closing by DER leaves many questions unanswered
abstract: Not only did the PA Department of Environmental Resources reject East Huntington Township's request to expand its landfill, it decided to close Y&S Maintenance Inc. The hauling service operated is the main refuse collector for the landfill. Scottdale Borough Manager Barry Whoric says the borough recently signed a 3-year contract with the company. Connellsville Mayor Casimir Zabela says the city is in its third year of a 3-year contract with the company and sees no reason to panic.

headline: Inventor Says Water-Filled Barriers Could Save Highway Lives
abstract: Plastic barriers filled with water are being installed on a section of interstate construction.  The new barriers are touted as safer than concrete barriers, which often cause major damage to cars or bounce them back into traffic.

headline: Courtroom Conditions Are Part of the Problem
abstract: The bad conditions of City Hall as a courthouse, as well as the hindering backlog of cases discredit the city's criminal justice system.

headline: When the state is killer
abstract: In light of the PA Legislature's passage of a bill providing for execution by lethal injection, Ralph David Samuel, clerk of the Advisory Committee of the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting of Friends writes that citizens of a democracy are all responsible for the actions of a government, especially in the case of the death penalty. Samuel says that in order to deny responsibility for PA murders, citizens ended public executions and now search for a "humane" method of execution. Samuel argues that the state's only logical justification for the death penalty is retribution.

headline: It's a deficit
abstract: The editorial board discusses PA Governor Casey's proposal for a balanced budget by funding the PA Economic Revitalization Fund (PERF) through a $94 million bond rather than through the general fund.  The editorial board believes that this will end up creating a deficit for the state because the bond is a loan that will need to be repaid.

headline: Viewing Harrisburg
abstract: New York investment house Drexel Burnham Lambert Inc paid its employees roughly $260 million in bonuses just weeks before declaring bankruptcy.  The company claims the payments were guaranteed before bankruptcy but creditors say the rewards seemed excessive.

headline: Crystal Unclear. Will Tuesday's Disaffection Become Rejection at the 1992 Polls?
abstract: The article suggests that though it is a mistake to project the results of the 1990 midterm elections forward to the 1992 Presidential election, results indicate deep dissatisfaction with the federal government. Though most incumbents won, many margins of victory were smaller. The article says that PA Governor Robert P. Casey impressed many with his million-vote victory margin and suggests he might consider the Presidency.

headline: Jubelier, Mikula to pair off in fall
abstract: PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelier and Democratic Altoona City Councilman Alan Mikula both received their party's nominations for the fall election in Tuesday's primary.  Mikula is the former mayor of Altoona.

headline: State Awaits Census Results
abstract: PA officials are awaiting the results of the preliminary census population reports to determine how many US House seats PA will lose.

headline: If teams go, revenue and prestige go as well
abstract: Possible plans to move the Sixers and Flyers sports franchises to New Jersey would have a devastating economic impact on the city of Philadelphia.

headline: Revenue drop clouds state's fiscal outlook
abstract: State tax collections fell $70 million below expectations in May, but budget Secretary Michael Hersock promised the state would end the year with a balanced budget. Republicans in the Senate are criticizing PA Governor Robert Casey's administration for attempting to conceal the problem.

headline: Pa. delinquent with $1 million for Berks Heim
abstract: PA has fallen behind on $122 million in Medicaid payments to nursing homes, hospitals, and pharmacies, $1 million of which is owed to Berks Heim, the county nursing home. The state is usually behind by a couple weeks on payments, but this time it is considerably later than usual because of cash flow problems.

headline: New SAT doesn't grade well on end to bias, critics say
abstract: The College Board changed the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT) to allow the use of calculators, offer longer reading passages and reduce emphasis on multiple-choice questions. Critics argue that the changes will do nothing to reduce bias against black and Hispanic students, females, and those from low-income families. The change was made to ensure consistency between testing and school curriculums.

headline: Landfill critic quits waste authority
abstract: Former chairman of Dauphin County's Intermunicipal Solid Waste Authority stepped down from his post in disappointment, as his fervent opposition to a closed landfill was ignored when the county decided to build a new landfill next to it.

headline: Governor delivers highway package
abstract: Gov. Casey announced $9.2 million in improvements for Route 119 from the Uniontown Bypass north past Connellsville.

headline: Court-sanctioned sobriety checkpoints are intrusive and accomplish little
abstract: Columnist Charles Krauthammer sees the recent US Supreme Court decision upholding the constitutionality of sobriety checkpoints as an unfortunate victory for Jurists Against Drunk Driving. In Krauthammer's view, sobriety checks are a lazy way of addressing results rather than roots. The Court's decision violates the constitutionality of the 4th amendment--the right to be left alone.

headline: When the violence is from within the home
abstract: Victoria Branworth, a free-lance writer, writes on the problem of domestic violence and the fact that it is little addressed in the nation. Domestic abuse is the nation's most underreported crime, in part because the legal system does not have severe repercussions for the aggressor, and in some states a woman can't even press charges against her spouse for battering. She points out that there is some hope, however, in a bill being prepared by US Senator Joseph Biden (D-Del), which would require uniform response from law enforcement and judicial officials regarding domestic violence. Arrests would be mandatory and sentencing stiffened.

headline: IUP economic impact on county at $155 million
abstract: Indiana University of Pennsylvania means millions of dollars and thousands of jobs for Indiana County, a new economic study reports. It reported that spending by IUP students had the single largest effect on the county's economy.

headline: Violations existed before sale to Rite Aid, witness says
abstract: In the Ohio trial of Rite Aid and president, Martin Grass, attorneys say he is being harassed because of the success of the Pennsylvania based chain. But Melvin Wilczynski testified Grass tried to bribe him in exchange for his resignation from the Ohio Board of Pharmacy. At the time, Wilczynski owned Lane Division of People's Drug Stores, which Rite Aid is acquiring. Rite Aid received citations for failure to erect security barricades around pharmacy sections of stores during the transition.

headline: Cumberland GOP leader accused of trick
abstract: Cumberland County Republican Chairwoman Patricia Saylor is accused of distributing misleading literature in her campaign for Republican State Committee, seven other committee hopefuls charged.  The controversy is over the fact that Saylor is circulating poll cards that list herself and other candidates as "Republican endorsed" when Cumberland's Republican Committee has not issued any sort of formal support.

headline: Jubelirer sweeps to 5th Senate term. A 'smashing victory' over Mikula.
abstract: PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert C. Jubelirer won re-election to his fifth term against Democratic opponent Altoona Councilman Alan R. Mikula. Mikula volunteered to run at the request of the PA Senate Democrats in order to make Jubelirer spend money and to keep him out of other key Senate races. Jubelirer's victory will perpetuate his adversarial role against re-elected Democratic PA Governor Robert P. Casey on issues such as tax reform.

headline: State borrowing talks to resume
abstract: Auditor General and gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer refused to give the go-ahead for tax-anticipation notes for PA until Governor Casey includes a statement that the state's surplus was less than reported.  Talks are resuming between the camps on the issue.

headline: PA ranks 5th as home to top U.S. companies
abstract: Forbes magazine released its 22nd annual directory of the 500 biggest US companies.  Pennsylvania is home to 43 of the major companies ranked in the list.

headline: Revenues dip $4 million
abstract: PA state tax revenues for September were $4 million below estimates, making the tax revenue for the year so far $47 million, or 1.8%, below projections.  PA Governor Casey's administration says that the September numbers were essentially right on target, but Republicans are predicting a total of $100 million shortfall for the year.

headline: Pa. doctors challenge overcharge legislation
abstract: Groups of doctors have filed suit against a state legislation, which prohibits doctors from charging over the set Medicare fee for senior citizens.  The doctors claim that the state cannot make legislation involving Medicare, which is a federal program.

headline: New site readied for HACC
abstract: Students at Harrisburg Area Community College's Lebanon Campus will return to classes temporarily held at the Lebanon County Area Vocation-Technical School after the Cumberland Street campus burned down. HACC expects to remain at the location at least through the spring 1991 semester.

headline: Landfill foes gear up to battle Tri-County
abstract: Tri-County Sanitation of Hazleton submitted the second part of its application to the PA Department of Environmental Resources to become the largest landfill operator in PA, amidst protests by Save Our Local Environment II (SOLE II). Carl Zbegner, a DER engineer in the Wilkes-Barre Bureau of Waste Management, says the landfill may not be economically feasible. Otherwise, he sees no problems with part II of the application. SOLE II member Tom Meyers says the group will hire its own engineer to look into landfill logistics.

headline: Greyhound Buses Running in PA, Union Says Numbers Inflated
abstract: Greyhound  has some buses operating in Pennsylvania but customers are urged to double check as some union members have not returned to work.

headline: Crime bill police groups appeal to Senate to approve assault weapons ban
abstract: Lyle Swenson, president of the National Sheriff's Association spoke out against assault weapons in a news conference, while the US Senate debated a bill that would ban nine military-style assault weapons. The bill is opposed by members of the National Rifle Association. The bill has been reshaped by Democrats in the Senate to include provisions regarding the death penalty and use of evidence in warrantless searches.

headline: Who will pay for prisons? Referendum asks if state should
abstract: York County commissioners, including Commissioner Ronald Fitzkee, president of the county's Prison Board, and prison officials are urging support of a referendum that will allow the state to loan $200 million to counties to construct and upgrade prisons. Loan regulations would be established by the PA Commission on Crime and the PA Department of Corrections. The PA State Association of County Commissioners is concerned about overcrowding and decreasing state funding, but warns against federal mandates. York County Prison will begin an expansion project regardless of the results of the referendum.

headline: Lake Erie takes another home
abstract: Erosion from Lake Erie is forcing the Torrance family to demolish their house on the waterfront and move to a less picturesque location.  The house went from 30 feet from the shore 35 years ago to 10 feet today.

headline: Wary eye kept on skies
abstract: Rising waters could cause problems and locals are evacuating their homes. Numerous routes were closed in Butler and Armstrong counties were closed throughout the day. Officials are concerned about the flooding getting worse.

headline: Cumberland Valley back to 'normal' after teacher strike
abstract: After a three-day teacher strike, classes resumed yesterday in Cumberland Valley, and officials say that morale is high and there are no bad feelings between teachers and students or administrators.

headline: Jubelirer to GOP: Gear up for a tough year
abstract: PA Senator Robert Jubelier, president pro tempore of the PA Senate, called upon GOP to gear up for a tough year. He believes Republican voters may be apathetic. He also discussed tax plans that are steps to a fairer tax system that he claims is completely different from PA Governor Casey's. He criticized the Governor for wasting a surplus. Jubelier was also very concerned with rural economic development and gaining attention for them.

headline: State can't afford 4 more years of Casey
abstract: Peggy Madigan, president of the Pennsylvania Council of Republican Women, writes in support of Barbara Hafer's candidacy for governor against incumbent Democrat PA Governor Robert Casey, who Madigan says seems like a "robot reciting how wonderfully well off we are," while Hafer is a straight-talking, sensible candidate.

headline: Clean-air bill: Where whispers mean millions
abstract: Lobbyists filled the hallways and floors surrounding the House Energy and Commerce Committee rooms, waiting to hear the finalized version of the Clean-Air Act--arguably the biggest piece of legislation the 101st Congress has considered.  The bill is likely to be presented to the full House by May and includes looser federal deadlines for the coal industry, as well as provisions that require other states to help defray the costs of cleaning up the heavy emissions from Midwestern industries.

headline: Revenues for state take a dip
abstract: PA revenues fell 2.5 percent, $21.3 million below the official estimate of $869 million in October. Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer says that PA Governor Robert P. Casey's covered up a $189 million deficit at the end of the last fiscal year and that a tax increase is inevitable. Casey spokesman Vince Carocci said the shortfall was a reflection of the national economy and that Casey would not rule out the need for raising taxes.

headline: Pa. drug-treatment insurance law not used effectively, advocate says
abstract: An insurance law prescribing drug and alcohol treatment in Pennsylvania is not being used as effectively as it should be, says Deborah Beck, president of the Drug and Alcohol Service Providers Organization of Pennsylvania.  Beck also offered insight into pending legislation covering involuntary commitment of juveniles with drug and alcohol problems.

headline: Older Upper Merion Teachers sue over raises
abstract: A group of more senior teachers at Upper Merion Area School District have asked Federal District Judge Franklin Van Antwerpen to void the contract negotiated for the upcoming school year on the grounds of age discrimination. The suit was filed against the school district and the Upper Merion Area Education Association. The more senior teachers accuse the contract of granting higher pay raises to younger teachers.

headline: Landfill owner's credibility
abstract: Alden H. Cover of the Environmental Justice Coalition writes that Modern Landfill operations should be stopped before it receives an expansion permit. Tonnages of waste were falsely reported in Erie County and the incident was to result in an investigation of all Waste Management Sites. Cover says when the York County Solid Waste Authority is ready to use the landfill, it will already be filled to capacity.

headline: Group backs Hafer's transit proposal
abstract: The Committee for Public Mass Transit Survival, a citizen's group, has backed Barbara Hafer's plan to use 2 cents of a proposed 6-cent gas tax increase to fund mass transit, and the other 4 cents to highway maintenance.

headline: Crime victims' fund faces financial crisis. Audit suggests better budgeting.
abstract: An audit by the PA Legislative Budget and Finance Committee reported that the Crime Victims Compensation Board faces a financial crisis and will likely run out of operating funds before the fiscal year ends. The committee urged the board to seek supplemental funds and to improve its budget-request procedure. The program is faced with the loss of about $750,000 in federal funds because the Legislature did not enact federally required changes to include victims of drunken driving in grant eligibility.

headline: Widow starts group to lobby for change
abstract: Maura Irby started the Irby Foundation after her husband, James, a motorcycle policeman, was killed by a parolee during a traffic stop. The parolee had been convicted of child sexual assault and sentenced to 15 years in prison, but served 13 months. Now Maura is on a quest to collect statistics to lobby for change in the Texas parole and prison system. She says the Texas system has been termed a "country club" for criminals, and has met with legislators to lobby her cause.

headline: Land cost clouds jail plan
abstract: Relations between City Council, the Urban Redevelopment Authority, and the county have become strained over plans to build a new justice complex and prison. The county must meet a federal deadline of 1992, but has to wait for the city to approve the existing plans. CSX Railroad, owner of the property, is threatening to increase its asking price from $4.3 to $6 million if a decision is not made by year's end. County Commissioner Tom Foerster said it is unlikely an agreement will be reached by then.

headline: York group unfazed by takeover
abstract: Despite being turned over to the federally chartered Resolution Trust Corp. (RTC), the Heritage Savings Association will continue operating, said PA Secretary of Banking Sarah Hargrove. President and CEO of the First Capitol Bank in York, Thomas Capello is pleased. The Office of Thrift Supervision is not authorized to approve federally assisted transactions requested by Capello in a pitch to acquire Heritage, in which Capello urged that Heritage be turned over to RTC.

headline: Cuomo Proposes 2,000 Layoffs, Major Cuts
abstract: New York Governor Mario Cuomo has proposed firing 2,000 state workers and eliminating 4,000 other state jobs through attrition and early retirement in 1990 to deal with the city's fiscal problems, most of which would come from the prison and mental health systems. Cuomo also proposed cutting $200 million from the state school aid package to mixed reactions. About 60 percent of the Cuomo plan is subject to approval by the PA Legislature, while the rest could be done administratively. The state's credit rating dropped to its lowest point ever in 1990.

headline: Judge hears Dietterick case
abstract: Commonwealth Court Judge John T.J. Kelly Jr. heard arguments but did not make a decision on PA  Representative G. Scott Dietterick's request to be removed from the general election ballot, 2 and a half weeks before the election, and one week after Dietterick was convicted of forgery and other crimes for falsifying insurance documents. Luzerne County Commissioner James Phillips and Anne Vernon are both hoping to be allowed to take Dietterick's place on the ballot if he is indeed removed.

headline: State Christmas tree lighted in Harrisburg
abstract: Two-year old Elyse Casey with help from grandfather PA Governor Robert Casey, light the state's Christmas tree. More than 500 people jammed the Capitol rotunda to witness the lighting of the councilor.

headline: As the clock winds down, Republican hopefuls gear up
abstract: In Pennsylvania's 120th legislative district, five candidates are vying for the Republican nomination for state representative.  Over the next few weeks, candidates will be trying to distinguish themselves by conducting forums, door-to-door visits, rallies and phone calls.  The winner of the Republican primary election will face Democratic candidate Phyllis Mundy of Kingston.

headline: Rifts in the region's economy
abstract: There are signs of a potential economic recession in the Philadelphia area, i.e. a decreasing number of jobs and decreased retail sales.

headline: Pa. may provide test site for wildlife rabies vaccine
abstract: The National Wildlife Federation is asking Wistar Institute of Philadelphia, PA,  to hold off on testing a proposed rabies vaccine on PA state gameland until a trial on a Virginia island is completed in August. Said member Jane Rissler, the full effects of the vaccine are not known and could be potentially harmful to the environment. The US Department of Agriculture has requested Wistar test the vaccine on bears and porcupines to determine the vaccine's effects on these animals.

headline: Oregon considers tax credits to aid private schooling
abstract: The most ambitious school-choice plan to make it to the ballot-box will take place in Oregon, where a proposal would grant tax credits for tuition to private school and expenses for home-schooling.

headline: Landfill plan concerns residents
abstract: Antrim Township residents met with representatives of the PA Department of Environmental Resources to voice their concerns about a proposed expansion of the Community Refuse Ltd. Landfill, citing potential health and safety issues, and hazardous waste dumping. Teresa Schnoor, code enforcement officer and landfill inspector for Antrim Township, and a representative of the Antrim Township Supervisors, John Lisko, said the landfill is in violation of zoning ordinances and other requirements.

headline: Hafer brave to suggest gasoline tax increase
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer is telling voters they can have better highways and mass transit as long as they are willing to dig a little deeper into their pockets. The legislature just voted against using the gasoline tax to fund highways. PA business groups also want gas taxes raised.

headline: Criminal justice sites compared
abstract: This chart shows the square footage, cost and cost per square foot of potential sites where new Philadelphia justice centers may be built.

headline: 'Widow's tax" relief vetoed by governor
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey vetoed a bill that would have eliminated the state's "widow's tax," which is paid by surviving spouses on inherited property and assets that were not held in joint ownership.  Under the bill, the 6% tax would have been decreased by 1% each year until it was eliminated.  Casey's veto has prompted immediate criticism from Senate Republicans.  Casey has called the bill "a giveaway to the rich."

headline: Land cost clouds jail plan
abstract: The city and county are facing a 40 percent increase in the cost of the land for the proposed Downtown criminal justice complex. If the city does not buy the riverfront site by December. 31, CSX Railroad, will increase the price from $4.3 million to $6 million. The county said they would build their own jail if the deal with the city didn't work out.

headline: Advance for Yearend Editions
abstract: A look back at the events in the month of December revealed US soldiers in Saudi Arabia were specially provided with Hershey's chocolate bars. The PA government is facing a deficit approaching $1 billion, which could mean layoffs and cuts to welfare and other programs.

headline: Cut! Legislatures trimmed across nation
abstract: Across the nation, proposals to limit lawmakers' terms are appearing on ballots for this November's election. Many people feel that lawmakers are entrenched and that incumbency is too much of an advantage, and they want politicians to stop making careers out of legislative work. Some legislators are starting to join the cry and are pulling to add the measures to ballots and calling for a constitutional convention to address the issue on a national level.

headline: Judge narrows bond act order
abstract: PA Supreme Court Judge Lawrence Kahn modified an order he made last week prohibiting New York Governor Mario Cuomo from speaking about his proposed $2 billion bond act.  Cuomo is under attack for allegedly promoting the passage of the act illegally with state funds.

headline: State cost-cutting should begin with LCB examiners
abstract: PA Senator John J. Shumaker writes to explain the legislation he introduced that would eliminate 13 "patronage" positions on PA's Liquor Control Board, which were deemed unnecessary by Auditor General Barbara Hafer's recent audit of the board. The legislation would save taxpayers $657,000 a year.

headline: The Abingtons
abstract: Stephany Malyska, along with the other students who won Pennsylvania's Recycling Poster Contest, attended a reception in the capitol building.  At the reception, PA Governor Robert P. Casey signed a proclaimation declaring April Earth Month and spoke to the youngsters individually.

headline: Sales Tax Collection to Improve, Panel Told
abstract: David Donahoe, Revenue Secretary, claims improvements in sales tax collection will allow the state to make up its shortfall and end this fiscal year in the black.

headline: Pa. to get AMA drug award
abstract: One of Pennsylvania's anti-drug programs is being recognized for excellence by the American Medical Association.  The award recognizes the state's efforts to improve adolescent health with its Student Assistance Program.  The program combines efforts of the Education, Health, and Public Welfare departments.

headline: PA. Official:  Blacks Misplaced in Special Ed
abstract: A state education official asserts that black children are being placed into special education programs faster and more often than white children, even at times against the childrens' best interests.

headline: Landfill Proposal
abstract: At the end of a town meeting to inform Conyngham residents about a proposed township landfill, supervisors declared they planned to adopt an ordinance that will reject or control any proposed landfills.

headline: Hafer calls for 65 mph speed limit
abstract: Saying most drivers ignore the 55 mph speed limit on the PA Turnpike, Hafer suggested raising the limit 65 on certain portions of the road to determine the effects of the change.

headline: Critics say bias spurs police focus on blacks
abstract: Critics are accusing police nationwide of prejudice against blacks in the war on drugs. Though blacks comprise only 15 percent of users, they make up 41 percent of those arrested for drugs, statistics which the Police Foundation finds discriminatory. Officers say drugs are harder to track in white neighborhoods, requiring more time, resources and money. Columbus, Ohio police commander John Rockwell says police are merely responding to areas in which complaints are made.

headline: Window's tax bill vetoed
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey vetoed a bill that would have eliminated PA's "widow's tax," an action which prompted immediate criticism from PA Senate Republicans. Casey called the bill "a giveaway to the rich." The 6% tax is paid by surviving spouses on inherited property or assets that were not in joint ownership, and the bill would have decreased the rate by 1% each year until the tax was eliminated.

headline: Landscape of change
abstract: Philadelphia has spend about $200 million in projects to renovate the northern part of the city. The project include construction of townhouses and rental units intended for low-income residents.

headline: All veterans deserve flag
abstract: Letter to the editor criticizes the PA County Code that only allows veterans who have served during active duty to have a flag placed on their grave for Memorial Day.  When flags are less than 60 cents when ordered in bulk, there doesn't seem to be a reason why all veterans can't have flags on their graves.

headline: Debate Issues
abstract: The article gives a brief representation of PA Governor Casey's and his Republican challenger Barbara Hafer's positions on various issues taken in the gubernatorial debate.  The issues include education, abortion, taxes, auto insurance, the widow's tax, legislative taxes, and the Philadelphia financial crisis.

headline: Judicial issues on docket
abstract: The PA House and Senate have before them a set of bills regarding the state's judicial practices. Three key issues expected to be brought up are judicial discipline, merit selection of judges, and regional elections as an alternate to merit selection. They will soon begin to negotiate the state's budget for the upcoming fiscal year.

headline: State ethics body clears township official
abstract: The PA Ethics Commissioner cleared North Versailles Commissioner Paul Homanai of charges he exploited his position in addition to his job with the PA Department of Revenue. Homanai had been hired to help the East Allegheny School District reduce $2 million in outstanding taxes but was charged with basing his consultation improperly on information to which he was privy because of his job and elected position.

headline: Casey Adviser to Keynote Local PSU Commencement
abstract: Sondra Myers, cultural adviser to Governor Robert P. Casey, is slated to be the commencement speaker for The Pennsylvania State University's Worthington Scranton Campus graduation exercises.  Myers is a nationally recognized leader in the arts and humanities.

headline: Saving for a rainy day
abstract: PA Senator James C. Greenwood wants to use some of the $125 million “rainy day funds” to pay for child protection programs. PA Governor Robert P. Casey said that he will not initiate the Rainy Day expenditures the Republican-controlled Senate has proposed, his decision is supported by the PA Economy League (PEL). The PEL says that the funds are for emergencies and not funding ongoing programs, raising taxes while the state has a tax surplus would not be responsible.

headline: Pa-hospitals
abstract: A report by the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council revealed the fiscal condition of the state's 289 hospitals, which operated at an excess of 330 million dollars more than their $12.5 billion budgets. Philadelphia, which experienced the worst year, was one of nine regions to report operating losses. A spokesman for the Hospital Association of PA says the situation has worsened due to the state's delays in making medical assistance payments.

headline: Pa. training of directors is needed
abstract: Calling for a more intensive training program for newly elected school board members. It calls the two round, five hour course inadaquate training, especially for someone dealing with the $60 million annual operating budget of the Reading School Board.

headline: Landfill response
abstract: The author of the letter criticizes the PA Department of Environmental Resources' response to a public meeting held regarding the proposed expansion to the Modern Landfill in Windsor Township as late and unsatisfactory. The author says that if the York County Solid Waste Authority processed only local garbage, there would be no need for an expansion. The author hopes that only the townships that would be affected by the landfill would be involved in the ratification of the plan.

headline: Hafer plugs gas tax for transit, highways
abstract: Touting her plan to raise the gas tax to help fund Southeastern PA Transportation Authority and improve state highways, Republican gubernatorial hopeful Barbara Hafer made a brief campaign stop in Bucks County to court support of local GOP leaders. She visited the county courthouse, meeting with the commissioners and the GOP row officers.

headline: Crosses evident at event
abstract: A traditional three-barred Eastern Orthodox cross led the procession of Ecumenical Patriarch Dimitrios  into the Cambria County War Memorial Arena for his visit here, but many other forms of the cross were evident. The clergy and faithful wore Greek crosses with four arms of equal length, Celtic crosses and the more familiar crosses used by other branches of Christianity.

headline: Winner of child-care leave legal fight feels other men will follow
abstract: This week the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a man's right to a child-care leave when an employer grants the same benefit to women. In 1981, Gerald Schafer requested a leave-of-absence from the Pittsburgh School Board after the birth of his child. The board turned him down, and Schafer soon took his complaint to the PA Human Relations Commission, then the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and finally the US Department of Justice which filed this suit against the school board.

headline: Legislation on impact fees may end developers' suit
abstract: David D. Reel, executive director of the Home Builders Association of Bucks/Montgomery Counties, said the organization will likely drop its lawsuits against 28 municipalities if PA Governor Robert P. Casey signs two impact-fee bills passed by the PA Legislature. Written largely by PA Representative Donald Snyder and regarded as a compromise, the package is still opposed by the PA State Association of Township Supervisors. The legislation allows municipalities to assess fees for transportation systems, water and sewer improvements, and parks and recreation.

headline: Area military enlistments unaffected by Gulf crisis
abstract: Area military recruiters say that there has been no change in the number of people enlisting in the military since the Persian Gulf crisis began, though they have been getting calls of support, veterans seeing if they can get back in, and concerned parents worried that their children could be sent to Iraq.

headline: Debate night
abstract: PA State Representative Robert Freeman and Republican challenger Brian Leidy held a televised debate last night in their race for the 136th district seat.  They clashed over their policies about minimum wage, which Leidy believes hurts poor people by increasing the cost of living. Freeman supports the minimum wage, and would increase it "when necessary."

headline: Juniata voter registration up
abstract: Voter registration is up slightly in Juniata County since the May primary elections, but down a few voters since last November. Voter registration has closed for the November 6 election, in which two Juniata County residents, incumbent Daniel Clark and Democratic challenger Danny Martin are fighting one another for the 82nd Legislative District seat.

headline: State GOP Expects $50,000 from Quayle Visit
abstract: Vice President Quayle's day trip to Pennsylvania is projected to raise $50,000 for the Republican State Committee as well as the images of candidates like Auditor General Barbara Hafer.

headline: Barbara Bush to speak at Penn
abstract: Barbara Bush, the nation's 38th first lady, will be the University of Pennsylvania's commencement speaker on May 14th, marking the school's 250th anniversary.  The content of her speech is unknown, but Bush has been a staunch advocate of literacy since her husband took office.

headline: 'Sin taxes' effective, but unfair
abstract: Editorial discusses how the government uses tax deductions to encourage certain kinds of behavior. For example deductions for giving money to charity and reverse by taxing things like smoking with sin taxes. It believes that eventually the sinners will call enough and call out against being taxed. It does say that sin taxes do work to get people to quit and raise revenue, but they are unfair.

headline: pa-hospitals
abstract: General hospitals in PA barely took in enough operating revenue to pay bills for the fiscal year. It was only one of nine regions to report operating losses.

headline: PA. underfunding education
abstract: The board believes that PA's budget is out of balance, and cites that as the only possible explanation for why the Casey administration refused to reconsider its underfunding of public education. For example, school boards in Manheim Townships, Eastern Lancaster County, Columbia and Ephrata will all have to increase property taxes. Although the state is providing more dollars, the percentage of money for public education has dropped despite increased education costs. Poorer school districts stand to suffer greatly.

headline: Landfill Space Adequate - DER
abstract: Ed Shoener, the regional direction of the state Department of Environmental Resources explained that they will be more strict in reviews of new applications now that Northeastern Pennsylvania has adequate landfill space.

headline: Heinz: Casey must act
abstract: US Senator Heinz is calling on PA Governor Casey to help defeat a bill in the Senate that would force PA to create a tax to support South Eastern PA Transportation Authority, or risk losing 25% of federal highway funds.  Casey plans to stay out of the matter, as it is a federal issue and not a state bill.

headline: Cumberland backs inmate earned time
abstract: Cumberland County Prison inmates who behave and work to better themselves could have their sentences cut under an “earned-time” program endorsed by county commissioners. Herbert Motter, deputy warden, said that the officials support the plan as a way to avert prison crowding and discipline problems. The inmates’ times are cut by 5 days a month if they follow prison rules and attend classes to educate them and show improved behavior. Fourteen other PA counties have similar programs.

headline: Witness alleges payoffs
abstract: A former narcotics agent with the Philadelphia police testified that Police Inspector William T. Bergman was given $7,000 to $10,000 stolen during property searches by One Squad Narcotics officers.

headline: Let's Build That Justice Center
abstract: One of the few things that everyone agrees on in Philadelphia's City Hall is the need for a new justice center, though there is disagreement over where and when and how to build and pay for it.  The editorial stresses the need for the government to decide on a plan so that it can begin construction, because otherwise the total costs will only rise.

headline: Area reservist braces for possible orders
abstract: With thousands of military reservists on alert, families are waiting anxiously to see how many and who will be called for duty.

headline: Delays plague West's bid for U.S. attorney post
abstract: President George Bush nominated James J. West to become U.S. attorney for the Middle District of PA. His name then was to go before the Senate Judiciary Committee, which had to conduct a background investigation, and then to the full Senate for a vote. However, since Congress adjoined without making a decision on the nomination, West's name will now go back to the president for re-nomination. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter called for public hearings after receiving complaints about West from former PA Auditor General Don Bailey.

headline: Kevin Street pleads guilty in car death
abstract: Kevin Street, son of former PA Senator T. Milton Street, pleaded guilty to vehicular homicide while under the influence of alcohol, receiving stolen property, and aggravated assault. Under a plea agreement with the District Attorney's Office, Street will receive a mandatory sentence of three to six years in prison. Street was represented in court by his uncle, Philadelphia City Councilman John F. Street.

headline: State GOP regroups in 'mighty' Pa.
abstract: GOP conservatives have announced the formation of "The October Group", an organization who wants to return the party to its conservative principles and resign those who engineered Auditor General Barbara Hafer's gubernatorial campaign. A spokesman for the group said Hafer's support of abortion and increased taxes alienated social conservatives in the party. The author of the letter suggested that Hafer's billing of PA Governor Robert P. Casey as a "redneck Irishman" alienated rural residents. The PA Legislature adopted a state song last week.

headline: Ex-Congressman Seeks One-Time Return to Politics
abstract: Charles Diggs Jr., the former Democratic Congressman from Michigan, is running for the Maryland Legislature.  Diggs was ousted from Congress after 25 years for his participation in a kickback scandal, and is hopeful that voters will remember his accomplishments more than the scandal that sullied his name.  Diggs plans only to serve one term so he can help redraw Maryland's political district lines; he claims that blacks are very underrepresented in several areas of the state.

headline: State faces $959 million in red ink
abstract: PA Governor Robert P Casey told the PA General Assembly the state faces potential deficit of $959 million this June. A tax increase may be necessary, but is a last resort. Casey is currently examine spending cuts to reduce deficit. Revenues have fallen and spending has gone over. Welfare in the recession has exacerbated the spending.

headline: Panel probes Pitt cancer research
abstract: The National Institutes of Health is looking into an accusation that a University of Pittsburgh doctor faked results in research on immunotherapy, or the strengthening of the body's defenses. Dr. John Hiserodt in turn accused his superior of stealing his work, and said that the school's Pittsburgh Cancer Institute ousted him to gain the federal money allocated to his projects. The NIH is looking into both accusations.

headline: Parents' coalition wants seatbelts in school buses
abstract: Parents of students on a bus in an accident asked the Pittsburgh School District's board to require seat belts in regular sized buses. The school board complies with federal law, which mandates seatbelts be available in smaller buses, but there is no federal or state law requiring seatbelts for regular sized buses. The PA General Assembly has 2 bills pending which would change that requirement, but a National Academy of Sciences study shows the measure would not be cost effective.

headline: Landfill suggested at Benjamin mine
abstract: A waste management company wants to convert a former strip mine in southern Clearfield County to a solid waste landfill to serve area counties. Residents of the area are opposed because they are afraid it will be bad for the groundwater supply.

headline: Here We Go Again
abstract: An editorial expressing that SEPTA's most recent fare increases allows the transit agency to demand its rightful share of government aid.

headline: DA: No evidence of coke decline
abstract: Sharon DA James Epstein says that there is no evidence in Mercer County for the supposed decline in cocaine and other drug use, though fortunately there are fewer reports of heavily armed dealers.  Epstein wants to be able to give grants directly to police departments to hire more officers for high-crime areas.

headline: Witnesses with protection. Ex-offenders win guilty verdicts- and bitter attacks.
abstract: Federal prosecutors used nine protected witnesses in a recent organized-crime case, the most ever used in one case by the U.S. attorney's office in Western PA. Stanton Levenson, president of the PA Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, said the convictions based on testimonies do not outweigh the program's negative impact on society. Ninety-seven percent of those enrolled in the witness-protection have extensive criminal records.

headline: OIC Likely to Lose Weatherization Funds
abstract: The state Department of Community Affairs plans to consolidate Cumberland and Adams Counties' weatherization services, cutting the Carlisle Area Opportunities Industrialization Center's program for low-income families.

headline: Army forcing retirees into service
abstract: The Army is looking for more volunteers. They are even searching out retirees, especially those with medical skills. As the buildup of US forces in the Persian Gulf surges toward the 400,000 level and the United Nations deadline nears for an Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait, the Army is digging around for support.

headline: Democratic aspirants reject liberal doctrine
abstract: Democrats Dianne Feinstein, running for the governor of California, and Paul Hubbert, running for governor of Alabama, are both breaking with the standard Democrat platform. Feinstein supports the death penalty, and Hubbert is against prisoners' rights, two departures from traditional Democratic platforms that they are using to their advantage in their general elections, despite Democrats' opposition to their positions. The two candidates represent a small but growing trend of Democrats to defy certain positions that may have hurt candidates, especially presidential presidents, in the past.

headline: King Blvd. to be Market Street again
abstract: Harrisburg voters chose to change Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard to Market Street in a referendum. A group of mostly white residents used a little-known state law to get the issue on the ballot after a compromise failed to win a majority vote on the City Council. Harrisburg is now one of the few major cities that does not have a major thoroughfare named for King, said Lynn Cothren, spokesman for the Martin Luther King Center for Non-Violent Social Change.

headline: State GOP Sour on Dems Over City's Fiscal Pickle
abstract: Republicans are criticizing the Casey administration for not doing more to help the city of Philadelphia in its fiscal debacle.  Casey's press secretary said "attempts to politicize this issue makes [sic] it more difficult to resolve."

headline: Insurance law blocked--again
abstract: Portions of Pennsylvania's new sweeping auto-insurance law were blocked by a Commonwealth Court judge on Monday. Two provisions of the law--one setting a cap on medical costs and one barring doctors from billing any party other than an insurance company--were blocked by an injuction.  The Casey administration has appealed the injunction.

headline: State unemployment rises to 5.5 percent
abstract: The Pennsylvania unemployment rate rose by .6% last month, which is worrisome but doesn't mean the state is in a recession, according to Penn State University business analyst William Anderson.  The state, at 5.5% is still slightly below the national average, 5.7%.

headline: Panel urges aid to poor for Medicare
abstract: A congressional study commission plans to recommend that the government help low-income elderly people pay Medicare charges. The Pepper Commission is also expected to call for including more preventive services in Medicare and increasing the amount that commercial policies supplementing Medicare must pay.

headline: Parents' group gives state schools a 'B'
abstract: In a recent report by a new parents' organization gave the PA school system a 'B' grade, which has some people encouraged that the state is improving its education system.

headline: Lawmakers boost OUE membership
abstract: Two PA state legislators spoke to members of the Watsontown Area Business Association about their opposition to a US Pollution Control hazardous waste incinerator. The USPCI did not expect businesses to get involved. Four different sites are proposed for incinerators. Local businesses are not trusting that the technology will stay the same for 50 years and after the 50 years the government will no longer take responsibility and they will be left with a pile of ash.

headline: Herman to move on audit
abstract: Borough Manager William Herman is taking steps to correct long-standing faulty auditing procedures.  The borough has been asked to refile its audits for the last three years.

headline: Defense Contractor Charged with Shipping Government Bad Bomb Fuses
abstract: Glenn Clement, a United Chem Con Corp. supervisor, was charged with sending over 200 defective bomb fuses to the government.

headline: Woman in right-to-die case slips closer to death
abstract: Nancy Cruzan's condition deteriorated from serious to critical, 11 days after a feeding tube was removed from the permanently unconscious woman at her parents' request. Critical is the last stage before death. Cruzan has been in a persistent vegetative state since a 1983 car accident. The tube supplying food and water was removed December 14, 1990,  when a probate judge granted her parent's wish t let her die. A Florida minister is seeking an order to resume feeding.

headline: Living Ellis Island, 2 Takes
abstract: Ellis Island Immigration Station opened to the public two months ago after a $160-million restoration of the main building. Deputy Superintendent of the Statue of Liberty National Monument Tom Bradley said more exhibitions will be added to the area by the beginning of 1991. Bradley said the National Park Service hopes to give visitors access to more of the island, and later, access to some un-restored parts of the main building.

headline: Army may lay off workers
abstract: If the Department of the Army approves proposed layoffs, 150 workers at the Tobyhanna Army Depot in Monroe County could lose their jobs. The cuts were proposed by the Army Material Command in Alexandria, VA which faces a shortfall of money of more than $100 million.

headline: Democratic Comptroller Candidates Agree on Bond Issue
abstract: Both Democrats in the primaries for New York state comptroller support the $2 billion environmental quality bond act being put up to voters this November.  The Republican incumbent opposes the bond act, saying that the state shouldn't go into debt more than it is already.

headline: Labeling of the Governor
abstract: An opinion piece reproaching Barbara Hafer's crude labeling of Governor Casey and refusal to apologize.

headline: State House candidates focus on different issues
abstract: The two candidates for Lancaster's seat in the PA state House focused their attention on two different issues in separate press conferences yesterday.  Democratic City Councilman Mike Sturla called for programs that would encourage development in the city, such as new water line construction, as a means of preserving farmland from development.  Republican attorney Peter Hahn, called for programs to help with the in-home care of senior citizens, to relieve their property tax burden, and to lessen the threat oh physical violence toward them.

headline: Volusia County grand jury rules 2 Live Crew, others obscene
abstract: A Volusia County grand jury found 2 Live Crew's album "As Nasty As They Wanna Be" obscene.  This declaration effectively bans the sexually explicit record in Volusia County.  Four other Florida counties and two counties in Pennsylvania have also banned the album.

headline: State Budget
abstract: Governor Casey and the Pennsylvania General Assembly will soon begin deciding appropriations from next year's state budget.

headline: PA-Prudential
abstract: Prudential, a NJ company, is phasing out its H-M-O plan due to lack of participation in the Pittsburgh area. Prudential will honor all of its contracts, which mostly expire in August 1991.

headline: Parents, teachers are partners
abstract: Shamokin area schools held open house programs as part of their observance of American Education Week, and some administrators reported a noticeable increase in the number of parents attending. The editorial board commends these parents who show strong interest in their children's education. The board believes communication lines should remain open between teachers and parents throughout the year.

headline: Lead's dangers a top concern
abstract: The article warns of the dangers of lead in drinking water, saying that the American Academy of Pediatrics declared that exposure to lead was the top environmental hazard to children.

headline: High Speed Rail Bill
abstract: Rep. Geist of Blair said that it would cost an estimated $3 billion to build a high speed rail line between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.

headline: Department's survey has 5 sets of questions
abstract: Summary of the state Board of Corrections survey which consists of five sets of questions dealing with general attitudes toward prison overcrowding, specific methods of reducing crowding, alternatives to incarceration, and a one year/one time tax increase to address the overcrowding problem.

headline: Woman in state right-to-die case dies before feeding tube removed
abstract: 63-year-old Ruth Ragona died Tuesday of complications from pre-existing conditions as a stroke victim. Her husband asked permission from the Lackawanna County Court to remove his wife's feeding Tube, citing the case of Nancy Cruzan as a precedent for the case. Ragona died during the 30 appeal period though the court granted the request. The case was expected to have statewide impact as PA does not have a law addressing such requests.

headline: Mall Option Extensions Sought
abstract: Department store owner Al Boscov explains to property owners of United Cerebral Palsey of Scranton an offer to extend sales option agreements on properties needed for construction of a mall in downtown Scranton.

headline: At the Gap
abstract: Soldiers at Fort Indiantown Gap of PA looked forward to a bleak Christmas until a call was made to Father Francis Bach at the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary Catholic Church. The support, encouragement, and outreach of the church's parishioners overwhelmed the soldiers with encouragement.

headline: Democratic Comptroller Candidates Agree on Bond Issue
abstract: Both Democrats in the primaries for NY state comptoller support the $2 billion environmental quality bond act being put up to voters this November.  The Republican incumbent opposes the bond act, saying that the state shouldn't go into debt more than it is already.

headline: Labor Can't Choose in 4th District
abstract: The AFL-CIO ended up supporting neither candidate for the 4th district Senate seat being contested by Joseph Rocks and Allyson Schwartz.

headline: State House Set to Tackle Parental Leave Legislation
abstract: The state House is voting this week on a bill providing most Pennsylvania workers with unpaid leave for medical and family-care reasons.

headline: Abortion becomes a quiet issue in primary campaigns
abstract: In the 22nd Legislative District of Pennsylvania, riverboat gambling, auto insurance, and health care costs are all issues that have been considered during the primary campaign for state Legislature.  Candidates say there has been little discussion about abortion--an issue many thought would dominate this year's primary election.  This has not stopped two political-action committees from endorsing and printing slate cards of candidates they support.

headline: State budget OK'd
abstract: The partisan wrangling that had been expected to precede the adoption of a new state budget was avoided, and the absence of a struggle seems the result of an enlightened attitude by the Republicans who control the PA Senate. It authorizing the spending of $12.27 billion during the fiscal year that began July 1. The total is an increase of only 1.7 percent and reflects a recognition by both PA Governor Robert Casey and PA Senate and House leaders that revenues sources are falling off.

headline: P-G editors: Liability or stupidity?
abstract: Letter criticizes paper for advocating a change in the product-liability laws and they failed to factor on tens of thousands of Americans who have not been injured or killed by defective products. He believes the papers should urge state government to fund other programs to decrease insurance costs like classes to help smokers quit smoking.

headline: Parochial Schools Promised 'Fair Share' of Funds
abstract: Donald M. Carroll, state Secretary of Education address concerns of non-public school systems that all schools, both public and non-public, will receive a fair share of funding.

headline: Leaf recycling law has some municipalities up a tree
abstract: Despite laws requiring municipalities to use large-scale composting to recycle leaves, many municipalities do not have such a program.  Some potential reasons behind this are a lack of a suitable location for a composting area or the lack of large-scale leaf-collecting equipment.

headline: High-speed Rail Gains Support Across U.S.
abstract: Interview with Bob Casey, executive director of the High Speed Rail Association in Pittsburgh, about goals and concerns of high-spreed rail development in the state and country.

headline: Despite orders, guard let troopers in prison
abstract: A guard at the Camp Hill State Correctional Institute opened the gate to state troopers despite prison administrators not wanting to do so. The guard, Sgt. Paul A. Beck, testified to the Senate Judiciary Committee that he asked permission three times to send troopers into the facility to help quell the riot, before bypassing the administrators and admitting the police.

headline: Women in DA's office find no barriers
abstract: Women working in the District Attorney's office in Allegheny County have reported that the office is a uniquely gender-equal workplace, that everyone is treated the same, which cannot be said for many other places.

headline: Marina Planned
abstract: The Urban Redevelopment Authority has scheduled a news conference to announce the construction of a new 325-ship marina for pleasure boats on the southwestern shore of Washington's Landing in Pittsburgh.  The authority's board of directors will vote on whether or not to proceed with the project.

headline: Breakwaters work expected to resume next week
abstract: The Army Corps of Engineers expects the Presque Isle breakwaters project to resume next week after being inactive for 7 weeks due to the lack of armor stone, then to other unrelated delays.

headline: Democratic hunting grounds
abstract: David S. Broder believes Republicans concerned in elections. Republicans face tough candidates in Florida, Texas and California gubernatorial races. Already Governors William Clemets, Bob Martinez, and George Deukmejian have been forced to increase taxes. In Florida, former San Francisco Mayor Diane Feinstein will challenge Governor Pete Wilson, while former Charlotte mayor Harvey Grant will challenge US Senator Jesse Helms. Poles  former Senator Lawtown Chiles ahead of Texas Governor Bob Martinez.

headline: Labor Delegates to Vote on Endorsements
abstract: The AFL-CIO has already endorsed Gov. Casey and his running mate, along with three US Congressmen, and will soon vote on endorsements for three state Senate seats and 29 House seats.  The organization will also soon voice its support of the Temple Association of University Professionals in their strike against Temply University.

headline: State labor chief cutting through red tape
abstract: State Secretary of Labor and Industry Harris Wofford describes his history with PA Governor Bob Casey, Wofford's record, the new comprehensive job centers being opened by the state, and how the state will adapt to federal legislation mandating equal rights for disabled persons. In Johnstown, where many see problems with labor and industry, Wofford says case studies of the school districts have revealed the town is on a positive path. He is encouraged by the path the state is on as a whole.

headline: Parents to fight closing
abstract: As part of a cost-saving package that could save the Wilkes-Barre Area School District more than 350,000 dollars, school board members are considering shutting down the Wilkes-Barre Township Junior High School.  The board is also reviewing other cost-cutting measures, such as closing other schools, laying off workers, consolidating curricula and raising property taxes.  Some residents plan to protest the closure.

headline: State budget race enters the home stretch
abstract: The PA General Assembly is required by the state constitution to pass a budget by June 30th. Senate Republicans are making the demand that PA Governor Robert P. Casey free at least $20 million from the state’s Rainy Day fund to enhance child welfare programs in the state. The budget is said to contain little surplus money and the debate will be over how to divide the limited state funds.

headline: Philadelphia health officials eye earlier measles shots
abstract: Dr. Robert Sharrar, an assistant city health commissioner, said new guidelines will recommend that parents have their children vaccinated for measles when they reach six months of age, instead of the usual 15 months.
