Sharrar said the city has already had an increased number of measles outbreaks and hopes the recommendations, based on the Centers for Disease Control's guidelines, will ward off an epidemic. Sharrar said if the recommendations are adopted, the city is likely to provide free vaccines for young children.

headline: Penn State "Buys" Wooded York Site
abstract: The Pennsylvania State University's York Campus is developing recreational facilities in nearby Rotary Woods which they bought from York for a bookkeeping price of one dollar.

headline: Legislators blamed for backing Act 108
abstract: The writer attests that state legislators must stop the construction of a Concord's planned hazardous waste disposal plant in Clarion County.

headline: High-speed trains for Pittsburgh backed by Japan
abstract: A Japanese consortium is hoping to combine business with goodwill in helping to finance a high-speed magnetic levitation train system in Pittsburgh.

headline: Dietterick's lawyer wants talks out
abstract: The attorney for PA Rep. G. Scott Dietterick, who faces re-election this year, filed a request for statements made to the investigating PA Attorney General by his client to be kept out of trial. Dietterick is charged with forging school district busing insurance coverage. The request was accepted by Luzerne County President Judge Robert Hourigan and will be ruled upon by the presiding judge. A previous attempt to have charges dismissed because county detectives who arrested Dietterick did not have the power of arrest were denied.

headline: 'Yes' urged on volunteer loans
abstract: The editor of the newspaper urges voters to support a referendum allowing the state to loan $25 million to volunteer fire, ambulance and rescue companies to modernize facilities and purchase equipment at a two percent interest rate. The author says that  financially strapped volunteer companies often have to look to inadequate local fund-raising and municipal support to pay for constantly rising equipment prices.

headline: Mayor reopens Grant St., says more to come
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Masloff attended a ceremony reopening Grant Street, a project that lasted six years.  Just before the ceremony, she unveiled a $146 million capital budget for 1991 that emphasizes the redevelopment of downtown Pittsburgh.

headline: Carnegie gets OK to Move Sub Here
abstract: The Carnegie Science Center got the approval of the Secretary of the Navy to relocate a World War II sub, the USS Requin, to  Pittsburgh and use it for scientific demonstrations.

headline: Democrats confident of victory
abstract: Democrats in Northumberland County are confident of PA Governor Robert Casey's victory in the upcoming gubernatorial elections, though several say that Democrats can't become complacent or take the race for granted.

headline: Lancaster Mayor Calls for GOP Counsel's Resignation Over Remark
abstract: Mayor Janice Stork has joined other female officials in demanding that Republicans fire their counsel, Stephen MacNett, for saying of Gov. Casey that he "has learned that there is a third purpose for women. Not only do they cook and blank, they vote".

headline: State opens regional office for deaf
abstract: An office was opened in Scranton, which will work with state and local agencies to help deaf and hearing impaired citizens live and work as independently as possible.

headline: City policy requires employee drug tests
abstract: Johnstown Mayor Herb Pfuhl unveiled a new policy last week that mandates drug and alcohol testing of city employees.  All employees will be tested, and if a test result is positive, the employee will be required to take a leave and enter a treatment or assistance program; if the employee does not enter the program, he or she will be fired.

headline: State budget set for a vote
abstract: Legislators and PA Governor Casey are working towards approving a budget by the midnight deadline tonight. Senate Democratic Leader Robert Mellow expects the measure to pass. Casey spokesman Rod Snyder noted there is still work to be done. Vital issues include funding mechanisms for special and basic education. Other vital issues are social service programs, drug prevention programs, and economic development. The Legislature approved 40 spending bills to fund state related universities.

headline: Philip Morris taking heat as sponsor of 'Bill of Rights Tour'
abstract: At a Capitol news conference, representatives of health organizations and community groups condemned Philip Morris Company's "Bill of Rights Tour" for indirectly promoting smoking among youths who visit the exhibit. PA Senator Michael Dawida used the occasion to announce plans for legislation that would restrict smoking in public places and raise the state's 16-cent tax on cigarettes to support anti-smoking programs in schools. William Godshall, director of the Pittsburgh-based Smoke-Free Pennsylvania group, said Philip Morris has a history of suppressing individual rights.

headline: Penn State Can Avoid Future Student Unrest, Students Say
abstract: Penn State student leaders say administrators can avoid future unrest if they actually pursue their self-stated goal of a more diversified enrollment. Much of the decline in black enrollment has been linked to the spring 1988 takeover of the university's telecommunications building by students, a move designed to call attention to a perceived lack of attention to black needs. Retention studies show that most black students who leave Penn State after one or two years transfer to Temple or Pitt.

headline: Loan could fund Spring Twp. Sewers
abstract: About 50 homes and businesses along Jacksonville Road in Spring Township could have sewage service in the next year if the board of the PA Infrastructure Investment Authority approves a $1.5 million low-interest loan for the Spring-Benner-Walker Joint Authority. A PENNVEST spokesman said that staff recommended the project, along with 45 other projects for sewer and water system improvements, as one the board should approve at its quarterly meeting. Malfunctioning septic systems have posed health problems in the area for a number of years.

headline: Highway Contract
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation has awarded a $28.9 million contract for excavation and foundation work on the final stretch of the Uniontown bypass in Fayette County, most of which was built in the '70s, but a 3.4-mile stretch remains to be built. The contract was awarded to Gust K. Newberg Construction Co., a Chicago company which submitted the lowest bid.

headline: Don't Relax Drug Laws, Preate, Others Argue
abstract: State Attorney General Ernie Preate, Jr. and other citizens advocated the continued outlawing of drugs and narcotics.

headline: Young, black and in danger
abstract: In relentlessly increasing numbers, this generation of the city's poor, young black men are ending up on drugs, in shelter, in jail or in the morgue. They have even been called a species in danger. They account for one out of every five people in homeless shelters. It has become an epidemic.

headline: Mayor to VisionQuest: Stay out of Cressona
abstract: Controversial youth-rehabilitation program VisionQuest is being chased out of town by Cressona residents who say they don't want delinquent youths housed at the center to cause trouble in town.  Other areas housing a VisionQuest center have had incidents with runaway program members.

headline: Casey to be at brig commissioning
abstract: PA Governor Casey is scheduled to attend and speak at the commissioning of the US Brig Niagara at Erie in a few days.  The 177-year-old ship was recently reconstructed and has been named PA's official flagship.

headline: Democrats encouraged by turnout at dinner
abstract: A high turnout to the Democrats' annual dinner at Martin's Banquet Center at the York Fairgrounds gives Democrats some extra confidence going into the elections in November. About 300 people showed up to the dinner, where PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel and PA Representative Michael Bortner spoke.  A few speakers poked fun at Bortner's opponent for a PA Senate seat, Republican Representative Donald Dorr.

headline: Lansford men meet Gov. Casey
abstract: Two men who served in the Civilian Conservation Corps attended Gov. Casey's "Capital For a Day" events at Colton Point State Park.  The men want to plan a reunion of CCC members.

headline: State Reps Get an Extra $350 a Month for Office Rental
abstract: State House leaders voted to raise the amount members get for district office expenses from $450 to $800 per month to go toward rentals, telephone costs and utilities. The change would enable lawmakers to pay for office costs out of one account. The increase was approved during an informal meeting of the House Rule Committee and was made by consensus. If all House members took full advantage of the change, the bill would total $852,600 per year in additional expenses.

headline: Recycling now in curriculum
abstract: School districts across Pennsylvania must comply with the new state recycling law that applies to municipalities.  As a result, many school districts have set up pilot recycling programs.  Additionally, school districts across Lancaster County have been educating students on recycling--something that Manhiem Township science teacher Richard Brown has been doing for nearly 20 years.

headline: State lawmakers expect fierce budget war
abstract: PA Sen. Ralph Hess predicts a fight over PA's $12.3 billion budget. He owes his prediction to how little money is available. PA Governor Casey has hinted at a tax increase. Commonwealth Cause President Don Eberly warned government is less efficient than the market, urging cuts rather than taxes. The state is planning to withhold reimbursements for special education until the end of the next fiscal year, forcing many schools to raise property taxes. The budget is a big deal in elections.

headline: Plan gets care for terminally ill on release from jail
abstract: Allegheny County prison warden Charles Kozakiewicz announced a revision of the county's jail policy in order to ensure adequate provisions are made for released prisoners with a terminal illness. Medical prison personnel are required to notify the warden and work with the county Health Department, the mental-health and mental-retardation drug and alcohol program, the behavior clinic and bail agency to ensure adequate medical care and housing are available.

headline: Penn State Museum Acquires 16th Century Painting
abstract: A 16th century painting by Michele Tosini, “Madonna and Child with St. John” was acquired by the Penn State University Paler Museum of Art.

headline: Local group lobbies for Fairchild bill
abstract: The members of Organizations United for the Environment, advocates for the Fairchild Bill, which requires a safety zone between prisons and hazardous waste facilities, met with state legislators.

headline: Highway Maintenance to Hit Record Level
abstract: Gov. Casey has proposed a record $690 million for highway maintenance in his 1990-91 budget. The money will pay for resurfacing highways as well as repairs to road shoulders and guardrails.

headline: Former Johnstown editor charged anew
abstract: Charges of harrassment and impersonating an assistant state attorney general have been refiled against former editor of Johnstown Tribune-Democrat Theodore Beitchman. Bucks County officials originally charged Beitchman made the calls to a couple involved in a civil lawsuit against his brother, however the case was dismissed by a Bucks County magistrate for insufficient evidence. Officials say they will present new witnesses at a preliminary hearing.

headline: Youths abusing cough syrup
abstract: Teenagers have been abusing dextromethorphan, a substance contained in Robitussin DM and other legal, OTC medicines.  Some pharmacists and doctors are seeking to put more limits on the drug so that kids won't be able to get it as easily.

headline: Mellon Bank considers job cuts
abstract: As part of a streamlining process initiated by Mellon Chairman Frank Cahouet, Mellon Bank announced it some employee layoffs could result. The company employs 8,000 people in Pittsburgh.

headline: Environmental research center planned for Johnstown
abstract: Plans to open a National Defense Center for Environmental Excellence under the US Department of Defense were announced in a contract with the University of Pittsburgh by acting University president Daniel DeVos. Johnstown Area Regional Industries Inc. announced it has hired Robert Murphy to help local business procure defense contracts. DeVos credited US Rep. John Murtha with earmarking money for the center and choosing Johnstown as its site.

headline: Democrats Endorse Casey for Re-election
abstract: Governor Casey and Lt. Governor Mark Singel received unchallenged endorsement for another term in office from Democrats.

headline: Last-minute Dover bargaining set
abstract: Dover Area School District teachers have voted to strike starting Tuesday, the first scheduled day of classes, if an agreement is not reached on a new contract during a bargaining session scheduled for today.

headline: State revenues down $47 million
abstract: According to PA Governor Casey's administration, PA state revenues are $47 million below estimates.  The administration claims that the shortfall is temporary and will be corrected by later collections, but Republican state Senator Richard Tilghman, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, has said that the state will eventually face a $1 billion deficit.

headline: Argall spends day at mining site
abstract: As part of a Special District Workday program, state Representative David G. Argall spent the day working at Lehigh Coal and Navigation Company sites along Route 209.  Under the Special District Workday program, Representative Argall spends at least one day a month working as an unpaid employee for local businesses and industries, or with state and local government agencies.

headline: State lawmakers work to meet deadline on budget
abstract: PA Legislative aides say approval of the budget is close. Lawmakers continue to work with PA Governor Casey's administration to ensure his approval. The proposal will be less than initially thought after the state's revenue shortfall and the sluggish economy. The biggest issues are spending for special education and the state's prison system. The PA Senate Appropriations committee has approved 40 spending bills that grant state aid to several state and state-related universities.

headline: Plan to aid addicts
abstract: #NAME?

headline: Penn State selects president nominee
abstract: An educator with a reputation for quiet leadership and a balanced commitment to education and research was nominated to be the 15th president Pennsylvania State University. Joab Langston Thomas will begin his new duties September 1, 1990, the day President Bryce Jordan retires. Thomas, an accomplished botanist with a long list of published works, has been teaching biology at Alabama since he stepped down as president of that institution.

headline: Local recycler gets loan to upgrade equipment
abstract: Claws Refuse of Wysox will be receiving a $45,000 loan from the state to expand their recycling facilities.  The assistance comes from the Environmental Technology Fund, recently created by PA Governor Robert P. Casey.

headline: Historical markers dedicated on turnpike
abstract: Two historical markers were dedicated at the original service plazas of the Pennsylvania Turnpike, which marked its 50th anniversary yesterday.

headline: Goode asks D.A. to reopen probe of shop killing
abstract: At a press conference, Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode asked District Attorney Ronald Castille and Police Commissioner Willi Williams to review the shooting of a black man inside a Korean sandwich shop. The homicide was ruled self defense. Executive director of the Philadelphia Human Relations Commission Leah Gaskin, head of the Korean Association of Greater Philadelphia Daniel Yun, Councilman Lucien Blackwell and Ward Leader Vivien Miller attended. Justice Nicholas D'Alessandro issued a restraining order for store owner against protestors.

headline: A worthwhile handout
abstract: Panhandlers have become so overwhelming in cities that people are less likely to give to them and less likely to feel sympathetic to their plight. A new program is being proposed that would have people give beggars' tokens for a free meal instead of regular change.

headline: Member aids member on the PHA board
abstract: One board member of the Philadelphia Housing Authority turned to another board member's law firm for a lawyer to file for the incorporation of her non-profit tenants group.  It is reported that there was no conflict because the group is a non-profit, the law firm made no profit in the transaction.

headline: Former Defense Chief Looks at Post-Gulf War World
abstract: Discusses opinions in regard to the war, defense policy, and the Middle East of former Defense Secretary Frank Carlucci III.

headline: Democrats Lead in Governor Races but GOP Takes California, Michigan
abstract: The article details the election results of governor races across the nation. PA Governor Robert P. Casey Jr. won over Auditor General Barbara Hafer. Hafer had attacked Casey for passing legislation restricting abortion rights.

headline: Law abused contended by Oravitz
abstract: Joseph V. Oravitz contends the experience with Act 195 clearly indicates the law has not met its intended purpose, to promote a orderly and constructive relationship preserving the public interest in labor relations. With almost 800 teacher strikes since the law was created does not seem to him to meet the guidelines. He believes there was be some penalty for striking.

headline: State says bills being paid despite sluggish economy
abstract: A spokesman for PA Governor Robert Casey said that more than $200 million in delayed payments to fund county service is being sent out this week, but that delays in the borrowing of nearly half a billion dollars in tax anticipation notes could delay the next round of payments. Casey's Republican gubernatorial challenger and Auditor General, Barbara Hafer, is blocking the sale of the TANs, charging that Casey plans to use some of the money to bail out the financially floundering Philadelphia.

headline: Lead paint: A fiscal fiasco
abstract: Lead poisoning is a serious problem that can be cured by removing lead from all buildings.  Yet, the U.S. Government spent only 3.9 million dollars last year to help children poisoned by led.  For 10 billion dollars, we could solve this problem, and this should be our priority.

headline: State residents see income rise 7.8%
abstract: Penn State's Center for Regional Business Analysis found per capita income increased 7.4 percent in the state of PA, with an overall increase of 7.8 percent. Service industries continued to lead as areas in which the largest gains occurred. PA account fro 4.8 percent of US personal income last year.

headline: Poll shows conflicting consumer attitudes on health care
abstract: Three out of four Pennsylvanians are happy with their health insurance and medical care, but many believe the country is heading into a health-care crisis. 88 percent of state residents endorse attempts by the federal government to assure that everyone has access to health care. But 61 percent believe the government programs are costly and wasteful.

headline: Penn State Trustees Say Big Ten Move Benefits Entire University
abstract: Penn State trustees are defending the university's decision to join the Big Ten conference against sports interests, as the Big Ten provides many more academic resources.  They also say that joining the more powerful conference will be beneficial for sports programs as well.

headline: Make recycling effort, businesses told
abstract: Business and industry can make the state's mandatory recycling law work best by participating in all three stages of the recycling loop. They should sort recyclable materials, get those materials to a processing plant and bolster the market for recycled goods by buying them. This was the theme at two Recycling and Business forums held to help business leaders prepare for compliance with Act 101.

headline: House Oks Bill to Boost Crash Fines for Truckers
abstract: The state legislature passed a bill aimed at truckers driving on Route 22's Cemetery Curve that imposes higher fines on commercial drivers whose actions cause accidents

headline: Drug czar pats state on back for war on narcotics
abstract: Federal drug czar William Bennett congratulated the PA Legislature for passing a string of anti-drug measures without waiting for federal funding, but still suggests that lawmakers can still increase the state’s drug fighting. PA state Senator Gerald LaValle said that he was surprised that Bennett did not mention PA Governor Robert P. Casey in his acknowledgement of PA’s efforts. Bennett suggested that he Legislature could toughen the state’s mandatory sentencing laws by requiring stiffer penalties according to the type of drug and proposed a fee be paid by convicted drug offenders to help fund drug treatment programs.

headline: ACLU takes city to court over children's services
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union filed papers to include the city in a federal class-action suit against local courts and state officials for failing to fund child social services mandated by the federal government. The suit alleges that the state city and city failed to provide adequate services for 6,000 foster care children.

headline: New plant could be boon to Conrail, official says
abstract: A spokesman for Consolidated Rail Corporation, Conrail, announced plans for a new cogeneration plant in Altoona which should help locomotive shops in Juniata be more competetive in addition to providing jobs locally and boosting the area's enterprise zone economy. The use of local vendors and payment of real estate taxes has county commissioner John J. Ebersole agreeing the cogeneration plant, which will allow Conrail to produce its own steam and electricity, is a win-win situation.

headline: Grant to probe Pa. bases, says Casey
abstract: PA Governor Casey announced an additional $10,000 in funding for an economic study of the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard and air station.  The shipyard is on a list of bases for potential closure.

headline: Democrat's pro-flag stand draws GOP blandishment
abstract: Republican State Committee Chairman Anne Anstine invited Democratic State Committee Chairman Charles Vizzini to attend a GOP meeting after Vizzini was booed by members of his party for suggesting they vote on a resolution to support a constitutional amendment banning flag burning. Anstine said Vizzini, a veteran, should in essence consider joining the Republican party. Vizzini, who has known PA Governor Casey for a long time, has no intention of doing so and has declined her invitation.

headline: Law Professor Contradicts McDermott in Libel Case
abstract: Patrick McGinley testified to Common Pleas Judge John Lavelle that PA Supreme Court Justice James T. McDermott, though he said otherwise, voted in favor of a law firm that had contributed to his 1981 election campaign. McDermott alleges that the Philadelphia Inquirer's series called "Above the Law", which concluded that members of the PA Supreme Court routinely ignored judicial canons of ethics, implied that he fixed cases.

headline: State senate contest heats up in York County's 28th district
abstract: The state senate race between PA Senator Mike Bortner and his Republican challenger Donald Dorr is heating up, as the candidates each are accusing the other of negative campaigning.  One major issue is Bortner's nay vote on an amendment to a bill which would require a label be put on music recordings that signified if it is explicit in nature, presumably helping parents to monitor what their kids are listening to.

headline: null
abstract: This cartoon depicts a large trash dumpster that is full of refuse.  The trash in the dumpster is labeled "Casey Recycling Plan" and "Excuses."  The front of the dumpster says "can'ts" and is positioned next to a much smaller, empty bin labeled cans.  The dumpster is sitting in front of a sign that says "Allegheny League of Municipalities."

headline: State revenues miss goal
abstract: State revenue collections were below expectations for the third month in a row, but PA Governor Casey said that it would have little effect on the budget.  Casey is looking for ways to redistribute tax funding so as to avoid having to increase taxes next year.

headline: Rally targets city's high-risk drug areas
abstract: An anti-drug march led by PA Governor Casey made its way through several high-risk areas of Harrisburg yesterday.  Community and church leaders spoke with Casey at the end of the march about the importance of fighting drugs.

headline: Penn State wants out of a cracker box, into a complex
abstract: Penn State's decision to join the Big 10 comes with plans to construct a new basketball stadiums in order to allow for the school to host the games. PA Governor Casey's signature is needed to release $38 million approved by the PA Legislature. Capitol Budget Office spokesman Rod Snyder believes the release is unlikely given a number of other state projects. Senior Vice President for development and university relations, G. David Gearhart says state funds are crucial to completion of the project.

headline: Make trash exporters pay
abstract: The writer supports the DC Appropriations bill because it carries an amendment forcing garbage-exporting states to pay a fee in order to send their trash to another state.

headline: House passes water, transportation money bills
abstract: In a rush to finish budget work before the election break, US House members passed a transportation spending ill and an energy and water spending bill amounting to a total of $33 billion. They also passed $8.4 billion for military construction projects, which will include new housing for families of servicemen and women. The bills were created as a reconciliation between separate bill already passed in the House and Senate separately, and they will go to the Senate next for approval.

headline: Drug Policy OK'd in New Brighton
abstract: The New Brighton School Board stamped their unanimous approval on three state-mandated policies on drugs and suicide.

headline: Bill hopes to eliminate liens on welfare recipients' homes
abstract: Philadelphia State Representative David P. Richardson Jr.'s bill removes PA Department of Public Welfare home liens. Liens established amount to total welfare received which must be repaid before a house is sold or willed. Outstanding liens will keep the bill from passing, says general counsel to the PA Senate Republican Majority Stephen C. MacNett. The Unemployed Council of Southwestern PA is lobbying for passage. Critics say liens are not applied to recipients of Aid to Families with Dependent Children. PA Governor Casey's administration has not indicated if it will support the bill.

headline: No 'gloom and doom' in local economic poll
abstract: According to the Greater Pittsburgh Chamber of Commerce's annual economic survey, a large majority of area businesses expect a sales increase and to hire more employees in the next year. Ralph Bangs of the University of Pittsburgh's Social and Urban Research said that a national recession would have little effect on the city's economy, citing Pittsburgh's diversified local economy, lack of suffering commercial real estate and investment industries, and undergoing major development projects. The survey was conducted before the release of recent pessimistic economic statistics.

headline: Guard hails copter changeover plan
abstract: CH-54 Sky Crane helicopters are being de-activated to make way for medium lift Chinook helicopters. It will bring new life to PA's Army National Guard units.

headline: Democrats re-elect chairman
abstract: Two years after taking over a troubled Lebanon County Democratic Committee, Franz Messerschmidt was re-elected as its chairman.  He wants to continue efforts to find more people interested in serving as county committee members and interest more young people. He is trying to improve the nuts and bolts of the party and fundraise more.

headline: Lawless keeps up offensive
abstract: Democrat John A. Lawless criticized opponent PA Representative Joseph A. Lashinger for his inaccurate statements about Lawless' voting registration record and his relations with his former employer, Bell of PA. Lashinger, seeking re-election to an eighth term, is investigating a flier from the group "Republicans for Decency 1990", an organization not registered as a political action committee. Lawless is encouraging a state investigation of Lashinger's activities as a member of the Madison Bank board of directors.

headline: State Senate quickly confirms Stengel as newest county judge
abstract: The PA Senate very quickly moved to confirm attorney Lawrence Stengel to a Lancaster County judgeship.  The procedure was sped up in part because the legislature will not be in session next week and PA Senator Gibson Armstrong pushed for the vote to be held this week.

headline: Hafer forbids employees from seeking office
abstract: Pennsylvania Auditor General Barbara Hafer has banned her employees from political activity that interferes with their duties; employees are also banned from running for political office.  The purpose of the law is to prevent even the appearance of a conflict of interest and requires those running for office to take a leave of absence and resign once elected to office.  In response to Hafer's rule, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees filed a complaint with the PA Labor-Relations Board.

headline: State sells most of $495 million in TANs
abstract: Most of the $495 million in tax anticipation notes blocked by Barbara Hafer for a week or so have now been sold, allowing the state to pay its bills to the Education Department.  The interest rate on the notes was unaffected by the delay.

headline: Rates at Lysock View to rise in February
abstract: Rates at Lysock View will increase by $5 daily beginning February 1, 1990. The increase is for self-paying patients at the nursing home. It was recommended by Complete Care Services, the Blue Bell firm.

headline: Pitt faults Casey program for 6% in-state tuition hike
abstract: University of Pittsburgh officials say their tuition increase proves PA Governor Casey's tuition-challenge program did not work. Casey administration officials say the increase would be higher if not for the program. The challenge appropriates a bonus to universities which stay within a 6 percent increase, raised from 4 percent last year to make up for lower than expected state subsidies. PA Rep. Ron Cowell agreed with the Casey administration's assessment. Professors got a 4 percent raise due to a tight budget, which president of the United Faculty teacher's union Philip Won says is totally inadequate.

headline: Manufacturer hopes to expand plant
abstract: North Annville Township supervisors asked that Barrey Borrell, despite the award of a permit from the Lebanon County Planning Department for the expansion of his printing plant, refrain from proceeding until the township solicitor reviews the proposal. Supervisors were not sure the expansion was in accord with the residential zoning. A sewerage module submitted for subdivision of a farm was also passed along to the solicitor. Police Chief Randall Gingrich reported 49 incidents in the past month.

headline: House Safe SEPTA?
abstract: An equipment malfunction is alleged to have caused a subway crash which provides an impetus for the $4 billion upgrade of SEPTA.

headline: Drug searches
abstract: PA State Police are instituting a traffic checkpoint on Route 81 for drugs, saying interstate highways are often used for illegal drug transport. Police would not reveal whether or not the first of the checkpoints resulted in any finds.

headline: Bush cuts go beyond HHS fat
abstract: In the desperate rush to find places to out funds in the federal budget the worst thing the Bush administration could do is undermine the ability of government agencies to carry out essential programs in an efficient and competent manner. But it may be happening. Funding may damage Social security, Medicare and other federal health programs. Or it may damage Low income home energy assistance programs. The editorial board believes the government should not ignore serious problems that only it can do things about.

headline: NYC City Cutting $338 Million, Eliminating Jobs to Close Budget Gap
abstract: New York City Mayor David N. Dinkins announced $338 million in cutbacks, including a reduction of 5,500 city jobs through layoffs and attrition due to falling tax revenues. He is expected to announce another proposal to close the growing $1.6 billion budget gap. Communications Workers of America demonstrated against the announcement. A plan to save Philadelphia from fiscal crisis is expected to be announced.

headline: House panel limits troop cut
abstract: The US House Appropriations Committee is breaking ranks with the overall House over the reduction of US troop levels abroad, proposing a troop cut of 77,000, rather than the 129,500 approved by the House.  The Appropriations Committee's would also halt production of B-2 stealth bombers and about halve President Bush's $4.7 billion for the Strategic Defense Initiative.

headline: Dennis announces resignation, cites area ties
abstract: Edward S.G. Dennis Jr. resigned as Assistant US Attorney General to work at the law firm of Morgan, Lewis in Philadelphia. Dennis denied that he was resigning in protest of the management style of US Attorney General and former PA Governor Dick Thornburgh. Dennis supervised the inquiry into a leak of the investigation of US Rep. William Gray III of PA, and Thornburgh's plan to merge 14 organized crime strike forces under the US Attorney General's jurisdiction. President Bush will nominate Robert S. Mueller III in Dennis' place.

headline: Lawmakers float pay raise idea but say it won't sail
abstract: Some PA state lawmakers say that their colleagues have been quietly talking about raising their salary, but that the discussions will not amount to anything.  PA lawmakers are paid $47,000 a year, which makes them the second-highest-paid General Assembly in the nation, second only to New York.

headline: State should adopt merit selection for judges
abstract: Urging the Senate Judiciary committee to endorse a plan that would appoint PA judges based on merit. It had previously endorsed such a plan, but then abandoned it in favor of regional elections.

headline: Hafer Meeting
abstract: Top Pennsylvania Republicans met today with Barbara Hafer--their choice for the part'y gubernatorial candidate.  Party officials refused to criticize Hafer for her remarks about Governor Casey being a rednecked Irishman and stated that Hafer's campaign will focus on the issues.  State Auditor General Hafer says she wants to focus on Governor Casey's handling of dedicated funding for SEPTA.

headline: State tax collections below official estimate
abstract: Revenue Secretary David L. Donahoe said General Fund collections for October totaled $838 million, which was 2.5 percent below the official estimate. Fiscal year-to-date collections are $3.4 billion, which is 2 percent below estimate. The article goes on to list other tax income revenues.

headline: Reaching a boiling point
abstract: District Director for PA Senator Edwin Holl, Ken Fody, describes his visit with constituent Linda Brackin as unique. Brackin, frustrated with a series of events in which the state misplaced paperwork and delayed making payments on hospital bills, came to the office threatening to shoot someone if the office did not find a way to get a brace for her son approved by the PA Catastrophic Loss Benefits Continuation Fund. Fody was able to get confirmation from the CAT Fund that the brace was approved.

headline: Program helps pregnant teens stay in school
abstract: A program at Williamsport High School allows girls to stay in school while learning to be mothers. The teens can enroll in an elective course that will help them deal with their pregnancies and teach them how to properly care for a baby. Students who receive this kind of class are more likely to stay in school. Fathers are usually met with separately.

headline: Maryland man charged as poacher
abstract: Charges filed with District Justice Robert Philson by the PA State Game Commission include possessing a loaded gun in a vehicle, using a vehicle to hunt, hunting without a license or in off season, and running a live poaching operation across state boundaries. Charles Garlitz faces up to $4,544 in fines and will also be charged by the US Wildlife Service. PA wildlife conservation officer John Smith says the investigation uncovered a major poaching operation.

headline: Inspectors to check cards before cars
abstract: PA drivers have to turned their insurance card over with their owner's card and car keys at the service station. Mechanics won't do any work with out it.

headline: Drug stand is reversed
abstract: St. Joseph Hospital has reconsidered its decision to pull out of the business of treating Berks County Prison inmates for drug and alcohol problems, but now has to submit a proposal along with several other treatment agencies that have offered their services after St. Joseph pulled out last month.

headline: Cabinet Profile - Pubic Welfare
abstract: Brief career history of John F. White, pictured right. Boasting a long career in health and human services, White was in the Philadelphia Urban League, became a state representative, then Philadelphia City Council chairman.  He was appointed secretary of the Public Welfare Department in January 1987.

headline: Officials aim for zoning balance with ordinance up for adoption
abstract: There is a new proposed zoning ordinance for Springettsbury Twp., which has not had its zoning ordinances comprehensively reformed since 1980.  The new ordinance proposal contains 10 zones rather than the previous 8, and one of the intents of the new plan was to "save some of the township from being developed," according to township planner Mary Beckman.

headline: In Memory
abstract: A photo catches two Department of PA Veterans of Foreign Wars employees laying flowers at the 71st Annual PA Veterans of Foreign Wars convention.

headline: Depot credit unions ease layoff blow
abstract: Federal credit unions say that they will work with the 1070 employees who have received layoff notices to help soften the financial blows dealt by the process.

headline: Lawmakers gobble up PAC money: "Dishonesty" not allowed
abstract: In a speech on the budget summit, US Representative Robert Toricelli made a partisan attack on President Bush, stating that he was "intellectually dishonest in the last election." Representative John Murtha, Toricelli's fellow Democrat who was presiding over the debate, was forced to rule on comments made by his fellow party member.

headline: State Suffers Net Loss in U.S. Funds, Study Says
abstract: U.S. Census Bureau study indicates that Pennsylvania pays a larger share of federal taxes than it receives in federal funding.

headline: Casey supports funding to save student loans
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Robert P. Casey says he will support spending 10 million dollars in the next fiscal year to help the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency keep its non-subsidized guaranteed student loan program intact.  Without the funding, the loan program could collapse in July.

headline: State tightening belt, but expects no tax hike
abstract: Republicans, including PA Senate Appropriations committee chairman Richard Tilghman, are accusing PA Governor Casey of deliberately misleading the public during his re-election campaign in regards to the state's budget deficit. State Auditor General Barbara Hafer said Casey overstated revenues and understated expenses. However Budget Secretary Michael Hershock said he does not believe a tax increase is likely.

headline: Relief on way for nursing homes
abstract: The PA Welfare Department says it may have some relief for PA nursing homes facing cash crunches because of delayed state aid. The state department is about a month behind its payments and owes nursing homes nearly $52.6 million for caring for low-income people. Nursing homes will be unable to meet payrolls and pay mortgages if the state doesn't pay up soon. Lower than expected tax collections have worsen the problem.

headline: Program helps pregnant teens stay in school
abstract: Wiliiamsport Highschool teacher Janelle Boerckel recently was presented with a family service award by the Family and Chidlren's Services of Lycoming County, a private non-profit counseling serivice supported by United Way. Dr. Gary W. Ledebur, director of community and student services in the PA Education Department said high school programs which provide expectant mothers lessons in pre and post-natal care in addition to financial planning and other resources, are on the rise in the state.

headline: Mayor calls on DER to inspect foul odor
abstract: There is a gut-wrenching smell allegedly coming from the Scranton Sewer Authority Plant in Minooka, which now being investigated by the PA Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Insurance-discount law has a catch for elderly
abstract: A new auto law allows senior citizens to take a driving course to reduce his auto-insurance. They are having trouble finding places where the course is offered. The state only helps set the standards for the courses, but does not provide them. PennDOT is trying to approve as many new ones as it can to help reduce the demand.

headline: Drug task force raids Hampden Twp. party
abstract: Members of the Tri-County Drug Task Force raided a party in Hampden Twp. this weekend as part of a three-month drug dealing investigation, and found a half-ounce of cocaine, a variety of drug paraphernalia, $1000 in cash, several thousand dollars in negotiable bonds, and a small amount of marijuana. Officials said that arrests will hinge on lab results for the drugs.

headline: Casey cuts in social programs will mean cuts in area services
abstract: Clinton County Commissioners said that the PA Department of Public Welfare's resolution to cut back on expenditures will require county governments and their taxpayers to increase payments. PA Governor Robert P. Casey's deficit budget will require cuts to Clinton County's human services, including the Welfare Department.

headline: Ohio cities dominate economy index; Northeast continues to decline
abstract: According to a survey by Alphametrics Corp., which measured real personal income and employment, cities in New England and the Mid-Atlantic region continued their economic decline, while several areas of Ohio showed a rebound.

headline: Memorial team sues over revision
abstract: The PA architects who won a design competition for a Korean War Veterans Memorial filed suit to prevent construction of what they consider to be a replacement plan. They are asking for $500,00 in damages for breach of contract. They believe they are being deprived of worldwide renown and professional advancement.

headline: Depot workers' long days remain
abstract: Workers at the Defense Depot Mechanicsburg have been working 12-hour shifts and 7-day weeks since the beginning of Operation Desert Shield in Saudi Arabia.  The DDM ensures American military personnel have everything they need, from aspirin to boots and sunglasses.

headline: Lawmakers gobble up PAC money: Heroes 1, Zeroes 0
abstract: The Consumer Federation from America rated members of the US Congress on their voting records on consumer issues. The only PA lawmaker on either of the CFA's "heroes" and "zeroes" lists was US Representative Tom Foglietta, who was rated a "hero."

headline: State teachers earn an average of $33,338
abstract: An overview of the results of a study by the PA Education Department.  The results include data about salaries, gender discrepancies, an years of service.

headline: Tax-exempt fight widens
abstract: The Hospital Council of Western Pennsylvania has filed suit in federal court to stop local governments from bullying hospitals into making payments in lieu of taxes.  The suit was filed against Allegheny County and the cities of Pittsburgh, Erie and Johnstown.

headline: Tax Flap
abstract: PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer said that PA's deficit has reached nearly $237 million, and wants Governor Robert Casey to announce it to investors when trying to sell $475 million worth of tax anticipation notes to get the state some spending money.  Casey, a Democrat running against the Republican Hafer in the upcoming gubernatorial election, said that it's too early to say whether there is a deficit. Hafer won't allow the state to sell the tax notes until the Casey administration promises that the money will not be used to help bail out Philadelphia, which is nearly out of money.

headline: Report: health care can hurt
abstract: A study conducted by the US House Select Committee on Aging found that rising health care costs are consuming increasing amounts of America's elderly's income. The report found that retirees will see their health care costs rise 1.5 times faster than their income.

headline: Progress Made, But Suit Goes On
abstract: Penn State University administrators say they could be, and will be, doing more to attract and retain minorities. Chairman of the President's Council on Undergraduate Recruitment and Retention Jerry Covert suggests that black students use the Penn State Commonwealth campuses as a springboard to Pitt and Temple Universities, leading to low retention rates. Penn State is charged in a discrimination suit saying the university hasn't complied with a Human Relations Commission ruling against it.

headline: Mayor wants landfill action
abstract: Scranton Mayor Jim Connors is pressing the PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) to take action about problems between the Keystone landfill, the city, and the Scranton Sewer Authority (SSA).  The city continues to take its garbage to Waste Management Inc. which costs taxpayers about $1 million more per year over the Keystone tipping fees.

headline: Is it safe up there?
abstract: The editorial notes that the South Eastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority transit system has been especially crime-free recently, but worries that the criminals that had been operating in the subways have now moved to the streets.

headline: Drug War gets funds
abstract: a PennFree grant of $1.49 million has been awarded to the Alllentown and Bethlehem areas. The money will be spent to fight the war on drugs.

headline: Cash crunch delays state payments to nursing homes
abstract: The PA Welfare Department said that since PA is short on cash, 620 nursing homes will have to wait for their monthly checks from the state. The state is already 2 weeks late in issuing about $60 million to nursing homes, and Welfare Department spokeswoman Vicki Smink said that "we hope to issues the checks in about 2 weeks." Nancy Rorem, deputy director of the PA State Association of County Commissioners, said that state payments have been slow in many other areas, not just nursing homes. PA Governor Robert Casey's budget secretary Michael Hershock had no comment on the funding problem.

headline: Outreach worker gets council support
abstract: Outreach worker Clair Sexton has been approved for continued funding from York City and County for his one-the-street substance abuse and AIDS counseling program.  York City nearly used the funding to hire a bilingual AIDS counselor, but decided to continue funding Sexton instead.

headline: Military Cleanup
abstract: After a year of legal fighting, Commonwealth Court Judge David W. Craig gave the Navy Ships Parts Control Center in Hampden Township a timetable for action to remove a polychlorinated biphenyls contamination.

headline: Depressing duo: Trump and Phila.
abstract: The piece notes the similarities between Philadelphia's and Donald Trump's financial situations, in that they're both in debt and running out of cash, and that Mayor Goode and Trump will likely see no real personal loss, while employees and citizens suffer.

headline: Lawmakers gobble up PAC money: PAC men
abstract: According to Common Cause, US Representative Peter Kostmayer was the leading PA lawmaker in contributions from special-interest political action committees (PACs). Other top recipients of PAC funds in the US House were Majority Whip William Grey, Paul Kanjorski and Doug Walgren.

headline: State to pay one big bill this week
abstract: A spokesman for PA Governor Robert Casey said that more than $200 million in delayed payments to fund county service is being sent out this week, but that delays in the borrowing of nearly half a billion dollars in tax anticipation notes could delay the next round of payments. Casey's Republican gubernatorial challenger and Auditor General, Barbara Hafer, is blocking the sale of the TANs, charging that Casey plans to use some of the money to bail out the financially floundering Philadelphia.

headline: School tax hike is asked
abstract: Because of salary increases, last year's tax-rate limits, and state-mandated asbestos removal, the York Suburban School Board is proposing a tax increase.  If the increase is adopted, the average taxpayer could expect to pay roughly 190 dollars more in taxes during the 1990-91 school year.

headline: Tax Measure Approved
abstract: The PA State Senate Republican majority approved legislation intended to give a tax break to homeowners and businesses in the state. The Democrats say that the bill, which passed 26-22, could lead to higher taxes.

headline: Report: HealthPass cost is far more than expected
abstract: A report prepared by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services found that the costs of the insurance program HealthPass have been greatly underestimated and a retroactive rate increase of 9.2 percent appears likely. HealthPass, funded by state and federal governments and administrated by Healthcare Management Alternatives, provides medical care to low-income residents of Philadelphia. The report also shows that physician compliance and medical care standards are below acceptable levels.

headline: Proposals to Cut School Taxes Drastically Are on Ballots in Several States
abstract: Gubernatorial races across the nation have major initiatives on the ballot to cut school taxes. Education experts argue this will have negative consequences on the national movement to improve education. The article examines in detail proposals in Nebraska, Arkansas, Massachusetts and Oregon.

headline: Monroe Studies Recycling, Out-of-County Garbage
abstract: To operate at full capacity, a Monroe County incinerator would have to intake out-of-county garbage in the winter.  There is concern that a strong recycling program would not remove too much flammable trash from the incinerator to make a waste-to-energy facility impractical.

headline: Killer Highway
abstract: Many local officials and legislators want efforts to be taken quickly to have the Conchester Highway widened so as to prevent further accidents and fatalities.

headline: Drunk Driving Checkpoint
abstract: Police conducting a sobriety check point to a Klu Klux Klan member saying the member thinks the police are infringing on his civil liberties.

headline: Connellsville care home appeals to remain open
abstract: PA state Welfare Secretary John White is deciding whether to overturn a decision by subordinates that might force the Hillcrest Personal Care Home in Connellsville  out of business for violations reported. The home's owner, Dr. Godofredo Perez, appealed to the Office of Hearing and Appeals to reverse the closure.

headline: PA Farmaid
abstract: Nineteen PA counties have contributed $2.4 million to support farmland preservation efforts in 1990. The state Land Preservation Board has allocated $25 million.

headline: Navy depot plans to cut 51 temporary jobs
abstract: The Navy Ships Parts Control Center in Hampden Twp. will lay off 51 temporary employees as a result of an expected decrease in funding.

headline: Despressing duo: Trump and Phila.
abstract: The piece notes the similarities between Philadelphia's and Donald Trump's financial situations, in that they're both in debt and running out of cash, and that Mayor Goode and Trump will likely see no real personal loss, while employees and citizens suffer.

headline: Lawmakers gobble up PAC money: Ripon wrangle
abstract: US Representative William Clinger, a prominent Republican centrist, exerted his influence over the Ripn Society, a group of moderate and liberal Republicans. Clinger backed Washington attorney Don Bliss, who won an internal election to become president of the organization.

headline: State treasurer reiterates: No to Phila. Bonds
abstract: PA Treasurer Catherine Knoll writes a letter to the editor defending her position on wiring money to Philadelphia. She will not purchase City of Philadelphia notes. She will expedite payments to all municipalities.

headline: Educators Leading '90 Event
abstract: All of the area's environmental groups are planning educational campaigns for the 20th anniversary of Earth Day on Sunday.  The coalition behind these campaigns has come under criticism because it is accepting corporate donations without judging the firms' environmental values, however.

headline: Tax reform rears its head in Harrisburg
abstract: There is a debate on PA local tax reform which is up for vote in the PA Senate. Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer has written a new tax plan which PA Governor Robert P. Casey supports; the author though points out that these are changed stances from the previous year and this is part of the election season in PA. Jubelirer's plan tries to reduce local government reliance on property taxes by allowing local voters to approve increases in wage taxes.

headline: Researcher: Niacin Most Cost-Effective Drug to Lower Cholesterol
abstract: A team of researchers from the University of Pennsylvania found Niacin, the least-commonly used drug in cholesterol reduction, to be the most cost effective for moderate reduction. Niacin is one of six drugs recommended by the National Cholesterol Lowering Program. Lovastatin, was proven to provide the most significant reduction, however it is significantly more expensive.

headline: Proposed arts center escapes ax
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey included a proposal on behalf of the Pocono Arts & Convention Center in the 1991 capital budget, calling for an $11 million arts and convention center.  Bond money, as opposed to general fund budget monies, must be used in order to build the center.  The proposed center is meant to raise revenue for the Poconos.  A final decision has not yet been reached regarding the future of the convention center.

headline: Montco plans to develop an 'environmental agenda'
abstract: The Montgomery County Commissioners ordered the county Planning Commission to develop an 'environmental agenda' for the 1990s. The commissioners voiced concern over increasing development and the environmental impact.

headline: It's still the worst...Our readers say Five Points is the intersection they love to hate
abstract: Readers wrote in with their opinions and voted that the Five Points intersection in Montgomeryville, PA is the worst in the region due to its frequent overcrowding. There was no consensus on the worst stretch of highway.

headline: Editor says he was set up
abstract: Theodore Beitchman, former editor of Sports Illustrated, Rolling Stone, and the Johnstown Tribune-Democrat newspaper, said criminal charges that he impersonated PA Deputy Attorney General William Finnegan resulted from a "set up." Beitchman allegedly threatened a Bucks County resident who his brother owed money by claiming to be Finnegan on the phone.  Beitchman plans to prove his innocence at a hearing in Bucks County next week.

headline: Continued funding for poor urged
abstract: In response to a directive by PA Governor Robert Casey to cut operating and additional costs of the PA Department of Public Welfare, a coaltion of activists, including the PA Council of Churches, the Lutheran Coalition of Public Policy, and the PA Jewish Coalition recommended the budget for programs remain consistent and that taxes be raised to meeting decling revenue.

headline: Pa. breaks economic slump
abstract: A US Commerce Department Bureau of Economic Analysis study reveals PA is overcoming its post industrial slump after 2 decades. State per capita income in PA surpasses national trends. Keith Laughlin, staff director for the Midwest Northeast Institute warns against being overly jubilant. Per capita income is misleading since the overall change is in population. Nonetheless, analysts predict huge job growth and economic gains for the state in the coming years.

headline: Navy wavers in backing Phila. yard project
abstract: The US Navy showed signs of wavering in its commitment to the Philadelphia Navy Shipyard's most important program, aircraft carrier overhauls. The US Senate Appropriations Committee withdrew, then restored $113 million for the Philadelphia yard's overhaul of the USS Kennedy, scheduled for 1993.  The decision on whether to continue with the planned overhaul will now rest with Defense Secretary Dick Cheney.

headline: Deterrent for future thieves
abstract: Each day peels off a new layer of the savings and loan scandal, bringing federal investigators closer to the core but not closer to a solution to this most expensive taxpayer-funded boondoggle in US history. Congress is being too reactive. They are trying to tighten enforcement by assigning more federal more federal agents to S&L oversight.

headline: Lawmakers hit limits to terms
abstract: Only a few PA lawmakers support a national movement that to pry secure politicians out of their jobs. A group called Americans to Limit Congressional Terms is trying to limit the number of terms for members of the PA Senate and House of Representatives. The aim is to get better politicians who are doing to the job well and not just for the money.

headline: State troops do well in desert
abstract: PA General Services Secretary David L. Jannetta, back from a tour of duty in the Persian Gulf, said PA troops are performing well in the Operation Desert Shield mission despite harsh weather conditions. In honor of Veteran's Day, Jannetta, is sitting in for PA Governor Robert P. Casey to deliver the governor's Saturday radio address. Jannetta says that heat, crude living conditions, bad food, culture shock and fear of chemical warfare are making life in the gulf challenging.

headline: In '70, It Wasn't Hippie Guru's Eco Trip
abstract: Although Ira Einhorn played a role in Earth Day 1970, it was a minor one.  Einhorn, who is now wanted by police for questioning in the slaying of Holly Maddux, was, in 1970, the leading voice of the Philadelphia counterculture movement.  Although he did not take part in the planning of Earth Day 1970, he was allowed to be master of ceremonies for a portion of the rally in exchange for his cooperation in getting the counterculture people to join the rally.

headline: Tax would harm charities
abstract: Senior Vice President of Marketing and Corporate Relations for the Capital Health System, which includes the Harrisburg Institute of Psychiatry, Ernest McDowell hopes the Derry Township School Board will rethink its amusement tax proposal for the Lady Keystone Open. As is, only 17 of the proceeds go to charities, including the Keystone Sports Foundation. An additional amusement tax would decrease the amount of money available for distribution to the Health System.

headline: Rite Aid; Chairman Grass predicts firm's vindication
abstract: At a stockholders meeting for Rite Aid, the nation's largest pharmacy-drug store chain, discussion of the ongoing bribery trial of company president Martin Grass, son of Chairman and CEO Alex Grass, was brief. Allegations made during the trial in Ohio include bribery of a state pharmacy board member, Melvin Wilczynski. Alex Grass said the company, based in PA, would be vindicated and that the trial would have no effect on its ability to fill third party prescriptions, including Medicare.

headline: Protesters want more funds for state school districts
abstract: An estimated 2,000 rallied at the PA state Capitol to push more funding for local schools. Groups said the state should pay an equal proportion of the costs of basic education to keep property taxes low. Right now the state only pays 40%.

headline: Montgomery County and waste authority target of suit by FBI
abstract: Browning-Ferris Industries, one of the county's major trash haulers, filed a federal anti-trust lawsuit against Montgomery County and the Waste System Authority. The suit seeks a court injunction to prevent the implementation of the county's municipal waste management plan. The plan would require all waste from the 24 municipalities in the eastern end of the county to be disposed of exclusively in the Pottstown Landfill. The Pottstown Landfill is managed by the Waste Management Inc. who would charge BFI $47 per ton and the authority would charge an additional $6 ton surcharge. The suit claims violations to BFI's civil rights and federal anti-trust laws.

headline: Jogging around; Welcome, Governor
abstract: In a quick tour of western PA, Governor Casey attended three ceremonies which promise positive economic development for the state, including a trucking company which will employ over 500 people, construction of an extension to Beaver Valley Expressway, and the addition of a learning center to the Penn State-Beaver Campus.

headline: Execution Blocked By Beaver County Court
abstract: The execution of Charles Cross was blocked by a common pleas court, and Cross' attorneys have three months to file a relief petition.  Only one death warrant remains active of the 9 signed by PA Governor Casey this summer, and the execution is scheduled for November 13.

headline: Day Care Operators Complain Of New State System
abstract: Some Philadelphia day care operators are speaking out against changes adopted by the Welfare Dept., which spread the state's day-care subsidies to twice as many agencies, leaving some centers that depended on subsidies strapped for cash.

headline: Panel hears plea for restrictions on Church Farm site development
abstract: A citizens group spoke out against a planned development to the House Select Committee on Land Use, saying that the state's open, green space needs to be perserved.

headline: Niagara commissioned
abstract: PA Governor Casey attended the commissioning of the U.S. Brig Niagara, from which Commodore Oliver Perry commanded sailors in the Battle of Lake Erie in the War of 1812.  The ship is part of an effort to redevelop Erie's waterfront.

headline: Did Hafer sink the local Republicans?
abstract: John Thompson, chairman for the Republican Committee of York County, attributed the GOP's losses in the 28th state Senate District to Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer's 2-1 loss to PA Governor Robert P. Casey. The GOP maintained its majority in the PA Senate, safeguarding its say in next year's congressional redistricting. Thompson said he was uncertain if Senate candidate Donald Dorr's loss to Democrat Michael Bortner would have any effect on elections for York County offices, including the election of county commissioners.

headline: Lawmakers Study Possible Federal Role In Philly Fiscal Crisis
abstract: US Senator John Heinz and Representative Lawrence Coughlin are working to get federal help for Philadelphia's financial woes, though the government will not be able to make a direct appropriation.

headline: State's cash flow problems spread
abstract: Pennsylvania is late with its payments to hospitals, pharmacists, and nursing homes due to cash flow problems. PA Governor Robert Casey's administration is placing some of the blame on Auditor General (and Casey's Republican challenger in the upcoming gubernatorial election) Barbara Hafer for refusing to sign tax anticipation notes, which would allow the state to borrow $475 million in order to continue payments. Hafer places the blame on Casey's "mismanagement" of the state.

headline: AIDS' reach is statewide doctors say
abstract: Doctors in Pennsylvania say that AIDS is a statewide problem--not one that is confined to inner-cities or homosexuals.  They also argue that education about its transmission is still the best way to fight its spread.

headline: Taxpayers can choose up sides on state budget
abstract: An article discusses the state's budget approval process, which resulted in PA Governor Casey approving a budget submitted 12 hours post-deadline. Republicans are claiming a tax increase will be necessary as the budget was so trim, however many agree Casey will wait until after elections to initiate an increase. If precedent is followed, the same rush to pass legislation before the budget is approved will take place next year during the same.

headline: RPH applauded for scoring high
abstract: The Robert Packer Hospital was rated number one of 12 regional hospitals with over 100 beds, with cost of care, results of treatment, and average length of stay taken into account in the rankings.  The ratings came from a report by the Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council.

headline: PSEA also targets equity
abstract: The president of Pennsylvania State Education Association writes to praise the Patriot's editorial which supported raising the minimum salary for teachers.

headline: Mountains of Trash
abstract: In Lackawanna County there are two landfills less than 10 miles away from each other. The staggering amounts of trash and the long-term effects of burying such trash permanently make a commanding environmental concern. Some claim the landfills are safe, but environmentalists say there is no such thing as a safe landfill. They are worried about toxic chemicals getting into the landfills.

headline: Judge Orders Resort To Stop Charging on Toll Road
abstract: The PA Commonwealth Court has ruled that a Pocono resort, Vacation Charters Ltd., must stop charging tolls to drivers who travel a 2.2 mile stretch of its road.  Vacation Charters Ltd. must file for a permit room the PA Public Utilities Commission to continue collecting tolls.

headline: Expensive tailoring
abstract: A few years ago, Philadelphia Mayor Goode accepted 24 suits at large discounts, drawing a legal investigation by the Ethics Commission.  The legal bills for his defense, paid by the city, amount to about $60,000 for two private attorneys, while it would have been more cost-effective to use staff attorneys already being paid.

headline: Disabled and caretakers rally for more money
abstract: Carol Marfisi, who has cerebral palsy, and her attendant Delores McCloud joined Carl F. Odhner, president of the PA Coalition of Citizens with Disabilities, to encourage PA Governor Robert Casey and state lawmakers to earmark $15.5 million for attendant care in the new state budget. The coalition stated that increasing the combined federal-state allocation would eliminate a 500-person waiting list for attendants. According to Odhner, attendant care is cheaper than placing a disabled person in a nursing home.

headline: Payment policy: City of Philadelphia, Department of Finance
abstract: The article is Philadelphia's temporary payment policy, including prioritization of payments and the process of payment. The policy has been instituted because of the current financial situation of the city, which could run soon out of money.

headline: PA Financial News
abstract: Congressmen representing PA, Delaware and New Jersey aree requesting a meeting with Defense Secretary Richard Cheyney to discuss the fate of the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, which he has slated for closure.

headline: Dietterick: Wrong name on papers may be administrative
abstract: PA Representative Scott Dietterick testified that he's not guilty of forging another insurance agent's name on an insurance certificate during his years as an insurance agent, because even if he had signed another agent's name to the certificate, "it was a strictly administrative type of thing." Dietterick is accused of wrongdoing in relation to three insurance certificates he gave to school districts from 1984 to 1987.

headline: LCB jobs abolished, but not right away.
abstract: The PA General Assembly voted to abolish the Liquor Control Board hearing examiner positions, which are widely regarded as wasteful and unnecessary. The legislation, if signed by PA Governor Robert P. Casey, is not effective until July 1, 1992, when the LCB was scheduled to end anyway. The LCB recommended abolishing the position when it offered a business plan for cutting agency costs in 1988. Auditor General Barbara Hafer said the examiners work about three days a month and are paid $50,000 a year, plus benefits.

headline: State's revenues dip another $21.3 million
abstract: State revenues dipped to $68.2 million, or about 2 percent, below estimates of $858.9 million as of the end of October. Republican gubernatorial candidate Auditor General Barbara Hafer has focused on revenue shortfalls in her campaign against incumbent PA Governor Robert P. Casey and has said that a tax increase is inevitable. Casey spokesman Vince Carocci said the shortfall is a reflection of the national economy.

headline: Sony to manufacture tubes in ex-VW plant
abstract: Sony is planning to open a manufacturing plant in Southwestern Pennsylvania.  The manufacturing site will be located at an old Volkswagen factory and will be leased to the company for 21.1 million dollars over 20 years.  The state of Pennsylvania has been trying to lure companies to the site and is offering Sony a generous package of low-interest loans and training grants.

headline: The State/ Aid Cuts Expected
abstract: President Bush's proposed 1991 budget includes large funding cuts for PA programs.

headline: Sayre research labs dedicated
abstract: U.S. Congressman Joseph McDade helped to secure a $2 million appropriation from the Department of Defense for the construction of three new research laboratories in the Guthrie Research Institute. McDade, who was making a re-election campaign stop, said the institute was an "emerging force in cancer research."

headline: PSEA also targets equity
abstract: The president of PSEA writes to praise the Patriot's editorial which supported raising the minimum salary for teachers.

headline: Mountains of Trash
abstract: Lackawanna County disposes of trash in Empire Landfill and Keystone Landfill, both of which are being tested by the US Environmental Protection Agency and the PA Department of Environmental Resources to ensure they meet standards. The tests by both levels of government remain satisfactory thus far. Traces of numerous unsafe compounds were detected in the aquifer below Keystone, but the service provider for the area uses surface water, allowing the landfill's continued operation.

headline: Lawmaker calls for House vote on bill dedicating funds for transit
abstract: PA State Rep. Gordon Linton will call for a vote on an amendment to dedicate a funding source for mass transit, despite Rep. Stephen Friend's announcement that he and several Republican colleagues will refuse to vote for it unless PA Governor Casey authorizes Rainy Day Funds for special education. Friend has presented a lose-lose situation, said Linton. The amendment initiates a gas tax. The funding mechanism means the South Eastern PA Transit Authority would not be guaranteed 70 percent of available.

headline: Ex-Stable Operator Fined in Cruelty
abstract: District Justice Jules Melograne of Whitehall Township in Allegheny County, found Sophia Lake, operator of the Allegheny County-owned stables for the past 22 years, guilty of 11 of 20 counts of animal cruelty. Lake was fined $100 for each offense at Valley Brook Stables and an additional fee for court costs. Under the maximum sentence, Lake may also have received 90 days jail time for each count.

headline: Education Change Should Consider Children's Welfare
abstract: An editorial expressing concern that changes in the way handicapped children are identified and taught in the public school system are based mainly on cost when it should be based more on the children's welfare.

headline: People with AIDS can't find affordable housing
abstract: People with AIDS often have trouble finding affordable housing because of the costs and requirements of AIDS treatment.  Various groups and task forces are looking for ways to make affordable housing more accessible.

headline: Pa. reservists prepare to ship out to Gulf
abstract: Members of five PA Army Reserve units prepared for rotation to Saudia Arabia as part of Operation Desert Shield. They are among 19 Army Reserve units in the Northeast to be called up in the expansion of U.S. troop strength to the Persian Gulf.

headline: Disclosure of Ritter's campaign account sought
abstract: Congressional hopeful Richard Orloski is attempting to get US Representative Don Ritter to disclose the working of an undisclosed campaign account.  Ritter says Orloski is trying to make it into something it isn't.

headline: Leadership Vacuum. Smoke and Mirrors.
abstract: The Lackawanna County Court revealed it rejected the Scranton government's request to issue $4 million in bonds because city officials had engaged in deliberate deficit budgeting. The editorial board accuses Mayor Jim Connors of doing the same thing by banking on $3 million in revenue from the proposed refinancing of the Scranton Sewer Authority and hiring new full-time police officers despite the budget deficit. The board urges PA legislators to veto the mayor's budget plan and force him to engage in cost-reduction talks with employees.

headline: Sterner to Seek Seat in House
abstract: Harrisburg bureau chief for the News-Item, Al Sterner is planning to resign so he can run for the state House of Representatives.

headline: Democrats say Hafer code is aimed at one candidate
abstract: State Democratic lawmakers claim that Auditor General Barbara Hafer's new code of conduct barring her employees from seeking elected office is aimed at protecting a specific House incumbent.  House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese says he received information that Representative Jess Stairs requested the rule to block political competition.  A spokesperson for Hafer found the charge of DeWeese odd because Stair's challenger, civil servant Rodd Durbin, would not be affected by the rule; the rule is not retroactive.

headline: Toward making Phila. competitive
abstract: Dianne Reed of the PA Economy League writes in response to an article written by PA Budget Secretary Michael H. Hershock regarding studies about state aid to local government. The PEL analyzes data from the US Bureau of the Census, and does not analyze state spending that does not go through local governments. Reed asserts that less emphasis should be placed on increasing the tax burden in Philadelphia, so that the city can remain competitive with other Northeastern US cities.

headline: School district opposes burner
abstract: Montgomery School Board said yes to banning the burner, a hazardous waste treatment and disposal facility proposed by USPCI of PA. The board believes the facility would involve unknown and unnecessary health risk to the children of the district. Other board business is also discussed.

headline: Pupil test results rise statewide
abstract: PA Department of Education Testing for Essential Learning and Literacy Skills Exam (TELLS) scores are listed for several districts, many which show significant improvement over last year though a number also stayed the same. Harrisburg schools improved for the first time in five years just as Superintendent Donald M. Carroll Jr. has resigned to become PA Education Secretary. Former PA Education Secretary Thomas Gilhool used testing scores as a measure of a school's academic achievement. Department Spokesman John Clark notes the scores are impressive as the exam was made harder this year.

headline: Nations agree to ban ocean dumping
abstract: Delegates from 43 of the world's largest industrial nations adopted a ban on dumping industrial waste at sea.  Member nations are expected to prosecute flagships violating the ban and to develop and promote cleaner industrial processes, waste treatment and recycling. The United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union voted against the resolution, but indicated they would voluntarily comply.

headline: Maglev supporters reel in private funds
abstract: Western PA will have to pin its hopes for building a high-speed, magnetic levitation train system on funding sources other than the federal government. It still could attract private investors. A number of area corporations have joined the City of Pittsburgh and Allegheny County to build a 19 mile demonstration rail link between downtown Pittsburgh and the Pittsburgh International Airport. The group hopes for a more extensive system that could serve communities within a 150-to-200 mile radius of Pittsburgh. The main barrier to this is funding, thus private funding is being sought heavily.

headline: Fallen firefighter remembered.
abstract: Firefighters from across the state joined yesterday in remembering Timothy Stine, who was killed while battling the fire at the Lebanon campus of Harrisburg Area Community College. He was the first firefighter killed in the line of duty in Lebanon in 40 years.

headline: Free rides home planned for drinkers in Beaver
abstract: In Beaver County there is going to be a year-round taxi service to get people home who have had too much to drink from the bars. This is a program patterned after one in York County and allows bartenders to judge who should have the free ride home, The Alert Cab Program.

headline: Philadelphia may end up borrowing 100-Million dollars less than it had hoped
abstract: Crucial negotiations with area banks continue as Philadelphia officials, led by Mayor Wilson Goode, attempt to secure loans in lieu of declining tax revenue. Goode estimates at the current loan projections that the city will only last until January 4th before going bankrupt. Merrill Lynch Capital Markets may not participate in the loan, meaning Philadelphia would end up with $100 million less than was originally hoped.

headline: Panel recommends spending $403 million on Osprey
abstract: The US House and Senate armed services panels have recommended that $403 million be spent on the production of the V-22 Osprey aircraft in 1991. The Osprey is an aircraft that can take off and land like a helicopter, but can reach the speeds of a plane. The Osprey is produced by Bell Textron Helicopters in Fort Worth, Texas and Boeing Helicopters in suburban Philadelphia. President Bush's administration has made efforts to remove the Osprey's funding from the national budget, but Congress has restored it twice.

headline: Don't limit lawmakers' terms -- vote
abstract: The editorial opposes the idea of term limits in state legislatures and in Congress, because although it does remove "lousy" legislators, it would also remove effective ones.
