Instead, it urges people to support campaign finance reform, and to vote, and become well-informed so they can vote intelligently.

headline: Leading pro-choice lawmaker says she will vote for Bob Casey
abstract: Leading pro-choice legislator PA Representative Karen Ritter endorsed pro-life PA Governor Robert P. Casey for re-election, saying he supports many of the same workers rights issues that she does. Despite opponent Republican Auditor General Barbara Hafer's pro-choice position, Ritter criticized her "incompetence" and exploitation of abortion to further her political career. Ritter said the key to passing future abortion rights legislation is to elect more pro-choice lawmakers and that Casey's position as governor will not have much of an effect.

headline: Stetler gets big win in state House race
abstract: In the 95th District, Democrat Stephen Stetler won over Republican Michael V. Z. Summers. Stetler accused Summers of not paying York's business and mercantile tax and not filing a return for more than six years and questioned his "skimpy" voting record. Stetler viewed crime, drugs and education as his priorities and was endorsed by the PA State Education Association PAC. Summers prioritized low taxes, cutting government waste and no state bailout of Philadelphia's fiscal crisis.

headline: Federal Judge Blocks Attempt to Have Bayh Questioned for Trash Suit
abstract: Two Pensylvania trash haulers are suing the state of Indiana over its new out-of-state trash law.  The law prohibits the importation of trash and the plantiffs claim that the law violates their constitutional rights of due process, free commerce and equal protection.  A subpoena for Indiana Governor Evan Bayh, an official named in the suit, was quashed by a U.S. District Court Judge on Tuesday.  The trial is set to begin on Tuesday, but attorneys for the state have asked for a delay until June 4th.

headline: Two Votes Show Tax Increases Face Wary Public
abstract: In light of a referendum by California voters which approved a gas tax for the PA transit system, some analysts predicted a more tolerant attitude toward taxes. Director of public finance for the Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations, commissioned by President Reagan and Congress, Robert Ebel disagrees. Marshall Taylor, for the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, says people have reached their tolerance limit. Last November, Pennsylvanians voted down a tax increase.

headline: Senate panel adds apprenticeship proposal to midwife bill
abstract: A key PA Senate committee has approved a bill that would allow lay midwives to operate legally in PA if they first assist 50 births and undergo a two-year apprenticeship. Currently only doctors and licensed nurses are allowed to deliver babies under state law, but members of the state's Amish and Mennonite religious sects have traditionally relied on midwives to assist home births. Amish don't permit young persons from going to school past 8th grade, so the Amish cannot become registered nurses. The apprenticeship program gets around this rule.

headline: Record tax hike on board agenda
abstract: Southeastern Superintendent Luther C. Natter placed most of the blame on a proposed school board tax hike on the state's failure to reimburse schools. Other plans in the budget include raising teachers' salaries, adding new staff positions, a construction project, higher transportation costs, and increased special education costs. The budget will increase property taxes by 3.5 mills per property, ranging in an increase from around $260 to $300 dollars depending on the school district.

headline: Neighbors to meet about landfill site
abstract: The York County Solid Waste Authority is planning a public meeting with Chanceford Township and Lower Windsor Township residents to discuss plans to locate landfills in the townships. Lower Windsor Township supervisors have opposed a landfill, saying its proximity to Rexroth recreation park would pollute small streams flowing into Fishing and Cabin creeks and that the road system to the site is inadequate for truck traffic.

headline: Magnetic Rail Consortium Eyeing Deal With West German Company
abstract: A public-private consortium developing magnetic rail transportation in Pittsburgh said it is nearing an agreement with the West German company Transrapid International of Munich to build a magnetic rail train running from downtown Pittsburgh to the Greater Pittsburgh International Airport.  The proposed agreement between Maglev and Transrapid could lead to exclusive manufacturing rights in North America.

headline: Fayette Camp Investigated by Court
abstract: The PA Department of Welfare is investigating the Pressley Ridge School amid accusations of physical abuse. Allegheny County Judge Eugene Strassburger III scheduled a hearing on the case. The child advocate's unit of the Legal Aid Society asked Strassburger to remove about 12 youths from the school, a move that was denied pending the results of the investigation.

headline: If I had a Hammer
abstract: Habitat for Humanity builds houses with people, not for them. It has been active since 1986 and works with people who need homes, but cannot afford them. They have to not only work on their own home, but also other houses Habitat is working on. Habitat doesn't receive any tax money for their work, instead using individual, corporate and church donations, private foundation grants and revenue from fundraising.

headline: Philly Finances-Brite, 250 Hay Bill Provides Horse Laugh at Budget Session
abstract: Philadelphia Finance Director Elizabeth C. Reveal and six aides worked through a list of 931 new bills totaling $12.5 million and tagged $7 million for payment. Priority went to spending for vital services, such as police, fire, foster care, prisons, food and hay. City officials hope to float a short-term note issue for about $300 million in the next few weeks, without which the city will run out of money within a month. The city projects a $229.5 million deficit for the fiscal year.

headline: Peace groups in city protest gulf military buildup
abstract: Protesters gathered on the steps of the Federal Building in Harrisburg to protest the US military buildup in the Persian Gulf, which some say could lead to a US-Iraq war.  The protesters want more diplomatic talks and for the United Nations to bring in a peacekeeping force.

headline: Don't look now, but contract time coming up
abstract: After the November election, the state will begin contract talks with unions of workers under the governor's jurisdiction.  The piece notes that the next budget will need something in it to pay for salary increases to the workers of those unions.

headline: Leagl bill 'staggers' county commissioner
abstract: Montgomery County commissioner Rita Banning, a Democrat, revealed the county paid over a million dollars this year to firms representing the county in legal matters. She claims the high numbers are a result of Republican county commissioner and chairman Paul Bartle trying to save face. Almost half the funds spent were in relation to a federal and county lawsuit filed which charged Bartle with political corruption. The suit was later settled for a mere $9,000.

headline: The focus is on Laurel Crest
abstract: Cambria County Commissioner Ron Stephenson yesterday lambasted The Tribune-Democrat for what he called a "one-sided" view of the operations at Laurel Crest Manor.

headline: Senator Specter backs tax credit for speedy rail service
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter says he will propose a 10 percent tax credit for the development of high-speed railways.  Such a credit will help spur private investment in projects like the 500 million dollar system proposed for Allegheny County--a system that will afford Pennsylvanians a 2 hour and eight minute ride from Pittsburgh to Philadelphia.

headline: U.S. 'sin taxes' may require more sinners
abstract: Congress recently passed a comprehensive tax package to help raise the billions needed to cut the national debt with the intent to target as many groups as possible in order to spread the burden around. "Sin taxes", those levied on tobacco and alcohol, will be increased. Liquor Control Board Chairman James Goodman said increased alcohol prices may accelerate the decline in consumption of alcohol.

headline: Senator Lauds AIDs Program Vying for Federal Grant
abstract: U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter promised to help bring federal money to a cooperative effort by two children's hospitals that treats families affected by AIDs.

headline: Reformer proposes 5-year training program for teachers
abstract: John Goodlad of the University of Washington proposed a plan requiring five years of college for public school teachers, who would then receive a bachelor of pedagogy degree, as a means of improving the quality of elementary and secondary education. Goodlad, who directs the Center for Educational Renewal, will attempt pilot programs at the University of Washington.

headline: Neville Island 'Poison Park' doesn't look like waste site
abstract: The planned Ohio River park on Neville Island is likely to be designated a federal toxic waste site after the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) listed it as a potential Superfund site last October.  The 32-acre site was donated by the Hillman Co. and the local subsidiary The Neville Land Co. maintains that the park poses no danger to local groundwater contamination.

headline: Maritime Administration says Litton site should be a shipyard
abstract: The maritime branch of the US Department Transportation has recommended that the former Litton complex be used as shipyard. The state had previously chosen the complex as the site of a berth and maritime museum for the newly restored US Brig Niagara. The maritime administration does not offer any financial support in the letter.

headline: Federal officials open bids for Union prison
abstract: Bids are in for the first stage of construction of a federal prison complex in Union County.  The complex will begin with a minimum-security prison, and will then add medium and maximum-security sections as well.

headline: Group seeks funding boost for state poor
abstract: Spokesmen of the PA Coalition for Human Services have called on the PA Governor and PA Legislature to increase funding for the poor and disadvantage. They were not criticizing the current charitable efforts, but believe it is more than charity that enables homeless to become more than statistics. They would like to get rid of workfare, because many affected are unemployable. They would like an income tax increase of .1% that could raise $!50 million for the needy.

headline: PIDA loans will create jobs
abstract: Loans from the Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority, in conjuction with private investment, will help create about 800 jobs in 13 PA counties.

headline: Perry's Flagship to Anchor Erie Waterfront
abstract: The US Niagara, which was Commodore Oliver Perry's flagship in the defeat of the British in the Battle of Lake Erie in the War of 1812, has been given a permanent berth along the Erie waterfront.  It is part of an effort to revitalize the waterfront.

headline: Don't tell me...it shows in your face- Some dame is breaking your heart
abstract: This political cartoon shows a bartender addressing an elephant symbolic of the Pennsylvania GOP upset over unpopular Republican gubernatorial candidate Auditor General Barbara Hafer.

headline: Legislative candidates debate tonight in Lebanon
abstract: Candidates for the PA House seats for districts 101 and 102 will meet in a debate co-sponsored by the Lebanon League of Women Voters and radio station WLBR. Republican incumbent Representative George Jackson and challenger Edward Krebs are competing for the 101st district, and Republican incumbent Nicholas Moehlmann will face off against Ed Arnold for the 102nd district.

headline: The PA gubernatorial debate
abstract: The cartoon depicts a man watching the debate between PA Governor Casey and challenger Barbara Hafer, saying "The big question is: will Casey bore me to death before Hafer self-destructs?"

headline: Recycling Day
abstract: President Bush does not deserve to be called the environmental president, and it's time for him to come clean.  The president continues to resist Democratic efforts to cut solid waste and improve recycling.  With the 200 billion dollars he has committed to the S&L bailout, he deserves to be called the savings and loan president.

headline: U.S. unemployment reaches 2-year high
abstract: The US's unemployment rate increased for the third straight month in September, and reached 5.7%, the highest level since the spring of 1988.  Some economists are predicting even higher rates in coming months.

headline: Senator Proposes Boosting Cigarette Tax
abstract: PA Senator Michael Dawida said he will propose an increase in the state's cigarette tax to help pay for anti-smoking programs in schools and communities when the PA Legislature opens next year. Dawida said he also planned to draft a bill to tighten the state's clean air law and to ban teachers from smoking in schools. Dawida's comments came during a news conference where anti-smoking advocates criticized the Phillip Morris Cos. Inc. for sponsoring a nationwide tour that highlights the Bill of Rights.

headline: Reibman, Grucela hit the books. Candidates air education views.
abstract: Easton Area High School teacher Richard Grucela is running against PA Senator Jeanette Reibman in the race for 18th District Senate seat. Grucela, endorsed by the Easton Area Education Association, favors merit pay for teachers and welfare payment cuts to parents whose children are absent from school. Reibman, supported by the Pennsylvania State Education Association, started the PA community college system and has served as chairman of the senate's education committee.

headline: New caster will reduce pollution of air and water, save energy
abstract: A continuous slab caster to be installed at the USX Corp.'s Edgar Thomson plant will be cleaner and will run with less energy.  Air and water pollution will be decreased as a result of the new equipment.

headline: Mexican Firm eyes 100 GE locomotives
abstract: Congressman Tom Ridge of Erie says he is confident that a Mexican leasing company will soon purchase 100 new locomotives from the General Electric Company's Transportation Division in Erie for around $160 million.

headline: Federal prison plans approved
abstract: The director of the US Bureau of Prisons has approved a federal prison project in Union County which will build minimum, medium, and maximum security prisons, all part of the same complex, starting this fall.  The minimum security prison will be built first and is expected to house 900 inmates.

headline: In Volunteerism, Few Answer the Call of an Uncertain Trumpet
abstract: An opinion expressing sadness at the decline of civic engagement and skepticism at the expectation of younger generation to volunteer and develop a sense of community spirit.

headline: Pine Grove Township preparing for sewer hookup
abstract: Township Supervisor John Brown announced to the borough council that Pine Grove will attempt to connect five surrounding areas to its sewer system at once after receiving a grant from Schuylkill Township and applying for a loan from the Farmers Home Association. The connecting areas would include Marstown, Ravine, Brookside, Pleasant Valley and Paradise. Brown suggested the board begin feasibility studies to decide how much to charge residents for use of the system. The council also addressed other matters.

headline: Reserves activated; danger pay OK'd
abstract: 62 Army reserve units and 3 Navy reserve units nationwide have been called for active duty, including 2 from Western PA.  Defense Secretary Dick Cheney has approved "imminent danger pay" for troops in the Persian Gulf.

headline: Door-to-door census to continue in city
abstract: Due to understaffing, the Harrisburg US Census Bureau office will continue door-to-door field visits for beyond the national deadline, said Sandra Domeny, Harrisburg District Manager. Especially in minority communities, return of forms is low, with an average of 86 percent across the city. Nevertheless, in these smaller communities, some numbers have not even reached 50 percent. The overall return rate is better than that of Philadelphia however, which has a response rate of 77 percent.

headline: Legislature has $94,000,000 Left Over
abstract: A legislative report indicates that the General Assembly ended the last fiscal year with a $94 million surplus.

headline: Stish blasts McMonigle on pro-life flier
abstract: After months of criticizing PA Governor Robert P. Casey's administration, Republican PA representative candidate Joseph McMonigle has been spreading a potentially illegal and unauthorized flier calling him a part of the pro-life "Casey/McMonigle team". Casey does not support McMonigle. Incumbent opponent PA Representative Tom Stish said the McMonigle violated campaign laws, which call for a disclaimer on election materials saying who paid for the advertising. McMonigle has criticized Stish for being endorsed by labor unions.

headline: Superfund making progress in PA
abstract: An official with the federal Department of Environmental Protection says that the superfund program is making porgress with the problem of hazardous chemicals in Pennsylvania.  The state has about 100 superfund sites and most of the projects are in active remediation.  Roughly 12 of the 100 sites have been cleaned up.

headline: We can get better
abstract: The editorial comments on the economic state of Warren County, PA, and the US. The unemployment rate in PA and the US has increased in recent months, but Warren County's is near a record low for August, unfortunately due to a decrease in the labor pool rather than an increase in jobs. It says that economic trends usually are slow to reach the county, but that the inevitable effects could be lessened by improving the school system, encouraging development, and improving infrastructure.

headline: Senior citizens applaud passage of MOM bill
abstract: Senior citizens with Medicare are now protected from certain charges by the Medicare Overcharge Measure (MOM), which prevents doctors from charging more than the approved Medicare rate for certain doctors fees.

headline: 'Remember the children', Marywood grads told
abstract: Marywood College's 590 graduating seniors and advanced degree recipients were told to have responsibility and advocacy throughout their careers at commencement ceremonies Sunday.  PA Governor Casey's wife, Ellen Harding Casey, spoke at the ceremony.

headline: New Leachate Plan Advances
abstract: Mayor Jim Connors proposed a modified agreement between Keystone Landfill and the city emphasizing an alternative resulting in treated leachate going through another treatment and getting dumped in the Lackawanna River.

headline: Midstate in Brief. Bids opened for upgrade of Routes 11-15.
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation opened bids for a project to widen a section of Routes 11-15 to four lanes. PennDOT spokesman Rich Scheon said that the apparent low bid by Eastern Industries Inc. is approximately $2 million higher than the estimate, but that is not expected to prevent the contract from being awarded. The two lowest bids were separated by less than $20,000.

headline: Feds Arrest Florida Man Connected to Plane Filled With Cocaine
abstract: Federal officials in Miami arrested a second man, Jack D. Malone, in connection with a stolen plane carrying $140 million worth of cocaine that made an emergency landing at the Allentown-Bethlehem-Easton Airport. Police have captured only one of the three men who fled the plane after it landed, Harold Hill, and are looking for three other suspects.

headline: Legal services group may lose federal aid
abstract: Neighborhood Legal Services Association which provides legal assistance to the poor, could loose federal money because it refuses to give a federal agency access to personnel files.

headline: Pittsburgh Delegation Pushes Ramp Funding With Casey
abstract: Stadium officials, supported by the Steelers and the Pirates teams, are optimistic about Governor Casey's acceptance of their proposal for state funding to build new pedestrian ramps at Three Rivers Stadium.

headline: Senate appropriations panel endorses defense bill
abstract: The US Senate Appropriations Committee has approved a $268 billion defense bill that leaves President Bush's 1991 budget request for the B-2 stealth bomber intact.  The bill has 2 provisions relevant to the Philadelphia area: $113 for a program at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, and research funds for the V-22 Osprey, an aircraft being developed by Boeing in Ridley Twp.

headline: Dorr gets low grade from group that lobbies on consumer issues
abstract: Citizen Action of Pennsylvania, a group that lobbies on consumer issues, gave a low score to Representative Donald W. Dorr based on votes he made on Medicare overcharges, mandated family and medical leave, the minimum wage and other legislation.

headline: Lepore's decision closes three-year political career
abstract: For reasons which may never be known, the five-member court of Fayette County asked for the resignation of District Attorney Alphonse P. Lepore Jr. in what is the first such request in the history of PA according to the PA District Attorneys Association. It was originally believed Lepore would fight the request however PA Senator J. William Lincoln read Lepore's resignation statement at a press conference. Lepore will continue to serve as coordinator of the Fayette County Central Task Force.

headline: Stopgap for cash crisis
abstract: Philadelphia is searching for ways to gain more revenue so that it can potentially avoid the predicted budget shortfall.  Mayor Goode and City Council are having difficulties drumming up enough investors, and may have to use money from the city's pension fund.

headline: Incinerator regulations put on back burner for month
abstract: A proposed amendment to Pennsylvania's statewide plan for commercial medical waste incinerators would give the state more latitude in denying permits.  Under the amended plan, the state Department of Environmental Resources would not issue a permit for an incinerator unless the owner could show that 70 percent of its waste would come from the 28 county Central Zone in which it would be built.  Until a final plan is approved, a statewide moratorium on commercial medical waste incinerators is in place.

headline: With little to stop Pa.'s 1991 budget, it just might be adopted on time
abstract: As budget negotiations continue between PA Governor Casey and the General Assembly, the PA Budget Secretary Michael Hershock revised earlier predictions that the state would finish its fiscal year in a deficit. Elected officials want to use Rainy Day Funds, decreasing the state's bond ratings. Casey refused. Most recently a block of Republicans banded together to defeat a bill to fund mass transit through a gas tax in order to force Casey's hand, criticizing his plan to use the PA Workman's Insurance Fund to meet operating expenses.

headline: Smokeout, 130.
abstract: PA Health Secretary Mark Richards and Miss PA, Marla Wynne, spoke at the state Capitol as a part of the American Cancer Society's Great American Smokeout, intended to call attention to the health hazards of smoking. Richards said that the yearly economic cost of smoking-related illnesses is $247 for every PA resident.

headline: Restoration of intermediate health classes urged
abstract: A teacher writes to the paper to emphasize the importance health-education classes in schools, which could be discontinued at Shawnee Intermediate School.  She writes that the classes are important in providing students with knowledge about health risks pertinent to their age group that they would not likely obtain otherwise.

headline: Nitrates harm water supply
abstract: Southern York County communities rarely exceed the 10 milligram-per-liter limit on nitrates in their water supply. But levels come close, says James Gillespie of the PA Department of Environmental Resources. Borough officials report findings to residents and offer free bottled water until the levels decline. Farming contributes, but has declined as a nitrate source said county agricultural extension director Anthony Dobrosky. Railroad Borough council President Jon Berdoll says they will apply for funding from the PA Infrastructure Investment Program. The community also received federal aid.

headline: Mifflin-Juniata-Snyder MADD chapter gets charter
abstract: In order to become an official chapter of Mothers Against Drunk Driving, a group must have twenty dues paying members, answer 20 questions concerning local statistics, DUI laws and MADD national, and elect officers. Recently, the Mifflin/Juniata/Snyder MADD group was founded. First Vice President Karen Goss maintains that the group is not out to prohibit alcohol, but merely to raise awareness and change laws to impose stricter penalties for those DUI.

headline: Felons in the Food Chain. How to Execute and Save Energy.
abstract: The editorial board addresses PA Governor Robert P. Casey's decision whether or not to sign a bill to use lethal injection instead of the electric chair in death penalty cases. The board says injections are more humane, but still have a few kinks to be worked out. The board suggests that criminals should be turned into mulch to be used as compost for vegetable gardens.

headline: Local facilities get by
abstract: Administrators of local nursing homes said they've been getting by since the PA Welfare Department began falling behind on its monthly Medicaid payments. The county has been able to meet all bills and payroll. 95% of Cedar Haven's residents are receiving some kind of assistance from Medicaid, which translates into $500,000 a month. The payments have been late for about six months now. They believe they will just have to wait it out.

headline: Plan scorned: Irked Tinicum doesn't want stadium, pro sports teams
abstract: Tinicum township Commission President Adam German wants the commissioners in Media, PA to discuss their plans for a new sports complex which is proposed for Tinicum.  German claims that most of his constituents don't want the stadium and feel that their concerns are being ignored. The proposed stadium would fit 23,000 people which is almost five times the number of people who live in Tinicum.

headline: Soldier sought in major bust of stolen arms
abstract: Former Army sergeant John Tubbs is wanted after authorities found a massive stockpile of stolen military weapons and explosives in a warehouse raid. Authorities said the cache may have been intended for use by members of the white supremacist group Aryan Nations. U.S. Representative Curt Weldon and U.S. Representative Tom Foglietta of Philadelphia called for a probe by the House Armed Services subcommittee after a Patriot-News investigation revealed that soldiers have been stealing military weapons and selling them on the black market.

headline: Fayette DA to step down
abstract: Fayette County District Attorney Alphonse Lepore did not attend a press conference held to announce his resignation from office. After the primary Lepore said he will resign to allow a successor to be appointed by the court.

headline: Let the people have a say
abstract: The editorial shows frustration at the political process in which the writer feels he has no control.  He believes that there should be ballot questions on abortion, the death penalty, pay raises for lawmakers and other issues, rather than having to factor in such issues when voting for candidates, and sometimes swinging a vote based on one issue.

headline: Stretton wins handily over Don Hadley
abstract: Samuel Stretton, Democrat, won the democratic nomination for the 5th Congressional District. The results were 5,889 to challenger Donald Hadley's 618.

headline: Towns hope plant eases pain
abstract: Residents in Mount Pleasant PA are excited to hear that Sony Corporation of America is planning to open a manufacturing plant in Westmoreland County.  Sony is going to convert an abandoned Volkswagen plant 3 miles from Mount Pleasant into a high-tech television tube factory.  This is a shot in the arm to an area whose economy was depressed by the closing of Volkswagen's factory.

headline: Worker count hits record
abstract: The PA Job Service announced record employment for Pittsburgh, at 948,000 during the month of June. The rate of unemployment fell in the state overall as well. Nationally, unemployment has risen in the past few months. Most of the increase in PA are in the areas of service industries, retail trades, construction and federal census workers. A marginally significant decrease in the number of those willing and able to work from May to June was also noted in the Job Service report.

headline: State charges two with Medicaid fraud
abstract: Two nursing home operators have been charged with Medicaid fraud, as they charged many private purchases to the nursing home account in order to receive more Medicaid reimbursement.

headline: Rhoades wants education panel
abstract: PA Senator James Rhoades (R) wants the legislature to set up a special commission to help overhaul the PA school curriculum to make it more performance oriented and more effective in today's world. Thomas Gentzel of the PA School Boards Association said the PA Education Board is already working on a study of curriculum requirements and reform.

headline: No Charges Expected In Medical Waste Probe
abstract: No charges or fines are expected as a result of the apparently accidental disposal of medical waste bags at the Lycoming County Landfill, according to Daniel T. Spadoni, a PA Department of Environmental Resources spokesman. The bags were discovered as a part of "Operation Trashnet", in which state officials check landfills to ensure state regulations are being met. The waste was traced to the Sunbury Municipal Authority Solid Waste Transfer Station, and then to a Sunbury-based regional laundry service.

headline: Montrealer Jumps Tracks Near Zoo
abstract: An Amtrak train derailed as it approached Philadelphia’s 30th Street Station, near the Philadelphia Zoo. The accident injured the engineer, but there were no immediate reports of injuries to passengers.

headline: Fire destroys HACC-Lebanon. Collapse of roof kills fireman, problem in furnace suspected.
abstract: A firefighter was killed and a city block evacuated when the campus of the Harrisburg Area Community College caught on fire. Lieutenant Mark S. Singel, at the scene with officials of the PA Emergency Management Agency, said state resources would be made available for assistance. The fire was attributed to a defective furnace in the 150-year-old building.

headline: Losing bidders protest over HealthPass pact
abstract: Two of the three unsuccessful bidders for a new five-year pact to run the HealthPass program for low income Philadelphia residents have filed formal protests asking state Public Welfare officials to reverse their decision. The protests have been filed by Birch and Davis Managed Care Corporation and by Maxicare Corporation. The two firms are seeking reversal of the June 21 decision by state Welfare Secretary John white Jr. to grant a new five year contract to Healthcare Management Alternatives, the firm that has been running HealthPass for the past year. The contract is expected to exceed $1 billion.

headline: Plants' suitor has solid track record
abstract: NS Group Inc has managed to survive the up and down economic cycles that have plagued the steel and energy industries and are negotiating to buy two closed Babcock and Wilcox steel mills. They have previously bought and revitalized steel mills.

headline: Spending bill gives $20M to area depot
abstract: The US House Appropriations Committee set aside $13.2 million for the transfer of operations in the Lexington-Bluegrass Army Depot to the Tobyhanna Army Depot. But, the Pentagon is revising downward initial job projections for the facility, and the legislation discourages a second round of base closings supported by Defense Secretary Dick Cheney which could bring jobs to the facility. Jobs won't be available for those laid off in light of the Army Material Command's budget shortfall.

headline: Fayette DA to step down
abstract: The Fayette County court's recent publication of its request that District Attorney Alphonse P. Lepore Jr. resign was not accompanied by an explanation for the request. Calling the situation a very difficult one, PA Senator J. William Lincoln stepped in to lend aid. Lincoln read Lepore's resignation statement during a press conference for which Lepore was absent. According to the statement, Lepore will resign but remain in office until after the primary when the court can appoint a new assistant DA.

headline: Lieutenant governor hopeful stumps in Mifflin County
abstract: Barbara Hafer's running mate, Harold Mowery, spoke in Lewistown about campaign tactics and other issues.

headline: Study shows Walker isn't PAC'ing it in
abstract: US Representative Robert S. Walker takes less campaign money from special interest groups than any other congressman from PA, except for William Gooding, who does not take campaign contributions political action committees. The findings were released in a report by Common Cause, which stated that Walker took $111,364 from political action committees from 1983-1988. The article includes a complete listing of Walker's campaign contributions

headline: Rural program takes root in legislature
abstract: A series of policy initiatives known as ROOTS, or Rural Opportunities Offer Tomorrow's success, is intended to address problem areas in rural education, economic development, health care, and access to state programs.  The legislative package, which has bipartisan support, will act as a rural renewal in the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: null
abstract: The federal Third Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that women's health clinics may sue anti-abortion protestors even if they have not been the target of demonstrations. The panel said that clinics in Chester, Allentown and Philadelphia could join a suit against abortion protestors because they were potential targets. The suit was filed by the clinics after a series of July 1988 demonstrations by Operation Rescue.

headline: State Medicaid Program Faces $20 Million Deficit
abstract: The chairman of the US Senate Finance and House Appropriations committees said that they will ask House Speaker R. Clayton Mitchell Jr. and Senate President Thomas V. Mike Miller to take another vote on the emergency regulations to eliminate payment for home health care services, personal services and reimbursement of the cost of transportation to health facilities for people under Medicaid.

headline: SAT scores level after 2 years on the decline
abstract: PA's Scholastic Aptitude Test scores leveled off in 1989 after two years of declines. Pennsylvanians averaged 886 on the verbal-math test. PA is 17 points below the national average of 903. PA is ranked 16th of the 22 states that use the test.

headline: No dumping near wells allowed
abstract: The editor is writing about the Towanda Municipal Authority’s wells being closed because of unauthorized dumping occurring is welcome but questions why the site was open from the beginning.  The writer believes precautions in the area should be taken, such as making sure the gates are closed securely and that no unauthorized persons can get in, in order to protect the community’s drinking water.

headline: More optimism for Route 202 buyers
abstract: The Route 202 bypass project has been included in the state's proposed budget in order to preserve a 1-mile0long corridor in Montgomery Township from development. The right of way is worth more than $1 million, but will make the town loses its easement. Public reaction is mixed.

headline: Firefighter perishes in HACC blaze
abstract: Volunteer firefighter Timothy Stine was killed in a fire that demolished the historic Lebanon campus building of the Harrisburg Area Community College. Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel arrived at the scene to view the damage of what was called "one of the most devastating fires in the history of Lebanon." The fire was attributed to a faulty oil-fired boiler in the basement of the building.

headline: Mentally ill children to get aid, White says
abstract: State Public Welfare Secretary John F. White proposes state funding for residential treatment of mentally ill children, so parents do not have to give up custody. White said he will ask for an unspecified amount of residential treatment of mentally ill children in his budget request for the year at the Department of Public Welfare (DPW). PA Governor Robert Casey is thought to support this request because right now these programs re only funded though county welfare agencies.

headline: Remaking Phil.: Hard choices are called for . . . But some see that as an opportunity
abstract: If Philadelphia is to recoup lost revenue, it may require workers to fill out wage forms identifiying $4.4 million in revenue for the city of Pittsburgh which otherwise would have been lost. Philadelphia also struggles to earn revenue because of its status as a county and city. The Chamber of Commerce's Pizzi warned problems in Philadelphia will spill into the surrounding suburbs. Executive director of the Community of Seventy Frederick Voight said an economic boom is needed to improve prospects.

headline: State Air National Guard sent
abstract: Member of the PA Air National Guard trained to refuel jets mid-air will be sent to Saudi Arabia to speed up the movement of US troops through the area.  Marines from the Willow Grove Naval Air Station will be stationed on the West Coast to replace Marines sent to the Middle East.

headline: Goode backs state supervision
abstract: Bowing reluctantly to demands from business leaders and state legislators, the Philadelphia Mayor Goode administration formally endorsed the creation of a state authority the would take some control over city spending in return for bailing Philadelphia out of its financial predicament. It does not address the city's immediate cash crisis and administration officials continued to negotiate with bankers. The city will not be able to meet its Jan 4 payroll.

headline: Lieutenant governor to speak at fall dinner
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel will be the keynote speaker at the Annual Democratic Fall Dinner on Saturday. PA Representative Jeffrey Coy of Shippensburg will also speak, and County Chairman A.D. "Zan" Beattie will be the master of ceremonies.

headline: Summers inspiring voter
abstract: The author of the letter, never before registered to vote, has been inspired to do so by Republican candidate for the 95th District, Mike Summers. The author appreciates Summers' individual attention to voters' concerns.

headline: Rolling on the river
abstract: State Representative Frank Gigliotti introduced a bill that would legalize riverboat gambling in Pennsylvania.  The legislation would allow riverboats to offer slot machines, blackjack, dice games and roulette wheels.  The bill also requires voters in each community to approve a ballot referendum before any gambling can take place.

headline: ‘Campaign Operatives’ Blasted as Senate Debates Flag Amendment
abstract: A constitutional amendment against flag burning is being moved toward a Senate vote, while critics of it say that it is already dead and being debated only as ammunition for use during election time. The US House of Representatives rejected the amendment, which would have allowed the federal government and the states to ban flag burning.

headline: State newborns to get AIDS test
abstract: In an effort to track the AIDS epidemic, the state Health Department will begin testing all newborns in PA for the AIDS virus. The tests will be funded by a grant from the federal government's Centers for Disease Control. The babies' mothers will not learn the results, as universal screening cannot be achieved without the subjects' anonymity. Secretary of Health Dr. N. Mark Richards acknowledged that the lack of notification is an "ethically touchy issue".

headline: Save the children, early
abstract: A bill approved by the PA House Education Committee Tuesday would deliver services to mentally handicapped children earlier in life.  PA Representative Ronald Cowell, chairman of the House Education Committee, supports the bill and PA Governor Robert Casey has proposed a 64% increase in spending in this area.

headline: North end homes picked for pilot recycling program
abstract: 3,279 homes have been selected to be in a pilot curbside recycling program to begin July 10. A borough-wide recycling program will begin Sept. 4. PA requires any town with more than 10,000 residents to have a recycling program by Sept. 26, 1990.

headline: Municipalities donate funds for Routes 322/422 study
abstract: A group of municipal and private-sector officials meeting with the PA Department of Transportation were told local communities must demonstrate broad-based community support for a project to improve traffic conditions on Routes 322 and 422 in Dauhin and Lebanon Counties. Several companies gave $5000 to support a research initiatve identifying solutions to congestion. Participants hope efforts will force PennDot to put the roads on its 12-year plan.

headline: Firefighters
abstract: An anonymous member of the paper's staff writes about current legislation in PA which would give active volunteer firefighters pensions when they reach 65 years of age, following 20 years of service. However, the pension plan would create numerous problems, such as volunteers serving 20 years in different departments, underfunding in smaller departments, and the plan's application to ambulance personnel, diving teams and fire police. The author suggests a plan similar to the PA Bureau of Forestry, which pays its members for the time spent fighting fires.

headline: New Pa. Welfare Aide Draws Fire from Rep. Richardson
abstract: PA Rep. David Richardson and 2 Philadelphia lawmakers drafted a letter to PA Governor Casey protesting the appointment of Gerald F. Radke as deputy secretary of the PA Department of Welfare. The letter demands a meeting between Casey and Welfare Secretary John F. White, Jr. to discuss Radke's alleged conflict of interest, as the firm with which he was employed contracted with the DPW to handle drug prescription claims for HealthPASS. Richardson has denounced Radke for his involvement in the cuts carried out by Thornburgh.

headline: Resort land swap draws pros, cons
abstract: A PA House panel heard sharply divergent opinions about a proposed land swap between the state of PA and developers of Hidden Valley resort in Somerset County. The bill remove a federal roadblock to the exchange. Trade would be sound environmentally and would help a firm that is already the Western PA county's largest employer.

headline: VA chief says aging vets to get top priority
abstract: Veterans Affairs Secretary Edward J. Derwinski visited Erie and told veterans that the facilities will begin to focus more on geriatric medicine and long term care to meet the needs of the aging veteran population.

headline: Goode Backs State Supervision
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode reluctantly accepted demands from business leaders from whom Goode was seeking loans to carry the city until taxes are received. Under demands, Philadelphia will be overseen by an independent review commission comprised of PA legislators to ensure the city  takes steps to deal with its finances. City councilman were split in supporting the issue, Commissioner David Cohen against the measure while John Street favored it.

headline: Limiting hostile takeovers
abstract: Editorial board approves of the state legislature's passage and PA Governor Robert Casey's signing of a bill designed to prevent hostile corporate takeovers in Pennsylvania.

headline: Susquehanna Twp. Picks commissioner
abstract: After the death of Susquehanna Township commissioner John Micka, both former commissioners George Searight and Leah Kleiman became interested in filling the vacant seat. The eight member Republican board appointed Searight over Kleiman because Searight is also a Republican. District Justice Raymond Shugars swore in Searight. Searight has served as an officer in the Pennsylvania Pharmaceutical Association and as chairman and treasurer of the Republican Party.

headline: Officials endorse regional jail idea
abstract: Due to overcrowding in federal, state and local prisons, a Williamsport Firm's proposal to build a regional prison has received a positive reception from two Northcumberland County Commissioners.  Under the current proposal, Buckingham Associates would operate the prison through a not-for-profit agency, or lease the entire facility to a government agency.  A spokesperson for Governor Casey said the state has not been contacted about the project yet.

headline: … considers suit against menorah
abstract: Soviet immigrants celebrated Hanukkah openly with a 10-foot high menorah on a plaza in front of the Capitol. The ACLU has sent two representatives to see if this crosses any lines of separation of church and state.

headline: State officials reduce the AIDS budget
abstract: The PA Legislature reduced the PA Department of Welfare's budget for AIDS, specifically in the Department's Pharmaceutical Benefits Program said director of Legislative Affairs for Philadelphia's AIDS Activities Coordinating Office (AACO), Renee Brody. The cut came because Legislators say the program has enough federal revenue to continue operations at the status quo. Brody said despite PA's state rank of AIDS cases as 7th, PA Governor Casey's $5.3 million allocation is embarrassingly low.

headline: School aid changes to be studied
abstract: PA Education Secretary Donald Carroll will create a commission to solve the issue of the budget for public schools, but the results will be instituted for '91-'92. School boards are calling for the PA Education Department to contribute 50 percent of school budgets, but the state average is 42.7. The Leechburg Area School District closed in a 1 day protest of funding which forced the District to raise property taxes. Carroll was in Armstrong County with PA Governor Casey.

headline: NRC to hold hearing on waste-disposal plan
abstract: The federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission announced a public meeting in Philadelphia to discuss a policy proposal which ceases to require companies to dispose of low-level radioactive materials in hazardous waste sites, allowing material to be disposed of in public landfills or recycled. US Rep. George Miller, who opposes the proposal on the grounds that full effects of low-level radiation are yet unknown, has scheduled a hearing of the issue in the House energy and environment subcommittee.

headline: New I-81 Interchange Asked on Transportation 'Wish List'
abstract: The Lackawanna Regional Planning Commission submitted a 'wish list' to the PA Department of Transportation. The list contains over 60 projects, however area PennDOT community relations director Rolly Keisling warned inclusion on the list does not mean PennDOT will approve and fund the projects, though that is what the Planning Commission hopes for.

headline: Fleeing inmate caught after downtown chase
abstract: Larry White, a prison inmate of the Huntingdon State Correctional Institution, testified in a trial for a fellow inmate before attempting to escape with sheriff's deputies in pursuit. The testimony occurred in the Court of Common Pleas before Judge W. Terrence O'Brien. White was caught and charged with assault by a prisoner, assault on a police officer, and escape. He was arraigned before Common Pleas Judge Joseph James.

headline: Pennsylvania in number one
abstract: PA Representative Jim Distler writes to praise Pennsylvania for being the top state in the nation as far as its services to the elderly. He also discusses the possibility of moving some lottery-funded programs for the elderly to the state's General Fund in order to protect the solvency of the lottery fund for elderly. Much of PA's funding for programs for the elderly is provided by lottery proceeds.

headline: Rhoades wants '911' system
abstract: PA Sen. James Rhoades said a House-Senate conference committee approved amendments to a bill establishing a statewide 911 service. The legislation heads to the full House and Senate for approval. The PA Department of Community Affairs, the PA Emergency Management Council, and the PA Public Utility Commission must give approval before counties hold meetings to gauge citizen reactions. The program will be funded by a charge on monthly telephone bills, capped according to the population of each county.

headline: VFW post commander Witmer to be honored by veterans group
abstract: Glenn E. Witmer will receive the Dauphin County Outstanding Veteran of the Year. He is a the definition of a busy man. He remains very active in veterans groups and the community.

headline: Drug czar pats state on back for war on narcotics
abstract: State Rep. Nick Colafella supports a proposal by federal Drug Czar and Director of the Office on National Drug Control Policy William Bennett, to charge addicts fees to help fund treatment. Bennett commended PA for its leadership against drugs, however his failure to mention PA Governor Casey led to criticism by PA Sen. Gerald LaValle, who assumed it was due to upcoming  elections. PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer is challenging Casey.

headline: Limiting terms of representatives a flawed concept
abstract: Author believes the proposal to limit terms of representatives is a flawed plan, undemocratic in spirit and counterproductive in practice. One of the fundamental tenets of a democracy is that people should have the right to choose those whom they want to represent them in office. Limiting terms would weaken the powers of Congress because so many would be novices or lame ducks. Fewer than one-third of the House serve longer than the proposed 12 year term limit.

headline: Taxpayers seek a level playing field in effort to limit terms
abstract: Former Representative John Kennedy, president of Kennedy Railroad Builders and founder of Citizens for the Common Wealth, criticized a recent letter by former Lieutenant Governor Ernest P. Kline attacking Kennedy. Kennedy defended his rejection of a bill that would place limits of legislators' terms. He believes that the state debt, teachers strikes and high benefits and salaries for legislators are all issues that taxpayers want to be remedied.

headline: States under siege
abstract: A report released by the National Governors Association shows that the combination of a sluggish economy and other pressures are hurting revenues in all 50 states.  The other pressures affecting state revenues are federally-mandated increases for Medicaid, increasing education costs, prison overcrowding, and a shift in the burden of transportation funding from the federal government to the states.  Governor Casey, who up until this point has refused to entertain the idea of a tax increase, may have to consider such an option to increase revenue as the state's surplus dwindles.

headline: A key foe on abortion backs Casey
abstract: PA Representative Karen A. Ritter, the legislature's leading abortion-rights activist, endorsed pro-life gubernatorial candidate PA Governor Robert P. Casey. Democratic voters are torn over supporting the incumbent with whom they agree on many social issues but oppose on the issue of abortion. PA Senator Jeanette Reibman, also an abortion-rights supporter, supported Casey.

headline: State pays county for Medicaid
abstract: The PA Department of Welfare made good on its promises that $60 million in payments to nursing homes statewide were "in the mail," as York County received $600,000 for the York County Hospital & Home at Pleasant Acres, which will now be able to meet payroll.

headline: School aid formula could cost N.Va. $85 million.
abstract: A panel appointed by Virginia Governor L. Douglas Wilder has recommended transferring $85 million in state school aid from wealthier Northern Virginia districts to poorer systems downstate. North Virginia officials said this drain on local school budgets could force either substantial tax increases or reductions in education programs, including fewer class offerings and teacher layoffs. Educations say their goal is to increase overall state spending rather than just to re-divide the current offerings.

headline: Nuclear Hangover
abstract: Editors are angered by sloppily enforced nuclear regulations. In addressing clean-up, the US Energy Department raised the projected cost of waste disposal by 50 percent, a number equal to half the PA budget. In other states, the Federal Bureau of Investigation has raided facilities looking for violations of environmental laws. The problem is worsened by President Reagan's failure to address it when it surfaced. This would have been a lot cheaper if people had adhered to regulations in the first place.

headline: New lane, light needed at Route 61 intersection
abstract: PennDOT has announced that an extra lane and a traffic light will be constructed at an intersection on Route 61 by next summer, earning rare praise for the department from residents.

headline: Food-stamp fraud sting reveals abuse of system
abstract: In a sting by undercover agents from the US Department of Agriculture's Office of Inspector General, agents arrested 13 residents of York county for illegally trading drugs for food stamps as well as 14 Harrisburg residents. Among those arrested are Robert Richardon who was the Deputy Director of the Harrisburg Concerned Citizens Organizations. Also arrested was Orus Patterson, a former state House staffer.

headline: Senate and White House near pact on child care, lawmakers say
abstract: According to US Senate leaders, the Senate and White House are near an agreement on a $13 billion child care bill that would provide matching money to states seeking to set up programs to train childcare professionals and to subsidize state-regulated childcare centers.

headline: Saidel against larger loan deal
abstract: Philadelphia City Controller Jonathan A. Saidel said he would oppose Finance Director Betsy C. Reveal's attempt to sell $325 million in short-term notes, citing the city financial plan he made with Mayor Wilson Goode and PA Supreme Court judges that agreed to selling $250 to $300 million.  Reveal says the larger package is needed to assure investors that the city will remain solvent. Saidel said the loan would leave taxpayers with unnecessary interest payments and that he would not deviate from the original plan.

headline: A creaky computer system
abstract: 20 years ago a computer system was created to go through the filings of thousands of insurance companies and identify those with high risk insolvency. It is still the way state regulators examine the companies. The system used to catch 90% of those that went under, but now it is only catching 75% and 25% of those aren't really in trouble. New systems are being explored.

headline: Dueling candidates aim for votes
abstract: Two photographs, one is of PA Governor Robert P. Casey at a state shoot in Tower City, talking to a prospective voter and the other photo is Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer talks to the public relations director of PA State Shooters Association at the state shoot in Elysburg.

headline: Most local voters stayed at home
abstract: The tri-county area of Venango County, Clarion County and Forest County experienced very low voter turnout for primary elections to US Congress, PA General Assembly, and gubernatorial offices. Candidates for US Congress and the PA General Assembly mostly ran unopposed, while PA Governor Robert Casey won the Democratic party nomination and PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer won endorsements in Venango and Forest Counties. Cindy Callihan, chief registrar of Clarion County stated her disappointment at the low turnout.

headline: Teacher strikes stir ire over public-worker unions
abstract: Act 195 granted collective-bargaining rights to an estimated 500,000 employees on the state payroll. It was passed almost 20 years ago, but symbolically celebrates its anniversary while the state is embroiled in a labor contract battle with a group of teachers. The consensus is that teacher strikes are at the core of the resentment to public-employee unionism. Even the legislature is aimed at somehow restricting the right teachers have to strike.

headline: Local officials say state should pay for its mandates
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode spoke to the state Senate's Local Government Committee and argued that the state needs to shoulder the financial burden for services it forces city and county governments to handle.  The chairman of the committee, Senator Frank Pecora, is pushing for a state constitutional amendment that would make compliance with state-mandated services optional if full funding is not provided.  The city of Philadelphia joined a class-action lawsuit earlier in the year, contending that state funding for childrens' programs has fallen short for six years.

headline: A place for banquets, black pride
abstract: Bishop Frank C. Cummings response to a lack of opportunity for the black community in banquet facilities, was to open up First District Plaza, now home to the city's largest black owned banquet facility. President of the PA Chapter of the National Coalition of 100 Black Women, Francine Cheeks, said the Plaza has historical and economic significance. The project was financed through bank loans, a federal block grant, and Self Help Inc.

headline: State recommends measles vaccine
abstract: The PA Department of Health recommends that students in grades 7 through 12 be vaccinated a second time for measles due to the number of outbreaks in the past few years, said spokesman Bruce Reimer.

headline: School board rejects Mont Alto offer
abstract: The Waynesboro Area School Board has rejected an offer from Mont Alto Borough Council to buy the community's former elementary school, and school director Nelson Rock said the board may consider selling the school at a public auction in November.  Rock did say that the board is willing to consider a counter-offer from the borough.

headline: One-man show?
abstract: A bill which passed the PA Senate and is pending in the House, would establish a $1 million annual appropriation for grants awarded to owners of properties threatened or damaged by sinkholes. It would also provide the PA Department of Environmental Resources' Bureau of Topographic and Geologic Survey to speed up its identification of sinkhole locations. Currently, it is the job of one man, Bill Kochanov, who hopes the money will be used to hire additional surveyors to finish the project faster.

headline: New law cracks down on backhauling
abstract: PA Senator Edwin Holl writes about the new law prohibiting "backhauling," or the practice of carrying food in the same trucks used to transport garbage, saying that it has already caught a few "unscrupulous" truckers in the few months it's been in effect.  He supports the creation of a hotline that would allow citizens to report this practice if they see evidence of it, a tool he says would be useful in conjunction with random spot checks.

headline: Frankford pharmacist convicted in drug case
abstract: Louis Brickman, a 65-year-old pharmacist in the Frankford section of Philadelphia, was found guilty of illegally trading in federally restricted drugs. Prosecutors contended that Brickman ordered large amounts of controlled substances, threw away invoices documenting the deliveries, and tried to cover up by keeping a file of forged prescriptions. Brickman's sentencing hearing will be on Nov. 29 and he is free on $10,000 bail.

headline: Senate Prevents WIC Cutback
abstract: The Senate approved a measure early to prevent nearly 250,000 poor pregnant women and infants from being cut from federal program designed to highest-risk babies a healthy start. The food or vouchers that can be used to buy food at local stores. The states administer the program using federal funds.

headline: Salvation Army determined to locate space for homeless
abstract: Captain Leroy Lyle of the Salvation Army says that they are planning to build a third floor on their current facility in order to provide emergency housing for 12 people, and they are hoping to use a building in the Edgemont section of Susquehanna Twp. available for emergency housing of another 12 people, though the latter measure is being opposed by some residents, who feel that the shelter would bring more homeless people to the area and make it unsafe.

headline: A time of mixed feelings
abstract: The Scrantonian Tribune, a well-established regional newspaper, sold some of its assets to the Lynett family, which publish The Morning Times and The Sunday Times. The Morning Times will now become known as the Tribune, and the editorial board hopes to serve the widest possible audience with the name change.

headline: Duke Says He'll Announce For Governor Next Month
abstract: Louisiana Representative David Duke is among a number of men running for Governor during this election campaign. Previously, Duke received 44 percent of the vote to incumbent Bennett Johnston's 54 in the race for US Senate. Duke is criticized for past leadership of the Ku Klux Klan and sale of Nazi literature from his public office as recently as 1989. Duke predicted he will be in a runoff against former Governor Edwin Edwards or incumbent Governor Buddy Roemer.

headline: Norristown agency leader answers her critics
abstract: The PA Department of Community Affairs suspended federal aid to the Montgomery County Opportunity Board, citing several problems, chief among them the process by which Frances V. Pierce became executive director and the way the board's makeup changed. Critics say Pierce does not have the education or experience to run the board. Shortly after being elected, Pierce voted not to renew the appointments of several board members whose terms were up, despite the board's custom to reappoint members who wanted to keep serving.

headline: Teachers endorse Gov. Casey
abstract: Pennsylvania State Education Association has given their endorsement to PA Governor Casey, who spoke at a rally Wednesday.  Casey has supported educational reforms and a increase in the minimum salary for teachers.

headline: USA'a best environment: New England
abstract: A recent study reports that New England--led by Vermont--has the United States' healthiest environment, while the South has the worst.  The study used thirty-five indicators to determine the healthiest environment.

headline: Abortion Appeal
abstract: A federal appeals court expanded a permanent injunction barring anti-abortion protestors from disrupting Philadelphia-area clinics. The order came after the anti-abortion group Operation Rescue announced its intention to demonstrate at several city clinics during that week. U.S. District Judge Clarence Newcomer previously dropped several clinics from the protective order after they failed to prove they had been targets of protests. Today's opinion determined Newcomer erred in dismissing several of them.

headline: State rejects nursing home planned in Upper Macungie
abstract: PA Health Secretary Dr. N. Mark Richards rejected a request to build a $5 million, 120-bed nursing home in Upper Macungie Township, citing inadequate documentation to justify need and financial feasibility. A spokesman for the Department of Health said it was the first of 120 nursing homes proposed for the state by an Ohio architectural firm to be acted upon. Opposition to the plan also came from at least three nursing homes in the Valley, who claimed there were sufficient long-term care beds in the region.

headline: School District opposes burner
abstract: During a meeting of the school board, Superintendent of Montgomery School District read a second draft of a resolution by the board opposing the site and construction of a hazardous waste incinerator near the school, saying the facility is contrary to the school's policy of nurturing future generations of youth, in addition to posing economic risks and transportation hazards. The school also reviewed a proposal for computer education among other items on the agenda.

headline: Only northwest quarter  of city to recycle in '90
abstract: Mandatory recycling will begin in the northwestern quarter of Pittsburgh by October 1991. The recycling program will no start in the entire city until more than a year after the deadline. The entire city was supposed to be recycling by Sept. 26 1990 according to state mandate, and since they will not the city faces to lose $246,000 in state grants.

headline: New Route 901 opens in county. Businessmen eye opportunities for industrial, economic growth.
abstract: The opening of Route 901, a safe and truck-accessible link to Interstate 81, will allow for industrial and economic development in mountainous Schuylkill County and has the support of state Representative Robert E. Belfanti Jr.  The project was first proposed in 1982 and has been supported by Shamokin City Council, the Ashland PA General Hospital board, and Ashland and Mount Carmel merchants.

headline: Freeman Fired For Role in Prison Melee
abstract: Corrections Commissioner David Owens Jr. fired the suspended superintendent of the riot-damaged Camp Hill prison. Gov. Casey had recommended the action.

headline: Senior citizen day-care/respite  center opens in Lebanon
abstract: PA Department of Aging Secretary Linda M. Rhodes and Lebanon County officials have helped to open the state's first county-run adult day-care/respite center.  The facility built next to Cedar Haven which is the county home is operated by the Lebanon County Area agency on Aging.

headline: Say no to courthouse, solicitor urges Phila.
abstract: Philadelphia's City Solicitor Charisse Lillie urged the rejection of a private developer's proposal to build a courthouse at the old Bulletin Building at 30th and Market Streets, saying that the legislation for the courthouse violates local and state bidding laws by granting the developer, Daniel Keating, exclusive rights to build the courthouse in return for city money and property.

headline: CBS ends all-talk format at Philly's WCAU radio
abstract: CBS suddenly replaced its longstanding news and talk station, WCAU-AM, with oldies music and sports calls, laying off about 50 to 60 workers.

headline: Easy state OK predicted for flag amendment
abstract: After US Supreme Court overturned a ban on flag burning by Congress, politicians in Washington vowed to amend the constitution. Members of the PA Legislature vowed to do the same. PA Rep. Jeffrey Piccola, PA Senator M. Joseph Rocks, and PA Rep. Larry Kenney expect the measure to pass. Gubernatorial candidate and PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer supports an amendment. However PA Rep. Paul McHale is concerned about the unconstitutionality of a possible ban.

headline: Lobbyists provide vital data but is price too high?
abstract: Ralph and David Tive are lobbyists for whom Common Cause director for PA Barry Kauffman hopes regulations and restrictions will be tightened. Kauffman says because of loose reporting laws in PA, lobbyists disclose only a percentage of what they spend in securing votes from the Legislature. PA Sen. Michael Dawida notes it is harder for lobbyists to use money as an influence given salaries and provisions for Legislators. Michael McLaughlin, for the PA Task Force on Product Liability, says lobbying is over exaggerated.

headline: Teacher's pension board to discuss loan to Phila.
abstract: The head of the PA School Employees Retirement System's Board of Pensions, Bernard Freitag, warns against Philadelphia bashing in light of the city's current fiscal crisis. Citing the Pension's 16 billion fund, Freitag argued the $50 to $100 million loan requested by the city is fractional. Bernard was encouraged by PA Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll's assurance that state funds to the city would first go to lenders. The Pension Board's nine members are expected to meet to discuss the loan tomorrow.

headline: Demotions spark union interest
abstract: AFSCME is attempting to organize Montgomery County employees.  The employees would be represented by separate collective bargaining units.  Currently, organizing committees are forming.

headline: Abortion foes cause a drop in rural services
abstract: A study by the Alan Guttmacher Institute found abortion services in rural areas fell since 1977, said author Stanley Hershaw. President of the National Right to Life Committee, John Wilke said the decrease is a reflection of public opinion in small towns. Executive director of the Nation Abortion Rights Action League Kate Michelman says abortion rates have remained the same since 1980, with a higher percentage of abortions performed out of state in those states with large rural areas.

headline: State revokes license of Phila. nursing home
abstract: The PA Health Department has revoked the license of the River's Edge Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Northeast Philadelphia, citing mistreatment, abuse and failure to properly report and investigate charges of sexual assault on patients.  The department has also ordered that the management immediately be replaced at the facility and that current patients be sent to other homes.

headline: School district rejects church's call for Halloween ban
abstract: A church group attempted to convince the Avonworth School Board to stop celebrating Halloween in schools, as they claim the holiday has "satanic overtones."  The school board is ignoring the request, saying that the celebration is harmless fun and does not have religious affiliations.

headline: Opinion: Blair, city face wrath of DER
abstract: Editorial board comments on the PA Department of Environmental Resources' decision to force Blair County and the City of Altoona to develop a plan for a recycling system.  The city has given the Blair County commissioners this responsibility.

headline: Nigerians Nabbed with 1.6 Ponds of Heroin
abstract: The US Customs agents found 1.6 pounds of heroin in the luggage of two Nigerian nationals entering the United States from Canada. US Attorney Stephen Markman said that the heroin was found during routine inspection of a passenger bus that was stopped at the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel.

headline: Get rid of bad guns by law, not lawsuits
abstract: DC City Council wants to make  the person who pulled the trigger responsible but also the manufacture of the gun, and distributor. If approved it will be the first law of its kind. It has already had a record 445 murders this year. Other cities around the country and breaking records as well. The editorial claims that the proposed law will not help because it is not comprehensive.

headline: State settles lawsuit over child welfare; Agrees to seek extra $40M to help counties' services
abstract: PA Welfare Secretary John White announced Monday that the Casey administration has tentatively agreed to settle a lawsuit by seeking an additional $40 million for county child welfare services over the next six years.  White said the money and budget changes are part of a proposal to settle a lawsuit that accused the state of short-changing county-run child welfare programs.

headline: Shelter Service Inc. nets $890 in donations
abstract: The Mifflin/Juniata Board of Realtors organized a community service fundraiser and raised $890 for Shelter Service Inc. of Lewistown, a homeless shelter hoping to buy a new building, as their current building is deteriorating.

headline: Conrail has wrong data
abstract: VP of Bell of Pennsylvania Daniel Whelan writes in response to Conrail's claim that the Altoona area "has a phone service that would not be able to meet the demands of a service center."  Whelan contends that the Altoona area's phone service has access to excellent technology, and would have been able to provide all of Conrail's requirements.

headline: Election '90
abstract: The article details election results in the 82nd and 171st Legislative Districts by county, precinct and ward. Republican Daniel F. Clark and Democrat Ruth C. Rudy won the districts respectively.

headline: Local Electors Spurn 'Vote 'em Out' Talk; Incumbents Succeed
abstract: Despite a national diagnosis of anti-incumbency sentiment, Lycoming County voted to re-elect PA Governor Robert P. Casey and PA Representatives Alvin C. Bush and Thomas W. Dempsey. Local electors went against the overall state mandate to borrow $200 million to improve county prisons but endorsed borrowing to enhance volunteer fire, ambulance and rescue companies.  U.S. Congressman George W. Gekas, who ran unopposed, also saw his plurality shrink. Voters in Montgomery and Porter Townships opted to switch from paper ballots to voting machines.

headline: Teachers to strike in Dover
abstract: Teachers in the Dover Area School District plan to begin striking today, as there are still several stumbling blocks in contract negotiations.

headline: Casey
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Robert P. Casey held his first re-election fundraising dinner.  The dinner was hosted by two of Governor Casey's longtime frineds--both of whom are Northcumberland County Commissioners.  At the event, the governor was asked why 6.1 million dollars earmarked for Children and Youth agencies was not released; he stated that the money was not released because the state legislature did not pass a bill broadening the definition of child abuse.

headline: Abortion foes rally in D.C.
abstract: Abortion opponenst rallied in Washington D.C. on the 17th anniversary of Roe v. Wade

headline: State's new prenatal-care program runs into criticism before it begins
abstract: The PA Department if Public Welfare is preparing to start a new Medicaid program to provide the most comprehensive health care ever for pregnant women in the state. Hospital administrators criticize the plan, calling it an 'administrative nightmare'. Under the plan women would get far more than the routine medical exams. A health worker would be assigned to each woman who would make sure she kept appointments to counseling sessions on drugs use, smoking, nutrition and classes on parenting.

headline: School spending reaction mixed
abstract: PA Rep. Bruce Smith is dissatisfied with the budget approved by the Legislature and PA Governor Robert Casey. After last year, this year's increase is too tight to keep school districts from raising taxes, Smith says. He attributes it to elections. York County school superintendents participated in a rally in Harrisburg seeking more aid for basic and special education. Dr. David J. Krauser, superintendent of the Northeastern School District, said the increase in state education funding is short of what is necessary.

headline: OUE offices relocated; meeting set
abstract: The Organizations United for the Environment has relocated to an office space in a trailer belonging to Gregg Township supervisors. OUE's fast growing membership has made more accessible facilities a necessity. The group is spearheading the effot to keep USPCI from building a hazardous waste incinerator in the Susquehannah Industrial Park. OUE will host speaker Diana Steck of the Citizen's Clearinghouse for Hazardous Waste at their next meeting.

headline: No plaudits for city transit aide
abstract: T.J. Dorricott Jr., a member of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, criticizes Philadelphia Transportation Director Denise L. Goren's recent letter blaming service cuts, the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority's inability to understand market needs and shortcomings in service quality for the 6 percent drop in City Transit Division ridership. Dorricott argues that Mayor Wilson Goode's inability to provide SEPTA with the city's local subsidy share represents a greater threat to riders of the transit system. Dorricott argues that Goren should have pushed for a local 0.5 percent sales tax to be dedicated to SEPTA.

headline: Getting permits should be tougher
abstract: The editorial says that obtaining a permit to own a firearm should be more difficult and be more closely monitored, in light of a recent story about a man who had been treated by a psychiatrist for 15 years, was the legal owner of a concealed handgun. It says that getting a gun is too easy in PA, and points out that the National Rifle Association has prevented the US Congress from banning possession of automatic assault weapons, even though they are not hunting rifles.

headline: State, waiting figures on aid, fears there won't be enough
abstract: PA officials still don't know how much in federal energy assistance funds the state will get to support its Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, despite the fact that an agreement has been reached on the federal budget. Even if the state receives as much as it did last year, it may not be enough due to the increased costs of heating oil because of the crisis in the Persian Gulf.

headline: State aid for Philadelphia?
abstract: a shaping up that would have the full faith and credit of the state backing up $300 million or more in bonds floated by financially desperate Philadelphia, which without a large infusion of funds may be unable to pay its bills by the end of the month. The editorial wonders if the state can afford to give such a large amount when they already are taking out loans to pay their own bills. The editorial believes Philadelphia has to reform or it will continue down this path.

headline: Consumer Advocate, Bell Say Refunds Shouldn't Pay for 911
abstract: PA state legislative leaders are urging the chief administrative law judge for the Public Utility Commission (PUC), Judge Allison K. Turner, to support a proposal to use $24 million in Bell of Pennsylvania consumer refunds for a state-wide 911 emergency telephone system.  Bell of Pennsylvania and the state consumer advocate believe it would be unfair to customers to use their refund money to pay for 911.

headline: Election holds importance in perilous times
abstract: Robert Lee Smith of Camp Hill writes to urge people to register to vote and to vote in the upcoming November elections for PA governor, senators and representatives, and US congressmen and senators.  Smith says that there are challenges at the state and national level and voters need to choose their leaders wisely.

headline: Local lawmakers not impressed by lobbyists' 'wining and dining'
abstract: Local lawmakers say lobbyists play an important role in the legislative process but fail to impress anyone with their wining and dining. Luzerne County legislative delegation agree want laws that regulate lobbyist spending to be tightened. They want full disclosure of what lobbyists spend while wooing lawmakers.

headline: Teachers union lessons
abstract: Editorial board discusses the teachers' strike in Spring Grove and whether or not the contract issue has been fully resolved.

headline: Casey begins bid in coal country
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey began his re-election campaign by holding a fundraiser in Northcumberland County last night.
