The governor told supporters that he intends to stimulate industrial growth in Pennsylvania's coal region; he also wishes to reduce auto-insurance costs, improve water quality, and end drug abuse.  The state Democratic Committee endorsed Casey's candidacy for re-election on Saturday.

headline: Abortion law to be decided in court
abstract: Pennsylvania's controversial Abortion Control Statute is being challenged in court by the ACLU.

headline: Strike notice issued
abstract: Hospital director of public relations Michael Peckman, District 1199P of the National Union of Hospital and Health Care Employees, local President David Thomas, union negotiator Fran Campo

headline: Senator Fights to Keep Rocky Statue at Philadelphia Art Museum
abstract: Democratic Senator Vincent J. Fumo said he has introduced a resolution to keep the 8 foot 6 inch, 2,000 pound statue of the fictional boxing champion Rocky Balboa permanently at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. A spokesman for the museum said they believe it is a 'movie prop' and does not belong outside an art museum.

headline: OUE speaker says burner fight can be won
abstract: Dr. Paul Connett spoke of the effects of hazardous waste incinerators, as well as how to keep them from coming into a particular area, at an Organizations United for the Environment (OUE) meeting.  For the past several months, OUE has been rallying support for local communities to oppose the installation and operation of a hazardous waste incinerator in Susquehanna Industrial Park in Gregg Township.  The proposed incinerator would be constructed and operated by USPCI Inc. of PA.

headline: No Way to Run a Transit Business
abstract: An editorial criticizing SEPTA and the funding of mass transit, suggesting that local governments find ways to increase subsidies so riders are not charged more.

headline: Glutted Probation System Puts Communities in Peril
abstract: The Federal Justice Bureau reports a 5 percent increase of those on probation from the year before. Executive director of the National Association of Criminal Justice Planners, Mark Cuniff, says probation is the dominant sentence for drug related criminal activity. Officers are overloaded with casework, paperwork, and investigative work, making communities less safe. More importantly, it is unpopular for politicians to call for more funding for probation as the public perceives it as being soft on crime.

headline: Taking care of the care-givers
abstract: A new state-sponsored program in PA will soon provide financial and other forms of support to disabled people and their families in order to lighten the burden of care-giving for those taking care of the disabled.

headline: State funds flow to area
abstract: State money was flowing into Beaver County yesterday, including $8 million in low-interest loans to restart 2 former Babcock & Wilcox plants, a $1.4 million grant for water, sewage and an access road for a proposed industrial, research, and office park, a $1.55 million loan for the purchase of 15 acres of the H.H. Robertson site in Ambridge, and a $600,000 grant to the Beaver County Corporation for Economic Development.

headline: Examining the death of WCAU-AM
abstract: CBS's elimination of WCAU-AM, which was a staple of radio history, has some people wondering if AM radio will continue to garner attention.  Until it was cancelled, WCAU had been losing money since the late 1970s.

headline: Election Results
abstract: The article details the result of PA governor, lieutenant governor, PA Senate, PA House of Representatives and U.S. Congress elections. It also lists the results of two bond issues, allowing the state to lend money to county prisons, volunteer fire companies and ambulance services to update their services.

headline: Local officials upset with state of federal government
abstract: Several local officials, including Juniata and Mifflin County Commissioners, are disappointed and upset with the federal government's spending in the past, and are fearing budget cuts, causing local governments to have to pick up the slack.  The US House just rejected a $500-billion deficit reduction package.

headline: Teamsters come up short in USAir union vote
abstract: Although the Teamsters union apparently lost a 2 year battle to represent employees of USAir, receiving only 34.2 percent of votes to designate the union as the offical bargaining agent for USAir employees, the National Mediation Board has overturned the results based on illegal interference by USAir. The union has until January 3 to provide evidence of interference, with USAir given until January 23 to respond. USAir is confident management acted within the law in its actions.

headline: South Mountain veterans home sought
abstract: There are hundreds of veterans in Pennsylvania who do not have families to take care of them in their twilight years.  It is time to let our state representatives know that we Pennsylvanians support a veterans home at the South Mountain Restoration Center.  The appropriation of six million dollars, the amount needed for this home, has been sitting on the governor's desk for two years; we need to send a message of support and get the appropriation passed.

headline: Abortion not biggest issue to U.S. voters
abstract: Despite earlier predictions that abortion would be a critical issue in the 1990 elections, voters were generally more concerned with economic and tax issues. PA voters replaced a pro-life PA Senator with a woman who ran a health clinic that performed abortions. Nationwide, election results gave no clear view of American's overall position on legalized abortion, with victories split between pro-life and pro-choice legislators.

headline: Study finds 13 percent in work force uses drugs
abstract: According to statistics extrapolated from national substance-abuse studies shows that 13% of the work force in a five-county Pittsburgh area use drugs other than alcohol.  The problem could cost employers up to $1 billion a year in absenteeism, accidents, medical benefits, theft, and workers' compensation.

headline: Senator proposes education task force
abstract: PA Senator James J. Rhoades has unveiled a proposal to create an education task force that would examine and revamp what kids learn and how buildings are used.  The task force would be charged  with improving curriculum, making schools more accountable, developing incentives for schools that meet or exceed certain standards and sanctions for those that don't.  The task force would have to submit recommendations to the governor, education secretary, and legislature by July, 1992.

headline: OUE speaker sees defeat of USPCI
abstract: The Organizations United for the Environment, led by John O'Connor of the National Toxics Campaign in Williamsport. are fighting against the hazardous waste incinerator proposal and the USPCI.

headline: Oh, the lives they'll save
abstract: Janis Avon of Bethel Park writes to support a bill in the PA legislature that would suspend the drivers' license of anyone arrested for drunken driving, even before a trial or conviction.  She also seeks to dissuade lawmakers and the media of the idea that, as stated in a previous Pittsburgh Post-Gazette article, the public is "indifferent" to the problem of drunken driving.

headline: Goode says child funds are not lost
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode tried collecting a state matching policy for services for abused and neglected children. The city has funded the state shortfall in the past. However, Goode joined other counties in a suit, expecting to win funds he prematurely awarded the Department of Human Services. In a settlement with PA Governor Casey's administration, there is now a deficit. City Council refuses to refinance bonds, causing Philadelphia Citizens for Children and Youth to criticize Goode, who vows to restore the budget.

headline: United Way organizes 'major push' to meet goal
abstract: United Way of the Capital Region, with ten days to go in its 1990 annual fund drive, will begin a "major push" to meet its $7.575 million goal. The drive has reached 55 percent of its goal so far. Senior Vice President for Resource Development, Bruce Mohler said that as the economy slows down, contributions to the United Way slow down as well, but that the impact of that economic slowdown causes needs to go up.

headline: State Grants for 2 City Businesses OK'd
abstract: The Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority approved loans for two Lancaster city projects.

headline: Pitched fight over Caller ID rages on and on
abstract: PA Commonwealth Court ruled Caller ID is unconstitutional. The PA Public Utilities Commission plans to ask the PA Supreme Court to allow Bell Atlantic to offer it. Similar arrangements were made in other states to allow the company to offer the service in conjunction with blocking technology. Anti-blocking technology could gridlock the system, says director of the PA attorney general's public protection division Dan Clearfield. Call tracing has been described as dangerous by the American Civil Liberties Union.

headline: Elections to be focus of shows
abstract: The article shows a lineup of the day's TV news shows regarding the upcoming election and who will be on them.

headline: Local Republicans stood by Hafer when others didn't
abstract: York County Republicans were among the few who supported PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer in the her primary election against fellow Republican gubernatorial contender Marguerite "Peg" Luksik. Hafer won York County with 52% of the vote. State Senator Ralph W. Hess stated that, from talking to people at the polls, abortion was less of an issue than was Hafer's personality. He also believes that Republican voters will support the Republican nominee regardless, once PA's financial problems under current governor Robert Casey are better publicized.

headline: Teamsters for Casey, Singel
abstract: John P. Morris, president of the Pennsylvania Conference of Teamsters, announced that the union would support PA Governor Robert P. Casey and PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel for re-election. Morris said that Casey's record shows support for the interests of the 140,000 Teamsters living in PA. The Teamsters believe both candidates' records reflect concern for working-class people.

headline: What's fertile and environmentall sound?  Sewage sludge
abstract: A Compost of sewage and sludge from Washington and its suburbs is being used to fertilize soil at the White House.  Although it is popular to use sludge this way in Washington, returning sludge to the earth is controversial in Pittsburgh.  In Pittsburgh, some believe that sludge should be incinerated to generate electricity, while others argue that such incineration is bad for the environment and say that sludge should be used as fertilizer instead.

headline: Abortion Pill:
abstract: The American Medical Association has announced it favors testing and possible use of the controversial French abortion pill, RU-486. The Association maintains the pill may be a safer and cheaper method of abortion. John Wilke, President of National Right to Life found this policy stance outrageous.

headline: Study Finds Addicts Must Wait for Care
abstract: According to a National Association of State Drug and Alcohol Treatment Disorders survey, addicts must wait an average of 45 days for residental treatment.

headline: Shameful verbal scores
abstract: The editorial notes that verbal scores on the SAT are lower than ever, at an average 424 out of 800.  It stresses that schools and parents need to take more interest and spend more effort educating children even in simple reading and writing.

headline: Our Opinion: Differences Resolved: DER, Harhunt Together
abstract: Judge Chester Harhunt and the PA Department of Environmental Resources (DER) are finally in agreement about the Keystone Scranton Sewer Authority's transportation of leachate from the Keystone Landfill.  DER and Judge Harhunt have clashed over ways to transport the leachate from the landfill in the past.

headline: O'Hara man sues PennDOT over son's death
abstract: The father of an O'Hara man who was killed during a landslide on Freeport Rod has sued PennDOT for failing to properly maintain the road. He is seeking damages for the loss of projected earnings and his son's mental and physical suffering.

headline: Group Will Help Victimes of AIDS
abstract: Home 4, a group of Lambertville, New Jersey volunteers will help AIDS victims find housing.

headline: Welfare Savings
abstract: At a Lebanon Valley Chamber of Commerce breakfast, Ed Adams, manager of the Lebanon Job Center, and executive director of the Lebanon County Assistance Office Francis Ulishney outlined services for job seekers and employers. The Assistance office has saved the county over $1 million in helping to place people receiving assistance in jobs. However, medical assistance needs are dramatically increasing.

headline: State officials hear complaints about Warminster
abstract: Two officials from the state Department of Community Affairs listened to complaints about the town of Warminster and possible investigations into the town's administration, specifically concerning money management.

headline: PUC Approves $40 million Bell refund, nixes 911 funding
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) approved a $40.2 million refund for Bell of PA customers who used deceptive marketing practices to sell optional services. The plan to use a chunk of the money for an emergency telephone system was rejected.

headline: EMS union protests job cuts
abstract: Pittsburgh's paramedic union is upset with Mayor Sophie Masloff's plan to cut positions in the Emergency Medical Services Bureau as a part of her 1991 budget. The city believes the cuts won't impair emergency service or employee performance in light of an aggressive public education campaign and rescheduling in the bureau. Richard McClelland, president of the Fraternal Association of Professional Paramedics, said the plan will put even more strain on an understaffed and overworked corps of paramedics.

headline: London: I'm Not Out to Destroy Republican Party
abstract: Herbert London, NY gubernatorial candidate for the Conservative Party, attacked the Republican candidate for acting "wimpish," and says he [London] will revive the Republican Party.

headline: Televised debate fails to rivet GOP faithful
abstract: Few of the 475 gathered Republicans at the Penn Harris Motor Inn yesterday for the Cumberland County Republican Committee's annual campaign dinner were actually watching the gubernatorial debate between PA Governor Casey and Republican challenger Barbara Hafer.  The majority chatted with each other and ate.

headline: A difficult line to draw
abstract: While we find it unaccepatable that some Pennsylvania employers are not sensitive to the needs of working mothers, we also think that a whole-hearted embrace of the parental leave bill will hurt small business.  The bill, as currently drafted, requires employers with 10 or more workers to provide 18 weeks of unpaid leave in any two year period and calls for them to continue health benefits as well.  The law should be amended so that it protects small businesses.

headline: Abortion protesters sent to state prison
abstract: Two abortion protesters were convicted and sentenced to up to two years of prison time for blocking the entrance to a clinic and refusing to promise not to participate in further demonstrations if placed on probation.

headline: Summer alert: Best rabies protection is prevention
abstract: The concern for rabies increases with the warmer weather, the state total so far is 218 cases. The PA Health Department officials state that the most recent human death to rabies in PA was in 1984. Any bite from a wild animal should be immediately cleansed with soap and large amounts of water and medical attention should be received, physicians must report bites to the proper authorities.

headline: She says it's time the educational system was changed
abstract: Letter to the editor upset about school board actions. They voted for teacher raises against voters wishes. They also make school like a prison. The author class for the board to resign so they can be replaced with people who will do what's best for the children. She also calls for taxpayers to unite against the board.

headline: Out-of-state trash isn't the problem
abstract: The editorial says that despite the "drama" of trash-laundering scandals about bringing out-of-state trash into PA and who did what wrong, the problem is the questionable legality and wisdom of restricting out-of-state trash in the first place.

headline: Older drivers face restraints. One in four tested can't pass.
abstract: Twenty six percent of senior citizen drivers in PA randomly selected to take medical and vision tests have not had their licenses removed and another 23 percent have had restrictions placed on their licenses. As the result of a state law requiring insurance companies to offer discounts to older drivers who take accredited courses, some are taking classes such as 55 Alive, sponsored by the American Association of Retired Persons.

headline: Governors Drugs
abstract: Governors oppose relinquishing federal funds to their states to fight the drug problem and praise President Bush's willingness to increase his budget request to combat drugs, but Philadelphia Mayor Goode wants funding for cities.

headline: WIC Needs Funding
abstract: In the opinion of the editors, though PA is doing a good job on a state level in ensuring the federal food supplement program, Women, Infants and Children (WIC), is doing well, the US Congress could allocate more money to the program. In PA, a bidding system for such items as baby formula allows the state to cover over 22,000, with a plan to increase that number. Other states however have not fared so well as Congress continues to allocate money to other projects.

headline: state program to offer some cheaper mortgages
abstract: PA Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll announced a $100 million program yesterday that will provide assistance to first-time home buyers, single-parent families and veterans get a cheaper mortgage when buying a home.

headline: PUC seeks to fine Bell for service cutoffs
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission plans to fine Bell of Pennsylvania for improper cutoffs of phone service to dozens of customers who were behind on their bills, though some had already paid the overdue bills or had not yet reached a mutually agreed deadline.  The PUC legal staff determined that Bell should be fined $1.1 million for the violations.

headline: Endorsements
abstract: The article lists the editorial board's endorsements for PA representatives in the U.S. House, PA House, PA Senate, governor and statewide ballot questions. It also lists endorsements for New Jersey representatives in the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statewide ballot questions.

headline: Long-awaited arts center in limbo
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey met with Pocono lawmakers to discuss obtaining state support to build a year-round center to host conventions. The state has passed capital budgets authorizing $17 million to build orchestra shell but Casey has to approve it. Current capital authorization gives the state Department of Environmental Resources oversight to build arts center.

headline: Temple and faculty resume negotiations
abstract: Officials at Temple University and its faculty union met for about 10 hours yesterday and planned to begin negotiations again today, bringing about the first bargaining session since a Common Pleas Court Judge ordered professors back to work on Oct. 2, which ended a 29-day strike.  The issues of wages, benefits, and the professors' pay rate for make-up classes still need to be discussed and resolved.

headline: Medical waste five-feet thick
abstract: PA Department of Environmental Resources officials are attempting to discover the origins of medical waste along the banks of the Auburn Dam.  Originally, inspectors thought the waste was from a private resident, but upon more serious examination investigators realized that the extent of the waste and the seriousness of the problem was much greater than originally thought.  The DER and local residents staged a two-day cleanup of the Dam; investigations into the source of the waste continue.

headline: Abortion rights supporters, from left, Mary Robinson
abstract: A photo depicts abortion rights supporters Mary Robinson, Celeste Behrend, and Dave Tessitor holding a sign thanking Project Multitude anti-abortion demonstrators for coming out. For each picket displayed, $183.00 was pledged to the Vivian Campbell Fund of Women's Health Services, Inc., the abortion clinic being protested.

headline: Tainted eye drops and tragic results
abstract: An eye drop concoction made by a Pittsburgh pharmacy was infected with bacteria and has lead to blindness and eye infection in those, usually patients recovering from cataract surgery, who have used it. The PA Health Department and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration are investigating the pharmacy. State law prohibits the manufacture or sale of any drug that has been adulterated or prepared in unsanitary conditions that cause contamination.

headline: Smaller classes
abstract: The editorial board states that children's' declining performance in school is the US' most profound problem. A host of factors contribute to this, such as "the breakup of the family, working parents and school curricula overloaded with educationally irrelevant material." State Representative Ron Cowell is sponsoring a bill which would create state-assistance incentives for smaller classes in kindergarten through 3rd grade, the time range at which children are more likely to retain basic knowledge.

headline: pa financial briefs
abstract: Officials from the Ambridge Water Authority and Harmony borough will meet to discuss hydrant fees, maintenance and unpaid bills. The authority has claimed it will shut off water if it does not receive payment for unpaid bills.

headline: On first day of new fares, riders put in their 25 cents
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority increased its base fare by 25 cents, which most riders opposed, but some of whom believe it was necessary. John Pepe of Center City Philadelphia believes that SEPTA needs more state funding, while Leslie Willis believes that SEPTA's general manager Louis Gambaccini could stand to take a pay cut. SEPTA's $667.3 million budget for the upcoming fiscal year included $2.5 million in service cuts.

headline: Green Light To Evict Drug Trafficker From Public Housing Units
abstract: Senator Roxanne H. Jones said the Senate Urban Affairs and Housing Committee has approved a measure providing for the eviction of drug traffickers from rental units and public housing projects. Jones said the measure is likely to reach PA Governor Robert P. Casey for approval before the end of the legislative session. The bill would allow landlords to terminate the leases of individuals convicted once on drug trafficking charges or convicted twice on drug possession charges, and those who possess drugs on the premises.

headline: Without basics, family survives on the edge
abstract: A profile on a family living in extreme poverty. Cheryl Banks' family was given gifts by a local gift drive, but they are useless to her because she cannot eat them or house herself and her family with them. They do not even have heating in their home. City employees are trying to move her and her family elsewhere. The city was impressed by how she maintained a normal lifestyle under horrible conditions.

headline: Steelers, Pirates team with City on Walkway
abstract: While meeting with Governor Casey, Pittsburgh officials, supported by the Steelers and the Pirates, proposed the building of a ramp from Point State Park to Three Rivers Stadium, arguing for its effectiveness in relieving pedestrian and auto traffic as well as parking hassles during stadium events.

headline: State panel agrees on 911 funding plan
abstract: The PA state Legislature is expected to approve a plan that allows counties to impose telephone-bill surcharges and use the money to buy and operate state-of-the-art 911 systems. Members of the House-Senate conference committee agreed on the plan and under the plan the county governments could recover the costs of implementing emergency telephone systems through the monthly fee on every telephone line in the county.

headline: Erie County GOP Leader Calls it Quits
abstract: Assemblyman Thomas Reynolds is the front runner in a contest to succeed Victor Farley as Erie County GOP chairman.

headline: Lottery Fund going broke; Casey to tap reserve
abstract: PA State Lottery Fund is so close to going broke that PA Governor Robert Casey plans to spend a $120 million reserve to continue paying prescription-drug discounts, property tax rebates, and other benefits to senior citizens. Republican budget analysts believe this would violate a state law that they say freezes the money to ensure public confidence in the Lottery Fund, which finances the programs for the elderly. Without the reserve the Lottery Fund will run out of money to cover a number of programs for the elderly.

headline: Tested in primary, Singel finds easier going in general election
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, who had to borrow money near the end of the May primary election for television ads that he felt would help ensure victory against his opponent, is spending considerably less in the general election, as he and PA Governor Robert Casey are expected to soundly defeat Republican challengers Barbara Hafer and her running mate, Harold Mowery, Jr.

headline: Day cares not just for kidding around
abstract: Two West End day-care centers offer innovative and trend-setting programs.  For Kid's Sake Learning just expanded its school-age program, which includes bilingual lessons, and the Ark II Nursery School just unveiled a pre-kindergarten program for 5 year olds who missed the age cutoff for entering kindergarten.

headline: Abortion showdown a tossup. Tuesday gains, losses split between camps.
abstract: Recent PA legislature elections across the nation saw victories for both abortion-rights and pro-life candidates. The most visible anti-abortion activist in the PA legislature, Stephen F. Freind, was victorious even though he was targeted by the National Abortion Rights Action League. Last year, PA enacted one of the nation's most restrictive abortion laws.

headline: Teens face greater risk of getting AIDS
abstract: Teens' promiscuity puts them at risk for AIDS and tighter blood screening is needed according to the National Academy of Science. High teenage pregnancy rates and drug use makes them a high risk group, since sex and drug use are the two main ways HIV is spread.

headline: State universities, faculty sign ratified pact
abstract: Officials of the State System of Higher Education and leaders of the 4,000-member Association of PA State College and University Faculties met to sign a three-year contract to raise faculty salaries by 20 percent to end a year of negotiations. Other provisions included salary limits for coaching positions, limits on the use of graduate assistants and teaching associates, and the assessment of a representation fee for non-union members.

headline: PA to Philadelphia hasten recycling
abstract: The state would like Philadelphia recycle faster. PA Department of Environmental Resources told officials it is not thrilled with their target date of expanding curbside recycling into the rest of the neighborhoods by February 1992. The entire state is supposed to be recycling by September. The city pushed back its expansion schedule this year in the face of budget problems and uncertainties in ordering special trucks.

headline: On-time expressway vowed
abstract: State officials vowed that the Southern Expressway project, a 7.5 mile highway to the new airport terminal in Pittsburgh, would be finished on time, despite ongoing delays and foreseen obstacles.  PA Governor Casey said that the project will greatly aid Western PA economically.

headline: Green Suggests Plan to End Prisoner Overcrowding in City Hall Cellroom
abstract: Philadelphia Sheriff John Green has proposed renovation in City Hall to reduce overcrowding in the cell room that prisoners use to await trial. Mayor W. Wilson Goode was presented the proposal and his administration has presented a suggestion for a new courthouse that would provide prisoner-holding space.

headline: Without basics, family survives on the edge
abstract: Cheryl Banks has been living for three years in an apartment without heat or water. Her absentee landlord, whom Banks has not seen in over a year, owes $1500 in backtaxes to the city and $1800 in unpaid water bills. City workers in the district of Councilman John F. Street met Banks last month for the first time and are attempting to move her and her children to a low-income housing project through the city's Relocation Program.

headline: Stoystown gets funds
abstract: Picture of PA Representative Leona Telek delivering a check for $7,000 to Stoystown Borough Council. The money will be used to resurface the tennis court at the town's recreation park.

headline: Sunday Grit publishes last edition today
abstract: The nation's original good news newspaper will publish its final Sunday edition. Local competition is the root cause. It will continue to publish its upbest weekly. It began being published in 1882. It's peaked circulation was once 1.5 million but now is only 400,000.

headline: Evans for Penna.
abstract: The editorial board hopes that anti-Philadelphia sentiment won't affect the vote in the PA House over whether Representative Dwight Evans (D., Phila) becomes the new chairman of the appropriations committee, saying his election would strengthen both the Democratic party and state government. The board suggests that details are need on the budget cuts and tax proposals raised in Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode's financial rescue plan. The board believes that city leaders need to build political consensus around the rescue plan, including more support by PA Governor Robert P. Casey.

headline: Low Voter Turnout Likely
abstract: Discusses the upcoming gubernatorial election and how the issue of abortion has driven much of the politics leading up to the campaign.  Governor Casey has signed one of the strictest abortion laws in the country and is strictly pro-life while his likely Republican challenger, state Auditor General Barbara Hafer is pro-choice.

headline: The Barbara Hafer Victory Dance
abstract: The cartoon shows a defeated-looking woman lying on the ground after having tripped, calling it the "Barbara Hafer Victory Dance".

headline: Dunmore Official Seeks Status of Keystone Landfill
abstract: In an effort to determine the status of the Keystone Sanitary Landfill, Michael J. Carr, chairman of Dunmore's Department of Public Works, wrote a letter to the PA Department of Environmental Resources.  Knowing the status of the landfill will help with future budgeting and waste-disposal arrangements; Dunmore offcials assumed the site would be open this January.

headline: Abortion-rights advocates rally
abstract: Abortion-rights advocates rallied outside the Delaware County Pro-Life Coalition offices.

headline: Temple firm on payments for health benefits
abstract: Temple University, which is facing an ongoing strike by its professors, is remaining firm on its position that all employees should pay a $260 co-payment for healthcare benefits, so as to drive healthcare costs down.

headline: Sobering statistics for colleges
abstract: With college tuition costs continuing to rise, state funding decreasing, and high school graduation rates declining, colleges will have to start paying more attention to controlling costs and providing better undergrad educations if they hope to continue filling their classrooms to capacity.

headline: Pa. halts school's pit burning
abstract: Moravian Academy in Bethlehem Twp. has been asked by PA Department of Environmental Resources officials to stop burning refuse in pits on campus, a practice the school officials say has been going on for decades.

headline: Opinion on Route 30? Let 'em have it
abstract: York County citizens will have the chance to tell the PA Department of Transportation how they feel about the Route 30 bypass. The meetings are scheduled by the York County Planning Commission.

headline: Guards: New riot brewing
abstract: Some officials at the Camp Hill prison have warned of an outbreak of violence on the Oct. 25 anniversary of last year's riots, though prison spokesman John Palakovich said that despite warnings, the prison is secure and under control.

headline: $20,000 grant or Tableland Services Inc.
abstract: PA State Secretary of Community Affairs Karen A Miller has announced more than $2.4 million in employment and community conservation grants, including one for Somerset County. The grants are designed to help community-based organizations across PA develop and expand delivery of grass-roots human service programs. Tableland Services Inc. will receive $20,000 to provide, pre-vocational training, job counseling, skills training, and remedial educational classes for 25 low-income residents.

headline: Strittmatter hoping to get state money for local stadium
abstract: PA Rep. Strittmatter hopes the House will approve $11.4 million for a Lancaster baseball stadium and franchise. PA Governor Robert Casey would have to approve, which Lancaster Mayor Janice Stork says may be likely in an election year. Strittmatter admitted it would be better to fund the project privately. He has been working with the Bring Baseball Back to Lancaster Committee to write House Bill 2556, which includes the request for funds in a match from the PA Department of Community Affairs.

headline: Sunday Grit publishes last edition today
abstract: This Sunday marks the last edition of the Sunday Grit, a newspaper traced back to 1882. The decision to cease Sunday publication, though weekly circulation will continue, was made after the Grit's cross-town rival, The Williamsport Sun-Gazette was bought by a West Virginia company that announced it planned to begin publishing a Sunday edition. Stauffer Communications Inc. president John Stauffer said the town is not big enough for two Sunday publications.

headline: Everything's going off without a hitch
abstract: The cartoon depicts the Hafer campaign car traveling down a precarious mountain road, and a GOP trailer coming off it's hitch and falling off a ledge, signifying that Hafer is losing Republican support.

headline: Luksik almost got to be star
abstract: In one reader's opinion, Republican gubernatorial candidate Peg Luksik missed out on being the primary winner because she is not a real Republican. The only reason she ran against Barbara Hafer is because of Hafer's pro-choice stance. Note that she first went to PA Governor Casey as a spokeswoman of the people's concerns, and only went to the Republicans after she was ignored.

headline: The city GOP takes second best
abstract: The author of the article criticizes the Philadelphia GOP for clinging to leader Billy Meehan despite consistent election losses. He suggests that the City Charter, which guarantees the minority party two of the City Council's seven seats, gives the Republican Party no incentive to try very hard in elections. He believes this system weakens the ideal of a two-party government.

headline: Takeover billl advances
abstract: Legislation that denies corporate raiders short-term profits from takerovers, as well as voting rights, passed the state House Business and Commerce Committee.  The bill requires management to consider employee and community interests in deciding takeover offers, and was introduced, in large part, to help Armstrong World Industries fight off a hostile takeover attempt.  Critics of the legislation argue that it insulates bad management from potential sanctions and does nothing to prevent future job losses.

headline: Abortions increase in Pa. in 1989
abstract: The PA Health Department reported that the number of abortions performed in PA rose by 1.1% between 1988 and 1989.  The Health Department also released other statistics, including that over 94% of the abortions were performed during the first 14 weeks of pregnancy, and that women between age 20 and 24 accounted for 33% of the total abortions.

headline: The hidden drug is the most dangerous
abstract: Calling for more attention to be paid to the problem of alcoholism. While the drug war is necessary, people are not enough aware of the dangers of alcohol.

headline: Sony, government units agree on taxation rates
abstract: Southmoreland School District will receive $753,000 each year for three years, among other school districts, from Sony Engineering and Manufacturing of America (SEMA) in lieu of taxes, a decision made by the Southmoreland School Board, the Westmoreland County Planning Commission, the Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority and PA Secretary of Commerce Ray Christman.. Sony will lease a plant owned by the Development Authority at a cost of $21 million over the next 20 years. The district previously received funds from Volkswagen.

headline: Pollution law gets tougher
abstract: The revised Clear Air Act mandates that the US Environmental Protection Agency set air pollution standards for coke plants. The law orders the industry to meet extremely stringent emission standards based on the impact that those fumes have on the health of a plant's neighbors. Congress did give the coke industry to delay those standards for 30 years. To take advantage of the deadline plants must reduce their emission to the level that can be achieved by the best plant.

headline: Opinions differ on transit summit
abstract: South-Eastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority (SEPTA) officials and PA Senator Edwin G. Holl ignored requests from commissioners from Bucks and Montgomery counties for a transit summit with PA Governor Robert P. Casey to discuss SEPTA's growing financial troubles.  Senator Holl believes the two commissioners should have contacted local legislators before going to the Governor.

headline: Guida drug-case answers lead to more questions
abstract: New information of the federal investigation into alleged cocaine use of Richard Guida may raise as many questions as it has answers. A government request to withdraw a plea agreement in which Guida admits to using cocaine from 1983 through 1989 was accepted by US District Judge Edwin Kosik. Some questions raised are: Why did an internal investigation fail to uncover his drug use, why did it take three years to start an investigation, are there any other public officials suspected in the case, and why are federal authorities spending so much time focusing on a cocaine use investigation and not larger cases?

headline: $5 million in Franklin Field improvements needed for bid
abstract: Diane P. Hovenkamp, vice president of the Philadelphia Sports Congress, estimated that improvements to Franklin Field at the University of Pennsylvania to attract the 1994 World Cup will cost about $5 million. Hosting qualifying games in Philadelphia would have a positive economic impact on the region. The improvements include adding backs to the bleachers and making the field natural grass.

headline: SU arts center part of state's latest wish list
abstract: The PA Legislature's $2.2 billion state capital budget, it's wish list of spending projects, was sent to PA Governor Robert P. Casey for approval. The governor's office, which decides which projects become reality, spends only about $150 million annually. The list includes improvements at Shippensburg University, including a new arts center, Penn State's Mont Alto campus, Scotland School for Veterans Children and South Mountain Restoration Center. Funds are also proposed for a new welcome center on I-81 in Franklin County and an expansion of an information center in Fulton County.

headline: Cicippio family marks anniversary
abstract: The Cicippio family observed the 4th anniversary of Joseph Cicippio's kidnapping in Beirut, where he is still held hostage.  They preserve the hope that he will someday be released.

headline: Ex-Bush Aide Denies Wrongdoing in Lobbying for S&L Buyer
abstract: A former aide to then-Vice President Bush, Robert Thompson, is being investigated for any illegal role he may have had in James Fail's takeover of 15 Texas S&Ls.  Officials say that the deals were not conducted "on the up and up."

headline: Luzerne County Results
abstract: The chart shows the voting outcomes in the gubernatorial and PA House and Senate elections by political party in Luzerne County.

headline: The Deal That Almost Was
abstract: A map of the number of properties delineated by ward, owned by the bankrupt Harrisburg Restoration Association, Ltd. Is paired with a photo of developer John O. Vartan, who was attempting to purchase 450 of properties from the Association.

headline: Extension of Federal Contract Eyed
abstract: A ceremony was held at Grunman to commemorate the manufacturing of its 50,000th mail truck, which was part of a contract the company received to manufacture 99,150 delivery trucks.  At the ceremony, two assistant postmaster generals announced that the U.S. Postal Service is interested in extending its 1.2 billion dollar contract with Grunman; the postal service is very interested in the firm's newly developed, four-wheel-drive mail truck.

headline: Abortions increase statewide
abstract: The number of abortions in PA climbed by more than 1% in 1989, but  Bucks County's abortion rate decreased, according to statistics released by the PA Department of Health.

headline: Top health insurers' rates climbing
abstract: Capital Blue Cross and Pennsylvania Blue Shield, the state's two largest health insurance providers, have raised rates consistently over the past decade to keep up with skyrocketing costs of medical care.

headline: Special ed funds uncertain
abstract: Centennial Schools Superintendent Harry Harhigh is upset about the 1990-1991 budget because of the uncertainty of the state funding for special education programs. The PA Department of Education has said that there will be no special education reimbursement, which is a loss of $1.4 million.

headline: Packer employees hit the road to clean up trash, litter
abstract: The weekend, some Robert Packer Hospital employees will be participating in cleaning up areas of roadway as part of PennDOT's Adopt-A-Highway program.  66 employees from 11 departments will be helping pick up little from roadsides for an hour an a half on Saturday.

headline: Optimism fades for highways
abstract: In 1950, following WWII, the Montgomery County Planning Commission designed an expressway system to handle projected traffic congestion. The expressway never materialized says director Arthur Loeben. It received support from PA Rep. Robert Godshall, who said it would keep truck traffic out of municipalities. Local officials have opposed roadway proposals to protect private properties. Dan Miller of the PA Department of Transportation says the '70s saw many proposals die as a result.

headline: Guida was deceptive about officials' use of cocaine, FBI says
abstract: Former state prosecutor Richard Guida candidly identified his drug activity with a high-ranking public official, but flunked a lie-detector test when he said he knew of no cocaine use by any other state or local official, federal investigators said here in court. He lied to conceal two ex-girlfriends' drug use.

headline: 2 firms, ousted by Rouse project, file suit alleging broken promises
abstract: Two businesses forced to move by a developer are filing suit, saying that he didn't live up to his promises of financial reimbursement for moving and relocation expenses.

headline: Supervisors seeks changes in bill on impact fees
abstract: Township supervisors across the state are levying for the PA legislature to change a bill so that it favors them more than builders on the issue of impact fees.

headline: Delco firm 1st in US to get Iran's permission to help rebuild
abstract: The Iranian government will allow a Delaware County construction executive to lead a group of 13 Americans to Iran to build temporary shelters for victims of the June 21 earthquake. Film Applicators of North America uses polyethylene to build temporary shelters for storage and construction sites. A State Department official said that he knew of no similar US effort that Iranians have allowed. The policy is normally to be hostile to Americans.

headline: Ex-official discusses early years
abstract: Christ Zervanos headed the PAe Bureau of Labor Relations, the commonwealth's voice in Act 195 for the first 16 years of its 20 year life. He remembers a time before the act and believes the past 20 years under the act have lead to mutual growth between both unions and the state.

headline: Lynch vows to defeat party-backed candidate
abstract: Longtime state Sen. Francis Lynch said he would run for his seat despite receiving a no-confidence vote from Democratic party leaders in the area.

headline: The governor's race is run in the media
abstract: Because the floods of TV ads for incumbent PA Governor Casey do not mention his challenger Barbara Hafer, and Hafer doesn't yet have enough money for TV ads, much of the campaign is being run through the media and through interactions between the campaigns rather than the actual candidates.

headline: Albany Urges Making Cuts in Local Aid
abstract: In Albany, New York state leaders have proposed a 1 percent cut in financial assistance to local governments to help fill a projected 1.5 billion dollar budget gap for 1990-91.  The measure would save the state approximately 200 million by cutting 1 percent of the state's contributions to schools, Medicaid, revenue sharing and other programs.

headline: Abortion's unlikely lightning rod rallies.
abstract: President of Planned Parenthood, Faye Wattleton will speak at the 60th anniversary dinner of the Pittsburgh chapter. Last week, the organization asked the Supreme Court to strike down federal regulations that require recipients of federal family planning money to tell nothing about abortion except that it is wrong. Earlier in the year, AT&T Co. cut off its annual donation to the organization.

headline: Tuberculosis making 'shameful' comeback
abstract: Tuberculosis cases are up 9% compared to a year ago according to the Centers for Disease Control. Drugs to fight TB were developed three decades ago and the disease has been on the decline since then, until now. A part of the disease's resurgence is due to the increasing number of cases of AIDS, and AIDS patients' susceptibility to TB.

headline: Special education funding in York County
abstract: The PA legislature voted to switch to a reimbursement system of excess special education costs, which has caused costs to spiral since it is a blank check system. Apparently if one looks at the actual numbers there is less money flowing into the system. Editorial shows the cash flow decreases in special-education from the 1989-90 school year to the 1990-91. It averages a 46.3% decrease all over the county.

headline: Panel backs water-rate revision over Goode officials’ objections
abstract: A Philadelphia City Council committee challenged the Goode administration’s authority over water rates and approved changes to give residents more of a voice in determining their water and sewer bilks. The Rules Committee sided with Community Legal Services and the Consumers Education and Prospective Association to urge the council to adopt measures to curb the rate setting powers of the water commissioner. Under the proposed law the examiner would issue an opinion on the commissioner’s suggested rates and then the PA Water Department would be required to adopt the recommendations of the hearing officer unless they were without material support.

headline: ORO Expected to Get Nod In Rail Bid
abstract: A private consortium's proposal to design and build a high-speed rail across the state was up for a vote before the Ohio High Speed Rail Authority. It is expected that the Ohio Railway organization will be named to determine if such a rail link is feasible.

headline: Guilty
abstract: Two former state prosecutors pled guilty to cocaine charges yesterday.  Richard Guida pled guilty to cocaine distribution, and W. Michael Trant pled guilty to cocaine possession.

headline: A Downtown whipping boy
abstract: PA Governor Casey vetoed a $105-million dollar expansion proposal for the Pittsburgh David L. Lawrence Convention Center which some vendors and city officials say is vital for the center, ranked 41st in space for exhibitors, to remain competitve. However, some vendors complained that catering and management at the Center are too much to deal with, even writing a letter to Mayor Sophie Masloff.

headline: Tampella Keeler upgrade gets go-ahead
abstract: Tampella Keeler, an industrial boiler manufacture, has decided to proceed with a $10 million modernization of its plant in the city's industrial park. One factor in the decision was an agreement reached late last week with the union that represents 125 of the company's 220 workers, where a contract was reached till 1995.

headline: null
abstract: A photo depicts PA Governor Robert Casey presenting a plaque and Savings Bond. On hand for the ceremony are Smokey Bear and Director of the PA Department's Office of Natural Resources Terry Fabian.

headline: Expect City Loan Request Next Week, Pension Board Told
abstract: As the city of Philadelphia warned employees of missed paychecks as the city continues its cash crunch, major parties work behind the scenes. Merrill Lynch, PA Governor Robert Casey, Mayor Wilson Goode, the Philadelphia Board of Pensions and Retirement, and the PA Public School Employees Retirement Board met to negotiate a short term cash infusion. Finance Director Elizabeth Reveal's representative said inability to resolve repayment terms could scuttle the transaction.

headline: Lyons to run again for 96th district House seat
abstract: Democratic City Councilman Jon Lyons announced he will run for the 96th district state house seat being vacated by Republican Marvin Miller Jr.

headline: The never-ending scandal
abstract: Continuing scandals in the judicial system, particularly concerning the Roofers' Union, are providing an even more compelling case for judicial reform.

headline: In reckless pursuit of wealth, mankind is poisoning earth's environment
abstract: This article asks if anything can be done to save our environment.  While we are aware of the problems that exist and the actions we must take to solve them, the author is not optimistic that we are willing to make the sacrifices necessary to save the environment.  We are too wedded to pecuniary, rather than spiritual, interests.

headline: ACLU wants official punished for prayer
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union requested that Downingtown High School board president Robert G. Elderedge write an essay about the separation of church and state. US District Judge J. Hutton Jr. had asked for prayer to be eliminated from graduation after a suit was filed by two students, but he slipped in a prayer.

headline: Women who eat large meals said socially unappealing
abstract: A study conducted by researchers from Lafayette College found that it's not socially advantageous for women to eat large meals in public. In the study, a woman was filmed eating four meals of different sizes and compositions. Student volunteers who viewed the film rated the woman as significantly more feminine and having more social appeal when eating a small meal.

headline: Special education rules will take effect July 1
abstract: The PA House is preparing for an overhaul of the state's special education system. The PA Senate rejected the regulations, but the House took no action so the rules will take effect on July 1. House Minority Leader Matthew J. Ryan said he couldn't understand why the regulations will go into effect since they were rejected by both chambers' Education Committees, and the PA Independent Regulatory Review Commission.

headline: Panel urged to help keep mob out of waste industry
abstract: Attorney General Ernie Preate said the state needs to begin checking backgrounds of waste haulers that use PA landfills to keep organized crime out of the nearly $1 billion-a-year business.

headline: PA Financial News
abstract: The chief of the Souteastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority says he is reorganizing the mass transit agency in order to provide better service.

headline: Hafer criticizes prison staffing.
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate and PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer criticized low guard staffing and inmate overcrowding as part of a three-year review of the Department of Corrections released this week. Hafer said the department relied too heavily on overtime pay to make up for its low staffing and urged it to correct 58 percent overcrowding. Corrections spokesman Ben Livingood criticized the report as politically-timed.

headline: A Hot Time in the Old Town. Center City's Swinging Again.
abstract: The editorial board notes that hundreds of new shops, luxury hotels and mini-hotels are being joined by dozens of new restaurants in Philadelphia, giving the city a vibrant night-life.

headline: The city has a housing plan
abstract: A response from the Philadelphia Director of Housing and Community Development Edward Schwartz to criticisms against his agency for a lack of a comprehensive housing plan, which he claims they have.

headline: Ann's secret weapon: The aunts
abstract: Ann Richard's victory over Clayton Williams for the Texas governorship is credited to her popular appeal in the female constituency and her ability to raise money without turning to corporations. William's campaign is estimated to have spent $37 million, overshadowing Richards' $11 million campaign.

headline: Expenses not to Hafer's taste
abstract: PA Auditor General and Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer accused PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel of using state funds totaling $1,995 for two events not related to state business, which Singel denied, though has reimbursed the state "to remove even the slightest doubt." Singel also accused Hafer of manipulating the Auditor General's position for political motives, as she found time amid a huge backlog of audits to look into the Lieutenant Governor's office only week before an election.

headline: Making the state more efficient
abstract: PA Representative George Saurman has betrayed his own words. Saurman has come up with Penn Search, a way to help state government control allocate spending. He doesn't want any ideas too irrational i.e. anything to do with reforming the PA Legislature.

headline: The November of our discontent. State voters send message to Capitol.
abstract: At least 15 state legislative incumbents were defeated in a move that some say is a reflection of the national "anti-incumbency movement". Analysts say the election results could force an examination of legislative perks and benefits, campaign finance reforms and term limits. Republicans suggested their incumbents were hurt by GOP gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer's poor showing against PA Governor Robert P. Casey.

headline: Woman accused of juggling Lake sewer accounts implicates 2 officials
abstract: Former Harveys Lake Municipal Authority secretary Gloria Anne Marie Evans accused two board members of directing her to credit unpaid sewer accounts.  She accused authority President John McManus and authority Treasurer Terry Jones of instructing her to mark sewer accounts as paid, even though sewer fees has not been paid.  Correale Stevens, Luzerne County District Attorney, said that his office will investigate the allegations and will follow up on any provable evidence.

headline: Lead Peril Restated At Throop
abstract: Throop residents living near the former Mayor Battery plant gathered Thursday to hear Dr. John F. Rosen, professor of pediatrics at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine at New York City's Montefiore Medical Center discuss test results from first phase of lead testing for residents.

headline: Adams re-elected
abstract: Harvey Adams Jr. has been elected to an eight two-year term as president of the Pittsburgh NAACP. Adams was opposed by Edward Blackmon. He is also director of police for the city Housing Authority.

headline: 'War on AIDS'; Senate bill deserves support
abstract: The editorial board supports the U.S. Senate's passage of a bill to provide $2.9 billion to help finance AIDS care and support facilities in cities that are hardest hit by the epidemic.  The board also criticizes President Bush's inaction on the issue.

headline: SSHE chancellor asks employees to join budget fight
abstract: The PA System of Higher Education (SSHE) Chancellor James McCormick is seeking the aid of 10,300 employees at the 14 state-owned schools to lobby for a budget increase.  The request comes at a time of a tight state budget and PA Governor Robert P. Casey's administration hopes that that SSHE will understand the budget constraints they face.

headline: Parsons named to DER post
abstract: PA Department of Environmental Resources Regional Director A. Paul Franklin announced the appointment of William P. Parsons as assistant regional director of the DER's Williamsport office. Parsons' duties will include administering environmental protection programs in 14 counties in north central PA.

headline: Pa. Fall/Winter travel  package available now
abstract: The 1990-91 "Pennsylvania, America Starts Here" fall/winter travel package is now available through the state Department of Commerce. The free package includes a 24-page travel guide-book to PA, a vacation and trip planner, and an official PA Department of Transportation state highway map.

headline: He Wants AIDS Decision Before Death
abstract: Attorney Clarence Billy Cain sued Hyatt Legal Services for demoting him because he has AIDS hopes a federal judge will rule on the case before he dies.

headline: Affordable housing is scarce. Study, Economy here may suffer.
abstract: A study by the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission found that in 81 percent of the municipalities contained in the PA/New Jersey region, median-priced housing units were unaffordable for families earning the median income. Among the detrimental effects on employers this affordability gap will cause are mandated higher wages, the need to assist employees in finding housing, lower attractiveness to young workers, decreased productivity from commuters, and increased employee tardiness, absenteeism and turnover. PA is not mandated to provide specific quotes of affordable housing by price, only to have zoning laws that permit different kinds of development.

headline: The dream of their own home becomes nightmare
abstract: Four New Frontiers Real Estate agents were convicted of conspiracy and filing false reports with the Department of Housing and Urban Development for government-insured mortgages. New Frontiers improperly backed mortgages for low-income workers that ended in foreclosures by exaggerating their incomes. The buyers were left with debilitating credit ratings.

headline: null
abstract: Gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer attributed her election loss to a lack of grass-roots pro-choice organization, the major parties' reluctance to support female candidates and PA Governor Robert Casey's popularity. Hafer said she would not rule out a second try for the governorship in 1994, expecting that by then, the state will be in a bad financial situation.

headline: Ex-senator gives up seat, not power
abstract: Former PA Senator Jenry Hager is speculated to have more power now than when he was representing Lycoming County. He is the president of the PA Insurance Federation and is one of the registered lobbyists in Harrisburg. He is considered one of the most influential lobbyist around.

headline: Mall Option Extensions Sought
abstract: Local officials and Mayor Jim Collins, PA Governor Robert Casey, US Rep. Joseph McDade, and former Governor William Scranton were present to negotiate property for a mall. Property owners were offered an extended 6 months of sales agreements and 8 percent interest on purchase prices. Developers want more than 6 months, and await a PA Supreme Court ruling on litigation between property owners and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. Financing was secured from the Public School Employees Retirement Board.

headline: The President and Politics of the Flag
abstract: The White House appears to be playing "good cop" "bad cop" over a constitutional amendment banning flag desecration. President Bush was criticized when he visited a flag factory in the campaign against Democratic Presidential nominee Michael Dukakis. Chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee Edward J. Rollins supports using the flag amendment as a values issue, but some Republicans think it has lost steam since the Supreme Court ruling.

headline: Want a Comfortable Old Age?  Plan for Care, Experts Advise
abstract: With the average cost of nursing-home care reaching 30,000 per year, experts agree that individuals should plan early for long-term care.  Experts say that even middle-aged persons should familiarize themselves with Government and private programs so they have enough information to make an informed decision about care.

headline: Killing off health-cost panel won't solve much
abstract: Edward Hibbard of Delaware Valley Business Coalition on Health in Philadelphia criticizes PA Senator Richard A. Tilghman's legislation to terminate funding for the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council.  He hopes that the support of business, labor, and the insurance/hospital industries will persuade Senator Tilghman and the legislature to continue funding for the council.

headline: AIDS discrimination often lurks behind cloak of compassion
abstract: AIDS advocates say patterns of discrimination are changing as overt bias is replaced by subtle prejudices involving denial of basic health care. Many AIDS discrimination are probably not reported. Only 149 case of 13,000 went on to court. One reason is that many problems are handled by state or local anti-discrimination agencies.

headline: Washington Hospital Workers End Strike
abstract: Dietary workers, nurses aides, technicians, and other staff members at Washington Hospital ended their strike  and won a pay raise.

headline: State education
abstract: Officials say that PA's public schools have improved over the past 4 years due to the hard work of teachers and administrators, not as much because of PA Governor Casey's actions. Casey's administration did advance several education programs and teachers' minimum salaries increased from $6,000 to $18,500, but local property owners had to pick up a lot of the slack in local taxes.

headline: Pennvest loan approval clears way for projects
abstract: The Municipal Authority of Ralpho Twp. will hold meetings with contractors to organize two upcoming projects, since yesterday members of the Pennvest Board of Directors authorized a $486,698 low-interest loan for the authority. The money will be used to fund two projects, one for painting a large storage tank and the other making repairs and replacements of lines in Elysburg's water distribution system.

headline: Pa. Turnpike gears up for Labor Day travelers
abstract: The PA Turnpike is readying for busy roads during Labor Day weekend, opening all possible lanes for traffic.  State Police are also gearing up for the weekend, with efforts to crack down on the seatbelt law and increased patrol cars.

headline: Helping East bloc police move to a different beat
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner Williams spoke yesterday to the leaders of Czechoslovakia's national police.  Eastern bloc countries with new governments are seeking to change the reputation of their police system.

headline: Also moving general news circuits
abstract: A deal for a stadium for the Philadelphia Flyers and 76ers on the site of JFK Stadium is nearly complete, with assurance to PA Governor Robert Casey teams will remain in PA. Philadelphia Deputy Commerce Director Christopher Cashman said there are no guarantees. The stadium, with its 120 luxury boxes, is one of 3 National Basketball Associatoin arenas designed to provide teams income. The city and state have agreed to fund construction, though Philadelphia's finances are shaky.

headline: The Mall
abstract: Money is the only real issue hindering plans for the proposed $85 million Lackawanna Avenue Mall

headline: null
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey cut the ribbon for a 2.5 mile section of the Bayfront Parkway in Erie, a $20 million project that is expected to help lure jobs and tourists the Erie waterfront. Casey also participated in the groundbreaking of two other highway projects, while his opponent in the upcoming election, Republican Barbara Hafer, was in State College and Altoona for media interviews and a fund-raiser.

headline: Ex-state Sen. Zemprelli Indicted
abstract: Former Democratic state Senator Zemprelli, along with four others, was indicted on charges associated with conspiracy and defrauding investors of over $57 million over 10 years.

headline: Mandatory pension contribution lowered. County reduces amount to 5%.
abstract: The Dauphin County retirement board voted to reduce the mandatory contribution that workers must make to their retirement funds from 9 percent to 5 percent. Employees could still contribute up to 15 percent, but only the 5 percent mandatory amount would be a tax write-off, said County Controller Thomas E. Washic. The retirement board was also asked to increase the cost-of-living rate by 25 retirees, which officials said the board was unlikely to grant.

headline: The Real Bob Casey Committee
abstract: The clipping is a picture of PA Governor Robert Casey and an invitation to a "Homecoming" celebration for Casey on Oct. 6 at the Montage Mountain Ski Lodge.  The event is being put on by The Real Bob Casey Committee, and tickets are $50.

headline: Bill targets deceptive use of mail
abstract: A bill under consideration in the U.S. Senate would give the U.S. Postal Service new power to prosecute individuals who mail documents that appear to be federal documents but are not.  The bill is designed to protect senior citizens from being taken advantage of, and was drafted largely in response to mailings distributed by several groups that former U.S. Representative Mark Siljander joined after losing his re-election bid to Congress. One of the mailings asked seniors to contribute to a fund to fight the Catostrophic Health Tax.

headline: Limit Care to Curb Med Cost?
abstract: The editorial board reports that for more than a decade, government and private industry have unsuccessfully tried to restrict quickly increasing health-care costs. Some Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs) are limiting or eliminating coverage for those they think may require extensive medical treatment. The rise in health-care costs has been reflected in increases in the cost of health insurance premiums.

headline: Amended 'living will' bill falters in Legislature
abstract: PA Senator John Peterson said that last-minute House amendments killed a bill that would allow Pennsylvanians to end artificial life-support if they become terminally ill. Peterson said the changes in the "living will" legislation raised too many questions that could not be resolved before the end of the legislative session. The most controversial amendment ruled that life-sustaining treatment would have to be continued to a pregnant woman regardless if she had a living will and was strongly supported by anti-abortion advocates.

headline: Well
abstract: The idea of school health centers arose from a June 1986 report by a School District Task Force on Adolosecent Pregnancy and Planning. Deputy superintendent in the division of school management, Helen Faison, said establishment of centers was impeded by decideing what services to offer and how to fund them. Health care officials stressed students will not be charged for services, instead relying on parents' insurance, the government, and center sponsors, such as Pittsburgh New Futures.

headline: State s big on education but short on funding it
abstract: School boards and school administrators are less than enthusiastic when the department of education and the legislature funds any new program to benefits students. They know sooner or later the funding will disappear and they will be left with a program will be left for them to fund and they will become the bad guys when taxes have t be raised. The class reduction program seems to be headed towards the same fate.

headline: Phila. Ash reported in the mail from Haiti
abstract: The Khian Sea sailed the world for two years trying to find a place to dump 13,000 tons Philadelphia's incinerator ash. It dumped 3,000 tons of ash in Haiti labeled as fertilizer and now its being mailed back to the US to the US Environmental Protection Agency and Philadelphia Mayor Goode.

headline: Park-and-ride commuter service planned
abstract: Starting in November, a park-and-ride commuter service to New York City will be established in Monroe County. Russ Albert, president of Marshalls Creek Electric, unveiled his plan for a 100-car park-and-ride lot on Route 447 next to the Pocono Grand Hotel.  The service will charge customers $35/month to park in a reserved space and to use the bus or carpools and a small building housing restrooms and other amenities.

headline: Heroin seized on train
abstract: Amtrak officials and the federal Drug enforcement agency announced the arrest of two men carrying 19 pounds of heroin onboard a Broadway Limited train headed for New York. Amtrak officials said the arrest was their biggest bust ever. Spokesman Cliff Black said officials were becoming more sophisticated and successful in their drug investigations.

headline: Arena upgrade in works. Need for new building hinted.
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council members gave tentative approval to spend $5.9 million in city and county funds to upgrade the Civic Arena as part of an extended lease agreement that will keep the National Hockey League Penguins at the center. Paul Martha, president of the Civic Arena Corporation said the city should consider either expanding or replacing the arena after the new agreement runs out in 1995.

headline: The risks of business with a city on the brink
abstract: Many firms and non-profits that do business with the city of Philadelphia are demanding more assurance of payment or are having to delay or cut back on services due to lack of payment from the city, which is getting closer to insolvency.

headline: null
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode, PA Senator Vince Fumo and PA legislators Dwight Evans and Robert O-Donnell will reveal their proposal to avoid a fiscal collapse in Philadelphia. The plan calls for creation of a local sales tax, cuts in city spending and the floating of long term bonds. The city also plans to get loans from local banks, the PA treasurer and the municipal pension fund. Bell of PA has agreed to pre-pay its taxes to stave off the cash crisis.

headline: Extra Censory Perception
abstract: Cartoon depicts a psychic coming up with the numbers of unreturned census forms in Newark while a chart with tallies to date for some of the major U.S. cities hangs behind the census worker.

headline: Many in GOP can’t back Barbara Hafer
abstract: The Republican state Auditor General Barbara Hafer is getting opposition in her campaign for governor against PA Governor Robert P. Casey from members of the GOP. State House Representatives from the GOP have said that they cannot support Hafer in her campaign, especially because of her pro-choice stance on abortion. PA State Representative Richard Geist said that a liberal faction of the Republican party brought in Barbara Hafer and she has a lot of work to get the support of the more conservative republicans.

headline: The Scene; Comebacks: Who knows what 10 years will bring?
abstract: Columnist Clark DeLeon compares former President Jimmy Carter's dismal term in office to Philadelphia Mayor Wilson Goode's. At least Carter's exit was relatively quick and painless. Goode is a lame duck with 18 months to go. However, it is hard to imagine him winning awards in political obscurity as Jimmy Carter has done.

headline: Gettysburg man will bring new world to Mrs. Bush
abstract: Kennneth Bucher, a resident of Adams Acounty who learned to read at age 50, was invited by Ellen Casey to speak at a literacy conference in Harrisburg.  First Lady Barbara Bush, a long-time activist in the literacy movement, will be at the event; Bucher is scheduled to meet her.

headline: Long-term health assistance plan should include home-based care
abstract: Calling for a national program to assist people in need of long term care.

headline: At Capitol abortion-rights rally, dead teen's parents hit consent law
abstract: At an abortion-rights rally in the Capitol Rotunda, Karen and Bill Bell, whose 16-year-old daughter Becky died after having an illegal abortion, spoke against "consent laws" which require minors to receive the consent of at least one parent before having an abortion.  Becky had not consulted her parents and had an illegal abortion, which was the cause of her death, according to a coroner.  Abortion-rights supporters are trying to energize their base, anticipating the election 5 weeks away.

headline: Wetlands Bog Down BMH Plans
abstract: A plan to build a health-care facility is facing problems, as the proposed location is located in a wetlands area.  The facility may have to be built elsewhere.

headline: State Senators Question Proposed Budget
abstract: State senators grilled Secretary of Education Donald Carroll about a budget proposal that forces local school districts to raise property taxes and might subject the state to lawsuits from poorer districts, but Carroll defended the Department of Education's $6.4 billion request.

headline: Philadelphia unveils plan to reduce garbage
abstract: Philadelphia officials presented a proposal to more than halve the amount of garbage the city sends to landfills each year by the year 2000 by increasing recycling and composting, and limiting the amount of trash produced.  The city now produces 2.6 million tons of trash and hopes to reduce that to 1.2 million tons.  The proposal will now go to City Council.

headline: PAT riders understand but don't like 15 cent fare increase
abstract: Pittsburgh Port Authority Transit riders understand the reasons for the 15 cent fare increase for monthly passes, however they do not like it. The increase is a result of the cost of oil related to the Persian Gulf crisis. The cost of diesel and other fuel products in addition to the oil, which goes into tire manufacturing, are reasons cited by PAT for the hike. The system will among the most expensive in the nation, but less so than Philadelphia's Southeastern PA Transportation Authority.

headline: High-profile policing
abstract: Editors note heroic acts by officers of the Philadelphia police department. Editors mention officers John Simon and Frederick Roth, who needlessly roughed up an arrestee however. The man later died in custody. The editors believe it is important to carry out the investigation currently being operated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the force's Internal Affairs unit. Pursuing the truth will not detract from the heroism of fallen officers, it will only add to it.

headline: At another, the disorders of drug culture
abstract: The Philadelphia Housing Authority's Schuylkill Falls development is among the worst public housing in the city. Manager Robert Byrd is reluctant to evict tenants even if they are arrested despite a US Housing and Urban Development eviction mandate in such situations. Marshall Johnson, son of a tenant, just recently did time in a Juvenile Detention center. The development is plagued by drug trafficking. The geography and layout of the complex makes it difficult for police to effectively pursue criminals.

headline: Three Dead in Collapse of Wall
abstract: Three people were killed and eight injured in the collapse of a brick façade on Market Street in Philadelphia.  The collapse was likely caused by signs and other items hanging from the improperly anchored wall.

headline: null
abstract: The article details the election results of the PA governor, 103rd, 105th and 106th Legislative District election results by precinct. It also details the result of a vote to change King Blvd. to Market Street in Harrisburg.

headline: Facing a Problem Head-On
abstract: An editorial urging voters to evaluate Republican representative William Adolph on his whole term, rather than the recent DUI and speeding charges which he publicly admitted to receiving, when he runs for re-election.

headline: Marathon talks held on loan
abstract: As Philadelphia Mayor Goode, Finance Director Benjamin Blakney, and City Controller Jonathan Saidel continued addressing the city's financial crisis, a meeting was held involving PA Governor Casey's assistant G. Edward DeSeve and Ian D. Lanoff, special counsel to the city pension board. The city is attempting to persuade the Pennsylvania School Employees Retirement System's pension board to invest in city loans, but Lanoff warned of legal entanglements if the board pursues the option.

headline: The Streets stonewall action on unpaid fines
abstract: Father-and-son Traffic Court employees T. Milton Street and T. Milton Street Jr. were suspended from their jobs for having a total of $3,436 in unpaid traffic tickets and refused to post $50 each to obtain a hearing to contest the violations. The elder street Said they would file a protest with the PA Supreme Court, saying it was unconstitutional to require poor people to put up money to get a hearing. The elder Street alleged that Traffic Court President Judge George Twardy promised that he would help Street pay the fines.

headline: Some darts and some laurels
abstract: This article applauds Bucks County for allocating funds for an enhanced 9-1-1 system.  It also criticizes Montgomery County for refusing to spend money on a much needed 911 system.  Montgomery Couny Commissioners are hopeful that the state will provide funds for the system.

headline: Lottery Fund going broke; Casey to tap reserve
abstract: The drain on the PA State Lottery Fund has been the Pharmaceutical Assistance Contract for the Elderly Program, which has seen costs of state aid in prescription drugs double since the inception of the program. PA Governor's Casey's plans to use lottery reserves for rebates to senior citizens will bankrupt the lottery next year unless operational procedures are changed. Budget Secretary Michael Hershock's projections differ from Robert Bittenbender's, chief budget analyst for Senate Republicans.

headline: Attorney General to recruit Blacks
abstract: According to PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr., David E. Gibson "has been assigned to affirmative action duties." Preate wants more blacks and other minorities recruited for positions in the Office of the Attorney General, such as administrative positions and investigators.
