Gibson is president of the Central Pennsylvania chapter of the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement Officers.

headline: Why parental leave is needed
abstract: This is an article from a woman who works as a teacher in Philadelphia and has a daughter that was diagnosed with leukemia and has faced inadequate support for working and caring for her children. Fewer than 20% of the firms who responded to a 1985 US Chamber of Commerce survey had formal maternity leave plan and the US General Accounting Office estimates that fewer than one-third of women workers are employed by firms that provide six week disability leave. She believes that people should not have to decide between caring for their children and their job and that the US Senate and House of Representatives should continue to work on the bill that allow workers to fulfill family and work responsibilities.

headline: State Student Loan Program in Trouble
abstract: State officials warned that the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency, which gives 55,000 students financial aid every year, could collapse by June.

headline: Pickup fees won't go up as much as expected
abstract: Borough Manager Terence Farren said Grove City residents will pay less in fees for the new garbage-pickup contractor hired by City Council. Under the old contract, residents paid based on collection rates which were lower than anticipated. Farren warned the fee might go up or down based on the tonnage collected by BFI. He noted however, that rates may decrease when recycling is implemented, as plan the city opted to implement earlier than mandated by law.

headline: Penna. ACLU sees threat in drunken driver rulings
abstract: US Supreme Court rulings that allow police greater freedom in trying to stop drunken driving are being said to be assaults on personal freedom says the American Civil Liberties Union. The Court ruled that police did not violate a PA driver’s rights when he was videotaped in his answers without warning him of his rights to an attorney and remain silent due to drunk driving. Lou Raider, manage of the PA Alcohol Highway Safety Program for the PA Department of Transportation has said that the number of drunk driving arrests has increased 14% since 1985.

headline: Hitchhikers' Trial
abstract: Westmoreland County Common Pleas Judge Charles Loughran Jr. sentenced Robert Cravener to between 8 and 16 years in prison, also sentencing Gary A. Yockney to between 7 and 14 years in prision. The two were hitchhiking when they were picked up by a 17-year-old-girl, whom they then raped, beat, and stabbed. The girl managed to flee to a nearby home after being left for dead.

headline: At Veterans Stadium, interest in grass grows
abstract: Philadelphia Phillies president Bill Giles hired a team of experts to study the implications and process of returning Veteran Stadium to nature. Currently, the stadium is equipped with Astroturf, however, a trend that is seeing stadiums return to grass has Giles interested in a state of the art sod system called Prescription Athletic Turf, a system of heating coils, peat, sand, and irrigation pipes that comprises "Super Grass."

headline: Township Must Permit Group Homes for Disabled
abstract: U.S. district judge Maurice Cohill, Jr. ruled that Moon Township must allow group homes for the disabled in the municipality.

headline: null
abstract: The article details the state legislative election results in PA by district.

headline: Fact-finding could avert teacher strikes
abstract: Officials say that if proper measures are taken for teachers contract negotiations, teacher strikes could be eliminated in the state.  In other news, discussion about the state's "sunshine law," or open meeting law, which the state legislature wrote for local governments but does not abide by itself.

headline: Marino avows neutrality in re-election bid
abstract: Montgomery County District Attorney Michael D. Marino announced his re-election bid at a press conference held yesterday.  Marino wishes to remain neutral even though he will seek endorsement by the Republican Party.  The GOP's 14 area leaders will meet in January to draft the remainder of their recommended county slate.

headline: The Wimp vs. The Whiner. Governor's Race: Profiles in Courage.
abstract: Stu Bykofsky supports neither gubernatorial candidate PA Governor Robert P. Casey nor Auditor General Barbara Hafer due to their lack of support for Philadelphia in this humor piece. The author argues that, though Philadelphia has the highest wage tax and the highest real estate transfer tax in the nation, it is not getting its fair share from the commonwealth.

headline: Nuclear plant alert criticized
abstract: The Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency's response to a full alert at the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station has come under criticism from some local officials.  Luzerne County Emergency Management Executive Director Jim Siracuse told reporters that surrounding counties should have been notified of the full alert at the station, which occurred last month.  Meanwhile,  Joseph L. La Fleur, director of PEMA, argued that the agency acted properly--stating that the decision not to inform neighboring counties was a discretionary move.

headline: Medicaid ruling may force health-care showdown
abstract: Editors see politically difficult choices to be made, as the US Supreme Court recently affirmed a lower court ruling which requires states to increase their rate of payment to hospitals for Medicaid patients. A lower court ruling in PA is expected to cost the state $5 million this year and $33 million next year in increased reimbursement rates in a state already facing a budget deficit. Lawsuits alone cannot address this issue, what is needed is legislation to resolve the health-care crisis.

headline: Black Corps of Engineers Workers Allege Decade of Bias
abstract: Three black employees of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers allege the Pittsburgh office of racial harassment and discrimination, claiming years of complaints have been ignored.

headline: Women AIDS Victions, 2 Takes
abstract: The latest report by the Federal Centers for Disease Control places the number of women infected with AIDS at 12 percent of the total number of victims, more than 5 times the number reported 2 years ago. In PA, women represent only 8 percent of the total number of those infected with AIDS. The Lehigh Valley AIDS Long Range Planning Coalition recently found 30 percent of its HIV positive patients were women. Doctors expect the percentage of women infected in PA to rise.

headline: State suit in school strike draws criticism, praise.
abstract: The state Department of Education filed suit in Commonwealth Court in an effort to force the New Castle Area school board to bring striking teachers back to work, with the support of the PA Federation of Teachers. Joseph Oravitz, the executive director of the PA School Boards Association, criticized the decision, saying it undermined the school board's efforts. The PA Supreme Court is in the process of ruling on an appeal that would outlaw teachers' strikes in the state.

headline: Pine Creek Opposes Clarion Waste Sites
abstract: Pine Creek Township supervisors adopted a resolution opposing the proposed waste treatment facility in Clarion County, among other local news.

headline: PennDOT Alert
abstract: A list and map of area construction by PennDOT is given with dates for when construction will be going on.

headline: Holiday duty cuts for Pittsburgh police
abstract: Pittsburgh city officials have ordered police officers who volunteered for duty on Christmas and New Year's Day not to work this year. Assistant Police Chief Donald Aubrecht said the city did not need all the manpower that was scheduled and in addition, the $300 per day premium pay which the officers received was becoming a burden on the city's premium pay budget. Out of the $56 million budget for 1990, $5.8 million went for premium pay.

headline: Author of Sullivan Principles tackles homeless problem
abstract: Reverend Leon Sullivan, author of a set of codes of conduct for US companies in South Africa, has established the first Human development Center in North Philadelphia. The center is meant to help homeless people, which Sullivans states is the biggest problem in America, by preparing them for life in mainstream society, instead of traditional facilities which provide food and shelter. The City of Philadelphia provided the facility, and Sullivan plans to take his idea to the federal government after 6 months.

headline: UPS gets state grant
abstract: The Schuylkill Economic Development Corporation has been awarded a $100,000 grant for business infrastructure development, which it will use to improve road and utility service access to a new UPS distribution center.

headline: null
abstract: The article includes a picture and information about the candidates for the PA's 199th District seat in the state House. Republican Ron Turo and Democratic Representative John Broujos' age, background, and positions on issues are included.

headline: Fairchild has commodity calendars
abstract: PA Representative Russ Fairchild announced residents of the 85th Legislative District may obtain free copies of the 1991 PA Commodity Calendar at his district office. The calendar is produced by the PA Department of Agriculture.

headline: Martin Predicts 'Productive' Relationship With Organized Labor
abstract: The American Federation of Labor - Congress of Industrial Organizations has not responded warmly to President-elect George Bush's hasty nomination of Lynn Martin as Secretary of Labor. Martin predicted she would have a very productive relationship with organized labor, however the AFL-CIO gave her a 29 percent rating, the amount of time Martin voted "right" in decisions involving labor as a Congresswoman from Illinois. Martin supported Bush in the presidential election.

headline: The winds of change
abstract: Times have changed for the better with the advent of democracy according to the editorial board. Despite having a 2-1 advantage in number of registered voters, Republicans, who also outspent Democrats by the same margin, lost three seats to democrats in elections. The only local representative to go unscathed was a US House Representative. The county GOP did not get very much bang for its buck.

headline: Medical Groups Sue to Challenge PA Auto Insurance Law
abstract: Medical groups and three private physicians challenged the constitutionality of parts of Pennsylvania's new auto insurance law.

headline: Black people urged to make selves heard
abstract: C. Delores Tucker, chairwoman of the Democratic National Committee's black caucus, spoke at the 56th annual NAACP state conference, and said that the defeat of the civil rights bill in the federal government was due to a lack of involvement of the black community in supporting and demanding that the bill be passed. President Bush vetoed the bill and the Senate failed to override his veto by just one vote.

headline: Yale Study Shows Drug Helps Alcoholics
abstract: Yale University Researchers have published the preliiminary findings of a report that find that a drug used to treat heroin addicts, Naltrexone, may also help alcoholics.

headline: State Treasury rescues student loan fund
abstract: State Representative Sam Morris writes about a financial arrangement between the PA Treasury Department and the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency. The Treasury Department is investing $200 million to maintain PHEAA's student loan program for the benefit of students from middle-income families for the upcoming academic year. Morris commends Treasury Secretary Catherine Baker Knoll for instigating the arrangement.

headline: Plant's neighbors fatalistic about air
abstract: Residents of areas near the Clairton Coke Works comlain of air that "burns when you breathe."  The neighborhood has the most polluted air in Allegheny County.

headline: PennDOT blamed for property damage
abstract: A property owner on Lloyd Street contends the PA state Department of Transportation caused at least $61,689 damage to his home as a result of North Scranton Expressway expansion. PennDOT officials counter that while construction may have aggravated problems at the residence, it was not the direct cause of the damage. In addition, officials said they have tried to address other concerns of property owner Roy Howarth, but have not been able to finish the agreed upon work because Howarth refuses to grant access to the property.

headline: Homosexual encounters at rest stops pose problem for police
abstract: A few rest stops on Interstate 83, such as two near Exit 13, seem to attract illicit homosexual activity, and police must be careful to avoid harassment in crackdowns.  Truckers and police agree that adding more lights to the dimly lit stops would significantly reduce the illicit activity.

headline: Band-aid solutions?
abstract: Dauphin County's efforts to help the homeless this winter are merely a Band-Aid for the problems and ignore permanent solutions according to a Harrisburg minister. He believes the city is planning short-term solutions that will eventually turn into long term. He has been posting copies of a declaration that talks about the plights facing the homeless like the 25 area homeless people who have died in the past two years. The county agrees something needs to be done but they don't know what.

headline: USPCI seeks 'meaningful' participation from public
abstract: USPCI of Pennsylvania announces it will work with more than the Host Community Working Committee to pursue the meaningful public participation required for the granting of a certificate of public neccessity.

headline: null
abstract: The article lists financial disclosure information of PA's 23 congressmen. Most congressmen have holdings in either property of companies. Others receive payments from various associations, such as Robert Borski, who earned speech income from the American Trucking Associations. William H. Gray III earned the most, with an income of over $350,000.

headline: Fairchild has commodity calendars
abstract: PA Representative Russ Fairchild said residents of the 85th district may obtain a free copy of the 1991 PA Commodity Calendar at his district office. It features recipes using products grown in PA.

headline: Masloff amusement-tax plan draws flak
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Sophie Masloff and her administration are questioned on their decision to hire Raymond P. Pepe to lobby the Legislature to reduce or eliminate the city's 10 percent amusement tax. Pepe's law firm employed now PA Governor Robert Casey. Legislators, including Rep. Tom Murphy and State Sen. Michael Dawida resent Masloff's strategy, saying the money allocated for Pepe could have gone for other advocacy resources. State Sen. Michael Fisher will consider an elimination or reduction of the tax in exchange for tax increases in other areas.

headline: There are PACs in abundance
abstract: The article notes that the ratio of PACs to legislative committees in PA is 3 to 1. The two best financed PACs include LAWPAC, the political arm of the PA Trial Lawyers Association, and PACE, the PAC for the PA State Education Association. However, interests represent a wide spectrum, even including the deputy sheriffs of Allegheny County!

headline: Medical plan rated 1st
abstract: Consumer Reports magazine named Capital Blue Cross and Pennsylvania Blue Shield the best in the country, below only Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota, in a survey of over 50 policies nationwide. The rating is based on questions of affordability, comprehensiveness, and availability. The company however, only sells insurance in the state of PA.

headline: Black Revs Urge Guv to Up Aid
abstract: The Black Clergy, a politically influential group of reverends from Philadelphia, wants Governor Casey to increase funding for the city and not take African-American support for granted as he seeks re-election.

headline: York Officials Report Progress in Controlling AIDS Spread
abstract: Last year in York County there were fifteen new AIDS cases but fewer people tested HIV positive which indicate some progress in controlling the disease.

headline: State:  School Till Dry
abstract: Donald M. Carroll, Jr., state Secretary of Education states that schools must raise taxes, cut programs, or curb costs in the coming academic year, painting a dismal scene for local districts.

headline: Politicians blamed for not eliminating gypsy moth scourge
abstract: Letter to the editor who does not believe politicians efforts will help the gypsy moths. They do not spray consistently for the moths. The taxpayers money is being spent on useless and not effective sprays.

headline: PennDOT blasted at Route 30 hearing
abstract: Property owners will be affected by lane additions proposed by the PA Department of Transportation  in West Manchester Township. Some businesses will lose portions of their properties via eminent domain, in which the state acquires properties for the public good by paying fair market value. John Rautzahn, PennDOT plans development manager, said he did not expect residents to agree with the agency's proposals.

headline: House agrees 'chair' out, chemicals, in.
abstract: If PA Governor Robert P. Casey signs a bill passed by the PA House and Senate, PA will use lethal injection instead of the electric chair for all death-penalty cases. A spokesman for the PA Correction Department said it was unlikely that the state would be in a position to use the new method for convicted murderer Raymond Whitney, assigned to be executed December 11th. The opponents of the bill included both legislators who oppose the death penalty and its strongest advocates.

headline: BASF to expand Monaca plant, add pollution controls
abstract: BASF Corporation said it will build a $29 million latex plant next to its existing latex facility. The corporation said it will also spend another $14 million for environmental improvements at the 36-year-old complex, including emission control and reductions in solid waste and waste water. This will lead to 24 new employees.

headline: Veterans' center begins work on 192-bed nursing facility
abstract: A $5.8 million renovation project is underway at the Southeastern PA Veterans' Center outside Spring City.

headline: null
abstract: The chart lists the gubernatorial election results between PA Governor Robert P. Casey and Barbara Hafer by precinct.

headline: Fairview board refuses to meet with citizens
abstract: The Fairview School Board refused to schedule a public meeting to discuss a contract that will raise teacher salaries and fringe benefits up to 40% over 4 years. A citizen's group, Citizens Concerned About School Taxes (CAST), has been questioning the contract, which they say the board has not made fully public. The board said that nothing constructive could be accomplished in an open public dialogue.

headline: Mayoral candidates vie for scarce dollars
abstract: The 1991 Philadelphia mayoral primary, with 11 candidates currently in the running, has created the most competitive and complicated fund-raising environment in the city's political history, party officials and fundraisers said. Middle-level businesses, traditionally relied upon for funding, are reluctant to contribute so soon after the 1990 election and in light of the city's fiscal crisis. Candidates are relying on their connections to PA and U.S. Representatives to build name recognition.

headline: There's little new at the polls
abstract: Valley voters should expect a new electronic voting machine in Springdale polling place and a low voter turnout. Waning interest in the gubernatorial race between PA Governor Robert P. Casey and Barbara Hafer is expected to lead to decreased interest in the state House race as well.

headline: Medical-aid fuss called preview of budget battle
abstract: PA Senator David Brightbill and Democratic counterpart Senator Michael O'Pake clashed over a supplemental appropriation designed to bail out the bankrupt state medical assistance program.  Senate Democrats believe there is funding in the budget to support the medical assistance program while Senate Republicans do not.  The flare-up occurred at the 13th Legislative Forum sponsored by the Berks County Chamber of Commerce.

headline: Both sides agree: 'Roe' in danger
abstract: The recent ruling by the US Supreme court, upholding notification of a parent or parents in the case of an abortion for a minor proves the issue of abortion is just a volatile as when Roe v. Wade was first decided. In PA, a case making its way through the courts concerns a law passed which requires spousal notification and mandates a 24 hour waiting period. Olivia Gans, president of American Victims of Abortion sees the recent Supreme Court ruling as a victory for pro-life supporters.

headline: York-area panel urges action on drug report
abstract: A commission which issued a report on York County's drug problem is urging quick action, as the report has a "short shelf life."

headline: State's budget for TELLs is sadly deficient
abstract: President of the PA State Education Association, John Yarnovic, applauds an editorial noting defects in the state funding for TELLS, for which a remedial program for students with low scores on statewide tests was developed. The PA Department of Education publishes TELLS scores to pressure districts to improve pass rates. But the most recent budget eliminates these funds. The legislature cannot expect school districts to fund programs alone--if state funding disappears, so will the programs.

headline: PPG Fines
abstract: The federal government wants to fine PPG Industries and Nippon Paint $1.7 million for the illegal handling of seventeen chemicals in violation of the Toxic Substances Control Act two years ago.

headline: PennDOT crew thanked
abstract: Anne Joyce of Lake Ariel, PA writes into the Scrantonian Tribune to defend Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) workers who were recently criticized in articles published in the newspaper.  Joyce discusses the recent actions of PennDOT workers that saved the life of a child and calls for their recognition.

headline: House Committee Approves Boot Camp Bill
abstract: The state House Judiciary Committee unanimously approved a bill that suggests military-style boot camps as a solution to overcrowded prisons in Pennsylvania, restricting eligibility to inmates with sentences between two and five years.

headline: Bell Atlantic donates shelter space for 40 men
abstract: Bell Atlantic announced that it would donate and heat a Center City building to the nonprofit agency Project Home as an emergency shelter for up to 40 chronically homeless men in Philadelphia this winter. Mayor Wilson Goode hailed the initiative as the sort of corporate-government partnership needed to solve the city's estimated homeless population of 30,000 to 35,000. The men will have access to mental health services, employment counseling, drug-abuse and alcohol-recovery programs, and computer literacy classes.

headline: Weldon denies misusing federal development funds
abstract: US Rep. Curt Weldon denies allegations confirmed by former director William Tancredi, saying Weldom mismanaged US Community Development Block Grant funds. The audit, conducted by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development, alleges Weldon granted no-bid contracts to friends and political supporters out of the Partnership for Economic Development in Delaware County. The Federal Bureau of Investigation is also investigating Weldon and the agency.

headline: "Capital For A Day: Schedule Announced
abstract: Wellsboro and Tioga County will host PA Governor Casey's program "Capital for a Day." The Governor, Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, and members of the cabinet will attend various functions in the community to understand the needs of residents. The agenda includes a luncheon with elected area officials.

headline: Family-leave bill is sent to Bush
abstract: The Senate passed a bill President Bush has threatened to veto. The bill mandates businesses with over 50 employees must offer 3 months time off to employees for childbirth or family emergency, while continuing to provide health benefits and holding their job. Business associations oppose the bill. If vetoed, it is not expected to survive in either chamber. Sen. Orrin Hatch opposed the bill, while a number of Democrats, including Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell, support it.

headline: McAvoy's loss more than political
abstract: Rosemary McAvoy, a pro-choice Republican candidate for the 106th District seat in the PA House of Representatives, not only suffered defeat in the race. During the campaign, her car was sabotaged, her children's cats were stolen, and a home she is trying to sell was vandalized. The board states that participants in political races should not become victims.

headline: They're on Ticket To Ride Coattails
abstract: While candidates for lieutenant governor win nomination on a separate column in primaries, they run as part of the governor's ticket on the main ballot. Democratic Governor Casey's running mate is Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel. Republican Auditor General Barbara Hafer's running mate is PA Representative Harold F. Mowery Jr.

headline: Medicare costs would still go up, but not as much
abstract: In a bill passed by the US House and being debated by the Senate, the elderly would still be paying more for Medicare, but the increases would not be as high as those in the budget bill rejected by the House last week.  In other Congressional news, a 2-cent-per-gallon tax on refined petroleum products would not apply to heating oil, and jobless workers would not have to wait two weeks after losing a job to apply for unemployment.

headline: Both sides see impact on Pa. cases
abstract: Reactions were mixed across PA on the abortion issue decided by the US Supreme Court. President of Chester County Citizens Concerned About Life, Alberta Horrocks, was pleased, but Planned Parenthood of West Chester director Rae Force said the ruling reduces the rights of teens. The ruling allows Ohio to mandate one parent of a minor to be informed, while in Minnesota, both parents must be notified unless a minor can convince a judge otherwise. In PA, where District Justice Daniel Huyett will review abortion legislation, the consensus is that the state's one parent legislation will be upheld.

headline: Younger women are targets of smokeout
abstract: The American Cancer Society's 14th Annual Great American Smokeout will be held to encourage tobacco users to quit. This year, the Pittsburgh unit of the society targeted young female smokers for special attention.

headline: Student shortage felt by colleges across U.S.
abstract: Many colleges nationwide are seeing dropping application rates as a result of a decrease in numbers of graduating high school students.  Even high-tier schools like Stanford and Notre Dame have seen application numbers fall.

headline: Preate to take a look at West Side Landfill Fiasco
abstract: State Attorney General Ernest Preate Jr. will tour the West Side Landfill in Plymouth Township to get a sense of the problem there. Citizens and municipal officials have labeled the site an environmental crisis. The Landfill is struggling financially.

headline: PennDOT defended
abstract: A York County resident believes criticism of the PA Department of Transportation is unwarranted. Granted, the agency is slow-moving and construction is a hassle for many, but it is necessary to plan for the growth of the area. The agency has a responsibility to seek the opinion of the local government and public opinion, in which the agency could improve, but the construction is a necessary part of the agency's job.

headline: House shoots down bill to protect gays
abstract: PA Representative A. Carville "Peck" Foster opposes House bill sponsored by Rep. Babbette Jospehs to include sexual origin-motivated crimes under a law imposing heavier penalties for hate crimes. The only York Representative to vote in favor of the bill, Michael Bortner, was surprised more Representatives opposed a law protecting people from hate crimes. Gubernatorial candidates PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer and Governor Robert Casey support the bill, which failed to pass.

headline: Bell Atlantic donates space for homeless shelter
abstract: Bell Atlantic Properties, a subsidiary of the telephone company, has turned over a former retirement home to Project HOME for use as a homeless shelter while the agency searches for a permanent home. Bell Atlantic have paid for renovations to the first two floors of the build and will also pay for heat and other utilities. The agency will receive $2 million in federal grants and $25,000 in contributions from Bell Atlantic to acquire a permanent shelter.

headline: Why unify the port?
abstract: The editorial states the importance of unifying the ports along the Delaware River under a single authority to provide economic studies and marketing and stronger representation for the businesses.

headline: $1.4 Billion In Cuts for Va. Detailed
abstract: $1.4 billion in budget cuts in Virginia were announced, one-fifth of which will be sustained by local governments.  Effects include college tuitions increasing, state employees losing jobs, and cuts in funding for jails and cultural projects and arts.

headline: Feather bows from fray
abstract: Lebanon County commissioner Feather announced he would not participate any further in the Commission's decision to choose a site for a County Airport now that the most likely site has been named as Millard. The decision will be up to commissioner and chairman Rose Marie Swnager and commissioner William Carpenter. Feather, who previously worked to help select and establish the county's aviation advisory committee, said he may resign as a commissioner, drop Eastern Land Development as a client, or withdraw himself from the process of decision making.

headline: McDade and Mowery special Towanda luncheon guests
abstract: U.S. Congressman Joseph M. McDade and Lieutenant Governor Candidate Harold F. Mowery Jr., gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer's running mate, spoke at a Bradford County Republican Party luncheon. McDade praised the new federal budget package, a result of Republican efforts, for maintaining strong national defense funding, citing American troop presence in the Middle East. Mowery criticized PA Governor Robert P. Casey's administration's budget policies.

headline: Thievery by Lawyers Is On The Increase With Duped Clients Losing Bigger Sums
abstract: Bar officials attribute the increasing trend of lawyers stealing from clients to tough economic times, the high cost of practicing law, substance, and the influence of television shows that portray lawyers leading glamorous lives. Special funds set up by state legislatures and bar associations to reimburse bilked law clients are facing unprecedented losses. PA's fund paid $1.7 million in 1990, up from $720,000 in 1989.

headline: Medicare's gaps criticized
abstract: The Senate is considering a measure which would put a cap on Doctor's fees in response to frustration from senior citizens who say they must pay out of their pockets hundreds each year in such fees.

headline: Capitol steps provide a forum for pair's daily messages
abstract: An article describes two fixtures on the steps of the Capitol, where a man seeking military disability benefits due to his service in WWII attempts to convince passers-by to sign a petition lobbying congress. Nearby, another woman lobbies tourists to sign a petition to pass a constitutional amendment banning flag burning.

headline: Your Turn; For the patients
abstract: A response to the letter "nurses deserve more" criticizing the actions of nurses at Neshaminy Manor House and saying "patients deserve more".

headline: Students
abstract: In a spontaneous protest of a school board policy in which up to 11 teachers and 4 staff members could get fired, 200 to 250 students of Apollo Ridge High School boycotted classes.

headline: Progressive attitude
abstract: The editors commend the efforts of Mount Carmel Township Supervisors, whose township is not subject to the PA Municipal Waste Planning, Recycling and Waste Reduction Act, but who are promoting recycling nonetheless. The township's Mount Carmel Landfill was closed in April, providing residents and supervisors with an incentive for rethinking trash disposal in light of higher fees.

headline: PennDOT gets tough
abstract: The editorial praises the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, which after dealing with contractor Tri-State Asphault Corp. for over a year, has fired the company for poor performance on the resurfacing of 5.6 miles of Route 51.  Potholes started showing on newly paved sections, several accidents were caused because of a too-slick surface, and the project was supposed to have been finished last year.  Over 200 cars were also damaged by protruding manholes and other structures on the road.

headline: House votes aid to S&L prosecution
abstract: The US House of Representatives approved a $10.5 billion spending bill that would give the Justice Department an extra $75 million to use in prosecuting fraud at the nation’s savings and loans. The $75 million was part of a bill that provides half the money for the coming fiscal year for the Departments of Commerce, Justice and State. The largest chunk of the bill goes to the State Department operations for the fiscal year.

headline: Bill would help pay for services at developments
abstract: The Pa House of Representatives is expected to pass a bill that could help communities meet costs of providing municipal services to new developments. The House Local Government Committee amended and approved the bill, which will allow municipalities to charge the fees from real estate developers.

headline: Wofford opens Job Center in Emporium
abstract: PA Secretary of Industry and Labor opened a PA career center in Emporium. This center, a satellite of St. Mary's, is a cooperative effort between service organizations, community-based industry, the state, and the North Central PA Regional Planning and Development Commission. Active organizations will include the Office of Vocational Rehabilitation, the Office of Employment Security, the Army, Navy and National Guard, and the Cameron County Assistance Office. Borough Secretary Don Sestina praised the state for contributing to the US Rapid Response Team.

headline: ...fraud scandal widens: Ex-aide to Pa. Congressman McDade indicted for bribery
abstract: A former aide to PA State Representative Joseph M. McDade was indicted Thursday for allegedly using bribes, gifts, and influence to steer $69.2 million in contracts to Lancaster-based United Chem-Con Corp.  Raymond S. "Tim" Whittig of Rockville, Maryland served as counsel to the House Small Business Committee and received payments from Chem-Con.

headline: Feds Probe Illegal Contributions to Casey, Others
abstract: The FBI and a federal grand jury are investigating allegations that James J. Curran Jr., head of Reading Anthracite Coal Co., made illegal campaign contributions to PA Governor Robert P. Casey, U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, former Governor Dick Thornburgh and other politicians. The investigation centers on allegations that Curran gave cash to employees in return for their checks, which were then given as campaign contributions. Both PA and federal election laws prohibit shielding the source of contributions and using corporate money for donations.

headline: McIntyre Among 1,000 Delegates To Protest at AFL-CIO Convention
abstract: Robert McIntyre, a Scranton union leader who was a candidate for the presidency of the AFL-CIO, was among one of 1,000 people to walk out of the convention of the 1.2 million member Pennsylvania AFL-CIO.  McIntyre and others claimed that the rules were being changed to allow an influx of Pittsburgh area union members to become delegates to support his opponent William M. George.

headline: This is a butter idea
abstract: It is appropriate that the Peanut House be saved, even if the cost is going to be salty. (These days you can't get anything for peanuts.) While this was being debated, my wife and I were talking to Mary Jane and George Leader, and we all agreed that Ellen and Bob Casey should be consulted for a Goobernatorial opinion. (Thank goodness we shelldom run into problems like this.) At any rate, history is going to be served. Now, all we have to worry about is whether the peanut is sturdy enough to survive and move, or is the peanut brittle?

headline: Mental health: York judge to hear Dauphin services suit
abstract: A York County judge will decide if Dauphin County can get records from the agency handling case management for its 4,000 mentally ill and retarded citizens court officials said. The county must show compelling reason for why they are doing this. The issue arose when the county proposed competitive bidding for case-management services.

headline: Cardinal issues abortion warning
abstract: Cardinal John O'Connor announced politicians who support abortion legislation and/or public funding for the procedure risk excommunication from the Catholic Church. New York Governor Mario Cuomo was "profoundly disconcerted" by the statement. Cuomo personally opposes abortion but supports a woman's right to choose.

headline: Ag secretary ambivalent on farm subisdies
abstract: Secretary of Agriculture Boyd Wolff says that he has mixed feelings about farm susidies, as he strongly believes that farmers need a strong foundation, but also believes that most farmers would do all right in a free market system.

headline: Students get little attention
abstract: Columnist Tony Perry writes about the Temple University professors' strike, saying that despite the fact that the teachers have a right to use whatever tactics will result in the best work conditions, it was clear that Temple University and the union did not have the students' best interest in mind during negotiations.  The University has lost about $4 million in tuition from students that have left in frustration since the strike began.

headline: Protect wetland, owners
abstract: A judge in Erie recently reduced the taxable value of two one-acre wetland plots to $1 each. A similar case in Monroe County awaits Judge Ronald Vican's opinion regarding unbuildable acreage in Stroud Township. The editorial board believes that best option in resolving the matter is to refer to the Clean and Green Act that allows qualified landowners to lower their tax assessments by leaving their property undeveloped.

headline: PennDOT given $2 million to widen 202
abstract: U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter announced a $1.8 million federal grant to PennDOT to widen route 202 in King of Prussia.

headline: Housing Police
abstract: The Pittsburgh Housing Authority has approved the arming of it police with semiautomatic pistols.

headline: Block grants awarded
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey has announced that $829,643 in community development funds have been awarded to five municipalities, Frackville, Girardville, New Philadelphia, and Coaldale.  The funds are part of $36 million being distributed through the Community Development Block Grant program.

headline: Work on state Capitol may hamper visitors
abstract: Various construction projects going on in the state Capitol building make visiting the building confusing and difficult.  The projects should be over in September.

headline: 1,800 sign petition for Market Street
abstract: More than 1800 registered voters signed a petition to change the name of Re. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard back to Market Street. The number of signatures will most certainly force the issue to come before Harrisburg City Council. Nonetheless, the Council will most likely place the issue on a ballot referendum. Supporters of the status quo say the petition is racially motivated. Councilman F.M. Richard Simons favors a return to Market Street in favor of what he views as the voice of the people.

headline: Female candidates need more funds, Ferraro says
abstract: Former vice presidential candidate Geraldine Ferraro says that while women candidates "bring another dimension to the political process", they face problems in raising money and overcoming  incumbents' re-election successes. She believes that the work force still has more opportunities for men, citing inequalities in salary and top management. A former Democratic U.S. congresswoman from New York, Ferraro is considering a possible campaign next year for U.S. Senate.

headline: Mediation chief likes law as it is
abstract: Thomas Quinn steps in when the parties in labor disputes step out and away from the bargaining table. Quinn has been directing the state Bureau of Mediation for the past 10 years. He says 96 percent of potential strikes are solved without a strike. The 4 percent that don't is low for the tension around. Teachers are the only ones that have the muscle to have a successful strike.

headline: Thornburgh can't avoid controversy
abstract: Former PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, now the US Attorney General, has become involved in another scandal. His deputy, Donald B. Ayer, resigned last Friday stating that Thornburgh mishandled an investigation in an attempt to protect one of his longtime aides. The board asserts that Thornburgh, who handled the Three Mile Island crisis very well after only 3 months in office in 1990, should "begin mending his fences as quickly as possible."

headline: Mentally ill children to get aid, White says
abstract: PA state Public Welfare Secretary John F. White said he will propose state funding for residential treatment of mentally ill children, so that parents are no longer forced to relinquish custody of their children just to get help. He called the absence of residential treatment the most glaring weakness in the mental health system. He will include a request for funding in his budget request for the year beginning July 1, 1991.

headline: Cardinal's threat raises church-state questions
abstract: Cardinal John O'Connor's article threatening Catholic politicians with excommunication should they favor abortion or public funding for it has caused an uproar. Some believe the Cardinal's comments appeared to be aimed at New York Governor Mario Cuomo, with whom O'Connor has repeatedly clashed. New York Representative George J. Hochbrueckner said O'Connor does not realize his position means no Catholic representatives. NYU Law Professor Burt Neuborne said the comments revive the issue which dogged JFK during his campaign.

headline: Agriculture secretary visits Bradford County
abstract: Boyd Wolff, PA Secretary of Agriculture, visited Bradford County as part of PA Governor Robert Casey's Capital for a Day program in Wellsboro. He was an honored quest at a picnic at Mount Pisgah State Park, where he offered some comments on his work in Harrisburg. He said he was impressed by what he saw on his visit.

headline: Students give illiteracy fight in York a blue-ribbon effort
abstract: Students helped the illiteracy fight by inserting blue ribbons in the York County Literacy Council's September newsletter.  September 8 is International Literacy Day, and Gov. Casey has designated September as Adult Literacy Month in PA.

headline: Protest Scenes
abstract: The photograph shows a crowd chanting while waiting for Department of Environmental Resources representatives.

headline: PennDOT ignores local conditions when doing its work
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation has shot itself in the foot again. PennDOT did not prepared for the street rod invasion last weekend. Traffic was horrible because PennDOT had reduced Route 30 to one lane traffic. They have been inconsiderate for most of their actions and do not notify locals of plans before hand.

headline: I CAN'T BELIEVE IT.  I FORGOT TO HAVE CHILDREN!
abstract: Cover of a blank greeting card issue in 1986; part of the piece on career costs for women.

headline: Blueprint for the future
abstract: Raymond Brown, a member of an 11-member panel sponsored by the American Institute of Architects that converged on North Philadelphia to study its problems and offer solutions, said he was inspired by the people he was sent to help. The panel, which calls itself a Regional/Urban Design Assistant Team, wrote a blueprint for revitalizing the community.

headline: Work-at-Home Idea, Using High-Tech, Still in Infancy Here
abstract: While many industrial experts predict more and more will start "telecommuting" to work via home offices, area business are only beginning to explore this possibility.

headline: 100 years ago, election in state was a crazy-quilt
abstract: The article details the unprecedented election results of 1890 in Pennsylvania. Voters elected Robert Emory as the first governor re-elected to a second non-consecutive term. The lieutenant governor race attracted more votes than the gubernatorial race. GOP head Matthew Stanley Quay's forced nomination of PA Senator George W. Delamater led to "open revolt" among Republican leaders.

headline: Fill up, don't feed Philadelphia's rat hole
abstract: The editorial suggests that the state or federal government step in and take over Philadelphia's finances in order to restore a state of stability to the city, instead of bailing Phila.'s government out with money.

headline: Medical Overcharges, 150
abstract: The PA Senate amended a bill that does not allow doctors to charge senior citizens more than the fees set by the federal government. The amendment was approved 29-19 but the bill still needs a final vote in the Senate and then a PA House of Representatives vote on Senate changes.

headline: Tomorrow:
abstract: The newspaper announces it will follow today's article on lobbying with a second article on reform efforts coming from the Legislative and private sectors.

headline: Mentally ill shortchanged
abstract: Letter that believes PA Governor Casey's budget for mental health services is totally inadequate to even care for those currently being served. With no new funds the governor plans to serve 2,624 additional people. Obviously this will not be enough.

headline: Career costs
abstract: Story focuses on the career and lifestyle choices that women in the workforce have to make.  Many women who are successful in their careers are single and without children and this piece focuses on the changing roles for women in the workforce.  Often, women are forced to choose between career or family, while men are not.

headline: Alternative fuels aid farmers in cutting cost
abstract: The Bureau of Forestry has allowed farmers and others to cut dead or downed trees for firewood with a permit for 70 to 80 years. Many are converting to wood burners to save fuel costs. Last year, 330 permits were sold and this year there were between 400 and 500.

headline: Students take a pass on make-up classes
abstract: The teacher's union which went on strike October 1st was ordered back to work 6 weeks later by a judge who insisted teacher's work while negotiations were ongoing. Since then, a date for negotiations to resume has not been set. In order to avoid losing state funding for failure to meet the 180 days of required education by the state, William Penn Schhol Disctrit and Southeast Delco School District held classes during the Christmas holiday, seeing absentee rates of 60 percent.

headline: Radon tests/Legislative mandate goes too far
abstract: The piece claims that mandatory Radon testing is stepping over the line, and that if a homeowner wants to have the tests done, they may, but the government shouldn't require it.

headline: PennDOT opens anti-litter campaign
abstract: The PA Transportation Department announced a $400,000 campaign to convince people to stash their trash the right way. Litter is estimated to cost $5 million a year to clean up. Instead of spending money on new highways and bridges it has to spend money on the mess left behind.

headline: In anti-drug fight in Germantown, neighbors see their efforts pay off
abstract: The efforts of residents of a neighborhood in Germantown have seen their anti-drug efforts pay off, as protests against a house on their street that was being used as a crack house and a drug dealer's home base succeeded in garnering enough attention to merit judicial action against the owners. The neighbors don't want to create trouble and drama, but say that they just want to be able to live peacefully and without the threat of drugs on their neighborhood.

headline: Bond ratings
abstract: A chart displays the possible ratings allocated to bonds by two major rating firms, Standard & Poor, and Moody's Investors Service. Both firms have dropped the city of Philadelphia's bond ratings to the lowest possible rating still considered "investment grade," just above speculative ratings.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon of a "Same Old Racket Liquor Store" being disguised by a ":Wine and Spirit Shoppe" front.

headline: 11th District
abstract: This chart shows the election results of the PA House race between Joseph Steighner and William Neel Jr. in the 11th District by township and ward.

headline: Fill vacancies in public view
abstract: The PA Sunshine Law allows the opportunity for public officials to meet in private but the author doesn’t think that they should push the options to the limit. However, in the case of the Altoona Area School Board elections the board members met in private to talk about how they would fill the vacancies and the author thinks it would have be interesting for the public to have seen the process. The author asks that the selection process of officials be in front of the voters more.

headline: Mellow's anger unwarranted
abstract: Letter from James H. Broussand, a member of Citizens Against Higher Taxes, speaking out against PA Senator Robert Mellow's negative response to the groups' actions to hold legislators accountable for their "anti-taxpayer" votes.

headline: Tough times for polls
abstract: The editorial points out that no matter who is elected on the state and local levels this November, they are going to have to increase taxes and cut budgets because of the economic slump in the Northeast and Southeast US and the crisis in the Middle East.

headline: Midstate in Brief. Casey signs AIDS-test privacy bill into law.
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey approved a bill that would guarantee confidentiality and counseling to people tested for the AIDS virus. The compromise bill, which both the House and Senate approved, would require health care providers to receive written consent from a patient before performing the test, ensure that the results remain private and require providers to offer patients counseling regardless of the results. Casey said he hoped the law would encourage more residents to get tested.

headline: Carpools offered to help ensure La. Abortions
abstract: An Arkansas abortion rights group offered to arrange car pools for Louisiana women seeking abortions should the restrictive bill pass and become law. The bill outlaws most abortions and punishes doctors with up to 10 years hard labor.

headline: Bottle bill would help Pa. farmers
abstract: The editorial praises PA farmers' continuing efforts to get the legislature to enact a state deposit law for bottles and cans, which have been unsuccessful in the past.  This time, the PA Farmers Association is attempting to get the question put to voters on November's ballot.

headline: Students to Hold March, Rally on Environment Issues
abstract: The Student Environmental Action Coalition is sponsoring a rally to voice important environmental concerns in which students from sixteen colleges and universities around Pennsylvania will march from City Island to Harrisburg.

headline: Ralph W. Abele, 68, an environmentalist
abstract: Ralph W. Abele was recognized as a leading environmentalist, having worked as the executive secretary of the General Assembly of PA's joint pollution control and conservation committee, helping to establish the PA Department of Environmental Resources and an independent Fish Commission. Abele harshly criticized both PA Governors Dick Thornburgh and Milton Shapp, as well as President Reagan for their environmental policies. Abele served on the board of directors for the National Wildlife Federation. Federation President John Hair calls him an inspiration.

headline: PennDOT schedules 2nd meeting on Route 30
abstract: York County Planning Commission Director R. Jack Dunn encourages interested residents to contribute to a plan and design meeting scheduled by the PA Department of Transportation for improvements to US Route 30. In the past few months, attendance at PennDOT meetings has increased as residents have become interested in the estimated $10 to $20 million dollar project.

headline: In West End, a disturbing rise in crime
abstract: The rural West End has seen an increase in violent crimes, which some say is related to an overall increase in population and influx of people from cities. State police have also seen an increase in residents carrying weapons. Monroe County Coroner Robert Allen said that violent crimes were up everywhere.

headline: Business people discuss homeless
abstract: 42 businessmen and women met at Betheseda Mission to discuss the problem of homelessness in Harrisburg, expected to rise 10 percent in the cold winter months. At the luncheon's conlusion, the Capital Area Relief Effort announced $20,000 was pledged. The group's goal is $230,000 by February, which Dauphin Chairman Wiliiam King said is reachable. Sponsors include Boscov's, The Patriot News Co., and the The Dauphin Deposit Bank and Trust Co.

headline: 10 firms told to cut rates
abstract: The Insurance Department temporarily rejected rate proposals from nine companies that wanted to be exempted from the state's new car insurance law. Another company, Home Mutual Insurance, was ordered to comply with the law, which requires rates be sliced by 10 percent for all motorists and 22 percent for those who give up their right to sue in most accidents. The 10 companies has sought to sidestep the rate cuts.

headline: 12th indictment in defense probe
abstract: Raymond S. Wittig of Rockville, MD has been charged in an eight-count federal indictment on counts of racketeering, conspiracy to defraud the United States, bribing public officials and filing false tax returns in connection with his work with United Chem-Con Corporation of Lancaster County, PA.  Witting had been hired as a lobbyist to Congress for the company.

headline: Final count a relief for congressman. Goodling glad control of redistricting stays split
abstract: U.S. Representative William Goodling was relieved that the GOP maintained its control of the PA Senate, safeguarding its say in next year's redrawing of congressional districts. PA is expected to lose two congressional seats, going from 23 to 21, based on preliminary U.S. Census figures. Split control between the GOP-led senate and Democratic PA Governor Robert P. Casey will make gerrymandering more difficult.

headline: Merit Selection? Why Ruin a Good Thing?
abstract: A cartoon depicting an elephant and a donkey in judge robes. Underneath them there is the line, "Pennsylvania's Party-Picked Judiciary."

headline: Treasurer won't buy notes, approve loan for Philadelphia
abstract: Treasurer of the PA Commonwealth Catharine Baker Knoll writes to the editors that she resents their factual inaccuracy in the editorial stating her administration has flip-flopped on  its policy regarding the purchase of City of Philadelphia Temporary Loan Notes. She reiterates her refusal to advance funds to the city in addition to refusing to purchase loan notes from the city. Knoll has however, agreed to expedite payments lawfully due to cities statewide.

headline: Montco kids hang up on drugs...
abstract: Members of the Montgomery County delegation of PA legislators welcomed children of Bell of PA employees to the State capitol. The children met with the 11 representative and gave their pledges not to use drugs or alcohol to help ensure a drug-free future. The photo shows the legislators with the children.

headline: Casey's pro-life victory
abstract: The author of the letter argues that the main issue in PA's recent gubernatorial election was abortion and wonders why PA Governor Robert P. Casey's landslide victory is not billed as a pro-life victory. The author claims that media polls that report that 50 to 60 percent of Pennsylvanians are pro-abortion are biased and unfactual. The author claims that unless Republican party leaders realize that 70 percent of the state is pro-life, their candidates will not win.

headline: Bovine TB-free status reinstated
abstract: After a labor-intensive investigation and testing of nearly 12,000 cows, Pennsylvania's status as a bovine TB-free state has been reinstated, according to Agriculture Secretary Boyd E. Wolff.  A case of bovine tuberculosis was found in a dairy farm In 1989, and the Bureau of Animal Industry and federal animal health officials followed by testing all cows that could have come into contact with the disease.

headline: Study challenges county to plan for 21st century
abstract: PA Senator Terry Punt established the Punt Commission on Business and Educational Partnerships to review Franklin County's educational systems. The commission devised 10 areas of improvement for educational systems to emphasize, including stronger encouragement for students to stay in school, more opportunities to explore business-exchange programs, and early intervention for failing students. A chief recommendation is establishing of a nonprofit to oversee the commission's recommendations.

headline: Ray of hope
abstract: Art Davis, Secretary of the Department of Environmental Resources gave indication that the hazardous waste incinerator proposed for Gregg Township is subject to environmental, social and economic considerations in addition to meeting siting criteria. Critics argue that the incinerator's close proximity to a federal penitentiary complex and the Lycoming County Landfill will discourage business and housing developments. The editorial board believes that local residents should double their efforts to fight the burner.

headline: PennDOT wins anti-litter award
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation's anti-litter programs won a distinguished service citation from the Keep America Beautiful organization and the Federal Highway Administration. The department's programs include Adopt-A-Highway, Keep Pennsylvania Beautiful, Litter Brigade, a recent advertising campaign and its wildflower planting program. PA was one of three states recognized.

headline: Incompetent or corrupt? Prison officials were one or the other
abstract: Editorial board comments on the importance of protection for key trial witnesses who are currently in prison for other crimes in light of the stabbing of a  murder trial prosecution witness serving time in Holmesburg Prison.  Prison officials failed to report this matter to the city police department.

headline: Businesses to get loans
abstract: PA Minority Business Development Authority low-interest loans totaling $700,000 have been approved for six projects that are expected to create 49 jobs and retain 99 jobs. In Dauphin County, a loan of $75,000 was approved for Omega Waste Services. In York, $100,000 will go to Celsius Transit Communications.

headline: 14 bars charged with gambling
abstract: Fourteen bars in York and Adams counties have been charged with liquor law violations in connection with last December's gambling raid by state police. A spokesman for the PA Bureau of Liquor Control Enforcement said the citations were issued based on information provided by the state police criminal investigations unit. Evidence uncovered in the sweep was reviewed administratively for potential liquor law violations.

headline: 18th U.S. House District. Vote total by municipality.
abstract: The article details the vote totals by municipality of the 18th U.S. House District election.

headline: Finance Expert Announces Bid for Mayor
abstract: Municipal finance expert Sam Katz announced his candidacy for mayor of money-troubled Philadelphia. District Attorney Ron Castille encouraged Katz to run, though he has also been mentioned as a potential mayoral Republican candidate. Democrats Peter Hern and former district attorney Ed Rendell already have announced they are seeking the party nomination.

headline: Mezvinsky's 300-hour submarine campaign surfaces
abstract: Comments on the upcoming lieutenant governor race and how candidate Edward Mezvinsky, Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel's pro-choice opponent, has avoided the campaign trail and the media up until this point.  Phillip Berg, a lawyer from Montgomery County, is the other pro-choice candidate in the race.

headline: Truth be told, new Pa. governor will have to hike taxes, Hafer says
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer visited State College, and said that if elected, she would raise taxes in order to deal with the state's financial situation, and contended that incumbent Governor Casey would have to if he wins. She also committed another campaign taboo, mentioning the possibility of her defeat. She said that "if I go down, I'm going down telling the truth."

headline: New state AIDS official predicts funding decline
abstract: Pennsylvania's top AIDS officials believe that they will have a tough time trying to get more money to fight the disease with President Bush and PA Governor Robert Casey vowing to hold the line on new taxes.  Casey has asked the Legislature to increase AIDS funds to the Health Department by about $133,000 next year to $2.8 million.

headline: Charges of Racism Cloud Real Issues
abstract: An opinion referencing the Camp Hill prison riots and expressing the gravity of charges of racism and how it may oftentimes cover up the real issue at hand.  Nowadays racism is taken lightly and used as a political manipulation.

headline: Bucks will have $2.7 million for farmland preservation
abstract: Bucks County Finance Director Stanley Allen said Tuesday the county expects to have at least $2.7  to million on hand by the end of the year to purchase development rights to agricultural land for farmland preservation. The county is expected to have at least $550,000, the state will match that with a grant. The program is intended to slow the rate farmland development.

headline: Study: School Real Estate Taxes Up the Most
abstract: Rising costs associated with teacher contracts and diminishing state aid are largely responsible for an $8 million increase in Lycoming County school real estate tax levies in the past five years, according to area school officials. Dr. Oscar W. Knade Jr., superintendent of the Williamsport Area School District said the state's wealthier districts receive 140- to 150-percent of their state entitlement, wile poorer districts struggle to receive even 100-percent.

headline: Recycler reduces rubbish
abstract: John Bergold, the duty director for Wilkes Barre's bureau of recycling, believes his efforts are being appreciated. He has numerous awards lauding Wilkes-Barre's leading role in reducing rubbish. They been a model in the state. Even though rubbish is growing recycling has reduced city stench by 15%. City residents have increased recycling in huge numbers. Five years ago 1.5% of home stacked papers in front of their houses, but now 63% of homes stacked papers. Critics say more can be done though.

headline: Pittsburgh gets rail center
abstract: Conrail will open its customer service center in Pittsburgh and not in Altoona despite a push by U.S. Representative Bud Shuster. Conrail justified the position, saying that it employs around 250 more customer service personnel in Pittsburgh and that putting the center in Altoona would be very costly. Conrail guaranteed $12 million in outside contracts for the locomotive section of the railroad's Juniata shop.

headline: Infighting among Pa. high judges continues
abstract: Justice Rolf Larsen of the PA Supreme Court is attempting to have the chief justice Nix excluded from the disciplinary hearing for Larsen because of a "long and tiresom vendetta" between the two.  Larsen has accused Nix of misconduct in three lower court cases.

headline: CAP classification will aid low-income programs
abstract: Lebanon County commissioners went ahead with plans to attain Community Action Program designation for the county. The designation would allow a community action agency to serve as an umbrella organization that serves as an incentive to use a variety of funding to tackle a wide range of social problems. Two of the main sources of funding that will be handled by the CAP will be community service block grants and emergency community services homeless grants. The editorial board approves of the program and hopes that it will cut clerical and processing costs.

headline: 1990 in Review: Top 10 business stories in Western Pennsylvania
abstract: Reports on the top 10 business stories in western PA included the announcement of a Sony plant's opening and a report on the labor market which has experienced growth over the national average. USAir continues to hit financial turbulence while several companies, including USX Stell, Equimark, and Aristech Chemical Corp. battle political maneuvers and potential takeovers. Battles continue in the courts over several publicized pension agreements including LTV Corp.

headline: 1990 primary to be remembered for surprises
abstract: Discusses how political newcomer, Marguerite Luksik, came within 50,000 votes of defeating Republican front-runner Barbara Hafer, Pennsylvania's auditor general in the gubernatorial primary.  The issue of abortion divided the candidates, with Luksik being pro-life and Hafer pro-choice.

headline: Financial forms released in D.C.
abstract: The article lists summaries of 1989 financial disclosures of US Senators and Representatives. Senators are allowed to keep earnings from speeches up to 40% of their salaries, while Representatives may keep up to 30% of their salaries. Senators and Representatives listed come from PA, New Jersey and Delaware.

headline: Midstate in Brief. 2-verse state song to be official in 60 days.
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey signed a bill designating "Pennsylvania" as the state song. The song, written by two Philadelphia men and selected from among more than 200 entries, was reviewed by a panel of music experts. Though some legislators disapproved of the song, it passed both the state House and Senate.

headline: Tulli, in an impressive field
abstract: Republicans in the 106th state House district have several viable candidates to choose from in the May 15th primary.  The Patriot-News editorial board endorses Frank Tulli specifically, the Republican party's endorsed candidate.  In addition to Tulli, Middletown Mayor Robert Reid, Swatara Township Commissioner Dominick Costanza, Rosemary McAvoy, Donald Cappetta, and Gregory Ricci are also running.

headline: Niacin will cheaply lower cholesterol, Penn researcher says
abstract: Dr. Terry Jacobson, from the University of Pennsylvania which published findings on Niacin in the December issue of the Journal of the American Medical Association this month, found Niacin is the cheapest and easiest way to lower cholesterol, if drug treatment is offered as a solution rather than diet as the National Cholesterol Education Program prescribes. EAS

headline: Churches ask for open door for disabled
abstract: Wife of former PA Governor Dick Thornburgh, Ginny, created the position of director of religion and disability for the National Organization on Disability. She hopes to persuade churches, synagogues, and other religious organizations to accept disabled persons rather than making them feel less welcome or valuable. Ginny, visiting the Pope with husband and US Attorney General Dick Thornburgh, requested the Pope pay special attention to the issue.

headline: Carter to speak at Pa. Holstein Association
abstract: Former President Jimmy Carter will speak at the PA Hostein Association's annual meeting and convention Feb. 22. Carter agreed to speak at the request of a dairy farmer he befriended while fishing in Pennsylvania.

headline: Study-group approach makes grade
abstract: A new approach to education involving organized group activity and projects is proving to be a valuable resource, especially for blacks and Hispanics.  Blacks and Hispanics only make up a tiny proportion, compared with the population percentages, of math and science students at universities.

headline: Recycling brings rules by the ream
abstract: A new law to go into effect in 1992 will require two thirds of the state's local governments, including cities, towns, and large townships, to enact recycling programs for at least three materials. It is up to each local governance how to devise, solicit, and pay for its program, though state grants may be sought. Altoona, Logan Township, Hollidaysburg and Tyrone are meeting with county planners to devise recycling plans.

headline: Plants: Casey on track
abstract: PA Governor Casey's pledge to support rail service for the Wellsboro area pleased plant managers. Casey has asked the PA General Assembly to provide $500,000 to purchase and operate the section of track feeding the airway, which current operator Conrail intends to abandon. The tour of the plants was part of Casey's "Capital For A Day" program. President of Local 1001 of the American Flint Glass Workers, Mark Christman, also stressed the importance of rail service to the area.

headline: Inmate Loss Reimbursement Decision was Shortsighted
abstract: An opinion piece supporting reimbursement for inmates who lost property in the wake of the October riots at the State Correctional Institution at Camp Hill.

headline: Casey: 'Engel is investment opportunity'
abstract: The York County work force is responsible for a high-tech Austrian manufacturer locating in the area. PA Governor Casey believes Engel makes a statement about job investment in PA.

headline: 2 state bills get last-minute action. Video-poker plan hits Casey's desk.
abstract: The PA Senate approved a bill that would legalize video poker machines and sent it to PA Governor Robert P. Casey. Casey has had a long standing opposition to increasing gambling laws and has vetoed previous wagering bills. If Casey vetoes the bill, the Legislature would not be in session to override it. Profits from the machines would be split between the bar owners, the host municipality, school districts, the PA lottery and the PA attorney general's office.

headline: 1990 state population totals
abstract: A chart of population totals by state is listed, along with their rank in 1980 and 1990 as well as the change in the number of people and percent from the past decade's measurement to the present.

headline: Firms to prepay wage taxes
abstract: Several Philadelphia businesses and universities, including some of the city's largest employers such as the Univ. of Pennsylvania and Bell Atlantic Corp., have agreed to prepay about $50 million in wage taxes to help the city through its budget crisis.  This deal alone will not save the city, but will simply delay the date that Philadelphia will run out of cash unless other deals and adjustments are made.

headline: Mikula knocks on doors in his quest for a Senate seat.
abstract: The article details the door-to-door campaigning efforts of PA Senate candidate Alan Mikula against powerful PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert C. Jubelirer. Mikula does much of his election work from home and is faced with campaign financing issues.

headline: U.S. House OKs job-leave bill
abstract: The U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation guaranteeing almost half of American workers up to 12 weeks a year of unpaid job leave to care for newborn children and family members who are seriously ill.

headline: As oil price rises, dealers are falling.
abstract: The number of Philadelphia gasoline stations dropped from 2,187 in 1972 to 1,791 in 1987, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Sharp increases in the cost of gasoline and a shift by major oil companies away from domestic production and into refining and marketing have made gasoline retailing more competitive. New federal safety regulations require station owners to upgrade underground storage tanks and carry more insurance to pay for leaks and spills. The Petroleum Marketers Association estimates that at least 20,000 independent service-station owners will go out of business over the next few years as a result of the legislation.

headline: City considers extending job benefits to gay couples
abstract: The City of Philadelphia awaits a study by administration representatives, unions, the Civil Service Commission and the Philadelphia Lesbian and Gay Task Force to decide if it will offer benefits to gay and lesbian couples, and unmarried heterosexual couples. Mayor Wilson Goode refuses to support the matter until its legality is examined, referring to a PA Supreme Court ruling on a law department memo, denying benefits to unmarried and/or same sex couples. Task force director Rita Adessa says that interpretation of the case is inappropriate and hopes benefits will be extended by executive order.

headline: Casey signs pet, littering bills
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey signed bills to prevent dangerous dogs and litterers. The pet law requires owners to register dogs that are deemed dangerous by a district judge. The littering bill boosts penalties for people who scatter trash on roads, railroad right-of-ways and state waterways.

headline: Sturla unveils plan aimed at improving education system
abstract: Mike Sturla, Democratic candidate for the PA House, unveiled a 10-point plan to strengthen the state's education system, including changing the state's reimbursement formula for building new buildings vs. renovating old ones. He also wants to prepare public universities for increased enrollment, as private university tuitions continue to increase.

headline: Recycling business booming, and many trying to cash in
abstract: Article detailing how the recycling plant works. Communities all over PA are turning to the low-tech world of recycling to help ease the price of trash disposal.

headline: Police STEP over the border
abstract: State police in eight states are participating in EIGHT STEPS, a program beefing up highway patrols to help encourage and enforce highway safety.

headline: Inmates Deliver Strong Message About Drugs
abstract: Lehigh County Prison inmates wanting to share stories of their drug abuse with the public appeared in a video made by Muhlenberg College and the county corrections department.

headline: Center City Plan Gets Some Praise - and Criticism
abstract: The Center City Plan's lofty goals of controlling crime, homelessness, littering, and street vendors was met with praise but also concerns of diminishing quality of life

headline: 2 steelmakers to help can recycling efforts
abstract: Two of the region's steelmakers, USX Corp. and Weirton Steel Corp., are making moves to make recycling easier and more attractive to residents.  USX  has donated 75 "reverse" vending machines, which dispense pennies for inserted cans, and Weirton has increased the price they will pay for cans.

headline: 1990; The Year in Review:Budget troubles galore, new democracies in Europe and year-end worries of war
abstract: Over the past year, President Bush ordered troops into the Persian Gulf to reduce gas prices. PA Governor Casey was re-elected in a landslide only for Pennsylvanians to discover a budget deficit of nearly $1 billion dollars. In Philadelphia, Mayor Wilson Goode experienced financial difficulties as the city neared bankruptcy and was forced to seek loans. New Jersey residents were incensed by taxes levied by Governor Jim Florio and British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher was disposed from power.

headline: First ladies earn share of spotlight
abstract: Patriot News columnist Nancy Eshelman comments on the impact that politicians' wives, specifically Barbara Bush and Ellen Casey.  Eshelman write in response to women at Wellesley College's objection to the fact that Mrs. Bush is slated to speak at graduation.  Eshelman believes that many politicians' wives have significant influence while their husbands are in office.

headline: Minimum salary plan for teachers is poorly timed
abstract: Opinion believes that the time is not right for PA Governor Robert Casey's proposal to increase the state's minimum salary for teachers to $21,000. Voters will not support it during the recession. Another time it would be a great idea to appreciate our teachers with higher salaries.

headline: U.S. House vote
abstract: The article details the election results by precinct of the 14th, 18th, 20th and 22d District U.S. House races.

headline: Carter: American lives could be toll in gulf
abstract: Former President Jimmy Carter said at a talk at Moravian College that if sanctions or negotiations fail to end the Persian Gulf crisis, Americans will pay with lives, high oil prices, or both. He warned against the fallout of Invading Iraq, but lamented at the apparent likelihood of an invasion.

headline: City considers extending job benefits to gay couples
abstract: The Philadelphia Lesbian and Gay Task Force is supporting a proposal that would give gays and lesbians job benefits reserved for married couples but the City Law Department is expected to rule that the change is illegal. Philadelphia Mayor Goode and representatives of the task force met and Mayor Goode said that he would not take a position on the proposal. In 1984 a PA State Superior Court upheld a lower court ruling that gays could not enter into common-law marriage.

headline: Comparison of Lancaster County, Montgomery County, Md. and Manheim Township
abstract: The chart shows 1990 population, population increase in the 1980s, acres in land, acres in farmland, acres having agricultural zoning, acres permanently saved and yearly value of farm productivity for Lancaster County, Pa., Montgomery County, Md. and Manheim Township, according to the Maryland National Capital Park and Planning Commission and Lancaster County Agricultural Preserve Board.

headline: Superintendent urges students to say no to steroids
abstract: Dr. Robert Bohn wants to be sure students are aware that the illegal use of steroids is not permitted in the Mifflin County School District. The superintendent recommended to members of the school board at their committee-of-the-whole meeting that specific reference to steroids be included in the school district's medication and drug and alcohol policies plus the Student Handbook.

headline: Recycling center
abstract: Workers begin installing the conveyor belts at a new recycling center scheduled to open on Sept. 24.

headline: Port Panel Split as PA Vows to Block Teams' Move
abstract: State residents on a regional port authority vowed to block new train routes and highway ramps that could carry 76ers or Flyers fans to games if the teams transferred to Camden.

headline: Inmates drill in hard style of bootcamp
abstract: Following prison riots at the PA Correctional Institution in Camp Hill, a New York prison is being watched by all levels of government, including from abroad. The prison reduces sentences for those who complete a boot camp program, saving taxpayers millions.
