PA Legislators are also considering instituting this style of prison to reduce tension and problems of overcrowding. A bill to introduce a similar approach by PA Rep. Dwight Evans has the support of PA Governor Casey.

headline: Center Open
abstract: Pictured is PA Secretary of Industry and Labor Harris Wofford, presenting a $2 million federal grant for a Punxsutawney program to w assist unemployed coal miners. Present are Michael Lawrence of the North Central Planning Council; Albert Stanton and Robert Mowrey, who assisted in organizing the program; Frank Campbell, a miners' counselor; and State Rep. Paul Wass.

headline: 68 firms in state forgo anti-takeover-law protections
abstract: 68 of 300 PA corporations have chosen to opt out of the legislation amongst the strictest anti-takeover regulations in the country. Opponents say it proves the law, which forces corporate raiders to surrender profits from a sale of shares within 18 months of a failed takeover attempt, strips shareholders of rights and entrenches bad management. President of the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry, Clifford Jones, supports the law and helped guide it through the legislature.

headline: 2 defeated Democrats given higher salaries
abstract: 2 former Democratic Representatives, Connie Maine and John Pressman, received contracts from House Democrats to help new legislators get settled in government. Maine will be organizing training programs for new employees in district offices, as well as doing general consulting to eliminate waste and inefficiency. Pressman will assist members computerizing their offices. House Republican Minority Leader Matthew Ryan said his party will employ three legislators who also lost elections.

headline: Fisher outdrawing Freind: GOP primary challenger reports more campaign cash than incumbent
abstract: Ellen Fisher of Haverford has raised substantially more campaign money than incumbent state Representative Steve Freind, her opponent in the May 15th primary.  Of the three candidates running for the seat, Fisher has raised the most as of May 4th.  Many of the groups who donated to Fisher and Freind fell on one of the two sides of the abortion issue; either pro-life or pro-choice.

headline: Minority grants still a hot topic
abstract: An announcement by assistant US Secretary of Education for Civil Rights, Michael Williams, making scholarships for minorities illegal, touched off a reaction from interest groups and college officials, including the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and the National Association of Independent Colleges and Unviersities. Williams amended his earlier statement Tuesday by declaring all scholarships safe for the next 4 years.

headline: Union Boss Stout Convicted in Racketeering Case
abstract: A federal court jury convicted Earl Stout, former union boss of District Council 33 of the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees in Philadelphia, of embezzlement, racketeering, and conspiracy.  The jury also convicted two co-defendants, including Stout's son William.

headline: Cause Proped in Low-level Alert at Pa. Nuke Plant
abstract: The Susquehanna nuclear power plant reactor that experienced a 6 1/2 hour alert over the weekend will not opearte until plant and federal officials determine the cause of the electrical problems that triggered the emergency.

headline: City cracks down on gay-bashing
abstract: Harrisburg Police officials are increasing foot patrols near an area where there are are several gay bars in an attempt to cut down on anti-gay assaults and gay-bashing.

headline: Farmers brace for new law
abstract: Groups are calling for farmers to do more to protect waterways from runoff polution.

headline: Survey: Employers to hire fewer grads
abstract: According to a report by the College Placement Council, Inc., employers expect to hire fewer entry-level college graduates, and they predict more competition for select graduates in the future. This decline is due to increased competition for top graduates, a widening gap between the best and worst students and a decline in company loyalty among new college hires.

headline: 'Recycling judge' takes on PepsiCo
abstract: The city's self-appointed recycling judge has removed his robe and put on the gloves against one of the country's soft drink giants over its use of cans containing steel. He is sparring with Pepsi over its use of cans made of steel and aluminum, bimetals cans as they are known.

headline: Private Group Gets Contract
abstract: The Ohio Railway Organization will spend $1.5 million on forming a construction plan for a high-speed passenger rail system in Ohio.  This is the third attempt to construct a high-speed railway system in Ohio.

headline: Inmates have suggestion for easing prison tensions
abstract: A member of the State Correctional Institution at Huntington is writing about the currently over its maximum capacity at the Institution. The writer states that even though the PA State Correctional Institution is still receiving inmate transferred from other prisons that were even more overcrowded, which leads to bad conditions in the prison. The writer believes that the society needs to know about the problem and find a solution.

headline: Change impact-fee bill
abstract: Municipalities are fighting to change a PA House bill concerning impact fees, saying that the bill favors developers too much.

headline: 9.1 percent rate increase not enough, Aetna says
abstract: The PA Department of Insurance granted Aetna Life and Casualty Company a 9.1 percent premium increase as part of an agreement which Aetna will comply with the rollbacks mandated by the state’s new auto insurance law.

headline: 2 state bills get last-minute action. House limits 'living will' proposal.
abstract: A bill that would enable terminally ill people to reject artificial life-support was passed in the PA House but likely will not be passed in the PA Senate before the legislative session ends. The Catholic Church succeeded in having three restrictive provisions amended into the legislation. Donna Malpezzi, counsel to Senate Majority Leader F. Joseph Loeper said it is unlikely that the two chambers will have time to reach agreement on the amendments.

headline: Fisher wins majority whip spot in Senate
abstract: In the Republican caucus, PA Senator D. Michael Fisher was elected to the majority whip spot, Robert Jubelirer was re-elected as Senate President Pro Tempore, Senator F. Joseph Loeper was re-elected as majority leader and Senator Frank Salvatore was elected as caucus secretary. The secret ballot was held shortly after the defeat of GOP gubernatorial nominee Barbara Hafer to PA Governor Robert P. Casey. Senator Roger Madigan's challenge of Jubelirer was the first of its kind in 20 years and was a move intended to express the dissatisfaction of some with the direction of the party.

headline: Money Diverted
abstract: Former Pittsburgh Attorney Ronald Mckay has plead guilty to diverting about $670,000 of his clients' money into his personal care home business, he will be sentenced March 28th.

headline: Union expected to issue strike notice
abstract: The reunion representing 181 employees at Brownsville General Hospital is expected to issue a strike notice to go into effect Wednesday informing the hospital that a walkout will occur midnight July 21 unless a contract settlement is reached. Meanwhile a new round of bargaining talks have been scheduled for July 16.

headline: Consumer advocate: Cut utility's rate hike
abstract: The state consumer advocate says Pennsylvania American-Water Co. deserves less than one-fourth of its proposed $21 million rate hike. Consumer advocates believe they should receive slightly less than $4.5 million. Pennsylvania-American's territory includes about 3,300 customers in Bangor and Roseto boroughs and parts of Plainfield, Upper Mount Bethel and Washington townships. expert witnesses have determined the company has overstated its plant additions and other expenses.

headline: City Hall to Skip Christmas Trees and Menorahs
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff has decided to keep the City Hall's decorations free of Jewish and Christian religious expression. The American Civil Liberties Union brought a federal case against Allegheny County and the city of Pittsburgh for a nativity scene that had been set up in front of a courthouse. The Supreme Court ruled that government bodies could display menorahs and Christmas trees because they contained secular elements.

headline: Farmers still optimistic, agriculture leader says
abstract: PA Secretary of Agriculture Boyd Wolff said PA farmers are still optimistic, despite two years of low yields.  Farmers are faced with increasing regulation on land from the PA Department of Environmental Resources, and some farmers are attempting to unionize to bring up the price of milk.

headline: Tax package provides new grant for child care
abstract: Congress passed a tax package that includes new grant programs for childcare and increases tax credits for low-income families with children. US Senator Christopher Dodd (D-CT), one of the authors, said the has is "extremely satisfied" with the package.

headline: Recycling law to affect business
abstract: Erie Area Chamber of Commerce President Donald F. DiPlacido urged businesses to attend a seminar hosted by the Northwestern PA Energy Center, the PA Department of Environmental Resources, the City of Erie, the Erie County Planning Department and the Northwest PA Industrial Resource Center. The seminar will address the Municipal Waste Planning, Recycling and Waste Reduction Act.

headline: Project leaves roadways abloom
abstract: Thanks to a new PennDOT program, many spaces next to highways are now adorned with wildflowers along the road.

headline: Inmates works for early release
abstract: 11 prisoners are being allowed to take part in a unique approach to corrections call the Earned Early Released Program. For each five days a prisoner works he receives one day off his jail term. Prisoners are eligible for the program if they are not in jail for violent crimes, sexual assaults or drug dealing. Judges can nominate them and prisoners can decline. People are waiting to see the results of the program very intently.

headline: Chill out, Chilton Borough
abstract: Chilton is the name of a proposed 73rd municipality in York County, a new borough developers hope to carve out of Monaghan Township. Double M Development Company blocked by the township in its efforts to construct a 227-unit housing development and golf course, has gone to court to get a referendum on the ballot which would give township voters the chance to approve the secession. The proposed new borough would be 492 acres. The town will lose revenue though. The new borough is going to cause a headache, but very unlikely at the same time.

headline: A Creaky Computer System
abstract: The National Association of Insurance developed the Insurance Regulatory Information System, or IRIS, as a computerized finanaical system to sift through insurance company filings and identify companies in danger of insolvency. At its inception, the system identified companies that later became insolvent at a rate of 90%. However, accuracy has decreased to 75%, with some healthy companies targeted. Efforts are being made to fortify the system against misleading data entries.

headline: 246 thirfts in jeopardy, agency says
abstract: Nearly 250 savings and loans nationwide are expected to fail and are candidates for government takeover.

headline: Florio raises taxes and the ire of taxpayers, who punish party
abstract: New Jersey Governor Florio pushed $2.8 billion in tax increases through the state legislature after telling voters he would not raise taxes in his 1989campaign. US Senator Bill Bradley almost lost his Senate seat because of the backlash. The governor blamed the previous administration for leaving him with a deficit.

headline: Montco COP Elects Nahill Chairman
abstract: The Montgomery County Republican Committee elected state Rep. Charles F. Nahill Jr. as chairman to fill the vacancy left by the resignation of Frank W. Jenkins. Nahill defeated Frank Bartle, 384-311, in a special committee meeting Wednesday night.

headline: Union head see law giving teachers more responsibility
abstract: Albert Fondy sees Act 195 as the vehicle giving public employees the right long-accorded other workers, and not as the culprit responsible for work stoppages. He said opponents of the limited right to strike accorded public workers too often focus on school teachers and fail to recognize the annual number of teacher strikes have been decreasing. He claims if the schools are better all the kids learn more and the public will be more receptive to teachers.

headline: Cuffs Run: place to store the juice
abstract: The Mid-Atlantic Energy Engineers Ltd. proposes a hydropower to ease a run on energy as the area becomes more developed. The energy warehouse is designed to store energy and redistribute  it more suitable to demand. Cuffs Run, as the proposed site it titled, would buy cheap energy during periods of low demand and sell it at higher prices during periods of high demand. The US Council for Energy Awareness predicts demand to exceed supply within a year or two. An inadequate supply will cause rotating energy blackouts for the east coast.

headline: City wants proof of contract bias
abstract: As a step towards a new minority contracting program in Philadelphia, the city will commission a study to find whether Philadelphia companies have discriminated against minorities and women.  Findings from the study would be used in designing a new minority contracting ordinance.

headline: Farmers still optimistic, agriculture leader says
abstract: State Secretary of Agriculture Boyd Wolff said PA farmers are still optimistic, despite two years of low yields.  Farmers are faced with increasing regulation on land from the DER, and some farmers are attempting to unionize to bring up the price of milk.

headline: Tax-exempt status of city universities challenged.
abstract: The City of Pittsburgh would like to see the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University lose tax-exempt status on some of their buildings in the city.

headline: Recycling not as difficult nor as time-consuming as you may fear
abstract: This opinion discusses how necessary recycling is to solve the waste crisis. Feelings of accomplishment outweigh the frustrations of recycling. The article gives helpful tips for recycling. Highlights include cleaning cans and removing the metal rings. She suggests progressively recycling more and more but taking it step by step.

headline: Proposed US 30 improvements
abstract: A map depicts a section of US Route 30 from Mount Zion Road to Hanover Road. Areas for improvement are highlighted. Improvements include widening the road in several places as well as adding interchanges and ramps.

headline: Innocent man sues Philadelphia over rape and murder convictions
abstract: Matthew Connor, who spent 12 years in jail for the 1978 rape and murder of the 12-year-old Corinthia Fields, was recently released following evidence presented by Philadelphia District Attorney Ron Castille that proved his innocence.  Connor is now suing the city of Philadelphia and former city officials, including former prosecutor Joseph McGill, who, among others, he said is guilty suppressing evidence and intimidating witnesses in his case.

headline: Chill Out, Chilton Borough
abstract: Editors want developers of a proposed home development and golf course, Susan and Richard Mummu, who have proposed a ballot referendum allowing part of the township to secede and become Chilton borough, to modify  plans to meet township standards and build the dvelopment as part of Monaghan Township. This would ensure safety and environmental preservation of Yellow Breeches Creek, which the PA Department of Environmental Resources may deem a flood plain.

headline: A dubious prosecution unravels
abstract: Editors hope prosecutors in Ohio would make better use of taxpayers money than to prosecute corporations for aggressive but legitimate pursuit of their company objectives. Rite Aid and president Martin Grass were charged with bribing New Jersey Pharmaceutical Board member Melvin Wilczynski to resign. Judge Lilliam Greene dismissed the case when it was determined a check given by Grass to Wilcynski was for the exact amount of a buyout of the latter's company. Rite Aid is based in PA.

headline: 3 of Hafer campaign offices omitted from expense reports
abstract: PA Governor Casey's campaign revealed a discrepancy between reports filed with the PA Bureau of Elections and those filed by PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer's campaign manager Patrick Killian. Hafer's campaign has not revealed how offices or phones are being funded. Killian says he is waiting to report a total figure, but noted phone lines will be reported as having been donated at reduced or no cost. Casey's phone costs exceed $3000. The state mandates disclosure of "in kind contributions" exceeding $250.00.

headline: Florio raises taxes and the ire of taxpayers, who punish the party
abstract: After telling voters during his 1989 election campaign he saw no need to raise taxes, New Jersey Governor Jim Florio, faced with a deficit for which he blamed for New Jersey Governor Kean, raised the sales tax, doubled the income tax for the upper brackets, increased aid to local school districts and the poor, and eliminated aid to the wealthiest districts. Taxpayers responded by nearly voting Christine Todd Whitman into office and instituting a Republican Camden County government.

headline: Moody's downgrades Philadelphia bonds
abstract: Moody's Investment Service has downgraded Philadelphia's ratings on long-term bonds, which will make it more difficult for the city to raise funds to help avert its current financial crisis.

headline: United Way drive reaches 35% of goal
abstract: The United Way of the Capital Region has raised 35 percent of its $7.575 million goal. United Way is an umbrella agency that raises funds for more than 50 human-service organizations and many of its grants go to meet the needs of the homeless. The division chairman reported that some area firms exceeded their corporate and employee-campaign goals this year.

headline: Critics scorch NRC plan for radioactive waste
abstract: Director of the Safe Energy Communications Council Scott Denman's suggests low-level radioactive waste be used in manufacturing. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission proposed ways to get rid of radioactive waste which concurred with Denman's. Jonathan Becker of Public Citizen opposes the policy. Environmental Protection Agency estimates 1 death per 10,000 people a year from it. The PA Senate is considering restricting radioactive disposal to designated sites only.

headline: Consciousness raising
abstract: Editors hope the findings of the Philadelphia Human Relations Commission regarding inequitable provision of services for the Latino community heat up the city mayoral campaign. Rev. Thomas A. Ritter was impatient, as were other Commission members, with excuses for low numbers of Latinos in the city's work force. Latino city councilman Angel Ortiz testified as to the mistrust in the Latino community Judge Edward J. Bradley was criticized by the Commission for the lack of Latinos in the court system.

headline: Farmers tell senators it's tough making it
abstract: US Senators John Heinz and Arlen Specter are attempting to get an idea of what farmers need or want from the 1990 farm subsidy bill before the US Senate. Regional farmers had differing views on federal subsidies. Specter and Heinz promised to fight for the region's fair share of subsidies, most of which go to states in the south and west. 14 states produce more than PA, however 33 states receive higher subsidies.

headline: Taxpayers stuck with project's bills
abstract: 19 years ago, the state pressured Federated Medical Resources, a consortium including Temple, Hahneman,  and Thomas Jefferson universities, the University of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia Medical College, to build a research facility rented from the state. Now, the state evicted FMR and forgave $4 million in rent in exchange for 77 acres of land worth less than the money owed, pending approval by the PA Legislature. Taxpayers are being stuck with paying the rest of the money.

headline: Recycling on the half shell
abstract: The author of the letter, a worker at Genpak Corp., reacts to a recent editorial that addressed McDonald's shift away from foam packaging, denouncing the company's move to a non-recyclable, non-biodegradable paper wrap. The author says that foam clamshells are recyclable and don't contain any ozone-depleting chemicals. The author claims the Environment Defense Fund and Ralph Nader haven't offered any alternative that's good for the environment. Genpak Corp manufactures and recycles foam packaging.

headline: Rail Track Examined for Clues
abstract: Investigators are trying to figure out the cause of a 29-car train derailment that forced an evacuation and fouled an Allegheny river tributary.  Over 110,000 gallons of crude oil and sodium hydroxide were spilled into Buffalo Creek after the derailment.

headline: Jury names 4 in North Huntingdon ticket-fix scheme
abstract: A grand jury recommended 2 North Huntingdon commissioners, Phil Abbott and James Tempero, and 2 police officers, William Sombo and Sergeant Donald Austin be charged in connection with a widespread ticket-fixing scheme. Westmoreland County District Attorney John Driscoll expects to file charges in January. The scheme was first discovered during an audit of District Justic Raymond Tubbs' office.

headline: Choosing North Philadelphia
abstract: The article details a small trend of black professionals living in- and trying to rebuild North Philadelphia, a predominantly poor and black area with a reputation for crime, where few middle-income families go to buy homes. Experts estimate that six out of every ten people who live there are impoverished. Many of these professionals, including Germaine Ingram, grew up in the neighborhood. In 1988, Mayor Wilson Goode developed the North Philadelphia Revitalization Plan- a document outlining steps needed to improve housing, economic and social conditions in the area.

headline: Above the law
abstract: Editorial board is concerned about new legislation proposed by PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf that would ban all insurance companies who leave the auto insurance market in PA from writing new policies in other insurance areas.  They are also concerned about the insurance companies' decision to stop coverage in light of a new bill signed by Governor Casey that would reduce auto insurance rates in PA.

headline: 41% of lottery take goes to programs
abstract: More than $1.5 billion was realized from the sale of PA Lottery tickets last year. PA state Deputy Revenue Secretary Karl Ross broke down the distribution of each dollar spent on the lottery. Percents goes to the retailer, 50 to cover prizes, 2 cents to vendor, 2 to administration, and 41 to elderly programs.

headline: Florio Says He Won't Take Pay Increase; Tax Wars Continue
abstract: New Jersey Gov. Florio went on air on a radio show to announce that he was not taking the pay raise given to him by state law, and to take calls from listeners and promote his tax reform plan.

headline: Most Seniority
abstract: US Senators Roberty Byrd and Strom Thurmond are the longest-serving and highest-ranking Senators to currently hold office. In the US House, Jamie Whitten and William Broomfield have the most seniority.

headline: Unmasking the fallacy of the 'women's vote'
abstract: Election efforts did not see gender voting in the primary election between California gubernatorial candidates Diane Feinstein and Attorney General John K. Van de Kamp. In fact, the greatest difference occurred not between groups of men and women, but among groups of women themselves. Those who decided early voted overwhelmingly for Feinstein, while those deciding with three weeks left were more apt to vote for her than those who made a decision within three days of the primary.

headline: Electric car needed
abstract: Stephen A. Copetas of Mt. Lebanon writes to support the idea of developing widespread production and use of electric cars in the US, saying that it would be a much cleaner method of travel and would lessen dependence on oil and gas.

headline: Controversy surrounds flag-burning amendment
abstract: There is a debate about whether or not an amendment should be added to the Constitution concerning the burning of anything that represents the United States flag. One of the arguments is that adding the amendment limits the First Amendment’s protection of the freedom of speech. Many are suggesting that fines and/or prison terms be used instead of amending the Constitution.

headline: How a Maryland county uses TDR's to preserve farms
abstract: James Delaney, a Maryland attorney believes that Montgomery County's transfer of development rights program serves the public's interest by preserving farmland, and that it provides farmers with fair compensation for having the value of their land reduced through agricultural zoning that limits development. Critics of TDR say that the program is unfair to farmers who lost development potential without getting enough money in compensation. They also charge that the Maryland program has been poorly established and has resulted in overcrowding in certain communities. Should the program be implemented in Lycoming County, PA, it would be under local control.

headline: Teacher-pay falsehoods
abstract: Gary John Diclemente of Hershey writes to dispel what he calls the false notion created by the media that teachers in school districts are paid high salaries.  He says that they still earn less than many other professions, and blaming teachers for increased taxes is just a politically driven action.

headline: Recycling programs take root at local level
abstract: The process of implementing a curb-side recycling program is exemplified through the community of Babylon in Long Island, New York. A program must be designed simply without hopes for economic benefit, and with the support of the community. Panis Skislak, communications chairman for the National Recycling Coalition says communities should consider whether or not there is a market for certain recycled goods in their area before adding them to the list of recycled items.

headline: Railroaded on transit
abstract: US Representative William Gray III (D-Phila) seems to have succeeded in forcing PA to adopt a dedicated tax for funding mass transit, especially the Southeast Pennsylvania Transit Authority. Gray inserted a provision in a transportation appropriations bill that would have denied PA of $142 million in federal highway aid unless the special fund for public transportation was created. The editorial comments that this is essentially taxation without representation, since the federal government is requiring that the state enact a tax, and PA's voters have little to no say in the matter.

headline: Jury names 4 in North Huntingdon ticket-fix scheme
abstract: A Westmoreland County grand jury has recommended that two North Huntingdon commissioners and two police officers be charged in a widespread ticket-fixing scheme. They recommended each man be charged with obstruction of justice and conspiracy in connection with almost 500 alleged ticket-fixing incidents. It was done as favors for friends and political allies rather than for personal gain.

headline: Cities must reclaim streets from homeless
abstract: Actor, lawyer, writer, and economist Ben Stein writes that as a city, Philadelphia cannot afford not to help the homeless or those affected by the homeless problem.

headline: Aetna, state reach pact on car insurance
abstract: Aetna Insurance Corporation stopped its departure from PA due to pending outcome of rate case before the state Insurance Department. The Robert Casey Administration made an agreement with the company to rule within two weeks of Aetna's request to sidestep rate rollbacks in the state's new car insurance law.

headline: 41% of lottery take goes to programs
abstract: Over 50 percent of PA State Lottery revenue goes to prizes, while only 41 percent goes to programs to aid senior citizens, the original purpose for the creation of the state-run lottery. The breakdown is given by state Deputy Revenue Secretary Karl Ross. The most money is used by the Pharmaceutical Assistance Contract for the Elderly. Money from the fund is also distributed to local municipalities for transportation systems and county-run agencies such as recreation centers.

headline: Foes of merit selection are jockeying for best shot at bill
abstract: The debate on whether appellate judges should be elected or appointed is underway this week in the legislature. Many groups are attacking it from all sides. Amendments to the bill are being fought off, but the bills future is in doubt. It will be more likely to pass if all judges have to be approved by 2/3 of the PA Senate.

headline: Mourners spill out of chapel for Sigmund service
abstract: Thousands of people attended the funeral of Princeton Mayor Barbara Boggs Sigmund, which was held in a Princeton University chapel. Speakers praised her selfless personality and the way she dealt with her cancer. NJ Governor Jim Florio also spoke at the funeral.

headline: US drug czar lauds state Legislature
abstract: Director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy William Bennett addressed the PA Legislature, drawing criticism from PA State Senate Democrat Robert H. Mellow and House Majority Leader H. William DeWeese for not crediting PA Governor Robert Casey with establishing the Pennfree program. Democrats believe Bennett did not mention Casey in light of upcoming elections. Bennett also met with PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr, saying local governments are critical in the fight against drugs.

headline: Energy Department to Release Health Records of Nuclear Plant Workers
abstract: The Energy Department has agreed to make public the health and occupational records of 200,000 people who have worked in the most dangerous plants in the government's nuclear weapons production complex.  The Three Mile Island Public Health Fund , formed to study the health effects of radiation after the 1979 accident at the power plant, sued the Energy Department for release of the records in 1987.

headline: Court ruling fails to unleash wave of abortion restrictions
abstract: More than 40 states are considering nearly 350 abortion related bills in the year after the US Supreme Court gave states permission to curb abortions. Only PA, South Carolina, West Virginia and Guam passed restrictive legislation. Predictions are that the Webster case will lead to a flood of restrictive abortion measures. Both sides believe one state's law might provide the Supreme Court with a vehicle to take down its Roe vs. Wade decision.

headline: License action pleases Grange
abstract: Legislative director of the Pennsylvania State Grange Brenda Shambaugh is pleased with PA Governor Casey's approval of legislation to allow farmers to transport loads within 150 miles of their farm without a commercial license.

headline: Teachers beat boredom, win kids
abstract: York City educators developed a pilot project, called Flex, that emphasizes child-centered teaching and hands-on learning without costing more than traditional education. The program involves 178 students in sixth through eight grade, selected at random. Parents signed contracts to support the program and teachers had to apply to participate.

headline: Recycling recommendations offered
abstract: Recommendations for implementing a recycling program including which materials to choose and what type of collection system to utilize, were presented to members of the Punxsutawney Recycling Task Force and Borough Council. The engineering consultants presented outlines on various types of materials that can be collected for recycling. The borough must choose three types of materials to be collected and recycled from borough households next fall.

headline: Rains breed gaping pothole
abstract: Heavy rains and warming temperatures contributed to a large pothole on Route 63 near Lower Salford Township that damaged at least six cars over the course of the night and early morning. Police lit flares and placed warning cones near the eight-inch deep pothole after discovering two cars ahd blown tires, four more were stopped to examine damage to their car and six hubcaps were lying near the pothole site.

headline: Larsen Accuses Chief Justice of Misconduct
abstract: PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen has accused Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. of misconduct and formally charged him with violations in two court cases the Philadelphia Inquirer reported.  The formal charges accuse Nix of violating the code of judicial conduct in cases before the Supreme Court in 1980 and 1986.

headline: City Dares Investors to Take a Big Risk
abstract: Philadelphia's disclosure statement concerning the $400 million temporary loan note issue states that the issue is unsecured, uninsured, and high-risk.  The city is attempting to take measures to reassure investors that the loans will be repayed.

headline: Agents happy over Harleysville move
abstract: Harleysville Mutual Insurance Co. may start accepting new customers for auto insurance again, following the state's decision to allow the company to follow less stringent guidelines than defined by the new state auto insurance law. Local insurance agents are hopeful that the company will decide to start accepting new contracts soon.

headline: 44 named to Pa. Heritage Affairs panel
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel announced the reappointment of 22 members and the appointment of 22 new members to the PA Heritage Affairs Commission. The commission, which deals with cultural pluralism and ethnic issues, will include six members from ethnic groups previously unrepresented.

headline: Foglietta takes lead for House
abstract: U.S. Representative Thomas Foglietta was headed to an easy victory over North Philadelphia lawyer Willis W. Berry Jr. in the First Congressional District primary yesterday.  In the only other congressional primary in the area, Donald T. Hadley was trailing minstream Democratic Samuel C. Stretton in the 5th Congressional District. Also includes election returns for U.S. House races and State Senate races.

headline: Mowery jumps into ring, raps Singel on riots
abstract: Rep. Harold Mowery, recently announced as Republican gubernatorial candidate's selection for Lt. Gov., criticized current Lt. Gov. Mark Singel for refusing to send National Guard troops to the Camp Hill prison riot. Lt. Gov. Singel defended his actions, saying that no loss of life or escapes occurred, and saying that Mowery's "shoot from the hip reaction would have gotten people killed."

headline: USX never conspired, lawyer says
abstract: USX Corp., USW District 36 Director Thermon Phillips and union aide E. B. Rich are involved in a federal case in which their company is accused of granting undue pensions to them in exchange for their work negotiating a contract. USX denies the charges. Vice President of labor relations Thomas Sterling testified Rich has remained a critic of USX, which changed a policy resulting in the pension payments after the contract was negotiated. US Judge E.B. Halton is presiding.

headline: EPA says link is weak for cancer, electric fields
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency has reported that some caners may be caused by energy fields created by electrical flows down power lines and through home appliances. The preliminary report states that 60-Hertz magnetic fields from power lines and other sources in the home are a possible but not proven cause of cancer. The strongest evidence comes from the EPA studying children who lived near electrical power transmission lines.

headline: Court ruling’s effect in PA is disputed
abstract: There is disagreement over the legal implications for PA from the Supreme Court rulings on paternal involvement in abortion; some say that there was an opportunity for the PA Governor Robert P. Casey to implement the state’s own parental consent law which requires unmarried girls to gain permission from at least one parent and others saw little impact. Various groups, such as the PA Pro-Life Federation, the Christian Action Council and the PA Catholic Conference see it as a morale booster at least. Legislators propose that Casey petition from federal court the implementation of the PA parental consent provision.

headline: Many farmers fear possible legislation
abstract: Farmers such as Jack Dehoff fear the effects of the US Congress's 1990 farm bill on York and Adams Counties. The bill places new environmental regulations on the use of chemicals and pesticides in farming, which some assert would be harmful to the agriculture industry. Chester Young, district supervisor for the PA Department of Environmental Resources, states that certain agricultural practices produce contaminated ground runoff, especially nitrates from fertilizers. Tom Wolfe, president of the York County Farmers' Association states that homeowners, not just farmers, contribute to putting pesticides and chemicals into the ground.

headline: Teachers strikes end in Fayette, Allegheny Counties
abstract: An agreement has been reached in resolving the teachers' strike in the Laurel Highlands School District, Fayette County, and teacher's are back to work at South Allegheny High School (Allegheny County), though around 200 students may face disciplinary measures in light of their protestation of the teachers' tactics, which involved a nightly decision on whether to strike the next day.  Students say that it seriously disrupts their education and the unpredictability is very frustrating.

headline: Recycling Recommendations Offered
abstract: The Punxsutawney Recycling Task Force and borough council heard recommendations from a Pittsburgh-based engineering firm authorized to conduct a study and aid in securing funding for the borough to implement a recycling program through the utilization of an $8,000 state grant. The borough must identify three materials under state Act 101, which are to be collected and recycled by next fall in order to minimize landfill wastes.

headline: Raise taxes
abstract: Barbara Hafer, Republican candidate for governor, has espoused a rise in the state's gasoline tax of 50 percent, or six cents per gallon. The tax would be used solely to improve our roads. The paper agrees with this tax increase as it is a fair way to tax because it levies on its users.

headline: Law removing tax on widows overdue
abstract: The editorial expresses support for the removal of the "widow's tax" on in inherited property from a deceased spouse. A bill allowing for the tax's removal has received nearly unanimous votes in the PA House and Senate, and several groups are urging PA Governor Robert Casey to sign the bill, though Casey has expressed opposition to the bill.

headline: City deals for funds as Hill housing is given priority
abstract: In Pittsburgh the Masloff administration has placed a proposed major housing project in the Hill District on its priority list. The plan it is to put a mixture of low and moderate-income housing in the mostly poor Hill District, and the city has been moving ahead with zoning and planning approvals from agencies. The city has chosen McCormack, Baron and Associates Inc. to build and finance the project.

headline: Alcoa opts for takeover law; Ludlum rejects most terms
abstract: Aluminum Company of America, despite threats from major pension funds to boycott is stock, has elected to be covered by the state's anti-takeover law. Alcoa became the first major Pittsburgh corporation to be covered by the law. They claim they acted in the best interests of the stock holders.

headline: 87th-seat GOP race heated; Unlinke contest in neighboring 88th District
abstract: The Republican primary for the West Shore's 87th District PA House seat has been filled with controversy while the GOP campaign in the neighboring 88th District has been quiet.  The controversy in the 87th district involves county GOP Chairwoman Pat Saylor accusing Hampden Township Commissioner John V. Thomas of running a deceptive campaign.  Rest of the article discusses the candidates' campaign contributions and issue positions.

headline: For lieutenant governor
abstract: The editorial board supports incumbent PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel's nomination on the Democratic primary ballot for lieutenant governor, despite Singel's anti-abortion views.  Singel's opposition is Edward Mezvinsky, a former state Democratic Party chairman.

headline: Mowery: Casey should be concerned
abstract: Despite polls and analysts indicating that incumbent PA Governor Robert Casey will win by a wide margin against Republican challenger Barbara Hafer, Lieutenant Governor hopeful Harold Mowery said that Casey should be concerned about a comeback win for Hafer.  Mowery said that the fact that Casey started his television ad campaign earlier than most candidates do is a sign of his fear of Hafer and is proof that the Republicans still have a chance.

headline: Venango House Results
abstract: The article details the House election results between Slaughenhaupt and Black in Franklin, Oil City, and the boroughs and townships.

headline: Exxon put at bottom in mine safety
abstract: Exxon Corp. compiled the worst safety record in 1989 among the 20 largest US underground coal producers.  The corporation is contesting the findings, saying that the firm used incorrect data.

headline: Court says flag-burning ban violates right to free speech
abstract: The Supreme Court struck down a federal law protecting the American flag, igniting an impassioned debate in Congress that could quickly lead to passage of a constitutional amendment the would prohibit flag desecration. With in hours President Bush called for an amendment that would make flag-burning a criminal offense. Thursday is flag day. The Supreme Court found that burning the flag is protected by the First Amendment

headline: New Egg Creates Confusion, Skepticism in the Dairy Aisle
abstract: C.R. Eggs Inc.'s introduction of an egg purported to not raise the cholesterol levels of consumers has been met with skepticism and low sales. The special feed given to hens, low in saturated fat and enriched with vitamin supplements, has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, but the FDA is still reviewing the company's findings.

headline: Teachers to strike in Penn Delco
abstract: Teachers in the Penn Delco School District voted overwhelmingly to strike until a contract settlement is reached.  The move affects about 3,000 students, and administrators plan to keep the schools open.

headline: Recycling Reducing Demands on Landfill
abstract: Stephen E. Schopfer, Lycoming County Solid Waste Department business manager said that the amount of municipal garbage from Lycoming County is continuing to decline since the start of curbside recycling in April, but there is no steady, monthly pattern. The overall goal of the state recycling and waste minimization law is to reduce the amount of waste going into landfills and incinerator plants by 25 percent this decade.

headline: Rally Around Osprey
abstract: Legislator Curt Weldon from Delaware County officially launched a massive effort to help salvage the V-22 Osprey military aircraft program which has been cut from the Pentagon's budget request for the second consecutive year.

headline: Lawmakers look for consensus on school violence
abstract: After the Littleton, Colorado shooting massactre, talk shows in Harrisburg, blame the internet, free access to firearms as the main cause for the increased rates of violence in the country. The lack of consensus among the lawmakers will pose to be a challenge for th legislators in Harrisburg.

headline: City gets consent signing on fair housing violations
abstract: The Philadelphia commission on Human Relations signed seven consent orders and decrees against violations of the city's fair housing laws during the summer.

headline: Amid fiscal crisis, a prosperous Philadelphia
abstract: Philadelphia has become two cities: a staggering government with the worst municipal credit rating in the US and an economy that despite the recession continues to do decent business. The city has been trying to anything they can, but local business owners wonder what the fuss is over. The state is unlikely to help it very much to get out its debt.

headline: 8th District
abstract: This chart shows the election results of the PA House race between Howard Fargo and Don Megnin in the 8th District by township and ward.

headline: Former Mayor Says He's Going to Run Again
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Frank Rizzo plans to run for mayor again, saying that Mayor Goode's administration lacked leadership, which he could bring to the table.

headline: Mowrey: Hafer has beaten odds before
abstract: Republican candidate for Lieutenant Governor, PA Rep. Hal Mowrey, believes he and gubernatorial candidate and Pa Auditor General Barbara Hafer can unite the Republican party to win this fall against incumbent PA Governor Casey and Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel. Mowrey criticized Casey's 1990-91 budget and defended Hafer, who was formerly elected Allegheny County Commissioner. Hafer has been criticized for her proposal to raise the gas tax to fund mass transit.

headline: Vending machine pays for cans
abstract: Some "reverse" vending machines are being installed in Pittsburgh that dispense pennies when people put an empty can in. The machines are being used to promote recycling.

headline: Fruehauf Trailers to Shut Down Middletown Plant in May
abstract: The Fruehauf Trailers Middletown plant is scheduled to shut down on May 15 and is being replaced by a new facility somewhere else.

headline: Court supports 2 abortion parental-notification laws
abstract: The US Supreme Court upheld a law requiring doctors to contact a parent of a minor before an abortion, as well as a Minnesota law in which both parents must be contacted. A teen may ask a judge to make an exception if she can prove herself mature enough to make a decision. Dissenting justices say the system is cumbersome. The National Abortion Rights Action League's Kate Michelman opposed the ruling, while the National Right to Life Committee's James Bopp considered the ruling a victory.

headline: Pa. farm markets 'defined'
abstract: A proposal to revise the definition of farm market won full House approval last week in Harrisburg. The bill now goes on to the PA Senate. It would protect some farm markets from local governments prohibitions and nuisance lawsuits. Under the law 50 percent of what is being sold must be grown on a farm. Additionally, farm markets must be seasonal, sell at retail prices and offer only agricultural crops or commodities from PA.

headline: Temple fines 3 students for April fracas
abstract: According to Temple University spokeswoman Kathy Gosliner, three students involved in a racial fracas on North Broad Street, right next to Temple's campus, will be fined and disciplined. The incident occurred when several white members of the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity chased after several blacks, whom they suspected had broken windows at the fraternity house, with sticks and bats. Furthermore, university police came under fire from black student leaders, who allege that the university police used excessive force in trying to quell a crowd of people outside a dormitory after the building's alarm was set off. Temple plans to fire 5 police officers involved in the incident, while some suspect that the officers' union, Local 511 of the International Union of Plant Guard Workers, may dispute the firings through union grievance procedures.

headline: Recycling spreads
abstract: The editorial praises the recycling efforts in PA throughout the past few years, and suggests that Bedford County local leaders ought to start recycling programs or join a larger umbrella program, even though no Bedford County communities will be required by law to begin recycling plans this or next year.

headline: Rapid Transit
abstract: Calling for a Harrisburg area community wide commuter-rail system.

headline: Lawyer Layoffs
abstract: The Office of the Public Defender in Maryland plans to fire forty public defenders in January to help make up the state budget deficit. According to chief public defender in Cencil County, Jane Carins Murray, the cuts will put courts in even worse shape. She also said it made no sense to exempt police and firefighters from budgeting cuts, noting that public defenders are used in almost 75 percent of cases.

headline: City releases housing report
abstract: Philadelphia's Office of Housing and Community Development released a report showing that it has greatly improved its yearly rehabilitation rate despite reduced federal funding since 1984.  It hopes that the report will encourage more private investments in the programs.

headline: An Awakening Giant
abstract: The appointment of Jospeh (Fred) Hamilton as marketing director of the PA Liquor Control Board accelerated changes in the board's approach to the PA control system. With Hamilton have come better selection including specialty wine shops and superstores, better shopping environments, and price promotions. However, Hamilton is careful to adhere to the moderate policies of PA Governor Casey in light of such groups as Mothers Against Drunk Driving and Students Against Drunk Driving.

headline: A Capital Idea
abstract: Berks County residents agreed with Governor Casey and his Cabinet members that the Capital for a Day program boosted community morale.

headline: Frank Clark, former congressman, challenging incumbent Representative Joe Kolten
abstract: Former U.S. Representative Frank Clark of Bessemer, Lawrence County is challenging incumbent Representative Joe Kolter of New Brighton in the Democratic primary for Pennsylvania's 4th Congressional District.  Clark pleaded guilty in 1979 to mail fraud and income tax evasion but does not think this will affect his candidacy.  Gordon Johnston of Brighton and John Loth of Edinburg are challenging each other in the Republican primary.

headline: Mrs. Fulmer buys ad time for Hafer--on Fulmer stations
abstract: Judith Fulmer, executive director of HGF Organization Inc., which owns several PA radio stations, has purchased $50,000 worth of advertisements on those stations for Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer.

headline: Vietnam veteran nominated judge
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey nominated Attorney Hugh F. Mundy to the PA Senate for appointment to the Luzerne County Court of Common Please to fill the vacancy created by the resignation of Judge Bernard J. Podcast. The confirmation may not be passed before the Senate adjourns for the year. Mundy, who has not been heavily involved in Democratic Party politics, was chosen from a list of six names that the Judicial Nominating Commission submitted.

headline: Gas: A new kind of price war
abstract: Comments on the rising price of gas in relation to the Iraq/Kuwait turmoil, but notes that when the price of oil went down, he didn't see the price of gas mirror that drop.

headline: Cross-shaped items on state tree allowed
abstract: A federal judge ruled the cross-shaped ornaments on the Christmas tree in the Capitol rotunda did not represent a violation of the constitutional separation of church and state. The few cross-shaped ornaments on the tree out of 1,000 ornaments did not indicate a state support of Christianity over other religions, which would be a violation of the First Amendment.

headline: Pennsylvania Non-Farm Jobs Show Typical Winter Decline
abstract: Non-farm jobs in Pennsylvania, including retail, government, education, manufacturing, and construction all declined this winter season.

headline: Temple strike wreaks havoc
abstract: The editorial criticizes the Temple University administration and faculty for so far failing to resolve a 5-week long strike, because of which classes will soon be cancelled, causing students to lose valuable money and time in the education.  It also criticizes the state for not getting involved to help resolve the issue.

headline: Recycling start-up is granted $200,000
abstract: Reading has received a state grant of more than $200,000 to finance two components of a mandatory recycling program. The PA Department of Environmental Resources is the one overseeing the grant program which is a $7.6 million program that is being distributed to municipal and county recycling programs throughout PA.

headline: Re-elect Bunt to represent 147th district
abstract: The editorial board endorses PA Representative Raymond Blunt Jr. to the 147th district seat against opponent Bernard McCollum for his ability to both represent his district's needs and compromise with the needs of PA as a whole. McCollum wants a share of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority with no tax increase and supports the right of teachers unions to strike. Blunt would support a designated tax for SEPTA if half of the tax went for mass transportation and supports efforts for a constitutional amendment that would negate striking provisions and mandate arbitration.

headline: Lawyers closely watching a case about ethics
abstract: An ethics case involving a law firm and a large maritime company is being watched by lawyers statewide, as the standing decision by the PA Superior Court is being touted as giving lawyers free reign to engage in conflicts of interest and other misconduct.

headline: City reports steady gains on housing
abstract: Despite declining federal funding, the Philadelphia Office of Housing and Community Development has continued to improve its number of units rehabilitated, due to increased state and private funding.

headline: An international vision
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners are seeking to make the county more active in international commerce by considering the possibility of constructing a world trade center in the area.

headline: A chance to support families
abstract: The editorial commends the 10 Republicans in the PA state House that broke party lines and helped pass a bill that would require most PA businesses to offer more family leave for workers.  Under the legislation, businesses of at least 10 workers would be required to offer up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave, though with benefits, for birth or adoption of a baby, or to care for a sick family member.

headline: Franklin's Legacy
abstract: Mayor Good is reconsidering using the Franklin Fund, a gift left by Ben Franklin, to fund community events such as the 4th of July festival. He ought to use it to fund hospitals and a college and a museum.

headline: Murphy offers bill to merge row offices
abstract: PA State Representative Tom Murphy introduced a bill that could lead to a merger of three elected Alleghany County row offices into one appointed office. The merger is thought to cut costs and to improve efficiency. The General Assembly will most-likely not consider the bill before the summer recess due to the attention on the state budget at the time.

headline: Viewing Harrisburg
abstract: Michael Blood, an Associated Press writer, believes that although ballot proposals are being set up in many states to allow the public to choose whether their legislature will have finite term limits, Pennsylvania will likely not have such a ballot question this November. Many states are allowing voters to decide the issue, since the general public in recent years has begun to distrust "career lawmakers" and has noticed that incumbents are nearly impossible to unseat.

headline: Gasoline prices
abstract: Gasoline prices are at record levels in Maryland and are continuing to increase.  This month's AAA survey shows that prices have increased by 24 to 28 cents since the invasion of Kuwait.

headline: Divisive abortion politics bring Iowa Democratic primary to a boil
abstract: Abortion has become the center-stage issue in the primary gubernatorial elections in Iowa, where the National Abortion Rights League has pledged to defeat the only anti-abortion Democratic candidate, Attorney General Tom Miller. The Iowa Right to Life Committee is also actively participating, according to committee head Marlys Popma. Pro-choice gubernatorial candidates won elections in New Jersey and Virginia in 1989, which were viewed as "primers for the new political era" spurred on by the US Supreme Court's decision to give states more power on restricting abortion.

headline: Pet Lovers Urge Protection for Animals
abstract: Pet owners are lobbying for a "lemon law" for pets, which is designed to force pet shops and breeders to go through more rigorous veterinary procedures before being allowed to sell the animals as pets.  Shop owners opposed the legislation, as it will significantly drive up their costs, and they feel that it's too distrusting of the pet-shop business.

headline: Testimony continues on Temple strike injunction
abstract: Common Please Judge Daniel Lehrer continues to hear arguments from Temple University, which is attempting to force striking teachers back to work or to cancel the 60% of classes which have not yet met this semester.  Faculty and students stand to lose significant amounts of money if classes are cancelled.

headline: Recycling: County Hopes To Have Recycling Center Ready for Operation by Sept. 26 Deadline
abstract: Construction on Lackawanna County's $3.5 million recycling center may come down to the wire on the Sept. 26 deadline for mandatory recycling programs in various communities.  Officials say that even if the plant isn't complete yet, the communities will still be able to begin their programs, and the materials will be stored until the plant is finished.

headline: Regional Airport takes off
abstract: York County commissioners want to form a regional Susquehanna Valley Regional Airport Authority, including Perry, Cumberland, and possibly Adams, Dauphin, Lancaster and Lebanon. Murray Friedman, chairman of the Air Transportation Authority of York County said while he expects resistance from the community to a York airport, it is needed. A spokesman for the Federal Aviation Administration said approval by the FAA and the community is necessary before construction begins.

headline: Legalize Them?
abstract: An opinion expressing opposition to the decriminalization of illegal drugs in America to lessen the drug problem.

headline: City Says Its Homeless Policy is Nothing New
abstract: Mayor Goode's administration clarified that Philadelphia's policy toward the homeless has not changed, they will simply enforce existing policy to maintain order and uphold citizens' rights.

headline: An offer too good to be true
abstract: Fred Bailor of Lewistown writes to detail his experiences digging around about a mail and phone scam to get peoples' credit card numbers and to warn readers not to fall for such tricks.

headline: A day in the life of a caseworker
abstract: Supporting Daughin County  Youth and Childrens Services employees in their demands for a pay raise.

headline: Freind may face GOP opposition
abstract: Ellen Fisher is considering challenging Rep. Stephen Freind in the Republican primary this spring. Fisher is a pro-choice Republican, Freind is known as one of the biggest abortion foes in the PA House.

headline: Murray goes on the attack to unseat incumbent Art Hershey in 13th district
abstract: Dorthea Murray's campaign against PA Representative Arthur Hershey for the 12th Legislative District seat represents the resurgence of the county Democratic Party. Murray has prioritized tax-reform, municipal day care, environmental issues and senior citizen care and has been sponsored by the Gray Panthers. Hershey, a farmer and member of the House Agriculture and Rural Affairs committee has also worked on behalf of the environment, tax reform and senior citizens, though he is charged with over-representing the interests of farmers.

headline: Viewing Harrisburg
abstract: Some critics see incumbent PA Governor Casey's campaign spokeswoman's comments arrogant or cocky, as she has repeatedly dismissed Casey opponent, Barbara Hafer, as a single-issue candidate.  Casey maintains that he will still need to campaign hard, despite a significant lead in fund-raising and predictions that the election will be a rout.

headline: Gasoline Up to $1.20 at Area Pumps
abstract: Gas prices in Philadelphia are continuing to rise, as uncertainty reigns in the Persian Gulf.  Prices also rose recently because of a slight decrease in national crude oil stockpiles.

headline: Editorial uninformed
abstract: PA Representative Thomas Caltagirone corrects misinformation and misconception about House Bill 1141 which editors said meritted a veto by PA Governor Robert Casey. The conception by the American Civil Liberties Union that the bill, which would allow police to compile electronic records during investigations, would also allow infringement on the privacy of innocent citizens, is incorrect. In addition, the bill wishes to bar obscenity with no redeeming value, not obscenity in general.

headline: Pigeon shoot's backers say event to continue
abstract: Organizers announced that they will continue the Fred Coleman Memorial Shoot, a live-pigeon shoot held to raise money for community parks, fire companies, libraries and children's sports leagues. Community leaders said the estimated 300 demonstrators who protest the event every year give it a negative image. Protesters say the shoot is a senseless slaughter that should be banned

headline: V-22 Osprey under fire. New study questions needed.
abstract: A study on the V-22 Osprey aircraft that concluded it is too heavy and vibrated excessively in early tests has ranking Republican U.S. Representative Bill Dickinson calling for a more in-depth study of the costs and need for the program. The General Accounting Office reported that it is unknown if production of the V-22 can begin in 1992 due to "the program's status and high concurrency." The V-22 is made partly by Boeing Helicopters in Ridley, PA- Delaware County's largest employer.

headline: Recycling; Trash program will add $5 to Hummelstown residents' bills
abstract: Hummelstown Borough Manager Michael O'Keefe expects residents will pay an additional $5 per month for recycling services once the borough institutes a state mandated curb-side recycling program. Because of the borough's contract with Waste Management Inc., the cost is less to borough residents than those in nearby areas. The borough also discussed its pavilion construction project, to which the Fuzzy Few Organization agreed to donate should the costs exceed $5000.

headline: Reject airport-area town houses, planners urged
abstract: The South Middleton Twp. Planning Commission members unanimously recommended that the township reject a plan for a town-house complex near the flight path for Carlisle Airport.  Township engineer Bud Grove said that the height of the proposed buildings would give aircraft only a 10th of a foot margin of error during a "worst case" landing at the airport.

headline: Lethal injection passes: Called 'the reasonable thing to do'
abstract: The PA House of Representatives passed a bill replacing the electric chair with lethal injections as the sanctioned mode of state executions, which will now go to PA Governor Robert P. Casey for approval. PA Commissioner of Corrections Joe Lehman testified in favor of the bill, demonstrating support within the Casey administration. McCandless Township Representative Elaine F. Farmer voted against the bill, citing difficulties in administering the injections due to the deteriorated veins of many drug addicted prisoners.

headline: City Says Pitt Residence Violates Zoning Law
abstract: The city and county are still challenging the tax-exempt status of University of Pittsburgh's president Wesley Posvar's official home as it violates city zoning laws because of collegiate business conducted there.

headline: Anti-takeover Law Would Preserve Shareholder Rights
abstract: An editorial urging the House to pass an anti-takeover bill despite immense criticism against it to improve Pennsylvania businesses, shareholders' interests, and subsequent business climate.

headline: A familiar tale of financial woe, but this time it's from Scranton
abstract: Scranton, unable to float a $4 million bond as expected, cannot both pay its bills and meet its payroll for the rest of 1990. Mayor James Connors said he would delay bill payments to avoid tax increases and previous threats of laying off half of the city's police and firefighters. Connors' plan hinges on refinancing the city's quasi-independent sewage authority so it can take the authority's $2.3 million reserve fund.

headline: Friendless Florio
abstract: Gov. Florio of New Jersey suddenly seems to be alone in his support of a tax reform proposal, faced with vocal tax protesters.  He is receiving little help from groups and individuals who originally helped form and promote the proposal.

headline: Murtha, McDade top Congress list of military giving
abstract: John Murtha and Joseph McDade received more donations from defense contractors than any other member of Congress.  The pair hold the two most powerful positions on the Defefnse Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee.

headline: Viewing Harrisburg. An AP News Analysis.
abstract: Recently re-elected to a second term, PA Governor Robert P. Casey will likely change the composition of his Cabinet. The author suggests that Transportation Secretary Howard Yerusalim, Environmental Resources Secretary Arthur Davis and Corrections chief Joseph Lehman will likely remain in the Cabinet. The author suggests that Insurance Commissioner Constance Foster, Banking Secretary Sarah Hargrove and Community Affairs Secretary Karen Miller will return if they want to. Department of Public Welfare Secretary John F. White Jr., Aging Secretary Linda Rhodes, Revenue Secretary David L. Donahoe and Commerce Secretary Raymond Christmas are likely to leave the Cabinet.

headline: Glassport waste incinerator proposal withdrawn
abstract: Glassport Electric Company has withdrawn a proposal to build an incinerator in Glassport due to the influence of residents who spoke out against the plan.  The incinerator would have burnt hospital waste to create electricity.

headline: Education level hikes the black-white gap
abstract: John Jacob of the National Urban League is talking about the difference in education between African Americans and whites. He believes education is important in achieving with employers.

headline: Preservation program gains support
abstract: The state Agriculture Land Preservation Board is trying to push a bill through the General Assembly so that it can pay farmers for purchase of development rights or easements of their land. The program was set up to limit development by paying farmers to keep their property in agricultural use. The Senate is trying to approve legislation to extend guidelines until regulations are in place and PA Senator Edward Helfrick thinks the bill will set up regulations faster.

headline: Three school districts still on strike in Pa.
abstract: Teachers in three school districts returned to classrooms, leaving three unions still on strike.  Nearly 5000 students and over 400 teachers are still affected by the three strikes.

headline: Regional Air Quality Pact Signed
abstract: State, city, and county officials signed a pact during the National Governors' Association convention with goals that could help improve air quality in the region.

headline: Residents Rip I-83 Proposal
abstract: Residents of Shrewsbury Township oppose a new interchange on Interstate 83 south of Exit 1 for the second time in two weeks.

headline: Local men linked to Camp Hill riot
abstract: Two Bedford County residents were among nine inmates charged for crimes committed during the riot at the Camp Hill state prison.

headline: City tours offer view of housing for poor
abstract: Sponsors of the No House Tour, including Harrisburg Fair Housing Council, Catholic Charities, Christian Churches United, and the Hunger Action Resource Team attempt to open the eyes of participants to the problems of poverty and homelessness in Harrisburg. For Patrick A. Zlogar of the PA Bankers Association, the experience was eye opening. Stops on the tour include the Harrisburg Welfare Rights Organization building. Tour leader Kay Pickering hopes to prompt legislative action as well as promote awareness.

headline: Auto insurer predicts big loss
abstract: Nationwide Insurance Co., the third-largest auto-insurer in PA, announced that the company could lose up to $70 million in the next two years as a result of rate rollbacks mandated by the state's new auto insurance law. Despite the predicted losses, Nationwide plans to stay in PA, where it covers over 800,000 vehicles. The company has filed suit challenging various parts of the law.

headline: A 'legal aid society' comes to rescue with supplies
abstract: The Philadelphia Law Department has run out of paper supplies, a reflection of a cash crisis that could push the city into insolvency by December 1st. The Department of Human Services and other city law firms and businesses donated free paper, pads and file folders to the department.

headline: Funding Announcement Pleases Business, Civic Leaders
abstract: Scranton Mayor Jim Connors is pleased the PA Public School Employees Retirement Board will be the guarantor for a new mall. Austin Burke, president of the Great Scranton Chamber of Commerce, said construction represents tax revenue, praising PA Governor Casey and PA Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll for their involvement. He credits Mike Washo, director of the city's Office of Economic and Community Development, for keeping the US Department of Housing and Urban Development, involved.

headline: Musto plan would cut non-paying contractors
abstract: PA State Senator Raphael J. Musto introduced legislation to ban general contractors from receiving state or local government contracts if they fail to pay subcontractors on a timely basis. Those wishing to bid on government jobs would be investigated by the PA Department of General Services to determine if they have legitimately paid subcontractors.

headline: Voices/ How long should people wait before they can buy a handgun?
abstract: Different citizens' opinions about how long a person should wait before buying handguns. They all mention the need for background checks.

headline: Hot Stuff; Coal-related firms boom
abstract: Coal-related businesses in upper Dauphin County have experienced dramatic sales increases due in part to rising oil prices stemming from Iraq's August 2nd invasion of Kuwait. A ton of anthracite coal can provide as much heat as 180 gallons of oil at nearly half the price, though it is not as popular due to necessary ash cleanup.

headline: Faye Wattleton, the former nurse-midwife who is Planned Parenthood's president, will speak at 60th anniversary dinner of the Pittsburgh chapter today at 5:30 p.m. at the Vista International Hotel.
abstract: The picture is of Faye Wattleton, the president of Planned Parenthood. The byline announces Wattleton's upcoming speech at the 60th anniversary dinner of the Pittsburgh chapter of Planned Parenthood.

headline: PSU Farm Show exhibit aimed at more than farmers
abstract: The 75th annual PA State Farm Show in Harrisburg will feature among others, an exhibit by the Pennsylvania State University which focuses on biotechnology and waste management. B. Alan Snider, Penn State professor of agriculture and extension education emphasized the changing nature of 4-H programs as more and more urban youths take an interest in participation. Guy Temple, a Union County extension agent, also commented on the focus of the Farm Show.

headline: Trade-school fraud probed
abstract: Auditor General at the US Department of Education John Thomas testified for a US Senate Committee that trade and technical schools continue to employ fraud. Loans to students attending trade and tech schools amount to 22 percent of program borrowers. However, from this same pool come 44 percent of those who default. President of the National Association of Trade and Technical Schools Stephen Blair said schools with fraudulent practices account for 5 percent of trade and tech schools.

headline: Residents plan to protest expansion of plant
abstract: Residents plan to attend a University of Mount Bethel Township planning and zoning commission meeting to protest construction of a Formica factory. Residents complain the Wildon Industries plant located on Route 512 emits an odor and they don't want to increase it with another plant. The PA Department of Environmental Resources has investigated the smell, however residents say the odor is not constant. Wildon Industries needs permission from the planning and zoning board before it can begin construction.

headline: Road Checks: Putting Drunken Drivers to the Test
abstract: Police say drivers can expect to see many more sobriety checkpoints. The National Highway Traffic Safety Board wants to make them a regular feature of highway driving. A. James McKnight, president of the National Public Services Research Institute, says studies show sobriety checks significantly reduce the incidence of drunk driving. Groups such as Mothers Against Drunk Driving are credited with changing public attitudes toward drunk driving. The American Civil Liberties Union has denounced sobriety checkpoints.

headline: 'Living will' backed
abstract: The Reverend Thomas J. Tobin, general secretary and vicar general of the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh and a member of the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference Adminsitrative Board, clarifies that the PA Catholic Conference opposed recent living will legislation because it eroded Catholic rights and others in the common wealth, not because it is opposed to living will legislation. The Conference attempted to amend the bill, which was overwhelmingly passed by the PA House, but not the Senate.

headline: City's Enterprise Zone to Expand by 135 Acres
abstract: State officials declared that Lancaster's enterprise zone, a targeted area for development, has undergone a 135 acre expansion.

headline: Auto-insurance forms self-explanatory
abstract: The author of the letter expresses satisfaction with the unpopular state insurance-reform law, saying forms were easy to understand and fill out, and explains her own insurance situation. The author argues that it is fair for those wishing to maintain the right to sue for emotional damage to pay for it.

headline: A man who knows tells how to choose judges
abstract: Former New Jersey Governor Thomas Kean criticizes the US Senate for using "litmus tests," which they condemned years ago, on Supreme Court nominee David Souter.  Kean says that Souter is clearly qualified, and nominees should be confirmed based on merit, not political positions.

headline: Gallen takes jab at Demos, Hafer
abstract: PA Representative James J. Gallen, a Republican campaigning for re-election, criticized Democrats at all levels yesterday, though he jabbed at Republican gubernatorial candidate Barbara Hafer as well because of her pro-choice stance on abortion.

headline: n/a
abstract: US Rep. Joseph McDade has co-sponsored a resolution expressing the sentiment of Congress against a proposal by the US Postal Service to eliminate Saturday mailing and one-day first-class delivery. The resolution, if passed, would not be binding on the Postal Service, which has also received criticism for its planned rate hike. The US Chamber of Commerce says the hike may overwhelm many small businesses.

headline: Voinovich Visits Cleveland, Celebrezze Stumps Among Plant Workers
abstract: Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate George Voinovich said that despite his opponent's remarks to the contrary, Democrat Anthony J. Celebrezze Jr. wants to repeal property-tax-limiting law House Bill 920.  Celebrezze criticized Voinovich's tax abatements to steel companies, a move he says leaves outlying neighborhoods behind.

headline: Limerick employee falls ill, plant declared unusual event
abstract: The Philadelphia Electric Co. declared an "unusual event" at the Limerick nuclear power plant in Montgomery County, since a worker who suffered a heart attack while on the job was transported to the hospital while still in his contamination clothing. Hospital officials checked for contamination and found none. Regulations require the reporting of an unusual event when a worker leaves in his/her contamination clothing. The worker was performing maintenance in Unit 2, which has been shut down since mid-Sept. for refueling.

headline: FBI's top-ranking black field agent named to investigate racial case
abstract: The FBI has named the only black agent in charge of a bureau field office to investigate racial allegations against the bureau by Donald Rochon, another black agent.  The FBI has reached a legal settlement with Rochon, which called for this investigation.

headline: PSU Farm Show exhibit aimed at more than just farmers
abstract: Pennsylvania State University exhibit at the PA Farm Show will focus on everything from biotechnology to waste management. This is a responsive to the ever urbanizing world. The issues should be interesting to both urban and rural residents. Professors believe that people will become more comfortable with biotechnology when they understand it is a more precise way of conducting animal and plant breeding.

headline: Treasurer loans PHEAA $200 million for student loans
abstract: PA Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll announced that she has agreed to loan $200 million to the state's student loan agency.  The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) signed a promissory note to borrow the money.  Knoll made the announcement in the Capitol rotunda along with PA Governor Robert P. Casey.

headline: Resort sewage fouling water
abstract: A luxury resort in the Laurel Mountains in Fayette County, owned by Joe Hardy, founder of 84 Lumber Co., is dumping as much as 75,000 gallons of raw sewage a day into a mountain stream and lake.  The PA Department of Environmental Resources is seeking to levy fines against the resort and to address the problem itself.

headline: Route 51 resurfacing may resume Tuesday
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation expects the resurfacing of the last 2.5 miles of Route 51 to resume as early as Tuesday, as PennDOT is reviewing bids from contractors now and paperwork could be signed tomorrow.  The original contractor, Tri-State Asphalt Corp., was fired by PennDOT last week.

headline: Local state jails set to add inmates
abstract: The state prisons at Dallas and Retreat will begin doubling up more cells to accommodate 125 new inmates during the next few months. The measure is part of an effort to maximize jail space and add 1,179 beds in the state's 15 facilities.

headline: City's takeover of homeless program causes concern
