abstract: Payments to key witnesses for information for a book about the Susan Reinert murder case seriously questions the ehtics of a well-know author, Joseph Wambaugh, according to another author, Loretta Schwartz-Nobel.  In 1987, both authors found themselves in a virtual race to deliver manuscripts to their respective publishers on the compelling murder case.

headline: Car subleasing business is sued by state bureau
abstract: The state attorney general's Bureau of Consumer Protection sued Resource Financial Group Inc., a car subleasing business, and three of its officers, for costing consumers at least $11,000 in unexpected charges.

headline: Casey Still Rankled by Slight
abstract: Try as he might, Pennsylvania governor Robert P. Casey could not keep hidden the wound he still nurses after he was denied the opportunity to present the antiabortion message to the Democratic National Convention last month.

headline: Most want to know what went unasked
abstract: The second debate of the presidential series certainly was an unusual experiment.  It offered an opportunity for 209 citizens- undecided voters all- to question the three major candidates on the issues they feel are important.  However, the Patriot-News feels that they did not ask the questions most people wanted to ask, although their questions were intelligent and perceptive.

headline: When Democrats Throw Down the Gauntlet, It's Often 'Read My Clips'
abstract: As detailed claims and counterclaims fill the air, the candidates have been outdoing each other in trying to cite supposedly objective analyses to validate their proposals and discredit those of their rivals.

headline: Abortion law's effect could be limited
abstract: If the US Supreme Court upholds Pennsylvania's restrictive abortion act, activists on both sides agree, the number of arbotions probably will go down.

headline: Coal mine safety record achieved
abstract: Underground mines in Pennsylvania went trhough 1991 without a fatality or serious injury, for the first time in more than 200 years, according to the state Department of Environmental Resources.  Pennsylvania now becomes the first state to eliminate deep mine fatalities for an entire year- nine years ahead of a target date of 2000 to end them nationally.

headline: Even behind bars, veterans gather
abstract: Though Commer Glass is in prison for life without parole, he was, first and foremost, a retired US Army Infantryman.  And as vice-president of Veterans of Graterfor, Vietnam Veterans of America Chapter 466, a group he co-founded in 1980, Glass helped lead a quiet, somber morning service for 150 people in the prison chapel.

headline: Cogen plant fires up opponents
abstract: Despite assurances by Foster Wheeler officials, Hanover Township residents attending a public meeting expressed fears about controversial facility.

headline: Casey's Anger Was Not a Factor Here
abstract: The local ties are one reason Mrs. Clinton wanted a celebration to be held in Scranton.  Another reason that is not being mentioned might be that Clinton did well here despite Governor Robert P. Casey, a Scrantonian, never endorsing him, over the abortion issue.

headline: 'Motor-voter' bill called 'auto-fraudo'
abstract: The Senate passed the "motor-voter" bill, compelling states to automatically register voters when they apply for drivers' licenses or government benefits.  Senator Mitch McConnell called it "auto-fraudo" and there were some partisan concerns too.

headline: Where Anita Hill Is the Silent Third Candidate
abstract: At a roadside inn near Scranton, a dozen campaign workers sat briefing Senator Arlen Specter, Republican of Pennsylvania, on how a certain woman was threatening his bid for re-election.

headline: Abortion 'railroad' planned in case Roe overturned
abstract: Abortion rights supporters say it will work like the Underground Railroad that secretly transported slaves escaping to the South.  Buth they're calling it the "Overground Railroad" and if the Supreme Court eoverturns legal aboritons, they say their volunteer network will be used o transport pregnant women from states that restrict and ban abortion to those where it is legal.

headline: Commissioners investigating slap, future of LETA program
abstract: Terry L. Kauffman and Brad S. Fischer, two Lancaster County Commissioners,  met with Shaki Wilson, the 19-year-old downtown cleanup crew member who said he was struck last week by the owner of Café 111.  Wilson was supervising a crew of Clean and Green Team members who were employed by the Lancaster Employment and Training Agency (LETA) when the confrontation occurred.

headline: Ex-Notre Dame Coach to Get Drug Policy Job
abstract: Former Notre Dame basketball coach, Digger Phelps, will join the office of national drug control policy as a liason with the Bush Administration's "weed and seed" initiative.

headline: Connelly eyes IPO, but lawsuit rattles Gold Coast casino effort
abstract: Pittsburgher John Connelly's Davenport, Iowa-based gambling company is planning to go public with a $70 million stock sale, public documents show.  Connelly's President Riverboat Casinos Inc. needs the proceeds to pay off debts and expand its gambling operations into Mississippi and St. Louis, but the efforts could be complicated by a lawsuit filed against him by a Texas competitor.

headline: Casey's rating takes a plunge
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey's job approval rating is the 14th lowest of the nation's 50 governors, according to a poll conducted alst month for Thomson News Service.

headline: Mowery a proven leader
abstract: Hal Mowery was a proven and effective leader during his term as a state legislator, so he deserves support for election to serve as state Senator in the 31st District.

headline: White House hopes trip polishes image
abstract: President Bush- his foreign policy credentials tarnished by lingering problems in Iraq, Haiti, Panama and China- looks to restore his image as world leader with a European tour beginning July 4.

headline: Abortion Rights Strategy
abstract: Abortion rights groups expected the Supreme Court to overturn Roe v. Wade in June, and they were prepared with legislation to undo the damage.  The Freedom of Choice Act was designed to protect by statue abortion rights that since Roe have been protected by the Constitution.  Though the court weakened, not overturned, Roe, the idea would have been complicated by several factors anyway.

headline: Communities in state resist incinerators
abstract: USPCI, a subsidiary of Union Pacific Railroad Inc., wants to build a commercial hazardous waste incinerator less than 2,000 feet from Clyde Peeling's Reptiland.  Clyde challenges whether USPCI can be trusted to comply with the laws governing operation of an incinerator, and is not willing to take the risk with his family.

headline: Expert: Health care in city jails is sick
abstract: Medical care in the city's prisons is so poor that some inmates have died from lack of proper care, according to a 68-page report by Robert L. Cohen, a prison medical-care expert.  He concludes, "The medical care system in Philadelphia jails is in disarray."

headline: CoreStates to acquire bank-service firm
abstract: CoreStates Financial Corp. said that it would acquire a small New Jersey bank-service firm in a move designed to expand the Philadelphia bank's fee-based corporate business.

headline: Cash 5 to debut in April
abstract: By mid-April, Pennsylvania will launch a new cash jackpot game- Cash 5- to try to bolster sales.  The game will offer top prizes of $250,000  for picking five of 39 numbers.

headline: 'Mr. Pennsylvania' turns to poetry
abstract: While his friends hope he'll live to be 100, Peter Cyrano Wambach at 76 has put together a sprightly volume of 128 more or less poems that mark an incredible journey.  But it's hardly his swan song, since the one-time radio personality, newspaper columnist, politician and bon vivant still possesses his powerful personality.

headline: Who gains from Perot's exit?
abstract: Texas billionaire Ross Perot surprises supporters by announcing Thursday he's abandoning his run for the White House.  Bill Clinton is the early beneficiary of Ross Perot's departure from the presidential race.

headline: Abortion: case or cause?
abstract: In arguing against Pennsylvania's Abortion Control Act in the US Supreme Court, an attorney for Planned Parenthood put case before cause by suggesting that, to uphold the Pennsylvania law, the court would have to dispose of Roe v. Wade, the 1973 decision legalizing abortion.  It is understandable that supporters of legal abortion want to energize the effort to secure protection for abortion rights in case Roe is overturned.  But they shouldn't concede the battle in the court before it is lost.

headline: Company's goal- Turn sludge into pay dirt
abstract: A sludge treatment company has concocted a way for communities to turn their sewage into something akin to pay dirt, a commercial fertilizer that looks, smells and acts like soil.

headline: Fathers demand fairness
abstract: Women and children are not the only ones affected by the child support system.  Fathers are also frustrated because while they pay hundreds of dollars in support a month, the current system requires no accounting of how the money is used.  As a result, they have no idea how much of the money they pay actually goes to their children.

headline: Court agrees to hear tavern appeal
abstract: The state Supreme Court has agreed to hear an appeal from owners of a former Mechanicsburg tavern, Paradise Hotel, that lost its liquor license after the Liquor Control Board ruled it a "nuisance bar."

headline: Cash-rich congressman
abstract: Out of the expected 150 congressmen retiring or being booted off Capitol Hill this year, about two dozen House members could walk away with their pockets stuffed with cash.  Locally, Republicans Richard T. Schulze and R. Lawrence Coughlin are still holding purses, which they should hand in and retire honorably.

headline: Mrs. Clinton finds gem in area
abstract: A Lower Paxton Township artist may have a personal stake in the presidential election.  If Democrat Bill Clinton wins, paper jewelry designed by Anna Marie Ginocchi Enders may be headed for the White House.  The word is that Hillary Clinton would ask Enders to design accessories for her inaugural outfit.

headline: Why do state legislators smoke, eat, sleep on the job?
abstract: In a trip to the capitol, a junior in high school writes about how Senators and House members smoked, ate and slept with a complete lack of respect for the speaker.

headline: Abortion: From the Courts to the Voting Booth
abstract: The Supreme Court listened to both sides of the endless debate over abortion, with ruling on the Pennsylvania case of Roe v. Wade due by the beginning of July.  If the Supreme Court is no longer going to protect a woman's right to make this decision, if 50 states are going to be allowed to make 50 different lawas, if a woman's rights are to become a matter of geography, if ever election is going to include a referendum on abortion, it's time to find out.

headline: County motorists may face tougher emissions tests
abstract: Car and light truck owners in Centre County might be required to have a special test of their vehicles' tailpipes later this year under a 1990 federal law.

headline: FBI increasing efforts in probing health-care fraud
abstract: Estimating that health-care fraud is costing billions of dollars and hitting those least able to protect themselves, the Department of Justice is doubling the number of FBI agents investigating such crimes and setting up special prosecution units in 12 cities, including Philadelphia.  In addition to the 46 FBI agents working on health-care investigations, 50 agents will be moved to such cases from counterspy and counterterroism assignments.

headline: CREDC names interim chief
abstract: Clifford L. Jones, former president of the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry, will become interim executive vice president of the Capital Region Economic Development Corp. on Nov. 16.  He will join CREDC as the organization seeks a replacement for William Graf, who is resigning.

headline: Census Bureau seeks comment on '90 count for federal funding
abstract: After an outcry from Northeast and Midwest lawmakers whose states stood to lose millions in funding, the Census Bureau has decided to seek public comment on whether to use adjusted figures to disburse federal dollars to state and local governments.  The agency is considering five options.  Using one set of figures, Pennsylvania would be the biggest loser.

headline: Ms. Outsider is challenging Mr. Insider in Pennsylvania
abstract: Last May, when Lynn Yeakel won the Democratic primary with a video-tape ad of Senator Arlen Specter interrogating Anita Hill, there were many who assumed it was all over.  In the afterglow of her victory, with all th rosy hype about the year of the woman, some assumed she would easily beat the veteran Senator, but the race is tough.  The sharp differences make the race one of the most interesting political studies of '92.

headline: Wife far outearns husband
abstract: Bill Clinton has relied on his talented wife, Hillary Clinton, to pay most of the family's bills.  He publicly questions where he'd be without her.

headline: Abortion-rights rally in DC draws 500,000
abstract: In one of the largest demonstrations in the nation's capital, an estimated half-million abortion-rights advocates marched in an outpouring of political strength aimed at presidential, congressional and statehouse races in November.

headline: County rethinks subsidy
abstract: Bucks County intends to get out of the recycling business.  After spending more than $1.8 million in the past three years to subsidize the recycling of aluminum, glass and newspaper, the county wants to lease its collection center in New Britain Township to Otter Recycling in Bristol, a private operator.

headline: Fire Power- A Single Family Makes Many of Cheap Pistols That Saturate Cities
abstract: The three companies that make the Raven, Jennings and Davis guns are all owned by members of the Jennings family, where George Jennings is the patriarch of the secretive clan in southern California that has made a fortune from a market of mystery.  The family's pistols have been selling cheaply to the nation's criminals and kids, but Jenning's offers no apology.

headline: Deal to buy USAir stake is imperiled
abstract: The failure of British-American talks on freer competition between the two countries' airlines has left a cloud over the proposed $750 million deal between British Airways PLC and USAir Group Inc.

headline: Census guesstimate costly to Pennsylvania
abstract: The Census Bureau's adjustment, although it may not be accurate, would be costly, especially for Pennsylvania, which would lose $40 million a year.

headline: Murphy silent after squeaker
abstract: Austin Murphy, incumbent Democrat, barely survived the struggle of his political life in Tuesday's election, defeating Republican William Townsend, a political newcomer, by less than 3,200 votes.

headline: Willie who? This time, crime talk doesn't pay
abstract: It was a typical day, based on the most recent crime statistics, and the presidential candidates spoke mainly of other things.  Its rising rate seems to parallel a sense of American decline, but this year's race is not concerned with such talk.

headline: Administration Partly Lifts Abortion Advice 'Gag Rule'
abstract: In a partial reversal of a longstanding and controversial policy, the Bush administration will permit doctors at federally funded family planning clinics to advise pregnant women on abortions.

headline: Court sides with Rapho in dispute over landfill
abstract: An order issued Friday and signed by Judge Michael J. Perezous dismisses Maleable Castings Co.' appeal, saying that the firm "has not carried its burden of persuading" officials that the landfill should be approved.  The landfill was to be placed in Rapho Township.

headline: For Savitz, it was a life of promise and success
abstract: The arrest last week of Edward I. Savitz followed six months of apparently poor coordination and lack of cooperation between police, child welfare workers and archdiocesan school officials- all of whom had received reports that he was paying teenagers for their underwear, feces and sexual favors.

headline: Dealers get clear shot at licenses
abstract: More than 12,000 licenses to buy and sell firearms have been issued in the state.  ATF has been regulating the licenses to control the dealer.

headline: Challenger knocked out on technicality
abstract: Democratic congressional hopeful Joe Hayes' petition to get on the ballot was rejected because he collected signatures about a month too early, leaving him three days to collect 1,000 signatures from registered Democrats.

headline: Murtha, Kolter back Foley
abstract: Representatives Joseph Kolter and John Murtha said they still support embattled House Speaker Tom Foley, despite increasing criticism and a demand from a member of his own party that he resign because of his handling of recent congressional scandals.

headline: Winners, losers
abstract: Fortune's up for Al Gore, the Tennessee senator who clearly wants to be president, and fortune's down for Robert P. Casey, the governor who continually argues that the Democratic Party needs to moderate tis abortion-rights stand by backing more restrictions and who was spurned in his efforts to speak on the issue at the convention.

headline: An Abortion Law Ruling May Provide a Boost to Anti-Abortion Forces
abstract: Though less than a third of voters think abortions should be illegal, they could be a plus for Bush in a race agianst two abortion-rights backers.  Opposition to making abortion ellegal rose in the WSJ/NBC poll to a 10-year high of 65% of voters.

headline: DER backlog stymying 'thousands' of projects
abstract: Millions of dollars in Schuylkill County projects are caught in the slow-grinding wheels of the state Department of Environmental Resources, which is understaffed by about 400 workers.

headline: For women of fashion who plan on stashing
abstract: What with all the problems a working woman encounters- pay inequalities, the "glass ceiling," family obligations- the last thing she needs to worry about is what to do with her handgun.  For women who need clothing that allows them to hold a handgun, Linda Mutchnick established PistolERA, manufacturer of "firearm-capable clothing" for the well-dressed woman.

headline: Eager to work-anywhere
abstract: The Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce held a two-day job fair that brought in more than 6,000 job hunters.  Many of the companies have experienced downsizing and hiring in the job market is tight.  Even unstable businesses attracted applicants because of new college graduates and lay-off victims.

headline: Challenger: Rep. Goodling 'liberal'
abstract: Independent congressional candidate Tom Humbert says US Representative William Goodling is a "liberal in disguise" and is not holding to the positions his constituents support.

headline: N.J. ballot issues
abstract: South Jersey voters may not have a lot of closely fought political races to occupy them next Tuesday, but they will be challenged by three ballot issues of more-than-routine interest.  The Inquirer recommends how NJ voters should vote on the three issues.

headline: Winners, losers
abstract: Lynn Yeakel, the Democratic Senate contender, was climbing in the polls and getting national media attention and new endorsements.  All the signs of a candidate gaining ground.

headline: Banquet location fractures Steelton
abstract: Some members of Steelton Borough's black community are upset that a banquet honoring Steelton's high school basketball championship team, which is made up mostly of African-American students, is being held in the local Moose Club, which has no black members.

headline: DER estimates superfund site clean-up outside of Meadville at $28.9 million
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources said clean-up for the Avtex Fibers state superfund site outside Meadville wil cost an estimated $28.9 million, opting for Alternative 3, which involves solvent extraction of contaminants at the site.

headline: Former city fire official cleared in state ethics case
abstract: A divided Commonwealth Court has cleared Thomas W. Hitchings, a former Pittsburgh Fire Bureau captain, of illegally serving as a paid consultant in a lawsuit filed over a fire he investigated.

headline: Former Liquor Store Opens At Seneca Street Site
abstract: The Pennsylvania Wine and Spirits Shoppe opened at its new home on Seneca Street after being transformed to meet the industry's changing needs and latest trends.

headline: Chance of strike at USAir growing
abstract: Officials of the union that threatened to strike USAir last week are talking tough again and recommending that its members reject the company's final offer and vote to strike by the end of the week.

headline: Nahill won't run again for seat in state House
abstract: State Representative Charles F. Nahill Jr., the seven-term legislator who chairs Montgomery County's Republican organization, announced that he would not seek re-election after 23 years in elective office.

headline: Wofford screened for vice president
abstract: In late March, US Senator Harris Wofford said he wasn't interested in sharing the Democratic ticket with Bill Clinton, but now Wofford's office has been cooperating with Clinton aides screening prospective vice presidential sources.

headline: Barr Attacks Abortion-Rights Bill
abstract: Attorney General William P. Barr said a bill that would forbid states to impose restrictions on most abortions goes far beyond the standard set in Roe vs. Wade, the Freedom of Choice Act, and he questioned Congress's authority to enact such a change.

headline: DER fines wrecking company $18,500
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources ruled that US Wrecking Inc. committed "knowing and willful" violations of asbestos regulations in razing a city building in February 1988, giving the company an $18,500 fine.  The firm failed to notify the DER prior to the demolition.

headline: Founder of scam gets 21 months
abstract: The founder of a massive pyramid scheme, Fredrick Taft, who authorities said defrauded 27,000 people in 30 countries was sentenced to one year and nine months in prison.

headline: Economy bites into a dream
abstract: After learning he was dying of cancer, John Swalley Sr. closed his shop, the Blandon Sub Shop, after six years of business to ensure his family was left with something to keep them going after he was gone.  With the economy at such a slunder, people couldn't afford to spend what they used to at the sandwich shop.

headline: Checks Still Matter
abstract: Congress members hoping the Los Angeles riots and Ross Perot might have overshadowed outrage over bounced chekcs got little solace this week.

headline: NEA gives its support to Clinton
abstract: Democratic presidential candidate Bill Clinton will be endorsed by the National Education Association, the nation's largest teachers' union, with the "highest percentage of vote" ever given by the group.

headline: Women of all ages have helped open the doors
abstract: Katherine M. Keefe writes in response to BJ Philips' column about the absence of young women at Lynn Yeakel's victory celebration, saying that the 20- and 30-somethings can be relied on by Lynn Yeakel and other candidates for their supply of meaningful contributions- their votes.

headline: Beliefs
abstract: Within a few months the Supreme Court will almost certainly rule on the constitutionality of a Pennsylvania law that hedges access to abortion with a number of conditions.  Whatever the decision, both parties will make abortion an issue in the general election.

headline: DER out of control, critics charge
abstract: After a case where a coal mining company was shut down by the state Department of Environmental Resources in which the owner claims was punishment for making the departmentment look bad, legislators who oversee DER believe the agency is out of control and its personnel are almost impossible to fire for incompetence and favoratism.

headline: Fugitive in '74 slayings is found in Puerto Rico
abstract: Sandy Basile was convicted of helping kill two people in a Montco bar.  She had escaped from the State Correctional Institution in Muncy in 1982, but after 10 years on the lam, Basile finally was found by authorities, living a new life as a wife and mother in rural Puerto Rico.

headline: Empire Landfill principals are top officials of firm buying hotel
abstract: A check of corporation records has shown that previously unidentified officers of the Empire Sanitary Landfill in Taylor are owners of the firm that wants to buy the Lackawanna Station Hotel.

headline: Cheer Up, America! The Future Only Looks Bad From Here
abstract: The article talks about how our current predictions about the future will be as wrong as those in the past and explains how to use simple graphs and charts to make an outlandish prediction for the future.

headline: Negotiators see progress in workers' comp talks
abstract: House and Senate negotiators, continuing to work behind closed doors to forge a compromise on workers' compensation reform, said that they were optimistic about reaching an agreement by the end of the session.

headline: Worth Repeating
abstract: Bill Clinton admonishes his Wharton hosts: The Wharton School is home to much of America's economic potential, and has produced many of our best corporate leaders.  Yet it is also a powerful symbol of where our country went wrong in the 1980s.  Together, we must bring an end to the something-for-nothing eithic of the '80s.

headline: Black clergy finally confronts AIDS crisis
abstract: When the Reverand J. Jerome Cooper came down from the pulpit to deliver a eulogy beside the casket of a 21-year-old parishioner, he confessed that the church had failed.  Its deacons had refused to give communion to a dying man, and Mr. Cooper himself had washed his hands after every visit to the man's hospital bed.  From that day on, he vowed he would never again let the church discriminate against anyone suffering from AIDS.

headline: DER seeks your ideas
abstract: In the southeast region of the state we are in severe non-attainment for ozone and commute trips are a significant contributor to this air pollution problem.

headline: Fund-raiser bilking Pa., Preate says
abstract: A fund-raising campaign falsely claiming to help the state police enforce drinking and seat-belt laws has bilked Pennsylvanians of more than $100,000, State Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. alleged yesterday.

headline: Expansion goes outside crayon lines
abstract: Tom Muller, overseer of the Crayola line at Binney & Smith factory in Easton, joined the company in 1990 and began to update and expand the lineup.  He expects 80 new or revised products next year.

headline: Choice: issue or political hot potato?
abstract: All three presidential candidates say a major overhaul of the nation's primary and secondary schools is long overdue.  All agree there must be some type of national standards or testing.

headline: Networks play censor with political videos
abstract: The Republican convention in Houston ends tonight, but early reviews are already in.  To be precise, early movie reviews are in, and the networks have rated the Republican's move R: restricted to viewers watching CNN.  Like the Democrats, the Republicans have made a movie about their nominee to show at their convention.

headline: Yatron to leave office
abstract: After 24 years as a US Representative in the Sixth Congressional District, Gus Yatron is retiring from in December when his current term expires.  Although he served most of his career without controversy, some has derived after he was accused by his former district aide, Elwood J. Broad, for extorting kickbacks from Broad and other members of the Congressional staff.  He was accused by Broad for stealing funds for personal purposes, although Broad withdrew allegations in October.  Under federal law, Yatron must retire if he wants to convert campaign funds into private use.

headline: Black Contractors in Md. See Share of Set-Asides Slipping
abstract: Of the top 10 minority contractors for the Maryland Department of Transportation, only two are black.  The pattern has prompted growing concern among black contractors that a program designed primarily to offset the effects of discrimination against African Americans is failing.

headline: Down by the river, they watch for the invader
abstract: The hunt for the dread zebra mussel- a clingy, crusty critter that clogs water intakes throughout the Great Lakes region- is on this year in the Delaware River.

headline: Funeral procession goes through area of slaying
abstract: A funeral procession passed slowly through the drug-plagued Harrisburg neighborhood, where Damian A. Walker was recently shot to death.  The slain man's father said that the procession went that way to draw attention from members of the community.

headline: Firm May Publish Daily Newspaper
abstract: Webb Communications Inc. is considering starting publication of a daily newspaper serving the Williamsport area, said James Webb, chairman of the company, which was created after Webb bought Grit Publishing's offset printing operation earlier this year.

headline: Citizens Jury call Yeakel ad offensive
abstract: Senate candidate Lynn Yeakel's most controversial tlevision ad- a commercial calling US Senator Arlen Specter the 'most obnoxious man in the Senate"- was criticized as "very objectionable" by a panel of 16 Pennsylvania voters, called Citizen's Jury.

headline: New teacher contract does little for reform
abstract: Philadelphia school teachers walked around the Civic Center Monday night, waiting for the president of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers to arrive with a contract proposal they could vote on.  If it didn't happen within the hour, they'd all be on strike.

headline: Yeakel gets heat; Specter, warmth
abstract: Lately Lynn Yeakel has experienced something new- angry voters and tough questions.  An d the long-besieged Arlen Specter has experienced at least one day of political grace.

headline: Black Expo: They came to deal, and to dream
abstract: Three black women, Carolyn Miller, Ginger Newman-Askew and Margaret Benjamin had the dream to have a small business of their own.  They attended the Black Expo USA at the Philadelphia Civic Center, which is a mixture of trade show, business convention, and music festival.  They plan to open a consulting practice for small businesses.

headline: Downington won't sell waterworks
abstract: The Downingtown Borough Council has spurned Philadelphia Suburban Water Co.'s offer to buy the local waterworks, slowing the regional utility's march through Chester County.  PSW's bid was turned down as cash-poor.  Now fast work is needed to meet a deadline on a new plant.

headline: Good law must have funding, crime panel told
abstract: Adequate funding for law enforcement enables Massachusetts authorities to keep organized crime out of the popular form of charitable fund-raising.  Raymond G. Hotte, manager of the Massachusetts State Lottery Commission, testified before the PA Crime Commission with two days of hearings on organized crime's infiltration of bingo in Pennsylvania.

headline: Firms get OK to cut insurance
abstract: A rapidly growing number of victims of cancer, AIDS and other serious illnesses are discovering that under recent court interpretations of a law that was originally intended to protect employees' benefits, their insurance coverage can evaporate when they need it most.

headline: Citizens Jury's fault
abstract: The 17 voters from eastern Pennsylvania on the Citizens Jury evaluating our choices for US Senate didn't even consider Arlen Specter's grilling of Anita Hill and his essentially rubber-stamping all but four of the more than 500 Reagan-Bush nominations of federal judges to lifetime appointments.

headline: Nixon has other plans
abstract: Though his last political convention was in 1972, some convention planners had suggested this might be the year to welcome him back for the Republican National Convention.  Nixon wrote to Bush's campaign chairman, Robert Mosbacher, saying he won't be attending.

headline: Yeakel is speaking new political language
abstract: Lynn Yeakel, symbol of women's aspirations to political paower, up against Arlen Specter, Republican, and- ever since he grilled Anita Hill on national television- symbol of men who just don't get it.  A key to to her campaign is that Lynn has been talking in plain language, and Arlen talks in political double talk, and people are sick of it.

headline: Casey still talking against abortion
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey last night moved into a new phase in his campaign against abortion with a speech opposing the proposed federal Freedom of Choice Act.

headline: Envronment quiz- Which state agency is an island?
abstract: Ralph Haurwitz gves a humorous quiz on environmental issues in the Pittsburgh area.

headline: Graterford guard accused in drug smuggle attempt
abstract: Nathaniel Butler, a corrections officer at the State Correctional Institution at Graterford was detained today after he was found carrying marijuana and pills during a routine strip search, a prison official said.

headline: Fund pool insuring agency
abstract: A $4 million pool originally set up by the stae Legislature to insure private bank depositors now is insuring the state agency that onws the state-created Marian State Bank, Philadelphia.

headline: City courts seek ban on union
abstract: Philadelphia court officials have asked the state Supreme Court to bloc an election that would give court workers a chance to decide whether to join a labor union.  The Pennsylvania Labor Relations Board plans to hold an election, and the lawsuit asks the state Supreme Court to rule that the PLRB has no jurisdiction over the Philadelphia courts- on the ground that the courts are an independent branch of government.

headline: No balance
abstract: Congressional Democrats let us know this week exactly what they think of the proposed Balanced Budget Amendment.  By a comfortable margin, the Senate voted to continue stalling tactics, in effect killing the issue for the year.

headline: Yeakel laments the focus on her country club membership
abstract: Though new to politics, Lynn Yeakel states that there's a lot of room for improvement.  In rebuttle to issues mentioned of her country club membership, which could signify bigotry, Yeakel says it is a diversion from real issues.

headline: Court sets precedent over truth
abstract: The 5-4 ruling by the US Supreme Court on the Roe vs. Wade abortion decree should worry all Americans- wether supporters or opponents of abortion rights.  The opinion is at war with itself.  And an opinion so divided cannot last.

headline: Farmers in county fear nutrient management bill
abstract: Local farming organizations are mobilizing to stop an 11th-hour legislative effort that would put nutrient management legislation on the state books before the legislative session ends.  Farmers, conservationists and lawmakers have worked for more than four years to craft a bill to help keep the state's manure from washing down the Susquehanna River and polluting the Chesapeake Bay.

headline: Grenades from Gap probed
abstract: Police in Washington County and investigators from Fort Indiantown Gap are investigating as to how three simulator grenades got from the Lebanon County base to the Washington, PA, area where they were detonated early Wednesday.

headline: Gannett ups ante with printing plan
abstract: The Gannett Co., publisher of the North Hillls News Record and the Valley News Dispatch, has reached an agreement to buy 10 acres in Marshall Township's Thorn Hill Industrial Park for a new printing and production plant.  While Gannett officials deny that the acquisition is part of a plan to expand the North Hills News Record into all of metropolitian Pittsburgh, industry analysts say that that is a very real possibility.

headline: City Democrats back Buxton for 103rd
abstract: Although former District Justice Michael A. Stewart presented himself to the Democratic City Committee as a candidate for the 103rd Legislative District's House seat, the endorsement overwhelmingly went to Ronald Buxton.  Stewart was removed from office by the state Supreme Court on account of accusations that he violated elections codes and played favoratism with employees.

headline: No Winner in First Round Of McDade Corruption Case
abstract: The first round of US Representative Joseph M. McDade's corruption case ended in a draw Thursday when both sides lost the initial battle.  In separate 12-page rulings, a federal judge in Philadelphia refused to dismiss an indictment against McDade and denied a government request to disqualify some of the congressman's lawyers.

headline: Yeakel Taps More Voter Anger
abstract: Lynn Yeakel, a women's rights activist outraged over the treatment given to Anita Hill, especially by Republican Arlen Specter, won a stunning upset victory in Pennsylvania's Democratic Senate primary- and the right to challenge Specter in the fall.

headline: Diane Allen accuses CBS of sex, age bias
abstract: Saying that Channel 10 management has "crushed my caeer," WCAU-TV anchor Dianne Allen has filed a federal age and sex-discrimination complaint against CBS.

headline: Farmers want paid for wildlife damage
abstract: Farmers would like to receive compensation from the state- similar to a program in Wisconsin which collects a $2 additional fee on hunting licenses to help pay for crop damage- for losses from the growing number of deer herds, flocks of wild turkey and fur-bearing animals that are not being trapped.

headline: Group tracking 'all
abstract: A solution to the drug problem in poor neighborhoods is called Youth Build Harrisburg, which is helping carve a future clean of drugs and full of promise.  Working since June on a plan to attack the area's social ills, the coalition founded by John O. Vartan will spend the month listening to Harrisburg residents talk about the problems in the city and suburban neighborhoods.

headline: Getting down to business
abstract: The Casey administration is trying to find a buyer for Bethlehem Steel Corp.'s Johnstown plant, with 1,700 jobs at stake.

headline: City draws fire for quick shift in employee funds
abstract: Philadelphia city officials have abruptly shifted the investment of $27 million in retirement accounts for about 13,000 city workers, prompting a flood of complaints from city workers in recent days.

headline: Nomination and celebration
abstract: Democrats traveled back to the future Wednesday, honoring fallen Kennedys before staking their claim to the White House on another young man.  Putting aside the disputes that still divide them, delegates to the party convention finally performed the two jobs they came here to do: with high hopes and a touch of trepidation they nominated Arkansas Governor Bill Clinton for president.  And then they celebrated.

headline: Yeakel to speak tonight
abstract: Lynn Yeakel will give what could be the most important, and certainly the most widely watched, speech of her life when she addresses the Democratic National Convention.

headline: Disabled Americans deserve open doors
abstract: Hopefully, when the Americans with Disability Act goes into effect, it will open doors to the millions of disabled citizens in this country.  The law's intent is to make getting a job and going to stores and public places as easy for a handicapped person as it is for others.

headline: Finding wildlife in the big city
abstract: When Rich Shire joined the Pennsylvania Game Commission in 1985, it was the Big Woods he longed for- vast, rugged land with more deer and bears than people, a far cry from his boyhood on the streets of Tacony.  Naturally, they assigned him to Philadelphia.

headline: Gunmen anxiously await end of reign
abstract: In Mogadishu, Somalia, the gun has been the only national law for almost two years, feeding the nation bullets at the expense of food.  US Marines will be landing in that capital to try and rid the nation of their weapons.  Gunmen are fearful of the Marine landing, but most Somalis are preparing to welcome with open arms and hearts.

headline: Glass Plant Plans Advance
abstract: Progress is being made in efforts to reopen the dormant Foster Forbes Glass Plant on Route 8.  If the plant opens, the production rate could be as much as 1.3 million glass containers a day.

headline: City talks put focus on Labor Day events
abstract: When city employees and teachers preparing for possible strikes, organizers of the city's Labor Day parade promised "the biggest damn parade you've ever seen in this icty," with 1,000 marchers and national-level speakers.

headline: Non-profit non-starter
abstract: Pennsylvania courts continue to provide unsatisfactory guidance on how taxing bodies should deal with tax-exempt institutions.  Particularly, Hamot Medical Center would owe $800,000 in property taxes if it doesn't appeal against the Commonwealth court that reported Hamot should lose exemption because of compensation packages and perks.  Legislation must develop fair, uniform and specific rules for how non-profit institutions should help pay for the services of local government so most non-profit organizations don't end up losing their exemption like Hamot.

headline: Yeakel's crime: Being a daughter
abstract: Hardy Williams, endorsing Senator Arlen Specter, has taken a cheap shot at Lynn Yeakel by visiting the sins of the father upon the daughter for the sake of the re-election.  If there's anything to be learned from all this, it is that Arlen Specter really likes his job, that he's scared to death he might lose it and that he's willing to do anything to keep it.

headline: Don't back abortion rights, Casey urges Dems
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey is scheduled to formally urge the Democratic Party to embrace thos who oppose abortion.  Much of the governor's notoriety on the issue resulted from the state's abortion control being challenged in the US Supreme Court, a dispute over which the court is expected to issue a ruling in June or July.

headline: Firm fined for unapproved toxic-waste device
abstract: The firm building a commercial hazardous-waste incinerator in East Liverpool, Ohio, has agreed to pay a $129,000 penalty for beginning to install unapproved equipment at the site.

headline: Guns-for-cash swap seems a drop in the bucket
abstract: A program run by the Philadelphia Anti-Drug/Anti-Violence Network, swaps money for every gun someone hands over, and then destroys it.  Scores of people turned in more than 150 weapons duringthe first week of Philadelphia's second gun turn-in.

headline: Good rebound by Pa.'s bigger institutions
abstract: Advocates of the sky-is-falling scenario in the nation's financial sector got little support yesterday, as more major commercial banks reported fat profits for the third quarter in 1992.

headline: City wins delay on pension fund
abstract: Judge Abraham Gafni approved a deferrment of $19 million in payments by Philadelphia to its pension board, allowing for a boost in the city's weekly cash balance.  Lawsuits by the municipal, police, and firefighter's unions brought about the action on the pension payment.

headline: Not youngest
abstract: Bill Clinton, 45, and Al Gore, 44, are not the youngest major-party ticket in presidential politics,, at least considering their combined ages.  In 1920, Democrats nominated Ohio Gov. James Cox, 50, and running mate Franklin D. Roosevelt, 38.

headline: Yeakel's victory one for Anita
abstract: Lynn Yeakel stomped the opposition, winning the right to give Senator Arlen Specter fits in the fall.  The emotional force behind Yeakel is something Specter still doesn't seem to understand.  There he was, being a good soldier for his party, abusing Professor Anita Hill enthusiastically, but a lot of people were watching, and most were furious.  A lot of them were women like Lynn Yeakel who stayed mad and are in the process of getting even.

headline: Don't be afraid of feminism
abstract: Feminism has become a dreaded term, but all women and men who believe women deserve an equal chance to live a full life should be brave and call themselves a feminist.

headline: Flaws Masked By Prosperity
abstract: California is struggling to overcome deep-seated problems that were masked by years of healthy economic growth, problems of deteriorating schools and roads and, at least in the opinion of many businessmen, environmental and other regulations that are oppressive.  A kind of economic vertigo has set in whereby the forces that drove the California boom in the last decade, like its sizzling real estate market and immigration, have turned into negative factors.

headline: Have an unwanted horse?  Donate it to state police
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Police yesterday asked the public to donate unwanted horses to law enforcement.  State Police Commissioner Glenn Walp said horses have been an important part of the department fo ryears and are still used in crowd control and searches for missing people.

headline: Hamilton Bank merging
abstract: Hamilton Bank will be merged next year into CoreStates Bank, the prinicpal subsidiary of CoreStates Financial Corp.  The merger will enable CoreStates Hamilton Bank to operate as a division of the nationally chartered CoreStates Bank, rather than under its state charter.  Hamilton Bank is the only CoreStates bank that operates under a state charter.

headline: Clinton Aides say Polls Indicate That Bush Has Boxed Himself Into a Corner
abstract: As Democratic presidential nominee Bill Clinton prepares for a Texas bus tour with running mate Albert Gore Jr., his aides express growing confidence that the Republican convention in Houston last week will ultimately make it more difficult for President Bush to win the election.

headline: Noteworthy
abstract: Labor leaders will join Casey at the dedication of a new state monument, "The Pennsylvania Worker," art work on alcohol awareness is on display now in the Capital Rotunda, and the State Employees Combined Appeal is seeking contributions for charitable giving and caring kicks off today.

headline: Yes, 128 Clinton Fees and Taxes. Count Them.
abstract: A loud chorus of pundits says the Bush-Quayle campaign has twisted the facts in compiling a list of 128 taxes and fees raised during Bill Clinton's tenure as Governor of Arkansas.  The Bush-Quayle campaign assembled its list of 128 by taking records of tax and fee increases out of a handbook printed by the Arkansas Legislature.  No one disputes the numbers anymore- even a Clinton aide recently put the actual total at 127.  The list is included in the article.

headline: Eugene Beard: NAACP Disappointed With White Media
abstract: African-Americans have not made any substantial gains in the city's major TV or radio stations, in regards to employment and advancement, members of the Pennsylvania Branch NAACP said at a press conference held earlier this week at the main office.

headline: Golf course's water blamed for illnesses
abstract: Notices to boil water were posted Tuesday afternoon at the Cumberland Golf Club after nearly 40 people reportedly became ill.  Two large groups- PPG and Holly Milk Cooperative- and several individuals who have held golf outings at the club in the last two weeks have reported peoople becoming sick about a day after the outings.

headline: He seeks refuge in his name
abstract: Jay Smith clings to the same old lines, denying that he ever saw Susan Reinert away from Upper Merion High School or that he knows more than any courtroom observer about her family's obliteration.

headline: Hargrove ties Gov. Casey to closing of bank
abstract: State Banking Secretary Sarah W. Hargrove on Wednesday directly tied Governor Robert Casey to the seizure of Tobias Knoblauch Private Bank, testifying that he personally asked for federal help in clsoing the bank and getting insurance for the successor.

headline: Clinton and Yeakel won believers in the primary
abstract: The Inquirer feels good about the outcomes of the Pennsylvania primary, including Bill Clinton and the upward climb in what might be called his "esteem ratings," and for Lynn Yeakel, whose campaign was able to take off so rapidly, probably because there were hundreds, even thousands, of people in Philadelphia and across the state who knew her and who knew that she is real.

headline: Noteworthy
abstract: Retiring Representative A. Carville "Peck" Foster, presided over the House, an honor being accorded in recent days to members who have announced their intentions of making this term their last.  Also, the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority has issued $32.5 million in revenue bonds to fund more than 20 clean-water projects in the commonwealth.

headline: Yet Another Suit
abstract: US District Judge Edwin M. Kosik dismissed the last suit filed by the Architectural Heritage Association against the Mall at Steamtown project because the preservationists did not bother to file any support for their allegations.  Now, AHA spokesman Nancy Bisignani states, the group is simply trying to force the city and the mall developers to come clean on the exact details of their development agreement.

headline: Ex-Catholic teacher's jobless appeal denied
abstract: When Catholic teacher Maria Wesley decided to marry a divorced Protestant in a Presbyterian church in 1989, she was fired by a Pittsburgh parochial school for "public rejection" of Catholic doctrine.  Pennsylvania court ruled that she could not collect unemployment benefits.  Then the Supreme Court refused to hear her complaint that she was deprived of her constitutional rights.  Other action in the Supreme Court for the day include affirmative action, Miranda rights, segregation, and a libel lawsuit.

headline: Green thumbs up for N.J., 4 others
abstract: New Jersey is the best of states and Nevada is the worst when it comes to protecting the enviornment, according to City & State's exclusive analysis of how well the 50 states take care of their air, land and water.  Profiles of the best, worst and detailed survey results are given.

headline: Heard on the Hill
abstract: Ronald A. Sell, executive director of Pennsylvania Partnerships for Children, announced that nearly 442,000 children in the state were identified as poor, representative of 15.4 percent of Pennsylvania children.

headline: Holtzman spreading capitalizm in ex-communist nation
abstract: With a new company and friends in high places, Kingston native Marc Holtzman's Hungarian gamble is starting to pay off.  Holtzman is busy spreading capitalism through Hungary, where Lenin's ideas failed.

headline: Clinton breezes to victory in Pa.
abstract: Bill Clinton, hyped by his rousing final rally before a mob at Phildadelphia's City Hall, had borrowed a high school band's saxophone and tootled an upbeat "Satin Doll."  Maybe jazz and rock 'n' roll fan Clinton should have played "Sunny Side of the Street" or "Bobby McFerrin's "Don't Worry, Be Happy," after his blues were wiped away in Pennsylvania.

headline: Noteworthy:
abstract: Derek E. Gordon has resigned as executive director of the Pennsylvania Council on the Arts.  The State Health Care Cost Containment Council has pushed back until April the release of its controversial report comparing doctors who perform heart bypass surgery.  Also, Lt. Governor Mark Singel, in a speech to the Disabled American Veterans in Monroeville, asked them and their colleagues to work aggressively for passage of the $10 million bond issue referendum to fund a bonus for those who served in the Persian Gulf.

headline: Your place again?
abstract: Instead of renting out the top floor of a hotel like most presidential candidates would do, Jerry Brown is more likely to visit your place, a guest room.  By visiting people literally where they live, he saves money and gets to exchange ideas with "real people."

headline: Face-off in Buffalo
abstract: Abortion-rights proponents made a show of force at downtown clinics, while abortion foes vowed to close the clinics in memory of "Tia"- a hand-sized fetus they brandished at a news conference.  But the emotionally chardged atmosphere was heightened by threats of force from the militant National Women's Rights Organizing Coalition.

headline: Greene Township rules recycling firm violates law
abstract: Kipini Industries, a recycling firm in Greene Township, has lost its appeal to a township ruling that its operation violates a local ordinance.

headline: Heard on the Hill
abstract: State Police Commissioner Glenn A. Walp commented on the direct link between the New York La Cosa Nostra and drug trafficking in Pennsylvania following a drug bust in the Poconos resulting in 23 federal indictments.

headline: In Center City, there's life after 5
abstract: Ther sidewalks were still crowded hours after the Center City skyscrapers had disgorged the usual evening rush of scurrying office workers, briefcases and bags swinging by sweaty sides.  It was the launch of the Center City District's program to woo people back to the streets, the shops and the restaurant tables until at least 8 pm.

headline: Clinton derides Bush as 'fearmonger'
abstract: Bill Clinton yesterday scorned President Bush as an untrustworthy "fearmonger" whose criticism of the Democrat's economic plan "flew in the face of the plain truth."

headline: Noteworthy:
abstract: Harrisburg is playing host to approximately 300 delegates and guests from across the state who are attnding the Pennsylvania League of Cities' 93rd annual convention.

headline: You're just using us
abstract: Chelsea Clinton slipped into school through the back door last Monday and avoided most photographers on her first day back since her father's election, accompanied by the Secret Service detail.

headline: Fellow patient silences baboon-transplant protesters
abstract: Protesters were silenced by a man with liver disease who angrily defended the use of a baboon liver to save a man dying of hepatitis.  A 35-year-old man underwent the world's first baboon-to-human liver transplant at the Presbyterian University Hospital Sunday.

headline: Hazardous waste found beneath Conestoga Pines
abstract: State and federal environmental officials are looking for the source of hazardous chemicals found in groundwaer below Lancaster's Conestoga Pines Park.

headline: Holly questions 911 policy
abstract: Mt. Holly Springs Borugh Council is siding with borough firefighters skirmishing with county officials over ambulance calls.  Fire Chief Ivan Bretzman says for two months the fire company has been sending a fire truck as a backup when an ambulence is called.  The fire company only wants to be summoned for life-threatening situations.

headline: In this war, the winner gives out the cash
abstract: In one hot turf battle, the battle of the networks, New York and Philadelphia teams are scrapping for dominance.  Not the networks on TV, but the ones that link banks' automated teller machines (ATMs).

headline: Clinton Forces Wrestle With Challenge to Allay Voters' Unease About the Candidate's Character
abstract: Now that Governor Bill Clinton has no credible challengers for the Democratic nomination, top Clinton operatives are concluding that the governor's campaign must follow two parallel tracks: The Clinton forces have to move quickly and crisply to clinch the nomination, positioning themselves for a national convention that is the kickoff of a general-election campaign rather than the conclusion of a messy primary fight, and at the same time, Clinton must shift his attention to President Bush and move the focus from questions on himself to those of larger issues about the future of the country.

headline: Now it's a new faction protesting Act 195
abstract: Seventy five people, representing thousands of taxpayers in eight Northeastern Pennsylvania taxpayers' groups, marched on the Capitol to protest the might of the teachers' unions.  Act 195, the bill that gave teachers the right to strike, was passed by state legislature, meaning it had wide public support.  It's fascinating to hear disgruntled taxpayers echo the same "union-busting" statements that their bosses used to say.

headline: Boaters organize to fight Presque Isle Marina fees
abstract: 75 boaters joined to complain about the new slip fees (rates have nearly doubled) at the Presque Isle Marina in an attempt to get the costs lowered.  State Rep. Karl Boyes plans to propose legislation that would amend the Independent Regulatory Review Act, which would require agencies to seek approval for fee increases.

headline: Finally- living will law is long overdue
abstract: Pennsylvania's living will law is stuck at whether pregnant women should be exempted from the law.  Under the law, doctors would be forced to ignore those women's living wills and keep the patients alive if their pregnancies could be brought to term.  Though this portion of the law may disappoint some people, far more people will benefit from this law than will be harmed by it.

headline: How Much Do We Care?
abstract: Growing numbers of Americans now accept that there are major problems with the environment, and most say they're pitching in to help: 93% of the respondents in PARADE's nationwide survey said they personally are "doing something to help the environment" such as recycling waste or conserving electricity.

headline: Homicide suspect seized
abstract: Rufus Carter, a Youngstown, Ohio, man was arrested in connection wtihthe fatal April 25 shooting of Gregory Holder of Bulger, Washington County, in Broadhead Manor, police said.

headline: Insurance company worth saving
abstract: Two members of former management of National Security General Insurance Co., clear up clarify some points about a recent front page story on the liquidation of the company.

headline: Clinton forecast positive
abstract: Hillary Clinton, wife of Democratic presidential candidate Bill Clinton, talks confidently of when her husband is elected president, not if.  During a brief stop in Reading, she dismissed the negativity surrounding the campaign of the Democratic front-runner by saying her husband presents an approach to solving problems that is non-partisan.

headline: Now Let's Put Limits On Campaign Spending
abstract: Though the New York Times wrote about people being tolerant of Ross Perot's campaign spending, it is appalling the vast sums of money he poured into his television blitz of self-promotion.  The message is clear- the Presidency of the United States is for sale, and anyone with enough bucks, qualified or not, could enter the bidding.  Legislature must limit campaign spending for all candidates.

headline: City Beautiful
abstract: Harrisburg is blessed with a magnificent array of parks, each with its own allure and personality, that are largely the legacy of the City Beautiful Movement that thrived here around the turn of the century, but lost its vigor after WWII.  Mayor Stephen Reed has tried getting it back by creating a long-term, step-by-step rebuilding of the city park system and restoration of a park ranger patrol, which have brought a dramatic turnabout.  The latest round of investments is a clear commitment to make the parks even better.

headline: Gray defends vitality of NAACP
abstract: Those who believe the NAACP has lost touch with young blacks have forgotten the organization led the fight for civil rights, former Philadelphia Congressman William H. Gray said yesterday.

headline: Retirees get scary surprise: Cutbacks of medical benefits
abstract: While many big, old firms with thousands of retirees have promised for years to pay all or part of retiree medical expenses not covered by Medicare, almost none has set aside money to cover those costs.  Now those open-ended promises are converging with ballooning medical costs and growing numbers of retirees to create a financial flash point that threatens to blow holes in the profitability of many companies.

headline: In Greene County, it's a life of poverty
abstract: For many people in rural Greene County, wedged against the West Virginia border in the remote southwestern corner of Pennsylvania, life is often a small, secluded piece of hell.  It is life under a tin roof, or in a tiny trailer, with no shoes for the children, no water for the toilet, no electricity to light the darkness.

headline: How could he have not known?
abstract: Though Johann (Hans) Breyer says he knew nothing of the death factories for which he guarded at Auschwitz and Buchenwald and that he was drafted into the Nazi SS against his will, Historians say he must be wrong.  Breyer was alleged to be a member of the Death's Head Battalion, a division of the SS that guarded concentration camps, in a lawsuit filed by the US Justice Department.

headline: Integrated Circuit will acquire California firm
abstract: Integrated Circuit Systems Inc. said that it would acquire another semiconductor firm, Avasem Corp., in a stock transaction that could be worth nearly $20 million.

headline: Clinton hopes Keystone State gave him key
abstract: When Democratic presidential front-runner Bill Clinton came to Harrisburg, he took time to be interviewed by the Patriot-News, and the transcript of the interview is given.

headline: Now, Pa. supporters go to work
abstract: While Paul Tsongas' and Pat Buchanan's supporters could boast that their guy did good in their local campaigns, each candidate had a few setbacks as well.

headline: City calls off ration plans after study
abstract: Harrisburg officials have called off plans for water rationing after a new study shows that the DeHart Dam, the city's water source, is actually deeper than originally thought. The city will urge residents to voluntarily conserve water, to help preserve dwindling supplies.  The city's dire straits are being echoed across Pennsylvania, which is suffering through its 10th consecutive month of below-normal rainfall.

headline: Help for aged sought by churches, synagogues
abstract: Hoping to tap the activism of synagogues and churches, the Jewish Healthcare Foundation, the county and local religious leaders announced plans to marshal 300 to 500 volunteers who will help the elderly with daily tasks.

headline: School nurses assail bill as bad medicine
abstract: Even the routine parts of being a school nurse are not so easy as people think, say the state's 1,700 school nurses.  The nurses are suddenly eager to explain that- especially to state legislators- because of a proposed bill that would allow school districts to hire nurses with less education.  Districts also would be allowed to provide nursing services through local health-care agencies and could assign an unlimited number of students to one nurse.

headline: Incinerator fight draws rock singer into debate
abstract: The fires burning against the start-up of a hazardous waste incinerator were fanned even brighter last night when rock singer Richard Marx added his voice to the outcry.  Marx met with Waste Technologies Industries officials at the incinerator before joining local organizers and a group of hunger strikers at a rally to speak out against the incinerator.

headline: In racially mixed neighborhood, deadly confrontation
abstract: Keith Duczkowski, was a former Golden Gloves boxer, a roofer, the kind of guy his oldest brother said wouldn't start trouble but would not back down from a fight, and William Taylor, was a ninth grader who brought a loaded .22-caliber sawed-off pump rifle to his midterms at the Audenreid Senior High School.  Their paths crossed at a tiny store in Grays Ferry, and resulted in Duczkowski being shot twice and bleading to death.

headline: Kennametal is advised to go on the offensive
abstract: Allegations that Kennametal Inc. illegally traded with Iraq has forced the business to look to local politicians for advice to keep their business alive.  County Commissioner Ted Simon said the company must attack- go on every ABC and NBC news program and clear things up.

headline: Clinton plans for fast start
abstract: At Clinton campaign headquarters, there's talk already of ripping the sign from the strategy room and hanging it in a Clinton White House: "It's the economy, stupid."  That simple credo, Bill Clinton's compass toward election, would guide the Democrat in the early days of a presidency that would launch a revolution in Washington much like Ronald Reagan did 12 years ago.

headline: Number of area jobs takes a sharp plunge
abstract: Nearly 77,000 people were knocked off payrolls last year in the eight-county Philadelphia area, the Bureau of Labor Statistics announced.  The 3.5 percent decline in payroll employment was the largest single-year decline in the 40 years that records have been kept.

headline: City man takes flood problem right to the top
abstract: Local Mill Run flood control advocate John D'Andrea has had the dream since 1964 for someone to dredge and channel Mill Run to keep it from eroding the backyard of his home.  Mayor Daniel J. Milliron listened to D'Andrea's assessment and pledged to talk with the Department of Environmental Resources for help against the flooding.

headline: High Court At Abortion Juncture
abstract: The Supreme Court, one vote away from eliminating the constitutional right to abortion, wrestled with the implications of such a historic step as it considered a challenge to a Pennsylvania abortion law.  The justices remained largely silent as American Civil Liberties Union lawyer Kathryn Kolbert established abortion as a fundamental right but were far more active in quizzing Pennsylvania Attorney General Ernest Preate Jr. about the individual provisions at issue.

headline: Since '88, AIDS infection rate among state women has tripled
abstract: While the number of Pennsylvania men diagnosed yearly with AIDS has leveled off, the infection rate of women has tripled since 1988.

headline: Incinerator fight unites residents
abstract: Many Beaver County residents have become involved in the fight against a hazardous wasted incinerator about to go on line in East Liverpool.

headline: Indictment: Group sold $57 million in cocaine
abstract: A federal indictment made public announced that a Philadelphia cocaine ring poured into the area an estimated 2.5 tons of cocaine that rang up more than $57 million in proceeds in less than three years.

headline: Last call for Edgewater
abstract: The future of Edgewater Steel Co., which entered Chapter 11 protection last year, likely will be decided this week when US Bankruptcy Court conducts a Sept. 17 hearing to sell the firm.

headline: Clinton plans unlikely to affect midstate economy soon
abstract: President-elect Bill Clinton's bold economic blueprint will have little immediate impact on Pennsylvania or elsewhere, midstate representatives say.  Clinton still has to deal with Congress.

headline: Of Mideast politics and an election
abstract: Jews are debating Arlen Specter's and Lynn Yeakel's positions.  So are Arab American leaders, who are upset at both sides- in Yeakel's case, for refusing to meet them.  Arab Americans are angry at Specter for distributing a letter that they say plays on Jewish fears and Arab stereotypes.

headline: Dam plan continues to cloud river's future, group claims
abstract: The proposed Harrsburg Hydroelectric Project continues to make the Susquehanna one of the most threatened rivers in the United States, threatening the waterway's ecosystem and setting back efforts to restore important fisheries, according to American Rivers, based in Washington, DC.

headline: High court denies Americans the right to fight out, and settle, the abortion issue
abstract: If the Supreme Court were a National Commission on Everything, we should be overjoyed that it has promulgated an abortion policy that is not only sensibly moderate but that caputres what national consensus exists on the issue.  Unfortunately, the Supreme Court is not a national commission.  It is the nation's ultimate constitutional authority.  And the damage it does to the Constitution in its zeal to legislate correct abortion policy is profound.

headline: Society faces questions of health, cost
abstract: The life-expectancy gains that have occurred throughout the developed world this century had their roots in revolutionary inventions now taken for granted- antibiotics, water and sewer systems, hospital care for women giving birth.  This arises questions like how long do people want to live and who will pay for the cost of old age?

headline: Incinerator licensure hits a snag
abstract: The Clinton administration, in an early show of commitment to environmental protection, will try to stop testing at an Ohio hazardous waste facility that some local residents say is dangerous.

headline: It Was One More Car Theft- Until Chase Killed an Officer
abstract: A car theft in Prince George's County led to a tragic chain of events, resulting in the death of Prince George's police Sgt. Roger P. Fleming, when he chased the car for eight miles at high speeds, and died when his patrol car spun out of control and hit a tree.

headline: Lawsuit says Vartan failed to turn over CCNB stock
abstract: Susquehanna Township businessman John O. Vartan faces a second lawsuit from a brokerage firm claiming htat he failed to turn over a block of CCNB Corp. stock after execution of a sales order.

headline: Clinton Releases '69 Letter On His Draft Deferment
abstract: Arkansas Gov. Bill Clinton made public a 22-year-old letter in which he thanked an ROTC recruiter "for saving me from the draft" during the Vietnam War.  Clinton decided to release the letter to because it had been leaked to ABC News as part of a "dirty tricks" campaign by "George Bush and the Republican Party."

headline: On edge in California
abstract: Anger is mounting as the nation's richest state begins its 37th day without a budget.  Lobbyists are crowding the Capitol, trying to stop cuts to their favorite state programs.  The state is out of cash, facing an $11 billion deficit and because it is budgetless, it can't even borrow money.

headline: Delco may weed out garden program
abstract: Sod may be all that is planted at the Delaware County-owned park, Rose Tree Park, and parking spaces all that are harvested if the county council decides, perhaps by the end of this month, to do away with the park's community garden program.

headline: High Court, 5-4, Affirms Right to Abortion But Allows Most of Pennsylvania's Limits
abstract: By the narrowest of margins, and in words reflecting anger and anguish alike at its continuing role in the center of the storm over abortion, the Supreme Court reaffirmed what it called the "essence" of the constitutional right to abortion while at the same time permitting some new state restrictions.

headline: Solution to national health care will have political cost
abstract: The solution to national health care requires a price, but not in reference to money, a political cost is at stake.

headline: It's time to clean up our act
abstract: Politicians and scientists of the developed world have been preaching "environmentalism" for mor than 20 years, yet the world environment has continued to deteriorate overall, especially because of the pollution generated by those same countries.  Also, they expect that we will remove th barriers in the world economic and trading system that make sustainable developemnt in the Third World difficult.  Environment plus development plus democracy.  The triad needs to be put into effect.

headline: Law to thwart stalking of people considered
abstract: State law does not do enough to protect the targets of stalkers who harass, maim and murder, advocates and vicitms told the House Judiciary Committee.  The panel is considering legislation that would make it a crime to stalk someone.

headline: Lawsuit: Horizon bigwigs blew it
abstract: A lawsuit claims top administrators' of Horizon Financial, a defunct savings-and-loan depositor, money into risky multi-million-dollar deals.

headline: Clinton scolds Bush over family leave
abstract: Bill Clinton chided President Bush yesterday for threatening to veto the family leave bill, calling it an example of how the Republicans were reluctant to have America catch up with the world.  The bill passed by Congress would require employers with more than 50 workers to allow employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave annually to deal with matters including the birth of a child, adoption or a sickness in the family.

headline: On stage, little left to chance
abstract: The Democratic National Convention this election year is being held at Madison Square Garden, and though it might be fine for basketball, it's lousy for politics, too small and loaded with technical nightmares.

headline: New fee increases go into effect at state parks this year
abstract: Patrons visiting state parks in 1992 will see an increase in fees for camping and other services, the first price adjustment since 1986.  The park service says they need the increasing because their costs are going up as well.

headline: Hispanics feeling at home
abstract: Hispanics are more eager to take full part in US society than they are in preserving their distinct ethnic identities, a sweeping new survey finds.  Results of the Latino National Political Survey show US residents of Mexican, Cuban and Puerto Rican descent fit firmly within the national mainstream- debunking the stereotypical myth that they resist assimilation.

headline: Some experts fear cost-cutting moves
abstract: Experts, such as Edward N. Hibberd, president of the Delaware Valley Business Coalition, say that Gov. Casey's proposal to move basic functions of the Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council to the stae Insurance Department is hazardous to the council.

headline: Keep kids lead-free
abstract: In neighborhoods across Philadelphia and the suburbs, dust form lead paint is a danger to a generation of children.  But parents can do a lot to help protect the kids by testing and cleaning.

headline: Jamaicans confront Williams
abstract: Jamaican community leaders attacked the city's Police Department for what they cited as two recent incidents of police brutality.  Police commissioner, Willie L. Williams, had a meeting with the Jamaican Progressive League to discuss a review of police behavior.

headline: Lawyer: Insurance behind bank seizure
abstract: State Banking Secretary Sarah W. Hargrove seized Tobias Knoblauch Private Bank on April 17 not because of its condition, but because she and the governor's office wanted to close the state's private insurance pool despite the Legislature's hold on it, the private bank's attorney asserted.

headline: Clinton Sees Bush Engaging In Empty Talk on Families
abstract: Governor Bill Clinton, adding his voice to the theme of family values that has occupied President Bush and Vice President Quayle this week, said the White House has engaged in "cynical election-year politics" designed to avoid taking a leadership role in resolving the problems of families.

headline: Other voices
abstract: Several people speak out on issues involving politics and candidates.

headline: Parks lack lifeguards
abstract: Local state parks are closing lakes to swimmers next week because lifeguards are going back to school.

headline: In N. Phila.'s heart, fire destroys a temple of unity and self-reliance
abstract: The Universal Negro Improvement Association building in Philadelphia was destroyed by a four-alarm blaze.  The group plans to rebuild by funding through book sales or some sort of benefit.

headline: St. Christopher's Hospital to dedicate AIDS clinic
abstract: St. Christopher's Hospital for Children will dedicate its new clinic for treating children and family infected with the AIDS virus in a ceremony at 2pm tomororw.

headline: Landfill Owner Sues Township
abstract: The owner of County Landfill near Leeper village filed suit in Clarion County Court challenging the validity of an ordinance enacted last May 6 by Farmington supervisors Lewis Culp, Henry Lencer, and Janet Ochs.

headline: Judge disputes 'cut-rate justice' in homicides
abstract: The recent Inquirer articles and editorial concerning homicide cases in Common Pleas Court left the impression that indigent homicide defendants in Philadelphia are inadequately represented, unfairly convicted and often erroneously put to death.  That is not the case at all.

headline: Lending Hope
abstract: As Washington policy makers struggle in the aftermath of the Los Angeles riots for ways to create more jobs and business opportunities for African Americans, some minority enterprise experts suggest thath they take a look next door at the program Stanley Tucker has developed in Maryland, a multi-faceted, profit-making program designed to funnel investment capital to minority businesses.

headline: Clinton Struggling to Cope With 'Slick Willie' Image
abstract: In a private session with the editorial board of New York Newsday, Bill Clinton was confronted with the issue of his marijuana 'smoking but not inhaling' comment.  The questions persist: Is he the "Slick Willie" who evades unpleasant questions and tough issues, or an empathetic leader with a solid metal core?

headline: Our gift to the new mayor: A lot of free advice
abstract: The Inquirer asked for suggestions for the next mayor which were printed on the day of Edward Rendell's inauguration.  Some suggestions: concentrate on opportunities rather than problems, earnings for the homeless rather than handouts, more governmental support to school systems, and get cops out of their cars and in the public.

headline: Parks moves toward fresh water service
abstract: Supervisors have taken a step toward bringing water service to residents of 72 homes along Airport Road by applying for a $298,000 grant.  Armstrong County officials held a public hearing on the application for Community Development Block Grant money to help offset the project's estimated $378,000 cost.

headline: Joining the hate-crime fight
abstract: The A-K Valley Community Relations Council had its first formal meeting with a gathering of more than 25 concerned citizens.  The group initially formed as an ad hoc committee responding to the March 20 beating of a 14-year-old black youth, Beau Cannon, in Harrison Township.  The group raised money for the family and conducted a survey of the community response to the incident.

headline: State bar will backfire
abstract: New York's new health insurance bill could help provide affordable coverage to people with small-group or individual insurance with higher risk, but it does nothing to address the more than 2 million New Yorkers without insurance or the high health care costs.  By charging everyone the same rate, you can expect rate hikes of 30% or more on smalle employers, and many will drop coverage.

headline: Leak at Sovereign Oil has city over a barrel
abstract: A three-acre site a half-mile east of Temple University, an abandoned motor-oil processing plant called Sovereign Oil, inspired the US Environmental Protection Agency to summon, for the first time, new powers under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 to get the plant mopped up.
