And while the city and state governments have demanded in court for years that the Sovereign Oil Co. site be permanently cleaned, its owners have packed up, left and declared that they are broke.

headline: Judge scolds state in conduct of Capitol granite case
abstract: Common Pleas Court Judge Sebastian D. Natale sharply criticized the state attorney general's office for its conduct in a case against two men who supplied granite for an addition to the state Capitol.

headline: Liquor aides get 5th of chance- sort of
abstract: Chalk up a victory- sort of- for the hearing examiners in the latest legislative battle over those controversial positions under the state Liquor Control Board.  The House approved a bill that would protect five of the hearing examiner positions, jobs some say are wasteful and unneeded.

headline: Clinton tackling GOP already
abstract: Bill Clinton, mindful of Michael Dukakis' mistakes four years ago, is taking on many of the Republican Party's favorite issues early, hoping to define himself for the fall campaign before President Bush does it for him.

headline: 'Our Obligation Is To Define the Liberty of All'
abstract: Excerpts are given from the opinion for the Supreme Court in Planned Parenthood of Shoutheastern Pennsylvania v. Casey.

headline: Peace Garden in city park 'to plant ideas, flowers, trees'
abstract: A two-block area of Riverfront Park called The Peace Garden is the founder's hopeful reminder to push for peace and preserve the Earth.  The purpose is to plant ideas as well as flowers and trees.  A dedication to the garden was held Sunday that attracted people of all ages.

headline: Justices to Rule on Pennsylvania Abortion Limits
abstract: The Supreme Court agreed to rule on Pennsylvania's restrictive abortion law, setting the stage for a decision before the November election on the future of the constitutional right to abortion.  The appeals court siad the new standard for testing abortion laws appeared to be whether they impose an "undue burden" on women- proposed by Sandra Day O'Connor but that has never been adopted by a majority of justices.

headline: State Protection in Insurance Failures Put to Test
abstract: Althought 47 states have now approved a plan to resolve the biggest American life insurance company failure in history, New York State Officials are threatening to block it, saying it treats customers unfairly.

headline: Mirror ignored DER's progress
abstract: The Department of Environmental Resources has made unprecedented progress during the past five years to make our drinking water safe, to clean up hazardous waste sites, to recycle our trash, and to protect our natural resources, yet the Mirror unfairly and irresponsibly characterized the entire department based upon comments from a few disgruntled employees.

headline: Judge talks about curtailing services
abstract: Judge Carson V. Brown, a Clinton County judge said curtailing services might be a way to draw attention to the state's failure to fully fund the court system.

headline: Liquor, wine prices going up
abstract: The Liquor Control Board voted to increase by 2.5 percent the price on all wine and liquor items carried in the State-Store system, effective Aug. 21.

headline: Clinton Vows Continuity, Stability
abstract: Bill Clinton, about to lay claim to the most powerful office on Earth, warned other countries against stirring up trouble as he assembles the first Democratic administration in more than a decade.

headline: PA governor's race faces wide open field in 1994
abstract: The presidental election has eclipsed all things of passing interest to most Pennsylvanians- including the race for the governor's mansion in 1994 when Robert P. Casey steps down.  To date there are at least seven state politicians with the ambition, influence, or the right of succession, who have indicated their interest in, or who have been asked to consider running for the governor's job, including Dwight Evans, who could become PA's first black governor.

headline: Peaceful creek engulfed in whirlpool
abstract: The Yellow Breeches Creek, once peaceful, is now home to a battle between those who want the creek designated as a scenic river under the PA Scenic Rivers System and Robert M. Mumma, who wants to build Chilton, a championship-calibur golf course and 350 homes.

headline: Leaders of Top U.S. Religions Join on Welfare Revision
abstract: Organizations representing the nation's main religions are combining their moral authority to help change US social welfare policies.  The effort is described as the first time such a wide spectrum of American religious agencies has tackled jointly such a broad concern.

headline: Stiffer nursing home regulations proposed
abstract: Nursing homes that don't meet federal standards could be fined thousands of dollars per day in addition to being kicked out of the Medicare and Medicaid programs under rules proposed by the Department of Health and Human Services.

headline: More Waste Dumped In River Here
abstract: More than 400,000 gallons of screened sewage poured into the Allegheny River while workers attempted to lower an exposed main near Veterans Bridge, but City Engineer Ghris Sporer isn't unhappy with the results.  She explained the main did drop some and that the discharged sewage will not damage the river or pollute drinking water.

headline: Judges face loss of colleague
abstract: There was a noticeable emptiness in the Dauphin County Courthouse around Courtroom 4, were Judge Herbert A. Shaffner Jr., killed in a plane crash, usually presided.

headline: Local B&B Owners Happy with New State Legislation
abstract: Late June was a time of celebration for the Endless Mountains Visitors Bureau and local bed and breakfast owners when Governor Robert P. Casey signed legislation addressing the unique needs of these establishments.

headline: Clinton vs. Bush
abstract: The Daily News came up with 10 good reasons why the monster lead that Bill Clinton has in the national polls will- or will not- vanish.

headline: PA labor unit asks high court to spurn city on fact-finding
abstract: Philadelphia city officials are showing a "cynical perspective" toward state labor law by asking the state Supreme Court to prevent fact-finding in the city contract talks, the state labor relations board contends.

headline: Preserving history
abstract: New Castle residents and officials are being encouraged to preserve the city's architectural past by renovating and reusing rather than razing and replacing its buildings.

headline: Lemont's Smith named to commission
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey appointed Susan Smith of Lemont to the Pennsylvana Commission for Women.  The commission is a state agency created to promote equal opportunity for women in all aspects of life.

headline: Stop cheating kids
abstract: A tax meant to expand health coverage for children was passed and the money was collected, but the legislature didn't know how to spend it.  Six months have been wasted.  It is time for Governor Casey and his Senate foes to sit down and hammer out a workable compromise- to show that government can respond to the real problems of real people.

headline: New York's wandering trash finally comes home to be buried
abstract: Nearly a month after 2,200 tons of New York City trash left for a Midwest dump, the oft-rejected load returned yesterday, having chugged about 3,000 miles to reach a resting place 20 miles from  home.

headline: Judiciary reform measure advances
abstract: The cause of state judicial disciplinary reform is making its ponderous way through the legalities involved in amending the constitution.  This is not a fast or easy process, and it whould not be.  But the need for such action is clear.

headline: Lukens Posts Loss Of $8.5 Million For Fourth Quarter
abstract: Lukens Inc., troubled by both a prolonged strike at its main steelmaking facility and seasonally soft sales to industrial products companies, posted a loss of $8.5 million, or $1.07 a share, in the fourth quarter.  The company specializes in steel-plate manufacturing, and has subsidiaries in corrosion-protection, safety products and materials-handling equipment businesses.

headline: Clinton wants, and gets, his MTV time
abstract: The TV campaign war may have only just begun.  On Wednesday alone, presidential candidates armed up four new unconventional apearances, including Bill Cllinton, who wants his MTV- an hour of it.

headline: Pa. Democrats hang on to control of State House
abstract: Pennsylvania Democrats are much relieved in the wake of last week's election.  There had been fear that because of reapportionment and other factors, they might have lost control of the House- bad news, especially for the city.

headline: Protection may be on the way for a stretch of the Delaware
abstract: The Delaware River Greenway supports the preservation of the open space along the river, but if environmentalists and some politicians get their way, up to 40 miles of the Delaware River could be protected through the federal Wild and Scenic Rivers Act.

headline: Message spins out of control
abstract: Perot's weekend gaffe- addressing an NAACP audience as "you people"- seemed to seal a pact between the largely liberal black establishment and the Demcoratic ticket of Bill Clinton and Al Gore.  "When he said that 'you people' business, he put a tremendous gulf between us," said Joseph Duff, president of the Los Angeles NAACP.

headline: Success rates of state's heart surgeons analyzed
abstract: A state agency, the Health Care Cost Containment Council, will release a report that analyzes the outcomes of heart surgery across Pennsylvania for the purpose of publicly comparing physician performance.  The study will evaluate heart surgeons' mortality rates, adjusted for patient age, gender and condition.

headline: Nimby- State must control site rules
abstract: A bill that passed in the House would allow host counties and municipalities to hold public hearings on state permit applications for hazardous sites.  The NIMBY (not in my back yard) mindset is too powerful, nobody wants hazardous waste dump in his backyard.  Therefore, the state and federal governments should remain the final and only arbiters in these matters.

headline: Justices to make Miranda decision
abstract: The Supreme Court agreed to decide whether to severely restrict federal-court reviews of state convictions that may have been obtained in violation of the Miranda rule.  Such a step, which the court appears likely to take, would mark a substantial further contraction of the jurisdiction of federal judges to review petitions for writs of habeas corpus from state-prison inmates.

headline: Merchant's fight with vendor stirs Germantown protest
abstract: Since last Thursday, a small group has stood at the curb in front of the SMA Discount Store in the 5600 block of Germantown Avenue, urging potential customers to spend their money elsewhere.  The standoff renews an old Philadelphia confrontation between street vendors and store owners and dramatizes the more recent tensions in some neighborhoods between Korean merchants and their black customers.

headline: Clinton won't say anything on VP search
abstract: When Democratic presidential candidate Bill Clinton names his running mate, probably later in the week, he'll also tip his electoral strategy against President Bush and Ross Perot.

headline: Pa. Dems need arithmetic course
abstract: The Democrats had trouble counting votes when the party got together to choos its favorites in the April 28 primary election.  The only close endorsement contest, for auditor general, tallied up 187 votes to 167, a total representation of 35 more than delegates who were authorized to vote.

headline: Protersters find dead birds on Casey's lawn
abstract: People who joined a 24-hour environmental protest outside the Governor's mansion noticed something unusual on its grounds- dead birds.  Dan Wittig, who coordinated the Greenfire Coalition's role in the March on Harrisburg, said a security guard explained that the birds are being poisoned intentionally, because Gov. Robert P. Casey thinks they are too dirty.

headline: More court challenges on abortion
abstract: The Supreme Court's long-awaited decision on a Pennsylvania abortion case is expected to be issued tomorrow, but it is unlikely to be the justices' final word on the issue.  Three more cases heading toward the hgih court, from Utah, Louisiana and Guam, will directly ask the jjustices to decide if abortion is a constitutional right.  Those states have all sought to ban abortion, with limited exceptions.

headline: Supreme Court refuses Pa. Appeal of Medicaid reimbursement order
abstract: The US Supreme Court let stand a ruling that said that Pennsylvania's Department of Public Welfare's payments were inadequate and violated federal regulations after PA officials appealed.  Public Welfare officials said a settlement with the hospitals in May had increased Medicaid reimbursement rates.

headline: North Middleton group wins ruling on trash-pact fight
abstract: Commonwealth court has given a North Middleton Township group the legal means to continue battling a controversial trash collection/recycling contract approved by township supervisors.

headline: Killings sap coroner's budget
abstract: A string of violent murders, four women and a child during the first three weeks of February, has taken its toll on York County Coroner Kathryn Fourhman-Olewiler by exceeding her budget for a forensic pathologist for the year.

headline: Meridian's owners plan to brace frame
abstract: The owners of the fire-damaged One Meridian Plaza building told city officials they would begin installingaddional steel bracinginthe skyscraper as early as next week, but the officials reserved judgment on whether that would satisfy them that the structure is safe.

headline: Clinton woos the disillusioned in distressed factory towns
abstract: In each case, the votes from smaller cities, coupled with more affluent suburban areas, have combined to overwhelm the traditionally Democratic vote of the region's major cities.  But now, after years of economic difficulties, the Democrats believe they can win here.

headline: Pa. GOPers in but-kickin' frame of mind
abstract: Pennsylvania Republicans, after four daily doses of GOP hoopla, head home today rejuiced, reborn and crowing about a re-emergence.

headline: Scenic River Law Signed
abstract: President Bush signed legislation to include 85 miles of the Allegheny River in the federal Wild and Scenic Rivers system.  The law also directs the US Forest Service to study the Clarion River and Mill Creek for possible inclusion in the system.

headline: NAACP 'Irrelevant'
abstract: "You people" blew it- when you criticized Ross Perot for his use of the term "you people" while addressing the National Association for Advancement of Colored People.  You said, "Perot should be seeking to unite Americans rather than splitting them into groups."  Yet Americans have already split themselves into groups based on race, gender, sexual preference.  If the NAACP isn't for the jobless, dispirited young blacks, then whom is it for?

headline: Surgical scorecard
abstract: The novelty of posting the "batting averages" of Pennsylvania's heart surgeons has attracted considerable attention to a report released last week by the state's Health Care Cost Containment Council that reviewed nearly 15,000 heart-bypass operations.

headline: Officials begin Cumberland bug battle
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources already began to spray the leaf-eating gypsy moth caterpillars on 2,944 acres in state parks and forests across Cumberland County.

headline: L.A. on long road to recovery
abstract: Citywide, more than 4,000 people have applied for aid since disaster application centers opened after the Los Angeles riots of violence and looting.  Business owners are ready to rebuild, and agencies are open help get the process started.

headline: More Sony delays for Westmoreland
abstract: Japanese electronics giant Sony Corp. is expected to again delay the full startup of its Westmoreland County television plant, this time until 1995 or 1996, knowledgeable sources report.

headline: Clinton, Gore coming to town?
abstract: Jeff Blum, the Northeast coordinator for the Bill Clinton-Al Gore presidential campaign, is optimistic hae and the local staffers working with him have a real good shot at getting one or both of their candidates to come into the Wilkes-Barre area some time in the weeks ahead.

headline: Paul Kanjorski for United States Congress
abstract: The Times Leader endorses US Representative Paul E. Kanjorski for re-election to Congress for one simple reason: Kanjorski has been a creative and effective congressman, one who has won wide support throughout the district.

headline: Using wood to peer at the past
abstract: As a National Park Service official looked on approvingly, Bill Callahan spent Memorial Day calmly drilling holes in the rafters of Independence Hall, looking for core samples that could hellp him determine the exact age of Philadelphia's best-known building.

headline: Once again, men speak for women on issues vital to women
abstract: So far, a disturbing commonalty exists among those stating what is reasonable when it comes to women's access to abortion.  The commonalty is: the comentators are all men.

headline: Tougher Measures To Fight TB Urged By New York Panel
abstract: Wading into one of the most contentious issues in modern medicine, a panel of 34 scientists, ethicists and public health leaders yesterday released a report calling for broad new measures to stem the rampant spread of tuberculosis in New York City and around the nation.

headline: Old tires clutter Rochester property
abstract: Rochester Township Commissioners Said they are tired of being dumped on.  The township plans to begin cracking down on people who are illegally dumping their trash in the community.

headline: Landsdowne architect aided Nazis, Justice Dept. charges
abstract: A retired Lansdowne architect, Jonas Stelmokas, who has been a leader of Philadelphia's Lithanian community for four decades, was accused by federal authorities of serving as a high-ranking officer in a volunteer unit that helped the Nazis murder Lithuanian Jews and other unarmed civilians in 1941 and 1942.

headline: New GM credit card gets mostly favorable reviews
abstract: After cosiderable hype, General Motors Corp. yesterday unveiled a new credit card to generally favorable reviews from industry analysts.

headline: Clinton/Gore
abstract: Governor Bill Clinton, going against the grain of conventional policitical thinking, has strenthened the Democratic ticket by selecting Tennessee Senator Albert Gore Jr. as his running mate.

headline: Paul Tully Is Dead at 48; Top Democratic Strategist
abstract: Paul Tully, the political director of the Democratic National Committee and one of his party's pre-eminent strategists, was found dead in Little Rock, Ark., today.  He was 48 years old.

headline: Venango County Supporting Try For Recreational Funds
abstract: Venango County commissioners gave their support yesterday to a grant application that ultimately could deliver almost $1.2 million in new funding to help create a recreation rails-to-trails system in the Venango and Clarion counties.

headline: Opening an abortion debate
abstract: Governor Robert Casey is engaged in a singular quest this election year to open up a debate within the Democratic party on the abortion issue.

headline: With health care for all
abstract: York and Adams counties are different form many other areas in Pennsylvania and across the nation in that health care, including emergency care, prescription medicines and regular medical and even dental care in some instances, is available for the uninsured.

headline: Once Derided as the Garbage State, New Jersey Gets Tough on Polluters
abstract: In an effort to curb pollution in New Jersey, state officials are attacking polluters criminally.  "If you have intentional violation of environmental law, bribery, serious health issues, an ongoing crime, lots of dollars involved," Edward Bordon, the Camden County Prosecutor, said, "then you're a criminal in New Jersey."

headline: Latino inmates organize to better their lot at Graterford
abstract: LACEO, the Latin American Cultural and Educational Organization, a group co-founded by Ray Yabor, a veteran of Graterford Prison in Montgomery County, addresses the problems that Latinos face at Graterford.

headline: News brings common feelings
abstract: Bethlehem Steel Corp. plans to exit the bar, rod and wire business, leaving 1,978 people without jobs.  The company would need $150 million worth of improvements to stay in business.

headline: Clinton: 'It's time to change America'
abstract: Excerpts are given from the prepared text of Democratic presidential nominee Bill Clinton's acceptance speech at the Democratic National Convention.

headline: Pecora seen at core of delay on judges, district justices
abstract: A handful of Western Pennsylvanians who want to be county judges or district justices have found themselves held hostage by a political impasse in the state Senate.  Democrats say confirmations have been stalled by Denator Frank Pecora of Penn Hills, who recently defected from the Republican Party to the Democrats.

headline: A Philadelphia view from an outlander
abstract: Philadelphia's projected five-year budget deficit is $1.2 billion, but with the burly new mayor, Edward G. Rendell, his strategy of lots of little savings could produce solvency.

headline: Operation Rescue heads for Louisiana
abstract: An $8,000 fense constructed around the Delta Women's Clinic- Baton Rouge's only abortion clinic- that drew the most fire from Operation Rescue executive director Keith Tucci.  Up to 5,000 abortion opponents are expected by police in the city, despite Louisiana's 1991 abortion bill, one of the USA's toughest.

headline: Wofford lays out his national health plan
abstract: For too long, the health-care debate has been symbolic of the frustration most Americans feel with politics and polititcians today- with Washington's failure to make hard choices and respond to the real problems they face in their daily lives.  Sen. Harris Wofford and Sen Tom Daschle have joined to introduce legislation that would provide all Americans with health insurance throughout their lives, regardless of where they live or work.

headline: Other peregrines of note
abstract: Peregrines now fly in Philadelphia and a growing number of other Eastern cities, thanks to biologists' work to bring them back from virtual extinction east of the Mississippi in the 1960s.  Best known and longest established are probably the falcon pairs in Baltimore.

headline: Latinos confront abuse
abstract: Domestic abuse cuts across al racial and socioeconomic lines.  But experts say a prevailing "macho" culture and limited resources for women seeking help accent the problem among Latinos.  Hotlines and services that are bilingual are helping to taking a public, and long overdue, stand against domestic abuse, especially Latinos.

headline: 'No bar, no problem'
abstract: The closings of several bars in Allison Hill have made the neighborhood relieved of drugs, crowds, alcohol and threats.  Area residents are thankful for the closings for business and personal purposes.

headline: Clinton's Fund Raising Falling Short
abstract: With his lock on the Democratic presidential nomination all but secured, Bill Clinton has begun merging his fund-raising apparatus with that of the Democratic National Committee (DNC).  But both Clinton and the party leadership face a tough financial challenge as they head into the general election campaign.

headline: Pecora switches, becomes a Democrat
abstract: In a move for political survival, Sen. Frank Pecora of Penn Hills switched his party registration to Democrat.

headline: Activists ask PA to nullify $35M bond issue
abstract: The Bristol Township Taxpayers Association, a newly formed taxpayers group, has filed a complaint with the state asking it to reject the school board's $35 million bond issue.

headline: PA abortion law defended
abstract: A large majority of people agree with the provisions that the Supreme Court may make on the abortion law, and it is only a small group of radical feminists who vociferously are against them.

headline: Wofford says health care top issue
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford states that national health insurance will probably be the focal point in the 1992 presidential campaign.  Woffard compared his dream for national health insurance to Social Security and said studies show $200 billion would be saved annually -much of it in paperwork- if there were a centralized insurance system.

headline: PA Senate passes bill that would set air-pollution fees
abstract: Senators voted unanimously for sweeping air-pollution controls that will help the state meet federal guidelines in the Clean Air Act amendments of 1990.

headline: Lawyer to fight double charges
abstract: A federal public defender, D. Toni Byrd, is attacking the government's double prosecution policy of those who possess a gun while involved with illegal drugs.

headline: Clinton's mandate: Battle the economy
abstract: If President Clinton listens to Valley voters, and those across this nation, he'll move quickly to put an aggressive economic plan into action during his first 100 days.

headline: Pa., N.J. are key to Clinton, Bush prospects
abstract: A scant 23 days before the election, President Bush is in trouble in both Pennsylvania and New Jersey, two shining prizes coveted by his campaign and that of Democrat Bill Clinton.

headline: Attention: The Sky Is NOT Falling in Philly
abstract: For almost two years, Philadelphia has been urban America's Chicken Little, sounding repeated warnings that its government could go broke any day.  Now suddenly its leaders have turned optimistic, launching an unorthodox experiment in urban comeback just as the sky was about to fall.

abstract: According to AIDS researchers, women are now contracting the virus at about the same rate as men.  In the age of AIDS, women must learn to be demanding and insistent about their health.  And they must teach their daughters to do the same.

abstract: Pennsylvania sued an Ohio firm for $270 million to recover the costs of removing asbestos from state buidlings, the state attorney general's office said.

abstract: Senate-passed legislation that would change the way judges are disciplined has come under attack from lawyers' groups that are charging that the proposal would undermine the state Supreme Court.

headline: On the waterfront: an urban boom
abstract: A year ago Philadelphians seemed agreed on one point: The Delaware River would never make it as a tourist attraction.  Isolation and inaccessability made the harbor seem a hopeless entertainment proposition.  But this summer Philadelphia's waterfront bustles with everything from suburban singles on the make to tourist families to empty-nesters who live in the new condos at Pier 5.

headline: Close the Vietnam Book Now
abstract: As evidence mounts that Americans may have been left behind when the United States pulled out of Vietnam, that nation's communist government once more is refusing to cooperate in laying the question to rest.

headline: Paterno addresses problems
abstract: Penn State football coach Joe Paterno last night addressed the recent rash of lawlessness by members of his team, using his weekly radio call-in show as a forum.

headline: Be flexible, activists ask mayor
abstract: Environmental groups are asking Mayor Rendell to help clear up the daily commute.  They're proposing that he give an estimated 28,000 city workers a chance to change their schedule in an attempt to cut the pollution that wafts from commuters' cars.

headline: Peaceful protest to be held today over King case
abstract: Because Rodney G. King has become a symbol of the frustration and despair of blacks, community and religious leaders said they planned a protest rally for this morning because they didn't want his case to be forgotten.

headline: 800 Adams County farmers seek drought relief
abstract: More than 800 Adams County farmers are seeking some form of federal drought relief assistance, but few farmers expect to see any substantial payments to help offset losses, estimated by some to be as high as 80 percent.

headline: Permit Awaited For Water Project
abstract: Residents in Victory Heights will have a public water system in operation by early next year if the township is able to start the project in late summer.  The startup date depends on whether the township receives a water allocation permit.

headline: Letter links Yunkin to Show killing
abstract: Defense attorneys in the Lisa Michelle Lambert murder trial produced a letter they say proves her one-time fiance killed 16-year-old Laurie Show, then convinced Lambert to shoulder the blame.

headline: Pennsylvania LCB gets shot
abstract: The state-controlled liquor system received a warming shot of good news last week in Harrisburgh when a committee of review pronounced the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board both increasingly efficient and sensitive to its customers' needs.

headline: Closed-door talks center on Sunbridge
abstract: Mercer County Commissioners and representatives from Mercer County Area Angcy on Aging Inc. met with state Secretary of Aging Dr. Linda M. Rhodes in Harrisburg to discuss problems with the agency and Sunbridge personal care home.

headline: Paterno grabs the stick
abstract: Whatever path the Penn State Nittany Lions take after several alleged incidents occurred with football players, it's a trip that has become much more of a challenge than coach Joe Paterno or anyone else ever could have expected.

headline: Big tax hike expected in Mt. Holly
abstract: Mt. Holly Springs Borough Council President John Bitner says the borough property tax may have to be increased by as much as 52 percent next year.

headline: Personal commitments to racial justice, equality sought
abstract: Leaders of an emerging Social Justice Coalition will ask borough residents to "take the pledge," and make personal commitments to racial justice and equality.  The coalition's unity pledge, to be circulated later this spring, is the group's first step toward breaking down fear and mistrust and building bridges between white and black residents.

headline: American farmhand- he's a dying breed
abstract: On the nation's farms, federal statistics show, the hired man is a vanishing breed.

headline: Plant operator, DER deny dumping of toxics
abstract: The general manager of Trooper Ink of Tinton Falls, NJ, refuted published reports the company is discharging toxic chemicals from its satellite facility in Bridgewater Township into the Montrose Sewer Authority plant.  Gary Collichio siad that allegations in a Susquehanna County weekly newspaper cannot be true because the Bridgewater plant does not use any toxi-based inks in its manufacturing.

headline: Lineup time at the Roundhouse
abstract: Philadelphia's next police commissioner should be an individual with an imposing presence and the ability to hold the respect of his commanders and the cops on the street, management skills, a sensitivity to the city's diverse neighborhoods and a willingness to live with the fiscal realities of the 1990s.  Thes are among the major qualities that a 19-member search committee is looking for in a successor to Willie L. Williams, who is taking over the beleaguered Los Angeles Police Department.

headline: PETCO breaks ground for plant
abstract: International relations involving Sweden, Japan and the United States got a shot in the arm as officials of the Pennsylvania Extruded Tube Co. broke ground for a $45-million plant for PETCO in Lackawanna County.

abstract: State Representative Kenneth J. Cole filed a civil lawsuit in Adams County Court agaisnt his opponent Stephen R. Maitland, charging the Republican 91st district candidate with slander, libel and defamation of character.

abstract: The school distrct admnistraton and the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers have been constructng a new teacher's contract for the past few months.  Some people want both sides to settle so that the city employees' unions won't wage freeze or extract givebacks by Mayor Rendell.

headline: City panel rejects creating 3 black-majority districts
abstract: City Coucil's reapportionment panel has rejected a plan to creat three black-majority districts, saying it could backfire.  Instead, the panel recommended that the current nine council districts, which include two with a majority of black voters, be changed slightly.

headline: Police class mostly white males
abstract: The city's first police class since the elimination of quota hiring is likely to be made up of almost entirely of white males with a few black males and no women.

headline: Bird Shooting Is a Sport
abstract: Pigeon shooting is a sport and shoots are held throughout Pennsylvania and other states.  Shoots are held almost every weekend for about 10 months of the year in PA.  Though people have the right to protest and to be against the sport, the activity at the Labor Day pigeon shoot event was out of hand, with protesters screaming at children about their parents being killers.

headline: Polymer cleanup proposed by U.S.
abstract: Federal Environmental Protection Agency officials have proposed a Superfund cleanup of the St. Jude Polymer Corp. site to remedy contamination left behind by a mirror manufacturer.

abstract: Drugs are sold and abubsed throughout the city of Philadelphia and its suburbs.  But nowhere is the trafficking more blatant or the money bigger or the menace greater than in the drug corridor known as the Badlands.

abstract: Reports of financial troubles at Ohio-based Phar-Mor Inc. have resounded at two area shopping centers that are shaking off their own problems.  The 300-store Phar-Mor chain sought Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

headline: Colo. 'tax revolt' hard to interpret
abstract: Colorado voters shook the state on Election Day when they passed a measure that stripped government of its tax powers and gave them to the people.  Today, both government officials and residents are scratching their heads over how to interpret what has been called the nation's most radical tax-limitation measure.

headline: PEL Plan Gets Nod From Wolkoff.. But
abstract: Myron Wolkoff, president of a city taxpayers' group, today endorsed the Pennsylvania Economy League's financial recovery plan for municipal government, but did not close the door completely on an alternative strategy being prepared by Mayor Jim Connors.

abstract: The Greater New Castle Chamber of Commerce exists no more, and in its place is the Lawrence County Chamber of Commerce.

headline: Polish-American promoted ethnic respect
abstract: Efforts to make people aware of their cultural heritage should not make a community divisive but should bind us together.  Thaddeus Kosciusko was born a citizen of Poland and came to America for the belief in freedom.  His instilled ethnic respect by his will which requested that Negroes be given liberty in his name, which led to a "Colored School" in New Jersey named after its benefactor.

headline: Erie County farmers saving topsoil
abstract: Since it takes 200 years to form an inch of topsoil, free advice on how to protect topsoil is being offered by the Soil Conservation Service of the US Department of Agriculture.  Erie county farmers are taking advantage of the tips and as a result, they are improving water quality, preserving term productivity, and ultimately, their farm profits.

headline: Possibility of chicken manure pollution has residents concerned
abstract: Ralph Hoerner and Ed Selbert, two residents of Conewago Township, are concerned that chicken manure from an area farm may be polluting Spring Creek.

headline: Lots of money, little to show
abstract: For more than a decade, we've been treating the drug problem as if it were merely a matter of curbing supply by catching dope dealers.  Billions of dollars were dropped on the War on Drugs, yet in Pennsylvania, 54 counties spent no money at all on "costs associated with school, public and other community drug awareness educational programs."  It's a wonder why we're losing this war.

headline: Phila. firm proposes a different life for a Chester County hotel
abstract: The Oxford Hotel, also known as El Conquistador, once the anchor of a bustling rural crossroads, became known as a fist-fighting and pick-up joint that attracted a rowdy clientele.  Now, a development partnership with a flair for forging deals has dropped onto Oxford's tiny stage; ready to turn the old hotel into something a bit more staid: apartments for the elderly.

headline: Compassionless budget
abstract: A letter written by a Philadelphia resident states how the Inquirer's editorial on Gov. Casey's budget was much blessed by the poor.

headline: Penn State gets ready for speech by Bush
abstract: President Bush is scheduled to deliver what is billed as a major economic address on the lawn in front of Old Main, Penn State's administration building.  Football coach Joe Paterno will introduce Bush.  Immediately following the speech, Bush will attend a $250-a-ticket fund-raising luncheon at the Nittany Lion Inn on campus.

headline: City aims to cut fees it must pay to raise money
abstract: Searching for ways to cut costs, the Rendell administration is taking aim at two powerful political constituencies: investment bankers and bond lawyers. Financial advisors say they want to reduce the professional fees for bond sales and other financial transactions by negotiating more aggressively with underwriting and legal firms and by giving repeat business to those that do the best work for the least money.

headline: Priest's action, not beliefs, being punished
abstract: Reverand John Osterhout and other abortion protesters in Lehigh County Prison are confusing strongly held beliefs with their illegal actions.  They were charged with disorderly conduct, trespass and defiant trespass after disrupting daily operations at the Allentown Women's Center, which crossed the line of the law.  They are not being punished on account of their beliefs but instead, their actions.

headline: Farm Show steer fetches record price
abstract: A black Angus steer called Milli Vanilli shattered previous State Farm Show records when he was purchased by Hoss's Steak and Sea House for $25,000 at a carnival-like auction of the show's top livestock.  Hoss's plans to donate him to the Bedford County Rotary Club.

headline: Power line proposal jolts Armstrong
abstract: Gary Nelson owns a timber filled property that lies in the path of a controversial 500-kilovolt transmission line that would stretch from Beaver to Dauphin County.  The contractor who provides Nelson with aerial spraying against gypsy moths says he can't guarantee full coverage if the project goes through.

headline: Lycoming County beats average for collections
abstract: The Lycoming County domestic relations office continues to beat national averages for collecting support payments.

headline: Politicking in malls
abstract: Mall owners point out that these public-looking places are, in fact, private property that they bought and paid for.  As a result, they say they have the right to restrict activities that might normally take place in a public place, such as leafleting, petitioning, proselytizing and the like.

headline: Confidence is Failing
abstract: A survey by Penn State found 15 percent of the 829 adults surveyed said they never trust state government to do the right thing; however, a 1990 survey shows that no one said they never trusted government.  Also, truck traffic on the Pennsylvania Turnpike has declined by 1 million vehicles last year and overall us is down.  Officials say the drop is due to the recession.

headline: Pennsylvania House spending
abstract: Running the US House cost roughly $700 million last year.  USA Today took an in-depth look at congressional spending and published a member-by-member accounting for members' expenses in 1991.

headline: City Hall needs more of Saidel's addy-tood
abstract: City Controller Jonathan Saidel has a serious "addy-tood" problem.  Let's hope it catches on.  Saidel attacked the city Water Department's proposal for a 24 percent rate increase.  He slaughtered it.

headline: Pro-choice advocates vow to open doors
abstract: Pro-choice advocates may open their doors to women who need a place to stay during the mandatory 24-hour waiting period.  Abortion rights activists hope to establish a network to provide overnight accommodations.

headline: Farmers look forward to bountiful harvests
abstract: After weeks of bountiful rainfall, Lt. Governor Mark S. Singel lifted what he called "the longest declared drought emergency in Pennsylvania history."  Things are looking better for farmers this year, with many seeking alternatives to adapt to the weather pattern changes.

headline: Public vs. private recycling debated
abstract: Lycoming County faces a dilemma.  Should it try to save money by processing and shipping recycled materials collected at curbs and drop-off sites, or should it continue to use private enterprise?

headline: Lynch agrees to hire 26 workers for prison
abstract: Erie county Executive Judy Lynch said that new prison guard jobs authorized at the Erie county prison will be filled by people already working for the prison as per diem employees.

headline: PPG adapting to weak economy, chairman says
abstract: The surge in PPG Industries Inc.' first-quarter profits could be a sign the recession is ending.  But even though PPG's profits last year were battered by slumps in housing starts and auto manufacturing, PPG employees and managers learned an important lesson- how to do the little things that make money in tough times.

headline: Congress Daily Makes Mark on the Hill
abstract: The newsletter Congress Daily reported of an incident between Senators Daniel Patrick Moynihan and Christopher S. Bond about an argument and an alleged shove.  As a tip service, gossip sheet and legislative tracking device, the Daily has become the space-age version of the wire service ticker: up-to-the minute news delivered the day it happens.

headline: Pension changes urged
abstract: Advisers to Mayor Rendell have recommended changes in the disability system for city employees that they say could eventually save taxpayers more than $20 million a year.  Proposed changes, "will probably affect less than 10 percent of city employees" because "most do not abuse the benefits system." Therefore, the disability reform would free up city funds so that other health benefits can be saved in a time of fiscal austerity.

headline: City receives $430,000 bill for financial advice
abstract: The company advising Mayor Rendell on financial matters, Public Financial Management Inc., has billed the city nearly $430,000 for preparing a five-year recovery plan, assisting city labor negotiators and performing other work over the last six months.

headline: Pro-choice or pro-Bush? You can elect to be both
abstract: To the surprise of many pundits and to the disappointment of many Democrats, the 1992 Republican National Convention ended as it began- on an upbeat note.  Abortion may become the defining issue in the campaign, but there is room in the GOP for those who advocate choice.  You can be pro-Republican and pro-Bush and not give up a belief in the right to choose.

headline: Federal program looking for new farmers
abstract: The Farmers Home Administration is looking for a few good potential farmers to apply for its "Guaranteed Farm Ownership Loans for Socially Disadvantaged Persons" program.

headline: Radioactive sites
abstract: The Senate Government Operations Committee released a list of 45,361 radioactive-contaminated sites.  Removing the contamination not only represents a problem of tremendous scale, more importantly it raises a difficult issue of removing the radioactive material and storing it in a way that will not pose a new hazard for the public and for future generations.  The country is beginning to confront the true cost of the nuclear age of discovering that- whatever the benefits- it is very steep, indeed.

headline: Marchers protest sexual violence
abstract: For the second annual "Take back the night rally" activists who marched against sexual violence carried signs reading, "Sexual Vilence Kills" and "Rights for Victims."  Some 200 strong, they marched from the University of Scranton Commons.

headline: PSFS becomes shining jewel in Mellon's crown
abstract: Mellon Bank, which took over the Philadelphia Savings Fund Society's 27 local branches after federal regulators on Friday shut down the bank's parent, Meritor Savings Bank, is now arguably the biggest bank in town.

headline: Congressmen call for citizen policing
abstract: Two area congressmen, Robert E. Andrews and Curt Weldon, urged the US House to turn the job of policing its ethics over to a citizen commission that would assume much of the power of the current House ethics committee.  They say it will help restore confidence in a Congress battered by the scandal over members' checks and allegations of wrongdoing at the House post office.

headline: Pension system appeals troubling
abstract: A legal time bomb with a potential multi-million dollar impact on the state's pension system, and Pennsylvania taxpayers, ticks ominously somewhere within Commonwealth Court.  An appeal pending before the court challenges the state's two-tiered retirement system for legislators that gives pensions to those elected prior to March 1, 1974 at a rate 3.75 times greater than other lawmakers.

headline: City set to tap visiting pros' pay
abstract: Mayor Rendell is expected to announce today that he is going ahead with his plan to collect wage taxes from athletes and entertainers who come to town to perform.  Overall, Philadelphia could gain as much as $10 million a year.  Local targets already include lawyers and doctors.

headline: Push-Me-Pull-You
abstract: A cartoon of an elephant with heads on both sides is drawn, titled "GOP" and one side is labeled pro-life, the other pro-choice.

headline: Holden hopes to join panel on agriculture
abstract: Following a suggestion made by a farmer, Tim Holden, Democratic candidate for Congress, took some time to learn about farming, won the general election and now plans to seek a spot on the House Agriculture Committee.  Holden will be the first Pennsylvanian on the panel in 19 years.

headline: Residents decry incinerator as testimony in Montco ends
abstract: The state Department of Evnironmental Resources concluded testimony this week on a request by a Montgomery County pharmaceutical firm, Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc., to build an infectious-waste incinerator at its world headquarters.

headline: Mayor fills 2 safety posts
abstract: Mayor Masloff changed the Public Safety Department guard, naming Louis DiNardo as the department director and Earl Buford as her police chief.

headline: PSFS is seized by U.S. regulators and sold to Mellon
abstract: Government regulators seized the Philadelphia Savings Fund Society's parent company, putting an end to the 176-year-old institution that was once the area's largest and best-known bank.  The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. (FDIC) immediately sold off 27 branches and all of the bank's deposits to Mellon Bank Corp.

headline: Construction workers support Specter
abstract: Sen. Arlen Specter won the support of the Pennsylvania Building and Construction Trades, a major Pennsylvania building and construction workers' union, an endorsement that one union leader said could mean up to $200,000 in contributions to his re-election campaign.

headline: People ask why Kolter's failing to carry out job
abstract: US Representative Joe Kolter is getting a $125,000 salary plus expenses paid by taxpayers to represent them until January.  But some people, from farmers to small business advocates, are wondering what Kolter is doing to earn his paycheck.

headline: County Considers Joint Purchasing Program
abstract: The state Department of Community Affairs has called on the Butler County commissioners to take the lead in putting together a program that could save millions of dollars each year through regional joint purchasing.

headline: Rallies for, against abortion set
abstract: Abortion-rights advocates headed for the nation's capital in preparation for a march and rally three weeks before the Supreme Court takes up a Pennsylvania case that anti-abortion and abortion-rights groups have said could undermine, if not overturn, Roe v. Wade, the 1973 decision that legalized abortion.

headline: Lancaster County girls in the spotlight as Farm Show queens
abstract: Governor Robert Casey accepts a gift of a chicken and eggs from the state Poultry Queen at the 76th annual state Farm Show in Harrisburg.

headline: Roadside kills
abstract: Dead deer on roadsides are familiar sights in the state.  More than 40,000 killed annually, but the state has never defined whose job it was to clean it up.

headline: 'Men Who Care Day'
abstract: More than 20 men took off work or rearranged their schedules to attend a program to honor fathers and others who are male role models to a group of first graders at the Camp Curtin Early Childhood Center, for the first "Men Who Care Day," held by the class.

headline: Racing bill ups the ante for riverboat gambling
abstract: A bill introduced by Rep. Frank J. Gigliotti would increase the tax on the receipts of companies that run horse racing, adding a 10 percent tax to the current 1.5 percent levy.  If enacted, the race track industry would go out of business.  Claims have been made that Gigliotti's bill was created in an effort to get legislative attention on a former bill of his that did not pass known as the "riverboat bill."

headline: Contractor seeks Foster's post
abstract: Michael L. Waugh, a Shrewsbury Township supervisor and building contractor, is the third Republican to announce plans to run for the House seat beign vacated by Rep. A. Carville Foster.  Waugh listed the state's budget crisis and reforms of the local tax structure, education system and health insurance as his top priorities.

headline: 'People First' Platform Adopted
abstract: Democrats reached outside the sealous atmosphere of Madison Square Garden in a bid to connect with the lives of ordinary Americans through an untraditional platform that "promotes people first."

headline: County may lose $200,000 annually
abstract: Unless state legislators act to restore funding cuts for court related services in this year's budget by Governor Robert P. Casey, Indiana County will continue to lose $200,000 annually in reimbursements, according to Commissioner James McQuown.

headline: Supreme Court: Abortion Decision '92
abstract: National statistics from the Alan Guttmacher Institute are given through graphs and charts on who is having abortions and where.

headline: Non-agriculture jobs up
abstract: The number of non-agricultural jobs in the state increased in June for the fifth consecutive month, to 5.05 million, state Department of Labor and Industry analysts say.

headline: Sewage treatment plant started
abstract: Ground-breaking ceremonies Thursday morning signaled the start of the Blairsville Municipal Authority's $5.4 million secondary sewage treatment plant project located 1.5 miles west of the borough in Burrell Township.

headline: Navy investigator had been suspended
abstract: Agent Laney S. Spigener, a Navy investigator who was removed from the Tailhook sexual harassment probe, had been suspended for misconduct related to a romantic relationship during his last tour of duty.

headline: Radisson to reopen as Embassy Suites
abstract: The Radisson Suite Hotel, which went out of business so abruptly last year that guests were evicted in mid-stay, is reopening under the Embassy Suites name, the building's owner announced.  The Radisson closed amid a wide-spread slump in the hotel buisness, with the recession and an oversupply of hotels pushing down occupancy rates in Philadelphia and many other cities.  It will get a multimillion-dollar facelift before reopening.

headline: Conventional wisdom
abstract: Generally, the Republicans seemed to be having "we" and "they" problems on opening night.  In the end, former President Ronald Reagan put it best: "We are all equals in the eyes of God, but in America that's not enough.  We must be equal in the eyes of each other."

headline: Per diems peeve Perugini
abstract: Republican legislative candidate Louis R. Perugini made a splash when he announced some old news in a new way.  He held a press conference in Harrisburg to denounce the expense money state lawmakers get simply for showing up each day.

headline: County spending must be reviewed
abstract: Gov. Robert Casey hit with a big state tax increase, and the Beaver County Commissioners raised the county tax, then enfoced a personal property tax.  Beaver County is fed up with taxes and waste of tax dollars.

headline: The Constitution guarantees choice
abstract: Choosing abortion or childbirth without government interference is a fundamental constitutional freedom and should have the maximum protection of our courts.  If Roe v. Wade is overturned, states would produce a crazy quilt of inconsistent and discriminatory state regulations, thus replacing a uniform American right with a host of new, bewildering legal dilemmas.

headline: Protests, 114 arrests mark annual Hegins pigeon shoot
abstract: At the annual Labor Day pigeon shoot at Hegins Park, 114 animal rights activists were arrested.  Activists began lining up in the parking lot about 6:30 am chatting among themselves and taking pictures of one another holding signs.

headline: Sierra Club gives the nod to Clinton
abstract: Governor Bill Clinton was formally endorsed for president by the Sierra Club in Pinnacle Mountain State Park, Arkansas, only the second such choice in the 100-year history of the nation's oldest environmental organization.

headline: Neighbors voice shock over arrest
abstract: Etta Mumford was put in jail, charged with the murder an ddismemberment of Calvin Stanley, her 3 1/2-year-old foster child.  Her neighbors simply cannot believe that a woman- whom they recalled as so kind and conscientious- could commit the horrible act she has been accused of.

headline: Referendums on gambling OK'd
abstract: The state House Finance Committee approved legislation that would allow communities to hold referendums on small games of chance every two years.

headline: Conway bid dead for term
abstract: If Maryann D. Conway's nomination to a Schuylkill County judgeship dies, as expected, next week, Governor Robert Casey will nominate her again in January.

headline: Perman awaits Dermody, but Barch hasn't given up
abstract: Novice politician Frank Perman looks forward to challenging state Representative Frank Dermody.  Perman defeated Spence Barch for the Republican state House nomination, but Barch refuses to concede the election until he reviews precinct results.

headline: Cranberry Tax Boost Is Still Up In The Air
abstract: Cranberry school directors continue to whittle away at a budget that calls for a hefty tax increase and also are trying to finalize negotiations with the Service Employees International Union.

headline: The Fading Freedom Of Choice Act
abstract: During the Democratic presidential primaries, all five of the contenders made a pilgrimage to Washington to assure Kate Michelman, executive director of the National Abortion Rights Action League, that they surely supported the passage of the Freedom of Choice Act by Congress.  The law would provide statutory protection for Roe v. Wade no matter what the largely misogynist Supreme Court decided to do.  FOCA would go beyond Roe v. Wade to ensure the right to choose.

headline: 'Set-aside' farm is praised
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey called it a great day in the history of farmland preservation during a visit to John Angermier Jr.'s farm in Jefferson Township.  Thanks to the state Agriculture Preservation Board, the land can only be used as farmland as the Angermiers have sold all development rights to the board.

headline: Spilled cargo traces currents
abstract: A severe storm two years ago has given scientists unusual tools for studying the currents of the Pacific: shoes.  The shoes went from mere footwear to tools of science on May 27, 1990, when the freighter Hansa Carrier ran into heavy weather and 21 cargo containers were lost overboard.

headline: New boss picked for youth center
abstract: The state Department of Public Welfare ended a national search by picing Leverne Alford, a juvenile center administrator from West Chester, to head the troubled Youth Development Center in Bensalem.

headline: Sears, accused of auto-service overcharges, offers credits
abstract: In an effort to regain public trust, Sears Roebuck & Co. announced that it will offer $50 coupons to nearly one million customers of its auto service centers, where New Jersey and California investigators alleged that consumers had been through unnecessary repairs.

headline: Cosby helped buyo out Berndt
abstract: Bill Cosby does a lot more for Tmeple than serve as a free pitchman in its TV ads.  He also buys out its football coaches.  The comedian, the school's most famous alumnus and trustee, helped pay the cost of buying out coach Jerry Berndt an dhis nine-member staff.

headline: Perot appeared at a thinly attended Dallas rally.  He danced, sang, bantered, and denounced pollsters.
abstract: While Bill Clinton and George Bush jet-hopped across the country, Perot spent the last day of the campaign in his home town.  At a rally, Perot bantered with supporters and sang songs on the stage at Reunion Arena.

headline: Dispute over washing machines remains ensnarled in litigation
abstract: Despite apparently winning the battle to keep their washing machines, 35 Hall Manor residents still are ensnarled in litigation.  The Harrisburg Housing Authority refuses to concur with the residents' motion to dismiss the legal action they brought in US Middle District Court here but preserving the right to refile it.

headline: US is Allowed Supporting Role on Pennsylvania Abortion Law
abstract: The Supreme Court granted the Bush administration's request to argue in support of the Pennsylvania abortion law when the politically charged issue comes before the high court in April.

headline: State snaps back at bungee craze
abstract: The state Department of Agriculture, which regulates amusement rides, acted correctly last week to impose some common-sense standards on the latest American craze- bungee jumping.  The state has a proper interest in seeing- to the extent possible- that such confidence has some basis in fact to avoid what some people view as fun from turning into tragedy.

headline: State bottle bill for litter would include many spin-off benefits
abstract: Rep. John Broujos has once again introduced the bottle and can bill, yet Pennsylvania's lawmakers still block passage of the bill, unlike most other Northeastern states.  Such a law will encourage recycling efforts, create spin-off jobs in the retunable container industry, and enhance Pennsylvania's reputation as an environmentally responsible state.

headline: No-bid courhouse contract called political patronage
abstract: Peter Aborn, a former top city official in the $224.5 million prison-courthouse project, has alleged that political patronage prompted the Rendell administration to award a multimillion-dollar no-bid contract to Daniel Keating III, a Villanova developer.

headline: Seeking a better RIDC
abstract: Last week, a special committee of the Business Times chaired by state Representative Thomas Murphy, was preparing to go public with a report critical of the Regional Industrial Development Corp. of Southwestern Pennsylvania..

headline: Coslett fund-raiser
abstract: There will be an outing for Republican state representative candidate Keith Coslett form 1 to 5pm today at Sacred Heart Grove in Dallas.

headline: Perot candidacy beginning to look better and better
abstract: Congress and the president responded to the ailing economy and exploding national debt with playpen politics, making H. Ross Perot look good as a candidate for presidency as an independent.  But as an idealist, people see Perot as an overreach, and say that he couldn't achieve hardly any of what he promises.

headline: Down in flames- Tax revenue at One Meridian
abstract: After One Meridian Plaza went down in flames, the owner, E/R Associates, hasn't paid its annual tax bill for 1991 and won't pay the 1992 bill until the issue of the building's market value is resolved.  This is depriving the city of millions of dollars in property taxes.

headline: The True Pro-Life Position
abstract: President Bush ordered establishment of a Government fetal tissue bank, accepting only tissue from miscarriages and ectopic pregnancies for research, but that tissue is usually defective or diseased, rarely being suitable for such research.  By acting as if taking tissue for research from abortion encourages abortions, Bush is turning his back on the many Americans for whome fetal research represents a new chance at life.

headline: State, humane society nearing dog agreement
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture has recently taken two major steps toward getting the Crawford County Humane Society to resume its acceptance of stray dogs from the department.

headline: State inspectors leave Pottsville in dark on lead
abstract: Lead-poisoned children in Pottsville who were screened by the state Department of Health office in Schuylkill County were returned to their contaminated houses and their cases were never reported to the city, as the local code requires.

headline: Nomination for federal bench approved
abstract: The Senate Judiciary Committee yesterday unanimously approved the nomination of Montgomery County Common Pleas Judge Anita B. Brody to the US District Court in Philadelphia.

headline: Sharon Steel to lay off 500 workers
abstract: Debt-laden Sharon Steel Corp. said it was laying off another 500 workers, bringing to about 1,300 the number of employees let go this year.

headline: Council to hire attorney, rely less on city solicitor
abstract: City Council, which threatened for months to hire its own attorney because of conflicts with the acting city solicitor, unanimously made that move last night.  Council members, saying they need someone to review complicated information for them, approved hiring a part-time attorney and will interview candidates Nov. 5.

headline: Perot insists he did not let his supporters down
abstract: Ross Perot appeared on television to say he did not believe that he had let his supporters down by bailing out of the presidential campaign.  He also indicated he will not throw his support to either Bill Clinton or George Bush.

headline: Flushing deadbeats
abstract: Whenever the city makes a sweep for tax delinquents and code violators, as it did with impressive results recently along a Northeast Philadelphia commercial strip, it sends a powerful signal to others who aren't current on taxes, license fees and the like.  So the special push on Castor Avenue by city inspectors and Revenue Department investigators could have a lucrative, ripple effect upon the city's coffers.

headline: They're out to shop till stigmas drop
abstract: The women of the Lesbian Visibility Project target suburban shopping malls for evenings of "consumerism and consciousness-raising" about the lifestyles of women who are gay.

headline: The river runs rich
abstract: It is a struggle to make the rocky red clay of northeastern York County produce crops.  So, when Geary Huntsberger bought part of his father's farm there in the late 1940s, he began looking faround for other, richer land on which to grow corn.  He found it in the middle of the Susquehanna River.

headline: State- Mine fire will devour all
abstract: The last holdouts, 58 people, who plan to fight the state's move to get them out of the borough of Centralia should wake up and smell the fumes, Jack G. Carling claims, chief of disaster programs for the state Department of Community Affairs.  The underground mine fire will someday encompass the whole town.  It's hard to predict when, so residents should consider their health and safety and move out of there.

headline: Nurse fired, helped inmate with mail
abstract: Giving three stamps and three envelopes to a Dauphin County Prison inmate so he could send some poetry to a New York magazine cost Julie Shomper her nursing job at the jail.

headline: Siemens shows interest in 2 of GTE's area plants
abstract: A German light bulb manufacturer may be interested in buying a division of GTE Corp. that has plants in St. Marys and Warren in northwestern Pennsylvania.  David Tedone, manager of public relations at Sylvania Lighting Division headquarters, said it is impossible to answer questions concerning whether GTE would close down its lighting and precision materials operations if a sale is not made, but he did say it was highly unlikely.

headline: Council: Expediter not expedient
abstract: With little fanfare or flourish, Council members issued a civic announcement remarkable for its simplicity and revolutionary nature: Say no to The Expediter.  The Expediter is a moonlighting Philadelphia Housing Authority employee who was recommended by a city employee.  But there are lots of them, ready, willing and able to expedite.

headline: Perot Investigated Bush's Activities
abstract: Ross Perot, after months of dickering with then-Vice President Bush over a plan Perot thought would provide information about US servicemen still missing from the Vietnam War, concluded that Bush had let him down.

headline: For city property, the fixes won't be in for a long time
abstract: Philadelphia's city-owned buildings, roads and bridges are aging fast, with lack of money to maintain, repair and replace city property.

headline: Tioga group wants rights panel member to resign
abstract: A group of Tioga residents demanded the resignation of the Rev. Peter H. Park from the Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations for his involvement in a dispute involving a Korean-American merchant and an African American woman.

headline: 50 lose jobs when clothing factory closes
abstract: The Toby Sportswear sewing factory that has operated in York since the mid-1970s is closing, putting roughtly 50 people out of work,

headline: State planning a second look into relocation
abstract: State officials have decided, after meeting with a crowd of angry residents, to take a second look at their effort to relocate 80 stubborn residents of Centralia in Columbia County.  Residents are threatened by subsidence and poisonous gases resulting from an underground fire that has been burning for 30 years.

headline: Officer of Montco S&L is guilty
abstract: The vice president of Hill Financial Savings Association, David W. Foulke, has pleaded guilty to bank embezzlement in the loss of $42 million in loans, federal prosecutors said.

headline: Sluggish economy leads to more business failures
abstract: Business failures increased by double-digit percentages in July and over the first seven months of the year, compared with 1991.  Leading the pack were New York and California.  The recession has weakened many firms that many can no longer survive at the current slow pace of economic growth.

headline: County commissioner not a shoo-in for Schuylkill County Court vacancy
abstract: Maryann D. Conway may be the governor's choice for Schuylkill County judge, but her confirmation faces obstacles in state Senator James J. Rhodese, a feuding Senate and a ticking clock.

headline: Perot power zaps county
abstract: The Lawrence County branch of Pennsylvanians for Perot plans to have 3,000 to 4,000 signatures on petitions by mid-July.  The way things are going, the committee doesn't have far to go to reach its goal.

headline: From decay, purpose blooms
abstract: As bureaucrats cut to the bone at City Hall, fine-tuning Mayor Rendell's five-year plan to save the city from bankruptcy, some wonder if City Hall could really do anything to support their neighborhoods.  Surprisingly, the answer seems to be yes- at least from the experience in the Norris Square section of West Kensington.

headline: Towns target abortion
abstract: Nearly 1,100 midstaters who opose abortion formed a "Life Chain" on Front Street, joining a nationwide event that its organizers called a "statement of faith."

headline: Building Trades' view
abstract: Thomas Miller, President of the Pa. Building and Construction Trades Council, rebuts the remarks of John Morris, president of the Pennsylvania Conference of Teamsters, regarding a brawl breaking out at the statewide AFL-CIO Convention in 1990.

headline: State Recycling Focus Turns to New Markets
abstract: The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania has made a commitment to environmental responsibility through the implementation of its statewide recycling policy.  The response of the citizens of the Commonwealth has been overwhelming and raw materials ready for recycling have been collected at impressive levels, but we must do more.

headline: On probation, but hardly free
abstract: About 32,000 Philadelphians are on probation, instead of in prison, for scores of crimes, more and more of them involving drugs.  Nearly 6,000 are under the most common form of probation-"moderate supervision."  One of their probation officers laments that some on probation think "they've beat the charges."

headline: Small Businesses, Key To Urban Recovery, Are Starved for Capital
abstract: Corporate America has wailed about a credit crunchrestraining it in recent years, but it has gone through nothing like the credit starvation that is a governing condition of inner-city business.  Here there are all the usual worries that go with rlunning any business, plus the myriad woes of the ghetto.

headline: County controller sues opponent in election
abstract: Beaver County Controller Richard Towcimak filed suit against state Representative Susan Laughlin over an election brochure she mailed to residents in her district accusing Towcimak of losing $250,000 in state checks.

headline: Perot resembles Bush more than either of them could comfortably acknowledge
abstract: Perot has too few ideas to be either a liberal or conservative, but he has the mentality that has gotten liberalism into lots of trouble.  Perot resembles Bush more than either could comfortably acknowledge.  And Bush has failed because he believes in nothing much other than the process that proved its merit by producing him as president.

headline: Indiana, Moscow now sister cities
abstract: Officials from Indiana Borough and Moscow, Russia, signed documents establishing a sister-city agreement which will encourage the exchange of citizens, ideas and economic technical assistance between the two cultures.

headline: Two parties differ on abortion issue
abstract: What happens to the laws on aboriton may depend on who is elected president.  President Bush and Governor Bill Clinton have very different views on abortion- Bush wants to make abortion illegal again and Clinton wants to keep the right of women to choose.

headline: Canonsburg union faces challenge in May vote
abstract: Service employees at Canonsburg General Hospital will vote on decertifying the Service Employees International Union, the union that represented them during a bitter, 150-day strike that turned into a battle over replacement workers.  The National Labor Relations Board has scheduled the vote.

headline: States With Acute Smog Problem Sign Ozone Pact
abstract: The governors of 12 Northeastern and mid-Atlantic states and the Mayor of the District of Columbia agreed today to a regional plan to help their governments meet tough new Federal laws on ozone pollution.

headline: On racial issues, Bradley lifts his stock
abstract: Bill Bradley, the same person who spent years reveling in the intricacies of Third World debt and the Strategic Oil Reserve, barely 12 hours after the stunning acquittal of four Los Angeles police officers, banged a Senate podium 56 times- one for each blow to the body of Rodney King, at the hands of those four officers.  Now, many favor him as a candidate for vice president.

headline: Sports car manufacturing company locates in Monessen, gains investors
abstract: Young entrepreneur David Allinder, after months of discussions, finally has taken his first formal steps toward becoming a manufacturer of his own DeLorean-style, stainless steel-bodied sports car in the Monongahela Valley.

headline: Court approves redistricting plan
abstract: The PA Supreme Court upheld a congressinal redistricting plan that splits the Pocono region between two U.S. House districts instead of the current three-way alignment.

headline: Perot says he'd serve just 1 term if elected
abstract: Presidnet Bush and Bill Clinton grappled in a presidential debate last night that was more polite than revealing, more cautious than caustic.  Independent Ross Perot, trailing badly in the polls, continued to play the role of the feisty outsider, tagging both Bush and Clinton as part of the political establishment that has contributed to government gridlock.

headline: Inequality in procedure cheats some, not others
abstract: Twenty years after Bucks County's last reassessment, two Bensalem houses lie at opposite ends of the township, tree miles and worlds of fairness apart.  They are mute reminders of how, over two decades of runaway development in the county, assessments have steadily slid out of whack.

headline: Volunteers mobilize for end-runs of state abortion statutes
abstract: Since June 29, the day the US Supreme court held a Pennsylvania law requiring minors to get approval for an abortion and requireing all women to receive counseling and wait 24 hours before getting one, more than 100 letters have been sent to the "Overground Railraod," a group who wants to help transport women to other states where they can have abortions without such harsh restrictions.

headline: Caterpillar denies union busting
abstract: Caterpillar Inc. officials discussed their contract talks with counterparts from other companies last month in a meeting the United Auto Workers said may be an attempt at union busting.

headline: Steel state's No. 2 polluter in '90
abstract: Bethlehem Steel's Bethlehem plant emitted more toxic pollutants in 1990 than all but one comparable facility in Pennsylvania, federal data shows.

headline: Opening a new world to inmates
abstract: The Prison Literacy Project, an eight-year-old program that brings volunteers into the stae prison to work with inmate tutors and students to break bonds of illiteracy, has helped the 40-60 percent of inmates who could not read past fourth-grade level at Graterford, Pennsylvania's largest prison.

headline: State court rules medical center in Erie is taxable
abstract: Commonwealth Court issued a decision that Erie's Hamot Medical Center was not entitled to a property tax exemption because it didn't operate 'free from profit motive' and didn't provide enough 'purely public charity.'

headline: Court Case Sould Pave Way For Legislative Pension Boost
abstract: While it is too early to declare the winners in the November elections, it is already obvious that many citizens consider themselves to be the losers.  Voting studies inform us that citizens are disappointed with their electoral choices, nervous about their political futures, and in the mood for major changes in governmet at all levels.  Incumbents are the primary targets of voter antipathy.

headline: Perot steers clear of mixing politics, POWs
abstract: After 23 years seeking a spotlight for POWs, Ross Perot is refusing to testify before a Senate committee looking into the possibility that prisoners of war presumed dead in Vietnam are still alive.

headline: Laughlin hasn't given up fight to repeal personal property tax
abstract: State Representative Susan Laughllin plans to continue to fight Beaver County's personal property tax.  Laughlin's efforts seemed popular with most of the approximately 50 people at a meeting Thursday night at the Beaver County Courthouse.

headline: Voters and abortion
abstract: Despite Pennsylvania's leadership in the fight to restrict abortion, most voters in the state's primaries- on both sides of the aisle- oppose the overturn of Roe vs. Wade, the 1973 Supreme Court ruling that legalized abortion nationwide.

headline: Caterpillar shutdown threat held as credible
abstract: Caterpillar Inc. announced last month that only significant savings in labor and other expenses would save the York plant.  Caterpillar told workers at the plant and distribution center that the company's contract proposal guaranteed them job security for six years, yet six days later they were told the plant would probably close.

headline: Study: State Needs Toxic Waste Incinerators
abstract: The draft of the state's new Hazardous Waste Facilities Plan says that the hazardous waste incinerators used to "treat" hazardous wastes are especially needed in Pennsylvania and that the state should rely on commercial waste handling companies to meet that need.

headline: Overtime reduced at 'high-security' YDC
abstract: YDC overtime expenses during a recent 12-month period plunged 52 percent- the same time the number of juveniles living at the site decreased dramatically.  Meanwhile, state Department of Public Welfare officials decided to make the Youth Development Center strictly a high-security facility for now.

headline: State Insurance Department Cuts Workers' Comp Increase In Half
abstract: The state Insurance Department cut by half the 52 percent rate increase requested by the state's insurance industry, which has been pending for over a year.

headline: Crumbly is viable
abstract: Though Iris Crumbly's eligibility to run for the 103rd District is in question because of where she lives, she is a viable, outstanding candidate, who shouldn't have to defend herself against trivial accusations.

headline: Perot's local supporters eager for him to re-enter the contest
abstract: Ross Perot's candidacy attracted thousands of volunteers, but the bomb came on July 16 when he announced he would not run.  Even after the announcement, the faithful have stuck behind Perot.

headline: Lebanon official's actions probed
abstract: City Treasurer Jack Miller submitted insurance papers to Lebanon County more than a year ago that falsely showed that his cab company had the coverage necessary to meet th e requirements of a contract with the county, documents show.

headline: Women will get photos, drawings
abstract: Photographs and drawings will be included in the mandated material to be provided to women in Pennsylvania wanting an abortion, a state Health Department spokeswoman said.

headline: Creating new jobs called biggest issue
abstract: Creating new jobs should be "the biggest, single issue we're talking about in this country," US Labor Secretary Lynn Martin said during a visit to the midstate.  Martin praised President Bush's proposed $3 billion job-training and education program, while admitting it probably will go nowhere before the November election.

headline: Superfund listing adds 28 houses
