abstract: The federal government has added to its Superfund cleanup list 28 houses in Delaware County that are tainted with radium from a processing plant.  Superfund listing frees up money for further study and a cleanup plan, thought the entire process will take years and millions of dollars, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

headline: Postscript to Delco's gang era
abstract: Police are still looking for answers to four of the five unsolved mystery deaths of five young women at Robert Marconi's mansion from 1975.  Robert Nauss, Marconi's buddy, received a life sentence in 1977 for hanging and dismembering his girlfriend, the fifth of the five slain girls.  Marconi suffered chest pains on Jan. 18 and died later that day.

headline: State insurance fund offers sound package in workers' comp
abstract: In response to a letter from Dec. 16- writer gives credit that the letter makes a point about the effects of investment income, but says that the comments about the State Workers' Insurance Fund and the governor's proposal are inaccurate.  Gov. Casey's four-point proposal addresses the major cost drivers in Pennsylvania's system.

headline: D.C. Vote Set on $100 Limit to Campaign Donations
abstract: District voters will decide this fall whether political candidates should be forbidden to receive campaign donations that exceed $100.  In a move that could bring dramatic change to how political campaigns in the District are waged, the city's election board ruled yesterday that a proposal to slash the current contribution limit of $2,000 will be put to voters on the November ballot.

headline: Perot's Man On Wall St.
abstract: Kenneth Langone, one of Ross Perot's closest friends, could be thrusted into the limelight if Perot becomes president.  He could even be offered a key post in a Perot administration, perhaps influencing national economic policies.

headline: Local tax caps scrutinized
abstract: The state House Finance Committee will hold a public hearing today to discuss a bill that would remove local tax ceilings, allowing local governments to set their own tax rates.

headline: Wade got $5.8 million for parts of minority cable-TV franchise
abstract: James N. Wade, a well-known black business leader, got more than $3 million in cash last year when he sold a majority interest in his Philadelphia cable television franchise to a white-owned New York firm.  The sale brought strong protests from some city and community leaders, who said the franchise should remain with a minority-owned firm.

headline: Cronin: Fiery leader of Philadelphia labor
abstract: In a recent television interview, Philadelphia union leader Thomas Paine Cronin was captured talking about the progress of labor negotiations with the city.  Pay attention to Tom Cronin's mouth.  As the days drag on and the possibility of a strike by municipal workers draws closer, Cronin's mouth promises to be one of the chief weapons in the war of words and deeds that has already seen its early skirmishes.

headline: Testing the waters
abstract: Kate Kauffman is a volunteer for ALLARM- Alliance for Acid Rain Monitoring, where she tests water to measure the effect acid rain is haing on Pennsylvania's lakes and streams.  ALLARM is building a foundation of information about the health of the sate's water systems.

headline: Parole report cites $46 million saving
abstract: The State Board of Probation and Parole released a report, "Changes in Parole Policy: Impact and Performance," outlining the new policies and programs that the agency implemented during 1990 and 1991.

headline: State Oks new anti-fraud insurance rules
abstract: Regulations approved by the Independent Regulatory Review Commission would protect people from insurance fraud and financially troubled health maintenace organizations.

headline: Dance Marathon tops $1.1 million mark
abstract: Penn State's Dance Marathon, the largest student-run philanthropy in the nation, raised $1,141,145.38 for young cancer patients, topping the $1 million mark for the first time in the event's 20-year history.

headline: Perot's plan faces resistance
abstract: If the voters turn to Ross Perot, he promises to use the presidency as a "bully pulpit" to provoke some fundamental changes in government.  Campaigning as a can-do businessman who knows how to get things done, Perot describes a presidency that would be highly confrontational with Congress to force the Washington political establishment to adopt his programs.

headline: Mayor's panel: revamp agencies
abstract: A radical restructuring of the city's confusing myriad of housing agencies, including the Philadelphia Housing Authority, has been recommended in a draft of a mayoral commission's report.  The commission charges the primary problem with the city's housing effort is a lack of coordination among the agencies charged with doing the job.

headline: Who owns the right to speak?
abstract: When Governor Casey was speaking about being a "pro-life liberal," prochoicers shouted him down.  If the crowd hadn't interrupted Casey, the press would have been able to report that pro- and anti-choicers engaged in a polite and civilized discussion on this issue and all supported free speech.

headline: Evenflo Staff Offers Concessions
abstract: Workers at the Evenflo-Crator plant here have offered to take concessions in order to keep the plant within commuting distance of Tionesta.  A petition was given to Robert Till, vice president of operations at the Ravenna, Ohio, plant, yesterday.  Till was at the Tionesta plant for a safety inspection.

headline: The Bridge Game
abstract: Out of your nickels, dimes and quarters, the Delaware River Joint Bridge Commission has buildt a $122 million empire ruled by favoritism, intimidation, and unaccountability.

headline: Pension board to retired cops: Give us $$ back
abstract: Hundreds of retired police officers and firefighters were notified yesterday that they have been receiving $50 a month more than they are entitled to and will have to return the overpayments to the Board of Pensions and Retirement.  The 411 and 144 firefighters would have to repay an average of $2,200.

headline: State says four partners broke law
abstract: Attorneys for the state Department of Banking claim the four general partners of the former Tobias Knoblauch Private Bank violated state law, gave each other preferential interest ratres and overdraft protection, had too little loan documentation, and took the bank to the brink of collapse.

headline: Day for non-politicians
abstract: Although the presidential primary gets the headlines, there are othehr offices at stake in the election and at least one is generating heat- the neck-and-neck contest between Lt. Governor Mark Singel and Lynn Yeakel for the Democratic senatorial nomination.  The "non-politician" has always been a factor in elections, but usually as spoiler or the occasionally successful reform candidate.  But now voters are actively seeking out the non-politician.

headline: Perot's workers deny allegation
abstract: Bill Clinton said that a reported attempt by Ross Perot's camp to hire away one of his consultants for $600,000 appears "highly political."  Perot spokesman James Squires called the incident "absolutely unbelievable" and said no one authorized to make such an offer did so.

headline: Nanticoke: Ex-mayor sees bankruptcy by summer
abstract: Former mayor John Haydock said he is concerned the city's deficit will rise to more than a half a million dollars at the end of 1992 because Nanticoke ended 1991 with a shortfall of about $200,000, according to councilman Mark Yeager.  A balanced budget was insured by an inflation of city revenue numbers for '92, which practice wil insure Nanticoke's financial doom.

headline: With its latest abortion decision, the Supreme Court further muddied the waters
abstract: The Supreme Court's refusal to overturn the extremism of Roe vs. Wade is commended as "moderation."  Still, liberals did not get the decision they wanted.

headline: For unions, city: swing, hit & miss
abstract: This will be known as the summer when the labor games went into extra innings for days and days and days.  Everybody got some hits, but no runs were ever scored.

headline: 'Tis season for saving; here's how
abstract: Green holiday suggestions are given from Environmental Defense Fund, and from the book "The New Green Christmas."

headline: Perry formalized court-cost agreement with Juniata
abstract: Perry County commissioners formalized the informal, approving an agreement that requires Juniata County to help pay court system costs.  "We've always had an understanding on this, but we've never had anything in writing," Commissioner Jeffrey A. Conrad said.

headline: State to demand funds
abstract: State Banking Secretary Sarah W. Hargrove has decided she will seek to force five depositors of the defunct Tobias Knoblauch Private Bank- who were hastily given back $1.5 million in uninsured deposits just moments before Hargrove seized the bank April 17- to return the money to the state.

headline: Daylong din greets Council
abstract: Though they say John Street is lord and master of City Council, even he couldn't prevent a rowdy band of housing activists from disrupting yesterday's council meeting.

headline: PHA award: Politics?
abstract: A personnel firm with strong local political connections is expected to win a contract to assist the Philadelphia Housing Authority in filling at least the top 20 jobs at the agency, informed sources say.

headline: Norristown school taxes to rise 11%
abstract: Norristown Area School District residents will be paying about 11 percent more in school taxes to fund the budget adopted.

headline: Women are poised to make House history
abstract: Female politicians saw the door to the US Senate, currently an institution that's 97% male, open wider.  A record 11 women, 10 Democrats and one Republican, have won party nominations to the Senate this year.

headline: Governor has sound plan for Workers' Comp reform
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey made tough decisions in his Workers' Compensation plan, but he characterized the Senate Republicans handling of his reform package as if "they put it through a sausage machine."  Without reform, the alternative will be companies moving out of the commonwealth and many workers left without jobs.

headline: To save bay, curb Maryland development and Pennsylvania cows
abstract: The article on the Chesapeake Bay would be amusing if it weren't so serious.  The gathering of the "great powers that be"- all supposedly dedicating themselves and the resources at their disposal to the cleaning up of the venerable Chesapeake Bay.  A condo complex, Coast Guard station and new homes are taking away the serenity of the shoreline and EPA rules are arbitrary.  As long as development is allowed to go on unabated right on the shoreline of the bay, it will continue to deteriorate.

headline: Pointing fingers at the past
abstract: George Bush, Presidnet for three years, vice president for eight years.  Does he bear any responsibility for the state of economic and race relations in this nation that helped fuel the Los Angeles riots after the Rodney King police brutality verdicts were returned?  Not according to spokesman Marlin Fitzwater, who suggested that you have to go back to the 1960s to find the responsible party- the Democratic Party.

headline: State wineries ae hopeful
abstract: Even if a settlement is reached and the US government backs down on its threat to tack a 200 percent tariff on European white wines, wineries in Pennsylvania will benefit from the added exposure.  An dif the triffs are applied, Keystone state wineries can expect sales to increase as wine drinkers turn to domestic alternatives.

headline: DCA's Miller, Connors Take Off the Gloves
abstract: The gloves, which have been softening the debate over Scranton's financial recovery plan, came off Friday as a state cabinet member and Mayor Jim Connors verbally bare-knuckled each other.

headline: Philadelphia lawmakers divided on speaker
abstract: Democrats count Robert W. O'Donnell in their delegation.  Some have lined up behind his opponent, Bill DeWeese, for the top House position.

headline: Politics will yield to local interests
abstract: With the budget process nearing the midnight June 30 deadline, expect ideological differences between Democrats and Republicans to give way to political pragmatism and local interests.

headline: Annual Mammogram Needed, Experts Say
abstract: Women 65 and older are twice as likely to develop breast cancer or die from it as women ages 40-64.  Yet, according to the National Cancer Institute, these women are not receiving annual mammograms, a screening procedure that can detect cancer early.

headline: Initial jobless claims decline by only 2,000
abstract: the number of first-time claims for unemployment insurance edged down in early June, the government said in a report reflecting the painfully slow recovery from the recession.  The Labor Department said 407,000 Americans filed applications for benefits, down from a revised 409,000 a week earlier.

headline: Toxic emissions abound, but it's improving
abstract: Though area companies blew 2.8 million pounds of toxic chemicals into our air in 1991, Joe Pezze, air quality manager for the Pittsburgh office of the state Department of Environmental Resources, insists the air is getting better.

headline: Police charge foster parent with murder
abstract: Etta Mumford, who insisted she loved her missing foster child, was charged with murdering th boy and dismembering his body, parts of which were found in her basement freezer.  The 3-year-old boy died of blunt trauma to the body, the medical examiner ruled.  An investigator said she admitted dismembering him, but not killing him.

headline: States are right to bar health-care cherry-picking
abstract: States tackled a menace- "cherry-picking," insurance companies' questionable practice of insuring only those who need it least, luring the youngest and healthiest with low rates and denying those who need it most.  New York and Iowa are banning insurers from cherry-picking in groups with fewer than 50 members.  They are good examples to follow.

headline: Deadline is 10 days to prevent new crisis
abstract: A core group of eight legislators- with three to four others occasionally participating- is meeting bhind closed doors to largely decide how Pennsylvania will spend more than $14 billion in state tax dollars the next fiscal year.

headline: Philadelphia redefines its role as the employer of last resort
abstract: Philadelphia seems poised to bear a strike by the two blue- and white-collar public worker unions representing its 16,000 non-uniformed employees.  Bargaining is still under way between the unions and the Rendell administration.  In its struggle with its union, will Philadelphia be setting the pattern for the nation?

headline: Property tax relief plan unveiled
abstract: Lt. Governor Mark Singel and tow Democratic lawmakers unveiled a new property tax relief proposal yesterday.  But Governor Robert P. Casey said it looked like a tax increase and he will veto any tax increase.

headline: A lurching start for new agency
abstract: Hampered by the lack of medical records, adequate space and essential supplies and equipment, a new community mental health center, the Charles R. Drew Center, opened in North Philadelphia, with hundreds of clients relieved just to be there.

headline: Injured workers benefit from returning quickly to jobs
abstract: At Chrysler, managers and medical and legal experts meet weekly to design temporary jobs for injured workers.  "At home, workers sit around, gain weight, lose tone, and they have all the psychological baggage that comes with being unproductive," says Dr. Sue Parkins, a director of St. Vincent Medical Center.

headline: Trash station concessions sought by Silver Spring
abstract: Silver Spring supervisors came to the Cumberland County commissioners seeking concessions to offset the "detriment" of a county plan for a trash-transfer station in the township.  But Supervisors Karen Best and Jan LeBlanc came away with only one "no" and indefinite promises from commission Chairman Earl R. Keller to review the matter.

headline: Police commissioner summoned to court over grand jury leaks
abstract: Police Commissioner Richard Neal will be asked to a Common Pleas courtroom next week to discuss- and possibly, launch an investigation of- leaks of grand jury testimony from "a high-ranking police source" to reporters, attorney Mark E. Gottlieb said yesterday.

headline: Supermarket bank opens
abstract: One-stop shopping takes on a new dimension today with the opening of a Pennsylvania National Bank branch in the Giant supermarket at Colonial Commons in Lower Paxton Township, the area's first supermarket bank.

headline: Dear Guv: Here's how to change your image
abstract: A letter written to "Guv" a.k.a. Governor Bill Clinton gives him advice in a mocking manner about the presidential election.

headline: Phone-poll tally nixes Warren
abstract: When asked if Commissioner's Chairman Andrew L. Warren should run for governor, 147 readers called in with no-votes while only 34 respondents encouraged Warren to run.

headline: Region counts on airport to create economic victory
abstract: In an aging, former coal-mining village west of Pittsburgh known as Midway Borough, where home mail delivery and public sewage still are notably absent, residents are finding themselves talking on the street about economic growth, perhaps from plans for the new Pittsburgh International Airport.

headline: A strange contraption
abstract: New Jersey legislature has put together a health-care plan that only Rube Goldberg could love.  The health-financing mechanism has a distinctly slapdash, experimental look, that robs Peter to pay Paul, dipping into the state's unemployment fund to pay hospitals that treat the uninsured.

headline: Issues remain to be resolved by GM, union
abstract: Last spring's boardroom revolt at General Motors Corp. forced company executives to speed up the pace of sweeping cutbacks.  Buth this month, 2,500 workers in GM's Lordstown, Ohio stamping plant stood up against the company's aggressive restructuring plan.  Their nine-day strike shut down nine assembly plants, idled 42,900 workers and cost the company an estimated $75 million.

headline: Trash station site: Silver Spring
abstract: Cumberland County Solid Waste Authority is ready to act Monday on the purchase of a Silver Spring Township 79-acre tract on which it plans to build a trash transfer station and composting facility.

headline: Police department remains alive, well
abstract: Rumors have been passing that the borough police department was disbanding; however, the police unit remains intact.

headline: Surprise! Regional banks look for commercial loans
abstract: Regional banks are scrambing to add commercial loans to their balance sheets before year-end, reversing the practice of recent years.The turnabout mainly reflects continued improvement in the banks' capital ratios, which has enabled them to be more aggressive in making new loans.

headline: Defeated once, he'll run again
abstract: John P. Murtha of Johnstown, who lost the US Rep. in the 1990 primary election, announced his second bid for a congressional seat.

headline: Picketing for checks pays off
abstract: Constitution Bank was foreclosing on their employer, Die Cut Specialty Inc., but the Center City bank's employees' paychecks bounced, forcing the employees to picket outside, demanding their money.  State Representative Ralph Acosta served as a representative for the workers.

headline: Residents not amused by tax bill
abstract: Homeowners near the roar of the Pocono International Raceway in Tunkhannock Township an din the shadow of the Big Two ski resorts in Kidder Twonship likely will pay higher township property taxes if a controversial bill, tailor-made for those special-interest groups, becomes law.  And homeowners in the Weatherly and Jim Thorpe area school districts could face a double tax whammy.

headline: Absence of health insurance paramount parental concern
abstract: Pennsylvania legislators are slated to begin a special session that will include working out a health insurance program for needy children and reforming the woerkers' compensation system.  For families around the state, an agreement can't come too soon.

headline: Jobless claims rise after GM shuts plants
abstract: The number of Americans filing first-time claims for unemployment benefits shot up by 69,000 in the third week in July as the labor market was jarred by temporary layoffs in the auto industry, the government said yesterday.  The layoffs lasted only two weeks as a result of a decision by General Motors Corporation to shut all of its plants in late July.

headline: Trying a new way to kill PCBs
abstract: The contraption with the fancy name sits next to an old landfill on an island in the middle of the Saginaw River, looking a little like someone threw it together in a hurry after a late-night brainstorm.  If the gas-phase thermochemical reduction reactor annihilates PCBs the way it is supposed to, no one will care what it looks like.

headline: Police officer waives hearing on drugs
abstract: Robert A. Silks, a veteran city police officer, who spent a month in drug rehabilitation, waived his preliminary hearing on charges he bought $50 worth of cocaine in Lemoyne.

headline: The American Dream: Fired Up and Melted Down
abstract: For USX Corp. workers, steel was their ticket, good for paying off mortgages, sending children to college, lifting families above the stations to which they were born.  Despite decades of decline, few prepared themselves to live without it.  USX Corp. closed most of its massive Fairless Works here on the Delaware River.  Now the ex-workers are stalled, or more frightening, shifting into in reverse.

headline: Deficit battle takes on political tones
abstract: The federal deficit reared its ugly head Thursday as an increasingly potent political issue in this year's presidential and congressional elections.

headline: Pitcher makes pledge for pools
abstract: Every time Terry Mulholland wins a game, he's pledged $1,000 to the Philadelphia Recreation Department, a donation the Phillies organization will match.

headline: Tax bill takes bite from future collegian, too
abstract: Before 1992, Beaver County collected the personal property tax only from people who voluntarily reported they had assets that could be taxed.  This year, the county paid the Central Tax Bureau to use state income tax records to find people who owed the tax and to collect from them.

headline: AIDS- Families are dying
abstract: Philadelphia's two hospitals, Children's Hospital and St. Christopher's Hospital for Children, have developed a team approach in response to the extraordinary needs of children and parents with AIDS.  The Barrone family became infected with the HIV virus after the mother was infected by her former partner, an intravenous drug user, and passed the virus on to her two children and new husband.  Mary and her first son have died from the illness, but Ray and the other child, Baby Ray, are seeking help from the AIDS team of St. Christopher's.

headline: Jobless-benefit claims tumble
abstract: The number of new claims for jobless benefits shrank in early October for the third straight week, retreating to the lowest level in more than two years, the government said yesterday.  Still, analysts noted that applications for unemployment insurance are volatile and remained wary about whether the report portended substantial improvement in the labor market.

headline: Valley Forge is threatened again
abstract: Valley Forge National Park's creek, Valley Creek, may be threatened as Rouse and Associates wants to build, at the headwaters of Valley Creek, a housing development and sewage treatment plant that will dump more than 500,000 gallons of treated water into the stream daily.

headline: Police plan fails, and siege ends in death
abstract: Marseilles Desire Ebron, after fleeing from police, was surrounded by officers as he stayed in his broken-down car for nearly ten hours.  When police moved in to make a siege, the plan went awry, Ebron fired at an officer, and nine officers rushed to the car, killing Ebron with six shots.

headline: The best wheels
abstract: Statistics compiled by a marketing research company, RL Polk & Co., say that more than three-quarters of Western Pennsylvanians still prefer cars with American nametags.

headline: Deliberative democracy
abstract: At the Sheraton Society Hill Sunday morning, citizen's jury questioned the two Pennsylvania candidates for the United States Senate, and it was a portrait of demcracy the way democracy is supposed to be.  Seventeen ordinary citizens questioned Arlen Specter and Lynn Yeakel about three central issues: education, health care and the economy.

headline: Pittsburgh/State digest
abstract: A brief compilation of what's happening in the Pittsburgh area: Rep. Karen Ritter proposes to update sexual assault laws, senior citizens with limited incomes will benefit from a law that will eliminate part of widow's tax, and Gov. Casey unveiled that legislation would ban out-of-state trash and shipping garbage to other states.

headline: The people's parks
abstract: If council approves, city government will stop being the obstacle and start becoming the organizer of citizen efforts to improve 863 parklets, playgrounds and ballfields around Pittsburgh.

headline: Albany Seeks More Money for Child Health Insurance
abstract: Child Health Plus, a program that began last year, provides insurance for primary and preventive health care at low or no cost for poor children up to the age of 13.  Governor Mario Cuomo and the Democrats who control the Assembly now want to double the program's budget by passing legislation that would allow them to raid the state's Bad Debt and Charity Care pool.

headline: Lesson learned- Plan ensures UC Fund's solvency
abstract: There is a new plan for a tax that will keep the Unemployment Compensation Trust Fund in the black.

headline: Waste sheds- State would limit imported trash
abstract: The Casey Administration made Pennsylvania the first major state to adopt a trash recycling program, called a 'waste shed,' where PA is self-sufficient of properly disposing all the waste the region produces internally.  In promoting this self-sufficiency, the plan seeks to exclude trash coming in from other states.  Although it will reduce the energy employed in the transportation of garbage, legal challenges are faced.  It may violate the 'interstate-commerce clause' of the US Constitution, but may also be discluded from the clause as garbage isn't a commodity in the usual sense.

headline: Police see more cases of hate crime in Pa.
abstract: Violence based on a victim's race, religion, ethnic background or sexual preference jumped 60 percent in Pennsylvania last year, according to a report released by the Attorney General's Office.

headline: The gift of thrift
abstract: Emma Chappell, who found enough money from investors to start the United Bank of Philadelphia, discusses current issues in banking and the economy. Her bank represents the first time an African American community has pulled together and opened up their own financial institution since the early 1900's.

headline: Democrat Casey gets GOP plug on abortion stance
abstract: Governor Casey didn't get to the podium at the Democratic convention in New York, be he made it at the Republican Convention- at least in name.

headline: Plot against Specter?
abstract: The Inquirer's May 7 story on Senator Arlen Specter was absolutely incomprehensible, looking as if it deliberately meant to injure Specter.  While the story says that Senator Specter "faced potential criminal liability," it did not quote how the lawyers had no information that he did anything illegal.  How can the inquirer justify that omission?

headline: Township with 57,000 residents will finally be put on the map
abstract: State cartographers will finally put the town of Bensalem, which is north of Philadelphia, on the official transportation map in April of 1993.  The town has 57,000 residents, several major highways, and two shopping malls, yet has been excluded from the map for nearly 300 years.

headline: Bill must contain health care costs
abstract: Governor Casey is right in taking a stand against rising health care costs in his support of a House bill setting limits on medical care fees for workers' compensation cases.

headline: Lives Once Solid as Steel Shatter in Changed World
abstract: About 2,000 workers were laid off when USX stopped making steel at Fairless Works, and now they must cope not only with a grinding recession but also a post-industrial society that often treats laid-off industrial workers as if they were factory rejects.

headline: Waste unit foes given tips
abstract: Three dozen opponents of a hazardous-waste incinerator in Union County received pointers last night from the Allenwood Fire Company on how to break the law without getting into serious trouble.  The lessons in civil disobedience were arranged by Organizations United for the Environment, a citizens' group that claims 17,000 members.

headline: Police seize house
abstract: A house, barn and 2.1 acres of land in this township will be the first property in Schuylkill County to be seized and auctioned off because of drug violations.  The property, which belongs to Rodney and Deborah Fidler, will be sold at a public auction.

headline: The lonely struggle of a North Philadelphia business
abstract: In the midst of all the failure in clothing-based manufacturers in Philadelphia, Richard Seitchik's business, W. Seitchik and Sons, business is booming.  However, the placement of the factory in a dangerous community with high taxes, makes the business less than ideal.

headline: Democratic Governor Urges Pro-Life in Party Platform
abstract: Democratic Governor Robert P. Casey lectured at Notre Dame Law School, saying that millions of Democrats believe their party's dead wrong on abortion.  They refuse to knuckle under to the party line.  Gov. Casey cited exit polls from the 1988 elections.

headline: Political Talk
abstract: Sidney Blumenthal, writing for the New Republic, stated, "Perot seems to be able to do everyhting because he is not a politician; Clinton can't do anything because he is."

headline: Cunningham takes his TV show into really fearsome territory
abstract: Randall Cunningham, Eagles quarterback, traveled to Graterford Prison to tape his weekly television show.  The tough guys that Randall came face to face with were chosen by prison authorities for their leadership in sports activities.

headline: Blue Cross enlists Keystone in new managed-care push
abstract: In response to fierce competition from other insurers and the demand by employers for more tightly controlled health care plans, Blue Cross of Western Pennsylvania and Pennsylvania Blue Shield are planning to use a health maintenance organization as a subcontractor to deliver services for future members of a new insurance plan.

headline: Miners protest PCA decision at Tunnelton
abstract: Members of Local 1378, United Mine Workers of America, were  holding informational demonstrations today at the local branch office of the Pittsburgh National Bank and at the Greensburg PNB office, near the Westmoreland Mall on Route 30.

headline: Waste unit pins delay on wording
abstract: Citing "terminology" snags, Cumberland County Solid Waste Authority is delaying action on a $1.4 million option to buy a Silver Spring Twp. Site for a trash-transfer and composting station.

headline: Police, fire budgets supported
abstract: Police and fire commissioners told City Council that their proposed budgets were adequate but left little room for further deductions.

headline: The USA's most troubled banks
abstract: For the third year, USA TODAY analyzed the financial shape of the nation's banks and savings banks.  Listed are the 375 banks that fail one key measure of finanical health: their problem assets exceed their capital and reserves for loan losses.

headline: Democrats Can't Hide Cultural Liberalism
abstract: Media conglomerate Jeff Greenfield thinks he has an explanation for why Bill Clinton needed 53 minutes to accept the Democratic nomination.  What he had to do, opined Greenfield, was to pre-empt every charge the Republicans might subsequently throw at him.  But the spirit of the new moral wave within the Demcoratic Party can't be concealed behind a 53 minute speech.

headline: Political telegraph alive with scenarios on who may fill spot on county board
abstract: The county treasurer, a former commissioner and the county sheriff are among the names being mentioned to replace Maryann D. Conway on the Schuylkill County Board of Commissioners if she becomes county judge.

headline: Fantastic e-e-e-lastic
abstract: Bungee jumping was an ancient rite of passage by the aborigines of New Guinea.  Modern-day bungee jumping caught on when jumpers leaped off the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco.

headline: Blue Cross Strives to Regain Fiscal Health
abstract: With Blue Cross plans all over the country in financial trouble, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of New Jersey is fighting to regain the financial health it enjoyed until the 1980's, when changes in the state's system of payin gfor health care, combined with an explosion in expensive medical technology, threatened to bankrupt the insurer.

headline: N.E. Philadelphia accident leaves 1 dead, 7 sick
abstract: A worker was killed and seven other men were hospitalized last night after what police called an industrial accident at Mrs. Paul's Kitchens in Northeast Philadelphia.

headline: Water levels below normal at Kutztown Borough wells
abstract: In a Kutztown borough well the water level is down about 4 feet from its normal level and 6 feet lower than last year at this time, prompting Kutztown officials to publicly remind residents to conserve and cut back on water usage.

headline: Possible drug links probed as third body found
abstract: The body of a man was found yesterday in Highspire- the third victim in as many days whose death may have been tied to illicit drugs.  The other two deaths- both attributed to gunshots- have been ruled homicides.

headline: Timing of Damascus sale is 'uncertain'
abstract: The sale of Damascus Tubular Division of Sharon Steel Corp. is one of the conditions placed by the Pennsylvania School Employees Retirement System in lending Sharon Steel $30 million.

headline: Democrats dissent, to Clinton's chagrin
abstract: For a couple of hours Bill Clinton's tightly scripted-for-TV "Conformity Convention" was threatening to turn into a rowdy Animal House.  No doubt Clinton's steering the train- and some passengers are raising nervous hell.

headline: Politics aside, Hamilton's top VP pick
abstract: If you could simply hire a President instead of electing one, Representative Lee Hamilton of Indiana could be a top choice.  He could certainly do the job; it's the political campaign to get it that does him in.  If Clinton wants him, Hamilton is there.

headline: Fort Hunter steps back in time for a spot of tea
abstract: A dozen Hampden Township Junior Girl Scouts yesterday donned their gest dresses and manners to attend a formal "Victorian Tea" at the Fort Hunter Mansion.  The Girl Scouts were accompanied by 150 other tea guests.

headline: Bucks County bars begin stocking free condoms to promote AIDS discussions
abstract: Bowls containing a colorful assortment of condoms at the Great American Grill in Kitnersville are the hallmark of a group Cliff Ruebner, bar owner, formed six months ago called the Council for AIDS Awareness and Education.  The group has stocked three other bars with free condoms and hopes to expand to 11 more.

headline: No Daily Papers Means Bad News for Pittsburgh
abstract: Pittsburgh, In this city of 370,000, residents have been living without their two daily newspapers since May 17, when the 627 drivers who deliver them walked off the job amid a bitter labor dispute, forcing the morning Post-Gazette and the evening Press to stop publishing.

headline: Water rates rising for Beaver Falls customers
abstract: Beaver Falls Municipal Authority customers will have to look past the immense rainfall over the past couple months to understand why water rates will be increased 3 percent this month.  Authority Manager Norman Van Dyke said the Aug. 20 rate increase was prompted by a lack of rainfall in the first quarter of the year.

headline: Preate's drug-arrest data questioned
abstract: In announcing his bid for re-election, Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. boasted of his success in the war on drugs.  But his claims of increased drug arrests have been questioned by potential challengers, perhaps prompting a war of statistics.

headline: Troubled Md. Insurer Ousts Three Officials
abstract: Blue Cross-Blue Shield of Maryland, struggling to repair its image with regulators and congressional investigators after losing $120 million on its subsidiaries, dismissed three high-ranking executives, including the insurer's second highest officer an dits chief financial officer.

headline: Democrats for top state offices plunk funds into television ads
abstract: Democratic candidates for attorney general and auditor general are converting campaign contributions into tv exposure, hoping to broadcast their messages into Pennsylvania living rooms.

headline: Poll has Singel leading Colville
abstract: A recent poll conducted for Lt. Gov. Mark Singel's US Senate campaign showed  him leading his chief opponent, Allegheny County District Attorney Bob Colville, by nearly a 2-1 margin.  Singel got 40 percent and Collville 22 percent, while 38 percent were undecided.

headline: Ginny Thornburgh's continuing career
abstract: It comes as something of a surprise to learn that Dick Thornburgh and his popular, almost unvelievably sweet-natured wife are currently struggling with one of those thoroughly modern long-distance relationships, with their home being in Pittsburgh, and Dick being in Washington, DC.

headline: Bush health plan: Access for all
abstract: An interview with HHS Secretary Louis Sullivan shows that the USA faces tremendous problems if it doesn't act now on health-care reform.  Sullivan also gives the US a health-care report card and Sen. Lloyd Bentsen comments on Pres. Bush's proposal on health care.

headline: No gains seen in USAir talks
abstract: USAir and representatives of its ground-crew workers met separately with federal mediators yesterday, the third day of a strike by 8,300 members of the International Association of Machinists.  No progress was reported.

headline: Wetlands work earns awards
abstract: Two employees of the state Department of Environmental Resources, Larry Oliver and Michael Tarconish, have been granted the 1992 Pennsylvania Interagency Wetlands Enforcement Award.

headline: Prison getting a face-lift
abstract: Lewisburg Federal Penitentiary is a maximum-security institution with nearly 1,400 inmates.  $35 million will be spent to renovate portions of the prison.

headline: Unhealthy games
abstract: For Pennsylvania's workers and leaders of tomorrow- its children- there was some good news and some bad news last week.  Governor Casey announced that insurance carrriers in the state would be required to cover childhood shots, but the state Senate delayed passage of a modest plan  to cover some the state's vast number of uninsured children.

headline: Democrats form state chapter
abstract: The organization that fed Democcrat Bill Clinton most of his campaign ideas- the Democratic Leadership Council- now has a Pennsylvania chapter.

headline: Polls
abstract: Polls are given showing Clinton, Bush and Perot's placings from sources Washington Post-ABC, New York Daily News/The Hotline and CBS News.

headline: Going for the gold at Hershey
abstract: Five of the eight teams representing Eastern Pennsylvania in the state championship basketball tournament at the Hersheypark Arena are Capitol region teams.

headline: Bush plan: Little change
abstract: President Bush's plan to fix the nation's health-care system, at 93 pages, includes 20 existing private-sector proposals.  The plan's greatest weakness is the lack of a firm idea of how to pay for it.

headline: Overtime pay soars, official's report shows
abstract: The amount of overtime Lycoming County paid to employees has more than tripled in three years.  County Controller David C. Raker said some of the increase can be attributed to the commissioners' decision to pay double time and a half to those who work holidays.  Previously, they received time and a half.

headline: Who's afraid of toxic waste?
abstract: Mid-American Waste Systems Inc. has acquired land adjacent to its Valley Landfill along the Pennsylvania Turnpike in Penn Township, even though the property is known to contain buried drums of hazardous waste.

headline: Prison will house aobut 1,600
abstract: The state correctional institution at Clearfield is called a 1,000-cell facility, but according to Ben Livingood, spokesman for the Department of Corrections, the facility will house from 1,500 to 1,600 prisoners.

headline: Vartan leaves legacy of sharing good fortune with noble causes
abstract: John O. Vartan, a business maverick and a developer who has amassed some 500 properties, announced that he had decided to pull up stakes in the city an dmove to Princeton, NJ.  In his wake, he leaves behind a sizable record of charitable giving.

headline: Democrats' Health-Care Debate Resolved Little But Focused on Anger on Flaws in Current System
abstract: A Democratic debate on health care reform focused rather on angry attacks of the current system rather than on specific plans.  The moderator, Senator John Rockefeller insists that he isn't worried that presidential candidates haven't yet found their clearest voice on the subject.  He claims that the debates are helping the candidates gain confidence to take on President Bush on the issue and, "Public anger is our greatest ally."

headline: Poor Excuses
abstract: The poor are receiving very little attention in this year's presidential election, and the candidates must address issues concerning the poor.

headline: In the Flyers' bid for Eric Lindros, the dollars make sense
abstract: With seeming disregard for all reason, two hocky clubs are now clamoring to spend up to $20 million just for the right to negotiate with Eric Lindros, a 19-year-old who has never skated a big-league shift.  That is more than any sports team has ever paid another for a player.

headline: Bush's plan to omit specific financing
abstract: President Bush, seeking to avoid what an aide called "a lot of slings and arrows," will omit a specific financing plan for the health care proposal he will unveil.  Instead he will suggest some "examples" of how the program can be paid for and call on Congress to choose among them or offer its own ideas.

headline: Pay equity gap smallest in state, local govt.
abstract: In government as well as in private industry, men continue to earn considerably more than women for jobs of similar skills and responsibilities.  But the gap in state and local government is substantially smallerthan it is in the private sector or the federal government.

headline: Wrap it up with three R's
abstract: Environmental concerns needn't be abandoned in the bustle of the holiday season.  Remember your three R's when you wrap presents: recycled, recyclable and reusable gift wrap and trim.

headline: Prisoners in peril
abstract: In a U.S. Supreme Court ruling of cruel and unusual punishment in a case where a prisoner was beaten by a prison guard while the supervisor watched, two justices dissented. They justify their opinions by saying that the resulted injury was not "serious" and that the Eighth Amendment protects agains cruel and unusual punishment in the terms of sentences and other formal penalties.

headline: Wal-Mart to announce site for warehouse, distribution center
abstract: Wal-Mart Inc. will announce the site for a warehouse and distribution center either in Spring Township or in Clearfield County that will employ about 450 people initially.

headline: Democrats here out-registering Republicans 5-1
abstract: In what could turn out to be a major boost to the political fortunes of Governor Bill Clinton and his ticket, Democrats are out-registering Republicans in Philadelphia by a ratio of more than 5-1.

headline: Preate and Kohn trade attacks in a taped TV debate
abstract: The candidates for state attorney general attacked each other's record and aspirations during a taped-for-TV debate yesterday in which the most common refrain from both was: "That's not true."

headline: It's a real fight to get this scene filmed
abstract: The Battle of Gettysburg flared again yesterday and, from the looks of things, it was a shutout for the Confederacy.  As they did 129 years ago, thousands of Confederate troops led by General George E. Pickett marched across an open field an dup the slopes of Cemetery Ridge.  The scene was part of the filming of the Turner Network Television miniseries, "The Killer Angels."

headline: Cardinal O'Connor in hospital
abstract: Cardinal John O'Connor, leader of New York's Roman Catholic Archdiocese, fell ill at a political dinner Thursday and was rushed to the hospital, where he was admitted for tests.

headline: Press unions keep hat in ring with proposed funding
abstract: The International Brotherhood of Teamsters, along with other unionized workers at the Pittsburgh Press, said it wants to join in a financial venture with potential buyers of the strike-bound daily newspaper.

headline: Wright Says Concord Trying To Thwart Him
abstract: State Representative David R. Wright said Concord Resources Group is trying to thwart his request that he be allowed to testify in support of the state Department of Environmental Resources' rejection last month of the firm's Phase I siting permit application.

headline: Prisons ordered to institute TB policy
abstract: US District court Judge Jan E. DuBois ordered the state prison system to put into effect its new policy against tuberculosis, examining inmates and guards on a regular basis for the disease.

headline: Washington Steel reorganization is a first
abstract: Because US Enterprise Corp. agreed to sell its sole operating company, Washington Steel Corp., the company came out of the court proceedings with expanded credit and with roughly the same amount of bank debt it had going in.

headline: Democrats open shop for ticket
abstract: Officials at ribbon-cutting for Luzerne county Clinton/Gore headquarters talk of delivering victories in November races.

headline: Preschool screening impresses Mrs. Casey
abstract: Ellen Casey took time Friday morning to learn about the preschool screening process conducted as a group effort by four Mercer County agencies.  The screening is a prevenative concept designed to pick up problems that may inhibit development in the early stages when the problems are more easily corrected.

headline: Jumps for chumps?
abstract: Plunging 60 mph from a 15-story height is not for the faint of heart.  It may also not be good for your health, as bungee jumping could dislocate joints, stretch and tear ligaments and cause traction injuries.  Spinal injuries may result, and the fear can result in a panic attack.  Still, the fear of physical danger is the allure of bungee jumping.

headline: Casey hails passage of health-care plan
abstract: After two years of tough negotiations on a landmark heath insurance plan, thousands of poor Pennsylvania children soon can afford to get sick.  The House passed a children's health insurance plan that its author promises will be studied and duplicated in other states.

headline: Publication could begin by mid-June
abstract: The unions affected by the strike against the Pittsburgh Press Co. may begin their own newspaper.  As editions of the Allegheny Bulletin, the strike-prompted paper produced by the Press, reach area mailboxes, local union officials have called on an experienced publisher to plan their own newspaper.

headline: WTI incinerator debated on national TV
abstract: Citizens fighting the Waste Technologies Industries incinerator in East Liverpool took on the US Environmental Protection Agency on national television overnight.

headline: Probe continues into shooting of 2 police officers
abstract: State police last night had no new information about a shooting on Monday that left two borough police officers wounded and a 20-year-old man dead after he opened fire on them in a borough alley.

headline: Weekend visitors like city, poll shows
abstract: Pittsburgh's sports teams, tourist attractions and shopping give it regional appeal to tourists.  The Greater Pittsburgh Convention & Visitors Bureau conducted the survey to examine visitors' attitudes about Pittsburgh and to determine the effectiveness of the bureau's weekend advertising program.  The study also found thatmost weekend visitors find Pittsburgh affordable, friendly and to be a good family destination.

headline: Democrats pour it on in auditor general race
abstract: With only four days to go before Pennsylvania voters cast their primary ballots, the Democratic race for the state auditor general nomination is a maad dash around the state.

headline: Preserve the Crime Commission Or Lose Vital Line of Defense
abstract: As commissioners appointed to the Pennsylvania Crime Commission by the governor and our legislative leaders of the House and Senate, the public and our lawmakers should carefully reconsider the budget that was recently passed by the House of Representatives.  The House budget puts the Crime Commission out of business.

headline: Liberty Bell history
abstract: The recent letter about the Liberty Bell fails to inform the readers that the bell never ahd true historical importance after it was installed in 1752.  The real emblem of the Revolution was the traditional red liberty cap (worn as a freedman's badge in ancient Greece and Rome), as many contemporary drawings and paintings prove.

headline: Companies join to cut high health-care costs
abstract: Across the county, the American Hospital Association counts 140 business coalitions on health care using their buying clout to reduce costs and improve quality.

headline: Roofers Local 30-30B to pay $350,000 fine
abstract: A federal appeals court has ordered Roofers Local 30-30B to pay $350,000 in contempt-of-court fines for illegal picketing in 1989 and for intimidation of dissident members seeking union office in 1987.  The order was the result of an agreement between the union and government officials on how to punish the union's violations of court orders dating back to 1978.

headline: WTI plant is a threat to area
abstract: Thanks to Dr. Robert C. Knapp for his efforts to help bring attention to Beaver County's plight with the Waste Technologies Industries plant.

headline: Probers tied to falsifying of evidence
abstract: Two key investigators in the Susan Reinert murder investigation were accused of fabricating evidence at an unrelated murder scene just months before the Reinert case began.  The inverstigators were accused of planting fingerprints at the scen of the murder of Helen Elizabeth Horn, who was found beaten and strangled to death in her Gratz home March 22, 1979.

headline: WLR is buying Round Hill Foods
abstract: Round Hill Foods, a turkey-processing operation based in New Oxford, Adams County, is being purchased by WLR Foods Inc. of Hinton, Va., for about $8 million.  The acquisition, expected to be closed Dec. 1, will make WLR Foods the second-largest turkey processor in the nation.

headline: Democrats rally support for candidates
abstract: Democrats cheering on Democrats seemed the purpose of the Hanover Area Democratic Club's annual meeting.  The guest speaker for the evening was Democratic State Rep. Dwight Evans of Philadelphia, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee.

headline: President predicts 'the fight of our life'
abstract: Receiving the Republican nomination yesterday for the second time, George Bush now sets out on a come-from-behind campaign that could restore his political stature or dump him into the history books as a rejected president.  The latest surveys show that Clinton held his lead over Bush through the first two days of the convention, despite a barrage of Republican attacks on the Democratic ticket.

headline: Murphy films in Harrisburg
abstract: A Hollywood crew is in town at Capitol Hill through the weekend to shoot scenes for a new Eddie Murhpy movie- which some say reverses political reality- about a con-man turned congressman.

headline: County might tax hospitals
abstract: Pennsylvania's courts have recently ruled that some hospitals may have to pay real estate taxes.

headline: Senate's version of reform won't help workers' comp
abstract: Leo McDonough's commentary on workers' compensation reform not only misses the point, but it also advocates the notion that a so-called "reform" bill passed last month by the Senate will be anything short of disastrous for all employers in this state.  Controlling health care costs and keeping the insurance industry in check is the path to real reform.  Restricting worker benefits to save premium dollars is pure fantasy.

headline: Yeakel picks up Sierra Club backing
abstract: Democratic US Senate candidate Lynn Yeakel made the comment about how jobs, health care and other top issues won't matter if the nation doesn't stop abusing the environment, after accepting the endorsement of the 18,000 member Pennsylvania chapter of the Sierra Club, one of the nation's top environmental lobbying groups.

headline: Ramona freed, and unMOVEd
abstract: Seven years after the inferno of Osage Avenue, Ramona Africa is a free woman.  The lone adult survivor of the 1985 MOVE blaze in which police bombed he house, killing six adult cult members san dfive of their children, was charged with riot and conspiracy.

headline: Worker bids for machine shop
abstract: Gregory Lunko of Lower Yoder, a 27-year employee of Bethlehem Steel Corp., is currently a buyer handling machine-shop services for Bethlehem's Bar, Rod & Wire Division and soon will be out of a job as the steelmaker phases out the division.  He has asked Bethlehem to sell the machine shop to him.

headline: Democrats See Hope of Taking Ohio From GOP, But Republicans Insist They'll Prevail as Usual
abstract: In election after election, Democrats vow to win on this critical Midwestern battleground of presidential politics.  But each time, the Republicans snatch victory away every time.  The GOP has won Ohio in every presidential election since the Lyndon Johnson landslide of 1964 except when Jimmy Carter took the state in 1976.

headline: Presidential debates running short of time
abstract: Political parties set up a panel to make scheduling easier.  It hasn't.  And there might not be a single debate this year.

headline: Rave: Dancing the night away
abstract: Raving has arrived: a dance-till-dawn phenomenon that started in London two years ago, quickly migrated to Los Angeles, and this summer hit the East Coast hard, including Philadelphia.  Almost by definition, a rave is illegal.  Every weekend, the parties rove from space to space without city dance-hall and alcohol permits.

headline: Democrats Offer a Health-Care Plan
abstract: Seizing the initiative on a politically charged issue, House Democratic leaders unveiled a health care proposal intended to contain costs and insure more than half of the 30 million Americans not covered by health insurance.

headline: Signs spell no strike- now
abstract: The Pennsylvania Labor Relations Board plans to shuffle the deck.  If the board agrees to a municipal union's request for fact-finding, the showdown between Mayor Rendell and labor would be postponed for up to 60 days.

headline: Ambitious energy bill emerges with changes
abstract: The most ambitious federal energy legislation in more than a decade finally emerged from a House-Senate conference early yeasterday, different in important respects from the original version in either chamber but still loaded with novel provisions.

headline: Ramona not the one to talk about justice
abstract: It's horrible enough that five children died and a neighborhood was destroyed in the MOVE debacle: now a lie is being enshrined in its aftermath.  The lie is that Ramona Africa, the only adult survivor of the MOVE fiasco, has credibility to speak about justice; the lie is that Ramona Africa has legitimate credentials to deliver lectures about right and wrong.

headline: Workers' comp rate hike would put jobs at risk at worst possible time
abstract: The Pennsylvania Insurance Commission dropped another bomb on the state's business community by approving a 24 percent rate increase in workers' compensation premiums.  Insurers may profit, but businesses will not.

headline: Democrats slam the opposition at area fund-raiser
abstract: The candidates of the Cambria County Democratic Party gathered with 500 party regulators for a breakfast buffet and to buffet Republicans.  The affair's primary purpose was to unify Democrats behind the endorsed candidates for the April 28 primary.

headline: Prime Time TV
abstract: A brief list of politicians who will be appearing on tv is given.

headline: They make beautiful music together
abstract: For more than 25 years, Roy and Gene Clair have been creating high-volume sound systems for acts from Japan to America in the quiet little farm town of Lititz, PA.

headline: Diverse group to meet on ideas for crisis Rx
abstract: In this election year of discontent, the number of potential solutions to the nation's health-care crisis has been exceeded only by the number of town meetings organized by politicians and television commentors to address the volatile issue of national health care.  This week, the Harrisburg region gets into the fray.

headline: Stalemate predicted in session
abstract: Last year, workers' compensation insurance cost Hampden Twp. Taxpayers a cool $180,000.  If the insurance industry is granted the 52 percent it has requested from the state, the math is enough to give township Manager John Bradley Jr. fits.

headline: Area's Motorists to Get Cleaner, Costlier Gasoline
abstract: Beginning Sunday, the fuel Washinton-area motorists will pump into their cars is going to cost a bit more, give them slightly fewer milers per gallon, and smell and possibly look different from traditional gasoline.  According to federal law, additives that create this new gasoline are required to be blended into gasoline to reduce emission of toxic carbon monoxide.

headline: Rapists and AIDS: The dilemma over testing
abstract: The National Victim Center conducted a survey where rape-crisis counselors nationally found that fear of "getting HIV," the human immunodeficiency virus that casues AIDS, is now the fastest growing concern among rape victims.  In 1990, Congress passed a law that tells states: Either enact mandatory testing for convicted rapists by the end of next year or lose some federal aid.

headline: Appropriations Panel Votes to Cut 10,000 Naval Jobs
abstract: The House Appropriations Committee, angered by the Navy's handling of an investigationof sexual assaults during a Navy and Marine aviators' convention last year, voted to eliminate 10,000 positions from Navy headquarters, twice the number it had originally considered cutting.

headline: Democrats suffer a setback in Senate
abstract: Republican Paul Coverdell's narrow victory over US Senator Wyche Fowler Jr. in a Georgia runoff election has dashed Democratic hopes of increasing the party's majority in the Senate.

headline: Privatizing services: Easier said than done
abstract: Having made privatization a major theme in his campaign last year, Mayor Rendell is trying to privatize as many as 20 city services at projected savings of almost $30 million a year.  To date, he hasn't succeeded in privatizing anything, although it hasn't been for lack of trying.

headline: TV stations characterize cartoons as educational
abstract: It might seem like an ordinary television cartoon, but the Saturday morning adventures of Bucky O'Hare, a rabbit in space who fights alien toads with guns and lasers, is in fact "educational and informational," according to what a New Orleans television stateion WGNO told federal regulators as it documented its efforts to comply with the Children's Television Act.

headline: Doctors with AIDS keep lethal secret
abstract: A request for federal lawmakers was given by a dying woman: Require that physicians and dentists regularly test for AIDS, and restrict those who are infected from performing invasive medical procedures.  The National Commission on AIDS declared that it sees no reason why AIDS-infected medical professionals should restrict their practice.

headline: Taco Bell work to start
abstract: Construction of a Taco Bell drive-through restaurant is set to begin at the site of the former Hill Financial office at 32nd and Market streets in Camp Hill.  The restaurant will create about 30 full-time and part-time jobs.

headline: Coal association opposed to Tunnelton coal sales
abstract: The Pennsylvania Coal Association is objecting to a request by Pennsylvania Power & Light Co. for a non-appealable order form the Public Utility Commission that would permit the Allentown-based utility company to purchase coal from the new owner of the Tunnelton Mining Co. when the mine resumes production.

headline: Rash of slayings plagues York police
abstract: A recent slaying of a 19-year old mother and her 7-month-old girl bring February's total to 4, following the murder of a 19-year-old pregnant woman whose unborn child died with her.  Another killing of a 22-year-old woman and her unborn child was discovered on Feb. 8.  York police are alarmed at the spurt of violence in their community.

headline: Billionaire's commitment to 'people we left behind'
abstract: Several people commend the billionaire Ross Perot for his dedication to Prisoners of War.

headline: Democrats' taxing ways
abstract: According to Clinton and Gore's way of thinking, President Bush is solely responsible for everyhting that has happened in this country in the past three-plus years.  If this were so, we have to assume that the Democratic-controlled Congress merely rubber-stamps everything the president wants.

headline: Public interest group shows PAC contributions growing in House
abstract: Off-year election contributions to House members from political action committees grew by 22 percent in 1991 from the off-year of 1989.  And a majority of members seeking re-election got more than half of their money from the special interest groups, said a study released by the public interest group Common Cause, which opposes the donations.

headline: Utah wins title of 'Most Livable State' while Pennsylvania comes in at No. 30
abstract: Utah won the title of America's 'Most Livable State' because of its educated citizens and low taxes, simply having what people and companies are looking for.  Pennsylvania was rated 30th.

headline: Elderly abuse a concern
abstract: Doctors should routinely ask elderly patients if they are being abused or neglected, and most physicians will find some who are, the American Medical Association says.

headline: Truckers gear up for strike
abstract: Freight railroads shut down today coast-to-coast and Amtrak stopped passenger service except through the Boston-to-Washington corridor after the Machinists union went on strike against CSX Transportation.  The dispute involves unions representing about 20,000 carmen, engineers, dispatchers, machinists and other employees.

headline: County won't rush power line stance
abstract: The Beaver County Commissioners listened for about an hour Thursday afternoon before quieting supporters and opponents of a proposed 268-mile high-voltage power line.

headline: Recession's cost: Lives
abstract: The economy may be killing us.  A study out today says a poor economy in 30 selected cities is responsible for more murders, more deaths from stroke and more fatal heart disease.  Another report blames the recession for 1,170 more suicides in the USA.

headline: Gekas wins Army vow to guard Gap ammo
abstract: Guards have again been posted around the clock at the ammo supply area in Fort Indiantown Gap that houses tons of ammunition, rockets and plastic explosives, after an agreement was hammered out yesterday between Army officials and US Representative George W. Gekas.

headline: Dems at Senate helm
abstract: Democrats seized control of the state Senate yesterday in a stunning turnaround that makes six Philadelphia senators committee chairmen and gives the Dems total control of the Legislature.  Without public warning, Senator Frank Pecora switched allegiance from Republicans to Democrats and supported a series of Democrattic-run votes to oust GOP leaders.

headline: PUC figure accused of influencing power vote
abstract: Robert Sugarman, a Philadelphia attorney, wants Public Utility Commissioner Joseph Rhodes Jr. to disqualify himself from the biggest power-line case in state history, alleging Rhodes discussed the matter with governor Robert P. Casey on the eve of a crucial PUC vote.

headline: Vincent calls himself out
abstract: Commissioner of baseball Fay Vincent yesterday bowed to the pressure and requests of 18 team owners by resigning effective immediately, thereby completing three turbulent years in office.

headline: Encouraging statistics on breast cancer
abstract: Breast cancer is the disease most women fear most.  But new findings described this month in The Journal of the National Cancer Institute paint a much more optimistic picture.

headline: Union swaps 101 jobs for modernizing
abstract: Union members at Bethlehem Steel Corp.'s Steelton plant have voted by a 3-to-1 margin to sacrifice wage increases for two years an dgive up 101 jobs in exchange for more than $70 million worth of new plant equipment.

headline: Cutbacks put pressure on heating aid for poor
abstract: 70,000 people in Philadelphia, and 500,000 statewide, are expected by state officials to seek help from the program to pay for gas or oil, to pay their electric bill, or to get their heaters working.  This winter's budget for assistance, though, is 21 percent less than last year's.

headline: Recreation director is a man of the people
abstract: Philadelphia Recreation Commissioner Michael DiBerardinis explains how his department can make a difference in the lives of the city's children.  He is unswerving in the blief that the Recreation Department can help prevent and defuse such volatile conflicts- and, with the help of communities, improve the city itself.

headline: Harsco to merge its defense unit with FMC's
abstract: Harsco Corp., a Camp Hill company that makes combat vehicles, said it had agreed to merge its defense operations with those of FMC Corp.'s Defense Systems Group.  The combined company would have estimated sales of about $1.2 billion in 1993.  Both firms want to curb costs and boost efficiency.  Shrinking defense budgets are driving them to it.

headline: Dems give Singel big edge
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark Singel won the overwhelming endorsement of the Democratic State Committee in his quest for the party's U.S. Senate nomination, despite the lack of support from Gov. Robert Casey.

headline: Quayle attacks 'cultural elites'
abstract: Vice President Quayle invoked the "family values" theme in attacking "cultural elites" in Hollywood and the media who "think fathers are dispensable and parents don't have to be married or even of the opposite sex."  He said, "To appeal to our country's enduring, basic moral values is to invite the scorn and laughter of the elites culture- I wear that scorn as a badge of honor."

headline: Expanded medical coverage proposed
abstract: Representative Roy Reinard, a Bucks County lawmaker, has proposed legislation that could allow some Pennsylvanians to join the state's Medicaid program for long-term health care without first having to deplete their assets.

headline: Union workers labor along beneath the city's ax
abstract: Since May 15, the Rendell administration has sent out a stream of formal letters to various local swithin the city's white-collar and blue-collar unions, warning that the city is "contemplating" contracting out jobs, and more letters are coming.

headline: Energy policy is going backward
abstract: For the first time in recent history, energy is a front-burner issue on Capitol Hill.  Unfortunately, a number of bills in Congress threaten to move the nation's energy policy backward rather than forward.

headline: Rockwell pleads guilty to 10 counts
abstract: Rockwell International Corp. pleaded guilty to 10 criminal counts of hazardous-waste violations while it ran the Rocky Flats nuclear weapons plant.

headline: Navy facility to get new chief
abstract: Captain Richard D. Vroman, currently serving as director of the Supply Corps Detail Division in the Bureau of Naval Personnel in Washington, DC, will return to Pennsylvania to assume command of the Navy Fleet Material Support Office in Hampden Township.

headline: Departing politicians reveal plans
abstract: As the last days of the legislative session have finally ticked away, a group of lawmakers- Republicans and Democrats- are turning their attention from packing amendments into proposed legislation to packing their bags.

headline: Quayle labels Democrat ticket
abstract: Vice President Dan Quayle's top aide siad that the Democratic ticket of Bill Clinton and Al Gore is "McGovernism with a Southern face."  William Kristol, Quayle's chief of staff, was referring to the failed 1972 Democratic ticket headed by liberal George McGovern.

headline: Filling Health Care Gaps
abstract: Overcoming fierce resistance from segments of the state's medical community, the Minnesota Legislature has enacted the most far-reaching legislation in the country to expand access to health care insurace for hundreds of thousands of its citizens.

headline: Weis Markets Granted Permanent Injuction Limiting Union Protest
abstract: The picketers at Weis Markets on River Avenue may continue to picket as long as they stay in the two parking spaces nar the front of the store. County Judge Clinton W. Smith has ruled.  Although Local 23 of the United Food and Commercial Workers' Union will abide by the judge's decision, "We think it is absolutely wrong, and will challenge the error," Peter Marks, local president, said during a telephone interview.

headline: Expedited PUC step is denied
abstract: More than a year after the application for a 268-mile power line was filed, the state Public Utility Commission yesterday voted not to review the proposal on an expedited basis.

headline: Rodney King issues plea for an end to violence
abstract: Police stepped up arrests of looters, arsonists slowed their fiery rampage and residents of charred communities struggled to get food yesterday, the thrid day of rioting that killed at least 35 people.  Rodney King, the man whose videotapedbeating touched off the worst US rioting since 1968, made an anguished plea for peace.

headline: POW-MIA activists protest; Bush tells them to 'shut up'
abstract: Several dozen angry relatives of American servicemen missing in Southeast Asia shouted down President Bush yesterday as he addressed a convention of POW-MIA activists, prompting the perturbed chief executive to tell the protesters to "shut up and sit down."

headline: DeWeese's tourism panel clips 'award'
abstract: The Pennsylvania Leadership Council has bestowed one of its highest honors on House Speaker-elect H. William DeWeese, who wants to boost the travel and tourism industry in the state by creating a new House Committee of Travel and Recreation.  The council doesn't much like the notion and has named DeWeese as the winner of this year's Golden Paperclip Award.

headline: Quiet Convention?
abstract: Democrats, usually gearing up about now for free-for-alls on the floor of the convention, are predicting a relatively smooth four nights in New York City next month.

headline: Florio Offers Plan to Pay Health Costs
abstract: Facing a 30-day deadline for changing the way New Jersey pays for its uninsured residents' health coverage, Governor Jim Florio today proposed subsidizing private healthcare groups like health maintenance organizations to cover those residents.  But Mr. Florio left it to legislators to find a way to pay for the new coverage.

headline: Worker's comp
abstract: Without a doubt, the best way to reform Pennsylvania's bloated and unwieldy worker's compensation system would be to chuck the whole thing and start from scratch. Unfortunately, that would not be practical.  What Pennsylvania needs is a law that would control costs, end abuses and streamline the system.

headline: Fairview meeting scheduled
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission, responding to complaints afrom York County residents and at least one elected official, has agreed to hold a public hearing in Fairview Township on a controversial power line project.

headline: Scrambling brings problems
abstract: After Harrisburg officials began using police scramblers, many citizens are upset and feel like they're in the dark and traffic information is impossible to find.  Mayor Stephen R. Reed leads the team of police and have begun scrambling every transmission, from felonies in progress to the location of malfunctioning traffic signals.

headline: Retooling for Peace
abstract: The nation's defense acquisition budget, which peaked at more than $90 billion a year in the mid-1980s, is down to $54 billion in fiscal 1993.  Congress and the Pentagon already have agreed to delay, scale back or completely scrap some big-ticket hardware items.

headline: Dick's Next Step
abstract: Could Dick Thornburgh make it again?  Pittsburghers have been wondering ever since the former governor lost the election to Harris Wofford.

headline: Race for the statehouse
abstract: The governor's race in Washington, featuring an unabashedly liberal former congressman and an arch-conservative state attorney general, best illustrates the stark contrasts facing voters in the 12 states with 1992 gubernatorial elections.

headline: Funds delay freezes AIDS services
abstract: In Lancaster County, where the incidence of AIDS has risen 427 percent since 1988, the only public agency providing AIDS services is operating in a budget-crisis mode.  The Lancaster AIDS Project workers, four months into their fiscal year, are waiting for $61,000 in federal funds, one-third of their total budget.

headline: Workers' Compensation: A caring attitude can reduce costs
abstract: Costs of job injuries doubled, to $70 billion, in the last five years.  But Raytheon says a safety training program cut its accident rate 33% this year.

headline: Foes promise no surrender
abstract: Up and down the proposed route for a 268-mile paower line proposed by General Public Utilities Corp. and Duquesne Light, farmers and professionals, parents and business people, homeowners and developers argue vehemently there is more at stake than a 200-foot corridor.

headline: Secret state report fertile bed of suspicion
abstract: The state Department of Public Welfare should release the report on a four-month investigation it made into Cambria County Children and Youth Services because as long as the report is held from public disclosure, the doubts and suspicions will incubate and grow.

headline: Small Lebanon County firm fears effect of defense cuts
abstract: PRL Inc., a defense contracting company, waits to see how federal budget cuts will affect the company's projects.

headline: Discovering the middle class
abstract: Hypocrisy in both the Democrat and Republican Parties is evident as they only discover the American middle class on an election year.

headline: Read this
abstract: People who rely on television as their major source of political news generally don't vote.

headline: Health Care Giveaway
abstract: Pat Rooney, head of Golden Rule Insurance Co., claims that the reason for America's health care crisis is not that medical care costs too much but that we spend too much on it.  He proposes that if the employer gives each worker an allowance, tells him to shop around and keep the rest, then the cost of medical care would drop.

headline: Workers Keep Union
abstract: Vernango County workers voted by slightly more than two-to-one to retain representation by the Pennsylvania Social Services Union.

headline: Full impact
abstract: Hearings began yesterday in Millersville on a proposed cross-state power line, the outcome of which will have a profound influence on how Pennsylvania meets its electric needs for the 1990s and beyond.

headline: Senate to debate privacy of records in adoption bill
abstract: The debate over how much information adoptees should be able to get about their birth parents is expected to be rekindled as the state Senate handles an adoption bill already passed by the House.

headline: State must prepare for defense plant cuts
abstract: For many years Pennsylvania's defense-related industries have played a key role in developing and building the world's most advanced military hardware.  They have also played a key role in the state and local economies, providing thousands of jobs and generating payrolls worth millions of dollars.  Pennsylvania must act aggressively to help ensure the survival of its defense-related industries.

headline: Doing your primary duty
abstract: Even if you feel like you lose no matter how you vote, you should work past your ennui and get to the polls.  There are a number of interesting and important races this time.

headline: Realpolitics
abstract: A weekly report on Campaign '92 is given, which includes polls on crime and city issues with relation to the presidential candidates.

headline: Health Care Rationing Could Be Approved
abstract: The state of Oregon's controversial plan to set up the nation's most extensive experiment in rationing medical care still has a good chance of approval by the Bush administration, despite criticism in a recent draft report for Congress.

headline: Annenberg Institute, courted from abroad, will stay in Phila.
abstract: Rebuffing approaches from two universities in Israel, officials at a scholarly institute in Philadelphia with a world-renowned collection of religious documents have decided to affiliate with the University of Pennsylvania.  The decision marks an end to independent status for the nonsectarian institution, which was founded in 1907 as Dropsie College and is now known as the Annenberg Institute.

headline: Group backs big power line to aid economy
abstract: Calling it a boost for the state's ailing economy, a group of business and labor leaders will urge construction of a 250-mile power line to carry electricity from coal-fired plants in southwestern Pennsylvania to consumers in Eastern Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

headline: Sensible and overdue
abstract: State Senator Albert Belan's plan to bill lawbreakers for work done at Pennsylvania's crime labs is a great idea.  The surprise is that such an arragnement hasn't already been instituted.  Belan's proposal is sensible.  The early betting is that it will be easily approved- as it should be.

headline: They suspect pills caused aches, bleeding, fatigue
