abstract: At least five Gulf War veterans who served with the 131st Transportation Company of the Pennsylvania National Guard, Williamstown, say they are suffering from medical problems they believe are a result of the war.  Several speculate their illnesses resulted from pills they were told to take as a precaution against chemical warfare.

headline: Don Bailey may seek auditor general post
abstract: Former state AuditorGeneral and ex US Rep. Don Bailey confirmed that he has been circulating nominating petitions to become athe Democratic nominee for state auditor general.

headline: Recollections: Kennedy, Kefauver and me
abstract: Bill Clinton talks about what made him fall in love with American politics and how he is still thrilled by the process nearly 40 years later.

headline: Health care, business killer
abstract: For many small business owners, the cost of health care, not the list of leading economic indicators, is what really determines whether they will survive another year.

headline: null
abstract: Two kids on a swingset are talking about the teacher strike bill, with the teacher's union against state legislators.  They mention how at the same time, these are the guys who want to teach moral values in school.

headline: Last delay for Florence mines
abstract: It will be at least the middle of June before Florence Mining Co. can reopen operations and begin supplying coal to the Conemaugh Generating Station, after having to wait out a 30-day public notice petition.

headline: She has lost the key to open prison doors
abstract: Jeanne D. Bonney spent the last six years helping people get out of jail, working as executive director of the Philadelphia People's Bail Fund.  However, the end came two weeks ago, when she was reassigned to special projects, and therefore, cannot continue to do for prisoners what she was once relentless about.

headline: U.S. 'must act,' Bush tells world
abstract: President Bush, presenting to the United States a military mission that he described as "God's work," said he was dispatching American troops to Somalia to save thousands of innocent people from death by starvation.

headline: Dr. Dennis says take a pol and call him in the morning
abstract: Dr. Dennis is asked questions by politicians and offers advice.  As more of a lampoon, Dennis' article talks about events that had occurred that deal with the politicians' past decisions, and he gives advice that could be viewed as what the people want or just the comment of a smart-alic.

headline: Reconsidering privatization of state government services
abstract: The federal government and an increasing number of state and even local governments are ignoring problems and letting deficits soar.  Privatization is an alternative that an increasing number of governments are going to be considering.  Many of the current functions of state government were successfully handled by private enterprise in the past.

headline: Health Care: The Rhetoric And Reality
abstract: Democratic senators at a news conference blasted President Bush on health care.  Both Bill Clinton's and Bush's plans alter the health industry to make it easier for businesses to buy insurance for people with preexisting medical conditions and for employees to carry their existing insurance with them to a new job.

headline: $63 million school windfall
abstract: In the twilight of President Bush's term, the Department of Education has poured an additional $63 million into the types of programs he was advocating when he took office four years ago as the self-described "education president."

headline: Letter on energy inaccurate
abstract: Joseph Winton's letter on energy contained a number of inaccuracies.

headline: Sixth marijuana suspect is scheduled for hearing
abstract: David Fred Douty faces a preliminary hearing on drug charges stemming from an investigation that led to the seizure of more than 400 pounds of marijuana in Lower Paxton Township.  He was the sixth member of a drug-trafficking ring broken by the Dauphin county Drug Task Force and other area police agencies.

headline: War heroes' home under siege
abstract: Two veterans, who live together in Peach Bottom Township in a group home for US military veterans, might soon have to find a new place.  The township is suing the facility's owners, saying they are operating the place illegally because the land it sits on is zoned for farming, not for something like this.

headline: Economy, ideology: Parties trade places
abstract: In the 1992 election, it appears that the political parties have traded places.  The Democrats are now debating whose economic policy makes the most sense for the largest number of Americans, while the Republicans compete for the favors of the smallest, most ideological wing of their party.

headline: Recovery plan meeting fails to materialize
abstract: The ritualistic meeting between Mayor Jim Connors and Charles W. Watters of the Pennsylvania Economy League, scheduled for Wedensday, never happened because each side was waiting for the other to call.  The simple failure to communicate seemed symbolic of the relationship between the two, which has seen fierce political and legal combat centering about the competing financial recovery plans they have prepared.

headline: Health Council gets boost
abstract: The 30 staff members of the state-run Health Care Cost Containment Center will undoubtedly spend the next four weeks dwelling more on stretch run activities in the legislatrue surrounding the passage of a state spending plan than on the rising cost of health care in state.  Governor Robert Casey has proposed both cutting funds to the six-year-old council and merging its operations into the state Insurance Department.  Such a move would leave as many as 20 staffers without work.

headline: 600 residents vent anger at board
abstract: Armstrong School District directors attemted to conduct a business meeting for more than four hours Monday night, pestered by about 600 screaming residents, unbearable heat and flying gnats in the Jr. High gymnasium.  Discussion could not get past one fundamental issue: whether the school district has the authority to deconsolidate.

headline: More utility cutoff notice urged
abstract: Utilities would have to give hospitals annd nursing homes 37 days' notice before cutting off service, under a measure proposed yesterday by the state Public Utility Commission.

headline: Small victories in war on drugs
abstract: Dealers once owned Fourth and Cambria.  Now the law-abiding have their corner back- and the drug trade has moved a mile away.

headline: Cable bill shows inept Congress
abstract: We have seen, heard or read conflicting advertisements in recent weeks about the impact of the cable regulation bill called "the Cable Television Consumer Protection Act."  Though the legislation passed overwhelmingly in both the House and the Senate, the act was not carried out as it should have been, and instead, special interests stood in the way of passing legislation that would benefit cable TV customers.

headline: Egolf has integrity to be representative in 86th
abstract: Allen Egolf, who is a candidate for state representative, 86th District, and is a man of quality, integrity, and decisiveness.

headline: Redistricting mess stymies Republicans
abstract: Redistricting cases before the state Supreme Court and Legislature are delaying county political decisions and amy hinder timely preparation of April 28 primary ballots.  Until matters are legally resolved, the committee will not meet to choose candidates for local and state offices, Cumberland County Republican Committee Chairman Patricia Saylor says.

headline: Health officials admit error, rescind a PA policy on AIDS
abstract: Pennsylvania health officials said that they were rescinding a new policy requiring drug and alcohol treatment programs to report people suspected of having AIDS.

headline: A bold new goal for schools
abstract: During a visit to Philadelphia, President Bush promoted a plan that would make tax dollars available to pay for private and parochial school tuition.  Last year, the Pennsylvania legislature rejected a form of school choice.

headline: N.J. utility lays plans to plug itself in city
abstract: Atlantic Electric Co. had the idea if it attracted more businesses to South Jersey, it would expand its customer base and help the regional economy at the same time.  The utility company found that many of those companies were just across the Delaware River, and so Atlantic Electric will begin a marketing campaign directed at companies in 25 industries it thinks are a good fit for South Jersey.

headline: Speed Demons
abstract: Four commentaries, in regard to a woman's opinion about a police officer pulling her husband over on Christmas day, each react with different opinions from their own experiences.  One sympathizes with the woman who felt that the cop was unjust, while the other three find the patrolman to be correct in his issuance of a traffic violation.

headline: Cable TV rates unlikely to fall
abstract: Cable company officials say not to expect a decrease in monthly bills, despite Congress passing legislation this week allowing government re-regulation of the industry.  In fact, several companies said, expect an increase.

headline: Ellwood Forge waits on OK for move
abstract: Elwood City Forge wants to move its finish machining crankshaft division to Hermitage, and the only thing it's waiting for is the approval of that Mercer County city's officials.

headline: 'Region 2000'
abstract: President Bush's 1989 Summit contained six goals with two ingrediants to ensure success: leadership and broad-based community involvement.  Translating the goals to workable plans is proving a challenge.

headline: Health officials expect test results in meningitis case
abstract: Several students at Edinboro University have contracted meningitis, an inflammation of membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.

headline: A bridge from the street to stage
abstract: Abigail Adams, the associate artistic director at People's Light and Theater Company, and her students are conducting an experiment called the Chester Project.  It aims to find out what can happen when teenagers from dying neighborhoods meet the lively art of theater, when they move from hanging out under street lights to performing behind footlights.

headline: National Fuel Seeks Rate Hike
abstract: National Fuel Gas has filed for a purchased gas cost increase which would raise the typical residential customer's bill by about 8.5 percent.  The utility is blaming recent rapid increases of natural gas prices as well.

headline: State official: City facing racial violence
abstract: The gravity of racial tension in Allentown and its potential for violence has prompted the Governor's Advisory Commission on Latino Affairs to convene its first-ever hearing, commission Executive Director Lillian Escobar-Haskins said.

headline: Caller ID violates law, court rules
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court said that Caller ID- the service that lets subscribers see the phone number of an incoming call- would violate the state Wiretap Act "and cannot now be offered in Pennsylvania."

headline: End Attained, Clinton Mutes Talk of Middle-Class Tax Cut
abstract: The saga of Arkansas Governor Bill Clinton's middle-class tax cut is an instructive story of politics and economics and how the two intersect in a presidential campaign.

headline: Registration Deadline Set Monday For Election
abstract: Monday is the lst day to register before the November 3 general election.  Eligible voters must re-register at the county courthouse if they have not voted at least once during the preceding two years.

headline: Health panel approves two bills
abstract: The House Health and Welfare Committee approved legislation that would improve health care in rural and inner-city areas, and partially forgive student loans for Pennsylvania doctors who work in those areas.

headline: A heap of good for gardens
abstract: Marian Luongo, coordinator of Penn State's community composting education in Philadelphia, offers information on composting if a city strike ensues.

headline: NBC program focusing on TMI accident in '79
abstract: Producer Gloria Sykes and the cast and crew of the new NBC series, "What Happened?" want to explain to viewers what happened at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant on March 28, 1979.  They were in midstate recently filming interviews for the TMI episode of the series, which is scheduled for broadcast at 8:30 pm Nov. 6.

headline: State plans to drop inmate-care pacts
abstract: Amid warnings of a growing tuberculosis crisis in its prisons, investigations into the death of an inmate at Camp Hill and a lawsuit in federal court, the Department of Corrections intends to terminate the cotnracts of all companies that provide prison health care.

headline: Casting a smaller net
abstract: The low-budget WYBE studios, home of Philadelphia's alternative public broadcasting, can give viewers informative programming where people can live call-in the show that deals with prisons, prisoners and what the problems are nationally and locally with those relevant issues.

headline: End to California Budget Crisis Seems Near
abstract: California's long budget ordeal appeared near an end as aides to Governor Pete Wilson and Assembly Speaker Willie L. Broown Jr. crafted details of a compromise on education financing.

headline: Reluctant Clinton backers speak out
abstract: The typical mood of a small random sample of voters in central Pennsylvania was against Presidnet George Bush for re-election.  They were reluctant Bill Clinton backers, not really liking any of the candidates, but choosing the lesser evil.

headline: Health woes inhibit learning, health officials at schools say
abstract: Legislation to provide health insurance to needy children is just the first step in addressing a serious heath crisis among poorer youths, school health officials said yesterday.  An increasing number of children are unprepared to learn in Pennsylvania's classrooms as a result of inadequate health care.

headline: A National Curriculum- Fairness in Uniformity
abstract: An advisory panel to President Bush recommended that the US adopt voluntary national curriculum standards and national tests after the British national curriculum has won wide acceptance as a way of raising standards and insuring equal education opportunity.  Problems arise with the differences between Britain and the US, such as multiculturalism.  Support for the testing system is strong, but struggles occur in teacher training and time consumation.

headline: PE will pay $131 million for napping technicians
abstract: Philadelphia Electric Co. said it would pay $131 million to three other electric utilities to settle claims from the case of the napping nuclear technicians, after the Nuclear Regulatory Commission ordered the plan to shut down.

headline: State Sues Boarding Home Operator To Allow Facility Inspection
abstract: A boarding home operator, Mae Biel, accused in a civil proceeding of converting more to her own use than $1 million in assets belonging to one of her tenants, is being sued by the state Department of Public Welfare for allegedly refusing to allow its representative access to her facility.

headline: Families, society agonize over issue
abstract: A vast national study aims to answer some of the most emotionally charged questions in science and society today: Do working mothers imperil their children's inner security and future happiness?

headline: Erick Weil (Who?) begins '94 race
abstract: Erick Weil, Centre County, had officially announced his candidacy for the 1994 Governor's race.  He said he will not accept any money from anybody for his campaign, nor will he pay for any advertising.

headline: Remap snag could delay Pa. Primary
abstract: Further delay in the selection of a plan to redraw Pennsylvania's congressional districts oculd force the state to postpone a portion of the April 28 primary into the summer.

headline: Health-Care Costs Dampen Hiring
abstract: This could be the first recovery crippled by medical costs.  Employee benefits- health insurance in particular- have become so expensive that manufacturers are increasingly coping with weak demand by cutting payrolls, not overtime.  And laws meant to discourage overtime might now be having the opposite effect.

headline: A program that deserves to live
abstract: Widener University put millions of dollars into a unique job training program called Project Transition.  The money has been well spent and the program has succeeded in finding a lot of people employment; however, studies show that similar programs fail because they didn't have enough money to keep the program going.

headline: Penelec Rates May Decline By 3.2 Percent
abstract: Bills paid by penelec customers could decrease by 3.2 percent in April because of two filings made by the company with the state Public Utility Commission (PUC).

headline: Students walk security gantlet at troubled Chester school
abstract: At Chester High School in Delaware County, the first thing students see each morning is a metal detector and a police officer.  Police guard the cafeteria.  Parents monitor the halls.  Outside doors are locked.  Still, crime finds a way in.

headline: Media mergers may casue revolution
abstract: Dubbed the digital revolution, the coming merger of today's computer, communications, media and home electronics market could transform the way people get news, communicate, sh op, learn and entertain themselves.  Under plans being developed by IBM, Time Warner, Apple Computer and Microsoft, consumers would carry pocket-sized devices to send and receive messages, read news reports, take notes or look up a fact or phone number.

headline: Erie, Pennsylvania
abstract: The first of 6 public hearings on health care reform will be in Erie on Dec. 16, Governor Robert P. Casey said.

headline: Remarks by Freind on Israel draw fire
abstract: A high-ranking Republican, Robert Jubelirer, and several Jewish organizations rebuked Senate candidate Stephen Freind for comments made aobut Israel and religion during a televised debate Monday night.

headline: Healthcare for Everyone Is Goal of Sen. Wofford
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford, who is credited for bringing healthcare into the national political debate, last spring introduced his plan for repairing the nation's healthcare system.  The Pennsylvania Democrat wants healthcare to be available to everyone, believes people should be allowed to choose their own doctor and thinks prevention and wellness are important.

headline: A promise is kept at Temple
abstract: Former Temple University basketball star Mark Macon slam-dunked one for education as he proudly received his bachelor's degree along with 6,000 other Temple graduates at the Civic Center.  "I know basketball won't be forever," said Macon, now a guard for the Denver Nuggets.  "I promised my coach, family and myself that I would get my degree."

headline: Power line will benefit the region
abstract: The signal that Pennsylvania is sending out to businesses is that Pennsyvlania is ambivalent about new investment.  If southwestern Pennsylvania is to recover, we must strengthen the region's surviving industries, such as power production, so all the people of southwestern Pennsylvania can participate in a brighter future.

headline: Study slams city prison health care
abstract: Several inmates have died in Philadelphia prisons, where AIDS has gone untreated, tuberculosis is unchecked and other ailments are mis-diagnosed, according to a report prepared as part of a federal lawsuit.

headline: Phone outages in PA raise questions
abstract: Calling failures with MCI and Bell of Pennsylvania have brought increased scrutiny by the Federal Communications Commission, which has empaneled a new Network Reliability Council to address accountability and reliability in the industry.

headline: ESU puts projects, jobs on ice
abstract: East Stroudsburg University is biting the fiscal bullet in the face of declining state aid this week as officials froze two top administrative posts and cut other costs.

headline: Rendell makes a splash in Forbes
abstract: Mayor Rendell's face-off with Philadelphia's municipal unions has won him two pages of favorable copy in the Nov. 9 issue of Forbes magazine.

headline: Health-research spending to include more minorities
abstract: The federal government plans to spend $45 million in the next year to increase minority health research, after decades of doing little to study the health problems of blacks and hispancs.

headline: A Safe Haven for Learning
abstract: A project proposal written by Concerned Black Men, Inc., called Project 2000, asks for charity to fund Safe Haven- where children in inner cities are given tutors and learn discipline and are attentive and eager to learn.

headline: Power line: Both sides to air views
abstract: Proponents of a planned 500,000-volt electrical transmission line say the project will create jobs and further the area's economic development.  Opponents say the line will devalue their property and harm both humans and animals in its path.

headline: Suit is filed over AIDS protest
abstract: Paul J. Arcure, co-owner of the Waldorf Café in Center City Philadelphia, filed a federal lawsuit yesterday against the city and the Police Department for injuries he claims he suffered Sep. 12 during a protest by AIDS activists at an appearance by President Bush in Philadelphia.

headline: Physicist finds no cancer link in soaring electricity use
abstract: David Jackson, a particle physicist from the University of California at Berkely, concludes there is no proof that exposure to electromagnetic fields causes cancer.

headline: Events That Affected Finances
abstract: A list is given of events over the past few years that may have had an effect on Cranberry School District's financial crisis:

headline: Renegades are trying to liven up the parties
abstract: Folks in Pennsylvania are disgusted this year with the Republican and Democratic parties.  In the state legislature, 26 House and four Senate candidates have no opposition, which indicates insurgents and their organizers have certainly not turned the political process upside-down.  But in a couple of spots, the nontraditionalists are working hard.

headline: Helping to beat breast cancer
abstract: Mercy Hospital, the National Cancer Institute and the National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project are looking for aobut 100 local women to participate in an national survey that could help end the scourge of breast cancer.  They would be part of a nationwide long-term study of the drug, tamoxifen, involving 16,000 women at high risk for breast cancer.

headline: A shift in school board
abstract: When Philadelphia's Board of Education met to approve its $1.27 billion operating budget and $106 million capital budget on May 29, an unusual exchange took place- there were split votes, debates and disagreements.  Board members asked hard questions.  They wanted to know about priorities.

headline: Proposed power line may go through park
abstract: The proposed path of a 268-mile power line goes through a protected park in Beaver County, possibly complicating the controversial case before the Public Utility Commission, an official said.

headline: Suspect described as artistic, educated
abstract: A gunman, police say Jose Guadalope Cruz, shot his 16-year-old girlfriend, and six family members inside their Adams County Farmhouse.  A total of three died in the shootings, and four others survived with injuries.  Cruz has been charged with three counts of criminal homicde, four counts of attempted homicide, four counts of aggravated assault and one count of burglary.

headline: Pittsburgh Papers Halt Publication After 2 Days
abstract: After two days of publishing in the face of stiff resistance from striking deliverers and flagging public support, the Pittsburgh Press Company today indefinitely suspended its effort to print and distribute the city's two newspapers.  Elected officials and civic leaders, who criticized The Press's decision to publicsh, said they also hoped the cessation of publication would lead to a quick settlement.

headline: Excerpts From Supreme Court Arguments on Pennsylvania Law
abstract: The article includes a compilation of some excerpts from the oral argument today before the United States Supreme Court in the case of Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Robert P. Casey, as provided by Alderson Reporting Company.

headline: Rep. Foglietta is named to appropriations panel
abstract: US Representative Thomas M. Fogglietta announced that he had been named to the House Appropriations Committee, which, because of the panel's responsibility for approving all government spending, is one of the most influential committee assignments in Congress.

headline: Hold drug makers criminally acountable
abstract: DES, a drug given to women between 1940 and 1971 to prevent miscarriages, was linked to cervical cancer and is accountable for reproductive disorders.  The makers of silicone implants are also making headlines for unscrupulous practices.  These companies whould be held responsible for their actions.  Yet, they simply walk away.

headline: A teacher of year who's been there
abstract: Denise Pitts-Downing, who grew up on welfare, raised by her grandmother, quit school at 15 to work as a chambermaid and who didn't earn her high school diploma until she was 29, was named yesterday as Philadelphia's Teacher of the Year at the district's annual Celebration of Excellence Awards Ceremony.

headline: PUC judge rejects 'X-ray vision' case
abstract: A Public Utility Commission judge, George M. Kashi, has decided to dismiss the case of Dianna McPheat, a woman who testified that electromagnetic fields from a power line near her house allowed her to see through things.

headline: Teen drinking rates linked to unsafe sex, crime, injuries
abstract: The more teen-agers drink, the likelier they are to be perpetrators and victims of crime, to suffer injuries and to practice unsafe sex, according to the latest in a series of reports on underage drinking released by Surgeon General Antonia C. Novella.

headline: Toll-Free Phone Calls
abstract: The debate between the newspaper and an opposing view is given about the need for regulations to prevent charges on 1-800 lines.  One view says the Federal Communications Commission should enact new rules to guarantee that calls to 800 numbers are toll free, and the other says that the proposal for unneccessary rules is the work of a rotary-dial mind in a touch-tone world.

headline: Ex-CIA agent to challenge Rep. Kanjorski
abstract: Michael A. Fescina, a 25-year veteran of the US Central Intelligence Agency plans to run against US Rep. Paul Kanjorski for the 11th Congressional District seat, stating his long-time interest in world affairs prompted him to run for office.

headline: Republican 31st District
abstract: Republican John Hopper has bowed out for the 31st District senatorial race, leaving Rosemarie Peiffer and John Kennedy in the running for Republican candidate, and for the Democratic side, Bill Duncan as a possibility.

headline: Horizon Hospital and Primary Care plan joint effort
abstract: The newly formed Horizon Hospital System announced that it's teaming up with Shanango Valley Primary Health Care Center to provide "alternative" health care services in the Shenango Valley.  They will offer an occupational medicine program to local business and industry, as well as develop a primary care physician network in underserved parts of Mercer County.

headline: All in the Family
abstract: Twenty-nine state police cadets who recently finished a 19-week training school were presented with graduation certificates by relatives in the law enforcement field.  A list of cadets and relatives/presenters follows.

headline: PUC screens plans to cut electric use
abstract: An investigation that could bring far-reaching changes in what electric companies do to promote energy conservation is quietly under way at the state Public Utility Commission.  Everyone in the state who pays an electric bill could be affecte dby the case, which the state's electric utilities hope will alow them to place a small surcharge on monthly bills to pay for energy-conservation projects.

headline: Teen gets life term in murder of Show
abstract: Tabitha Faith Buck, 18, was sentenced by a Lancaster County judge to life in prison for the second-degree murdar charge in the death of Laurie M. Show, 16.

headline: American Business Starts A Counterattack in Japan
abstract: After spending much of the 1980's struggling to survive against its Japanese competitors, Harley-Davidson Inc. has joined hundreds of American companies in challenging Japanese manufacturers by revving up its sales on their home territory.

headline: Executive advice
abstract: Before too long, City Hall may look as if it's been occupied by the Chamber of Commerce: Upward of three-dozen corporate executives have begun to catalog the city's computer and information-processing needs.

headline: Republican candidate asks LaGrotta to drop from Race
abstract: George R. Reese Jr. asked Frank LaGrotta to withdraw from his race for re-election because Reese believes he is "testing the intelligence of the voters by running for his state House seat and for Congress.  No incumbent should assume or be allowed to have that much political power."

headline: Hospital costs oversight panel may expire
abstract: The Casey administration is drafting a bill to abolish the Health Care Cost Containment Council and move its functions into the state Insurance Department.

headline: And Schools in Maryland
abstract: There was a good bit of grumbling two years ago when Maryland released the first of the annual report cards- evaluations not of students but of the state's school districts and individual schools.

headline: State Pressure on U.S. over Nuclear Waste
abstract: Florida's utilities regulators have accused Washington of "squandering" $3 billion of electricity customers' money in a fruitless search for a place to put nuclear waste.

headline: Teen jobs doubled
abstract: Thousands of young Philadelphians are scheduled to begin federally funded part-time summer jobs- and there's still room for as many as 1,400 more, thanks to the federal aid to cities bill passed last month in the wake of the Los Angeles riots.

headline: Canada cultivates new trade ties here
abstract: After nearly abandoning Philadelphia five years ago, the Canadian government is back with a new mission: to open markets for Canadian firms in the Delaware Valley.

headline: Exemplar of 'Family Values' To Address GOP Convention
abstract: President Bush has said his campaign is going to be about "family values," and if the message has not been clear enough, it will be at the Republican National Convention.  The ultimate symbol in family values- Barbara Bush- will deliver a prime-time address at the Houston convention next month, a party official said in confirming news reports yesterday.

headline: Republicans' 'Electoral Lock' Is Looking Much Less Secure
abstract: For a generation, Republicans began most Presidential campaigns with the comforting knowledge that the South and much of the West were conservative bastions.  This dominance of the Sun Belt, where more and more of the votes and the people are, gave the party an enormous edge in winning the Whtie House- what many analysts described as a lock on the Electoral College.  Yet in the 1992 election, the Republican base looks decidedly shaky.

headline: Hospital death reports
abstract: Allegheny County Coroner Joshua Perper called for a law (which is already a bill undergoing approval) that would require hospitals to report their fatal mistakes.  Based on his own study, Perper found that the accidental deaths in Allegheny County hospitals called "therapeutic misadventures" are being underreported.

headline: Any boost in state aid for education is likely to be negligible
abstract: Pennsylvania high schools and colleges expect small or negligible increases in state aid next year as the annual debate heats up over the state budget.

headline: State utilities belatedly join in EMF issue
abstract: When a judge with the Public Utility Commission recommended banning use of a new power line until the commission sets standards for electromagnetic fields, he caught many of the state's utilities off guard.  Six utilities have put the PUC on notice that they want to have a say in the controversial Philadelphia Electric Co. case, which has generated national attention and put the PUC in the middle of the simmering EMF controversy.

headline: Teen saw porn video; 2 aides reprimanded
abstract: The athletic director, Harry Beaudet, and the maintenance supervisor, Oliver Giorgi, at Triton High School in Runnemede have been reprimanded for not intervening when a pornographic video was shown on school property to an audience that included a 16-year-old student.

headline: Study says U.S. workers are the world's top producers
abstract: US workers are more productive than their Gernam or Japanese counterparts, largely because of America's highlly competitive and open trade environment, the authors of a new study conducted by McKinsey Global Institute, said.

headline: Exit poll: It's economics, not race
abstract: Recently the movement of people out of cities- in many cases done to change where their children will go to school- appears to be more an issue of money than race.  Those who can afford to leave, of whatever race, often do.

headline: Retirees to receive insurance assurance
abstract: The Casey administration is polling some 3,700 retired state workers and beneficiaries to assure that the state will pick up a penalty imposed on them by the federal government for late enrollment in the Medicare Part B program.

headline: Hospital Merger Praised
abstract: Oil City and Franklin hospitals have merged to become the Northwest Medical Center.  Neil Todhunter, chief executive officer of the new hospital, commented that the merger was the best cure for Venango County's health woes, and separately, one hospital probably would not have survived.  Increased revenue, significantly lower spending, and no layoffs are all positive effects that were evident within the first few months of the merger.

headline: Applications up despite fewer high school seniors
abstract: Although the number of high school seniors is down, applications at Penn State University are up slightly from a year ago.

headline: State's northwestern oil drillers fear rules may dry wells
abstract: Small operators in northwestern Pennsylvania, the world's oldest oil field, are struggling against two forces- low prices and strict environmental regulations.

headline: Teenage son of city aide shot to death
abstract: The 15-year-old son of Sultan Ahmad, the head of the Mayor's Office of Community Services, was shot to death- blasted numerous times by a shotgun- as he walked home from school along Hunting Park.  Homicide Lt. Thomas Quinn said police had not determined what prompted the shooting of the boy.

headline: Matter of Principles
abstract: The Federation of United irish American Societies picketed outside the courhouse to drum up support for the MacBride Principles, which seek to help Catholics in strife-torn Northern Ireland.

headline: Exit polls give quick results
abstract: Exit polls, networks taking a survey as people leave the polling place, have been used for more than 20 years, and enable networks to find the results of an election and project a winner before the votes have been counted.

headline: Rhoades goes for top post
abstract: Schuylkill County's state senator, James J. Rhoades, is seeking a key leadership role in setting th edirection and policies of the Republican-controlled state Senate.  He has been busy contacting all 26 members of the Senate Republican caucus lobbying their support for him to serve as Majority Policy Chairman.

headline: Hospital picketed by nurses
abstract: Three weeks after staging a one-day municipal work stoppage, District Council 33 finds itself on the receiving end of a picket line.  Union-owned John F. Kennedy Hospital said it will ask a Common Pleas judge today to order more than 100 registered nurses off the picket line and back to their jobs at the Northeast Philadelphia facility.

headline: As More Earn Equivalency Diploma, Its Value Is Debated
abstract: A new study says that those who passed the General Education Development test are no better off than high school dropouts who did not take the test.  And as that educational level becomes more common, more questions are being raised about the long-term value of the test.

headline: Tentative deal could save jobs at Tunnelton
abstract: A tentative three-way deal between mining, steel and power companies reached Wednesday in Harrisburg could save the jobs of about 250 coal miners.  The three companies involved are the Tunnelton Mine, Mon Valley Steel Inc. and Pennsylvania Power and Light Co.

headline: Teenager convicted of murder
abstract: Donnell Drinks, 18, who said he was induced into crime by a former Philadelphia police officer- his girlfriend- was convicted yesterday in Common Pleas Court of first-degree murder in the 1991 slaying of a Northern Liberties man during a robbery.

headline: Signs publicizing minister's speech are called anti-Semitic
abstract: The widespread posting of signs in Philadelphia heralding a speech titled "Are Jews Hiding the Truth?" has been condemned as anti-Semitic by leaders of the city's Human Relations Commission and leading Jewish organizations.  The signs tout a free Saturday speech by Haleem Asadi, a minister of the Lost-Found Nation of Islam mosque.

headline: Expect a political fight over jurist replacement
abstract: Capitol insiders and others say the selection of a replacement for Philadelphia Justice James McDermott, who died at his home Sunday, will be tangled in the usual partisan knots between Democrat Governor Robert Casey and the Republican state Senate.

headline: Rhoades urged to support nomination
abstract: Senator James J. Rhoades is once again playing party politics regarding the confirmation of Maryann Conwar for judge of Schuylkill County court of Common Pleas.  Senator Rhoades is against confirming an extremely qualified woman.  He should think of Schuylkill County's needs first and put politics aside.

headline: How drug companies minimize R & D risks
abstract: Drug companies spend three times the average of other industries on research and development.  They cushion the risks, absorb the costs and still manage to be the nation's most profitable business.

headline: BCCC needs $30M
abstract: Bucks County Community College hopes to raise almost $30 million from private sources over the next five years if a feasibility study shows public support for the plan.

headline: Town meeting scheduled
abstract: The Regional Environmental Alliance will sponsor "Our Region Under Siege," a town meeting on the poetential impact on the area of current and proposed incinerators and a potential 500,000 volt electrical power line, in the laboratory classroom auditorium at Penn State Beaver campus.

headline: The Anguish of Asking A Court for an Abortion
abstract: Such hearings, with a teenage pregnant girl trying to get permission from the court to have an abortion, are routine in the Cambridge court, where a smooothly oiled system linking lawyers with pregnant girls under 18 years old helps hundreds of teenagers each year tell a judge what they will not tell their parents.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon shows a man in a business suit with bushy eyebrows holding a mask that looks similar to him.  The mask is shouting, "Clinton, Clinton Clinton!"

headline: Few resist low road to office
abstract: The Republican National Convention established a theme and style for President Bush's reelection campaign: ethics, not issues.  It is dismaying how quickly that approach has been picked up by local candidates from both parties.

headline: RNC Hopeful Says No To Clinton Honeymoon
abstract: E. Spencer Abraham, one of a growing list of candidates to head the Republican Party, yesterday sent Republican National Committee members a four-page letter vowing that the GOP's mission every day for the next four years should be to hold Clinton's feet to the fire.

headline: Independent crisis center
abstract: The article titled, "Mentally ill held in jails, study says," referred to communities doing an excellent job of handling the problem, but unfortunately, the article referred to Norristown State Hospital instead of the award-winning Exemplary Program at Montgomery County Emergency Service Inc.

headline: Beaver Falls must give pupil compensatory education
abstract: Commonwealth Court upheld Tuesday a state order that the Big Beaver Fallls Area School District provide "compensatory education" to a student because it failed to place her in a proper special education program.

headline: 470 miles of PA turnpike add up to one big paint job
abstract: It takes thousands of gallons of paint and millions of pounds of glass beads that are mixed in to improve reflectivity to touch up the lines on the 470 miles of the Pennsylvania Turnpike.

headline: The Last Casualty
abstract: Jimmy Berghaier, who once was Philadelphia police stakeout officer, became "Jimmy the Broom," in a process that occurred over years and in a single instant.  His story is told of how he was accused of firing shots that scared children into a burning house, which ended his career as an officer.

headline: null
abstract: A cartoon where the television states, "And in Harrisburg, the state legislators are stalling again on a budget."  The man watching TV proclaims, "If there's one thing I can't stand, it's summer reruns on TV!"

headline: Fill 'em up
abstract: Governor Robert Casey proposed legislation to establish four regional 'waste shed' areas within the state, with the shipping of garbage across their borders being prohibited.  Federal courts have ruled states cannot restrict interstate commerce, even as garbage; therefore, if Casey's proposal becomes a law, it is likely to be challenged in the courts.

headline: Ron Brown's grail: Democratic unity
abstract: Ron Brown was once thought of by Democrats that he would damage irreparably any chance the party had of blocking George Bush's re-election, but now is probably one of the very few people in the entire country that can be given credit for putting Democrats in position to win the White House.

headline: Infant Health Problems Cost Business Billions
abstract: US Companies and their employees pay about $5.6 billion a year to care for babies born prematurely or with other complications to mothers covered by insurance plans.  Infants at risk of major medical problems at birth aren't just a big problem in poor urban and rural areas, but pose enormous human and economic costs for US businesses as well.

headline: Bill to give Aliquippa more leeway on tax rates dies as session ends
abstract: Legislation to give Aliquippa School District the ability to tax land at different rates than buildings fell victim to larger political battles over special education and education reform.  But Representative Susan Laughlin, boosted by the bill's success in the House, vowed to try again when the General Assembly returns to Harrisburg in January.

headline: After the sky fell
abstract: A woman tells the story of how her son was badly injured when a plane crashed into his elementary school.

headline: The strike lands in court
abstract: The state Supreme Court- without explicitly addressing the constitutionality of the second-class county Port Authority act's barring third-party intervention in labor disputes- decided that the city had standing to institute a complaint in court over the hardships created by the current situation.

headline: null
abstract: As a visiting football team is entering their locker room, a man is begging for money to put in his box labeled 'wage tax,' and he is wearing a sign that says, "Phila."

headline: Finally, Casey's getting his shot
abstract: Governor Casey returns to New York City this week for what's billed as "the speech the Demcorats wouldn't allow"- his well-known views against abortion.

headline: Ross Perot, Though to Many a Political Unknown, Emerges in Poll as a Formidable but Elusive Force
abstract: As a presidential candidate, Ross Perot is unannounced, untested and endefined- and still ranks higher than any independent candidate in modern history.  A new Wall Street Journal/NBC News poll shows Mr. Perot drawing 26% of the vote against the likely two major-party nominees- just four percentage points behind Gov. Bill Clinton, at 30%, and 12 percentage points behind President Bush, at 38%.

headline: Is health reform ailing?
abstract: Politicians agree that there is a major need for health insurance reform but debate on the shape that reform should take.  The evolving choices include the single-payer system (government-run and tax-financed), play-or-pay system (employer offers coverage or pays taxes), or the incremental reforms (fix insurance market, cover children, and expand access).

headline: Bill would halve school strikes
abstract: The number of teacher strikes in Pennsylvania should drop by one-half or more, under a teacher-strike reform bill that will soon become law, state Education Secretary Donald M. Carroll Jr. said.

headline: Airplane-crash drill held
abstract: The Harrisburg International Airport held a mock disaster- a drill required by the Federal Aviation Administration every three years.  The airport stayed open during the drill, so sirens weren't sounding and ambulances weren't moving at emergency speed.

headline: The title of 'Mom' says it all for Gill
abstract: Nancy Gill should have the superlative "Most Super Mom" who, after 65 foster children, three adopted children and five children of her own, was chosen to receive a top award from the Pennsylvania State Foster Parent Association.

headline: Board asks for fact-finder in teacher talks
abstract: Cornwall-Lebanon school board members have requested PA state fact-finder Lynne Mounts to present a report in teacher contract negotiations. Richard Sterner of the PA State Education Association said major issues are wages and tuition reimbursement. Teachers are hoping to exhaust all legal avenues to pursue demands before striking.

headline: Firm with connections could get $750,000
abstract: Capital Partnerships, a lobbying firm that employes the daughter and a former aide of US Representative E.G. "Bud" Shuster, stands to earn $750,000 for work on behalf of a client with the business before a committee on which he serves.

headline: Ross Who?
abstract: Comedian and perennial presidential candidate Pat Paulsen came in second in North Dakota's GOP primary, even beating Ross Perot.

headline: Non-traditional chief turns hospital around
abstract: Tom Pregent, Muncy Valley Hospital's chief, considers himself odd and admits to a non-traditional approach- but points out that it has turned around the rural Lycoming County hospital.

headline: Board wary in accepting school pact
abstract: Assurances of more state funding helped ease board members' concerns.  Still, at least $11 million in Philadelphia school cuts will be needed next year.

headline: Airport officials plan for growth
abstract: The Allentown-Bethlehem-Easton Airport Authority took the first steps yesterday toward targeting land for expanding a growing airport hemmed in by suburban sprawl.

headline: The year of the murderer
abstract: James McClure examines the murders in York County last year, one of the most deadly years in the history of the country.

headline: Boys on bus
abstract: The Democratic campaign takes to the road Friday after a post-convention rally- in decidedly country-and-western fashion.  Bill Clinton and Al Gore will be going by bus to small towns and cities for the six-day tour.

headline: Firms lavish big bucks on conventions
abstract: The corporate gang's all here- from oil companies and Baby Bells to Philip Morris and bankers.  Business interests have lavished Republican convention-goers with festivities.  The companies, most of which have donated to both parties' conventions this year, insist their motivation is not to buy political influence but rather to help the host city put on a good show.

headline: Running in place: '92's latest odd twist
abstract: It is hard to tell whether the 1992 presidential campaign is all but over or hasn't really begun.  In the month since the Republican convention, the campaign has failed to produce a serious discussion of issues or even the normal barrage of charge and countercharge.

headline: Lyme disease cure risky, study shows
abstract: Allegheny and Butler county residents who have been bitten by ticks but aren't sure if they have contracted Lyme disease should not be hasty about getting treatment.  That's the conclusion of a recent study by the University of Pennsylvania on the possible side effects of the drugs used to fight Lyme disease.

headline: Budget approved by HACC
abstract: Harrisburg Area Community College officials are predicting they may be one of the few institutions of higher learning in Pennsylvania able to boast of not raising tuition this year, as the delegate body approved a $26.6 million operating budget for the school's 1992-93 academic year.

headline: AMP lawyers warn GM
abstract: Attonreys working for AMP Inc. have alerted General Motors President John F. Smith Jr. that they may sue the Detroit-based automaker over the cleanup costs of a contaminated site in Lower Allen Township.

headline: They displayed the pain and anger of victims of rape and incest
abstract: On clotheslines strung around the LOVE statue in JFK Plaza and between a dozen trees, women hung out dirty laundry- some 150 T-shirts decorated with the pain of rape and incest.  More than 300 people joined in the rally to protest violence against women, one of 18 planned around Pennsylvania.

headline: null
abstract: Results are given of candidates in the 31st Senatorial District, and 199th, 86th and 103rd Legislative Districts in chart form.

headline: Florio Agrees To Revisions In School Act
abstract: Under pressure from political and legal challengges to the sweeping school financing changes he made barely a year ago, Governor Jim Florio has agreed to a largely Republican-inspired revision of the plan.

headline: Satellite Pitch
abstract: You had to hunt the skies to find it, but President Bush took to the airwaves Wednesday with a pitch for the balanced budget amendment.  The speech, sent out via satellite, was aimed at "anybody who wants to use it," said spokesman Marlin Fitzwater.

headline: Mammography law
abstract: On Sept. 3, the Mammogram Quality Assurance Act became effective.  Because a mammogram is the single most effective tool to detect breast cancer in its earliest and most curable stages, this act is important to the health and lives of all women.

headline: Budget cutting draws wrath
abstract: As Pat McCue addressed the Neshaminy School Board with some 600 parents and studnets looking on his hands shook slightly, but his words were unwavering.  McCue said he felt the entire special education program of the district's is at risk.  The board has set up a special hearing to listen to more comment.

headline: An incentive to enlightenment
abstract: Currently, convicted teens may lose their licenses for an amount of time for drinking, but since there is no connection between underage drinking and motor-vehicle laws, Representative John Broujos' proposal would opt out the license suspension if the teen attended an education series.

headline: They wonder if anyone cares
abstract: Vandals, almost always outsiders, usually young people from the suburbs, come to center-city Philadelphia for nights of revelry, where they take people's belongings right off their front porch.  "They don't live there so they don't care," is the reasoning.

headline: null
abstract: The text is given from Governor Bill Clinton's campaign speech delivered at the University of Pittsburgh branch at Johnstown, PA., on April 22, as transcribed by the New York Times.  Issues covered include the economy, the need for partnership, health care, education, and citizens' responsibility.

headline: Foe blasts Nickol for newsletters
abstract: State Representative Steven R. Nickol "blatantly misused" tax money in sending newsletters to York and Adams County residents who are not in his redistricted 193rd House Districkt, Nickol's Democratic challenger, Wayne Lau, says.

headline: Scolded by Dems, Acosta again toeing party line
abstract: Democratic state Representative Ralph Acosta must be getting dizzy.  He steps over the party line to endrose Republican Senator Arlen Specter, then steps back and says he's going to endorse Democratic candidate Lynn Yeakel.  That followed the party's threats to shun him and cut off his flow of Election Day street money.  Then he slips out of Democrat City Committee headquarters, but once again slipped in with the Democrat committee.

headline: 'Managed-Care Networks' Show Promise
abstract: Corporate America's most comprehensive strategy to stanch hemorrhaging health costs is beginning to show promising results at many large companies, a report by benefits consultant Towers Perrin says.

headline: Bush backs college aid plan in visit to Dieruff High School
abstract: President Bush, calling for a revolution in education, promoted a plan to give $25,000 in college student aid to every American, ripped Congress for protecting the status quo and praised local educational reform efforts in the first visit to the Lehigh Valley by a sitting president in 43 years.

headline: Bill on $120,000 intersection plan for Station Square to be submitted
abstract: City council members will submit legislation to spend $120,000 to design a new intersection on West Carson Street that is necessary for the expansion of Station Square.  The intersection will be just west of where the base of the Duquesne Incline is on Carson Street, and will lead onto a new internal road that will form the new western entry to the Station Square complex.

headline: Ticked-off agent mashes thousands of fake watches
abstract: An investigation of a trafficking of courfeit watches that started at the Silver Spring Flea Market resulted in the seizure of 60,000 watches so far and the conviction of four area men on copyright violations.

headline: null
abstract: Two advertisements thank Governor Robert P. Casey for recognizing Sharon, PA, as "Capital for a Day" and welcoming him to the area.  One is from AFL-CIO, and the other is from Sharon Tube Co.

headline: Foglietta fuming over check list
abstract: The House ethics committee says Rep. Thomas M. Foglietta had an account at the infamous bank and bounced two checks.  Foglietta denies he ever had an account, never mind bouncing a check in one.

headline: Scranton 'implosion' makes way for mall
abstract: Officials in Scranton blew up two blocks of Lackawanna Avenue, preparing the downtown district for a new shopping mall.

headline: Managing Medicaid
abstract: State medicaid officials are eager to take advantage of cost control techniques offered by managed care health plans.  But advocates for medicaid patients oppose the easing of safeguards against possible abuses.

headline: But in some areas, sharing works
abstract: At St. Hugh's parish in Kensington, about 20 school district classes are held inside operating parochial school buildings as part of a district lease for space.  According to school principals and other officials, it's a program that works well.

headline: Bill seeks to tighten seat-belt law
abstract: Under current law, officials can only ticket drivers for not wearing their seat belts when they've been pulled over for another violation, but under legislation proposed by state Reps. Katherine McHale and Gordon Linton, police can pull over drivers solely because they or their passengers weren't belted.

headline: To help battle addiction, he advocates the use of a drug
abstract: Howard Lotsof sampled a drug called ibogaine, derived from the root of an African shrub, and Lotsof claims this drug treats addiction.  He said that ibogaine erased his dependency on heroin and cocaine without the agony of withdrawal- a claim endorsed by other addicts who have tried it.

headline: $100,000 pledged to aid Floridians
abstract: 87,000 homes in South Florida were destroyed by Hurrican Andrew, four times the number of buildings in Harrisburg.  Aid in the form of money and volunteers to help Floridians rebuild their homes and lives, is pouring in from throughout the midstate.

headline: Foglietta's offices doing double duty
abstract: Members of Congress who are seeking re-election are supposed to separate their legislative offices and their campaign operations.  But what happens when a member has no campaign office- or even a campaign telephone?  That is the situation facing Representative Thomas M. Foglietta.

headline: Searching for New Jobs, Many States Steal Them
abstract: In state capitals across the nation, just as in Washington, government leaders are casting about for approaches, new and old, to reinvigorate their economies.  And the key to that, where ever it is tried, is creating jobs.

headline: Merck Chairman Opposes Democrats'  Health Proposal
abstract: P. Roy Vagelos, chairman of Merck & Company, spoke agaisnt health care legislation that he said might endanger American leadership in medical research and innovative technology.

headline: Casey asks Pitt to make cuts rather than increase tuition
abstract: Gov. Casey has urged the University of Pittsburgh to meet reduced state funding with lower spending rather than a tuition increase.  Casey suggests that the school use its reserves or cut operations rather than raise rates for students.

headline: Bill to upgrade state's rail lines sent to Casey
abstract: The state House and Senate voted to spend $38 million to upgrade railroad lines across the state, enabling "double-stacked" railroad cars and oversized industrial products to traverse the state'e rail lines.  Governor Robert P. Casey has backed the project and is expected to sign the bill.

headline: Top court: Jury selection biased
abstract: A new trial will be held for Grover Dinwiddie, a former police officer prosecuted for several robberies.  Dinwiddie, a black man, claims the jury makeup was biased as there were 10 whites and only two blacks.  The blame is being directed to the trial judge, Stanley L. Kubacki for failing to ask the prosecutor, Marc Gottlieb, his reasons for six peremptory challenges to strike five blacks from the jury.

headline: 1 in 4 mark $1 box to boost campaigns
abstract: Only one in four Pennsylvanians marked the $1 presidential campaign check-off on their federal tax returns, but participation in the state was still among the highest nationally, the Federal Election Commission reported.

headline: For Clionton, chronic hoarseness- and silence- come at an apt time
abstract: After two weeks of extended silences, the audio portion of Bill Clinton's slowed-motion presidential campaign remains muted.  Events and interviews in Pennsylvania, which holds its primary Tuesday, are still being postponed and even canceled to give the candidate's much-abuse vocal cords a rest.

headline: Searching for the cheap seats
abstract: A sparsely populated state like Montana or Idaho has cheap seats for someone running for state legislature.  House seats in both state are flat-out bargains- winning one consumed less than $5,000 on average four years ago, and hasn't gone up much since.

headline: Monsour Medical Center struggling to stay open
abstract: Monsour Medical Center in Jeannette, Westmoreland County, fell under court supervision after several suits of mismanagement.  A repayment schedule has been established for the debt of $31.7 million.  The only solution would be for the medical center to affiliate with another hospital, and according to the attorney for Monsour, negotiations are in progress.

headline: Casey must heed call to support science education
abstract: Pennsylvania is playing a key role in a growing federal commitment to strengthening technological education, while at the same time enhancing educational opportunities for disadvantaged students, but Governor Robert Casey plans to cut funding to PA's colleges and universities.  We as a state should be investing more in higher education.

headline: Bills would boost enforcement
abstract: Police would have greater powers to enforce the state's mandatory seat belt law and more children would be required to use car safety seats under legislation proposed by state Reps. Katherine McHale and Gordon Linton.

headline: Troopers launching a 'Language Line'
abstract: Poly-lingualism takes the airways as the state police inaugurate a program of using a telephone translator service to help communicate with people who cannot speak English.

headline: 123-page financial report details billionaire's wealth
abstract: Texas billionaire Ross Perot, estimated to be the 13th richest person in the USA, provided a peek into the heady world of high finance when he detailed his personal fortune for the Federal Election Commission.  His 123-page file was the largest ever plunked down on the desk at the FEC.

headline: For Swing Voters, Not Much Choice
abstract: A Washington Post-ABC News poll of US voters suggests that where President Bush rates high, his opponent, Arkansas Gov. Bill Clinton, does not, and vice-versa, leaving a split decision between swing voters, those who will ultimately decide the election.

headline: Sen. Fumo tips his hat to O'Donnell
abstract: Senator Fumo, representing the First District in the state Senate, speaks of his unwavering loyalty to former Speaker of the Pennsylvania House, Bob O'Donnell and of O'Donnell's successes in the House.

headline: More Doctors Go Where the Patients Are: Home
abstract: Doctors in the New York region and throughout the nation are once again turning to one of the oldest forms of medical care: house calls.  Pushed by insurance companies looking for ways to cut down on expensive hospital stays, they are climbing stairs to take the blood pressure of elderly patients too weak to make office visits, or dropping in on mentally ill patients who might not keep a regular appointment.

headline: Casey proposes realigning aid to school districts
abstract: Twenty-four school districts in Allegheny county would receive more state aid for basic education than they are getting now, and 19 would get less under Gov. Robert P. Casey's proposed budget for 1992-1993.

headline: Blind couple's concert plans hit roadblock when bus driver balks
abstract: Sharon O'Brien and her husband, both blind, won tickets to a concert, but when they tried to get on the tour bus, the driver would not let them on with their guide dogs.  With the help of Ted Young, state president of the National Federation of the Blind of Pennsylvania, they are preparing to file a legal complaint with the US Justice Department that will detail the encounter and seek monetary damages.

headline: Troopers' stations due for renovation
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey has released $4.7 million to renovate and expand three state police headquarters.  Those receiving funds include Troop "N" in Hazleton, Troop "J" in Lancaster and Troop "M" in Bensalem, Bucks County.

headline: 1988 platform: Promises made, but largely unkept
abstract: An advance guard of Republicans spent last week debating and writing the party platform on which President Bush will seek re-election.  By the end of this week, after the GOP convention officially approves its work, almost nobody will read or remember what the platform committee did- except for the intense debate over abortion.

headline: Foundation sees upsets, continuity
abstract: The Commonwealth Foundation has weighed in with its spin on the year that was, calling 1992 a year of "convulsions as well as a period of continuation of many powerful policy trends."  The foundation, based in Harrisburg, is a non-profit that focuses on government and education reform.

headline: Sen. Specter deserves 3rd term
abstract: Had it not been for his aggressive questioning of Anita Hill during the Clarence Thomas confirmation hearings last year, Senator Arlen Specter would have a comfortable lead over a Democratic "suit."  His time serving as a US Senator proved him worthy of the position.  Arlen Specter should return to the Senate for a third term.

headline: N.J. court considers issue of 'wrongful birth'
abstract: Judy Hummel is suing her obstetrician and the hospital, St. Michael's Medical Center in Newark, on behalf of her daughter, saying she had a "wrongful birth" and although the time was before the landmark decision of Roe vs. Wade, Hummel should have been granted an abortion to save her own life.

headline: Casey takes aim at school fund surpluses
abstract: Gov. Robert P. Casey claims that 90 percent of Pennsylvania's school districts have squirreled away a total of $600 million for a rainy day, and it's time for those institutions to put up the umbrella, because it's raining.

headline: British firm expected to give USAir stability
abstract: The proposed alliance between British Airways and USAir is expected to bring some financial stability to the domestic airline and promises to open up more international air routes.

headline: Two men slain as gunfire erupts on N. Phila. Street
abstract: Two men were fatally wounded yesterday when gunfire erupted during an argument involving them and two others on a drug-infested street in North Philadelphia's Fairhill neighborhood.

headline: 2 candidates push reform at West York debate
abstract: The first step in reforming Congress is to elect a new representative from the 19th Congressional District, say Democrat Paul V. Kilker and Republican Tom Humbert, two of the three candidates for the position.

headline: Foundation sues Turgeon for $250,000
abstract: The John Crain Kunkel charitable foundation has filed suit against Dauphin County Judge Jeannine Turgeon and her embattled law firm, claiming her former partner, Michael Q. Davis, embezzled nearly $250,000 intended to erect a memorial.

headline: Sen. Specter Lobbies For Burner Exclusion
abstract: Federal officials have joined Pennsylvania leaders in calling for a ban on construction of hazardous-waste facilities near federal prisons, according to US Senator Arlen Specter.

headline: N.Y. probes surgeon in Giuffre case
abstract: New York state health officials have begun an investigation of Dr. Leonora Weissman, a surgeon who was barred from a North Philadelphia hospital in 1988 after an investigation of what Pennsylvania authorities called unnecessary surgery and improper treatment.  The NY Health Dept is looking into whether or Weissman misrepresented her past on her application to the James C. Giuffre Medical Center.

headline: Casey, schools disagree on how to use surpluses
abstract: Local school district surpluses have emerged as a bone of contention in a budget battle between Gov. Robert P. Casey and the education community over state support for instructional costs.

headline: Bypass plans draw cheers from officials
abstract: Suburban and county officials said they are generally pleased with an elaborate plan to widen a section of Route 30 and restructure interchanges.

headline: U.S. Panel Faults States' Child Support System
abstract: A Federal panel said that the states' system of collecting child support was a "cumbersome, slow-moving dinosaur fed by paper," and urged Congress to play a role.  Congress seems more interested in child support legislation.  Senator Richard C. Shelby, Democrat of Alabama is pressing a measure that would make it a Federal crime for a parent or a legal guardian to cross a state line to avoid child-support payments.

headline: 2 to probe state justices
abstract: A former US attorney, Edward Dennis, and a former attorney general of Maine, James E. Tierney, will lead an investigation into allegations of wire tapping, kickbacks and conniving by Pennsylvania Supreme Court justices.

headline: Fox, Mezvinsky to clash for Coughlin's House seat
abstract: Republicans and Democrats took opposite tack in the race to replace US Representative Lawrence Coughlin, with GOP voters picking veteren officeholder Jon D. Fox and the Democrats choosing rookie Marjorie Margolies Mezvinsky.

headline: Sen. Stapleton fund-raiser ties questioned
abstract: An upcoming fund-raiser for state Senator Patick Stapleton has his opponent, Republican Lance Alexander, questioning the incumbent's ties to special interests.

headline: Nicotine Patches' Link To Heart Attacks Probed
abstract: The Food and Drug Administration is investigating reports that people who smoked while wearing nicotine patches suffered heart attacks.

headline: Catholic crisis to reignite vouchers
abstract: The crisis of Philadelphia's Catholic high schools seems almost certain to put the issue of tuition voucers for private schools back squarely before the General Assembly after the Nov. 3 election.

headline: Community feels railroaded
abstract: Some residents living amid the massive reconstruction of SEPTA's commuter lines through North Philadelphia fear that the reconstruction money train won't make enough stops in their neighborhoods.

headline: Urban policy is back on the agenda
abstract: When President Bush tours the riot scarred city of Los Angeles, the nation will turn to him for answers.  Some will see a gritty leader committed to controlling the decline and violence in their neighborhoods.  Others will see the architect of that decay and despair.

headline: 2nd Dem wants to challenge Goodling for seat in Congress
abstract: York County resident Paul V. Kilker is challenging Paul E. Ritchey in the Democratic primary for the 19th District seat in Congress.  The winner is expected to face incumbent William F. Goodling, a nine-term Republican who has not yet formally started a re-election campaign.

headline: Frankly embarrassed
abstract: Rep. Rick Santorum has been a scourge of special privileges for members of Congress, and he is the leading user of the so-called franking privilege.

headline: Senate backs voter registration via mail
abstract: The Senate approved legislation to make it easier for millions of Americans to register to vote by requiring states to allow registration by mail and to enroll voters automatically when they apply for driver's licenses.

headline: Now, health insurers compete for poor clients
abstract: Competition among health care insurers has come to the low-income residents of South and West Philadelphia, a situation that makes state officials gleeful because it holds down health care costs.

headline: Catholic school group revives voucher issue
abstract: A coalition of teachers, parents and alumni got a political boost last night in the effort to keep 10 area Catholic high schools from closing or merging.  And a dormant attempt to get the state to help parents pay to send their kids to private schools emerged as one key to the coalition's strategy.

headline: Commuters in Pittsburgh riding out a transit strike
abstract: About 2,700 bus and trolley operators walked off their jobs in Pittsburgh, leaving commuters with nothing but finding their own ways to get around.

headline: Urban rescue
abstract: The Badlands, one of the worst drug neighborhoods in the country, located in a section of North Philadelphia, is the peacetime equivalent of a "free-fire zone" where authorities carry out surprise "crack attacks" in which entire blocks are bulldozed in the ongoing war against illegal drugs.  We had better find a way to deal with the Badlands of urban America, or the neglect and rot they represent are going to spread and consume whole cities.

headline: 32 reporters called by Bush campaign
abstract: One recent day, each of the 32 reporters in the Capitol  newsroom were called from Washington, DC, by "the Bush-Quayle Campaign '92" people inviting them to cover a news conference the next morning.  Massachusetts Governor William Weld was expected to say nice things about the president and vice-president.

headline: Friend-ly persuasion
abstract: Stung by attacks from state Rep. Stephen Friend, his GOP primary challenger, Sen. Arlen Specter has moved a briefing for his contributors from the White House to a Washington hotel.

headline: Senate rejects insurance chief; Casey berates GOP
abstract: Acting state Insurance Commissioner Cynthia Maleski, of Natrona Heights, failed to win Senate confirmation to the post Tuesday.  The rejection, by a 25-21 vote, re-ignited the political warfare between Governor Robert Casey and state Senate Republican leaders over the worker's compensation reform issue.

headline: NRC cites Mercy Hospitals
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission cited Mercy Catholic Medical Center for allegedly violating federal radiation safety requirements, imposing fines double the normal penalty for the hospital's failure to report known violations. Hospital officials, having since hired a full-time radiation safety officer, say violations occurred primarily in documentation and that no patients were adversely affected. The NRC is concerned violations could have led to misadministration of radioactive medicines in deviation from the prescription by 10 percent.

headline: CD gets its checks back as refunds prove taxing
abstract: The Central Dauphin School District would like to give $455,000 back to taxpayers.  But some taxpayers think this is too good to be true and are sending back their $10 checks.  Some are even writing their own checks for $10 and sending that to the district, thinking that it's a bill they have received.

headline: Conrail cancels pact with firm in union dispute
abstract: The company that operated Conrail's Harrisburg terminal has lost its contact with the railroad amid a dispute with the Teamsters union, and Conrail said it canceled its contract with the Pennsylvania Truck Lines Intermodal Inc..

headline: US director of prisons resigns, cites ill health
abstract: Federal prisons director J. Michael Quinlan, under investigation in a politically sensitive case involving Vice President Quayle, is resigning immediately because of ill health, Attorney General William P. Barr announced yesterday.

headline: 34 Million View Final Session
abstract: About 34 million Americans watched the Republican convention on Thursday night, roughly the same numer that watched the final night of the Democratic convention in July.

headline: Fully open budget process would only reveal its tediousness
abstract: The general public is more concerned with the results of the annual state budget ritual than the process.  A fully open and participatory budget process is more disorderly and drawn out, and since few people, press or public, are much into tedium or boredom, many of the most important governmental decisions are unattended, unreported, and/or unread.

headline: Senate rivals' assets a question of balance
abstract: Arlen Specter's backers tout his seniority.  Lynn Yeakel's followers cite her close ties to Bill Clinton.  Seniority or majority- which one gives a senator more clout?

headline: Nurses say Nancy 'seems' alive, shouldn't be cut off from food
abstract: Nurses who have cared for Nancy, who is permanently brain damaged, are opposing a request by Nancy's parents to stop life support.

headline: Central Dauphin district taxpayers given no credit
abstract: The Central Dauphin School District was forced to move ahead on preparing 1992-93 tax bills for mailing by the July 1 deadline, all except those for non-public transportation reimbursement.  Without knowing how much more that is, the district can't determine how much money will be rebated or credited to taxpayers.

headline: Conrail ordered to open up its rail network to a rival
abstract: The Interstate Commerce Commission said that Conrail must negotiate to give the Delaware & Hudson Railway access to Conrail's tracks within the city of Philadelphia.

headline: Utah firm again wins state contract
abstract: Pennsylvania finds it necessary to contract with a company in Utah to handle an arm of the commonwealth's tourist promotion program because it’s the "lowest or best bid" thing that governmental bodies use to make sure the contractor signed gives the most for the buck.

headline: 3712,116 register to vote in Montco, a county record
abstract: A total of 371,116 Montgomery County residents are registered to vote in the November election- the highest registration in the county's history.

headline: G.O.P.'s Platform Reveals Conservativies' Dominance
abstract: The platform the Republicans will adopt at their convention and the drafting session this week illustrate the degree to which diehard conservatives are in control of party affairs.

headline: Senator without a pause
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter, a big-time Philadelphia politician for three decades, started out as a prosecutorial wonderboy, a crusading reformer, locking up corrupt magistrates and Teamsters.  After a nine-month tour with the Warren Commission in Washington, he switched parties and was elected district attorney twice.  Then he lost four elections until 1980 when he grasped a six-year term in the US Senate and was re-elected in 1986.

headline: On health care issue, states take initiative
abstract: Frustrated with the federal government's paralysis in the face of runaway health-care costs and the inability of millions to get the insurance they need, individual states are slowly moving to address these problems.

headline: Chester parents ask court to intervene
abstract: As students returned to Chester High School yesterday in the wake of two days of unrest last week, a parents' group asked a federal court to appoint a special administrator with power to overhaul Chester-Upland schools.

headline: Court backs order ending transit strike
abstract: The state supreme court yesterday affirmed a judge's order that ended a 28-day transit strike and sent 2,700 bus and trolley drivers back to work.  The court rejected the arguments of Local 85 of the Amalgamated Transit Union, which said the April 10 order unfairly deprived members of the right to strike without submitting the dispute to binding arbitration.

headline: Violence begotten of violence
abstract: Anger and outrage at a verdict that acquitted white cops of using excessive force in beating a black motorist is understandable.  But the public violence that broke out in Los Angeles in response to a stunning jury verdict will serve no useful purpose.  And there is no reason for anyone to believe that torching LA will do anything but pile one more oppressive burden on a community that finally snapped when it was wronged one more time than it could bear.

headline: 3-way presidential race can be healthy for USA
abstract: Win or lose, Ross Perot's candidacy can serve an alienated public well.  Warnings of government chaos or constitutional crisis are greatly overblown.  An independent candidate is not to be feared but is a challenge to the major parties.

headline: Gadzooks! Another forlorn jackpot
abstract: State officials for the Pennsylvania lottery said yesterday that a $6.9 million jackpot- the second unclaimed ticket in the last month- could expire this week.
