headline: Serious problems facing state businesses were given scant notice
abstract: Nearly 700 business people came to Harrisburg to the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business & Industry's Tax Summit on January 29.  Instead of talking of reform and giving them reasons to remain in PA, presenters just spoke the past to each other in partisan bickering.  Attendees wanted to hear that their political leaders appreciated the situation and were prepared to work together to correct it, but instead got political fingerpointing.

headline: One State's Utopian Dream
abstract: Long ago, in 1995, the state of Coltuckin undertook health care reform.  Historians credit Coltuckin with the first step toward the nationwide system Americans enjoy today.

headline: Children at Risk program expanding in area schools
abstract: Family and Children's Service of the Capital Region has been providing services to at-risk children and their families under the Children at Risk in Education program for six years in the Harrisburg School District and for the past year in the Steelton-Highspire School District.  Early intervention with at-risk students provides dramatic results in the kids' attitudes and is very much needed among school districts.

headline: Crash is a new setback for beleaguered Osprey
abstract: The fatal crash of a V-22 Osprey tilt-rotor aircraft could be the biggest setback yet for an experimental program that has been hounded for 3 1/2 years by funding problems but that has been free of any known technical flaws.  The accident was the second in less than 14 months for one of the gangly looking Marine Corps aircraft.

headline: Warden in Perry quits post
abstract: After a turbulent year at the helm of Perry County's prison, Warden Robert A. Shull has resigned to "pursue personal interests and family obligations."  Commissioners said Shull deserves credit for taking the prison "from zero to where it is now."

headline: 4th District Democrat: Veon
abstract: Democratic voters in the 4th Congressional District who are not satisfied with the kind of representation offered by five-term Representative Joe Kolter are flush with choices.  Democrats in the 4th District- with their job-development, transportation and human-needs problems- could do better.  They could nominate Mike Veon.

headline: Generally, they're feuding
abstract: Don Bailey, a candidate for the Democratic nomination for state auditor general, has filed a federal lawsuit charging that US Attorney James West holds his post illegally and should leave office.  Bailey, who served as auditor general 1985-1989, said that West is serving illegally because the US Senate hasn't acted on his 1989 appointment.

headline: Session did well, Singel declares
abstract: Speaking during a discussion of the session that just ended and the one that will begin next month, Lt. Governor Mark Singel touched on a variety of topics including the feud between Senate Republicans and Democrats, his legislative agenda and speculation about his political future.

headline: Pew gives grants to 57 groups
abstract: The Pew Charitable Trusts announced that 57 area organizations would be awarded grants totaling $5.9 million for providing services to vulnerable adults, including the homeless, people with mental and physical disabilities, victims of domestic violence and individuals with chronic health conditions.

headline: Christian Activists Set Their Sights on School Board Seats
abstract: Local school board races have become the new battleground for politically conservative Christian activists who believe that the public schools must be purged of their prevailing "atheist" philosophies in favor of a biblically based approach to education.

headline: CSX plans bypass Fayette railyard
abstract: CSX Transportation plans to start interdivisional runs in May that could force between 150 and 200 railroaders to move their families from Connellsville in order to keep their jobs.

headline: Welfare system subsidizes addicts' heroin purchases
abstract: Pennsylvania taxpayers have been financing heroin buys for junkies who have discovered how to make the welfare bureaucracy work for them.  Law enforcement officials say addicts have been pooling their government drug treatment payments and have been using this pooled money to buy heroin in Harlem.  Police say they use some of the heroin and sell the remainder.

headline: A campaign to have pools open on time
abstract: Mayor Rendell and Recreation Commissioner Michael DiBerardinis announced a "Pull for the Pools" campaign, a public-private effort to raise $225,000 to get the pools open on time and avoid what has become an annual embarrassment for the city: hordes of vacationing schoolchildren with no place to swim.

headline: Goode starts dishing again, with a rumor on Rendell
abstract: Former Mayor W. Wilson Goode elevated the chitchat on the street to quiet speculations when he told a radio talk show host that he thinks Mayor Rendell may be a candidate for governor in 1994.  Rendell's people say that he's not interested in other employment.

headline: Setting priorities- spending state tax dollars
abstract: Gov. Robert P. Casey's proposed $14.2 billion General Fund budget has been broken apart by who wins and who loses, and stats on where the money comes from and where it goes are given.

headline: Pharmaceutical firms say new PACE bill unwarranted
abstract: Secretary of Aging, Linda Rhodes, has charged that the PACE prescription drug rebate of 12.5 percent enacted last year will turn out to be a net loss for fiscal year 1991-1992.  In response, a proposed bill would require drug manufacturers to give PACE rebates, for which pharmaceutical firms say the new bill is unwarranted.

headline: Church and state, public and private
abstract: The President's educational policy, which would give public money to students who well might then turn around and use it to matriculate at private institutions, is baffling.  What our public schools need is support at every level.

headline: CSX wraps deal for P&LE assets; years of toil for local railroad end
abstract: CSX Corp., and $8.6 billion, Richmond, Va.-based transportation company, bought Pittsburgh & Lake Erie Railroad assets through an affiliated company.  The deal, in the works since February, followed several failed attempts in recent years by the local railroad to sell the company as a going concern.

headline: When a court judges its judges
abstract: Never before have justices of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court disciplined a colleague, or even asked to- until now.  In a 2-1 decision, the Supreme Court ordered that Justice Rolf Larsen be publicly reprimanded for "providing information to a Common Pleas Court judge relating to a matter that was pending before her."

headline: A Cheerleader for the Cities
abstract: York, Pennsylvania's, Bill Althaus may be the typical mayor of a typical American city- but his duties with the US Conference of Mayors in this election year will be anything but ordinary.

headline: Goodling challenged to show all checks
abstract: US Rep. William F. Goodling was challenged by his opponent, Democrat Paul Kilker, to release his checks and bank records dating back to 1975.  Goodling is accused of bouncing 439 checks in a 39-month period without the fees.

headline: Sharing is caring
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey has made a habit of withholding endorsements in the primary.  But he still cares enough to share his opinions.  In recent weeks, he has routinely shared his apprehension about Bill Clinton with reporters.  He did care enough to share some kind words though.

headline: Pitt doctors broke practice-plan income rule
abstract: Under a practice plan set up through corporations who collect payments from patients treated by University of Pittsburgh physicians, doctors could keep fees equal to their base salary, but through most of the 1980s, physicians kept at least $5 million in patient fees that should have gone toward education and research at the Pitt School of Medicine.  Eventually, Pitt officials say, they cracked down on the practice plans.

headline: City schools
abstract: Sunday through Wednesday news is given on schools in the city of Harrisburg.

headline: Cuomo Presses Legislators To Act on Transit Bailout
abstract: Seeking to salvage a small victory from what increasingly seems a lost cause, Governor Mario M. Cuomo proposed that the Legislature return to Albany this month to earmark $125 million for a mass-transit bailout aimed at preventing fare increases next year in New York City and several upstate cities.

headline: When city clams up, it hurts all
abstract: The police in Harrisburg, under the supervision of Mayer Stephen R. Reed, are scrambling their radio conversations and saying it is to keep criminals from knowing what the police are doing.  When the city shuts out the media, it also slams the door on citizens who depend on them to keep them informed about everything from traffic jams to murders.

headline: A Congress in decline
abstract: Members of Congress are walking away from their jobs in droves, sending perhaps the clearest signal that something is terribly wrong in Washington.  We can sit and wring our hands about the need for a new and improved Congress or we can put those hands to work building it, starting with the primary election on April 28.

headline: Goodling No. 24 on 'worst abusers' list
abstract: US Rep. Bill Goodling confirmed that he was apparently the unidentified 24th congressman on the House Ethics Committee's 24 "worst abusers" of check-writing privileges at the House bank list.

headline: Should non-teaching coaches get less?
abstract: Palmyra teachers this week took their case against a wage freeze for non-teacher coaches before a state labor relations board haring examiner.  A PLRB spokeswoman said a decision will take one to two months.  It may be appealed to the full three-member board and later to the courts.

headline: Plan offers basic coverage for all
abstract: Saying the health-care crisis has been "diagnosed to death," Robert P. Casey yesterday unveiled a wide-ranging blueprint to restructure Pennsylvania's health system, to ensure that all residents have access to affordable medical care.

headline: City schools' security chief defends search for weapons
abstract: Stanley Rideout, chief of security for the Pittsburgh area school districts, says he's not apologizing to anyone for using metal detectors and pat-downs to stem the flow of weapons in Pittsburgh public schools.  Rideout said he's convinced that randomly held searches are the only answer to keeping the street violence from entering the schools.

headline: Dickinson Twp. seeks state help on bridge
abstract: Dickinson Township officials hope a state grant will save the township money on the construction fo a bridge on Stuart Road, after supervisors unanimously agreed to apply for funding through the state's 12-year transportation program.

headline: Why Philadelphia won't get outsider to lead police
abstract: A nationwide hunt for a new police commissioner has narrowed the field to five- all veteran commanders from Philadelphia.  Fat chance that Mayor Rendell will turn the search to an outsider because an outsider would not look twice at the job.  There is no money in it.

headline: A Democrat for the 18th
abstract: The reconfiguration of the 18th Congressional District through reapportionment was tempting for Democratic candidates, with 11 lifetime Democrats hoping to win the nomination and challenge incumbent Rick Santorum, who is running unopposed in the Republican primary.  The Post-Gazette would like to endorse David Levdansky for that Democratic nomination of the 18th District.

headline: Goodling wins fight 'for name'
abstract: With the US House bank scandal plaguing him during the 19th District's three-way race, US Representative William Goodling calls this year the toughest of his life.

headline: Shuster disputes House ethics panel report of overdrafts
abstract: Millionaire Rep. Bud Shuster has become the latest Pennsylvania congressman to pre-emptively disclose his dealings with the now-defunct House bank, reporting that the House Ethics Committee claims he wrote 38 overdrafts over a 39-month period.

headline: Poll: Most want national health plan
abstract: Nearly 60 percent of Americans support a national health insurance system, a new national survey shows, and nearly as manyt people are willing to pay $600 a year to finance it.

headline: Civilians-to-be: You're out of the Army now
abstract: For those soldiers who are finishing time with the military and becoming civilians, the Transition Assistance Program (TAP) offers aid in the adjustment back into civilian life.

headline: Driving, Harrisburg style
abstract: The driving privileges that state legislatures attain are driving the citizens to frustration.  The Legislature must reform its absurd auto-leasing privileges.

headline: Williams back in LA for more interviews about top police post
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner Willie L. Williams arrive in Los Angeles for two days of interviews with the city commission that is selecting the next police chief of Los Angeles.  Williams tops a list of six finalists seeking to head the department.

headline: A desperate move
abstract: Retired Army Col. Eugene Holmes must have the longest fuse in America.  Twenty-three years after Bill Clinton wrote him that famous letter thanking him for "saving me from the draft," Col. Holmes is suddenly furious.  He's accusing the Democratic presidential nominee of purposely defrauding the military.

headline: Goodling's amendments shut out
abstract: Legislation introduced by US Representative William F. Goodling, aimed at easing the post-Cold War transition for defense contractors and former military personnel, will not reach the House floor.  The Democrat-controlled Rules Committee refused to allow the York County Republican to introduce three amendments to the 1993 Defense Department appropriations bill under consideration.

headline: Sign the 'Motor-Voter Bill'
abstract: The so-called 'Motor-Voter Bill,' which has passed in the Senate, would make it easy for citizens to register to vote automatically by combining voter registration with other routine government encounters.  President Bush threatens to veto this.  There is no valid excuse for not trying to include as many Americans as possible in the electoral process.  The president should sign the bill.

headline: Prescription Program Saved
abstract: State Secretary of Aging Linda Rhodes joins Governor Robert Casey at the Senior Citizen's Center for signing into law a bill that would save the state's prescription program for the elderly.

headline: Colleges in Virginia
abstract: Virginia's public colleges and universities, among the most enviable in the land, hae some unenviable choices to make.  They must decide how to preserve their stature in the face of rising demand and declining state funds.

headline: Facing the bridge crisis
abstract: As civic and public officals begin to appreciate what effect the rapidly approaching closing of the Fort Pitt Bridge and Tunnel, which handles more than 140,000 vehicles each weekday, will have, there is suddenly a lot of scrambling for some miracle solution that will provided an alternate route so smooth-flowing that the loss of this connection will be hardly noticed.

headline: Williams in L.A. for interview
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner Willie L. Williams is one of the 12 semifinalists to replace Los Angeles police Chief Daryl F. Gates and is in Los Angeles interviewing.  If chosen, Williams wold head an 8,300-member department.

headline: A Golden Parachute
abstract: A Selinsgrove man comments on how ex-mayor Jessie Bloom was granted the position of rural-advisor to the governor with a significant pay and benefit package for her, "useless job lacking any responsibility."

headline: GOP attacks in Arkansas
abstract: A week before the Democratic National Convention, President Bush's campaign Monday unleashed a torrent of criicism of Bill Clinotn's economic and environmental record- signaling the intensity of the contest ahead.

headline: Signs of distress are rising in suburbs
abstract: The crash of the high-flying '80s has hit suburbanites hard.  Many are deep in debt, anxious and uncertain of the future.

headline: President Unveils Health Care Plan
abstract: President Bush unveiled an election-year health care proposal that he said would "preserve what works and reform what doesn't" rather than fundamentally change the nation's health delivery system.  The proposal is built on government subsidies to help the poor and middle class purchase health insurance and cutting health care costs through a series of reforms.

headline: Colleges learning a lesson in free-market economics
abstract: A suit was filed against several Ivy League universities, alleging they violated federal antitrust laws by lowering costs by preventing a bidding war for students.  Since the universities signed a consent decree, offers of generous financial aid packages have been offered to many more students, allowing students the chance to choose among offers.

headline: Fix for pike interchange
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission plans to spend an estimated $9 million to $11 million next year to improve and expand the Allegheny Valley interchange in Harmar.  The turnpike should be ready to bid the project sometime this winter.

headline: Wilson warns violence could happen anywhere
abstract: California's Governor Pete Wilson warned the racial violence that devastated Los Angeles could happen anywhere: "I wouldn't limit it just to inner cities."  The Republican blasted "cynical efforts" to politically exploit riots and backed President Bush's calls for personal responsibility.

headline: A grass-roots approach by Jewish Democrats is urged
abstract: Democratic party bigwigs and Jewish leaders told about 500 delegates at the Democratic National Convention that the key to victory this fall is grass-roots campaigning, door-to-door style.

headline: GOP chairman assails Hillary Clinton
abstract: GOP Chairman Rich Bond sharply attacked Hillary Clinton yesterday, suggesting the wife of the Democratic presidential nominee "has likened marriage and the family to slavery."  Bill Clinton labeled the remark "pitiful."  He said it proved the Republicans had no plans of their own to talk about.

headline: Singel urges companies to expand into E. Europe
abstract: Lt. Governor Mark Singel yesterday praised Pennsylvania businesses that are expanding to post-communist Eastern Europe and encouraged other companies to do the same.

headline: Program helps teens make it
abstract: State-funded and hospital-administered Teen-Age Pregnancy and Parenting Project, TAPP, addresses costs and health issues with young mothers.

headline: Community service needed for diploma
abstract: Starting next school year, students attending Schuylkill Haven will be the first in the county who must complete a community-service requirement to graduate from high school.  The program will require students in the Schuylkill Haven Area district to volunteer for 64 hours over four years to give aid to local community groups, such as fire and ambulance companies, nursing homes and government agencies.

headline: For Pittsburgh, a Model Airport at an Immodest Price
abstract: Opened last month, the new Pittsburgh International Airport is the nation's most expensive since the Dallas/Fort Worth International opened in 1974, but represents a new age of efficiency.

headline: Witness, on stand, tells of light-bulb torture during '88 police raid
abstract: Bland Griffin Jr. took the witness stand and testified that he was repeatedly burned with a light bulb and beaten as police officers ransacked his Grays Ferry home in an unsuccessful 1988 drug raid.

headline: A land mine for Yeakel?
abstract: Lynn Yeakel's biggest problem may not be Arlen Specter.  Democrat Yeakel continues to have to grapple with questions concerning her failure to pay city wage and business taxes for 10 years while she worked in Philadelphia as a consultant.

headline: GOP headquarters
abstract: The George Bush-Dan Quayle Campaign '92 people locally will open a Republican headquarters at 7 pm Tuesday at the Hotel Sterling on West Market Street in Wilkes-Barre.

headline: Singel wins Erie County, loses to Yeakel statewide
abstract: Mark Singel easily defeated political newcomer Lynn Yeakel in Erie County, but Yeakel crushed the lieutenant governor in statewide balloting to win the Democratic nomination for US Senate.

headline: Public wants all available health care but isn't willing to pay
abstract: The only problem with the health care system in the US is that the public refuses to pay for all the available health care.  The Health Care Financing Administration came up with a  system of fee schedules for Medicare fees benefits approximately 60% of physicians and for 40% benefits no one.

headline: Condom debate flares as school board reviews courses on sexuality
abstract: The battling over the role of public schools in teaching students about responsible sexual behavior flared at a Philadelphia Board of Education meeting, when school officials unveiled a beefed-up curriculum designed to encourage abstinence.  Opponents immediately branded the curriculum stating too little, too late after the board decided in June to make condoms available to students in high school.

headline: Four-lane Route 40 still possible, PennDOT official tells FA-PAC
abstract: Fayette County probably will not get an expressway from Uniontown to Brownsville, but plans for a four-lane road still may be in the works.  PennDOT said they couldn't imagine how the state could upgrade Route 40 to make it safer while keeping it historical so building a road parallel may be the solution.

headline: 'You name it' and district justices probably handle it
abstract: District justices handle traffic offenses, listen to criminal and summary cases, issue arrest warrants and impose fines and/or restitution.  They accept guilty pleas, hold arraignments and preliminary hearings in criminal cases, and decide landlord-tenant matters and other civil actions involving amounts under $4.000.

headline: A letter to Tuesday's winner
abstract: Art Carey writes a letter to the President-to-be on behalf of the nation on what they seek in their new president.

headline: Gore accepts No. 2 position, says Bush, Quayle must go
abstract: Senator Al Gore accepted the second spot o the Demcoratic ticket by delivering a speech that blended adulation for Bill Clinton with attacks on White House policies.

headline: Singel, in LV, blames GOP for hard times
abstract: Lt. Governor Mark Singel used a state unemployment office as a backdrop for a campaign speech blaming 12 years of Republicn leadership in the White House for the nation's economic woes.

headline: Putting Price Tags On Lives In Oregon
abstract: The debate is not over.  Although the president, in the most humane act of his administration, has rejected the Oregon plan, there are intimations from below that Oregon may yet get its way if it can sufficiently cosmeticize its proposal so the plan will appear to be in consonance with the Americans With Disabilities Act.

headline: Condom Debate Widens
abstract: Officials in Maryland and Virginia are being urged to allow distribution of condoms in high schools, at a time when D.C. Mayor Sharon Pratt Kellyis pushing a similar initiative to try to stem the rising number of AIDS cases among the city's teenagers.

headline: Funding for tougher drunken-driving laws
abstract: A new federal highway program offers states millions of dollars to implement tougher drunken-driving laws, including stricter standards for determining when motorists are legally intoxicated.  In general, a state must meet four of the five requirements to receive a grant.

headline: 2 programs in LIHEAP
abstract: LIHEAP is split into two components, a cash program and a crisis program.  The cash program assists low-income people by sending money toward their heating bill directly to the utility.  The crisis program provides emergency assistance when a household has had its heat turned off or is in eminent danger of having it turned off.

headline: A nationwide movement is being started to reconnect the people to their politics
abstract: American voters, the nation's top election officials were in town to tell us this week, are not so much apathetic as angry; not so much ignorant of the issues as disconnected from the process that could address them.  The question is whether the politicians want us reconnected.

headline: Gov. Rendell? Not a chance, says Fast Eddie
abstract: Even before his masterful handling of negotiations with the city's unions, some political mavens were talking about Ed Rendell for governor.  When asked if he would consider it, Rendell answered no way, saying he had no interest in running.

headline: Skewed spud spelling found in state Capitol
abstract: It turns out that the vice president, Dan Quayle, who earliers this week became the butt of jokes for spelling the word potato wrong- he spelled it potatoe- isn't the only one who has trouble with spuds.  The Capitol cafeteria, which serves the tubers every day in every way, committed the same error as Qyayle in its printed menu, reading, "Double Stuffed Baked Potatoe."

headline: Questions Raised on Drug Used in Breast Cancer Study
abstract: Thousands of healthy women taking part ina new large-scale trial to see if a potent drug can prevent breast cancer are being inadequately informed of the risks.  Opponents of the study said the Government had not informed participants of recent research that cast doubts on the drug's safety.

headline: Consolidated school district may break up
abstract: The Kittanning and Ford City consolidation of school districts to some has been a success, but to others, a disaster.  The state Board of Education has not yet ruled on whether the district may break up.

headline: Getting to the station
abstract: For many people, the road to Station Square, the city's most vibrant nightsopot, is the Smithfield Street Bridge.  That will change, though, when PennDOT vwfina rhw long-awaited rehabilitation of the historic span next year.

headline: 31,660 get welfare here, increase of 35% in 2 years
abstract: In the past two years, the number of people inrolled in one or more of the public assistance programs has soared 35 percent in Lancaster County, to its highest level ever.  Under the 1992-93 budget unveiled recently by Gov. Robert P. Casey, welfare spending is projected to climb about 5 percent next year, to just over $4.8 billion.

headline: A president-in-training
abstract: Bill Clinton's friends and critics agree that if this complicated and guarded man is anything, he is a politician.  And has been since grade school, high school- since anyone close to him can remember.

headline: If I can make it there
abstract: It was the first nationwide gathering of the latest political movement- lunch with Ross Perot, the people's billionaire.  Perot took 340 people to lunch to solicit advice for his gestating political platform and to map campaign strategy.

headline: Skinner Shuffles Post
abstract: White House Chief of Staff Samuel K. Skinner unveiled a complex new structure to help President Bush make domestic policy, a move privately derided by Republicans whose restiveness over the operation of the White House and the reelection campaign has turned in the direction of despair.

headline: Merchantville closer to switching schools
abstract: Merchantville is one step closer to sending its hgih school students to Haddonfield Memorial High School instead of Pennsauken High School.  In a strongly worded 86-page decision, a state administrative law judge said that Pennsauken had failed to prove that it would suffer if Merchantville students went to Haddonfield.

headline: Contain costs
abstract: The State College Area school board is negotiating with representatives of the teachers' union, which will probably propose additional unjustifiable increases in teachers' salaries.  School board members should take whatever action required to stop the rapid upward spiral of school district budgets and the tax rates necessary to support them.

headline: Gov. Casey sending us a message?
abstract: Just when it appeared that the Route 222 bypass project around Reading might shift into a higher gear, along comes a political move that could delay the badly needed roadway as well as other highway projects in Berks.  Berks has waited too long- in some cases more than 20 years- to see these prjects completed.  We cannot aford to let them go for another 20 years.

headline: ACLU is seeking new ruling
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union will ask a federal court judge to reconsider his decision of limiting the scope of a child welfare suit against Philadelphia and state officials.  The ACLU is attempting to represent the failings of the child-welfare through 16 cases in hopes for reform

headline: A real loss
abstract: Several proposals have been made to reduce the size of the Legislature.  A recent Philadelphia Inquirer article provides plenty of ammunition for reform.

headline: If It Takes All Kinds, The Candidate's Staff Has Got What It Takes
abstract: Bill Clinton's eclectic campaign staff is clearly the most effective on the Democratic side this year, on significant reason Clinton now appears on the verge of the nomination, six weeks after the conventional wisdom pronounced him dead.

headline: Snakes alive! We're privy to Clinton's life as a kid
abstract: Democrat Bill Clinton has been coping with even more political din than usual.  In an interview program sponsored by the San Francisco Examiner, Clinton was talking to reporter Chris Matthews, about why "the roots from which I came have still not come across to most people in this country."

headline: Midstate projects get funding
abstract: A $50,000 grant to the Central Penn Technology Council is among funding for several midstate projects approved recently by the Ben Franklin Partnership.  Members of the 3-year council, which encourages technology-based industry throughout the midstate, will provide matching funds for a 1992-93 budget of almost $220,000.

headline: Convention Center's new art plan still makes some unhappy
abstract: The Pennsylvania Convention Center Authority has changed how it plans to spend its $2 million art budget, but advocates for local artists are complaining that they are still not getting a fair chance.

headline: Introductory high-speed rail
abstract: Swedish State Railways has taken a different approach to high-speed passenger trains from the more-famous Japanese "Bullet Trains" and French TGV, the fastest train in commercial operation anywhere in the world.  It has designed a train that tilts as it goes around curves, providing smoother performance and higher speeds on conventional tracks.

headline: Aging parents less able to care for the disabled
abstract: No one knows how many aging parents in this country are caring for disabled adult children in their homes.  Men and women didn't have the choices today's parents have.  Many simply disappeared into America's neighborhoods with their children.

headline: A rebellion in Illinois GOP bastion
abstract: In a sumptuous suburb eight miles outside of Chicago, it is Republican turf.  The loyal women of Hinsdale would be talking up the GOP presidential nominee, much the way they devoted themselves so tirelessly to the garden clubs and PTA.  But not this year.

headline: In 77th race, Mike Radis
abstract: Mike Radis and Bill Patton, both seeking the Democratic nomination in the 77th state House district, are two strong candidates, and voters will have difficulty choosing between them.  Whichever they choose, Democratic voters can't go wrong, but Mike Radis is likely to be more in tune with voters' interests.

headline: So, who's 'reckless'?
abstract: To discredit Bill Clinton's foreign-policy ideas, President Bush needs to have some of his own.

headline: MIT on trial in accusation of price-fixing
abstract: Massachusetts Institute of Technology is scheduled to stand trial this week in an antitrust case in which the federal government accuses it of conspiring with other schools to fix tuition and aid offers.

headline: Critics say state lied about test anonymity
abstract: Representatives of local parent and taxpayer groups accused state education officials of lying abou the use of personal student information being gathered on a new state test.

headline: Harrisburg West pike work to start
abstract: After 32 years, the Harrisburg West Interchange of the Pennsylvania Turnpike is ready for a face-lift, and the Turnpike Commission  has hired Frederic R. Harris Inc., a Philadelphia firm, to handle the design work.

headline: Anemic safety net ends up more costly
abstract: In an editorial from Feb. 27, the Patriot has once again attacked general assistance welfare recipients by resorting to the stereotype that the majority are able-bodied with all the skills necessary to be employed.

headline: A reliable vote
abstract: Despite what some disappointed congressional candidates seem to be suggesting , the Pennsylvania AFL-CIO doesn't have to be fair.  The organization's executive committee endorsed state Representative Mike Veon for Pennsylvania's 4th District seat in Congress.  The move is to solidify union clout on Capitol Hill, to enhance the AFL-CIO's Washington power base.

headline: Governor balks on sales tax
abstract: Republican legislative leaders made an unsuccessful, last-ditch bid to convince Democratic Governor Jim Florio to enact a bill lowering the sales tax from 7 to 6 percent on July 1.  The Governor is expected to conditionally veto the bill, setting the stage for a political showdown by forcing the Republican Legislature to seek its first override.

headline: Solving local job woes a difficult task, candidates say
abstract: The candidates vying for the 46th Legislative District seat in the state House, Victor Lescovitz and Susan Miscovey-Berton, agree that western Pennsylvania has a serious economic problem- Beaver County alone has the highest unemployment rate among the state's 15 major labor market areas.

headline: Money awarded for teen parent program
abstract: The Erie School District has been awarded a $248,000 state grant that will be used to expand its school program for teenage parents with the goals being to keep more teenage parents in school so they graduate and to help them get jobs so that they become self-sufficient.

headline: Deal reported with teacher accused of sex harassment
abstract: A Middletown Area School District teacher accused of sexually harassing female students has been allowed to strike a deal to prevent being fired and losing his retirement benefits.

headline: Heard on the Hill
abstract: JD Fogarty, deputy executive director for finance with the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, stated, "In order for the road to pay for itself, tolls would have to be three times the rate set by the commission."  He was commenting on the $1.25 rate fixed for traveling the full 13.5-mile length of the Amos K. Hutchinson Bypass.

headline: Brrr: Heating assistance slashed
abstract: The state's Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program fudning has been cut 21 percent- from $123 million last year to $97 million this year.  Betty Hicks, Cumberland County administrator of the program, says that she expects requests for energy assistance to increase this year, but some people who need assistance will not get it.

headline: A sampling of blacks finds support for Rendell
abstract: Mayor Rendell's televised address last Friday on the city's "last and best offer" to the city's blue and white-collar workers may have altered the apparent racial split among Philadelphians' support for the unions.

headline: Governor recycles the same ideas from '91
abstract: A year from Gov. Casey's State of the State address, PA still wallows in an economic recession but again the governor sprinkled his annual review speech with economic programs intended to at least give the state a peek out from under crushing fiscal circumstances.

headline: Some states' systems thwart voter sign-ups
abstract: More than a dozen states have voter-registration systems that keep people out of the election process, the League of Women Voters said yesterday.

headline: Montco pol throws block at Haverford
abstract: Thanks mostly to blocking tactics by Senator Richard Tilghman of Bryn Mawr, Haverford State Hospital hasn't had a full board of trustees since 1987.

headline: Deconsolidation would put CD back on track in educationd
abstract: The Ed.D.'s are experts in only one category- they all know how to build a bureacuracy.  The only way we're going to get education back on track is through smaller units.  Therefore, The Central Dauphin School Board should break up the jointure and sell the Administration Building to AMP.

headline: Heard on the Hill
abstract: Senator Edwin Hall  made the statement, "A familly of obviously limited resources were trying to muster enough money to purchase sandwiches, but thy were unable to come up with enough to buy one for each family member."  He was telling of what he saw at a turnpike restaurant and why he is urging the Turnpike Commission to add minimarts at the plazas to allow low-income travelers to buy the makings for nutritious meals.

headline: Clinton Economic Plan Targets Poor Families
abstract: Extolling the virtues of free enterprise like a Republican speaking to a local Rotary club, Democrat Bill Clinton today chose a poor, inner-city neighborhood in DC as the backdrop to unveil the details of a $1.5 billion-a-year plan to encourage poor people to save, start their own businesses and revitalize their communities.

headline: A Specter aide finds article wanting
abstract: In a May 31 article concerning Senator Arlen Specter and US Attorney Michael M. Baylson, The Inquirer outrageiously spreads innuendos while admitting that absolutely nothing improper has occurred.  Although Senator Specter responded to a request from the writer, Emilie Lounsberry, for an extensive interview, she left out the most important points.

headline: Graded on a curve, Bush flunks
abstract: The founding father of Reaganomics, Arthur Laffer, says President Bush's economic performance has been a disaster.  "I really think Bush does not deserve to be re-elected," Laffer said.

headline: Southeast Delco teachers' union approves pact after long impasse
abstract: Teachers in the Southeast Delco School District voted yeaterday to accept a tentative contract granting them a 6.5 percent raise each year over six years.

headline: Most would bar strikes by teachers
abstract: Depite passage of recent legislation limiting teachers' right to strike during a school year, most Pennsylvania residents do not believe teachers should have that right at all, accoridng to a Pennsylvania State University poll.

headline: Deer Lakes halts 'outcomes' plan
abstract: Deer Lakes has added its name to a growing number of school districts that have postponed state-mandated action on new education proposals.  Directors voted Monday night to halt the planning process that marks the beginning stages of transformation to outcome-based education.

headline: Heritage group sets two completion dates
abstract: Lackawanna Heritage Valley Authority will soon be in the market for red ribbons to cut after setting completion dates Thursday on its first two construction projects.  The rail passenger boarding platform at the Scranton Iron Furnaces will be dedicated May 23 two days of ceremonies coinciding with Memorial Day and the resumption of rail excursions at the Steamtown National Historic Site.

headline: Coatesville bashing?
abstract: Some assessments penned by the director of the Chester County Assistance Agency and distributed to members of a task force fighting the proposed closing of the Coatesville welfare office seem to confirm that the move isn't predicated solely on economic issues.  They also seem to contradict the idea that the decision isn't what the director called "Coatesville-bashing."

headline: A speech by Terry Waite at Phila center canceled
abstract: A speech by former hostage Terry Waite, scheduled for tonight at the Charles and Elizabeth Gershman YM and YMHA has been canceled due to low ticket sales.

headline: Greenwood needs GOP: Gift of Persuasion
abstract: James C. Greenwood, the Republican candidate for Bucks County's congressional seat, needs to do only one thing to win in November: persuade most of his fellow Republicans to vote for him, which will not be easy.

headline: Specter and Yeakel will go at it tomorrow in debate on live TV
abstract: Television viewers will see Republican Arlen Specter and Democrat Lynn Yeakel live in their first and probably only televised debate, which will broadcast from Pittsburgh at 7pm tomorrow night.

headline: Museum celebrates expansion downtown
abstract: The Museum of Scientific Discovery, in addition to this year marking its 10th birthday, on Tuesday, will celebrate a grand opening.  It has expanded to inlcude space not only on the third floor in Strawberry Square, but also areas on the first and second levels.

headline: Did Archiocese wait too long on schools?
abstract: In 1988, fear that Catholic schools' days are numbered rang out in a national Catholic magazine.  Today, Catholic educators across th country are far more upbeat, with a much brighter vision for the future of Catholic schools.

headline: Improved state rail system is urged
abstract: Local industries said they are losing business to foreign competitors, and will continue to do so, unless Pennsylvania improves its railroads, which are too low and not wide enough to accommodate the heavy equipment companies manufacture and ship.

headline: Dueling with The Day Care Lobby
abstract: Child care at home amounts to a huge unregulated industry, and it is one the states are finding very hard to handle.

headline: A spirited race shaping up for NJ governor
abstract: The New Jersey governor's race has attracted some of the biggest guns of American politics.  Two major challengers are lining up troops an dmoney to take on a tax-scarred incumbent.  The race has begun to revolve around a single issue: Jobs.

headline: Greenwood savors a tough victory over Kostmayer
abstract: State Senator James C. Greenwood had worked so hard and fielded so many congratulatory phone calls by yesterday afternoon that he did the only sensible thing a congressman-elect could do: he went for a leaf-kicking walk with his two daughters.

headline: Specter appeals for unity
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter, facing a tough re-election fight and worried about preserving his Republican base, tried to recruit Pennsylvania's GOP anti-abortion leaders to his banner.  The effort was generally rebuffed, according to two participants in the private session.

headline: Nepotism charged at community college
abstract: Community College of Beaver County has been saddled with AJ University, A for Albanese and J as in Javens, because two of its trustees have those names.  It has also been nicknamed because it employes five members of the Albanese and Javens families, and they are not the only trustees with kin working at the college's campuses in Center and Chippewa townships.  The number of kin at the publically financed college is too many, according to Representative Michael Veon.

headline: Diplomas Guarantee Less
abstract: The link between education and worker performance is hard to measure.  Research suggests that a high school diploma or its equivalent is less of a guarantee of basic workplace competence than it used to be.

headline: Lawmaker, wife injured in car crash
abstract: State Representative Thomas C. Corrigan Sr. and his wife, Annabelle, were seriously injured yesterday morning when their car slid off a rain-slicked roadway in Pemberton, NJ.  Annabelle Corrigan was treated for spinal injuries while Thomas Corrigan suffered injuries to his left arm.

headline: Florio signs sweeping changes in welfare law
abstract: Governor Florio signed legislation that includes a controversial provision denying welfare mothers increased payments if they have more children, extended now to the state of New Jersey.  If the program wins federal approval as state officials expect, it will initially take effect in the three counties with the most welfare recipients: Essex, Hudson, and Camden.

headline: A third choice in Pa.
abstract: There is a third choice in Pennsylvania's senatorial election this year.  His name is Dr. John Perry, and because of a petition drive that secured 48,000 signatures, he is our only alternative to two candidates who are nearly indistinguishable.

headline: Groups seek to give the homeless power through the ballot box
abstract: The National Coalition for the Homeless has asked the Board of Elections to review the interpretation of the law for who can vote to include those who do not possess an an address of a nighttime shelter.

headline: Specter crime-fight talk 'hypocrytical,' Democrats say
abstract: Republican Senator Arlen Specter talks up his record as a crime fighter and says his Democratic opponent, Lynn Yeakel, is "really on the extreme" because she opposes the death penalty.  Democrats say Specter is a bit hypocritical for not mentioning his previous job as a defense lawyer.

headline: New Futures, old problems
abstract: Pittsburgh New Futures, a coalition of city, school, business and community leaders trying to reduce teen pregnancy and dropouts and boost student achievement and employment, has failed to reach most of the 1991 goals the city had set in its application.

headline: Discussion becomes racial policy review
abstract: An impromtu discussion of racial policy in the Reading School District developed among leaders gathered in the high school which addressed the district's curriculum, hiring policy and disciplinary problems.

headline: LCB plan targets drinking, driving
abstract: Cumberland County officials helped the state Liquor Control Board launch a new campaign that targets drinking- and drinking- and driving.  The county agreed to place a bright yellow bumper sticker on all county-owned vehicles and marked municipal police cars.  Its message- "Impairment begins with the first drink.  Never drink and drive."

headline: Food program bills unpaid
abstract: Commissioner Vern L. Eppinger is threatening to stop the county surplus food distribution program for elderly and low-income citizens unless the controller pays the bills for it.  Controller Richard Cini, however, claims that the money budgeted to cover the $18,189 in outstanding bills has already been spent by Eppinger.

headline: A vote for Perot is a vote for Bush
abstract: All Ross Perot wants is a piece of the resentment vote, which could be considerable this time.  The trouble is that a vote for the colorful liar from Texas is a vote for George Bush, the guy who deserves all that resentment.

headline: Hafer appointments were so political
abstract: Just three days after her re-election, Auditor General Barbara Hafer created two $83,900-a-year jobs at the top of her department for her campaign manager, David Sanko, and a former campaign aide, Patricia Jardine.  If nothing else, these appointments, and the arguments used to justify them, diminish Hafer's stature.

headline: Specter discounts the static from the Thomas hearings
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter states that he does don’t believe that the election is in any way a referendum on the Justice Thomas hearings.  His women's issues record is matchless, he says.

headline: New high school, expansion of 3 other buildings approved
abstract: An eight-year battle over building and renovation plans in the Lewisburg Area School District apparently has ended.  The school directors have adopted a $27.7 million comprehensive facilities plan which calls for construction of a new high school, renovation and expansion of three other buildings and the closing of another.

headline: Drexel starts swap with China silk firm
abstract: Drexel University announced that it had signed a five-year agreement with a major Chinese silk company, exchanging design tips for fashion internships.

headline: Leetsdale overpass gets needed funding
abstract: Leetsdale will likely be getting a new overpass above a dangerous railroad crossing.  State and Allegheny County officials have agreed to provide $4 million for the overpass, which would connect Broad Street with Buncher Industrial Park along the Ohio River.

headline: For many people, welfare means survival
abstract: The state Department of Public Welfare reports a record number of people are now relying on the government to help them survive.  Welfare is not only assisting those who are unemployed; there is an increased need for working people to turn to the government for help in food and medical bills.

headline: Acting on impulse
abstract: After Ed Rendell's landslide victory, he established just how temperamental, passionate, and brave he is.  The story goes over several notable points in Rendell's career that show the attributes that made him a great mayor.

headline: Hafer says Singel spending improper
abstract: The state Auditor General's Office says spending improprieties shown in the latest audit of Lt. Gov. Mark S. Singel may have been minor but are a recurring matter.

headline: Specter endorsement doesn't surprise Friend
abstract: Rep. Stephen Friend says he isn't surprised that the Republican State Committee overwhelmingly endorsed the re-election bid of Sen. Arlen Specter.  Friend comments that the people who voted for the bid of Specter weren't representative of the party and for what it stands.

headline: Noteworthy
abstract: State Representative Michael Sturla will be among the scheduled speakers at a scoial-sercices workshop at Millersville University.  Also, the state Board of Education approved changes to controversial public school reforms that were previously approved by the board's council.

headline: Education series flawed
abstract: The series of articles which describes the "Capital Region 2000 plan for Education" has some serious flaws of fact and reasoning.  Educators, students and the public have to change their attitudes and the idea of stack 'em deep and teach 'em cheap must be eradicated.

headline: Limo services blast 'gypsy' operators
abstract: Miffed limousine-service operators from around the state came to the Capitol to warn limo renters that "gypsy" operators are taking them for a ride in more ways than one.  About two dozen limo operators said the problem with uncertified, fly-by-night services is getting so bad that the "bad guys" are nearly outnumbering the honest services.

headline: Grant is announced
abstract: Berks County has received $195,000 to provide drug and alcohol services for child welfare agency clients as a part of a $3.6-million statewide grant program.

headline: Ad watch
abstract: Nicole Weisensee analyzes Arlen Specter's and Lynn Yeakel's television advertisement attacks on each other.

headline: Hafer says WAMs need fiscal review
abstract: In an effort to improve the overall accountability of state funding, Auditor General Barbara Hafer said that her department will conduct a detailed review of the Legislative Initiative Program, more commonly known as "Walking-Around Money" or WAMs.

headline: Specter fights for intelligence panel post
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter has honed his radar on the Senate Intelligence Committee.  After taking a two-year leave of absence from an eight-year appointment to the panel, he's launched a bid for the post of ranking Republican.

headline: Noteworthy:
abstract: Representative Thomas R. Caltagirone is coordinating a demonstration of non-toxic retardants by a former Reading Fire Department official.  The Sierra Club has scheduled a "Toxics Use Reduction Summit" conference at Harrisburg Area Community College.

headline: Educator Cites Need to Keep Higher Education Affordable
abstract: A major challenge for higher education in the 1990's is to keep college open, accessible and affordable to students from all economic circumstances and backgrounds, the president of Harvard University said today.

headline: MADD tree is in memory of road-slaughter victims
abstract: A white pine tree was planted by Mothers Against Drunk Driving as "a special rememberance" for the victims of drunk driving, a crime that last year killed more people than gunshot wounds.

headline: Hector: Get a job, any job, but don't accept welfare
abstract: A letter in response to a story of "Hector" who doubted value of taking a low-wage job vs. welfare payments: Something is horribly wrong with the welfare system that allows able-bodied people to sit around and have others support them for the simple reason that they can’t find the 'perfect job.'  Welfare was never intended to serve this purpose.

headline: Advice for city and union negotiators: Don't look at the trees
abstract: For the leaders of Philadelphia municipal unions: a recommended reading  is an article in the Feb issue of Skiing Magazine entitled " Learning to Learn," which in it can be seen that skiing and negotiating are strikingly similar.  Both are learning experiences in which people must go against their initial instincts and do things in ways that may at first seem awkward, but will evenutaly become natural, enabling success.

headline: Hafer strong; 4 Democrats at odds
abstract: Although Barbara Hafer's disastrous bid to unseat Gov. Casey two years ago was unsuccessful, with the April 28 primary coming up, she appears to be in a strong position to prove that reports of her political death were greatly exaggerated.  Four Democrats are vying for the Democratic nomination.

headline: Specter gets big boost from Philly Dem
abstract: Democratic state Senator Hardy Williams endorsed Republican Arlen Specter in his re-election bid for the US Senate, marking a first for Philadelphia politics.

headline: OBE delays frustrate educators
abstract: Whle opponents to outcomes-based education are celebrating a partial victory in Harrisburg, some educators are frustrated by what they see as another delay in the educational system.  Governor Robert Casey, yielding to opposition headed primarily by conservative groups, asked the state Board of Education to put off approval of 57 state outcomes until January, when the board had planned to vote today.

headline: Erie School District might cut programs to balance budget
abstract: Joseph Rodriguez, superintendent of the Erie School District, said the district's estimated $4 million deficit will force district officials to pare all but the most essential programs to balance the budget for the 1992-1993 school year.  The state's financial crunch has created most of the problem for the district by reducing education subsidies.

headline: Maglev, transit budget cuts draw fire in Senate
abstract: Several senators made it clear that they're concerned that the 1993 Bush budget cuts mass transit funding by a third and eliminates a demostration project for a magnetic levitation train, even though Transportation Secretary, Andrew Card, appears to be assured.

headline: Home heating assistance to begin on Nov. 30
abstract: The state Welfare Department next month will begin accepting applications for assistance with home heating costs.

headline: AFL-CIO leaders Decide It's Time to Endorse Clinton Presidential Bid
abstract: AFL-CIO endorsed Arkansas Governor Bill Clinton for the Democratic presidential nomination in an effort to put to rest any idea of a brokered convention and allow the party to begin focusing on the general election contest against President Bush.

headline: Hafer wants WAM accountability

abstract: Trying to regain momentum, Jerry Brown returned Monday to traditional themes- national health care and employment.  Although Bill Clinton is considered the favorite, Brown said he hopes he can duplicate Sen. Edward Kennedy's upset win over Jimmy Carter in the 1980 Pennsylvania primary.

headline: In California, wind's not blowing Bush's way
abstract: Ontario, Calif., the city 40 miles east of Los Angeles- the kind of burgeoning suburb that has become a weather vane of both California and national political winds- offers little good news for Bush one week before Labor Day, the traditional start of the fall campaign.

headline: Making room for some old laws
abstract: An unveiling of a collection at Temple University includes books that contain laws written in 1773.  William Rawle, founder of the country's oldest continuing law firm, acquired these books and now his descendants own them, and the books will be kept at Temple University.

headline: SEPTA, union realized strike hurts everyone
abstract: Louis J. Gambaccini, SEPTA's general manager announced the details of a new contract with 5,149 members of Transport Workers Union Local 234, barely averting a strike that would have left 450,000 Philadelphians without their usual transportation.

headline: Welfare bill: Reform or politics?
abstract: Pennsylvania House Republican leaders have unveiled a six-bill legislative package proposing sweeping reforms in PA's welfare programs.  Democrats will argue that the "package" is more "political" than "welfare reform."

headline: Area lawmakers say they don't abuse car leasing
abstract: Several lawmakers in the Scranton area say that the car leasing perk of state government is not abused by them.  They say that while some lawmakers do go overboard, not everyone takes advantage of the car leasing perk.

headline: High Court Invites Move By Congress On Mail-Order Tax
abstract: The Supreme Court handed over to Congress the delicate task of deciding whether states can tax sales made by national mail-order companies, thus taking a course likely to prolong rather than settle this multibillion-dollar debate.

headline: Stop complaining
abstract: The retired state employees were not forced to accept free coverage so they should stop complaining.  They still have a choice.

headline: In Harrisburg, 81-year Statehouse coverup continues
abstract: Things will stay as they were in 1911 outside the state Capitol, when sculptor George Grey Barnard covered up the male marble statues on the statehouse lawn after onlookers become outraged at his depiction of male genitalia.  The Capitol Preservation Committee considered a $2.6 million project to restore the aging nudes.

headline: Many public school recruits
abstract: The University of Pennsylvania's president, Sheldon Hackney, appreciates the support of the Inquirer, and comments on the suit brought over their Mayor's Scholarship program that they actually provide more scholarships to students from Philadelphia than the number for which they are legally bound.

headline: SEPTA's impasse
abstract: A strike for Philadelphia's transit authority, SEPTA, would mean another cut out of the city's already struggling economy, amounting to an estimated cost of $2.5 million a day.  This is not the case of a greedy union, so SEPTA general manager Louis Gambaccini ought to find room for agreement that doesn't break SEPTA's bank and gives the workers a decent deal.

headline: Welfare cuts costs, not people
abstract: In Pennsylvania we propose to conatin costs, not by ripping holes in the safety net, but by preserving core services and expanding others that help the poor move from welfare dependency to self-sufficiency.

headline: Area legislators voice differing views
abstract: State legislators and political candidates voiced opposing views on Monday's Supreme Court decision.  Several quotes are given by candidates.

headline: High school leaders vote to go with Perot
abstract: America's high school leaders have picked Ross Perot as their choice for president.  More than 1,500 student leaders, meeting at the annual National Association of Student Councils, gave Perot 41.5 percent of the vote.

headline: Strong Perot vote could send election all the way to House
abstract: The prospect of Ross Perot running an independent campaign for president this fall has led electoral mathemeticians back to dusty sections of the US Constitution.  They are consulting that rarely used provision outliing the manner by which Congress- not the people- elects the president.

headline: In their own words
abstract: Quotes are given of what presidential candidates George Bush and Bill Clinton stated regarding defense, jobs and the environment and on urban renewal at separate addresses.

headline: Many vote to keep others out
abstract: Those who are fighting to keep Little Flower Catholic High School for Girls open, rejected the suggestion made by Superintendent Constance Clayton that the School District lease space in three Catholic high schools on the archdiocese's hit list.

headline: Shuster pledges support
abstract: US Representative Bud Shuster, has promised to push for a bypass of a commercial section of Rutes 11-15 in Snyder County.  He told members of the Route 15 Coalition that he will work for the proposed bypass around Hummels Wharf and Shamokin Dam.

headline: Welfare office staff hits plans for move
abstract: Local welfare office workers and some other local residents are upset that the state is planning to move its welfare office to the 103-year-old Masonic Temple at 1115 11th Street.  The vacant, decaying building doesn't have enough room or parking for the office's approximately 150 employees plus clients, they said.

headline: Armstrong executives take pay cuts up to 25 percent
abstract: Top executives at Armstrong World Industries Inc., based in Lancaster, accepted salary cuts of up to 25 percent in 1991 due to weaker financial performance last year.

headline: Hillary Didn't Want Confrontation
abstract: Hillary Clinton was warmly received at the pre-election dinner of the Lackawanna County Democratic Committee on Tuesday at Fiorelli's in Peckville.  Governor Robert P. Casey avoided the dinner, lest his appearance imply acceptance of the abortion-on-demand policies of Clinton.

headline: Strong, weak points
abstract: Each of the three candidates brings his own strengths and weaknesses to Sunday night's first presidential election.  Each candidates' are listed.

headline: A Deal's Undoing Stirs Deficit Fears
abstract: Sixteen months ago President Bush preached about doing something to stop mortgaging the future of young people, but today, Bush seems willing to borrow a little more from the young people's futures to protect his own.  In three interviews Bush claimed that his "essential" budget compromise of 'no new taxes' with Congress was a "mistake."

headline: In this corner, Vincent Fumo
abstract: Democratic state Senator Vincent Fumo is investing heavily in Democrat Bill Keller's campaign for state representative in South Philadelphia, according to finance reports filed yesterday.  Fumo's campaign lent $20,000 to the Keller campaign, and a political action committee associated with Fumo lent the campaign $37,500.

headline: Maybe Pitt doesn't need state funding
abstract: If the University of Pittsburgh can spend $92, 550 on the installation of a university president, maybe it doesn't need any funding help from the state budget.  The alumni association has pledged $10,000 toward the cost of installing J. Dennis O'Connor, and if more is needed, private funding should be sought.

headline: State aid for transit won't rise, Millar is told
abstract: Rep. Dwight Evans, the chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, told PAT General Manager William Millar that he shouldn't expect any increase in state aid for mass transit next year.

headline: Welfare plan shortsighted
abstract: State House Republicans are right- the welfare system needs to be overhauled.  But they need to fine-tune their reform proposals.

headline: Army, VA urged to probe complaints
abstract: Pennsylvania's two senators and a congressman are demanding explanations from the Army and the Department of Veterans Affairs because of complaints from injured members of the 14th Quartermaster Detachment about inadequate medical care, paperwork delays, or the level of disability awards.

headline: Home Free
abstract: In Houston this Sunday, a merry group called the Independent Committee for Ethics will be treating the media to a guided tour of the legal residences of George Bush.  He was driven to his home of Texas in a bid to avoid a capital gains tax back in 1981, when Bush insisted that Maine was his home, describing his seaside estate as his prinicpal residence.  Yet the IRS, generally knowing a vacation home when it sees one, sent him a bill for $198,128.

headline: Supreme Court does justice to practice of perks
abstract: The Supreme Court is the unrivaled perk palace of the federal judiciary, but court members do not have the kind of ugly public controversy over their trappings of office that has engulfed the House and executive branch.

headline: A declaration on end of recession
abstract: The US recession technically ended several months ago, but the final nail in its coffin may be struck Dec. 21 when the National Bureau of Economic Research meets.  The private research organization of highly regarded academics has become the de facto "official" monitor of when US recessions begin and end.

headline: In this race, all's fair in love and in presidential politics
abstract: Mary Matalin, deputy manager of President Bush's campaign, and James Carvill, a top strategist in Bill Clinton's campaign, are significant others in their non-political lives, but currently they are tending to business, which means they are working mightily to elect their chosen candidates.  And that has created a highly distasteful situation.

headline: Penn State trims expenses, considers 'clustering' as state-aid slide continues
abstract: Higher education in Pennsylvania is at a fork in the road, where rising costs, declining state support and changing student bodies are forcing universities to re-evaluate programs and organizational structure.  The commonwealth's largest institution of higher learning, Penn State, is well along in its own process of self-examination as it looks to trim expenses by 10 percent over the next three years.

headline: State sees return on investment
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey saw the return of a $1.25 million investment into a state highway project five years ago at R.D. Werner Co., Sugar Grove Township, when state lawmakers, local union leaders and company management broke ground on a $2.5 million, privately financed plant expansion.

headline: When assistance is cut off, she faces desperate times
abstract: A woman has been on General Assistance for most of her adult life, angry with politicians who cut GA without fully considering the consequences for people like her.

headline: As Bush Ratings Sink, Some Sense Parallels with Carter in 1980
abstract: After an impressive foreign-policy victory, the president looks like an ineffectual leader, saddled with a weak economy, dropping like a stone in public opinion polls and suffering fromm a debilitating ideological challenge within his own party.  President George Bush's situation is looking much like that of Jimmy Carter's in 1980.

headline: Honoring PA's veterans- if they'll pay for the medals
abstract: Pennsylvania wants to honor veterans with a special medal, but state leaders say the former soldiers would have to pay for the recognition.

headline: Survey Finds Newsrooms Discontented
abstract: In a study sponsored by the Freedom Forum, a foundation endowed by the sewspaper publisher Frank E. Gannett, researchers documented what may be unprecedented discontent inside newsrooms and a basic discomfort among journalists with what ends up inside their newspapers and on the airwaves.

headline: A rival tax plan debuts
abstract: House Democrats finished work on a bill that would squeeze the rich and cut taxes for just about everyone else.  Bush promised to veto any Democratic income tax increase that reaches his desk, even though his own budget contained about $23 billion in increased taxes and fees.

headline: In Year Of Outsider, Yeakel Just Might Win
abstract: Lynn Yeakel took the Democratic primary with a videotape of Senator Arlen Specter interrogating Anita Hill, thus forming the Year of the Woman.  A tough race still ensues, but the outsider could just preside over the insider.

headline: Pilot program allows merchants to pass savings onto schools
abstract: When a new program in Beaver Falls kicks off this fall, area schools could find themselves with free globes, dictionaries, computers, microscopes, band equipment and other supplies if city merchants participate in Power In Education, a national program based in Pittsburgh.

headline: Subway worker's widow sues SEPTA
abstract: The widow of a SEPTA worker killed 2 years ago in an accident on the Broad Street subway has sued the transit authority an dfive individual employees under the federal civil rights law. Doris Beerhalter, whose husband, Michael, was hit by a SEPTA train while he investigated reports of malfunctioning signal lights, filed the report one day before the statute of limitations expired.

headline: When Giving Up Welfare For a Job Just Doesn't Pay
abstract: One of the most commonly denounced problems in welfare policy is that many mothers cannot earn much more than the welfare system alone provides, and some actually earn less.  Many working mothers also lose health insurance, for themselves and their children.

headline: As GOP prepares, the mood is somber
abstract: Republican delegates readied for the opening of the GOP convention in a more somber mood than usual, schasised by the sour economy, their intra-party fight on abortion and the low standing of President Bush in public opinion polls.

headline: Hospital ready to build funds for expansion
abstract: More than six years since first announcing plans for a major renovation and expansion, Memorial Hopital is set to start its community fund-raising campaign with an invitation-only kickoff celebration.

headline: Survey Indicates Blacks Strongly Back Democrat
abstract: A survey released yesterday suggests there is enthusiastic support among blacks for Democratic presidential nominee Bill Clinton, seeming to contradict earlier predictions that black support for Clinton was begrudging at best.

headline: All those coins add up-to millions and millions
abstract: Through good economic ties and bad, the bistate commission has proved to be a thriving moneymaker (total assets of $122 million) that shows no signs of slowing down despite its original mission to make crossing the upper Delaware free for commuters.

headline: Incumbents Hafer, Knoll atop polls
abstract: Latest poll results show incumbents Auditor General Barbara Hafer and Democratic state Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll with commanding leads over their respective challengers, Craig Lewis and Lowman Henry.

headline: Principals' contracts at issue
abstract: A three-member arbitration panel met in the Palmyra School District administration building to begin a process aimed at resolving a dispute with the district's principals.

headline: Va. Panel Reduces Proposed Bond Issue for Roads
abstract: The Virginia General Assembly, a kepy committee of the House of Delegates, slashed $132 million in transportation projects from a proposed bond issue and rushed the measure to the floor for a vote expected later in the week.

headline: YMCA is looking for new quarters
abstract: The Altoona YMCA has decided to look for a new home an dis considering converting its aging Lexington Avenue facility into low- and moderate-income housing.

headline: Ask LaGrotta about foes
abstract: State Representative Frank LaGrotta, is not at a loss for words when it comes to describing his three opponents, US Rep. Joseph Kolter, state Rep. Michael Veon, and Ron Klink, in the upcoming Democratic primary race for Pennsylvania's Fourth Congressional District.

headline: Hospital saga has happy ending
abstract: The state and a community group signed an agreement for reopening the former Philipsburg State General Hosptal.

headline: Tabloid Politics, the Clintons and the Way We Now Scrutinize Our Potential Presidents
abstract: For Bill Clinton, the issues regarding his rocky marriage remain before the voters- questions about honesty, character and judgement.  The 1992 election should become known as the Tabloid Campaign because of the all-too-familiar charges of philandering.  A comic is attached regarding facts and tabloids in debate.

headline: Balance the federal budget?
abstract: The public concentration on the House bank scandal and other congressional miscues has forced Congress to face not only its own fiscal problems but the nation's dismal deficit.  Whether they do anything or not not, senators and representatives realize that they must at least recognize an escalating $4 trillion federal deficit or risk being voted out of office.  And so, movement is solidly toward a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution.

headline: Incumbents won't resign early
abstract: Senator James C. Greenwood says he may be willing to resign his Senate seat ealry if he wins his bid for Congress this year- but not if it means turning over control of the chamber to Democrats.  The aspirations of both Greenwood and Senator H. Craig Lewis for higher office have raised the possibility that Bucks County willl be without a voice of its own in the state Senate for at least two months next year.

headline: Private school ponders
abstract: Students at the Friends Select School, a private Quaker School at 17th Street and the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, have asked school officials to consider making condoms available to them.

headline: Traffic prognosis: clogged arteries
abstract: During the first week of the 19-day Port Authority Transit strike, drivers made a strong effort to avoid the Golden Triangle.  But slowly, traffic has been returning downtown, disrupting travel considerably and this week threatening to develop into the gridlock officials feared when the strike began.

headline: $5.5 Million Grant Targets Lead Poisoning
abstract: The Fannie Mae Foundation, an arm of the Federal National Mortgage Association, yesterday donated $5.5 million to create the National Center for Lead-Safe Housing, with the goal of protecting children from toxic exposure to deteriorating lead paint foundi n much of the country's older housing.

headline: Aspiring to Govern
abstract: The policy advisers that Bill Clinton has cultivated, or who have cultivated him, are a diverse lot who share a common ambition: to wield power within the next Administration or influence it from without.

headline: House balks at subpeonas
abstract: House Speaker Thomas S. Foley said that the Justice Department has issued far-reaching subpoenas for House Bank records, including those of members who had no overdrafts.

headline: Tailhook is trying to polish its image
abstract: Spurned by the Navy and fearful of becoming forever identified with drunken debauchery, the Tailhook Association has hired a public-relations consultant and launched an ambitious attempt at image-polishing.

headline: Budeget countdown: 47 days
abstract: The tranquil mood over the opening of the budget season ended when House Republican Leader Matthew J. Ryan accused House Democrats of abruptly closing what he said had been an open budget process.

headline: Inmate camp's fate hangs on public hearing
abstract: Several of the 11 counties that are members of the SEDA Council of Governments questioned whether the economic development organization should proceed with plans to build a proposed regional inmate work camp in the Sproul State Forest.

headline: Program helps truckers pass exams
abstract: An innovative curriculum, developed by the Institute for the Study of Adult Literacy, in Penn State's College of Education, allows for commercial truck and bus drivers to use computer courseware that provides interactive basic skills instruction as an aid for the new federally mandated licensing exam.

headline: Transit programs to help disabled tainted by fraud
abstract: A federal transportation audit found fraud and fat profits among private companies hired by local transit systems to pick up people who cannot ride regular buses or subways.

headline: 115 Communities Listed 'At Risk'
abstract: There are 115 municipalities throughout Pennsylvania, most in the western part of the state, identified as "at risk" for financial difficulties.The 115 affected municipalities include cities, townships and boroughs and represent five percent of the total municipalities of the state.

headline: Assistant to Governor visits Ellwood City
abstract: Robert W. Grotevant, special assistant to Governor Robert P. Casey, emphasized that "there will be a tax decrease" for Pennsylvania residents for the new fiscal year during an informal press briefing at the Ledger office.

headline: House Bank Crusaders Feel the Heat
abstract: When the House meets again next January, will the "Gang of Seven"- the brash crusaders against the House Bank- all be there?  All but one of the seven Republican freshmen are threatened with defeat in their first reelection campaigns.

headline: Tailhook spurs women's election-year ire
abstract: The Tailhook scandal in which Navy officers sexually assaulted 26 women and then engaged in a cover-up just grows and grows.  And with it the "Anita Hill Factor" in the 1992 elections grows exponentially.  With national discontent at a 26-year high, voters are sending a strong signal of their own to incumbents of both parties: "We'll remember in November."

headline: Budget battles raging
abstract: This year's budget season looks suspiciously like the recession-plagued campaign from the spring of last year.  A year of fiscal 1992 tax increases, which pumped $16.2 billion worth of new revenue into state coffers, and a slew of budget cuts failed to balance finances in 35 states.  Conditions in those states forced governors to propose spending cuts of $5.7 billion over the last 12 months.

headline: PSEA does political homework
abstract: Though the Pennsylvania State Education Association slogan is "Quality Education: Our Commitment, Our Challenge," its interests are far from wholly altruistic, since the union protects the economic needs and desires of teachers, seeks to preserve their professional their professional status and job security.

headline: Unblocking Access, for now
abstract: Port Authority Transit company might make all disabled persons within a certain distance of fixed transportation routes pay full fares for Access rides, until other ways of complying with the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act are fully explored.

headline: 25,000-seat amphitheater to be built on Camden waterfront
abstract: A $12 million amphitheater will have 7,000 sheltered seats and 25,000 seats altogether.  The theater will be built on a 14-acre site alon g the river south of Ulysses Wiggins Park in Camden.  It will share parking with the new aquarium.

headline: Attacks by fax captivate media
abstract: It used to be that presidential candidates made their attacks directly.  Then they left the matter to "surrogates."  This year, the Bush-Quayle campaign is employing a high-profile "fax attack," a strongly worded anti-Clinton missive sent to newspapers across the country.

headline: House endorsements
abstract: The Tribune-Review lists its endorsements for the Pennsylvania House of Representatives.
