headline: Talking heads
abstract: The tease goes on.  Bill Clinton and President Bush teams go courtin' Ross Perot and his volunteers, but Perot won't decide until Thursday if he'll get back in the race.

headline: Budget Countdown: 12 days
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey yesterday certified the state's official revenue estimate for the 19992-1993 fiscal year, predicting the state will receive $14.587 billion from tax and other revenue.

headline: School Boards Need Guidance
abstract: Gov. Casey made a speech before the Pennsylvania Association in which he said future balanced budgets are possible if schools would control costs, and do not depend on routine increases in local taxes or special appropriations lacking accountability for payment, and that local schools expect either the state or their own taxpayers to pay for administrative pay raises and/or elaborate programs.  If local school boards and the school administrations continue to ignore the temper of the times, publice discontent may arise and bring some of the facts of life to their attention.

headline: Union leaders rejected proposal for 1-year contract
abstract: Leaders of the bus-trolley drivers union rejected a proposal for a one-year contract during the 11th hour attempt over the weekend to head off a strike of Port Authority Transit.

headline: A homeless program gets high marks
abstract: A program called the Homeless Family Initiative, which is run by the Philadelphia Health Management Corporation (a nonprofit public organization), although it ended two years ago, shows a high rate of success that advocates for the homeless say the city should consider adopting some of its methods.

headline: Attacks vicious in debate
abstract: During a debate that focused more on attacks than issues, state Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll called her oponent a hypocrite yesterday and Lowman Henry accused her of unethical behavior.

headline: House members travel to San Juan
abstract: Two state House members, Ruth Rudy and Louise Bishop, traveled to San Juan at taxpayers' expense for the annual conference of the National Order of Women Legislators in Puerto Rico, which included a crise to the Virgin Islands.

headline: Talks lag on judge discipline
abstract: As the legislative clock ticks toward summer recess, efforts to change the way that Pennsylvania discipline judges have become snagged, raising fears among advocates that overhauling the system will take two more years.

headline: Budget countdown: 14 days
abstract: The Budget 11, a group of legislative leaders, scheduled a sit-down for the first serious interparty, interhouse session on seeking a compromise over differing views on how the state should spend $14.2 billion over the next fiscal year.

headline: School choice remains issue here
abstract: This year, Pennsylvania lawmakers doused the idea of giving parents a $900 voucher good towards tuition at any non-public school in the state.  The plan was killed on constitutional grounds.

headline: Unused rail lines can serve two purposes
abstract: Railbanking is a critical tool to the preservation of this nation's elaborate system of unused, although not necessarily abandoned rail lines.  Railbanked lines, while saved for future transit or freight use, can be used for recreateion in the interim.

headline: A suburb grapples with changing identity
abstract: To their chagrin, Cheltenham Township residents have found that a 60-foot-wide avenue doesn't protect them from is happening in the city of 1.6 million on the other side.  Cheltenham is a magnet for Koreans who want to be near their North Philadelphia businesses, changing the suburbs into a community that is aging, racially diversifying, and increasingly influenced.

headline: Auditor general race: Watching the watchdog
abstract: The race for state auditor general, a job referred to as Pennsylvania's fiscal watchdog, is taking a strange turn this year.  The incumbent, Barbara Hafer, says that her office and campaign car were the target of politically motivated break-ins, possibly to pilfer an audit report she intended to keep under wraps.

headline: Issue of Adjusting 1990 Census Is Revived
abstract: A year after the Bush Administration decided against adjusting the 1990 census to compensate for an undercount in the inner cities, the adjustment issue is back.  The question this time is how to adjust the biennial population updates that Congress uses to distribute tens of billions of dollars to state and local governments annually.

headline: Task force to push for public hearing
abstract: Despite fears that it won't sway an impending decision by state officials, a task force formed to halt the closing of the Coatesville welfare office is forging ahead with plans for a public hearing on the matter within 30 days.

headline: Budget hearings get a fresh perspective
abstract: Traditionally, the annual Senate Appropriations Committee public hearings are held with only state government "insiders."  However, this  year the Appropriations Committee heard testimony from the Pennsylvania Economy League (PEL), a non-partisan private sector expert on finance and budgets.

headline: School equality in 1992 falls under scrutiny
abstract: During a program honoring the 38th anniversary of the landmark Brown vs. Topeka Board of Education decision, many African American students and former students spoke of their experiences as the minority in predominantly white school districts.

headline: USAir-British Airways Talks Stall
abstract: President Bush and British Prime Minister John Major failed in weekend talks to bridge diffferences that threaten British Airways PLC's proposed $750 million investment in Arlington-based USAir Group Inc.

headline: As more national stores move in, Chestnut Hill debates its future
abstract: Weeks of demolition and months of construction to follow will cap a two-year tussle between Wheeler Development Group of Washington and the Chestnut Hill community over what was going to be built on the site, which had been vacant for more than three years.

headline: Back Kilker in 19th
abstract: The 19th Congressional District has a high profile race..for the first time in years.  There rarely has been any competition for the seat in the last three decades.  Paul Kilker is the better choice for the 19th Congressional District.

headline: It isn't Hillary, it's the children
abstract: Hillary Clinton's attackers are firing wildly and racing from the scene.  In their zeal to exploit a politics of division, Clinton's critics created the specter of a Willie Horton in our own homes- the litigation-happy child.

headline: Teacher honored by Bush
abstract: Etheletta L. Charles, from Montour County, who went from teaching in a classroom to tutoring illiterate adults was selected yesterday by President Bush as his 859th Point of Light.  Each day President Bush recognizes a Point of Light, a person who successfully addresses social problems through volunteer service.

headline: Budget proposal passed
abstract: The House narrowly approved an unusual two-option budget plan for 1993 that includes proposals to double the defense spending cuts proposed by President Bush and to funnel as much as $12 billion into programs next year.

headline: School strikes most in 9 years
abstract: The largest number of teachers' strikes in nine years idled more than 100,000 Pennsylvania students last year, according to information compiled by the Pennsylvania School Board Association.

headline: When someone dies on the tracks, the train operator is a victim, too
abstract: At SEPTA, half the drivers of the Broad Street subway have hit and killed someone on that line, operators say; some have killed more than one.  Whether it be a kid playing on the tracks, a passenger taking a shortcut, a drunk falling from the platform, or a suicide "jumper," the life of a train operator is victimized with the trauma that the operator experiences.

headline: Businessman hailed for 'extensive community involvement'
abstract: Receiving the York County Bar Association's Liberty Bell Award "is one of the nicest surprises you can get, " said the 1992 recipient Thomas W. Wolf.  Wolf, president of the Wolf Organization Inc., was honored for his "extensive commmunity involvement" that has "stimulated a deeper sense of individual responsibility so that citizens recognize not only their rights, but their obligations to the community."

headline: Backers want Bush to fish for Baker aid
abstract: Bush-Quayle campaign officials had their minds on Wyoming yesterday, where, they are convinced President Bush will ask his old political friend James A. Baker III to shelve diplomacy for politics.

headline: It was down to two
abstract: Bill Clinton's vice presidential choice came down to selecting between Tennessee Senator Al Gore and former Massachusetts senator Paul Tsongas.

headline: Teachers go back to work
abstract: Classes were back in session in North Schuylkill School District yesterday, signaling the end of a nearly month-long teachers' strike that could resume if arbitration produces no results.

headline: Budget tricks work no magic
abstract: In a time of fiscal crises, last year's $3 billion state tax increase failed to live up to expectations, becoming an easy target for those who hope to score a few political points.

headline: School talks break down in Abington
abstract: Contract talks broke down last night in the Abington school district, and officials said schools would be closed today for the expected strike.  The teachers union had said last week that it would go on strike at 6:45 am today if no settlement had been reached, and school officials notified parents that the schools would be closed if a strike occurred.

headline: Who decides highway project funding?
abstract: Politics are undoubtedly a part of highway funding decisions, but with the State Transportation Commission being evenly divided between parties, they claim to keep partisan politics out of their decisions.

headline: Cheaper and better technology illuminates the city
abstract: The Philadelphia light show glows from high points like Liberty Place to the Ben Franklin Parkway and the renovated 30th Street Station.  There are neon sculptures that add some funky rays to our stately and historic surroundings, as well as old favorite bright spots like Boat House Row and City Hall.  Three Foundation for Architecture volunteer guides created this Philadelphia illuminated tour last year and then created a two-hour bus tour on city lights.

headline: Bad employment figures mean bad news for the President
abstract: The lates discouraging economic news couldn’t have come at a worse time politically for President Bush.  He leaves the country this weekend, in the middle of the presidential campaign with his approval ratings falling, for an economic summit in Europe.

headline: It's Keno to the Rescue in Md.
abstract: The nation's newest gambling craze, which uses one of the oldest kinds of lottery, is headed for Maryland.  As Governor William Donald Schaefer looks for money to fill a budget shortage, his is counting on a new lottery game that officials say will look familiar to anyone who ever played keno in Las Vegas.

headline: Teachers in 2 Adams districts to work while talks continue
abstract: Teachers in two Adams County school districts have agreed to work under the terms of the old contracts while negotiations on new agreements continue, and talks reached an impasse in two other county districts.

headline: Bush Accepts Some Blame for Economy In a New Hampshire Campaign Stop
abstract: President Bush made his first re-election campaign appearance in New Hampshire and accepted part of the blame for the 'free fall' in the nation's economy.  He vowed to keep the 1990 budget agreement in place to maintain caps on federal spending, and had said his proposals would include individual retirement accounts, a cut in capital gains tax rates, extension of the research and development tax credit, and a good health program.

headline: Schools defend research projects
abstract: The funds for projects at Marywood College, Pennsylvania State University, and Carnegie Mellon come from more than $684 million set aside by Congress for non-competitive awards to colleges and universities in fiscal 1992.  Some observers say the increasing number of earmarked projects reflect the financial problems of higher education and efforts by lawmakers to bring money home to their districts.

headline: Workers- PennDOT sold jobs
abstract: A state grand jury is investigating alleged job selling and Democratic Party patronage in the Pennsylvania Transportation Department, according to workers who were subpoenaed.

headline: City eyes $750,000 to restore property
abstract: Harrisburg will receive $750,000 in state and federal funds from the Home Investment Partnership Program to buy, restore and sell vacant property for new homes, a project called Capital Corridor Project.

headline: Baker's courage and vision will revive White House
abstract: Jime Baker had tears in his eyes when he said goodbye to the State Department he has served so well, but his savvy and directness will bring the White House to life with a swiftness that few expect.

headline: Judge asked to rethink decision not to oust lawyers for McDade
abstract: Joined belatedly by their star witness, prosecutors yesterday asked a federal judge to reconsider his refusal to disqualify the defense team for US Representative Joseph McDade in his trial on bribery and racketeering charges.

headline: Term limits, the big election winner, is no more restrictive than the Bill of Rights
abstract: Term limits won in all 14 states that voted on them last Tuesday, in 13 of the 14, term limits got more votes than Bill Clinton got.  Term limitation, another openness-enhancement, is no more "anti-democratic" than the Bill of Rights.

headline: Bush insists the nation is in a recovery
abstract: President Bush said Wednesday- as he often does- that economic recovery has begun.  Jeff Faux of the Economic Policy Institute, a labor-backed think-tank, has little sympathy: "He's going through the difficult routine of trying to distance himself from conditions he created."

headline: Schools plan personnel cuts
abstract: Philadelphia school officials released a detailed list of 373 personnel cuts that they're making to plub a projected $24 million deficit in the budget that begins next year, but no teachers are expected in the layoffs.

headline: Yes, we have no bananas
abstract: The War of the Banana Counters is over, the Port of Wilmington has own, and in the aftermath there are a few lessons for the Port of Philadelphia to ponder.  The episode occurred when the Port of Wilmington discovered recently that the Delaware River Port Authority (DRPA) was spreading promotional literature in Central America claiming that the Ports of Philadelphia are "the largest banana port in the USA."

headline: City fund was beneficial
abstract: Lenora M. Smith, in announcing her candidacy for state representative in the 103rd legislative district, said that $7 million was given to people who won't bring anything back to the city; however, it helped finance many community and economic development projects in the city.

headline: Barbs, sparks, fur fly in a South Phila race
abstract: Guy Ciarrocchi and Robert Donatucci, for state House of Representatives, quarrelled in wordslinging combat for the campaign.  Ciarrocchi has challenged Donatucci to a debate, but the incumbent isn't biting.  "Not with his lies, his innuendos," he said during a recent interview.

headline: It's the Candidate, Stupid!
abstract: Bill Clinton and Al Gore probably assembled as good a staff as anyone has ever put together for a Presidential campaign.  But the dirty little secret is that they would have won with the staffs assembled by Michael Dukakis or Walter Mondale.  It has always been our belief that consultants don't win elections; candidates do.

headline: The battle goes on; Senate rejects local justice nominee for 2nd time
abstract: Attorney Steven D. Guinter was rejected as Governor Robert P. Casey's nominee for the post by the Senate, leaving the local district justice seat officially vacant.

headline: Bush Says Economy Is Not as Bad as People Think
abstract: Hours after his Democratic rival began broadcasting a television commercial accusing him of misjudging Americans' economic pain, President Bush told a national radio audience today that the economy was not nearly as bad as people believed.

headline: Schools say tax rebates unlikely
abstract: A Commonwealth Court ruling requireing school districts to rebate extra funds received from the state does not affect most area school districts, officials say.  Act 25 requires rebates from districts that received funds over their budgets.

headline: 13-year-old sut on trout could be cast out of court
abstract: Whether there will be a trial will be determined today when visiting Columbia-Montour County Senior Judge Jay W. Myers holds a hearing on a defense motion to dismiss the 13-year-old lawsuit about if sediment from the quarry has gotten into Antes Creek, affecting the trout population, due to inactivity.  The plaintiffs are fighting the dismissal , claiming it has teken years to obtain expert evidence to prove Antes Creek has been damaged by sediment from a stone quarry.

headline: City is sued to force housing in Fairmount
abstract: Both the US Justice Department and a local public-interest law firm filed coordinated federal lawsuits that accuse the city of Philadelphia of failing to provide housing for the mentally ill homeless.

headline: 'Bargaining' brochure a waste of time, money
abstract: A brochure released by an agency created by Governor Robert Casey, Pennsylvania Schools Cooperation Committee, is dubbed, "A Guide to Bargaining for Better Education."  It is downright ridiculous.  The Pennsylvania State Education Association doesn't need or want a brochure to tell its contract bargaining experts how to get more money for its members.

headline: It's Their Party: The Democrats' Midsummer's Nightmare
abstract: In story form, the article looks at how Democratic candidates handled the Democratic National Convention.

headline: The Case Against Casey
abstract: Comparing Roe v. Wade with Planned Parenthood v. Casey, the New Republic must conclude that the Reagan and Bush justices on the Rehnquist Court- the archconservative dissenters as well as the compromising majority- are even less principled than their Burger Court predecessors.

headline: California's Budget Impasse Leaving Suppliers in Lurch
abstract: California is on their 42d day without a budget.  Because the state has run out of money to pay its bills, the thousands of vendors who supply state menatl hospitals, schools, prisons and other institutions with nearly everything from syringes to eggnog are beginning to hurt.

headline: Scores up slightly on SATs in '92
abstract: High school seniors nationwide averaged slightly higher scores on the Scholasstic Aptitude Test this year, halting at least temporarily a worrisome decline blamed on television, immigration and inadequate education.

headline: 2 awarded $309,513 by judge
abstract: A Dauphin County judge has awarded $309,513 in attorneys fees to two men, Carl H. Lunderstadt and Bradford C. Bernardo, who were acquitted of fraud in connection with the sale of granite to Pennsylvania for its Capitol addition.

headline: City's next target: Cars parked around City Hall
abstract: Mayor Rendell and City Council President John F. Street vowed yto do away with one of the most prized perks in Philadelphia officialdom- free parking on the plaza around City Hall.  They state that the area has become intolerably cluttered, even unsafe for pedestrians.

headline: Beaver County precincts hand victory to Laughlin
abstract: In the midst of all the hullabaloo at Javy's in Ambridge Tuesday night, Susan Laughlin grinned like a Cheshire cat in a pink jacket.  Although only 54 percent of the Beaver County precincts were in, reports showed Laughlin was leading by a 3-1 margin for her second term as state representative.

headline: Jackson re-emerges as pivotal '92 player
abstract: Reverand Jesse Jackson's role in the 1992 elections is pivotal, with the ultimate fate of Bill Clinton's candidacy hinging on whether Jackson is on board and happy in his work.  Ross Perot's candidacy is also taking (white) votes away from Clinton, so if Jackson supports Clinton, he may be able to confiscate the (black) votes to make up for the ones he lost.

headline: The Character Issue
abstract: The wondrous aspect of the vice presidential debate was to have Vice President Quayle raising the so-called character issue in supposed favor of George Bush and against Bill Clinton.  Yet the president in whose behalf this standard of steadiness was invoked has been the ultimate chameleon in all his years in national politics.

headline: Casey tires of fighting utilities' tax breaks
abstract: After months of insistence, Governor Casey said that he'd given up pushing the legislature to fix a mistake in state law that has allowed elecitric companies to escape paying about $77 million more in taxes annually.

headline: Scranton students score in average range of state assessment
abstract: Students in the Scranton School District scored in the average range in 70 percent of the areas tested under the new state assessment system last spring.

headline: 2 jailed for non-support of children sue county
abstract: Francis A. Marsico, the brother of an area state legislator, Rep. Ron Marsico, and another man briefly jailed for supposedly not paying child support are suing Dauphin county over how it enforces collections.

headline: Clinton's economic program is welcomed by U.S. mayors
abstract: Bill Clinton told mayors that his economic plan would create jobs and investment dollars to rebuild cities, drawing an enthusiastic embrace from urban leaders seeking federal help in the aftermath of the Los Angeles riots.

headline: Being Hollywood's host could mean big bonus in attracting other movies
abstract: Long after the filming stops and Eddie Murphy and other stars leave the capital city, this week of playing host to Hollywood could mean a bonus for Harrisburg.  Ron Jury of the state Department of Commerce said the location work here this week for the movie "The Distinguished Gentleman" could have a lon-term effect by attracting other films to the city.

headline: Jerry Brown's last stand at convention tonight
abstract: Renegade political holdout Jerry Brown was busy penning his speech Tuesday in preparation for an uninvited- and unpredictable- appearance before Demcoratic convention delegates today.

headline: The darkest hour at the register
abstract: Jeff Dougherty works the night shift at the 7-Eleven at 23rd and Passyunk in South Philadelphia.  He has undergone several stick-ups, but continues to go back to work regardless.  The benefits he sees in his work make it worth the occasional robber and the night work.

headline: Centre County unemployment at 6.1%
abstract: According to the state Department of Labor and Industry, Centre County's unemployment rate for November was 6.1 percent, the second consecutive month it was lower than a year ago.  For the month, Centre County had the seventh lowest unemployment rate of the state's 40 labor market areas.

headline: shaking Our Lady of Confidence
abstract: Our Lady of Confidence, a parochial school for mentally retarded students, is at risk for parceling kids out to different classrooms in different parishes.  This week, officials from the Office of Catholic Education reassured parents that Our Lady of Confidence will survive- somewhere.

headline: 3 fugitives in car crash, flee
abstract: Three fugitives from Perry County Prison wrecked a stolen car in Clinton County and fled the scene.

headline: Commissioners OK $6.7 million for bond projects
abstract: Cumberland county commissioners yesterday sanctioned a $6.7 million bond issue to finance several projects and agreed to buy a downtown bank for $1.02 million for conversion to county offices.

headline: Beleaguered Jacksonville ends status as borough
abstract: Residents of Jacksonville, the beleaguered little place in Indiana County in western Pennsylvania, took the somber step last week and disbanded the borough's government.

headline: Jesse on the whinepath
abstract: Some may be convinced that Jesse Jackson is on the Republican National Committee's payroll.  The Rev. Rainbow seems intent on making life miserable for the Democratic presidential ticket.  But there's nothing that says party leaders have to respond to Jackson's crabbing.  And if they're smart, they won't.

headline: The debate degenerates
abstract: In his televised debate with Sen. Arlen Specter, state Rep. Stephen Freind displayed an in-your-face aggressiveness that is well within the bounds of acceptable political combat, but his post-debate behavior was not.

headline: congress will be eager to act on economic plan
abstract: With a radically different Congress, eager to act, the next president will have a quick opportunity to tackle America's economic problems and to try to contstruct a comprehensive health-care system.  Tax cuts, too, were promised, but the huge budget deficit stands in the way.

headline: Six Area Firms Launch Day-Care Programs for Children
abstract: Six Washinton-area businesses announced yesterday that they are investing more than $2 million to fund 16 projects to care for workers' children, including a science and technology summer camp in Silver Spring and a program to care for children on school holidays.

headline: 33 lb. Of cocaine a month
abstract: Joseph Dragone admitted that he was a cocaine dealer to the US Drug Enforcement Administration saying he imported several pound to Western PA about a dozen different times.  An agreement was made between the US attorney's office and federal prosecutors that for exchange of info he wouldn't be charged, but days after the deal was finalized, Dragone backed out.

headline: Commissioners support state bond issue referendum
abstract: Indiana County Commissioners want voters to authorize the state to borrow $350 million to continue funding grants and low-interest loans through the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority.

headline: Better mammograms demanded
abstract: About 100 women, Governor Robert P. Casey and his wife and top legislators from both parties at an emotional Capitol Rotunda rally, urged the General Assembly to set statewide standards for mammogram testing.

headline: Jobs for the area? Kanjorski staffers aren't even local
abstract: Paul Kanjorski has a strange slant on how to create jobs for his home congressional district.  While the latest numbers show more than 10 percent of the workforce around here is unemployed, Kanjorski has managed to keep his office payroll top-heavy with out-of-towners.

headline: The Democrats Slog On
abstract: Though Bill Clinton plainly has his work cut out for him, and the Democratic party is prickly, skeptical and perverse, he won four states, which together, is impressive.  He keeps chugging along.

headline: Consumers are showing confidence in economy
abstract: Economic indicators in the vital areas of consumer outlook and houisng offered more evidence of a continuing recovery from the long national recession.  A report by the Conference Board said consumer confidence in the economy jumped sharply in May for its third straight monthly advance.

headline: State education officials delay new regulations
abstract: The state Board of Education is scheduled to act Nov. 18 on new regulations establishing what students will be expected to elarn in school, according to a Department of Education spokesperson.  A decision expected early in September was postponed due to the amount of information to consider from hearings on the issue.

headline: 400 state jobs are up for grabs
abstract: Schuylkill County's newest prison, the State Correctional Institution/Mahanoy, is making 400 jobs available for when it opens next year.  A job fair will take place where an informed estimate of 6,000 are expected to apply.

headline: Council approves ordinance that requires smoke detectors
abstract: Dillsburg Borough Council unanimously approved what could be the first of several fire and building codes by passing an ordinance requiring smoke detectors in all residential units.

headline: Bill Clinton began the day running hard.  He was to cover eight states before going home to Little Rock
abstract: Exchanging high-fives with Teamsters, teenagers, homemakers and men in business sutis, Governor Bill Clinton began an arduous 4,100 mile, eight-state election eve campaign finale with a raucous breakfast rally at a Northeast Philadelphia diner.

headline: Judge offers redisticting plan
abstract: A Commonwealth Court judge yesterday recommended that the state Supreme Court approve a congressional redistricting plan that would eliminate the seat of at least one Republican while severely jeopardizing the re-election chances of another.

headline: The Economy's Final Report Card Before Election
abstract: With a publication of the gross domestic product, a week before election day, President Bush may get one final chance to contend that the ecoomy has finally begun to emerge form the rare limbo between recession and recovery in which it has hovered since mid-1991.

headline: Democratic Governors, Bush Tangle on Budget
abstract: Democratic governors interrupted President Bush's piitch for his economic program to accuse him of budgetary gimmicks, creating a "sewer of debt" and of favoring the rich.

headline: State going after LIU boss
abstract: The Department of Education will be filing a formal complaint that may cost Luzerne Intermediate Unit 18 head Kevin O'Connor his job.

headline: 5 out-of-state men charged after major marijuana bust
abstract: More htan 900 pounds of marijuana with an estimated street value of $5 million was seized and five alleged out-of-state "major-level drug dealers" arrested, state police Commissioner Col. Glenn A. Walp said.

headline: Council expected to approve project
abstract: John O. Vartan decided not to take City Council's suggestio to bring revised plans for his Forum Place high-rise project before planning commission for a once-over.  Now the decision whether to give an initial go-ahead to the $82 million project will fall back into the hands of City Coucil, which is expected to vote on it Tuesday.

headline: Bill Clinton clearly best hope to bring the nation together to tackle festering problems
abstract: There is no question that Bill Clinton is up to the challenge of the presidency.  It's time to change course.  The country needs a fresh start, a new vision and vigorous leadership.  Bill Clinton is endorsed by the Patriot News because he is clearly the best hope among the three candidates to bring about an American revival in the 1990s.

headline: Jury set to decide on firing of voter registration clerk
abstract: A federal court jury has been asked to determine if the fired Snyder County voter registration clerk was a whistleblower or power hungry media star.  Delight F. Swinefold is seeking damages over her firing saying she was fired in violation of the whistle-blowing law for compiling a list of 31 alleged state Election Code violations.

headline: The great bungee binge
abstract: Just as people are getting used to the idea of bungee jumping, both Pennsylvania and New Jersey temporarily banned it, citing safety concerns after two people died in bungee jumping accidents in the United States.

headline: Democrats' tax-cut bill does little, indicating the status quo really suits them
abstract: Dan Rostenkowski, chairman of the tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee, created a bill that Paul Tsongas states "is not serious either as economic stimulus or distributive justice.  It just scratches the legislative itch to have a tax bill every year."

headline: State leaps into education reform
abstract: Education in Pennsylvania has taken a step toward the 21st century with the adoption by the state Board of Education of new regulations designed to recognize some basic truths about the learning process.

headline: 8 county attorneys seeking judge post
abstract: At least eight county attorneys, three of them women, are seeking to fill the open judge's seat on the Lancaster County Court bench.  They are applying for the position left vacant by the death of Judge Louise G. Herr, who died April 30.

headline: Despite Aid, a Queens Bakery Is Shutting Down and Moving
abstract: The Taystee Bakery plant was forced to close, although it received government aid.  An estimated 500 people lost their jobs at the factory, and many are heading to Pennsylvania to see what those factories have to offer.

headline: Bill Clinton: Born to Run..and Run.. and Run
abstract: Bill Clinton was first elected as governor in 1978 at age 32, lost a bid for reelectionin 1980, but ran again in 1982 and was victorious.  From the start, perserverence has been his trademark.

headline: Just do it
abstract: Voter turnout continues to decline so people must understand that change starts with themselves.

headline: The Mirage of Campaign Reform
abstract: We've spent the past 20 years talking about how to keep money from corrupting the political process.  The more we talk, the worse the problem seems to get.

headline: Economy isn't slipping again, forecasters say
abstract: According to a survey of some of the nation's top forecasters, the economy is not dipping back into recession.  The consensus is that the economy will grow at an annual rate of just 0.5 percent in the January-March quarter.  Despite the teeter-totter of the economy, economists suggest a modest recovery by summer.

headline: State Squelches Deconsolidation
abstract: The state education department has turned down a request by the Armstrong School Board to reverse the consolidation of its school system, saying the change would be detrimental to education.

headline: A lawyer's long trail of alleged deception
abstract: A. Terry Daly, a lawyer with offices in South Philadelphia, was arraigned Aug. 7 on 26 criminal counts stemming from the grand jury's probe into his handling of six lawsuits over the last six years.  In each case, the grand jury alleged, Daly persuaded accident victims to lie in an attempt to defraud heavily insured defendants who had nothing to do with the accidents.

headline: Disabilities act beginning to have impact
abstract: Public accommodations provisions of the Americans with Disabilities Act went into effect in late January, causing a major impact on how public places, businesses, airports, and hotels accommodate those with disabilities.

headline: Bill Clinton's next big hurdle: The Speech
abstract: Bill Clinton is headed for another Democratic National Convention and another vital moment.  He will take the convention podium to claim the presidential nomination for himself.

headline: Justices receive a hefty pay hike
abstract: The state Supreme Court might face an unprecedented crisis of confidence amid charges of criminality, but its members are, nonetheless, getting a hefty pay raise.  Governor Casey yesterday signed without comment legislation raising salaries for six Supreme Court justices.

headline: The mouse that roared
abstract: A mouse that made Stephen Gogola lose control of his Volvo, crashing into a utility pole and causing him back and neck injuries, died in the accident, which story is much like that of President Bush.  With Bush's wars and lagging economy, local leaders are asking whether or not Bush will kill the mouse by dragging state and local Republican candidates down with him.

headline: Economy stirs: Building picks up as inflation quiets
abstract: Two government reports suggest that the nation's economy may be stumbling to its feet with a higher level of home construction and minimal rises in consumer prices.

headline: State's decision is best for district and residents
abstract: The ruling by the state Department of Education allowing Reynolds Area School District to keep $68,000 from an original $116,000 overpayment makes good common sense.  Dividing that amount among taxpayers- after spending $17,000 to refund the money- would have been an unwise use of their money.

headline: A man on the edge- who fell
abstract: Marseilles Desire Ebron, a man who has been in and out of prison since juvenile years, fell from that edge early yesterday, shot dead in his car by police after a 10-hour roadside standoff in Huntingdon Valley.

headline: Fairfield Fire Company receives $50,000 state loan for new building facilities
abstract: The Fairfield Community Fire Company has received a Volunteer Loan Assistance Program check for $50,000 from Pennsylvania Lt. Gov. Mark S. Singel.  The low-interst lloan will help pay for a recently completed quarter-million-dollar building which houses the fire company's apparatus.

headline: Blair is given unfair order
abstract: The state has Blair County by the throat, wanting the county to raise probation officers' salaries, but at the same time the fiscally troubled state wants to cut the budget for probaton officers.

headline: Kanjorski threatens to subpoena White House aides
abstract: Congressional Democrats attacked White House perks, as five aides to President Bush boycotted a Capitol Hill hearing on the subject.  US Rep. Paul E. Kanjorski, chairman of the House subcommittee on human resources, threatened to subpoena those officials if they continued to refuse to testify.

headline: The odd couple of city politics
abstract: Three months into office, Mayor Edward Rendell has found a friend in Senator Vince Fumo, though Fumo was asked last spring about the crowded Democratic mayoral field, and he was certain of one thing, "I won't support Eddie."  They confer regularly on budget issues, mayoral appointments and a wide array of other matters.

headline: Forest County Taxes Up
abstract: Forest County Commissioners have adopted a budget for 1992 that increases real estate taxes four mills.  Until this budget year, certain cash reserves allowed the county to balance the budget without increasing taxes, but this year new mandates and costs for housing prisoners, health insurance, court fees, and improvements to the courthouse property, make the tax increase inevitable.

headline: Student defaults costly
abstract: CareerCom Corp. announced yesterday that 19 of its schools could lose their access to federal student loans or financial assistance programs due to high student default rates.

headline: A new generation of killers, feeling no blame and no shame
abstract: After interviewing 18 teenagers charged with murder, the Inquirer found that this generation of youth has a more casual attitude toward human life, saying a single murder is no big deal.  The cases represent a trend toward teenagers imitating remorseless, senseless violence portrayed in movies and television.

headline: Former Samters Building Being Readied for Fall Debut
abstract: The former Samters and Jon York building is fast becoming home to a host of state agencies, where the plan calls for a complete renovation of the building, with exterior rehabilitation designed to meet historic preservation standards established by the secretary of the interior.

headline: Both hopefuls claiming most experience in 101st
abstract: Both State Representative Edward H. Krebs and Republican Lebanon County Commissioner Rose Marie Swanger are vying for the seat that covers a portion of Lebanon County, and both claim they have the most experience in that area, the 101st District.

headline: Kanjorski's statement regarding his bad checks
abstract: The complete transcript of Kanjorski's statement along with some previous comments is given.

headline: The Perot Factor
abstract: A three-way race among Independent Ross Perot, President Bush and Democrat Bill Clinton raises the possibility that there will be no clear-cut winner on Election Day.  How could a deadlock occur?  What would happen next?  A guide is given based on the Constitution and election laws on how we choose the president.

headline: Goodling, Gekas seeing upward trend in economy
abstract: US Representative William F. Goodling says a sure-fire method to jump start the economy is to keep Congress at home.  Games being played in a political year don't help the economy, it doesn't help the United States, and the longer the House and Senate members stay home, the greater the hope for an all-out recovery.

headline: Students are left out of teacher pay wrangle
abstract: Any serious discussion of educational matters has been notably absent from all the wrangling over a new wage schedule for Dallas teachers.  The teachers, students and taxpayers in the Dallas School District deserve a fair and speedy resolution to the current contract dispute.

headline: A refuge for the illicit
abstract: For  years, drug dealers at Richard Allen Homes have been terrorizing residents, some of whom suspect collusion between the dealers and workers at Philadelphia Housing Authority.

headline: Giving her all to help others
abstract: Rev. Justine Hall pastors a church, runs a homeless shelter, rents aprtments to homeless families and people with AIDS, and in a project she calls "Broad Street," she runs an all-purpose help center for the needy to be housed in a vacant storefront church.

headline: Both sides confidently await judge's verdict in Flaherty budget suit
abstract: Common Pleas Court will decided whether city Controller Tom Flaherty's claim that his office can't survive a $506,000 budget cut is indeed valid.

headline: Keeler rises to top pulpit in U.S.
abstract: At a time of much debate over the direction of the Catholic Church, Archbishop William H. Keeler brings a reputation as diplomatic trouble-shooter to his new position as American Catholicism's chief spokesman.

headline: The Perot Factor: Who'll Get Hurt?
abstract: Ross Perot's candidacy could determine the election's outcome, but whether his name on the ballot most helps President George Bush or Bill Clinton is uncertain.

headline: Governors prescribe welfare, budget cuts
abstract: Governors across the country emphasized solutions to the biggest deficits state governments have ever faced.  Some focused on cutting welfare grants, while others spoke of cutting state agency-spending and laying off workers.

headline: Students rap plan for cuts
abstract: Students frustrated over proposed cuts in state funding to their universities rallied in the Capitol, saying tuition hikes resulting form the reductions could force them to drop out of school.  In his 1992-1993 budget, Governor Robert P. Casey proposed cutting funds to the 14 state-owned universities by 3.5 percent, or $13 million.

headline: A riot post-mortem
abstract: While it is being left to other bodies to reflect on what steps are needed to address the social causes of urban rioting, an inquiry being launched into police handling of the tumult in Los Angeles could provide much needed information on how such uprisings can be controlled.

headline: GM closing puts 500 in Bucks out of work
abstract: About 500 Bucks County area residents will be thrown out of work by the end of the year when General Motors closes its Mercer County, NJ parts supply plant.

headline: Bounced checks were tradition when GOP was in charge, too
abstract: A third of all members of Congress have bounced checks at the House bank, some repeatedly and by more than their monthly salary, the General Accounting Office warned the speaker of the House.

headline: Kelly Proposal For Pay Raise Is Rebuffed
abstract: DC Council members denounced a proposal by Mayor Sharon Pratt Kelly to increase her $90,709 salary in exchange for a ban on accepting speaking fees, calling it unnecessary and insensitive amid the city's money crunch.

headline: The presidential election has cost taxpayers $173.7 million
abstract: Taxpayers have paid $173.7 million for this presidential election, paying for everything from the conventions' confetti and balloons to the candidates' advertising.  It is the cost of democracy since 1976, when the nation agreed to finance its presidential election to control excessive spending and remove some of the reliance on rich, special-interest donors.

headline: Governors Report Grim Fiscal Status
abstract: Despite three years of budget cuts and tax increases, states' finances are still in turmoil as a result of the nation's weak economy, the National Governors' Association said today.

headline: Students seek better future through recycling
abstract: Every family with kids at Washington Elementary School has a cloth bag to fill with paper, and then the children haul them to the school recycling shed, where a group of students sort it.  The children are a start to an effort to make the world a pretty good place through recycling.

headline: A selective review
abstract: On the eve of the 19th anniversary of the Roe vs. Wade decision, the court agreed to hear arguments on the Pennsylvania law, but it did not say that it would re-examine the case, rather it indicated that it would confine its inquiry to the constitutionality of the provisions of the Pennsylvania law.

headline: If HUD buys it, it's $8M
abstract: John Kromer, acting director of the city housing office, took a novel approach to resolve a long-running dispute with the US Department of Housing and Urban Development over allegations that federal grant money was misspent.  It took whopping number crunching, but it looks like Kromer's idea will save the city $8.2 million.

headline: Brandon will face Steighner
abstract: Ron Brandon, the Republican nominee challenging incumbent state Representative Joseph Steighner, says he needs to do two things to unseat the Prospect Democrat in November: organize his campaign and raise money.

headline: Kennedy a watch dog
abstract: The campaign of state senatorial candidate John Kennedy has been impressive.  It's refreshing to have a person who will stand up against the strong mmajority and fight for the taxpayer.  We now have an opportunity to put Kennedy in a key leadership position where he can be a watch dog for the taxpayers.

headline: The terms of endowment from Rowan
abstract: Wearied by speculation and controversy, industrialist Henry Rowan made public the previously unreleased document that outlines his plan to give Rowan College of New Jersey $100 million over the next 11 years.  And it's deceptively simple.

headline: Homeowners Can't Afford Hefty Property Tax Hike
abstract: At a time when Governor Casey is calling for restraint and cutbacks in school spending plans, the Oil City school administration plans a tentative $346,000 increase in spending, of which about 80 percent is meant for salary increases.  Raising taxes on homes is the most common way of getting revenue, but sooner or later the taxes will become too much for owners to bear.

headline: Susquenita board faces pay decision
abstract: The average salary of teachers in Susquenita School District would rise to slightly more than $40,000 by the start of the 1994-1995 school year under a proposal recommended by a state-appointed fact finder.  The school board, which rejected the fact finder's proposal, would rather see teachers take a one-year wage freeze.

headline: A top prosecutor's style again under scrutiny
abstract: The state Superior Court said that in a recent case that brought Barbara Christie her most famous victory, critics may have been right who said she was overzealous and had ice water in her veins.  The appellate court threw out the murder convictions and ordered a new trial for mob figures Raymond Martorano and Albert Daidone on the ground that Christie engaged in prosecutorial misconduct.

headline: HUD releases funds for town houses
abstract: The US Department of Housing and Urban Development has released $2.8 million in grant money for Harrisburg developers to use in construction of the Washington Square Phase II development.

headline: Braun lead shrinks in Ill. Senate race
abstract: Illinois US Senate candidate Carol Moseley Braun tried to rekindle her romance with voters Monday in her first debate with Republican opponent Rich Williamson in Peoria.  But her campaign's honeymoon is clearly over.

headline: Kennedy campaign impressive
abstract: Senatorial candidate John Kennedy has had an impressive campaign.  We now have an opportunity to put Mr. Kennedy in a key leadership position where he can be a "watch dog" for the taxpayers.

headline: The Third Wheel That May Help This Shebang Run Better
abstract: Seven predictions about the '92 presidential election: There will be fewer negative ads, less divisive politics, more people involved and higher turnout.  Ross Perot is actually helping the two main parties by being a candidate.

headline: In House, lips read no new taxes
abstract: House Democrats started the legislative budget ball rolling early this year by introducing an election-year spending plan that is even a bit stingier than Governor Casey's $14.2 billion proposal.  Appropriations Committee chairman, Dwight Evans, said, "There's no tax increases."

headline: Teachers approve 5-year pact
abstract: Teachers in the York City School District have overwhelmingly approved a new five-year contract, ending more than a year of bargaining marked by two strikes.

headline: Ackenheil Engineers gets corrections-related deal
abstract: The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Department of General Services has hired Ackenheil Engineers Inc. to provide engineering services for a $35 million project involving renovation to the State Correctional Institution.

headline: I'm leaving today
abstract: Despite two years of promises that there would be no sweeps of the homeless from the Madison Square Garden area for the Democratic National Convention, advocates for the homeless said dozens of people were being pushed out of the neighborhood.

headline: Brown or Perot? Spare us the implausibility- Democrats need someone real
abstract: Numerous polls show Clinton's negatives so high that his nomination could be considered a forfeiture of the election, meaning 16 years would pass between competitive campaigns.  If Democrats cannot send forth a serious challenge to an unserious presdient, then the world's oldest political party must be considered exhausted, and the day of the buccaneers- Brown and Perot- will be at hand.

headline: Kerrey Takes Early Lead Over Harkin in S. Dakota
abstract: Sen. Bob Kerrey and Sen. Tom Harkin put their presidential ambitions on the line in the South Dakota primary today, with Kerrey being considered the front-runner.

headline: The Thomas-Hill confrontation is showing up in primary voting
abstract: Lynn H. Yeakel's stunning victory in the Pennsylvania Democratic primary makes it clear that Anita Hill's testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee in the Clarence Thomas confirmation hearings sruck another blow toward making th US Senate a more representative body.

headline: In search of real tax reform
abstract: Representative Jim Gerlach's attempts at tax reform do not address the basic problem and would only expand the ability of taxing authorities to play games by providing an expanded range of taxing options.

headline: Technology education replaces 'shop' class
abstract: Some Valley schools have discarded industrial arts and modernized the name "technology education," which integrates computers, science, math and English with traditional industrial arts projects.  Tech Ed classes are now attracting both college-bound and vocational-technical students.

headline: Advocates urge prison AIDS work
abstract: Healht officials should target prison inmates for education on AIDS because inmates are at higher risk for the disease and they are literally a captive audience, AIDS prevention advocates said.

headline: In the Mon Valley, community groups duel for turf, clout
abstract: The Mon Valley Initiative, a community-development group sponsored largely by Pittsburgh-based foundations, this month received a public slap from the Steel Valley Regional Planning Commission for allegedly attempting to position itself as "the voice of the Steel Valley."  A group perceived as "the voice" of the valley would control most of the grant funds and have the power to decide which communities and projects received assistance.

headline: Brown Relishes Outsider's Role
abstract: Edmund "Jerry" Brown set the limit in his quest for the Democratic presidential nomination to dramatize his message that campaign spending by the rich and poerful has corrupted the American democratic system.  Throughout his career, Brown has often been a trailblazer.

headline: King-sized promotion of Yeakel: Just talk?
abstract: Larry King, the CNN talk show host who interviewed every presidential candidate and helped launch Ross Perot's candidacy, was promoting Lynn Yeakel last week.  Yeakel, a Democrat who narrowly lost her Pennsylvania Senate race against incumbent Republican Arlen Specter, appeared on King's show with Sens.-elect Dianne Feinstein and Carol Mosley Braun.  King told his viewers to expect Yeakel to have a "high-ranking" appointment in the Clinton administration.

headline: The Ultimate Town Meeting: Dialing D for Democracy
abstract: Whatever else you may think about Ross Perot, he's got an acute sense for the national mood and he's far ahead of the political pack in recognizingan idea whose time has come: "electronic town halls."  But we don't have to wait for President Perot to call the first meeting.  If we start immediately, we can do it yet this summer- in plenty of time to influence both the national political conventions and the fall campaign.

headline: Jobless Picture Gloomy
abstract: The national unemployment rate is holding at a worrisome 7.3 percent, and the state's is high but dropping.  However, Venango and Clarion counties are facing some severe increases.

headline: The Choice Debate
abstract: School choice is spreading across the landscape of American education, from the use of magnet schools to aid desegregation, to the statewide, comprehensive system of choice.  Looking downstream is key to understand the repercussions of allowing such extensive choice in education.

headline: Aftermath: 'We have nowhere to go'
abstract: The story is told of Peggy Burton and twelve children in her custody after a fire ripped through the third floor of her South 14th Street home, leaving the family with nowhere to go.

headline: Jubelirer hopeful
abstract: A Senator speaks about their efforts to improve the job climate in our area through the Pittsburgh Symphony project in Bedford County, and comments how it is quite surprising that the Mirror would use the word "quiet" to describe their position.  The senator says it is enormously frustrating that the Casey administration has not lived up to earlier funding commitments, but work to land this project continues, and state funding has not been ruled out.

headline: Brown says US is facing a crisis greater than Russia
abstract: Former California Governor Edmund G. Brown Jr., who is seeking the Democratic presidential nomination, was interviewed at The Tribune-Democrat during his campaign stop in Johnstown.

headline: Kiski told to rehire part-time officers
abstract: The twonship must reinstate with back pay six part-time officers laid off in February when the township converted to a full-time force of three men, the state Labor Relations Board has ruled.  The ruling likely will cost the township at least $20,000.

headline: The week's headlines
abstract: Wofford was interviewed by Clinton for the Vice President slot, Casey was denied his convention speech, Yeakel leads in poll, and Specter was backed by the Philadelphia AFL-CIO.

headline: Jobless rate up, local staff busy
abstract: Unemployment in Pennsylvania increased to 7.1 percent for December after hovering at 6.5 percent for two months.  The unemployment rate for Pennsylvania in December was the same as the current national rate.

headline: The cost of education
abstract: Taxpayers, teachers, school board members and superintendents are struggling to answer the question of whether the cost of education is out of control.

headline: Aiming to lessen Mischief Night's toll
abstract: Mayor Aaron A. Thompson told a group of about 35 officials and residents assembled in front of two houses on State Street, "What we're trying to do is not take Mischief Night away from the children, but remove arson from Mischief Night," as he and others nailed up signs with warnings of the Adopt-A-House program, begun by officials in Camden.

headline: L&I says crackdown is 'a business census'
abstract: The city's Department of Licenses and Inspections launched store-by-store inspections on several blocks of North Fifth street, the start of a citywide crackdown to enforce business licenses and zoning regulations.

headline: Brown's luster faded under bright lights
abstract: After disappointing returns in the New York primary and a close race in Wisconsin- a state Jerry Brown's aides thought they'd win- Brown's tone changed from circus-like to serious.

headline: Klein had promise of post
abstract: Five people who applied to become Susquehanna Township Treasurer were out before they even submitted their resumes.  A month before the full board of commissioners knew of the vacandy, the spot was promised to former commissioner James M. Klein.  That the commissioners did not bring Klein up as a candidate in front of the entire board is offending, according to the other commissioners.

headline: The Woman Who's Doing It All
abstract: Marjorie Margolies Mezvinsky is busy with her campaign, children and career, and getting elected is hardly the candidate's only worry.  Not that she looks worried.  She claims that if she's elected, it will be because she's different, that people want her to be different for them.

headline: Legislatures Face the Fiscal Gloom
abstract: The Maryland General Assembly opened the 1992 session upon the state's tightest financial squeeze ever, prompting legislatures to raise taxes.  In Virginia, a 28 billion dollar budget cuts state agencies, increases college tuition, and proposes a new tax on health-care.  The beginning of a new fiscal year on both states causes budgets to be reviewed and amended, and the General Assemblies are prepared to face political consequences.

headline: The news from our schools is exceptional
abstract: A teacher expresses his pride in the community of Harrisburg and in the students of Harrisburg area school districts.

headline: Alleged Date Rape Is College's Topic A
abstract: Last year, a freshman named Katie Koestner drew national attention to the College of William and Mary when she publicly claimed that she had been raped by a fellow student.  Today that incident- which college administrators found to be a sexual assault, not a rape- is still topic A at the school.  Although the case helped spotlight the problem of acquaintance rape at the college and elsewhere, the undergraduates there are deeply divided on the issue of whether or not she was raped.

headline: Living civilly in an urban hell
abstract: Though the neighborhood in North Philadelphia is drug users, the homeless, and criminals, a Philadelphia Housing Authority house serves as a safe-haven for the Thomas family.  The Thomas family dreams of leaving their unsafe neighborhood, and have received a vow from their local councilman, Daniel P. McElhatton to find them a safer house.

headline: Buchanan Defends Focus On 'Values'
abstract: President Bush's campaign may be trying to moderate its approach to "family values," but not Patrick J. Buchanan, who said yesterday that Republicans would be mistaken to back away from social conservatism.

headline: Klink Bows out of Beaver County Dem Endorsement Race
abstract: Despite indications that he has considerable grassroots support in Beaver County, 4th district congressional candidate Ron Klink says he will bypass seeking the endorsement of the county's Democratic Committee.

headline: 'The Worst Political Coverage in My...Memory'
abstract: The problem today with election coverage is reporting the campaign as if it were a horse race (it isn't) and reporting the candidates as if they were actors in a soap opera (they aren't).  The idea of liberty is perhaps the freedom that has suffered the most from the gradual degradation of the freedom of the press.

headline: Living standard
abstract: The Commerce Department reported that the income growth of Americans last year was the lowest it has been in 30 years.  It also was the first time since 1982 that inflation outpaced income, 4.4 percent to 2.4 percent.  No single remedy is going to reverse this course but there are a number of things that would help.

headline: These drugs skits proved all too real
abstract: The debut kicked off of a project designed by students from Olney and Central High Schools and Little Flower Catholic High School for Girls, which was developed to have elementary students role-play drug deals to teach them of the danger.

headline: An inconclusive inquest
abstract: The open inquest that was held to bring out the full story surrounding the fatal shooting of a 26-year-old man by police in Wilkinsburg established what did not happen, so the post-gazette presents some evidence of what went on.

headline: Lock Haven Officials Seek Committeeman For Enterprise Zone
abstract: City Council is looking for someone to serve on its Economic Enterprise Zone Committee.  Former councilwoman and Mayor Diann Stuempfle resigned from the committee this week.  Stuempfle represented industry on the seven-member committee, which works to help economic development job recruitment.

headline: Bucks state senator appears to have ousted auditor Hafer
abstract: Bucks County State Senator H. Craig Lewis apparently unseated Pennsylvania Auditor General Barbara Hafer yesterday, according to early returns.

headline: Kudos to Casey
abstract: Robert P. Casey did a great job in his speech about Democrats and pro-life, paving the way for Democrats who don't want to leave their party, but who see abortion as a dilemma and choose pro-life.

headline: They're talking about
abstract: Governor Casey's face superimposed atop a color illustration of the pontiff as a button has been rumored that it will head to the Demcoratic National Convention where it will likely be a popular piece of political paraphernalia.

headline: Lower Swatara stabilizes budget
abstract: Frank Linn, president of the Republican-controlled Lower Swatara Board of Commissioners moved to reopen the 1991-1992 budget to deal with a 19 percent tax cut instituted by his Democratic predecessors.  He regards the tax cut as an irresponsible booby trap set by the Democrats to force the Republicans to increase taxes.

headline: Those low SAT scores are the SAT's fault
abstract: When Scholastic Aptitude Test scores declined again in 1991, despite increased workloads and higher grade-point averages in US high schools, the experts were quick to point their fingers.  The major factor behind the drop in scores is the SAT itself.

headline: An urban manifesto
abstract: For the Los Angeles riots featuring violence and looting, some believe the reason for this is the failed social welfare programs of the 1960s and 1970s.  But bashing earlier programs won't do much good; what's needed no is leadership to ouline constructive policies and rally the nation behind them.

headline: Lowball strategy
abstract: When City Council gave the green light for the convention center in October 1984, the city's Redevelopment Authority began to plot a strategy of how to buy out almost 200 businesspeople and property owners who would be displaced by the massive project.

headline: Budget bill lacking, candidates say
abstract: A bill before the state House that would give the public a voice on school board budgest is a good idea, but is not all it's cracked up to be, according to three legislative candidates, state Rep. Bob Allen, Michael A. O'Pake, and Edward M. Koval.

headline: L.A. aftershocks
abstract: The first returns are in on the Los Angeles riot and, if the White House thinks that sending Dan Quayle out to congratulate the LAPD is going to be enough to satisfy Americans (black, Latino, Asian and white) this year, the President's team had better think again.

headline: They're talking about
abstract: Inside the Capitol, they're talking about the opening of the political TV advertising campaign- and taking bets on which candidate will be the first to take the low road.

headline: Mixed signals on the economy
abstract: The US economy clearly left the recession behind in the first three months of 1992, but a plunge in new-home sales last month demonstrated the wobbly underpinning of the fledgling recovery.  Nevertheless, consumers expressed a surge of optimism about the outlook for jobs and business: The Conference Board said consumer confidence reached a seven-month high in April.

headline: Through the Middle
abstract: As the debate rages over school choice, some reformers are quietly charting a middle course that they hope will shake up the education establishment without destroying public schools.

headline: Appraiser admits false auto claims
abstract: Richard Melton, a senior appraiser at Travelers Insurance Co., pleaded guilty to racketeering and conpiracy charges in connection with the submission of hundreds of phony insurance claims that netted him more than $350,000.

headline: Man with plan won't take 'no' for an answer
abstract: A 37-year-old architectural and urban designer from Dryden, N.Y., is doggedly promoting Market Square, his idea for a "world-class plaza" at the convention center, all over Philadelphia.  City officials have never liked the design and insist it is impractical and too expensive, buy public support grows by the month.

headline: Burns, on tape, says he bribed city councilmen
abstract: Wilkes-Barre businessman Joseph Burns boasted in a tape-recorded 1987 conversation that he was bribing Wilkes-Barre city councilmen to eliminate back taxes on the Percy Brown's building.  The tape was given to officials by Mary Anne Magnifico, a nightclub dancer who tape-recorded the conversation with Burns.  All councilmen deny taking any bribe from Burns.

headline: Labor market looks bleak, survey finds
abstract: Even if the Ispat Group were to start hiring locally in the first quarter of next year, Manpower Temporary Services says it would not reverse the negative findings of its Employment Outlook Survey for the Johnstown area.

headline: They're talking about:
abstract: Inside the Capitol they are talking about the dance performance by students in the Rotunda marking "Day of the African Child," proclaimed by Gov. Casey.

headline: More woes on budget in Camden
abstract: There's a hole in Camden's budget- a $12.2 million holde.  And unless it's filled, there might be more layoffs.

headline: Tuition soars, but profs teaching less
abstract: A congressional subcommittee investigating the soaring cost of college tuition is discovering that one of the reasons for the outrageous cost of college is that professors are disappearing from the classrooms to do more research.  When teaching loads are half of what they were a generation ago, that means it takes twice as many professors to get the same courses taught.

headline: Arresting ARD
abstract: Three men charged with theft of money from the University of Pittsburgh Golden Panther booster club and food-service operation were recommended by the district attorney's office to be in a program that allows for a maximum two-year probation and a clean record once the sentence is served because the case fits the rules for ARD- Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition.

headline: Miller Blasts Mayor For PELPlan Stance
abstract: State Community Affairs Secretary Karne Miller came to town today to rip Mayor Jim Connors for putting th city adrift on a sea of red ink by refusing to accept the Pennsylvania Economy League's plans for financial recovery.

headline: Bush Ad Courts Perot Supporters
abstract: A full page ad in yesterday's USA Today was titled "An Open Letter To Every Perot Supporter in America" and signed "George Bush."  The president praised Perot supporters as "an important voice in determining the future of our country" and for having "articulated the frustration of working Americans with government."  And he invited Perot followers to "study what we say we will do.  And what we've really done."

headline: LaGrotta should be returned to office
abstract: Democrat Frank LaGrotta faces an election challenge from Republican Douglas Maffatt.  The incumbent has done much to merit his re-election to the state House.

headline: Thornburgh named to key U.N. post, vows to improve organization's efficiency
abstract: Former Attorney General Dick Thornburgh was named to a top administrative job at the United Nations and promised to help make the world body more efficient in the post-Cold War era.  The U.N. is poised to play a more important role than ever before in securing global peace and promoting economic and social progress throughout the world.

headline: Number of jobs drops
abstract: The number of non-agricultural jobs in the state fell by 133,000 in January, according to state Department of Labor and Industry analysts.

headline: Two deserving champions
abstract: The Patriot commends two very deserving championship teams from around the area, Scotland School and Cumberland Valley High, for their state football championship wins.

headline: At shelter this year, a full house
abstract: The families who have taken up temporary, emergency, life-saving residence at the Women Against Abuse shelter in Philadelphia know that they are a long way from home.  During the time of the holidays, one would think women would want to keep their families in their homes, yet the capacity at the shelter this season is crowded.

headline: Monroe delays borough decision
abstract: Monroe Township supervisors say they will anounce April 23 whether they will spend the money to oppose the creation of the proposed Ashcombe Borough.  Ashcombe Products Co. proposes to turn 506 acres of farmland in the southeast corner of Monroe Township into a separate municipality so it can develop a 1,324-unit development and golf course.

headline: Bush blames Democrats' 1960s policies for riots
abstract: President Bush is blaming the Los Angeles riots on the failed Democratic social-welfare programs of the 1960s.  Bill Clinton, meanwhile, is treading a narrow line intended to hang onto a fragile coalition of minorities and blue-collar whites who feel threatened by the prospect of further violence.

headline: Latino Dem Acosta likes Specter
abstract: In a water-torture strategy to dampen support for Lynn Yeakel,  Senator Arlen Specter's re-election campaign has announced another endorsement from Democrat state Representative Ralph Acosta, the state Legislature's only Latino.

headline: Three-Way Race Forces Politicians to Rethink Strategies in States That Used to Be Sure Bets
abstract: The three-way presidential race is prompting politicians at all levels to rethink not only their strategies and tactics but their entire sense of the political terrain.

headline: Optimism on economy falls
abstract: US business executives' optimism about the economy eroded in the last three months, according to a survey released by the Confederence Board.  The board's Business Confidence Index was 62, down 8 points from the previous three months.  But the current level matches the figure for the first three months of 1992, the economic research group said.

headline: Undermining public school system
abstract: By offering to subsidize private schools, you are undermining the public education system completely.  You will have the people paying taxes to send the best students to private school.. Only the poor students will remain in the public ones.

headline: Authorities call arrested man a bomb expert
abstract: To federal, state, and local authorities, Joe O'Donnell is believed to be artful in munitions, since he pread word around Northwest Philadelphia that if you wanted a bomb built, he was the man to see.  Police arrested him and found two pipe bombs in a stolen Ford truck.

headline: Murtha: Firm studies Fruehauf site
abstract: US Representative John P. Murhta promised to bring jobs to Fayette County, and said 400 may be on the way as a defense contractor is considering building tanks in the vacant Fruehauf plant.

headline: Bush Campaign Ads Withdrawn
abstract: As if Bush's reelection campaign didn't have enough problems, it had to withdraw two new advertisements over the weekend and replace potentially embarassing graphics that showed the presidential seal.

headline: Lawyers feed the campaign that bites them
abstract: Republican leaders have suggested in recent speeches that lawyers overwhelmingly support Democrat Bill Clinton.  But a recent analysis suggests that the big money from the legal community is actually going to the Republicans.

headline: Thrust & parry
abstract: For ever issue raised, US Sen. Arlen Specter has an answer, whose 12 years in office were spent innoculating himself against every possible political disease.

headline: Peace Tax Fund backers give views to Rep. Goodling
abstract: The proposed US Peace Tax Fund would allow taxpayers conscientiously objecting to war to earmark their taxes for other purposes.  Under the legislation, a Peace Tax Board of Trustees would spend the percent of the budget earmarked for military purposes for "peace-enhancing purposes." The percent of the budget spent on non-military programs would be returned to the Treasury.  A group of midstate residents met with US Representative William F. Goodling in an attempt to win him over to the idea.

headline: Universities use Total Quality Management
abstract: Total Quality Management is an approach most often associated with business and industrial communities.  Increasingly, however, it is applied to institutions of higher education.

headline: Auto Thieves Have Wide-Ranging Tastes
abstract: As carjacking spreads across the country, no car makes or models seem to be immune.

headline: Nearly 100 jobs to be created
abstract: Nearly 100 jobs are expected to be created over the next three years by mid-state companies whose expansion plans have been approved by the SEDA Council of Governments, a regional economic-development organization based in Harrisburg.

headline: Bush complains of 1992 rule: 'Be ugly, be nasty' in politics
abstract: A day after questioning the patriotism of Democrat rival Bill Clinton, President Bush yesterday complained that the rule in politics this year is "be ugly, be nasty, and everything goes."

headline: League of Women Voters begins registration drive
abstract: While the various political parties and candidates are beginning their campaigns in earnest, another group has jined the race in a campaign against voter apathy.  Over the weekend, the Berks County League of Women Voters will begin its most aggressive campaign to date in order to see that as many people who are eligible to vote are registered in time to cast their ballot in the Nov. 3 general election.

headline: Time may be running out for Wherry, McMahon
abstract: Time appears to be running out for lawmakers to untangle a partisan dispute that has prevented Greenville lawyer Michael Wherry and other nominees for county offices from taking office.  Since being nominated by Gov. Robert Casey for Mercer County's third judgeship in January, Wherry has twice been unable to win the necessary two-thirds majority of votes to win confirmation.

headline: Personal property tax is an injustice
abstract: The Personal Property Tax, enacted in 1913, was designed partly to encourage investment in Pennsylvania businesses, but has been somewhat outdated by today's financial instruments.  There are a number of complexities in the tax, and there are varying points of view about its repeal.

headline: Voices
abstract: Harrisburg area teachers, PTA members, other school officials and area residents speak out on parents' perceptions of the public school system in Harrisburg.

headline: Bail raised on suspect in city sex, HIV case
abstract: District Justice Joseph S. Solomon doubled the bail for Lisa Star Mallery, who allegedly agreed to perform a sex act with an undercover officer knowing she had tested positive for the virus that causes AIDS.

headline: No wrecking ball for these walls
abstract: The Philadelphia Athletic Club is being dismantled with care, part by part, floor by floor.  The operative words used are "controlled demolition."  Over the years, the building served as basketball venue, wedding site and workout headquarters.  But when wreckers are finished in mid-June, it will be nothing more than a vacant lot.

headline: Bush depends on convention to swell rating
abstract: An army of Republicans trooped into Houston yesterday for their nominating convention, hoping President Bush will use the next five days to revive his sagging presidency and carry the fall battle to the Democrats.

headline: Legislative Battles Swirl Around Tax Hike, Business
abstract: Last summer's budget impasse and the record high tax increase in which it culminated has Republican candidates, Tom Bonello and Ron Brandon, in two local legislative districts on a mission- knock Democratic incumbents who raised taxes out of office in November.

headline: Today's convention schedule
abstract: Eastern Standard Times are given of upcoming events for the day involving the Democratic National Convention.

headline: Retail sales are strong for 2d straight month
abstract: Retail sales rose 1.3 percent to a seasonally adjusted $157.7 billion in February from January, the Commerce Department said, a sign that consumers appear to be leading the nation to an economic recovery by starting to spend again.

headline: We're glad board listened to the parents
abstract: The concerted effort by the parents of children in the Roxbury School succeeded in getting that school taken off the closing list and encouraged openness of a proposed Eastside School on a remote hilltop in Stonycreek Township, by the Greater Johnstown School Board listening to the parents and taxpayers.

headline: Beer case plea deal has fallen through
abstract: A Dauphin county judge yesterday refused to enforce a plea agreement that would have virtually dismissed what was once billed as a major racketeeringcase against the owners of Beer World.  Thomas McGough, attorney for David Trone, whose company serves as a consultant to the Beer World distributors, charged that political pressure applied to the state attorney general's office led the prosecution to back out of the deal.

headline: One voice of optimism for PHA
abstract: John Paone, the Philadelphia Housing Authority's executive director praised the authority, unleashing a blizzard of facts, figures and optimism in an attempt to put a little polish on the agency's badly tarnished image.

headline: Bush edges closer to Clinton
abstract: President Bush, who trailed Bill Clinton by 15 points two weeks ago, has narrowed the gap to nine in the latest USA TODAY/CNN/Gallup poll.  Bush, now behind 51%-42%, made gains with men, Republicans and independents.

headline: Legislative failures brought on session
abstract: Governor Casey wouldn't have had to call the General Assembly into special session this fall if the well-paid legislators didn't drag their feet so much.
