headline: Trial in '91 election smear letter delayed again
abstract: The Cumberland County trial of a Hampden Township man, W. Gregory Rothman, accused of helping send an election-eve smear letter in the 1991 county commissioner race has been delayed for a third time.

headline: Revenue update
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey prepared a spending plan for the upcoming budget year.  He said he would not raise taxes again and has been putting money in reserve in case the economy worsens.

headline: Which choice?
abstract: In the business of school choice, in Bill Clinton's acceptance speech,  he called for "more choices for young people in the schools they attend," with a quick addition of, "the public schools they attend."  That's the safe position for a Democrat to take.  The Philadelphia Inquirer believes President Bush has an approach that will better serve the kids.

headline: 'Beyond bricks and bars'
abstract: As jails overflow, the lock-'em-up credo is drawing unlikely criticism- from prison officials themselves.

headline: PICA sells bonds, lifts city's finances
abstract: In a boon to Philadelphia's shaky finances, the state oversight board sold about $480 million in bonds to erase the city's past deficits and pay for long-delayed repairs to roads, buildings and bridges.  Bonds were offered by the Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority (PICA).

headline: Bush fails to make his case with TV networks
abstract: President Bush, frustrated by an inability to drive his campaign themes home and daunted by Ross Perot, wanted to command voter attention in tonight's press conference.  But the strategy- to bypass media filtering and make his case directly to millions of voters in prime time, much as Perot has done with talk-show appearances- fizzled.

headline: Legislative leadership major issue
abstract: In Pennsylvania this election year, the stakes are bigger than the deficit, abortion rights and the economy.  The 1992 election is about control.  The reins on the General Assembly are up for grabs, and both parties are trying to get a grip.

headline: Tsongas 'advises' Clinton, Bush, Perot
abstract: Former Massachusetts senator Paul Tsongas isn't going to be nominated this week, but he's offering advice, not only for Bill Clinton, but Ross Perot and President Bush as well.

headline: Senate votes to scale back business taxes
abstract: On the eve of Gov Robert P. Casey's budget announcement, the state Senate passed a bill that would save businesses $468 million in taxes over the next three years.

headline: Yeakel at Rosemont: Mixed reaction
abstract: Liberal arts colleges are perhaps the last places in this country that promote free thought and exchange of often conflicting ideas.  So Ofelia Garcia, the president of Rosemont College, should be praised for her effort to promote the development of young minds by inviting Lynn Yeakel to speak at her college.  Another letter speaks of how Yeakel's position on abortion and how that advocates legalized murder, thus making her not the right choice as a graduation speaker at Rosemont College.

headline: 'Boot camp,' more beds proposed for prison
abstract: Dauphin county officials may build a 200-bed 'boot-camp' syle minimum security prison and add about 100 beds to its existing jail as part of an $11 million expansion project.

headline: Pittsburgh best city in region in house prices
abstract: Pittsburgh remains the most affordable city in the northeastern United States in which to buy a house, according to survey findings published by the National Association of Realtors, which shows that the median price of a house in the Pittsburgh metropolitan area jumped 8.4 percent, from $69,000 to $74,800.

headline: Bush gains delegates to clinch GOP race
abstract: Bill Clinton swept Pennsylvania with command.  President Bush won enough delegates in PA to put him over the top and claim the GOP nomination.  Turnout was among the lowest ever for a presidential primary in the state, with the dismal showing following a national drop-off of 18 percent in other primary states compared with 1988.

headline: Legislators left much on agenda
abstract: Governor Casey and Senate President Pro Tem Robert Mellow last week committed themselves to something that should have been done long ago: reforming the state's workers' compensation system when the Legislature returns in January.

headline: Tsongas didn't want to play hardball
abstract: Paul Tsongas only chance to beat the other candidates in the presidential primary would have been to exploit their weaknesses, but he didn't want to play hardball, and so he got hit.

headline: Singel proposes 10% cut in U.S. income tax rate
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark S. Singel said federal income taxes should be cut 10 percent for most people, saving many families about $400 a year.

headline: York students turn up the heat
abstract: Students at York's William Penn Senior High School walked out of class to protest their teachers' threatened use of selective strikes in order to turn up the heat on union negotiations with the school district.

headline: Buck no killer, family says
abstract: Tabitha Buck's family refused to believe she could be part of anything as monstrous as the brutal stabbing of Laurie M. Show.  The 18-year-old Tabbi they know worked hard, had goals.  And she's no murderer.

headline: Planner's plea: keep district intact
abstract: Deconsolidation in the Armstrong School District could hurt the local economy by discouraging people and businesses from locating in the county, says the Armstrong Council for Community Development, a group devoted to expanding the tax base and attracting jobs.

headline: Bush has domestic priorities
abstract: Volume one of George Bush's presidency told the tale of overseas adventures and foreign policy triumphs.  The second volume, if there is one, promises to be the saga of George Bush discovering America.

headline: Legislators pretend to be in Congress
abstract: Typecasting is the show biz word for a person whose reel life mirrors his real life, as in 34 House members and eight senators being party of a reception crowd scene for the Eddie Murphy movie being shot at the Capitol.

headline: Tuesday's election is a pivotal one
abstract: Tomorrow's voting could reverse the downward trend of recent elections.  Democracy will be the real winner on Tuesday.

headline: Speaker calls for equitable state taxes
abstract: After watching events that led to approval of the 1992-1993 state budget, John Dankosky, the head of the Pennsylvania Business Roundtable, says it's time to establish a commission to develop a blueprint for a more equitable state tax system.

headline: 3 judges hear trash case
abstract: Concerned Citizens of North Middleton has made a second attempt to break North Middleton Township's contract with trash hauler J.P. Mascaro and Sons.  The group is fighting the township's three-year contract with Mascaro because all households pay the same $38.61 per quarter for pickup of trash and recyclables regardless of volume.

headline: Buck to be tried as adult in killing
abstract: Tabatha Faith Buck- the alleged accomplice in the stabbing death of Laurie Show- will be tried as an adult.  Through her attonrey James Cullen, Buck, now 18, withdrew her request that her case be transferred to juvenile court.

headline: Proper management, not shutdown
abstract: Southwark Plaza, a troublesome housing development in the Philadelphia area, as proposed by State Sen. Chaka Fattah, deserves revamping.  Although extremely expensive, the council wants it for many more reasons than those who object.

headline: Bush mixes trade talk and Columbus
abstract: President Bush introduced his latest political strategy "Theme of the Week" with a talk about trade that invoked Christopher Columbus and Richard Nixon but had little other substance.  In a speech opening AmeriFlora '92, an international flower show honoring Columbus, Bush spent less time talking trade than he did introducing guests at the Columbus, Ohio, event.

headline: Legislators use newsletters to keep in touch with people
abstract: Communicating, the need to keep in touch with the constituent pulse, is the word that underpins the rationale for legislative newsletters.  Despite all the high-tech and electronic gadgetry available to gaining entrance into the voters' homes, virtually every incumbent legislator continues rely heavily on the US Postal Service for access to households.

headline: U.S. officials may assume PHA control
abstract: City and federal officials were discussing a possible federal takeover of the Philadelphia Housing Authority, capping days of intense negotiating and posturing by city politicians and years of mismanagement at the public housing agency.

headline: State budget goes to Casey for approval
abstract: Governor Casey made a final review of a no-new-taxes budget in preparation for signing the document before the 12:01 a.m. deadline marking the start of the fiscal year.  The governor was expected to sign the Republican-written budget, but only after using his line-item veto to reduce spending in certain areas, crafting a spending blueprint closer to his own specifications.

headline: A battle brews over waste plan
abstract: Doug Kepler, head of a citizen's group called protect Environment and Children Everywhere, said to state officials at a public hearing that residents would not let Concord Resources Group Inc. build an incinerator and landfill in Millcreek Township.

headline: Budget cuts won't hurt state prison in Woodward
abstract: The state Department of Corrections may not be able to open four new state prisons next April due to budget cuts, but these cuts do not impact the 1,000 cell state prison slated for Woodward Township in Clearfield County.

headline: Recycler looks for funding
abstract: A proposal by Morrisville Paper Co. to move onto borough land to operate a $140 million de-inking and recycling plant sailed unopposed through a brief public hearing devoted to  helping the company secure low-interest loans.

headline: Bush proposals window dressing
abstract: George Bush's State of the Union message implies that he really believes tht the recession is easing offa nd will cure itself because his program, because his program doesn’t offer much in the way of change for economic policy.

headline: Lewis lists things he'll do if he beats auditor Hafer
abstract: About once a week since the end of summer, State Senator H. Craig Lewis has stepped up to a podium in the Capitol Rotunda to tell reporters what he would do if elected Pennsylvania's next auditor general.

headline: U.S. Rep. Goodling: Checks no scandal
abstract: A small-business owner took US Representative Bill Goodling to task on the issue of the House banking scandal during a town meeting at the Salvation Army in Carlisle.  Goodling responded that he never changed his story.

headline: State 'budget' leaves too many holes to fill
abstract: The good news is that Governor Casey signed a budget Tuesday night that calls for no tax increase.  The bad news is that this budget is far from complete.  It isn't complete, and some issues should have been addressed in the document signed by Casey.  Instead, lawmakers have chosen to delay- once again- the difficult decisions.

headline: A tortuous tale of an exceptional little creek
abstract: After much lobbying, the Environmental Quality Board voted to grant the Valley Creek stream "exceptional value status" which will place it under the state's most protective regulations. The PA Department of Environmental Resources has stricter restrictions for granting protective status than the U.S.  Environmental Protection Agency allows, and the Raymond Profit Foundation is suing the EPA for not enforcing such standards on the DER.

headline: Bush deploys 5.000 to help
abstract: President Bush sent 1,000 federal riot police and SWAT forces to help protect the streets of Los Angeles and put 4,000 military troops on standby to quell America's worst urban violence in nearly a quarter century.  The Justice Department, meanwhile, opened a grand jury investigation to determine if white police officers who beat black motorist Rodney King could be charged with federal civil rights violations.  It was the acquittal of the four officers that triggered the riots.

headline: Renovation to shelter a family
abstract: Outreach Inc., a program that helps Harrisburg's homeless, rehabilitates buildings that are otherwise vacated for the homeless to reside in.  Outreach retains ownership and hopes to earn enough from rent to pay the utilities and taxes.

headline: Bush rejects debate with 1 questioner
abstract: The Bush-Quayle '92 campaign, which for months has accused the news media of negative reporting, now says President Bush won't debate Bill Clinton unless a panel of reporters asks the questions.

headline: Libraries get tough shake from Casey
abstract: Hundreds of library officials and supporters were forced to rally in the Capitol Rotunda for the money Gov. Robert Casey proposes to cut from their state funding.

headline: U.S. Sought Clinton Files at Embassies
abstract: A senior State Department official this month ordered the US embassies in London and Oslo to conduct "extremely thorough" searches for files on Bill Clinton's years as a graduate student in England, including any documents relating to the Democratic Presidential candidate's draft status and citizenship, according to department officials.

headline: State cuts could mean less University services
abstract: In response to the 3.5 percent budget cut slated for Penn State in Gov. Robert P. Casey's 1992-1993 budget proposal, the University may cut services and programs and possibly increase tuition.

headline: Activists Planning Protest At Sunday Pigeon Shoot
abstract: A pigeon shoot scheduled Sunday morning near Waterford in Erie County has driven some outraged persons to call the Pennsylvania Game Commission and register their protests.  But Bob MacWilliams, information officer at the Game Commission's Northwest Regional office in Franklin, said the commission is not affiliated with the pigeon shoot in any way.

headline: Carjacking Spreads to Nation's Suburbs, Raising Fear There Are No Safe Havens
abstract: Responding to a wave of carjackings, President Bush this week urged that carjacking be made a federal crime punishable in some cases by life imprisonment and, if a victim is killed, by the death penalty.

headline: Santa Monica Grows Hostile to the Homeless Who Consider It Home
abstract: Today, Santa Monica is fiercely at war with itself over the swelling homeless population that dominates some city parks and sidewalks, harasses pedestrians fo rmoney and commits crimes ranging from public urination to murder.  The city council and police, who have tried to help, responded to fear of crime by firing the district attorney, Robert M. Myers, bearing much of the blame for the homeless' coming to the area.

headline: Bush rides the rails
abstract: The rich irony in watching President Bush enjoying the joys of train travel during a supposedly Trumanesque "whistle stop" tour of the Midwest recently is that few presidents have done so little to help train travel.

headline: Like-Minded Delegates See a Frightening America
abstract: Delegates who came to the Republican National Convention favoring Patrick J. Buchanan have limited exposure to the unlike-minded where they live: Mesa, Ariz., a quiet, conservative town with many mobile retirement homes and Christian churches.

headline: Unanimous House renames rest room
abstract: The House, in a display of unanimity and in a spirit of cooperation, passed a resolution by a resounding 192-0 vote to rename the women members' lounge in honor of the late Representative Anita Palermo Kelly.

headline: State economic woes traced to last decade
abstract: A report by the Northeast-Midwest Congressional Coalition suggests Pennsylvania's current economic ills were gained in the borrowing boom of the 1980's.  Significant declines occurred in areas of manufacturing, transportation, communications and public utilities, and government.  Bright notes go to the state's chemical industry, food, and kindred products.  Pennsylvania State University economist William D. Anderson reflects that the recession is not hitting PA relative to the nation because every other state and industry is feeling it.

headline: Airport may no longer stand in the way of landfill permit
abstract: The Federal Aviation Administration had said that the expansion of the Tri-County Industries' landfill could cause safety problems at the airport, but a Tri-County lawyer says that the industry may be underway in getting a state permit.

headline: Case against Peruto 'valid,' prosecutor says
abstract: US Attorney Michael M. Baylison yesterday defended the aborted mail-fraud presecution of criminal lawyer A. Charles Peruto Jr. and said he would have preferred that a federal judge who threw out the case allow the jury to try to reach a verdict.  The case ended when US Disrict Judge Thomas N. O'Neill Jr. said the prosecution had not proven a crucial point required under the federal mail-fraud statute: that Peruto had used the mails to advance an alleged scheme to get out of paying 30 parking tickets.

headline: Some Republicans embracing Renaissance fund program
abstract: A state program to aid economically distressed steel towns that has long been supported by Democratic lawmakers appears to be catching on with some Republicans.  The so-called Renaissance program has targeted money into areas that have been sending Democrats to Harrisburg for decades.

headline: Bush tackled not only opponent Clinton, but also the opinion polls.  He spoke with Cardinal Bevilacqua.
abstract: On the last day of what he called his last campaign, President Bush was exuberant, angry, confident, imploring, nostalgic and absolutely determined to prove the opinion polls wrong.

headline: New Philly mayor deserves union help
abstract: Mayor Edward G. Rendell faces probably the most difficult financial situation for any city in the country today, and workers unions should face up to reality and see that he is calling for sacrafices in other areas that would actually bring them into line with other workers across the country.

headline: Union leader charges meddling by PICA in city contract dispute
abstract: Officials of the Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority improperly interfered in contract talks Wednesday when they warned that delays could lead to mass layofffs, the president of the largest municipal union, James Sutton, charged yesterday.

headline: States should learn, change budget ways
abstract: Reacting to the economy- the deep recession on both coasts and the economic slowdown elsewhere- most state governments since 1990 have done their damnedest to avoid raising taxes and have minimized either drastic tax hikes or spending cuts.  Instead, many report they have begun to drain their reserves, either the rainy day (budget stabilization) or general fund, according to the numbers in City & State's seventh annual financial survey of the 50 states and the District of Columbia.

headline: Amish to decry nutrient management bill
abstract: A bill aimed at controlling manure runoff into the Chesapeake Bay will come under more scrutiny as state legislators meet with the Amish community.

headline: Case could set precedent
abstract: When three Commonwealth Court judges decide whether a citizen group has standing to sue to break a contract between hauler J.P. Mascaro and Sons and North Middleton Township, they may be breaking new ground.

headline: State launches 'Save Our Cities'
abstract: State Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll announced the invetstment of $50 million in state funds to help create jobs and low-income housing at the same time, which is a part of the 'Save Our Cities' program, which could help rid poor urban areas of unemployment and squalid housing.

headline: Bush throws book at Clinton record
abstract: The Green Index, a state-by-state snapshot of the nation's environmental health, accuses President Bush of "regulatory cowardice."  The Bush campaign is using the book to bash Arkansas Governor Bill Clinton, but the co-authors of the book are wondering why.

headline: OIC to mark 25 years of Carlisle service
abstract: The Carlisle Area Opportunities Industrialization Center has worked hard for 25 years to give the disadvantaged, downtrodden and under-educated a decent shot at the working world.  So, the agency is holding a party- a Silver Anniversary dinner, at the Embers Convention Center in Middlesex Township.

headline: Union leader: Benefits not excessive
abstract: In response to an editorial that commented that Mayor Ed Rendell thinks that union benefits are out of line, this letter states that municipal union benefits are necessary for union members and their dependents to live in dignity and to afford reasonable protection.

headline: Stealing Congress's Thunder
abstract: Richard G. Darman, director of the Office of Management and Budget, added a section called "allowance" to the budget Congress designs for itself, instead of totalling the budget requests of the legislative branch agencies.  By doing this, Darman is reducing the total budget that Congress requests.

headline: Area is not secure enough, area man claims
abstract: A Mechanicsburg boater, Wayne B. Fenicle, who has participated in Kipona Drag Boat Races since 1958 said he won't race today because of his concerns about the safety of the course.  But race organizers and a spokesman for the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission say safety is their top priority.

headline: Case took many strange twists, turns
abstract: The murder of Susan Reinert happened during a weekend in 1979.  The police investigation took years before two men, fellow educators at the suburban Philadelphia high school where Reinert taught English, were tried for the crime and convicted.  A timeline is given of happenings with the case.

headline: The Arena: Partnership to the 42-million-dollar man: 'Put a plan on table, ball is in your court'
abstract: Is Joseph J. O'Donnell the Wilkes-Baree Arena Project's 42 million dollar man?  O'Donnell is a self-described local independent real estate development consultant who claims to be capable of securing $42 million from anonymous investors for construction of a 10,000-12,000 seat civic arena/convention center at Highland Industrial Park in Wilkes-Barre Township.

headline: Bush Tries to Recoup From Harsh Tone on 'Values'
abstract: A month after the Republican Convention, much of President Bush's campaign is still directed at avoiding the harsh tone of the "family values" oratory in Houston, which party strategists have agreed was a mistake that damaged Mr. Bush's re-election effort.

headline: Little-Heard Clinton Speech Shows Shackles on Candidates
abstract: Bill Clinton's 14 minute speech that was cut up by news stations and papers, illustrates the difficulty candidates face in commjnicating a sustained thought to voters, for all who do not attend the affairs.

headline: Union mulls Press purchase
abstract: While no one was surprised to hear the Press Co. is for sale, the property has attracted some local interest.  Local 211 President Joe Molinero said the Teamsters might be interested in buying the paper.

headline: Such charity merits taxation
abstract: Henry Rowan has given away great sums without being charitable.  Others have done the same, given money with discriminatory strings attached.  Ultimately, charity money gives benefactors tax breaks, which then the public must pay.

headline: Bald eagles choose a reservoir in Chesco to feather their nest
abstract: For the first time, along the upper fringes of the Octoraro Reservoir in southwestern Chester County has become home to a bald eagle chick.  Fittingly, the bird flew from the nest for the last time on the Fourth of July.

headline: Center City dentist loses lawsuit accusing ABC news show of libel
abstract: A federal court jury yesterday rejected a Center City dentist's claim that he was libeled and falsely portrayed as a "charlatan" by the ABC news show 20/20.  After barely a half-day of deliberations, the jurors said that ABC's show had not libeled Owen J. Rogal, a dentist who specializes in treating TMJ, a chronic jaw-muscle pain caused by grinding teeth.

headline: The convention center is rising- and so are its costs
abstract: When the price was first put on the Pennsylvania Convention Center in July 1983, the developer, the Reading Co., touted a $309 million project.  Today, Reading is no longer the developer, and its successor, the Pennsylvania Convention Center Authority, says the project will cost a whopping $522 million.

headline: Bush volleys hit some PA targets
abstract: When President Bush took highly publicized aim at what he called wasteful federal spending, he shot at a half-dozen Pennsylvania projects for which money had been earmarked.

headline: Local Perot backers say yes
abstract: Everett Laws was going against the tide at the gathering of local Ross Perot supporters but the event's organizers were insisting that he be heard, that no voice be silent.

headline: Union settlement has white collar workers upset
abstract: Several hundred members of the American Federal Government Employees Local 2004 filled a field at the former New Cumberland Army Depot last night for a much-awaited vote on a settlement of a 4-year-old asbestos case.  The offer was accepted, but only wage grade employees are eligible for the differential pay, general schedule white-collar workers cannot collect in the settlement.

headline: Tax collectors paying taxes?
abstract: The resolution of a battle between two bureaucratic giants, the Social Security Administration (SSA) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), is leading to a paradox of sorts: tax collectors not paying taxes- at least a portion of the taxes they have previously paid.  So, who will be paing the taxes? You, throught the taxes you pay your local governing authorities.

headline: Beetle may have us pining for Christmas trees
abstract: An insect could be the Grinch that steals Christmas.  The pine shoot beetle, a European import, is munching its way through pine trees in six states, threatening nurseries and Christmas tree farms.

headline: Cheers and jeers
abstract: Wiley Rowland McKellar III announces cheers to the Head Start program of the Martin Luther King Jr. Center of Allison Hill, the 84-year-old Harrisburg woman who called the police on a con artist, to Elaine Chao, director of Peace Corps and to District Justice Joseph Solomon for his practial approach to students' parents.  Jeers were given to the AIDS Coalition on Prisons and Jails and to slack-jawed Florida hinterlanders who tried to sell freshwater to hurrican victims in Miami.

headline: Truly moving, Mr. HUD head
abstract: Michael Smerconish, chief of the regional Housing and Urban Development office, and his right-hand man, Elton Jolly, have taken up temporary residnece at Southwark so they can find out what it's like to live in public housing.  The embarassing part of it is the apartment had to be spruced up in a jiffy, just before their arrival, while people who've waited for years for repairs look on in wonder.

headline: Bush waffles on Specter 'done deal' for youth jobs
abstract: When US Senator Arlen Specter boarded Air Force One yesterday, he believed Phladelphia would have enough federal money to offer summer jobs to about 11,000 poor young people, twice the number originally expected.  But President George Bush said while he favors the program, he didn't know where the money would come from.

headline: Looking Out for No. 2
abstract: The quadrenniel guessing game has begun in earnest, and if he puts his ear to the window of the governor's mansion in Little Rock, Bill Clinton can probably hear the buzz all the way from Washington.  With a suspenseless Democoratic convention looming, the last mystery of Clinton's presidential candidacy is his choice of a running mate.

headline: Union workers to foot the bill
abstract: As medical costs spiral higher, union members can expect to start footing the bill just as white-collar workers have been doing for years.

headline: Tax plan's impact on rich, poor
abstract: President Bush's tax proposals would bypass the poor, help the middle class and shower money on the very rich.  The benefits are definitely for the middle class to upper-income categories, and the financing is from middle-class and in some cases, lower-income people.

headline: Berwick battles DER over sewer plan
abstract: When dealing with the Department of Environmental Resources, the Berwick Township Supervisors are discovering that the more the state agency gets, the more it wants.  Seven months after placing a building moratorium on the township, the supervisors are still battling with DER over the adoption of the township's updated Act 537 sewerage disposal plan.

headline: Chester lawyer enters attorney general race
abstract: Arguing that Pennsylvania needs an attorney general who will battle utilities and drug dealters, Joseph Kohn, a Chester County lawyer, announced that he would seek the Democratic nomination for that office.

headline: Wal-Mart to create 500 jobs at center
abstract: Wal-Mart, America's largest retail chain, laid plans for a $30 million distribution center that will create at least 500 jobs in Clearfield County, one of Pennsylvania's weakest economic regions.

headline: Bush's Big Speech
abstract: President Bush's State of the Union speech is billed as the most important address of his life and the pressure is on Bush to revive national confidence, but also to prevent rebellion on the Republican right.  The officials who put the president into a trap are still in control of policy.

headline: Majority in midstate leans toward U.S. cars
abstract: In the latest Patriot-News/WGAL Viewfinder Poll, 51 percent of midstate residents surveyed said that if they were to buy a new car today they would be less likely to buy a foreign car than they would have been a year ago.  This may be due to increased animosity between the US and Japan as the recession and election-year politics fuel the two countries.

headline: Unworthy disparagement
abstract: John Vartan's announcement for his imminent departure from the Harrisburg community stirred him up some enemies, but he should be commended, not condemned, and everyone should make a supreme effort to persuade him not to leave the community because of what he had done for Harrisburg in the past.

headline: Taxes down to earth
abstract: The Pennsylvania Economy League, a non-profit, non-partisan group will examine Gov. Robert Casey's proposed budget and will offer suggestions to  legislative leaders.

headline: Bill aims to punish tactics that disrupt hunting
abstract: State Senator Bill Haines of New Jersey wants to stop anyone obstructing lawful hunting with legislation that provides for fines and imprisonment.  The bill passed the Senate last week and is awaiting action in the Assembly.

headline: Child abuse cases down slightly here
abstract: Beaver County received 249 reports of children being beaten, bitten, burned, poisoned, drugged, drowned, suffocated, shaken or otherwise abused in 1991.  That's 1.5 percent decrease from the 292 cases reported in 1990.  The figures reverse a 5 percent increase seen between 1989 and 1990.

headline: We need a visionary
abstract: Harrisburg needs a developer and visionary such as John Vartan.  He would require no tax dollars, create many jobs and most of all make Harrisburg a lovely city.  Hopefully there is still a chance to convince Mr. Vartan to develop in Harrisburg.

headline: Bush's Muddy Message
abstract: Bush campaigners are confident that natural forces favor them.  Bush's plan is less to attract voters than to portray Clinton in a way that repels voters, principally by associating him with the Democratic Congress.

headline: Majority of Voters Say Parties Have Lost Touch
abstract: In 1992, the idea of "political party" has almost not content for a large swath of voters- and the few images voters do have of both Republicans and Democrats are almost all negative.

headline: Update
abstract: The governors of six states have joined Governor Robert P. Casey in fighting to limit the amount of trash that crosses state lines.

headline: Tentative budget that boosts realty tax is approved
abstract: Schuylkill County commissioners, blaming changes in state funding, approved a tentative 1993 county budget that raises real estate taxes to their legal limit to meet more than $2 million in increased costs projected for next year.

headline: Bill seeks to preserve section of Delaware River
abstract: The US House of Representatives approved legislation that would place 32 miles of the Delaware River under federal protection.

headline: City man sentenced in drug death
abstract: Terrance Hamilton Sr. was sentenced to 2.5 to 5 years in state prison yesterday after pleading guilty to causing the death of a friend through a drug overdose.

headline: What will it take?
abstract: Urban enterprise zones are all the rage, but the actual proposals won't do enough.

headline: Bye Bye Bubba
abstract: The Bubba Theory, win over Bubba, the stereotypical white Southern male and thereby rack up a base of electoral college votes that allows you to win the national election, has been successful for the past two decades, but it seems the South has joined the American mainstream, so there is a need for revision on the Bubba Theory.

headline: Manheim official to see new 37th seat
abstract: Patrick M. McGeehan, a Republcan and a Manhem borough councilman, is entering the race for Lancaster's new seat in the state House of Representatives.

headline: Vacationing Casey could be the key
abstract: On the one hand, national party leaders were praising the rising political fortunes of some Pennsylvania Democrats.  On the other, they were snubbing, spurning and alienating one state Democrat whose help or lack of help could mean the difference between victory and defeat in Pennsylvania, Robert P. Casey, who was vacationing the week Bill Clinton and Al Gore toured Pennsylvania.

headline: The future looks bright to CoreStates' economist
abstract: With thousands of job cuts looming and the economy growing ever so slowly, the wager made by economist Carol A. Leisenring, that in five to 10 years, the nation will consider the corporate restructuring of today a "major watershed" in the transition to a global economy, might seem a poor bet.

headline: Board revises waste-site rules
abstract: The state Environmental Quality Board revised the criteria used to determine if and where hazardous-waste facilities, such as incinerators and landfills, may be built in Pennsylvania.  The biggest, and most controversial change, is the state Department of Environmental Resources' projection that Pennsylvania will need the capacity to burn as much as 101,000 tons of hazardous wastes by the year 1997.

headline: City police lieutenant is charged with running a prostitution ring
abstract: Lt. Joseph Kelly Jr., a Philadelphia police lieutenant, has been charged with operating a prostitution organization after an eight-month investigation that also resulted in the arrest of his wife and 12 other people.

headline: Zoning will allow institute's expansion
abstract: A $16 million expansion of the Rehabilitation Institute in Squirrel Hill, which has been studied for several years, could begin this summer now that the Zoning Board of Adjustment has given it their blessing.

headline: Cabbie, press those pants, mousse that hair and follow that car!
abstract: It was finishing school for cabbies.  For a few hours, courtesy of Phila-Pride, the cabbies were treated like consummate professionals who had something of value ot contribute to the revitalization of their city.

headline: March to highlight plight of US cities
abstract: The nation's big-city mayors, saying cities have been ignored too long by Congress, by President Bush and by presidential candidates, plan to call attention to their complaints by marching on Washington next month.

headline: View From the Booth: A Faulty Bush Speech
abstract: All week long, newscasters, television commentators and even Republican officials had been billing President Bush's acceptance speech at the National Convention as his last, best hope to explain why he shouldn't lose his job.  Mr. Bush's task, they said, was to lay out a compelling vision for the future and clear plan for tackling the nation's domestic problems.

headline: The politics of the budget
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature is too slow, secretive, and contentious as it is, and during budget season those qualities are more pronounced, as legislators from two political parties must work together to develop a $14 billion spending plan.  The key to reforming and resolving these issues is owrking across party lines to develop a framework acceptable to both Republicans and Democrats.

headline: Bottled bottle bills
abstract: Bottlers, supermarket owners and labor groups would have us believe it's bad for the economy, bad for woerkers to extend so-called "bottle bills."  Such laws are in effect in 10 states, and those states report an astounding 80 percent return rates on bottles and aluminum cans, and have drastically curtailed roadside litter, without economic ill effect.

headline: City stock sale protests Ice-T album
abstract: Philadelphia's municipal pension fund is selling $1.6 million in Time Warner Inc. stock to protest an album by rap star Ice-T that includes an explicit description of anti-police violence.  Ice-T said he did not intend to advocate violence against police, but rather to convey the rage engendered by police brutality.

headline: $36 million withdrawn after state seized banks
abstract: Depositors withdrew about $36 million from two banks set up by the Pennsylvania Department of Banking after their predecessors were seized by the state in April.

headline: Call for change echoes back 25 years in Pa.
abstract: Like today, people wanted change in government a 25 years ago.  But unlike today, Pennsylvanians were willing to do more than beat their chests and berate the system.  They launched an all-out effort to rewrite the state constitution, a document they believed was the root of the state's ills.

headline: Marilyn Quayle targets Perot
abstract: President Bush's main opponent now is Texas billionaire Ross Perot, a man who makes "outrageous" comments, and not Democrat Bill Clinton, Marilyn Qayle said during a visit to the midstate.

headline: Views on Presidential Performance
abstract: The National Journal posted opinion polls from noted sources on several issues regarding President George Bush's performance on each.  Results are given.

headline: The state budget crossroads: Time to redefine government
abstract: The state budget ws passed this year, on time, with no tax increase.  The version passed is actually that proposed by the Republican caucus, althought he Democrats would have liked to see more discussion of funding for certain programs.  Every year it is the same Republican-Democrat sniping from Harrisburg incumbents.  It is time to redefine our government and give it back to the people rather than a particular party.

headline: Bush pitches strike three and environment loses
abstract: President George Bush has been trumpeting the Clean Air Act as his top planet-friendly deed- while quietly letting 40,000 large utilities, oil companies and factories ignore, in effect, the new law.

headline: City, firefighters sign 3-year accord
abstract: Masloff administration officials reluctantly signed a three-year fire arbitration award, saying it would result in almost immediate layoffs in other departments.  An arbitrator mediating the contract talks awarded the Pittsburgh Fire Fighters Union a three-year contract calling for a 5 percent increase this year, 5 percent next year, and 4 percent in 1993.  In addition, the arbitrator approved union demands for increases in longevity pay, special duty pay, retiree health care and life insurance.

headline: $49 Million Contract To Begin Keno in Md.
abstract: The Maryland Board of Public Works gave a $49.1 million contract to a Rhode Island firm to launch a keno lottery game in January, one of the largest non-competitive awards in state history.

headline: 'Cameo Appearance' Arranged For Sununu at the Convention
abstract: John H. Sununu, who once thought he would accompany a triumphant Presient Bush to a coronationat the Republican National convention, will have a "cameo appearance" at the convention, where he will conduct a brief speech.

headline: Marilyn Quayle to endorse Mowery in visit
abstract: Vice President Dan Quayle's wife, Marilyn, is traveling to Camp Hill to endorse Republican candidate Harold F. Mowery Jr. for state Senate.

headline: Volunteers have no doubts they can get Perot on the ballot
abstract: Supporters of Ross Perot need to get 37,216 signatures to get Perot on Pennsylvania's ballot, and in a two-day effort by volunteers of Dauphin County Perot people, they expect to easily surpass their goal.

headline: 'This budget is built on choices-stark choices'
abstract: Choices that Gov. Robert P. Casey told the Legislature in his annual budget message include an increase in state spending with a cut in federal funding for AIDS research and millions of dollars in cuts for the state funding for the arts.

headline: Bush seeks to boost EPA funds
abstract: President George Bush will ask Congress for a 6 percent increase over last year's Environmental Protection Agency budget for toxic cleanup, sewage treatment, and air and water quality programs.  The proposal falls short of the $6.9 billion needed for the cleanup effort next year.

headline: Commissioners hope state sill fund lockups
abstract: Mercer County Commissioners Joseph F. Fragle and Olivia M. Lazor siad they believe the state will give the county half the money it needs to open a jail for women and to put a regional lockup  in the Shenango Valley.

headline: 20,000 expected for dedication of facilities at Horseshoe Curve
abstract: Now the Horshoe Curve bodes to represent more than mere history to the economically bleak Altoon region: It could mean the future.  $5.8 million in federal funds will be available to create a tourist center at Horshoe Curve 18 months in the making.

headline: Campaign '92
abstract: Results are given by community for Democratic candidates running for US Senator.

headline: Marilyn talks of Perot
abstract: Questions about Ross Perot dogged the vice president's wife on a campaign visit, while a lone protester hawked the Texas billionair as the answer to the country's problems.  Marilyn Quayle attended a ceremony down the street from the Capitol to name the state Republican headquarters after Geowrge Bloom, a longtime Republican leader who died last year.

headline: Voter turnout markedly low
abstract: After a long day in Philadelphia shaking hands and wallets, a subdued Bill Clinton claimed victory less than two hours after the polls closed in yesterday's Pennsylvania Democratic primary.

headline: Trenton Budget Makers, After Three Years of Crisis, Gear Up for More Austerity
abstract: After three straight years of fiscal crisis, beleaguered New Jersey budget makers may be abou tot tangle with the worst budget yet.

headline: Candidate Kohn visits proposed mine site
abstract: Joe Kohn, a Democratic candidate for Attorney General, visited a proposed mine site at Hosterman's Pit cave in Centre County.  The Penns Valley Conservation Association applauded Kohn's presence but the Nittany Grotto Chapter of the National Speleological Association is trying to stop the quarry.

headline: Conaboy To Retire As Chief Judge
abstract: After 30 years on the bench, chief federal Judge Richard P. Conaboy has decided to retire from regular active service as a US District Judge on September 1.

headline: A big affair for small businesses
abstract: Tuesday will bring one of the more unconventional entries to the region's fair season- the annual Small Business Fair.  This one is strictly business, a venue for suits, box lunches, exhibit booths and business cards rather than T-shirts, corn dogs, concession stands and Ferris wheel tickets.

headline: Campaign continues for beaten Buchanan
abstract: Despite meager showings in Tuesday's Michigan and Illinois primaries, Pat Buchanan said Wednesday that he'll continue his campaign in Connecticut, North Carolina, and California.

headline: Mario Cuomo's Abortion League Logic Inconsistent
abstract: In a conversation that resembled a college campus debate, Governor Mario Cuomo referred to his "strong" Catholic faith, which has persuaded him that unborn babies are persons.  But, as he has declared in his writing and speeches, he said what he learns form the church should be kept separate from his duties as governor.

headline: Voters fail issues test, survey finds
abstract: As Election Day approaches, a new survey indicates that many voters still lack basic information about President Bush, Bill Clinton and their records.

headline: Unemployment drops
abstract: The beginning of the normal spring hiring season helped push the unemployment rate for the four-county Pittsburgh area down slightly in March, the first reduction in the index since October.

headline: Casey signs bill on water, sewer funds
abstract: Gov. Casey signed legislation that authorizes a referendum on another $350 million bond issue to PennVest, which would provide loans to local government and water and sewer authorities in the 1992-93 fiscal year.

headline: Court returns killing case
abstract: The controversial case of a 9-year-old boy charged with shooting and killing a 7-year-old girl was ruled by the state Supreme Court that a judge improperly blocked the transfer of the case from criminal court.  District Attorney Jim Gregor believes the boy should be tried in juvenile court, but Common Pleas Judge Ronald Vican ruled that the boy should be tried as adult.  The Supreme Court did not rule on which court the boy should be tried in as of yet.

headline: A big boost for firms entering marketplace
abstract: There are among scores of products that soon may be in the marketplace thanks in part to the Ben Franklin Partnership, a low-profile venture between the public and private sectors whose raison d'etre is to spur  high-technology growth in Pennsylvania.

headline: Campaign Treasurer Bristles At Charges
abstract: A disgruntled constituent has forwarded to the state attorney general's office allegations that state Rep. David R. Wright of Clarion improperly received 21 contributions totaling $4700 during his 1990 campaign.  D. Merle Wetzel, treasurer for the Wright for Assembly Committee, bristled at Briggs' charges.

headline: Mary Lewis elected GOP chairman
abstract: Cumberland County Republican Party members unanimously elected county Register of Wills Mary Lewis as the new county chairman Monday.  Ms. Lewis succeeds Pat Saylor, who after serving one two-year term decided not to run again.

headline: Voters Have Mixed Views of Campaign They Largely Ran
abstract: On election morning, it is customary to trot out a familiar cliché- that, after the hoopla, the campaign is now in the hands of the voters.  Funny thing, this year: It's been that way all along.  Charts are given on how voters rated the '92 campaign.

headline: Unemployment Figure Climbs To 8-Year High
abstract: Unemployment in the United States reached 7.5% last month, the highest level in nearly eights years

headline: Casey waste bill may be buried
abstract: When the US Supreme Court struck down a Michigan ban on out-of-state trash, it sounded the death knell for a similar law sought by Governor Robert P. Casey, according to a group that represents the nation's trash-disposal industry called the National Solid Waste Managers Association.

headline: Contract to improve adoption process
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey announced a $4 million contract with the Pennsylvania Council of Children's Services for a program to improve the adoption process and encourage the adoption of children with special needs.

headline: Amoco to cut 8,500 jobs by end of '93
abstract: Amoco Corp. said it would slash 8,500 jobs by the end of 1993, joining other big US corporations that are axing thousands of jobs in restructurings prompted by the nation's sluggish economy.

headline: Can a paper clip cast a vote? Question argued before court
abstract: Rep. Richard Hayden jammed his voting lever to record "yes" to every vote taken on the day he would be absent.  His vote was key as the $14 billion state budget was passed by one vote.  Other legislators say his vote should be void and although legislators are immune from prosecution, your immunity leaves you when you leave the House floor.

headline: Mayor eases stance on voter purge
abstract: Mayor Rendell said yesterday he has had a change of heart about purges of voters who sit out two elections- and instead will push to have names of nonvoters removed every four years, or every presidential election.

headline: Where Candidates Are Today
abstract: A list is given of where Democrats Jerry Brown and Bill Clinton along with Republicans George Bush and Pat Buchanan are going to be appearing today.

headline: Vindication for a 'Stupid' Report
abstract: How many times can Maryland Governor William Donald Schaefer go before local officials and call for more budget cuts, and how many times can he trot out projected deficit figures based on estimates he himself questions?

headline: Casey's trash ban set back by court
abstract: This past January, Governor Robert Casey asked the General Assembly to approve legislation that in effect would ban trash hauled in from other states to Pennsylvania-based landfills.  The proposal now lies in the House Appropriations Committee and could, if enacted into law, stop cold about 3 million tons of trash currently being trucked into the state's 47 operating landfills each year.

headline: Cop/firefighter unit to sue city over benefits cut
abstract: The Police and Fire Medical Association, claiming the city "arbitrarily" slashed $95,000 from this month's benefits payment, planned today to file a lawsuit.

headline: Amphitheatre could be local entertainment jewel
abstract: The Bud Light Amphitheatre will be placed on the grounds of the former Hanson's Amusement Park in Harvey's Lake, Pennsyvania, and will renew the glimmer of Harveys Lake's glamorous past, allowing for more diversity to Northeastern Pennsylvania entertainment.

headline: Candidate is hoping to fix things
abstract: Freddy Friedman believes the federal government is in disrepair, so she is among five Democrats in the April 20 primary seeking nomination for the seat now held by Republican Arlen Specter in the US Senate.

headline: Mayor Rendell paints grim fiscal picture
abstract: In the strongest language to date on the city's anemic financial condition, Mayor Rendell said yesterday that "service cuts are inevitable" and predicted that "almost everyone will have something near and dear to them taken away."

headline: Women, minorities packing their bags for Capitol Hill
abstract: Not only will a voice for change be blowing through the White House come January.  Capitol Hill may never be the same.  Women and minority canddidates were elected Tuesday in record numbers.

headline: 1,600 gather to honor King memory, message
abstract: Political, spiritual, and community leaders gathered to honor the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., at the 10th annual luncheon hosted by the Philadelphia Martin Luther King Jr. Association for Nonviolence.

headline: Centralia residents plan lawsuit to protect coal rights
abstract: The Columbia County Redevelopment Authority faces a second lawsuit filed by Centralia residents fighting the state's  decision to force them from their homes, according to Mayor Anne Maire Devine.

headline: Council hears 2 sides on police review
abstract: Most police insist the "curbside justice" system that they sometimes administer to suspects works now.  Critics are pushing City Council for an independent review board.

headline: Appliance Store plans to close 10 weak stores
abstract: The Appliance Store announced that it would close 10 of its money-losing stroes as the first step in its restructuring in US Bankruptcy Court.

headline: Candidates exhibit late inning strain
abstract: Yesterday, the candidates were running on adrenaline, and showing- under the strain- a lot about themselves.  In Pennsylvania, the focus has been on the battle for the state's 23 electoral votes, as well as a US Senate race that has captured national attention.

headline: McDade Has Lunch in D.C. with Gorbachev
abstract: Embattled US Representative Joseph M. McDade was among a group of House and Senate leaders who were meeting over lunch this afternoon with former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.

headline: Waiting in the Wings for 1996
abstract: Vice President Dan Quayle, despite a decent approval rating, lacks public speaking skills, which produces doubt among voters that he would suffice as president.

headline: 2 G.O.P. Groups Ask Party To Drop Anti-Abortion Plank
abstract: Republicans seeking to force their party to withdraw its anti-abortion plank from the platform began a six-state road trip to their convention city, vowing that "we will not be silenced in Houston."  Platform committees have defeated abortion-rights proposals by 2-to-1 margins at the last three conventions.

headline: Centralia residents sue for coal proceeds
abstract: The borough of Centralia sued the state of Pennsylvania yesterday, saying residents facing eviction orders because of an underground mine fire should be paid their share of the town's coal reserves.

headline: County balks at funding AIDS hospice
abstract: Citing concerns about the stability and fundingof the Montgomery County AIDS Task Force, the county commissioners delayed a decision on partially funding a proposed hospice for AIDS patients.

headline: Area biotech firms are thinking global
abstract: The region's biotechnology community, young though it may be, has been quick to recognize the importance of global thinking, reaching across the ocean with the help of a 10-year-old association.

headline: Candidates in 15th District offer voters very clear choice
abstract: When they talk about issues, Democratic state Representative Nick Colafella and his Republican opponent, Dale Laughner, take positions that for the most part reflect their party affiliations and their status as incumbent and challenger.  Their views are given on issues such as government, education, jobs, taxes/spending and the environment.

headline: McDade indictment detriment to state
abstract: The federal indictments handed up against US Representative Joseph M. McDade of Scranton, for selling out to lobbyists and contractors, has significantly tarnished his previously sterling image, and his effectiveness to Pennsylvania has been impaired.

headline: Wall: A test of wills
abstract: Ross Perot, who began as the largest individual contributor to the Vietnam Memorial, tried to undermine the project through threats and intimidation when an unconventional design was chosen, according ot several people involved in the project.

headline: 77 arrested in abortion protests
abstract: More than 500 anti-abortion protesters jammed sidewalks outside a women's clinic, waving photos of dismembered fetuses, singing hymns and shouting Bible verses.  Seventy-seven protesters, including 15 children, were arrested, most on disorderly conduct charges.

headline: Checking out the trash patrol
abstract: Governor Casey visited a Trashnet checkpoint at Interstate 90 and Route 97 in Summit Township.  Casey called for federal legislation that would allow states to regulate the flow of trash from out-of-state sources.

headline: Court right to block pay to constables
abstract: Pennsylvania constables serve warrants and papers in civil suits.  Sometimes they transport defendants, provide courtroom security or performother services.  Fees are set by state Legislature, and before this year, the last time fees were increased was 1972.  This year the constables wanted a pay raise in the form of higher fees and the Legislature obliged.  This month, the new fees took place throughout the commonwealth, except in Lehigh County.

headline: Armstrong closing 3 out-of-town plants
abstract: Armstrong World Industries Inc. announced a global streamlining plan Tuesday which includes closing three North American manufacturing plants, scaling back operations at other plants and writing off land, buildings, equipment and other undisclosed assets.

headline: Candidates mum on U.S. decline
abstract: George Bush has behind him substantive accomplishments in foreign policy.  But he seems not to realize that there is also an American soul at home that desperately needs tending.  Bill Clinton seems to be who Americans will vote for as a reluctant first choice, and Ross Perot is an imperfect vehicle for change.  Qualities such as analysis of the problem and then pure will sadly are not evident in this campaign.

headline: McDade lawyers seek delay in bribery trial
abstract: Citing a need to examine more than 400 hours of wretapped conversations and a roomful of other evidence against their client, attorneys for US Representative Joseph M. McDade are seeking a three-month delay in his trial on bribery and racketeering charges.

headline: Watch the spin
abstract: George Bush may not have any principles or platform or reason for being, but he has good handlers.  They've got him out front, whining about victroy despite the fact that a quarter of his own party thinks he's so pitiful that a bad columnist who admires dictators is preferable.  With Bill Clinton in the running, these tactics may just not work for George Bush.

headline: A New American Compact: Caring about Women, Caring for the Unborn
abstract: A list of sponsors that are anti-abortion is given along with a statement about liberty and boundaries and urges people to have respect for human life.

headline: Cheers and Jeers
abstract: Cheers go to federal officials for giving the go-ahead on a project by PennDOT, for Elizabeth II who is becoming a taxpayer for the first time and for Judge Joseph Kleinfelter for ordering the cessation of late-night, BYOB parties at the former Vanity Bar.  Jeers go to Edward Lessick Jr. who falsified military orders and for coal region developer Louis Beltrami for seeking Luzerne Country for a landfill site.

headline: Court spectators say jurors face tough decision
abstract: The Seneca County jury considering the case of Laurie Lee Kellogg face a difficult time deciding whether she plotted with four teenagers to kill her 43-year-old husband or wether she planned only to leave him after learning he allegedly sexually molested two teenage girls.

headline: Ater Six's fate rests with judge
abstract: A federal judge is expected to rule today on whether Philadelphia formal-wear maker After Six Inc. can close its plant and sell its assets to a Baltimore company.Meanwhile, the trustees of the Amalgamated Insurance Fund, filed a suit in US District Court in Philadelphia seeking to put part of the sale proceeds aside for the workers' underfunded pension and insurance funds.

headline: Candidates Seek Matching Funds
abstract: The presidential primary season is over, but Democratic nominee Bill Clinton's campaign is still working hard on getting federal matching funds to pay off bank loans.  Clinton submitted  arequest to the Federal Election Commission asking for $1.8 million from the fund.

headline: Meet Perot's Fans: They Crave Change, Not Specific Proposals
abstract: Ross Perot, still unannounced for presidential campaign, has supporters fueled by a combination of idealism and frustration among voters that cuts across political learnings, social class and individual issues.

headline: We don't want pros
abstract: The attitude expressed by state Rep. Frank LaGrotta will eventually force the voters' decision on term limitations, stating that only he can represent the public.  Hopefully the voters of the 4th district will listen to all the opponents' voices.

headline: Rally of the day
abstract: The Lancaster Branch of Demonstrate Against Drug Dealers turned over 12,000 signatures in support of increasing the penalty for anyone selling drugs within 1,000 feet of a school building.

headline: 1st public health care hearing draws reform backers, detractors
abstract: Vice President Al Gore, filing in for Hillary Rodham Clinton at a marathon of hearings on health reform, promised that the administration's developing plan would give all Americans "freedom from fear" about whether they will receive proper care.  Some business owners that attended were worried that the increase cost would drive them out of business or cause the price of their goods to skyrocket.

headline: Uncle Sam has become the biggest spender on health care
abstract: The article discusses a study by the Health Care Financing Administration that shows that the government has become the biggest purchaser of health services, for the first time surpassing the private sector and individuals.  This will most likely increase our federal deficit and create a need for increased taxes.

headline: State glosses over inflated price tag
abstract: If you're planning on joining a new state program to pre-pay for college tuition, make sure you read the fine print.  Even then you might not get the full story.  The state Treasury Department, in a brochure explaining its program, doesn't fully disclose that the state is charging higher prices than today's actual tuition costs.

headline: Press On, PennDOT
abstract: ABC NEWS asked in wonderment last week why nearly $500 million is being spent on the Lackawanna Industrial Highway.  That's a fair question.  The project, after all, is publicly funded, with federal higway funds funnelled through the Pennsyvlania Department of Transportation.  The problem is that, having asked a fair question, ABC did little to fairly answer it.

headline: Pineda says their strategy is all wrong
abstract: Santiago Pineda was beaten by a group of drug dealers after Pineda yelled for them to get away from his property.  Since then Task Forces by police have been formed, and the town holds meetings to discuss ways of keeping them and their children safe, along with keeping drug dealers away.

headline: City floats casino plan on a sea of myths
abstract: The article criticizes Philadelphia Mayor Rendell's plan to bring riverboat gambling to Philadelphia. The nostalgic image used to market riverboat gambling is dishonest, since they will actually use barges and not boats.  Gambling has also historically been associated with dirty politics and crime.  However, Rendell says it will bring thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue to the city.

headline: Chartiers Valley vote ends strike
abstract: Chartiers Valley teachers voted 132-37 to return to work today while contract negotiations continued.  Classes for students also will resume today, but two hours later than usual starting time to give teachers a chance to prepare their rooms and study plans.

headline: GOP suit to unseat Stinson fares ill
abstract: PA State Senate Republicans are trying to unseat Senator William Stinson from his election to the Second District Senate seat and have brought it up in front of a seven-judge panel; usually courts do not get involved in legislative affairs. The Republicans are arguing that Stinson was able to vote on issues that he had a personal interest in and that Senator David Heckler was not seated quickly enough to vote. The Democrats maintain control of the Senate even though it is spilt 25-25 because acting PA Governor Mark Singel is the Senate President.

headline: Questions dog a firm selected to reform city workers
abstract: Mayor Rendell's administration says it will reform the system that compensates and treats disabled city workers.  The reform includes a loan to pay the claims adjustment company of Riley & Fleming more than $1 million a year to investigate claims of injured city workers to determine whether they deserve compensation.  Riley & Fleming, however, has been under investigation many times and been involved in scandals.

headline: They plan to give a historic home its rightful place in the sunshite
abstract: The Trappe Historical Society bought the Muhlenberg house for $250,000 and will use $200,000 from the Pew Charitable Trusts, plus a $50,000 commitment from local supporters to restore the house to its original glory.

headline: Reform the system, foster parents of slain boy urge
abstract: A three year old child was killled by repeated blows to the head just days after being returned to his biological parents.  Both biological parents are in jail awaiting trial for the case, but the foster parents are furious because they claim the warning signs were there.

headline: 2 boroughs seeking state grants to help start family centers
abstract: Norristown and Pottstown want to create a family center in each borough, which people could go to for a variety of different services. Montgomery County commissioners promised $50,000 to each center, and the Norristown Area School District has committed $50,000 for the Norristown center.  The rest would need to come from a state grant from PA Governor Casey's "Children's Cabinet", headed by the state secretaries of health, education and public welfare.

headline: Uniontown physician appointed legislative liaison by group
abstract: Dr. Cataldo F. Corrado, director of emergency medicine, Uniontown Hospital, has been appointed by the Pennsylvania State Legislative Committee of the American College of Emergency physicians as Pennsylvania State Legislative Liaison. He will be responsible for interfacing with the state legislative liaisons to advise them of important state regulations and proposed bills that deal with issues respective to emergency medicine.

headline: State schools had to turn 9,000 away, officals say
abstract: Chancellor of the State System of Higher Education told ta Senate committee yesterday that 13 of the 14 state-owned universities had to turn away potential students.  The school say they need more funding in order to keep facialty and the buildings in usable condition.  Gov. Casey says he feels the school have enough money to opperate as is.

headline: Privatizing urged to improve roads
abstract: The Federal Government's top highway official, Rodney E. Slater, administrator of the Federal Highway Administration, proposed today that private businesses operate portions of the 42,500-mile Interstate System, charging tolls and providing money to repair decaying highways and bridges.

headline: Pittsburgh financially raped us for having our car stolen
abstract: The city of Pittsburgh's administration financially rapes stolen car victims by charging them money to get their cars back from the impound after they are found with no notification of how to pick it up prior to impounding.

headline: Clinton to ease lending regulations on banks
abstract: The Clinton administration is loosening bank lending rules in an effort to ease a credit shortage blamed for holding back the economy.

headline: Citizens plead for help for the handicapped
abstract: Hillary Rodham Clinton listened to citizens plead, often emotionally, for health-care changes to help the handicaped, the dying and the uninsured.  Mrs. Clinton chairs a White Hose task force working towards a May 3 deadline to produce a plan to provide halth insurance for all while bringing runaway costs down.

headline: Gore in Phila. To 'learn,' raise money
abstract: Vice President Al Gore came to Philadelphia where he spoke in Hawthorne to people; such as US Senator Harris Wofford, Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, and City Councilman Joseph C. Vignola. Gore listened to complaints about the drug problem in the Martin Luther King housing project and has lead Mayor Rendell say he will look into it. Rendell is having Philadelphia compete for one of five grants for about $100 million each that would be given to big cities.

headline: Quote...Unquote
abstract: A list of six quotes from the week including Pennslyvania Attorney General Ernest Preate protesting Gov. Robert P. Casey's plan for a large staff increase at the state enviornmental department.

headline: Voters asked to back parks
abstract: Public parks and other forms of recreation will receive a boost in Pennsylvania, if voters approve a bond issue on the November 2 ballot.  State voters will be asked to approve a $50 million bond to help pay for improvements in parks, historic sites, libraries, museums and scenic areas.  The measure also calls for establishing a regular source of revenue for these important programs.  This bond issue makes sense.

headline: Release prisoners on time, not early
abstract: In Pennsylvania, a prisoner does not get off for good behavior.  That goes for all sentences.  At least not yet.  Last week, in the state legislature's rush to pass all the bills it put off the rest of the term, the Senate approved a sentencing-reform package that includes a provision allwoing inmates to earn time off for good behavior.

headline: 2 nations impose limits; 1 doesn't, and pays a price
abstract: In a study of healthcare in three countries, Canada, Germany, and the United States, a Philadelphia Inquirer reporter spends 24 hours in each of three hospitals to examine patient care, attitudes towards the health system by patients, problems encounted by doctors and administrative staff, and government spending and regulation of health care. The articles reports on the trade-offs made by different countries according to their priorities.

headline: USAir files lawsuit against Blue Cross
abstract: USAir has sued Blue Cross of Western Pennsylvania, claiming that the health insurer overcharged it by more than $15 million over nearly four years because of administrative lapses.  The lawsuit, filed in US District Court in Pittsburgh yesterday, claims that the overcharges resulted from errors that included double paying of claims, payments in excess of plan-authorized amounts and payments to those not covered by the plan.

headline: State seen at risk in education
abstract: The National Education Association and Pennsylvania State Education Association are both management and union and we are losing to both.  The state House voted to give school districts the right to choose whether or not to adopt Outcomes Based Education, a right that was ours all along but was removed by appointed educrats and the PSEA.

headline: PUC Oks bridge plans
abstract: The Public Utility Commission on Thursday approved plans for PennDOT to rehabilitate the deteriorated Route 588 bridge over the Beaver River between Beaver Falls and Eastvale.

headline: Police set to enforce new law on car seats
abstract: Police might get some resistance from parents who are now required to secure their toddlers in car seats, but it's the children who will probably complain the most, a local police chief said.  The Child Passenger Protection Act, which went into effect Aug. 21, requires all children younger than 4 to ride in a federally approved child safety seat.

headline: Clinton's proposal would take a heavy toll on small insurers
abstract: The future of America's health insurance industry could mean a hefty cost for small business owners, probably shutting most down.  For large companies that could stay alive, they will have to narrow their geographic market, sell different kinds of coverage and forge new alliances with hospitals, doctors and other insurers.

headline: City goes on a spree of debt refinancing
abstract: Rates are low.  Its bond rating has rebounded.  So the city of Philadelphia is floating, and hopes to save $95 million.

headline: Gore-Perot showdown tonight could make or break NAFTA
abstract: Vice President Gore will confront populist billionaire Ross Perot tonight in a TV debate likely to be remembered as a make-or-break test of the North American Free Trade Agreement- and a riveting political slam-dance.

headline: Quotes of the Week
abstract: Nine quotes from various citizens, including the PA House speaker and the Warrior Run School Board president. There is also a cartoon that goes along with a quote about the Endeavor from Mission Control.

headline: Voters' decision on Key 93 crucial to state parks
abstract: State Representative Bill Lloyd said unfit conditions have become the norm across the state in recent years as lawmakers, faced with tight budgets, cut back on maintenance at taxpayer-owned facilities such as Laurel Hill in Somerset County and Bushy Run Battlefield in Westmoreland County.

headline: Rendell still thinks the police can monitor themselves; he's wrong
abstract: It is more than a little sad that even before the police advisory board is put into place, its number one proponent, Councilman Michael A. Nutter, and Mayor Rendell remain seriously at odds.  Obviously, the two men have major differences, not only over the basic concept, but also concerning the board's independence, its structure, its responsibilities and authority.

headline: 2 offices for HMO doctors to open
abstract: This year, as the fall enrollment season begins, the rapidly growing HMO is taking matters into its own hands.  HealthAmerica of Central Pennsylvania plans to open two physician centers in the Harrisburg area in January, and possibly more sites later in York, State College and Lancaster.

headline: Vying views emerge on health care
abstract: Hillary Clinton has a difficult task to mediate between two camps of thinking between social reformers wanting to expand society's safety net and assure health care for all and the so called deficit hawks that are afraid the price of $230 billion is too much and in turn will hurt the economy.

headline: State using pension funds
abstract: PA Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll is completing plans to provide millions to school districts for construction and equipment. The Treasury Incentive for Education Program is one of several which uses state pension funds. The state employees pension fund has also agreed to provide money to the PA Linked Deposit Program, which provides low-cost loans to small businesses.

headline: Quiet corner can be deadly to the unwary
abstract: A quiet corner housing farms, an ice cream shop, and a cemetary, is the site of twenty accidents involving either towing or Cumberland County emergency response vehicles and state police. Monroe Township Manager Thomas Stubits is hopeful that under the federally funded Safety and Mobility Initiative Program, plans to install a light and other warning signs will improve the safety of the intersection.

headline: Preate fights rent-to-own deals
abstract: PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. and the Bureau of Consumer Protection filed a lawsuit against Rent America with the Commonwealth Court for its violation of the 18% cap on interest rates.

headline: Companychanges mind on plant use
abstract: International Wood Products Inc. said yesterday it will not use the former Masonite Corp. plant in Northumberland  County borough for its lumber operations  because the loan process through the Pennsylvania Industrial Development  Authority's deadline to prodive additional information about  investors could not be completed on time.

headline: 'Clean & seal' bags another
abstract: To call the South Philadelphia rowhouse a "wreck" would have been too kind. So why did Ken Skinner call the abandoned dwelling on Carpenter Street near 21st "a good house"?  As chief of Department of Licenses and Inspecitons' nine "clean and seal" crews, he has seen a lot worse.

headline: Gov. Casey gets a new pair o f custom-fit cowboy boots
abstract: Gov. David Walters of Oklahoma presented Gov.  Casey of Pennsylvania cowboy boots in a custom of the host to present gifts to the colleagues during the National Governor's Association conference.

headline: Races Being Decided by Voters
abstract: A major indication that the turnout would be low in Scranton was the fact that Lackawanna County Bureau of Elections was not receiving a lot of calls on election day. Normally, lots of people call up with problems and questions. This was expected to be a down election to four years ago when five candidates where vying for the democratic mayoral nomination, compared to only two this year.

headline: Voters to decide $50 million bond issue
abstract: Voters throughout Pennsylvania on November 2 will vote yes or no on a proposed $50 million bond issue from which proceeds would be used for parks, recreation areas, conservation efforts, libraries, historic-site preservation and some deferred maintenance projects at state-owned universities.

headline: Rendell's grandstanding
abstract: When City Council overrode Mayor Rendell's veto of the Police Advisory Board it, in a sense, told Ed to go to his room and not come out until he understood that citizens have police rights, too.  Then Ed bolted from his room like a defiant spoiled brat who just realized that if he didn't start grandstanding, he might not get those big toys (casinos and a new Charter) he's been asking for.  Standing on his 20 years of questionable law enforcement experience, Ed threw a tantrum in the Daily News.

headline: 25% of top teens admit sexual activity
abstract: They are the nation's best and brightest high school students.  Yet what they say in a recent national survey apparently mirrors the thoughts of their generation.  One-fourth of those who responded to the survey said they are sexually active.  A third of the students said they have considered killing themselves.

headline: We are already tracking medication errors
abstract: In Steve Twedt's recent series "Medication Errors," he makes a compelling argument to collect medication-error incidents for the purpose of identifying trends that can be shared among health professionals to create a safer system.  However, he falls short in reinforcing the point that there is already a national system to report errors: The USP-ISMP system.  The answer lies in building on that program.

headline: State wants to cut some school funds
abstract: Casey wants to cut subsitides to community colleges for non-credit courses such as basket weaving or basic welding.  Instead, the money will go towards coures that will be used to obtain a degree or admittence to a four year college.

headline: Rail transit decisions
abstract: It could be many years before a light-rail system emerges as a credible and financially feasible option for serving the commuting needs of the Harrisburg region.  But even if light-rail isn't a viable prospect today or anytime soon, decisions made today could either enhance or hinder the ultimate realization of this exciting transportation alternative.

headline: Preate Praised
abstract: PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr.'s public protection division won a national award from the American Bar Association for recovering $97 million for Pennsylvania consumers.  He also won praise for his work on President Clinton's crime-fighting proposal as the chairmen of the criminal law committee for the National Association of Attorneys General. However, the Pennsylvania Crime Commission is investigating Preate on charges that he took campaign contributions from illegal video poker operators in return for promises to not prosecute them.
