headline: Consumbers helped scuttle West Va.'s state store system
abstract: West Virginia couldn't stop the flow of liquor over state lines prior to 1990.  Its state-operated stores had trouble competing, especially with neighboring Maryland's privately run system.  Today, West Virginia stores openly court Ohio customers through price comparison ads in an Ohio newspaper.  As for illegal transport of alcohol from West Virginia into Pennsylvania, "that's Pennsylvania's pproblem," said Ron Moats, deputy commissioner of Wester Virginia Alcohol Beverage Control.

headline: Clinto: Back plan or show a better way
abstract: Clinton began to travel to gather support for his tax increase plan.

headline: Gov. Florio's Lead Slips As N.J. Contest Tightens
abstract: New Jersey Governor Jim Florio's once-comfortable lead over Republican challenger Christine Todd Whitman has eroded substantially over the past 10 days, as the two head toward Tuesday's election in a climate of deep voter dissatisfaction.

headline: 'Ragin' Cajun' cookin' for Florio
abstract: It's the candidate, stupid!  That might be how James Carville is feeling the week before Election Day as he shies away from media attention.  He's got plenty of it these past two years, and he didn't get to be a famous political strategist, after all, by getting more ink for himself than for his candidate- this year, New Jersey Governor Jim Florio.

headline: 'A big mistake'
abstract: The Lawrence County Commissioners explained yesterday why they did not negotiate further with Wal-Mart Inc. for the sale of county-owned property.  Despite the possibility that the company is looking at land elsewhere, commissioners were chastised by John Graziani.  The commissioners disagreed with his criticism and defended the Wal-Mart dealings.

headline: Reno urges 'new day' in drug war
abstract: U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno wants to allow non-violent convicts an opportunity to work their way out of the federal prisons by completing job-training and drug-rehab programs. She is also looking into the possibility of repealing federal mandatory-minimum drug sentences.

headline: 2-organ transplant eligibility tightened
abstract: If an organ-procurement policy established yesterday had been in place a month ago, Governor Robert P. Casey might still be waiting for a new heart and liver.  The new policy calls for heart-liver transplant candidates to be placed on separate waiting lists for each organ.  Making it to the top of one list would automatically boost them to the top of the other list.

headline: We Need A New System Now-Mere tinkering with health care won't do the job, says Mrs. Clinton
abstract: President Clinton's appointment of wife Hillary Clinton to chair the Task Force on Health Care Reform is seen as risky by pundits, Hillary knows. However, it is her belief that the current system has failed the American people, costing more and covering less than it should. Hillary wants a complete overhaul of the system rather than what she calls mere tinkering with the edges of nonaspects.

headline: Static on school metal detectors
abstract: Hand-held metal detectors will be used for screening weapons in city high schools.  But the Board of Education had some worries that there would be civil liberties lawsuits if they did not create a specific document outlying the proper procedures of the mental detectors.  In other news the Board discused the sexual assult of one of their teachers on a 9 year old girl.

headline: Rethink the DUI campaign
abstract: How many drunks is a seat cushion, bearing a picture of a silly duck wearing a "DUI" T-shirt, going to get off the road?  This is the question being asked by Dauphin County commissioners as they ponder the larger issue of whether the taxpayers are getting their money's worth for the $10,000 being spent to promote sobriety on the highways.

headline: Preate urges end to 'bug' sweeps
abstract: Months after nighttime security sweeps of legislative offices were conducted in the Senate, an attorney general report from Ernie Preate Jr. has been released calling for state police to end the practice.

headline: Consumer protection bill's back
abstract: A new bill in congress will give consumers protection from erroneous credit reports by allowing one free copy of personal credit reports per year.  They will also create a toll free number to report error and give the Federal Trade Commission more power to enforce the protection of costumers.

headline: Clinton delivers eulogy at father-in-law's funeral
abstract: President Clinton gave the eulogy at his father-in-law Hugh Rodham's funeral in Little Rock, Arkansas. Vice President Al Gore, the US Justice Department's Webb Hubbell, White House Chief of Staff Mack McLarty, and other White House staff members were in attendance. The burial and a second funeral is to take place in Scranton, PA, Rodham's hometown.

headline: In a race for votes, Phila. is last lap
abstract: A win for Democrat William Stinson or Republican Bruce Marks in the Second Senate District special election will be more than a personal victory: It will finally put to rest months of legal and political maneuvering between Republicans and Democrats for control of the Pennsylvania state Senate.

headline: Reed foe's son called for hearing
abstract: Supporters of Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed are trying to throw the Rev. James A. Bishop off the Democratic primary for mayor by having his son testify against him in court.  Bishop surmises that they the supeana for his son is related to gathering signitures for his canidicy, but says that this is the dirtiest politics he has seen.

headline: A Hurtin'-city welcome
abstract: Scranton, PA, officially declared a financially distressed city by the state, did its best to host the Clinton family for the funeral of Hugh Rodham, Hillary Clinton's father. Despite previous hype, rain kept away the crowds, though a Scranton police detail of 140, at $150 a day was on guard. Local volunteers had readied the neglected cemetery, whose owner was imprisoned for stealing cemetery funds.

headline: Reno: Center to reduce 'turf wars'
abstract: U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno pledged that the new National Drug Intelligence Center will help eliminate "turf wars" that occur between the federal agencies in fighting drug trafficking.

headline: 5 agencies will share AIDS funds
abstract: Philadelphia has ended its policy of awarding money from the federal Center for Disease Control on a competitive basis. Five local agencies will share the $237, 665 the government granted. Two local agencies failed to qualify for the federal funding, but the Rendell administration has agreed to cover the loss.

headline: What's in it for the neighborhood? Jobs? Neglect?
abstract: Like a wave.  That's how some neighborhood residents said the University of Pennsylvania's $2.1 billion proposal to build a hospital, ambulatory care facility and research park complex on and near the site of the Civic Center would hit West Philadelphia.

headline: Strike extends break in Pine Grove district
abstract: Pine Grove Area School District teachers have mounted a strike that will last up to 10 days over contract agreements and a proposed retiree health-care plan.  Due to Act 88, the school must provide 180 days of education by June 15 regardless of stikes or any other interuptions, and therefore an injunction by the district my be filed against the teachers.

headline: Relocation will add to  congestion
abstract: The proposed relocation of Pennsylvania National Insurance Co. to Hampden Twp. should be reconsidered because of the traffic increase of 600 'one-occupant vehicles' into the already gridlocked streets and highways.  The company should relocate to a  place with public transportation.

headline: Preate: Larsen illegally purchased Rx drugs
abstract: a 10-month, $800,000-plus probe of alleged crimes on the state's Supreme Court has resulted in charges that Justice Rolf Larsen illegally obtained prescription drugs to hide his emotional problems.  State prosecutors yesterday hit Larsen with 27 felony counts for what they called a decade-long scheme of using his doctor and court employees to get him anti-anxiety drugs like Valium and Librium.

headline: Don't bank on those savings from lower cable fees
abstract: Consumer groups rejoiced in April after federal regulations ordered a $1 billion rollback in cable TV rates, the first step in implementing a tough new cable law.  But now those groups and some legislators worry that the law's promise of lower monthly cable fees, better service and more video competition is being jeopardized by resourceful cable industry lawyers who have the law tied up in nearly half a dozen courtrooms from New York to California.

headline: Clinton follows computer maps to White house
abstract: Clinton's campaign contained state of the art mapping equipment that was updated daily.  It showed figures on which advertising was working and other crucial information for the campaign.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: Perry County Commissioner Billy Roush led a contingent of his colleagues in a plea for the PA Legislature to reform revenue-poor counties tax structures, which is the official position of the PA State Association of County Commissioners.  House rookies in the PA legislature are breaking tradition and becoming more vocal in their first term

headline: Reed plant closing will affect families
abstract: need pg 67 of Feb. 1

headline: Allegheny County deserves home rule
abstract: The editorial board argues for home rule by Allegheny County to cut down on the lengthy legislation processes for county operations. Previously home rule has not been supported by voters against sweeping changes, however the current proposal is adoption of the Second Class County Code without structural changes. The board believes it is time for the county to govern itself, as the 19th century political structure requiring it to go through the Legislature is outdated.

headline: Reputed Phila. Mob boss' getaway in New Jersey
abstract: John Stanfa has moved from southern Philadelphia to Burlington County, New Jersey.  Both Pennsylvania and New Jersey police as well as the FBI have recognized his move, but the motive is unknown.

headline: 5 Blues' overhead takes 8% of expenses
abstract: Pennsylvania's five Blue Cross and Blue Shield plans together spent $214 million last year on administrative costs.  That's about 8 percent of their total expenses.  It is also enough money to fund a big city hospital for one year or a city health clinic for the next 20 years.

headline: When the system fails
abstract: Dr. Andrew Krantz's 15 years of chiropractic practice near Atlanta had engendered a familiarity with hospitals, how the various disciplines within their walls worked together, and what might happen if they didn't.  So when Rose, his 82-year-old mother visiting from Philadelphia, was hospitalized last year, Krantz took no chances.  Despite all his precautions, an error- a mix-up with insulin given rather than penicillin- killed his mother.

headline: Students find empathetic ear
abstract: A profile of Maria Perez a former high school drop out, teen mother, and drug addict is now a prime example to help kids at Harrisburg Area High School where she is a guadence counciler.

headline: Repair records falsified at USAir
abstract: USAir is under federal investigation for falsifing mechanics' records.  In two instances the mechanics' said they made repairs, when they didn't, to save the company money.  This endangers the public safety of aviation.

headline: Preate: Sunday Times story 'untrue, unfair, unbelievable'
abstract: The Sunday Times reported that Attorney General and former Lackawanna County district attorney Ernie Preate is being investigated by federal officials for unreported campaign contributions given to him by a corporation that manufactures video poker machines. The story also stated that the Pennsylvania Crime Commission turned over evidence to federal authorities.  Preate claims all accusations against him are false and that he is a victim of a political vendetta.

headline: Don't harass newsletter
abstract: Pennsylvania's insurance department, a toothless watchdog where real insurance companies are concerned, has nevertheless managed to sink its gums into a charitable newsletter run by Amish and Mennonites.  The Christian Brotherhood Newsletter publishes names of those who need help paying medical bills and subscribers then make donations.  The insurance department declared that this constituted an unlicensed insurance company, and sprang into action.

headline: Clinton pounds Specter on jobs
abstract: Republicans filibustering the Clinton economic stimulus package are skeptical of earmarks, questionable projects, and increase in the deficit. However, the White House is putting pressure on several Northern Senators, including US Senator Arlen Specter, citing the number of jobs the stimulus plan will create to aid what has so far been a jobless recovery in PA.

headline: Investigate misuse of WAMS
abstract: Once again Vincent Fumo and Dwight Evans are under fire because of their use of WAM (Walking Around Money).  State Auditor General Barbara Hafer is not doing this for political purposes.  She and most Pennsylvanians are concerned about the accumulated power and wealth of two state legislators, Fumo and Evans.

headline: Retired teachers at odds with PSEA
abstract: On September 27, about 5,000 retired school employees from all areas of Pennsylvania held a rally at our State Capitol.  These folks were representative members of the Pennsylvania Association of School Retirees (PASR), the largest school employee organization in the state and in existence for more than 50 years.  The Pennsylvania State Education Association-Retired, via PSEA has sent a letter to its members urging them to work against PASR.

headline: Bailing out the city
abstract: The writer believes the one percent raise in sales tax in the county (Pittsburgh) was done by the politicians to help them with their duties and not to use on city facilities. He does not think the money will be given back to the people, but will be given to city officials and the bureaucracy.

headline: Respect family's privacy
abstract: It seems unfair that the media sensationalized a young man's death, Michael Rozgonyi.  They don't know the whole truth so they shouldn't be allowed to broadcast what appears to be a biased opinion.

headline: A cluster of sudden deaths puzzles county coroners in Pa
abstract: Indiana County coroner Thomas Streams asked members of the PA State Coroners Association to report sudden deaths preceded by flu-like illness after 6 cases have recently been recorded. The PA and Montgomery County Departments of Health are investigating the deaths. Rather safe than sorry, Streams has sent blood samples to the  Federal Center for Disease Control and Prevention.

headline: When the workplace is a health hazard
abstract: Subtle toxins poison millions, especially in small businesses.  Often they're oblivious.

headline: Students struggle to get courses
abstract: Overcrowding in the state community colleges is the product of the number of students doubling over the last five years and the classroom space not changing.  The growing enrollment is causing some to want Pennsylvania to increase the amount of money it gives to the colleges, which Gov. Casey is considering.  The colleges are also considering raising the cost of a credit hour by $2.

headline: Residents make pleas to close Tullytown ramp
abstract: Several have died on the Old Route 13-Route 13 ramp in Tullytown.  Opponents aren't willing to wait for a redesign.

headline: Presumed Innocent
abstract: Mumia Abu-Jamal, once a WHYY-FM reporter, was convicted in 1982 of murdering a Philadelphia cop, Daniel Faulkner, and has gotten a lot of attention since being put on death row. A member of MOVE, he was supported by PA state Representative David Richardson and PA state Senator T. Milton Street and even has had numerous organizations, such as Amnesty International, appeal to PA Governor Robert P. Casey to take him off of death row. The PA courts and US Supreme Courts have held to his guilt.

headline: Don't wager on floating casinos
abstract: Powerful politicians in Pittsburgh and Erie are pushing for the Pennsylvania Legislature to legalize riverboat gambling.  There are many excellent reasons why they shouldn't succeed, but we'll have to pull out all the stops to scuttle their effort.

headline: Clinton proposes ways to cut federal spending
abstract: The government-issued ashtray- which had to meet 10 pages of regulations- may soon be a thing of the past.  President Clinton sent congress legislation yesterday overhauling the government's purchasing rules to allow agencies to buy more off-the-shelf goods.

headline: Governor displayed courage in Hazleton
abstract: Governor Bob Casey was in Hazleton May 27 and 28 for "Capital for a Day," events, though he had health problems and he also appeared to be ill.  The governor displayed immense courage during his two days in Hazleton.  He had to be tired, but he carried out his duties as head of the state.

headline: Singel seeks to carve out larger niche
abstract: While PA Governor Casey is recovering from his heart-liver transplant, PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel is acting in his place.  Some question what his political future will hold once Casey is able to return.

headline: Buffalo board takes heat over sewer suit
abstract: A member of Buffalo's township municipal authority criticized the board of supervisors for failing to reveal the details of a lawsuit between the authority and its former engineering company.  W.E.C. Engineering Company claims that the municipal authority didn't pay for some of the work the company did for the authority's sewer system.

headline: Review support payments
abstract: The new law that will take effect in January 1994 will require mandatory wage attachments for child support payments.  Once again the dutiful, hard-working individual who is willing to pay to support his children is punished because of the deadbeats.  This system is grossly unfair and must be reviewed.

headline: A Consumer's Guide: How Different Groups Would Be Affected
abstract: A guide is given on the new health-care plan that President Clinton has drafted for how the program will work for you in your particular situation.

headline: When yellow fever held Philadelphia in its deadly grip
abstract: Article discusses the yellow fever plague that struck Philadelphia in the late 1700s.

headline: Students walk ot over vo-tech firings
abstract: Several hundred high school students walked out of classes at the Milton Hershey School yesterday as part of a protest against the dismissal of six administrators.  Milton Hershey's board wanted to make room for new blood.  Protesters see a sinister, secret board.

headline: Ribbon cut on bypass section
abstract: A 3.15-mile road that took 40 years to build is expected to open to traffic on Wednesday.  Politicians who stepped to the microphone on Friday during a ribbon-cutting ceremony to mark the near completion of the Uniontown Bypass spoke on the cooperation and perserverance needed to win highways.  The Uniontown Bypass originated in the 1950's as a way to eliminate traffic congestion in Uniontown.

headline: Prevention, not prison, best remedy for violence, parole officers told
abstract: In the same way that more and better lung surgery will not reduce the rate of lung cancer, putting more people in prison will not reduce violence in America, an assistant dean of the School of Public Health at Harvard University, Deborah Prothrow-Stith, told 1,200 probation and parole officers at their convention in Philadelphia this week.

headline: Eatery play areas may be regulated
abstract: Pennsylvnia's not clowning around.  Chuck E. Cheese, McDonald's and other restaurants may end up accountable to the state for their playgrounds' safety.  An Agriculture Department advisory committee is considering whether to recommend the department take jurisdiction over such play areas.

headline: Clinton stumps for health plan, Florio
abstract: Saying that curbing urban violence is critical to controlling health-care costs, President Clinton came to New Jersey yesterday to stump for his national health-care plan and give a boost to Governor Florio's re-election campaign.  Clinton also called for a national ban on assault rifles.  Not coincidentally, Florio's assault rifle ban is one of the cornerstones of the Democrat's re-election campaign, with Election Day little more than three weeks away.

headline: Governor hopeful chides Democrats, blames party for loss of jobs in state
abstract: Earl Baker, the Chester County state senator and former state GOP chairman, was in Lancaster Friday to announce his candidacy for governor.  Flanked by his family and state Representative Art Hershey, Baker criticized the Democratic administration for driving jobs out of Pennsylvania.

headline: Reform requires sustained push
abstract: It's vital that the allegations of misconduct swirling around state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen don't overshadow fresh disclosures that prove the need to revamp the court itself.  Let's get started now.  The Legislature should take the lead by scheduling a constitutional convention devoted solely to fixing the court.

headline: Cities take a variety of approaches to tax-delinquent properties
abstract: All over the country, cities struggle with the problem of residents who can't pay their property taxes.  But the way these cities handle tax-delinquent properties is as different as their weather and regional accents.  And even when cities have a choice, as Pittsburgh does, they are guided by vastly different philosophies.

headline: Rival justices sit side by side
abstract: State Supreme Court justices Larsen and Zappala, whom have been in the national spotlight for accusations toward one another ranging from judicial misconduct to attempted murder, were for the first time since these accusations have been made public they sat next to one another to hear a case on the Supreme Court.  Neither uttered a word to the other, but the tension was obvious in their body language.

headline: A day in the life of 3 doctors
abstract: Family doctors in Canada and Germany have less access to high tech than US counterparts. Though they are paid less, and their access to technology and pharmaceutical prescriptions regulated, their satisfaction is greater. In the US, only 30% of doctors provide primary care, while in Canada there are waiting lists for some services, and in Germany the government mandates primary care to decrease costs.

headline: White House seeks home care for all disabled
abstract: President Clinton has tentatively decided that every severely disabled American should have insurance coverage for long-term care at home. The new $15.4 billion-a year benefit is to be included in the core package of medical insurance benefits being designed by the administration. The long-term care is expected to be supported by the AARP.

headline: Study Finds Most Students Lack Reasoning Skills in Mathematics
abstract: When it comes to mathematical problem-solving, most American students just don't get it, the Department of Education said in a report issued Wednesday.  The department's National Center for Education Statistics said only 16 percent of fourth graders, 8 percent of the eighth graders and 9 percent of the high school seniors correctly answered mathematics questions requiring problem-solving skills in a nation-wide test.

headline: Robinson, Wagner call Conrail route threat to city
abstract: Two local officials, City Council President Jack Wagner and Frank Brooks Robinson, chiarman of the Public Auditorium Authority, warned that a disaster affecting a large section of Downtown is imminent unless Conrail relocates its train tracks and railroad bridge that run near the David L. Lawrence Convention Center.

headline: Prison board buys sneakers made in China
abstract: Looking to save money, the Luzerne County Prison Board voted 4-1 Monday to buy as many as 1,200 pairs of shoes from China rather than an American-made product.

headline: Fidelity is taking name of its parent
abstract: Fidelity Bank is changing its name to First Fidelity to match its New Jersey-based corporate parent, officals said yesterday.  A similar move is under way at a Pittsburgh-based PNC Bank Corp.

headline: Clinton talks of his wish to inspire
abstract: Presdient-elect Clinton gave an inspiration speech to those at Howard and Georgetown Universities on Martin Luther King Jr Day.

headline: Governor hopefuls warm up
abstract: A panel of gubernatorial candidates including PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, PA Representative Dwight Evans, PA Senator Earl Baker, PA Senator Mark Fisher, and PA Attorney General Ernie Preate was hosted by the Commission for Independent Colleges and Universities. The members discussed plans for higher education and state aid to public and private schools. The only official gubernatorial candidate, US Representative Tom Ridge, was not present.

headline: Region struggles to return to normal
abstract: Things are getting back to normal after the weekend's extraordinary snow storm that left two feet of snow.  The death toll has risen to 12, all but one from heart attacks while shoveling snow.

headline: City budget no bitter pill, sources say
abstract: Mayor Rendell will plans to announce today that the extreme measures he had been talking about for the last few months to balance the city's budget may not be needed.  The reason for this is a larger than expected tax revinue.  He plans to privatize some health care facilies, lower then number of firefighters on latter trucks from 5 to 4, and erase about 1,000 city jobs, most of which are vacant.

headline: Robbed and shot, he's loyal to borough
abstract: Monessen Mayor Robert Leone said that a $111 robbery in which he was shot and wounded was one of the reasons he decided to sell his service station at Eastgate Plaza. Leone was the first witness in the case again Gary Lee Warrington, one of the two suspects charged in the robbery-shooting; Eugene A. Robinson is also awaiting trial on similar charges.

headline: A disservice to sonograms
abstract: Sonograms can provide parents with choices.  It cannot change complications with the baby that have already developed, but it can provide the parents with preparation for the complications.  The fields of radiology and sonography are done a great disservice when phrases like "$200 baby photo shot in the womb" are used to describe an exam which is a meticulous, detailed survey of the fetal anatomy by skilled specialists.

headline: White House Tries New Numbers To Bolster Health Plan's Appeal
abstract: Struggling to convince Americans that its health care plan would save most people money, the Clinton Administration today produced its third set of predictions of how many Americans would pay more, or less, for health insurance.

headline: Support libraries privately
abstract: Elizabeth Larson believes that when hard-pressed governments have to make choices, libraries cannot be a priority, despite what the American Library Association may argue. The government should be fighting crime and protecting the lives and property of its citizens. In Larson's view, community spirit should be what keeps a library open, not people looking to score a free read, or schools looking to supplement their own shortcomings.

headline: Route 30 bypass work expected to begin in '96
abstract: A new plan adopted by the PA Transportation Commission will widen Route 30 two years earlier than planned.

headline: Prison hostage freed
abstract: Ohio State Coorectional Facility guard Darrold Clark was released from hostage after prisoners made an emotional appeal for their demands via live radio broadcast. Prisoners said they are willing to die, but hope to successfully negotiate with the Federal Bureau of Investigations for better conditions, removal of the warden, and better health care. Though officials have been granting prisoners good faith payments, the Ohio Funeral Director Association's mass casualty disaster team is on site.

headline: Fighting back
abstract: Sharon Steel workers want the banks that hold liens on the corporation to open the vault and let back wages spill out.  Taking their plight to the streets, the United Steelworkers of America Local 1197 began picketing Mellon Bank offices over the past two weeks.

headline: Clinton Unveils Plan to Restrict PAC influence
abstract: President Clinton proposed a bill that offers public subsidies for television commercials for Congressional candidates who limit their spending and seeks to reduce the influence of lobbyists and political action committees. The bill will keep the limit of $5,000 for House candidates and lowers the limit for Senate candidates to $2,500 that they can receive from PACs.  Congressional Democrats to keep the limit at $5,000 fearing they would not be able to be re-elected with the cut.  Article includes a chart showing all of Clinton's campaign proposals.

headline: Governor of Oklahoma Says He Won't Seek Second Term
abstract: Governor David Walters, who pleaded guilty last month to violating the campaign financing law, said on Monday that he would not run for a second term next year.  The governor, a 41-year-old Democrat, cited family considerations for his decision.  His Oct. 21 guilty plea was "not the determining factor" in his decision, he said.

headline: Reinventing government? Ask Philly
abstract: When it comes to "reinventing government," the current Clinton-Gore buzzword, Philadelphia is well ahead of the curve.  For most of the past year and a half, Philadelphia and the Rendell administration have been praised as a national model for redefining and re-tooling government to make it perform better and cost less.

headline: City politics is still a boys' club
abstract: Jane R. Eisner, a member of the Editorial Board, points out the lack of representation of women in the Philadelphia government. She believes that Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell is not doing his part to bring women into his administration and support them the way people thought that he would. When Councilwoman Happy Fernandez attended a budget meeting with Rendell, she was the only woman in room full of men. The author believes women are not being incorporated into the government enough.

headline: Robbery ends in shootout
abstract: Robbery victim was killed after an off-duty police officer startled two armed robbers which started a 30 shot shoot-out, leaving one of the two robbery victims dead.

headline: A health-care plan for all women
abstract: Even before the President's speech, health guru Ira Magaziner said they were prepared to accept a plan without abortion coverage.  It took a spine-stiffening visit from the Congressional Women's Caucus and a pre-emptive press conference to get the administration back on track.

headline: White House vows it will soon send health plan to Congress
abstract: The White House sought yesterday to blunt mounting attacks on its health plan by promising that the long-delayed blueprint will be delivered to Congress soon in final legislative form.

headline: Supporters push forward a bill to put OBE into law
abstract: A legislative fight over the controversial outcome-based education plan took a twist as Senate committee passed a bill that would put into the law the new rules for public schools.  Opponents, including Gov. Casey, have argued that outcome deals too much with values and attitudes.

headline: Route 30 bypasses rejected in study
abstract: A study by Gannett-Fleming Inc. which cost $1.1 million in tax money declared that the effect from a by-pass of Chambersburg or Gettysburg would have a minimal effect because the finial destition for  most of the traffic that congests these towns is Chambersburg or Gettysburg.

headline: Prison opens new building
abstract: Despite thousands of new cells, state prisons in Pennsylvania will remain overcrowded until the Legislature adopts sentencing reform, the Camp Hill state prison superintendent said Tuesday.  To some degree, keeping the prison population down is contingent upon state legislators reducing reliance on mandatory sentencing.  If that doesn't happen, Camp Hill and other prisons statewide will be just as overcrowded after the expansion.

headline: Firms invited to use Penn State Research Park
abstract: Penn State Research Park is not yet open for business, but university officals were in Harrisburg last week to drum up interest among midstate businesses, giving them the message that Penn State Univeristy offers world-class professors, facilities and results, including inventions by faculty members that are available for licensing by business who see a a way to market them at a profit.

headline: Clinton, Florida-Bound
abstract: President Clinton will join the exodus from Washington this Labor Day weekend, jetting to south Florida to check on reconstruction a year after Hurricane Andrew devastated the area.

headline: Gov't gimmies will get us
abstract: The federal budget is being taken up and in danger due to entitlement programs;  Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security unemployment compensation, and farm-price support. President Bill Clinton was meeting with others to look into this problem. One problem is that many people depend on these programs, including the elderly, and do not want to have their taxes raised in order to pay for them.

headline: Reinventing stirs state's officials
abstract: Ted Gaebler, coauthor of the book Reinventing Government that has stirred government offical from President Clinton to state reps, has been meeting with bureaucrats to talk about his view.  He believes that more power must  be given to the lower end government workers to save money for the government.

headline: 'Clean and Green' participants save green
abstract: The 'Clean and Green' program is saving a combined total of $250,000 annually in county tax for large land owners, such as farmers and forestry.  It is not taxing them on the value of the land according to the market, but rather according to land use.  If the farmer wants to sell the land or develop it they must pay the county the back taxes up to seven years plus six percent interset.

headline: What price welfare?
abstract: How can one not afford a rent raise in an apartment complex, yet five families in the same complex, who are on welfare, can afford the raise?  Talk about injustice.  The whole welfare system needs to be changed.

headline: A hospital drug mix-up turns into fatal error
abstract: A St. Clair nurse, believing she was reaching for a single-dose, 100-milligram syringe of the heart drug lidocaine, instead picked up a similar-looking 2-gram syringe.  The injection delivered 20 times the prescribed dose, killing Ed Wolf Jr. within hours.  The facts of Wolf's death were made public in 191, 13 months after he died, when St. Clair came under state scrutiny following two other unusual overdose deaths.

headline: Will Casey give repeat performance?  Stay tuned
abstract: PA Governor Casey says that in spite of his heart-liver transplant, he will resume his duties as Governor as soon as he feels physically able.

headline: Susquenita board to vote; classes resuming
abstract: The School board is voting today on a tentative four year contract settlement that would end the three day strike in Susquenita school District. The three day strike will push the last day of classes from June 15 to June 18.

headline: Rt. 23 expressway study will take 2-3 more years:  PennDot considering corridor north of existing road
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation began a study in the mid-1990 hoping to finish the proposed Route 23 expressway in Lancaster County in one year, and now say that it will not be completed for another 2 to 3 years.  PennDot says it may revise the route for the corridor north instead of south of the existing road.  3 PA governors have failed to make a decision on the road and now the estimated $762,000 cost is being revised upward.

headline: Prisons change procedures after accidental releases
abstract: The Dauphin County Prison will slow admission procedures for inmates next year, a move prison officials hope will reduce the chances of suspected criminals being released accidentally.  The prison will admit one police department and its prisoners at a time, ending the practice of processing the paperwork on several prisoners at the same time so each officer who brings a suspect can leave more quickly.

headline: Fly the open skies
abstract: Great Britain and the U.S. will begin talks in May to revamp agreements that guide international airline service which the editorial board believes will result in the world's air carriers being unshackled from anti-competitive government politics on both sides which is evident from the difficulty USAir Group Inc. had in completing a recent agreement with British Airways.

headline: Collingdale audit finds little problems, not big: Hafer: Borough should learn from error of its ways
abstract: In the state audit of Collingdale's pension plans for both police and non-uniformed borough employees, they have found a string of poor accounting practices that PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer said she hopes Collingdale's will improve the management of their pension funds.

headline: Group recommends against 7 state judicial hopefuls
abstract: The Pennsylvania Bar Association announced the ratings of 22 statewide judicial candidates, saying they could not recommend seven of the candidates running. The lone female in the group did not receive a recommendation and claimed that the results were sexist; she stated in the past two years, three women have been rated, two of them not receiving the recommendation. The Bar Association says they will give reasons to why they rated candidates the way they did.

headline: Rendell and City Hall: A natural fit
abstract: Rendell's successes since sworn into office last year as mayor of Philadelphia include improvements in finance, labor, economic development, imagine, and intergovernmental relations.  Although Rendell has made many improvements there are still many to be addressed including urban problems, crime, poverty, budget cuts, and layoffs.

headline: Dangerous financing
abstract: The new 'creative' financing Mayor Stephen R. Reed is using to slow the city's debt of $15.4 million is dangerous.

headline: Willing adopters feel held back by DHS
abstract: On any given day in 1989, 50 to 60 boarder babies were housed in Philadelphia hospitals.  Today there are few, if any, boarder babies because the city's Department of Human Services, along with a consortium of foster care agencies, launched a campaign to recruit foster families, particularly those interested in caring for drug-affected babies.

headline: A job well done
abstract: Steve Twedt's series "Medication Errors" provided us with a thorough, focused and objective examination of a complex subject.  Possibly most important, the series is working as a catalyst to promote further intense examination by each hospital and group action among Western Pennsylvania hospitals.

headline: William Penn opens health academy
abstract: Many of the future African-American doctors, nurses and health professionals who are now North Philadelphia high school students will someday be able to look back and say "thanks" to William Penn High School, Hahnemann University, Workforce 2000, and a group of local politicalns and business professionals who took an early interest in their futures by opening a new Health Academy from William Penn High School.

headline: TAP plan a worthy gamble
abstract: Pennsylvania is rolling the dice with its new Tuition Account Program, but it's a gamble on the future of the state that is well worth taking.

headline: Rt. 65 section closing for year
abstract: The state Transportation Department reminds motorists that rebuilding of the Eckert Street Bridge on Route 65 (Ohio River Boulevard) will begin after 9 am Tuesday for the duration of one year.

headline: Probe centers on crime panel
abstract: Lawmakers are threatening to cut out of the budget the Pennsylvania Crime Commission, which is mandated to investigate organized criminal activity an public corruption within the commonwealth and report it to the PA General Assembly. Lawmakers are unhappy that the commission prints citizens' names without enough evidence to prosecute them and think that their $2.5 million budget is too large.

headline: Foglietta opposes gambling along the Delaware
abstract: Conjuring up images of garish, Las Vegas-style neon casting an unsavory glow on Philadelphia's historic landmarks and traditions, Representative Tom Foglietta yesterday declared his strong opposition to riverfront gambling as a solution to the city's economic woes.

headline: Commissioners pass pay raise ordinance
abstract: Cumberland county commissioners yesterday unanimously passed a pay raise ordinance for elected officals.

headline: Grudge Match: State Senate makes pettiness an art
abstract: Now that the Democrats have a one vote control of Senate they seem to be using it to gain petty advantage and personally attacking the Republicans with votes about office space and parking spaces rather than voting on legitimate legislature.

headline: Rendell berates Specter
abstract: Members of the Mayor's Commission for Economic Development at the Philadelphia Naval Base yesterday tentatively approved a Rendell administration report that assumes the Navy Yard will close in 1996.  Mayor Rendell, meanwhile, scolded US Senator Arlen Specter for his weekend complaints that the report undermines a lawsuit aimed at forcing the government to keep the yard open.

headline: Countians seek reform on tax
abstract: Berks Countians told a state Senate panel Tuesday they want some relief from burdensome property taxes.  But most were not certain in what form that relief should come.  Nearly 125 people, most of them elderly, packed into the Berks county Senior Citizens Center auditorium to discuss local property tax reform with state Senator Michael A. O'Pake, who has written one of the bills being considered by Harrisburg, and Senator Michael M. Dawida, the chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, which is considering the measures.

headline: null
abstract: Sept. 22 BIG (Beaver Initiative for Growth) begins intensive lobbying in Harrisburg for 18 projects they support in promise of jobs for Pennsylvania through legislative funding.  Now, who of sane mind would oppose such projects in view of Pennsylvania's problematic economy?

headline: A matter of Life and Death
abstract: The issue of health care in the United States is beginning to question whether it should continue to provide prolonging life procedures. Many experts are beginning to say that it is costing the US Health Care system too much and it is not beneficial, but those receiving the treatment do not agree with eliminating the coverage and care.

headline: Wofford expects bipartisan support for health plan
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford said that he gained new hope that President Clinton's health care reform package would win bipartisan support and be enacted before the end of 1993.  Hillary Rodham Clinton, head of the president's health care task force gave a briefing for a bi-partisan group composing of half of the US Senate.

headline: TAP questions and answers
abstract: Some questions and answers are given about the state Treasury's Tuition Account Program.

headline: SEPTA chief defends management
abstract: Louis J. Gambaccini, the general manager for SEPTA in Philadelphia, defends the budget and the efficency cost of the transit system against a previous letter written on the Editorial pages.  He claims SEPTA is one of the most cost-effective, top ranked, explains how railwork is essential, and how money is being spent to make SEPTA better.

headline: Program may bounce DWI suspects who lie
abstract: The Pa Supreme Court ruled that convicted drunken drivers who lie about prior offenses may be thrown out of a special program that allows them to be put on probation without ending up with a criminal conviction.

headline: For SmithKline plant, the phaseout drags on
abstract: Company executives of the pharmacuetical firm SmithKline Beecham had hoped to close the plant soon after announcing that moving the drug production elsewhere and selling various drug-making rights to other companies would save money. However, because the US Food and Drug Administration enforces strict guidelines on transferring drug production, the plant is experiencing a long slow decline towards its final close.

headline: Common Pleas judge winner withdraws from November race
abstract: Katherine B.L. "Karin" Platt, a Republican lawyer who won a slot on the Democratic ballot for Common Please Court judge, withdrew from the race so that she would not be running against fellow Republicans.

headline: Hafer campaign dismisses Rollins
abstract: Political strategist Ed Rollins, embroiled in election controversy in New Jersey, lost his entry in the 1994 Pennsylvania governor's race yesterday as Republican Barbara Hafer dumped him as her campaign consultant.

headline: Rendell: 'Both sides' violated law in Second Senate District voting
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell spoke out that both parties committed voter fraud in the Philadelphia Second Senate District. Rendell though does not believe that all the blame should be on William G. Stinson and that the PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. would be able to handle the case without the assistance of the US Justice Department. Accusations surrounding the election include the misuse of absentee ballots on both side; however the PA Supreme Court has said that city commissioners should hear the case before it would reach the state Supreme Court.

headline: County budget display a big joke
abstract: Roger C. Spitz, a Carlisle borough council member, is tired of hearing public officals in Dauphin County say that people do not look at the budget and therefore do not care.

headline: A market that's now a peach of a place
abstract: Merchants and city officials yesterday toasted the Philadelphia Regional Produce Market, which has completed a $20 million modernization.  The market, where grocers and restaruants buy fresh produce early in the morning, was known as the Food Distribution Center until its renovation, completed last summer.

headline: A model for curbing U.S. drug costs?
abstract: In an attempt to cap prices on new, name-brand perscription drugs, some look to Canada's national price control board as a model.  The drug companies say that this would be a 'grave mistake' because unlike Canada the U.S. has generally favored less government intervention and a higher relience on private health care.

headline: Wofford plan would help retirees keep benefits
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford said that he is proposing a "stop-gap" measure in Congress to help retirees who lose their medical benefits as a result of corporate cross-cutting.  In a statement, Wofford cited a study by the consulting firm A. Foster Higgins that found two-thirds of US companies plan to reduce retiree health beneftis or shift more costs to retirees.

headline: Tax Reform
abstract: The editorial is in response to the PA Senate committee's tax reform proposal that does not include school districts. They believe that even if it is a political necessity, the PA Legislature cannot ignore the problem of school district taxation much longer.

headline: SEPTA's 'better than driving' a hard sell
abstract: According to its new marketing cmpaign, SEPTA wants to be known as "Better Than Driving."  But Philadelphia area commuters seem to be saying "We Don't Think So."

headline: Rock hurlers prompt I-83 travel warning
abstract: The message from state police is clear: Stay in the right-hand lane when traveling on Interstate 83.  Unsuspecting motorists have been injured by large rocks lobbed at their vehicles.  State police have received reports of 16 rock-throwing attacks since November 13.  Most of the incidents occurred between 6 and 9pm between the extis 7 and 10 on the outskirts of York.

headline: For SmithKline plant, the phase-out drags on
abstract: Company executives of the pharmaceutical firm SmithKline Beecham had hoped to close the plant soon after announcing that moving the drug production elsewhere and selling various drug-making rights to other companies would save money. However, because the US Food and Drug Administration enforces strict guidelines on transferring drug production, the plant is experiencing a long slow decline towards its final close.

headline: Complacency perceived
abstract: The disparity between the needs of the people versus the people in power becomes obvious when little offhand remarks are made like the one by Governor Robert P. Casey when he recently left the hospital, showing that he is so far above the average person that it is impossible for him ot reach down and fulfill the needs of the people.

headline: Hafer picks former Reagan manager to run her campaign
abstract: PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer chose Ronald Reagan's campaign manager to head her 1994 gubernatorial campaign.

headline: Rep. McDade Spared From Ouster by Rule
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph M. McDade will be allowed to keep his committee posts in spite of being indicted with racketeering, conspiracy and taking bribes. This is because the new rule says that Representatives will have to step down if accused of criminal crimes will only apply to future cases and will not be used retroactively.

headline: County wants to tax Schenley golf course
abstract: The Masloff administration has been shocked to learn that the city-owned facility of Schenley Park gold course, which for decades has been tax-exempt property, has been shifted into the taxable category.  The unexpected move by Allegheny County's Board of Property Assessment, Appeals and Review could worsen the already shaky relations between city and county governments.

headline: Account for $5.1 million, HUD letter orders Delco
abstract: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development has issued a letter to Delaware County, demanding that it prove it didn't misspend $5.1 million dollars in funds the Department of Housing and Urban Development granted.

headline: A New Framework for Health Care
abstract: To control medical costs and provide secure coverage to all, President Clinton has proposed a vast restructuring of the health care system, to be phased in over several years.  The strategy is to make consumers conscious of the true cost of their care and, by fostering competition among plans, to force the plans to cut costs and offer better service.

headline: Women press role in health reform
abstract: Women in Congress and other activivists are pushing hard to ensure that women are not left out of the national health-care reform.  Womne's health advocates insist that a basic health benefits package fully covers reproductive health care, from Pap smears to prenatal care to abortion.  But many pro-life advocates do not want the government to pay for abortions.

headline: Taxpayers can't afford to lose private schools
abstract: PA Senator Mike Dawida talks about a bill in which he and PA Senator Hank Salvatore introduced which would offer the same educational opportunities for children of moderate income as those with higher incomes. The wealthy have always had choice of where to send their children to school, this bill will help provide the poor with that same choice.

headline: Shift in depot exit plan sought
abstract: Opponets of a new road that could be built to improve access to the New Cumberland Defense Distribution Depot believe they have come up with a better idea that would have a new interchange off of the turnpike below valuable wetlands the depot owns.  The turnpike commission is worried that will cost too much money and the residents of Marsh Run Road would have to put up with increased traffic.

headline: Rolf Larson: Inadvertent Judicial Reformer
abstract: PA Justice Rolf Larsen never set out to reform the PA Supreme Court, but his response to misconduct charges and startling counter-accusastions may ultimately do more to reform than decades of good-government moralizing. Larsen's accusations against Supreme Court Justices Stephen Zappala and Ralph Cappy are so surprising that merit selection of PA judges has been introduced in both Houses of the PA legislature to allow the governor to apoint all state appellate judges.

headline: Freshening up the great indoors
abstract: A state Senate committee held hearings in Pittsburgh yesterday on a bill that would bank smoking in bingo halls and shopping malls, at public meetings and convention halls, and at factories and restaurants, no matter how small.  In fact, the bill, which is intended to protect people from second-hand smoke, would forbid smoking pretty much anywhere indoors except in bars and homes.

headline: Computer workers may feel the byte
abstract: The federal Defense Department decided to keep the Naval Aviation Supply Office open, but was forced to lay workers off in order to do so when they consolidated 158 data-processing centers into fifteen "megacenters".  U.S. Representative Robert Borski and U.S. Representative Bob Livingston are attempting to force a study of the plan, arguing that the Pentagon cannot consolidate the data centers without approval of Congress.

headline: Hafer reimburses Phila. For pensions, disabilities
abstract: PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer gave Philadelphia officials a $4.5 million reimbursement for disability payments the city made to retired and disabled police and firefighters.

headline: Repeal, don’t replace, tax
abstract: PA Senator Melissa Hart, Minority Chair of the Senate Finance Committee, writes that in agreement to the editorial boards criticisms of the PA Senate Finance Committee's action on legislation changing the county personal property tax because the arbitrary tax is inequitable and burdensome to families that save and invest.  She says that Republicans were united in favor of repealing the personal property tax.

headline: Ding-a-ling, ding-a-ling - its your deficit calling
abstract: The city of Philadelphia spent $90,000 in late fees for the phone bills.  They called directory assistance 271,650 times last year instead of looking numbers up in the phone book which cost $95,000.  No one knows who made the calls and even prison immates are taking advantage of the disorganization by making long distance calls and having the city foot the bill.

headline: Adams County gets $288,988 for migrant and year-round farmworker housing project
abstract: Adams County will receive $288,988 to construct and rehabilitate 19 housing units for migrant and year-round farm workers which was awarded by the Pennsylvania Department of Community Affairs. The program represents a partnership between county fruit growers and two local nonprofits, Rural Opportunities Inc. and the Adams County Housing Authority.

headline: A plan for (almost) everyone
abstract: The $700 billion healht-care reform plan proposed last night by President Clinton would guarantee cradle-to-grave health insurance to virtually all Americans through regional health-insurance alliances.  Under this so-called managed competition, alliances and large self-insured corporations would bargain with doctors and hospitals for the best deals, presumably bringing down prices.

headline: Year later, no disabled businesses
abstract: After a year since the Americans with Disabilities Act went into effect businesses are cooping with the results, which aren’t as bad as they expected.  Although there have been lawsuits against companies and individuals alike the benefit of the Act has heavily outweighed the cost.

headline: Teacher contract delayed
abstract: An arbitration panel appointed to try to resolve stagnant teacher contract talks in Susquenita School district has scheduled a secound meeting.  The teachers want $7,900, the school board $4,700, and the arbitration panel found that $6,800 would be appropriate.

headline: Shifting Route 18 carries a price
abstract: PennDOT must do all it can to accommodate Geneva College's request that Route 18 be rerouted without offending the school's neighbors.  The route that the college has proposed doesn't come without a price.  Hopefully PennDOT, the college and the homeowners can work out an agreement that will be in the best interests of all involved.

headline: Rules on huge propane tanks needed, judge says
abstract: After the PA Department of Labor and Industry's Industrial Board approved construction of two propane tanks relying on technological which failed in a New York explosion, the Schaefferstown Area Quality of Life Committee went to the Commonwealth Court. Judge David Craig ordered written standards of operation, public hearings and reports, and approval by independent regulatory review. PA Senator David Brightbill opposes adoption of Fire Protection Association standards as a solution the company is considering.

headline: From two small ships, port optimism blossoms
abstract: After local importers, exporters, and other maritime businesses gathered together to form Ship Philadelphia First under the approval of PA Governor Robert Casey in response to being formally dropped as a port of call by the Trans Atlantic Agreement, the city scored a deal with the American Contract Freight Line. The association in the industry has since led to a rise in interest among other companies, proving the cartel that once abandoned the city's industry is on shaky ground.

headline: Concourses swept clean
abstract: For a week, ominous rumors swirled among advocates for the homeless: The city would hire a private security force to drive the homeless from Center City subway concourses, sweeping them not into shelthers, but into the cold night.  It turnout out differently.

headline: Hafer says $34 million missing
abstract: A report on money used for legislative pet projects shows some funds were improperly expended or spent in violation of state contract terms, Auditor General Barbara Hafer said yesterday.  Hafer released a long-awaited audit of the Department of Community Affairs, the conduit for most of the legislative initiative grants, known as "walking around money" or WAMs.

headline: Reporting deserves credit
abstract: Reporter Mary Niederberger attended the Parenting with Humor Power seminar and wrote a feature story that reflected the fact that she listened diligently to the content and carefully analyzed it.  Ms. Niederberger's informative and upbeat style was a pleasure to read.  Her examples were well-chosen and well-expressed.

headline: Don't forget manufacturing
abstract: Two stories in last weeks Pittsburgh Business Times created an interesting irony. One of the stories detailed the efforts of Alcoa to find new office space for top executives, while the other explored the winners and losers among Pittsburgh's publicly held corporations for the first four months of this year. Alcoa repositions itself by downsizing its white-collar work force; the city of Pittsburgh should pay extra attention to Alcoa and not take its presence for granted because it does a lot for the city.

headline: Aid for Vartan Village
abstract: There is now no doubt that the City of Harrisburg is willing to assist the Vartan Village project of rebuilding an uptown neighborhood.  Mayor Stephen Reed has pledged land, manpower, and cooperation to a project led by several religious leaders and a developer.

headline: A Senator Finds Strong Support On Health Care
abstract: Returning to the issue he brought to national prominence in 1991, Senator Harris Wofford today found strong and unexpected support among small-business men for the idea of requiring employers to pay health insurance premiums for their workers.

headline: A hands-off approach to farming
abstract: The U.S. Census Bureau reported that only 56% of farmers farm their own land.  44% of farmers rent their land to others, and 6% both farm and rent their land.

headline: Teacher's class day less frantic
abstract: In intensive scheduling, which makes classes longer but has students going to less classes, teachers throughout the country are seeing improved attendance and grades. The teachers who are part of the intensive scheduling schools say that it makes the day less hectic and is successful.

headline: State drivers give pike good grades
abstract: A survey coducted a Penn State University Harrisburg rated the Pennsylvania turnpike in six catigories.  The overall  satifaction of those polled was up from last year, but in  other polls Pennsylvania roads  are among the worst in the nation.

headline: Rules wall off state child abuse funds
abstract: The Pennsylvania's Children's Trust Fund, created in 1968 by the Legislature to fund programs that prevent child abuse through the PA Department of Public Welfare, is much like Ruth Wernicks's Exchange Club Center for the Prevention of Child Abuse in Lehigh Valley/Pocono Mountains.  Wernick expressed her disappointment that the PA Child's Trust Fund only gave grants to create new programs and not to help existing programs that already work.

headline: Gorell seeks backing to open new window-making company
abstract: Former Season-all Industries co-owner Wayne Gorell plans to start a new window manufacturing company that could be up and running with more than 200 employees by next spring.  Gorell said this week that what he needs to make the factory a reality are some financial assurance from the state- specifically from the Department of Commerce- to back local banks willing to help finance the venture.

headline: Contributing facts
abstract: Knowing who contributed to the candidates in the mayoral race will make it easier to make a wise decision. Perhaps knowing who contributes to our future judges will allow voters to make more informed decisions there.

headline: Hafer still plans to retain Rollins
abstract: Auditor General Barbara Hafer says Ed Rollins, the GOP political strategist under fire after the New Jersey gubernatorial election, is still scheduled to be a consultant for her campaign next year.

headline: Reshuffled deck
abstract: Republicans had to be feeling good after Tuesday's impressive showing in Pennsylvania, where their candidates swept to victory in three appellate races and mamy have regained control of the state Senate, and in most of the headline races around the country.

headline: Ex-Greene County officials recount efforts for progress
abstract: Former Greene County commissioner Lloyd "Odie" Rohanna knows full well the price paid for progress.  Before a crowded gymnasium on hand to dedicate the new state prison in Greene County on Tuesday, Rohanna repeated a belief he held three years ago that the prison represented a glimmer of economic growth in a county ravaged by unemployment.

headline: Ballpark figures
abstract: Monica Lewis reports on Erie's plans to build a new stadium for its minor-league baseball team.

headline: A shift on early retirees
abstract: President Clinton's proposed health-care plan would spare businesses billions of dollars in costs for early retirees but would shift the expense to taxpayers.

headline: Adams County on endangered farmland list
abstract: Adams, Lancaster and York counties are at risk of losing highly productive farmland to population growth and development, American Farmland Trust officials said Wednesday.  The Mid-Atlantic/Chesapeake Bay area was listed fourth among the 12 most threatened agricultural regions in the United States for losing farmland.

headline: Teachers take case to parents
abstract: Carlisle Area School District parents going to Back-to-School nights at Crestview and Mooreland elementary schools were greeted by picketing teachers Monday night.  Some people did not stop to accept leaflets, and there were a few acts of overt hostility.  But there were also acts of support.

headline: State nixes road funding
abstract: Two Clearfield Township supervisors say that state road repair funding requriements are keeping the township from fixing the roads in an acceptable manner.  The supervisors, Mike McConnell and Alice Krug, last month agreed to treat approximately 15 miles of roads with dust oil and stone, rather than the usual seal coating.

headline: Ruling says traffic judge drove aide to breakdown
abstract: In a very 'bizarre and abnormal' case Molly D'Errico was rewared with money to compensate her for time lost at work and expenses for her continued stay at a mental hostipal because of the harrassment she received at work by a Philadelphia City Traffic Court Judge.

headline: Group aims to drum up business
abstract: Falls township has created a development committee with a small, $2000, budget in order to try to expand the industry of the township.

headline: Convenient gambling
abstract: The innovation by state lottery officials is self-service vending machines that dispense tickets as fast as the player can insert his money.  The state has ordered 1,000 of the machines and has begun installing them in "high-traffic outlets."

headline: Hafer unqualified
abstract: If Barbara Hafer wants to waste her time running for governor again, let her do it at her own expense and not while she continues the charade of pretending to serve as our auditor general.  Better yet, let's pay her to go back to her home state of California and audit them for a few years.

headline: Residency, feud, deficit spur debate
abstract: When voters go to the polls Tuesday to select Lancaster's next mayor, they can choose among a Democratic incumbent struggling to bail the city out of economic trouble, a couty commissioner who won his post as a Democrat and then became a Republican, and a third-party candidate who may or may not actually live in the city.

headline: Flinty Shenandoah refuses to bend to bankruptcy
abstract: A native of Shenandoah, PA, when Joe Valento became a borough council member only for the town to file for bankruptcy, his response, to give $100 dollars of his own money towards the debt, led to the creation of his I Love Shenandoah Fund as more donations came in. The PA Department of Community affairs recently proposed rescinding the town's distressed status as the debt is expected to be paid off in three years.

headline: Bill Bradley and Henry Cisneros have a shot at creating a sensible urban policy
abstract: David S. Broder, 1973 Pulitzer Prize winner, thinks US Senator Bill Bradley and Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Henry Cisneros might have a shot at creating sensible urban policy. Rather than wait for Congress to sort through the blockade of a Community Development Grant, the two are working with the White House and Urban Institute on a proposal for enhanced enterprise zones of bureaucratic cooperation that would lift entire neighborhoods into the mainstream.

headline: After all, they fought Medicare, too
abstract: Physicians make a lot more money than most Americans, and they should.  Many doctors see the critical need for health-care reform, and know it won't happen without some new limits on their own incomes, just like when Medicare was introduced.  Turns out that, once they were forced into Medicare, the country's doctors learned to love it.

headline: Ag-equipment personnel upbeat
abstract: Farm equipment dealers as well as farmers are optimistic about this year.  The 77th Pennsylvania State Farm Show will draw a crowd of farmers anxious to buy after last years good crop season.  Also on their minds is a bill in US legislation that may give them a tax break when barrowing money for equipment.

headline: The  merits of "Sponsor-A-Scholar"
abstract: The Executive Director of Philadelphia Futures writes to the newspaper encouraging people to sponsor a student through her organization. Philadelphia Futures sponsors students who show great promise but can not afford to go to college.

headline: State plane put to use
abstract: According PA Department of Transportation records, after PA legislators met to cast their vote regarding the budget, eight of the legislators used the state plan to return to their districts.

headline: Russian roulette game kills teen, Chesco police say; friend charged
abstract: A game of Russian roulette between a group of 17 year olds, who were drinking beer, ends in the death of one child.  The victim allegedly put a single bullet in the gun, spun the barrel, then put the gun on the table.  James Burr, son of former county police officer, then picked up the gun and Anthony Glasco leaned his head to the gun.  One shot to the head killed him.

headline: Hershey takes lead among confectioners
abstract: Hershey Foods Corp. has solidified its ranking as the top confectioner in the world, winning a market share at midyear of 26.5 percent, according to a recent issue of Advertising Age.

headline: Conventional panel seeks an end to 'outmoded' rules
abstract: The Convention Center Authority issued a challenge to the unions whose members set up displays on its premises and proposed a new set of work rules to make the facility more "user-friendly" to exhibitors.

headline: Hafer vs. Fumo - coming soon
abstract: Fumo, the Democractic Sen. Of Philadelphia will have a chance to ask Hafer, the Republican Auditor General questions in  a Senate pannel.  It may be cordial or an intense exchange including topics of backed audits and more politically driven attacks between the two Pa politicans.

headline: Reward for a job poorly done
abstract: Steven Berry, disgraced State Department operative, was exposed during the recent presidential campagin attempting to dig up dirt on the then candiate Bill Clinton's passport files.  Berry was only demoted, not fired from the Bust administration and beginning today he will report to Sen. Jesse Helms as a minority staffer for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.  In some government circles is pays to be sleazy and dishonorable.

headline: Government must pay bills on time
abstract: PA Representative Victor Lescovitz is trying to pass a bill that would require local governments to pay interest if they are late in paying their bills to certain small businesses. The bill would require local governments to pay bills by the deadline set out in contracts, or within 30 days of getting an invoice. The senate should pass this measure as quickly as possible.

headline: Bottomed out
abstract: An analysis released by the University of Pittsburgh's Center for Social and Urban Research is consistent with the US Census Bureau's finding that population decline is now moving in the opposite direction, however slowly. The news is helpful to marketing and promotional campaigns, which believe the population increase will bring higher paying jobs to the area.

headline: After three hours of testimony, doctor waives hearing
abstract: A Connellsville doctor charged with nine counts of Medicaid fraud faces an Oct. 28 arraignment in Dauphin County Court.  Dr. Godofredo Perez was charged in August for allegedly writing prescriptions for drugs that were not medically necessary for patients he was treating.

headline: Animal research: Consciences clash
abstract: Is the Hershey Medical Center a place where miracles are born from animal research?  Or is it a modern-day chamber of horrors?  It is in this atmosphere of goriwng militancy that US Representative George Gekas lobbied yesterday for a federal law that would further protect those who work with animals- from researchers to farmers- from extremists in the animal rights movement.

headline: The media outnumber onlookers
abstract: A disapointing crowd of only a handful of people came to greet the first and second women of the whitehouse at Penn State Harrisburg.  A class from the local elementary school outnumbered the college students that choose to attend.

headline: State troopers flying high in effort to nab speeders
abstract: Average motorists using the interstate highways in Pennsylvania probably are not aware of this, but their speed often is being monitored from an airplane.  A trained observer joins a pilot on board a single-engine Cessna 182 "Skylane" to monitor the speed of traffic on wide-open, more rural sections of the interstate, and can then issue traffic citations.

headline: Same judge clears him after earlier conviction
abstract: Mark Irvine, a Baldwin Borough man, has earned the distinction of being convicted and found not guilty by the same judge.  The FBI is investigating the case for possible civil rights violations as part of a larger investigation or possible case fixing in Allegheny County Common Pleas Court.

headline: I call it discrimination
abstract: When renewed efforts to enforce the Allegheny County personal property tax began, it caused somewhat of a ruckus with the public.  The county has singled out the owners of stocks, bonds and mutual funds, while exempting the owners of savings bonds, certificates of deposit, money market certificates and interest bearing accounts of banks, savings and loan and trust companies.  This is direct and deliberate discrimination and should therefore be illegal.

headline: Converting Clinton plan into real jobs
abstract: Elizabeth Cleveland and other Americans question how Clinton plans to inact the economic changes he has promised.  Clinton says he will have a short-term plan to increase government spending on education and infrastructure with a longterm plan to increase tax-code changes and federal spending priorities.  Some economists claim that if anything does change it will not be seen for at least a year.

headline: Hafer, Fumo to square off
abstract: Auditor General Barbara Hafer has a meeting with Sen. Vincent Fumo that is sure to become heated because they are going to discuss the WAM grants, which is a sore spot for most legislators.  Hafer publically threated to have the legislature audited for its use of the WAM funds, which she believes are poortly spent.  The political ramification of making those records public would hurt many of the politicians.

headline: Ridge aims for governor's mansion
abstract: GOP Congressman Tom Ridge of Erie has been the first to announce candidacy for governor of Pennsylvania.  An interview with Ridge was done by John O'Donnell, editorial page editor.

headline: Greene County insulted from afar
abstract: Greene County and its good residents have been grossly insulted- at length.  The length is the distance between Greene County and the great city of Philadelphia from whence the insult emanated.  The editor of the Philadelphia Inguirer discussed the writings of Lani Guinier, challenging Guiner's definition of "authentic," black, elected officials.

headline: Brightened outlook for a blighted area
abstract: Pittsburgh's Lower Hill District is being fixed up with the largest city housing construction project since the 1960s, Crawford Square. Potential residents of Crawford Square are screened carefully and this is a step towards making the once crime-ridden, unsafe area the place that it once was in the 1930s and 1940s. With the help of the Hills Project Area Committee, the Crawford Project is becoming a successful reality.

headline: Agency sounds alarm to danger of huffing
abstract: Nearly one-fifth of American high school seniors have tried to get high from some kind of inhalant, according to a 1991 study by the National Institute on Drug Abuse.  Inhalants rank fourth in popularity among school children, behind alcohol, tobacco and marijuana, but ahead of LSD and cocaine.  Attractive because it is cheap and the products themselves are legal, yet it causes more irreversible physical damage than other drugs, and can kill on the first try.

headline: Borough puts claws in animal-control base
abstract: A Mechanicsburg, PA Borough amended its animal-control ordinance to include not just dogs, but cats. No dog nor cat may befoul, defile, or corrupt any public sidewalk or private property, according to Councilman Gerald Forry, who supported the amendment. It also includes provisions against noise disturbance by cats and their running free throughout the neighborhood.

headline: Trashing Penn's daily
abstract: The editorial board views the trashing of an entire press run of University of Pennsylvania's campus newspaper by African American students as arrogant, given freedom of expression. Black students claimed to be victims of "institutional racism." Penn's President Sheldon Hackney, set to leave for a new job at the National Endowment for the Humanities, did not condone the actions, and though the editorial board agreed with Hackney, it suggests he figure out how Penn got into this mess, and how it can get out.

headline: State, fed laws hamper ISTEA
abstract: Remember ISTEA, the Intermodel Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991, the law designed to allow the states to spend highway money on transit and toehr non-highway transportation needs?  Congress passed the laudable bill nearly two years ago, but officials say insufficient funding and other glitches have throttle their attempts to be flexible with highway money or meet increased transit needs.

headline: School violence begins at home
abstract: Poor parenting and too many hours in front of the television are the major reasons why some children beat up their classmates, experts on school violence said yesterday.  William Modzeleski of the US Department of Education said that while violence in schools was on the rise, parents shouldn't be afraid to send their children to school.

headline: IBM loses $285 million, quarterly revenue drops
abstract: Chief Exectutive Officer Lou Gerstner of International Business Machines Corporation, faces a third straight quarterly loss, fifth in the last nine. The operations loss is blamed on competition, decreased demand, and slumping global economies, and does not bode well for IBM, says analyst Peter Burris of the International Data Group. Accounting charges for successful restructuring, $11 billion, increased the loss, over hardware and main frame sales declines.

headline: Corporations upbeat on economy
abstract: The nation's economy is stronger than it looks and should grow at a moderate 3 percent rate through the end of next year, according to an upbeat report issued yesterday by the chief executive officers from 100 of the largest corporations.

headline: Half time, half pay
abstract: A man writes into the newspaper criticizing PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel for refusing to call the Senate back into session until November. He says that if the legislators only work for half a year, they should have their salaries cut in half, rather than raised as some of the legislators have proposed.

headline: Ridge amendment left $100 error
abstract: Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. isn't the only gubernatorial candidate who has amended his campaign reports.  Backers of his GOP primary rival, US Representative Tom Ridge, amended a campaign report for Ridge's Fund for Pennsylvania Leadership to correct a report balance that was off by $18, 031.  Trouble was, the corrected report was also off, by $100.

headline: Ignore panhandles, don't insult him
abstract: The author says the city's anti-panhandling campaign shouldn't be accused of not providing jobs or drug treatment.
