A survey of panhandlers by the Center City District did not turn up any information that was not already known, but people should just ignore them so that the point of panhandling goes away.

headline: Bruise on a peach
abstract: The editorial board thinks Mayor Ed Rendell's push to buy a deteriorated Reading Terminal headhouse fronting the PA Convention Center, will create a perfect landmark by which to guide tourists. Philadelphia dean of city planning Thomas Bacon agrees; the renovations will put the building in keeping with its surroundings. The city is willing to cover some costs, but is also looking to benefit from public and state financial contributions.

headline: AIDS hspice planned near St. Joseph's Hospital
abstract: A new facility will be built in North Philadelphia for people in the middle and later stages of AIDS.  Calcutta House, a non-profit organization, which will be running this project, has another facility within Philadelphia.  Funding will come from the federal, state, and local governments as well as the Connelly Foundation.

headline: Conemeadow Farm recognized
abstract: Conemeadow Farm near Tunnelton has been named a Take Pride in America Conservation Farm for its use of sound soil and water conservation practices.  Operated by Edward Kuckuck, Conemeadow Farm will be recognized during a ceremony.

headline: Tuition account program
abstract: More than any Halloween goblin, the cost of a post-secondary education is a specter that can scare you.  Pennsylvania has taken a step to ease a young parent's fears.  Early last year, state Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll introduced the Pennsylvania Tuition Account Program, which allows a parent to lock in today's tuition rates for tomorrow's education.

headline: States of war over bidding
abstract: A prolonged skirmish over new cars for SEPTA's Market-Frankford line show signs of mushrooming into a border war between Pennsylvania and New York state.  The New York State Senate unanimously passed a resolution this week threatening economic sanctions against Pennsylvania companines if SEPTA fails to award a $285 million contract for new cars to the low bidder, ABB Traction, of Elmira.

headline: Schools aim to curb violence among pupils
abstract: Philadelphia School District officials announced a $150,000 initiative to quell the violence in city schools.  The money will pay for a three-day citywide forum Nov. 16-18, titled "It Takes a Community to Raise a Child."  It will also be given as mini-grants to community and anti-violence organizations to conduct programs in schools.

headline: In high-level jobs at nonprofits, charity really pays
abstract: An investigation by the Philadelphia Inquirer reveals that many nonprofit executives are paid comparable to for-profit companies, some making far more than even top government officials and the President. Nonprofits defended the high compensation as necessary to retain those most competent for the job. Nonprofit agencies are tax exempt for the community services they provide, however critics are suspicious of no-interest loans and benefits executives use for large personal purchases, such as homes.

headline: Could N.J. stem state of decline?
abstract: Peter Leo writes that he has a solution to Pennsylvania's chronic problem of decreasing population due to residents moving to other states, and our state not attracting immigrants, and is one of only 9 states to lose population in the 1980s.  His resolution is to attract New Jersey residents, because more than half want to leave.

headline: Harassment suit dismissed
abstract: A federal lawsuit filed by a Harrisburg real estate developer, William G. Basonic, against a host of county, state and federal officials alleging they conspiered to violate his civil rights for more than 20 years has been dismissed.

headline: Ridge off to a fast start in '94 race
abstract: Erie Repulican Tom Ridge seems to be making all the right moves fr an obscure congressman who wants to be governor.  He was the first person to announce his candidacy for '94.  He's raised more than a million dollars.  And he's lined up the support of key state Republicans.

headline: Inside the Capitol-Local tax reform hearing scheduled
abstract: In a public hearing on local tax reform, to be held in the Student Activity Center of Penn State Harrisburg's Capital Union Building, PA Representatives Jeffrey Piccola, Ronald Marsick, Trank Tulli, and Peter Zug are hoping to hear from the region's government, education, business leaders, and the general public on local tax reform and restructuring ideas.

headline: Business regs on fall agenda
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Rendell's administration created a legislative wish list concerning local businesses.  The list includes proposals that would allow the city to shut down businesses that don't receive proper permits and proposals that would reduce taxes for certain businesses.

headline: AIDS is up dramatically in city
abstract: AIDS cases in Philadelphia have been increasing and according to Richard Scott, director of Philadelphia's AIDS Activities Coordinating Office, and other health officials it is due to an expanded definition of AIDS adopted by the federal government. The increase in cases has those in charge of providing care worried  and acting Health Commissioner Estelle Richman pleaded with minorities to get tested for HIV and get treatment.

headline: Eulogy for a way of life
abstract: The article recounts the plight of the Montgomery County, PA Holl family farm as the owners are forced to sell it to developers in order to pay inheritance taxes. However, the date of sale continues to be pushed back even as the Township approves development plans. Ralph Grossi of the American Farmland Trust views the loss of the farm as a loss for the whole community.

headline: Tuition Assistance Plan should Help Many To Attend College
abstract: State Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll recently introduced a tuition program to help make college more affordable for Pennsylvania families.  Representative Edward Staback echoed that statement when he said, "With the Tuition Account Program, people can lock in a price today to pay for tomorrow's tuition."

headline: Superfast train takes smooth final test run
abstract: Amtrak yestserday staged a final test run of its X2000 high-spped train from Swedish State Railways for passiengers of travel agents before it gets publicly tested for the next 3 months between Washington, D.C. and New York.  The train will run at top speeds of 155 m.p.h. and can turn corners %30 to %40 faster than traditional trains.

headline: Schools would hand off strip searches to police
abstract: Most Valley school officials say they will continue to call police to strip-search students despite a proposed bill that would allow them to do it.  The bill was approved by the House Education Committee Tuesday and moves on to the full House.  To become law it must also pass the Senate and be signed by the governor.

headline: Indal sale won't stop Season-all closing
abstract: Parts of Indal, Ltd., the Toronto-based parent company of Season-all Industries, have been sold, but an Indal spokesman said the sale cannot reverse last week's closing of Indiana's Season-all plant.  Economic development officials of Indiana County, however, interpret the news of the sale as verification there are no inherent deficiencies with the local factory.

headline: Council chief files suit charging 'intimidation'
abstract: Newville Borough Council President James Shelton is sueing Councilman Bruce Miller for intimidation.  It is the latest in an outgrowth of a continual battle between warring council factions.

headline: Harrisburg uses obscure tax lure
abstract: Harrisburg's mayor, Stephen R. Reed, pulled out his 'unusual and creative widget' for the first time in city history allowing a lower level of tax as an incentive to keep Pennsylvvania National Insurance Cos. From moving to another area.  The mayor says it would lose no tax revinue because it would continue to collect what it did from the old sight, plus keep the jobs associated with the business.

headline: Ridge opens long tour
abstract: U.S. Representative Tom Ridge is making a tour of Eastern and Central Pennsylvania as part of his campaign to win the Republican nomination for Governor.

headline: It's cuts or more taxes, city warned
abstract: City Council President Street and Mayor Rendell yesterday offered a bleak alternative for critics of the budget by announcing the additional taxes that would be required to balance the budget with the current expenditures.

headline: Builders say environment is killing them
abstract: After being flooded by complaints about rising lumber costs and its effect on the home building industry, US Senator Arlen Specter met with the local Philadelphia chapter of the Builders Industry Association. Costs have more than doubled in under a year, perceived by home builders as the result of northwestern logging bans. Specter sympathized with builders and will continue to meet with US Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt for a compromise between environmentalists and logging companies.

headline: AIDS units are fearful of impact
abstract: Former City Health Commissioner had promised AIDS group leaders he would help to make up for the federal money lost in a competitive bidding system mandated by the Center for Disease Control, but now that he has resigned, AIDS groups are concerned about how this will happen.

headline: Farm Show: Birds, cows, pointsettias
abstract: At the 77th Pennsylvania Farm Show one can buy everything from 8 ounce birds to 1,600 pound cows all under one roof.  In addition to the aggricultural sales there is icecream, food, and learning centers.  It is considered Pennsylvania's version of a state fair.

headline: Tuition costs at a glance
abstract: Several graphs show the premiums built into the state Treasury Department's Tuition Account Program for state-owned and state-related universities and community colleges.

headline: Superhighway isn't super
abstract: The proposed Mon-Fayette expressway would just add to the already threatened Downtown with its spaghetti-like ramps to here and there.  The benefits would most likely go to highway contractors and a few developers.  Another superhighway is no longer an adequate solution to the urban transportation problems.

headline: Screening keeps guns out of felon's hands
abstract: States with waiting periods and background checks for handgun purchases similar to those in the Brady bill have stopped tens of thousands of felons and other prohibited individuals from buying weapons through registered gun dealers, a random survey shows.

headline: Industry residents want access to sewer lines
abstract: A group of 20 Industry residents came to the council meeting to talk about extending sewer lines.  The president of the council  thought it not possible due to high cost, but they are looking into loans and community reaction.

headline: Council gives 3-days' notice on motions
abstract: Council is required to submit motions regarding Babcok & Wilcox three days before the regular council meeting.  "In my opinion, I don't think they should throw it on council as a last-minute thing," said Jim Andring, council president.  Andring requested the action in a Sept. 8 memo to council members.

headline: Harristown counts on $13.1 million
abstract: Harristown, a non-profit organization, reconstructing Harrisburg's downtown for the last decade was forced to open their records to the public due to a Pa Supreme Court ruling stating that if a company receives more than 1.5 million from the state it must keep its records open to the public.

headline: Ridge to announce governor candidacy
abstract: Ridge, U.S. Rep., to announce his governor candidacy earlier than most do in order to gather momentium in hopes of scarring other potentional canidates from attempting to run.

headline: Just a hunch: Opening day will have to wait
abstract: A source in the City Hall law library has a copy of a recent correspondence that had been routed to the office speaking about the trade school that is meant to open in August is missing books on locksmithing and asks for help in the matter.

headline: Building hope with hammer and nails
abstract: The Philadelphia Housing Authority started a program called the Apartment Renovation Team that will buy materials and hire trades people directly from union halls to repair decaying public housing buildings through a contract with the Philadelphia-area Building Trades Council. It was approved by the U.S. Department of Housing and  Urban Development after a year.  The program will also train public housing residents and give them a job repairing the housing.

headline: Amsco International cuts jobs
abstract: Amsco International's medical products group said it will eliminate 100 to 150 jobs in coming months and take a $2.2 million charge in the second quarter to cover the costs of layoffs.

headline: Hold the sensationalism
abstract: In assuming that the purpose of Barbara White Stack's series "The Animal Cops" on humane agents was to inform the public that humane agents are not answerable to a specific government body, the she made her point.  However, in doing so, she cast a negative image on humane agents in general.

headline: Tuition outpaces earnings, aid
abstract: The cost of higher education continues to outpace income, inflation and financial aid this fall, even as colleges and universities slash services, according to the College Board.

headline: Supervisors demand PennDOT attendance
abstract: Neshannock Township supervisors want Pennsylvania Department of Transportation officials to address the township's stormwater problems at a public meeting.  The supervisors believe the problems have been caused by inadequate stormwater management controls on the highway. The county included the project as a priority on its list of projects and the list was submitted to the PA Transportation Commission, but the project was omitted. PA Representative Frank LaGrotta reserved funds for the project but it never materialized.

headline: Second person taking drug dies after liver transplant
abstract: A second participant in the clinical trial of Eli Lilly & Co.'s experimental drug treatment plan for hepatitis B has died.  The 42-year old Virginia resident, who received a liver transplant Sunday, died two days later.

headline: Industry to boost spending
abstract: Economists say strong corporate profits and low interest rates are behind the US Department of Commerce announcement that American businesses plan to increase investment in new buildings and equipment by 6.6 percent this year, the biggest rise in four years.

headline: Council's ideas get attention
abstract: The US Housing and Urban Development has promised rent reform as currently HUD bases rent charges on income.  Reform is needed so families need not be split simply to avoid higher rent charges.

headline: Hart aide mulls race
abstract: Phil English, chief of staff for PA Senator Melissa Hart, is considering running for the United States House of Representatives. He was a former city controller, and he ran unsuccessfully for the position of state treasurer.

headline: Ridicule follow-up
abstract: Democrats mocked Auditor General Barb Hafer's report on mismanagement in the legislative initiative grant as being "much ado about nothing". However, the Casey administration recently ad mitted it hadn't provided Hafer with a full account of its grant program involvement, causing a discrepancy of $7.6 million.

headline: Merger of public services in the air
abstract: Pittsburgh and Allegheny county officials gathered montsh ago to discuss the once-taboo subject of merging some city and county services.  But they are taking slow, cautious steps toward cooperation, and officials warned that no one should expect anything to happen overnight.

headline: Building's owners vow to clean up
abstract: The owners of the former One Meridian Plaza have agreed to speed up the process of ridding the fire-gutted building of its contaminated contents, paving the way for eventual rehabilitation of the structure.  The cleanup promise was made in a meeting Tuesday between Philadelphia city officials and attorneys for the building's owners.

headline: An AIDS hospice threatens to close
abstract: Betak, a Philadelphia PA AIDS hospice, has announced plans to begin closing if state funding is not increased within the next few months. The AIDS activist community and other local organizations are outraged at the state for a funding lag and lapse and is threatening action. PA Senator Allyson Schwartz is lobbying for funding but has no deal from the state as of yet.

headline: Holstein hoofs it to title of top dairy cow in show
abstract: Dr. Alan McCausley of Elizabethtown, a former professor of reproduction at the New York State Veterinary School at Cornell University, won the Supreme Champion Dairy Cow award yesterday at the State Farm show.

headline: U.S. high court lets limits on student housing stand
abstract: A challenge to a Lower Merion ordinance restricting college student housing was turned down by the US Supreme Court yesterday, allowing township officials to limit both the number of student sliving together and the location of homes with students.

headline: Tarentum Bridge work won't make deadline
abstract: The completion of the Tarentum Bridge will not meet the PA Department of Transportation December 15 deadline. The delay could fuel an investigation by the PA State House Transportation Committee, since the E. Smalis Painting Company has not met the second deadline. The company says that they could not use their equipment due to restrictions set by the Alleghany County Health Department and this is what delayed them.

headline: Senate rejects limit on Death Row appeals
abstract: The Senate yesterday rejected a bill offered by Senator Arlen Specter that would have placed time limits on post-conviction appeals in federal court by inmates on Death Row.  By a 65-34 vote, the Senate tabled Specter's bill, which effectively kills the measure for the rest of the year.

headline: Insurance executive urges reforms
abstract: Dennis Chookaszian, chairman and chief executive director of CAN Insurance Cos., says that government reforms are needed to bring down insurance costs. The fact that similar claims can now result in very different awards causes higher insurance premiums. He says there is a need for a federal tort system, but it is unlikely to happen due to the fact that President Clinton has strong support from trial lawyers. He also believes workers' compensation reform is needed.

headline: Counsel delays Larsen session
abstract: Counsel for the state Supreme Court Justice Larsen succeeded yesterday in delaying the justice's session with the grand jury investigation allegations of misconduct on the high court.

headline: Hasty swearing-in called 'hypocrisy'
abstract: Republicans yesterday questioned the hurry-up swearing-in of William Stinson to the Pennsylvania Senate, but the Democrat was undeterred and began establishing roots here in a new office.  Steven C. MacNett, general counsel for Senate Republicans, called the certification of election results showing Stinson the winner over Republican Bruce Marks "illegal."  He said sufficient time was not permitted for appeals.

headline: Rizzo statue contributions used to pay campaign debt
abstract: Stephanie Eglin sent money that she was told would help errect a statue of the late Frank Rizzo, but instead it went to pay off his campaign debt.  She has filed a claim with the City Commissioner's office and is upset that she was decived.  The family of Rizzo says there was a problem with who the check was adressed to and the statue project has been all but abandoned.

headline: Modified tax reform urged
abstract: County commissioners from the state's 67 counties sit down to talk with Singel, the lieutenant governor over tax reforms.  The reforms would give the counties an optional 1 percent personal income tax or 1 percent wage tax, but proposes counties share 75 percent of the income from either levy with schools, townships and boroughs.

headline: CCD has more changes in store
abstract: The Center City District yesterday unveiled an ambitious $35 million plan to improve the downtown "streetscape" in what officials call the next logical step toward making Center City clean, safe and attractive.  The plan calls for refurbished sidewalks, safer lighting, bolder landscaping and more detailed signage, along with guidelines for retail storefront improvements and outdoor building lighting to be provided by property owners.

headline: Apparent heart attack strikes judge in chambers
abstract: A federal judge was in Presbyterian University Hospital yesterday after he collapsed in his chambers from an apparent heart attack.  Judge Donald J. Lee was in serious condition in the hospital's cardiac care unit last night, a hospital spokesman said.

headline: Humane agent ban proposed
abstract: A Fayette County legislator plans to introduce a bill this week that would bar humane agents from exercising their powers on farms.  The proposal, by Representative Richard Kasunic would make the state Department of Agriculture responsible for determining whether farm animals are abused.

headline: Use some common sense
abstract: The writer does not think that the Boggs Avenue School should be opened up for the most disruptive high school students in the city.

headline: Teachers see what truckers can't
abstract: Driver education teachers got a trucker's-eye view of a car-truck relationship Thursday in Middlesex Township.  Some said they came away with an entirely new perspective.  While acknowledging there are some "discourteous" truckers, a 15-year truck driver Ulysses Bell told teachers that truckers have as many, if not more, complaints about motorists as motorists do about truck drivers.

headline: Senate votes to shut down Pa. Crime Commission
abstract: The PA Crime Commission was abolished by a bill that was passed by the PA State House and Senate, it is now waiting to be signed by Governor Robert P. Casey; according to the deputy secretary for legislative affairs for the Casey administration. Until its June 30, 1994 completion any work will go to the PA State Police. The commission really came into trouble with its feud with State Attorney General Ernie Preate J and Casey limiting its budget to only half-year's appropriation.

headline: Insurers find new global market
abstract: In foreign country after foreign country, US insurance firms find new business.  Just in time.  Sales are flat here.

headline: County changes made official
abstract: Allegheny's two Democratic commissioners, Tom Foerster and Pete Flaherty, pushed through a sweeping job change involving the transfer of 13 individuals in the county government, against the voice of Republican minority commissioner Lawrence Dunn. Dunn called the move political, pointless, and potentially disastrous, as people were moved to departments completely outside their expertise.

headline: Hatching a plot
abstract: The Hatch Act has been a law for more than half a century that has promoted good government by restricting political activities by federal employees.  The federal congress voted 333-86 to relax the law, with the backing of Clinton.  Now federal employees will be allowed to run for local government.

headline: Robert Maynard rose to the top, but he reached down to help others
abstract: Reporter Robert Maynard died, and the article discusses his accomplishments and commends his character. He was a very successful journalist and founded the Institute for Journalism Education and taught many aspiring women and minority journalists.

headline: More scrutiny on security in schools
abstract: Fights, stabbings, and shootings have plagued Philadelphia Public Schools.  The recent increase has caused many to search for a solution.  Besides the placement of metal detectors the only thing being done by the government is finger pointing and criticism with limited positive results.

headline: City housing appeal leaves nun 'astounded'
abstract: A week ago, Sister Mary Scullion thought her wait was over.  A federal judge had issued an order that seemed to end the three-year court battle that had stymied Scullion's plans to open a 48-unit residence for formerly homeless people.  But it's not over.  On Monday, the city appealed federal Judge Louis Pollak's order that required the city to grant a zoning accommodation to permit renovation of a building at 1515 Fairmount St. for her Project HOME.

headline: At area medical schools, limited choice of fields seen
abstract: President Clinton's health care reform plan doesn't go so far as to tell students what they'll do for the rest of their lives.  But it downs use an unprecedented level of government intervention to channel student sinto what are now lower paying and lower prestige medical fields.

headline: Law gives tax break for land conservation
abstract: In the hurry-flurry that marked the rush for recess by the Legislature, the House passed a bill on to the Senate that has importance for Pennsylvania farmers.  Sponsored by Representative Bruce Smith, the bill would provide farmers with tax relief for land restricted to agricultural use by state law.

headline: Valley schools mull state education proposals
abstract: A news conference held by PA Senator Melissa Hart and other Republican senators is expected to discuss proposed changes in the state's education system providing districts with options in order to adjust to economic hardship. Under discussion are plans to extend tenure award evaluation periods, certification and sabbatical leave, and mandatory furlough. While changes would ease burdens, some teachers are concerned about quality effects in poorer districts.

headline: Temporary convenience
abstract: The editorial views attempts in the Harrisburg region to ameliorate the growing traffic congestion with plans for road and traffic pattern improvements as only a temporary fix to the problem. In the meantime, the construction will only increase congestion. After surveying the region's growth statistics, the article concludes investment in a light rail system, while steep at first, may prove to be more beneficial than construction in the long run.

headline: SERT team acted properly, report says
abstract: Members of a state police SERT team acted according to regulations when they shot Robert Fortunato, 39, of Indiana, on December 31, 1992, according to a preliminary report of an investigation of the incident by the state Bureau of Professional Responsibility.

headline: Investigation of British  Air-USAir deal sought
abstract: Three U.S. airlines filed  a petition that proested the 'repackaged version' of a scuttled proposal for Brittish Air to gain  21 percent of the voting stock for USAir.   This, the U.S. Transportation  Secretary said, would be a violation of federal law against foreign control of a U.S.  airline.

headline: Couple claims jackpot
abstract: A "private" western Pennsylvania couple too frightened to leave home with a winning lottery ticket claimed the $52.1 million Super 7 jackpot yesterday, positioning themselves to become the largest winners in state history.  Their identities remained secret while lottery officials put the ticket through a series of tests for authenticity.

headline: Health care: Where's the middle?
abstract: The four-inch-thick, 5 3/4-pound "Health Security Act" is another testament to polticial maneuvering, this one by President and Hillary Clinton.  It appears cobbled together form the agendas of dozens of interest groups, politicians and vested interests.

headline: Rollins is not the issue, race-based voting is
abstract: The statements made by Ed Rollins on paying African American clergy to suppress New Jersey's urban vote, thus aiding the election of Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Todd Whitman, conjure up visions of Willie Horton, David Duke and former President Reagan's warnings of "welfare queens."  It is another patch in a sizable Repbulican quilt of race-based politics.  Or is it?

headline: Murphy deputies will start early
abstract: Two of Pittsburgh Mayor-elect Tom Murphy's deputies will be hired by the city. Deputy Mayor Sal Sirabella has to still find a residence in the city in order to fulfill the residence requirement, while Deputy Mayor Thomas Cox has already found an apartment. These jobs are being given so that they can gain experience in city operations.

headline: Community combats homelessness
abstract: Bethesda Mission has been helping the homeless for nearly 80 years.  Their short-term goal is to have a facility to give shelter to and feed the homeless, but their long-term goal involves rehabilitation and then integration into independent living.

headline: Back to Smoke and Mirrors
abstract: The gnomes on the health care task force were faced with a riddle.  The president wanted it all.  He wanted to provide every American with a generous package of health-care benefits.  At the same time, he wanted to cut health-care spending.  The president wanted to extend coverage to the 37 million who now lack health insurance.  But he didn't want to raise taxes to pay for it.  What was a policy wonk to do?

headline: Leaving the land behind
abstract: The number of farmers under the age of 25 has dropped in the in the last 10 years.  The cause for this is the lack of profit potential as well as the difficulty of starting a farm.

headline: Valley teen-agers split time between school and work
abstract: Officials say students aren't euipped with the skills needed in today's work force, but not according to 30 seniors at the Deer Lakes Junior/Senior High School, who get job training in a special program run by the school.  The district and local businesses work together to provide work experience to eligible seniors.

headline: The highway to heaven
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike has too many tractor-trailers and it is dangerous.  The posted speed limit is 55 yet they go 65 to 75.  When going downhill one must speed up to 80 to get out of their way.  Its terrible!

headline: She killed, now wants inheritance
abstract: After euthanizing her elderly mother, Bernice Cotlar and her sister attempted to complete a suicide pact. However, Cotlar survived, and was convicted of the third degree murder of her mother. Her attempt to claim inheritance after her sister's death has outraged other heirs. Court hearings on Cotlar's eligibility to claim inheritance from her sister after heirs allege Cotlar murdered her are underway as the PA Slayer's Act forbids killers from inheriting from victims.

headline: Is CoreStates next to fall to out-of-town owners?
abstract: Philadelphia could potentially lose its last locally headquartered major bank, CoreStates, as the pace of bank mergers accelerates.  Under one scenario, the acquisition of CoreStates by either of two Pittsburgh-based bank holding companies is a definite possibility.  But a CoreStates spokesman, insists the bank expects to stay independent for at least several years.

headline: 'Crack house' shut down
abstract: Councilman Jim Ferlo entered what he called a "notorious crack house" in Lawrenceville and threw couches, chairs, tables and other furniture onto the sidewalk.  Ferlo said he would nail shut the doors and windows to the privately owned house.  He said he was justified in removing a public health and safety hazard.

headline: Heard on the Hill
abstract: Pennsylvania's Secretary of Aging is trying to market Pennsylvania as a wonderful place to retire to, in hopes of attracting more elderly settling down here.

headline: Rollins swears that he was lying
abstract: It was all a lie, Ed Rollins said under oath.  The controversial Republican strategist testified yesterday that he was simply tring to "one-up" his Democratic counterpart, James Carville, by boasting that Republicans had sought to suppress the minority vote in New Jersey's November 2 gubernatorial election.

headline: Murphy promises change
abstract: State Representative Tom Murphy promises change to the city of Pittsburgh if elected mayor.  He pledged a more rapid and coordinated response to complaints about vacant lots and vacant houses.  He repeated a campaign pledge to hold public meetings in every neighborhood.

headline: Convention Center spawns idea for new aid site for homeless
abstract: A 'reception center' is likely to be added to the Convention Center for homless to come for food, shelter, and sevices including drug and alcohol counseling and employment adivce.  It will benefit the homeless in obvious ways and will benefit the city as a whole by removing the unsightly homeless individuals from the streets.

headline: Before Clinton's heatlh plan there was Casey's proposal
abstract: When Clinton reveals his plan for health-care reform, he will be playing catch-up to Pennsylvania, where the debate over health-care reform is much further advanced.  A universal-coverage health-care reform plan has been on the table for months in Pennsylvania.  Debate already is well under way.

headline: License humane agents
abstract: Barbara White Stack wrote a great series on humane agents called "The Animal Cops."  The groups of untrained, self-appointed humane agents should be licensed and bonded by the state.  State lawmakers should start an investigation to protect the people of Allegheny County.

headline: Vow aids HACC in passage of budget
abstract: Receiving the minimum votes needed to approve the Harrisburg Area Community College's 1993-1994 budget, registration resumed and classes were no longer set to be canceled. The School Districts in the area disagreed with the budget because of a 6.5 percent raise for faculty. Students and teachers expressed relief at the vote, which passed because of John Sweikert of Williams Valley School District's promise to past HACC president Kenneth Woodbury not to vote against the HACC budget.

headline: There are valid reasons not to raise speed limit
abstract: Some in the PA Legislature have made an effort increase the maximum speed limit, but PA Governor Casey says he will veto the measure.  Casey says that keeping the maximum speed at 55mph save lives and energy.  The editorial board argues that if the speed limit is increased to 65mph fast drivers will just drive faster than they already do and agree with Casey.

headline: She's not an agent of revenge
abstract: It's no accident that defense lawyers happily march defendants before Judge Lisa Richette in her non-jury trials.  For every defense lawyer who sings Richette's praise for her compassion and fairnes, there's a victim's family walking away in tears and anger.

headline: Is new USAir-British Air deal in the wings?
abstract: British Airlines seems to be one step closer to purchasing 20 percent of USAir for a reported $340 million.  This would be the first time USAir has turned a profit since 1988 and some see this buyout could help the economy in Pittsburgh.  Others believe this is just another sign that the economy is breaking from the recession the better.

headline: Cut costs, not benefits, Clinton tells session
abstract: As a favor for Majorie Margolies-Mezvinsky for voting last-minute for his budget package, President Bill Clinton attended a controversial daylong conference. There he spoke about the deficit and that controlling healthcare costs and not cutting benefits would solve the problem. Clinton said that changing Social Security in a big way could create a new class of elderly poor, and that behind every entitlement program is a person.

headline: Hearing nothing interesting
abstract: The hearings for Ruth Bader Ginsburg to become the newest Supreme Court justice had about them something of the new rules aobut gays in the military: Don't ask, don't tell.  Basically, it was a question of a woman who was not talking before a committee composed mainly of men who cannot shut up.

headline: Rollins: GOP Cash Suppressed Black Vote
abstract: Republican political consultant Edward J. Rollins said yesterday that the successful guvernatorial campaign of Christine Todd Whitman in New Jersey spent roughtly $500,000 in "walking around money" largely to suppress black voter turnout.

headline: Nuclear fuel a hot potato
abstract: Shipments of radioactive fuel may pass through Philadelphia.  Philadelphia Mayor Rendell supports this but many Philadelphia city council members do not.  Another possibility is to take a route through New York.  This is largely a political issue due to upcoming elections.

headline: Beverly found unfair
abstract: Beverly Enterprises, the nation's largest nursing home chain has been orderd to end widespread, unlawful reistance to union organizing.

headline: Midstate price index
abstract: An itemized listing of housing utilities, food, fruits and vegetables, dairy, miscellaneous items, household and other items with differences between the posted fourth 1992 quarter and first 1993 quarter indicates a total loss of 40.99 points on the Midstate price index.

headline: We live in a world of negatives, as reaction to recent news tells us
abstract: Politics in the last year has been so filled with negatives it has almost to the point of irony that it needs to be examined.  The budget problems and defict has been an issue in elections for the past four presidency yet nothing has been done.  Education is the answer, some say, but no one knows what to do with the education system.  We need to hear more ideas and impliment the good ones.

headline: Trains and highways
abstract: States with large, congested urban areas should commit more federal funds to mass transit.  Indeed, the 1991 federal Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act, known as ISTEA, was intended to do just that.  But the law's not working in Pennsyvlania, where mass transit is still a stepchild to highways.  The Federal Highway Administration reports that Pennsylvania has obligated only $10 million of ISTEA funds for mass transit, or less than 4 percent of the funds coming to the state that could be sued for either purpose.

headline: Shooting blanks
abstract: It is our right under the 200 year old Constitution and Bill of Rights to carry arms.  The gun is not the problem, because that is only an inanimate-object, but rather the gun use.

headline: Is Wal-Mart interested?
abstract: State Representative Frank LaGrotta is disappointed that Wal-Mart Inc. has decided to look at other properties instead of making a second offer on a tract in Shanango Township.  However, the county's chance for a Wal-Mart retail store may not be completely lost.  There is speculation among local officials that the company may be eyeing a site on the south side of US 224 in Union Township.

headline: Cut Taxes 30 Percent? Whitman's Top Statehouse Allies Say Not So Fast
abstract: Within an hour of hearing Governor-elect Christine Todd Whitman repeat her pledge to reduce the New Jersey income tax by 30 percent over the next three years, the leaders of the State Legislature began distancing themselves from their fellow Republican's plan.

headline: Hearing set on election challenges
abstract: the state Supreme Court yesterday said it was up to the city Board of Elections to rule on allegations of absentee ballot fraud in the disputed state Senate race in the Second District.  The ruling took the case out of the hands of Common Pleas Court Judge Eugene E.J. Maier, who had been assailed by Republican Bruce Marks for a series of rulings that Marks said showed against him.

headline: Ross takes job in San Diego
abstract: Philadelphia City Health Commissioner Dr. Robert Ross is leaving to become director of health services for San Diego County.

headline: Officials rip reform-plan tax additions
abstract: A proposed tax reform is oppossed by some of the Cumberland County commissioners.  There are multiple plans to raise taxes: One plan raises earned-income tax whereas another chooses sales tax and tax on motels, hotels, and like rentals.

headline: Bill shows his cards
abstract: President Clinton held up a wallet-sized plastic card last night, and said that it represents a revolution.  The red-white-and-blue card, he said in a nationally televised speech to Congress, would guarantee "health care that can never be taken away.  Health care that is always there."  Clinton unveiled his long-awaited plan that he said would reform "the costliest and most wasteful health care system on Earth without any new broad-based taxes."

headline: Non-farm jobs grow
abstract: The number of non-agricultural jobs in Pennsylvania increased in Februrary to 5.04 million, the state Department of Labor and Industry says.

headline: Weighing public vouchers for private schooling
abstract: Backers of Proposition 174 of California's Nov. 2 ballot are calling their opponents names.  A favorite is "educrats" meaning professional educators out to protect their monopolies in public education.  Educators, they say, will lose their grip on schools if voters approve the measure- which gives parents $2,600 per child to send them to private or even religious schools if they want.

headline: Trains safer than trucks
abstract: The recent Conrail derailment Downtown was surprisingly characterized as "a major catastrophic accident waiting to happen."  Train derailments in Pittsburgh are infrequent and have not resulted in a single injury or hazardous-material release in recent memory.

headline: Shooting down assault weapons
abstract: The author does not approve of people trying to repeal Philadelphia's ban on assault weapons. She gives various reasons that people give in support of allowing assault weapons from being carried and disproves each of them based on her opinion that they are more harmful than helpful.

headline: Journalists on the front lines of litigation
abstract: Publishers of litigation newsletters are looking for the next hot legal topic. PA business entrepeneur Leonard Andrews capitalized on the bankruptcy preceedings of Penn Central Railroad, producing a specialized newsletter covering it and other bankruptcy proceedings. This venture spawned the creation of numerous other specialized legal newsletters and three similar companies. Owners of the two most prominent companies are constantly competing to find the next legal topic with newsletter potential.

headline: Cutting fat from federal government
abstract: The Clinton administration hopes its proposal to streamline government will save $108 billion by the end o ffiscal year 1999.  Charts show annual savings and where the savings would come from.

headline: Heinz gives symphony $20 million boost
abstract: With a $20 million head start form the Heinz Family Endowments, the Pittsburgh Symphony Society kicked off a capital campaign yesterday to raise $70 million by its 1995-96 season.  With an additional $11 million in unspecified gifts, the symphony has commitments for $31 million- or 44 percent of its goal.

headline: Row officers get extended 5% increases
abstract: The Dauphin County Commissioners yesterday gave themselves- or their successors- and other lected county officials raises of 5 percent each year through 2000.

headline: On road tour, charter plan is widely panned
abstract: In 13 public hearings- at a rate of two and three a day- the Philadelphia Independent Charter Commission's proposed reforms to the icty's 1951 Home Rule Charter were hammered from all sides.  The final charter reform will likely propose giving the mayor the power to appoint park commissioners, subject to Council review.  A nominating board was also suggested.

headline: Blount home check bounce
abstract: After program director Irwin Banks quit Mel Blount Youth Home and was not replaced, Judge Gene Strassburger and the Legal Aid Society of Pittsburgh's Georgene Sirosky investigated. Physical abuse and insufficient funding discoveries caused Strassburger to set a deadline for hiring a program director. The Home, also monitored by the PA Department of Health and Welfare, said checks bounced once due to failure to grant funds on time by Allegheny County Children and Youth Services.

headline: Pennsylvania dog breeders need stricter state regulation
abstract: Pennsylvania shares in a distinction that should shame state residents and lawmakers by its designation by the Human Society of the United States as a "puppy mill" state, for its lax in standards for dog breeding, where thousands of sick and under-nourished farm-bred dogs are released into an already over-populated dog community.  The state legislature should take steps to rid Pennsylvania of the "puppy mill" distinction.

headline: West Shore chief: HACC crying wolf
abstract: School District Superintendent Larry Sayre says after speaking with Howard Simmons, executive director of the Middle States Association of Colleges and Education, he is confident controversy over pay raises and the school districts' failure to approve the Harrisburg Area Community College Budget thus far will not result in loss of accreditation, as alleged by HACC President Mary Fifield. The Board of Trustees revised the budget and will meet with district delegates, however the controversial raises remain unchanged in the new proposal.

headline: Troopers' copter rescues area pilot from craft in river
abstract: A police helicopter crew rescued a pilot whose single-engine plane lost power and crashed into the Susquehanna River near Highspire.

headline: Shooting reinforces concerns
abstract: The shooting death Wednesday of a rookie McKeesport police officer, Frank Miller, is a reminder to law enforcement officials that even a routine call- something as minor as a traffic stop- can turn deadly in seconds.

headline: Journalists on the front lines of litigation
abstract: Publishers of litigation newsletters are looking for the next hot legal topic. PA business entrepreneur Leonard Andrews capitalized on the bankruptcy proceedings of Penn Central Railroad, producing a specialized newsletter covering it and other bankruptcy proceedings. This venture spawned the creation of numerous other specialized legal newsletters and three similar companies. Owners of the two most prominent companies are constantly competing to find the next legal topic with newsletter potential.

headline: Dares lawmakers to publish 'earnings'
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate voted to recess with pay until November 22 at a cost of about $60 million to the taxpayers.  On June 23, the vote was 24 Republicans against the recess and 24 Democrats for the recess.  Acting Governor and Lt. Governor Mark Singel, as president of the Senate, voted for the recess.  That's greed and exercise of power and money.

headline: Here's some suggestions for cleaning up Legislature
abstract: The author believes that the PA state Legislature needs to be overhauled since PA has one of the most partisan legislatures in the nation and all the lawmakers are concerned with is re-election. The suggestions he makes are: campaign finance reform, tougher lobbyist disclosure, end grants for local projects, reduce partisanship, end seniority system for committees, limit the number of bills each legislator can file, require committee vote for every bill, reduce the size of the Legislature, term limits, reform of perks and expense accounts, permit open television coverage of Senate and House, end taxpayer-financed "newsletters," and voter initiative and referendum.

headline: Rowdy FOP meeting ends with a rumble
abstract: Anger over a new police contract and disclosures abou the Fraternal Order of Police leadership erupted into a brawl at a union meeting, with a shoving and shouting match involving at least 30 officers.  Harsh words were hurled at FOP president John J. Shaw.  Then came quarreling; then, the brawl.

headline: Opening before ceremony
abstract: The article discusses the opening of the Keystone Games, something like a state olympics. Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed started it as a way to boost the economy by bringing money to Harrisburg.

headline: Blue Cross asks to hike premiums
abstract: Most of the 227,000 people who buy Medicare supplemental insurance from Blue Cross of Western Pennsylvania will see their premiums rise 11 percent next year under a proposal filed with the state Insurance Department.  Blue Cross is also proposing to replace its current Medicare prescription drug coverage with a policy that provides less coverage.

headline: Pigeon shoot background
abstract: Some facts are given about the 60th annual Labor Day pigeon shoot at Hegins.

headline: Where the Belmont students are today
abstract: In 1987 George and Diane Weiss took on 112 sixth graders at Belmont Elementary school, which is an inter-city school with low graduation rates, but this group of sixth graders, now seniors has done well compared to standards.  About half will be attending a four-year colleges; half will be attending two-year schools; 18 have been held back, 30 had dropped out, and two have died, and one is in prison.

headline: Truck detours cause a commotion
abstract: Spurred by a steady stream of citizen complaints, City Councilman Charles McLaughlin said recently that he was considering introducing an ordinance that would fine truckers for going off the route.

headline: Shrinking police force battling rampant crime in Chester
abstract: The violent crime continues to be a problem in Chester and the police force is dwindyling.  In a city of 42,000 there were 23 murders, 66 rapes, 499 robberies, and 1,407 aggravated assaults and a police force of less than 100.

headline: KBL's new fees will only alienate baseball and hockey fans
abstract: KBL's plan to charge bar owners a $1-$3 per seat fee for showing its sporting events is just another in a series of recent moves that will weaken the link between area residents and local sports teams.

headline: Debate moves to July 9 hearing in federal court
abstract: For another month, residents can play lotteries from California to Texas to Illinois- without leaving the Valley.  That ends July 19.  On that Monday, legislation sponsored by Rep. Leo Trich Jr. of Washington goes into effect that prevents Pic-A-State, Ps. Inc. from selling receipts for out of state lottery tickets.

headline: Hetzberg's his name
abstract: The editorial board of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette endorsing Sophie's choice for City Council in District 2. In their editorial "Council District 2: Daniel" they conveniently eliminated the other candidates on the ballot.  The committee members of District 2 overwhelmingly endorsed Alan Hertzberg by a vote of 61-3.

headline: Rules panel members take perk: All 16 file for daily expense tab
abstract: 16 members of the House Rules Committee claimed per diems, daily unvouchered expenses that the panel voted behind-closed-doors to increase last month.  13 of the 16 submitted per diem claims for more than half of the 19 legislative sessions from January 5 to March 31. A chart is included showing the number of per diem claims made and the total amount claimed by each member.

headline: Parking lot bids draq uproar
abstract: Mayor Masloff's administration has caused an uproar in the city's parking industry by trying to shift the management of four major parking lots and five city-owned garages.  Critics say it appears that the mayor is aiming for a "political deal" to help some of her allies.

headline: Blue Cross cost plan OK'd
abstract: State Insurance Commissioner Cynthia M. Maleski yesterday gave Blue Cross of Western Pennsylvania approval to use a range of new options when contracting with hospitals that will hold down health care costs for the insurer and its policyholders.

headline: Puppy lemon law
abstract: Michael deCourcy Hinds' article on the lancaster County puppy mills, grossly missed the mark, for this controversy has not now, nor has it ever been an "animal rights issue."  Also to romanticize how the Amish treat their animals does little to call attention to the horrible and inhumane conditions that exist in these mass breeding facilities.

headline: Would Pa. 'bonuses' to poor schools continue next year?
abstract: As a reaction from the suit from the Pennsylvania Assocaition of Rural and Small Schools Gov. Casey has provided a $100 million 'bonous' for poorer schools districts.  No one is really upset that the governor will be giving more money to poorer schools, but some of the wealthier districts that are having their funds frozen are worried.

headline: Trucking firm plans Lower Swatara
abstract: Georgia-based trucking company Watkins Motor Lines Inc. told township commissioners last week that it plans to build a 150-bay terminal in Lower Swatara Township that will bring between 300 and 500 jobs to the area.

headline: Sick and tired of it
abstract: My right to bear arms is being infringed upon by the Bradly Bill and the Staggers Amendment which requires background checks upon the purchase of fire arms.

headline: Lawmaker wants to end WAMs
abstract: Another Pennsylvania lawmaker called for the abolishment of Walking Around Money yesterday, saying funds saved by abandoning the controversial program should be sued to lower state taxes on small business.  State Senator Harold F. Mowery has proposed legislation to eliminate WAM and use the funding to again give small businesses a tax break after a money-losing year.

headline: Deciding on reporting off is enough to make you ill
abstract: Getting sick in the work place is most common amongst teenagers, but the government is the leading industry for taking sick days from work.  The recession has cut down on sick days in all types of work because of fear of being layed off.

headline: HHS chief: 'I love what I'm doing'
abstract: Most of America's social burdens fall on the shoulders of one person in the Clinton administration: Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala.  Although Shalala is responsible for practically every major change on Clinton's agenda, she says she doesn't consider herself stressed.  Only lucky.

headline: Ruling clouds Larsen future
abstract: Whatever the outcome of the criminal charges against the now-suspended State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen, he faces the continuing threat of an impeachment resolution in the Legislature that could lead to his permanent removal from the bench.

headline: Phila. Looks for ways to make up lost taxes
abstract: No longer do state and federal tax exemptions mean an automatics local tax exemption for nonprofit agencies. Cities throughout PA are questioning the tax subsidies obtained from private citizens that allow nonprofits to remain tax exempt. The city of Philadelphia is currently examining a plan to institute Payments in Lieu of Taxes or Services in Lieu of Taxes to capture a portion of the estimated 95 million tax dollars the city loses in exemptions. Many nonprofits are contesting in court.

headline: Blue Cross elderly, individual rates will rise Jan. 1
abstract: For the elderly and individual subscribers of Independence Blue Cross the cost of health insurance will increase between 7 percent and 20 percent. The PA State Insurance Department approved the rate hikes for senior citizens purchasing supplemental Medicare coverage and individuals with basic hospitalization and Major Medical plans.

headline: Shirtsleeve owners have roots in picking
abstract: Michael and John Pia, owners of Kaolin Mushroom Farms, the largest mushroom producer in Kennett Square, have faced business threats before through foreign market competition. Now that a quarter of their farm's workers are on strike, Michael Pia has displayed a calm presence among the community and concern for his workers, though failing to understand the strikers grievances. Workers say Pia is unaware of the abusive conditions in his plants.

headline: Year-round schools
abstract: The York City School District has all fo the usual problems associated with urban school districts, including a low rate of expenditure per pupil and a high dropour rate.  But it also has an asset too few districts seem to have- an administration bold enough to try radically different approaches in an attempt to break out of the sad regularity of student under-achievement.  Superintendent Jack C. Van Newkirk proposed  to abandon the traditional school year, with its 2 1/2 month vacation period, for a year-round calendar.

headline: US Route 30 resurfacing project begins in York County
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation set up construction work zone signs along a nine mile section US Route 30 in western York County Tuesday for a resurfacing project between the Adams County line and a point just west of Pa. Route 116.

headline: Singel announces $780,000 in support of youth services
abstract: Acting PA Governor Mark S. Singel announced $780,000 in support of state summer community youth service programs.  Funding was administered through the PA Department of Labor and Industry.

headline: Lawmaker wants to require accurate repair estimates
abstract: PA Representative Thomas Caltagirone is pushing a bill to require accurate repair estimates and fines to repair shops that don't comply. Caltagirone says the bill was created because of the hundred complaints he usually receives each year about repair shops grossly overcharging customers.

headline: Dem judicial candidate cites background as asset to post
abstract: Allegheny County Judge Jerry Bigley is a Democratic candidate for the 9 member, 10 year term Commonwealth Court. Bigley believes past experience practicing law and presiding over lower courts help him understand the working man, an advantage given Bigley's prediction that appellate courts will be flooded by worker compensation cases due to pending legislative reforms. Bigley favors an activist judiciary and is against merit selection, believing it is the people's right to select who will serve.

headline: High court is no help
abstract: The state Supreme Court yesterday rejected a request by Republican Bruce Marks to intervene in the special state Senate election that he says was stolen by Bill Stinson.  Marks had asked the court to throw out the Philadelphia Board of Elections' certification of Stinson as the winner of the election.  In a separate action, petitions filed by 54 voters asked the court to take the case away from Common Pleas Court, which failed erlier to overturn Stinson's election.

headline: Salvaging of bases praised
abstract: Congratulations to Mayor Ed Rendell and the congressional delegation for a spectacular job.  Convincing the Base Closure and Realignment Commission to consolidate operations in Philadelphia, saving over 8,000 jobs, is city/state/federal cooperation at its best.

headline: Pleasures of Pittsburgh
abstract: Pittsburgh is not the dreary city of the past but rather a shimmering Oz of glass and metal and marble, set among green hills in the Y of two great rivers.  In Pittsburgh one can see great urban architecture, fine museums, and ride trolleys to Mount Washington.  Pittsburgh's greatest export is knowledge itself because it is home to thousands of scientists, and many research and development facilities, colleges, and hospitals.

headline: Bombed clinic to resume work
abstract: Planned Parenthood patients will soon be able to receive a full range of family planning services at a rented agency rebuilds in the wake of a firebombing three weeks ago.  For the past several weeks, Planned Parenthood has been providing only limited services- pregnancy testing, birth control injections and birth control pill distribution.

headline: State lawmaker will sell farm development rights
abstract: The Chester County Agricultural Land Preservation Board will receive development rights to a farm owned by PA Representative Arthur D. Hershey. He will likely receive $500,000 for selling the development rights.

headline: null
abstract: Fishing in the Chesapeake bay is great after going through a declining period during the 1980's The bay stretches just under 200 miles, from around Norfolk, Virginia almost to the Pennsylvania line 30 miles north of Baltimore. More than 40 significant rivers and thousands of streams root the bay intimately.

headline: USAir  seeks approval of BA pact
abstract: USAir plans to implement 'seamless'  service with Birtish Airways out of Philadelphia to a number of cities starting  May 1.  Seamless service will give passengers flying BA from London to cities such as Rochester, NY one ticket that will read BA instead of two.  The codesharing will  simplfy the processes of transfering passengers from BA planes to USAir planes and increase revinue USAir claims.

headline: Singel: building prisons not answer to PA crime problems
abstract: Moments before he cut the ribbon on one of the country's most sophisticated prisons, acting Governor Mark Singel cautioned Tuesday that Pennsylvania can't build its way out of its prison overcrowding problem.  Speaking before an audience of 400 state and local officials assembled for dedication ceremonies in the gymnasium at the new State Correctional Institution at Greene, Singel stressed the need for better law enforcement, crime prevention and education.

headline: Lawsuit a mighty big load for local gondola maker
abstract: Johnstown America Industries Inc. is suing Trinity Industries over a patent that Johnstown holds on a railway car for coal and utility industries.

headline: Demand a solution
abstract: Our highest court is an embarassment.  Let's demand a solution from our responsible elected officials.

headline: Hospital workers to vote
abstract: Service employees at Monongahela Valley Hospital, who face a contract extension deadline tomorrow, are scheduled to vote on a proposal described by management as a final offer.

headline: Santorum gauging run at Wofford
abstract: U.S. Senator Harris Wofford is beginning his campaign for re-election by sending out newsletters and touring Pennsylvania. Several Republicans have expressing interest in running against him, but Representative Rick Santorum will most likely be the nominee, as his tour of Pennsylvania has indicated he has much support.

headline: Population growth seen
abstract: The impact on Clarksburg, VA and the surrounding communities will be profound.  The population of Clarksburg decreased by about 5,000 from 1980 to 1990, and now stands at 18,500.  Harrison County, of which Clarksburg is the county seat, lost 10,000 residents during that decade.  Projections for the year 2000 show Harrison County will add at least 10,000 residents, and Marion and Taylor, nearby counties, are expected to increase in population by 18 percent or more by the end of the decade.

headline: Bringing up baby taxes families without coverage
abstract: With President Clinton due to announce his reform package next week and the focus on health care nationally, the Courier Times went into the community to find out how people in Bucks County are managing to take care of their medical needs.

headline: State livestock put on display
abstract: The 37th Keystone International Livestock Exposition will open at the state Farm Show Complex on Thursday.  The five-day show, coming on the heels of the Pennsylvania All-American Dairy Show, is sponsored by the Pennsylvania Livestock Association in cooperation with the state Department of Agriculture and the Pennsylvania Farm Products Show Commission.

headline: 14 men charged with extortion in landfill deals
abstract: Five reputed Luchese crime family members threatened violence to make $3 million illegally at landfills in Pennsylvania and New York, an indictment unsealed yesterday says.  The indictment said 14 men extorted money from legitimate vendors and engineering firms and even bullied two engineering firms into not reporting to authorities that tainted and illegal wastes were being dumped.

headline: Visitors Information Center opens at airport
abstract: A new Visitors Information Center, to handle tourist inquiries from up to 100,000 visitors a year, has opened at Pittsburgh International Airport.

headline: Single moms find the trip rewarding
abstract: A sharply increasing number of educated and professional women are having children on their own since 1980, says a Census Bureau report released July 13.  Though most reviews media-wise have been negative, women find the experience rewarding.

headline: Let's put a cork in State Stores
abstract: After moving to Philadelphia, everybody said that if you are going to live here, you need to know directions to the best out-of-state liquor stores.  Reason being, the State Store in Philly offered the most overpriced booze, and it had a terrible selection of wines.  The liquor marketing system is dumb and a bad use of scarce law enforcement resources.

headline: Democrat may end up taking the fall
abstract: US Representative Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky, a freshman Democrat, cast the deciding vote for President Clinton's budget, and thus, jumped off a cliff.  And one of two things will happen: she'll hit the rocks and die politically, or the waves of history will turn her into a political superstar.

headline: Hospitals, lawmakers linked to tobacco; Legislators accept tobacco-firm money
abstract: Records of the PA Bureau of Elections show legislators receiving thousands of dollars both from Philip Morris and RJR Nabisco, top tobacco companies. Bill Godshall, executive director of SmokeFree PA, said the tobacco lobby is one of the most powerful forces in Harrisburg. Though Representative Matthew Ryan failed to recollect any legislation in which the industry tried to sway votes, the newspaper reports several.

headline: Santorum gauging run at Wofford
abstract: Wofford is starting his re-election campaign for United States Senate by sending out newsletters and touring Pennsylvania.

headline: Private-sector lessons for the government
abstract: Pittsburgh hosted the Inc. 500 conference which brought the CEOs of the country's fastest growing companies to town. Local government officials can learn from the way that these people due business.

headline: Casey hailed for offering health-care reform, but...
abstract: PA Governor Casey's new healthcare proposal received mixed reviews. Nearly everyone praised his effort for trying to insure the 1.2 million uninsured Pennsylvanian residents. No new taxes would be required his plan; a portion of everyone's premium would go into a fund to pay for coverage of the unemployed. The plan would guarantee a certain level of health benefits for every citizen, with businesses, working people, and the state and federal governments paying the cost.

headline: The Fido and Fluffy bill
abstract: Kathleen D. Curran writes that she supports Senate Bill 583, Pet Population Control Act, has been introduced in the PA General Assembly and that it will help reduce the population of unwanted stray cats and dogs by encouraging sterilization by having a one cent per pound surcharge on all dog and cat food sold in PA that can be received as a rebate if their pet was sterilized.

headline: 3 deer hunters die on 1st day of hunt
abstract: A Fayette County woman was killed in a shooting accident, and at least two people died of apparent heart attacks yesterday as thousands of hunters took the day off and walked into Pennsylvania's woods for the first day of antlered deer season.

headline: With state help, Collegeville aims to make Route 29 a straight shot
abstract: The Collegeville Borough Council is working with the state Department of Transportation to fix Route 29 so it runs straight through the borough, officials said at the council's October 6 meeting.  The project's estimated cost is $500,000, according to Clarence W. Huling, council president.

headline: State eyes pyramid schemes
abstract: A classic and dangerous get-rich-quick plan is cropping up in the Wyoming Valley, and justice officials ask the public's cooperation.

headline: Lifestyle Insurance says it has halted operations
abstract: Lifestyle Insurance Services Company is closing its three Pittsburgh offices and has went out of business.  This is due to an investigation by the PA Insurance Department.

headline: Democratic leader miffed
abstract: The state Senate Ethics Committee could be dragged into an ongoing partisan feud over whether that chamber should be in session this fall.  Democratic Leader J. William Lincoln of Fayette County is contacting other members of his caucus to ask whether they would like to file a complaint over GOP Leader Robert Jubelirer's petition to bring the Senate into special session.

headline: House aims to erase image of character flaw
abstract: The Legislative body of Pennsylvania is better than before, but a long way from where we expected it.  The new bills that were passed to regulate the actions of representitives in such things as travel budgets do not do enough, but are an improvement.

headline: Santorum urges campaign lid
abstract: US Representative Rick Santorum yesterday fired the first salvo of the 1994 campaign when he challenged Senator Harris Wofford to sharply limit campaign contributions from individuals and political action committees who are not from Pennsylvania.  Santorum urged that all candidates agree to raise at least 60 percent of their campaign money from contributors and PACs that are in the state.

headline: Red Cross lays off 14, reduces programs
abstract: Already facing a budget deficit, the American Red Cross Pittsburgh-Allegheny County Chapter learned this week that its United Way allocation for fiscal year 1994 would be $216,000 less than last year.  The combined loss forced the local chapter to lay off 14 people, or 37 percent of its 38-member staff.

headline: Clinger believes president should seek bipartisan help
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill F. Clinger Jr. criticized President Clinton's deficit reducing package, claiming he bullied several Democrats into voting for the bill and that the bill did not have bipartisan support. He suggested that in the upcoming issue of health care reform, Clinton seek bipartisan support.

headline: Two county farms included in state easement program
abstract: The Pennsylvania Agricultural Land Preservation Board approved 27 farmland preservation easements in 12 counties including two in Chester County. Under the program, the state and counties buy development rights from farmers to guarantee that their farms will remain as agricultural land.

headline: 3 environmental groups share $25,000 windfall
abstract: Attorney General Ernie Preate also stopped in Greensburg Tuesday to present $25,000 to three Westmoreland County environmental groups.  The money was obtained by Preate's office through the prosecution of National Waste and Energy Corp., Pine Valley Drive, Plum, which operates the Valley Landfill in Penn Township, Westmoreland County.

headline: WAMs under heavier fire
abstract: Growing, statewide consternation over the extent, political implications, and possible wrongdoing in the so-called WAMs program operated out of the state's General Assembly might drive lawmakers to pass HB 1516.  But don't bet on it.  The bill proposes to replace the current WAM program with a blue-ribbon panel of non-legislators that would review all grant applications and make awards based upon merit.

headline: Some police can't win with Scheib
abstract: Liberty police no longer bother handing out traffic citations because Judge Raymond L. Scheib routinely tosses out traffic cases as part of a political feud.

headline: Lukens restructures
abstract: Lukens Inc., after acquiring Washington Steel Corporation a year ago, restructured its steel operations, creating separate operations companies for its steel and carbon productions. The company also announced executive changes and reviews of non-steel operations, some or all of which they may divest.

headline: Democrats support finance reforms
abstract: For 14 years, Representative Allan Kukovich ahs been trying to push campaign finance reform through the state House.  Now, the Westmoreland County Democrat has some major backers.  A bill setting caps on candidates for statewide office and providing public financing has the backing of both House Speaker H. William DeWeese and Majority Leader Ivan Itkin.

headline: House director to begin duties
abstract: Susan Cohen will begin her duties tomorrow as co-executive director of the PA House Bipartisan Management Committee. Cohen will fill the vacancy created by Russ Faber who left to return to his old job.

headline: School board offers contract to Clayton
abstract: The Board of Education voted yesterday to accept the retirement of Superintendent Constance E. Clayton on Aug. 31, and, with one dissenting vote, offered her a contract as acting superintendent until Nov. 30.  The Pennsylvania Public School Employees Retirement System must now decide whether Clayton may serve in the interim post and still qualify for a state retirement incentive that would boost her $87,000 pension by about $7,000.

headline: Reforming our  taxes
abstract: The state politicans said they wanted to hear what people had to say about tax reform and they got an earfull Friday at the allegheny County Courthouse during a Senate Finance Committee hearing.  The complaints came in a varieity of ways but all wanted lower taxes; most emphasising the increased property tax.

headline: Businesses would pay bulk of Casey's health-care plan
abstract: Governor Casey says that not one penny of additional tax money will be needed to provide health insurance. To compensate businesses will pay at least 90 percent of the premium for a basic health-care package for full time workers and 45 percent for part-timers. Some business owners think that the governor does not have the right to do this.

headline: When it hits close to home
abstract: 90 percent of the population needs and uses humane and animal-control agents.  They are essential to the well being of not only animals, but also of people.

headline: 4-state pact set to reduce runoff taint
abstract: Time, cooperation and money will be needed to meet goals of reducing nutrient runoff into rivers that feed the Chesapeake Bay, state environmental officials say.  A multi-state agreement calls for Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia and Washington, DC, to develop strategies for a 40 percent reduction in nitrogen and phosphorus entering the bay by the year 2000.

headline: Wanted: Airport money
abstract: Cumberland County Transportation Authority needs to raise its share of money needed to fun the study of air transportation needs. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) will fund most of the study, however small remaining portion needs to be raised locally. The study will look to see if the Carlisle Airport can be made safe enough to remain in its current location or will have to be moved; which consultants have already began looking into other sites and will be presented (as made permissible under the state Sunshine Law).

headline: Specter introduces career criminal bill
abstract: U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pa offered a bill that could send career criminals to federal prisons.  This would encourage longer sentences for career criminals so that the prisoners would be out of the overcrowded pa prison system.  The critics point at statistics that show the federal prisons are operating at nearly the same level of overcapacity that the state is.

headline: Lukens to add $86 million mill to Conshohocken plant
abstract: Lukens said it will invest $86 million to improve efficiency and expand the companies product line to include coiled plate that will be up to 102 inches wide.  This will make them one of the premire steel companies in the world accounting for about %5 of the nation's steel production.

headline: Democrats tackle bill on deficit
abstract: Democratic negotiators began work yesterday on a compromise version of President Clinton's deficit-reduction plan, agreeing that the outcome would determine whether their party could govern the nation.  Republicans watched from the sidelines because they oppose the bill's tax increases, which would fall mainly on the well-to-do.

headline: House joins McDade in his appeal
abstract: US House of Representatives attorney and the US Representative Joseph M. McDade argued that federal corruption charges filed went against legislative areas protected by the Constitution. Charles Tieger, acting general counsel for the House, told a panel of US Third Circuit Court of Appeals that it was a breach in separation of powers, going against the "speech or debate" clause of the US Constitution.

headline: School strikes and public militancy
abstract: In teacher strikes of the past, one scene has been familiar.  Once a strike lasted beyond a certain time, parents would appear outside negotiating sessions, demanding an agreement be reached no matter what the cost.  In Upper St. Clair last week, parents were on the streets with picket signs, but they were telling the school board not to settle on the teachers' terms.

headline: Reform-plus
abstract: The writer does not think lawmakers should question whether the proposal to raise the state's six-percent sales tax, approved by the PA State Senate, is beneficial to constituents. The writer questions how something that is good for the people of Alleghany County cannot be good for those in Bloomfield, Penn Hills, McCandless, Coraopolis, and East Liberty. The benefits of the increased sales tax are tax reductions, providing for additional tax cuts or necessary purchases from a source that only comes 75 percent from Alleghany County residents.

headline: Casey adviser says reform plan isn't the best
abstract: A disenchanted adviser to Governor Robert P. Casey said the governor's health care reform plan would bring socialized medicine to Pennsylvania.  Casey's plan would put government in charge of health care by having employers pay health insurance premiums to a state board, which would then pay health care providers.  The Pennsylvania Health Care Committee did find two major problems in considering health care reform in Pennsylvania.

headline: 4,000 attend UMW rally at Red Barn
abstract: The United Mine Workers of America's battle for "Jobs with a Future" is the most important labor strike in 50 years, according to speakers Sunday at a UMWA Solidarity '93 Rally at the Red Barn Sportsmen's Club.  The coal miners received moral and financial support from an estimated 4,000 people at the day-long rally.

headline: A real bumper crop of dumps
abstract: A new dump may come to northeastern Lancaster County.  This one will be used for hazardous waste.  There has been community outcry that they do not want another dump, but their representative states that the market is too strong in their area from such an operation and he needs to back the company in order to help the community.

headline: West Busway/Wabsash HOV work speeds ahead
abstract: Port Authority Transit has hired Baker Engineers Inc. of Beaver as the lead consultant to do the preliminary design for the proposed 7.2 mile West Busway/Wabash High Occupancy Vehicle project.  The PAT board hired the Maguire Group to prepare a final environmental impact statement under the same five-month deadline.

headline: Squabbling has negative impact on high court
abstract: Lawyers and interest groups representing the best interest of the people in the courts both agree that the squabbling in the State Supreme Court has made a mockery of the system.  It is embarrassing and not fair to those who are waiting to hear a trial that such acquisitions are taking place.
