Some say that the judges need to take a break and figure out the problems between them before hearing another case.

headline: Madoff: Limit video poker
abstract: Councilwoman Michelle Madoff introduced legislation in City Council that would limit minors' access to video poker machines.  It would prohibit electronic gambling devices in any city business not licensed by the PA Liquor Control Board.

headline: Democrats to join Arlen event
abstract: Several Democrats are expected to attend a fund-raiser hosted by Senator Arlen Specter.  Apparently the three-term Republican has these events annually- to which he invites campaign donors- and routinely invites top Democrats to speak.

headline: House leaders sued over perks increase
abstract: Common Cause of Pennsylvania and the Pennsylvania Leadership Council took PA House leaders to court yesterday over their secret approval last month of a boost in lawmaker's perks. The are arguing the way that the Rules Committee increased expense allowances from $88 to $110 a day for legislators meeting in Harrisburg violated the Sunshine Act. The suit seeks to block the per diem increases.

headline: Senate battle 3 weeks away
abstract: A constitutional crisis could erupt in three weeks when the Republicans attempt to shorten a plannned five-month recess and reconvene the state Senate.  At issue is which party controls the upper chamber.

headline: Regionalizing assets
abstract: The cultural and recreational facilities of the Pittsburgh area are among its most valuable assets.  And though they benefit the entire region, the way they are maintained is becoming more and more inequitable.

headline: Casey bill would ensure health care
abstract: PA Governor Casey proposed a Pennsylvania Health Security Act which would guarantee health care to all Pennsylvanians. The plan would also create a statewide system of managed-care networks, would provide security to Pennsylvanians who already have adequate health care and would preserve their right to see the physician of their choice. Casey estimated that his proposal would cut healthcare costs in Pennsylvania by $710 million in its first year; however that number does not factor in the cost of providing health care to the uninsured.

headline: '90s' best career bets
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry conducted a study indicated where there is likely to be job growth in the coming decade.  Health care is the fastest growing field, and manufacturing jobs will continue to disappear.

headline: A tradition that should end
abstract: As most Pennsylvanians enjoy the last holiday of summer today through traditional leisurely pursuits, some "sportsmen" in Schuylkill County are engaged in another traditional activity that is a continuing embarrassment to the entire Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, the Fred Coleman Memorial Shoot.  Each year about 250 participants kill about 7,000 pigeons that are released from cages.  One need not be an animal rights extremist to recoil in horror at the misuse of animals at Hegins.

headline: What are we teaching children about safety?
abstract: PA Senate Majority leader J. William Lincoln is trying to pass a bill that would require students to wear seatbelts on school buses. The bill is reaching opposition because it would require about $5 million a year to do this. This is a bad message to children saying that you only have to wear seatbelts sometimes; Somewhere down the road it could lead them to the mentality its ok to break the law sometimes.

headline: Stanfa's Son Shot in Ambush
abstract: The sone of reputed Philadelphia crime boss John Stanfa was shot and wounded yesteday morning in a daring rush-hour ambush in which his father was believed to be the prime target.  The shooting was being viewed in law enforcement circles as a stunning escalation of a mob war that has left three people dead and two others wounded this year.

headline: Mandated Insurance Face Fight
abstract: Small businesses are making an emotional 11th-hour appeal to head off the Clinton Administration's plan to require all companies to pay for health insurance for their workers.  They claim the costs will affect wages, the company's output, and their ablity to hire new employees.

headline: Democrats urge retention of six statewide judges
abstract: The Democratic State Committee has endorsed six judges for retention to statewide courts.  Meanwhile, one of the retention candidates, Justice Nicholas Papadakos, endorsed Democrat Judge Russell Nigro for the Supreme Court.

headline: House offers members new auto option
abstract: A much-ballyhooed reform of auto-leasing arrangements for state lawmakers may turn out to be little more than a new option for House members.  House leaders of both parties unveiled the option Monday, hailing it as a way to save up to $1.4 million for the state's taxpayers.  Any lawmaker who wishes to participate in the new arragnement will be assigned a state-owned vehicle, rather than making his or her own private auto-lease arrangements at public expense.

headline: Senate candidates accent negatives
abstract: The race for the second state senatorial district went into high, screeching gear last week as Republican candidate Bruce Marks and Democratic candidate Bill Stinson took potshots with negative mailings and television ads.  Whover wins the district will tip the political balance to ne partyor the other in the state Senate.

headline: Rendell and other mayors tell D.C.: Put up, or shut up
abstract: Mayor Rendell and other area mayors yesterday joined a nationwide effort by local officials to generate public opposition to federal directives that mandate action by local governments but are accompanied by, no money.  Rendell said unfunded mandates from Washington in such areas as environmental, health and safety policies are forcing local governments to spend scarce funds and leaving mayors and other local officials with diminished discretionary powers.

headline: Casey feeling good, speeds return plans
abstract: Governor Casey emerged from a three-week hospital stay yesterday, saying he had beaten back the infection that put him there and now was speeding up his plans to return to power.  He emerged yesterday looking thin but healthy.

headline: Against closed shops
abstract: Joseph Brocker, President of Adyn Raytor, is against closed shops. Brocker argues that in America, employees should not be forced to pay initiation fees and union dues for memberships they may not even want. Additionally, companies cannot afford strikes which automatically shut down their operations until negotiations are settled with unions.

headline: All charged up about the dangers from electric power lines
abstract: Panels of lawyers and activists spent two days in Pittsburgh recently to plot strategies for blocking power-line projects, grumbling about how mainstream environmental organizations and scientists dismiss the peril the panelists call "the environmental issue of the '90" a threat that they equate with to asbestos, tobacco smoke and lead paint.

headline: What Went Wrong on the Flight to Quantico
abstract: On July 20, 1992, a Bell/Boeing V-22 Osprey en route to Quantico, Va., crashed unto the Potomac River just short of the runway.  The diagram shows how the tilt-rotor plane works, what went wrong, and how it is being fixed.

headline: State gun law vote possible today
abstract: The PA House of Representatives could pass legislation that would prevent local governments (Pittsburgh and Philadelphia) from banning assault-style weapons. Opponents of the bill include; PA Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel, PA House Majority Leader Ivan Itkin, and Pittsburgh City Council President Jack Wagner. Proponents of the bill include; the Allegheny County League of Sportsmen, the National Rifle Association, and the PA Federation of Sportsmen's Clubs and they say that local bans on assault-style weapons are confusing and poorly drafted.

headline: Md. Insurance Commissioner Implicated in Taking Favor
abstract: Jana Greer, senior vice president of Sun Life Insurance Company of America, alleges that Maryland Insurance Commissioner John Donaho accepted a free limo ride from an official whose company he represents. Having been implicated in accepting gifts before, Donaho had barred himself and his staff from further acceptance. Maryland Governor William Donald Schaefer referring to Donaho's appearance before the US Senate as disappointing.

headline: Dennis' seductive logic
abstract: Andre L. dennis, chancellor of the Philadelphia Bar Association, made terribly misleading points in his June 14 letter to the editor.  Mr. Dennis is being, at best, disgenuous in his torturous, seductive logic advocating the merit system for the selection of judges in Pennsylvania.

headline: House Oks jobless-aid extension
abstract: US House passes a bill, promoted by Clinton, to extend jobless benefits for the longterm unemployed by a vote of 254-161.

headline: Senate confirms 2 district justices
abstract: The PA Senate confirmed Barbara Nixon and Ronald Haskell, Jr., to appointment as district court justices. The nomination process was briefly held up after debate by two democrats who later changed their minds and voted for the confirmation. Nixon will resign her position as York School Board President, as both nominees are eligible to be sworn in immediately.

headline: Revamp property tax
abstract: As local governments ponder where to get the money to pay for their programs and services, attention turns each year to the vast amounts of tax-exempt real estate in Pennsylvania.  Local governments would be better off persuading state governments to force school districts off the property tax, and force municipal governments off the wage tax.

headline: Casey health plan unlike Canada's
abstract: In Amy Neff's interview of Jay Tolson, who chaired Governor Casey's Health Care Reform Task Force, his assessment of the governor's proposal is highly misguided, though he is a much respected man.

headline: Agencies advise miners
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry and the United Mine Workers of America Local 1368 offered an informational session to advise miners who were laid off by BethEnergy Mine 33.  The funds administered by the Alleghenies Planning and Development Commission are low due to a poor economy.

headline: An alliance dedicated to saving green land
abstract: In recent weeks, a diverse group of the area's business, civic and environmental leaders called the Green-Space Alliance, has begun pushing the notion of creating a beltway of green through Philadelphia and its four suburban counties in Pennsylvania.  The group envisions a regional network of open space and more environmentally sensitive development.

headline: Will beltway's four lanes meet traffic needs?
abstract: Before the first cubic yard of dirt is moved, the question already is being asked: Is the interstate-81 Connector through Hampden Township being underbuilt?  The highway represents the missing segment of the so-called "Capital Beltway."  But it will be only four lanes, and highway officials are making plans to widen the reaming four-lane sections to six.

headline: State police feeling county growing pains
abstract: State police must take over areas where there are no local police. This is the case in southeast Pennsylvania, where an increase in population and its proximity to Philadelphia creates a strain on the state police, who are now stretched too thin.

headline: Mellon's mega-merger
abstract: The Mellon Bank Corporation acquired the nation's sixth-largest mutual fund company, Dreyfus Corporation. This merger will put Mellon as the top of the bank mutual fund field and together will generate annual revenues over $3 billion.

headline: Devilish endorsement
abstract: While even an indictment hasn't hurt Hutchison, state Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. can't even join a fraternal club without getting flak.  Preate decided to join the Masons, something that wouldn't sound too controversial considering there are more than 170,000 of them in Pennsylvania.  However, Preate is Catholic and the news that he was joining got enough publicity to rile his monsignor back in his hometown of Scranton.

headline: House Oks own probe of Larsen
abstract: The state House yesterday took a major step toward an impeachment proceeding aimed at Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen, adopting a resolution called for an investigation of Larsen's conduct on the bench.

headline: Senate confirms Hackney for Humanities position
abstract: The United States Senate confirmed former University of Pennsylvania president Sheldon Hackney as head of the National Endowment for the Humanities.

headline: Saying 'no' was right thing
abstract: Sometimes deciding against doing something is more important than any number of decisions to initiate actions.  A case in point is Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed's veto of a proposal to have the city obtain three military surplus helicopters for the police department.  There is no tellinghow many dollars or how much grief this common sense decision may have saved the city.

headline: Casey takes silent tack on health care
abstract: PA Governor Casey and President Clinton both plan announcing major health reform plans before summer begins, but the two are going about it differently. The Casey administration has been mostly silent on the issue since a governor's task force issued its health reform recommendations in November. In contrast Clinton's plan has been on the front-page of the news virtually every week.

headline: At least 125 laid off at Ingersoll
abstract: Between 125 and 150 steelworkers at Ingersoll-Dresser Pump Co. will not be recalled to wrk this week or anytime soon, following settlement of a 106-day strike.  Workers hired after July 29, 1968, will not be recalled to work at the Phillipsburg plant.

headline: Animals destroyed at wildlife park
abstract: An argument between the state officals and the park owners can not take back what happened to the 850 mammals that were killed at Lake Tobias wild animal park from exposure to highly contagious 'Mycobacterium Bovis Tuberculosis'.  The state officals said they would have tested the aminals for free when the outbreak started, but the owners were unwilling to pay for the animals capture.  The owners claim the state officals were unwilling to test the animals.

headline: You make me choke
abstract: A letter is written to Walter Goldburg in response to his letter saying that a clean air delay will not save Mon Valley.  Port Vue is tired of do-gooders from Washington telling them how to live.  They have no qualms about using government to punish little communities like Port Vue out of the way.

headline: State police want to be biggest force in the world
abstract: the Pennsylvania State Police are trying to become the largest accredited police agency in the world. The 3, 814 member force is being reviewed for accreditation to see if they meet the 733 professional standards that would apply. You have to meet every standard or you don't get accredited.

headline: Midstate price index explained
abstract: The article attempts to explain the midstate price index, modeled on the US Consumer Price Index. The survey uses sixty-seven regularly purchased goods, not including items such as furniture, insurance, cars, or large appliances. Items surveyed are from both the East and West Shore areas, with food prices based on monthly amounts to balance food and utility bills.

headline: DeWeese takes aim at Murphy
abstract: PA House speaker H. William DeWeese accused Pittsburgh mayoral candidate Tom Murphy of hypocrisy in a memo circulated after Murphy declined an increase in per diem compensation for legislators, Murphy saying such decisions should be approved in public. However, before running for mayor, Murphy twice profited from such increases approved in precisely the manner of DeWeese's request. The memo was circulated to House leaders and committee chairmen.

headline: House panel fails to take OBE stand
abstract: Though a PA House panel deadlocked on two votes to recommend for or against outcome based education before an independent regulatory review commission vote, the senate committee voted to recommend the standards. PA Governor Robert Casey approved the move and urged the regulatory commission to pass the legislation. However, opponents of the bill say they will continue to thwart the legislation in coming budget talks, and would support it only if the adoption of standards is voluntary.

headline: Senate GOP gives up its effort to reconvene
abstract: Senate Republicans, finally seeing the aimlessness of shouting into the political wind, have given up their quest to convene the Senate before the chamber's scheduled November 22 return.

headline: Slow road home
abstract: For Allegheny County residents who believe changes in local government should be made locally, not in Harrisburg, the dawn of home rule for the county will come none too soon.  That's why there may have been momentary disappointment this week when state Representative Ivan Itkin agreed to "slow track" the bill.  The idea would give Allegheny County the same powers of self-determination enjoyed by the growing number of homerule communities in Pennsylvania.

headline: Casey unveils overhaul plan for healthcare
abstract: IN one of his last major acts before undergoing a heart and liver transplant, Governor Casey introduced a proposal to overhaul the state's health care system.  Under the proposed legislation nearly all Pennsylvanians would be insured, no matter their income or whether they had changed jobs, lost jobs or become seriously ill.

headline: AT&T to add 180 new jobs here
abstract: AT&T said it is creating 180 new customer service jobs in downtown Pittsburgh and will offer them to long-distance operators whose positions are being eliminated, in part, because of a decline in calls to Cuba.

headline: As deer numbers soar, battle strategy shifts
abstract: After much internal debate, the Pennsylvania Game Commission appears to have undergone a change in attitude, allowing municipalities to assume some control over their deer destiny, after the size of the herds continued to grow.

headline: Zoning for future railroads
abstract: There needs to be more industrial zoning near the railroads in case of an economic-development that may arise in connection wit ha proposed regional light-rail commuter system.

headline: State prison system is falling victim to unabated growth
abstract: Pennsylvania's prison inmate population will continue to grow and spending for corrections will spiral steadily upward if current policies remain unchanged, Corrections Commissioner Joseph D. Lehman said recently.

headline: Museums-turned-merchandisers: Where does tax exemption end?
abstract: For-profit retailers are decrying the opening of nonprofit retail stores in public venues, allowing nonprofits to sell items in what for-profit companies say are commercial ventures which should not be covered under the museums' US government tax-exemptions. Ventures include showing films in museum theatres, gift shops, and direct mailing, almost all of which examples are tax exempt because the museums claim they are tied to educational museum programs.

headline: Diary vote disappoints Specter
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter yesterday said he had voted to limit the Senate Ethics Committee access to the private diaries of Senator Bob Packwood because the panel's investigation into charges of sexual misconduct against the Oregon Republican could be delayed for years by court action.  In an action sharply criticized by his 1992 Democratic opponent, Specter joined five other senators Tuesday night in voting against a resolution that Packwood comply with 8,000 pages of a diary he has kept.

headline: House Post Office case nears deadline to indict
abstract: The US attorney for the District of Columbia is facing a critical decision in the investigation of Representative Dan Rostenkowski in the House Post Office scandal.  With the current grand jury's term expiring this month, according to legal sources, new US Attorney Eric H. Holder Jr. must decide whether there's enough evidence to indict Rostenkowski now.

headline: Senate likely to be huffy
abstract: The PA Legislature returns to session and Majority Leader J. William Lincoln plans to run the daily calendar. One issue to be looked at is the Crime Commission. The Senate will have a partisan atmosphere due to the fighting over the election of Senator William Stinson and acting Governor Mark Singel doesn't know if anything will be accomplished. Republicans in the Senate have sued every Democratic senator and Singel in Commonwealth Court, which the president of PA Leadership Council, Sean Duffy, says is a sad state of affairs.

headline: State should reject county 1% sales tax
abstract: The authors do not believe that the PA State Legislature should give Alleghany County the authority to impose a 1 percent sales tax increase. They believe this is especially bad since there is a county tax increase for many property owners in 1994 even though the 1994 county budget keeps the property tax rate at the same level. The authors believe the increase in sales tax would pit counties against each other and be difficult for businesses to keep track of since it is only for Alleghany County citizens.

headline: Casey: Promoting women's health
abstract: DuBois Regional Medial Center's Breast Health Awareness Day was held to spread awareness on breast cancer prevention and intervention. PA First Lady Ellen Casey was the keynote speaker and because one of her nieces died of breast cancer at age 35. She cited that breast cancer was the leading cause of death for women 35-52 and that one in 10 women is diagnosed with it.

headline: Bill would provide supplemental funds
abstract: The chairman of the House Appropriations Committee said yesterday that he introduced legislation that would provide additional funds for state programs, agencies and jobs.

headline: At last, Pennsylvania known what and where its plants are
abstract: PA's trees are recovering and the state has more trees than it did 100 years ago, but due to the white-tail deer and other disruptions the state is loosing many of its understory shrubs and bushes. As part of the Flora of PA project a database of all the plants known to grow in the state is being compiled. The database shows that along with plants that have gone extinct there are also exotic new ones being found in the state.

headline: null
abstract: The cartoon depicts a dog holding an organized crime sign pointing two gentleman in a certain direction.

headline: State's new stalking law unties officers' hands
abstract: The stalking law that went into effect June 23 is heralded as the law that will uncuff police officers' hands.  Pennsylvania became the 41st state to implement the law intended to prevent stalking from escalating into a physical confrontation.

headline: NAFTA a gamble with litte protection for workers
abstract: There is little question, however, that the approval of the North American Free Trade Agreement will impact upon state governments throughout the nation.  The high price will be paid when families are placed out of work and become increasingly dependent on government agencies.

headline: Did Demos promote fraud in Philly Senate election?
abstract: At the rate Pennsylvania is descending into the political mire, it soon may join its eastern neighbor high on the list of most corrupt states.  If one case of fraud were sufficient to throw out an election's results, the Karne Deloach case would seem to be plenty.  But Pennsylvania courts have ruled previously that to overturn an election the challenger must prove more than just fraud.  Fraud must be extensive enough ot change the outcome.

headline: House returns to session
abstract: The Dispatch gives a look at some bills that may be considered by the state House this week when it reconvenes after recess of several months.

headline: Senate Majority Leader won't run again
abstract: Senate Majority Leader J. William Lincoln confirmed yesterday that he would not seek re-election next year.  Lincoln, 53 was elected majority leader last fall when Democrats seized control of the Senate with the party switch of Senator Frank Pecora of Berks County.

headline: Tax collection left unsolved
abstract: An emergency meeting of Susquehanna Twp. Municipal and school board officials yesterday resulted in no change in the status quo.  The tax office remains closed.  The township's treasurer- the person responsible for collecting taxes for the county, school district and township- resigned Monday during the office's busiest time of the year.  Treasurer Donald Lauver left after complaining about low pay.

headline: Casey's insurance plan due shortly
abstract: The Casey administration is not going to wait for health-care to be resolved in Washington they are expected to send the health reform plan to the legislature within the next 10 days. PA Governor Casey's plan is very similar to the one Clinton is trying to pass in Washington. The main goal is to provide options for people who live in medically underserved areas.

headline: Canadian labor leader takes swipe at NAFTA goals
abstract: One may assume that when it comes to labor's position on the North American Free Trade Agreement, the issue boils down to the potential loss of jobs to low-wage Mexico.  It ain't that simple, says Leo W. Gerard, a Canadian national director for the United Steelworkers of America.  At a press conferencein Pittsburgh early last week, in which he rattled off a litany of concerns in rapid-fire fashion, Gerard said labor's opposition to NAFTA goes far beyond possible job losses.

headline: Authority receives '92 financial report
abstract: The article is a report on a meeting of the Freeland Borough Authority. At this meeting they received its 1992 accounting report.  Freeland councilmen Steve Jordan and Ronald Briggs and the Authority also inspected the new authority building.  It was also announced the sewer plant is running well and that lead pain in barrels has been disposed of under PA Department of Environmental Resources guidelines.

headline: null
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court is claiming that a professor's sales of audiotapes of arguments before the court is in violation of an agreement by which the professor could only use the tapes for teaching, but not sell them. The newspaper feels the Supreme Court is wrong.

headline: Stories of five slain officers
abstract: Behind each of the names on the National Law Enforcement Officers Memeorial in Washington is a human story- about someone with family and friends, strengths and flaws, whose life was cut short.  Here are a few of the stories from among the hundreds of Western Pennsylvania officers whose names are carved into the walls.

headline: New operator to be sought for Mann center
abstract: The Fairmount Park Commission voted yesterday to look elsewhere for someone to manage the Mann center after consistant losses from the non-profit organization that currently runs the outdoor facility.

headline: Distortions screen the truth about NAFTA
abstract: The trouble with all the hoopla about NAFTA is that there are so many distortions and exaggerations nobody knows what to believe.  When you confuse the American people like this, they usally take the safe road and maintain the status quo.  That would mean NAFTA goes down the chute.

headline: House vote likely on workers' comp
abstract: The Senate seeks to trim $3 billion on the cost to companies for workers' compansation in a vote this week.  The House will likely have a strong resistance to the new amendments.  It is anotehr test of how productive the Pennsylvania legislative system is.

headline: Senate poised to pass service plan
abstract: After a week-long Republican filibuster, President Clinton's national service program, which would allow students to work off college costs with community service, was approved by the Senate.

headline: Taxpayers dunked
abstract: Over Mayor Masloff's objections and in defiance of good judgement, City Council has abolished fees at Pittsburgh's 32 swimming pools.  That may be nice for the people who use the pools, but it's terrible for those who have to pay for them.  Evidently it didn't occur to council that in many cases these city residents are one and the same.

headline: Casey's proposed health-care plan ignores importance of home care
abstract: Stephen W. Holt, the president and CEO of the Visiting Nurse Association of Greater Philadelphia, writes to comment on PA Governor Casey's health-care reform initiative. He commends Casey for initiating reform he believes will  continue on to the national level. He also believes the proposal will guarantee health care access to everyone and give consumers the ability to choose their own doctor and insurer. However, he feels that provisions regarding home care are limiting and not specific enough.

headline: Chesco mushroom strike takes on larger life
abstract: A mushroom strike for respect and dignity of Mexican workers has received local, state, national, and international attention, including area interest groups such as the Farmworkers Support Committee, Philadelphia Mexican consul, and union organizer Ventura Gutierrez. With recent and pending state and federal legislation, including the North American Free Trade Agreement and an amendment to the PA 1978 farm workers act to increase labor protection, the small strike has great potential.

headline: B&W dumping wasn't very neighborly
abstract: Babcock & Wilcox of Apollo has not been a good neighbor of Kiski area residents.  That was obvious last week, when the state Department of Environmental Resources reported the company violated federal law over a period of eight months by discharging pollutants into the Kiski river.

headline: $60M fuel-fraud ring broken: 13 suspects in N.J. tax scam linked to mob
abstract: 13 suspects labeled as mobsters in association with Mafia members and Russian émigrés were accused of running the largest fuel tax scam in U.S. history with 101 counts of federal indictment charges. The groups joined with John Gotti's Gambino crime family have skimmed more then $60 million in state and federal taxes on gasoline, diesel fuel and home heating oil.  US. Attorney  Michael Chertoff says that this case is reflect traditional organized crime.

headline: Students get SADD's message
abstract: In a dramatized simulation of the aftermath of a crash involving a drunken teenager and a schoolmate, emergency personnel and police officers worked to clean up the scene and rescue those involved while students from Iron Forge Educational Center watched. The simulation was put together with help from Students Against Drunk Driving and Chase Pyers, ambulance chief assistant, to discourage students from drinking and driving as prom approaches.

headline: No need to impose antitrust law, businessman tells state
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Judiciary Committee is considering a bill already passed by the Senate that would enact an antitrust statute. It would also allow the state attorney general to investigate and prosecute cases of conspiracy to create monopolies.  It is sponsored by Senator H. Craig Lewis. Speaking on behalf of the Pennsylvania Business Roundtable, Jay H. Tolson claims that Pennsylvania is too small an area within the global economy to enact such a law.

headline: Divided GOP backs Castille for court
abstract: The Republican State Committee met yesterday to decide who to endorce for the state Supreme Court race, backing Ron Castille over Zoran Popovich.  The issue of gays in the military came up as a side note to a meeting that was supposed to be exclusivly about the Pa Justice to endorce.

headline: How Pennsylvania Insures Health
abstract: "The States' Stakes in Clinton's Health Plan" graphically illustrates that Pennsylvania is one of only five states with a rate of uninsured workers of under 10 percent.  And Pennsylvania has, by far, the largest population of the five.  There are several reasons why Pennsylvania has maintained a low rate of uninsured workers compared with most other states, despite the economic dislocations that have occurred statewide in the last decade.

headline: Senate puts politics before people
abstract: The League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania is dismayed that the state Senate has adjourned until late November, effectively shutting down the legislative process.  By adjouning until after the special elections to fill two vacant seats, the Senate has put political considerations ahead of the needs of Pennsylvania citizens.

headline: Three big-city mayors show the way to survival for cities on the brink
abstract: The gradual implosion of America's big cities is one fo the clearst examples of a problem that cannot be solved by the federal government.  Since 1965, Washinton has spent about $2.5 trillion on aid to cities- the equivalent of 25 Marshall Plans.  The result being worsening racial tensions, escalating crime, crumbling bridges and sewer pips, and deteriorating services continue to force millions of city dwellers into safer, cleaner, lower-taxed suburbs.  Despite the cities' plight, mayors believe most of the answers to problems begin at home.

headline: Challenges given to caregivers
abstract: Promoting good health among the elderly hinges on good communication, says a Philadelphia-based specialist in health literacy, Janet Ohene-Frempong.  Ohene-Frempong spoke before a packed room during a four-day, state-sponsored training conference for health workers last week.  Called PrimeTime Health, the program challenges caregivers to promote healthier lifestyles for Pennsylvania citizens.

headline: Coal strike negotiators to talk again
abstract: Negotiators for the United Mine Workers and the Bituminous Coal Operators Association will return to the main bargaining table by tomorrow to seek an end to strikes that began five months ago.  Herb Fishgold, an associate of Bill Usery, the former Labor Secretary appointed to mediate the dispute, yesterday said the two sides were successful in smaller-scale meetings last week.

headline: B&W facing $2.4 million in new fines
abstract: Babcock & Wilcox Co. could face up to $2.4 million in fines for polluting the Kiski River.  B&W violated the federal Clean Streams Act when it dumped water that contained too much dissolved iron, sediment and an extremely toxic chemical, TCE, into the Kiski River, according to the state Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: ..Legalize drugs
abstract: It is time to seriously consider legalizing drugs because it will reduce crime, create revinue, make the drugs safer for the user, and increase agricultural production.

headline: Suit of Steel
abstract: Best-selling romance novelist Danielle Steel is making news, but it has nothing to do with her books.  She's gone to court to prevent a biographer from using information about her 15-year-old son, who was the focus of a nasty custody battle in 1985.

headline: Odd Reservations About Indian Gaming
abstract: President Clinton spoke with a forked tongue when asked about Indian gambling reservations.  His low regard for the way 58 tribes in 18 states are generating nearly $6 billion this year in gambling revenue is well out of line with the intent of the 1988 Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.  It is a tad late for moralizers to preach that money from these gambling operations is a breakdown in standards that should not be sanctioned.

headline: Don't ignore Olasz
abstract: As questionable as the placement of state Representative Richard Olasz in an Accelerated Rehabilitative Disposition program might be, it does dispose of the two felony charges against him.  The House should weigh taking action against the Democrat.

headline: HUD administrator will join city law firm
abstract: MichaelSmerconish,the federal offical who attracted controversy through his takeover  of t he troubled Philadelphia Housing  Authority, announced yesterday t hat he w as resigning.    This leaves many questions unanswered about the direction the PHA will be heading and whether anything  will be done to keep the federal control over it intact and whether it will be  in  worse shape than before  the takeover.

headline: Senator addresses recyclers
abstract: Sen. David J. Brightbill was the only member of the PA General Assembly who voted against the state's mandatory recycling laww because he is concerned that in the short term, it would cost municipalities money instead of saving them money.  He is committed to making it work now that it is a law and met with those concerned with recycling this week.

headline: The Scene In Philadelphia and Its Suburbs
abstract: Clark DeLeon writes about the hot, humid weather in center city and lack of rain.  Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell was honored by the Philadelphia Advertising Club as the Person of the Year.  Marc Howard of Action News and Channel Sox humorously attacked WCAUTV general manager and vice president Gene Lothery while the two introduced the mayor.  A picture shows two signs at a gas station near Kennett Square, Chester County's mushroom growing capital, where you can buy both diesel and mushrooms.

headline: Children's health plan touted
abstract: Four local state representatives joined to publicize the opening of a new statewide health insurance program aimed at helping children of the working poor.  The program, known as the Children's Health Insurance Program, will use $21 million collected since 1991 through a 2-cents per pack cigarette tax.

headline: Cost of living
abstract: The struggle to make a living has assumed a dimension these days far beyond sweat-of-the-brow labor.  A study by Northwestern National Life has found that the workplace has become, for many workers, far more dangerous than the streets when it comes to violence.

headline: Baden needs a fire station- fast
abstract: City council placed some of its members on a search committee with representatives of the Baden fire department for the purpose of finding a new fire station.  The article also states that work on the Berry Street water line, drainage and road resurfacing project will begin. The article also mentions that the PA Department of Environmental Resources has granted the borough six new sewer connections for homes.

headline: 10 face oil tax fraud charges
abstract: Federal investigators discovered that the Zorawar Truck Center in Clarion County was evading federal and state excise taxes on each gallon they sold at the pumps. By evading taxes the company was able to sell at a lower price and gain more customers. A federal grand jury in Pittsburgh charged ten people in connection with the scheme, which was discovered in a three year investigation called "Operation Diesel Storm."

headline: Supreme Court to appeal ruling ordering Guarino reinstatement
abstract: Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Angelo Guarino was removed from court while overseeing a felony trial, after the PA Supreme Court suspected Guarino reneged on promises, encouraged by the American Civil Liberties Union, to punish jury evaders. Guarino appealed and was ordered reinstated by Senior US District Court Judge Ramond Broderick on grounds he was not granted due process. The PA Supreme Court failed to comply, waiting on a Third US Circuit Court appeal and stay.

headline: Offbeat games for bars
abstract: M.T. Entertainment Specialties, the company that brought us Velcro Wall-Jumping have come up with a new game to entertain patrons at bars, Human Bowling.  Its sure to bring in higher profits as people wait in line to be strapped inside of a large, circular, metal cage then be rolled towards oversized bowling pins.

headline: Don't let the door hit you
abstract: When President Clinton fired FBI Director William Sessions last week, he called him twice, once to tell him he had been fired and a second time to remind him that the dismissal was "effective immediately."

headline: I'm walking
abstract: Mike Barrett is on a road he hopes will lead to the Massachusetts governor's office in 1994.  He is walking 300 miles across the state, campaigning in offices, stores and city halls.

headline: Senator plays hardball
abstract: A federal judge ruled that major league baseball teams should not be exempt from the nation's anti-trust laws.  U.S. Senator Howard Metzenbaum is lobbying for a bill in line with that ruling, but U.S. Senator Arlen Specter is against it.

headline: Unfairness marks assessment rates
abstract: At least 22 Pennsylvania counties put unfair tax burdens on the owners of the lowest priced homes by assessing those homes at much more than they're worth, the Post-Gazette found.  Twelve Western Pennsylvania counties are among those which overassessed such properties, according to a computer-assisted review of more than 130,000 residential sales in Pennsylvania in 1992.

headline: City health officials: Medicaid cuts hurt
abstract: Medicaid cuts are going to hurt the poor and be worse for the city in the long run by costing more in emergency room visits and needless hospitalizations.

headline: Defending the mushroom industry
abstract: Defending the integrity and quality of Kaolin Mushroom Farms, President Michael Pia corrects misstatements by a columnist and sets the record straight about working conditions, company attitude towards workers, discrimination, and benefits. Pia blames paid union organizer Ventura Gutierrez for the strike and alleges threatening and intimidation tactics have been used by Gutierrez. Pia defends his right to bring in replacement workers for the security of his company and other employees.

headline: Bill to set Earth Day permanently on April 22
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey is expected to sign a bill to formally declare April 22, Earth Day. In the past, special legislation has had to have been introduced in the House and passed through the senate to enact a resolution declaring earth day. This bill will eliminate the process in a ceremonial culmination of this year, which includes activities sponsored by the Earth Day Coaltion and the PA Department of Environmental Resources in the state Capitol.

headline: 2 boards appointed on judicial misconduct
abstract: As a grand jury is wrapping up its investigation of the state's highest court, acting Governor Mark Singel yesterday appointed 10 people to two newly created boards that will handle allegations of judicial misconduct.  Singel named six members to the Judicial Conduct Board and four members to the Court of Judicial Discipline, two panels that were established by referendum last spring.

headline: Surgeon General Suggests Study of Legalizing Drugs
abstract: Surgeon General Joycelyn Elders made a statement that legalizing drugs may reduce violent crimes. President Bill Clinton does not stand behind this stance and the White House spokeswoman Dee Myers issued a statement saying that Dr. Elders had been "talked to."

headline: Pennsylvania lags behind nation, chamber official says
abstract: Julianne Nolan, director of local services of the PA Chamber of Business and Industry, says PA has become a paradox because the state has the highest business tax rates in the country, it offers a good transportation system, ample water systems and qualified workforce, but PA has not kept up with the growth of the rest of the nation, which may be due to the numbers of elderly in the state.

headline: Dr. Ross's legacy
abstract: The newspaper praises City Health Commissioner Dr. Robert Ross.

headline: Imaging
abstract: Technology columnist M. J. Richter investigated imaging technology capabilities and its use by governments to determine if the technology could integrate data and document management. Examining the PA Department of Public Welfare, and government uses in New Jersey, North Dakota, New York, and Texas, Richter discovered several uniquely designed systems which integrated both data and document imaging in ways which saved hundreds of thousands of dollars and hours of time.

headline: Senator rides high in spite of indictment
abstract: A grand jury indictment isn't supposed to help a politician in the polls, but Texas Senator Kay Bailey Hutchison is far from ordinary.  Hutchison charmed a group of supporters of Senator Arlen Specter in Washington last week only days after a Travis County, Texas grand jury indicted her on five counts of misusing state employees, destroying government records and tampering with evidence to conceal records from prosecutors when she was Texas' state treasurer.

headline: United Way groups face strict review
abstract: The 72 nonprofit agencies that rely on the United Way of Allegheny County for annual funding soo will have to prove that they've done just aobut everything they can to get money from toehr sources first, particularly from the federal government.  In a comprehensive study to begin this summer, the United Way also will weed out duplicative programs with suggestions that the nonprofits could either consolidate or coordinate services.

headline: City lead-poisoning cases soaring
abstract: The number of children identified with lead poisoning in Philadelphia grew eightfold last year, to nearly 5,000 cases.  The city Health Department said tougher medical standards and more aggressive screening accounted for much of the increase.

headline: Employers and workers find advantages to new programs
abstract: As more and more mothers return to work, companies are finding child care services are more than morale boosters for working parents.  Such on-site facilities help lower employee turnover and often lead to higher productivity.

headline: Bucks water tainted with lead
abstract: Lead levels in tap water from the Lower Bucks County Joint Municipal authority have tested more than three times higher than the healthy limit allowed by federal law. They are one of five Pennsylvania systems where lead levels in the tap water exceed healthy levels and has been ordered to correct the hazard by the federal government.

headline: 2 of 3 YDC juveniles to face trial as adults
abstract: Two of the three juveniles who fled from the Youth Development Center and allegedly destroyed property will be tried as adults in Perry County Court, a judge ruled Thursday.  Jason Hockenberry, 17 of Mifflin County, and Jeremy Archer, 15, of Mercer County, were certified as adult defendents and remaded to the prison in lieu of $150,000 bail each after a preliminary hearing before Perry County Judge Keith Quigley.

headline: Suspect led 3 lives, slaying reveals
abstract: Steven Michael Kennedy, originally James Gregory Sheaffer, who went by the name of Stephen Jaye Fresno when he was township commissioner in 1989 was charged with the murder of his wife.  He was found hitchhiking in Oklahoma wearing a bloodstained shirt, two days after his estranged wife was stabbed in her apartment.

headline: Pennsylvania offers Mack aid
abstract: In an effort to assist struggling Mack Trucks, the PA Legislature and Governor's Response Team proposed a $9.15 million loan. PA Senator Roy Afflerback and Representative Charles Dent were optimistic about the proposal, which could help the company, provided a Mack's United Auto Worker's union vote approves concessions by the company. Mack is also hoping the Legislature will reinstate a "net loss carry forward" tax allowing companies to reduce taxes on net income by losses.

headline: Fayette resort honored by state agency
abstract: Nemacolin Woodlands has been selected by the Senior Employment Services of the Area Agency on Aging as the statewide winner of the Outstanding Large Employer award for 1992.

headline: Impasse ends on benefits for jobless
abstract: Democrats broke the GOP logjam on the extension of benefits.  The Senate resumed debating the bill.  The measure would assist long-term jobless people.

headline: Senator Santorum? Just asking
abstract: After last weeks primaries U.S. Representative Rick Santorum is looking to become a senator. He has started an exploratory committee to help make his decision. He would run against the incumbent Harris Wofford who many republicans think is very beatable.

headline: We don't need a new tax
abstract: The writer does not think that raising the sales tax in Allegheny County will be helpful and will only hurt the population numbers in the area.

headline: Clapping for Health Reform
abstract: The applause that greeted President Clinton and his wife, Hillary, from both sides of the Congressional aisle Wednesday night signaled more than mere politeness.  It was the sound of an emerging bipartisan consensus for health care reform.

headline: Foley: Workmen's fund has surplus
abstract: An independent actuarial report concluded that the State Workmen's Insurance Fund is capable of paying all present and future claims against it, says PA Labor and Industry Secretary Tom Foley.

headline: Car-pool plan released: Aims to cut pollution
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources has a new commuting arrangement in an effort to curb solo communing around the city and cut air pollution by getting one-fourth of cars off the road in the morning rush-hour in Bucks, Montgomery, Delaware and Chester Counties. Article includes map showing the targeted areas.

headline: 2 paramedics first to arrive
abstract: Two paramedics were the first to arrive on the scene of a shooting that involved two police officers.  The paramedics helped the two wounded police officers into hiding before the police arrived and then took the two injured officers to the hospitial.

headline: Tackling the horrors of child abuse
abstract: Clergy would be exempt from reporting cases of child abuse divulged during a religious confession or a confidential conversation under a chid abuse bill adopted by the state House.  The House voted 198-0 Tuesday to approve the first overhaul of Pennsylvania's child protective laws in nearly two decades.

headline: Personal income, sales of new hows increase slightly
abstract: Due to the 5th coldest February on record consumers had to dip into savings to pay for heat.  The weather also was a factor that held back a rebounding new-home sales, which grew only 4.6 percent.  The federal report that was released yesterday gave an overview of a slowly rebounding economy.

headline: Former local priest's view clouded by time and distance
abstract: Reverand Robert P. Hubal's letter is difficult to understand unless you consider it as simply a diatribe against the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh.  The letter is replete with innacuracies.  His view of the Diocese of Pittsburgh is obviously seriously clouded by distance and time.

headline: Impeachment process likely to move forward
abstract: Unless he resigns, State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen will probably become the first jurist in nearly two centuries to be impeached by the House of Representatives and forced to stand trial before the Senate in an attempt to keep his job.

headline: Sharp NAFTA debate
abstract: Vice President Al Gore called the North American Free Trade Agreement a good deal while Ross Perot cited lost jobs without uplifting Mexicans in their debate on "Larry King Live" just a week before the pivotal House vote will be made on the controversial trade agreement.

headline: Well-to-do township is skeptical of tax plan
abstract: In Birmingham Township, Chestser County, one of the most weathly areas surround Philadelphia where the average household income is over $100,000 the new tax increase targeted at them is upsetting.  They feel under attack and volnerable because they claim to be working rich and not watch-the-trust-fund-grow rich.  Others feel they need to do their part to help, but wish he could cut spending before increasing taxes.

headline: Clinton appeals to elderly
abstract: Senior citizens should support the Clinton health care plan because without it many won't get the medicine they need, President Clinton told a packed house at Ambridge High School Wednesday.  Clinoton hammered on health issues facing senior citizens as he pitched his plan on the first anniversary of his election.

headline: Ford City PPG pickets go home
abstract: Striking workers from the closed PPG Industries plant here have agreed to stop picketing.  Roy Albert, an international vice president of the Aluminum, Brick and Glass Workers International Union, said an agreement was reached in Armstrong County Court on Tuesday.  Picketing stopped Wednesday.

headline: Chesco hires consultant on landfill
abstract: The Chester County commissioners voted 2-1 to hire an outside consultant to review the records of the  Chester County Solid Waste Authority.

headline: 22 face charges in probe of drugs
abstract: The Franklin County Drug Task Force and the Chambersburg police split into teams of five and swept the neighborhood in a successful drug bust of crack cocaine dealers in Chambersburg yesterday.

headline: Take close look at impeachment, panel advises state lawmakers
abstract: A grand jury has rejected every one of state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen's allegations against his fellow justices and "strongly recommends" that state authorities consider throwing him off the court.  Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. will release the grand jury's 249-page report on its 11-month investigation.

headline: Pittsburgh Brewing Co. says it'll keep clock ticking
abstract: Time will keep on ticking for a landmark on Pittsburgh's South Side- the giant clock on the side of the old Duquesne Brewing Co. building.  Pittsburgh Brewing Co., maker of Iron City Beer, has agreed to rent the clock for the next five years for $5,000 a month, city Finance Director Ben Hayllar said.

headline: Goodbye, Dr. Ross
abstract: The newspaper editorial board discusses the resignation of Philadelphia Health Commissioner Robert K. Ross from his position. They criticize him for evading the requirement that he lives in Philadelphia, and mention that his salary was well below those of city officials in other cities. They commend the Rendell administration for its use of competition to distribute federal funds to AIDS groups.

headline: In Ross Perot's Wake, some 1992 Supporters Now Form New Parties
abstract: The article discusses Ross Perot's run for the presidency. It discusses the difficulties of running as a third-party candidate and suggests that since the Patriot Party is more likely to draw in conservative rather than liberal voters, the fact that Ross Perot is running will probably help President Clinton, because conservative votes will be split between the Republican and Patriot Party.

headline: Show some reverence
abstract: The Post-Gazette fails to show reverence for the hgih court of our state.  Is this how we want to portray the justice system to a developing mind?

headline: York County commissioners OK pay boosts
abstract: York County commissioners will be paid more than $60,000 a year in 1999, but they still won't be getting as much as commissioners in neighboring third-class counties.  Under a pay schedule commissioners approved yesterday, commissioners and row officers will get 5 percent wage boosts in 1996 and 1997, and increases of 8 percent in both 1998 and 1999.

headline: Clinton gets an earful on health care
abstract: President Clinton yesterday heard health-care horror stories from Americans- and health-financing fears from small business owners- as the White House began selling the health plan the President will formally present to Congress on Wednesday.

headline: From rhetoric to reality: Unions knock out Press
abstract: The Pittsburgh Press went on strike on May 17 when news broke of new distribution system that would eliminate 450 drivers of their job.  The leader of the union did a very good job of using the press to get his message to the public in hopes that a settlement could be reached in the favor of the workers.  The stike resulted in the loss of many jobs.

headline: Chlorine rules to spare rivers
abstract: the Pennsylvania Environmental Quality Board approved rules that municipalities and businesses must meet chlorine standards for all waterways, whereas currently limits are set only when the state finds a chlorine-related toxic problem. House and Senate committees and the Independent Regulatory Review Commission must review the rules.

headline: 29 states' officals join in urging child-proof caps on mouthwash
abstract: Officals from 29 states yesterday urged the federal government to require childproof caps on mouthwash which would prevent most of the 10,000 calls posion control gets per year of children under 6 ill due to mouthwash.  It would add an estimated 2 cents per bottle to impliment and may prevent the premature death of toddlers across the country.

headline: Taking life on day at a time
abstract: Thomas Harrington holds his 2-year-old son Shahid during a news conference to announce that he and his three children will be the first family to move into the city's first housing for homeless fathers and their children.

headline: Port may lose half Chile fruit business
abstract: As public officials, union leaders and businessmen angrily blame each other, the fractious Philadelphia port is dancing with disaster- the loss of up to half the city's precious imports of Chilean fruit.

headline: DRPA fires operator of its new yard
abstract: Fed up with labor problems, Delaware River Port Authority commissioners agreed to fire the Illinois firm running its new container transfer yard in South Philadelphia and run the yard itself. Word of the decision caused Teamsters Local 107's picket line, previously incensed at management's refusal to negotiate a labor contract, to disband. Conflict remains however, as the Teamsters fight for jurisdiction over the port against the International Longsharemen's Association.

headline: In spruced-up Senate digs, dirty PA politics predicted
abstract: The newly renovated Senate chamber is ready for today's long-awaited session, the elegant room buffed to the hilt with new carpeting, polished marble, vanished mahogany and retouched guilding.  Just in time for a brawl.  The atmosphere in the Senate has been bad the last several years, but now it is downright poisonous.  Republicans, doing a slow burn for a year, appear ready to explode.

headline: Sick? Moi?! Case of mistaken identity
abstract: Clark DeLeon clears up as to why his article did not appear on his designated day.  His daughter was sick and he was the designated caretaker.

headline: null
abstract: The newspaper praises the band "The Kinks", who recently played at the I.C. Light Amphitheatre.  They call Ray Davies one of the best songwriters to come out of the 1960s, for his song about a person of ambiguous sexuality.

headline: Clinton Is Going on the Road To Rally the Public on Health
abstract: President Clinton today kicked off what White House staffers are calling "health care a-go-go," a nationwide blitz of talk show appearances, radio call-ins and visits to local diners intended to anser one question: What does the President's health care proposal mean to me?

headline: How they voted
abstract: Article shows how local legislators voted.  In the PA House of Representatives were votes on workers' compensation, prescription penalties, and the Sunrise Act.  In the PA Senate were votes on workers' compensation and unattended children.

headline: Chlorine spill kills fish
abstract: According to the PA Department of Environmental Resources, a discharge of chlorine from an apartment complex's pool into a pond killed 26 fish on Saturday. The owners of the Bryn Mawr apartments complex are holding the firm that was hired to clean the pool responsible.

headline: 3 get jail rerms for their roles in insurance fraud
abstract: Three appraisers were convicted and sentenced to prison after a federal investigation revealed a network of 64 people involved in fraudulent insurance claims for chemical particle damage to car paint by the Marcus Hook refinery. US District Court Judge Curtis Joyner and Assistant US Attorneys Lee Dobkin and Michael Holston questioned the motives of the Travelers Insurance Company employees involved, saying despite cooperation prison sentences were necessary to prove that insurance fraud will not be tolerated.

headline: Teacher accused of sex abuse
abstract: Gregory J. DiFonzo, a music teacher, was charged yesterday with child abuse, involuntary deviate sexual intercourse and corruption of a minor.  A search warrant was given to police who then found the videotape that has DiFonzo telling a blindfolded 9 year old girl in his classroom to test the kinds of reeds by feel.  The girl is duped into performing oral sex for several minutes.

headline: PPG drops the ax on 360 at Ford City
abstract: An unnerving calm hovered over town Wednesday when PPG announced it was closing its plant in Ford City.  PPG- the plant that spawned the birth of Ford City 105 years ago- announced Wednesday that it is closing its doors for good, leaving 360 workers out of jobs.

headline: Economy residents want no part of Crows Run project
abstract: 300 Economy residents made it clear Tuesday night that they don't want a proposed Crows Run highway running through their community.

headline: Indecent exposure
abstract: Kenneth Lakeberg, father of Philadelphia's conjoined twins, and his wife had to decide the fate of the two little babies, one of whom had to die to let the stronger one live.  We should be praying for baby Angela and leaving her parents alone.

headline: Signed into law
abstract: Several bills are noted in which Lt. Governor Mark Singel, who is acting governor while Governor Casey recuperates from a heart-liver transplant, last week signed into law.

headline: '93 class looks anxiously ahead
abstract: The class of '93 is comparable in many ways with the 1960s.  The babies of the baby boomers are coming to age as the 'fast-forward' generation.  Instead of 'make love, not war' they may be saying 'spend less, waste less' as a response of the economic ressession.

headline: Clinton Lobbies for Lawmaker, Health Plan
abstract: President Bill Clinton and other top officials conducted a tutorial about the federal budget and talked about his plan for a health care plan. Clinton does not want to eliminate Social Security and Medicaid because many elderly would find themselves in poverty, but the spending on Medicaid and Medicare needs to be curbed. Many are unsatisfied with the budget plan that US Representative Majorie Margolies-Meszvinsky helped to pass because of the tax raise.

headline: Initial jobless claims up 25,000 in latest week; 3d straight gain
abstract: The number of new claims for state unemployement has risen by 25,000 in the last week.  Economists are confused because the number of jobs continues to increase.  Many think this is a phase that will quickly become balanced in the coming months.

headline: City water bills to climb again
abstract: The Water and Sewer Authority in Pittsburgh is raising rates on water bills by 4 percent. While some board members approve the increase, Ann Davis said that she did not because it would be an extra burden on the elderly who are on pensions and Social Security. One reason for the increase is tougher federal standards on drinking water that require the authority to buy expensive equipment.

headline: 3 police officers put on leave after shooting
abstract: Three midstate police officers are on administrative leave and one is assigned to desk duty as a result of Sunday's shooting of a Middletown man during stand-off with police. The police received call that the man was holding his wife and child hostage and when they responded the man came out and started firing at the police; the man was shot 6 times and is listed in critical condition.

headline: Teacher: Nude photos take 'for years'
abstract: A former city schoolteacher charged with taking nude and seminude photos of two female students, 10 and 13 years old respectivly.  He was also charged with drug possession when police searched his house and found marijuania.

headline: Preate's office investigating IRA fees at Dauphin Deposit
abstract: State Attorney General Ernie Preate's office is investigating whether Dauphin Deposit Bank & Trust Co. can now renege on paying customers a "guaranteed" 10 percent annual interest rate with no fees on an individual retirement account option the bank offered on a limited basis.

headline: Editorial board failure
abstract: The recent endorsement of several incumbent city school board members by the editorial board, shows that they have a lack of understanding of the real issues. The school board members must encourage the administration to find creative ways to operate within budgetary constraints.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: The number of lobbyists registering to ply their trade in PA dropped to 767 in 1992, the lowest in four years according to Common Cause/Pennsylvania which may be because of the confusion over which lobbyists are subject to the state's new sales tax on services.  The state treasury is losing at least $10 million annually because of a 64-year restriction on how tax money may be invested according to PA Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll.

headline: Singel deals losing hand to riverboat gambling
abstract: Lt. Governor Mark Singel said this week that he would not sign a riverboat gambling bill into law as long as he is acting governor.  He indicated, however, that he would study the issue if he were elected governor in his own right.

headline: A heartfelt concern
abstract: In Ron Bitting's letter, it is a shock he could write such a thing.  His comment about Rich Hrivnak was a low blow.

headline: Clinton May Not Meet Deadline on Health Plan
abstract: Several factors are causing the delay of President Clinton's health care reform to be submitted for congressional review, including the absence of task force leader Hillary Clinton in the wake of her father's current illness, a lawsuit imposing cumbersome review of all task force proceedings, and failure to streamline the reform into concise terms. Health care legislation will not be passed within the year as Clinton had previously asked of Congress.

headline: Japan's Employment System Straining
abstract: The Japanese system of lifetime employement with one company may be seeing its last days.  With the changing economy those aged 50 and older may be finding little hope in keeping the manager positions in their own company.  Traditional the Japanse corporations have retained their loyal employees for a lifetime: 64 percent of all Japanese men aged 45 to 54 have worked moere than 20 years with the same employer, compared to 33 percent in the United States.

headline: Clean Air Controversy Could Cost State Car Buyers
abstract: It is doubtful any Pennsylvania resident would want state lawmakers to abdicate their responsibility to govern to the Califronia Legislature.  Homegrown and resident lawmakers know better what issues and solutions are best for citizens.  Yet Governor Robert P. Casey's administration has long supported the so-called "California Plan" on reducing dangerous automotive emissions.

headline: 300% filing fee increases upset state's court official
abstract: Court officials acroos Pennsylvania are objecting to a 300 percent filing fee passed by the ledgislature.  The fees are going to go towards increasing the judges pay as well as go to the state's general fund.  William M. Carlin Jr., secretary of the state Prothonotaries and clerks of Courts Association wrote in a letter that he doesn't 'care what the state calls it, it is a tax against a few.'

headline: Testimony opens in ACLU's suit against prisons
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has filed a class-action lawsuit against the PA prison system and the case has gone before US District Judge Jan DuBois. According to the ACLU there is a high level of using excessive force against inmates, which some say results from increasing the prison population since 1980. The PA State Department of Corrections has opened five new prisons in 1993.

headline: Premiums still high despite auto-insurance law, agents say
abstract: Despite some benefits, Pennsylvania's 1990 auto insurance law has not cured high premiums in Philadelphia and its suburbs, witnesses tod a House committee yesterday.  Most insurance companies are not writing personal auto coverage in Philadelphia and the four suburban counties.  Drivers are being forced into the more expensive assigned-risk plan.

headline: Editorial views from elsewhere
abstract: A sampling of editorial opinion from other newspapers is given.  Included are editorials from the Clovis News Journal on the federal gas tax, The North County Blade-Citizen on Samalia, the Cincinnati Enquirer on health care, Charleston Daily Mail on retirement, and the Williamsport Sun-Gazette on state pensions.

headline: Inside the Capitol:  Noteworthy
abstract: When Marie Lederer takes her oath of office in the House tomorrow, she becomes the fourth member of her family to serve there.

headline: Singel eyed for position in Clinton administration
abstract: Singel, Lt. Gov. of Pennsylvania, has been contacted by Clinton aids with talks of a post possibly in the Energy Office.  Singel says he has not been the one pursuing contact and has not received any official offers.

headline: Baseball owners vote to break each league into three divisions
abstract: Major-league owners voted to break each league into three divisions next season- a vote that will have a dramatic effect on everything from the long-hallowed significance of the regular season to which teams the Phillies will find themselves battling in the standings next summer.

headline: Clinton may seek lid on doctors fees and liability suits
abstract: The Clinton Administration officials are considering asking Congress to impose restrictions on medical malpractice lawsuits and limits on doctors' fees.  This will be complicated and hotly debated legislature in an attempt to curb the outrageous price of health care.

headline: Jobless claims sink
abstract: Though the number of Americans filing jobless benefit claims saw its sharpest rise in the past eight weeks, Bruce Steinberg of Merrill Lynch blamed it on the shortened work week and said the labor market was improving at galacial speed. US Department of Labor statistics appeared to match his claims.

headline: Commissioners make collusion claim vs. DER
abstract: In Lewisburg, PA, Union County commissioners claim a conspiracy between the PA Department of Environmental Resources and the Hazardous Waste Treatment Council, seeking federal review. Pam DiSalvo of DER cites compliance with the county's desire to reduce overall hazardous waste as evidence against a conspiracy, but commissioners remain convinced that recent regulatory reviews of hazardous waste have unnecessarily increased the need for new facilities.

headline: 42 fire deaths in first two months continue a puzzling trend in city
abstract: Philadelphia officles are puzzled why there have been so many fire deaths in the first two months of the year; more than any other city in the country.  It is during this time the Rendell is proposing to cut funding and lower the number of firefighters per truck.  The Firefighters union says that is a direct corrilation to the number of deaths, but most others disagree.

headline: The Assault on Juvenile Crime
abstract: As the House and Senate continue hammering out the details of a federal crime bill, our represenatives in Washinton would be well-advised to pay attention to what is being said back home about the crime problem.  Throughout the ocuntry, district attorneys are naming juvenile crime as the number-one crime problem and reform of the juvenile justice system as their top priority.

headline: Prime Rate Cut to 5 1/2% By Morgan
abstract: Morgan Guaranty Trust Company reduced its prime lending rate to 5 1/2 percent from 6 percent yesterday, the first among the nation's largest banks to take that step.  While the rate cut matters little to Morgan's customers, millions of individuals and small businesses could benefit if other banks follow.

headline: Elderly poor show a sharp increase in some PA areas
abstract: The number of Pennsylvania's elderly population who are poor and living alone continues to grow at an alarming rate in rural and central city areas, according to a recent Pennsylvania State University report.  All this comes at a time when the state's supply of younger workers who generate the revenues needed to help supply the funding need to support programs for the elderly is diminishing.

headline: Inside the capitol: GOP senators face minority status
abstract: When the legislature convenes tomorrow Republicians will shift to minorty status in the senate while continuing their minority status in the house.

headline: Singel fires a firm warning shot in city gun-control controversy
abstract: PA Acting Governor Mark Singel has put gun control in the light as a major campaign topic by stating that he supported a statewide ban on assault-type weapons and that he would veto any legislation attempting to prevent local governments from banning them. The National Rifle Association has already warned that they will not support Singel's stance. The author believes the other gubernatorial candidates should state their stance on the issue for the public to know.

headline: Beware! Congratulations: You win scam tips
abstract: Beware of scams this year including calls, letters, and fake charities.  Lists 10 warning scams that have been used on people in Pennsyvlania.

headline: Clinton Outlines Health Care Plan Paid by Employers
abstract: President Clinton spoke at a meeting of the nation's governors and revealed his health care plan.  It would require all employers to provide health care for every employee, but employers would have five to seven years to achieve this.  Some of the costs for this plan would be covered by increased taxes on cigarettes and liquor.

headline: Kanjorski eyes jobs from technology
abstract: US Representative Paul Kanjorski has developed a bill that aims to develop a program to commercialize technology held by the federal government. Kanjorski argues that the US needs to create new jobs to compete in the global marketplace and under the Technology Commercialization and Credit Enhancement Act of 1993 the technologies would be transferred into new business and employment opportunities. With $9 to $12 million as many as 250,000 new jobs could be created.

headline: Concord May Drop Plans
abstract: Due to what sources says has been a huge financial loss for Concord Resources Group, it will drop its fourth appeal of a PA Department of Environmental Resources rejection of a proposal to operate a commercial waste incinerator and hazardous waste disposal site in Millcreek Township, Clarion County. The site proposed contains wetlands and a gas well which are grounds for automatic disqualifications by the DER.

headline: 5 judges endorsed by Allegheny County Bar Association
abstract: The Judicial Merit Selection Committee of The Allegheny County Bar Association requests public support of five jurists who are candidates in the "Yes-No" Judicial Retention Election Tuesday.  They are Pennsylvania Superior Court Judges Joseph A. Del Sole and Patrick R. Tamilia and Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas Judges Robert P. Horgos, Alan S. Penkower and Paul R. Zavarella.

headline: The IRS, an enforcer that can't keep up
abstract: The Internal Revenue Service does not have the staff or money to adequately police nonprofit businesses, so they operate unfettered, an 18-month investigation by the Philadelphia Inquirer revealed. Federal legislation in favor of extending the definition of a charity has moved to block enforcement action against selected nonprofits engaged in commercial activities. The article cited numerous examples of the legal and political battles waged against IRS attempts to revoke tax exemptions.

headline: QED orders internal inquiry
abstract: QED Communications has hired a Pittsburgh law firm to review past business practices and determine whether any improprieties exist in the operations of the parent firm of television stations WQED and WQEX.

headline: Elders is no Ginsburg
abstract: A man praises Clinton for his appointment of Ruth Bader Ginsburg to the position of associate justice of the Supreme Court and says it is no surprise she was quickly confirmed by the Senate.  He discusses the anger Christians have expressed over Clinton appointing Dr. Joycelyn Elders the surgeon general due to her pro-choice and anti-Catholic comments.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Heard On The Hill
abstract: A spokeswoman for Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Ridge was quoted as saying, "It's beyond belief.  We're going to pay m much closer attention to our filings as we had in the past", in reference to Attorney General Ernie Preate's regaling of campaign reports.

headline: Singel growing into the governor's chair
abstract: The longer Mark S. Singel serves as acting governor, some say, the more he does for his own political chances.

headline: Bishop acted outside of council
abstract: Lutheran Bishop Guy Edmiston left a false impression with the people who read the advertisement which appeared in the newspaper October 29.  The bishop did not act with the blessings of Synod Council when he took out a paid advertisement rejecting the draft of the Synod Council of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of America (ELCA) statement on human sexuality.

headline: Clinton Plan envisions 'Health Security Card'
abstract: Details of President Clinton's healthcare reform plan to give all Americans a health security card that would guarantee them health care benefits regardless of income, health, jobs status, address change are being revealed. Proposals include requiring companies and employees to contribute to health care plan costs, acceptance of Medicaid by all health plans, and competition among health plans according to benefits above the federal minimum, with special provisions for rural and inner-city areas.

headline: Key issues in coal talks reportedly resolved
abstract: The United Mine Workers and the nation's largest coal operators have agreed on how to resolve the key issues that triggered the union's 6-month strike, sources said yesterday.  However, at least some members of the Bituminous Coal Operators Association balked at a union demand that the companies rehire strikers who were fired for alleged picket line violence, the sources said.

headline: Conemaugh cleanup only a start
abstract: At a town meeting in Johnstown, organized by community leader Richard Mayer and US Representative John Murtha, citizens were asked for input on the US Army Corps of Engineers plan to clean up Conemaugh River basin. Farmers reported as many as 75 cattle dead from the pollution. Colonel Carl Alvord said citizen input is needed in order to identify the most polluted areas, largely due to coal mines,  in a study and plan which should be released next year.

headline: 850G for a probe to turn up pills
abstract: After spending almost a year and close to a million dollars probing what's been called the worst court in the country, a special counsel and the state attorney general have come up with a small-potatoes drug case against one justice.

headline: The IRS, an enforcer that can't keep up
