abstract: The Internal Revenue Service does not have the staff or money to adequately police nonprofit businesses, so they operate unfettered, an 18-month investigation by the Philadelphia Inquirer revealed. Federal legislation in favor of extending the definition of a charity has moved to block IRS enforcement action against selected nonprofits engaged in commercial activities. The article cited numerous examples of the legal and political battles waged against IRS attempts to revoke tax exemptions from nonprofits.

headline: Singel set to back mandate
abstract: Acting PA Governor Mark Singel supports the Casey administration's proposal requiring all businesses to provide health insurance to their employees.  He says he will work to move the bills through the PA Legislature.  Businesses strongly object to this and claim that it will destroy small business, but President Clinton and Singel say that rapidly rising health care costs hurt businesses much more.

headline: Elections director predicts low turnout for Nov. 2
abstract: Mark Wolosick's forecast for next month's election in Allegheny County is that it won't be a record low turnout, but it could come close.  Wolosick, the county's elections director, projected that 42 percent of the county's voters would go to the polls Nov. 2.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Heard on the Hill
abstract: PA Governor Casey replies, "I feel good" whenever asked about his recovery from surgery.

headline: Singel is a part-timer
abstract: It is interesting to not that acting Governor Mark Singel's comments about Pennsylvania having a part-time General Assembly come on the heels of Pennsylvania having a part-time governor.  Mr. Singel did not seem so eager to voice his hidden agenda when he was Senator Singel.

headline: Casey going home today
abstract: Doctors at Presbyterian University Hospital said they couldn't be happier with Governor Casey's recovery and expected to discharge the governor today, six weeks and a day after his heart-liver transplant.

headline: Clinton rejects linking bullet tax, health reform
abstract: President Clinton yesterday ruled out financing his health-care plan in part with an increased tax on ammunition, an idea proposed by Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan last week.  But the President raised the possibility of pushing for a ban on some of the more lethal bullets Moynihan had complained about.

headline: Labor leaders march on Consol
abstract: National labor leaders and community activities are marching to support  the 60,000 coal miners whose contract extension expires May 3. Consol Inc.'s joint leaders Du Pont and Rheinbraun AG of Germany will be negotiating requests from the union and from the company says Joseph Uehlein, assistant to the president of the AFL-CIO's Industrial Union Department.

headline: Conservancy will attack river pollution
abstract: US. Representative Paul Kanjorski scientific brainchild, Earth Conservancy, will put its high-tech equipment to a new environmental use, cleaning the Susquehanna River. Kanjorski received $700,000 in federal seed money to construct wetlands to help purify contaminated water. The river is currently listed among the nation's 25 most threatened rivers.

headline: A family full of gunshot victims
abstract: Street violence began exploding in Homewood two years ago and has effected a number of families, including the Greens. Dion Green had been raised by his mother to always prepare for the worse, and the worse happened when he was shot in the neck and paralyzed from his mid chest down. This all happened because Dion called someone by their wrong name.

headline: The justice system fails in stalking the stalkers
abstract: For people under the power of a stalker, the state's new stalking law was heralded as the be-all and end-all to their problems.  The law, signed by acting Governor Mark Singel defines stalkers as people who threaten others.  Yet little can be done because the Stalking Law isn't any different from other laws- unless police can catch the stalker, prosecutors have no case.

headline: Residents try to stem liquor flow
abstract: Local stop 'n go shops specializing in beer seems to draw minors and drug dealers like bumblebees to a rose, and area residents have come up with a strategy to harass certain stop 'n goes and slow the growth of new ones.

headline: Election's over, but flawed court system remains
abstract: The 1993 election is over and Pennsylvania has a new Supreme Court justice but despite the election of Mr. Ron Castille, Pennsylvania still has many problems.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Heard on the Hill
abstract: Pennsylvania House Speaker H. William Decease is quoted as saying, "As long as I am involved at the head of my branch of government, it is appropriate that I share a memento with Pennsylvanians.  I shouldn't give them a set of golf clubs, but a pen doesn't seem to be egregious". This is in defense of his spending thousands of taxpayer money on souvenir pens and tote bags with his name.

headline: Singel on the road
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel, acting as governor during PA Governor Casey's recovery from a heart-liver transplant, is attending the annual meeting of the National Governors Association.

headline: Cartoon:?
abstract: "Have we asked philadelphia for advice?  They've had expereince in boming children."  A political cartoon with solders aiming at a small village on their shirts it reads 'WACO'

headline: Clinton's prescription
abstract: Surrounding President Clinton's health-care reform proposal, he had to blunt the attacks coming from small-business groups, as well as sectors of the insurance industry and medical profession.  The President had two tasks- seize the moment and confound the skeptics.

headline: Laborer' s union backs health plan
abstract: Yesterday, the Laborer's International Union became the first labor organization to publicly endorse the Clinton administration plan of health care for all, which the president will introduce next week in a speech to Congress.

headline: Contractor hired to clean up contamination
abstract: One hundred companies responsible for soil and groundwater contamination at a Newberry Township site have hired a contracting firm to do work to clean it up.  The PA Department of Environmental Resources is overseeing the project under authority of the Hazardous Sites Cleanup Act, proposed by PA Governor Casey and signed into law in 1988.

headline: A lawsuit takes aim at city gun ordinance
abstract: A Philadelphia gun business with more than $1.3 million in annual sales has filed a lawsuit in Common Pleas Court, challenging the "validity and constitutionality" of Philadelphia City Council's recent ban on assault and semiautomatic weapons.

headline: The law according to Lisa
abstract: Ask a Philadelphian to name a judge, any judge, and chances are the answer will be 'Lisa Richette.'  No other judge has inflamed controversy the way she has in 25 years of public life.  Her decisions in criminal cases prompted ex-Mayor Frank Rizzo to name her 'Let 'em-Loose Lisa.'  But insiders say the criminal justice system could not operate without her.

headline: Riverboat gambling's a bad bet for the gamblers- and the city
abstract: The decision to bring riverboat casinos to Philadelphia boils down to one question: Do you want to live near one?  Philadelphia is such a large city that most of us don't consider a few abandoned docks along the Delaware to be anywhere close to our neighborhoods.  Putting riverboats at the river's edge has, to borrow a phrase used by Mayor Rendell in another context, an "intrinsic historical value."  For much of this nation's history, urban dockside areas have featured businesses that victimize unwary travelers and drunken sailors.

headline: Ellen Harley may run
abstract: PA Representative Ellen Harley may run for U.S. Senate against U.S. Senator Harris Wofford, who is up for re-election.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Heard on the Hill
abstract: Sen.-elect Harold Mowery, R-Camp Hill, called a news conference for today to announce the first in a series of proposed legislative reforms to restore the public's confidence in state government.

headline: Singel outlines aggressive plans
abstract: Acting Governor Mark Singel hasn't yet officially announced his 1994 candidacy for governor but he is mapping out a "to do" list for the administration he is making into his own after taking power June 14, when Governor Robert P. Casey underwent a heart-liver transplant.

headline: Casey recovering slowly, normally
abstract: Governor Casey continues "progressing normally" more than two weeks after his heart-liver transplant.  Casey is walking and gradually becoming more active.  He may undergo another heart biopsy later this week.

headline: Common cancer test doubted
abstract: New text results that were published in the Journal of the American Medical Association confirm pre-existing doubts about the effectiveness of fecal occult blood tests.  These blood tests are a way to cheeply test for colorectal cancer, but are so uneffective, finding only 30% of cases, that they are not worth using as a test.

headline: Landmark ruling near on repretitive work injuries
abstract: The court case between the Occupational Safety and Health Administration against Pepperidge Farm for 'callous indifference' towards the safety of their employees will set new precidence in restricting the ability of OSHA's power to police.

headline: Conway folks must boil water
abstract: For at least the next several days, residents of one Beaver County community will have to boil their water for cooking or drinking.  The water supply in Conway, a town of about 2,500 people, has been contaminated with fecal coliform bacteria, which, if ingested, could cause headaches and diarrhea, borough Secretary Sandra Brandenburg said.

headline: A leg up on child support
abstract: Under legislation last spring, the General Assembly passed a law which gives courts the ability to go after the professional licenses of parents delinquent in their child-support payments.  Under this new law, counties also may choose to publish the names of parents in child-support arrears without fear of retribution, and we have strengthened the legal ability to go after delinquent parents in other states.

headline: The leave bill  is a net, but many workers will fall through it
abstract: The family-leave bill gives employees of companies with more than 50 employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave to care for a newborn or adopted baby, or care for themselves or a family member with a serious illness.  Some business owners complain that the government should not interviene and that they will lose productivity if they can not count on all workers  being there.  Others say that they may need to stop highering those most likely to request this type of leave, which is woman of childbearing age.

headline: Rollin' on a river?
abstract: When it comes to gambling, is Pennsylvania missing the boat?  Some lawmakers say yes.  Representative Frank Gigliotti argues that state residents are gambling elsewhere and we are losing valuable revenue for our state, county and municipal governments.  That seems to be the prevailing opinion in the Legislature, but not a unanimous one.

headline: EMILY'S List trips over finance law
abstract: Ledgislation is being raised that will prevent campaign finance loopholes that have made groups like EMILY'S List, a group of democrats that support woman canidates who are pro-choice, very successful.  The loophole is in 'bundling' where an organization gathers the maximum $1,000 checks per indivdual and compounds then into packages of tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars towards on candidate.

headline: Inside the Capitol: House leader holds ecumenicial service
abstract: House majority leader Ivan Itkin, D-Pittsburgh is having an ecumenical service for members and their family before tomorrow's swearing in.  He will be serving in his first term in the House from the 159th District.

headline: Singel refuses to swear in new senator
abstract: PA Senate Republican leader Robert Jubelier has sent letters to acting PA Governor Mark Singel asking him to swear in the newly elected Republican senator David Heckler, but Singel has refused to do so until the Senate reconvenes.

headline: Casey, wife visit son for holiday in Scranton
abstract: Governor Casey spent the Labor Day holiday back at his old stomping grounds in Scranton, returning to his hometown for the first time since his June heart-liver transplant.  Saturday night they spent three hours at an engagement party for their son, Patrick, at a restaurant outside of Scranton and spent Sunday at their Scranton home.

headline: Despite Hillary Clinton's lobbying, questions remain on health care
abstract: Hillary Rodham Clinton's three days of congressional testimony left a trail of unresolved questions about how the administration's helath-care-reform plan will meet its goal of coverage for all Americans.  Altough lawmakers appeared to be impressed with Clinton's savvy, skepticism ran high about White House claims that universal coverage could be financed largely through savings and that the plan would make health care less bureaucratic.

headline: Life on the edge
abstract: As of September, there were 1.75 million Americans who had been out of work for more than half a year.  That's a lot of people going a very long time between paychecks.  The House of Representatives responded to the numbers and the constituents they represent by approving the third extension of the extended unemployment benefits program begun under President Bush.  The vote is an indication of the consensus around the need for the benefits beyond the normal 26 weeks of unemployment compensation.

headline: Creek debris poses flood threat
abstract: Houston area homeowners got a taste of major flooding on Sept 6-7, 1990, when 6 inches of rain fell within 12 hours, putting a good part of town under water.  They haven't the stomach fro another helping.  A more immediate concern is the pile of tree trunks, limbs, discarded tires and other refuse hung up on a bend in the main line of Chartiers Creek.

headline: A Marine veteran's slide ends on a S. Phila. Street
abstract: Kenneth McClary was once a strong intelligent Marine who eventually became a vagrant of his former town. He was shot and killed by a Philadelphia Police officer after throwing bottles at his head. Many people who knew him from his youth were very upset by his death. According to his mother McClary was never the same after coming back from the marines; he was eventually diagnosed with schizophrenia.

headline: The lowdown on the high court
abstract: Like two people passing eachother on the escalator, Supreme Court Justices Stephen A. Zappala and Rolf Larsen find themselves heading in opposite directions.  Zappala has been the court's rising star.  Larsen seems to be on a steady descent.

headline: Sears to convert catalog stores
abstract: Sears, Roebuck and Company announced it was pulling out of the catalog business and converting 350 of 2,000 catalog stores to small retail stores by the year's end. Fifteen of these stores, which will primarily sell appliances, electrongics, and law and garden equiptment under independent dealers, will be located in PA, including Sometset and Kittanning.

headline: Empower workers, author says
abstract: Author, Ted Gaebler, tells the Pa Senate that they need to work more efficently by trusting public employees more.  In a system he calls "de-layering", more responsibility would be given to the workers to come up with ideas and produce with the money given to them.  His book was praised by both republicans and democrats.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Noteworthy
abstract: John F. Graham, former director of capital projects for Allegheny County, has been appointed deputy executive director/chief engineer by the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission. He will be replacing James B. Wilson.

headline: Singel rules out a Washington job
abstract: Singel, Lt. Gov., announced that he will take his name out of consideration for the Clinton administration's Energy Department job because he will be able to do the most good for Pennsylvanians from Harrisburg.  Critics don't think he would have gotten the job even if he stayed in the running and others believe he is best staying in Harrisburg for his potential run for Governor in 1994.

headline: Deaths
abstract: List of well known people that died in 1992.

headline: Cost council studies Philly hospitals
abstract: Two hospitals, Springfield Hospital and Crozer-Chester Medical Center, operated by the Crozer-Keystone Health System had the highest average charges in 1991, according to a state survey of 27 hospitals in suburban Philadelphia.

headline: Mack Trucks, union urge workers to OK concessions
abstract: Mack Trucks Inc. and United Auto Workers are urging employees to accept a contract in order to save their jobs. The company, which is currently losing $10 million a month, plans to relocate various branches without layoffs in order to add three years to an agreement with workers against foreclosure, along with other concessions. If a majority of some 3000 UAW workers do not approve the contract, Mack Trucks will cut operations in some facilities and close its Allentown, PA headquarters.

headline: Critic blames mines for river's pollution
abstract: Phil Patz, former Yough and Cheat Rivers guide in Johnstown, PA, is familiar with area pollution, and cautioned to the US Army Corps of Engineers in a public meeting that their Comprehensive Plan to clean up the area could not happen overnight. A lot of the pollution seems to be coming from area mine leaks, despite efforts to plug them. Patz and the Keystone River Runners of Indiana County will be involved in a cleanup project of the Conemaugh River on May 8th.

headline: A teen against Brady Bill
abstract: The Bradly Bill will only hurt us common folk who won't be able to defend ourselves because criminals will get guns anyway.

headline: Va. Hous Weakens Handgun Limit Bill
abstract: Virginia House of Delegates weakened a bill limited handgun sales in the state, which had a one-gun-a-month policy.  The amendment allows individual says to surpass the one-gun-a-month policy.

headline: Sears to convert catalog stores
abstract: Sears, Roebuck and Company announced it was pulling out of the catalog business and converting 350 of 2,000 catalog stores to small retail stores by the year's end. Fifteen of these stores, which will primarily sell appliances, electronics, and law and garden equipment under independent dealers, will be located in PA, including Somerset and Kittanning.

headline: End notes
abstract: Biopsy test results from Pennsylvania Governor Robert P. Casey- who underwent heart-liver transplant surgery nearly three months ago in Pittsburgh- show that his new heart is functioning properly, with no sign of rejection.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Singel lends an ear and winds up late
abstract: The article notes that Acting PA Governor Mark Singel and Clinton both are known for being late to events, mostly due to the fact that they are both personable and will stop to listen to those who wish to speak to them. Singel was late to a news conference to sign a proclamation changing the state constitution, and he was also late to another news conference.

headline: Singel: Government obligated to education
abstract: Lt. Governor Mark Singel told a ballroom full of teachers, legislators and business leaders from across the country that the most important obligation of government is fostering education at the Education Commission of States, which is holding its two-day annual convention at the Hilton Hotel in downtown Greensburg.

headline: Eagles haven't been distracted
abstract: The eagles are set to play their rivals the Dallas Cowboys in the NFL playoffs.

headline: Critics say deploying  fewer paramedics  will cost lives
abstract: Rendell's  proposal  to  save money by adding EMTs to the support teams of the city's 20 paramedic vans comes  under  fire  by many in  the  field saying that this move is  not  just a mathematical equation, but lives will be lost that otherwise would have  been saved because  of the unskilled replacements.

headline: Madigan Angry With Developments Regarding Workers' Compensation
abstract: State Senator Roger A. Madigan, angry with developments in the workers' compensation reform arena, called on Acting Governor Mark Singel to fire any administration employee who gets out of step with the administration's opposition to compensation insurance tax hikes.

headline: Curbside recycling to expand
abstract: Philadelphia's effort to bring curbside recycling to ever neighborhood and every home will take a major step forward today, when recycling trucks begin to roll through West Philadelphia for the first time.  Over the next two weeks, the city will pick up buckets of bottles, cans and newspapers from 104,000 homes in West Philadelphia neighborhoods.

headline: A tokin' liberal
abstract: A man writes into the newspaper advocating the legalization of marijuana, saying that he is a responsible user of it.

headline: The Scene: In Philadelphia and Its Suburbs
abstract: Philadelphia firefighters have put up a billboard in their 'save a child' campaign to make the public aware about fire dectectors.  Two Temple films students are planning to make a non-profit movie based on a Steven King Novel in Philadelphia.  A lawyer in Chicago charged with embezzlement is blaming it on the need for theorpy for having to constantly fly to Philadelphia.

headline: Seven Scenarios Under Clinton's Proposal
abstract: Hypothetical scenarios are given assuming that the Clinton plan goes into effect as proposed.  They are based on the average price for family health insurance in the Washington area and are based on calculations that take into account different personal situations.

headline: Environmentalist to guide Heinz gifts
abstract: Franklin Tugwell, an environmentalist who maneuvers in the power jungle of Washington DC, and preserves tropical rainforests in Costa Rica, has been named as the new executive director of the Howard Heinz and Vira I. Heinz Endownments.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Singel to see pope but still run state
abstract: Acting PA Governor Mark Singel is leaving the state to meet with Pope John Paul II, along with President Clinton. He will also attend the National Governors Association, where Clinton will unveil his national health plan.

headline: Singel's poll favorite
abstract: Lt. Governor Mark Singel has released a poll that shows him to be the front-runner in the Democratic primary for governor next year.  The poll shows Singel winning 34 percent of the Democratic vote, followed by former US Senate candidate Lynn Yeakel at 21 percent.

headline: Gov. Casey undergoes more post-transplant tests
abstract: Governor Casey returned to the Univeristy of Pittsburgh Medical Center for another heart biopsy and various tests relating to his heart-liver transplant operation.

headline: Department's lack of staffing to delay new state law
abstract: A new Pennsylvania workers' compensation law faces delays because the PA Health Department lacks the staff to approve all the organizations that will oversee patient care. Also causing delay is a lawsuit by the Pennsylvania Orthopedic Society over certain provisions of the law.

headline: Mine workers president looks to workplace change
abstract: Far from standing on its last leg, the United Mine Workers of America is winning its struggle for change in the workplace, its president, Richard Trumka, said Wednesday.  Trumka, whose union is striking the nation's major coal producers, cited a labor-management agreement at the Maple Creek coal mine in western Pennsylvania as an example of positive change.

headline: Deer pose less peril than hunters
abstract: Local officials should not allow hunting advocates to prevail in a matter of general public sagety.  Discussions at a Valley Forge meeting of possible ways to prevent deer-casued auto accidents and other effects of deer overpopulation seem to favor hunters' interests over those who are opposed to shooting and, more specifically, opposed to shooting in their own neighborhoods.

headline: Abortion terrorists
abstract: The acts of the pro-life movement are terrorism.  Their tactics of violence, threats, bombings, and murders are terroristic even if they are not from a foreign land.

headline: Theft of tractors, mowers adds up to $8 million haul
abstract: A tractor theft ring with an attraction to John Deere models has stolen more than $8 million in machinery during the past four years.  The thieves have preyed on farm machinery dealerships near interstate highways in five states, including Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio, West Virginia and Virginia.

headline: Shoe plant shutdown will idle 175
abstract: Workers at Penn Footwear Corp., one of the last shoe manufacturers in the Wyoming Valley, were told Monday afternoon that they won't have jobs two months from now.  Ther permanent plant closure affects 175 employees.  Penn Footwear founder William Davidowitz and his three sons attributed the closure to an inability to compete with foreign imports, primarily from the Far East.

headline: Erie mayoral race close in early returns
abstract: With 10 districts reporting out of 152 Erie Mayor Joyce Savocchio held a six-vote lead over Chris Maras. Maras, is a consultant who is in his second council term; he is a former city comptroller and has lost two previous mayoral campaigns. Savocchio is running for her second term.

headline: Inside the Capitol: They're talking about
abstract: Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky cast the deciding vote to get the president's budget passed in the House after he promised to hold a budget summit in her Montgomery County district.

headline: State should tell counties about changes
abstract: Thomas D. Evans of Cambria County lost the election seeking a nomination for township tax collector.  If he had won he could have been disqualified for not knowing about a change in the township code.  Evans wasn't told about the township code change requiring a one-year residency in the municipality, because the bureau personnel weren't told.

headline: Herbert Stewart, ex-Cumberland comissioner, dies
abstract: Herbert Stewart, dies at age 68 at the Masonic Homes.  He led a colorful life as a county political in the 1960s and 1970s.

headline: Doctor says MRI would benefit Carlisle Hospital
abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) at Carlisle Hospital would allow profits from the procedure to benefit the hospital rather than private operators or hospitals outside the area, says Dr. Herbert C. Perlman, head of radiology at the hospital.  Those profits would go back into the hospital and enhance local services and possibly reduce patient bills, says staff radiologist Rand J. Cuthbertson.

headline: Miners' wives trying to help
abstract: Wives of laid off union coal workers are holding meetings to find out what needs to be done in order to find a buyer for the mines so that their husbans can have jobs again.  They are having state reps. speaking at their meeting and plan to get in touch with the Casey administration.

headline: Delco '92 recycling less than increase reported to state
abstract: When the state recently released recycling figures for Delaware County, officials rejoiced.  The county had met the state's 25 percent recycling goal- five years early.  Based on numbers provided by the county officials, state analysts said the county had recycled 26.2 percent of its municipal waste in 1992.  However, a review of county and state records shows that percentage of recycled county waste actually declined, reason being double counting and other errors.  The county will resubmit.

headline: Absence becomes presence in 2 affected households
abstract: The ordeal of families of murder victims is well-documented.  The families of those who kill face an ordeal as well- particularly when a crime shocks a small community.  Absence is the presence in these families.

headline: This time the NRA is in the cross hairs
abstract: After victories in New Jersey and Virginia, two very different states, for the gun control lobbies some believe the NRA is now in trouble.  The victories were in one-gun-a-month legislature and the Bradly Bill, but NRA officals aren’t worried at these setbacks.

headline: Silo is closing 45 of its stores, cutting 570 jobs
abstract: Silo, a Philadelphia based electronic store, will close 45 of its stores in seven states citing millions in operationing losses in recent years.

headline: Even a hot beach beats the 'burg
abstract: Being at the beach is much better than being in Harrisburg.  Nancy Eshelman gives 25 reasons as to why the Atlantic coast beats the edge of the Susquehanna.

headline: Inside the Capitol: They're talking about
abstract: PA Governor Casey is continuing to recover from his surgeries and appeared at Strawberry Square to sign autographs.

headline: Some Republicans to offer hsopitiality
abstract: The Inauguration week for President-elect Bill Clinton comes with mixed hospitality from the Republicans in Washington.  Some are not letting partisanship stop the calibration and welcoming in the conciliates into their offices whereas some are more bitter and will be friendly, but not go out of their way to welcome in the new leadership.

headline: Here's Why Casey's Heart-Liver Transplant WAS Fair
abstract: When Governor Robert Casey was placed on the wiating list for a heart transplant he was a very sick man.  Nonetheless, people have questioned the speed with which he received his transplant.  The ensuing controversy has promoted public debate about organ donation and transplantation.  Governor Casey should not be punished for who he is when, in all likelihood, someone with less stature in the same need would have received the transplant as quickly.

headline: Doctors assailed in antitrust move
abstract: The Federal Trade Commission used antitrust law today for the first time to challenge two joint ventures formed by doctors who sent patients to medical equipment companies in which the doctors had invested.  The commission, the two companies and 28 doctors agreed to settlements intended to reduce the doctors' financial interest in the two businesses, which supply oxygen and oxygen equipment fo ruse by patients with heart and lung diseases.

headline: Moonlight union decides future
abstract: United Steelworkers of America Local 8025 vote to decide whether or not to accept concessions the Moonlight Mushroom say are need to keep the farm open. One of the possible aspects could be downsizing Armstrong County's largest employer from 967 workers to 550 workers.

headline: Delco industrial park is tainted
abstract: Soil at the Delaware County-owned Riverbridge Industrial Center here contains "elevated levels" of dangerous PCBs and other contaminants that will need to be cleaned up, said the county's executive director.  Such contamination at the 53-acre site has been suspected for years, but was only recently confirmed.

headline: Across Philadelphia, slow burn, brutal toll
abstract: At least 41 people have died in Philadelphia during the oppressive hot spell that is coming to an end.  City officials label a death as heat-related even if heat is only one factor.

headline: Those who knew brothers puzzled by killing
abstract: MUST GO BACK AND FIND.   PG. 22/23

headline: Simulcasting supported
abstract: Richard Guida, a philadelphia resident, supports the passage of the state Senate bill allowing simulcasting in Pennsylvania of full racing cards from out-of-state tracks.

headline: Ex-authority member ordered to repay salary
abstract: The state Ethics Commission has ordered Daniel Zontek to repay $2,550 to a Westomoreland County sewer atuhority, claiming Zontek got the money by voting himself a salary improperly.  The commission ruled that Zonteck, as a member of the Western Westmoreland Municipal Authority, sidestepped state law regarding compensation for authority members.

headline: Inside the Capitol: They're talking about
abstract: The latest amendment to the state constitution since 1988 was enacted by PA Lieutenant Governor Singel.  It will ratify the judicial reform changes approved by voters.

headline: Sour End to Strong Year
abstract: The 103d Congress more or less ended a productive first session today, but on a note of ill will that made it clear that the legislative paralysis of recent years had been diminished but not vanquished.  Party divisions were raw and obvious during the budget battle in the summer and clear against today as minor differences held up a popular gun control measure.  Democrats sought to trap the Republicans into blocking it, or giving up ignominiously.

headline: If an image is worth a thousand words, imagine what imaging is worth to you
abstract: An advertisement for Unisys info imaging cites benefits beyond paperwork reduction and enhanced productivity to efficiency, promising a solution for whatever organization your current system relies upon.

headline: Dollars and Sense
abstract: A list is given of what the health-reform plan would cost, and a chart shows where the money would come from.

headline: Moonlight workers face contract vote
abstract: Moonlight Mushroom employees could know Friday if they will lose their jobs this year.  That's when union members are set to vote on contract concessions proposed by Moonlight.  The company says the concessions, amounting to about $6,000 a year for each employee, are needed if the mushroom mine is to remain open.

headline: Delco unloads a costly white elephant
abstract: PA Delaware County officials boasted in 1984 of the purchase of an incinerator they planned to install in Middletown Township to provide energy. However, despite victory in Middletown v. Delaware County, and the incinerator was retired to a storage facility. Nine years later it has been sold to Ralph Petruzzo to use at his egg carton plant in exchange for payments totaling $2 million to universities comprising the Center for Solid Waste Systems and Technology.

headline: Admiring from afar
abstract: City Councilman Jack Wagner's proposal to ban automatic and semiautomatic weapons in the cty is agreeable.  Such guns serve no legitimate purpose for self-defense, hunting or target shooting.

headline: Tighter abuse law weighed
abstract: The House this week is expected to consider legislation that would overhaul the state's law on child abuse.  The legislation, the first major revision of the state's Child Protective Services Law in nearly 20 years, would expand the definition of child abuse.

headline: Singel Warns Firms
abstract: Newspaper praises acting PA Governor Mark Singel for making a public appeal to private insurance companies to file reductions in workers' compensation rates by the end of the month. This was in response to rumors that some companies might ask the PA Insurance Department for a rate increase.  The Pennsylvania Compensation Ratings Bureau said they are in the process of determining its rates.

headline: Excerpts from The Larsen Testimony
abstract: Following are excerpts from a transcript of grand jury proceedings on Sept. 9, 1993, at which Justice Rolf Larsen was questioned by John Charles Dodds and Edward S. G. Dennis Jr., special deputy attorney general.

headline: Inside the Capitol: They're talking about:
abstract: The legislature's return tomorrow.

headline: Sovereignty threatened
abstract: Look who's promoting NAFTA; David Rockefeller front-men Henry Kissinger and Jimmy Carter.  Why would Rockefeller muster his top guns to push NAFTA?  Frightening is NAFTA's theft of our sovereignty.  We hire people in Washington to run things for us.  If our hired hands give authority to non-elected international tribunal, we would lose control of our commerce and destiny.

headline: 'If anybody asks, I'm back'
abstract: Governor Casey is helped on the treadmill yesterday by physical therapist Chris Wells, recovering from a heart-liver transplant.

headline: Drug error system pushed
abstract: US Representative William J. Coyne said he planned to introduce legislation this month to establish a mandatory centralized reporting system for medication errors.  After reading a Post-Gazette series on hospital medication errors, Coyne said, "I think there is a need for a national attempt to address this problem, and I'm hoping that we'll be able to get enough support to do something."

headline: Moonlight: Singel stops in
abstract: The union has blasted the company during the past several weeks unwilling to negotiate.  Asked if the company has offered to push back Monday's shutdown deadline for Moonlight Mushrooms Inc., there has been no indication yet of doing so.  Although Lt. Governor Mark Singel has pledged the full support of the state to keep Moonlight open, as Armstrong County's largest employer, he said he made no specific promises to Sylvan Foods or the union.

headline: DER Leader Gets Grilled Over Burner
abstract: Forces proposing a planned hazardous-waste incinerator in northern Union County finally got a chance to publicly question last night Arthur A. Davis, secretary of the state Department of Environmental Resources, the state's top environmental official, but they spent most of the time "prosecuting" him and his aides.

headline: Aide convicted of killing a nursing home resident
abstract: A nurse's aide at a Montgomery County nursing home was convicted yesterday of murdering a 90-year-old resident by striking him on the face so hard that his brain was injured.  The verdict stunned defendant Wendy Palmer and her lawyers.  Attorneys for both sides said it was the first time a nursing home attendant in Pennsylvania had been found guilty for murdering a resident.

headline: Time and again, murder hits close to the same homes
abstract: In Philadelphia the same few neighborhoods are affected by multiple homicides. These homicides leave a lasting affect on the communities and the people. Even though those responsible are brought to court, it does not help those who experience the loss. The article discusses the cases of Ella Davis, Lawrence Hollerway, Wadell Edwards, and David Parker.

headline: Socking it to the restaurateurs
abstract: The new 'sin-taxes' impossed by the federal government are to be activated the average person will be hurt.  Taxing alcohol is going to be taxed an additional 25 cents per ounce.  The more you tax the less people will go out.  The less jobs will be needed the worse the economy.  Hasn't the government ever taken economics 101?

headline: Exertion costs lives of many residents
abstract: Pennsylvania has the highest number of known storm related deaths from the latest blizzard.  The state is asking money from the federal government in the amount of $60 million to help with emergency snow plowing costs.

headline: Inside the Capitol-Noteworthy
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey receives the distinguished public service award from the American Society of Highway Engineers at the 31st annual convention tomorrow in Balitmore. The award recognizes Casey for his efforts to create jobs by accelerating public works improvements during recessionary times.

headline: Specter rips report
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell and 28 members of a commission to study the future of the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard have a report on the issue. US Senator Arlen Specter says that the report undermines the bargaining position that Specter and a group of regional political and union officials have with arguing the legality of the proposed shutdown with President Clinton's administration.

headline: It's what makes us great
abstract: Part of what makes America great is that the average citizen is armed!  Armed people are citizens; unarmed people are subjects!

headline: Drug inventors honored
abstract: The Intellectual Property Owners Association yesterday named developers of a prostate gland shrinking drug "Inventors of the Year". The two men, Gary Rasmusson and Glenn Reynolds of Merck & Company, received approval of Proscar by the US Food and Drug Administration last year. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company employees were also honored for development of the Aquatred tire.

headline: Mushroom pact loses, plant closing is looming
abstract: The 950 workers who grow and harvest Moonlight brand mushrooms yesterday voted for the second time to reject the concessionary contract and accept the closing of Armstrong County's largest employer.  Gary Walker, president of Moonlight Mushrooms Inc., said he was disappointed with the vote but would proceed to shut down the mushroom farm in an orderly way.

headline: DER official offers 2 dates for meeting
abstract: A state Department of Environmental Resources official has offered two dates for agency secretary Art Davis to meet with a citizens advisory group studying a hazardous waste incinerator proposed in Gregg Township.  The suggested dates were in late September.

headline: Aimed at teens, abstinence gets a sexy sell
abstract: York County observed its Great Sex-Out Day yesterday in an effort to impress upon unmarried teenagers the joys of abstinence.  The Teen Pregnancy Coalition of York County ran the event which gave information on teen pregnancy and listed activities teens could engage in instead of sex.

headline: To protect a child
abstract: For the first time in 20 years the state House of Representatives has approved a major revision of the commonwealth's child-abuse law.  Representative Kevin Blaum of Wilkes Barre, its prime sponsor, expects no less from the bill than a dramatic reduction in the number of children killed and seriously injured as a result of abuse.  He is absolutely right in suggessting that government commitment to genuinely protect children is a critical first step.

headline: Square changes dramatically
abstract: A fight by Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed to keep Penn National Insurance from moving to the West Shore ends as construction plans are announced for the city's former run-down, but now up and coming Market Square. Businesses in the way of construction have mixed feelings and plans, from resentment and retirement, to optimism and relocation, and even support from the Historic Harrisburg Association for attempts to keep the façade of the Senate Hotel.

headline: Ex-teachers protest over pension woes
abstract: They stood in the rain to make their point, nearly 3,000 of them, mostly retired school teachers who came to demand a boost in their retirement checks and head off what they fear is a raid on their pension funds.  It was the first time the 56-year-old Pennsylvania Association of School Retirees staged such a rally, said Anna P. Simpson, a former Philadelphia school teacher and the group's president.

headline: Inside the Capitol-They're talking about:
abstract: Inside the Capitol, discussion of PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr.'s contention that the PA Crime Commission is out to get him in its probe of his connection to video poker operators is ongoing.

headline: Specter ruges probe of state campaign
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter has jumped ino the disputed 2nd Senatorial District election on behalf of his protégé, Republican Bruce Marks, calling for a criminal investigation of possible abuses of absentee ballots by Democrat William Stinson's campaign.

headline: Liver-transplant surgeon's book gets new life
abstract: The book "The Puzzle People" written by a transplant surgeon Thomas Starzl has starting selling in large numbers since PA Governor Casey's heart-liver transplant.  A movie may even be made based on the book.

headline: Eating Well
abstract: Two reports within the last year on breast cancer and diet have provided discouraging news for women who work hard to keep their fat consumption down, hoping to avoid a disease that affects one in nine American women.  Neither study showed a correlation between the level of fat consumption and the incidence of breast cancer.

headline: Mushroom workers reject givebacks for 3rd time
abstract: A penny a pound was not enough to persuade employees of Moonlight Mushrooms Inc. to back down yesterday and swallow contract concessions to save Armstrong County's largest employer.  A tally of the balloting showed 378 votes against the contract and 357 for it.  It was the third time the members of United Steel Workers Local 8025 voted down contract concessions knowing their jobs hung in the balance.

headline: DER officials suspect newer gasoline spill at site
abstract: Water samples by the PA Department of Environmental Resources revealed traces of a gasoline chemical used since the early 80s. Officials suspect the area, the site of a massive spill cleanup two decades ago, may have been exposed to another spill within the last decade, and have requested records from a Hampden Township oil company site to determine if leakage has occurred. This comes as a local developer attempts to have the area re-zoned for a potential mobile home site.

headline: Alleged attack on smoker lands law student in court
abstract: Nigel J. Cohen, a second-year law student at the University of Pittsburgh, is getting a lesson on the inner workings of the criminal justice system.  Call it a jailbird's-eye view.  Common Pleas Judge Paul F. Lutty Jr. revoked Cohen's bond Wednesday afternoon when the law student refused to help Assistan Public Defender Charles Clerk select a jury for Cohen's trial on charges of simple assault and resisting arrest.

headline: Tracking the elusive judge
abstract: A reporter for the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette tracks Joseph O'Kicki, a PA judge convicted of corruption and conspiracy, and an international figutive, to Yugoslavia where O'Kicki's wife and two sons now live and where O'Kicki is believed to be hiding. Family neighbors say they have frequently seen O'Kicki. His wife, who has changed her last name and filed for divorce, refuses to account for discrepancies in her story that she does not know where the fugitive is hiding.

headline: Star Lake part of international amphitheater deal
abstract: It'll be business as usual next year at Star Lake, even though the amphitheater is part of an agreement signed by three entertainment giants Monday.  Blockbuster Entertainment Corp., Sony Music Entertainment and PACE Entertainment Corp. announced the formation of a joint venture partnership to develop and operate musical concert amphitheaters in North America, Europe and other international markets.

headline: F.W. de Klerk: 'We are making peace'
abstract: Remarks by F.W. de Klerk at Independence Hall are given recorded by KYW Radio and transcribed by The Inquirer.

headline: Investment rewards
abstract: The dramatic increase in the compensation paid to those responsivle for managing the $22 billion fun of Pennsylvania School Employees Retirement System should be questioned.  They will now make $160,000 a year, which is more than the governor makes.  Public servants should have incentives such as bonuses for successful performance, but this is a rediculous.

headline: Specter to receive award
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter is one of two lawmakers selected by the Blinded American Veterans Foundation (BAVF)to receive tis annual George "Buck" Gillispie Award for Congressional Service.  The award, which will also be presented to Representative Time Penny of Minnesota, is named in honor of Gillipsie, a blinded WWII veteran who has devoted more than 40 years toward helping in the rehabilitation of visually impaired veterans.

headline: Meeting draws many of world's top minds to city
abstract: The American Philosophical Society in its 250th anniversary celebration in Philadelphia, will host distinguished minds from all over the world in a feast of knowledge, including the King of Spain, Juan Carlos 1, who will be honored with the presentation of the Thomas Jefferson Gold Medal. Nobel Laureates, renowned physicists, scientists, and humanities contributors will meet to celebrate interdisciplinary dialogue, one the of the key foci of the Society.

headline: Economists have little faith in cost controls for health care
abstract: Clinton wants to impose price controls on the health care industry by capping prices of medicine, doctors, and hospitals.  History teachers and economists agree that it won't work.  They point the th Nixon and Carter Administrations and the failures associated with their economic price controls.

headline: Organizer's goal reaches over border
abstract: Farmworkers union coordinator Ventura Gutierrez, recruited by the Farmworkers Support Committee, is counting on a mushroom strike in Chester County, PA to create a union for farm workers there. Gutierrez has met with PA state Representative Mark Cohen, Philadelphia City Councilman Angel L. Ortiz, Mexican Deputy Consul Carlos Giralt-Cabrales, and other leaders to create support for plans to organize a network of Mexican farm worker unions that spans both borders.

headline: DER raises a stink over Chesco mushroom-compost odors
abstract: Pennsylvania's Department of Environmental Resources yesterday warned a Chester County farmer that his mushroom compost business is violating the state's air-pollution laws.  This is new ground for the DER because the $246 million mushroom industry, has traditionally been exempt because it is an agricultural enterprise.  Only a warning was issued, but the DER said it will follow through on the threat if the situation isn't improved.

headline: Amendment OK'd to forbid unfunded mandates
abstract: The Senate voted 48-0 to pass a proposed constitutional amendment that would bar the state from imposing costly new mandates on local government without giving them the resources to pay for the orders. The proposal must be approved by the House and then voted again in the next session of the Legislature; voters would ultimately decide the issue in a referendum.

headline: Tragedy hit a lively street
abstract: Six children perished early Sunday morning at 2015 Oakford St., in Point Breeze.  Neither the mother of one or the mother of the other five were in the house when the fire hit.  Yesterday, saddened neighbors said that although the six children were boisterous and fun-loving, they lived under difficult circumstances.

headline: State must reverse trends in manufacturing decline
abstract: As David Passmore sees it, it is too early and too dangerous to give up on Pennsylvania's manufacturing industry given the economy. Though some say the decline in manufacturing jobs PA by over half a million follows national trends, Passmore argues PA has led that trend. Over those who would invest rather in the service industry, Passmore cites 900,000 manufacturing jobs and recent restructuring, incentives, and tax reform as reasons to be more optimistic and loyal to the industry.

headline: Fat of the land
abstract: There's no denying that the clout of Senator Robert C. Byrd has had a lot to do with decisions to undertake more than $800 million in federal projects in West Virginia.  In fact, the Appropriations chairman has promised to bring more than $1 billion in spending home by 1995.

headline: It takes two to reduce partisanship
abstract: Pennsylvania House Speaker Bill DeWeese criticizes the Republicans in the PA General Assembly for being partisan, based on statistics that show they are more likely to vote along party lines.  The newspaper points out that there are other measures of partisanship in which Democrats are just as guilty,

headline: Specter vows to find energy aid
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter assured state officials yesterday that he would work to get more federal energy aid to needy Pennsylvanians.  "This is a matter of higherst priority, where people not only suffer from cold, there are deaths which result and many people are faced with the alternative of heat or eat," Specter said.

headline: Mrs. Brian P. Walsh
abstract: St. Paul's Church, Scranton, provided the setting Saturday for the wedding of Karen Louise Chandler and Brian Patrick Walsh, both of Harrisburg.

headline: Education about AIDS is critical to prevention
abstract: Nationally, the trend is that AIDS is becoming more heterosexual and female in its profile.  Which suggests that high school-age men and women are increasingly at risk, which is why so much emphasis on AIDS education is targeted at these groups.

headline: Pa. House passes fourth version of workers' compensation plan
abstract: The House has passed its fourth version of a workers' compensation bill that reverses key provisions of a Senate-approved plan aimed at reducing the $3 billion annual cost of permiums for buisnesses.  The lobbying betrween Teamsters union officals and a Philadelphia legislator became violent as it led to shoving and heated words.

headline: DER says its hands tied by courts in issue of out-of-state burner waste
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Resources does not encourage incinerator companies to import waste, despite an internal memo from 1990 that says DER should not restrict out-of-state waste, a DER spokesman said Friday.

headline: Amishman held in 'gruesome' slaying of wife
abstract: Gruesome murder of an Amish woman allegedly committed by hurt husband with a blunt object and a knife left her naked and disemboweled body in their house.

headline: Tranquilizers not addictive, drug experts say
abstract: The prescription drugs prosecutors charge state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen illegally obtained to hide his emotional problems are mild tranquilizers.  The "abuse potential" of the tranquilizers is "quite low," an expert in psycho-pharmacology said.

headline: State Oks insurance rates
abstract: The Pennsylvania Insurance Department approved a 9,3 percent average rate decrease for Insurance Services Office and a 0.2 percent average decrease for Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co.

headline: Father, son finally share a life
abstract: 11-year-old Dantay Davis and his father, Todd, have always stayed in touch, but until lasty year they hadn't lived together since Dantay was 1 year old.  Last year Todd Davis finally stepped in to rescue Dantay from a life of being shuttled around from one relative to another.  It may have started out a little belatedly, but they are a family now.

headline: It was nothing special
abstract: In visiting Albridge to see the president speak three weeks ago, the "special guest pass" that was received turned out to be a worthless piece of paper.  It turns out that these were issued all over Western Pennsylvania and only allowed you to stand in line on a first-come, first-in basis behind the many VIPs and school students that the president wanted in the audience.

headline: St. Pat Parade Committte Names Judge Munley as 'Man of the Year'
abstract: Lackawanna County Judge James M. Munley has been named 'Man of the Year' by the St. Patrick's Day Parade Committee of Lackawannna County Inc.  He has been on the bench since 1977 and is very active in the community.

headline: Phillies are NL champs
abstract: Those Phillies- who won over this city with belly-flop catches and inside pitching, with the reckless joy with which they played the game- are the National League champions.  They defeated the Atlanta Braves last night to claim the league pennant for the first time since 1983.

headline: Effective health reform must include physician-hospital integration policy
abstract: Mac Thornton, chief counsel to the Inspector General, US Department of Health and Human Services, was in Pittsburgh to address the issue of health care reform, and the integration of the health care delivery system in various parts of the country.  His office has the responsibility to enforce the anti-kickback statute of the Social Security Act.

headline: Pa. official says PGW locked out workers
abstract: Jack F. Rudy, an official of the PA Department of Labor and Industry, ruled that a work stoppage by 1,800 Philadelphia Gas Works employees was the result of a blackout by the city-owned utility, thereby entitling the workers to unemployment benefits.

headline: DER: Poultry operation must improve
abstract: Wellington Farms poultry processing plant has only partially fulfilled an agreement with the state to improve its waste-water disposal system.  Levels of waste producsts released into the plant's septic system exceed levels set in a March agreement with the state Department of Environmental Services.

headline: Ammonia leak kills 2 workers
abstract: Adams County Coroner Patricia Lineback identified two people who were killed by the ammonia line break at the Knouse Foods Cooperative Inc. plant. With the help of the State Police and local fire police the village of Orrtanna was evacuated as a precaution. The situation was handled also by the Adams County Emergency Management Agency.

headline: Trial on Hanover disturbance still on hold
abstract: After being notified that the US District Courts did not have money available to pay for the civil jury trials, US District Judge William Caldwell removed the lawsuit filed by 17 plaintiffs about two nights of racial disturbances in York County. Since, the  director of the US Courts Administrative Office, L. Ralph Mecham, has said  that the money was still available for civil jury trials, but the trial has not been rescheduled.

headline: Taxpayers will become big winners
abstract: Every day Pennsylvania loses millions of dollars that are wagered by its citizens in out-of-state gaming parlors.  The problem is that other states reap the windfall and Pennsylvania gets zero benefit.  This leakage, based on the income statistics from states that have authorized riverboat gambling, is enourmous.  These are reasons that legalized gaming, and expecially riverboat gaming, must be considered as good public policy.

headline: Federal probe of Preate reopened
abstract: The U.S. Attorney's Office in Harrisburg reopened the investigation of campaign contributions to PA state Attorney General Ernie Preate. He is accused of accepting campaign contributions from operators of illegal video-poker machines and protecting them from prosecution.  He claims the allegations are a political attack by the Pennsylvania Crime Commission.

headline: It's a two-way street
abstract: The residents of Allequippa Terrace say that good design not only underlies a better quality-of-life environment, but it good design requires a committed client- in this case, the Housing Authority of the City of Pittsburgh.

headline: Start reform with Larsen's exit
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen has lost all credibility as a fair, temperate and competent jurist.  The only legitimate service that he could now perform for the troubled high court is to resign, so that the long overdue business of judicial reform can get under way.

headline: Quilt events
abstract: Lebanon Valley College will hold a series of itemized events as part of the Names Project AIDS Memorial Quilt display, including k-12 AIDS education, a film "Long Time Companion", a candlelight vigil, and a play, "Party of Two."

headline: End run seen on health-care law
abstract: As Pennsylvania tries to keep down health-care costs by limiting expensive new technologies, some legislators have attempted to use their power to bypass state regulators.

headline: PGW strike (lockout?) casting pall on her wedding
abstract: As of yet, no solution to end the Philadelphia Gas Works lockout.  This means the union workers are on the street picketing to get back to work, because their company illegally enforced a contract not approved by union officials.  One daughter of a worker is getting married at the end of the month, and the lockout has been a little more than inconvenient for her family.

headline: Dirty water: State firms 2nd in U.S.
abstract: Pennsylvania is second only to Texas in the number of water-polluting businesses.  The U.S. Public Interest Research Group reported that eighty-six PA companies violated Environmental Protection Agency laws.  The report attacked the national system for monitoring discharges into lakes, streams, and rivers, saying that federal licenses do little to protect the environment.

headline: Another product of terror outside an abortion clinc
abstract: Dr. David Gunn was murdered by Michael Griffin, dressed in his Sunday best, at an aboration clinic.  Few seemed surprised about the assassination after the rising tention between clinics and the pro-life zealots.

headline: Trial to start in death of Norristown officer slain on domestic call
abstract: The jury is being picked for the trial of a Norristown man accussed of shooting a police officer.  He admited under oath that he shot the police officer, but claims that he didn't know it was the officer and believed it was the son of his longtime girlfriend.  His court appointed attorny asked the jury not be allowed to hear the confession because it was taken illegally.

headline: The game in the stands
abstract: The Philadelphia Convention and Business Bureau has targeted black business in an effort to boost the $2.7 million the Penn Relays bring the regional economy. The event has become a rite of passage for African Americans, some of whom even witnessed Jesse Owens compete here before the Berlin Olympics. The Relays, while a multicultural event, bring out many black sororities and fraternities in their finest, helping to make Philadelphia the number one tourist destination for African Americans.

headline: 'Federalist Papers' and Mezvinsky
abstract: Representative Marjorie Mezvinsky's vote on the Clinton tax package prompted a re-read of the Founding Fathers' description of her job, described in "The Federalist Papers" by Hamilton, Madison and Jay in 1787.  If Mezvinsky wants to "pooh-pooh" the Founding Fathers, maybe we have to "pooh-pooh" Mezvinsky, or the rest of the House of Representatives.

headline: Judge asks delay in new lottery ban
abstract: A federal judge, Sylvia Rambo, asked if Pennsylvania's new law banning the sale of receipts for out-of-state lottery tickets can be delayed four days to give the court time to decide whether the law is constitutional.

headline: State ads misleading
abstract: It is intriguing that Pennsylvania is engaged in a high-profile attempt to woo new business to the state by touting what is supposedly a favorable economic climate here.  Advertisements have been appearing on television an din the print media which would lead one to believe that everything is coming up roses; nothing could be further from the truth.

headline: Rendell prviews Hanks film
abstract: While city officials were finishing up the operation to clear the homeless encampment from Centere City subway concourses Saturday night, Mayor Rendell was sleeping in the White House.  Rendell had been invited to Washington by President Clinton for a special screening of the movie "Philadelphia," which stars Tom Hanks.

headline: Erie hospitals consider forming HMO
abstract: Two hospitals in Erie have proposed forming their own health maintenance organization called the Alliance Health Network, which would be the only HMO in the area since 1989. They are awaiting approval from the PA Health Department.

headline: PGW union says it will strike if company imposes contract
abstract: The union that represents most of the Philadelphia Gas Works says it will strike if the company follows through on a contract that would cut starting pay and impose higher individual costs for health insurance.

headline: East Penn Twp. blocks plans for plant to treat contaminated soil
abstract: The plans of two Tamaqua-area businessmen to construct a contaminated-soil treatment plant in East Penn Twp. In Carbon County were dealt another setback when township supervisors on Tuesday refused to extend a lapsed building permit for the plant.

headline: Anti-Drug Law Puts Landlords on the Spot
abstract: A new city ordinance in Fort Wayne, Indiana, can prosecute and find landlords who knowingly allow drug activities by tenants to continue without eviction. Under the ordinance, the landlord is notified of each of three steps of investigations concerning suspects, with 30 days to take action against tenants before being fined as much as $2500 a day. Mayor Paul Helmke hopes the ordinance will enhance the city's approach to battling drugs, now focused on drug dealers.

headline: Troopers cracking down on sex activity at Moraine
abstract: State Police are cracking down on sexual activity in Moraine State Park after receiving complaints about homosexual activity in the park from rangers and employees. Park Manager Larry Adams made it clear that homosexuals are not being targeted because of sexual orientation. Sergeant Al Brown says police will continue visits to the park after having made four arrests on their past visit.

headline: The RTC is accused of fraud and mismanagement
abstract: Congress thought the $500 billion savings and loan scandal was a disaster for taxpayers, but yesterday senators heard more than a few horror stories about the Resolution Trust Corp., the agency created to clean up the mess.  Senate witnesses said losses might toal millions.  The attorney general will be asked to investigate.

headline: Fees weighed for some using public defender
abstract: Some low-income criminal defendants in Dauphin County would pay $25 to $50 for a public defender's aid under a plan offered by Chief Public Defender Scott Evans.  Evans' plan would seem to coincide with a proposal Lycoming County commissioners are considering.

headline: It's time for Senate to get back to work
abstract: Summer's over, and it's time for the Pennsylvania Senate to get back to work.  There's a lot to do, and little to justify staying in recess until Thanksgiving as acting Governor Mark Singel and the other Democrats clearly intend to do.  A five-month summer break is much too long, and the Senate GOP is correct in calling on their Democratic colleagues to cut it short.

headline: State approach to offering economic development help needs overhaul
abstract: In the last 15 years, Pennsylvania has lost 1.5 million manufactuing jobs, facing a growth rate of only around 8 percent, while the nation grew by 30 percent.  Due to this, Pennsylvania has had the worst manufacturing record among states in the Northeast and Midwest.  Meanwhile, this dismal performance has, for the most part, been downplayed.  We have to set government policies in motion that make it desirable to live off our economic capital and allow for centralized control of an ever-shrinking capital pool.

headline: Saying It With Flowers
abstract: In an effort to get the New York Assembly to pass the budget on time so that his wife Sandra Galef would be home to celebrate their 30th wedding anniversary, freshman Democrat from Westchester Steven Galef sent a red rose and a note to all 149 of her colleagues, urging them to pass the budget on time. However both Galefs were disappointed as it was passed five days late, and Mrs. Galef was not at home to celebrate.

headline: Experts call Harvard plan wave of future
abstract: In a renovated 19th- century Army barracks, in the working class neighborhood of Watertown, the Harvard Community Health Plan (HCHP) has assembled a complete staff of family doctors, gynecologists, pediatricians, surgeons and specialists of every description. The nonprofit HCHP, a type of Harvard Plan, is its own health insurance company, and the Harvard Plan is considered one of the country's best HMOs.

headline: Pickers' work is fast, filthy, and grueling
abstract: 142 of Kaolin Farms' Mexican mushroom workers have been on strike seeking recognition of a union. Time is money for these workers, who complain that recent stipulations by Kaolin have slowed worker production capacity. Workers live in crowded, often dangerous areas with little extra money and only the barest essentials.

headline: East Rochester homes to connect to sewer system
abstract: Within the next year, nearly 50 households in East Rochester will be forking over money to be attached to the borough's sewer system.  Residents will pay $500 each to be connected to the new lines, which are mandated by the state Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Anti-graffiti group lashes back as Saidel releases critical audit
abstract: The Philadelphia city controller's office issues its official audit of the Philadelphia Anti-Graffiti Network, accusing the agency of misuse of city funds and poor record-keeping.  Timothy D. Spencer, the network's executive director said in an interview that he disagreed with the report and accused Controller Jonathan A. Sadel and his auditors of exaggerating and having their own agenda.

headline: Troopers' new barracks
abstract: Public tours are available of the new state police barracks serving the Belle Vernon area. The barracks will hold 46 troopers.

headline: Towns discover risk in gambling-The riverboat sails away.
abstract: In the town of Deadwood, South Dakota, hopes to raise revenue to pay for municipal programs are tied to the gambling business, but also means an increase in crime and social ills. Competition continues to grow between cities on the Mississippi River for riverboat gambling contracts. Cities are worried about losing tax revenue that is a vital part of the their budget from casinos and tourism.

headline: Firm may sell out-of-state lottery tickets in Pa.
abstract: A federal judge struck down yesterday a Pennsylvania law that bans residnets from playing out-of-state lotteries through outlets in the Commonwealth.  In a precedent-setting decision, US District Judge Sylvia H. Rambo said the law restrained interstate commerce in violation of the US Constitution.

headline: Jeannette puts $600,000 on hold
abstract: Jeannette officials were to accept a $600,000 loan repayment from New York investor Abraham Zion today, but the transfer apprently is on hold.  State Senator Eugene Porterfield, who is holding the $600,000 check, said an attorney for the city has advised council not to accept the money for now.

headline: State Association honors Jim Green
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Association of County Commissioners named County Commissioner Chairman Jim Green "Member of the Year".

headline: Senators' buyer sought a team for N.Y.
abstract: The prospective buyer of the Harrisburg Senators is a sports entrepreneur whofailed last year to lure a minor league baseball team to Long Island, N.Y.  Van Farber has a tentaive agreement to buy Harrisburg's Class AA Eastern League franchise for $3 million from Jerome Mileur, who moved the team to Harrisburg from Nashua, N.H., before the 1987 season.

headline: Experts doub mammogram benefit for women under 50
abstract: A new study finds that women under the age of 50 that are getting mamogram testing are not any more likely than woman that wait until age 50 to start maogram testing to prevent the cancer.  This is being highly debated against other testing results of the United State, Canada, and Sweden.

headline: Plum workers should take time to cool off
abstract: Plum wokers including garbage workers, road crews, and mechanics, should go back to work instead of remaining on strike for the public's safety and health.  The stikes occurred because the borough is thinking of going to an outside garbage collector and didn't renew the contracts with the garbage collectors.

headline: Environmental doomsayers proven wrong
abstract: The scare of global warming is almost entirely perpetrated by nerds who never go outdoors, but ruin their eyes staring at green numbers on a black screen.  Environmetalists convinced the nation to endorse costly policies designed to reduce greenhouse emissions.  Gradually, data supporting the optimists mounted.  The feedback is good news, meaning the Earth is stronger than many realized, and catastrophe is not around the corner.

headline: Area killer's date with death scheduled
abstract: Frederic J. Jermyn, the Mechanicsburg man convicted of first degree murder in the death of his mother in August 1985, is scheduled to be executed in a month.  The Department of Corrections has set the execution for 10 pm December 7 at the State Correctional Institution at Rockview in Centre County.

headline: Turn crime commission's cases over to state police, local lawmaker urges
abstract: Accusations of Attorney General Ernest Preate Jr. (a candidate for governor) have caused many to want to get rid of the PA Crime Commission. Rep. Mike Veon wants the sentence to be carried out even though the House Appropriations Committee has tried to stop it and there is still $1.2 million in the 1993-1994 budget allotted to it. Sponsored by Judiciary Committee Chairman Thomas Caltagrione, the bill calls for commission to report quarterly activates to the PA House and Senate judiciary committees.

headline: Video-rental giant branches out
abstract: Blockbuster is branching out, saying with its vast distribution network, that it only makes sense to own some of the rights that go with its videos. Blockbuster's expansion is vertical-branching into the entertainment business and building video stores abroad. Recently, plans have been announced to partner with Virgin Atlantic Airways in construction of music outlets.

headline: 'First couple' a fact of life
abstract: When the two presidnts visited Ambridge last Wednesday, they were referred to by several radio and television reporters as "the first couple."  That clearly implies that Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton share the duiteis of the president of the United States.  When was the last time you ever heard any American president and his wife being referred to as "the first couple?"  Never.

headline: John Street Introducing Ed Rendell
abstract: Accompanying an article is a photograph of lead of City Council John Street, introducing Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell at his inauguration in 1991. Rendell had backed Street's primary foe and withheld support as Street pushed to head the Council. Once both were in office, the two quickly reached an accord.

headline: State certification in justice races overblown
abstract: State certification which is a big issues in the District Justice race is being blown way out of proportion. A district justice who isn't an attorney must take a four-week course offered by the state and pass a two part exam before taking office. Voters take these tests to be worth more than they really are, they should look at the candidate with the best experience.

headline: The Scene In Philadelphia and Its Suburbs: The sad state of an NFL holy war
abstract: The author makes fun of the fact that there is a hatred in Texas of Philadelphia and their sports teams.

headline: Filling a need on Hill-Old hospital renovated for elderly
abstract: The Pittsburgh area Urban Redevelopment Authority, along with several non-profit organizations including the Hill House Association and the Allegheny Union Baptist Association, is using funds from the Allegheny Department of Health and Human Services to renovate an abandoned hospital into homes for elderly and families to encourage interaction. The PA General Services Administration is also providing funding for the project.

headline: PNI unions set strike date
abstract: The Council of Newspaper Unions has voted unanimously to strike the Daily News and Inquirer at noon Monday unless a contract settlemtn is reached before then with Philadelphia Newspapers Inc., which publishes both newspapers.

headline: EPA list gives broader view of wastes
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency included for the first time chemical waste disposal information. Previous reports to the EPA included pollutants released into the environment but not wastes shipped to other places for treatment, recycling or disposal. Delaware gets more toxic chemical wastes than any other state; more than 7000 tons of waste are shipped from other states to Delaware each year.

headline: Assault seen as mischief gone awry
abstract: In the Northern Home for Children, which is a home that takes in abused and neglected children, six 13 year old boys sexually assaulted three others. The director of the home says it’s a prank that has gone wrong and is not a usual act. The six alleged perpetrators were charged with involuntary deviate sexual intercourse and aggravated indecent assault.

headline: U.S.-born baker's citizenship on trial
abstract: Nikolaus Schiffer was on the stand today in a trial that is set to determain his status in the United States.  Schiffer, 73, was a SS guard in a concentration camp during WWII and lied about it to regain entry to the United States.

headline: Wagers on water
abstract: Pennsylvanians are no strangers to gambling, yet some have an emotional breakdown when they hear of legislative proposals for riverboat casinos.  As if floating game halls would cost the state its gambling virginity.

headline: First lady's health pitch is hit on Hill
abstract: Hillary Rodham Clinton yesterday opened the white House drive for health care reform on Capitol Hill, telling Congress that she knew first-hand about the flaws in America's medical system as a mother, wife and citizen.  Mrs. Clinton, only the third first lady ever to testify at congressional hearings, laid out broad principles for reform before standing-room-only audiences at two House committees.

headline: Judge a report by its cover
abstract: Sid Cato, an annual reports consultant itemizes a list of what to look for in a good annual report, including total honesty by the company, an engaging cover, use of the first person singular, readability and clarity, and attractive graphics and pictures.

headline: State Democrats gather for patry's day in sun
abstract: Pennsylvania Democrats including Wofford and Casey, attended the inauguation of President Clinton in Washington.

headline: U.S. Catholics often at odds with the pope
abstract: The Pope is visiting the United States for World Youth Day events in Denver.  The article discusses the fact that American Catholics have a greater tendency than others to disagree with the Catholic Church on certain issues. The Pope has previously criticized American Catholics for altering the religion to fit their own conscience or beliefs.

headline: Final act of love
abstract: A gravely ill father who left his bed to attend his son's season final football game at Carnegie Mellon died hours after returning home, his son, Jarrod Siket, said yesterday.

headline: Pony Express drivers walk off job
abstract: Delivery drivers for Pony Express struck the company's depots in various locations as part of a nationwide campaign by the Teamsters union to negotiate a first contract. The strike effected Pittsburgh businesses: Mellon and PNC banks. The strike is about low wages and minimal to no benefits received.

headline: EPA proposing alterations to Safe Drinking Water Act
abstract: The Clinton administration yesterday proposed changes in the Safe Drinking Water Act aimed at improving the nation's drinking water supply while helping small water companies comply with government standards.  If Congress accepts the administration's proposals, Americans could end up paying an additional fee on their water bills to help finance clean water programs.

headline: At this boys' home, discipline's key
abstract: Ex-Steeler, Mel Blount, started a home for troubled inner-city youths. The boys who live there must rise early, do farm work, go to school and study, and go to bed early.
