He also frequently uses corporal punishment for those who misbehave, which has resulted in Children and Youth Services of Allegheny County pulling out some of the children under charges of child abuse, and a family court judge ruled he would not be allowed to see them. Blount was forced to make his home a private rather than public facility.

headline: Unify crime fight
abstract: Vice President Al Gore will reveal a proposal to create a federal "Directorate of Central Law Enforcement" that will unite several different law-enforcement agencies.  The editorial board believes this to be a good idea because it will make the government more efficient in fighting crime, but objects to the name of the program, which it feels invokes images of a "Big Brother" police state.

headline: Weirton delays steel can plan
abstract: Plans to launch a new lightweight, recyclable steel can by Weirton Steel Corporation in conjunction with overseas companies have been pushed back to the second half of the year after early estimates that the can would have been on the market earlier in the year.

headline: First Wofford challenger steps forward
abstract: Gettysburg businessman Robert Monahan Jr. on Wednesday filed federal documents in Washington declaring himself a candidate in the 1994 Pennsylvania senatorial election. He is the first Republican to step forward to seek the seat held by incumbent Democrat Harris Wofford. PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer and U.S. Rep. Rick Santorum are also considering getting in the race.

headline: Judge races
abstract: Pennsylvania voters will elect one judge each for the state's Supreme, Superior and Commonwealth courts.

headline: State Employee-Protection Laws
abstract: Many states have passed laws protecting employees participating in legal activities off the job (including "high risk" recreation activities such as mountain climbing and sky diving). Michigan is the only state to have passed a law against employee weight discrimination. Other states have passed laws protecting smokers and the right to engage in legal activities, including Minnesota, Wisconsin, Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Wyoming, Main, Connecticut, New Jersey, North Carolina, Kentucky, Indiana, Illinois, North and South Dakota, Louisiana, and several others shown on a map.

headline: First lady decries health insurers
abstract: Hillary Rodham Clinton yesterday accused the health insurance industry of greed that has driven the nation "to the brink of bankruptcy," and of lying to the public about the president's plan to protect its profits.  The first lady denounced television advertisements run by the Health Insurance Association of America against the administration's health care plan.  She said that its message that the plan "limits choice," a theme of one of the industry's advertisements, was false.

headline: PPG Springdale pact angers Creighton workers
abstract: PPG industries has signed a contract with 175 workers at its Coatings and Resins plant, further angering picketing glassworkers at the Creighton site.  Under the terms of the new contract, member of Local 112, representing workers at the Springdale plant, wil receive a $1.05 pay increase over a three-year period.  The agreement was ratified October 30 by the union.

headline: EPA sets standards for controlling radon
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency set standards controlling the amount of radon in homes, an odorless, colorless, naturally occurring gas that is the second leading cause of lung cancer. The EPA urged homeowners to ask for radon test results and for sellers to reduce the level of radon. Radon resistant features suggested by the EPA could save 200 lives over the next five years.

headline: Attorney general's office seeks to keep transcript from Larsen
abstract: The PA State Attorney General decided that Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen has no legal right to a transcript of his grand jury testimony about allegations of criminal misconduct on the court. Larsen has asked for these to help him in the possible impeachment hearings by the House Judiciary Committee.

headline: Volunteer firefighters to receive benefits
abstract: More than $677,000 will be distributed to municipalities throughout Washington County for the benefit of volunteer firefighters in each community.  Auditor General Barbara Hager said that 65 of 67 municipalities in the county will receive allocations totaling $677,241.

headline: What about the victims?
abstract: Another murder has occurred in Florida to a tourist, yet television stations only seem to care about the impact on the Florida tourist industry, rather than focusing on the victim.

headline: Floor rules tie up House
abstract: The first day of discussion on the floor of the house since the election is new procedure including two important issues: a 24 hour notice before they vote on bills and expenses that will be paid for the reps for travel expenses and car leases.

headline: Judge strikes down prevailing-wage law
abstract: U.S. District Court Judge Edwin M. Kosik struck down a Pennsylvania law requiring contractors on state-financed public works to pay their workers the prevailing wages for the locality in which the project is built.  The PA Department of Labor and Industry plans to appeal the decision.

headline: State House rules rebellion long overdue
abstract: The adoption of rules governing the day-to-day floor agenda is well overdue.  The majority party is resistant to any change because it will limit their power to control the agenda completely, but this is needed, no matter who is in power.  It will effect how long representatives have to look at bills before they vote as well as limit the amount of closed door talks by senior leaders.

headline: First lady turns focus back to health care
abstract: First Lady Hillary Clinton took a brief leave of absence from her vigil by her father Hugh Rodham's side, whom sources say remains in critical condition, to give a speech at the University of Texas on health-care reform. President Clinton has also visited his father-in-law. Rodham's condition has delayed the release of Hillary's health care reform proposal and will continue to do so unless his condition improves.

headline: Proposed contract
abstract: Included is what Sylvan Foods and Moonlight Mushrooms Inc. are asking from union workers in their contract proposal.

headline: EPA sued to enforce water law in Penna.
abstract: The Raymond Profit Foundation, a Bucks County environmental group, is filing a federal suit against the US Department of Environmental Protection for not forcing the PA Department of Environmental Resources to have stronger standards to protect waterways.

headline: Bail allowed for two in Roofers killing
abstract: Nine years after being condemned to life in prison for ordering the gangland murder of Philadelphia Roofers Union boss John McCullough, reputed mob figures Raymond 'Long John' Martorano and Albert Daidone may be coming home.  A judge ruled they needed a new trial because of misconducts during their first trial and set bail at $2 and $1.5 million respectively, which is low compared to the $20 million bail the prosecutor wanted.

headline: Waiting for justice
abstract: Just as the characters in the play "Waiting for Godot," so too, the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina wait for help which perhaps will never come.  Even though television provides us with vivid documentations of the brutal mutilation of children and the unmerciful suffering of defenseless men and women, our world leaders do not act.  Shame on them for holding out hope that help may be on the way and then condemning these suffering people to wait.

headline: What are best methods to preserve, promote?
abstract: Americans have convinced themselves of the moral and career value of such frivolity- if they manage to squeeze in a little business.  That's good news for Bucks County, whose tourist commission expects spillover business from the new Philadelphia Convention Center.

headline: Larsen mum on Zappala till Oct. vote
abstract: Larsen accussed Zappala of 'gross misconduct' only after Zappala and Cappy voted in October to reprimand Larsen more misconduct.  Larsen has be subpoenaed to appear before a statewide grand jury next month to answer questions.

headline: Judging from campaign- change needed
abstract: After the last week of campaigning, we're even more convinced Pennsylvania needs merit selection of statewide judges.  Talk about voter confusion.  And negative, soundbite campaigns.  They certainly weren't the kind of campaigns worthy of state's highest judges.

headline: State justices cling to cloaked expenses
abstract: Seven years ago, state Senator Richard A. Tilghman gave a whole new meaning to "Remember the Alamo."  During an acrimonious hearing over the issue of how the Supreme Court's seven justices refused to itemize their expense accounts, the Montgomery County Republican said: "I see seven people defending the Alamo."  State Senator Vincent Fumo, a fellow member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, scolded Tilghman for the remark, disagreeing with the comparison of the jurists to the heroic defenders of the Alamo.

headline: For Consumers, System Would Offer a Menu of Choices
abstract: For all the mind-blurring, quasi-technical talk swirling around President Clinton's health care proposal, from the consumer's point of view it would create a surprisingly simple world.  Several features include the use of one plastic identification card, one medical claims form and one set of minimum benefits for everyone.

headline: Rate cut only start of insurance reforms
abstract: An order to cut workers' compensation rates by up to 6.7 percent represents just the first step in controlling costs to guard against claims for on-the-job injuries, state officials said yesterday.  Businesses, for instance, could get an additional one-time rate reduction of 5 percent by establishing a committee to evaluate safety  in the workplace, said Labor and Industry Secretary Tom Foley.

headline: Ex-plant manager charged
abstract: Former Keystone Cement Co. plant manager James Longenbach has been charged with tampering with records and two counts of unlawfully using a computer to avoid environmental regulations at the facility.

headline: Barb:
abstract: To those paranoid legislators and other officials in Harrisburg who kept calling in the state police to conduct security sweeps of their offices- to uncover listening devices that never were there- and a laurel to state Attorney General Ernie Preate for moving to end the security sweeps; it has cost taxpayers too much money and has tied up state troopers whose services could have been better used elsewhere.

headline: 'Wake up,' teen-ager tells mayor of Phila.
abstract: After a schoolmate was shot to death, a 16-year-old Norht Philadelphia boy wrote a letter with a strongly worded invitation for Mayor Ed Rendell to visit his neighborhood.  Jerron Faison wrote, "Wake up Rendell, instead of talking about Reading Terminal Market and Wednesday nights in Center City, take a drive through my neighborhood and see if your conscience lets you sleep at night."  Faison's letter was published in a Philadelphia Daily News supplement about children and violence.

headline: What's the Communications World Coming To?
abstract: An advertisement by Greyhound Financial Corporation attempts to convince customers that they will find reliable communications financing with the company, which has an experienced staff of responsive professionals to accommodate acquisition and recapitalization financing.

headline: Larsen's defense pulls no punches
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court is having its share of trouble as Rolf Larsen tries to clear himself of misconduct charges.  His best defense seems to be a good offense as he has accused the other justices of wrongdoing as well including Fumo and his passenger Justice Stephen Zappala trying to run him down.

headline: Judicial races top ballot in PA today
abstract: Pennsylvania voters go to the polls today to elect a new justice to the troubled state Supreme Court and to decide whether another justice who is already on the court should be allowed to stay for a second 10-year term, even though he could only serve for one year.

headline: State lawmakers live inside a fantasy world
abstract: Imagine a worker that has been unproductive in the last four months, gets $47,000 a year plus $110 a day to show up to work, a company car and is complaining they need a raise.  Pennsylvanian legislatures are ripping off the taxpayers because they are doing just that.

headline: For Low-Income Families, Health Care Costs Have Twice the Bite
abstract: A study by the Economic Policy Institute referencing the National Medical Care Expenditure Survey by the Agency for Health Care Policy and Research of the Department of Health and Human Services revealed low-income families pay 20.5 percent of their income on average for health care expenditures, twice as much as high-income families, with more out of pocket payments, and higher spending on premiums. However, low-income families paid the least taxes applied to health expenditures.

headline: Regional wages below state average
abstract: Some workers in Central Pennsylvania earn less than those who do the same job in other parts of the state, according to a report issued by the state Department of Labor and Industry.  "In all but 14 of the surveyed occupations, statewide average annual salaries wee considerably higher than regional," the report states.

headline: F-16s may soon buzz state parks, forests
abstract: Air National Guard fighter pilots could begin-low level combat training over Pennsylvania wilderness areas if the Federal Aviation Administration approves.  Secretary of the PA Department of Environmental Resources is fighting the proposal on the grounds that it will harm local wildlife and be disruptive to residents of the area, but the Air  National Guard's plan has already been approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

headline: Beaver jail controversy takes center court
abstract: 12 members of Beaver filed suit to stop a 21.5 million dollar jail being contructed, claiming the commmissioners are eroding the town's taxbase by buuying three properties needed to accommodate the jail.

headline: Warden tells panel larger staff needed
abstract: Warden George A. Wagner alerted the Berks County Prison Board on Wednesday that he has insufficient staff to comply with court orders and treatment for inmates jailed for failing to pay child support, and he appeals for $1.3 million in additional funds to boost his staff.

headline: When going got tough, the tough got going
abstract: The storm showed the resolve of some of the cities workers in both the public and private sector.  In the baby ward of the hospital some workers pulled 40hrs over the weekend.  Tollboth workers had to stick it out as well as nurses at a retirement home and countless  jobs across the state.

headline: Lawmaker wants to curb legal fees
abstract: Carlisle freshman state Rep. Albert H. Masland will introduce two bills tomorrow aimed squarely at the wallets of his colleagues in the legal profession.  They will both aim at reducing the amount of money lawyers can make from insurance and injury claims so that in theory the malpractice rates as well as the price the insurors must pay will go down.  That should have a direct effect on the cost of primiums, but he doubts the bills will pass.

headline: Judicial reform stalled
abstract: Robert B. Surrick, the Patriot Party's candidate for the PA Supreme Court, writes that praises the Patriot's articles about there not being much difference between candidates for the Supreme Court race.  He says that 5 candidates are from Allegheny County and 2 from Philadelphia County, and the other 65 counties are shut out.  Surrick has testified twice before the PA House and Senate Judiciary Committees about reforms that will end the corruption and arrogance of the PA judiciary.

headline: State Legislature: Lawmakers don't deserve pay hikes
abstract: The editorial board writes that PA state lawmakers shouldn't entertain any thoughts of boosting their own pay, instead they should concentrate on the business of the state. They write that since the Legislature's return in January they have done little and focused on light issues instead of welfare reform, workers' compensation reform, and education reform.

headline: Fraud epidemic costs Medicare millions
abstract: Two columnists discuss a study by the General Accounting Office that discovered that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is common and extremely costly.  The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has also failed to create a team to combat this fraud, which allows it to continue.  Even when cases against fraud are pursued, it will often take years to settle, the punishments are mild, and the health agency doesn't regain all the money stolen from it.

headline: Season-all may close local plant
abstract: In order to cut its loses in the manufacture of commercial windows, Season-all Industries, Inc. is studying what the company calls the possibility of dropping that product line and concentrating just on the residential window market; this move could close the Indiana plant. This could effect the jobs of more than 530 local hourly and salaried employees with an estimated payroll between $8 and $10 million.

headline: Falls awaits ruling today on question
abstract: The Township of Falls and Falls Solicitor Michael Sellers must try to convince a Bucks County President Judge Kenneth G. Biehn to allow a ballot question asking voters whether or not they support Waste Management Inc.'s proposed 153-acre landfill expansion after they had sued the county Board of Elections challenging the legality of the voter poll..  Judge Biehn says he believes the question is illegal because it amounts to a non-binding referendum improperly authorized buy the Bucks County Commissioners.

headline: Behind the settlement in deaths of 4 foster children
abstract: The city of Philadelphia settled out of court for $1.6 million dollars to the mothers and family of children killed in a fire in 1989.  The fire was started by Lakeya, a 14 year old sibling of one of the victims, who is serving an eight-year sentence for murder and arson.  Some Philadelphia taxpayers feel that the city gave in too easily and is writing too many checks instead of finding out where the problem lies.

headline: Was Judge Richette injudicious or was she just b eing Richette?
abstract: Judge Richette had lunch with a defense lawyer, and long time friend, during the week they were to be in a trial together.  Some would quesiton this, but I believe that is just Richette's way of acting.  She doesn't think of how things look and doesn't care.  That is one reason she's one of Philly's best known judges.

headline: Whitman sale Okd by judge
abstract: Whitman's Chocolates will close its Northeast Philadelphia plant after U.S. District Judge Donald W. Van Artsdalen refused to halt the sale of the company to a rival candy-maker despite arguments made by the PA Attorney General's Office.  The new owners are an affiliate of Russell Stover Inc. will move the factory to the Midwest and will cause the lost of 700 jobs in the area.

headline: Lawmakers not serious about reforming taxes
abstract: We have serious doubts about the sincerity of state lawmakers initiating any kind of tax reform legislation- either in this session or the next.  Recent history on this issue doesn't lend itself to optimism.  Past history of tax reform initiatives indicates that lawmakers are gun-shy about undertaking anything this comprehensive and controversial.

headline: Just A Start
abstract: The editorial board says that President Clinton convincing Congress to pass his deficit-reducing bill was only the beginning of his duties.  They say he will have to convince Americans to support it as well, so that he will be elected a second-term and be able to carry out his plan.

headline: State Senate's strange days
abstract: A special election to fill a vacant Senate seat resulted with a win by Republican David Heckler, making 25 Republicans and 24 Democrats in the Senate.  However, the Dems continue to control the Senate because Heckler has not yet been sworn in.  Then after their recess, another special election will take place in which a Democrat is favored to win.  Dems oppose Heckler taking seat, so Heckler may have to wait four months to take his seat.

headline: Generic drug bonanza
abstract: The experation of the pattants for expensive prescription drugs is making a huge market out of generic brands and saving the individual money.  Over the next year a number of important perscription drugs will become generic leaving a scamble for the stocks of generic compies, some rising %50 in anticipation.

headline: Sole proprietor cries out for workers' comp controls
abstract: A passionate letter to the editor that complains about the new workers compensation laws.  This small business owner stats that due to the new random increases she can no longer afford to pay her employees .75 an hour over the minimum wage.  She feels that the legislature should look out for the people, even those that don't have the time or money to have lobbyists.

headline: Falls Twp. Residents to vote in May on landfill expansion
abstract: Falls Township supervisors are hoping to gain guidance from residents on the proposed re-zoning for landfill use by including the question on the Falls Municipal primary ballot. The proposal, submitted by Waste Management Inc. was already submitted to the PA Department of Environmental resources and the township. Despite the vote, the referendum is non-binding on the commissioners' final decision.

headline: Beware Rules Abuse
abstract: New rules on reporting child abuse adopted by the state House could prove to be a mixed blessing for children and the child welfare and justice systems in Pennsylvania.  The bill, sponsored by Representative Kevin Blaum, a Wilkes-Barre Democrat, passed unanimously by the House, now moves on to the Senate for consideration.

headline: We've become prisoners of our violent society
abstract: What used to be irrational has become an everday experience.  With terrible regularity, peole do get shot from passing cars.  It is sad and shameful to live in a time when life has so little value, when people are killed for jackets or shoes, for wearing the wrong colors, or standing on the wrong corner.

headline: Winding Down
abstract: The information is an itemized list of pharmaceutical drugs which have been transferred to other drug production sites of SmithKline Beecham, drugs for which production rights have been sold, and drugs which must still be moved from the firm before it can close.

headline: Lawmakers plan bipartisan assault on the old order
abstract: As it stands right now the leaders of the legislature have closed room discussions then expect a vote on bills within 20 minutes.  Rank-and-file state lawmakers are taking a stand and belive they should be allowed appropriate time, 24 hours, to read bills before they vote on them.

headline: Justice's role not advocacy, Ginsburg says
abstract: Greeted cordially by the lawmakers who will judge her nomination, Supreme Court nominee Ruth Bader Ginsburg pledged yesterday that while she rose "on the shoulders" of women's rights pioneers, advocacy is not her vision of a justice's role.

headline: State shenanigans embarrassing
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark Singel sounds like a petulant child who has just lost the classroom presidency.  I am angry that as a taxpayer I'm going to have to pay for special elections for Bucks County because my lieutenant governor is playing politics.

headline: Giving Addicts Clean Needles Cuts Spread of AIDS, US Study Finds
abstract: The Federal Government's first comprehensive study of whether giving clean needles to addicts can help prevent the spread of AIDS has concluded that it does, and that the Government should finance a significant expansion of such programs.

headline: State ranks 5th in death on the job
abstract: Pennsylvania ranked fifth in the nation in the number of workplace deaths during the 1980s, according to the first federal study to pinpoint workplace fatalities by state.  The study, to be released today by the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health, examines the worker death toll in each of the 50 states.  NIOSH wants state governments to find ways to prevent the biggest killers of their workers.

headline: Female hunters take to the forest
abstract: In PA more of the million hunters are starting to be women. The PA Game Commission does not have a separate list of female license buyers and male license buyers, but nationally the increased amount of female hunters is seen.

headline: Biden's bad bill
abstract: This week the US Senate is scheduled to debate whether it sould impose stringent restrictions on a constitutional right of ancient origin- the right to petition for writ of habeas corpus. Senator Joseph Biden of Delaware has introduced a "habeas reform" measure that supposedly addresses both the public's concern and some of the more egregious effects of the Supreme Court's rulings, while simultaneously providing adequate counsel for death-row prisoners.  Unfortunately, the bill falls far short of these laudable goals.

headline: Wheels of justice grind up reason
abstract: Lee Brown, 22, was charged with drunk driving when she was riding her bicycle down the wrong side of the road and hit a car head on, breaking her arm.  Her case has been going up and down the legal system and the tax payer is who pays for these stupid trials because she is using a public defender and the DA is prosicuting.

headline: With Gambling Expert in Capital, a Casino Rolls
abstract: As a boom in legalized gambling rolls across America, no politician has stepped up to the table with more prescience and gusto than Governor Edwin W. Edwards of Louisiana, a rather fabulous crap-shooter who likes to risk $5,000 a roll in the casino and far more in the state House.

headline: Lawyer and doctor face charges in alleged insurance fraud
abstract: A grand jury contests that Terry Daly, a lawyer, and Dennis B. Zaslow, an osteopath were invovled in a cooperative act of racketeering, fraud, theft, perjury, and records tampering.

headline: Juxtaposing two sides of presidency
abstract: The inauguration of Clintion while bombs go off in Iraq makes for an interesting transition of power in the White House.  Being president has both the glamour of a movie star and the frustration that comes with bombing civilians in Iraq that are both occuring right now as the transition from the Bush to Clintion adminstration occurs.

headline: State should free municipalities to do their job
abstract: A transcript of a testimony presented before the House Appropriations Committee and the Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee on the problems of rural governments, considers the challenges Patton Township has had to face. Phil Park, chairman of the board of township supervisors, believes local governments deserve more credit and freer reign and attention to tax structure reform by both committees. Park also cites loopholes and micro-legislation as obstacles for growing municipalities.

headline: Governor to remain hospitalized
abstract: Governor Casey will have to spend as much as another week in the hospital to clear up what his doctors say is bacteria that entered his bloodstream as a result of a virus.

headline: Strike expected at York-area agencies
abstract: Workers of Children and Youh Services as well as Agency on Ageing are planning to strike as soon as Monday if a better offer isn't received.

headline: Further hearings for WTI?
abstract: The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency is expected to rule on whether a hazardous waste incinerator in East Liverpool, Ohio, can begin limited commercial operation as a contract revision between Von Roll Inc. and Waste Technologies Industries, or whether the decision must undergo further public hearings as a contract modification. The US Environmental Protection Agency approved the plan earlier in the week, the site of which is located 30 miles northwest of Pittsburgh.

headline: Bill Would Honor Cops, Firefighters
abstract: State Representative Gaynor Cawley has introduced legislation which would create a holiday honoring the state's firefighters and police officers.  The legislation, which was referred to the House Committee on State Government after its introduction earlier this month, would make each Aug. 7 a holiday known as "Firefighters' and Police Officers' Memorial Day."

headline: Who is a deadbeat?
abstract: In the "Payday for Deadbeats" editorial, the Post-Gazette failed to mention why these fathers fail to pay their "meager" child support, and failed to mention mothers who fail to pay their fair share.  The fathers are looked down upon in our courts.

headline: Yes to riverboat gambling
abstract: The newspaper advocates legislation that would allow riverboat gambling. The editorial board says it will greatly improve the economy of Pittsburgh and they support legislation authored by State Representative Frank Gigliotti that would allow it.  Governor Robert Casey has consistently opposed such legislation.

headline: Ledgislator pushes to impeach Larsen
abstract: House Representative, Christopher K. McNally (D. Allegheny), has drafted impeachment proceedings against State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen.  House Democratic leaders believe that there should be no impeachment until there is a proper investigation into the charges by the State Attorney General.

headline: Keeping faith amid the Rescue
abstract: In the Operation Rescue protest at the Elizabeth Blackwell Health Center in Center City, it was evident that people of good faith and good conscience can differ.  Right and wrong are not as simple as Operation Rescue believes.  Morality is complicated.

headline: State tax reform must be a priority
abstract: Leaders in the state House of Representatives are playing with the proposal to try to enact serious tax reforms before the end of this year.  Come on friends, stop talking about it and do it.  Schedule action on taking some of the heat off property owners across Pennsylvania, and enacting more fair methods of raising the money required by counties, municipalities and school districts.

headline: Guidelines address HIV-infected health workers
abstract: When a hospital finds out that an employee is infected with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, it should form an expert panel to decide if the person's duties should be restricted and whether patients should be notified, according to guidelines being issued this month by the state Health Department.

headline: Striking miners picket
abstract: Striking coal miners in the United Mine Workers Union are being accused of shooting a non-union subcontractor.  They insist they are innocent.

headline: Inventory: A roster companies rue
abstract: Many companies are putting a lot of money into new production methods, switching to non-toxic chemicals and adding pollution-control devices to escape the roster of chemical emitters. Plants in Saint James and Uncle Sam, La., registered the highest annual percentage of pollution increase of any factory in the USA.

headline: Bill would protect off-job smokers
abstract: A bill promoting smokers' rights went down in flamse sEdnesday in the state House, but it is expected to rise from the ashes next week after an important change.  The legislation would ban the firing of employees simply because they smoke, drink, or take legal drugs off the job.

headline: Who says justice must be slow?
abstract: In a case where two felony charges held against state Representative Richard Olasz, the so-called wheels of justice never moved so fast, and this hasty sequence speaks of pre-arrangement and secrecy.

headline: A Civil War unit from Pa. gets its due
abstract: The clash of armies is the topic of Gettysburg, a four-hour film that premieres Friday.  In the movie, the Irish regiment is brought to life by a group of Philadelphia-area Civil War buffs, grass-roots historians awho are dedicated to giving some overdue credit to those Philadelphians who held the wall.

headline: Ledgislators seek to correct mah in filling fees
abstract: The Act 167 that passed last year raised the filling cost of misdemeanors and felonies by $6 and $12 respectively.  The problem is that the federal government rose what it gets out of those fees to $7 and $13 which leaves the counties to pay the difference of $1 for every filed misdemeanor or felony.  The counties are trying to get that changed and it looks like legislation may pass.

headline: Kudos for the scoop on the high court
abstract: The Post-Gazette should be tahaked for their research and commended for publishing the series on the happenings of the state Supreme Court justices.  The paper has uncovered the flagrant waste and should lead the way with suggestions to the Legislature for controls.

headline: Stately tree lights up
abstract: A picture of Ellen Casey, wife of PA Governor Robert P. Casey, and her granddaughter lighting the state Christmas tree.

headline: Guv looks fit in video
abstract: A little more than five weeks after a double-organ transplant, Governor Casey made his first "public appearance" yesterday, via satellite.  A state-produced video showed Casey looking at photos of a picnic he attended last weekend, doing some exercise and walking in a hospital hallway.  He looked better than expected.

headline: The passing of a way of work: Northeast Phila., a place of good jobs.  Or so they thought.
abstract: Within four years, a tide of plant closings and reductions-in-force eroded the working neighborhoods in Northeast Philadelphia leading to change economic conditions from industrial to service and increases in crime.  Companies closing and laying-off include Empty Glass, Canada Dry, Mrs. Paul's Kitchens, Naval Aviation Supply Office and Sears. Article includes map showing the neighborhoods affected by the closings.

headline: Greene advisory committee reviews new solid waste management plan
abstract: The Greene County Solid Waste Advisory Committee reviewed chapters 7 and 10 of the draft of the new solid waste management plan.  According to Shirl Barnhart, vice chairman of the committee, the draft states that municipalities will be required to pass and ordinance requiring the orderly disposal of solid waste.

headline: Bills target lawyer fees, damages
abstract: PA Representative Al Masland has introduced a two-bill package designed to limit lawyers' contingency fees and damages awarded from delays in settling civil cases.  The first bill would establish specific limits that lawyers could charge on a contingent-fee basis for their services and the second is aimed at limiting delay damages in civil actions and proceeding against municipal governments and the state.

headline: Who's on states' death row
abstract: In PA there are 3 females on death row and 165 males. The race make-up on the PA death row is 4 Hispanics, 61 Whites, 101 Blacks, and 2 Asians.

headline: "Hello, David"
abstract: A poem is given about a nurse in the Vietnam War who meets and takes care of an injured soldier.  The poem is taken from "Visions of War, Dreams of Peace," a collection of writings from nurses who served in Vietnam.

headline: Legislators fill hiatus working out agendas
abstract: The Senate is not due back in session until Monday, Nov. 22, so there is no formalized agenda as to how much floor work is scheduled for the remainder of the year.  Note, however, that the following Monday kicks off deer hunting season in Pennsylvania and that, traditionally, is a short-work week.

headline: Labor gives Singel warm welcome
abstract: Acting PA Governor Mark Singel spoke at a breakfast meeting hosted by Sheet Metal Workers Local 12.  He spoke in front of 82 labor leaders and tried to solicit their support for his campaign for governor.  Labor leaders speak highly of him and will most likely endorse him as a candidate.

headline: States face $2 billion refund
abstract: Officials in Virginia and other states believe they have several legal options to avoid paying nearly $2 billion in tax refunds the US Supreme Court has ruled are owed to federal government.

headline: 3rd year of slow growth under way, reports show
abstract: The US Department of Commerce is reporting modest gains for the fifth advance in six months according to its Index of Leading Economic Indicators. While the gains point to positives; increased demand, a possible increase in the labor force, and rising prices for raw materials, a decline in building permits and consumer confidence are offsetting increased potential growth.

headline: Guvs get green light
abstract: The National Governors' Association met in Washington to discuss health care.  Each state, including Pennslyvania, is working on improving their health care systems.  President Clinton spoke at the meeting to try to push his health reforms.

headline: The state has agenda on workers' compensation carrier
abstract: Jerome Silverstein writes that the controversy concerning PA workers' compensation is part of an agenda whose aim is to remove insurance carriers from the workers' compensation business and that a cost-of-living adjustment should not be used to create a premium.  He calls for reform.

headline: Greene Township holds off on waste recycling facility permit
abstract: The Greene Township Supervisors are waiting for the response of the owner of a waste recycling facility to conditions stipulated before granting him a permit to operate in the township; the township was set to give it to Peter Kipin, the president, before he didn't attend their meeting. Kipin applied for a permit in February to operate a recycling facility that would process 43,000 tons a year at the firm's 41-acre site.

headline: Boot camp gives cons a way out
abstract: The state prison system has created a boot camp in order to solve overcrowding in the state's prisons. Judges can recommend convicts for the camp as an alternative to prison when they are sentenced, and the PA Department of Corrections picks who will go there after psychological and physical screenings. Convicts are not forced to go to the camp, but can elect to. Prisoners of the Quehanna boot camp serve six month sentences rather than a two-to-five year prison sentence. Prisoners of the boot camp are put through exercise and work regimens, and also receive counseling, education, and group therapy.

headline: Will the changing nature of charity change our society?
abstract: Family Services of Western Pennsylvania has been serving this region for more than 100 years.  But the furture threat of the changing nature of community philanthropy is troubling.

headline: A court ruling removes S&L's accounting break
abstract: A federal appeals court reversed a ruling that would have forced the government to pay the nation's sixth largest savings and loan as much as 1.4 billion dollars. The ruling affected Glendale Federal Bank which claimed that the U.S. owed it money.

headline: Legislators returning to uncertainty
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey has been delayed returning to office since he had a heart-liver transplant in June; he told acting PA Governor Mark Singel he would return before the end of the year. The PA House of Representatives is voting on the fate of the Crime Commission and Representatives have been switching which side they support (Democrat and Republican). Republicans are also challenging any votes by PA Senator William Stinson because they think he did not actually win the election.

headline: Lame-duck etiquette
abstract: Mayor Masloff is doing her successor a legitimate service by not invoking her right to reappoint commission and authority board members whose terms are expiring during the last months in office.  Keeping these board members in suspense for a few months about their future with the incoming administration strikes us as preferable to having a soon-to-depart mayor deprive her successor of an opportunity to name his or her own appointees.

headline: State's story running out of room
abstract: On the dimly lighted fourth floor of the state Archives Building, rows of cartons filled with mounds of papers line hundreds of shelves.  This is where you'll find the Pennsylvania story- from the advent of William Penn's grand experiment to the highs and lows of the Thornburgh administration.  But while the state's history isn't ending, the space to hold it is.

headline: 4th-quarter results won't be so bad overall, economists say
abstract: Overall there will be an improvement in the market lead by retailers and bankers.  Those dependent on the condition of the market, such as automakers, have yet to bounce back.

headline: Have a living will?
abstract: The health-care rationing debate is complicated about who decides when or whether to withdraw life support and that most elderly people do not make it known in writing. Most elderly do not have a living will for family to refer to in life support situations.

headline: Activities continue despite strikes
abstract: Teachers and school officials in the strike-bound Bethel Park, Chartiers Valley and Upper St. Clair school districts can't aagree on many contract items, but they have concurred on one issue- extracurricular activities.  Despite weeks of canceled classes, hundreds of South Hills students still make regular trips to their schools each day to participate in sports, band and other activities.

headline: Grow green with NAFTA
abstract: The North American Free Trade Agreement will help to clean up- not pollute- the environment.

headline: Brightening Easton's dark side
abstract: Police Chief John Border vows the city will clean up its Downtown before the Crayola Visitor Center becomes a reality.

headline: Witness: Probe worried Burke
abstract: Robert B. Burke, who was under federal investigation for insurance fraud and racketeering, is now accused of hiring a man to murder Donna Willard.  He ordered the murder because Donna Willard was subpoenaed to testify against him.

headline: At long last, women veterans stand in their place of honor
abstract: More than 11,000 US military women, most of them nurses, were stationed in Vietnam during the war.  Many were reunited here, at the dedication of the Vietnam Women's Memorial in Washington, the first monument in the capital honoring women in the military.

headline: Legislators to look at local teacher talks
abstract: Republican state legislators will focus on unsettled teacher talks in Carlisle and Big Spring school districts this week as part of a two-day hearing on public education.  A newly formed subcommittee of House Republicans will hold the hearing in Harrisburgh's Main Capitol Building Thursday and Friday on the costs and financing of public education in Pennsylvania.

headline: Landlord focus of grant-fraud probe
abstract: Federal investigators are looking into whether Haverford businessman Patrick H. McCrystal misused Philadelphia Housing Development Corp. (PHDC) grants totaling $325,000, officials involved in the probe said.

headline: State's youngest candidate must wait for vote totals
abstract: The state's youngest candidate will have to wait until later this week to see if voters in New Ringgold gave him a chance to serve on borough council and to test election laws that require office holders to be at least 18 years old.  Andrew Belsak, 16, ran as a write-in candidate for one of the two open borough council seats, after no one else in the tiny farming community of 321 residents campaigned for the posts.

headline: A quiet triumph
abstract: The budget for the first time in recent memory passed without inordinate bloodshed and is delicately balanced.  Rendell did a fabulous job getting a fair budget to the councle months before it was due.  They made minor changes and passed it unanimously.

headline: Hawaii offers look at state of full coverage
abstract: President Clinton says Hawaii proves his heatlh care reform proposals can achieve affordable and universal care.  A look is given at how the Hawaii health-care plan works- and sometimes doesn't.

headline: After 16 years, the state notices a tutoring agency
abstract: Barkan's Tutoring & Testing Service, tucked into the back end of the Red Barn Mall, is nearly invisible, yet parents and students know about it.  In April, a state regulator drove through Hatboro, found Barkan's and told its director that the tutoring center was subject to a flurry of state private-school regulations.

headline: Harmony needs sewer lines, report says
abstract: Harmony Township Commissioners set up a meeting with the township municipal authority and an engineer to determine how to implement a plan to create new sewer lines. The township must also expand the Baden sewage treatment plant, and are mandated to do so by thePA  Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Bringing humanity to inhumane times
abstract: The Police Department has met with representatives of Families of Murder Victims Inc. to talk about how the homicide department treats the families of the victims.  The organization believes the police become numb to the pain the families are going though and need to have more training in family care.

headline: Wofford and Reno need to put violence on the front burner
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford and US Attorney General Janet Reno did little to provide a problem-solving environment.  The chose, instead, to assuage anger.  We have a crisis, a nightmarish epidemic of violence.  This complex societal problem arises as a result of years of neglect by our leaders.  Our leaders are out of touch with reality.

headline: Kuwait won't forget
abstract: Parents of 95 US troops killed in the 1991 Persian Gulf War's Iraqi Scud missile attack were grateful for the therapeutic trip to the country where their children were killed. Connie and Robert Clark were comforted by the warmth and care of the Kuwaiti people, thankful their daughter died for such kind and grateful people. Darlene Mayes was amazed at the generosity of the people and the royal treatment she received, and thankful that she was not alone in her grief.

headline: Legislators to promote
abstract: House Speaker H. William DeWeese and Senator F. Joseph Loeper usuall sit on different sides of the aisle.  A planned 10-day tour of Finland, Germany and Belgium, however, has brought these two together to promote a major player in the state's economy.

headline: Landmarks left in limbo by court delay
abstract: Two years ago, the state Supreme Court told Philadelphia officials that if they wanted to declare a movie theater a historic landmark, they would have to compensate the owners for the accompanying restrictions on development.  A sweeping decision declared the preservation law unconstitutional.  The ruling casued an outcry, and the justices agreed to reconsider their ruling, but nothing has been heard from the court since then- leaivng the law on historical preservation in Pennsylvania in limbo.

headline: Stations get more access in Pa. House
abstract: Starting Monday, House Speaker H. William DeWeese said that both commercial and public television cameras will be able to record bot sound and video during floor sessions.

headline: Are Cash-Starved States 'Looting' Medicaid Coffers?
abstract: Federal efforts to close loopholes in the Medicaid law under which the Federal government establishes criteria for matching state contributions have failed plug all holes. Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, PA and other states are moving millions into programs and qualifying for matching grants, only to redistribute funds once grants are received, using the surplus to ease state deficits. The PA legislature is considering loopholes to use to gain over the $520 million grant that kept the governor from raising taxes and making budget cuts.

headline: Health Benefits and Care: Who Will Get How Much?
abstract: By channeling most consumers through the same purchasing aliances, the Clinton plan would go a long way toward providing equal access to medical care for all Americans.  But some people with ihgh incomes or better benefits at work would still be better off than others.  As with many things more services bring higher price tags.

headline: An Opportunity for the '90s
abstract: LearnRight is an outgrowth of The Learning Center in State College.  As its own entity, including teaching licenses, will provide valuable services comprable to Sylan Learning Center, but long term private school atmosphere.

headline: Hazardous waste incinerator opponents fighting each other
abstract: The battle to put an end to plans to build a hazardous waste incinerator in Union County took a new twist last week, with opponents fighting among themselves and accusing county officials of criminal wrongdoing.

headline: Brothers held on counts after fatal carjacking
abstract: Two brothers, 18 and 16, were charged with murder, kidnapping, theft, robbery, conspiracy and other charges for a fatal car-jacking in philadelphia leaving one person dead.

headline: Woman was killed in apartment, probers believe
abstract: The local police said that they have conlcuded that a missing city woman was not killedi n her car, but in the Lower Paxton Twp. Apartment where her badly beaten body was found on March 5.

headline: Letterkenny layoff aid sought
abstract: Due to national military consolidation the Army has announced plans to lay off 450 depot works and 50 employees of Depot Systems Command.  The Casey administration will apply for a $1.1 million federal grant to help train and provide job-assistance to 500 employees expected to be layed off this year at Letterkenny Army Depot.

headline: Legislature's size burdens state taxpayers
abstract: Citizen Michael D. Ostroff commends The Patriot for continuing efforts to expose costs borne by PA taxpayers, of funding a bloated legislature, having also written to PA Senator John Shumaker, PA Representative Ron Marsico, and Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel. Ostroff recommends the number of legislators be reduced and their pay based on a six month session. In his opinion, legislators income is supplemented by lucrative law practices and other professions; additional perks and raises are unnecessary.

headline: Larsen gives grand jury his view
abstract: Justice Rolf Larsen offered a lengthy closing statement yesterday during his fourth and probably final appearance as a witness before a grand jury investigating the state Supreme Court.  The closing statement was apparently Larsen's opportunity to give the grand jury his perspective on the investigation.

headline: The Aftermath at Waco-President orders inquiry and backs Reno
abstract: After allegations that he attempted to distance himself from the fallout events in Waco, Texas, President Clinton held a press conference to discuss the issue with reporters, announcing he had approved actions by Attorney General Janet Reno. Nevertheless, he ordered a full investigation of the Federal Bureau of Investigations and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms,  in order to achieve accountability before the American people.

headline: Area jobless rate climbs to 5%
abstract: The unemployment rate in the Harrisburg area inched up to 5 percent in August but continues to show little movement since a sharp drop in February, state labor analysts say.  The August data, the latest available, show the area's seasonally adjusted unemployment rate increasing from 4.9 percent in July.

headline: Health care glossary
abstract: A compilation of terms associated with health care services and their definitions.

headline: Analysist says deficit could double in decade
abstract: Analysist warns that if there isn't a drastic change in policy which would including higher taxes and trimmer programs the deficit could double in the next ten years.

headline: High-level trouble
abstract: As state officials involved in managing low-level radioactive waste have learned, regional cooperation doesn't always produce regional solutions.  Nine multistate compacts designed to create regional disposal sites for less contaminated classes of nuclear waste remain active, and a 10th, involving Maine, Texas and Vermont, is on the drawing board.

headline: Buyback
abstract: Call it voluntary gun control.  In Philadelphia, for the third year straight, the city is getting unneeded, unwanted and potentially dangerous firearms out of circulation.  And no one is arguing that it violates a constitutional right.  The "Turn in a Gun" program rought in 970 revolvers, single-shot pistols, semiautomatic handguns, rifles, shotguns and other arms at $20 apiece.

headline: Woman's ID confirmed
abstract: It was a bloodbath after two detectives discovered the body of a 41-year-old city resident in the closet of her ex-boyfriend.  Resident James N. Bell shot the two detectives who made the discovery, critically wounding them both before the was shot and killed by one of the detectives.

headline: New VA director vows more services for veterans in speech to Legion
abstract: Veterans Affairs Secretary Jesse Brown pledged a new era in an administration often under fire for its performance, saying he wants Veterans Administration employees to know they better deliver, or else.

headline: Lesson one: Why teachers are on strike
abstract: A Bethlehem-Center school board member criticized the pay raise demands of striking teachers yesterday while a union official complained that the district's salaries were among the lowest in Washington County.  And in the strike-bound Upper St. Clair School District, teachers issued a statement defending their salary requests.

headline: Lighten up, folks
abstract: The people who wrote recent letters regarding Tom Hritz's columns need a sense of humor.

headline: Stinson declared winner, sworn in to state Senate
abstract: Democrat William Stinson was sworn in as a state senator yesterdayj, less than an hour after the Philadelphia Board of Elections declared him the winner of the bitterly disputed 2nd Senatorial District race.  About 50 Democrats assembled in the Senate chambers at the Capitol for a hastily called ceremony to make Stinson's election official and assure, for the time being, a Democratic majority in the Senate.

headline: Benefits or Bust
abstract: A chart and pie chart about the percentage of the budget spent on the entitlement programs and how that compares to the spending on other aspects in the nation.

headline: Health care package reviewed
abstract: A successful managed healthcare plan must emphasize primary care and have academic health institutions among its providers, according to members of Pennsylvania's medical community who met Tuesday with state Senator Hardy Williams.  Williams, chairman of the Public Health and Welfare Committee, discussed Governor Robert P. Casey's proposed helath-care package in an informal session with physicians, nurses and health-care administrators in Pittsburgh.

headline: And he's wrong on renters
abstract: Regarding Tom Hritz's "Let Parents Pay Education Costs," though he has the right to say any stupid, misinformed thing he please, it is irresponsible of the Post-Gazette to let him perpetuate the myth that non-homeowners get a free ride on property taxes.  Rental property is not tax-exempt.  Renters have to take a lot of grief from their more affluent "neighbors" who, like Mr. Hritz, castigate them and even threaten to withhold rights and privileges because they can't afford the down payment on a house.

headline: How the report was compiled
abstract: For the second year, City & State's Environmental Survey of the States takes a comprehensive look at how the states are responding to current environmental challenges.  Comparisons of state performances in various categories are tabulated and shown in charts.

headline: Camden's 1992 homicide toll sets a grim record
abstract: There were 50 homicides in 1992 is an increase from the 37 from the previous year.  The majority of the homicides are minority on minority crimes involving firearms.  Camden Police Detective Lenny Hall believes the best way to curb the violence is to "flood the streets" with police officers, but he admits with some ambivalence that there is always a risk that more police on the street could intensify the atmosphere of hostility that fuels the rage that fuels the violence.

headline: Wrong mob, Mr. Neal
abstract: Police Commissioner Richard Neal has declared war against the mob violence in South Philadelphia.  He should wage a war in West Philadelphia and North Philadelphia.

headline: Nursing home for veterans finally opens

abstract: Leechburg Area School Board president Earl Freilino will remain on the board for two more years, sidestepping a federal law that would have forced him off the board in December.

headline: Reject NAFTA pollution
abstract: The North American Free Trade Agreement could significantly or wholly reverse the actions of our environmental laws from past decades.  NAFTA could seriously undermine efforts to make the US environment cleaner and safer.

headline: Community fights back against gunfire rending society's fabric
abstract: Last week the Post-Gazette featured a four part series in response to the increasing crime in Pittsburgh. Many people wrote back with their various responses, they had a common thread which was the hope of slowing the mayhem that strikes hardest at the city's young black men. The city is working hard to help the situation get better.

headline: Flexible child care adds flex to lives
abstract: According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 75% of mothers of school-age children are in the work force.  This trend has created a need for convenient day care, and the number of day care facilities is increasingly rapidly.  A day care center business, Kids Kart Express Inc., is seeking permission from the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission to expand into Montgomery County.

headline: AT & T buys largest U.S. cellular net
abstract: American Telephone & Telegraph Company said that it will buy McCaw Cellular Communications Inc. for $12.6 billion in stock. Bell Atlantic Corp. said that this will cause less competition and therefore higher prices for consumers. The Federal Communications Commission said it will keep an open mind to any lawsuits filed against AT &T.

headline: Lottery bill makes a valid point
abstract: The editorial board does not support the reasons that Washington County Representative Leo J.Trich had given for a proposed lottery bill that would ban other states' lottery tickets to be sold to Pennsylvania residents that recently failed in the House.  He argued that other states do not allow PA lottery tickets in their state and the editorial board argues that if someone in PA wins, then the state still profits from the taxes on their winnings as well as the winner spending their money.

headline: Support home rule
abstract: In an itemized list of the top five reasons to support home role for Allegheny County, the editorial board includes citizen access to active roles in government through petition and ballot questions, a shortened legislative process as the county will no longer need to go through the PA Legislature, provisions for county aid to struggling municipalities, control over personnel issues relative to local taxes, and ability of voters to quickly and efficiently fill expired terms of local officials.

headline: Clinton vows to seek more budget cuts
abstract: In a speech Presdient Clinton promises to add deeper spending cuts into the budget before increasing the taxes.  The republicans are united in voicing their dislike in the budget sighting a lack of adiquite cuts.  The democrats are mixed, but wholy united in support of Clinton's package.

headline: Health Planners' Radical Idea: Same Coverage for All
abstract: President Clinton's health care plan to standardize a benefits package would standardize minimum benefits currently left up to the states. Numerous interest groups are pushing for coverage of specific benefits, such as women's groups, the elderly, and mental health advocates. The Clinton Administration has yet to propose how the costs of such a plan would be covered by the federal government or by businesses of varying size.

headline: Bring a weapon to school and you're out, House bill proposes
abstract: Any student caught with a weapon on public school grounds or on the bus faces automatic expulsion for the rest of the year under legislation approved by the House Tuesday.

headline: Rep. Ridge proposes plan to divide DER
abstract: US Congressman Tom Ridge wants the state Department of Environmental Resources broken into two departments.  Representative Ridge said at a press conference that he proposed a four point plan to overhaul the DER by breaking it into two cabinet level departments.  He said a cabinet level department is necessary to better manage the state's parks and forests.

headline: Confessed carjacker: Partner started it all
abstract: William Sahw and Craig Watson highjacked a BMW and became the first to be caught committing an armed carjacking after the crime was made a federal offense.  If convicted they will likely face 25 years in prison.

headline: Food stamp cushion encourages welfare cuts
abstract: States across the country are cutting benefits to the poor, but the federal government picks up some of the tab.  Because federal food stamp program allocates money depending on income the reduction in state welfare actually increases the amount of food stamps they are elligable to receive.

headline: AT&T, British firm in dispute-British Telecom wants to provide long-distance service in the US. AT&T wants to do the same over there.
abstract: In an effort to level the playing field, the American Telephone and Telegraph Company has asked the Federal Communications Commission to withhold a license to operate in the US from British Telecom until the Clinton Administration can come up a coordination plan in the global telecommunications market. Both companies have said they are happy to compete with one another as long as each gets equal access to the other's market.

headline: Lottery ought to let more fulfill dreams
abstract: When the lottery jackpot gets up into the tens of millions it should be divided among more winners.  There could be a somewhat bigger prize for the firs winner and still a number of big prizes for the next closest tickets.  If part of the fun of the lottery is seeing dreamsm come true for people like us and you, then more winners would make all of Pennsylvania merrier.

headline: Surrick runs for job he wants to abolish
abstract: Robert B. Surrick thinks a deeply politicised, sharply factioned, nearly dysfunctional Pennsylvania Supreme Court can be saved only by abolishing it.  So Surrick, one of three candidates in the November 2 court election, is out there hurling grenades.

headline: Collections for March come in above estimates
abstract: The PA Department of Revenue Secretary Eileen McNulty reported average general collection of state revenue from various taxes to be above estimates for the month of March. Corporation taxes accounted for a large chunk of this revenue, while other areas of revenue including income tax and realty transfer taxes were below estimates.

headline: Health unit hit on return of funds
abstract: A Senate Appropriations Committee member lambasted the Health Department for returning $2.3 million to the treasury and for not fighting for $5.8 million more that the governor had put away for their use.  The money that was promissed to some non-profit organisations as well as a number of loan forgiveness program have not received their money.  As of now, the Health Department can't explain the numbers, nor do they have accurate figures.

headline: Business plans don't add up, Ptt critics say
abstract: The University of Phiitsburgh's plan to start an undergraduate business school is drawing critcism from Ed Nicholson, president of Robert Morris College, where 4,500 of 4,800 students are business majors.  Morris claims that this is a poor way to allocate public funds because the amount of business students has dropped by 50% in 5 years and there are plenty of undergraduate schools of business in western Pennsylvania.

headline: Representative Murphy seeking changes in hardrock mining law
abstract: The federal government and taxpayers are lsoing millions each year because of archaic mining law which haven't been changed in over a century.  However, Congress is mounting two challenges to the hardrock mining law, created in 1872 when prospectors loaded up their mule team and headed west in search of gold and silver.

headline: Court rejects case that piqued Larsen
abstract: Three weeks ago, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court quietyly resolved a matter that has been the focus of the court since Larsen accussed two of his fellow judges of intentionally delaying the trial and other, criminal offenses.  The Supreme Court refused to hear the case Commonwealth v. David Lee Yohn, a convicted murderer.

headline: Getting Food to hungry children
abstract: With funding from the United Way of Southeastern PA, Trudy Gay, program director of the Wharton Square Program at the Wharton Square Recreation Center, operates one of four programs designed to feed children in the poorest section of Philadelphia that might otherwise go hungry. In addition to feeding hungry children, Gay also teaches them respect, responsibility, and cooperation they might not otherwise learn.

headline: Automatic rate hikes are cut off
abstract: The state Senate's Communications and High Technology Committee wisely acted to drop automatic annual rate increases from legislation linked to Bell of Pennsylvania's proposal to rewire the state for video services.  Moving the bill to the Senate floor by a 12-1 margin, the committee suggested instead a formula by which Bell and the other telephone companies in the state could seek "price stability"- seeking annual rate increases of the inflation rate minus 2.25 percent.

headline: Lottery stakes draw lines
abstract: The lottery reached a jackpot of $35 million, which drew huge sales of lottery tickets.

headline: Take the high road
abstract: The current four-month shutdown of the state Senate by the Democratic Party is not one of the party's stellar moments.  In a bald political bid to hang on to its razor-thin majority, the Democrats, through a decree by Lt. Governor Mark Singel, unnecessarily delayed until last July a special election to fill a vacant seat in Bucks County, to keep the Republicans from control of the Senate for the time.

headline: Congress may meet on budget
abstract: United States Congressmen Harris Wofford and Tom Ridge are introducing bills that would reduce spending to ease the budget deficit, as advocated by President Clinton.  U.S. Senator Bob Kerry suggested a special session be called to meet on creating the budget.

headline: Health-care bill passes in Wash.
abstract: Washington state's Governor Mike Lowry signed a new health care plan that could be used as a model for the Clinton administration. The new plan will provide all 5.1 million Washington residents with health insurance by 1999 and will also seek to control health-care costs by capping insurance premiums.

headline: Cleric rebuts Temple professor on school vouchers
abstract: Some of the statements in Temple professor of law Burton Caine's letter truly amazes me.  Vouchers and tuition tax credits are all a means to an end, implementing the human rights of the parents as specified in the United Nations Declaration of Universal Human Rights, which recognizes that parents have a prior right to direct the education of their children.

headline: Revisiting the riverfront
abstract: The water of the Delaware River along Philadelphia's riverfront may be cleaner than a year ago, but the entertainment definitely isn't.

headline: Court resolves custody battle
abstract: Desperate to have a child, when Patrick O'Malley and his reconciled wife Rebecca learned a brief relationship during their separation had left Pampena Connor pregnant, the three planned for the O'Malley's to adopt the child. After the adoption fell through however, the O'Malley's were arrested and accused of kidnapping the child in a custody dispute. Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Joan Orie threw out the charges and granted custody to Connor and her husband.

headline: Heard on the Hill
abstract: Casey threatened to veto House-approved legislation that would eliminate more than 120,000 Pennsylvania residents from the "transitionally needy" welfare program.

headline: Bell outlines fiber-optic proposal
abstract: At stake is a multibillion-dollar communications network that proponents say will bring Pennsylvania into the 21st century.  At issue is how the system will be built, who will pay for it and who will have access to it.  Bell of Pennsylvania will start addressing those issues today when it files a plan with the state Public Utility Commission outlining how the company would build and pay for the fiber-optic network.

headline: Ludlum exec asks Congress for assistance
abstract: Secretive foreign steel cartels threaten the American steel industry, and Congress should do something about it, Allegheny Ludlum Corp. President Robert Bozzone told a congressional panel Thursday.

headline: Taking bets
abstract: Right now, Ed Rollins and Mike Murphy are working together to help Republican Christie Whitman win the 1993 New Jersey governor's race.  But when they get to Pennsylvania, they're on opposite sides.

headline: Deficit becoming too big to tame
abstract: Senator Harris Wofford sat with three voters to talk about the national debt and, when the time came to cut to the chase, the puzzle became just where to cut.  But at $4 trillion and rising, the national debt is simply too large to lay on a table.  For Pennsylvania's junior senator, questions of national debt and the yearly budget deficit that feeds it presents a slippery dilemma.

headline: Health-care bill puts off full coverage
abstract: The health-care reform bill President Clinton will deliver to Congress today retools dozens of provisions in his earlier draft, and delays by a year the goal of full insurance coverage for every American.

headline: Building a future
abstract: The recent dedication of Brossman Hall at Millersvielle University is both gratifying and ominous.  The new facility houses one classroom, several laboratories and 10 faculty offices.  It was built thanks to the generosity of the Brossman family, which has provided significant financial support to the university over the years.

headline: Rush Subsidence Aid, Legislators Are Asked
abstract: Scranton Police Chief George Murphy is writing to the city's federal representatives asking that they do whatever they can to free funding for the Office of Surface Mining to combat a subsidence problem centering in the 500 block of Noth Washington Avenue.  There has yet to be evacuations, but the water to the city may be comprimised if there are any more sink holes which would put the city in danger.

headline: Country's drug unit runs out of money
abstract: The 14-month-old Indiana County Drug Task Force is bankrupt after being underfunded by state by $28,000.  Most of the money went to paying police overtime and for 'buy money'.  They are asking the state and local government for more money because they have 45 cases open which could produce as many arrests.

headline: Heating aid cuts could hurt many needy
abstract: Some low-income families in Pennsylvania may go without heat this winter due to the shrinking budget of a federally funded program that helps the needy pay home heating costs.

headline: Bell still hanging up in public
abstract: A columnist discusses the study done by the Public Utility Commission that shows Bell of Pennsylvania has the worst customer service performance rating in Pennsylvania.  The telephone company also fails to comply with customer service regulations, particularly in instances where customers don't pay their telephone bill.

headline: Madigan Sees Uphill Fight For Lieutenant Governor
abstract: State Senator Roger A. Madigan says he faces an uphill fight in a nomination for lieutenant governor next year.  Madigan, speaking at a luncheon of the Williamsport Lycoming Council of Republican Women yesterday, said 10 or 11 other people are reported to be considering a run for the number 2 spot on the GOP's gubernatorial ticket in next spring's primary election.

headline: Tax reform dead issue until 1995
abstract: Tax reform appears to be dead until 1995.  The Legislature's wrok on the controversial legislation was shelved until November.  Could the Legislature surprise us and do it before '95? Sure.  But don’t hold your breath.

headline: Differences
abstract: The article briefly outlines the major differences between two local tax reforms in PA, one by the House Local Tax Reform Caucus and the other called Senate Bill 182 sponsored by Senator Mike Dawida.

headline: Health-care debate falters
abstract: Health care consumes one-seventh of our national income and that guarantees President Clinton's plan for health-care reform to be one of the most far-reaching proposals this country has considered.  Martin Feldstein, former head of the Council of Economic Advisers, says Mr. Clinton has underestimated the cost of the plan by $120 billion.  Let's hope the quality of the debate picks up.

headline: Campuses That Stress Teaching and Community
abstract: Pennsylvania's 14 state-woned universities have grown in stature and visibility, generally known as places where teaching and communities are strong.

headline: Saegertown turns attention to another toxic cleanup
abstract: With cleanup scheduled to start at one of Saegertown's hazardous sites, borough and government officials have turned their attention to another toxic area on the south side of town.  Steve Donohue of the Environmental Protection Agency updated the status of the proposed cleaunup of the former GATX Industrial site.  Visiting from Philadelphia, he addressed Saegertown Borough Council at its Monday night meeting.

headline: County program seeks to help kids in own homes
abstract: A new county program created by the Northampton County Department of Human Services makes caseworkers available 24 hours a day in order to keep children in their own homes rather than in placement.

headline: Hired gun had cleaned up D.C.
abstract: The article discusses Rick Barnes, who worked as Philadelphia's disability programs manger for Philadelphia Mayor Rendell.  He then worked for the Washington Metropolitan Transportation Authority where he hired a private firm to handle claims management (a strategy Rendell adopted).  He greatly improved the state of disability programs in Washington.

headline: Cable TV scrambles to meet new pricing
abstract: Due to a new federal price cap on cable 9 of the 10 Harriburg area cable stations are offering new inexpensive offers for cable.  For as little as $9.95 a month a perscriber can get the basic 11 channels.  The federal government is saying that this will offer other options to those that can not afford the more expesnsive channels, but the cable companies doubt many will downgrade.

headline: Maintaining contact
abstract: Julia H. Grimstad, President of the Board of Driectors of CONTACT Pittsburgh, Inc., writes to commend the Pennsylvania Psychological Association for selecting CONTACT Pittsburgh, Inc. to receive tis prestigious 1993 Public Service Award at its recent statewide convention held at the Westin William Penn.

headline: Taxpayers' group yields in standoff with GOP leaders
abstract: START, a conservative taxpayers' association, withdrew Herschel Elias's candidacy for school board. They withdrew his nomination because he acknowledge that he had plead guilty in 1984 to federal misdemeanor charges of supplementing the salary of an official of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

headline: Economy's Growth Rate Perked Up in 3rd Quarter
abstract: After a stutter-step early this year, the U.S. economy picked up speed in the three months from July to September as growth hit a 2.8 percent annual rate despite continued defense spending cuts and farm losses, the Commerce Department said yesterday.

headline: Health-care future shock arrives
abstract: A new rule, FASB 106, by the Financial Accounting Standards Board will force companies to show the estimated future cost of retiree's health care.  There is major backlash from the corporate world who will go from showing positive yearly gains to record loses.  As a result, some companies are cutting the benefits to retirees.

headline: Casey at bat late in education-reform game
abstract: Casey was silent on education reform to long and by the time he gave his oppinion the momentium of the reform 'outcome based education' was unable to be changed.

headline: Second report on waste facility due
abstract: The next report by ChemNuclear Systems Inc will be presented later this week to the Commonwealth to determine the best place to have Pennsylvania's first low level radioactive wast storage facility.

headline: Couple files complaint
abstract: An interracial couple in East Hanover Township has filed a complaint with the PA Human Relations Commission against Lower Dauphin School District, charging the district of subjecting their son to harassment by refusal to provide a safe and unbiased atmosphere or adequate medical care. The complaint seeks adoption of a school violence and discrimination policy under federal Civil Rights Law, reparations, counseling and training for staff and students, and school security.

headline: Hunger on rise in state, aides to needy say
abstract: Food banks across PA and the nation are seeing a growth trend in the number of needy people they serve. With 14.2 percent of the population in poverty according to the US Census Bureau, most food banks service the elderly and children, arguing that the stereotypical addict does not comprise their customer base, rather mothers or parents with young mouths to feed. Food banks include the Ecumenical Food Pantry, and the Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank with research by the PA Coalition on Food and Nutrition and the Food Research and Action Center.

headline: Character Recognition: How Computers Read
abstract: Unisys account manager David Mills explains the difference between optical character recognition and intelligent character recognition. OCR systems available are accurate about 50 percent of the time, although a more expensive machine can be up to 95 percent accurate. ICR systems are more accurate and fine-tuned that OCR systems, with greater potential for future technological development, says Frank Iacono, technical program manager.

headline: Make-believe reform
abstract: Having taken a 180-degree turn away from his longtime support for merit-based appointment of appellate judges in Pennsylvania, state Senator Stewart Greenleaf is offering a package of alleged reforms that would do little for the flawed system of electing these judges.  Don't be lulled into thinking that Senator Greenleaf is offering real judicial reform.

headline: Taxpaying strike foe lives to fight for causes
abstract: Last week, Carolyn Rapaport was an interested taxpayer who, in a passionate speech, had urged school board members to stand tough against the demands of the teachers.
