By yesterday afternoon, she emerged as the undisputed leader of a grassroots effort that has pitted residents of the usually quiet South Hills community against the striking Upper St. Clair Federation of Teachers.

headline: Fisher urges special session of cut corporate taxes
abstract: PA Senator D. Michael Fisher announced he would run for governor and promised that if elected, he would make a cut in the state's corporate income tax.  He asked Acting PA Governor Mark Singel to convene a special session of the General Assembly to reduce the corporate income tax.  Tom Ridge is also planning to run for governor and has come up with a plan to reduce school violence. Sam Katz is planning to run for governor as well.

headline: Health-care plan injected with rival doses of rhetoric
abstract: The article discusses the rhetoric from both political parties regarding President Clinton's health plan.  There is much bias on each side, and because the details have not been worked out,  no one is sure what the effects of his plan will be.

headline: Casey stresses basic subjects
abstract: Gov. Casey warned the state board of education that refusing to pass key changes in the curriculum guidelines, which include a focus on reading, writing and arithmetic, would be a harmful for the education system of Pennsylvania.  The plan would shit the way schools measure progress from the current system which specifies the number of courses a student must take to the student's ability to reach certain goals in areas such as writing and mathematics.

headline: Silver Spring poultry firm gets new name
abstract: Wellington Farms Inc., which ran a poultry processing plant in Silver Spring township, is out of business.  An identical business, however, has sprung up.  Assets of Wellington Farms, which was under fire from the township and the state Department of Environmental Resources, were sold and Pheonix Poultry as formed.

headline: Court Critic takes aim at amendment
abstract: Citizen William T. Reil has filed against the inclusion of a measure to replace the Judicial Inquiry Review Board with a two tiered, more public, and less Justice controlled system on the primary ballot, calling the measure unconstitutional. Reil alleges that the placement of the measure on the primary rather than the election ballot intentionally reduces voter awareness. Though controversial, the new system is supported by the PA Bar Association and Pennsylvanians for Modern Courts.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Noteworthy
abstract: The PA Department of Public Welfare will take public comments on its heating assistance program.

headline: Complaint prompts cable TV refund pledge
abstract: More than 20,000 state consumers will get surprise refunds from cable-television companies.  Twenty-nine cable operators settled a state attorney general's complaint by promising to refund money to consumers who prepaid their cable bills but canceled service before the billing period ended.

headline: Mandela gets vows of support
abstract: Philadelphia's black political leadership rose at dawn yesterday to put aside differences an djoin forces to raise money for one of the most important elections of modern times- Nelson Mandela's bid to forge a new, multiracial government in South Africa.

headline: Teacher talks continuing in 4 districts
abstract: Teacher contrac negotiations in at least one local school district are becoming tense as representatives continue to bargain.  Teachers in Allegheny Valley, Apollo-Ridge, Armstrong and New Kensington-Arnold have been working while negotiations continue with respective school boards.  But in Armstrong, tempers are beginning to flare.

headline: Foundations build a giant nest egg
abstract: By distributing only the minimum required by law as investments grown at a faster rate, tax exempt foundations have become huge warehouses of wealth where more money is stockpiled every year. Critics argue taxpayers are subsidizing these organizations unnecessarily and urge laws requiring higher taxes, larger grants, and/or maximum lengths of establishment be imposed. Some foundations argue the current requirements are necessary in order to long-term sustainability of the organization.

headline: Health-care reform seminar scheduled
abstract: Health-care reform will be the subject of a seminar from 8 am to noon Thursday at the Harrisburg Hilton and Towers.  The seminar, sponsored by the Pennsylvania Economy League, will look at how corporations can prepare for health-care reform, trends in benefit plans, and cost-management programs to control expenses.

headline: Center residents balk at teacher raises
abstract: Resident backlash against teacher requests for salary increases has spread to Center, Beaver County.  Echoing the sentiments of citizens in Allegheny, Washington and Westmoreland school districts who decried pay raise proposals, Center taspayers are urging school board members to hold the line on teacher salaries.

headline: Sludge spill  angers York residents
abstract: A truck carrying 12 tons of sludge from Philadelphia spilled half of its load on Route 124 outside of York, Pa.  The sludge left the road very slick and caused a collision leaving one injured.  The sludge has since been cleaned up, but resdients are upset.

headline: Cover-up alleged in '85 slaying
abstract: A state police cover-up put an innocent Gettysburg man behind bars six years ago, said an attorney who is attempting to prove his client's innocence.  Gregory Brent Harner was convicted in 1987 of killing a high school classmate two years earlier only because police withheld evidence at the trial, said his attorney, Farley Holt of York.

headline: Inside the Capitol: State caterers told to donate food
abstract: New administrative policy forces vendors of prepared food for any commonwealth function to donate the excess food to one of some 50 charity organizations across the state.

headline: Imaging: An Expanding Horizon
abstract: State and local governments are realizing the potential of imaging systems, a technology that is growing so fast, it sometimes cause governments to structure around the imaging system, says Frank Iacono of Unisys. Mordechai Beizer, Vice President of Sigma Imaging Systems, Inc., cautions that imaging works best on tasks for which an organization has to move around large numbers of small documents, helping to save on transportation and control costs.

headline: Many variations in mayors' race
abstract: Mayoral primaries will be held in the state's 28 third-class cities, which are cities that have less than 100,000 residents. The candidates differ on many views throughout the different races.

headline: Teachers pact near in Franklin
abstract: Negotiators for the Franklin Regional School District and its teachers union have tentatively agreed to a one-year extension of the old contract with a 5.5 percent pay increase.  In the Hopewell Area School District, a strike was averted because union and school officials agreed yesterday to a state mediator's request for a one-week cooling off period and a resumption of negotiations next week.

headline: Foundations build a giant nest egg
abstract: By distributing only the minumum required by law as investments grown at a faster rate, tax exempt foundations have become huge warehouses of wealth where more money is stockpiled every year. Critics argue taxpayers are subsidizing these organizations unnecessarily and urge laws requiring higher taxes, larger grants, and/or maximum lengths of establishment be imposed. Some foundations argue the current requirements are necessary in order to long-term sustainability of the organization.

headline: Health-care regulations exist for a good reason
abstract: The editorial board agrees with the call for an in-depth investigation of the accidental death of an elderly nursing home patient, disciplinary action against the home if warranted, and better enforcement of existing laws. The board says health care workers can go ahead and complain about rules and change them if possible, but in the mean time they had better follow all laws to the letter so as not to make mistakes that end up with deaths and investigations.

headline: Changing the way teachers train
abstract: Outcome-based education is gaining influence in Pennsylvania schools, where students may be required to perform certain tasks to graduate.  The PA House of Representatives voted for such requirements to be optional for school districts, but this will most likely to be opposed by PA Governor Casey.  In order to students to meet these requirements, the PA Board of Education will establish new rules for certifying teacher-training programs and teachers themselves.  The PA Education Secretary warns that these changes will be controversial.

headline: Small-scale pollution may be a big problem
abstract: On February 26, 1992 an inspector from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency tested five drains in the service bay of Keystone Dodge Used Cars in Quakertown finding that crankcase oil and other automotive fluids have been put down the drain, which were carried to a septic tank creating a threat to underground drinking water.  The EPA is beginning to crackdown on the improper disposal of toxic wastes.

headline: Crash involving 3 police officers investigated
abstract: A two-vehicle accident earlier this week involving all three of the borough's police officers has crippled the police department and sparked public questions over the late-night mishap in this Perry County community.

headline: L & l stages a weigh-in
abstract: The Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections began dropping by the kitchens of various steak houses to see if the meat and poultry entrees actually weigh what the menus say. The L & l can impose up to a $200 fine for every piece of meat or poultry that weighs less that its advertised weight.

headline: Localities must act on control of cable
abstract: Communities big and small are scrambling to decide if they want to regulate basic cable television service.  A Federal Communications Commission rate freeze is scheduled to expire Novemeber 15 and many municipal officials suddenly are struggling against time to understand the complex federal law and FCC rules that authorize them to check rate increases and demand rollbacks.

headline: Marks is ordered to back up charges by today
abstract: Republican Bruce Marks has until 9 am today to produce the names of more than 500 people he says filed fraudulent absentee ballots in Tuesday's Second Senate District special election and the reason the votes should be disqualified.  Otherwise, his complaint could be thrown out of court.

headline: 'Technical' or not, they're violations
abstract: Now that there's a criminal investigation of the Bruce Marks/Bill Stinson state Senate contest, the election antics that we've come to expect in Philadelphia may not seem so amusing.  Some small fry will get caught in election-code violations, and it will be interesting to see what happens if they're granted immunity and start to talk about the people who directed Democrat Stinson's remarkably successful absentee-vote effort.

headline: Foundations: Grants vs. Assets
abstract: A bar graph contrasts market value of foundation assets with total grants, adjusting for inflation in billions of dollars. In 1982, for every $83 in assets, foundations granted roughly $6. In 1991, foundations grant roughly $9 for every $163.

headline: Heed Warning Signs
abstract: The writer urges people to have loved ones (women) to have routine physical exams, especially routine mammograms. He has lost his wife due to her having breast cancer and widespread metastasis.

headline: Children sought for Pitt study on absence due to fear of school
abstract: Researchers for a University of Pittsburgh Medical Center study are recruiting children ages 7 through 17 whose fear of school causes high absenteeism.  After an evaluation, the children enrolled in the 12-week study will be divided into two groups, both of which will undergo behavioral therapy one day each week.

headline: Smokestacs' fallout includes some ill-will
abstract: Residents are upset with Bellefiel Boiler Plant because they claim that there is fallout from the smokestacks.  There have been seven complaints in two years that claim that there is sometimes black suit on the ground which is especially evident after fresh snow.

headline: Crime bill's main goal should be saving the children
abstract: The $22 billion federal anticrime package moving toward passage in Congress has some good things in it.  But the bill owes too much to the latest mass hysteria about crime, and it will do almost nothing to defuse the nation's real crime bomb.

headline: No lien on me
abstract: A photograph of a woman celebrating with the Mon Valley Unemployed Committee over a state law that removes liens against the homes of welfare recipients.

headline: New market for wastepaper hailed
abstract: The International Paper Company mill began converting old newspapers, magazines, and catalogs into pulp to make printing papers in Clinton and Lycoming County. The farmers are worried though because they use papers as bedding for cows. Clinton County Solid Waste Authority and International Paper are sympathetic to farmers though and will work to see they are not affected.

headline: Marks loses bid to decertify vote
abstract: Republican Bruce Marks went to court to testify that PA Senator William Stinson stole the special election vote, but Common Pleas Judge Mark I. Bernstein turned down his motion to decertify the election. Marks complained that he was not given an outside judge because he could not get a fair hearing from "Philadelphia judges."

headline: Texas Dems should follow N.J.'s lead and drop charges
abstract: The author believes that the Travis County (Texas) district attorney should drop charges that Texas Republican Senator Kay Bailey Hutchison used state phones and employees for private business for state treasurer. He believes that the charges are to suppress Hutchison's re-election bid.

headline: Going on Offensive, Whitman Plans Cuts In New Jersey Taxes
abstract: Christine Todd Whitman, the Republican candidate for govenor of New Jersey, announced an economic plan today with a promise over the next three years to make the most sweeping tax cuts in state history, to reduce the size of government and to create 450,000 jobs.

headline: Help needed to buy medicines, HELP Ministries says
abstract: HELP Ministries of Christian Churches United says it has exhausted its budget for emergency medication and transportation needs for the next two and a half months, inhibiting the Harrisburg Hospital Social Work Department, which refers up to 15 people monthly. The Ministry, concerned about rising health care costs and persons without health care, will consult with the United Way, which has also failed to meet its budget for the last three years.

headline: City school hearings draw 1,000
abstract: About 1,000 people attended five public meetings over the past two weeks on a plan for instituting sweeping changes in the Pittsburgh Public Schools.

headline: Solution to waste divides families, EPA
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency confirmed their fears and told a family who were sure they were secure in their Delaware County town of Lansdowne: that decades ago, their home was built with sand containing radioactive materials.  A tentative plan called for tearing down their home- along with 18 others and 10 nonresidential buildings in four nearby towns- to guard against a fire or construction work releasing radioactive dust into the environment.

headline: Crime Commission under fire
abstract: Earlier in the month, the Pennsylvania Crime Commission revealed it had been investigating allegations that PA Attorney General Ernie Preate, Jr. took campaign contributions from illegal video-poker operators in the 1980's in exchange for veiled assurances not to prosecute them. These charges have caused the commission to come under a lot of fire from various congressmen who believe they handled the situation very poorly.

headline: Noteworthy
abstract: PA Secretary of Aging Linda Rhodes is advising young and old to watch "Elder Abuse: Whose Problem?".

headline: PUC hearings on Bell plan
abstract: The Public Utility Commission has scheduled hearings in 10 communities to receive public comment on the proposal Bell Telephone Co. of Pennsylvania for an alternative form of regulation.  Bell has asked the commission to approve a "price stability mechanism," the deregulation of six services and a plan for modernization of its network by the year 2015.

headline: Marsico tries again on prevailing wages
abstract: PA Representative Ron Marsico is continuing hi efforts to repeal the state's Prevailing Wage Act, which he says drives up the cost of governmental capital construction projects. He is proposing that municipalities be given the option of being excluded from the law in order to be better able to afford construction projects.

headline: Thanks anyway, PG
abstract: Gloria Novak was not mentioned as a candidate for the legislative seat to be vacated by Tom Murphy, but the ommission could be to her advantage.  In previous races for City Council, the Post-Gazette consistently failed to recognize two of the eventual winners as viable candidates, so Gloria Novak can confidently look forward to a vicotry at the polls in May!

headline: House backs  budget deadline plan
abstract: A package of legislation was overwelmingly approved by the House yesterday.  The bill included a push by republicians to offer a plan to freeze senior citizens' property taxes.  The proposal will force a deadline to get the budget complete as sell as set up a commission to review the budget and a forecasting board to assess the budget from different state departments.

headline: Hershey strives to develop permanent artificial device
abstract: With the electrically powered heart, patients won't be tethered to machines, stay for months in the hospital or be required to take expensive and sometimes dangerous medications for the rest of their lives.  That's the future according to Gerson Rosenberg, who is leading a team of Hershey Medical Center researchers trying to make the next quantum leap in artificial heart development ready for clinical trials by the turn of the century.

headline: City schools learn a beleaguered district can shine
abstract: To the community of Farrell, with its school district being the state's sixth-poorest, nearly three dozen Harrisburg officials ventured last week in search of answers that have so far eluded the city's own beleaguered district.  The town of Farrell is dying and decaying, yet somehow, the school district blossoms.

headline: State Fines Two Companies
abstract: Two businesses, Chromographic Processing Co. and CNG Transmission Corp., have been fined for violating state air pollution rules, the Department of Environmental Resources said.

headline: Criminal Controll Beats Gun Control
abstract: If there's one bumper sticker that emerged from Tuesday's election, this is it: Criminal Control.  Criminal control trumps gun control when voters can choose between two candidates clearly associated with those alternatives.  The criminal control issue is a reality that is going to start sinking in among the people who actually have to run for office, like Jim Florio or Mary Sue Terry.

headline: On Welfare, Wisconsin Leads, Beltway Straddles
abstract: President Bill Clinton is talking to reform the welfare system in the United States. Wisconsin though is the leader in welfare change stating that in 1998 all welfare programs will be abolished. President Clinton is not likely to be as radical because he is not willing to be as harsh.

headline: Technology centers help businesses prosper
abstract: In an effort by President Clinton to help the waning defense industry convert technology to commercial use, centers like the Midwest Manufacturing Technology Center are providing businesses much needed consulting advice, from efficient floor plans to new equipment. Sponsored by the US Department of Commerce, the Center is one of several supplanted around the nation by state and federal funds.

headline: Matta decries pension shortfall
abstract: Unfunded pension obligations are a "bomb hanging over the city of Pittsburgh," Republican mayoral candidate Kathy Matta said yesterday.  Matta said a high-level commission should be formed to look into a "pension mess" in which the city's unfunded liability has grown to nearly $440 million.

headline: The 1,200 students in Clairton are all Governor Caseys
abstract: It was wonderful that Pennsylvania's governor was given the opportunity for a new lease on life.  Pray that students have the same opportunities and consideration as the governor was allotted in his time of distress.  The 1,200 stuents in Clairton School District are all Governor Caseys with their lives and futures on the line.

headline: House gives narrow approval to Clinton's budget proposals
abstract: The House of Representatives approved the heart of President Clinton's budget plan today with a vote of 219-213. To lower the Federal budget deficit the measure would raise the taxes of almost all Americans except the poor, amounting to about $250 billion over five years.

headline: Hillary Clinton's image has transformed with health-plan effort
abstract: Hilary Clinton, who was once described as cold, power-hungry and a radical feminist, transformed after the president presented his health plan to Congress and the nation.  As chair of the Health Care Task Force, an unpaid, unelected position, she traded in her selfishness for the country.

headline: Clairton can teach a valuable lesson to toher school districts
abstract: We are all aware of the crisis this summerin the Clairton School District.  We lost busing and elective courses and suffered a major cutback in the sports program.  In spite of that, our schools are open, our kids are given the best education possible with the limited resources available and we still have hope.  Perhaps this lesson in cooperation can spread throughout the area so that all children, everywhere, may benefit.

headline: State police at Carlisle warned of tainted water
abstract: State police at the Carlisle barracks are under orders not to drink, wash or come into contact with the water there by the US Department of Environmental Protection.  DEP conducted a test of their well water after a complaint and found high levels of volatile synthetic organic chemicals according to barracks commander Sergeant Fred Scott.  They believe the water was contaminated by illegal dumping before the barracks was build, which seeped into the groundwater.

headline: DA wants death warrant signed
abstract: Martin D. Appel, convicted of killing of three people during a East Allen Township bank robberty seven years ago, has been sitting on death row.  Acting Governor Mark Singel has requested that action be taken immediately to execute the death.

headline: Pa.  Sues firm  over rentals
abstract: American Home  Rentals  Inc.  Is being sued by the Attorney General's office for a  scam that targeted the poor  looking for low income housing by taking an average  of $400 in fees and not doing  anything in return.

headline: Wireless data service still in works
abstract: Bell Atlantic Mobile trumpets its new wireless digital data services as a potential billion-dollar industry wthat will change people's lives.  But two weeks after its announcement that the new and untested technology will debut here early next year,  Bell Atlantic Mobile remains a billion dollars short of its projection.

headline: Matta spies issue in Philby remark
abstract: For now, it would seem, a dead British spy is the principal issue in the Pittsburgh mayor's race.  Republican candidate Kathy Matta assailed Democratic front-runner Tom Murphy yesterday for a speech Sunday in which he said he was impressed by Kim Philby's "commitment to change" and urged the audience to be "committed, as Kim Philby was, to revolution."  Philby is notorious for having passed British and American secrets to the Soviets for nearly 20 years while working at the top level of the British intelligence service from the mid-1930s to the mid-1950s.

headline: The candidates
abstract: An intemized list of 1994 PA gubernatorial candidates includes a brief description of political involvement for each candidate. Candidates include PA Senator Earl Baker, PA Representative Dwight Evans, PA Senator Mike Fisher, PA Attorney General Ernie Preate, US Representative Tom Ridge, and PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel.

headline: How Whitman Sees the Bottom Line
abstract: Christine Todd Whitman, the Republican candidate for governor of New Jersey, laid out proposals to cut state taxes and spending.  The total state budget for this year is $15.5 billion.

headline: HIV precautions called adequate by dental official
abstract: Dentists are treating their HIV patients with relative confidence thanks to safety procedures that have become routine, like wearing protective gear, and because it’s a federal law. This is after a dentist was suited by the American Civil Liberties Union for refusing to treat an HIV patient for a cracked tooth.

headline: Clayton announces retirement, but might stay through November
abstract: Superintendent Constance E. Clayton, whose forceful persona has dominated the city schools for more than a decade, will retire Aug. 31, but will likely stay on as interim superintendent until Nov. 30.

headline: State urges cleanup of faulty sewage systems
abstract: Faulty sewage systems in northeast PA are contaminating groundwater with disease-carrying parasites. The PA Department of Environmental Resources has begun enforcing regulations to get townships to adopt on-lot management laws to regulate sewages systems hooked up to rural homes.  Ron Harlan, supervisor in Wetmore Township says that these regulations are an unfair financial burden to the poor.

headline: Dad gets 235 years in children's abuse
abstract: Rickie Gaddis was convicted last fall on 157 charges that he raped his daughter over an 18-month period and endangered the lives of all his children.  He was sentenced to 235 years and $1.71 million in fines.

headline: Pa. seeks new bids for welfare office
abstract: A planned increase in caseworkers has led the state to seek new bids fro a larger site to house the county's welfare office.  The state Department of Welfare has decided to add caseworkers in Chester County as part of a regular statewide rotation.

headline: A vote for free trade couldn't come at a better time
abstract: Three events, all cocurring in the next 30 days, together will help determine the strength of our economy and the standard of living of the American people as we enter the 21st century.  The first event is today's climactic vote on the North American Free Trade Agreement.  NAFTA is one of the gr3eat foreign policy opportunities of this generation.

headline: Maybe Philadelphia Is Governable After All
abstract: Newly elected Mayor Ed Rendell knows how to play the game of politics, making friends with city council members, easing tension, and tweaking the budget enough to create a maximum reduction in the deficit with minimal pain. Rendell has worked with officials to create the image of a government that listens, though his political power is tightly controlled. The PA Intergovernmental Authority is concerned budget cuts will not meet long-term 5 year goals.

headline: The curious case of Judge Thomas Cooper
abstract: The charges lodged against Judge Thomas Cooper when he appeared before the General Assembly during the winter of 1811 read like something out of "Bizarre Tales of the Bench and Bar."  Now, nearly two centuries after Cooper became what historians say was the last judge in Pennsylvania to be removed from office by the legislature, it looks as though the "Bizarre" book might get an addendum.  The General Assembly is again taking a look at removing a jurist.

headline: If not this plan, what?
abstract: Clinton asks the republicans, If not this plan, then what?  Those in favor of the 'trickle-down' theory of economics will not like this plan, but there could not have been any more spending cuts without political fallout.

headline: HMO to 'grade' own docs, hospitals for consumers
abstract: US Healthcare Inc., the Blue Bell-based HMO, said yesterday it is taking the first step toward developing a report card that compares the performance of cotors and hospitals in its statewide network.  The HMO's "report card" would be available to consumers and employers, the company said.  The data are designed to measure the quality of services provided to US Healthcare members by the doctors and hospitals they use.

headline: Clinton Proposes Service Program to Aid Students
abstract: President Clinton has outlined a plan to overhaul the way students pay for college, offering students up to $10,000 for college for two years of community training and change the way students can borrow directly from the government as a campaign appeal towards the middle-class.  He also said that his National Service Trust Act will help community service jobs.

headline: Stubborn coal miners continue to dig in as industry slowly dies
abstract: An reporter explores the dying town and coal mines of Portage, PA. A depressed area, the future looks bleak, although stubborn coal miners refuse to leave. Having braved explosions, layoffs, and labor unions, the mine's biggest challenges now come from the PA Department of Environmental Resources and other government regulators says Bruce Brunett, Portage Township Supervisor.

headline: Dad, 77, ordered to pay $50,000
abstract: A Bucks County judge has ordered a Florida man, Franklin Hayes Bullock Jr., to cough up 34 years worth of delinquent support payments totaling almost $50,000.

headline: Proposal likened to goals of FDR
abstract: Social Security was the beginning.  Over the last half-century, government has moved to protect the welfare of citizens.  President Clinton's proposed American Health Security Act ranks with the sweeping goals of Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal and Lyndon B. Johnson's Great Society.

headline: Area educators debate NAFTA
abstract: Opponents of the North American Free Trade Agreement say it will result in companies relocating to Mexico, where wages are lower and environmental standards more lax.  But if companies wanted to go to Mexico they would have already done so, tow college professors maintained Tuesdyanight at a discussion of NAFTA at the University of Pittsburgh at Johnstown.

headline: Mayor may be bound for diplomatic trail
abstract: Mayor Masloff may be offered a position by President-elect Clinton to become 'ambassador-at-large'.  The mayor has put off running for re-election until she hears from Washington.  She would be working with the Eastern European countries to help local governments implement democracy.

headline: The final reel?  Politics threatens Pittsburgh Film Office funding
abstract: The Pittsburgh Film Office may run out of funds after Memorial Day because the state is going to stop funding the film office.  The debate has been between the Department of Commerce, legislative inniciatives, and local government.  None of the three want to fund the film office and therefore it may no longer exist in a few months unless it merges with another department.

headline: Index of leading indicators
abstract: Various indicators in the Index of Leading Ecomic Indicators left the index at a seasonally adjusted 153.6, up 4.3 percent from a year ago, and up 10.3 percent from ten years ago as shown in a chart.

headline: HMO touts 'one-stop shopping'
abstract: Keystone Health Plan East is forging ahead with a plan that would link the HMO with at least 15 group physician practices in the area, offering "one-stop shopping" for members.  Yesterday, Keystone, a for-profit unit owned by Independence Blue Cross and Pennsylvania Blue Shield, broke ground for the first of the centers on Delaware Avenue, just south of Washington.

headline: Clinton service proposal popular
abstract: Clinton's plan to give students an option of doing community service activities to help pay off college loans comes off popular in Pa.  Students would be givent the option to do work within inner-cities or rural poor for $8,000 for the first year to help pay off their student loans.  Some students don't think it will work because it would be easier to pay off loans by working a higher paying job in the private sector.

headline: Survey finds states still going green
abstract: The trend toward tougher state environmental laws continues, and a few states that had been unresponsive to toxic dangers have jumped on the green bandwagon, City & State's second annual Environmental Survey of the States has found.

headline: Damages for harassment made easier
abstract: Workers do not have to prove that sexual harassment severely damaged them psychologically or seriously hurt their work performance, the high court ruled.

headline: Proposal to freeze benefits dropped
abstract: Clinton dropped the proposeed plan to freeze Social Security benefits for rich and poor alike for a year in the face of feirce opposition and instead turned to a plan whicn proposes that middle- and upper-income recipients pay taxes on more of ther Social Security benefits.

headline: Clinton warns against rejection of NAFTA
abstract: Surrounded by the bounty of free trade, President Clinton warned yesterday of an ugly side to rejecting an economic pact with Mexico.  He predicted a new flood of illegal immigrants from Mexico and more competition from Japan and Germany.

headline: Mayor missed deadline
abstract: Whaterver happned to Mayor Rendell's assurances that the homeless situation in the 13th Street subway concourse would be handled before the city's Convention Center opened?

headline: The flight to Erie
abstract: The reputation of Pennsylvania's courts is such that nothing could shock us.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Déjŕ vu on federal budget passage
abstract: Pennsylvania's budget was passed along strictly partisan lines, with all the Republicans opposing it and all but one Democrat supporting it.  The federal budget was passed in a similar fashion, by two votes in the House and one vote in the Senate.

headline: Holy Spirit expands catheterization unit
abstract: Holy Spirit Hospital in East Pennsboro Township has opened the first heart catheterization lab on the West Shore.  The diagnostic lab will allow low-risk Holy Spirit Hospital patients to undergo the heart tests without being transferred to other hospitals.

headline: College cost up here; but lags national rise
abstract: College costs in Pennsylvania are rising at 6.5%, which is 3% above the inflation rate of 3.5%.  However, it is a smaller increase than the 10% rise in college costs nationally.

headline: Test models inaccurate, WTI hearing is told
abstract: Test models cannot predict the health risks of a suspected cancer-causing chemical that the Waste Technologies Industries hazardous waste incinerator will emit said enviornmental officals.  They believe the test won't properly messure the amount of exposure to potential cancer causing agents whereas WTI operators say the plant will safely destroy 99.99 percent of all the material it handels.

headline: 'Deadbeat dad' crackdown is useless
abstract: It is more costly than helpful to go after 'deadbeat dads' because the crackdowns are ineffective.  Even if they do work those that are caught would be mostly teenagers, with limited money to help support anyway and it futher undermines the instiution of marriage and sweetens the financial incentive to have more out of wedlock births.

headline: Protest against hunger
abstract: The failure of Congress to reinstate the House Select Committee on Hunger prompted a Hunger strike by Ohio Chairman Tony Hall, and protests in Pittsburgh, among them US Representative William Coyne and representatives from Food Bank, Just Harvest, A Center for Action Against Hunger, the Hunger Services Network, and the Lutheran Services Society. The protestors wanted to raise political awareness about the importance of monitoring hunger issues.

headline: Free trade foes spar at local NAFTA hearing
abstract: Business and labor faced off in Pittsburgh yesterday over the proposed North American Free Trade Agreement, as Pennsylvania lawmakers conducted the first of several hearings to gauge the trade pact's impact on the state economy.

headline: Mayoral candidate calls panel a 'social club'
abstract: Gary Henderson said he won't seek the democratic City Committee's endorsement for his run for Mayor of Pittsburgh because "that's a social club for the Catholics and I'm not a Catholic".  The tention had been buildling since his last run for office.

headline: The Gov. Whose Time Has Come
abstract: Newly elected New Jersey Governor James Florio saw support vanish when he raised taxes literally overnight without publicizing his budget. Florio toured the state defending his policies but only seeking to make more enemies. However, with the Clinton victory and recent Republican missteps in fostering Bush support and attempting to override a gubernatorial veto on assault rifles, Florio's ratings have risen over other gubernatorial contenders including Christine Whitman.

headline: Job seekers struggling
abstract: Layoffs. Layoffs. Layoffs.  That seems to be the extent of news on the economy's health.  Nonetheless, beneath the appearances of a pink slip blizzard, something surprising is happening: job growth.

headline: Hospital to defend plan for service
abstract: Carlisle Hospital and Heatlh Services will make its case tomorrow for the addition of a $3 million magnetic resonance imaging service at Carlisle Hospital.  Hospital officials, who have been criticized recently for their involvement in money-losing, non-hospital subsidiaries, say the MRI proposal is one of three new hospital-based projects aimed at upgrading facilities.

headline: College drops newpaper case
abstract: The University of Pennsylvania said yesterday it won't take disciplinary action against nine students who confiscated copies of the student newspaper in an April 15 protest.  Interim President Claire Fagin and interim Provost Marvin Lazerson accepted a special faculty officer's recommendation not to proceed any further with the case.

headline: The One That Slipped In
abstract: Blair Horn, of the New York Public Interest Group, was upset by the quick passage of a bill to eliminate new, strict emissions standards for cars sold in New York during a NY Legislature budget meeting. Thomas Jorling, Commissioner of the NY State Department of Environmental Conservation said that the potential law would inhibit the ability to meet the Federal Clean Air Act provisions, costing the state its federal transportation funds.

headline: Death row gets another killer
abstract: Frederic Jacob Jermyn, a Cumberland County man convicted of killing his 80-year-old mother, was put on death row yesterday, and the warrant was signed by acting Governor Mark Singel, his first authorization of a death warrant.

headline: Retiree age might rise
abstract: The retirement age, already scheduled to rise from 65 to 67, may have to be increased further because so many baby boomers could live into old age that it would overwhelm the Social Security system, the new Social Security commissioner said yesterday.

headline: It opens the door for U.S. businesses to flee wages, standards and protections
abstract: In the final days leading up to the vote in the US House of Representatives, pro-NAFTA forces are trying to sell it to the American people as primarily a tariff-reducing agreement that will make it easier for US-made products to be sold in Mexico.  But NAFTA's primary focus is not tariffs, nor is it the opening of the Mexican consumer market.  If it were, US corporate interests wouldn't be lobbying so furiously to get it passed.

headline: Mayoral candidates urged to hire women for top posts
abstract: The Women's Leadership Assembly, a group representing more than 30 women's organizations in the city, has issued a challenge to the three major mayoral candidates: Hire women for one-half of all city leadership positions.

headline: The Governors' Untouchable Subject
abstract: The article discusses the meeting of the National Governors' Association and the fact that many governors are seen as possible Presidential candidates, though at the meeting none of the governors would discuss a potential future bid.  Carroll A. Campbell, Pete Wilson, William F. Weld, and John Engler are all Republican governors thought to be planning to run to be their party's nominee.

headline: Jobless Rate Underestimated, US Says, Citing Survey Bias
abstract: The Government has been substantially underestimating unemployment for at least a decade or more, particularly among women, the Labor Department reported today.  As part of the biggest revamping in the 53-year history of the Government survey that determines the nation's official jobless rate, researchers at the Labor Department have discovered a bias in the survey under which many women who were seekign jobs were erroneously described as homemakers, and therefroe not counted as being in the workforce.

headline: Hospitality in place
abstract: Philadelphians should be proud of the organization, Hospitality Philadelphia, which welcomes guests to Philadelphia.  The company hosts guests in private residences and gives them behind the scenes tours of establishments in Philadelphia.

headline: Colleges link service, scholarships
abstract: While President Clionton's National Service Porgram, which Congress approved in September, will create an opportunity for students to finance their educations through community service, many colleges around the country have long had programs that tie financial aid to volunteer activity.

headline: There's nothing anti-business about cleaning up the water
abstract: It is time that this nation's chemical and industrial polluters learn that the public waterways are not their private sewer systems for disposal of their industrial wastes.  But to listen to a spokesman for the chemical industry, an effort in Congress to strengthen weak clean water laws is an affront to apple pie the American way.

headline: Death warrant signed
abstract: A Mechanicsburg man will be put to death in December unless the US Supreme Court stops the execution.  Acting Governor Mark Singel Tuesday signed a death warrant for Frederic Jacob Jermyn, who was convicted of first degree murder in 1986.

headline: Real welfare reform
abstract: The PA House approved a Republican concept of welfare reform last week that would remove more than 40,000 individuals from General Assistance, while the Democrats wanted a plan of providing job training to the able-bodied and to seek more federal funding.  The editorial board asks where the reform was in their plans and calls for a plan that will cut the cycle of dependency and poverty.

headline: Midstate enterprise flourishes in Mexico
abstract: Business ties already bind the United States and Mexico- ties that are multiplying and strengthening even as Americans debate what kind of economic relationship the two countries should have.  Debate over a proposed North American Free Trade Agreement has turned a spotlight on Mexico.

headline: Mediocre and mellow
abstract: President Clinton would come off sounding a lot better if he had mediocre, mellow, middle aged people writing his speeches instead of the young and brilliant. This would broaden his appeal to more people.

headline: The HACC budget
abstract: A breakdown of the votes of 22 school district delegates to HACC lists 12 members voting in favor of the vote, 9 voting against, and one delegate absent from the vote.

headline: Keys to tax reform success
abstract: John Manna, political reporter for the News, suggests tax reforms begin with lowering property taxes and increase wage or income taxes. However, local officials do not have authority to raise wage taxes unless they have drafted a home rule charter, which few have. Manna suggests requiring a limit on property tax increases, perhaps by prohibiting increases for a few years after new tax levies, and limits for subsequent hikes to the annual inflation rate.

headline: Hospitals accused of excessive charges
abstract: Five hospitals in Pennsylvania are being sued b attorneys Stephen R. Bolden and John Dodig for practices that are violations of the Racketeering Influenced and Corrupt Organization Act, the Sherman Antitrust Act and the 14th amendment by charging $1 per page and an administrative fee for printing pacients medical records.  The suit claims that the hospitals are doing this in order to prevent malpractice suits.

headline: Colleges relying on part-time teachers
abstract: Across America, colleges and universities are increasingly dependent on part-time teachers, cheap labor in budget-conscious times.  With federal, state and local governments tightening outlays for education, with the public demanding that tuition be kept down, school administrators increasingly can't do business without part-timers.

headline: This one will take PA drivers' breath away
abstract: Good news! You will be paying more for your next new car if some do-gooders concerned about your right to breath cleaner air have their way.  Pennsylvanians for Clean Air want the Legislature to mandate additional "smog-reducing" equipment on every new car sold in our state.

headline: Debate over jail belongs in public, not courtroom, solicitor says
abstract: Beaver County Solicitor Dale Fouse said he wants to get the discussion about the $21.5 million jail into a public forum rather than a courtroom.

headline: Reform as a code word
abstract: Representative Matthew Ryan refers to a House vote to control welfare spending.  What the House really did was simply reclassify people, without real cause, making them ineligible for welfare.

headline: NAFTA- a special report
abstract: The North American Free Trade Agreement would eliminate trade barriers between the three nations.  Some facts are given for what the people need to know about it.

headline: Mellow Bill prompts 25 teachers to retire in Parkland
abstract: 25 employees in the Parkland School District, many teachers according to Jeffery Grim, the district's business manager, have told administrators they plan to retire in August under the provisions of the Mellow Bill. Superintendent Gary McCartney commented on losing a lot of talent in one year to the bill that allows public school employees who are least 55 years old and have had 10 year of service the opportunity to receive higher pension payments if they retire before August 31, 1993 created by PA Senator Robert Mellow.

headline: The Heart That Didn't Die
abstract: The article discusses the life of Mike Lucas.  He was from an impoverished area and had difficulty keeping employment.  He was the type of person PA Governor Casey had promised to help in campaign speeches, and when Lucas died, his heart and liver went to Governor Casey who was suffering from a genetic disease.

headline: No jobs, no riders; mass transit hit
abstract: The country's lackluster economy has been tough not only on workers but also on the public transit agencies that carry many of them to and from their jobs.  With unemployment rates higher in large urban areas than elsewhere, public transit agencies, typically found in those same areas, are particularly at risk.

headline: Hospitals' exemption from tax is in peril
abstract: The protracted struggle between hospitals and local governments over taxes and municipal services has been largely a two-sided argument- but that's about to change.  Initiatives pending in Washington, DC, and in Harrisburg could have a significant impact on the tax-exempt status of Pennsylvania hospitals.

headline: Colleges score with tax-free income from big-time sports
abstract: Without congressional oversight, the Internal Revenue Service grants colleges tax exemptions for all commercial football broadcasts as "educational" ventures. Critics argue revenue is not used to substantiate education, rather to underwrite less profitable sports. Thus the National Collegiate Athletic Association and College Football Association have earn millions  tax-free, while other nonprofits are denied exemption for commercial ventures under the Unrelated Business Income Tax.

headline: Today's course: Advanced trash
abstract: Lower Merion's new trash policy is too complicated to be successful and includes five categories of trash.

headline: Defusing a crisis at M.L. King
abstract: Parents, police, and security guards were in full-force at the Martin Luther King High School where African American and Jamaican students have been battling each other and drugs are an issue. Members of Mantua Against Drugs were also there, as well as members of the Philadelphia Anti-Drug/Anti-Violence Network.

headline: Shelter no place to raise children
abstract: More low-income housing in Bucks County would go a long way toward solving local homelessness.  So would better public transportation and cheaper child care.  These services were at the top of Nancy Stroukoff's list for ways to eliminate the Red Cross Homeless Shelter, which she directs.  And all, she said, would increase the quality of life for the shelter's most precious resident's- the homeless children.

headline: NAFTA will boost economy, US labor secretary says
abstract: Labor Secretary Robert Reich said that he expects lower-skilled assembly-line jobs with US automakers will move to Mexico if the North American Free Trade Agreement is approved.  But he said that overall, the industry should see an increase in jobs as it sells more cars south of the border.

headline: Metamucil man
abstract: In Debuque, Iowa, last week, Senate Republican Leader Bob Dole said his age would not hinder a 1996 presidential bid.  "They may be ready for the Metamucil generation after four years of Clinton," Dole said.

headline: The holiday passed by and some eggs were never found.
abstract: A cartoon depicts the tired and somewhat dejected looking face of PA ex-Judge Joseph O'Kicki on an egg hidden behind a tree in a rural landscape as the sun sinks.

headline: Nothing Personal
abstract: It is unjust that securities tax isn't being collected.  Last year 40,000 persons who filed a return which totaled $12 million dollars would have failed to pay if not for more intense investigations.  If they do not collect this tax rigorously it may give the idea that other taxes can be avoided, whether out of ignorance or defiance.

headline: Hospitals to discuss prevention
abstract: A hospital in the Pittsburgh area has called on 100 Western Pennsylvania hospital executives to convene a regional forum on preventing medication errors.  The call for a regional forum by St. Clair Memorial Hospital in Mt. Lebanon was spawned last week, when hospital executives met to dicuss the content of the series.

headline: 'Consumer Challenge' is met
abstract: The finals of the first "Consumer Challenge," sponsored by the state attorney general's office, featured four-student teams from Harrisburg Academy and Camp Hill High School.  Camp Hill claimed the championship.  Afterward, Renardo Hicks, director of the Bureau of Consumer Protection, praised the students from both schools.

headline: Underground dump fire feeds on itself, evacuates residents
abstract: An underground dump fire in granville forces local residents to evacuate their hosue.  The fire has been burning for over a week.  The fire is in the process of being put out using a million plus gallons of water.  There is some delay because the ground is becoming too soft to use digging equipment to find the fire.

headline: DHS had abuse reports on Port Richmond boy found in basement
abstract: A 3-year-old boy whom police found naked in the basement of his Port Richmond home with a broken leg, bruises and cigarette burns on his body had been the subject of frequent reports of child abuse and neglect.

headline: Singel tours rehab center, lauds vocational program
abstract: Acting Governor Mark Singel visited a vocational rehabilitation center in Harrisburg yesterday and said he was committed to continuing welfare reform efforts by helping people to move from welfare to work.

headline: Singel: Developing European partnership
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel discusses how he met with business and government leaders in Great Britain, Poland, and Belgium to initiate several large-scale, joint venture, and academic-business research partnership efforts between European and Pennsylvania business and universities. The ultimate object was to sell Pennsylvania as a player in the global economic marketplace. This is a step in the right direction in achieving economic success in the world marketplace.

headline: Mezvinsky caved in to pressure
abstract: Representative Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky didn't "represent" her constituents as the "Federalist Papers" would have dictated, according to a recent Guest Opinion contributor.  Our Founding Fathers were invoked to show that politiciasn should be restrained by the need to be dependent upon the electorate.

headline: The Hush Rush Law
abstract: Members of Congress may not care for the attention, but despite a few excesses, talk radio has become a thriving part of the new, wired-up democracy.  Rush Limbaugh, the Godzilla of talk radio, has 20 million listeners a week.

headline: Number of jobs drop
abstract: Job numbers down in non-agricultural fields by 20,600 in Pennsylvania in December according to state Department of Labor and Industry analysts report.

headline: Hospitals, lawmakers linked to tobacco; Hospitals have investments totaling more than $800,000
abstract: Three Harrisburg hospitals have investment over $800,000 in tobacco companies, saying the hospitals have no investment policies, and arguing there is no conflict with investments and responsibility to public health and reducing smoking related deaths. Bill Godshall of SmokeFree PA and other critics argue investments contradict the hospitals' purpose and recommend, along with George Yanoshik, vice president of the American Cancer Society's PA division, a review of nonprofit health investment policies.

headline: Crestwood will battle for more aid
abstract: Several Crestwood Area school directors and taxpayers are forming a committee to lobby for an increase amount of state subsidies the district recieves.  Gov. Casey has increased the education budget by $100 to the neediest schools, but Crestwood hasn't increased aid in 3 years although their student population has increased by 200 students in the past year.

headline: Valley farmers favor some type of controls on deer herds
abstract: Area farmers have been forced to contend with crop damage from marauding deer for years.  Some suburban residents also are rooting for hunters this season, hoping dmage to landscaping around their homes can be curbed by reducing the deer herd.  The issue has come to a head in Fox Chapel, where council recently voted to allow limited archery hunting this year.

headline: Drug  Companie' Profits Finance More Promotion Than Research
abstract: The drug companies are spending more in advertising than in research and development which leads some to believe that they are abusing their powers and profiting too much.  The drug companies defense is that many of the products they spend millions on in research never make it to the shelves.  Schondelmeyer of the University of Minnesota  wants the drug companies to make their budgets public.

headline: State can't lien on welfare recipients' dreams anymore
abstract: The Pennsylvania legislature repealed a law that allowed welfare liens on welfare recipients' homes.

headline: State won't wait to reap benefits
abstract: Don't expect Pennsylvania exports to Mexico to boom as soon as the ink dries on NAFTA, but it won't be too long until some businesses see substantial benefits, state manufacturing lobbyists predicted as they awaited the US Senate's expected weekend vote on the trade pact.

headline: Midas pays $51,250 to settle case
abstract: The operators of 12 Midas Muffler shops in the region have reached an agreement with the state attorney general's office over allegations that certain needed repairs weren't made, while some that weren't necessary were performed.  Midas, while denying any wrongdoing, will pay $51,250 to settle the case.

headline: The latest: Casey to be back Nov. 29
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey is expected to return to power Novemeber 29, not next Monday when the Legislature returns, according to the Capitol rumor mill.  Why then?  The governor's son, Patrick, is getting married Nov. 26 and logistics would make it easier for Casey to return to the job after the long Thanksgiving weekend.

headline: Passing on the buck?
abstract: Pennsylvania taxpayers will have a chance to pass on $50 million in state spending when they go to the polls Novermber 2.  If approved, the money from the bond issue would be allocated among several state agencies.

headline: Hospitals, lawmakers linked to tobacco; Hospitals have investments totalling more than $800,000
abstract: Three Harrisburg hospitals have investmented over $800,000 in tobacco companies, saying the hospitals have no investment policies, and arguing there is no conflict with investments and responsibility to public health and reducing smoking related deaths. Bill Godshall of SmokeFree PA and other critics argue investments contradict the hospitals' purpose and recommend, along with George Yanoshik, vice president of the American Cancer Society's PA division, a review of nonprofit health investment policies.

headline: Crisis aversion
abstract: The Harrisburg Area Community College has boosted delegate participation, but the funding process still awaits reform.

headline: Valley garages worried about lost business
abstract: The PA State Department of Transportation is giving the Arizona company Envirotest Systems Corporation the job of emissions testing in compliance with the federal Clean Air Act. While not implementing the system would cost the state about $1 billion in US highway money many are angry about the losses that local businesses will face from no longer running the emissions tests. The new tests will also be a lot more extensive and could result in more cars failing.

headline: Drug violence hits home: Resident beaten and shot after confronting dealers
abstract: Santiago Pineda a resident in Hunting Park in Philadelphia has fought to keep drug dealers away from his home and children by calling the police several times and was beaten and then shot twice.

headline: State implementing new hospital payment rates
abstract: Despite a review board's rejection, the state Public Welfare Department is moving ahead with new reimbursement rates for hospitals treating poor people.  The Independent Regulatory Review Commission turned down the regulations 3-1 Friday.

headline: The issues NAFTA raises, minus the spins
abstract: What you may not have heard, are the unadorned facts about the North American Free Trade Agreement.  Those facts, looked at objectively, suggest that the deal, which gradually eliminsates most of the trade barriers among the United States, Mexico and Canada, would be neither the disastrous economic blow predicted by its opponents nor necessarily the economic boom promised by its supporters, according to economists who have studied the treaty.

headline: Midstate clout
abstract: Not that Republicans seem poised to take over the US House, but if they ever did, you could be seeing two central Pennsylvania faces running the show.

headline: The legal eagles hit a head wind
abstract: Lawyers face a new era as the '80s grow dim.  Cost-conscious clients, new billing policies and layoffs chill the atmosphere.

headline: Poll: Congress not spoiling to get tough on budget
abstract: Poll says that Clinton will face tough opposition on several important fronts, such as raising the gasoline tax, cutting taxes for the middle class and creating a civil rights bill for gays.  The budget deficit remains to be an issue that will most likely be gridlocked due to partisan differences despite public disguist.

headline: Hospitals, Seeking Simplicity, Mostly Welcome Health Plan
abstract: If for no other reason, hospitals generally welcome President Clinton's proposal to overhaul the health system because nearly everybody would carry basic coverage and hospitals could rely on a regular stream of income.  More-over, hospital administrators hope that the Clinton plan to draft a single uniform insurance claim form would reduce the mounds of paperwork.

headline: CV teacher contract approved
abstract: Over objections of several taxpayers and two school directors, Cumberland Valley School Board Monday approved a two-year contract with the district teachers union.

headline: Warminster must replace welands filled in to build golf course
abstract: Eight acres of federally protected wetlands were destroyed when the 133-acre Five Points Golf Course was built in 1988.  When the wetlands were filled in, flooding occurred, and now the township must replace those wetlands in another section of the watershed, Department of Environmental Resources officials ordered.

headline: Fired officers win suit
abstract: Clearing three of four Westmoreland County Commissioners, a jury awarded punitive damages to two North Huntingdon officers who claimed they were fired after disability leaves and disagreements with Police Chief Charles Henaghan. The township claimed the officers dismissal was due to unsatisfactory evaluations by the Chief, however in a video, Thomas Krause, the convicted commissioner, referred to the officers as useless.

headline: State Pushes Change
abstract: The newspaper commends PA Governor Robert P. Casey for his implementation of the federal Americans With Disabilities Act.  He ordered improvements to be made to parks that are accessible for people with disabilities. He ordered every state agency to follow the federal law.  He also issued an order to people working in state government to not say or write "disabled person" in their work, but instead "person with disabilities".

headline: Trading away future
abstract: We send American jobs to Mexico, so they can make more money, so they can afford to buy American products, which aren't made here anymore.  Somehow linking ourselves with one of the poorer countries of the world is supposed to bolster our economy.  Doesn't appear to be so.

headline: Military suffers from low morale
abstract: Military morale has dropped greatly in the last year since they earned victory in the Gulf War. Members are facing the biggest staff reduction in decades and they are contending with a seemingly disillusioned public. Many military men are threatened at the prospect of gays in the military, causing some to threaten to quit.

headline: The missing element of the recovery: Jobs
abstract: Due to government fees and regulations it is becoming more profitable for employees to replace humans with machines so that while the economy is recovering employmenet is not increasing.  One example of that is the law that says companies of over 50 employees must give paid leave.  Some companies are capping at 49 so they won't have to pay the extra expense.

headline: Recession hit the region harder, head of Phila Fed tells senators
abstract: The Federal Bank has released numbers that show Pa, De, and Nj have been slow to recover from the recession.  Even into the second year of recovery all three are still losing jobs whereas nationwide the number of jobs have increase substancially.

headline: How hot was it? A sultry 98, with no relief in sight
abstract: Meteorologists are now warning that the worst heat wave in at least two years is likely to continue to next week.  Yesterday's official high, 98, tied the record for the date.  The heat can pose a serious health threat.

headline: Despite revisions, OBE wrong for state
abstract: PA Senator Michael Fischer writes that he thanks the Patriot for writing about outcome-based education when the PA Board of Education had ignored it.  He writes that he opposes outcome-based education because it is the wrong direction for education and it has failed in trials.

headline: Washington Twp. Oks building of sewage plant
abstract: In Washington Township supervisors voted in favor of a sewage treatment plant that the Pucketa Creek Watershed Association and its supporters do not agree with. The supervisors submitted a proposal to the PA Department of Environmental Revenue and any letters expressing opposition are being submitted to the Department as well.

headline: First, Clean up the court
abstract: The PA Supreme Court is a mess and needs to be quickly changed in accordance with the accusations of Larsen against Zappala and Cappy, including attempted murder.  If they are guilty, wholly or partly, they must be impeached.  If they are not, Larsen must be impeached for making up the accusations.  Besides the short-term problems, the Supreme Court has too much power and needs to be limited to deciding cases.  No longer should it have administrative or legislative powers.

headline: States slice into programs
abstract: States continue to cut into the benefits provided by the government for the poor.  This year money was cut from the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program.

headline: Travel tax on block
abstract: The White House, still short of the votes needed to pass a free-trade act with Mexico and Canada, signaled yesterday it was open to a compromise that would eliminate a proposed travel-tax increase.  But the administration and its congressional allies asserted that they were gaining ground even though controversy over the proposal to raise fees on airline and cruise travel is cutting into support.

headline: Ministers in an Uncomfortable Spot, Defending Their Honor
abstract: Whether one believes Edward J. Rollins Jr. when he said this week that the campaign of Christine Todd Whitman had funneled money to black ministers so they would not urge their congregants to vote, or believes Mr. Rollins when he later retracted the comments, angry ministers say one thing is clear: Mr. Rollins has diminished the credibility of the black clergy at a time when blacks can least afford it.

headline: The new business leaders aren't from Philadelphia
abstract: A columnist writes that he believes Philadelphians are too modest, and that their lack of ambition has resulted in many Philadelphia institutions disappearing, and the fact that many Philadelphia financial institutions and businesses are run by people not native to Philadelphia.

headline: Sales pitch
abstract: The opinion piece discusses President Clinton's televised presentation of his economic plan.  This plan would increase taxes on the rich, decrease taxes on the poor, increase the gas tax, and both add and eliminate expenses.  The plan is meant to reduce the deficit.  The writer feels his plan will achieve its goal, but that it did not go as far as it should have.

headline: How to get latest info on cancer
abstract: People with access to a fax machine now can get the latest information about cancer by calling a computerized data bank maintained by the National Cancer Institute. NCI is a government agency that has a broad mission to educate the general public and physicians about the causes, prevention, diagnosis and treatment of cancer.

headline: Direct lending for college loans a dubious idea
abstract: Jay Evans, the president of the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency writes about President Clintons new proposal which is a far-reaching series of changes in student financial aid. He wants to create a national service initiative and direct federal loans that would eliminate banks, other lenders and guarantee the PHEAA from the programs. Evans thinks that the direct service is a great idea but he is worried about the direct loans. He believes they will end up being more costly to the students and the schools. The PHEAA has offered seven proposals that they think would help.

headline: Waste disposal site opposed
abstract: Greene County commissioners said Thursday they will pass a resolution opposing a proposed low-level radioactive waste disposal site that will be placed in one of Pennsylvania's 67 counties.  The request for a resolution came from Mary Potter, a member of Greene County Citizens United, who presented a draft of a proposal she asked commissioners to consider.

headline: Flimflam king skips his day in court
abstract: Street hustler Nick Ward scammed thousands of dollars from Philadelphians using made up predicaments and problems. Given his previous record, Ward, in violation of parole, would have been arrested had he appeared for his hearing. Former assistant district attorney Anthony Vocci, defense counsel, believes the city will not pursue the arrest warrant, but prosecutors are confident Ward will resurface.

headline: Support voiced for the National Service Trust Act
abstract: A woman writes to the newspaper urging representatives in Congress to support the National Service Trust Act, which would allow people to earn money for college by doing community service.  She feels this program will pay for itself in the benefits gained from the community service.

headline: Control by the elite
abstract: The North American Free Trade Agreement is not about free trade.  It will not abolish restrictions on trade in North America, but rather creates more than 30 appointed committees, councils, working groups, secretariats and sub-committees to rule on trade matters previously the sole domain of the elected Congress.

headline: Miss Penn National Insurance makes a choice.
abstract: A political cartoon shows a woman on a dating show, her two potential suitors hidden from her, choosing bachelor number one. The woman is named Miss Penn National Insurance, and the bachelor, whose jubilance is evident, Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed.

headline: The PG favors serfdom
abstract: The editorial on postal and federal workers was a real hatchet job and the paper receives favored postal treatment as a second-class mailer, making the attack more unsupportable.  The Postal Workers Union deserve and expect Hatch Act reform and have earned it.

headline: Santorum, Coyne tackle tax measure
abstract: US Representative William Coyne, D-Oakland and US Representative Rick Santorum, R-Mt. Lebanon on the House Ways and Means Committee are at opposite ends of the political spectrum of a major bill that calls for tax increases and some spending cuts, which is at the heart of President Clinton's plan for trimming budget deficits.

headline: HUD chief's son's malformed heart rebuilt
abstract: Surgeons yesterday rebuilt the malformed heart of John Paul Cisneros, the son of Housing and Urban Development Secretary Henry Cisneros.  The 2.5 hour operation created a four-chambered heart that is expected to perform normally.

headline: Discipline is a local decision
abstract: There are competing interests in the effort to ban corporal punishment from Pennsylvania's public schools.The concept is that local people can best determine what works best to educate their own children.  The decision on how discipline is to be maintained should likewise be a local decision.

headline: Waste proposal unveiled
abstract: A dozen members of the Adams County Solid Waste Advisory Committee and municipal officials met Wednesday night to hear a presentation on a new anaerobic co-composting system.  The meeting was held in an effort to expose those present to a variety of solid waste disposal opitons, according to county commissioner Richard Waybright.

headline: Focus on crime control
abstract: Micheal Fuoco's article misses the point and 'spins' it to promote fear and ignorance rather than respect and knowledge of firearms.

headline: The end of Welfare?
abstract: Columnist William Raspberry may wonder what would happen if the welfare program was ended, but his observations of Ohio's Learning, Earning, and Parenting program make him reluctant to find out. The LEAP program gives incentive and punishment to young mothers who return to school for a diploma. Unfortunately, as New York's Manpower Demonstration Research Corporation has found, not everyone does what others feel is in their best interest.

headline: Coyne visiting Asia
abstract: U.S. Representative William Coyne and other members of the U.S. House Ways and Means trade subcommittee are visiting China, Hong Kong, Japan, and Vietnam.

headline: Mixing Medicine and Politics
abstract: Two Philadelphia doctors are under question for multiple offenses and abuses at a Philadelphia nursing home.  Most of the questing that is outside of the home deals with the relations to political donations and investments in the tens of thousands.  With all this being said and countless civil cases and government investigations Mayor Rendell still renued their city contract.

headline: The Philistines have a history of cutting the heart out of the city
abstract: The architectural and historical theme park that once was in the vicinity of Front and Walnut Streets is now just about gone.  And thanks to the recent end run around the historical commission, the Elisha Webb Chandlery, is one of the last to go.  Nowadays, the streets where Philadelphia first got started are boring and barren.

headline: Senate committee approves county referendum option
abstract: Pennsylvanians could vote on whether they want higher income or sales taxes in exchange for lower property taxes under a bill approved by the PA Senate Finance Committee. The legislation represents the latest bid for statewide tax reform and was sent to the full Senate.

headline: Hype has produced 'health-care crisis'
abstract: It’s unbelievable the amount of press the 'health-care crisis' is receiving in the press.  In any system of medicine there will be those that suffer, but one must look at our system and see who is suffering and why.  The media enjoys throwing statistics out that fan the flame of resistance, but under further review we have one of the most impressive medical care in the world.

headline: District hints at tax hike
abstract: Board of Education President Rotan Lee yesterday said the School District of Philadelphia may have to request a tax increase to fend off an expected $49 million deficit facing its 1995-96 school year.  The suggestion came after Irv Davis, the district's managing director, reported the district had pared an expected $30 million deficit for the 1993-94 school year to $16.8 million.

headline: Waste Technologies' plant delays wounding local firms
abstract: The litigation and controversy surrounding Waste Technologies Industries, a hazardous waste incinerator seeking a commercial operation permit in Ohio, is hurting local chemical firms. Federal and state laws and regulations are hiking the costs of waste disposal. With controversy continuing and involvement of Greenpeace and the Coalition for Responsible Waste Incineration, local plants say the future is dim for small companies, which cannot afford to meet regulations larger companies can.

headline: Foot patrols draw praise
abstract: With a beat officer on the streets of every neighborhood, Pittsburgh citizens find the streets are running a lot smoother.  These "community-oriented" police aren't supposed to invade crack houses to slap on handcuffs and arrest suspects.  They're supposed to fulfill the stated goal of Public Safety Director Lou DiNardo and Police Chief Earl Buford- to form a police partnership with communities.

headline: The subway vagrants
abstract: Although no one wants the cronically homeless to freeze to death it is wrong to allow them to squat in the subways causing an  unbearable stench.  The best solution is to give these people  a warm building  where they can continue their self-distructive ways away from the public, because most  of these people have  been 'red-tagged' from shelters for disruptive behavior.

headline: Croatian president urges US action
abstract: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, visiting the US, spoke to the Croation Fraternal Union, repeating a popular theme of Croats who want more outside involvement in the region. Tudjman plans to press President Clington, the United Nations,  and other world leaders to lend air strike support against the Serbs, whose violent seizure of much of former Yugoslavia has been costly for Croatia.

headline: MMM goes to Washington
abstract: MMM, Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky, a democrat has won a seat in US House in the 13th district PA.  It is an area that has 2-1 Republicans.  Summary of her professional and personal carreer in route to becoming a congresswoman which included Harvard, publishing books, working in the media, and raising a family.

headline: The question of questions: An experiment in polling
abstract: Results of H. Ross Perot's mail-in survey in the 1992 presidential campaign are compared with those for the sam equestion given to a national sample by Yenkelovich & Partners, a more neutrally worded version of the question submitted to a national sample and still another version given to another naitonal sample by the Gordon Black Corporation.

headline: Serious budget-cutting
abstract: If Congress really wants to reduce the federal deficit, here are two ways to do it.  The first serious package of spending cuts offered for the upcoming debate was the "Penny-Kasich Plan."  Just last week, a bipartisan group of senators, including New Jersey Democrat Bill Bradley, introduced the "Kerrey-Brown Plan"- a somewhat similar plan with slightly greater savings.

headline: In Scope and Vision, Health Plan Defines Clinton Presidency
abstract: Nothing the president has done- or is likely to do- better defines aspirations of the Clinton presidency than the massive health care plan delivered to Congress yesterday.  Woven through the 1,300-page health plan is a liberal's passion to help the needy, a conservative's faith in free markets and a politician's focus on the middle class.

headline: District says teachers may not strike
abstract: Susquenita School District officials and Curt Rose, a representative of the PA School Boards Association and Susquenita's chief negotiator have told teachers they are expected in the classroom, not on the picket line a day after teachers called a strike for that day.  District officials moved to prevent a year-end walkout, arguing that new state laws governing negations prohibit it.  Board President Ronald C. Brown delivered the letter to union president Pam Cananaugh.

headline: What a waste in Chester County
abstract: The Chester County commissioners had a problem.  The Solid Waste Authority was already in the red, and things were only getting worse.  In all, more than $9 million was needed to get the finances under control and put the trash system on a solid footing for the next decade.  Obviously, something had to be done.  Fortunately, Chester County had the money to do it, namely a $16 million budget surplus.

headline: FOP sues city over contract, seeks preliminary injunction
abstract: The Philadelphia Fraternal Order of Police is suing the city over an alleged invalid and illegal police contract. The suit alleges that the arbitration process between the FOP, the neutral arbitrator, and the city arbitrator was conducted in a corrupt manner.
