Mayor Rendell's chief of staff David Cohen says the victory for Rendell in trying to reduce the city's labor costs did not violate the arbitration process.

headline: They put heat on state
abstract: A handful of needy folks and citizen advocates planned to spend last night in the Capitol rotunda protesting cuts in a government home-heating program.  Under sponsorship of the Philadelphia-based Consumer Education and Protective Association, the group also held a late-afternoon news conference to call for state lawmakers to pick up the slack on a federal program losing funding.

headline: Exporting prisoners one hard-cell idea
abstract: Representative Peter J. Daley suggests that prisoners farmed out to such supposedly willing nations as Turkey, South Korea and Mexico could be housed for as little as $6 per prisoner per day in comparison with current domestic rates of $60 to $100 daily, and came up with a proposal of farming out prison inmates to foreign countries.  Serving foreign time would reinforce the sometimes forgotten idea that jail time is hard time.

headline: MMM's Top Ten
abstract: The day after Vice President Al Gore schmoozed with David Letterman, he appeared at a breakfast fund-raiser for Montgomery County Congresswoman Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky.  Noting that Big Al had unleashed his own Top 10 list on Letterman, MMM offered her own Top 10 list, explaining why she voted for Bill Clinton's budget.

headline: The race for governor does have issues
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel writes about the 1994 race for governor asking that the candidates and the press enlighten the public instead of entertaining them.  He summarizes the measures he's introduced as a candidate to promote economic security in Pennsylvania including local tax reform, campaign finance reform, a Community Reinvestment Act, and etcetera.

headline: Smoke and Mirrors-Clinton Budget masks deficit, rather than cutting deep enough to reduce it
abstract: The article criticizes President Clinton's $1.5 trillion budget proposal reducing the deficit growth rate yet still increasing the total. The critic questions Clinton's fiscal integrity and environmental dedication, after revealing less spending on the Land and Water Conservation Fund for National Park Services than he had criticized Bush for, more for the Drug Enforcement Administration, and less for the Federal Bureau of Investigations. US Defense Secretary Les Aspin referred to the budget as treading water.

headline: Indiana Medicaid won't pay for some of Lakeberg twins' care
abstract: Indiana's Medicaid office will not pay for the medical care that the Lakeberg twins had in order to be separated after birth. The office is arguing that since the surgery happened at the Philadelphia Children's Hospital it is not at liberty to pay the bill.

headline: Districts sue again for funds
abstract: The School Boards Association went back to the Commonwealth Court to force PA to release funds withheld over outcome based education. The PA Department of Education says the stalemate in the Legislature has prevented the release of funds. So far, two amendments have been added to the bill, with the final version being blocked twice by opponents over objections of the school districts who are extremely disappointed, said PSBA spokesman Thomas Gentzel. The PA Secretary of Education also expressed his disappointment with the current situation.

headline: What's in a landfill?
abstract: The newspaper asked its readers to respond to the question of whether landfills were safe, and several wrote in to give their opinions.

headline: Gag order is issued in air-crash lawsuits
abstract: A Montgomery County judge has ordered that any settlements of lawsuits from the fatal 1991 mid-air crash over Merion Elementary School that killed US Senator John Heinz be kept secret.  The order by Judge Paul W. Tressler, who is overseeing the civil suits, forbids plaintiffs, defendants and lawyers from disclosing "the fact and amount of any settlements."

headline: Those on dole should work, poll says
abstract: President Clinton wants to reform welfare by imposing a two-year limit on benefits.  After this time, a person must work in order to receive benefits. Welfare recipients would also need government-funded job programs, education, day care and health care in order to work however.  The majority of people polled for this article favored including the work requirement after two years.

headline: Israel's cost to the U.S.
abstract: Person writes in to the newspaper to criticize the federal government for cutting back on domestic programs, while simultaneously sending billions of dollars of aid to Israel.

headline: Modest reforms are a start-Newcomers in Legislature get lesson in power
abstract: Newcomer PA House representative Albert Masland is relieved at recent reform, the first in 15 years to examine perks abused by congress members, though he knows the reform is modest at best. As a member of the most partisan Legislature in the nation, Masland has seen laws passed in force by rules virtually mandating uninformed voting. He is hopeful the House can move on towards more pressing issues of reform.

headline: The Right Choice: Pittsburgh mayor is stepping down
abstract: Mayor Masloff announced that she will not seek the Democratic nomination to run for re-election as mayor.  At age 75 she has gracefully declined to run again.

headline: State gains new fiscal muscle on its debt, tax 'take'
abstract: New Jersey's budget for the year 1994 is looking better thanks to a decision by the federal government to allow the state to defer one year repayment of $96 million debt left by the Kean administration.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: The Capitol cleared in six minutes for a fire drill that was staged while the PA Legislature was in session, according Michael D. Brooks, institutional fire and safely specialist in the PA Department of General Services.  AIDS service organizations, including the South Central AIDS Assistance Network, brought their plea for more money for AIDS education to the Capitol and are seeking $1.5 million increase or three times as much as PA Governor Casey Proposed in the 1993 budget.

headline: Don't abandon libraries
abstract: The editorial takes the position that cash-strapped governments are making a mistake by taking books out of people's hands. While budget cuts for libraries may be less politically painful than welfare or life essentials, hindering learning and success is not a wise strategy. Libraries alone should not bear the pain of budget sacrifices.

headline: White House Issues An Order to Bolster Recycling of Paper
abstract: After months of wrangling between environmental groups and the paper industry, the Clinton Administration yesterday issued an executive order requiring Federal agencies and the military to buy paper made from at least 20 percent recycled fiber by the end of next year and 30 percent by the end of 1998.

headline: Gallo's Humor
abstract: Conditions in the most poverty stricken, drug ridden streets of Northeast Philadelphia might be too much for any other Narcotics Field Unit, but not former Marine and Lieutenant John Gallo's. Frustrated by the Philadelphia prison cap forcing him to allow busted dealers back on the street the next day, Gallo continues his work in the community with tenacity that is both surprising and respected by various community anti-drug groups, commanding attention even from the American Civil Liberties Union and law enforcement at the federal level.

headline: Thousands of Fayette welfare recipients see liens lifted
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey signed legislation to remove liens on the homes of welfare recipients.  Thousands of Fayette County welfare recipients can now secure loans for home improvements. This came about through lobbying efforts of groups like the Mon Valley Unemployed Committee.

headline: Mandela? De Klerk? What's the P.C. dilemma?
abstract: We Americans have a lot of nerve preaching racial tolerance to South Africa.  Perhaps we should recommend that South Africa take care of its indigenous population with the same genocidal dispatch in which we annihilated ours.  Philadelphia, the birthplace of this imperfect American experiment, is exactly the place where Nelson Mandela and FW de Klerk should come together to ponder the wondrous possibilities and inevitable heartaches that lie ahead for the people in the country they love.

headline: Mon Valley Young Woman of Year named
abstract: Kristina Carlstrom of West Mifflin has been chosen as the Mon Valley Young Woman of the Year for 1994.  Carlstrom, a senior at West Mifflin Area High School, was chosen Sunday from among 19 finalists from seven public and parochial high schools in the Mon Valley.

headline: The right place, the wrong man
abstract: Steve Lopez is not sure US Senator Arlen Specter, given his reputation as a supporter of the National Rifle Association, is the right man to lead the cry for an investigation spanning several executive offices, from US Attorney General Janet Reno to the Oval Office, considering his track record for investigations and the pain of Senate Judiciary Committee officiators. Lopez hopes Specter's publicity will increase pressure to discuss his opposition to President Clinton's emergency stimulus plan with Mayor Ed Rendell, which Rendell supports.

headline: State must reject its 'comfortable concepts'
abstract: John Dankosky, executive director of the Pennsylvania Business Roundtable in Harrisburg, writes that PA needs sound tax policy, balanced environmental regulation, effective public education, and more state government accountability to survive economically in the 21st century.  He says the State Tax Commission needs to develop a long-range tax strategy to fund state and local government and evaluate the impact on PA's private and public sectors.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Health-care plan before Senate panel
abstract: Various PA legislative committees will be meeting. The Senate Public health and Welfare committee will meet to discuss health care reform.  The House Education Committee will continue its review of improving vocational education programs offered in the state.  The House Labor Relations Committee will discuss legislation regarding workers who go on strike or are fired. The House Judiciary Committee will hold a public hearing regarding product liability.

headline: Dropout rate in Pa. schools declines third straight year
abstract: The dropout rate in PA school fell for the third straight year n 1991-1992 in grades 7-12, dropping from 2.59 percent to 2.5 percent. The Allentown, Bethlehem and Easton city school districts are higher than the state average and the Philadelphia City School District had a 7.8 percent dropout rate.  Pittsburgh School District had a 5.4 dropout rate.

headline: Workers' literacy is crucial to job safety
abstract: Occupational-safety and environmental-protection experts say many occupation accidents occurred because the people involved could not read.  Many saftey experts and literacy professionals believe there is a close correlation between low educational levels found among some American workers and occupational and environmental safety.  Many cannot read the labels that would protect them.  Chemicals are a key worry.

headline: Gearing up
abstract: To put it charitably, the General Assembly has not taken much of an interest over the years in accusations against state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen, preferring to leave a myriad of questions about the justice's ethics to the now-defunct Judicial Inquiry and Review Board.  But as a state grand jury winds up its investigation of Justice Larsen's behavior and of sensational accusations he has made against some of his colleagues, that passive attitude is changing.

headline: Volunteers modestly accept honors
abstract: Community volunteers honored by the The Volunteer Center, The Junior League of Harrisburg Inc., and the Patriot-News Co. were recognized for services work in institutions, hospitals, and other private and public facilities. Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, who presented the awards, said this kind of service goes far beyond the scope of any government program and needs to be encouraged. A former rehab client won the Junior League's Challenge Award.

headline: Mexico has changed
abstract: Cyrus Hitz' comments on NAFTA omits the fact that Mexico has experienced dramatic changes.  That nation's decades-old tradition of protection and intervention have been replaced with massive privatization and deregulation, and like the US, needs exports to boost economic growth.

headline: Money for votes? Of course
abstract: Ed Rollins, the political manager who out-strategized White House guru James Carville in the recent New Jersey gubernatorial race; when asked a question, he is compelled to blurt out the dangerous truth.  His need to expose the existence of what pols have long called "walking around money"- henceforth to be known in the annals of psychiatry as Rollins' Compulsion- has provided the healthiest revelation in politics this year.  His 'strategy' is nothing new.

headline: The Rollins Cloud's Silver Lining
abstract: It's been two weeks since Ed Rollins, a consultant to New Jersey's Republican Governor-elect Christine Whitman, gave America's political community a bad case of indigestion with his offhand breakfast remarks that he spent $500,000 in "street money" to discourage black ministres and Democratic workers from getting voters to the polls.  But amid all the partisan outrage on one side and the denials on the other, some key points have been ignored.

headline: Steil wrong on budget
abstract: State Representative David Steil's comments show how much he has to learn about being honest with the people he represents.  He is quoted as telling business people in Bucks County that the new state budget does not make an investment in economic development.  Nothing could be further from the truth.

headline: Insurance pros strain to solve long-term care
abstract: Long term insurance is growing in popularity as more and more people contemplate spending their final years in nursing homes; the insurance is very complex though doesn't always work the way it's supposed to. Pennsylvania recently has adopted regulations for long-term care insurance sold to the commonwealth that provide consumer protection.

headline: Easton woman is Warren's top teacher
abstract: Johnette Lyn Bennett of Easton, a science teacher at North Warren Regional High School in Blairstown has been selected by the County Review Committee through the County Superintendent's Office to be recognized as the 1993 Warren County Teacher of the Year through the Governor's Recognition Program.  She will now compete for the State Teacher of the Year.

headline: WTI is again allowed to burn
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and PA Department of Environmental Resources have given Waste Technologies Industries permission to restart commercial incinerator operations based on tests that show pollution control equipment is effective.

headline: Grand jury and Larsen becoming adversaries
abstract: PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen cooperated fully with a grand jury when the grand jury began investigating his allegations about the corrupt behavior of other justices on the state's high court, but has stopped cooperating since evidence led the grand jury to begin investigating Larsen himself.

headline: Welfare bill isn't 'reform.' Scrap it.
abstract: The welfare reform legislation is disgraceful. Reform implies change for the better but the bill before the state senate guarantees increased hardship for those at the bottom of Pennsylvania's economic well. PA Governor Casey is also sending mixed messages about his feelings on the bill.

headline: That sucking sound: Prez sucked in
abstract: Right from the start, selling the North American Free Trade Agreement to Congress has been an uphill fight.  The combination of anemic economic recovery, persistently high unemployment and the ravings of a big-eared fraud about a "giant sucking sound" has made NAFTA anathema to Americans scared for their own jobs- and to the finger-in-the-wind types who pass for political leaders.

headline: Montco GOP sings the blues
abstract: The Montgomery County GOP is struggling as the democrats seems to be holding strong in what was once a Republican stronghold.  In addition to the election problems the lack of funding the GOP is reciving has been detrimental.

headline: The Scene In Philadelphia and Its Suburbs: All the better to see your shame
abstract: The author makes fun of Channel 12 family therapist John Bradshaw's cosmetic surgery.

headline: Stimulus fans work 2 ways
abstract: Lobbyists, including Ralph DeGennaro, budget analyst of Friends of the Earth and York, PA Mayor William Althaus, president of the US Conference of Mayors, are working two fronts: make sure Senate Republicans accept President Clinton's stimulus package, and prevent the administration from ditching favored packages. Critics claim the stimulus is laden with pork-barrel spending, and the administration's Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Henry Cisneros has hinted at compromise.

headline: Is managed care unmanageable?
abstract: President Clinton will present his health care reform plan next month.  However, the article says that the states will make changes to the health care system on a state level before the federal government does.  PA Governor Casey's plan involves cutting costs by using a system of completing managed-care n networks that offer health coverage for all except the elderly on Medicare. Doctors would be paid predetermined fees and the system would emphasize preventative care. The state legislature is just beginning to analyze his plan.

headline: Educating campus in crime
abstract: As 24,050 University of Pennsylvania students began a new semester last week, crime in the university's economically depressed West Philadelphia neighborhood was at an all-time high.  To combat the threat, campus policing has reached a new level of sophistication and saturation.  Part of that effort is an orientation program for parents entrusting Penn with their children's care.

headline: 1 grade drops at N-plant
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission gave the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant top grades on maintenance, engineering and plant support, but said operations need some improvements.  A newly released report card noted weaknesses in operators' performance of infrequently performed activities during a refueling outage and weaknesses in communication and teamwork.  The operations grade dropped a notch from Category 1 to 2.

headline: Grant to fund boot camp for teen offenders
abstract: The Harrisburg-based Abraxas Foundation and Cumberland County have won a $300,000 federal grant to establish a boot camp in the Adams County woods for teen offenders with drug and alcohol problems.

headline: Welfare Lien removal sought
abstract: Members of the MonValley Unemployed Committee are seeking PA state legislation to remove welfare liens on homes of welfare recipients. Allegheny County Commission Tom Foerster told the Committee he agrees with their efforts to repeal the PA law establishing liens in the amount of welfare received, expected to be paid once recipients go off welfare. The Committee says liens are causing credit damage and are unrealistic.

headline: null
abstract: A specially designed, interactive video wall will allow visitors to play the role of their state legislators.  Seated at the voteing desks, visitors will see an issue presented on a video screen, complete with comments from lobbyists and constituents, and an actual debate or simulation debate from the floor.  Voters will then vote on the issue by touching "Yay" or "Nay" on the video screen.

headline: More for themselves
abstract: The editorial board notes that no new legislation of substance has reached the PA governor's office since session began, but that both sides are united in trying to raise salaries and perks of the job. The editorial board is thankful the House Rules Committee ended some double-dipping concerning leased cars and mileage and a stopped expense reimbursements to $34 for those legislators within 50 miles. However it is irksome to the board that most legislators consider reimbursement a supplement to their pay.

headline: The Scene In Philadelphia and Its Suburbs: Entitlements?! Of Course you know this means war!
abstract: The writer makes fun of the conference that was held at Bryn Mawr College that discussed Social Security, calling for generational warfare. The writer believes that US Representative Majorie Margolies-Mezvinsky made a wise choice trading a vote on a "more-of-the-same" deficit budget for 1994 to be the first to know about the Social Security battle to come in the future years.

headline: Targets of ire by public don't cost that much
abstract: An article examines the $1.5 trillion budget proposed by Clinton and discounts theories that most of the money is going to areas the public views as unnecessary. In reality, the real big spending items are Social Security, Defense, Healthcare, and interest payments. For fear of re-election however, congress is unable and or reluctant to make significant cuts on any of these big ticket items.

headline: Is Pa. drug review hurting elderly?
abstract: The Pharmaceutical Assistance Contract for the Elderly program was created to review drugs to make sure patients are receiving the right medications at the right dosages.  If a patient wants to obtain a drug that is not yet approved, the state will not pay for the patient to buy that medication.

headline: Education chief to try again for names on tests
abstract: In baseball, it's three strikes and you're out.  But yesterday, after a committee of the State Board of Education rejected a proposal to require students to put their names on tests designed to assess how well schools are doing their jobs, state Education Secretary Donald M. Carroll Jr. said he will make another pitch in January.

headline: 26 Pa. counties to receive $471, 949 for nuclear emergency preparedness
abstract: The Pennsylvania Emergency Management Council approved a total of $471,949 for 26 counties to help support on-going nuclear power plant emergency preparedness and response programs.  PA Lieutenant Governor Mark S. Singel is the chairman of this council. The funds are allocated by the Radiation Protection Act.

headline: Gun battle
abstract: In a heated public hearing on the Wagner bill, which would ban assault rifles and other semiautomatic weapons in the city, supporters told stories of loved ones beingshot with the kind of weapons that Wagner wants to ban, and opponents spoke of loved ones preventing crimes because they carried guns.

headline: Welfare panel hears the appeals for overhaul
abstract: The article discusses President Clinton's welfare-reform task force that met to hear testimony from women on welfare.  President Clinton's goal is to get people off welfare, but many who get off of welfare face great difficulties afterwards.

headline: null
abstract: Cartoon about the Pittsburgh Regatta.  District justices are mentioned.

headline: More than 15,000 in state lost jobs
abstract: The number of layoff's during the second quarter of 1992 was up 10.4% from earilier that year.  15,125 had lost their jobs between April and June 1992.

headline: The Scene in Philadelphia and Its Suburbs: Stinson-Marks? Isn't that a housing project?
abstract: According to the author everyone knows about the PA Second District state Senate election and the candidates William G. Stinson and Bruce Marks.

headline: Tax breaks send steel mill south
abstract: Tax breaks in Kentucky apparently led Canadian steelmaker Dofasco Inc. to locate a steal mill there instead of western Erie County. The state did everything possible to make the Erie site attractive but it just wasn't enough.

headline: It can be done
abstract: The editorial board writes that stories from Germany and Canada proves that a modern democracy can provide health care for all of its citizens, which is important while the Clinton administration tries to launch their health care reform.  The American Medical Association opposes the reform due to salary caps and the administrative nightmare it may ensue.

headline: Education leader calls for support
abstract: Grassroots support is necessary to achieve President Clinton's education goals, US Education Secretary Richard Riley said Thursday.  He called Clinton's "Goals 2000: Educate America" proposal a partnership between federal and state officials, and local communities that takes a bottom-up approach to education reform.

headline: After TMI break-in, sides differ on need to increase security
abstract: Witnesses want an increase of security, posibly from a private agency, but law makers and the company at Three Mile Island Nuclear Plant don't see the need.  A break-in at the nuclear plant in which the driver of a car smashed throw a door and then into a turbine room and was not found for 4 hours is what has caused the new talk of security or lack there of.

headline: Gun control an issue at city, county state levels
abstract: While police data raises questions about how effective a Pittsburgh City Council gun-control initiative would be, Allegheny County Commissioner Pete Flaherty is pushing for the proposal.  And state legislators have begun looking for their own ways to try to quell rising violence on the streets.

headline: Welfare reform coming
abstract: While the Clinton Administration struggles to get its welfare reform effort under way, a few states are racing ahead with proposals of their own to fulfill the president's campaign promise to place strict time limits on benefits.

headline: A Clinton aide predicts 'historic breakthrough'
abstract: President Clinton's chief counselor, David Gergen, said yesterday that Congress and the White House appeared on the verge of a "historic breakthrough" in reforming the health-care system.

headline: 'Motor voter' bill becomes law
abstract: President Clinton signed into law a landmark measure requiring states to ease voting registration, ending a hard fought battle by Democrats, and advocates for young, disabled minority Americans. This law requires states to allow registration by mail, as well as when citizens apply for or renew a driver's license, visit welfare and other government agencies or stop by a military recruiting office.

headline: The Scene In Philadelphia and Its Suburbs: The Knowxville strut, or memories of Manayunk
abstract: Greater Kennsington String Band went to the Knoxville, Tennessee Santa Claus Parade and taught the locals the Mummers Dance.

headline: Tax loophoes for the rich: The worm at the heart of the Clinton economic plan
abstract: Charles Krauthammer views President Clinton's new economic plan as a corrupt attempt at political patronage, given the government's level of involvement in the private market and various tax loopholes and indulgences for states and industries 'on-board' with the plan. In Krauthammer's opinion, the massive state expansion into the inner-workings of the economy is a reversal of the heralded 1986 tax cuts and a sign that the current economic plan needs to be reviewed.

headline: It is Temple's site or none, Shriners Hospital officials testify
abstract: If the setting had been the Old West, somebody with an itchy trigger finger surely would have snarled that Philadelpia wasn't big enough for the three of them.  Instead, the battle over a proposal to build a new pediatric-care facility in one of the city's most impoverished neighborhoods took place inside a cramped hearing room on the eighth floor of the state Health and Welfare building.  So, the combatants had to make do with lawyers.

headline: Education nominee Riley rips tax dollars for school choice
abstract: Secretary of Education-designate Richard Riley said he would oppose any project which parents could pay for private schools with pulblic dollars.  The Clinton White House will not consider any such program either.  The Bush Administration promated such a program.

headline: Cheaper mortgages hold down living cost
abstract: The US Department of Labor reported a lesser inflation growth rate for the month than in months previous, with estimated annual inflation matching the previous year's 3 percent. However, almost all items surveyed for a price index in the Harrisburg area saw a decrease in rates, with mortgage rates decreasing the most. The only downturn to the news are petitions to the PA Public Utilities Commission by utility companies to raise rates.

headline: Gun control won't stop urban violence, but it's a start
abstract: Controling guns will not prevent violent crimes, but would be a good step in the right direction.  The NRA has lost two minor legislative battles in Virginia and in New Jersey, yet still have a strong grasp of influence on the issue.  Clinton hopes that they will pass the Brady Bill which will not infringe on the rights of people to own guns yet will still keep them out of the hands of criminals.

headline: Convention Center's not accessible to all?
abstract: Advocate groups for the disabled such as Disabled in Action of Philadelphia are angry that the Philadelphia Convention Center does not comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act. They are requesting that Pennsylvania Convention Center Authority officials renovate the building so that it is more accessible to the disabled.

headline: A Clinton Pitch Aimed at the Middle
abstract: Bill Clinton rose to national prominence as a self-proclaimed New Democrat, promising to build on the legacy of Roosevelt and Truman and Johnson with new approaches to old problems rather than relying on tired old formulas.

headline: Motor-voter pushed
abstract: A legislative hearing before the PA State Government Committee to discuss purging from the system registered voters having not voted for two years as well as other ballot and election changes will be held in the Allegheny County Courthouse. Federal legislation that would automatically register drivers license applicants to vote is currently pending and will also be discussed, as the state must approve the enactment before its implementation in PA.

headline: The Scene In Philadelphia and Its Suburbs: The sound of silence goes unnoticed
abstract: The bell on top of the PNB Building in Philadelphia has not been ringing due to repair work being done to it.

headline: Tax plan hurts the rich, helps the poor
abstract: The article discusses who would benefit from or be burdened by Clinton's deficit-reducing plan.  The richest 1.2% will face a large income tax increase, but no one else will be affected.  A 4.3 cents a gallon increase on gas will be imposed.

headline: It's an honor
abstract: President Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton will visit Beaver County Wednesday to promote the Health Security Act.  The Clintons selected the perfect location to talk about the impact of health-care reform.

headline: English: Kids' language of choice
abstract: Children of the USA's most recent immigrants- Latin Americans and Asians- not only prefer English, but many are abandoning their parents' native tongue, according to a new study.

headline: Coal industry creates jobs and economic strength, as well as electricity
abstract: Ted Clutter, the direct or communications at the PA Coal Association, reports that a recent study by Adam Rose, head of mineral economics at Penn State University funded by a PA Coal Association grant, quantified coal mining's benefits to the PA economy finding that coal mining creates a "multiplier effect" which stimulates production, income and employment in nearly every sector.

headline: Gun-permit case stirs debate on the right to know
abstract: The Erie Times is entitled to some data on applicants for gun permits, the court said.  The National Rifle Association disagreed.

headline: Cool air coming to public housing
abstract: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development will now allow public housing to provide air conditioning. The Department will not give housing authorities extra money to install air conditioning, but housing authorities can choose to pay for it with existing funds. The tenants will have to pay the cost of operating air conditioning.

headline: A look at teacher salaries
abstract: Teacher salaries have risen consistently in recent years, but still alg behind those in most other white-collar professions, according to the American Federation of Teachers.  Charts show teacher salaries across the world and show other professional salaries in the United States.

headline: Motor-voter pushed
abstract: A legislative hearing before the PA State Government Committee to discuss purging rfrom the system egistered voters having not voted for two years as well as other ballot and election changes will be held in the Allegheny County Courthouse. Federal legislation that would automatically register drivers license applicants to vote is currently pending and will also be discussed, as the state must approve the enactment before its implementation in PA.

headline: The wrong way to settle teacher contract negotiations
abstract: State Senator Robert Jubelirer's letter proposing that all teacher negotiations be conducted in public was fascinating.  Clearly, he is one more politician pandering to the teacher-bashing mentality that sweeps this state every autumn and has reached a level that surpasses all rhyme or reason.

headline: Tax reform, once again
abstract: The tax reform for local government has been an issue that has been of concern of the people for a decade without much done about it.  Any time a politican tries to reform the tax system it is quickly ruled out in Harrisburg to the frustration of many.

headline: It's not too good to be true
abstract: Pennsylvania's health care coverage for children of low-to moderate- income families was launched in May, funded by a 2-cent-per-pack cigarette tax on cigarettes levied in 1991 by the state Legislature.  Under the program, insurance for children is free or half cost, depending on a family's income and size.

headline: Equality, not choice, holds the key to educational excellence
abstract: America's current status as the first industrialized nation in the world where children are the poorest segment of the population has been caused in part by the willingness of adults to abandon responsibilites to the next generation  The absence of a national ethic of commitment to meeting the needs of all children has unquestionably resulted in disenfranchised and angry students in our schools.  We need renewed state and federal effort to reform school financing so the rights of all children to adequate education are fully protected.

headline: Coal prices sent soaring
abstract: The forces of nature have combined with a United Mine Workers strike to force a "substantial" surge in the price utilities are paying for one-time purchases of coal.  Eventually as many as 700 laid-off union miners may be recalled at the three mines of CONSOL operations.

headline: Guns in schools not the half of it
abstract: The violence in junior high and high schools is bad, but the streets are worse.  In an interview with four juveniles it is discovered that guns are everywhere and that if they don't get oyou in the schools, they'll get you outside.  It is rediculous to hold a magnifying glass to the schools, when outside they are dropping like flys.

headline: County gets development grant
abstract: The PA Department of Commerce Secretary Andrew Greenberg presented the Indiana County Development Corporation with a $100,000 check at a conference hosted by PA state Senator Pat Stapleton to finance economic development strategy. He also agreed with an assessment of the Indiana County Office of Planning and Development that most new jobs will come from existing businesses. President of the Indiana County Visitors and Convention Bureau, requested that state officials give the county more of the money they are entitled to for promoting local tourism attractions.

headline: null
abstract: The author is remarking on how Ellen Casey, PA Governor Robert P. Casey's wife, is the one that lit the Capitol Christmas tree and not Acting PA Governor Mark Singel. The author says it shows Casey is not willing to hand everything over to his surrogate as he recovers.

headline: Move sparks exchange
abstract: A heated exchange occurred between members of the Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County when commissioner Richard Vidmer and Terrry Marolt voted to replace Robert Smouse with Robert Miner, a certified public accountant of Donegal Construction Company. Ted Simon accused the two of caring more about to whom appointees belonged along with accusations by Smouse that the pair started their election campaigns early.

headline: There is strong support for election of judges
abstract: PA Senator writes to the newspaper about his proposals for judicial reform. The newspaper wrote an editorial about his proposals and implied that Pennsylvania citizens would rather a system where judges are appointed by merit rather than elected.  The Senator says that Pennsylvania citizens have voted against merit selection.  His judicial reform proposals would have judges elected but would limit lawyer and law firm contributions and would lift the gag rule on judicial candidates and rotating names on the ballot.

headline: The deficit: It depends on how you look at it
abstract: President Clinton's budget proposes the biggest deficit-reduction in history, yet despite decreasing the deficit growth rate, it will continue growing annually. Critics argue a faster deficit reduction could cause a recession. Clinton's budget directer Leon E. Panetta, and Susan Tanaka, vice president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, say the next budgetary issue is health care reform.

headline: It's simple, really
abstract: None of the controversy surrounding the "quick" double transplants of a heart and liver recently performed on Governor Casey would have occurred if there were a sufficient supply of life-saving organs.  While that may seem obvious, the shame is that with a little effort and better understanding, the need to ration scarce organs could be greatly reduced.

headline: Ex-CMU deans call for 'revolution'
abstract: Robert Cyret, one of six former deans at Carnegie Mellon's Graduate School of Industrial Administration, as a panel member dedicating the department's newest building, called for innovation, saying the school was no longer unique in its teaching strategies. Former dean Allan Meltzer called for a revolution. Among other panelists were  former deans Elizabeth Bailey, Herbert Simon, George Leland Bach, Dennis Eple, and current dean Robert Sullivan.

headline: Electromagnetic foes to gather
abstract: About 250 people are expected to attend a conference this weekend sponsored by opponents of high voltage power lines.  The National EMR Alliance, a New York-based group that organizes local opposition to electromagnetic fields, will bring leading power line opponents to the South Hills on Friday and Saturday.

headline: Guns-for-cash program collects 155 weapons
abstract: Cash the city collected from the sale of a drug dealer's confiscated 1989 BMW was used to collect weapons 'no questions asked' from city resdients.  Residents could turn in guns and receive $30.  Those who ran the program called it a success because they colleted 155 guns, yet they admitted most of them were old and more likely to hurt the people shooting the guns than those who the gun was pointed at.

headline: Covenant signing is urged
abstract: Developer Jonh O. Vartan and local religious leaders are asking community residents to commit to their vision for rebuilding city neighborhoods by signing the Inheritanace Covenant, which has advice for safe, happy, and healthy lifestyle.

headline: null
abstract: William A. Mattiford writes a quick poem describing how we will lose jobs here if we go along with NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement.

headline: Mr. Clinton comes to Ambridge, and other notable tales
abstract: Some notes are given regarding the presidential visit to Ambridge Area High School in Beaver County.

headline: They'll still vote the old-fashioned way in the Senate
abstract: The state Senate is spending $46,500 on a system that will alow votes to be recorded electronically, yet its 50 members will continue to announce their yeas and nays the old-fashioned way, by individual voice vote.  The installation is taking place during the multimillion-dollar renovation of the Senate, whose members have elected not to use an electronic tote board that could shorten a laborious, arcane process to the time it takes to flip a switch.

headline: The wrong target
abstract: It was inevitable, after years of economic pain in the form of downsizing and givebacks and declining income and job losses, that the labor movement and rank-and-file workers would find a vehicle to express pent-up rage, anxiety and fear.  Unfortunately, opposition to NAFTA is the wrong vehicle.

headline: Job prospects generally rosy in health care industry
abstract: Chances are getting better to find a job in the health care industry across western Pennsylvania and the rest of the country.

headline: Fifth-graders hear lesson on Senate
abstract: Fifth-graders at Greenwood Elementary School strained to see out the wondow as state Senator Melissa Hart arrived Wednesday.  Hart visited the classroom as part of student teacher Mary Lou Rethmeyer's community education project- in which students are learning about all the elements that make up their community, including family, business and government.

headline: Energy assistance slashed
abstract: The US Congress cut its funding for PA's Low-Income Heating Assistance Program from $134.6 million in 1986 to $96.4 million. Due to these cutbacks, PA has been forced to make cuts in eligibility  and Cathy Regets, energy supervisor for the Fayette County Board of Public Assistance said fewer Fayette County residents would qualify for funding.

headline: Handgun found in boy's coat
abstract: At the Swatara Junior High School a boy was found to be carrying an unloaded semiautomatic weapon, according to Swatara Township Police Sergeant Robert Simmonds. The boy, who's name is unfamiliar with police, has not had any indication of violence before and did not threaten anyone.

headline: DCA is willing to give city second chance on Fairlawn
abstract: The state Department of Community Affairs will give the city of Scranton another chance to document how it spent $225,000 on the Fairlawn Apartments project.

headline: 19 say ballot signatures forged
abstract: Two absentee voters hadn't lived in the city- or the state- for two years.  Another had moved from the Second district in May.  Others could have gone to the polls.  Antonio Batista, father of Niltha Schloeffel, compares the signature on an absentee-ballot form with her signature on another form.  Schloeffel said it's not her signature.

headline: Mrs. Clinton now shepherd of bill
abstract: Hillary Rodham Clinton shifted yesterday from supervising the preparation of the White House's health care plan to becoming its chief negotiator in the tough bargaining that lies ahead.  The first lady, cast in an unusually prominent role, signaled the White House's willingness to compromise with Congress even before her husband formally introduced the 1,336-page measure to House, Senate and Cabinet members in a ceremony on Capitol Hill.

headline: They're talking about:
abstract: PA Senator Francis Lynch's illness might have an effect on the Democratic leadership's hopes of sending a budget to the House by week's end.

headline: They're talking about:
abstract: The PA Senate will amend the PA House-approved supplemental appropriations bill with a $15.2 billion general fund budget and have the next year spending package on Casey's desk by the end of the month.

headline: Key elements of health progran unresolved
abstract: State officials yesterday disclosed a revised schedule and other details about a health program planned for 620,000 low-income Philadelphia area residents, but acknowledged that key elements, such as whether contractors will have to be licensed, still are not resolved.

headline: Filling their dance cards
abstract: Four of Pennsylvania's universities will be in the NCAA basketball touritment.  Those teams are Temple, University of Pennsylvania, Temple, and Pittsburgh.

headline: Energy levy won't curb energy use, analysts say
abstract: President Clinton's proposed tax on oil is said to help protect the environemnt and reduce dependency on foreign oil, but experts don't think either will happen.  The tax is too low to have any real impact on either.  It is just another means of te government collecting more revinue and because it is phased in, most won't even notice.

headline: Happy Valley's low-crime status questioned
abstract: According to District Attorney Ray Gricar, "The popular misconception of Happy Valley as a totally safe and peaceful community is incorrect.  There is danger here just like there is in any other community."

headline: DCA, WAM sometimes cross paths
abstract: Auditor General Barbara Hafer's recent WAM grant audit singled out the state Department of Community Affairs, which processes more grants than any other state agency, for failing to monitor the program.  The audit cited 1,500 alleged contract violations in which there was little or no accountability for $15.5 million worth of grants.

headline: 2 TV networks could air segments of fugitive judge
abstract: Judge O'Kicki, 62, was declared a fugitive on March 8 after he failed to show up for a bond revocation hearing in Northampton County.  Both America's Most Wanted and Unsolved Mystories are looking into doing a story on the fugitive judge.

headline: Mrs. Heinz passes
abstract: Teresa Heinz's elaborate walts around the issue of whether to run for the US Senate ended unexpectedly yesterday when she turned in her dance card.  So much for the speculation that she would seek the seat once held by her late husband John Heinz.  Her statement was at once a tribute to what is right about America and a warning about what is wrong.

headline: Thieman favored for U.S. attorney
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford recommended that President Clinton nominate Pittsburgh lawyer Frederick Thieman as U.S. attorney for Western Pennsylvania. Wofford also recommended several other democrats to fill the two U.S. district court vacancies in the Western District. The choices will be sent to the president for review by the White House and Justice Department.

headline: Unemployment rates up slightly
abstract: Unemployment rates for Franklin and Fulton counties went up slightly during May.  The counties had a 6.4% unemployment rate for the month compared to a 5.9% mark in April.

headline: Key health care plan issues
abstract: President Clinton's health reforms would alter the way Americans get heatlh insurance and force sweeping changes on the health care industry.  A look at some of the issues is given.

headline: Finland: A Free School System With Very Few Cracks
abstract: Finland's education system is considered to be a good one without any real problems, according to a study by the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development. One major incentive to stay in school is that there is a high unemployment rate in the country.

headline: Four Schemes
abstract: A brief explanation of the four schemes used in order to evade $15 million in federal and excise taxes on diesel fuel. The schemes center around heating oil and diesel fuel which are chemically the same, since heating oil is not taxed.

headline: Hard time
abstract: The editorial board does not feel federal guidelines assure time fits the crime, especially in the case of "career criminal" James Battles, recently sentenced to 22 years in federal prison on the basis of previous convictions, this time for dealing less than a gram of heroin. The board called for revising guidelines to take into account kinds of drug convictions leading to careet-criminal designation, and emphasis on drug programs. US District Judge Gustave Diamond expressed frustration, feeling his hands were tied.

headline: DRPA officials: Port-unity talks to stay private
abstract: The discussion over whether to unite the Philadelphia and Camden ports stays behind closed doors, under no violation of law, argued Delaware River Port Authority chairman Reverand Nicholas Rashford. The board has argued that designing a strategy in the public eye would be impossible. However, others familiar with the discussion have said the closed door policy is due to discussion of patronage and not to strategic economic planning.

headline: 2 ways to campaign for mayor-Wagner knocks door-knocking Murphy
abstract: After a slow start, the election campaign for the Democratic nomination for Pittsburgh Mayor heats up between PA House representative Tom Murphy and City Council president Jack Wagner. Murphy has been the front-runner, however recent allegations of ghost voting raised by Wagner might hurt Murphy's old fashioned, door-to-door campaign which refuses to respond to Wagner in accord.

headline: Murphy leads in Pittsburgh mayor's race
abstract: PA Representative Tom Murphy defeated City Council President Jack Wagner in the democratic Pittsburgh primary for the mayoral election. The winner of the democratic primary is almost assured to become the mayor because Pittsburgh has a strong democratic majority. Murphy will face the lone Republican candidate, interior designer Kathleen Matta, who made an unsuccessful run last year for the state House.

headline: Third-Party Candidate Vows Non-Traditional Campaign to Reform Court
abstract: Robert B. Surrick, the Patriot Party for state Supreme Court, predicted yesterday that sweeping judicial reforms are imminent, measures he believes will break the stranglehold exerted by the "big-city political machines" of Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.

headline: Which grants are WAMs?  Depends on who you ask
abstract: The use of WAM grants, which are grants earmarked by individual legislaters to fund projects that could not receive money through normal channels.  Gov. Casey has earmarked a certain amount of money for specific grants and has therefore taken some money from those that expected the annual grant.  They are upset and confused.

headline: Lab to pay $2.4 million
abstract: Med-Check Laboratories Inc. of Ross has agreed to pay $2.4 million to settle a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Justice Department for defrauding Medicare by getting doctors to order unnecessary blood tests.  The settlement was reached before any suit was filed on behalf of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

headline: France: A Method of Teaching that Produces Readers
abstract: According to a report by the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development, the fourteen year olds in France and Finland are the most proficient readers in their age group in the world. The schools in France achieve this by trying to make the students as comfortable as possible around words.

headline: Gas prices increase by less than tax hike
abstract: A survey conducted yesterday morning by AAA West Penn/West Virginia shows that many Western Pennsylvania gas stations didn't pass on the entire 4.3-cent federal tax increase that went into effect yesteray.  The survey showed that the average price of regular unleaded self-service gas was up 3.4-cents a gallon.

headline: He says an officer robbed him; police say he lied
abstract: Xavier Gallon has accused police of stealing $3,000 and returning it to him through the black market.  He withdrew his complaint and the police sued him for filing a false police report.  The trial is pending procedural delays.

headline: DRPA Oks $50 million in non-port projects
abstract: The Delaware River Port Authority's board voted to spend $50.45 million in surplus bridge-toll money on major improvements on both sides of the river. They compiled a list of projects that adds up to one-third of the economics development money the bistate authority expects to be able to spend during the next five years.

headline: 2 welfare offices gave out $324,000 in overpayments
abstract: Chester County's two state welfare offices handed out about $324,000 in overpayments during a period of nearly three years, according to audits by State Auditor General Barbara Hafer's office.  But that figure represents a tiny fraction of the money disbursed by the two offices during that period.

headline: My days with JFK
abstract: In 1993, during the year of unhappy anniversaries, the 30th of John F. Kennedy's murder in Dallas brought US Senator Harris Wofford to reflect on what it was like working with him, what might have been different in the country if he were living today and how he would face the challenges of today.

headline: Thurgood Marshall, ex-justice and rights activist, dies at 84
abstract: Thurgood Marshall dies at 84 after a long period of poor health.  He retired from the courts in 1991 after a long standing record of helping protect the rights of minorities and the liberity of all American.

headline: You need sharp eyes to see recovery in Pa.'s factories
abstract: It's hard to believe that an economic recovery is underway in Pennsylvania.  Last week's unemployment rate showed that the number of jobless in the state had climbed for the third straight month, with most of the job losses in manufacturing.  Amid the continuing losses, a glimmer of good news surfaced in the Harris Industrial Directory, indicating that employment in Pennsylvania's industrial sector improved slightly over the last year and the number of new manufacters in PA grew, a sign the industrial sector is on the rebound.

headline: Let's cover health care for women, state urged
abstract: Democratic Sen. Allyson Schwartz unveiled her plan, Pennsylvania Women's Health Security Act, which proposes to have the government cover the cost for women at or below 300% the poverty level to see doctors for preventive services.   These would include gynecological exams, pree-natal care, second opinions concerning hysterectomies, and other female problems.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: Lottery sales are down.  Hess, then executive director of the Senate Enviornmental Resources and Energy Committee handed out business cards that had Japanese on the back from when he traveled to Japan.  A conference called 'Censorship '90s Style: It could Happen Here' will be held today to discuss case studies from museums, libraries, and schools.  Tax reform is needed said Rep. Edward J. Haluska.

headline: Higher output, lower costs are generating more interest in windmills
abstract: The article discusses the possibility that wind energy will be used more often in the future.  The price of using wind power has now fallen below that of conventional methods, and could drastically reduce pollution.  The technology is expected to continue to advance because of the federal Energy Policy Act of 1992 that o offers tax incentives for building windmills. Pennsylvania could potentially use wind energy along Lake Erie, the Allegheny Mountains, and the northeaster part of the state.

headline: Hearings being moved to Baltimore
abstract: The U.S. Executive Office of Immigration and Review has moved the hearings for some of the Chinese illegal aliens being held in York County Prison will be moved to Baltimore as the result of a lawsuit by five Pennsylvania newspapers. The newspapers are suing because the immigrants, feeling they were not receiving a fair trial, requested open hearings, but the press was denied access by the U.S. Executive Office of Immigration.

headline: Finding jobs for homeless
abstract: This summer, members of the Homeless Program Committee of the Greater Philadelphia Urban Affairs Coalition plan to talk to corporations and ask for help with a project meant to assist 300 homeless individuals and 300 homeless families over the next three years. The committees are requesting job training and jobs.

headline: 20,000 are due cable refunds
abstract: Twenty-nine Pennsylvania cable-television companies will return thousands of dollars owed to subscribers and reform their refund policies, according to an agreement by state Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr.  About 20,000  cable subscribers will receive refunds of one cent to $10.

headline: N. J. GOP candidates pay taxes for illegals
abstract: Two Republican candidates for governor, Christine Todd Whitman and her primary opponent W. Cary Edwards , paid tax liablities yesterday stemming from their employment of illegal immigrants that had worked for them in the past.

headline: Today: An overview
abstract: For the next week there will be an article in the paper on the following topics at the Federal level of government: the economy, health care, cities, education, crime, and the environment

headline: null
abstract: St. Louis joins seven cities nationwide, according to Gay and Lesbian Task Force spokesman Robert Bray, to adopt a code protecting citizens against sexual orientation and other discriminations, giving the city's Civil Rights Enforcement Agency and Civil Rights Commission the power to investigate claims, jail convicts, and administer fines. Claude Rogers, executive director to the Civil Rights Enforcement Agency, says the changes have not provoked intense reactions in St. Louis.

headline: Let's emphasize wellness, nursing spokesman urges
abstract: The best way to avoid the high cost of health care is never to get sick.  Stay well.  The problem is, many insurance compaines don't cover wellness visits such as prenatal care, annual physicals, mammograms and other health screenings.  Doctors, insurance company officials and hospital officials all said the federal government should emphasize wellness when it considers a national health-care plan.

headline: Grants in all shapes, sizes
abstract: WAM grants this year go to nearly 5,000 groups ranging from over $100,000 to under $10,000.  These grants go to organizations such as the Mid-Atlantic Air Museum in Berks County to the Little League Baseball Museum in South Williamsport.

headline: March price rises fuel inflation fears
abstract: According to the US Department of Labor's Producer Price Index, prices charged by producers jumped .4 percent in March, matching February's rate. The volatile food and energy sectors in the first three months of the year represent the worst inflation rates per quarter since the end of 1990.

headline: High court investigation under wraps
abstract: The gran jury investigating the state Supreme Court met in Harrisburg last week, but no one is saying what it did, or when the results of their inquiry will be released.  Investigators were expected last week to submit a final report to the grand jury for a vote.

headline: First Enterprise Money Arrives
abstract: Senator Pat Stapleton of Indiana, PA, on Wednesday delivered a check for $40,000 to county commissioner Tom Cayne as the first drawdown on a $110,000 annual grant to the Greater Indiana Enterprise Zone.  The grant, from the state Department of Community Affairs, will be used for administration of the lcoal Enterprise Zone, which provides initiatives to improve the local business climate and create new jobs.

headline: 3 key issues unlikely to revive soon
abstract: Three issues that are unlikely to surface again in the Legislation for some time include workers compensation, a statewide fiber optics system and local tax reform.  Workers comp and fiber optics are considered settled issues by those who wond the battle, and they are not likely to bring them out for any needed adjustments.  As for tax reform, who wants to run as an advocate of higher taxes?

headline: N.J. does spot-checks on farm vans
abstract: The Labor Department pulled over loads of blueberry pickers.  Violations were plenty.

headline: Trail littered with broken promises
abstract: When Christopher Columbus bumped into the New World in 1492, anthropologists and histornians now estimate, North America contained 10 million-50 million Indians, members of perhaps 400 tribes that functioned as independent nations.  Half a millenium later, the US government and the remaining 300 Indian tribes are committed to an uneasy relationship again, based on the notion of tribal sovereignty.

headline: 3,000 U.S. Greeks convene in city
abstract: The Order of Ahepa, which stands for American Hellenic Educational Progressive Association, is meeting in Pittsburgh.  It will honor U.S. Senator Paul Sarbanes, U.S. District Judge Gustave Diamond, and Allegheny County Commissioner Tom Foerster, among others.

headline: Local mom: 'We scratch and claw.'
abstract: The Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) provides free or low-cost health insurance for children of working parents who earn up to $33,723 per year.  It will begin in May, and will accommodate about 30,000 Pennsylvania children.  The Pennsyvlania State Insurance Department says slots are filling rapidly.

headline: Gun incidents don't sway teachers
abstract: There have been gun incidents in the Harrisburg, Central Dauphin, East Pennsboro, West Shore, Shippensburg, and Susquenita school districts. Area teachers are unwilling to view the incidents as more than isolated acts and will not let it deter them from teaching.

headline: Milestone, but no finish line
abstract: The owner of Three Mile Island, General Public Utilities, has disposed of 2.2 million gallons of radioactive water by evaporation.  The water was a remnant of the 1979 accident that destroyed the nuclear reactor.  A company spokesman declared that the process of cleaning up the accident is over, but the editorial board of the newspaper disagrees and says that there is still radioactive uranium fuel in the reactor that must be removed.

headline: Homeless, mentally ill man shot dead by officer
abstract: A Philadelphia police sergeant is under investigation after shooting and killing a homeless man who threw a bottle at him. The homeless man was shot as he was preparing to throw another bottle at the police officer. The officer tried using mace originally but it was not effective. City Council is schedule to vote on a civilian over site bill, which is adamantly opposed by police.

headline: For the homeless, hope comes via phone
abstract: An estimated 400 homeless people living in six Philadelphia shelters can now use voice mail to help find jobs and living quarters.  Now, when making the rounds of potential employers or landlords, a homeless applicant can leave the voice-mail number.  This will make it easier for potential employers and landlords to reach the applicant, and enable the applicant to conceal that he lives in a shelter.

headline: 35 shopping days 'til
abstract: State buildings and grounds workers clean up after erecting a 25-foot blue spruce with the aid of a cran on the steps of the state Capitol.  The tree is one of three to be erected around the Capitol for the holiday season.

headline: NAFTA is still short 18 votes
abstract: President Clinton remained at least 18 votes shy of vicotry yesterday ss he headed into the final 48-hour stretch run before the cruical House vote on the North American Free Trade Agreement.  Both sides said they are confident of victory tomorrow, but neither appeared to hold firm commitments from a majority of House lawmakers.

headline: Tree destroyer pardoned
abstract: The state Board of Pardons has voted unanimously to pardon a Florida doctor for blowing up a tree nearly three decades ago when he was a student at Franklin and Marshall College in Lancaster.  Dr. William Hearn sought the pardon so his criminal record wouldn't hurt his career opportunities.

headline: Abortion adversaries unite for a common goal
abstract: Anti-abortion activist Loretto Wagner and abortion-rights supporters in a St. Louis clinc have teamed up to push for better prenatal care, adoption reform and help for drug addicted pregnant women.

headline: Most midstaters back strict smoking limits
abstract: Two-thirds of central Pennsylvanians support the Casey administration's plan to ban smoking in state buildings and further restrict the practice in most public places, according to a new Patriot-News/WGAL Viewfinder poll.

headline: HACC baord backs budget, tuition plans
abstract: Harrisburg Area Community College has given a preliminary approval to a 30.1 million dollar budget plan which results in a 4% tution increase for students in 1993-94.

headline: Nuclear drill prepares county
abstract: Emergency evacuation of the area near the power plant in Luzerne County on Tuesday night.  The drill was a simulation of a radioactive leak.  Everything went smoothly.

headline: Homeowners dealing with backyard digging
abstract: Slava Kulikov is suing Toll Brothers in Bucks County Court for damages done by construction outside her home that resulted in unsafe levels of methane.

headline: For yourths, program offers another chance
abstract: Raymond Garland, 19, has decided to change his life after dropping out of higschool at 17 to sell drugs and guns.  He now attends YouthBuild, a national program just starting in Philadelphia that allows dropouts to return to school for their diplomnas and learn contruction skills by rebuilding homes in their community.  The program is funded by grants by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development as well as state and local funds.

headline: 5 in Phila. On U.S. attorney short list
abstract: Three Philadelphia Common Pleas Court judges and two lawyers, all democrats, are finalists for the position of US attorney, the region's highest ranking federal law enforcement officer. US Senator Harris Wofford is expected to make the decision within the week. The finalists are veterans in the field, some having served with the US Attorney's Office previously, and one as Philadelphia District Attorney with close ties to influential Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell.

headline: NAFTA vote sale
abstract: If it is wrong for Ed Rollins to use campaign funds to persuade black preachers not to support Jim Florio in New Jersey, why is it right for Mr. Clinton to use public funds to buy House votes for NAFTA?

headline: Triumvirate of Toms
abstract: The three Toms, Tom Murphy, being invested as the probable next mayor, Tom Foerster, Allegheny County Commission Chairman, and Tom O'Brien, board chairman of PNC bank- working together- can fill Pittsburgh area's need for leadership.

headline: Abortion foes protest at clinic by chaining themselves to cars
abstract: 10 anti-abortion protesters locked their necks to automobles that were pressed against the door of a clinic making it diifficult for police to move the cars or unlock the protesters.  The clinic remained opened and the protesters were arrested.

headline: Linking of Universal Health Coverage To Cost Containment Endures Scrutiny
abstract: It is the great chicken-and-egg question of the health-care reform debate: Which comes first, universal coverage or cost-containment?  President Clinton, during his major health-care address to Congress in September, made his own view perfectly clear.  Unless every American has adequate medical benefits, he declared, "Wed will never be able to fully put the brakes on health-care inflation."

headline: HACC session threatened if budget deadlines missed
abstract: In a move threatening the Harrisburg Area Community College's twelve week summer session, the college's Board of Delegates voted against the budget proposal, primarily due to a 6.5 percent raise in pay for teachers. An emergency session will vote to trim the budget by about $68,000 a savings for school districts who pay a third of the cost of tuition. However, many delegates say they still will not vote to approve the budget, which threatens HACC accreditation.

headline: Nuclear engineer seeking damages from Westinghouse
abstract: Terry Dysert, a nuclear engineer who says Westinghouse Electric Corp. fired him in 1986 for reporting safety violations at a Georgia facility, asked a court yesterday to award him damages.

headline: Hospitals bracing for attacks
abstract: Welcome to the modern metropolitan hospital, where saving lives today can be a life-threatening situation tomorrow, and where security- for patients, workers and visitors- is now a primary concern, especially with gang-related violence on the rise.

headline: Friends, enemies and affordable housing
abstract: Bucks County has created programs to build more affordable housing. Some object to this, however, stating that as poorer families move into a county, the services required to help them cost the county and wind up hurting it economically. The county is also having problems acquiring funding, as some state and federal agencies don't feel Bucks County is poor enough to require low-cost housing.

headline: 60G raised for Rizzo monument
abstract: The more than 400 people who gathered at the landmark banquet facility at 8th and Catharine streets plunked down $75 apiece to eat, drink and help raise money for a larger-than-life statue of the late Mayor Frank L. Rizzo who, in many eyes, was larger than life himself.

headline: NAFTA's promise
abstract: November 17 looms as a significant moment in the economic history of the United States as the House of Representatives decides- either out of fear or optimism- the fate of the North American Free Trade Agreement.

headline: Tumor Humor
abstract: The Senate Judiciary Committee was dubbed a meeting of the "Cracked Head Club" when Senator Arlen Specter arrived wearing a "Pennsylvania" baseball cap to hide the scars from recent surgery to remove a brain tumor.

headline: Abortion uproar threatens reforms
abstract: President Clinton has brought abortion to the forefront by promising to cover it under his new healthcare reform package. Even though abortion is just a tiny part of the health package it is still receiving the most attention and criticism. This has turned nation's Roman Catholic archbishops against them.

headline: Lobbying makes AIDS top disease
abstract: AIDS Awareness Day was supported by President Clinton and the US Postal Service who printed a red-ribbon stamp. The author believes that the only reason AIDS is in the spotlight versus other diseases is that they have a lobbying voice, and does not believe this to be right.

headline: Health Watch: College Students Quizzed
abstract: Study from West Chester University researchers, in the Journal of Health Education, indicates that most education majors, tomorrow teachers, will be ill-prepared to deliver the facts about because their training programs pay little attention to public health issues such as AIDS.

headline: Nuclear power plant official admits failures
abstract: Operators of a nulcear power plant "missed the boat" by failing to correct a 7-year-old refueling problem, a plant official told federal regulators.  Less than a month after a shipment of radioactive fuel struck the Unit 1 reactor wall at the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station near Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania Power & Light Co. officials said they had never looked closely at a piece of equipment that kept on breaking in the refueling process.

headline: House adopts child-abuse bill
abstract: Representative Jeffrey Piccola said the House of Representatives has unanimously approved child-welfare legislation that would enact a series of reforms, including an expanded definition of child abuse to cover those children who are at risk of being abused.  In a statewide radio broadcast, the Republican chairman of the House Judiciary Committee said, "Protecting children from abuse is difficult. Preventing it still harder."

headline: H'ford gets grant to repair damage
abstract: PA Representative Greg Vitali announced that Haverford will receive a $100,00 state grant from the PADepartment of Community Affairs to repair thirty-two homes that were damaged by foundation settlement.

headline: 7 Democrats seek hot seat in primary: Ethics charges, other controversies spotlight normally placid race
abstract: Seven Democrats are competing in the May 18 primary for nomination to the open seat on the PA Supreme Court.  Justice Ralph Larsen will be heard by the PA Legislature for impeachment over charges that he violated the canons of judicial ethics by Justices Stephen Zappala and Ralph Cappy and Larsen has in turn accused Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr., of a litany of ethical lapses.  The article includes pictures and biographies of the seven candidates.

headline: Navy yard gets 'hope' from court
abstract: Thanks to a federal appeals court decision the Philadelphia Navy Yard and its 7,000 workers may have a chance for a future. The decision sent the case back to the U.S. District Court for a hearing on the merits. Lawmakers in the tri-state area had filed the case when the Navy and base-closure commission had broken the law when it decided to close the yard.

headline: Turn on the bulb, Spotlight; Santorum voted for his constituents
abstract: The writer thinks that US Representative Rick Santorum should not be criticized for voting against the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), since it is what his constituents wanted him to do. The writer also thinks that President Bill Clinton should not be praised for supporting NAFTA and getting the House of Representatives to pass it.

headline: Abortion-rights group holds rally
abstract: Abortion-rights group holds rally in support of doctors that are not resigning after the murder of an abortion doctor in Flordia.

headline: Making health plans prove their worth
abstract: A group of large employers and H.M.O.'s will introduce a standardized report card system for all health plans.  This will allow employers and employees to see how plans perform in different area such as vaccinations of children, prenatal care for pregnant women, etc.  The Clinton administration, who will soon reveal their health care reform package, are impressed by the program and it may influence national health care.

headline: Here are academic and core goals students would aim for under OBE
abstract: The article lists academic and core goals of students under an outcome-based education plan, including communications, mathematics, science and technology, environment and ecology, citizenship, arts and humanities, career education and work, wellness and fitness, home economics, self-worth, information and thinking skills, learning independently and collaboratively, adaptability to change, ethical judgment, and honesty, responsibility and tolerance.

headline: PE to get nuclear fuel from Long Island reactor
abstract: There is a large public outcried against the proposed shipping of nuclear feul from Long Island to P.A. via trian through major cities.  The private sector proposal would save the state millions of dollars over 12 to 15 years.

headline: House arrest for embezzlement causes furor
abstract: Abington Township tax collector was sentenced to house arrest by Montgomery County Judge Samuel W. Salus for stealing more than $200,000 from taxpayers.

headline: Homewood gets city aid for coliseum, offices
abstract: The Homewood-Brushton Revitalization and Development Corp. received $100,000 from the Pittsburgh Urban Redevelopment Authority to renovate the Greater Pittsburgh Coliseum.  Money will also come from the PA Department of Community of Affairs and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

headline: 9 seek one Supreme Court seat
abstract: Pennsylvania voters will be voting to choose nominees for each party for PA Supreme, Superior, and Commonwealth Courts. Seven Democrats and two Republicans running for one Supreme Court seat and one third-party candidate, Robert Surrick.  The Supreme Court seat was vacated after the death of Justice James T. McDermott and PA Governor Casey appointed Frank Montemuro Jr. to hold the seat.  The article gives an overview of the election and provides a chart showing the candidates for each position.

headline: Negotiations fail in Upper St. Clair teachers strike
abstract: Negotiations in the strike-bound Upper St. Clair School District broke off yesterday and no progress was reported.  Neither side altered its position during the talks, which lasted about 1 1/2 hours.

headline: Two meetings on proposals set
abstract: State officials will hold two meetings to explain a proposed state plan to curb commuting by lone drivers by the PA Department of Environmental Resources at the Valley Forge Convention Center and the other at the Strawbridge & Clothier auditorium.

headline: Leonard gets a jump on the fall
abstract: Thomas Leonard is quietly running for mayor of Philadelphia. He will not be on the ballot in the primary but will be on the ballot come the General Election in November. Leonard plans to reserve his resouces and generate voter interest.

headline: All problems are equal
abstract: The writer believes that African-Americans will be kept outsiders of the American business community if they continue to think that they prohibit them from learning how to do business.

headline: Mammogram guidelines elicit debate, confusion
abstract: The National Cancer Institute (NCI) had debates about the effectiveness of mammograms for woman under the age of 50.  They concluded, from recent research, that woman over the age of 50 yearly mammograms could reduce the risk of breast cancer by 30%.  Yet woman under 50 it has not shown to be as affective.

headline: Here are the basics of pact
abstract: The basics of the Cumberland Valley School District's agreement between the school board and the teachers union are outlined.

headline: PEO position clarified
abstract: The press secretary of the PA Energy Office is writing to clarify the PEO's stance on the transmission line application that is pending before the Public Utility Commission. At the time the PEO is neither for or against the proposal.

headline: House panel seeks OK for probe
abstract: The House Judiciary Committee yesterday moved one step closer to impeaching Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen by deciding to ask the full House for subpoena power and the authority to launch an investigation of Larsen.

headline: Housing plan crawls at Highland Building
abstract: A Commonwealth Court decision improves the chances of turning a vacant 13-story building in East Libety into housing for the elderly.  But don't expect any immediate construction activity.  The state appeals court last month gave the go-ahead for the proposal to convert the turn-of-the-century Highland Builiding into 120 apartments for senior citizens.  The court rejected several owners of nearby businesses to stop the project.

headline: A bad ratio for fund-raising
abstract: The newspaper criticizes telephone pitches asking people to contribute money to supplement the pensions of retired state troopers.  They say that it is run by the American Association of State Troopers, not the Southwestern Pennsylvania Troopers Association, who also fundraises, and has a greater number of state troopers than the former.  The state attorney general also objects to the fact that the fundraising is done by professional solicitors, and not the organization itself.  Moreover, state troopers enjoy a lucrative pension, and the vast majority of money raised goes to the telemarketing company, not the state troopers.

headline: New priorities in federal budget will benefit our states and citites
