abstract: The Clinton administration is giving more power to the local and state agencies to decide how to solve the problems within their district with the help of federal money.  It is a welcomed step that governors and legislatures are excited about, although some question the modivation or results.

headline: U.S. Is Asked to Probe Failed Arkansas S&L
abstract: The Resolution Trust Corporation has asked federal prosecutors in Little Rock to open a criminal investigation into whether a failed Arkansas savings and loan used depositors' funds during the mid-'80s to benefit local politicians, including a reelection campaign of then-governor Bill Clinton.

headline: Anti-abortion protester plans to fight fine
abstract: An abortion oppenent, Rev. Phillip Beachey of Bloombield, will fight his citation of not getting a permit to protest on rights of his freedom of speech.  A loosly organized group of 40 peacefully picketed an area where U.S. Supreme Court Justice Harry Blackmun made an appereance.

headline: Mayo Clinic among the wealthiest
abstract: When President Clinton on Wednesday singled out the Mayo Clinic as a model of a health organization holding down costs, he was unwittingly praising one of America's largest and wealthiest medical networks.  But its very size and wealth raise some of the issues Clinton is purporting to address.

headline: Hoarding Michener art for safekeeping
abstract: A state-of-the-art storage vault has been built for the newly expanded James A. Michener Art Museum in Doylestown.  The museum will reopen on Sunday.  The room is constructed to hold 80 racks as well as store sculpture and works on paper.

headline: Plant is Evacuated
abstract: 200 workers at the Power X. Company power plant were evacuated after cleaning solvent backed up in a drain and spilled inside the building.

headline: House passes gun bill after long struggle
abstract: A Senate showdown is the next step for the Brady bill.  It would require a waiting period to purchase a handgun.

headline: HUD to the rescue?
abstract: The editorial board approves of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's plan to fix the poor-quality public housing in Philadelphia. They support the HUD's restructuring of the Philadelphia Housing Authority's board, but they also suggest that the HUD suspend all bidding on PHA contracts, hire the deputy director of the PHA through the board from among the nation's best housing and urban-planning professionals, and support new and promising ideas.

headline: A Better Way: Lawmakers should vote a perk hike
abstract: PA House Speaker H. William DeWeese has been pushing to increase the salaries of state lawmakers from present $47,000 a year to the mid-$50,000 range by 1996 because their salaries are not adjusted for inflation.  The editorial board suggests that DeWeese went about the pay increase in the proper manner by putting it through the PA Legislature for vote.

headline: New tactics reported in 2d District race
abstract: Democratic workers came to a senior citizens home and set up to sign the residents up for absentee ballots for the 2nd District race, but there are accusations by the residents that they were not handled the right way. These accusations are part of the scandal surrounding the election of Senator William Stinson in November. Others, non-senior citizens, are coming forth about how they were forced to fill out absentee ballots and never selected who they wanted to vote for.

headline: U.S. on the road to reform
abstract: The promise of health care reform was a key ingredient in Bill Clinton's recipe for victory over George Bush.  And there is little doubt the issue helped win Harris Wofford one of Pennsylvania's seats in the US Senate.

headline: Battle lines are drawn over waistlines, pastimes
abstract: Appearance still plays a role in how some employers perceive a person's skills and level of competence, especially in the area of weight. United Airlines made what their officals claim was an image and health motivated decision to enforce weight standards for flight attendants. The American Civil Liberties Union says discrimination causing the Association of Flight Attendants to file a complaint with the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is common despite state and federal laws prohibiting infringement of civil liberties.

headline: Medicaid endangerments
abstract: New thinking is needed in order to fix the Medicaid/Medicare problem that we are facing and the way the Casey administration is going things will not get better soon.  If they make cuts to the doctors and hospital the poor will suffer more.  They are having similar problems at the federal level.

headline: Hopeful Start for Profit-Making Schools
abstract: Harlem Park and eight other Baltimore public schools have been taken over by a private company that runs them for profit.  The Baltimore City School District, unable for many reasons to improve the schools, ceded them to Education Alternatives, Inc., which receives the same annual allotment for each student as the public schools.

headline: Plant's rating not affected by break-in
abstract: A break-in last February at Three Mile Island had no effect on the report card the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued to GPU Nuclear, the plant's operator.  TMI earned the highest mark possible in three of four categories, including the one that covers security and emergency preparedness.

headline: Improved communication is first order of business in wake of police shooting
abstract: Two police officers were wounded in a gun battle in Lower Paxton twp.  The officers were on a missing persons investigation and had very limited communication with the local police.  It took a long time for medical help to arrive to attend their wounds because of the bad communication.  The city needs to improve its communication between police departments and its officers.

headline: HUD's homeless aid seeks to skirt shelters
abstract: Housing Secretary Henry G. Cisneros described a new $20 million homeless-aid program yesterday as a way to circumvent shelters and connect homeless people with the services they need to survive.  The program will have a test run in the District of Columbia next year and be introduced in other US cities afterward, he said.

headline: A blow to workplace poison rules
abstract: Government regulations on hundreds of toxic substances at workplaces that were voluntarily bained by the industry in 1968 may be back in the work place because of a Clinton administration decision not to appeal a federal court ruling.  The court claimed that the Occupational Safety and Health Administration could not justify scientifically each change in standards.

headline: Newman TV ads had no place in campaign
abstract: Joseph Mistick should get the vote against Sandra Schultz Newman for Commonwealth Court judge, strictly as a reaction to Ms. Newman's television advertisements.  Her unsupported, thinly veiled accusation of criminal behavior has no place in a legitimate political campaign.

headline: unabated in corporate economy
abstract: need pg. 77 of Feb. 1

headline: Bishop Discuss a Health-Care Stance on Abortion
abstract: The nation's Roman Catholic archbishops held a private meeting in Chicago to discuss what stance they will take toward a national healthcare plan if it covers abortion. The secrecy surrounding the meeting seemed to indicate that church leaders were having difficulty with a question that poses political perils. Church leaders warned the Clintons that including abortion would be a "moral tragedy."

headline: Medical costs building
abstract: The article discusses the fact that the PA Department of Health continues to grant large sums of money for almost any project regarding hospitals, nursing homes, and health care technology. This trend will raise the quality of health care,  but it will also raise health care costs to the point where few will be able to afford it.

headline: Horns locked on veterinary school funding
abstract: Gov. Robert P. Casey supported cutting funding to the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine in 1992.  He is still facing controversy from the agricultural community which claims this problem is still unresolved.

headline: Power fails in heat wave
abstract: Surgical teams broke out flashlights, workers sweltered in offices and subway passengers stumbled in the dark after three power lines that serve threee city neighborhoods and two Uptown institutions failed in rapid succession.  The unique three-in-a-row blowout shut down power to Mercy Hospital in the midst of surgery and canceled classes for 2,500 students at Duquesne University.

headline: In the mean time..
abstract: More stringent gun control will not increase our security and safty because it only regulates those that committ crimes with guns they lawfully own.  Society would be safer with more law abidding citizens carrying arms.

headline: 'I Love Shenandoah'-Former mailman's fund drive spurs town's recovery
abstract: 72 year old Shenandoah Valley native Joe Valento loved his town so much, that when as a borough member he discovered the town was filing for bankruptcy, he gave $100 of his own money. Valento's act spurred a barrage of community and nationwide donations,  leading to his creation of the "I love Shenandoah Fund." The town, with help from the PA Department of Community Affairs, has been removed from the distressed areas list and is on its way to recovery, much to Valento's efforts.

headline: A detail or two Clinton won't share with you
abstract: As you listen to the president's speech on health care tonight, don't forget that the devil's in those details that won't be a part of his speech.  Once more, as he did throughout his campaign for the presidency, Bill Clinton wants everyone to buy "The Plan" without providing them with those all-important implementation details.

headline: News Groups Appeal Ruling Allowing Task Force Secrecy
abstract: Six major news organizations, including the Associated Press, the Radio-Television News Directors Association, and the American Society of Newspaper editors have joined other interest groups appealing in federal District Courts the workings of President Clinton's health care task force. Citing an error in the ruling of Judge Royce C. Lamberth, groups are arguing in their accepted brief that closed meetings undermine the intent of the law to provide openness and accountability of government.

headline: Union charges to be heard within 6 weeks
abstract: The teacher union of Carlisle charges Carlisle Area School Board based on the terms of a contract.

headline: Black leaders accept ruling
abstract: Black leaders emerged from a meeting with Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Robert E. Dauer,  satisfied with his explanation of why he had dismissed charges stemming from a cross-burning incident and agreed to help him work to toughen the state's Ethnic Intimidation Act.

headline: Medical treatment to Medicaid patients lags, a study says
abstract: Patients with traditional commercial fee-for-service plans or HMO plans are more likely to receive surgery and treatment than those patients with Medicaid a study shows. The authors of the study think that financial incentives play a role in deciding whether to operate or not.

headline: House acts to kill education standards
abstract: The house voted 139-61 to nullify the 'outcome-based education' standards adopted by the State Board of Education last month.  Governor Casey was concerned with the effect of teaching cultural diversity, AIDS education and living skills such as child care, but failed to get it out of the suggested legislation.

headline: Power line poses environmental disaster
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey supports one of the most needless environmental disasters ever proposed, a 268 mile high voltage GPU/DQE transmission line, which is not needed, only wanted. At a technical hearings in April, a GPU/DQE witness admitted under questioning that this line was purely economic. It will cause hundreds of property owners to lose viable land.

headline: In ursuit of safer schools: Security studied in wake of assault
abstract: The parents meet with the administration after a 10 year old girl was raped in a school bathroom by an intruder said to be between the ages of 19-24.  A 'buddy-system', private security gaurds, parent watch-team, and video cameras were all brought up as options to help the situation.

headline: Ignore the whining in Edgewood and extend the PAT busway
abstract: People are crying over the Port Authority's planned extension of the East Busway, yet it will benefit a great many people.  For a community to not want a bus stop on the busway is one thing, but to try to halt the entire project is another and is inherently unfair to communities that welcome the project.

headline: A holiday or infamy?
abstract: Amid the memorial ceremonies, there may be controversy; there has been talk about declaring Pearl Harbor Day a national holiday.  Thos ewho think it sould be will sy it's a day to honor the soldiers and sailors who died that fateful day in Hawaii; those who don't will argue that many private and public employees get too many holidays already.

headline: Night of surprises
abstract: In the election of 1993, a breakdown of some of those elected in Pennsylvania and surrounding states.

headline: Unpredictable justices
abstract: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Byron White is set to retire and Clinton has the privilage of picking a new justice.  In the past the justices, rightly, don't always go along with the social ideology of those who put them on the bench.  Clinton changed his tone from finding a 'pro-life' justice to finding a justice that has good judgment, wide experience and has a 'big heart'.

headline: Blacks get short end of kidney transplants
abstract: Black Americans awaiting kidney transplants are caught in the crosshairs of cultural bias and transplant ethics.  Kidney disease afflicts a greater percentage of African-Americans than any other ethnic group in the United States, but statistically blacks wait longest to receive the organs for transplant.  The reason for the paradox lies in the genetic-matching used to determine who gets the next available kidney.

headline: Merger fever hits hospitals
abstract: Three smaller hospitals and two large ones in the Philadelphia area are talking separately about linking up with one another.  Their sizes may vary, but the reasons behind the discussions are remarkably similar.  They are trying to cut back on costs and duplicating services, to focus on their strenths, to continue to provide quality health care in the region.

headline: House expects OBE fireworks
abstract: A show down is expected in the Pa House after the State Board of Education approved Outcome-Based Education plans which would shift the emphasis of education to what students can demonstrate they know instead of how much time they spend in the classroom.  Those who object say the reforms have not been proven successful, could be costly and require students to lear objectionable values.

headline: Power off
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission (PUC) has been stalling on making a decision about whether or not Duquesne Light could sell its excess electric power to the General Public Utilities Corporation in New Jersey. The New Jersey Board of Regulatory Commissioners made a decision not to have GPU allow it and the writers believe this failed transaction would be more accepted if it had been the PUC to rule it was not allowed versus the other state's commission.

headline: Inmate who owes $35 million to be freed, deported
abstract: An inmate of a federal prison in Union County who owes the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. more than $35 million could soon be a free man in Argentina.  Jacobo Finkielstain is to be released next Sunday from the Low Security Institution at Allenwood and immediately deported as an illegal alien.

headline: Jobless mom: What recovery?
abstract: The US Department of Commerce announcement of economic growth does not convince an unemployed single mother of two. Kathleen Bancroft was a shoe department manager at Ames, a local department store chain which is closing numerous East Coast locations. Now she worries about finding another steady full-time job with health benefits as the future looks bleak.

headline: A lesson for teachers in unions' hard times?
abstract: A bunch of white-collar workers has bested the tough, entrenched Teamsters union.  The National Education Associateion reports having more members than the Teamsters.  It's probably no surprise that teachers have taken the lead in union membership- and therefore potential lobbying power.

headline: Nigro gets backing to run for Pa. court
abstract: After a four hour session of raw politics and open horse trading, the state Democratic Party yesterday endorsed Philadelphia Judge Russell M. Nigro for state Supreme Court in a vote 189-182.  Munley was a close second and when a motion to make the vote for Nigro unanimous there were shouts of 'No' from the crowd.

headline: Unreasonable logic
abstract: The editorial "Unreasonable Fear" was highly inconsistent with the messages we are daily subjected to by the media, including the Post-Gazette.  While in agreement with the message of the editorial, it contains many contradictions.

headline: Both sides in abortion fight claim support
abstract: The 'Cities of Refuge' project, conducted by Operation Rescue, an anti-abortion activist group, has ended in the Philadelphia area and will now move on to another city.

headline: Metropolitan Area News in Brief
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey is showing signs that his amyloidosis is getting better. Casey had liver and heart transplants in the spring and has been hospitalized twice since then due to illness.

headline: Images from a presidential visit
abstract: Photographs were taken of President Clinton's and first lady Hillary Clinton's visit to the Beaver County area, particulary Ambridge Area High School, to promote the new health care proposal.

headline: PUC judge suggests Philly power line receive go-ahead
abstract: A Public Utility Commission judge ruled that there is too little evidence of the potential health risks of electromagnetic fields to warrant setting minimum standards for power lines. Therefore the Philadelphia Electric Company will be allowed to turn on a 230,000 volt transmission line through Bucks and Montgomery counties.

headline: Inmates tell of idleness, violence
abstract: A class-action suit has been filed against the PA prison system by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). The complaint is that the increase in population has lead to overcrowding in the jails and there are not enough jobs for the inmates, leading to more violence.

headline: Jobs issue puts blemish on town's economic rebirth
abstract: The addition of Willamette Industries, Inc which is a paper and wood products company in Johnsonburg is coming with mixed feelings.  The construction of the new plant, which will alter the skyline, is the issue of big debate.  Although the cost of $450 million will surely help the community many members are made because a lot of the workers are coming from other areas instead of locally.

headline: A lesson in PR
abstract: Clinton should be grateful for his early crash in the polls and the nasty personal attacks he suffered in the press.  His early faux pas prepared him to sell health-care reform.

headline: Nigro nips Musmanno
abstract: Article is a list of several political stories.  Philadelphia Common Please Judge Russell W. Nigro narrowly won the Democratic primary for the PA Supreme Court. PA Governor Casey is recovering from a heart-liver transplant. The PA House Judiciary Committee hopes to remedy the fact that Pennsylvania is the only state without its own anti-trust laws. Two PA top Democrats urged Congress to approve President Clinton's economic plan.

headline: Update public authority law
abstract: The showdow government needs to see the light in Pennsylvania.  The commonwealth has 2,800 public authorities, which are largely invisible bodies that are used primarily as vehicles to raise large sumes of money to provide services that are self-supporting.  There is too much money in these public authorities and the people need to have more say, by voting on who they are and how they spend money.

headline: Casey suggests reform deletions
abstract: Casey suggested in a letter to the state Council of Basic Education that it deletes three categories in the OBE plan: Appreciating and understanding others; Personal, family and community living; Wellness and fitness.  The OBE supports were outraged by Casey's letter and claimed that Casey was merely giving into an extremist view of the religious right-wing.

headline: 'Monster Cigarette Tax' of Up to $2 a Pack Is Said to Gain Support
abstract: President Clinton is reviewing proposals to raise federal taxes on cigerettes as high as $2 a pack to provide money for health care.  This will discourage young smokers from ever starting, but big tabacco lobbists are fighting the new tax.  They claim this tax unfairly focuses on the lower income population rather than taxing the wealthy.

headline: Improving image of schools is a high hurdle
abstract: Any conversation about Wilkinsburg inevitably turns toward the borough's public school system.  School Superintendent Walter Watson knows how some perceive his district of 1,871 students.  A large number of students identified as impoverished, and so with that comes some other problems that cause certain kinds of judgements by the public.

headline: PUC member leaving at critical time
abstract: Wendell Holland will be, in March, the second member of the five person board to step down from the state Public Utility Commission.  Amid controversy about the 268 mile power line project proposed by General Public Utilities and Dquesne Light that has raised nearly 9,000 complaints from opponents.  Some question the timing of his resignation and look for Gov. Casey for answers.

headline: Inquest in Carlisle killing to open
abstract: Three police officers who confronted and shot a Berks County murder suspect last month are among those called to testify at today's coroner's inquest into the death of Steven Ficula. The inquest was called by the coroner in an attempt to find out whether the death was justified or was the result of either criminal action or criminal negligence on the part of the Carlisle Patrol.

headline: Katz out of the bag
abstract: All anyone knows at this point, the 76ers are not bound for Spectrum II, the new, state-of-the-art arena that has been projected for construction on the former site of JFK stadium.  "The deal is gone," said Harold Katz, the Sixers' owner.  Katz, who has been negotiating for more than five years with Ed Snider, the founder of Spectacor and owner of the Flyers, to become a tenant in a proposed, new building, has withdrawn from the project.

headline: 'A new phase'
abstract: Governor Robert P. Casey and his wife, Ellen, are greeted by the press upon arrival yesterday at Capital City Airport in Fairview Township.  Casey, returning home form a three-week hospital stay in Pittsburgh due to a viral infection, indicated he's moving closer to resuming his official duties.

headline: Nigro's fund raising twice that of Castille
abstract: Philadelphia Common Pleas Judge Russell W. Nigro appears to be on his way to winning the fund-raising battle in the race for state Supreme Court.  The Democrat has raised more than twice as much as Republican candidate Ronald D. Castille since the primary elections in May, according to campaign expense reports filed this week.

headline: US officials launch probe in 2d District
abstract: The US Justice Department plans to investigate whether anyone's rights were violated in the Second Senate District race.  Both William Stinson's and Bruce Marks' campaign workers said they welcomed the scrutiny.

headline: Caught in a conflict
abstract: A man writes into the newspaper to criticize the editorial board for supporting abortion, but opposing abortion based on the sex of the fetus. He says that in the future genetic testing will allow parents to discover physical and mental ailments present in the fetus, so if the editorial board believes abortions based on such issues are wrong, than it is admitting that a fetus is a person deserving of protection.

headline: Most immunized here, but state rate just 66%
abstract: The state Department of Health says only 66 percent of Pennsylvania's children are properly immunized by their second birthdays.  But the figure might not be nearly that high in Cumberland County.  Department of Health spokesman Richard McGarvey says the state doesn't keept track of the immunization rates in individual counties.  But area pre-schools, day-care centers and school districts say almost all children are properly immunized.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Noteworthy
abstract: PA Education Secretary Donald Caroll Jr. announced that twelve state teachers have been nominated for the 1993 Presidential Awards for Excellence in Science and Mathematics.

headline: PUC told to rescind decision
abstract: Rep Frank LaGrotta has called on the Public Utility Commision to rescind its descision to move a team of lawyers from PUC headquaters to another building and promised to call for a 'legislative investigation' by the house if not done.  He believes it was payback because the lawyers had been leading the fight against the proposed GPU-DQE powerline.

headline: It's a long walk to death row
abstract: Acting PA Governor Mark. Singel signed the death warrant for Fredric Jacob Jermyn, but he has gotten a stay. 168 people have been condemned to death row, but no one has been executed since before the US Supreme Court struck down the death penalty in 1972 and then the PA Legislature reinstated it in 1974. The American Correctional Association says that there are 2,760 prisoners sentenced to death by states and 4 facing death sentences in the nation.

headline: Land set for mall on sheriff's block
abstract: There was a foreclosure on land that was to be a large mall in Fairview Twp.  The reason for the foreclosure was that 8376 Associates could not pay the $3 million in loans and could not find retail stores that wanted to be in the proposed mall.  This is bad news for Fairview Twp who expected 2,000 temporary construction jobs and 2,000 part time and full time jobs once it opened, in addition to an estimated 1.1 million dollars annually in taxes from the property.

headline: A new way to vote?
abstract: Since you can easily shop from home these days- even order a gourmet meal delivered piping-hot to your doorstep- why not vote from home?  It wounded reasonable to the Hispanic voters approached by Democratic workers going door-to-door in the hotley contested Second Distict state Senator race.

headline: No overtime
abstract: The writers believe that the PA Crime Commission should not be saved at the last minute by the bill proposed by House Judiciary Committee Chairman Thomas Caltagirone to appropriate $1.2 million to the agency and file quarterly updates to the House and Senate judiciary committees. They believe the commission is redundant and since it does not have prosecution powers, so it is a waste of money.

headline: VA's value
abstract: The staff of the Lebanon VA Medical Center, regardless of all the hundreds of emergencies and needs that come through its doors at all hours of the day or night, in spite of anything and everything, its staff MAKES the time to help every veteran on an individual basis.  That is not an easy task.

headline: Censorship charge is off the mark
abstract: The way People for the American Way tells it, America's schools are under siege by "religious right" groups waging a national censorship campaign.  Book-banning zealots have tightened classroom freedom, imposed a religious orthodoxy on schools, harassed educators and disrupted schoolwork.  It is all part of "the broader assault on free speech emerging in the arts, television, films, music, politics and elsewhere."

headline: Mother of girl needing lungs pleads to public for organ donors
abstract: Sandra Fuller, whose daughter will die if she does not receive a lung transplant, made a public plea for people become organ donors.  She supports legislation being considered by Pennsylvanian legislators that would presume Pennsylvanians want to donate their organs at death unless they or their families have previously prohibited it.

headline: Inside the Capitol-College students urge more funding
abstract: Students from 14 PA owned universities gathered in the capitol to plead for more funding to universities, arguing a delay of $60 million by the Legislature was leading to hazardous conditions in some university buildings. The students were met with a letter of welcome from PA  Budget Secretary Michael H. Hershock and a report of money PA spent on institutions since Governor Casey took office.

headline: Radiation monitors installed within 2 miles of plant
abstract: Five radiation monitors that will provide measurements of radioactivity in the region surrounding Three Mile Island were installed at shore locations.

headline: Leader in drug gang sentenced to 23 years
abstract: Edwin Ramos a self confessed cocaine dealer whose business nearly ruined the Spring Garden community begged for mercy as the judge sentenced him yesterday in US court.  He received 23 years in prison, to run concurrent with a 13-year sentence he has already received for a related crime.

headline: Leaders take city's room temperature
abstract: Developer Donald Pulver wants to construct a hotel, parking garage and movie theatre complex on Market street and is willing to put up half of the 47 million dollar cost but cannot find others to invest more than an additional 10 million as well. Pulver revealed his problem and plans yesterday at a forum and received some optimism but few solutions.

headline: A Phila. Mother tells Clinton a bill on leave is needed
abstract: Beware of scams this year including calls, letters, and fake charities. Clinton talked on the phone with Joann Mapp and 10 others across the nation for a half an hour about Family-leave bill that he may have the opportunity to pass into law.  It involves being able to take off non-paid leave for family or personal medical emergencies.

headline: No worker in U.S. should be poor
abstract: Poor people in America do have a lot more stuff than poor people in many other countries.  Most have telephones and TVs, after all, and many have cars.  The Census Bureau says there are more poor people in the coutnry than at any time since 1962, and that the poverty rate is the highest in 10 years.  The face of the poor has changed, and that change poses difficult and disturbing questions.

headline: Veon works to have Hatch Act repealed
abstract: PA Representative Mike Veon called for an appeal of a half-century old law that bars state civil service employees from partisan political activity. The bill would allow state workers to engage in partisan politics as long as they did it on their own time. State restrictions currently apply to about 60,000 civil service workers and about 10,000 government employees.

headline: Chinese horror story told
abstract: About 60 people listened quietly last night as Zi Zi, a citizen of the People's Republic of China, described what he called "the dark days of my life" while undergoing "six years of slavery" in a Chinese labor camp.  He was one of several speakers at a public forum held by the York County Bar Association on local efforts to gain asylum for Chinese detainees being held at the York County Prison.

headline: Mrs. Clinton says health status quo will cost more
abstract: First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton insists that the country cannot afford to delay reform of its health care system. Stating, unless congress approves a package this year that, Americans will pay an additional $100 billion next year and not receive any more care. Clinton heads a 500-member White House task force set to make public a massive package next month containing sweeping reforms of the nation's health care system; the plan not only is expected to provide insurance for those uninsured but also offer proposals to cut the soaring cost.

headline: Inside the Capitol-Heard on the Hill
abstract: PA Governor Casey is quoted after education changes he supports cleared the House and Senate Education committees.

headline: Rail shipments fuel charged debate in Council
abstract: City Council seemed to be suffering radiation sickness yesterday as members bashed on another and the mayor over the imminent passage of 33 rail shipments of partially spent nuclear fuel rods through the city.  Or perhaps it ws simply because of a light agenda and nothing else to talk about.

headline: 'Ivan' still divides Jews and Ukrainians
abstract: A former Nazi guard, who had immigrated to the United States, was stripped of citizenship and deported.  The Israeli court has overturned convictions of him as a war criminal. It is unsure what his fate will be.

headline: Let's put people to work
abstract: Tom Croft, the executive director of a regional intermunicipal jobs authority in Pittsburgh, writes to the newspaper to disagree with those who say the area doesn't require federal assistance. He says that four Steel Valley Authority member communities are bankrupt. The SVA has created 700 jobs but still needs federal assistance to fix the local economy and create more jobs.

headline: A roller-coaster ride to joy for fans
abstract: With a final, strike-out pitch from heart-stopper Mitch Williams at 11:17 last night, Philadelphia exploded in pent-up jubilation.  For with a 6-3 victory, this underappreceiated city wrested its first pennant in 10 years, its fifth of the 20th century.

headline: Non-Minority Firms Cannibalizing Minority Business Opportunities
abstract: In 1987, PA Governor Robert Casey established the Office of Minority and Women Business Enterprise under the Department of General Services. To be certified by the OMWBE, a business must show it is owned or operated by a minority or woman. State contract bidders having a nondiscriminatory history are then given a list of contractors from which to choose. Secretary of General Services David Janetta disputes PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer's finding that the agency was non-compliant in its hiring practices according to its guidelines.

headline: Vince Fumo Goes A-Courtin'
abstract: Nobody has a bigger say about who gets to wear a black robe in Philadelphia than Vince Fumo, the city's most powerful politician.  What exactly is he looking for in a judge?

headline: Christian group keeping to the right
abstract: This was to be a conference where the Christian Coalition broadened its political image, but today Pat Buchanan brought 2,000 Christian conservatives to their feet with a vow to rebuff Republican moderates and never "raise a white flag in the cultural war."

headline: New heart, liver doing 'extremely well'
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Robert Casey's doctors say he's done extremely well with a new heart and lover.  He shows no signs of transplant surgery's most serious complication- the body's rejection of new organs.

headline: Interception
abstract: That trouble erupted at the end of the Westinghouse-Peabody football game at South Stadium Thursday night doesn't mean that the school board should be ready to cancel oather athletic events or even consider staging them someplace else.

headline: Rendezvous in Oil Country
abstract: There's a crude reason- the bubblin' kind- to visit Emlenton in Western Pennsyvlania.  Today it's a boom town that dozed off, a pleasant base for exploration of the region where the state's oil industry began.

headline: Jail terms unlikely in PHA bribe scandal
abstract: Most of the former public employees and private contractors caught up in the latest Philadelphia Housing Authority bribery and bid-rigging scandal won't be going to a real prison for their crimes, a federal judge hinted yesterday.  But they will be hit hard financially, with fines and restitution totaling more than $1 million, and will spend short periods in halfway houses or under house arrest, US District Judge Norma L. Shapiro suggested.

headline: Let's rethink affordable housing
abstract: Policy makers in Bucks County need to take a hard look at where and how to solve the problem of providing affordable housing. The county faces a severe economic crisis because the labor force needed to perform our lower-paying service functions can't afford to live in the county. It is questionable why the county continues to focus its affordable housing efforts in the municipalities that can least afford it.

headline: A scary tale has happy ending
abstract: President Clinton sat in the Rose Garden yesterday morning, listening to 15 Americans tell stories about their frustrating- and sometimes heartbreaking- experiences with the nation's health-care system.  But for the teller of one story, there wan an unrevealed happy ending.

headline: Nonprofits lobby like everyone else
abstract: Though federal tax codes and election laws prohibit charities from participating in political activies, nonprofits have established Political Action Committees awarding thousands and millions of dollars to congressmen each year in the form of speaking fees, honorarium, and other perks. Congress has since passed a ban on the speaking fees for members of the House, however, legislators still accept trips paid for by PACs. An estimated $43 million from the health industry alone went straight to lawmakers.

headline: Voices
abstract: Quotes from people about Vartan's covenant.

headline: Cities prep for rallies
abstract: The anti-abortion group Operation Rescue is apt to receive stern greetings in other cities besides Philadelphia when it begins its latest crusade Friday.

headline: New stat staff health plan eyed
abstract: The agency that manages health benefits for 290,000 state employees, retirees and their dependents is developing a major new insurance plan that directs members to networks of specially selected hospitals and physicians.  The Pennsylvania Employee Benefit Trust Fund wants to guide more workers into managed care.

headline: It isn't fair to give students a false sense of accomplishment
abstract: The writer of the letter believes that the Pittsburgh Public Schools should not lower the requirement of having a 2.0 or better GPA in order to participate in afterschool activities. He believes that doing so is placing activities above learning, since a 2.0 or C is already and average score, and showing kids they should not aim for above average.

headline: Showdown time nears in hospital controversy
abstract: One week from today a final decision is expected on the controversial consolidation plan for Franklin and Oil City hospitals. The proposed plan would eliminate acute-care and emergency department services at Oil City; those services would be consolidated at Franklin, which is eight miles away. In turn, Oil City would become the center for most outpatient services. The plan is widely opposed in Oil City.

headline: Jail to become county's criminal courthouse
abstract: The Allegheny County commissioners are planning to transform the Allegheny County Jail, a national historic landmark designed by Hobson Richardson, into a court designated for judges' chambers, jury selection rooms, holding cells, probation services, the Bail Agency, and etc.

headline: Litany of lost jobs must be brought to an end
abstract: The editorial wants answers to questions concerning how to restore the dwindling Philadelphia job market. Citing examples of failed efforts at employment by city and government strategies, the editorial also believes looking to the hospitality industry to save the job market will be unsuccessful. The author looks instead to the private sector's potential to take advantage of a strong improvement in the national economy.

headline: A Stish in time
abstract: The editors think Tom Stish, a 3 term PA Representative, is a turncoat. Campaigning as a Democrat, accepting $35,000 from his party, endorsed by PA Governor Robert Casey, he changed his status to Republican upon re-election. The board thinks the motive was the swing in power to Republicans in the US House, now led by Speaker Newt Gingrich. The board agrees with lame duck PA House Speaker William DeWeese; Stish would have left the Democrats with more honor had he died.

headline: Odds go against Clinton's quest
abstract: No one who has tried to fill out a Medicare claim form, get the Internal Revenue Service or the Social Security Administration on the telephone, apply for a government contract or grant- no one, in short, who has ever been hogtied by federal red tape- can disagree with President Clinton's description of the government: "The government is broken, and we intend to fix it."  The bureaucracy is bloated, wasteful and inefficient, but no one who has followed past efforts to solve the problem can be confident that this president will succeed.

headline: Volunteers honored
abstract: Last week, both men, Larry Holt and Terry Patterson- along with 19 other volunteers from across the state- were honored for their work by state Agriculture Secretary Boyd Wolff.  Wolff presented certificates to the volnteers as part of the annual observance of World Food Day.

headline: Civil Disobedience takes rightist twist
abstract: America's latest episode of civil disobedience produced typically compelling visuals: anti-abortion demonstrators blocking a suburban clinic until police took them away.  What the cameras didn't pick up was the leaders of Operation Rescue conferring with police behind the scenes to plan what happened next.  People who break laws to make statements are making a redefining protests, using techniques developed in the left wing for the right wing.

headline: New ways of doing business as doctors
abstract: The rapid rise of HMOs and other forms of managed care is forcing many doctors to merge practices in order to save money.  Many area doctors have become convinced that the individual practitioner is deader than the dinosaurs.

headline: Ius are redefining mission
abstract: Pennsylvania has cut special-education costs so that disabled students are encouraged to attend regular schools rather than Intermediate Unit schools.  The PA House Education Committee has heard hearings on the merits of Intermediate Units and is deciding how much money should be granted to them. Intermediate Units could help the PA Department of Education by taking over some of its responsibilities to disabled children.

headline: USX gets OK to sell services to new Fairless Works tenants
abstract: The PA Public Utilities Commission is considered a linchpin in USX's plan to lure tenants to the one-thriving 2,000-acre site, according to Robert Dunsek Sr., a consultant working with USX in the redevelopment. PUC will allow them to sell electricity and other utilities to businesses that move into the closed partition of the USS Fairless Works steel mill.

headline: Jails set to snuff out inmates' smoking
abstract: Pennsylvania jails show mixed reactions to banning tobacco in their respective correctional facilities, but several are ready to move to a smoke-free environment.

headline: Low-income housing complex gets $200,000 grant for repairs
abstract: The Snyder County Housing Authority has received a $200,000 grant from the state Department of Housing and Urban Development which it will use to improve the 40-unit Shade View Apartments, a low-income housing complex off Essex Road.

headline: A super editorial
abstract: The Post-Gazette editorial on the super-collider was very well written and showed that the author had done his homework.  Please keep up the fine science coverage.

headline: O'Donnell promises cleanup of rundown city house
abstract: Gubernatorial candidate Bob O'Donnell has vowed to clean up a rundown house he co-owns in Harrisburg and sell it for $1 to a community group or person willing to maintain it.  O'Donnell, a state legislator and former speaker of the state House, called the city codes enforcement office yesterday to say he would hire a contractor immediately to fix the problems with the house at 100 N. Third Street.

headline: Vote for Darkins, Matta advises black audience
abstract: Republican mayoral candidate Kathy Matta is urging black voters to support Duane Darkins, one of her rivals in the mayor's race- if for no other reason than that he's not Democrat Tom Murphy.

headline: Clinics and Klansmen
abstract: Congress must act to protect women from 'pro-life' zealots by nullifying the decision from the Supreme court that would allow federal marshals to protect woman going to a clinic for an abortion.  The law that was in the Supreme court was based on a law passed in the 18th century which protected black Americans seeking to vote from the intimidation of the Ku Klux Klan.

headline: North Phila. Elderly home to lose funds
abstract: Elderly home will lose funding from Medicare and Medicaid in 23 day 'fast-track' program because of the inadequate care the elderly patrons have been receiving with respect to "just about every aspect of the facility".  There are worries that it will be difficult to find places to put the patients once this elderly home closes and if they do it may cause trauma to the sick patients.

headline: Join together to force change in schools, communities
abstract: The recent stories, editorial and letters to the editor regarding efforts to improve Harrsiburg's schools by duplicating changes in the Farrell School District bring to light one of the most important ingredients of successful schools- parental and community involvement.  Such involvement is usually the item that distinguishes successful schools from those lost in a downward spiral of dispair.

headline: Utilities serve area well
abstract: Utilites often draw criticism from people who think their rates are too hgih, or they don't pay their share fo taxes, or they are unreasonable to deal with, but area residents should be proud of their gas and electric utilities.

headline: Johnstown hails U.S. drug center opening
abstract: A new federal center called the National Drug Intelligence Center was created to collect and disseminate information on drug traffickers.  The Bush administration sought to establish this to bring together the departments of Defense, Justice, Transportation and others to fight drug trafficking more effectively. U.S. Representative John Murtha was the influence behind the center being located in Pennsylvania.

headline: Making progress at PHA
abstract: A class-action lawsuit against the Department of Housing and  Urban Development that sezed control last may of  the public housing in Philadelphia is ignoring all the good that has been done at the Philadlphia  Housing Authority.  People have been hired and fired  based on  mirit which is a great step  to reach the goal of  housing more than 80,000 Phialdelphian

headline: A talk with Frank was like a chat with a friend
abstract: Two years after his death, a radio colleague recalls the days when ex-Mayor Frank Rizzo's special charm went over the airwaves.

headline: Official guidance for the lost
abstract: The Allegheny County government hired a consultant to plan and design a "government information system" to help people find their way around various buildings that house government offices. The county sought outside help for the study in hopes of finding a creative solution.

headline: Vote forecasters are calling for a low turnout
abstract: The only contests in the Philadelphia primary are for five seats on Philadelphia Common Pleas Court. Nine candidates including four sitting judges, are vying for 10-year terms on the bench. For the fifth seat, three lawyers are running without backing from either party for a seat on the court. The District Attorney race and the controllers race are both uncontested.

headline: Clinton avoids public clash over abortion
abstract: Pope John Paul II visited America to speak against abortion and for family values. In spite of President Clinton's support of abortion rights, he praised the Pope and the two had a cordial private meeting.

headline: Noteworthy:
abstract: PA Governor Casey was honored by the Association for Retarded Citizens due to his years of support for programs for people with mental retardation.

headline: Judge lauds school district recovery
abstract: Erie County Jduge George Levin, when asked aobut the current financial health of the Erie School District, can smile.  Nearly three years ago, Levin granted the 12,000-student district reluctant approval to float bonds to pay for $14.1 million in unfunded debt.  Now, as the district registers some of its best financial news in a decade, Levin can't help but smile and take some of the credit.

headline: Why Pennsylvania Needs the Transmission Project
abstract: The proposed high voltage line is designed to make electric power supplies in Pennsylvania more cost competitive and reliable.  U.S. Steel is a large user of this electric power as are the people of western Pennsylvania.  U.S. Steel believes that it will help all Pennsylvania's if the GPU-DQE Transmission Project is allowed.

headline: Judge calls for quick settlement of home dispute
abstract: Litigation has stalled the planned Fairmount Avenue facility.  US District Court Judge Louis H. Pollak instructed the parties to negotiate.

headline: Maryland lures Wal-Mart plant
abstract: Wal-Mart was offered financial incentives like tax abatement and a low-interest mortgage payment plan, new roads leading to nearby Interstate 81and a hungry, hard-working labor force.  The Schuylkill Economic Development Corp. (SEDCO) also provided a new sewage collection system and about 11 acres of land at what industrial developers consider a good price- a little under $20,000 an acre.  But a good price could not beat what Hagerstown, Md., offered: free land.

headline: A third party is coming
abstract: The writer says that by President Clinton voting in favor of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) it shows that neither the Republicans nor the Democrats represent the interests of the average working Americans. The writer wants to create a third party that would be led by a coalition of working people of America who want to have safeguards against selling out to corporate interests.

headline: Officials accounts of situation differed
abstract: In Washington as government officials explained what went wrong in Waco, Texas, contradictions concerning officials' patience, fear of a mass suicide, and the day of the week became apparent. The article lists comments made by Federal Bureau of Investigations Director William Sessions contrasting Attorney General Janet Reno's statements, FBI Agent Bob Ricks statement in contrast with  Reno's, and Reno's statements in contrast with what Texas rancher Melanie Felton was told.

headline: Vote out Borski, Fumo
abstract: A man calls for people to vote out U.S. Representative Robert Borski and PA Senator Vincent Fumo for their anti-labor stands.

headline: Clinton ends Most Abortion Bans
abstract: Clinton makes it easier for women to get abortions by raising funding for abortions, lifting bans on different types of abortion programs, and by allowing abortions in military facilities.  Those who voted for him were happy that he came through with his campaign promises so quickly, in just his second day of office.

headline: Official: heatlh care plan 'monumental' for Pennsylvanians
abstract: The Clinton health care plan is a significant piece fo legislation that will restore control to an out-of-control system, a spokesman of the Clinton administration said Monday during a Penn State forum on health care reform.

headline: Judge's rulling to help special-needs students
abstract: The ruling from  U.S. District Judge Sylvia  H. Rambo ordered the state Department of Education to work with school districts to help them develop m ore programs for special-needs students so whenever  possible, they can be educated in a regular classroom setting rather than a private school.

headline: YMCA says line would destroy campground
abstract: Recreational consultants say a proposed 268-mile cross-state power line will deprive children of the joys of a 220-acre campground by creating an eyesore and potential health hazards.  A cable-television company says the project will interfere with broadcast signals it pics up and re-transmits to customers.

headline: Judge Ginsburg's turn
abstract: Though Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg may be a shoo-in as a Supreme Court Justice, the public will benefit from hearing her story.

headline: Meridian Plaza-Patience is wearing thin: Fix the city's towering eyesore
abstract: The author of this editorial thinks it is time for the public interest in the appearance of the city of Philadelphia to get some respect. The article welcomes Mayor Rendell's intervention in a lawsuit between the owners of a charred downtown skyscraper and its insurer to speed up the process and raise the quality of the city's image. Licenses and Inspections Commissioner Bennet Levin is also threatening action against the neglected building.

headline: A tight Senate race in 2d District
abstract: Democrat William Stinson and Republican Bruce Marks were locked in a tight race yesterday in their campaign to win the legislative seat that would determine whether Democrats or Republicans control the state Senate.

headline: Off-year primary
abstract: Most voters in Tuesday's primary may not have had full knowledge of the referendum on judicial discipline but they understood it meant change from the discredited system that’s currently in place. It was enough to convince an overwhelming 82 percent to cast their vote in favor of the new two-tiered disciplinary system. Harrisburg's Mayor Stephen Reed assured himself a fourth term in a landslide victory.

headline: Vote out Borski, Fumo
abstract: Man criticizes U.S. Representative Robert Borski for costing thousands of people their jobs.  He mentions PA Governor Casey's $700 million investment to improve the highway system.

headline: Clinton gives compromise on gay ban
abstract: President Clinton delivered a policy that would allow gays to be in the military as long as they don't engage in homosexual activity.  He noted that advocates on both sides will be displeased.

headline: Officials here wary of governor's plan
abstract: Agreement wasn't in the vocabulary of the health insurers, insurance agents and legislators who gathered yesterday to discuss Governor Casey's state health-care plan.  The Senate Public Health and Welfare Committee held what it called a focus-group meeting on the issue at Independence Blue Cross.  The committee will hold such meetings across the state this month.

headline: Let parents pay education costs
abstract: In Michigan, the governor signed legislation that eliminated property taxes as a source of funds for public education.  The state plans to find another source of funding.  The columnist argues they should not find another source, and require parents to pay for their child's education themselves.  He advocates eliminating free public education in Pennsylvania and the rest of the country, as well as medical care, pension, and welfare.

headline: $3 million PAT cut worries county
abstract: County offices were generally pleased with the proposed budget by Casey but were worried about the cuts to the Port Athority and public transportation.

headline: Judge on the lam phones in sick
abstract: Josephi F. O'Kicki, a Pennsylvania judge who was tried in 1989 on public lewdness charges and convicted of corruption has vanished.  He never showed when he was supposed to be in court to begin his sentence of 2 to 5 years and pay $300,000.  Some think he is sick in the hospital while others think he has fled to his homeland of Slovenia.

headline: Mobile home owners say rules are unfair
abstract: Residents of mobile home parks are angry over their homes being taxed as both homes and vehicles. They also pay real estate taxes for services they do not receive, since mobile home parks are privately owned.  Many resident-landlord disputes also occur.  The state legislature has considered these issues before with little success, but the state finance committee will hold a hearing to listen to the concerns of mobile home owners.

headline: A time for courage
abstract: If the North American Free Trade Act dies, the prospects for workers will get bleaker, not better.  And so will America's politics.

headline: Old feuds, rivalries crowd out issues in PFT race
abstract: The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers union will have an election for the president, but many teachers don't see the point in even voting.  The races in the union always seem to turn into old political battles between old foes and don't focuse on the issues at hand including class size and resources, many teacher say.

headline: With, but not of Perot
abstract: A person writes into the newspaper to correct the newspaper's statement that United We Stand is a political party in support of presidential candidate Ross Perot. The person says that they are not a political party, but a non-partisan citizens organization.

headline: Clinton Signs Law Protecting Religious Practices
abstract: President Clinton today signed into law legislation requiring the Government to meet stringent standards before instituting measures that might interfere with religious practices.  The new law, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, overturns a 1990 Supreme Court ruling that set a looser standard for laws that restrict religious practices.

headline: Officials Predict Deluge of Suits On Health Plan
abstract: Even before President Clinton sends a formal legislative proposal to Congress, the Administration is preparing for a flood of constitutional and civil rights challenges to his health care plan.  Officials at the Justice Department and the Department of Health and Human Services say the Administration is only beginning to understand the potential wave of legal challenges.

headline: Liberals and 'choice'
abstract: School choice is an interesting idea.  What's galling, is the incredible self-righteousness of choice advocates- their insistence that choice is the only and obvious solution to what ails the nation's schools.

headline: $76.4 million in US funds granted for SEPTA projects
abstract: Federal agencies have awarded a total of $76.4 million for SEPTA rail improvements.  The federal Department of Transportation and the Federal Transit Administration supplied the funding, which was announced by US Representative Thomas M. Foglietta.

headline: Judge rejects plea that she quit case
abstract: Judge Jeannine Turgeon will not step down from the case although the public defenders Colin Kelly Lydon and Bryan S. Walk said her ruling earlier this week on their request for a non-jury trial uncovered bias on her part.  The trial is for a possible cerial killer who is charged with two murders and an assult.

headline: New bond issue means goodies for a few firms
abstract: The state agency overseeing city finances yesterday started the train frolling as it prepares a second bond issue worth millions in fees to politically connected law firms and financial experts.  In advance of its plans to borrow as much as $815 million on the city's behalf, the Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority board picked 15 consultants and said more would be selected in a few weeks.

headline: Absentee ballots
abstract: The Bruce Marks campaign has called attention to a problem in voting.  It's wrong for non-eligible voters to vote absentee ballots.  It is unfair to those who did go to the polls to count the votes of those who are lazy, whose ballots were made available by Democratic party workers.

headline: Open Bargaining-Citizens might consent to secret talks if they knew what was being negotiated
abstract: An editorial argues that secret contract negotiations between teachers and the school board do not allow taxpayers input. The author suggests that a public declaration of initial negotiations terms followed by intermittent declarations of proposals in public hearing is preferable to public negotiations. If taxpayers could comment on proposed deals, they may be inclined to allow the negotiation process itself to stay private, as the author recommends.

headline: Women told of hurdles in politics
abstract: Ruth Rudy, a sixth term Democratic House member, says its more difficult for women to hold office and the statistics demonstrate it.  The ones that do get in are usually because of the name reconition that their fathers or husbands have generated and once in office they need to do twice as well to get re-elected.

headline: Club could be expelled from state's federation
abstract: The midland Sportsmen's Club in Ohioville could face expulsion from the Pennsylvania Federation of Sportsmen's Clubs if the statewide group determines that the local club's membership policies are discriminatory. Federation officials are conducting an investigation into the club's practices of not admitting African Americans and women as members.

headline: On the front lines of US healt-care delivery, there is hope mized with anxiety
abstract: David Broder is convinced the Clinton health care reform plan must be examined by pracitioners such as John Polk, senior vice president of the Council of Smaller Enterprises, who hopes tax policies will allow individuals to purchase health care before taxes, and who is concerned about regulation of small firms competition. M. Orry Jacobs, senior vice president of University Hospital, recommends cost cutting incentives and state and local flexibility, while Cleveland's Free Clinic operator Marty Hiller advocates preventative health care incentives and a Canadian style system.

headline: Library/youth aid exchange
abstract: The editorial board says that the Pennsylvania Corps program, best known as the Conservation Corps, administered by PA Governor Casey's Office of Citizen Services is a quiet success of the Casey Administration.  The Summer Youth Service Corps for disadvantaged youth is a service-learning programs in schools under the heading of School-Based and Literacy Programs.  Casey has now announced a Library Corps to assist cash-starved libraries.

headline: 6 bills aimed at road safety
abstract: Calling the work zones on Pennsylvania's highways a "twilight zone of death and destruction," Representative Ronald S. Marsico yesterday announced a wide-ranging six-bill package to help make them safer.  Marsico would amend the state Vehicle Code to make speeding, careless driving, reckless driving, following too closely, drinking and driving and illegal passingin work zones punishable by automatic $1,000 fines.

headline: Judge says he fled to achieve justice
abstract: Convicted Cambria County ex-judge Joseph O'Kicki called WWCP-TV on Friday via an international telephone operator to explain that he fled so he could "fight for real justice in PA" and because he would not receive adequate medical care for cancer and heart problems in prison. After being sentenced to 2 to 5 years, O'Kicki skipped bail and has been a fugitive since, unable to appeal while on the run, said prosecutor Lawrence Claus of the PA Attorney General's office.

headline: New boost for housing
abstract: The Richard Allen Homes will be helped by the Philadelphia Housing Authority (PHA) due to the $46.2 million award given by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell had already promised to help the troubled PHA earlier in the year.

headline: Ad wars begin over health-reform plan
abstract: It was D-Day Plus One in President Clinton's campaign for sweeping health-care reform, and the smell of money- not munitions- was in the air.  Backers and foes have launched a multimedia drive to win over the American people.

headline: Optional plan evades savings on state cars
abstract: Some reform, that state House plan on group leasing for lawmakers' cars.  It would be optional.  That, is no reform, because individual lawmakers would will be allowed to lease cars for as much as $650 a month as they are now.  The plan is unacceptable, and area residents ought to tell their lawmakers so.

headline: Zimmerman retiring from Hershey Foods
abstract: Richard A. Zimmerman, chairman and chief executive officer of Hershey Foods Corp., Wednesday announced that he plans to retire at the end of the year.  He terms the change a planned, orderly succession.  Under his leadership, Hershey overtook competitor M&M/Mars for the nation's top spot in chocolate making.

headline: Conditions of life in L.A., cynicism temper the joy
abstract: At the site of a race riot a year before and the beating of Rodney King by police, today there is peace in light of two federal guilty verdicts for officers involved. While the courts have yet to rule for two other officers, citizens and members of the Brotherhood Crusade and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People held peace signs and NAACP executive director Benjamin Chavis praised the verdict. Racial cynicism however, was still evident.

headline: Oregon gets OK to allot services
abstract: Oregon will become the first-ever explicit attempt to ration medical services, launching a controversial program to cover every indigent person in Oregon but reducing the array of medical services available.

headline: Local OBE option is a bad idea
abstract: If the idea of permitting local school boards to decide whether to adopt outcome-based education (OBE) principles or to continue with present education procedures and goals becomes law, we fear the state's public education system will be in worse shambles than it presently is.

headline: A storm to remember
abstract: The Blizzard of '93 will be remembered for its deep snow, at least five deaths, eerily empty roads and heroic efforts of rescue and kindness.  PennDOT crews had major arteries passable by mid-day and a state of emergency was declared by Gov. Casey.

headline: Judge sides with Shaw in FOP fight
abstract: A Common Please Court judge struck down an effort by the Philadelphia Fraternal Order of Police to remove John Shaw from his post as chief of the union.

headline: New management for city garages
abstract: The Pittsburgh Parking Authority plans to save the city $217,000 by changing the management of three large surface lots and two parking garages.

headline: Adversaries polite, but cool
abstract: As Liberty Medal ceremonies ran long on Sudnay, President Clinton left his seat between South African President FW de Klerk and African National Congress President Nelson Mandela, departing to tour Midwest flood damage.  Their rivalry was evident.  It was also clear, in their comments and body language, that de Klerk needs Mandela.  Mandela does not need de Klerk.

headline: Oregon votes via mail
abstract: All of the registered voters participating in Oregon's June election did so by mail, over an 180day period.  The mail ballot saved the state hundreds of thousands of dollars and increased voter "turnout, " according to election officials.  And Oregon made history as the first state to hold such a statewide vote-by-mail election.

headline: Voters should think twice about Murphy's admiration of Philby
abstract: Civilization does indeed exist in the Fox Chapel area.  The suburbs may well lie boyond Tom Murphy's understanding, but what the voters need to worry about is whether large areaso fo the city lie beyond his understanding.  As for his bizarre comments about Kim Philby and his commitment to change and revolution: Philby's commitment was to deliver Western Civilization to Josef Stalin and his Soviet successors.  Philby sold out allies and had only disdain for the liberty of the individual.

headline: Contempt for minorities showed in two campaigns
abstract: Ace Moore, associate editor of The Inquirer, believes the actions in the Philadelphia Second Senate District race do not show that the city is advancing. He says that if the Democrats targeted African Americans and Hispanics into wrongfully election William G. Stinson to the PA Senate, this shows a lack of respect and equality for both groups and believes the Democrats should be punished if this is the case because it is disenfranchisement.

headline: Organ donation bill makes sense
abstract: The revised version of the organ donor bill that was passed by the state House judiciary committee is a positive step toward alleviating the serious shortage of transplant organs.  At the same time, the bill no longer contains the "implied consent" language for large organs that we found so troubling.  Under that provision, all citizens would be considered potential organ donors unless they specifically declined.

headline: Making schools accountable
abstract: California's voucher initiative, Proposition 174, would give parents about $2,600 per child to send them to any qualified school they want.  Among fears shadowing the measures are ones that it will violate separation between church and state by allwoing parents to spend tax money at religious schools.  Mary Jane Veirs, on the board of her children's Catholic school in Riverside, Calif., says the measure will force public schools to be better and more accountable.

headline: Airport authority still awaits OK on U.S. aid for study
abstract: The Susquehanna Valley Regional Airport Authority's please for federal funding for a study to see if it is nessiary to build another airport in central Pennsylvania has yet to be answered.  The FAA is being asked to finaince 90% of the cost, which is over $200,000.

headline: Judge to rule in expulsion over fake gun
abstract: Cumberland Couty Judge Kevin A. Hess expects to rule by week's end on whether a Lemoyne Middle School student expelled for bringing a fake gun to school can return to the classroom.  However, Hess aid during a hearing yesterday he probably won't void the one-year expulsion unless he finds the West Shore School Board violated the boy's rights or its own disciplinary policies.

headline: Next time, write about the success stories of public housing
abstract: The Executive Assistant of the Pittsburgh Housing Authority wrote into the newspaper complaining about an article that harshly criticized housing projects.   She says the article was one-sided and that public housing has helped many people, and tenants have become successful.

headline: Aesthetics do count
abstract: The erroneous date on the statue of the late Mayor Richard. S. Caliguiri should be corrected.  But you're wrong to think that "aesthetic perfection is less important than factual accuracy."  The entire granite base should be replaced and people are willing to contribute to help have the statue be made right.

headline: O'Reilly Ireland's richest
abstract: The former Irish rugby player Tony O'Reilly, H.J. Heinz Company Chairman, was named the richest man in Ireland, with wealth valued at $292.3 million. Most of the wealth is held as shares in the Pittsburgh based Heinz.

headline: Voters' suit over distric is dismissed
abstract: A lawsuit filed with the U.S. District Court challenged the redistricting that dropped a state senator from the Pittsburgh area to a newly created district in parts of the four counties near Pottstown.  The lawsuit was dismissed because no one was being denied the right to vote and it was the right of the legislature to format the voting districts.

headline: Counseling limits may be lifted today
abstract: President Clinton is expect to mark the day the 20th anniversary of legal abortion in America, but revoking his predecessors' restrictions on abortion counseling at federally supported clinics.  The Anti-abortion supports are making their annual march on the Supreme Court for the first time in years without the support of the president.

headline: PA continues with own plan
abstract: The Casey administration, never friendly with President Clinton, is pushing its own health-care reform and hopes to have at least part of it through the Legislature by the end of the year.

headline: Many area teachers lack contract
abstract: Teachers in 10 area school systems are scheduled to return to work without a contract this year, and in three districts, it's an all too familiar feeling.  In the Pennridge, Tamaqua and East Penn school districts, teacher resumed classes last year without a new contract and worked the year amid tumultuous negotiations, including a strike in Pennridge.  The union leaders and school boards have been negotiating for 20 months.

headline: Airport bond refinanced
abstract: Westmoreland County commissioners approved an airport authority's request to refinance a $3.7 million bond issue for improvements to the county airport in Latrobe and at Rostraver Airport.

headline: Judgment Day
abstract: Kathy Hendricks, claiming she developed multiple sclerosis after being injured at a Kenny Rogers concert, has won a $900,000 judgment against the singer's production company.  She was knocked over by some chairs as security guards were escorting Rogers onstage.

headline: Nuns plan fund drive for nursing home
abstract: The Sisters of St. Joseph of Baden yesterday announced a $3 million fund-raising drive to build a 120-bed nursing home on the grounds of their convent in Beaver County.  Villa St. Joseph will be a skilled and intermediate care home for low-income elderly people and will have a special 30-bed unit for people with dementia.

headline: Afta NAFTA
abstract: Well, NAFTA has passed the half of Congress where only a few weeks ago it had gone to be buried.  Bill Clinton can take deep bows for resuscitating the accord, which we thought all along to be- on balance- a good one.  But he'd created his own anti-NAFTA monster.  He let the Ross Perots and Lane Kirklands define the pact.  Clinton beat the monster he helped create, an dnow he must call on a nation's patience.

headline: Oust State Lawmakers
abstract: Referring to a letter to the editor by PA Senator Robert Mellow, citizen Walter Mazzola remarks on the lack of attention to a referendum's consequences for the elderly, saying Mellow was too busy worrying about effects of a referendum on children's education. Mazzola notices Mellow had no rebuttal for an editorial about high paying legislative salaries, and suggests a referendum that would vote overpaid politicians out of office.

headline: WAM 'buys' Hope for Eisenhower birthday
abstract: Twenty-four years after his 1969 death, state taxpayers paid $100,000 to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the birth of this country's 34th president, Dwight D. Eisenhower.  The money to underwrite the festivities was split into three WAM parcels, for some reason.

headline: Course uproots racism
abstract: There is a new class being taught once a week by volenteers in Brooklyn's Bensonhurst section about sterotyupes and race relations for the highschool.  It began as a way to cope with racial violence in the area that spurred the killing of Yusuf Hawkins, a black teenager who was killed for being in a white area.

headline: PACE Still Hurting
abstract: The state Department of Aging has begun to monitor prescription drug usage by older Pennsylvanians enrolled in the Pharmaceutical Assistance Contract for the Elderly.  The agency says the program is designed to protect patients from overdoses and conflicting prescriptions, but the program was born of the need to save money.

headline: Metropolitan Area News in Brief
abstract: Senate Majority Leader J. William Lincoln yesterday urged the State System of Higher Education to reconsider its decision, announced Thursday, to boost tuition at its 14 state-owned universities in 1993-94.

headline: All aboard, Greenfield!
abstract: The writer is thanking PA Representative Ivan Itkin for restoring bus service and that with the cooperation of the Port Authority Transit the service will resume shortly.

headline: Judicial proposal has some opposition
abstract: There is some opposition from both the Common Cuase of Pennsylvania and Robert Surick, a canidate for state Supreme Court for the May ballot question on judical discipline.  The amendment itself, which the legislature adopted, would replace the much criticized Judicial Inquiry and Review Board to discipline judicial members.

headline: Old Park looks for new friends
abstract: Residents near Riverview Park outside the University of Pittsburgh are hoping for increased community and city efforts to restore the dilapidated grounds of the park. Park history reveals a changing tide of effort and attention to its grounds, now waning once again. North Side Councilman Dan Onorato and North Side Partnership coordinator Ralph Hogan are hoping to fund improvements in the coming year.

headline: Age, experience among concerns to GOP hopefuls
abstract: The fight is on between Republican hopefuls Popovich, State Superior Court Judge, and Castille, a Philadelphia laywer.  The state Republican committee has endorced Castille by a 180-57 vote.

headline: Out-of-state lottery ticket firm alleges Pa. wants a monopoly
abstract: The Pennsylvania Lottery's new scratch-off game is called Monopoly.  And, according to Scott McLean, that's what the state lottery is and wants to continue to be: a monopoly.  The owner of Pic-A-State, a company that sells out-of-state lottery chances to residents of the Keystone state, Mclean has watched Pennsylvania legislators try to vote him out of business.

headline: WAMs furor
abstract: WAMs, for "walking around money" are spent by lawmkers who call them "legislative initiative grants."  At best, the controversial pockets of cash sprinkled through the state budget are innovative, flexible and expedient ways of getting cash to senior centers, local governments, art centers and charities overlooked by conventional funding programs.  At worst, they are unaudited and sometimes untraceable cash gifts.

headline: Court limits restraints on abortion blockades
abstract: The Supreme Court decided 5-4 that the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 could not be used to protect women going to get abortions at clincs from the protesting of anti-abortion supporters such as Operation Rescue.  The abortion-rights advocates must rely largely on state courts and local police to enforce state criminal laws and illegal protests.

headline: Painful choices are inevitable with health reform, analysts say
abstract: The draft of President Clinton's health-care reform plan calls for sweeping changes in the way medical services are delivered, dramatic savings from government and private insurance plans, and the promise that the patient- a bloated health-care system- will make an amazingly swift recovery.

headline: Monessen teachers contract approved
abstract: While negotiators in several Western Pennsylvania school districts wrangle over teacher contract proposals, those in the Monessen City School District have quietly reached a settlement.  Monessen school board members on Tuesday approved a three-year agreement that teachers approved last week.

headline: Amtrak puts its fast train of future on display
abstract: A passenger train using a twist and a tilt is vying with a system promoted by a Pittsburgh corporation to become Amtrak's next generation.
