Called the X2000, it senses curves and adjusts the tilt of cars accordingly so the train can travel up to 40 percent faster on the same track than the trains Amtrak now operates.

headline: Judicial reforms taking effect
abstract: Acting PA Governor Mark S. Singel signed a proclamation that will institute a new judicial discipline system, which will replace the Judicial Inquiry and Review Board.  The Pennsylvanians for Modern Courts lobbied for this judicial reform.

headline: Push is on for early Pa. sales tax increase
abstract: Allegheny County lawmakers are pushing for the PA State Legislature to approve a 1-cent-per-dollar sales tax increase  to finance regional attractions in the area (such as park, libraries, Pittsburgh Zoo, and Three Rivers Stadium). Rick Staford, executive director of the Allegheny Conference on Community Development, hoped the legislation would be introduced before the PA Legislature left for the holidays.

headline: Aide to Foerster named in lawsuit
abstract: A former Allegheny County employee, Beverly Assaro, claims in a federal lawsuit that she was fired a year after she was sexually harassed by Wayne Fusaro, executive assistant to Commissioner Tom Foerster.

headline: Oversight lacking for WAM gifts
abstract: It's called "walking around money."  That makes it sound a little like a grandparent who jingles change in his pokcet, doling out a uqarter here and there.  But WAMs amount to more than spare change, and the Washinton Legal Foundation last week asked Pennsylvania legislators to turn over documents that show which officials gave what to whom.

headline: Want some fries with that?
abstract: Campaign stops, where you fill up on the chicken dinnerrs at banquets and fast food on the road, can be fattening.  Just ask President Clinton, who is constantly hounded by jokes about his weight and penchant for french fries and fast food.  Sandra Schultz Newman, a candidate for Commonwealth Court, is more upfront, telling a GOP crowd she's gained 25 pounds since the campaign started.

headline: Tops in child care? Calif. gets the nod
abstract: Working Mother magazine reports on the quality of child care and ranks California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin.  They were based on the best health, safety, and funding for child care as well as ratio of teacher to children and availability.

headline: Differing Jewish view
abstract: As a Jew myself, I am mad that Rabbi Susan Marks' letter said that her 'traditions and beliefs' lead her to favor abortion rights.  I believe that the Jewish 'religious left' should not claim that my religion dictates their political views.

headline: Passavant Hospital offers baby-sitting class
abstract: Teen-agers and young adults who want to learn how to be a good baby sitter can get helpful tips from "Smart Sitters," a course being offered next month at North Hills Passavant Hospital.

headline: Monitoring sensitivities at Penn
abstract: The newspaper mocks the University of Pennsylvania for deciding its employees acted inappropriately in the way they attempted to stop black students from stealing the press run of the Daily Pennsylvanian.  It seems racial remarks were made. The Public Safety Task Force is mentioned.

headline: Authority to consider need for second airport study
abstract: In order to properly estimate the need for a second airport in the mid-state area within the next twenty years there must be more studies.

headline: Jury finds attacks on peers baseless, urges his removal
abstract: The statewide grand jury that recommended 27 felony charges against Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen also suggests that Larsen be removed from the bench in a report that shreds his credibility.

headline: Parkway messed
abstract: The editorial board supports nonprofits, the PA Department of Transportation, Allegheny County government, Allegheny West Authority, and Penn-Dot's efforts to break ground on the Three Rivers Parkway Project. The project will raise the aesthetic value of the parkway view, generate economic stimuli, and bring new development and commercial regulations. As no single authority exists for the project, it will be proposed one community at a time, but diverse backing, the board does not foresee a problem in approval.

headline: All but Specter salute nominee
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter injected the only cool note in an otherwise-warm reception federal Appeals Court Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg received at the opening of her confirmation Supreme Court hearings yesterday.

headline: PA justices cloak court in intrigue and politics
abstract: Justices Rolf Larsen and Nicholas P. Papadakos of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court met at a park bench in downtown Pittsburgh to discuss Larsen's fear that the court chambers were bugged.

headline: Was vote newsworthy?
abstract: Although the "Inside the Capitol" item regarding "miscast votes" by a group of Central Pennsylvania House Republicans on a resolution was technically correct, it is curious the writer found the mishap so newsworthy, especially, as the article noted, because an immediate move to correct the votes was made as soon as the mistake was realized.

headline: Two unions courting workers at USAir
abstract: Two big unions, the Teamsters and the United Steelworkers, sensing employee discontent at USAir over its plans to eliminate 2,500 full-time jobs and reduce benefits, are mapping separate campaigns to organize thousands of customer service workers.

headline: 'Don't do it - but if you do...'
abstract: When people discuss how to teach teenagers sex education the view points are completely opposite. Some feel that abstinence only is the best method while others feel that they are going to experience sex and hence should be taught so they can be responsible. Research is showing that the best method might be both, this way they know about sex but they are still taught to refrain from it.

headline: Paying for Mental Health
abstract: By approving a bill last week that would funnel more state money to community mental  health programs, the Legislature boxed Governor Mario Cuomo into the most awkward of corners: It forced him to threaten to veto a major initiative whose underlying principle he has long supported.  Seeking a way out, Mr. Cuomo has found a way to buy time, a maneuver that strenthens the possibility that a compromise can still be forged.

headline: Move problem kids in and you can kiss me goodbye
abstract: The writer does not agree with the Pittsburgh School Board's idea to send the city's problem teenagers to Mount Washington. The writer believes that Mount Washington is already full of problem teenagers and that having them all in one school will not solve the problem.

headline: Bill is aimed at BA-USAir deal
abstract: Two congressman have introduced legislation that would revoke British Airways' right to link flights with USAir and invest more money in the U.S. carrier.

headline: Jury gives Miller death sentences
abstract: In a case of double murder Joseph D. Miller was sentenced to death, ignoring his claims that he didn't deserve to die.

headline: Patton and Heinz Hall
abstract: A man writes to the newspaper praising Anne King Patton for helping fund the changing of Loew's Penn Theater into Heinz Hall. Loew's Penn Theater was going to be destroyed, but the man talked to county commissioners and the Allegheny conference on Community Development, who in turn discussed it with Anne Patton, who received the funding.

headline: All the Same: Incumbency Party looks out for No. 1
abstract: The editorial board suggests the manner in which state lawmakers have raised per diem from $88 to $110 shows the power of the incumbent party, consisting of both Republicans and Democrats.  The per diem expenditure amount was raised in the PA House Rules Committee without a role-call vote, making it easier for them to avoid their constituents know who voted yes or no.

headline: Pa. GOP moves to grab lead in Senate
abstract: Just when you thought it was quiet in the legislature, Senate Republicans made another attack yesterday in an enduring political feud.  A swearing-in ploy would give Republicans a 25-24 edge, challenging a previous arrangement.  Democrats were fuming.

headline: What makes David run?
abstract: David Cohen holds no title defined by the city charter, but he is without question the most powerful appointed official in the Philadelphia Mayor Rendell administration. Cohen has decentralized the management which gives everyone a lot more freedom to do what they want. Cohen and Rendell have a great relationship allowing them to work very well together.

headline: Tyson Foods opts not to reopen plant destroyed by fire
abstract: 475 employees are now unemployed after a six-alarm fire destroyed the Tyson Food poultry processing plant in Chester County last week.  The social services offices are getting swamped with unemployment applications as well as others seeking help in a time when they no longer know where their next pay check will come from.

headline: Ed blasts abortion foes
abstract: Mayor Rendell yesterday sharply criticized a group planning anti-abortion operations here, saying his administration would not tolerate the blockading of abortion clinics.  Rendell called the tactics of Operation Rescue, which has targeted Philadelphia and six other cities for a 10-day "Cities of Refuge" blitz beginning Friday, as "the antithesis of a democratic society."

headline: Penna. Action Line
abstract: This article had two questions asked in it: about the flu season and unemployment benefits. The PA State Department of Health predicts that the flu season will be bad and that those who are health professionals, chronically ill, or elderly get the flu shot. The US Congress approved legislation to extend the federal Emergency Unemployment Compensation program (EUC) until February 4, 1995.

headline: Moving On
abstract: Two college presidents are moving on: University of PA's Sheldon Hackney to the National Endowment for the Humanities, and Ronald Temple to chancellor of eight Chicago community colleges. Both men leave well respected, Hackney having instituted community involvement and organized a successful fundraising campaign, and Temple having raised respect, awareness, and enrollment for Community College of Philadelphia. The editorial wishes them both the best.

headline: Bridge paint job has been big headache
abstract: The authors are glad that the PA state Transportation Committee is investigating the Tarentum Bridge painting project since it has taken a lot longer than expected and disrupted citizens. There are still questions that need to be answered for the authors, since the project has caused a lot of other problems for people in the area. They commend PA state Representative Terry Van Horne for requesting the investigation and PA state Representative Joseph Petrarca (of the House Transportation Committee) for getting the probe started.

headline: Jury looks into Rxs for Larsen
abstract: Investigators conducting the criminal inquiry of the Pennsylvania Supreme court are examining whether Justice Rolf Larsen obtained prescription drugs through his employees.

headline: PIDA approves loans
abstract: Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority approved its highest monthly loan total, $16.5 million, in 15 years for 22 projects across the state.

headline: All wet?
abstract: The writer addresses the Republican community's disapproval of the Clinton wetlands policy. The policy requires federal permits to drain and fill a greater variety of wetlands, and Republicans claim this will cause property values to go down, and therefore decrease property-tax revenue. The writer claims that the Clinton's definition of wetlands hasn't expanded much and that it will protect the Alaskan coastal lands. He also says that by leaving certain wetlands unprotected as Republicans advocate, it will lead to flooding and the costs to fix it, thereby hurting the economy in the long-run.

headline: Pa. governor wants HDTV job creation
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey wrote President Clinton expressing strong support for US Labor Department Secretary Robert Reich's suggestion that the Federal Communications Commission consider job creation when imposing a broadcasting standard. Testing revealed such close similarities between HDTV, Zenith, and General Instruments that they collaborating on system development. FCC Commissioner James Quello said jobs should be a factor in setting the standard.

headline: What they're hoping to gain
abstract: President Clinton touts his health-care plan as giving the system major surgery, but many Philadelphia area residents are asking whether they will be on the winning or losing side of the fight for reform.  The hopes, fears and concerns of six people are given.

headline: Union takes strategic advantage in coal talks
abstract: The Bituminous Coal Operators Association could end the United Mine Workers' selective strike against Peabody Holding Co. In.c subsidiaries by giving the union information it wants about association members.  It was an impressive political maneuver by striking over the association's refusal to provide requested information.

headline: Equal rights in the womb
abstract: A man writes into the newspaper to protest pro-choice sentiments, saying that while women deserve full rights, so do unborn children.

headline: Pennsylvania's uncovered children
abstract: The state's new Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) began in May, with Governor Bob Casey and wife Ellen enrolling the first children May 3.  A graph shows estimates of children who need qualify for CHIP and who will be served divided into regions.

headline: New standards proposed for U.S. schools
abstract: While proposals to revamp the US health-care system are grabbing national attention, another vital reform is working its way through Congress almost unnoticed.  The loftily titled "Goals 2000: Educate America Act," passed this month by the House, establishes an ambitious framework of standards and goals for US student achievement by the year 2000.

headline: Bridge plan in doubt
abstract: A state historical commission has recommended shelving 5-year-old plans to replace Treichlers Bridge because the project would damage the historic Lehigh Canal.  The recommendation means PennDOT will have to submit an alternative bridge design.

headline: Jury report puts high court at a crossroads, officials say
abstract: Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen had inflicted acts of "judicial terrorism" on his fellow jurists, according to special prosecutor Edward S. G. Dennis.  State Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. said the grand jury report led to "one inescapable conclusion: Justice Larsen must now be removed from office.

headline: Plan expected to create winners, losers
abstract: The Clinton reform plan will have an enormous impact on the Philadelphia area health-care industry, the region's largest employer.  Based on interviews with industry executives and consultants, the likely winners and losers are given.

headline: Allen for judge
abstract: When you go to the polls November 2, you'll be electing five judges for the Court of Common Pleas and two for Municipal Court.  For the fifth seat, Jacqueline F. Allen is recommended, she will make an excellent judge.

headline: Pa. House changes its ways
abstract: In a vote of 189-8 the state Hosue passed new rules that would change procedural opperations, such as the amount of warning time the members must get before a vote is to take place, as well as cut down on the perks received by members of the legislature.

headline: When the minority represents the majority-Republicans in Congress took the voters seriously
abstract: In William Safire's opinion, the Democrat's attempt to steamroll an economic plan that included payoffs to Democratic mayors and personal projects increasing the deficit Clinton promised to cut in half has united a Republican minority that will insist upon the will of the people being heard. The Republican filibuster represents the voters standing strong on reducing the deficit and taxation for unnecessary pet projects, the economic promises on which Clinton was elected.

headline: Unions extend contract to avoid strike
abstract: Leaders of the 10 unions at the city's two major newspapers voted to extend their contracts indefinitely and day-by-day, to continue negotiations and avoid a midnight strike deadline.  Philadelphia Newspapers Inc., the publisher of the Philadelphia Inquirer and Daily News, immediately accepted the offer.

headline: Failed concept-Busing Phialdelphia kids across town won't improve neighborhood schools
abstract: The editorial disagrees with forced busing as a desegregation tool, in the Philadelphia School District citing general unhappiness, a decrease in the quality of available education, and a lack of community unity and pride in local neighborhood schools. Citing the federal government's abandonment of forced busing, the author wonders why the PA Human Relations Commission has renewed its interest. The rejection of forced busing by the PA Commonwealth Court has the author hoping for a better solution.

headline: Pitt will test new AIDS drug
abstract: An experimental drug will be tested on 20 AIDS patients at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, doctors said Tuesday.  Like AZT, the current standard treatment for AIDS, the new drug is intended to block an enzyme required for the virus to mature.  The problem with AZT is the virus eventually develops a resistance to the medication.  Doctors hope this will not be the case with the new drug, called L-735,524.

headline: No Substitute for Professionalism When It Comes to Good Education
abstract: It's not even Thanksgiving and the Williamsport Area School District already has been unable to find substitute teachers 33 times, inlcuding nine times at Williamsport High School.  The resulting scenario is one of classes being combined or other teachers in a particular subject filling in during planning periods, a situation in which "teaching and learning suffers," according to WHS Principal Philip M. Thomas.

headline: Bridge unveiled as part of bus way
abstract: Allegheny County and Port Authority officials announced that they plan to finish the initial stage of the proposed airport bus way by 1997, with a bridge from Downtown to the south shore of the Monongahela River. Howard Yerusalim, state secretary of transportation, said that the project is expected to take 10 months during the 1997-1998 construction seasons.

headline: Just do it
abstract: A man writes into the newspaper advocating the decriminalization of drugs, stating that people can obtain them whether they are legal or not, and that legalizing drugs would save the government and taxpayers a lot of money.

headline: Port authority agrees to waterfront land deal
abstract: The Port Authority decided yesterday to pay developer Ronald Rubin $4.25 million for just over 7 acres of land on the waterfront in south Philadelphia.

headline: Althaus cites family, won't seek 4th term
abstract: York Mayor William J. Althaus said he will not run for a 4th term which leaves the election wide open for other canidates.  He would not be interested in serving in congress, but would be interested in being governor, although he would not run for the position.

headline: Pa. House leader details Republican agenda for reform
abstract: Representative John E. Barley, a state House Republican leader, said Thursday that his party members will begin legislative maneuvers to force votes on reforms concerning business, government, welfare and family issues.

headline: When whites outnumbered they usually retain control
abstract: Whites are a minority in Harrisburg and 2,000 other US cities, counties or towns, but in most of those places, they keep a tight grip on political and economic power.  This was the finding of Associated Press reporters who checked out many of the communities where the US Census Bureau found blacks or Hispanics were in the majority.

headline: United to trim jobs and flights
abstract: United Airlines posted large fourth quarter 1992 loses and will, as a result, cut staff, limit routes, and management will take a salary cut.  The staff of United Airlines believes they can not take any more pay cuts.

headline: For the gays, it is one step ahead
abstract: A gay man formerly in the Navy writes about the Clinton Administration's "don't ask, don't tell" policy regarding gays in the military.  He says that it is an impressive step towards greater acceptance towards gays, but that this should not be accepted as a final solution.  He argues that policy is still not sufficient.

headline: Plan seen as 'frightening' or 'realistic'
abstract: President Clinton's healthcare reform plan is a bold leap into the unknown.  For consumers dogged by ever-increasing medical costs and fears their coverage will one day evaporate, the sweeping plan may sound great.  But the administration's plan is a hybrid of untested ideas, economic assumptions and, critics say, wishful thinking.  It's a $700 billion, five-year experiment of daunting proportions- and an intimidating political risk.

headline: OBE takes another step toward schools
abstract: Parents want answers about the new outcome-based education system being taught in schools. The new reforms require students to show they have attained skills in communications, mathematics, science and technology, and other components. Opponents across the state are deciding what step they will take next to halt the reform package

headline: Clinger announces more funding for Lycoming Airport
abstract: U.S. Congressman Bill Clinger announced that the House Public Works and Transportation Committee has approved a bill that will in crease funding for the Williamsport-Lycoming County airport by $100,000 a year for three years.  Other small airports nationwide  will receive similar funding. Clinger also authored a bill that would set up a commission to review all mandates.

headline: Justice Larsen's Drug Case Leaves Disturbing Questions
abstract: The man who was heir apparent to the position of chief justice on the oldest appellate court in the land has been indicted on drug charges and relieved of his duties on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.  But the case that has been made against Rolf Larsen is not the end of the troubling controversy that has besmirched the high court.  Instead, it has given rise to many disturbing questions and speculation.

headline: Pressure, threats to buy unwanted homes
abstract: People who look to the Logan Assistance Corp for help often end up getting in trouble. The corporation tends to force people into buying homes that they would not want to buy. Logan Assistance Corp says that they have done nothing wrong and there should be no reason for the investigation that is currently going on.

headline: America: What works
abstract: A look at how the federal government is doing to solve the nations problems.

headline: Pa. lawmakers grade 100 days
abstract: There was a general consensus, though harder to come by for Republicans, that President Clinton receives high marks for effort in his first 100 days in office, though marks for achievement are low. PA Representative Austin Murphy said Clinton's effort is larger than past presidents' 100 days, while PA Representative John Murtha conceded Clinton has been accessible if overambitious. Republicans are disappointed with what they view as lack of effort to reach across party lines in various proposals.

headline: Where are the liberal protestors?
abstract: Sean Duffy, the president of the PA Leadership Council, believes that the liberals in Philadelphia should be speaking out during the William G. Stinson and Bruce S. Mark election controversy. He believes that the dilemma in the PA Second Senate District shows that equal voting rights still have a long way to go and should lead to nonpartisan protests because fair voting should be wanted by all Americans.

headline: USW leader foresees lengthy strike
abstract: A union leader at Hankison Corp. of Canonsburg expects the current labor dispute to last longer than the nine-week strike six years ago.  The 91 members of United Steelworkers of America Local 6546 went on strike Thursday, one week after their six-year contract expired.

headline: Gay rights is a tough sell in Pa.
abstract: Homophobia of constituents and failure of politicians outside of Philadelphia to support legislation amending the 1964 Civil Rights Act to include discrimination based on sexual orientation are reflected by Politicians' absence from a gay rights march, and no comment by all but US Senator Specter, who had a hard time taking a stance given the mixed constituency he represents. Lancaster County Representative Robert Walker is against legislation, though optimists hope Specter and US Senator Harris Wofford will "do the right thing" when it comes to voting.

headline: Plan will have massive effect on area workers
abstract: The Clinton health-care reform plan will shake the foundations of the Philadelphia area's largest industry- health care itself- and could threaten the stability of many other businesses throughout the region.  At stake are jobs.  Lots of jobs.

headline: Options to ease overcrowding call for tax increases
abstract: Due to the expanding student population, the Downingtown Area School District has decided it must build new schools or expand its existing ones.  This means taxpayers will have to pay at least $206 more a year.  The school district is considering six different plans, but each will be costly.

headline: Cameron fix-up runs into $1.69 million
abstract: Synchronized traffic signals, wider streets, and more turning lanes at one of the city's busiest and congested intersections will cost $1.69 million. The project is necessary because of the number of different destinations accessible from the intersection, including PA state police headquarters, and the US Postal Service. The project is a welcome solution for Harrisburg Traffic Safety Unit's Sergeant Michael Butler.

headline: Justices of Ohio's high court often fight
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has nothing on the Ohio Supreme Court who has more fame for the fighting between justices than the decisions they make.  The charges against one another in Ohio include a fist fight between two justices, rumors that one consulted a psychiatrist about his sanity, accusations of leaking cases, and sweeping their office for hearing bugs that they believed other justices may have placed to electrically eavesdrop.

headline: Princely tribute
abstract: A proposal has been advanced for renaming a short stretch of roadway near Three Rivers Stadium after the popular Pirates broadcaster, the late Bob Prince.  Joe Gordon, the Steelers' communications director, noted that the stadium is home to both football and baseball teams and so it might be better not to use the name of a figure of just one sport.

headline: 'An egg is an egg' state agency claims
abstract: The PA State Attorney General's office has sued Eggland's Best Inc. for false advertising of low cholesteral eggs. Barbara Anthoney, chief of the attorney general's public protection bureau argues that vice president of medical and quality assurance for Eggland Dr. Jeffrey Garwin's study results were flawed. Scott Ballin of the American Heart Association agreed that Eggland advertising implied its eggs had lower cholesterol than other brands.

headline: Pa. Supreme Court race pulls crowd
abstract: Nearly a dozen judges and layers have expressed interest in Pa. Supreme Court opening even with the chaotic happenings between Justices Zappala, Cappy, and Larsen.

headline: Where's the other side?
abstract: Barbara White Stack's unbridled power ramblings concerning humane agents in her article paints a most convincing picture, even though it only covers half of the canvas.  Seems that the artist ran out of colors when it came to the positive side of the work.

headline: Where do you stand on issue?
abstract: In Senator Roger Madigan's recent letter, he spends three columns in the paper trying to justify a workers' compensation rate increase for insurance companies-money that comes right out of the pockets of Pennsylvania business- while reminding us how hard he worked on workers' compensation reform in Pennsylvania.  You can't have it both ways on this issue, Roger, no matter how much your instincts tell you to straddle the fence.

headline: Guinier: U.S. not discussing race issues
abstract: President Clinton withdrew his nomination of Lani Guinier to the nation's top civil rights post after deciding that her views on voting rights were not compatible with the administration's.  Guinier addressed the annual convention of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and received the President's Torch of Courage Award at the NAACP's annual meeting.

headline: Plan would affect virtually everyone
abstract: President Clinton's health plan would affect virtually everyone in some way.  Listed is the expected impact on various segments of society.

headline: Outcome-based education promises skilled workers
abstract: Business people are excited for the results of the proposed Outcome-based education because they feel it will produce workers that have accomplished something, not just sat in school for 180 days.  The only debate among the business people is about the 'values' that will be involved with the outcome based learning, which the business people have mixed feelings about.

headline: Canadians steer clear of Pittsburgh
abstract: The interstate 79 is horrible throughout the Pittsburgh area and cost the Mancuso family 5 tires in 10 days because of pot holes.  They refuse to drive through that area again on their trips from their native Canada to Flordia.

headline: Juveniles benefit from family-like rehab programs
abstract: Juveniles with serious criminal records, averaging 11 felonies apiece, go to facilities like Last Chance Ranch in Florida where they spend their time going to school, doing work around the ranch, playing basketball, and enjoying the benefits of what some are calling a family atmosphere.  This 6 to 12 month program costs 30,000 dollars as compared to the $100,000 it costs the state for incarcerating the teens, but the success rate in more then double.

headline: Rendell pushes rehab proposal
abstract: Rendell is pushing a year-old plan to renovate vacant housing it hopes will take care of housing problems in Philadelphia using federal funding it is already receiving.

headline: An end, a start in trash battles
abstract: A voluntary sidewalk clean-up near Penn fails.  But an assessment-based sweep of South Street begins.

headline: Pa. to N.Y.: Drop Dead
abstract: Just as the Middle East finally seems on the verge of peace, the world now faces another troublesome hot spot- an area of fierce regional loyalties, intransigent eleted leaders and a long history of factionalism between partisans.  We speak of the battle between Pennsyvlania and New York centered on SEPTA, Pennsyvlania's largest public transit agency, and New York state legislators, who are threatening to block the government purchase of Pennsylvania-made goods.

headline: Whither NAFTA?
abstract: The Great NAFTA TV debate is history.  Ross Perot was testy and Al Gore was calm and prepared.  The matchup offered dueling data, less-than-gripping graphs, little genuine illumination and no clear knock-out punch.  But all that is beside the point.  The central question is: Whither NAFTA?

headline: Where work meant minding the masters
abstract: The Rendell administration's privatization plan kicks off at the Art Museum and 85 guards loose their jobs.  45 will find other work within the government, 10 will be employed as gaurds with the private securaty company (with big wage cuts), and the rest will have to find work.

headline: Having Doubts About Disabilities Act
abstract: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), signed by President George Bush in 1990, is coming into question for not being effective. Laura Cooper, a national independent living consultant to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, says that requests for accommodations may not be filled for a long time. The ineffectiveness of the ADA is angering many Americans with disabilities who need to work for a living.

headline: Poem pleads for end to cruelty
abstract: International business student Stanton Cheah plans to read his poem entitled "We Pray" as one of the events scheduled to raise AIDS awareness while the Names Project AIDS Memorial Quilt is on display at Lebanon Valley College. Cheah hopes to educate others about preventing the disease as well as raise the level of compassion for AIDS victims and awareness.

headline: Paint splashed in library after Blackmun's speech
abstract: Vandals splash red paint in the library at Dickinson School of Law after U.S. Supreme Court Justice Harry A. Blackmun spoke against using a 'litmus test' for picking new justices.

headline: Changing captains
abstract: The ports on the Delaware River have just about gotten themselves to the point where they can fight back and take cargo from their East Coast competitors.  The mere possibility that this could really happen over the next few years is amazing given the history of non-cooperation between New Jersey and Pennsylvania, but a tentative merger of the two states' port agencies was announced recently by Gov. Florio and acting Pennsylvania Gov. Mark Singel.

headline: Killing crime panel would be 'travesty,' lawmaker says
abstract: The chairman of the PA House Judiciary Committee. PA Representative Thomas Caltagirone, tried to argue to save the PA Crime Commission from being stopped and instead giving its duties to the state police Bureau of Criminal Investigation. The commission was hurt when it named Attorney General Ernest Preate Jr. bad  for not punishing illegal video poker operations in exchange for campaign contributions. The Legislature provided only enough funding for the commission in the 1993-1994 budget to operate through December 31.

headline: Rendell to head housing in Philly
abstract: The US Department of Housing and Urban Development claims the Philadelphia Housing Authority has breached its contract with the federal government by failing to provide "decent, safe, and sanitary housing". The HUD demanded the PHA board be restructured.  Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell will become the chairman of the Authority and City Council President John Street will be vice chairman.

headline: An unethical wrist slap
abstract: It is unthinkable that Representative Richard Olasz of West Mifflin got away with his attempted thievery so lightly.  Those members of the General Assembly who said they were concerned by the situation should be.

headline: Pack it in
abstract: Poor Bob Packwood.  Not only has the Oregon Republican made a mess of his Senate career, but he has also sullied his reputation, perhaps irrevocably.  The controversy over Sen. Packwood's diaries has so clouded perceptions that it threatens to obscure the issue that prompted the Senate Ethics Committee's investigation of him in the first place: sexual harassment.  Resign senator, if not for your own sake, then for the sake of your state and your country.

headline: Whitman brother testifies
abstract: Governor-elect Christie Whitman's borther, a top official in her campaign, testified yesterday that Republicans worked hard at "keeping the vote light" in New Jersey's urban areas on Election Day.  Webster B. "Dan" Todd Jr. said he advised Whitman on how to curtain support for Governor Florio in Newark and Camden.  He said the campaign devoted a "fair amount of planning and effort" to keeping a referendum on legalized sports betting of the November 2 ballot, fearing the casinos would spend money in heavily Democratic areas to get out the vote.

headline: Workers' comp fund banking on reforms
abstract: The State Workmen's Insurance Fund, the largest provider of workers' compensation in Pennsylvania, is banking on recent reforms to stop- or at least slow- its hemorrhage of money.  And what a flow it has been: In 1987, the fund showed a surplus of $379 million.  At the end of 1992, the fund's surplus had dwindled to $30.6 million.

headline: Historic case for 2-parent kid care
abstract: In a new book by Mary Frances Berry entitled "The politics of Parenthood: Child Care, Women's Rights and the Myth of Good Mother" she looks at the history of who has traditionally looked after the children between the parents. In previous times father would look after more but now mothers tend to spend more time looking out after them.

headline: Poor to get managed health-care benefits
abstract: Come October 1, 1994, the 620,000 low-income people on Medical Assistance in Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery and Berks counties will all be in a managed health-care program that will be responsible for their health-care needs.  The Pennsylvania Department of Welfare got approval late last week for its Heatlh Choices program from officials at the US Health Care Financing Administration, which is part of the US Department of Health and Human Services.

headline: Parents have no option, except to start saving
abstract: With college costs growing faster than inflation, by the time a child born in 1993 attends college, the cost for four years at a private college or university will be close to $200,000.  You've got to begin preparing for an expense like that as early as possible.

headline: Construction Credibility
abstract: It's no secret the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has an image problem.  The number of reports of highway workers leaning on shovels instead of using thme makes all those Elvis sightings look like isolated instances.  With that less-than-flattering reputation, the last thing PennDOT needed was another blemish on its credibility.  But that's what has happened.

headline: Killing fields
abstract: Nothing really conveys the horror of this reality: a 14-year-old girl shot in the head and criticially wounded at 2:35 pm while walking down the street in the East Hills.  The tragedy of Sophia Hall and her 16-year-old brother- who was choked to death in March- is not merely a personal one.  It is a tragedy of American society that there are hundreds and thousands of Sophia Halls.  That the homes of many city dwellers are more bunker than refuge.  That the playgrounds are headquarters for drug dealers.  The the streets are free-fire zones.

headline: Rendell under attack for homeless-aid cuts
abstract: Councilwoman Jannie Blackwell led an attack on Mayor Rendell's proposed cuts on the homeless program by saying they were morally wrong because they will leave people out in the cold by taking away the number of emergency beds within the city.  Rendell's staff claims that the number of beds taken away by the $1.7 million cut will be more than made up for with perminant housing as well as transitional housing.

headline: And they're off in governor race
abstract: Four out of five Pennsylvanians don't have a clue yet as to who he is.  But US Representative Tom Ridge is emerging as an early favorite in next year's Republican primary for governor.  Ridge, a six-term congressman from Erie, has the backing of some of the state's top GOP leaders.

headline: Packwood going to court over subpoena
abstract: The courthouse is the next stop for Senator Bob Packwood as he resists a Senate demand for his diaries in an ethics probe of alleged sexual misconduct and possible criminality.  Packwood will file papers in federal court within two weeks to fight the subpoena, his chief of staff Elaine Franklin said yesterday.

headline: Whitman manages to steady campaign
abstract: Christine Todd Whitman, after lsing her footing, is now up and tottering.  The big question is, can she regain her balance and lengthen her stride in time?  With Election Day now 12 days away, the Republican is well behind Governor Florio and must go all out to pull ahead of him by November 2.

headline: Workers' efficiency soared in '92
abstract: U.S. workers productivity is up 2.8 percent in the last year, which is the biggest increase in the last 20 years.  Although productivity has risen the amount of hours worked has lowered which shows that the demand for jobs is reducing even though more is being produced.

headline: In Calif., longshorewomen
abstract: Due to a lawsuit establishing discrimination against women by the International Longshormen's and Warehousemen's Union, an agreement with the Pacific Maritime Association stipulated 35 percent of all new hires must be women until fulfilling a 20 percent quota. Currently, women comprise 10 percent of the work force, and their treatment has improved as their ability to keep up with the backbreaking labor has been proven. No one working for the Union takes their high paying job for granted.

headline: Predicting a Flood of Lawsuits
abstract: Administration officials drafting proposed legislation say they are concerned about how to provide remedies for consumers who are denied what may become a new Federal right: the right to adequate health care.

headline: Parents protest conditions at Cramp school
abstract: Cramp Elementary school is true to it's name- cramped.  And its overflowing condition finally sparked a pair of protests yesterday.

headline: Construction funds for Ghost Town Trail OK'd
abstract: Indiana County commissioners approved earmarking $79,700 in matching funds for a $397,500 grant from the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation for the purpose of constructing a limestone base for the Ghost Town Trail.

headline: Killing of pro-abortion doctors
abstract: The press has put the murder of David Gunn, the aboritionist shot to death in Pensacola, in the blame of all pro-life movement participants.  This is wrong because he had a background of violance and wasn't even very active in pro-life protests.  Most likely the people that will pray for the family of the murder victum are pro-life protesters themselves because they are not selective in their stand against murder.

headline: Salutes and Boots
abstract: Salutes for the week go to the operator of the Civic Arena in Pittsburgh for its new smoking policy, to Beaver and Vanport Township for considering a merger of their police departments and to a compromise that shows the needs of nature and business are not necessarily incompatible.  Boots go to those who continue to oppose the normalization of diplomatice and economic relations between the United States and Vietnam and to state Representative Pete Daley, who wants to incarcerate the state's inmates in foreign jails.

headline: Appeal filed over 2nd ballot spot for Evans
abstract: The fight over whether Dauphin County Chief Public Defender Scott A. Evans- already a county judicial candidate on the Republican ballot- can appear on the Demcoratic side is on its way to the state Supreme Court.  Robert B. MacIntyre, who was an unsuccessful Republican judicial candidate in the primary, filed the appeal yesterday, taking the place of Representative Jeffrey E. Piccola, who initially was handling the challenge on behalf of 15 Democrats.

headline: Painful Lessons for Mexican Labor
abstract: Standing almost in the shadow of Mexico's twin volcanoes, long lines of new Volkswagen Beetles- remarkably unchanged from those sold in waves in the United States until the 1970s- give an impression of steadiness and continuity.  But that belies the turmoil that has shaken Volkswagen de Mexico during the last year and may be a precursor to the painful transition that all Mexican businesses are aobut to undergo, with or without a North American Free Trade Agreement.

headline: Whitman releases reports on final weeks' spending
abstract: Senior Republican officials, facing accusations that the party paid $500,000 to black ministers and Democratic Party workers to suppress voter turnout in urban areas, yesterday released records that they said proved the charges were untrue.  But the campaign finance reports, for the waning days of the governor's race, leave many questions unanswered and probably will do little to still the storm of controversy over the issue.

headline: Workers rally at endangered plant
abstract: Union workers of the bankrupt Shenango Group Inc, a steel producing plant, have been holding a vigil.  They want to have an employee buyout with stock options so that the plant can continue to operate.

headline: In support of women making their own decisions
abstract: Operation Rescue arrived in Philadelphia July 8 for a 10-day "Cities of Refuge" campaign.  The group's goal of blocking clinics that provide abortion services clearly did not meet with the success the members had anticipated.  Those who support women's rights to choose an abortion have to remain organized and ready for Operation Rescue's campaign.  At the Elizabeth Blackwell Helath Center, they respect women's ability to make moral decisions for themselves and support those decisions.

headline: President to limit federal subsidies in health program
abstract: To control the cost of his proposal for universal health insurance coverage, President Clinton has modified it to limit Federal spending on subsidies for low-income workers, small businesses and early retirees, Administration officials and Congressional aides said today.

headline: Pay now, go to college later
abstract: The state syas it's getting 400 calls an hour and that 150 people have signed up in just the past week for a new program that allows parents to lock in today's college tuition rates for future use.  Apparently none of those calls are coming from Bucks County, where guidance counselors said they know little about the program, have received no information about it from the state and have learned all they know from the media.

headline: Construction of mall could commence within one year
abstract: Construction of a shopping mall on the north side of US 224 in Union Township could begin within 12 months, Peter Gerney said, a spokesman from the development company.

headline: L.V. program has to go
abstract: Project Child, a member of the Child Abuse Prevention Coalition of the Lehigh Valley/Pocono Mountains, will be on its own on October 31, 1994 when its three-year grant from the Pennsylvania Children's Trust Fund runs out and it will need alternative sources of funding to continue its 24-hour hotline for troubled parents and child abuse prevention education.  Virginia Jensen, executive director of Project Child believes they will survive with a combination of funds from the county and other local sources.

headline: Shelter owner won't run it
abstract: Mohammed "John" Mizani, who was asked by the city to run a proposed homeless shelter in spite of the fact that a previous shelter he ran failed, decided to back out of the deal because he felt the city was requiring he offer so many services that the project would bankrupt. He will rent the shelter to the city but won't take part in its operation. The city is now negotiating with Sylvestor Outley, who may run the shelter. Outley had previously run a homeless shelter that offered drug rehabilitating and counseling, but it was forced to change to a short-term shelter, which many believe was a gesture to Philadelphia Mayor Rendell.

headline: Appellate ruling keeps 3 council candidates on ballot
abstract: A Commonwealth Court upheld a lower ruling allowing three Democratic Harrisburg City Council candidates to remain on the primary ballot. The candidates were not among those endorsed by Harrisburg mayor Stephen R. Reed. In the judges' opinion, although the candidates filed late financial statements with the city clerk, their promptly filed Dauphin County statements revealed they provided adequate access to information by voters.

headline: Parting Shots
abstract: A person writes into the newspaper to criticize state legislators for bullying Philadelphia's transit authority into giving a railcar contract to West-Mifflin based AEG Westinghouse, even though AEG demanded more money than the winning bidder.  The writer of the letter wonders why Allegheny County politicians would want to waste the money on a company that is moving to Washington County.

headline: Who elected her?
abstract: Hilary Rodham Clinton is organizing a national health care plan.  She is aid to be a critical advisor on judicial nominations.  She may lead the charge to overhaul the welfare system.  Observing all this, a growing number of citizens have made the hostile query: "Who elected her?"

headline: Wounds still deep at Caterpillar-Discord continues in year since UAW strike ended
abstract: The United Auto Workers strike ended unsuccessfully for the union. After federal mediation broke down, UAW workers were forced to return tot their jobs, fearing replacement. President Clinton has promised a federal ban on permanent replacement of strikers. For now, conditions in the Caterpillar factory remain hostile although workers are hopeful upcoming union elections will allow negotiations to resume.

headline: Increasing abortions
abstract: Claude Lewis' May 17 column criticized PA Governor Casey for protesting too much about the abortion issue before the National Press Club. However, Mr. Lewis failed to describe the reason for the Governors remarks. The reason is that President Clinton's actions and proposals would greatly increase the number of abortions our country sees. Lewis should be joining Governor Casey in his criticisms of the President not criticizing the Governor himself.

headline: Private surgery facility denied state certificate
abstract: The proposed New Castle Ambulatory Surgical Center has suffered a setback because the application for a Certificate of Need was denied by the PA State Department of Health. The facility was not consistent with the new State Health Plan.  PA Representative Frank LaGrotta, who was opposed to the center, said that the was the first Certificate of Need denied by the state in 10 years.

headline: Penn finally discovers Philadelphia high school grads
abstract: Memories of the sometimes bitter controversy over the number of Mayor's Scholarships the University of Pennsylvania was to award to Philadelphia high school students may have gone on the back burner this week.  During a City Hall reception Monday, Mayor Edward Rendell, City Council President John Street and University of Pennsylvania Interim President Claire Fagin greeted the first class of Mayor's scholars selecte dunder Penn's expanded recruitment program for local students.

headline: Cooling off period ends for pilots, Flagship
abstract: Negotiations between AMR Corp. affiliate Flagship Airlines and 1,100 American Eagle pilots dragged on last night in an 11th-hour bid to solve a long-standing dispute before the midnight expiration of a 30-day cooling-off period.

headline: Land acquisition for new prison complete
abstract: Land purchase documents for property at the site of the future state prison, the Clearfield State Correctional Institution, were signed at the district office of PA Representative Camille "Bud" George. Reverend John Neyman for the St. Barbara's Polish National Church, President Paul Wild, Secretary Treasurer Judi Matia and Larry Kanour of Power Contracting of Osceola Mills R.D. transferred land to the state to PA Department of General Services Secretary David L. Jannetta.

headline: Signs of distress
abstract: East Pittsburgh has applied for "distressed status", and the PA Department of Community Affairs has offered advice to help Pittsburgh's economy. They recommend Pittsburgh contract out for part of its police protection, get involved with surrounding communities to carry on a joint public-works program, and share a trained municipal administrator with other boroughs. The Department of Community Affairs reccomends other areas in financial distress take on similar measures.

headline: Area firms, unions add pressure
abstract: Midstate companies and union have made their voices heard on both sides of the NAFTA debate.  Representatives of AMP Inc. traveled to Washington last weed urgining legislators from Pennsylvania and North Carolina to vote today for the North American Free Trade Agreement.  On the other side of the debate, midstate unions have sent delegations to Wahtington to urge NAFTA's defeat.

headline: Partisanship in Harrisburg getting worse
abstract: The Speaker of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives writes into the newspaper to criticize the partisan nature of the House.   He sites statistics that show that Republicans are more likely to vote along party lines.  He says that he will try to reach out to the Republicans and come up with bi-partisan solutions.

headline: Who's practicing overzealous party politics?  Democrats plead innocent
abstract: The PA Speaker of the House of Representatives writes an opinion piece criticizing the Republicans in the General Assembly for having a greater tendency than Democrats to vote along party lines.

headline: Board eases nepotism policy
abstract: The West Shore School Board boted last night 6-3 to adopt a new policy that relaxes the rules of nepotism to allow relatives of school board members and administrators to be hired by the district.

headline: It's just too late
abstract: There is now a new approach to second-and third-trimester abortions.  It is D&X (Dilation and Extraction) and has led pro-lifers to use this development in an attempt to kill the Freedom of Choice Act.  Dr. Martin Haskell explained the process.  D&X is legal; the target of the Metzenbaum scissors, which slice the skull, evacuating contents, is not yet a "person," not yet human enough to be protected by the Constitution.

headline: Public health systems will change, but how?
abstract: The future of public health after health-care reform remains cloudy, even if a reform plan calls for the continuation of local public health systems, as is likely.  But what is not as clear is how some of the programmatic aspects of a traditional public health department- immunizations and senior services, for example- would be treated.

headline: Penn protesters balk at proposal for scientific-research complex
abstract: Protests broke out with signs that read things like 'Johnny Can't Read, Johnny Can Kill' during a meeting between University of Pennsylvania and representatives from the Pentagon.  The Pentagon is planning to partically fund a new science building at the University of Pennsylvania that will replace a 19th century building.

headline: County is pleased with the possibility of more state funds
abstract: Allegheny County officials received an increase in human services funds in the Democrats' budget. The spending plan will help avoid the shortfall in state funding for the Port Authority. State operating subsidies provide about half of the PAT's budget, which is about $211 million. The Democrats plan would increase overall funding by $4.8 million.

headline: Larsen again slated by jury
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen will make his fourth appearance before a grand jury investigating the court, a signal that his attempts to quash the secret investigation may have failed.

headline: Site of apartments for elderly disputed in Greenfield
abstract: A local community group has launched a proposal for federally subsidized 40-unit apartment building to house low income elderly in Greenfield; the only problem is the local residents don't want it nearby. Local officials have been seeking a suitable site for years and this current one seems like the perfect place. People in the neighborhood don't want the apartment building there because they feel it will diminish the character of the community.

headline: Area leaders in Harrisburg for meeting
abstract: The possible closing of Indiana's Season-all plant should be near the top of the list of topics for discussion when a group of Indiana business leaders meet with the Pennsylvania Commerce Secretary.

headline: Patriot Party holds first meeting
abstract: The Perot-inspired New Patriot Party had their first State Committee meeting in which they outlined some of the parties goals which including reforming the government to have less lobbiest, minizing government, and making government be more accountable and responsible.

headline: Who's stalking Perot?
abstract: We don't doubt there may be some nutbag who wants to take a shot at ol' Ross Perot.  Such are the risks of celebrity these days.  Turn the pressure up and you can be sure that he'll go public with the latest conspiracy.  The plot du jour: A half-dozen Cubans are planning to take him out as he struggles to sqeeze off a few one-liners at Vice President Gore's case for the North American Free Trade Agreement.

headline: 4th-graders to dive into outcome based math
abstract: Fourth-graders in some Pennsylvania schools will participate in a math test where they must come up with the best way to construct an aquarium and fill it with fish.

headline: Journalistic trailblazer
abstract: The article praises the life of Robert C. Maynard who recently died at age 56. He was the first African American to own a major daily newspaper and founded the Institute for Journalism Education, an organization which trained minority journalists.

headline: Questions and answers concerning breat cancer
abstract: Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in American women.  Risk Increases with age and family history increases the chance.  It can be detected by lumps in the brest but the best way in a mammography.

headline: Penn State plan is unveiled
abstract: Using a state grant, the Delaware County campus of the Pennsylvania State University will get a new $3 million academic building.

headline: County projects included on state's road repair list
abstract: The state transportation committee has approved several road and bridge projects for the 1992-2004 12-year transportation program.  The state prioritizes two p projects and reviews their progress every two years, and then the list is updated.  The article goes on to list some of the projects.

headline: Larsen faces drug charges, is suspended
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen was charged yesterday with illegally using court employees to obtain prescription drugs for his use.  The rest of the court sweiftly relieved him of his duties.

headline: Site of vets home under fire
abstract: PA Governor Robert Casey declared the building of a new veterans' home, but the land he designated for it is part of a state park.  The Friends of the Poquessing Watershed, an environmental group, are fighting Casey's decision.

headline: Area Votes in Congress
abstract: Votes in US congress this week were as follows: voted against ending the Special Committee on Aging, voted for bill HR 920 providing extra weeks of jobless benfits for the long-term unemployed, and overhauluing the Hatch Act.

headline: Patriot Party tries to gain more attention
abstract: The Patriot party is trying to attract Ross Perot as its presidential candidate in 1996. Tim Holloway, the party's state vice-chairman says they have plans to help spread the base of the party. He hopes that  these plans will help bring in Perot.

headline: Who's worst
abstract: In New Jersey's governor's race, Republican Christie Whitman has TV ads calling Democratic Governor Jim Florio "the worst governor" the state has ever had.

headline: 6 of midstate's school districts lack contracts
abstract: With the new school year approaching six Pennsylvania mid-state school districts still do not have a contract with their teachers. 115 districts state-wide are without contracts.  This is because teachers are striking for better pay and benefits.

headline: Judge refuses to disqualify self
abstract: The plantiffs in a suit over Pennsylvania's Abortion Control Act want Senior U.S. Deistrict Judge Daniel H. Huyett to withstain from participating in the case due to bias about abortion.  They sight previous rulings and quotes from his past, but he claims that he is not bias and will not step down.

headline: Rabid raccoon bites child
abstract: A rabid raccoon bit a 4-year-old girl in her back yard Sunday, making her the first person exposed to rabies in Allegheny County this year.  State Health Department officials have taken several hundred calls from people afraid that they might have been exposed to a rabid pony at the Peters Township Community Fair.

headline: Penn's Fiscal Plan Would Cut 3 Departments
abstract: Citing the kinds of tight finances that are squeezing campuses nationwide, the University of Pennsylvania has moved to eliminate three departments- religious studies, civilization and regional science- and absorb their faculty in other departments.

headline: Departments merged
abstract: Commissioners in Westmoreland County approved a consolidation plan under the Department of Public Works. The new department will oversee the bureaus of parks, weights and measures, engineering, and building maintanence, cutting costs and eliminating duplication of services, said administrative aide to the commissioners John Pallone.

headline: Larsen makes converts
abstract: Larsen, a PA Supreme Court justice, has made accusations of wrongdoing from justices that are wired to case fixing within the PA Supreme court.  There needs to be more discipline within the court system, which should be enacted upon by the legislative branch.

headline: Spirit unbroken, members rebuild
abstract: The building in which the Marcus Garvey movement group, Universal Negro Improvement Association, has called headquarters for over 40 years has burnt in Philadelphia.  They plan to rebuild it and hope to inspire the rest of the community to improve the neighborhood.

headline: Argall rules out run for Congress
abstract: State Representative David G. Argall confirmed Tuesday he will not be a candidate for the Republican nomination in the 6th Congressional District race next year.  Argall, whoe 124th District straddles the Berks-Schuylkill county line, was expected to be the GOP standard-bearer in the ifrst challenge to freshman US Representative Tim Holden.

headline: Patriot Party will campaign to oust Justice Papadakos
abstract: The new Patriot Party is an offshoot of citizens supporting Ross Perot that opposes the retention election of Justice Nicholas P. Papadakos to the PA Supreme Court. Some of their reasons are that Papadakos employed his son Peter-Clyde and pays him a high salary, he is above the mandatory retirement age of 70, and in 1989 he voted to increase his own pension.

headline: Whose friends hurt most?
abstract: George F. Allen, the Republican candidate for Virginia governor, hasn't run a sterling race to date, yet he has made a spectacular leap in the polls, from 30 percentage points behind this spring to 17 points ahead in one recent survey.  It isn't so much what Mr. Allen or his opponent, Democrat Mary Sue Terry, have or haven't done in the campaign that has counted.  Rather, it is that Ms. Terry is in the unfortunate position of being linked to state and national Democratic leaders who are wildly unpopular in many corners of the state.

headline: A  letter on Temple's graduates is given an "F"
abstract: Temple University Professor George Ingram writes in reply to Penn State Univeristy Professor David Milby to defend Temple from remarks made that the students from Temple University do not help the urban community  once they graduate.  He lists Floyd Alston and the Sister Mary Scullion as people/organizations from Temple that are making a difference in Philadelphia.

headline: Keep up the embargo
abstract: Cuban people have been suffering shortages for many years- not only of medicine, food and material goods, but also of dignity, freedom and human rights.  Only fools would think that the problems of this once rich and beautiful island coul dbe solved by a collection of some medicine and food which will not even reach the Cuban people.

headline: Rationing: It's when medicine plays the odds
abstract: President Bill Clinton's health-care reform plan does not deal with rationing of treatment that may not actually cure or prevent death. Examples of elderly patients not given treatments to prolong life and twins joined at the heart are given as cases where rationing would affect patients.

headline: Phila. district throws book at school discipline problems
abstract: Expulsion is back- not only in Philadelphia but, perhaps soon, in every school district in Pennsylvania.  Earlier this month, the state House passed 160-36 a measure that would force all 501districts to expel any student caught with a weapon.

headline: Disabled seek improved transportation
abstract: Two young women who use wheelchairs told the Fayette County commissioners Wednesday that it is difficult for them to live an enjoyable and independent lifestyle with the county's current transportation options.

headline: Larsen pleads not guilty to 27 felony drug charges
abstract: During Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen's first court appearance as a criminal defendant, his attorney did not dispute the fact that Larsen had used employees to obtain prescription drugs for him.  But William Costopoulos argued yesterday that there was nothing illegal in Larsen's actions, which resulted in 27 felony drug charges being filed against him last week.

headline: Snider-Katz deal seen still doable
abstract: City and state officials are quietly trying to nudge Sixers owner Harold Katz and Flyers owner Ed Snider back together in a deal for the proposed $134 million Spectrum II.  But neither Mayor Rendell nor Governor Casey are holding out the possibility that they'll provide anything beyond the approximate $15 million in public money already committed to the project.

headline: Arlen's hat nixed on voice vote
abstract: Arlen Specter gets some comments on a "Pennsylvania" baseball cap he wore with his business suit.

headline: Pay Packages of Nonprofit Executives
abstract: As reported on Internal Revenue Service tax forms, a listing of pay package values of Nonprofit executives includes compensation exceeding $400,000 in some cases. In other cases, compensation may be closer to $1,000,000.

headline: Wife of Kenna may run for state seat
abstract: County Commissioner Joseph Kenna's wife, Barbara, is considering running for the 155th District legislative seat.

headline: A tale of 3 cities
abstract: The Philadelphia Art Museum is joining with a museum in Paris and one in London to exhibit a major Paul Cezanne retrospective in 1996, the only one in the US. The author says it may seem hard to justify spending on art when other services are being ignored, but a city without cultural institutions may not be one worth protecting.

headline: Lawsuits against abortionists urged
abstract: A year-old anti-abortion group in Texas has designed a glossy kit for lawyers on how to sue doctors who perform abortions in what the group says is a new tactic to launch large numbers of malpractice and damage lawsuits.  During the last two weeks, Life Dynamics in Lewisville, Texas, has mailed the 72-page guide to 4,000 lawyers nationwide.

headline: Restaurant rating system gets a C
abstract: The Allegheny County Helath Department officials say the system they use to grade area restaurants is unfair to restaurant owners.  The department today will propose new regulations for an estimated 9,000 food purveyors, including scrapping the A-B-C health rating system for restaurants.

headline: Phila. Schoolboard names an acting superintendent
abstract: The Board of Education named Theresa Lemme to serve as acting school superintendent until a permanent replacement is found for Constance E. Clayton.

headline: Disney's cut won't redeem forgettable film
abstract: A scene that occurred in the movie "The Program" has happened in real life.  If you haven't already seen it, The Walt Disney Co. has decided you never will.  After a teen-age boy was killed and two others were seriously injured while trying the highway stunt in two separate incidents, the scene will be edited out of the film.

headline: Larsen ready to talk in probe
abstract: State Supreme Court justice Rolf Larsen has told investigators that he would cooperate with them in the criminal investigation of Cappy and Zappala, both Supreme Court justices.  Larsen accused them of giving preferential treatment to cases in which they both had interest as well as illegal wiretapping.

headline: State audit of city program delayed until mid-October
abstract: The state's audit of New Castle's Community Development Block Grant program isn't expected to be completed until mid-October, according to a representative of the Department of Community Affairs.

headline: Armstrong County looking beyond Moonlight's closing
abstract: When Moonlight Mushrooms closes in January, Armstrong County will lose $30 million the mine pumped into the local economy, said County Commissioner and Chairman Jack Dunmire.  But he said he isn't giving up.

headline: Pay Packages of Nonprofit Executives
abstract: Listed are the amounts of total compensation for executives of nonprofit organizations, as reported on Form 990s filed with the Internal Revenue Service for the years noted. Not included on the list are individuals whose compensation is given in the accompanying article. The list, derived from 6,000 IRS forms, gives a representative sample of each major category of tax-exempt groups. Local organizations are in boldface type.

headline: Williams quits over controversy
abstract: Controversy over an emerging history of fraud, assault, forgery, and fabrication have led to the resignation of Bucks County Redevelopment Authority and state GOP committeeman Robert Williams. Republicans in his party, colleagues, and the Young Republicans National Federation are relieved at Williams decision, which has brought bad publicity to the party. Williams has served parole for both federal and state convictions.

headline: Acting Gov. Singel: Improving math skills multiplies economic competitiveness
abstract: Acting Governor Mark S. Singel speaks of the Pennsylvania 24 Challenge math program, involving over 250,000 students, and draws a parallel between mathematic and science education and how jobs are demanding such skills with advanced technology.

headline: Let them exercise their choice
abstract: When voices are silenced by a government and media machine that allegedly support free speech and the right to assemble, then a few of the less-balanced are bound to go ballistic, literally.  Pro-life activists could make women who are considering abortion think more about the reality and seriousness of their decision.  Protesting is their right.

headline: Retailers sue drug companies
abstract: The nation's biggest drugstore chains filed a broad antitrust lawsuit accusing leading pharmaceutical companies of colluding to drastically mark up the prices they charge neighborhood pharmacies.  The lawsuit, filed in US District Court in Harrisburg, accuses seven drug makers of charging pharmacies up to 1,200 percent more than other drug buyers such as hospitals and health maintenance organizations.

headline: Poorer students will be left behind with 'choice'
abstract: Annette Palutis, President of the Pennsylvania State Education association writes about how the idea of school choice has been floating around Congress in Pennsylvania a lot lately, specifically  with the bill that Senator Dawida introduced The idea is that a parent would get to chose which public school they would send their children too. Much of the impetus for this legislation comes from the closing of parochial schools due to troubled finances of inner city parishes. Many people feel that these choices would benefit children of more affluent families but would hurt the children of poorer families

headline: Don't sell Stage II of the light-rail system short, PG
abstract: The writer believes that the proposal of the Stage II of Port Authority Transit's Light Railway Transit System would provide for the greatest savings in travel time, lowest subsidy per rider, and a completion of the system envisioned in the 1970s. Stage II has been supported by the Port Authority, LS Transit Systems, and the Southwestern Pennsylvania Regional Planning Commission (SPRPC) and hopes that they will be able to persuade the Federal Transit Administration to fund the project.

headline: Larsen resumes grand jury testimony
abstract: Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen made another appearance yesterday before the state grand jury that is investigating the hgih court, and his attorney said he was uncertain whether Larsen had concluded his testimony.

headline: State comes calling for city's $1M check
abstract: The city of Meadville is investing $1 million dollars in a special program designed to help local municipalities earn a greater financial return on their investment. Meadville became the first city in the state to enroll in the program. By doing this the city would save 5,000 dollars on investment fees compared to investing with a private firm.

headline: Ask not what the city's $9 can do for you, jurors
abstract: John Wind proposes the option for jurors to put their jury stipens of $9 a day towards the government office of their choice.  He believes most would do this and if 100 jurors per day donated $9 it would generate another $250,000 annually for social programs.

headline: Peabody Students Talk With Secretary of Commerce
abstract: The picture shows PA Secretary of Commerce Andrew Greenberg meeting with students from the Youth Entrepreneurial Training Program.

headline: Willingness to sacrifice, skepticism
abstract: Clinton's tax increase of the rich from 31 to 36 percent plus a 10 percent surtax on those making $250,000 or more is greeted with surprising willingness to contribute.  Clinton's speech on health care told American's that they must accept responsibility and take a tax increase.  Some of the wealthy are worried that they are being targeted unfairly.

headline: Legislation will help reduce pollution
abstract: Environmentalists and farm organizations are praising the nutrient management bill passed unanimously by the Senate and approved earlier by the House, and is expected to by signed into law by Governor Casey soon that is expected to cut by millions of tons the pollution that flows into the Susquehanna River and, ultimately, the Chesapeake Bay.  The measure was sponsored by PA House Majority Caucus Chairman Representative Jeffery Coy.

headline: Let's set an example
abstract: Perhaps those Christians who are expending so much energy on the negative aspects of the reorganization in our diocese could think about better utilizing that energy on the values and teachings of Christ.  Let's focus on the positive aspects of reorganization and show our young people by example, what being a Christian is all about.

headline: Risky behavior should cost, survey says
abstract: If you smoke, abuse alcohol, use illegal drugs or engage in unsafe sexual practices, most Pennsylvanians want you to pay more for health insurance, according to a study released yesterday.  The survey of 600 residents, commissioned by the Pennsylvania Medical Society, found that most people are unwilling to tolerate hgiher heatlh costs driven by their neighbors' unhealthy behaviors.  The message from the survey was simple: If you take risks, then you- not society- should pay for it.

headline: Population shift could mean less money for Phila. schools
abstract: Due to the potnetinal loss of the federal Chapter One, the Great Society prgram from Philadelphia schools to the schools out west, where the census said are in worse poverty, schools such as Birney School in Logan will have to make changes.  Part of the changes may be cutting some kindergarden programs because the $1 million loss of federal aid will substancially hurt the effort to educate the urban population.

headline: Dozens of major, minor road projects ahead
abstract: Major road projects are planed by PennDOT in districts 10,11, and 12, which include various parts of the Valley.  The projecets are plnaned for the next 10 years.

headline: Larsen testifies for second day before grand jury
abstract: PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen will likely return for a third day of investigation by a grand jury of his allegations of illegal wiretapping, kickbacks and other charges against Justices Stephen Zappala and Ralph Cappy. Larsen is facing impeachment and allegations of attempting to influence a lower court. William Costopoulos, attorney for Larsen, said Larsen is fully cooperating and that his client's aim was not to indicte anyone, but to fulfill a request by the jury that he appear.

headline: State sends $500,000 for Fayette development
abstract: A grant by the PA Department of Commerce will act as a revolving loan for Fayette County, said commissioner Fred Lebder. For now, the money will go to Berkley Medical, a medical supply plant, creating 110 new jobs in the county. PA Representatives J. William Lincoln and Larry Roberts are excited about the grant, announced by PA Governor Casey, and credit Fred Lebder's work in getting attention from Harrisburg.

headline: Asking if a Plan Goes Too Far
abstract: From Roosevelt's New Deal to Johnson's Great Society, ambitious new social programs have faced constitutional challenges from people arguing that the Government exceeded its legitimate powers.  Federal officials expect similar challenges to Mr. Clinton's health plan.

headline: Penchant for secrecy
abstract: Senator Jim Rhoades and Congressman Tom Ridge have done our state a great service by fighting for the right of Pennsylvanians to place important issues on the ballot for decision.  Unfortunately, the Democrat leadership of the state House has been loath to even discuss initiative and referendum, preferring instead to hide in the shadows of smoke-filled rooms when it comes to making important decisions.

headline: Wofford basking in health care glory
abstract: This past week was like Christman for US Senator Harris Wofford.  After a couple years of waiting, he got the political gift he'd been hoping for.  Wofford was elected two years ago, saying, "We need national health insurance, and we need it now."  At last, a Democratic president was singing from Wofford's songbook last week.

headline: Legislative opposition to proposed emissions regulations expands
abstract: A move to have Pennsylvania challenge federal authority over imposing anti-pollution regulations appears to be growing among state legislators.  Legislators claim the Environmental Protection Agency has been inconsistent  and ridiculous on their new regulations.

headline: Life as a moral marathon
abstract: A man writes in to the newspaper to criticize the Catholics for a Free Choice for advocating changes in the positions and guidance of the Catholic Church.

headline: Robodoc joins staff at Shadyside Hospital
abstract: Shadyside Hospital is one of five US hospitals chosen to test the first robotic tool that performs orthopedic surgery and see whether it might make hip replacement surgery less brutal.  Called Robodoc, the computerized surgical arm, cuts with far more precision than the hand o feven the most skilled surgeon and may reduce the risk of a patient's leg being broken when artificial hip joints are installed, hospital officials said.

headline: Portugal: A Lack of Discipline Keeps Math Scores Low
