abstract: As in the United States, Portugal is working to raise its significantly lower mathematics scores. One of the main reasons thought to be the cause of the low math scores is that there is a lack of discipline among students and teachers and not a lot of support from home; this is also a complaint about the United States.

headline: Driver killed in roadwork zone
abstract: Lance Kohlhaas, a Hampden Township man, was killed yesterday when his car was crushed underneath a tractor-trailor rig on Route 283 near Elizabethtown, the latest in a string of of fatal accidents in a construction zone.

headline: Larsen's allegations about surreptitiously recorded conversation
abstract: Exerpts from a state grand jury report regarding Justice Rolf Larsen and others are given.  Among the allegations in Justice Larsen's Petition for Recusal is an allegation that Justice Zappala "illegally andn surreptitiously tape-records telephone conversations."

headline: State wants to help troubled firms
abstract: If your company is starting to have problems such as shipments, sales and employment falling off the PA Department of Commerce and Labor and Industry want to hear them. They are trying to help companies with technical assistance, public loans and grants, new equipment, and other things. The state announced they have agreed to invest 80,000 dollars into a pilot program developed by the Steel Valley Authority to identify troubled companies in 10 south-western Pennsylvania counties.

headline: Aspin sued over closing city sites
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and five members of Congress sued Defense Secretary Les Aspin seeking a court order compelling defense officials to release all information used in deciding to recommend closing four facilities in the city. The suit contends that Navy officials have refuted to provide Specter's office with complete documentation of the closure recommendations.

headline: Pennsylvania
abstract: A multi-agency task force was formed to develop a state plan on heat emergencies in Harrisburg.  Recent record temperatures caused more than 100 deaths statewide, nearly 90% of them people 60 or older, records show.

headline: Wofford headed for TV stardom
abstract: Senator Harris Wofford's staffers apparently are downplaying it, but there's no getting around the fact that Wofford scored big time in the national political image department when President Clinton addressed a joing session Congress on September 22.

headline: Most of W.  Pa. found unfit for toxic dump
abstract: State environmental officals yesterday released a report eliminating much of Western Pennsylvania as  a potential site for a low-level radioactive waste  disposal  facility that is  estimated as a $70 million project.  Due to delays it is now estimated it will not be completed  before Gov. Casey's second term in 1995.

headline: 'Life Chain' draws over 1,300 pro-life supporters at 5 sites across county
abstract: The "Life Chain" came to Lancaster County Sunday afternoon, as pro-life supporters lined the roads in five locations.  More than 1,300 people here participated in the national event, begun six years ago in California.

headline: Running a fever
abstract: The health care industry is a problem that has been noticed nationwide and the Clinton Administraion will almost certainly make changes.  Although there are problems the health care industry is the largest percentange of our GDP and restricting it may hurt the economy more than it helps.

headline: Poverty stricken district is lauded
abstract: A cycle of poverty is happening in Harrisburg school districts, and former Governor George M. Leadery is ready to try to break it, using Harrisburg as a demonstration project.

headline: DRPA fires operator of its new yard
abstract: Fed up with labor problems, Delaware River Port Authority commissioners agreed yesterday to fire the Illinois firm running its new container transfer yard in South Philadelphia and run the yard itself. Word of the decision caused Teamsters Local 107's picket line, previously incensed at management's refusal to negotiate a labor contract, to disband. Conflict remains however, as the Teamsters fight for jurisdiction over the port against the International Longsharemen's Association.

headline: Latest crime bill misses the point
abstract: The people who don't believe you can solve problems by throwing money at them just wound up and tossed $23 billion at crime.  They also decided to execute more people for more things and to let those we don't execute rot in some brand-new prisons for longer.  As crime bills go, it wasn't a bad one, though.  The way things work, most of the money will go to places it's least needed, but that's politics.  Some of it has to trickle into places like Philadelphia.

headline: State's heartland is struggling
abstract: In rural Pennsylvania, a way of life is being threatened by increasing poverty and economic decline in rural areas. Rural legislators are hard-pressed to find the muscle to make changes to the situation. Shelter Services, Inc., with a state and federal agency grant of only $54,000 has seen an increase in the number of families it services, says Linda Eby, who worries that while cities deserve the funding they receive, rural areas are all too often forgotten.

headline: Aspin's Hear Condition Said to Have Worsened During Past Two Years
abstract: Defense Secretary Les Aspin's heart condition has gotten worse over the last two years, officals say, since it was discovered two years ago.  He has yet to had over his work to his deputiy, but has been told by doctors that he  must reduce his work load for the next few weeks.

headline: Pennsylvania
abstract: In Harrisburg, Private universities statewide would get $73.5 million in the 1993-94 budget, in a package before the PA Senate. PA Governor Casey said the state cannot afford it. A fabric mural made by survivors of sexual assault and abuse is hanging in the state Capitol this week as part of the Sexual Assault Awareness Month.

headline: Wofford needs a shot of courage to lend NAFTA his support
abstract: Thirty years ago, Harris Wofford helped John F. Kennedy start the Peace Corps, a promising initiative in United States international policy.  Now an apparently more cautious Sen. Wofford has declared that he will not support the North American Free Trade Agreement, citing Pennsylvania jobs as the reason for his opposition.

headline: Local environmental group launches clean water effort
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Interest Research Group, an environmental advocacy organization, started a clean water campaign in which it asked East Brandywine and Caln to help them convince President Clinton and U.S. Representative Robert S. Walker to make clean water a priority.

headline: Lifting the ban
abstract: Lifting the ban of homosexuals in  the military by Clinton is not to agree with the lifestyle of  homosexuals, but simply to end the bias against  gays and treate them  like any  other  citizen  with rights and privialges.

headline: Saint Mary bars USH patients
abstract: Starting today, the doors of Saint Mary Hospital will be closed to patients insured by U.S. Healthcare.  Contract negotiations broke off late yesterday afternoon, and it is unlikely that the two sides will continue to try to reach an agreement.

headline: President of CCP lands job in Illinois
abstract: Ronald J. Temple, Community College of Philadelphia president, has accepted a job overseeing eight community colleges in Chicago. As with CCP, Temple hopes to strengthen the Chicago education program, become involved in economic development of the city, and encourage business and industry partnerships. Temple was a popular CCP president who helped bring the college greater financial stability.

headline: Effort made to cut highway slaughter
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has launched an education effort called Truck Smart to help reduce the amount of accidents between truckers and motorists. PennDot will be distributing informational pamphlets.

headline: 'Laughing gas' a serious matter
abstract: Until recently, police didn't know it was illegal to possess nitrous oxide.  But the gas can be deadly.

headline: Street of broken dreams
abstract: Mill Street once was full of thriving small businesses, but now many shops have had to close due to increasing competition from stores like Wal-Mart and K-Mart, as well as indoor malls. The Mill Street Business Association, a group representing about half of the merchants there, is forming an economic development committee to help this problem.  They're lobbying town council to reinstall a floating dock at the Market Street whart that they hope will bring more foot traffic to the area.

headline: Audit hassle is political retaliation
abstract: PA Governor Casey's budget secretary, Michael Hershock, wants to hire an outside accounting firm to conduct the state's two biggest annual audits, which examine how the administration spends federal funds. The problem with this is that Pennsylvania already has an instrument in place for this, PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer. It is a possibility that Casey is seeking outside help in order to punish Hafer for embarrassing the governor by uncovering financial mismanagement in his administration. This is not the appropriate way for Casey to settle a political score.

headline: Pennsylvania least likely to be a non-native's home
abstract: The US Census Bureau released figures that shows the Pennsylvania has one of the lowest percentage of non-native (non-Pennsylvanians) among its population with less than 1 of 5 born in another state.  This shows that Pennsylvania isn't attracting any new works says Gordon DeJong, a sociologist at Penn State University.

headline: Wofford 'Very Close' To Announcing Judicial Picks
abstract: US Senator Wofford is very close to announcing his choices for nominations to vacant judicial and U.S. attorneys posts. The process has been delayed slightly because of informal background checks the senator has made on candidates recommended to him. Luzerne County Judge Patrick Toole and Scranton attorney Thomas Vanaskie are widely rumored to be the front runners for the two vacant judgeships in the Middle District of Pennsylvania.

headline: Local plant OK if reactivated, state official says
abstract: The amount of emissions calculated to be released through the planned reactivation of the FR Phillips Power Station are higher than what would be normal for a more modern plant, but still at a reasonable level.

headline: Magnificent Anderson-A racial pioneer, her music was her way
abstract: The article pays homage to deceased African American singer Marian Anderson, the personification of grace on and off stage. Anderson was famous for singing on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial before a large crowd including First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt, after being barred from entering Constitution Hall by the Daughters of the American Revolution.

headline: Saving Shriners
abstract: There is a debate over whether or not the PA Department of Heath should have approved the request to allow a new children's hospital at Temple University's North Philadelphia medical center, when there is already the Saint Christopher's Hospital. Mayor Edward Rendell and City Council President John Street have tried to come up with a compromise for the situation. The authors think one good thing has come from the decision though, making sure the Shriners hospital stays in Philadelphia.

headline: Private colleges seek higher-education policy debate
abstract: The Commission for Independent Colleges and Universities has a new Public Purpose brochure.  The two key recommendations concerning the state's outdated policies on higher education are: The state should develop a long-range strategy to achieve its higher education goals in the most cost effective manner possible, and Pennsylvania should allow the State System and state-related institutions to set their own tuitions.

headline: Farm Show routes listed
abstract: PennDOT has created suggested alternative routes for the state Farm Show this weekend in hope of preventing gridlock.

headline: Learning to Turn a Life Away from Crime
abstract: The Washington, DC prison system is trying a new program to try to reduce the amount of criminals who leave jail and return. The program is focused on counseling the inmates and teaching them to stop their criminal ways.

headline: SU repairs on list of 'wish list' projects
abstract: The state lawmakers' annual wish list includes $60 million in various projects at Shippensburg University and $83,000 to purchase trackless trolleys and related equipment for Chambersburg Area Transit.  Legislation is pending on acting Governor Mark Singel's desk authorizing $2.1 billion of lawmakers' proposed projects across Pennsylvania in the state capital budget.

headline: Bar gives ratings of judge hopefuls
abstract: The Pennsylvania Bar Association announced its evaluations of the candidates for the three statewide courts yesterday and they were immediately denounced by Judge Doris Smith. She stated that not only where they far from being impartial, the work was politically motivated. Three candidates received the highest recommendation, two democratic candidates and one republican.

headline: Pennsylvania waits on Casey, a state in limbo
abstract: The governor had a heart-liver transplant months ago and hasn't returned to work.  The lieutenant governor, who's acting governor, is seen a sa caretaker but yearns to put his mark on things for a run for governor himself next year.  Now it's time to shape a $15 billion state budget and the legislative agenda for next year.  But who's agenda will it be?  Who's really in charge here?

headline: Wofford, Bentsen tout plan on N. Side
abstract: When President Clinton's emissaries fanned out across the country yesterday to sell his health care reform plan, Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen and Senator Harris Wofford came to Pittsburgh to take on one of the toughest assignments: pitching it to small businesses.

headline: Luzerne sludge-dumping dispute: The waiting begins
abstract: All the people can do now is wait after the township meeting in Luzerne Township where Teslovich wants to gain a permit to allow him to dump sewage on his 120 acre farm.  Residents displayed united voice of concern about the proper percedures and the risks to the health of the community.

headline: Mayor is angered by letters from Klan
abstract: Mayor Betty J. Eiceman is enraged over a letter sent out by the Ku Klux Klan to Lebanon residents that contains a veiled threat.  The letter invited residents to join the Klan, and said that any Jews or minorities who attempted to join would be "dealt with in a most Klannish way".

headline: Scores march, rally against health cuts
abstract: A protest of 100  people marched from West Philadelphia District Health  Center to the city morgue, where they said many poorand unisured people would end up if the Rendell administration went through with plans to cut servieces in the health department.   Backed by Citizen's Health Advisory Committee residents protested against the privitization of one of the city's distric health centers as well as other changes in policy.

headline: Private funding vital to survival
abstract: Johnny Majors returned to the University of Pittsburgh this year to try to rebuild the football team he once led to the national championship.  Jimmy Stewart is a beloved, hometown figure to folks in Indiana, home of Indiana University of Pennsylvania.  Both come to Pennsylvania with private funding.  In this day and age, with state and federal assistance to high education dwindling, private fund-raising efforts are becoming increasingly important to public colleges and universities.

headline: First, we need bridges within the bureaucracy
abstract: Relief for the Bridgetown Pike Bridge may take some time as the system for bridge repair goes through many processes and lots of time to get to the final product.  The best solution would be to ask lawmakers to smooth the regulatory road for PennDOT and minimmize the inconvenience for residents.

headline: Legislation proposed to aid victims of child abuse
abstract: Jenny Shifflet, director for the Lebanon county Sexual Abuse Center, has seen an increase of about 75% from last year in the number or people seeking help through her agency.  Many of those seeking help are adults that were sexually abused as children, but these victims have little legal recourse to seek damages from their abusers.  Shifflet hopes that the new legislation sponsored by PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf will pass as they are introduced at a Capitol new conference.

headline: Suit charges Bensalem keeps handicapped out
abstract: Community Interactions- Bucks County, Inc., a non-profit firm which provides group homes for the mentally handicapped, filed a federal lawsuit against Bensalem officials for violated the Fair Housing Amendments Act for refusing permits for two proposed living facilities. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development granted $628,000 to the firm to build these homes, which now can not  be built.

headline: Barn's history worthy of saving
abstract: Nancy Eshelman missed the mark with her negative comments on the preservation of the Star Barn.  The importance fo this barn and other landmarks of our agricultural heritage should not be glibly discounted.

headline: Pennsylvanians, including the PG, don't appreciate what we have
abstract: Casey's recent State of the Commonwealth address was not a waste of time as your editorial stated because it outlined an aggressive and ambitious public agenda for Pennsylvnia.

headline: Women lobbyists still fight subtle forms of sexism
abstract: The article discusses problems female lobbyists face.  Many report that because a lot of business is conducted in bars or other social settings, male legislators will make sexual advances or not take them seriously.  The article includes quotes from female lobbyists of different interest groups.

headline: Mall Associates plan to treat contaminated soil pile on site
abstract: Instead of transporting 1,000 tons of lead-contaminated soil across the state to Ohio, Madiera Plaza Associates will have the soil treated on site to render it non-hazardous before removing it from the parking lot of the mall in Muhlenberg Township.

headline: Midstaters generally approve of Clinton, except on gay ban
abstract: South-central Pennsylvania overall approves of the job Clinton has done in his first two weeks as President but disagree with him on lifting the ban on gays in the military.

headline: Secondhand smoke listed serious risk
abstract: The government offically reconized second hand smoke as a leading cause of cancer among non-smokers.  These finding are predicted to bring about lawsuits and changes in policy towards smoking in public.

headline: Private schools plead case for budget
abstract: Private schools for severely disabled children were represented by dozens of their students urging PA legislators not to approve a plan by PA Governor Robert Casey to strip schools of their funding. Supporters argue the plan would change the negotiator of funding for private schools from the state to local school districts, plans to ameliorate that process currently underway in the PA Department of Education. Opponents like PA Representative Dennis O'Brien say that process would mark the end of such schools.

headline: Freeman supports PennDOT's study of 'Valley Special'
abstract: The state Department of Transportation's decision to study a possible Lehigh Valley passenger train route has gotten a thumbs-up from state Representative Robert Freeman.  Freeman was concerned about reports the state wanted to use money earmarked for the "Valley Special" train on another train route that would run into Philadelphia.  But PennDOT Secretary Howard Yerusalim calmed his worries with a recent letter.

headline: Legislator's bill goes after a questionable question
abstract: State Representative Anthony H. Williams introduced a bill recently that would have required people applying for marriage licenses in Philadelphia to state their ethnic origin, not only their race, as is now required.  What he ended up with was legislation that requires neither.  And that's fine with him.

headline: Taking a convention approach to growth
abstract: Pittsburgh convention officials read the numbers and weep.  In the increasingly intense battle between cities for lucrative convention business, they see themselves falling further and further behind.  What does Pittsburgh have to compete?  The 12-year-old, 130,000-square-foot David L. Lawrence Convention Center.

headline: Base list OK with Clinton, officials say
abstract: President Clinton will approve without change an independent commission's list of 35 major and 95 minor domestic military bases to be closed, aides said yesterday.  Under the current federal base-closing law, Congress cannot alter the list.  If it does not reject the whole list within 45 legislative days, the bases must close.

headline: Pennsylvania's government is in disarray
abstract: Acting Governor Mark Singel this week met with Governor Robert P. Casey's Cabinet in a rare public session.  It was intended to show that things are owrking smoothly in Casey's absence.  But what's going on behind the scenes belies the image of hormony and tranquility that Singel and Casey staffers would have you believe.

headline: Work or campaign
abstract: U.S. Rep. Tom Ridge as well as state Attorney General Ernie Preate, and Lt. Gov. Mark Singel have or are planning to run for governor.  They can not rule such a time consuming political race without sacrificing their duties they are currently elected to carry out.  If they should be taken seriously they should resign from their present office to remove any conflict of interest.

headline: Marking a revolution
abstract: The environmental revolution began in Pennsylvania on Aug. 23, 1965, the day Governor William Scranton signed into law HB 585, which brought coal companies under the Clean Streams law.  In the next three legislative sessions the Legislature acted with revolutionary zeal to enact legislation to protect the environment.  After the enactment of that legislation, nothing in Pennsylvania's environmental world would ever be the same.

headline: N.J. women going out for political fair share
abstract: Linda Bowker, the head of an organization to recruit feminist women to run for office is gather money and support in N.J. to back women running for office.

headline: Seeking AIDS vaccine, using people in tests
abstract: Government sponsered research on AIDS vaccines at Hopkins University is giving 330 drug users an experimental vaccine that will hopefully prevent the virus.  Some worry that this will promote risky behavior and increase infection rates.

headline: Professors' daydream
abstract: The author writes that PA Education Secretary Donald Carroll said to a group of ninth graders that their education would be more like college and that he feels that this is one reason outcome-based education should not be implemented in PA.

headline: Geneva College asks PennDOT to reroute Route 18
abstract: Geneva College no longer wants a major highway running across campus.  Campus officials unveiled a plan Thursday to reroute Route 18 away from the main part of the campus.  The plan also would eliminate a sharp S-curve that has been the site of numerous accidents in which trucks have tipped and dumped their loads.

headline: Legislators tour new prison
abstract: The state prison in Pottsville and four other new ones are expected to put hardly a dnet in the state's overcrowding problem.  But Pennsylvania has no intention of building more prisons once the new ones are filled in 21 months.  The answer is not more prisons, says state Representative Thomas R. Caltagirone, but a change in the state's sentencing structure.

headline: Three Amway seminars head elsewhere
abstract: The organizer of four motivational seminars fro Amway sales representatives that have been planned for the David L. Lawrence Convention Center had decided to move three of them to other cities after Ben Novack Jr. of Convention Concepts Ltd. Found out that the Public Auditorium Authority voted to bar retail sales of clothing, jewelry and other items at seminars. Joseph McGrath, head of the Greater Pittsburgh Convention &Visitors Bureau said that the cancellation will cost up to $4 million in revenue.

headline: B-C teachers, board hold late-night talks trying to avoid strike
abstract: Members of the Bethlehem Center Teachers' Association (BCTA) met with school directors through late Sunday night in an attempt to reach an agreement and avert a possible strike.  Negotiators were still meeting in the Beth Center Elementary School at presstime, and no word was available as to whether any progress had been made in the 11th bargaining session between the two sides since January.

headline: Pennsylvania's high court, in upheaval, hits a low
abstract: PA Supreme Court justice Rolf Larsen is being investigated for allegations that he used aids and clerks to obtain prescription drugs for him and that he had out-of-court contact with lawyers. The House Judiciary Committee is expected to approve a bill that would end electing judges in PA and create a merit process. PA House Representative Christopher McNally says that the PA House plans to begin impeachment proceedings and PA Governor Robert P. Casey believes he should resign.

headline: Worker proves he's one of a kind
abstract: In the ugly throes of budget woes, the Casey administration sent 2,000 state employees packing two years ago, abolishing jobs it felt were no longer necessary.  Yesterday, one of those workers, Eugene A. Cherney, got revenge- and the Casey administration got a scolding, courtesy of Commonwealth Court.  Only when the state laid him off did PennDOT realize how much it needed him.

headline: Mateer gets power to move tire plant
abstract: The board of directors of Polymer Enterprises Incorporation has authorized Donald Mateer II, the president and CEO of Polymer, to take the steps necessary to find a new location for Indiana's tire manufacturing company. At a meeting the PA Department of Commerce Mateer said the company would move if the state could not find a solution for the company's dispute with the PA Department of Environmental Resources, Fish and Boat Commission, and the Environmental Quality Board. The dispute arises over the company's discharge of warmer water than acceptable in the Whites and Marsh Runs.

headline: New look at abortion law urged
abstract: Abortion-rights advocates today will ask a federal judge to reconsider a challenge to Pennsylvania's abortion law, arguing that the U.S. Supreme Court changed the standard for measuring its constitutionality.

headline: Seeking to Bypass Comment Periods
abstract: If Congress approves Mr. Clinton's health plan or anything like it, the Government will have to issue scores of regulations.  The Administration wants to issue emergency rules, without the usual opportunity for public comment, because it sees an urgent need "to assure access to health care for millions of Americans and to reduce the runaway growth in health care spending."

headline: Program helps save for future
abstract: The Tuition Account Program, a state program that would allow for parents to pay today's tuition rates for college courses their children would take years from now, is being touted by state Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll as the most flexible program of its kind in the nation.

headline: Get Tougher: Upping the stakes on drunken driving
abstract: The Governor and Legislators should follow the recommendations of the commissioner of the Pennsylvania State Police by becoming more strick with drunk driving.  Lower the rate from .1 to .08, zero tolerance for under 21, and zero tolerance for commerical drivers would all help save lives.

headline: Let me remain in US prison, con artist asks
abstract: Convicted con artist Thomas Hugh Akins, now serving time in a federal maximum security prison, is petitioning for an extended stay in the federal prison and a harsher federal sentence in exchange for serving part of his sentence in a PA state prison. Attorney Charles Sheery has negotiated with Somerset and Westmoreland county officials who are willing to accept the terms in exchange for the extended stay. US District Judge D. Brooks Smith will hear the case.

headline: Thousands Welcome New Mall
abstract: The Mall at Steamtown, described as a "new heart" for Scranton, opened Saturday with a ceremony combining mutual admiration among its movers, beauty queens and comedy, including a routine involving Governor Robert P. Casey.

headline: Beaver native to guide Senate outsider's race
abstract: At 29, Sean McBride, the youngest campaign manager in this year's US Senate race, was named to manage the campaign of Republican Senate candidate Robert Monahan.

headline: Florio's Rating Starts Slipping, But He's in Lead
abstract: Governor Jim Florio's standing with the voters has begun to erode in New Jersey's race for governor, according to the latest New York Times/WCBS-TV News poll, but he still maintains a comanding lead over Christine Todd Whitman.

headline: Pension manager's pay plan attacked
abstract: The PA Public School Employees Retirement System officials have hired a consulting firm to evaluate private investment firms and propose a competitive pay scale for the PSERS. Officials call it an effort to attract and retain the best, however the effort has upset the Catherine Baker Knoll, Secretary of the Treasury, believes the raises are excessive, and PA Representative Stephen Maitland argues officials should not be allowed to set their own salary.

headline: Yeakel hopes to be next governor
abstract: Lynn Yeakel, who lost a race for US senator last year, has formed a committee to support her candidacy for governor in 1994.

headline: Meadville water advisory continues
abstract: Meadville Public Works Director Joseph Chriest said an advisory asking residents to boil drinking water will be continued due to fecal coliform bacteria that were found in two more city water locations.  The city needs three consecutive days to clear the readings and lift the ban.

headline: New Middle Ground
abstract: Wednesday's vote by the House of Representatives to retain a 16-year ban on federal fudning for poor women's abortions reveals a political truth about the issue that advocates on both sides have yet to fully grasp.  That is, simply, that the issue unexpectedly has evolved in a way that has created what once was impossible- a political middle ground on abortion- an island in a tumultuous sea created by the Supreme Court's validation of the Pennsyvlania Abortion Control Act and public reaction to it.

headline: Service cutbacks spark hospital feud
abstract: PA Senator John E. Peterson, chairman of the Health and Welfare Committee, hopes that administrators and physicians at Oil City and Franklin Hospitals can resolve their differences so that a legislative hearing to air the fiscal facts of the hospitals to discuss whether a merger between the two is necessary. The Hospital Association of Pennsylvania wants to take part in the hearings, as well.

headline: Programs teach peaceful solutions
abstract: Peace Grows Inc. has started an Alternatives to Violence program which teaches teachers and students non-violent conflict resolution. Pittsburgh school districts include it in their educational programs, and the Youngstown police force took courses as well.

headline: 'Ghost Riders' Are Target of an Insurance Sting
abstract: The New Jersey Insurance Department has set up sting operations to catch people who run onto trains and buses when they crash and then file insurance claims for injuries they never sustained.

headline: Let's end the war
abstract: A man writes into the newspaper to praise Mayor Masloff for advocating the decriminalization of drug use.  He says that there will be drug addicts whether drugs are legal or not, and that must adults would use drugs responsibly. He points out negative consequences of the "war on drugs".

headline: Three Rivers plus
abstract: In the last two years, enough Pittsburghers have watched Orioles games at Baltimore's fabled new Camden Yards to share this common though: Why can't we have a handsome, friendly baseball park like that on the banks of the Allegheny?  That's the same thought that Mayor Masloff had out loud, pre-Camden Yards, several years ago.  The mayor has committed her staff to developing a plan for a not-so-expensive facelift at Three Rivers stadium.

headline: Best judgment, not party loyalty, counts
abstract: The spirit of fairness and objectivity warrants sharing some facts about the level of partisanship that exists among House Democrats and Republicans.  We should strive to cast more of our votes according to our best judgment and not according to blind party loyalty.  Ultimately, we can achieve only so much if Republicans continue to practice the kind of extreme partisanship that is reflected in their voting record.

headline: Foe's breakfast not to GOP taste
abstract: Democrats are charging $5,000 a plate for a breakfast with the house leadership.  The GOP thinks that is boardering on obscene to charge more than $1000 and that those people paying for the breakfast are buying influence.

headline: Perot backer creates 3-way race for seat on top court
abstract: Robert B. Surrick, a Chester County lawyer and member of the Patriot Party, is running as a third party candidate for the PA Supreme Court.

headline: Yeakel says she might run for governor next year
abstract: Democrat Lynn Yeakel, who came close to unseating US Senator Arlen Specter last year, said yesterday that she was seriously considering running for governor next year and would make her decision "within the next few weeks."

headline: Mission fizzles
abstract: A group of about 20 protesters demonstrated outside the government buildings in Washington trying to call attention to their resentment with the proposed hazardous waste incinerator in East Liverpool, Ohio.  They failed to get a meeting with the president's environmental advisers, but vowed to kepe the heat on the new administration.

headline: No Foregone Conclusions in Fargo
abstract: North Dakota abortion clinics argue unconstitutionality of the law requiring a lecture and 24 hour waiting period for an abortion, which was upheld in a PA ruling, Planned Parenthood versus PA Governor Casey, because of North Dakota's limited abortion facilities and availability. US Supreme Court Justices O'Connor and Souter have signaled interest in a review of the case. A law such as the Freedom of Choice Act would eliminate a lot of abortion litigation in individual states.

headline: Shalala: Health card will be key to access
abstract: US Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala says the current health care task force will propose a singular, all encompassing piece of legislation that will allow the bill to be passed by Congress in the current year. Shalala described the proposal as a fundamental change in structure and in financing of the existing system. The issue of illegal aliens, who would not have access to a card entitling them to basic health care, is being discussed.

headline: PSEA out of Control
abstract: In response to Union Member Mr. Richard Riter who says on regards to the strike in Susquenita School District, you have to be pro-education or anti-education and if you don’t feel that way you shouldn't be here. That statement summarizes the attitudes of many of the rank and file of the Pennsylvania State Education Association; the belief that the public  should really has no say in what is going on in the school district.

headline: Gripes & sour grapes
abstract: Rumors are flying at the Port of Philadelphia concerning the likelihood that a consortium of Chilean fruit growers, who now unload some 4.8 million cases of fruit at the Port of Philadelphia, will move to Wilmington, DE, or some other East Coast port, where costs are cheaper.  Just because this sort of rumor surfaces every year, port insiders warn, doesn't mean that this won't be the year it comes true.

headline: Let's use self control
abstract: Education is the way to combat violent crimes.  Punish those that committ crimes with guns and teach those who want to properly use weapons in gun training classes.

headline: Total Federal Regulators vs. Private Sector Job Growth
abstract: It is a chart released by the Heritage Foundation that shows how job growth increases when there are fewer federal regulations and decreases when there are more federal regulations.

headline: Beyer Easily Defeats Farris; GOP Poised for Legislature Gains
abstract: The Democratic Party's 12-year domination of Virginia politics collapsed yesterday as Republican George F. Allen won the governor's race and his party captured the attorney general's office and appeared likely to gain additional seats in the legislature.

headline: For 'author' North, no ghost of dissent
abstract: Oliver North's ghostwritten book about his recent return to Vietnam "One More Mission," is helping him rise up in the candidacy for a US Senate race in Virginia.

headline: Perot is not sounding beaten
abstract: Ornery and defiant in the face of defeat, Ross Perot vowed yesterday to make his organization "bigger and stronger" in time for retribution against congressional supporters of the North American Free Trade Agreement.  Perot also said the NAFTA experience would only intensify his desire to delve into health care and other political battles, and he coyly suggested he might soon drop is opposition to turning his organization into a third political party.

headline: York Mayor Althaus is a man of contradictions
abstract: York Mayor Althaus is set to retire from politics after a 12 year career as mayor.  He claims to have no intention on running for governor or state legislature, but rather to spend more time with his family and enter the private sector, being a lawyer by trade.  He has done a lot of great things for the city including balancing the budget, creating the adopt-a-city program, and being highly respected among democrats and republicans.

headline: Municipal recycling programs grow by heaps and mounds
abstract: Pennsylvania has become more aggressive in solid waste managemnt and the results have shown it to be a success.  The entire government has been invovled from the elgislature to Gov. Casey and local government.

headline: No school=no job=prison
abstract: Having learned from his failure to take school seriously, and his struggle to graduate, African American Richard Jones III urges his fellow brothers and sisters to take advantage of their education. Having witnessed kids skipping school in a local business, Jones suggests the business think more critically about instituting measures to keep kids in school rather than making money. In Jones' view, without an education, a job is impossible and prison is likely for inner city African Americans.

headline: Singel fires warning shot on workers' comp rates
abstract: The Pennsylvania Compensation Ratings Bureau is planning to ask the PA Insurance Department for a rate increase.  Acting PA Governor Mark Singel is warning them ahead of time to not ask for such an increase in light of the new reforms designed to lower the rates. One such reform was a bill the legislature passed that capped medical fees for doctors and hospitals treating workers' comp patients.

headline: PSU professor to lecture on burnout
abstract: Robert Munzenrider, a Penn State Harrisburg associate professor of public administration, will lecture on the topic of job burnout/ job stress to a public audience.

headline: Harborcreek pedestrian safety a hot issue
abstract: After road safety issues were raised in a town meeting, township supervisors Donna Mindek and David Bossart vowed to work with the PA Department of transportation to make a section of a Route 5 safer for both motorists and pedestrians. Not only is it difficult to see pedestrians because of a narrow berm, soft embankment, and brush, but conditions also make it easy for cars to overturn. Supervisors and residents were pleased with the session.

headline: Let's use self-control
abstract: Common sense and good judgemnet of adults is the first step to stemming the child on child gun violence.

headline: Use of homeless shelters still high
abstract: According to Patty Richwine, spokeswoman for Harrisburg-area shelters and soup kitchens are operating at near or full capacity while its supposed to be the slow season.  Bethesda Mission has housed two over capacity in its Men's Shelter and Shalom House for women had to turn down 20 single-mother families in April.

headline: Big Bills, Little Time
abstract: There was little time for deep thought or serious objection to the passage of two important New York State bills--a transportation financing package, and a constitutional amendment to change the way the state borrows money. Democrats did not have a problem with the nature of the proceedings, though some Republicans voiced objections.

headline: For edgy Clinton aides, it was like sweating out the election
abstract: The Clinton Administration is anxiously waiting for the Senate vote on his economic plan.  It will most likely come down to the sole vote of currently undecided Nebraska Senator Bob Kerrey.

headline: Perot rallies midstate troops
abstract: Ross Perot, leader of United We Stand America, spoke to a crowd of supporters and said that he would make sure no members of Congress who voted for the North America Free Trade Agreement would be re-elected in 1994.

headline: You can have Manhattan, the Bronx and Staten Island, too
abstract: New York native Mayor Rendell, in the Big Apple, finds worms.  He'd rather be in Philadelphia.

headline: Oust hydrophobic yuppie
abstract: Back in 1891 an out-of-control bureaucrat with the "United States Board of Geographic Names" decreed that no town in the United States could end with a Scotch "H."  Similarly, another bureaucrat insisted that Pittsburgh's water supply could be contaminated because it is open to the sky.  He has, therefore, decreed that it must be enclosed.

headline: Operation Rescue's criminal acts violate the rights of others
abstract: Operation Rescue has come to Philadelphia, hoping to harass women who want to have abortions and to disrupt the lives of all Philadelphians.  In other cities, these extremists have engaged in violent and threatening activities designed to frighten and intimidate women from excercising their constitutional rights, but they go too far and violate the rights of others.

headline: Smoking?
abstract: Cartoon with two children in the back of a car smoking cigarettes and the dad driving, not smoking,  with the caption "Hey kids, put those cigarettes out - there's a cop coming!"

headline: Q & A / National Service Program
abstract: Questions and answers to the national service program that Clinton has proposed that would allow students to do community service to repay their federal loans.

headline: Holiday offers traffic, heat
abstract: The Fourth of July weekend seems to be stacking up this way: cheaper gas, lots of heat and one self-evident truth- a load of traffic.  In fact, so many people will be taking to the road to celebrate the holiday that it brings to mind the words of social philosopher, author and critic Lewis Mumford, who once said that our national flower is the concrete cloverleaf.

headline: Link sought in city death, other killings
abstract: A resident of Harrisburg, Dale Bloom, was murdered in his home. His death may be linked to the killings of five other homosexuals.  Sean Darrington was arrested for murder and the theft of Bloom's car, and Chief Deputy District Attorney is considering seeking the death penalty.

headline: We may be laughing all the way to the unemployment office
abstract: Participant in the General Public Utilities-Duquesne Light Transmission project Joseph Bresnei appreciates political cartoonist Tim Menees' humor, but believes there are more serious advantages to the project that is Menees' subject, such as the economic benefits the project will bring to the region. Maybe Menees could sketch lines of unemployed workers instead of mineralizing a project designed to bring jobs to the area and stimulate industrial growth.

headline: Billboard barons thankful to Shuster
abstract: A new billboard is erected every 30 minutes in the United States.  The barons of the outdoor advertising industry know who to thank: Representative Bud Shuster.  A seemingly routine congressional "reauthorization"- in which Congress renews funding for existing programs- is an example of the billboard industry's clout.  This story can be told through a war of words between two old enemies, environmentalists and the billboard industry.

headline: For Phila. Officials, the pay's the thing
abstract: PA Governor Casey must find a replacement for city health commissioner, but may have trouble finding someone to fill the position, because of the low pay Philadelphia officials receive in comparison to officials of other cities.  He had trouble filling the head of the PA Department of Human Services for this reason.

headline: Perot's liberal critics are ignorant of economics, so they back NAFTA
abstract: The attack on Ross Perot shows the intellectual bankruptcy of American liberalism.  If thousands of jobs have already gone south of the border, imagine the result of NAFTA- the loss of millions of jobs.

headline: You do it! No, you!!
abstract: Candidates in the crowded race for Pennsylvania governor have been trying to get some of the competition to run for US Senate next year instead.  None of them are having any luck.

headline: Panel hears debate about tougher auto-emission standards
abstract: The federal Ozone Transport Commission held a hearing to debate whether the Environmental Protection Agency should require twelve northeastern states to adopt strict vehicle-emission standards that are currently enforced in California. The Commission heard testimony from the automobile and oil industries as well as environmental and health groups such as the American Lung Association.  A Pennsylvania advisory commission, appointed by PA Governor Casey, voted last month to recommend that the state delay action on the standards until 1995.

headline: Parents of gays face fears, find understanding
abstract: Facing the fact of a son or daughter's homosexuality challenges family relations in many ways, say the parents of gay sons and daughters.  Even when they are supportive, parents often have no prior experience with gays- though they may be only too familiar with society's harsh views of homosexuality.

headline: Some Answers to Questions About How Plan Will Affect Consumers
abstract: Some questions and answers are given concerning the potential impact of President Clinton's health care reform proposal, compiled from inforamation by benefits experts Frank McArdle of Hewitt Associates and John Erb of A. Foster Higgins & Co.

headline: Reform: Students to prove they've learned
abstract: Education reform is underway which would require students to show they have mastered some skill before graduating high school.  Opponents of the Outcome Based Education (OBE) claim that the government is imposing values onto their children.  One section of the testing required for graduation if this is made into law requires the teachers to judge the 'honestly and work ethic' of the student.

headline: Housing, toll road action sought
abstract: Concerned citizens of Fayette County are asking the County Commissioner to dismiss the board members of the Fayette County Housing Authority, claiming they have violated various elements of the Sunshine Law. The Commissioner also sent a letter to the PA Department of Commerce requesting funds for pump station rehabilitation, roadway reconstruction and street lighting at the Fairchance Industrial Park.

headline: Logan resident held for murder trial in Olney woman's death
abstract: Police interrogated Frank Bines who admitted to burglarizing and then murdering an 87-year old woman for $20 worth of cocaine.

headline: Wreckers' tools expose long-hidden log structure
abstract: The demolition crew ripped off the roof and peeled away the skin of a pseudo-brick asphalt shingles and exposed foot thick timber stacks two stories high.  Some say this house was over 200 years old and is now cleared for the 18-space parking lot that will serve a new restaurant.

headline: Black-vote tricks N.J. race denied
abstract: Governor-elect Christie Whitman's campaign manager said yesterday he "went too far" in claiming that the campaign paid black ministers and Democratic workers to suppress voter turnout.  Whitman denied that such payments were made.

headline: Forget presumed consent
abstract: A woman writes to the newspaper to say she opposes the bill that presumes consent to organ donation unless otherwise stated.

headline: Perspective/Classified: It's the law now
abstract: Recap of all the bills past in 1992.  There were 248 bills past of which 238 were signed into law by Casey.  None of the 10 vetoed were overridden.

headline: 'You promised'
abstract: Mary McGroy, a syndicated columnist for the Washington Post talks about how President Clinton had about 200 peopled outside the White House protesting the toxic-waste incinerator in East Liverpool Ohio. Among the protestors was Martin Sheen, whose mother lives in Ohio. Most of the demonstrators seemed to be Clinton voters and they seemed more disappointed then angry. She ultimately believes that WTI protestors are the wrong type to have.

headline: Panel to hear arguments in Greene dispute
abstract: A three-judge Commonwealth Court panel Monday heard arguments in a Greene County garbage hauling dispute that could further define the state's new solid waste management law.

headline: Penn dumps speech code and plans a new approach
abstract: In her first major act as interim president, Claire Fagin said yesterday that the University of Pennsylvania is abondoning its bitterly debated, widely ridiculed racial harassment policy.  Brought to widespread attention last spring by the now-infamous "water buffalo" episode, the so-called hate speech code became a national and local symbol in debates over political correctness and free speech.

headline: Some radiologists say benefit exists and will emerge in time
abstract: The National Cancer Institute decided to stop recommending regular mammograms for women younger than 50. This comes after researchers have found that there is inconclusive statistics as whether a yearly mammogram is effective in preventing breast cancer in women younger than 50; since the evidence is so strong for women older than 50. However, many individual doctors still are trying to prove that women in their 40s should have mammograms and that it can prevent cancer from spreading.

headline: Reminder: Schools are for learning
abstract: We have long been concerned that the public school system would lose sight of its primary mission: education.  Schools, above all, are for learning.  Learning requires books- and all children deserve the chance to learn.  Until that becomes the uppermost priority of public education, the system will continue to deteriorate and be challenged by voucher advocates- who argue that private schools can do better at educating our young because public schools are no longer trying.

headline: ICE Train woos Amtrak
abstract: The Intercity Express Train arrived in Pittsburgh.  It moves at an average speed of 155 to 175 miles per hour and its fastest speed is 250 miles an hour.

headline: LRBSA Action Boosts Planned Federal Prison
abstract: Efforts by Lackawanna County officials to get a planned $60 million federal prison built received another boost Monday when the Lackawanna River Basin Sewer Authority agreed to work on extending sewer service to the targeted tract.

headline: Annual reports losing their glitz
abstract: Critic Sid Cato held off on categorizing the year for the quality of annual reports until he has finished his reviews. However, companies such as United States Steel were forced to scale back their annual reports to save money, a response Cato says sends a negative message to investors. Bell Atlantic Corporation and Pittsburgh National Corporation Bank disagree, saying their scaled back reports reflect responsible spending to investors.

headline: Blackwell wants pair axed
abstract: U.S. Rep. Lucien Blackwell has written a pair of letters to the white house offering reasons that Smeronish and Jolly, both officals in the Philadelphia Housing Authority.  The letter have had no effect except to 'embarrass' Blackwell.

headline: Former manager claims bands treated properly
abstract: Don Brown Jr., manager of the recently closed Club Met which filed for bankruptcy, responds to claims that the club renegotiated contracts with bands after shows. Referring to claims that several bands were not paid in full, Brown insisted that bands playing at the club were content, citing multiple appearances by different bands as evidence.

headline: Petition presented on Larsen
abstract: An investigation into possible impeachment of state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen started yestserday but is likely to be a slow process in which the committee will 'methodically' review the allegations then confer with house leaders.  He is being accused of a decade-long record of misconduct.

headline: You wanted change?
abstract: The strongest theme in voting around the country was the continuing demand for change- in leaders, policies and the process itself.  Fine, but the winners in the big races better turn out to be quick learners.

headline: Park Construction halts in Bensalem after DER request
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Resources asked Bensalem officials to cease construction on a city park so that additional soil and water tests can be done on the land to ensure that it is safe to build a park on it. The Raymond Proffitt Foundation , an environmental activist group, pressured the DER to order more testing of the grounds.

headline: Penn takes cowardly route
abstract: George Will points out inconsistencies in Penn University President and President Clinton's nominee to head the National Endowment of the Humanities,  Sheldon Hackney on treatment of racist motivated incidents at UPenn. A recent trashing of the newspaper by black students over right wing politically incorrect articles received neutral comments by Hackney. Yet an incident involving a Jew and African Americans was treated severely, though Will argues there were no grounds for prosecution.

headline: Speaks, collapses in council chambers, 'the place he'd pick'
abstract: Former Monroeville Councilman Miles Span, known for his feisty and outspoken style, collapsed Tuesday in council chambers, moments after finishing one of his trademark speeches on problems in the municipality.  Mr. Span was pronounced dead of an apparent heart attack later at Forbes Regional Health Center in Monroeville.  He was 75.

headline: Require consent for psychological testing, lawmaker urges
abstract: Representative Lawrence Curry, a Montgomery County lawmaker, has proposed legislation forbidding school districts from conducting psychological testing of students without permission from their parents.  A violation of the proposed law could cost a school district 15 percent of its state aid.

headline: In the dark on I-95
abstract: A man writes to the newspaper to criticize the Pennsylvania Turnpike, PA Department of Transportation and Federal Highway Administration for barring citizens from witnessing their meetings.  This is in violation of the Open Meetings Act.

headline: Lt. Gov. Signel signs first death warrant
abstract: Lt. Governor Mark S. Singel yesterday signed his first death warrant as acting governor, ordering a Cumberland County man to die by lethal injection the week of Dec. 6.

headline: null
abstract: The cartoon is making reference to the inevitability of gambling becoming legalized in Pennsylvania.

headline: Bradford McKean advises the freshpersons
abstract: Bradford McKean speaks to the Patriot-News senior Capitol correspondent about the reasons for coming back to Capitol Hill before they are required.

headline: Former mayor's leadership hailed
abstract: Former Harrisburg mayor harold A. Swenson was honored yesterday for his efforts to save and rebuild the city in the wake of the devasting Agnes floods in 1972 by re-naming the Walnut Street Bridge to Swenson Plaza.

headline: Petrarca: Woman's arrest breaks state's Sunshine Law
abstract: State Representative Joseph Petrarca said the arrest of a Leechburg woman in a public meeting broke the state's Sunshine Law.  "We just passed a law in Harrisburg a couple of months ago that said to give citizens a reasonable amount of time to speak in a public meeting," said Petrarca.

headline: You, too, can be a campaign tool
abstract: Steve Lopez makes up a humorous "quiz" showing how citizens could be of assistance to politicians in the next election.  Majority of the questions reflect the Bill Stinson race for the Second Senatorial District.

headline: Perry defends waste disposal plan
abstract: Perry County commissioners are trying to convince the state Department of Environmental Resources officials its waste handling plan complies with state law.  DER contended last December the plan violated state law because all of Perry's trash was directed to a single landfill.

headline: Politics dingy at best
abstract: Why do people get bent out of shape when it is reported that Republicans handed out monies so that a group did not vote?  In the past, the Democrats have given money to black leaders for casuse so as to deliver the black vote.  What is the difference?

headline: Special Treatment
abstract: The author is angry that the two doctors, supporters of Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell and former Mayor Wilson Goode, are allowed to continue working for the Philadelphia Nursing Home (PNH). The author thinks that the doctors, Gene R. Newtown and Theodore Burden, are not providing proper care and that Rendell is not looking at how the taxpayer feels.

headline: Residents take turns asking questions about plans
abstract: About 50 residents of Beaver Falls' College Hill section gathered Thursday evening in Geneva College's student center to hear what the school's plans to re-route Route 18 would do to their homes.

headline: Inside the Capitol: PennDOT to hold emissions hearings
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's plan to expand the state's auto emissions inspection program will be discussed at three public hearings. It will require vehicle owners from twenty-five counties to have their vehicles' emissions systems inspected once every two years.  If their automobiles' do not meet requirements, they will be required to spend up to $450 to make repairs.

headline: Man charged in kidnap was state prisoner
abstract: A Landisburg man who has a history of psychiatric and drug problems was charged with kidnapping his 21 year-old former girlfriend.  The state police had to use tear gas to get him out of the basement where he was staying.  After capture he threatened that he would get them once he got out of jail.

headline: null
abstract: The PA House Judiciary Committee will hold a hearing on KBL's plan to charge taverns a barstool fee for showing televised Penguins games as entertainment.

headline: Brady bill impasse stymies Senate
abstract: Adjounment of Congress was blocked yesterday by deadlock over the "Brady" handgun bill as the Senate- its members already scattered across the country- was put on notice to be ready to return next week for another attempt to pass the legislation.  But, even as word of the unusual recall of the Senate was spreading to the farflung members, negotiations resumed to reach a comprovmise that might spare the senators from having to return to Washington after Thanksgiving.

headline: Former state pol makes list of sorts
abstract: Quotes from politicians of the week show a lighter side to politics.  The poll numbers are showing that people still feel we are in a recession and find only our presence in Somalia more worrisome then the economy.

headline: PHA chief rebuts critics on firings
abstract: Elton Jolly, special master of the Philadelphia Housing Authority, returned fire yesterday to critics who claimed that he had racial and political favoritism in his reorganization of senior managemtn at the low-income housing agency.  Jolly challenged anyone to match their record of service and fight to end racism against his.

headline: Zappala top star in state judiciary
abstract: A mispoken word here or there has done nothing to dim the reputation of Associate Justice Stephen A. Zappala of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court who is viewed by many as the fastest-rising star in the state's judicial firmanent.  He is widely respected not only for a scholarly approach to problem-solving, but also for never forgetting his roots, US Circuit Judge Carol Los Mansmann said in a recent introduction.

headline: Progress cited along Chesapeake Bay
abstract: The Deputy Director of the Chesapeake Bay Program Office, Jon Capacasa, writes to the newspaper in response to a column that cast a pessimistic light on cleaning up the Bay. Capacasa says that changes are already taking place to clean up the Chesapeake Bay.

headline: Race harassment charged in York
abstract: Murdaugh, the chairman for the York Chapter of the NAACP, is sueing police for violating his rights when they stopped him Sunday night and took his picture.  He claims that they will use his photo in a police lineup without his concent in a rape case.

headline: State assistance to the elderly defended
abstract: The Pennsylvania Pharmaceutical Assistance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) program is the largest of its kind in the country.  So far, many aging advocates and physicians are supporting the PACE action.  They view the program as a service to them not against them.

headline: Rhoades praises states' college tuition program
abstract: Senator James J. Rhoades praised Senate Republican Leader Robert Jubelirer and State Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll for the early success of the groundbreaking Tuitiion Account Program (TAP).  TAP guarantees parents who purchase tuition credits at Pennsylvania's state-owned or community colleges at today's prices that their investment will grow to meet the future enrollment costs.

headline: Inside the Capitol: State car auction includes two corvettes
abstract: The PA Department of General Services is auctioning two corvettes seized by the Office of the Attorney General.  They are also a auctioning Pennsylvania Department of Transportation 4-by-4 trucks.

headline: Mass. gives juveniles hand instead of a cell
abstract: Dozens of innovative programs for juvenile offenders are being tested on small scales all across the nation.  But justice officials are paying particular attention to Massachusentts, which has a statewide and long-running program that appears to be a success.  While spending far less per delinquent than most states, Massachusetts has achieved one of the nation's best records at deterring juvenile crime.

headline: 2 banks announce purchases
abstract: Two mid-atlantic banks, PNC and First Fidelity, have announced acquisitions in New York and New England yesterday, in order to expand the traditional boundries of both of these companies in a time when the market is showing a slow down in banking and a good time for expansion.

headline: Brutto was always on the Hill to check egos
abstract: Patriot-News capitol correspondent Carmen Brutto covered the Capitol for 32 years- only two of the state's 250-plus lawmakers have been around longer.  He retired Wednesday, still in his prime, after 43 years of reporting, and many of the state's top honchos came by his desk to wish him well and pay their respects on his last day.

headline: Fortuituous discovery
abstract: In response to 'Pennsylvania least likely to be a non-native's home' I believe that it could be that the low percentage of incoming people living here is to be accounted for by the high percentage of natives for whom Pennsylvania's attractive features make it easy to resist the blandishments for moving elsewhere.

headline: Phila.'s odd power couple
abstract: In a rare allocation of power, Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell often defers to lead City Councilman John Street who in return has delivered 17-0 votes supporting the Mayor's budget cuts and agendas. Having supported Street's opposition for the position, Rendell's deference comes as a surprise. However, the power sharing pair, in addition to Rendell's Chief of Staff David Cohen, have made national headlines in their successful campaign to pull the city from the brink of financial ruin.

headline: Zappala's and Fumo's meeting at Zappala's vacation home
abstract: Exerpts from a state grand jury report regarding Justice Rolf Larsen and others are given.  In particular, this excerpt focuses on a meeting between Sen. Fumo and Justice Zappala at Fumo's vacation home, five days before the City of Philadelphia filed the Pennsylvania Labor Relations Board case.

headline: Protesters quiet during pigeon shoot
abstract: The Eastern Pennsylvania valley had its most peacable Labor Day pigeon shoot in years yesterday as animal-rights groups decided to make less noise and send fewer people.  Having declared success in drawing attention to the event in past years, activists focused more this year on retrieving wounded birds and providing them with medical treatment.

headline: Racial discord jars Boyertown
abstract: After two centuries of unspoiled German heritage, traditions die hard in Boyertown, a working-class borough on the eastern edge of Pennsylvania Dutch country.  But in the last few years, as the Route 422 Expressway attracted new businesses and industries, it also brought a diverse array of newcomers.  The result has been a sharp rise in the number of sometimes-violent clashes over race, culture, style and creed that are being played out in the cafeterias and hallways of the Boyertown public schools.

headline: State cutback threatens HMC poison center
abstract: The Central Pennsylvania Poison Center at Hershey Medical Center will reduce services if state funding is not received. The allotted $1.52 million a year has not been given to the three centers across the state. Since 1990 four centers have been forced to close due to the lack of funding.

headline: Rich districts, poor districts
abstract: The Pennsylvania state Legislature allocated $130 million to school districts that are particularly poor or facing special problems.

headline: Intersection draws several complaints
abstract: A Patton Township intersection has gotten many complaints to the township Chief, Gary Davenport, since a fatal car accident. Davenport  said that he would pass the complaints about the intersection on to the PA Department of Transportation. The PA Department of Transportation is already investigating the accident that occurred at the intersection.

headline: Mayor hopefuls agree on war against crime
abstract: Tom Murphy says people have offered to protect him as he door-knocks his way around Pittsburgh in hopes of becoming mayor.  Murphy estimates that in the past four months, there have been 10 homicides within a mile of where he lives.  Murphy and his two opponents in the November 2 race have sketched out asimilar strategies for dealing with spiraling gang- and drug-related crime.

headline: 2nd cut-rate airline wants to serve Pittsburgh
abstract: A startup airline being developed by the operator of a charter service in California, AirTrain Corp., is seeking federal permission to operate daily cut-rate flights from Pittsburgh to Philadelphia and Detroit beginning next April.

headline: Bucks election pivotal
abstract: PA State Democrats are backing Tom Lingenfelter, founder and president of Heritage Collectors' Society Museum and Gallery, for a special sate Senate election this summer in Bucks County. The PA Senate election is July 13 to fill a vacancy created by PA Republican Senator Jim Greenwood's election to the U.S. House last fall. The election is critical because the Senate is now split 25-24 in favor of the Democrats.

headline: Four clinch city spots in low turnout
abstract: Yesterdays primary had very low turnouts because the only elections that were contested were those for Common Please Court. The races for District Attorney and city Controller were uncontested. The four sitting judges who were endorsed by both parties appeared to have easily swept aside challengers.

headline: Philly vote vital to Hart
abstract: State Senator Mellissa Hart visited Greenwood Elementary School to discuss her job with a fifth-grade class.  She could gain a considerable amount of clout in the state government if Republican Bruce Marks ultimately wins the seat- shifting the balance of power to the GOP.

headline: Zerbe step, revamping link denied
abstract: Retirement of HERCO's president has nothing to do with recent internal restructuring that elinated more than 50 jobs.

headline: Drug-related slayings worry York
abstract: Drug-related slayings of two men were only a matter of time in York says Police Chief William Smith. Smith says it is important to realize that drug traffickers are armed, but that the general public should not worry since assailants are known to one another and police are pursuing numerous leads in these two cases. York County Coroner Kathryn Fourham said James Johnson bled to death from gunshot wounds.

headline: Religious leaders bless city in ecumenical service
abstract: A gathering of religious leaders from various conferences, also including Lieutenant Colonel Israel Gaither of the Salvation Army, met to bless the city of Pittsburgh on Holy Saturday before Easter. The leaders prayed for the city Bishop Alden Hathaway of the Episcopal Diocese says has a spiritual problem.

headline: State health care plan resubmitted
abstract: State Public Welfare Secretary Karen F. Snider recently  announced that her department has resubmitted a plan to the federal government that would allow the state to provide comprehensive managed health care to more than 620,000 medical assistance recipients in southeastern Pennsylvania.

headline: Ridgway Library going to the head of its class
abstract: The Ridgway Library building, which for twenty-five years has been empty, will now be converted into Philadelphia's High School for the Creative and Performing Arts.

headline: Legislators back 'Valley Special'
abstract: Four Pennsylvania legislators are protesting the possible diversion of money from a project that would return computer rail service to the Lehigh Valley to another rail service. The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation says enough money is available for both.

headline: Minus Mr. Larsen
abstract: It's amazing, yet not surprising.  Criminal charges were brought yesterday against Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice Rolf R. Larsen, as the first fruits of a 10-month state grand jury investigation of the Supreme Court justices' conduct.  Justice Larsen, it might be noted, is next in line to be chief justice of that court.

headline: 3 charged over phony insurance
abstract: Three men accused yesterday at a federal grand jury trial of phony health insurance plans that affectd 2,400 employees in 14 states.  They collected $260,000 in premiums but only payed $4,558 in claims.

headline: Cleveland Amory writes legislators
abstract: Every House member returning to work yesterday got a hand-delivered letter from Cleveland Amory, president of the Fund for Animals, urging them to pass legislation that would ban live pigeon shoots.

headline: From Holt, it's an olive branch shrewdly held
abstract: Unprecedented things are happening on the Philadelphia waterfront.  An old labor antagonist is offering jobs to a union he's been accused of trying to bust.  And a young leader, considered an upstart by the union's old guard, is risking political fortunes by listening to the deal.  In his own angry, indignant, take-it-or-stick-it way, businessman Thomas J. Holt is, indeed, extending an olive branch to the International Longshoremen's Association leaders he has fought for years.

headline: Pitts decries state's business climate
abstract: Thursday night, state Representative Joseph R. Pitts covered a number of topics in one of a series of scheduled constituents meetings.  Pitts briefed residents of West Bradford and Newlin on issues ranging from regulation of workmen's compensation and the decline of manufacturing in Pennsylvania to outcomes based education and road maintenance.  It was the first in a series of six information sessions Pitts plans to schedule for his constituents.

headline: 3 more monuments slated at Gettysburg
abstract: The three monuments to be added to the Gettysburg Military Park will be honoring Masons, Marylanders, and a Confederate major general.

headline: Edward Savitz, main figure in sex scandal, dies of AIDS
abstract: Edward Savitz, known as 'Uncle Eddie' or 'Fast Eddie', died of AIDS a month before his trial was set for allegations of sexual molestation of four tennage boys.  He was thrown into the spotlight after his bizarre sexual fetishes were uncovered.

headline: Reno Backs Legislation Limiting Protest Tactics Against Abortion Clinics
abstract: Attorney General Janet Reno testified before the Labor and Human Resources Committee said that a bill designed to protect women and health care providers from violent attacks at abortion clinics is necessary and constitutional. The bill would make it a federal crime to use force or physical obstruction to prevent a woman from obtaining an abortion, or to damage medical facilities because they offer abortions. Opponents argue that it would violate freedom of speech guarantees and put a clamp on the antiabortion movement.

headline: State revokes personal care home's license
abstract: The PA State Department of Public Welfare announced it has revoked the license of the Colonial Estate Personal Care Facility after a patient was strangled to death at the facility by a posey, a restraining device.

headline: Rochester teachers get raises, grant concessions
abstract: Teachers in the Rochester Area School District have a new contract that calls for average annual pay raises of $2,500 but also includes benefits and work schedule concessions.

headline: Lincoln Highway group starts fund-raising journey: Money targeted for park
abstract: The state has appropriated $150,000 to plan for a Lincoln Highway State Heritage Park Corridor along US 30 spanning through Franklin Fulton, Bedford, Somerset and Westmoreland counties.  Joann Zeigler, local coordinator of the park said the plan would identify mechanisms, strategies and resources that could be used in creating the park.

headline: More prison alternatives needed, advocate says
abstract: State Corrections Commissioner Joseph Lehman wants to keep nonviolent prisoners out of the commonwealth's jails.  Lehman, a strong advocate of jail alternatives, says he will ask the state Budget office to strip up to $17.4 million from his budget to make money available for more county alternatives to prison.

headline: A brave merger
abstract: An announcement came last week by Tele-Communications Inc. and Bell Atlantic that they intend to merge.  With this merger, do newspapers have a future?  The answer is yes; the largest news and advertising gatherers in their regions should continue to be so if they continue to invest in news and advertising gathering and keep up with the needs of their customers.

headline: Bureaucrats up, but jobs down, group says
abstract: The Heritage Foundation, a think tank based in Washington found that more bureaucrats equals fewer jobs and less bureaucrats equals more jobs. The reason is simple, when the federal government orders companies to do more little things they have less money to spend on expanding the company.

headline: From homelessness to honor
abstract: President-elect Bill Clinton had lunch with Benjamin Edwards, a former homeless man, as one of the 50 inspiration people the Clintons and Gores had met on the campaign trail.  When Edwards and Clinton first met, Edwards shook Clinton's hand and wouldn't let go until he told his story about 12 years being homeless and how he needed Clinton to win so he could get a job.

headline: Pittsburgh pension plan underfunded
abstract: When Pittsburgh Mayor Sophie Masloff leaves office in January, she will leave behind a balanced operating budget  but also a deficit of nearly half a billion dollars in one critical city account.  That deficit is in the pension fund, which city owrkers depend upon for their retirement pay.  The account is not only drastically underfunded; it is by far the most cash-poor pension fund of any large US city covered in a recent survey.

headline: 3 sculptures, memorial spark renewed debate
abstract: There is a debate whether the use of Harrisburg's Riverfront Park for art displays and memorials, such as the newly proposed holocaust memorial is appropriate.  Some find the park too cluttered with manmade objects whereas the opposition feels it is good to display the art and monuments where people will see them.

headline: Effort to save sister's life sends siblings to court
abstract: Diagnosed with a rare genetic kindney disorder in 1986, Gregory Cooke has been on dialysis since then.  His body has already rejected one kidney transplanted from a cadaver and he believes he is in this position for one reason: he wanted to save his sister's life.  Last month, a sympathetic Philadelphia jury agreed, awarding Cooke $5 million in a lawsuit against the surgeons who performed the transplant.

headline: Selling goods, not stereotypes
abstract: The article discusses the fact that marketers are realizing stereotypes about the buying habits of minorities are inaccurate.  There is no homogenous "African-American", "Asian" or "Hispanic" market, so marketers must focus on the differences between sub-groups (such as African Americans in the north or south) in order to effectively advertise to these groups.

headline: States Are Reluctant Partners In Clinton's Big New Venture
abstract: President Clinton's health plan creates a mind-boggling array of new duties for the 50 states, which would be responsible for carrying out Mr. Clinton's promise to guarantee insurance coverage for all Americans.  A handful of states have developed innovative programs to control costs and expand insurance coverage, but it is unclear whether others have the political commitment or expertise to arrange insurance for all of their resident's under Clinton's proposal.

headline: Rumors abound Clayton may go
abstract: Schools Superintendent Constance Clayton is rumored to be leaving her position as superintendent of New York City public schools for a job possibly in Washington or Philadelphia.

headline: Looks like a choice among three evils for the new Mon Bridge
abstract: In the article, "3 Designs in Running For New Mon Bridge," all designs are uninspired solutions, and in a city so rich in bridge engineering, how could they be saddled with one of those three solutions?  Is this the best that the talent of this area can muster?
