headline: Muncy Prison Experiencing Aging Facility, Older Inmates
abstract: Sixty-three years after the State Correctional Institution at Muncy opened as a reform home for women, the facility is showing its age.  Although most housing units, treatment facilities and education buildings remain in good condition, tings like sidewalks, roof and gutters need to be repaired.

headline: A German spin in Delco
abstract: Today, politicians and other dignitaries will gater at the plant in Concordville, Delaware County, as the German manufacturer Pilz GmbH marks its entry into the US market as a maker of compact discs.

headline: Bush honors last point of light
abstract: Bush reconizes in his "Daily Point of Light" individuals or groups in the country who have impacted the community through volunteer work.  46 Pennsylvanians were mentioned over the last four years and some of their stories are told in the article.

headline: Frustrated by Capitol 'politics as usual,' Rep. ken Lee says he'll leave Legislature
abstract: Frustrated by a system he paints as crippled by inertia and politics as usual, state Representative Ken Lee announced that he is quitting the legislative rat race.  First elected in 1988, the three-term Republican lawmaker from Tunkhannock says he'll go out the way he came in- fighting for reform.

headline: Plane extravagance
abstract: Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen, in his testimony to grand jury, made allegations that a private flight to Erie, Senator Vince Fumo explained, came out of Philadelphia's "wealth of perks."

headline: '93 centennial offers great excuse to park yourself in a Penna. Park
abstract: Mike Shoup, travel editor, reports on his favorite state parks of the 113 in PA, including Nockamixon State Park and Parker Dam State Park. Shoup also mentions various outdoor activities offered by park services, including nature walks, wildlife hikes, water rentals, and more, especially in light of the upcoming centennial celebration of the state's park system. Shoup recommends renting park cabins built by the Civilian Conservation Corps and the PA Conservation Corps.

headline: Emboldened by alliance, the fraud squad emerges
abstract: PA state attorneys general in the National Associations of Attorneys General are working together to take over some of the responsibilities of the federal Consumer Product Safety Commission and bring other issues to the Commission's attention.  They are more effective at regulating product safety than the federal agency.

headline: Separate, unequal and still in court
abstract: The desegregation of city public schools has been one of the longest-running desegregation cases in the nation, one that began in 1968 and still awaits resolution in the Commonwealth Court.  The problem of unbalanced spending in areas of urban, predominately black, schools compared to that of the predominately white Northeast schools is apparent, but the solution voluntary integration by providing voluntary transportation to either schools has had, at best, mixed results.

headline: Syringe confusion leaves a trail of deadly mix-ups
abstract: A Pittsburgh Post Gazette investigation of medication errors found that deaths and injuries began surfacing shortly after lidocaine concentrate syringes went on the US market in 1976.  Reports to the US Food and Drug Administration, medical journal articles, licensing board actions, lawsuits and news accounts show such mix-ups have happened repeatedly since 1977.  The tally: At least 42 people killed, and at least 27 injured.  In at least five other overdose cases, the fate of the patient wasn't reported.

headline: School aid reallocation proposed
abstract: The Clinton administration asked Congress yesterday to spend more on programs for poor school children and change the way the money is distributed.

headline: MADD salutes officers
abstract: Throughout the commonwealth and across the country, Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) works closely with law enforcement to support their efforts at ridding the highways of drunked drivers.  Law enforcement is one element in MADD's campaign to save lives from being wiped out by a drunken driver.  It is the responsibility of every one of us to fight drunken driving.

headline: Murderer of officer set to die
abstract: In a bizarre turn of events, Walter Baker, on trial for the murder of Norristown police officer Thomas Barone, pled guilty against the advice of his attorney and then ordered his defense to rest midway through the trial. Baker made no attempt to defend himself prior to sentencing, in which Montgomery County Judge Salus convicted him of first degree murder and sentenced the former Army sharpshooter to death.

headline: A sloppy name, but porky profits
abstract: At New Pig Corp., a small but fast-growing maker of products for cleaning and controlling industrial messes, the eqully messy marketing puns, goo-guzzling absorbents and hog-style humor are drawing customers in.  Its sales are grwoing by more than 20 percent a year, and profits are increasing at an even fast rate.

headline: Cable war of nerves heats up with WPXI ad move
abstract: WPXI-TV will use tomorrow's telecast of the Steelers-Los Angeles Rams football game to kick off its campaign against cable operators who refuse to pay for carrying its signal.

headline: Galloping on the paper trail
abstract: Investigators from Attorney Genral Ernie Preate's office spent a second day yesterday inventorying and carting away every piece of paper associated with the scandal-ridden election in state senatorial district 2.  They hope to finish today so they can get down to the real business of determining whether anyone broke the law in the November 2 election.

headline: Plans prepared  to let the homelss  use old military bases
abstract: The  Clinton administration is drafting  an eexecutive  order to allow  surplus military  bases  near cities to be used for shelters  for the homeless.

headline: A fitting anniversary tribute
abstract: This year marks the 100th anniversary of Pa park system and it just may happen that legislation will create a Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fun, initially funded by $93 million bond issue with 15 percent of the Realty Transfer Tax assigned as a sorce of funding.  This project is called 'Key 93".

headline: Even in prison, they call him 'Mr. Tayoun'
abstract: Jimmy Tayoun, the former city councilman who's now in federal prison for paying and taking bribes, is in a minimum-security prison with no barbed wire at the gate.  There, he's writing, teaching and working out.

headline: State agrees to stall cuts in Medicaid funds
abstract: A class-action lawsuit was filed on Dec. 31, 1992 that stated the cuts to Medicaid within Pennsylvania violated the Americans with Disablilities Act, the federal Medicaid Act, and the due process clause of the 14th Amendment.  They were successful in their injunction which stalls the implication of the legislation for 120 days.

headline: The flu bug has landed in the region, health experts warn
abstract: The Type B/Panama flu has arrived in two known cases in Philadelphia, both of which were children.  Its not to late to get a flu shot and people should be warned that if they are at high risk the flu is deadly.

headline: School board accepts reports
abstract: The Shippensburg Area School District passed a 5% increase in teachers saleries in a vote 6-3 costing the school district over $300,000.

headline: Many speak for legalizing city jitney service
abstract: Speakers at a public hearing yesterday criticized service by the Yellow Cab Co. and expressed support for a North Side man who wants to legalize and expand his jitney service.  A dozen people, including Pittsburgh City Councilman Duane Darkins and Wilkinsburg Mayor Bob Pitts, testified at the hearing.  The state Public Utility Commission, which regulates taxis, held the hearing because Yellow Cab is protesting Curtis McCoy's application for a licensed taxi service.

headline: Murders increasingly are the American way of death
abstract: In the United States murder is becoming a way of life.  What was once settled with a handshake is now being handled with a handgun.  In 1991 24,020 murders were the highest ever.

headline: A suburban push to sell city tourists on side trips
abstract: The suburban counties surrounding Philadelphia to include their attractions in their tourism offices as well as in the Philadelphia International Airport.

headline: Call for audit isn't supported by candidate
abstract: Dan Bradley, one of three North Allegheny school director candidates endorsed by a group seeking an audit of the districts finances, stated that he disagreed with that action. The Patriot Party contends that the board approved a $54 million dollar budget but then filed information claiming they only had a $51 million dollar budget.

headline: Game commission working on a multi-faceted agenda
abstract: Game Commission Executive Director Peter S. Duncan undergoes a question and answer segment regarding the commission's agenda.

headline: Political strategists are today's kingmakers
abstract: Strong-willed and flamboyant Mark Hanna twisted ethical standards as well as arms in guiding the political campaign of his malleable but likable candidate- and go him elected to the White House.  The candidate was William McKinley.  The top issue was the gold standard.  The year was 1896.  Hanna's story demonstrates that the phenomenon of campaign managers with higher profiles than some of their clients is nothing new in American politics.

headline: ACEDC asks Gettysburg for business park water
abstract: An Adams County Economic Development Corporation asked Gettysburg officials to expand borough water and sewer service to the proposed business park site in Straban Township.  At a special meeting, ACEDC Executive Director Robert Hendricks asked the borough council and Gettysburg Municipal Authority to expand its township service area to the business park site at the US Route 30 interchange of US Route 15.

headline: Everyone did it, contractor claims
abstract: There was Stephen Shemin, housing contractor, owner of PB Stevens & Co., standing in the middle of a federal courtroom yesterday explaining how corrupt business was done at the Philadelphia Housing Authority.  At the PHA, corruption was a way of life, and he had been a part of it form ore than 20 years, Shemin confessed.

headline: Study of HIV in gays spurs worries
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh released an alarming new study that showed in the 536 gay men that had joined the study had the same rate of infect at 22% as men eight years ago had.  That may show that the STD prevention and information has not stopped to curb the spread of the disease in the gay community.

headline: Stigma underscored
abstract: For the one million Pennsylvania residents who are affected by a serious mental illness and their family members, the indictment of Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen for allegedly asking others to pick up his prescribed drugs for clinical depression presents a disturbing picture to people who share the nightmare of this illness.

headline: School contracts at a glance
abstract: Summaries of the progress of school contracts are given for districts in Allegheny, Beaver, Fayette, Washington and Westmoreland Counties.

headline: Monroeville toll site curtails long parking
abstract: Pennsylania Turnpike authories said that they will need the space along the shoulder of Monroeville Interchange toll plaza to park construction equipment for the current project they are working on.  After the construction is complete the ban on parking at that spot will continue to be ban for safty reasons.

headline: Neighborhoods are fighting back
abstract: Neighborhood watch groupos in Philly and across the country are ganging up to stop drugs, prostitutes, and hustlers from consuming their neighborhoods.  The success stories are plentiful including Sandtown, Link Valley, Wilshire, and Philladelphia's own Spring Garden.  More success can come to other towns in the people work together with police to imporove their neighborhood.

headline: A Winning Hand?
abstract: Casino gambling has become an oasis in an economic desert for many Indian tribes.  In the eyes of tribal leaders, it could be a key to giving Indians greater control over their own destiny.

headline: Calling all candidates for a special election
abstract: PA House Speaker H. William DeWeese decided to schedule a special election to fill two vacancies in the state House.  One seat is empty because Representative Gordon Linton resigned after being appointed by President Clinton to head the Federal Transit Administration. Neither party has yet chosen a candidate.

headline: George W. Davidson Jr., 67 ex-Carlisle mayor, councilman
abstract: Former mayor and councilman of Carlisle, George W. Davidson Jr. died May 4, 1993 at 67.  He was also the director of Cumberland County's Tax Claim Bureau and long time clerk, manager and part-owner of the former Kronenberg's clothing store and was remembered by his friend Earl Keller, Cumberland County Commissioner.  Also mentioned in the obituary section is Max Worthington Jr. and Geraldine Heim.

headline: Politics is not baloney
abstract: State Senate Republican Leader Roberty Jubelirer was quoted in news article as saying that political stuff is baloney when it comes to real things in life.  The political stuff is not a lot of baloney.  It is important and affects thousands of people's lives.  Until we elect idealism, integrity and conviction we will continue to be thought of as baloney.

headline: Allegheny plans scenic development on rivers
abstract: Where once a line of ugly industrial sites stood along the banks of the three rivers residents might one day be able to bicycle along 172 miles of scenice riverview trails.  That's the snapshot of the future Allegheny County land use planners would like to see.

headline: Excerpts of Larsen testimony
abstract: Justice Rolf Larsen testified befroe the special grand jury four times.  During his appearances, he was questioned extensively by prosecutors about the lengthy list of allegations he had made against fellow Supreme Court Justices, their relatives, attorneys and others.  What follows are excerpts of the Larsen testimony on which the grand jury based its conclusions.

headline: Tasco takes issue with an editorial
abstract: The Inquirer editorial of Feb. 12 concerning the law of protesters interference with access to reproductive health-care facilities is misleading.  If the federal government won't protect the rights of the patients at legal health care institutions it is the responsibility of the state and local government to protect the rights of the patients, not just the rights of the protesters.

headline: Studies Show Futility of Rushing Some Heart Victims to Hospitals
abstract: It is futile, and economically wasteful, for emergency medical owrkers to rush heart attack victims to the hospital after efforts to resuscitate them in the field have failed, two major studies, done in Memphis and Houston, have found.

headline: School district needs help on guns, Outen says
abstract: The discovery of two guns in Harrisburg City schools is sad, but not shocking, schools Superintendent Randolph G. Outen told a packed city school board meeting last night.  And, he told a room of concerned parents and faculty, the district cannot tackle "the problem of kids and guns" alone.

headline: Motorist fights to see radar reading
abstract: A Harrisburg man, Paul B. Owens, is trying to get out of a speeding ticket using a novel approach: He sasy the officer should have had to show him the radar reading when he was stopped.

headline: 'Never mess with a man in jail again'
abstract: BuSandra K. Biddle was arrested for smuggling drug to her boyfriend in Lewisburg Federal Penitentiary and will serve 2 years on probation.

headline: After Bhopal, Congress got busy
abstract: Appalled by the chemical accident that killed 2,500 people in Bhopal, India, and chilled at the news that similar disasters had barely been avoided here, Congress passed the Emergency Planning and Community Right to Know Act of 1986, ordering states to devise way sto avert chemical catastrophes.  Congress, however, did not provide funding to make the act work properly, emergency-planning officials say.

headline: Calling Sen. Specter
abstract: As the US Senate heads into the final round of action on the crime package this week, we hope that Senator Arlen Specter can resist the appeals of those who want to weaken the Brady Bill.  Hopefully, Senator Specter will vote for reasonable restriction rather than ratcheting up the violence.

headline: Gephardt vows to oppose NAFTA
abstract: House Majority Leader Richard A. Gephardt yesterday dealt a serious blow to President Clinton's hopes to win congressional approval of a free-trade pact with Mexico and Canada by vowing to actively oppose it.

headline: Pollsters Enlist Psychologists In Quest for Unbiased Results
abstract: A survey by Ross Perot has become a textbook case of how readily results of a survey can be manipulated by the pollster, a point too easily forgotten in a day when polls have become a fisture of the information landscape  as a quick pulse reading of the body politic.  But survey researchers, seeking to minimize such biases in their results, are continuing to raise questions about the way they ask questions.

headline: Bond issue for parks appeared to be a winner
abstract: A $50 million bond issue to improve the state's parks and recreational attractions appeared to be heading for victory last night.  The referendum was passing with a 64 percent to 36 percent reatio, with 25 percent of the state's precincts counted.

headline: Experts on Catholic canon law say parish lawsuits doomed to fail
abstract: Attorney David McMullin has filed suits against Bishop Donal Wuerl saying that Wuerl violated the state law because he didn't obey canon law whne he closed certain parishes.  Experts of canon law say McMullin is like an amateur.

headline: The dream of inclusion is not yet fulfilled
abstract: Today, the dream of inclusion is only slowly being realized.  Just as the Civil Rights Act of 1964 did not change the condition of blacks overnight, the Americans with Disabilities Act has not suddenly transformed the lives of people with crebral palsy, paraplegia, mental illness and other impairments.

headline: Study find 8th grade drug use is up
abstract: In a report which disturbed Secretary of the Department Donald Shalala, the US Department of Health and Human Services released results of a University of Michigan survey showing a statistically significant increase in drug use by eight graders. Though drug use among high school seniors continued to decline, principal investigator Lloyd Johnston attribute the increased use among eighth graders to lack of federal and media attention to drug use.

headline: School incident report
abstract: William T. Bergman, in his final appearance as executive director for school safety for the School District of Philadelphia, told the Board of Education yesterday that schools often under-report serious accidents.  Bergman said some incidents are not reported because officials fear they will be judged by the number of incidents in their schools.

headline: Move over, truckers
abstract: Representative Thomas Fee introduced legislation last week to prohibit large trucks from traveling in the passing lane unless they are passing other vehicles.  Fee said it was a safety hazard as well as an inconvenience.

headline: New judge puts brake on  drivers' appeals
abstract: Senior Judge Robert A. Doyle was sour one moment, grandfathery the next, presiding over a procession of motorists trying to overturn PennDOT's suspension of their licenses.  Most brought attorney's, but some bravely went it alone.

headline: Airing Nations Air
abstract: Nations Air, the latest upstart to seek a no-frills niche in the cutthroat airlines industry, is offering low fares and millions of dollars in annual payroll with 150 local jobs.  Allegheny County officials will study the proposal carefully, pros and cons.  The proposal is intriguing enough to deserve an unprejudiced evaluation.

headline: Calls workers a model group
abstract: The young health workers spending their summer by immunizing inner-city kids served as a brief TV backdrop for US Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala in North Philadelphia yesterday.  The publicity helps them to help kids.

headline: Getting your Irish up
abstract: Saint Patrick's Day has become another excuse for the ethnic equivalent of WASPs for an extra holiday.

headline: Poor voter turnout expected
abstract: It's Election Day, when voters are called upon to flex the muscles that make democracy work.  History tells us, however, that three out of four Pennsylvanians will continue to let those muscles atrophy.  Off-year elections such as this one, with low-profile state judicial elections at the top of the ticket, typically yield voter turnouts that would make the Founding Fathers cringe.

headline: Brewed on grant
abstract: A cartoon depicts Jim Ferlo suggesting to save the Highland Park Resevoir rather than using it for those who need water.

headline: Ex-police major tied to tax case leaks
abstract: Former New Jersey State Police officer Maj. Joseph Craparotte is under a federal investigation along with many other in a major multi-million dollar tax-evasion scheme.  He is believed to have leaked information to suspects about the investigation into the tax-evasion of $14.8 million in diseal-feul tax.

headline: The Eagles and a tale of two cities
abstract: The Philadelphia Eagles win in the playoffs has shifted all focus to the game and away from differences such as race, gender, and sexual preference.  Compared to Cincinnati’s problems with religion, free speech, and the Ku Klux Klan which is consuming the people attention and dividing them, Philadelphia’s winning football team is bringing Philadelphians together.

headline: Study finds patients unhappy with HMOs
abstract: A nationwide study found that HMO patients were unhappy with their treatment.  They complained of long waits, difficulty scheduling an appointment on short notice, doctor appointments that were too short, and a decreased interest of doctors in their well-being. The study is important in light of President Clinton's health care reform plans, which would offer incentives for people to enroll in health maintenance organizations.

headline: School pact vote today
abstract: After a nine-day strike, Penn Hills teachers will vote on a labor contact reached under the supervision of Common Please Judge David s. Cercone.

headline: M'sex Oks 'disposable' industry
abstract: A "disposable" concrete company, that will leave after finishing its work, has a contract with the PA Department of Transportation to repair a section of I-81.

headline: New prison ready for inmates
abstract: The PA State Correctional Institution/Mahanoy will be ready to accept inmates in two months as the state deemed the project substantially complete. The prison will be medium security and have around 1000 cells; it is expected to create 400 full time jobs in Schuylkill County.

headline: Also in business . . .
abstract: Pittsburgh businessman John Connally is expected to make a donation to Duquesne University's Center for Entrepeneurship. Northwest Airlines agreed to purchase USAir's Baltimore-London Route as Delta Air Lines takes an $82.5 million dollar writeoff. Weirton Steel Company announced its first-quarter results would be affected by a pretax accounting charge in the hundreds of millions.

headline: Can Rendell, Street work magic on public housing?
abstract: Walking down a City Hall corridor last week, Mayor Rendell ticked off the reasons why it wouldn't be a burden assumnig the leadership of the Philadelphia Housing Authority in an effort to turn the beleaguered agency around in the next two years.

headline: Giants versus Phils: But were we shut out?
abstract: The Phillies continue to be the only team in major league baseball who have not been SHUT OUT by an opponent this season.  So who cares they didn't win yesterday, at least they scored.

headline: Post office punch
abstract: US Senator Arlen Spector is going to try and prevent the death of the $200 million federal office center at 30th and Walnut Street. In an announcement last week U.S. Postmaster General Marvin T Runyon Jr said that the project was canceled due to the Postal Services "fiscal responsibilities." Spector said that Runyon does not have the right to unilaterally and arbitrarily cancel the project without consulting Congress first.

headline: Bull's-eye on Star Barn
abstract: Nancy Eshelman's column hit the bull's-eye on the side of the Star Barn.  Simply because something is old does not mean we have to restore or preserve it.  It's understandable to preserve the Star Barn if it were the only unique barn left in Pennsyvlania, but it is not, nor is it even unique for its star.

headline: Ex-police officer charged with drug trafficking
abstract: Bernard L. Hont, a former Pittsburgh police officer, imprisoned in 1988 after his conviction as the mastermind of a burglary ring that operated while he was on and off duty, has been charged with drug trafficking and operating illegal gambling machines in his North Side bar.

headline: Va. Assembly Kills Fairfax Proposal To Add 2 Minority School Board Seats
abstract: A proposal to add two seats to the Fairfax School Board for representation of the county's growing Asian and Latino communities was killed in the General Assembly today, capping a bitter debate about civil rights and party politics by a vote of 51 to 48.

headline: Study says substance abuse takes 20% of Medicaid's hospital money
abstract: The abuse of tobacco, alcohol and drugs is responsible for $1 of every $5 Medicaid spends on hospital care, and will add more than $7.4 billion to Medicaid inpatient hospital costs in 1994, according to a study by the Center on Addiction and Substance Abuse at Columbia University recently released.

headline: School playground safety gets political eye
abstract: State Representative Ron Cowell, chairman of the House Education Committee, says he will propose legislation to promote playground safety on school grounds.

headline: Narrow road will stay that way
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation decided to leave Wissahickon Avenue as it is, rather than widening it.

headline: Night in the city
abstract: After the murder of a shopkeeper during Philadelphia's "Make it a Night Program" when shops stay open late, Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell in a press conference argued the killing appears not to be random. The city beefed up security and despite public perception, crime declined since last year. The editorial board urges boldly addressing crime, but notes shopkeepers can not be blamed for not participating in the event, though empty streets beget crime in a downward spiral.

headline: Amazing Maise  Maze is not-so-corny idea
abstract: Don Frantz financed and came up with the idea of creating the world's largest maze.  All proceeds will go to Red Cross efforts to aid flood victims in the Midwest.

headline: 'Capital city syndrome' is nationwide
abstract: null

headline: Ginsburg's potential
abstract: Out of President Clinton's portfolio of new-direction nominees has come Ruth Bader Ginsburg, likely successor to retiring Justice Byron White on the US Supreme Court.  Unlike previous new directionists, however, Judge Ginsburg shows a welcome political survivability and the potential to be a true consensus builder once confirmed to the court, as almost surely she will be.

headline: Postal probe splits Santorum, Klink
abstract: Both Representative Rick Santorum and Representative Ron Klink are adamant that they want to get to the bottom of the House Post Office scandal as quickly as possible.  Both are dertermined that any wrongdoers be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.  Beyond that, they agree on virtually nothing about the Justice Department's investigation into the scandal in which former Representative Joe Kolter and House Ways and Means Chairman Dan Rostenkowski have been publicly implicated.

headline: Can mill towns revive?
abstract: Cheap transportation by rail and water, coupled with easy access to coal and markets, made this region's river valleys the soul of American heavy industry from the late 1800s through World War II.  These assets are no longer so valuable.  The question now is how much will it take to replace those assets with new, equally valuable ones that might bring something to replace the 77,000 manufacturing jobs lost to the valleys over the past 20 years.  Or shold the valleys turn themselves into something else?

headline: Ex-policeman pleads guilty to drug charge
abstract: Thomas J. McAleer, a former Philadelphia police officer pleads guilty to extoring more than $14,000 from Kensington drug dealters and distributing some of their heroin and crack.  He faces 27 to 33 months in prison.  He was caught because of a federal crackdown on drug-dealing organizations in the 2200 block of North Palethorp Street.

headline: Va. Lawmakers Avoid Battle Over Abortion
abstract: To avoid another battle about abotion in the Virginia congress early every major bill dealing with the subject - from measures that would limit abortion rights to those that would protect them - was killed.  It is an election year so many are taking a more modest stance or simply ducking questions.

headline: Subscribers, lawyer defend newsletter
abstract: Christian Brotherhood Newsletter subscribers said yesterday they got into the newsletter's health-care program mainly to help other Christians in need, not to find a cheaper way to insure themselves.  And despite no guarantee that their medical bills would be paid, they said, they are confident the program is just as reliable as any inusrance contract.

headline: School ruling seen as likely to spur tax increase
abstract: Higher taxes appear inevitable to obtain funding parity between the state's 30 poorest school districts and the wealthiest school districts, the head of a bipartisan state commission working on solutions to school funding problems said yesterday.

headline: New brand of taxi driver
abstract: Professional cab drivers, such as Anthony Teagle, are supporting a new system that requires Philadelphia cab drivers to be certified and display photo-identification cards in their vehicles made by the PA Public Utility Commission.  The certification system is trying to clean up the Philadelphia taxi industry by creating a new dispatching system and setting certain flat fees.

headline: Obituary: D. Quinlan; lawyer and former judge
abstract: Judge Daniel L. Quinlan, 70, died Friday at Bryn Mawr Hospital.  He was a lawyer and active in the Democratic party.

headline: An alluring offer from New Jersey
abstract: Spectacor says the offer that was rejected by 76ers owner Harold Katz was sweetened with increased revenues and a rent reduction.  Still, it doesn't appear comparable to an offer New Jersey is reported to have made to woo both the 76ers and the Flyers to Camden several weeks back.

headline: Capitol Duties
abstract: A picture of PA Representative Thomas B. Stish as he stands in the gallery overlooking the House of Representatives chamber in the Capitol.

headline: Give Cohen more credit
abstract: The comments in the article "Cohen, Smith Coast to Victories" about incumbent City Councilman Dan Cohen's win over challenger Alan Convard were puzzling.  Reporter John Bull referred to Convard as feeling "disillusioned" and quote him as having said that voters evidently didn't want change.  Change to what?  Mr. Cohen deserves some credit at the time of his re-election!

headline: Powell has cash on mind, Murtha says
abstract: Hillary Rodham Clinton was not the only superstar in Washington's frimament last week.  Colin Luther Powell, who wears his stars in sets of four on each shoulder, was also in orbit from the White House to Capitol Hill as he made his way through a round of farewells before he retired on Thursday.

headline: County shelves radio upgrade for 911
abstract: The Chester County Association of Township Officials met to discuss plans to update a radio dispatch system for the county's Department of Emergency Services with an $8 million operating cost. Originally, the municipality and county would split the cost 20/80. However, former chief of Westwood Fire Company and treasurer of Chester County Fire Chiefs Association, Ronald Scott is concerned about radio costs cutting into its budget and believes the county should pay for 100 percent of costs through taxes.

headline: Face drugs, crime head-on
abstract: Block meetings are being formed as residents confer about keeping their area of Hunting Park safe as a reaction to the beating of Santiago Pineda in May by a dozen alleged drug dealers after Pineda ordered them away from the front of his house.s

headline: They couldn't take the heat
abstract: Three years ago, AT&T, which had supported Planned Parenthood for 25 years, withdrew its funding under pressure from the Christian Action Coalition, an anti-abortion group.  This was despite the fact that much of Planned Parenthood's mission- and 96 percent of its expenditures- are devoted to education and preventative helath-care services, specifically designed to avoid unwanted pregnancies and the need for abortions.

headline: Surgeon fighting to keep Pitt chair
abstract: A University of Pittsburgh surgery professor who is at odds with the school's medical center officials has vowed to fight to keep his tenured position here.  Dr. Norman Wolmark, who traces his difficulties to 1990, had been chief of surgery at Montefiore Hospital since 1986 and has watched his authority erode and his research funds evaporate.

headline: School weathers curriculum turmoil, but needs strong leader to go forward
abstract: Just when it appeared that things were back on track at the Milton Hershey School, the private institution lost its new president before he ever ste foot on campus.  Arthur Levine, whose installation had already been scheduled for Aug. 29, told the Hershey School board that he could not take the job because of family problems.

headline: New Cumberland is placed on East Shore in state map
abstract: The new Pennsylvania road map has incorrectly placed New Cumberland in East Shore township because it was too crowded on the map to place the correct title over the correct location says the press secretary for the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: Officer in killing to be fired
abstract: According to Philadelphia Police Commissioner the police officer who shot and killed a mentally ill homeless man has been suspended and will be dismissed from the force. The commissioner said that the officer could have resorted to less drastic measures in order to subdue the man. The shooting occurred after the homeless man threw a bottle at the officers head and was about to throw a second one.

headline: Another great day for shopping
abstract: In an effort to boost weekend business sales, downtown Pittsburgh merchants held a second "great day to shop" promotion which included giveaways by many merchants. Jacques Kahn, executive director of the Golden Triangle Association, said the first promotion held a month earlier appeared to be a success, however it was difficult to measure given that department stores had additional special promotions during the same weekend.

headline: Carmen Brutto, longtime capitol reporter, retires
abstract: The longtime Patriot-News Capitol reporter and columnist Carmen Brutto was as much a part of the halls of state power as the marble columns, the towering gold-leaf paintings, the legislative pay raises.  At 70, after more than 30 years "on the hill," he retires today.

headline: Give Heckler a promotion to Senate
abstract: Voters in Bucks County's 10th state Senate District will choose a new senator Tuesday, in an election unusual for more than its middle-of-the-summer date.  The timing of the winner's swearing-in hasn't been set, but it won't be before November.  And he or she will serve only through next year.  The only real choice is state Representative David W. Heckler, the Republican candidate.

headline: Power Dressing
abstract: When New York General Assembly Speaker Saul Weprin threw grungy looking clothes, forgot his identification, and tried to get past Capitol guards for a meeting, he had to be rescued by a longtime Capitol elevator operative who made a positive identification of Weprin.

headline: Fragile battle flags saved
abstract: The Capitol Preservation Committee opened the state Textile Laboratory to show off some of the 400 Civil War flags that men from regiments throughout PA carried during the war. They were once housed at the Capitol Rotunda, but were not being preserved properly and were withering.

headline: Fair-housing laws have agents changing pitch
abstract: Fair-housing laws are forcing real estate agents to watch their words as some are being accused of 'steering' clients away from certain areas.  Racism is the shadow of steering, hidden by phrases such as 'good neighborhood', 'high crime', or giving the opinion that a certain person shouldn't live in that area for unspecified reasons.  Real estate agents argue they have a responsibility to tell their clients of the statistics of an area, good or bad.

headline: Tougher law for crack offenses angers civil rights activists
abstract: Civil rights activists such as the National Rainbow Coalition are protesting the federal law that sends people caught with crack cocaine to prison while hose with powder cocaine can get probation. It treats one gram of crack cocaine equal to a hundred grams of powder cocaine, though the substances are similar, and civil rights activists says the law disproportionately harms poor African Americans.

headline: TB Cases Spreading Rapidly Among Children, Report Says
abstract: Tuberculosis cases among children under 15 have increased 35 percent since 1985, as parents and other adults spread the lung disease in their homes, the Center for Disease Control and Prevention reported today.  Doctors are concerned because they see few ways to protect children.

headline: Schools are open in Bethel Park
abstract: The strike by Bethel Park teachers generated a great deal of ill will from borough residents, but little of that acrimony was shared by the students as they finally got into their classrooms.

headline: No relief in sight, state lacks funds
abstract: Interstate 83 has gotten worse over the years.  A road designed to carry 35,000 vehicles a day now is overwhelmed by 90,000.  Already, residents whose properties back up to I-83 are making their own noise about the need for sound barriers for the heavily populated stretch between Union Deposit Road and Route 22.

headline: O'Kicki in a land where borders are made to cross
abstract: Slovenia is a good place for wanted PA ex-judge Joseph O'Kicki to have fled from the US Federal Bureau of Investigations, with borders shared by four other countries. Even more difficult however, is what to do with him if he is caught, as Slovenia and the United States have yet to sign an extradition treaty. Slovenian officials may know where he is, as all citizens carry identification for large transactions and register a permanent address, however they are protecting his privacy.

headline: Area Companies Benefit From State Ben Franklin Funding
abstract: Woolrich Inc., the renowned Clinton County clothing manufacturer with nine plants in four states, is "revolutionizing" the way its workers work so their jobs won't be shipped overseas.  Grays Run Technology's Inc., a small firm housed in a "business incubator" in the Williamsport Industrial Park, hopes to launch its first standard product.  Both efforts got a boost when the companies received about half of $300,000 in economic development money for the 1993-1994 fiscal year.

headline: Carville sorts through defeat, ponders future
abstract: Could it be that after finally losing a big one- New Jersey- James Carville, the hard-knocking, face-eating Hannibal Lecter of Democratic politics, is actually becoming a wuss?

headline: Giving Government a Makeover
abstract: The public is frustrated with a government that does not seem to be working efficiently given its fiscal crisis. As a result, officials at all levels of government across the nation, including President Clinton, are being forced to reinvent the way government operates. The National Academy of Public Administration has created the Alliance for Redesigning Government in response to a political and social culture that is ready for change.

headline: Preate campaign audit: oops!
abstract: The campaign committee for PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. failed to report 238 campaign contributions because of clerical errors.  Preate has been investigated before by the Pennsylvania Crime Commission for links to illegal video-poker operators.

headline: Historical Society unveils expansion project
abstract: The Cumberland County Historical Society has found room to expand and is paying $250,000 from Mary Kollas for several adjoining lots and two parking lots.

headline: Father accused of endangnering children is freed on bail
abstract: Michael Axten, 35 of Port Richmond, left his four children in an unheated car, in mid-20 degree weather, for over an hour while drinking in a bar.  He was arrested with a bal of .17, nearly twice the legal limit to drive, and charged with four counts of endangering the welfare of children.  He was released on $15,000 bail.

headline: Urban activists boycott civil rights march
abstract: The National Urban Peace and Justice Movement, an activist organization of youth gangs, is protesting the civil rights march in Washington D.C. They say that problems in the inner cities are not taken seriously by the march organizers and their representatives were denied permission to participate in the program.

headline: Temple, Shriners hospital plan Okd
abstract: A $68 million plan to build two hospitals, in conjunction with Temple University, in North Philadelphia were approved by the state Department of Health. Saint Christopher's Hospital for the Children is not pleased because this plan includes funding for a new pediatric hospital that they say will come in competition with their existing facility.

headline: Schools close if Mich. City doesn't OK $20.7M
abstract: Bay City, Michigan may have to close its schools. Already in financial trouble, city schools will now be unable to operate due to the legislation signed by Michigan Governor John Engler that eliminated property taxes as a source of funding for public schools.  Voters will have to approve $20.7 million for education in order for schools to remain open, and this vote may not pass.

headline: Not Like the Movie: 3 Take a Dare, and Lose
abstract: Like the hero of the new movie "The Program," two teenagers from Pennsylvania and another from Long Island lay in the middle of two different roads at night, apparently to prove they had nerves of steel.  Unlike the move hero, they did not walk away unharmed.  One was killed almost instantly and the two others were critically injured.

headline: Olasz gets light penalty in auto-leasing 'sham'
abstract: The PA Ethics Commission ruled that State Representative Richard Olasz violated the state Ethics Act twice by using the House's auto-leasing allowance to buy cars for cheaper prices.  Although he could be forced to pay $18,864 and face jail time, he may only wind up paying $6,288 with no jail time or criminal record.

headline: Bad news from 3 top companies
abstract: Three of America's top companies, IBM, Boeing and Pratt & Whitney have announced massive corporate cutbacks.  IBM, Boeing, and Pratt & Whitney have slashed 55%, 35%, and 11,000 jobs cut respectivly.

headline: Casey aims to aid poor
abstract: Casey's budget focused on keeping taxes down while increasing spending towards prisons, health care for the poor and poor school districts.  While there was no tax increase there was a 'tax correction' of %13.6 to electric companies, which will get passed directly to ratepayers.

headline: Go West, Ms. Hafer
abstract: If Barbara Hafer wants to waste her time running for governor again, let her do it at her own expense, not while she continues the charade of pretending to serve as state auditor general.  Let's pay her to go back to her home state of California and audit it for a few years.

headline: Preate campaigner
abstract: Mike Hudome has been appointed director of the Ernie Preate for Governor Exploratory Committee.  Hudome is expected to be campaign manager once Preate becomes a declared candidate, probably later this fall.

headline: Indian artifacts abound on property
abstract: Rev. Park Smith has found bones in his mountainous back yard in Juniata County which he claims are indian remains.  Archologists are interested in the find, but he has decided to hand over the site to a Bible College.

headline: FBI gave a warning; then began its assault
abstract: The Federal Bureau of Investigations gave cult leader David Koresh a warning before the FBI began using armored trucks to ram holes in the wall of the compound where Koresh and his cult had held forth under seige for the past 51 days. The FBI released non-lethal gas, asking members to exit, however agents were met with gunfire. The cult members lit fire to the building with only one member exiting, resulting in what FBI spokesman Bob Ricks said was a massive loss of life.

headline: Valley school districts try, but fail, to recruit minorities
abstract: An absence of minority teachers and administrators isn't for a lack of trying to recruet them, said four Valley superintendents.  Though the recruiting effort is rigorous, the effort fails, and minorities simply don't apply for the openings.

headline: The case for Jersey children's hospital
abstract: A recent article raised the question of whether or not tow proposed new children's hospitals were needed in the Delaware Valley.  As far as the Southern New Jersey Regional Children's Hospital in Camden is concerned, it is felt that both the need and evidence supporting the development of this institution is overwhelming.

headline: Schools in Bucks are more crowded
abstract: In Bucks County public school districts, the housing market, new constrution and population shifts seem to explain the more crowded schools, while private schools point to tuition hikes and changing recruiting techniques to explain why they grew or shrunk.

headline: Officials do an about-face
abstract: Transportation officials are now convinced that there needs to be construction of a four line highway between Brownsville and Uniontown to cope with the heavy amount of local traffic.  A survey of those on the road was taken and most were local traffic going between the borough and the city.

headline: One hostage freed, one found dead
abstract: A prison riot at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility, which may have begun due to racial tensions, has left seven white inmates, one black inmate, and a prison guard dead thus far. One of eight guards held hostage was released after negotiators agreed to a ten minute radio broadcast by an inmate. The broadcast, one demand among a number centered on gaining media access, called for the Federal Bureau of Investigations to negotiate the situation.

headline: BCCI case: There were bad guys- and just guys
abstract: A Temple University of Law symposium is asked about The Bank of Credit and Commerce International: "Was this the most criminal bank in the world?  Or just the most investigated bank in the world?"

headline: Casey could return to job before yule
abstract: Governor Casey will probably return to work sometime between Thanksgiving and Christmas, his wife Ellen, said at a news conference in Pittsburgh yesterday.

headline: Going it together
abstract: President Clinton has called for bi-partisanship and pleaded with Republicans to work together with Democrats to solve issues.  He will need bipartisan support for three upcoming issues: the ratification of the North American Free Trade Agreement, streamlining the federal government and reforming the health care system. The editorial board agrees that our nation's problems require cooperation from both parties.

headline: Preate 'campaigns' in Valley
abstract: It seems the state attorney general is concerned with more than just crime these days.  Attorney General Ernie Preate made a stop at Hill Crest Country Club Tuesday night to speak at the Strong-Land Chamber of Commerce's annual meeting.  Chamber officials had touted that his speech would focus on anti-drug efforts, but Preate spent more time talking about tax reform for businesses and criticizing leadership in Harrisburg.

headline: Justifying the means
abstract: The trees are falling in part of the 11,300 acres of forest and trout streams along the Allegheny River that were purchased this year by the Pittsburgh-based Western Pennsylvania Conservancy.  To help swing the $8 million purchase, the converancy in June sold the timber right son 9,600 acres to Indurstrail Timber and Land Corp. under a 10-year contract.  The sale of the timber rights is just one disuputed aspect of the unusual land acquisation.

headline: Federal suit pits a city law firm against a lawyer with AIDS
abstract: A young lawyer is filing a federal lawsuit against his former employer, Kohn, Nast & Graf, for violating state and federal laws banning discrimination agaisnt people with AIDS, when he was told to look for a new job upon learning he tested positive for the HIV.

headline: Villified by bishop
abstract: The ELCA bishop and his staff have demonstrated their Central Pennsylvania suburban mortality with their advertisement decrying a humane approach to the understanding of all people as human and deserving of God's grace.

headline: The Challenge: Winning Trust, Lowering Costs
abstract: The article discusses HMOs, or Health Maintenance Organizations, which may play a large role in President Clinton's health care reform plans. Studies show that lower costs but are less popular with consumers than traditional health insurance .The article discusses different experiences of those who have used HMOs.

headline: Schools in Minneapolis Try a Cooperative Approach
abstract: Peter C. Hutchinson is slated to become a Superintendent of the school system in Minneapolis, even though he has not climbed the latter (teacher, principal, central office administrator). He is not the only businessman to be coming into school districts nationwide, some urban school districts are turning to corporate executives to assist with their management and fiscal issues. There is a new trend throughout the country of trying different methods to improve the level of education.

headline: One man tries to stop death at intersection
abstract: Brian Ems, at 6 am yesterday, was at the intersection of Route 13 and Old Route 13, where just the night before another crash sent six people to the hospital.  He crafted a sign "Caution. Thirteen dead ahead," now embedded near the entrance to the ramp that leads from Old Route 13 south and crosses over Route 13 north.

headline: One Nation under Hamp is divided
abstract: Kenneth Hampton, leader of the gang 'Hamp's Nation', was arrested for a number of charging involving drug trafficking, possession of illegal firearms, and distributing cocaine.  Along with Hampton, a number of his relatives were arrested around the city for similar charges.  This federal drug bust has claimed to stop a nortoriously dangerous gang that used violence frequently.

headline: Bedford Springs resort proposed
abstract: The Pittsburgh Symphony backed out of its plans to buy The Bedford Springs Hotel. Bedford County commissioners have hired a consultant to help market and sell the hotel.

headline: Casey has 2nd biopsy
abstract: Governor Casey underwent a second heart biopsy yesterdy as a routine check to see wether his body is rejecting the transplanted organ.  Results of the laboratory analysis will not be available until this afternoon.

headline: Gondola for parades imported courtesy of taxpayers' money
abstract: Pennsylvanians are in the restoration business- whether they like it or not- thanks to the state's history-conscious legislature.  Taxpayers are underwriting the costs incurred by the Italian Heritage Society of America in Pittsburgh to restore an imported gondola the society uses in parades and at ethnic festivals.  The cost?  About $30,000, according to the Department of Community Affairs.

headline: Preate caught between position and politics
abstract: During his run for re-election, Democratic PA Representative David Wright was accused by the state attorney general's office of violating ethics laws by awarding state contracts to a company he owned. Though no arrests were made, Attorney General Ernie Preate called a newspaper and advised fellow Republicans to keep the investigation public. He is being accused of using his position to go after Democrats. Preate is under investigation himself by the FBI and Pennsylvania Crime Commission under charges that he solicited campaign contributions from illegal video-poker operators.

headline: Lawmakers tour
abstract: Touring the Gettysburg National Cemetary and the Visitors Center at the Gettysburg National Military Park included many state officials who came to Gettysburg to study the impact of the battlefield on the local economy.

headline: Financing of inmate facilities arranged
abstract: Dauphin County Commissioners voted to sell $20 million worth of bonds raising money to expand their overcrowded county prison and build a larger juvenile detention center. Previously, taxes had also been raised by 19 percent to help foot the bill. Plans include increasing courthouse security, building a new juvenile detention center, adding more beds to the prison with the construction of an addition, and relocating the county's 911 service.

headline: Voting rights appeal
abstract: A Pittsburgh voting-rights group will take its fight for three black-majority districts for City Council to a federal appeals court.  The Citizens Committee for Full and Fair Empowerment has filed a notice that it will appeal a decision issued Aug. 6 by US District Judge Donald E. Ziegler.

headline: The G.O.P. Alternatives
abstract: Republicans in Congress have professed their willingness to work with President Clinton on health care reform.  But a number of Republican plans have also been put forward.  A comparison is give between the Clinton Plan, Chafee Plan, Gramm Plan and the Alternative House Plan.

headline: Schools of thought
abstract: If we are to enjoy another renaissance, the development of a new, regional approach to secondary education is certainly worth thinking about.  By any objective standard, the way things are now organized does not make any sense.

headline: Our express wishes
abstract: The 31st Ward Citizens Council of Pittsburgh has been opposed to the Mon Valley Expressway since 1987.  They have been sincere, vocal and objective, but have been ignored by the Pennsyvania Turnpike Commission.  They have been unable to generate the kind of public debate that they hope may now be commencing.

headline: 'Only the best': Local residents pin on trooper's badge
abstract: Sally A. Worst graduated from her police cadet class and became a state trooper. She was one of only four women in her class.

headline: Block riverboat gambling
abstract: The writer does not believe that riverboat gambling should be passed by the PA Representatives and urges people to contact theirs to stop the legislation. She believes that it does not provide the economic gain or lower taxes that it promises and adds more problems.

headline: Casey picks Adler for judge vacancy
abstract: Louis J. "Larry" Adler of Susquehanna Twp was appointed to  succeed County Judge Herbert A. Schaffner, who was killed in a plane crash.  The appointment must be confirmed by the state Senate.

headline: Good night, Gracie
abstract: Goodnight to the editorial staff as they clean out the barn.  Ross Perot predicted a "giant sucking sound," but little did he know it would be initiated by the Post-Gazette's news organ on Aug. 26 ("Say Good Night Ross").

headline: Preate gets more press as no show
abstract: Eight of the 12 candidates for governor showed up at a conference sponsored by the Pennsylvania Newspaper Publishers Association last Friday.  But journalists were most curious about who didn’t show up, particularly Ernie Preate Jr.

headline: Park to showcase history, beauty
abstract: A plan to create an Oil Region Heritage Park in Venango and Crawford counties includes proposals for a "living history" museum and boat rides on the Allegheny River.  The park would showcase the history and natural beauty of the Allegheny River and Oil Creek valleys.

headline: Fired agent sues Preate, attorney general's aides
abstract: Robert E. McCormack, an agent who was fired from the state attorney general's office, has filed a multimillion-dollar civil racketeering lawsuit against top officials in the office, claiming he was dismissed for trying to enforce the law in an office that didn't want that.

headline: 'We need resources'
abstract: Nelson Mandela, the leader of the African National Congress collected much as Philadelpia shuttled, fed, photographed and applauded him.  He also left much behind.  In his visit, Mandela skillfully laid the groundwork for a continuing city effort to bring to his long-oppressed people the power they have so long waited to regain.

headline: The One That Got Away
abstract: New York Senator Michael Tully, Jr.'s attempt to attach a last minute Medicaid reimbursement plan to a Federal-State grant matching program for ailing hospitals was met with immediate resistance from the New York Assembly. In the last minute passage of bills, the New York Assembly passed one bill while the New York Senate passed another; the NY Legislature adjourned and left the hospitals with nothing.

headline: Schools seek ways to make up days
abstract: Due to the severe winter weather there have been many school days missed by students at local schools.  The school districts are looking for ways to make up the days so that they meet the 180 day requirement set by the state.

headline: Pa. could lose millions of dollars for highways under Gore plan
abstract: A four-line proposal buried in an appendix to Vice President Al Gore's plan to streamline the government has alarmed Pennsylvania lawmakers, who fear it could cost the state millions of dollars in federal highway money.

headline: PA rape counselors to help in Belgrade
abstract: Rape crisis counselors from Pennsylvania plan to travel to the Serbain capital of Belgrade in March to teach volunteers how to counsel rape victims.  Kathryn Geller Myers, a spokeswoman for the Pennsylvania Coalition Against Rape, said counselors had to be taught sensitivity and the importance of telling rape vicitms they should not blame themselves for the crime.

headline: British Airways may seek smaller stake
abstract: British Airways is attempting to buy 25 percent of USAir.

headline: Casey says he's ready to go home
abstract: If things go as he hopes, Governor Casey will leave the hospital this week and return to Harrisburg.  No date has been set, but the governor said he is looking forward to leaving the hospital, where he has been for six weeks since receiving a new heart and liver.

headline: Goodling bill recommends cut in support to U.N. opponents
abstract: U.S. representative William Goodling introduced a bill that would cut all U.S. economic support funds and military education, training and financing to countries routinely voting against the U.S. position. If the law was in place this year, the U.S. would have cut $241.4 million in security assistance to 48 countries.

headline: Preate poll shows Singel, Preate leading
abstract: Republican Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr., who last month flew across the state to announce that he is thinking seriously about running for governor, released snippets of a poll that he had commissioned to assess his chances.  The poll showed Preate as the front-runner in the Republican gubernatorial primary and Democratic Lt. Governor Mark Singel would be ahead in his respective party.

headline: Plowing state roads proved very costly
abstract: The Blizzard of '93 left a big expense for the local governments.  They are hoping that the federal government will reemberse them for the funds spent for the plowing, some of which were more than their entire winter budget.

headline: Fired officers win suit
abstract: Clearing three of four Westmoreland County Commissioners, a jury awarded punitive damages to two North Huntingdon officers who claimed they were fired after disability leaves and disagreements with Police Chief Charles Henaghan. The township claimed the officers dismissal was due to unsatisfactory evaluations by the Chief, however in a video, Thomas Krause, the convicted commissioner, referred to the officers as useless.

headline: Wofford confounds activists on both sides of abortion issue
abstract: While U.S. Senator Harris Wofford believes women have the right to an abortion, he voted against a bill that would include abortions under health care coverage.  This angered many pro-choice Democrats. He said, however, he would work to add amendments to the bill on the Senate floor in order to make it similar to Pennsylvania's Abortion Control Act.

headline: The only choice for patients at health centers: Patience
abstract: The patients are tired of waiting, some for up to two hours, for their medication from state health centers.  Rendell, as part of his budget balancing package, has proposed to privatize one of the health center and use the staff from that one to fill in gaps in the other facilities.

headline: Senate committee approves New Bolton Center funds
abstract: Funds for the University of Pennsylvania's New Bolton Center were part of a package approved by the PA Senate Appropriations Committee to send the $73.5 million in funding for private universities in the 1993-1994 state budget before the full PA Senate.  The article lists which private schools are affected by the package.

headline: Paving around poles absurd
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation decided to widen and repave Claremont Road due to increased traffic.  The Pennsylvania Power & Light Co. was told to move the poles on the side of the road to allow for it to be widened.  However, it failed to do so in time, and the contractor widened the road around the poles so that the poles are now in eight feet away from the edge of the road.  The person writing the opinion piece criticizes both the PA Department of Transportation and the PP & L for allowing this to happen.

headline: Parents can get help for truants
abstract: An advertisement that tells parents having problems with truant children are told to call members in the school district or call for a copy of the Philadelphia Citizens for Children and Youth report.

headline: Casey glad Mack will stay in Pa.
abstract: PA Governor Casey is happy he was able to keep Mack Trucks Inc. in Pennsylvania; he had to reach into the state's pockets for 9.15 million in state financing to keep the Allentown-based truck making company here. The company employs 2000 Pennsylvanians.

headline: Casey says Pa.'s finances healthy
abstract: Gov. Casey, in his annual State of the Commonwealth address, yesterday said that the recession seemed to be ending and that the state's finances seemed to be heading in the right direction.  Is speech was impassionate and his opponents said it was what they expected from such a lame duck governor.  He proposed no new major ideas, but simply ran of statistics of the economy and rhetoric of how it has improved.

headline: GOP adds amendments to House bill
abstract: Republicans pushed a measure through the PA House to cut off aid to 40,000 able-bodied welfare recipients and Democrats warned that the amendment was too harsh.  The original bill won bipartisan support to be passed through.  PA House Republican Leader Matthew Ryan said that they should discontinue welfare to those who are able-bodied, which would move PA welfare closer to how it was chartered under former PA Governor Thornburgh.

headline: Preate seeking governorship
abstract: State Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. told a group of Berks County Republicans he is running for governor and will battle any obstacles, such as lack of funds or attacks on his character, to get there.

headline: PSFS executive suite is just a memory
abstract: The celebrated 33rd floor of the PSFS building is empty, its modern furnishings are now in storage.  The building is a National Historic Landmark and the furniture may be subject to the same treatment as the buildling, meaning it can not be destoryed and must stay with the building.

headline: Proposal would ban smoking in cars with kids
abstract: Rep. Peter J. Dale announced a proposal yesterday that would change state law to prohibit smoking in a car with a minor under 16 in the car.  The penalty would be a $50 fine.  The ACLU says its an invasion of privacy and disrespecting the parent-child relationship.  The Tobacco Institute agrees with the ACLU and says 'it borders so closly on a police state'.

headline: Woman wins bias complaint with marshals
abstract: The US Marshals Service has agreed to pay $37,400 in back wages and legal fees to a woman whose discrimination complaint has jeopardized the reappointment of US Marshal Eugene V. Marzullo to a fourth term.

headline: Under Clinton Health Plan, All Employers Would Pay
abstract: President Clinton health advisers have decided that most of that burden should fall to employers, a senior White House official said. The administration plans to propose that all employers pay part of their employees health coverage Officials have estimated that it would cost $30 billion to $90 billing to cover the 37 million uninsured. Other tax schemes are being considered to help as well.

headline: Shame on the school board
abstract: The content, tone and unprofessional character of the Upper St. Clair school board's "Negotiations Update" is appalling. Not everyone in the community supports the corporate-business approach that the board has taken in the negotiation.  There are those of us who can do without the ribbons, banners, loaded and biased surveys, picketing, honking and polemical propeganda.

headline: Pursue airport road project
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation didn't approve funding for a road that was to be built near the Wilkes-Barre-Scranton International Airport.  The editorial board feels this is a mistake, because it would help the economy of the area,  and they support the airport's plans to pursue state funding for the project.

headline: Parole officer was struck down while doing his job
abstract: Police officer shot allegedly by Dodson in self defense after Dodson pointed a gun at two Postal Inspection Service investigators who had come to question him.  After a breif scuffle Dodson shot officer Ed Jones in the shoulder.

headline: Business fueled by employee incentives
abstract: Across the country companies are moving towards profit-sharing schemes where employees can get a bonus based on performance.

headline: Casey wishes Clinton the best
abstract: Casey claims he is still friends with Clinton dispite the fact that they havn't spoken since April when Casey choose not to endorse Clinton in the Democratic primary for president.  Casey asked to speak at the Democractic National Convention about his pro-life stance and was rejected by the Clinton advisors and replaced with an nemiesis Republican who was pro-choice.  Since then Casey has avoided the Clintons while they were campaigning in P.A.

headline: GOP chief: Clinton plan could boost Republicans
abstract: Clinton's tax increase gives the GOP a great oppurnity to rebound after losing the elections.

headline: Preate Shows He Has a Sense of Humor
abstract: PA Attorney General Ernie Preate showed that he still had a sense of humor as he was roasted by six persons at a Scranton Kiwanis Club program. The probe of Preate's campaign expenses by the crime commission provided much of material for the jokes.

headline: PUC delays Gettysburg Railroad ruling
abstract: Just when it seemed a done deal, the state Public Utilities Commission has once again delayed a final ruling on Gettysburg Railroad's re-locating a storage building closer to the battlefield.

headline: PUC aims to combat drugs by phone
abstract: John Hanger, a commissioner of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, says he will do what is necessary to help police departments that are fighting the selling of drugs over payphones. A law was passed that mandated two-way payphone service, but the PUC has pushed for exceptions that allow either the removal of a payphone or a conversion to one-way service if necessary to fight drug sales.

headline: Writings imperil Justice selection
abstract: The Clinton administration is facing a potential divisive confirmation battle over C. Lani Guinier, its choice to head the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division because of law review articles she wrote expressing what critics contend are radical views on civil rights enforcement. Guinier is a University of Pennsylvania law professor and veteran voting-rights litigator for the NAACP.

headline: The science of health
abstract: Strong school health-education program will benefit our children, not tear the community apart, by teaching them ways to stay healthy and providing them information on a variety of illnesses.

headline: Smaller budgets, bigger classes
abstract: Francesca Karpel thinks the public schools her children attend in northern California are just fine.  But she's convinced they won't stay that way if voters approve Proposition 174, giving parents $2,600 in tax money to send their kids to private or religious schools.  "We'll lose at least 10% of our budget, and class size will balloon by five to seven children per class," she says.

headline: PEL Recovery Plan
abstract: Cartoon of a car marked 'commuter tax opposition driving off the edge of an unfinished bridge.  The bridge has a sign pointing forward (off the bridge) that reads 'PEL recovery plan'.

headline: PG reporting of violence at football playoff game is biased
abstract: Similar stories between riots at football games made very different headlines though the situations were quite similar.  The story of the game between Peabody and Westinghouse made front page.  The game between North Hills and North Allegheny, however, was limited to a two-inch spot on the front of the Region section, probably because no reporters were injured at that game.  If the Post-Gazette is going to report similar stories, then it should do so without bias.

headline: Business group backs NAFTA
abstract: The Pennsylvania Business Roundtable, which represents senor executives of 40 major corporations that employ about 220,000 in the state, has attacked the notion that jobs will be lost to low-wage countries under the North American Free Trade Agreement Act, claiming that there are numerous benefits of the agreement.

headline: Casey, Singel join foes of NAFTA
abstract: Governor Robert Casey and acting Governor Mark Singel have joined a growing legion of Democrats and labor leaders in the state in taking a stand against the North American Free Trade Agreement.

headline: GOP governor hopeful talks to police here about crime
abstract: Republican state Senator Mike Fisher is making crime an issue right from the start of his 1994 gubernatorial campaign.  "The number one issue on the minds of the people is jobs and the economy," Fisher said in Lancaster before a law-and-order crowd.  "But the issue that falls right behind that is safe streets in Pennsylvania."

headline: Preate wants judge to reconsider ruling on out of state lottery sales
abstract: U.S. District Judge Sylvia Rambo ruled that a Pennsylvania law banning out-of-state lottery sales was unconstitutional.  PA Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. asked the federal judge to reconsider her ruling.

headline: Reed unveils controversial statue
abstract: Mayor Reed of Harrisburg unveiled a statute by Boris Blai that is now being displayed in Harrisburg Reservoir Park.  It has incited controversy since it is a statute of a nude woman.  The statute is part of an effort by the city to improve the park; they also planted over 70,000 plants, trees, and flowers. Future improvements to the park will include the construction of a nature center, park ranger station and an observation tower, as well as the expansion of the children's playground.

headline: Questioning focuses on job performance in harassment trial
abstract: Attorney Kathleen Frederick appeared to be firm and direct Tuesday as she responded to defense questions about her mental stability, professional competence and sex life.  Frederick is suing the Pittsburgh-based law firm of Reed, Smith, Shaw and McClay for sexual harassment.  She claims to have been fired in 1990 after ending a reluctant sexual relationship with an influential partner in the firm's Philadelphia office.

headline: Wuerl suit appalling
abstract: It is appalling that some are suing Bishop Donald Wuerl for closing the churches.  How ironic that the Constitution of the United States mandates separation of church and state and the state is now being petitioned to intercede between Catholics and the bishop.

headline: The wrong impression
abstract: In the recent series "Medication Errors" the entire story is not told.  Reporting that errors are running rampant with little or no corrective actions is irresponsible.  To imply the entire medical profession is careless is equally unfair.  Medication errors are rare.

headline: Special at the diners
abstract: A public television special documentary looks at diners in central Pennsylvania. Some of the diners include the East and West Shore Diners, Red's in Lewistown, Ye Old College Diner in State College, and Peg and Bill's in Williamsport.

headline: PennDOT right: Refuse to fund others' errors
abstract: PennDOT has a secret plan to save taxpayers hundreds of thousands of dollars.  The agency will not install a traffic light or other safegurads at the Route 13 ramp because "accidents are caused by driver error."  Perhaps PennDOT is suggesting that traffic lights are too expensive to install or maintain.

headline: Phila to celebrate Constitution signing
abstract: Philadelphia, the birthplace of the US Constitution 206 years ago today, this morning will again play a unique national role- this time launching the first-ever "Sea to Shining Sea" celebration of the signing of the Constitution.

headline: Business leaders press for help in export market
abstract: Business leaders want more help from the state government to promote international commerce in Pennsylvania.  Under the proposal by the House Business and Economic Development Committee the state would provide grants to establish centers to help businesses of 250 or fewer employees wishing to enter exporting.

headline: Casey's counsel resigns his position
abstract: James Haggerty has submitted his resignation, effective June 15, as Governor Casey's general counsel. Haggerty told Casey he was doing because he wanted to spend more time with his family and his private life and career. Casey named Richard Spiegelman, executive deputy general counsel, to replace Haggerty when the resignation takes effect.

headline: GOP group eyes issues
abstract: Key republicans met yesterday at the Majority Coalition which began a series of national hearings, spearheaded by US Senator Arlen Spector; the goal is to broaden the parties appeal. The coalition believes the Republican Party should stand for lower taxes and take no positions on social issues such as abortion and homosexuality. They are trying to reach out to women, labor and minorities.

headline: President Clinton Resurrects Candidate Clinton and His Proposals for a ' New Democrat' Agenda
abstract: The Clinton administration is increasingly turning back to the "New Democrat" ideas of candidate Clinton. Legislative proposals to fashion these ideas into reality are rapidly moving to the surface. The difficulty of turning a New Democrat agenda into reality is best illustrated in welfare reform, which is one of the most controversial and complicated proposals on the agenda.

headline: Save Norristown dam
abstract: The board of governors of the Norristown Boat Club express concern over the fate of the Barbadoes dam in Norristown.  Removal of the dam would have a devastating effect on the river, essentially ruining it for fishing and boating related activities.  And it could have a severe impact on property values along the river.

headline: Rabe F. Marsh Jr., 87, retired federal judge
abstract: Retired US District Senior Judge Rabe F. Marsh Junior died of heart failure. Appointed by President Truman, the former Westmoreland Attorney General, County Sports Hall of Fame inductee, and award recipient of the Westmoreland County Bar Association, was 87. Rabe Jr. presided over cases including Frank Mazzei, former PA Representative extortionist, crime boss John LaRocca, and Communist Party leader Steve Nelson.

headline: null
abstract: Political cartoon of a man on an operating table covered by a blanket reading  "Health Care", while incompetent surgeons (one wearing a hat that says "PA", look over him.  A caption reads, "Alright.. who's got the manual?" It seems to be criticizing health care in Pennsylvania.

headline: To keep their privacy, they run the risk of pregnancy
abstract: Many young women are so afraid of the pelvic examination that they risk getting pregnant- and sometimes do- before getting up the nerve to submit to the innocuous, albeit uncomfortable, procedure.  The problem led the Family Planning Council of Southeastern Pennsylvania to study whether medical harm would result from allowing teenagers to start the pill, but postpone the exam.  The results were so positive that the federal Food and Drug Administration endorsed the approach.

headline: Special ed funds passed by house
abstract: The House members voted 168-32 for legislation that provides the mechanism to distribue special education fudning to the 501 public school districts by changing the formula to give less money to the Pittsburgh school district as well as the Education Department and more to other schools.

headline: PennDot video on blizzard response called a snow job
abstract: In March, a blizzard dumped more than 12 incehes of snow on area roads, and the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation left some Lower Bucks residents stranded for four days.  But a new videotape produced by PennDot explains: "In everything in life, someone is going to be first and someone is going to be last.  The same is true when it comes to plowing the roads."  But according to state Representative Matt Wright, "That's the sugercoated version."

headline: Phila. Crime rate drops for 3rd year
abstract: Philadelphia police commissioner Richard Neal credited the work of the city's police officers and cooperation with other agencies including the Federal Bureau of Investigations and the District Attorney's Office for the 11 percent decrease in crime from 1992 to 1993.
