The suits contend that leading drugmakers are charging independent drugstores and chains more than prices paid by hospitals, health maintenance organizations and mail-order sellers. A spokesman for the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America said that prices were set in the marketplace.

headline: Don't mislead public about waste site
abstract: The editorial board says that Pennsylvania is now required to house a low-level radioactive waste disposal facility somewhere in the state, but the selection process should be free of the type of misleading statements made recently by a representative of the firm that will select a site. Matt Shields of the Chem-Nuclear Systems Inc. firm charged with building the facility, told a Bedford County audience that a small does of radioactive exposure "jump starts your immune system." The editorial board says that PA must except the facility somewhere in the state and live with it, but asks that no one say that "a dose a day is good for anyone."

headline: Cost hard to estimate for plans
abstract: Pennsylvania has several three strike bills in congress. They all result in life without parole but they differ in crimes involved, innmates added due to the crimes and costs. The bills are being sponsored by various congressmen.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; Food Stamp Payment
abstract: For a two-person family, between $143 and $206 is allotted per month in food stamps. For Aid to Families with Dependent Children, the maximum for a 3 or 4 member family is $275 or $327 per month respectively.

headline: As governor's race closes, candidates stop in strongholds
abstract: As PA GOP gubernatorial candidate Tom Ridge campaigned with a heavy anti-government, anti-tax emphasis in central PA, Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel was appealing to the Democratic base in and around Scranton, Wilkes-barre, and Philadelphia. Despite trailing in the polls, Singel attempted to derive media attention in these areas, even using humor, urging Democrats to bring friends and pets to the polls in order to get the vote out.

headline: Legislators sponsor election reform bill
abstract: Two members of the PA House sponsored a bill that would not let legislators vote on their own contested elections, that if there are open seats special elections would be held quickly, and special election winners who have been certified begin working right away.

headline: Voter became Singel-minded, after we praised Ridge with faint damns
abstract: A letter writer calls the Philadelphia Daily News's "underwhelming endorsement of Tom Ridge for governor" a "coin-flipping editorial collaboration with the Inquirer...you seem to think it is good journalism to have the city's two big newspapers endorse opposing candidates" The letter writer adds that Ridge is dishonest and that he will vote for Singel over Ridge.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Noteworthy
abstract: The PA Health Department's Youth Against Tobacco Campaign had 8,500 kids vow to not smoke at the Farm Show.

headline: Fayette eleventh in recycling
abstract: In a report by the PA Department of Environmental Resources for the State Legislature, it ws discovered that Fayette County, said director of Fayette County Solid Waste Management Vincent Vicites, has the 11th best recycling participant percentage out of 67 counties. In the 10-County Southwestern region of PA, Fayette County has generated the highest percentage of the waste stream recycled at 20.7 percent.

headline: Council demands curfew 'impact study'
abstract: Pittsburgh's City Council is already debating the introduction of Mayor Murphy youth curfew bill. The council gave unanimous approval to Council President Jim Ferlo's bill requiring the mayor to do an "impact study" on the effects of a nighttime curfew for youths. The council also wants to know what effect is projected on city police recourses. The Council appears to be divided on the curfew concept.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; Forcing welfare moms to work; Critics hit plan
abstract: David Kass of the Children's Defense Fund worries about Learnfare, a pilot program in PA designed to deny Aid to Families with Dependent Children unless their children have good attendance at school. Cathy Dishman, a mom on welfare, says it is difficult for kids to go to school when they realize they are different. President Clinton's new reforms include denying assistance to families on welfare for 5 plus years, denying cash assistance after 2 years, and denying additional aid to mother's who have more kids on welfare.

headline: As His Term Winds Down, Casey Refuses To Let Up
abstract: Despite only a few weeks left as PA Governor, Robert Casey leaves Harrisburg by plane and attends a ground breaking ceremony at the site of his proposed American Street Corridor Industrial Park, where he mentions the funding his administration provided. Taking several interviews, Casey then speaks at a luncheon for Sheet Metal Workers Local 19. Back in Harrisburg, Casey has a personal training session, as he is recovering from transplant surgery. He caps the day with a dinner for the PA Council of Churches.

headline: Let's start lying to the vote wizards
abstract: Voter turnout was low in yesterdays primary because there was nothing to get excited about.

headline: Voter turn-off helping GOP
abstract: Most political scientists, including former president of the American Political Science Association Charles Jones, expect low turnout at the polls during elections, driven by President Clinton's approval ratings, campaign ads, and disinterest. Curtis Gans of the Committee for the Study of the American Electorate at American University, believes Democrats may have a stronger showing if voters get scared of the prospect of Republican control of both Houses, as the trend indicates.

headline: Is Gephardt bill a dessert topping or floor cleaner?
abstract: U.S. Representative Richard Gephardt's health care reform bill highlights the inherent contradiction of government meddling in the health care business. The provision adds a third major section to Medicare and it has nothing to do with the elderly. The bill illogical and should not get passed.

headline: E.P.A. Affirms Health Dangers from Dioxin
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency has affirmed the health dangers from exposure to the chemical dioxin, but hasn't declared it a known cause of cancer in people.

headline: Court order halts pay for Larsen
abstract: The Court of Judicial Discipline ruled that PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larson will be suspended without pay because he was found guilty of using employees to obtain prescription drugs.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; Pennsylvania children in poverty
abstract: Although the total number of children in PA has dropped by 300,000, the number living in poverty has grown by over 6,000. In 1979, there were approximately 425,000 living in poverty. In 1989 however, the number rose to over 432,000.

headline: As the elections near, Democrats return to black base for support
abstract: Worried about rejection in the forthcoming election, the Democratic Party is returning to an old standby: black voters. Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson, just two months removed from saying he might run against President Clinton, has been out campaigning for the Democratic National Committee to get out the black, urban, and labor vote. A recent survey has only a core group of blacks over 50 still considered to be solid for Democrats.

headline: Letters To The Editor: Beware of easy money
abstract: State and municipal politicians must raise revenue for the city, but are confronted by residents who won't accept higher taxes. And higher taxes make it more difficult to be re-elected. The survey by Hospitality Franchise Systems soothed politicians fears with results showing residents support riverboat gambling, however this citizen feels if something is too good to be true, it probably is. New Jersey afterall was hit by the highest tax hike in its history after collecting casino revenue.

headline: Voting guide for gays
abstract: The League of Gay and Lesbian Voters based in Pittsburgh did not endorse any candidates but rated the candidates on issues of interests to gays in a guide published and distributed throughout the state.  In the race for governor, Democrat PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel and Republican US Congressman Tom Ridge both got high marks, while in the Senate race Democrat US Senator Harris Wofford got high ratings where Republican challenger Rick Santorum did not.

headline: Let's get universal health care  before granting the right to die
abstract: Art Caplan, the director of the Center for Bioethics at the University of Pennsylvania, discusses how the efforts for universal health care have died but the drive for legalizing euthanasia continues. On November 8, the citizens of Oregon will have the right to vote on a bill that would legalize euthanasia. In response to this, Caplan believes that a society that is not ready to offer a decent package of health care to all its citizens is not ready to offer them a death prescription.

headline: E.P.A. urges compromise on Auto pollution
abstract: Top officials of the US Environmental Protection Agency urged state officials and leaders of the auto industry to reach a new national compromise on tailpipe pollution standards in the next few weeks. They are proposing tough auto emission standards.

headline: Court: 'No" is not enough in rape cases
abstract: The PA Supreme Court ruled that for someone to be convicted of rape, there must have been "forcible compulsion" and victims just saying "no" does not count.  Victim counselors are upset at the ruling.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; Poverty
abstract: A pie graph of 1990 reveals 18 percent of America's full-time workers who had a family of four still did not make enough money to keep their family out of poverty. 13.5 percent of Americans live in poverty, including 11 percent of Pennsylvanians. In PA, 42 percent of females who head households and 58 percent of those with children under five live in poverty.

headline: At last, Congress gets to be a TV director
abstract: In Congress, C-Span can no longer air wide-angle camera shots of the chambers during "secials orders," only letting viewers see the Congressmen speaking, but not the presence or absence of an audience.

headline: Letters To The Editor; A bad sign of the times
abstract: President of the Realtors Association of Metropolitan Pittsburgh, May Lynne Deets, is disappointed by city Planning Commission and Chairman Tom Armstrong and Historic Review Commission Chairman John DeSantis expectation that the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette comply with proposed legislation limiting advertising signs on buildings.

headline: Vulnerable Clinton to stress cooperation
abstract: After winning a majority in the US House and Senate yesterday, President Clinton is left vulnerable, his agenda subject to change as he tries to practice bipartisan politics. No doubt Clinton will likely face competition from within his own party for the Democratic nomination the 1996 elections. The mood of voters seems to be a repudiation of Clinton and his policies, though the White House denies this observation.

headline: Letters to the Editor
abstract: Barbara Coombs Lee, Chief Petitioner of Oregon Right to Die for the Oregon Death with Dignity Act, Measure 16, feels Dr. Kass' concern that the act garnts physicians undue power is unwarranted. The patient, not the doctor, Lee argues, retains the right to determine how much suffering they want to endure and allows the patient to request aid from a physician.

headline: Eco-tip
abstract: The pesticides on some flea collars finds effectiveness in permanent nerve damage. The pet absorbs the chemical into its system until its tissue reeks of the toxin, paralyzing the bugs. Adding brewer's ear and garlic to pet food works just as well. The source is listed as 50 Simple Things You Can Do to Save the Earth.

headline: Crime is state's 2nd worst problem, survey finds
abstract: The results of the crime victimization survey were released and some of the results show that 1 in 3 people do not want to be out alone at night, 4 of 10 said they have a gun, and 1 in 12 has been a crime victim in six months.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; State may have answer in part; Outlay triples in 6 years but can't match demand
abstract: Though provided with federal funds to fulfill the requirement of providing job assistance programs to recipients of Aid to Families with Dependent Children under PA Governor Casey, money for New Directions has gone to other companies for out-sourcing. An ex-official noted the Legislature must extend funds to counties, where caseworkers are currently understaffed. New Directions is not aggressive in recruiting clients, meeting the federal requirement of 20 percent participantion statewide by welfare recipients.

headline: At this time I would like to introduce this nation's most powerful leader. . .
abstract: Cartoon shows President Bill Clinton being introduced at a conference or meeting by the host who says, "At this time I would like to introduce this nation's most powerful leader."  President Clinton has a confused look on his face and thinks to himself, "Hillary's here?" implying Hillary Clinton, the first lady, is the most powerful leader in the nation and President Clinton will do what she says to do.

headline: Letters:  Hafer's reform plan
abstract: Letter to editor from PA Auditor General Barbara Hafer comments on article that stated she has criticized lack of accountability in regard to walking-around money.  Hafer states she wants to inform readers that she has also been pushing for reform package calling for abolition of walking-around money and ability to independently audit legislative and judicial branches of PA government.  Hafer states she hopes that those not connected to PA government will no longer be able to distribute state money and that secret PA government spending will come to end.

headline: Wage inflation barometer soars
abstract: Wage inflation shot up at the fastest pace in three years during the first quarter. The Clinton administration insists that this is an aberration not a hint of spiraling prices.

headline: Letters to the Editor; Doctor-Assisted Suicide Gives Patient 'Freedom'
abstract: A citizen opposes the editorial page written by Dr. Leon Kass supporting the view that Oregon had given physicians the frightful license to prescribe death in assisting suicides by a ballot referendum. The citizen points out that the advance of modern medicine now allows docters to keep patients alive far beyond their capacity of suffering or necessity. She counters that allowing a patient to starve to death is less humane than actively ending a human life if the patient so desires.

headline: Emission retreat brings lawsuit
abstract: The PA Legislature's tabling of the federally mandated Clean Air Act until a system similar to the hybrid model in California can be adopted, prompted the Philadelphia Clean Air Council to sue in a US District Court. Joseph Minot, executive council director, is attempting to force the US Environmental Protection Agency into enforcing the act over the PA Department of Transportation. PA Governor Casey lashed out at EPA regional administrator Peter Kostmayer for backing off on the mandate.

headline: Crime report draws local ire
abstract: State and local officials do not agree with a study by the American Legislative Exchange Council, concluding tougher sentences and more prisons will deter violent crime. PA Department of Corrections spokesman Ben Livingood cites increases in statistics to prove his point, while Westmoreland County Judge Debra Pezze says answers are in creative sentencing approaches, advocated by Deputy Superintendent of the PA Correctional Institution Neal Mechling. Policeman Joe Nixon agrees.

headline: Welfare: A View From the Inside; State may have answer in part; Too often traning leads to the low-paying jobs
abstract: The nature of the jobs for which welfare recipients are trained, and the strategy to move them off welfare is in question. Carmella Perkins is suing the PA Department of Public Welfare, alleging it thwarted her attempts to move off welfare by failing to provide assistance for schooling. As a low-paid secretary, Perkins may be caught in the "cycle," the 40 percent of those who return to welfare within a year of leaving the program, LaDonna Pavetti of the Urban Institute says.

headline: Audit is a political weapon
abstract: PA State Auditor General Barbara Hafer has questioned the independence and objectivity of the Big Six accounting firm which audited her department, citing criticisms of the way the audit was conducted. Hafer writes t the Butler Eagle to say that she believes the audit report of her office was a political document strongly influenced by the governor's office and possible exaggerated.

headline: Letters; Readers divided over national as well as local races
abstract: A citizen criticizes the public for being duped by the media in the race between Dianne Feinstein and Michael Huffington in California. Another is against US Senator Harris Wofford's re-election to US Senate because he failed to institute health care reform. Two citizens find PA representative Rick Santorum unworthy of election to US Senate based on ties to the National Rifle Association and comments regarding the National Service Corps.

headline: Waiting, then celebrating.
abstract: A photo of Governor-elect Tom Ridge and Brett Schweiker, 6, captures the celebration of the news of Ridge's election victory just before 11 p.m. Tuesday night on the 8th floor of the Avalon Hotel in Erie, PA. Minutes later, Brett's father, Lieutenant Governor-elect Mark Schweiker and Ridge went down to their victory party in the hotel ballroom.

headline: Letters to the Editor; When is an Embryo Human?
abstract: A biologist and pharmacuetical consultant with a PhD thinks Father Richard John Neuhaus needs to keep religion out of science. F.M. Sturtevant details the process of implantation up to appearance of human life in embryo form, which Sturtevant says is a 14 day period. The response by Neuhaus was prompted by the release of a recommendation by the National Institutes of Health which advocated research on the pre-embryo prior to the 14th day.

headline: Emissions program attacked
abstract: local Libertarians are hoping that the issue of auto emissions will help get them into power this November. They are questioning the newly passed federal Clean Air Act which will make counties across the country adhere to stricter auto emissions standards. They question the data the US Environmental Protection Agency used in formulating the law.

headline: Crime state's fastest growing issue
abstract: A survey of Pennsylvanias shows that 1 in 4 are afraid to go out alone at night and 1 in 12 had been victims of crime in the last 18 months.  Many people also keep small guns in their homes.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; State may have answer, in part
abstract: PA welfare officials praise the program instituted by PA Governor Robert P. Casey, providing welfare recipients with job training. State Secretary of Public Welfare Karen Snider calls New Directions a national model,  though officials admit that many graduates continue receiving welfare, and getting a job does not mean recipients will stay employed. New Directions serves only 1 in 5 recipients of Aid to Families with Dependent Children, too meagerly staffed to make a huge impact at the county level.

headline: Awaiting Rendell's response
abstract: Facing negative publicity over the Philadelphia's 911 system's inadequate response to multiple calls of rioting, Mayor Ed Rendell said a timetable for investigation would be revealed on the Today show. City Councilman Brian O'Neill, representing the Fox Chase neighborhood, is invited to attend made suggestions regarding the time table and disciplinary action. Ronald Mauldin, head of the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees Local 1637 said workers were scapegoats.

headline: Levering joins House Republicans in signing of 'contract with America'
abstract: Fred Levering, a candidate for the 6th Congressional District has joined his Republican collegues in signing the Contract with America. The document is a pledge, that states if the Republicans take control of the U.S. House after the November general election, taxes will be lowered, an inititation of term limits will be done, a balanced budget amendment will be produced, and welfare reform will be proposed within the first 100 days of taking office.

headline: Walker, Gekas win praise as cost-cutters
abstract: The Conservative National Taxpayers Union analyzed 895 U.S. House bills sponsored during 1993 and revealed that U.S.Representatives Robert S.Walker and George Gekas ranked 3rd and 4th, respectively, as the members who proposed more spending cuts than spending that year.

headline: Lose the insurers
abstract: A letter writer says that if the US switched to a single-payer health care system like in Canada, administrative costs could drop from about 25 percent to about 13 percent. The writer says the insurance industry, which "does not provide on iota of health-care service, needs to be eliminated to enable efficient administration of health care to all Americans."

headline: Emissions tester will halt training
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency's Peter Kostmayer held off on sanctioning PA for a 3 month delay in implementing mandatory central emissions testing, which could mean loss of federal highway funds and expansion obstacles for pollutant companies. Central tests inconvenience motorists, the Legislature ruled, however a recent attempt by California to implement a hybrid system involving local repair shopes was more expensive. Envirotest, Inc., test administrator, has halted employee training.

headline: CYS is committed to protecting children, but cannot shoulder all blame for failures
abstract: Melvin Pirchesky and Barbara K. Shore of Allegheny County Children and Youth Services,  Advisory Board Chairperson and Vice Chairperson respectively, responds to claims by the Post-Gazette that the organization cannot honestly review and learn from its own mistakes. They also state that the "no comment" given to the Post-Gazette was not "an unnecessarily thick cloak of secrecy meant to hide deficiencies" but was just in compliance with PA laws forbidding the agency to talk about specific facts surrounding individual cases. Pirchesky and Shore add that "the epidemic of child abuse and child neglect is not caused" by the Children and Youth Services, and they invite the Post-Gazette to help them become the solution.

headline: Welfare: A View From the Inside; State may have answer, in part; Advocates see a need to build on past success
abstract: Ronald Shell, executive director of Pennsylvania Partnerships for Children is one of many who acknowledged progress has been made concerning welfare, but the state and federal government could do more. It is up to Governor-elect Tom Ridge to extend the PA welfare program New Directions to adequately staff county offices. Thus far, neither the state nor the federal government have prioritized spending to make the Family Support Act effective.

headline: Bad votes extended to the booth
abstract: The paper has uncovered ballot fraud in the 2nd district other than by absentee ballot.  This time votes were cast on machines in the 6th Division of the 42nd Ward by people who were out of the country, out of the district, or dead.  Documents show non-matching signatures.  Election official wrong doing can be traced to Linda Papanikolaou, Fani Papanikolau, and Ethel Kaplan.  Some voters are bringing a lawsuit to the judge handling the 2nd district case.

headline: Liberal, conservative
abstract: Neither US Senator from Pennsylvania broke the 50 percent mark in ratings compiled by the American Conservative Union.  Senator Arlen Specter got a 46 percent rating from the American Conservative Union, while Senator Harris Wofford  was scored at 16 percent.  In the House of Representatives, Representative Rick Santorum, Wofford's opponent, received an 81 percent rating and gubernatorial candidate Tom Ridge received a 61 percent rating.

headline: Walkout would join seven others
abstract: If Deer Lakes District teachers strike Wednesday, they will be the 8th district in PA to do so. 3 out of 5 strikes thus far have ended in teachers returning to work without settlement, said Wythe Keever of the PA State Education Association. Westmoreland County's district has enlisted the help of arbitrator Ronald Talarico. Union and school board represetnatives from the Leechburg Area have exchanged propsals on a few remaining issues. Other districts are continuing negotiations as well.

headline: Losing sight on health reform
abstract: The paper believes that health care reform is necessary because it can hurt people and the country.  They see too many without healthcare and rising costs.

headline: End the shoot
abstract: A letter to the editor writer criticizes the pigeon shoots on Labor Day as an "atrocious and barbaric," and singles out PA state representatives Richard Cessar, Richard Olaz, Joseph Petrarca, and Herman Milhalich for voting against banning the pigeon shoot in an effort that got defeated 99-93 on the floor of the PA state House.

headline: DA withdraws Erie drug case
abstract: A women was arrested on charges of possession of drugs. The charges were dropped when it went to court because the judge ruled the arresting officer lacked the probable cause to stop the defendant's vehicle and search her purse.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; State may have answer, in part; With New Directions, state was out in front
abstract: In 1988 when President Reagan signed the Job Opportunities and Basic Skills Training program mandating states provide education, job opportunites, and skills to Aid to Families with Dependent Children recipients, New Directions, was proposed by PA Governor Robert P. Casey. However, the program is understaffed, reaching 20 percent of welfare recipients despite contracting with nonprofits like the Susquehannah Employment & Training Corporation, a study by the American Public Welfare Association revealed.

headline: Ballot fraud is no cause for ridicule
abstract: Walter J. Ruchniewski writes an opinion stating that he is "appalled by Dan Geringer's willingness to print so many untruths and practically condemn the man who fought voter fraud."  Ruchiniewski said that the voters of the 2nd Senatorial District should applaud Senator Bruce Marks for Marks's actions against the absentee ballot scam last year headed by City Commissioner Margaret Tartaglione.

headline: Libertarian tells voters less is more
abstract: Don Ernsberger he libertarian candidate for Senate believes that the Republicans and Democrats don’t' give voters much to choose between. Ernsberger believes that less is more, a smaller amount of government will be much more beneficial.

headline: Waves of Change
abstract: A bar graph shows the changes in gains of US House seats by both major parties from 1894 under Cleveland, to 1992 under Bush. Democrats gained under Truman, Johnson, Nixon, Regan, and Bush, while Republicans gained under Johnson, Carter, Reagan, and Bush as well, though at times more or less significantly than Democrats.

headline: Louisiana Took 'Every Federal Dollar We Could Get Our Hands On'
abstract: Louisiana claimed all state money spent on hospitals, for Medicaid and non-Medicaid patients, under the Medicaid hospital subsidy.  Some of the money was used in drug treatment programs.

headline: Environmental causes languish in this Congress
abstract: There are only a few weeks before Congress adjourns for the year and there are still six important pieces of environmental legislation that are stalled. A lot of these pieces are not expected to pass after the break because Congress will most likely become more conservative in the November elections.

headline: Death penalty For justice, not vengeance
abstract: PA district attorneys want the courts to sign death warrants that the governor has not signed.  The paper argues that the death penalty is not cost effective or a proved deterent.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; The kids might be little but embarrassment isn't
abstract: According to the research organization Child Trends, Inc.,  Aid to Families with Dependent Children kids are more than twice as likely to fail in school and are more likely to have serious behavioral problems. Critics claim the Family Support Act of 1998 failed in addressing the impact of welfare on kids. In PA, the AFDC support levels have not increased in 4 years. Ronald Sell, executive director of PA Partnerships for Children, is alarmed at cuts proposed by Republicans.

headline: Ballot-box justice
abstract: South Africans had been deprived of their right to vote for 300 years and now they understand truly how important it is.

headline: Like Time Pressed Americans everywhere, Desperate Incumbents are shopping by Mail this Election Season: Carville&Rollins-Campaign Outfitters
abstract: The cartoon pokes fun of election campaigns, advertising a mail order catalog called "Carville&Rollins-Campaign Outfitters." Among items listed are a "Fold-O-Porch" for that "down-home feeling" candidates need when making commercials-this way they don't have to travel home. Other items sold are "inflatable extras: fill out that constituency crowd with the diversity that makes America great!" and Flannel shirts, "perfect for that 'Outsider Look' at your district's fall festivals."

headline: Welcome home, Leland?
abstract: The paper believes that it is a continuing sign of corruption when Leland Beloff was unanimously elected Democratic chairman of a South Philadelphia ward.  He was just released from prison for tying city government with the mob and forging absentee ballots.  The paper supports Philadelphia officals like Mayor Rendell for denouncing the move.

headline: Low-income heath care coming
abstract: The Department of Public Welfare is implementing HeathChoice, a healthcare service for Medicaid patients, in six counties in southeast PA provided it has enough bidders.  The Hospital Association of Pennsylvania and the Delaware County Medical Society both oppose this plan because they don't think it has been thought out enough and that patients may be far from doctors.

headline: Environmental group 'nervous' over new site location
abstract: The Sierra Club in North Carolina is unhappy with Chem-Nuclear Systems' plan to put low-level radioactive waste near Raleigh, NC.

headline: Defusing the boob tube
abstract: Steve Connelly of Spruce Run Technologies invented the "C Chip", or "Choice Chip" allowing parents to pick and choose to block programs deemed too violent for kids. The chip is an alternative to legislation proposed in the US House by Edward Markey, whose "V chip", or "Violence Chip" would automatically block violent programs. The National Coalition on Television Violence endorses the C chip because it gives control to consumers, said Vice President Mary Ann Banta.

headline: Welfare: A View From the Inside; Welfare
abstract: 10 percent of the federal budget is spent on welfare. 33 percent of the PA budget is spent on welfare. In PA, 16 percent of the budget goes to Medicaid.

headline: Battles heat up in some city wards
abstract: Philadelphia's 69 Democratic ward leaders are up for election on Tuesday. Many of them face stiff challenges. Don't count them out though, Ward elections can be raucous and unpredictable.

headline: Locked schools are squandered
abstract: New Jersey Senator Bradley sponsored a bill in Congress that would open up schools, specifically gyms, on evenings, weekends, and summers for public use.  The author agrees and believes it would be a positive force in the neighboorhoods.

headline: Welcome to the revolution, Alvin
abstract: Councilman-elect Alvin Stewart is already in contention with Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell. Rendell's plan to cut funding for city services to provide a safety net for 5,000 otherwise homeless men and women angered Stewart, as voters are without representation since the death of former Councilman Herb DeBeary. Stewart agrees with Rendell in keeping people off the streets, however he is skeptical, along with the rest of the nation, how taxes and social programs may be cut while endless prison and military spending ensues.

headline: Managed-care rights proposed
abstract: Member of the PA House of Representatives is introducing House Bill 1866 to reform health care.

headline: EPA maps cleanup of Alsco Park soil
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency is going to put down a rubber coating, sand, soil, and seeding on Alsco Park in Harrison because of the dumping of toxins like lead, arsenic, and DDT.  Atochem will pay much of the $14 million cost.

headline: Delco wants definition in guard benefit fight
abstract: Delaware County is going to appeal to the State Supreme Court for a definition of a "park guard" to determine whether or not they have to pay for park officer's injuries under the heart and lung act.  They say he was a security guard at the time.

headline: Welfare: pay now or pay later
abstract: The author suggests that for fewer women to be collecting welfare they would need better access to publically funded contraceptives and abortions.

headline: Big wins for LoBiondo in 2d District, Andrews in 1st
abstract: Both New Jersey State Assemblyman Frank LoBiondo and Democrat Robert E. Andrews won easy victories over opponents. Shrewd politicking helped LoBiondo, who defied his party in the primary and won a huge victory, seemingly unstoppable. Andrews' landslide victory and moderate to conservative version of the Democratic platform makes him a candidate to keep an eye on, especially for future statewide elections.

headline: Lottery pot takes too long to build
abstract: Pennsylvania needs to increase the lottery prizes on a week to week basis if there is not a winner. Compared to other states Pennsylvania's prize pool is very small.

headline: Wesley wants back on
abstract: Dennis Wesley is asking a US District court to put him on the Democratic Primary ballot until his court challenge is done.  He was taken off when his petitions were circulated by someone who was not registered to vote.

headline: Medicare proposals 'upsetting,' elderly say
abstract: President Clinton proposed Medicare cost savings could prove to be dtrimental to hospitals. Allegheny Valley Hospital is currently reimbursed 91 cents for every dollar if this happens they could lose an extra 24 cents on every dollar.

headline: EPA shouldn't impose sanctions on state
abstract: The editorial board finds it unfair that in the battle between the PA Legislature, Governor Casey, and the US Environmental Protection Agency, the Legislature's refusal to immediately implement federally mandated unfunded central emissions testing, supported by Casey, may result in federal sanctions withholding highway funds from the state. Though Monroe County is not required to implement the program, its bypass would be affected by loss of funds. The board thinks both sides could do better at negotiating.

headline: Dirty talkin'
abstract: The author believes that Lisa DePaulo, a writer for "Philadelphia Magazine," who included Mayor Rendell's sexually suggestive comments to her in a profile for the magazine, was correct in including the comments in the article, but should have been clear in interviews afterwards that she was not actually offended and was bantering with him at the time.

headline: Welfare-plan protest
abstract: A group of people have set up "Caseyville" on the Capitol to protest welfare cuts that will hurt the poor and homeless.

headline: Billy Meehan was a man of his word
abstract: Elliot Curson regrets the fact that the press never got to know the real Billy Meehan who was the late counsel to the Republican Party. He always did the best that he could to help people that came to him in need of help. He was very known and respected in the world of politics; he was a man of his word and never went back on it, after all that was his idea of politics.

headline: Lucyk seeks eight term as state rep.
abstract: Profile and legislative goals of State Representative Ed Lucyk who is seeking reelection.

headline: What Really Bothers Working Women
abstract: A recent study conducted by the U.S. Labor Department and the Courier Times found that salary inequities and high stress are the two issues that irritate the majority of working women in Lower Bucks.

headline: Mental health group eyes unity
abstract: In Westmorland County, mental health and mental retardation services will be centralized under one organization.  This is to allow service options from different agencies to be available to all patients.  The centralization also opens up the county to federal grant money.

headline: EPA: Lead testing ignored
abstract: The US Environmental Protection Agency filed "notices of violation" to 223 water system operators in PA for failing to test for lead and copper during the latter half of 1993.  This was in violation of the federal Clean Drinking Water act that requires the tests because lead and copper in drinking water poses serious health issues.  AMP Incorporated, which received four notices, said the PA Department of Environmental Resources advised them to test during the beginning of 1994 instead of 1993.

headline: DNA test clears suspect in girl's rape
abstract: DNA test results corroborating a victim's identification of the man who raped her, failed to support her claim. After a bizarre citizen arrest, 21-year-old Colin Winterle was jailed for 3 months awaiting DNA results. Winterle maintained innocence, said his lawyer, Jerome H. Mallon. Mimi Rose, head of the district attorney's office, said the evidence speaks for itself, Captain Eileen Bonner of the Police Department's Sex Crimes Unit admitting DNA can go either way in a case.

headline: Where audit findings go far beyond numbers
abstract: PA State Auditor General Barbara Hafer writes to discuss the importance of state audits and how those audits are beneficial to the state. Hafer reveals that her department's previous Single Audit report of federal funds shed light on the PA Department of Public Welfare's weakness in controlling the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP). The report noted a total of $5 million in LIHEAP funds voluntarily returned by vendors. Hafer says people must look beyond the number to understand the audits.

headline: Bitterness remains despite return of teachers
abstract: Officials are hoping that a court agreement that sends Shenandoah Valley School District teachers back to their classrooms will help the troubled district get back on track. Teachers agreed in county court to return to work in compliance with state law that requires strikes to end in time for a district to provide 180 days of education by June 15. Both parties are expecting non-binding arbitration this week to try to settle differences over salary hikes, health-care benefits, and work hours.

headline: Luksik begins TV ads
abstract: Independent gubernatorial candidate Peg Luksik says she will begin television advertising tomorrow on cable television stations throughout the state.

headline: What would James Madison think of Lani Guinier?
abstract: It was sugged that in future elections to give minorities a more fair chance, everyone who votes gets as many votes as there are canidates. For instance if there are 12 canidates running you get 12 votes to allocate however you please. However, this would go directly against the very idea of representative government.

headline: Mother's love beyond measure
abstract: Michelle Mower, a single mother of a child with Schwachman-Diamond syndrome, which keeps her marrow from making blood to fight infections, spent the past 18  months talking to doctors and caring full-time for Jennifer. Yesterday, Mower gave her child a quarter of her liver after a bone marrow transplant failed due to blockages to Jennifer's liver. The surgery is the first performed in the area between a mother and child. Mower's mother worries whether insurance will cover hospital bills.

headline: Expect nuke dump to land in a rural area
abstract: State cosultants will pick three communtiies as potential sites for nuclear tests. One of these sites will eventually become the location for an above-ground waste facility to house contaminated items. This could cause protets and civil dissobedience in the communties picked.

headline: DNA tests clear suspect in rape
abstract: 21 year old Frank Winterle was released from the Philadelphia Industrial Correction Center yesterday after DNA evidence failed to pinpoint him as the rapist of the 12 year old who identified him. Charges against Winterle by the District Attorney's office under Lynn Abraham were dismissed by Common Pleas Court Judge Arnold New. Winterle was released despite a pending hearing involving unrelated drug possession.

headline: Who are the mothers on welfare
abstract: Data about mothers who receive welfare from the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC), shows that AFDC mothers are less likely to work than others, were teens when their first child was born, and shows that only about half are married to the father of their children.

headline: Black legislator endorses Ridge
abstract: PA Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Ridge yesterday won the endorsement of a black Philadelphia legislator, Democratic PA Senator Hardy Williams, who called on fellow Democrats to look past party lines. In return, Ridge promised to work with the black community if elected. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Mark Singel has the support of several black legislators, including Democratic Representatives Dwight Evans and Vincent Hughes of Philadelphia.

headline: Luksik deserves your support
abstract: A letter writer supports independent gubernatorial candidate Peg Luksik, who "in the past ten years fought relentlessly for the rights of families." The writer adds that Republican Tom Ridge voted for the federal Clean Air Act of 1990 and Democrat Mark Singel implemented it while acting governor, which will result in repairs on failing cars costing about $450 for an extremely small improvement in air quality.

headline: When Casey Called, NatWest Listened
abstract: PA Governor Casey made a personal plea to NatWest Bancorp to relocate to Scranton, PA.  NatWest did just that.

headline: Mothers-to-be getting care here
abstract: A study on Pennsylvania prenatal care showed that more people in Lancaster get prenatal care and those who are poor are less likely to have prenatal care.

headline: Explosion at chemical plant triggers fire
abstract: An explosion at United Chemical Technologies, Inc. started a fire that burned out the building, caused 39 casualties, required some local resident evacuations, and closed parts of I-95 and the Pennsylvania Turnpike.

headline: 'Doe' walks a publicity tightrope
abstract: The lawyer known as Scott Doe has allowed his first name to be used in court and his face has been seen regularly in photographic and TV coverage of the federal trial, in which Doe accuses his former employer of firing him because he has the virus that causes AIDs. This illustrates the conflict between the public's right to know and the individual's right to privacy in the courts today.  24 civil suits in Southeastern PA have been allowed to proceed with the plaintiffs using the "John Doe" pseudonym since 1989-seven so far this year.

headline: Yearly income comparison
abstract: For a family of three, the median income in 1989 was $33,470. In 1993, the poverty level stood at $11,890. Aid to Families with Dependent Children provided a family total aid per year of $7,692. Working instead at minimum wage, such a family could have made $300 more than relying solely on AFDC aid.

headline: Blackwell lost his touch in D.C., they say
abstract: Lucien Blackwell who was a very popular in Philaelphia politics due to his populist ideologies became a poor fit in congress.

headline: Luksik offers more
abstract: A citizen views millions of dollars spent by gubernatorial candidates Mark Singel and Tom Ridge a waste in light of their negative campaigns. Independent Party candidate Peg Luksik's campaign has cost a tenth of Singel and Ridge's and her audiences come away refreshed, hopeful, and more informed. The cost of her campaign is less because the money comes from ordinary citizens who want a Pennsylvania shaped by family-centered values.

headline: When times were tough, Shapp was at his best
abstract: On the death of former PA Governor Milton Shapp, the editorial board reminds people of all the good Shapp did, despite his administration's association with corruption, with which Shapp was never directly linked. The board recounts his genuine concern for those affected by the Johnstown flood and his success in resolving a truckers strike that had potential to affect the entire Interstate. Shapp came to office with a deficit but left with a surplus, instituting statutes for responsible government.

headline: New life for health reform in '96
abstract: Marcia Angell, the executive editor of The New England Journal of Medicine talks bout how the health care reform effort came to an end without any success. The democrats of course blamed the republicans but the fact doesn't change that our health-care bill is rising and we aren't doing anything to stop it. Health-care reform was not passed because lobbyists  poured vast amounts of money into defeating the reform.

headline: Gov. Tom Ridge has a solid and sensible environmental agenda
abstract: Former secretary of Department of Environmental Resources Cliff Jones, Former director of Pennsylvania of State Parks James Seif of the Regional III Administration of the US Environmental Protection Agency, and Richard Thorpe formerly of the Bureau of Foresty recognize and support the vision of PA Governor-elect Tom Ridge to restructure environmental regulation by the Department of Environmental Resources in creating a Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

headline: Domestic-violence homicides fall; tough measures credited
abstract: The number of domestic violence murders has falledn 18% since the 1970s and murders of black women have fallen 41% since 1976.  But assaults have risen by 2 million cases in ten years to 1990.  Domestic violence education, laws, and shelters are credited with the drop.

headline: $600,000 state loan will create 30 jobs
abstract: A $600,000 state loan by the Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority was announced by Fay-Penn Ecomonic Development Council, to be given to the Greater Uniontown Industrial Fund, which will loan it to Rugged Liner Incorporated for the construction of a warehouse facility that will allow the creation of 30 additional jobs. Interested applicates may apply at the Unionwotn Job Service Cneter.

headline: Bob O'Donnell, Later
abstract: Former speaker of the house Bob O'Donnell lost his job and talks about wanting to run for Governor of Pennsylvania.

headline: Luksik scrimping to make final push
abstract: Independent Peg Luksik has been outspent by opponents Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel and US House Representative Tom Ridge. Yet, she believes she can win, based on the success of her previous gubernatorial campaign, in which she stunned parties by winning 46 percent of the vote. Luksik says her success thus far is based on trust from supporters, her party independence, and her 1-800 numbers throughout the state, available for voters to call for updates and to leave messages.

headline: Where business and politics meet
abstract: The New Jersey State Democratic Party was trying to figure ways to raise 5 million dollars to help get Jim Florio elected governor, as well as a few other people. Business man Irv Richter decided to donate 100,000 dollars to the cause, which is one of the largest individual contributions in New Jersey history. Florio eventually got elected and nominated Richter's wife for a Camden County Judgeship which caused some controversy. New Jersey has now changed the law so the most an individual can contribute is 25,000 dollars.

headline: Nicotine study hushed, lawmaker says
abstract: A former researcher for Phillip Morris discovered in 1983 that nicotine was addictive but the company kept him from publishing the report, even after he had left Phillip Morris.  The surgeon general did not declare nicotine addictive until five years later.

headline: Group wants 'authority' removed from Greene solid waste plan
abstract: Residents of Greene County voiced their concerns at the last meeting of the county solid waste committee. The residents were concerned with the mentioning of the nearly defunct Greene County Solid Waste Authority in the county's third solid waste plan. The meeting was held to review the third plan draft.

headline: Drug task force benefits from helping smash ring
abstract: Special Agent Joseph Wolf of the Harrisburg office of the US Customs service presented a check to York County Drug Task Force coordinator Bob Kessler in the amount of $6,647.  The money represents the county's share of the money hauled in by local and federal law enforcement in the wake of the arrest and conviction of 35 people involved in a drug smuggling operation from Jamaica to New York.

headline: 5 steps a barrier to wheelchair-using movie fans
abstract: The United Artists's Capital City Mall Cinema in Lower Allen township is not wheelchair accessable. Theotis Braddy, the executive director of the Center for Independent Living of Central Pennsylvania, plans to portest this.

headline: Both friends and foes pay respects to Nixon
abstract: Former President Richard Nixon's body lies in state at the Nixon Library and Birthplace.  His funeral is April 27, 1994.

headline: Luksik: Children not a hindrance
abstract: Independent candidate for PA governor Peg Luksik has made family issues a keystone of her platform, while in some voters' minds Luksik's own family is an issue. Luksik, 39, is the mother of six, five boys and a girl, ranging from 12 years of age to 4 months old. Some voters have asked Luksik how she intends to be a state executive with young kids, which she has answered that "John Kennedy used to meet heads of state with his children around. There's this notion that you put your kids her and your life over there. That’s the sort of thing that is destroying our families."

headline: Where the money came from
abstract: It a chart showing the leading health and insurance political action committees ranked by contributions between January 1, 1993 and July 31, 1994. The American Medical Association was the most at $1, 363,474 and the Podiatry PAC was the least at $348,370.

headline: Norristown is shot down in struggle over bankrupt hospital
abstract: A federal judge rejected the Borough of Norristown's attempt to bankrupt Sacred Heart Hospital to prevent its purchase by Montgomery County. The County is supposed to by the hospital for 7.05 million dollars at the end of the month.

headline: Government blamed for wetlands loss
abstract: Though landowners complain about delays and difficulty obtaining permits from the government to destroy wetlands, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation reports that only 10 percent of applicants were turned down between 1991 and 1993. The region is losing thousands of acres per year despite a 1988 promise by officials to allow no net loss in acreage. Some officials recommend closing loopholes and improving enforcement to protect wetlands.

headline: Drunken-driving center needs aid, may be shut
abstract: A centralized center to process drunk drivers in Lycoming County is in danger of  closing if the municipalities don't help pay costs.  A shortage of funds is due to the collection of less than the total of fees charged to guilty parties.

headline: A commitment to growth
abstract: Business's need to be assured that people in a town really want them there. The best way to do that is if a business makes its money by the community they should give back to the community.

headline: Both sides put spin on latest ruling
abstract: Recent testimony in the Stinson-Marks absentee ballot election fraud case has Philadelphia city commissioners knowing they helped with absentee ballots and that both Democrats and Republicans are agreesive with absentee ballots.  Also Marks had a camera on during a deposition because of alleged abuse by Stinson lawer Charles Peruto.  Judge Newcomer is trying to determine if there is evidence for another election or not.

headline: Mandelas address: Glory and hope
abstract: Mandela's speech preaches hope for a better and more glorious life for all. He is thankful for the transistion into having their first democratic elections and for the fact that South Africa is now a free nonracial, nonsexist country.

headline: Whitman captures attention
abstract: Since winning the election, New Jersey Governor Christie Whitman is receiving praise for her tax cuts and her easy, open way with the public.  Even democrats, including PA Governor Robert P. Casey, have said the republican Whitman has done a great job and could very well end up on the republican ticket for President.

headline: No-smoking now in style at the mall
abstract: Franklin Mills Mall is the latest mall to ban smoking in the Philadelphia area.  This trend has become popular after the US Environmental Protection Agency released a report linking second-hand smoke to cancer.  Margaret M. Barnes of the Philadelphia division of the American Cancer Society confirms there is considerable evidence that second-hand smoke presents a substantial health problem.

headline: Greene officials consider starting over on solid waste plan
abstract: A second rewrite of the solid waste management plan for Greene County is needed because the first was rejected.  The rewrite was coming after a lawsiut was filed.

headline: Dunn restricts CYS until he gets report
abstract: County Commissioner Larry Dunn ordered Allegheny Children and Youth Services to report on a case by case basis the complaints aired against the agency during the last public hearing. As CYS failed to submit the report, Dunn will not permit the agency to speak at the next public hearing. Dunn says the failure to submit the report further invalidates the agency, which inaccurately announced it was granted access to the National Criminal Information Computer System by state police.

headline: A different focus
abstract: PNC Bank economist Paul Flora believes that Pittsburghers would feel better about themselves economically if they stopped comparing conditions to the way they were a quarter of a century ago instead focused the region's current relationship to the rest of the nation. The Pittsburgh area now ranks 12th among the 30 largest metropolitan statistical areas in per capita income.

headline: Brave South Africa voters should inspire Pennsylvanians
abstract: It is amazing how in South Africa voters are standing in mile-long lines to vote; they have truly realized the central concept of democracy. In Pennsylvania half the people eligible to vote aren't even registered.

headline: Mark S. Singel, Democrat
abstract: Biography of Mark S. Singel, current PA lieutenant governor who won 1994 Democrat gubernatorial primary with 31 percent of the vote in a seven-person field.

headline: Whitman Maintains a High Profile, Sunny Side Up
abstract: For the first seven weeks in office, New Jersey Governor Christine Todd Whitman traveled around the state talking to citizens.  The true test begins soon with figuring out how to pay for her tax cuts as one of the her priorities.

headline: Notorious center for retarded to be phased out under accord
abstract: A long saga of abuse and neglect of mentally retarded residents at the Embreeville center came to an and when state officials announced that the facility would be closed in three years. The closure settles a lawsuit by U.S. Department of Justice against the commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

headline: Group drops Susqeuhanna from list of threatened rivers
abstract: The Susquehanna River is not on the 1994 list of the 30 most endangered and threatened rivers in the US by the American Rivers.  The group said this is less to do with reduced threats but with other rivers in the country becoming more threatened.

headline: Early treatment essential for kids who abuse others
abstract: Professionals say that juvenile sex offenders may have up to a 90% success if rehabilitated when young.  The chances of rehabilitation go down as the person gets older.  They receive intense therapy and are taught to emphasize in rehab that can be two years or more.

headline: An arena for the future
abstract: The paper believes that the Philadelphia City Council should put up the requested $2 million towards the construction of the Spectrum II.  It would lead to more jobs and $12 million per year in taxes as well as growth of surrounding businesses.  The owner of the Flyers and the Sixers will sign leases to keep the teams in Philadelphia for 29 years.

headline: Brown's Crime Issue Rebuttal: Daughter Raped, Son Mugged
abstract: California state treasurer Kathleen Brown, in her campaign to unseat Republican Governor Pete Wilson, turned the issue of crime on the incumbent, mentioning that her daughter had been raped and son mugged., and saying that her commitment to being tough on crime should not be questioned. Brown, behind in the polls, also challenged Wilson about lying about his ability to balance California's budget without a tax increase, while Wilson countered that Brown's economic plan would require new taxes, and that she does not understand the problem of illegal immigration.

headline: Mary McGrory, syndicated columnist
abstract: Mary McGrory writes that President Bill Clinton was right to applauded two well-known Republicans, William Bennett and Jack Kemp, for condemning the illegal immigration proposition number 187, which would deny illegal's health care and exclude children from public schools.

headline: Who'll listen?
abstract: A member of the racist United States of America Nationalist Party wants to speak at the Bucks County Community College and the paper believes that no one will care to go.

headline: Nursing home neglected ill resident, affidavit says
abstract: Geriatric and Medical Centers owned Tucker Nursing Home is being investigated for poor patient care when William Young was brought to the hospital for bed sores so infected, some bones could be seen.

headline: Harvey's Lake getting keeper trout this year
abstract: The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission is going to stock keeper-sized trout in Harvey's Lake.  Additionally they will add fingerling trout to build the trout population and stop stcking walleyes that reduce trout populations.

headline: Editorial about guns enrages reader
abstract: Only 1 percent of the homicides committed in the U.S.are commited with the 19 now banned firearms. More Americans are killed each year by automobiles than firearms, yet they are not banned.

headline: Around the Rivers-Apollo
abstract: The Apollo Area Economic Development Council, a community group hoping to pull the area out of its economic slump, released the results of a $32,000 study team leader Paul Farmer hoped would spark "discussion, debate and disagreement." The study included recommendations for storefront awnings, an industrial park construction site, and the general refurbishment of the downtown shopping area.

headline: Clinger mulls impact of expected GOP gains in Congress
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Clinger has stated that if Republicans come close to control of Congress, four Democrats are likely to switch parties. Cliner was in DuBois to address the annual meeting of the Route 219 Association and stated that if the control in the House is not clear there will be gridlock in Congress.

headline: McDade appeal rebuffed
abstract: U.S.Representative Joe McDade, who was charged with racketeering and conspiracy after accepting gifts and trips in exchange for diverting government contracts to specific groups, has lost another round in his quest to get the charges against him dropped. McDade is headed to the U.S.Supreme Court where, if he loses there or if the court declines to take his case, he will face trial.

headline: Wire to wire
abstract: Lt. Governor Singel and U.S. representative Ridge campaigned the longest and spent the most money and it resulted in a win for both

headline: Official wants criminal penalties for nursing-home neglect
abstract: PA House members want to have the ability to prosecute care-givers for negligent care.  The move comes from recent deaths and hospitalizations of elederly residents of Geriatric and Medical Centers' nursing homes.

headline: Hritz shows his ignorance of auto-emission inspection program
abstract: Howard Yerusalim, PA Secretary of Transportation, writes that Tom Hritz's previous opinion piece "left no doubt that he doesn't understand the state's auto emission inspection program.  Yerusalim adds that PA Governor Robert Casey's recent veto of a bill that would have interrupted PA's auto-emissions testing program was an example of "what he has done for the past 30 years in public life; he made the tough, but responsible, decision for the people of Pennsylvania." Had Governor Casey had made a different decision, the US Environmental Protection Agency would, by law, "impose draconian sanctions."

headline: Effectiveness of '3-strikes' plans questioned
abstract: Some people question the '3-strikes' plan saying too many people would fall under the rule and the US does not have the prison space.

headline: Assessing remedies
abstract: Legislation has been introduced to the state legislature to lessen the property tax increases on homes that have been revalued.

headline: Burns sworn in to Murphy's  old House seat
abstract: Barbara Burns was sworn into a PA House seat opened by Mayor Murphy.

headline: McDade may miss key position
abstract: A US House Republican Conference rule bars indicted members from serving as chairmen, affecting those elected after 1992, not including Representative Joseph McDade. The next likely Speaker, Newt Gingrich, said it is unlikely McDade will serve, while McDade said he would probably be elected. Representatives Robert Walker of Lancaster County, Tom Delay, and Bill McCollum are all vying for majority whip, though the Washington Post reports Walker leading.

headline: Wofford deserves a full term
abstract: The editorial board endorses US Senator Harris Wofford over PA Representative Rick Santorum, saying Wofford has demonstrated support for the elderly and health care reform. Rick Santorum, however, favors raising the social security age and would allow insurance companies free reign over whatever health care program congress decides. The board would like  Wofford to pay more attention to the area and be more conscientious about answering constituent mail.

headline: One lives, one dies as organ drama unfolds
abstract: Next in a series of articles about the problems and personal stories of liver transplant patients.

headline: Iron bars preseve nature's balance
abstract: The PA Game Commission, Bat Conservation International, and Heritage Conservation are trying to put grates on all the entrances to the abandoned Durham Mine.  The gates would allow bats to fly in and out but keep out partiers who kill the bats and destroy their habitat.

headline: Enforce drinking laws - but not at all cost
abstract: The paper believes that while the three legislators have a noble goal to cobat underage drinking, taking away our Constitutional rights for a warrant before search and arrest is not the way to solve the problem.

headline: At PHA, a face of optimism makes lingering frustration
abstract: The Philadelphia Housing Authority fixed up a high rise in West Philadelphia; the agency is trying to improve conditions for its 48,000 residents. This comes after the US Department of Housing and Urban Development set high goals for the agency. The PHA has rehabbed 702 units since January, compared with 260 in all of 1993.

headline: Burrell schools reach accord
abstract: The Burrell School Board and the local teachers' union will vote Wednesday on a new contract. The teachers were set to strike on September 16 but called it off when both parties agreed to a week of good-faith bargaining.

headline: Medal set for Czech President in Philly
abstract: Czech Republic President Vaclav Havel receives the  Philadelphia Liberty Medal.  We the People 2000 confers the medal and award annually to individuals or groups that have contributed to freedom or equality.  Havel led the 1989 Velvet Revolution that freed his nation from the Soviet Bloc.

headline: Wofford gets support from anti-gun group
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford picked up the support of two teachers unions and a gun control advocacy group, Handgun Control, Inc., the chairman of which, Susan Brady, praised Wofford for support of sensible gun control legislation and standing up to special interests. Rick Santorum campaigned in Philadelphia with US Senator Arlen Specter. Santorum argued that teamwork with Specter would convince city and local officials to stop the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard from closing.

headline: Pols finding reform may be too costly
abstract: President Clinton wants to introduce a plan that would provide all Americans with healthcare. The congressional Budget Office says this would be rather costly.

headline: Lawmakers see 'revolving door' in auto program
abstract: Some lawmakers are concerned that a Pennsylvania Department of Transportation supervisor, who had a role in developing an enhanced auto emission testing program for Pennsylvania, is now working for a company that will run the program. State officials say there is nothing illegal about this but it poses an appearance of conflict that should have been avoided.

headline: Ex-officials of FOP deny kickbacks
abstract: John Shaw, the former head of the Philadelphia's police union, the Fraternal Order of Police, and two of his former aides denied charges that they received kickbacks in return for awarding exclusive contracts to provide personal legal services, insurance and printing business.

headline: Audit finding will cost city . . . as bill comes due
abstract: The paper believes that the city of New Castle is learning that state and federal grants will have to be handled professionally in the future so as not to repeat the current problem.  The city's Community Development Program is being audited by the state Department of Community Affairs over $2.2 million.

headline: Business Group Splits With Clinton
abstract: The Business Roundtable did not endorse President Clinton's health care bill, instead it supported another.  Clinton also lost support of the National Governors' Association.

headline: Mezvinsky out-Fox-ed
abstract: US Democratic incumbent House Representative Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky was replaced by Jon Fox, whom she defeated 2 years earlier, with 87 percent of the vote in and only 46 percent of votes compared to Fox's 48. In her concession speech, Mezvinsky said it was her vote for President Clinton's budget package, which she had promised not to support, that cost her the election.

headline: Wofford our choice
abstract: Comparing a sincere, wisened Democrat to a brash, young conservative Republican, the editorial board supports US Senator Harris Wofford for the US Senate. The article cites his success in raising the issue of health care reform to a national level, assembling an anit drug force in Lancaster, and helping people retain jobs. Wofford has also been endorsed by several unions and interest groups, including the PA State Education Association and the PA Federation of Teachers.

headline: Pennsylvania planning to expand CHIP program
abstract: As of October 1, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is expanding the Children's health Insurance Program, or CHIP, to include 14 year olds. With this addition the program will cover 2400 more children in the northeastern Pennsylvania area.

headline: Justices Decide Incinerator Ash Is Toxic Waste
abstract: The Supreme Court ruled in a 7-2 decision that any toxic residue created by burning household and industrial waste in municipal incinerators must be treated as hazardous waste and not dumped into ordinary landfills.

headline: Familiar crime package has drawn mixed reviews
abstract: President Clinton called for crime legislation in the State of the Union Address.  Some of what he wants is to fund states for more police officers, enact the "three strikes" sentancing, and ban semi-automatic weapons.

headline: Baldwin, KBL put stadium on list
abstract: Pittsburgh Penguins owner Howard Baldwin and KBL President Bill Craig have both been trying to buy the Pirates and now the Three Rivers Stadium, where the Steelers and the Pirates play.

headline: But there isn't any cereal...
abstract: Cartoon showing a frustrated girl with a box of "Campaign Flakes" cereal, with "Free Gimmicks Inside" on the box. The girl says "but there isn't any cereal," commenting on all the gimmicks that came with the box, but the lack of actual substance.

headline: Midstate delegation a mix of lifestyles
abstract: For many congressmen renting apartments in Washington D.C. is too much money and not worth it for the limited time they spend there.

headline: Wofford, Santorum focus in crime, guns
abstract: US Senator Harris Wofford said of opponent Rick Santorum in the race for US Senate, that he has been pocketed by the National Rifle Association, citing Santorum's recent flip-flop and vote against the crime bill. Santorum claims the bill was a social-welfare bill designed to pay off President Clinton and Wofford's constituencies. Santorum campaigned with US Senator Arlen Specter recently, receiving endorsement from the PA Anthracite Council and Mayor Dan Guydish in Hazelton.

headline: Perot group backs modest health proposals
abstract: Ross Perot's organization, United We Stand America, endorsed a House measure by Representative J. Roy Rowland and Representative Michael Bilirakis that contains an array of insurance revisions but is far from President Clinton's universal health care proposal.  Empower America has also started an ad campaign to weaken the Clinton universal health care plan because they feel it is like socialized medicine.  Both groups say people would be stripped of their right to choose a doctor they want under Clinton's plan.  Perot's group is advising to pass the issues everyone agrees on this year, and revisit the issue the following year after the elections.

headline: Kostmayer shifts for solutions
abstract: Regional Environmental Protection Agency administrator Peter Kostmayer addressed local Southwest Philadelphia residents about the noise and smell that local trucks make as they drive by on their street. Kostmayer said he will launch a major study to see what he can do about the problem.

headline: Family comes home to aftermath of attack
abstract: Joan Smith and her five children are residents of Fishtown. Last week five white men broke into her home shouting racial slurs and attacked her and one of her children with a baseball bat sending them to the hospital. Many of her neighbors think that she should stay in the neighborhood but she doesn't know if her and her family can handle it.

headline: Braman sells the Eagles for $185 million
abstract: Norman Braman sold the Philadelphia Eagles to Jeffrey Lurie for $185 million.  Braman has had a contentuous past with other owners and the Philadelphia government, and Lurie wants to improve that relationship.

headline: But Who's Going to Protect the Little People?
abstract: With the White House in the distance, in front of which stands a sign reading "Perks and Privilege", a limo carrying a disconcerted donkey in a tux, drinking champagne, has stopped at the curb. A valet wearing a jacket with "the voters" inscribed on its chest, is escorting the donkey out of the car. "But who's going to protect the little people," the donkey asks.

headline: Migrant apple-pickers content to the core
abstract: Every year a group of migrant Mexicans come to Bedford County to help with the apple picking season. The work is very strenuous but the minimum wage they receive is far better than any money they would receive back in Mexico. Bedford County welcomes their services.

headline: Wofford's Pennsylvania Woes
abstract: Three years ago Wofford was leading a universal health care bill and was extremely popular. Today, he is struggling to keep his Senate Seat against PA Representative Rick Santorum. According to a poll the two candidates are in a statistical dead heat. Clinton's advisors have been consulting on the Wofford re-election bid which is the only Senate race they are involved in.

headline: Pharmaceutical firms trying a new formula
abstract: Drug companies are trying to change their role from just producing medicine; SmithKline Beecham bought up a company that handle prescription-drug benefits so they can manage how patients use drugs. There are mixed reactions about this, some say patient care will improve others worry about higher prices and intrusion into personal lives.

headline: Landfill's neighbors lament
abstract: Residents who live near the Empire Landfill are complaining do to the lessening conditions of the landfill.  The Senate Environmental Committee is trying to place federal limits on the amount of garbage states are able to export to their neighbors.  They want states to become more self sufficient.

headline: Female guards allege abuse
abstract: Five female prison guards and a female nurse at the Schuylkill County Prison have filed a federal complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission claiming they were sexually harassed and discriminated against for more than five years by a male supervisor, John Kling, of the prison.  This was a week after the Local 429 of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters filed a similar complaint with the EEOC asking to have Kling removed.

headline: Casey Hails Caparo deal
abstract: A speech given by PA Governor Robert Casey marked an 8 year long effort by the governor to help the town of Farrell regain economic opportunity. Under the terms of the final contract with Caparo Inc., the company will reopen a closed steel mill with a $2 million PA Industrial Development Authority loan and a $4 million Economic Development Partnership Fund loan. Farrell Mayor Eugene C. Pacsi said it would be hard to top what Governor Casey has done for the town.

headline: Campaign '94/Ad Watch
abstract: Tim Reeves of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette evaluates the fourth ad by Republican Gubernatorial Candidate Tom Ridge on crime, and the second to focus on Democratic opponent Mark Singel's record on the state Board of Pardons. Reeves concludes that the assertions made in the ad are accurate, except for the case of Richard Klinger, who Singel voted three times for clemency.  PA Governor Casey denied two of the requests for Klinger's clemency, not three as the Ridge ad argues, although the third request is pending.

headline: Misspelled name irks Thornburgh
abstract: Former Pennsylvania Governor and US Attorney General Dick Thornburgh's name was misspelled in campaign literature by Representative Rick Santorum, in the Washington Post, in a Wall Street Journal editorial, and on C-Span.  Accoridng to a senior aide, this happens a lot and bothers Thornburgh.

headline: Wolf in sheep's clothing
abstract: City Controller Saidel, in response to a possible loss of his position with the re-write of the City Charter, sent a false and alarmist letter saying that retitrees may lose their pensions without him in the job.

headline: Polyclinic, Harrisburg hospitals decide on merger
abstract: Capital Health System and Polyclinic Medical Center, two of the largest health care providers in central Pennsylvania, have decided to merge their institutions. The merger would result in a non-profit health care organization that would retain the two hospitals but divide health services between them in an attempt to reduce the costly duplication of services that have been responsible for rising health costs.

headline: LaValle to EPA: Give state good emissions deal
abstract: Senator Gerald LaValle wants PA to renegotiate with the US Environmental Protection Agency over its emssions testing proposal after California received reduced standards after it missed the deadline.

headline: Ferlo drops lawsuit plan
abstract: City Council President Jim Ferlo is no longer going to sue two lawyers for his perception of their weak prosecuting of gang youth.  He was not supported by Mayor Murphy and most of the council.

headline: Cities and states working with airline industry; See it as good business sense and good politics
abstract: Air South is scheduled to take off in South Carolina after residents had complained about their airline service.  Air South will benefit from $3 million of grants from Columbia and a pledge of $12 million in low-interest loans, backed by federal housing funds. Dennis Gabriel, a South Carolina Commerce Department official, said the federal Housing and Urban Development will not challenge the idea as long as most of the airline's 700 jobs went to low and moderate-income people.

headline: Campaign '94; Tomorrow's Senate Races
abstract: A map of the US is shown according to states held by Democrats, open seats, and those seats held by Republicans. The candidates in each state are listed, along with retiring candidates. Incumbents are marked with an asterik.

headline: More blacks, Hispanics heading to the GOP
abstract: The Wall Street Journal in an editorial wrote that "a record number of black and Hispanic Republicans are running for Congress this year And indeed surveys have begun to show that younger black and Hispanic voters have less faith in government than their elders, and have weaker ties to the Democratic Party."

headline: Woman of '92 Running Anew For a Pennsylvania Position
abstract: Lynn Yeakel had a much easier time running for Senator against Arlen Specter; as a novice she only lost by 3 percent because she was able to focus on one issue. Running for governor is a lot different though, she has no single issue to rely on; she is one of six democrats running in the primary.

headline: Post-Casey-surgery rule stirs debate
abstract: Governor Casey, when he went to the University of Pittsburgh Mideical Center, was put at the top of the transplant list, needing both a heart and liver.  Some were upset about the quick response, while others have waited for years.  Now there is a new system where patients are put on transplant lists for all organs they need and to get either, they must be at the top of at least one.

headline: Limiting out-of-state trash recieves majority backing
abstract: PA Govenor Robert Casey has asked state lawmakers to pass legislation in order to restrict the amount of incoming waste into the state. The measure has gathered 16 of 21 Pennsylvania House members support. The bill would also give governors and counties the ability to limit out-of-state waste.

headline: Fight criminals, not gun owners
