The City of Harrisburg also cleared the snow from the streets, requiring 50 cars to be towed.  Governor Casey sent a letter to President Clinton saying Pennsylvania may ask for federal disaster relief assistance for three weeks of snow, subzero temperatures, and the earthquakes near Reading the previous week.

headline: 6.2-mill tax boost and layoffs loom in Stork's budget
abstract: According to Mayor Janice C. Stork of Lancaster, a $6.2 million tax increase, layoffs at City Hall, and a new amusement tax may be needed to balance a $23 million budget for 1995.  Peter I. Hahn, chairman of the three-member finance committee of the City Council, said the Republican-controlled council would not support a tax increase unless it accompanies spending cuts. Stork says 85 percent of the city budget pays for personnel, so deep cuts would mean reduced services for the city.

headline: Senate panel wants to keep milk board
abstract: The Senate Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee yesterday approved continuing the Pennsylvania Milk Marketing Board with a few changes.  Additionally, the committee also approved a bill to create an Agricultural Product Development Commission and another bill to retain the State Farm Products Show Commission.

headline: Winter Cleanup Bills Piling Up Faster than Near-Record Snow
abstract: Lackawanna County spent $533,000 over budget to clean up from the winter weather but will be receiving federal disaster money.  Wyoming County is over budget as well but is not on the list to receive federal money.

headline: How to keep dangerous criminals behind bars
abstract: Across the country just 3 percent of all felony arrests go to trial and 97 percent are plea bargained or dismissed. This is important because unless the defendant goes to trial sentencing provisions aren't truly mandatory. Too many criminals are reaching these plea bargains and not receiving the full prison time that they deserve.

headline: Parking order hurts man with wheelchair
abstract: An executive order by Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed suspended the issuing of additional reserved parking spaces for people with disabilities.  Reed cited that over half of the spaces already issued are being misused.  This is creating problems for people like Lynda Singleton, who have a legitimate reason for needing a space.  Reed gave officials 90 days to formulate new eligibility criteria.

headline: Clinton, Major stress unity for U.S., Britain
abstract: President Clinton and British Prime Minister John Major visited the Pittsburgh area and denied rumours of a strained relationship.

headline: Patrick Fallon, Libertarian
abstract: Biography of Patrick Fallon, a Libertarian who ran against US Representative Joseph McDade in 1980.

headline: Assessment cap could raise tax havoc
abstract: A possible new tax law that would be retroactive to January 1, would allow a 5% property assessment cap for people who have lived in Alleghency County for at least three years.  Officials say that tax bills would have to be mailed and refunds sent to homeowners later.

headline: A memo from Wall St.
abstract: Wall St. warned Pittsburgh that it could get a lower bond rating after announcements of a $22 million deficit.

headline: The Pitfalls of Puppy Love (And Other Dog-Law Perils)
abstract: Basil Miller is the dog warden for 10 counties under the PA Department of Agriculture.  He has cought and returned many dogs in 18 years.  The most common calls are for dogs running loose without leases and bites are a risk.

headline: With deer everywhere, Abington seeks a plan
abstract: In recent weeks, 25 deer have been killed on Abington township road, prompting the township to contact a deer management consultant. Under PA law, the Game Commission granted authority to municipalities to hire deer-control agents to shoot deer out of season and in higher numbers. Commissioner Nicholas Turco reminded residents that the plan was not a deer hunt, the board can choose not to accept recommendations by the consultant, and the residents would have the final say.

headline: I am against this prison cap because my sister did not get justice when she was shot in a crossfire by a 30-year-old man.
abstract: A letter writer says that she is against the prison cap because her sister did not get justice after getting shot by a criminal, and that something should be changed about the cap now because no person should be on the street for doing a crime.

headline: Pennsylvania Project Aims at New Jersey Commuters
abstract: Developers from New Jersey are building new homes in Lower Makefield Township, PA.  Its closeness to the New Jersey border is meant to attract those who work in NJ but want a more relaxed community.

headline: Close Races In House
abstract: Asked what party they would support during the election of US House Representatives, the margin of difference between Republican and Democratic responses decreased to a mere 3 percentage points. It appears Republicans, provided polls are accurate, are in the best shape since the Reagan landslide of 1980 going into elections. That landslide occurred with a margin of difference between parties at 2 percent.

headline: Pay raises down in state
abstract: A survey done of 97 Pennsylvania companies showed that all but the to executives in the state are getting annual raises slightly smaller than the national average.

headline: 'Be Loyal, By Local' drive slated
abstract: The greater Carlisle Area Chamber of Commerce leaders believe all the ingredients for the next round of economic growth are in place. They are about to begin a low-cost, high-visibility public-awareness campaign aimed at reminding everyone within its service area about the merits of buying locally. This should help businesses make new sales to customers already in there backyard.

headline: All things being unequal
abstract: An indepth look at the disparity of state, local, and federal taxes in proportion to income of those in different classes.  Those making more pay a smaller propotion of their income in taxes on more expensive items, like property and cars, than those who earn less.  Some states have flat taxes to combat the problem.  Corporations are paying a smaller proportion of taxes.

headline: With low prices, dairy farming is no cash cow
abstract: Dairy farmers are unable to turn a profit on dairy farming, paying 1990 prices for machinery and getting 1960 prices for milk, which has not kept up with inflation or rising costs of living. A report by the US Census Bureau revealed a decrease in the number of farms counted by the Census of Agriculture. Unable to get by, many farmers, like Nelson Stoltzfus, are getting out of the business. Alan Stock of the PA State Cooperative Extension in Chester County observed milk prices do not account for machinery prices.

headline: 6 plead guilty in plot to avoid diesel tax
abstract: 6 men pleaded guilty and two not guilty to selling heating oil, that is chemically the same as diesel fuel and not taxed like diesel is, at truck stops in Pennsylvania.

headline: I feel safer ... I think
abstract: In a recent article in the Pittsburg Post-Gazette it said that Murder rates are up but serious crime is down in our country. Is this saying that murder isn't a serious crime?

headline: Phila. Employers unable to keep up with U.S. job rise
abstract: Philadelphia economy is not bouncing as quickly out of the recession as people had hoped. Last year 3000 jobs were added in the Philadelphia area which is the first year over year increase since 1989. In the city, however, the number of jobs coninue to fall.

headline: Coalition's pamphlets urge Christians to vote
abstract: The Christian Coalition compares 33 million voters guides for distribution to the guides provided by the League of Women Voters, though drawing fire from the League, which disapproves of the comparison. The guides include candidates for US Senate, the PA House and Senate, and gubernatorial candidates. Representative Jim Detweiler said the group, originally founded by Pat Robertson,  is trying to diversify its members, mostly white fundamentalist churches.

headline: Peas-in-pod candidates vie for guv
abstract: Democrats are relying on voter turnout to give Lieutenant Governor and gubernatorial candidate Mark Singel an edge over Republican Tom Ridge, who has recently reached beyond his Republican voter base and is shown to be ahead in the polls. Both politicians say they are in favor of cutting taxes, their agreements on other issues making it hard for voters to choose between the two. In the last week, both campaigns have used abortion as an issue to attempt to garner more votes.

headline: Billboard battle
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Murphy urged Allegheny County Commissioners not to renew a lease to Martin Media Co. for a sign that advertises an alcoholic beverage atop a parking garage. Murphy argues his administration has attempted to protect the beauty of the skyline, however his efforts are disjointed, as a recent lease to Mellon Bank for billboard advertising shows. Barry Heffner of Martin Media argues the sign helps keep people in the area employed and does not detract from the skyline because of its relatively low height.

headline: Another tax-cut scam
abstract: The paper believes that while the Congressional Republican budget plan is less than President Clinton's, they are spending far too much on national defense and a tax cut to people making less than $200,00 a year, costing $20 billion.

headline: Air traffic controllers criticize plan
abstract: The National Air Traffic Controllers Association union at Capital City Airport in Fairview Township is criticizing the Federal Aviation Administration's plans to contract service to private contractors, causing workers to move in order to keep their jobs. The plan is part of Vice President Al Gore's effort to improve efficiency. The agency has been contracting service to low-activity towers since 1982, but will save $200,000 through the expansion of the program.

headline: A chilling surprise in utility bills
abstract: Because of cold temperatures in January, heating energy bills are up 50%.  Gas and oil bills are up as well.

headline: 'I have clear conscience'
abstract: Philadelphia Police Department 911 operators defended actions the night of Edward Polec's death, at a press conference held by the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees Local 1637. The 3 were fired by Mayor Ed Rendell, who, questioned about racial motivation in response to workers claims, said he followed recommendations of Police Commissioner Richard Neal, and would have fired all 11 operators under investigation had his decision not been made rationally.

headline: Phila. has plenty of room for new stores
abstract: The Department of Commerce of the city of Philadelphia have encountered problems trying to find new stores to open in their new business development plan in North Philadelphia.  Gerri Walker, chairwoman of the North Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce, said the area has not seen any investment from 1960 until the present. The city is seeking $100 million in federal empowerment-zone funding for venture capital and loan guarantees for North Central Philadelphia

headline: Comments start a row
abstract: Richard Gibson called the college rowing event, the Dad Vail Regatta, segregated and the president of the event a neanderthal at the Fairmount Park Commission.  He thinks that the race should have minority participants if it is to be held annually in Philadelphia.  City Council President John Street agreed with him.  There are few rowing options available to minorities in the area.

headline: Peg Luksik, Constitutional
abstract: Biography of the Constitutional Party's Peg Luksik, a housewife with six kids who challenged Republican Barbara Hafer in 1990 gubernatorial primary and lost by less than five points.

headline: Charitable tax
abstract: The editorial board agrees with Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell's plan to exact voluntary payments from the city's major nonprofit organizations that are tax-exempt.  While they would be voluntary payments, the city is threatening to appeal the tax-exemption of any nonprofit that doesn't volunteer to contribute.

headline: Budget was slow getting to Hill
abstract: President Clinton's 1995 budget was delivered late to Congress and Congressmen did not have early warning of buget cuts.

headline: Aunt Jemima to depart for Iowa
abstract: The Quaker Oats Company plans to stop production of Aunt Jemima syrup at its Shiremanstown plant, eliminating 40 jobs, as part of efforts to streamline operations.  The bulk of the operation will be absorbed by a facility in Cedar Rapids, Iowa.  The Shiremanstown plant employs about 470 workers and also makes various brands of cereals and granola products.

headline: Auto, gasoline dealers to discuss impact of 'reformulated' gas
abstract: Automobile and gasoline dealers are meeting today with community officials to discuss the "reformulated" gasoline that will be sold in Erie County starting December 1.  Critics of the reformulated gasoline, mandated in the area by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), say that it will cost more, reduce engine performance, and produce less mileage per gallon.  The EPA classified Erie County as an ozone "non-attainment" area, which means the county must meet federal regulations for reducing pollutants.

headline: 'I'm going to O.J. you,' abusers say; Probers of spouse beatings still wonder why such cruelty exists
abstract: US Senator Alren Specter visited the Harrisburg YWCA to meet with women seeking shelter from domestic abuse.  Specter, a  former district attorney, is lobbying for more money for the domestic-abuse network in light of the O.J. Simpson trial.

headline: Planning can save rural characteristics
abstract: The columnist suggests that communities should decide what they want to preserve and then restrict development, through processes like zoning, based on that evaluation.

headline: Commission, Preate meet in private
abstract: PA Attorney General Preate, the Pennsylvania Crime Commission and the federal grand jury supervising Judge Gates met behind closed doors about the investigation into Preate's alleged taking of campaign contributions from video poker operators for beneficial judicial outcomes.  Preate is currently running for governor.

headline: Pennsylvania Congress races seem unexciting
abstract: Many of the Pennsylvania congressional seats seem to be much in the favor of incumbents and as a result races are not attracting attention.  Even if Ronald Reagan, presidential candidate, wins in a landslide in November the state delegation in Pennsylvania is not expected to change much if at all.

headline: Charter panel to try again
abstract: The Philadelphia Independent Charter Commision is trying again to change the referendum that  would change Philadelphia's Home Rule Charter. The commision is asking that any votes cast on the charter question be voided.

headline: Casey proposes to slice CNI; others seek loss carry-forward
abstract: Governor Casey propsed to lower the corporate net income tax by 20% over 3 years in his State of the Commonwealth address.  Others want faster and larger reductions and the loss carry-forward ability.

headline: Benefits dispute may head to court
abstract: The 2,482 PECO Energy Co. employees who agreed to waive their rights last month to file for unemployment compensation in return for either buyouts or early-retirement benefits may have a problem. To qualify for a buyout worth three weeks pay for every year of service up to 65 years, or qualify for early retirement at 50 or older with 5 years of service, workers had to sign a waiver saying that they could not qualify for unemployment compensation and could not sue the company. Many workers claim the company used coercive tactics to force workers to take the packages.

headline: B&W foes send judge videotape
abstract: Local activists sent a video to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission showing the location of the Babcock & Wilcox to houses in an attempt to shut the location down.

headline: Impact of election unclear
abstract: Lower Burrell Crime Watch Pioneer Judy Luniewski believes safer streets start with stronger families. Allgheny County District Attorney Robert Colville pushed President Clinton to include in his crime bill money for programs addressing social ills some say cause crime. However, according to political analyst Terry Madonna and National Fraternal Order of Police spokesman Richard Boyd, Governor-elect Tom Ridge will put social solutions in the background and focus on simpler instantaneous results.

headline: Prices of homes within reach of more in Bucks 'Affordability gap' narrows for buyers
abstract: Housing in Bucks County is less expensive because of lower interest rates, property values, and economic situation.

headline: Committee meetings:
abstract: A listing of meetings for the state House Judiciary, Appropriations, Insurance, Urban Affairs, Agriculture & Rural Affairs, Legislative Budget and Finance, and Aging & Youth Committees; the Local Government Commission and the Subcommittee on Crime & Corrections; and the Senate Finance Committee.

headline: Pennsylvania house votes to impeach a state justice
abstract: State Supreme Court justice Rolf Larsen that was convicted of drug charges. The house voted 199-0 to impeach him. If the senate votes to impeach him he would be the first Pennsylvania elected official in 183 years to be impeached.

headline: City residents can provide enforcement
abstract: Edward Deslauriers is the councilman who urged Lower Burrell Mayor Dennis Kowalski to introduce the "Handicapped Parking Patrol." The need for such a patrol is imperative, there is no confrontation involved and you are doing a service by helping the people out who need help. The issue is not about getting even with the violators its simply in place to help the disabled.

headline: Clear message: Feds should cut the budget deficit
abstract: An overwhelming majority of people in northwestern Pennsylvania, according to an Erie Daily Times public opinion poll, want the federal government to reduce the budget deficit.  91 percent of 386 residents surveyed said that Washington must trim the deficit, with only 2 percent disagreeing and 7 percent having no opinion. 80 percent of respondents disagreed with increasing taxes, while a plurality of 48 percent disagreed with decreasing military spending, 68 percent disagreed with less spending and decreased benefits for Social Security.

headline: Blacks lost jobs and a generation with manufacturing's demise
abstract: Affirmative action programs seemed to give blacks a chance, but with economic downturn, those hired most recently were the first fired in the steel unions. Programs like the Bidwell Training Center, Inc., and Bobby J. Hunt's hair design training center attempt to equip blacks with skills to combat the high unemployment rate of nearly 19 percent, compounded by living in what former boxer Nate Smith now an advocate for blacks calls, "the most racist city in America."

headline: Court blocks passing TMI bill  to public
abstract: A PA appeals court overturned a 1993 decision by the PA Public Utility Commission allowing Metropolitan Edison to charge ratepayers for the costs of decommissioning Three Mile Island Unit 2.  Ratepayers already paid $246 million of the $1 billion clean-up after the 1979 nuclear accident.

headline: In Pittsburgh, memorial service unites hundreds in grief
abstract: The city of Pittsburgh held a memorial service for the 132 victims killed in the crash of Flight 427.

headline: Prices of homes within reach of more in Bucks What's good for buyers, not so good for sellers
abstract: People selling their houses are making less money or selling for less than the purchase price, but the low costs and interest rates are allowing for easier buying.

headline: Congress facing generational shift
abstract: In the United States Congress of 1995, a majoity of the representatives from Pennsylvania will have been born during or after World War II.

headline: Pennsylvania Justice Facing Impeachment by Legislature
abstract: Due to drug convictions, State Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen faces faces a chance at impeachment.

headline: County disaster squad largely unused
abstract: Allegheny County has spent $1.2 million on an emercency disaster response team, Delta Team, whose expertise and equipment is rarely called on by federal or state officials.  This is in addition to traditional emergency services.

headline: Consumer Spending Is Brisk
abstract: Retail sales, which account for about 1/3 of the economy jumped .8 percent in the month of August. This means it should more than double its second-quarter growth peace of 1.4 percent. This could mean the economy is not slowing as much as the Federal Reserve would like.

headline: Cat ads seek new workers
abstract: Workers at Caterpillar Inc. in York County have gone on strike while the company has advertised for new workers.  There has been long standing tension in contract negoatiations between Cat and the United Auto Workers union.

headline: Cutoffs zoom while winter approaches
abstract: The federal government has not renewed funds for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program. John Hangar, a PA Public Utilitiy commissioner has advocated increased federal and state funding for the program, which gives 7 percent of its budget to PA residents, the second highest amount in the nation. Aggressive campaigns are ongoing by heating companies to terminate contracts of residents who have failed to pay, before PA prohibits termination of services on December 1st.

headline: In this sue-happy nation, we shun our own responsibility
abstract: The editorial "We Train Autistic Children to be Included in life" was great. Parents should be responsible enough to restrict their children from going on rides. They should not hold the amusement parks responsible

headline: Regatta continues to rock boat
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell supports the Dad Vail Regatta and says that he disagrees with allegations by Park Commissioner Gibson that the regatta is racist.

headline: Congressional reform on back burner, again
abstract: Congressional reforms like  committee strength and size and especially campaign finance reform have been rejected by Congress, although much of the public believes they are a problem.

headline: Pennsylvania: Largest GOP State
abstract: Though Republicans approve of his switch from Democrat to Republican after elections, swinging control of the PA House to Republicans, Democratic House Speaker William H. DeWeese and Representative Robert Belfanti publicly denounced Tom Stish. Stish accepted $35,000 from the Democratic National Committee and was endorsed by PA Democratic Governor Robert Casey. Some allege Stish violated the Legislative code of ethics, his opponent complaining to the Attorney General.

headline: DeWeese to miss toll road hearing
abstract: People are scheduled to gather at Pittsburgh City Council to let them know how they feel about the Mon-Fayette Expressway being built. Most of the areas legislators were there, but House Speaker H. William DeWeese will not be.

headline: Economy keeps growing; pace likely to slow
abstract: Economic growth in the spring was stronger than earlier estimated, the government reported, but analysts said the pace was likely to slow. Much of the increase in the gross domestic product was caused by the biggest buildup of inventories seven years.

headline: Comparable worth
abstract: Colorado US Representative Patricia Schroeder could introduce a "Fair Pay Act" in Congress with hopes to eliminate the gender gap in pay amongst workers with the same skills.  Under the Act, a woman can sue her employer for paying her less than a man with the same job.  Economists and the US Chamber of Commerce fear this act would really hurt businesses.

headline: Dates to remember
abstract: Suggestions and dates for government and private investigations into the health concerns for the areas around the Apollo and Parks nuclear fuel plants.

headline: Indecent exposure? Don't tailor TV to the youngest common denominator
abstract: The Federal Communications Commission recently enacted a sweeping ban to protect children from indecent television programming, however it was repealed by a three-judge panel and is now under review by the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. The editorial board disagrees with the ban, favoring a lesser ban which would bar indecent programming from 6am to 8pm, still allowing adults to view what they please.

headline: Regional Food Bank Expected To Create 180 Jobs
abstract: The Department of Community Affairs Housing and Community Development program awarded the Commission on Economic Opportunity $1.042 million to create the Northeast Regional Food Bank in Luzerne County.  The project is also expected to create 180 jobs.

headline: Congresswoman trails, poll says
abstract: A Millersville University poll released yesterday showed Republican candidate John Fox is leading incumbent Democratic US Representative Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky by 7 percentage points for the 13th congressional seat in Montgomery County, with Fox having 39 percent and Margolies-Mezvinsky receiving 32 percent, with 22 percent undecided.  Fox's largest support comes from voters who have a negative opinion of Margolies-Mezvinsky.

headline: Pension benefits could bakcrupt City of York
abstract: New York City Mayor Charles Robertson believes pension adjustments for police and fire workers made by city officials in the 1960s destined higher taxes. After scaling the plan back in the '70s, a complaint to the City Council led officials to agree to binding arbitration found in favor of the defendant which will raise taxes $3.6 million, or force budget cuts and layoffs. Robertson urges union officials to reconsider, threatening to appeal the arbitration.

headline: Drink tax passes as two switch votes
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council passed a 10% tax per alcoholic drink.  Revenue of $5-10 million will go towards public education.

headline: Fed boosts rates again to slow down economy and ward off inflation
abstract: To stabilize and prolong the current growth in the market, the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee yesterday raised the interest rate .75, the highest increase in a day in 14 years. Economic analyst Paul Getman, of West Chester, PA, said while the impact on the South and Midwest may be positive, for PA, behind the overall growth curve, it will hurt more than help the economy.

headline: Early impact of NAFTA slight
abstract: The US Department of Labor has certified that 4.825 people for special benefits because they lost jobs as a result of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) between the US, Canada, and Mexico. Vic Trunzo, division chief for the Labor Department's Trade Adjustment Assistance Program cautioned there is not enough data yet to measure the impact of NAFTA.  These numbers were much less than skeptics, like Ross Perot, had anticipated, but the PA Department of Labor and Industry says the data could say more about individual companies than about NAFTA.

headline: Demand-side management is energetic Pennsylvania policy
abstract: Pennsylvania has a high consumption of electric energy and the Public Utility Commission is requiring electric utilities to create plans to conserve energy.  Any solutions like energy-efficient lighting and emergency generators will cost money for customers, but less than a new power plant would.

headline: Insanity defense's day in state court could be over
abstract: The US Supreme Court refused to hear a case from Montana where insanity was not allowed to be used as a defense, therefore allowing the ruling to hold.  Opponents say that striking the insanity plea will punish those actually insane and those who have sucessful insanity defenses are required to go to mental institutions and are not on the streets.

headline: Rendell backs deal
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell supports the sale of the Philadelphia Eagles to Jeffrey Lurie.  The city will not receive income taxes from curent owner Norman Braman because he lives in Florida.

headline: Conservative PAC nod goes to Luksik
abstract: Independent PA gubernatorial candidate Peg Luksik picked up the endorsement yesterday of a conservative political action committee from Washington D.C. Paul Weyrich, founder of the Free Congress PAC, said Luksik is the gubernatorial candidate who best represents mainstream American values, and that the group would help Luksik financially in her independent campaign.

headline: Perils of privatizing
abstract: Evan Sutton, business agent of AFSCME Distich Council 33 Local 488 in Philadelphia, wrote a piece about neglected facts in an Oct. 6 article about the privatization of the Philadelphia Nursing Home. Sutton points out that the union signed up 200 new employees into the union, and said that Mayor Rendell's chief of staff David Cohen did nothing to make sure that the nursing home employees-victims of the privatization-found other city jobs, but that it was him and City Council President John Street. Sutton added that "privatization stinks" and that if money is being saved by the city, where is it going?

headline: Electrical fire destroys library in Atglen Borough
abstract: PA state Fire Marshal Richard O'Brien said an accidental, electrical fire that destroyed a library in Atglen Borough.  The building was home to the Borough government offices, but they were able to save files from fireproof file cabinets said Borough Manager Gail Murphy.

headline: GOP weighs variety of ways to cut funding
abstract: To support the Contract With America under incoming House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Representative John Kasich outlines $176 billion in budget cuts to ensure a balanced budget. The cuts over 5 years, coupled with Republican calls to increase military spending cannot be successful without reducing the size of the government workforce and programs. The Kasich proposal targets welfare programs, crime prevention, farm, education, and transportation aid, and environmental protection programs.

headline: Employers of Amish seeking insurance exemption
abstract: The Coalition for Employers of the Amish is asking Congress to continue letting the Amish and their employers be exampt from paying into Social Security and Medicare, even under new legislation.

headline: DER distributes supplement on low-level waste program
abstract: A full brochure describing the state Low-Level Radioactive Waste regulatory program was distributed to 90 newspapers. The brochure outlines the regulatory process; highlights legislated provisions; defines low-level radioactive waste from, among others.

headline: Inside the Capitol-Heard on the Hill
abstract: PA Senator Vincent Fumo, chairman of a select committee on gun violence, hopes to make final recommendations on Wednesday regarding gun violence, however it is unlikely those recommendations will include any type of weapons ban.

headline: Rendell touts life in big city
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell appared is going to appear in an infomercial to talk about the joys of living in Philadelphia. He wants to help premote people living in the city. The commercial is for HomeStart which is a compnay whose goal is to make it possible fo ryoung professionals who are income rich but not have much cash to become home buyers.

headline: Cuba-born DeGarcia represents American success story
abstract: This article profiles the life of Harrisburg City Council President Orlando Francisco DeGarcia.  DeGarcia has worked his way up the collective ranks since fleeing from Cuba in 1962 and is often characterized as a true American success story.

headline: Perot Factor Still Percolates
abstract: Many of the voters who did not vote for President Clinton in 1992 still highly dissaporve of him. Republicans hope to garner some of the Perot support into republican support in the next election.

headline: Gen. Moses?
abstract: After watching the television coverage after the crash of 427, August Hoffman is puzzled on how to address Delta Team general Joseph Moses. Our county commissioners chose a man who has a major ego trip.

headline: GOP win ignites tax-cut fervor
abstract: In lieu of their "Contract With America," Republicans are tossing around a lot of proposed tax cuts, including plans by Representative Dick Armey to introduce a flat tax, Senators Pete Domenici and Samm Nunn's introduction of a bipartisan Universal Savings Allowance for tax-free savings and dividends, a consumption tax , a middle-class tax cut favored by Clinton, a capital gains tax, and a new tax system for IRAs. All of the cuts must determine how taxes will affect the budget.

headline: Final offer: Going once, going twice
abstract: The International Ladies' Garment Workers Union and most of its striking Leslie Fay employees rejected their contract offer.  They are striking because Leslie Fay plans to move production to Honduras.

headline: Electric enlightenment?
abstract: In a recent article in the Pittsburgh Post Gazette it listed the cost for per killowatt hour for electricity from Duquesne Light Company at about 9 cents when in reality it is 12.75 cents. This is one of the most expenisve residential electric-service providers in the country.

headline: Is every lawmaker pushing a crime bill?
abstract: There are over 70 crime bills proposed in the Legislature with varying provisons to prevent crime.

headline: Rendell's urban plan gives city even more impetus
abstract: An opinion by Richard Smoot, the president and CEO of PNC Bank in Philadelphia, supporting Mayor Ed Rendell's economic plan for the city.  He believes that private businesses and government should work together and businesses should invest in the community, including poverty stricken areas.

headline: Democrats agree on goal, differ on timing
abstract: Senate Majority Leader George J. Mitchell and House Majority Leader Richard A. Gephardt said they will stay in session for as long as it takes to pass the health care reform legislation without rushing it.  However, the Democratic leaders are not sure on how long of a phase-in period to achieve universal coverage should be.  While the White House and President Clinton have pushed for a two to three year period, Mitchell said a six to eight year period is being considered.  Gephardt thinks four to five years makes sense for the country.

headline: Philadelphia a must for a Democratic primary win
abstract: Philadelphia and its suberbs are extremely crucial for the democrats running in the Gubernatorial primary. The five canidates all appeared at the annual Jefferson-Jackson Day dinner in hopes of gaining any advantage they could.

headline: Give us money, Dave
abstract: Philadelphia Chief of staff David Cohen is approving checks to people who have met and been horrified by Patrick Gallagher who is our loutishly horny former prison commissioner. The Daily News Editorial Board believes they are entitled to some money as well.

headline: Group wants state budget tossed
abstract: Common Cause, a citizens advocacy group, has filed a lawsuit asking that PA state's current budget be thrown out on the grounds that it was enacted unconstitutionally. Common Cause is also urging a PA Court to make permanent a temporary injunction which bars the state from spending any of the $20 million included in the budget for about 150 "walk around money-" (WAM) appropriations.

headline: Heinz workers reject contract offer
abstract: The United Food and Commercial Workers Local 325, representing Heinz workers in Pittsburgh, rejected the new contract offered by the Heinz Company.

headline: Even at 1 AM., blasts of TMI sirens alarm few
abstract: People are becoming accustomed to false alarms blasts from three Mile Island nuclear power plant. If there is a real emergency things could get very bad because no one ever believes that they are real.

headline: Kids killing kids; When will we say 'enough'?
abstract: The editorial board writes that patchwork local laws leave too many loopholes between jurisdictions, so gun violence is rising even as more laws are put in place. Only comprehensive national controls can, according to the board, make us safer.  The editorial board also asks Congress to authorize the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to begin collecting credible data on gun violence in order to frame effective gun laws.

headline: Ridge commits to hotel project
abstract: Campaigning in Scranton with Mayor Jim Connors before addressing the Chamber of Commerce, gubernatorial candidate Tom Ridge committed to honoring the PA budget allocation of a $10 million matching grant to the city. Ridge encouraged the city to consider coming up with $5 million from private investors to match the $5 million in federal funds. Ridge also discussed the completion of several other Scranton projects and ridiculed opponent and Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel.

headline: Democrats Agree They'll Lose Seats-Worry Is, How Many?
abstract: In the upcoming November election, democrats could lose the house for the first time in nearly four decades. The majority in the senate will also be very close. A lot of this is due largely to the fact of the unpopularity of President Clinton.

headline: Philadelphian's newest heir: Hillary Clinton
abstract: A wealthy Philadelphian Henry Freeman, Jr. willed that first ladies of the United States would received $12,000 in "pin money" a year.  Even though he died in 1917, the first person to get money was Hillary Clinton because all heirs had to be dead.

headline: Inequities in assessments remains
abstract: Homes in Pennsylvania's Allegheny County have not been properly assed for their values in determining property taxes, with many being undervalued.

headline: Governors' Dilemma: Budgets Out of Control
abstract: Governors have let state budgets get out of control due to imbalance, taxes, and more spending.  PA Gov. Bob Casey received a "D" grade for fiscal policy.

headline: Incentive to strike must be removed
abstract: Pennsylvania has heard the title of School Strike Capital of America; no other state comes close to the more than 800 strikes Pennsylvania has seen. This changed with the passage of Act 88 which restricted school employers right to strike. Still this has not stopped it completely; Pennsylvania must stop effectively rewarding teachers for going on strike by making it financially difficult.

headline: Hartford Uses Corporate Tax Breaks for Clean-Fuel Cars
abstract: The state of Connecticut announced a new law that says any commercial fleet operator that wanted to convert vehicles from ozone-spewing gasoline to cleaner fuels like natural gas or electricity would get a big tax break; Oklahoma is the only other state that has a similar law. The tax break would be around 50 cents for every dollar spent on conversion.

headline: Judge Orders Removal of Larsen
abstract: Because of obtaining prescription drugs from employees, Judge O'Brien of the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas removed State Supreme Court Justice Larson from the bench.  The House has already impeached Larsen and the Senate will still vote to do the same.

headline: Singel offers praise for cancelled project
abstract: Lt. Governor Singel gave support to the modernization of a steel plant in South Bethlehem that had been cancelled.

headline: Contributors deny they're buying favors
abstract: The upcoming Gubernatorial election is going to lead to some of the nastiest commercials in Pennsylvania history. The money for these commercials comes from campaign money. Those donating the money often are looking for influence in the process but both campaigns deny that accusation.

headline: Pittsburgh needs bailout
abstract: Pittsburgh is going to get a loan of $10-15 million to help run the city whose $27 million deficit was just revealed.  Other plans to save money include watching programs and not filling vacant positions.

headline: Kenney couldn't stop drink tax, so wants bars to keep a cut
abstract: Philadelphia Councilman James Kenney will introduce a bill proposing restaurant owners who are forced to institute a 10 percent sales tax on all alcohol should receive 1 percent of tax collections. Former president of the Licensed Beverage Association Bill Pawliczek said the bill was the least the city could do. Kenney was not sure how other council members stood, but that in his view, it was similar to the school district's method of paying the city to collect taxes for it from the state.

headline: Hart's in the right place
abstract: The writer supports State Senator Melissa Hart's tax reform bill that would require referrendums for tax increases.

headline: Job-sharing helps worker balance family, job needs
abstract: Two mothers found a job as covice presidents for a movie producer. The two of them will work the same job and this is called job sharing; it enables them to spend more time with their families.

headline: Inflation gauge
abstract: In midstate Pennsylvania, mortgage rates dropped to 6.6%.  Also falling were gas prices, at about $0.90 per gallon.  Rising are utility rates for water and natural gas, food costs especially for produce, and some telephone providers for improved 911 service.  Water rose because of federal water-quality guidelines and gas prices fell even with a tax increase of $0.04 per gallon.  Not changing were electricity rates.

headline: Judge rules to allow new taxi firm
abstract: An administrative law Judge allowed a new Pittsburgh tax company to start in the city. This taxi company will help provide better service for the residents of Pittsburgh's black neighborhoods.

headline: Stadium Spat
abstract: The paper believes that the new policy at Three Rivers Stadium requiring those in luxury boxes to only eat stadium food is silly.

headline: Control of Pa. House is up in air
abstract: Both parties await returns for PA House and Senate results. Republicans are expected to retain the Senate, while Democrats cling to a precarious lead in the House. The Republican party is optimistic given the tide sweeping the nation as well as US Representative Rick Santorum's victory over US Senator Wofford. Matthew J. Ryan will most likely become Speaker of the House, although a power struggle may occur for House majority whip.

headline: Political ties evident in city election jobs
abstract: Employees on the Board of Elections are suppoesed to be non-partisan but many have politically active family members or take a temporary leave a absence from partisan politics while they are on the Board.

headline: Levy on parking appealed by city
abstract: The city of Harrisburg has filed an appeal on the parking tax of the Harrisburg School District, accusing the district of being financially irresponsible and claims the district has refused offers from the city to help straighten out its financial affairs. The tax is a 15-percent levy on the patrons of non-residential parking facilities in Harrisburg. The school district is also under fire for another tax to levy on those who lease tax-exempt property for commercial use.

headline: House Oks spending plan
abstract: The $15.7 billion state budget was passed by the PA House and only needs to be signed by Governor Casey.  It includes welfare reform, a cut in business taxes, and education equity funding.

headline: Labor board accuses Sprint in mass firing
abstract: A week before La Connexion, a Sprint subsidy, workers were to vote on unionizing, they were told the plant was closing immediately and that they must leave. The National Labor Relations Board asked a federal court to force reopening the company and reinstating workers. Sprint maintains the subsidy was a financial failure, but statements from officials and documents validate the NLRB's conclusion; the company closed to eliminate unionization with Communications Workers of America.

headline: Met-Ed seeks OK to pass on energy charges
abstract: The Metropolitan Edison Co., an energy company, requested permission from the Public Utility Commission to charge customers for the incresed cost in energy.

headline: Judge: Sheriff can't bill inmates for warrants, trips
abstract: Lebanon County Judge Robert J. Eby ruled that Lebanon County Sheriff Michael J. DeLeo will no longer be able to bill county prison inmates for the costs of having his deputies serve warrants on prisoners or drive inmates from the jail to the courthouse.  The ruling stems from a lawsuit filed by county prison inmate Timothy Anspach.  Eby said taxes pay for these duties and the sheriff should not be paid twice.

headline: Snider's persistent chase ends in vindication
abstract: Flyers president Ed Sniders persistence in trying to get a new stadium built finally ended in success. They began working on a new stadium that will house both the Flyers and Sixers two years from now.

headline: Controlling the spin spins out of control
abstract: PA Gubernatorial candidates Tom ridge and Mark Singel are taking divergent viewpoints on nearly every issue. Both campaigns are trying to put a lot of negative spin on the other candidate to help gain the competitive edge.

headline: Politics as usual on motor-voter law
abstract: Pennsylvania is among the states that have failed to implement a motor voter law that would make it easier for millions of people to register to vote. The PA State House has passed legislation on the matter twice and the state budget includes $1.2 million to establish such a system but the Senate has yet to pass one. The Scranton Tribune says its time for the State General Assembly to stop playing politics and pass the legislation as soon as possible.

headline: Murphy's method
abstract: The city of Pittsburgh is facing a huge budget deficit, 345 million in total. Former mayer Masloff didn't try to fix the problem he instead tried to mask it. New mayor Tom Murphy knows he needs to act quickly to start to develop plans to fix this problem.

headline: House set to vote on new state budget
abstract: The PA House of Representatives is expected to approve the budget for the state.  The version expected to pass is the Republican one that was created by Republicans from the House and Senate, Democrats from the Senate, and members of the Casey administration.  The budget will then move to the Senate.

headline: Leslie Fay plight examined
abstract: Five US Congressmen held a hearing of the House Labor and Education Subcommittees on Labor Management Relations in Wilkes-Barre to listen to concerns about Leslie Fay moving its factories to Honduras and taking jobs from Pennsylvania.

headline: Notice of Proposed Rate Change
abstract: Columbia Gas of Pennsylvania, Inc. asked the PA Public Utility Commission to raise gas prices 9.34%.

headline: Justices blast drug profile arrests of 2
abstract: The search of two men at a train station  profiled as being drug couriers was deemed an illegal search, causing the evidence and profile to be unusable.

headline: Spectacor ahead in the game
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council tentaively approved the Spectrum 2 project on the site of a current Temple University parking lot.  Temple is having problems getting Council approval for a new parking building in the area.

headline: Counsel stand debated
abstract: Representative Rick Santorum, a Senatorial hopeful, accused his opponent Senator Harris Wofford of not calling for a special counsel to investigate a land deal in Arkansas by President Clinton and First Lady Hillary Clinton.  Wofford's press secretary said that Wofford did ask the White House to investigate and has announced it publically.

headline: Poll finds Philly most hostile
abstract: A study conducted by Dr. Redford Williams of Duke said that Philadelphia was the most hostile city in America.The study took participants from 10 cities across the country and gave them a hostility test; Philadelphia scored the highest.

headline: Norristown human relations panel will get training
abstract: The Norristown Human Relations Commission will offer public training and orientation session on Saturday. The nine-seat volunteer panel has been accused of leaking confidential information and failing to process complaints properly. The session will concern what the commission can and can't do to help with its struggling image.

headline: Jobless rate falls to 6%
abstract: As reported by the US Department of Labor, the national unemployment rate fell from 6.4% in April to 6% in May.  191,000 more people were employed.  Pennsylvania and Philadelphia rates were down as well.

headline: Leslie Fay: a sign of the times
abstract: The columnist believes that Leslie Fay moving production overseas is following in the current trend in business.  Also seen are fewer unionized workers, part time shifts, fewer employees, greater wealth gap, and less heath insurance.

headline: NRC examines possible safety violations at Drexel
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has cited Drexel University for a dozen possible violation of safety rules concerning the handling of radioactive materials. Drexel officials said they are taking steps to correct the problems.

headline: Larsen drug use debated
abstract: Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larson is on trial for obtaining perscription drugs under his employees' names.  His defense argues that he has a mental illness which is treated with therapy and drugs and he just wanted to shield that from the public and the media.

headline: State audit of program completed
abstract: PA's Department of Community Affairs finished their audit of the community development block grant program in New Castle.  The results are not yet public.

headline: County puts low priority on officials' pay raise
abstract: The Alleghency County Salary Board is considering a raise for county directors and deputy-directors to counteract higher paying offers elsewhere.  Opponents say that the $265,000 will be paid with a higher sales tax.

headline: Poll Gives Pataki His First Lead
abstract: For the first time a poll on the New York State governor's race shows that the challenger, George Pataki has a statistically significant lead. The poll consisted of 901 probable voters and it was done by A Daily News / Harris Poll.

headline: Organizations ask for funds from asset district
abstract: Sixty-seven  organizations, including gymnastics teams, volunteer fire companies and folk music groups, submitted 1995 funding requests totaling nearly $22 million. $53 million are to be disturbed by the new Allegheny Regional Asset District.

headline: Jobless rate here tumbles in February
abstract: Metropolitan Pittsburgh, which encompases six counties, had a drop in employment in January and February due to bad weather cutting constructions jobs.

headline: Ludlum talks on again
abstract: Allegheny Ludlum Corp. is trying to restart negotiations again with United Steelworkers union. The company has lost 3500 employees to a strike that began April 1. The workers want stronger guarenteed benefits; they are remaining unified and won't go back until there is a contract.

headline: Nuclear legacy puts residents under a cloud
abstract: People living around the Apollo and Parks nuclear fuel plants are worried about long term heath concerns because of radiation.  The editorial suggests monitoring with a federal report, a health study, and intependent investigation.

headline: Larsen fights effort to suspend pay
abstract: State Supreme Court Justice Larson wanted to plead his own case against his suspension from the court and pay at a Court of Judicial Diciline hearing.  He was not allowed because he already had council.  He was convicted for conspiracy in having employees get prescription drugs for him.

headline: State OKs grants for local townships
abstract: PA Governor Robert P. Casey on Friday announced that Springfield Township was one of 27 communities statewide to receive a portion of more than $8.1 million in Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding.  Springfield will get $350,000 for installing water lines, while three Greene County townships received grants totaling $820,000, including Aleppo, Center, and Washington townships.

headline: Court Offers 3 Options in Voter Fraud Case
abstract: The Federal Appeals Court for the PA 2nd Senate District election ballot fraud case gave US District Judge Newcomer three options: count valid votes and declare a winner, have a special election, or have no one fill the seat.

headline: Poll: Preate, Singel leading
abstract: Ernie Preate Jr. is narrowly leading Tom Ridge in the republican primary for governor. Lt. Gov. Mark Singel has a large lead and is favored to win the democratic primary.

headline: Pa. panel to discuss land use planning
abstract: PA Representative P. Michael Sturla is co-sponsoring a bill which would require local governments to establish their planning rules and policies in coordination with county and state government plans.

headline: Local tax reform revived
abstract: The PA State House Finance Committee approved a proposal to let local governments increase sales and income taxes if 95% of the profit is used to lower property and nuisance taxes.

headline: Ludlum: Strike at what price?
abstract: The largest employer in the Allegheny Valley, a mill Allegheny Ludlum Corp., is running the risk of a workers strike with two unions approving one and the end of talks with the steelworkers union.  The contracts are good until March 31, 1994.

headline: Oily eyesores to be razed
abstract: The ugly oil tanks at the abandoned Sovereign Oil Company are headed for the dump. Officials today planned to announce the impending demolition them. For years oil oozed out of the ground coating the street when it rained, causing trouble for local residents.

headline: Larsen must pay part of probe costs
abstract: Allegheny County Judge W. Terrance O'Brien ordered former PA Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen to pay $38,875.16 to the state and $811.50 to the county court.  The costs stemmed from the investigation to prosecute Larsen on charges related to prescription drugs.  Senior Deputy Attorney General Lawrence Claus estimated the total costs at $1 million.

headline: Susquehanna Twp. Manager quits
abstract: Longtime Susquehanna Township. Manager Miles Cughey submitted his resignation last night calming that he was too ill to continue serving the residents of the community. He managed the township for more than 20 years.

headline: Crime bill worries governors
abstract: US Governors told President Bill Clinton that they did not want money from a crime bill if the money would come with too many rules and stipulations.

headline: Polls: Texas race a tossup
abstract: The two most recent polls of the Texas gubernatorial race show a tossup, with Governor Ann Richards up only one point and two points in the Mason-Dixon and Rice University polls, respectively.

headline: Permit for concert to be needed
abstract: A board of supervisors in Cumberland Country have moved against a heavy metal rock concert because of zoning technicalities. Many local residents are angry with this.

headline: Senator airs his views on Clawges
abstract: The Chairman of the state Senate Judiciary Committee wants the Bucks County District Attorney to charge the former Police Chief Clawges for having sex with 4 of 12 women who were teenagers at the time while he was an officer.

headline: Medicaid Grows Into 'Budgetary Time Bomb'
abstract: The new budget for Medicaid had been worked out in mid-October of 1990 and it included $2 billion in federal funding over five years.  Some expressed disapointment because it was supposed to be a deficit-reduction budget.  The rest of the article outlines the history of Medicaid and how it expanded.

headline: Ludlum's salaried workers spared ... for now
abstract: Allegheny Ludlum has said they won't lay off any more salarried workers unless the strike lasts months longer. The strike started March 31 when their contract expired; the workers want more than the 50 cent an hour pay raise that they were offered.

headline: Propane fuels a growth spurt by revived UGI
abstract: UGI corp. is making a comeback from its once glorious past. They have transformed themselves from a diversified energy company into a holding company tightly focused on two core businesses. They focus on Pennsylvania gas and electric utilities, and its rapidly expanding AmeriGas propane distribution network.

headline: Larsen showed 'clear intent to bypass' law, prosecutor says
abstract: The state Attorney General has filed charges against state Supreme Court Judge Rolf Larson for purchasing prescription pills through other people.

headline: Trump's cash bolsters bid for potential gaming site
abstract: Donald Trump has offered to pay a $3.3 million loan on a piece of property on the Delaware River that he wants to develop into a casino.  Initially the property was to be sold by Royal Bank.  The opponent to the plan is First Lehigh Bank which has a $4.5 million mortgage on part of the land.

headline: Crime problem an easy target, but hard to hit
abstract: In the PA gubernatorial campaign between Republican congressman Tom Ridge and Democrat Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel, the issue of crime has undergone "the political equivalent of strip-mining." During a campaign filled with half-minute attack ads, researcher Alfred Blumstein of Carnegie Mellon was "stuck by the similarity" between the crime position papers of  the Ridge and Singel campaigns. Back-and-forth 30-second ads have buried any hopes of a discussion of crime's root causes.

headline: Pols: Dems ignored blacks
abstract: No one can fault African American voters for Tuesday's election of a Republican PA governor and US Senator. Black turnout matched overall turnout. Even so, pols yesterday blamed incumbent US Senator Harris Wofford and Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel for failing to address blacks until too late, Ridge receiving leading endorsements. Ridge literature nonetheless insulted blacks and kept many from voting. Alan Gould, Singel's campaign manager, believes dissatisfaction in Allegheny county caused the results.

headline: Phila. liquor-tax vote set for today
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council is to vote on a 10% per drink liquor tax that would raise $3-20 million for public schools.

headline: Sentencing study treads cautiously
abstract: A mandatory minimums study shows that drug offenders serve more time than more violent criminals.

headline: Middle-of-the-road approach puts emphasis on investment
abstract: President Clinton, in creating the new federal budget, managed to give money to those he thought who needed it while not overspending.

headline: More workers fired over union drives
abstract: Under the Federal Wagner Act of 1935, it is illegal to fire someone for exercising the right to "form, join, or assist" a labor union.  However, employers have been increasingly firing workers who contribute to a union drive, because the Wagner Act does not have any harsh fines or charges for employers who fire workers.  The Act, enforced by the National Labor Relations Board, makes employers give the jobs back to the workers with back pay, plus interest.

headline: PUC set to probe 'rolling blackouts'
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission is investigating the blackouts during the bad winter weather of January.

headline: Lawmakers to tackle remaining legislation
abstract: 6 days to discuss pending legislation before unfinished business "dies" and must be reintroduced during the next term will most likely result in omnibus bills. The Senate will try overriding several PA Governor Casey vetos, including one rejecting stricter emissions tests. Many bills concern crime, including efforts  to morph a PA ban on 19 assault weapons into a federal ban. The Senate overrode a Casey veto on rolling back weapons bans in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.

headline: U.S. says no bias in siting of shelter
abstract: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development cleared Delaware County of discriminatory housing charges involving the placement of an Upper Darby shelter for the homeless. A complaining was filed by the residents of the Cobbs Creek neighborhood in West Philadelphia alleged that the shelter's placement was discriminatory, racially motivated, and would have a negative effect on the area.

headline: Dark cloud of anarchy
abstract: The United States is heading in a direction that they think is true democracy, being able to say whatever you want whenever you want.  This, however, could lead down a road to anarchy.

headline: Population conference faces issues that may determine the quality of all our lives
abstract: It's good to see that the U.S. is voicing its opinion on population control in the U.N. Conference on Population and Development. It is obvious that population growth is out of control and that something needs to be done.

headline: Pittsburgh should build heath-care priority model
abstract: The author believes that regions in Pennsylvania should join to asses a "hierarchy of needs" of the citizens for healthcare to determine what can and needs to be available.

headline: Sheriff given grant to fund AIDS training
abstract: The Department of Community Affairs has given the Berks County Sherrif's Department $10,000 for the training of and equipment for police officers who interact with HIV/AIDS sufferers.  They will get rubber gloves, a mask, hazardous waste bags, glasses, and a first-aid kit.

headline: Midstate employers scrounging for entry-level workers
abstract: More than three years of steady economic growth since the end of recession in 1991 is producing some pinches in the labor market, economists say. This is true in the Harrisburg area, which even in the worst of times has one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country. Employers are having to use more money or special recruitment efforts to do find entry-level workers, and Bill Ogan of the Harrisburg Job Service Office says his office corkboard is filled with job notices, showing a demand for workers that hasn't been seen for five years.

headline: Prism, Fisher ink workers' comp deal
abstract: Fisher Scientific Co. expanded its contract with a division of Veronabased Interppose Group inc.  They did this for assistance in managing the early stages of workers' compensation cases. The new contract with Prism will add seven Fisher sites across the U.S..

headline: Pulling the plug on utility jobs
abstract: Peco Energy is set to reduce its payroll by offering early retirement and separation incentives, this will cause them to lose more than a quarter of their workforce. In 1992, the federal government passed an act aimed at the eventual deregulation; this would open the utilities to competition. Thanks to these factors, utilities stocks have been on a long slide for the last year.

headline: Lawsuit will test Pa. veterans' preference law
abstract: The PA state Supreme Court will hear arguments for the case of Gordon Brickhouse, a Vietnam veteran who has not yet won a teaching assignment in the Spring-Ford School District in western Montgomery County. The Commonwealth Court in May 1993 sided with Brickhouse and upheld the law that gives veterans preference in getting hired for state jobs. The law will remain in place unless the PA Supreme Court rules against it, or if the state legislature amends it.

headline: Welfare: A View From The Inside; Hope in Hall Manor? Just ask the children
abstract: Justin and Ashley Harris, living in the Hall Manor city housing project, have big dreams despite being kids on welfare. Justin wants to be a cop when he grows up, to take all the drugs and crime off the streets. Ashley wants to be so rich, she could buy a mansion and build a playground that all of the kids in the neighborhood could play on.

headline: Dark forecast for election
abstract: It's primary day in Pennsylvania. Tom Hritz talks about the lack of quality canidates to vote for and the lack of purpose behind passing some of the bills that they want to pass.

headline: Post has few duties
abstract: The role of the Pennsylvania Lieutenant Governor is thought to be ceremonial but he is President of the Senate, Chair of the Board of Pardons, and second in the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Council.  The politically dificult job comes with a good salary, a house, and other perks

headline: Property owners get word
abstract: Most of the homeowners are willing to sell their homes, as long as they are offered a fair price, in a section of the Leechburg Area School District for school expansion.

headline: Shooting victims' shoes make silent statement at Capitol
abstract: Pat Bell took a pair of her sons band shoes to Washington yesterday as a part of a march. The march consisted of 38,000 pairs of shoes, representing the 38,000 people whom had worn them before they had been killed by guns in the last year, including Pat Bell's son. The shoes were offered as a challenge the National Rife Association in hopes of getting tougher gun restriction laws.

headline: Mistake deletes $90 million
abstract: A mistake in the budget paperwork deleted $90 million in mass transit funds from the budget.  A quick vote in the House and Senate will put it back in the budget.

headline: Private Industry Council job training draws fire
abstract: Philadelphia's Private Industry Council was set up to harness the efficiency of the private sector to find jobs for the unemployed. Many activists say the agnency if failing.

headline: Rupture of pipeline likely to raise prices of gas this weekend
abstract: Gasoline prices soon could jump as much as four cents a gallon after two Texas pipelines exploded Thursday, cutting off one-fourth of the East-Coast's motor fuel. Floodwaters broke the Colonial Pipeline where it crossed beneath the San Jacinto River, turning the waterway into an inferno. Larry Goldstein, president of the Petroleum Industry Research Foundation Inc., warns that while supply is not a concern for consumers, price will be.

headline: Legalized gambling has already come to Philadelphia, but sadly, our mayor is using prison workers as chips.
abstract: Jim Moran, director of the Philadelphia Area Project on Occupational Safety's and Health, says that lifting the prison cap will be every prison guard's worst nightmare, while doing nothing to stop crime in Philadelphia. Moran adds that housing more prisoners means more costs and increased taxes, but the worst part is the potential for prison riots. Moran asks Philadelphia Mayor Rendell to look for serious alternatives to incarceration, at least for non-violent crimes, combined with some prison building.

headline: What People Are Saying
abstract: Several comments are printed in reaction to the selection of John J. Rigas, head of Adelphia Cable Communications Company, as the potential owner of the Pittsburgh Pirates. Comments are from former Mayor Sophie Masloff, Anne Swager, executive driector of the American Institute of Architects, and Kay Ray of the Penn Hills Senior Citizens Center, among others. The consensus is strongly supportive of the sale to a local businessman with a vested interest in keeping the Pirates in Pittsburgh.

headline: Darkins alerts council that hel'll return
abstract: City Councilman, Reverand Duane Darkins said at his church that he was not finished on the City Council and would be returning.  He is suffering from lymphoma but says that he watches council meetings on TV and keeps up with issues dealing with his Public Works Committee.

headline: Preate hoping probe will be closed
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General Ernie Preate, Jr. is being investigated for actions while he was Lackawanna County District Attorney.  He is accused of overlooking video poker opperators for campaign money.  He believes that the case is about to be closed in his favor by U.S. Attorney for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, David Barasch, a former appointee of Preate who also worked under Preate's current top deputy, Walter Cohen.  Preate wants the case to be closed so he can run for governor of Pennsylvania in the Republican Party primary.

headline: Residents must guard 'regional assets'
abstract: The powerful Regional Assets District Boad has been appointed for Allegheny County. They will decided how they spend the 53 million they got in the new 1 percent sales tax increase.

headline: Shootout shakes peaceful Narberth
abstract: Narberth police officer Frank Carafa was wounded in a shootout with two men wearing bulletproof vests and ski masks who had robbed an Acme supermarket and fled on bicycles. Carafa was the first Narberth police officer ever shot in the line of duty. Carafa and one of the suspects are currently in stable condition while the other suspect escaped and is still at large.

headline: Pa. budget will take form in private meetings
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature is working on creating the budget for the $15.7 billion they have, looking at welfare and taxes.  There will also be possible consideration on the signing of death warrants and assault weapons as well as bills on judicial, welfare, and tax reform.

headline: Rail strikers ordered to work
abstract: A federal judge ordered striking Conrail employes back to work yesterday. The 4000 workers who maintain the railroad's tracks walked off their jobs over saftey concerns.

headline: Search for lethal pellet centers in scrap yard
abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission believes that a box of radioactive pellets of Cesium 137 were sent to a PA scrap yard by accident.

headline: Legislation on rapes takes shape
abstract: A bill sponsored by PA Representative Karen A. Ritter has undergone changes that would overhaul the state's sex-crime laws.  William H Ryan, Jr., the immediate past-president of the PA District Attorneys Association, said the changes have moved the legislation in the right direction.  The bill still includes a politically popular provision that would specify that victims of rape need not have resisted their attacker for prosecutors to obtain a rape conviction.  Ryan's comments were made after a House Judiciary Committee meeting in which lawmakers, prosecutors, and victims' rights groups engaged in a far-ranging debate about the bill.

headline: Why all the secracy over BRW negotiations?
abstract: The paper belives that the city of Johnstown should not have signed a confidentiality agreement with BRW Steel Corp. and the Pennsylvania Economy League over the possible purchase and reopening of the Bethlehem Bar, Rod and Wire Division mills.  They believe the public has the right to know information about a loan that the city would provide and that the city can be sued if BRW believes there was a confidentiality leak.

headline: David Letterman on the Massachusetts Senate race
abstract: David Letterman joked about the Massachusetts US Senate race, saying "Ted Kennedy told voters, he said 'Hey, don't judge me by my past record because I was drunk at the time.'"

headline: President didn't have mandate to win reform
abstract: President Clinton implosion of health reform has become a prime exhibit of his shortcomings as a leader. Some political leaders thought Clinton did a good job in trying to get universal health care while others think he failed greatly. However, the Clintons have vowed they won't forget about the 39 million uninsured Americans.

headline: Reverse gear
abstract: The paper believes that Allegheny County should have thought about how the public would react to a new $623,000 lease for 59 cars after it announced that it would be reducing the ammount of employees who can use county cars and the number of cars the county holds.

headline: Should Marijuana Be Legal?
abstract: A report on marijuana and its medical uses, risks, and possible legalization future.  It is a sticky part of the plant Cannabis sativa, is used to reduce pain and nausea in patients, some harm comes from accidents while high, and some say it should be medicalized while others are worried about it leading to other drugs.

headline: Pa. is back on track with tax collection
abstract: Because of poor winter weather, Pennsylvania had not collected all due taxes, but is now on schedule.

headline: Striker bill loses a key vote
abstract: The Senate failed again to pass a bill that would ban businesses hiring replacement workers during strikes.  Richard Lesher, president of the US Chamber of Commerce, said it was a major blow to organized labor and would not talk of compromise.  During the seven year debate, unions say replacement workers give management the upper hand in negotiations while businesses say a ban on replacement workers would upset a current balance between workers and their employers.

headline: Splitting atoms and hairs
abstract: Experts are tying to identify where a waste disposal facility can be built in Pennsylvania. There are differing opinions on the safety threats on low-level radioactive waste disposal, some believe it can be very hazardous while others believe its not at all.. Right now, radioactive waste in Pennsylvania is being temporarily stored where it was created.

headline: Legislators attempt to close loophole
abstract: The House Judiciary Committee sent a bill to the House that would band people 17 or younger from having firearms except in certain circumstances, like licensed hunting.

headline: Wild, wild west
abstract: The editorial board writes that they would hate for North Fayette Township to get a reputation for being "easy" for new developers, and should reconsider the Three Rivers Parkway Project, whose goal is to improve the look of the Parkway West so that it will be more appealing to commuters, occasional visitors, and even prospective developers.  The editorial board argues that while the township is understandably "hot for new development," the project's restrictions are reasonable enough to believe that any developer would be willing to meet the conditions.

headline: Debatable barriers
abstract: One of the best ways to learn more about the two gubernatorial candidates is to watch them debate. Debates differ depending on who is sponsoring them, for instance the debate sponsored by the League of Women voters allowed all five candidates to debate, which is not a normal occurrence.

headline: President Leads Swearin-in Of New Crops Volunteers
abstract: President Clinton swore in the first 15,000 members of Americorps, the domestic Peace Corps that he promised to create. Clinton's goal is to make America a better place.

headline: Revision to heritage study caught in government's web
abstract: The Erie County Council voted to revise the Natural Heritage Inventory without deciding who would do revisions.  The orginial study has been paid for and does not have any implications except that it counts all of the different kinds of plants and animals.

headline: Signing warrant the governor's job
abstract: The paper believes that Governor Casey should be signing death warrants for those sentanced, no matter his personal beliefs.  They also believe that legislation to have judges sign the death warrants is not needed and should not pass.

headline: Rep. Robert Walker paid more '93 taxes
abstract: U.S. Representative Robert.S. Walker and his wife, had an income topping $200,000 in 1993.They paid $46,342, equally 23% in federal tax, according to the partial copies of their 1993 income tax returns.

headline: Teachers, board to share contract session tonight
abstract: Parents and teachers are hopeful a contract might be successfully negotiated tonight, otherwise expecting a strike from the Deer Lakes School District union. Chief negotiator Glenn Sutton, also the negotiator during a 1991 11-day strike, is also hopeful. However, students worry about canceled activities, parents about the possibility of childcare. Teachers have already shown willingness to strike by refusing to participate in an Open House because of lack of negotion progress.

headline: States sue Energy Dept. for federal nuclear waste repository
abstract: 20 states, including Pennsylvania, have sued the US Energy Department because lack of location to dump nuclear waste requires it to be stored at nuclear power plants.  States have collected $10 billion in taxes for a facility that will not open until 2010.

headline: Letters To The Editor; Bang, bang, you're wrong
abstract: A citizen argues Tom Hritz in his column "Toy Guns Loaded with Imagination" has an invalid argument. According to Hritz, toy guns are a developmental stage of the imagination. The citizen thinks this is a stereotypical assumption and believes it does more harm than good to allow boys to imitate the violence they see on TV and in the streets. Left to themselves, boys who never saw guns being fired would probably not conjure this action up in their imagination.

headline: Zone in Bethlehem has lured business over past 11 years
abstract: Bethlehem has had a state Enterprise Zone since 1983 and it has been great for the city. In order to qualify for its Enterprise Zone grants, the city has to show that areas benefitting were economically depressed. Enterprise Zone grants also help to attract or leverage other state funding to improve the city's infrastructure.

headline: Defections by men to GOP helped ensure rout
abstract: Despite support among women for Democrats, in elections this year, the defection of white males to the Republican party cost Democrats a number of seats. Analysts say many men simply had a problem with President Clinton, bothered by his support of homosexuals in the military, his stance on health care, and caused by their own empathy for hard line Republican issues like crime and taxes.

headline: Presidents assemble for Nixon farewell
abstract: The current and past presidents all assembled in Yorba Linda, CA for former President Richard Nixon's funeral yesterday.

headline: Saved from the tax collector
abstract: The editorial board says that justice was served last week when the Dauphin County Board of Assessment Appeals refused to permit the county, municipalities, and school boards to tax 10 facilities that provide housing and nursing care for senior citizens, a ruling that saved hundreds of seniors form having to pay steeply higher rents and forcing the facilities to pay local property taxes. The editorial board adds that this experience should galvanize the state Legislature to promptly revisit an address local-tax reform early next year.

headline: Singel pushes crime stance in W-B visit
abstract: In a campaign visit to Wilkes-Barre, PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Single received an endorsement from Mayber Lee Namey and promised to work with Police Chief Joseph Coyne on implementing increased radar scanning. Singel portrayed himself as tough on crime, with a record to prove it, despite attacks by Republican candidate Tom Ridge. Singel argued Ridge placed too much emphasis on issues that would not really affect policing crime in the streets.

headline: Reports point to stronger economy
abstract: The increase in sales of new houses shows that the economy is doing well.

headline: Workers OK after chemical exposure
abstract: Ten workers from Supelco Inc. had to be hospitalized after they became ill from the odor of chemical compound. The plant was forced to evacuate 150 workers for about 15 minutes, but everyone including those who were hospitalized were fine and back to work by early afternoon.

headline: Taking the plunge for power
