abstract: The author feels that Governor Tom Ridge's proposal to expand the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) is a good for senior citizens.  The proposal would raise income limits for those eligible for the program.  The author encourages law makers to support the proposal

headline: False Issues: Task for report is off the mark
abstract: PA Improve Management Performance & Cost Task pitch efficiency as the answer to the issue of reports stating getting rid of waste and fraud can save PA money.

headline: Commissioners turn to the state for help with $3.9M C&Y deficit
abstract: Monroe county commissioners told the state that they cannot absorb the projected $3.9 million deficit from its Children and Youth services agency, and will be forced to raise taxes if the state does not help.  The article details the request and why its needed.

headline: Hospitals lingering on life support
abstract: Hospitals in Philadelphia and its suburbs are in bad financial situation, and this is the bottom line of the report that is published by PA Health Care Cost Containment Council. Main difficulties are caused by cuts in state and federal funds. The article gives more details about the report.

headline: Ryan against waste facility
abstract: PA State Association for Township Supervisors Executive Director B. Benneth Greider invited supervisors to attend a seminar regarding how to acess the resources and finacial assistance for a low-level radioactive waste facility. The Ryan Township Supervisors went on record opposing the low-level radioactive waste facility.

headline: Harrison woman ends welfare trend
abstract: The story is about welfare reform and its consequences on people who are struggling to make for a living. This story is about the a Harrison woman and her teaching career, her raising of two kids and her family tradition of being on welfare. This is not stopped by the welfare reform.

headline: Families split in reaction to Andrezeski apology
abstract: State Senator Anthony Buzz Andrezeski was often times in airways because of advertisements, but this time he went on airways to apologize for his advertise (some of them were referring to the Bain murder case). Families of victims from the murder case are accepting his apologies differently.

headline: City fears '96 federal grant will be cut
abstract: Federal budget causes a change in the amount of annual block grant received by city which may lead to devestating funding cuts.

headline: Hospitals pay big $$$ in buyouts of doctors
abstract: Hospitals in Philadelphia and its suburbs are involved in an intense, big-bucks buying binge as they scoop up private practices for hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash and perks, and put doctors on their payroll. The baying spree is changing the region's medical landscape. An article further discusses possible impacts of these changes on patients, quality if medical care, etc.

headline: Seven years later, Dysart boil-water notice is lifted
abstract: After seven years of letter writing and battles with the state, users of one of the smallest water systems in Cambria County can stop boiling the water. The old reservoir has been replaced with a small water tank and well. The project was sponsored by the State Department of Environmental Protection.

headline: Hearings set on job crisis
abstract: A hearing will be held at the Philadelphia City Council to look at the challeges that will be caused by tougher state and federal wellfare laws that will send thousands into the job market.  Feather Houstoun, Secretary of the Department of Public Welfare, will testify.  The article details the hearings planned for the day and what they will entail.

headline: FEC rules Waldholtz should get a refund
abstract: The Federal Elections Commission says U.S. Representative Enid Greene must repay $1.8 million in illegal compaign contributions to her former husband, Joe Waldholtz, even though Greene says Waldholtz stole the money from her father.

headline: Commuter tax might stay put
abstract: Johnstown's commuter tax may be in place at its current level until the year 2000 as part of the city's continuing path toward financial recovery. This was one of more than 20 ideas city council members discussed as they began forming an amended recovery plan. An article lists other ideas as well.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Health secretary bill wins approval
abstract: A bill that would eliminate the requirement that the secretary of health be a medical doctor has been sent to the House floor for an expected vote. The article talks more about the current law that regulates this matter and it describes recent resignation of the state Health Secretary.

headline: Sewer authority may go it alone on Portage Township work
abstract: A year after an agreement was signed by Mainline communities for joint sewer service, one town is tired of waiting and is going ahead on its own. The Portage Area Sewer Authority has applied to the state PennVest loan board for about $2 million needed to extend sewage service to the Munster Road and Jamestown areas of Portage Township.

headline: Heat available for needy
abstract: South Central Community Action Programs (SCCAP) is collecting donations to help people in need reduce their heating costs this winter.  Rising oil prices will make it harder for poor families to pay their bills.  Federal assistance is also available through the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Prrogram (LIHEAP).

headline: Final wish comes true
abstract: Representative William Clinger, who spent much of his final years in Congress overseeing high-profile investigations into the Clinton administration, wanted to leave without a bang. The PA Republican's final legislative achievement: a low profile bill declaring a river"wild and scenic.

headline: Conservation agency to see more funding
abstract: An additional $10,000 may seem like a drop in in a bucket in the county the size of Cambria, but to officials of Cambria County Conservation District it is a vote of support. The state will give money to Cambria commissioners to help defray the cost of operating the district.

headline: Malpractice fund abolition sought
abstract: The fund that helps doctors and other workers in the medicine field deal with enormous amounts of malpractice suits is rising the premiums rapidly in the recent past. Therefore, some organizations argue that doctors should not pay for these high premiums because the real problem are unreasonable lawsuits. Some legislators will try to address this issue by changing the current law.

headline: Sludge plan seeks storage rights
abstract: A proposal to use municipal sludge to reclaim abandoned strip mines in northern Cambria County includes a request to store the waste at the mine site until it can be spread on the ground. The sludge would come only from the Pittsburgh area sewage treatment.

headline: House approves shift on welfare
abstract: The House approved on July 19 the bill that would end the Federal guarantee of cash assistance for poor children and instead giving states power to run their own welfare and work programs. The bill with the vote of 256-to-170, similar to the one taken up in the Senate on July 19, would make the biggest changes in welfare policy since the New Deal.

headline: Fisher helped benefactor win bid
abstract: State Attorney Mike Fisher intervened to help political benefactor win a city bridge repair, despite the fact the PennDOT recommended rebinding. Political benefactor, Ruscitto, gave $9,000 toward Fisher campaign to win the state's top law enforcement position. Some other state official helped Ruscitto.

headline: Council vote on state grant will cost city
abstract: Four members of city council did a disservice to a city and taxpayers by opposing a $10,000 match for establishing six historic districts in Altoona. City will pay at least $25,000 or more on the same purpose in the next year.

headline: Managed care big business in Valley
abstract: Many employees are switching recently from traditional fee-for-service health insurance, to managed care insurance. Employers want to cut costs and to provide better coverage for employees and these are the reasons for that. An article offers national statistics about people who switched to the new managed care, and some information about new insurance plans (providers, deductible, etc.).

headline: Small-game season opens smoothly
abstract: There were more than five inches of snow fall in northwest Pennsylvania during the opening of small-game hunting season. The Wildlife Conservation Officers in Green County did not report any serious hunting injuries or problems. The season has started off smoothly.

headline: House-Senate panel to tackle welfare bill
abstract: The Senate voted down a bill passed by the House at the beginning of May that would have retained benefits for everyone but reduced benefits for many.

headline: Flood victims told: nothing is impossible
abstract: The Plot Neighborhood Association and Scranton city officials have said they will exhaust every possible lead to fix the river's hot spots from Grace to Race streets. PNA president, Tom Preambo says that federal authorities have even been contacted on the matter.

headline: Goodbye, culm banks
abstract: There are many calm piles throughout Northeastern PA and most of them are in Luzerne County. They will be cleaned in next two decades. There are many potential usages of these areas and these are described in more details in the article (golf fields, housing land, etc.).

headline: Medicare 'Glitch' Startles Outpatients with Big Bills
abstract: Morris Jalazo is fairly savvy about Medicare, the government-sponsored health benefits program serving nearly 38 million older and disabled Americans.  He knows it is illegal for Pennsylvania hospitals to charge Medicare beneficiaries more than the customary 20 percent of what Medicare deems appropriate for inpatient services.  What he didn’t know was that the law does not apply to hospital outpatient services.  Members of the American Association of Retired Persons call it a glitch in the Medicare law that allows hospitals to shift the costs and bill beneficiaries far more than their fair share.  Legislation is needed to stop over-billing for outpatient hospital services.

headline: Smog may not trigger sanctions
abstract: Western PA will probably avoid additional restrictions on industrial emission even if this area has excessive smog level this summer. Official from Environmental Protection Agency said that recent agreements with PA and Philadelphia based Clean Air Council to produce a smog control plan here will give the agency some latitude in interpreting the Clean Air Act.

headline: In protest on AIDS care, 50 go to an officials home
abstract: 50 protestor went to the home of Feather Houstoun, secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare, and drapped a large banner over her house demanding that she delay enrollment in HealthChoices, a program for people with HIV and AIDS.

headline: Focus protection on those truly at risk: Fishing for votes
abstract: Legislation introduced by PA State Representative Bruce Smith, if passed by the PA House, would protect fishers from harassment acts that are already illegal under general anti-harassment statutes. The Daily Record says the bill is just a way for politicians to pass feel good legislation and garner more votes for the next election.

headline: Expert: Don't jack up city taxes
abstract: Commonwealth Court Judge Doris A. Smith will decide if the state,  city, or both should pay for reforms she has ordered in the city schools desegregation case. City Solicitor, Joseph Dworetzky estimates the cost of 1 billion. Robert P. Inman, professor of finance and economics at the University of Pennsylvania, says this would further burden the most heavily taxed residents of the commonwealth.

headline: Mrs. Ridge dedicates new cancer center
abstract: Michele Ridge, wife of Governor Tom Ridge gave the dedication address for the hospital's Community Cancer  Treatment Center.

headline: State acts to protect waterways
abstract: The head off court-ordered federal regulation of state rivers and streams, PA's environmental agency has proposed changes in its water-quality ratings system that eventually would make it impose greater restrictions on what pollutants could be discharged into more of the state's waterways.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Amnesty, LIHEAP tied up together
abstract: Representative Mark Cohen lobbed another grenade at the governor's office for its handling of LIHEAP. This time he used the Tax Amnesty Program to make his point. He said the Governor expanded the Amnesty program for seven days but did not expand days for needy families to sign up for the LIHEAP.

headline: Foes derailing "mag-lev" system
abstract: Two PA legislators (Kukovich and Geist) have proposed a high speed railway system (named Mag-lev) with trains running more than 300mph in Pittsburgh area. There are many opponents of this idea, and the conclusion is that opponents are coming from business that would be hurt if this system is established. Author of the text argues in a favor of the system.

headline: Expert: Don't jack up city taxes
abstract: If taxes are raised to pay for court-ordered school reforms, it should be state not city taxes that get lifted. This is the opinion of professor from economics school. He also argued that private business in Philadelphia already have high taxes and it would not fair to impose more taxes on them.

headline: No sure bet for seniors
abstract: The author states that the delay on the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) debate has been due to party bickering.  Democrats are charging that the Republicans are delaying to get higher copayments for PACE participants. The author encourages senior citizens to question their lawmakers about their motives behind the PACE program.

headline: State bows out on Bell Mountain
abstract: State Department of Environmental Resources has decided that rock crashing into Wal-Mart store on Bell Mountain is not within its jurisdiction, and it will be up to Dickson City to force a correction of what is now a public safety matter. Thus the borough government must demand a quick resolution of the problem before someone gets hurt by failing rock.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Welfare marchers meet with Ridge
abstract: The Kennsington Welfare Rights Union, camping out in the Capitol Rotunda, met with Governor Tom Ridge to discuss the changes in welfare and how that will affect the poor.  They were unable to come to any agreement.  The group later went to the Governor's mansion to protest, but were told they could not enter.

headline: Fuss over the flood
abstract: U.S. President Bill Clinton has signed the disaster declaration for Pennsylvania, less than four hours after federal emergency officials received a faxed request from PA Governor Tom Ridge. The Post-Gazette says that there are procedures for getting the aid and PA needs to fully complete them before criticizing others for not doing enough.

headline: Game farm owner charges retribution
abstract: The Blackhawks were just recently informed about their requirement to have an occupancy permit after living in their mobile home after a year.

headline: Nursing home tries to correct problems
abstract: The Manor facility may lose the state and federal funding if the deficiencies that are determined before are not corrected until the April 30th. The article talks about the deficiencies in more details.

headline: State line, not distance, key to moving costs
abstract: For a residential move within Pennsylvania, the cost is almost the same, but the difference comes when your move crosses the state. That determines whether o not your move is regulated by the state Public Utilities Commission.

headline: Jockeying on welfare
abstract: Congress would produce a final welfare measure acceptable to President Clinton but stopped short of endorsing the legislation approved by the Senate and House. The House approved its bill 256-170 with the support of 30 Democrats. The Senate bill was adopted 74-72 with the support of 23 Democrats.

headline: Gerow, Goodling give views on incumbents
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Goodling decides not to debate his Republican challenger Gerow, and laughs at the suggestion that he has taken politcal advice from Senator Dan Delp, R-Manchester Township to avoid debates. Goodling urged voters to send him back to Washing to finish the business of the Republican Congress.

headline: History/ Legislators allege Ridge deception
abstract: The issue is last year approved law that balances rights of property owners and historical preservation interests (main change in the bill was that property owners will not be forced anymore to conduct expensive archeological digs, because for the first time the state would pick up the tab for more expeditious studies). The problem is that administration did not provide the money for this, and many lawmakers are angry on Governor Ridge and his administration.

headline: Our opinion:  The dilemma
abstract: The editors opine that Governor Tom Ridge's proposal to expand the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) is at odds with his desire to cut costs.

headline: State Officials pushing Congress for trash bill
abstract: PA officials including state Sen. David "Chip" Brightbill, R-Lebanon will be joined by officials pushing for congressional legislation that would limit trash imports from other states.

headline: Medicaid Budget Cuts Opposed at Hearing
abstract: Proposed cuts in Pennsylvania health and welfare programs will hurt the state financially and punish the poor, according to opponents of the budget revision.  About 150 people attended the third of five statewide public hearings called by Governor Ridge on his proposal to eliminate Medicaid health insurance for 175,000 recipients.  The state should concentrate on helping the unemployed find jobs.  Programs should be cut after people are employed.  The state is unable to afford the rising costs of medical and social care according to the Department of Welfare and Department of Aging.

headline: Get a grip
abstract: Republicans tightened their control in PA House and Senate. Although on national level, they lost, in PA they became stronger. Governor Ridge will now have much better opportunity to implement his agenda. The article has more details about PA elections and results across the state.

headline: Hospital payments could be ending
abstract: The 625,000 annual payment Johnstown agreed to pay the local government in lieu of taxes may end if Senate Bill 355 passes the House. The bill that list five criteria that must be met for an entity to receive tax-free status.

headline: Pa. House votes for 2-day stays for births
abstract: The state House voted unamimously to end so-called "drive-through deliveries" by requiring that health insurance policies provide for minmum hospital stays of 48 hours for mothers and infants after birth. The bill awaits approval by the Senate.

headline: State to start spraying for gypsy moths May 1
abstract: The PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources announced it will be spraying for gypsy moth and select forest insects in 24 PA counties on May 1, conditions permitting.

headline: Off welfare, but sinking in debt
abstract: A state program to provide subsidized day care funding to parents with low income salaries would not have any money available until some time in December of 1996. The program director says that they  would not be able to help everyone who was on the waiting list due to a large number of people.

headline: Gingrich's woes cloud conference
abstract: The Hershey bipartisan conference  funded by a &700,000 grant looking to resolve matters in a civil manner and bring the expectancy of about 300 lawmakers has some skeptics such as Democratic Chief Deputy Whip John Lewis, D-Ga due to the Gingrich ethics case.

headline: Local Lawmakers Back Tax Reform Measure
abstract: If the state Senate does not act in the next few days in regards to tax reform, they will have to start all over next year.  The Republican controlled Senate drafted and passed a 100-page complex tax reform measure which was pared down in the state House to only one page, courtesy of an amendment sponsored by Democrats Mike Veon and Frank Dermody.  The amendment called for school districts not to "levy real property taxes for any purpose."  By a vote of 160-36, the amended measure passed overwhelmingly in the House and will take effect one year after the governor signs it.  The amendment now goes to the state Senate for final approval.

headline: Pennsylvania Hospital for an alliance with Penn
abstract: After 245 years of independence, the nation's first hospital will become a part of University of Pennsylvania Health System. Offer of the Jefferson Health System was turned down, and many doctors from the hospital will move to the Thomas Jefferson University Hospital.

headline: The acid (rain) test
abstract: Last month PA Department of Environmental Protection announced that 1995 acid rain fell 20 percent in western PA, and by as much as 25 percent in other sections of PA. This is a very good news, but researchers from Penn State University showed the evidence that says even these lower rains have negative impact on some fish species in some stream areas. More details about those research reports are presented in the article.

headline: PACE eligiblity being expanded
abstract: The state senate voted to expand provisions in a bill that would increase the number of low-income senior citizens eligible for the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE).  The article details the changes to the program including increased limits on income.  The bill must still be signed by Governor Tom Ridge.

headline: Goodling gets new opponent
abstract: U.S Representative William F. Goodling, 11-tern incumbency, is the largest target of Barton L. Baron, a 53-year old manager at York's Harley Davidson plant and one of York's newest Reform Party members.

headline: Make Sure Reform Just Shifts Taxes: Beware Most Regressive Tax on Sales
abstract: In this editorial, it is vital that new legislation be confined to shifting the local tax burden away from real estate, where appropriate.  More Pennsylvanians than ever are on fixed incomes and local school districts still are dependent primarily on local real estate taxation.  The revenue gap between affluent and needy school districts has grown, and older Pennsylvanians are struggling harder than ever to meet their tax obligations.  Tax reform would give districts, and possibly municipal and county governments the ability to shift the tax burden away from property and toward income and consumption.

headline: PACE changes questioned
abstract: The author opines that changes to the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) will hurt senior citizens by reducing their choice of pharmaceuticals to generic ones.  Additionally, the author feels that by restricting brand name drugs, the proposed changes will hurt the pharmaceutical industry in Pennsylvania, which employ many residents.

headline: Streamlining
abstract: After a year of coping with large deficits at township's recycling center. Franklin Township Supervisors are scrambling to streamline the operation. The decided they will seek for a grant from state Department of Environmental Protection. The grant would be used to purchase the system that automates the sorting of aluminum cans.

headline: PG Energy offering assistance
abstract: Pennsylvania's Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program provides financial assistance in need and on a "first-come, first-serve" basis.

headline: Goodling survives again
abstract: Charles Gerow, the challenger who fought to tie U.S. Rep Bill Goodling to the national crises of confidence in government, gave Goodling his worst primary fight in more than 20 years, winning Cumberland County and small pockets of York County.

headline: No Property Taxes?  House Stirs Cauldron
abstract: Lawmakers approved a measure that would revoke the authority of school districts to assess property taxes unless the Legislature adopts some sort of tax-restructuring plan within a year.  The amendment would eliminate property taxes as a form of revenue for the school districts.  Senate leaders called the House’s action disappointing and intend to act before the legislation session ends on Tuesday.

headline: Park Dedication In Honor Of Sen. Roxanne Jones
abstract: St. Joseph Hospital officials will honor the late Senate Roxanne by naming its park after her. The article has details about honoring ceremony, people who will attend and sponsors of the ceremony.

headline: Supervisors lead fight against sludge processing project
abstract: The Young Township supervisors and Citizens Against Sludge Processing (CASP) are appealing a state permit for Pitt Mining Co. to process and distribute sludge on an abandoned mine site near this small township village. They fear of possible affects of heavy metals in the sludge on the private water supplies. Also, they are not satisfied with information they are getting from Department of Environmental Resources.

headline: Pretzel favors major culling of welfare
abstract: The Governor's $16 billion budget proposal called for removing 260,000 low-income people from the program for a savings of $250 million. State House Majority Leader John Pretzel said that many of those targeted to be cut from state medical assistance were able-bodied people aged 22, 25.

headline: GOP asks for the dirt on Clinton
abstract: A memo sent by two close allies of House Speakear Newt Gingrich - Rep. Bob Walker, R-Lancaser and Rep. Jim Nussle, R-Iowa asked the committee and subcommittee chair to come up with anything in the files that raises ethical or other negative issues about the Clinton administration.

headline: No sure bet
abstract: A state lawmaker proposed giving school districts and municipalities a split of a tax paid at off-track-betting facilities, but the author argues that the proposal is an example of inequity. The tax would come from off--track-betting facilities, but the unfairness lays in the fact that the school next to facility would benefit from this, while other schools would not benefit.

headline: Region's hospitals less busy
abstract: According to a survey of the Hospital Council of Western PA patients and employees are down. Vice prisident of finance for council, Walter K. Wayne reports 3,100 fewer full time jobs at 79 hospitals this was the largest quartery decline recorded since tabulations began 13 years ago.

headline: Supervisors seek state grant
abstract: Supervisors from Blair Township are seeking state money to help resolve sewer and flooding problems. The are seeking $20,000 from the Department of Community Affairs for the separation of the stormwater and sanitary sewer in the Fort Fetter area.

headline: Protest of Welfare Cuts at Governor's Mansion: 140 Mile March By Welfare Rights Activists
abstract: Advocates from the Kennsington Welfare Rights Union (KWRU) peacefully protested Governor Ridge's new welfare reforms at the Capitol Rotunda.  The article details their protest activies, including a 140 mile march to Harrisburgh

headline: GOP come-ons arrive in the wrongest of mailboxes
abstract: Babette Joseph, state representative from Philadelphia, democrat, is one of the most liberal members of the PA General Assembly. She received, by mistake, the invitation to participate in a Republican event, where Bob Dole will also attend. The invitation has provided one of the most prominent and best places in the event, and the article talks more about the mistake that Republicans made.

headline: Opinion: A Poll on Confidence
abstract: .The members of the House decided that they will never tackle a major problem-tax relief for the property owner-without creating a penalty if they don’t.  So what the lawmakers decided was that if they don’t reform the property tax structure that funds counties, municipalities and school districts within a year, then the authority of school districts to assess property taxes will be revoked.

headline: Ridge making PACE expansion a priority
abstract: During a fundraising event in Erie, PA, Governor Tom Ridge stated that he hopes the legislature will pass his proposal to expand the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) by increasing the income limits for senior citizens.  The article detailed other issue that the Governor talked about including a controversy over pigeon shooting, Coast Guard issues, and a meeting in Canada about health care costs.

headline: Suspension extended for environmental watchdog company
abstract: The Environmental Compliance Organization has yet to submit details of how $450,000 of taxpayer' money was spent to monitor cleanup and razing of the Babcock & Wilcos nuclear fuels processing plant in Apollo in 1983. As a result the state has extended it's 90 day suspension for good cause.

headline: Protesters, sign removed from House
abstract: Lance Haver, educational director of the Consumers Education & Protective Association in Philadelphia and six others were involved in a squabble centered on decorum and the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP which got his sign that read "Lack of heat --- for any rason -- is an emergency confiscated and escorted out of the building

headline: GOP incumbent, running under a cloud, steps aside
abstract: Representative Wes Cooley (R., Ore), an outspoken conservative facing allegations that he lied about his war record and marriage is under pressure by Newt Gingrich and other Repblicans to sep aside for antoher GOP candidate.

headline: Our View Ridge Needs to Speed Local Tax Reform
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge must call a special session of the Legislature to deal with school tax reform.  Voters overwhelmingly told state lawmakers that their top priority is property tax reform.  All lawmakers from Valley were re-elected; therefore, it is time for them to fulfill their promises to work for local tax reform.  The issue isn’t a simple one.  That’s why it is suggested lawmakers devote two or three weeks to public debate and discussion about it.  We hope the debate will be aired on television and heavily covered by newspapers, which would allow the public to weigh different proposals.  After years of campaigning for tax reform, a statewide income tax should replace about half of the revenues raised through local property taxes.  Currently, the state funds less than 40 percent of most schools districts budgets.  So local property taxpayers bear the largest burden for education, but it is the state’s responsibility to see that all Pennsylvania children get a quality education.

headline: Ridge to discuss senior prescriptions
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge will discuss his changes to the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) at a Senior Citizens Center.  He will also meet with Olympians from Pennsylvania.

headline: The woods are lovely, dark and deep-and thick with deer
abstract: Ridley Creek State Park gets into the news at this time of the year because of its regulated deer hunts. Peter Landry, a writer in Bryn Mawr, writes about the beauty of the woods and the deer within them.

headline: Ridge to sign welfare reform plan into law
abstract: The Senate voted 26-23 to pass the plan that would require employable, single individuals between the ages of 21 and 58 who have no dependent children to work at least 100 hours per month at minimum wage in order to qualify for medical benefits.

headline: GOP leaders declare success
abstract: Legislative session hailed as among the most productive in the state's history. They reformed welfare and workers compensation, cracked down on crime, cut business taxes and so on. But these are the words taken from Republicans. Democrats actually have different opinions. An article lists several comments from both sides.

headline: Reform Revived: One Way to Smart-Sizing Allegheny County Government
abstract: Three commissioners have reached an agreement on how to reshape Allegheny County government.  The Compac 12 task force recommends an elected country executive and an elected part-time council, most of whose members would represent geographic districts.  8 out of 10 of the county’s elected row offices would be eliminated, but their functions would be formed, after some reorganization by county employees in the executive branch.  The changes would require both legislative and voter approval.  The county’s Republican administration has already moved ahead on two other ComPAC 21 recommendations.

headline: Ridge's RX for state's prescription program
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge plans to expand the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE), funded through the state lottery fund.  The article details the plan including raising income limits for eligibity and mandate the use of generic drugs when available.

headline: Three towns get state recycling grants
abstract: Two PA state legislators ( a senator and the representative) announced that Larksville Borough, Nanticoke city and Newport Township have been awarded the state grants for recycling education programs. The article has more data about the ways the grants will be spent, and some information on others, possible towns that could soon be granted the similar grants.

headline: Senate approves sweeping change in welfare policy
abstract: The Senate approved a welfare bill on July 23 that would end the longstanding Federal guarantee of cash assistance for the nation's poorest children and give states to run power their own welfare. The vote was 74 to 24.

headline: GOP Primary Schedule
abstract: The article is actually a chart-schedule of GOP primary election across the US. There is information about dates, methods and different details related to different states and primary elections.

headline: Residents Should Demand Tax Reform
abstract: Many Allegheny County homeowners were pleased when the county commissioners froze property assessments, upon which real estate taxes are based.  The commissioners pledged to study ways to revise the assessment system while assessments were frozen for five years.  Rising assessments have been a common complaint among Valley residents in Allegheny County.  Some residents of the Quaker Valley School District, where assessments have been a hot issue for several years, have sued the county claming the assessment freeze is unconstitutional.  They believe they will be paying a disproportionately higher share of taxes while owners of under assessed property get an unfair tax break.  In addition, they want the entire system reformed.  Allegheny County, along with residents from other area counties, must actively support local tax reform in Harrisburg.

headline: Saylor blasts Armstrong for not keeping up the PACE
abstract: Bill Saylor, running for state senate, state that his opponent, Senator Gibson Armstrong, should not have voted to adjourn the legislature before expanding the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE) to increase income limits.  Saylor feels this will hurt even more senior citizens.

headline: Throop council Oks Keystone expansion
abstract: Council on Monday voted to notify the PA Department of Environmental Protection

headline: Seniors Dislike GOP Medicare Plan
abstract: The way to cut Medicare costs is to get rid of fraud, eliminate tax breaks for the rich and stop raiding the program to balance the budget, senior citizens opposed to the Republican Medicare reform plan say.  Sixty-three seniors who attended a forum Friday by Senator Rick Santorum left the presentation on the Republican plan unconvinced that it is the way to go.

headline: Gore touts Dems at Poplar development
abstract: With the first phase of the Poplar Nehemiah housing development as his backdrop, Vice President Al Gore and the assembled Democratic brass yesterday touted their horns about new homes, new jobs and the hope for new life in North Central Philadelphia.

headline: Stair succeeds in Briar Creek supers' race
abstract: Republican Gary D. Statir defeated democratic opponent Wayne H. Heller in the race for a three-year term as a Brair Creek Township Supervisor.

headline: Senate panel tries to combine PACE proposals
abstract: The state senate Aging and Youth Committee tried to combine two proposals to changes in the Pharmaceutical Assitance Contract for the Elderly (PACE).  One change is to raise income limits for eligibility and mandate the use of generic drugs.  The other is to allow for higher income limts with deductibles and copayments.  The pharmaceutical lobby testified that the proposal of generic drug use would stymie drug inovation.

headline: Tire dumps: Is Bucks at risk?
abstract: Tire dumping is illegal but just not limited to Bucks County, where junk tires are stored and burned.

headline: Setting an SSI standard
abstract: Hundreds of thousands of families are in limbo, not sure of the Supplemental Security Income money they receive to help care for their disabled children will continue. The main reason is that the law has changed, so that the administration has more flexibility to assess the meaning of the bill. Author argues that some fair standards should be developed, and that families who really need the help, should get it.

headline: Governor Ridge's latest Motto?
abstract: The drown picture shows the badge where Governor Ridge and Presidential candidate Doll are presented together. The message is that Ridge will be a candidate for a vice  president.

headline: State House Should Pass Tax Reform
abstract: Local officials and residents should be calling on their state representatives to make sure a Senate-approved property tax bill passes before Nov. 30.  All levels of government need to get away from relying so much on property taxes and onto the more equitable way of people paying based on how much they earn or spend.  The bill passed by the Senate last December would allow countries to impose up to a 0.5 percent income tax, municipalities up to 1 percent and school districts up to 2 percent in exchange for an equal reduction in property taxes.  Counties also would have the option of putting on a 1 percent sales tax in lieu of the income tax.

headline: Senate votes to allow new mothers to stay in the hospital for 48 hours
abstract: The Senate voted with broad bipartisan support according to Representative Gerald B.H. Solomon. Senator Bill Frist says the legislation guarantees a safe have for at least 48 hours after a mother's delivery.The problem is some illnesses don't develop until the second day after a woman has given childbird.

headline: U.S. EPA to monitor Elrama cleanup
abstract: Residents living near the former Elrama School site, where the cancer-causing chemical benzene was dumped in the 1940s, complained of ill health, now the EPA will monitor the cleanup of the hazardous dump site.

headline: Shrinking safety net cradles hearts and hopes of children
abstract: About 10 million of the poor children account for two-thirds of the beneficiaries of welfare checks, and 5 million more get other forms of welfare. In sixties and seventies welfare could lift children to the threshold of poverty, but in nineties because of inflation and budget cuts welfare benefits are worth half as much as they were in 1970, according to the House Ways and Means Committee.

headline: Governor stays mum on possible campaign
abstract: PA Governor Ridge stayed mum on his standings as Bob Dole's possible running mate. He is one of possible candidates for Vice President position. Ridge was disappointed because Republican Party abandoned the tolerance language in abortion. He thinks the move can only hurt Bob Dole, and he thinks this is not consistent with Dole's support for principle of tolerance.

headline: State to decide whether Nanty Glo can save by consolidating services
abstract: A state agency has been asked to study borough operations to determine if money can be saved by combining municipal services. Borough manager says he wants an outside agency to study operations in the borough, before making any larger decisions.

headline: Study finds problems with nursing in state
abstract: Three months of public testimony about nursing quality in PA hospitals from nurses, doctors, and hospital administrators yielded one conclusion for some legislators - something is wrong. House Health and Human Services Committee held several hearings to examine the situation in hospitals. The Committee issued the report with several recommendations, and one of them for example is to create an avenue for nurses to report dangerous or inadequate medical care without jeopardizing their jobs.

headline: Valley sites not suitable to rules for waste damp
abstract: According to the federal law, each state should take care of its nuclear waste and the special facility should be built to deal with such a waste. Valley is one the  list of potential places for such a facility and the article lists the reasons explaining why Valley should not be chosen.

headline: So Far, States Aren't Rewriting the Book on Welfare Plans
abstract: The article states that most states who have already filed their welfare programs with the federal government are not making drastic changes, but simple ones or extensions of new programs.  The article details how states get block grants from the federal government.  The article also details the changes in California and Arizonia law, while mentioning other state laws.

headline: Governor, secretary off course
abstract: In Pennsylvania, the Governor appoints the secretary of education and the appointment is confirmed by the state Senate. Governor Tom Ridge and Education Secretary Eugene Hickok are the originators of a majority of the proposals currently on the legislative table in regards to education. There is a photograph of the author of the article Robert Zellers.

headline: Tax Rate Reform Advances: Compromise Gives Break on Residential Property
abstract: The House and Senate have been volleying different measures that would amend the state constitution to allow different tax rates to be imposed on different types of property.  The compromise reached would allow tax breaks only on residential property, essentially allowing homeowners to get a tax break without handing businesses a windfall.  The constitutional amendment sets the stage for a separate tax reform bill, which would allow local governments to reduce property taxes and switch to a system that relies on income taxes.  The moved marked a compromise forged to speed action on the constitutional amendment, which must be passed by both the House and Senate a second time before it can be put before voters for their approval in a referendum question.  The earliest this could happen is in the May 1997 primary election.

headline: Study questions heart attack aid
abstract: PA doctors are not prescribing enough aspirin, clot busters and other drugs known to make a significant difference in survival of heart attack patients, a major new study shows. The text gives info about measures that should be taken in order to deal with this situation.

headline: Waste dumping in river OK'd
abstract: The Department of Environmental Protection has approved a water and sewer authority's plan to discharge industial waste into Franklin Cove on the Delaware River. Environmentalists said the plan adequately protects the river.

headline: Somerset grant helps counseling for seniors
abstract: The PA Department of Aging has awarded a grant to the Area Agency on Aging of Somerset County to pilot a peer counseling program between elderly people.

headline: Governors Group Finds Agreement on Medicaid Plan
abstract: Leaders of the nation’s governors said that they had agreed on a bipartisan proposal on Medicaid, one of the major stumbling blocks in the budget impasse between President Clinton and Republicans in congress.  The governors, at a conference of the National Governor’s Association, said they had also made progress toward a compromise on welfare.  By themselves, the governors cannot alter Medicaid or welfare policy now set by the Federal Government.  But both the White House and Republican leaders in Congress have been looking to them for suggestions about how to overcome the current impasse.  Under the bipartisan Medicaid proposal offered by the governors, each state would receive a lump sum of federal money, know as a block grant, to finance health care of the poor.  However, it would guarantee a package of medical benefits, to be defined in Federal law, to millions of poor people.  The proposal thus strikes a compromise between the desire of many Democrats to keep Medicaid as an entitlement and Republican demands for block grants.

headline: Street courteous
abstract: Council President John Street was just demonstrating human courtesy when he sent a written apology to Jack Myers, the School District's director of financial planning, for a racial jest he made  (by mistake) at Mayer' expense. Mayer doesn't feel he is offended and thinks the apology is not necessary.

headline: Welfare cheat
abstract: Governor Ridge's reform splits people in two categories: those who need a little help to get a job and those who underserved dregs feed off the taxpayers. Those who want to work can easily travel to where jobs are and do not have to contend with physical and mental impairment. Those who are able to work and do not are not entitled to health care. However, in Pennsylvania welfare reform cuts 220,00 people from medical assistance and requires payment of a $150 deductible from every childless adult (including those who are unable to work).

headline: Waste Giant to Pay $3m Fine
abstract: Browning Ferris Industries has agreed to pay a $3 million fine to federal authorities in Philadelphia for Clean Water Act violations, fraud, and conspiracy.  It will also contribute another $1.5 million toward area environmental restoration projects and another $642, 311 to several municipal sewage treatment plants victimized by the scheme.

headline: State House ready for battle
abstract: A  monumental battle is expected in the state House on Monday, when members will begin to debate welfare system changes that some Republicans call the toughest decision of their careers. The bill is supported by Governor Ridge and the bill would remove 2260,000 able-bodied people from medical assistance. The bill is introduced to lower the raising costs of free government welfare.

headline: Groups call state lax on voter law
abstract: With the presidental election less than two months off, the federal government and a coaltion of civic groups complained yesterday saying that the state is hindering voter registration for the poor and diaabled that a national law was supposed to make effortless. The account that state does not offer enough opprtunities to poor and disabled to register.

headline: The State, the County and US
abstract: The state legislature has a responsibility to provide a flexible, fair system of taxation to enable county governments to collect revenues without impoverishing taxpayers.  The personal property tax is unfair because it penalizes people who have the inititative and wherewithal to save.  Real estate tax is unfair because it penalizes property owners who work hard all their lives.  Northumberland County commissioners fearful that the courts may eventually outlwaw the personal property tax, favor approval of legislation that would allow for imposition of a county sales tax of up to 1%, which would be coupled with a decrease in the real estate tax.

headline: Berks, Montgomery residents sickened by cyclosporine  parasite
abstract: A single-celled creature called cyclosporine may have caused 14 cases of flood positioning in Montgomery and Berks counties - 40 percent of the reported cases in PA attributed to the region. The article has instructions and preventions measures for avoiding parasite. People who suffered food poising ate strawberries or raspberries before coming ill.

headline: Waste racism suit filed
abstract: The environmental group Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living and several individual plaintiffs filed a federal civil right lawsuit in federal court charging that the state Department of Environmental Protection with practicing environmental racism. The recent decision at the state level to place the waste facility in Chester motivated citizens to react this way, because in the past they were often times exposed to unfair treatment from the state.

headline: State legislature approves "tough" new welfare bill
abstract: Both House and Senate approved a measure that mollifies Governor Ridge's proposal to control Medicaid costs by removing from the program poor adults without dependent children who are healthy enough to work.

headline: GSA chief likes what he sees
abstract: U.S. Congressman Paul Kanjorski and Wilkes Barre Mayor Tom McGroarty hosted U.S. General Services Administration Acting Administrator David Barram at the Stegmaier Brewery which is being redeveloped.  All parties agreed this is the type of rejuvinatino cities need throughout the country.

headline: WVW Taxpayers Urged To Support Tax Reform Bill
abstract: The Wyoming Valley West Citizens’ Action Group heard from two out-of-town speakers at their meeting.  Lois Kopcha, a Lake-Lehman School Board member, and Isadore Berley, from Crestwood School District, told the group about financial woes in their district, while Berley distributed a memo about Senate Bill 2.  The bill would allow local voters to decide whether to keep the current tax system, which relies on property taxes, or shift to a system based on wage or income tax.  It would also give voters the power to approve school tax increases and major school bond issues.  The House Finance Committee made changes to the bill, removing the provisions that would call for a vote on tax increases and bond issues.  Both Kopcha and Berley asked taxpayers to contact local representatives and urge them to pass the bill in its original form.

headline: Concern grows as farmland shrinks
abstract: The number of farms in Delaware County is decreasing in last couple of decades and the number of used acres is decreasing as well. Soon, the voters of the county will have an opportunity to decide whether the County should borrow the $100 million to preserve and restore the open space. An article also has several quotes and opinions from local farmers.

headline: Watershed Lands
abstract: Many hunters are angered now that previous watershed land used for hunting has now been closed in PA, Writer Jerry Palko says that watershed lands do pose a liability and it is unlikely that hunters and local and state officials will not be able to come to an agreement on the matter before this hunting season.

headline: State warns elderly to prepare for the future
abstract: The state will have a high concentration of senior citizens through 2020 though the growth of the elderly population is projected to lag behind every other state in the nation.

abstract: Barbara Hafer (Republican) has won the race for PA state Treasurer. There indications that she was helped by Philadelphia city Democrats in her campaign. The article examines those claims, and  showes that some well known city Democrats were not involved in helping Hafer (like Ciafrani and Bob Brady).

headline: Drought's reduced harvests bring disaster declaration
abstract: Last's year drought resulted in fewer apples, smaller pumpkins and less corn for farmers in Bucks and 45 other counties in the PA. Following the drought, federal government decided to declare those areas as disaster areas, and to allow farmers from those areas to apply for low interest loans.

headline: Waterways protections enhanced
abstract: The federal Environmental Protection Agency has set new water quality standards for Pennsylvania that are intended to increase protections for lakes, rivers, streams and wetlands.

abstract: The legislation signed on May 16, 1996 would issue strong work requirements for those on public assistance and cuts medical benefits for thousands. There is a photograph of Republican Bill Robinson who campaigned to defeat the bill.

abstract: Barbara Hafer, has started her fall campaign for state treasurer with a blast at Mina Baker Knoll. Hafer released her tax returns for last 4 years, and charged Knoll for her promise to do the same (but so far she did nothing). The article has more details about both of them, especially about their recent careers.

headline: Farm transfer info available at show
abstract: Pa is facing a defining issue in agriculture that will affect future generations and the state of the PA's number one industry. The main problem is that among 44,000 farmers in PA, almost half are 55 or older, and some prediction that soon there will be less farms because. There should be a solution that transfer farms to younger generations.

abstract: The paper argues that the envirionments needs to be protected is seen as a positive by companies looking to locate to pristine locations.  They site Vermont's history of environmental laws.

abstract: After the nation decided that the welfare system had much failed, congress and President Clinton overhauled it and handed the states new rules in October of 1996. Most states found that they  had to be more frugal. Through the year of 2002, the Federal Government was supposed to cut about $10 billion a year from what it would have spent under the old welfare system.

headline: Hafer tours county courthouse
abstract: State Auditor General Barbara Hafer, the Republican candidate for state treasurer, toured the Schuylkill County Courthouse. She had several discussion with local officials about current investigations. She has also laid out the plan with a focus on six issues, that she will follow if reelected.

headline: Farmers: New law an economic burden
abstract: Area farmers are organizing a letter-writing campaign in hopes of persuading the state to provide options to a new law requiring safety inspections for large farm vehicles. The are afraid the measure would force them to get rid off the old vehicles and that can be a new burden for them.

abstract: The Environmental Compliance Organization of Ashland, Va., a waste management consulting firm is under temporary suspension from contracting and subcontracting with federal government for hiring a company for $450,000 in 1993 to monitor cleanup of nuclear fuels, the monitoring never took place.

abstract: The Luzerne County Assistance Office will hold a forum to address the changes in the wellfare law, including what "able-bodies" means in terms of receiving welfare payments.

headline: Hafer: Knoll no help with new post
abstract: Barbara Hafer (newly elected State Treasurer and former State Auditor General) and Catherine Baker Knoll are back at battling (they had hot political battle in the last elections). This time Hafer is complaining to Governor Ridge that incumbent Knoll (mother of Catherine)  does not cooperate in transition process by not providing too many information about new job to Hafer, and Knoll claims that this is not true and that Hafer has more information than she needs.

headline: Farming viable if it's business, professor says
abstract: Professor from Cornel University gave a talk in 46th annual meeting at PA Farm Bureau and he emphasized that, in order to succeed, farmers have to treat farming as a business. The reason is that market is changing rapidly, specific consumer demands are changing, technology is changing, and all that has to be taken into consideration when planning the business. If that is taken into account, then the farmers can be successful.

abstract: Insufficient criminal background checks of all people hired to read gas meters led to an incident that took place in Penn Township when a woman was raped by a gas meter.

headline: Welfare overhaul will affect county residents
abstract: The overhaul of the American welfare system, signed into law by President Bill Clinton, will affect 2,200 people on cash assistance in Armstrong County.  The new law sets a five year time limit for familes receiving benefits and a two year limt for "able-bodied" adults.  The article details both federal and state wellfare reforms.

headline: Hazleton-Area Race Democrats' Priority
abstract: Todd Eachus said state Democrats have earmarked his race against Republican Representative Tom Stish as the party's No. 1 targeted contest statewide.  Tim Potts, press secretary for state Democratic House Leader H. William DeWeese, democrat from Greene, said the Eachus race and three or four races in the Lehigh Valley are the party's key targets.  The Republican Party hold a one-seat majority, 102-101, which came after Stish defected from the Democratic Party in 1994.

headline: Puppy lemon law entitles consumers to refund
abstract: A new state senate bill proposed by Sen. Stewart Greenleaf would obligate pet stores and breeders to refund customers if a pet gets sick or dies within ten days of the purchase.  Customers would also get a refund if the pet is found to have a hereditary disease within thirty days of the purchase.  The customer can choose to be refunded the purchase price, have the breeder pay the veteranarian bills up to the purchase price, or replace the pet.  The article details the bill's history in the legislature.

headline: Bright sparks
abstract: PA's political and business leaders bemoaned the state's high, anticompetitive electricity rates. In the final days of the legislative session, lawmakers in Harrisburg considered doing something that promised to bring pieces down. The State Senate debates a bill to deregulate the $10 billion industry, enabling residential and industrial summers to choose their electric utility much like that they now choose their long-distance.

abstract: Governor Ridge supported a report given by task force commission that concluded state should help building stadiums that will be privately owned. Main support for the state funding would come from selling of state-liquor stores. An article analyzes whether this is fair (giving public money to private stadiums), and argues more against such a proposal.

headline: He Enjoys the Race
abstract: Sterling Fritz and Stan Saylor are running for the 94th Legislative District.  Although Saylor beat his 1994 Democratic opponent with 79 percent of the vote, probably the widest margin in York County’s modern political history, Fritz remains realistic, but hopeful that he can pull off a win.  Fritz is a moderate, who is hoping to get the support he needs from Republicans.

abstract: Campaigns running in the 190th, 181st, and 186th State House Districts are reported upon.

abstract: A federal judge threw out more than 2,000 damage suits filed against the operators of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant, saying the plaintiffs had offered a "paucity of proof". The main point is that in the 17 years of the accident plaintiff did not provide enough evidence to continue with trial.

The Senate Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure Committee considered a bill that would require a contractor to conduct criminal history background checks, drug tests, and psychological evaluations of its employees before allowing the workers to have any contact with customers.

headline: Competition for electricity benefits us all
abstract: A bill in the state Legislature would remove the monopolistic boundaries separating electric utility service areas and allow electric companies to compete for customers. The competition would spur lower electric rates for residential and business customers.

headline: Asides
abstract: On September 26, 1996 Governor Ridge met with a group of homeless people who were protesting at the Capitol.

headline: House Candidate Offering to Donate Pay
abstract: Richard G. Gallo promises to donate his $47,000 annual legislative salary to charity if voters elect the Indian businessman to the state House of Representatives.  He is seeking the Republican nomination for the 62nd legislative district.  So far, no other Republican has announced a candidacy for the post, which represents parts of Indiana and Cambria counties.  If he is successful in the primary, he will face Democrat incumbent Sara Steelman.  Since he gets a paycheck from his business he doesn’t think it is fair to have two salaries.  He will donate the money to organizations such as unemployed families, homeless shelters, soup kitchens, and organizations helping the less fortunate.  Gallo hopes to eliminate property taxes, opposes gun restrictions and wants to boost funding for local governments and Indiana University of Pennsylvania.

abstract: The $5.1 million complaint filed by the state Public Utility Commission against National Utilities Inc. on request for a 49 percent rate increase.

abstract: The company  has decided not to build facility in PA and  that move might created more than  1,000 jobs in the Chambersburg area. PA was one of the several state considered for the new facility which would produce potato, tortilla and corn chips. The PA was ruled out in large part because of high workers' compensation insurance rates.

This legislation hit the tightly regulated, $200 billion-a-year electricity industry, spitting its normal alliances.

headline: Dunn Says He'll Back Allocation for Events
abstract: Commissioner Larry Dunn supported the request for $250,000, from the Pittsburgh Federation for events and promotions.  It is expected to be approved by the commissioners.  Commissioner Bob Cranmer opposes the funding because he doesn’t believe the federation’s events, which include the First Night celebration on New Year’s Eve, result in people staying overnight in Downtown hotels.  At first Dunn was against the funding, but changed his mind after he and Mayor Murphy reached an agreement to move forward with $10.5 million in renovations to the Civic Arena sought by the Pittsburgh Penguins.  Murphy agreed to support $500,000 allocation from the Allegheny County Regional Asset District for Capital improvements for Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Hall in Oakland.  In exchange Dunn said he would back a $500,000 Regional Asset District Allocation to improve access to city and county libraries for people with disabilities.  The Regional Asset is funded through a county wide sales tax.

This is the result of the recent law that is passed in order to reform workers' compensations because they were too high. Now, the law should be implemented.

abstract: Citizens groups claim that the fees set by stenographers to copy transcripts from Public Utility Commission are too high and hinder their right to have access to public record.

headline: Fayett's fortunes continuing the help that will produce a turnearound
abstract: Fayette County with its lowest per capita income in the state is trying to invigorate its approach to tourism in hopes of creating jobs and other business opportunities with the use of various grants and loans by the federal Appalachian Regional Commission, to boost the economy.

abstract: State Representative James Shaner will square off against political newcomer Michael Cavanagh and former legislator Eugene Saloom in the April 23 Democratic primary for the 52nd Legislative District seat.  Shaner is seeking his second term in Harrisburg.  Cavanagh, is making his first venture into the political area, while Saloom, is looking to return to Harrisburg after serving 20 years in the state House. The article talks about how each one responded.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Ridge thanks many on workers' comp
abstract: Governor Ridge signed into law workers' compensation reform bill. He praised both Republicans and Democrats inn reforming the 1915 law. The bill should create much better climate for business in PA.

headline: How Do We Rate? Local Economy Trails Other Cities
abstract: Pittsburgh has lost industries, jobs, young people and a fair amount of confidence in the future.  But there were also good things happening.  Pittsburgh Post Gazette isolated 12 factors that economists say are good indications of a region's business vitality.  Then they compared the results with 14 similar sized regions in the U.S.  The goal was to determine the weaknesses and strengths, and aid regional discussions on ways to do better.  The 12 economic categories were profit, gross metro product, new and expanded facilities, construction, business stress, startup, initial public offerings, average annual pay, exports, job growth, and quality job growth.

headline: Inside the Capital; What makes special sessions so special?
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge is calling for a special session of the legislature, for the second time since taking office. This session would be called to deal with the weather related disasters, both blizzards and flooding, that ravaged the state in early and mid-January.

headline: No. 2 state union approves contract
abstract: The state employees' second largest union, the PA Social Services Union has approved a new three-year deal. According to the contract pay raise will be 8% in the next three years. Most of the workers in the union are from state Department of Welfare, and few other departments.

headline: Murtha fears heating oil crisis
abstract: U.S. Representative John Murtha is asking the federal Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary to investigate a potential price and supply crisis in the home heating oil industry which may become a major problem this winter.

headline: Inside the Capitol - State authority OK's $7.2 million in loans
abstract: Thomas Hagen, Community and Economic Development Secretary announced that $7.2 million in business loans have been approved by the PA Industrial Development Authority, and the measure will help retain more than 750 jobs and could create another 400 jobs. The loans are targeted toward manufacturing, industrial research and development, agricultural processors etc.

headline: Inside the capitol - Council PRIME'd for an IMPACT
abstract: Politicians like to make committees. One of the last ones in the task force created by Governor Ridge with a task to recommend better ways to operate state government. The commission made a lot of recommendations and now new commission is formed to implement these recommendations. There are more details about the commission in the article.

headline: Private enterprise tries to cure ills of workers comp system
abstract: The article talks about the new Governor's proposal to deal with PA's workers compensation system. The system is a large barrier to business that want to come to PA. An article lists Governor's details of reform, but at the same time there is an issue of health care facilities management that can save a lot of money as well.

headline: PUC approves water rate hike for suburban Bethlehem users
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission approved on no September 19 of 1996 a are increase of 16.6 % for Bethlehem 11,00 water customers who live outside the city.

headline: Lawmaker calls grant program a WAM revival
abstract: The Dept. of Community and Economic Development is currently distributing applications used to tap into state programs providing funding for economic development, community services, community development, and job training. The secretive legislative initiative process of grants awarded have been said by Rep. Ander Carn, D-Philadelphia that Gov. Ridge is not circulating the money.

headline: Inside the capitol - DCA death vote postponed again
abstract: The planned dismantling of the Department of Community Affairs was postponed again. Instead of voting, the bill is sent to the Appropriations Committee for fiscal analysis. The article talks more about the provisions in the bill.

headline: Reformed workers' compensation system should benefit all sided
abstract: In comparing with some surrounding states PA has very high workers' compensation rates and that has negative impact in business. The reform is starting in PA, and is causing the dispute between labor and business. The author argues in the favor of the reform and concludes that if all sides look rationally at the issue, they would agree that the reform is needed.

headline: PUC bill lost in "black hole"
abstract: The House bill 2737 that could have been amendment to Title 66 to force the election of Public Utility commission members mysteriously disappeared having never made it out of committee.

headline: Lawmakers vote to dismantle DCA
abstract: Two state democrats broke ranks with the democrats in the state House and voted in favor of the plan to dismantle the state Department of Community Affairs. The legislation passed the House, and the voting was most along party lines. The bill would move most of the functions to the Department of Commerce.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Governors hedges on VP eligibility
abstract: Speculations that presidential candidate for Republican Party Bob Dole could invite PA Governor Ridge for vice president are launched. The Governor, however, is denying that Dole invited him, and says: "if I am to decide and give a list of potential candidates for vice president, I would not be on that list".

headline: Ridge hears workers' compensation woes
abstract: The main goal in spring for PA governor Ridge is to reform the workers' compensation and the main reason is that PA is not competitive in comparison with some other states. The article also lists the details of the reform proposal.

headline: Quarry talk kicks up dust
abstract: The public hearing held to discuss the quarry's expansion proposals had a xrow split 50-50 over a plan to exand a quarry near John C. Rudy Park. If the facility were expand the nuisances of dust, loud nouises and vibrations would not only continue but get worst.

headline: Loans for two area companies could lead to 200 jobs
abstract: Cannaught Laboratories in Swiftwater and Huxley Envelope in Mount Pocono are the beneficiaries of two loans from the Industrial Development Authority to aid in their planned construction projects, expansions could generate more than 200 new jobs.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Hafer launches a bitter response
abstract: Auditor General Barbara Hafer assailed Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll for allegations she made against Hafer and her staff in a lawsuit. The lawsuit accused Hafer and her staff of spending tax dollars on lavish business dinners, alcohol and personal items. Hofer said the lawsuit is politically motivated.

headline: Ridge vows 2nd round in workers' comp reform
abstract: Governor Ridge has promised a major legislative assault on the state's workers' compensation program, saying the system for helping injured workers is costing too many healthy employees their jobs. He said that change is needed in this domain, because no economic development program is possible with this costly compensation.

headline: Ridge says competition is needed among electric utilities in state
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge called fro enactment pf a plan that would permit electric utility competition in Pennsylvania. Public Utility Commission chairman John Quain said that Pennsylvanians pay 15 percent more for electricity than the national average, and the plan would allow to lower costs due to competition.

headline: Marketing a marriage
abstract: PA Economy League has done a study that anticipated many benefits of joining two tiny boroughs Wall and Wilmerding in Turtle Creek Valley. There are many benefits from this, but the final approval would have to come from referendum in both boroughs. An author of the text argues that PA Economy League and other interested parties should send a message through both communities, if they want combination to happen.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Lottery winner decries state law
abstract: A Johnstown man who won $28.6 million in the Florida Lottery criticized PA's law stopping a company from allowing the people to play another state's  lottery without traveling there.

headline: Ridge: Worker comp rate reform to pay off
abstract: With the recent passage of a workers' compensation reform Governor Tom Ridge decllared business throughout PA should see 10 percent to 15 percent decreases in worker's compensation rates by the end of this year.

headline: Small generations open competition
abstract: The 1978 law gave independent power producers to compete for their customers. The concept of the law required qualified facilities to use quality resources. The law still requires utilities to purchase energy from qualifying facilities at a price not exceeding a utility's avoided costs.

headline: McGroarty asks Specter to Cut through Flood-Aid Red Tape
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter mad a brief stop in Wilkes-Barre to hear the city’s request to have the federal government waive Community Development Block Grant Guidelines to facilitate flood recovery.  The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) will fund at least four flood mitigation projects the city has outlined in its Disaster Survey Reports.  However, one project has been determined that it is not eligible for FEMA funding.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Mellow says open another window
abstract: Senate Minority leader Mellow said that General Assembly should consider enacting another round of early retirement incentives for state workers to save more money for the state budget. He supported and sponsored the series of bills with the similar intention.

headline: Steelworkers push for merger to create largest U.S. union
abstract: The United Steel Workers of America would like to join forces with the United Atuo Workers and the International Association of Machinists creating the largest union in the U.S.

headline: State takes on regulation
abstract: Competition in Pennsylvania's electric utility industry assumed rough shape in Harrisburg, in a meeting called by Governor Tom Ridge and attended by major power companies' decision makers.

headline: Mobile home dwellers vent over large increase in rent
abstract: John Schwartz, owner of the mobile home park off Middletown Road sent certified letters to his residence to inform them of the large hike in rent. The Liberty Mobile Home Park in Hempfield Township must fork over $325 a month instead of $120 to $145 they now pay

headline: Inside the Capitol - Preate's legal bills out under scrutiny
abstract: As former Attorney General Preate reported to prison, his successor began a review of the bills Preate passed along to the state. Most of the reviews will be directed to the spending of his predecessor.

headline: Target: Workers' comp
abstract: Recently Frito-lay company decided not to build plant in PA because of high workers' compensation rates. One of the lawmakers has proposed a bill that would introduce a reform in that domain, but the Governor Ridge did not support that. An author of the article is arguing in the favor of the reform in this domain, and the reason is that this is the only way to attract business in PA.

headline: The crisis over nuclear waste
abstract: The crisis over the storage of nuclear waste moved one step closer to meltdown last week, as PA joined the coalition of 22 other states insisting that the federal government make good on its promise to build a centralized storage site for high level nuclear waste. The federal government promised years ago it will do something, but so far nothing is done.

headline: 'Opportunity Outreach' Program Unveiled by
abstract: Allegheny County is open for business as its departments of Economic Development and Minority, Women, and Disadvantaged Business Enterprise unveiled their new "Opportunity Outreach" program.  The program is different from past programs because it is outside the norm for the Department of Economic Development.  The major significance of this program is that it will allow women and minorities the chance to do business.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Schweiker tapped for Lt. Gov. post
abstract: Lt. Gov. Mark Schweiker has been elected to serve as eastern region chair of the National Conference if Lieutenant Governors. He said he will then be able to promote PA among state and national officials and showcase the progress the Ridge administration has made in areas of improving job climate and workers compensation, welfare and education.

headline: U.S. budget cuts endanger summer youth jobs programs
abstract: At least 2,000 young people counting on getting the jobs through Pittsburgh and Allegheny County programs this summer may want to start looking elsewhere. The federal congress has eliminated the money for these programs and local officials are trying to find a help from private companies now.

headline: The spark of change
abstract: Thanks to changes in federal law, increased competition in electric rates is on the way. Pennsylvania now can move to accommodate itself to the competitive environment that is coming.

headline: Our View: Senior citizen housing choices grow in Valley
abstract: The editors feel that there has been substantial growth in retirement communities and personal care homes for senior citizens. They detail several new homes that are opening.

headline: Inside the Capitol - Senate committee backs breakup, 6-5
abstract: The planned breakup of the Department of Community Affairs took its first step toward reality when a divided Senate committee approved the move proposed by the Governor Ridge. The voting was tough and it divide the committee and the Republican reasoning for this vote was that this measure would help municipalities functioning better. However, the fate of the proposal is far from certain, especially in the House.

headline: Union sues over workers' comp changes
abstract: Claiming that the state constitution was violated when changes to workers' compensation law were adopted, PA's largest labor union sued the state in Commonwealth Court. Labor leaders opposed the bill, which they say will make hard for workers with severe injuries to get compensated.

headline: Utility chiefs: states will lead deregulation
abstract: Deregulation of the US electricity industry is supposed to be accomplished by the states and not by the federal government. Proposals in Congress would require utilities to provide other power producers access to their transmission lines.

headline: Penguins Stalemate Criticized: Murphy Blames Baldwin, Commissioners for Impasse
abstract: Howard Baldwin, owner of the Pittsburgh Penguins, is considering all options, including a move of his National Hockey League team out of Pittsburgh, unless he gets financial relief from the city and county.  The Penguins are seeking $10.5 million in revenue-generating improvements to the arena and also want the city and the county to reimburse them for $10 million in renovations made to the facility two years prior.  The city wants to use $1.5 million a year from the Allegheny Regional Asset District to help finance the improvements and to reimburse the team for the previous work.  County Commissioner Bob Cranmer has balked at using RAD money to help make the debt service payments, estimated at $2.3 million a year.  The county wants the Penguins to divert $1.1 million a year from revenues generated by the renovations for that purpose.  There have been no final resolution, and Baldwin and the county have engaged in a public spat over their differences.

headline: Investigator hired to probe Preate bills
