Fisher denies he made a pressure in order to help his friend get a job.

headline: Some argue proposal may close competitors
abstract: Pennsylvania State University's proposed restructuring is expected to bring major improvements to the institution and benefit its students, but officials at other area colleges and universities are condemning the plan. Opposition says that what is good for the Penn state is  not necessarily good for other colleges. The Penn State's idea is to take two-year feeder campuses and turn them into the four-year colleges.

headline: Shuster prepares bill aimed at better disaster notification
abstract: Representative Bob Shuster, R-Everett, chairman of the House Transporatation Committee is preparing legislation that would require airlines to use trained personnel to notify families of an accident.

headline: Ridge hawks Pa. products on TV
abstract: On commercial TV channel, QVC, Pennsylvania week will take a place soon, and this will be an opportunity to advertise products from PA. As a part of the week, PA Governor Ridge and Democratic state representative will show up.

headline: Pretzel campaign falls short for Dem
abstract: State Representative Alan Butkovitz fell short in a bold attempt to unseat veteran Representative Dwight Evans, a fellow Philadelphian, for Democratic leadership of the House Appropriations Committee.

headline: Some teacher sabbaticals eliminated by state House
abstract: Sabbaticals cost school districts $200 million a year, which amounts to an unfunded mandate. The state House did away with travel sabbaticals and terminal sabbaticals for employees near retirement. Governor Tom Ridge favors eliminating guaranteed sabbaticals for teachers who have put 10 years of work in.

headline: Slimmer budget trims PennDOT's roadway plans
abstract: Two years ago funding was in place for all modes of transportation however due to federal budget cuts The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has to change funding plans.

headline: Telephone lines too busy in 412 code
abstract: Area code 412 is expected to run out by the middle of 1997. the ?state Public Utility Commission weighs two alternatives: an "overlay" option of adding a new area code or splitting up the existing 412 area code assigning one section a new area code number.

headline: Prevailing wage costs taxpayers
abstract: The article  talks about the measure that is approved by the state Senate, that again confirmed the state "prevailing wage". This is the wage that has to be paid to the constructors of public projects that are paid by tax dollars. And the problem is that all municipalities have to be the same wages as in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia. The measure costs PA taxpayers too much, is the conclusion of the author.

headline: State bucking national student enrollment trend: Education Department study estimates 2.2 percent drop in number of pupils in 10 years
abstract: PA will have the 10th sharpest drop among states in student enrollment over the next 10 years, according to the U.S. Education Department. Student enrollment will drop to 1.79 million students in 2006 from 1.83 million students in 1996. Meanwhile, pupil amounts for the nation are expected to soar.

headline: Some people just should not drive
abstract: There are many cases that some people (especially elderly) are not able to drive safely because of medical reasons, and so far, law was pretty soft toward them. For example, if they were supposed to retest for medical reasons, they could wait up to the expiration of driver license, which could be up to 4 years. Author of the article strongly favors tougher law on this issues, which would rule that people who are not able to drive safely, should be prohibited from driving.

headline: Uliana challenges ad in Bell bill
abstract: Senator Joseph Uliana received a notice tucked inside his October phone bill, informing him about the phone company's internet service provider, Bell Atlantic.net. Uliana asked to stop financing ads for bell's Internet service saying that Bell was breaking the law by distributing eye-catching handbills.

headline: Primary Races in Just One Legislative District
abstract: In legislative district, the 63rd House, there is competition in the primary election.  The district covers Clarion County and about a third of Armstrong County.  Three Democrats and three Republicans vying for the seat to be vacated by Democratic David Wright.  On Democratic ballots will be Gerald Borovick, a Monroe Township supervisor; Ralph Seigworth, an elementary school principal for the Clarion-Limestone School District; and Shirley Hagar, the former notary and clerk of courts for Clarion County.  On the republican ballots will be Fred McIhattan of Know, a legislative aide to Senators. Tim Shaffer and John Peterson; Greg Mortimer of Rimersburg, register and recorder for Clarion County, and Sal Mazzochi, a realtor, of Clarion.

headline: State lawmakers prise Erie school district
abstract: State House of Representatives' Education Committee received a tour of the Erie School District.  The legislators praised the school district's "innovative programs and committed educators."

headline: Speed raised on 119, 442
abstract: Lt. Louis Hutcherson, commander of the state police in Indiana, joined PennDOT District Engineer Donald R. McNeal in unveiling the 65 mph speed limit sign along the eastboind lanes of Route 422, east of the Oakland Avenue (Route 286) interchange.

headline: Wire service
abstract: Net 96 is an effort to wire America's public schools to the internet. Schools look for sponsors to purchase a $400 kit containing wire, jacks, other equipment and volunteers to design a plan.

headline: Privatization of state LCB opposed
abstract: Sabo, running for the 183rd District of the PA House is campaigning against privatization of the PA Liquor Control Board.

headline: State of Education: Pennsylvania must re-examine higher education policies
abstract: There has been no meaningful discussion on financing of higher education for the last 20 years. Higher education is engaged in a zero-sum game where this year's winners are next years losers. Governor Ridge should create a blue-ribbon commission to explore how to provide PA with a long range vision for higher education, which the state is currently lacking.

headline: State car registry fee one of lowest
abstract: Car registration is one of the cheapest ones in the U.S. An article offers statistics about situation in some other states. The situation regarding some other fees related to the vehicles is presented.

headline: Mexico, state seek trade deal
abstract: PA is negotiating with Mexico to open agricultural trade through the port of Philadelphia, which promises to be a cheaper entry point for produce headed to East Coast markets than San Diego or Houston said Mexican government officials. The article continues with more details about expectations from Mexican government officials.

headline: Profiles in Power
abstract: The article talks about most powerful players in state Capitol. Among them are governor, and many influential lawmakers. Many of them have different definition of power. An article analyzes many of them  individually. There are also some politicians that are mentioned  and that are not incumbents anymore.

headline: State report leaves school districts on edge: Panel doesn't address funding inequities
abstract: A report by a special commission appointed by Governor Tom Ridge failed to respond to the disparity between poor and rich districts. The commission was formed in response to an order from a Commonwealth Court judge, who is reviewing a lawsuit filed by 214 school districts that contend state aid is not fairly dispersed. PA ranks among the top five states for funding disparities between rich and poor school districts.

headline: Study criticizes turnpike management
abstract: The study done by Deloitte and Touche Consulting Group has said that the management and especially finance in the PA Turnpike Commission are very poorly managed. Some employees have no job descriptions, make more money than they should, are never evaluated and are promoted for no good reason. Those are only some fallacies of internal management in the Commission.

headline: Goodling criticized detainee policy
abstract: Representative Bill Goodling is speaking out against Chinese detainees at the York County Prison urging President Clinton to end the three year detention because it is embarrasing to him that the illegal immigrants are being held in the city that claims to be the first capital of the United States.

headline: Promises to keep
abstract: Bob Dole is a presidential candidate of Republican Party in the coming elections, and one of the main aims, if he gets elected, is tax cut. However, he explained at the event with Veterans of Foreign Wars that the tax cuts will not mean reduction of benefits and help to them.

headline: State's Oversight of Charter Schools Is Scant, Teachers Union Says
abstract: Charter schools operate largely outside of the public schools administrators control and some state laws that govern them are too weak. This is the opinion of national teachers union. The problem is that current laws do not hold those schools accountable for student performance, and they do not require teachers to be certified.

headline: The Ivan Itkin Turnpike
abstract: The cartoon depicts in sarcastic way the bad management of PA Turnpike Commission.

headline: 20th Congressional District
abstract: Mike McCormick or Peters announced his candidacy for the 20th Congressional Distrit. McCormick's focus will be on advocating balancing the federal budget, welfare, social security and medicare benefits.

headline: Public comes out ahead
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge signed three bills to change some practices of the Delaware River and although it may not mean much to the vast majority of Pennsylvanians the public still comes out a winner.

headline: Status quo on schools
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge had the chance to show that he is serious about education for both the rich and poor. He blew it. A Commonwealth Court judge ordered the governor to set-up a commission to study education funding in PA. The governor's proposal did not satisfy the PA Association of Rural and Small Schools. The association wants the state to eliminate local school taxes, institute a statewide 2.5 percent earned income tax and dole it out equitably.

headline: Throwing the money at a problem
abstract: Already criticized as a sanctum of political patronage and subject of a proposal to combine its functions within those of Penn DOT, the turnpike commission is on spending spree, trying to straighten malfunctioning. The commission already spent some money on consulting services and it is expected to spend even more.

headline: A closer look at each region
abstract: A map shows income inequality throughout the United States.

headline: Question of influence
abstract: Mike Fisher, newly elected highest state prosecutor got a $9,000 donation during campaign from Louis Ruscitto. Ruscitto, got a job from city of Pittsburgh to repair the bridge at Schenley Park, and the question is whether Fisher influenced somehow this decision. The case is now in the Common Pleas court.

headline: Step right this way
abstract: A bus tour through a Philadelphia public school in a struggling neighborhood, highlights the advanced abilities of the young bright students work dilgently in ther underfunded school which raises the question of how much more outstanding they would if there were more funds available to them.

headline: Thumbs Down
abstract: The badly needed widening and repaving of Route 413 in Bristol Township is off.

headline: Boys, Boys
abstract: Presidential campaigns of Clinton and Bob Dole are using some very dirt practices and words, and in all those fights, the victim is truth. Dole is accusing Clinton for highest taxes in history, while Clinton is accusing Dole for voting many times for tax increase. The problem is that both of them are using words that are away from the truth, and this is not fair because of voters.

headline: Rating judicial candidates
abstract: The new Pennsylvania Judicial Evaluation Commission,  should provide voters with more useful, credible information to help in choosing among statewide judicial candidates. Under the new system the commission will release explanations for its rating of each candidate.

headline: Student Squeeze
abstract: As Penn State fees top $10,000, debt threatens to strap public college grads. The college expenses are raised in the middle of the state legislature's pulling in the reins on funding. This is expected to have a significant impact on the number of applicants. Also these new burdens are likely to be manifested in many other ways.

headline: Tomorrow Center is one of many new concepts being evaluated for turnpike
abstract: The letter is written by executive director of PA Turnpike Commission, and he opposes previously published facts about PA Turnpike Commission and its construction of Cranberry interchange (the main issues is financing of the project). The second issue discussed is related to construction of Tomorrow Center. Some people think that building the center is waste of time, but the director thinks that the project is good one, because it supports tourism and this is second most important industry in the state.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has signed a measure allowing the public to attend meetings when local government bodies discuss filing a vacancy in an elected office.  He believes that the public should have the right to hear the discussions.

headline: Ray attacks new Specter brain tumor
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter underwent a specialized radiation therapy for a benign brain tumor regrowth, from which he had in 1993.  He stated to well-wishers that he feels fine.  The article details the medical procedure.

headline: Students felt the reform
abstract: Former Governor Robert Casey introduced a requirement for high school students: to do at least 30 hours of community service in order to graduate from a high school.

headline: Transportation for elderly funded to tune of $459,000
abstract: State grants provided by the Dept. of Transportation totaling $459,000 will help ensure that older residents of Butler, Clarion, Lawrence and Venago counties have access to low cost public transportation through the "Shared Ride" service.

headline: "Prevailing wages" hit taxpayers in wallet
abstract: Laborers in school projects are one of the biggest expenses in the school district budget because state law mandates they be paid a prevailing wage based on the collective bargaining agreements with unions and in a given region. Some Republican Party people and taxpayer groups are against this practice, but the problem is that all law proposals to deal with this issue were without success.

headline: Reed wants effort to be bipartisan
abstract: Harrisburg mayor Reed comments recent visit of presidential candidate Dole to city. Dole praised President Clinton on his standings on small business (cutting regulations referring to them), and Reed emphasized that regardless of the fact that they (Reed and Dole) can have different standings on different issues, they can agree on some issue (small business in this case).

headline: Students must have computers
abstract: State Representative Mike Veon has proposed a $2.5 billion program to put a computer on every students desk within 10 years. Some are concerned about the price tag of the proposal. The information age demands this type of investment to prevent a digital divide. As Veon says, "Can we afford not to do it?"

headline: Trash truck checks to be daily
abstract: One of every five waste hauling trucks failed a recent state inspection crackdown, prompting the industry to announce yesterday it will voluntarily inspect its trucks every day.

headline: "Worthless" session costs taxpayers plenty
abstract: PA General Assembly last week met for a couple of days, but several topics on the agenda that were discussed were completely worthless. Topics were minimum wage and telemarketing fraud measure.

headline: Reform killed in Harrisburg
abstract: In Harrisburg the influence of lobbyist and special interests groups are not as widely known leaving the public to some degree in the dark about money and its influence on legislation. Rep Allen Kukovich, a Westmoreland County Democrat has introduced campaign finance reform legislation in Harrisburg during every legislative session and to no avail this time Philadelphia Republican Georg Kenney stopped it, by calling for a statewide referendum on riverboat gambling.

headline: Study says privatizing schools hasn't worked
abstract: A study by three New York University researchers examing public policy issues were surprised with negative results showing privatizing schools had no dollar savings, no improvements in test scores and no rduction of education bureacracy.

headline: Truckers criticize Geist's toll plan
abstract: Truckers and truck stop operators are not happy with a local proposal to from local lawmakers to make Interstate 80 a toll road. They argue that the that tolling the road would drive a lot of trucks out of PA. However, there are some truckers who think the opposite way. The article lists more details about the proposal.

headline: 136th District rivals speak to the issues
abstract: Democrats in the 136th PA House District will have three candidates to choose from in the primary while Republicans have only one candidate.  The candidates are profiled.

headline: Rendell backs Fattah's urban policy bill
abstract: The American Cities Investment Act, as the bill is called, has won favorable support from across the country. Introduced by U.S. Representative Chaka Fattah (D-2nd) and co-sponsored by 25 members of Congress, including Republican U.S. Representative Chistopher Shays of Connecticut, the bill (H.R. 3349) offers a powerful financial tool to help rebuild cities nationwide.

headline: Tackling reform school by school
abstract: When Bob Shawartz, a Harvard grad whose been an educator, principal, policy advisor to a mayor and a governor and head of education programs at Pew Charitable Trust, was asked if he knew how to improve student achievement in urban areas, he said not for an entire system. There is a growing consensus that top-down systematic eduation achievement solutions are not working . A school by school approach is needed. Charter schools have focused on reaching the most difficult students. Charter schools are in 24 states, but not PA.

headline: Turnpike faces hard questions
abstract: A state representative from Allegheny County has proposed a bill that would merge the PA Turnpike Commission and state Department of Transportation. The main reason for this proposal is better efficiency and use of tax dollars. An author of the article thinks that Turnpike Commission should not be abandoned fully, but some changes related to the effectiveness can be made.

headline: 5th Dist. Hopefuls Rate Ridge, Gambling
abstract: Four Republicans and one Democrat trying to succeed retiring 5th District state Representative Jim Merry, a Republican, offered varying views of Governor Tom Ridge’s first year in Harrisburg and the proposed legalization of river-boat gambling during interviews with Erie Daily Times.  Vying for the GOP nomination are, in order of drawn ballot position, Erie County Council Chairwoman Tracy Seyfert, a professional psychologist; Conneautville businesswoman Carol Bocan, a member of the Conneaut School Board; Albion-area businessman Clayton Schulze; and Edinboro May Clifford “Kip” Allen, owner of the Edinboro Hotel.  The winner will face Democrat Bill Knupp in the November general election.

headline: Rendell lends name to Hoeffel's campaign
abstract: Democratic congressional candidate Joseph M. Hoeffel is running against freshman Republican U.S Rep. Jon D. Fox and has sought the endorsement of Governor Rendell, the mayor of Philadelphia.

headline: Teacher sabbaticals not a legislative matter
abstract: The state House Education Committee dropped the ball when it approved an amended bill restricting some teacher sabbaticals, but removed a provision granting school districts the power to make decisions. The main argument in the article is that if the state is going to mandate that teachers be granted sabbatical leaves, the state should pay for those sabbaticals.

headline: Turnpike tunnel bypass plan draws foes
abstract: Somerset County town, Berlin, in Allegheny Mountains, has a population slightly above 2,000 and those people are afraid that they are lacking the support for their voice. They think the proposed bypass PA Turnpike plan can cause water supply problems to them (the bypass would be the solution for the problems that exist with turnpike tunnel that exists near Berlin).

headline: A change in chiefs
abstract: The Supreme Court can now work on remaking itself in wake of Robert N. C. Nix Jr.'s announcement to step down at the end of the year; Justice John P. Flaherty will succeed him.

headline: Rep. Stish Agrees to Debates with Challenger Eachus
abstract: State House candidate Todd Eachus challenged incumbent Tom Stish to a debate.  Stish agreed to it.  Eachus, the Democratic challenger issued the challenge in a press release.  He wants to have 4 to 6 debates on a myriad of issues.  Stish is seeking a fifth two-year term representing the 116th Legislative District. Stish also said the number of debates would have to be negotiated.

headline: Teacher Standards Called 'National Shame': Bipartisan Commission Cites Inadequate Training, Poor Treatment
abstract: A national bipartisan commission found that about 25 percent of high school teachers lack college training in their primary classroom subject; that nearly 40 percent of math teachers are not fully qualified for their assignment ; that 500 of the nation's 1,200 education schools lack accreditation; and that three in 10 teachers quite their jobs within 5 years. Toughening teacher standards is hard due to a lack of consensus on what approach to take. The study also found that the notion that teacher unions are adamantly against reforms is a 'myth.'

headline: Turnpike would lose tax share under bill
abstract: A state senator introduced legislation to take away $42 million in annual state tax money provided to PA Turnpike Commission and use the money for local road and bridge repairs. The movement is partly motivated by recent report suggesting turnpike revenues have grown faster than operating expenses and inadequate disclosure  - in the eyes of some lawmakers.

headline: A Coattails Reversal From '94 Races
abstract: There was a time when many democrats ran from Bill Clinton now they want to be pictured side by side to him. Never before has there been a stark role reversal in the dynamic between Presidential candidates and Congressional candidates

headline: Re-politicizing of PennDOT now?
abstract: Governor Thornburgh started with policy of hiring people for state offices on the base of professionally, and not on the base on partisanship. Governor Casey (Democrat) continued that policy, but current Governor Ridge is stopping that policy, and this is apparent in recent PennDOT hiring. An author of the article argues against such a policy, and lists some examples to support his statement.

headline: Teachers air concerns about special education
abstract: Dr. Thomas Connor, superintendent, and Debra Sestili, director of pupil personnel services wallked th crowd of more than 40 teachers at a Washington School District budget workshop which turned into a forum about special education and needs of teachers and students.

headline: Wayne roads, bridges could be better if
abstract: Edward J. Coar, county's director of planning, spoke on behalf of the county commissioners in Bethlehem on the state's 12-year transportation program claiming roads and bridges could be in better shape without a gas hike if PennDOT would stop diverting millions to excessive historical, archeological and environmental studies.

headline: A Democrat for the 44th
abstract: Profiles of those running for the 44th House District are given and the paper endorses Sharon Chauvet Braun.

headline: Representative Walker lashes out at Intell for 'vendetta'
abstract: U.S. Representative Robert S. Walker outraged over articles written by Intelligencer Journal which he stated were not correct.

headline: Teachers fear unruly kids
abstract: This very long article talks about the recent rise of the violence in the schools. There is a list of recent violent incidents in the schools and the discussion with teachers, police officers and other officials about this problem. General assessment is that kids are more violent and they are coming to schools more violent. Some of the teachers are afraid to talk about this issues because they are afraid that publicizing this topic might influence their jobs.

headline: White takes up green
abstract: If winter continues as it has, Pennsylvania Department of Transportaion spokesman Steve Chizmar says projects for the year may go $20 million over budget. PennDOT faces other challenges with fatigue drivers, a dwindling salt supply and are further exploring a pilot program using solar salt.

headline: A Democrat gets stroked by the GOP
abstract: This is a satiric story about animal taken to the GOP event in Pittsburgh, as a part of Bob Dole and Kemp campaign. The article depicts in satiric way all the details from the event.

headline: Republican candidate for attorney general pulls out of race
abstract: Montgomery County District Attorney Mike Marino yesterday announced he will not seek the Republican nomination in the state attorney general race. The reason for that decision is that he is expecting not to get GOP endorsement at the January GOP state committee meeting.

headline: Test critics decry trend
abstract: The Saturday-morning test taken on October 26 of 1996 by college-bound students for 70 years, reemerges as a major factor in deciding who gets into college.

headline: Board flattens road kill proposal
abstract: Inmates at the Clarion County Jail won't be finding venison on their dinner menu, as the County Prison Advisory Board has flattened a proposal to obtain road to kill to feed jail inmates. The proposal was made to save the Prison system money but failed to be approved.

headline: A Given: Citizens Have a Right to Be Heard
abstract: In this editorial the state Senate voted to amend the state’s Open Meetings Act, also known as the Sunshine Law, specifically to include school districts.  The law was changed in 1993 to require that “political subdivisions” and their authorities provide for a “reasonable opportunity” for public comment at regular and special meetings.

headline: Republicans retain state House with large majority
abstract: An article is an analysis of recent elections, where Republicans strengthened the control of PA House. Their leaders however, did not set the agenda for the next two years.

headline: BILL FUNDS SEPARATE CLASSROOMS FOR DISRUPTIVE STUDENTS
abstract: Unruly students who disrupt class may be temporarily or permanently removed and placed in classes of their own under a bill passed unanimously by the House yesterday.  The bill, sponsored by Representative Jesse Stairs, Republican-Westomoreland, authorizes actions many school districts have already taken.

headline: TIRE RECYCLER LOST PERMIT, DEP SAYS
abstract: The state has revoked a tire recycling company's permit for a "history of noncompliance."  The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) announced that it revoked the E-Z Ship Recycling Inc.'s permit to operate the tire recycling facilties in Pennsylvania.  The state cited E-Z Ship for conducting an illegal tire processing operation at Export Tire Co. in Export from November 1996 - February 1997.

headline: Slayers' execution is stayed by judge
abstract: The murderer Bernard McGill's execution was stayed and three others on death row are expected to have their executions postponed.

headline: Legislature friends supporting Brosius
abstract: Gov. Ridge forced Charles C. Brosius to resign from Secretary of Agriculture despite support by many in the legislature.

headline: BILLS WOULD PROVIDE ACTIVITIES FOR HOME-SCHOOLED STUDENTS
abstract: School districts would be forced to open extracurricular sports, choirs, clubs and plays to home-schoolers under a pair of bills introduced in the House.  Representative Susan Laughlin, Democrat-Beaver proposed changing the state's Public School Code to prohibit exclusion of home-schoolers when it comes to sports.  Representative Mark McNaughton, Republican-Harrisburg would take it further by opening the door for home-schoolers to join school clubs, choris and bands and act in theaterical productions.  Both bills have been sent to the House Education Committee and would affect all 501 of the state's school districts.

headline: TROUT FISHING REALLY BEGINS AFTER OPENING DAY
abstract: Seasoned trout fisherman call the first day of trout season as "amateur day" because that is the day that people play at trout fishing and go out for an easy catch but will not be seen again until next year.  The seasoned fisherman think the best fihsing is often June-July.  The Fish and Boat Commission has determined that there is a certain segment of the license-buying public that enjoys fishing for trout as soon ast he fish are taken from the stocking truck.  Therefore, to provide a "put and take" fishing experience, some Saturday trout stockings are planned.

headline: Some gave all
abstract: 85 state troopers will be honored at the State Police Academy in Hershey. They will each be dedicated on the Memorial Wall.

headline: Lessons in losing Congress race
abstract: The election system is based on perceptions, not issues, and how much money a candidate can raise. The money used for campaigns could be put to better use.

headline: BILLS:  LET PUBLIC IN ON TEACHER PACTS
abstract: The Legislature is considering two bills to allow more public knowledge about "early bird" teacher contracts, in which a district and teachers reach an agreement before most taxpayers understand the implications.  A measure introduced this week by Senator Melissa Hart, Republican-McCandless,w ould require 72-hour notice of school board meetings where a vote on a teachers' contract will occur.  The other bill, which would open negotations to the public, is being sponsored by Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer, Republican-Altoona.

headline: TURKEY SEASON IS ADJUSTED IN PENNSYLVANIA
abstract: The 1997-98 hunting seasons approved by the Pennsyvlania Game Commission include changes in the fall turkey season and in a special youth hunt for squirrels.  The change in the turkey season is designed to eliminate confusion among sportsmen about dates.  Rather than wait until the last minute to announce changes in turkey season, they are making a more liberal turkey season all together.

headline: SPECIAL INTERESTS PACK PUNCH
abstract: State Representative Greg Vital, 166th District writes an opinion column talking about a major piece of tort reform legislation The bill was drafted by lobbyists for the Pennsylvania Medical Society and Pennsylvania Trial Lawyers' Association and was first presented to the House two hours before the vote.  Vital suggests that legislators did not even consider the needs of the taxpaying public.  He believes that mindset reflects the excessive influence of special interest groups in Harrisburg.

headline: Luck of draw prevails in glare of publicity
abstract: The glare of television camera lights caused the numbers for the lottery to be misread. The Pennsylvania lottery did not pay for any incorrect number winners.

headline: Boosting the arts
abstract: The National Endowment for the Arts has made questionable funding choices, but does many worthwhile projects. Proposed legislation wants to dismantle the NEA, but two congressmen are working to preserve it.

headline: VOLANT MARKS 32ND YEAR OF TROUT RELEAST IN NESHANNOCK CREEK
abstract: Volant will observe two events Saturday that have made the first Saturday in March the community's own unique holiday for the past 32 years.  The date traditionally is the day the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission stock the Neshannock Creek with a variety of trout in preparation of the opening day of trout season April 12.  This event has become a popular spectator event since it began in 1965.  Saturday is also the day that the Volant Volunteer Fire Company hosts the semi-annual all-day pancake and sausage fare at their firehall.

headline: State Bar Association condemns death penalty
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Bar Association sees capital punishment as discriminatory and not applied fairly.

headline: MAHER BEST CHOICE FOR THE LEGISLATURE
abstract: This editorial recommends that John Maher, the Republican candidate be elected to fill the state House seat left open by the death of Representative Albert Pettit, 40th Legislative District which comprises Peters Township, Upper St. Clair and parts of Bethel Park.

headline: BUREAUCRACIES DON'T EDUCATE KIDS
abstract: A state's commission's report on how to put children first in Pennsylvania's urban schools makes 17 recommendations, many of them good.  Most of them deal directly with what children learn, how to compare the progress of children, and schools and who is to be held accountable and how.  But other recommendations do not make sense and fail to recognize that inadequate funding is a critical problem for Children Achieving.

headline: VOLUNTEERS ACCOMPLISH GOAL:  REMOVE TIRES FROM RIVERBED
abstract: Recently, thousands of discarded tires were discovered along the west bank of the Susquehanna River in the vicinity of the Black Diamond Bridge, on the Edwardsville side of the river.  Hundreds of volunteers answered the call for help in cleaning up the mess.  The clean up drew about 150 people and was coordinated by the Riverfront Parks Committee.  Community members, the Luzerne County Correctional Facility, the State Correctional Institution at Retreat, the Susquehanna River Watch, and Edwardsville Borough removed about 1,500 tires that were filled with mud and silt.  State Representative Standly Jarolin (D-119th) is asking Governor Ridge for $10,000 in emergency grant money to recycle or dispose of the tires.

headline: State begins hotline giving parents' criminal background
abstract: A woman whose ex husband killed her two children created a hotline to help parents obtain information about criminal charges of other parents.

headline: Maher drops bid for Supreme Court seat
abstract: A law school professor asked Governor Ridge to be removed from the running for a spot on the state Supreme Court.

headline: CAPITAL AREA INTERMEDIATE UNIT GETS STATE GRANT
abstract: The Capital Area Intermediate Unit was among the 43 charter school planning-grant recipients announced yesterday by Governor Tom Ridge.  The $21,000 grant is the second awared to the Intermediate Unit.  The first, a $15,000 grant was awared in January and was intended to help the intermediate unit plan and develop a new arts magnate school for the region's students.

headline: VOLUNTEERS BRAVE COLD WATER TO STOCK TROUT
abstract: On Thursday, the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission led a convoy of about 20 vehicles, mostly volunteers, to help disperse 5,400 fish into Bull Creek.  The high, swift waters were 10-12 inches above normal but that did not stop volunteers from wading into the creeks with hip waders in water termperatures of 42 degrees.

headline: State court bucks a step closer
abstract: There will be a multiyear phase-in for funding of county and local courts which could save Philadelphia millions a year.

headline: McDade's legal bills continue to accumulate
abstract: McDade was aquitted of bribery charges, but his legal fees are still large. He has used campaign contributions and rewarded contracts to help pay his legal fees.

headline: CARONE SAYS BAD TEACHERS MUST IMPROVE
abstract: Representative Robert Godshall, Republican-Montgomery County and Representative Pat Carone, Republican-Lancaster suggest it is unfair to blame teachers for failures of the public education system.  Godsall said that most of all, parental responsibility is sorely lacking.  Carone agrees with the Ridge administration that the state needs to re-examine how well Pennsylvania universities are preparing college students to become teachers.

headline: VOLUNTEERS MAKE A CLEAN SWEEP OF AREA WATERWAYS
abstract: Volunteers conducted a River Sweep in Southwestern Pennsylvania according to Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) staff.  Five sites in Washington County were selected for the cleanup.  In all, the nine-year-old sweep follows 2,700 miles of the Ohio River watershed through six states.  More than 1200 volunteers worked in Pennsyvlania and collected more than 55 tons of trash, including 300 tires.

headline: State FOP reiterates radar-gun, cancer link
abstract: The Fraternal Order of Police believe that radar guns can cause health issues and are opposed to allowing local police use them.

headline: McHale urges remembering 'other' America
abstract: US Representative Paul McHale wants us to remember that even in this time of a strong economy there are plenty of Americans that are poor and hungry.

headline: Casey to kick off voluntary audit of Millcreek schools
abstract: Auditor General will start off a performance review of Millcreek School District by holding a town meeting and informational session. Millcreek is one of twelve school districts looking to gain more from each dollar.

headline: Water rates vary with settlement
abstract: Scranton are residents will receive a lower water bill because of the settlement of the Pennsylvania-American Water Company's rate-hike case. Other areas of the state would see an increase, some as high as 17 percent.

headline: State fults Lancaster officials in abused infant's death
abstract: A baby was killed and raped by his mother's boyfriend.  The state Office of Children , Youth and Families said it will conduct a performance audit of Lancaster County's Children & Youth Services because of the incident.

headline: Miss. Deal raises Pa. cut, official says
abstract: Mississippi received a larger than expected settlement against the tobacco industry which caused the estimates for a settlement for Pennsylvania to increase.

headline: CEASE FIRE - CCBC LEGAL WARS CAN BE AVOIDED
abstract: The Community College of Beaver County and two school districts have gone to court over sponsorship-related issues.  This opinion piece calls for the county commissioners to have the power to remedy this situation instead of taking it throught he courts.

headline: WATER SAMPLES REVIEWED
abstract: State environmental officials are reviewing hundreds of samples from water supplies and underground fuel storage tanks throughout the region because of allegations that testing at an East Stroudsburg company was done incorrectly or falsified.  Hess Environmental Laboratories blames a former employee for the problems and says it is cooperating with an investigation by the U.S. attorney's office and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in Philadelphia.  Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) officials said it is too soon to say whether public health may have been affected.

headline: State House sends fetal homicide bill to Ridge.
abstract: Gov. Ridge is expected to sign a bill governing making fetal homicide a crime.  The state House approved the bill  171-23.

headline: MR. CLINTON'S BLOW FOR REFORM
abstract: President Clinton threatened to call a special session if Congress adjourned without acting on campaign finance reform.  Democrats and Republicans reached an agreement permitting a vote on the McCain-Feingold reform legislation as early as next month.  Mr. Clinton had a selfish motive to deflect attention from the Justice Department's investigation into the White House telephone solicitations by himself or Vice-President Gore.  The drive for reform should not deflect attention away from an impartial investigation into whether the President or anyone else violated exisiting laws last year.

headline: CHALLENGES ABOUND IN URBAN EDUCATION, LOCAL OFFICIALS TELL PANEL
abstract: New City schools Superintendent Dale Frederick testified before the Urban Education Commission which will make its recommendations to the state legislature in January.  Commission members challenged city school officials to tell them about programs that work.  Frederick advised them that quality and safety are the two issues that dominate urban education.

headline: WORK TO BEGIN SHORTLY ON CREEK
abstract: Work to rehabilitate the lower portion of Sterry Creek including the replacement of the Constitution Avenue Bridge could begin any day.  The project's designer, David Greenfield of the Bureau of Abandoned Mine Reclamation in the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (EPA) said the contractor has been given permission to start the project.

headline: State man charged in school bond case
abstract: An investment adviser hid the losses of 75 school districts that invested in municipal bonds from his company.

headline: Murtha taking threats on himself seriously
abstract: Donald Lee Fenton threatened US Representative John Murtha. Representative Murtha did not use to take threats seriously but does now.

headline: CHANGING MINDS
abstract: Outside Turner Elementary School in Wilkinsburg swirls the debate over whether the public school can be run by a private company.  But inside the walls, Alternative Public Schools of Nashville continues to build its version of an urban elementary school for about 375 pupils.  Known as the Turner Initative, the program includes an extended school year that only ended on Thursday.Two years ago, the Wilkinsburg school board signed a five-year contract for the for-profit company to run the school, including ousting the union teachers and hiring its own staff.

headline: WORKERS PULL COAL CARS FROM RIVER
abstract: Workers pulled four coal-filled rail cars out of the Susquehanna River after they fell into the river whena  section of the Rockville Bridge crumbled and part of an 82-car freight train derailed.  The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the derailment which dumped 500 tons of coal into the river.  The derailment also ruptured a fuel line on the bridge which dumped an unknown amount of diesel fuel into the river - anywhere from 600 to 9,000 gallons.  Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) officials say there is no evidence that the fuel or coal harmed the fish or waterfowl.

headline: State police crime lab may close
abstract: A study suggests that the state police should close six crime labs located throughout the state. Those working at the Lawrence Park lab are concerned about their job safety.

headline: Musham saga reflects Democratic woes to woo candidates
abstract: Bettye Martin Musham considered running for governor, but quickly changed her mind. The Democrats still do not have a viable candidate for the race in 1998.

headline: CHARTER SCHOOL APPLICATIONS REQUIRE CAREFUL CONSIDERATION BY SCHOOL BOARDDS
abstract: According to Thomas Gentzel, assistance executive director, governmental and member relations, of the PA School Boards Association, commentaries alleging that school boards are stifling charter schools is unfair.  Contrary to this supposition, the PSBA supported the enactment of a charter school law because it would create a means of providing these new public schools with more flexibility.  PSBA did not support ACT 22 of 1997 which allows charter schools because of technical deficiencies.

headline: 2 PUC judges in Peco case are replaced
abstract: The Public Utility Commission dismissed two judges who were not valuing the public's opinion in the Peco Energy case.

headline: State police leader scans high tech
abstract: The State Police Commissioner is finding new ways of fighting crime with new high-technology.

headline: NAYSAYERS:  STEP IN WRONG DIRECTION
abstract: Four local lawmakers voted "no" to the charter school bill that passed the House last week, although at least two say they support the concept.  Republicans Steven Nickol of Hanover, Todd Platts of Springettsburg, and Bruce Smith of Dillsburg and Democrat Stephen Stetler of York, were among the 57 members of the state House who voted against the charter schoos.  The measure passed 137-57.  The naysayers believe the bill usurps the authority of local school boards.  This bill removed the authority from the local level and gave the responsibility to the state, according to Representive Stetler.

headline: CHARTER SCHOOL EYED FOR SOUTHERN COLUMBIA AREA SCHOOL DISTRICT
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge and the state legislature approved charter schools for Pennsylvania to strengthen public education.  Southern Columbia Area School District Director Guiy Schlesinger announced during the board's work session that the Central Susquenhanna Intermediate Unit (CSIU) has taken the first initiative in the area to establish a charter school with SusQ-Cyber Charter School.  With SusQ-Net, the CSIU will be able to transmit classroom instructions to the consortium schools through telecommunications equipment.

headline: 3 firms drop parts of electric pilot
abstract: Three companies who had previously signed up for the electric competition pilot have now dropped out of the residential programs. There are various reasons for the three companies to drop out of the program.

headline: State police to assist borough officers
abstract: The Borough of Greencastle does not have enough local policemen so the State Police will assist the borough with police duties.

headline: Nearly ousted in scandal, she is now judging other judges
abstract: Esther R. Sylvester, who previously had extortion charges against her dismissed, was appointed to the judicial discipline system.

headline: CHARTER SCHOOL MEETS DEADLINE
abstract: The Armstrong School District now has in hand the application for a charter school within the district presented by the Community Dedicated Charter School Group.  The group is dedicated to providing a community-oriented lifelong learning environment for grades 6-12 and the school will most likely be located in the former Worthington High School now being used as a community center.

headline: 3 GPU plants are up for sale
abstract: GPU Genreation will sell its non-nuclear generation unit due to the deregulation of the electric utitlity. GPU believes most of the jobs will be retained by the new owner.

headline: State Supreme Court may decide high-tech issue
abstract: A Supreme Court will hear a case that relates to various laws on police searches including the use of high-tech heat sensors.

headline: Network a bias culprit
abstract: Top congressional aides tend to be males because of the friendships they have with the politicans. Other say that more woman congressmen will lead to more female top congressional aides, but the editors believe this change will be too slow.

headline: CHARTER SCHOOLS BILL RAISES QUESTIONS
abstract: A quick survey of parents, school board members and administrators shows there is support for the idea of charter schools in the Valley but that unanswered questions overshadow optimism about the proposal.  Undera  bill which Governor Tom Ridge is expected to sign into local law, local school boards may opt to create charter schools that give emphasis to a chosen curriculum.  But even though local taxpayers would foot the bill for the charter school, the school board's control over it ends with approving the charter.  The school board would not control day-to-day operations including things such as the classes taught, length of school day or year, and who teaches.

headline: Activist urges PUC to educate public
abstract: An environmental activist feels the Public Utility Commission is not doing everything it can to educate the public on the electric competition program that is being conducted.

headline: State to construct DNA laboratory in Westmoreland
abstract: Governor Ridge has plans to build a DNA laboratory to help the state police with sexual crimes.

headline: New Coal Queen meets the House
abstract: The Coal Queen Sondra Hambrosky was introduced to the House by her representative Lawrence Roberts.

headline: CHARTER SCHOOLS NOT ABOUT ELITISM
abstract: A new report by the U.S. Department of Education might move forward the debate on charter schools in Pennsylvania.  The report shows that about half the pupils in 428 charter schools in 25 states are minority pupils.  The study found that charter schools are popular with low-income parents because the schools are not allowed to charge additional tuition.  Charter schools might be useful to improve the quality of education for at-risk pupils in public school.

headline: Bailing out on the public
abstract: Despite being considered 'mortal enemies,' Senator Vince Femo and PECO Energy have a proposed deal to help PECO reclaim part of the $6.7 billion in stranded costs they have lost.

headline: State troopers now share county and interstate duties
abstract: State police troopers who use to only be responsible for itnerstate duties will now take on investigating and other police matters.

headline: New Sunshine Act would radiate light
abstract: A new updated version of the Sunshine Act is expected to be voted on by the state House of Representatives. The editors approve the new version of the law.

headline: CHARTER SCHOOLS WILL TAKE WORK
abstract: Pennsylvania has approved legislation authorizing the establishment of charter schools.  The charter school law presents an exciting new opportunity for students, parents and educators who may want to choose educational approaches which may not be available or appropriate in other schools in their school district.  The charter school law also presents an opportunity for Sugar Valley to remain an isolated educational community.

headline: Blackout hits Pa.'s report on utilities
abstract: The Public Utility Commission releases a yearly report card on Pennsylvania's utilities. This year the report is being altered due to the utilities continuing to limit the amount of information the public can know.

headline: Sticky issue over amendment
abstract: A proposed amendment to the constitution allowing videotaped testimony of minors and to eliminate the defendant's right to face his accuser was approved by the public in a referendum and is now being taken up by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. Some lawyers feel that the two ideas should have been separate referendums.

headline: No big winners in state court contests
abstract: The Pennsylvania court races were split between Democrats and Republicans even though Democrats were expected to fair well.

headline: CHESTER UPLAND MANDATES ATHLETE DRUG TESTING
abstract: The Chester Upland School District has become the first in the Philadelphia area to require mandatory random drug testing for student athletes.  A spokeswoman for the Pennsylvania School Boards Association said that she knew of five amonth the 501 school districts in Pennsylvania, none in southeastern Pennsylvania that required mandatory drug testing.

headline: Consumers will soon get power to choose electric company
abstract: PECO Energy customers will soon be able to choose which company they can receive their electricity from.

headline: The Mercury News Comes Clean
abstract: The San Jose Mercury News admitted that its articles claiming the CIA was involved in a drug trade were below the newspapers standards and apologized to its customers.

headline: No governor, Senate races for Singel
abstract: Former Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel will not challenege Governor Tom Ridge in the upcoming gubernatorial race, but will run for a spot on the US Senate.

headline: CHURCH-STATE DIVIDE NARROWED
abstract: In keeping with its recent trend of lowering the wall between Church and State, a narrowly divided U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school teachers may provide remedial education to students in parochial institutions.  The court reversed a 12-year-old decision forbidding taxpayer-funded teachers to tutor children in religious schools.

headline: Co-ops plan electricity choice effort
abstract: Two of Pennsylvania's rural electric cooperatives will have their own pilot program similar to the program now in place for the major electric companies in Pennsylvania.

headline: The Real Story
abstract: Eliot Ness was a crime fighter in Chicago, but spent the end of his life in Pennsylvania.

headline: OBITUARIES:  Kay Wright, former state education chief
abstract: Kay Wright, 61, of Chestnut Hill, former acting state secretary of education died Friday.  Wright, served as state commissioner of basic education in 1984, was appointed secretary of education in 1986 by then Governor Dick Thornburgh to replace a secretary that resigned.  She served for six months until the end of Thornburgh's second term.

headline: CLINTON TAKES GOVERNORS TO TASK OVER EDUCATION
abstract: With his major education initiative stalled in the statehouses, President Clinton lashed out at the nation's governors for "dragging their feet" on improving school standards and began bypassing them by signing up some of the largest cities for his new testing program.  Clinton's vision of a nationwide series of tests in reading and math to improve achievement in an increasingly global marketplace depends largely on the cooperation of officals outside Washington.  Clinton has tried to persuade state leaders to voluntarily adopt his testing regime.  However, more than six months after first issued his challenge in his State of the Union address, he has enlisted only six states for such testing.  One of the cities participating is Philadelphia.

headline: Critics say PECO cut is too small
abstract: PECO Energy will cut its electricity rates by 4 percent, but others want them to reduce their rate by at least 30 percent.

headline: They want justice for their sister
abstract: The killer of Sandra Lindsay and five others is still on death row ten years after conviction. Efforts are being made to change his sentencing, but the relatives of Sandra Lindsay are pushing for his execution.

headline: Officials optimistic, realistic about iron works
abstract: The Cambria Iron Works project was approved to be a part of Governor Ridge's budget. Those involved are encouraged, but realize that state legislators now will have to work towards getting money released for the project.

headline: Closing arguments set Sept. 8 for schools' suit
abstract: The closing arguments for 200 school disticits who are suing the state is scheduled for September 8th.

headline: Crutchfield says she'll stay at PUC another month
abstract: Lisa Crutchfield had said she was going to leave her position on the Public Utility Commission at the end of the month, but has decided to stay on for another month.

headline: Townships ready to balk at bill for police
abstract: The new budget would require municipalities with a population of 9000 or more to pay for state police protection.The 23 municipalities are banding together to avoid paying the charge.

headline: Openness is still the best policy
abstract: First Lady Hillary Clinton's health task force meeting in 1993 was ruled that it should have been opened to the public. A judge fined the government four years later for not opening it to the public. The fine came four years too late and did not benefit the public.

headline: COLONIAL DISCUSSES WRITING CHARTER SCHOOL POLICY
abstract: Colonial School District School Board Vice-President Jack Pinheiro would like the district to write up a policy for future applicants of charter schools.  He recently attended a conference of the Pennsylvania School Board Association (PSBA) which recommended school districts have such a policy in place.

headline: Deregulation foes hope to fuel cause
abstract: The grassroots coalition for industry, labor, and consumer groups will have a summit in Washington DC to try to slow the pace of industry deregulation.

headline: U.S. courts lack authority to declare local convicts 'innocent'
abstract: "Friend of the court" brief filed by Attorney General Mike Fisher criticizes the federal government for overturning the conviction of Lisa Michelle Lambert. She was convicted by the local courts in Lancaster.

headline: OUT OF THE INKWELL - THANKS GOVERNOR
abstract: This is a political cartoon that depicts Governor Ridge with a large pen dipping it into an inkwell.  The pen is entitled, "veto" and hooked on the end of the pen is a "third party candidate."  The State G.O.P. is standing on the opposite side of the inkwell being splashed with ink.  The inkwell is entitled, "Excessive Burdens on the 1998 Ballot."

headline: COMMUNITY COLLEGES NEED STATE BOARD
abstract: When Pennsylvania approved the formation of community colleges in the 1960s, it established a three-way funding formula:  one-third by the state, a thrid from the sponsoring community, and a third from the students in the form of tuition.  The role of community colleges has changes sinced then and the formula is no longer adequately supporting many of the programs.  The state's 15 community colleges service about 400,000 students each year.  But the state subsidy only covers the education of just more than 71,000 full-time students.  If enrollment drops below projection, the community colleges must reimburse the state and this year the giveback may be $5.2 million.  To complicate matters, local support has shrunk to twenty percent of costs which has forced tuition to rise to about 40 percent of cost.  Educators and lawmakers are in discussion in regard to correcting the problem.  One step is a proposal to form a statewide community college board.

headline: Electric-choice pilot plan defended
abstract: Dusquesne Light Company backs its proposal for the deregulation of the electric industry. The pilot program for electrical competition would allow Dusquesne customers to save 10 percent.

headline: UNIT INSTANTLY ANALYZES BLOOD
abstract: The State Police have purchased 17 cell-phone-sized instruments called Intoximetere RBT IV so troopers can conduct breath tests on the roadway.  The portable devices cost about $2,000 each.  Until now, troopers have been using a desktop machine called an Intoxilyzer.  The department is seeking federal and state funds to purchase more Intoximeteres.

headline: Pa. attorney general eyes Saidel payment
abstract: An investigation is being conducted into City Controller Jonathan Saidel's campaign check given to his aide and girlfriend for the purchase of a luxury home.

headline: COMMUNITY COLLEGES NEED SUPPORT
abstract: President Clinton has proposed an education program that calls for every qualitifed student to complete at least two years at the post-secondary level.  This goal is reachable with a sound community college system.  Pennsylvania's community college system has funding problems that challenge its ability  to meet such need and the funding problem is fundamental.  Members of the state Board of Education testified before the Pennsylvania House and called the system "fragile" and in need of an overall.

headline: Electricity war has plenty of sizzle
abstract: The Public Utilities Commission heard proposals from PECO Energy and Enron Corporation about providing electricity to southeastern Pennsylvania. The competition between the two is bitter.

headline: Violent crime down, no thanks to three strikes
abstract: The three-strikes law is harsh in states like California. The state Supreme Court ruled against the rigidness and now the law be altered to  only include repeat violent or serious offenders.

headline: Pa. Democrats on the run
abstract: There are various factors that have caused the Democratic Party to not be able to field a candidate against Governor Ridge and Senator Specter. Ridge and Specter are excellent campaginers and fund-raisers. The cost of challenging an incumbent is extremely high.

headline: Conduct surprise inspections of day care centers in Pa.
abstract: Proposed legislation that would require unannounced inspections of day cares has a good chance of being passed and should be supported.

headline: Electricity, telephone services to be offered
abstract: Allegheny Power Systems plans to offer telephone services as well as electricity. It hopes the combination will allow it to retain most of its customers after the deregulation of the electric utility.

headline: W-B lauds decrease in crime
abstract: Wilkes-Barre crime rate dropped after a harsh year the year before. New aggressive programs are cited for the reason.

headline: PANEL RECOMMENDS STIFFER RULES ON DISCLOSURE FOR STATE LOBBYISTS
abstract: A legislative panel unanimously agreed to stiffen public-disclosure rules for lobbyists and sent the bill to the Senate for an expected vote.  Under the measure, lobbyists and lobbyist firms will have to register with and report their expenditures to the State Ethics Commission, except lobbyists who earn less than $2,500 per quarter and those firms that spend less than $2,500 per quarter.  Critics believe the rules should be toughened.  The bill will repeal the 1961 Lobbying Registration and Regulation Act which requires lobbyists to report expenditures but contains loopholes.

headline: CONSULTANT:  GNA SHOULD TRY TO AVOID STATE TAKEOVER
abstract: Nick Staresinic, a state educational consultant working with Sto-Rox and Clairton school districts, both distressed and locaed in the western portion of the state, addressed a group of Greater Nanticoke Area (GNA) School District parents, residents, students and officials at Luzern County Community College.  Staresinic told the audience that life under a board of control would be a very painful solution and best avoided if possible.  If a board takes over, there will be a total budget reconfiguation, the board can control raised taxes; cut programs, staff, and all transportation except for special education students.  Every sports program would be cut and students will use out-of-date textbooks because new ones will not be ordered.  Students can also be consolidated to one building.  He notes that a control board will take complete control of purse strings.

headline: Electric choice: What's deal on watts?
abstract: The state's CHOICE program is not consumer-friendly. Electricity providers are allowed to provide services to various areas, but most do not offer residential services in many areas.

headline: 'Weed-seed' plan touted
abstract: "Weed and Seed" program aims to control crime and improve high crime neighborhoods.

headline: Pennsylvania got less from U.S. in '96
abstract: Pennsylvania was the only state in the midwest and northeast that received less funding from the fedearl government in 1996.

headline: CONTINUE EDUCATION FOR TEACHERS
abstract: The state House Education Committee will continue its debate on legislation to require continuing professional development for Pennsylvania's approximately 100,000 public school teachers.  Currently, public school teachers receive their permanent teaching certificate once they have taught successfully for three years and have earned twenty-four credits beyond their bachelors degree.  After that there is no requirement for teachers to continue their professional development.  House Bill 159 would require teachers to complete either 12 college credits, 12 district-approved credits or 360 hours of professional activities (or a combination of the three) every five years to maintain an active teacher certificate.  The legislation sponsored by Representative Joe Conti, Republican, Bucks is expected to be heavily amended.

headline: Electric deregulation full of promise, but consumers will just have to wait
abstract: Deregulation is usually a positive, but has its drawbacks. The deregulation of the electricity industry can be seen as a good thing, but at the moment is confusing.

headline: WILLIAMS ASKS STATE GRANTS FOR FIRE FIGHTING SAFETY EQUIPMENT
abstract: Volunteer fire companies could be eligible for $5,000 state grants to purchase safety equipment under legislation co-sponsored by Pennsylvania Representative Connie Williams (D-149).  The one-time grants are only to be used to purchase safety equipment and are one-time grants.

headline: PENNSYLVANIA PROBES OVERSIGHT OF GIRARD COLLEGE
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives has begun an investigation into the Board of City Trusts and its administration of Girard College and will hold hearings in January.  The House Judiciary Committee chairman, Thomas P. Gannon, Republican-Delaware said he received a written request from House Majority Leader John M. Perzel, Republican-Philadelphia.  Perzel said that a series of incidents have raised serious questions about how the board is being run.  Board members said they welcome a state investigation and were confident in the results. Girard, reputed to be the wealthiest man in American when he died in 1831, left the bulk of his estate to building a boarding school for fatherless children in North Philadelphia.

headline: COUNCIL, SCHOOL SYSTEM:  A NEW UNITY
abstract: City Council opened hearings into the school district budget with the usual animosity between the two sides refocused on a different villain - the state.  Both sides say a new unity was forged by last week's announcement that the city will sue the state to change the way it funds schools.  The suit seeks $52.8 million for the next fiscal year and millions more after that, charges that the state has shortchanged the district since 1991 when its funding formula changed from a per-capita system to one based on property values and income levels.

headline: Electric deregulation may mean better deals
abstract: The Public Utility Commission is allowing 5 percent of the electric consumers the option of choosing their electric company. The savings could be up to 10 percent annually.

headline: York initiates effort to arrest serious crime
abstract: Law enforcement from every level is sending more officers to high crime neighborhoods to crack down on serious crime.

headline: PENNSYLVANIA PROFESSORS EARN TOP PAY
abstract: Full professors at the 14 state-owned universities earn high salaries when compared to other state-owned schools.  Last week, the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education Board of Governors approved a three-year contract with the Association of State College and University Faculties.  The contract for the 5,500-member union freezes wages the frist year and calls for raises of 2 and 3 percent in the following years.  The average salary in 1996 for full professors at the 14 universities was $72,000.  The base salary was $58,205.  The American Association of University Professors ranks the salaries earned by Pennsylvania's professors in the 98th percentile when compared with institutions across the country.

headline: DETAILS SLOW CHARTER SCHOOLS
abstract: The concept of independent public schools created and operated by parents, teachers, or business people is one that the Pittsburgh school an union officials find intriguing.  Board President Ron Suber is worried that charter schools will drain state funds from regular city public schools.  Albert Fondy, President of the Pittsburgh Federation of Teachers believes that some groups will try to use charter schools to circumvent teacher contracts and to establish schools with extreme, separatist agendas.

headline: Enron trying to 'prostitute' Pa. regulation, Peco says
abstract: Peco Energy refuses to make a deal with Enron. Enron wants to become the electric supplier for anyone in the area that does not choose a supplier when the competition begins.

headline: Access to justice requires legal aid funding
abstract: There is popular support for tax dollars to be used to pay for legal aid for the poor; however, Congress does not support this measure and cut the funding of Legal Services Corporation.

headline: Peterson ready for Congress
abstract: John Peterson and Joseph Pitts, former Pennsylvania legislators, were sworn into Congress.

headline: DRESS CODE MIGHT HELP IN SCHOOLS
abstract: School dress codes are back on the table in the State legislature and though they might not be for everyone, it makes sense fo rthe state to allow them.

headline: Enron's electricity rate plan greeted by questions
abstract: Enron wants to play a major role in the electricity business in Philadelphia and promises to greatly reduce electricity rates. This caused smixed reviews.

headline: Advocates to talk to Philly's homeless
abstract: Project HOME will conduct a survey from the homeless in Philadelphia about welfare reform and shelter services.

headline: PETERSON WORKS TO ENSURE ACCESS TO HIGHER EDUCATION
abstract: John Peterson, U.S. Representative, Republican from the 5th District, has hired a veteran Washington staff, rented a spartan apartment and settled in on Washington but says his heart is still in Pennsylvania.  He denies that he intends to become a "Washingtonian" and stated that he and his family are local and will remain so.  He reiterated his tops goals to included improving educational resources in his district, protecting rural interests in health care reform and seeking more highway improvement assistance.

headline: Early intervention programs for children are too important to shortchange
abstract: Funding for early intervention programs for the development of infants and toddlers with disabilities will be cut under the governor's plan to get out of the federal EI program.

headline: Erie GPU customers to take part in deregulation program
abstract: Roughly 5 percent of GPU customers in Erie will be allowed to try a new pilot program which will give them the opportunity to shop around for their electricity.

headline: Domestic violence presents welfare dilemma
abstract: States are worried that if they waive the requirements of new welfare legislation for abused women they will put themselves at risk of losing millions of federal dollars.

headline: Phone books criticized
abstract: State Representative Donald Synder feels the current phone book is inadequate and is missing some government agency numbers. He wants GTE to issue new ones.

headline: EDUCATION COSTS RISE TOO FAST
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Goodling, Republican-Seven Valleys has a soft spot for education.  When Republicans gained control of Congress in 1994, Goodling elevated to the chairmanship of the House Education and Workforce Committee.  This year, the committee will look at how to curb college tuition costs without sacrificing quality.  The costs of higher education have escalated far in excess of the rise in income in America.  A General Accounting Office Study of public four-year colleges found that tuition rose 234% between 1980-81 and 1994-95, almost three times as much as median household income in that period.  Goodling's committee will explore whether the government, through its programs to make higher education affordable is the culprit for such a rise.  When someone else is picking up the tab, are administrators and parents as cost conscious as they should be?  In Pennsylvania, the state gave millions to Penn State University and other state-related schools, and they don't have to itemize how it is spent.  This is wrong.

headline: Fumo gets Peco to cut rates
abstract: Peco will cut their rates by 10 percent if the company would be allow to recover '$5 billion in underperforming assets.' State Representative Vicent Fumo sued Peco after their attempt to reorganize.

headline: Helping flood victims
abstract: Paradise Elementary School filled an 18-wheeler with clothing, shoes, health care items, and toys for those affected by the floods in Ohio.

headline: Plevel: 'I'm not going to resign'
abstract: A number of Beaver County row officers are calling for the resignation of the Democractic Party Chairman in order to 'bolster their power base for the 1999.'

headline: EDUCATION FORUM SLATED FOR SUNDAY
abstract: The issue of values and character education in public schools will be the topic of discussion at an area church.  Allison United Methodist Church is hosting the discussion which will feature speaker James Noseworthy, a United Methodist Church official and an expert on public policy issues and education.  A panel of local educators will discuss the issues and answer questions from the floor.  The panel includes Robert P. Miller, superintendent of South  Middletown  School District; Mara Donaldson, professor of religion at Dickinson College; Ann Cook, teacher of gifted students in Carlisle Area School District; and state Representative Al Masland, Republican-199.

headline: Gathering fees could be explosive legislative issue
abstract: Gathing fees are put together for one price for gas customers; however, with the deregulation of the gas utility, these fees might be broken up and could cost consumers more.

headline: Saved from the brink
abstract: Legal aliens in Pennsylvania will still receive their welfare benefits despite reform to have their benefits cut.

headline: POLITICS STAND IN THE WAY OF CUTTING EDUCATION COSTS
abstract: David Rhone, a former deputy superintendent of a surburban Philadelphia school district states that politicians only make recommendations that are politically motivated and thus do not cut education costs.  His opinion is based upon the state hearings of the House Select Committee on Higher Education which consisted of five members (3 Republicans and 2 Democrats).  He stated that the majority report (Republican) made several recommendations that if implemented would have saved money; however, the minority report (Democrat) avoided any recommendations for savings, had no accountability, or future goals, only "meaningless political comments."

headline: EDUCATION NEEDS NEW FUNDING
abstract: Senator Allyson Schwartz, Democrat-Philadelphia proposes that enacting a new funding system for education is necessary.  She states that state mandates must be accompanied by adequate funding.

headline: George asks PUC for electric bill refunds
abstract: State Representative Camille George is trying to get back money for volunteer fire companies and seniors who paid more than the law required for electricity.

headline: SCHOOL BREAKFAST IDEA SHOULD GROW
abstract: About two decades, when the costs of providing food stamps to welfare recipients began to soar,w e offered the suggeston that instead of giving the equivalent of cash to people who needed food, we should just give them food.  We couched our suggestions in the context of reviving soup kitchens.  And we were criticized from those that said we robbed people of their dignity.  We were outgunned in the days of liberal ascendancyh when most Americans were convinced that the "Great Society" would eradicate poverty.  Today we know better and have hit on an idea that draws praise from recipients and providers alike and that idea is school breakfasts.  Not all youngers who need school breakfasts are from poverty and may just be from working families.  Surprisingly there has been little crticism of school breakfast programs on the grounds they are demeaning.  Food stamps may be useful for families whose misfortune takes them out of the self-supporting category because of illness or emergency but for people whose upbringing has not included the knowledge or the habit of good nutrition, food stamps are not what is needed.  Food is what is needed.  We like school breakfasts becausee they deal in honesty and if food is needed, food is provided.

The Commission recognized that Pulice did not intend to transgress the Ethics Law but that intent is not required to sustain a violation.  They further said they will take no further action. In addition to a highly publicized 11-county question on raising the sales tax a half cent for seven years to finance sports stadiums and economic development projects, there are three state-wide referendums.  There is a question on property tax reform; a referendum that would alter the composition of the state Board of Pardons and require a unanimous vote to recommend changes in sentences involving life in prison or the death penalty; and a statewide question on absentee voting.  If past history holds true, one in four voters will ignore the referendums.

headline: HAFER NOW PROMOTES TAP AS GOOD INVESTMENT
abstract: A year after then-Auditor General Barbara Hafer sounded warnings about the soundness of the state-run Tuition Account Program (TAP), Hafer now treasurer, is preparing it to promote the college savings plan as a good investment for families.  TAP essentially allows parents to pre-pay their children's college tuition at close to today's rates, no matter how before their children are ready to enroll.  TAP was a source of contention during last year's bitterly fought treasurer's race when Hafer ran against former Katherine Baker Knoll's daughter Mina.  Baker-Noll created TAP.  Treasurery spokesman Robert R. Gentzel said that the problem was the questionable tax status.  It was unsure at that time if the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) would slap a 34 percent tax on the fund's profits and that would have caused the fund to collapse.  Since that time, Congress intervened and passed a law exempting such accounts from having to pay federal corporate taxes on earnings.  As a result, Hafer is much more willing to promote TAP.

The education nominating committee, which submits names to Rendell for consideration, met fo rthe first time yesterday and presented 12 names to fill four seats on the nine-member board that would be vacant as of Monday.  At issue is the possible nomination of Louis Esposito, whos Board of City Trusts administers the $375 million estate orginally left to the city 166 years ago by merchant-banker Stephen Girard.  A recent series of articles by  The Inquirier have raised questions abou the board's management of Girard's fortune.

headline: HEY PROFS; CHECK WITH YOUR DOCTORS
abstract: This opinion piece notes that college costs rose three times the rate of inflation and the public is being ripped off.  The authors note that the same thing could said for health care four or five years ago and professors ought to look at the medical doctors' earnings to see what might happen to theirs.  They note that for the past two years, actual earnings for medical doctors have declined and they blame this on managed care which  was preceeded by year after year of increases in the cost of health care, two to three times the inflation rate.  They warn college professors that the same thing could happen to them.

Both are important to the 19th Legislative District because it is apparent that PA needs an overall economic plan to carry it into the twenty-first century.  During the past several years, Pennsylvania's state's economic position in comparison to other states has slipped.  The author, Bill Robinson believes the Democratic plan called "Pennsylvania Can" is more comprehensive.
