headline: HICKOK'S PLAN WOULD IMPROVE STATE'S TEACHERS
abstract: State Secretary of Education Eugene Hickok proposes that one way to get better teachers is to raise the standards for teachers.  His proposals include: require a B average after three semesters of college before allowing a student to enter teaching courses; require prospective teachers to take more college courses in the subjects they will teach rather than just courses in how to teach; require a higher cutoof grade on the teacher certification exam; and require teachers to be certified every five years.  The Pennsylvania State Education Association, the teacher's reunion is resisting the recertification requirement.  A recent "report card" issued in Education Week rated PA in the middle overall, despite teachers being the fifth highest paid in the nation.

headline: INNOVATION PREVAILS AT STATE'S CHARTER SCHOOLS, BUT WILL THEY REALLY WORK?
abstract: Pennsylvania charter schools share taxpayers' dollars with public schools but are exempt from most state regulations.  Teachers need no state certification and are not bound by state curriculum rules.  The schools must submit annual reports to their local school board and students are required to take state assessment tests.  Nationally, internal conflicts among school boards, principals, parents and teachers and funding dilemmas are not uncommon according to a report published by the Hudson Institute, a conservative think tank based in Indianapolis.

abstract: State Representative John A. Lawless, Republican-150th District, says the ever-increasing tuition at Pennsylvania state universities is funding a "backdoor socialism."  He said that tuition hikes are nothing but greed and defied any one to tell him where $1.5 billion in education dollars went.  He said the money is going to university-run businesses such as buying a law school or Geisinger Health Care.  He said universities have unfair financial advantages and that is what makes their businesses socialist.  He notes that there is "no direct correlation betweeen the amount of money spent on education and quality" and points to the parochial system to prove his point.

headline: MOBILE HOME PARK DRAWS TENANTS' IRE
abstract: Several residents complain about the conditions at the Blue Jay Mobile Home Park.  They told reporters and elected officials that they live in fear of retaliatory evictions for complaining about water quality, excessive trash collection fees and dilapidated trailers.  Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) stated that residents have problems with water pressure and outages for years and they do not get cooperation from the owner.  The owner, Gene Rubel has neglected to pay sewer fees to the borough as he claims he has a contract which allows him to pay reduced fees.  The borough is awaiting a court date so that they can have sheriff's sale to pay off Rubel's debt believed to be between $20,000 and $40,000.  DEP is also pushing Rubel to fix the underground distribution line and storage tank problems.

The plan allows new tax-funded schools operating free from most government mandates.

Eugene Hickock, the state's secretary of education had scheduled a hearing on the matter but cancelled it when it was determined that he probably does not have jurisdiction.  Kelly was originally suspended without pay and has received her back pay and is now receiving her annual salary.

headline: PUC should pay attention
abstract: Administrative Law Judge Louis G. Cocheres ruled that the Public Utility Commission should not allow PECO's 'request for the securitization of $3.7 billion in stranded costs.' The ruling came much earlier and was much harsher than expected.

headline: New stadiums not answer for growth
abstract: According to supporters of the Regional Renaissance Initiative, Pittsburgh must raise their sales tax to help fund stadiums because without a professional sports team, the city's economy will slow down. Houston, Texas survived a move by its football team and became one of the fastest growing cities in the United States.

headline: Senators press for hearing on Massiah-Jackson
abstract: Both Pennsylvanian US Senators are holding a special hearing in Philadelphia to discuss the nomination of Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson to the federal court.

headline: LEECHBURG AREA HOME-SCHOOLING POLICY VINDICTIVE
abstract: Leechburg Area School Board's vote to block home-schooled students from taking part in after-school activites smacks of vindictiveness and pettiness.  Last week, the board voted to revise its policy and ban home-schooled pupils from participating in sports, music, or other after-school programs.  School Board President Chuck Pascal said that there was way to determine whether a student was eligible as far as grades, attendance, and discipline standards.  Home-schooling of children is legal in Pennsyvlania.  The pupil's progress is checked annually through standardized testing and reviewed by a certified teacher.

headline: PUC vote supports consumer savings
abstract: The Public Utility Commission plans to help cut Philadelphia's electric bills by 15 percent. The PUC will give a larger "shopping credit" than PECO Energy allowing consumers to save more money.

headline: OFFICIALS SUPPORT SLUMLORD MEASURE
abstract: Fifty-one cities in Pennsyvlania, including McKeesport, Duquesne and Clairton would be able to sock slum landlords with $63,500 in fines and year's jail time under a proposed House bill.  State Representative Jim Caorio, D-Irwin urged passage of House Bill 1924 which he and 19 other state legislators are co-sponsoring.  The bill would establish a maximum $1,000 fine in third-class cities for violations of building, fire, health or safety codes.

headline: SHRAWDER STEALS GAVEL FROM GEIGER
abstract: A single vote has apparently knocked District Justice Robert Geiger off the bench after 18 years and put challenger Marvin Shrawder in his place.  But a call for recount is likely given Shrawder's thin 2, 121-to-2,120 victory.  Shrawder, is a paralegal from liberty township.

headline: LEGISLATION PLANNED TO HELP SCHOOL DISTRICTS GET LOANS
abstract: State Representative Camille "Bud" George, Democrat-74, Houtzdale, announced that he intends to introduce legislation to provide no interest loans to over 50 school districts in Pennsylvania that were involved in the Devon Capital Management Investment scam.

headline: PUC: Duquesne Light pilot running aground
abstract: Duquesne Light Co. is losing time to enroll in the new customer-choice pilot program due to the company missing deadlines.

headline: Proposed plan for Three Rivers will not work
abstract: The plan to alter Three Rivers stadium into a baseball field will not work due to its current design. A plan to build a new baseball field and then turn Three Rivers into a better football field should be considered.

headline: Shut out? We want to hear your story
abstract: The editors of the Observer-Reporter want to know if anyone has had trouble getting public records from any level of government.

headline: LEGISLATIVE LOGJAM: GIVE SCHOOL BOARDS, EDUCATION DEPARTMENT ABILITY TO VARY SCHEDULES
abstract: It is time for the state Legislature to give up the reins in controlling when and how long schools are in session.  A bill passed the House of Education Committee that could give Redbank Valley School District in Clarion County the ability to have classes on Saturday and to use an hourly total to meet the state's requirements.

headline: PUC's Crutchfield Withdraws Name for Reappointment
abstract: The Vice Chairman of the Public Utility Commission has decided to not be reappointed for the position. PECO Energy and Bell Atlantic have both tried to keep her on the board.

headline: Public leaders come through for Altoona
abstract: State Representatives and Senators plus a US Representative worked together to obtain funding for the Blair County Double-A baseball team's new stadium and infrastructure near the new stadium.

headline: Singel makes the right choice to step aside
abstract: Former Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel will not run again against Governor Tom Ridge which is a wise move. He understood the mismatch and knew the timing was not right to run for Governor.

headline: LEGISLATOR URGES MORE AID FOR COMMUNITY COLLEGES
abstract: State Representative Mike Veon (Democrat-Beaver Falls) said that community colleges face the "worst crisis in their 35-year history."  He blames an outdated state funding formula and diminishing local support for severe underfunding, increasing tuition, and reduced enrollments.  Veon proposes to change the state funding formula by increasing it by $100 per student to a total of $1,310 per student.  He would also include $6.6 million to replaced outdated and worn out equipment and restore the state reimbursement for work-force development.  Dr. John Pisano, Vice-President for academic services at Lackawanna County Community College stated that he and others in the community college system support Veon's proposal.

headline: QUARRY CAN BEGIN OPERATION IN FAYETTE
abstract: Amerikohl Mining Inc. of Butler received the final approval to quarry limestone at Jim Mountain near Normalville but not before local opponents had their say during a Fayette County Planning Commission Meeting.  Amerikohl will mine on a 570-acre tract in Springfield Township with haulage trucks using Route 11 for access.  At issue was the fate of Amerikohl's land use plan.  The state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP); Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) and the county's zoning hearing board have already approved the controversial project.

headline: Readshaw unveils stadium funding plan
abstract: State Representative Harry Readshaw proposed a plan to sell $4 lottery tickets to help benefit senior citizen programs and pay off bonds used to help build stadiums.

headline: Sources: Kaiser to quit Cabinet post
abstract: The rumor is that Insurance Commissioner Linda Kaiser will leave her cabinet position. She would be the fourth cabinet level member to leave the Ridge administration.

headline: LEGISLATORS RETURN TO HANDLE ISSUE-FILLED 3-WEEK AGENDA
abstract: Legilsators return to Harrisburg to tackle a laundry list of unfinished business before officially taking off for the summer.  Charter schools legislation is on the agenda before the recess.  Almost everyone claims to support the concept of charter schools, but lawmakers and the Ridge administration have been unable to agree on how they should operate.  Under the legislation being considered, groups of parents, teachers, community organizations, and other "not-for-profit" groups would be allowed to establish independent schools that would be funded by state and local taxpayers.

headline: Rate case has impact across Pa.
abstract: The Public Utility Commission is having a hearing to debate how much PECO can charge its customers to help recoup the stranded costs. PECO is trying to influence the Public Utility Commission through lobbying and campaign gifts.

headline: RIDGE WELCOMES CTS TO LOWER PROVIDENCE
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge toured Clinical Trial Services (CTS) in the Valley Force Corporatate Center and praised the owners of the pharmaceutical packaging and distribution company for locating the $12 million dollar facility in Pennsylvania.  Employment is expected to increase to 12 employees by the end of the year and to grow to 200 workers in two years.  This comes on the heels of similar tours with SAP American Inc in Newtown Square, IKON Office Solutions in Chester County and SmithKline Beecham in Philadelphia.  These projects are generating more than 4,000 technology jobs in Pennsylvania.

headline: 'SPECIAL' DAY IN PETERS TOWNSHIP
abstract: A special election is being held in Peters Township, Wahsington County, and Upper St. Clair and parts of Bethel Park in Allegheny County to elect a successor to Representative Albert Pettit, a republican who died in June.

headline: Literacy advocates appointed by Ridge
abstract: Five local literacy activists are on the new Pennsylvania Adult Basic and Literacy Education Interagency Coordinating Council.

headline: Ridge deserves blame, too
abstract: PECO Energy is receiving much criticism from the consumers over the deregulation process. The Delaware County Daily Times believes that Ridge should be blamed over the inadequate time given to deregulate the industry.

headline: RIDGE'S ATTACK ON SUBURBAN SPRAWL CAN DEFINE HIS LEGACY
abstract: Ridge's 21st Century Environmental Commission has made reducing suburban sprawl one of the state's top environmental priorities early in its year long deliberations.  Suburban sprawl is the phenomenon of homes and businesses moving out of built-up areas and paving over farms and fields.  Ridge officials say it has led to abandonment of cities and despoiling of William Penn's woods.  The best way to best way to slow sprawl is to empower counties or groups of municipalities to plan together in regions.  Ridge favors an incentive-driven approach that would entice communities into regional planning.

headline: Specter blasts VA for inaction on Gulf ailments
abstract: The Senate is investigating Persian Gulf syndrome. US Senator Specter wants to pick of the pace of the slow investigation.

headline: Local educators back drug tests for athletes
abstract: Bedford Area School Board is looking into becoming only the fifth school district in Pennsylvania to require drug testing for its student athletes.

headline: Unions seek to pull plug on electric deregulation
abstract: Unions are very active in want to repeal the deregulation of the electriticty utility in Pennsylvania.

headline: SECTION 8, PART 2:  STILL NO RENDELL
abstract: Mayor Rendell did not attend last month's City Council hearing on the Section 8 housing program because he feared a publi battle tinged with racial and class undertones.  Today, as City Council again takes up the subject of the federal rent-subsidy program, the Rendell administration is again passing up the opportunity to testify.  Rendell is under fire for suggesting that about 50 percent of participants live in clustered housing (in contrast to the 15 percent now).  Critics say this is reinventing the ghetto.

headline: Specter gets Democratic challenger for next year
abstract: Linda Rhodes, the former state Secretary of Agining, announced she will challenge Senator Alren Specter in the 1998 US Senate election.

headline: LONGER CLASSES HELP LEARNING, SCHOOL'S STUDY FINDS
abstract: Afgter a four-year study of block scheduling, Hatboro-Horsham High School administrators have found that students do better in longer classrooms.  Their data show improvements in SAT scores, Advanced Placement courses and college admission rates.  Increasing numbers of high schools in the region are adopting block scheduling which more closely resembles college course scheduling.

headline: Utilities Deregulation
abstract: Pennsylvania is one of seven states that is deregulating the electric utility industry. There are mixed reviews over the positives of deregulation.

headline: Steel explains rejecting bid for bream mill
abstract: Bethlehem Steel Corporation explained that it rejected an $85 million offer to reopen a Bethlehem beam mill because the plan would not have benefited anyone. Many are protesting the decision.

headline: Specter is pro at raising funds
abstract: US Senator Alren Specter does not enjoy fund raising, but excells at doing so. He is well ahead of any Democratic candidates to face him in the 1998 election.

headline: MANAGEMENT OF MISBEHAVIOR TAKES TACTICS
abstract: A three county survey of public and private schools in rural to urban settings found that educators managing student misbehavior in both traditional and non-traditional ways.  Most school discipline policies begin with after-school detention, followed by in-school suspension, out-of-school suspension, and then expulsion.  McKeesport High School has a time-out center.  Security guards and metal detectors are used in Woodland Hills.  Police are called in to deal with serious offenses.

headline: Utilities wait to learn their fate
abstract: The Public Utility Commission is debating over how much PECO Energy and PP&L can be allowed to pass off to their customers the stranded costs from the deregulation process.

headline: The earth is sinking!
abstract: An abanoned clay and coal mine is sinking causing the houses and buildings underneath it to crack apart.

headline: Specter speaks out
abstract: US Senator Arlen Spector wrote into the Washington Post describing testimony by Attorney General Janet Reno. She claims that the FBI withheld national security information from President Clinton.

headline: MANUFACTURING OFFICIALS SAY SCHOOLS NOT DOING THEIR JOB
abstract: The U.S. manufacturing industry is growing faster than its foreign competition but is still plagued with high training costs because American schools aren't doing their job, two top industry officials said.  The National Association of Manufacturers President Jerry Jasinowski said that we have a major educational problem in kindergarten through twelth grade and that it is only getting worse.  He notes that a significant number of entry-level employees lack necessary skills and sixty-five percent of companies spend as much as five percent of their payroll on worker education and training.

headline: Water rate 'hike' cuts bills
abstract: The Public Utility Commission allowed a rate hike for water which actually will low the water bills for the Pennsylvania-American Water Company consumers.The rates will increase by 17 percent in other areas of the state.

headline: Thrown for a Loss
abstract: Voters in the Pittsburgh area do not want to help support building a new convention center and two new stadiums with a tax increase. Minneapolis area voters voted to require a referendum when a project will cost more than $10 million dollars.

headline: Specter threatens to block budget
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter has sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader saying if he does not restore $1.5 billion for elderly medical costs, he and others will block the budget. US Senator Rick Santorum has joined Specter in attempting to block the budget.

headline: MATTER OF DEGREE:  FOR-PROFIT SCHOOLS CAN NOW HAND OUT A BETTER SHEEPSKIN
abstract: Pennsylvania has become the 50th state to let for-profit schools of higher learning grant academic degrees.  This means they will have to meet the same academic standards set by the state for schools that already issue academic degrees.

headline: Airport gets aid for runway work
abstract: New Castle Municipal Airport was given a grant to renovate the deteriorating runway.

headline: TIMES' EDITORIAL CRITICISM UNJUSTIFIED
abstract: The Ridge Administration is proud of its partnership and investment with Tosco Corporation and its workers.  Through the Governor's Action Team, the Commonwealth of PA worked with the employer, the workforce and the Delaware Community to reopenthe refinery in Trainer Borough and to bring renewed employment opportunies and future job growth to area workers.  The alternative would be zero jobs and an unproductive, abandoned facility to the community.  An editorial entitled, "Monday Morning Quaterback" missed that point and instead criticized the Ridge for winning 360 jobs for the community.

headline: State agents padlock business for tax debt
abstract: W.J. Exley Repair Company has had its company's assets seized because of it owed the government $100,000 and withheld taxes.

headline: Midland boss wants longer tuition deal
abstract: Midland School District and East Liverpool City School District want to extend their tuition agreement. East Liverpool City students can attend Midland under the current agreement.

headline: BACKHAUL UPDATE
abstract: A Clinton County trucking company that carried food products in trucks used to haul sewage sludge and automobile shredder fluff has forfeited a truck and a trailer to the state and agreed to pay fines and costs totaling nearly $120,000.  Under a plea agreement, Donna and Mary Powers, owners of the company will pay $98,000 to the Department of Transportation's Motor License Fund for violations of the state's backhauling law. The company will also pay $16,820 to DEP and $5,004 to state police as reimbursement for their investigative costs.

headline: UPS:  ROAD EXPANSION EQUALS NEW EMPLOYMENT
abstract: Jointed by county officials, Governor Tom Ridge hailed the extension of Hog Island Road as an investment that will allow businesses to expand and employment to grow.  The main benefactor appears to be United Parcel Service which announced plans for future job development and anticipating more than 7,000 new jobs in the next five years.  Additionally, Ridge said that he is committed to providing transportation to the facility for Chester residents that are expected to be hired at the facilitity.

headline: STATE AUDIT CRITICAL OF KEYSTONE CENTRAL
abstract: Auditor General Robert P. Casey, Jr. has released an audit of Keystone Central School District which found "insufficient record keeping" in reports the district filed with the state.  The reporting errors caused the state to reimburse Keystone Central $28,006 more for public transportation than it was entitled to receive.  Additionally, because an administrator's certificate lapsed and another administrator did not have a proper certificate, the district will be fined $6,930 by the state.

headline: MORE CREDITS REQUIRES FOR GRADUATION
abstract: The District's school board voted unanimously to raise the minimum number of graduation credits for graduation in 1998 from 22 to 23.  They added credit does not have to come from any specific course.  The adoption is part of the district's recently adopted strategic plan, approved by the Pennsyvlania Department of Education.  The plan calls for raising the number of credits to 26 over the next six years.

headline: 'BIG BORTHERS' PLAYING OFF DEATH OF PRINCESS DIANA
abstract: In the wake of Princess Diana's fatal car crash, there's a move under way on Capitol Hill to tighten the legal standard for drunken driving nationwide, as was done for awhile with the speed limit by setting it at 55 miles per hour.  The authors have no problem with PA legislators determining that lowering the permitted blood alcohol level is good for PA but they protest such a move by U.S. senators whom they believe are trading on the shock value of the charismatic princess's death to make the federal government more intrusive in our lives.  They are trying to force the states to lower their blood-alcohol standards by withholding federal highway dollars if they refuse to comply.

headline: Vox populi matters on 'stadium tax' issue
abstract: Jack Markowitz does a conversation between Caesar and Conservativus Veritas over the funding for two new stadiums in Pittsburgh.

headline: State auditors may analyze schools districts' efficiency
abstract: Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr. plans to add performance audits of school districts to the list of tasks state auditors will have to accomplish.

headline: NATIONAL TESTING FOR SCHOOLS DIVERTS NEEDED RESOURCES
abstract: This editorial notes that the majority of American schools do not perform as well as they should but also argues that national testing will deprive them of the resources they need to make improvements.  Instead, they argue for standardized state tests.

headline: CCBC's air traffic controller program flies high again
abstract: The FAA is to hire 70 air traffic controllers from Community College Beaver County. CCBC has an agreement to train air traffic controllers and then have them hired by the FAA, although in recent years the FAA has not hired many from CBCC.

headline: Ways sought to turn Conrail demise into growth
abstract: Governor Ridge and executives from CSX and Norfolk Southern held a meeting to discuss how the breakup of Conrail can be turned into an economic growth. CSX and Norfolk Southern are buying Conrail and plan to breakup the railroad company.

headline: State court hopefuls nonjudgmental on air
abstract: Supreme Court hopefuls Thomas G. Saylor and Joseph A. Del Sole criticize each other on experience and fund raising after a televised debate.

headline: NUMBERS GAME IS MATTER OF QUALITY
abstract: As class sizes rise, individual time is reduced and this hurts kids, according to educators.  Despite consensus that this is so, there remains a wide range of class sizes in the 15 Delaware County school districts.  Money is a major factor.  The districts with the lowest class sizes spend the most money per pupil.  But that is expensive and why state lawmakers defeated a plan last month to reimburse schools who reduce their elementary class size to 20.

headline: Conservation and development can co-exist
abstract: There is support and opposition to the proposed new Route 202. The opponets claim that the new highway will displace the bog turtle, an endangered or threatened species.

headline: null
abstract: There is a man that represents the electric companies moving around three bowls and saying 'you look like a man who can spot a bargain.. Watch closely and I'll tell ya what I'm gonna do..' The person watching has a shirt that saying PA. Consumer.

headline: State Democrats would benefit all Pennsylvanians
abstract: Ivan Itkin, the House Democratic Whip, argues that the Patriot News has misinformed the public on the value of the state Democrats.  He criticizes Governor Ridge for helping big businesses and says Democrats have new ideas to help Pennsylvania.

headline: 'OLD' SCHOOLS OWE A CHANCE TO THE NEW
abstract: State lawmakers passed a law that allows the formation of charter schools.  If the experience of the proposed LeHigh Valley Charter School for the Performing Arts is any indication, there are some problems with the law.  So far, the school has received approval from 3 school districts and rejection by four with little input from those trying to start the charter school.

headline: DUI COUNT CONVICTION A SOBERING  EXPERIENCE
abstract: Cumberland County District Attorney Skip Ebert states that most people cannot financially afford a DUI.  Dauphin County Senior Deputy Districut Attorney Fran Chardo states that the consequences of drinking and driving are more well known but the average driver still does not realize excactly how much one costs.  The DUI alone (without damages and injuries) still can cost several thousand dollars.

headline: 2 local banks nix ATM surcharge
abstract: Merchants Bank of Pennsylvania has decided to not charge ATM surcharges. The ATM surcharges have grown throughout the country and most banks now charge at least $1.

headline: State Dems to meet, still searching for governor candidate
abstract: The Pennsylvania Democratic Party will meet to discuss furture candidates for the governor race. Two hopefuls are no longer going to be considered for the nomination.

headline: OPINION:  OFF THE MARK, STATE'S FUNDING POSITION FLAWED
abstract: In their closing arguments in the school funding lawsuit brought by 217 rural and poor school districts, lawyers for the state argued the issue does not belong in court, that any disputes should be taken to the General Assembly.  The flaw in this argument is that neither the Legislature nor the Ridge administration wants to address the problem in any meaningful way.  The authors hope Commonwealth Court understands that.

headline: EIGHTH DUI ARREST ATTRACTS LEGISLATIVE ATTENTION
abstract: Two state lawmakers citing a man's record of seven DUI's and one jail term for killing a motorist while drinking and driving want PA's sentencing laws bolstered.  Curtis Ireland, of suburban Pittsburgh served 3 1/4 years in jail for killing a man in 1986 while he ws drunk and driving.  Now he is facing an eighth charge aqfter being stopped by police as he tried to avoid a DUI checkpoint.  Republican Senator Melissa Hart has introducted stiff penalties for people who repeatedly drink and drive.

headline: 3 COUNTY COMMISSIONERS OPPOSE SLOT MACHINE AT RACETRACKS
abstract: Carbon County Commissioners Tom Gerhard, Charles Getz and John Mogilski wrote to state legislators urging them to defeat slots.  They noted that the counties and citizens of Pennsylvania are still wating for tax reform and the legislature seems to by busy assisting racetrack owners and those affiliated with them over the citizens of Pennsylvania.  They also sent copies of their letter to Governor Tom Ridge and others in state government.

headline: STATE ETHICS PANEL CLEARS LAWYER
abstract: A state legal ethics hearing panel has recommended that all disciplinary charges against legal reform advocate Robert Surrick be dropped.  Surrick gained prominence in his battles with now-impeached state Supreme Court Justice Rolf Larsen over issues of corruption in the state courts.  This is the third time in 13 years that Surrick has been brought up on ethics charges connected to his efforts for change.  The earlier cases were dropped or dismissed.  Surrick is seeking the GOP nomination for Superior Court.

headline: OPINION:  STRENGTHEN SCHOOL, WORK PARTNERSHIP
abstract: In this opinion piece, the authors noted that cooperative education program, in which students alternate class time with months of full-time work in their career choice, should be promoted.

headline: Extra $31B paved the way for passage of road bill
abstract: The US Senate voted to approve a six year highway funding bill by increasing transportation funding by $31 billion. However, US Rep. Chris Shays opposed the decision, saying it did not make sense to add more money without deciding where it will come from, as other programs will inevitably receive cuts. However, the Senate has promised not to take the money from the anticipated budget surplus. The highway bill has popular support among lawmakers however, allowing pork to be brought home to all 435 House districts for various local projects.

headline: A SURE LOSER: RIDGE SHOULD CUT OFF THIS SLOT-MACHINE GAMBLE
abstract: There is not way to make the introduction of thousands of slot machines at Pennsylvania's four horse tracks sound like good public policy.  It is not.  Racetracks and lotteries are enough for the state.  Slot machines are among the most addictive of forms of gambling.  The legislators ought to worry about the fact that the public's entertainment dolloars - now spread among restaurants, professional sporting events and theaters will not be diverted to the one-arm bandits.  A statewide referendum is an easy way for legislators to wiggle out of their moral responsibility to stop an expansion of gambling.  Any referendum campaing should tell the truth. Slot machines will cost more for regulation, law enforcement and social services.  If approved, the nast consquences will be felt state-wide.

headline: State help on Wharton election probe needed
abstract: There is criticizm of Fayette County for having the FBI investigate balloting issues in Wharton Township for the primary election.

headline: OUR VIEW - GET ON CHARTER BUS: EASTON SHOULD LEAD THE WAY FOR GETTING THE PROPOSED CHARTER SCHOOL FOR THE ARTS
abstract: The proposed Lehigh Valley Charter High School for the Performing Arts has found a site at Fifth and Northampton streets.  This is the now a closed arts gallery next to the State Theatre and is an ideal location for a school of 50 talented teenagers who have accesst to the State's facilities.  The State Theatre is a precious resource that can be used with other pooled resources to support such a charter school.

headline: Fewer road projects slated for weekend
abstract: Governor Ridge wants to keep highway construction to a minimum over the Memorial Day weekend due to the increased highway traffic.

headline: ADDING SLOT MACHINES RAISES MANY CONCERNS
abstract: Pennsylvanians should be wary of allowing slot machines at racetracks.  Representatives of the tate's four racetracks say slot machines are necessary to help the tracks compete with those outside the state.  The lack of slot machines makes it harder for tarcks to draw spectators and horses.  No one wants to see the tracks suffer, but we are concerned with the expansion of gambling in the state.  If slots are allowed, blackjack may follow.  Gambling is a thorny issue.  The editors caution the state and its residents to be very cautious before allowing slots.

headline: State Judiciary
abstract: Various people deserve the endorsement for positions on the Supreme Court, Commonwealth Court and Superior Court.

headline: OUTCOME-BASED EDUCATION FEARS FUEL PLUM DEBATE
abstract: Plum School District officials are considering having a special panel discussion on the district's strategic plan to calm parents' fears about learning outcomes.  Parents are worreid that the outcomes the district included in its plan will change Plum schools and introduce the teaching of values and attitudes they don't like.  Parents want to ensure the Department of Education does not force the district to teach undesirable outcomes.

headline: Free-market expansion
abstract: U.S. Airways, a major employeer in Pittsburgh, is planning to order new jetliners and engines in addition to building a new midwestern hub and additional terminals in Philadelphia. U.S. Airways is growing and strengthening its company.

headline: AN ADDICTION:  GETTING HOOKED ON VIDEO POKER GAMES
abstract: It's a sure bet that a proposal to ban video poker machiens in Pennsylvania will get nowhere.  State Representative Joseph Battisto, Democrat, Monroe County wants his colleagues to ban video poker machines, which he claims are similar to illegal gambling devices - like slot machines - because of their ability to hook players and drain their money.  The machines are supposed to be for entertainment only but can easily be converted to gambling.  His opponents say better enforcement, not banishment is the solution.  Battisto is right.  It is too bad his colleagues don't agree.

headline: STATE SENATE CANDIDATES SPENT $3.66 PER VOTE IN '97 ELECTION
abstract: The three candidates in the Senate special election on November 4 spend nearly $171,000 on the race.  For those keeping track, that comes to $3.66 per vote.  It is about 17 percent more than was spent in a similar election campaign in the 10th District in 1993, another three-way race.  On paper, Democrat Karen Ritter of Milford narrowly outspent former Representative Joe Conti, Republican-Doylestown, according to campaign expense reports filed with the State Election Bureau.  Constitutional Party candidate Jay Russell of Churchville spent a fraction of what Conti and Ritter spent.  Uncounted is all of the assistance that Conti received from the Republican State or Senate Republican Campaign committees for polling, mailings and campaign staff.  Conti raised more money overall than Ritter and was able to stash away nearly $48,000 for his expected 1998 bid for a full four-term election.

headline: PA CONSIDERING CHARTER SCHOOLS
abstract: Whether or not Pennsylvania teachers, parents and other groups should be allowed to establish charters schools and if so, what rules will govern these charter schools, is likely to come up for a vote in the General Assembly sometime this year.  At the end of 1996, there were 481 charter schools operating in the United States, and 16 in the District of Columbia.

headline: Good idea, wrong use
abstract: Sen. Allen G. Kukovich does not agree with the current proposal for a magnetic levitation transportaion system, although he does feel there is a great need for one in Pittsburgh.

headline: Area braces for shuffle in banking
abstract: First Union bought CoreStates and local branches are waiting to see how their jobs will be affected. There are multiple banks within a small area in the Lehigh Valley so closings are imminent.

headline: State's clout to shrink further
abstract: Pennsylvania, compared to other states, is growing slowly and will lose some of its seats in the House.

headline: PUSHING NEIGHBORHOOD SCHOOLS
abstract: A neighborhood schools referendum in Pittsburgh showed that residents want their children to attend public schools close to home. Residents voted 3 to 1 on the neighborhood schools ballot question. Two Pittsburgh legislators, Representatives Harry Readshaw (Democrat-Carrick) and Frank Gigliotti (Democrat-Brookline) introduced a bill to require that city school directors implement a school integration plan assigning pupils to the appropriate grade level closest to their home unless busing sstudents to a school farther aways is necessary to rectify violations of the equal protection clause of the U.S. Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment.

headline: HEARINGS TO BE HELD ON BUS SEAT BELTS
abstract: Legislators concerned about school bus safety will hold hearings this summer on how seat belts on buses can protect students.  Senate Bill 784 which would require all buses to be equipped with seat belts, was introduced by Senator Steward J. Greenleaf.

headline: ARMSTRONG COUNTY GOLF COURSES SAVE $1,575 IN PROGRAM
abstract: There have been public protests about Armstrong County golf courses being in the Clean and Green Program.  The program was designed to keep land for agricultural or forest use.  A check of the county assessment showed that three golf courses are in the state program:  Kittanning Country Club, Lenape Heights Golf Course and Apollo Lakes Golf course.  These three courses saved a total of $1,575.14 in county property taxes by being in the program.  Jim Bronder of the Taxpayers Fair Play and Ethics Committee said that he though permitting golf courses in the program was unfair to taxpayers becaseu the law was designed to help farmers not elites.

headline: STATE'S DATA BELONGS ON THE INTERNET
abstract: Pennsylvania Secretary of State Yvette Kane testified to a House committee about plans to computerize state records and make them available on the Internet.  Those record include information about registered charities and licenscing boards for professions such as barbers, doctors, real estate agents or funeral directors.  Governor Tom Ridge wants those records to include campaign finance reports and is seeking an extra $370,000 in the budget this year to put campaign reports on the Internet.  Any effort to do this is a step forward.

headline: PANEL TO INVESTIGATE HIGH COST OF COLLEGE
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Goodling (Republican-Seven Valleys), Chairman of the House Education and the Workforce committes; U.S. Representative Buck McKeown, Republican-California, chairman of the the subcommittee on Postsecondary Education, Training and Lifelong Learning; and Dr. George Waldner, President, York College, co-author an article that explains that Congress will update and improve the Higher Education Act, which provides student loans, grants and other federal financial aid to about one out of every two college students.  They note that the federal government will provide an excess of $35 billion in federal student aid this year but many parents still cannot afford college because of its spiraling costs that go up two to three times the rate of inflation each year.   They use York College of Pennsylvania as an example of keeping costs low and quality high.

headline: Holden asks panel to set aside money for bypass project
abstract: US Representative Tim Holden wants to earmark some transportation funds for the extention of Warren State/Route222.

headline: ATMS - quick, convenient and costly
abstract: ATM fees and surcharges are growing rapidly due to the cost of running an ATM. Various Senators are proposing legislation against ATM surcharges. Two of the biggest banks in the area, Mellon and PNC Bank, want to preserve the surcharges.

headline: STATUE LEAVES CAPITOL PERCH TODAY
abstract: The statue of the bronze woman atop the Capitol is due to come down to the public for the first time since it was erected.  It will then be shipped by flatbed to Connecticut where it will be restored as part of a $12 million restoration of the Capitol.

headline: PARENTS WARY, HOPEFUL ABOUT CHARTER SCHOOLS
abstract: Although many parents did not know anything about it until they were asked, the Philadelphia parents generally seemed pleased with the new charter school bill signed into law last week.  Pennsylvania is now one of 27 states to have authorized charter schools, small, publicly funded instituitons, started by parents, educators, or community leaders.  They purpose of custom-designed charter schools is to provide more flexible, creative ways of educating children without many of the impediments of public school systems.

headline: House leader will support funding area road projects
abstract: US Representative Nick Rahall from West Virginia has offered to fund three transportation projects in Pennsylvania.

headline: AUTHORITY SEEKING RIDGE'S HELP IN RECOUPING MONEY
abstract: The Waashington County Authority is seeking help from Governor Ridge in recouping money from a company that defaulted on a low-interest loan.  In December 1994, the authority loaned Nicon Holdings Buildings $100,000 to start Genesis Plastics, Inc.  The plastic recycler was expected to employ 380 people.  The company agreed to pay back the loan in 180 installments but filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy owing the authority $87,710.  The state made two loans to the company totally $5.5 million  and the state department of Economic Development advised the authority to satisfy the mortgage lean and write off the balance owed.

headline: Still vacant
abstract: Eight months after the retirement of Chief Justice Robert N.C. Nix Jr. the position on the state Supreme Court is still open and may not be filled until the January elections.

headline: PENNSYLVANIA 4TH GRADERS' MATH SCORES RATE A C-PLUS
abstract: Pennsylvania's fourth graders score above the U.S. average, but not near the top of the pack on a national mathematics report card that shows the nation's students making steady progress in this decade, according to federal officials.  Education Secretary Richard W. Riley released findings from the 1996 National Assessment of Education Progress (NEAP), Math Report Card for students in grade four, eight, and twelve.  Pennsylvania did not participate in the eight-grade math testing.  No data specific to states was available for grade 12.

headline: If state divests two airports, viability will require marketing
abstract: Expansion of HIA and Capital City is difficult given their location and resources. The airports need to be updated and marketed for the privatization to be successful.

headline: Banking on more with less
abstract: There is concern over how the merger of First Union and CoreStates banks will affect local business and low income neighborhoods who have benefited from CoreStates being a Philadelphia-based and pro-business bank.

headline: Strassburger urging voters to check his record
abstract: Strassburger has had a success record as a depty solicitor in Pittsburgh and now is vying for one of the Democrat nominations for the state Superior Court.

headline: PHEAA INCREASES AVAILABLE GRANTS
abstract: State Representative Stanley Jarolin, Democrat-Luzerne has announced that the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency will award about 8,000 additional grants to financially needy colleg and university students during the 1997-98.  This is do to a revised formula.

headline: Link to Heritage
abstract: The Public Utility Commission halted the dismantling of abandoned railroad bridges to review the need to destroy them. It came three weeks too late to save bridges for a proposed rails-to-trails project in Lancaster County.

headline: Bill would ban automatic teller machine surcharges
abstract: Rep. Eugene McGill proposed a bill that would eliminate surcharges at ATMs. The banking industry is against the proposal and view it as an attack by credit unions.

headline: STUCK IN THE NET
abstract: Thursday was the deadline for statewide judicial candidates to file their latest set of expense reports.  As of this writing, we are not aware of any candidates for Supreme, Superior or Commonwealth court have failed to meet this deadline.  However, not one of the 12 judicial candidates bothered to make that information available to citizens through the Internet.  Representative Greg Vitali, Democrat-Haverton introduced legislation to require candidates for statewide office to file their campaign finance reports electronically and to have the Pennsylvania Election Bureau make the information available on the Internet.  Governor Tom Ridge said candidates for state-wide election will be able to voluntarily file campaign expense reports electronically next year.  The 12 judicial candidates have been notified of Vital's offer, they should take him up on it.

headline: PHILADELPHIA BEGINS CHARTER SCHOOL ERA
abstract: On August 21s, the Philadelphia School Board of Education gave conditional approval to four of the five applicants who petitioned the body to start up Charter Schools or the 1997-98 school year.  All four schools were granted conditional approval pending compliance to specific uniform preconditions set by the Board of education such as minimum and maximum enrollment, verfication that the applicant is not-for-profit, and evidence of leases or deeds for physical plants and facilities.

headline: Lumber contract was wrong move
abstract: Butler County purchased lumber for a bridge project without bidding for a lower cost.

headline: BOEING JOBS RUMORS FLY
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge, along with a legislative contigent, made an unannouned stop at the union hall of Boeing Helicopters' organized workers to ease anxiety surrounding the planned Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger, all of which has been fueled by the recent transfer of some Boeing work to other sites.  Ridge noted that there is always speculation after a merger but that he has been assured by Boeing that for the time being, jobs are not being transferred out of PA.  The union has a collective bargaining agreement that runs into 1999.

headline: SURPLUS BRINGS RAY OF LIGHT
abstract: Another benefit of the $500 million-plus state surplus is that it has prevented the Legislature from making excuses for not computerizing campaign finance report.  In the past, several legislators claimed they rejected computerization because it would cost too much.  This year, there is a budget surplus so there are not excuses.  Credit goes to Governor Tom Ridge who supplied his own campaign records on computer discs and since his election has advocated a universal system.  The new system will work for greater integrity.

headline: PITT REJECTS UPJ'S CHOICE FOR POSITION
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh has rejected the Johnstown campus' choice for  a new vice president for academic affairs, sayhing UPJ didn't have enough female candidates on the list.

headline: Marsico's bills say loudly: Slow down
abstract: Proposed seven-bill legislation for improving highway safety especially in construction zones.

headline: Bond ratings must not slow county program
abstract: Allegheny County bond rating might be lowered. The county commissioners must find a way to improve the county finances in light of the tax cuts.

headline: Swing.. And a Hit!
abstract: Pennsylvania Congressmen have an excellent record of recording votes with an average of missing less than 1 in 10 votes.

headline: PITT RESHUFFLES ACADEMIC DECK
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh is forging ahead with the largest reshuffling of academic resources in 40 years.  They are moving people and money to higher-priority areas such as computer engineering and bioengineering and away from classical fields.  Pitt has a long-term plan to move the university forward and recommendations include eliminating 400 of 9,600 jobs and setting aside five percent of the annual budget to enhance funding of high-priority programs.

headline: MASCARA MAKES CASE FOR ROAD IMPROVEMENTS
abstract: U.S. Representative Frank Mascare (Democrat) said that if southwestern Pennsylvania is to survive as a region, it needs an adequate transportation system.  He told participants of the Airport Area Development Corporation that a lack of easy-to-use road systems has contributed to many problems in the region such as businesses being reluctant to locate in the region.

headline: Business could save Pirates if it wanted to
abstract: Business leaders turned to the government to help keep the Pirates in Pittsburgh. With all of the possible creative solutions to funding a new stadium, only two (increase in sales tax or a sports lottery) are being told to the public as the only possible solutions.

headline: The time is right
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature will not reform the current way that Supreme Court judges are elected. Instead of a state wide election, reformers want a regional election.

headline: PLANNING BEGINS TOWARD NEW CHARTER SCHOOL
abstract: Bridgeton parents and community members are determined the doors of Bridgeton Elementary School will open again soon as a charter school.  About 100 people are meeting to write the charter school's mission statement and to prepare its planning application that are due to the state Department of Education by July 25.  A school consolidation plan closed the Bridgeton School on June 11.  Community leaders and parents have maintained that the community school is paramount to educating students.

headline: New airport road a path to jobs
abstract: A new highway is being constructed that would link the Wilkes-Barre-Scranton International Airport to a nearby industrial and office park.

headline: CARBONDALE WOMAN STEPS UP OTB FIGHT
abstract: The building permit for an off-track-betting facility at the old Monarch Pallet property was approved by the city's building inspector last month but that is not stopping Councilwoman Mary Lil Hayslett who opposes an OTB facilty in the city.  She states that she will go to court to have a public zoning hearing on the matter.

headline: Thornburgh, Casey to lead Capitol rally
abstract: Two former Governors will hold a rally at the Capitol to support a local property tax reform referendum.

headline: POOR NONURBAN SCHOOL DISTRICTS RECEIVE SHORT SHRIFT IN NEW JERSEY
abstract: The New Jersey Supreme Court ruled that the most recent state school funding system, adopted by the legislature in December 1996, is unconstituional as applied to poor urban districts.  The state aid formula must enable the 28 urban "special needs" districts to spends as much per child as is spent in the state's most affluent districts, the court said.  This ruling will not benefit the thousands of students in nonurban districts, most in South Jersey.

headline: NEW ROAD TO CUT TRAFFIC, ELIMINATE FLOODING
abstract: When the Rose Street Extension in White Township is completed this fall, the new road should not only allenviate traffic snarls at the Oakland Avenue - 13th Street intersection but also should eliminate chronic flooding on Wayne Avenue.

headline: CASINO ODDS ARE STACKED AGAINST YOU
abstract: Casinos hire some of the smartest advertisers, marketers, mathematicians and game designers , all focused on getting you to lose money and have a good time doing it.  Their strategies run the gamut, from liquor to maze-like floor plans that discourage wandering.  At the core of gambling's success is people's desire to take risks for potentially big rewards.  But big payoffs are rare.  Your chances are you will lose.

headline: CORPS OF ENGINNER WEIGHS REDUCING LOCK, DAM SERVICE
abstract: The gates of eight Allegheny River locks are not expected to shut permanently anytime soon.  After 1999 federal cuts occur, the Army Corps of Engineers is considering closing or cutting back operations at Locks and Dams 8 and 9 and reducing services at Locks and Dams 2 through 7.  The corps would rather cut service that close a lock, which would require an act of Congress and might take years.

headline: Possession is 100% of the law
abstract: A new law will allow school districts to impose a fine on students caught on school property with tobacco products. Previously, there was just a ban on smoking on school property.

headline: Pa. troopers warn speeders
abstract: The State Police will be devoting more time to Operation Centipede to help slow down speeders and keep the highways safe during the Labor Day weekend.

headline: Commissioners say you can be sure about jobs if it's Westinghouse
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners are convinced that Westinghouse will keep their businesses in the Pittsburgh region despite Westinghouse's original desire to make their industrial businesses a new company.

headline: CREEK PROJECTS ON TRACK
abstract: Flood-weary Keyser Valley residents may not have to wait much longer.  Work on a flood-control project for Lindy Creek and Keyser Creek in West Scranton that will help those living on the east side of Keyser Avenue could begin this summer.

headline: PRIVATE SCHOOLS TAKING HIGH-TECH STEPS
abstract: Many Lower Bucks parents sacrifice to pay tuition so their children can attend private schools.  School officials admit the are behind in computer technology, but parents say they get something more in return.  Many parents say that they are willing to give up elaborate computer labs, elaborate vacations and expensive cars to avoid the problems that public school kids face.  They also say the religious instruction, discipline and higher standard of education is an advantage of private and parochial schools.

headline: PennDOT opens road hotline
abstract: PennDOT will have a hotline for updates on road coniditions in the winter.

headline: Committee eyes licensing law for counselors
abstract: A Senate committee wants to require a master's degree or doctorate and to pass an examination to become licensed for personal counseling. Currently, there is no license requirement to practice counseling.

headline: Developers sued by state
abstract: Piatt Partnership is being sued for selling land without properly warning customers about the well water problems.

headline: PROPOSED DISTRICT BREAKUPS ENDORSED
abstract: A bipartisan panel approved a controversial report on reforming urban education that recommends the breakup of the Philadelphia School District and the closing of the Chester Upland School District.  The 44-page report now goes to the House and Governor Tom Ridge for consideration.  Representatives of the Pennsylvania Federation of Teachers, the teachers' union blasted the report and vowed to fight key proposals which include a pilot program to offer 3,000 urban students "opportunity scholarship," also called school vouchers.  Others lauded the report's recommendations for smaller class sizes for kindergarten through grade three and alternative schools for disruptive students.

headline: Plan to link rails-to-trails scuttled by state agency
abstract: A judge ordered three former rail crossing removed which eliminated the first looking rails-to-trails path.

headline: Counselors seek own license board
abstract: A rally is being conducted by the Alliance of Counseling Professionals to urge the creation of a Board of Professional Counselors. State Senator Jeffrey Piccola will join the Alliance.

headline: FLOOD FUNDS INCLUDED IN FEDERAL ACT
abstract: A flood control project along Mill Run and the extension of sewage treatment to residents of Snyder Township are two projects included in the 1998 federal appropriations act.

headline: PROPOSED RULES CAN MAKE GOOD TEACHERS BETTER
abstract: The state Board of Education wants to make the public school teachers keep up with developments in their field.  The board wants the Legislature to require a teacher to complete six credits of academic courses or participate in 180 hours of conferences, workshops or teacher mentoring every five years and require new teachers to undergo a performance assessment every five years.

headline: Ridge orders road work kept to minimum
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge order all road work to be kept to a minimum during the Labor Day weekend due to the increased traffic. He wants the roadways to be as safe as possible.

headline: DON'T ALLOW RACETRACKS TO ADD SLOTS
abstract: Some lawmakers, racetrack officials and those associated with horse racing want to legalize slot machines at the state's four horse racing tracks.  Horse racing revenues last year were $22 million.  Wagering at the state's four tarcks has dropped 15-20 percent over the last two quarters which State Racing Commissions Executive Secretary Richard Sharbaugh says is the result of the availability of slot machines at racetracks in Delaware and West Virginia. This is not sufficient reason to bring them to Pennsylvania.

headline: FOREST'S TIMBER SHOULD BE USED, NOT JUST SAVED
abstract: The environmentalists are exaggerating in order to create their own private parks on public land.  The issue is timber cutting on the Allegheny National Forst and on other state and national forest lands.  They propose that cutting any tree is bad and the authors disagree because the multiple use concept  (using the forests to provide timber resources, for watershed protection, and a suitable environment for hiking, hunting, fishing and camping) makes sense.

headline: PUBLIC FUNDING OF PRIVATE SCHOOLS IS A BARGAIN
abstract: Larry Hicks states that Pennsylvania taxpayers spend $120 million dollars to support private eduation by way of transportation, textbooks and LIU services.  According to a report published by Penn State, there are 336,093 private school students in Pennsylvania.  That $120 million dollars comes to $357.04 spent per student.  In contrast, if those students come back to public schools, taxpayers will pay an average of $6,147 per student.

headline: Ridge pushes for I-80 toll
abstract: Representative Phil English does not want to make interstate highway 80 a toll road; however, Governor Ridge wants I-80 to become a toll road.

headline: GUARANTEES FOR LIVE RACING IN PENNSYLVANIA SLOT-MACHINE BILL
abstract: This letter by Salvatore M. DeBunda of the Pennsylvania Thoroughbred Horsemen's Association notes that the proposed bill does not threaten the continuation of live horse-racing but does the opposite - it guarantees that live racing will continue and that a portion of revenues will be used to support horse breeding in the state and to support disability and pension benefits for jockeys and employees.

headline: FORT LIGONIER FOCUS OF RESTORATION
abstract: A reconstruction project estimated at $2.3 million is currently underway at Fort Ligonier to restore the historical bastion to its original state.  The fort Ligonier organization was founded in 1946 to re-create the British fort that originally stood on the site and it has raised more than $2 million so far in individual donations and grants.  The organization also received $100,000 Keystone Historical Preservation Grant.

headline: PUBLIC SCHOOLS RIGHT TO BE WARY OF STATE
abstract: This is a public opinion piece that notes that for the second time in eight years, the state is revising its standards for public education and educators are less than enthusiastic because many school districts have spent the past three years redesigning their curricula to fit Governor Robert Casey's mandate of "outcome-based education."  Now that Governor Ridge is in office, he has, under political pressure, done away with those plans.

headline: Shuster to push $32 billion in transportation spending
abstract: US Representative Bud Shuster is pushing for a $32 billion transportation bill. The bill would go against the balanced budget and favors funding for the Northeast states.

headline: Hoteliers back room-tax boost to expand concention center
abstract: A 40 percent tax increase on hotel and motel rooms was supported by the Greater Pittsburgh Hotel Association. The revenue would help aid the cost of expanding the Convention Center.

headline: Funding available to complete trails for hiking, biking
abstract: $16 million was awarded to complete multiple trails in Western Pennsylvania.

headline: RECOUPING THEIR MONEY:  "THE SOONER THE BETTER"
abstract: Several local school districts and towns got word that they can access some of their own money.  They had invested with John Gardner Black of Tyrone and is investment companies, Devon Capital Management, Inc. and Financial Management Sciences, Inc.  In September, the federal Securities and Exchance Commission (SEC) file da civil complaint against Black, alleging Fraud.  The SEC believes Black mayh have lost $70 million of the $233 million invested with him and froze his assets.  A federal judge in Johnstown agreed Monday to release about half of that money, $121 million so that the investing schools and municipalities would not be in financial straits.

headline: STATE CHECKS TRASH HAULERS
abstract: Truckers arriving at Mountain View Reclamation landfill in Upton on Wednesday were greeted by state workers conducting surprise inspections.  The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) handed out 23 citations to 19 drivers in the daylong inspection.  Violators can be fined as miuch as $1,000 for each offense.  Antrim Township supervisors were also on site and hope the inspection will help.

headline: HOUSE KILLS RACETRACK SLOT VOTE PROPOSAL
abstract: The state's horse racing industry lost as the state House scratched a last-ditch effort for a vote on a bill calling for a November referendum to permit slots at the state's four tracks.  The Senate had approved it - but the measure stalled in the house because Governor Ridge promised to veto it.

headline: Grant will help extend trail
abstract: A grant was provided to purchase an abandoned railroad to turn it into a trail.

headline: REPORT CARDS FOR SCHOOLS IN STATE
abstract: Comparative rankings of teachers is difficult because they have such varied areas of expertise.  It is difficult to evaluate individual teachers and it is difficult to evaluate entire school systems.  Inter-school ratings should be brought out into the open.  Though it might not be possible to determine the best school district in Pennsylvania, it should be easy to pick out the failing ones.  It is being done in Alabama and should be done in Pennyslvania.

headline: TACKLING DUI WILL REQUIRE STRONGER EFFORTS
abstract: Pennsylvania (and other states) should have little tolerance of those who drink and drive.  Lowering the legal blood alcohol level, better enforcement of laws and public education campaigns are all need to curb this problem.  PA police will boost their efforts to curb underage drinking by posing as shoppers at places that sell alcohol.  Called "Cops in Shops," the program will begin soon.

headline: INK MAKER COMING TO COUNTY
abstract: Gellner and Company, Incorporated, a New Jersey-based research and development firm dedicated to the formulation of various printing inks for the graphic arts industry will begin manufacturing water-based polymers in a new plant in Hometown early next year.  This new plant will start with 10 employees.  Gellner checked out several sites in four years in South Carolina and five Schuylkill County industrial parks before choosing Tamaqua Industrial Development Enterprise's (TIDE) Tidewood East Industrial Park in Hometown, Rush Township.

headline: HAWK MOUNTAIN GETS $100,000 GRANT
abstract: Representative David Argall (R-Schyulkill/Berks) and Senator David Brightbill (R-48th) announced that Hawk Mountain Sanctuary in Kempton has been awarded a $100,000 state grant from the Pennsyvlania Historical and Museum Commission.  The grant will be used to support continuing the positions of a full-time educator and biologist on the staff and to offer a first-time teacher internship.

headline: RHOADES TALKS SCHOOLS
abstract: State Senator James Rhoades, Republican-Monroe/Carbon/Schuylkill told Pleasant Valley Concerned Citizens that with all the available information, no one can learn it all and this is why we need statewide standards for what students should know by a given age and tests to see if they meet those standards.

headline: Traffic relief?
abstract: Heroin and cocaine have been transported from Detroit to New York, but many have avoided traveling on Interstate 80 because of the state police patroling the highway.

headline: Insurance sales at banks nears House approval
abstract: Proposed legislation would allow consumers to get insurance from state-chartered banks. Various other stipulations are attached to prevent exploitation.

headline: INDIANS JOIN ANTI-CASINO EFFORT
abstract: Chuck Gentlemoon told an anti-gambling coaltion at the Capitol that the Eastern Lenape Nation of Pennsylvania is against gambling.  He notes that different tribes remain split on the issue but he notes that many people suffer and gambling money is not trickling down to reservations that have gambling.  Nationwide, gambling is allowed on Indian reservations if the laws of that state permit gambling in general.  There are no reservations in Pennsylvania, Gentlemoon said.

headline: RIDGE HOPES TO AVOID PREDECESSOR'S WOES WITH SCHOOL STANDARDS
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is trying to set statewide academic standards for what public school students should learn in their core subjects of reading, writing and math.  He wants to avoid the pitfalls encountered by Governor Robert Casey. Ridge is staying out of "outcome based" education that became emeshed in a culture war and is more focused on objective criteria  in hard-core subjects.

headline: TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC:  MUCH TALK ABOUT IT
abstract: Traffic on Route 611 cannot handle the additional cars from a proposed off-track betting site at what is now Mikels Motors, a Stroud Township official said.  Supervisor and Roadmaster Jim Decker said at the Horse Racing Commission hearing that there is too much congrestion at two intersections near Mikels Motors.  About 1200 cars drive through the strip everyday, said Decker, citing a traffic study conducted by the developers of a proposed mall slated to go across the street form the proposed site.  He said that more than $1.35 million is needed to reduce the congrestion and no mechanism is in place to get such funds.  The township is not getting any money from the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation for improvement.  Other citizens said that another location would be much better for a betting parlor.

headline: IS MORE GAMBLING WORTH THE GAMBLE?
abstract: Governor Ridge seems to acclept the pro-slot machine argument that allowing slots at racetracks will halt the exodus of gamblers to neighboring states.  Republic Paul Clymer's position is that no amount of added revenue is worth the social cost more gambling would exact:  the addiction, the crime, the broken families and the resultant increased load on the welfare system.  Clymer notes that casino gambling in Atlantic City has made a lot of money for casino owners but has done nothing for Atlantic City or the people that live there.  The authors do not believe that the supporters of expanded gambling have made a convincing case - they never discuss the drawbacks.

headline: Iron works quagmire
abstract: Debate goes on whether the Cambria Iron Works should be saved and preserved. Those trying to preserve the Iron Works want to make it into a historial site used for tourism.

headline: RIDGE PUSHES HARD FOR CHARTER SCHOOLS
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has been pushing hard for legislation that would lead to the creation of charter schools in the state.  Representative Dwight Evans, Democratic-Philadelphia has introduced an educational reform package designed to improve the city's schools, in part by creating local councils that would be made up of parents, teachers, and other community members who would make many of the decisions about the schools are run.

headline: Troopers tag 8,300 on traffic charges
abstract: 8300 have been ticketed under the new highway-safety enforcement programs, "Centipede" and "Tag-D."

headline: Job picture turns cloudy in banking
abstract: Mergers have caused a loss of jobs in the banking industry around Philadelphia. More layoffs are expected with the union of CoreStates and First Union.

headline: Kanjorski vows to assist Bloomsburg with flood protection
abstract: Congressman Paul E. Kanjorski is seeking to obtain funding for a flood control project in Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania.

headline: RIDGE'S REWARD PROGRAM FEELS UNFINISHED
abstract: Education Secretary Eugene Hickok supported Governor Tom Ridge's $10 million dollar reward program to provide cash to schools for improving academic performance and graduation rates. Senator Allyson Scwartz, Democrat - Philadelphia said she is concerned that poorer districts would have less chance of gaining state funds under such a program.

headline: With 40,000 deaths yearly on roads, more dollars should go to prevention
abstract: Highways fatalities account for 94 percent of all transportation deaths, however, highways safety accounts for only 1 percent of the Department of Transportation budget.

headline: JOGGING AROUND
abstract: Gone on Gambling:  Here's some more fodder for those who oppose expanded legalized gambling.  The Economist, a news weekly reports a "1995 study conducted by the Iowa Department of Human Resources found that 5.4 percent of the state's population had a gambling problem, up from 1.7 percent before the state introduced riverboat gambling."  Gambling has become the fastest growing cause of personal bankruptcey, and 28 states now have programs for compulsive gamblers.  All this makes the gambling industry's efforts to paint itself as family friendly rather ludicrous.  Now matter how you look at it, the expansion of legalized gambling isn't healthy.  For the state to sanction this in the name of econmic devleopment is betryal of public trust.

headline: MARITIME MUSEUM TO OPEN TO PUBLIC IN AUTUMN
abstract: The Erie Maritime Museum on the eastern bayfront will open to the public sometime this fall but probably won't be finished until April 1998, state officials said.  Amy Riggleman, press secretary for the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission said that no firm date has been set.

headline: RIDGE'S STANDARDS WIN PRAISE
abstract: School administrators may not like rewriting curriculum every time the state's political winds change, but academic standards proposed by the Ridge administration do not seem to be causing the problems that surrounded their predecessor, outcomes-based education (OBE).  Many administrators are praising Ridge's plan as concrete and tangible, in contrast to OBE, which many believe is vague and difficult to measure.

headline: Without state grant, airport will close down
abstract: Mid-State Regional Airport Authority believes it needs a grant from the Governor's Action Team in order to maintain operations. The Authority has tried to make multiple changes in their budget in order to overcome the highcost of running the airport, but mas made mistakes concerning the insurance policy.

headline: LAWMAKERS EYE GAMBLING ISSUE
abstract: Lawmakers plan to put a three-way gambling quesiton on the ballot this fall.  Statewide voters may decide on the merits of gambling at the same time they consider a constitutional amendment to allow business and residential property to be taxed at different rates.  The latter is considered a key component to enacting a local tax reform law.

headline: MUSEUM COMMISSION CLEANING HOUSE
abstract: It is cleaning time for the state's Historical and Museum Commission and today it will auction off the bayonets, double-barrel shotguns and other items from its collections.  Money made will go toward the purchase and restoration of the museum's 2.5 million other artifacts.  State auctions are held almost every year as a way of opening space and raising money for museums.

headline: SCHOOL BOARD NIXES CHARTER PROPOSAL
abstract: The Spring Grove School Board voted against a proposal to make the district a charter school district.  But board member Dean Snyer, acting as  a private citizen, filed an application to make the change from public school district to charter school district.  He said he may bring a litigation against the school board for its failure to hold a public hearing as required.

headline: null
abstract: A political cartoon reading 'State law takes effect, mandating prosecution of students using tobacco at school immediately, a co-conspirator is charged.' Joe Camal is smoking with two police officers saying 'I'd recognize those yellow teeth anywhere.'

headline: Lenders Trying to Impose Fee on Most Creditworthy
abstract: Credit Card companies are starting to charge a fee for those cardholders who pay in full their balance each month.

headline: New well to assist cleanup
abstract: There is an effort to clean up the Little Schuylkill River which is severely polluted.

headline: SCHOOL COMPUTERS MOTIVATE, BUT DO THEY EDUCATE
abstract: The nation's schools will spend a record $5.2 billion on computers and related technology this year, an increase of nealry a billion dollars from over a year ago.  Computers are the teaching tools of tomorrow.  But will the technology help them learn?  No one seems to know, according to an in-depth report published last week by Education Week, a leading publication on education issues.  Technology is changing so fast that it has been almost impossible for researchers to examine the impact.  Though they are known to motivate, they may also be hi-tech toys.

headline: 16 to testify at hearing on jail break
abstract: A public hearing will be conducted on the escape of six inmates from Western Penitentiary. Testimony will be taken from 16 people.

headline: Many others left the Valley station
abstract: Union Pacific Corporation will move its corporate headquarters from Bethlehem which reminded others of when Bethlehem Steel Corporation and burns Philp and Company left the area creating many lost jobs.

headline: PERMIT ISSUED FOR REPAIR OF FLOOD-PRONE DAM
abstract: State environmental officials issued an emergency permit for work on the East Bangor Dam, where flooding has caused constant problems for residents and railroads through December.  The permit directs Northeastern Equity Associates, owners of the property where a drainage problem has caused repeated flooding, to begin remedial work within 15 days.  The permit was issued in response to a Commwealth Court Order requested by the Department of Environmental Protection.

headline: SCHOOL DISTRICTS' FEAR OF COMPETITION HOBBLES CHARTER SCHOOL INNOVATIONS
abstract: According to the Commonwealth Foundation, a growing number of parents and educators attempting to build better public education through charter schools are finding that some local education leaders are simply beating them up. Rather than embracing the new approach to public education represented by charter schools and sincerely encouraging school leaders to support true innovative key statewide education groups - particularly the Pennsylvania School Boards Association, have helped create the environment of difficulty and derision that too many charter applicants are facing.  This trade association, funded by taxpayer dollars and claiming to support the reduction of school mandates, has effectively hobbled the creation of schools that would operate with few mandates and provide new options in public education for the children of the taxpayers who support their well-funded association.

headline: 1997 Had Most Executions Since Penalty's Return
abstract: A record high number of executions were carried out in 1997. The 74 was the most since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976.

headline: May be the mother of all bank mergers
abstract: First Union and CoreStates are planning on mergering together creating the largest bank in U.S. history. Philadelphia is planning to be majorily affected by the merger.

headline: President forwards letter
abstract: A letter from President Clinton was sent to the residents of the Wyoming Valley describing the damage from Agnes and the new construction of better levees.

headline: SCHOOL DISTRICT'S WORDS MISLEADING
abstract: Jack Steinberg of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers commends an editorial endorsing the adoption of a new city-wide standard as a positive step toward improving the education of the city's public school children; however, he feels that it does not go far enough in ensuring that priorities are put into proper order.  He states that academic standards are meaningless if the priorities are not correct.

headline: 3 AGENCIES PROBE SCHOOL INVESTING
abstract: Three federal agencies are conducting a criminal investigation of a Blair County investment advisor who has been accused by the Securities and Exchange Commission of defrauding Pennsylvania school districts and municipalities out of $71 million.  The U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Internal Revenue Service will scrutinize a lengthy paper trail to reconstruct how John Gardner Black, 53, of Tyrone lost at least $50 million while trading in securities in 1995.  The SEC accuses him of taking $2 million from his clients and using it to settle a personal lawsuit and to pay salaries, office rent and personal expenses.

headline: MINNESOTA CHAIN IS TARGETING WAL-MART AND KMART HERE
abstract: Target is making an aggressive eastward expansion from Minneapolis to the Atlantic.  In time there will be more than 40 between here and the suburbs of New York City as Target moves head-to-head with its big-boy rivals, Wal-Mart and Kmart.

headline: READSHAW LEADS MONUMENT REPAIR BATTLE
abstract: Representative Harry Readshaw (D-36) is working on legislation to permanently fund the preservation of monuments and markers to Pennsylvania soldiers who fought at Gettysburg. There are 111 such monuments and markers.  Over the years many have fallen in to disrepair and neglect.

headline: SCHOOL STATS EASIER TO FIND, BUT SOME ASK IF THEY MATTER
abstract: Pennsylvania recently released reports for each of 3,167 schools that comprise such numbers as enrollment, economic status of students, education spending, dropout rates and academic test scores.  Previously, such reports were available only to educators.  The state redesigned the information and has released it for mass consumption on CD-Roms, the World Wide Web, and on paper.

headline: A dozen death warrants Ridge cited in his '94 campaign still not signed
abstract: Gov. Ridge has signed only 7 of the 21 death warrants he claims former acting Gov. Singel was slow in signing.

headline: MINNESOTA COURT UPHOLDS STATE JURISDICTION OVER GAMBLING WEB SITE
abstract: Minnesota has the right to regulate Internet activity, the state Court of Appeals ruled in a widely-watched case involving a Las Vegas company's gambling site on the World Wide Web.  The site's operator stated he will appeal.  The case stems from a push by Attorney General Hubert Humphrey III to block the gambling operation from soliciting business from Minnesota's resdiences on the Internet.  Kerry Rogers, president of Granite Gate Resorts claims Minnesota lacks jurisdiction because he has not mailed or advertised anything in Minnesota.

headline: REGION REMEMBERS 20 YEARS AFTER FLOOD
abstract: This weekend marks the 20th anniversary of the 1977 Johnstown Flood and area groups are planning services to remember those who lost their lifes and those that were left behind to rebuild.  Thirty-nine people in Tanneryville died as a direct result of the Laurel Run Dam collapsing.

headline: School voucher programs are not the answer for Black students
