abstract: The support of school vouchers is growing in the Black community, especially amongst the poor. The editors do not believe that vouchers will be the most beneficial to the students in the poorer school districts. The editors' solution would be to improve the public schools and increase parental involvment.

headline: A heartless drug law can be nullified
abstract: The Monroe and Lehigh County District Attorneys is will prosecute any individual with marijuana even if it is being used for medical use, but is not actively pursuing such cases. There is debate over whether the law should be changed for these cases.

headline: Murphy vetoes bill boosting video poker
abstract: Saying the legislation would have resulted in increased illegal gambling, Pittsburgh Mayor Murphy vetoed a bill that would have allowed restaurants and taverns to increase the number of video poker machines and other amusement devices on premises. The reason was that these games are considered pure betting devices. He wants state law to regulates this matter before allowing it in the city.

headline: Ridge releases $3.4 million for Delaware Canal repairs
abstract: Two projects to help revitalize the Delaware Canal State park received funds.

headline: SCHOOL WEAPONS ACT NEEDS REVISION
abstract: Under the American system of education, schools, their governance and operation are predominately a local concern.  Locally elected school boards set policies and hire administrators who carry out these policies.  The temptation to impose rules and requirements is great and grows as the political climate heats up.  As a result of the 1995 "Safe Schools Act", Harrisburg School District's administrators find themselves taking draconian actions against some kids whose crime was a lapse in judgment, simple oversight, thoughtlessness or forgetfulness.  The Legislature is not considering revising the law to introduce greater common sense into the process.  This is a welcome change.

headline: A new old role for caseworkers
abstract: A new project is being conducted in Allegheny County to evaluate and change the Allegheny County Children and Youth Services, particularly the caseworkers attitudes and behaviors.

headline: Name game to be in play again
abstract: The CoreStates Center and Spectrum will be renamed becausing of the merger of CoreStates with First Union. The sponsor has a deal in place for renaming of the sports complex in situations as this.

headline: River can be the tie that binds
abstract: The breathtaking Allegheny River needs to havae a celebration to expose the river to other people in the state. The river is underused and would benefit greatly from a summit.

headline: SCHOOL WEAPONS LAW UNDER FIRE
abstract: Pennsylvania's 1995 safe schools act is being interpreted so differently in each district that justice isn't always done for those caught with weapons, superintendents said at a legislative hearing on Thursday.

headline: Adoption the focus of local gathering
abstract: About 700 come together for the Adoption in Pennsylvania conference held in Lower Swatara Township. The message of the conference is to recognize the need for more caring families.

headline: New insurance options for consumers are approved
abstract: Three topics are covered in this article. Community-based charter schools will be able to be set up. Consumers can now go to state-chartered banks for insurance policies. Ten southwestern counties can vote on a tax increase to help fund regional economic development projects.

headline: Salutes & Boots
abstract: The Beaver County Times salutes Gov. Tom Ridge for adopting a smoking ban in all state-owned buildings. They also salute Rep. Harry Readshaw for working towards preserving the monuments and statues at Gettysburg National Military Park. The boot was given to Rep. Ivan Itkin for trying to stop the change of government for Allegheny County.

headline: SCHOOLING PENNSYLVANIA ON STATE TUITION PROGRAM
abstract: Two students enter Pennsylvania colleges this fall as the first to use the Tuition Account Program (TAP) that was set up in the fall of 1993.  Now four years later, they are set to reap the benefits of what is billed as a conservative, low-risk way for families to put money away for college.  State treasurer Barbara Hafer is planning some changes in the way TAP is administered and believes it was oversold as the best way for families to save when she believes it is one way to save.

headline: An attempt to make jury duty less of a trial
abstract: Proposed legislation would allow for a juror to serve only one day unless picked for a longer trial. It also calls for various other bonuses for jurors.

headline: NUMBER OF SLOTS ISN'T THE ISSUE
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge noted that the concept of placing slot machines at the state's four horse tracks makes some sense to him.  The governor expressed reservations about the number of slots, calling the proposed 3,000 per track as too high.  The stage is now set for the horse racing industry to get what it wants at the expense of Pennsylvania businesses and citizens.  The fundamental issue is that the best number of slots is zero.  The state has no obligation to bail out the horse racing industry.  The notion that slots create new economic activity is bogus.  All it does is take money out of the pockets of citizens and line those of the track owners.

headline: SANTORUM SUCCESSFUL IN BATTLE FOR GETTYSBURG FUNDS
abstract: U.S. Senator Rick Santorum said he was successful in convincing the chairman of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on the Interior to include $1,052,000 for preservation efforts in the Gettysburg National Park in addition to the $3.6 million funding request for the Park's operation.  Santorum said it was sort of an easy sell as the chairman is a Civil War buff.

headline: SCHOOLS AWAIT STATE SUMMARY OF '96 SKILLS TEST
abstract: In February 1996, thousands of Pennsylvania students took a standardized test that area educators said would provide a snapshot of how the state's public schools were performing.  More than a eyar later, a school-by-school summary has yet to be released.  Fifth, eighth, and eleventh graders in public schools were tested in math and reading while sixth and ninth graders completed a writing assessment.  The testing program is called the Pennsylvania System of School Assessment (PSSA) and costs $4 million dollars annually.

headline: Appeals court strikes down Ohio limit on late abortions
abstract: A fedearl appeals court ruled against a 1995 Ohio law that bans late term abortions using the dilation and extraction method, citing there must be a concession for women whose life is in danger.

headline: OFFICIALS SCRAMBLE FOR SHIP GAMBLING LEGALITY
abstract: The executive director of the Erie-Western Pennsylvania Port Authority is in the state Capitol this week trying to determine exactly where state and federal law stands on vessels that are equiped with gaming devices.  Raymond Schreckengost met with six members of the Erie County legislative delegation and said it is important to get the legal issue cleared up because there is a proposal to provide daily ferry service from Erie to Port Colbourne, which is 10 miles from the new Casino Niagara at Niagara Falls, Ontario.  The ferries will likely be equipped with gaming devices, most likely slot machines that patrons could begin playing once the vessel steams about 10 miles across Lake Erie to Canadian waters where gaming is allowed.

headline: Smoking banned in state Capitol
abstract: A smoking ban in the Capitol was adopted.

headline: SCHOOLS LOSING INVESTMENTS ARE OUT OF LUCK
abstract: School districts, including three in the midstate, caught short of cash because of millions of dollars disappeared from investment accounts should look elsewhere for money to pay their bills, trustee Dick Thornburgh said yesterday.  The former governor, now a practicing attorney in Pittsburgh, is sorting out a wide-ranging school finance scandal for a federal judge.  He met with 200 school officials, including some form the midstate.

headline: As Texas Executions Mount, They Grow Routine
abstract: The death penalty in Texas is being routiney carried out and it considered common. The state is breaking its own records for number of people executed.

headline: OFF-TRACK BETTING IN THE CARDS
abstract: Pocono Downs horse racetract in Wilkes-Barre announced plans to develop an off-track betting facility along Route 611 in Stroud Township.  Pocono Downs has signed a contingency lease to occupy Mikels Motors, a Oldsmobile-Cadillac dealership at 1061 N. Ninth Street.  They will file an application with the Pennsylvania Horse Racing Commission.  If Pocono Downs gains approval, renovations would begin immediately.

headline: State grant to fund study of watershed
abstract: A study to examine the watershed of the Tinicum Creek will awarded a grant.

headline: SCHOOLS SET A $500 BOUNTY ON ILLEGAL STUDENTS
abstract: School officials frustrated with out-of-towners who illegally slip their children into the district, are putting bounties on the students.  Beginning in August, local constables will get $500 or each verified non-resident student they find.  Non-residents must pay $10,000 in tuition to send their child to this Buck's County school district.  Many students are attending illegally from places such as Trenton, New Jersey, across the Delaware River.

headline: Attorney confident Pa. smoking suit will continue
abstract: The attorney who filed a lawsuit against the tobacco industry still feels the class-action lawsuit has a good chance for a settlement. The lawsuit represents the millions of smokers in Pennsylvania.

headline: OTB PARLOR NO SURE BET
abstract: The state Supreme Court has granted an appeal of a June 1996 Commonwealth Court decision upholding plans for the Concorn Turf Club, an off-track betting parlor and restaurant proposed for the former Eric Theater site on Route 1.  The appeal was filed by a citizens' group, CONTACT II and Soutco, a manufacturing company whose property abuts the proposed site.

headline: STATE MAY ORDER SAFETY MEASURES AT LOW-HEAD DAMS
abstract: A bill to prevent drownings at low-head dams in Pennsylvania was approved by the state House of Representatives.  If approved by the Senate, the bill will require dam owners to post warning signs and buoys at 351 dams across the state, including 23 low-head dams in Lancaster County.  The billw as prompted by the drowning in 1994 of a 14-year-old York boy, said Representative Todd Platts, the York County Republican who introduced the bill.

headline: Seneca may bring courtroom to school
abstract: A district justice will allow for a campus court to be held at Seneca Valley School District for one day per month. The cases held at campus court will be related to the new law banning tobacco products on school property.

headline: Atty. Gen. bolsters drug task force program in Pa.
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher is altering the Municipal Drug Task Force program to help the war on drugs.

headline: PERZEL SIGNALS SHIFT IN GAMBLING STANCE
abstract: In his most direct comments to date on gambling expansion, House Majority Leader John Perzel recently said he supports the concept of riverboat casinos, slots in race tracks and video poker machines.  The Philadelphia Republican's comments came during a televised call-in show.  He said he will support a statewide referendum on gambling in November.  Governor Tom Ridge has insisted on a ballot before he wold consider any gambling bill.

headline: State Oks grants for recreation
abstract: Various townships in Franklin County are to receive grants to help determine improvements needed for recreations sites and programs.

headline: Shippensburg school board memebr challenges vote by phone
abstract: A Shippensburg school board director challenges how the school board used telephone to approve the budget.

headline: BAR ASSOCIATION UNIT TO STUDY ETHICS OF CAMPAIGN GIVING
abstract: The American Bar Association plans to spend nearly a year looking at the ethics of campaign giving by attorneys.  A task force will study whether lawyers should be prohibited from appearing in court before judges whose elections they helped finance.

headline: Pittsburgh losing last vestige of big steel
abstract: LTV Steel will close their plant in Pittsburgh. The closing strips away at Pittsburgh's identity as the Steel City.

headline: State panel gets look at Presque Isle
abstract: The Conservation and Natural Resources Advisory Council visited Presque Isle on an ideal weekend.

headline: SILVER BULLET:  CHARTER SCHOOLS THE LATEST FAD
abstract: The Issue:  State law makers are considering charter schools legislation.  We Suggest:  These schools will not improve public education because they ignore the underlying societal problems facing our schools.

headline: Behind the grim statistics on child abuse
abstract: The Dept. of Public Welfare came out with a report that shows the number of child abuse cases in Cambria and Somerset counties dropped; however, for ever one reported case of abuse five go uncounted.  In the opinion of the newspaper there needs to be more education, more protective services and money directed at the problem.

headline: RACETRACK BILL OPENS CASINO DOORS
abstract: Governor Ridge had it right when he said that a proposal to allow up to 3,000 gaming devices at each of the state's four horse racing tracks "seems like a heck of a lot more about building casinos thant it does about saving racetracks."

headline: State parks visits decline in 1996
abstract: Visitation of Pennsylvania's state parks declined in 1996.

headline: State exercise plan for elderly honored
abstract: The Department of Aging Peer Education Program Promotes Independence was honored with the Special Population Health Education/Promotion Award at a ceremony in Harrisburg.

headline: Bill offers standards for crime victim restitution
abstract: Criminals must pay restitution to their victims, but the amount given is not regulated and the counties rarely investigate what should be paid.

headline: RACING INDUSTRY HOLDS RALLY AT STATE CAPITOL
abstract: About 200 people involved in the horse-racing industry rallied at the Capitol in hopes of jump-starting a bill legalizing slot machines at tracks.  The bill has been stuck at the House gate where Governor Ridge has questioned details of placing 1,500 electronic slot machines at Philadelphia's Park in Bensalem and each of the state's other three race tracks.

headline: State rivers compete for nation's top 10 spots
abstract: A number of rivers in Pennsylvania are trying for a spot on the "American Heritage Designation Initiative." 10 rivers will be chosen to receive help from the federal program.

headline: Smoking fines burn hole in some students' wallets
abstract: A new law imposes a fine for having tobacco products on school property. The school districts can keep the money from the fines.

headline: Bill to tighten restitution passed by House, 190-1
abstract: Proposed legislation to tighten the restitution process easily passed in the House and now will go to the Senate.

headline: RANDY BISH:  ONE-ARMED BANDIT VERSUS TWO-ARMED BANDIT
abstract: This is a political cartoon depicting a picture of a slot machine entitled "One-Armed Bandit" next to a picture of a man with "Pa Politician" on his chest and underneath, the caption "Two-Armed Bandit."

headline: Susquehanna River focus of press conference today
abstract: A public meeting is being held to discuss the American Heritage Rivers Initiative which could help clean up the Susquehanna River.

headline: RIDGE ADDS CAFETERIA INSPECTION TO BUDGET
abstract: Governor Ridge has approved spnding for school cafeteria inspections in the state's new budget.  The spending plan for the fiscal year starting July 1 sets aside $686,000 for cafeteria inspections under the Department of Agriculture budget.

headline: SOCIAL WORKERS COULD EASE TEACHERS' MULTIPLE BURDENS
abstract: Teachers must deal with many issues such as lack of parental involvment, age-inappropriate behavior, kids on an off medication, teenagers with dirty clothes and a host of psychological issues need attention..  Social workers could relieve them of some of this burden.

headline: Bill would forbid contactiing kids for sexual favors
abstract: Rep. Matthew Baker has sponsored a bill that would bar pedophiles from being able to contact children via the internet, mail, or in person.  Legislators in the House will vote on the measure soon.  The bill has received the support of the PA District Attorney's Office and PA Catholic Conference.

headline: Reprieve in works for iron works?
abstract: Various officials will meet to decide the future of the Cambria Iron Works. Locals want to have a plan that would make the Iron Works a historical site and an industrial plant.

headline: Volunteers free trees from prison
abstract: "Operation Tree Rescue" saved half a million trees from a former nursery where a prison is planning on being built.

headline: All branches equal, but legislative's $111 million more equal
abstract: The legislature says how much money they are appearing to save during appropriation hearings, but keeps a $111 million surplus in case of governor cuts because of political pressure.

headline: SOON, PEOPLE CAN FIND OUT MORE ABOUT PUBLIC SCHOOLS
abstract: Education Secretary Eugene Hickok's recent announcement that computer data on Pennsylvania's public schools is being made available on the Internet and on CD-Rom is more important in spirit than in substance.  What is more important is the attitude of Hickok and the Ridge administration that this is information all parents should have.  It represents a sharp shift in PA.

headline: Bill would OK no-warrant 'roving' telephone taps
abstract: Proposed legislation would no longer require prosecutors to obtain a warrant in order to tap a telephone if the person is trying to evade police surveillance.

headline: Ridge may seek referendum on state stores
abstract: Governor Ridge wants to privatize the state liquor store and is waiting for the Legislature to back his proposal. He would be willing to ask the public if they would be willing to have the state auction off the licenses for the liquor stores.

headline: Allegheny charter looks into the future
abstract: Allegheny County is planning to change the three-commissioner form of government to an elected chief county executive and a 15 person county council plus make Allegheny County home-ruled.

headline: ANALYST GIVES FISCAL NOD TO RIDGE
abstract: A top fiscal analyst says New Jersey Governor Christie Whitman is "fiscally wildely liberal" compared to Governor Tom Ridge.  Hal Hovey, the former budget director of Ohio and Illinois who now edits "State and Budget and Tax News" defines fiscally conservative management is management that hedges against risk, that has a low probability of unexpected surprises that would require cuts in services or increases in taxes, that fully funds or comes close to fully funding its pension funds.

headline: SPRING-FORD PARENTS FIELD CALLS
abstract: State investigators were conducting telephone interviews from a long list of parents yesterday in their audit of the special education department of the Spring-Ford Area School District.  Parents have complained that during public meetings that administrators have not returned phone calls or kept written or oral promises in students' individual education programs.  They also have said that the district has not provided adequate transportation for special-needs children or followed time line for services set by law.  Afeter received a number of formal complaints filed against the distict over these and other issues, the state Bureau of Special Education announced its investigation earlier this month.

headline: Bills focuses on unmarked police cars
abstract: Proposed legislation would ban unmarked police cars from stopping vehicles for moving violations. There are concerns over people imitating unmarked police cars, stopping motorists, and causing harm to those motorists.

headline: Ridge opposes ban on ATM surcharge
abstract: The Ridge administration feels a ban on ATM surcharges would put state banks at a competitive disadvantage.

headline: ARAD budgets groups' funding
abstract: Allegheny County will receive a larger than expected budget increase for Regional Asset District, an agency that funds regional parks, libraries, arenas, and cultural facilities.

headline: Both houses squeeze Casey appropriation
abstract: The Senate cutback a grant to Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. It is much lower than an original request due to a low budget increase.

headline: STATE BLOCKS PAINTING'S REMOVAL
abstract: A $300,000 replica of a painting depicting George Washington's historic crossing of the Delaware River is in the middle of a battle between the state and a tiny foundation that owns it.  Commonwealth Court Judge Joseph T. Doyle issued a temporary restraining order Friday to prevent the historic painting from being removed from its Buck's County location until a hearing can be held.  The Washington Crossing Foundation that owns the painting, wants to send it to New York for restoration but will not guarantee its return to Pennsyvlania.  The Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission requested the court order saying that the foundation is contractually required to give one year's notice before removing the painting.

headline: Bills on elder adbuse signed by governor
abstract: Gov. Ridge signed into law a meaure that would help protect the Pennsylvanian elderly from elder abuse and provide protection for whistle-blowers.

headline: Ridge tours on bike state's northeast
abstract: Gov. Ridge is trying to promote tourism with Pennsylvania by taking his annual bike tour.

headline: Bipartisan embrace saves bid for county reform
abstract: A referendum for ComPAC 21, which at first looked like it would never have  worked, will allow voters to approve a county charter that would change the structure of Allegheny County government.

headline: Budget increases annoy DeWeese
abstract: Rep. DeWeese argues that Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr. did not receive a fair increase in budget compared to Republican leaders.

headline: STATE CAN LEARN FROM OTHERS TO GET BEST FROM CHARTER SCHOOLS
abstract: In 1992, only California and Minnesota had passed legislation allowing charter schools.  At the end of 1996, half the states were operating charter schools with more to follow, including Pennsylvania.  Enough experience has been gained in the past five years that Pennsylvania has an opportunity to implement what has worked in other states and avoid some of the problems they have experienced.  A survey by the Education Commission of the States (ECS) and the University of Minnesota Center for School Change at the Humphrey Institute for Public Affairs found that the biggest barriers in starting a charter school have been the lack of start up funds, finances, and problems related to facilities.

headline: Board seeks help to retain Waymart's forensic services
abstract: The forensic services of Waymart might be replaced by those offered by other places. The Susquehanna County Prison Board is trying to keep Waymart's forensic services available to inmates.

headline: SENATE OKS REFERENDUM ON SLOT MACHINES AT TRACKS
abstract: The state Senate approved a measure that would allow voters to decide in November whether to allow slot machines at the state's four horse racing tracks.  The prospects for passage appear uncertain in the House.

headline: BROWNSTONE TO APPLY FOR GRANT TO BUY LEAF VACUUM
abstract: Brownstone Borough officials will apply for a grant to buy a leaf vacuum to alleviate problems between people who prefer to burn yard waste and others who don't like smoke.  Officials are seeking a state grant that would fund 90 percent of the cost of a leaf vacuum according to Borough Council.

headline: Budget passage tied to school funding
abstract: The new budget easily passed because of the promise of more funding for urban school districts.

headline: STATE EARMARKS $100 MILLION FOR TEMPLE
abstract: Governor Ridge dedicated Temple University's new Apollo arena on Tuesday.  Ridge guaranteed Temple University $100 million in funding from the state's capital budget in annual increments of $20 million over the next five years.  Temple officials are states that they have never been able to do any long-range planning based on state money because it has been year-to-year and this way they can plan.  The Apollo is a 10,205 seat arean they hope will anchor a Broad Street entertainment complex.

headline: BOARD TO TACKLE CASE SURROUNDING COLLIE'S SHOOTING
abstract: The Fish and Boat Commission's Firearms Discharge Review Board met in a closed meeting to discuss the case of a volunteer deputy Jacob Wishard who shot and killed Martha Eng's border collie last year at Colyer Lake.  Wishard claims the dog bit him twice, Eng disputes that and said the dog was at least six feet away from Wishard and is a show dog and had a canine good citizen (CGC) certification.

headline: Shutdown of Hazelwood works could signal twilight of coke's era
abstract: LTV's Hazelwood Coke Works, the last Big Steel plant in Pittsburgh, will be shutdown. The coke-making part of steel production is expensive and not environmental friendly. New ways are being used for steel production.

headline: COMPAC'S CHIEF TO MEET AGAIN WITH QUARRELING SENATORS
abstract: Duquesne University President John Murray will today with Allegheny County's state senators in an effort to resolve their reamining disagreements over plans to revamp county government.  Murray, who headed the Committee to Prepare Allegheny Country for the 21st Century (ComPAC 21) has emerged as the principal broker between quarreling legislators.  Murray and several of the senators who attended a meeting said the county lawmakers had reached accord on a variety of issues that had divided them.

headline: Great Lakes states losing federal funding
abstract: The Great Lake states saw a lower rate of return from their tax dollars while Pennsylvania had the best return from the federal taxes.

headline: STATE LAWMAKERS REVISE PUBLIC SCHOOL WEAPONS POLICY
abstract: State lawmakers have passed legislation revising a recently enacted state law banning weapons in public schools.  The changes are designed to make it easier for local school officials to administer and close some legal loopholes.  The plan was included in a larger bill amending other state school programs and is expected to be signed by Governor Ridge.

headline: Caging the sex predator
abstract: A new law labels sexual predators and brings harsher penalties on them including making his name and photograph available if sexual predators are paroled.

headline: SLOTS A BAD BET
abstract: For years, the gambling industry has been stalking the Pennsylvania legislature trying to expand gambling and hoping to rake in the dollars that gambling brings.  The latest is a prosposal to allow slot machines at race tracks.  Proponents say it is needed because Delaware and West Virginina now have slots at their race tracks and that is hurting Pennsylvania tracks.  They say slots will bring $752 million a year and 35,000 jobs.  This seems awfully high and if horse racing is in such dire straits, won't this just kill it off?  If passed, more poor peole who can't afford to blow their paychecks will.  Atlantic City is not paved with gold but with crumbling ashpalt and trash.  The editors encourage York's House delegation to reject the slot-machine proposal.

headline: COUNCIL VOTES TO HAVE LAND APPRAISED
abstract: Ebensburg Borough Council planned during its meeting to have land appraised for a landowner who wants to either purchase the plot or lease it from Ebensburg.  The land is being sought by the landowner to offer in a bid by the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP).  DEP is leaving its current offices and is searching for larger quarters.

headline: House favors cut for state advocate
abstract: The House decided to reduced the state's consumer advocate budget despite having a large surplus.

headline: STATE MIGHT NIX TUITION AT COMMUNITY COLLEGES
abstract: Massachusetts is pondering a proposal to eliminate tuition at its 15 community colleges.  The idea which needs approval from the Legislature and governor would make the two-year schools accessible to immigrants, minorities and the poor.  According to a state report, Massachusetts' community colleges are the second most expensive in the nation and cost an average of $2,530.

headline: Calling for 911 system changes
abstract: In 1995, two people died because ambulances were sent to wrong addresses. Proposed legislation would establish a 911 service on cell phone and impose a charge as what is done on land line customers.

headline: SLOTS IN PENNSYLVANIA:  MORE GAMBLING MEANS MORE CRIME
abstract: Pennsylvania's state senators and the governor are negotiating the details of a proposed legislation to allow slot machines in Pennsylvania.  Meanwhile, top law enforcement across the nation are publicly warning and actively campaigning against the expansion of gambling in their respective states.  Attorneys General from five New England states and New York issued a joint statement warning their states against expansion of legalized gambling because it is coupled with a high price tag which gambling proponents ignore at their own state's peril.

headline: County nears sale of tax liens to collector
abstract: Allegheny County's property tax liens are being sold to GLS Inc. to help with their budget deficit. The private company will now have the right to foreclose on the private citizens' liens.

headline: RAD to spend less money in '98
abstract: Allegheny Regional Asset District's 5 percent budget decrease for 1998 is due to the unusually large 1997 budget and varies budget cuts.

headline: STATE OFFICIAL WON'T TAKE KELLY'S CASE
abstract: For the second time, the Secretary of Education, Eugune Hickok has refused to hear the case of Bridget Kelly, the suspended Stroudsburg High School principal who is seeking reinstatement.  Hickok stated that he does not have jurisdiction and that the matter belongs before the school board.  Kelly was suspended based upon charges made by former superintendent Alfred Arena who left last November after accepting a $300,000 buyout on the remaining years of his contract.  The charges include incompetence, willfull neglect of duties, persistent negligence and will violation of school policy.  Kelly denies all charges.

headline: Campus crime
abstract: Colleges in Pennsylvania have found ways to make their crime statistics seem lower than they really are. There is a push to change how universities report their crime rates.

headline: SLOTS WANTED BY PENNSYLVANIA TRACKS
abstract: State Senator Robert Tomlinson, a Republican from suburban Philadelphia introduced a bill in the Legislature to try and stem the loss of revenue from Pennsylvania horsetracks to West Virginia.  His measure would allow the four Pennsylvania horse tracks to have 3,000 slot machines each.

headline: County parks help sought
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner is trying to receive more funding in order to hire more policemen to patrol County parks; however, the final budget for 1998 has been approved.

headline: Senate defeats challenge to balanced-budget bill
abstract: The House postponed the vote on a balanced-budget admenedment. The Senate voted against one of the balanced bill admendments.

headline: STATE SYSTEM ENROLLMENT INCREASES THE FIRST TIME IN 5 YEARS
abstract: Reversing a five-year decline, enrollment in the State System of Higher Education (SSHE) has incrased by 56 students for a total of 94,237 students for the fall of 1997.  Current enrollments are 0.56 percent higher thant he fall of 1996.  African-American and Latino students increased by five percent at System universities while student Asian student population increased by 13 percent.

headline: CAMPUS CRIMES DECLINE, IF YOU BELIEVE THE NUMBERS
abstract: Campuses in Pennsylvania appear a lot safer in 1996 but the State Police Uniform Crime Report (UCR) is suffering from a credibility problem when it comes to campus crime.  According to Temple University, the UCR shows Temple's theft rate plummeted 90 percent but it was discovered it was a typo - 339 thefts were reported but only 33 made it to the UCR.  State Police confirmed the error and admits it is responsible for about one-quarter of the 10 percent decline in serious campus crime statewide.  Without the error, state police say the actual decline would have been 7.5 percent. Additionally, all colleges were not represented.  Penn State-Beaver's supervisor of campus police said that they hand-carried the UCR numbers to state police and they were not put into the system.   State police spokesman Jack Lewis admits that there were problems but said the fundamental problem is that UCR reporting is voluntary and that major cities like Wilkes-Barre do not report.  Lewis said a fundamental fix would be requiring all schools and municipalities to report.

headline: SMART MONEY'S ON RIDGE

Advocates have tried repeatedly to get casino gambling on riverboats, slot machines at race tracks and video poker in taverns through the General Assembly. abstract: Pennsylvania Treasurer Barbara Hafer is trying to raise the visibility of the state's Tuition Account Program (TAP), the college-savings plan of which she offered a scathing critique only last year as auditor general.  In her new job, she runs TAP which allows parents to buy tuition credits for their child's future attendance at college at close to today's prices.  She has dramatically improved disclosure about the plan, its costs and penalities, including making clear that participants are paying a premium over current tuition when they purchase credits, something was not explained previously. abstract: The total tax burden in many of Pocono Area school districts, once below the state average, have climbed to near the middle of the pack, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Education. The annual massacre is a fund raiser for a park association in the town which should switch to clay pigeons.  Every year, the bloodfest occurs on Labor Day.  Each year, the Legislature is presented with a bill to outlaw pigeon shoots.  Just as regularly, the bill languishes in committee because many legislators are afraid of offending the state's large and active pro-gun lobby.  Outlawing pigeon slaughter would do nothing to restrict the rights of legitimate sportstmen.  It would add to the law that prevents cruelty to animals.  A Legislature with backbone would outlaw these cruel spectacles and put Pennsyvlania among the ranks of the vast majority of states that outlaw pigeon shoots.

headline: A RIVER RUNS FOUL
abstract: Local anglers have confirmed that one of Pennsylvania's top five trout streams, the Little Juniata River in Blair and Hunington counties has been severely damaged by an unknown pollution source.  Officials from the Department of Environmental Protection and the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission speculate that sometime between September 1995 and September 1996 an unknown pollutant nearly wiped out the aquatic macroinvertebrate population of the river.  The aquatic macroinvertebrates - mayflies, caddisflies, crayfish, stoneflies, hellgrammites, and others - make up the food base on which the river's brown trout feed.  Such feeding allows the trout to grow quickly.  The Pennsylvania Boat and Fish Commission has cancelled stocking of fingerling brown trout because of the lack of such food.

headline: BEAR KILLED ILLEGALLY, SELF-DEFENSE RULED OUT
abstract: For the first time in 50 years, a black bear was killed in Cumberland County this year.  Unfortunately, it was on the last day of antlerless deer season and almost a month after the end of bear season.  According to the Game Commission's Southcentrla Region, the 250 pound male was illegally shot in Colonel Denning State Park by Ron Miller, 26 of Newville. Miller was fined $800 for killing the bear plus an $800 restitution fee.  Also cited for "aiding or assisting to transport a bear unlawfully taken" were Ronald Miller, 56 and Tracy Burkholder, 33 both of Newville.  Miller claimed he shot the bear in self-defense.  However several deer hunters witnessed the incident and reported it to the park office.  One hunter also videotaped the defendant loading the bear into a truck belonging to the older Miller.  After the killing, Miller called the Game Commission's office to report killing the bear in self defense.  An investigation revealed that several hunters saw the bear and the bear was no aggressive.
