headline: Court says states can limit abortions to licensed doctors
abstract: The Supreme Court has decided only licensed doctors may perform abortions. Fourty-one states already have laws limiting abortions to licensed doctors.

headline: DRILLING PROJECT SAFE, SAYS EPA
abstract: A Superfund site in Palmerton is scheduled to be tested for heavy metals contamination in the water.  The federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sais that the drilling project will not cause in contamination to drinking water sources.

headline: FORMER ATTORNEY GENERAL CHARGED WITH DRUNKEN DRIVE
abstract: Former state Attorney General Leroy Zimmerman has been charged with drunken driving after being stopped by a Susquehanna Township police officer.  Zimmerman served as Dauphin County's district attorney for 15 years before being elected attorney general.  His arrest will pose problems for local prosecutors as Zimmerman is well-known within the Dauphin County District Attorney's office.  District Attorney John Cherry said a special prosecutor from outside the county could be appointed.

headline: An unsettling secret PECO deal
abstract: PECO will cut their rates by 10 percent if a lawsuit against them by Senator Fumo is dropped. The author is wary of PECO claiming to be making this deal on the behalf of the consumer.

headline: DOH CLEARS COVINGTON IN CONCERN OVER CANCER
abstract: The state Department of Health has determined that Covington area does not show any indication of a "cancer problem" according to an update by the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP).  The cancer study and elevated blood lead levels in children were health issues raised by residents at a DEP hearing.  A cancer epidemiologist reviewed data and noted that the rate of cancer is the township was much lower than would normally be expected.

headline: DUMPS' CLEANUP IS LIKELY TO COST ABOUT $5 MILLION
abstract: The owner of a former steel company that dumpted asbestos, sludge and lead-laden industrial waste on property in Economy and Baden will spend about $5 million cleaning up the contaminated sites.  California-based Robertson-Ceco Corporation expects to start cleaning up a 2.5 acre dump on Legionville Hollow Road in the fall, the company's Pittsburgh attorney Dave Pusateri said.  The state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) ordered the cleanup 10 years ago.

headline: Frivolous litigation draws fine
abstract: A Williamsport computer-service firm will be fined because of frivolous litigation after a bad business deal.

headline: An Unworthy Speaker
abstract: House Speaker Newt Gingrich is to be fined $300,000 for his ethical conduct in misleading the House to spend money.

headline: EMS alliance DOA
abstract: The Northern York County EMS Alliance fell apart when one of the main partners decided to not join.

headline: DUNCANSVILLE CITED FOR WORK AT SEWER PLANT
abstract: Duncansville Borough and its municipal authority have been cited for a violation of the authority's recently expanded and upgraded wastewater treatment plant.  The state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) violation notice was issued because a "bypass" was left in when the plant was expanded in 1996. DEP wants the bypass, which carries diluted sewage from the plant to Blair Gap Run, eliminated.

headline: Gekas urged Reno to seek death penalty for CIA spy
abstract: US Representative Gekas is pushing to reject the sentence reduction for a spy and asks for the death penalty.

headline: Anti-shutdown bill aims to avoid disaster
abstract: US Representative Gekas criticizes a couple of columnists on their criticisms of the Republicans and the White House on their debates over the anti-shutdown bill and the Disaster Relief Bill.

headline: Ex-dentist eyes decision on license
abstract: The state Board of Dentistry will decide if Dr. Joseph Mazula will be able to practice dentistry in Pennsylvania again after a boy died after being given anesthesia by Dr. Mazula.

headline: ELK SURVEY SHOWS A SEEMINGLY STABLE HERD
abstract: The January 1997 elk survey produced a population estimate of 312 elk.  This year's estimate is believed to be conservative because areas outside the primary range are not known.

headline: Gingrich Considering Loan to Pay $300,000 Ethics Penalty
abstract: Gringrich will tell the House Republicans how he plans to pay the ethics penalty before going public with his decision. He has made no public appearances and plans to resolve the issue soon.

headline: Cappabianca named minority chairman of agriculture panel
abstract: Cappabianca, a Representative from Erie, is named the Democratic chairman of the state House Agricultural and Rural Affairs Committee. The 'nemesis' of Cappabianca was ordered to reassign committee chairmanships forced a new House rule giving chairmanships by seniority.

headline: Forget day-care research--trust your instincts
abstract: There is plenty of day care research being conducted. Many of the studies find different recommendations, but the best policy is to just trust your instincts.

headline: ENVIRONMENT WATCH:  FORD HONORS DEP'S WORK VS. POLLUTION
abstract: A program designed to clean up polluted industrial sites and put them back to use has netted the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) a $20,000 grant from the Ford Foundation.

headline: GLASSPORT:  AID FOR FIREFIGHTERS SOUGHT
abstract: State Representative Richard Olasz appealed to Governor Ridge for financial assistance for volunteer fire departments that lost equipment in a devastating industrial fire last Friday.  In a letter sent to Ridge, Olasz, D-West Mifflin, asked Ridge to provide state money to help the fire companies replace that was lost in the fire at Glassport Industrial Center.  Hoses, helmets, breathing apparatus, boots, coats and other gear were contaminated with acids and other chemicals.  The damage forced the Reliance Hose Company in Glassport to take both of its firetrucks out of service.  Olasz said the firefighters need assistance to replace contaminated equipment and for medical examinations to check for exposure to harmful chemicals.  He also asked Ridge for assistance for businesses and employees affected by the fire.

headline: Casey awaits test results
abstract: Former Governor Robert P. Casey is still recovering from pneumonia in Pittsburgh.

headline: GAME DAY TO FOCUS ON PREVENTING INJURIES
abstract: A statewide organization that focuses on preventing injuries to children under the age of 15 will sponsor "Gear up Games" from 1 to 4 on City Island.  The free event is sponsored by the Pennsylvania Safe Kids Coalition in conjunction with the state Department of Heatlh, Harrisburg Senators and Eat 'n Park.

headline: EPA OFFICIAL SAYS PENNSYLVANIA IS NATION'S PAY TOILET
abstract: Pennsylvania in general and Lancaster County in particular are becoming the nation's "pay toilet," a federal environmental protection official told Democratic lawmakers Wednesday.  Hugh Kaufman, a senior engineer for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) urged that Pennsylvania's laws governing sewage sludge disposal be strengthened.  He said the state's current laws barely meet the EPA's minimum standards, which is making the state a dumping ground for sludge from surrounding industrial states.

headline: Grant will help D.A. drive against domestic violence
abstract: Delaware County has received an a grant to help stop domestic violence and help with previous cases.

headline: Casey looks for story behind audit numbers
abstract: Auditor General Robert. P. Casey Jr. is planning to conduct performance audits of government programs, nursing homes, and school districts.

headline: Arbiter: County must pay laid-off worker
abstract: An arbitrator has ruled that back pay is owed to a former Democratic committeewoman who was fired based on her political and union affiliations.

headline: Health care hearings vital for residents
abstract: Hearings will be conducted on managed health care. There is concern that Health Maintenance Organizations are forcing hospitals to rush the discharge of patients and cut costs.

headline: EPA SAYS IT TOLD WEISENBERG OF ANTI-SKID SLAG BAN IN '95
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) says it mailed Weisenberg Township a notice that it had barred an anti-skid material from roads at the same time it notified other municipalities and agencies and cannot explain why Weisenberg did not receive it.  They are investigating Weisenberg's use of high-temperature metal recovery slag, also known as iron rich material (IRM) after EPA banned it in February 1995 as it contains high levels of lead and cadmium.

headline: GUN LAW COULD DISARM COPS, CHIEFS SAY
abstract: More than 60,000 police officers who have been convicted of domestic abuse coul dhave their firearms taken away or lose their jobs because of a new federal gun control law estimates the National Chiefs of Police Association.  Police groups are lobbying for changes in the domestic abuse amendment to the Gun Control Act of 1968 which made it illegal for anyone convicned of misdemeanor domestic abuse to possess a gu n.  That includes convinctions before the law went into effect.  The Fraternal Order of Police wants to stop the ban from being applied retroactively.  The National Assocation of Police Organizations wants police to be exempt.  Advocates for victims of domestic violence oppose any changes or amendments to the law to make exceptions.

headline: Casey unwell, forgoes La Sale ceremony
abstract: Former Governor Robert P. Casey will not  participate in the La Salle University graduation ceremony due to illness.

headline: Attorney General selects Philadelphia lawyer to head unit
abstract: Alexis Barbieri will now be the head of The Public Protection Division.

headline: It's time to focus on alcohol and tobacco
abstract: District Director of the Pennsylvania Council on Alcohol Problems states that alcohol must come under the same kind of fire as tobacco. More anti-alcohol campaigns should be done and government funded.

headline: EPA TO WITHHOLD MONEY UNTIL STATE CLEANS UP CLEAN AIR ACT
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has announced that it will withhold $411,600 - 8 percent of the state's $5.5 million federal air quality program grant - until the state agrees to report all "signficant violators" of the Clean Air Act.  The DEP's own Citizens Advisory Council agreed with a federal audit's conclusion that the department failed to report air polluters and inentionally withheld such information from federal regulators.

headline: Gunpowder on hand
abstract: Gunpower was found on the hand of a man who violated his parole and was shot to death by police. Police claim that proves he shot at the police, but his lawyer claims that the powder on his hand was because he was shot in the hand.

headline: CASEY'S IDEAS TO FIGHT FRAUD WORTH A LOOK
abstract: It is difficult to blame the four local school districts involved in the statewide investment scandal.  This is primarily a case of fraud, where an investment advisor misrepresented the type and value of investments he was making with school districts' money.  Auditor General Robert P. Casey, Jr. had some good ideas.  He said the type of investments made by John Gardner Black's companies were not allowed under the Public School Code.  Authorities say that Black invested in mortgage derivatives but told districts that their money was in guaranteed investments and he greatly overestimated the worth of the investments.  Casey does not see that the law needs to be changed, just enforced.

headline: Attorney to run for governor
abstract: Attorney Philip J. Berg is running for governor despite failed attempts at the seat in 1990 and for the lieutenant governor seat in 1994.

headline: It's time to focus on alcohol and tobacco
abstract: In light of various alcohol abuse issues, Robert L. Nissly argues that alcohol should come under the same scrutiny as tobacco. A tough anti-alcohol campaign should be targeted towards children and adults.

headline: EXPERTS:  FIRE SHOULDN'T HAVE LASTING ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS
abstract: Investigators doubt there will be any long-term environmental problems associated with the massive tire fire in Washington's east end.  Heavy equipment is being used to scrape away about 8 inches of topsoil laced with tire chunks and oil, and the blackened earth is being trucked to Arden landfill in Chartiers Twonship, which is also accepting the tires.  Other hazardous workers are treating the water that remains at the closed National Granulating Company, Inc. plant before it is released into a nearby stream.  The tire fire which burned for 10 days was the largest to have occurred in Pennsylvania.  A 15-year-old Washington youth pleaded guilty to setting the fire.

headline: Halt all executions, state bar group asks
abstract: The Pennsylvania Bar Association wants to stop all death penalty executions until it can be administered without discrimination.

headline: Census notes population drops in Pa., Pittsburgh
abstract: Since 1990, the population of Pennsylvania dropped 20,000 people which was the most of any of the states.

headline: Aviation authority offers HIA workers assurances about jobs
abstract: The Susquehanna Area Regional Aviation Authority will establish terms of employment for the 70 state employees that work at Harrisburg International Airport once a firm is hired to manage the airports. There is concern over the loss of jobs for those state employees.

headline: LYME DISEASE ON RISE LOCALLY
abstract: Bucks and Montgomery counties are ranked in the top 10 in the country for incidents of Lyme Disease, according to at 1995 study done by the Lyme Disease Foundation. The highest incident rate occurs in adults in their 30's and 40's.  The disease is contracted by being bitten by a black-legged tick or deer tick as they are commonly known.  The tick attaches itself to the skin and needs 24 hours to transmit the disease.

headline: FARMERS PUSH FOR DEPOST FEE TO END BOTTLE, CAN DUMPING
abstract: One bottle thrown along a country road can cause hundreds of dollars of damage to farm equipment or ill a cow, yet rural roadsides are littered with countless of them.  Farm and environmental groups throughtout the state are urging the Pennsyvlania Legislature to approve a bill that would set a 5-cent deposit fee on soft drink bottles and cans.  They hope the deposit fee will prevent the bottles and cans from becoming dangerous roadside litter that causes millions of dollars in damages to the agricultural economy each year.

headline: Heidnik competent for execution
abstract: A Common Pleas Court found the murderer and sadist Gary Heidnik is mentally competent to be executed.

headline: City's Democrats look to Foglietta
abstract: Representative Thomas M. Foglietta, a Democratic from Pennsylvania, has been nominated to be the next ambassador to Italy. His nomination will require a special election for his seat on the Philadelphia's First Congressional District.

headline: BILL TRIES TO BOLSTER WEAK STATE LAW
abstract: The gaming industry spent $1.1 million pushing its cause in Massachuseets in 1995 but in Pennsylvania, home of four major race tracks and a renewed push for riverboat gambling, the industry spent just $1,093?  Teachers unions, schools boards and others spent more than $1.1 million influencing legislation in Washington.  Pennsylvania's 20 year old lobbyist reporting law is considered one of the weakest, if not the weakest in the nation.  Former Attorney General Tom Corbett labeled lobbying an $80 million industry, many lobbyists fail to file any reports.  Senator David Heckler, Republican Doylestown and the watchdog group, Common Cause are pushing the Lobbyist Disclosure Act in various forms in both the House and the Senate.

headline: LYME DISEASE THREAT SHOULDN'T TICK YOU OFF
abstract: Protect yourself but don't panic if you get bitten by a tick.  That's what city and state officials are urging in light of new statistics that show that more people are being infected with Lyme's disease and that the Philadelphia region is being hit especially hard.  The number of Lyme disease cases reached over 16,000 in 1996, a 41 percent increase over 1995 according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).  Pennsyvlania reported the third-highest number of cases after seeing a 50 percent jump in the same period.

headline: FISHERMEN TO FACE CHALLENGE AT DEEP CREEK
abstract: The Pennsylvania Fish Commission will not be stocking Deep Creek Lake for the upcoming trout season.  The lake is due to be dredged and the Commission is afraid the fish will be sucked up during the dredging operation.

headline: Helfrick's bills to limit use of death penalty
abstract: Proposed legislation would eliminate the death penalty. There is also proposed legislation to eliminate the death penalty for minors and mentally ill.

headline: Clean up mess in Upper Chi
abstract: Kathrynann Durham tried to give her appointed poistion as the Upper Chichester township solicitor to her husband, but resigned after the scandel. The man who was first thought to be receiving the position was evenutally appointed.

headline: BILL WOULD MAKE VOTE FOR NONE AN OPTION
abstract: Representative David G. Argall (Republican) proposes that voters have a "none of the above" option on their ballot.  He prposes that this would clean up campaings and attract a better class of candidate. Argall was one of several government experts testifying before the House State Government Committee on a bill he is sponsoring that would allow voters in the state to nullify a political contest by casting a vote for none of the above.  This means that if "none of the above" gets the highest number of votes in the race, the results would be thrown out and a special election called.  One expert testified that in Nevada, a similar option has led to cleaner campaigns and higher-caliber candidates since it was introduced in 1976l

headline: Milestone Pact
abstract: Pennsylvania and roughly 30 other states are suing the tobacco industry for medical related expenses paid for by Medicaid. 12 of the 30 states have already had their class-action suits filed.

headline: FISHING LICENSE SALES DOWN
abstract: The Fish and Boat Commission took in almost $12,900 less in license fee revenue during the first seven months of this year compared to the same period last year.

headline: Hershey site to again offer officer training
abstract: Municipal law enforcement training for police officers can now be taken at Hershey and four other regional training centers.

headline: COLLEGES, FACULTY REACH ACCORD
abstract: Negotiators for faculty and management of the 14 state universities have agreed on a three-year contract after resolving disputes and use of temporary faculty. The State System's board of governors will wait until after a vote by the 5,500 member union before balloting to vote on the agreement.

headline: Blacks Grab Six Judge Nominations in Low Turnout
abstract: Unedorsed Black candidates did well in a low turnout primary while endorsed Democratic candidate did not do as well as expected. All endorsed Republicans won their races in the Superior Court. Western Pennsylvania candidates faired better than the Philadelphia counterparts.

headline: Nursing home status discussed for Internet
abstract: Proposed legislation to allow information on long-term care facilities to be available through the internet or calling a toll-free hotline.

headline: FOWLS BEFOUL LAND, WATER:  WATCH YOUR STEP; CANADA GEESE ARE HERE TO STAY
abstract: Many members of the goose family from Canada have decided that Pennsylvania is a nice place to settle down.  All of these no-longer migrating Canada geese have golfers teed off, health officials worried and park visitors dodging goose droppings.  According to the Pennsyvlania Game Commission, the breeding pair population of geese has risen from 11,000 in 1989 to 89,000 in 1996.  Local governments and private recreation parks are using novel approaches such as on-sight dog patrols, netting and scaring them with noise makers.

headline: High court overturns law limiting death-sentence appeals
abstract: The court systems ruled against legislation that would simplify and speed up the process for long death penalty appeals stating it would create more procedural and administrative problems.

headline: COLLEGES, UNION NEAR DANGEROUS CONTRETEMPS
abstract: The union representing 4,000 faculty members at Pennsylvania's 14 state-owned colleges is poised to take a strike vote.  A strike at the schools serving 93,000 students is not imminent and there has never been a strike previously.  Our recommendation is to take a play from the book of former President Reagan.  Governor Ridge should fire striking college faculty members because the "do-little'work, earn-big-bucks status of too many (although not most) faculty members at the nation's colleges."  The system is lousy though not the fault of the faculty - they just took advantage of it and the system needs a major overall.  A faculty strike would provide a significant, albeit unpleasant, opportunity to start on that overall.

headline: Blackwell's hat in ring
abstract: Even against strong opposition and having been previously voted out of office, former US Representative Lucien Blackwell is going to run for the 1st Congressional District seat held by US Representative Tom Foglietta.

headline: Pa. gives nursing home last chance
abstract: State Department of Health officials will give Cobbs Creek Nursing Center one more chance to pass inspection before its 160 residents must be transferred next month.  State and local officials closed the West Philadelphia nursing home to new admissions, effective tomorrow, because of serious quality-of care problems discovered in two inspections last month.  Medicare and Medicaid payments for residents will end on passes and unannounced inspection.

headline: GAME COMMISSION HEAD GETS POWER TO BAN BIKES, HORSES
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission has formally approved a new rule that gives the head of the agency sole authority to ban bicyclists and horseback riders from state game lands.  He or she will no longer have to seek input from fellow commission members or the public before deciding a game land is off-limits to certain groups.

headline: In jail, there's no recidivism
abstract: More children are being tried as adults for violent crimes; however, a study reveals that those in the adult court system go on to repeat crimes more often than those tried as juveniles.

headline: COMMISSION TACKLES PROBLEMS FACE BY CITY SCHOOLS
abstract: A special state commission made up of legislators, educators, labor leaders and business hopes to change the failure of urban schools.  In April, the House voted 195-3 to create a 17-member commission to examine the problems of city schools.  Its members were handpicked by Republican and Democratic leaders.  The commission will hold its first meeting in Harrisburg and State Education Secretary Eugene Hickok will testify.

headline: Bortner refuses to gloat over ex-foe's woes
abstract: The former 1994 opponent of Senator Daniel S. Delp refuses to gloat over the sex scandel Senator Delp now faces.

headline: Pa. joins states suing tobacco firms
abstract: Pennsylvania and 23 other states are suing tobacco manufacturers for marketing their products to children.

headline: GAS STATIONS, OTHER AREA BUSINESSES FACE BIG COSTS TO REPLACE AGING TANKS
abstract: Gas station and business owners trying to meet strict regulations on underground storage tanks may get some help from the state.  Legislators are working on a bill that would provide loans to help tank owners remove or upgrade them by the deadline.  If improvements are not made, owners face fines of as much as $10,000 per day.  Only about 30 percent of tanks are in compliance statewide.

headline: Inmate suit claims injury by broken toothbrush
abstract: A prisoner claims he was hurt after swallowing part of his toothbush. He had warned prison officials about the toothbrush and is now seeking damages.

headline: CONGRESS TO AGAIN TAKE UP TERM LIMITS
abstract: The House plans to try again to pass a constitutional amendment limiting the terms of members of Congress but it is expected to fail as it did two years ago.  The issue is alive because it is popular among voters.

headline: Brownell wants to meet with Springirth
abstract: The New Public Utility Comission member, Nora Mead Brownell,  wants to meet with the utility rate case activist. Brownell was easily confirmed with all of the Republican senators voting in favor of her.

headline: Pa. late to join tobacco assault
abstract: Pennsylvania joined 24 other states in bringing a lawsuit against the tobacco industry. The tobacco industry had already put an offer down before Pennsylvania joined; therefore, the law firms representing Pennsylvania will have no work to do, but will receive millions.

headline: GRANT IS JUST BEGINNING OF CLEANUP
abstract: The federal Envrionmental Protection Agency is sending Bucks County $200,000 to check for contamination in approximately 180 different abandoned industrial sites.  Bucks County Redevelopment Authority officials state that the grant will be used to find the sites and determine what problems, if any, exist at those sites.  The sites will be cataloged.  The author of this opinion piece thinks that is a good thing for Bucks County.

headline: INVESTIGATION EXPANDED INTO SCHOOL INVESTMENT FIRMS
abstract: A federal criminal investigation into two Blair County investment firms is underway in conjunction with civil allegations that the firms defrauded scores of investors, including 18 school districts, out of up to $71 million.  The U.S. Postal Inspector's Office and the U.S. Attorney's Office in Pittsburgh head the problem of Devon Capitol Management, Inc. and a subsidiary, Financial Management Sciences, Inc., both of Tyrone.

headline: Congressmen need to boost Internet use
abstract: Only half of the Representatives from Pennsylvania have webpages while the national average of the House is 75 percent.

headline: Bucks CEO mulling race for governor
abstract: Bette Martin Musham, a Bucks County CEO of a marketing and design compnay, is considering to be a Democratic candidate for the Governor race in 1998.

headline: PHYSICIAN GENERAL PUTS THE FOCUS ON THE PEOPLE
abstract: The State's first physician general, Dr. Wanda Filer said that her priority is to return the focus of health care to the people it is supposed to serve.  Filer's new job as physician general was created by the Legislature last year.

headline: GREENE DUMPS SLUDGE PLANS
abstract: Plans to use sewage sludge as fertilizer to help reclaim an abandoned mine dumb in Cumberland Township have been called off.  Afer received notice that sludgewould be used to restore vegetation at the site, township supervisors wrote the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) and asked for a meeting.  They received a letter from DEP indicating that Alcosan, which was participating in the project, will not be applying sludge to the site.

headline: Investigator: Slaying of 'unarmed' man was avoidable
abstract: Parole officers are being investigated for the fatal shooting of a man in front of his girlfriend and children. The man, who was unarmed, had violated his parole.

headline: COUNTY REFORM PARTY LOOKING FOR CANDIDATES
abstract: The Reform Party of Lackawanna County is looking for candidates, particularly anyone interestedi n school board and district justice positions.  As a result of a recent 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling, the Reform Party is permitted to cross-file candidates in the same races that major parties can.

headline: BUILDING DEMOLITION POSTPONED
abstract: Demolition of the fire-ravaged state Transportation and Safety Building, originally slated for August has been delayed at least for several months, the state Department of General Services announced.  The delay was caused by a 1990 lawsuit the state files against the maker of asbestos materials in the building.

headline: Poll supports rise in cigarette taxes for tot health care
abstract: According to a new poll, Pennsylvanians are overwhelming in favor for an increase in cigarette taxes if the money is used for children without health insurance.

headline: GREENE LANDOWNER GETS GRANT TO CLEAR TIRE DUMP
abstract: About 200,000 used tires dumped on property along Route 18 in Jackson Township, Greene County, will be cleaned up with a $53,000 state grant awarded to an Aleppo Township man.  The grant from the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) was awarded to Walter A. Alger of Aleppo R.D. 1.  He purchased the 60 acres of property in 1996, tires and all from Don Keller who permitted the tires to be dumped there.  Money for the tire clean up comes from the Waste Tire Pile Remediation Program, a program signed into law by Governor Ridge in December 1995.

headline: Judge allows smokers' suit to go forward
abstract: A US District Judge allowed a lawsuit by Pennsylvanian smokers against the tobacco to continue. Other lawsuits against the tobacco industry are looking for the same approval from the court systems.

headline: COUNTY TEACHERS AVERAGE $46,000
abstract: Lackawanna County's public school teachers are earning slightly less, on average, than others in Pennsylvania this year, but more than teachers nation-wide.  The average salary for classroom teachers in Lackawanna County is $46,341 according to figures released by the Pennsylvania State Data Center in Harrisburg.

headline: Campaign Fund Raising
abstract: Campaign finance reform will be discussed when Congress comes back to session.

headline: Saultes & Boots
abstract: Proposed legislation would allow nonprofit trusts to set aside money to provide care in the way of living expenses, medical care, and other services for people with disabilities.

headline: HAZARDOUS WASTE TO BE CLEANED UP IN PULASKI
abstract: Land surrounding the former Metcoa Plant on PA 551 in Pulaski Township, polluted with hazardous waste, is scheduled for clean up in the coming weeks.  Nearly 200 companies, mostly in the metals and chemical industries have agreed to help pay for the cleanup of the property where a scrap metal processing planed operated from 1976 to 1983.  A consent decree to pay $1.95 million was signed by 187 defendants linked to the pollution of the land, formerly owned by Pesses Co., just outside of Pulaski, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced.

headline: Jogging Around
abstract: The aging criminals in prison cost taxpayers three times as much as a younger criminal.

headline: County touted for air center
abstract: US Senators Specter and Santorum are working towards getting a Fedearl Aviation Administration facility built in the Pittsburgh area.

headline: CAMPAIGN REFORM IS REALLY NEEDED
abstract: A new study shows a consistent correlation between campaign giving and voting outcomes in Congress. The editors say this is absolute proof that campaign financing reform is badly needed.

headline: STATE SHOULD OPEN DOCTORS' RECORDS
abstract: Pennsylvania is not among the states that allows residents to find background information on their doctors.  There needs to be more information about physicians.  States are passing laws to open doctors' disciplinary records and malpractice histories because current laws in most states bar consumers from getting that information.  That is wrong.

headline: HEGINS AGAIN
abstract: Lying on a road with your arms encased in 10-gallon containers filled with concrete is effective at stopping traffic but as a way of halting the annual Hegins Labor Day Pigeon Shoot, it’s a bummer.  Ask the seven animal rights activitists who linked arms and stretched out for 10 hours in a circle on Route 25 in Schuylkill County, blocking the main street leading to the shoot out.  The did irritate local residents, raise the hackles of motorists, and give various police officers and fire officials overtime to remove them.  But the shoot itself went on with 10,000 people watching shotgunners mow down hundreds of pigeons to raise about $40,000 for the park and local charities.  Neither side has really garnered legislative support so it will probably be repeated next year.

headline: Jury clears Peco of discrimination in worker's suit
abstract: Peco Energy was cleared by a fedearl jury of all race discrimination and harassment charges brought on by an African-American employee.

headline: Court election in fall could play supreme role in shaping Congress
abstract: Republicans are expected to have control of the Congress and retain the position of Governor after the 1998 election. This means the GOP is expected to have control of the reapportionment of district lines.

headline: CAMPAIGN 'REFORM' JUST SOUNDS FURIOUS
abstract: This editorial suggests that for all of the sound and fury emanating from Washington, D.C. about reform of campaign funding is just that - sound and fury, signifying nothing.  There are more than 70 bills  pending in Congress that have something to do with campaign reform but the only one that has received any real support has been one authored by conservative Rep. John T. Doolittle, a California Republican, that would essentially remove all restrictions on campaign financing.  This bill has received 54 co-sponsors.

headline: Specter against raising cigarette tax
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter does not want to raise the cigarette tax. He also feels funding children's health and discouraging smoking should be separate issues.

headline: HICKORY HILLS NEEDS SEWER, PIPE REPAIRS
abstract: A sewer plant needs expansion and pipelines need repairs at the Hickory Hills housing development in Foster Township.  The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) spokesman, Mark Carmon stated that the plant has problems and needs upgraded.  The plant is too small, it overflows and sends untreated sewage into waterways.

headline: Jury probes billing for Preate defense
abstract: There is an investigation into the report that former Attorney General Ernie Preate Jr. billed taxpayers for his own personal defense.

headline: Court worker deserves post
abstract: Jean A. Damin is replacing James McNulty as clerk of courts after his death. The editors agree with the appointment of Damin.

headline: CAMPAIGN REFORMERS RALLY AT CAPITOL; SENATORS UNMOVED
abstract: Arguments made at the state Capitol by state-based campaign finance-reform advocates failed to change the positions of either Senator Arlen Specter or Senator Rick Santorum.  Specter continues to review a proposal that would limit campaign donations and Santorum called it "a horrible piece of legislation."  The bill, touted by the Project Independence Coalition at a rally in the Capitol, would give candidates some free broadcast time, some reduced-cost broadcast time and chepater mailing costs in exchange for limiting their campaign spending and fund raising.  U.S. Senators John McCain-Republican, Arizona and Russell Feingold, Democrat, Wisconsin has said their proposal is constitutional and will reduce the impact of money on politics.

headline: State Capitol Roundup: Cutting medical red tape
abstract: Three issues discussed in article- The first issue is a proposed increase in hunting fees for residents and non-residents. The second portion of the article is about the creation of a 10 page document for doctors to join a HMO. The last issue is about two proposed elder abuse bills to end home-improvement rip-offs.

headline: HIDDEN DRAKE REPORT HAS LEGISLATOR FUMING
abstract: A report by a federal public liaison on the Superfund cleanup of the former Drake Chemical Plant in Lock Haven is finished but the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) will not let anyone see it and that has elected officials and a local environmental group fuming.  The report was prepared by a national ombudsman Bob Martin and is thought to be critical of the Drake cleanup so far and Martin will not release a second copy of the report without EPA approval.  Local officials believe that Martin is being pressured by EPA to change his report and Martin is refusing to do so.

headline: Lackawanna Judge Munley on anti-smoke bandwagon
abstract: A Lackawanna County judge has banned smoking for multiple defendants sentenced to the county prison.The new county prison is expected to restrict or ban all smoking.

headline: DELP PAYS BACK $50 TO SENATE FOR DINNER TAB
abstract: Senator Daniel S. Delp, R-York has reimbursed the state for a $50 dinner which two women from a York County escort service say he bought them and his aid at taxpayers' expense over last Labor Day weekend.  Delp paid the $50 tab two days after the Patriot-News made an inquiry to the Senate clerk's office asking to see Delp's bills.  The newspaper had been inquiring about the women's claim that they went on an August 31st boat trip with delp as part of their duties with the now-defunct Platinum Escorts Inc. and ended up spending the night with Delp and his aide.  Delp intitially offered a credit card receipt for the dinner to support his claim he had dinner with other friends that evening.  He submitted that bill to the Senate and said it was a dinner with three constituents over "banking issues."

headline: CAMPAIGN REFORMS DRAW YAWNS
abstract: U.S. Represenative Bob Borski has been making frequent stops in his Northeast Philadelphia congressional district.  He observed that no one seems to care about news reports that the White House has been "selling" nights in the Lincoln bedroom or that China sought to funnel illegal campaign funds to the Democrats.  Instead, they are focused on issues that affect their wallets.  Many say this is because voters are cynical, have more pressing concerns, and are confused over what money in politics is all about.

headline: State to join tobacco-makers suit
abstract: Pennsylvania will file a lawsuit against the tobacco industry for medical related expenses the state has been forced to pay for state smokers.

headline: HUNTERS' LAND
abstract: Because the Legislature let die a $7 increase in the price of a resident Pennsylvania hunting license, the state Game Commission will not have the money to add to the state's public hunting grounds this year.  It is the first time in at least 20 years that the commission will not be purchasing property for the State Game Lands system.  The inability of the Legislature and various sportsmen's groups to agree on a fee increase during the 1996 session has left the Game Commission strapped to the point that it may not be able to field a full complement of Wildflife Conservation Officer trainees this year, much less aquire new game lands.  Only an active program of land acquisition under the State Game Lands program can assure a future of happy hunting in the Keystone State.

headline: Lancaster County D.A. seeks the return of woman to prison
abstract: The Lancaster County District Attorney Office wants to have the acquittal of Lisa Michelle Lambert, who was previously sentenced to life in prison, overturned.

headline: Democrat won't take on Ridge
abstract: Former Lieutenant Governor Ernest P. Kline wil not run for a statewide office. He was not intimidated by Ridge's fundraising power, but it was family obligations that will keep him from running.

headline: Candidates come out at Democratic party
abstract: Senator Robert Mellow will hold his annual Democratic party. He hopes to promote former Lieutenant Governor Ernie Kline as the next Democratic candidate to run against Governor Ridge in the 1998 election.

headline: Tackle teen drinking
abstract: The editors feel Gov. Ridge should not use the issue of underage drinking as a way to maintain control of the state liquor stores. They also argue that underage drinking is still a major problem in Pennsylvania.

headline: HUNTING FOR CHANGE:  GROUP SQUARES OFF WITH GAME COMMISSION ABOUT DEER HERD FEARS
abstract: A group of hunters angered over the decline of white-tailed deer has a challenge for the state:  pay  more attention to the needs of hunters and clean up the Game Commission.  Sportsmen in Schuylkill County say the doe population may eventually be wiped out if the Commission continues its license policies.  They say officers aren't enforcing laws against poachers and a law requiring hunters to report kills.  But a wildlife officer says the Game Commission is doing its job properly and the doe populiation remains plentiful statewide.  About 45 distraught sportsmen and sportswomen have formed "Pennsylvania Whitetails Forever" and met to air their gripes over what they say is the Game Commission's constant refusal to allow hunters more input into the way the system works.

headline: Late News
abstract: A state trooper raped a woman and left her gagged in her home. The trooper apparently had problems in the past, but the Governor and the state police headquarters were not aware of them. The Patriot News feels someone should have informed the higher-ups of the previous problems.

headline: Democrats Facing Mountain of Debt
abstract: The Democratic National Committee has a debt of $16 million from campaings, legal bills, and lack of fund-raising.

headline: Candidates Surfacing
abstract: Various lawyers are vying for the vacancy on the county court. The former county court judge did not receive the appropriate amount of 'yes' votes to retain his seat.

headline: Toughening the Tobacco Deal
abstract: A new deal would hurt the Food and Drug Administration being able to regulate the nicotine amount in cigarettes and impose penalties on the tobacco industry. President Clinton is requiring the changing of these two policies before signing any deal.

headline: I'MDOING WHAT I CAN - HUNGER STRIKER HOPES TO CHANGE THE WAY ANIMALS ARE TREATED
abstract: Dawn Ratcliffe, a North Carolina woman is behind bars at the Schuylkill County Prison as the result of charges stemming from an incident at the 1996 Fred Coleman Memorial Pigeon Shoot in Hegins.  Today marks her 20th day of a hunger strike that she hopes will prompt Pennsylvania lawmakers to vote on a bill that would stop pigeon shoots.

headline: Law on prosecuting shoplifters stronger
abstract: A new law would not prohibit would-be-shoplifters from removing anti-theft devices from merchandise.

headline: Democrats find help in GOP ranks
abstract: A former organizer of the Young Republicans is now returning to help spark a youth movement in the Democratic Party.

headline: THUMBS UP TO HART'S TEACHER BILL
abstract: Two bills were introduced in the state Senate to allow the public more input into school teacher contracts.  Senator Melissa Hart, Republican-McCandless, introduced a bill to require schools to give the public 72 hours notice of a meeting in which they will vote on a teacher contract.  The other bill, proposed by Senator Robert Jubelirer, Republican-Altoona wants to allow the public to sit in on school district teacher negotiations.  Even state Secretary of Education, Eugene Hickok is against Jubelirer's bill.  This article states that Hart's bill is a good idea, Jubelirier's is not.

headline: Unhealthy secrecy for Healthy Start
abstract: 40 more communities will join the 15 urban areas to be included in the Healthy Start program to help fight infant mortality. A study was conducted on the effectiveness of the program, but the results were not shared with the public.

headline: 'IT'S BEEN A REAL FIGHT' : STATE DENIES PLAN TO OPEN FLY-ASH DUMP IN AMBRIDGE
abstract: The state will not allow an Ambridge fly-ash dump to reopen according to a state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) spokeswoman.  Besty Mallison said the state has denied Gab Sacco's application for another permit for the fly-ash dump.  He has 30 days to appeal; however, Mallison said that the dump will not reopen.  The state's denial of the application for a new permit brings an apparent end to the 14-month battle between Sacco and the grass-roots group Harmony Against Dumping-It (HAD-IT).  Sacco announced last year that he wanted to reopent he dump which had been inactive for nearly 20 years.

headline: Lawmakers want to put perverts in psych wards
abstract: Proposed legislation, the Sexually Violent Predators Act, to put the most violent sex offenders in a psychiatric ward or a mental hospital after their prison terms.

headline: Democrats in Bucks fill post
abstract: Philadelphia school teacher John Murray will replace retiring Democratic party chairman Milton Berkes.

headline: TILL DEATH DO WE PART
abstract: Pennsylvania Senator Rick Santorum led his fellow Senate Republicans last week to passage of an entirely appropriate ban  on partial-birth abortions.  A few days later, Santorum was among the Republican majority that voted against a 43 cents per package increase in the tax on cigarettes that would have been used to provide health insurance for 5 million low-income children.  The Republicans also failed to pass President Clinton's proposal for a $5 billion dollar program to help states and local school districts repair crumbling schools and build new ones.

headline: YOUTH STATUS REPORT IS LESS THAN GLOWING
abstract: Data shows that dropout rates have risen but abuse cases have dipped.  Births to unwed mothers are up but more teenage mothers are getting prenatal care. Joan Benso, executive director of Pennsylvania Partnerships for Children, which along with the University of Pittsburgh, released "The State of the Child in Pennsylvania."  The report tracts changes in the status of children in Pennsylvania's 67 counties by examining 15 indicators of well-being between 1990-95.

headline: JESSUP DRILLING SLATED
abstract: Exploratory drilling along Blakely Street and possibly First and Second avenues will take place on the public right-of-way and not on private properties.  Geologist Michael Walsh said the boreholes will be drilled to a depth of about 100 feet to locate voids and determine the general surface conditions in the area.  Walsh said his Department of Environmental Protection's Bureau of Abandoned Mine Reclamation authorized the drilling in light of several minor subsidences that have occurred over the past three years.

headline: 'Lawyer for Ever Child' great idea
abstract: The Philadelphia Bar Association has created a volunteer group called A Lawyer for Every Child. The group's mission is to help chronically ill and disabled children fight for their Supplemental Security Income which is being threatened under the new federal welfare law.

headline: Democrats starred as entertainers
abstract: The Democrats during a gas tax vote in the Legislature made fun of various Republicans and referenced other popular people.

headline: Two families sit out congressional race
abstract: Lackawanna County natives William Scranton and Robert P. Casey's sons will not run in the race to replace U.S. Rep. Joe McDade.

headline: Ag Progress Day in bloom Tuesday
abstract: A showcase of agricultural technology and research will take place in Centre County to promote precision agriculure.

headline: L. TOWAMENSING FEARS EPA DRILLS
abstract: Lower Towamensing Township supervisors have joined a growing chorus of people concerned that the federal Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) plan to test Palmerton's water may do more harm than good.  The EPA plans to drill 88 deep wells in 50 areas as part of the Superfund clean up activities in the Palmerton area that has been on the EPA's Superfund list since 1982 because of high levels of lead, cadmium and other heavy metals in the soil.  Area residents fear the agency mahy pollute the water system when it digs.

headline: Legal deals for tobacco industry worry Fisher
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher does not want to be able to limit people's ability to sue the tobacco companies.

headline: Democrats tighten fund-raising rules
abstract: Democrats are changing how campaign fund raising will be done. There will be new restrictions on contributions which will be tougher than the law requires.

headline: Union endorses Saylor for justice
abstract: A Union endorses Superior Court Judge Thomas G. Saylor for his run to be named to Supreme Court.

headline: Area dairymen put strike plans on hold
abstract: The board of the Progressive Agriculture Organization has agreed to push back the decision over a milk strike. The PAO wants to protest the high loss of revenues. US Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum are trying to have how the price of milk is determined changed.

headline: LEECHBURGH RECYCLING PROGRAM RECEIVES STATE RECOGNITION
abstract: Leechburg Borough's recycling center is helping southwestern Pennsylvania and the entire state reach its recycling goal of recycling 25 percent of what is discarded.  Leechburg's program has been profitable and in 1996, the center grossed $9,000.  The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) has toured the center and the Pennsylvania Borough Association plans to feature the center in its October issue of its magazine.

headline: Legislation focuses on sex offenders
abstract: Proposed legislation would not let sexually violent predators back into society and place them in mental hospitals.

headline: Dems seek viable slate for 1998
abstract: The Pennsylvania Democratic Party promises to be able to create a 'viable' ticket for the governor and US Senate elections in 1998. The party is having difficulty finding candidates for the races.

headline: Voter registration hits record number
abstract: Pennsylvania has a record number of voters which is now over 7,000,000.

headline: CHALLENGES TO FARMERS TO BE DISCUSSED AUG 14
abstract: State Representative Raymond Bunt Jr, R-147 of Schwenksville said the House Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee is interested in hearing about challenges and problems encountered by farmers and agribusiness representatives at an upcoming meeting in Centre. County.  The Committee will meet Aug 14 at Rock Springs during the penn State University's Ag Progress Days.  The meeting will be from 10 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Special Events Building.

headline: LETTERS: OPPOSE HIKE IN HUNTING FEE
abstract: Jean Oswald, Director of Unified Sportsmen of Pennsylvania writes that Pennsylvania Game Commission has rquested a hike in hunting license fees.  Oswald opposes any fees because he says that the Game Commission is inefficient and can manage what monies it receives better before raising such fees.

headline: Letter calls for return of Einhorn
abstract: Various members of the US House of Representatives are urging the French President to extradite Ira Einhorn.

headline: Dems, minorities blast Ridge over his nominee to PUC
abstract: Democratic lawmakers are upset with Governor Ridge for not nominating a minority to the Public Utility Commission saying he is insensitive to the poor.

headline: VOTERS CAN OPEN DOOR TO REFORM ON TAXES BUT SLAM IT SHUT ON LIFERS
abstract: When voters go to the polls Tuesday, they will get the opportunity to open the door to property tax reform, bolt prison doors, and write themselves absentee ballots for more convenient voting in the future.  The first referendum question is a chance to launch property tax reform by deciding whether voters will permit legislation to allow local governments to discount home assessments for tax purposes.  The amendmentment would limit the amount the property tax can be reduced in any community and prevent local governments from raising millage to make up the difference.  The second ballot question will make it harder for a prisoner sentenced to death or to life in prison to receive a pardon or a commuted sentence.  The third constitutional amendment would let voters cast absentee ballots if they cannot vote because work or other business requires them be out of their home municipalities on Election Day.

headline: Cold destroys most of peach crops
abstract: The peach and apple crops in Pennsylvania have been severely damaged or destroyed from the subzero degree weather experienced in April.

headline: LICENSE ALLOCATIONS HEADLINE CHANGES IN DEER HUNTING SEASON
abstract: There will be some major changes regarding deer hunting in the state of Pennsylvania this year.  Gone are the bonus licensees and surplus licenses for non-residetns and muzzleloader hunters.  One major revision is a change in the anterless deer license application system.  Statewide, a hunter may apply for and receive only one antlerless deer license unless he or she plans to hunt in special regulation counties such as Allegheny, Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery or Phladelphia.

headline: Literacy program targets state inmates
abstract: Proposed legislation would require a literacy plan for all state prison inmates.

headline: Dept. of Wrong?
abstract: The Corrections Commissioner in Philadelphia should not tolerate how the Community Correction Center is being administered. Background investigations and an audit should be done according to the writer's of the Philadelphia Tribune.

headline: WATCHDOG'S WEB SITE KEEPS TABS ON POLITICIANS
abstract: Common Cause, a political watchdog group. Launched an interactive Internet World Wide Web site earlier this month that's dedicated to giving citizens access to detailed campaign finance information.  The site contains federal campaign finance information, congressional voting records and an interactive feature that allows users to send e-mail and faxes to members of Congress.

headline: EMERGENCY LOANS AVAILABLE FOR FARMERS
abstract: Butler County is among 46 Pennsylvania counties declared natural-disaster areas by the U.S. Department of Agriculture because of the drought this spring and early summer.  Farmers in the state's other 21 counties will be eligible for emergency loans because they are contiguous to those designated counties according to state Agriculture Secretary Samuel Hayes, Jr.

headline: LICENSE INCREASE LEGISLATION INTRODUCED
abstract: Representative Bruce Smith, York County has introduced legislation in the state House that would provide the Game Commission fee increases for most of the hunting licenses it sells.

headline: Louisiana maps license to chill no-fault divorce
abstract: Louisiana is now offering an optional covenant marriage which would require premarital counseling and virtually eliminate getting an easy, no-fault divorce.

headline: Despite murky semantics, Kanjorski's vision is clear
abstract: Congressman Paul Kanjorski has not always made great decisions, but has a great vision for the Susquehanna River becoming a "Heritage River."

headline: Weighing the scales of justice
abstract: Mark C. Shultz was appointed to the 16 member board who oversees and disciplines lawyers who violate the code of ethics or laws.

headline: Emergency loans available for farmers
abstract: Famers in 22 counties are eligible for emergency loans due to loss of feed because of the drought.

headline: Logging practices in state reviewed
abstract: A study will be conducted in the summer to determine if Pennsylvania's forests are being sustainable while logging. The certification could provide extra money from marketing.

headline: Make those probing abuse accountable
abstract: State Sen. Greenleaf introduced a bill that will make it a crime to report false allegations of child abuse.  This, however, does not protect against the therapy some children are put through that implants false memories of child abuse into their memory.

headline: DEVELOPER TRIES TO HALT THE SALE OF DIXMONT PROPERTY
abstract: A Pittsburgh developer has filed suit to halt the state's second attempt to sell the expansive but chemically contaminated Dixmont State Hospital campus.  Kilbuck Associates filed the action in Commonwealth Court, arguing that the state cannot sell the former hospital because it has already agreed to sell it to Kilbuck.

headline: Well-intended amendment fails
abstract: An amendment proposed by US Senator Arlen Specter to have the Congress and states to set limits on campaign spending was easily defeated. Despite the promise of changing campaign spending, it would have created more problems.

headline: Ex-Demo leader resigns over DUI charge
abstract: Ronnie L. Reichart, a former leader of the Columbia County Democratic Committee, resigned from his poisiton at the state Agirculure Department after being arrested for DUI for the second time.

headline: MAKING WAVES
abstract: Recreational boaters are flocking in record numbers to Pennsylvanias rivers and lakes and it is occurring in the unlikeliest of places - a region 300 miles from the nearest ocean, hours from the Great Lakes and in an area where the boating season is relatively short and the winters brutal.  Pennsylvania Point, created by the convergence of three rivers has become a busy place for the enforcement arm of the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission.

headline: Man picked to head state drug unit
abstract: James Caggiano has been named head of the Bureau of Narcotics Investigation.

headline: Disclosure on-line
abstract: State Representative Greg Vitali has created a website tracking campgain reports. He is attempting to obtain all candidates information on political contributions for the website.

headline: What's in a name?
abstract: A highway near Scranton might be renamed after a controversial and current US Representative. The editors feel this is unjust especially since Representative McDade is currently seeking re-election.

headline: FARM BUREAU CHIEF BACKS "BOTTLE BILL"
abstract: The president of a state-wide farm organization voiced strong support for legislation to put a refundable deposit on beverage containers purchased in the state.  Guy Donaldson, an Adams County fruit farmer and president of the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau, called for passage of House Bill 922 during a hearing of the House State Government Committee.  The legislation would put a deposit of at least 5 cents on beverage containers.

headline: Man charged in waste dumping
abstract: Christopher Tate was charged with dumping hazardous waste on a National Historic Site in Juniata Township.

headline: Marinelli execution stayed
abstract: Marinelli, who was convicted of beating and shooting a man to death, had his execution stayed by a Philadelphia judge

headline: DONATION RECORDS ON DISK COMING
abstract: A relatively small state approation of $370,000 will be used for bringing the state Elections Bureau into the computer era.  Governor Ridge predictes that the process of making things accessible will revolutionize campaign finance spending.

headline: ALLIANCE FISHING FOR PEOPLE POWER TO PROMOTE RIVERS
abstract: The Kiski-Conemaugh River Basin Alliance is a specially formed partnership with six watershed groups to conduct a studey on how to improve waterways in the streams of Fcambria, Somerset and three nearby counties.  The alliance was formed in conjunction with the Stonycreek-Conemaugh River Improvement Project, Conemaugh Valley Conservancy, and Loyalhanna, Blacklick Creek and Roaring Run watershed associations.  A study will develop a program to conserve and improve river resources and will be turned over to the state in 1999. The study is the first step towards having the basin entered in the Pennsylvania Rivers Registry, making it eligible for state grants.

headline: Farm easement deadline nearing
abstract: Application are being taken for Bedford County's new agriculutral easement purchase program which will try to keep the best soils in farming.

headline: MARCH MEETING TO DISCUSS DEER HERDS
abstract: State Game Commission officials will attend a public meeting 7 p.m. March 13 at the Ulmer Planetarium.  Lock Haven University, to answer concerns about the supposedly low deer population in Northcentral Pennsylvania.  The meeting is at the insistence of state Senator J. Doyl Corman and state Representative Michael Hanna.  The alleged low deer population is keeping away hunters and having a negative effect on the economy.

headline: Mentally ill youths a dilemma for CYS
abstract: The Dormont family's son, who is mentally ill, accused his parents of child abuse.  Though there was no actual abuse, Child and Youth Services of Allegheny County took the child away because he was deemed not to be "controllable."  A judge then upheld a decision to put the child into a mental health home the parents did not want for their child.

headline: Don't allow public officials to be secretive
abstract: The article is a coversation with Joseph T Leighton who is the director of government affairs for the Pennsylvania Newspaper Publicshers' Association and an editor from the Chambersburg Public Opinion. The discussion is about the Sunshine Law.

headline: BABBITT ENDORSES PARTNERSHIP AT GETTYSBURG
abstract: U.S. Secretary of the Interior, Bruce Babbitt endorsed a public-private partnership to build a new visitors center and museum in Gettysburg National Military Park. Babbitt told an audience of about 600 gathered in the National Military Cemetery in memory of the 134th anniversary of President Lincoln's Gettysburg address that he welcomed debate from preservationists on the issue.

headline: Farming remains state's top industry
abstract: Farming is Pennsylvania's top industry. Farmers have been able to produce much more than in previous generation due to developing technology.

headline: MARSH LOST TO RUNWAY TO BE RESTORED
abstract: Work has begun to restore 26 acres at the John Heinz Wildlife Refuge at Tinicum tidal marsh.  The restoration is intended to mitigate the loss of 23 acres of wetlands during runway expansion at nearby Philadelphia International Airport.

headline: Middletown: No $$ for state cops
abstract: The Middletown Township Council adopted a resolution refusing to pay for services by the state police. There currently is a proposal in the budget to require all municipalities to pay for state police services.

headline: ELBY WILL ATTEND SUMMIT PHILLY
abstract: Daniel Potter Elby, co-founder and executive director of Alternative Rehabilitation Communities, Inc. and a York County resident will be one of five official representatives of the commonwealth at the Presidents' Summit for America's Future.  Elby was selected to attend the summit to be held next week in Philadelphia by Governor Tom Ridge.

headline: BRANDYWINE NOW WILL BE TREASURED
abstract: First Lady Michele Ridge joined representatives of the Pennyslvania Historical and Museum Committee last week to officially declare the Brandywine Battlefield as the state's first Commonwealth Treasure.  The designation is in recognition of extraordinary historic significance.  In addition to the awared, the Brandywine Battlefield will receive a $50,000 grant from the Commonwealth Keystone Preservation Grant Fund to assist the Brandywine Task Force in planning and development.

headline: Feds should do better by PA dairies
abstract: Farmers have been hurt by the changes in milk prices. US Senator Arlen Specter has been fighting to help farmers receive a more fair system of establishing milk prices.

headline: MORE SLUDGE HEADED FOR OUR LAND?
abstract: State Representative Camille "Bud" George, D-Houtzdale, held a hearing July 9 to discuss the expanding use of sewage sludge in the commonwealth.  The meeting featured rhetoric aimed at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) and the staet Department of Environmental Protection's (DEP) role in regulating and monitoring the land application of sludge.

headline: More cities have curfews, with mixed results
abstract: A growing number of cities are imposing a curfew on the youth to help reduce juvenile crime.

headline: End judicial guessing game
abstract: The way that judges are selected to the state Supreme Court needs to be changed. The editors believe that the judges should be picked based on regional elections to cut down on the number of candidates voters have to choose from.

headline: BROCHURE GRANT AWARDED
abstract: Schuylkill County has received a $20,000 grant to develop a full-color brochure highlighting area anthracite attractions.  The grant was awared by the state Department of Conservation and Natural Resources through its Heritage Park grant program.

headline: Five Monroe farms will get easements
abstract: Pennsylvania's Farmland Preservation program has purchased fives farmers in Monroe County to insure they will continued to be farmed.

headline: MORE TIRES HAULED FROM SUSQUEHANNA
abstract: The State Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) coordinated the second major clean up of the Susquehanna River of the summer.  DEP received assistance from various groups and organizations including the PA National Guard; Luzerne County Road and Bridge Department; Wilkes-Barre City; PennDOT and Alliance Landfille.  The tires, found near the Black Diamond Bridge in late July, were dug out of the river in August by volunteers.  DEP has been investigating where the tires came from.

headline: More kids going to prison
abstract: Children 15 or older are now tried as an adult for serious crimes. Concerns are raised over what crimes should remain in juvenile court and if these youth offenders should try to be rehabilitated in juvenile courts.

headline: END OF MANDATES IS GOOD NEWS FOR PENNSYLVANIA SCHOOL BOARDS
abstract: The Legislature is looking to remove several current mandates such as court-ordered bargaining; the prevailing wage; and seniority-based furloughs.  Each mandate would be eliminated under legislation working its way through the state House and Senate.  By freeing boards of mandated burdens, school boards could regain dominion over the districts they were elected to administer.

headline: Ceremony marks start of levee-raising project
abstract: Twenty-five years after a horrible flood in Wyoming Valley, the levees will be raised along the Susquehanna River.

headline: Hayes visit leaves dairy farmer cold
abstract: Farmers are struggling with the demand for lower milk costs by processors, but having increasing costs for production.

headline: New reservation system coming to Pa. state parks
abstract: A toll-free hotline was set up to make reservations for campsites in Pennsylvania.

headline: Murder or muddle?
abstract: A law was passed calling it muder if an assaulted pregnant woman has a miscarriage. Editors want lawmakers to decide if killing an unborn baby is murder or not. Currently, in aborition it is not, but assault it is.

headline: English chief of staff describes 'unique position'
abstract: Corry Rotary Club had Representative Phil English's chief of staff as the guest speaker at their monthly meeting. At the monthly meeting, he spoke of what Representative English was doing for his constituents.

headline: Clinton creates river program, but it lacks funding
abstract: The American Heritage Rivers Program was created, but has not received funding. The program will work to help communities revitalize rivers.

headline: HE'LL GET $734,000 NOT TO SELL THE FARM
abstract: Upper Makefield Supervisor William Gunser has made sure another farm will stay a working farm in the township.  He discovered the famr next to his Highland Avenue land was being sold so he went into debt and bought the 131-acre hay and soybean farm.  He then applied to sell the development rights to the state and county-funded Agricultural Land Preservation Fund.  Bucks County Commissioners approved the county's portion of the purchase for $100,000.  The state will pay Gunser $634,000 for its share of an agricultural easement that will prevent development.  Gunser also sold the rights to his 95-acre farm for an undisclosed amount.  He states that he is not doing it for personal gain but to entice farmers in the area to do the same thing so that farms will remain as they are.

headline: NEW THREAT:  LEAKING UNDERGROUND GAS STORAGE TANKS
abstract: Leaking underground petroleum storage tanks could be endangering the environment and small business owners.  The federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) estimates there are 1 million underground petroleum tanks at 370,000 sites nationwide.  The EPA said 325,000 of those tanks have leaked, and about 60 percent of the leaks contaminated underground sources of drinking water.  Half of Americans get their drinking water from underground sources.

headline: Murtha menace to stsand trial
abstract: A man accused of threatening to kill US Representative John Murtha and an insurance company employee will stand trial for making terroristic threats and harassment.

headline: Ex-Rep. Hayes tops field of ag hopefuls
abstract: Former House Majority Leader Samuel Hayes Jr. is a top candidate to replace the Agriculture Secretary.

headline: Clinton invited to help preserve Gettysburg Park
abstract: State Representative Harry Readshaw asked President Clinton to help preserve the  monuments, artifacts, and buildings at Gettysburg National Park. He also wants Clinton to come and see the damage first hand.

headline: Holden battles to reverse milk price subsidy change
abstract: Rep. Holden is concerned for farmers in his district because of the court decision to change the milk subsidy which is based on the idea milk is cheapier to produce in Wisconsin.

headline: NEW YEAR, NEW LICENSE
abstract: Fishing anglers are reminded that they need a new fishing license for the new year (1998).

headline: New jail dress code suggested
abstract: State Senator Tim Murphy wants to create a different dress code for inmates since the six escaped from prison were so easily able to change into civilian clothes.

headline: FACULTY AT 14 STATE UNIVERSITIES SET STRIKE VOTE; TALKS GO ON
abstract: The union representing faculty at 14 state universities has called for strike authorization vote but is also continuing to negotiation.  The strike authorization vote will let union leaders determine when to call a walkout, said Jim White, union president.  The 5,500 faculty belonging to the Association of Pennsylvania State College and University Faculty have been working without a contractd since a two-year extension ended in June.  Unresovled issues include the number of temporary teachers being used at the schools and a proposed health insurance co-payment for new campus hires.

headline: Conflicting opinions expected at Presque Isle meeting
abstract: A hearing will be conducted about the Presque Isle State Park's Resource Management Plan. It is expected to be a heated debate.

headline: Milk Bills on the Mark
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter has proposed legislation that would help correct the current formula of setting wholesale milk prices.

headline: NO EASY ANSWER FOR BAKERTON:  STILL LOOKING FOR WATER TO REPLACE DAM
abstract: Bakerton residents still have no idea when or how a new water supply will arrive once their reservoir is empty.  West Carroll Township supervisors and water officials met Thursday with their Carrolltown counterparts to discuss the Bakerton situation.  The state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) ordered the Bakerton Dam Reservior drained after it failed an inspection.  Carrolltown offered to help provide water to West Carroll Township but cannot provide more than 25,000 gallons daily when the need is 135,000 gallons of water per day.

headline: New rite of passage happening in court
abstract: Pennsylvania and 40 other states have made a law that would try anyone 15 years old and older as an adult in violent crimes. Some feel the juvenile courts have lost their purpose and those under 18 should be tried in juvenile court.

headline: FBI STUDY PLANNED ON FAYETTE SUSPICIONS
abstract: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has agreedto look into allegations of voter fraud in Fayette County in response to a request by county commissioners Chairman Vince Cicites, Harry Albert and Sean Cavanagh.  In dispute are 8 absentee ballots from residents of Bouras Personal Care Home, Inc. where residents are supposedly mentally incompetent.  Family members are supporting Cavanagh's contention that this is so and a deliberate fraud.

headline: MILK BOARD RESPONDS TO FARMERS' RALLY
abstract: A day after dairy farmers rallied for higher milk prices in Washington, the Pennsylvania Milk Marketing Board voted to hold an emergency hearing next month on the price Pennsylvania diary farmers receive for their milk.  The milk board will decide whether to continue a temporary 30-cent price support for the state's 11,000 dairy farmers, who say that lower federal prices and weather conditions have hurt their businesses this year.  The board has the authority to set retail prices in Pennsylvania and sets a premium that is over and above a base formulate price determined by the federal government.

headline: NO MOVEMENT ON LICENSE HIKE
abstract: The state Legislature is nearing their summer recess and a bill that would hike hunting license fees has not yet been scheduled for consideration by the House Appropriations Committee where it has rested since April.

headline: No More Trails in Absentia
abstract: A proposed law will allow for retrials for those tried in absentia. This is being proposed due to the French's refusal to extradite Ira Einhorn because he was convicted in absentia.

abstract: US Representative Bud Shuster is under investigation for receiving campaign contributions from Boston businessmen in exchange for legal help.

abstract: A Nuangola Borough resident contacted Senator Specter's office to try to get help for the Borough's sewage treatment plan. The resident wants the borough to separate its sewer and water systems.

abstract: There was no evidence found saying that Mayor J.D. Varner conducted 'official oppression' in a case about a custody dispute.

abstract: A program is being conducted for homeowners to help them dispose of a variety of pesticides.

abstract: Congressmen Jon Fox and Carolyn Maloney have proposed legislation that would allow only the Bureau of Labor Statistics the authority to create the Consumer Price Index.

headline: PROPOSED LEGISLATION WOULD BOOST FARMLAND PRESERVATION
abstract: Montgomery County's farmland preservation program may benefit from legislation that passed the state House this week and is now before the state Senate.  Under the proposed legislation, interest money paid by property owners penalized for opting out of a preferential tax assessment program would be earmarked for farmland preservation programs.  Adams County state Representative Stephen Maitland authored the bill that includes Montgomery County state Reps. Ray Bunt, R-147th District, Joseph M. Gladeck, Jr., R-61st District, and Ellen Bard, R-153rd District as cosponsors.

headline: ODOR PROBLEM HALTS SPREADING OF SLUDGE IN RUSH TOWNSHIP
abstract: A stench is hanging over Rush Township and has residents upset.  The Rushton Mining Site owned by Pittsburgh Power and Light is where the mining company disposed of its mind refuse.  Such refuse is not conducive to growing vegetation and the area must be re-vegetated so they applied for a permit to put bio-solids (sludge) on the site according to Department of Environmental (DEP) officials.  The sludge was stored on site over the winter and one of the stockpiles turned septic, causing the horrific odor.  DEP has stopped the spread of the sludge until they can get the odor under control.

headline: Officials try to save crime lab
abstract: Law Enforcement Officials are working towards keeping the police crime in Wyoming open. A chairman on the Governor's task force will examine the inefficiency of closing that state police lab.

abstract: The State Farm Show Complex is in desperate needs of major repairs. Despite the needed repairs and growing competition, there is great attachment to the Farm Show.

headline: OFFICIALS RAISE ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERNS ABOUT CONSTRUCTION SITE
abstract: Construction on a new Insalaco's supermarket has caught the eye of environmental officials.  The Monroe County Conservation District has referred Blakeslee Corners Group, which is building the shopping center on the southwest corner of Routes 940 and 115, to the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection for enforcement.  District Technician Victor Motts said the problems on the site stem form the fact that construction of the building area pad is occurring before structures designed to channel and contain stormwater are built.

abstract: The Luzerne County district attorney and a group of local police officers are going to plead with the state police Commissioner to keep the crime lab in Wyoming open.

headline: OIL SPILL MAY HAVE ORIGINATED AT JS STEEL
abstract: Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) authorities are investigating the possibility that an oil spill contaminating Oak Grove Run near Avis might have originated at the Jersey Shore Steel Mill.  Officials said they are investigating rumors that the spill was deliberate when employees poured the material down a drain before demolishing a building on mill property.

abstract: A court decision will lower the cost of milk by taking out transportation costs from the subsidy received by farmers. Famers, who are already struggling to pay their bills, are concerned by the decision to make the cost of milk even lower.
