abstract: The former state House of Representatives speaker will be a special counsel for the Thorp Reed & Armstrong law firm.

headline: SENATE RESOLUTION GIVES SUPPORT TO DAIRY FARMERS
abstract: The United States Senate adopted a resolution seeking to separate the pricing connection between cheese and milk as the first step toward obtaining financial relief for dairy farmers who have seen a 25 percent cut in their revenues since September.  Dairy farmers are to meet today to determine if they are satisfied enough for the moment to maintain the flow of milk to the nation's grocery shelves.  The resolution was sponsored by Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum in response to dairy farmer complaints that they face financial ruin unless osmething is done to permit them to charge more for their product.

headline: PALMERTON RESIDENTS SAY EPA IS RUINING THEIR ENVIRONMENT
abstract: Residents of Palmerton are upset that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) still has their operations set up at an old playground.  The EPA says it makes since to be there as the site has an address wehre equipment can be shipped to the on-site crew.  Residents disagree because children cannot use the playground while the EPA is there.  The EPA is there to do residential clean up as Palmerton is a Superfund site due to lead, cadmium, zinc and other industrial residue contamination.

headline: P.S. to lawmaker: The South lost the Civil War
abstract: The editors of the Courier-Express disagree with Rep. John Perzel who wants to allow the changing of sentences of previous convicted and freed sex offenders. A judge ruled on this issue against the sentence changing under "Megan's Law."

headline: Fox returns from trip to China
abstract: Two US Representatives from Pennsylvania believe if relations were strengthened with Asia, Delaware Valley could be a leader in technology.

headline: Senate resolution gives support to dairy farmers
abstract: The US Senate easily passed a resolution urging the change of how the price of milk is determined. The resolution was proposed by the two Senators from Pennsylvania, Specter and Santorum.

headline: PA'S $12 MILLION PLAN TARGETS TIRE PILES
abstract: Pennsylvania's top environmental cop is ready to spend $12 million  to pay private businesses to clean up about 36 million scrap tires dumped throughout the state.  The plan was unveiled in Marlborough Township in Montgomery County in a junkyard littered with more than 300,000 old car tires.  These illegally dumped tires will be the first to go under the program - they will be converted into fuel chips by a Conshohocken firm that was awarded $280,000 from the state to clean up the tires.  DEP Secretary James Self noted that the scrap tires throughout Pennsylvania pose a fire risk and public-health hazard.  Much of the impetus behind the program was a fire last year that burned thousands of tires dumped beneath Interstate 95 in the Port Richmond section of Philadelphia.

headline: Pa. facing more civil liability
abstract: The 1992 Supreme Court decision on state liability has caused the Attorney General to pay out large settlements including a $1,000,000 case involding PennDot.

headline: Fox will face GOP challenge
abstract: An anti-abortion activits is going to oppose US Representative Jon D. Fox in the Republican congressional primary.

headline: Specter offers dairy plan
abstract: Sen. Spector wants to pay farmers based on production since current pay is under production costs.

headline: PERRY COUNTY GROUP SEEKS STATE OFFICIALS' EAR IN SLUDGE DISPUTE
abstract: A group of Perry County residents plans to meet with state officials  to make another bid to win a years-long battle to force a sludge-spreading operation from their Carroll Township neighborhood.  Their aim is to prevent the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) from renewing a permit for a holding pond on property Commonwealth Disposal, Inc. of Harrisburg has used for drinking water sludge storage and application.  DEP officials claim that the sludge which is largely mud processed out of drinking water is not dangerous and that the site located west of Sherman's Dale has received special monitoring due to residents' complaints.

headline: Pa. House OKs tighter dispatcher standards
abstract: The state House of Representatives has passed a bill creating tougher standards for 911 dispatchers. The legislation would require a minimum training and certification for emergency dispatchers.

headline: Gekas continues to pursue shutdown-prevention measure
abstract: US Representative George W. Gekas is to proposed legislation against a government shutdown in case of the failure to pass the budget.

headline: STATE FARMING PROGRAM AT ISSUE IN SOMERSET; MEETING SCHEDULED
abstract: State Representative William Lloyd will convene a public meeting to consider whether Somerset County should participate in a state farmland-preservation program.  As part of the program, the state pays $20 to $30 million a year to selected farmers across Pennsylvania for the difference between their value of their farms for agricultural purposes and their potential value with commercial or residential development.  Farmers opting for the program are required to place restrictions on their deeds assuring their farms are never developed.

headline: PORTRAYAL OF EPA CALLED INACCURATE
abstract: The author of this letter states that a previous column inaccurately portrays the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) as being opposed to Pennsylvania's policy for encouraging self-audits.  Instead, he argues that the EPA encourages states to develop self-audit policies.

headline: Pa. must ID witnesses to executions, court says
abstract: The courts ruled that death row inmates will not be able to find out what chemicals are used to kill them; however, an inmate may find out the names of those who will witness his or her execution.

headline: GOP caucus takes up touchy issue
abstract: The Senate Republican caucus discussed sexual harassment for a sensitivity training. This was necessary after allegations of sexual harassment by a former state Senator.

headline: STATE PEACH CROPS FEARED DAMAGED
abstract: This week's sub-zero temperatures apparently decimated the state's $24-million-a-year peach crop and may have made a dent in the $50-million-a-year apple business, according to agriculture experts and farmers.  Peaches were vulnerable because they went into full bloom during last week's unusually warm weather.  George Green, an agriculture professor at Penn State University's center in Biglerville, PA said up to 90 percent of peaches may have been killed but stopped short of dooming the crop.  Green said that anywhere from 20 to 100 percent of the apple crop may have died.

headline: POTPOURRI:  FALL STOCKINGS BEGIN, PHEASANT RELEASES, BASS CHANGES CONSIDERED
abstract: The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission will stock 148 bodies of water across the state with 140,825 legal-sized trout as part of the fall trout stocking program; the Pennsylvania Game Commission is in the process of releasing 45,870 hen pheasants on state gamelands and other properties enrolled in the agency's access program; the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission is recommending major changes in the structure of the bass season in Pennsylvania.

headline: Pardons unit denies Philly killer hearing
abstract: A Philadelphia killer will not have his case heard by the state Pardons Board. A referendum, which is expected to receive court challenges, makes it harder to those on life in prison or death sentences to receive clemency.

headline: GROUP FORMED TO PROBE BLACK
abstract: A task force of state senators, representatives and the state treasurer was appointed to investigate investments made by John Gardner Black of Blair County and his companies, Devon Capital Management and Financial Management Services.  The task force will be chaired by state Treasurer Barbara Hafer and include state senators Melissa Hart, chairwoman of the Senate Finance Committee, and John Wozniak, and state represenatives Fred Trello and karl Boyes, chairman of the House Finance Committee.

headline: TAX PROGRAM NO HELP TO ARMSTRONG FARMER
abstract: Farmer David Daugherty admits he is puzzled about the county's interpretation of the state's Clean and Green program.  He's paying more taxes under a program that is supposed to help him pay less.  The Clean and Green program lets farmers or landowners with 10 or more acres who keep their land as farmland or woods pay a lower tax rate than if the land were developed.  But Daugherty says his tax rate is higher under the program.  He appealed his assessment to Armstrong County commissioners who denied it.

headline: PROPOSAL WOULD ALLOW YEAR-ROUND BASS FISHING
abstract: The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission is considering a proposal that would allow a three-tiered season that provides for year round fishing for large-mouth, small-mouth and spotted bass.  There will be a public comment period about the proposal.  The preliminary apportionment of federal excise taxes on hunting equipment shows that Pennsylvania receives more than $4 million, behind only Texas and Alaska.  The states must kick in 25 percent of the cost of any projectc.  The PA Game Commission is in a budget crunch and the author notes that this is unfortunate because "they are not making anymore land."

headline: Part-time prosecutors' raises upheld
abstract: Courts have ruled that part-time district attorneys are allowed back pay for the raises given to judges that were not given to them.

abstract: Sam E. Hayes Jr. is the new Secretary of Agriculture for Pennsylvania. The Department of Agriculture has a variety of responsibilies including food inspections.

headline: PROPOSED LAW WOULD INCREASE FINES FOR LITTERING NEAR FARMS
abstract: State Representative Jeff Coy is proposing a new law that will increase the fines for littering in agricultural areas and provide money to remove litter and compensate farmers.  Littering has long been a problem for local farms because discarding bottles and cans can damage machinery and injure livestock. Coy's bill is an alternative to a controversial bottle bill which has been discussed for over a decade.  Farmers support the bottle bill which would create a refund system for bottles and cans, similar to what is in effect in other states.  But manufacturers, retailers and recycling advocates oppose the bill.

headline: Piccola locks horns with bar association
abstract: Sen. Jeffrey Piccola is sparing with Pennsylvania Bar Association President Vincent Grogan over the Bar Associations' efforts against the Pardons Board referendum. The referendum would require a unanimous vote instead of a majority for a life or death sentence prisoner to receive clemency.

headline: Harmar supervisors agree to seek outside state audit
abstract: A petition was drawn up by employees for an outside audit of Harmar.

abstract: The Department of Labor and Industry has not heard an appeal of the unemployment compensation filed by workers of the Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corporation's Allenport plant. State Representative Peter J Daley is trying to speed up the process.

headline: REMOVING ANTLERLESS DEER HELPS CONTROL HERDS
abstract: Wildlife managers remain convinced that removing antlerless deer is the best method for controlling deer herds.  The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission has agreed to consider changes in bass fishing regulations.

headline: KEEP EYE ON TAB FOR NEW MONTOUR JOBS
abstract: The editorial questions the wisdom of corporate welfare - the practice of states and local governents providing low or no cost loans and other freebies to businesses in exchange for creating new jobs.  They note that as the Wall Street Journal has pointed out, many of these jobs wind up costing States and locales more in taxpayer dollars than the jobs are worth.  Residents of Mountour are encouraged to watch negotiations with Alden Industries that is considering taking over a vacant Textron plan near Danville.

abstract: Representative McDade worked towards getting $30 million in funding for South Central Pennsylvania Environmental Infrastructure Program and Army Corps of Engineers projects in seven counties.

headline: PLUNGE IN NUMBER OF VOLUNTEERS PLAGUING MANY FIRE DEPARTMENTS
abstract: Over the past ten years, Pennsylvania fire companies have witnessed a crisis that affects every community in the commonwealth.  The number of men and women who step forward to volunteer has been spiraling downward and local fire chiefs have been nearly powerless to stop it.  Fire chiefs say that volunteer fire membership is at its lowest ebb in fire service history.

headline: Holden backs tough bill to reform campaign finances
abstract: US Representative Tim Holden has proposed legislation that would toughen campaign financing. The bill would set spending limits, impose fines, and outlaw soft money.

headline: SANTORUM KNOCKS EPA:  WANTS DRAKE SHUT DOWN

Michael McCabe, regional administrator for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency asking for suspension of clean up operations at the Drake Chemical Superfund site in Lock Haven.  State Senator J. Doyle Cornam recently issued a public statement urging the state to shut down testing operations at the site until state over sight can be reestablished.  Santorum noted that the EPA must understand that it cannot come into a state and "run a steamroller over the very legitimate concerns of local and state officials."

Plum and Penn Hills were mandated in 1988 by the state Department of Environmental Resources (DER) to share the Plum Creek facility and Plum will pay for expansion and upgrading.

headline: STUDY SAYS TEEN EMPLOYMENT UNHURT AFTER BOOST IN FEDERAL MINIMUM WAGE
abstract: Eight months after the federal minimum wage was increased to $4.75, a liberal think tank reports that earnings among low-wage workers rose and widespread job losses did not materialize as opponents had predicted.  In a study entitled, "The Sky Hasn't Fallen: An Evaluation of the Minimum Wage Increase," the Washington, D.C. based Economic Policy Institute reports that job opportunities for teen-agers and young adults was not adversely affected.

headline: SEWAGE SERVICE SET FOR MOTEL

Authority members agreed to submit to the state Department of Environmental Protection (EPA) certification which indicates an estimated 7,200 gallons of sewage a day from the motel will not overburden the borough's treatment plant within the next five years.

headline: Prison shakeup necessary
abstract: Top officials at a Pittsburgh prison where six inmates escaped were demoted or fired. The movement was necessary in order to change the security and how the prison will be ran.

headline: IGNORING THE CONSTITUTION
abstract: There's an unconscionable arrogance to the Pennsylvania state legislature which goes beyhond the usual condenscension elected officials so often exhibit toward the general public.  Galling as that behavior is, it is surpassed by the General Assembly's flaunting of the state Constitution in a manner which indicates that our elected lawmakers have little regard for the law.  The recent passage of a bill that tightens restrictions governing third-party access to election ballots provides a perfect case in point.  The bill passed the House at 1:30 a.m. onJune 12.  The restrictions contained in the bill were introduced the night before at a Senate Rules Committee meetings.  There were no hearings held nor were most of the rank and file given an opportunity to reviewit.  How appalling.

headline: 'Voluntary comp time' bill is a bad bet for working families
abstract: Lawrence A. Collins believes the voluntary compensation time that is being proposed in the Congress will hurt workers and help employeers eliminate the 40 hour work week.

abstract: Cherokee Biotechnology Inc., a company from North Carolina that wants to build a soil processing facility in Chester to clean nearly 300,000 tons of contaminated dirt, has been denied permits to do so by the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP).

abstract: A new program by the Community Corrections Center is allowing well behaved and clean inmates to live in a dorm like setting and receive counseling if they had less than six months left on their sentence. It is a way to help them readjust to a civilian lifestyle.

headline: IN BRIEF:  USED STATE CARS SOLD
abstract: The state will be auctioning off 220 used vehicles at 10 a.m. on August 21 in the Commonwealth Garage.

These results from the Third International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) were hailed by President Clinton and leading educators as a promising sign that American students are gaining on a national goal to be the first in the world in mathematics and science achievement by 2000.

headline: 5 CITY SCHOOLS TO TRY LESSONS
abstract: Pittsburgh Public Schools will be the first district in the state to pilot an education program designed to get businesses and community groups involved in promoting positive character traits among children.  While character education is not new to local school districts, producers of "Your Environment Character Education" say their program is unique because it encourages parents, businesses and community groups to participate in its activities.  It is also integrated throughout curriculum so you needn't a another time set aside for it.  The program has material for preschool through twelth grade.  It is being offered on a trial basis in 30 schools in Ohio, Arkansas, Kentucky, North Carolina, South Carolina and Pennsylvania.

headline: STATE AND COUNTY OFFICIALS TOUR SITE OF WEEKEND TIRE FIRE
abstract: Officials of the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) and the Erie County Health Department, accompanied by State Police, toured the site of a weekend blaze that burned part of a pile of 30,000 tires.  The fire borke out in southwestern Erie about 3:30 p.m. Saturday and was not extinguished until Sunday afternoon.

School Board Presidents Mary Beth Sweeny stated that negotiators for the Indiana Area Education Association, the teachers' union, refuse to show the contract to their membership.  The schoo board maintains that it is a good offer and want the teachers to see the proposed contract.

abstract: Pittsburgh is proposing building a black history center dedicated to Black culture, history, art, and artifacts.

A DEP emergency response team assessed the area after the fatal accident involving the tanker trunk hauling the petroleum to a nearby business.

They encourage school districts not to throw out the strategic plans but to incorporate the new standards into them.

headline: STATE FINDS NO VIOLATIONS IN CITY'S DUMPING OF COMPOST

Erie City Councilman Mario Bagnoni disagrees and stated that the city is using the park for a dump.  He took water samples and has sent them to the county health department.

headline: A POISON PILL FOR CHARTER SCHOOL BILL
abstract: Governor Ridge badly wants the General Assembly to approve legislation allowing the formation of charter schools and he appears to be willing to accept a bill containing a poison pill - a last minute amendment allowing charter school clusters in Philadelphia.  This amendment is the brain-child of Senator Vincent Fumo, Democrat-Philadelphia who wants to create charter clusters - several schools offering kindergarten through the 12th grade within political boundaries, such as wards and precincts.  This introduces a political aspect to the measure that is at odds with the philosophical concept of charter schools.  This is a prescription for mischief and patronage.

headline: STATE GRANTS AVAILABLE FOR WASTE TIRE CLEAN-UP
abstract: State Representative Lynn B. Herman (R-77) of Philipsburg announced that state grants to clean up waste tire piles are available and cautioned that the deadline is quickly approaching.  He urged individuals, companies and municipalities who want to clean up priority sites (those with 10,000 or more waste tires) to apply quickly.

headline: Residents in uproar over new parole office
abstract: Residents near the new Probation and Parole Board office are protesting the opening.

headline: Kirkland running for Foglietta's seat
abstract: Former Congressman Lucien Blackwell and state Representative Thaddeus Kirkland are both running for the Congressional District seat vacated by the departure of Tom Foglietta who was appointed to be the ambassador to Italy.

headline: A SUB?  THERE'S THE RUB
abstract: Pennsylvania School Districts are scrambling to fill a critical shortage of substitute teachers.  Many school districts are having to resort to "emergency substitutes," those not certified to teach in Pennsylvania.

headline: STATE TO HOLD DEER HUNT AT FRANCES SLOCUM STATE PARK
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources will conduct a regulated antlerless deer hunt at Frances Slocum State Park, Kingston Township on Monday, December 15, to help control the deer population in the park.

headline: Revoking outside work for lifers right decision
abstract: A referendum is being voted on to no longer allow inmates with life sentences the opportunity to work outside of the prison.

headline: Kirkland thinks D.C.
abstract: With the anticipation of US Representative Tom Foglietta being nominated to be the ambassador to Italy, state Representative Thaddeus Kirkland is considering running for his seat in the 1st Congressional District in Philadelphia.

headline: AILING GNA SLASHES TEACHERS
abstract: The Greater Nanticoke Area School Board layed off five teachers, including a board member's wife, and made other cuts that will curtail music and sports programs next year.  The district, threatened with a state takeover if it does not curb runaway spending, also put eight teachers, including three of four music teachers, on part-time status.  Superintendent Anothony Perrone said that if the state takes over the district, it could lay off up to 50 teachers.  The state has forecast a $3 million dollar deficit by the end of 1998-99 if the district does not contain spending.

headline: State to undergo smallest gypsy moth spray program
abstract: Due to the decrease in gypsy moth population, the state will do the smallest gypsy moth spray since 1972.

headline: Ridge signs 3rd death warrant for Saranchak
abstract: Gov. Ridge signed the third death warrant for Daniel M. Saranchak, a man who killed his grandmother and uncle.

headline: Kovach seeks Pettit's seat
abstract: Tom Kovach will run in the special election to replace the late Representative Al Pettit.

headline: Anti-drug lessons might fall short
abstract: DARE and other anti-drug programs may be out of date and ineffective.

headline: STATE URGES PEOPLE TO TEST HOMES FOR RADON
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) is urging Pennsylvanians to test their homes for radon, an invisible gas that is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in the United States.  High levels of radon have been found in all 67 Pennsylvania counties.

headline: Ridge signs his 70th death warrant
abstract: The death warrant for Miguel Rios has been signed by Gov. Ridge, marking the 70th death warrant signed since Ridge has taken office.

headline: Lawmakers encouraged to support sale
abstract: Gov. Ridge was finally able to sell the state-owned airports. There is a promise of economic and industrial development even with a $18.9 million debt between HIA and Capital City. A concern is over the pensions for the state employees that work at the airports. Concerns also include the environmental issues surrounding HIA and the exclusion of Lebanon and Lancaster counties in the deal.

headline: APOLLO-RIDGE TO OFFER DRIVING TESTS IN SCHOOL
abstract: The Apollo-Ridge school board approved a plan that will allow ARIN Intermediate Unit, which provides the district's after-school driver's education program, to administer a final skill examination and provide a license to students who pass.  Apollo-Ridge is the only school district in the Valley and one of 29 in the state to implement the pilot plan which is developed by PENDOT and the state Department of Education.

headline: STATE'S MINING CHANGES ASSAILED
abstract: A state citizens advisory panel has urged the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) to abandon "emergency rulemaking" that could eliminate a mining firm's responsibility to prevent or minimize susidence damage to water, gas or electric utilities.  The panel is concerned that the proposed changes could shift the costs of preventing or fixing the subsidence damage to utility ratepayers.

headline: RISE IN YOUTH SHOOTINGS PROMPTS STRICTER PA SAFETY PROPOSAL
abstract: The steady rise in unintentional shootings and suicides among young people nationwide has prompted two state legislators to push for stricter safety regulations for handguns.  State representatives Andrew Carn, D-Philadelphia and T.J. Rooney, D-Northampton, introduced separate legislation that requires gun owners to have safety locks on their weapons and to personalize handguns so only those authorized may use them.

headline: LAWMAKERS PONDERING NEPOTISM
abstract: Nepotism, the practice of public officials using their position to hire relatives is not something that area legislators are eager to fix.  Some area school board members admitted they twisted arms to get family members jobs.  State Senator John Wozniak, Democrat - Westmont wants to review a Kentucky law that forbids school board members and administrators from serving in districts where relatives are employed.  The Kentucky reforms also gave school superintendents total hiring powers.  Represenative Michael Hanna, Democrat-Centre and Clinton counties plans to introduce a bill that would excuse school board members from voting on labor contract and salary issues if the decision will affect a family member.

headline: APPLICATIONS AVAILABLE FOR AGRICULTURE EDUCATION LOAN FORGIVENESS PROGRAM
abstract: Applications are now available for the Agriculture Education Loan Forgiveness Program, the Pennyslvania Higher Education Assistanced Agency (PHEAA) has announced.  The program was established in 1992 by the Pennsylvania General Assembly and is funded by a state appropriation.  This year's appropriate is about $177,000.  The program will repay up to $2,000 per year of PHEAA-guaranteed student loans for each year the borrower is employed full-time in an agriculture-related field.  Borrowers are limited to a lifetime maximum of $10,000.

headline: TENDING TIMBER:  STATE PROGRAM HELPS OWNERS OF WOODLANDS SAVE TREES, WILDLIFE
abstract: The Pennsylvania Forst Stewardship Program, managed by the state Bureau of Forestry, allows local landowners with five acres or more to get financial help and other help in managing their woodlands. There are a lot of potential clients because only 5 million of the 17 million acres of forest in Pennsylvania are state-owned.  The remaining 12 million acres are owned by about 500 private landowners.  The average parcel is 24 acres.

headline: Ruling could cut charges against teen
abstract: A 17 year old could face only one county's worth of charges after committing crimes in multiple counties because of a Pennsylvania law allowing a defendant to be prosecuted for the same crimes in only one county.

headline: LAWMAKERS PONDERING NEPOTISM
abstract: Nepotism, the practice of public officials using their position to hire relatives is not something that area legislators are eager to fix.  Some area school board members admitted they twisted arms to get family members jobs.  State Senator John Wozniak, Democrat - Westmont wants to review a Kentucky law that forbids school board members and administrators from serving in districts where relatives are employed.  The Kentucky reforms also gave school superintendents total hiring powers.  Represenative Michael Hanna, Democrat-Centre and Clinton counties plans to introduce a bill that would excuse school board members from voting on labor contract and salary issues if the decision will affect a family member.

headline: Arts Grant
abstract: A state grant was given to the Chambersburg Council for the Arts for its Summer Concert and Enrichment Series in the Park.

headline: Study will put great value on Pennsylvania's forests
abstract: A study will be conducted on Pennsylvania's public forests. Certification would be very important to the forests in Pennsylvania.

headline: Sad Truth
abstract: Due to allegations of sexual harassment against former state Senator John Peterson, sensitivity training will be provided to all senators and staff. The Patriot News feels the training does not truly reflect the seriousness of sexual harassment especially when it is being done by such high level officials.

headline: LAWMAKERS STAND UP FOR MOR LOLLYGAGGING
abstract: This opinion piece states that state lawmakers sunk even the simplest election reform.  The bill the state Legislature passed would have forced the Legislature to schedule special elections in a timely fashion. The legislature tacked on an amendment that made it harder for third-party candidates to get on the ballot and this sunk when Governor Ridge refused to sign it and rightly so.

headline: Auditor questions Midland school deal
abstract: The Auditor General is investigating the legality of an agreement for Midland sending student to a high school in Ohio.

headline: TIRE DUMP OWNERS FINED
abstract: The owners of the Marlborough Township property being cleared of thousands of tires by the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) have been fined $530,000 in Montgomery County Court.  The tires were actually dumped by former tenant Raymond Coakley who faces criminal charges in the matter.  The township solicitor accuses the owners, Edward and Marie DeLoach of allowing Coakley to dispose of the tires.  The DeLoaches, an elderly couple, deny the charges and said that they told Coakely not to dump the tires.

headline: SCHOOL WEAPONS LAW NEEDS REWRITING
abstract: When the Pennsylvania House committee charged with reviewing and revising the state's school weapon's law next week, there is nothing more helpful than for the lawmakers to resist the temptation to micromanage the law or the schools.  They caused the problem in the first place by recent get-tough legislation and the result has not been to reduce crime but rather to increase the costs of law enforcement and imprisonment.

headline: Lawson may get role in campagin
abstract: A report says that Lynn Lawson will be Gov. Ridge's campaign spokesman. Lawson has previous experience in running election campagins for various GOP members.

headline: BACKGROUND CHECKS MAY HAVE LOOPHOLE
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Education is being ask how a former Hempfield Area School District teacher who pled guilty to molesting children landed a teaching job later in New York. According to a spokesman, the problem is that if a teacher accused of a crime resigns before being convicted, the school district is not required by state law to notify the Department of Education of the alleged offense.  Thus, it is very possible for one later convicted to maintain their teaching certificate.

headline: TIRE DUMPS INELIGIBLE FOR AID
abstract: Local officials in Richland and Springfield townships have learned that they are not eligible to apply for money to clean up tire dump sites.  That is because sites that Richland and Sprinfield Townships want to clean up are already on the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) ineligible list as there are already state enforcement actions on going against the sites in question.

headline: Should the innocent pay for the BAC test?
abstract: Rep. Surra proposed legislation against making those found to be below .05% BAL to be forced to pay for the testing.

headline: Legislators honor city soup kitchen
abstract: The Daily Daily Bread is being honored by the House of Representatives for its excellent service in Central Pennsylvania.

headline: The President's Budget
abstract: New York Times praises President Bill Clinton for his tight and balance budget proposal.

headline: Bipartisan HMO reforms unveiled
abstract: Eager to shatter a partisan impasse on Capitol Hill, Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pa., and fellow moderate senators yesterday unveiled a package of managed care reforms that would provide patients with greater rights to challenge decisions by their health plans and guarantee the power to collect limited financial damages in federal court.  The bill, whose sponsors include a coalition of influential Democrats and Republicans, is an attempt to forge a bipartisan consensus on reforming managed care at a time when few lawmakers have displayed any inclination to make the necessary compromises to pass a bill and gain President Clinton's signature.

headline: Attorney general speaks during Waynesburg commencement
abstract: Waynesburg College graduates had Attorney Mike Fisher as their ceremony speaker. Award winners and honorary degree recipients are noted.

headline: Consumers balance cost vs. pollution
abstract: According to studies done by the Natural Resources Defense Council, electric generators in the U.S. are responsible for a significant amount of air pollution, and in PA, where 60 percent of power plants are fueled by coal, compared with 38 percent nuclear, the American Lung Association estimates about 73 percent of the state’s population faces health risks from high ozone levels, and PA receives the most acid precipitation in the nation. PA power plants have been criticized for contributing to pollution levels, yet most comply with state and federal regulations, and many have taken some serious steps to do good things for the environment. Nuclear power plants produce little air pollution, but environmentalists have criticized them because of the potential for accidents, and overall, electric companies must balance costs and the desire to protect the environment when making decisions on how to best serve their customers’ demands.

headline: Helping teens master the art of driving more safely
abstract: The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety finds elderly drivers have a high risk for accidents and are often targeted for retesting. At a lawmaker's symposium, PA legislators will explore stricter standards for younger drivers. The PA Department of Transportation reports 13 percent of 16-year-old drivers in the state are involved in accidents. Transportation Secretary Brad Mallory warns the state must be ever vigilant about its driving standards. PA Rep. Anthony DeLuca supports mandatory road training.

headline: Both questions get a 'no' vote
abstract: Pocono Record urges voters to say no to the two proosed constitutional referendums on crime.

headline: Underage DUI Arrests
abstract: Since Act 31, commonly known as the "Underage Drinking Law" went into effect on May 24, 1988 the number of underage drunken drivers involved in PA has declined.

headline: Critics say bankruptcy bills threaten child support
abstract: Pending bill sponsored by U.S. Representative George Gekas and Senator Charles Grassley would force debtors who file for bankruptcy to pay more unsecured debts, such as credit card debts. However, critics argue the bills will make it harder for women to collect child-support and alimony payments from ex-husbands who file for bankruptcy because they will have competing payment interests. A spokesman for Gekas assured there are safeguards, but others disagree.

headline: Commissioners face legislative showdown - Lawmakers stand fast on home rule committee
abstract: Allegheny County Commission Chairman Bob Cranmer wrote to PA House and Senate leaders, asking them to help break their deadlock over the appointment of a panel to draw 13 new charter council districts; however, legislators, including Senate Minority Leader Robert Mellow and Senator Leonard Bodack, responded quickly that they were unwilling to change their list of nominees, which includes four white males. There have been concerns about the lack of female and minority representation on the panel, and Commissioner Larry Dunn refused to approve the four nominees unless they promised to vote in a minority woman as the fifth member. State Representative John Maher is considering introducing legislation pertaining to the issue, but as of now, the panel would have until October 23 to create the new districts.

headline: Luksik remains confident of victory
abstract: Best known as the only pro-life gubernatorial candidate, Peg Luksik is trying to become the first third-party candidate since 1910 to finish ahead of a Republican or Democrat gubernatorial candidates.  Polls in the city and the state show her far behind Gov. Tom Ride , who registered 66 percent in each poll, followed by Democrat Ivan Itkin, in the mid-teens.  So far, Luksik's support has yet to graduate from the single digits in any poll.

headline: Surra featured speaker at Democratic dinner
abstract: At a Democratic spring banquet, PA Representative Dan Surra voiced his support for U.S. Senate candidate William Lloyd, and he admitted that it would be tough for gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin to defeat Governor Ridge because of Ridge’s huge financial advantage. However, he did criticize Ridge and the Republican Party for rushing the state’s budget, granting a $3.5 billion tax cut for big businesses, allowing the environment to suffer and for raising taxes when there was a $700 million surplus. Surra will be unopposed in the upcoming election, and he took time to highlight some of his accomplishments in the House.

headline: The State Budget by the Numbers
abstract: Highlights of Governor Ridge's proposed general budget, in millions of dollars. The general fund is not only source of revenue for these departments, but is the one over which the state has control.

headline: Bipartisan Support Grows For Managed Care Patients
abstract: It is an election year, and Congressmen have been flooded with complaints about health insurance providers, which has helped crate a bi-partisan consensus on the need to enact legislation to help protect managed care patients by guaranteeing emergency room coverage, allowing for a timely and affordable appeals process for denied coverage and granting an assurance that consumers will be given all the information about possible treatments. President Clinton supports legislation, and a number of different Congressmen have developed or are working on legislation to reform health care, but the exact details are still a source of contention between the two parties. Health insurance companies have been lobbying against the legislation, but there is a clear consensus on the need to reform, so it will be difficult for there efforts to be successful.

headline: Audit confirms fiscal problems in North Penn
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey's investigation of North Penn School District reveals financial mismanagment in excess of $1.4 million.

headline: Deer hunts no longer horrify suburbanites
abstract: In many deer-saturated states in the East and Midwest, game wardens and town councils are hiring professional sharpshooters or rounding up bands of experienced hunters to reduce white-tail herds that are roaming through urban parks and forest preserves and residential areas.  And surprisingly, residents in many suburbs and some cities aren't resisting.  As recently as 10 years ago, the concept of stalking deer in metropolitan parks and neighborhoods was practically unheard of.  But no longer.

headline: Here's an issue for Pa. lawmakers
abstract: Pocono Record suggets that lawmakers being to open another full-service state transportation center like the one in Snydersville.

headline: Brill gets prison time and Megan's Law designation
abstract: Terence P Brill became the first defendant in Wayne County Court to be sentenced under the Megan's Law provision for sexual abuse crimes. Under this statue, Brill must register with local law enforcement authorities when ever he changes his address for the first 10 years after he is released from prison. He was convicted of sexually abusing a girl almost weekly.

headline: Unfair rap
abstract: Sunday school teachers might be shocked, but it happens sometimes that a Philadelphia judge will cuss amid the rough-and-tumble of court-room sparring.  It doesn't mean these judges are bad people. Honest.

headline: Crossing state lines in drive to uncover insurance fraud   Some Pa. motorists fake N.J. residency for lower rates. Investigators comb the streets to find them
abstract: Although New Jersey has some of nation’s highest car insurance rates, there rates are significantly cheaper than those for residents of Philadelphia and New York City, and insurance officials estimate that there are thousands of people who often go to great lengths to lie about having residency in New Jersey to obtain these cheaper rates, which ultimately causes the state’s insurance rates to go up. The New Jersey Legislature imposed stiff fines to try to address the problem, but it had no effect, so the New Jersey Division of Insurance Fraud Prevention uses a seven member unit to search Philadelphia and New York City for potential rate-evaders. These individuals drive through sections of the cities searching for and recording New Jersey license plates numbers, and the information they obtain is then used to determine whether the car is illegally registered.

headline: Congress candidates from GOP debate tax
abstract: Five of the six Republican candidates seeking the party’s nomination to represent the 15th Congressional District in the U.S. House, including Larry Grello, Bob Kilbanks, Joe Pascuzzo, Nick Sabatine and Pat Toomey, support the implementation of a flat income tax, while the other candidate, state Senator Joe Uliana, wants to keep the current graduated income tax. With the graduated income tax, higher incomes are taxes at higher rates, whereas the flat income tax would tax everyone equally. Uliana claims the flat tax is not fair and would create a huge federal budget deficit; however, the other candidates claim it would tax everyone more equally by eliminating loopholes and deductions in the current system; though there was disagreement on which exemptions should still be permitted under a flat tax system.

headline: Luksik's cry 'local control' draws volatile mix together
abstract: Peg Luksik is the Constitutional Party’s gubernatorial candidate, and she met with people from Green Township to voice her support of their objections to a proposed exit off Interstate 81. Luksik is stressing "local-control," and she is trying to secure the votes of people who feel disenfranchised and angry towards the government. She may be able to secure votes based on single issues; however, she faces a challenge in convincing many alienated voters to vote again, and she must find a way to convince the rest of the population, which may not agree with some of these single issues, to vote for her.

headline: Talks on state university pact have touch of Harvard. State System negotiators to meet with faculty reps over contract for 5,500
abstract: Representatives from the State System of Higher Education and its 5,500 faculty members, represented by the Association of PA State College and University Faculty, attended a seminar at Harvard University last spring to learn how to handle contract negotiations better and avoid a strike. The two sides must replace the current contract that will expire on June 30, but the union’s president, William Fulmer, sees people in the state government, especially Education Secretary Eugene Hickok, as a complicating factor because of efforts to cut down on costs. The union lowered pay demands for its last contract in order to limit the use of non-tenured faculty, so salaries, according to Fulmer, must be addressed.

headline: State gives consumers way to avoid fraudulent charities
abstract: Residents can research charities on the internet to ensure that they are legitimate. The website also trlls information on the contributions, fundraising, and demographic infomation on the charity.

headline: Blame game continues
abstract: Two federal lawmakers were killed, and their alleged killer, Russell Weston, has a history of schizophrenia, but he refused to take his medication. In response to the murders, Dr. Jill Taylor, a mental health expert, said that doctors, social workers, families and even neighbors need to pay more attention to the needs of mentally unstable people. However, the authors of the editorial are clearly tired of society being blamed for an individual’s actions, and they claim that if Weston is convicted and not taking his medication is deemed as a contributing factor to the murders, he should be held accountable for his choice to refuse medicine.

headline: Audits of schools show errors, weakness
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey releases an auditing report on Rockwood Are School District snd Somerset County Area Vo-Tech Schools. Financial overpayments by the districts may cause them to lose some funds next year.

headline: Deer report cards on the rise
abstract: The Game Commission's Bureau of Wildlife Management has collected about five percent more buck season report cards than last year, while doe season report cards have come in 16 percent higher than 1997.  Deer aging teams examined over 47,000 deer at meat processors during and shortly after the  two seasons, including over 18,000 bucks and more than 29,000 does.  In comparison, aging teams in 1996 checked approximately 16,000 bucks and over 20,000 does.

headline: High-Speed Hopes
abstract: A proposed bill would create a high-speed intercity rail passenger service traveling through Johnstown.

headline: Client status unclear in bail bondsman's license loss
abstract: Susquehanna Twp bail bondsmen Jesse Rawls Sr.'s application for renewal of his bondsman license has been rejected by the state, leaving his clients with an uncertain future.  At issue is $170,000 in judgments against Rawls filed in the Dauphin County Courthouse-bail the county says was to be forfeited after various defendants failed to appear in court.  Neither the county district attorney's office nor Rawls' attorney were able to say how many defendants Rawls is handling, and Pennsylvania law is unclear what those individuals need to do when Rawls' license expires at the end of the month.

headline: Violence puts schools on edge
abstract: The authors of the editorial claim school violence has changed over the years, and it is no longer enough to simply "get tough" on students who commit serious crimes because this approach often comes too late. Spring-Ford Area School District and PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf are considering policies that would require teachers and students to report threats of violence to school officials, and the authors sadly believe these controls are needed. In the authors’ opinion, it will be tough for school officials to differentiate between the actual trouble students and those who are just tough-talking, but children must become aware that it is unacceptable to even joke about violence.

headline: Dean to head No Dice
abstract: Evan Stoddard of the South Side, an associate dean at Duquesne University, is the new president of No Dice, a local organization that opposes efforts to legalize gambling casinos in Pennsylvania. City officials have been willing to consider establishment of gambling casinos as part of an overall policy of giving people more venues for entertainment in the city. No Dice is a nonpartisan, nonprofit citizens group formed several years ago to oppose the legalization of riverboat casino gambling and other forms of gambling in the state.

headline: Congress Hunkers Down for Protracted Struggle Over Whether Clinton Will Serve Out His Term
abstract: Congressional Democrats are becoming increasingly nervous about Kenneth Starr’s report on President Clinton’s sexual relationship with Monica Lewinski, and questions remain about what kind of impact the report will have. Clinton has vowed not to reign, but an impeachment process would almost certainly last until next year, and many Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, are urging the President to speak more to ease the public’s concerns. Congressmen are debating procedures for receiving and evaluating Starr’s report, and most Democrats believe there’s nothing to gain from having Clinton resign; though many are concerned about Clinton’s impact on their re-election bids in the upcoming election.

headline: Many clues, little certainty in the Senate on impeachment: As usual in the body, senators are not speaking in unison. Expect the minority Democrats to be heard.
abstract: Democratic Senate minority leader Tom Daschle and Republican majority leader Trent Lott have both been vague on how they plan to deal with the potential impeachment of President Clinton; however, Senator Robert Byrd did tell the White House not to interfere. Some Democrats are calling for a quick bipartisan censure of Clinton, while most Republicans, including Pennsylvanian U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, argue the Senate should at least convene a hearing and then decide which course of action to pursue. Democrats have enough members in the Senate to prevent Clinton’s impeachment conviction if a hearing is held, but the impact a hearing could have on the presidency is unknown.

headline: Tangretti again comes under attack
abstract: Beating the drum of scandal again Tuesday, Republican candidate for the state House of Representatives John W. Bush Sr., upped the ante- calling for the resignation of incumbent Tom Tangretti. But the allegations Bush made are false according to Tangretti and others.

headline: State may tighten subsidies for child care
abstract: PA Child Care Campaign and Auditor General Robert Casey, oppose the proposed subsidized regulations on child care. The regulations are believed to hurt low-income families in various ways.

headline: Blue Cross lowers cost of health plans
abstract: Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield will continue to offer its KeystoneBlue HMO and SelectBlue point-of-service programs; however, the PA Departments of Health and Insurance approved the company’s new CommunityBlue program, which will offer lower-cost health care coverage to nine southwestern PA counties. Blue Cross Blue Shield introduced the new program in the midst of rapid change in the region’s health care system, and it is designed to fulfill the needs of cost-conscious consumers who are willing to use a selective network of hospitals and physicians to reduce costs. The new coverage should cost by about 10 percent less than the other programs, and the network of coverage includes 21 hospitals, nearly 1,000 primary care physicians and about 2,600 specialty physicians.

headline: Axing Huck is off Mark
abstract: The authors of the editorial disagree with the PA National Association for the Advancement of Colored People for calling on "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" to be removed from required reading lists in PA schools. They argue the book can be a powerful piece of literature if someone tries to understand its underlying adult themes and use of irony, and they ultimately believe educators should be making curriculum decisions.

headline: Deer targeted in city parks - Fairmount Park commissioners for the first time talked openly of killing most of the destructive animals
abstract: Several Fairmount Park commissioners are openly calling for the killing of deer in Wissahickon and Pennypack Parks because of overpopulation that is destroying much of the parks’ flowers, shrubs and small trees. Commissioner Mary Mason is still undecided on what to do, while the Friends of Wissahickon group is conducting a study and trying to garner support for eliminating some of the deer population. The Fairmont Park Commission would have to obtain a permit from the PA Gaming Commission to kill deer, but because of Philadelphia’s status as the only fully urban county in PA, with not legal hunting anywhere, nobody is certain how the permit process would work.

headline: High-speed rail in Western Pa. gets $5M boost
abstract: A federal transportation bill will provide $5 million in funds that will be used for design and assessment of a high-speed railway system.

headline: Business is slow in execution chamber
abstract: Death Row is explored in terms of number of people currently on PA death row, number of executions occurring in PA, and the PA appeals process. There is a current battle on the appeals process between the state legislature and the courts.

headline: Vote 'no' - twice
abstract: The Philadelphia Inquirer urges voters to say no to two constitutional referendums on crime.

headline: Demolition provides opportunity for drill
abstract: The demolition of the Transportation and Safety building wwill be the site of a search-and-rescue training mission for state emergency workers.

headline: Congress: California's 22nd District
abstract: Facts about the 22nd district including: population, largest cities, economy, home to, and presidential vote.

headline: Marriage not a single issue   Bachelors in the running for mayor
abstract: Three of the likely mayoral candidates for Philadelphia in next year’s election, former Philadelphia Housing Authority chief John White Jr., state Representative Dwight Evans and City Councilman Frank Rizzo, are all bachelors. Rizzo, who does have a girlfriend, said being single has advantages because he can dedicate all his time to his work, whereas a spokesperson for Evans said marital status should make no difference as long as a person has strong leadership skills. The candidates denied that being single would leave anybody more susceptible to scandals, and White’s spokesman made a distinction between White and the other candidates because his wife died, and he has children.

headline: Tax collectors block efforts to streamline
abstract: A bill to centralize tax collection was killed after tax collecters protested at the Capital. New legislation is in the works to unfiy and cost-effectively collect state and local taxes.

headline: State should back child services
abstract: York county Children and Youth Services Department is required by the state of PA to provide a variety of services but are not being allocated the appropriate funds by the state to do so.

headline: Bond agencies batter AHERF
abstract: Moody’s Investor Service continued to downgrade the credit ratings of Allegheny Health Education and Research Foundation’s (AHERF) hospitals in the Philadelphia area. AHERF has been considering to sell its Philadelphia hospitals, but after a deal fell apart last month, it could be forced to file for bankruptcy since its monthly losses total an estimated $27 million. Vanguard Health Systems has continued to pursue purchasing some or all of the hospitals.

headline: Belle Vernon board hears complaints on state assessment test
abstract: At the Belle Vernon Area School Board meeting, a father of an eighth-grade student complained about a standardized test that was administered in the school a month ago. The PA Department of Education requires several tests to be administered without school officials being able to review their content, and the state has $10.4 million available to reward schools that improve their scores. After the public meeting ended, the board was expected to discuss the high school band director, who was suspended for "inappropriate" contact with a student.

headline: DEP will not reduce state water standards
abstract: PA industries reported discharging 22.8 million pounds of toxic chemicals into waterways in 1996, which was second highest in the nation, yet the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) had proposed loosening restrictions by easing standards on discharge limits for many toxic chemicals and allowing a general permit to discharge all toxic chemicals. However, the DEP announced it would not loosen standards after a public outcry, including complaints from the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and Clean Water Action.

headline: Highway bill gets green light
abstract: The six year transportation bill passed by lawmakers will give Pennsylvania $1.3 billion dollars for roadway improvements, which is up 46.8% compared to the last proposed bill.

headline: Call for stiffer penalties for arson draws a mixed reaction
abstract: Public outrage continues to grow as the fifth church in four weeks fell victim to arson, and PA Representative Peter Daley announced his proposal make arson a Felony Two, which would increase the maximum prison sentence from seven to ten years. While Monessen Valley Fire Chief Tim Billick supports the proposal, he believes it should apply to all arsons, not just churches; however, he said the major problem is most smaller communities don’t have the resources to thoroughly investigate arson cases. Local clergy had mixed opinions on how to deal with the problem.

headline: Where have all the judges gone?
abstract: Allegheny County judges are arriving late, leaving early, and calling for recesses in their courtrooms. Involved parties are frustrated wit the slowmoving system and judges do not believe their work ethic should be questioned.

headline: Designer offers diection to boost state tourism
abstract: A sign project is being constructed to help tourist get around popular PA sites.

headline: Congressional race could get ugly
abstract: The 10th District race between Democrat Patrick Casey, son of former Governor Casey, and Republican Paul Sherwood has been relatively quiet over the summer; however, it is expected to become one of closest and most heated battles. U.S. Representative McDade is leaving office after 36 years, but most of his elections were either easy victories or uncontested. Casey, Sherwood and Reform Party candidate Tom McLaughlin have all begun their fall campaigning, and the first debate is scheduled; though McLaughlin has yet to be invited.

headline: Maryland's Republicans Strain to Fill State Ticket: Only 1 GOP Candidate Is Considered Strong
abstract: Traditionally, the Democrats have been the dominant party in Maryland politics, and this year, Republicans are struggling to find strong candidates to challenge. Maryland’s Republican Party chairman, Joyce Terhes, insisted the party would field strong candidates, but the reality is they are running out of time and any candidate they field would be unlikely to defeat the powerful incumbents: Attorney General Joseph Curran Jr., Comptroller Louis Goldstein or U.S. Senator Barbara Mikulski. The only candidate who is considered strong enough to challenge is Ellen Sauerbrey, who is challenging Governor Parris Glendening, and Sauerbrey could actually benefit from the weak party candidates because it could keep some Democrats away from the polls.

headline: Tax cuts are in the air in governor's race
abstract: PA will collect a record $18 billion in taxes this year, and tax relief remains one of the major issues for the gubernatorial election. Incumbent Governor Tom Ridge claims he’s saved the public $2.6 billion by cutting taxes over the past four years, and he has said that he will continue to do so in the future; though he offered no specific plans. On the contrary, Democratic challenger Ivan Itkin has called on providing funding to school districts, which could cut local property taxes in half, and Constitutional Party challenger Peg Luksik favors the elimination of the state’s inheritance tax.

headline: State slaps Big 33 foundation with $18,000 fine
abstract: The state has fined the Big 33 Scholarship Foundation $18,000 after uncovering 24 charity-law violations. In the wake of violations, Big 33 officials admitted they misled people about how donations would be used and made inaccurate statements on reports filed with the state. Other mistakes they characterized as clerical errors.

headline: Borski says Pennsylvania needs a patients bill of rights
abstract: U.S. Representative Bob Borski released data that shows that six million Pennsylvanians will lack adequate patient protections unless Congress passes legislation to create a patients’ bill of rights. He said the bill will offer people the protections they deserve, and he feels that a federal bill is necessary because the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 limits each state’s ability to offer the necessary protections alone. He also singles out women as being important for a number of reasons and hopes that the leadership in Congress will stop blocking his proposed bill.

headline: Bevilacqua unhappy about lack of vote
abstract: Cardinal Anthony Bevilacqua, Philadelphia’s archbishop, expressed his disappointment with the PA Legislature for failing to vote on a bill that would have provided publicly funded vouchers to be used by parents who want to send their children to public, private, religious or charter schools of their choice.

headline: Deputy system to be reviewed: Game Commission committee to focus on entire program
abstract: The PA Game Commission, in an informal agreement with PA Senators Helfrick and Hart, will undergo a thorough review of its deputy program, which employs 854 paid volunteers that receive one week’s training and one year probation under a full-time officer before being allowed to patrol. These deputies have been highly criticized for a number of reasons, and the license fee bill, which is awaiting Governor Ridge’s signature, has a provision that would require nearly every deputy to take their citations to full-time officers for approval. The bill also contains an increase of $11 million in annual revenue for the agency that has helped quiet internal criticism.

headline: Highway bill no way to help
abstract: U.S. Representative Bud Shuster inserted a provision into the $203 billion highway bill to make a portion of the PA Turnpike free, which he thought would encourage locals to use the turnpike and reduce construction delays on the nearby Route 30. However, the authors argue the provision has no business being in the bill, which awaits President Clinton’s signature. They claim it violates the turnpike’s operating procedures, it will cost merchants along Route 30 to lose business, and local residents can avoid the construction on their own.

headline: Capital fire alarm turns out to be false
abstract: Asecond firm alaram, which counded in the Harrisburg Capital Building, was a false alaram and is belieevd to be pulled by someone in the basement. An investigation is underway.

headline: Voters must decide whether prosecutors can ask for jury trial
abstract: Pennsylvanians will have the opportunity to vote in the November 3 election on a constitutional amendment to allow judges to deny bail to certain suspects, as well as on a more controversial amendment that would allow prosecutors to ask for a jury trial after a defendant waives that right. Proponents of the jury trial amendment, which includes Governor Tom Ridge and Attorney General Mike Fisher, argue that the amendment will prevent defendants from searching for a sympathetic judge that would be more lenient on them. Critics of the amendment believe that it takes away an important right of defendants and would give prosecutors too much power.

headline: Do AMP and legislators defeat democracy in takeover fight?
abstract: Opinion piece about whether or not the legislature protecting AMP with a law is democratic. AMP did not use capitalism to help its shareholders and had the government intervene. They knew if AlliedSignal took over they would be completely changed due to their own bad management.

headline: Congressional race heats up
abstract: PA's primary election is just a month away, and the race is heating up for the 10th Congressional District seat currently held by retiring Congressman Joe McRae. The primary is only a formality for the Democratic party this year, as Scranton attorney Patrick Casey is the lone candidate for his party's nomination. The Republican party's pick will be a little more difficult, because eight party members are running for the nomination.

headline: Mascara, Murtha say they'll vote against Clinton's impeachment
abstract: Representatives Frank Mascara and John Murtha say that while they do not agreee with President Clinton behavior they will not vote for impeachment.

headline: Taxes a key concern of state legislators
abstract: PA Representatives Merle Phillips and Russ Fairchild spoke at a breakfast event, and Fairchild focused on the tax reform that passed the state House. The reform is only applicable to school districts, but four local schools have to fix some problems first. Both legislators expressed the need for cooperation in support of the Central Susquehanna Thruway proposal, while Phillips said the state was in solid financial shape, and the federal government is requesting all states to lower their blood alcohol level for Driving Under the Influence charges.

headline: State warned it may lose federal money - The lack of a statewide child-support operation jeopardizes the $796 million
abstract: The Clinton Administration notified PA that it is in jeopardy of losing $796 million in federal welfare and child-support funding for failing to comply with a 1988 federal law requiring all states to implement a statewide child-support system, despite an extension of the original deadline by two years. PA has implemented pilot programs in several counties and is considered one of the best states in recovering child-support money; however, it is nowhere near full compliance with federal regulations, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said they are serious about cutting the funds unless Congress passes another extension, which it is considering. Governor Tom Ridge will file for a formal appeals hearing, and the state Legislature recently took its own action to crack down on parents who refuse to pay child support.

headline: Brightbill in hospital to fight off leukemia
abstract: PA Senator David Brightbill, who was nominated for re-election, has been hospitalized with a rare but treatable form of leukemia. He expects to return to work after a seven-day chemo therapy treatment for hairy cell leukemia, which his doctor said is easily controlled.

headline: Big Charter school increases expected
abstract: Pittsburgh area has four new charter schools planning to open and additional charter school applications are being filed.

headline: Doe license allocation is up: Game Commission also modifies youth deer hunt, lengthens several seasons
abstract: Despite objections from some commissioners, the PA Game Commission approved the allocation of 797,200 antlerless deer licenses, which is a substantial increase from last year. The Commission also modified the junior license allocation process, and hunters under the age of 17 will be allowed to hunt both sexes of deer only on the two Saturdays of buck season. In addition, the Commission extended the hunting seasons for rabbits, squirrels and pheasants, and a list of the set seasons is provided in the article.

headline: Highway bill paved with pork
abstract: US House Budget Chairman John Kasich has been at the forefront of the effort to balance the budget, however his efforts appear to have been thwarted by a $218 billion highway bill scheduled for a vote today. Kasich says the bill is filled with pork. The bill was put together by Transportation chairman Bud Shuster. To achieve bipartisan support, the bill is filled with provisions for federal funding in almost every district. A top aide to President Clinton said the bill's provisions were getting out of hand. Citizens Against Government Waste Opposes the pork spending in the bill.

headline: Capitol security to grow - State earmarks $4.8 million for new measures
abstract: PA Department of General Services Secretary Gary Crowell said the state plans to spend $4.8 million on new security measures for the state Capitol Complex, including increased surveillance and electronic screening devices that will automatically close and lock doors if weapons are detected. The security upgrades follow an incident in July, when a gunman killed two police officers in the U.S. Capitol building. PA House and Senate officials, including Senate Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer, expressed support for the new security measures, and Crowell vowed to not let the new features inhibit the public’s access to the buildings.

headline: Votes of note
abstract: Senator Arlen Spector voted agaisnt a bill restricting attorney fees in the tobacco settlement, while Senator Rick Santorum vote for the bill.

headline: Gambling Lobby Stacks the Deck
abstract: Opinion on the gambling lobby and how it controls Washington politicians. Two sitting governors lost elections partially because of their opposition to gambling. They also helped pick the leadership in Congress. The author believes this is too much power for one group to hold.

headline: Congressional Roll Call Report
abstract: In addition to the Senate’s passing of a $250.5 spending plan for the nation’s defense, the article provides information on how the U.S. House voted on several different bills, and it lists how each Pennsylvanian from the House voted on each issue. The House upheld President Clinton’s executive order that bans discrimination in the federal workplace based on sexual orientation, it approved a campaign finance reform bill sponsored by Representatives Christopher Shays and Martin Meehan, and it voted to continue a $9.4 million program that attempts to send anti-Castro programming to the Cuban people. In addition, the House voted against Clinton’s plan to use sampling along with direct counting for the 2000 census, it upheld a plan to repay $475 million to the United Nations, and it increased spending by $109 million to an agency that provides free legal counsel to the poor.

headline: Mason: Choose or lose
abstract: In order for Philadelphia to elect an Africa American mayor, it is believd that the many individuals planning to run should select one person for the job so that all black voting suport can go to one candidiate.

headline: Taxpayers fund gym for House, Senate
abstract: The PA House and Senate plan to open a workout facility in the East Wing addition to the Capitol, but the gym will only be open to members of the Legislature and their staffs. State Senator Jane Earll said she wouldn’t use the facility because it’s ridiculous for taxpayers to pay for it, and state Representative Karl Boyes also said he wouldn’t use it. It will cost $49,344, and Susan Cohen, co-executive director of the Bipartisan Management Committee for the House, said the gym is necessary in light of the growing awareness of the need to exercise.

headline: Tax privilege - The state House should reject special treatment
abstract: The authors support two provisions in a PA Senate bill focusing solely on Allegheny County; however, the two provisions occur in the same bill as a measure sponsored by Senator Melissa Hart to grant senior citizens tax breaks over property reassessments. The authors oppose the measure because it only provides relief to senior citizens, even though there are no real statistics showing elderly people are being forced out of there homes because they can no longer afford to pay reassessed property taxes. The authors propose two alternate ideas that would protect the elderly while also ensuring the other half million property owners in Allegheny County are treated fairly.

headline: Campaign focuses on expanding CHIP
abstract: PA Senator Allen Kukovich went to Seton Hill Day Care Center in Greensburg to promote the Children Health Insurance Program (CHIP), which provides health insurance to children whose parents cannot afford to purchase it themselves. CHIP covers 70,000 children, but Governor Ridge said that another 122,000 are eligible yet not participating. The program is funded with federal dollars and a 3-cent state cigarette tax.

headline: Burden lies with applicants
abstract: Eric Barron, a member of the State College Area School Board, believes the charter school law is essentially and unfunded state mandate, so if the board accepts a charter school application in the future, it would almost certainly cause a tax increase. The state law sets very specific guidelines on how to evaluate applications, so Barron believes all applicants must provide evidence that they are financially sustainable, demonstrate innovative educational contributions, offer improvements for the entire district and are equally accessible to the entire community. Barron believes the school board owes it to the taxpayers to evaluate any charter school applications carefully, and they will only approve an application that fulfills all of these criteria.

headline: Don't politicize deer season
abstract: There is a movement in Harrisburg to move the authority to regulate the length of hunting seasons and the limit on the number of deer an individual can kill from the PA Game Commission to the Legislature. The authors of the editorial hope the movement fails because wildlife management takes a lot of skill and expertise, which many lawmakers simply don’t have. The authors believe the Game Commission can increase the deer population without interference from the Legislature.

headline: Highway Bill's Bounty Isn't Always in Dollars
abstract: A $217 billion US House Transportation bill includes provisions for special interests, including weight limits in the trucking industry, and eligibility for Chick-fil-a to display signage on federal highways. The latter provision was inserted by US Rep. Mac Collins. Sugarcane growers hope to benefit from a provision allowing 100,000 pound loads on federal roads, as permitted on state highways. The Association of American Railroads opposes exemptions for weight limits in trucking. The bill contained a moratorium inserted by US Rep. Bud Shuster against using GPS to check driver hours.

headline: Capitol shootings leave local public servants on edge
abstract: After a fatal shooting of two policemen at the U.S. Capitol building, PA Representative T.J. Rooney is sponsoring two gun control bills in the state House, one of which would make it a misdemeanor to bring a gun into a municipal building. New Jersey Senator William Schluter said his state probably has enough security in place to protect elected officials, and Governor Christie Whitman has a security detail with her at all times. At the local level in PA, a man shot himself inside a South Whitehall Township building in March, and three local Easton lawmakers said they believe Easton has enough security in place, but sometimes, it can still be scary being an elected official.

headline: Waiting for justice
abstract: Allegheny County judges are critcized for their ineffiencient behavior and time-consuming tactics.

headline: Drug HQ here should be safe
abstract: Philadelphia officials say they're watching the merger talks between pharmaceutical giants SmithKline Beechman and Glaxo Welcome, but have no reason to fear the SmithKline's plans for expansion in the city are threatened. There's no reason to believe SmithKline's North American headquarters, under construction at 17th and Vine Streets, won't move ahead.

headline: Congressional, House Races Highlight Tuesday Primaries
abstract: In the upcoming primary, voters will nominate a number of important candidates for office, but Governor Ridge and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker will run unopposed, and Ridge is expected to defeat any Democratic challenger easily in the fall. Philadelphia Democratic Chairman Robert Brady is the favorite to win a special election and the nomination to represent the 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House, Anthony Hardy Williams will try to win the 8th Senatorial District seat vacated by his father and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter expects little opposition in his primary or the general election. A number of races for state House seats to represent different areas of Philadelphia are discussed, but the 188th District race between incumbent Representative James Roebuck and his challengers could be especially heated.

headline: Mayor gives Ridge nod over Itkin for governor: Mayor insists praise not 'endorsement'
abstract: While introducing Governor Ridge for a $15 million check presentation towards Downtown developments, Pittsburgh Mayor Murphy offered strong words of praise for Ridge, and he criticized his own party’s gubernatorial candidate, Ivan Itkin. Murphy wouldn’t go as far as to formally endorse Ridge, but his words spoke loud enough and comes as even more bad news for Itkin, who is far behind in the polls and had Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed defect from the party to endorse Ridge recently. Murphy’s words were a bit surprising, but he does have a long history of poor relations with Itkin.

headline: Tax-subsidized stadiums are bad for business and worse for future
abstract: Allegheny County subsidizes stadiums despite the public's referendumn decision. Allegheny County residents are moving out.

headline: Study shatters the stereotype of the needy in midstate
abstract: The South Central PA Food Bank conducted an interview and released a survey that found charitable food recipients are either very young or very old, they are overwhelmingly female and white, and many work but don’t make enough to provide for their families. In both the central PA study and national studies, charity recipients were found to have little or no health insurance, and they often skip doctor’s appointments and have to choose between eating and paying for rent. The South Central PA Food Bank’s warehouse accepts food donations, which are distributed to member agencies that feed an estimated 194,000 people a year throughout the region, and while unemployment rates are low, many people require assistance because low-paying positions often don’t provide living pay wages.

headline: Casey asks Ridge to fire health secretary
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey calls on Govenor Tom Ridge to fire Daniel Hoffmann because he has failed respond to allegations of nursing home abuse and nursing home complaints.

headline: Campus Drinking
abstract: Consumption of alcoholic beverages at the University of Virginia is high, especially among fraternities and sororities and among white students.

headline: Emissions escape halts soil burning
abstract: OHM Remediation Services Corporation has a contract to incinerate contaminated soil at the former Drake Chemical Company, but it was forced to halt its efforts by the PA Department of Environmental Protection because dust from incinerated soil was seen to be leaving the facility, which is a violation of the state’s Air Pollution Control Act. A similar problem was detected during the beginning phases of the project but was thought to have been corrected. A citizens group is trying to file a lawsuit in Clinton County Court to try to stop the incineration process, but the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and Clinton County Commissioner Dean Buttorf feel that the problem can be fixed by early next week.

headline: Highway Funds Will Help Concert Jams
abstract: US Rep. Joseph McDade said he inserted provisions for improvements to I-81 using federal funds. The insertions were made in a $217 billion transportation bill, which was recently passed by the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. The bill will still need approval from the full House and Senate.
