The projects in question must also be included for renovation by the PA Transportation Commission so that federal funds could be matched by state funds, said district engineer for the PA Department of Transportation Charles Mattei. Approval from local officials is also needed.

headline: 'Caravan of Conscience' traveling rally stops at state facility in Waynesburg
abstract: About 170 protesters gathered at the State Correctional Institution in Waynesburg Greene County, to criticize the death penalty. The march, called the Caravan of Conscience was organized by a Philadelphia group joined by dozens of members of the Mayette County Brudehof communities and other death-penalty abolitionists from across the state.

headline: Warning label lakes punch vs. spousal abuse
abstract: A state lawmaker wants to put warning labels on marriage licenses to discourage domestice abuse. The propsal takes critisim and offers suggestions for supporting domestice violence groups and shelters.

headline: Elsewhere, they're keen on keno
abstract: Keno is a gambling game that has become very popular other places in the US. Article gives background on how to play and how people pick their numbers. The PA Legislature is considering letting keno into the state. Counties would vote if they want to allow it in their county.

headline: Conklin-Corman, Thompson-Hanna races in spotlight
abstract: Four candidates attended a breakfast meeting where they answered questions on taxes, education and health care in front of 50 guests of the Chamber of Business and Industry of Centre County. Incumbent 76th PA District Representative Mike Hanna and challenger Glenn Thompson Howard were present, as were the two candidates running for the 34th District state Senate seat, Scott Conklin and Jake Corman, whose father just retired from the seat. While the candidates shared similar opinions on many issues, such as the link between improving education and attracting new jobs, the candidates also tried to distinguish themselves based on record and level of experience.

headline: McDade bill to scrutinize prosecutors 'unworkable'
abstract: Represnetative Joseph McDade passes legislation that would require federal prosecutors to follow ethic rules of the state. This legislation comes with great opposition.

headline: Tears in Happy Valley
abstract: PA Senator Robert Jubelirer wants PA Attorney General Mike Fisher to punish sports agent Jeff Naley for giving former Penn State star running back Curtis Enis a $400 suit in a scandal that ended his college football career.

headline: Testimony: Welfare system needs more flexibility
abstract: About ten past and present welfare recipients spoke to the Interfaith Coalition on Poverty, a group of leaders from different churches across the Lehigh Valley that has been exploring the issue of poverty. Ray Schlecter, the director of operations for the Department of Public Welfare, heard the testimony, and he agreed with many others that the system needs to be more flexible in helping individuals on a case-by-case basis. The testimony of several women is provided in the article.

headline: Casey outlines solutions to fix nursing-home care
abstract: PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. released a report on nursing homes that identifies, among others, six general needs that must be addressed, including a recommendation for the state Health Department to begin issuing report cards on every nursing home in the state. Casey suggested the idea to Governor Tom Ridge’s administration last spring, but the administration and Health Department have been reluctant to do so. In addition, Casey questioned whether the Health Department was imposing tough enough sanctions against facilities that violate regulations, he called for increased inspections, and if the state doesn’t listen to any of his suggestions, Casey has been working with U.S. Attorney David Barasch, who wants to sue nursing homes that don’t provide quality care.

headline: Candidates differ on funding, control of schools
abstract: PA Senator David Brightbill, who was selected by fellow Republicans for the third highest leadership post in the Senate as the majority whip, is seeking his fifth term to represent the 48th District, and he will face Democrat Lenny Marrella, a retired school administrator and Army Reserve officer. Marrella wants more money to be spent on education, and he believes the state should require classroom sizes to be smaller, whereas Brightbill believes local teachers and school boards should be left alone to make those types of decisions themselves. Both candidates support a $40 million proposal to construct a dam across Swatara Creek, and Brightbill has taken credit for helping to secure funding for a $12 million railroad overpass construction project in Lebanon, and he said PA must find a way to make cities more attractive places to live in.

headline: EPA sides with dam opponents   Agency: Plan would ruin Swatara habitat
abstract: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) wrote a letter to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers opposing Pennsylvania’s plans to build a dam on the Swatara Creek because it claims the dam would destroy several wetlands and woodlands in the region. The Corps is expected to decide whether to build the dam by the end of the year, but the EPA could essentially veto the decision if the Corps votes to build the dam. State Senator David Brightbill has been an advocate of the dam for years, and he criticized the EPA for overlooking the people in the community who would greatly benefit from the dam; though he remains hopeful that it will still be built.

headline: Highway project 'not pork--its survival'
abstract: A dangerous section of Route 10 in West Virginia may get an overhaul thanks to a bill by the US House that appropriates $218 billion for transportation projects across the nation. The Congressional Accountability Project condemned the bill as pork. The USA Today however, finds that rather than being a pet project, improvements now possible for Route 10 have been lobbied for hard by residents and local officials. Shuster has indicated he may be willing to compromise in House-Senate negotiation. Senators are inclined to drop the long list of local projects.

headline: Casey seeks change in laws on children
abstract: State Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr. releases child welfare investigation findings and calls for immediate reform in PA state child welfare laws.

headline: Warning: This column mocks overzealous cautions
abstract: Representative Charlie Dent's proposed bill for warning labels on marriage licenses is harshly criticized. Representative Anthony Williams's proposed bill on licenses challenges by Congress is harshly critized.

headline: Emphasizing deal of the arts
abstract: Philadelphia can use arts and culture as a major tourism venue. The city must find better ways of funding the arts to help consumers with costs.

headline: Constituents keep those cards and letters coming
abstract: Consitiuents flodded the office of Representative Bill Gooding with messages concerning the impeacement vote of President Bill Clinton. Gooding's pro-impeachment vote could not be swayed.

headline: McHale accepts apology
abstract: The White House issued an apology and assured U.S. Representative Paul McHale that it was not the source of a false tip aired by television reporter Geraldo Rivera that McHale had lied about his military service. McHale accepted the apology and doesn’t blame Clinton for it. However, he suspects one of the president’s political advisers provided the tip because he was the first Democratic congressman to call for Clinton’s resignation after he had admitted to misleading the country about his relationship with Monica Lewinski.

headline: Term Limits Give Neophytes Legs to Run
abstract: The 1992 Arkansas term limits bill has inspired many new people from a variety of different backgrounds to seek election to the state Legislature, and half of the state’s 100 House seats will be open in this year’s election, which gives new hope to Republicans who are badly outnumbered in the House. While there have been some successes in states like Maine and California, many of the 18 states that passed term limits are beginning to confront the effects of the laws they passed in the early 1990’s, and the results could have a profound effect on whether national efforts can regain momentum. Critics of term limits argue the high rate of turnover creates a lack of experience in government, but proponents believe limits increase accountability, and they hope they will encourage legislators to tackle risky subjects such as ethics reform.

headline: Thornburgh defends plan to reimburse bilked districts
abstract: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission accused John Gardner Black of improperly investing his clients’ funds and losing $71 million, which led to his remaining funds being frozen. Former Governor Dick Thornburgh recommended that all of Black’s clients, including Northern Lebanon and Cornwall-Lebanon, evenly share $95 million in frozen funds, but the proposal must be approved by U.S. District Court Judge Donetta Ambrose. While Thornburgh believes the return is fair, Northern Lebanon is proposing a different formula that would spread total losses out more evenly and return $5.9 million more than Thornburgh suggested, and Cornwall-Lebanon took precautions in investing its money, so it doesn’t think it should have to pay any investigation costs

headline: Casey to Health: Protect citizens
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey wants the Health Department to upgrade their system, investigation nursing home abuse charges, and begin responding immediately to complaints. Gov. Tom Ridge pledges $1.4 million to the Health Department to assist in correcting the current problems.

headline: Central seen as flagship for year-round education
abstract: Students at Central Elementary School in Allentown are on vacation under the year-round calendar. Many of them have chosen to attend the school's remediation and enrichment sessions during vacation. School districts from all around the country are eager to learn about the program. It has turned around what was once one of Allentown's most troubled schools. About 4 percent of schools are now year round.

headline: Experts at odds over why Pa.'s tops in trash imports
abstract: PA imports more trash than any other state, and the garbage industry claims that it’s simply a matter of economics, whereas critics believe that the state’s weaker environmental laws have allowed it to become a dumping ground for other states. In 1978, the U.S. Supreme Court decided that trash can only be regulated by Congress under the interstate commerce clause, and PA Senator Raphael Musto and Representative Tom Tigue believe that the federal government should enact legislation that would solve the problem and make other states more responsible for their own trash.

headline: Highways and Heaches
abstract: Montogomery County will receive $400 million over the next four years for road projects, but traffic delays and congestions will get worse as construction begins.

headline: Changes to the law do affect divorce rates
abstract: Maggie Gallagher explores why divorces end up being bitter and nasty.

headline: When manufactured justice masks injustice
abstract: Mumia Abu-Jamal's latest appeal to the Sumpreme Court is denied. The 22 issues brought up by Jamal and his lawyers are dismissed as being unable to be fully proven.

headline: Employment rises for fifth time in '98
abstract: The number of people employed in PA hit a record high last month, 5,464,600. It is the fifth increase, according to statistics released by the US Department of Labor and Industry. Strong growth occurred in durable goods manufacturing, construction, finance and service industry. The service industry picked up 5,600 jobs.

headline: Consultant seeks GOP nomination
abstract: Marketing consultant John Schnatterly will challenge incumbent John Maher for the 40th District seat in the PA Legislature. Maher won the seat in a special election held September. 9 to fill the vacant seat left when Albert Pettit died of cancer.

headline: McHale being shipped to top job in the Navy?
abstract: U.S. Representative Paul McHale, who decided to retire from Congress at the end of the year, has been contacted by Pentagon officials for the position of Secretary of Navy. Defense Secretary William Cohen wants McHale for the position, and McHale said he would accept if nominated. However, current Navy Secretary John Dalton has given no indication that he will be leaving the position.

headline: The candid Cranmer
abstract: Local resident is upset over a campaign mailing he received from County Commissioner Bob Cramer about his candid self.

headline: Tufts University's ranking of state welfare policies
abstract: Tufts University’s Center on Hunger and Poverty evaluated the 50 states’ welfare policies to judge how reforms are likely to affect the poor’s financial status. The article provides a list of rankings, and PA is ranked fourth best.

headline: Casey urges 6 steps in nursing-home care
abstract: Auditor General Bob Casey release a report, Improving the Quality of Care, to the public about nursing home care. He proposes six steps to fixing current problems and urges Govenor Tom Ridge and Congress to begin working on the issue.

headline: Change in state law may save taxes on school construction
abstract: Contractors are charged a sales tax on all items they purchase that will become a permanent part of a building, and schools are exempt from that tax; though contractors often include it in the final bills which schools pay. In order to retrieve the money paid in sales tax, Dallas School District is using the services of Chartwell Advisory Group. However, the State Legislature passed a bill that could make those services unnecessary in the future because the bill would allow contractors themselves to be exempted from paying the sales tax if they tell suppliers that they are doing work on a school building.

headline: Final decision may be near on Game bill: House, Senate to review license increase, agency's accountability
abstract: House Bill 1994, which would increase hunting licenses by up to $7 and generate about $11 million for the PA Game Commission, passed the House and Senate game committees last week and could be considered for final vote. The bill also includes provisions intended to make the Game Commission more accountable and track complaints better; though critics believe it doesn’t go far enough. Key Senate leaders and Representative David Levdansky are calling for an amendment that could change the powers given to the agency’s deputies, who are paid volunteers that receive the majority of public complaints, but stripping most deputies of their power could cause a serious hardship for the Game Commission.

headline: House begins work on license reform
abstract: PA Rep. Richard Geist believes it is time to change the way the PA Department of Transportation administers the junior licensing system. Geist is chairman of the House Transportation Committee. Safety advocates stressed the need for strict graduated licensing standards. Possible changes to the system include increasing the time a permit holder must wait until taking the driver's test, parental notification of violations, strict guidelines and harsher suspensions for reckless drivers, and being crash and violation free to earn an unrestricted senior license.

headline: Charting Mumia case
abstract: The contoversials case of convicted murderer Mumia Abu-Jamal is examined and a television appearance on ABC 20/20 is scheduled.

headline: Aging Agency Cleared - State: Death not cause by caseworkers
abstract: Local woman upset over treatment her father received while under the care of the Area Agency of Aging. Investigation into the matter clears the agency of wrongdoing.

headline: Erie County women would trade stamps for ATM card
abstract: Three Erie County women who receive food stamps from the state all said they’d be happy to get rid of food stamps in favor of an electronic banking debit card. They all said that it’s embarrassing to have people watch them rip up food stamps when paying for groceries at the grocery store, and the favor the debit card, which would make purchases more anonymous. The state is scheduled to make the switch to debit cards this August.

headline: Democrats appear to make gains
abstract: Republicans kept control of the Senate, but Democrats won most of the close contests, and Republicans fell short of their overall goals. However, U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich did point out that Republicans were able to maintain control of both the House and Senate for a third consecutive term. Most incumbents from both parties won easily, including Pennsylvanian U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, and both Jeb Bush and potential 2000 presidential candidate George W. Bush won their gubernatorial elections.

headline: McNaughton outpolls two challengers
abstract: Representatives. Mark McNaughton is well on his way to gaining a stranglehold on his 104th House District seat as he outpolled Republican challengers Sally Klien and Matt Napiltonia. The real battle was for second place after he took in 60%.

headline: The DA's main squeeze
abstract: Frank Ford, an 82-year-old Philadelphia radio host, could be an extremely influential figure in the politics of the city because he could potentially influence his wife’s decision on whether to run for mayor of Philadelphia. His wife, Lynne Abraham, is current District Attorney, but polls show that she would likely beat any candidate that both the Democratic and Republican Parties could offer in the upcoming mayoral election. Ford believes his wife has already made up her mind, but he offered no clue as to what the decision will be; though he personally doesn’t think she’d be happy as the mayor.

headline: United Way has banner 50th year
abstract: In 1947 volunteers from the Greater Greenville Community decided to expand to become the Northern Mercer County United Way. Now in its 50 year, the group the group gathered to celebrate its most successful year. Over $244,000 was raised in the 1997-1998 fundraising campaign.

headline: CAT Fund started to help pay large malpractice settlements
abstract: The CAT fund, started by doctors and hospitals, is being used to help curb the cost of malpractice awards. The fund is not supported by tax dollars.

headline: Change of policy will benefit local university
abstract: The newspaper’s editorial board gives praise to the State System of Higher Education (SSHE), which owns 14 universities in PA, for admitting it made a mistake by raising out-of-state tuition for the universities nearly a decade ago. The decision resulted in fewer out-of-state students, which drove down enrollment and hurt funding. The editorial boards is pleased that the SSHE will now allow each university to determine its own out-of-state tuitions.

headline: Free Boating Courses
abstract: There will be two safe boating courses offered by the Game Commission office. They will be free to the public, and information on how to register is provided.

headline: House bill earmarks gas taxes for trails
abstract: The PA House Tourism and Recreation Committee held a hearing on a bill that would divert $16 million in gasoline tax revenue away from roads and bridges to finance trail projects. It’s estimated that drivers of snowmobiles, all-terrain vehicles and similar vehicles pay about $16 million a year in gas taxes, so state Representative Robert Godshall wants to ensure their money is spent to benefit them.

headline: Check cashing scheme probed
abstract: Authorities uncovered a check-cashing scheme throughout Harrisburg banks by a bank teller's suspicions about a customer in the bank and a routine traffic stop on the customer while driving a vehicle. A women was arrested in the connection with the scam.

headline: Antifreeze tragedy bound to happen?   State Representative blames lax DPW oversight
abstract: PA Representative Russ Fairchild was critical of the state Department of Public Welfare because of an incident at Step By Step home, where four mentally retarded adults swallowed antifreeze and were rushed to the hospital. He criticized the agency for insisting that mentally retarded adults living in state-owned homes eventually be moved to group homes. A spokeswoman for the agency said they are not forcing anybody into group homes, and the welfare department is investigating the incident for possible violations of state regulations.

headline: Evans floats idea: Riverboat gambling to pay for stadiums
abstract: State Rep. Dwight Evans is proposing legalizing riverboat gambling in the city as a way to raise funds to build new sports facilities for the Eagles and Phillies. Evans suggests the plan would allow money to be raised for stadiums without increasing taxes and address other top issues in the city: schools and local development. The city will need to come up with perhaps as much of $200 million to cover its share of he costs of two new stadiums.

headline: Democrats Appear Vulnerable in Senate Races
abstract: Since President Clinton’s election in 1992, Democrats have lost 11 seats in the U.S. Senate, and Republicans now hold a 55-45 majority, yet there is a chance that Republicans could win the close senatorial races to obtain a 60-40 majority, which would allow them to block a Democratic filibuster if no party members broke rank. According to recent estimates, in order to reach the filibuster proof majority, Republicans would have to retain five of their closely contested seats and pick up six Democratic-held seats, where their best chances would be in the closely contested races in Illinois, California, Kentucky, Nevada, Wisconsin, Washington and South Carolina. Many incumbent Democrats are facing serious challenges because of Clinton’s scandal, changing voter demographics and their own personal failures as senators, and the race in California between incumbent Senator Barbra Boxer and Matt Fong is a prime example of the vulnerabilities incumbent Democrats face in the upcoming election.

headline: Meckley ends hike through Schuylkill County: Holden says he travels through district at every chance
abstract: John Meckley, who is challenging incumbent U.S. Representative Timothy Holden, has already walked 50.5 miles throughout the Sixth Congressional District as part of his "No Tax Hike." Despite being told that Schuylkill County is very Pro-Holden, Meckley remains optimistic and has vowed to spend as much time as necessary in the county. Holden said that all the money from the federal budget surplus should go towards paying back funds borrowed from the Social Security trust fund, and Meckley assured that the Social Security system would be saved.

headline: The entomology of political words
abstract: During a budget hearing in front of the Philadelphia City Council, District Attorney Lynne Abraham broke the tension by poking fun at her friend, Mayor Ed Rendell. Rendell’s spokesman humorously showed that the mayor was not offended.

headline: Welfare Reform Act of 1996  directly affected recipients
abstract: The Welfare Reform Act of 1996 brought direct changes to welfare recipients by setting time limits on how long welfare recipients can collect cash assistance and requiring them to be in job training programs or have part-time jobs. It also cut the number of people receiving public assistance in Indiana County, yet the number of applicants remains the same, and many recipients are receiving less. PA Representative Sara Steelman said that finding adequate transportation to get to work can be a big obstacle for welfare recipients, and there are some cases in which people lose money by working because of drops in public assistance payments.

headline: Certain states will be hit harder than most by spending cutbacks
abstract: Medicare’s new cost-containment strategy is aimed at curbing skyrocketing costs from home health care coverage, and it will impose an interim payment system for home health service that will basically roll back prices to 1994 levels. A handful of states, mostly in the South, have had some of the largest increases in home health service spending, whereas many states in the Northeast and Midwest have had relatively small growth in comparison. There has been criticism of Medicare’s new proposal because it calls for cutbacks in all states and will not close the disparity that exists between many of them, so states that were able to control spending in home health services feel like they are being penalized for good spending practices while others are being rewarded for bad spending practices.

headline: Charter schools differ in approach   Lewisburg League of Women Voters hold symposium on option
abstract: Last year, the PA Legislature passed a bill that allows charter schools, which are independent, publicly funded schools that don’t have to follow most state mandates. At a meeting of Lewisburg League of Women Voters, some speakers were worried that charter schools would abuse funding and only allow certain groups of students to attend. Tim Daniels, a policy specialist from the state Department of Education, said charter school can offer different alternatives for at-risk students, and both he and a representative from the PA School Boards Association voiced their support for charter schools.

headline: Game Commission at its limit
abstract: The state Game Commission already in disfavor among lawmakers, just can't seem to get it right.  Provided with $475,000 in state funds to build four radio towers in northwest Pennsylvania, the commission constructed the towers to specifications that make them incompatible with the statewide communications network.  That violated the terms under which the commission received state funding for the towers, according to Secretary of Administration Tom Pease.

headline: House returns proposed pickup-riding ban
abstract: A bill that would have banned riding in the back of pickup trucks was referred back to the transportation committee by the House. Several other bills, relating to school buses, parole boards, pension plans, and a consititutional amendment were passed by the house.

headline: Checkpoints checkmate drug dealers
abstract: According to the authors, the blocks along Somerset and Cambria in North Philadelphia have been considered some of the worst areas for drug activity; however, William Colarulo, who became captain of the 25th Police District last summer, began an extremely effective policy. Colarulo set up 24-hour checkpoints and removed abandoned cars that were often used to store drugs, which has provided a strong deterrent against drug crimes. The authors claim this approach could provide a blueprint for the rest of the city’s crime-fighting measures, and it could lead to greater community involvement.

headline: As welfare time limits near, many states are unprepared
abstract: Since welfare reform was passed by Congress two years ago and recipients began facing requirements to search for work or lose benefits, the number of welfare recipients has dropped substantially, and states have saved about $4.7 billion. However, the authors take a look at the numbers more closely and argue it’s far too early for state’s to be celebrating the success of these reforms. They claim states need to invest the welfare money they’ve saved to enact programs that target the reasons why people need public assistance and help find employment for those who will soon lose their welfare benefits.

headline: Evans floats idea: Riverboat gambling to pay for stadiums
abstract: State Rep. Dwight Evans yesterday tried to breathe life into the stadium debate with an old idea: legalize riverboat gambling in the city as a way to raise funds to build new sports facilities for the Eagles and Phillies.  Evans, who is seeking the Democratic nomination for mayor, said his plan could raise $100 million a year, of which $50 million would be devoted to public education, $30 million to community development, and $20 million toward paying off $100 million borrowed to finance two new stadiums.  The plan would allow money to be raised for stadiums without increasing taxes, he said, and at the same time address other top issues in the city: schools and local development.

headline: Democrats benefited from Goldwater in York
abstract: PA Rep. Steven Nickol remembers volunteering on Sen. Barry Goldwater's campaign for president in 1964. Goldwater died Friday. That year, York residents voted for a democrat, the only time between 1952 and 1998 that Republicans lost the county. Chairman of the county Republican committee John Thompson remembers the party took a beating in York that year.

headline: Mellow solicited for U.S. House seat
abstract: PA Senator Robert Mellow was contacted by U.S. Representative Dick Gephardt to try to encourage him to run to replace U.S. Representative Joe McDade. Gephardt is searching for a Democrat to challenge the rumored Republican candidate, Scranton Mayor Jimmy Connors. Mellow said that his focus right now is on recruiting Democrats to run for PA Senate; though he has not closed the door on running for federal office.

headline: The Gang of Five: What it means for its members and what its members say it means
abstract: US Rep. John Perzel said his most recent political involvement is due to his strong belief in the value of what he is fighting for. US Rep. Dwight Evans says his impetus is that something is wrong and needs to be fixed. Us Rep. John Taylor says his only agenda is to get things done! US Rep. Anthony Williams says his involvement in the Gang of Five is due to his reputation for getting straight answers from House leadership and the Governor. US Rep. George Kenney says his satisfaction is derived from getting things done.

headline: What can be done
abstract: The editorial begins by describing the recent sermon of Reverend Jody Silliker, whose volunteer work has exposed her to many families and small children that suffer from extreme hunger. The authors of the editorial agree with Silliker that more needs to be done to help the nation’s starving children, and they offer several suggestions, including the expansion of the federal food stamp program and school breakfast programs. In addition, the authors criticize the 1998 federal budget for reducing food allotments to soup kitchens and food pantries, and they ask people to support food charities year round, rather than just at Thanksgiving and Christmas.

headline: Chidren's may bid for one hospital
abstract: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia took its first formal step toward a possible bid to acquire the most attractive hospital in the financially wounded Allegheny health system. Children's filed a notice with U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Pittsburgh in which it indicated a serious interest in buying St. Christopher's Hospital for Children. The Pennsylvania attorney general has moved to become an unsecured creditor in the Allegheny bankruptcy, seeking to recover charitable assets apparently spent in an attempt to avoid financial collpase.

headline: Charter schools gain some acceptance
abstract: Since Governor Tom Ridge signed the charter school bill into law a year ago, six charter schools have opened, twenty-six will open in the fall and three more will open next year; however, the law is very ambiguous in many ways, which has caused disputes and uncertainty. Charter schools can set their own agendas and operate free from state regulation, but they must be approved by local school districts. As part of the negotiation process to pass the law with the PA School Boards Association, Ridge agreed to wait two years to put in an appeals board, and PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola is working on an appeal board now, which should help solve some disputes and clear up many uncertainties in the future.

headline: Game Commission expected to increase doe licenses in '98
abstract: Deer hunters across the state, and especially in Luzerne County, did very well in the 1997 season according to the Pennsylvania Game Commission.  But PGC biologists feel the deer herds are still 40 percent above habitat ability to support them; therefore the commission wants to increase doe licenses by 158,000 over last year's allotment.  Statewide, hunters harvested 400,000 deer during the 1997 season, an increase of 13 percent over 1996, a 10-year low harvest total.

headline: How democracy should work
abstract: Editors believe democracy means that people have the right to protest an effort to change plans imposed on them by the government if they do not like them. A plan to close Route 501 for construction on Route 30 was devised after the PA Department of Transportation and contractor Balfour Beatty blamed one another for delays. PA Sen. Gibson Armstrong and Rep. John Barley developed the plan without consulting the people or the local government. After hearing complaints, PennDOT revised its plans. Editors believe if PennDOT keeps the lines of communication open, more conflict will be avoided.

headline: Child abuse reports decrease in county
abstract: Fayette, Greene, and Washinton Counties in PA show significant statistical decrease in child abuse reports.

headline: Attend conference
abstract: The photo depicts Governor Tom Ridge with Beth Bamberger, administrative assistant for the Warren-Forest Area Agency on Aging, and Peter Carnovale, the agency’s executive director, at the Governor’s Conference on Aging Issues in Hershey. Ridge was the main speaker at the event, and he said PA is completely committed to assisting the state’s senior citizens.

headline: Farming Locally, Thinking Globally
abstract: When Senator Chuck Hagel visited the TL Irrigation Co. here, the big topic was an impending shopping trip by a delegation from China. A reporter from a local television station wanted to know about Asia's financial turmoil. What about funding for the International Monetary Fund, a manufacturer of cattle watering troughs asked Hagel over hot turkey sandwiches at a Lions Club lunch at the OK Café. He was asked about almost everything before he left. Republicans are fighting isolationism as trade booms.

headline: Despite Healthy State, Maryland Governor Struggles to Gain Foothold
abstract: The good times are rolling in Maryland, but the strong economy may not be enough to get the Governor re-elected. Governor Parris Glendening is struggling to project an image that voters will support according to a survey recently given. His opponents are also hitting hard even though he has had a successful term.

headline: Michele Ridge to speak in Erie
abstract: Governor Ridge’s wife, Michele, will be the speaker at an Erie Kiwanis Club meeting and is expected to speak about what it’s like being the wife of a governor.

headline: The Gingrich game: Stand-up lawmakers keep throwing themselves in front of Speaker's volleys at campaign reform
abstract: According to the editorial, House Speaker Newt Gingrich’s attempts to kill campaign finance reform by introducing amendments to the Shays-Meehan bill are failing because the House keeps rejecting them. The authors criticize local Republicans Joseph Pitts, Curt Weldon and Christopher Smith for voting in favor of the latest amendment to weaken the bill. The Shays-Meehan bill would prevent parties from accepting unlimited contributions from special interests, and the authors of the editorial commend four regional Democrats and four Republicans, including Pennsylvania’s Jon Fox and Jim Greenwood, for supporting the bill.

headline: WIC program expands
abstract: More families will qualify for federal WIC programs under the new changes in household income limits.

headline: Children's Health Program
abstract: No child should be without health insurance.  Yet the reality is that there are some 330,000 uninsured children in the state, according to Pennsylvania Partnerships for Children.  In June, the legislature passed a measure that expands the Children's Health Insurance Program to benefit an additional 122,000 children.

headline: Charter schools on a learning curve
abstract: Two Philadelphia charter schools, which are publicly funded but privately operated, recently ran into some problems. The authors believe these problems were to be expected, and they highlight the complexity of running a school. West Oak Lane Charter had a number of different problems, but they were ultimately resolved, and there is still a waiting list of 200 to get in.

headline: Game Commission keeping a close ear on grouse population
abstract: The type of land that is suitable for the ruffed grouse has been disappearing along much of the eastern part of the U.S., which has caused their population to dwindle. Since 1975, the PA Game Commission has been maintaining a habitat conducive for grouse, and their numbers grew substantially; however, in the past two years the grouse population unexpectedly began dropping again. It is difficult to explain why the population dropped and how to reverse it, but Bill Palmer, a biologist for the Game Commission, is recommending the habitat remain closed to hunting for at least 15 more years to allow more extensive studies.

headline: I-81, PennDOT both need help to improve
abstract: Public Opinion is upset that it has taken so long for PA Department of Transportation to improve I-81 between Exit 8 and the Cumberland County line. The Public Opinion wants stat officials and PennDOT to start adressing the issue sooner rather then later.

headline: Child Welfare, adoption reform bills ready for co-sponsers
abstract: State lawmakers seek sponsers for a bill to constructed to reform the current PA laws regarding child welfare in adoptions and foster care systems.

headline: Attention sports enthusiasts: Social Security number now required for 1998-1999 state hunting licenses
abstract: The federal government passed a number of laws that require a person applying for any recreational license, such as hunting or fishing licenses, to provide their Social Security information, so they can track down parents who fail to pay child support. PA Representative Sam Smith, who wrote the opinion piece, believes it is an intrusive policy, but despite his objections, the General Assembly passed legislation that requires the state Game and Fish Commissions to obtain the information due to threats from the federal government of denying over $800 million in funds. Smith doesn’t believe that the practice will actually track down parents who owe child support, and the Game Commission, at this moment, will not require social security information if all other information is given.

headline: Financial venture to aid city residents - Credit union hopes for site near enterprise zone
abstract: The Greater Harrisburg Credit Union should open sometime later this year, and it is expected to primarily serve small businesses and individuals with low income to help them with financial services and obtaining loans. Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed said one of the most challenging aspects of poverty is that many people don’t have access to financial services, so the credit union will help serve an "underserved need" of the city. The credit union’s task force has about $60,000 of the $110,000 needed for anticipated start up costs, and U.S. Senator Rick Santorum and several local authorities have already pledged to deposit funds in the bank.

headline: Conti has no problem with write-in
abstract: PA Senator Joe Conti said that he has no problem with Democrat Kathie Brown getting the required 500 write in votes to run against him in the general election. Brown said she would use the write in campaign to find out the concerns of Bucks County; though some of her major concerns would be reforming public education and managing growth. As of now, Conti has no challenger in the Republican primary or the general election, and Bucks County Democratic Chairman John Murray supported Brown and didn’t want to just give Conti the election.

headline: Minor parties gaining members
abstract: 8.5% of voters are turning to thrid partiea and away from Democrats and Republicans. The trend of third party voters is said to be growing and anticipated to continue.

headline: The online Legislature is overdue
abstract: Through the state department's website, www.state.pa.us, you can get tax forms, driver and vehicle information, stat budget data, links to state agencies and departments, even travel and tourism tips, but you cannot find out what the representatives are doing themselves. The paper believes in more transparency for elected officials.

headline: Yes, a Surplus Would Help but Tough Choices Remain
abstract: Applying projected budget surpluses to the financial problems of Social Security could help make fixing the retirement system easier the Washington has feared, but would not eliminate the need for politically excruciating choices, White House officials and members of both parties said. Congress would still have to wrestle with raising taxes, cutting benefits, increasing the retirement age or making other unpopular decisions to shore up Social Security.

headline: CHIPping away to insure county children
abstract: For about 8,000 children in York County seeing a doctor just isn't that simple.  Their parents have no health insurance and can't afford to take them to the doctor for every cough or sniffle.  Many of those 8,000 children would qualify for either Medical Assistance or the Pennsylvania Children's Health Insurance Program, local experts believe.  In June, Gov. Tom Ridge raised the income and age limits for CHIP, making more families eligible.

headline: Classroom certification considered
abstract: A new certificate program could help professionals, to teach K-12 grade without having to have a degree in education. The program would help to get quality teachers in the classroom and fill a need for teaching positions.

headline: Game Commission makes poor decision on anterless licenses
abstract: Given the high level of public interest in our white-tailed deer, the Pennsylvania Game Commission staff devotes a good portion of the nearly $10 million it spends on wildlife management and information and education each year to putting together and promoting public understanding of a scientific deer management plan.  Gov. Tom Ridge appointed George Venesky of Luzerne County to fill a vacancy on the eight -member commission, and the state senate confirmed that appointment last month.  At the summer meeting July 13-14 in Harrisburg, Venesky was one of four commissioners who voted against a proposal to allow hunters to purchase two anterless deer licenses in 1998.

headline: I-83 spilt at Route 581 lands on HATS study list
abstract: The Transportation Improvement Program had several amendments added to it, inclduing studies on I-83 split at Route 581 and cost sharing plans with HATS and Amtrak.

headline: City case against gunmakers gets ammo
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell is still weighing the chances of success for a lawsuit against gun manufacturers; however, a key member of his legal team that is preparing a city lawsuit resigned and said the city has a strong case. Attorney David Kairys refused to give many details, but he did say gun manufacturers knowingly produce, market and distribute significantly more handguns than they expect to sell to law-abiding citizens, which creates a public nuisance by flooding the market with guns for criminals. A member of the PA Federation of Sportsmans’ Clubs said Kairys is wrong, and gun sales have been federally regulated since 1968.

headline: Bill puts day care workers under microscope
abstract: PA Representative Robert Godshall sponsored a bill that would provide much greater regulation over day care providers, but the legislation may not be passed before the summer recess if lawmakers can’t find an agreement over a controversial provision in the bill. That provision would require employees of small day care centers responsible for the care of three or fewer children to undergo criminal background and child-abuse checks. The state Department of Public Welfare opposes the provision, and the Ridge administration backs an amendment to allow self-certification.

headline: Fire companies stand to benefit from proposed law
abstract: A bill passed the PA House of Representative and is awaiting the Senate’s vote that would give local fire companies more options to raise money. The bill would increase the number of available temporary alcohol permits and would also give organizations an entire year, rather than the current 90 day time frame, to take advantage of the permits. Representatives from the Freeland Fire Company and Butler Township Fire Company agreed that events where alcohol is served are the most profitable, and they are hopeful that the law will be approved because it will make their fundraising efforts much easier.

headline: Corlazzi says he's ready to upset the apple cart
abstract: Joseph Corlazzoli said he's fed up with the waste, unfairness, and unresponsiveness in all levels of government today. And he speaks from first hand experience. His experiences with the IRS, Children and Youth Services, and the local sewage authority and other governmental agencies prompted him to run for office to fix things.

headline: Mitman has promise: Facing fellow novice Steve Samuelson, the GOP hopeful has business savvy
abstract: The authors of the editorial are disappointed that another representative for the 135th State House District, PA Representative Lisa Boscola, is running for the state Senate because she is beginning to yield some influence, and both her potential successors are political novices. They, however, give the newspaper’s endorsement to Republican Mark Mitman over Democrat Steve Samuelson because they believe Mitman can communicate his positions better, knows how the government can promote business growth and has a better potential for the future. Both candidates views on abortion, how to spend the state’s budget surplus and the educational system are also described in the article.

headline: Toomey bucks national trend: Inside sources say Roy Afflerbach was out-hustled and out-campaigned
abstract: Republican Pat Toomey defeated Roy Afflerbach surprisingly handily for a seat in the U.S. House as the representative of the 15th Congressional District, which has about 16,000 more registered Democrats than Republicans. Afflerbach’s campaign manager, Kevin Geary, attributed the loss to three main factors, including a disadvantage in funding, but other Democrats said that Afflerbach simply didn’t work as hard as Toomey to reach out to voters, while others claimed the campaign was mismanaged by Geary. Afflerbach is unsure of what he will do in the future but said his biggest regret was not emphasizing his accomplishments in the state Legislature.

headline: $2.5 million grant earmarked for Logan, Allegheny townships
abstract: U.S. Representative Bud Shuster announced an additional $2.5 million in federal grants would be given to the Altoona region for sewer and water infrastructure improvements. Altoona received $3 million last year, and Shuster said the funds will help facilitate the construction of the new convention center and will allow development in several surrounding areas.

headline: Choice, affordability key to health reform
abstract: Republican U.S. Senator Rick Santorum, who represents PA, is writing this letter to garner support for the Republican Task Force’s version of the "Patients’ Bill of Rights," which he claims offers accessibility, affordability and individual choice. He claims that medical savings accounts, which allow people to buy insurance policies to set aside tax-free money, will help increase the number of insured Americans. He also discusses a proposal which would create an internal and independent external review process that would handle grievances, he says the proposal is not intended to interfere with state regulations, and he criticizes the Democrat’s version of the bill

headline: Clinton supports Fattah's education bill
abstract: President Clinton gave support to U.S. Representative Chaka Fattah’s 21st Century Scholars Act of 1997 in his State of the Union Address. Fattah is hopeful that he will be able to pass the bill, which calls for students in areas with high poverty and dropout rates to be notified that if they stay in school and achieve the necessary grades, they will be guaranteed to receive the Pell Grant to pay for them to go to college. Fattah pointed to statistical evidence that shows students are much more likely to achieve success if they are notified about incentives such as the prospect of a paid education in the future.

headline: Game Commission president faces investigation
abstract: Don Elder, a sportsmen’s advocate, accused PA Game Commission President George Miller of illegally using a driveway on state gamelands, illegally using state equipment and using his position as a board member to make land transactions with groups he had a personal interest in. The agency’s northwest regional director, H.L. Harshaw, filed a report to Executive Director Don Madl, who sent the report to the governor’s office, where it ultimately was submitted to the state Ethics Commission for an investigation. While admitting to making two mistakes, Miller denied the accusations and accused Harshaw of feeding information to Elder, while on the other hand, Harshaw said he had nothing to gain from feeding information, and he claimed Madl knew about the problems Miller faced last year, which Madl denied.

headline: I-95 in Philly also targeted in House Bill
abstract: A bill funding imporvemnts for Conchester highway also includes funding for improvements of I-95.

headline: City considers suit citing guns as a nuisance
abstract: Lawyers for Mayor Rendell have prepared a lawsuit that would try to force the nation’s gun makers to reimburse the city of Philadelphia for costs incurred by the city due to gun use, but Rendell must decide whether he wants to invest an estimated $1 million to take the lawsuit to court, which could have major political ramifications if he chooses to run for governor in 2002. Gun crimes have been a major problem in Philadelphia, with 80 percent of the city’s 420 homicide victims killed by guns, but gun makers have denied responsibility and are trying to convince Rendell not to file the lawsuit. Previous lawsuits claiming gun-makers should pay costs under product-liability laws have repeatedly been shot down by courts; however, the new lawsuit would contend that guns have created a public nuisance.

headline: Blowing the lid off fraud - City grand jury investigates food-stamp trafficking
abstract: A Philadelphia grand jury investigation has led to 11 arrests of workers at four businesses for purchasing food stamps at a discounted price in order to redeem them later at full value. According to the Welfare Reform Act of 1996, all states must distribute food stamp benefits by using electronic debit cards, which is intended to cut down on fraud and eliminate the stigma of using food stamps.

headline: First Union, First Fidelity
abstract: Following mergers, First Union and its predecessors closed branches in low-income neighborhoods. They opened new branches mostly in wealthier ones.

headline: Costs rose 5.2% here for workers' health benefits
abstract: According to an annual study done by Mercer/Foster Higgins, the cost of health benefits for workers in the Philadelphia area rose by 5.2 percent in 1997, the second biggest increase of any city in the country. Roel Hoekstra, a consultant for Mercer, said this could be attributed to the fact that most employers in the region had already shifted employees to some type of managed care programs, which left few options for saving money. The study also found that national costs will likely rise between 5 and 7 percent, which will likely be caused by a national migration toward managed care policies; especially policies that are more expensive because they offer choice, and Hoekstra predicted that coverage for retired workers would be one of the biggest future challenges.

headline: Money flows to Specter, despite his huge lead   In a lopsided race, contributions are more about lobbying than electing, watchdog groups say.
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter has now raised his campaign funds to $6.3 million even though his challenger in the upcoming election, PA Representative Bill Lloyd, has only raised a couple thousand dollars, and several political watchdog groups said the money Specter received was more about lobbying than it was about getting him elected. Specter recently received contributions during a visit to Puerto Rico, which could be explained because of his role as the chairman of the Veterans Affairs Committee, and Specter’s positions a member of the Judiciary Committee and as chairman of an appropriations committee that handles many federal health care funding could explain why many of his top contributors gave him money, including bankers, chiropractors, hospitals, lawyers and the health care industry. His record shows he has voted against some of his big campaign contributors in the past, and the article examines his voting record in a number of different areas.

headline: They didn't improve my life
abstract: Larry Hicks talks about the General Assembly and what it has not accomplished during the 1998 session.

headline: 2 mortgage lenders join forces to provide low-interest loans to first time home buyers
abstract: The large amount of money needed up front when purchasing a new home has always been a major deterrent for people interested in home ownership.  Now, two major government sponsored mortgage assistance providers are joining forces to help low and middle income residents purchase their first home.  Congressman Paul Kanjorski was on hand for Wednesday's announcement that assistance programs from Fannie Mae and the Federal Home Loan Bank of Pittsburgh could now be combined to make ownership possible for a larger segment of the population.

headline: Concern over hantavirus growing
abstract: Two deaths in PA in the last 13 months have been attributed to the hantavirus, which is an often fatal disease that can be transmitted to humans by direct contact with wild rodents or their saliva, urine or droppings. While the chances of getting hantavirus are very low, health officials still said the public should assume the virus can be found anywhere and take the necessary precautions.

headline: Clinton to Seek Boost in Funds For Education
abstract: President Clinton will propose increasing education spending by $15 billion over the next five years, and he has said the increase won’t affect the balanced budget agreement. The costliest of the five year proposals is a $7.3 billion plan to train more teachers in hopes of reducing class sizes, but billions of other dollars will be spent on increasing school constructions, introducing more technology into schools and informing younger students about college opportunities. Clinton will also call for $200 million in new funding to aid Hispanics, Vice President Gore announced a plan to train more workers in high-tech jobs, Democrats are hoping to take advantage of their support of Clinton’s education proposals for the upcoming election and an increase in the minimum wage is being considered.

headline: Game Commission shoots holes in rifle ban
abstract: A proposal to ban high-powered rifles for deer hunting in 14 counties stalled this week after sportsmen's groups shot down the idea.  The Pennsylvania Game Commission yesterday decided to send the proposed rifle ban to a special committee for further review.  Sportsmen's groups supported the decision, saying the proposed ban was poorly crafted in the first place.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Head on the Hill
abstract: There is a quote from Dr. John Lawrence, the PA Medical Society President, who is urging the governor to veto a bill that would repeal the state’s law requiring motorcyclists to wear a helmet.

headline: City's gun czar backs News' campaign
abstract: When it comes to gun violence, Deputy Mayor Richard Zappile is looking for a lockdown.  As the Daily News launches its campaign against gun violence today with the distribution of free gunlocks, Zappile applauded the program.  The devices work much like the Club on car steering wheels, immobilizing the gun's bolt, cylinder or slide.

headline: Boon or bust: Any left for us?
abstract: Most parents of baby boomers like the Social Security program and want it to continue for later generations. However, because so many more people will be retiring in the coming years, concerns have arisen that social security will run out. By 2012, what is paid in to social security will not equal what is paid out. Analysts estimate that by 2029, reserves will be depleted and payment problems will arise. The American Association of Retired Persons is plead the president is attempting to keep the system financially sound. Seniors now have the option of electronically deposited Social Security checks.

headline: First Union-CoreStates merger critics get deals
abstract: The Senator and the plumber, the factory owner and the graphic artist, all are getting their say today in an unusual Federal Reserve public meeting on First Union Corp's plan to absorb Philadelphia's CoreStates Financial Corp in the most expensive bank merger ever. Part direct directory, part interest-group politics, the hearing follows four months of complaints groups about the loss of CoreStates, the area's biggest private employer, leading lender and most generous corporate contributor to charity. The Fed this week published a list of the witnesses who will be testifying.

headline: Counting on Congress
abstract: Philadelphia Inquirer talks abou the large number of people not counted in the 1990 census, and argues that lawmakers should find a solution so that all residents are accounted for in 2000.

headline: More than governor's race rides on election outcome
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is all but assured of winning reelection this year, and the biggest question has become whether he will win big enough to put himself in a good position to be considered as a potential vice presidential candidate on the Republican ticket in two years. It remains unknown what his margin of victory will be over candidates Ivan Itkin and Peg Luksik and how big of a win would be needed to put himself in an advantageous position, but most political analysts agree that winning with less than 50% of the popular vote would be a serious setback. Pennsylvania’s role as a "swing" state could help Ridge’s cause, while his future will also rely heavily on who wins the Republican presidential nomination, which is still a big question mark.

headline: They Sally forth, Mark every Matt
abstract: The author critiques the campaign signs of candidates Mark McNaugthon, Sally Klein and Matt Napiltonia, who are seeking the Republican nomination to run for the 104th PA House seat. She also writes about the governor for giving the Whitaker Center in Harrisburg $3 million, which she claims should please voters and represents an ambitious goal to draw 500,000 people a year to the center. She also claims that times have changed since people applauded in support of McNaughton while he cried during a rally when recalling the death of his 4-year old son.

headline: An unlikely team scores for the city - The mayor and governor sold selection officials.
abstract: Republican Governor Tom Ridge and Democratic Mayor Ed Rendell worked together to convince the Republican Party to hold its 2000 National Convention in Philadelphia. Despite differences in political orientation, the two have worked together on numerous occasions to deliver results, while they’ve still been able to hold on to their own political identities. There have been many issues in which the two hold opposing viewpoints, yet they seem to have a mutual respect for one another that has allowed them to work together effectively.

headline: Condom access shows no effect on teen sex rate
abstract: Researchers surveyed 1,945 students at a high school in Los Angeles, and they compared the students’ responses to questionnaires about sexual behavior before and after a program was put into place to make condoms available at school. The results found students were no more likely to engage in sexual behavior, but the use of condoms by sexually active teens increased. Previous studies yielded similar results in New York, Philadelphia and Seattle, but some people still claim condom programs send the wrong message to teens.

headline: Coalition responds to restructuring report
abstract: The Philadelphia Coalition for Education Reform and School Choice came out in favor of a report released by the PA House’s Urban Education Commission that called for more school choice. While the coalition disagrees on some details, it is in favor of providing school vouchers to help parents send their children to private schools, and William Palmer, an education advocate, said too many people are wrong in assuming that the Black community opposes school choice because it is minorities who suffer the most in public schools. State Education Secretary Eugene Hickok and the Ridge administration favor school choice programs, and Representatives Dwight Evans, John Perzel and Anthony Hardy Williams were all involved with the commission.

headline: Game Commission to act on new hunting proposals
abstract: Starting Sunday and continuing through Tuesday, the Game Commission will hold its spring meeting at the Riveredge Motel and Conference Center near Reading.  At this meeting the proposed 1998-99 hunting and furtaker seasons and bag limits, along with anterless deer license allocations, will be acted upon by commissioners.  The proposed allocation for Schuylkill County is 17,900 anterless deer. This is up from last year's allocation of 10,000.

headline: Interchange dispute should focus on safety, budget constraints
abstract: Cost and design are big factors in the three-highwat intersection project in Summit Township. Butler Eagles urges PennDOT to and residents to come a consensus on safety and budget issues.

headline: City's most sought-after cameraman
abstract: Gibson Ivery, who videotaped the alleged beating of a suspect by city police officers, made nearly $1,000 by offering the footage to several news stations. However, the footage doesn’t show what led to the incident, so many local television executives have been cautious to put the video into the same category as the Rodney King tape. Channel 17 decided not to air the footage because it lacked context, and Larry Kane, who has been an anchor for 23 years, hopes the public doesn’t jump to conclusions because the Philadelphia Police Department, though not perfect, has handled event crowds effectively for years.

headline: Borski backs social security conference
abstract: US Rep. Robert Borski supports President Clinton's White House Conference on Social Security and is committed to working closely with Congress and the Administration to finding a solution for the future of the program. Growing concern over the financial solvency of the program as baby boomers come of age is leading to serious debate over the future of social security.

headline: Fisher to probe system finances
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher plan to investigate and auit the Allegheny health systems o determine is financial mismangement has occurred.

headline: County Democrats fire up party faithful
abstract: Lancaster County Democrats are getting dupport from their party and believe they have a chance at unseating Govenor Tom Ridge in the next election.

headline: More than governor's race rides on election outcome
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is all but assured victory in his upcoming reelection bid over Democrat Ivan Itkin and third party candidate Peg Luksik, so the real question is whether he will win big enough to boost his credentials for a possible vice presidential nomination in the 2000 election, a position he has expressed interest in. While numerous analysts gave different estimates on the margin of victory needed to put Ridge in a good position, everyone agreed he must at least win 50% of the vote. Ridge’s fate will rest largely on who wins the presidential nomination, but Ridge could be an attractive candidate because PA is considered to be an important swing state.

headline: They're lining up to replace Joe
abstract: Joseph McDade is retiring from congressional office and there are several individuals planning to run for his seat.

headline: and Walker for the GOP
abstract: Republicans seeking a candidate to face Representative Doyle in November have two credible choices in the primary. Both have experience at the local government level that would serve them well. Their differences are less defined by political attitudes than they are by age and experience. Dick walker would abolish the Department of Education and is a fiscal conservative who the paper endorses for the Republican nomination.

headline: Consider organ donations-help save lives
abstract: Since this is National Organ Donor Awareness Week, it is a good time to evaluate how we are doing.  The good news is Pennsylvania is a model for organ donation in the country -- because it requires hospitals to inform donor organizations of an impending or potential death.  Then it is up to the donor organization to approach a family for permission.

headline: Colleges Aim to Control Thinking, but Not Drinking
abstract: Prosecutors had considered bringing charges against the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) over Scott Krueger, a freshman who drank himself to death at a frat that is recognized by the university; however, MIT’s president cited a 1979 decision by the Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The court basically said that universities cannot act in place of parents, and students are responsible for their own decisions, which the author agrees with; however, she cites numerous examples where MIT and other universities did act in place of parents to regulate students’ speech, beliefs and even moral values. She believes the actions of such schools are hypocritical, and she calls on them to stop trying to regulate "the hearts and minds" of students.

headline: Game Commissioner to vote on proposals that have drawn ire from hunters
abstract: Hunters have been voicing opposition to the liberalized seasons and bag limits proposed by the Game Commission. The proposals being considered by the Game Commission include allowing hunters to take two gobblers during the spring gobbler season and junior hunters to take either a buck or doe during the rifle deer season. Other proposals would increase hunting hours, permit the use of underwater snares for beavers, add two weeks to the general small game season, and extend the late season on rabbits and squirrels.

headline: Intersection now safer?
abstract: The York Dispatch praises PennDOT for putting a four way stop at the inersection of Route 177 and 382.

headline: Clearfield County looking for ways to collect housing costs from inmates
abstract: State Act 342, a state law implemented in July, 1996 that is meant to teach inmates responsibility, mandates inmates who are incarcerated for more than 3 days should be charged at least $10 a day for room and board. Clearfield County Prison Warden Sam Lombardo is considering adding these costs on top of existing fines and costs, which would allow Clearfield County to collect over $640,000 without needing to add a new position or use the services of a collection agency. In other prison news, Greg Collin was promoted to become the new work release coordinator for Clearfield County Prison, which is a big program that helps employ a third of the prison population for work release programs.

headline: Britain embracing welfare reform
abstract: Britain’s New Deal Program, an important part of Prime Minister Tony Blair’s overhaul of the nation’s welfare system, has been operating in Swansea, Wales and 11 other areas on a three month trial basis. Though the program differs from the American approach, both welfare systems operate on the principle of trying to get people off of the nation’s welfare system. Britain’s program targets 18-24-year-olds by providing them with personal advisers to help them obtain employment, and the program is significantly less harsh than programs in the United States, where a 1996 welfare reform law set a five-year lifetime time limit for government assistance and requires recipients to work.

headline: Former AGH leader's home on market for $1.375 million
abstract: The palatial Sewickley Heights home of Sheriff Abdelhak, the ousted chief executive officer of Allegheny Health, Education, and Research Foundation, has been put on the market for $1.375 million.  Abdelhak was replaced as the foundation's chief executive officer in June by Anthony Sanzo, his longtime lieutenant.  The foundation, the parent of Allegheny General Hospital, filed for bankruptcy in July, staggering under $1.3 billion in debt.

headline: County GOP Endorses All Local Candidates
abstract: The Dauphin County Republican Committee held its annual meeting to endorse candidates before the upcoming primary, and they endorsed U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, U.S. Representative George Gekas and PA Representatives Ron Marsico, Frank Tulli Jr. and Peter Zug for reelection. The committee also endorsed Representative Mark McNaughton over Dauphin County Commissioner Sally Klein despite a court decision that recently went against McNaughton. Klein vowed to continue her campaign and has criticized the committee’s chairman, Bob Dick, of intimidating committee members into voting for McNaughton.

headline: More than governor's race rides on election outcome
abstract: It is more and more certain that the eyes of the political world will be trained on Gov. Tom Ridge Nov. 3 to determine if the Republican chief-executive has the strength the muscle his way onto the GOP national ticket in 2000.  The question is not whether he wins or looses the upcoming gubernatorial election --a victory over rivals Ivan Itkin and Peg Luksik is all but certain-- but the margin of his victory. Most political analysts believe that Ridge needs at least  55 percent of the popular vote to be considered for the vice presidential nomination.

headline: They're working for us
abstract: Opinion piece about how the author is proud of how the PA Legislature is handling the budget surplus. She loves the idea of working on tax reform. Small businesses could really use the help.

headline: Another big raise for lawmakers?
abstract: According to the editorial, Congress gave itself a $3,072 pay raise a year ago, and there was no public outcry. However, sources are saying that U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich has contacted senior members from both parties about another pay raise of $3,554 to compensate for cost of living adjustments, and President Clinton gave his support. The authors of the editorial think it’s ridiculous for Congressmen to seek a pay raise for cost of living adjustments when they already make $140,000 a year, plus benefits.

headline: Could board members have saved AHERF?   Attending parties is often nonprofit directors' main job
abstract: The Allegheny Health Education and Research Foundation (AHERF) has filed for bankruptcy, and many people are wondering what the foundation’s board members knew and if they could have done anything to avert the financial crisis. Some people have blamed the board’s failure to act, or its ignorance of the impending crisis, on "social appointments," where many nonprofit board members are often chosen from prominent lawyers, bankers and business executives who have other responsibilities that prevent them from dedicating much time to overseeing the organization and keeping it out of trouble. For the most part, board members from AHERF have refused to comment, and people in the article compared the responsibilities of board members of for-profit companies against those of nonprofit organizations.

headline: Committee makes very few substantive changes to proposed academic standards
abstract: A committee of the PA Board of Education made very few changes to new academic standards under which all public school students would be required to learn. Earlier this month, legislators and others submitted a flurry of suggestions on the new rules for reading, writing, and math that the board passed in April. The standards are designed to replace the controversial Outcome-Based Education, which had been cicatrized for being too vague.

headline: Game commissioner was outside line of duties
abstract: The conviction of a Venago County man on a drunken driving charge has been overturned because a state game commission agent overstepped his authority, a state appellate court has ruled.  Superior Court Judge Joseph Hudock ordered the case returned to Butler County, where Brent Carlson of Kennerdell had been arrested Oct. 14, 1995.  District Attorney Tim McCune said Monday that his office will not retry the nor will any further appeals be filed by his office.

headline: It's a go: Route 202 expansion gets green light
abstract: Route 202 bypass project has been approved and is scheduled to be constructed in an effort to reduce traffic congestion. Opponents of the expansion are worried the highway will increase development in the area and bring about even more traffic.

headline: Clinton's Legal Team Awaits the Public's Response to His Risky Political Gamble
abstract: President Clinton testified before a grand jury that he didn’t lie during the Paula Jones lawsuit by denying a sexual relationship with Monica Lewinski because he didn’t believe the "intimate" contact he had with Lewinski fit the lawyers’ definition of a sexual relationship, which allowed him to avoid admitting to lying under oath. Kenneth Starr released a report on his investigation into Clinton, and the White House and other critics claimed the report was so filled with embarrassing sexual details that were unnecessary and intended to damage the President politically. However, Starr said Clinton’s attempts to hide behind legal interpretations of a sexual relationship forced him to include many sexual details to prove he had lied under oath and obstructed justice.

headline: Child care proposal keys drive to capital
abstract: Philadelphia mothers, and college students, went to Harrisburg to present Gov. Tom Ridge with a petition against the parent co-pay for welfare day care.

headline: Good deals for good drivers
abstract: If you have a clean driving record, you might consider shopping around for a new insurance policy.  Some local insurance agencies say good drivers stand to save the most from insurance providers' recent good fortune.  Fewer accidents and safer cars have helped slow cost increases on some auto insurance policies and have brought about decreases in others, say state Department of Insurance officials and a spokesman from the country's largest auto insurance provider.

headline: County Republican Committee hold February meeting
abstract: The Bradford County Republican Committee met and was called to order by chairman Matthew Brann, who recommended the committee follow suit with the State Committee and endorse Governor Tom Ridge, Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter for reelection. Brann also discussed the retirement of U.S. Representative Joseph McDade and recommended the committee hold another meeting to interview candidates to replace him in the 10th Congressional District. State Representatives Scot Chadwick and Matthew Baker will seek reelection, and some other details were discussed during the meeting.

headline: Morganelli is supporting Pa. governor
abstract: Northampton County District Attorney John Morganelli, one of the county’s leading Democrats, went to Governor Ridge’s kickoff campaign because he supports Ridge’s bid for reelection. He said he would vote for anybody who is pro-law enforcement, and he claimed Ridge passed more crime legislation in two years than former Governor Casey did in his entire eight years. He acknowledged he has a good relationship with Ridge and said he was glad Democratic State Chairman Mark Singel resigned because the party is in shambles.

headline: Third GOP candidate to run for Waugh's House seat
abstract: Joyce Keesey will formally announce that she will be running for the 93rd District seat in the PA House, joining two fellow Republicans, Ronal Miller and Barb Metzler, as well as the only Democrat to declare as of now, Jeffrey Sanders. The seat is open because of Representative Mike Waugh’s decision to run for the state senate. Waugh will battle Tom Skehan for the Republican nomination for the 28th Senatorial District seat and would likely face Jackie Kramer if he manages to win the primary.

headline: Anti-abortions license tasks OK'd
abstract: Florida lawmakers give the okay for a license tag to display a choose life abortion message. The money collected from these speciality plates would go to services for needy mothers and adoption services.

headline: County hiring practices prhibited
abstract: Childre Youth and faily agency and Mental Health/Mental Retardation agency are investgated for violating state-mandated procedure for hiring practices.

headline: Community Voices - 22 districts for the city?
abstract: A proposal was recently made by the PA House Legislative Commission on Restructuring Pennsylvania’s Urban Schools to divide the Philadelphia School District into 22 smaller districts that would each have their own elected school board officials. School District Superintendant David Hornbeck opposes the proposal, and the newspaper asked people to write in their opinions, which are printed in the article. Of all 24 responses received, only one person supported the proposal, and many of those who opposed the plan commented on the lack of funding for the district.

headline: Game Commission's spending on radio towers draws criticism
abstract: PA lawmakers are concerned that the PA Game Commission will continue with plans to rebuild its own system of radio towers despite a statewide radio system that is being developed and is already paid for in bonds. The Game Commission has said that it is only making upgrades to its system and will transfer to the statewide system when it’s ready, but Representative David Levdansky is dubious considering the Game Commission built new radio towers that don’t meet statewide standards and cannot be used as part of the network. Some officials believe the Game Commission is trying to protect its status as an independent agency, but Senator Edward Helfrick doesn’t see any threat and believes the agency’s actions will only cost hunters money.

headline: It's full speed ahead for new light-rail line
abstract: The New Jersey Department of Transportation included about $48 million in the capital budget, which is expected to be approved by the state Legislature in July, towards the controversial $450 million construction of a new state-of-the-art light-rail line that will connect Trenton to Camden and potentially other parts of the state. The New Jersey Transit’s plan has been met with considerable opposition, and while critics have argued there won’t be enough riders to make the system worthwhile, most cities with light-rail passenger lines claim the number of passengers has exceeded expectations.
