The article provides an analysis of several cities’ light-rail transit systems, and despite much criticism, New Jersey’s plan continues to move along.

headline: Clone debate: Science vs. morality
abstract: Dr. Richard Seed claims that he can clone humans by the middle of next year for profit by using similar techniques which were used on the cloned sheep nine months ago in Scotland. However, bioethicists, pro-life advocates and theological professors don’t see any moral or medical benefits to cloning, and many experts don’t believe Seed has the expertise to actually clone humans. Critics of Seed pondered how scientists would justify sacrificing hundreds of human embryos for cloning and why cloning a child would be necessary since thousands are awaiting adoption; though some doctors feel that cloning done right would be the same as vitro fertilization.

headline: Child-care changes will aid more families
abstract: PA Senator Harold Mowery Jr., the author of this opinion piece, criticizes a previous editorial for its depiction of new regulations for subsidized child care. While Mowery acknowledges that fewer families will technically be eligible to receive subsidized child care under the regulations, it will actually enable 4,000 additional children to be subsidized because there are currently thousands of eligible children on waiting lists. He claims low-income working families will continue to receive subsidies, but they will simply have to pay larger co-pays, which will allow thousands of less fortunate families to receive subsidized child care and ultimately get off the state’s public assistance.

headline: Hartford cuts PA auto rate
abstract: The Hartford Financial Services Group, one of the nation’s largest insurance providers, reduced automobile insurance premiums in PA by an average of 2.9 percent for customers who purchase their insurance through independent agents. The Hartford has had success with cost containment programs, so it will offer the reductions, as well as ‘Harford Premier,’ a lower priced program for customers with clean driving records. It will also expand eligibility for higher risk drivers, and customers can lock into these new rates for a full year by purchasing an auto policy that can include a number of features.

headline: County Republicans busily jockeying for position   Commissioner race drawing plenty of attention among those in GOP
abstract: The four year terms are set to expire in 18 months for the three incumbent Dauphin County Commissioners, Russell Sheaffer, Sally Klein and Anthony Petrucci, and it unknown which of the three will seek re-election, which has prompted many Republican candidates to consider running. The candidates are evaluating the past Republican House primary when PA Representative Mark McNaughton overwhelmingly defeated Klein and Matt Napiltonia, and important lessons can be learned: to win the Republican nomination for commissioner a candidate must prove they can fund services without increasing taxes and oppose a landfill to appease voters in the north. Important politicians from the region have given their support to different potential candidates, and winning the county committee’s endorsement could be extremely important.

headline: Mrs. Clinton to visit Philadelphia in support of Margolies-Mezvinsky
abstract: First lady Hillary Clinton will visit Philadelphia for several fundraisers, which will include one for lieutenant governor candidate Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky that is expected to raise $200,000.

headline: This reviewer gives Schwanger 2 thumbs down
abstract: David Schwanger's expression looked like that of a little boy on his way to the dentist at a candidates forum, which is not a good way for a candidate to appear. He is in his first race for public office. He was honest about his lack of experience.

headline: Apportionment commission may wait until last minute
abstract: It appears that the four members of the Allegheny County apportionment commission, all white men, will wait until the final day to make their selection of a fifth member for the commission. Meetings for this week were cancelled because two of the members, Joseph Mistick and Edward Zemprelli, decided to privately interview four candidates, all black women, rather than hold public meeting, which had been previously agreed upon. The other two members of the commission, Keith Schmidt and Robert Owsiany, were disappointed and felt their colleagues had reneged on their deal.

headline: Delay urged in privatization of 60 health centers in state
abstract: State Health Secretary Daniel F. Hoffman last week recommended the plan to privatize the state health centers be delayed to allow further evaluation.  Hoffman said his recommendation is consistent with the findings of a report for the Health Department prepared by the University of Pittsburgh Graduate School of Public Health.  That report suggested another year is needed to collect information that would assess the feasibility of privatization, effectiveness, cost and staff preparedness.

headline: Continuing Education for Teachers Not a Bad Idea, Professionals Say
abstract: Proposed legislation requireing teachers to continue their education throughout their career seems to be favorable among professionals. PA is one of only 5 states in the country not requiring teachers to do this.

headline: Got deer meat? It may be illegal
abstract: Rep. Bruce Smith, a York County Republican, said Monday he is introducing a bill allowing hunters to keep venison in there freezers for one year.  Currently, deer meat may be kept frozen only until the end of the license year in which it was taken.  That means venison from the last hunting season must have been disposed of by June 30.

headline: Jobs born as Conrail dies
abstract: CSX and Norfolk Southern are expected to gain final approval to jointly purchase and divide Conrail, which dominated railroads throughout the Northeast for the past two decades. With the breakup of Conrail, CSX and Norfolk Southern will be able to offer direct service between almost every market east of the Mississippi River, and the improved service is expected to bring 1.1 million additional truckloads of cargo to the rail each year. In preparation, the two companies are already hiring 3,100 train crew members, and the Community College of Philadelphia has joined three other schools in offering training programs to help produce workers for these new positions.

headline: Colleges run bars to battle binges Officials try to control drinking by keeping it on school grounds
abstract: Since 1996, there have been a number of deaths linked to binge drinking at colleges, and a national survey found that 42 percent of college students had engaged in binge drinking, which constitutes having five or more drinks in a row, within two weeks of the survey. While many colleges have responded by enforcing stricter penalties and bans on alcohol consumption at school functions, others have responded by creating bars run by the colleges. Proponents of the idea argue that college drinking cannot be stopped altogether, so the college run bars could offer a way to oversee the drinking environment and encourage safe drinking habits.

headline: Children's rights suit settled by the city
abstract: After a long battle, the ACLU preveils in court, granting the public the right to know how DHS is serving the children and the public.

headline: High stakes for mutual insurers
abstract: After nearly 120 years of friendly competition, two small New Jersey mutual insurance companies are in a Chester County courtroom battling each other in a breakup that has large financial implications for 42,000 policyholders.  Millions more policyholders in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and throughout the nation also could be affected as more mutual insurers attempt to reorganize as publicly traded companies.  That's what Mercer Mutual Insurance Co. wants to do.

headline: County split on Ridge
abstract: After four years under PA Governor Tom Ridge, there is general agreement among business leaders and law enforcement officials that life in Montgomery County is better now than when he took office. Others would not agree. He seems to have only focused on the economic side of governing and not the human side.

headline: Mundy coasts to 5th term in 120th District
abstract: Phyllis Mundy was re-elected by a significant margin over Bill James to win her fifth term as the 120th District’s representative in the PA House. Mundy commended James for running an issue-oriented campaign when she defeated him two years ago; however, this time was different. James made several controversial accusations against Mundy, and Mundy was able to raise a lot more money.

headline: Ticket-splitting, backlash propelled Hoeffel
abstract: Joseph Hoeffel defeated Jon Fox for the U.S. Representative seat. Fox's handleing of the impeachment rrial and republican party issued seemed to sway voters against Fox.

headline: Appropriations the plum: Candidates want seat on critical committee
abstract: During a debate at the University of Scranton, Democrat Pat Casey, Republican Don Sherwood and Reform Party candidate Tom McLaughlin, who are all running for the 10th District seat in the U.S. House, all said they would, given the choice, select the Appropriations Committee as their committee assignment if elected. U.S. Representative Joseph McDade is retiring after 18 terms representing the 10th District, and he was able to secure millions of dollars for the district thanks to his position as the senior Republican on the Appropriations Committee. The candidates also debated the issue of Social Security, and this was the last debate before the election.

headline: Delayed investigation of nursing home death feeds criticism of agency
abstract: PA Auditor General Bob Casey has released two audits since March that criticize the state Health Department for delays in investigating complaints at nursing homes and for enforcing weak sanctions for violations. He cited an example where the Health Department waited 101 days to launch an investigation into a 90-year-old woman with broken bones, but since then, Health Department Secretary Daniel Hoffman ordered the department to begin all investigations within two days of receiving a complaint. Casey also cited poor oversight because his audit found the number of sanctions imposed by the Health Department has been decreasing while nursing homes have grown in numbers.

headline: Convicted former solicitor owes money to school districts
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. told 33 PA vocational schools and school districts, including West Shore, Harrisburg and Susquehanna Township, that they are entitled to nearly $60,000 from Charles Steele, who was convicted in federal court of padding legal bills between July 1992 and April 1993. Steele overcharged his clients on a number of occasions, and Casey warned the schools that they may have been overcharged at other times which weren’t part of the investigation. West Shore and Susquehanna Township schools have already filed their claims for reimbursement.

headline: INSIDE THE CAPITOL
abstract: Joanne Denworth, president of the PA Environmental Council, is quoted, claiming state agencies should locate facilities downtown to reuse and restore them whenever possible, instead of abandoning them.

headline: Jubelirer wants Route 30 meetings in public
abstract: PA Sen. Robert Jubelirer believes it is essential that meetings to design a 5 lane Route 30 project through Mile Level are public, not closed, as officials with the PA Department of Transportation suggest. Congressman Bud Shuster said he was stunned to hear the meetings might be closed. In Hollidaysburg, closed meetings led to the project being stalled. Eventually, its funding was earmarked elsewhere.

headline: Columbia should get facts before defending agency
abstract: The commissioners of Columbia and Montour counties were asked for comment because the agency has come under fire again from families who are left feeling bruised by their dealings with protective-services officers.  The strong show of support for the agency must certainly have buoyed the morale of the agency staff.  But to the average citizen, the assessment seemed premature and reflexive.

headline: City welfare plan calls for 15,000 jobs - The initiative will provide for training, expanded public transit, and job counselors.
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell will use $55 million from Philadelphia’s share of the federal Welfare-to-Work grant towards his plan that’s aimed at getting 15,000 Philadelphians off public assistance and into jobs over the next two years. The plan, Greater Philadelphia Works, will include at least 40 businesses providing welfare recipients with jobs or training as well as the addition of new transit lines to transport them to job centers, and Rendell hired former CoreStates bank president Rosemarie Greco to head the Private Industry Council, a nonprofit job training agency that will oversee the project. These efforts come in response to new federal and state welfare laws that put time limits on how long a person can receive public assistance, and while Rendell believes his plan is a good start, he thinks Philadelphia needs more federal funding because there simply aren’t enough jobs out there to satisfy all welfare recipients who will lose their benefits.

headline: House bill a victory for credit unions
abstract: Legislation reversing a US Supreme court decision and allowing credit unions to keep growing sailed through the House after weeks of intense lobbying by the 70 million-member industry. The Credit Union Membership Access Act will allow the nearly 800 federally chartered credit unions in PA to continue to serve more than one group in the membership.

headline: Democracy leads to bad art
abstract: Dave Gilmartin talks democracy about Pennsylvania's commemorative coin design choices and the state motto.

headline: Munley picked for federal bench
abstract: President Clinton made the long-awaited much-anticipated nomination of Lackawanna County Judge James M. Munley to the federal bench on Thursday.   Judge Munley, of Archibald, is in line to serve as a U.S. District Court judge in the Middle District of Pennsylvania.  Depending on the calendar, his nomination could come before the Senate Judiciary Committee as early as a month or two from now.

headline: To Debunk Those Dems..
abstract: Newt Gingrich is attacked Democrats for their stance on issues, especially following the Clinton scandal.

headline: Area campaign officials noted
abstract: PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola was named chairman of Dauphin County’s reelection campaign for Governor Tom Ridge and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker. Several co-chairs were also named, and they will all represent the Ridge campaign throughout the county.

headline: Democrats recast physician-general job
abstract: Although it's a medical-advisory post, the job of Pennsylvania physician general continues to radiate charges of political meddling.  The turmoil began last week, after Dr. Wanda Filer of York said interference from the Republican Ridge administration prompted her to abruptly quit as the state's first physician general.  Those arguments spilled over into the state Senate yesterday.

headline: Costs become prohibitive factor at private schools
abstract: Joe Szabo had to take his children out of a private Catholic school because he could no longer afford to send his children there. Costs prohibit many parents from sending their children to private schools, but there is a bill being considered by the Senate education committee that would allow public funded vouchers to be given to parents to help reduce the costs. State Senator Ed Holl and state Representative Robert Godshall support some sort of voucher plan, and the Philadelphia Archdiocese are also calling on vouchers to help parents send their children to Catholic schools in the area.

headline: Governor: nuclear waste not, want not
abstract: Jim Hodges, who is running for Governor of South Carolina in two years, has vowed to prevent out-of-state low level radioactive waste from being accepted at the state’s Barnwell storage facility. The possibility of the site being closed in the future could potentially persuade the Appalachian States Compact, composed of PA and three other bordering states, to renew efforts to build a dump site within the region. Hospitals and other industries that rely on the Barnwell site are especially concerned, and the nuclear power industry is closely monitoring the situation; though they are better prepared to store nuclear waste on site if required.

headline: Kiski expressway dead, StrongLand says - Chamber bases conclusion on Harrisburg visit
abstract: After meeting with top officials from the PA Department of Transportation, StrongLand Chamber of Commerce members concluded that the proposed $125 million Kiski Valley Expressway was dead; however, a spokesman for the department denied that anything like that was said during the meeting. Nonetheless, StrongLand abandoned its support for the Expressway project and joined the Alle-Kiski Coalition, hoping a more regional group could attract more state funding for transportation projects, especially the widening of Route 356. PA Representative Joe Petrarca believes the Expressway project is not only alive, but it would fit perfectly into a long-range plan to create a beltway around Pittsburgh, yet StrongLand will continue to push for the Route 356 project and a more regional approach.

headline: Community group grills city officials
abstract: Philadelphia Interfaith Action had been highly critical of former Police Commissioner Richard Neal for eliminating a successful community policing program. They hosted at event at a Baptist Church to again lobby for the programs, but they were accused of trying to ambush public officials into accepting their demands.

headline: Congress losing focus on child care issues
abstract: Child care for families in PA is a growing problem that needs solutions. Congress should be taking a more active role in low income families with child care needs.

headline: House ready to roll the dice
abstract: Owners of the state's four tracks, including Penn National Race Course, say they continue to lose business to slots at tracks in neighboring states. The state House is poised to vote today on referendums for riverboat casinos, video poker and slot machines at racetracks. However, Governor Tom Ridge did not like some of the specific proposals, and said he would veto the bill.

headline: Democracy needs choices for voters
abstract: Bucks County Courier Times talks about low voter turnout in Bucks County and wonders where third party and Democratic candidiates are, as Republicans are out in full force.

headline: Museum would boost economy
abstract: Steven Kauffman, chairman of Carlisle Area Chamber of Commerce, and Cumberland County Commissioner Earl Keller agreed that if the Carlisle area is chosen as the site of a national U.S. Army museum, it would bring huge economic benefits to the region. PA Representative Al Masland believes the museum could secure the War College’s presence in Carlisle. Masland and Governor Tom Ridge will both try to lobby for the museum, but ultimately, the decision will be up to Congress.

headline: Tobacco Industry Steps Up Flow of Campaign Money   Proposed Settlement Leads to Record Giving Even as Political Opposition Grows
abstract: The tobacco industry gave $4.5 million to Federal candidates and national political parties in 1997, which was the most the industry ever gave in a non-election year, and they have spent over $58 million lobbying the past two years for a bill that would cut smoking rates in return for the industry getting more protection from lawsuits. Despite the increased spending, the bill’s future is still a big question mark, and even the top recipient of campaign contributions, Thomas Wiley, has been critical of the industry, while many Congressmen, including Representative Richard Gephardt, Senator John McCain and Representative Michael Bilirakis, have stopped accepting contributions. Members of the Commerce, Agriculture and Judicial Congressional Committees have received the most in campaign contributions, and Republicans have received more money than Democrats.

headline: Area Lawmakers Give Views on Iraq, Clinton: Legislators United in Support for Troops
abstract: U.S. Congressmen united to support American troops and air strikes in Iraq aimed at weakening its leader, Saddam Hussein; however, they were far from unified in their opinions on whether or not President Clinton should be impeached. Republican Representatives Frank Wolf and Thomas Davis III said they would vote to impeach Clinton because he committed perjury, whereas Democratic Representative Albert Wynn defended Clinton, claiming the impeachment was a result of the Republicans’ hatred of him. Both the Senate and the House remain deeply divided, mostly along party lines; though some moderate Republicans, such as Representative Constance Morella, have yet to make a decision on the issue.

headline: Department of Health
abstract: Political Cartoon on the Department of Health's failure to investigate nurshing home complaints quickly

headline: Countdown to meltdown
abstract: Days after lawmakers passed a bill threatening a takeover of Philadelphia's schools, Superintendent David Hornbeck remains optimistic a compromise can be reached. The business group that administers the school district's funding supports S. 494, supports provisions that may allow reorganization of the district's finances and the removal of restrictions from labor contracts. Hornbeck earlier sued the state for more funding, saying the district could run out by next March. Executive Director John Claypool disagrees with Hornbeck's funding philosophy.

headline: Guv candidate Itkin almost gets trashed
abstract: According to staff for gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin, PA Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) Secretary James Seif was going to throw a bag of trash at Itkin during a speech in which he harshly criticized the agency and Governor Tom Ridge. Ridge had given a speech and called for a three year halt on permits for new landfills, and Itkin gave a speech afterwards where he suggested that the DEP and Ridge were looking kindly on landfill requests in exchange for campaign contributions. Seif’s staff admitted that the secretary had gotten emotional when the integrity of the DEP staff was questioned.

headline: L.V.'s worst highways identified
abstract: The International Roughness Index is being used by PennDOT to test Pennsylvania roads for bumps, surface problems, and additional transportation concerns.

headline: Congress considers 'Aimee's Law'
abstract: The U.S. House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime is considering passing "Aimee’s Law," which would require states that release violent criminals who go on to commit a crime in another state to pay financial restitution for court fees and the victims’ families. The proposed law is in response to Arthur Bomar, who was paroled from Nevada but is now accused of raping and murdering Aimee Willard in PA. U.S. Representative Curt Weldon supports the proposed law, which he claims would hold states accountable for the release of violent criminals.

headline: Direct deposit catches on in Valley
abstract: The US Treasury Department has proposed granting senior citizens the option to receive Social Security through paper checks or electronic deposit. US Rep. John Murtha said the proposed change is expected to be approved soon, with the Social Security Administration to provide more information on direct deposit options and low-cost accounts. Other agencies have not yet decided whether they will follow the same practice. The switch to direct deposit is a result of the government's goal to go paperless in terms of checks, by 1999 with the exception of tax returns.

headline: Industry may have bounced tough bill
abstract: Last year, as bipartisan momentum began building in the legislature to regulate the state's check-cashing industry and cap its unlimited fees, a not-so-curious thing happened. People at the cash-checking companies opened their checkbooks. They focused their money on PA Senator Frank Salvatore who sits on the Senate banking committee. In a previous session, he had effectively blocked Senate consideration of a House measure they feared.

headline: Democrat Dabrow sets sights on 187th District seat-again
abstract: After losing two years ago, Arlene Dabrow will again run against incumbent PA Representative Paul Semmel, who also faces Todd Gummo in the Republican primary. Dabrow believes that Semmel is not addressing a number of the 187th District’s problems.

headline: Nasatir announces challenge to Holl
abstract: David Nasatir stopped at Lansdale Train Station to announce he would be challenging PA Senator Edwin Holl for the 24th State Senatorial District. He said that the train station was finally being repaired because it’s an election year and claimed that Holl brought his district less than 1% of all state funds, which Holl adamantly disputed. Nasatir also criticized Holl for not supporting two health care bills, as well as a proposal to eliminate ATM surcharges, and Holl defended himself on these issues, claiming more information is needed for each of them

headline: Today's racial problems being called more 'subtle'
abstract: About sixty teachers from Beaver Falls Middle School committed three hours of their in service day towards discussions on race relations. PA Representative Mike Veon attended the discussions, which were similar to conversations he’s been holding monthly at Geneva College. At the session, teachers focused on a wide range of issues pertaining to race, ranging from an examination of their own personal beliefs to how the police and media make race an issue when it should not be.

headline: Ask representatives to change the rules
abstract: PA Reps. Edward Krebs and Sara Steelman recount the public outcry over H. 907, which passed with an obscure provision inserted last minute that would allow the state's debt ceiling to be increased without congressional approval. They point out that the public should be concerned that the legislative process has evolved such that uninformed votes occur and surprise tactics are frequently used. A 24-hour rule to prevent last minute amendments is frequently suspended. Citizens should demand a reform of the legislative process so that the will of the majority is not subverted.

headline: Diabetes hits state harder than average
abstract: A new study by the Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment council says diabetes was a factor in more than 14 percent of all Pennsylvania hospitalizations in 1997, a rate much higher than the national average.  The council says it hopes the study will help discern the impact of a new law that could help estimated 1.1 million Pennsylvanians suffering from the disease.  Signed by Gov. Tom Ridge in October, the law requires insurance companies to pay for medical supplies and equipment for diabetes.

headline: CR lawsuit sparks Sunshine Law reform
abstract: PA Senator President Pro Tem Robert Jubelirer sponsored a bill intended to clear up the language of the state’s Sunshine Law, and it now awaits Governor Tom Ridge’s signature. The Sunshine Law requires governmental bodies to deliberate in public; however, a Bucks County Court ruled the language of the bill was vague as to whether school boards would be subject to the law. The PA School Boards Association said almost all school boards have still complied, but Jubelirer’s revision clearly specifies that school boards do fall under the law.

headline: Hasay plans legislative assault on state game commission
abstract: PA Representative George Hassay is angry at the PA Game Commission and is drafting legislation that would give the authority to set kill limits, as well as the length and dates of seasons, back to the legislature. Hassay claims that hunters throughout the state have complained about dwindling deer herd numbers, yet the Game Commission announced it would raise the number of antlerless deer licenses to about 900,000 for the upcoming hunting season. Hassay believes the agency's independence is a problem, and he wrote a letter Don Madl, executive director of the Game Commission, to voice his dismay.

headline: Lackawanna Ave. parking lot top candidate for project
abstract: Plans for a multimillion dollar transit system in downtown Scranton are being made and positions of parking lots and centers are being drawn out.

headline: Consider negative side of gun rules
abstract: The state Legislature needs to be careful that it doesn't get ahead of technology and common sense with laws designed to keep unauthorized people from firing handguns.  The House Judiciary Committee has approved a bill that would require safety devices on new and many older guns within a few years.  If the bill is enacted, a Handgun Safety Standards Commission would within a year set statewide standards, which would be enforced four years later.

headline: Disabled-parking measure introduced
abstract: In response to complaints he received from businesses about people illegally parking in handicapped spaces, PA Representative Stephen Stetler has proposed a bill that will remove information about fines and being towed from parking signs. He simply wants the information to tell drivers handicapped spaces are solely for people with disabilities. In other news, PA Representatives John Perzel and Mike Veon will be guests on a PA Television Network show.

headline: Insurance pays off: Proper coverage eases pain for storm victims
abstract: The Federal Emergency Management Agency rejected Governor Ridge’s request for financial aid for victims of a tornado storm; however, the reason the request was rejected is that damage assessors found that most people in the area had adequate insurance coverage. Montgomery County Commissioner was surprised that no federal aid was given, but the author of the editorial is thankful that nobody in the area was hurt, the damage wasn’t more severe and most residents were wise enough to purchase sound insurance plans.

headline: Democrat Fund-raiser said to name China tie
abstract: A Democratic fundraiser has told Federal investigators he funneled tens of thousands of collars from a Chinese military officer during President Clinton's 1996 re-election campaign. After federal law foreign governments are forbidden from contributing to US campaigns.

headline: National GOP committeewoman to speak at annual spring brunch
abstract: The Venango County Republican Women’s Council will hold its annual spring brunch, and it will be open to all Republican voters and candidates in the upcoming election. National Republican committeewoman Christine Toretti, who also serves in the board of governors for the State System of Higher Education and the board of directors for a Federal Reserve Bank, will be the guest speaker.

headline: Trio vies for 93rd GOP Seat
abstract: When state Representative Mike Waugh decide to run for state Senate three Republicans stepped up for his seat. Each of them is dedicated to tax reform and community service. They are Joyce Keesey, Barbara Metzler, and Ron Miller. The winner will go on to oppose Democrat Jeff Sanders in the general elections

headline: At GOP meeting, Rendell pitches Phila. For 2000 convention
abstract: The nonprofit group Philadelphia 2000 paid $30,000 towards the costs of holding a reception for about 130 Republican National Committee members at a golf resort in California, and Mayor Ed Rendell travelled to be there, hoping to persuade committee members to choose Philadelphia as the site of the 2000 Republican National Convention. Rendell, a Democrat, said that while Philadelphia is predominately Democratic, PA is one of the most Republican states in the nation, and he even wore an elephant tie to prove how serious he is about luring the Republicans. With the addition of the Convention Center and CoreStates Center, Philadelphia now has the capacity to host the event, but it will face tough competition from 24 other cites that have submitted proposals to host the event.

headline: Diabetes patients ask legislators for a little help
abstract: Over 40 diabetes patients met at Mercy Hospital to discuss their problems with the insurance companies and urge the PA Senators to vote on a bill that would require all PA health insurance companies to pay for preventative diabetes measures. Preventative measure can cost diabetes patients without coverage over $3,000 a year, but Marianne McAndrew, a Registered Nurse at Mercy, said that prevention and continual monitoring are essential for keeping symptoms under control and could reduce health care costs if covered.. She told people to contact Governor Ridge and their Senators to vote on House Bill 656, which has been stuck in committee.

headline: Cream of the Classroom
abstract: The Tribune-Democract explores the new proposal for changing educational standards for students graduating from college in Education.

headline: Hasay threatens to strip the power from game commission
abstract: State Rep. George Hasay has once again put the Pennsylvania Game Commission on notice that if it does not voluntarily reform policies regarding deer and turkey management, he will legislate changes to protect the Commonwealth's wildlife.  In a recent letter to Don Madl, executive director of the PGC, Hasay bluntly told him that four things need to be done to prevent the continuing decline of the state's deer herd and the threat of the same thing happening to the state's turkey flocks.

headline: Late 199 completion date eyed for Southwest Beltway
abstract: Larry King of the PA Department of Transportation told the Great Hazleton Chamber of Commerce's Governmental Task Force that the project to build a Southwest Beltway is on track. King met with members in PA Sen. Ray Musto's office. Over the years, local governments, including Luzerne County, have pitched in funding for the project. Another project also receiving attention is Hazleton Mayor Michael Marsicano's proposal to renovate Broad Street. The PA Department of Transportation has received funding from the federal government.

headline: Constitutional amendments still face challenge
abstract: Voters passed two constiutional amendments on crime, but the passage of the amendments bring more challeneges and questions on the legality of the changes.

headline: Discuss senior centers
abstract: The photo depicts PA Representative Jim Lynch reviewing information on the state’s network of senior citizens with Margaret Sleeman, co-coordinator of the Northwest Region of the PA Association of Senior Centers.

headline: IRA holders petition over new fees
abstract: Dauphin Deposit Bank is seeking to impose new fees and conditions on almost 5,000 high-interest individual retirement accounts that have been the subject of drawn-out litigation, and customers and the state attorney general's office aren't happy about it. A petition filed in Cumberland County Court by lawyers for the account holders seeks to block enforcement of six pages of amendments mailed out at the end of January. One of the changes appears to give the bank the right to collect its litigation legal fees from customers or their accounts.

headline: Democrat switches parties, will take on Shuster
abstract: Monte Kemmler, who lost to U.S. Representative Bud Shuster in the general election two years ago, has decided to switch parties and challenge Shuster again in the upcoming Republican primary. He lost badly in the previous election but blamed it on a  huge disparity in spending. Two Democrats, John Henry and Paul Politis, have announced plans to seek the Democratic nomination.

headline: Nealon in line for Eagen's post
abstract: Democratic attorney Terrence R. Nealon was nominated Thursday by Republican Gov. Tom Ridge to fill former Judge Frank Eagen's seat on the Lackawanna County Common Pleas Court.  If confirmed by the state Senate, Mr. Nealon would follow in the footsteps of his father, senior U.S. District Judge William R. Nealon, whose judicial career was launched  by an appointment to the county bench in 1960.

headline: Trying for No. 2
abstract: Row officers in Allegheny County are scehuled to compete for the No. 2 spot in the Democratic Committee.

headline: Attorney general's office to interview fighting commissioners
abstract: The PA Attorney General’s office will handle the investigation of Fayette County Commissioners Sean Cavanagh and Harry Albert III to avoid any conflict of interest with the District Attorney’s office. The two commissioners were involved in a fight that sent both to the hospital, and the investigation will determine if any charges should be filed.

headline: Docs protest mismanagement, crisis: Encouraged after CEO is replaced
abstract: Doctors and medical staff at Allegheny University’s hospitals and medical schools in Philadelphia drafted a letter of criticism to be sent to Allegheny management. The draft had been prepared before an announcement that Anthony Sanzo had replaced Sherif Abdelhak as Allegheny’s chief executive and president. Most seemed cautiously optimistic over the leadership change and had harsh words of criticism for Abdelhak.

headline: Dean at University of Pennsylvania chosen as 12th president of Lehigh
abstract: Lehigh University chose Gregory Farrington, dean of the School of Engineering and Applied Science at the University of PA, to become its next president. His wife, Jean, was in charge of a staff of 22 at Penn’s Van Pelt-Dietrich Library Center, and she was given a position as a special projects librarian at Lehigh. Farrington spoke to a crowd of about 100 for an official coronation ceremony, and Penn’s President praised the work of him and his wife.

headline: Hearings set on year-round bass fishing plan
abstract: Four public hearings will be held in Harrisburg, Wallenpaupack High School, Berks County and Monroeville over the PA Fish and Boat Commission’s proposal to allow year-round bass fishing. Currently, there is a period of three months where fishing is prohibited, but the Fish and Boat Commission suggested a change to allow more opportunities for fishing. In order to protect bass from vulnerabilities, there would be limited harvest periods in the winter and fall, which would be followed by a catch-and-immediate-release-only period.

headline: Late 1999 completion date eyed for Southwest Belt
abstract: State officials plan that the Southwest Belth project will be completed by the end of winter in 1999.

headline: Conviction still haunts DA
abstract: York County District Attorney Stan Rebert is still working on a 10 year old case, trying to investigate, try and convict a man believed to be guilty of murder.

headline: Don't punish success - Let states keep savings from welfare-reform efforts
abstract: According to the authors, Wisconsin Governor Tommy Thompson and Indiana Governor Frank O’Bannon, the nation’s governors have transformed the welfare system since the passage of welfare reform legislation two years ago. The caseloads across the nation have dropped 30%, and states have helped welfare recipients find employment and get off public assistance. The authors believe the federal government must allow the states to keep left over federal funding that they’ve saved, so they can reinvest it to ensure continual success and prepare for any challenges in the future.

headline: Is vote sought to expand gambling?
abstract: The gambling industry, in its haste to expand gambling in this state, is promoting the passage of legislation this session in the General Assembly that would allow a voter referendum to be offered to Pennsylvania voters.  The referendum would present three ballot questions to voters, asking them to vote yes or no on the question of slot machines at racetracks, riverboat gambling and electronic gambling devices or machines at bars or clubs.

headline: Democrat who hoped to challenge Shuster admits forging signatures
abstract: US Representative Bud Shuster got help from a surprising quarter in contesting the validity of signatures on an opponent's nominating petitions, the opponent fussed up. Democrat Paul Polities of Mechanicsburg admitted he forged three signatures and falsely swore he circulated petitions that he did not.

headline: New challenge awaits state GOP
abstract: Republicans face challenegs in the upcoming local 1999 elections.

headline: Trying for No. 2
abstract: Two Allegheny County row officers are challenging to win the Number 2 spot in Pennsylvania’s Democratic Committee, and state Representative Christine Tartaglione is expected to be re-elected as the committee’s chairwoman.

headline: Auditor General Casey to hold fund-raiser in Erie next week
abstract: PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. will be in Erie for a fund-raiser next week that will be hosted by several Erie attorneys and Democratic officials. Casey’s father was the former governor of PA, and his brother is running his campaign operations. Casey has been mentioned as a possible gubernatorial candidate in the 2002 election, and he is trying to raise funds to pay off a loan he used to fund his last election.

headline: Docs seek state hospital aid
abstract: Hospitals in Pennsylvania are being driven by a "bottom-line mentality" that seems to care more about profits than patient care, a physician's group charged yesterday.  In recent years, the amount of money being spent on health care in the state has remained the same, but the amount of care seems to be dropping, Lee McCormick, president of the Pennsylvania Medical Society, told state Democratic law makers.  McCormick, whose group represents 19,000 doctors throughout the state, said reliance on the bottom line has led to the recent collapse of on health-care system --- Allegheny --- "and more will follow."

headline: Despite tight budgets, schools pay top dollar for top doctors    Million-dollar salaries are not uncommon for revenue-generating specialists at the area's four major medical schools
abstract: Philadelphia’s four major academic medical schools, Allegheny, Temple, Thomas Jefferson and the University of PA, are paying their top faculty over a million dollars each year, which is significantly higher than what faculty in similar positions throughout the Northeast U.S are being paid, and this comes a time when health care reimbursements are dropping and pushing the schools towards budget deficits. In a competitive marketplace, these schools have to pay top dollar to attract top tier doctors, most of whom are skilled surgical specialists that have the ability to attract larger numbers of referrals. Top administrators are also well compensated, and the article provides a large table that compares some of the highest paid faculty and administrators from the four medical schools with the Northeast average for similar positions.

headline: Hess Announces Grant For Taylor Township
abstract: PA Representative Dick Hess announced that the PA Department of Environmental Protection has awarded Fulton County’s Taylor Township a $28,423 state grant to update and revise its official sewer plan. The township will be expected to match the grant for a project that will cost about $56,856.

headline: Lawmaker supports Kiski Valley highway
abstract: PA Representative Joseph Petrarca, the author of this opinion piece, is writing to voice his support for funding the construction of the Kiski Valley Expressway, and he refutes claims that money would be better spent to simply fix Route 356. He believes Route 356 is unfixable, citing opinions from the PA Department of Transportation and private engineering firms, and he believes the Expressway should be the region’s top priority project. According to Petrarca, the Expressway would also fit nicely with state Representative Tim Pesci’s Northern beltway plan for Pittsburgh, and he urges people to support him as he pushes for funding.

headline: Convicts must take victim impact instruction
abstract: A new bill passed by Representative Daley will require certain convicted felons to participate in a victim impact instructional program before being eligible for parole or release.

headline: Driving toward independence
abstract: Mike Fullerton, a job developer for the York County Public Assistance office, was behind an idea to help welfare recipients overcome a common barrier to finding employment, transportation. Two local car dealerships and an anonymous donor have donated three used cars to be used by welfare recipients to get them to work and off of public assistance. PA Representative Steve Nickol presented one woman with a car, and Fullerton will try to keep the program going, provided people are willing to continue donating cars.

headline: Just in time
abstract: Workers' Compensation Bureau goes modern. Faced with impairment reviews and other, additional administrative functions, the state's Workers' Compensation Bureau finds itself in the middle of a timely effort to modernize its processing capabilities. Attorneys, business and carriers should soon see a marked change in efficiency in the processing of claims, and other information. It couldn't be more timely.

headline: Democratic Allies Mount Counteroffensive on Social Security
abstract: US Sens. Edward Kennedy and Earl Pomeroy are drafting legislation to address the viability of Social Security, and hoping to slow or reverse the momentum gained by the idea of partial privatization. Pomeroy favors allowing the Social Security Administration to directly invest in the market. The AFL-CIO opposes partial privatization and has begun a grass roots campaign to educate its members on the risks involved. The National Organization for Women plans to make defense of the current system a priority in the next year. President Clinton has not adopted a position on the debate, making it difficult for liberals to support a particular policy.

headline: New chance to reform campaign law
abstract: U.S. Representatives Christopher Shays and Martin Meehan introduced a bipartisan bill that would prohibit parties from accepting soft money, which is unregulated money given to parties, but House Speaker Newt Gingrich has prevented the bill from being voted on in the past. A discharge petition is gathering support that could force the bill onto the House floor for consideration, and Gingrich appears to have reversed course and will allow the House to vote on the bill. Most Democrats have signed the discharge petition, but Jon Fox and Jim Greenwood are among some Republicans who have not, and the authors of the editorial remind them that in numerous polls Americans have supported campaign finance reform.

headline: Two Troops Take on Armey - Majority Leader Fights for Post
abstract: U.S. Representative Bob Livingston worked quickly to secure enough support to succeed House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who announced his resignation from the leadership position. However, Majority Leader Richard Armey is trying to fend off two challengers to his post, Representatives Steve Largent and Jennifer Dunn. As of now, it is difficult to determine where each one stands because voting is done in secrecy.

headline: Auditor general lags in fund raising
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey has funding problems for his upcoming campaign. He is holding more debt then the State Treasurer and the Attorney General.

headline: Donor wants gift moved if a firm buys Allegheny: Her $3.4 million endowment could go to Penn. It now funds a Graduate Hospital post.
abstract: Emilie de Hellebranth, the donor of a $3.4 million endowment fund to Allegheny Health System’s Graduate Hospital, said she would seek to move the money to the University of PA if the hospital is sold to a for-profit company. Vanguard Health Systems Inc. and Tenet Healthcare Corp., both for-profit companies, have placed bids on Graduate Hospital and seven other Allegheny hospitals in the Philadelphia area. The de Hellebranth fund and many others funds are under scrutiny because Allegheny, which has filed for bankruptcy, apparently moved millions of restricted funds without consulting the donors first.

headline: District to offer more after-school - Using federal money, seven programs will be expanded and 27 others created, Hornbeck said
abstract: Philadelphia School District Superintendent David Hornbeck announced the district will give a total of $170,000 to schools and community groups for the expansion of seven after-school programs and the creation of 27 others around the city. The money is available through the federal Safe and Drug Free Schools grant. The announcement comes after last months State of the Union address in which President Clinton unveiled his $55 million grant for after-school programs; though Philadelphia’s grant isn’t being paid with that money.

headline: House agency hears of wildlife officers' improper, abusive conduct
abstract: The hunting and wildlife agency has been criticized for everything from its annual doe license allocations to the way it raises pheasants.  At a hearing before the House Game & Fisheries Committee in Harrisburg a week ago, testimony was heard on varied charges, including a tale of a raid on a remote Cambria County hunting cabin where seven suspects in the illegal shooting of a doe were reportedly held for nine hours by four deputies.  A woman involved in the case went on record saying she was confined, also for nine hours, in a PGC vehicle where she was sexually and verbally harassed and threatened.

headline: Lawmakers OK money for area road projects
abstract: The PA Legislature approved a new highway construction capital budget that included a number of new projects for Erie. The federal government will also contribute to some of the projects. US Rep. Phil English brought home $21.2 million for a project which recently broke ground. PA Gov. Ridge was there for the ceremony. PA Rep. Karl Boyes said the passage of the bill is a crucial first step. The PA Department of Transportation now has the revenue to make things happen.

headline: Council targets laser pointers
abstract: The Uniontown City Council passed a resolution intended to curb the inappropriate use of laser pointers by calling on businesses that sell them to educate buyers about the risks of improper use. Two law enforcement officers recently had a laser pointer aimed at them, which could be mistaken for a laser rifle site. The individual responsible for the incident faces simple assault and disorderly conduct charges, and Mayor James Sileo said he’s contacted PA Representative Larry Roberts about making laser pointers illegal.

headline: Effects of Welfare Time Limits Documented - In Florida Study, Most Who Had Lost Assistance Were Working After Six Months
abstract: Two years ago, Congress changed the nation’s welfare laws by establishing a five year time limit on benefits, but it also allowed states to shorten time limits, which Escambia County, Florida chose to do. The county became the focus of the first controlled scientific study on the impact of welfare time limits, and while the study found that most people who lost their benefits were working within six months, it also found time limits didn’t encourage people to leave the welfare payroll any faster than they would have if they hadn’t faced time limits. The findings could be good news for the rest of the nation’s welfare programs; however, the authors of the study cautioned that more time is still needed to judge the results, and time limits could have a different impact in other locations.

headline: Justice Department tell First Union to sell nine Lehigh Valley Branches
abstract: Department of Justice orders First Union to close nine branches in Lehugh Valley due to antitrust issues after the acquisition of CoreStates Corp.

headline: Democratic endorsement crucial to Itkin
abstract: PA Representative Ivan Itkin has been campaigning longer than any of his challengers to become the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, and if he doesn’t receive the endorsement of the Democratic State Committee, it would be a slap in the face which could potentially end his campaign. As of recent history, the endorsement has not helped candidates win elections, which could explain why challengers Phil Berg, Don Bailey and William Kiesling don’t care too much about winning the committee’s support. Itkin has made it clear that he wants the endorsement since last June, and he has been dealing with poor attendance at campaign rallies, the inability to raise much money and criticism that he’s too boring to energize the party.

headline: New Dem chair will find disarray
abstract: Mark Singel, who decided to step down as the chairman of Pennsylvania’s Democratic Party, has drawn a lot of criticism for the troubles of the party, and the author of the article agrees he made a lot of mistakes but argues he did some things rights, and Democratic leaders for the past twenty years are all responsible for the current state of the party. State Senator Tina Tartaglione will take over for the time being, but she is not expected to remain chairwoman for long, which could open the door for state Representative Mike Veon. The incoming chairman will face tough challenges considering Democrats don’t control either branch of the Legislature, Philadelphia-area residents have had poor voter turnout recently and Democratic candidates for governor and U.S. Senator, Representatives Ivan Itkin and Bill Lloyd, face uphill battles in their elections.

headline: Two years, many challenges
abstract: A time line of two year term of Chester Upland's Superintendent Joseph Lapchik.

headline: Auditor: Lincoln U. mismanaged. State report alleges bid-rigging, nepotism and waste
abstract: PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. released a report that found Lincoln University’s top administrators, including President Niara Sudarkasa and her husband John Clark, had mismanaged and wasted funds, which led many trustees to call for her resignation without severance pay. According to the report, Sudarkasa used university funds to pay for personal lawyer fees, and she spent $531,000 on the presidential residence without the board’s approval. PA Senator Vincent Fumo will press the Attorney General to investigate criminal charges against Clark for bid-rigging by paying thousands of dollars for projects without soliciting more than one bidder, and state senators have withheld $11 million in funding from the university because of these problems.

headline: Don't Dilute State HMO Bill
abstract: Republican lawmakers recoiled in horror back in 1993 and 1994, as the Clinton administration put together a proposal for national health care.  Instead,  American health-care consumers now are faced with a capitalist-style monolithic bureaucracy - the managed care industry.  Health maintenance organizations have grown steadily since the demise of the administration's plan.

headline: District to see if uniforms might fit: Wilkes-Barre Area to study issue after Ridge signs law allowing mandatory uniforms
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge signed a bill that allows school districts to establish mandatory uniform policies, and Wilkes-Barre Area School District Superintendant Jeff Namey is seriously considering adopting a uniform policy. A survey of students found mixed results, and some parents are in favor of the idea because some families cannot afford to buy brand name clothing for their children, which can result in them being ridiculed by classmates. The Scranton School District will mandate uniforms in one or two of its elementary schools, and many districts are sending out surveys to determine how students, parents and teachers feel about the issue.

headline: House bucks blame for new license rule
abstract: Seeking political cover, the state House Tuesday passed a resolution blaming Congress for a requirement that applicants for hunting licenses must provide their Social Security numbers.  But the resolution won't change anything.  Hunters will be asked for the information when new licenses go on sale this month.

headline: Leaders stress highway's importance to area's future
abstract: 56 local leaders representing the Mon/Fayette Expressway and Southern Beltway Alliance travelled to the nation’s capital, where they met with national highway advocacy groups and lobbied for funding for the highway. U.S. Representatives Bud Shuster and Jon Fox have both pushed to pass a transportation bill that would take the Highway Trust Fund off the federal budget, which would allow all of the money generated by the gas tax to be spent entirely on road projects, rather than on balancing the budget. Advocacy groups cited the benefits of increased spending on the nation’s roads, and while many congressmen, including Senator Rick Santorum and Representative Frank Mascara, expressed their support for the proposal, leaders are hoping to get enough votes to pass the bill and override President Clinton’s likely veto.

headline: Counting out crime
abstract: A city wide recount of crime statistics is being called for in Philadelphia. The numbers are inconsistent and officials want accurate numbers to find accurate solutions for crime reduction.

headline: Emlenton resident receives highest Girl Scout award
abstract: Kayne Alden was awarded the Gold Award in Girl Scouting, the highest achievement attainable in Senior Scouting, and PA Representative Scott Hutchinson presented her with a citation he sponsored in the state House. The article also includes a photo of Alden and Hutchinson.

headline: Keno proposal tied up is Legislature
abstract: A measure introduced five months ago that would allow keno games to be played in PA to raise funds for new stadiums is languishing in a Legislative committee. The measure would legalize the casino game, Revenue from the game could then be used for regional projects such as sports stadiums. It is now tied up in the Legislature.

headline: Democratic Headquarters
abstract: The photo depicts PA Representative Lawrence Curry, Montgomery County Commissioner Joseph Hoeffel and Doris Prosser at a ribbon opening ceremony for the Democratic headquarters in Jenkintown. Prosser will direct the headquarters, and Curry is seeking reelection, while Hoeffel is running for the U.S. House.

headline: New law brightens the light
abstract: Reform to the Sunshine Law will give the public more access and more rights to comment and confront government issue directly affect them.

headline: U.S. BOMBS IRAQ
abstract: President Clinton announced that U.S. and British forces had launched major missile strikes against Iraq in response to reports from United Nations weapons inspector Richard Butler that alleged Iraq’s President, Saddam Hussein, continued to obstruct inspection efforts. The announcement delayed Clinton’s impeachment vote, which had been scheduled for the next day, and many Republican members of Congress, including Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, criticized the timing of the attacks, while incoming House Speaker Bob Livingston said he’d leave it up the public to make their own judgment on the timing. According to a poll, 74% of Americans approve of the president’s actions, and Congressmen Dick Gephardt, Tom Daschle, Newt Gingrich and former president George Bush all expressed support for the military strikes.

headline: Average teacher pay up 2.2%
abstract: The average salary for Pennsylvania teachers is the sixth highest in the nation. The national slaary average for teachers in up 2.2%.

headline: Don't Minimize Care Findings
abstract: The findings from the Health Departments audit are scheduled to be released. The regulations of the agency are to be examined.

headline: Dodging bullets
abstract: Last year, while he was in Camden County Youth Center, Jason Nigro helped produce a newsletter. Using the nickname "Shaggy" Nigro wrote and illustrated the poem shown on the page describing life in his neighborhood. Early this year, he went to adult prison for armed robbery.

headline: House leader vows to stop Ridge on landfill limits
abstract: Rep. John Perzel vowed to stop an attempt by PA Gov. Ridge to limit the amount of garbage which can be deposited in landfills, as well as stop new landfill permits. The House Maj. Leader is using his leadership position to bottle Ridge's proposal up in committee. PA is the nation's leading importer of garbage, receiving 25 percent of all sold municipal waste from other states. Trash importing has become an issue in the gubernatorial campaign. Challenger Ivan Itkin has accused Ridge of being soft on waste hauling because of their contributions to his campaign.

headline: Learner's Permit
abstract: Patriot News talks about the lack of driver education, parental responsibility, and reckless driving of teenagers and urges that PA Department of Transportation and state lawmakers get involved in this matter.

headline: County detectives got no summons
abstract: Over a six year period, detectives in Allegheny County received parking tickets but did not pay them. They all failed to received notification summons.

headline: Fisher launches task force in attempt to protect elderly
abstract: Attornet General Mike Fisher launches a task force to study, educate, and enact legislation to protect PA elderly citizens from multiple types of mistreatment

headline: Keystone of pill mills   Drug manufacturers are flocking to Pennsylvania
abstract: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, drug employment has increased by 25 percent nationally, or about 52,000 jobs, but it grew by 36 percent in PA, or 7,200 jobs, from 1986 to 1996, making PA second to only California in job creation for the industry. Several years ago, the drug industry appeared to be heading for trouble; however, it reversed course and improved its public image by investing heavily in research, restructuring to cut costs and focusing more on marketing in order to generate more revenue through increased sales rather than high prices for drugs. About 80 percent of the state’s industry is located in the Philadelphia region, where Merck & Company, one of the nation’s top pharmaceutical companies has seen extensive growth recently, and the biotechnology firms have also grown substantially.

headline: Democratic Party Singled out
abstract: The Democratic nominee for govenor, Mark Singel, has resigned as Committee Chairman. Observer-Report says this move furthers the argument that Democrats are in serious trouble in Pennsylvnia.

headline: New York State Legislators Quietly Clamor for Pay Raise
abstract: New York’s state legislators will return to Albany to vote on the new party leadership positions, but while they’re in town, they may take up the issue of giving themselves pay raises, which they would have to pass before January 1st to take effect in time for the next two-year terms. While most legislators privately support pay raises, they are often hesitant to address the issue in public, but when they do, they are often careful to refer to raises as "cost of living adjustments." The big question for most of the lawmakers is how they can approve a pay raise without angering the public, and they must also be able to secure the support of Governor George Pataki.

headline: U.S. Senate: Specter, Lloyd to clash in November
abstract: It appears as if PA Representative Bill Lloyd, who has served for 19 years in the state House, has won the Democratic primary and will challenge the incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, who has served for 18 years in Congress, for his seat in the U.S. Senate. The unofficial results of the primary showed Lloyd with 48 percent of the vote, and his closest challenger, Richard Orloski, with 26 percent of the vote, whereas Specter gained a majority of the votes in his primary with 66 percent of the vote. Many of the votes were made on a name recognition basis, and Lloyd will face a difficult task in defeating Specter in the upcoming election, considering Specter's huge campaign chest advantages.

headline: Bad vote by Goodling
abstract: The authors of the editorial are pleased that the U.S. House passed the Shays-Meehan campaign finance reform bill, but they are extremely disappointed at U.S. Representative Bill Goodling for voting against it. If the bill passes the Senate, which is highly uncertain, it would require the sources of funding for issue advocacy campaign to be disclosed, and it would prevent national parties from raising soft money, which is unregulated money that often is illegally funded to campaigns for specific candidates. The authors claim Goodling’s opponent, Charles Gerow, benefited substantially from the use of soft money in the past election, which makes Goodling’s vote to follow the Republican leadership even more disappointing.

headline: Gambling rider put brakes to bone disease proposal
abstract: The bill was on the fast track, and its supporters spoke enthusiastically on the House floor of the benefits of a state public-awareness program about the bone disease.  The bill had passed the chamber unanimously a year earlier and was on a return trip from the Senate in June on its way to the governor.  But then the mild-mannered, silver-haired lawmaker from suburban Philadelphia's Bucks County stood up to point to page 21 of the 22-page bill.  Tacked on by the Senate were a couple of unrelated paragraphs extending the life of simulcast betting at the state's four horse-racing tracks.

headline: Don Sherwood
abstract: Profile on Don Sherwood including age, address, party, employment, family, education and community service.

headline: Hunter ed right on target
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission has released an astounding figure for the 1997 hunting seasons. Only one person has died as the result of a firearm accident. The total is the lowest of any hunting season since the commission began keeping records in 1915. Statistics show that hunter-education programs reduce the danger of hunting.

headline: Letterkenny targeted for truck school, highway center
abstract: If the House transportation bill is singed into law, the new Letterkenny Opportunity Center business park could receive $11.3 million over the next five years towards a truck driver training facility and an "intelligent traffic system" for monitoring traffic and alerting motorists of accidents on Interstate 81 and the PA Turnpike. According to a spokesman for the PA Department of Transportation, the state is trying to make use of the Letterkenny Army Depot, which is being downsized by over 1,000 jobs. The development of an electronic message system is still in its initial phases, but the system would coordinate emergency responses among state and local governments in central PA.

headline: County drug court to open
abstract: Alleghney County Drug Court is opening. The court will focus on rehabilitation for non-violent offenders.

headline: Gingrich wants commission to study Social Security reform
abstract: A day after President Clinton called on Congress to tackle Social Security, U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich gave a speech near Atlanta, and he said he would push for a national commission on retirement to improve the Social Security system. His other goals included a safe, drug-free environment for children, a quality education system and a smaller government that collects no more than 25 percent of taxpayers’ income, which he believes could be accomplished by using the budget surplus to begin giving small tax breaks. He expressed opposition to bilingual education programs, and he seemed sympathetic to the idea of allowing workers to invest money that now goes into Social Security.

headline: Lawmakers hope to put an end to bailout trend
abstract: After hearing stories about millionaires who have filed for bankruptcy, U.S. Representative George Gekas is sponsoring legislation that will strengthen bankruptcy laws and make it more difficult for a person to qualify for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. Gekas believes too many people take advantage of bankruptcy laws because they are too lenient, and it is unfair for consumers because retailers ultimately pass the costs of bankruptcy onto them. U.S. Representative Curt Weldon is likely to support the bill, and U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts is still undecided.

headline: Democratic, Republican leaders expect low turnout for election
abstract: Chester County Republican and Democratic leaders are both predicting that the upcoming November election will likely have the lowest turnout of all major races across the country with estimates between 35-40 percent of registered voters. The Republican Chairman, Alan Novak, blamed the "Motor Voter" law for failing to encourage registered voters to actually vote but also said that people tend to vote less when they’re pleased with how things are going. The Democratic Chairman, John Beemer, didn’t seem too optimistic about the party’s chances in the upcoming election since they are substantially outnumbered in terms of registered voters, and he offered his own suggestions for increasing voter turnout.

headline: News from central Pennsylvania
abstract: Relatives and friends are mourning for Earl Max Downs, the Democratic challenger against PA Representative Todd Platts in the November general election. Downs died Monday after suffering a heart attack in a convenience store.

headline: Ultra right can take GOP to the margins
abstract: According to the editorial, the Republican Party’s relatively poor showing in the recent elections was the catalyst that brought on House Speaker Newt Gingrich’s resignation. Extreme conservatives accused Gingrich of being too willing to compromise with President Clinton, whereas moderates blamed Gingrich for pushing the attack against Clinton when voters had clearly grown tired of it. The authors believe that if right-wing conservatives prevail, it will deeply divide the party, and they argue Republicans would be best served to move more towards the center.

headline: Barrasse's Delay Freezing Others
abstract: District Attorney Michael Barrasse cannot decided if he wants to run for the U.S. Representative position being given up by Joseph McDade.

headline: Drug chains drop HMO - Keystone Mercy slashes reimbursements
abstract: The largest Medicaid Health Maintenance Organization, Keystone Mercy Health Plan, announced it will pay pharmacists less money to fill prescriptions for its members. However, CVS and Eckerd pharmacy chains said the payments are too low, so they will no longer fill prescriptions for subscribers of Keystone Mercy. Rite Aid will accept the new payments, but it has been accused of accepting lower payments to take over the market by driving small stores out of business.

headline: Don't bet on Ridge blinking in school crisis
abstract: The Philadelphia school district tried to force the state to provide an additional $100 million by threatening to close the schools, and the Superintendant made accusations that racism has played a factor in why the district hasn’t received full funding. The author believes these incidents strengthened Governor Tom Ridge’s resolve, and he worked with the PA Legislature to pass a bill that would allow a state takeover of the school district if it fails to pass a suitable budget. The author believes Ridge, who has proven critics wrong in the past, will not back down, and his support of school reform, which is supported by Democratic parents, could actually win him improbable support from city voters.

headline: Hunters recall encounters with commission officers
abstract: 23 readers responded to a July 19 article about the Game Commission's failure to track public complaints.  Almost all of the readers were critical of agency actions.  Many had complaints about officers or deputies.

headline: Local officials eager to see plan proceed
abstract: Officials want Johnstown passenger rail services to proceed with development but cost is posing a problem.

headline: County Judgeship Maneuvering Starts
abstract: Now that the 1998 general election is over, attention is turning to Lackawanna County's vacant judgeship.  The opening was created last month when Judge James M. Munley of Archibald was sworn in as U.S. district judge after serving on the county bench for 20 years.  Judge Munley formally resigned his county post on Oct. 23, technically giving Gov. Tom Ridge until Jan. 20, or 90 days to nominate a successor.

headline: Go Slow
abstract: US Sen. Rick Santorum urged caution in considering reform to Social Security in a speech at the conservative Heritage Foundation. Santorum is chairman of a Senate Republican task force on Social Security and editors believe people should listen to him. A survey revealed most young Americans think government should be responsible for ensuring people have retirement money. However, the ideas being considered in Washington are just the opposite. Santorum favors partial privatization. The Senator is right that the current system cannot be fixed no matter what is done, but his idea is a hard sell.

headline: Lawmakers vow to save Suburban General
abstract: PA Senator Edwin Holl and Representative John Fichter wrote a letter to Governor Tom Ridge asking for the state to provide $1 million to help finalize the merger between Suburban General, which is struggling financially, and Mercy Health System. U.S. Representative Jon Fox has already promised to push for federal support for the merger, and Holl and Fichter hope that Ridge can take some money from the state’s "Rainy Day Fund" to help facilitate the merger. Both Holl and Fichter denied their petition has anything to do with the election in three days, claiming it is about protecting the nearly 1,000 people employed by the hospital.

headline: Democrats brace for Clinton's turbulence
abstract: Democrats are hoping that Clinton can assure the country of the future so they can get re-elected. His poll numbers are still high and people are happy about the economy, but worried about the future. Possibilities are discussed.

headline: News from the Pennsylvania General Assembly
abstract: A measure to name a section of Allegheny Avenue in Philadelphia after former PA Senator Roxanne Jones, the first black woman to serve in the Senate, was approved and awaits Governor Ridge’s signature. A quote disputing the need to publicly fund new stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh is provided, and House Republican Ellen Bard will hold a news conference on her legislation to reform the system of local tax collection. House Republican Dennis O’Brien will hold a news conference to announce legislation handling the $11.3 billion settlement reached with the tobacco industry.

headline: Unclaimed property list includes Santa
abstract: Treasury Department is looking for lists of people who have unclaimed proerty in the state.

headline: Court clerk shouldn't be left hanging
abstract: The Altoona Mirror argues that Govenor Tom Ridge and Senate memebers should approve Jean Damin as Cambria County's new clerk of courts.

headline: EMS contribution
abstract: The Emergency Health Services Foundation donated $1,200 for EMS equipment to West Shore ALS Services. In the photograph, Cynthia Ehlers, president of EHSF, presents the check to William Brandmore Jr., executive assistant to PA Senator Harold Mowery, and Representative Pat Vance.

headline: Earning teacher certificate can prove to be expensive
abstract: For those who have a college degree and decide they want to obtain teacher certification, it can be expensive. Carlow College offers programs, but it usually takes three semesters to receive certification, which could cost up to $13,000. People in these programs come from a wide variety of backgrounds, and they must complete teaching exams, like all other teachers, to obtain their certification.

headline: Hunters recall encounters with commission officers
abstract: The PA Game Commission has been criticized for not keeping track of public complaints against its officers and deputies, and Dr. Terry Smith wrote a letter to Governor Tom Ridge to voice his concerns. In addition, 23 people responded to a July 19 article in the newspaper, and almost all had complaints about the agency or specific complaints about officers or deputies. While the Game Commission denies its officers acted inappropriately, the article details some of the complaints the newspaper received about deputy wildlife officers, including an 80 year old man who claims he was assaulted five years ago, a retired police officer who was arrested and another man who was investigated after hunting in New York.

headline: Linda Tripp, beware
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge signed a bill that will update Pennsylvania’s wiretap law. It will expand the list of offenses that a wiretap can be authorized for and will expand the definition of "electronic device" to include new technologies.

headline: Court lets states try '3-strike' offenses
abstract: In a 5-4 decision, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a state does not violate the double jeopardy clause of the constitution by holding trials or hearings on the three strikes laws, which hand out tougher punishment for repeat offenders. Justice Sandra Day O’ Connor wrote the majority opinion, and Justice John Paul Stevens wrote the dissenting opinion. In addition, the Supreme Court decided not to hear a Salt Lake City school religion case, refused to hear a Massachusetts religion case, and rejected arguments for compensation to citizens who lost money due to the 1979 Iranian Revolution.

headline: Green Party candidate talks Social Security
abstract: Green Party candidate Bill Belitskus, who is challenging 5th District U.S. Representative Peterson, said that all of the revenue collected from Social Security should go into Social Security trust funds. He is against Peterson’s proposal to partially privatize Social Security, and he believes the system will fail once the baby-boomer generation retires if more money is not saved. He cites a number of areas of wasteful government spending and claims the government is using Social Security revenue to hide the fact that the rest of the government is operating under a deficit.

headline: Legislation could force building and loan to close
abstract: Legislation now on PA Governor Tom Ridge's desk could cause one local building and loan to close up shop within three years. The bill eliminates the PA Savings Association Insurance Corp., a group that essentially acts as the FDIC for small building and loans. Without the PSAIC, building and loans would have to either consolidate, buy the FDIC insurance or dissolve.

headline: Democrats face gubernatorial mountain
abstract: Recent statewide elections suggest tough proposition to unseat Ridge. Democrats are trying to find a way to unseat the governor, but this is getting unlikely. The only recent success story if Governor Robert Casey for the democrats. History has been examined and re-examined trying to win a role model for this difficult election.

headline: News from the Pennsylvania General Assembly
abstract: PA House representatives returned to their 92-year-old chamber after $5 million in renovations were finished. Representatives Andrew Carn and William Robinson will hold a news conference on legislative action on stadium financing, and fun facts on PA and Philadelphia publishing are provided.

headline: Union dues in politics remain issue
