abstract: If a measure is approved in California that would require labor unions to ask all their members for permission to use union dues for political purposes, it could encourage Republicans in the House to push for a national version. However, a bill would face an uphill battle since most Democrats would oppose it, and 52 Republicans from labor districts, including Representative Phil English, opposed a dues restriction bill earlier this year. Unions claim it would be next to impossible to get permission from all their members, and Representative Chris Shays has proposed a compromise where unions simply have to announce that anyone who pays dues can request the portion of their dues back which is used for political purposes.

headline: Courting change
abstract: If the state House and Senate cannot agree on the chairman of the next Legislative Reapportionment Commission, the PA Supreme Court would choose with a 4-3 majority; however, Republicans are trying to pass a constitutional amendment that would require a 5-2 majority, which would mean at least one Republican justice would have to support the choice.

headline: Experts debate lawsuit's impact on medical costs
abstract: Experts argue over the medical CAT fund and over large sum jury award for malpractice cases.

headline: East Wing becomes vocational showcase
abstract: In observation of Pennsylvania Vocational-Technical Education week, area students set up booths in the Capital building to demostrat their skills.

headline: Hunting a dying game that needs alterations: Man discusses ways to keep the sport alive
abstract: Dave Henderson spoke at a conference for the Outdoor Writers Association of America, and he painted a very dim picture for the future of hunting. The author of this piece, Terry Brady, agrees that the future of hunting is uncertain; however, he is pleased that Governor Tom Ridge is hosting the Governor’s Symposium on North America’s Hunting Heritage in PA, and he says that all hunters should attend the event. Vernon Ross, the Governor’s Sportsman Advisor, describes some of the activities and information that will be available at the event, and he believes that anyone who attends will learn valuable lessons on how to carry on the tradition of hunting, so future generations can continue to enjoy it.

headline: Local commuters feel sting of strike
abstract: For about an hour yesterday morning, hundreds of commuters at Bucks County train stations waited for trains that never arrived. The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority strike wasn’t supposed to affect them; however, service was temporarily shut down after strikers from the Transport Workers Union Local 234 blocked the entrance to train yards, preventing nonstriking workers from entering. Service began again early yesterday afternoon after SEPTA obtained a federal court injunction against the pickets.

headline: Court may lift Bible tax break
abstract: PA state sales tax exeption for certain religious items may be changed by the state Supreme Court. If religious items were taxed, PA could see a revenue increase of $1 million per year.

headline: Hands across the water: A bistate approach to jobs - A regional planning commission study urges a joint Pa. and N.J. effort to help those on welfare get work
abstract: According to a study by the Delaware Valley Regional Panning Commission, there are four major barriers that prevent welfare recipients in PA and New Jersey from being able to cross the state line in search of jobs. Marilou Wernecke, manager of comprehensive planning for the commission, said that 94 percent of welfare recipients don’t have access to cars, so they must rely on public transportation systems; however, it is often too expensive for welfare recipients to commute between the two states because they have to pay two fares each way. Wernecke is developing goals and strategies to help coordinate public transportation between PA and New Jersey, and she gave credit to a pilot program in PA that provides weekly transit vouchers for people on welfare who are searching for jobs.

headline: Legislation OK'd to protect AMP
abstract: The PA Senate agreed to shelter AMP Inc from a hostile takeover despite the second largest shareholder denouncing the action and most shareholders desiring to sell the company. The bill would require an eight-month waiting period following a takeover bid before shareholders could vote on a merger. Any vote for a merger must be unanimous and must be taken at the company's annual meeting. The law would expire after eight months.

headline: Democrats Fear Loss of Black Loyalty
abstract: Democratcs running for high office in diverse states are facing a loss of black votes, which is usually the highest supporting Democratic votes.

headline: No contests for Mascara, Stout, Daley
abstract: U.S. Representative Frank Mascara, PA Senator Barry Stout and PA Representative Peter Daley were all unopposed in the past election and were reelected easily. A brief summary of each one’s political career is provided in the article, and both Mascara and Stout vowed to continue fighting for the Mon/Fayette Expressway and Southern Beltway Project.

headline: 'Unknown' Dems
abstract: Post-Gazette talks about the lack of enthusiam Democratic have been able to get from voters. Post-Gazette hopes that Democrats get their voices together, get a good leader, and get their message heard.

headline: Courting Change
abstract: PA Supremem Court is being reapportioned and Republicans seeks to take control of it away from Democrats.

headline: Fair or fraud?
abstract: Plenty of other people are paying medical bills medical bills they don't owe, too, either because they're billed twice or they're billed for care that is covered by their health insurance.  As in Mooney's case, the amount for any one patient seems insignificant.  Collectively, though, the amounts may be quite large.

headline: Educating the educators
abstract: There should be more requirements and follow-ups on requirements of educators in Pennsylvania. The current legislation, House Bill 2100, may be an effective measure.

headline: Hunting ban misses mark
abstract: Due to pressure from sportsmen throughout PA, the PA Game Commission decided that it will collect more information before voting on its proposal to ban high-powered hunting rifles during deer season. Sportsmen questioned why the rifles were banned for deer but not small game and wondered why population dense regions were treated the same as sparse regions. The authors of the editorial are pleased with the Game Commission’s decision and believe that sportsmen cannot be ignored.

headline: Lots of credit to share for success of the beltway
abstract: Standar-Speaker talks about the new Southwest Beltway project and is happy with Govenor Tom Ridge, lawmakers, and PennDOT for finally getting the project started.

headline: Courts may take action agaisnt Shallenberger
abstract: PA courts want to take legal avctions agaisnt an 82-year old man, convicted of child molestation. Courts claim the man established a youth group with is a violation of his court order.

headline: Hearing to address impact of welfare reform - Panel to hear testimony, issue recommendations
abstract: A Community Hearing on Welfare Reform will be held in Monessen, and community leaders will hear testimony about what’s working and what isn’t working with Pennsylvania’s new welfare laws. Renee Warner, who has been relying on welfare assistance for the past 16 months, will testify at the hearing about the misconception that everyone on welfare is lazy, and she will talk about some of the obstacles in the system that make it difficult for welfare recipients to improve their conditions. According to a report compiled after a hearing in Aliquippa, the three major concerns were a lack of adequate transportation, caseworkers not informing recipients of special allowances they may be eligible to receive and inadequate information provided by caseworkers regarding Temporary Assistance for Needy Families options.

headline: Legislation to benefit credit unions
abstract: The US Senate dealt a setback to the banking industry by agreeing to legislation that would reverse the effect of a US Supreme Court decision and again allow credit unions to expand their memberships. It ends a bitter lobbying battle between the nation's banks and credit unions. Banking representatives argued that credit unions, which are exempt from federal income taxes and most state taxes, were using that advantage to grow at the expense of banks. The legislation grants credit unions limited authority to expand their memberships.

headline: Democrats focus effort on people power
abstract: Paul Politis, who is conducting a write-in campaign to challenge U.S. Congressman Bill Shuster for the Democratic primary, and former PA auditor general Don Bailey, who is challenging Ivan Itkin and William Kneisling for the Democratic gubernatorial primary, spoke at an annual Democratic Committee dinner. Politis admitted to forging signatures before, and there is no one to challenge Shuster in the primary. Bailey criticized Governor Ridge, and both candidates are at serious financial disadvantages compared to Governor Ridge and Congressman Shuster.

headline: No deal: Legislature fails to forge shield for AMP
abstract: AMP Incorporated is facing a $10 billion hostile takeover from Allied Signal Incorporated, so its president asked the PA Legislature for help in fending off the takeover. However, the state Senate’s leadership, Senators Joseph Loeper and Robert Jubelirer, refused to consider a bill passed by the House, and House Majority Leader John Perzel refused to consider a bill passed by the Senate. Fortunately for AMP, a federal judge’s decision will bide the company more time, and its president is hopeful that the Legislature will agree to pass a bill for Governor Tom Ridge to sign.

headline: Unregulated Money Rolls in While Politicians Call for Ban
abstract: Parties are aggressively expanding their efforts to raise and spend the largely unregulated political contributions known as soft money, even suing Federal elections officials in an attempt to remove the last restrictions on those donations. The two political parties pursuit of such money, generally made by wealthy individuals, corporations, and labor unions has already captured $94 million for Congressional elections this year, despite calls from President Clinton and members on both sides of the aisle for a ban on soft money.

headline: Courting cynicism
abstract: Post-Gazette criticizes Allegheny County for their deficits and 21.2% pay increase for Commwealth Court administrators.

headline: Family's dog fought with rabid racoon
abstract: After a fight with an infected raccoon, a local families dog was quarentined for 5 months. Rabies in animals and humans is examined and discussed in terms of effects, prevention, and treatment.

headline: Education focus of Pitts response to Clinton speech
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts gave a speech on national radio and television immediately after President Clinton’s address. Pitts spoke about American students’ math scores, which were lower than 14 other countries, and science scores, which were lower than 11 other countries. He also advocated his bill, Dollars in the Classroom, which would require 95 percent of federal funding be spent on classrooms, rather than the current rate in which 35 percent of all funding is spent on bureaucracy.

headline: Hunting fee hike gets ok
abstract: The state Senate has approved a bill that would increase hunting license fees to generate an extra $11.4 million for the Pennsylvania Game Commission starting next year.  In exchange for the added funding, the bill would curb some of the commission's law enforcement powers and require the agency to become more accountable to lawmakers and sportsmen.  The measure passed the Senate by a 43-5 vote yesterday.

headline: Magazine says Pa. roads improve
abstract: Overdrive, a trucking magazine, had rated the PA Turnpike and Interstate 80 as the nation’s worst roads based on a number of different factors for the past six years, but this year, an interstate highway in Alabama took over that distinction. Overall, truckers still voted Pennsylvania’s roads as worst in the country, but the state also received twice as many votes for the most improved category. A representative for the magazine travelled to PA to test out the roads, and she was pleasantly surprised with their conditions, which pleased PA transportation officials who have spent millions of dollars upgrading the state’s roads.

headline: Credit spread all around
abstract: Thanks to the efforts of Governor Tom Ridge and PA Senators Michael O’Pake and David Brightbill, Reading’s police force will receive a $500,000 crime-fighting grant from the state.

headline: House Democrats attack child-care plan for poor
abstract: State lawmakers are upset with Governor Ridge's  plan to raise costs to mothers for child care subsidies. Mother would pay more on co-payments and require criminal background check of providers.

headline: Legislature holds on gambling votes
abstract: All bets are off in the state House, where there will be no votes before session ends next week on referendums to expand gambling in Pennsylvania.  Under pressure from House GOP leaders, horse racing officials who wanted a referendum to allow slot machines at their tracks yesterday decided to postpone their work until the new year.  Supporters of riverboat casinos, video poker and keno also appeared to back down for now.

headline: Democrats Object  Clinton Says Matter is Now Up to Congress and the People
abstract: After a debate that lasted over three hours, the House of Representatives voted 258-176 to begin a full-scale inquiry into the possibility of impeaching President Clinton, which could eventually lead to a House vote on whether the Senate should begin a trial. The vote was mostly along party lines, but 31 Democrats joined Republicans in voting to begin the inquiry; many of whom are in close races in the upcoming election and fear being viewed as blindly following their party. President Clinton said the matter is now out of his hands, the Black Caucus was especially critical of the Republicans’ impeachment investigation and the article provides numerous quotes from representatives who spoke during the debate, including Paul McHale of PA, who is the only Democratic U.S. Representative to call for Clinton to resign.

headline: No evidence for Democrat surge
abstract: There's no evidence that the Democrats are closing on the Republicans. Several pollsters agree the Republicans are on course to pick up seats on Nov. 3. Democrats have handle budget issues and government shutdown more skillfully than the Republicans have.

headline: 'Up-or-down' vote leaves public out of process
abstract: According to the author, the Republican-controlled PA Legislature and Governor Tom Ridge are keeping the minority party and the public in the dark on nearly every controversial issue. For example, the Senate voted on a bill that would allow school district voters to decide whether to shift nuisance taxes and a portion of property taxes to local wage taxes; however, there were no public hearings on the issue, and Democrats complained they didn’t receive significant details on the bill until the day before the vote. Democrats have been especially critical of Republicans for using the Senate Rules Committee, which allowed Senator Melissa Hart to easily insert the tax reform amendment, and Senate Democratic Leader Robert Mellow, who voted against it, said Republican techniques go against the democratic process.

headline: Cox withdraws, says Livingston will be next speaker
abstract: U.S. Representative Chris Cox withdrew as a candidate for speaker of the House, so Representative Bob Livingston will almost certainly succeed Newt Gingrich as Congress’s top leader. Gingrich, who many have blamed for the party’s loss of five House seats in the past election, made the surprising announcement that he would be stepping down and would not seek re-election. Cox offered his support for Livingston, and while Majority Whip Tom DeLay will most likely retain his leadership position, Majority Leader Dick Armey faces mounting criticism and the very real possibility of being unseated by several potential challengers, including Representatives Steve Largent, Jennifer Dunn and Dennis Hastert.

headline: FDA panel Oks tamoxifen to cut breast cancer risk
abstract: Women who are healthy but at high risk of getting breast cancer should be allowed to take the drug tamoxifen to reduce their risk even though the drug can cause serious side effects, government scientists said yesterday.  The decision by advisers to the Food and Drug Administration was a reluctant one, because tamoxifen doubles women's risk of uterine cancer, triples the risk of a potentially deadly blood clot and increases the chances of cataracts --- all in women who don't have breast cancer.  In a second potentially critical advance against breast cancer, the advisory panel also recommended that thousands of American woman be allowed to us a genetically engineered drug that promises to help stave off an advanced form of the disease.

headline: Education for teacher makes sense
abstract: The Valley News Dispatch explores the possiblity of recertification requirements for teachers in Pennsylvania.

headline: Hunting forum begins
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is concerned about preserving hunting in Pennsylvania for future generations. Over 700 people from across the country and Canada are expected to attend the Governor's Symposium on North America's Hunting Heritage. The symposium will talk about recruitment programs, as well as the ways to boost the image of hunters in the non-hunting public's eye.

headline: Maglev project must move forward
abstract: Bill Robinso believes that Pennsylvania should adopt a new Maglev transportation system as it would benefit the economy.

headline: Crime bills fail to pass in term
abstract: In September, PA GOP leaders introduced over a dozen bills to fight school violence, however, in a popular election year which should have ensure their safe passage, the bills failed to be addressed. Once a top priority of House Maj. Leader John Perzel, competing interests and unrelated issues derailed original plans. Proposals included millions for school security and mandatory sentencing for juveniles. The Senate ignored or gutted most of the bills, Sen. Jeffrey Piccola saying he preferred identifying classroom troublemakers and removing them. School violence never became an issue in elections.

headline: Labor-backed seniors pan Santorum plan to privatize
abstract: As President Clinton discussed the future of Social Security, nearly 2,000 senior citizens converged on Capitol hill to oppose plans such as US Sen. Rick Santorum's proposal to partially privatize the system. Before a crowd of mostly retired Steelworkers Organization of Active Retirees, House Minority Whip David E. Boniour said such proposals would weaken the system, not strengthen it. The system is projected to run out of reserves by 2032. More than 350 Pennsylvanians met with US Rep. Phil English, congressional staffers and representatives of the National Council of Senior Citizens.

headline: Licensing system is targeted for overhaul  LCB chief wants to get rid of town quotas
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board (LCB) has introduced a proposal that would get rid of its quota system which sets a specific number of liquor licenses that are allocated for each township. The LCB estimates 5% of available licenses throughout the state are not being used; however, there are many high-demand areas where it is exceedingly difficult or expensive to obtain a liquor license. A "resort area" exception to the quota system is being abused, so the LCB also proposed a non-transferrable economic development license, which could be purchased by restaurants that make 70% of their revenue from food sales; however, the proposals have been challenged by many current owners of liquor licenses because the value of their licenses could be severely depreciated.

headline: Democrats outnumbered
abstract: It appears that the number of registered Republicans out numbers the number of registered Democrats, which may cause concerns for the upcoming election.

headline: No pacts in 56 state districts
abstract: Act 88 is believed to have reduced the number of teachers that have gone on strike. Of all the teachers currently negotiating contracts with their school districts only 3% are predicted to go on strike.

headline: 'Up-or-down' vote leaves public out of process
abstract: Brad Bumsted write about the stuggles a minority party in Congress faces when arguing for or against bills.

headline: Cranberry votes can bring power
abstract: Cranberry is one of the fastest growing municipalities in southwestern PA, but most of its residents move there from other places, so the theory goes that they tend not to vote in most elections because they lack attachments to local politics. One of the township's supervisors, Richard Hadley, has been working with a committee to increase voter turnout by publishing occasional newsletters. Increased voter turnout could potentially give Cranberry more political power that could lead to increased state and county funding.

headline: Filer lists her priorities in letter to legislators
abstract: Wanda Filer resigned as the state’s first physician general, and during public interviews, she harshly criticized Governor Ridge’s Administration for ignoring her, not inviting her to staff meetings and reprimanding her for not being a team player. State Senate Minority Leader Robert Mellow congratulated Filer for her work, and Representative Elinor Taylor was extremely critical of the Ridge administration, whereas Ridge has been virtually silent over Filer’s resignation and is searching for a replacement. Just before resigning, Filer wrote a five-page letter to all 253 state legislators, and in the letter, which is printed in the article, she makes some final policy recommendations on ten different issues, including diabetes monitoring, mandates, tobacco, Pennsylvanians with no health insurance, emerging infectious diseases, school health and school based health centers, state community health centers, telemedicine, managed care and reproductive health.

headline: Education tops ridge's priorities
abstract: York County's state lawmakers looked first in the thin, staple-bound booklets titled "Basic education Funding." Most of PA Governor Tom Ridge's general budget proposals were contained in a much chunkier book, a glossy volume the size of a metropolitan phone directory. But many legislators still had not broken its jacket late Tuesday afternoon. Ridge's budget proposal for 1998-99 would increase funding for PA's local school districts by $120 million, a 3.5 percent increase, and direct the bulk of it to poorer districts.

headline: Hunting license controls criticized
abstract: PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. found that the PA Game Commission doesn’t have sufficient controls to prevent the issuance of new licenses to hunters who have had their permits revoked or suspended for a number of different reasons. John Shutter, assistant director of the agency’s law enforcement bureau, acknowledged the problem does exist, but only a couple dozen are given out each year, and the agency is looking into a computerized system for the future. Casey’s audit also found problems with other areas of the Game Commission, but Shutter laughed off some of these findings as extremely minor.

headline: Maglev technology, funding cause concerns
abstract: Allegheny county is looking into establishing a magnetic levitation transit system to transport riders between Grant Street to the Civic Area. There are some concerns about the technology.

headline: Crime prevention conference slated
abstract: An African-American crime prevention conference will be held in Philadelphia and is expected to turn out more than 500 participants.

headline: Legislator fights fees on seniors' checks
abstract: PA Representative George Hasay is introducing a resolution urging the elimination of fees on the bank accounts of senior citizens who receive Social Security or other government benefits via an electronic deposit into their bank accounts. Electronic banking will make accessing money easier, and it could save the U.S. government millions of dollars a year. However, Hasay said many banks assess fees for services that had previously been free, which he wants the federal comptroller of currency to develop regulations to end.

headline: Liquor law change on tap after fire company raid
abstract: The PA House approved a bill sponsored by PA Representatives Steven Nickol and Stephen Maitland which was made in response to an incident in February where Buchanan Valley Fire Co. was charged with selling alcohol without a license at a fundraiser. The bill is intended to make it easier for non-profit organizations to sell alcohol at fundraising events if they obtain special occasion permits. However, Robert Kimple Jr., president of the fire company, doesn’t believe that the fire department should be required to obtain a special occasion permit because he believes alcohol is offered for free to anyone who chooses to drink, whereas the PA State Police consider it to be selling alcohol if tickets are required to attend the event.

headline: Democrats seek candidate to face English
abstract: Tom Talarico was approached by a number of different people to consider running against incumbent U.S. Representative Phil English, but he decided that he would rather continue his work as an Erie attorney. Larry Clemens, a Mercer County educator, has emerged as a potential Democratic candidate against English, yet his spokeswoman said that he is still only considering running. The Democratic Party is still searching for a candidate, and former PA state Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll approached a number of female candidates who have taken themselves out of the running.

headline: No quick response on lobbying reform
abstract: The loss of eligibility by Curtis Enis to play football at Penn State for accepting gifts from a sports agent, has led to new legislation. PA Gov. Rendell signed a bill that will require agents operating in PA to register with the PA Athletic Commission before the month's end. However, the regulations on lobbyists, editors point out, are much more difficult to enact. A law was eventually approved that upgrades rules on reporting lobbying expenditures and limits gift-giving by this source to our elected representatives. Perhaps what is needed to ensure an adequate address is a lobbying scandal.

headline: us
abstract: There is a quote listed by PA Senator Leonard Bodack, who tried to require HMOs to pay for diabetes supplies. He basically says that he’s disappointed that it did not pass, but that’s not the end of it.

headline: Credit union bill could cost government
abstract: Representative Paul Kanjorski's prosed credit union bill is causing concern because it may end up  costing the government $217 million in costs.

headline: Finding health policy in Pennsylvania is no easy task
abstract: What if you need health insurance and don't know how to go about it?  Your options differ dramatically depending in what state you live in.  New Jersey has a setup that makes finding the best deal on health insurance easy.  Pennsylvania and Delaware have a system that makes finding a good deal almost impossible.

headline: Education-assistance bill back on track: An affirmative-action amendment that had threatened the measure was likely to be defeated.
abstract: A bill is being considered in Congress which would provide aid for middle-class and low-income students who are pursuing post-high school education. The bill would also incorporate a number of other provisions that are described in the article, and it has a good chance of being passed and signed by President Clinton. Clinton said that he would veto the bill if it included an amendment sponsored by U.S. Representative Frank Riggs to prevent universities from using affirmative-action when admitting students; however, the amendment seemed to be heading towards defeat in the House last night.

headline: Hunting revenue generates millions in Pennsylvania
abstract: According to a recent study conducted for the International Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies, hunting supports more than 20,000 jobs in Pennsylvania. According to the economic analysis, the state's 879,000 hunters spent $757.4 million in 1996 and supported 20, 243 jobs across the state. County Commissioners in the Elk County last week threw their support behind a park where tourists could see the animals.

headline: Magnetic levitation train may head to Pa.
abstract: Federal transportation legislation has already committed $55 million to study the feasibility of magnetic levitation trains or maglev, and eventually, a winning proposal will be given $950 million by the Federal Railroad Administration for the construction of a maglev system. Maglev trains use magnets to propel them to speeds of over 300 miles per hour, and if Maglev Incorporated’s proposal is accepted, PA could have a system that stretches from Pittsburgh to Philadelphia. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter backs the proposal, and he recently travelled to Germany to ride the only operational maglev system in the world.

headline: Criminals who love to hunt turn to state for guns
abstract: One guy ripped off $60 worth of items from a snack bar 38 years ago. Another broke into a store and swiped some cigars in 1956. And a Marysville man broke into a car in 1970. Since then, all three have acknowledged their illegal activities and led crime-free lives. But such misdeeds are incredibly coming back to haunt hunters. People convicted of crimes cannot own guns, so hunters don't know what to do. They are asking the Pardons board for help.

headline: Local kids' welfare system OK in state fine scare
abstract: PA may have to pay a $4.5 million federal fine because of the state’s delays in implementing a new computer system that takes care of the collection and disbursement of child support payments and helps find the location of parents who are delinquent in their payments. However, Huntingdon County is one of 45 counties throughout the state that already has the program. President Clinton and Congress have agreed to ease financial penalties for states putting in a "good faith effort" to implement the system, and the PA Public Welfare Department is working to comply with federal regulations.

headline: Liquor license reform possible in Pennsylvania: Ruby Tuesday's may be stalled
abstract: As of now, a Ruby Tuesday’s restaurant cannot obtain its liquor license because each municipality has a specific number to give out, and Norwegian Township, where the restaurant is being built, has no more available licenses. However, a bill being sponsored by Frank Serfafinni and potentially cosponsored by State Representative Bob Allen could change the regulations by making the distribution of liquor licenses a countywide quota system, which would allow the restaurant to obtain an open license from nearby Tremont Township.

headline: Democrats seek Senate vote on lobby disclosure
abstract: PA Senate Democrats will force a vote on a lobby disclosure in the Appropriations Committee. Supporters say there is little chance the measure will work however. PA has what is widely regarded as the nation's weakest legislative lobbying disclosure law. The discharge resolution is expected to be sponsored by Sen. Minority Leader Robert Mellow and Minority Whip Leonard Bodack. A spokesman for Sen. President Pro Tem Robert Jubelirer says the approach by Democrats usually is taken in the case of legislation that is forgotten, which is not the case with the lobby reform bill.

headline: No regrets for Neal on eve of his last day - Says he was "honored" despite controversy
abstract: On the evening before Richard Neal’s last day as Philadelphia Police Commissioner, he held a press conference, where he said he doesn’t have any regrets or bitterness from his five and a half years on the job. He said he had already wished incoming commissioner, John Timoney, the best of luck, and he offered some words of advice to his successor. Neal, whose career began walking the beat in West Philadelphia in 1962, has accepted consulting positions with Drexel University and Penn’s Landing Corporation, and at the conference, he did face a difficult question about Drexel’s decision to hold an All-Star baseball game after recent shootings.

headline: Veon sweeps to eighth term in 14th Legislative District
abstract: Matthew Heidorn lost to Democratic incumbent Mike Veon for a seat to represent the 14th Legislative District in the PA House; however, he said he didn’t care because he had planned to move to Ohio next year anyway. He’s been planning to move since May, but Republicans convinced him to stay in the race nonetheless. Veon won the election easily, which Heidorn claimed could be explained by his own lack of effort, whereas Veon saw the vote as the result of his track record and dedicated campaigning.

headline: Cullen Makes It Official: Democrat Running For McDade's Seat
abstract: Joe Cullen failed to defeat U.S. Representative Joseph McDade two years ago, but he is challenging again for the Democratic nomination for a seat in the 10th Congressional District now that McDade is set to retire. He plans to release a five point plan next week on how to wisely use the anticipated federal budget surplus. His key competitor is Patrick Casey, the son of former Governor Robert Casey, and he believes that voters will look past his famous name to choose the most qualified candidate.

headline: First do no harm
abstract: The movers and shakers in the health-care industry in Pittsburgh, the ones with the vision for the future and the power to do something about it, are pretty much all thinking about market share.  And that's an unsettling reality.  It has brought us to this pass: The insurer that covers two-thirds of the region's families and the hospital conglomerate that controls nearly half of the acute care beds are in a test of wills that could leave thousands without access to the care they need and want.

headline: Embattled university president resigns
abstract: Lincoln University President Niara Sudarkasa resigned less than a week after PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. released a report criticizing top administrators for mismanaging and wasting funds, such as spending $532,000 on the president’s house. The state has withheld $11 million in funds for the university, and Casey recommended withholding the money until the university fixes problems identified by the audit. PA Senator Vincent Fumo was pleased that Sudarkasa resigned, but he is calling on the Attorney General to begin a criminal investigation.

headline: Hunt's on for data
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission has unveiled a new project that will reward hunters luck enough to harvest ring-necked pheasant an aluminum leg band. The commission thinks its $3 million investment in the pheasant program would pay better dividends if more hunters bagged more birds. Commission officials have revealed that they expect to dole out between $55,000 and $110,000 in rewards.

headline: Major work planned on Route 28 near Etna
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is scheduled to begin construction on one of the most dangerous intersections in the state, Route 28 near Etna.

headline: Crossin snubs state ethics law
abstract: Luzerne County Commissioner Frank Crossin violated Pennsylvania’s ethics law by voting to approve a $1,500 payment to his own insurance company. Crossin said his insurance company has been selling bonds to county tax collectors for years, and he didn’t realize he was violating the law when voting. If any county resident files a complaint, the state Ethics Commission would have to investigate, but the agency’s executive director, John Contino, said the commission usually doesn’t seek criminal or civil penalties unless someone knowingly breaks the law.

headline: Maryland Session A Success For Poor - Reversing Trend, Spending Increased
abstract: Maryland has changed course after years of cutting funding for social programs, and the General Assembly and Governor Parris Glendening have passed numerous plans to benefit poor families. The booming economy has allowed Maryland to cut income taxes and expand the income tax credit for low-income people, which helps the working poor. Overall, advocates for the poor agree the current legislative session has been overwhelmingly successful, and in addition to the tax credit, the state expanded health insurance coverage to 60,000 poor children and pregnant women, created a new emergency food program, doubled funding to prevent homelessness, set aside $850,000 to provide food assistance to pregnant women and small children and expanded property tax breaks for low-income elderly and disabled people.

headline: Lobbyists politiked for AMP
abstract: When John Perzel was first elected state House majority leader, he decided to introduce himself to the biggest private employer in the Harrisburg area. Perzel set up a meeting with Swatara Twp-based AMP Inc. He was cordially greeted by company leaders, but was soon curtly told the company really didn't have much need for state government. AMP, it was explained, is an international company that mostly deal in Washington. A few weeks ago they met again. But this time it was AMP CEO Robert Ripp who wanted the meeting. He was seeking legislative support to strengthen the state's anti-takeover law to fend off a $10 billion hostile takeover from AlliedSignal.

headline: Democrats' small gain could give Ridge grief
abstract: Despite Governor Ridge’s landslide reelection victory, Republicans were unable to capitalize in the state House, where Democrats picked up one seat. Representative H. William DeWeese, the House’s ranking Democrat, hoped to capitalize on the momentum, but House Majority Leader John Perzel’s spokesman reminded them that Republicans still retained control of the House. The reelection results won’t make it easier for Ridge to pass some controversial issues he intends to pursue, including a plan to allocate at least $300 million to build new stadiums and a proposal to provide vouchers to parents, so they could send their children to a school of their choosing.

headline: No title
abstract: The photo depicts PA Representative Rod Wilt and three 4-H members, who met with legislators and toured the state capitol building.

headline: Veteran area lawmaker campaigning to replace Pa. House Democratic Leader - Tigue faces uphill battle
abstract: PA Representative Thomas Tigue is trying to unseat House Democratic Leader William DeWeese, but according to Representative Joseph Battisto, he faces an uphill battle. The 100 House Democrats will elect their leadership on November 24th by secret ballots, and while Democrats are the minority caucus, House Majority Leader John Perzel has needed their help to pass major pieces of legislation. If Tigue wins the post, Barrett and Coolbaugh Townships would be represented by both the House minority leader and Senate Minority Leader Robert Mellow.

headline: Cullen will run again for the seat
abstract: Joe Cullen will announce his intent to run for Congresssional district 10.

headline: Florida Alters Care's Balance
abstract: Florida is one of the nation’s leading states in efforts to address concerns with health maintenance organizations (HMOs), and it has passed laws that make it easier for someone to seek emergency care, file grievances and see certain specialists, including dermatologists, without obtaining a prior referral. Congress is debating legislation that would mandate many of Florida’s HMO laws at the national level. The number of people on HMOs in Florida, especially in Miami, is extremely high when compared to the majority of the rest of the nation, and while many have benefited from Florida’s laws, health insurance companies’ costs have risen substantially because of them.

headline: END GAME - Lawmakers snub worthwhile bills
abstract: According to the editorial, the PA Legislature’s final days will likely be dominated by school vouchers, stadium financing and the expansion of legalized gambling; however, there are many other bills of equal importance that won’t be addressed and face little opposition, including bills dealing with the child welfare system, school violence and various others. The authors agree with statements made by state Representative Katie True and Senator Alan Kukovich, and they feel far too often legislation is created to further political agendas.

headline: Ill-gotten game
abstract: Hunters and fisherman have long complained that Game Commission officers run roughshod over them out in the field.  They have wide latitude in conducting searches for contraband or illegal game.  They don't have to get warrants to search vehicles or people, and they aren't held to the same standards of probable cause as other police officers.

headline: Making I-80 a toll road would help give Pennsylvania better roads
abstract: The authors support the addition of tolls on Interstate 80 because it’s a premier road, and it is already a toll road in Ohio. They argue that even with the decision to raise the gasoline tax, which was approved by Governor Tom Ridge and the PA Legislature, the PA Department of Transportation still doesn’t have enough money to properly maintain all of the state’s roads. They dispute claims from U.S. Representative Phil English and truckers who oppose tolling the road, and they suggest tolling I-80 would bring much needed revenue from out-of-state travelers.

headline: Custody and Cruelty: A judge runs roughshod over a mother's rights
abstract: Judge Robert C. Reed takes harsh critcisim for terminating the rights of a young mother because she may become unfit in the future and private citizens seek adoption of her child.

headline: Monroe's welfare-to-work effort performs well
abstract: Monroe County Board of Assistance spokeswoman Terry Blair told members of the Welfare Reform Task Force that the county scored well in the number of people who have left public assistance and the number of these people who have found work. She said the county performed significantly better than average throughout PA.

headline: Local credit unions confident Congress will step in
abstract: PA Credit Union League is hoping Congress will step in and help credit unions who took a hit from the Supreme Court ruling banning them from extending membership to individuals outside of company's.

headline: Democrats still behind in quest for cash
abstract: Governor Ridge has spent 15 times more than all four Democratic gubernatorial candidates have even raised, and he has raised $1.5 million since the beginning of the year compared to PA Representative Ivan Itkin, who is the leading Democratic fundraiser with less than $40,000 raised. Don Bailey has raised $11,750, William Keisling raised $1,050, lieutenant gubernatorial candidate Marjorie Margolies Mezvinsky raised $12,375 and gubernatorial candidate Phil Berg’s campaign is likely over due to a court ruling. According to one political analyst, it seems like nobody inside or outside the Democratic Party has much interest in the Democratic candidates.

headline: North Hills mystery: Why is the able Rep. Orie facing a primary challenge?
abstract: The authors of the editorial question why PA Representative Jane Orie is being challenged by Douglas Yauger in the upcoming Republican primary election, and they endorse Orie. Orie is supported by House Republican leaders, but Yauger is supported by PA Senator Melissa Hart, which Orie believes could be traced to her decision to break party ranks and come out against a proposal supported by Hart to raise the county sales tax to fund regional projects. A difference between the two candidates is that Yauger believes the Regional Asset District tax is unconstitutional, whereas Orie recognizes it serves a purpose.

headline: Video arraignments low priorty in crime, delinquency spending
abstract: Butle Eagle makes suggetions to the Pennsylvania Crime Comission on ways to wisely spend money and their time and effort should be devoted to imprtant criminal issues.

headline: DA Fits GOP Profile
abstract: Republicans want District Attorney Michael Barrasse to run for a U.S. Representative seat but Mr. Barrasse has not yet decided if he will run.

headline: Flu more prevalent this season
abstract: Health officials in 44 states have reported above average cases of the flu, and it is causing more severe illness than usual. Scientists are pleased that it has been over a month since the last case of bird flu; though they remain wary that it could strike again. There were 18 confirmed cases of bird flu and six deaths, but they were all limited to Hong Kong.

headline: Federal spending bill includes funds for arts center
abstract: The Whitaker Center for Science and the Arts is less than a million dollars shy from its $51 million fundraising goal after President Clinton approved a spending bill which includes $1.75 million for the center. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter played a key role in getting the center the funds. The Whitaker Center will be the nation’s first place to house science and the arts together, and it also will receive funding from the Allied Arts Fund.

headline: Improvements at Kooser State Park
abstract: New Enterprise has donated the use of a track-hoe machine and an operator for a project to remove eight feet of silt from the bottom of Kooser Lake. The project at Kooser State Park should improve fishing and swimming, and fish have already begun moving upstream into Kooser Run. The PA Fish and Boat Commission will also restock the park by adding 1,300 trout to the lake and 1,100 to the stream in time for the opening of trout season.

headline: Mandatory driver ed
abstract: The authors argue Bethlehem lawyer Mark Sigmon made a compelling case for mandatory driver education courses in Pennsylvania’s schools at the PA Department of Transportation’s Young Driver Symposium. As of now, some schools have such programs, while others do not; however, state Representative Steven Nickol said he can’t envision funding driver education courses until there are improvements in their quality. The authors believe the only way to improve the quality of driver education courses is to make them mandatory, so the state should provide funding to do so.

headline: DA under fire, again
abstract: York County District Attorney H. Stanley Rebert had assured the defense attorney for Carlos Gene Moose Jr. that he would not use a statement from a jailhouse informant; however, he called that informant to the stand, and his statement was used to convict Moose in 1988. Seven years later, Moose’s conviction was overturned because of the statement, he pleaded guilty to lesser charges, and Rebert was reviewed by the state disciplinary board, which decided not to discipline him. The state Supreme Court looked at the case and decided upon a new definition of the law that classified Rebert’s actions as "reckless," and they told the disciplinary board to review Rebert yet again in a confidential opinion that ended up going public in 1995.

headline: Moving Beyond Simply 'Saving' Social Security
abstract: President Clinton changed the budget debate by suggesting any part of the new budget surplus go to social security. Saving social security has long been a goal of US Senator Kerrey, who suggested cutting the payroll tax to allow citizens to privatize social security. Where the idea was once unpopular, it is now supported by a number of Senators, including John Breaux and Patrick Moynihan. Kerrey argues salvaging social security is also the key to saving Medicare. Kerrey's proposal relies on allowing individual wealth to foster so that social security and Medicare will not be utilized.

headline: Lock Haven's mayor might have conflict of interest: LCB to rule whether owner of hotel licensed to sell liquor can hold office.
abstract: Harold Yost has been Lock Haven’s mayor for three years; however, he could be forced out of office because of a PA Liquor Control Board (PLCB) regulation that prohibits an elected or appointed public official from having an interest in an establishment where liquor is served. Yost owns the Eagle Hotel, which serves alcohol, but he was told by the PLCB six years ago that there was no conflict in interest while he was running for City Council. Yost doesn’t believe there is a conflict of interest, but he said he will give up the position as mayor if the PLCB makes him choose between it and his restaurant.

headline: Democrats Strike Gold Using Direct-Mail Drives Aimed at Small Donors Amid Probe of Big Givers
abstract: Ever since the Democratic Party lost control of Congress in 1994, it has been increasingly reliant on small donors through mailing drives to raise money for the party’s congressional elections. During the first six months of this year, Democrats have raised $9.9 million from small donors, composed largely of seniors who donate modest amounts of money. The money has helped offset losses from big corporations, which may be scared off by the possibility of a special investigation into illegal campaign financing in the 1996 election, and the mailing campaigns require a significant amount of researching and experimenting to reach out to potential donors.

headline: Northeast Finally Gets Commissioner
abstract: After over two years, northeastern PA finally has a representative on the PA Game Commission to replace Commissioner Edward Vogue. Last year, Andy Mizzanti was nominated, but area politicians and sportsmen clubs opposed him, so he was not confirmed by the state Senate. However, George J. Venesky was nominated by Governor Ridge and was confirmed by the Senate.

headline: Video poker: Stick with legal or illegal
abstract: PA Supreme Court strikes down video poker convictions for two Allegheny County men. It is time for video poker to have a set legal status in PA.

headline: Dan Quayle Is Right Again
abstract: The author, Charles Krauthammer, says that Dan Quayle was right during a 1992 vice presidential debate with Al Gore for repeatedly saying "Bill Clinton has trouble telling the truth." Krauthammer calls the Republican Party stupid for releasing video tapes of Clinton during Kenneth Starr’s investigation, which despite showing a number of instances where Clinton perjured himself, still managed to put him in favorable light. Krauthammer says Clinton has encouraged numerous people to lie, and the honorable thing for him to do would resign, which Clinton has no intentions of doing.

headline: Get in the game
abstract: Allegheny’s bankrupt health care system is trying to sell its Philadelphia hospitals to the highest for-profit bidder to pay off creditors, but the authors believe the organization lost all its credibility, which makes an independent perspective needed. They believe the sale of the hospitals to nonprofit ownership would be best for the community, and they think that U.S. Bankruptcy Court Judge M. Bruce McCullough should extend the auction deadline to allow nonprofits to make a bid on the hospitals. Mayor Rendell supports the nonprofit route, and the authors urge PA Attorney General Mike Fisher to become more active in the process.

headline: Fewer Children Per Care Provider Is Good for All
abstract: A Florida study shows that the lower the ratio (child care provider: child) the better child behavior was and the better teacher turnover rates were.

headline: Independence a must for the PGC
abstract: The PA Game Commission receives all of its money from hunting license fees, fines and federal taxes on sporting equipment, so it doesn’t receive any money from the state’s budget. The Commission, however, is asking the General Assembly to approve an increase in license fees, but lawmakers may be hesitant to approve the increase due to a number of complaints, mostly about the Commission’s law enforcement branch. The authors of the editorial believe that increased accountability could help weed out the few bad officers, and they hope the Commission continues to retain its autonomy to prevent control by legislators.

headline: Medics, doctors ask Ridge to veto revised helmet law
abstract: Doctors are hoping that the motorcycle helmet law will not be repealed, as there are too many health concerns associated with it.

headline: Dam safety bill awaits Ridge's signature
abstract: The PA Legislature passed a dam safety bill that awaits Governor Tom Ridge’s signature. The bill was drafted by Representative Todd Platts following the death of Joseph Keller, who died after jumping into the Conewago Creek to save a girl. The bill would require dam owners to install buoys and sings warning the public about the dangers of swimming near dams, and it would fine dams that don’t comply.

headline: New welfare debit cards making life harder for some recipients
abstract: The PA Department of Public Welfare began replacing food stamps with new debit cards in January, and while most people seem to support the new debit cards, it is causing problems for many of the state’s elderly and disabled populations. Disabilities’ issues only affect about 15 to 20 percent of the state’s food-stamp recipients, but organizations for the disabled argue the state has an obligation to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act by making the system more easily accessible. A spokeswoman for the Welfare Department said accommodations would be made for those in need.

headline: McCall addresses stadium funding issue
abstract: PA Representative Keith McCall clarified the House of Representative’s position over the repeal of bill that had been previously passed. McCall said the original bill was never intended to provide funding for stadiums in Pittsburgh, but a small group of people misinterpreted it. McCall gave the Local Government Commission and Governor Tom Ridge credit for working to repeal the bill.

headline: Democrats to slug it out for key positions in the House
abstract: 15 State lawmakers are currently campagining for 7 lHouse Democrat leadership positions.

headline: Not ready to adjourn
abstract: Despite the protests of PA Senator Jack Wagner, the Senate approved a resolution to adjourn for the summer, with Republicans supporting the resolution and Democrats opposing it.

headline: Vitali, Kelly to square off at debate
abstract: The two candidates for the 166th District seat in the PA House, Democrat Greg Vitali and Republican Joe Kelly, will have a debate sponsored by the Hilltop Civic Association. After Kelly canceled a debate sponsored by the League of Women Voters due to concerns that he would be treated unfairly, Vitali agreed to attend the Hilltop Civic Association’s debate, which he had previously declined.

headline: Dance away Valentine's Day
abstract: Johnny Yudichak holds a Valentine's dance fundraiser for his campaign against Stanley Jarolin for State Representative.

headline: Good news I: Pa. program to insure more children
abstract: The state government had a surplus of over $650 million last fiscal year, and it has put some of this money toward the state’s Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP), which provides health insurance for children whose parents don’t qualify for medical assistance but cannot afford to purchase health care. The increased spending of $15 million by the state could be matched by $600 million in federal funding over five years, and the money will be used to expand the age and eligibility requirements of CHIP. In the editorial’s opinion, the state is spending its money wisely, and hopefully, parents will take advantage of these benefits.

headline: Forum will look at teacher salarues
abstract: Dickinson College hosts a forum to discuss the findings of a study comparing teacher salaries in the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: It's time to catch up
abstract: The "Right to Hunt and Fish"  Amendment to the PA Constitution was introduced by PA Senator Bill Slocum, and the Governor’s Sportsmen Advisory Council will meet to discuss Senate Bill 1233. The PA Fish & Boat Commission is considering changing the regulations on Kettle Creek from Delayed Harvest Artificial Lures Only to Delayed Harvest, Fly Fishing Only, which is endorsed by Bill Sabatose and the Kettle Creek Watershed Association; though anglers are encouraged to share their opinions. In addition, Tom Ridge nominated Rozell Stidd for the PA Fish & Commission Board of Commissioners, Robert Gilford is being considered to fill a vacant spot of the Board of Commissioners for the PA Game Commission, there will be a Walleye Anglers Team Challenge and there will be an upcoming 3-D archery event.

headline: Meetings with mediator called, SEPTA outlines contract proposals
abstract: 5,200 workers for the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority have been on strike since June 1, which affects about 435,000 people. Union negotiators recently stormed out of a bargaining session, while SEPTA officials published a highly critical advertisement in Philadelphia’s daily newspapers that apologized for the union’s behavior and listed the offers SEPTA is making. A spokesman for Governor Tom Ridge said both sides will meet with a state mediator separately to discuss the issues, and the Democratic National Committee, which is looking at Philadelphia as a potential site for its 2000 convention, cut their visit to the city short because of the strike.

headline: Death Penalty Action Week
abstract: List of events for Death Penalty Action Week.

headline: New Welfare: Poor pay for the poor
abstract: PA is changing the current welfare system dealing with child care co-pay. Families may see an increase in co-pay, as other families will see a decrease.

headline: Medical savings account usage low
abstract: The insurance industry reacted quickly to a new federal law that was intended to promote the use of medical savings accounts (MSAs), which allow depositors to withdraw money for medical expenses without it being taxed. The actual demand for these type of accounts has been much lower than the industry anticipated, but Senator Rick Santorum, who first introduced a bill to Congress to create MSAs, believes that the demand will continue to increase over time. The PA Insurance Department expects more people to file for MSAs after they realize the money they could have saved after filing for taxes this year, and there are some insurance companies that have done reasonably well in selling MSAs.

headline: Democrats want to meet once again
abstract: After being asked by Republicans during a PA House Education Committee meeting why the Democratic caucus was holding a meeting since the House was set to recess at the end of the day, Representative Ronald Conwell, a Democrat, joked, "It’s to find out what we did." In other news, PA Secretary of State Yvette Kane became the fifth cabinet secretary under Governor Tom Ridge to resign. She was nominated by President Clinton to serve as a U.S. District Court judge.

headline: Not ready to adjourn
abstract: While lawmakers voted to end session early and resume in Septemeber, Senator Jack Wagner argued to keep session ongoing to consider important building code legislation.

headline: Vote now on state lobby reform
abstract: Editors believe lawmakers, back from a long recess, are more focused on the upcoming election and have submitted proposals to cater to constituents rather than substantive business. This includes a package of school violence bills by House Republicans. House Maj. Leader John Perzel is refusing to schedule a vote on the state's lax lobbying regulations. Perzel claims he is withholding a vote to prevent Democrats from sabotaging the bill. Democrats say Perzel just does not want to lose lobbying money. PA voters deserve a clearer picture of how special interests are influencing lawmakers.

headline: Dates to remember for primary election
abstract: Important dates from the PA Department of State are provided for the upcoming primary election.

headline: GOP, Democrats duel over HMO reform plans
abstract: There has been a rush for both Democrats and Republicans to address problems with managed health care plans, which political consultants have advised will be a key issue in this year’s national elections. Both parties claim that they want to improve HMO regulations; however Mark Merritt, vice president of the American Association of Health Plans, is skeptical of their intentions and believes they’ve turned health care into a political battle. The two parties disagree on number of issues, including accountability, specialists and an expansion of Medical Savings Accounts, and a number of House and Senate leaders from both sides are working to produce a bill to vote on.

headline: Fox measure would increase exemption for college savings
abstract: U.S. Congressman Jon Fox introduced the Education Savings Account bill to help families save for college. Under current law, a tax-exempt amount of $500 can be put into an account to save for college each year, but Fox’s bill would increase that amount to $5,000 a year. Fox is concerned that parents aren’t saving enough money early to send their children to college, and the president of Gwynedd Mercy College hopes his initiative helps show parents the importance of saving money for college.

headline: Judge upholds confiscation of wolf hybrids
abstract: Judge H. William White agreed with the PA Game Commission’s decision to confiscate two wolf hybrid cubs that were purchased illegally. The two people who purchased the cubs argued in court that they should be returned to them because they were domestic animals and therefore, didn’t violate the state game law’s requirements for a special permit and restrictions for "exotic animals." Since the cubs were only 25% dog and 75% wolf, White considered them more dangerous, so the cubs will not be returned to their owners and could potentially be euthanized by the Game Commission.

headline: Mild weather saves money for PennDOT
abstract: At this time last year, the PA Department of Transportation had spent $233,000 and 3,330 hours on cleaning up roads due to wintery conditions, but so far this year, winter has been quite mild. The mild weather has saved PennDOT thousands of dollars, and its workers have been able to focus on other roadwork. However, Ernie Pyle, the agency’s county coordinator, warned winter was far from over, and he offered some suggestions on how motorists can help prepare themselves for wintry weather.

headline: Decline in Gun Violence Bypasses Philadelphia
abstract: While homicide and violent crime rates are declining throughout most of the nation’s cities, the number of homicides has remained steady in Philadelphia at about 400 a year for nearly a decade, and a majority of these deaths have been attributed to high-powered handguns used by people under the age of 23. Despite a slight drop in the homicide rate for the first four months of this year, the problem has gotten so pervasive that Mayor Ed Rendell has appointed a deputy mayor to coordinate local and Federal efforts to slow the flow of weapons into the city, and a violence task force he created four years ago and many community leaders agree that drugs are the main reason for so much gun violence. Many experts blame the increasing availability of guns on a 1995 state law that eliminated Philadelphia’s ability to refuse to issue a gun permit if the applicant couldn’t demonstrate a "reasonable need" for the gun; however, defenders of the law, including state Senator Vince Fumo, claim the real problem is the city’s lax enforcement of the law’s provisions.

headline: Parties disagree on Social Security action as White House conference nears
abstract: Republicans and Democrats are skeptical to believe a bipartisan compromise can be reached during President Clinton's White House Conference on social security. US Sen. Rick Santorum says the White House still has a lot of work to do in the trenches. The Clinton Administration is unwilling to submit a blueprint for reform to Congress, unsure of the consensus within both chambers. The public is invited to view the opening and closing statements at the conference via satellite feed at their local Social Security Administration offices.

headline: Mellon sues to block bid from Bank of New York
abstract: Mellon bank files legal suit against the Bank of New York for their $23.22 billion takeover proposal. Mellon shareholders favor the takeover.

headline: Democrats without direction
abstract: Democrats are having difficult times within their party and with getting new ideas out to the public. Republicans are doing a good job of getting out messages to the public.

headline: Pa.'s political landscape remains much the same
abstract: All state lawmakers seeking re-election to their seats won. Thirteen departing members either lost bids for higher office or retired. Political issues during the election included welfare reform, workers compensation and tax cuts. PA Go. Tom Ridge was also re-elected. Republicans have maintained their lead in the Senate. That majority in only narrowly maintained the House. However, House Maj. Leader John Perzel does a good job of garnering Democratic votes when he needs them. The PA School Reform Network says the issue was hurt from not receiving attention in the election.

headline: Voter apathy appalling here and across Pa.
abstract: Voter turnout for the state primary elections could set a record low, and Wayne and Pike Counties also had an extremely low voter turnout. The authors of the editorial are disgusted that voter turnout is so low; especially given that Memorial Day Weekend is approaching. The authors are upset that soldiers have given up their lives for rights like voting, and the believe that non-voters should be ashamed for throwing away these rights by not voting.

headline: Dauphin County GOP candidates talking trash
abstract: People have long complained that politics is a dirty business and that candidates are often more fluent talking trash than discussing the issues. That notion appears to hold some truth in Dauphin County's 104th state House District. The hottest issue is a trash heap located in amid the rolling hill and farmland Upper Paxton and Washington townships.

headline: Intimidation of doctors by AGH parent alleged
abstract: Creditors of Allegheny General Hospital’s bankrupt parent foundation, the Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation, asked U.S. Bankruptcy Judge M. Bruce McCullough for permission to speak with hospital doctors after the foundation allegedly threatened to sue them. The meeting was intended discuss the options for creditors to recover the $1 billion still owed to them by the foundation. Eight of the foundation’s bankrupt Philadelphia hospitals recently shifted ownership to a for-profit hospital chain.

headline: From Harrisburg: fishing, PIAA, disaster assistance
abstract: According to the author, PA Representative Rod Wilt, the PA Game Commission is restocking trout in preparation for the April 18th opening of trout season, and the PA Legislature was in Harrisburg for the final week of budget hearings and committee meetings. The House Education Committee held an informational meeting on the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association, which is being investigated by the state Senate after several questions arose pertaining to a lack of oversight. In addition, Representative Matthew Baker has proposed the creation of a PA State Emergency Disaster Assistance Fund that would provide homeowner loans for communities that suffer from natural disasters but don’t qualify for federal aid.

headline: Landfill lawsuit question: Can state ruling end federal case?
abstract: Jefferson County Solid Waste Authority solicitor Robert Ging filed a motion in U.S. District Court in Erie on behalf of Jefferson County and Pine Creek Township to dismiss a lawsuit filed by Khodara Environmental on behalf of Eagle Environmental. Eagle filed the suit after a federal law was passed that allowed the local airport authority to veto two proposed land fill sites due to air-travel safety concerns, which Eagle thought was unconstitutional. Ging hopes that the judge will throw out the lawsuit because the state Department of Environmental Protection upheld the suspension and revocation of their landfill permits because of environmental reasons, but the case is still far from being settled.

headline: Monroe 2020 asks PennDOT to enforce billboard regulations
abstract: Monroe County 2020 Task Force, which was created to coordinate economic development throughout the county, has asked the PA Department of Transportation to help control the number of billboards in the region by enforcing regulations and ensuring all billboards have been properly registered. But according to Paul Goida, an administrator for PennDOT’s district office, the agency is responsible for monitoring hundreds of billboards in six different counties, so local municipalities may be best suited to ensure each billboard is in compliance with regulations. PA Representative Joe Battisto has sponsored a bill that would allow counties to create uniform billboard ordinances, and Monroe 2020 is working on the same issue.

headline: Delp gets curfew break to attend shuttle launch
abstract: After PA Senator Dan Delp pleaded guilty to hiring a teen-age prostitute and providing her with liquor, which resulted in a Dauphin County judge sentencing him to two years probation and ordering him to pay for court costs as well as perform community service, he has kept an extremely low profile and has refused to talk to the media for months. The judge also imposed a curfew, but he was granted special permission to travel to Florida to witness U.S. Senator John Glenn’s second shuttle launch. PA Representative Stan Saylor said he is often absent from the Legislature, but he did surprise members of the York County Transportation Commission by showing up to a recent meeting, his last as a state Senator.

headline: Pennsylvania eyes cuts in subsidized day care
abstract: According to a plan by Governor Tom Ridge and the PA Department of Public Welfare, thousands of the state’s working poor would no longer be eligible for subsidized day care because the state plans to lower the eligibility income limits to provide subsidized day care for parents who are even poorer and are trying to get off welfare. According to Community Services for Children, which provides child care subsidies for Lehigh County, 198 out of the 1,175 kids currently enrolled would no longer be eligible under the new regulations, and critics argue the new plan will backfire by encouraging the working poor to leave their jobs because they can no longer afford day care. House Democratic Leader William DeWeese, state Representative Dwight Evans and Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. all oppose the plan.

headline: Merger will be tough to stop
abstract: Opponents of First Union's proposed $16.6 billion takeover of CoreStates availed themselves of a rare Federal Reserve Board hearing to put their criticism in the record. The opponents point approvingly to CoreStates' good record of community investment and engagement and say that First Union is arrogant, negative, and even incompetent. The paper wonders if halting the merger is the right thing to do.

headline: Demos discuss debating
abstract: Allentown Dr. Richard J. Cusick has called for three debates before the May 18 Democratic primary. He, along with Allentown lawyer Richard Orloski and PA Representative William Lloyd, are all seeking the nomination to challenge U.S. Senator Arlen Specter.

headline: Pa.'s population erosion: PA lost the most people of any state in past year, and could lose two congressional seats.
abstract: New federal population data was released which confirmed PA had lost more residents than any other state for the second straight year. The loss of residents could potentially cost PA two House seats after the 2000 census is taken and seats are redistributed. Pennsylvania’s overall population growth is only 1 percent; far below the national average of 8.7 percent.

headline: Voter turnout low in midstate
abstract: Throughout Pennsylvania’s midstate region, polling places reported low voter turnout for the state’s primary election, and even regions voting in the 104th State House primary and the 19th Congressional District primary, considered two tight races, reported poor voter turnout. Some of the major issues for voters in the 104th District were a proposed landfill expansion, taxes and abortion, which impacted voters’ choice between candidates Mark McNaughton, Dauphin County Commissioner Sally Klein and Matt Napiltonia. U.S. Representative Bill Goodling was challenged by Charlie Gerow for the second straight 19th Congressional District election, and at some polling places, supporters gathered signatures to oppose the consolidation of two Dauphin County high schools.

headline: Day's Events Could Narrow Credibility Gap  Clinton Aides, Scholars Urge Forthright Disclosure
abstract: President Clinton has been very skillful in using language that is able convey different impressions to groups with entirely different views on issues, and he has used his rhetoric to defend himself on many subjects in the past, including his use of marijuana, promises to cut middle class taxes, tax increases on the wealthy and not being drafted to serve in Vietnam. Clinton has adamantly denied having sexual relations with Monica Lewinski, and his advisers said that covered intimate acts short of intercourse, but he is now considering admitting to having "sex play" with Lewinski, but claiming he didn’t lie under oath in the Jones case because his actions couldn’t be considered actual intercourse. Clinton’s use of rhetoric has set traps for himself in the past, which he has been able to get out of, but it is now beginning to hurt his credibility, and many scholars are urging him just to tell the truth this time.

headline: Growth of HMO enrollment in the North Hills
abstract: The graph shows the growth of HMO enrollment in the North Hills, which has been steadily increasing since 1992.

headline: Fumo's tactic could backfire
abstract: PA Senator Vince Fumo and others have threatened to shut down the Philadelphia School District if Governor Tom Ridge and the state don’t increase its funding to make up a $95 million budget deficit, which is more than Erie School District’s entire budget. According to the authors, Philadelphia already receives more than its fair share of state funding, and Commonwealth Court threw out a lawsuit filed on the district’s behalf. The authors claim Erie School District has had to make some budget cuts, and if Fumo and others don’t work with the state by cutting spending, they will have themselves to blame for a shutdown of Philadelphia’s public schools.

headline: Landlords are fined over lead hazards
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency yesterday proposed fines against four landlords -- including two in Philadelphia-- for failing to tell their tenants about lead paint hazards.  The fines are the first civil penalties sought under a 1992 federal law that requires sellers and landlords to inform buyers and tenants about the dangers of lead-based paint in homes built before 1978.

headline: Moon
abstract: 246 truck and bus licenses have been canaceled as a result of drivers not responding to a retest prder.

headline: Delp goes to court
abstract: PA Senator Dan Delp sat quietly in Dauphin County Court while his attorney, Paul Killion, and Senior Deputy Attorney General Anthony Forray battled for three hours in front of Judge Richard Lewis. Killion, who is hoping to have all charges thrown out, argued against the legislation that led to the existence of the state attorney general’s office, and he argued the charges of patronizing prostitutes and supplying alcohol to a minor should be separate from a charge of theft. Forray countered Killion’s arguments against the legislation, and he argued that all the charges are inextricably tied together.

headline: Philadelphians join national Social Security dialog
abstract: Standing before a number of elderly constituents, US Sen. Bob Borski complained about the government's use of social security funds for other programs. Social Security is expected to go bankrupt by the year 2029. Borski disagrees with the federal government's policy of using social security funds to balance the federal budget. President Clinton held a town meeting on Social Security in Missouri before dropping in on a town meeting in Philadelphia via satellite. Clinton has asked Congress not touch the budget surplus until a better plan for Social Security is in place. Santorum favors partial privatization.

headline: Mergers Create 2 Banking Giants
abstract: NationsBank Corp. and BankAmerica Corp. said they would join forces in a $60 billion merger to create a banking behemoth that would cast a shadow over all but a few megabanks and usher in a new era of nationwide banking. The deal was announced at the same time two other big banks said they had agreed to a $29.5 billion merger, creating the fifth-largest bank. Analysts said the merger wave will reshape the banking landscape for years to come.

headline: Dems miffed at Singel: He denies rift with party forced him to quit post
abstract: Mark Singel, who was chairman of the PA Democratic Party, decided to step down from the position. Some party members were considering voting Singel out as chairman over anger that his law firm represents Republicans and for comments he made about gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin. Singel denies this played a role in his decision, but several others disagree, and Singel has expressed interest in running for governor or senator some time in the future, which state Representative Mark Cohen believes could be as early as 2000 or 2002.

headline: PAC endorses Rogan
abstract: VIEWPAC, an organization which provides financial assistance to qualified female Republican candidates running for the U.S. House, endorsed Mary Rogan. Rogan is the only female running for the 10th District’s Republican nomination and would be the state’s first ever Republican congresswoman if elected.

headline: Women's caucus to sponsor debate
abstract: Democratic Women's Caucus will sponsor a debate of Democratic candidates seeking statewide offices.

headline: Debate turnout deflates Democrats: 8 candidates aggressively seek votes despite poor attendance in Hershey
abstract: Eight PA Democratic candidates attended a debate in Hershey, but most state committee members didn’t show up, so the crowd was disappointingly small; however it didn’t stop the candidates from aggressively debating. Gubernatorial candidates Ivan Itkin, Philip Berg and William Kneisling all bashed Governor Ridge, and they all said they’d do more for schools, public education and the defense of working people and unions. Incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter was criticized by his challengers, Bill Lloyd, Rick Orloski, Rick Cusick and Harry Liller, and the senatorial candidates focused on creating jobs, tax reform, health care and Social Security.

headline: Handling of CHIP program questioned
