abstract: Pennsylvania became a pioneer in 1992 when it started the Children's Health Insurance Program designed to ensure all children access to health care.  Now, many are questioning whether the state is beginning to slacken in its leadership role.  Under Gov. Robert P. Casey's administration, the Legislature created CHIP to serve children of working parents who could not afford health care coverage.  Funded by a two-cent cigarette tax, it was one of just a handful of such programs in the nation.

headline: Good, efficient colleges possible
abstract: George Waldner, York College’s President and a member of the National Commission on the Cost of Higher Education, spoke at House subcommittee chaired by Representative Pat Carone to explore ways to keep higher education affordable. He discussed an efficiency index he developed for the university and said universities can improve efficiency without hurting the quality of education. Representative Tom Druce asked Waldner if he’d be willing to fill out an efficiency report, which he said he’d be happy to do if it required no more than four to five hours to complete.

headline: Lawmaker pushes broader reform
abstract: Legislation on the table for Tuesday's House hearing on the Game Commission falls far short of what is needed to bring more accountability to the agency, and Allegheny County lawmaker said.  The committee Tuesday will examine the allegations of law-enforcement abuses at the agency and will consider bills to curb the powers of Wildlife Conversation Officers and deputies.

headline: Motorcycle helmet law repeal opposed, backed
abstract: The proposed repeal of the Pennsylvania helmet law has many backers and opponents telling there side to Govenor Tom Ridge.

headline: Despite punishments, debate continues at SCI Greene
abstract: Waynesburg prisons guards are charged abusing inmates. Some guards charges are still pending while a number of guards have had charges dropped with no penalities.

headline: Poll: Most favor heating aid for poor
abstract: A poll released by the Campaign to Keep America Warm shows eight percent of Americans support government funding for a low-income heating and assistance program. The US Housing Appropriations Committee is slashing $1.1 billion in funds for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program. US Sen. Arlen Specter is urging legislators to restore funding to the program. US Rep. Phil English plans to offer an amendment to restore the program's funding by making small across-the-board cuts elsewhere.

headline: More banks levying ATM surcharges
abstract: Non-customer surcharge fees at ATM machines are rising.

headline: Dems pick staewide candidates
abstract: Democratic Party Leaders have endorsed Ivan Itkin, Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky and Bill Lloyd. Their individual platforms are also mentioned.

headline: Parties focus on Lehigh Valley
abstract: Lehigh Valley has become a site for politics with the upcoming election. Legislators are flooding the area to ensure party control by promoting their party's nominee in Lehigh Valley.

headline: Voters Services checks write-in votes
abstract: Luzerne County Voters Services attempted to retrieve the write-in rolls from five machines based on a complaint by Democratic PA House candidate Richard Kamus. After opening the write-incompetents on two of the machines that had been used, it was discovered that the write-ins rolls were still there and had not been turned in. None of the write-in rolls were thrown away.

headline: Del-Nero's the newest Democratic candidate
abstract: James Del-Nero will be the new Democratic candidate for state Representatives in the 157th District. Del-Nero, who lives in the borough, was chosen by party committee members to replace John Jasienski Jr. He was found dead in the garage of his Phoenixville home.

headline: Health care reform bill may be headed to Ridge
abstract: Legislation establishing a "bill of rights" for managed health care patients could be on Gov. Tom Ridge's desk by tonight.  Legislators agreed late Monday to expedite the issue before adjourning the General Assembly for a three-month summer recess by combining three issues into a bill Ridge has reportedly agreed to sign.  The proposed legislation would prevent health maintenance organizations from summarily denying coverage for medical treatment.

headline: Grading the states
abstract: PA was among the top 14 states in a study that rated academic standards, teachers, educational climate and school funding. Some selected categories include: academics, teachers, learning climate, adequacy, funding allocation, and equity.

headline: Laws, 'green' thinking lead to increase
abstract: Residents of the North Hills in Allegheny County have been recycling much more than 10 years ago, and counties throughout PA have met or exceeded the goal to recycle 25% of all municipal waste set by the state’s Municipal Waste Planning and Waste Reduction Act. Most waste collection companies have been able to keep costs down while offering recycling collection options to residents, and both Butler and Allegheny Counties have recycled significant amounts of waste. Allegheny has set a new goal of recycling 35% of its waste by 2003, and a table of recycling percentages in the North Hills is provided in the article.

headline: Motorists get a break due to court's ruling
abstract: Due to reciprocity agreesments between ststes, many motorists arrested in other states between January 1. 1995 and December 9, 1996, will get a break from license suspensions.

headline: Detail how police, schools deal with crime on campus
abstract: Since more violent crimes are being committed by juveniles, school districts are being forced to call on law enforcement officers much more often than in past years. Governor Ridge highlighted the need for cooperation between schools and law enforcement officers by vowing to cut off school safety grants for schools without memorandums of understanding, which are agreements between school districts and police on how to cooperate to deal with criminal activity in schools. The authors of the editorial claim most Lancaster County schools have signed memorandums, and Police Chief Michael Landis has called for even tougher police-school cooperation.

headline: Poor will pay more for kids' day care
abstract: PA Representative Jeffrey Coy and several other Democrats held a press conference asking Governor Tom Ridge and the state Department of Public Welfare to modify its regulations that encourage parents to send their children to unregulated day cares. Under the regulations, mothers who send their children to state-supported day care would pay $10 less in co-payments if they agree to send their children to unregulated day care. Critics argue a child’s wellbeing will be in jeopardy because unregulated day cares don’t require criminal background checks.

headline: N.Y. Bank challenges Mellon to beat offer
abstract: Bank of New York seeks to takeover Melon Bank. Melon bank is fighting the takeover, while Bank of New York is obbying shareholders for support.

headline: Dems pin slim hopes on House: State GOP seems to have lock on governor, U.S Senate races
abstract: Republican Governor Tom Ridge is expected to win easily, and Republicans have a seemingly insurmountable hold over the PA Senate, so Democrats are hopeful that they can take control of the state House, which is controlled 104-99 by Republicans. A political science professor at Millersville University said that the chances of this happening after the upcoming election are "fair to poor," yet it is still possible. A number of key House battles are described in the article, including the Lehigh Valley’s four open House seats, and Democrats, such as Representative Thomas Catlagirone and Representative Stephen Stetler, admitted that the party faces challenges but remained hopeful over their chances of winning control over the House.

headline: Parting shots
abstract: The authors don’t believe Governor Tom Ridge will have to implement his school takeover plan, but if he does, they believe Rosemarie Greco would be one of his top choices to run things. Michael Nix is seriously considering challenging Philadelphia City Councilwoman Donna Miller. The Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation said a decline in private source funding will require staff cutbacks, and Alan Brown was laid off from his position as deputy director of operations.

headline: Wash. Allows lying among candidates: A political consultant says winning-and losing-by lying will continue
abstract: The state of Washington’s Supreme Court ruled that a law prohibiting lying in political campaigns is unconstitutional because it violates the First Amendment guarantee of free speech. A political consultant doesn’t expect the ruling to have much of an impact on elections, and he believes some candidates will win by lying and some will lose because of it. While the majority of the court took the First Amendment position, the minority argued the decision will harm the electoral process.

headline: Delp blames media's 'inaccurate' stories
abstract: After months of denials, PA Senator Dan Delp pleaded guilty to patronizing a teen-age prostitute and giving her liquor, and he will receive two years probation, 400 hours of community service and $4,000 in fines. In a court-ordered apology, Delp apologized to his constituents and fellow Senators, but he still blamed the media for inaccurately covering the story. He will not seek re-election, but a court imposed curfew could make things interesting when the Legislature convenes later at night during the Fall session.

headline: Health care union rallies over staffing
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey visit a protest site where demonstrators rallied over the shortage of staff in nursing homes and rising injury rates in nursing homes.

headline: Group to meet on alleged Girard abuses
abstract: The Black Clergy of Philadelphia and several PA legislators are sponsoring a public meeting today over allegations that several students at Girard College have been abused and poorly supervised. One of the participants will be an attorney for a former student who has filed a lawsuit claiming he was sexually abused by other students at the school; however the school’s board provided a statement that denied any wrongdoing and supported the school’s staff. The state House Judiciary Committee is conducting an investigation, and according to state Representative Leanna Washington, the meeting is in response to complaints by numerous parents about alleged misconduct, including sexual activity, drug use and attempted suicide.

headline: Luksik urges factory farm moratorium: Candidate discusses proposed pig operation
abstract: Peg Luksik, who is running for governor as the Constitutional Party’s candidate, said the state government should bring large livestock operations to a halt in PA until related environmental and health questions are answered. She announced this to a group called the Swatara Township Opposing Pig factories, which opposes a hog farm that has been proposed in the area. Luksik told the group that environmental regulations, such as nutrient management regulations, aren’t strictly enforced, and the state should make a distinction from small and large-scale livestock operations to prevent corporate agriculture from taking advantage of lax environmental laws.

headline: Needy Bridge to be repaired
abstract: The Dorantown Road Bridge needs improvemnts to fix holes that cause a danager to traveling residents.

headline: Did you lock your gun?
abstract: Have you locked your gun today?  You should.  Child safety locks are cheap -- about $12 to $15-- and have been proven effective in keeping little hands from pulling the trigger of big guns.  Moreover, it will help keep liberal do-gooders and conservative yahoos from trying to pass tough gun-control laws or harsh juvenile justice laws every time a tragedy such as the one in Jonesboro, Ark., occurs.

headline: President presses debate on change in social security
abstract: President Clinton says he believes the social security crisis could be solved without raising payroll taxes, during the first of 4 regional conferences on social security this year. However, Clinton did not close the door on privatizing social security. Clinton called for Congress to set aside the budget surplus to address social security. Aides confirmed he would support partial privatization if it could be ensured that all retirees were guaranteed benefits. US Sens. Rick Santorum and Bob Kerrey backed private accounts during the conference. Other suggestions include increasing the retirement age.

headline: New law kills amusement tax proposal
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge signs Act 50 into law, making tax cap on amusement park taxes void.

headline: Dems push Republicans for budget concessions
abstract: President Clinton and congressional Democrats kept the focus on education as they pressed Republicans for concessions in a federal budget deal. With the public's approval of Congress declining in opinion polls, republicans sought to end the budget dispute by giving ground. They were negotiating terms not dollars in both cases.

headline: Party bosses lied about record
abstract: PA Representative Thomas Yewcic of the 72nd Legislative District is the author of this piece, and he is writing in response to the Cambria County Democrat’s decision to "dump him" and hold an open primary. He claims that party leaders lied about his voting record on a bill to require companies to give notice to workers of shutdowns. He believes he was dumped because he would not blindly follow orders from party bosses and made his own decisions on what he felt was right.

headline: WASH: into payola
abstract: Mrs. Jones’ lawsuit against Clinton for allegedly putting her in a dead-end government job after refusing to have sex with him in 1991 was thrown out by Judge Wright, which clearly pleased the president, who found out the news in Senegal today. The decision is likely to please the majority of Americans, who continue to give high approval ratings of the president in polls; however, both Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and Independent Counsel Kenneth Starr said the Jones’ decision will have no impact on Starr’s investigation into whether Clinton had a sexual relationship with Monica Lewinski and then lied under oath to cover it up. Clinton has been hit with more allegations of sexual misconduct recently, and Jones’ lawyers will almost certainly file an appeal; though it could prove difficult to overturn Wright’s decision.

headline: Jobs top candidates' priorities: Conklin, Corman, Hanna, Thompson among those discussing issues at forum
abstract: Jacob Corman and Scott Conklin, who are running to represent the 34th District in the state senate, as well as Glenn Thompson and incumbent Representative Mike Hanna, who are vying for the 76th District’s seat in the PA House, appeared at the Meet the Candidates Night to debate issues such as Social Security, medical care, welfare reform, education, the budget surplus and jobs. Each candidate presented their thoughts on the issues and defended their positions. In addition, Green Party candidate Bill Belitskus, who is challenging Congressman John Peterson, presented his thoughts, as did Dean Snyder, the Constitutional candidate who is challenging U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, and the Libertarian candidates for governor and lieutenant governor.

headline: Health Department's upgraded Web site still falls short on some kinds of data
abstract: The Health Department is crowing about its upgraded, user-friendly Web site, but some believe there is a problem.  Health officials are saying the website (www. health.state.pa.us), will help Pennsylvanians, via interactive communication, better address health care needs.  But while the new Web page is a step in the right direction, it falls short on some kinds of information, such as data on nursing home care that is less than that which would be required under legislation pending in the House and Senate.

headline: GV student's work wins Capitol acclaim
abstract: U.S. Representative Curt Weldon co-chairs an annual art competition where high school students can submit their artwork for a chance to be displayed for one year at the U.S. Capitol. Weldon, along with celebrity guests and hundreds of students, attended the kickoff event to this year’s 17th Annual Congressional Art Competition. Garnett Valley High School student Michael Kenney was chosen to represent Weldon’s district at the event for his collage, a unique portrait of the famous musician Neil Young.

headline: Man wants to bring 'Green' movement to Poconos
abstract: Skip Mendler, an advocate for the Green Party, will host three meetings as part of the "Green Politics in the Poconos" series. Mendler has been actively involved in the Green Party and is hoping to find out if people in the area are interested about green issues. He said the Green Party is about more than the environment and politics, and it currently is working on ways to make it easier for smaller parties to field candidates.

headline: Neither motorists nor states need more annoying tolls
abstract: According to the editorial, Arkansas, PA and Florida are thinking about adding tolls to sections of interstates in their respective states, but the authors think this is a bad idea. First of all, they claim drivers already overpay to drive, considering $13.4 billion of the $86 billion collected in federal highway revenue, including the fuel tax and user fees, is spent for "nonhighway" purposes. Secondly, they argue tolls cause traffic backups and accidents.

headline: Domestic violence bill up for debate
abstract: One out of every four women reporting to the emergency room is a victim of domestic violence, according to a 1997 article in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Victim's advocates in PA say the proportion of victims is about the same in this state population, although women who are beaten or hurt by a partner seldom report it. A bill pending in the state house attempts to get at the root of this problem. It mandates screening for women seeking health after a beating. Medical professions are open to any method of screening they would like.

headline: Retire the system
abstract: Editors believe President Clinton does not have what it takes to save Social Security. In their opinion, the solution is to institute private retirement accounts. Social Security has no savings component. It will go bankrupt by 2030. Every American should save for their own retirement. A recent survey by the Heritage Foundation reveals minorities and the poor put more into Social Security than they will ever get out. Social Security taxes and Medicare eat up 15.3 percent of a person's salary, leaving little left to save.

headline: News from the Pennsylvania General Assembly
abstract: PA Senator Roy Afflerbach introduced a bill that would require insurers to explain their reasons for denying insurance coverage, and the state Senate unanimously approved Governor Tom Ridge’s request for $123.1 million in tax cuts for business and low-income workers. A quote from PA Senator Jack Wagner is provided over a failed amendment to cut the state’s income tax by one-tenth of a percent, which Wagner supports. In addition,  Harrisburg author William Keisling is expected to announce that he will run for governor of PA.

headline: Dems savoring afterglow from primary sweep
abstract: Members of the state Democrats are patting themselves on the back after the way their endorsed candidates for statewide office swept all the nominations in the May 19 primary. It marked the first in quite awhile that the chosen slate actually came out on top in a primary.

headline: Party's rally cry: Less government intrusion
abstract: Republican Tim Holloway, who is challenging Democratic U.S. Representative John Murtha, said President Clinton should get his day in court, but he criticized House Republicans for dragging out the scandal and Murtha for calling on all Americans to support Clinton. Peg Luksik, an independent challenger to Governor Tom Ridge, condemned attempts by the state to build stadiums in Pittsburgh, and she challenged Ridge’s claims of economic success in PA. Both candidates, who are endorsed by Westmoreland County's Reform Party, focused on government intrusion on education, business and environment.

headline: Washington County
abstract: Rose Ann Master, elected by the Washington County Democrats, will serve as their new chair.

headline: John Morgan Makes A Difference for GOP In the Odd State Race: An Expert on 'Block Voting, He Maps Races for Clients Wary of Granola Crunchers
abstract: John Morgan, a staunch supporter of the Republican Party, has become a treasured asset for Republicans who have utilized his ability to analyze historic voting patterns and the underlying demographic trends. He has spent the last 30 years creating a huge collection of political maps, which use, among other things, census data, national ancestry and the proportion of state natives, and he is currently consulting the Republican Parties in 14 different states. He advises national candidates, as well as state candidates, correctly predicted the Republican Party would pick up over 50 U.S. House Seats in the 1994 election and predicts that from 10 to 22 House seats would be picked up by Republicans in the upcoming election.

headline: Health Gap
abstract: Pennsylvania has gained some national recognition as a health-care innovator in recent years .  Unfortunately, its success in following through on its ideas would appear to leave much to be desired.  The Pennsylvania Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) launched during the Casey administration on legislation long pushed by now-state Sen. Allen Kukovich, D-Westmoreland, is widely credited with being the model for similar programs in other states and a new federal children's health insurance program.  Some 61,000 Pennsylvania children, mostly of working parent, are enrolled in CHIP, the highest number ever, though an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 are eligible.

headline: HACC swears in president. Baehre installed as college's 6th leader
abstract: Edna Baehre, who had previously been vice president for instruction and educational service at Elgin Community College in Illinois, was sworn in as the sixth president of Harrisburg Area Community College. Five people offered Baehre their congratulations, including PA Education Secretary Eugene Hickok. Hickok pledged Governor Ridge’s continued support of the college, and he predicted success for the college in the future.

headline: Mountains of trash
abstract: According to a report by the Congressional Research Service, PA was a net importer of 8.4 million tons of waste, making it the top trash importer in the nation. The authors of the editorial claim that disposal fees are low, which makes PA attractive for states like New York and New Jersey. However, the authors are concerned about the future if PA continues to accept so much out-of-state trash.

headline: New drunk driving law another tool to save lives
abstract: With far too many people still dying on our nation's roads as a result of drunk driving, both state and federal drunk driving laws are getting tougher and must continue to do so. One law passed last year created a new charge, aggravated assault with a motor vehicle, aimed directly at drunk drivers. This second-degree felony is just one more thing that those who drive drunk need to worry about, in addition to jail time, fines and loss of driving privileges.

headline: 'Don't ask, don't tell' wins likely last appeal
abstract: A federal appeals court in New York upheld the Clinton administration’s "don’t ask, don’t tell" policy on gays in the military, and the Supreme Court is not expected to hear the case over the policy’s constitutionality. The Lambda Legal Defense and Education Fund was clearly disappointed with the ruling but vowed to continue fighting to stop discrimination against homosexuals. According to the policy, homosexuals can remain in the military if they don’t discuss their sexual orientation, and superiors aren’t supposed to ask about it.

headline: Rep. George attacks welfare debit card plan
abstract: The PA Department of Public Welfare is implementing its new program to replace welfare benefit checks with new debit cards that recipients can use to make purchases. State Representative Camille George sent a letter to the Welfare Department’s Secretary, Feather Houston, that was harshly critical of the department’s plan to charge a 50-cent surcharge after the fourth transaction. George has been an outspoken critic of all automated teller machine fees, and he vowed to take action in the House if changes aren’t made.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell plans to speak with the developers of two proposed casinos in Philadelphia about moving the projects. The proposals were approved by the gaming control board in 2006, but some residents and lawmakers, including Mayor Michael Nutter, oppose the casinos being built.

headline: Dems take aim at GOP
abstract: Butler County Deomcratic Committee held a dinner to introduce Democratic candidiates and talk about the party's platform.

headline: Past Praised, Future Pondered as McDade Says Goodbye
abstract: The Greater Scranton Chamber of Commerce honored U.S. Representative Joseph McDade, who will retire in January after 18 terms representing the 10th Congressional District. McDade said he’ll miss representing the district’s constituents, and the Chamber’s president, Austin Burke, said life will go on without McDade, but he will be sorely missed. Burke estimated McDade’s economic influence brought in over $1 billion in capital investment and wages for the district.

headline: Web watch
abstract: For the first time ever, Pennsylvania’s official homepage will broadcast Punxsutawney Phil’s prediction on whether there will be six more weeks of winter.

headline: Jubelirer appoints Corman to Senate Finance Committee
abstract: Jake Corman will officially be sworn in as a member of the PA Senate on January 5, but Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer already announced Corman has been appointed to the Senate Financing Committee for the 1999-2000 legislative session. The position will help Corman shape tax policy, and he said he plans to advocate reducing the inheritance tax and enacting tax reform. In addition, Corman was appointed to several other committees in the Senate.

headline: Health-care bill of rights in the works
abstract: The PA House will likely consider a bill that would establish an independent review system to consider appeals from patients who are denied coverage for treatment under their managed health care plans. By 2000, 80 percent of Pennsylvanians are expected to be enrolled in such types of plans. Representative Nick Colafella, who is the ranking Democrat on the House Insurance Committee, doesn’t think that the proposed bill goes far enough, and he will try to incorporate nine other amendments, which are described in the article.

headline: Hafer to talk about tuition option
abstract: State treasurer Barbara Hafer will talk about the PA Tuition Account Program at Butler County Community College. The program allows families to create accounts and receive tax benefits to pay for their children to go to college in the future.

headline: Murtha delivers $4.2 million check for East Huntingdon sewage system
abstract: U.S. Representative John Murtha presented the East Huntingdon Township Sewage Authority with $4.2 million in federal funding from the Environmental Infrastructure Pilot Program. For a while, the PA Department of Environmental Protection has imposed a moratorium on the township that has prevented housing and commercial development projects from beginning construction. The funds will be used to build a new sewage treatment system, and Murtha hopes it will allow the projects to move forward on their proposals.

headline: News of barriers disquiets residents on West Shore
abstract: The House Republican Caucus got a $15 million line iten to include in the budget, a pilot program for "safetey and sound barriers" that the Department of Transportation must enforce along Interstate 81.

headline: Don't outlaw cider that tastes good
abstract: In response to a young child who died in 1996 after drinking cider, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration passed a new rule that requires labels on all unpasteurized cider containers. The author feels that one death in three years is nothing to get alarmed about, and even the PA Agriculture Secretary admitted that she couldn’t think of any serious illnesses caused by cider in the state. The new regulations could hurt small cider makers, and the author believes unpasteurized cider tastes better, and he wants the choice of drinking it.

headline: Rep. Kanjorski hits GOP 'raid' on Social Security Trust Fund
abstract: Representative Paul Kanjorski criticizes Republicans for their stance on Social Security. Kanjorski argues that Social Security should be preserved and not raided for tax cuts.

headline: Nonprofit credit unions should be able to grow
abstract: The US Supreme Court announced that it had ruled in favor of the banking industry regarding an "unfair competition" lawsuit five banks had filed against AT&T Federal Credit Union in North Carolina many months earlier. AT&T Federal Credit Union had been accepting new businesses into its field of membership to sustain a level of healthy growth. The plaintiff banks claimed that AT&T Federal Credit Union was accepting new members, who otherwise would have no other option than to do business with banks.

headline: 'Dialing for voters' ripped
abstract: Tax dollars are being used for a telemarketing use during the Deleware County election. Lawmakers have varying points of view on the tactic.

headline: Pennsylvania Democrats, where are you?
abstract: There are upcoming elections in PA for governor, U.S. Senator, all 21 congressional seats, half the state Senate seats and all the state House seats, and the author claims that it has disappointingly become a Republican dominated, one-party show. Other than some strong Democrats in Philadelphia like Mayor Ed Rendell, she feels like the party has not even tried to offer new ideas and have allowed Governor Ridge and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter to scare off any well-funded competition, leaving little known challengers like Ivan Itkin and William Lloyd, respectively. According to the author, many Democratic strategists seem to be content allowing the Republicans to take over for the time being, but she is unhappy with their efforts.

headline: Weldon set to vote yes on perjury articles
abstract: Representative Weldon says he will vote for the impeachment of President Clinton.

headline: Judge chronicles her fight to stay upbeat
abstract: PA Common Pleas Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson was nominated for a federal bench, and she had to undergo a controversial U.S. Senate confirmation, but ultimately, she withdrew her name from consideration yesterday. She allowed the newspaper to release some of her written thoughts from February 12 to March 16, and during the time period, she tried to remain positive while enduring heavy criticism; especially from Philadelphia District Attorney Lynne Abraham, who submitted cases to the Senate that she claimed show Massiah-Jackson had an anti-prosecution bias. Massiah-Jackson tried to defend her record and passed the Senate Judiciary Committee, but near the end of her written account of the grueling process, she was considering whether to withdraw before a final vote was taken by the entire Senate because she clearly didn’t have enough votes to be confirmed.

headline: HIV and name reporting
abstract: Randal Forrester, director of Persad Center, criticizes the Post Gazette's article on HIV and name reporting, as lacking sufficent information and rushing to judegment about the issue.

headline: Hafer wants safeguards for school investments
abstract: Pennsylvania Treasurer Barbara Hafer lays out a six point plan to financially protect school districts from bad money managers.

headline: New gasoline reduces smog - A cleaner-burning fuel will debut in area gas stations this summer
abstract: The Pittsburgh region is in danger of joining Philadelphia as being classified by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as a “serious nonattainment” area because of its poor air quality, which would trigger business and emissions restrictions, so in order to improve air quality, all gas pumps in Allegheny and six other surrounding counties will be required to sell Reid vapor pressure gasoline. RVP gas contains less ozone-producing gasses, and it would only raise gas prices by a cent or two; however, some have called for the use of reformulated gas, a more expensive gas type that could reduce ozone emissions even further, but contains a chemical believed to contaminate groundwater. PA Representatives Richard Olasz and Joseph Petraca have introduced bills that would ban both types of gas, and the state Department of Environmental Protection plans to compromise by banning just reformulated gas.

headline: Nightmare returning to Schuylkill
abstract: The expressway repavedment project from Passyunk to Montgomery Drive is scheduled to be completed by the end of October, according to PennDOT.

headline: Drop in crime rate due to many factors
abstract: The PA State Police recently delivered some good news about crime. The number of serious crimes in the state decreased 5.5 percent in 1997 compared with 1996. Some credit goes to laws passed, a strong economy, an aging population and more police on the streets.

headline: Rework the contract
abstract: Editors are thankful the unpredictability of Wall Street is causing some to second guess privatization of Social Security. In their opinion, basic retirement security ought to be more stable. In addition to the pitfalls of the stock exchange, investors may become victims of scams as well. To editors, the point of the system is that it guarantees a retirement check. Editors suggest Social Security be reworked as a standard pension plan which saves for the future, not pays out as money is put into it. In addition, the government should not use social security to balance the budget. The system should partially invest in the stock market, but not make it the priority of private individuals.

headline: Nonprofit status key to mergers
abstract: Thanks to the ambiguity in state law, none of the mergers that vaulted AHERF from second place in Pittsburgh's health care market to the largest hospital system in Pennsylvania was ever reviewed by the state.  The attorney general's office would have relished the opportunity to review the mergers.  And the office is responsible for reviewing major transactions involving nonprofit organizations to "ensure that the public interest in the charitable assets . . . Is fully protected."

headline: District office key to service, Allen says
abstract: Former mayor and current PA Representative Bob Allen said he would make the 125th district accessible to its citizens. He will offer numerous services at the district office to help constituents with variety of different issues.

headline: Pennsylvanians deserve to know more about who spends what in Harrisburg
abstract: According to the editorial, PA has one of the weakest lobbying disclosure laws in the nation, and lobbyists have been able to avoid reporting how much they spend trying to influence the state Legislature. Over $100 million a month is spent lobbying Congress in Washington, and the authors claim extensive lobbying is also going on at the state level, which PA Senator Clarence Bell referred to as "horrible." The Legislature is considering a bill that would require lobbyists to disclose more details on what they spend, and the authors argue that if the bill is passed, elected officials will be more weary and will try to avoid appearing as if they’ve been bought by special interests.

headline: Welfare defends security switch
abstract: A state Department of Public Welfare official reacted angrily to allegations by a security firm that contended to the termination of its contract to guard the Haverford State Hospital grounds was bogus.  Central Security Agency of Philadelphia was replaced by Foulke Associates of Media.  Springfield GOP boss Charlie Sexton, Republican Gov. Tom Ridge's political confidante, replaced Central.

headline: Judge targeted anew
abstract: With her nomination to the federal bench hanging in the balance, Philadelphia Common Pleas Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson launched her defense yesterday, rallying against the "misinformation and mischaracterizations" of her career.  But Massiah-Jackson again had to fight last-minute allegations from District Attorney Lynn Abraham, whose office sent a 65-page report to the Senate Judiciary Committee a day before the hearing with a new round of allegations against the judge.  Some of the material involved 20-cases that had never been mentioned publicly, and Massiah-Jackson was not expecting to answer questions on those cases.

headline: HMO Backlash
abstract: The author tells a story about his personal frustration with his family’s health-maintenance organization (HMO), and he cites a statistic from the Kaiser Family Foundation that found complaints about health insurance to Congressmen outweighed positive stories by a 7:1 ratio. Despite these statistics and personal frustrations, he still believes that the managed-care system is much better than the pay-for-fee system in the past, and he feels that the current system was responsible for slowing soaring health care costs. In the author’s opinion, more regulation of health care is definitely needed, but most problems will work themselves out over time, and foolish, overbearing regulations would be detrimental to sound national policy.

headline: Hanna wants state dropout age raised to 18
abstract: PA Representative Mike Hanna is supporting proposals to raise PA's school dropout age to 18 and lower to 6 the age at which students must begin school. Under current law, students are not required to start school until age 8 and can drop out when they reach age 17.

headline: Official explains expressway delays
abstract: The Mon-Fayette Expressway/Southern Beltway project is stopped because of an endangered spotted owl, which resides in the area.

headline: No heartbreak-Ridge                                                                                                                        Governor guarantees bypass funding
abstract: A Berks County transportation committee asked the state for $104.4 million for the $205 million Warren Street extension and Lancaster Pike widening project, which would be a considerable percentage of the state’s overall transportation budget; however, Governor Tom Ridge and Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory vowed to fully fund the project. The extension has been on the table since the 1950’s, and it was nicknamed "Heartbreak Ridge" after Ridge cut it due to lack of funding in 1996. Fortunately for the project, the PA Legislature approved an increase in the state’s gasoline tax and registration fees, which generated an additional $550 million, and state Representative Sheila Miller said she hopes the project receives all the funding it needs.

headline: Drug task force to get $65,000 per year
abstract: Wahington County will receive $65,000 in funding for the Drug Task Force.

headline: Ridge administration begins energy assitance program
abstract: On behalf of Governor Tom Ridge, PA Public Welfare Secretary Feather Houston announced cash grants and crisis grants will be available for the upcoming winter to help families needing help paying for home-heating fuel sources and furnace repairs. The grants are federally funded and are available through the state’s Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program. The program is expected to assist 300,500 households this winter and has $62.8 million in available funding.

headline: Our biz climate not hottest - Survey sez high taxes, bad city schools hurt
abstract: Greater Philadelphia First sent out surveys to gather information on businesses’ perceptions of Philadelphia, and it received feedback from 137 corporate executives and 58 business editors and reporters from across the county; however, the two groups viewed the city’s major economic industries much differently. Substantially more business leaders viewed the region’s biomedical and pharmaceutical industry, which has been growing rapidly, as one of the region’s most important economic activities, whereas a significant percentage more of business writers viewed hospitality and tourism as a major regional business activity. Overall, Philadelphia was praised for its educated work force, efficient transportation and good quality of life, yet it compared poorly to several other cities because its business climate was criticized for having high taxes, bad public schools and a high overall cost of conducting business.

headline: Dole bemoans 'lack of leadership' during Gettysburg College visit
abstract: Former U.S. Senator and presidential candidate Bob Dole addressed Gettysburg College students, and he said the lack of leadership is threatening the chance to curb tobacco use among the nation’s youth. While the tobacco industry reached an agreement with state attorneys general, including PA Attorney General Michael Fisher, for a $368 billion settlement last June, a $516 billion Senate plan has been met with stiff opposition by tobacco executives, and Dole believes the two sides need to find a compromise to get the deal done. In addition, Dole praised independent counsel Kenneth Starr for his investigation of President Clinton, but he refused to accuse Clinton of any misconduct.

headline: Pension boost approved for state retirees
abstract: The PA Senate approved a pension boost in the form of cost-of-living-adjustments for retired teachers and other state employees, pushed by Sens. Allen Kukovich and Melissa Hart. Approval is also expected by the House. The increases range from 1.86 percent to 25 percent. Retired teachers and other public school employees have stepped up pressure on lawmakers to consider the issue in recent years.

headline: Wellsboro Cross Country champs meet Gov. Ridge during Capitol visit
abstract: PA Representative Matt Baker hosted the 1997 state champion Wellsboro Area High School Girls Cross Country Team, which impressively won 82 straight dual meet victories in the past six years. Members of the team, coaches and the school principle were all given a tour of the state House and Senate chambers, and they were introduced to Governor Tom Ridge and U.S. Senator Rick Santorum. The article includes a photos of the team along with Baker and Ridge.

headline: Judicial Temper
abstract: The defenders and the detractors of Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson's star crossed nomination to the federal bench could go on waging their ideological wars and racist-intoned recriminations for years.  That will only ensure that the next such judicial review will be equally politicized.  Or they can work together - with Democratic district attorneys John Morganelli of Northhampton County and Lynne Abraham of Philadelphia taking a lead role, along with Republican Sen. Arlen Specter - and offer an African-American woman whose record can pass muster in the Senate.

headline: HMO reform focus of conference
abstract: PA Representative Lawrence Curry held a press conference along with six panelists from the health industry and one consumer to discuss State Bill 91, which was signed into law by Governor Ridge despite Curry’s vote against it. The panel agreed with the spirit of the bill but focused on three troublesome areas that the bill failed to include. Emergency room coverage is guaranteed in a "medical necessity," which is vague in the language of the bill, mental health coverage is not included, and another issues was not addressed that could put a strain on independent pharmacies that compete with chains.

headline: Head of the class  Congress' new student-aid bill is a smart move
abstract: The editorial board is pleased with Congress for finally getting past all the distraction to pass a bipartisan education bill. The bill, which President Clinton is expected to sign, will cut student loans by 1 percent, provide incentives to get teaching graduates to teach in rural or inner-city schools and offer incentives to universities if they can guarantee their teaching graduates are proficient in core subjects. It also includes a proposal from U.S. Representative Chaka Fattah that will notify students in low-income areas that they are eligible for federal aid to help them go to college.

headline: Our viewpoint: DEP is making progress
abstract: The authors claim that the PA Department of Environmental Protection has developed a reputation as being more interested in enforcing regulations than it is in working with the community to actually solve environmental problems. However, they believe the agency is taking a step in the right direction by at least saying it would consider granting alternatives to traditional septic systems for areas where soil conditions are unsuitable for their use. The authors give credit to the PA Rural Electric Association, as well as the organizations which are providing funding, for working to develop alternative septic systems.

headline: No more freebies: $EPTA's back in business
abstract: As a consolation for the strike, the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority has been offering free service to commuters since the transit strike ended. But today, commuters will begin paying again; though Fridays will continue to be free for the remainder of the month. Several riders said they understood fees had to be reinstated, while others weren’t as understanding.

headline: Drug-crime squad gets $25,000 state grant
abstract: PA Senator Joseph Uliana presented Stroudsburg Mayor Jonathan Mark with a ceremonial check for a $25,000 state grant to be used by an interdepartmental police squad to get better bullet proof vests and special training. The Special Entrance Response Team, which includes 18 officers from three different police departments, will use the money to focus on drug arrests and hostage situations.

headline: Ridge wary of charity tax credit plan
abstract: Republican Governor Tom Ridge was cool to a proposed state tax credit program, aimed at shifting support for the poor away from government welfare to community-based charities. The bill would give individuals a credit toward their state tax liability in return for certain charitable donations to help the poor. Incentives for increased private support will reduce taxpayer-financed welfare costs.

headline: PA Bank Merger
abstract: CoreStates Financial Corp. bank branches in PA that maybe sold if First Union Corp. purchases the Philadelphia-based bank. If approved, it would be the biggest bank merger in US history.

headline: Dole, GOP focused on 10th District: Former senator says house seat 'is one of the key races'
abstract: Republican Bob Dole, who lost the presidential election in 1996, spoke at a political rally in Scranton to support Don Sherwood, who is battling Democratic candidate Pat Casey and Reform Party candidate Tom McLaughlin in one of the closest races for a seat in the U.S. House. Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich has already had two fundraisers for Sherwood, and Dole said that Republicans throughout the country are following the 10th Congressional District race closely. He praised Sherwood for his stand on Social Security, Medicare and taxes, told the crowd he expects Sherwood to do a fine job for the district and managed to dodge questions about Clinton’s impeachment.

headline: Petard: Polities did more than forge three names
abstract: A spokesperson for Congressman Bud Shuster tells The Daily News a former Democratic candidate for Shuster's congressional seat did much more than forge three signatures on nominating petition. At the same time it has been learned from the state Election Bureau that Paul Polities has formally withdrawn as a Democratic candidate for Congress and will not appear on the May primary ballot.

headline: What election taught Polities
abstract: Letter to the editor from former candidate Paul Polities. He discusses his lessons from the campaign including humorous statement from people when they found out he was running.

headline: Justices Deal Setback to Method Of Funding Legal Aid to the Poor
abstract: Many states fund legal aid for the poor by using money from interest payments that lawyers earn while they hold onto clients money. The states contend that this is acceptable because clients wouldn’t actually earn interest on any of the funds that are collected; however, Washington Legal Foundation filed a case that says the interest payments are private property. The Supreme Court agreed that the interest payments are private property; though they didn’t go as far as to say that the practice is unconstitutional.

headline: HMO system works
abstract: A more appropriate title for the July 12 article ("National surveys reveal greater frustration with HMOs") would have been: "The system works for Pennsylvania HMO members."  The basis for the article was the case of a Lancaster family dissatisfied with a coverage decision made by their HMO in regard to their young son.  Unlike any other health insurers in Pennsylvania, HMOs are required to have a consumer-specific grievance process with an ultimate appeal to the state Department of Health.

headline: Helping Aliquippa
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey proposes three ways in which the Aliquippa School District could save more then $760,000 in spending.

headline: Pa. deer kill total rises
abstract: Sportsmen took nearly 400,000 deer during Pennsylvania's 1997 hunting seasons, rebounding from the 10-year harvest low posted in 1996. The antlerless harvest was an interesting lesson in antlerless license adjustments. Elimination of surplus antlerless licenses limited many hunters to one antlerless deer and resulted in many unsold antlerless licenses in counties with large allocations during the 1997 seasons.

headline: No more Ice Mine Cut detours
abstract: Rumors about Route 120 closing again are not true. PA Department of Transportation says that the Route will remain open with no plans to close.

headline: Eliminate age restrictions
abstract: Opinion piece about how juvenile's heinous crime belong in adult court. Gives examples of heinous crimes that should be treated as adults to help prevent teens from committing these crimes. Age restrictions should be gotten rid of so that justice can be served.

headline: Santorum plan on Social Security is criticized
abstract: A democratic candidate for US Senate, Rep. William Lloyd, writes that US Sen. Rick Santorum's suggestion to privatize social security is merely another way to line the pockets of investors. He reminds people that social security was never designed to replace private savings, but was instead intended as a safety net in lieu of financial catastrophes like the Great Depression. Lloyd believes the first step in saving social security is to stop using it to balance the federal budget and start putting it in a Trust Fund.

headline: PA Insurance Department launches toll-free hotline
abstract: According to PA Insurance Commissioner Diane Koken, a new toll-free number will allow consumers easier access to obtain information from the state’s insurance department, leave messages for a department representative and request brochures or insurance complain forms.

headline: Don't Eliminate PACENET
abstract: PA Senator Robert Mellow and Representatives Kevin Blaum and Todd Eachus want to extend the eligibility requirements for the Program of All Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE), and they want to eliminate PACENET, an extension of PACE that requires a $500 copay for prescription costs. They justify this because the Lottery is running a surplus, but the authors argue the Lottery is unpredictable. They believe PACENET is reasonable in requiring copays based on income, and they argue it’s important for the long-term financial stability of the entire PACE program.

headline: Peterson announces bid for re-election
abstract: US Representative John Peters of Pleasantville formally announced his campaign for a second term at a news conference here today. It is expected to be an easy campaign for Peterson. No other candidate has filed nominating petitions as of the deadline last Tuesday.

headline: What might happen if Clinton left office: Some say the presidency would be damaged, with a thinner separation of powers.
abstract: The article examines the potential ramifications if President Clinton resigns or is removed from office in the future. Some scholars believe it would take years for future presidents to restore the public’s trust in the office, whereas another scholar said that leaving Clinton in office if he did commit perjury would result in undermining the Constitution. Other scholars warned that the impeachment and removal of Clinton from office would set a dangerous precedent by showing that one party can use its power in Congress to remove a President from the opposing party, which would erode the separation of powers between the two branches of government.

headline: Kanjorski votes against inquiry: Congressman says impeachment not proper reprimand for president
abstract: U.S. Congressman Paul Kanjorski voted to oppose launching an inquiry into the impeachment of President Clinton; however, he is on the losing side, and the inquiry will begin. Kanjorski criticized the partisanship of the vote, and he doesn’t believe that the founders of the Constitution intended for impeachment to be used against presidents for personal matters. He agreed with a proposal from former President Gerald Ford to issue a strong public censorship of Clinton which he would not be permitted to respond to.

headline: HMOs dealing from a stacked deck
abstract: If an HMO harms you by denying or delaying treatment that your health plan should cover, what can you do?  In most states, almost nothing, when you have an employee plan.  You can sue doctors and hospitals, but federal law prevents you from suing the plan itself.  Advocates of "patients' rights" are fighting an uphill battle in Congress to give injured people (or their survivors) a right to sue their HMOs.  Advocates of insurance companies are successfully blocking them; saying that lawsuits would increase everyone's health insurance costs.

headline: Here's what's wrong with this program
abstract: The School-to-work Opportunities Act is an attempt to use federal mandates and funding to browbeat the public schools into changing their mission. The school-to-work plan is to train children in specific jobs to serve the work force and the global economy instead of to educate them so they can make their own life choices. It de-emphasizes traditional functions of society.

headline: Pa. forests get high marks from group
abstract: Pennsylvania’s 2.1 million acres of state forest became the largest woodlands to be certified as "well managed" by Scientific Certification Systems of Oakland, one of six worldwide accredited companies that offer third-party certifications of sustainable management techniques. PA Governor Tom Ridge said that the certification will increase the value of wood products because many customers want environmentally sustainable products. The Department of Conservation and Natural Resources was pleased with the certification, as was the Western PA Conservancy; though its president, Larry Schweiger, said that deer herds threaten PA forests, and the Game Commission needs to take action.

headline: No secret: Roadwork overdue
abstract: Joe Halberstein talks about long overdue transportation projects in Bucks County and the new transportation bill that will begin address the problems.

headline: Enhanced infant crib safety is goal of Rubley bill
abstract: PA Representative Carole Rubley introduced legislation aimed at reducing the number of infants killed or injured from unsafe cribs. Each year, over 13,000 infants are injured in the U.S. because of them, and over the past five years in PA, five children have died from serious injuries suffered in faulty cribs. The bill puts forward eight dangerous features of an unsafe crib, and it would make it illegal to sell or remanufacture them.

headline: Santorum's high-level discussion on Social Security
abstract: US Sen. Rick Santorum chatted with President Clinton on board Air Force One about the future of Social Security. Santorum favors partial privatization. The two are in favor of a bipartisan approach to fixing Social Security. The American Conservative Union rated US Rep. William Coyne a "perfect liberal." PA Rep. John Peterson rated the most conservative of PA members. US Rep. Murtha is among the highest recipient of funding from companies attempting to gut the endangered species act. Murtha says he continues to support the act.

headline: Pa. and insurance firms in a regulatory circle   State aides often come from industry jobs. Critics say public confidence is at stake.
abstract: The past five PA Insurance Commissioners, who are each briefly described at the end of the article, worked for or represented the insurance industry before being appointed; however, many people believe the regulators of the insurance industry should be independent, and they are concerned they will act in the best interests of the insurance industry, rather than in the best interests of the public. Diane Koken presented Provident Mutual Life Insurance’s petition to change its corporate structure from a company where policyholders own the business to a publicly traded company owned by stockholders, and she was appointed days later by Governor Tom Ridge to become the state’s new Insurance Commissioner; though she has promised not to make a ruling on the Provident petition as the new commissioner. Two lawsuits have been filed against the petition because policyholders could stand to lose out on many benefits if it is approved, and many people have been critical about the secrecy of the process in which Provident and the state Department of Insurance worked together during preliminary phases of the company’s proposal.

headline: Don't let apathy be a big winner
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge faces no Republican primary challenger and has $5 million to spend, whereas Democratic primary contenders, Ivan Itkin, Don Bailey and William Kneisling, have $130,000 to spend combined. Itkin is the party’s endorsed candidate, yet he hasn’t received much money, which is a sign that Democrats see Ridge as unbeatable and would prefer not to waste money campaigning against him. The authors of the editorial hope that Ridge’s popularity doesn’t lead to voter apathy in other Republican primaries; especially the important 13th Congressional District race in which incumbent Jon Fox faces Melissa Brown, Michael McMonagle and Jonathan Newman.

headline: Peterson To Vote 'Yes'
abstract: Local U.S. Representative John Peterson will join most Republicans in the House and vote for the impeachment of President Clinton on charges of perjury. Representative Joseph McDade, who will retire shortly, has not yet decided on the issue. Peterson said he will vote to impeach Clinton because nobody is above the law, and he expects the impeachment to narrowly pass the House.

headline: What others are saying: State seniors get a voice
abstract: Senior citizens in PA are getting more of a voice in Congress, as US Sen. Rick Santorum was recently named co-chairman of the Senate task force on Social Security. Pennsylvania has the 2nd highest concentration of the population of senior citizens in the nation. The task force will work to educate the public and lawmakers about preservation of the system. As more employees become eligible for retirement, Social Security is looking at bankruptcy by 2029. Editors hope PA receives prime treatment when ideas are solicited.

headline: Kanjorski: Impeachment process amounts to persecution
abstract: Representative Paul Kanjorski talks on the impeachment of President Clinton and the partisaness of Republicans during the trial.

headline: HMOs posted losses totaling $768 million last year, study finds
abstract: Health maintenance organizations, the health-insurance plans that spearheaded the growth of managed care in Philadelphia and nationwide, lost $768 million last year, according to a new study of the industry.  The study by Florida-based Weiss Ratings Inc. found that 1997 was the third straight year of declining profits in the HMO industry and the first year the industry as a whole suffered financial losses.  Nationwide, 57 percent of HMOs lost money last year.

headline: Hickok to students: Revere Constitution
abstract: Education Secretary Eugene Hickok, who carries a copy of the constitution with him in his pocket spoke with Cheltenham townships high school students.

headline: Pa. plans to stomp litterbug: State program urges drivers to turn in tipsters and snitch on trash-dumpers
abstract: The problem of littering has shown no signs of declining since the 1950s Keep America Beautiful Campaign began, so the PA Department of Environmental Protection has responded by calling on motorists to call in to report motorists who litter. The PA Resources Council will then issue the offenders a reminder to not litter to raise awareness about the evils of littering. It remains to be seen whether the program is having any significant effect, and the Keep America Beautiful Program will bring back its infamous American Indian Commercials to try to curtail littering.

headline: No tolls on I-80 - yet
abstract: Gov. Ridge and his adminstration discussed the possiblity of turning I-80 into a toll road but have recently decided against it.

headline: Ex-Judge to get day in court
abstract: Bribery and other criminal charges against former Lackawanna County Judge Frank Eagen were held over for trial Friday following a marathon preliminary hearing in Central Court.  Mr. Eagen showed no emotion when senior Luzerne County Magistrate Leonard Harvey declared, after listening to more than seven hours of testimony, that he found the government had presented sufficient evidence to send the charges to trial.  The former judge's attorney, William Costopoulos, was repeatedly frustrated in his attempts to attack the credibility of government witnesses, especially Mr. Eagen's chief accuser, Philip Bosha.

headline: Senator finds students aren't rapt by Social Security issue
abstract: Students at Schenley High School were hard for US Sen. Rick Santorum to sell on privatizing social security. Students generally saw the issue as distant to their present situations, goals and concerns. Santorum is co-chairman of a Senate Republican task force on Social Security. President Clinton has called for a bipartisan national discussion on the future of Social Security. Santorum was joined yesterday by representatives of the urban League of Pittsburgh and Economic Security 2000, a DC based nonprofit. Santorum proposes partially privatizing social security.

headline: Pa. debates out-of-state OTB renewal
abstract: Lawmakers must decide by year's end whether PA's horse racing industry can continue its lucrative practice of telecasting big-name races in other states. The simultaneous telecast of races from tracks and off-track betting parlors. They attract clients who like to have dinner, watch races on the big screen and place bets. Five years ago a law was enacted that allowed them to simulcast races from out-of-state tracks.

headline: Don't let GOP leaders delay reform
abstract: The authors criticize House Republican leaders like Newt Gingrich and Tom DeLay for trying to prevent and delay campaign finance reform, which could threaten their party’s chances of raising more money than the Democrats for the upcoming election. They especially criticize Delay for claiming reform efforts could threaten the First Amendment's guarantee of free speech. There are 11 different proposals, but the authors call on the House to use the Shays-Mehan amendment, which outlaws the use of soft money and requires disclosure about issue advocacy ads, to be used to amend a bill being considered sponsored by Representative Asa Hutchinson.

headline: Peterson tops Belitskus to win 2nd term
abstract: Congressman John Peterson won a second term in House U.S. District 5, to defeat his opponent Belitskus by a large margin.

headline: What's holding up reform?
abstract: Despite support for SB -1, a lobbying disclosure reform bill, the PA House leadership has failed to bring the bill to a vote with only about 12 days left in the legislative session. PA's lobbyist law is widely regarded as one of the worst in the nation. Lobbyists are not required to disclose which laws they are attempting to influence. Some lobbyists fail even to register and many do not disclose expenses. Officials suspect lobbyists disclose much less than they actually spend. Barry Kaufman of Common Cause believes a critical piece of information for the public is data on the pressures exerted on it.

headline: Keep Constitution first and foremost
abstract: Courier-Express discusses the Supreme Court's decision to disallow the President to veto individual items passed by congress. Courier-Express criticizes Ridge for his support of the decision being passed on theory and not on facts.

headline: Hoeffel outlines rights of patients
abstract: Democratic congressional candidate Joseph Hoeffel III outlined his proposed Patient’s Bill of Rights in a press conference yesterday, where he also called for the need to develop national standards.  Incumbent U.S. Representative Jon Fox said that he’s already addressed many of the same issues in different pieces of legislation. Hoeffel’s 13-point proposal would, among other things, allow patients in managed care programs greater choice and flexibility in choosing plans and doctors, allow access to emergency care without prior authorization, establish an appeals process for denied medical coverage and allow doctors to inform patients of all treatment options.

headline: Hire teachers for their skills, not their degrees
abstract: The Public Opinion explore Govenor Tom Ridge's new teaching proposal, allowing individuals without teaching backgrounds to teach students in the state of Pennsylvania.

headline: Pa. to host hunting symposium
abstract: "Hunter Recruitment and Retention" will be the theme of the fifth Governor's Symposium on North America's Hunting Heritage when it convenes Aug. 12-15 at the Hershey Lodge and Convention Center.  Pennsylvania's hosting of the symposium will mark the first time it has been held east of the Mississippi River.  According to a letter sent out by Gov. Tom Ridge's office, as many as1,000 delegates are expected to gather in the mid-state for the symposium.

headline: North Strabane
abstract: PennDOT has planned to improve the one mile stretch on Route 19 between Weaver and McClelland roads.

headline: Ex-state official quits job in Maine
abstract: Laurence J. Reid, former PA employee, quits his job in Maine to resolve charges faceing him in PA. Reid is accussed of taking gifts and not reporting them while working for the Department of Corrections.

headline: Sensible protection or burden?
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey wants PA legislators to approve a bill that would require all child care providers recieveing state funding to undergo a criminal background check. State welfare authorities do not support the bill.

headline: Pa. law is pill that calms takeover mania
abstract: In the hostile takeover dance between AlliedSignal and its target, AMP Inc, PA's tough laws are calling the tune. AlliedSignal, a worldwide maker of aerospace and automotive parts based in New Jersey, launched a hostile takeover bid Aug. 4 of Harrisburg-based AMP, the world's largest manufacturer of electronic connectors. AMP employs approximately 1,800 in York and Adams counties. AMP was ripe for takeover, because sloe earnings growth due to Asian crisis and a failed expansion bid brought AMP's share down to around $30.

headline: Double Duty
abstract: In a preview of a regular House race that could unfold in the fall, two candidates in the 58th Legislative District are running tomorrow in a special election to fill the unexpired term of Representative Herman Mihalich. The Monessen Democrat died in Sept. The pair who would like to replace him are Republican Shaun Bannon and Democrat Ted Harhai. Both are concerned about jobs.

headline: Phila. Offers sweeter deal to PHA pick - Mayor Rendell offered the Detroiter more job security, even if lawsuit against him succeed.
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell added more incentives to his offer to get Carl Greene, head of the Detroit Housing Commission, to take over as head of the Philadelphia Housing Authority. Greene had accepted the job last month, but he changed his mind after tenant leaders and City Council members opposed his hiring. According to the new contract, which was approved by the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation, Greene would be paid an annual salary of $160,000 with the possibility of a 10 percent performance bonus, and he would be guaranteed a three year contract regardless of the outcomes of three lawsuits that have been filed against him.

headline: When politicians' private lives were private
abstract: The article examines the differences between presidents in the past who were accused of sexual improprieties, including John F. Kennedy, Thomas Jefferson, Grover Cleveland and Andrew Jackson, with the current situation that President Clinton is dealing with. While in the past, there was more of a line drawn between private and public life, the new age of 24-hour television coverage and the Internet has blurred that distinction.

headline: Keep eye on Starr, Specter tells rally
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, who is seeking reelection in an upcoming election, spoke at a fund-raising event at Fox Hill Country Club to try to add more money to his campaign chest that had $3.9 million in it last month. He said that it was too early to talk about impeaching President Clinton, but it is at least possible. He also said that PA should reelect him because he is third in line to chair the Appropriations Committee, which is a very powerful position that could result in PA getting extra funding.

headline: Home Safe
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey's report on the Health Departments treatment of nursing homes is examined. The politics of Casey and the situtaion may be influencing the issue.

headline: Homestead exemption act meet: more questions than answers
abstract: A meeting was held between Clarion County commissioners Keith Martin and Sally Minich, county chief assessor Robert Lieberum and the county’s school district superintendants over the new homestead and farmstead exemptions, which will allow school districts to cut property taxes in return for raising the earned wage tax. However, the school superintendants left with more questions than answers, and most agreed they would cautiously investigate before deciding whether they wanted to make the change. Lieberum expressed concerns about the time line given to school districts based on the new legislation, and he said he isn’t sure how the state expects the county to pay for all the work that would need to be done to determine a median assessed value for each school district.

headline: Parents say dust making kids ill
abstract: Dust falling from the ventilation system at Wrightsville Elementary has prompted school officials to embark on an extensive effort to clean up the school's air units, and hire an air quality specialist to assure that no one is in danger. State health department officials said the department contacted the school as soon as it received the complaint. One parent has filed a complaint with the state's Department of Health.

headline: Official sees flowers in intersection's future   Beautification plan promoted
abstract: PA Representative Nick Colafella has brought the PA Department of Transportation, the Western PA Conservancy and local businesses together on plan to beautify an intersection along Route 18 in Beaver County by planting thousands of flowers. The Route Eighteen Community Advisory Panel has offered $10,500 towards the estimated $25,000 project, and it will enlist volunteers for planting. The state Transportation Department offered $7,500, and Colafella is hoping to obtain the remaining funds from local businesses; though someone still would need to be in charge of maintaining the flowers after planting.

headline: Extension granted on rifle-check program
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate yesterday overwhelmingly granted the state police an 18 month extension before they must start instant computer background checks on buyers of rifles and shotguns.  However, the state police may not need all the additional time and could have the system in place a few weeks after the July 1 deadline, agency spokesman Jack Lewis said. Unisys Corp., the company installing the system, has said it could have it ready by the deadline, but the department did not want to the chance and requested the extension.

headline: Should government help the Lord take care of his own?
abstract: Proposed legislation seeks to provide credit to those agencies and or organizations that spend more then 75% of their budget on directly heping lower-income and poverty stricken individuals.

headline: Panel to vote on Measure to Tighten Bankruptcy Law
abstract: With the number of personal bankruptcies soaring, the House Judiciary Committee considered a controversial bill today, promoted by the banking and credit-card industries to make it more difficult for people to declare themselves legally broke. By defeating several changes proposed by Democrats, the republicans in control of the committee signaled that they would pass the bill. The bill would require an income test of those filing bankruptcy and would constitute the first major change to bankruptcy law in two decades.

headline: Doyle faces Democratic, Republican challengers
abstract: Incumbent U.S. Representative Mike Doyle is seeking re-election, but he will face Democratic challenger Mary Beth Hacke, who lost her 1-year-old son and her second cousin in tragic shooting incidents, and she will try to spread a message focusing on fighting violence among the nation’s children, which could resound well with voters due to her personal tragedies. Two Republican challengers, Dick Walker and Craig Stephens, are also vying to defeat Doyle, and many critics of Doyle have criticized him for not being proactive enough in Congress and for switching back and forth between parties on several different occasions in the past. Two U.S. Representatives from PA, Frank Mascara and John Murtha, have given their support for Doyle to be named to the powerful House Appropriations Committee, and Doyle cited several of his accomplishments in Congress, including his efforts to bring technological jobs to the city of Pittsburgh.

headline: Phillips plans to run for 10th consecutive term
abstract: Representative Merle H Phillips announced that he will be a candidate and seek re-election to his 10th full term as a member of the PA House of Representatives.

headline: Where the bucks are   Instead of kissing babies, aspiring rep Bob Brady hobnobs at fund-raisers
abstract: Bob Brady is expected to easily win a special election to replace U.S. Representative Tom Foglietta, who is now the ambassador to Italy, and although he faces tougher competition from PA Representative Andrew Carn in the Democratic primary for a two-year term to the same position, he is still the overwhelming favorite to win. From now until the May 19 election, he will attend one or two fundraisers nearly every day and is expected to raise an astounding $500,000 in a month, which is far more than any of the incumbent U.S. Representatives from Philadelphia were able to raise during a two year time period. He will also retain his position as Philadelphia’s Democratic Committee chairman, so many ambitious lawyers and politicians are contributing to his campaign in hopes of being rewarded with Brady’s support in the future, and while some claim Brady is catering to the wealthy, he said he is still making an effort to meet with ordinary citizens from the district.

headline: Klink challenger unveils federal tax reform plan
abstract: Mike Tarsal, Republican candidate for the 4th district, used Tax Freedom Day as a platform to reveal his proposal to reform the federal tax structure. Tura's tax initiative calls for an end to the IRS, implementation of a flat tax, elimination of the tax on capital gains, elimination of the inheritance tax, and elimination of the multiple taxation of savings and investments.

headline: HOME-CARE DENIAL IN MEDICARE CASES IS RULED IMPROPER
abstract: U.S. judges have ruled in thousands of recent cases throughout the nation that elderly Medicare beneficiaries are unfairly being denied coverage for home health services. Medicare often denies home health services if they feel patients are stable and not homeward bound, but many critics and doctors claim these patients require home health services and would deteriorate quickly if they do not receive them. The director of the Center for Medicare Advocacy has won many such cases and claims there is a major problem; however, Medicare officials, who are under pressure to reduce fraud and abuse to control skyrocketing costs, claim anyone who is denied service has a fair chance to appeal their case; though it often takes over a year for an appeal and the decisions usually only apply to the past.

headline: House subcommittee examining methods to control college tuition
abstract: PA colleges produced an excess number of teachers to fill open positions, not enough technical students graduated to fill the industry’s demands and only 30% of students graduated in four years. The PA House Education Committee’s Subcommittee on Higher Education is holding hearings on how to reduce costs of higher education, which is a response to Representative Tom Druce’s resolution. If the state allocates $1.6 billion a year for higher education, Druce believes they should get something in return from the investment, and the subcommittee is searching for ways to ensure state funding is spent better, such as trying to ensure different universities aren’t competing over programs, making colleges more accountable and rewarding those that keep costs down.

headline: Penalty fits the lab's misdeed
abstract: William Hopkins Jr., former president and owner of Hess Environmental Laboratories Inc., is expected to be sentenced to 15 to 21 months in jail for billing customers for water and other environmental tests that his company never actually performed. The author believes that he should receive jail time because his actions endangered the health of the public, and it may cause environmental contamination that cannot be determined for years.

headline: On Route 30
abstract: PennDOT is finsihing the project on I-83 and is ahead of schedule on the Route 30 project.

headline: Extreme injustice
abstract: Legal justice is the art of the good and the fair, goes the Latin saying.
