Thursday's decision to try, for a third time, two suburban Pittsburgh police officers in the death of motorist Jonny Gammage is neither justice, good, nor fair. Newly appointed Allegheny County District Attorney Stephen Zappala Jr says his decision is consistent with last month's ruling by PA Superior Court Judge James Rowley. The judge rejected a defense motion for a directed verdict of acquittal now-retired Brentwood Police Lt. Milton Mulholland and Baldwin Police Officer Michael Albert. Then the jury is now deadlocked. He believes there is still evidence the jury needs to hear.

headline: Should Social Security go to private accounts?
abstract: President Clinton's administration opposes privatizing social security. This month, as town hall meetings with members of the US Congress begin, including US Sen. Rick Santorum as a panelist, editors hope new insight will be gained on how to solve the impending social security crisis. Polls show nearly 80 percent favor privatizing social security, however only 46 percent would take advantage of private accounts, unwilling to trust Wall Street. New ideas are needed on how to improve government handling of social security funds.

headline: Pennsylvania invest a lot in tourism, too
abstract: Mississippi lawmakers have appropriated $2 million specifically to put The Splendors of Versailles exhibit on display at the Mississippi Arts Pavilion in the capital city of Jackson. Half of that sum goes to the French government to finance ongoing restoration work at the royal palace. Officials hope tourists will flock to see the treasures and then take sides trips in the state. States use tourism as a way to increase revenue and PA itself spends $11 million a year to attract tourists.

headline: Doyle for the Democrats
abstract: Profile of Mike Doyle who is the democrat running for re-election for the 18th District. He is known for fighting for improvements for the city of Pittsburgh. The paper decided to endorse Mike Doyle for his bid for re-election.

headline: Philly mayor's support of foes irks politician
abstract: For years, PA House Democratic Leader William DeWeese has complained that Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell has financed his political opponents in the state House and Senate. In particular, he’s complained that without support from Rendell and state Senator Vince Fumo, Representative Alan Butkovitz, an outspoken challenger to DeWeese’s authority, wouldn’t have been able to finance his bid to become House Democratic Appropriations chairman. Despite the criticism, Rendell surprisingly gave DeWeese $100,000 towards his campaign.

headline: Whether Ridge runs or not, state will pay
abstract: Dennis Barbagello tells Pennsylvania Residents that if Govenor Tom Ridge runs for reelection or for the presidential nomination, taxpayers will still hold the bill for his campagin efforts.

headline: Klink says Turzai's workers dogging him
abstract: U.S. Representative Ron Klink has accused his challenger, Mike Turzai, of unfair politics after being harassed by staff from Turzai’s campaign. Two men from Turzai’s campaign with a camera first tried to enter one of Kink’s campaign events, and later in the week, they surprised Klink and his chief of staff by jumping out of a corner and asking questions about Klink’s alleged extramarital affair. Turzai’s staff also flew over Klink’s home to take photos, which drew more criticism from Klink; though Turzai said his staff was only trying to seek answers, and he is trying to make an issue out of his opponent's home.

headline: Hospital bailout ruled out: The governor said the Allegheny "system can't stand under its own weight."
abstract: After a meeting that included Governor Tom Ridge, Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell and Allegheny Chief Executive Officer Tony Sanzo, Rendell and Ridge promised to accelerate funds that had already been promised to the Allegheny health system; however, Ridge acknowledged it was barely even a short term solution. Ridge ruled out a bailout of the health system, which is now $371 million in debt after its massive expansion and acquisition of numerous hospitals. Vanguard health Systems Inc. is reportedly negotiating to purchase nine Philadelphia area hospitals, and Allegheny may have to lay off workers or file for bankruptcy.

headline: House vote expands terroristic threats
abstract: Threatening someone via the Internet would be a crime punishable by prison time under a bill approved by the state House of Representatives this week. The legislation, written by state Representative Charlie Dent, was drafted in response to an incident earlier this year in the Bethlehem Area School District in which students threatened teachers on a Website. The definition of terroristic threats to include next new technology.

headline: PennDOT to help Game Commission remove deer carcasses from highways
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is now contracting with private entrepreneurs to remove deer killed in collisions from many state roadways. PennDOT became involved at the request of the Game Commission when the volume of deer killed on the state's highways reached a saturation point beyond what Game Commission officers could routinely handle.

headline: On the Bus
abstract: Allegheny Cunty Transit Council member speak out about the proposed rerouting of downtown buses.

headline: Family Situations
abstract: Living arrangements for juvenile offenders in PA shown in a pie graph. 46% live with just their mother.

headline: Social Security Investment Plans Weighed
abstract: The Clinton administration is considering an approach to Social Security reform which involves stock market investments. Democrats and the party's key constituencies are displeased. Five plans have emerged, each of which involves stock investments, however they vary in the degree to which Social Security would rely upon them, and just who may do the investing. Three versions would mandate privatization, while two would allow privatization on a voluntary basis. Two plans would divert payroll taxes from the program's trust fund. Some plans would raise the retirement age.

headline: Phila. Rates not top-dollar
abstract: Say you have $10,000 and are shopping for a certificate of deposit, a low-risk way to invest your cash. Here's a tip don't shop just in Philadelphia. A one-year CD in Milwaukee, and you'll be ahead by $77 on average when your certificate matures, pocketing $548 in interest versus $471 if you invest in a CD here. Why do Philadelphia banks pay low rates? It is because Philadelphians put up with them.

headline: Dozens of House Democrats Seem Likely To Vote for GOP Impeachment Inquiry
abstract: The White House tried to garner support for a Democratic proposal to end the impeachment inquiry by December 31 into allegations that President Clinton committed perjury, obstructed justice and tried to coerce witnesses to cover up his affair with Monica Lewinski. However, thirty to sixty House Democrats, mostly conservatives or those involved in close races, are likely to vote for an open-ended Republican plan, and the Republican plan is expected to be approved later today. In addition, Senator Robert Byrd told the White House not to tamper in the process.

headline: Physician General mustn't be quitter
abstract: Not everyone is cut out for politics and one of the people who is apparently not well-suited to that challenge is Pennsylvania's very first physician general, Dr. Wanda Filer.  She recently resigned after just 15 months on the job.  As anyone who has ever played the game knows, politics is an art form that requires a wide variety of skills, including but not limited to statesmanship, leadership, compassion, cooperation, negotiation, insight, mind-reading, information gathering and analysis.  Many doctors we know use those same skills.

headline: White House show interest in Reed
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed may have lost support from Democrats by endorsing Republican incumbent Governor Tom Ridge for reelection, but that didn’t stop the White House from inviting him to a reception as part of a two day conference on community empowerment. Reed had to decline because of a prior speaking engagement; however, the White House called twice urging him to reconsider. He’s enjoyed a close relationship with President Clinton but couldn’t explain the strong interest in his attendance.

headline: Kwak nationalization bill headed to full Senate vote
abstract: A comatose Korean immigrant shot in a robbery came one step closer to naturalization as the Senate Judiciary Committee cleared legislation. Supporters are optimistic despite a tight time frame and a number of other pressing issues. Kwak had already passed oral and written exams required for citizenship, but was injured before he could take the oath of allegiance. US Attorney General Janet Reno agreed with the US Immigration and Naturalization Service officials who refused to nationalize him without his having taken the oath. Legislation in the Senate was sponsored by US Sen. Arlen Specter.

headline: Hospital foundation shifted research unit's funds, audit shows
abstract: A yearlong buying binge by Allegheny General Hospital's parent corporation ended in May 1997 with the acquisition of seven hospitals in two states, and one of the region's biggest physician practice groups.  While the Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation was busy buying up hospitals, however, $13.1 million was withdrawn from Pittsburgh affiliate Allegheny Singer Research Institute, according to U.S. Bankruptcy Court records. The money was shifted to other "affiliates" according to an audit for fiscal 1997 submitted to the court.

headline: How Good Teaching Can Affect Student Scores
abstract: Teachers play a large role in student performance. In fact they could account for an up to 40 percent difference in performance in average student test score gains, making teachers roughly as important as family and background.

headline: PennPIRG takes environmental concerns door-to-door in Erie
abstract: Members of the PA Public Interest Research Group are running a door-to-door campaign in Erie to get people involved in the organization’s environmental defense campaign and to ask them to encourage U.S. Representative Phil English of Erie to vote against several pending bills in Congress. The organization’s leader, JoAnn Kester, accused English of not being a leader in dealing with environmental issues in Congress, and she wants him to vote against bills that would repeal legislation that uses money from taxes on the chemical and petroleum industries to clean up Superfund toxic waste sites. English’s administrative assistant defended English’s stance on the environment.

headline: One year after gas tax, construction buzzing along state roads
abstract: Thirteen months have passed since PA Gov. Tom Ridge approved a gas tax and hike in vehicle registration fees to fund infrastructure renovations. An additional $400 million is also available, and motorists are beginning to appreciate the changes they see. This is good news for the PA Department of Transportation, which has gone from rebuilding 70 to 110 miles a year.

headline: FBI vows caution in training: Responds to Gekas in wake of botched E-town incident
abstract: Deputy FBI director Robert Bryant promised to be more careful in the future and issued a formal apology to the group of teens who were accidentally detained by the FBI during a training mission in Elizabethtown, PA. U.S. Representative George Gekas received the letter from Bryant, and he was basically pleased, believing the incident had truly been an accident. However, a Harrisburg lawyer is filing a lawsuit on behalf of one of the teens who was briefly detained.

headline: Social Security Proposals
abstract: The White House is examining five different proposals concerning the future of Social Security. The plans each involve privatization to some degree. They include the 21st Century Retirement Act, the Moynihan-Kerrey plan, the Kasich and Roth plans, the Ball Plan, and the Feldstein Plan.

headline: Philadelphia losing corporate muscle - Fortune 500 HQs are packing bags and leaving town
abstract: When CoreStates Financial was bought by First Union earlier this year, it became Philadelphia’s third loss of a Fortune 500 corporate headquarters since May 1997, and the city is now home to seven Fortune 500 companies, ranking eighth among the top 10 cities, despite being the nation’s fifth most populated city. Many experts believe these corporate headquarters are important because they help spur development in the services sector, which creates jobs for top bankers, engineers, consultants and corporate lawyers, and they also benefit charitable organizations in the region by making large donations. According to one analyst, the city spent three times as much money promoting tourism as it did promoting business, and Philadelphia’s image as a union town and its rather small airport may also create an anti-corporate headquarters atmosphere.

headline: DUTY TO DEBATE: A Goodling-Gerow showdown would give primary voters vital aid
abstract: The authors of the editorial criticize incumbent U.S. Representative Bill Goodling for his refusal to debate his primary opponent, Charles Gerow. Conventional wisdom is that Goodling’s refusal to debate is sound politics, and Goodling says he is proud to stand on the record of thousands of votes he’s cast while in Congress. However, the authors believe that if he is truly proud of his record, he should be willing to defend it in a public debate, and they suggest the public should consider voting for someone else if he doesn’t agree to do so.

headline: PIAA Time needed for a study
abstract: The authors were glad to see the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association (PIAA) vote to move the state football championship from Altoona to Hershey; however, the move angered PA Senator Robert Jubelirer, and they are now concerned that the decision was made for the wrong reasons. The PIAA had a surplus of $4 million last year, and Hershey is refusing to say how much it bid to get the football game, which are both troubling to the authors. They believe there are too many questions that must be addressed, and they support Senator Jim Rhoads’ proposal to create a task force to investigate the PIAAA.

headline: Who Should We Blame for Impeachment?
abstract: The author is tired of people passing the blame of Clinton’s impeachment onto others, and he claims that Clinton deserves to shoulder the blame because he had many chances to tell the truth. The author cites numerous opportunities where Clinton could have avoided impeachment if he simply told the truth. In the author’s opinion, the House Judiciary Committee gave him one last chance to tell the truth, but he again lied, which left the Republican majority with no other choice but to begin the impeachment process.

headline: Landfill donations filter in
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge called for a three year halt on landfill expansions, but House Majority Leader John Perzel said that he would not allow such a bill to come to a vote. Perzel’s spokesman said that the decision has nothing to do with the $5,000 in campaign contributions that the House Republican Campaign Committee received from Waste Management Employees Better Government Fund, which operates 17 PA landfills. He said that it would be unfair to change the rules after operators had already submitted expensive expansion applications, and other representatives who received money from the company also said the donations have had no effect on their decisions.

headline: Hospital giant to alter course
abstract: The Allegheny health system's top official said this week that the organization had concluded  that its long-standing strategy of aggressive expansion hasn't worked and its business approach would substantially change.  Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation chief executive Sherif S. Abdelhak acknowledged that the system could no longer grow larger and larger.  Instead, he said, Allegheny would focus on treating certain high-dollar disease categories, such as cancer and heart disease.

headline: Inpt period to start for school standards
abstract: Final public comment period for the Pennsylvania proposed academic standards is scheduled to begin.

headline: Pennsylvania deer herd still in jeopardy today
abstract: A major insurance company is targeting the whitetail deer in television commercials.  The farmers do not want to the deer.  And it seems that the Pennsylvania Game Commission is bent on helping them rid the state of whitetail deer.  The Game Commission consistently advertises our deer density to be at least 1.2 million.  Yet, according to its own statistics, there were only 822,400 deer in Pennsylvania going into the 1997 hunting season.

headline: Orphan rail line scorned no more
abstract: PennDOT and additional companies are prosing upgrades for Amtrak's Keystone route.

headline: Fired up over instant gun checks
abstract: In an effort to uphold its own restrictions on buying guns and to save local gun dealer extra fees, Pennsylvania implemented a statewide instant gun check on Wednesday, said Jack Lewis, press secretary for the State Police.  The plan has been in the works, for almost two years, he said.

headline: 3 state agencies show interest in QS building
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation’s district engineering office will move into Oil City after renovations are complete at the former Quaker State headquarters later this summer, and three additional state agencies have also expressed definite interest in moving into the building. The agencies have not been identified, but the PA Job Center may a potential tenant. The new agencies will help attract more Downtown traffic, which should help increase usage of the municipal parking ramp.

headline: Philadelphia, rest of America brace for possible retaliation
abstract: Amid fears that there could be retaliatory strikes from terrorists in response to U.S. missile strikes against terrorist operations in Afghanistan and Sudan, security across the nation and abroad has been tightened to protect American interests. According to a recent poll, only 10 percent of Americans fear a terrorist attack; however, specialists have warned that there have been retaliation attacks in the past, and they urged American businesses throughout the world to take the necessary precautions to protect their employees. In PA, Three Mile Island, Philadelphia Airport and Philadelphia’s symbolic tourist sites, such as the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall, will remain on constant alert, and the State Department has closed down and evacuated several embassies around the world.

headline: Easy races do not slow campaign spending
abstract: In their last elections, 111 members of Congress steamrolled no-name, no-chance opponents by an average margin of 41 percentage points. Each winner spend between $400,000 and nearly $6 million while cruising to victory. They spend because they can not because they need to. Examples of wasteful spending are given.

headline: Piccola To Host Govt. Seminar
abstract: PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola will host his third annual Good Government Seminar at Harrisburg Area Community College to allow students to engage in discussions with people involved in the different processes of government. Panelists from a wide array of professions will be in attendance, including PA State Police Commissioner Paul Evanko, Heath Secretary Dan Hoffmann, Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory and numerous state legislators.

headline: Why Clinton Lied
abstract: According to the author, the question of why Clinton lied about his relationship with Monica Lewinski has often been overlooked, yet there is a big difference between lying due to personal embarrassment and lying to prevent more damage from the Paula Jones lawsuit. The author claims the only real difference between Lewinski and Jones is that Jones refused Clinton’s sexual advances, whereas Lewinski accepted them, and job arrangements were made in return for her signing a sworn affidavit and lying about the relationship, which may have destroyed Jones’ case. The author makes a comparison between Nixon’s Watergate cover up and Clinton’s attempts to conceal the truth because a low crime was transformed into an impeachable offense in both cases, and they both used the government to try to cover up their actions.

headline: Language obstacle lowered for Puerto Rican Statehood
abstract: Supporters of Puerto Rican statehood achieved significant progress yesterday when a compromise softening the English-language requirement was forged. The House approved an amendment by US Rep. Dan Burton which encourages Puerto Rico to promote the teaching of English, however the amendment was a bipartisan substitute for a much stronger measure proposed by Rep. Gerald B. H. Solomon which mandated English as the official language. If the bill becomes law, Puerto Ricans must hold a plebiscite to determine their status, whether statehood or an independent commonwealth.

headline: Hospital honors lawmaker for service
abstract: Suburban General Hospital’s Board of Directors honored PA Representative David Mayernik for his service as a hospital board member for the past nine years. The chairman of the board praised Mayernik for helping to deliver two state grants for the hospital. In March 1997, the hospital received a $350,000 grant for Phase I of a rehabilitation services renovation process, and in June of the same year, it received $400,000 for the second phase of the project.

headline: Internet-Hookup Group for Schools draws Political Fire
abstract: Ira Fishman is head of Schools & Libraries Corp., one of two nonprofit groups that the Federal Communications Commission established last year to dole out $2.56 billion a year to help link the nation's schools, libraries and rural hospitals to the Internet. The subsidies were praised, by Republicans and Democrats alike when lawmakers mandated them in the Telecommunications Act of 1996. But now there is a ruckus how the organization is carrying it out. Republicans claim it is a bloated new bureaucracy.

headline: Pheasant Surprise
abstract: The Pennsylvania Commission, in an effort to continue to re-introduce pheasants to the state, has approved payment of reward bands to study the harvest rate of the birds for the 1998-99 season. The commission unanimously passed the motion at its summer meeting in Harrisburg. The study hopes to determine the percentage of released game-farm pheasants that are harvested, the cost per harvested bird, and to find the differences in harvest rate by time of release, land ownership and hunting zone.

headline: 'P' in PennDOT not for 'pathetic'
abstract: Despite the heap of criticism the public often throws at the PA Department of Transportation, the authors believe the agency does a lot of things well, and far too often, people only remember the agency’s mishaps. While there’s still room for improvement, the authors believe PennDOT does a good job while operating on a limited budget.

headline: Fisher says community involvement may be best way to reduce violence in schools
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher supports a community-wide response to violence in schools, and he spoke to Allegheny County officials about school violence, which has become a national concern after 19 people were killed in schools throughout the country last year, including PA, where a 14-year old killed a teacher and wounded three others. Fisher proposes a number of different ways to address school violence. Many of his proposals call for tougher punishments for students who bring weapons onto school grounds, increased penalties for parents of children who commit violent acts and increased efforts by law enforcement and school district officials.

headline: 93rd State House Race
abstract: Three question survey filled out by the three candidates for the 83rd House seat: Joyce Keesey, Barbara Metzler, and Ron Miller. The questions are Do state nursing home regulations need to be changed to give the Department of Health more regulatory power over nursing homes? Urban sprawl is one of the toughest issues facing your district. What is your top idea to reverse sprawl? Do you support privatizing state liquor stores?

headline: PhilEx spurns Chicago for Amex
abstract: Choosing New York over Chicago, the board if the Philadelphia Stock Exchange voted to join the American Stock Exchange. The decision, if ratified by the members, would move the exchange to New York and likely bring it under the control of the National Association of Securities Dealers, the powerful brokerage alliance that runs the Nasdaq stock market and is slated to acquire the Amex this month. The non-cash deal would grant the Philadelphia exchange's 505 members and more than 100 members firms, from national giants to locally based contenders, the right to continue buying and selling Philadelphia's mix of stocks and options on Amex's New York trading floor for the next 12 years.

headline: Ed through with politics - I'm tired of the crap,' mayor laments
abstract: When asked about the potential political ramifications that could arise from the possibility that the city of Philadelphia will file a lawsuit against gun manufacturers, Mayor Ed Rendell said the possibility of him running for governor is so remote that he isn’t considering any political consequences. He has shown some interest in the past about running for governor after his mayoral term ends, and he hasn’t ruled out running for office again. However, he said he’s grown tired of the demands of politicians, interest groups and the critical news-media, and there are many careers he’d enjoy pursuing outside of politics such as teaching, practicing law or getting involved with sports.

headline: Pippy passes muster on residency rule
abstract: A PA Commonwealth Judge ruled that state Representative John Pippy did meet residency requirements when he ran for and won a seat in the House in 1996 because he qualified for a military exemption based on his service. The judge also ruled that despite a recent law which was passed, judges still have the right to remove candidates from the ballot under given circumstances. In addition, Governor Ridge will tour the Whitaker Center for Science and the Arts, and Paul Cain was named director of the Veterans Affairs Bureau.

headline: Wilkes-Barre Man Unopposed for Republican Nod
abstract: A Wilkes-Barre man has announced he is seeking the Republican nomination for the 11th District US House Seat. Stephen Urban is currently running unopposed for the party nod.

headline: Not standing for it
abstract: While PA House chambers are undergoing ceiling renovations, all members are gathering in a small conference room. Votes are being calculated by members standing up for no and sitting down for yes, the constitutionality of this is in question.

headline: Hospital passes surprise checkup
abstract: Inspectors walked unannounced into Allegheny University Hospitals, Hahnemann in downtown Philadelphia on Friday, checked staffing levels, examined the amounts of drugs in the pharmacy and food in the pantry, talked to administrators and patients, looked at records and concluded patient care is not being compromised  by its parent foundation's billion dollar bankruptcy.

headline: Investing in the Future, States Spend More on Preschool Education
abstract: Many different studies have shown that children who attend full-day kindergarten and preschool are much better prepared to succeed in school in the future, which could save money in the long run and has prompted many states to provide more funding to early education programs. A federal study found that children age three to five were much more likely to be enrolled in prekindergarten programs in households with incomes above $50,000 than households making less than $30,000, so states are working especially hard to provide more opportunities to low-income families. New York, New Jersey and Connecticut began spending tens of millions of dollars last year to create more early education opportunities, but there have been some limitations on what these states have been able to provide.

headline: Proposal targets reducing state archery safety zones
abstract: A proposal by recently appointed Game Commissioner Stephen Mohr to reduce the statewide size of safety zones for archery hunting is a bad idea, according to a report by Keith Snyder, chief of the Game Commission's Hunter-Trapper Education Division.  Mohr, requested a report on extending the hunting day to a half hour after sunset, a move agency staff oppose based on research conducted at Franklin and Marshall University.  Except in special regulation areas, such as Allegheny County, state laws sets the safety zone for all hunting and trapping activity as 150 yards from any occupied building.  Mohr wants to make the statewide safety zone for archery hunting 50 yards.

headline: Pa. officials are hitting the road
abstract: PA Department of Transportation officials, including Secretary of Transportation Brad Mallory, took a ride in search of crumbling concrete and bumpy expressways. Mallory identified Route 22 as the most glaring point of need. PennDOT engineers use the International Roughness Index to score a road. Route 378 and 309 received good scores. More roadwork could be in store if federal funding comes through. Mallory blasted critic who accused US Reps. And Sens. Of pork barrel spending. The funding for 22 is short.

headline: Fisher visits are to announce arrests in state burglary ring
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher visit Cambria County and announces the two men responsible for the 52 burglaries there have been found and will be charged.

headline: A bigger center for a growing convention trade? Officials say they have hopes but no money. Meanwhile, they're busy attracting folks to the city's current facility.
abstract: Robert Butera, executive director of the PA Convention Center Authority, said the Philadelphia Convention Center is becoming increasingly popular, so he is ordering a feasibility study to look into expanding the facility; though he doesn’t want expansion talk to prevent convention planners from booking events now. Mayor Ed Rendell is calling for an expansion, and he is working with Governor Tom Ridge; however, the project could cost between $200 million and $300 million, and there are several competing projects across the state as well as in Philadelphia. As of now, there is no money set aside to expand the Convention Center.

headline: PIAA Ticket Prices Under the Gun Again
abstract: Increased ticket prices for high school games sponsored by the PIAA is straining students, fans, and families that try to follow their teams' tournament games. Students can only get the discount price if they attend the school selling tickets. With two games a week the prices can hit hard easily.

headline: Educated adults under 30 believe area has little to offer
abstract: According to the latest U.S. Census data, PA residents between the ages of 20 and 30 are increasingly leaving the state, while at the same time, the number of retirees is increasing. Many of these young adults believe the area has little to offer, and they leave for higher-paying jobs in other states. Envision Capital Region recently identified this trend as one of the midstate region’s biggest problems, and many businesses in the Harrisburg-area and across the state are searching for ways to convince this age group to remain in PA.

headline: Pippy's Republican foes had switched their party affiliation
abstract: Three registered Republicans are challenging that PA Representative John Pippy does not meet the constitutional residency requirements to represent the 44th District in the House; however, they switched their party affiliation from Democrat to Republican the same day they filed the challenges in Commonwealth Court. Two of the challengers are lawyers employed by Democrats, which makes it especially difficult to believe that the leaders of the party didn’t’ know about the case. House Democratic leader H. William DeWeese has also filed a lawsuit over the constitutionality of a law which was passed that takes away the right of voters to challenge constitutional qualifications of candidates.

headline: Williamsburg Native Running Against Specter
abstract: Tom Lingenfelter is challenging incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter in the upcoming election, and he is related to a number of different families in the Doylestown area, which he speculated could help him do well in the upcoming primary. He criticized Specter for being too liberal and said that the Republican Party deserves to be represented by a true Republican. The rest of the article provides a brief history of Lingenfelter’s life, including his education, military background, athletic career and scholarly work.

headline: Of RAD and home rule
abstract: Allegheny County will let voters decided on changing the current setup of county government. The proposed home rule carter leaves open debate as to whether the RAD tax can be removed legally if a new setup is chosen.

headline: Hospitals beware
abstract: Geisinger Medical Center is a key part of the Penn State health system, but it announced spending cuts and a hiring freeze because it lost $10.5 million in four months. According to the editorial, if top medical facilities are struggling financially, there must be something seriously wrong with the health care system that cannot be addressed by health maintenance insurance plans. In the opinion expressed by the editorial, the future of health care is seriously in question, but people must voice their concerns and not sit back idly.

headline: Jefferson schools investigate energy-saving technology
abstract: Steel Center Area Vo-Tech and Mon Valley schools are considering taking advantage of the PA Guaranteed Energy Savings Act, which was passed two years ago. According to the law, a contractor can install energy saving additions to buildings, and it will be reimbursed by the money that is saved in energy costs over a ten year period. If the plan is accepted by the school board, Landis & Staefa Inc. would install $1.2 million in improvements, the school would be expected to save $2.3 million in energy costs over a ten year period and Landis & Staefa would eventually be paid back with no additional funds being spent by the school district.

headline: Recycling efforts faltering in Phila.
abstract: Philadelphia’s recycling effort fell from 49,000 tons of paper, glass and aluminum in 1995 to 44,000 tons last year, so it didn’t meet the state’s goal of recycling 25 percent of the city’s solid waste, and it lost a $500,000 grant from the PA Department of Environmental Protection. Across the city, only 6.5 percent of residential trash and 19 percent of commercial trash was recycled, and Streets Commissioner Lawrence Moy was grilled by questions from angry City Council members. Moy attributed the low percentages to three main factors, including competition with scavengers who take recyclables to make a profit themselves.

headline: Panel adds Routes 61, 442 to highway funding plan
abstract: Several Pennsylvania Counties will receive funding for raod improvements and highway studys.

headline: Fisher: State making progress on tobacco
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher is negotiating with 7 states on the recent tobacco settlement and says that the states are making progress.

headline: Accidents may not fan flame for stadium funding
abstract: The collapse of a railing at the Army-Navy football game in Philadelphia and a fence collapse at Three Rivers Stadium near the end of the Pittsburgh Steelers game are unlikely to have an effect on the PA Legislature’s consideration of a $300 million stadium financing bill. The accidents come only days after Governor Tom Ridge vetoed a controversial bill that could have allowed funding for Pittsburgh stadiums, which most legislators complained they didn’t understand when they voted. Ridge will continue to push the Legislature to pass a separate financing bill, but several legislators didn’t think the recent accidents would convince the Legislature to act.

headline: PIAA's site change draws fire
abstract: Senator Robert Jubelirer takes issue with PIAA director Bradley Cashman over the choice to move championship games from Altoona to Hershey.

headline: Education is first in voter priorities
abstract: Education tops the list of issues likely to influence the November midterm elections, but voters also see and agenda of big problems for Washington to tackle that includes Social Security, overhauling the tax system and protecting the rights of patients according to a new Washington Post- ABC news poll. Two issues that are timely for Congress are campaign finance reform and tobacco legislation, but rank low in voter's mind.

headline: Plan 'B' Hits a Snag
abstract: Attention of House members was focused on defeating a measure by minority leader Bill DeWeese to  fund the construction of two new sports stadiums by raising the state's public debt ceiling. Although the measure failed, a clause had been inserted into another matter of routine business which allowed PA Gov. Tom Ridge to raise the debt ceiling without Legislative approval. PA Local Government Commissioner Virgel Puskarich said he had no idea what the ramifications of the bill would be when he asked the Legislature to address it. Pittsburgh and Allegheny officials saw the bill months ago and Steeler's lobbyist Chuck Knolling viewed it without suggesting changes. Ridge has pledged to veto HB 907

headline: With partisan discord, House begins historic impeachment debate
abstract: During the second day of debates, the House considered four different articles of impeachment against President Clinton, and while most Republicans support impeachment, many Democrats urged its delay while American forces are at risk in military action against Iraq. Democrats called for a vote on censoring the president as an alternative to impeachment, and they criticized Republicans for putting partisan interests ahead of the nation’s, but Republicans rejected their plea. At least one of the impeachment articles is expected to pass, which would set of the second impeachment in U.S. history, and the day became filled with even more drama after Representative Bob Livingston, who is set to become the new speaker of the House, announced that he had also had extramarital affairs.

headline: Office-holders' abuse of public trust has no political boundaries
abstract: The author says that the recent suspension of the director of the Luzerne County Office of Emergency Management Services and two of his assistants for making money by using a privately owned firm for county services is especially disappointing because the office has been doing a good job for years, and he believes it could represent a larger problem. Public officials use their positions to hand out jobs to friends and family, insert tax exemptions that are personally beneficial, do nothing to reform campaign financing that allows special interest funds to flow into their pockets and grant exemptions and favors to special interest groups who they favor. While the actions of the three Luzerne County men are strictly prohibited, the author wonders why similar abuses of public office for personal gain are allowed.

headline: Hospitals get a 2d for-profit firm's bid: Tenet Healthcare would buy Allegheny's 9 Phila area hospitals. Terms were not disclosed.
abstract: Tenet Healthcare Corp. became the second for-profit hospital firm to bid on all of Allegheny’s Philadelphia area hospitals, but it is unknown whether their offer will surpass Vanguard Health Systems’ offer of $502 million. Allegheny filed for bankruptcy, claiming $1.3 billion in debts, so any deal for the hospitals must be approved by the federal Bankruptcy Court. The Allegheny system’s main facility, Allegheny General Hospital, operates in Pittsburgh and was spared from the bankruptcy filings; however, Moody’s Investors Service told major bondholders that Allegheny General has also been seriously weakened by the financial troubles.

headline: Klock addresses school violence
abstract: Citing the recent school shooting in Edinboro, Erie County and student's Internet threats against Bethlehem Area School District teachers, Democratic state House candidate Robert Klock last week called for a tougher stance on school violence. At a news conference in front of Northampton High School, Klock said an increase in violence in schools both locally and nationally in the past two years calls for a quick action to protect students. He favors a zero-tolerance policy on guns in school and a proposed 72-hour psychological evaluation for offenders.

headline: Ridge gets report on the environment
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge was given the 21st Century Environment Commission’s report, and it identified controlling sprawl as the state’s top environmental priority. There was little hype concerning the report, which could be explained by Environmental Secretary James Seif being out of the country. The report identifies several other recommendations, and on a different note, the article describes a Pittsburgh Steelers commentator’s references to the PA Department of Transportation.

headline: Panel plans testimony for transportation hearing
abstract: Fayette County's Public Participation Panel met to start planning the county's testimoney to the State Transportation Commission Hearing as required by PA Department of Transportation.

headline: Fix it up
abstract: Current problems with contractors lead state lawmakers and Attorney General Mike Fisher to propose legislation requiring all contractor in PA to register in PA. The legislation also included provisions for contractor fees to the state and criminal penalities for contractors.

headline: Activists gear up for brawl over 'sprawl'
abstract: The efforts of advocates, known as anti-sprawl activists, are gaining momentum in promoting land development controls, and even PA Representative John Barley, a property-rights advocate, noted that many municipalities are making it difficult for developers to begin new projects. There has been a backlash from organizations such as the PA Builders Association, which issued reports claiming growth controls will impede economic growth and cause housing prices to skyrocket, and two PA think-tanks released reports that show little support for the creation of regional governments, an important part of anti-sprawl activists' plans to monitor development. The PA 21st Century Environment Commission released a report that identified controlling land growth as the key environmental issue of the future, but critics of the report claim Pennsylvanians have the right to live anywhere they choose.

headline: Playing Poker
abstract: A state Superior Court panel wisely has affirmed an Allegheny County judge's rejection of a parochial legal hypocrisy. Authorities have spent the last few years attempting to crack down on video-gaming machines. A sound initial ruling from Judge McGregor and Superior Court's affirmation this week places every community and every video-gaming vendor on notice.

headline: Election officials: Voting numbers rise with population
abstract: Voting registration in the Pocons has increased 4% and other areas continue to see an increase in registered voters as the population increases.

headline: Plan B will escape new rules
abstract: Unless the debate over whether to provide state funding for new stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh goes well into the end of next year, which is highly unlikely, lobbyists will not be required to report how much they’ve spent lobbying the issue. The law was passed to force lobbyists disclose how much they spend trying to influence legislation, but the first reports will probably not be required until October. In the meantime, Governor Tom Ridge is expected to continue trying to persuade the state Legislature to approve raising the state’s debt ceiling to provide funding next year.

headline: Wogan questions the legality of opponent's business holdings
abstract: PA Representative Chris Wogan said his opponent in the Nov. 3 election, Bill McKeown, is breaking the law by having an interest in beer distributorship and delicatessen with takeover beer. McKeown responded that he has an interest only in the beer distributorship. The conflict began when he filed a statement of financial interests with the State Ethics Commission.

headline: Official Increases Chances of Picking Winner
abstract: Mayor Steve Capelin has left three hopefuls for GOP nomination in the 10th district scratching their heads by disavowing his previous statements of support for each of their candidacies. He says he has not arrived at a formal decision yet.

headline: House GOP Plans Health Care Rights Bill
abstract: In light of growing national concern over managed health care programs in an election year, House Republicans unveiled their plan to enact reform for patients’ rights, which is a change from eight months ago when most rejected President Clinton’s call for Congress to pass a "bill of rights" for patients. The bill will include some of Clinton’s themes, such as requiring insurers to cover more emergency expenses and establishing a system to address grievances, but House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Representative Dennis Hastert have included some conservative measures that have drawn criticism from Democrats, as well as the powerful Health Insurance Association. Representative Charles Norwood Jr. has agreed to abandon his bill to support the new version, and the bill could unite the party, while it could also make the debate over health care reform even more partisan.

headline: Lapchick steps down
abstract: Months of flip-flopping debate and controversy are over. Chester Upland School Superintendent Joseph Lapchik quit for good, but offered barely the shadow of an explanation. Lapchik and Thomas Persing, the new chairman of the control board, issued a joint statement saying the bound by an agreement not to comment further. Just last month, Lapchik had agreed to stay until a successor was found, expected to be in early 1999.

headline: Ridge: Game Commission probe on target
abstract: Republican Gov. Tom Ridge said Wednesday he agrees with a legislative effort to make the Pennsylvania Game Commission more accountable to hunters, the legislature and the public.  Ridge, in an interview with the Tribune-Review, urged the Game Commission, an independent state agency, to adopt a system for tracking public complaints against Wildlife Conservation Officers and deputies as one step toward accountability.

headline: PAT joins maglev project - Route between Pittsburgh, Greensburg under study
abstract: The Port Authority of Allegheny County agreed to administer a $416,000 federal grant for Maglev Incorporated to develop a high-speed magnetic levitation train from Greensburg to Pittsburgh International Airport. Congress has included $10 million in its six-year, $204 billion transportation spending bill towards the design of a maglev system that could stretch from Pittsburgh to Philadelphia, and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, who rode a maglev train in Germany, supports the plan.

headline: For Starr, a big break fraught with risk
abstract: Kenneth Starr is the special counsel responsible for investigating President Clinton’s personal life, which includes the sexual-harassment suit that was filed against him by Paula Jones. Starr has spent $25.6 million since becoming special counsel in 1994, and he has been criticized for continuing to teach law at New York University, accepting a position at Pepperdine University and for his handling of the investigation of the death of former deputy counsel Vincent Foster Jr. While his investigation could topple Clinton’s presidency and repair Starr’s image, if the investigation concludes the allegations against Clinton are false, it could devastate Starr’s career.

headline: Africa Bill Passes in U.S. House of Representatives
abstract: The U.S. House passed the African Growth and Opportunity Act, which provide African nations with funding for debt relief and infrastructure projects. According to Congressman Charles Rangel, the bill’s co-author, the bill has broad support from Americans and Africans, and it will increase economic and trade opportunities for both Africa and the U.S. It will now go to the Senate where it’s expected to face some opposition because of textile issues.

headline: Political half-truths
abstract: The Tribune-Review criticizes the Allegheny Advances tax funded ewspaper for delivering partial truth stories to the readers.

headline: Elections may be crucial to Clinton survival, lawmakers say
abstract: Former presidential candidate Bob Dole and former White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta both agreed that the upcoming election could determine whether President Clinton faces impeachment charges or gets off with a reprimand. Panetta said that if Republicans gain seats, particularly in the U.S. Senate, Clinton will be in serious trouble of facing impeachment. The House Judiciary Committee will almost certainly begin its impeachment inquiry, and many leading Democrats criticized Republicans for diverting attention away from other problems and using the impeachment issue  to serve its own political agenda.

headline: Plan to cut government fails
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers are trying to pass legislation that would reduce the number of State Congressional members, after the 2010 census.

headline: Wogan turns down ACLU
abstract: PA Representative Chris Wogan declined an invitation to join the American Civil Liberties Union of PA. The invitation listed details on some of the organization’s lobbying efforts against "dangerous ideas," but Wogan has actively worked on several of these bills.

headline: Ohio governor hopeful comes to pa.: GOP candidate Bob Taft gets support from Gov. Tom Ridge, who is host for a fund-raiser in Pittsburgh
abstract: Bob Taft, Ohio’s Republican candidate for governor, traveled to Pittsburgh, PA for a fund-raising event held by PA Governor Tom Ridge that raised $35,000 for Taft’s campaign fund. Ridge has a commanding lead in his bid for reelection, whereas Taft is involved in a closer race, leading his opponent, Lee Fisher, by approximately eight or nine points. Former Ohio Governor George Voinovich, who had a fundraiser for Ridge four year ago, asked Ridge to help Taft,  and both Fisher and Taft have received money from out of state.

headline: In Texas, a Laboratory Test on the Effects of suing H.M.O.'s
abstract: To hear lobbyists and lawmakers in Washington tell it, giving patients the right to sue insurers that refuse to approve medical treatment would be either the death of managed care or the salvation of patients.  If Federal protection against such suits is eliminated, "you'd have business dropping health care coverage right and left," warned Mark Merritt, a vice president of the American Association of Health Plans.  Supporters of such a change argue that it is the fair thing to do.

headline: Law may benefit school district loans
abstract: PA school districts will be able to reduce costs from borrowing because of legislation that was signed into law by the governor. State Treasurer Barbara Hafer made the proposal in response to the recent scandal involving John Black in which school districts lost millions of dollars in investments. The law will allow school districts to get lower interest rates on bonds they are issued by having the PA Treasury directly handle the payments to bond agencies.

headline: Santorum, Peterson address forest issues
abstract: State Senator Bill Slocum, U.S. Representative John Peterson and U.S. Senator Rick Santorum spoke to a crowd of loggers and other concerned people at an open meeting in support of logging in Allegheny National Forest. Peterson said that 200 million acres of public land is designated for "multiple use" by the U.S. Forest Service, and he believes that timber from the forest should be marketed. Santorum criticized some environmental groups who opposed the use of timber, and all three answered questions on various different topics.

headline: PennDOT delays York Road project
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation has delayed its project to make traffic improvements at an intersection in Warwick Township because it ran out of engineering money. According to police, the intersection has been especially prone to accidents because there are no left-turn signals or left-turn lanes. Township manager Joseph Czajkowski plans to send letters to Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory, Governor Tom Ridge and state Representative David Steil, who has called the intersection the most important project in the district.

headline: Former New York Official To Lead Philadelphia Police - Shift Follows Complaints Over Crime Rate
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell selected John Timoney, who had been second in command of New York’s police force in 1995 and 1996, to replace Richard Neal as Philadelphia’s new police commissioner. While Philadelphia has never been considered one of the more dangerous cities in the country, its murder rates have yet to fall like most other cities, and it has faced accusations of brutality, corruption and numerous complaints from citizens that the police force isn’t trying hard enough to reduce everyday nuisances such as panhandling, graffiti and petty crimes. Critics have also pushed to allow the Police Commissioner to appoint and dismiss all department managers, which Rendell is considering putting on a referendum, and Timoney promised results after accepting the position.

headline: Alcoa turns over landmark
abstract: The Aluminum Company of America handed over the deed to its headquarters in downtown Pittsburgh, to use as below-market rent for nonprofit development and social service agencies. It will also double as a showcase to feature regional products, cultural attractions and development sites. President of the Southwestern PA Corp., Robert Kochanowski called the day historic. A $3 million grant from PA Gov. Tom Ridge's capital fund will help transition the building, which will house agencies such as the PA Economy League/Western Division, the Great Pittsburgh Chamber of Commerce and Action Housing.

headline: Politicians roll the dice on gambling
abstract: Gov. Parris Glendening was in an inner city church in Baltimore, Maryland discussing the evils of slot machines and the casino industry.  But Glendening's adamant stand has fractured his party, scrambled the usual political order and turned the Maryland governor's race into a referendum on gambling.

headline: Emergency Spending Bill Runs the Risk of Being Victim of Pork, Party Politics
abstract: A $3.1 billion emergency spending bill is at risk of being dragged down by pork-barrel and party politics. The Senate is already piling on add-ons for home-state voters. Another Senator is trying to add-on spending cuts to the bill for political purposes.

headline: Players
abstract: Profile on Bob Livingston including title, age, education, family, previous jobs, hobbies, and on leaving Congress.

headline: Wogan welcomes housing changes
abstract: PA Representative Chris Wogan said he’s happy with the Philadelphia Housing Authority’s promise to make changes in its operation of the federal Section 8 housing program. Wogan had been highly critical of the authority’s former executive director, John White, and he is pleased that new director, Carl Greene, plans to give preference to the working poor.

headline: On message
abstract: Percentage of registered voters polled who say the issue will be very important in their voting choices in 1998: improving education 77%, Social Security 68%, Crime 68%, tax system 66% economy 65%, campaign financing 32%, foreign affairs 36%, cigarettes 39% and abortion 41%.

headline: Independence no longer an option, doctors find: No longer able to beat 'em, area allergist plans to join 'em
abstract: Dr. George Kern has been somewhat of an anomaly in the medical community because he has been running an independent medical practice with Sam Babikian as his office manager. However, rising medical costs and problems with receiving reimbursement from health management organizations (HMOs) have led him to reconsider joining a network. According to Dr. Douglass Moeller, many doctors join networks because they are unfamiliar with how to run a business, networks allow them to concentrate efforts on providing care for patients, while reducing costs, and he expects nearly all physicians to be affiliated with a network in 10 years.

headline: Lawmakers support school's application for pool funding
abstract: Three PA Legislators, Senator James Rhoades, Representative David Argall and Representative Keith McCall, signed a letter that was sent to the state Department of Community and Economic Development in support of a grant application sent by the Panther Valley School District. The school district is trying to obtain funding to reopen it high school swimming pool, which has been closed for 13 years and would cost about $175,000 to reopen. A decision on the application should be made in the next few weeks, and Rhoades, who is chairman of the Senate Education Committee, said that projects like this improve the quality of education in schools.

headline: Sen. Ray Musto will be speaker at NE Alliance Retirees District 3 AFL-CIO dinner
abstract: PA Senator Ray Musto will be the main speaker at a dinner honoring local union leaders in Pittston Township. Musto, the long-time Democratic chairman of the Senate’s Environmental Resources and Energy Committee, is considered the Senate’s expert on environmental issues, and he has been responsible for some key environmental legislation over the years.

headline: PennDot engineer to retire, take new position with PAT
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation engineer, Henry Nutbrown, is leaving PennDOT and taking a position with the Port Authority of Allegheny County.

headline: Fox endorsed by lawmen
abstract: Local and county law enforcement officers have given their formal approval of incumbent U.S. Congressman Jon Fox. They based the endorsement on his initiative to fund bullet-proof vests for policemen and provide funding for 10 additional patrol officers in Lower Merion, as well as his support of a bill to provide funding for computerized systems on officers’ patrol cars and a bill that gives scholarship money to children whose have fallen in the line of duty.

headline: Altoona to get convention center - Shuster, Jubelirer key in getting governments to foot $60 million bill
abstract: In October, Altoona was awarded $16 million in state and federal funds to construct a 6,000-seat minor league baseball stadium, and yesterday, it was announced that the city would receive another $60 million dollars towards the construction of a convention center and surrounding roads. Governor Tom Ridge released $17.5 million in state capital funds for the convention center, and U.S. Representative Bud Shuster, who chairs the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, said $43.5 million in federal funds will go towards the construction of access roads and parking areas. PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer also played a key role in securing the funds.

headline: Politicians roll the dice on gambling
abstract: Virtually invisible on the national political scene until recently, gambling has erupted as a major issue this election year in a least 10 states. Maryland Governor Parris Glendening stood among ministers preaching the evils of slot machines and casinos. Casinos, lotteries, and racetracks have become the subjects of state controversies, some of which have created unusual alliances.

headline: Enthusiasm for local races cooled by Clinton scandal
abstract: Voters seem to be lacking interest in the upcoming election as un-opposed candidates run, candiadates are greatly leading their challengers, and the Clinton scandal is overshadowing local races.

headline: Poisonous atmosphere pervades Washington politics
abstract: The impeachment of President Clinton, which stems from his extramarital affair, and  Representative Bob Livingston’s announcement not to seek reelection two days after confessing to having adulterous affairs could be considered a fitting end to a rather horrendous year for the image of America’s politicians. The personal lives of politicians have become increasingly scrutinized by the media, especially by Hustler magazine’s editor, who offered $1 million for evidence of affairs with top politicians. While some political analysts agreed issues in the personal life could be detrimental to public service, others argued that a line must be drawn, and many of the intrusions into public officials’ live are unnecessary and unfair.

headline: World of difference on issues in governor's race
abstract: The article provides information about each gubernatorial candidate, Incumbent Republican Tom Ridge, Democrat Ivan Itkin, Constitutional Party candidate Peg Luksik and Libertarian Kenneth Krawchuck. Ridge will continue trying to lower business taxes while encouraging high-tech job development, and Itkin has criticized Ridge’s use of campaign contributions and will focus on providing more education funds to lower property taxes. Luksik is against abortion, and Krawchuck will adhere to Libertarian principles by trying to limit government interference.

headline: One Ridge to Another
abstract: The photo depicts Governor Tom Ridge and his wife, Michelle, during the Great PA Workout. Governor Ridge ran two miles, while his wife walked the two miles.

headline: Is an Allegheny bidder fading? Money picture continues shift
abstract: There is evidence that Vanguard Health, which made a $460 million bid to purchase the bankrupt Allegheny health system’s hospitals in Philadelphia, may be second guessing its bid. Allegheny has questionable budget sheets, and Vanguard’s chief financial backer, Morgan Stanley, has urged them to rescind or the lower the offer in order to reduce investment risks. Vanguard has denied second guessing the bid, but if it pulled out, it would leave Tenet Healthcare, who bid $465 million, as the only likely bidder; though there remains the possibility that both could walk away from the deal, leaving Allegheny with no bidders.

headline: Legality of voucher plan is debated before judge The Southeast Delco School District's plan was argued over at a Delaware County Court hearing
abstract: Southeast Delco School District budgeted $1.2 million of its surplus to provide vouchers to cover the costs of students who attend private schools in the area; however, a group of parents sued, and there was a hearing in front of Delaware County Judge Joseph Battle yesterday. School vouchers have become a national issue, so many advocacy groups from both sides were in attendance at the hearing. The plaintiffs’ lawyer argued school boards have no authority under the law to provide vouchers, whereas the school board’s lawyer said they have the right to enact innovative programs amidst concerns that rising taxes could be forcing many parents to shift their children from private to public schools.

headline: Sewer plant charges to be aired today   Officials to probe whether the Chalfont-New Britain Township Joint Sewer Authority may be allowing new hookups even though its plant is over capacity
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection, Bucks County Health Department and the Chalfont-New Britain Township Joint Sewer Authority will hold a meeting to discuss accusations that the authority is allowing new sewer hookups while its plant is allegedly operating well above capacity and is dumping untreated sewage into Neshaminy Creek. State Senator Joe Conti wrote a letter asking for a quick resolution, and it is unknown whether he was invited to join the discussions. A new development could generate thousands of gallons of sewage to be treated at the plant, and while many officials are concerned about monthly readings that show the plant is operating above capacity, authority officials claim those results were distorted by rainfall, and they have not been reckless in accepting new hookups.

headline: PennDOT expands agility Program
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation pilot program aimed at cutting costs is now available statewide, announced Deputy Secretary for Administration Robert Wonderling. The Agility Program allows state, county and local governments to develop temporary agreements to share resources across borders of jurisdiction.

headline: Freedberg's court could cut travels
abstract: For several years, Lehigh Valley residents with federal court cases have become increasingly familiar with traffic jams on the Schuylkill Expressway, that notorious highway to Center City Philadelphia.  Fewer federal judges have been handling cases in Lehigh and Berks counties because of illness and administrative duties of the judges here.  For Lehigh Valley residents, that has meant more travel to the U.S. Courthouse in Philadelphia.

headline: Anti-slumlord legislation final approval
abstract: The first of six proposed anti-slumlord bills was signed into law this week by Gov. Tom Ridge after mid-state lawmakers pushed it through the Legislature.  "These are landmark bills," said Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed, a Democrat, who said the bill was passed because of hard work by Sen. Jeffrey E. Piccola, R-Susquehanna Twp., Rep. Ron Buxton, D-Harrisburg and Senate Majority Whip David J. Brightbill, R-Lebanon.  The measure Ridge signed takes effect in late March.

headline: Power can corrupt when oversight is abdicated
abstract: Opinion piece comparing the PIAA meeting to the McCarthy investigation hearings. The PIAA doesn't evoke much sympathy around PA. Lawmakers originally got involved with PIAA because of its questionable site selections for state play off games, but after that meeting they will be digging deeper.

headline: Eppard indicted in peddling probe - Former Shuster aide accused of embezzling from campaign
abstract: U.S. Representative Bud Shuster’s former top aide, Ann Eppard, has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston for allegedly embezzling $27,500 from Shuster’s campaign committee and for accepting gratuities associated with the Big Dig, an $11 billion public works projects to dig a tunnel across the Boston Harbor. Eppard has denied all charges; however, the indictment alleges she conspired with another lobbyist, Vernon Clark, and received $230,000 in gratuities and loans to intervene on behalf of two Boston businessmen whose properties were being taken for the project. While several major newspapers have questioned the close relationship between Eppard and Shuster, who chairs the House transportation committee, Shuster has not been identified as a co-conspirator, and he has maintained Eppard’s innocence.

headline: 'Policy' cost a public servent
abstract: Dr. Wander Filer, Pennsylvania’s physician general, resigned from here post because of the inflexive policy of Governor Ridge’s office.  Dr. Filer sent a letter to the Legislature outlining areas of concern in Pennsylvania health issues. The proximate reason of Dr. Filer's resignation was because of a bill concerning diabetes.

headline: Worry stalks Saidel fund-raising gala
abstract: The mood at a fund-raising event for City Controller Jonathan Saidel was fairly solemn due to PA Attorney General Mike Fisher’s criminal charges against Diane Roca, Saidel’s former girlfriend and campaign treasurer, stemming from alleged campaign-finance abuses. Saidel easily won re-election last year, and he has been identified as a potential candidate for the 1999 mayoral election; however, his association with Roca could make him look very bad. Several Democrats have criticized Fisher, a Republican, for filing the charges based on political reasons, and they feel it’s a shame that Saidel’s image may be tarnished when no charges were even filed against him.

headline: Only 48% of eligible voters go to the polls
abstract: Despite the fact that more people are registering to vote in PA due to legislation that makes it easier to register, 48% of eligible voters in the state didn’t vote in the 1996 Presidential election between Bill Clinton and Bob Dole. The numbers grow even worse for election years that don’t involve presidential or gubernatorial races, and Millersville political science professor G. Terry Madonna believes that the poor voter turnout can be blamed on the general public’s cynicism towards politicians due to incidents such as Vietnam, Watergate and Clinton’s alleged sexual encounters. Registration barriers, limited voting to one day, lack of accountability for politicians, the power of incumbency and various other factors are also cited as reasons for why people don’t vote.

headline: Itkin campaigns for state intervention in Medicare battle
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center and Highmark Blue Cross have been involved in an ongoing dispute over a Medicare program, and gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin called on Governor Ridge to intervene to protect the 130,000 seniors who could be affected. The federal Health Care Finance Agency hasn’t increased funding enough to offset rising costs, which is at the heart of the dispute, and those involved refused to comment on the possibility of intervention but hoped to reach an agreement.

headline: Legislation Would Grant More Special Education Funding
abstract: PA Representative Jess Stairs and Senator Robert Tomlinson introduced separate pieces of legislation that would basically accomplish the same goal: providing more state funds for special education programs, with poor districts receiving the greater share of state funding. Stairs admitted that the legislation could cost up to $117 million to implement, but he assured school districts would still be required to raise substantial amounts of money to pay for special education. Stairs said his bill will make the distribution of special education funds more fair, so school districts that require funding the most will receive it.

headline: Shuster plans visit to utility job in Wood area
abstract: U.S. Representative Bud Shuster will be the keynote speaker for a kick-off ceremony for two projects that are underway in Robertsdale and Wood. The projects, which include a wastewater collection and treatment project as well as a water supply and environmental restoration project, are expected to cost $5.8 million. Shuster obtained federal funding to pay for some of the costs, and there will be several other speakers at the event.

headline: PennDOT hears 202 proposals
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation Administrator of District 6, Andrew Warren, says the purpose of PennDOT's plans to ease traffic with a 202 bypass is to alleviate traffic congestion. PA Sen. Edwin Holl has been involved in meetings. PA Rep. Joseph Gladeck believes the 202 bypass must be constructed in conjunction with improvements near route 63 at the Upper Gwynned/Montgomery Township line. Secretary of PennDOT, Brad Mallory, is to take part in the discussion. The Federal government is expected to announce approval or disapproval of construction plans in March.

headline: Full-court press: Toward a lasting solution on Common Pleas funding
abstract: The PA Supreme Court invoked its "King’s Bench" authority to take over jurisdiction in a court case involving a lawsuit by Judge Robert E. Dauer on behalf of the Common Pleas Court against three Allegheny County Commissioners for providing the court with inadequate funding. The authors of the editorial believe that the Supreme Court’s decision should send a powerful message to Governor Ridge and the General Assembly that they need to  make Pennsylvania’s judiciary system unified, which is a requirement in the state constitution and has been a demand of the Supreme Court for the last 11 years.

headline: Area legislators say Ridge takes right step with veto
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge vetoed a bill that could have allowed the state to provide $172 million in bonds for the construction of new stadiums in Pittsburgh. According to PA Senator Michael O’Pake, the Legislature didn’t intend for the bill to allow such funding, and Senator David Brightbill said Ridge made the right decision by vetoing the bill and ending any possibility of a long legal battle. State Representatives Sheila Miller and David Argall shared their thoughts on stadium funding, which died in the House but is expected to be considered again in January when the Legislature reconvenes.

headline: Proposal on vendors draws a protest - An ordinance would limit food vendors near Penn. Students and others are none too pleased.
abstract: A public hearing was held in the Philadelphia City Council over a proposed ordinance that would assign food vendors around the University of Pennsylvania’s campus to specific locations and would impose restrictions on operating hours as well as design standards. A representative for the university said vending had gotten out of control and was hurting some local businesses; however, several students showed up to protest because they often rely on vendors for quick, cheap meals, and many vendors spoke out against the ordinance because it could potentially force some of them out of business. City Council President John Street, who was one a vendor himself, assured vendors that they would still be protected under the new ordinance.

headline: Erie to be a major star in Gov. Ridge's new re-election video
abstract: A new campaign video for Governor Tom Ridge’s reelection bid will be unveiled at a Republican State Committee dinner, and Ridge officials are hoping it has the same effect as Reagan’s 1984 presidential reelection film, "Morning in America," which helped him win by a landslide victory. The polls show Ridge is in a strong position against little-known PA Representative Ivan Itkin, who is the only Democrat to announce candidacy as of now, but the film is intended to address one weakness. Most people know very little about Ridge’s background, so the film will focus on his early life in Erie, his service in Vietnam and his political climb to become elected governor in 1994.

headline: Policy of 'attack politics' has finally backfired on Clinton's White House
abstract: Patrick Buchnan, the article’s author, claims the White House’s use of aggressive tactics backfired, and it will all but guarantee that President Clinton is impeached by the House Judiciary Committee and possibly the entire House. In his opinion, Republicans were demoralized after doing poorly in the past election, and all Clinton had to do was offer them a reasonable way to back away from their calls for impeachment. According to Buchnan, the White House missed two open opportunities and arrogantly went on the attack against Republicans, leaving them with no other choice but impeachment, and he also says the Democrats have never even bothered to try to defend Clinton’s innocence.

headline: Writer Keisling is often alone, underfunded
abstract: Writer Bill Keisling is seeking the Democratic nomination to run for governor, but he has refused to raise or spend much money and is far behind his rivals, Ivan Itkin and Don Bailey, who he called "blowhards." Keisling's father was a politician and lobbyist, and he has said that he doesn’t care about the people that have called him a fool for running against nearly insurmountable odds. He has used his campaign to criticize the poor conditions of two Harrisburg schools, and he said he would consider his run a success if it results in even one broken window being fixed.

headline: Our Views: Prepare to cast your vote wisely
abstract: The authors believe that most Americans don’t pay much attention to elections until a few weeks prior to Election Day. In order to help provide more information, the authors claim the newspaper will increase its coverage of the upcoming election, which will include a number of key PA and national races, including the governor, lieutenant governor, U.S. Senator and the local representatives for the state House and state Senate. The authors are disappointed that less than half of eligible voters will show up to vote,  but they hope those who do vote take the time to make an informed decision.

headline: Legislature approves changes in managed health care
abstract: The PA General Assembly overwhelmingly passed a "bill of rights," which will soon be signed by Governor Ridge, that should benefit the five million Pennsylvanians who have managed health care plans. The bill provides a number of new benefits for doctors and patients that are meant to address complaints about insurers; however, President Clinton has proposed a national bill that could supersede it. There were some complaints about the language of the bill, Senators Robert Thompson and Jim Gerlach provided reasons for their support, and the bill will also increase low-cost health care coverage to up to 125,000 children.

headline: Legislation would help protect schools
abstract: PA Senator Melissa Hart is drafting legislation in response to the recent scandal involving John Garner Black, who allegedly lost $71 million of investments from school districts and municipalities. Hart’s legislation would protect school districts and municipalities from investment fraud in the future by establishing stricter investment regulations. The PA School Board Association has offered its own models for school boards to follow, and Association Assistant Executive Director Tom Gentzel is concerned Hart's proposal will be too restrictive.

headline: Smith sets his sights on reform
abstract: Hunters and other game-land users will take aim at the state Game Commission this week at a public hearing to review the agency's law-enforcement procedures.  Complaints from sportsmen and a recent series of articles in the Tribune- Review of Pittsburgh have alarmed lawmakers, who responded this month with a package of proposals to rein in the agency charged with reining in hunters.  The hearing before the House Game and Fisheries Committee on Tuesday will feature testimony from those who claim they were mistreated by the Game Commission's wildlife conservation officers and deputies.

headline: PennDOT is paving the way for more Bedford road jobs
abstract: In Bedford County, PennDOT will double the funds in 1999 for bridge and road projects.

headline: Fund-raiser for firefighter group fined
abstract: For the second year in a row, The Gehl Group of Fort Lauderdale Fla. Is fined by PA for using deceptive and misleading practices to rasie funds for firefighters.

headline: Artwork to add class to convention center
abstract: Artists would also benefit from the $809 million proposal for building two new stadiums and a larger convention center in Pittsburgh. The Public Auditorium Authority accepted a $500,000 donation from the Vira Heinz Foundation to be used to place artwork into the David L. Lawrence Convention Center after its expansion, and officials hope to get another $500,000 in donations, which would be matched by a $1 million state grant towards artwork. Across the state and country, it’s been common to provide funding for artwork to improve the appearance of new facilities, and an artwork committee will work closely with an architectural firm that’s designing the convention center’s expansion.
