headline: Regional industrial and education training center opens
abstract: The North Central PA Regional Planning and Development Commission recently opened the Industrial Technical Education Center in Ridgway, and PA Senator Bill Slocum and Representative Dan Surra were invited to speak at its opening ceremony. The center will offer both instructional and hands on training to high school graduates, so they will have the skills to work in the region’s important technological manufacturing sector. The center will, among other programs, offer training to prepare students for a career in powdered metal manufacturing, which is important because the region is already home to 40% of America’s powdered metal manufactures, and the industry is expected to grow substantially in the next few years.

headline: Evans behaving in a mayoral manner
abstract: PA Representative Dwight Evans, the first announced Democratic mayoral candidate for 1999, put pressure on the Philadelphia City Council to hire John Timoney as the new police commissioner, has gotten involved in talks with the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority and has ordered a study on the district’s troubled school system. Some have questioned whether he’s gotten involved in these issues to boost his name recognition for the upcoming election. While Evans can advocate ideas that he essentially doesn’t have to worry about the results for, his rival in the upcoming mayoral election, City Council President John Street, may be at a disadvantage because he’s the one who must implement changes and suffer the consequences of failure.

headline: Political Consensus: The Explosive Moment Was a Dud
abstract: President Clinton’s videotaped testimony before independent counsel Kenneth Starr aired yesterday, but almost everyone seems to agree that is wasn’t nearly as bad as Democrats feared and Republicans anticipated. Most U.S. Congressmen were hesitant to comment on the tape, and most Democrats throughout the country seemed relieved; though there is no indication the footage will slow the House Judiciary Committee’s impeachment inquiry or improve the Democrat’s gloomy outlook for the upcoming election. The opinions of numerous Democrats and Republicans from around the country are given in the article, and a common theme is the videotape is unlikely to have dramatically shifted the public's opinion in either direction.

headline: Wyoming County Man Running for Congress
abstract: Don Sherwood of Tunkhannock Township, who owns automobile dealerships and a forestry-equipment business, will seek the Republican nomination to run for the 10th District Congressional seat that will be left open by the retirement of U.S. Representative Joseph McDade, and he vowed to improve employment opportunities to keep younger people in the region. He will join at least four other Republican candidates, including Scranton Mayor Jim Connors, as well as two Democrats, one Patriot Party candidate and one Independent who will also run for the office. Saving Medicare and Social Security, overhauling the tax code, improving education and strengthening crime-fighting measures were some of the issues Sherwood said were important to him.

headline: OVERDUE    Lobbyists reform is a step forward
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is expected to sign a bill into law that will require lobbyists to register with the State Ethics Commission, file expense reports every three months if they spend over $500, identify lawmakers who receive gifts and meals costing more than $250 at one time or $650 a year and publish a directory of lobbyists. The authors clearly believe this is a step forward from the state’s "pathetically weak" past laws, and they especially give credit to state Senator Robert Jublierer and former state Senator David Heckler. However, they still believe the Legislature needs to work on campaign finance reform in the future.

headline: It's 'watchdog' vs. 'yardstick' in the inspection debate
abstract: The state Health Department is defending its decision to change the way Pennsylvania hospitals are inspected for license renewal.  State Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr. claims the change could diminish quality of care, because the inspections can be made every three years, instead of the usual two.  Health officials argue that the decision to allow the Joint Commission for Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations to conduct inspections eliminates duplication.

headline: Legislators go to bat
abstract: Elected officials are making every effort to ensure students' education will not be disrupted by the decision in the Wilkins- Penn Hills boundary case showing parents concerning have not fallen on deaf ears. The 665 feet boundary move has many concerned.

headline: State eyes $2.5 million to boost eco-tourism
abstract: Frank Felbaum, director of the state Wild Resource Conservation Fund, is an outspoken advocate for the creation of a network of wildlife viewing areas in PA, which he believes could be used to encourage people to spend money on trips to wildlife refugees and boost the state’s economy. The main proposal being considered would involve $2.5 million a year in spending to establish a wildlife network by developing sites, putting up maps and displays, as well as printing maps. Whether the idea becomes successful largely will depend on the future of the wild resource fund which faces a fiscal crisis; though officials are considering new options for raising money.

headline: PennDOT makes pitch for new program
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is pitching its new transportation idea, 'agility program.' The program would have PennDOT and various townships switch off projects and help each other with transportation issues.

headline: Gail Willard to push for Aimee's Law
abstract: The mother of a murder victim is pushing the U.S. Congress to pass a law in honor of her daughter, to make stricter parole requirements.

headline: Aye or nay
abstract: The pros and cons of H.B. 2446, which would allow the PA Department of Transportation to issue sports license plates and use the money collected to help fund arena and stadium construction projects are presented. Similar plans have succeeded in Florida, New York and Washington. Critics argue the state has no place in the arena/stadium financing business in the first place.

headline: Regulators guilty of malpractice
abstract: The failure of two of the state's largest medical malpractice insurers raises some serious questions about the effectiveness of state regulators.  After all, warning signals were being raised about one of the companies seven years before the state Insurance Department interceded.  Since the beginning of the year, PIC Insurance Group Inc. of Fort Washington, Montgomery County, and P.I.E. Mutual Insurance Co. of Cleveland, Ohio, have been placed in liquidation, the equivalent of a Chapter 7 bankruptcy, by the Insurance Department.

headline: Evans retains control of Appropriations Committee
abstract: PA Representative Dwight Evans of Philadelphia enhanced the legitimacy of his mayoral candidacy by defeating Representative Alan Butkovitz handily to retain his position as chairman of the House Appropriations Committee. Representative Harold James, chairman of the House Black Caucus, said the caucus worked hard to get Evans re-elected, and Butkovitz’s loss is seen as a defeat for state Senator Vincent Fumo, who had supported Butkovitz because he believes House Democrats have been split since Evans supported the removal of House Speaker Kenneth O’Donnell in 1992. William DeWeese, Michael Veon, Mark Cohen and other legislators were also re-elected to Democratic leadership posts.

headline: Political finance reforms OK'd: House approval of major campaign overhaul stuns GOP
abstract: Many House Republicans defied their leadership, and by a 237-186 vote, the House passed a bipartisan campaign finance reform bill sponsored by U.S. Representatives Christopher Shays and Marty Meehan that will likely be sent to the Senate for consideration. Once it gets to the Senate, it will face an uphill battle since Senator Mitch McConnell employed a filibuster in February to defeat a similar bill, and John McCain, who supported that bill along with Russell Feingold, admitted there aren’t enough votes to overcome the filibuster. The bill is meant to eliminate the 1996 campaign abuses in which both parties took advantage of loopholes to illegally promote their own candidates with "soft money" from big donors, unions and interest groups.

headline: Yes, Specter has opponent
abstract: Richard Orloski, who dropped out of the U.S. Senate race, is writing the letter to criticize the press’s coverage of the race. He defends Bill Lloyd, who is running against incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, and he criticizes the press for essentially giving Specter the election by not providing any significant coverage of the race.

headline: Pa. Dems tilt at impossible dream instead of facing realities of the '90s
abstract: Only two candidates endorsed by Pennsylvania’s Democratic state committee have been elected since Bob Casey’s reelection for governor in 1990, and the author criticizes the party for failing to realize that there has been a shift in public opinion towards a more centrist and smaller government approach to politics. The author attended a debate in Hershey in hopes of finding some reinvigoration to at least make the upcoming election interesting; however, only about 20 of the several hundred members of the committee actually showed up, and he concluded State Representatives Ivan Itkin and Bill Lloyd, the party’s endorsed gubernatorial and U.S. Senate candidates, were not up to the task of reenergizing the party. He concluded the Democratic Party held on to its outdated rhetoric and failed to adapt to changing public opinion.

headline: John Pezak, 84, former state legislator
abstract: John Pezak died of congestive heart failure at the age of 84. He had worked with the PA Revenue Department, and he served from 1964 to 1972 as the 175th District’s state representative. He was also involved in a number of organizations, including one that ran a Christmas party for mentally and physically handicapped children.

headline: Legislators reinstate funding to Lincoln University
abstract: Lawmakers grant $5.9 million o Lincoln University to keep the campus in business. After alleged financial mismanagement by University President Niara Sudarkasa, there is hope for Lincoln University to financially recover.

headline: Solutions to a tiring problem   Braddock waste-tire recycler calls for system to track tires from point of purchase in effort to make more available for recycling
abstract: Rochez Bros. Incorporated has a rubber recovery division that recycles used tires; however, the plant’s processing capability is struggling to be met largely because of people who illegally dump tires. The company’s general manager, Michael Deep, wants PA to develop a tracking system of tires from purchase to when they are properly disposed in order to cut back on illegal tire dumping and provide their company with more tires to recycle. The recycled rubber can be used for many different uses, and state Representative Tom Michlovic acknowledged that tire dumping in PA is a serious problem that is a public health hazard.

headline: PennDOT official a bridge support
abstract: Henry Nutbrown is supporting a construction bridge project on Route 28 expressway.

headline: Gekas meets with FBI officials on Elizabethtown training mistake
abstract: U.S. Representative George Gekas questioned FBI officials over a recent incident at an FBI training mission in Elizabethtown, PA. A group of teenagers was mistakenly arrested by an FBI SWAT team, but no blame was handed out by Gekas, who said the agents will ultimately be addressed by their superiors and Attorney General Janet Reno.

headline: Bait for new business needs a hook as well
abstract: Bucks County Courier Times praises Govenor Tom Ridge's idea of tax breaks for businesses investing in  failing communities, but urges lawmakers to have strcit rules about businesses staying in the community and not taking the money and moving elsewhere.

headline: Rep. George debates ATM fees
abstract: Reprsentative Camille George talks about ATM transactions, POS purchases, and associated bank fees for customers.

headline: Everyone shook hands with the governor
abstract: Governor Ridge attended a cocktail party at the Towanda Country Club, which raised money for his reelection campaign. Ridge was first greeted by the St. Agnes Student Council, and he spoke to hundreds of supporters who showed up for the event. The article provides the reasons for why many people attended the event to support Ridge, and PA Representatives Scot Chadwick, Matt Baker and Sandra Major also spoke.

headline: Political newcomers square off in 12th District race
abstract: Representative Pat Careone is retiring, and two newcomers to politics, Republican Daryl Metcalfe and Democrat Tim Tuinstra, are vying to win the 12th District’s seat in the PA House to replace her. The two candidates spent time in Saxonburg answering questions, and they both said they'd try to reduce local property taxes by increasing state funding. Metcalfe told one woman that he’d stand up against Ridge if he disagrees with him on issues, and Tuinstra felt voters want three things from him: obtain state funding for highways, ensure adequate support of school districts and make sure health care coverage is adequate.

headline: Yielding GOP, gleeful Dems usher in bill
abstract: The White House and congressional leaders from both parties all found something to crow about in the end-of-Congress budget deal that adds billions in federal spending from the schoolhouse to the Pentagon. But conservative House Republicans denounced the package as a came-in to Democrats' spending priorities. Democrats seemed to agree. Republicans choose their battles though to curry favor with the public for next months elections.

headline: Pa. desperately needs 'New Democrats'
abstract: New Democrats are coming out in force and winning election throughout the nation. Pennsylvnia New Democrats can prove beneficial to the state.

headline: Judge grants hospital merger petition: Penn State Geisinger/Hershey union is 'appropriate fit'
abstract: Dauphin County Judge Warren Morgan approved a petition filed by Penn State University to confirm the affiliation between the Milton S. Hershey Medical Center and the Penn State Geisinger Health System Foundation. Parts of Morgan’s opinion are given in the article, and comments are provided from Dr. C. McCollister Evarts, dean of Penn State’s College of Medicine, and Dr. Stuart Heydt, chief executive officer of the Penn State Geisinger Health System, who are both clearly pleased with the judge's decision.

headline: Let's save students, not money
abstract: Cecelia Burks, whose first substitute teaching assignment in the Philadelphia school system was with students in a Special Education Program, challenges Governor Tom Ridge and others who oppose additional public school funding to visit with the children in the program. She explains how decisions by the U.S. Supreme Court and the PA Supreme Court have contributed to the dire circumstances these students now face. She claims money that was the focus of President Clinton’s 1996 campaign could have been used to help these children, and without additional funds, she argues they are likely to drop out of school.

headline: Speakers urge better weather radar here
abstract: A crew team rowed on Presque Isle Bay two years ago, and the weather unexpectedly changed and sank two of their boats. Some of these crew members and others testified at a meeting before U.S. Representative Ken Calvert, chairman of the House Subcommittee on Energy and the Environment, in hopes of getting federal funding for the New Generation Weather Service. U.S. Representative Phil English of Erie said the new radar system needed to be installed and is awaiting authorization, while Erie Mayor Joyce Savocchio and others also supported its installation, claiming weather forecasting had deteriorated since a weather service office was moved from Erie to Cleveland in 1994.

headline: PennDOT optimistic about latest bypass plan
abstract: PennDOT officials are confident that their latest proposal for the Marshalls Creek bypass will meet the environmental regulations and be given the ok to proceed with the project.

headline: Gold behind bars
abstract: Cambria County is upset over the state's decision to ban the county from housing out-of-state inmates in their facilities, which would generate nearly $2 million per year.

headline: Bill's tax breaks provide incentive to live downtown - Aid to owners who renovate may slow rural development
abstract: PA Representative Thomas Tangretti introduced a bill in the House that would offer tax breaks to help owners of historic buildings in residential neighborhood fix up their properties. The state Legislature has recently tackled a number of measures focused on improving the state’s cities, and Tangretti’s bill goes along well with Governor Tom Ridge’s 21st Century Environment Commission, which recently called on the Legislature to improve the state’s cities and boroughs to help reduce sprawl development. The bill has the support of over 50 member of the House, including Representative Patricia Vance, and several historic conservation groups.

headline: Restaurants are fattening region's economy - As patrons belly up to the buffet, food service becomes the high-growth industry.
abstract: As Americans are increasingly eating out, the restaurant industry has expanded rapidly, and over the past five years, 11,000 new jobs in the Philadelphia region and over 1 million new jobs throughout the rest of the nation have been created by restaurants. However, researchers are concerned about the increase in restaurants because food eaten at restaurants traditionally contains many of the nutrients that are overconsumed and less of the nutrients that are underconsumed by most Americans, which may be contributing the nation’s rise in obesity rates. While restaurants have provided thousands of new jobs, most of them are low-paying jobs that don’t provide livable wages, which is another concern of many researchers, but ultimately, economists predict the restaurant industry will continue its strong growth.

headline: Everything points to Fox
abstract: Mary Crawford, spokeswoman for the National Congressional Committee, said the committee believes U.S Representative Jon Fox is in good shape to be reelected to represent the 13th District in PA. Polls show voters are generally pleased with their incumbents from Congress, and low voter turnout, President Clinton’s scandal and uninspired Democratic state races could be good for the Republican Fox. Hoeffel, Fox’s challenger, was narrowly defeated two years ago, but evidence from around the nation suggests that Fox should win even more comfortably this year.

headline: Political Notebook
abstract: Mike Turzai, who is the Republican congressional candidate for the 4th District, received the endorsement of the National Federation of Independent Business.

headline: York man wants Goodling donations probed
abstract: A York County man asked the Federal Election Commission to investigate campaign donations made to US Representative Bill Goodling by the National Republican Congressional Committee. In a complaint filed with the commission on May 8 Garry Kling says the NRCC has made or will make significant contributions to the Goodling campaign beyond the $5,000 in permissible primary contributions." The NRCC is a committee of the National Republican Party.

headline: Pa. lawmakers put some teeth in weak campaign finance law
abstract: PA is considered to have some of the weakest campaign finance laws in the nation, but Governor Tom Ridge is expected to sign a bill that will at least close some loopholes which allow lobbyists to avoid filling out spending reports. According to the new legislation, lobbyists would have to file public reports each quarter they spend more than $500 on lobbying, and they would have to identify lawmakers who receive gifts worth over $250 or hospitality that costs over $650. PA Representative Greg Vitali wants to take it further by requiring lobbyists to disclose what legislation they are trying to influence, and Representative David Levdansky wants to put caps on campaign contributions and spending.

headline: Klink pushes whistleblower bill to protect health care workers
abstract: U.S. Rep. Ron Klink, D-4th, of Murrysville has introduced legislation to protect people who work in the medical field from being punished for speaking out against practices that could harm patients.  "Health care workers have the best information day-to-day on the quality of care in a facility," Klink said at a news conference Friday at the offices of Local 585 of the Service Employees International Union.  The union represents about 6,000 health care workers in western Pennsylvania.

headline: Letters support defeat of bill
abstract: Over 4,000 letters will be sent to four state legislators from Lackawanna County, Representatives Gaynor Cawley, Fred Belardi, Frank Serafini and Ed Staback, asking them to oppose a bill that would allow the PA Department of Transportation to sell land to the Scranton School District for the construction of a new school. The land is situated on top of seven mines, and it is close to a site that caved in years ago, resulting in the death of a man. Opponents of the bill fear the school’s weight could cause the mines to collapse, and they also argue the school’s cost is so high because of the additional money needed to stabilize it.

headline: Spock wants License Fee Approved
abstract: Game Commissioner Dr. Nicholas Spock is calling on state legislators to get the Game Commission's request for a hunting license fee increase off the back burner and bring it up for approval. While the Game Commission is an independent agency that doesn't need legislative approval for most of its activities it does need that approval before license fees cab be increased. The last hunting license hike was in 1985 and it was not just the legislators who had problems with the increase.

headline: PennDOT planners look for input
abstract: PennDOT wants to shorten the transportation planning term that is currently 12 years long, and is holding a meeting in York County so offocials and residents can be informed and comment on the issue.

headline: GOP is blocking Senate bills
abstract: Opinion piece in response "Let's get real about crime war." In addition to the contents of that article we need cooperation form the governor and Republican Legislature. The governor believes the streets are safer, but he has obviously not walked the streets of Reading lately. We must prevent crime in the first place. Crime across the commonwealth is up, so we must do better.

headline: Break out the bunting - Straw hats off to those who landed the convention, and a welcome to GOP from the cradle of liberty.
abstract: The Republican Party announced they would be holding their 2000 National Convention in Philadelphia, which Mayor Ed Rendell and Governor Tom Ridge have both worked hard to achieve. The convention will increase media exposure to the city, bring millions of dollars in business and result in about 20,000 hotel rooms being booked, which could help jump-start the city’s tourism industry. The authors of the editorial are clearly pleased with the announcement, and they believe it provides an even greater incentive to push city construction and renovation projects.

headline: Ridge asks for disaster declaration
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge aska for federal disaster status and relief for Allegheny county after the June thunderstorms. President Cllinton has already declarred some counties federal disaster areas.

headline: Exodus from area registers as one of Pa's highest drops
abstract: According to the latest U.S. Census, county in Pennsylvania are seeing a large number of decreases in population.

headline: Political Potpourri - Rizzo leads tribute to local legend Bert Lancaster
abstract: Philadelphia City Councilman-at-Large Frank Rizzo Jr. organized a birthday reception at the City Council to honor Bert Lancaster, a long time promoter of youth sports in Philadelphia, and in other news, U.S. Representative Chaka Fattah was awarded Widener University’s 19th Annual Reverend Jesse Anderson Sr. Award for his commitment to education. Tommie Blackwell secured a large contribution in case he decides to run for the seat held by PA Representative Anthony Hardy Williams, who is expected to run for his father’s seat, and Dennis Morrison-Wesley has been harshly critical of the media for their role in his race against Bob Brady for the First Congressional District. In addition, two groups are cosponsoring a voter registration drive, there will be a grand opening ceremony for a campaign office for Thelma Peakes, and two local politicians will host an Easter Egg Hunt in Germantown.

headline: Yudichak succeeds Jarolin
abstract: John Yudichak, who defeated incumbent Stanley Jarolin in the Democratic Primary, handily won election to represent the 119th Legislative District in the PA House over Republican challenger Jean Sepling. He plans to try to raise standards in public schools, lower property taxes, allow people the freedom to choose their doctors without interference from their health providers and find ways to attract small business growth.

headline: Pa. legislators will do well in retirement
abstract: PA Representative Ivan Itkin, who lost the gubernatorial race, will receive about $75,000 a year as part of his pension plan for 26 years of service; however, Representative Leonard Gruppo, who was elected to the House six years after Itkin, will only receive $22,867 a year because the pension system changed after 1974. Some legislators have complained, including Representative Andrew Carn, and legislators could potentially try to pass pension increases during the "lame duck" session; though it is unlikely since Governor Tom Ridge has expressed no interest in undertaking the issue. The article provides some details on the pension system as well as a listing of estimated pension payments for several existing PA legislators.

headline: Klink sponsoring health-care meetings
abstract: Representative Ron Klink is hosting several meetings to discuss very important health care issues facing the nation.

headline: Libraries need dedicated Pa. fund support  Catching up is expensive
abstract: According to the editorial, some libraries have tough punishments for those with overdue books; however, the authors believe Lansdale Public Library’s "amnesty week," which allows all overdue books to be returned free of charge is a better approach. They also claim PA libraries are among the most underfunded in the nation. They believe Governor Ridge’s call to increase funding is a good start, but continual funding will be needed for libraries to catch up.

headline: Sportsmen's Sphere
abstract: The PA Game Commission will hold a meeting in Reading that the public can attend to discuss a number of proposals, and PA Senator Michael O’Pake will attend a legislative forum there. The author claims a proposal to allow junior hunters to kill antlerless deer during the two weeks of buck season will be controversial, he disagrees with a proposal to increase deer permits in Bradford County, and he expects two gobbler spring seasons and longer small game seasons to be approved. In addition, he discusses the opening of trout season, as well as a relocation project to move some wild elk from Elk to Clinton County.

headline: PennDOT plans early start on bridge
abstract: As part of plans to link Interstate 79 with the PA Turnpike, the PA Department of Transportation will begin widening the Route 228 bridge over Interstate 79 a year early to help reduce anticipated traffic backups that will come from the Cranberry connector project. The project is estimated to cost $65 million, and it will reduce traffic at the intersection of Routes 228 and 19, which PA Senator Melissa Hart said is the 10th busiest junction in PA. There are also two major developments proposed for the Route 228 corridor, including a shopping center and an office park.

headline: GOP state House members target violence in schools
abstract: According to House Majority Leader John Perzel, legislation aimed at stopping violence in schools will be a top priority for Republican lawmakers, who have unveiled 14 bills in which some of the main elements are described in the article. School violence has been a growing concern throughout the country, and it became especially evident in PA when a student killed a teacher and wounded three others in April. School District officials welcomed new legislation but warned it wouldn’t be a quick fix to the problem, and the House Democrats, as well as others, have proposed their own school safety measures.

headline: Building for the future: Ground broken for Juniata County Industrial Park
abstract: Former Juniata County Commissioner Ron Shearer spoke at a groundbreaking ceremony for Phase III of the Juniata County Industrial Park project, which is expected to produce 120 new jobs after it is completed. He introduced U.S. Representative Bud Shuster, who was instrumental in getting the U.S. Department of Commerce and Economic Development Administration to provide $812,000 for funding the project. Juniata Business and Industry Inc. purchased the land for the project from loans by the PA Industrial Development Authority and PA Power and Light Company, while the Appalachian Regional Commission and PA Department of Community and Economic Development each contributed $200,000 towards the project.

headline: Ridge offers no promises
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge emerged from a meeting with high-level Boeing officials unable to offer any assurances to the 6,400 workers here that their jobs are safe. The governor did provide the necessary relief on a day draped with another bleak backdrop of bad news for the plant, more layoffs next week, building demolitions and sale of 100 acres of land. Ridge pledged his continuing support to maintain Boeing's pre-Senatorial race in Ridley Township.

headline: Fahl launches bid for state House
abstract: Rima Fahl, the Republican candidate for the 132nd District seat in the PA House, announced the launching of her website, and she released a finance report. She has raised a total of $30,000 towards her ultimate goal of $70,000, and she is also launching a campaign to register voters and have them sign her nominating petition. Fahl is trying to win a seat vacated by Representative Charles Dent, who will be running for a state senate seat.

headline: Political Power Ball
abstract: PA Representative Nick Micozzie votes against organized labor more than half the time, according to the Delaware County AFL-CIO's questionnaire for candidates correctly. Getting labor's endorsement is far more complex than who the group of unions think is the best candidate. They must be able to raise money.

headline: Yudichak: 'The 119th is being left out in the cold..'
abstract: John Yudichak, who is challenging incumbent PA Representative Stanley Jarolin for the Democratic nomination to represent the 119th District, is trying to distance himself from his father’s relationship with Congressman Paul Kanjorski. Yudichak lost to Jarolin two years ago, but he claims Jarolin has failed in four major local areas: economic development, tax reform, infrastructure and community projects. He also criticized Jarolin for not informing his constituents properly, and Jarolin defended himself against some of Yudichak’s specific allegations, claiming Yudichak "has not done his homework."

headline: Pursue reform relentlessly
abstract: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott pulled the McCain-Feingold bill from the floor because it lacked the necessary number of votes. The bill would have banned the use of soft money, which is unregulated money that the authors believe is often illegally diverted into individual campaigns. All 45 Senate Democrats and seven Republicans favor reform, including Arlen Specter, and the authors urge campaign finance reform to continue to be pursued.

headline: Lack of children's medical insurance a fear for parents
abstract: According to statistics provided by the Pittsburgh Consumer Health Coalition, about 230,000 Pennsylvania children - one in 11- don't have health insurance.  But some of those kids are eligible for free or reduced-price coverage, said Ken Segel, senior program officer for the Jewish Healthcare Foundation in Pittsburgh.  It's just that sometimes parents don't know about it, he said, or are confused about which programs their children might be eligible for.

headline: Library funding still falls short
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is planning to ask for an extra $11 million in library funding for the 1998-99 state budget, but the authors of the editorial don’t believe it’s enough. Most of the money would be used to update computer systems, but the authors think libraries need more books and staff. They claim PA libraries are underfunded in comparison to other states, and they cite PA Representative Mike Veon, who wants to increase funding by $120 million.

headline: Spotlight to be shined on game commission
abstract: Sportsmen are expected to air their grievances against the Pennsylvania Game Commission with claims its enforcement officers violated their rights. Rep. Bruce Smith, chairman of the House Game and Fisheries Committee, said the hearing would examine legislation to curtail the commission's law enforcement powers. The Fish and Boat Commission is under fare less scrutiny because it is considered responsive by key legislative insiders.

headline: PennDOT re-administers thousands of tests for CDL licenses after discovering lax testing procedures and licenses for sale
abstract: Rebecca Bickley, PA Department of Transportation director of driver licensing, said 12 percent of truck drivers forced to retake their Commercial Drivers License exam failed to pass. The state had ordered 1500 drivers who received a license from Karchner Refrigeration Services Inc. to retake the test after the PA Attorney General's office determined drivers were tested improperly, some even paying instructors to pass them. The state's contract with Karchner has been canceled. If a driver fails the test, they do not get a second chance. Instead, they must reapply for a permit and repeat the process.

headline: Governor signs bill overhauling system protecting children
abstract: Two years after the brutal death of 16-month-old Maxwell Fisher, PA Governor Tom Ridge signed into law an overhaul of the state's system of child protective services. Ridge approved a package of bills designed to better protect children from abuse and neglect, and to move the most serious victims more quickly from foster care to adoption.

headline: Chester County firms join Team Pennsylvania
abstract: Chester County businesses are being asked to take part in Team PA, PA Governor Ridge's initiative is designed to help retain businesses in the commonwealth. Ridge has named the Uwchlan-based Chester County Development Council as coordinator for Team PA in Chester County. It is a comprehensive support network for business and industry concerns and needs.

headline: Ridge upbeat about area's marketability
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge missed the majority of the first day of Keystone Ride ’98 because he attended the funeral of a close friend; however he arrived during dinner and will begin biking in the morning. Ridge took the opportunity to address the group of bikers outside the Sony factory in Westmoreland County, and he claimed that PA is as attractive a location for international investment as any other place in the world. Sony employs 2,700 people in Westmoreland County and has invested nearly $600 million into two PA facilities.

headline: Family seats become assembly traditions
abstract: It is predicted that five PA senators and ten House members will be elected to office in the fall who are at least the second members of their family to serve in the General Assembly. State Representative Anthony Hardy Williams and Jacob Doyle Corman III are hoping to be a part of the growing trend.

headline: Politicians flock to funeral for an ally - Gov. Ridge was among 1,000 people who attended the farewell to Herbert Barness
abstract: Herbert Barness passed away at the age of 74, and over a thousand people attended his funeral, including Governor Tom Ridge, U.S. Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum, Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker and numerous PA legislators. Barness had served until his death as a Republican national committeeman, so he played a key role in helping many of the Republicans in attendance win their elections. Even Philadelphia’s Democratic mayor, Ed Rendell, showed up at the event with the Republican National Committee, which is considering Philadelphia as the site of its 2000 National Convention.

headline: $43 million renovation would help save history - But proposal is generating controversy
abstract: The National Park Service is hoping to build a new $43 million, 112,000 square foot visitor center at Gettysburg, but in order to do so, the Park Service plans to work with York County developer Robert Kinsley. According to plans, $30 million would be raised through private donations, and a nonprofit corporation would manage the new building for about 20 to 25 years; however, many historians and others are against the idea of allowing even more commercially managed enterprises into the park’s historical Civil War battle boundaries. The project has gotten support from the National Trust for Historic Preservation and Interior Secretary Bruce Babbit, but opponents continue to cite the failures of two past ventures by private enterprises, and they want the new visitor center to be funded completely by donations.

headline: Pa. promotions are criticized as ads for Ridge
abstract: There have been thousands of publicly funded promotional advertisements for the PA Departments of Health, Environmental Protection and most notably the Department of Community and Economic Development that have featured Governor Tom Ridge; however, many Democrats, including state Senator Robert Mellow, have criticized them for essentially being self-promotion advertisements for Ridge’s reelection. While they do promote Ridge’s work as governor, coordinators of the commercials claim they are useful in promoting the state’s accomplishments, and they are not being used to for reelection purposes. Many of the commercials are being used to attract out-of-state businesses to the state, but promotions featuring Ridge will cease after March 27; though many wish they would end much sooner.

headline: Large majority favor aid to need Pennsylvania children
abstract: PA Partnership for Children released a statewide poll that found 82 percent of Pennsylvanians believe the state government should guarantee sufficient food, shelter and health care for every child in PA. The exact figures of more specific data are published in the article, and 87 percent of Pennsylvanians also believe a portion of the state’s $400 million budget surplus should be used towards different children’s programs.

headline: Lincoln chief has ruffled feathers but made headway. Niara Sudarcasa is a key player in this week's Barnes shakeup. Under her, the college has made strides.
abstract: In 1987 Niara Sudarkasa became the first female president of Lincoln University, which is one of Pennsylvania’s state-related universities and is considered the nation’s oldest historically black college. Her abrasive personality and constant clashes have drawn criticism, and she is currently being investigated by PA Senator Vincent Fumo for using $530,000 to make improvements to the president’s house. Since Sudarkasa became president, she has increased enrollment and endowments substantially, balanced the university's budget, given pay raises, enacted new construction projects and has renewed Lincoln’s international ties to Africa, which even most critics of Sudarkasa can agree has helped repair Lincoln University’s image and has it moving in the right direction.

headline: State funds can help gas leak cleanup
abstract: PA Senator Edwin Holl and Representative Joseph Gladeck Jr. announced that additional funds with no cap would be available to the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) for its cleanup of a gasoline storage tank leak at Wagner’s Gulf station in Whitpain. The funds will be available under Act 13, which was signed into law by Governor Ridge this year, and will help the DEP continue the cleanup after the $1 million allotment from the Underground Storage Tank Indemnification Fund runs out. Joseph Feola, DEP acting southeast regional director, said the agency still needs to pursue additional funding in the future, and some of the cleanup efforts are described in the article.

headline: PennDOT Salt Pile May Be Source Of Contamination
abstract: PA Department of Transportation may be reponsible for the increase amount of salt in some residents water in Lackawanna County, due to the road salt and salt stockpiles used when constructing I-84.

headline: Governor Signs Papers for Crist Extradition
abstract: David Creek serving a 14 to 42 year state prison sentence for trying to kill his hearing impaired daughter to collect her life insurance, soon may be on his way to face first-degree murder charges. Governor Tom ridge signed papers last month to make way for Crist's extradition. He now faces an Erie County hearing, at which he can contest the extradition.

headline: City presses for fan $ - Up to 60,000 expected for A-10 tourney
abstract: The Atlantic Ten conference men’s basketball championship will be hosted in Philadelphia again this year, and it is expected to draw up to 60,000 visitors and generate up to $4 million in revenue for city businesses. In the past, the city has appeared to take the tournament for granted, but this year, city tourism officials, Atlantic Ten representatives and many others have come together to put a greater effort into marketing the event. The effort could be used as a model for next year when Philadelphia will host the tournament again as well as two other important basketball events.

headline: Ridge visit touts CorNet's success
abstract: CorNet International has been a Pocono success story, and Gov. Tom Ridge has noticed. It is will be the third in a series of events designed to showcase PA's emerging technology industry, which is the reason he is visiting CorNet, a developer of computer software revolving around sales force automation for a variety of industries.

headline: Fate of aging landmark American elm dividing community
abstract: An American elm that sits atop a hill just north of Pittsburgh is estimated to be 322 years old, and it has become a prominent landmark for Bellevue and surrounding communities; however, the tree may have to be cut down to prevent it from falling on a nearby apartment house or anyone close by. The tree is called the Lone Sentinel, and it is one of the largest known American elms in the nation, with a height of 110 feet and a circumference of 22 feet. Mayor George Malsch cut parts of the tree to buy more time, but ultimately, the tree is decaying, and the landmark that’s been able to survive for so long may have to be cut down.

headline: Politics Mostly Absent At Specter Meeting
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter didn’t mention anything about the upcoming election or his Democratic challenger, PA Representative Bill Lloyd, during a town meeting attended by 70 area residents, where he fielded questions ranging from President Clinton’s sex scandal to a number of different local topics. He spoke about the anticipated federal budget surplus, which he favors using to put towards Social Security, paying of the national debt and then providing tax cuts for the middle class, and he gave his support for a bill that would allow disabled people to receive federal assistance for in-home care. In addition to many other questions, Specter explained himself for initially criticizing Clinton’s decision to bomb suspected terrorist sites in Afghanistan and Sudan, and he voiced support for higher taxes on tobacco products and for the creation of a national Patients’ Bill of Rights to protect members of health maintenance organizations.

headline: $7 million surges into riverfront
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge delivered $7 million in state funding towards Allentown’s Lehigh Landing riverfront project, which all but guarantees the quick development of a national transportation museum on the property. Allentown Mayor William Heydt was clearly pleased with the grant, and Ridge said PA Representatives Patrick Browne and Charles Dent lobbied hard for the release, while he also took time to lobby for his plan to sell the state’s liquor store. The project is awaiting congressional approval of an additional $7 million in federal transportation grants, and in addition to the transportation museum, the $32 million project will include the restoration of several abandoned offices and warehouses.

headline: Pa. senators oppose spending package
abstract: Millions of dollars for PA was not enough to persuade the state's two Senators to back a $520 billion spending package. Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum criticized a process in which the four top leaders in Congress made most of the final decisions on behalf of 100 Senators and 435 House members. Both voted against the bill.

headline: Largest H.M.O.'s cutting the poor and the elderly
abstract: Citing losses and cuts in Government payments, the nation's biggest health maintenance organizations are quitting managed care programs for the poor and elderly.  Their retreat is most pronounced in Medicaid programs.  Health care analysts warn of a reversal of Government progress this decade in steering the poor into the mainstream of the health care system, both to provide good care and hold down costs.

headline: Litigation, solicitor costs burden on school districts
abstract: Woodland Hills School Board President John Wukich realizes many taxpayers in his district would be surprised and upset to learn Woodland Hills spent $359,533 last year just on legal expenses. But with the proliferation of school-related litigation in recent years, Wulkich does not see the high legal costs diminishing for any school district. Educational legal costs are rising nationwide.

headline: State hires contractors to carry off cariion
abstract: The State Game Commission has begun getting contractors to help with the removal of carrion from the busiest hghways in the state. The Game Commission has been unable to keep up with the large number of carcassess on roadways.

headline: PennDOT slated to begin work on I-80 next week
abstract: Montour County will get 7 miles of improvements on I-80 through a multi-million dollar project by PennDOT.

headline: Greenleaf works to bolster Megan's Law
abstract: As the PA Supreme court heard challenges to the constitutionally of Megan's Law, PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf took to the podium at the capitol to pitch a few enhancements. He was the primary sponsor of the 1995 law that makes all paroled sex offenders register with state police for 10 years and tougher sentencing. This has kept more sex offenders in prison for longer.

headline: City says 30,000 rooms available for convention The number, crucial to attracting Democrats or Republicans, is nearly double earlier estimates.
abstract: Mayor Rendell and other Philadelphia city officials announced that the region will be able to offer 30,000 hotel rooms when the city makes its proposals to try to lure both the Democratic and Republican National Conventions to hold their events in Philadelphia in 2000. The Committees usually require about 20,000 hotel rooms within a 30-minute drive, and the previous estimate for Philadelphia had been only 17,000; however, a more thorough analysis, along with the scheduled openings of several new hotels, boosted the estimate substantially. In addition, Rendell announced that Marriott International had bought the upper nine floors of the city’s historic Headhouse for $44 million, which it will use for 210 hotel rooms to supplement its nearby Philadelphia Marriott.

headline: Savers' Rewards
abstract: These are the average yields for various savings for various savings investments at leading banks and thrifts in the 10 largest metropolitan areas and the nation as of Jan. 14. A chart is given.

headline: Financial Flop
abstract: As the US investigates the potential privatization of social security, it should take note of the ongoing British scandal involving bad advice given to millions who were granted the right to privately invest their pensions. Actuaries now comparing British personal pensions to company plans are finding the personal pensions lacking. Though many insurance companies are admitting fault and compensating clients, many more have been fined for failing to act.

headline: Politics stymies sheriff's office: Kukovich forces Ridge to drop Thislethwaite confirmation for now
abstract: PA Senator Allen Kukovich, a Democrat, lobbied against Governor Ridge’s nomination of Republican Gary Thislethwaite as sheriff in Westmoreland County, which forced Ridge to withdraw the nomination. Kukovich said he would only endorse a candidate who did not plan to run for a full term in 1999, but there is speculation amongst Republicans that he won’t support any Republican for the position. It has been a struggle to fill the position after the resignation of Sheriff Gary Uhrin, and Ridge’s spokesman said he would likely renominate Thislethwaite.

headline: 18 state locales added to national historic register
abstract: Eighteen Pennsylvania sites have been added to the National Register of Historic Places.  The National Park Service administers the register as the official list of cultural resources that contribute to the understanding of the nation's historical and cultural foundations.

headline: Pa. voters face tame primary election scene
abstract: One of the more visible candidates for the Democratic gubernatorial primary, Phil Berg, was ruled ineligible to run, and the other three candidates, PA Representative Ivan Itkin, Don Bailey and William Kneisling are unknown to 65% of voters and have relatively little money to get their messages out. The Democratic race for the lieutenant governor nomination is between Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinky, Albert Penska and Ron Panza, and for the Republicans, Governor Tom Ridge and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker will be unopposed in their primaries. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter will face conservative Larry Murphy.

headline: Last day for AHERF practices
abstract: The Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation (AHERF) has decided to let go of over 80 physicians who work for the subsidiary called Allegheny University Medical Practices, and for many of these physicians, it is their last day working for AHERF. Many of the workers feel betrayed because they aren’t going to receive the severance and vacation pay that was promised to them; however, AHERF has agreed to return all of the assets of the practices in return for an agreement that the doctors won’t sue them for damages. The physicians could recoup some losses if they sell to another hospital, but as of now, they cannot due this because bankruptcy court hasn’t approved the transfer of assets.

headline: Lobbyists trying to sway younger minds
abstract: Energy lobbyists gathered at the American Petroleum Institute to develop a $6 million strategy to lobby against the treaty signed in Kyoto, Japan, which calls for reducing the emissions that cause global warming, and one proposed technique calls for targeting the nation’s children. Aiming messages at schoolchildren has become an increasingly prevalent lobbying strategy, and it is being used to get children to influence their parents and to leave a favorable impression with future decision makers. A 1995 study found that nearly 80% of corporate-sponsored educational material distributed to classrooms is in some way biased to the company or its economic agenda, but teachers are often not aware of this, so the National Education Association and other groups have established guidelines to try to ensure material advances educational goals, rather than industry goals.

headline: State is nation's dumping ground
abstract: Bill DeWeese, Democratic Leader of the PA House of Representatives, says that other states are taking advantage of PA, which recycles a quarter of its trash, by exporting 6.3 million tons of trash to PA landfills last year. He claims that he joined Representative George last year in cosponsoring a bill to place a halt on new landfill expansions, which Governor Ridge initially rejected but now is endorsing; though his endorsement will mean very little if the state Department of Environmental Protection doesn’t reduce the average daily amount of trash that is permitted into the state. DeWeese says that the problem of imported trash is continuing to grow, and he says that while Republicans such as Ridge and House Majority Leader John Perzel are in charge, the problem is unlikely to be resolved.

headline: PennDOT still optimistic about Exit 7
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation will continue its commitment to building an Interstate 81 Exit 7 in Greene Township, even though the township’s supervisor, Paul Ambrose, has led efforts against the construction of the exit, and opponents have threatened a lawsuit. According to District engineer Barry Hoffman, the department is still searching for a final site selection, and he hopes to have the exit done by the summer of 2000; however, there is historical farmland in the area, so the site must be approved by the National Register of Historic Places. Ambrose has also been critical of former Transportation Secretary Howard Yerusalem and U.S. Representative Bud Shuster, and the Exit 7 process has gone on much longer than Hoffman would have liked.

headline: Groups fight death penalty
abstract: It is only coincidence that the events of the upcoming Death Penalty week fall so close to the execution of Karla Faye Tucker. The six anti-capital punishment programs were planned months in advance. Her trial has ignited the topic to make the week more timely.

headline: City to consider zones for tax relief
abstract: The Keystone Opportunity Zone, which was promoted by Governor Tom Ridge, has drawn interest throughout the state, and seven midstate sites will be submitted to the PA Department of Community and Economic Development to be considered for the program. Through the program, all state and local taxes would be eliminated for selected sites to encourage development and help businesses survive in troubled economic areas. The program could benefit residents of public housing in Harrisburg and residents and businesses in Millersburg, Highspire, Lebanon, and parts of York and Franklin Counties.

headline: Senate panel to examine PIAA
abstract: The PA Senate is laying the ground work for an investigation of the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association that will surpass in both scope and intensity last week's session before a PA House panel. Ten members of a special Senate Committee on Interscholastic Athletics have been appointed and are investigating the policies, operate and financial status of the private, non-profit organization that governs high school sports in the state.

headline: Financial responsibility 'in limbo'  Legislation calling for state to pay salaries and benefits for certain county court administrators has not yet passed, leaving taxpayers obligated
abstract: The first of a four-phase state plan to take over the financial responsibility for county court systems was supposed to be implemented this month, and it would have the state pay $11.9 million for 165 key court administrators throughout the state. Luzerne County gave substantial salary raises to several court administrators; however, the state Legislature may not approve the state takeover until next year, so the county may have to cover all these costs in the 1999 budget plan. Despite the state paying some judicial salaries, the county’s taxpayers had to pay over $12 million towards judicial operations last year, and court administrators are appointed positions that pay very well.

headline: Poll: Democrats Gaining Support in Hill Contests
abstract: According to the most recent poll released by the Pew Research Center, support for Democratic congressional candidates has risen in the final days leading to the 1998 midterm elections, and no party has any clear advantage over the other. Last week, House Republicans took a gamble on a $10 million advertising campaign, which appears may have backfired. The Pew poll also found most registered party members would vote for a member of their party, about one-fifth of voters haven’t decided who they’ll vote for, Clinton’s job approval is 65% and most registered voters want their House representative reelected, while a separate poll predicted voter turnout to be lower than 1994.

headline: A pitch for Yuppie heaven
abstract: The demolition of the old Pennsyvania Department of Transportation building will propobably be replace by another state building just as the case has been over the fifty years.

headline: Deer could fear Gettysburg again
abstract: The deer population on Gettysburg National Military Park surprisingly doubled since last year, and the National Park Service, fearing the deer will destroy the battlefield by feeding on the crops and woodland, decided to reinstate their program to eliminate some of them. However, some local residents and animal rights groups have filed a lawsuit in federal court. The Park Service asked the PA Historic Preservation Office and the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation to review the deer management program, and they both found that killing the deer would have no adverse effect on the park.

headline: Lawmaker disappointed with Ridge decision    Sen. Murphy sought hearings on institution closings
abstract: Despite passing the PA General Assembly with nearly unanimous support from both the Senate and the House, Governor Tom Ridge vetoed a bill that would have required the PA Department of Public Welfare to hold a public hearing every time it plans to close a state-run facility for the mentally disabled or decrease the number of patients or employees by 10 percent. State Senator Tim Murphy was disappointed with the decision, and he hopes to still have a public hearing over the announced closure of Western Center in Washington County.

headline: Local leaders must take reigns of education reform
abstract: The author claims many surveys have shown that most Americans want to improve educational standards, yet there is no evidence of improvement over the past 25 years, and a Department of Education study found 29 percent of college freshmen required remedial classes for basic skills they should have already learned. The author points to a recent book for guidance called "Raising the Standards," which offers eight recommendations and describes how five communities worked to improve educational standards at their schools . The author of this opinion piece argues that in order to prevent America’s schools from continuing to fail, educational reform must come from the local level, and businesses need to take a bigger leadership role.

headline: State promotes youth, women during hunting conference
abstract: The fifth annual Governor's Symposium on North America's Hunting Heritage marks its first appearance on the East Coast.  About 600 participants are expected.  The last conference in Wisconsin drew 253 people.

headline: PennDOT surplus creates spat
abstract: State officials, Republican and Democrats, are debating the amount of surplus that PA Department of Transportation will have. All agree, however, that the surplus should go to fixing transportation problems in south PA.

headline: Gun background checks broadened
abstract: Gun shop owners on Monday began instant background checks of buyers of shotguns and rifles, but there were few opportunities to use the system.  Because Monday also was the first day of the antlered deer season, many hunters were outdoors, having already purchased their weapons.  As a result, many gun shops reported little or no business.

headline: City to get $20.3 million for homeless program
abstract: The city and several nonprofit organizations will receive $17.9 million next year from the federal government to help the homeless obtain housing and social services, the Clinton administration announced yesterday.  The city and nonprofits will also get another $2.4 million in emergency shelter grants that will provide short-term food and housing to the homeless.  In 1998, Philadelphia received $16.8 million in non-emergency funding for its 6,500 residents who were homeless or in transitional housing, and $2.6 million for emergency-shelter grants.

headline: Senate passes pro-AMP bill by 2-1 margin
abstract: The PA Senate passed legislation strengthening the state's anti-takeover laws, helping AMP Inc. to fend off a bid from AlliedSignal Inc. A House version of AMP legislation also passed, however unlike the Senate version, it can be amended. Sen. Jeffrey Piccola was grateful for the legislation's passage in the Senate. Gov. Tom Ridge favors legislation to protect AMP. An amendment threatening the legislation involves protecting Mellon and PNC banks from takeover, which Ridge opposes. Senators did not appear to hear warnings from Wall Street that the legislation will hurt the state's reputation.

headline: Fisher speaks to Republicans
abstract: Attorney Mike Fisher spoke to Elk County Republicans abut Govenor Tom Ridge's accomplishments during his term and his future election.

headline: Poll: GOP candidates keep edge despite souring opinion of Congress
abstract: According to a poll conducted by Pew Research Center, despite a drop in public opinion towards the Republican-controlled Congress, Republicans have a 5% advantage over Democrats in terms of Americans who are most likely to vote. The numbers are about equal for the larger group of registered voters who were polled, and the poll also found that the President Clinton’s impeachment is unlikely to have a significant effect on the upcoming midterm election. House Speaker Newt Gingrich predicted the Republican Party would  gain anywhere from 10 to 40 House seats, and the poll found Democrats have a 7% advantage among women over Republicans.

headline: ANF timber cutting moratorium threatens school, road money
abstract: School districts, local municipalities and various others are joining efforts to protest a federal court decision that prevented the U.S. Forest Service from following through with its Mortality II timber sale project. The project would have harvested timber in an area composed of 5,131 acres of dead or dying trees within the Allegheny National Project, which would have generated $2 to $3 million in tax revenue to fund schools and road projects in the surrounding four-county area. Local opposition groups claimed that the project violated federal environmental laws, but the lack of funding could hurt local townships, such as Jenks,  that were counting on the funds.

headline: DEP hears flood prevention ideas
abstract: PA Representative Joe Markosek, Senator Albert Belan and representatives from the offices of Representatives Tom Michlovic and Ron Conwell attended a meeting in Pitcairn where local officials proposed the use of detention dams to Mike Conway, an engineer from the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). There is $6.9 million budgeted to cement a channel to prevent flooding in the future, but Conway said the improvements wouldn’t be finished for five to eight years, which would leave the area vulnerable to flooding. Local engineers said the DEP’s plan would be inadequate if dams were not constructed to control the flow of water into the town, and it could provide a quicker fix as well.

headline: Lawmaker wants teen drivers to help out
abstract: PA Representative Mike Veon wants to require teens to have 50 hours of community service or have 50 hours of employment since their 15th birthday before they are able to apply for a junior driver’s permit. In other areas, the author writes about the speakers at commencement ceremonies for many of the universities from the state school system. He also discusses how the PA Corrections Department will have to pay Geisinger Medical Center over $200,000 for treatment of inmates, which he claims will result in the public paying for treatment through tax dollars rather than through higher hospital costs.

headline: Lt. gov's hooked on books
abstract: There are two photos of Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker from his recent visit to a fourth-grade class at St. Francis of Assisi. He read a book at the Allentown school to encourage children to read.

headline: State pumps money into area sewer projects   Fallowfield receives $8.7 million loan
abstract: State Senator J. Barry Stout and state Representative H. William DeWeese announced that low-interest loans worth $11.4 million were being granted for sewer improvement projects in four PA communities located in Washington and Green counties. Rices Landing Borough will receive $2.117 million, Brave Water and Sewer Authority will receive $115,000, South Strabane Township Sanitary Authority will receive $466,453 and Fallowfield Township Municipal Authority will receive $8.7 million towards various different sewer projects.

headline: PennDOT's ready for winter storms
abstract: PennDOT has supplies of snow plows and salt and are ready to combat transportation problems due to winter weather. The current traffic delay areas and SEPTA construction are also mentioned.

headline: Gun check helps nab suspect
abstract: A Washington County man, already accused of using a forged concealed weapons permit to buy a gun in 1997, is the first person to be arrested due to the new Pennsylvania Instant Check System for handgun purchases.  James Robert Schock, 28 of 141 Wisebecker Lane, Monongahela, was arrested Monday evening by West Mifflin police.  Schock was reportedly trying to purchase a Glock .40-caliber semi-automatic pistol from Outfitters Hunting and Shooting Supplies.

headline: Clear sailing expected for cruise-ship terminal - The character of the old Navy Yard building should shine through, even after renovation
abstract: Commissioners of the Delaware River Port Authority approved a $2.5 million loan guarantee to help renovate part of the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard to turn it into a terminal for cruise ships, and another $2.5 million in loans and grants will be provided by other sources, including Apple president John Mullen. In the past, the ability of cruise ships to operate has been hindered by a variety of factors, so the new terminal is already drawing interest. It will be located a few hundred yards from the planned construction of the new Kvaerner ASA shipbuilding facility, and it is expected to create 460 jobs and generate over $1.3 million in state and local taxes.

headline: Sequence of Funding is critical for Plan B
abstract: A question and Answer session on the new prosed staidums to be built in Allegheny County.

headline: Flynn Is Campaiging
abstract: Flynn is doing strong campaigning in Lackawanna County, where he previously received 30% of the GOP vote.

headline: Poll: Voters likely to back incumbents
abstract: According to a USA Today/CNN/Gallop Poll, 68% of those polled thought their incumbents deserved to be reelected, whereas only 16% said theirs did not, which could be advantage for Republicans since they have a 211-189 advantage over Democrats in the U.S. House. But nationally, the number of people who said they’d vote for Democrats was slightly higher than the number who said they’d vote for Republicans. The effect of the Clinton-Lewinsky scandal is still unclear; though both parties received low scores from the poll on their handling of the situation.

headline: Clinton offers something for virtually every Pennsylvanian
abstract: For residents of northeastern PA President Clinton's budget means more work on raising a levee to prevent flooding. For schools in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, it offers a chance to get special loans for construction projects. There's also money for navigational improvements in the Erie harbor and other water ways. The 1.73 trillion budget offers a little something for everyone in PA.

headline: Flood probability still exists
abstract: Representative Russ Fairchild and other members of the Susquehanna Caucus in the PA General Assembly gathered to discuss the flood outlook for the rest of the year, which shows the chances of flooding in central PA slightly above normal and northeastern PA above normal. The predictions were issued by the National Weather Service from the Susquehanna River Basin Flood Forecast and Warning System, which was created with federal funds due to the devastating effects of two hurricanes in the 1970’s. Fairchild said the system has saved a great deal of money in terms of damages and lives saved, and several other PA Congressman have written to Congress for $1.4 million in federal funding for the upcoming year.

headline: Laws would give consumers more control of managed care
abstract: The way managed-care companies do business in Pennsylvania appears on the verge of change as a result of legislation that would give doctors and their patients more control over healthcare decisions.  One bill would give doctors for the first time the right to appeal decisions made by committees that decide which treatments and procedures should be covered by managed-care plans, based on cost and necessity.  It would allow doctors and hospitals to act as advocates for their patients, a role they are not currently allowed to play, said Dr. Lee F. McCormick, a Pittsburgh family practitioner.

headline: Major has student aid applications
abstract: PA Representative Sandra Major said 1998-99 Free Applications for Federal Student Aid are now available and can be picked up her office or at school guidance counselors’ offices. They are the only applications needed to apply for PA state grant aid for the upcoming year. The PA Higher Education Assistance Agency has also mailed out many applications, and there are two different deadlines.

headline: State to suspend search for nuclear trash storage site
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection suspended the search for a suitable place to build a facility to dispose of trash contaminated with low-levels of radioactivity after spending nearly all of the $37 million that was allocated by the General Assembly. The amount of waste has substantially decreased within the Appalachian States Compact, which includes three other states that are expected to follow along with PA, and a dump in South Carolina has agreed to accept out-of-state trash. The dump could potentially last over 30 years, but some people are concerned that access to the site could be closed in the future, and PA may have been closer than ever to finding its own site.

headline: Pennsylvania is a wonner in road war
abstract: The recent six year transportation bill passed by Congress has left Pennslyvania with a large amount of money for various projects, due largely in part to Bud Shuster. The road plans are mapped out and statelawmakers And officials are pleased with the news.

headline: Gun checks go smoothly
abstract: When the state police's new instant checking system went into effect last week for prospective gun buyers, dealers in York were patient enough to give the new system a chance.  A federal computer system backup caused delays on the first day of the program --- July 1 --- making buyers wait a few hours before getting clearance to purchase handguns.  But since then, the Pennsylvania Instant Check system has been running smoothly.

headline: Commercial real estate a bright spot in regional economy - Big year for commercial real estate, with Mellon and PNC digging Downtown and retailers growing all over
abstract: 1998 was a big year for Pittsburgh’s commercial real estate market, with banks, department stores and various other projects beginning construction, and investors also came to the city in search of good deals. Wall Street’s uncertainty actually helped local investors tap into Pittsburgh’s real estate market, yet there were some weaknesses, considering there wasn’t enough interest to construct a new, multi-tenant office tower, and for the most part, Pittsburgh couldn’t attract businesses from outside the city. Next year, the construction of new stadiums for the Pirates and Steelers, which still faces a vote over state funding, will be a major focus, and commercial development in the suburbs could also heat up.

headline: Sherwood Receives Backing from Business Association
abstract: Don Sherwood, the Republican candidate to represent Pennsylvania’s 10th District in the U.S. House, gained the support of the National Federation of Independent Businesses, which has 1,900 members in the district. Several small business owners attended the "Rally in the Alley Event" to support Sherwood, claiming he would protect small businesses. The owner of the store where the event was held criticized Pat Casey, Sherwood’s opponent in the upcoming election.

headline: Foe assails Specter for doubting motive
abstract: Bill Lloyd, who is challenging incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter in an upcoming election, criticized Specter for the initial comments he made in response to President Clinton’s missile strikes against suspected terrorist bases in Afghanistan and Sudan. Specter had mentioned a New York Times article that suggested the president had conducted the attacks to shift focus from his recent admittance of having a sexual affair with Monica Lewinsky. Specter later backed off from those comments, and he said the action was "justified" in retaliation for the terrorist attacks on the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania this month.

headline: Pols seem unfazed as elections loom
abstract: Congressmen discuss how the impeachment of President Clinton will play out for Congressional elections.

headline: Clinton policy could create, and destroy, wetlands
abstract: President Clinton wants to increase funding for wetlands preservation programs and create 100,000 acres of new wetlands a year, but the newly created wetlands would basically be offset by losses in others. It remains unknown whether his proposal would help conservation efforts in the Poconos, which hold one-fourth of Pennsylvania’s wetlands, and Clinton’s proposal projects net gains in wetlands throughout the nation by 2005. Overall, Clinton is trying to ease restrictions on small development projects of wetlands while promising to tackle larger development projects, and he wants to offer incentives to farmers and others to promote wetland conservation.

headline: Frackville council to investigate parking and damage objections - Memorial field ball games take toll on neighbor's home
abstract: At a Frackville Borough Council meeting, Patrick O’Boyle complained that his home is being damaged by baseballs from the nearby Memorial Park. He also asked the borough to paint yellow lines to prohibit parking in some spots to protect children who play in the area. Members of the council said they would take up the issue during their next workshop session.

headline: Legal hurdle slows pursuit of automatic defibrillators
abstract: The American Heart Association’s latest thrust in the war on heart attacks has encountered a legal hurdle.  The association wants automatic external defibrillators to eventually be placed in airports, malls, businesses and other common areas.  The hurdle is that the law providing some legal protections for non-medical professionals (i.e. firefighters, police officers, volunteer ambulance or rescue squad members) who try, and in some cases, fail to improve the health of a distressed person---does not specifically address the use of external defibrillators.

headline: Mayor, cardinal at odds on vouchers
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell said he is still not inclined to accept a proposal by Cardinal Anthony Bevilacqua to have the Philadelphia School District offer students vouchers to attend parochial schools, which could remove 20,000 students from the district’s overcrowded public schools. Bevilacqua also said the plan would help the district financially. Rendell said he’s in favor of school choice, but only after the state provides adequate funding to level the playing field between public and private schools.

headline: State, hunters seek ways to build turkey population
abstract: Last fall’s harvest average for turkeys throughout PA was ten times higher than it was in Michaux State Forest, and the PA Game Commission, Bureau of Forestry and four local chapters of the National Wild Turkey Federation are concerned about the turkey population in the area. Game Commission officials believe that ATVs, such as four-wheelers, are causing hens to abandon their nests. An access road for ATV users will be closed until the end of the hatching season in hopes of addressing the problem, and a ban on the fall turkey hunting season in 1999 is also being considered.

headline: Pennsylvania is no highway to heaven, DOT head admits
abstract: PA Transportation Secretary Brad Mallory had to convince PA Gov. Tom Ridge to increase funding for the agency. He knows it has cost him political and public favor. It took two years to push through the Legislature. Mallory hopes to leave the roads better than when he came to them, encouraged by a recent poll by Overdrive Magazine, in which truckers agreed PA roads have improved. The additional revenue comes from a hike in license fees and a gas tax.

headline: Gun Lobby Safe
abstract: America continues to be safe for gun lobbyists, but not necessarily for kids who live in some houses where loaded guns are stored. The US Senate voted against a provision that would have required the inclusion of trigger locks in all new handgun sales. Even the Senators recognized that most Americans would look poorly upon their decision. They immediately passed a meaningless but politically face-saving measure that would require federally license gun dealers to stock trigger locks.

headline: Constitution Center gets panel nod
abstract: A U.S. Senate appropriations subcommittee approved a plan to provide $10 million towards the construction of the $130 million National Constitution Center in Philadelphia, and another $10 million could come from an appropriations subcommittee chaired by Senator Arlen Specter, a strong supporter of the project. Senator Rick Santorum and a spokesman for Specter both called it great news, and the subcommittee also included $3.5 million for a new Gateway Visitors Center and a new home for the Liberty Bell. The money will come as part of Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell’s $200 million renovation project, and the other sources of funding, including state, local and nonprofit foundations, are discussed in the article.

headline: Small banks form surcharge-free ATM alliance
abstract: Local PA banks create an alliance to form no-surcharge ATM for customers

headline: Foot-shooting 101
