abstract: It never fails that just before a key election- one of the two major political parties tries really hard to shoot itself in the foot. This time, it's the Republican who are imitating the Hatfield's and the McCoys. GOP moderates in Congress are up in arms about their party leader's staunchly conservative stands on issues from gay rights to free trade. At issue is a battle for the should of the party. It will tear the party apart.

headline: Pomona Grange hosts Legislative Banquet
abstract: Pomona Grange No. 35 held its 25th annual Legislative Banquet March 14 at Tuscarona Grange Hall. After dinner Grange Treasurer Harry Milliken presented a scholarship check in the amount of $200 to Joe Love, who is studying nursing at Indiana University of PA.

headline: Commercial development around Gettysburg
abstract: Map of Gettysburg and some of the plans for the region.

headline: Funds sought for site that greeted Lincoln
abstract: A special ceremony was held for the anniversary of President Lincoln’s famous Gettysburg Address, and at the ceremony, the deed to the Gettysburg Lincoln Railroad Station, where Lincoln was greeted 135 years ago, was transferred to the Gettysburg Borough. Through the efforts of PA Senator Terry Punt and U.S. Representative Bud Shuster, $800,000 in federal funding was approved for repairs to the station, but $200,000 in additional funding is needed to match it. Main Street Gettysburg will be in charge of efforts to raise the necessary funds.

headline: Legislation Would Stop Plan To Reduce Population in State Facilities For Mentally Retarded
abstract: According to Ed Scurry, a representative of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, legislation has been introduced in the PA House that would allow state-run facilities for the mentally retarded to admit more people. The legislation is an attempt to block Governor Ridge’s plan to reduce the number of patients in state-run institutions by half in the next five years. Scurry said reductions at the Polk facility could cost 86 union workers their jobs, and while most Republicans are hesitant to go against Ridge, state Representative Scott Hutchinson, a Republican from Venango County, has supported the bill.

headline: Meeting Encouraged HERCO
abstract: Altoona Area School director of public relations Tom Bradley said the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association could have saved people in his community time and effort if it had simply made clear a preference to move the state football championships to Hershey. Bradley said a letter from Hershey Entertainment and Resort Company vice president Jay Feaster to PIAA executive director Bradley Cashman gives him the impression that Altoona did not have much of a chance.

headline: Sticking point at 20 inches
abstract: The PA Fish and Boat Commission has already held two public meetings over its proposal to maximize fishing opportunities by allowing bass fishing year round, and the most common complaint was over the 20-inch minimum limit that would be set in rivers and streams in the fall through winter seasons. The limit is an attempt to make up for increased bass that are caught due to the extended season, but many argued that it is too extreme. According to the proposal, bass fisheries in rivers and streams would be regulated differently than in lakes, and the commission will not vote on the proposal until July after two more public hearing are held.

headline: Pennsylvania teen automobile deaths
abstract: A chart shows the number of teen auto fatalities each year from 1992 to 1996. The data was obtained via the PA Department of Health, Allegheny County Health Department, Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

headline: Gun-makers looming larger as focus of suit
abstract: Will Mayor Rendell lead a nationwide lawsuit against the gun trade?  It's beginning to look like that might happen.  The mayor has long been researching such a suit, while down playing its likelihood.  That changed last week, after a gun manufacturers' group rebuffed Rendell's plea to endorse a proposed limit on handgun purchases of one a month per buyer.

headline: Coyne, Ravotti cover some old ground at debate
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Coyne and his Republican challenger, Bill Ravotti took part in a debate last night, and they focused mainly on issues such as abortion, Social Security, regional job growth and educational spending. Ravotti spoke out against same-sex marriages and an Allegheny County Housing Authority plan to put in some low-income housing in Pittsburgh’s suburban neighborhoods. Coyne attacked Ravotti’s lack of experience, Ravotti blamed Coyne for slow job growth in the region and both tried to gain the upper hand over the question of Social Security.

headline: Some fear effects of bank deal
abstract: To Wall Street, it's the biggest bank merger ever. But it the worn brick neighborhoods along the Frankford El, church and community activists say First Union Corp.'s proposed $16 billion purchase of CoreStates Financial Corp. threatens to be the worst of a wave of mergers that has replaced local bank branches with high-price check-cashing agencies and what they call predatory finance firms. The eastern Philadelphia Organizing Project asked the Federal Reserve Board in Washington to reject the merger. It was the first of several protests that will seek to stop or modify the deal on grounds it threatens to cut the flow of credit to poor neighborhoods, in violation of the federal Community Reinvestment Act.

headline: For Ridge, two debates are enough
abstract: Two televised debates have been scheduled for the four candidates running for PA governor, incumbent Governor Tom Ridge, Democrat Ivan Itkin, Constitutional Party candidate Peg Luksik and Libertarian candidate Ken Krawchuk. The authors, however, are pessimistic about the chances of having more because Ridge enjoys a wide lead, and it would be politically foolish for him to have more. By having more debates, it could give the lesser known candidates more exposure time to lure away votes, and Ridge would increase his chances of making a major mistake that could alienate voters.

headline: Popularity poll
abstract: Poll results for Tom Ridge's state wide popularity, other candidates popularity, by party, by gender and by issues.

headline: Congress to order Park Service to release museum plan details
abstract: U.S. Senator Craig Thomas plans to ask the National Park Service to release all the details of a proposed $40.4 million Gettysburg battlefield visitor center and museum complex to the public. The Park Service is negotiating details with developer Robert Kinsley, and Kinsley’s plans were released to Thomas’s Energy and Natural Resources subcommittee as well as Freedom of Information Act requests; however, the financial details were blotted out. The General Accounting Office may be requested to conduct a review, and Senator Dale Bumpers has expressed some concerns about how the whole process is being conducted.

headline: Gettysburg ponders whether to cash in on its war history
abstract: Standing atop the National Tower, one can easily see the changes on the horizon. Below, the green rolling battlefield that saw 53,000 causalities in three days in July 1863 is a centerpiece gem rimmer by the blue-tinted South Mountain Range to the west and north and the Pigeon Hills to the east. Because the county is so rural, commercial development is targeted more toward drawing tourists than residents. Three projects, totaling more than $250 million, are among those awaiting final approval for construction. They include convention centers, mega-outlet mall, vistors centers, etc.

headline: Lessons from AHERF: Nonprofit acquisitions should have public watchdogs
abstract: According to the authors, two very important lessons can be learned from Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation’s aggressive expansion into Philadelphia, which has forced Pennsylvania's largest health-care system to file for bankruptcy. The authors claim the board of directors for a nonprofit hospital system should be more active, and the PA Attorney General’s Office should review mergers and acquisitions, which it currently does not do for a transaction involving two nonprofits. The authors believe PA Attorney General Mike Fisher should be able review the foundation’s bankruptcy case, and in the future all hospitals, including UPMC Health System in Pittsburgh, should be subject to external reviews.

headline: Middle schools targeted as weak link in education chain
abstract: Never has so much evidence about America's education failures pointed so convincingly in a single direction- middle schools. Fourth graders fare well by international standards, benefiting from several years of school reform. But US students stagnate in seventh and eight grades, leaving them unprepared and unmotivated for the stiff high school math and science class looming ahead. They need a better foundation.

headline: Still Selling Span
abstract: Danville officials try to stop protesters at the building site of the Danville-Riverside bridge.

headline: People to decide
abstract: Editors believe it is encouraging that the PA Department of Transportation is letting the people decide whether the Tunkhannock bypass should have noise barriers. Residents affected by the bypass have been invited to special public meetings next week. Editors encourage residents in noise sensitive areas to attend the meetings in order to make an informed decision.

headline: Guns and safety
abstract: Allegheny County Resident write the Post-Gazette to argue about firearms and tell citizens about the on going education of firearm safety.

headline: Cultural Center Still Waiting for Promised State Funds: Lawmaker reminds Governor Ridge the $8 million dollars still hasn't arrived.
abstract: It’s been almost a year since Governor Tom Ridge presented an $8 million check to the Scranton Cultural Center to complete renovations, but the money still hasn’t been released. Senate Minority Leader Robert J. Mellow wrote a letter to Ridge to see why the money is being held up. In total, the renovation project will cost $16 million, but it is clearly necessary considering the first floor collapsed shortly after Ridge’s presentation, causing the cancellation of a matinee performance.

headline: Sovereign Bancorp buying nine of CoreState's Valley branches
abstract: Sovereign Bancorp strengthened its foothold in the Lehigh Valley and moved itself into some new markets with the purchase of 95 bank branches from CoreStates Financial Corp. First Union, only days away from completing its purchase of Core States, was required by federal regulators to sell 32 branches because of anti-trust concerns resulting from the merger. First Union decided to shed an additional 63 branches, many of them in the northern and central area of the state, for business reasons.

headline: Foreign envoys get taste of Lancaster
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts organized a trip to Lancaster and Chester Counties for the diplomats representing several countries, including Malaysia, Argentina, Finland, Yemen and China. Gene and Anne Witmer, who founded a cultural exchange program in Lancaster County, hosted China’s deputy chief of mission, Xiaoming Liu, who spoke about improved relations between China and the U.S. and some common misconceptions about his country. At a dinner in Lancaster, the diplomats talked with various government officials, university presidents and county residents in an attempt to broaden everyone’s cultural understanding.

headline: Populist Party elects slate of officers
abstract: The Populist Party of Clearfield County elected officers and pledged their support to Peg Luksik for governor, James Clymer for lieutenant governor and Dean Snyder for U.S. Senate. Edgar Moore was elected county chairman of the party, and State Populist Party Chairman George Stryker praised Moore for his dedication to Christian morality.

headline: Congressman says Gettysburg project needs public money
abstract: U.S. Representative William Goodling is seeking $1.75 million in public funds toward the development of a new visitor center at Gettysburg National Military Park, which the National Park Service promised would be built without costing taxpayers’ dollars. The Park Service plans to form a public-private partnership with a development group headed by Robert Kinsley; however, it has refused to release a financial analysis conducted by Kinsley, and Goodling has argued the project cannot be done without using public money. The entire $40.4 million project would consist of a new visitor center and museum along with private commercial enterprises, but critics argue commercial developers will harm the integrity of the battlefield.

headline: Group works to purge 'Chiller Theater' runoff
abstract: Trout Unlimited works with a boot camp in PA to clean up acid mine drainage in Philipsburg.

headline: Likely disease source found
abstract: Allegheny County health officials have pinpointed a probable source of the bacteria that caused three workers at the Pittsburgh Technology Center in Hazelwood to contract Legionnaire’s disease: steam emanating from a nearby galvanizing plant.  Officials found a high concentration of Legionella organisms, the bacteria that cause Legionnaire’s disease, in the second cooling tower of Metaltech at 2400 Second Ave.  The company Is about 300 feet from the building at 2000 Technology Drive, where the three are employed.

headline: Monitoring the quality of new teachers
abstract: According of Education Week's state-by-state rating, many have to go in raising the quality of new teachers.

headline: Sunday Hunting Sought
abstract: According to Dave Lewonczyk, a columnist for the Sunday Times, the Pennsylvania Game Commission seems to think that by giving youth more opportunities to kill, it will recruit more of them into the sport. Lewonczyk continues by saying if killing is the only reason a child got into hunting, he nor you should want him out there. Lewonczyk also suggests that Pennsylvanians should be allowed to hunt on Sunday.

headline: Personal watercraft change coming: Fish & Boat may require operators to have boating safety courses certificates by 2000
abstract: Personal watercraft (PWC) are small, speedy motorboats that make up a small number of total boats registered in PA ; however, they are also the fastest growing aspect of recreational boating and have been responsible for a highly disproportional number of collisions and accidents. Since they have been involved in so many accidents, the PA Fish and Boat Commission is considering a proposal that would require any person operating a PWC on state waters to obtain a boating safety certificate by January 1, 2000. Dan Martin, the commission’s boating education program manager, believes the safety courses could help reduce the number of accidents and collisions.

headline: Guns blamed for Rise in Homicides by Youths in 80's
abstract: As homicide rates have dropped the past few years, criminal-justice experts have warned that they could soon rise again as a generation of super predator juveniles came of age.  But that fear is being called into question by new studies that show that virtually all the increase in homicides by juveniles in the late 1980's was attributable to crimes committed with handguns, not to a change in the nature of the teen-agers.  While the rate of killings by juveniles tripled from 1986 to 1993 and has fallen since, the rate of homicides by juveniles with other weapons has not changed.

headline: Delays plaguing 2 big hotel projects
abstract: The construction of a Hyatt Hotel at Penn’s Landing has been delayed because of a $10 million budget shortfall, and the conversion of another building into a luxury hotel across from the Philadelphia Convention Center has also been delayed. The hotels and their 940 rooms are a key component of the city’s efforts to boost tourism, create more jobs and increase the use of the Convention Center, but they could also play an important role in the city’s attempt to attract the Republican and Democratic National Conventions in the summer of 2000. Mayor Ed Rendell and the developers involved with these projects insist they will still be completed before the summer of 2000, yet others believe that deadline is questionable.

headline: Specter calls for hearings on First Union-CoreStates
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter is calling for public hearings to investigate the proposed merger between First Union Corporation, saying the venture may not only have a negative impact on the region, but may also carry antitrust implications. Specter contends that if the merger is successful , First Union will capture 33 percent of the Philadelphia market share and the largest number of depositors of any bank in the region. The Senator also believes that mega bank will invest less money in the city's low income communities, leading to their further deterioration.

headline: Fox extends thanks, appreciation
abstract: U.S. Representative Jon Fox is writing to the newspaper as he prepares to leave office. He thanks the people of Montgomery County for allowing him to serve them for the past four years, lists some of his proud accomplishments and wishes Congressman-elect Joseph M. Hoeffel III the best of luck in office.

headline: Post-ABC News Politics Poll
abstract: Poll results for: How the parties compare in top issues, congressional elections, and Bill Clinton.

headline: Counties, conservancies vying for land   Open-space programs pay for acreage. Once, some of that would have gone to green groups-for free.
abstract: Many local governments have been using open-space plans to purchase land at a reduced price to prevent it from being developed, including Bucks County, which recently bought 107 acres of farmland for $2.2 million dollars. However, these open-space plans have created a competition with conservancy groups that many landowners have donated thousands of acres of land to in the past for free. In order to compete, these conservancy groups, including Heritage Conservancy and Brandywine Conservancy, plan to target landowners that may feel uncomfortable dealing with the government, those who would actually benefit more from the tax write-off from donation and farms that don’t qualify for county plans.

headline: Hanging Rock near Valley Forge is now a national historic place
abstract: History buffs believe they have finally won a 70-year battle to save Hanging Rock from state highway officials who want to remove part of the boulder.  Hanging Rock, a Revolutionary War landmark, protrudes from the side of a hill along Route 320 near Valley Forge.  It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on Dec. 24.

headline: Local politician endorses free eye exam program
abstract: PA Representative Fred McIlhattan endorsed the VISION USA project, which is sponsored by the PA Optometric Association and the PA Vision Conservation Institute. The program is intended to provide free eye examinations and vision care to those who could otherwise not afford it. Information on how to apply for the program is provided in the article.

headline: More state funding is sought for Pa.'s community colleges
abstract: The PA House subcommittee on higher education, which is chaired by Representative Patricia Carone, released a study yesterday that recommends the state allocate $70 million more from its budget surplus for community colleges throughout the state. Under current law, the state, local governments and tuition are each expected to pay for one third of the costs of community colleges, but many local governments are strapped for cash and hesitant to raise taxes, which has made them unable to fulfill these obligations. The recommendation is supported by House Majority Leader John Perzel, but Governor Tom Ridge’s spokesman, Tim Reeves, said the governor has already allocated a 3.25 percent increase for community colleges in his budget proposal, and increasing funds by $70 million would be a rare and drastic increase in funding.

headline: Sunday Hunting Sought
abstract: Hunting land has disappeared over the last twenty years.  Even where there are still farms, they are being lost to no trespassing posters that are appearing in alarming rate.  Some farms are being posted to leasing and some are closed because a few slob hunters that ruin things for everyone.

headline: Phillipsburg bypass part of Transportation Act
abstract: Development and construction of a 27-mile dividied four-lane access relocation of Route 322 around Philipsburg is planned in the Transportation Efficiency Act.

headline: Guns plus children equals disaster
abstract: The seemingly endless debate of gun availability vs. gun control has flared up again over the past six months in light of five fatal shootings at schools or school events, most recently in Edinboro.  But while the arguments rage on, no one on either side would dispute that such highly publicized events are --- thankfully--- rare.  More frequent, but accompanied by little or no publicity, are the shootings --- both accidental and intentional --- that occur daily in the United States involving children who happen upon unsecured guns.

headline: Dems returning for a look-see
abstract: The site selection committee for the 2000 Democratic National Convention will return to Philadelphia on September 15, and officials are hopeful the committee chooses Philadelphia over Los Angeles. In addition, a committee will convene to review the results of a study commissioned by Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, and the hotel industry has agreed to a 1% tax increase on hotel guests to fund additional tourism promotions; though the City Council and PA Legislature must grant their approval. In other news, a hearing was held by the Zoning Board of Adjustment over Fresh Fields’ desire to build a foods market in Philadelphia, which is supported by many politicians from the city.

headline: Spector Seeks Halt to Bank's Merger
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter notes his concerns about the takeover of Corstates Corp. by First Union Corp. Specter notes that there will be job loss, removal of branches from much needed communities, and give Fist Union Corp too much bank control in PA.

headline: Fox goes out with a bang
abstract: U.S. Representative Jon Fox was defeated in the recent election by Joseph Hoeffel III to represent Montgomery County’s 13th District; however, he did cast four crucial ballots in favor of impeaching President Clinton based on his behavior in the Monica Lewinski affair. Fox said he’ll definitely miss the House, and he pointed out the balanced budget agreement of 1997, health care reform and grant money he secured for the county as some of the high points during his four years in Congress.

headline: Pottstown man on Libertarian slate
abstract: John Haley will be the Libertarian candidate for the 146th district seat in the PA House and will face Democrat Eileen McCaul and Republican Mary Ann Dailey; though Dailey’s primary victory is being challenged in court. The Libertarians also selected Patrick Burke to run in the 13th Congressional District race, Ken Krawchuk and Henry Haller to run for Governor and Lieutenant Governor and Jack Iannantuono to run for the U.S. Senate. The party qualified to run a candidate for the 12th district state senate election but has yet to officially choose a candidate, and Montgomery County has more Libertarians in office than any other county in the entire U.S.

headline: Rail-Trail Council Searching for State Funds To Restore Bank
abstract: The Rail-Trail Council of Northeastern PA will apply to the PA Department of Environmental Protection for approximately $30,000 to stabilize a section of the Lackawanna River’s bank. The council is developing a trail on 33 miles of land, and its director said it would meet with the Union Dale Borough Council about complaints it received over snowmobile use on the trail and trail-users parking on private property.

headline: Have a soda, support a park? Why not?
abstract: The author of the article believes that it is a good idea for PA to offer one soft drink company exclusive rights to sell its product at all state parks and museums in return for money to make improvements. The author cites a deal that was struck in New York with Coca Cola and believes that the proposal could raise money for the $100 million in funding needed to improve parks and museums throughout the state.

headline: Local politicians seek end to state hospital escapes
abstract: State Senator Edwin Holl and state Representative John Fichter have called for a meeting with PA Department of Public Welfare Secretary Feather Houstoun and others to discuss the problem of patients running away from Norristown State Hospital, where one patient ended up stalking a girl in October after running away from the facility. The welfare department has already hired more guards and supervisors, and the hospital’s superintendant, Aidan Altenor, said new security features have decreased the number of runaways substantially; though he admitted improvements could still be made, and he looked forward to the meeting. The local community has been working with the hospital to improve relations, and photo identification cards will soon be required for all patients.

headline: Nazareth may seek state audit on $54.5M debt
abstract: Nazareth Area School Board openly invites the state auditore genral to investigate the construction costs used by the Board. The Board also held elections for a new President and Vice President.

headline: Take aim at species-ism
abstract: Like sexism and racism, species-ism does serious harm and obscures important facts.  Destroying forest for suburban sprawl-does not eliminate deer habitat; it increases it.  Deer were far fewer when the area was all forest.

headline: Plan to realign Rt. 29 dogleg still up in air
abstract: There are plans to address the Route 29 dogleg that are causing traffic concerns. Proposed Plan 9 is facing issues with PennDOT, however.

headline: Half house security targeted
abstract: PA Representative Donald Walko has proposed legislation to increase half-way house security, following the increase in half-way house escapes.

headline: Development Council receives $325,000 grant
abstract: The Somerset County Economic Development Council has been awarded a $325,000 federal grant  to extend the infrastructure at the current Somerset Industrial Park. US Representative John Murtha announced the award. Council has never before received a federal grant. Council will apply for a PA Industrial Development Agency Industrial Park loan of $165,000.

headline: State holds onto wedding memories
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher's office has box of photgraphs and memoryies from a photographer in Bucks and Montgomery County. The photographer failed to deliver the services paid for by customers and is being investigated by the office.

headline: Fox loan hot topic of debate: 200 people attend GOP forum last night
abstract: All four Republican candidates for the 13th District Congressional seat, U.S. Representative John Fox, Jonathan Newman, Melissa Brown and Michael McMonagle, attended an hour long debate at Plymouth-Whitemarsh High School. The debate was rather subdued; however, it got a bit more heated when Newman questioned Fox over a $25,000 loan he received in 1992 that some believe was used to illegally bypass campaign contribution limits; though Fox claims the loan was a personal loan and was not used as part of his campaign. The candidates debated gun restrictions, abortion, affirmative action, campaign expense reform, term limits and a federal program aimed at drug addicts.

headline: President's own lawyers offer convincing argument for impeachment
abstract: The President’s lawyers used Alexander Hamilton’s definition of impeachment to claim that impeachment is only justified when the people themselves have to be protected from their own elected officials. However, the author cites two examples in which Clinton’s actions were so foolish and such an abuse of public trust that they could be considered to fulfill the criteria in the impeachment definition set forth by Hamilton and Clinton’s lawyers. According to the author, by having an affair with Monica Lewinski, Clinton put himself into a dangerous position in which he could have been blackmailed, and he also conducted official business on the phone while receiving oral sex, which was a severe abuse of public trust.

headline: Rivers of Steel Heritage flows to Armstrong
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker presented Armstrong County with a $25,000 grant, which became possible due to the county’s new inclusion into the state’s Rivers of Steel Heritage Area. County Commissioners Homer Crytzer and Jack Dunmire hoped the county would receive more money in the future, which is possible because the county is now eligible for money via the PA Heritage Parks Program. The article also provides information on other grant recipients, where a total of $350,000 was given to various members of the Rivers and Steel Heritage Area.

headline: Hikers want link for trail
abstract: Phoenixville is looking into applying for federal funds to connect a walkway to the 120 mile Schuylkill River Trail.

headline: Magee, UPMC merging
abstract: The Magee-Womens Hospital board of directors yesterday signed a letter of intent to formally join  forces with the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center Health System, a move that numerous hospitals have taken to ensure their survival in the competitive health-care industry.  Hospital officials have said in the past that they were discussing a merger with UPMC that would allow the health care giant to take over Magee without paying money to actually acquire it.  A press conference will be held at 1 p.m. today to discuss the specifics of the agreement.

headline: New board deserves grace period
abstract: The authors of the editorial believe that the new Board of Controls should be allowed some time to assess the details of Chester Upland School District in order to develop informed, educated decisions on how to tackle problems, such as the financial state of the district. They criticize supporters of Monica Washington for calling on the board to appoint her as personnel director quickly. For the time being, the authors hope that people can give the board some space and freedom to develop a plan, which the public would be able to freely debate in the future.

headline: TAKING IN THE TRASH   Virginia's Booming Waste Business   Industrial Waste At Incinerators Raises Concerns
abstract: Fairfax, Arlington and Alexandria invested $300 million into the construction of trash incinerating plants in the 1980’s and expected enough trash to be sent to the facilities, operated by the Ogden Corporation, to make them profitable; however, a U.S. Supreme Court decision made it cheaper for many customers to send their trash to landfills. In order to make up for lost revenue, the Ogden plants began accepting industrial waste from over 20 different states and Puerto Rico, but the state and  local governments provide different types of supervision over what is and is not acceptable to incinerate. Despite precautions, the Alexandria plant incinerated a restricted pesticide that caused burning eyes, noses and throats for its workers, state inspectors found a poorly stored hazardous waste in the Fairfax plant that was missed during inspection and there are concerns about air pollution as well as the possibility that ash produced could contain toxic residue.

headline: Politicians, 'pike execs to parley
abstract: State legislators, including Senator James Gerlach and Representative Don Snyder, will meet with PA Turnpike Commission officials to discuss two recent turnpike accidents. The day after the first accident, Vera Cruz Fire Chief Joe Sherman said the Turnpike Commission was more concerned about keeping the roadway open than it was about ensuring the safety of emergency responders, and two days later, a tractor-trailer crashed into an ambulance and rescuers who responded to the initial incident, killing one firefighter and injuring ten others. Sherman criticized how the Turnpike handles controlling the scene of an accident; however, Turnpike Marketing Director Bill Capone said state policemen are trained to take over accident scenes, and the Turnpike’s top priority has always been ensuring the safety of emergency responders, but they must still try to respect the wishes of toll payers by keeping roads open whenever possible.

headline: Harhart takes school violence prevention message to CNN
abstract: Cable News Network (CNN) visited a PA high school to interview state Representative Julie Harhart in recognition that PA has become a leader in efforts to curb school violence. Harhart introduced two bills which passed the House and have moved on to the Senate. The first bill would provide $80 million for schools to upgrade security systems and train staff, while the second would increase the penalties for assaulting a teacher.

headline: Disney's FUN CITY - What is Philadelphia getting in 2000?
abstract: In 2000, Walt Disney Company plans to open DisneyQuest, a five-story, 100,000 square foot mini-amusement park, in Philadelphia. While the plan is still in its initial phases, DisneyQuest would likely include many of the popular rides and attractions from Disney World as well as a huge arcade, an interactive zone featuring virtual reality rides, a Create Zone, where people can learn how to draw their favorite Disney characters and several other features. Mayor Ed Rendell played an important role in convincing Disney to locate in Philadelphia, which the company hopes will expand its market to people who cannot afford to travel all the way to Disney World; however, others have criticized the proposed location of DisneyQuest because it will be located close to the city’s historical landmarks.

headline: State sues Allstate for alleged bid to deter hiring of attorneys
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher files a lawsuit against Allstate Insurance for deceptively encouraging injuried parties to not seek counsel and to settle their claim.

headline: Fox's final days surge in importance
abstract: President Bill Clinton talks with Reoublican Congressmen on Iraq and Republicans discuss the possibility of impeachment for the President.

headline: Primary '98
abstract: Profiles of the three candidates for the 48th legislative district: Clemmy Allen, Tom Brown, and Joseph Corlazzoli and the seat itself.

headline: Salem receives $17,000 grant for park, road
abstract: Salem Township received a $17,000 grant from the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources to expand its community park and construct a new road that can be used as an alternate entrance for bigger events held at the park. Supervisor Larry Truitt confirmed the township would match the grant, and he praised PA Representative Fred McIlhattan and PA Senator Mary Jo White for their efforts.

headline: Internet to feature Gettysburg Address
abstract: A live Internet broadcast of Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, dedicating the Gettysburg National Cemetery, will be available tomorrow. It will feature the annual remembrance of Lincoln's speech. The Lincoln Fellowship of PA sponsors the annual Gettysburg Address.

headline: Major's budget amendment aids drug and alcohol services
abstract: Representative Sandra Major announced Thursday that the budget passed recently by the state House includes an amendment she sponsored to increase funding for drug and alcohol programs in the state. Major's amendment appropriates an additional $1.87 million in state funds for the programs.

headline: New education standards get OK from Fisher
abstract: New standards for PA school students in 3rd, 5th, 8th, and 11th wil require new more measureable standardized tests to judge performance level.

headline: The greening of the capital
abstract: Department of Enviornmental Protection dedicated its first 'green' state office building on Elmerton Avenue.

headline: Poor legislation
abstract: Pocon-Record talk about the prosed legislation to repeal the motorcycle helmet law and urges Governor Tom Ridge to reject it if passes.

headline: Harrisburg has strict sprinkler law
abstract: In 1987, Harrisburg did something remarkable: It passed a law requiring existing high-rise buildings to be equipped with fire-suppression sprinklers.  Such laws are rare because building owners usually object strenuously, complaining that sprinklers are too expensive.  Even more uncommon are communities that pass such laws without having a tragic fire.  Harrisburg had no major high-rise fire.

headline: Ed wants to put Vet sleep - Seeks 2 news parks; eyes sales tax if lottery fails
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell said Philadelphia’s professional sports teams need new stadiums to remain competitive, and for the first time, he said he intends to build two new stadiums for the Philadelphia Phillies and Eagles, rather than build one and renovate Veterans Stadium. Governor Tom Ridge’s stadium financing proposal for four new stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh would require the state, teams and cities to each provide one-third of the new stadiums’ funding, but in order to do this, the state Legislature would have to approve raising the state’s debt ceiling by $500 million. House Majority Leader John Perzel doesn’t believe there are enough votes in the House, and even if it does pass, Rendell would have to come up with the city’s one third funding, which he hopes to generate by having a regional sports lottery or adding a surcharge to the sales tax if the lottery fails to be approved.

headline: State tavern association pushes for referendum on video gambling
abstract: The rally, organized by the Pennsylvania Licensed Beverage Association, the trade organization for the tavern industry, attracted at  least 11 legislators and representatives of a number of others.  It was also one of the largest gatherings of the industry in the state's history, according to John Millrion, the association's executive director, with tavern owners on hand from 25 western Pennsylvania counties.  With more than 200,000 employed in 14,000 establishments statewide, the association is flexing its political muscle in a bid to force a statewide referendum next May on the legalization of video gambling.

headline: Fumo fuming over Cohen
abstract: PA Senator Vincent Fumo criticized David Cohen, Mayor Rendell’s former chief of staff, while attending a rally for Mayoral Candidate Marty Weinberg. Fumo had previously said that he and Cohen would raise $1 million to $2 million for a candidate to replace Rendell; however Cohen didn't want to take on the role. Fumo criticized Cohen for not having as much invested in Philadelphia, and Cohen took a shot back at Fumo.

headline: Principal seeks Democratic nod for 21st District U.S. House seat
abstract: Larry Klemens, principal of a Mercer County career center, announced his plans to seek the Democratic nomination to challenge incumbent Republican U.S. Representative Phil English, who has held the seat since 1994. He became the first challenger from either party, and he essentially said that English does not represent the views of most residents. Klemens switched form independent to Democrat three weeks ago and has not voted since 1992.

headline: SAVING GETTYSBURG
abstract: The photo depicts PA Representatives Frank Gigliotti and Harry Readshaw, who travelled to Gettysburg last week to accept a $65,000 pledge from Columbia Gas to restore the Peace Light Memorial, which President Franklin Roosevelt dedicated in 1934 to honor the 75th reunion of Civil War veterans.

headline: Internet to feature Gettysburg Address
abstract: An internet broadcast is scheduled to show Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, dedicating the new Gettysburg National Cemetary.

headline: MALPRACTICE MORASS   Discounts, court shift did in firm
abstract: PIC Insurance Group quickly rose to become Pennsylvania’s largest malpractice insurance provider by offering extremely discounted rates to doctors; however, the PA Medical Society Liability Insurance Company and John Reed, director of the PA Medical Professional Liability Catastrophe Loss Fund (CAT), warned the state Department of Insurance that their rates were too low and unsustainable. Ultimately, by January 1998, PIC didn’t have enough money to pay for claims, and its vice president attributed this to a change in the Philadelphia court system that resulted in claims being settled faster as well as to increased competition from another insurance provider, which also was declared insolvent this year. The CAT fund was nearly lost due to price undercutting by these two companies, but a 1996 law was passed to prevent companies from offering such low premium rates.

headline: News from the PA General Assembly
abstract: PA Representative Jess Stairs and Senator Robert Tomlinson introduced bills that would change the method for state funding of special education. A Senate committee approved a plan to establish an Internet site with information about long-term care facilities that would be controlled by the Aging Department. A quote by Tomlinson on funding of special education is provided, as is a fact about female composition in the PA General Assembly.

headline: Time for lawmakers to review procedures of game officers
abstract: A committee of the state lawmakers heard five hours of testimony this week from dozens of hunters, campers and other outdoor enthusiasts, alleging that game officers harassed them, conducted illegal searches and lied to them about their rights.  Clearly, there is enough information for lawmakers--- in this cases the state House Game and Fisheries Committee --- to delve further into these allegations.

headline: Pork-laden highway spending bill demonstrates worst, best of politics
abstract: US Rep. Bud Shuster helped to craft a massive transportation bill that recently passed the House. However, the bill gained bipartisan support because of the millions of dollars it allotted in pork spending. The $217 billion bill contains about $9 billion in pure pork. Transportation "demonstration projects" first originated with Shuster in 1976 when he had $3 million earmarked, resulting in the quick completion of a project. Since then, the number of demonstration projects has jumped to $14,000.

headline: Hearings on woes of Section 8 program begin in Coatesville - A Pa. House committee is delving into ways to weed out bad tenants and landlords while helping the poor.
abstract: A PA House panel began its first hearing in a series to look into problems associated with the federal Section 8 program, which provides subsidies to pay for at least 70 percent of housing costs to help move public housing tenants into the private sector. According to U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts, the panel’s findings could lead to reform at the federal level, and PA Representatives John Fichter and Timothy Hennessey both commented on the hearings, which began in Coatesville. There have been reports of both tenants and landlords abusing the program, so the panel will search for solutions.

headline: EDCNP Seeking Transportation Plan Input
abstract: The Economic Development Council of Northeastern Pennsylvania will hold a public meeting to release their straegic goals from now until the year 2018. The goals are outlined in the article.

headline: Storms hit hilltop Pittsburgh neighborhood
abstract: A series of severe thunderstorms stuck Western PA for the second straight day, leaving damaged homes, missing roofs and downed trees and power lines along its path. The National Weather Service received several reports of tornadoes, including one in Somerset County that may have resulted in the death of a 13-year-old girl, but it will investigate to determine if any tornadoes actually touched down. Over 33,000 homes in Allegheny, Beaver, Westmoreland and Fayette counties were left without power because of the storm, and according to a spokeswoman for Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy, four people were injured, but none were serious.

headline: Gap Between Party Funds Grows in Races for Congress
abstract: Republicans have exceed Democrats by more than $110 million in fund raising efforts.

headline: Privatization hot election topic
abstract: U.S. Senate challenger Bill Lloyd and incumbent U.S Senator Arlen Specter, as well as Roy Afflerbach and Pat Toomey, who are vying for Pennsylvania’s 15th Congressional District seat in the House, all agree that the government should stop spending Social Security surpluses and develop a fix to the Social Security system; though they different on how best to do so. Specter, Lloyd and Afflerbach are all opposed to the privatization of Social Security, whereas Toomey believes it would increase investment returns for retirees. Afflerbach believes the government should invest Social Security trust funds more aggressively, Lloyd wants to get rid of a cap that could raise $70 billion a year and Specter wants to see more studies but does not yet have specific plans.

headline: Some lawmakers against creating 'sixth' Great Lake
abstract: U.S. Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont is trying to designate Lake Champlain, which is located in his state, as a sixth Great Lake; however, U.S. Representative Fred Upton of Michigan introduced legislation to oppose Leahy’s efforts. By designating Lake Champlain as a Great Lake, Leahy would have a better chance of securing research funding through the Sea Grant program administered by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. President Clinton already cut funding for the program from $56 million to $50 million, and Upton is trying to secure the support of other Great Lake states, including PA.

headline: Just property?
abstract: Carla Messinger, founder of the Lenni Lenape Historical Society and Museum of Indian Culture in Allentown, wants the bones back to rebury then in Pennsylvania soil. That's where they belong, she says, not on some shelf collecting dust.  Yet her efforts remains ensnared in a web of bureaucracy that stretches from Harrisburg to Washington to Oklahoma plains.  On and off for the past six years, Messinger has tried to convince legislators in Harrisburg to pass a seemingly routine resolution that recognizes the Lenni Lenape as native people of Pennsylvania.

headline: Medical Practice Disclosure Act will foster full disclosure in state
abstract: The medical community speaks through economically and politically powerful groups such as the Pennsylvania Medical Society and the Osteopathic Medical Association.  In addition, the large number of physician organizations and medical malpractice insurance companies spend tens of thousands of dollars per year to insure that legislation beneficial to their views is passed.  The Peer Review Protection Act, which permits medical professionals to police themselves without any intervention by Pennsylvania Courts, has failed to protect Pennsylvanian citizens from medical malpractice and has hurt those who it was suppose to protect.

headline: On the right path
abstract: The Inquirer reviews the difficulties of finding good quality teachers in urban and rural school districts. The Pathways program is one alternative to the problem that is prodcuing good results and teachers.

headline: Trash-in, trash-out resolution pushed
abstract: Senator Leonard Bodack is introducting legislation that would control the flow of out-ofstate trash into Pennsylvania.

headline: Preserve freedoms
abstract: Lois Kaneshiki is writing in response to a previous editorial about the proposal to allow police officers to pull over a driver for not wearing their seat belt. While seat belts save lives, Lois argues the state has no right to regulate an individual’s personal decision not to wear a seat belt, and the proposal could lead to problems in areas where racial tension already exists.

headline: Heidnik's daughter to save father
abstract: Attorneys representing Philadelphia killer Gary Heidnik's daughter filed papers to try to stave off his execution. The PA Supreme Court rejected the latest appeal for Heidnik. He murder two women and tortured four others in the basement of his house.

headline: Economic development bill heads to Ridge
abstract: The PA House passed a bill sponsored by state Representative Joseph Gladeck to create 12 Keystone Opportunity Zones, which would make PA the second state in the nation to get rid of virtually all taxes in economically struggling areas to encourage development. Governor Tom Ridge is a big supporter of the plan, and he believes it will help spur development and the creation of jobs in areas that have been abandoned by businesses for years. The zones that win the state’s approval will also receive $250,000 in grants, and regional cooperation has been encouraged.

headline: Supreme Court deals blow to credit union expansion; banks hail ruling
abstract: Banks prevail in their legal suit against credit unions. Court rules that company credit uions cannot extend membership to individuals outsaide of the company.

headline: Geist promises funds, transportation
abstract: PA Representative Rick Geist will announce that he will seek reelection for an 11th term as the representative for the 79th district. As of now, he doesn’t have any challengers and would likely retain his position as chairman of the House Transportation Committee if he is reelected and Republicans maintain a House majority. He believes securing Altoona Area School District its fair share of funds and a road widening project were two of his biggest accomplishments the past two years.

headline: Prompt Ruling Vowed on Serafini Testimony
abstract: U.S. District Judge Thomas Vanaskie said he would rule promptly on the Time-Tribune newspaper’s petition to unseal documents relating to perjury charges against PA Representative Frank Serafini, who allegedly lied when he told a grand jury about money he received from his cousin. Serafini was indicted with four others for allegedly channeling $129,000 from a corporation to the campaign funds for former presidential candidate Bob Dole and other federal candidates. Attorney Frank McDonnel, who represents the paper, argued to the judge that the public deserves access to the documents due to the public nature of Serafini’s crimes.

headline: State offers grants for conservation projects
abstract: Local municipalities or organizations interested in undertaking conservation or recreation projects could be eligible for as much as $11 million in grant money. PA Senator J. Barry Stout is offering information packets which contain an application that must be returned to the state Department of Conservation and Natural Resources by October 31.

headline: Mine leaks: Study sees lode of cash
abstract: A study of mine drainage in Pennsylvania shows that some metals found in mine discharge could be sold and used for the mine cleanup.

headline: Medicare begins info campaign
abstract: Medicare+Cholice program is being advertosed to seniors in Alleghney County. Provisions and directions on the program are examined.

headline: Only 3 charter schools pass test
abstract: Four teams selected by Pittsburgh school officials to review eight charter school proposals have recommended that school board members approve only three of the applications. They are the Northways Urban Pathways Charter School and Urban League of Pittsburgh Charter School. The teams, which each were assigned two proposals to evaluate, advised city school board members not to grant charters to the five others for a variety of reasons that included little parent or community support and having budgets that seemed unrealistic.

headline: Turkey Brouhaha
abstract: Some members of the PA Legislature, including Vice-Chairman of the House Game and Fisheries Committee Ed Staback, are annoyed at the PA Game Commission. They believe the agency has put them in a difficult position by telling turkey hunters that they will be able to take more than one turkey in the spring and fall seasons if the legislature approves a turkey stamp that hunters have to pay for.

headline: Preserve old bridges correctly
abstract: Morning Call is praises Senator Arlen Specter and Jim Jeffords for finding a way to protect and preserved important bridges.

headline: Hess Receives Recognition By PA District Attorneys
abstract: The PA District Attorneys Association honored PA Representative Dick Hess for his commitment to public safety and support of law enforcement, criminal justice and victims’ rights legislation.

headline: Economic development official: NE region should work together
abstract: Although northeastern PA has higher unemployment than other areas of the country, it's a lot better off than it was 40 years ago. And Howard Grossman, executive director of the Economic Development Council of Northeastern PA, told a Greater Hazleton Chamber of Commerce Red Carpet Breakfast that officials have to work together as a region to make that progress continue. The region has to market all of its assets to stay competitive.

headline: Surcharges on ATMs fuel debate
abstract: Senator Alfonse D'Amato's proposed legislation to stop double ATM surcharges sparks debate and opossition from the banking industry.

headline: Gekas wants debate on Clinton impeachment to continue in '99
abstract: Representative George Gekas would like Congress to continue the Clinton impeachment trial into next year, 1999.

headline: Public wins right to comment before local officials vote
abstract: Provisions were added to Pennsylvania’s new lobbyist disclosure law that could force local governments who violate the state’s Sunshine Law to reimburse a person who files a lawsuit for legal fees. Local governments could do the same against people who file frivolous lawsuits, and another provision would require public comments be heard before a vote is conducted. These expansions of the Sunshine Law have been overshadowed by the lobbyist reform law sponsored by PA Senate President Pro Tem Robert Jubelirer, but the PA Newspapers Publishers Association still considers them to be a major victory.

headline: State parks join in open burning ban
abstract: On behalf of Governor Tom Ridge, the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources announced that all 116 state parks, along with all state forests and game lands, will observe a temporary ban on open fires and smoking. Extremely dry conditions have already caused several hundred acres of land to burn over the last few weeks, and 98 percent of wildfires are caused by people; often due to improperly extinguished campfires, careless burning of trash and cigarettes.

headline: Monahan files GAO complaint
abstract: Robert Monahan Jr. continues to claim that the National Park Service’s selection process for choosing a developer for projects at Gettysburg was flawed. An alternative developer was chosen for the projects, and Monahan has requested the federal General Accounting Office to conduct a full audit.

headline: Meeting Slated Thursday to Rally Support for Bill
abstract: Mercy Hospital, Scranton, will host a town meeting in support of House Bill 656, the uniform insurance coverage bill to improve care for individuals with diabetes in Pennsylvania, on Thursday from 7 to 9 p.m. at the hospital.  A similar meeting was conducted at Mercy Hospital, Wilkes-Barre, on March 2.

headline: Open the borders - Phila. Schools should end teacher residency rule
abstract: The authors of the editorial believe it’s difficult enough to lure qualified teacher to Philadelphia’s schools, which have larger classes and offer smaller salaries, but a residency rule makes it even more difficult. The residency rule requires all new teachers to live in the city, but the authors believe the requirement has reduced the number of qualified teachers in the city’s public schools and has forced the district to hire underqualified teachers to fill the gap. Instead of requirements, the authors think Philadelphia should offer more incentives such as student loan forgiveness plans and signing bonuses to help attract better teachers.

headline: Turkey hunters get less cluck for their buck
abstract: Pennsylvania currently allows hunters one bird per season, but the legislature can still establish higher bag limits in House Bill 1200, which would amend sections of the game code. The Pennsylvania Game Commission defeated a proposal to extend hunting hours by a half hour before sunrise and a half hour after sunset.

headline: Preventing turnpike tragedy
abstract: The authors, PA Representative Curt Schroder and Senators Jim Gerlach and Bob Thompson, are writing about the meetings they convened along with the Lionville Fire Company, Uwchlan Ambulance Corps, state police and the PA Turnpike Commission in response to the tragic death of David Good, who was killed on the turnpike after responding to an accident. As a result of the meetings, the Turnpike Commission has agreed to provide the fire company with early warning signs, it will work to establish an automatic gate at an emergency exit used by ambulance workers, and it will increase the number of training exercises offered to improve the functioning of the incident command system. In addition, the authority in charge of an accident scene will wear an identifying vest, and the PA Legislature is considering new proposals to try to prevent another tragedy from occurring.

headline: Hold open meetings
abstract: The York Dispatch questions private Court Task Force meetings as a possible violation of the Sunshine law.

headline: Economic studies don't support state-funding of sports stadiums
abstract: According to the author, a recent study found that 90 percent of central PA voters oppose state funding for new stadiums in Pittsburgh, and Allegheny County voters overwhelmingly oppose the plan to build new stadiums, yet Pittsburgh is still pushing the state Legislature to contribute $150 million to pay for one third of the cost of new stadiums. The author cites another study that shows the economic benefits of stadiums are nowhere near worth the investment, and he claims there is a major underlying problem that is greed in major league sports, especially baseball. Overall, the author says there are no moral, intellectual or philosophical reasons for funding new stadiums with taxpayers’ dollars.

headline: Tax doesn't amuse Naylor    Ski slope owner threatens to leave state
abstract: Irvin Naylor, the owner of Ski Roundtop and Ski Liberty in Warrington Township and Carroll Valley Borough, is threatening to relocate the ski resorts because of two bad seasons of warm weather and an amusement tax that he believes is unfair. While suffering $1.5 million in losses last year, Naylor had to pay $138,572 in amusement taxes to local schools and municipalities; however, PA Representative Robert Godshall has proposed an amendment that could ease the tax burden by amending the amusement tax from 4 percent to 1.6 percent for ski areas, bowling allies and golf courses and from 10 percent to 4 percent for all others. The local municipalities claim much of the money is used to clear roads to the ski resort, and they argue Naylor should raise ticket prices, which he doesn’t want to do in a competitive marketplace.

headline: Gekas: Support for impeachment fading
abstract: U.S. Representative George Gekas told a group of Lebanon County clubs that a vote to censure Clinton would be meaningless; however, he admitted the support for impeachment in the House, even among some Republicans, was weak. Gekas said he believes military action will likely be necessary against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. He also defended the Republican Party against accusations that they have been ineffective in their control of Congress, which he attributed to the use of the filibuster by Democrats in the Senate to stall and kill legislation that passed the House

headline: Punt takes his rest, plans to cast vote
abstract: Sen. Terry Punt suffered a mild heart attack but still made it to the polls and voted.

headline: State Parks Under Full "Open Swim" Policy This Summer
abstract: For the first time this summer, there will be no lifeguards at Beltzville State Park’s beach and others across PA. Some parents are concerned about safety issues, but the park management claims swimmers should be responsible for their own safety, and they can now swim anytime the park is open.

headline: Monahan's vision of Gettysburg
abstract: In addition to a hotel and conference center, Gettysburg entrepreneur Robert Monahan's $150 million plan for the now-defunct Adams County industrial park includes a museum and IMAX. Outside the museum will be a large reflecting pool lined with state flags, for a $3 fee, visitors will find theme areas all presented in a multimedia "sen-surround" sound.

headline: Mental health week focuses on stopping discrimination
abstract: The PA Mental Health Consumers Association (PMHCA) organized a rally in Harrisburg as part of this week’s Mental Health Awareness Week. According to Carol Shugerts, who directs a center for people with mental illnesses and dependency problems, the rally was intended to show Governor Tom Ridge and state lawmakers that mental health patients and their families face discrimination from insurance companies. The demonstrators support an anti-discrimination bill, and Vicki Darring, president of the PMHCA, said similar proposals in other states have yielded positive results.

headline: Our View: State must raise teacher standards
abstract: The U.S. Education Department estimates the nation will need an additional 2 million new teachers in the next decade due to a number of different factors. The authors of the article believe that now is the time for the PA Legislature to act and increase the standards for teachers before demand exceeds the supply of qualified teachers. They argue southwestern PA school districts have been able to attract more qualified teachers, but improving the statewide standards would still be beneficial, and action should come quickly.

headline: Upstream, Game Commission work draws conservationists' ire
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission apparently destroyed two colonies of the threatened plants and violated its own policy by bulldozing within 100 yards of a rare bird's nest site at Nescopeck State park, representatives of eight environmental groups. Game Commission policy bans such activities from within 300 yards of nests. Development plans for the park, amended over the past several decades, now include installing sewer lines, clearing land for parking and opening an environmental education center.

headline: Progress seen in SEPTA talks
abstract: Negotiators for the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority and the Transport Workers Union met for the third consecutive day. While they are still far apart on some issues, both sides expressed optimism about reaching a settlement that would end SEPTA’s 24-day strike, which has affected 435,000 commuters. Police are searching for the person responsible for shooting a SEPTA security guard with a pellet from an air rifle, and Mayor Ed Rendell made $100,000 in emergency loan funds available to help small retail businesses affected by the strike.

headline: Home protection laws on Geist's list
abstract: PA Representative Rick Geist had an intruder try to break into his home, and he is supporting a homeowner protection bill that would allow homeowners to use deadly force to protect their property under more circumstances. In addition, he is discussing a proposal to make owners of halfway houses responsible for crimes committed by people staying there, and he supports a bill that would implement tougher penalties for third time offenders convicted of theft charges. Geist will meet with PA Attorney General Mike Fisher and Altoona Police Chief John Treese this morning to discuss crime.

headline: Enterprise zone awaits funding OK   State grants would help Titusville Redevelopment Authority create 50 jobs
abstract: The Titusville Redevelopment Authority is still waiting to hear whether four competitive enterprise zone grants will be funded by the PA Department of Community and Economic Development. While the authority has not given any specific details to the public, money from those grants would be used to loan money to businesses for economic expansion. The authority has already had two successfully funded projects in the past through similar grants.

headline: Texas firm to buy Arco Chemical Co.
abstract: In an abrupt turnabout, Atlantic Richfield Co announced that it had signed "a definitive agreement" to sell Arco Chemical Co to a Houston concern, Lyondell Petrochemical Co in a deal worth $5.6 billion. The sale, which was approved by the boards of Arco Chemical and Lyondell, means that hundreds of administrative jobs at Arco Chemical's world headquarters in Newtown Square, Delaware County, will be lost, according to president and chief executive Marvin Schlanger. About 1,000 people work for the company in Newtown Square.

headline: Getting out the vote: A quiet but costly effort
abstract: You won't find big labor or the gun lobby advertising on TV this campaign season. But that doesn't mean they're not spending money to influence the election. They are spending money to get voters to the polls. This is more low profile, bt may help them win elections.

headline: Purdy hopes to challenge Marisco for House seat
abstract: State house Democratic employee Jay Purdy said he will seek hi spart's nomination to oppose Representative Ronald Marisco in the 105th District in Dauphin County. Acknowledging he is facing an uphill battle in a heavily Republican district, he said he is not looking for the easy way out.

headline: State representative calls attention to memorials
abstract: Civil War re-enactors and PA Representative Harry Readshaw took part in a ceremony to call attention to the deteriorating condition of many memorials on the Gettysburg battlefield. Governor Tom Ridge refused to support the use of state dollars for restoration projects, even though other states have raised money to restore their state’s monuments on the battlefield. Readshaw is leading the campaign to restore Pennsylvania’s 133 state-owned monuments, and a $65,000 donation and several smaller donations were presented at the ceremony.

headline: Park given battlefield land spotlighted in book, movie
abstract: Friends of the National Parks bought a six-acre wooded section of land that was of critical importance during the crucial Civil War battle of Gettysburg, and it is now part of Gettysburg National Military Park. The land is located on Little Round Top, where Union Colonel Joshua Chamberlin famously stopped advancing Confederates from taking the hilltop, which offered a strategic view of the entire battlefield. The site has been depicted in the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, "The Killer Angels," as well as the movie based on the book, "Gettysburg."

headline: Million Toddlers Said to Need Vaccination
abstract: There are approximatly 2 million children under the age of 2 who have not received vaccinations.

headline: Overhaul of PIAA recommended
abstract: Coaches, school officials, fans and journalists recommend a complete overhaul of the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association, which a PA Senate panel has been investigation for possible abuse of authority. 70 volunteers gathered into several groups to discuss what changes they believed were needed at the PIAA.

headline: Wastelands? Budget problems are making it difficult for state to manage its game lands
abstract: On May 11, 1905, after considerable debate among members of the Game Commission on the best ways to help Pennsylvania's wildlife, Gov. Samuel W. Pennypacker authorized the commissioners to establish game preserves on state forest land.  In almost eight decades since its creation, the game lands program has grown to include nearly 1.4 million acres.  "In an attempt to remain fiscally responsible and stretch our fiscal resources as far and as long as we've can, we've had to cut many program budgets," said Greg Grabowicz, director of the Game Commission's Bureau of Land Management.

headline: Putting brakes on teen drivers
abstract: New Castle News is agreeing with Pennsylvania Department of Transportation in that oarents should take more respobsibility when their young teenagers begin to drive, but New Castle News is cautiius about eays to do this and urges PennDOT to find alternate solutions to highway safety problems with teenagers.

headline: Homicides raise questions about gun legislation
abstract: According to police statement read in court during a preliminary hearing, the irate boyfriend who shot his girlfriend, told investigators he bought the weapon from someone on the streets.  Scenes such as the aforementioned question how effective the massive onslaught of gun legislation designed to reduce these incidents has been,  Recently enacted federal gun laws prohibit ownership, possession, receiving, shipping or transporting firearms (rifles, shotguns or handguns) or ammunition for residents who have been convicted of a crime punishable by imprisonment for more than one year.

headline: Feel-good-enomics
abstract: The plan to build two new stadiums in allegheny County is not feeling good for taxpayers who will foot part of the bill.

headline: The Companies at a Glance
abstract: Lyondell Petrochemical announced that it would acquire Arco Chemical. The two companies are profiled.

headline: Gingrich Is Admitting His Vision Is Blurred
abstract: U.S. House Republican Speaker Newt Gingrich’s vision helped Republicans win the majority in Congress in 1994; however, he admitted his vision seems to have blurred recently in light of the recent election in which Republicans had a net loss of five seats when most expected them to gain between 10 and 30 seats. The party’s poor showing has left him, along with House Majority Leader Dick Armey and conference chairman John Boehner, vulnerable to leadership challenges from within the party, and several potential candidates could pose a very real possibility of unseating them. Many believe the election was a backlash to conservatives, so the prospect of someone more conservative unseating Gingrich has drawn concern, but ultimately, many Republicans are angry with Gingrich, and the real question will be how many are angry enough to rebel against him.

headline: Put the Incivility Back in Politics
abstract: Geoffrey Fleger, a wealthy Bloomfield Hills Lawyer best known for defending Jack Kevorkian, stands little chance of being elected as governor of Michigan next month. The incumbent is well liked and has avoided negative campaigning unlike his opponent. Piece believes that voters are bored with polite politics and elections should include negative campaigning.

headline: Statewide test set for Emergency Alert System
abstract: As part of Weather Emergency Preparedness Week, the PA Emergency Management Agency and National Weather Service will conduct a statewide test of the Emergency Alert System today, with Lieutenant Governor Schweiker giving the message. The test follows three days of exercises that tested severe weather emergency response plans at the county level. Department of Emergency Services Director Bob Bish also urged families to develop an emergency plan that includes a kit with essential supplies, and state and county officials hope that the community develops and practices their own emergency response plans.

headline: Park Service Scales Back Gettysburg Development
abstract: Amid controversy over a proposal to allow commercial development inside Gettysburg National Military Park, the National Park Service and private developer Robert Kinsley decided to scale back the size of their original proposal by 20 percent, cutting the project’s overall cost from $40.4 million to $39.2 million. The Park Service wanted to try a public-commercial venture because they didn’t think Congress would provide enough funding to construct a new visitor center for a new museum and Cyclorama Center; however, strong public criticism over plans to allow commercial ventures inside the park convinced officials to scale back the operation. Kinsley set up the Gettysburg National Battlefield Foundation, a nonprofit group, to seek $27 million in donations for the project, and the additional $12 million will come from conventional bank loans.

headline: New facility for hospital under study: Carlisle trustees favor a smaller site
abstract: Carlisle Hospital has been in the same location for 82 years, but the hospital’s president, Michael Halstead, said that trustees have begun a series of planning studies on building a new hospital with a smaller inpatient capacity on vacant grounds the Carlisle Hospital and Health Services had purchased in 1995. According to estimates, it would cost between $53 million and $60 million to construct a new facility, whereas it would cost $46 million to renovate the current building, but a major drawback of renovation is that a modern hospital would have to be incorporated into an old building.  The studies are expected to be concluded by early next year to be voted on.

headline: Pa. grants to help some schools track finances
abstract: Several Lancaster County school districts received state grants to draft reports on how money is spent. According to PA Education Secretary Eugene Hickok, the reports will allow taxpayers and school officials to track how much money is spent on each grade, subject and building. If the program is successful, it may be expanded in the future.

headline: Water pollution from many sources is biggest threat   Nonpoint contamination is hard to trace, even harder to stop, officials say
abstract: Nonpoint source pollution is pollution that comes from so many different points that it is difficult to isolate any specific point, but according to Caren Glotfelty, a professor at Penn State, and a study done by the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) in 1994, nonpoint pollution represents the biggest threat to Pennsylvania’s waterways. Nonpoint pollution is extremely difficult to prevent because it comes from so many different sources, including runoff from farms, soil erosion from construction projects and even a farmer’s cow that walks into a stream, but nonetheless, the state DEP, the Fish and Boat Commission, Centre County’s Conservation District and numerous conservancy groups are trying to develop solutions to the problem. Unfortunately, it is difficult for these agencies to respond to many reports from the public in a timely manner, and between the branches that have the ability to enforce nonpoint pollution controls, there is not enough manpower.

headline: Rail Future
abstract: Patriot News says that if Maglev railway gets underway then Pennsylvania can reclaim the lead in technology.

headline: Hope in Bloomsdale-Fleetwing
abstract: An active, consistent police presence is essential to establishing and maintaining a safe, crime-free community, but it does not and cannot end there. The October 1995 drug raid carried out by federal and local law enforcement agencies, which resulted in more than 80 arrests shows what we can do. US Representative James Greenwood advertises what he is doing in congress.

headline: Firms consider project
abstract: Two businesses are considering moving into a section of the South Harrisburg Enterprise Development Zone, which is currently under construction. Businesses that move into the zone will receive state tax credits based on how many jobs they create. The head of the construction project said it should be ready to open by July, and a  spokesman for Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed said the mayor is extremely pleased with how the project is turning out.

headline: The Legacy of Milton S. Hershey
abstract: Milton S. Hershey, who founded Hershey’s Chocolate, was one of the top industrialists of his time, but he was a caring man and gave his entire fortune to create a school for orphans. Over four million people flock to Hershey PA, the site of Hershey’s first and largest chocolate factory, Hershey Theater, Hotel Hershey and Hershey’s amusement park, each year. Hershey Trust is now responsible for the school for orphans, which provides a college education and other financial needs for 1,000 children, and the trust has no intention of selling the 9,000 acres of land it owns; much to the delight of many locals.

headline: Gingrich stumps for Goodling
abstract: U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich accompanied U.S. Representative Bill Goodling to a fundraising event in PA, where he voiced his support for Goodling’s reelection and cited examples of him defending conservative principles in Washington. Gingrich spoke about other issues as well and said that 10 to 15 years of expected future federal budget surpluses could allow the nation to tackle problems with Social Security. PA Representative Al Masland introduced Goodling at a formal press conference, where Goodling said afterwards that his record spoke for itself, so he didn’t need to debate Republican primary challenger Charles Gerow.

headline: Races for 2 Senate seats key to GOP
abstract: PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola told Republican State Committee members that two midstate Senate elections are among the top priorities, and the overall goal is to increase the Republican’s control over the Senate by gaining 4 more seats by 2000, which would allow Republicans to confirm candidates for office without having to deal with Democrats. House Appropriations Chairman John Barley said he hoped to pick up one or two house seats, but the four open seats in Lehigh and Northampton counties will be crucial and a lot of money will be spent there. Republican candidates Pat Toomey and Don Sherwood were also discussed because their congressional races are expected to be extremely competitive.

headline: Susquehanna designated American Heritage River   Federal program selection will be economic boom for this region
abstract: U.S. Representative Paul Kanjorski led efforts to convince President Clinton that the Susquehanna River should be designated as an American Heritage River, and he happily announced that Clinton had in fact chosen it as one of 14 rivers. Although the Susquehanna wasn't among the 10 finalists submitted by a commission, Kanjorski was persistent in convincing Clinton, and the designation will allow the river to gain easier access to existing federal funds to help plan and achieve environmental clean up goals as well as economic development. A key part of the Susquehanna’s proposal to become an American Heritage River focused on cleaning up abandoned mine sites that contribute thousands of tons of pollution into the river each year.

headline: PennDOT wants to give you a house
abstract: Pennsylvania State Department of Transportation will give away a 140 year old historical home to the resident with the best proposal on what to do with the home and where to relocate the home.

headline: New HMO for PSGHS
abstract: The Penn State Geisinger Health System (PSGHS), which serves over 3 million Pennsylvanians, signed an agreement that will allow HealthAmerica members to receive services at any PSGHS site in 40 different counties. A similar agreement was made in June for Blue Cross’s subsidiary, First Priority Health, and Penn State Geisinger is hoping that the agreements will convince PA Attorney General Mike Fisher to approve the merger between Geisinger Health System and Penn State’s Milton S.
