Hershey Medical Center. Fisher held off on approval of the merger in the past due to concerns that it would monopolize health care, but these agreements are intended to alleviate these concerns.

headline: Pa.'s school uniform law not likely to strip local students of individual style
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge signed a bill in to law that will allow school districts to require all students to wear uniforms. According to PA Senator James Rhoades, the law does not require schools to impose a uniform policy, but it allows them the freedom to do so; though Stroudsburg school board members seem to be in no rush to adopt a mandatory uniform policy. Proponents of school uniforms believe they improve discipline, school safety and school spirit, whereas critics raise questions about the cost of uniforms and feel they could hinder students’ creativity.

headline: Waterway Cleanup Funds Promised by Rep. English
abstract: U.S. Representative Phil English introduced a bill in the House to ensure the full amount of money collected for the Abandoned Mine Land fund goes towards cleaning up abandoned mine sites. He’s proposing to take the fund off the federal budget, which the PA Department of Environmental Protection estimates would almost double the $22 million allocated to PA to help clean up the state’s 250,000 estimated abandoned mine acres.

headline: Regional Fatalies
abstract: Statewide, alcohol-related highway fatalities declined consistently between 1991 and 1996, dropping a total of 26 percent. Alcohol-related fatalities in the 12-county southwestern PA region dropped only 21 percent.

headline: Hospitals receive money to identify abuse victims when they seek treatment
abstract: Some PA hospitals will reicieve state funding to set up programs to identify domestic abuse vicitms.

headline: Former critic backs plans - Walko shifts gears, will support state funds for stadiums
abstract: PA Representative Don Walko had been one of the most outspoken critics against using taxpayers’ dollars to build new stadiums in Pittsburgh, and he had been highly critical of the Pirates and Steelers for not contributing enough money. However, he recently announced that he would support legislation to increase the amount of money the state can borrow to fund stadium projects. Governor Tom Ridge wants to fund no more than one-third of the cost of each new stadium, which could be up to $75 million per stadium, but time may be running out with less than 12 session days left before the Legislature adjourns for the year.

headline: The odds are against keno
abstract: Rep. Terry Van Horne is sponsoring a bill to permit the electronic gambling game keno in any of the state's 67 counties that secure voter approval in local referendums. State Rep. Paul Clymer contends that keno is highly addictive to many including low-income residents who hope to hit it big. Governor Tom Ridge is insisting on state-wide referendums.

headline: Gingrich whips up local GOP
abstract: Newt Gingrich visits Lehigh Valley to help raise money for Pat Toomey, who is seeking the ditrict congressional seat.

headline: Singel speaks at Democratic dinner: Party needs to focus on issues, not impeachment
abstract: Former PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Singel spoke at the Huntington County Democratic Committee Fall Rally Dinner, where he urged voters to focus on important issues like education, economic development and the environment as opposed to President Clinton’s impeachment hearing. He condemned Republicans for their role in the impeachment trial and criticized them for being indifferent and boring when it comes to many issues. He praised gubernatorial and senatorial candidates Ivan Itkin and Bill Lloyd, rallied Democrats to vote and told the group they should be proud to be Democrats.

headline: Susquehanna fails to make Heritage Rivers list
abstract: During his 1997 State of the Union address, President Clinton announced he would select 10 rivers to be designated as American Heritage Rivers, but Pennsylvania’s Susquehanna River was not among the final ten recommendations selected by a committee. U.S. Representative Paul E. Kanjorski of PA pushed for the Susquehanna, and he is disappointed that more rivers weren’t selected. Being designated as a Heritage River would bring economic and environmental opportunities to PA, and advocates are still working hard to persuade President Clinton to choose the Susquehanna.

headline: New law expected to help diabetics
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is expected to sign the PA Diabetic Control Act at the PA Medical Society’s meeting in Hershey. The law will require health insurance companies to cover the costs of diabetic supplies such as blood glucose monitors, test strips, syringes, needles and insulin. The bill is the result of the bipartisan legislative efforts of Senator Leonard Bodack and State Representative Matthew Wright, and it was voted on after the Health Care Cost Containment Council’s six month study on its economic impact on insurance companies.

headline: Panel assails student competency testing
abstract: Test results should not be the only basis for promoting student to the next grade or granting high school diplomas, says an expert panel in a report out that challenges widespread practices in states trying to boost achievement. President Clinton's1997 proposal to create voluntary national tests in reading and math, as well as his push for high academic standards nationwide, catapulted testing to the top of the national education agenda. The report also criticizes tracking and grade retention.

headline: Who complies with environmental laws?
abstract: In the past, the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) hasn’t had an efficient way of showing the public which businesses and local governments were complying with environmental regulations, but according to authors of the article, DEP Secretary James Seif and Gail Rockwood, a member of the Citizens Advisory Council to the DEP, Pennsylvania’s first on-line Environmental Compliance Tracking System is being developed. The authors claim the system will allow the public to easily view who is in compliance with regulations, which should increase accountability. The authors urge the public to take part in the process of developing the system by either attending a series of six public discussions or submitting written suggestions.

headline: Regulators Could Alter Conrail Deal
abstract: The Federal Surface Transportation Board is facing increased pressure to alter the planned $10 billion breakup of Conrail Incorporated, which would result in a joint takeover by two other companies. The industry has been criticized for botching mergers recently, so the proposed breakup will be scrutinized carefully, but ultimately, most analysts believe the breakup will be approved. The Surface Transportation Board’s decision will take on added meaning because it is up for reauthorization this year, and a group of 24 lawmakers, led by U.S. Senators Alfonse D’Amato and Daniel Moynihan of New York, are hoping the board prevents the railroad from becoming monopolized.

headline: House Oks anti-domestic violence bill
abstract: The PA House approved a bill established screening programs for domestic violence at 25 hospitals across the state. The legislation now goes to the Senate where Senator Mary Jo White, a Republican from Franklin, Venango County, said she will push for quick passage. It began as legislation to require hospitals, medical centers and clinics across the state to question all female patients about whether they have been a victim of spousal or partner abuse.

headline: Fourth and 10 for stadium funds
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is proposing to raise the state’s borrowing limit to provide one-third of the funding for new stadiums for the Philadelphia Phillies and Eagles and the Pittsburgh Pirates and Steelers, which would cost an estimated $300 million to $325 million. However, state Representative Donald Snyder, the third highest ranking Republican, and many other legislators believe the team’s owners should pay for all the stadium costs, not taxpayers. Ridge is trying to convince legislators of the economic benefits of the stadiums, and he claims raising the borrowing limit could open up to $200 million for other public projects throughout the state, but as of now, he doesn’t have the votes to pass a stadium funding bill.

headline: The odds are against keno
abstract: With projected revenue totaling millions Rep. Terry Van Horne, D-Westmoreland, is sponsoring a bill to permit the electronic game keno in any of the state's 67 counties that secure voter approval in local referendums.  The dollar signs are fairly jumping in Rep. Van Horne's eyes.  Based on revenues in state where  a fast-draw version of keno is legal, Rep. Van Horne estimates sales here could reach $400 million annually if all 67 counties participate.

headline: GLASS DOUBTS REILLY'S CHOICE
abstract: York County Commissioner Shirly Glass said that Commisioner Chris Reilly should have recused himself from last week's elections board meeting though she did agree with the board's conclusion. Glass said that Reilly's connections to District Attorney H. Stanley Rebert and state Senator Dan Delp, Republican-Manchester could lead to a public appearance of a conflict of interest.  The Board of Elections meeting concerned a complaint by the York County Democratic Party over a $1,000 donation sent by Delp's campaign committee to Rebert's.  The check was returned but was never recorded by Rebert's treasurer.  Republicans Reilly and Commissioner Bob Minnich met and reviewed the complaint finding no wrongdoing.  Glass, the only board's only democrat was on vacation and disagreed with the manner in which matters were handled.

headline: Reaction on Miller vote mixed
abstract: Bucks County Commissioner Sandra Miller, a Democrat, voted along with her Republican counterparts to join the Southeastern Legal Foundation and three other counties in a lawsuit against President Clinton’s proposal to conduct the 2000 census by avoiding the traditional head count method and using a statistical method instead. She based the decision on evidence that Bucks County could be undercounted, which would lead to less federal funding. Her vote drew mixed reactions from a number of Democratic leaders in the article, and there is a national concern amongst many Republicans that the new method of counting could hurt the party in upcoming congressional races.

headline: Timber sales should profit taxpayers
abstract: The authors of the editorial are disappointed that the U.S. Forest Service lost over $88 million on its timber sales, which is evidence that timber sales from the 192 million acres of national forests, including Allegheny National Forest, are not profitable. The authors believe that the Forest Service must find a way to make sales more profitable, but they must also walk a fine line to ensure that jobs aren’t lost in the logging industry. The authors believe that the Forest Service’s program of timber sales needs to be drastically overhauled in order to save taxpayers money, while also paying attention to environmentally friendly logging techniques and the needs of other outdoor activities.

headline: New law raising doubts
abstract: The Domestic Violence Health Care Response Act, which would require health care professionals to screen paients for domestic injuries, is dicussed in terms of the pros and cons of the legislation.

headline: Panel deals blow to city schools over funds
abstract: The Philadelphia School District filed a lawsuit alleging the PA Legislature and Governor Tom Ridge violated the state constitution by not providing adequate education funding to the district’s schools because the city couldn’t provide enough funding due to already high local tax burdens; however, Commonwealth Court ruled it did not have jurisdiction to interfere. School Superintendant David Hornbeck said he may be forced to shut down the city’s public schools without additional funding, but Ridge and the Legislature have continuously argued the fact that Philadelphia already receives a fair share of state funding, considering it receives 18 percent of public school funding for only 12 percent of the state’s students. Many other states have ruled on cases involving education funding, but House Majority Leader John Perzel said the court clearly understands its constitutional role.

headline: Who will challenge Hafer?
abstract: Based on the success of incumbents in the past election, if Catherine Knoll challenges incumbent Treasurer Barbara Hafer in 2000, she probably doesn’t stand much of a chance of winning. PA Representative Art Hershey will become the new Chairman of the House Environmental Resources and Energy Committee, and his main priority will be passing legislation requiring a deposit on bottles. Other priorities will include out-of-state trash in PA landfills and sewage disposal regulations.

headline: Rep. English must take the lead in pursuing county roads
abstract: Butler Eagle encourages Representative Phil English to do more then dicuss transportation issues with Routes 8, 228, and 356.

headline: House Oks update on wiretapping law
abstract: The House passed a bill that changed current laws on wiretapping for police. The bill has been sent to Govenor Tom Ridge's office.

headline: Globe Project Gets $500,000
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph McDade lobbied the federal Appalachian Regional Commission and announced that it had approved the release of $500,000 to convert the former Globe Store in Scranton into a headquarters for Diversified Information Technologies. The project is expected to create 650 jobs in Scranton over the next three years. In addition to the grant, the project will be financed by the PA Industrial Development Authority, bank financing, equity and $1.25 million grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Economic Development Administration, which is expected to be approved soon.

headline: US May Face enforcement Hurdles in Crackdown on Internet Gambling
abstract: Until this week, on-line gambling seemed a fairly safe bet: Many offshore Web sites run their operations with officials from their host governments. American magazines and newspapers display bold ads trumpeting the sites capabilities. Among tens of thousands of Internet users, placing a wager on-line seems as innocent as buying a book from a Web site. The federal government is beginning a crackdown on internet gambling, but faces a problem wit public opinion.

headline: Glatfelter hosts Kramer fund-raiser
abstract: Arthur Glatfelter, chairman of Glatfelter insurance Group, hosted a fundraising event for Democrat Jackie Kramer, who will face PA Representative Mike Waugh for the 28th District’s Senate seat. PA Senate Democratic Leader Robert Mellow could not attend due to a bad back. Glatfelter has supported many Democratic candidates, yet he also held a fundraiser for Republican Governor Tom Ridge three weeks ago.

headline: Redrawn voting district lines to remain
abstract: PA Commonwealth Court Judge Emil E. Narick denied a request to restore the old boundary lines from recent reapportioning of Susquehanna Township's voting districts. Dauphin County Judge Scott Evans approved the redistricting earlier this month. The plan placed two commissioners in the same ward and changed the neighborhood registration of a number of voters. State law requires municipalities to reapportion wards within a year after a federal census is conducted.

headline: Trail named after Rep. McDade gets cool reception
abstract: $3.5 million in funding to build the proposed 37-mile river valley trail through the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area is still pending in the 1999 federal budget, yet U.S. Representative Ralph Regula has proposed naming the trail after Representative Joseph McDade. However, some members of the park’s Citizens Advisory Commission were not pleased upon hearing the proposal. McDade has been accused of improving Pennsylvania’s section of the park at the expense of New Jersey’s portion, and some people don’t think it is right to single out McDade in naming the trail.

headline: New rules hurt home health-care agencies, doctors told
abstract: Home health-care agencies are being hammered by new federal regulations, and the level of services to patients has been cut more in this region than anywhere else in the country, said Stephen Holt, president and CEO of the Visiting Nurse Association of Greater Philadelphia.  A meeting of the Philadelphia County Medical Society subcommittee on aging, focused on helping seniors get access to quality health care.  Holt said that more than 1,300 agencies nationwide had closed since Medicare funds for home health care were reduced by the Balanced Budget Act of 1997.

headline: Panel: District failed special needs student
abstract: A state appeals panel ruled that Stroudsburg Area School District has to pay the $70,000 yearly tuition for a student with attention deficit disorder to attend a special school in Connecticut, which could cost the district thousands of dollars a year if other students take similar paths. According to the panel, the school district’s individual education program, required for special needs students, failed to address the boy’s problems, which prompted the mother to take him out of school. School officials are appealing the ruling because they claim they were never told by the mother about the boy’s problems; though the attorney representing him claims the mother repeatedly called the school to voice her dissatisfaction.

headline: Why aren't kids hunting anymore?
abstract: The Fund for Animals, Inc., a Maryland-based group, sent a letter to Gov. Tom Ridge claiming many hunters want to "clean up their sport" by getting rid of "contest killing events" such as live pigeon shoots. The future of hunting in Pennsylvania and elsewhere can only be assured if more young people are encouraged to take part according to organizers of the "Governor's Symposium on North America's Hunting Heritage." David Rockland, a market place research analyst, told symposium attendees to treat hunting, fishing, and other outdoor activities as a product that has to be sold to those who aren't already using it.

headline: Residents Must Wait for Noise Barriers
abstract: Scranton residents who are in need of noise barriers along Meadow Avenue and I-81 will have to wait, according to PA Department of Transportation. A meeting was held by resident to discuss the issue.

headline: House votes today on 'quality-of-life' bills
abstract: There are 25 different proposed quality-of-life laws in a bipartisan package set to introduced and voted on in Congress. The bills included a variety of things relating to prostitution, addicts, theives, etc.

headline: Gloomy Forecast
abstract: Besides announcing that it intended to lay off between 50 and 100 workers next week, the company confirmed that it planned to shut down five buildings. It would not say if the recreation center and a 100-acre parcel of land were for sale.

headline: Therapists see licensing bill as aid to profession
abstract: PA is one of 12 states without massage therapy regulations or licensure; however, the Senate is expected to consider a licensing proposal by House Majority Whip Keith McCall that passed the House with overwhelming support. If it passes the Senate and is signed into law by Governor Ed Rendell, massage therapy would join over 200 licensed professions in the state. The proposal would implement training requirements, and most massage therapists are pleased with attempts to finally license their profession.

headline: Godshall bill backs displays of flag - Tobaks happy with proposal
abstract: The Victoria Court Condominium Association and its management agent have asked Gloria Tobak to take down her American flag because it violates the association’s bylaws governing window treatments. However, PA Representative Robert Godshall is sponsoring legislation that would guarantee all Pennsylvanians the right to fly the U.S. or PA flag inside or outside their homes, regardless of any condominium or homeowner agreements. The bill may be introduced in the House this week.

headline: Reelect Tom Ridge
abstract: Although Tom Ridge has first year as Govenor was underwhelming, over his four years in office Mr.Ridge has grown markedly.  His list of accomplishments now ranges from lower taxes and budget surpluses to state leadership in cyberspace and helping seal the shipbuilding deal with Kvaerner.   The next governor faces daunting challenges from fax inequities to urban blight.  Tom Ridge is the best bet for handling them.

headline: What better location to honor vets? - Park cemetery makes sense
abstract: U.S. Representative Jon Fox introduced a bill calling for the creation of a veterans cemetery at Valley Forge National Historical Park. While the bill appears to be politically motivated in an election year, the authors still believe it is a good proposal because it would provide a closer military burial site for families in the region. They believe Valley Forge’s rich history makes it the perfect place for a veterans cemetery, and they urge Congress and the National Park Service to seriously consider the proposal.

headline: News from the PA General Assembly
abstract: A bill passed the PA House unanimously and will move to the Senate that would give $80 million in state funding for safety initiatives in school districts. Governor Tom Ridge is expected to sign a bill which would make Hospices that provide services for the terminally ill and their families licensed by the PA Department of Health. A fun fact about PA history is also provided in the article.

headline: Parent: Core matters
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Goodling is heading the U.S. House Education and the Workforce Committee, which has visited 26 schools in the past year and heard testimony from 200 witnesses in order to assess what works and what is wasted with federal education programs. The committee’s most recent meeting was in Fairview Township at Crossroads Middle School, and two parents voiced their support for York’s Core Knowledge education program. School officials and PA Education Secretary Eugene Hickok suggested reducing the paperwork needed for obtaining federal loans.

headline: Woodcock study may become reality
abstract: An effort to determine the impact of hunting in Pennsylvania on the woodcock population of the eastern U.S. may be back on track for a start in August.  The project was shot down by members of the Game Commission when first proposed last year because of the financial condition of the agency as it awaits legislation that would increase hunting license fees.  If approved at that time it would have begun last August.

headline: Residents see red in Summit signal dispute
abstract: Summit Township and Pennsylvania Department of Transportation cannot seem to make an agreement on who should pay the annual $10,000 in maintenance fees for traffic lights on Routes 422/68/38.

headline: Hunting, fishing proposal a sign of more basic problem
abstract: There is a pending proposal to amend the PA constitution to make hunting and fishing a basic constitutional right, and the author claims this may seem harmless, but it’s part of a larger problem in which the state Legislature has often tried to tamper with the state’s constitution. The author cites several recent constitutional amendments, including the controversial amendment that allows prosecutors to ask for a trial by jury and others that limit the basic rights of the accused. He also cites the "Homestead Exemption" amendment, which allows commercial, industrial and residential real estate to be taxed at different rates, and overall, he argues constitutional amendments take at least four years to undo, and the state shouldn’t be constantly changing the constitution and manipulating away Pennsylvanians’ basic rights.

headline: GOP lawmakers seek Plan B referendum
abstract: PA Representatives Tom Stevenson, Jeff Habay, John Maher, Jane Orie and Bill Robinson have all expressed support for putting the issue of whether the state should fund new stadium projects on a referendum question to let voters decide. However, the chance of stadium-financing being approved by voters would be very low, and Robinson doesn’t believe there is enough support in the Legislature to put the question on a referendum. Governor Tom Ridge has already promised $150 million for Pittsburgh’s proposed stadiums.

headline: Towns not amused by tax reform
abstract: New legislation has been passed in Pennsylvnia that will cap the amusement park tax.

headline: GOLD DIGGERS
abstract: The photo depicts PA Representative John Pippy and Senator Tim Murphy beginning work on the mall opening project in Carnegie using a golden shovel and jackhammer.

headline: Regional Voter Turnout Tops State's
abstract: The heated race between Republican Don Sherwood and Democrat Pat Casey in the 10th District Congressional Race helped make Lycoming County’s voter turnout of 46.7 percent of registered voters significantly higher than the state average of 33 percent. Tioga, Sullivan, Union, Northumberland and Clinton Counties also had significantly higher voter turnout than the state average. Sherwood has unofficially won the election by less then 600 votes, and the article provides some quotes from voters as well as two men who sat outside a polling station in a last minute attempt to sway voters’ choices in the election.

headline: When Blood Flowed Anew at Gettysburg, The Fur Flew, Too - To Some, Rangers' Campaign To Thin Park's Deer Herd Violates Spirit of the Site
abstract: The National Park Service complained that the deer population on Gettysburg National Military Park had again grown too high, so it planned to renew its deer conservation program; however, several local residents joined with animal rights groups in filing a federal lawsuit against the Park Service. The lawsuit argues that deer hunting on the battlefield violates the National Historic Preservation Act because it has an adverse effect on the battlefield’s historical character. However, the National Advisory Council on Historic Preservation concluded the park’s integrity wouldn’t be at risk from hunting, and the National Park Service expects the federal lawsuit to be defeated, which will allow them to push ahead on their deer conservation program.

headline: Norristown State Hospital feels the heat of a heat protest
abstract: Sweltering weather yesterday brought a group of protestors to Norristown State Hospital, where, they said, patients were enduring the heat without sufficient air-conditioning.  As the mercury approached 90 degrees shortly before noon, about 20 people with the Mental Health Association of Southeastern Pennsylvania carried "Cool It or Close It" signs near the hospital gates and urged state officials to witness the conditions for themselves.

headline: Parents, Student Question The State Of Public Schools
abstract: Philadelphia Schools Superintendent David Hornbeck said that he will make an effort to pass a reasonable budget, but if the state doesn’t provide $85 million to close a deficit, he will choose shutting down the district rather than lowering educational standards. However, the PA Legislature recently passed a bill that would grant Governor Tom Ridge the power to issue a state takeover of the district if it runs out of funding by March 1999, which would also replace Hornbeck with an education chief executive officer and would leave serious questions about the future of the district’s staff. Many have accused the bill of being a political maneuver, including City Council President John Street, and parents and student have also been highly critical.

headline: Young hunters get extra shot at deer
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission has adopted precedent-setting regulations allowing property licensed junior hunters to take antlerless deer on both Saturdays of the two-week buck season, as well as during the regular doe season. The original proposal was to give junior deer hunters the entire two-week buck season to hunt antlerless deer. The general consensus among Pennsylvanian hunters was that this wasn't an acceptable plan.

headline: Restrict teen licenses
abstract: Larry Hicks talks about the proposed teenage license law change presented by state Representative Anthony DeLuca. Hicks would like to see stricter laws around teenage drivers for safety reasons.

headline: Ideas abound for spending $350M
abstract: The state could have as much as $350 million left over this year, and local residents have plenty of suggestions for how to spend it. Ideas range from victims of child abuse to roads to supporting small business.

headline: GOP pushes funding for community building
abstract: The idea that community-based organizations are closest to problems and should therefore become the focus of solutions is gaining momentum, and this approach can be illustrated by Governor Tom Ridge’s Project for Community Building, which funds programs aimed at combating community problems. The Renewal Alliance is a coalition of Republican federal legislators committed to the principle of aiding community-based organizations, and it has introduced a legislative package. According to U.S. Senator Rick Santorum, the legislation would create charitable tax credits for donations to groups that fight poverty, provide tax relief and improve education to encourage business development in urban communities and offer grants to fund school choice vouchers.

headline: Trade trends
abstract: Plains states are Sending more and more goods abroad, particularly to Asia, the destination of 56 percent of Nebraska's and 35 percent of Kansas' exports in 1996.

headline: Golfing for dollars par for local political course
abstract: Public officeholders have been using golf tournaments to raise money for their political campaigns or for charity, and Luzerne County Commissioners Frank Crossin and Tom Makowski, District Attorney Peter Paul Olszewski, Wilkes-Barre Mayor Tom McGroarty and State Representative Raphael Musto are among many local politicians to host golf tournaments to raise money. These events can raise thousands of dollars, but they also provide good networking opportunities. Many officeholders will attend tournaments for other party members, and much of the profit from tournaments come from hole sponsorships.

headline: Register to vote and focus on state candidates
abstract: Public Opnion encourages Pennsylvania resident to go out and vote, despite the Clinton scandal. The Public Opnion urges voters to look at state candidiates and vote on their issues and their record.

headline: 3rd-class cities in line for tax shift
abstract: Third-class cities such as Harrisburg may see tax increases now that the PA Legislature approved tax reform for school districts. The governor, 25 state senators, and the House are up for re-election. Chief of Staff for House Majority Leader John Perzel, Thomas McCormac II says no one wants to raise taxes before an election. Cities in need of revenue may receive grants. General Counsel for the Republican majority, Stephen MacNett, said possibilities include raising the earned-income tax or converting the occupational privilege tax to a municipal services charge.

headline: Nursing home bill deserves fast track
abstract: A bill sponsored by PA Senator Edwin Holl that would make information about the state’s nursing homes available on the Internet is expected to be voted on by a committee on March 10. There is a similar bill sponsored by PA Representative Tony DeLuca. The authors support the proposal, and they hope the state Legislature acts quickly to pass it.

headline: PHEAA Board Increases State Grant Awards
abstract: The PA Higher Education Assistance Agency will provide an additional 6,000 grants to increase the number of PA students who receive them to 148,000. These grants are based on financial need and don’t have to be repaid. The agency’s board approved changes in its awarding formula, so more students can benefit from the budget, which was signed by Governor Ridge and provides a 7% increase from last year to the agency’s grant program.

headline: A British company wants TMI The Atomic Energy Act bans foreign ownership of U.S. nuclear plants
abstract: PECO Energy Company and British Energy have proposed a joint venture to purchase Three Mile Island, but whether the deal is approved will depend largely on how it’s structured. The Atomic Energy Act of 1954 bans foreign companies from owning U.S. nuclear power plants, so in order to comply with federal regulations, PECO said it would have 51 percent of the say over key decisions pertaining to the operational safety of the plant. Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman Shirley Ann Jackson has indicted that she is open to the proposal, but even with NRC approval, the deal would have to be approved by numerous other state and federal agencies.

headline: Resurfacing looms large on PennDOT slate - To avoid jams, much work scheduled at night
abstract: Additional revenue from an increase in Pennsylvania’s vehicle registration fees and its gas tax will be put to use this year, and overall, the PA Department of Transportation plans to spend $300 million on over 135 projects in District 8, which includes 5,400 miles of highway in eight different counties. A majority of the work will be on resurfacing projects, and these projects are largely scheduled to be done at night in order to reduce the impact on motorists. The article provides a description of many of these projects, and many resurfacing projects will utilize Ralumac, which is designed to improve skid resistance and reduce accident rates.

headline: In 2 languages, Timoney makes a pledge  "You have to trust us," the police commissioner said as he was sworn in. He vowed to work for all citizens.
abstract: John Timoney was sworn into office as the Philadelphia Police Commissioner, and at the ceremony, he promised to improve the responsiveness of the department. He impressed Councilman Angel Ortiz by speaking in Spanish to address the Latino community, which makes up 75 percent of the city’s poorest and most deadly neighborhood, Fairhill. Many police officers who worked with Timoney when he served for 29 years in the New York Police Department praised his achievements, and Mayor Ed Rendell also spoke at the event.

headline: Gov. Ridge gives Expressway 'jump start'
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge held a press conference to announce that the PA Turnpike Commission will invest another $338 million for the Mon-Fayette and Southern Beltway projects, which have been stalled for years. Many people, including Ridge, believe the projects will make access to Pittsburgh much easier, and they are key ingredients for the economic future of the region. However, PA Representative David Levdansky disagrees.

headline: Traveling businesses had generous friend in Pa.
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge and representatives from 28 PA businesses went on a trade mission to Japan, Singapore and South Korea, which the authors of the editorial criticize because the state paid as much as $7,000 for some individuals to make the trip. Some of the businessmen who went claimed they needed assistance, yet they also stated that they could stand to make lucrative profits in sales to Asia. The authors suggest that in the future businessmen should be given loans that must be repaid because they believe businesses should be responsible for paying to search for new business deals, and they also feel that it’s unfair to competing businesses that weren’t given money to go on the trip.

headline: Goodling a no-show at debate
abstract: A candidate forum at the Kingsdale fire house turned into a citizen debate about why a congressional incumbent will not debate. Republican challenge Charles Grow watched in delight at the meeting as people argued with Adams-York US Representative William Goodling's spokesman, Francis Coulson, about the need for debates.

headline: Registration edge toothless?
abstract: The county apportionment committee released its proposed lines for the new county council districts, and Democrats on the committee have complained that Republicans redrew the boundaries in an obvious attempt to make it easier for their party to win elections. Republicans on the committee haven’t denied this, but citizens don’t seem too upset based on two public hearings held on the proposal. Democrats hold a 2.4-to-1 advantage over Republicans in registered voters, but the authors looked into the past three major elections and found advantages in voter registration don’t necessarily reflect how the votes will turn out.

headline: A Column from the Senate by Senator Jeffrey Piccola
abstract: The PA Revenue Department extended the application deadline for the state’s Property Tax and Rent Rebate program, which is aimed primarily at senior citizens with average annual household incomes of less than $15,000. Each year, about 300,000 senior citizens receive a total of over $85 million in rebates from the program. PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola says that anyone who meets eligibility requirements could be eligible for up to $500 in property tax or rent rebate benefits, and he strongly encourages anyone who is eligible to fill out an application.

headline: Nursing home gripes lodged at Senate hearing
abstract: Julia Lindsey says she called the state Health Department several times in late 1996 to 1997 to complain about the poor care her 75 year-old mother was receiving in a Lancaster County nursing home.  Lindsey was one of several people, including two other York Countians, who testified at the hearing convened by the Senate Democratic Policy Committee.  Representatives from the Health Department were not asked to attend the hearing, prompting Gov. Tom Ridge's office to blast the hearing as a partisan "show" designed to embarrass the administration.

headline: PHEAA provides student aid, as well as loans
abstract: Elinor Taylor, Chairman of the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) Board of Directors, is writing to criticize a previous editorial’s limited definition of the PHEEA’s role in providing student aid and loans. Taylor cites the PA State Grant Program, Institutional Assistance Grants and State Work-Study Program as evidence of PHEEA’s role in providing aid to students of higher education. Taylor claims 150,000 students will be awarded grants for a total of $249 million, Governor Ridge and the General Assembly approved substantial increases for next year and PHEEA has been working hard to lower the cost of borrowing.

headline: A Column from the Senate By Senator Jeffrey Piccola
abstract: PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola commends the PA Public Utility Commission for its decision to keep all of Dauphin County within the 717 area code, and he has introduced legislation to require all future PUC decision to be based on county lines whenever possible. Schuylkill County lost out on the decision because it was split, but Piccola argues it simply made more sense for Dauphin County to remain intact. He also believes offering telephone numbers in blocks of 1,000 rather than 10,000 would help reduce the number of unused numbers.

headline: Ridge expected to announce road
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is scheduled to visit Hazleton, where he is expected to announce that construction of the Southwest Beltway will begin in September. A contractor confirmed the state had accepted its bid for the project, and the PA Department of Transportation said it would need to acquire 35 acres for the project. The beltway, which will connect State Route 309 to Interstate 81, had originally been proposed in 1969, but funding for the project wasn’t made available until June 1996.

headline: In a shift, Rendell embraces the 'Gang of Five' police critics
abstract: The "Gang of Five," which is composed of five PA legislators, including Republicans John Perzel, John Taylor and George Kenney and Democrats Dwight Evans and Anthony Williams, was harshly criticized by Mayor Ed Rendell in the past for meddling in Philadelphia’s affairs; however, he changed course dramatically and thanked the legislators for their suggestions for fighting crime in the city. The group promised their support in Rendell’s search for a new police commissioner, and they support his proposal to get the state police to take over the jurisdiction of patrolling the Schuylkill Expressway. The group offered several suggestions to improve crime fighting efforts, including a proposal to create tent cities to incarcerate low-level offenders during warm summer months to reduce the burden on prisons.

headline: Grant in store for USX site   $2.5 million will help defray cost of plant's $8 million infrastructure
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker plan to announce a $2.5 million grant to help build an industrial park at the former Saxonburg U.S. Steel Plant this year. Butler County Commissioner William McCarrier said the money would be helpful in offsetting some of the $8 million in expected costs for the project, and the project could create a place for about 3,800 manufacturing jobs. Ridge and Schweiker are working their way through Western PA to award at least seven grants to communities in four different counties.

headline: Trouble follows new fitness club owner
abstract: In West Manchester Township, a gym owner closes business without notice to customers, leaving him with penalites in the amount of $25,000. The replacing gym faced some difficulties when opening in the same building.

headline: Goodling backs colleagues in debate nightcap
abstract: Representative Goodling defends his fellow Congressmen and women from attacks and criticizms made during a debate.

headline: Rendell favoring Street as new mayor   He said nice things about others, too
abstract: Although Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell won’t formally endorse a candidate to be his successor in next year’s mayoral election, during a recent interview, he was critical of the media and others for viewing the election in racial terms, and he shared his thoughts on all the potential candidates; though he appeared to be leaning towards current City Council President John Street as his favorite. Rendell said that of all the black Democratic candidates, John White Jr., state Representative Dwight Evans and John Street, he thought Street was the only one capable of raising enough money to campaign effectively, and Lynne Abraham, a white district attorney, could win a sizeable segment of the black vote despite criticism from some of the black community. He discussed four others who have been projected as potential Democratic candidates, and of the three Republicans, John Taylor, George Bochetto and Sam Katz, Rendell felt Katz was the only one who stood out.

headline: A surprise tax-reform vote looms
abstract: State lawmakers will vote on proposed tax reform that would allow school districts to change the way taxes are collected and provide proerty tax relief to residents.

headline: Nursing Home Workers Urged Not To Give Up - State Auditor General tells them to continue fight for better working conditions.
abstract: Over 200 nursing home workers from over 40 nursing homes throughout PA gathered in Harrisburg to learn more about the process of unionizing their co-workers. State Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. urged them to continue to fight for better working conditions, and he called for comprehensive reform throughout the state to ensure patients are taken care of properly. In addition, State Senator Allyson Schwartz was there to announce she is sponsoring a reform bill for nursing homes.

headline: Phila. Area comes up big in state's cash art awards
abstract: Philedelphia resisdents are honored and praised for claiming more than half od the PCA awards in PA. A few winner's stories are told.

headline: A rival candidate for PUC
abstract: Timothy W. Merril Jr., president of Competitive Energy Strategies Co., confirmed that he is being considered to replace PA Public Utilities Commissioner John Hanger, whose term appointment expired a month ago. Merrill declined to say more until PA Gov. Rom Ridge makes an official decision on whether to replace Hanger, a democrat. In Philadelphia, the Clean Air Council expressed support for Hanger. Hanger has been in the news lately for his involvement in rejecting Peco's attempts to create rate deals with consumer groups and PA Sen. Vincent Fumo.

headline: Ridge nominates Wentz for State Transportation Commission
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge nominated Frederic Wentz for reappointment to a six-year term on the PA Transportation Commission. The commission is chaired by state Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory, and it includes 10 appointed private citizens as well as the majority and minority chairs of the House and Senate transportation committees.

headline: In the Super Bowl of jurisprudence
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher argues his first case in the U.S. Suprememe Court, involving the case of PA Board of Probation and Parole vs. Keith M. Scott.

headline: Harrisburg mayor tells local leaders how to revitalize economy
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed spoke at the Chamber of Business and Industry of Centre County, where he made a direct comparison between Harrisburg and State College and fielded questions from State College Borough Council members. He spoke about initiatives undertaken in Harrisburg to improve the economy such as tax exempt real estate, tax abatement, the improvement of historic districts and the creation of the downtown investment district. He offered suggestions for how State College could incorporate some of these initiatives, and he said they shouldn’t wait as long to act as his city did.

headline: Uncle Sam is making investments in state
abstract: Valley News Dispatch tells readers that money invested in the federal government showed a 3% return to the states.

headline: Goodling defends his decision to impeach: He said his decision is based on the premise that no man is above the law
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Goodling gave a three minute speech before the House, defending his decision to impeach President Clinton and calling it the most difficult decision of his 25 year political career. He downplayed the negative consequences of impeachment and countered Democratic accusations of Republican partisanship by saying it would actually be better politically for Republicans to have Clinton remain in office. Goodling urged other members to send the message that nobody is above the law.

headline: Rendell takes worldly view
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, who has a close relationship with President Clinton, believes that the President’s relationship with Monica Lewinsky is a private matter, and he can understand why the President would lie to protect his family. He cites numerous Presidents in the past, as well as the current French President, who have had affairs. He also calls for a change to the independent counsel law that allows Kenneth Starr’s investigation to continue, and he hopes that America can finally move past the issue, which he claims has made the U.S. a laughingstock around the world.

headline: Allegheny County property owners face tax change - 90 percent of taxpayers would end up paying more
abstract: Allegheny County’s commissioners are considering a proposal that would reduce the discount rate from 2 percent to .5 percent for property owners who file their taxes before the April 1 deadline. County Deputy Treasurer John Weinstein and Commissioner Larry Dunn are against the proposal because 90 percent of Allegheny County’s residents pay their taxes early to receive the discount, and it would cost them an estimated $3 million next year alone; however, it could help close the county’s anticipated $9 million deficit. A Common Pleas Judge ordered a 2 percent increase in property market values, so property owners would actually see a 3.5 percent tax increase next year if the discount rate is lowered.

headline: On Capitol Hill
abstract: According to information supplied by PA Representative Rod Wilt, the state House approved legislation introduced by Representative Patrick Fleagle that would allow paramedics to honor a terminally ill patient’s do-not-resuscitate order without getting physician approval first. Under a bill sponsored by Representative Ellen Bard, PA municipalities would have a standardized local tax collector system that would help crack down on fraud. A separate bill sponsored by Representative Jim Lynch could help prevent criminals from committing fraud using electronic access devices such as credit cards, debit cards and automated teller machine cards.

headline: Philadelphia schools plan to sue state for funding
abstract: Philadelphia School Superintendant David Hornbeck claims the district plans to file a federal lawsuit against the state of PA within the next two months for failing to provide adequate funding. The district could face a shutdown by 1999 without additional funds, and Hornbeck alleges the district hasn’t received adequate funds because of racial discrimination.

headline: A Tought Nut
abstract: Beaver County Times talks about natural gas deregulation and urges Pennsylvania lawmakers to make progress on this issue.

headline: Ridge vetoes motorcycle helmet repeal bill
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge vetoed legislation passed by Congress that would have repealed the motorcylce helmet law, but notes that he would sign a bill if it included eye wear protection for motorcyle drivers.

headline: Investigation continues into shooting of Civil War re-enactor
abstract: While participating in a Civil War re-enactment on a farm near Gettysburg, Clinton Epps was shot with an actual bullet through the neck, and state police are still trying to figure out if the shooting was intentional or simply due to negligence. Fortunately, the bullet missed his major arteries, but PA Representative Lynn Herman, a re-enactor himself, said each unit has a designated safety inspector that should have inspected all guns and prevented the injury. Freedom Township Supervisor Richard Varish said the incident was unlikely to affect future re-enactments.

headline: HIGH-RISE HAZARDS    Fire officials agree that sprinklers can save lives and minimize damage. But cost has been a major roadblock to more governments enacting laws mandating their installation.
abstract: Despite some tragic fires throughout PA in buildings that didn’t have sprinkler systems, at least 30 high-rise buildings in the Lehigh Valley and surrounding areas aren’t equipped with them, and tests conducted by the National Fire Protection Association have found that sprinklers can protect property and save lives. Regulations require most newly constructed high-rise buildings to install sprinklers, and retrofitting older hotels with sprinklers has become an important objective for fire safety advocates; however, opponents claim installation can be too expensive; though there are financial incentives to installing them. A deadly fire in One Meridian Plaza encouraged attempts to pass new sprinkler requirements, and apartment complexes for the elderly have been targeted as especially important high-rise buildings that should install sprinklers.

headline: US Steel to curtail operations
abstract: US Steel Group said its steel finishing mill near Philadelphia will idle most operations for at least a month because it is running out of orders. Blaming cheap imported steel for snatching market share, US Steel said hundreds of workers at the Fairless Works will be laid off and that production volume will be reduced by 70 percent. The mill employs 850, including those in a tin mill that will continue operating.

headline: Goodling invites Barbour: Haley Barbour plans to talk about Republican successes in Congress
abstract: Former Republican National Committee chairman Haley Barbour was invited by U.S. Representative Bill Goodling to speak at a York County Republican dinner event. Barbour plans to speak about the roles of parents and government in their children’s education because of Goodling’s position as chairman of the House Economics and Educational Opportunities Committee; though Goodling cannot attend the event because he will be in Congress for a vote. Barbour agreed with House Speaker Newt Gingrich that the investigation into President Clinton should not be hurried, and he shared his thoughts on how the issue could affect the upcoming election.

headline: Reno expands probe of '98 Clinton-Gore campaign ads, names Clinton
abstract: Attorney General Janet Reno has already launched 90 day investigations into campaign financing for both Vice President Al Gore and White House official Harold Ickes, and she decided to launch another 90 day investigation into whether President Clinton coordinated Democratic issue ads to help win his reelection in 1996, which would be a violation of federal financing laws. Any of the three investigations could lead Reno to appoint a special prosecutor to further investigate questionable Democratic financing operations in the 1996 election. The Federal Election Bureau released a preliminary report that Democrats violated federal election law regarding issue advocacy laws, and some Republicans are upset that Reno has yet to name a prosecutor.

headline: Anspach: Regionalize; Zug: Smaller is better
abstract: Republican incumbent Representative Peter Zug and Democratic challenger Charlie Anspach, who are battling for the 102nd District’s seat in the PA House, attended a debate last night. Anspach called for regionalizing services as a way of cutting the costs from 2,500 municipal governments, but Zug disagreed. Zug favored saving money from the budget surplus for the state’s Rainy Day fund and said the completion of Swatara State Park is the county’s most important environmental challenge, whereas Anspach said some of the surplus could be used to give tax relief to senior citizens and saw potential population growth in Lebanon County as the most challenging environmental issue.

headline: Open-Ended
abstract: Overall, SB100, which seeks to define patients' rights, is a good bill that will make HMOs more responsive to the health needs of their members than has often been the case.  But the bill came out of the House with a large number of amendments attached to it, some of them worthy, some of them not so worthy.  One of the most significant would require insurers to provide party of coverage for mental health afflictions.

headline: PIAA czar
abstract: A state Senate committee has the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association under a microscope trying to determine its controversial decision making process, and what does the PIAA do? It thumbs its nose at the lawmakers, and, with one sweeping decision, effectually tells the Senators to do all the investigating they want. In the end, the PIAA will decide how to run its own business.

headline: A warehouse club for gas and power
abstract: DTE Edison America wants to charge households $12 a month to buy power and gas from the company at wholesale. Later this month, 3.5 million electricity customers will become eligible to choose a new power supplier. Peoples Plus is trying to position itself as an alternative energy supplier. With the deal DTE offers, some Duquesne customers could lose money. DTE admits the deal would primarily save money in households where utility bills are higher than average.

headline: Road bonus awaits smooth operators
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation will allow for contractors to earn up to a 6 percent bonus if roads are smoother than specified in the official bid. Contractors could lose money if the roads are too bumpy.

headline: Iran Einhorn again arrested in France, his lawyer says
abstract: Fugitive Ira Einhorn, is arrested for the second time in France. Because of a new Pennsylvania law, France may consider extriditing him.

headline: House panel adds funds for production of Osprey
abstract: A key House panel has added nearly $100 million to White House funding for projects built by Boeing Co, a significant boost to the company, but one that is far from a done deal in the months-long legislative process. The House National Security Committee approved funding for eight V-22 Ospreys, which are built at the Ridley Township plant and by another contractor in Texas. If approved the increase would bring V-22 funding to more than $1 billion.

headline: Vicksburg wagers future on casinos
abstract: Tax revenue hasn't paid off for Mississippi River town. Four years ago Mississippi legalized slot machines to make more money off tourists. People are losing money they can't afford and leaving children out of the mix. They are ruining the historical significance of the area around them.

headline: Goodling opens campaign office in Gettysburg
abstract: U.S. Representative William Goodling nearly lost to Republican primary challenger Charles Gerow two years ago, and he will face him again this year, which has led Goodling to establish new campaign offices and Gettysburg and Cumberland Valley in hopes of generating higher voter turnout and support this year. Some Republicans in the district have criticized Goodling for not being conservative enough and for not pushing for enough reform, accusations that he adamantly denies. He said his role as the chairman of the House Education and Workforce Committee will allow him to exert considerable influence to enact reform, and he has refused to debate Gerow.

headline: RENOVATED
abstract: The photo depicts PA Representatives Paul Clymer and Sheila Miller and state Secretary of General Services Gary Crowell standing in front of the Commonwealth statue. The statue of a robed woman holding a staff was returned to the state Capitol after undergoing a nine-month restoration in Connecticut.

headline: Anti-windfall bill approved, sent to Ridge
abstract: Legislation aimed at Allegheny County, to stop windfall benefits from property reassessment and to expand property tax relief, has been passed by both the House and the Senate. The bill currently awaits approval by Govenor Tom Ridge.

headline: Osteoporosis testing fails to win council's backing
abstract: There's not enough evidence that widespread testing for loss of bone mass would improve the quality of life for women who have osteoporosis or significantly lower costs for its treatment, says a report released yesterday by the Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council.  The council concluded that it couldn't support legislation pending in the state Senate to require health insurers in Pennsylvania to include osteoporosis testing and treatment as part of basic coverage.

headline: PIAA Finances
abstract: Summary of PIAA finances for the past two years.

headline: Allegheny has advantage in 'power play' - Utility's low rates give it leg up as customers choose suppliers
abstract: Reverend Art Nelson and 1.8 million other electric customers in PA received letters from the PA Public Utility Commission notifying them that they were enrolled in the PA Electric Choice Program, which was made possible by the state’s effort to deregulate portions of the power industry. However, Nelson has found that his current supplier, Allegheny Power, still provides the lowest energy prices, and he criticized the PUC for not posting prices for consumers. According to former PUC Commissioner John Hanger, Allegheny Power’s low energy prices and a recent settlement that Allegheny’s West Penn Power unit received from the PUC make the company well suited for the competitive energy market, and it could be a long time before any competitor can beat or match their prices.

headline: Road improvements planned
abstract: Penn Township Commissioner James Lindsay hopes that everyone present at the recent meeting to discuss much-needed improvements on Harrison City-Export Road, Route 130 and the intersection where the two converge, follows through. They include Westmoreland County officials, US Rep. Ron Klink, PA Sen. Allen Kukovich and PA Rep. Jim Casorio. Officials from the PA Department of Transportation did not show up. County Commissioner Tom Bayla was present. Kukovich praised the township for passing an impact fee ordinance.

headline: Legislature considers measures to control sports agents
abstract: Agent Jeff Nalley violated the law by purchasing a suit for former Penn State football player Curtis Enis before his eligibility ran out, and the PA Legislature is trying to pass a law to punish agents who break the law. Senator J. Doyle Corman expects a bill to pass unanimously that would require agents to register with the State Athletic Commission to speak with an athlete after their eligibility is up. Agents who violate the law, whether they register or not, could be fined up to $5,000 for every infraction.

headline: House support not yet in the ballpark
abstract: Lobbyists for public funding of sports stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh failed to convince lawmakers to vote yesterday on raising the state debt ceiling to help fund the projects. However, the issue remains on the table until the Legislature ends its session on November 30th. A spokesman for House Maj. Leader John Perzel however, says the votes are just not there to approve the measure. Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell proposes a regional sports lottery or hike in sales taxes to provide additional funding. PA Gov. Ridge supports raising the debt ceiling.

headline: Wall Street Reaction
abstract: Since Dec. 12 just before it received the first bid, Luken's stock has gained 74 percent.

headline: Goodling to run for 1 more term: Area congressman plans focused race compared to '96
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Goodling will seek his final term and vowed to run his campaign differently than in 1996, when he nearly lost the primary to Charles Gerow. He decided that this will be his last term because his eligibility to chair the House Education and the Workforce Committee will expire after his term. He needs to raise campaign funds and is trying to displace allegations from Gerow that he is not conservative enough.

headline: Rep. Barley smiling about GOP efforts
abstract: Representative John Barley is is excited about the strategy of the GOP after a meeting with top House Republicans.

headline: Appeals court orders reassessment
abstract: Erie counted residents are getting a recalculated tax bill after the appeals court ruled that the real estate must be reassessed.

headline: Pa. ahead of pack on HMO reform
abstract: Federal lawmakers are continuing to debate plans to reform managed care plans, but PA has already passed a managed care law that applies to approximately 5 million Pennsylvanians. Some key provisions of the law include guaranteed access to emergency care without prior authorization, access for women to gynecological and obstetrical coverage without prior approval and a requirement for insurers to give patients decisions in a timely manner. The rest of the article provides some statistics on the growing discontentment over HMOs, the opinions of a number of different people and a more detailed explanation of the law which was signed into effect by Governor Tom Ridge on June 17.

headline: PIAA Finances
abstract: The PIAA Statement of Activity with revenue and expenses for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1997.

headline: Clearfield Chamber hears... What to expect from electric choice
abstract: Clearfield Chambers held a meeting with GPU Energy to help residents unbderstand the new electric choice program enacted by the state.

headline: Road Overkill
abstract: Editors believe Republicans are no different than Democrats when it comes to bringing home the pork for their constituents. This time, it is in the form of a $200-plus-billion transportation bill. Editors blame it on the fact that is an election year. Editors do not believe the spending pattern is consistent with Republican promises of reform. Stephen Moore of the Cato Institute called the bill a betrayal of conservative principals.

headline: It's time for some peace in war on booze
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge grants $560,000 to wage war on underage drinking, especially on PA campuses. The social war is critized for not being the most effective method to curb underage drinking.

headline: HUD grant will bring jobs to city
abstract: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development has granted a $40 million loan to Philadelphia that will create over 1,000 new jobs and redevelop the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, which closed in 1995. Kvaerner Philadelphia Shipyard Incorporated now has all of its $242 million in financing in order, and Mayor Ed Rendell cited a study that estimates the project could eventually create 13,500 jobs for the city. Housing and Urban Development Secretary said the grant is part of efforts to bring the benefits of the surging national economy to cities, and U.S. Representative Chaka Fattah, whose district encompasses Philadelphia, praised the grant for helping the city further integrate into the global economy.

headline: Weighing odds of slots in Pa.
abstract: If the state's tavern and restaurant operators get their way, patrons eventually will be able to play a hand or two of video poker while enjoying their favorite brew.  But local representatives of the two groups, who acknowledge talking with each other about the gambling issue, probably will pursue legislative approvals on their own.  Representatives of the Washington-Greene -Fayette Licensed Beverage Association -- the local arm of the Pennsylvania Licensed Beverage Association -- said recently they are continuing a 15-year campaign to legalize video poker machines.

headline: GOP behind before race even begins
abstract: Washington County Republicans have not yet found a candidate for the 20th Congressional District race. There are several additional positions being unchalleneged by Republican candidates.

headline: Rep. Blackwell opens re-election campaign
abstract: Democratic State Representative Lucien Blackwell, now running against state Senator Chaka Fattah, announced he was running for relection, opened several campaign headquarters, and attended campaign events.

headline: Apportioning responsibility
abstract: Allegheny County is rerapporting their districts as required by the new home rule charter.  The struggle between safe and competative districts, data used, and projections are posing serious problems to the redistricting efforts.

headline: Pa. is overwhelmed by surge in diabetes
abstract: Nearly one of every 11 Pennsylvania has diabetes.  That's one of the highest rates in the nation and a level that some have called epidemic proportions.  With its large elderly population, Pennsylvania is a veritable Rust Belt of diabetes.

headline: PIAA Probe Centers on Remittals
abstract: Members of a state high school athletics organization were reimbursed for a conference they attended in Colorado as if they drove from Harrisburg to Denver, though records show only three members arrived by car. They unanimously approved a system allowing themselves to use the IRS standard reimbursement for business use of a personal vehicle. The system is used even when executives and board members arrive by less expensive means of transportation.

headline: Competition must start with fairness
abstract: The authors of the editorial believe the PA Public Utility Commission, Governor Tom Ridge and the state Legislature have called for fairness in deregulating the energy market to provide more competition and cheaper energy rates for customers; however, they argue the PUC’s recent awarding of only $2.86 billion in stranded costs to the PA Power and Light Corporation is unfair. Stranded costs are debts incurred by electric companies by investing in power plants and other areas, and PP&L had asked to collect $4 billion. The authors believe the PUC’s decision was unfair because the Philadelphia Electric Company was awarded 70 percent of their stranded costs, while PP&L was only awarded 66 percent of theirs.

headline: Road repairs rolling into region
abstract: A 7 miles improvement project on I-81 in South Newton, Penn and Dickinson townships will cause an increased gas tax and construction delays on the interstate.

headline: Jay Smith, suing investigators, cites death row hardships
abstract: Jay Smith, former death row inmate, is suing State Police Officer for misconduct during the trial that originally landed Smith in prision for murder.

headline: Hustle begins for GOP 2000 convention
abstract: Some television production companies and members of the Republican National Committee’s site selection committee have already begun calling for hotel reservations in Philadelphia for the Republican National Convention, even though the convention is still 632 days away. Several key decisions still need to be made, including whether the event will be held in the First Union Center or the Convention Center, and Philadelphia 2000 has been flooded with requests from people looking for work as part of the massive project. The city proposed a $35 million public and private financing package when submitting its bid to be considered; however, a final contract detailing who pays for what must be negotiated and be approved by the Republican National Committee by January.

headline: Weighing odds of slots in Pa.
abstract: If the state's tavern and restaurant operators get their way, patrons will eventually be able to play a hand of video poker while enjoying their favorite brew. Representatives from the Washington-Greene-Fayette Licensed Beverage Association, the local arm of the Pennsylvania Licensed Beverage Association, said recently that they are continuing a 15-year campaign to legalize video poker machines. According to state Rep. Leo Trich Jr., it's probably only a matter of time until some form of gambling legislation dealing with slots machines is passed.

headline: GOP chair won't give up position
abstract: Luzerne County Commissioner Joseph Jones responded to a letter written by Sixth District Republican Party chairman Paul Defabo that called for Jones to resign from his position as chairman of the Luzerne County Republican Party. Defabo criticized Jones for not representing the best interests of the party because he didn’t support several Republican candidates openly as a county commissioner, which Jones denied. Jones attacked Defabo for supporting the previous Republican minority commissioner, who he claimed voted with the Democratic majority 99.3 percent of the time, and he vowed to do what’s best for the county regardless of partisanship.

headline: Rep. Guy Travaglio to seek third term
abstract: State Representative Guy Travaglio will seek re-election to his 11th District seat in the PA House. The two-term lawmaker will run for the Democratic nomination in the May primary. Some of his favorite achievements are detailed.

headline: Area Lawmakers Say Tax-Reform Bill Offers No Relief
abstract: Several of Lycoming County’s representatives in the PA Legislature voted against the controversial tax-reform legislation, and others reluctantly voted in favor of it; though they don’t think it does nearly enough to provide tax relief to homeowners or offer enough taxing options to local taxing entities. Representatives Brett Feese and Thomas Dempsey don’t think the legislation will help any of the school districts in their legislative districts, and they are outraged over a provision that provided tax breaks only to taxpayers in southeast PA. Senator Roger Madigan didn’t think the bill would be much of an improvement, but he still voted for it because "something is better than nothing," and while Feese believes the issue is dead, Dempsey is hopeful the Legislature will revisit the issue.

headline: Pa. school kids to get (another) shot in the arm
abstract: Millions of Pennsylvania school students will soon be required to stick out their arms to receive a second measles vaccination.  Health officials say the new vaccine requirement will help eradicate the disease by catching the small percentage of children who didn’t develop immunity with their first shot.  However, it will also boost to 12 the number of multi-dose vaccines mandated for school children and some people wonder: is this really necessary?

headline: PIAA renews director's contract
abstract: In the midst of a Senate probe, the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association board of control approved a five-year contract of $541,380 for Executive Director Brad Cashman, the Pittsburgh Tribune Review has learned. The PIAA board on April 3 approved the contract at $100,256 per year with 4-percent annual increases through 2003. The first year of the contract extension representation represented about a 5-percent raised for Cashman.

headline: Consumers get a break in their electricity bills
abstract: Standard-Speaker talks about the electric dereuglation in Pennsylvania and how it is saving consumers money on their electric bill. Standard-Speaker urges consumers to shop around companies for the best prices.

headline: Road safety dilemma
abstract: Moreland Health and Safety Committee is having trouble deciding what to do with Moreland, which has been the site of several deadly car accidents. Senator Greenleaf's proposed bill for harsher penalities for dangerous drivers is supported by the Intelligener Record as a possiblre solution.

headline: Judge Delays Lewinsky Deposition   Postponement Comes as Starr Subpoenas Other White House Aids
abstract: A U.S. District Judge postponed the deposition of Monica Lewinski, who had been scheduled to testify in the Paula Jones sexual harassment case against President Clinton this morning, in what would have Lewinski’s first public appearance since being linked romantically to Clinton. Lewinski first denied having a sexual relationship with Clinton; however, independent counsel Kenneth Starr obtained recordings made by Linda Tripp in which Lewinski not only admits to having a sexual relationship with Clinton, but says Clinton and long term friend Vernon Jordan both asked her to cover it up, which Jordan adamantly denies. Lewinski’s lawyer is seeking a plea deal in return for Lewinski’s cooperation, and Starr has filed numerous subpoenas and is trying to obtain White House visitor logs.

headline: Inaction in House stalls stadium bill
abstract: The PA Senate approved Governor Tom Ridge’s proposed bill to raise the state’s debt limit to help fund one-third of the costs of stadium projects in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia; however, the House’s Democratic and Republican leaders have failed to generate enough support for the bill, and if lobbying efforts by Ridge and Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell fail to deliver the necessary votes quickly, the proposal will have to reintroduced next year. Pittsburgh already has its share of financing in order, whereas Rendell is still considering Philadelphia’s money raising options, but ultimately, many legislators are hesitant to use taxpayers’ dollars to fund stadiums for multimillionaires. State Senator Vince Fumo voted against the bill because he feared Democrats wouldn’t get their fare share of contracts for the construction of the Philadelphia stadiums, but after being assured by Ridge’s aides that this would not happen, he contacted his colleagues in the House to support the bill.

headline: Weirton, USW call for steel import quotas
abstract: Steel producers and union leaders warned that the industry would continue to lay off workers and scale back plans to modernize unless the federal government intervenes to reduce the amount of Japanese, Russian and South Korean steel coming into the US. During a hearing of the Senate Steel Caucus chaired by Senator Arlen Specter, the chief executive officers of Bethlehem Steel and Weirton Steel painted a grim future for the US steel industry. They said declines in the steel industry profits, sharp reductions in production, and layoffs can largely be blamed on the stunning increase of steel imports during the past year.

headline: GOP governors' uncertain trumpets
abstract: The author of the article disputes the claim from Republican leaders that governors are the model for winning the upcoming 2000 presidential election. Although Republican governors did very well in the past elections, the author attributes many of the victories to incumbents riding a wave of strong economic prosperity into the office, and he also states that Governor Bush’s victory in Texas didn’t translate to pro-Republican votes in lower offices. Overall, the author believes that governors went against their Republican principles by spending heavily in good economic times, and their popularity will decline as soon as the economy stops booming.

headline: Rep. Reber won't seek re-election
abstract: PA Representative Robert Reber Jr. will not seek a tenth term, which will leave the race for the 146th District seat wide open to both parties. County Republican Chairman Frank Bartle was a little surprised and disappointed but vowed to search for viable candidates to replace him. Reber issued a written statement to explain his decision, claiming he wants to spend more time at his law firm and increase his involvement in sports organizations.

headline: Assume Nothing: Home-rule backers must sell their plan
abstract: The proposed home rule charter for Allegheny County must continue to be talked about or voters will lose interest and stop backing the charter.

headline: Pa. Senate plans hearings on hospital mergers
abstract: Spurred by the collapse of the Allegheny health system, the state Senate is planning September hearings to consider legislation that would strengthen the attorney general's authority to regulate the mergers of hospitals and other charities.  Lawmakers from both parties say there is a strong sentiment in favor of passing a law  before the 1997-98 legislative session ends in December.

headline: PIAA timing debated
abstract: After months of controversy the PIAA's State Board of Control has launched its own inquiry into allegations of unfairness and fiscal mismanagement. While he is heartened, the chairman of a Senate committee investigating the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association Control should hold its horses. The Senate is taking steps in the right direction by investigating the allegations of abuse of funds.

headline: Consumers will have power to think green - Buyers may opt for renewable electric sources
abstract: Pennsylvania’s Electric Choice program will be phased in starting January 1, and it will first give 33 percent of all electricity customers the option of choosing their electricity suppliers. According to the PA Department of Environmental Protection, about a third of the pollution that causes acid rain and smog comes from coal-powered plants; however, the Clean Air Council is hopeful that Pennsylvanians will use their new ability to choose alternative energy sources which receive the Green E certificate for being environmentally friendly. It’s possible there won’t be enough alternative energy sources to satisfy all Pennsylvanians’ desire to switch to clean energy, and the article provides a list of several electric generation suppliers certified by the PA Public Utility Commission.

headline: Road Stresses
abstract: Intelligencer Journal is hoping that the wish list of tranpsortation porjects that Lancaster County submitted to the State Trasportation Commission will be funded. The Intelligencer Journal is worried, though, about where the money will come from.
