headline: Judge finds order in new court
abstract: Judge Correale Stevens, who lives in Hazleton, served for nearly seven years as a Luzerne County Court of Common Pleas judge, but he was elected to serve as a judge for the PA Superior Court. As a Superior Court judge, he must review appeals ranging from traffic violations to murder cases and then determine the accuracy of rulings made by trial judges. Additionally, he listens to oral arguments in Superior Court locations throughout the state, and while these tasks are important, he said there are  a number of smaller details that he is and his staff of six are also responsible for which are important.

headline: Interim financing secured for new stadiums
abstract: PA Gov. Tom Ridge and Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy secured interim funding for the construction of new stadiums for the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Pittsburgh Pirates. The $18.5 million will keep the projects alive until the Legislature can revote in January on raising the state's debt ceiling. Pirates owner Kevin McClatchy had threatened to halt construction unless the interim funding came through. Without Legislative approval, Ridge could not release $80 million in public funding needed to complete the projects. The interim funding will be used to relocate seniors whose residence is Three Rivers Plaza, which will be torn down for construction.

headline: Whitman Focuses on Taxes And Insurance Premiums
abstract: New Jersey Governor Christine Whitman gave her first major speech since narrowly winning reelection last fall, and in her annual address to the state Legislature, she promised to address the state’s property tax and auto insurance rates, which are the highest in the country. She called for a statewide referendum to determine if voters want New Jersey to consolidate and merge some of its schools in order to reduce property taxes, and she drew a loud response when referring to a court battle with New York State over Ellis Island. In addition, she proposed major changes to the state’s Civil Service system, and this term, it appears Whitman may have to fight harder to win Republicans’ votes.

headline: GOP leaders say crisis will work in their favor
abstract: GOP members hope to capitalize on the President Clinton-Monica Lewinsky scandal in the upcoming election. PA Republican Committee Chairman Alan Novak said people will recognize the GOP as a party with morals and character. PA House GOP Leader John Perzel is convinced the scandal will be favorable for PA Republicans. Republican congressional candidate Mike Turzai is using the issue to attempt to unseat US Rep. Ron Klink.

headline: Rep. Ross announces UST guidelines
abstract: PA Representative Chris Ross announced that program guidelines and applications are now available for the Underground Storage Tank Upgrade Loan Program, which is administered through the state Department of Community and Economic Development to help owners of underground storage tanks upgrade their systems to comply with federal Environmental Protection Agency requirements. The new requirements will go into effect on December 22, and the rest of the article provides some specifics about the program, what exactly loans can be used for and contact information.

headline: Authority can condemn property
abstract: Maryland & Pennsylvania Railroad Preservation Authority, according to a court ruliong, now has the power to legally condemn parcels of land. This is an important case of eminent domain.

headline: Patient battles HMO for his life
abstract: James Holmes has liver disease and was set to have a liver transplant that would save his life; however, doctors discovered that he has a rare condition known as secondary pulmonary hypertension, which would cause him to die while under anesthesia. Holmes required an expensive medicine known as Flolan to relieve his hypertension and allow him to receive the transplant, but his health maintenance organization, Security Blue, told him that they would not cover the medicine because they only cover the cost for those with primary pulmonary hypertension. Holmes appealed the case three times but kept hitting dead ends, but fortunately, due to information that was sent by Dr. Srinivas Murali about Flolan’s effectiveness, the medicine will be covered.

headline: PIAA's practices under scrutiny: State Senate to open probe into state sports agency
abstract: PA Senator James Rhoades will chair a special committee which will investigate the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association (PIAA) and could possibly take away the PIAA’s autonomy by placing the independent agency under the state Department of Education. The decision to move the state football championship game from Altoona to Hershey made Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer especially angry, and the PIAA’s decision to grant Berwick football player Gus Felder eligibility to play and help his team win the Class AAAA state championship has also generated controversy. PIAA Director Bradley Cashman refused to be interviewed until after the hearings are finished, and the PA School Boards Association executive director defended the actions of the PIAA.

headline: Date set for water rate mediation session
abstract: The PA Public Utilities Commission set a date for its mediation session over the proposed 18.7 percent rate increase that the Susquehanna Division of Consumers PA Water Company requested to offset increased operated costs and earn a fair share on investments. If the three parties involved in the mediation session agree to terms, the case will not have to go before one of the commission’s judges. PA Representative Scot Chadwick and Senator Roger Madigan have both expressed opposition to such a large rate increase.

headline: Road-kill rage   Contractor hired to remove deer from highways here cries foul as PennDOT tries to save money
abstract: Each year, thousands of deer are struck and killed on roads throughout PA, and based on a recent agreement, the PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT) is responsible for picking up dead carcasses on all major highways, whereas the state Game Commission handles the responsibilities on all other roads. PennDOT has hired private contractors to remove many of the deer; however, Marie Blimline, who was hired by PennDOT for deer removal in Berks and Lancaster Counties, has criticized Lancaster’s PennDOT office for not calling her enough and for often leaving rotting carcasses on roads for weeks at a time. State Senator Michael O’Pake questioned PennDOT, but the head of the Lancaster Office disputed some of Blimline’s accusations, claiming he relied heavily on his own workers to clean up deer, which he said saves money.

headline: Judge sees disheartening results of breakdown of the black family
abstract: The disproportionate minority crime rate can be attributed to poverty and high crime neighborrhoods. It is apparent that some act be taken to effectively reduce the disparity.

headline: Kanjorski: Don't let old lodge languish
abstract: Bloomsburg town officials are considering buying the Moose lodge to prevent another incident like the Woolworth building, which was vacant for almost a decade after closing and just recently opened as Dollar General. U.S. Representative Paul Kanjorski toured the Moose lodge, and he said the building could be attractive for high technology companies looking to expand or relocate. The Moose club, which wants to relocate to a smaller building, was asking for $400,000 for the building, but state and federal funds could become available towards the purchase and renovation of the building.

headline: 'Buffalo Soldier Day' To Be Recognized In Philadelphia
abstract: The PA House unanimously passed a resolution sponsored by Representatives Rosita Youngblood, Dennis O’Brien and Louise Bishop that will designate February 20, 1998 as Buffalo Soldier Day in PA. Youngblood said the measure is intended to honor the thousands of African American soldiers who’ve fought and died in wars throughout the nation’s history. For years, black soldiers didn’t receive recognition for their service, and it took seventy years following World War I to award the first Congressional Medal of Honor to a black serviceman.

headline: GOP likely to retain control of House
abstract: After the election, Democratcs knew that the Republicans were going to regain control of the state House of Representatives.

headline: Rep. visits Merck
abstract: Representative Paul Kanjorski visits Merck and Co. to talk about job creation. His congressional opponent is also focusing on creating jobs.

headline: Belfanti derides tax reform - Measure not true change, rep charges
abstract: The PA Legislature passed a bill that would allow school districts to reduce property taxes and eliminate nuisance taxes in return for raising the local earned income tax; however, state Representative Robert Belfanti expressed his opposition to the bill, claiming it will offer very little property tax relief. He criticized Republicans for pushing the bill through in secrecy and for using procedural votes to prevent two Democrats from adding two meaningful amendments to the bill. Representative John Gordnor was also critical of Republicans for keeping many legislators in the dark over the bill’s contents, and he too voted against it.

headline: Patients' bill of rights proposed
abstract: As health maintenance organizations and other managed-care plans have proliferated, lawmakers lately have been reacting to a public concern about their impact on patient services.  Two bills pending in the Legislature aim to do in Pennsylvania what President Clinton has endorsed on a national level: create a "patients' bill of rights" to assure that cost cutting doesn't compromise care. Gov. Ridge added his voice this week, strongly urging the General Assembly to pass legislation this year affording similar consumer protection - and spelling out what he hopes to see in such a law.

headline: Pitts' 'Dollars to the Classroom' bill OK'd
abstract: The House of Representatives passed U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts' proposal, which would end 31 federal education programs and instead send grants totaling $14.3 billion over five years directly to the states to use at their discretion. Critics of the bill believe it will result in less educational funding, which Pitts denies, but it will face challenges in the Senate and a likely veto from President Clinton if it does pass the Senate. According to one study, PA would receive over $40 million more in educational funding, and Lancaster and Chester County schools would benefit significantly.

headline: DQE Calls Off Its Planned Acquisition By Allegheny Energy, Citing Regulators
abstract: The parent of Duquesne Light Company, DQE, announced it was calling off an agreement to be taken over by Allegheny Energy Incorporated because of the decision made by the PA Public Utility Commission to disallow stranded costs.

headline: Roadwork takes a right turn
abstract: Centre Daily Times talks about the 'agility plan' and thinks that the new Pennsylvania Department of Transportation plan might ctually make sense of the state's highways and get improvements done.

headline: Key Gun-Control Deadlines
abstract: A list of gun-control deadlines including July 1 when police begin checking purchasers of rifles and shotguns for criminal pasts. Would be purchasers would be approved or rejected immediately in a computerized instant-check system.

headline: KOZ and effect
abstract: Tribune-Review talks about the Keystone Opporunity Zones and how its passage is useful, although more can be done.

headline: House-passed bills will fund area projects
abstract: The US House of Representatives passed compromise appropriation bills funding Defense and Army Corps of Engineers programs for 1999 as including the Youghiogheny Reservoir and defense contractor in Windber. US Representative John Murtha said the conference reports represent a compromise between the different House and Senate bills passed earlier.

headline: GOP losses blamed on leadership
abstract: Former PA Representative Marty Laub blamed the Republican leadership’s handling of the impeachment situation for why his cousin, U.S. Representative Jon Fox, lost the past election to Montgomery County Commissioner Joseph Hoeffel. David Nasatir has been mentioned as a possible replacement for Hoeffel, but he’s drawn criticism for only moving to the county in 1996. Wendell Young IV, who lost a race against state Representative Joseph Gladeck, could have a good chance of being nominated for the position due to his union support.

headline: Representative Fairchild outlines concerns
abstract: A task force is voting on four proposals relating to the transition of the Laurelton Center; however, PA Representative Russell Fairchild wrote a letter to Governor Rendell outlining some other concerns that he hopes are kept in mind. These concerns are briefly described in the article.

headline: Bensalem seniors wants tax breaks
abstract: Bensalem Senior Citizens Association met to discuss the new Homestead Act and ways to reduce property tax for seniors.

headline: Patients' rights idea gains legislative support
abstract: Five years ago, when Sen. Allen Kukovivh first proposed a consumers' "bill of rights" for those enrolled in health maintenance organizations, his ideal fell on deaf ears.  Kukovich, D-Manor, was then in the House.  His Republican colleagues there dismissed his HMO proposal as little more than a ploy to replace private health insurance with a government-run, taxpayer-funded system.

headline: Pitts helps organize exhibit of president's stamp design
abstract: U.S. Representative Joe Pitts is a guest curator for the "Mail to the Chief" exhibit in the postal museum branch of the Smithsonian Institute. The exhibit includes eight stamps designed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt as well as some notes and concepts he had written for then Postmaster James Farley. Pitts, a stamp collector since he was 8 years old, drafted the text accompanying the exhibit and worked with the museum’s staff on its layout.

headline: Duquesne Light to sell electricity to area buyers
abstract: Duquesen Light Co. announces that it will sell 600 megawatts of electricity to suppplies looking to enegage in busines within the coverage area.

headline: Route 322 project gets $45M from Pa.
abstract: $45 million has been awarded by the state Legislature for safety improvement on Route 322.

headline: Lawmaker: Area isn't using available crime-fighting cash
abstract: New laws and grant programs have been passed by the state to help combat juvenile crime, but Columbia and Montour counties are not taking advantage of all of them. The money is out there for policing programs, school-based probation programs, and for teen court peer jury programs just to name a few. Some of the funding is only available for a short time, so it must be taken advantage of now.

headline: Lawmakers get input on making Berks count
abstract: Berks County’s state legislators met with local officials to discuss how to further the interests of the county in the PA Legislature. Senator Michael O’Pake told the group that a $3.9 million project to replace Felix Dam had been added to the capital budget, but O’Pake and Representatives David Argall and Samuel Rohrer explained that only the governor controls which projects are selected from the budget for funding. Representative Thomas Caltagirone said he was able to add a $10 million project to build a law-enforcement training center to the capital budget, and Senator James Gerlach gave an outline of his proposal to improve local land-use plans.

headline: In wake of controversy, area vets drop support of Clinton
abstract: The Southcentral Chapter of the Veterans of the Battle of Bulge, a local group of World War II veterans, rescinded its controversial resolution strongly supporting President Clinton. Several members dropped out of the group because of the original resolution, and many complained that politics should be left out of veterans organizations, while others said the resolution was improperly voted on and didn’t reflect the opinion of the group as a whole. The new resolution was passed without opposition, yet some members were not happy about it.

headline: GOP maintains narrow control of state House
abstract: After the recent election, Republicans in Pennsylvania held on to 103 Congressional House seats.

headline: Republican apologizes for campaign tactics
abstract: Republican Mike Turzai, who is challenging incumbent U.S. Representative Ron Klink, apologized for hiring a helicopter to shoot footage of Klink’s home and for having campaign workers confront Klink and an aide with a video camera. Turzai wanted the footage of his opponent’s home to show he built an expensive home since being elected; however, Klink said the helicopter terrorized his family. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette had called for an apology, and Klink enjoys advantages in fundraising and registration.

headline: Biggest tax bite yet to come
abstract: After the new real estate reassessments, residents will see a great increase in their property tax bills.

headline: TIFs can be terrific
abstract: Tax increment financing can help Allegheny County, PA in numerous ways. TIF guidelines, processes, and benefits are outlined.

headline: Patient's rights top House agenda
abstract: Legislation passed the Senate that would establish a patient bill of rights; however, the House has drafted over 48 changes to the bill, which could delay it from being considered for a substantial amount of time. The Senate’s version would establish a grievance procedure for those who feel they were unfairly denied care, an assurance that emergency medical services would be covered without prior approval, as well as services to improve care for women. Some of the House’s proposed changes are discussed, and the Senate will also consider expanding a program for children’s health insurance.

headline: 'Pledge Missing at VV'
abstract: School officials at Valley View School District were surprised after a parent asked why her two children’s classes weren’t reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. School Board President Robert Strony said that officials would look into the issue, but it doesn’t appear that it has been omitted for personal or legal reasons. Strony also said the board has yet to finalize a budget for the upcoming school year, but he anticipates future surpluses in the state budget, which could make it easier to not have to raise taxes

headline: Duquesne pulling plug on electricity generation - Company to sell plants but still distribute power
abstract: Duquesne Light Company submitted a proposal to the PA Public Utility Commission to abandon its plan to be taken over by Allegheny Energy Incorporated, and instead, it wants to sell off its power plants to focus on distributing power obtained from other electricity providers. An advocacy group has opposed the merger, but Allegheny Energy plans to take Duquesne Light to court to enforce the conditions of the merger, even though it could potentially purchase the power plants from Duquesne Light in the future. Problems arose from the deal because Allegheny Energy wanted to remain an integrated power utility, whereas Duquesne Light favored selling off its plants, and another rift occurred due to the issue of stranded costs, which are a power company’s investments in power plants and other equipment that they won’t be able to recover in a deregulated electrical market.

headline: Routes 422/68 crossing to get signals, lanes
abstract: Plans have been made to replace the danegrous areas on Routes 422, 68, and 38 with new safer designs.

headline: Lawmakers looking for ways to reduce prison costs
abstract: PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee, and he believes that PA could punish non-violent offenders in state prison more cheaply by making them work, putting them under electronic monitoring or placing them in halfway houses. Greenleaf is searching for ways to reduce the average $24,546 a year that is spent on inmates in state prisons, but Corrections Commissioner Martin Horn testified that he fears inmates could take advantage of opportunities with less supervision to escape. The prison population is expected to drop slightly next year due partially to new treatment options which are being used; though state prisons will remain largely overcrowded.

headline: Main Street program gets boost from grant to beautify Hatboro
abstract: PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf announced that the Department of Community and Economic Development had awarded the Borough of Hatboro a $210,000 grant. About $170,000 of the grant will be put towards a project to install Victorian-style street lighting in the central business district; however, the project was originally expected to cost $800,000, but recent cost estimates have risen to $1.1 million. Main Street Hatboro’s manager, Ruth Bernstein, will try to make up $238,000 from a federal loan as well as fundraising efforts, but she could be forced to scale back the project if these efforts fail.

headline: Missile defense thwarted in Senate
abstract: The U.S. Senate narrowly defeated a bill calling for the deployment of a national missile defense system, which Republicans hoped would pass in light of a congressional report warning of the dangers of relying on America’s intelligence agencies and recent missile tests by Pakistan, Iran and North Korea. However, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, sent a letter opposing the policy, and all but four of the Democrats voted against the defense system, fearing it would end all chances of establishing a strategic arms agreement with Russia. President Clinton is also against the defense system because it would violate the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with the former Soviet Union, but Republicans believe Democrats have put the nation’s security at risk, and they hope they are held accountable in the upcoming elections.

headline: GOP needs Black votes to keep majority
abstract: After losing five seats in the House to Democrats in last week’s election, the Republican Party was told by many strategists that it needed to change its image and develop a new message if it wants to retain its control over Congress in 2000. According to Linda Divall, Republicans must begin appealing to Blacks, Hispanics, Asians and women, while it must also find ways to mix traditional Republican values with solutions to problems in health care, education and other important areas. House Speaker Newt Gingrich announced his resignation from Congress after the elections, so new party leadership is needed, and Divall cited Texas, where Republican Governor George Bush was reelected easily, as an example that not all is wrong with the party.

headline: Republican enters race for House
abstract: A Hanover Township Republican announced he'll run for the 135th House District seat in the state Legislature. So far, Mark S. Mitman joins Northhampton County Council President Wayne Grube, a Democrat, in the race for the seat being vacated by Lisa Boscola.

headline: Bill to prevent Allegheny County tax windfalls OK'd
abstract: The PA Legislature approved a bill sponsored by state Senator Melissa Hart, and it awaits Governor Tom Ridge’s signature. The bill would protect Allegheny County residents against dramatic property tax increases due to property reassessments, and it would also change eligibility requirements to allow more low-income senior citizens into tax relief programs. In addition, it would set aside a third of the county’s hotel tax for the Pittsburgh Convention Center.

headline: Time for Ridge to share wealth
abstract: Scranton Tribune talks about the projected surplus for Pennsylvania and urges Govenor Tom Ridge to reduce income tax for residents.

headline: Penn State summit focuses on fighting underage drinking
abstract: A two day summit at State College boasts alternatives for campus weekend activities and various methods that can be used to discourage underage drinking.

headline: Plugged in
abstract: On Sunday The Times reported on the efforts of public schools in our region to incorporate computers into the classrooms. The need for schools to do so was driven home statistics to do so was driven home by statistics released by the state Department of Labor and Industry: Computers are where the jobs are. They are a solid base in the community.

headline: Electric Choice
abstract: Department of Community and Economic Deveolpment, Sam McCullough, voices his opnion that electric deregulation in Pennsylvani will attract businesses and provided great economic improvements to the area.

headline: Rt. 501 stoplight plan 'more palatable'
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation and Balfour Beatty Construction Corporation, which was contracted for an expansion project on the Route 30 bypass, agreed to hold off on closing Lititz Pike for at least two months by installing a traffic light at its intersection with Route 30. Balfour Beatty has already fallen behind schedule for the Route 30 project; however, it reached an agreement with PennDOT to try to speed up work, which the Federal Highway Administration approved. PA Representatives John Barley and Jere Strittmatter, two key private sector groups and several individuals interviewed for the article seemed pleased that PennDOT and Balfour Beatty had listened to their concerns, but ultimately, traffic is anticipated to get extremely backed up on Route 30 if many motorists don’t use alternate routes.

headline: Laws will aid PA children
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge signs three new bills to protect children in foster care by changing current rules for parental rights and increasing information sharing between counties.

headline: Markosek voted for HB 907 unknowingly, still undecided
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge vetoed the controversial House Bill 907, which many legislators approved without knowing that it contained language that would have allowed Ridge to provide $300 million for Pittsburgh’s proposed new stadium projects. PA Representative Joe Markosek said he too voted for it without knowledge of the bill’s hidden language, and he is still undecided on whether he would support legislation to raise the state’s debt ceiling to provide state funding for new stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh as well as various other projects across the state. The legislation will likely be considered next year, and Markosek said he will weigh the pros and cons in making his final decision.

headline: Museum Quality; New Army facility in Carlisle would be convenient to much of East Coast
abstract: With its deeps roots into America's past, Carlisle is an ideal spot for the U.S. Army Museum.  Officials today are set to unveil Pennsylvania's proposal to locate the facility adjacent to the Carlisle Barracks on land the Army has leased out for farming.  The Army, the nation's oldest service, is the only one without a museum.

headline: GOP pair removed from primary ballot
abstract: Tom Lingenfelter and Dan Snyder, who were the Republican opponents of PA Senators Joe Conti and Stewart Greenleaf, respectively, were removed from the ballot by Commonwealth Court Judge Dan Pellegrini. Pellegrini upheld challenges claiming the required signatures needed to run were obtained improperly, which will leave Conti and Greenleaf with no opposition in the upcoming primary elections. A separate hearing will be held for Lingenfelter because he was running a dual campaign against U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, and Snyder wasn’t present for the majority of his hearing after Pellegrini decided not to throw out his case.

headline: Republican retain House leaders slate
abstract: The Republican leadership of the PA House will remain unchanged following the re-election of Speaker Matt Ryan, Majority Leader John Perzel, Whip Donald Snyder and Appropriations Chairman John Barley. Other key Republicans were also re-elected.

headline: Boro officials worry tax reform falls short
abstract: The PA Legislature enacted tax reform that will allow school districts to ask voters to consider reducing property taxes and eliminating nuisance taxes in return for increasing the wage tax, and PA Senator Terry Punt and Representative Pat Fleagle believe the Legislature will work towards municipal and county tax reform in the near future. Chambersburg borough councilman William McLaughlin complained that the legislation doesn’t go far enough because it doesn’t provide the borough with property tax relief by giving it the ability to levy an income tax against the 12,000 people who work in the borough but live outside it. Representative Jeffrey Coy expects legislators to wait and see how the new legislation is implemented by school districts, so there are still many unanswered questions for local governments.

headline: Use federal trust funds as intended
abstract: Altoona Mirror criticizes the government for holding on to federal trust fund money to help balance the budget. Altoona Mirror suggests the trusts fundsmask a huge problem and should be released to intended programs, especially mining programs..

headline: Pennsylvania expects windfall from proposed tobacco deal
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher helped negotiate a $206 billion multi-state settlement with the four major tobacco companies that would bring PA an expected $11.26 billion over 25 years to offset the health costs of treating smoking-related illnesses. Anti-smoking advocates criticized the settlement for allowing too many loopholes for the tobacco industry, but those who negotiated the deal said it is a good starting point for Congress to act upon, which President Clinton vowed to try to do. If enough states agree to the settlement, which would offer them all lucrative financial compensation in return for settling lawsuits, it will be finalized, and the deal will also limit many types of advertising and require tobacco companies to fund anti-smoking efforts.

headline: Polls apart  - At odds on black & vouchers
abstract: According to a study by the Commonwealth Foundation, 64% of African American adults from Philadelphia favor school vouchers, even though conservative Republicans are voucher’s biggest supporters, and African Americans traditionally vote for Democrats. However, critics claim the poll’s wording influenced its results, and the results go against a statewide poll conducted by Mansfield University. PA Representative Dwight Evans, who supports a combination of vouchers, charter schools and School District reform, said the poll’s number indicate a growing frustration felt by most blacks.

headline: Electrical problem dims power lunches
abstract: An electrical transformer blew out two days ago, shutting off power to several different parts of the PA Capitol, including the cafeteria and several offices. A part to fix the problem is en route from Virginia. In other news, the PA Department of General Services will auction off 210 used state vehicles.

headline: School bus review welcome
abstract: Parents should weigh the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's plans to conduct a comprehensive review of school bus safety. Such a review is long overdue. All responsible persons agree. There is no way to make school buses crash-free, but we do have the obligation to take any steps that will improve safety and lessen the risk, such as seat belts.

headline: Lawyers face own secretive discipline process
abstract: The PA Supreme Court oversees the conduct of the state’s practicing lawyers, and it will investigate the conduct of James Persing and G. Robert Fitzpatrick, both of whom are facing criminal charges. The Disciplinary Board of the Supreme Court can offer a range of punishments for lawyers, ranging from private and public reprimands to disbarment; however, as a general rule, the proceedings are done in secrecy. Robert Surrick, a Chester County lawyer, believes that the proceedings should be done publicly, but others claim that the secrecy is important for protecting the reputation of lawyers since an estimated 70 percent of all complaints are thrown out as frivolous.

headline: Message to Ridge: Veto stadium bill - Many Valley taxpayers angered by funding ploy
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge must make a difficult decision on whether to veto a bill passed by the PA Legislature that would allow the state to fund new stadium projects in Pittsburgh. The bill, which was largely created to repeal unnecessary laws, contained an amendment that would essentially allow state-funded stadium projects; however, many lawmakers didn’t realize the amendment’s intentions. Most Tarentum Valley residents oppose using taxpayers’ dollars to fund stadium projects and agree the amendment was sneaky.

headline: No 'stamp' of approval for Postal Service - 'Omnibus' honor not what VFW had in mind
abstract: The Veterans of Foreign Wars was denied its request for a stamp commemorating its centennial next year, and instead, the U.S. Postal Service will issue a stamp honoring soldiers, firefighters and police officers who died in the line of duty. U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich, House Veterans Chairman Bob Stump and Representative Frank Mascara all sent letters to the Postal Service requesting the stamp, and the House passed a nonbinding resolution in support of it. President Clinton never responded to letters sent by the VFW.

headline: GOP pick for district justice hounded by past scandals
abstract: The man Gov. Tom Ridge might nominate to replace retired District Justice Robert Shaffer lost his license to practice law for three years in the early 1980s and just paid off the final $16,000 he's owed the IRS for years.  Those elements of F. Kirk Adams' background have his opponents crying foul.  They're trying to derail his nomination before Republican Ridge decides whether to submit the Ridley Park attorney's name to the GOP-controlled state Senate for confirmation.

headline: Republicans geared to rush Clinton testimony to TV screens
abstract: Despite some bipartisan cooperation in the House Judiciary Committee, Republicans are trying to release the video of President Clinton’s grand jury testimony, whereas Democrats believe it would be unfair to the President and are trying to block its release. Republicans have said the public should be able to view the video to help make their own determination on whether Independent Counsel Kenneth Starr’s accusations that Clinton lied before a grand jury are true, but many Democrats fear the video could damage his recent efforts to build up his image and apologize for an "inappropriate" relationship with Monica Lewinski. In addition, the option of censuring Clinton appears unlikely based on comments by some top Republican leaders, and the option of forcing Clinton to reimburse some of the costs of the investigation is being considered.

headline: Boscola's bill would ease seniors' tax load - The legislation would freeze property taxes for those age 65 who earn less than $65,000
abstract: PA Representative Lisa Boscola plans to introduce a bill that would freeze property taxes for people over the age of 65 who make less than $65,000 a year. The bill would save $65 million for 551,000 seniors and could help them remain in their homes. According to Boscola, her proposal would be a backup plan to the homestead bill, which allows school districts and local governments to lessen the tax burden on homeowners.

headline: Use surplus to pay down the debt
abstract: Opinion piece suggests that the surplus facing the federal government should go to pay down debt instead of tax breaks, funding current projects or starting new programs.

headline: Pennsylvania takes advantage of federal funds to boost children's health
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge requested an increase in $15 million to qualify for $80 million in federal funds for the Children’s Health Insurance Program, which provides health care for children whose parents can’t afford to buy it yet earn too much to qualify for welfare health benefits. A number of people praised Ridge because his proposal would triple the number of eligible children. However, some people were skeptical of Ridge and said he was essentially forced to do it, the federal government deserves most of the praise, and his efforts fell short because half of the state’s uninsured children will still remain ineligible.

headline: Pottstown schools 'raise the bar"
abstract: Students who want to pass a class or graduate from Pottstown High School will have to earn an A or B if new standards being championed by the administration are adopted. C's and D's won't count. They are tired waiting on the state to make new standards, so they are raising their own bar.

headline: End delays on storing nuclear fuel
abstract: Congress has failed to meet the January 31, 1998 deadline to begin accepting and disposing of used nuclear fuel, which was imposed when it passed the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982. Currently, the U.S. uses 107 nuclear power plants, including nine in PA, to produce 20 percent of the nation’s electricity; however, the plants have been required to store used fuel at their facilities, and an analysis on whether Yucca Mountain is suitable for storing material is still years away from completion. The authors claim by 2010, nearly 80 percent of all power plants will run out of storage space, and they urge the federal government to take action by designating temporary and permanent storage facilities.

headline: School bus review welcome
abstract: Parents should weigh the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's plans to conduct a comprehensive review of school bus safety. Such a review is long overdue. This is certainly an issue on which all responsible persons agree. There is no way to make school buses crash-free or completely injury-proof, but we do have an obligation to take any and all steps that will improve safety and lessen the risk.

headline: Legislation limits prisoner lawsuits
abstract: Governor Ridge is expected to sign a bill that will limit the ability of inmates in state and local prisons to file lawsuits, which PA Attorney General Michael Fisher estimates could save $3 million a year. The bill will require a filing fee from prisoners, and it will allow suits deemed frivolous to be thrown out. Any prisoner awarded monetary damages must first pay any victim restitution, and lawsuits by an inmate who has filed three prior frivolous cases will also be thrown out.

headline: Murphy has fences to mend
abstract: As the main architect behind Plan B, an $809 million plan for new stadiums for the Pittsburgh Pirates and Steelers and a new convention center, Mayor Tom Murphy’s political future may be in jeopardy because of Governor Tom Ridge’s recent veto of a bill that contained hidden language that could have allowed Ridge to provide state funds for the stadium projects. According to PA Representatives John Barley and Jeff Habay, Murphy’s credibility had been damaged, and while Murphy apologized for how he handled the situation, he’s blamed Philadelphia politicians for the failure to secure state funding. Ultimately, one political analyst said time could heal Murphy’s recent political struggles, and if the Legislature eventually does approve stadium financing, he could salvage his reputation.

headline: Outpatient clinics for veterans on way
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and Representative Ron Klink announced the Department of Veterans Affairs has approved the creation of community based outpatient clinics in New Castle and Ellwood City. Because of the new clinics, patients won’t have to travel to Butler to receive primary care.

headline: GOP refuses to give Democrats a break
abstract: Republican have been accussed of calling too man 'token' days so they racted against Democrats by not allowing them to take any breaks during the day.

headline: Republicans had the right issues; they should have run with them
abstract: The Republican Party held onto its control over Congress after the past election; but the author refers to it as an ugly victory because they did much worse than anticipated, which has led some people to speculate that Americans have rejected the far right conservatism of the party and are looking for more moderate candidates. However, the author disagrees, citing polls which show most Americans have very conservative views on issues ranging from work, family and taxes to religion, abortion and adultery. The author argues the results of the past election are a reflection of the party’s unwillingness to stand up for their conservative principles, and he feels it would be a terrible mistake for the party to become less conservative in the future.

headline: Commissioners: 'We have gone from chaos to order'
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners Bob Cranmer and Mike Dawida were present for the naming of the new Pittsburgh Pirates stadium. Absent was Commissioner Larry Dunn, a staunch opponent of the public funding used to finance the stadium. Cranmer and Dawida believe ousting Dunn as commissioner chairman helped put the County back on track. County Common Pleas President Judge Robert E. Dauer disagrees. County Controller Frank Lucchino believes County government has been calmer since the coup that ousted Dunn. Cranmer and Dawida still have much work to do in the budget.

headline: Work Force Development: Beware Remedies That Will Make Situation Worse
abstract: The author of the article criticizes House Bill 1800, which calls for the creation of a new bureaucracy that would oversee the spending of about $750 million each year on job training development for Pennsylvanians. First off, the author feels the proposal won’t allow changes in job demand for the economy to be taken into account, and he thinks government interference will reduce the choice of Pennsylvanians to receive training in areas which interest them. He also criticizes the bill because it would create a board of representatives that would try to push workforce development in their industry’s interest, while it would also create incentives for government officials to reward friends and political allies with positions on the board.

headline: Peterson discusses healthcare issues
abstract: U.S. Representative John Peterson met with the Deputy Administrator of the Health Care Financing Administration, Michael Hash, to discuss a number of concerns, including the reduction in payments to health care providers due to the 1997 Balanced Budget Act and the future of Medicare. Peterson also discussed the impact of the Balance Budget Act on rural America and said current policies are unfair to rural Americans for several different reasons. Home health care costs are covered unequally throughout different regions in the nation, and patients in rural communities often are forced to go to larger cites for treatment.

headline: Prison teachers want positions to remain positioned under the Department of Education, not the Department of Corrections
abstract: The Correctional Institution Vocational Education Association has twice thwarted attempts to transfer the oversight of educational programs for prisoners from the Department of Education to the Department of Corrections. Many teachers are concerned that the move would compromise the quality of education; though Department of Education spokesman Daniel Langan said the department supports the transfer because it would allow better management and would not impact education standards. Jeff Chiampi, a prison shop teacher, is afraid that GED testing from the Department of Corrections wouldn’t be as less highly regarded, and another teacher voiced her concerns and suggestions for reaching an agreement.

headline: Enron's end-run play - As Peco Energy plods toward deregulation, a tough challenger enters the market, short circuiting its plans
abstract: Last summer, Peco Energy Corporation had negotiated a settlement with consumer groups and PA Senator Vince Fumo that would guarantee Peco’s customers a 10 percent rate cut in return for Peco retaining its monopoly while the electricity market slowly opens up to competitors. Without help, Peco believes it will lose in the deregulated market, and part of the agreement would have required ratepayers to finance the $5.4 billion in stranded costs from building nuclear power plants. Just as the deal appeared to be heading for approval, Enron Corporation made a surprising move to challenge Peco by offering 20 percent rate cuts, and after each side spent millions lobbying, the PA Public Utility Commission dismissed Enron’s proposal as unworkable, but it also told Peco to modify its proposed settlement.

headline: Schuylkill rail plan chugs along
abstract: SEPT and BARTA are ready to move forward with with a proposal for a passenger service train on the Schuylkill Expressway.

headline: Legislature OK's bill on independent counsels
abstract: Senator Jeffrey Piccol's bill to hire independent counsels to investigate the Attorney General's office when there iare complaints of wrongdoing, has passed. Attorney General Mike Fisher supported the bill.

headline: New life offered to old homes
abstract: PA Representative Thomas Tangretti is the chief sponsor of a bill that would provide tax breaks to owners of historical homes for fixing them up. Proponents of the bill believe it would help preserve historical homes and stimulate older neighborhoods, especially in cities. The article describes several of the specific tax breaks the bill includes, and a spokesman for Tangretti said he’s unsure whether it will be voted on when the Legislature reconvenes September 28.

headline: Politicians kick off museum petition effort
abstract: Carlisle Mayor Kirk Wilson and U.S. Representative Bill Goodling were handing out petitions to local businesses in hopes of collecting between 10,000 and 12,000 signatures to show the area’s support for bringing the proposed national Army museum to the region. The Army is reportedly considering Carlisle along with Fort Belvoir, Virginia and possibly others for the site of the museum, which is expected to bring in a huge amount of tourists dollars to wherever it is ultimately located. Goodling will present the petitions to the Pentagon, and Governor Tom Ridge has also launched a campaign to bring the museum to Carlisle.

headline: GOP repairs image on Earth Day issues
abstract: In the 1996 elections, the image of Republicans was tarnished by accusations from Democrats that they were directly harming the environment, so the Republican Party has responded by improving its image and has issued a six-page list of environmental bills that it recently considered. Democrats have been forced to acknowledge the efforts of Republicans, so they have changed  their tone and are accusing the Republican Party of not being environmentally friendly enough. Democratic leaders, including House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, have criticized Republicans for not supporting some recent initiatives by President Clinton that Republicans claim will hurt businesses.

headline: Republicans hear attorney general urge them to vote
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher urges Republicans to vote in the upcomng election because the Clinton scandal should not be tolerated.

headline: Bureaucratic scheming
abstract: Taxpayers Local Control Act was supossed to bring about lower property taxes, but one year after its passage, citizens have yet to see the benefits of the act.

headline: Working families paying $1 billion more in taxes in Pennsylvania
abstract: Representaive William DeWeese writes that Republicans are decreasing economic opportunity for working families and increasing the amount of taxes that working families pay.

headline: Peterson says Security Blue's Medicare reimbursement cuts would hit rural areas hardest
abstract: U.S. Congressman John Peterson is urging Highmark’s Security Blue Medicare HMO to change its plans to decrease the amount it will pay hospitals for Medicare recipients’ coverage. He said the cuts could force rural hospitals to discontinue some services, which could require senior citizens to travel for hours to larger hospitals to get the care they need. According to Peterson, rural hospitals have already suffered budget cuts in Medicare reimbursements, and he has called on Security Blue to at the very least extend current rates for another year to allow senior citizens to search for alternatives.

headline: Professors debate merit review
abstract: Penn State professors, like college faculty around the country, are beginning a debate that could affect their own job security. It centers on whether to modify tenure, essentially a lifetime appointment, to give administrators and peers more opportunity to evaluate performance. Although supporters say the proposal will strengthen academic quality, critics fear it is a veiled attempt to make it easier to fire faculty members.

headline: Falling gas prices a tax boon
abstract: The recent decline in gas prices may help local municipalities using a back pay formula for fuel tax redistribution.

headline: Seat belt law gets second chance
abstract: Now that the recent election is over, a bill sponsored by PA Representative Robert Godshall that would allow police to stop and fine motorists $25 for not wearing their seatbelts will get a second chance. Currently, police officers can only issue seat belt citations to motorists who’ve already been pulled over for a separate violation, but Godshall and Pennsylvanians United for Safety, a coalition supporting the bill, have persuaded House Majority Leader John Perzel to allow the bill to come to a vote. However, Perzel has made no guarantees that the bill will pass, and Governor Tom Ridge and the State Police have been quiet on the issue.

headline: Legislature OKs bills for abused children
abstract: State lawmakers pass legislation to protect children in foster care by changing current rules for parental rights and increasing information sharing between counties

headline: New year begins: same old stuff?
abstract: Scranton Tribune proses some New Year's Resolutions for statlawmakers; democrats need to get back on track, economic development should be a key issue, and congress should strenghten open conduct laws for businesses.

headline: Promise Keepers will convene at the Vet
abstract: Promise Keepers, a Christian evangelical organization that claims to have helped 2.5 million men deepen their relationships with God and their families, will hold its first stadium event in Philadelphia. The event will be held in Veterans stadium, and it is expected to draw over 50,000 men. The organization has stopped charging admission, which has required it to survive off donations, and it takes its name from the seven promises a man is expected to commit himself to as a Promise Keeper.

headline: GOP retains fund-raising lead; soft monet to both parties soars
abstract: The Republican party has raised funds that far exceed Democrats but b oth parties have manged to increase th amount of soft money they received.

headline: Republicans Play to the Folks at Home
abstract: Republicnas in Congress are bringing various issues to the congressional floor to impress consituents. Some of the issues include, condeming Nazi-Soviet pacts, contraceptives for minors, agriculture purchases and many more.

headline: City tax cuts a real Laffer
abstract: Economist Arthur Laffer proposed an idea in the 1970’s that if the government lowers taxes, it may actually generate more revenue by encouraging citizens to do more of whatever is being taxed. Unfortunately, the Laffer curve didn’t work for President Ronald Reagan in the 1980’s when his tax cuts drove the federal government into a huge budget deficit, but since Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell took office and began lowering the city’s wage tax, wage-tax revenue has actually increased. The increased revenue could be attributed to a several other factors, yet the author believes it would be beneficial for the city to enact even greater tax cuts to see if the trend continues.

headline: Working poor deserve break on state tax
abstract: Valley News Dispatch applauds Govenor Tom Ridge for increasing the number of families who qualify for working poor tax breaks.

headline: Philadelphia doctors eye hospital purchase
abstract: Some Philadelphia physicians employed by Allegheny General Hospital's parent foundation have expressed an interest in buying the hospital in which they practice from the financially ailing foundation.  But an attorney representing 700 doctors who work at the Medical College of Pennsylvania Hospital said Wednesday that efforts to come up with a buyout proposal have been stalled by Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation's failure to provide him with the financial information he has requested.  Health care and consumer advocates yesterday also demanded financial data from the Pittsburgh-based foundation in the form of a state-ordered performance audit to determine how and why the nonprofit health system has $371 million in bond debt.

headline: Program gives prospective employers transcripts on job-seeking students
abstract: Hire Education, a program through the Somerset County, School-to-Work office, provides area employers with a means of requesting high school transcripts as part of the hiring process. The program encourages employers to request high school transcripts as one performance criterion when evaluating full-time and part-time job applicants who are in high school or are recent graduates. Schimpf says the local businesses have been very supportive of the idea and to date about 150 of them have registered with the program.

headline: Farmers urged to use extra care in filing for fuels tax refunds
abstract: State Treasurer Barbara Hafer is urging PA farmers to be careful when filing for this year’s liquid fuels tax refunds because a change in the law has made the process more complicated; though it should become easier by next year. Under PA law, farmers can be reimbursed for the state tax they pay for gas, diesel and other fuels. Some details on how to file properly are provided in the article, and each claim must include copies of paid receipts or a verification statement from the fuel dealer.

headline: Seat belts on buses are a good idea
abstract: A Pine eight-grader's suggestion that PA require seat belts in school buses could hardly have been more timely. Within just a few weeks of Mike Portuesi winning an essay contest called "There ought to be a law" an 11-year-old Butler boy was seriously injured when he stuck his head out a school bus window and hit a pole. A buckled seat belt might have kept him in place.

headline: Lesko death sentence upheld
abstract: John C. Lesko, convicted murdered, lost his final appeal to the PA Supreme Court to be removed from death row. Gov. Tom Ridge has 90 days to sign Lesko's death warrant.

headline: Newlin sees young people as region's change agent
abstract: CEO of Buchanan Ingersoll PC, William Newlin, Pittsburgh's second largest law firm, believes the city needs young people to stay and to grow. He also supports Plan B, under which 2 new sports stadiums in Pittsburgh will be built using public funding. Newlin also sees physical infrastructure and image enhancement as two areas in which regional cooperation is needed as reported by a syndicated columnist.

headline: Students urged to remember vets
abstract: Congressman-elect Don Sherwood was the keynote speaker at a Veterans Day ceremony at Lackawanna Trail High School. Sherwood, an Army veteran himself, reflected on his past experiences, and the high school band played a number of patriotic songs to honor members and veterans of the military who were in attendance.

headline: GOP unfazed by foes' plan to use tobacco issue in election
abstract: Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, are hoping the Senate’s rejection of an anti-smoking bill will become a key election issue that could lead to their party retaking the House. The bill was defeated largely due to the efforts of conservative Republicans who saw the bill as a massive tax increase that was intended to fund new federal programs. Republicans, however, don’t anticipate being hurt in the elections, and they are confident the public sees the bill as a government attempt to "grab more money."

headline: Republicans quietly using the 'I' word
abstract: Many U.S. House Republicans, including Pennsylvania’s George Gekas, reacted with skepticism to the party leadership’s proposal to name a special committee to prescreen evidence from Independent Counsel Kenneth Starr’s investigation to determine whether to begin impeachment proceedings against President Clinton on perjury charges. Speaker Newt Gingrich and Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde assured party members that no action would be taken "until and unless" Starr formally submits information to the House, but White House officials, who are trying to classify the investigation as a partisan attack against Clinton, asked why they are wasting time when other important issues still face the House. No matter how the Republican leadership handles the issue of impeachment, they are likely to face criticism, but some see the special committee as an "exit strategy."

headline: Clarion County lawmaker votes for tax reform bill
abstract: PA Representative Fred McIlhattan voted with the majority to approve a local tax reform bill, even though Clarion County, which he represents, voted against a constitutional amendment last fall to grant the Legislature the ability to enact the bill. The bill would allow school districts, with voter approval, to lower property taxes in exchange for raising the earned income tax to make up the difference. While McIlhattan admitted the bill isn’t perfect, he justified passing it because he also represents a portion of Armstrong County, which supported the constitutional amendment, and the tax shift is optional, so Clarion County wouldn’t have to approve it.

headline: 36 million abortions and debate still rages
abstract: Abortion rights supports and oppossers vocalized their stand and opinions on the issue. Statistical trend of abortion since 1973 are examined.

headline: Plan would start checkup on doctors
abstract: A hearing was held on PA Representative T.J. Rooney’s Medical Practice Disclosure Act, which would require the PA Department of State to collect data on all of the state’s licensed physicians and make that information public. Proponents of the bill, including the Citizens for Consumer Justice, believe that the information would allow people to seek out good doctors; however, critics, including the PA Medical Society and PA Academy of Family Physicians, believe that it is unfairly singling out medical practitioners and could provide misleading information. The PA Department of State believes that it would not be worth the cost, the committee's chairman, Representative Mario Civera, said that he will not allow the bill to be voted on in its current form, and Representative John Lawless opposed the bill outright.

headline: Proposal for new teachers isn't cure-all
abstract: $1.2 billion in federal funding has been allocated to hire 100,000 new teachers in an attempt to lower class sizes in first through third grade to 18 students, and PA would likely receive close to $51 million of that money. While hiring more teachers sounds good, the authors claim studies have been inconclusive and shown class size really doesn’t matter until classes reach 15 or fewer students. According to the editorial, more teachers would require more classrooms, which could present a challenge to low-income areas, higher-income areas like the North Hills would barely receive enough teachers to make a difference and the proposal could damage Pennsylvania’s attempts to improve the quality of teachers.

headline: Franklin is electrifying as utility-choice emcee
abstract: There was a ceremony at Franklin Institute in Philadelphia to kick off Pennsylvania’s first phase into deregulating the electric market. Governor Tom Ridge attended the event, and he said over 5 million electric customers will have the chance to save a billion dollars a year. A Ben Franklin actor, all five members of the PA Public Utility Commission and others attended the event, and 5.2 million electricity customers were to receive sign-up cards this week for the first year of the Electric Choice phase-in.

headline: Seat-belt advocates say cost is driving the school-bus debate
abstract: After a summer of strapping children into seat belts between visits to the beach, the zoo and day camp, parents may soon be watching them bounce around in the bus without restraints and why those buses don't have the same protection they have. A growing number of calls for seat belts on buses are not likely to result in any changes soon. Stories of accidents on buses are detailed.

headline: Let's give commish power to lead police
abstract: According to Fraternal Order of Police President Rich Costello, political influence over the Philadelphia Police Department is the worst he’s seen in 25 years, and City Councilman Jim Kenney agreed that about half of police transfers and appointments are politically motivated. The author claims charter and civil service rules tie the hands of police commissioners, which allows politicians to run the department, and there’s little agreement on what, if anything, should be done to fix the problem. Kenney and City Council President John Street disagree over the issue, but ultimately, the author thinks people should have faith in the new police commissioner, John Timoney, and he should be given the chance to effectively run the department without outside interference.

headline: NFL: A land of movers and takers
abstract: The author is highly critical of the National Football League’s franchises and owners for essentially trying to extort host cities into paying to build them new stadiums, and if the city refuses, they simply move on to other cities that will. He is also critical of the Philadelphia Eagles owner for demanding state funds for a new stadium, and he claims the state Legislature actually listened to its constituents by not approving a one-third stadium funding plan for the Steelers, Pirates, Eagles and Phillies; though backdoor legislation slid through which would provide the funding for the Pittsburgh teams. The author thinks it’s fair to fund the Pittsburgh stadiums because they’ve at least come up with the other two-thirds in funding, whereas Philadelphia has no defined plan.

headline: ALLTEL Seeks Changes
abstract: ALLTEL Pennsylvania Incorporated has filed a petition to the PA Public Utility Commission, asking for it to be allowed to impose a more flexible rate structure through alternative regulation. Alternative regulation allows the PUC to shorten the application process to allow companies to offer new services, such as caller Identification, call return and high-speed Internet. The PA Legislature and PUC created programs like alternative regulation to promote the spread of advanced telephone service in rural areas.

headline: GOP widens impeachment investigation
abstract: Republican House Judiciary Committee members decided to expand their impeachment investigation by examining whether President Clinton broke election laws, and they have ordered Attorney General Janet Reno to turn over internal memos, which could prove he broke the law but must first be approved by a federal judge. The Federal Election Commission determined that both Clinton and Bob Dole, who lost to Clinton in 1996, exceeded spending limits in the past election, and Democrats were extremely critical of Republicans for trying to add another charge a week before the impeachment vote was set to be conducted by the committee. The committee is still deeply divided by party lines over the question of impeachment, and the new charges could potentially set back a goal to have a final vote in front of the entire House by the end of the year.

headline: Republicans to face off at Monday's forum
abstract: All four Republican candidates for the 13th Congressional District, including U.S. Representative Jon Fox, Michael McMonagle, Melissa Brown and Jonathan Newman, will attend a debate at Plymouth-Whitemarsh High School. A previous debate fell apart after Fox said he would not attend. Newman wants Fox to come clean on a loans he accepted from a developer in 1992, and Democratic candidate Joseph Hoeffel won’t attend the debate.

headline: Coming up short - It's more telling what Gov. Whitman's restructuring tax plan does not include
abstract: The authors criticize New Jersey Governor Christie Whitman’s tax reform plan that calls for regionalizing local school districts and local governments, which Whitman claims would save $1.2 billion a year for taxpayers. The authors argue residents will be hesitant to cede local control, and they believe her tax reform plan fails to address the key issue causing such a heavy burden on local taxes, especially for senior citizens, which is the lack of adequate state funding. They do support recommendations to levy impact fees on developers and to limit teachers’ and public employees’ raises to the rate of inflation, but ultimately, they believe Whitman’s plan is a disappointment.

headline: 80 years of blazing trails
abstract: The Urban League of Pittsburgh will be celebrating eighty years in its struggle for racial justice, and the article provides a timeline of the Urban League’s long history as well as a list of eighty people who will be honored for their dedication throughout the organization’s eighty years. While some civil rights activists have criticized the Urban League for catering to the black elite, the organization has fostered some important black leaders, and Urban League supporters, especially in the business community, have praised the organization for working with businesses and helping people find adequate housing as well as quality jobs. In the future, the Urban League will try to boosts its membership, and it will also focus efforts on creating minority entrepreneurs and helping educate youths.

headline: President out at Allegheny health system
abstract: Sherif S. Abdelhak, the architect of the Allegheny health system's failed expansion strategy in Philadelphia, was ousted from his posts as chief executive and president by the organization's board yesterday in Pittsburgh.  Adding to the organization's disarray, Donald E. Kaye, chief executive and president of Allegheny's nine hospital Philadelphia area system and of its university, will resign Monday, a spokesman said.  Allegheny officials have not appointed a successor to Kaye.

headline: Proposed basic education funding
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge proposed about $3.5 billion in basic education funding for 1998-99. Here's how York County Schools fared.

headline: Gas-pump prices on 'fast-paced slide'
abstract: Gas prices in the United States are dropping and are at a low sale price due to various reasons.

headline: Senate Agrees to Lift Highway Spending by $26 Billion during the Next Six Years
abstract: Senators reached a bipartisan deal to boost highway spending by $26 billion in the next six years, clearing a major roadblock holding up Senate passage of the massive election-year construction bill. The deal, negotiated with the blessing of Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, would divert funds raised by a 4.3-cents-a-gallon gasoline tax from deficit reduction to highway-construction needs. The plan raises to $173 billion the amount committed to highway and safety programs under the bill now pending in the Senate.

headline: Local legislators support Republican initiative to curb school violence
abstract: House Republicans and PA House Majority Leader John Perzel unveiled a package of 12 bills to help curb school violence. Rep. Patrick Fleagle, a member of the House Education Committee, said legislators are recognizing school violence is prevalent everywhere, not just in the big cities. Rep. Jeffrey Coy, a democrat, does not want to make school violence a party issue and has scheduled a forum on the topic for his constituents.

headline: No more Camden Yards
abstract: The head of the Maryland Stadium Authority, which constructed the new Baltimore Ravens and Orioles stadiums, testified at a PA House hearing headed by state Representative Andrew Carn that while the economic impact of the stadiums has been "fabulous," team owners should contribute more towards future stadium construction projects. He endorsed a funding plan similar to Governor Ridge’s proposal to have the state, local area and team owners each pay one-third of the cost of building new stadiums for the Pirates and Steelers and Pittsburgh and the Eagles and Phillies in Philadelphia. Ridge hopes to convince the PA Legislature to support the one-third plan to keep the Pittsburgh teams from relocating, but the Legislature has been hesitant to accept some of his ways to generate funds.

headline: Area code grace period ends today
abstract: Today is supposed to be the last day that the 412 area code will serve most of western PA, but it could take an additional day or two for telephone companies to completely implement the change. The last court challenge was dismissed, and telephone companies have done their best to notify residents of the change. The old 412 territory will be split into two parts, and most residents inside Allegheny County will continue using 412, while most residents outside the county will use a new 724 area code.

headline: GOP, Dems agree: Outsiders' issue ads are killing them
abstract: Democrats and Republicans joined together in a court battle agaisnt special-interest groups that are hurting national campaigns because of the limitless advertising interest groups are doing. A judge will rile on the case soon.

headline: Republicans Use Spending Bills to Help Business Allies, Advance Social Agenda
abstract: With upcoming elections in November, Republican Congressmen are fighting to incorporate provisions in spending bills to help business allies and advance the party’s education and social agendas. Republicans voted along party lines to protect small businesses from National Labor Relations Board intervention, and they added new conditions to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. Alaskan U.S. Senator Ted Stevens is fighting a battle against American Seafood Incorporated, which is opposed by Senator Patty Murray, and some key budget recommendations in pending Congressional bills are provided in the article.

headline: Commissioners approve pay raises reluctantly
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners Bob Cranmer and Mike Dawida are forced by courts to approve a 21.2% raise for court managers. Commissioners originally agreed to the raise during a negotiation phase but later changed their mind.

headline: A call to involve more women in the realm of Pa. politics
abstract: Pennsylvania is lacking female officeholders and it is important that the state work together to esure that state positions are reflective of area demographic needs.

headline: President to Announce Health Care Protections
abstract: Despite protests from the insurance industry and Representative Bill Thomas, President Clinton will announce his plants to impose a "bill of rights" that would offer more patient protections to all 9 million federal employees and the 75 million Americans who are covered by government health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. In light of mounting criticism, he also urged Congress to develop stronger regulations of the health insurance industry for the approximately 180 million Americans who are covered by private insurers. Vice President Gore will submit an analysis of the federal agencies in order to determine which changes must be incorporated to ensure that each agency complies with Clinton’s new regulations.

headline: PSBA wants charter appeals board abolished
abstract: Since Governor Tom Ridge signed the charter schools bill into law in June 1997, six charter schools have been approved, and there will be twenty-nine more open by next year, but Ridge had to strike a deal with the PA School Boards Association in order to pass the law. As part of the deal, local districts must approve any charter school applications, and Ridge agreed to wait two years to institute an appeals boards; however, the School Boards Association now intends to lobby to delay or get rid of an appeals board altogether. They fear the state will use the appeals board to overturn school boards’ decisions and force them to use local funding for the creation of charter schools, whereas proponents of appeals boards claim they are intended to protect the interests of the local population.

headline: Gotta play to win
abstract: The authors of the editorial encourage all electric consumers to take the time to consider the different energy providers that are now available to choose from. They believe consumers can benefit if they are willing to put in the effort to consider the best electric deals that are out there.

headline: Senate Approves Measure to Fight Drunken Driving
abstract: The US Senate voted overwhelmingly to withhold federal highway aid to states that don't adopt a tough new national standard for drunken driving. The vote was a major setback for the liquor trade and restaurant and hotel industry, which had lobbied against the bipartisan measure as an unwarranted infringement of states' rights. The bill set the limit for ever state at .08% or they lose their federal highway funding.

headline: Pa. high court upholds Abu-Jamal conviction
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has unanimously upheld the conviction and death sentence of Mumia Abu-Jamal, a one-time Philadelphia radio commenter and member of the Black Panther Party, for the 1981 murder of a Philadelphia police officer. The ruling was made public yesterday and brings a definitive end.

headline: No-tax zones
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge is proposing the elimination of all taxes for businesses and residents in many of the commonwealth's urban and rural areas to spur economic growth. These so-called PA Keystone Opportunity Zones should prove a "dramatic enticement to attract private sector investment and ultimately create jobs and build communities." Twelve zones would be created statewide. Properties within each zone would have to be either abandoned, underutilized or unused to qualify for tax break.

headline: Area code proposed for faxes, cell phones - A lawmaker said traditional phone customers should not have a new code imposed upon them
abstract: PA Representative Tom Druce sponsored a resolution that led to House subcommittee hearings that will make recommendations to the state Public Utilities Commission on solutions for the problem that available telephone area codes will run out by the end of the year, even though telephone companies are holding thousands of unused numbers due to Federal Communication Commission regulations. The PUC is under a court-imposed deadline to act on a new area code, and it has proposed creating a new area code in Southeastern PA that would be used for all new phone lines once the old area code runs out. However, state Representative David Steil told the subcommittee that he’d prefer the new area code to only apply to cellular phones, pagers, computer modems and fax machines.

headline: Gore Attacks Republicans on Impeachment Steps
abstract: According to recent polls, there may be a backlash against Republicans for initiating impeachment proceedings against President Clinton, and Vice President Al Gore is jumping at the opportunity. While at a fundraising event for Democratic candidates in Minnesota, he criticized Congress for focusing on Clinton’s problems and not passing any significant legislation. He said the American population wants to move on, yet Congress continues to focus on impeachment, while passing the federal budget and other important problems have been ignored.

headline: REPUBLICANS VOW TO PRESS INQUIRY ON THE PRESIDENT
abstract: While the broadcast of President Clinton’s grand jury testimony actually increased his job approval rating, Republicans in Congress are hesitant to seek a deal, and the House Judiciary Committee will almost certainly recommend a full impeachment inquiry in early October, which would set up impeachment hearings to be held after the November midterm elections. The White House and leading Democrats are searching for a compromise short of impeachment that could satisfy the party and appeal to many Republicans, while Clinton’s lawyers are continuing to attack Kenneth Starr’s report, which cites 11 possibly impeachable offenses. Senator Arlen Specter of PA urged fellow Republicans to avoid the appearance of partisanship, and the party is trying to find a balance between trying to avoid alienating conservative Republicans by being too lenient and trying to avoid appearing too partisan by being overly aggressive against the President.

headline: Cooperation top vision in Harrisburg
abstract: Harrisburg’s Envision Capital Region program, which is similar to Schuylkill County’s VISION program, established four primary goals for its long term planning strategy. They include regional cooperation, improving education levels of the area’s residents, creating jobs and increasing job earnings. The details of these goals are compared with the benchmarks set by Schuylkill County’s VISION

headline: A diocesan diatribe: Ridge invitation an insult to church, pro-life
abstract: Pastor James Foster discusses why politicians, specifically Governor Tom Ridge, should always live and form opinions based on their religious beliefs.

headline: Proposed bill will affect local emergency medical personnel
abstract: A spokeswoman for House Majority Leader John Perzel said the House may consider a bill next session sponsored by Representative Patrick Fleagle which would allow doctors to provide a form, identity bracelet or card to a person who does not want to be resuscitated by emergency medical technicians. Currently, medics must resuscitate a person who has a do-not-resuscitate order unless they receive confirmation from a family doctor, which can be tough to do at the time of a crisis. Many medics feel the bill would make it easier for them to honor a person's wishes, but Mifflin County District Attorney Steve Snook believes it will make no significant difference.

headline: PSU, state to discuss campus expansion. Ridge wants to avoid litigation on decision against 4-year degrees
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has asked his top legal adviser to negotiate a settlement with Penn State University, which had its proposal to turn its Beaver, McKeesport and New Kensington branches from two-year to four-year programs rejected by PA Education Secretary Eugene Hickok. Hickok and leaders from other Western PA universities claim it would bring unnecessary competition among PA schools. Seven state legislators sent a letter to Hickok that claimed Penn State’s proposal would be good for the state because it would offer Information Science and Technology degrees.

headline: Hanger merits second term on PUC
abstract: Editors credit changes in utility bills to John Hanger, a consumer advocate on the PA Public Utilities Commission. Hanger was the mastermind behind the decision to remove regulation of utilities and instead move toward free competition, believing competition will foster rate cuts of up to 28 percent.
