Hanger was appointed by PA Gov. Robert Casey, however current Gov. Tom Ridge has yet to announce whether he will extend Hanger's position for another term. Editors believe Hanger has shown sensitivity to consumers and should be reappointed.

headline: Senate rejects helmet-law repeal
abstract: State Senate removed safety provisions for one bil and adding a list of additional privisons including, right turns at red lights, wheelchairs on sidewalks, and pick-up truck riders.

headline: Living in region isn't murder
abstract: Cambria and Somerset counties have low murder rates, which two veteran state police investigators suggest may be due to geography as well as local citizens' law-abiding natures. On average there are about three murders. The visibility of law enforcement helps keep it down.

headline: Official in push for no-tax zones
abstract: Johnstown is said to be one of the towns that will fall under the new Keystone Opportunity Zones. The district approval process is explained.

headline: Area codes give splitting headaches
abstract: At public hearings before the PA Public Utilities Commission, residents from Schuylkill and Bucks Counties expressed their concerns over the PUC’s proposed changes to regional area codes. The Schuylkill County Board of Commissioners urged the PUC not to split the county’s area code; however, eastern Dauphin County residents don’t want to give up their area code, and it isn’t technologically feasible to please both sides. The PUC made a tentative decision to overlay a new area code over existing area codes that serve Montgomery, Bucks, Lehigh and Northampton Counties, and while PA Representative David Steil agreed that a new area code is needed for wireless and nonvoice equipment, he disagreed with the overlay proposal.

headline: Gore to do Lehigh fund-raiser
abstract: Vice President Al Gore has scheduled a visit to the Lehigh Valley to reinvigorate the struggling PA Democratic party, which the region as the front line in its battle to regain the majority in the state House of Representatives Gore will speak to 400 to 500 Democratic campaign workers and contributors at Lehigh University's campus in Bethlehem.

headline: Resident has plan to end teacher strikes
abstract: Residents and some state lawmakers are looking into state-wide contracts for teachers to prevent strikes and to create uniformity in teacher wages.

headline: Council gives OK for tax breaks
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council gave preliminary approval to provide $33 million in tax breaks to four developers in the hopes of encouraging $164 million in development and the creation of 2,000 jobs. The tax breaks would allow the city to assess taxes based on the property’s value before being developed, which is usually much lower than after it’s developed, and the Rendell administration favors the system because it doesn’t result in any loss of money that the city is currently taking in. However, City Controller Jonathan Saidel and Councilman Michael Nutter are concerned that the city may be giving away too much of its future earnings, especially for school districts, whereas proponents argue these tax breaks are needed to spur development, and they will generate future revenue from alternative taxes.

headline: A journalist's religious awakening
abstract: The author claims he had an awakening when he realized that as a member of the press, he hardly ever touched on the subject of the right to worship, yet throughout the world, and especially in China, thousands of people are being persecuted for their religious beliefs.  U.S. Representative Frank Wolf and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter have sponsored a bill to impose mild, yet meaningful penalties against these countries through measures, such as ending non-humanitarian aid, and while the bill enjoys a wide range of support, there have been serious efforts to defeat it. The author criticizes President Clinton for his opposition to the bill, and he hopes the media begins covering more stories about the terrible persecution that Christians and other religious groups face around the world.

headline: Questions abound as state plans inquiry of hospital sale
abstract: Who will handle a $20 million nonprofit foundation created out of the sale of Berwick Hospital Center?  How will money be used?  These questions and others will be asked by the state attorney general's office as it probes the proposed $25.5 million sale of the hospital to The Quorum Health Group.

headline: Put gauntlet back on and wave bye-bye
abstract: The author is critical of Philadelphia School Superintendant David Hornbeck, Mayor Ed Rendell and the school board for creating a showdown with the PA Legislature and Governor Tom Ridge by threatening to shut down the district’s schools if the state doesn’t provide between $120 million and $140 million a year. He claims it was exceedingly stupid for the district to approve a million dollars in pay increases for non union teachers and for Hornbeck to announce a plan to spend millions of dollars on lowering class sizes when the district is already in poor financial shape. According to the author, there is bipartisan legislative support against Hornbeck’s threats, which are only hurting the district’s schoolchildren, and Hornbeck must go.

headline: Hefty PGW bonuses not out of line
abstract: Philadelphia Gas Works was a laughingstock according to this newspaper's editors, however that changed when Philadelphia Mayor Rendell raised the compensation rate. Moody's Investment Service recently gave PGW a favorable rating, crediting its new top management team. City Council however, was outraged at the generous bonuses received by management for their efforts. According industry standards, the bonuses and compensation at PGW pale. The team deserves their bonuses and the city's thanks.

headline: SEPTA asks strikers to come back - The authority offered the 5,500 idled workers only the prospect of a paycheck. The union said no.
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority’s offer to get striking workers back to work was refused by the Transport Workers Union, which said its workers had already engaged in negotiations without a contract, and they would not report back to work until they receive a new one. SEPTA’s chief negotiator said there’s little "wiggle room" for the existing offer, and top SEPTA officials met with City Council President John Street to discuss changes to a resolution that would ask Common Pleas Court to force the two sides to engage in round-the-clock negotiations. Some City Council members said they wouldn’t support the resolution if it forces striking workers to go back to work, there has already been legal action taken as a result of the strike, and seven members of Pennsylvania’s black legislative caucus criticized SEPTA’s attitude towards riders.

headline: Local Lawmakers cannot be sued
abstract: Eagle Times says the Supreme Court decision to bar individuals from suing lawmakers for policy decisions is good news.

headline: Officials interested in Ridge's tax plan
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge unveiled his proposed PA Keystone Opportunity Zones program, which would eliminate state and local taxes in twelve economically distressed zones to encourage growth. If the state Legislature approves, PA would become the second state in the nation to adopt such a program. Charleroi Mayor Ed Paluso, Monessen Mayor Ted Harhai and Donora Mayor John Lignelli all supported the plan to encourage local development and job growth.

headline: Area Codes-Divisions
abstract: The article details some of the new area code changes in Snyder, Northumberland, Schuylkill and Berks Counties as well as other sections of southeastern PA.

headline: Gore's visit shows Democratic imbalance: Itkin invited buy money goes to running mate
abstract: Vice President Al Gore invited Democratic gubernatorial candidate and PA Representative Ivan Itkin to join him at Kerotest Manufacturing Inc. However, the $250,000 that is expected to be raised by a nearby fundraiser afterwards will go into an account controlled by Itkin’s running mate, Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky, who agreed to join Itkin’s campaign if her consultant, Ken Smukler, controlled most of the operations for the statewide get-out-the-vote effort. Margolies-Mezvinky is expected to use much of the money to prepare for her planned campaign against U.S. Senator Rick Santorum in 2000, while Itkin is expected to have dwindling campaign funds by the end of September.

headline: resignation Was Prompted By Desire to Make a Point
abstract: After Larry Flynt, owner of the popular magazine Hustler, published an ad in  the Washington Post offering $1 million for anyone who could prove the sexual indiscretion of a member of congress, US Rep. Robert Livingston admitted to having a number of affairs and stepped down from his bid for Speaker of the House. Livingston attempted to separate his own indiscretion from that of President Clinton's, saying he had never lied under oath. Livingston will voluntarily resign in the next 6 months.

headline: County audit sought
abstract: Representative Joseph Preston wants Auditotr General Robert Casey to investigate and audit Allegheny County's funds and financial management before the new government is established.

headline: Abortion clinic must move out, judge declares
abstract: State College Medical Center, which performs abortion services, must move out of their leased space, as ordered by a judge. The original signers of the lease are not the occupants of the lease making the lease invalid.

headline: Remedies in reach
abstract: What does it mean to be a child whose parents can't afford private health insurance and missed out on government coverage?  Here's what it can mean, failing in school because you can't see the blackboard or hear the teacher.  And, as cost-conscious business trimmed payrolls and benefits through the early 90s, the number of uninsured children grew and grew - reaching 10 million plus.

headline: Questions arise over sleepwear standards
abstract: Editors agree that children are too precious to take risks on sleepwear and should be dressed accordingly. The federal flammability standard was weakened in 1996, no longer mandating clothing to be treated with flame retardant chemicals so long as the clothing fits snugly. However, since parents usually purchase clothing children can grow into, it is unlikely these standards will be met. Three house members want to return to the old standard, however the cotton industry opposes their efforts.

headline: In Council, a tangle over PGW's costs
abstract: A City Council meeting was held over spending by the Philadelphia Gas Works. Councilwoman Anna Verna criticized the company for wasteful spending on corporate customers and for paying too much for some of its employees. President James Hawes, who is leaving tomorrow to take a position in Atlanta, defended the company’s spending, claiming competitive salaries must be offered to attract qualified candidates and money must be spent to persuade potential clients to switch over from oil or electricity.

headline: SEPTA bias case begins - A class-action suit by five women targets the transit police's requirement on running
abstract: Five women have filed a lawsuit in federal court against the Southeastern PA Transit Authority over its requirement to run 1.5 miles in 12 minutes to become a transit police officer. The women, who couldn’t pass the test, allege it violates federal civil rights law by discriminating against female applicants. In addition, they claim it’s unfair because many current transit policemen couldn’t fulfill the requirement if they were forced to do so; however, a lawyer for SEPTA said the requirement is necessary because a transit officer may have to run significant distances as part of the job.

headline: Local lawmakers win immunity
abstract: Local lawmakers cannot be sued for individual votes, according ti a Supremem Court ruling. Even if votes are discriminatory or illegal in motive cannot be a liability for lawmakers.

headline: Panther Valley launches visioning process - 120 people take part in setting a course for future of area
abstract: 120 members of the Panther Valley Renaissance gathered at Panther Valley High School to take the initial steps in identifying important issues and setting goals for the region’s future. Discussion groups identified more jobs, historic preservation, tourism, downtown revitalization and image enhancement as the key issues confronting the area, and two borough council members expressed confidence that the meeting was a step in the right direction. PA Representative Keith McCall supports the program, and he expects future meetings to be held, so the group can continue developing and implementing its program.

headline: Bell Atlantic halts ISP fee payments
abstract: Bell Atlantic Corporation has stopped paying competing local phone companies for calls Bell customers make to Internet providers served by those local companies, and their refusal to pay what are known as termination fees for Internet-related calls is having an adverse effect on Internet service providers, who claim they are being refused service by local companies due to Bell’s decision. Ironically, Bell fought for the termination fees in 1996; however, these fees are now hurting them, and they argue they are disproportionately absorbing losses because Internet providers aren’t charged access fees. The Internet community and several alternative telephone providers have filed complaints against Bell to the PA Public Utility Commission.

headline: Gov. Bush's constituency
abstract: The U.S. Census Bureau predicts that by 2050 Hispanics will make up 25 percent of the U.S. resident population, so they will play an extremely important role in politics in the future; though their diversity could make it difficult to find a platform that can unite the entire group. According to the author, the Republican Party must clear up its image, and Texas Governor George W. Bush, who could appeal to Hispanic voters, may become the party’s next presidential candidate. The author, however, believes that the party cannot rely solely on Bush to secure Hispanic voters, so it must focus on education and other issues that could be appealing to the group.

headline: Restrictions are few for outside income
abstract: PA legislators are now the third highest paid state legislators in the nation, but the only rules regulating outside income are that legislators cannot be paid for giving speeches or receive bribes. In 1997, 155 out of 253 PA legislators reported outside sources of income. While they must disclose sources to the state Ethics Commission, they don’t have to report how much they were privately paid, and there is often know way of knowing whether they are paid by individuals or companies with an interest in state contracts, regulations or legislation. Legislative ethics in PA haven’t been a high priority since the state ethics law was rewritten in 1989.

headline: County to State: Thanks for money, where's the rest?
abstract: Washington County commisioners are set to receive $1.5 million from the state but are recieving a check for only $190,000. The anticipated projects are laid out but cannot be completed without the remaining promised funds.

headline: Abortion fight goes to D.C.
abstract: Pennsylvnia Attroeny General Robert Fisher urges Senate to pass legislation making it an offense to drive an underage female across state line for a no-parental-consent abortion.

headline: Removing the barriers   New state law provides new rights and protections for those under managed health-care plans
abstract: New legislation signed by Governor Tom Ridge last summer will go into effect at the beginning of next year, and it will give new rights to Health Management Organization (HMO) participants as well as many new protections. Under Act 68, there will now be a new appeals process, and one of the levels of appeals will be independent of the HMO provider. HMO providers will be required to allow women direct access to obstetric and gynecological specialists, there will be a an anti-gag clause requirement to ensure patients receive all pertinent information, and according to Paula Bussard, a senior vice president for the Hospital & HealthSystem Association of PA, the new law will clarify emergency care requirements, so people can use common sense in determining whether they should seek emergency care.

headline: Seavers to attend Penn symposium
abstract: Former President of Shippensburg University, Gilmore Seavers has been chossen to attend the first staewide symposium on William Penn's visions.

headline: In Montana, a Volt of the Blue - After State Deregulated, Utility Decides It Wants to Generate Different Business
abstract: Despite having reasonably cheap electric, the Montana Legislature approved deregulating the electric industry last year. However, Montana Power Company, the state’s largest utility, recently announced it would be selling off its generating facilities, causing many legislators to begin having second thoughts. A Department of Energy study predicted the Pacific Northwest can expect higher rates with deregulation, and many legislators are calling for a special legislative session to reverse or at least slow down the process of deregulation.

headline: SEPTA desperate to 'delight' suburbanites
abstract: With eight straight years of ridership declines, rapidly changing city and suburban demographics and an aging infrastructure that needs to be maintained, the Southeastern PA Transit Authority will have to make some big changes in the future to adapt and survive. SEPTA officials met with local leaders to discuss future options, and PA Representative Dave Steil suggested SEPTA could begin by providing rail transportation to New Jersey, which could help commuters who have to drive to Trenton to pick up a train for New York. In addition, SEPTA is considering several other options.

headline: Local 'White Out Day' fights drunken driving
abstract: Forty-four students who are members of the Youth to Youth anti-drug and anti-alcohol club painted white numbers on their faces, one every seven minutes to symbolize teenagers killed by drinking and driving as part of the annual White Out Day. They also were silent.

headline: Pennsylvania County Resume Its Growth - Recession now ended, Chester's lower costs plus roads prove lures.
abstract: Since the recession of the early 1990’s has ended, Chester County has again become one of the fastest growing counties in eastern PA, with population forecasts estimating an additional 80,000 residents by 2020 and plans approved last year to construct five million square feet of new commercial space. The county is conveniently located 45 minutes away from both Philadelphia and Harrisburg, and its location along the PA Turnpike and Route 30 makes it an attractive destination for businesses. The county’s two largest employers added buildings this year, and the article details other business activity, which is focused in the main corporate centers in West Chester, Devon, Exton, Downingtown, Coatesville and the tourism center in Brandywine Valley.

headline: Bridging the gaps in technology-and more
abstract: Last week, William Kennard, chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, spoke at the National Urban League convention in Philadelphia, and he spoke about the large digital divide that exists in the city and the nation. Far more white households have basic telephone service, which is needed for the Internet, than blacks and Hispanics, and there is also a huge divide between economic classes. However, the author is optimistic because of programs like the one going on at William Dick Elementary School, where teachers have volunteered their time teaching children valuable computer skills and have given them donated personal computers to take home.

headline: Gov. Inaugural Ball Scheduled For H'shey
abstract: The Four Tops, the Spinners and Mary Wilson and the Supremes will be performing a concert at the Hershey Lodge and Convention Center on January 18th to celebrate the inauguration of Governor Tom Ridge and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker. The swearing in ceremony and inaugural ball will be held the following day, and all Pennsylvanians are asked to donate nonperishable food for the "Inaugural Food Drive." There will also be luncheons to honor Ridge’s wife, Michele, and Schweiker.

headline: Rideg says crime shows need to bolster families
abstract: Givernonor Tom Ridge discusses several pressing criminal and welfare issues while fund raising in Berks County.

headline: Court rules tax unfair
abstract: State Supreme Court ruled  Montgomery Ciuntry personal property tax was unconsitituional, in the case brought by billionaire Walter Annenberg.

headline: Abortion foe working for God, he says Snell marks 10th year of protests, signs in yard
abstract: It has been 25 years since the U.S. Supreme Court legalized abortion, but Ed Snell is celebrating his 10th year as an anti-abortion activist. His home is decorated with anti-abortion material, and while he acknowledges the majority of the nation may not support his viewpoints, he is against all forms of abortion, including cases of rape and incest, and he claims to be doing "God’s work." The director of Planned Parenthood PA Advocates characterized Snell as a "hoodlum" who pretends to care about what is best for people, but Snell, who has been arrested on numerous occasions, continues his work and operates a telephone hotline aimed at convincing women not to get abortions.

headline: Researchers in limbo   Will AHERF problems hurt Allegheny General's research arm?
abstract: The Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation filed for bankruptcy, and many researches at Allegheny General Hospital are concerned that their parent foundation’s financial crisis will affect their researching opportunities. Doctor Richard Shannon, who is chairman of the Department of Medicine at Allegheny General, said the hospital’s research program is still strong, and cuts in research funding have been caused by industry trends, including falling reimbursements from health care. However, several researchers have left Allegheny General, and once promising programs, including a cancer research program, will not be receiving the funding that had been promised by the foundation.

headline: Recalling the lessons of a longtime educator - Ruth Wright Hayre became school board president. But former students and others say she never stopped teaching.
abstract: Ruth Hayre served Philadelphia’s public schools for over five decades, and she was the first black high school teacher, the first black principal, the first black female district superintendant and the first black woman named to the school board. Unfortunately, she passed away after battling a long illness, and many people from across the city paused to reflect on how many lives she had touched, including Mayor Ed Rendell and current School Superintendant David Hornbeck. In 1988, she donated much of her wealth towards the creation of a scholarship fund to pay college costs for 119 students at Wright and Kenderton Elementary Schools, and she will long be remembered for her contributions and dedication to Philadelphia’s schoolchildren.

headline: Light on savings  Here are the best deals on Electric Choice so far; but there's no reason to sign up right away
abstract: Pennsylvania’s new electric choice program was supposed to generate savings for customers by forcing electric companies to compete against one another; however, many companies that regulators thought would compete aren’t doing it, and there has been little effect for customers of Allegheny Power Incorporated and Duquesne Light Company. The PA Public Utility Commission has been disappointed with the results, but it’s still early, and there is no deadline for switching to a different company, so the situation could improve in the future. In addition, Energy Cooperative Association of PA is trying to expand into the Pittsburgh region, which could lead to rate reductions.

headline: SEPTA managers train to run rail lines amid strike
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority announced contingency plans to keep Philadelphia’s transit system running in case the Transport Workers Union orchestrates a strike if a new contract isn’t finalized, which would mark the first time the agency has ever continued service during a work stoppage. SEPTA would seek approval from city officials, including Mayor Ed Rendell and City Council President John Street, before operating city transit lines at the start of a walkout, but it has engaged in discussions with private security companies and has been training managers on how to run the lines. The union blasted SEPTA for its plans to continue offering service, and they warned the move would bring about a severe backlash from thousands of unions across the country.

headline: Lots of guns, but no nuts here
abstract: Opinion against Trent Lott who wants to arm the public against criminals stating this will end gun violence. Opinion tears apart his argument. Guns are like fire. They have their place, but it isn't on the street.

headline: Phila.'s new housing chief will have landmines to dodge
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell lured away Carl Greene from his position as head of the Detroit Housing Commission to take over the Philadelphia Housing Authority; however, many of Philadelphia’s tenant owners, who favored Fred Purnell for the position, have refused to meet with Greene, and things got even more dicey when an auditor sued him for sexual harassment. In Detroit, he had been remaking the image of public housing by demolishing over 4,000 homes, building 1,300 new units and filling the gap by awarding more public subsides for tenants to buy their own homes, which helped remove Detroit from the federal troubled list. The article provides some of Greene’s opinions on the problems that the Philadelphia Housing Authority is facing, and there’s no telling what kind of impact his unique managerial style will have in Philadelphia.

headline: Congress hangs up on Internet bill
abstract: If anything ought to be obvious, it's that classrooms should be wired to the Internet. Yet, scared by big telephone companies, Congress is on a rampage to undercut the federal program that accomplishes the task. President Clinton and Vice President Al Gore pressured Congress to include provisions in its huge 1996 Telecommunications Act to wire up the schools. Newt Gingrich added insurance that local telephone companies would have an advantage in getting into the long distance service business long before long distance companies could complete in local markets. Congress has been fighting over the little things instead of the big things.

headline: Gov. Ridge to name replacment
abstract: After the death of President Judge Bernard Schere, Govenor Tom Ridge and the Senate have 90 days to select a new President Judge.

headline: Ridge Accepts; Airport takes his name
abstract: Erie International Airport is scheduled for a name changed to honor Governor Tom Ridge.

headline: D.A. says her drug program won't die
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Lynne Abraham vowed to continue seeking $1.5 million for her Local Intensive Narcotic Enforcement program, even though the City Council passed Mayor Ed Rendell’s budget proposal without including any money for it. The budget passed with virtually no opposition, but Abraham was denied her funding largely in retaliation for her opposition to Common Pleas Court Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson’s nomination to become a U.S. District Court judge. Abraham, a possible mayoral candidate, was critical of the mayor and City Council for failing to approve additional funding, which she said would force her to shut down the program.

headline: Abortion has Ridge low-key in church Rights backer shuns Catholic speeches
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge, who is one of the most prominent elected Republicans of the Roman Catholic faith, has been criticized by many church members for his support of abortion rights. The Diocese of Erie, along with the National Conference of Catholic Bishops, have criticized pro-choice advocates, and they have issued a statement encouraging parishes and schools not to invite elected officials or candidates who support abortion rights to speak at Catholic-owned facilities. Ridge said he already began a practice of not accepting invitations to speak at Catholic events out of respect, and while he won’t change his stance on the issue, he does support Pennsylvania’s tough laws limiting legal abortions.

headline: Ridge may yet OK more mental health benefits
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge met with mental health advocacy groups, and he will begin reviewing mental health parity legislation that would increase mental health coverage and prevent health insurance companies from discriminating based on mental illness, which could provide a huge boost to efforts to pass a bill in the PA General Assembly. Congress passed the federal Mental Health Parity Act of 1996, but PA Representative Thomas Gannon, a sponsor of a state parity bill, said there are so many loopholes and exemptions in the bill that make it "meaningless." State Senator Joe Uliana is sponsoring separate legislation, but insurance companies and businesses are against any parity legislation because they believe it would increase costs substantially.

headline: Refunds for tuition account savers
abstract: PA Tuition Account Program is refunding many families for fees paid that are no longer necessary to maintaining the account.

headline: Lobbying campaign launched
abstract: Executives of Allegheny Energy Incorporated began lobbying to win approval for their proposed merger with Duquesne Light Company’s parent. According to Allegheny Energy Chairman Alan Noia, the merger would lead to lower rates for electric customers in southwestern PA. Allegheny Energy officials met with PA Senators Robert Jubelirer and Allen Kukovich, and Kukovich expressed support for the plan.

headline: SEPTA sides make strike preparations - Negotiations resumed, Mayor Rendell tried to speed things up. The deadline is midnight.
abstract: With citywide transit strikes set for midnight tonight, the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority and the union representing its workers are both preparing for a strike, which would impact about 450,000 passengers on an average weekday; however, Mayor Ed Rendell has urged the two sides to reach an agreement, and the City Council held a session on the issue. Negotiations have yet to focus on wages, and the article provides details on many of the key issues facing negotiators as well as a summary of what a strike scenario would mean for the city’s transit services. SEPTA’s operating officer implied that the recent vandalism of 30 buses is related to the labor dispute, and SEPTA is in the process of hiring security guards and training nonunion employees in preparation for a strike.

headline: Making peace in custody battles - Parents urged to find solutions outside of court
abstract: If a motion for child custody is filed in Monroe County, the parties involved must attend a four-hour co-parenting class, which teaches parents how divorce affects children and what they can do to make it easier on them. People filing for child custody are also required to attend a conciliation conference, where a judge helps facilitate communication between parents to develop a reasonable schedule that they can both agree on. Judge Linda Miller, who presides over Monroe County’s Domestic Relations Court, said she always hopes to reach an agreement between the parents, but if the case goes to court, she hears testimony from a number of different sources, including the children themselves in private, and she makes the best decision possible.

headline: Pike arts center money linked to stadium measure
abstract: The state has authorized millions of dollars for redevelopment assistance projects; however, it could be years before the projects receive money because Governor Ridge cannot move on any of them until the General Assembly authorizes more money for the redevelopment assistance fund. Governor Ridge’s administration has agreed to pay for one-third of the $300 million cost for new stadiums in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, as well as $175 million towards other unspecified projects throughout the state, but his proposal, which would allow the state to borrow about $500 million for redevelopment projects, failed to pass the state House. Other projects could rely on the ability to secure funding for the stadiums, including an arts center project in Pike County.

headline: Congress Moving Quickly to Try to Curb Cell Phone Abuses
abstract: Last week, the U.S. House passed a bill sponsored by Representative Sam Johnson that would outlaw cloning devices, which allow someone to intercept another person’s cellular phone information to be programmed into the new phone in order to have calls billed to the legal user’s account. The cell phone industry estimates it lost $650 million in revenue because of such devices, and Johnson was a victim. In response to an incident where a Florida couple taped a cell phone conversation between House Speaker Newt Gingrich and other Republicans, a separate bill was approved by the House Commerce Committee to make it illegal to modify electronic equipment to eavesdrop on cellular conversations.

headline: House, Senate work out HMO reform measure
abstract: Reimbursement for emergency room care, increased access to medical specialists and the establishment of an appeals process have been important topics of discussion in the PA Congress, but legislators have been unable to resolve them. Recent debate over amendments to legislation that did not make it to the floor for vote have focused on provisions that would allow patients to go directly to specialists without a referral, but Senator Stewart Greenleaf and others are hesitant to approve the amendments without considering costs. The issue could be an important topic in the upcoming gubernatorial campaign between Governor Tom Ridge, who has outlined 10 principles for patient protection, and Representative Ivan Itkin, who is strongly advocating the current legislation.

headline: Ridge and the GOP poised to do well in November
abstract: The low voter turnout in the primary election could possibly be attributed to Governor Ridge running unopposed and his widespread popularity; however, the editorial cautions the party not to take Democratic challenger Ivan Itkin lightly; though it does ultimately believe Ridge has done an extremely good job in office and deserves to be reelected. Lancaster Republicans won control of the mayor’s office and City Council last year, which has led to greater cooperation between the state and local governments, and in the editorial’s opinion, more could be done if Dave Schwanger can defeat incumbent Democratic Representative Mike Sturla to claim a seat in the state House. The editorial also praises PA Representative Katie True, who won her primary easily.

headline: Derry board wants occupation-tax relief for low earners - Township supervisors ask legislators to alter income level for exemptions
abstract: The Derry Township Board of Supervisors petitioned PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola and Representative Frank Tulli Jr. to raise the $5,000 yearly income threshold that qualifies someone to pay the occupational-assessment tax. At the current rate, many college students and people on fixed incomes have to pay $450 dollars of their income to the school district and township. Piccola said the Legislature is unlikely to consider the proposal unless it includes more comprehensive tax reform, but he did say school districts could opt to eliminate the occupational-assessment tax if they adopt a tax reform passed by the Legislature in April.

headline: Abortion plan blasted at breakfast: Former commissioner Huber steals spotlight meant for Lt. Gov. Mark Schweiker
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker and former Lancaster County commissioner Jim Huber spoke at a breakfast for the Lancaster County Americans for Christian Traditions In Our Nation. Schweiker focused on the accomplishments of the Ridge Administration but also voiced his displeasure over the PA Superior Court decision that ruled portions of Megan’s Law were unconstitutional. However, Huber stole the spotlight with his fiery speech against Planned Parenthood’s announcement that it would begin providing abortions in the city of Lancaster, and he urged people to unite and go to a meeting to support the decision to revoke Planned Parenthood’s building permit.

headline: Ridge right to press new 'bill of rights'
abstract: The author believes that Governor Tom Ridge is correct for pushing the Legislature to pass a "patients bill of rights" that would establish basic standards of care and coverage for all managed-care patients. One of every three Pennsylvanians is on such a plan, and the author believes that PA is falling behind other states and should incorporate the bill to shift control of individual patients’ care from insurers back to physicians.

headline: Rep. unveils Web site
abstract: PA Representative Rod Wilt unveiled his Web site.

headline: Marketplace meddling deserves to run out of gas
abstract: Independent gas stations have complained about being forced out of business by larger chains, and they have petitioned the PA Legislature, asking them to prevent all gas stations from selling gas below market value. The PA House Commerce Committee unanimously approved a bill sponsored by Representative John Gordnor to get involved; however, the authors believe the government should not interfere because criminalizing competition doesn’t make sense unless chains are engaging in price fixing, which nobody alleges. The authors believe gas should be treated like all other products, and they dispute claims that larger chains will be able to hike gas rates in the future by creating a monopoly over the gas market.

headline: SEPTA, Day One - Visiting GOP site committee shielded from TWU protest
abstract: After weeks of threats, 5,100 workers from the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority began their strike, leaving 400,000 daily commuters in search of alternate transportation, and contract negotiations aren’t expected to begin for at least a few days. The strikers were kept away from Republicans who were touring Philadelphia with Mayor Ed Rendell as part of their search for their national convention site. For the most part, the SEPTA shutdown was conducted in an orderly manner, and while SEPTA claims it’s in a financial crisis, union representatives believe these claims have been exaggerated.

headline: Marriage license warning urged
abstract: Representative Charles Dent's proposal for warning labels on marriage licenses is discussed from a domesic violence agency perspective.

headline: Plan B backed by RAD member
abstract: Daniel Griffin, member on the board, strongly supports the building of new stadiums in Allegheny County. Tax payer money will go to fund the project.

headline: Funds sought for high-tech forecasting
abstract: The network, which was installed in the wake of system failures during the 1972 Agnes Flood, includes 17 stream gauges and 40 rain gauges, all with satellite telemetry that can deliver data to forecasters.  However, the system has never enjoyed a dedicated funding source.  During the last few years, the agencies that operate the network --- the National Weather Service and the U.S. Geological Survey -- have seen funding fluctuate, ranging from $699,000 in 1996 to the current $1.12 million.

headline: Grants carry smell of political favors
abstract: In the race for governor, candidates must put their ideas for good government, their individual character and judgment to the test. In an ideal world, these would be the sole criteria for choosing though one would lead us. The reality is that a lot of money also gets thrown into the contest. Party loyalty also comes into play. Candidates need the support of their party's state Representatives and Senators to pull in the vote on election Day. An incumbent governor wields particular power regarding the last two factors. This violates the purity of the system.

headline: Ridge becomes Beatle face without a name
abstract: A political cartoon on the cover of New Republic magazine shows Govenor Tom Ridge but lists him as Govenor Tommy Thompson.

headline: Domocrats extending challenege
abstract: Democrat attack Govenor Tome Ridge and fellow Republicans with reasons to use the projected budget surplus to finally lower school property taxes.

headline: Abortion protest policy to be set
abstract: The ACLU represents a group of protesting clients who are being accussed of violating peacful protesting at abortion clinics.

headline: Ridge to sign bill regulating hospices
abstract: Hospices and their services will be licensed and tightly regulated under a measure expected to be signed into law by Gov. Tom Ridge Friday.  The governor's action would place Pennsylvania among 42 other states that license and regulate the facilities that provide services for terminally ill patients and their families  Sen. Allen Kukovich, a Democrat from Manor, was a prime co-sponsor of the bill along with state Sen. Mary Jo White, a Vanango County Republican.

headline: Report Undergraduates get shortchanged for research
abstract: The Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching released a report on 125 of the nation’s most prestigious universities, including Pittsburgh, Carnegie Mellon and Penn State, and the report found that many of these schools are neglecting their undergraduate population. The report claims many undergraduates are lured to these universities with promises of world-class professors and research, but many of these students end up being taught by poorly trained teaching assistants, and they never experience the research facilities. The report gives some recommendations, such as placing freshman taking the same courses in small living communities and encouraging undergraduates to take part in research with senior faculty; however, both Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon said they have already taken action and do not neglect their undergraduates.

headline: Missing this deadline could be dangerous
abstract: According to an opinion issued by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, the federal government is obligated to start disposing of spent nuclear fuel, which is stored at over 100 nuclear power plants throughout the country, by January 31, 1998. The authors of the editorial claim that President Clinton has failed to meet this deadline even though a surcharge for utility customers has raised about $14 billion towards the cause. The authors believe that the inability to deal with spent nuclear fuel poses a serious health concern, and they urge people to contact three U.S congressmen from PA or the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to urge them to begin constructing a storage facility in the Western U.S.

headline: Showdown over highway bill expected
abstract: The House and Senate are debating over what transportation projects to cover in the new six year transportation bill that was passed.

headline: Megan's law comes under scrutiny
abstract: Kenneth Kerekes Sr and his son wanted to make it clear the convicted sex offender wasn't welcome in their neighborhood. So when word spread that the ex-convict they intended to deliver their own brand of justice. They are now in jail for attacking a man they thought was the sex offender, but was not. This has caused criticism of Megan's Law which requires police release the name of sex offenders.

headline: Plan B backers remain undeterred in process
abstract: Supporters of Plan B, an $809 million development plan that would include millions of dollars towards the construction of new stadiums for the Pittsburgh Pirates and Steelers, vowed to continue pressing for the state to contribute, even though the plan suffered a setback by Governor Tom Ridge’s recent veto of a bill that could have allowed state funding. Lawmakers had complained that the bill contained hidden language that duped them into approving stadium financing. The Legislature failed to approve stadium financing in a separate bill, but supporters of Plan B hope the Legislature will have enough votes after it reconvenes in January to get a bill passed.

headline: Giants fight over local phone market
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge says he wants to bring true competition to the telecommunications industry, but until now, two major companies, Bell Atlantic-Pennsylvania and AT&T, have dominated the battle for the local phone market. AT&T has criticized Bell for controlling 98 percent of the local market, whereas Bell has said it’s open to local competition, but AT&T is blocking its access to the long-distance market. Two groups, including one headed by former state Senator William Lincoln, criticized Bell for failing to live up to its agreement to increase investment in the state in return for freedom from regulation, which Bell disputes, and the PA Public Utility Commission will mediate between AT&T and Bell to try to achieve the kind of local competition called for by the federal Telecommunications Act of 1996.

headline: Greenwood's GOP roots run deep   Seeking his fourth term in the House, Bucks County's congressman gained a reputation for a blend of social liberalism and fiscal conservatism
abstract: The beginning of the article is about how U.S. Representative Jim Greenwood, who is seeking his fourth term in the House against Democrat William Tuthill and three others, had his life shaped during childhood, where he first learned about the importance of family and began developing his Republican roots from his parents. Greenwood’s pro-choice and pro-environmental stances have moved him into a moderate Republican coalition in Congress, and he has developed a reputation for intermixing socially liberal policies with fiscally conservative policies. Greenwood refuses to accept contributions from political action committees, and one political science professor said he is one of the few moderates who could be elected to a leadership position for the Republican Party in Congress.

headline: Ridge brings Chamber good news on worker's comp
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge became the first governor in over 40 years to address the Greater Northeast Chamber of Commerce, where he announced that PA led the nation in cutting worker’s compensation rates. The chamber had lobbied four years ago for reform to curb skyrocketing costs, and the legislature passed a bill in response. The audience clearly supported Ridge’s suggestion that the state Department of Environmental Resources should be more cooperative with businesses, and Ridge also spoke about the controversy involving whether the state should pay more to fund Philadelphia schools.

headline: Dunn refuses approval of all-white committee
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Larry Dunn refused to approve a four member, all white committee nominated to carve the county into council districts. Fellow commissioners Mike Dawida and Bob Cranmer approved the nominations in order to see the task completed by the October 23rd deadline. Dunn is insisting the members reveal their fifth nominee, however the members are refusing. Dunn maintains he just wants diversity, however, critics say Dunnn has merely placed home rule in jeopardy. State rep. John Maher says he will introduce legislation to extend the deadline

headline: Abraham launched sneak attack against the judge
abstract: The resounding rejection by Philadelphia and National Lawyers Association of District Attorney Lynne Abraham's last minute sneak attack to destroy the appointment of the first African American female judge in Pennsylvania, has revealed Abraham's insidious motives and her disregard for the truth.  Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson's outstanding qualifications for the historic appointment to the federal court have been once more certified, after a careful review of 50 cases that were selected by Abraham as examples of her claim that Massiah-Jackson is not qualified for the appointment.  One of Abraham's deceptions is the pretense that a state association of district attorney's initiated the opposition to Massiah-Jackson and that they have played a major role in the decision to oppose her.

headline: Ridge wounded over nursing-homes charges
abstract: Auditor General Robert Casey criticizes Givernor Tom Ridge on his failure to respond to the allegations of nursing home abuse and neglect.

headline: Ridge program targets high-tech college grads
abstract: From now to 2005, over 10,000 computer related jobs are expected to be created in PA each year, but PA colleges are only graduating about 1,500 students a year in computer related fields, which prompted Governor Tom Ridge to take action. Ridge’s Sci-Tech Scholars program proposal would give up to $3,000 a year for three years to students majoring in technology related fields, but the students must promise to take a job in PA after graduation. Another proposal, the GI Bill for the New Economy, would provide scholarship money to students and workers who pursue associate’s degrees in high technology fields.

headline: PECO seeks ruling on deregulation issues
abstract: PECO Energy Company is hoping the Public Utility Commission will delay their deadline for allowing customers to swicth electric companies.

headline: Shuster bids goodbye with mixed emotions
abstract: Representative Bud Shuster helped negotiate a deal that elimated Conrail, but he had strong feelings about the situation.

headline: Megan's Law justifiably survives test
abstract: The Supreme Court rejected a constitutional challenge to the New Jersey law, which requires authorities to tell communities the whereabouts of convicted sex offenders. Rather than rule on an appeal of the law filed by sex offenders, the court simply decided to reject the appeal and leave open the possibly that it may some day fully preview and rule on the notification measure.

headline: Plan B battle goes to Capitol - Backers and opponents hit the lobbying trail
abstract: Several top officials from the Pittsburgh area are expected to travel to Harrisburg to lobby the PA Legislature to approve Governor Tom Ridge’s proposal to raise the state’s debt ceiling in order to provide funding for new stadium projects in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia. As of now, the proposal doesn’t have enough support to pass, especially due to the lack of support from mast central PA legislators, and if it doesn’t get approved before the current lame-duck session ends, it will likely be even tougher to pass once the Legislature reconvenes in January. Pittsburgh’s Plan B is counting on $300 million in state funding towards the expansion of its convention center and the construction of new stadiums for the Steelers and Pirates.

headline: Government-owned cable a success elsewhere
abstract: As Newtown Township supervisors look to start a local government cable TV service, they should be encouraged by the success of government owned Glasgow cable service in Kentucky. Glasgow competes with Comcast, and after 9 years, has just begun to break even. Comcast has slashed rates to remain competitive, but residents agree the service of their local company is better. It appears that localizing cable operations and running them by the government is much less about savings than it is about service. Newtown Township is looking for a private company to run its cable system.

headline: Grow must go through York County to get to DC
abstract: In two days, York County Republicans will pick the winner of their 19th Congressional District primary election and tell us a lot about the changing character of one of the misdate's fastest-growing areas. In 1996, York County, which nearly three of the district's every five Republicans registered to vote, rescued 24-year incumbent US Representative Bill Goodling from a shocking upset. Challenger Charlie Grow won his home turf by 1,000 votes. On Tuesday will find out if the voters have changed.

headline: Ridge can go higher
abstract: Bill McKinney, who attended school with Governor Ridge in Erie, claims Ridge has an overwhelming advantage over PA Representative Ivan Itkin, his only credible challenger, because Itkin has far less money to spend, and the Democratic Party is selling him short. Despite these advantages, McKinney hopes that Ridge is being careful to ensure that no mistakes are made by him or his supporters which could cost him in the future, but ultimately, he thinks Ridge will be counting votes to see how much he wins by rather than if he wins. He claims to be bothered by Ridge’s refusal to guarantee he’d complete his second term due to vice presidential aspirations because he believes vice president is a dead end position, and he feels that Ridge has the abilities to someday become President of the U.S.

headline: Dunn to lose SPRPC position
abstract: The Regional Planning Commission is scheduled to vote out Larry Dunn and replace him with Mike Dawida.

headline: Affirmative action faces extinction in Washington - Voters could end state programs for minorities, women
abstract: On November 3, citizens of Washington state will vote on Initiative 200, a referendum trying to ban affirmative action, and the results could have a ripple effect across the rest of the nation. John Carlson, an Internet talk-show host, is leading efforts to pass the referendum because he believes the state has no right to grant preferential treatment to anyone based on gender or race; however, his opponents have raised far more money and have the support of Governor Gary Locke, U.S. Senator Daniel Evans, most newspapers in the state and several key corporations and advocacy groups. Lobbying efforts against the referendum have focused on females, which studies show have benefited significantly from affirmative action.

headline: Rising costs create problems for managed health plans
abstract: Over 80 percent of employees are in managed health care programs, but despite a growing economy, the number of uninsured Americans is growing by about 1 million each year. Many states have developed a "bill of rights" to protect those in managed health care programs, but the states cannot help the 48 million people in other plans that fall under federal law, which U.S. Representative Charlie Norwood has proposed legislation in response to. The editorial’s opinion is that the Norwood’s legislation would pass if key leaders, including Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, would get on board, but the bill would still be imperfect and some people would be sacrificed by receiving limited care.

headline: Ridge releases more than $19 million for Penn State Projects
abstract: Governor Ridge announced the release of over $19 million from the state budget for Penn State projects. Penn State Harrisburg will receive 14.6 million for library and classroom constructions, and the University Park campus will receive several million towards a number of different projects.

headline: Peco thrives on wholesale deals - Its limber Power Team finds buyers for spare electricity
abstract: Philadelphia Energy Company’s Power Team has been able to take advantage of the deregulated energy market and Peco’s low cost, efficient nuclear power plants, and thanks to the Power Team’s strong performance, Peco reported an all time high in earnings for the third quarter. The Power Team specializes in making deals for the sale of energy on the wholesale market, and it has been able to sell excess power in the out-of-state market for lucrative profits. While the Power Team has been involved in some controversies, it has helped Peco thrive, and Peco intends to increase its generating capacity by investing in nuclear plants such as Three Mile Island.

headline: Shuster comes through with a cool billion
abstract: US Rep. Bud Shuster helped to award the PA Department of Transportation with $1.3 billion a year for the next six after talking with PA Transportation secretary Bradley Mallory about the state's need for federal funds. Shuster used his position on the transportation committee to help secure federal funding for about 150 special projects in the state. This will allow the state to shift some projects from state funding to federal funding.

headline: Minors and booze major concerns
abstract: The problem of underage drinking in the Far Northeast won't be solved overnight, but some people started to come up with a few solutions last week. Lt. Dave Marnien hosted an Aug 23 meeting on the topic at the 8th Police District. All agree underage drinking is a concern. It is happening outside of bars, so we need to attack it differently.

headline: Plan B gets green light
abstract: Allegheny County gets the needed six council votes to pass a $170 million taxpayer funded project to deveolp two new stadiums. The RAD board was able to pas after asking one member to step down and replacing the member with a Plan B suppporter.

headline: Governments at all levels trying to deal with Year 2000
abstract: One of the primary functions of state local governments is to ensure that its citizens have reliable electricity, pure drinking water, working sewer systems and functioning traffic signals, but this could all be threatened by a computer glitch known as the Year 2000 problem. Because the computers were made to see years is double digits in 2000 the year will be seen as 00 and computers will freeze up. PA is one of the only states on the way to becoming Y2K compliant.

headline: Grow says he will run again
abstract: Hampden Twp. Attorney Charlie Grow doesn't see his defeat to US Representatives Bill Goodling in the GOP primary as a loss, just a delay. Grow vowed to run again for 19th Congressional seat in 2000. The major factor in his loss was Goodling's 24-year tenure and his seniority in Congress.

headline: Ridge declines to discuss resignation of physical general
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge decided not to disclose the details behind the resignation of Physician General Wanda Filer, who often clashed with the administration and complained about how she was being treated. Ridge said he would search for a replacement, and the PA Senate unanimously adopted a resolution congratulating Filer for her service. Senator Robert Mellow criticized Ridge’s treatment of Filer and introduced a proposal to make physician general an independent post, which Ridge opposes.

headline: Ed wants to give back - Sets biggest wage-tax cut in budget, more money for schools
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell presented his budget to the City Council, and in addition to a 2.2 percent wage tax cut, it includes a proposal to begin taxing suburban businesses the same as businesses which are located inside Philadelphia. The budget, which drew positive reviews from Council members, won’t require service cuts, increases spending to allow the Police Department’s number of officers to reach 7,000 and provides money for after-school programs and health centers. It also gives the financially troubled School District a $15 million grant; however, Rendell said it’s not as much as the district needs, and he again asked the state for more funding.

headline: Agreement reached on disabled access
abstract: Attorney General Janet Reno announces a settlement with Wendy's Fast Food chains, that will allow better access for disabled persons in resturants.

headline: Rival plans heat debate on HMO reform
abstract: Backers fiercely defended two separate plans yesterday intended to protect patients from cost-conscious health care plans, setting up what could be one of the more politically charged debates during the remaining days of Congress.  President Clinton and congressional Democrats have pushed aggressively for a "patient bill of rights" intended to help consumers deal with HMOs' efforts to save money.  Democrats contend that Senate Republicans, who have kept the Democrats' measure from reaching the floor, began crafting their own version only after they realized their failure to take up the matter could cost votes in this fall's congressional elections.

headline: Ridge signs law to put tax reform into effect
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge sign a tax reform law that will gives school districts tax collecting options.

headline: Peco to eliminate 700 jobs in next 12 to 18 months
abstract: In response to the loss of its electric monopoly, Peco Energy Corporation will cut up to 700 jobs in the next 12 to 18 months. The PA Public Utility Commission rejected an agreement Peco had made with consumer groups that would have given the company $6 billion in stranded costs, assets that are expected to decline in value because of competition, and would have allowed Peco to maintain its monopoly for several more years. Peco is challenging the PUC’s ruling to award only $4.9 billion in stranded costs, and many of the layoffs will include workers in the company’s local distribution division.

headline: Shuster hosts hearing
abstract: Representative Bud Shuster holds a hearing for a listening session about a new act for the transportation department will which allocate funding for the next 6 years.

headline: More Schools Using Dogs to Sniff Out Drugs
abstract: A growing number of educators in the Washington area and across the nation are bringing drug-sniffing dogs into schools or are considering the idea as a tool to combat the recent rise in teenagers' use of illegal drugs. DC school officials launched an effort to search as many as two high schools a week. The searches were halted a year ago when police were told to focus on street crime.

headline: Plans for 'landing' park visitors in the works
abstract: Lawmakers pass legislation to continue the commission to promoting, preserving, and improving the Delaware and Lehigh National Corridor.

headline: GTE, Bell Atlantic Close to Merger - $50 Billion Deal Would Join Giants
abstract: Bell Atlantic Corporation is close to an agreement to buy GTE Corporation for over $50 billion, which would create the second largest phone company in the country, with combined revenue of $53 billion and service extending to 40 states and the District of Columbia. There have been over a dozen multibillion dollar U.S. telecommunications mergers since Congress passed the Telecommunications Act of 1996, and critics have argued the law has led to consolidation rather than competition, while industry executives have argued bigger companies will be able to provide services at a lower cost. U.S. Representative W.J. Tauzin blamed the merger on the Federal Communications Commission, which has barred Bell from getting into long-distance business, and PA Attorney General Mike Fisher will be investigating the merger in order to determine whether PA will approve the deal.

headline: Gruitza holds on to his seat for a 10th term in the House
abstract: PA Representative Michael Gruitza won reelection handily over Republican challenger James Lumpp, and he will represent the 7th District in the PA House for a tenth term. Lumpp only won two precincts, and his wife thanked his supporters and said the final vote represented the strength of the Democratic Party in the Shenango Valley. Gruitza promised to make economic development and the creation of jobs his top priority.

headline: Ridge draws mixed reviews
abstract: After four years under Gov. Tom Ridge, is Franklin County better off?  It depends on your perspective.  Local business leaders, police, and farmers offer an emphatic yes; educators have mixed feelings, while environmentalists and union workers give the governor a thumbs down.  The split is the result of an administration some say has focused primarily on making Pennsylvania friendlier to business.

headline: Farmers lobby for property tax break
abstract: Elliot Lengel, a dairy farmer from Mercer County, was at the Capitol to lobby Pennsylvania’s legislators to include farm property in the definition of a homestead when they draft bills to reduce local property taxes. Local tax reform has become a legislative priority since voters approved the homestead amendment last November to allow residential and commercial property to be taxed at different rates. State Representative Stan Saylor has introduced a bill that would allow some parts of farms to be included in the homestead definition, which would make them eligible for the homestead exemption.

headline: AIDS kills in silence in black communities
abstract: Racical disparity is dicussed in terms of causes and effects in African American communities. Proposed solutions and alternative to reducing the disparity are discussed, including Presdent Bill Clinton's propsed plan.

headline: Rural health group honors Baker as to Legislator
abstract: PA Representative Matt Baker was recognized by the PA Rural Health Conference as the 1998 Legislator of the Year. Baker helped establish the Partnership for Community Health and was instrumental in securing a state grant to help pay for the construction of a new hospital wing. He’s hosted a public hearing in Wellsboro with the House Health and Human Services Committee, and he played a key role in seeking approval for a Life Flight helipad.

headline: Ridge voucher plan: Private school for all
abstract: The Ridge administration, fresh off its landslide reelection victory, is proposing a voucher program that would offer children in "academically bankrupt school districts," such as Philadelphia, the option of attending a private school. If the bill passes the PA Legislation, which is a big question mark, it would almost certainly face a flurry of court challenges and would escalate tension between city schools and the state. Ridge’s pilot program could cost hundreds of millions of dollars over five years, and under the proposal’s provisions, it would theoretically allow every single student in Philadelphia to go to private school.

headline: Peco will reply to herbicide concerns
abstract: Local officials from Collegeville and Skippack have sent letters to the Philadelphia Electric Company in opposition to the company’s use of herbicides. Peco officials acknowledged that the use of herbicides in controlling growth has caused some damage; however, they argue that herbicides are a far better alternative than simply cutting down whatever vegetation threatens overhead power lines, and the chemicals have been approved by the Environmental Protection Agency and the state Department of Agriculture. Nevertheless, Peco has offered to meet with concerned local municipalities to discuss the issue.

headline: Shuster leads W.Pa. delegation in 1997 campaign fund raising
abstract: U.S. Representative Bud Shuster raised about $750,000 and spent about $500,000 last year, according to the Federal Election Commission, which was significantly more than any other members of the House from Western PA. New Enterprise Stone & Lime Company, which produces material for road construction, continued its support of Shuster, the House Transportation chairman, by giving him $7,000 last fall. The fund-raising/spending reports for Representatives John Peterson, William Coyne, Ron Klink, Frank Mascara, Mike Doyle, John Murtha and Phil English are also provided in the article.

headline: Mountain cabin fire kills at least 11 in Centre County - High school students, graduates are feared dead
abstract: At least 11 campers died from a fire that swept through a mountain cabin in Centre County, and the majority of the campers are believed to be current high school students and graduates of Line Mountain School District. The school was opened yesterday to help students cope. State police have yet to confirm the cause of the fire, but there’s speculation that it was caused by a gas furnace explosion.

headline: Players work Capitol during Stadium debate
abstract: PA Gov. Tom Ridge has promised to secure a third of the funds necessary to build four sports stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh through public funding. However, the measure is opposed by members of the GOP. Yet, Ridge does not want to be the Governor that lost major league teams to another state. Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy is trying to gain support from fellow party members whom he earlier alienated. Allegheny County Commissioner Mike Dawida found lobbying equally difficult. House Maj. Leader John Perzel has shown only lukewarm support for the measure.

headline: If you like, you can use your new area code now
abstract: Western Pa has just receieved the new area code 724. New phone books will have the new area code listed.

headline: Gubernatorial candidate campaigns in Indiana
abstract: PA Representative Ivan Itkin, who has chosen to forgo his 14th term in the House in order to run for Governor, still remains hopeful about his chances of winning, citing that 75% of the population recognizes his name now, and Constitutional Party candidate Peg Luksik could steal votes away from incumbent Governor Ridge. While visiting Indiana County, Itkin criticized Ridge for providing $3 billion in tax breaks for big corporation while raising taxes for the average citizen. Itkin said he would put money from growing budget surpluses towards increased funding of schools, which would reduce property taxes.

headline: Ridge has yet to replace state physician general
abstract: Eight months after the departure of Dr. Filer from her position as sate physician general, Gov. Tom Ridge has yet to select her replacement. Ridge officials say they are interviewing candidates and want to fill the position soon. But some say the state needs a top public-health doctor and Ridge has taken too long finding a replacement.

headline: Flaherty assails foundation on charter
abstract: City Controller Tom Flaherty alledges that home rule charter proponents sent out biased literature, not independent literature, on the proposed charter.

headline: All the fuss in Congress is about religion's role
abstract: The US Congress will address key legislation to determine the US domestic and international policy towards religion, including The Religious Liberty Protection Act, The Freedom from Religious Persecution Act, and the Religious Freedom Amendment. The first attempts to shield religious practices from governmental interference. The second creates an Office of Religious Persecution within the US State Department to determine whether other nations comply with standards for religious tolerance. The third amends the constitution to provide for more comprehensive religious tolerance.

headline: Sacred Heart shows off plans for community health care center
abstract: With only few remaining row homes and a possible eminent domain proceeding standing in the way, Sacred Heart Hospital officials Monday showed off artist's drawings of the Allentown hospital's $12.5 million Primary Care Center.  U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter, who helped secure $2 million in federal funds for the project, visited the site and thanked the hospital for its commitment to the poor of the community.

headline: Ridge wants $100 million to improve child literacy
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker, who are both seeking re-election, travelled separately to six cities in PA to promote a program aimed at improving reading proficiency for children before they reach fourth grade. According to a national survey, 39 percent of Pennsylvania’s 4th graders are below basic reading proficiency levels, and the percentage is more than double for students in financially disadvantaged schools. Ridge will ask the state Legislature to spend $100 million for his "Read to Succeed" program.

headline: PECO customer urged to get with the program
abstract: PECO Energy Co. has sent out forms to all customers that will help customers choose their electric supplier.

headline: Shuster to unveil transportation bill
abstract: Us Rep. Bud Shuster, chairman of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, is to unveil a $217 billion transportation bill today. A spokesman for Shuster said he hopes the House will pass the bill by April 1. Shuster wants the bill on the President's desk for signing by Easter. The bill may mean more money for PA and several Blair County road projects. The new legislation is known as the Building Efficient Surface Transportation and Equity Act, or BESTEA.

headline: Myth vs. Fact
abstract: Myths and Facts about sexual predators.

headline: Property values ordered higher
abstract: Judge Stanton Wettick orders Allegheny County to increase property values on homes within the county by 2% in 1999 and 2000. The effect should be to address properties that are both under and over assesed, but the proposal is taking some criticism .

headline: Midstate hurts for expert workers
abstract: One of the major themes in the recent Envision discussions on workforce in PA has been the need to fill positions in information technology firms, and Kevin Harter of the Technology Council of PA estimates the industry is about 11 percent understaffed. The President of Stoner Associates called on local firms to offer more internships and opportunities for students to test out jobs in the industry; however, this might not be enough since most college graduates in the region are lured away to more enticing areas in other states. According to the Information Technology Association of America, there are 346,000 vacancies in staff of software and computer technology firms throughout the nation, so the industry is struggling nationwide to fill positions.

headline: Habay for the House A competent incumbent who likes to have it both ways
abstract: The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette gives its endorsement to incumbent PA Representative Jeff Habay over Democratic challenger Tom Sunday to represent the 30th Legislative District in the PA House. While the paper does criticize Habay for trying to play both sides to gain a political advantage at times, they believe he is much more qualified than Sunday.

headline: Ridge Hosts Picnic, Mingles With Crowds At Conneaut Lake Park
abstract: Governor Ridge and his family spoke with residents from the area during a picnic at Conneaut Lake Park. He also addressed the crowd from a podium, where he spoke about lowering taxes, welfare reform, new academic standards in public schools, lowering the cost of workman’s compensation and computerized background checks for firearm purchasers. In his bid for reelection, Ridge recently received endorsements from Harrisburg Mayor Steven Reed and the National Rifle Association.

headline: For some jobs, Crossin is man to know
abstract: Claire Kelley, executive director of the Coalition of Luzerne County Taxpayers, was extremely critical of the County Board of Commissioners for allowing Commissioner Frank Crossin to provide the administrator of the Valley Crest nursing home with names of job candidates for over 150 positions without posting the jobs publicly. She also told the commissioners she expects to see a tax rollback next year because of a 25 percent increase in property taxes last year. County Chairman Tom Makowski defended the board against Kelley’s criticism, and in other board business, the commissioners are still trying to decide how to trim down some of requests made by over 50 county departments for the upcoming budget.

headline: Analysts: State lacks female legislators - Officials laying groundwork for women in politics
abstract: PA ranks 45th in the nation in the number of state legislators, and it has no female members in the U.S. House. State Representative Pat Carone attributed this to the state’s campaign laws, which offer powerful advantages to incumbents, and state Senator Melissa Hart said it’s more difficult for women to raise money, while Representative Jane Orie said women often don’t have as much time as men because of family obligations. The Women’s Network of the National Conference of State Legislators believes there are still too few female legislators across the entire nation, and Pennsylvania’s Commission for Women and many state lawmakers are working to get more women elected.

headline: Sale of 6 hospitals called off
abstract: The blockbuster deal that would have dealt six Allegheny hospitals to a for-profit company was declared dead yesterday when both sides acknowledged that they had failed to agree on price and other key points.  The joint announcement by Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation and Vanguard Health Systems Inc. came just a day before the proposed hospital's sale was to be the subject of a public hearing in Philadelphia organized by the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office, which overseas the sale of nonprofit institutions.

headline: Ridge's Library Deal Good Start  Equipment Upgrades Important, But Operating Funds Essential
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has proposed increasing funding for libraries by $11 million, but most of the money would go towards connecting libraries to the Internet and expanding funding for Access PA, which gives libraries money for lending books to people outside their areas of service. The authors of the editorial claim PA libraries are among the most underfunded in the nation, and the government is failing to meet commitments it has already made. While they agree Ride’s proposal is a good starting point, they hope the state Legislature adopts a broader spending plan proposed by Representative Mike Veon.

headline: PECO Energy is big winner in deal
abstract: Electric deregulation is moving forward in Pennsylvnia and the Public Utilities Commission and PECO Energy are said to be the biggest areas benefited.

headline: Shuster works out deal on highways
abstract: US Rep. Bud Shuster has outlined several key components of a $200 billion, six-year transportation funding bill he wants to see approved. These include a guarantee that gas taxes will only be used for transportation, tougher punishments for states that don't strengthen drunk driving standards, and billions for "high priority", or pork, projects. A House-Senate compromise has cut the original funding allocated from $217 to $200 billion.

headline: National death rate among teen drivers
abstract: A chart depicts the national fatality rate among teen drivers. It is rising among those ages 17-19, and declining among those age 16, and 20 years or older.

headline: Reed unveils City Towers upgrade plans
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed announced plans to renovate and upgrade the 25-story City Towers building, which has been vacant since being condemned by the city in 1994 after a water-main broke. Reed also criticized local banks for refusing to lend money for the renovation project. A new partnership of owners will spend $9 million to refurbish the apartment complex, and tenants could be moving back in as soon as this spring.

headline: Monitor checks weather in five are counties
abstract: Armstrong, Butler, Clarion, Forest and Venango Counties will now have access to 24-hour monitoring of weather conditions and storm warning because of the dedication of a weather radio transmission tower at Six Points. Central Electric offered its tower for the addition of a radio antenna, and PA Senator Mary Jo White and Representative Howard Fargo played a key role in securing $200,000 from the 1997-1998 budget towards the project. In addition, the article includes a photo of Fargo speaking with Larry Adams, manager of Central Electric, and Teresa Rossi, manager of the National Weather Service bureau in Pittsburgh.
