headline: Haley's ticket is government downsizing, taxes
abstract: John Haley is running for the 146th District seat in the PA House as a Libertarian candidate, and he claims that a key part of the Libertarian message is reducing the size of the government and the taxes which are used to fund it. He is realistic about his chances of winning the election, yet he remains optimistic and criticized the principles of both Republicans and Democrats. He is against taxpayers being forced by the government to pay for imposed social programs, such as welfare and public education, he favors sales taxes over income taxes, and he is an advocate for protecting the environment; though he does not favor the use of tax money to purchase public land.

headline: Ridge leading Itkin, 57- 22%
abstract: Governor Ridge with a chance to win a second term by a landslide margin, holds a seemingly insurmountable lead over Democrat Ivin Itkin and conservative third-party candidate Peg Luksik, according to the PA Poll. He is drawing impressive support from all parties.

headline: George, Slocum comment on property tax legislation
abstract: A tax-reform proposal passed the PA General Assembly that would allow voters to approve a shift in local property taxes to increases in income taxes and would require voters to approve any tax increases above the rate of inflation; however, state Representative Camille George was harshly critical of the bill, claiming it provides no tax relief. State Senator Bill Slocum voted in favor of the bill because he believes it gives local voters more choices and protections, whereas other legislators expressed disappointed that the state didn’t use its projected $500 million surplus to provide more tax relief. The bill also included a controversial provision to provide a slight tax credit for suburban Philadelphia residents who work in the city, which state Senator Roy Afflerbach opposed.

headline: Another reason to leave Allegheny County
abstract: Past African American state leaders have never come out of Allegheny County. Passage of the proposed home rule charter might make certain no African American is represented in Allegheny County government.

headline: Save it
abstract: Last week, Drexel University rejected Tenet Healthcare Corporation’ s deal to manage Allegheny University’s School of Public Health, and it remains unclear whether they will be able to find a partner before the November 5 rescheduled sale. The author, PA Representative Dwight Evans, believes Governor Tom Ridge should pledge continued government support. If a partner cannot be found, Evans argues, the state must fund the medical school to protect its jobs, student opportunities and research activities.

headline: Rivals argue education yardsticks  Some midstate educators back Ridge's standards over outcome-based scheme
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge claims to have gotten rid of outcome-based education in favor of student performance standards for reading, writing and math, whereas Peg Luksik, who is challenging Ridge as the Constitutional Party’s candidate, believes that Ridge simply gave outcome-based education a different name. Most educators support Ridge’s move to standards and believe the new standards make it easier for teachers to fit them into their curriculum; however, some do agree with Luksik that outcome-based education was essentially just renamed. Luksik is against outcome-based education because she sees it as federal attempts to "brainwash students," and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin agrees that the language isn’t much different, but he believes standards are better.

headline: Peco in trouble? Well, not exactly
abstract: Peco recently announced shocking cuts that sent its stock plummeting 14 percent yesterday, but the author believes they made exactly the right move. He believes Peco had to do some serious restructuring to improve its standing and adapt to the deregulating market. However, he is disappointed that Peco is trying to lay the blame on the PA Public Utilities Commission, and he fears Governor Tom Ridge will change the commission’s leadership, which could threaten electric deregulation and the potential for lower costs for consumers.

headline: Signs to give Capitol Beltway an identity
abstract: Like Interstate 465 around Indianapolis and Interstate 695 around Baltimore, Harrisburg has a beltway.  The problem is no one views it as such.  In the 30 months since it was created with completion of the Route 581 Connector, most motorists still see themselves as they did 20 years ago -- driving on Interstate 81 or Route 581, not a beltway.  The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation agrees the 26-mile loop needs one identity and today will unveil "Capital Beltway" signs during a construction briefing at the District 8 headquarters on Herr Street.

headline: New commissioner strategizes on crime
abstract: The Philadelphia Tribune interviewed Philadelphia’s new police commissioner, John Timoney, and the article includes his responses to several questions on what the African American community can expect and how he plans to deal with the city’s crime. Timoney, who served 29 years in the New York City Police Department, only saw himself as an outsider to Philadelphia in a geographical sense, and he didn’t see it as a problem. He reaffirmed his commitment to minorities, discussed some of New York City’s crime-fighting measures, including six or seven different strategies that were developed, and he planned to first conduct an analysis of Philadelphia’s crime problems, followed by the implementation of a deployment plan.

headline: Renovo awarded $20,000 grant for industrial park
abstract: According to PA Representative Mike Hanna, a $20,000 grant was awarded to the Clinton County Economic Partnership for repairs at Renovo industrial park. The grant was awarded by the PA Department of Community and Economic Development.

headline: PUC adds three area codes in eastern part of state
abstract: Due to the increased demand for telephone numbers, the PA Public Utilities Commission will add three new area codes to PA next year. The area code covering central and northeastern parts of the state will be divided in April, and two new area codes will be added to southeastern PA in June 1999.

headline: Hanging together
abstract: A bipartisan and interracial coalition of five legislators, nicknamed "The Gang of Five" has changed the PA Legislature's attitude toward issues confronting Philadelphia. They have helped to push through the creation of charter schools, a controversial law providing for state takeover of the city's schools, 24 laws aimed at quality of life, and a $500,000 audit of city school finances. Mayor Gov. Rendell does not seem to know how to react. Members of the "gang" include Rep. John Perzel, John Taylor, George Kenny, Dwight Evans and Anthony Williams.

headline: Ridge makes run official: Family tax at center of bid for re-election
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge officially kicked off his re-election campaign in front of 500 supporters, and he drew a good response from the crowd after announcing his proposal to eliminate the state income tax for families whose incomes are less than $25,000; though the crowd was less enthusiastic about his plan to establish the PA Achievement Awards. Ridge told the crowd about the many accomplishments of his administration during the past four years. There are, however, some promises that Ridge has not delivered on yet, and there was a scary moment when Dauphin County Commissioner Russ Sheaffer collapsed.

headline: Government officials, political leaders to air Schuylkill County Vision project
abstract: PA Representative David Argall invited the 124th District’s mayors, borough council members, township supervisors, school board members and party committee members to a meeting in Tamaqua to discuss the Schuylkill County Vision plan. Argall wants to hear their ideas and hopes for bipartisan cooperation on the project.

headline: Anti-mask law flawed, lawmaker says
abstract: PA Representative Benjamin Ramos introduced a bill that would make it illegal for anyone to wear a mask, hood or robe to hide their identity; however, a House lawyer said the bill’s current form would not stand up to a constitutional challenge. On the behalf of the Ku Klux Klan, the American Civil Liberties Union successfully challenged a Bedford County ordinance prohibiting them from demonstrating while wearing masks on public property, and in 1995, the U.S. Supreme Court reaffirmed the right to demonstrate anonymously. However, an ordinance passed the Georgia Supreme Court in 1951, and PA Representative Thomas Caltagirone believes PA could impose some restrictions without violating the constitution.

headline: Scrutiny of nursing homes expands
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge’s budget office is planning an audit of the PA Health Department’s new nursing home complaint resolution system, and the U.S. General Accounting Office is preparing to release a national audit of nursing home oversight for several states, including PA. Ridge’s budget office will be looking into the new system that was initiated in response to an audit by state Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. Casey’s nursing home task force, appointed in June, presented him with a list of recommendations, but any legislation would face tough odds in the Republican controlled state Legislature.

headline: Robbins lauded for legislation regarding agents
abstract: Yvette Kane is writing this letter on behalf of the PA Department of State to thank PA Senator Robert Robbins for his work in passing Senate Bill 425, which was signed into law by Governor Tom Ridge last week. Kane is pleased that the law will give the State Athletic Commission the power to register athletic agents who are trying to recruit Pennsylvania’s athletes. The law will also allow the commission to investigate complaints, and overall, Kane believes it will offer athletes protection from being taken advantage of by agents.

headline: Pennzoil Quaker St. join forces
abstract: Two of the oldest names in the motor oil business with roots deep in the heart of PA's oil fields will become one through Oil City and other northwestern PA communities. Pennzoil and Quaker State announced this morning that they have agreed to create a new publicly traded company by combining the motor oil, refined products and franchise operations of Pennzoil with those of Quaker State. A new name for the company has not been selected.

headline: Slocum funding for area transportation projects
abstract: State Senator Bill Slocum testified in front of the State Transportation Commission to encourage the start of transportation projects in Elk, Cameron, Clearfield, Jefferson, McKean, and Potter counties.

headline: New law frees up the state police to do what they are trained to do
abstract: Governor Ridge signed a bill that will shift the responsibility of inspecting underground storage tanks and equipment from the State Police to the PA Labor Department. The authors of editorial support the bill because they believe it will free up 100 state police marshals to investigate arson cases, which have been a growing problem in Wayne County.

headline: Ridge comes home with vision of future intact
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge spoke at a fund-raiser to promote the reelection of PA Senator Bob Robbins. He praised Robbins but also took time to highlight some accomplishments from his first three years as governor, including tax cuts, cuts in regulations, improvements in worker’s compensation and new economic development projects. He spoke about the importance of children for the future and vowed to continue to improve educational standards, including his proposal to require higher standards for teachers.

headline: Single area code 'feasible,' company says   If PUC asks, Commonwealth can achieve it
abstract: Commonwealth Telephone Company gave a report to the PA Public Utilities Commission that claims it’s feasible for the entire Schuylkill County to have the same area code, which is supported by Schuylkill County’s VISION, state Senator James Rhoades and state Representatives Bob Allen, David Argall and Edward Lucyk. The PUC had tentatively agreed to split the county into different areas codes, but it solicited public input over the issue. Rhoades and other local officials are hopeful the PUC will heed their advice, and a final decision is expected to be made by May 27.

headline: Harhai, Stepinsky seek nomination in 58th District
abstract: After former Monessen mayor James Sepesky decided not to run, current Monessen Mayor R. Ted Harhai will face Ron Stepinsky for the 58th PA District House Seat. While continuing to serve as mayor the past five months, Harhai has also held the seat after a special election following the death of Representative Herman Mihalich. Harhai appears to have a clear advantage in the upcoming primary election; though both candidates have faltered at times.

headline: Ridge offers help in fight with insurer
abstract: Gov. Ridge's re-election campaign stopped in Greensburg and nobody was happier about that than Sandy Smythe.  Smythe has been advised to have both of her breasts removed to avoid cancer, but her health insurance carrier has refused to pay for the operation and she's fighting to reverse the decision. After Smythe told Ridge about her situation during a brief encounter near the county courthouse, he promised her that his aids would look into the case to see if he could help.

headline: Gray area?
abstract: Alleghey County claims to be the second oldest county in the nation, but that information is misleading.

headline: Bid to block home rule panel rejected
abstract: Two Common Pleas judges rejected a bid to block implementation of Allegheny County's new home rule charter on the basis of a lawsuit submitted by three black main who claimed they were discriminated against in the process of setting it up. Justices Robert P. Horgos and Administrative Judge James H. McLean did not find that that the choice of Jeannie Riles-Pratt, an African American woman as a fifth apportionment commissioner to create 13 new county council districts was discrimination. County Commissioner had refused approve the commission for much of the summer, citing a lack of diversity.

headline: Semicure: CHIP expansion fills a big void
abstract: The Issue: Gov. Tom. Ridge has proposed a major expansion of the state's Children's Health Insurance Program.  We Suggest: Although the expansion of this program is welcomed, more than 100,000 children in Pennsylvania still will be without health-care coverage.  We all should be willing to chip in to provide health-care coverage for Pennsylvania children.

headline: Ruling Limits Speech Rights for Teachers: Appeals Court Decision on Play Broadens School Board Powers
abstract: In Boring v. Buncombe, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a North Carolina school board didn’t violate the rights of Boring, the school’s drama teacher, by disciplining her for putting on a controversial play even though she asked the principal’s permission to put on the play and obtained signatures from parents of students. The court’s majority opinion is that school boards have complete authority over teachers to control what is taught in the classroom, whereas the dissenting opinion is teachers have some First Amendment rights to freedom of speech in the classroom. Many civil liberties groups and teacher organization are concerned that the case will set a dangerous precedent which will make teachers afraid to answer any questions form students about controversial topics.

headline: Piping in the savings
abstract: The suggestion by Equitable Resources Inc. to allow Pleasant Hills residents to shop for their own utilities supplier quickly turned into a competitive race, as Columbia Gas, Peoples Natural Gas and Equitable began releasing more and more customers. Laws forbid utility companies from profiting for the gas they sell, so any differences in price are due to the supplies used to deliver the gas. Equitable is banking on the assumption that some customers won't want to take the trouble to shop around only to save $5 or $10 a month. Outside suppliers however, are allowed to turn a profit, and consumers save on taxes.

headline: Slocum Recommends Rt. 8 Improvements To State Commission
abstract: PA Sen. Bill Slocum testified before the PA Transportation Commission in support of projects in Warren, Forest and Venango counties. The projects were recommended by officials across all levels of state government and interest groups, including the Erie Metropolitan Planning Organization. Representatives from the Warren County Planning Commission and the Northwest PA Regional Planning and Development Commission also testified.

headline: New law tightens rules for parolees entering Pennsylvania
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge signed two bills into law sponsored by PA Representative Tom Gannon and Senator Stewart Greenleaf that were drafted in response to Arthur Bomar, a convicted murderer from Nevada who was allowed to enter PA on parole, where he was convicted of one murder and is suspected of another. The Probation and Parole Board will now receive more information on parolee candidates, and it will be able to refuse their entry into the state. There are other provisions in the laws regarding punishment of parolees who enter the state without authorization as well as those who violate their parole.

headline: Ridge expected to approve low-interest tank-removal loans
abstract: There is a federal deadline on December 22 that will require thousands of businesses to remove or replace underground storage tanks in an attempt to prevent them from polluting the groundwater. A bill sponsored by PA Representative James Lynch was approved by the General Assembly which will provide low-interest loans to businesses to help them comply with the regulations. A $1 million program for homeowners with leaky fuel oil tanks will also be offered if Ridge signs the bill, which he is expected to do.

headline: State to use PC software by Microsoft
abstract: By July 2001, all 40,000 desktop computer terminals used by state government workers will reply on Microsoft software to handle word processing, send e-mail, calculate or manipulate databases. State officials and representatives of Seattle-based Microsoft Corp. called the state's new three-year, $23.6 million contract to standardize state government software the first of its kind. About 15,000 of the state's desktop computers currently use Microsoft's word-processing software, and an equal number use Windows-based e-mail systems. Most of the state's desktop computers run on the Windows operating system.

headline: Harrisburg's Democratic mayor backs Ridge
abstract: Stephen R. Reed, long time mayor of this capitol city, broke ranks with his Democratic Party yesterday to endorse Gov. Ridge, the Republican incumbent in his reelection bid.  Reed, in his fifth term, praised Ridge as a governor who had paid attention to and invested state funds in urban areas.  He cited programs ranging from the cleanup of abandoned buildings to tougher penalties against juvenile criminals.

headline: Ridge promotes plan making it tougher to raise taxes
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge made a campaign fundraising appearance in Huntingdon County where more than 100 Friends of Tom spent the day either fishing, enjoying a meal or having a chance to talk with the governor. The fund-raiser was hosted by PA Senator Robert Jubelirer and a committee comprised of community leaders. He is also supporting his plan for a constitutional amendment that would increase the number of votes needed to raise taxes.

headline: Hafer rejects run for county executive
abstract: State Treasurer Barabra Hafer will not seek the position as Allegheny County's first executive.

headline: Bishops' abortion stance rekindles debate
abstract: Debate continues as Catholic churches and congregations think it unreligious for politicans to support legislation against their personal, church, and religious belieifs. Abortion is the central debate between the bishops and politicans

headline: Senator's forum spotlights issues on mental health
abstract: PA Sen. Vincent Hughes and his colleagues were shocked when PA House Chaplain Clyde Roach committed suicide. The Center for Disease Control revealed suicide is becoming more prevalent in the African American community. Legislators have gotten together to host a summit where president-elect of the PA Psychological Association Diane Salter spoke. Salter encouraged listeners to view mental help as a healthy choice rather than a sign that an individual is crazy.

headline: School audits uncover errors
abstract: Seven Montgomery County school districts were found to have errors after an audit by Auditor General Robert Casey. Missing transportation reports, retirement wages, bookkeeping records, and financial mismanagement are to blame for the errors.

headline: Plan to cut PP&L rates
abstract: Pennslyvnaia Power and Light Company will give customers a 4% cut in price rate. Additional companies may be giving customers rate cuts as much as 10%.

headline: Some outraged over lawsuit filed in bid to halt 202 bypass
abstract: Buckingham officials will file a federal law suit to reuire that the Route 202 bypass project does not begin until te effects of the roads on neighboring communities is examined.

headline: New trial OK's for Einhorn
abstract: State lawmakers pass legislation that would allow convicted killer Ira Einhorn the right to a new trial. This legislation was passed in the hopes that the French government would extradit Einhorn.

headline: Ridge eyeing Michigan's plan for tax-free zones
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is pursuing a plan that would eliminate all state and local taxes in some economically struggling areas to encourage development, and the PA House Urban Affairs Committee sent the proposal to create 12 Keystone Opportunity Zones to the full House for consideration. Michigan is the only other state to have adopted such a plan, and Jim Tobin, a spokesman for Michigan Jobs Service, describes many of the program’s successes throughout the article. While the program appears to be working well, the real test will be whether businesses remain when they have to begin paying taxes again, and some PA lawmakers have expressed other concerns.

headline: Those phone bill blues - FCC wants bills to be more understandable
abstract: The Federal Communications Commission wants phone companies to provide clearer bills, protect customers from being billed by third parties for things or services they never requested and prevent long-distance phone service from being switched without permission. The authors of the editorial support many of the FCC’s proposals to address these needs, which won’t become law until sometime next year, and they argue these changes are absolutely necessary in today’s age of deregulation and free competition in the phone industry.

headline: Harrisburg's turn - Legislators, stop the excuses: Study if you must, but now's the time to help Philadelphia's schools.
abstract: The authors of the editorial want the PA Legislature to take action in addressing the Philadelphia School District’s $85 million deficit, and if an audit is ordered, which is supported by PA Senators Richard Tilghman and Steward Greenleaf and Representative Dwight Evans, the authors hope it’s done quickly. They claim the district has already improved efficiency by eliminating 25 percent of its administration positions, and while Philadelphia uses less of its local taxes towards school funding, it only does this because it has to pay for various county functions such as courts and prisons. The authors are even willing to accept some kind of state oversight if it means the Legislature will address the school district’s financial troubles.

headline: Ridge pushes for an overwhelming victory
abstract: Despite facing a relatively unknown challenger like PA Representative Ivan Itkin, Governor Ridge has begun his second set of television ads, which many political experts believe is part of Ridge’s plan to win big to boost his chances of receiving the vice presidential nomination in 2000. Ridge has denied this, and regardless of his intentions, as of June 8 campaign filings, he had $5.1 million to spend compared to Itkin who only had $4,353. Ridge is trying to define Itkin before Itkin can define himself.

headline: Hearing date is set for county tax refund case
abstract: Billionaire Walter Annenberg lawsuit against Montgomery County for personal preoperty tax is scheduled to begin June 10, 1998. If Annenberg prevails, Montgomery County will have to refund more then $68 million in taxes.

headline: Black conservatives weave a Web of new connections - Groups reach political players, the young through Internet
abstract: Across the county, websites for several different black conservative groups have been established, which have helped these groups reach out to thousands of new people, especially young people, and have provided a forum for sharing ideas. For example, the conservative Center for New Black Leadership established a website for the organization, and on average, 4,300 people visit the site each week, an enormous increase from the 15 to 20 mail and phone inquires they used to receive. According to one organization, many black conservatives have grown tired of Democrats’ stereotypical portrayal of blacks, so they are using the Internet to network with other likeminded individuals to strengthen the Republican Party.

headline: SeniorBlue hears concerns from Holden
abstract: U.S. Rep T. Timothy Holden met with SeniorBlue officials Thursday in Harrisburg to express the disappointment felt by senior citizens across the Sixth District.  But the congressman said the discussion won't bring back prescription drugs or lower premiums to SeniorBlue subscribers.  Holden said SeniorBlue officials admitted that they didn't properly estimate the cost of supplying low monthly premiums with prescription drug coverage.

headline: School Choice movement clings to life
abstract: Governor Ridge’s proposal for vouchers to help parents pay to send their children to private schools failed to pass the Legislature, but a charter schools bill supported by both Ridge and PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf did pass, and six charter schools are now underway in the state. Charter schools receive public funding, but they are exempt from most state regulations and focus on different educational needs. Many people are pleased that parents will have more choice, but others are concerned that state funding of charter schools and the possiblity of vouchers for students to attend private schools could cause public schools to lose money.

headline: PP&L triggers 3 legal attacks
abstract: PA Power & Light Incorporated has filed three lawsuits in state and federal court, alleging the PA Public Utility Commission violated the company’s constitutional rights, misapplied state law and made a poor decision in the company’s recent restructuring case. The lawsuits stem from the PUC’s decision to only allow PP&L to recover between $2.5 and $2.8 billion of stranded costs from ratepayers, leaving over $2 billion up to investors. PP&L said it needed $4.7 billion to pay for stranded costs, including power plants and other investments that were made to provide power to the region’s customers.

headline: Somebody wake up PennDOT
abstract: Delaware County Daily Times taks about the unsafe roadways in the county, and urges PennDOT to take immediate action.

headline: News from the PA General Assembly
abstract: PA House Democrats called on Republicans to act on bills they drafted to enact tougher gun control standards, and Governor Tom Ridge nominated Ben Nartinez to the PA Board of Probation and Parole. Bills authorizing $461 million in spending projects for universities and medical groups were signed into law by Ridge, and two bills that will allow third-class cities to crack down on tax delinquents were also signed. A quote from Representative T. J. Rooney questioning why action has not yet been taken in response to a recent shooting is provided, motorcyclists will hold a rally to support a law which will allow helmets to be optional for drivers 21 or older and PA is one of the top ten states in worshipping.

headline: Ridge in town to talk Plan B
abstract: PA Gov. Ridge will meet with Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy, Pittsburgh Pirates owner Kevin McClatchy and Steelers Vice President Art Rooney II to discuss stadium financing, or "Plan B." Allegheny County Commissioners Mike Dawida and Bob Cranmer, supporters of the plan, may also attend. The plan depends on whether Ridge will come through with a third of the funding as promised. But, Ridge's hands are tied unless approval to raise the state's debt ceiling is granted. McClatchy insists he needs interim funding until another vote can take place in the Legislature.

headline: Hayes promotes agriculture in Republic of Korea
abstract: PA Agriculture Secretary Samuel Hayes Jr. finished up his visit to the Republic of Korea, which was part of Governor Tom Ridge’s trade mission to Asia in hopes of expanding Pennsylvania’s exports to the region. The Republic of Korea has the 11th largest economy in the world, and its market is expanding due to growth in the nation’s middle class. Hayes was accompanied by representatives from a Jefferson County wood and lumber producer, and he was pleased with the results of the trade mission.

headline: Hasay ready to deliver on campaign promises: Representative focuses on school safety, lower property taxes
abstract: PA Representative George Hasay, who was reelected after a tough challenge from Will Conyngham, promised to begin working to deliver on his campaign issues. He is planning to develop legislation to reduce property taxes, raise the income eligibility limit on the PACE program for seniors and target violence in schools. He also said PennDOT will put out a bid for a project he pushed for in Huntington Mills, and a railroad warning system will be installed in Mocanaqua.

headline: Ridge rolls to expected landslide
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge coasted to an expected easy re-election over Democratic candidate Ivan Itkin and Constitutional Party candidate Peg Luksik, and he downplayed speculation that he would be running for national office in two years; though he has not ruled it out. Ridge was never seriously challenged, yet he spent between $12 million and $13 million compared to Itkin’s $400,000, which Ridge acknowledged made it virtually impossible for Itkin to effectively compete. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter also won convincingly, but the Democrats could potentially make a net gain in Pennsylvania’s U.S. House elections if Joseph Hoeffel holds onto his narrow lead over incumbent Jon Fox.

headline: Here are three good reasons to vote for the home rule charter
abstract: Allegheny County Resident writes to the Post-Gazette urging voters to say yes to the new home rule charter electing one person as county executive.

headline: Black, white high school graduation rates equalizing
abstract: The Census Bureau released a report that found more women have graduated from college and high school than men in the 25-29 age group. The number of blacks in the same age group who graduate from high school has improved dramatically since 1940 and is getting close to equalizing the rate of graduation for whites. The Hispanic population is also improving on graduation rates, but it still remains far behind the others.

headline: Seniors attaCK Fox over Medicare bill
abstract: PA State Council of Senior Citizens gathered at the capital to protest Senator Jon Fox's sponsorship of a Medicare bill that would give doctors private contrcats without fee limits.

headline: School districts bullish on risk-free investment
abstract: School districts must make investments with tax payers money that are virtually risk free. These investments can be bonds, CD's, and securities.

headline: Proposed utility rate hike discussed
abstract: PG Energy has proposed increasing its rates by over 11 percent a year to cover upgrade costs, and if the PA Public Utility Commission approves the proposal, it would go into effect in December. The PUC has received a number of complaints, and at a public hearing on the issue, state Representative George Hasey Jr. said many of his constituents could not afford the increase, especially senior citizens. Four other area companies have recently had cases before the PUC, including Commonwealth Telephone Enterprises, Pennsylvania-American Water Company, Pennsylvania Power & Light Company and UGI.

headline: Specter discusses funding with airport authority
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter flew to Mount Alton to discuss how to improve air travel and safety with members of the Bradford Regional Airport Authority. Specter suggested increasing flights to Pittsburgh and Cleveland, and he addressed concerns about future federal funding by promising to use his position on the Senate Appropriations Committee to look into more federal funds for the airport. He also attended a town meeting at a hospital in Coudersport, where he discussed Medicare reimbursements and President Clinton’s alleged affair with Monica Lewinski.

headline: News from the Pennsylvania General Assembly
abstract: The PA Senate began deliberating the state’s $17.8 billion budget for the upcoming fiscal year, and Pennsylvania’s $307.9 billion economy makes it the 17th largest economy in the world. Senate Democrats have filed a lawsuit in Commonwealth Court to try to force Governor Tom Ridge to release a copy of an audit that justified the state to make a $156 million settlement with Envirotest Systems Corporation. PA Representative Katie True said she’ll consider drafting legislation based on recommendations from a report on improving problems in child protective services, and the aunt of a 16-month-old boy who died after being beaten and sexually assaulted by his mother’s boyfriend said she’s sorry it took his death to get lawmakers to act.

headline: Ridge plan: Waive taxes in rundown urban areas
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has proposed the creation of 12 Keystone Opportunity Zones, which would completely eliminate all forms of taxes in economically distressed locations for up to 12 years to help encourage development and create jobs. According to Henry Olsen of the Commonwealth Foundation, government policy underwrites and often encourages sustained poverty; however, the author claims local governments would have to address many of these problems when filing applications for the program. The author claims Ridge’s proposal is "refreshing" because the government is trying to improve people’s lives, rather than worrying about collecting taxes.

headline: Local companies tout importance of exports
abstract: Global exporting, inclduing a new goTRADE program, is being done throughout the states and is responsibile for a large portion of economic growth.

headline: Haverford State security contract switched to Ridge ally
abstract: Within hours of an outbreak of vandalism at the closed Haverford State Hospital last month, the state Department of Public Welfare had fired one security firm and hired another, headed by a prominent ally of Gov. Ridge, to patrol the grounds.  State officials say politics had nothing to do with the decision.  Foulke Associates Inc. of Media was awarded a no-bid emergency contract on Aug. 13, the day that rocks shattered more than 100 windows and four glass doors at the hospital.

headline: Ridge spends millions in ongoing campaign
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge spent an unprecedented $3.8 million in campaign funds between election years, making permanent campaigns a prominent feature in PA's political landscape. During the past three electionless year, Ridge spent more than any statewide officeholder spent to win election. Some money was spent for fundraising efforts and most of it went for trips and events to maintain his public image. He may be looking to run for president next year.

headline: 'Hershey Plan' details revealed at town meeting
abstract: PA Representative Frank Tulli Jr. helped negotiate a deal between the Derry Township Board of Supervisor, the Derry Township School Board and the Hershey Entertainment & Resort Company (HERCO) that will allow the township and school board to continue receiving revenue from HERCO at the same rate, even if the state Legislature passes a bill repealing the state’s amusement tax. The current amusement tax generates $2 million a year in taxes on tickets to Hersheypark and concerts, and without it, local property taxes would likely need to be increased. Two days before passing the agreement, 350 people attended a public hearing, and the article provides several details of the agreement as well as the public hearing.

headline: Can blacks be elected to new county government?
abstract: Black community members in Allegheny County struggle to get representation in and a member on the council and county government.

headline: Seniors held hostage
abstract: Clinton included a provision in the Balanced Budget Act that will more or less prevent seniors enrolled in Medicare from "private contracting," which refers to the practice of paying out of pocket for medical services that are also covered by Medicare. U.S. Senator Jon Kyl proposed legislation that would give seniors back the right to private contracting, and the author supports the proposal. The author disputes claims that it would destroy Medicare, and he believes that while private contracting would only be used in limited circumstances, it is a right seniors deserve to have, and it would help prevent the government from overly manipulating the system.

headline: School funding alternative
abstract: Letter to the editor against Nicolas Micozzie's 20-year term in office. He has spent much of his time putting band-aids on problems generated by the out-dated school property tax and inequity in funding for schools across the state, he has brought no real vision or urgency to this issue.

headline: PUC backs plans to cut electric costs
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission granted tentative approval to proposals that could begin cutting electric costs for most Duquesne Light Company and Allegheny Power customers by January. However, the savings are based on projected competition, which the PUC plans to promote by encouraging consumers to shop around in order to save money. The PUC won’t pay the two utilities as much as they wanted for stranded costs, which are costs incurred years before competition was contemplated, and Allegheny County vowed to challenge the decision in Commonwealth Court.

headline: Specter tests German maglev - Senator enthusiastic about rail plan here
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter rode a 250-mile-an-hour magnetic levitation train in Germany as part of his effort to bring a high-speed maglev rail system to PA. Maglev Incorporated is working with a German company to bring the technology to PA, and the first targeted project would be a connection between Pittsburgh International Airport and Downtown. Specter ultimately would like to see the train connect Pittsburgh to Philadelphia, which the train could travel in only an hour and a half, and Specter believes the project would create thousands of new jobs.

headline: No smokes? Inmates turn to Twizzlers and Little Debbies
abstract: Most new prisons that open are smoke-free, and existing prisons across PA and the country have been transitioning to smoke-free environments. While wardens still have to combat smuggling and some other problems, smoke-free prisons have largely been seen as successful and have made prisons healthier and cleaner. Some prisoners claim banning cigarettes amounts to cruel and unusual punishment, but allowing smoking can be detrimental to the health of workers and inmates who don’t smoke, and the usual cigarette based prison economy has been switching over to products such as snack cakes and licorice.

headline: Ridge pushes 12 'opportunity zones'
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge addressed the County Commissioners Association of PA about his proposed Keystone Opportunity Zones legislation, which would create 12 tax-free zones in economically struggling areas to encourage development and the creation of jobs. The legislation has already passed the state Senate, but Ridge urged county officials to contact their legislators to convince the House to pass it before the fall session ends. Ridge acknowledged there can be reluctance to give up tax revenue, but he said the areas aren’t generating any revenue now, so there would be no difference.

headline: Ridge's flight forced to turn around due to engine problems
abstract: A flight carrying Governor Tom Ridge and nine other members of his trade-mission delegation had to shut down one engine after encountering difficulties, but it was able to return to Tel Aviv, Israel to land safely. Ridge ended the Israel part of the trade mission by meeting with the chairman of TEVA Pharmaceutical Industries, which has its U.S. headquarters in PA, and he is expected to continue the technology trade mission in Scotland next.

headline: Head count is inaccurate and costly
abstract: The authors of the editorial believe that the U.S. district court panel’s decision to reject the use of extensive statistical sampling for the 2000 census should be appealed to Supreme Court. They claim it is extremely difficult to count everyone, and even the court panel admitted that the 1990 census missed a significant portion of minorities, while only failing to miss .7 percent of non-Hispanic whites. The authors believe that the issue should focus on getting a reliable count of the population; regardless of their political affiliation.

headline: Ridge touts Philly as site for Democrats
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge told member of the Democratic National Committee that Philadelphia would be the best place for the Democratic National Convention in 2000.

headline: Home rule propsal generates some heat
abstract: Meetings on the proposes new home rule charter for Allegheny County prove to spark heated debate among the public and government officials.

headline: Can 'Blacks only' primary wprk in this city?
abstract: Black leaders seek to have an all black primary to boost the chances of electing a black member of government in the Pittsburgh area and Allegheny County.

headline: Some physicians groups leaving AHERF
abstract: Some of the 211 physicians in Western Pennsylvania who sold their practices to the troubled Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation in recent years have already left the group.  Whether their departures are voluntary is unclear.  Dr. Richard Shannon, chairman of the Department of Medicine at Allegheny General Hospital said yesterday that discussions between AHERF and doctors in the practice plans had resulted in an unspecified number of physicians deciding to go it alone.

headline: School reform crosses political, racial lines
abstract: Members of the Philadelphia Coalition for Educational Reform and School Choice, two black Democratic state Representatives, Dwight Evans and Tony Williams, and white Republican state Representative John Perzel joined together in a press conference to support educational reform backed by Governor Tom Ridge. They all stressed the same message that educational reform must spread across racial and political boundaries. Part of the reform would involve state sponsored vouchers to offer parents more school choice, and overall, the authors of the editorial support the bipartisan, multiracial efforts to tackle educational reform.

headline: PUC gives final approval to PECO plan
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission gave its final approval to a plan for Peco, the state’s largest electricity company, to enter into the competitive electricity market. Under the plan, Peco customers could receive as much as a 22 percent reduction in their electricity bills.

headline: Spector plugs light-rail line
abstract: Senator Arlen Spector hopes to get a transportation light-rail line started between Philadelphia and Reading.

headline: No union status, probation folks told - Courts: Rights ended with contract
abstract: The Philadelphia court system notified two unions representing over 500 probation officers that since their contract had expired, any labor dispute would be resolved through "court personnel regulations" and not the grievance system that was used under the contract’s terms. The unions’ leaders are furious with the court’s decision and plan to hold a rally outside the Criminal Justice Center to protest. Chief Deputy Court Administrator David Lawrence said the court system was trying to conform with the way other counties operate by having unions negotiate with the executive branch, Mayor Rendell’s administration, yet an internal memo shows the court believes it still has a duty to regulate its workforce.

headline: Ridge signs tax-cut legislation on lawn
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge traveled to the bedroom community of Aldan, in Delaware County, where he stood on the front lawn of Frank and Judy Culbertson's home to sign legislation that will cut personal and business taxes by more than $220 million. The Culbertsons will benefit from elimination of the personal income tax on the net gain from the sale of their home.

headline: Specter: Caucus to press for hold on steel imports
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter said he and other members of the steel caucus are pushing for a commitment by President Clinton to quickly put a leash on steel imports that caucus members and the steel industry believe are being sold at unfair prices. Specter said congressional members pleaded in the meeting for the maximum effort to stop subsidized steel.

headline: Heading for prompt resolution
abstract: The authors of the editorial claim that members of the House Judiciary Committee must determine whether President Clinton lied under oath and if his actions can be considered worthy for removal from office. The committee is expected to vote along party lines, which would bring impeachment to the House floor to be voted on, The authors are against U.S Representative George Gekas’ suggestion to wait until next year to conduct the vote because they feel the American public is tired of the impeachment process, which has become a process of politics rather than law.

headline: Ridge touts Philly as site for Democrats
abstract: Members of the Democratic National Committee are in Philadelphia this week to explore the possibility of holding the 2000 Democratic National Convention in the city. Republican Governor Tom Ridge told members of the committee that Philadelphia would be a great place to host their convention. In other news, PA Education Secretary Eugene Hickok will visit Spring Grove High School to announce over $10 million worth of school performance incentives.

headline: Home Rule Slips in
abstract: 95% of yes votes in Allegheny County give the county a new home rule charter. The proponents and opponnents of the charter all had something to say about its passing.

headline: Cases point to Injustice of Justice system
abstract: One juvenile is killed and another injured by police. The circumstances of the cases point to recurring racism and injustice in the court system.

headline: Some physicians groups leaving AHERF
abstract: While the Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation goes through the bankruptcy process, some of the physicians in Western PA who sold their practices to the foundation have already left the network. Dr. Richard Shannon, chairman of the Department of Medicine at Allegheny General Hospital, said the decisions to leave the network were voluntary, whereas some health care consultants believe they were forced out. According to Shannon, new contracts will be issued to all physicians in the network.

headline: School sued as voucher controversy resurfaces
abstract: The Southeast Delco School District used some of its budget surplus to give grants to parents to send their children to private schools; however, the school is being sued. The Public Coalition to Oppose Tuition Vouchers is lobbying against public funding to send children to private schools, and Governor Ridge tried to pass a school choice program two years ago, but it failed to pass the House. PA Senator Allyson Schwartz also shared her thoughts on a proposed pilot program that would help send 3,000 children to private, religious or suburban schools.

headline: PUC needs consumer rep.
abstract: Editors believe PA Gov. Tom Ridge's decision to replace PA Public Utilities Commissioner John Hanger is unfairly influenced by the utility industry and should be rejected. Ridge declined to re-nominate Hanger, nominating Republican Mayor of Chester County, Aaron Wilson. Hanger has been making headlines lately for his involvement in defeating PECO's attempts to make customers pay cost-recovery charges. Wilson however, endorsed PECO's efforts. However, a PA law bars public officials from nomination to the PUC. PA Atty. Gen. Mike Fisher has been asked for a determination.

headline: Spend quality time on driving lessons
abstract: According to PA Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory, a law requiring parents to certify they have spent a certain number of hours teaching their teen-ager how to drive could and should be passed in PA by the end of the year. The American Auto Association Mid-Atlantic and the Insurance Federation of PA support the idea because teen drivers are disproportionately involved in accidents, and crashes are the leading cause of death for those aged 15-24. PA has already implemented a law requiring parental notification when a teen is cited for a serious traffic violation, and New Jersey recently passed a graduated licensing system.

headline: NRA can change elections when it targets candidate
abstract: Even if the National Rifle Association officials feel gun-shy in a city  where the mayor talks about suing gun makers, they should feel especially cozy, if not down right at home, gathering in Pennsylvania.  That's because when it comes to NRA political clout , Pennsylvania is a poster-state for gun policy, gun politics and gun lovers.  And as the NRA opens its annual convention today in Philadelphia, its power in this state remains locked and loaded.

headline: Ridge still attempting to find interim funding for stadiums
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge said he’s still hoping to come to an agreement with Pennsylvania’s legislative leaders on a plan to fund Pittsburgh sports stadiums sometime before December 21. The Pirates owner said he will stop writing checks for the design and engineering of a new ballpark unless the state guarantees it will provide some funding.

headline: A Weekly Report by Your Congressman George W. Gekas
abstract: U.S. Representative George Gekas wants to take time to honor some unsung heroes, beginning with fathers on Father’s Day, and he says June 26 will mark the 50th anniversary of the Berlin airlift, in which Allied forces flew thousands of missions and delivered nearly 24 million tons of supplies to the Soviet Union’s isolated portion of Berlin. He praises Gail Halvorsen, an American pilot who took part in flying mission, and Gekas believes the actions of Halvorsen and millions of others helped put America on course for more peaceful relations with Soviet-dominated countries. In addition, he cites this year as the 175th anniversary of the Monroe Doctrine and the 100th anniversary of the Spanish American War, which helped the U.S. rise as a foreign power and assert the Monroe Doctrine’s foreign policy.

headline: Heavy Players Support Area's Lottery Cash Cow
abstract: An analysis of lottery sales in Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia indicates that much of the market come from low-income, low-education players, which Maryland Governor Parris Glendening called "sad." In addition, minorities and people with lower incomes tend to make up higher percentages of heavy players, and low-income individuals tend to spend a larger percentage of their income on lottery tickets than more affluent individuals. In many upper class regions, no lottery ticket vendors can be found, and states have been criticized for targeting lottery sales to the people who can least afford to spare the money; however, there is no proof that states are purposely targeting minorities and lower classes, and states are searching for ways to entice higher-income players, often by using multi-state consortiums that offer bigger jackpots.

headline: Ridge wants Schiller back on court
abstract: Gov. Ridge yesterday nominated Montgomery County lawyer Berle M. Schiller, who just completed an interim appointment to the state Superior Court, to fill another vacancy on the court.  Schiller, a close, longtime friend of Sen. Vincent J. Fumo (D. Phila.) last year ran unsuccessfully for a seat on the Supreme Court.  His Supreme Court term expired this month.

headline: Hotel tax to be used for promoting tourism
abstract: Indiana County will set a 2% excise tax on overnight lodging. The tax will be used to generate tourism and is expected to bring in $130,000 a year.

headline: Cloning: Where's the Outrage?
abstract: The author believes that standard objections to the potential of cloning in the future, such as the argument that attempts to clone will result in deformed beings until cloning is perfected, will eventually phase out, and new things initially create fear but tend to become accepted over time. The author also delves into some issues of morality and claims that the issue can clash with pro-abortion arguments, as well as with arguments from those who defend single-parent or homosexual households raising children. He claims that Western societies have been working since the Enlightenment to normalize a long list of actions that used to be considered outrageous, and as a result, these societies have less moral standing to tackle ethical quandaries that are growing more and more complex.

headline: Specter expected to be released from hospital soon
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter is expected to be released from the hospital by Tuesday after being admitted to Thomas Jefferson University Hospital in Philadelphia after suffering chest pains. Tests for heart trouble came back negative for Specter, who is seeking re-election this fall.

headline: School uniforms legislation has General Assembly approval
abstract: The PA General Assembly approved a bill sponsored by Education Committee chairman James Rhoads that will allow schools to require their students to wear school uniforms. School uniforms will not be mandatory across the state, but each school will now have the option of requiring them. The bill was part of a larger education bill which will give the state authority to increase funding to schools in the PA budget, and it establishes a new mechanism to make sure that the Philadelphia School District will stay open for the entire 1998-99 school year.

headline: PUC: Utilities can merge before giving up lines - Allegheny Energy will have to give control of the lines to an independent operator by June 30, 2000
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission softened its stance and will allow Allegheny Energy Incorporated and Duquesne Light Company to complete their controversial merger before giving up their transmission lines to an independent operator; though they will be required to do so by June 30, 2000. The ruling came as one of the last made before Governor Tom Ridge replaces Commissioner John Hanger, who has criticized Ridge for succumbing to pressure from utilities, but consumer advocates in Pittsburgh have argued that the ruling will inhibit competition and lead to higher rates for consumers. Hanger said he was pleased with the requirement to force the companies to diverge the transmission lines; however, he hopes federal regulators, which still need to sign off on the merger, require stronger protections to ensure short term competition.

headline: Spped the trip
abstract: Pennslyvania Department of Transportation has made it easier for residents to register their automobiles but registering instantly at certain dealerships. Intelligencer Joural thinks the new plan is smart and a good simple solution.

headline: Ohio clemency issue gets top court backing
abstract: Supreme Court rules that states can have more leeway when deciding determining clemency issues for death row murderers.

headline: Ridge vows to press for early vote on new stadium bill
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge plans to press the PA General Assembly to vote early on a bill that would authorize over $300 million in funding for new sports stadiums in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia and would allocate about $150 million for other projects across the state. The bill died in the House before the winter recess without being voted on; however, a bill did pass that has a controversial provision that could potentially be interpreted to allow funding for the Pittsburgh stadium projects, which have already begun clearing sites and selling seat licenses. Governor Tom Ridge plans to veto the bill, and House Republican Leaders John Perzel and Matthew Ryan have threatened an investigation into whether the "stealth bill" was the product of a conspiracy to trick legislators into funding the Pittsburgh projects.

headline: For Einhorn, a quite village life
abstract: Ira Einhorn is found in France, living a relaxing life with his current wife. The U.S is trying to get extradition from France but has so far been unsuccessful.

headline: 'Help' on the Issues Raises G.O.P. Fears Of Voters' Backlash
abstract: Republican Party officials are concerned that the millions of dollars that will be spent by interest groups on their own independent advertising campaigns to promote Republican candidates could potentially backfire and even help Democrats in the upcoming election. Earlier this month, hundreds of thousands of dollars were spent on anti-abortion commercials to help defeat Lois Capps in a special election in California for the U.S. House; however, a poll indicates the advertising actually made people more likely to vote for Capps, the Democratic candidate. Gary Bauer, who heads the group that advertised the anti-abortion commercial, denied they played a negative role, but Republicans remain worried that advertising could backfire as it did for the Democrats in the 1996 election.

headline: Ridge's big bucks
abstract: Ridge campaign earns $36,418 in interest within the first three months.

headline: Jail fund guilty of overfeeding
abstract: The Allegheny County jail is accussed of providing daily free meals to 222 employees and non-employees, who should have been paying for meals.

headline: County council 'in ditch'
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Dunn showed up for a meeting and demanded women and minorities have representation on the council.

headline: Spending on Health Grew Slowly in 1996
abstract: Health spending increased in 1996 at the lowest rate in 36 years, but topped $1 trillion for the first time, the Government reported today. Such spending has been growing at the same pace economy for four years in a row, contrary to earlier projections, which showed health care eating up a bigger and bigger share of the nation's output.  The report, from the Department of Health and Human Services, describes pent-up pressures for a possible increase in health care spending in the near future.

headline: School vouchers opposed- Quakertown School Board adopts resolution against such legislation
abstract: Members of the Quakertown Community School Board unanimously approved a resolution affirming their opposition to legislation that would allow publicly funded vouchers to be given to help parents send their children to private schools. The resolution says such legislation would increase costs, could hurt support of public school funding and would violate the constitution. Copies of the resolution will be sent to the Legislature and advocacy groups.

headline: RATEPAYER BEWARE - PUC reopening of PECO decision could hamper success of electric competition
abstract: The authors are disappointed with PA Public Utility Commission Chairman John Quain’s announcement that he would convene a conference in hopes of ending Peco Energy Corporation’s legal challenges to the commission’s decision to allow Peco to recover $4.9 billion in uneconomic investments. While the authors don’t believe the court challenges or the conference will help Peco recover the $6 billion it is asking for, they are still disappointed with Quain’s decision. They believe the original settlement is a fair way to help Peco recoup some its losses and offer ratepayers recovery from years of high rates, and they hope Public Utility Commissioner John Hanger is reappointed in order to prevent the settlement from being overturned.

headline: Squeezing lemon law
abstract: According to the author, lobbyists for the automobile industry are trying to get Pennsylvania’s legislators to weaken the state’s current lemon law through two separate bills that are being considered in the state Legislature. The author claims these changes would offer consumers virtually no protection from faulty vehicles, and he urges voters to contact their local legislators in opposition to the bills.

headline: Out of control   Legal rules have changed, allowing federal agents, prosecutors to bypass basic rights
abstract: Congress, the Justice Department and the courts have combined to give federal law enforcement officers and prosecutors far more power than they have ever had in the past, and the article describes a number of different cases in which federal agents and prosecutors have abused their power to secure convictions by withholding evidence, setting up questionable sting operations, manipulating grand juries, relying on testimony from criminals with incentives to lie and manipulating charges against defendants to secure mandatory sentences. Many prosecutors give sentence reductions to prisoners who testify against others, which has led to a practice where prisoners buy information from others in order to testify against people they’ve never met, and some federal agents have even offered criminals protection from charges in return for evidence against their enemies. In order to correct the problem of abuse of power, U.S. Representatives John Murtha and Joseph McDade, who was acquitted of bribery charges after an eight year investigation, have proposed legislation, but the Justice Department remains strongly opposed.

headline: Ridge: Too much jobs credit?
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge may be receiving too many kudos from fellow Republicans on the success of his economic development strategies. Delaware County GOP officials have lauded the governor, praising his business-friendly policies for helping them lure companies here from the state of Delaware. According to the US Department of Labor, more than 20,000 new jobs were created in the Philadelphia area over the past year. The city was second to last in the state though only behind Pittsburgh.

headline: Holocaust settlement cash free of state tax
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge exempts Holocoaust's vicitms recieving settlements from the Swiss bank from paying state taxes on the money.

headline: Herman campaigning hard for re-election
abstract: Representative Lynn Herman faces no challengers in his re-election bid for the 77th District’s seat in the PA House, yet he is still campaigning hard to show he doesn’t take any votes for granted. He is chairman of the House Local Government Committee and the Joint House and Senate Legislative Data Processing Committee, and he said both are working on important legislation. He hopes to pass a statewide building code, consolidate local governments to make them more efficient and allow more state agencies, as well as the public, to access the House and Senate date processing center’s system.

headline: Ridge's garbage and trash talk leaves Itkin smelling like a rose
abstract: Democrat Ivan Itkin's gubernatorial campaign showed some spark last week, thanks mostly to the blunders of people working for his opponent.  Itkin held a news conference last Tuesday to blast Gov. Tom Ridge fro not doing enough to battle out-of-state trash. Ridge, not coincidentally, was holding a news conference of his own just a few yards away, calling for a three-year moratorium on new landfill permits in the state.

headline: Legislature OKs school tax changes
abstract: State lawmakers passed a bill that would reform proerpty taxes and let school district have a wage tax, if so desired.

headline: County's home rule panel to appoint minority woman - Decision comes after private meeting Monday
abstract: The four white men who were nominated to split Allegheny County into 13 home rule charter councils held a closed-door meeting and decided to appoint a minority woman as their fifth member. The private meeting technically didn’t violate Pennsylvania’s Sunset Laws, which require sufficient notice of public meetings and public access to governmental documents, and the appointment of a minority candidate is intended to address concerns about the lack of diversity in the group. The committee will have until October 23 to draw up the new council districts, and according to the recently passed home rule charter, there will be a total of fifteen elected council members and one county executive.

headline: State accepts center plans
abstract: After numerous violations before June, state and federal funds were cut off from William Penn Care Center in Penn Township. The center’s owners have spent over $500,000 to make up for costs, and inspectors from the PA Department of Health surveyed the facilities and approved plans that would bring them into compliance with regulations. State Representative James Casorio is pleased with the approval, and applications were filed to the federal Health Care Funding Administration and PA Department of Public Welfare in hopes of getting funding back.

headline: School vouchers touted for late-session haggling   'Opportunity scholarship' plan could include Harrisburg
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has unsuccessfully tried twice to pass a voucher bill through the PA Legislature that would provide vouchers to help many parents send their children to nonpublic schools. However, there is a growing number of states that are providing vouchers, and some believe the idea is gaining support in PA. There is speculation that several compromises may be offered before the end of the legislative session to help get the bill passed, yet there are still many legislators who fundamentally oppose vouchers.

headline: Rates would remain the same for PP&L customers under competition
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Utility Company granted tentative approval to a restructuring plan for the Pennsylvania Power-and-Light Company. Under the plan, customers would see a 10 percent reduction in their bills.

headline: Stairs support plan for funding bridge, road repairs from surplus
abstract: State Representative Jess Stairs is supporting proposed legislation that would require Pennsylvanai Department of Transportation to use any end of the year fiscal surpluses to immediately repair highways and bridges in south PA.

headline: Pa. coal town mourns deaths in cabin fire
abstract: County Judge William Wiest had two sons die in an 11 victim fire in the community of Madisonburg.  Centre County Coroner Scott Sayers reported that an autopsy revealed 4 victims died of smoke inhalation.

headline: Rooney pitches home scheme
abstract: PA Representative T.J. Rooney, who will face Catasauqua attorney Joseph Herber for re-election this year, has proposed a program that would allow families to purchase urban homes without the risk of losing money on the investment. The Neighborhood Home Equity Insurance Program would enable people purchasing homes in certain areas, excluding Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, to buy reasonably priced insurance protection. If the home has lost value when they try to sell it later on, the state would reimburse them for their losses.

headline: Pitts returns from tour of Algeria
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts returned home after travelling to refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria and visiting Algiers, where Islamic fundamentalists have recently massacred thousands. The political situation in northwestern Africa deteriorated 25 years ago when Spain withdrew form its colony, West Sahara, and 200,000 Moroccan soldiers immediately invaded the territory, forcing thousands of refugees to flee to Algeria. Pitts visited to encourage Morocco to allow free elections in Western Sahara, to permit international de-mining teams and to allow captured Moroccan soldiers to return home, and he said America has many key interests in the region, including trade and promoting democracy.

headline: High stakes in census case: How the Supreme Court rules in sampling dispute will seriously affect the political landscape.
abstract: The U.S. Census Bureau has proposed the use of statistical sampling for the 2000 census, and it claims that sampling would save money and reduce the undercounted percentage from 1.9 percent to .5 percent. Republicans fear that statistical sampling will hurt their party and have filed lawsuits against the proposal, whereas Democrats believe it could help their cause by counting those who were disproportionally not counted in the previous census: minorities in major cities. The U.S. Supreme Court must rule on the constitutionality of the proposal, as well as whether it violates the Census Act of 1976, and the decision could affect the distribution of House seats and the distribution of $100 billion in federal funds.

headline: Rivers get a 'Navigator'
abstract: Karen Hobbs is named the Susquehanna Heritage Program River Navigator.

headline: Legislature to begin debate on shifting school-tax burden - Last fall, voters authorized the lawmakers to act. The goal is to rely more on wages, not property.
abstract: Last November, voters adopted a statewide referendum to authorize the PA Legislature to pass tax-reform legislation with an exemption that would provide property tax-relief for homeowners, and legislative leaders outlined a bill yesterday that would allow school districts to reduce their reliance on property taxes by shifting more toward earned-income taxes. Senate Majority Leader Joseph Loeper said an agreement had been reached to initially concentrate tax reform on school districts rather than counties and local municipalities; however, Senate Minority Leader Robert Mellow complained about Democrats being left out of the process of developing the legislation, and he said the reform was simply tax shifting, not tax relief. According to the legislation, residents of a school district could vote on whether to shift taxes, and they could vote to approve or deny future tax increases, which Governor Tom Ridge insisted on adding.

headline: Countywide human relations commission?
abstract: Should there be a York County Human Relations Commission?  It is an interesting idea, one that York City adopted a long time ago, creating a commission that investigates and remedies cases of civil-and-human-rights violations in employment and housing.

headline: State funds anti-smoking campaign
abstract: The Wayne County Take Action For Tobacco Free Youth has received a $20,000 grant from the Pennsylvania Tobacco Prevention Network and the state Department of Health.  Anthony Delonti of the American Lung Association of North-east Pennsylvania said part of the grant would be used to help create smoke-free restaurants.  Members of TAFTFY will be doing surveys of local restaurants to see if the restaurant has a separate non-smoking section.

headline: School-choice issue to greet lawmakers in Harrisburg
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has twice failed to pass bills that would give publicly funded vouchers to parents to send their children to private schools, but voucher advocates are calling for another vote in the PA Legislature. Supporters of vouchers claim they will improve the educational system and allow parents more choice, whereas critics argue they would take money away from public schools and could lead to government interference into the affairs of private schools. Vouchers have been a bipartisan issue in the past, and lawmakers must consider what effects vouchers would have on their particular districts; though legislatures risk alienating constituents no matter which way they vote.

headline: Salutes & Boots
abstract: Beaver County Times Salutes PA Public Utlities Commissioner for commets about deregulation and Salutes Mark Singel for stepping down as PA Democractic Chairman. Beaver County Times Boots Attorney General Mike Fisher for being involved with the Fayette County Commissioners.

headline: Stairs supports plan for funding bridge, road repairs from surplus
abstract: PA Rep. Jess Stairs expressed support for a moved launched last week to appropriate any year-end PA Department of Transportation surplus for infrastructure renovations in southwestern PA. This year's surplus is projected at $150 million. The PA Transmission Commission is revising the state's "12-Year Plan." PA Rep. Richard Olasz, ranking Democrat on the House Transportation Committee, urges fellow legislators to reserve a PennDOT stimulus for long term projects to help move the state into a first-priority tier.

headline: Pa. Crime Guns
abstract: Top 10 state of origin for guns used in PA crimes based on a sample of firearms traces in 1997. 932 out of 1,519 were from PA.

headline: Santorum, Peterson pay visit to Stackpole Center, ITEC
abstract: U.S. Senator Rick Santorum and U.S. Representative John Peterson visited two projects managed by the North Central PA Regional Planning and Development Commission. They first visited the Stackpole Center in St. Marys where a brief presentation was held by Frank Kuntz, North Central’s board president, who described the project and the reasoning behind their request to Economic Development Agency for a $800,000 grant to help maintain perimeter roads. Santorum and Peterson then went to the Industrial Technological Education Center, which received its licensure to provide job training in the Die Setting program, and were joined by Ridgway Mayor Jim Martin and PA Senator Bill Slocum.

headline: null
abstract: The political cartoon pertains to questions about John Pippy’s residency and eligibility requirements to hold a seat in the state House.

headline: High, low spenders differ in approaches to House service
abstract: Of Pennsylvania’s 21 U.S. House Representatives, Representative Chaka spent the most on office-related expenses during the first nine months of 1997 at $661,000, whereas Representative George Gekas spent the least at $423,000. Collectively, the 21 House members spent $11.7 million, and the article breaks down the spending for each one. Each member is allocated a specific amount to spend, but they often return some of the money as a symbolic gesture, and both Gekas and Chaka believe they are spending their money wisely to serve their constituents’ demands.

headline: Roads meeting becomes Ridge rally
abstract: Local Democrats were leery of attending a meeting with Gov. Tom Ridge on Thursday about transportation issues, fearing the meeting really would be a Republican campaign rally.  The skeptics were right: although the event was sponsored by the Alle-Kiski Coalition, a proponent of Valley road projects--especially a $150 million bridge near the city--it was a rally for Republican candidates running in Tuesday's election. Other candidates attending the event included Lt. Gov. Mark Sweiker, state Sen. Melissa Hart, R0McCandless, and Mike Turazai, who is challenging US Rep. Ron Klink, D-Murrysville, in the 4th Congressional District.

headline: Many cabin fires caused by inattention
abstract: A recent fire began at a cabin in Centre County and killed 11 people, and Huntington County Emergency Management Director stressed the need for people to frequently inspect their cabins for problems that could lead to fires. The only cabins that are held to any significant state regulations are those on state property, which according to Marko Borne, Press Secretary for the PA Fire Commissioner’s Office, leaves most cabins under the authority of less stringent, local standards. There is pending legislation that could improve inspection standards and require all homes to be equipped with smoke detectors, but it could be a long time until these bills actually pass.

headline: Crowd expected for gay issue - City Council will consider extending its benefits package for employees.  The hearing is set for Wednesday.
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council will consider an extremely controversial set of bills that would grant gay and lesbian couples many of the same benefits as married couples. Hearings over the bills are expected to draw a huge crowd, and Cardinal Anthony Bevilacqua and the Urban Family Council will testify against the bills, while others will provide their own testimony in favor of them. The Council’s vote could go either way, but Councilman Michael Nutter, who voted against similar legislation five years ago, has changed course and supports the bills.

headline: State has Fought For-Profit Trend, Exec. Says
abstract: According to Steve Volla, chairman of Primary Health Systems, PA had been driving away for-profit hospitals in favor of non-profit hospitals in the past; however, a law was changed 18 months ago, and the competition of managed care organizations has begun to reverse the trend. According to an attorney with Community Catalyst, managed care makes it difficult for non-profit hospitals, and large commercial hospital groups have advantages that non-profits often cannot overcome. However, she claimed it's not always in the best interest of the community or non-profits to merge with for-profits.

headline: Schools embrace training  3 more support work force effort
abstract: Last week, PA Senator James Rhoads and Representative Bob Allen urged business and education leaders to work together to provide job training that would end up encouraging economic development in the area. According to Kelly Baldwin, work force development coordinator for the Schuylkill Chamber of Commerce, three local districts responded quickly and showed their commitments. Baldwin is expecting to work with the school districts to highlight available job opportunities in the region, and school officials have shown interest in job shadowing programs, career fairs and bringing business speakers into classrooms.

headline: Seeing the light
abstract: The authors of the editorial claim to have always doubted that the deregulation of the electric industry would be good for consumers, and they argue utility companies simply have too much power. Companies that want to buy power and resell it are finding that they must set prices higher than the utility companies that generate the power, and the PA Public Utility Commission reacted by freezing wholesale prices. For now, the authors urge those who are power shopping to compare prices carefully because it may not pay to switch companies.

headline: State and L. Nazareth differ over curbing
abstract: PennDot and L. Nazareth township are at odds over roads trhrough Ridgeview Estates subdivision.

headline: Pa. gun-check law faces new stumbling block
