abstract: Three years ago, PA passed a highly touted law treat rifles just like handguns, and to check their buyers for criminal pasts. The law was to take effect in 1996 and make PA one of a few states to check out such sales. But the state police said they weren't ready to enforce the measure and begged for a delay. The effective date was since pushed back to July 1 and could be possibly delayed again.

headline: Section 8 reforms in place, PHA chief says
abstract: The interim head of the Philadelphia Housing Authority, which administers the controversial Section 8 rent-subsidy program, told City Council members that the agency had already implemented many of the recommendations offered by Mayor Ed Rendell in a critical report. The program uses $66 million to provide subsidies for low-income and homeless individuals; however, critics blame the program for the decline of working-class neighborhoods, and Rendell bashed the Housing Authority for poor enforcement of housing regulations and for failing to control problem tenants and negligent landlords. Several Council members, including Michael Nutter and David Cohen, criticized Rendell for one of his recommendations, which some believe would be a hidden attempt to move minority tenants away from traditionally white neighborhoods, and for releasing the report a day before the Council’s hearing.

headline: A close shave! Politics at the razor's edge
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Bob Cranmer’s campaign advisors told him he should shave off his beard when campaigning for office, and the article examines the issue of facial hair in politics. PA Representatives Joe Markosek, Tom Michlovic and Jim Casorio all have moustaches, but the last president to have any kind of facial hair, other than eyebrows, was William Howard Taft in 1913. The author of the article poses three humorous explanations for the lack of beards in politics, including the maintenance factor, public appearance and the fact that not everyone can grow a nice beard.

headline: Hillary, Newt won for Dems
abstract: In light of the shocking election results in which Republicans lost five House seats, the author puts a lot of the blame on House Speaker Newt Gingrich. He claim’s Gingrich’s blunders have been serious enough for some House members to consider removing him as their leader. The author also gives a lot of the credit for the success of the Democrats to Hillary Clinton, who helped lead the party out from the darkness of her husband’s impeachment scandal, and after the election results, momentum for impeachment is waning.

headline: Roadside reminders
abstract: As part of an initiative from the York County Chamber of Commerce, "Vote: It’s Your Business" logos have been put on ten billboards to raise awareness and remind people to vote in the upcoming election.

headline: Millions at stake in Montco tax case
abstract: Walter Annenberg, a billionaire, is suing Montgomery County for personal property taxes. Many residents are waiting for the legal outcome.

headline: Deficiencies in public defender office cited
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union is filing a law suit against Allegheny County's Public Defenders Office. The county is accussed of being underfunded, overworked, and not providing adequate counsel to clients.

headline: State hearing on underage drinking held
abstract: Students in Northhampton schools are starting to drink alcohol as soon as they become teens. This includes all types of students. The Republican lawmakers were at the school for a hearing on underage drinking. The state needs to make alcohol more difficult to get for minors and give parents a better understanding of the liability they could face by allowing underage drinkers to have parties in their homes.

headline: Schools get grant totaling $400,000
abstract: A $400,000 grant proposal from Ridgway superintendent Fran Grandinetti was approved by the PA Department of Education’s Technology Literacy Challenge Fund. Included in the grant are Bradford, Kane, Cameron County, Johnsonburg, Ridgway and St Marys, which all formed a consortium for the purpose of brining technology to the classroom and linking the schools to share courses and experiences. Johnsonburg, St. Marys and Ridgway, which already have interactive televisions, will upgrade their computer labs for Internet use, and the other schools will use the money to purchase interactive television.

headline: Senate approves Wilson for PUC post
abstract: The PA Senate confirmed PA Gov. Tom Ridge's nomination of Chester Mayor Aaron Wilson to the PA Public Utility Commission. Wilson will replace outgoing Commissioner John Hanger, whose term had expired. Several dissenting Democrats expressed concern that Wilson should be given more time to understand the issues before the PUC before being catapulted to commission status, including Sen. Roy Afflerbach. A major issue facing the PUC is deregulation of electricity rates. Senate Maj. Leader F. Joseph Loeper defended Wilson and Ridge's nomination.

headline: State Capitol Roundup - REP. RONALD S. MARSICO 105th LEGISLATIVE DISTRICT
abstract: According to PA Representative Ronald Marsico, police can only issue citations to motorists on public roads who illegally pass a school bus that has stopped, with lights flashing, to pick up children. However, Marsico has introduced legislation that would give them the ability to pull over anyone who commits such an offense on any type of road. He believes the problem needs to be addressed because children in apartment complexes and other similar communities across the state are vulnerable under current law.

headline: Pa. issues apologies in shooting of collie
abstract: Melanie Eng was awarded $1,200 and given apologies over the shooting death of her border collie at Coyler Lake, an incident that ignited a flurry of criticism from animal lovers. Jacob Wishard, a volunteer deputy waterways conservation officer, shot and killed the dog after it ran towards him while he was trying to inspect Eng’s boat. The settlement also includes promises not to reissue Wishard a deputy commission, an agreement to train deputies in dog behavior and nonlethal means of protection and consideration of making dog access areas more accessible in light of newly passed restrictions

headline: Senate passes funding bill for battlefield - Compromise with House still needed
abstract: Two days after the U.S. House rejected a bill that included a provision to provide up to $1.5 million in federal funds to purchase the site of the Paoli Massacre, where 50 American soldiers were killed in 1777, the Senate unanimously approved more compromising legislation sponsored by Senator Arlen Specter of PA. The Senate’s bill would provide up to $1.5 million to purchase the land if a nonprofit group headed by Malvern Borough Manager Patrick McGuigan is able to raise at least $1 million on its own. The House could vote on the new bill as early as today, and U.S. Representative Curt Weldon, the original bill’s sponsor, felt much better about the chances of the new version passing.

headline: Another area lawmaker is left with no opponents on ballot
abstract: Incumbent PA Representatives Gary Haluska, Rick Geist, Larry Sather, Jerry Stern, Dick Hess and Camille George will have no opponents in the upcoming Republican primary election. Daniel Leventry had tried to obtain the required 300 signatures to run against Haluska; however, Leventry found out after a court challenge by Haluska that he did not have enough signatures to run. Leventry said that incumbents have huge advantages which make it extremely difficult for average citizens to get involved in politics.

headline: History and hoopla: How GOP convention came here - The city perfectly executed its pitch to both parties, finally luring the GOP.
abstract: Philadelphia was chosen over seven competing cities to host the Republican National Convention in 2000, and Governor Tom Ridge, Ed Rendell and countless others put a lot of hard work into convincing the site selection committee to choose Philadelphia. Besides the unfortunate timing of a strike by workers of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, officials operated a nearly flawless plan that provided site selection committee members with an opportunity to visit Independence Hall, tour the First Union Center, receive a fife-and-drum band greeting at the Liberty Bell and even watch sharks take part in the wooing effort by gobbling up competing cities in a skit at the New Jersey State Aquarium. The city’s efforts clearly left a good impression on committee members, and Philadelphia had to withdraw its name from consideration for the Democratic National Convention after being chosen by Republicans.

headline: Robbins Hoping For 3rd Term
abstract: PA Senator Robert Robbins is expected to make a district-wide tour to announce his plans to seek a third term to represent the 50th District. He had previously served in the state House, and the various committees that he chairs or serves on in the Senate are described in the article.

headline: More untaxed property found in Springbrook
abstract: Springbrook Township's year long investigation revealed that mmore then 40 properties had not been assessed and had not been charged taxes. The properties have been added to the tax roll and will benefit the North Pocono School District.

headline: Fewer Teens Receiving Abortions in Virginia - Notification Law To Get Court Test
abstract: Since Virginia past a law requiring minors to notify their parents before getting an abortion, preliminary statistics show that girls under the age of 17 received 20 percent fewer abortions in the state; though there is evidence that some girls are simply leaving the state to avoid the parental notification law. Nationally, teenage birth rates are down, and many anti-abortion advocates attribute this to behavioral changes caused by the parental notification laws, which eliminate the secrecy of a "quick fix," but pro-choice advocates refute this idea and claim birth rates have gone down because of increased use of contraceptives. Some parents support the notification laws, yet others fear the laws will encourage some children to avoid the laws by getting unsafe, back ally abortions.

headline: State HMO regulation will drive up costs
abstract: An estimated 67.5 million Americans are currently enrolled in a health maintenance organization (HMO). Nationally, HMO enrollment has increased by 85 percent since 1990.  Pennsylvania has the fourth-highest number of HMO members in the nation at more than four million.  Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries are also enrolling in HMOs and other network-based health plans in record numbers.

headline: Schools Lose Suit For More Money  Commonwealth Court says it has no jurisdiction
abstract: PA Commonwealth Court Judge Dan Pellegrini rejected a lawsuit filed by the PA Association of Rural and Small Schools (PARSS) that was trying to force Governor Tom Ridge to provide more funding for poorer, rural districts. PARSS is asking for more state funding to compensate for the fact that wealthier areas are able to generate more educational funding via property taxes than poorer districts, but Pellegrini said the court had no authority to intervene, and there was also no evidence to show students are receiving inadequate educations. Gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin criticized the court’s decision, whereas Ridge was clearly pleased and said the poorest districts are already awarded substantially more state funds than wealthier areas.

headline: Something is missing from choice
abstract: Gregory Karp talks about the 'hoice' with electric companies now allowing residents to pick their provider.

headline: State considers issuing new license plates
abstract: PA House legislators and staffers confirmed that new tags will be issued to motorists within the next 18 months, after police complaints that older plates are often hard to read, especially at night. PA Rep. Richard Olasz is the House Transportation Committee's ranking Democrat. The PA Department of Transportation will need over $1 million to carry out the reissuance. The reissuance is also due to a high number of suspected counterfeit tags. Legislators hope PennDOT will gain revenue, as those with counterfeit tags will be forced to go legitimate.

headline: Pa. joins fight for tobacco compact
abstract: PA expects to receive $11 million in a tobacco settlement, however, PA is still going on with the lawsuit in case the settlement does not come through.

headline: Senator pushes for mandatory smoke detector law
abstract: PA Senator Jack Wagner has proposed legislation that would require mandatory smoke detectors in all new homes and older homes that are being put up for sale. He cited the recent fire in a Centre County cabin that took the lives of 11 students as evidence for the need of a mandatory smoke detector law. Wagner’s bill comes at a time when the state Legislature is considering a statewide building code that would conform to the standards set forth by the Building Officials and Code Administration in 1996.

headline: $2.8 million a day in political funding not enough
abstract: Although the national Democratic and Republican Parties are raising $2.8 million a day, it is not enough for their ambitious plans, and both parties have been forced to scale back their campaign spending, which will result in the candidates themselves raising much of the money to spend on their elections. Between January 1, 1997 and October 15, 1998, Republicans raised $299 million and Democrats raised $192 million, which is much more than they grossed for the last nonpresidential election in 1994, but it is less than the huge amounts of money grossed for the 1996 campaign.

headline: Hoeffel, Fox face off in debate
abstract: Incumbent U.S. Representative Jon Fox and challenger Joseph Hoeffel 3rd held a debate, and the first question centered on President Clinton’s impeachment inquiry. Both claimed their party was responsible for the federal budget surplus and said it’s important to protect Social Security. Other topics included military spending, U.S. support of the United Nations, health care and abortion.

headline: Rodino and 400 historians say Clinton's act don't justify impeachment
abstract: Former Representative Peter Rodino, who presided over President Nixon’s impeachment hearings, doesn’t believe that Clinton’s actions justify his impeachment and could set a dangerous future precedent. The House authorized an impeachment inquiry three weeks ago, and hundreds of historians signed a petition condemning it. Arthur Schlesinger, who helped initiate the petition, said perjury charges could warrant impeachment but not when they involve one’s personal life, such as the charges facing Clinton.

headline: New Charter will be no threat to RAD
abstract: If the new home rule charter passes, the Regional Asset District and the RAD tax would legally remain part of Allegheny County.

headline: Fifth dimension
abstract: After the new home rule was enacted in Alleghnet County, four white males were nominated as part of the 5 panel council. Commissioner Dunn threatens to block the nomination is diversity is not reached on the council.

headline: State is lacking in laws for smoke-free initiative
abstract: Tony Delonti, the Chair of Take Action for Tobacco Free Youth, said PA smoking regulations are basically non-existent, and schools are the only public facilities where smoking is banned. The state Clean Indoor Air Law does have a provision that restaurants seating over 75 people should provide non-smoking areas, which most restaurants do provide. The group may be rewarded three Department of Health grants, one of which would fund a program to train up to 100 youth as anti-smoking advocates, and Delonti criticized Lackawanna County for spending money on cigarettes for prisoners.

headline: Schools to receive grades
abstract: The Ohio General Assembly passed a bill that will require the Ohio Board of Education to issue report cards on each school district’s performance. The report cards will review the performance of each school based on the percentage of students who pass proficiency tests, a minimum attendance rate and a three percent maximum drop out rate, and the schools will receive labels based on their overall scores. Proponents of the bill hope that it will raise educational standards and help inform parents about the performance of Ohio’s schools.

headline: Some states have trouble with electric competition
abstract: While Congress continues to debate mandating the deregulation of the $208 billion electric industry, 16 states have already deregulated to allow competition, and many other states are moving to implement competition plans or are seriously considering doing so. However, states such as New York, California and Massachusetts are running into problems with their deregulated markets, and state legislators and advocacy groups are searching for ways to promote more competition and provide cheaper energy for the average customer. One of the biggest sources of contention is who should pay stranded costs, debt still owed on nuclear plants and long term contracts to purchase power, but as of now, states have been awarding utilities full or major recoveries on their stranded costs.

headline: State considers options for Danville home
abstract: The state is considering whether Pennsylvania Department f Transportation is able to demolish certain homes on Factory Street to begin construction of the Dansville-Riverside Bridge.

headline: Pa. scraps 5-day wait for guns
abstract: Pennsylvania's five-day waiting period to buy handguns is history today.  Under the new, $3.5 million Pennsylvania Instant Check System (PICS) handgun buyers with no criminal record will be able to take their firearms home the day of purchase.  Except for the waiting period, however, little will change in the requirements, and handgun purchasers will still be subject to the same level of background checks.

headline: Senators wary on Mall plan - Rendell wants $65 million for the Constitution Center. It may be a tough sell
abstract: At the behest of Pennsylvania’s U.S. Senators, Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum, key Senators from the Appropriations Committee, including Ted Stevens, Slade Gorton and Pete Domenici, travelled to Philadelphia to meet with Mayor Ed Rendell over his plans to build a National Constitution Center, which he is counting on about $65 million in federal funding to complete. However, Stevens mistakenly believed the National Park Service was against Rendell’s proposal, and the Senators expressed concerns about the large amount of money Rendell is asking for. There were also concerns about having a non-profit organization running the Constitution Center; however, the Senator’s questionable stance will not affect plans to remake most of Independence Mall by creating a new home for the Liberty Bell as well as a new Gateway Visitors Center.

headline: ‘ROW, ROW, ROW YOUR BOAT’
abstract: The political cartoon pertains to Governor Ridge’s huge monetary advantage over his challenger, Ivan Itkin, in the gubernatorial election.

headline: Hoeffel, Fox sparring over their spending
abstract: Democrat congressional candidate Joseph Hoeffel III is putting a price tag on the hypocrisy he attributes to Jon D Fox, the Republican incumbent in the 13th District. The price tag is $54 billion. The $54 billion is the difference between $60.1 billion cost of legislation the Fox sponsored and the $6/07 billion cost of legislation he actually voted for. 89% of congressmen voted for more spending than he did.

headline: Rogan Announces Candidacy for 10th District Seat
abstract: Lackawanna County Republican State Committeewoman, Mary Rogan, officially kicked off her campaign for Congress in the 10th district on Tuesday at her home in Clarks Summit.

headline: New tax reform debate: Is a chicken coop a homestead?
abstract: A new proposed  legislative measure would allow the Homestead Act to include barns and nonresidential farm buildings to have a lower tax rate.

headline: Fisher supports curb on abortion transport
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher testified before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee in support of a bill that would make it illegal to transport minors across state lines for the purpose of getting an abortion and avoiding parental-consent requirements. The bill is a response to Rose Marie Harford, a woman who took the 13-year-old daughter of Joyce Farley to New York to get an abortion. Harford’s 18-year-old son impregnated the girl, and Farley was unaware of her daughter’s pregnancy.

headline: State physician flap irks Ridge
abstract: It was a made-for-television event that was supported to let Gov. Ridge highlight his support for a "patients bill of rights" to protect consumers enrolled in health maintenance organizations.  But it didn't work out that way.  Instead, the governor was peppered with questions about the resignation of Dr. Wanda Filer as the state's first physician general.

headline: Schools wary of teacher money
abstract: Local Pennsylvania school districts are cautious about the $662,982 received to hire more teachers. Schools districts are worried the ferderl government will discontinue the funding after the first year and school districts will be left with the bill.

headline: State electrified
abstract: Secretary of Community and Economic Development, Sam McCullough, writes to the Scranton Tribune about how important electric deregulation is to residents.

headline: State House passes bill to update vehicle code in PA
abstract: According to PA House Transportation Committee Chairman Richard Geist, the PA House passed a vehicle code, originally sponsored by Representative Merle Phillips, containing over 200 provisions for increasing safety, protecting school children and clarifying conflicting laws. The new code would cover a wide range of topics, which are described in greater detail in the article. Among other provisions, it would provide several restrictions pertaining to driving near school busses, direct the PA Department of Transportation to reissue new license plates and allow more seniors to qualify for cheaper vehicle registration renewals.

headline: Pa. Senators opposed gun-safety bill
abstract: Charlton Heston promised a more moderate, more mainstream national Rifle Association.  But judging by the recent acts of some NRA leaders, the association continues to shamelessly pin bull's eyes on any effort at promoting gun safety.  Worse yet, the NRA is getting the help of the U.S. senators who should know better -- including Pennsylvania Republicans Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum

headline: Senior complex receives funding
abstract: The PA Housing Finance Agency allocated $538,000 to fund a new senior citizen apartment complex in Chicora, and the project could begin construction by early June. The local housing authority will also seek tax credits and a $108,000 federal grant for the project, and Butler County pledged $250,000 towards the $2 million project. As of now, the Chicora Sewer Authority appears favorable to offering lower sewage rates for the project.

headline: 104th results chart political fortunes
abstract: One political career may have begun another seems to have been firmly established and another long career in politics may be a step closer to ending in the aftermath of the republican primary in the 104th House District. Representative Mark McNaughton won the hotly contested three-way race with a commanding 61 percent of the votes cast, demonstrating the kind of political muscle that will make prospective challengers think twice before taking him on.

headline: Holden gains 4th term in 6th District
abstract: Although official results are still not available, U.S. Representative Tim Holden won a fourth term to represent the 6th District by defeating John Meckley, his Republican challenger, handily. Meckley thanked party leaders and said "you haven’t seen the last of John Meckley" during his concession speech. Holden vowed to get back to work quickly, claiming he would focus on repaying all $650 billion that Congress owes the Social Security fund and working to secure more funds for a  proposed light rail line between Philadelphia and Reading.

headline: Ron Klink handily defeats GOP challenger for fourth House term
abstract: U.S. Representative Ron Klink easily defeated challenger Mike Turzai, receiving 64 percent of the 4th District's vote. The campaign had gotten bitter after Turzai hired a helicopter to shoot footage of Klink’s home and campaign aides got into a shoving match when Turzai’s workers confronted Klink with a video camera, which Klink believes widened his margin of victory. Klink cited his record in creating jobs and getting tougher on health maintenance organization during the election.

headline: No position on home-rule
abstract: Senator Bodack wrote to the Post-Gazette to say that the Democractic Committee has no official position on the proposed Allegheny home rule charter.

headline: Flag-desecration amendment revived by conservative group
abstract: Says executive director of the Citizens Flag Alliance, the organization is very hopeful a US Senate amendment to ban flag desecration will pass. Supporters are only three votes short of the 70 needed to pass the measure. The Family Research Council also supports the amendment. Congress earlier passed an anti-desecration measure which was struck down by the US Supreme Court. Supporters say the amendment would not infringe on freedom of speech.

headline: State wants case moved here
abstract: The state attorney general filed motions late yesterday to intervene in the Allegheny health system's bankruptcy proceedings and to move the case from Pittsburgh to Philadelphia  Consumer groups applauded the moves, while legal experts said the intervention was expected but doubted the case will be shifted to Philadelphia.  Attorney General D. Michael Fisher filed the two separate motions in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Pittsburgh.

headline: Schweiker visits NCC, tours Technology Hall
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker toured Northampton Community College’s Technology Hall and urged other educational institutions throughout the state and nation to use the college as a model to follow. Local industries donated much of the high-tech equipment that is used to train students at the college. Schweiker spoke about Governor Ridge’s endorsement of Brian Pest to fill the 137th House seat and Ridge’s new budget, which will include $74.5 million in new funding to develop Pennsylvania’s workforce.

headline: State may cut power of eminent domain
abstract: Pennsylvania’s move to allow greater competition in the electric power industry could have some unintended consequences. The state’s traditional eight utilities have been able to invoke eminent domain to seize a person’s property for the purpose of building a new power plant or transmission lines; however, the state’s efforts to increase competition have led to even more companies moving into PA to sell power. According to state Representative Ed Krebs, it is unclear whether these new companies would be entitled to exercise eminent domain, and state Representative William Lloyd hopes to address the issue when updating eminent domain laws.

headline: State must continue to fight drunken driving
abstract: State police stationed at the Butler barracks take the fight against drunken driving very seriously. That's one of the reasons the Butler station led all the barracks in PA by making 504 drunken driving arrests in 1997. State lawmakers must continue to toughen punishment for repeat offenders.

headline: Pa. Woman's Murder Conviction Upheld
abstract: PA judge rejects an appeal by a convicted female murdered, Lisa Lambert, that she received an unfair trail and is innocent of the accussed crime.

headline: Stadiums fall victim to phantom
abstract: The author says that in Harrisburg the truth isn’t always as it seems, and he discusses a notorious practice in the PA Legislature that seems to come around when the Legislative session ends every two years. This year, the Legislature passed a bill that contained hidden language that could have allowed Governor Tom Ridge to provide funding for stadium projects in Pittsburgh; however, Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy held a press conference that unveiled the bill’s hidden intentions, which brought on an outcry of disapproval and compelled Ridge to veto it. According to the author, Murphy’s actions may have doomed his chances of getting state funding for new stadiums for the time being, and Ridge will have to take the lead if there is any chance of resurrecting stadium-financing attempts in the future.

headline: 15th District Democrats withhold barbs
abstract: The two candidates seeking the Democratic nomination, Roy Offenbach and Janice McElroy, in the 15th Congressional District agreed on most issues discussed and unlike their Republican counterparts, avoided sniping at one another during a debate Friday night. They did differ on affirmative action and quotas and assault weapons.

headline: Holden: A day in the life of a Pennsylvania Congressman
abstract: The article describes the typical day of U.S. Representative Tim Holden, who was first elected in 1992 to represent the sixth district. Congress has already tackled his two main objectives, balancing the budget and reforming the welfare system, so he now plans to focus on the nation’s infrastructure problems, including a number of road and sewer projects in his district. Holden said he tries to pay attention to what his constituents care about, and he hopes to be re-elected this year, while his challenger, Assistant District Attorney John Meckley, said he plans to focus on economic development and brining more prosperity to the sixth district.

headline: ROTARY CHECK
abstract: The photo depicts representatives of the Rotary Club of Edge Hill presenting a check worth over $5,000 to PA Representative Ellen Bard for the Abington Trails project.

headline: Objective accelerating this city's renewal
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell included a 2.2 percent reduction in Philadelphia’s wage tax, and he focused on eliminating waste in spending, which the authors believe are steps in the right direction, but ultimately, they believe more still needs to be done. They claim the city’s wage tax continues to hurt the city’s economic development, and 66,000 Philadelphians will come off welfare within the next 18 months, with no clear source of income. The authors cite several examples of wasteful spending, and they believe that by eliminating the wage tax and encouraging more businesses, the city will be able to drastically reduce crime and improve the quality of education in public schools.

headline: Flexing their muscles
abstract: Leaders of the Million Woman March yesterday joined the campaign against District Attorney Lynne Abraham with a demonstration outside her office and calls for resurrecting a black power conference.  March co-founders Asia Coney and Phil Chionesu blasted Abraham's last-minute opposition to the nomination of Common Pleas Court Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson to the federal bench.  About 30 people gathered outside Abraham's office, handing out copies of the letter Abraham wrote two weeks ago to Sen. Arlen Specter in opposition to the judge's nomination.

headline: States blaze trail for anti-smoking laws   Their experiences can help Congress as it plays catch-up
abstract: While Congress is debating a bill that would increase cigarette prices, allow governmental regulation of nicotine and fine cigarette companies that fail to curb teen usage, many states are moving ahead with their own plans, which include raising cigarette taxes, preventing teen access to cigarettes, education programs and restrictions on smoking in public places. Despite efforts, Massachusetts and California, considered to have two of the toughest anti-tobacco programs, have only recently seen slight drops in teen smoking rates, while throughout the rest of the country, rates have increased by nearly a third in the past six years. Many states argue the importance of increasing tobacco taxes and educational programs, but evidence has suggested the best approach to reducing tobacco use is by targeting all smokers as opposed to focusing just on teens.

headline: Senate moves ahead in PIAA probe: Allegations abound that the group is too secretive
abstract: A special Senate investigation into the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association (PIAA), a nonprofit corporation that establishes and regulates rules for high school and junior high sports, held its second hearing and is considering instituting some type of state oversight panel. PA Senator Robert Jubelirer criticized the PIAA for being secretive and for trampling the constitutional rights of Pete White, a retired coach who spoke at the hearing to describe how he was forced to spend $2,000 to defend himself against a PIAA investigation that was based entirely on an anonymous letter. Many of the Senators are angry over the PIAA’s decision to move the state football championship from Altoona to Hershey; though they also cited a long list of complaints against the PIAA.

headline: State Oks releasing competing electric rates
abstract: Pennsylvania clears the way for comeptition between electric companies.

headline: State picks contractor for South-West Beltway
abstract: Tom M. Durkin and Son's won the bid for contracts to build new roads and make improvements along the South-West Beltway.

headline: Pa. Woman's Murder Conviction Upheld: Trial Judge Rejects Allegations That Lisa Michelle Lambert Was Framed; Appeals Planned
abstract: Lisa Michelle Lambert was convicted in 1991 of murdering sixteen-year-old Laurie Show, who was a romantic rival of her boyfriend. She claims that she was framed by the police and prosecution, and she was released from prison six years later by U.S. District Court Judge Stewart Dalzell, who found 25 instances of misconduct. However, his ruling was overturned by Lancaster County Common Pleas Court Judge Stengel, but Lambert’s lawyer still hopes that the U.S. Supreme Court will hear the case and release her.

headline: Stadium's financial future questioned - The county may take action to ensure it will never take over should project fail.
abstract: Northampton County Council Vice President Cindy Marakovits will introduce a resolution to ensure the county doesn’t get stuck owning the proposed baseball stadium in Williams Township if the stadium is found to be unprofitable. The county Industrial Development Authority sent an application asking the state for a $5 million grant to help build the stadium for Thomas Flaherty’s team, the Lehigh Valley Black Diamonds. However, County Executive Glenn Reibman has asked Governor Tom Ridge not to approve the grant because he doesn’t think taxpayers’ dollars should be used to fund it, and he’s worried about the stadium’s economic viability.

headline: 1905 case established government's right to require vaccinations
abstract: The 1905 U.S. Supreme Court Case Jacobsen vs. Massachusetts set the precedent that the government has the right to order vaccinations because the community’s right to protect itself supersedes the individual’s freedom to choose not to get vaccinated.

headline: Holden's district office besieged by calls
abstract: Representative Tom Holden received numerous calls from consituents about the upcoming impeachment vote on President Clinton.

headline: Roy Cornell wins 11th victory for 152nd House seat
abstract: PA Representative Roy Cornell won his reelection easily against Libertarian John Russo, so he will represent the 152nd District for the 11th time. No Democratic candidate challenged Cornell, which some Republicans viewed as a testament to the job Cornell is doing in office. Another area race between Fox and Hoeffel is much closer.

headline: Oh so slowly, Philadelphia rouses itself from its isolationist slumber
abstract: In the mid 1980’s, Wharton professor Howard Perlmutter’s plan to turn Philadelphia into an "international city" was met with little enthusiasm; however he is trying again, and this time, he’s found Philadelphians are much more aware of their city’s role in the global marketplace. The city’s international exports have increased substantially, and Philadelphia International Airport opened a new international terminal in 1991, which has acquired a good reputation. However, exports still fall below the nation’s average, the airport is ranked 21st nationally in passenger volume, despite serving the fifth most populous region, and Philadelphia still lags behind others cities as popular foreign tourist destinations.

headline: State a leader in land trusts   Pittsburgh-based conservancy guards largest acreage
abstract: According to the Land Trust Alliance, over 348,000 acres of land have been conserved in PA throughout the years, which ranks PA second nationally. The Western PA Conservancy, based in Pittsburgh, conserved 236,000 acres of that total, and its president, Larry Schweiger, described how the organization has been able to protect so much land from development during a phone interview. Nationally, 4.7 million acres of land have been protected.

headline: For Democrats and GOP, looking to church for votes
abstract: President Clinton and many other Democrats are attending predominately black churches on the final Sunday before elections, which could play an important role since blacks have consistently leaned Democrat since the 1960 presidential election. Republican candidates are more likely to benefit from the Christian Coalition’s $3.1 million effort to distribute information about candidates at conservative churches throughout the country. The Coalition claims that the information is nonpartisan, but many believe that it is consistently pro-Republican, which has led the Americans United for the Separation of Church and State to attempt to convince churches not to distribute the material.

headline: State's dilemma: What to do with $10B?
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher is hoping to finalize a multi-state settlement with the four major tobacco companies that is expected to bring PA about $10 million. Many states have filed lawsuits against the tobacco industry to try to recoup Medicaid costs caused by smoking-related illnesses, and the overall settlement is expected to reach $200 billion over 25 years. Several local organizations would like to use the funding for anti-smoking prevention programs, which Governor Ridge would also like to see, and state Representative Dwight Evans would like to put the money towards Medicaid, while the state Senate will have its own ideas on how to spend the money.

headline: Senate panel Oks academic standards
abstract: Critics of new statewide academic standards for public schools fired parting shots as the Senate Education Committee gave the standards a final round of legislative approval. The Senate panel endorsed the standards by a vote of 9-2, a margin more lopsided than last week's vote in the House Education Committee. The new rules specify skills which students are expected to master by each of four assessment stages in statistical analysis, number relationships, grammar, punctuation, literature and speechmaking.

headline: Still time to make electricity choice
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission extended the deadline to November 16 for choosing an electricity supplier, which will give customers more time to choose a supplier in time to see results on their January electric bills.  Many customers have been frustrated or confused with their choice because many suppliers have yet to announce their prices. Even if customers fail to meet the deadline, they will still be able to exercise their right to choose in time to see results on their bills by February or March.

headline: State police start checking for seat belts
abstract: State Police have begun using highway checkpoints to issue warnings to drivers in PA who aren’t wearing their seatbelts, but according to current law, officers can only issue tickets when they are citing a motorist for an additional offense such as speeding. PA Representative Robert Godshall is sponsoring a bill to allow officers to issue seat belt citations at any time; however, the PA chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union believes it would infringe on personal rights, while the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People fears the law could lead to minority drivers being harassed. According to the U.S. Transportation Department, 10,000 lives are saved each year by seat belts.

headline: Pact guiding Pa. prisons is thrown out
abstract: A consent agreement was reached after a suit was filed in 1970 against former PA Governor Milton Shapp’s administration by inmates who complained about living conditions and a lack of clear guidelines for registering complaints and appeals. The agreement established a code of conduct and set a number of guidelines, ranging from minimum health care standards to searches of cells and prison dress attire; however, U.S. District Judge Jan DuBois threw out the agreement and affirmed the U.S. Prison Litigation Reform Act, which was passed in 1995 to limit civil rights suits by prisoners. The American Civil Liberties Union in Philadelphia complained about the decision and believes the state will erode prisoners' rights over times, but many state officials believe the decision will allow corrections professionals to operate prisons more safely at their own discretion.

headline: Sports and business play the name game - New stadiums need the funding; corporations need the exposure.
abstract: Across the nation, more and more stadiums are taking on the names of corporate sponsors, and according to the Bonham Group, naming rights deals are worth a total of $1.37 billion, which is expected to exceed $2 billion by 2002. Naming rights deals have become popular for many stadiums, including the First Union Center in Philadelphia, because these deals can generate millions of dollars towards construction costs and other expenses. Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell has considered selling the naming rights of Veterans Stadium, and in addition, corporate sponsors have benefited from naming rights deals because they generate the same name recognition that would likely have cost millions of dollars more through television advertisements.

headline: 2 Philly Democrats to repeat caucus war
abstract: The Nov. 24 Democratic caucus election should be held in Gettysburg.

headline: Honor legislators
abstract: The Beaver County Chapter of the PA Association of School Retirees (PASR) hosted a breakfast to honor Beaver County legislators. The photo depicts PASR President Robert Wagoner, state Senator Gerald Lavalle, state Representative Susan Laughlin, state Representative Victor Lescovitz, an aide to state Representative Nick Colafella, state Representative Mike Veon and an aide to Representative Lescovitz.

headline: Rudy Dininni dies at 72, left mark on state House
abstract: Former state House member Rudy Dininni died at his home yesterday after a prolonged interest. Dininni is remembered as a man who cared deeply about the people he represented, said PA Sen. Jeffrey Piccola. As chairman of the House Transportation Committee, Dininni is well remembered for his accomplishments. Frank Linn, a Lower Swatara Twp. Commissioner, remembers Dininni for his charitable giving.

headline: Out at home
abstract: Although voters approved the adoption of home rule, the political process appears to have stalled in Allegheny County. Commissioner Larry Dunn held up the appointment of the apportionment commission. Then two members of the commission sought a fifth member beyond those nominated by the other three. And then, candidate Helen Faison, a former city schools deputy superintendent, took her name out of consideration. Jacqueline Hill has also withdrawn. In two biographies, a graduate certificate received by Hill was overstated. Editors believe Hill, who is both African American, female and Republican, would have brought the right mix of talent and diversity to the commission.

headline: Amusement tax repeal no joke
abstract: The PA Legislature is considering changing or repealing several local "nuisance taxes," including an amusement tax, which is paid by recreational establishments such as Pocono International Raceway. State Representative Joseph Battisto supports the elimination of the tax, but the authors claim that would only result in shifting the burden of taxes onto others. According to the authors, the need for taxes won’t go away, so the state Legislature and local governments should tell taxpayers where the tax burden will shift before they eliminate nuisance taxes.

headline: Four New Members Join D.C. Women's Hall of Fame
abstract: To commemorate Women’s History Month, four women were inducted into the District of Columbia Women’s Hall of Fame. The four women are Army Colonel Doris Browne, District of Columbia Council member Carol Schwartz, lawyer Brenda Smith and Superior Court Judge Mary Terrell.

headline: States still battle vs. managed care
abstract: As Congress considers new regulation of managed-care, states are continuing longstanding efforts to mandate benefits and patient rights.  Forty-two states passed managed-care regulation or benefit mandates in 1987, according to a survey released Thursday by the Blue Cross BlueShield Association.

headline: Sherwood steps down from TA school board
abstract: Don Sherwood stepped down as president of the Tunkhannock Area School Board, and he will be sworn in as the region’s Congressman on January 6, 1999. Sherwood performed his final duties and thanked everyone in attendance for allowing him to serve on the school board for over twenty years. Mike Burnside was named as the new president and Ray Mocium will continue as vice president.

headline: Tell public more about electric deregulation
abstract: Public Opinion talks about the deregulation of electric companies and urges that the public continue to be made aware of the deregulation process and progress.

headline: State reaps road rewards
abstract: US Sen. Rick Santorum and House Reps. Jim Grewood and Curt Weldon were surprised by an extra $140 million for projects in their districts, slipped into a House transportation bill by Rep. Bud Shuster, chairman of transportation. Shuster also chairs of the House Senate Conference Committee, which oversees final drafts of bills. Shuster added the $140 million after negotiations were over, and earmarked $3 million for tolls he had wiped out on the section of the PA Turnpike in his district.  The bill needed 400 individual corrections after its passage, angering watchdog spending groups.

headline: Pair mount Megan's Law Challenge
abstract: Two Cumberland County residents have joined a growing list of defendants questioning the constitutionality of Megan's Law. John Karns and Robert Dick recently were recently convicted of involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, one of a list of offenses that invokes application of PA's so called Megan's law. Megan's Law requires that individuals found guilty of sex-related crimes be ovulated by the State Board to Assess Sexually Violent Predators. If the individual is labeled a sexually violent predator he must register his address with the state police until he dies or is deemed no longer to be a threat. Some argue the law constitutes double jeopardy.

headline: Sports team owners seek stadium money - House OK could hinge on midstate delegation
abstract: The owners of the Pittsburgh Pirates and Steelers and the Philadelphia Phillies were in Harrisburg trying to persuade state legislators to go along with Governor Tom Ridge’s one-third financing plan to help build four new stadiums in the two cities, which would require the state to raise its debt level. Senate Majority Leader Joseph Loeper believes there are enough votes in the Senate to get it passed, and it may consider a proposal as early as today; however, House Majority Leader John Perzel’s staff was less optimistic about the chances of it passing the House. Governor Tom Ridge is trying to convince legislators from outside the two cities that money will also be available for projects across the state, but in order to convince the Central PA Caucus to vote along with the plan, $35 million for a Hershey arena may have to be included.

headline: 3 local Democrats against impeachment
abstract: Three Democratic U.S. congressmen from Westmoreland County, Frank Mascara, John Murtha and Ron Klink, have all announced that they will not vote to impeach President Clinton; though that has not stopped phone calls from flooding into their offices. Mascara said he didn’t see any evidence from Kenneth Starr’s investigation which would lead him to believe Clinton should be removed from office. He expects Republican House leaders will back down because they don’t want Vice President Gore to take over.

headline: House GOP to choose leaders by secret vote
abstract: In light of the poor showing by the Republican Party in the recent election, two of the four House Republican leaders face strong challenges to retaining their positions, and Representative Bob Livingston will be the party’s choice to take over House Speaker Newt Gingrich’s position. Majority Leader Dick Armey faces challenges from Representatives Steve Largent, Jennifer Dunn and potentially Dennis Hastert, while the chairman of the Republican Conference, Representative John Boehner, is being challenged by Representative J.C. Watts, the party’s lone black member in Congress. House Republicans will meet today to cast their secret ballots, and no one can yet be certain of what the outcomes will be.

headline: Rule by minority
abstract: Congressional failure to endorse a firm constraint on taxation is an old story that the House didn't alter when a supermajority requirement for federal tax hikes was defeated for the third straight year. The proposed constitutional amendment required the assent of two-thirds of the House and Senate and backing from 38 of America's state legislatures. Unfortunately, more than a third of the lower chamber voted to preserve the status quo. This is not ok to be ruled by a minority.

headline: Pa. court assails tax on stocks
abstract: The PA Supreme Court ruled that a tax on stocks and bonds unfairly discriminates against out-of-state companies; however, it didn’t rule the tax unconstitutional, and instead ordered Montgomery County Court to take up the issue. Most counties, including Lancaster, have gotten rid of the tax since it was first challenged three years. But if the court determines the tax is unconstitutional, counties could be ordered to refund the collected revenue, which would pose a serious challenge for most counties.

headline: 3 more States Stopped Taxing Poorest Families in '97, Study Says
abstract: Three states last year stopped taxing the incomes of families living below the official poverty line, but other state also scientifically cut taxes for the middle class and the rich in recent years continue to tax the incomes of poorest families, a new analysis of state tax laws shows. The survey was conducted by the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities. It research tries to help the poor get off of welfare and into the workforce.

headline: Gay killing spurs Pa. hate-crimes legislation
abstract: PA state Representative Lita Cohen would have preferred to jolt her hate crimes bills out of legislative slumber some other way, but when a gay University of Wyoming student, Matthew Shepard, was killed and hung from a fence and found 18 hours later after being mistaken for a scarecrow, Cohen's bills finally received attention. They require state police to monitor crimes targeting gays and lesbians. It also adds sexual orientation to the list of hate crimes.

headline: Steps taken to balance HMO goals
abstract: HMO's must now carry the following warning label: This managed care plan may not cover all your health-care expenses.  Read your contract carefully to determine which health care services are covered.  Requiring a warning label on HMOs?  This label symbolizes the current backlash against HMOs, based on oft-repeated horror stories about HMO abuses.

headline: Should school boards have say on charter schools?
abstract: According to the editorial, nearly all of the approved charter schools are located in urban or rural areas, and most suburban areas seem reluctant to try something new since suburban students already have huge advantages in opportunities over students in less privileged areas. However, the authors claim that in the growing global market, even the smartest suburban students are unable to compete in math and science subjects with students from abroad. They claim the state government has already given local school boards the power to approve or accept charter schools, and they ask their readers whether school boards should be given this power.

headline: The fight to make sure PGW works - Most say the management has made progress.
abstract: James Hawes and the rest of the new management team of the Philadelphia Gas Works, the largest municipal-run utility in the nation, have been credited with making substantial progress, including improved bill collections, a reduction in the company’s gas costs, improved response times for repairs and fewer complaints to the City Council. However, there has still been criticism, especially over the large bonuses given to Hawes and two other top executives, and the company faces many challenges in the future. Hawes has launched a large marketing campaign to target large customers who shop around and customers who have gas service but don’t use it for heat, while he must also address the problem of subsidies to the poor and elderly, which is draining profits.

headline: State roads must continue to improve
abstract: Valley News Dispatch is pleased that the Pennsykvania Turnpike is no longer rated as the worst road in the nation and that Pennsylvania roads were rannked among the most improvemed. Valley News Dispatch encourages PennDOT to continue road improvements in the state.

headline: Panel to overhaul crime reporting - A criminologist will head a Philadelphia effort to ensure accuracy by police
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner John Timoney has appointed Lawrence Sherman, a well respected criminologist from the University of Maryland, to head the Quality Assurance Review Committee, which will teach departmental auditors how to survey crime reports to ensure the city’s crime figures are being accurately counted. After taking over as commissioner, Timoney investigated the problem of police underreporting crimes to make the city’s crime rate appear better, and departmental auditors found that as many as 1 in 10 major crimes in the city were either downgraded or dropped entirely from the count. Mayor Ed Rendell supports the hiring of Sherman, and in addition to Sherman’s hiring, Timoney stripped two police captains of their commands due to underreporting in their precincts.

headline: Sprawl busters   Lawmakers seek ways to control growth
abstract: Urban sprawl has created many problems, and Governor Tom Ridge’s 21st Century Environmental Commission identified controlling sprawl as the state’s biggest challenge. Land is being consumed at a faster rate than population growth in some areas, and scatter development, where residential homes are scattered throughout isolated locations, have contributed to the problem. The PA Legislature is developing legislation which would reward local governments that create more efficient communities, and Ridge is hoping to provide incentives to keep developers away from precious areas such as farmland and natural areas.

headline: 3 local lawmakers vote against measure
abstract: Three lawmakers, Klink, Mascara, and Murtha from Pennsylvania voted agaisnt the new impeacment resolutions regarding President Clinton.

headline: House hopeful making promises in kickoff: Veterinarian in his second quest for Lloyd's seat
abstract: Bob Bastian, who has been a veterinarian in Somerset Township since 1968, formally announced that he would be running for a seat in the PA House to represent the 69th District, a position left open by longtime Representative Bill Lloyd’s decision to run against U.S. Senator Arlen Specter. Bastian lost to Lloyd in the 1996 election, and the Democrats have yet to find a candidate to run in Lloyd’s place. Bastian didn’t focus on issues during his announcement, but he said afterwards that pushing to complete Route 219 and paying closer attention to the needs of the business community will be important.

headline: 'Run like you're losing no matter' Unopposed incumbents on the campaign trail
abstract: Nationally, 52 Republican and over 30 Democratic incumbents face no opposition in their re-election bids, including Pennsylvania's U.S. Representatives Frank Mascara, Bud Shuster, John Peterson and George Gekas; though many will still run campaigns anyway. The non-competitive elections can often be attributed to the incumbents’ huge financial advantages, and Republican House leaders said that having so many incumbents running is definitely an advantage because it allows them to concentrate on other closely contested elections. While many claim the lack of challengers is evidence of voter contentment with incumbents, others are displeased with the lack of choice for voters and have proposed putting "None-of-the-Above" on ballots, so voters have an option to criticize even unchallenged incumbents.

headline: Pa. House of Representatives passes property tax control act
abstract: The PA House approved the School Property Tax Control Act, which will permit local school districts, with local voter approval, to eliminate nuisance taxes and reduce property taxes in return for implementing an earned income and net profits tax. The House also approved a bill intended to protect the rights of patients enrolled in health maintenance organizations, and it approved two bills dealing with military affairs. In addition, the House approved a bill providing licensure requirements for businesses dealing with asbestos abatement, and it supported greater regulation of tattoo artists and body pierces as well as 11 other resolutions.

headline: A rush to pay up
abstract: An estimated 44 million state and federal tax forms were expected to have been filed across the nation yesterday before last night’s tax deadline. A photo of a man receiving tax forms is included, and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and House Majority Leader Dick Armey made stops in the midstate to garner support for their tax proposals.

headline: Gay Scout finally gets a fair shake - N.J. court acts with courage
abstract: According to the editorial, James Dale was an ideal role model for Boy Scouting, yet he was relieved of his duties as an assistant Scout Leader because he had openly admitted to being gay. After eight years of battling in New Jersey courts, an appeals court ruled that Dale had been illegally discriminated against. The authors praise the court’s ruling, and they agree with the court’s majority opinion that homosexuals cannot be excluded from the Boy Scouts for not being "morally straight."

headline: Tenet Healthcare arrives with a burst of symbolism   The hospital chain will restore familiar names to 8 Allegheny hospitals it takes over today
abstract: Tenet Healthcare has restored the names of 8 Philadelphia hospitals that it has purchased from the Pittsburgh based Allegheny system, which became the largest nonprofit health care system to file for bankruptcy. Tenet faces a daunting task in trying to revive the struggling hospitals, but it began a $1 million advertising campaign under the motto, "Let the Healing Begin," and its hospitals will reopen this morning at ceremonies expected to be attended by Mayor Rendell, City Council President John Street, a representative for Governor Ridge and many others. Tenet’s entry into the Philadelphia area has drawn some concern because it didn’t renew some contracts of former employees, and it didn’t sign any formal agreements pertaining to charitable health care, but it breathes new life into the 8 hospitals, and it will try to reestablish a strong link between the hospitals and the community.

headline: Should we wire schools?
abstract: The Federal Communications Commission will vote on whether to suspend a small program, passed as part of the 1996 Telecommunications Act, that collects money from long-distance phone companies and uses it to offer discounts on the cost of hooking up schools and libraries to the internet. The program, known as the e-rate, has been contentious from the start, but lately, as it prepares to begin actually considering applications for the $650 million collected so far, it has become the focus of intense pressure.

headline: $1 million in state funds to go on track
abstract: Pennsylvania is giving $1 million in funds to support 11 rail-freight improvement projects across the state.

headline: State Roads Still Worst, But Better
abstract: Truckers rated PA roads the worst to drive overall, although a stretch of road in Arkansas was rated worst in Overdrive magazine. Last year, I-80 and the PA Turnpike tied for worst roads. However, this year, PA roads were voted most improved. PA Transportation Secretary Brad Mallory hopes truckers' impressions will improve.

headline: Penn State says underage drinkers to face sanctions
abstract: After a raid of Theta Chi fraternity house, that resulted in underage drinking citation, both police and Penn State vow the behavior will not go unpunished.

headline: Stadium bill frustrated by local politics
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge’s plan to raise Pennsylvania’s debt limit to provide funding for one-third of the cost of new stadiums for the Pittsburgh Pirates and Steelers and the Philadelphia Eagles and Phillies fell apart, and a big reason was because Philadelphia’s state legislators were angry at Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell for not seeking their input. Rendell admitted that he had made mistakes, but he recently held a productive meeting with some of these key legislators; though he admitted there aren’t enough votes to pass the funding plan even with their votes. The state Legislature passed a bill thought to be about fire-training; however, legislators and Governor Ridge himself were shocked to learn the bill’s language actually would permit funding for the Pittsburgh stadiums.

headline: 34th Senatorial District candidates asked views on negative campaigning
abstract: The candidates for the 34th District seat in the PA Senate, Connie Lucas, Jake Corman, Vicki Wedler and Scott Conklin, gathered for a debate, where they answered questions ranging from negative campaigning to term limits for legislators. Other topics during the debate included school vouchers, local tax reform, Mifflin County’s property reassessment, increasing cigarette taxes, creating jobs, ensuring accessibility to constituents, control of the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association and teacher contracts. While the candidates had varying opinions on many of the issues, there were some areas of agreement, and Monte Kemmler, who is challenging U.S. Representative Bud Shuster, also attended the debate.

headline: House panel gets an education in work training
abstract: A PA House Subcommittee on Work Force Development, which is chaired by Representative Robert Flick and includes local legislators Rod Wilt, Teresa Forcier and Tracy Seyfert, held a public hearing on proposed legislation over state-funded job training programs. Overall, the message was to make sure certain control of the programs remains local and educators are held accountable. James Brown, former assistant director of a vocational-technical school, supported the legislation to ensure workers have the technical skills to fulfill the demands of businesses; however, Warren County Commissioner Richard Campbell expressed some major concerns held by county commissioners.

headline: Running for office is no longer inexpensive
abstract: According to the editorial, Governor Ridge spent no less than $8.60 for every vote he received to be reelected in the past election, which is much more than the 50 cents Democrat Ivan Itkin and the $2.20 Constitutional Party candidate Peg Luksik spent to get each of their votes. The authors claim money undoubtedly helped Ridge win the election, and it becoming increasingly expensive for candidates to run for office at the local, state and federal level.

headline: Pa. Legislature still taking tenative steps toward local tax reform
abstract: Statelawmakers are propsing amendments that will allow the state to reduce local governments reliance on property tax. The legislation would propose alternative tax generating methods.

headline: Abolish school property taxes
abstract: Representative Dwight Evans writes an opinion on the need for school property tax reform. Evans notes the issues, problems, and possible solution to school property tax.

headline: GOP leaders assure Christian activists - At a meeting, Gingrich and his lieutenants pledged to push a conservative social agenda in the House.
abstract: Republican House leaders Newt Gingrich, Tom DeLay and Dick Armey had a three hour meeting with several Christian activists, which ended in an agreement to push for legislation restricting abortions, encouraging school prayer and limiting the rights of homosexuals. Many of the activists had accused Republicans of betraying their religious and anti-abortion supporters, including James Dobson, who threatened to withdraw his group’s support of the Republican Party. The House leaders agreed to establish a "values action team" headed by Representative Joseph Pitts of PA, and Gingrich promised quick action on proposals to ban partial-birth abortions, eliminate federal arts funding and get rid of a penalty that forces some married couples to pay more taxes than if they were single; however, these proposals will face stiff challenges, especially from President Clinton.

headline: Study: Name reporting does not deter HIV testing
abstract: Stduies conducted show that all states require name reporting for AIDS cases. HIV name reporting is not requird in all states, but, if mandated, it is believed that people would not be deterred from being tested because of name reporting.

headline: Showing off the past can be humbling
abstract: We're in something designated "Heritage Week" by the state Historical and Museum Commission.  John Schreffler is putting together an exhibit in the Dino Hall that will showcase -- probably beginning in June --  a dinosaur called Coelophysis.  It's been a painstaking process since its conception a year and a half ago.

headline: $54 million in road work due by 2001 - Legislators optimistic about county's chances
abstract: Schuylkill County’s Republican state legislators, Senator James Rhoades and Representatives Bob Allen and David Argall, will seek $54 million from the Transportation Commission for 12 different projects, which are listed in the article. Final approval is still needed, but the three legislators are confident, and Transportation Secretary Larry King travelled many of the roads last November.  Allen gave credit to Governor Ridge’s administration, and Argall credited the gasoline tax increase for generating additional revenue for the projects

headline: State, boro and fire company work to make intersection safe
abstract: The state of PA, Chambersbeurg Borough and Franklin Fire Company are meeting to decided what can be done to imprve safety on the corner of North Franklin and West King street.

headline: PennDOT cheated citizens, panel told - Property-condemnation law may be revised
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation was harshly criticized during hearings before the PA House Select Committee on Eminent Domain, which is examining whether the law regulating how the government can seize private property should be revised for the first time since the 1960’s. Former attorneys for PennDOT and people who have had their properties seized for road projects have complained about the agency pressuring appraisers in order to offer cheaper property compensation. State Representatives Ronald Marisco and Ivan Itkin were both troubled by the testimony over PennDOT’s alleged abuse of power, and while property owners can still take the agency’s offers to court to receive higher compensation, additional attorney’s fees and appraisals can be costly.

headline: Stadium funding in limbo
abstract: The PA Senate passed Governor Tom Ridge’s controversial one-third stadium financing plan for new stadiums in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, which would raise the state’s ability to borrow by half a billion dollars to help keep the teams from relocating. As of now, the House is apparently a few votes shy of being able to pass the bill. State Senators Richard Kasunic and Gerald LaValle opposed the bill, whereas Senators Barry Stout and Jack Wagner supported it.

headline: 93rd House District
abstract: Fact sheet about the three candidates running for the state congressional seat for the 93rd House District: Joyce Keesey, Barbara Metzler, and Ron Miller.

headline: House republican leader challeneged
abstract: Representative David Argall will challenge Majority Whip Leader Donald Synder for his position.

headline: Santorum releases hold on judgeships
abstract: Secretary of State Yvette Kane watched a speed bump on the way to her federal judgeship flatten out yesterday.  U.S. Sen. Rick Santorum, R-Pa., had been holding up the nominations of Kane and Lackawanna County Judge James M. Munley for appointments to U.S. District Court posts.  Sources said Santorum did so not to hamper Munley or Kane, but to strengthen his hand in negotiating over western Pennsylvania federal court vacancies.

headline: Pa. passes complex educational-tax reform plan
abstract: The new tax reform plan passed by legislators is cousing confusing amoung school districts, who most need to understand the reform.

headline: Act 50's local tax reform not of much help
abstract: Local tax reform, as outlined in PA's Act 50, is not beneficial to the taxpayers of Greenwood School District. This is the unanimous opinion of Greenwood school district based on their individual study of Act 50 and on lengthy presentation at the Oct. 14 board meeting. Greenwood's business manager Jennifer Lapina presented a comprehensive report on the various aspects and formulas involved in Act 50 and what it would mean to Greenwood residents.

headline: Gov. Ridge proclaims "White Cane Week"
abstract: In cooperation with the PA Association for the Blind, Governor Tom Ridge has dedicated the week of October 4-10 as White Cane Week. The white cane and dog guide are the two most common aides used by the blind and visually impaired people, who use them to get around public after hours of training. According to the White Cane Law, motorists must take certain precautions when a blind person is crossing a public street with a white cane or a guide dog, and the article offers some suggestions for how to courteously help the blind.

headline: Support For The Congressional Black Causus Task Force On The Tobacco Settlement
abstract: The National Black Causes gains support for a task force and legislation on African Americana and the settlements with tobacco companies.

headline: Stadiums, vouchers may wrap up session
abstract: The legislative session is about to end and residents are wondering if the issue of Stadiums and Vouchers wil be delt with before the close of session this year.

headline: 3 Projects to take off at Airport
abstract: Capital City Airport recieves state and federal grants in the amount of $855,000. The money is set to be used for three projects to improve and repair the airport.

headline: States need to fight federal plan for national IDs
abstract: U.S. Senator Diane Feinstein slipped a national-driver-license requirement into the Illegal Immigration Reform Act of 1996; however, the national licenses would require sensitive information, including Social Security numbers, so U.S. Representative Ron Paul has countered the bill with his own proposal to protect one’s privacy. Paul alleges noncompliance with the license requirement would essentially prevent someone from being able to function in society, and he has urged states to fight it. The PA Department of Transportation and Governor Tom Ridge are preparing to submit some sort of compliance proposal, but state Senator Gerald LaValle and Representative Richard Olasz have insisted that the Legislature review their proposal before it is sent.

headline: Pennsylvania program fights auto theft
abstract: Vehicle theft and related crimes are a huge problem in the US, especially in urban areas. In 1994, more than 1.5 million vehicles sere stolen in the US. Automobile theft costs everyone through higher insurance costs, incontinences, loss of property, and the psychological effects of being a victim of this type of crime. Act 171, reduces the incidence of car theft in PA. It does this by helping to establish, coordinate, and fund local and regional law enforcement and educational activities aimed at preventing automobile theft and supporting and improving automobile theft prosecution.

headline: Stadium funding puts lawmakers in a tough spot
abstract: PA House Maj. Leader John Perzel made it clear not to expect generous support form Republicans on a measure to fund sports stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh with public funds, raising the state's debt. Perzel would prefer to let Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy and Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell work it out with the Democratic caucus and PA Gov. Tom Ridge. Ridge supports raising the ceiling. The measure passed in the Senate, but failed in the House. Owner Kevin McClatchy received a stopgap measure of $18 million from Ridge after threatening to take his team out of state.

headline: A break for Brady
abstract: Representative Bob Brady's strongest opponent, Cody Anderson, pulled out of the Congressional race.

headline: House vote boosts Underground Railroad preservation
abstract: The U.S. House overwhelmingly passed legislation by Representatives Louis Stokes and Rob Portman to set up a National Park Service program to educate Americans about the importance of the Underground Railroad, which was used by black slaves to escape before the Civil War. Senators Mike DeWine and Carol Moseley-Braun offered a slightly different version of the bill in the Senate, but they are prepared to accept the House’s version in hopes of passing the legislation more quickly.

headline: Santorum: Clinton Responsible for Probe's Pace
abstract: U.S. Senator Rick Santorum feels that the investigation into President Clinton’s affair with Monica Lewinski, a White House intern, is finally headed where it should have been months ago. He blames the two for slowing down the investigation by not cooperating and claims that lawmakers and the American public deserve to hear the truth. He also speculates on what the result will be if Special Counsel Ken Starr finds that the President lied and wants to take a closer look, along with Senator Arlen Specter, into the special counsel law.

headline: Painless budget show how far city has come - Wage and business taxes are being cut again. Council is expected to approve.
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell released his $2.6 billion budget proposal, and it will almost certainly gain the approval of the City Council quickly. His plan includes no tax increases, no layoffs for the 23,000 city employees and would lower the wage tax by 2.2 percent as part of a five-year plan to cut wage taxes by 7 percent. He also proposed extending the business privilege tax to firms that do business in Philadelphia but are headquartered outside the city, and he said the city plans to sue the state because of racial discrimination for not providing adequate funds for Philadelphia public schools.

headline: Allegheny County officials back Hart tax reform bill
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners Bob Cranmer and Mike Dawida suppport Senator Melissa Hart's property tax reform bill.

headline: Group wants race dialogue in the schools and churches
abstract: PA Rep. Mike Veon has been encouraging people to engage in race dialogue. He has shirked duties in the House recently regarding welfare, tax and education reform to talk about race. He has done so because President Clinton has asked America to do so. PA is ranked fourth in number of hate crimes. Veon's consensus was to teach tolerance in schools, churches and cross cultural and multiracial events.

headline: Teen auto fatalities
abstract: A chart shows the number of fatalities in groups 16-19 from 1992 up to 1996 in Allegheny County. There were no more than 3 deaths per age group in all five years. The data is obtained from the PA Department of Health, Allegheny County Health Department, and the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

headline: State should set rules, requirements for investing
abstract: According to the Securities and Exchange Commission, John Black, a financial adviser, lost $71 million in investments for over 60 PA school districts and municipalities because of his risky investments. The debacle prompted PA Treasurer Barbra Hafer to recommend a six guideline plan that would provide some regulation over investments by school districts. The six points are described in the editorial, and the authors believe her points should be adopted by the General Assembly because they still allow local officials flexibility in investing funds, yet they would provide enough regulation to help prevent future incompetent advisers from losing millions of taxpayers’ dollars in the future.

headline: 5 chosen to confer on Rt. 61
abstract: Residents of Deer Lake have entrusted representatives to take a petition noting concerns about proposed road improvements to the PA Department of Transportation. While PA Sen. James Rhoades noted residents should have their say, he expressed the importance of the project to the county's future. Rhoades promised to help arrange a meeting with the district director for PennDOT, or if need be, even Secretary of Transportation Brad Mallory. The representatives hope to present their petition to county commissioners in the meantime. The residents' properties are slated for conveyance to the state.

headline: State's plates could soon feature deer
abstract: The PA House is considering legislation which will allow the state to issue a deer license plate to include the replacement of worn out plates, drawing praise from hunters. House Transportation Committee Chairman Richard Geist said the state Department of Transportation would be required to replace old and defaced plates throughout the state. President of the Cambria County Federation of Sportsmen's clubs, Dwight Weaver, said his group's parent organization started the push for the deer plates. The House Transportation Committee unanimously approved the legislation.

headline: Phila. will host conference on crime
abstract: Philadelphia will host a statewide conference next month on preventing crime in the African American community, and it will be sponsored by the Organized Anti-Crime Community Network, PA Senator Hardy Williams and PA Attorney General Michael Fisher. The conference will include workshops and panel discussions in which community members can speak with police and judges about inner city crimes.
