Reverend Eugene Rivers of Boston, an active clergy member in the battle against city gangs, will be the keynote speaker.

headline: State can draw line in sand on stadium issue - Player paydays out of control; now, owners want more money
abstract: The author cites the recent 7-year deal worth $105 million given by the Los Angeles Dodgers to pitcher Kevin Brown as evidence of how greedy owners of professional sports teams can be, and he resents the fact that owners pay their players millions of dollars and then turn around asking the state for taxpayers’ dollars to fund new stadiums. Governor Tom Ridge’s proposal to provide almost $350 million to build new stadiums for the Pittsburgh Pirates and Steelers and the Philadelphia Phillies and Eagles failed to pass the state House before the 1998 session ended, but he will reintroduce it next year. The author claims Pennsylvanians don’t want to pay for new stadiums, and he is tired of sports owners threatening to relocate if they don’t receive stadium funding, so he hopes Pennsylvanians call owners’ bluffs by not caving in to their demands.

headline: A donor, but not for favors
abstract: Peter L. Buttenwieser is the number 2 financial donor in America. His contributions usually go to Democrats.

headline: Housing author gets rehab money
abstract: U.S. Representative Phil English’s office announced that the Butler County Housing Authority received $472,504 in federal grants to help renovate public housing developments.

headline: Santorum: It's too early to bomb Iraq
abstract: U.S. Senator Rick Santorum said he’s not ready to support bombing Iraq, and he wants to secure the support of more Arab allies before taking any action. He also cautioned that retaliatory attacks against Americans are possible if air strikes don’t have support from Iraq’s neighbors. Pennsylvania’s other Republican Senator, Arlen Specter, said last weekend that any military strikes should first gain congressional approval.

headline: Palisades to consider reassessment
abstract: State lawmakers are looking into regular reassessment laws concerning real estate. A proposed 5 year reassesment law is causing some concern and generating many questions with school districts.

headline: Allegheny County officials back Hart tax reform bill
abstract: Bob Cramer and Mike Dawida, Allegheny County Commissioners, lend support to Senator Melissa Hart's bill that would completely reform the PA property tax system.

headline: Group is not fairly rating candidates
abstract: Project Vote Smart sent its "National Political Awareness Test" to many PA candidates running for office to survey their views on issues such as abortion, taxes and welfare; however, most candidates chose not to fill it out. This prompted the group’s president, Richard Kimball, to criticize the candidates for not being open. The author of the article cites two candidates who didn’t fill out the form but have been extremely open to constituent questions and public forums to share their thoughts on issues, so he believes Kimball’s criticism is unfair.

headline: Texas leads the way as states tackle
abstract: A number of states are closely watching Texas because it passed a law that allows patients to appeal a decision by health insurance companies to an independent external review board which makes a binding decision on whether the insurance company was justified in denying the approval of a treatment. Texas also has a law that allows patients to sue insurance companies for injuries that occur due to denial of treatment; though a case is pending in court that could decide its legality. The health insurance industry is lobbying heavily throughout the country against these types of laws, but a number of states have already enacted or have pending legislation for external review requirements, and the issues are beginning to divide a number of  groups into different coalitions.

headline: Some say state should raise the bar for tests
abstract: To be certified for teaching in PA, teachers must pass three different tests; however, some of these tests require only a 50 % average to pass. As part of the Governor Ridge Administration’s plans to increase standards for teachers, the minimum to pass will be increased for some of these certification tests. The state Board of Education also approved a proposal to raise the GPA requirements in college from a 2.5 to a 3.0.

headline: A Column from the Senate By Senator Jeffrey Piccola
abstract: PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola is writing about legislation he cosponsored and Governor Tom Ridge singed into law that transfers the ownership of the Harrisburg International Airport and Capital City Airport from the PA Department of Transportation to the Susquehanna Area Regional Airport Authority. He acknowledges Senator Harold Mowery and Representatives Frank Tulli and Bruce Smith for also co-sponsoring bills for the same purpose. He believes the transfer will allow the airports to grow and evolve as the region desires, without the government holding them back.

headline: State's roads to get grades
abstract: PennDOT lists the repair agendes and grades roads that need improvements. The information will become public.

headline: Philadelphia crime statistics misleading
abstract: The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s annual Uniform Crime Report has rated Philadelphia among the nation’s ten safest cities for decades, but after taking over as Philadelphia’s police commissioner, John Timoney became suspicious of the department’s crime statistics. An internal review discovered that nearly one in ten serious crimes were either being downgraded or excluded from incidents reports entirely. Timoney declared preliminary statistics from the first half of 1998 unreliable, and he refused to send them to the FBI.

headline: State clears CDC loans
abstract: The PA Department of Community and Economic Development decided not to investigate the Butler County Community Development Corporation even though there have been allegation that some board members and their friends received special consideration for loans and grants. Butler County Commissioner Bill McCarrier, who serves on the board, defended the agency’s actions, whereas Controller Jack McMillin said there should be some sort of oversight over the agency to ensure funds are spent properly.

headline: A Growing Number of Teens
abstract: The Census Bureau's projections show the number of children between 10 and 17 increasing in the coming years, reaching its highest level in three decades.

headline: How Delco Reps score with big labor
abstract: List of how the unions score the state Representatives from Delco county.

headline: Scandal undermines Clinton's agenda, giving GOP more say on host of issues
abstract: The White House sex scandal may impair President Clinton's agenda, allowing the GOP more say on a host of issues, including Clinton's proposed expansion of federal support for child care. It could also soften legislation for the tobacco industry. Clinton has shown amazing resilience in the past however, and even while preparing to be deposed in the Paula Corbin Jones sexual harassment case rolled out initiatives funded by tobacco revenues which put the GOP on the defense at the start of an election year. Peggy Taylor of the AFL-CIO believes Clinton will fare well if sticks to his agenda.

headline: Panel dots I's on county charter
abstract: The Allegheny County Charter Drafting Committee put the final grammatical touches and added statements on the document as the dealine for the charter arrived.

headline: Amusement tax repeal no joke
abstract: Pocono Record explores the proposed leguslative removal of 'nuisance taxes'. Pocono Record wants legslators to tell tax payer where te burden of revenue will be shifted if taxes are eliminated.

headline: Group tries to sell 'Huck Finn' up the river  Citing epithet, state NAACP wants Twain tale of school reading lists
abstract: At the PA State Conference of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, George Love called on school districts to ban "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" from required reading lists because of derogatory references that are made to African-Americans. According to Love, the language could potentially be damaging to the self-esteem of African-American children, so it should not be required, but he doesn’t have a problem with the book remaining in school libraries. The article provides details on whether the book is required to be read in several local schools.

headline: The rules are changing: Health care: What we have to fear
abstract: The editorial is a continuation of a series on health care. The series focused on some individual horror stories, the frustrations felt by doctors over the current system, as well as hospitals and medical practices that are being bought up by large corporations or forced to merge. Despite many of its imperfections, the editorial claims the system is working because it has reduced costs and the PA Department of Health reported a drop in the number of complaints, but the choices people face are changing and will be discussed in tomorrow’s editorial.

headline: Special Ed Boost Equals One Mill Here
abstract: Punxsutawney Area School District will receive $77,580 in new special education funding from the state, which is equal to the amount the district receives from a million dollars of real estate taxes. While the state budget was kept to a four percent increase despite a surplus, the 66th District’s school districts will receive an additional $3,532,190 in increased state funds, and the entire state will receive $383 million more towards education this year. Schools will also save from a reduction in the state mandated rate of contribution to the Public School Employees Retirement System, and schools will benefit because the budget was completed early.

headline: A 'load' of fun
abstract: Front-end loader drivers compete in a Pennsylvania Department of Transportation contest to test driving ability and agility.

headline: Suburban transit strike gets OK
abstract: About 100 members of the United Transportation Union unanimously authorized a strike if a contract agreement between the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority isn’t established by April 1. While the union’s president said things are going much better than in 1995, he characterized SEPTA’s insistence on hiring part-time workers as a deal-breaker. Other unions representing SEPTA workers have also authorized strikes, and there is speculation they may all walk out at the same time, which would have a crippling effect on regional transportation.

headline: Philly mayor appoints former NY cop to run department
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell selected John Timoney to replace Richard Neal as Philadelphia’s Police Commissioner, and he is hoping Timoney, a former policeman for New York City, can bring New York’s crime-fighting success to Philadelphia. According to statistics from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Philadelphia consistently ranks among the top ten safest cities in the country, but it falls short of New York City, and the Philadelphia City Council and several state representatives had been harshly critical of Neal for not focusing enough on drug dealing and nuisance crimes.

headline: State committed to local marina
abstract: PA Fish and Boat Commission President Sam Concilla released a statement which said the commission remained committed to North East Marina despite the fact that the marina is expected to need $800,000 to $1 million in improvements. The commission is possibly looking to privatize the marina, but it has not yet accepted two offers and will continue to run the marina if it cannot find a suitable offer. Another option that is being considered is to construct a township park near the site and share the costs with the local township; though Supervisor Roy Thomson didn’t believe the township had enough funds to do so.

headline: A lesson for everyone from the Greene hiring
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell described the search for a new director of the Philadelphia Housing Authority as one of the most open in the agency’s history. However, for a while, nobody really knew whether the director of the Detroit Housing Authority, Carl Greene, would accept the job because he went back and forth so many times. Greene finally did accept the position, and City Council President John Street, who had previously denied talking with Greene to lure him to Philadelphia, told reporters he had been talking with Greene’s lawyers.

headline: Hunters to air their problems: Record numbers registered to consider future of the sport and their roles in it
abstract: Over 500 participants have already registered for the Governor’s Symposium on North America’s Hunting Heritage in Hershey, PA, and Vern Ross, the Governor’s Sportsman Advisor, predicts even more participants. The number of registered participants already shatters the previous record, and Governor Tom Ridge will kick off the four-day event. The event will include a number of hands on activities and tours, and it will also include a number of speakers who will focus on efforts to preserve and promote hunting for future generations.

headline: Schneck is honored
abstract: Leroy Schneck received the National Leadership Award presented by the National Republican Congressional Committee. He was honored for his instrumental role in the Republicans’ balanced budget plan, and the photo depicts Schneck with PA Representative Jim Lynch, who gave him the award.

headline: Panel's accord breaks down
abstract: Allegheny County council has a difficult time selecting a fifth member before the deadline.

headline: Are House GOP tax cuts blessing or blunder?
abstract: For many conservatives, the plan by House Republicans to use expected budget surpluses for a huge election-year tax cut makes clever politics, reminding the GOP's staunches supporters what the party is all about. But for other republicans, the proposal summons memories of the 1986 election, when the GOP lost control of the Senate as Democrats used Social Security as a bludgeon.

headline: House leader says no to AMP
abstract: PA House Majority Leader John Perzel announced he won’t support a proposed bill intended to help prevent AlliedSignal Incorporation’s attempt to takeover AMP Incorporated, and he also won’t call for a vote on it. The bill is supported by Governor Tom Ridge and several midstate legislators, including state Representatives Bruce Smith and Mark McNaughton, who both criticized Perzel for not allowing the House to vote and vowed to continue to fight. House Minority Leader William DeWeese also opposes the bill, which will make it even more difficult to call for a vote, and AMP and AlliedSignal will continue to fight a legal battle in federal court.

headline: Time for Pa. to count HIV cases
abstract: According to state records, 8,219 Pennsylvanians have AIDS.  No one knows how many are infected with HIV because Pennsylvania, like 18 other states, doesn’t track the number of residents who have the virus that causes AIDS.   While keeping accurate records may, as some officials claim, get victims effective treatment earlier, keeping track would perform a more obvious service: it would tell us where in the commonwealth the infection rate is highest and what to expect in coming decades.

headline: Special education funding at issue again: Rep. Stairs conducting hearings throughout state on status of programs for handicapped students
abstract: PA Representative Jess Stairs, chairman of the House Education Committee, held his latest hearing at Westmoreland County Intermediate Unite as part of a series of hearings to gather information on the status of special education. The PA School Boards Association released a survey showing special education costs have grown significantly in the past five years, but the state only reimburses about 40% of the costs, which many school officials claim is driving schools towards debt and could result in higher local taxes or students in regular classrooms suffering cutbacks. Stairs and Senator Robert Tomlinson tried to enact special education reform last year, and school officials are calling for a solution.

headline: A report card for PennDOT
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation announced plans to begin issuing report cards for its employees; however, the authors believe the self evaluations are foolish and will be biased, so they offer their own report cards. They claim a section of Routes 11-15 is awful, Interstate 81 is extremely bumpy, and while PennDOT has made improvements since the gasoline tax was increased, they still have far to go. The authors think PennDOT should concentrate more on fixing highways than they do on trying to fix their image.

headline: Strike imperils far more than SEPTA
abstract: While most commuters in Philadelphia are getting by just fine during the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority strike, the author believes the strike’s outcome will be crucial to the city’s future. He acknowledges people who depend on SEPTA service to get to work have been hurt by the strike, and he believes the community should develop means of helping them, but beyond that, he argues SEPTA must get rid of the labor factors that lead to higher costs and cuts in service. He believes these factors must be addressed to make SEPTA’s service attractive in the future to middle-class riders, and he argues the city’s economic future depends on mass transit.

headline: Pigeon-shoot protest chain won't go to prison
abstract: Seven animal rights activists who formed a human barricade in 1997 to block a highway that leads into Hegins, where there is an annual bird shooting to raise badly needed funds for community projects, will not receive any jail time for the offense. They were convicted on only one of seven charges, but they could face stiff financial penalties for the thousands of dollars that their actions cost the local fire department and others. This year, no protesters attended the event, but the event’s organizer is concerned that the court ruling will lead to protests again next year.

headline: State grants awarded to help Corry
abstract: According to PA Senators Bob Robbins and Bill Slocum, three grants totaling $520,000 were awarded to help business development in the Corry Area Enterprise Zone. The grants will help three different companies create a combined 35 new jobs while retaining 13 others.

headline: A long-shot challenge: Newcomer to county says he'll fight Specter in GOP primary
abstract: Larry Murphy is the first and only person who has announced that he will challenge U.S. Senator Arlen Specter for the Republican nomination in the upcoming senatorial election.  Murphy criticized Specter for voting with President Clinton 59 percent of the time and for not representing the values of the Republican Party; however, it will be tough for him to win considering Specter’s huge advantages in name recognition, statewide support base and campaign funds. The Democratic Party is pleased that Specter will have to at least spend some money on the primary, and Murphy, despite the odds, remains optimistic and claims he has the "tentative endorsement" of former state Representative Stephen Freind.

headline: Hutchinson announces he will seek re-election
abstract: PA Representative Scott Hutchison will seek his fourth term to the state House. He is a member of several different House committees, was appointed to several other positions and is actively involved in several different House caucuses, including the local tax reform caucus. He was an important member of an investigation into the state’s mental retardation system, was instrumental in several key pieces of legislation which were passed and has received recognition from the Citizens Against Higher Taxes and the National Federation of Independent Business.

headline: School vote's success relies upon elections
abstract: With a school vouchers vote said to be coming after the Nov. 3 general election, PA Governor Tom Ridge and Lt. Governor Mark Schweiker repeatedly touted the House elections as vital to the plan's success. With republicans now holding a 104-99 majority, ever seat makes a difference.

headline: Petitions boost amusement tax abolishment opposition to 1,200
abstract: Over 1,200 people have sent correspondence to PA Representative Frank Tulli Jr. in opposition to a bill proposed by state Representative Robert Godshall that would eliminate the amusement tax in PA. Only six or seven municipalities in PA assess a tax on admission to entertainment facilities such as amusement parks and concerts, but Derry Township could stand to lose $2 million from the taxes it receives on tickets to Hersheypark and its concert facility, which could cause an increase in property taxes. Tulli has been working on a plan to maintain that source of funding even if the bill is passed.

headline: Armey: Goodling tax ally
abstract: US House Majority Leader Representative Dick Armey would replace the Internal Revenue Code with a 10-line tax form the size of a postcard. It probably won't come to fruitarian until there is a new president.

headline: House to vote today on prayer amendment
abstract: For the first time in 27 years, the U.S. House will vote on a proposed constitutional amendment guaranteeing the right to pray or express religious beliefs in schools and other public places; though even the strongest supporters don’t expect the two-thirds majority needed to move the amendment to the Senate. Opponents of the bill believe it would destroy the nation’s long standing tradition of separation between church and state, and both sides agree the amendment would have an effect beyond simply allowing prayer in schools. The bill is supported by the Christian Coalition and U.S. Representative Ernest Istook; however, Representative Chet Edward believes it’s unnecessary.

headline: To the editor:
abstract: PA Representative Ronald Marsico is submitting his written opinion to the newspaper in order to clear up misconceptions and show that he, the state legislature and Governor Tom Ridge are working hard to support the efforts of Emergency Medical Service (EMS) departments. He supports this claim by writing about $20 million in low-interest loans that will be made available for EMS departments, the creation of the State Fire Commissioner and a program to pay for children to go to college if a parent loses their life while serving in an EMS program. Marsico also cites an annual seminar and programs in local schools as evidence of his personal commitment to EMS programs.

headline: SSHE governors considering tuition rates
abstract: The State System of Higher Education (SSHE) Board of Governor’s will meet May 14 to discuss tuition rates for its state owned schools. Governor Tom Ridge and the General Assembly have both approved the state’s budget, and the SSHE will receive $425 million, which will force the Board of Governor’s to consider tuition increases or cutting spending in order to make up for $8 million not covered by the state’s allocation of funds. Clarion University of PA is also examining its budget and will find out more after the board’s meeting.

headline: Access gates proposed for 209 bypass
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation holds meeting to discuss 209 bypass proposals.

headline: Strobe light boosts road worker safety
abstract: An inexpensive red flashing strobe light is helping Pennsylvania Department of Transportation workers remain safe when working on roads at night time. PennDOT is thinking about making the device part of the statewide equipment for night workers.

headline: Police chases costly - Injuries prompt call for rules
abstract: In 1996, there were 1,410 police pursuits in PA, excluding Philadelphia, which resulted in nine deaths and over two hundred injuries, and nationally, 377 people died in about 100,000 high-speed police chases. Because of the number of crashes, there has been a push towards uniform police pursuit standards; however, many police departments feel these standards would restrict officers too much. The issue could become moot because of new technology that many police departments are beginning to use that’s designed to deflate a car’s tires, which could end many high-speed chases before they can lead to injuries to officers, those being pursued and innocent bystanders.

headline: State should act boldly on planning issue
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge’s 21st Century Environment Commission released a report that examined the problem of overdevelopment of land, but it acknowledged any solution would be difficult and would require the people and communities to take action themselves. The author believes that land development presents environmental problems for the future, especially in Dauphin County, and unfortunately, the state Legislature is unlikely to pass any significant land-use controls. He believes the commission did a decent job in identifying many problems, but ultimately, he thinks much more needs to be done to protect Pennsylvania’s land from being overdeveloped in the future.

headline: A Most Difficult And Personal Choice   Clinton Could Face Even More Jeopardy
abstract: President Clinton has admitted to an improper relationship with Monica Lewinski, but he continues to claim that he didn’t lie to a grand jury about the relationship because he didn’t have sexual relations with her in the way he believed the term to be defined. His defense of hiding behind legal definitions has angered many Congressmen, including Democratic leaders such as Senate Minority Leader Thomas Daschle, and they have called for the President to simply admit that he lied. However, if he does admit to lying, it could potentially leave him even more vulnerable to impeachment, and there’s a possibility that Kenneth Starr could indict him on criminal charges before or after he leaves office, so Clinton has basically backed himself into a corner with no great options to diffuse the situation.

headline: Hutchinson says Clinton should resign
abstract: PA Representative Scott Hutchinson said that President Clinton should resign because he feels it is pretty evident that Clinton committed perjury. He said it would set a double standard for anybody who testifies in the future if Clinton doesn’t resign. He also claimed the public should known the truth, and he disputed polls that show the American public supports Clinton.

headline: Schools hurt in investment scandal could recover more of their money  Settlements may be sought from 'third parties'
abstract: School districts that lost millions of dollars by investing their money with financial adviser John Black might get more of their money back if former Governor Dick Thornburgh, who was appointed to oversee Black’s frozen assets, is able to reach settlements with at least four unnamed third parties that profited from Black’s investments. Thornburgh has already released $133 million, and he recommended releasing another $95 million from frozen accounts to begin paying back some of the money lost by investors; though about 50 will have to settle for half of the funds they thought they had. Many school districts are encountering serious financial troubles due to their lost investments, and Thornburgh wouldn’t identify the third parties to protect the integrity of potential settlements.

headline: Powell says volunteer program on track
abstract: Retired General Colin Powell, who is chairman of America’s Promise, said his campaign to get corporations across the nation involved in volunteering efforts has already made a substantial impact, citing an increase in mentors for Big Brothers and Big Sisters programs, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s promise to help 3 million young people find summer jobs and a program by LensCrafters that has provided 100,000 free eye exams. He disputed contentions that the public has been losing interest since President Clinton and other past presidents met in Philadelphia a year ago to promote volunteerism. Powell plans to address 60 mayors in Chicago on how to get local governments more involved.

headline: Barriers block road to change
abstract: The article provides some problems Pennsylvania’s legislators face in developing local property tax reform, according to the PA Economy League. The concerns include the potential for counties to impose a sales tax, the issue of voter referendums, whether personal or earned income taxes should be used to offset property taxes and what exactly the definition of a homestead should be.  In addition, the issue of taxing farms needs to be addressed, the elimination of nuisance taxes could present challenges, and opponent fear the reform could create a confusing economic climate.

headline: How case shaped state politics - Abortion still big issue 25 years later
abstract: Since the U.S. Supreme Court legalized abortion 25 years ago, the Court has ruled on two PA abortion laws, including its decision on the 1989 Abortion Control Act under Governor Casey, which allowed new abortion restrictions such as parental consent for minors to get abortions and a 24-hour waiting period for all women. The PA Legislature has taken an active role in passing restrictions, and the issue of abortion frequently comes up in the state’s elections, including this year’s gubernatorial race between incumbent Tom Ridge and his potential challengers. While abortion rates have declined and the state Legislature has been active in the past, some anti-abortion advocates want more to be done, and one political consultant said PA tends to be more pro-life than almost all other states.

headline: Tobacco deal to give states $206 billion   Local health advocate: Not enough
abstract: 46 states have agreed to a $206 billion settlement from the four largest tobacco companies to offset smoking-related health care costs, and the companies also agreed to new restrictions on advertising as well as pay for $1.5 billion in anti-smoking ads. PA has been promised $11.259 billion over 25 years in return for giving up the state’s right to sue tobacco companies for past actions; however, the settlement provides far less restrictions than a version that failed to pass the U.S. congress, and Kevin Stewart, a local anti-smoking advocate argues the settlement is not nearly enough. The companies are expected to raise the price of cigarettes, which is expected to lead to a 10% decline in sales in 1999, and many health advocates are now calling on Congress to pass some tougher regulations in the future.

headline: State administers test for secondary school diploma
abstract: Don't allow the lack of a high school diploma keep you from meeting your educational or career potential. The Commonwealth Secondary School Diploma could help you reach your goals, according to PA Representative Herman, a member of the House Education Committee. The state department of Education issues the diploma to certify that the holder meets high school graduation requirements set by the State Board of Education. A candidate for the diploma must pass the General Educational Development test.

headline: Acute SEPTA anxiety - Who'll be hurt worst if trains, buses stop?
abstract: Two people who work at housing units in Philadelphia share their thoughts on the possibility of a strike by the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority. Both agree it would be a major problem for most of the tenants in their respective developments who rely on the transit service to get to their jobs. They argue that when SEPTA employees strike, it puts the entire city at a disadvantage.

headline: Studies: Deaths rise with speed limits
abstract: A study of all 50 states showed that as the speed limit on interstates increased, so to did the number of deaths by at least 8.2% overall.

headline: Police crack down on alcohol abuse around the county
abstract: Ferguson County police hold sobriety checkpoint and campus raids to fight underage drinking and driving under the influence.

headline: State slaps Scranton - State freezes funds after deciding city violated recovery plan
abstract: Scranton, which was declared financially distressed six years ago, is facing a budget deficit of at least $7 million, and the state sanctioned the city for violating its financial-recovery plan. The sanctions will hold up most of the city’s state funding until city officials can convince the state that they are making progress, but a $10 million state grant for the construction of a downtown conference center and the city’s garbage rates could also be affected. Several city councilmen blamed Mayor Jim Connors for messing up the city’s finances, but Connors defended himself and said reductions in wage and mercantile taxes approved by the City Council will likely go back to 1997 levels.

headline: A politician pulls strings for Ducky
abstract: According to the author, Bob Kilbanks, who began running for Congress years ago, has been embarrassed by the Federal Elections Commission, which deemed a $41,000 campaign contribution from his mother to be illegal and also found that his average annual income over the past five years was $1,825 a year. On the other hand, Ducky Miller quit school to work to support his mother at the age of 16, he has survived two battles against cancer, and after 16 ˝ years on Social Security disability, he vowed to get a job again. Kilbanks eventually helped Miller get a job with the PA Turnpike Commission, and the author says Kilbanks’ latest run for Congress should include the persistent, hardworking Miller at his side, instead of his rich mother.

headline: Hypocrisy on Campaign Funds
abstract: According to the editorial, Republican leadership in the U.S. House has complained about campaign abuses in the past election, yet they are trying to avoid changing the law regarding spending of soft money, the source of greatest abuse. The authors claim House leaders are attempting to offer fake bills that either wouldn’t pass or wouldn’t actually be reform if they did pass to kill reform and avoid blame, but these efforts are failing, as they did in the Senate, where a filibuster was needed to stop real campaign finance reform. The authors call on other House members to sign a discharge petition that would allow real reform to be voted on, and they suggest the Senate tries attaching their version of reform to another bill in the future.

headline: Schwanger promises money for city alleys
abstract: Lancaster City's alleys were the focus of a news conference held Wednesday by Dave Schwager, the Republican candidate for the 96th District seat in the state house. Schwager promised that, if elected he'll bring back $160,000 from the state to repair the alleys and two pieces of street cleaning equipment.

headline: Property tax reform is OK with the Senate
abstract: Property tax reform is passed by Congress, allowing school districts to raise wage taxes and eliminate nuisance property taxes.

headline: Battle between tax cuts gets underway
abstract: House and Senate Democrats are proposing a 3.5% cut in state income tax for 1999. Goveenor Tom Ridge has so far resisisted the tax cut proposals.

headline: Identify needs, disabled urged
abstract: Pennsylvania Coalition of Citizens with Disablilities held a meeting to discuss membership, education and health care.

headline: Tougher sanctions urged - Nursing home care was focus of forum
abstract: At a forum in Harrisburg last week, advocates for nursing home residents addressed many problems with the industry, and they were especially critical of the PA Department of Health and the U.S. Health Care Financing Administration for failing to impose tougher sanctions on facilities that violate regulations. PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr., who released an extremely critical audit of the Health Department’s oversight of nursing homes, attended the forum, and overall, the forum called for greater oversight, especially in low-income facilities. PA Senator Richard Kasunic has introduced five bills intended to improve state oversight and require nursing homes to provide information about their facilities to the public, while Representative Anthony DeLuca has introduced an alternative bill in the state House.

headline: State attorney general addresses ways to curb violence in schools
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher went to West Middlesex High School to talk about ways to prevent school violence and offer his recommendations, which will be presented to the General Assembly, along with input from four public forums, in September. He recommended a 72-hour "time-out" period for psychological evaluation after a student is caught with a gun in school, holding parents responsible for the actions of their children and raising the offense of bringing a gun onto school ground to a felony. He also stressed the need for cooperation between the community, law enforcement officials and school administrators.

headline: Agency will not release report
abstract: Concerns are being raised over the investigation into whether the PA State Transportation Department dealt fairly with property owners who were outted by road projects. The investigation is being tauted as unthorough and inaccurate.

headline: Summit may patch Rt. 30 dispute - Construction company, lawmakers, PennDOT look for solution to delays
abstract: Top executives from Balfour Beatty, the company responsible for an $83.8 million project to expand Route 30 near Lancaster, met with PA Representative John Barley and Senator Gibson Armstrong to discuss ways to speed up the project, which is already behind schedule. The PA Department of Transportation has fined Balfour Beatty $4.5 million for delays, but the company is suing PennDOT for questionable decisions that led to the delays. Local businesses have complained about lost revenue due to traffic buildup caused by the construction, so at the meeting, the legislators and Balfour Beatty decided to hold a meeting with PennDOT in early June to put aside difference and strive for a compromise to get the project done as quickly as possible.

headline: Police training may become law
abstract: Representative Thomas Caltagirone wants to pass legislation that rewuire police officers to undergo training in handling cases of persons with disabilities.

headline: Steelers hit pay dirt on personal seat licenses
abstract: The Pittsburgh Steelers permanent seat license sale has secured millions in private funding for a new stadium say team Vice President Art Rooney II. The team hopes to raise $37 million this way. The sale is a key part of the team's bid to raise $76.5 million toward the stadium's total cost, estimated at $233 million. PSLs are onetime fees fans pay for the right to purchase season tickets for a given seat for the life of the stadium. The Pittsburgh Auditorium Authority is the original owner of the PSLs and will hold the proceeds until they are needed to pay construction costs.

headline: A survivor, Casey makes time for family
abstract: Former Govenor Robert Casey celebrates 5 years of success after a heart and lung transplant. Casey shares his setbacks, victories, and family stories in the article.

headline: Impeach him, Gekas asserts
abstract: House Judiciary Committee member George Gekas, a Pennsylvanian from Dauphin County, believes the charges against President Clinton, including lying and obstruction of justice, are serious enough to warrant impeachment, but he warned that the evidence must be reviewed to validate Kenneth Starr’s report. Gekas plans to review the evidence, but as of now, he said it seems to corroborate Starr’s report. He also supports the release of most information and a videotape of Clinton’s grand jury testimony.

headline: Schweiker vs. Lynch: Lieutenant governor faces primary challenge
abstract: The authors of the editorial are surprised at James Lynch’s decision to run against incumbent Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker in the Republican primary, but they give him very little chance of winning due to several obstacles. They claim Lynch has very little name recognition, has much less money to spend and lacks the powerful Republican endorsements that Schweiker has as Ridge’s running mate. In addition, the authors claim Schweiker basically does what Ridge tells him to do, and Lynch has little criticism for both Ridge and Schweiker, so they wonder what his campaign strategy would even be.

headline: Property tax reform is OK with the Senate
abstract: The PA Senate approved a bill that would give school districts the option of increasing their earned income tax in exchange for eliminating nuisance taxes and reducing property tax rates, which the House is expected to approve and send to Governor Tom Ridge for his signature. If the shift is approved by school districts and local voters, local taxes would decrease for some, primarily retired senior citizen homeowners, and increase for others, primarily younger wage earners who pay rent; however, the PA School Boards Association said school districts would be extremely cautious in implementing the change. Senator Doyle Corman criticized the legislation for leaving out local governments, Representative David Steil would have preferred a personal income tax over an earned income tax, and Senator John Wagner criticized a provision that gives suburban residents who commute to Philadelphia a special tax break.

headline: Bogus tax 'reform' hurts most workers
abstract: Scranton Tribune criticizes Govenor Tome Ridge and lawmakers for passing a bogus unhelpful tax reform bill.

headline: James Introduces Resolutions for Justice
abstract: PA Rep. Harold James attended a National Black Conference of State Legislators to discuss the disproportionate share of African-Americans and minorities treated improperly by law enforcement. According to the US Department of Justice and the US House Judiciary Committee, African Americans make up roughly 13 percent of the US population but 72 percent of stopped motorists. Reports indicated that inmates at Holmesburg State Prison were subjected to medical testing.

headline: Transplant overhaul proposed: Health and Human Services action reignites debate over organ allocation
abstract: Due in part to the efforts of a former college friend of President Clinton, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) declared a change in the allocation of transplants, so the sickest people will receive transplants first no matter where they live, whereas before transplants were distributed based largely on location. The United Network for Organ Sharing, along with most of the 281 transplant programs in the country, have denounced the decision and claim that it will lead to fewer people receiving transplants. Some of the larger transplant centers, such as the nation’s largest at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, back the decision, and U.S. Senator Rick Santorum has vowed to protect the HHS and its Secretary, Donna Shalala, from any political fallout.

headline: State awards planning grants to seven more charter schools
abstract: Seven more charter schools have joined three others in Allegheny County that have been given planning grants of up to $25,000 by the PA Department of Education. Charter schools are independent schools that are free from most state regulations, but they must be approved by local school districts and receive funding from them. Some of the proposals include a school for youths with behavioral problems, an elementary school focusing on art and culture, a school that incorporates music into the learning process and a high school that would focus on applied biological sciences and communications.

headline: Aiming for first-class upgrade - The 33-outlet mall will be "the next generation" of airport retailing, officials say.
abstract: A new $135 million mall will open shortly at Philadelphia International Airport in Terminals B and C, which house US Airways’ concourses and are used by two-thirds of the airport’s clients. The new restaurants and shops will be a huge upgrade from before, and they will offer a wider variety of options at lower costs. It appears to be one of the world’s classiest airport shopping-and-dining malls, and it expected to generate $80 million next year.

headline: Teen drivers topic of study
abstract: A 16 year old driver who rounded a bend at 100 miles per hour, crashing into a car driven by a young pregnant woman, received the maximum sentence of loss of license for a year, a $500 fine, and community service. The PA Department of Transportation has now convened a symposium to make standards more strict. PA Gov. Tom Ridge ordered the closer look. The state Legislature is also reviewing the issue.

headline: Politicians to review school safety plans
abstract: To address school shootings, PA House and Senate members prepared legislation to toughen penalties for those who bring firearms to school property or assault a teacher.  Maj. Leader John Perzel said kids who bring firearms to school will be charged as adults. PA Gov. Tom Ridge and PA Atty. Gen. Mike Fisher support the proposals. The PA State Education Association supports a bill allowing schools to use force to stop violence. The PA Education Department is making grants available to install security cameras and hire guards.

headline: Steelers not a wash with cash for stadium
abstract: A question and answer session about the Steeler's financial position and the proposed new stadium.

headline: A Waste, All Right
abstract: After pleading guilty to hiring a 19-year old prostitute and providing her with liquor, PA Senator Dan Delp’s lawyers issued a statement claiming the investigation was a huge waste of taxpayers’ dollars. The authors say prosecutors dropped the most serious charge against Delp, alleging he spent $50 in state funds on the prostitute, and they believe the biggest waste of money was paying Delp’s salary as a senator. The authors also argue the investigation had a positive result in that it led to Delp choosing not to seek re-election.

headline: Impeachment Driving a Small Wedge Into G.O.P.
abstract: Republicans in Congress had hoped the scandal over President Clinton’s relationship with Monica Lewinski would split the Democrats, but as the House vote on impeachment approaches next week, it is actually dividing Republicans. The majority of Republicans will vote to impeach, yet there is a significant amount of them who are against impeachment or have yet to decide. Several Congressmen have proposed a tough censure of Clinton rather than impeachment, a split between conservative Southern and Northeastern moderate Republicans has emerged and several Republicans are concerned that if they vote to impeach Clinton, they could be voted out of office in the next election, which could threaten the Republican’s control over Congress.

headline: Second Setback for Advocates of Census Sampling
abstract: Federal judges ruled against the Clinton administrations proposal to use sampling in census data to find out characteristics of those who do not respond to census.

headline: Property tax vote expected next week
abstract: The PA House could vote on a bill sponsored by state Senator Melissa Hart that would protect Allegheny County residents against dramatic property tax increases after reassessments. A second part of the bill, if passed, would change eligibility requirements to allow more low-income senior citizens to participate in the county’s tax abatement program. The bill already passed the Senate, but it would have to be reintroduced next year if the House fails to take up the issue before the winter recess.

headline: Buck up
abstract: By offering $300 million cash for six struggling hospitals in the Allegheny health system, brash newcomers from Nashville have given the region's all important health-care industry quite a jolt -- and, at the same time a vote of confidence.  Not only does Vanguard Health Systems Inc. think it can operate the six hospitals successfully, but it is also going to try and make a profit.  At Graduate Hospital, that means turning around an $11 million loss in a recent three-month period.

headline: Jury Says Abortion Opponents Are Liable - Clinic-Closing Move Found to Violate Racketeering Law
abstract: A jury ruled that anti-abortion groups violated federal racketeering laws by using threats of violence and extortion to shut down abortion clinics in Wilmington, Delaware and Milwaukee. It is the first case in which civil provisions of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, which was passed by Congress to fight organized crime, were used against anti-abortion protesters, and the National Women’s Health Organization said the decision was a victory for abortion and is proof of an "organized campaign of terror" against abortion clinics. Anti-abortion activists plan to appeal the court’s ruling, claiming it violates their First Amendment Right to freedom of speech, and they never encouraged violence.

headline: U.S. and city reach pact on nursing home - The Justice Department will monitor treatment of patients at the Philadelphia Nursing Home.
abstract: After a three-year investigation, the U.S. Justice Department, Mayor Ed Rendell and the Philadelphia Nursing Home have reached a settlement to ensure the facility’s 450 patients are treated well. In 1995, the PA Department of Health found "deplorable" conditions at the nursing home, including physical abuse, sexual misconduct and neglect, which prompted a federal investigation that resulted in a civil complain being filed against the nursing home. Under the agreement, Rendell agreed to pay the federal government $50,000 to resolve a false-claim allegation, the Justice Department will monitor the nursing home for one year, and the city vowed to ensure the patients are protected from mistreatment in the future.

headline: State board to decide on college tuition rate
abstract: The State System of Higher Education is trying to fulfill its goal of not increasing tuition at the 14 state-owned schools next year; though tuition has increased every year since 1983-84. The Board of Governors asked Governor Tom Ridge and the state Legislature for $435 million in funding, and Ridge proposed $425 million, which would leave them $10 million short. The State System has enacted a number of money saving efforts, which have saved millions of dollars each year, but they’ll need to find some way to make up for the $10 million if more funding isn’t provided.

headline: Airport to get $2.2 million to upgrade people-mover
abstract: PA Department of Transportation Deputy Secretary Elizabeth Voras will present a $2.2 million check to the Pittsburgh International Airport for upgrades to its people-mover system. Meanwhile, Allegheny County Commissioners are preparing to begin a national search for a new airport director. In order to hire a high caliber person for the position, they expect to offer a larger salary than what was paid to the previous director, even though the county is trying to close a $9 million budget deficit.

headline: Teen drivers topic of symposium
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation wil hold meetings where safety and education experts will discuss the issue of teen drivers and how parents can help do something to curb the problem.

headline: Popularity of Ballot Initiatives Leads to Questions
abstract: Voters must decide whether to strike a law forbidding marriage between blacks and whites, which the US Supreme Court already ruled unenforceable. According to the Initiatives and Referendum Institute, citizens in 16 states will decide on 61 such initiatives and 170 measures dealing with constitutional amendments and bond issues. Many legislators oppose initiatives, as they can wreak havoc on state budgets. However some say legislators merely resent the usurpation of their own power. An Arizona initiative would abolish the IRS.

headline: Struggling to recover, South Allison Hill at last has a plan
abstract: A boarded-up brick row home decays amid rental properties on a block of South 13th Street.  Signs on the home warn passers-by not to loiter or dump trash.  And now there's a plan, an ambitious -- some  say unrealistic- vision for the neighborhood.  Goals are outlined in the preliminary South Allison Hill Community Action Plan.

headline: A welcome ally
abstract: PA Gov. Tom Ridge has announced support for a lobbyist disclosure bill, however that does not ensure its quick passage through the Legislature. The PA House leadership has made it clear it is no hurry to move on the bill. Nonetheless, editors welcome the governor's support.

headline: In city's House race, it cost less to win than lose: Sturla outspent by Schwanger
abstract: PA Representative Michael Sturla spent $84,766 to win reelection, whereas his challenger, Republican Dave Schwanger, spent $102,164 in a losing effort. Sturla spent more money on Election Day, and some of his contributors are listed in the article. When compared to last year’s election, less money was spent.

headline: Sen. Piccola meets over GOP position
abstract: Senator Jeffrey Piccola met with Dauphin Count District Attorney to ask him to force Michael L. Rozman to choose between two public service jobs.

headline: Putting the touch on those enjoying city's hospitality - But a likely increase in the tax hotel guests pay here---from 13 percent to 14 percent---is unlikely to put off travelers.
abstract: When New York City increased the hotel room occupancy tax to 21.5 percent, it deterred many businesses from holding conventions in the city; however, Philadelphia’s proposal to increase the tax from 13 percent to 14 percent is unlikely to have a similar effect. The PA Legislature granted approval to the City Council to raise the tax, which it is expected to do, and while the tax seems high, it is actually quite comparable in many other cities throughout the nation. The Greater Philadelphia Hotel Association has granted its approval of the tax increase because much of the additional revenue would be used to fund increased tourism promotions, and the money could potentially be used to fund an expansion of the Convention Center.

headline: Budget
abstract: Highlight of a package of tax breaks for 1998-99 in the federal budget.

headline: Latinos Are Far Behind In School, Report Says
abstract: According to a report by the National Council of La Raza (NCLR), the nation’s largest Latino advocacy group, Latino children are lagging behind in nearly every educational category from preschool to college, which is bad news for the U.S., considering the Latino population is expected to surpass African Americans as the largest minority group by the middle of the next decade. Latino schoolchildren have a significantly higher dropout rate than white and black schoolchildren, and they are far less likely to go to college than whites. The first lady, Hillary Clinton, spoke at a luncheon for the NCLR, where she told members closing the education gap is critical to both Hispanic and American prosperity.

headline: U.S. says doctor union is antitrust conspiracy
abstract: In a move with implications for physicians in Philadelphia and nationwide trying to fight fee cuts by insurers, the U.S. Justice Department has filed an antitrust complaint in Delaware against a union representing virtually all of that state's orthopedic surgeons.  The complaint alleges that the Federation of Physicians and Dentists "became the hub of a conspiracy to oppose and prevent proposed reductions in payments for orthopedic services by Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Delaware."  The Justice Department's action comes as hundreds of Philadelphia-area doctors recently joined the union to fight reimbursement cuts by Independence Blue Cross, the region's largest health insurer, which is not related to the Delaware insurer.

headline: State falls short in report card on education
abstract: A review of the quality of education in PA by Education Week magazine yielded less than impressive results; especially its C-minus rating on teacher quality. The magazine’s grade of teacher quality is based on state regulations that could improve quality, and Governor Tom Ridge and the General Assembly are currently exploring ways to raise teaching standards. The authors of the editorial claim that while the results aren’t impressive, there has been progress since last year, and they expect next year’s results to get better.

headline: Allocate Summit project money to save lives, property elsewhere
abstract: Pennslyvania Department of Transportation will stop reconstruction on Routes 422/68/38 intersection. Butler Eagle wants to know where the designated project money will go and hopes that the money stays in Summit Township.

headline: Teen driving rules under state review
abstract: PA Rep. Steven Nickol announced officials at the PA Department of Transportation have promised to be more vigilant and more rigorous in monitoring teen drivers, starting with parental notification for traffic violations. Nickol write Transportation Secretary Brad Mallory, asking for a full review of the state's junior licensing program. Meeting with the Bureau of Driver Licensing Director Rebecca Bickley and Deputy Secretary for Safety Administration Betty Serian, both acknowledge problems with PennDOT's system.

headline: Prisoners will run for midstate charity
abstract: The PA Prison Runathon will be held to raise money for Big Brother/Big Sister organizations. The Pardons Board rejected a request of convicted murder Hubert Blount to hold a hearing on whether his life sentence should be commuted, and  State College will host the annual National Governors’ Association meeting.

headline: Tax break proposed for renters
abstract: A state House panel yesterday put out the welcome mat for renters, including them in the list of groups benefiting from tax reform.  This move by the House Finance Committee represents a major expansion of the still-evolving plan and led one lawmaker to warn that the change could kill the reform movement.  The bill's sponsor, Rep. Stan Saylor, R-Red Lion, said the full House could vote on his plan in the next two weeks.

headline: Abortion rights group targets Fox in election
abstract: Planned Parenthood seeks to discurage voters from reelcting Representative Jon Fox, who has not been a strong pro-choice advocate for women. Fundraising and campaining against Fox are in the works.

headline: In NE, Ridge begins quest for four more years
abstract: Governor Ridge came to the Northeast Community Center in Philadelphia to announce to 600 supporters that he would be seeking reelection. House Majority Leader John Perzel and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker, who is also seeking reelection, spoke at the event, and Governor Ridge is highly favored to win the election against little-known PA Representative Ivan Itkin. Jobs, crime, education and taxes were the four main themes of Ridge’s speech, and he took credit for helping PA improve to 16th among all states in job creation, strengthening crime laws, toughening academic standards for teachers and signing bills to cut business and income taxes.

headline: Senate approves a nato expansion by a vote of 80-19
abstract: The US Senate voted overwhelmingly to expand the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to include Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. The vote was bipartisan. Supporters praised the decision for adding new forces to NATO and fostering democracy in Europe. Critics argued the vote merely redraws lines to form a new iron curtain. US President Clinton has supported the expansion extensively throughout his administration. The Senate defeated an amendment to force President Clinton to gain approval from Congress for the Bosnia mission.

headline: Quick vote possible on tax reform
abstract: Lawmakers are trying to quickly vote on a proposed tax reform bil for school districts before the session adjourns.

headline: Budget Surplus Sows Dissension on Capitol Hill
abstract: Congress will begin work in earnest this week on its tax and spending plans for next year, energized by the prospect of big budget surpluses but deeply unsettled about politically charged issues like taxes and Social Security. Already a rift has opened between House Republicans, who have remained aggressive and creative in looking for ways to cut taxes, and Senate Republicans, who are more cautious and appear inclined only to tinker with the balanced budget agreement hammered out. Democrats are positioning themselves as the guardians of the government's fiscal health.

headline: Longtime GOP supporter criticizes Ridge for stance on women's health
abstract: Elsie Hillman, who helped get Governor Tom Ridge elected four years ago when she was a member of the Republican National Committee, criticized the Ridge Administration for not doing enough to secure funding for women’s health issues, accusing him of being afraid of alienating party conservative because of the abortion issue. However, Tim Reeves, Ridge’s spokesman, said that critics should blame the federal government for giving the state less funding. A proposal by PA Representative Phyllis Mundy to increase funding for women’s medical services was rejected by the state House, and Ridge has yet to respond to letters written by four nonprofit family planning councils which wrote him letters of concern over the lack of funding.

headline: Unique stamp seeks to lick a killer
abstract: Breast cancer is considered the most commonly diagnosed form of cancer, and the U.S. Postal Service will begin selling Breast Cancer Research stamps. The stamps will cost eight cents more than regular stamps, but all of the extra money collected will be given to the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Defense Medical Research Program for breast cancer research. LeGree Daniels, a member of the U.S. Postal Service Board of Governors, supports the stamps and believes that they will also help raise awareness about the disease.

headline: State gives school district $55,000 to teach students to refuse sex
abstract: Twenty-four school districts across the state will receive funding under the governor's five-year Abstinence Education Initiative, including the Lackawanna Trail School District. The program primarily targets 9-14 year olds, teaching them how to say no to sex.

headline: Altoona Railroaders museum set to open: Exhibits to stress people who built Iron Horses
abstract: Altoona, which used to be the largest railroad town in the world, owes must of its existence to the old PA Railroad, and it will open the new Altoona Railroaders Memorial Museum to honor its historic past. The new museum will focus on the struggles and triumphs of railroad workers, and museum officials predict that it will draw 80,000 tourists a year and help Altoona’s tourist industry. Horseshoe Curve, which helped trains bypass the Allegheny Mountains, is located seven miles west of Altoona, and it is still one of the best places to watch trains since approximately 60 travel the curve every day.

headline: Thank You For Riding Septa
abstract: A politcal cartoon about SEPTA hazords and strikes.

headline: Privatization prevails
abstract: The PA Supreme Court ruled in favor of Delaware County’s privatization of its county prison, which should pave the way for future privatization of prisons in the future. Most of the former prison guards were rehired to work in the new facility, but their union filed a lawsuit against the county to protest the privatization. Unions representing prison guards are worried about the precedent this case may set across the state, and the private company now running the prison, Wackenhut, was clearly pleased with the ruling, and it is set to open a new $50 million prison in the next month.

headline: Tax incentives may be Chesco's solid foundation
abstract: The Keystone Opporunity Zones will creat new districts that would be exempt from Pennsylvania taxes for 12 years.

headline: Administration officials ride sport-utility craze
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge alternates between two Lincoln Town Cars, whereas the majority of his cabinet members have chosen Ford Explorers as their vehicles of choice. The Explorer and other sport-utility vehicles have been growing in popularity across the nation, and they are leased for the cabinet members from the PA Department of General Services.

headline: In Pa., many political races aren't races at all: This year, 84 of 228 legislative seats are uncontested. The GOP stands to benefit
abstract: Republicans Rod Wilt and Craig Dally both won their first elections to the state House two years ago in areas in which Democrats hold an edge in registration numbers, and surprisingly, no one has filed to run against them this year. 84 seats in the General Assembly, which is 37 percent of all open seats, will go unchallenged in the upcoming election, and 51 of those seats belong to Republicans. The Democratic Party is a long shot to defeat incumbent Governor Tom Ridge and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, so many believe they should focus their efforts on trying to regain control of the state House, which makes their lack of candidates surprising; however, Democratic party leaders have indicated that they'd prefer to concentrate their efforts on races they believe they can win as opposed to fielding unknown candidates for every race.

headline: Senate challenger says he is 'tired' and short on cash
abstract: Bill Lloyd, who is challenging the incumbent Arlen Specter for a seat at the U.S. Senate, spent most of the day in his apartment and appeared dejected after being told about bad poll results during the final week of the election. Lloyd has only spent $155,000 on his campaign and was forced to borrow $40,000, whereas Specter has already spent $4.2 million and still had $2.5 million remaining. Specter also became the first Republican to ever win the backing of the United Steelworkers of America, which dealt another blow to Lloyd’s already dim hopes of winning the election.

headline: Reality: Reform has its limits
abstract: Four months ago, Governor Tom Ridge signed a bill into law that allows school districts, with voter approval, to reduce property taxes by implementing a higher wage tax, but in order to so, all nuisance taxes would first have to be eliminated. The article provides the findings from a computer analysis that shows which school districts in five different counties would have the greatest incentives to consider adopting the new tax reform, which is optional; however, there is still disagreement on whether the tax shift would actually be beneficial. Taxpayers will have to evaluate which form of taxes they’d prefer, yet due to incomplete data, there are still many questions on what the effect of the tax shift would be on taxpayers as well as local governments.

headline: Can state cut its tax rates?
abstract: The defeat by Ohio voters this week of a referendum to increase the state sales tax by one cent on the collar reminded me of the PA legislature. Revenue from an increased sales tax in Ohio would have provided more money for schools and property tax relief for homeowners. One reason given for the overwhelming defeat was anti- tax sentiment. The proposal was the state legislature's response to a state Supreme Court ruling that found Ohio's system of funding schools unconstitutional.

headline: Massiah-Jackson's support grows; DA holds firm
abstract: Support for Common Pleas Court Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson to the federal bench is being stepped up as her confirmation vote in the U.S. Senate approaches next week.  The Black Elected Officials, along with a diverse group of some two dozen civic and religious leaders, held a news conference yesterday in City Hall to voice their support of the Common Pleas judge.  Members of the NAACP led a protest in front of the federal building in Center City to show their support for Massiah-Jackson and their continuing anger with Philadelphia District Attorney Lynne Abraham over her opposition to the judge's confirmation.

headline: Video confirms beating   Six state troopers reassigned; tape said to show stopped driver wasn't aggressor
abstract: Six state troopers are being investigated for the beating of Evan Gross, which a Carnegie Police Department vehicle captured on film. According to the officers’ report, Gross led the officers’ on a high speed chase, and after he stopped, he violently resisted arrest; however, four independent people watched the video and said the beating was "merciless, unprovoked and unnecessary." There were several other discrepancies in the officers’ account of events, and Gross will appear today in Common Pleas Court to determine if his mental health makes him a danger to himself and others because he had stopped taking his anti-depressant medication.

headline: State high court OKs searches of students' lockers for drugs
abstract: State Supremem Court ruled that school officials have a right to search student lockers because of valid reasoning. There is little expectation of privacy while in school.

headline: Amtrack is changing and ridership is growing
abstract: Acting President of Amtrak, George Warrington, tells readers that Amtrak is undergoing improvements and developments.

headline: Thankfully, Safety Course Requirement For Personal Watercraft Taken Seriously
abstract: The authors are pleased that the PA Fish Commission adopted new regulations that require operators of personal watercraft, such as Jet Ski, SeaDoo and Wave Runner, to attend a safety course to acquire certification. Based on the first session of the safety course in South Williamsport, the authors believe that people are taking the requirement seriously, which can help reduce the number of accidents and collisions that personal watercraft are involved in.

headline: Prosecution of psychic not in cards - Judge agrees with defense on jurisdiction, dismisses charges against Lebanon fortune teller
abstract: District Justice Hazel Swisher threw out a case against a psychic because her alleged crimes occurred in the city of Lebanon, which Swisher doesn’t have jurisdiction over. Lebanon County District Attorney Brad Charles vowed to refile charges against the psychic, Marie May, for violating a law from 1861 that makes predicting the future for money by use of cards or the examination of hands or heads, a third degree misdemeanor.

headline: Tax-Free concept explored
abstract: Department of Community Economic Development hosts a meeting to inform individuals about the new tax-free Keystone Opportunity Zones.

headline: AFL-CIO endorses Specter
abstract: Pennsylvania’s AFL-CIO, which represents about a million workers, broke a long tradition of supporting Democrats and endorsed U.S. Senator Arlen Specter in his bid for reelection for the first time ever; though its president, Bill George, did offer some praise to Specter’s challenger, State Representative Bill Lloyd. The union also endorsed State Representative Ivan Itkin for governor and U.S. Representative Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky for lieutenant governor. It harshly criticized incumbent Governor Tom Ridge for his record on labor issues, and a spokeswoman for Ridge defended some his actions.

headline: In Russia, a sign of hard times and of harder to come?
abstract: Hours before President Clinton admitted to having an inappropriate relationship with Monica Lewinski, Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, a close friend of the president, held a press conference to support Clinton, where he justified the actions of the president. He said Clinton’s credibility shouldn’t be hurt because it was justifiable for him to lie to protect his family, while he also said presidents have lied under oath in the past and it is not unusual for presidents to have affairs, citing, among others, Dwight Eisenhower’s relationship with his secretary. One expert called Rendell’s reference to Eisenhower "a bogus historical analogy," and other experts said that while presidents have lied to the public, they disputed that any have lied under oath.

headline: Senate hopeful rips opponent's NRA stance
abstract: U.S. Senate candidate Rick Orloski blasted State Representative Bill Lloyd, an opponent in the upcoming primary, for paying the National Rifle Association (NRA) over $7,000 during a past election. Lloyd defended the payment by claiming the NRA had a policy of not giving away its membership lists, so he paid them to send postcards on his behalf. Orloski plans to make the issue of gun control one of the key issues in his upcoming campaign to dethrone incumbent U.S. Senator Arlen Specter.

headline: Review & Outlook  Taxpayer Guarantee
abstract: The authors of the editorial believe that tax increases have gotten out of hand, and they support the Tax Limitation Amendment, which would add an amendment to the constitution requiring a two-thirds supermajority for any new tax to be approved. The U.S. House is set to vote on the amendment, but it supported the idea a year ago, and several public opinion polls show the public overwhelmingly supports the amendment. Many states have already adopted such requirements, and despite critics’ accusations that the supermajority requirement is anti-democratic, the authors support the amendment because they believe it will force proponents of tax increases to provide stronger arguments for why they are needed.

headline: City appeals tax-exempt rule
abstract: The city appeals to remove a tax-exempt status decision made by Allegheny County Board of Property Assessment.

headline: Misguided attack
abstract: PA Representative Jim Lynch is responding to Clark Moeller’s criticism of state Representative Baker for his support of House Resolution 417, a bill Lynch sponsored that urges Congress to propose a constitutional amendment to increase religious freedoms, including moments of silence in schools, the use of prayer at graduation ceremonies and many other activities. Lynch provides the actual language from the Religious Freedom amendment to dispute Moeller’s claims that the amendment would actually limit religious freedom, and he says some of Moeller’s claims are downright silly and untrue. Lynch supports the amendment because he believes it would reverse a number of U.S. Supreme Court rulings that have weakened the First Amendment’s Free Exercise of Religion Clause.

headline: Watching the system work for us
abstract: The invesitgation of the Health Department by Auditor General Robert Casey can prove to be helpful to nursing homes if the matters suggested are correceted.

headline: State legislators visit Penn State Hazleton campus
abstract: Penn State Hazelton hosted the 1998 special program for State Legislators, which was established to bring area legislators to the campus to exchange information about the campus and issues affecting higher education in general. Senator Raphael Musto, Judge Correale Stevens and Representatives Todd Eachus, George Hasay, Keith McCall and David Argall all attended the program. Discussions included the academic mission of the university, programs which are offered, innovative teaching and learning techniques and a final question session.

headline: Apollo joins other communities for Expressway
abstract: Borough officials of Apollo support the Kiski Valley Expressway.

headline: The end of the construction - Traffic stops for ribbon cutting celebrating completion of the Elmira Street Project
abstract: Police and firefighters stopped traffic in Athens Township for a ribbon cutting ceremony to celebrate the completion of the Elmira Street construction. Despite initial controversy, businesses along the street seemed pleased with the final results, and most of the money for the project, which exceeded $2 million, came from the state and federal transportation departments. All five township supervisors, PA Representative Scot Chadwick and Senator Roger Madigan attended the event.

headline: Protection for at risk children under study
abstract: Statelawers release a report with recommendations for improving children services and better protecting children who are at risk of abuse and neglect.

headline: Taxpayers may fund stadiums   Skepticism greets Ridge plan to finance arenas for pro teams
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has made new stadium funding a priority for the Pittsburgh Pirates and Steelers and the Philadelphia Phillies and Eagles; however, many legislators, including state Representatives Patrick Fleagle and Jeffrey Coy, are hesitant to increase the state’s debt to build stadiums for players and owners that make millions a year. Ridge is hoping to pay for one-third of the cost of the stadiums, which could cost up to $325 million and cost taxpayers $40 million a year in interest payments. Pittsburgh has been moving ahead on its stadium building plans, whereas Philadelphia is still trying to raise its share of funds.

headline: Allen says he's only one who's done something about jobs
abstract: With 17 years of experience representing mine workers and retirees, Clemmy Allen thinks he's ready to expand the role. Allen, a United Mine Workers of America Representative said he is the only candidate in the five man field seeking the democratic nomination for the 48th district legislative seat who has obtained grant money to retrain unemployed miners, lobbied legislators in Harrisburg and DC, and helped shape legislation that affects miners.

headline: Inadequate parking obvious at proposed state office building
abstract: The Department of General Services has, at long last, unveiled plans for the Keystone Building, which will replace the fire-damaged Transportation and Safety Building.  The Ridge administration had an opportunity to create a landmark building.  At a press conference unveiling the plans, DGS Secretary Gary Crowell made much of the design details intended to relate architecturally to the Capitol Complex's historic buildings.

headline: Senate votes to delay rifle check
abstract: The PA Senate passed legislation that would postpone the deadline for beginning criminal checks in the sales rifles and shotguns from next month to the end of next year. The only dissent came from Philadelphia Democrats. PA Governor Ridge is expected to sign it into law. State police are required to begin manual record checks on July 1.

headline: Ridge-Sweiker campaign on further property tax reform
abstract: More meaningful property tax reform is on the plate for Gov. Tom Ridge and Lt. Gov. Mark Schweiker should be the Republican team be re-elected Nov. 3. Schweiker agreed that homestead exemption act has its drawbacks but described the legislation as a positive start of tax reform.  School districts will begin to decide next year if they will stick with the old tax formula that relies heavily on property taxes or shift part of the district's tax base to an earned income tax.

headline: Colleges advised budget will have only 3.5% boost
abstract: State university presidents who threatened tuition increases if their institutions didn't get a 7.5 percent state spending boost will get far less when PA Governor Tom Ridge announces his budget proposal today. Ridge's month long series of budget announcements made education spending on of the few remaining mysteries of the 1998-99 state spending plan, which is not expected to contain new taxes. Universities will have to live with a 3.5% increase.

headline: Mother sued because son got girlfriend pregnant
abstract: 16-year-olds Leanne Detmer and Dallas Mills dated and had consensual sex, but Detmer got pregnant and had an abortion.
