Detmer’s parents have now filed a lawsuit in Lancaster County against Mills’ parents to have them pay $11,371 in medical expenses for the abortion and costs associated with their daughter’s depression because they claim Mills’ parents knew the two were having sex and did nothing to stop it. No trial date is set, and the idea of holding parents responsible for their children’s sex lives is new, but if the trial proceeds, parents may be forced to monitor their children’s sex lives more closely.

headline: Where there's smoke, there's ire
abstract: There is an anti-tobacco bill being considered in the Senate that would force the top five tobacco manufacturers to pay $516 billion over 25 years towards settling lawsuits, and while Clinton and other supporters of the bill say it’s intended to curb youth smoking, the tobacco industry claims it’s really just a huge tax increase being used to increase government spending. Tobacco manufacturers are going to begin a massive public-relations campaign, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the American Civil Liberties Union will also fight the bill; though their reasons have nothing to do with support for the tobacco industry. The bill would also limit advertising techniques, and the owners of convenience stores, which generate over $17 billion a year from tobacco sales, as well as smokers themselves could play a role in lobbying against the bill.

headline: State now unlikely to take over schools
abstract: In response to threats to close down the Philadelphia School District early if it didn’t receive additional funding, the PA Legislature passed a bill that would allow the state’s education secretary to take over the city’s public schools. However, the school board overwhelmingly passed its budget, and Superintendant David Hornbeck said the district has enough cash to keep the schools open for the entire 1998-1999 school year, so Governor Tom Ridge is unlikely to issue a state takeover of the district. The budget still includes a $55 million gap, which the district is exploring a number of different options to close, and Hornbeck said the state still needs to address its obligations to increase funding sometime in the future.

headline: Area gets slice of federal highway pie
abstract: President Clinton signed the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century, which will grant money to the California University of Pennsylvania, among other recipients, for a campus shuttle. President of the University, Dr. Angelo Armenti Jr., expressed the excitement of the University to be receiving the funds. US Rep. Frank Mascara sponsored that particular project. He also secured federal funding for a number of other local projects.

headline: The Fight Over Blood-Alcohol Limits
abstract: The US Senate has proposed a national legal level of intoxication of .08 blood-alcohol content. Most state have a limit of .10. The restaurant and alcoholic beverage industries are trying to kill the proposal. They contend .08 would cut into their business without scientifically reducing drunken driving.

headline: Put cameras in courtrooms
abstract: Eagle Times argues that there are no valid reasons to to keep cameras out of the courtroom and they should be allowed because the public has a right to know.

headline: There was no double-cross, but a need for timely cooperation
abstract: PA Senator Vincent Fumo, the author of this opinion piece, is critical of Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy for claiming Fumo double crossed him with regards to sports stadium funding projects. Fumo generally supports a proposal to provide state funding for stadiums in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, but he opposed the current bill, which passed the Senate, because he hadn’t received any assurances that a stadium authority in Southeastern PA would be bipartisan or nonpartisan, and an amendment requiring the teams occupying the stadiums to pay a revenue tax was defeated. Fumo says he contacted his Democratic House colleagues after learning that Governor Tom Ridge had agreed to his demands on the stadium authority, and he promises to work to pass a bill with broad support.

headline: Amendment to House bill angers Surra
abstract: According to current law, candidates who want to run for the PA General Assembly must sign an affidavit saying they meet all residency and age requirements, but a recent amendment was passed that protects a candidate’s affidavit from being challenged in court, which could ultimately allow any candidate to lie without penalty. State Representative Dan Surra is upset that Republicans were able to pass the bill because he believes it is intended to protect Representative John Pippy, who Democrats claim does not meet residency requirements. Governor Ridge is expected to sign the bill.

headline: Inauguration party to last 2 days
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker will be sworn into office during a two-day inauguration event. There will be a ball and a concert at the inauguration festivities.

headline: Senator Hardy Williams says this term is last
abstract: PA Senator Hardy Williams, who won a seat in the state House in 1970 after becoming the first African American to win against the established parties in Philadelphia, decided not to seek reelection. The sudden news became the biggest surprise of the day, and Williams’s son, State Representative Anthony Hardy Williams, will challenge for his father’s seat. A number of different elections are described in the article, including reelection bids by Governor Ridge, Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker and U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, and overall, there will be 21 congressional seats, 203 state House seats and 25 state Senate seats that will be up for grabs.

headline: Roadblock is broken; Dunn to OK nominees
abstract: Alleghney Conty council nominees are scheduled to be approved and later voted on to make the fifth member of the council. The candidates are all African-American Republican women.

headline: Commissioners show one way to reform taxes
abstract: Centre Daily Times thanks Centre County Commissioners for ending the occupational assessment tax but warn that tax issues are far from over.

headline: NAACP questions makeup of apportionment group
abstract: NAACP calls for diversity in the Allegheny County's new coucnil. Four members of the five panel council are white males and the fifth member has yet to be selected.

headline: White House Says Veto of 'Patient Protection' Bill is Likely
abstract: The White House said tonight that President Clinton would probably veto the version of "patient protection" legislation that Republican leaders plan to take up in the House of Representatives on Friday.  Mr. Clinton described himself as a champion of patients' rights.  But in a formal evaluation of the House Republican bill, the White House said, "It covers too few people, it provides too few patient protections, and it contains unnecessary and irrelevant provisions that undermine the chances for a bipartisan agreement on a patients' bill of rights."

headline: State offers free museum admission
abstract: William Penn established Pennsylvania 317 years ago, and Governor Tom Ridge announced that admission to 20 of the PA Historical and Museum Commission’s sites will be free as part of the celebration.

headline: Area lawmakers back new Danville bridge
abstract: The prosed new construction of a bridge on Danville Street is being criticized. State lawmakers are supporting the bill and PennDOT is being asked by residents to fight a lawsuit brought by Concerned Citizens Alliance Inc. to stop the construction.

headline: The last thing anyone wants to see is another traiffic signal on Route 11 between Bloomsburg and Berwick
abstract: Press-Enterprise endorses the installation of another traiffic light on Route 11, near Edgar Avenue but hopes engineers coordinate the timing off all the lights on the Route to make traffic flow easier.

headline: Race and the death penalty
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney is criticized by a local man for her dismissal of racial discrimination in capital punishment cases.

headline: 'They're not going to be able to do it'
abstract: City Council President John Street introduced a bill that would ban homeless people from aggressively asking for money and sleeping on sidewalks, but some Philadelphia merchants don’t believe the bill will have any significant effect. The article provides accounts from several city store owners and employees on their opinions towards the bill and homeless behavior in or around their stores.

headline: Americans less angry with Uncle Sam: But the confident level in government is still low, according to a nationwide poll
abstract: According to a three-year national poll conducted by Scripps Howard News Service and Ohio University, people are less angry at the government than before; however, they continue to have little confidence in it. Vice President Gore said "we still have a long way to go," and several experts were far from pleased with the findings, claiming voter anger has simply turned into cynicism. The booming economy has helped alleviate some of the anger, yet one expert believes there are still deep, underlying concerns about the government.

headline: Incoming Speaker's 'Art of Possible'
abstract: U.S. Representative Bob Livingston will succeed Newt Gingrich as speaker of the House, and he will bring a dynamically different type of personality to the position in hopes of uniting the House, which has gotten increasingly divided with Gingrich as its leader. Livingston grew up in New Orleans, attended Tulane University, became an assistant Louisiana state attorney general and eventually was elected to the House in 1977, where he developed a reputation for his notorious temper. He was nominated by Gingrich for the powerful position of chairman of the Appropriations Committee, and last year, he played an important role in the budget talks that led to an agreement for tax cuts and a balanced budget.

headline: Senator Robbins seeks third term in state office
abstract: PA Senator Robert Robbins concluded his bus tour of the district in front of over 100 supporters in Titusville to announce that he would be seeking his third term.

headline: Schools also must educate taxpayers
abstract: Altoona Mirror criticizes school districts for lowering the debt celiing and increasing higher income tax. Altoon Mirror suggets the school districts start educating the public about the need for funds instead of changing policies to avoid resident input.

headline: Consistent record of votes against major tax increases
abstract: PA Representative Mike Sturla is writing to correct some details that he claims Ted Byrnes failed to acknowledge in his recent letter to the editor. Sturla claims to have a consistent record of voting against major tax increases, and he says he has voted for tax cuts when feasible, regardless of which party was in power. He says he voted to introduce a 50 percent property tax cut to the House floor, which was blocked by Republicans, and he vows to continue to push the issue.

headline: NAACP says prisons need more black guards
abstract: NAACP says racial disparity among prison guards in PA may be contributing to unfair treament and abuse of prison inmates.

headline: Who would benefit under Pennsylvania's patients'-rights bill?
abstract: So you're in a Pennsylvania managed health-care plan. Thanks to a measure that was passed last week, you can look forward to being empowered with a new "patients' bill of rights" starting Jan. 1.

headline: State plan punitive, not constructive
abstract: The authors of the editorial believe the state’s proposed takeover of the Philadelphia School District, which was approved by the PA Legislature, is more bent on revenge and punishment than it is on providing a quality education for the district’s 215,000 children who attend public schools. According to the authors, under the plan, school days would get longer, but teachers won’t be paid extra, and local people would cede all control of the school district to a centralized government, which Governor Tom Ridge and state Education Secretary Eugene Hickok are not suited to handle. The authors claim the district’s problems are financial, not educational, and the state should approve an additional $85 million in funding, along with increased government oversight, rather than a complete takeover.

headline: Bedford buoyed by highway bill
abstract: Bedford County officials and PennDOT are looking into making a priority list for highways and other roads that need to be repaired with the $3 million in funds granted to the project.

headline: Toll road funds tagged to Highway bill
abstract: US Rep. Frank Mascara appropriated $20 million for the Brownsville-to-Uniontown section of the Mon-Fayette Expressway in BESTEA, or the Building Efficient Surface Transportation Equity Act. The bill, which allots $217 billion for transportation infrastructure, was approved by the House Transportation Committee. PA Gov. Tom Ridge announced $338 million has been committed to Mascara's project. PA Turnpike officials are seeking $500 million in federal funds. Mascara says the PA Department of Transportation is also involved in the project. BESTEA will now go to a House-Senate conference.

headline: Recently passed state legislation targets parole candidates
abstract: The PA Senate unanimously approved a bill created by Senators Stewart Greenleaf and Michael O’Pake that will give the state Probation and Parole Board the authority to reject parole candidates from entering PA from other states. PA had been required under the Interstate Compact to accept parolees if they met three loose criteria; however, those standards allowed Nevada murderer Arthur Bomar, who is now suspected of murdering a college athlete, into the state. The Board will now be able to review many different criteria to make a decision, and the state can now take action against parolees who enter the state unauthorized.

headline: To Lincoln National, region has a lot to like - No single factor persuaded the Fortune 500 insurance company to move headquarters here from Indiana.
abstract: Lincoln National Corporation, a Fortune 500 insurance company, decided to move its corporate headquarters from Indiana to Philadelphia, and its new chairman, Jon Boscia, said the city is perfect because it’s not too expensive or overcrowded, yet it’s not too small either. It also helped that Delaware Investments, which Lincoln owns, has been growing substantially in the region, and Delaware’s chief had a lot of good things to say about Philadelphia, including strong support from Mayor Ed Rendell, Governor Tom Ridge and others interested in attracting business to the region. A number of other factors played into his decision, such as the city’s transportation system, which helped Philadelphia be chosen over a long list of competing cities.

headline: An extraordinary year - 1998's events will seem more momentous as time passes
abstract: The author believes that as time passes, 1998 will be remembered as a truly remarkable year. First off, he believes the impeachment of President Clinton was an extraordinarily unique event, and secondly, he thinks there’ve been two particularly important events in southwestern PA: the decision to adopt a new form of county government by home rule and the public-private commitment to pursue development projects, including two new stadiums for Pittsburgh’s sports teams. While these issues have been extremely divisive, especially stadium-financing, the author believes Mayor Tom Murphy, Governor Tom Ridge and others will eventually be remembered well for the stances, even though they’ve faced criticism.

headline: Incumbents win ever race here
abstract: Lancaster voters embraced the familiar on election day sending incumbents back to office in every race. As they re-elected candidates ranging from Democratic state Representatives. P. Michael Sturla to Republican US Representative Joseph Pitts, voters made it clear they are happy with things the way they were.

headline: Senator Williams set to 'pass torch' to his son
abstract: PA Senator Hardy Williams will not seek re-election for a fifth term to represent the 8th PA Senatorial District; however, his son, state Representative Anthony Hardy Williams, is gathering petitions to run for his father’s seat. State Representative James Roebuck was surprised by the move, but he will challenge for the open seat while also seeking re-election for his seat in the House, and Tommie Blackwell, the son of former Congressman Lucien Blackwell, has been mentioned as a potential successor for Anthony Williams’ House seat. Hardy Williams became the first independently-elected African American to win a seat in the PA General Assembly in 1970 by winning election to the state House, and he has long been considered one of the most powerful voices for the African American community.

headline: Schools get control of crossing guards
abstract: Governor Ridge signed a bill that could allow school districts in 50 PA cities, including Lebanon, to take charge of their own crossing guards. Crossing guards have long been considered employees of the cities. However, due to an amendment from Representative Stephen Stetler that was inserted into the bill, third-class cities will have the option of allowing school districts to take over supervision of crossing guards.

headline: County leaders glad to see funds
abstract: Reaction to Governor Tom Ridge's $17.8 billion budget proposal ranged from enthusiastic endorsement to mild disappointment among Centre County's leaders. Penn State President Graham Spanier said he considered the $9.4 million increase for the university a positive sign.

headline: Not everybody is sold on racial harmony
abstract: Based on race relations discussions held by PA Representative Mike Veon at Geneva College, one would think that Beaver County is a place of racial harmony; however, the newspaper’s investigation shows a much different side. The paper has been asking for people to call in or write letters sharing their thoughts on race, and many of the comments, which are printed in the article, suggest the community is still divided over the issue of race. Several callers cited episodes of racism in the community, while others complained about the newspaper’s role in instigating the issue.

headline: Within Reach
abstract: There is no reason why a single child in Pennsylvania should be without health-insurance coverage.  That goal is within the state's grasp, and making it a reality should be a top priority of the Ridge administration.  More federal dollars are on the way for children's health care.  And more state dollars will be provided to match them.

headline: State senators grill Spanier over PSU budget request
abstract: Penn State University President Graham Spanier presented his $314.3 million budget request to the PA Senate Appropriations Committee, and while Spanier doesn’t expect to receive the entire amount, which would be $24.6 million increase from the past year, he hoped to get more than Governor Ridge’s proposal to only give the university $9.4 million more than the last year. Spanier said the additional money was needed to hire more faculty members, give employees salary increases and keep tuition increases to 3.2 percent. In addition to specific questions about funding, Senator Michael O’Pake asked Spanier whether the university was growing too large, Senator Raphael Musto asked him if a merger between two health systems constituted a monopoly and Senator Robert Thompson asked Spanier to explain progress on the university’s underage drinking problem.

headline: Behind the contract: 2 tough foes
abstract: After 40 days of strikes, a tentative contract settlement between the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority and the Transport Workers Union was announced. David Cohen, who negotiated city contracts for Mayor Ed Rendell in 1992, led SEPTA’s negotiation efforts, and while he commended the union’s president, Steve Brookens, he also said the new contract will be good for the future of SEPTA. Brookens became the target of harsh criticism, including a $15 million slander suit filed against him by PA Senator Vincent Fumo after the Democratic National Convention site-selection committee cut a visit to Philadelphia short because of the strike; however, union members never wavered in support for their leader.

headline: Too many license plates cause too many problems
abstract: The Public Opinion talks about the various license plates that PA residents can purchase, with a portion of the money going to a specific organizational fund. The editorial argues that state lawmakers should limit the number of licesnse plates by organizations or support only one state plate.

headline: Referendum draws strange bedfellows
abstract: Two prosed contitutional referedums on crime are proposed to voters. State lawmakers and local residents have concerns and questions about the referendums.

headline: Travaglio upset with Ridge, Murphy over passage of secret stadium bill
abstract: PA Representative Guy Travaglio was harshly critical of Governor Tom Ridge, Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy and Republicans over a bill that the state Legislature passed. According to Travaglio, members of the House believed they were voting to repeal a law pertaining to training schools for firefighters; however, the bill contained hidden language to exempt Pittsburgh stadium projects from the state’s debt ceiling, which could essentially lead to state-funding for the projects. Travaglio was angry over being duped into approving the bill, and before it was even passed, state Representative Frank LaGrotta criticized Ridge’s attempts to pass a separate stadium financing bill.

headline: An interview with Sen. Arlen Specter
abstract: The article provides the questions and responses during an interview with U.S. Senator Arlen Specter over the topic of President Clinton’s sexual scandal and the possibility of an impeachment trial. Specter said the issue deserves a bipartisan response, he expressed his apprehension over what an impeachment trial could mean for the country, and he spoke about the messages he has received from his constituents. He also spoke about his reaction to Kenneth Starr’s report, Congress’s frustration with being unable to address other important matters and his impression on whether the scandal has hurt the president’s ability to lead.

headline: Independent counsel promises to move quickly in Clinton investigation
abstract: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr said he would move as quickly as possible on his investigation into whether President Clinton had an affair with Monica Lewinski and then tried to cover it up, while Clinton again adamantly denied having a sexual relationship with her. Lewinsky signed a sworn affidavit that she didn’t’ have a sexual relationship with Clinton; however; Starr has a recorded conversation from Linda Tripp in which Lewinski says she did have sexual relations with Clinton, and both the president and Vernon Jordan, a personal friend, told her to cover it up. Around the time Lewinski was scheduled to testify in the Paula Jones case, Jordan was arranging job offers for her, and the president’s wife, Hillary, doesn’t believe the charges, while Attorney General Janet Reno refused to answer any questions.

headline: Senators Envision Swift Clinton Trial   Need to Call Witnesses Is Discounted
abstract: After Congress reconvenes on January 6, the U.S. Senate will hold the impeachment trial of President Clinton after the House presents its impeachment articles; however, there is no requirement to examine witnesses or even reach a verdict. Majority Leader Trent Lott and Minority Leader Thomas Daschle are discussing a timetable, and most senators agree the Senate doesn’t have the numbers to remove Clinton from office, which has led many to consider other options; though conservatives, including Rick Santorum of PA, do not want to make any decisions until after the trial has finished. Most senators would like to see the trial go quickly, so they’d prefer not to call witnesses, but there is disagreement on alternative options to removing Clinton from office such as a censure, financial penalty or a requirement that he admit he lied under oath.

headline: Schools told new tax law complicated
abstract: PA school districts are having complicated with Act 50. The tax reform requirements in the act are causes mulitple problems for school districts, and school officials are unhappy.

headline: County may trim property tax discount
abstract: Propsed changes in the Alleghney County may have tax payers losing the bulk of their discount for paying property taxes early. The considered 1.5% decrease in property tax discount is mocked as a tax increase and is engaging discussion.

headline: Obscenity law change could cause chaos
abstract: A PA House judiciary committee considered a bill that would allow communities to set their own standards on obscenity. A 1977 state law says the "community" is the state. That law uses a test as required by the US Supreme Court. The test uses community standards to determine obscenity. The paper believes this ends up limiting freedom of speech.

headline: Without Legislation, Price Rises Could Ease
abstract: The U.S. Senate’s rejection of a tobacco bill should slow the rising cost of a pack of cigarettes and allow greater tobacco advertising freedom, but the tobacco industry, which supported the $368.5 million pact in return for future protection for lawsuits, is claiming they did everything they could to cooperate with the government. Instead, the tobacco industry will continue to go to court to fight lawsuits from states and employee health pension funds that are trying to recoup money lost from health care spending on treatment for smokers. However, the environment should be more friendly than it was a year ago due to a number of court ruling that will limit the industry’s liability, but there are still powerful lawsuits against them, and some states are considering negotiating multi-state settlements on their own if Congress fails to act.

headline: State senators step up push to reform PIAA, fire director
abstract: PA Senators are threatening to dismantle the non-profit organization that runs interscholastic sports programs at 1,300 PA high schools. A special Senate committee said the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association must begin this week to change the way it does business. If it doesn't the legislation is prepared to create another agency to take its place.

headline: Bicycle tour links Lancaster museums
abstract: PA Representative Jere Strittmatter led efforts to create a 45.9 mile bicycle route through Lancaster County that takes bikers to the state’s three major museums, Landis Valley, the Ephrata Cloister and the Railroad Museum of PA. The Lancaster County Heritage Bike Tour was developed by Strittmatter, the Lancaster County Planning Commission and the PA Historical and Museum Commission, and it accomplishes three important goals by showing off Lancaster County’s beauty, getting tourists off the county’s major, congested highways and introducing visitors to the three museums. A map of the route is included, and most of the roads have very little traffic.

headline: Tougher DUI law nears decision
abstract: It's show time in the bitter, yearlong tug-of-war over a plan to tighten the nation's drunken-driving laws. House and Senate negotiators, meeting behind closed doors to develop the final version of a popular highway funding bill, will soon decide whether to include a proposal to lower the threshold for drunken- driving arrests from .10 percent blood-alcohol content to .08 percent. 35 states have the .10 standard.

headline: Rehabilitation may be hot topic for Legislature
abstract: Some state legislators say issues involving drugs and treatment centers will be top priorities the next two years. Suggestions include reviewing security at treatment centers, preventing courts from Sentencing offenders to far-away centers and requiring some convicted drug dealers to register their addresses with police. Rehabilitation centers offer a variety of programs that help drug and alcohol addicts break their habits. Some want courts to have offenders sentenced to treatment center closer to where they committed their crime. Some blame growing crime rates on rehabilitation centers.

headline: Trim welfare, along with taxes, to spur growth
abstract: To incumbent politicians the current economic climate couldn't get much better. It's been time since budgets looked this good. It's no surprise that so many trial balloons have been launched during the past couple of weeks. One of these ideas is to create 12 Keystone Opportunity Zones to help jump start economic development. The idea is to reduce taxes to help businesses.

headline: Battle brewing over residency of legislator: Election law change irks Democrats
abstract: PA Representative John Pippy was elected to the House in 1996, but House Democratic Leader William DeWeese and other Democrats claim he did not meet state residency requirements. Republicans have drafted a bill that would eliminate the need for legislative candidates to sign an affidavit swearing they meet residency requirements, which Democrats have threatened to walk out on in protest because they believe it’s an attempt to allow Pippy to seek reelection. Democratic Senator Allen Kukovich believes the bill could allow out-of-state residents to run for PA office, whereas Senate Republican Leader Joseph Loeper said the bill would strengthen the separation of powers between the courts and the Legislature.

headline: Inside the capital: Noteworthy
abstract: Republica leaders announce their appointments to 22 Senate committees.

headline: Shameless vs. spineless
abstract: The Tribune Review discusses the shock of Democracts that gained senates in the last elections. The Tribune-Review criticizes Republicans for not being unifed and persistent.

headline: Schools urge homeowners to participate in tax reform
abstract: Pike and Monore county residents can now fill out an application to decided qualification for homestead or farmstead property tax exemptions.

headline: Court says hospitals, now 'for-profit,' owe real-estate taxes
abstract: The PA Commonwealth Court ruled that since the Pinnacle Health System used leftover revenue to purchase physician practices in the past, they were actually for-profit institutions, so they were not considered exempt from real estate taxes and owed about $21 million in back taxes. Governor Tom Ridge signed Act 55, the Institutions of Purely Public Charity Act, in November to set five criteria an institution must meet to qualify for tax emption. York Health System has an arrangement where it makes payments in lieu of taxes, and although Act 55 makes it more difficult to prove an institution is for-profit, it is unclear what kind of impact the court’s ruling may have on other hospitals in the future.

headline: On the campaign trail Gubernatorial candidate: 'Give back life'
abstract: Peg Luksik, the Constitutional Party candidate for governor of PA, attacked the pro-choice movement and blamed the 1973 Roe vs. Wade Supreme Court decision to legalize abortion for a string of violence across the country, including recent school shootings. She said she is pro-life under all circumstances and spoke out against people who are pro-life but with exceptions such as rape or sexual abuse. Luksik is a mother of six and is the founder of Mom’s House, a national program that provides services to single parents.

headline: Wound Healer
abstract: It is difficult to fault Pennsylvania's first physician general, in fact the first state physician general in the nation, for resigning abruptly two weeks ago.  Dr. Wanda Filer, physician general for only 15 months, said she considered all 12 million Pennsylvanians as her patients.  To her credit, she was not about to let policy meisters in the Ridge administration influence her diagnosis.

headline: State should hang on to language requirement
abstract: The authors of the editorial are against a proposal from the state Board of Education that would get rid of a requirement that all students study a foreign language before graduating from high school. In addition to the benefits of learning a second language in the growing world market, the authors claim evidence suggests students who study a different language are more creative, better problem solvers and do better on the verbal section of Scholastic Aptitude Tests.

headline: Big jump in federal highway spending hits home
abstract: The new transportation bill passed will give Pennsylvania more than $200 billion dollars more then other states receieving funds.

headline: Traffic redesign irks SR officials
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has changed the design of Route 173 and 108 intersections to make traffic flow easier, however, residents are not happy with the new design and feel that it might cause more problems.

headline: Reject constitutional referendums
abstract: Beaver County Times urges voters to say no to two referendums which woud allow the prosecution to ask for a jury trial and deny bail for those accused of crimes that could end in a sentence of life if convicted.

headline: Up and Down: Job growth on a roller-coaster ride
abstract: The authors of the editorial are pleased that Business Facilities magazine ranked PA in the nation’s top ten states for high-tech business because it is a substantial improvement from last year, and high-tech jobs are good-paying jobs. However, they are unsettled by another study released by the U.S. Labor Department that rated Philadelphia and Pittsburgh 22nd and 23rd respectively in terms of economic growth out of the 23 major metropolitan areas in the U.S. The authors believe that Governor Tom Ridge is on the right path, but better coordination at the state, regional and local level is necessary to compete with other states.

headline: Battle in the 169th
abstract: Jack Noonan announced that he will be running to represent the 169th District in the PA House. No other Democrats are expected to run against him in the primary, and he will most likely face incumbent PA Representative Dennis O’Brien, who vowed to run a positive campaign which would highlight his efforts to help children with disabilities and strengthen criminal justice laws. Noonan said the district needs some Democratic representation since O’Brien, Senator Frank Salvatore and City Councilman Brian O’Neil all are Republicans.

headline: INSIDE THE CAPITOL - Heard on the Hill
abstract: A quote is provided from Miss Pennsylvania, Heather Busin, who spoke with PA House members.

headline: Sherwood aims to touch GOP voters
abstract: Pictured in his glossy campaign brochures, congressional candidate Don Sherwood reads to children, chats with an elderly woman, shakes hands with a officer, poses with a farmer and hugs his wife. Don Sherwood plans to get this in the hands of every Republican in the 10th Congressional District. He is one of eight running in the May 19 primary.

headline: Smithgall wants balance in city property-tax relief
abstract: Earlier this year, the PA Legislature granted school districts the ability to shift the burden of property taxes by implementing a higher wage tax, but the legislation left out counties and municipalities. The state’s third-class cities could be the next in line for consideration to provide property tax relief, but the Legislature doesn’t expect to consider any legislation until after the upcoming election. Meanwhile, Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed and Lancaster Mayor Charlie Smithgall want to see some sort of property tax relief for their respective cities.

headline: Dawida and Cranmer back off on tax discounts
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioners Mike Dawida and Bob Cranmer backed off their decision to reduce the discount available to taxpayers who pay their taxes early. The reduction was characterized by critics as a hidden tax increase. It would have cost $5 to $20 more for 90 percent of taxpayers, generating $3 million in revenue. The announcement came after County Deputy Treasurer John Weinstein said his office would not honor the Commissioner's decision. He and PA Rep. Donald Wilson said the reduction was in fact illegal. County Solicitor Kerry Fraas argued otherwise.

headline: Pastors must guide belivers in their provate and public lives
abstract: Pastor Jeffery Noble, of Oil City, critizes the Post Gazette for its lack of religious understanding concerning their editorial on Governor Tom Ridge's involvement with his church.

headline: $400,000 approved for farmland preservation
abstract: Montgomery County board votes to spend $400,000 to purchase development rights to county farm land, matching the amount received in 1997.

headline: State: School District must pay Bucks academy
abstract: Ronald Tomalis of the PA Department of Education sent a letter to the School District of Philadelphia that said the district had to pay for 264 of its students who are enrolled at the Mosaica Academy Charter School. The school district has refused to pay for the students because their district didn’t approve Mosaica’s charter, and they claim it could increase minority numbers in the district by sending resources to a predominately white school, which would be a violation of a court mandate to desegregate the district. Tomalis disregarded both claims and said the Department of Education would deduct the money from state payments to the district if they fail to pay the charter school.

headline: Big rigs banned from Route 125
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation lets truckers know that those carrying 102-inch wide trailers cannot drive on Route 125.

headline: Traffic signal due for busy West Nanticoke intersection
abstract: A traffic signal will be installed at Route 11 in Plymouth Township, and the bridge linking West Nanticoke and Nanticoke will be completed by late summer. PA Representative Stanley Jarolin announced the installation of the traffic light, and Commissioner Chairman Tom Makowski announced the county would contribute $45,000 for the project. Julie Golanoski gathered about 3,000 signatures for the projects in response to bad traffic buildup in the area.

headline: Rent rebate rip-off alleged
abstract: owner  of Candlelight Assisted Living is charged with filing rent rebates for residents who did not qualify for the rebate. Attorney General Mike Fisher claims the owner may have received more than $78,500 fraudulantly.

headline: Upstate financial authority hunts Harrisburg-area buys - Dauphin County forfeited deals like Northumberland's
abstract: The Dauphin County General Authority had been trying to acquire and develop land, but the Dauphin County Commissioners weren’t pleased with the deal, so they passed ordinances for tighter regulations to halt the authority’s proposals. However, the decision may have backfired because the Northumberland County Authority has moved in, and it is considering a deal to purchase the PA Department of Environmental Resources Southcentral Regional Office Building, four other buildings and the Whitetail Ski Resort and Mountain Biking Center, which the Dauphin Authority had originally tried to purchase. Dauphin County Commission Chairman Sally Klein was shocked at the news and believes the state may have to tackle the issues because of authority’s immunity from taxes give them too much of an incentive to purchase privately owned buildings.

headline: Before Starr and Congress, Clinton faces the biggest decision
abstract: President Clinton and his advisers are considering options on how to describe the President’s relationship with Monica Lewinski, which include continuing to deny the relationship, admitting partially to an improper relationship or completely admitting to a sexual relationship. The grand jury testimony could determine whether Clinton is impeached, and a majority of Americans already  believe that he lied under oath in the Paula Jones sexual harassment lawsuit case. Lewinski has admitted to a sexual relationship, and Kenneth Starr’s investigation is likely to release a report to Congress on whether the President committed perjury, obstruction of justice and witness tampering; though the House is considering a resolution that would make the information available only to the House Judiciary Committee.

headline: INSIDE THE CAPITOL - Heard on the Hill
abstract: The article provides a quote from House Minority Leader William DeWeese complaining that tax reform focused on shifting taxes, not reducing them.

headline: Sherwood and Casey are ready to clash
abstract: The three PA candidates running to represent the 10th District in the U.S. House are working extremely hard in the final weeks before the election, and all remain optimistic about their chances as they prepare for an upcoming debate. Republican candidate Don Sherwood believes he is still riding the momentum from his primary victory and pointed to endorsements from Government Tom Ridge, Attorney General Mike Fisher and Representatives Scot Chadwick and Matt Baker as extremely important. Democratic candidate Pat Casey’s Press Secretary said he is working hard, while Reform Party candidate Tom McLaughlin predicted a tight race.

headline: State might break impasse
abstract: Four Alleghney County council nominees are to draw lines for redistricting the county. If they fail to meet the deadline, legislative action may be taken.

headline: DESPITE AN EASING OF RULE, MILLIONS EVADE 'NANNY TAX'
abstract: After President Clinton withdrew Zoë Baird’s nomination to become Attorney General four years ago because she hadn’t paid taxes on her children’s nanny, Congress tried to simplify the process of reporting nanny taxes; however, their efforts to increase reporting actually backfired, and according to Internal Revenue Service estimates, less than 1 in 13 people actually obey the law, which takes away $1.2 billion a year from Social Security and Medicare taxes. Despite the lost revenue, the government does very little to actually enforce the law, and it is very easy to get away with. People who actually do pay the nanny tax are angry at the government for not trying to enforce the law, and while there are no immediate plans to change the system, tax specialists are considering some different options.

headline: Pennsylvania colleges facing federal inquiry   Probe seeks progress in minority enrollments
abstract: The Office for Civil Rights in the U.S. Department of Education is investigating Pennsylvania’s state-related and state-system schools to determine whether the universities have introduced enough policies to promote more racial diversity. The investigation is based on a 1980 federal circuit court ruling that PA and 18 other states still had segregated universities, a violation of Title VI of the 1964 Civil Rights Act. Officials from the PA State System of Higher Education, as well as Penn State and Pittsburgh, said the universities had tried to attract more diversity, and the inquiry could potentially find that PA no longer is in violation of the law; though it is not entirely evident how they will base this decision.

headline: Ag Sec: State farms need protection   State official addresses farm problems
abstract: PA Department of Agriculture Secretary Samuel Hayes spoke at the Wayne County Fair, where he said agriculture is Pennsylvania’s greatest industry, and he cited Pennsylvania’s Farmland Preservation Program for protecting 110,000 acres of land. He said the future success of agriculture will depend on preserving land, and he praised Wayne County’s agricultural success, especially in the dairy industry. The Department of Agriculture also regulates over 3,000 amusement rides in the state, and Hayes said PA has the best safety record in the nation.

headline: State's Act 88 helps schools keep spending under control
abstract: According to a spokesman for the PA School Boards Association, Act 82, which became state law in 1992, has helped reduce spending in school districts by limiting strikes by teachers. He also said state funding has been on the decline, and schools still rely too heavily on property taxes.

headline: Big Wheels busted
abstract: Philadelphia is doing surprise checks of trucks driving on interstates, to make sure they are in compliance with safety regulations.

headline: Transit issues: From Both sides of the table
abstract: The article publishes questions and answers from interviews of David Cohen, the lead negotiator for the Southeastern PA Transit Authority, and Steve Brookens, the president of the union that represents SEPTA workers. The two men addressed the current state of contract negotiations, the possibility of strikes and the fiscal shape of SEPTA, which is operating at a $150 million budget deficit. In addition, they spoke about drug and alcohol testing policies, inefficient workplace practices and how to increase ridership.

headline: Rep. Armstrong changes mind on jury trials
abstract: Represnetative Thomas Armstrong surprisingly voted against the prosed constitutional amendemtns on crime. Additional lawmakers speak out on their votes.

headline: Urban League President says opportunities are 'ripe' for Black business
abstract: At a breakfast meeting and press conference with Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, National Urban League President Hugh Price said the time is right for African Americans in the job market. The league will hold a conference entitled "Economic Power: Leveling The Playing Field" at the PA Convention Center. Those scheduled to speak include Vice President Al Gore, Mae Jemison of the Jemison Group and William E. Kennard, Chairman of the Federal Communications Commission. A job opportunity showcase will feature a career fair.

headline: Betrayal and Embarrassment
abstract: According to the editorial, the President can ask a lot from the American people, and in return, he owes them honesty and loyalty; however, President Clinton violated this trust by lying to a grand jury to cover up his affair with Monica Lewinski. The author believes Clinton has failed the American people by lying to them, which is an embarrassment to the nation and reflects Clinton’s personal character. In the author’s opinion, Clinton’s recent speech was not received well because Congressmen, the President’s staff and the American population found out that they had been lied to for seven months, and he didn’t even goes as far as to apologize for his actions.

headline: Insider or outsider?
abstract: The question of whether voters prefer a Washington insider or outsider is an element of both Iowa's second congressional district race and the GOP's looming 200 presidential race. A list of insiders and outsiders are given.

headline: Sherwood Endorsed
abstract: A Wyoming County businessman seeking the Republican nomination for the 10th District US House seat has secured some high-profile endorsements from elected officials here. Don Sherwood has said he has the support of Mayor Steven Capelin, Senator. Roger Madigan, and Representative Brett Fees.

headline: Tax deadbeats find a friend in Street
abstract: Editors believe City Council President John F. Street owes more to the owners of almost 16,000 tax-delinquent properties in his district than his obligation to the Philadelphia public schools or the neighbors of the tax dead-beats. It was discovered that Street excluded the properties from a program designed to get fast cash to the city by selling tax debt to investors and using private tax collectors instead of the city's inefficient Revenue Department. Street's defense is that he is saving the city from greedy speculators, but Editors don't buy it. PA House Maj. Leader John Perzel should question Street.

headline:
Despite promises, budget deal hardly easy
Politics and a secretive process contributed to the difficulties, but Pennsylvania avoided a shutdown and furloughs of workers.
abstract: The PA House and Senate finally passed a $28.3 billion budget that is over $1 billion more than last year’s, with most of the additional funds going towards education and social services. Governor Ed Rendell and top legislative leaders negotiated the deal; however, some criticized their lack of transparency in negotiations, and the budget was passed after the June 30 constitutional deadline. The economic downturn and a less than expected surplus forced some tough budgetary cuts, but a deficit was avoided; though some funds were transferred from special accounts to do so.

headline: Pennsylvania's role in the abortion debate is strong - In York, Adams counties reproductive rights have been historically a focus of debate, protests
abstract: PA has played an important role in the abortion debate, and it gained national attention when the U.S. Supreme Court considered the state’s 1989 Abortion law, which placed a number of restrictions on a woman’s right to abortion. The Supreme Court upheld most parts of the law, and abortion rights advocates said the law placed an undue burden on women, whereas pro-life advocates praised the law for providing women with information and for requiring a 24-hour waiting period to get an abortion. The debate continues, and there have been a number of local protests at abortion clinics, including some violent attacks; however, the PA Pro-Life Federation does not condone violence, and its director said that declining abortion rates, which are shown in a chart at the end of the article, are proof that the new law is working.

headline: Agents aim to wipe up on roosting at Capitol
abstract: The state Department of General Services is gearing up to end the birds reign of terror on sidewalks, vehicles and luckless pedestrians next week.  Starting Monday evening, Capitol Police and experts from the U.S. Department of Agriculture will use tape-recorded crow distress calls and firecracker-like shells to scare the birds.  The procedure will be repeated for four days, said Samantha Elliot, spokeswoman for General Services.

headline: State's decision doesn't shock area districts
abstract: PA Commonwealth Court rejected a lawsuit filed by the state’s smaller school districts that called for more state funding, which was disappointing for many people from Morrisville and Bristol Borough but wasn’t surprising. The lawsuit claimed that smaller, poorer districts aren’t able to raise as much money in taxes as more affluent districts, so the state should provide more funding to offset the differences. Attracting more businesses or getting more school volunteers could help reduce the tax burden for homeowners.

headline: Bikers win right to head trauma
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge signs the repeal of the motorcycle helmet law. The Eagle Times thinks that his decision is senseless and that lawmakers shouls now pass a law to assume responsibility for all bikers who ened up hospitalized from lack of a helmet.

headline: Transit talks end fifth day without strike
abstract: The potential for workers of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority to strike still remains a possibility, and both sides appeared frustrated after the most recent negotiations. Union negotiators from the Transport Workers Union Local 234 have vowed not to strike if progress continues to be made, but they have accused SEPTA of moving backwards in contract talks. SEPTA’s general counsel, David Cohen, criticized the practice of keeping SEPTA employees on payroll who have been unable to work for a significant amount of time due to injuries, and he said it’s time for the union to accept an offer because the public has grown tired of its actions.

headline: Report could affect county youth office
abstract: George Kovarie, the director of Berks County Children and Youth Services, is arranging a meeting with state welfare officials to discuss what needs to be done to make sure his agency’s license in renewed next year. The welfare department issued a critical report of the agency over its handling of the case of Maxwell Fisher, a toddler who was raped and murdered by his mother’s boyfriend, and the report also found the agency needs to hire more Spanish-speaking staff to serve the Latino population and require caseworkers to make more personal visits to children who are at high risk of neglect and abuse. Kovarie didn’t see a problem with the number of Spanish-speakers on his staff, and he said the state needs to provide more funding if it wants more personal visits to homes.

headline: Urban sprawl eating up farmland
abstract: Between 1970 and 1990, land use has grown far more than population growth, and between 1982 and 1992, PA lost 560,000 acres of land to development. Governor Tom Ridge created the 21st Century Environment Commission to investigate the problems caused by overdevelopment of land, and it has been conducting public hearings. At a hearing in Gettysburg, the commission’s executive director, Carol Collier, said that as of now, there is not much anyone can do to prevent development until the laws are changed, and a final report will be delivered by the commission to Ridge by September 15.

headline: Bid for presidency could deter candidate Ridge
abstract: Several key Democrats believe Governor Tom Ridge, who is seeking reelection, has aspirations to run for President in 2000, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin has already begun to criticize Ridge in what could become a major campaign issue if Democrats can convince voters that Ridge intends to pursue the presidency in two years. They cite his recent trade mission to Israel and Scotland, his attendance at various Republican functions throughout the nation and his pursuit to make Philadelphia home to the 2000 Republican National Convention as evidence of his presidential aspirations. They cite another trade mission scheduled later this year in Argentina, Brazil and Chile as Ridge trying to pad his foreign policy resume; though Ridge has claimed the trade missions are intended to promote PA abroad.

headline: Internships open in Pitts offices
abstract: U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts is accepting applications from 16th Congressional District college students who are interested in interning at his Lancaster, Kennett Square, Downingtown and Washington D.C. offices for the fall 1998 session.

headline: Sherwood Not Resting on Victory   Winner of GOP Primary Set for Battle with Casey
abstract: Don Sherwood is excited about his recent performance in winning the Republican nomination to run for 10th Congressional District’s seat in the U.S. House, which will be left vacant by retiring U.S. Representative Joseph McDade; however, he remains focused on the difficult task that awaits him, defeating Democratic challenger Patrick Casey in the general election. Sherwood is the owner or part owner of four car dealerships and a forestry equipment business, and he enjoys raising horses and still relies on advice from his father, who died in 1983. Sherwood expects that both he and Casey could spend over a million dollars each on the upcoming election, but he expects a significant amount of help from both national and local Republicans as well as the support of some long-term friends.

headline: Tax reform bill clears Legislature
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge is set to sign a Congressional bill that will provide tax reform and alter the way school districts collect taxes.

headline: Education spending sways Assembly
abstract: All but one of Butler County's lawmakers saw enough good things included in the new state budget to vote in favor of it. Most of those who voted for the budget had mixed feelings about it. Both sides criticized it, but compromised enough to pass it. The budget is good for low-income families and small businesses though.

headline: Peterson Works With Colleagues To Pass Child Custody Protection
abstract: U.S. Representative John Peterson is the co-sponsor of a bill that would make it a federal crime for a person to transport a minor across state lines to get an abortion and avoid state parental notification laws. PA law requires parents be notified if their child wants an abortion, which Peterson believes is important. He said the bill wouldn’t interfere with each state’s parental notification laws, and he commended his colleagues after the bill passed the House.

headline: Are purloined pigeons potshot o plat du jour?
abstract: Birdnappers are on the prowl in PA. they're pilfering pigeons from their lofts and spiriting them away in the night. They are actually homing pigeons bred for racing as far as 600 miles at speeds approaching 70 mph. Some are worth hundreds, even thousands of dollars. And owners suspect their pedigreed specimens are ending up as targets at pigeon shoots or on the menu at restaurants.

headline: States hold colleges responsible for results
abstract: A study by the Rockefeller Institute of Government Public Higher Education Program found that more states are beginning to treat higher education like businesses by requiring universities to prove results to ensure tax dollars are being spent wisely. 26 states already have such policies, and 35 are expected to have them set in place within five years; though researchers aren’t sure if this will be a long term trend. By doing this, states can set goals for universities, such as higher graduation rates or more diversity, and states could even use incentives to encourage universities to graduate more students in particular fields to meet the employment needs of the state.

headline: Bill included Rt. 61 projects
abstract: Congress manages to pass a six-year higway and mass transit bill, despite the House and Senate having different versions of the bill.

headline: Transportation bill approved in both the Senate, House
abstract: After a much publicized debate over the transportation bill, US Rep. Jon Fox announced it was approved in both houses. Controversy over the pork spending in the bill arose during the 13th District primary. The original $218 billion version was reduced during the House conference $205 billion to increase the bill's chance of receiving Presidential approval. The South Eastern PA Transportation Authority will be among funding recipients. The bill also provides incentives for states to cut down on drunk drivers.

headline: Reporting flaws taints crime report
abstract: The State Police Uniform Crime Report is not uniform and is responsible for miscalcualtions of county crime rates.

headline: Urban thinks it's time for a change for the 121st seat
abstract: Republican Stephen Urban, a 24-year old computer salesman and student, said it is time for change, and he will be running against incumbent Kevin Blaum, who is seeking re-election after 18 years as the 121st Legislative District’s representative in the PA House. Urban said he upset with the condition of the City of Wilkes-Barre and wants the state to do more to fill vacant downtown businesses. He supports "high tech" computer job development at the state level, and he admitted for many of the issues, he doesn’t have the solutions right now but will need more time to study.

headline: Big issues, little interest
abstract: In the governor's campaign, all the differences haven't made a difference so far. No major issue has emerged to dominate the campaign, to make voters warm up to candidates demanding answers. All of the issues seem important.

headline: Investigators request records on Shuster campaign spending
abstract: Two merchants from Boston said they had been contacted for invoices and other information related to U.S. Representative Bud Shuster, which seems to indicate there is an investigation into his campaign spending practices, yet Shuster and lobbyist Ann Eppard, who was his chief of staff for 22 years, have denied any wrongdoing and claim to have no knowledge of a federal investigation. As chairman of the Transportation Committee, Shuster controls billions of dollars in spending, and he spent $1.2 million on his 1996 campaign. Critics believe his spending bordered on illegal personal use of campaign funds, but the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Boston have neither confirmed nor denied the existence of an investigation.

headline: Sherwood says LA representative will get his vote to become speaker
abstract: Congressman Don Sherwoods states that he will vote for Congressman Robert Livingston to replace speaker Newt Gingrich, who resigned.

headline: Tax reform discussion due to start this week
abstract: Statelawmakers are responding to resident demands on lower proerty taxes. Lawmakers are discussing possible bill proposal to provide residents with proerty tax relief.

headline: Fast budget
abstract: The budget pass in only two weeks. It is the earliest passage in modern history. Republicans will use this in their campaigns. They don't want to admit how high the surplus will actually be so they are pushing it through fast.

headline: Pitts backs proposed amendment in support of prayer in schools
abstract: Since the day the nation's highest court declared officially-led prayer in schools to be unconstitutional, a debate has raged on the issue. More than three years after Speaker Newt Gingrich promised religious conservatives that the House would vote on a school prayer constitutional amendment, it appears Republicans are about to make good on that pledge. The House Judiciary Committee are scheduled a vote this week on religious freedom constitutional amendment that goes far beyond school prayer.

headline: Down on the farm
abstract: Agriculture is the largest sector in the Schukill County economy. In addition to the economic benefits, farming helps provide a massive amount of green space for animals to live in and people to enjoy the beauty of. The danger of loss of productive farmland to development and unwise farming practices has many people concerned, including those at the local, county, state and federal levels prompting programs from conservation to land preservation.

headline: Steps already available
abstract: Harrisburg resident writes in to encourage the Patriot-News to cover more law and practice of teaching. The resident suggets that Governor Tom Ridge has the power to increase standards in teaching, but has failed to do so.

headline: Bill would let police stop drivers for not wearing seatbelt - Hearing on measure set for next month
abstract: PA Representative Robert Godshall is sponsoring a bill that would allow police officers to stop and cite a motorist for not wearing their seatbelt, which the PA chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union views as an infringement upon an individual’s personal freedom. However, the PA Department of Transportation announced that mortality rates were up 19 percent since last year for people not wearing a seat belt, and Godshall argues drivers who don’t wear them end up costing society millions in dollars in medical expenses. A public hearing on the issue is scheduled for July 14 in Harrisburg.

headline: Transportation interests take new approach to setting mission in state long-range plan
abstract: Southwestern PA planning officials will work with the PA Department of Transportation and the State Transportation Commission on a new approach to gather public input for updating the state’s Twelve Year Transportation Program as well as the region’s four-year and long term programs. Ten county-based Public Participation Panels were created to work with transportation officials in hopes of increasing the public’s involvement. Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory and state Senator Barry Stout, who is Democratic chairman of the Transportation Committee and a member of the Transportation Commission, both welcomed public participation in coordinated hearings.

headline: Republicans plan package of bills
abstract: The PA Republican House leadership is hoping to give the party’s candidates a boost in the upcoming election by passing a package of bills, including several addressing school violence, a bill allowing the state to take over schools performing poorly academically, a requirement that state welfare recipients prove they’ve actively searched for jobs and the creation of a scholarship program for children of police officers or firefighters killed in the line of duty. In addition, state Representatives Tracy Seyfert and Linda Bebko-Jones will propose their own proposals before the fall recess. Republicans hope to extend their majorities in both chambers, and while Majority Leader John Perzel controls most bills that appear on the House floor, Democrats will try to attach some of their bills in hopes of getting of their legislation considered.

headline: Using sports license plates to pay for stadiums is a hotly contested topic Pennsylvania
abstract: Five years ago, PA Rep. Frank LaGrotta introduced Legislation to allow the PA Department of Transportation offer state license plates with professional sports team logos. The idea fell victim to political opposition and never made it through the General Assembly. LaGrotta has now reintroduced the legislation, the revenue of which would go into a Stadium and Auditorium Fund in the state treasury. PA Gov. Ridge identifies the plan as only a small part of a much larger picture that will need more funding.

headline: Bill could ease regulations for special occasion permits
abstract: Representative Steven Nickol introduced a bill last March to loosen restrictions on special occasion permits, which would essentially allow more flexibility for fire departments and other groups trying to raise money to serve alcohol at events. The General Assembly has added on a pile of amendments to the original bill, but it passed the Senate and could be ready for the governor to sign by the end of the week if it passes the House.

headline: It plays big on TV-and helped elect a governor. Wrestling has quite a hold on U.S.
abstract: Professional wrestling shows, such as the World Wide Wrestling Federation’s Monday Night Raw and TNT’s Monday Nitro, have been increasing in popularity, and they have invaded American pop culture and now politics with the election of former WWF star Jesse Ventura as Minnesota’s governor. Between 8 and 11 on any given Monday night, close to 10 million viewers are watching wrestling programs, and revenues from WWF’s licensed products generates over $500 million a year. These shows have been described as a man’s version of "soap operas," and some people are worried about children watching the violence on the shows.

headline: Shift by Rebel GOP Congressman Reflects Party's Split
abstract: A plan to expand the Julian Dubuque Bridge across the Mississippi River languished for more than a decade until last fall, when it was adopted by an unlikely patron: Representative Jim Nussle who has a reputation for putting fiscal conservatives over local projects. He says it’s a state sponsored project, not pork. Insiders say it’s the first sign of presidential aspiration.

headline: Tax Reform Lite - Less relief for taxpayers and more headaches for schools
abstract: The authors criticize a tax-reform bill that would allow school districts to cut property taxes in return for raising the local earned income tax because local governments were cut out of the deal, and they also argue Harrisburg should be providing more funding to school districts to reduce the burden on local taxes. Overall, the authors believe the bill will offer little, if any tax relief, and they are especially critical of a provision that gives residents in suburban Philadelphia who commute to the city special tax breaks. They believe the bill was designed to provide an election year boost for lawmakers, and they don’t think it’s the kind of reform Pennsylvanians wanted.

headline: Fed budget surplus: Legislators explore uncharted territory
abstract: Almost certainly the debate in Washington over the federal budget is about to take another turn, and the reason is the end of federal red ink. Both the Clinton administration and Republican leaders are giving voice to the prospect of an imminent budget surplus, if not this year then next. While President Clinton has been cautious when discussing the budget, other administration officials have pointed to the likelihood of a budget surplus sooner than the target 2002. Not since 1969 has there been a surplus.

headline: Plan for Tribal Casino Back fires on Fading Jersey Shore Town
abstract: In 1995, the Mayor and business leaders of Wildwood, a struggling resort on the Jersey shore, were certain that the path to prosperity ran through this parched corner of western Oklahoma. The idea seemed inspired: take a bit of city land and give it back to Oklahoma's Delaware Indians, whose ancestors were pushed out of New Jersey in the 1830's. The American Indians would open a casino, and Wildwood would finally tap into the river of dollars flowing to the resort casinos of Atlantic City. Instead it has been made a Federal case out of and the Native Americans are claiming the entire city is their ancestral lands and they deserve the entire city.

headline: Easement Program Preserving State's Farms
abstract: PA program places easements on farmland to ensure that the land is forever used for agricultural purposes. There is currently a waiting list to get easements and funding for the program is provided by a tobacco tax.

headline: Steps Launched to Curb School Violence
abstract: With the past school year's nationwide death toll at 19 there is little doubt that steps must be taken to stop students from taking weapons to school and opening fire on their classmates and teachers. State attorney general has called for a year of jail time for any student caught taking a gun onto school property. Some believe that is too severe.

headline: Boat operators should be licensed in Pa.
abstract: The author supports a proposal by the PA Fish and Boat Commission and believes that operators of motorized boats should be required to obtain licenses. In addition, the author supports a bill proposed by Senator Richard A. Kasunic that would require education and certification for the operation of these boats on PA waters. The author thinks that these types of boats can be extremely dangerous and urges lawmakers to approve the proposal.

headline: Transportation master faces himself in congressional race
abstract: Incumbent Republican U.S. Representative Bud Shuster will not only be unchallenged in the upcoming election, but he will appear as both the Republican and Democratic candidate on the ballot. His popularity comes from his ability to secure huge highway projects for the district, including the Bud Shuster Highway and the Bud Shuster Bi-way, which he regularly secures funding for. His former chief of staff was indicted for allegedly accepting $230,000 in illegal payments, and Shuster is being investigated by the House ethics committee; however, these troubles seem to have had no impact on how the district views him.

headline: Residents may get to vote in fall on issue of jury trials
abstract: Voter will face two constitutional referendums; to allow the state a right to request a jury trial and to deny bail to those whose crime could result in a life sentence if convicted.

headline: VISION interests Ridge's top aides
abstract: The PA Department of Community and Economic Development’s executive director, Denise Schlegel, has been so impressed with Schuylkill County’s VISION that she has scheduled a meeting for the VISION leaders to tell their story. Schlegel said Schuylkill County has become a leader in regional cooperation, and she invited nine other state departments to learn from their example. Overall, over two dozen of Governor Tom Ridge’s top administrators are expected to attend the session.

headline: Bill to fund Civil War monument restoration in Gettysburg shelved
abstract: After a few members of the PA House met with officials from the PA Historical and Museum Commission, they agreed not to act on Representative Harry Readshaw’s bill, which calls for the creation of a PA Military Monument Board within the commission. The board would require $250,000 to operate, but under the guidance of Governor Tom Ridge, the commission is trying to cut down on its bureaucracy, not increase it.  The commission would also prefer a private group to be in charge of monument restoration efforts in order to save taxpayers’ dollars, and Representative Stephen Maitland agrees that the creation of a new board would be redundant and unnecessarily costly.

headline: Itkin denounces treatment of workers across nation
abstract: PA Representative Ivan Itkin, who is challenging for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, spoke to striking workers at Tarkett Inc., a foreign owned company. Itkin criticized businesses for not paying their employees reasonable salaries when the economy is booming, and he charged Governor Ridge with catering to big businesses and allowing companies to leave the state while welcoming foreign companies to set up their businesses. Ridge’s press secretary, Lynn Lawson, countered that Ridge has brought nearly 250,000 jobs to the state, and he is trying to replace lost jobs by making PA a desired location for technology companies.

headline: Show us the money limits
abstract: According to the editorial, PA has one of the weakest lobbying disclosure laws in the nation, yet the state House leadership has still failed to allow the entire House to vote on a bill to strengthen these laws. When compared to other states, it is clear that PA lobbyists are able to avoid reporting thousands of dollars spent each year trying to influence the state Legislature. The authors believe Pennsylvania’s citizens deserve to know how much lobbyists spend and what laws they are trying to influence, so they urge the public to hold legislators accountable in the upcoming election if they fail to vote on the bill

headline: Tax reform plan still has tough road
abstract: The PA Legislature approved a tax-reform bill that would give school districts the option, with voter approval, of reducing property taxes in return for raising the local income tax, which would primarily benefit senior citizen homeowners at the expense of young adult renters. Governor Tom Ridge praised the bill, and state Representative Karl Boyes, the bill’s chief architect, said voters’ overwhelming approval of a referendum to allow residential property to be taxed at different rates than other properties is evidence of support for the bill; however, the author believes school districts will be hesitant to approve the change, and voters may still choose to reject it. Democrats in the House and the party’s three gubernatorial candidates agreed that the bill is simply tax shifting, not tax relief.

headline: Fight shapes up: Do you want tax cut or tax reform?
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin claims he wants to replace $2 billion of current school district property tax revenue with state funding over the next five years without raising taxes in order to cut local property taxes by 10 percent a year. PA House Majority Appropriations Chairman John Barley was critical of the plan, and he said the plan favored by Governor Tom Ridge and other Republicans would enact significant tax reform; however, Itkin said the Republican version of tax reform would simply shift one local tax to another. In order to accomplish Itkin’s plan, which was developed by House Minority Appropriations Chairman Dwight Evans, a number of state funded programs would have to battle for limited funds.

headline: Planned Parenthood clinic in jeopardy? - City starts review that could close it; group's CEO says effort 'bogus, political'
abstract: After learning that Planned Parenthood is planning to begin offering abortion services at its Lancaster clinic, Lancaster Mayor Charlie Smithgall and James Schelling, the city’s senior bureau chief of housing and structural inspections, announced the city will be investigating the clinic to determine if some of its testing operations violate city building and zoning laws. Planned Parenthood’s chief executive officer criticized the city’s actions as politically motivated, but Smithgall and Schelling disagreed, claiming they have a duty to uphold the city’s laws. It would be the first abortion clinic in Lancaster since abortion became legal 25 years ago, and U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts will speak out against Planned Parenthood later today.

headline: Farmers go to Harrisburg
abstract: PA farmers travelled to Harrisburg to meet with state legislators as part of the Harrisburg Legislative Tour, conducted by the PA Farm Bureau (PFB). The PFB recommended a separate "farmstead" exemption to legislation that would reduce property taxes, a requirement for state agencies to complete a property rights assessment before authorizing new environmental regulations, and it called on PA to join the Northeast Interstate Dairy Compact. The PFB also recommended the Legislation impose a refundable deposit on beverage bottles and cans to reduce littering, and it supported a number of current bills that are being considered by the General Assembly.

headline: Student accused of recording, sending out others' e-mail
abstract: Penn State Student Government Senate President Jason Covener was arrested by police for allegedly installing a program in student government computers that recorded students’ e-mails and allowed him to send those messages to other students. He awaits his preliminary hearing but claims he is innocent. The student government could vote to remove him from office, and the university will explore its own options, including a possible expulsion.

headline: Boscola rips PennDOT payment scheme
abstract: Representative Lisa Boscola is threatening to delay PennDOT's six planned higway projects in Lehigh Valley because the Route 22 project has gone over budget.

headline: Transportation safety bill goes to Ridge
abstract: The PA Legislature overwhelmingly passed legislation dealing with a variety of different transportation issues, but Governor Tom Ridge will take his time determining whether to sign it. Representative Richard Geist praised the bill, which would require motorized wheelchairs to stay of the road, prevent children under 18 from riding in the back of pickup trucks and impose various other restrictions pertaining to school busses and pickup trucks. In addition, the legislation included a provision sponsored by Senator Bob Mellow to increase the penalties for drunk drivers who kill multiple people in an accident.

headline: Richland seeking full cash payback
abstract: Richland school district is appealing a fraud case it sought against John Gardner Black and financial companies for the loss of $10 million in investments.

headline: Voting on stadiums? Imagine that
abstract: The author discusses San Diego and Denver, which are both holding public referendums to get approval to spend millions of dollars on new stadium projects, whereas in PA, the author claims Pennsylvanians will never undertake such a vote. According to the author, the subject of Philadelphia stadium financing is being discussed behind closed doors, so nobody, except a small chosen few, have any idea of what’s going to happen. The author believes pro-stadium advocates in San Diego and Denver have huge advantages because they’ve been able to raise enormous amounts of money, and people are led to believe the teams will leave town without new stadiums, yet citizens at least have the right to vote on the issue.

headline: Bittle won't run for 89th
