abstract: PA Govenor Tom Ridge takes out a small ad in Iowa thanking the current governor of the state for his service there.

headline: Specter to meet with foes of judge
abstract: Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pa., said he will meet next week with opponents of Common Pleas Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson to discuss her nomination to a U.S. District Court judgeship.  "We will listen to everything they have to say," said Specter, chief supporter of Massiah-Jackson, whose confirmation vote Jan. 28. Sen. Rick Santorum, R-Pa., also will attend, said Specter. If information developed then needs further investigation, Specter said, he would be willing to ask the Senate Judiciary Committee to hold another public hearing on the nomination in Washington.  This could delay the confirmation vote, he said.

headline: Using the Surplus to Patch Budgets, Not Public Works - Officials Defend Their Plans for a Windfall
abstract: For the second straight year, New York City is expected to have a huge budget surplus, and many public works, especially sewer systems and public schools, are in dire need of being fixed; however, city officials are planning to hold on to the $1.3 billion surplus. Mayor Rudolph Giuliani proposed using 73 percent of this year’s surplus to help close an expected $2.1 billion deficit for the next fiscal year, and the city plans to spend between $4 billion and $5 billion annually over the next five years on sewers, roads and buildings with funds from its capital budget, which is separate from the city’s operating budget. Some continue to argue more money needs to be spent now because the city’s public works are in such bad shape, while others believe the surplus should be used to pay of the debt that still exists from when New York City was forced to heavily borrow in the 1980’s.

headline: House passes amendment to reduce amusement tax
abstract: PA Representative Robert Godshall sponsored an amendment to reduce the state’s amusement tax, and it will be attached to a Senate bill intended to broaden tax exemptions for low-income people. Currently, municipalities and school districts can share amusement taxes as high as 10 percent, the highest in the nation. The amendment would cap the tax at 4 percent.

headline: Unity Day seen as statewide model
abstract: Daniel M Welliver, director of education and community services at the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission, Welliver see helplessness in the face of hate too often.  Thursday in Pennsylvania National Bank's Hollywood Theater conference room, Welliver gave kudos to those who helped organize a Unity Day in the face of a KKK rally on Schuylkill County's courthouse steps 26.

headline: Unlicensed dogs to be target of area visits by state dog wardens
abstract: Dog Law Enforcement Offices are looking for unlicensed dogs in Clearfield and Centre Counties.

headline: The Senator says: Specter discusses a variety of topics at session with students
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter travelled to Hazleton Area High School to answer questions from 550 seniors, and he urged them to make the best of their educational opportunities. He faced a number of questions on President Clinton’s alleged affair with Monica Lewinski, and he answered several questions on how the U.S. plans to deal with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. In addition, students asked questions about a wide variety of other topics, including teacher strikes, abortion, sending troops to Bosnia and Somalia, immigration, legislative pay raises, education and a proposed flat-tax system.

headline: Congress neglects need to fix more roads in the U.S.
abstract: Public Opinion argues that roads in the U.S. need attention from lawmakers. The editorial criticizes lawmkers for their lack of action and encourages them to use taxpayer money to fix Interstates and Highways.

headline: A 'cop's cop' arrives to police Philly
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell hired John Timoney to replace Richard Neal as Philadelphia’s new police commissioner, and he has already been meeting with officers, District Attorney Lynne Abraham, business leaders, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and members of the city’s clergy to discuss his vision for combating crime in Philadelphia. He also met with PA Representatives Anthony Williams, John Taylor and Dwight Evans, who were part of the "Gang of Five," which played an instrumental role in advocating change for the Philadelphia Police Department. Timoney, who served 29 years with the New York Police Department, will try to bring some of New York’s success to Philadelphia, and for the most part, those he’s met seem quite impressed with him.

headline: Speak out
abstract: The Issue: State Attorney General Mike Fisher said there is no need to expand the state's law on hate crimes. The paper suggests: Although the Legislature will have the final say Fisher has an obligation to speak against legislation he believes to be misguided.

headline: Activists, officials demand merger data from 1st Union
abstract: First Union Corp. has stepped up its campaign to gain public support for its proposed takeover of CoreStates Financial corp. But community activists and public officials continued to demand more information about the $16 billion deal. They again urged First Union to give details about the hundreds of branches and thousands of jobs is has indicated may disappear in the merger, and to release a federally mandated plan for making loans in poor neighborhoods, before the Feds public comment period ends  and the Federal Board of Governors begins with deliberating on whether to approve the deal. US Senator Arlen Specter and PA Attorney General Mike Fisher are working with federal agencies to investigate potential economic damage the state.

headline: Caltagirone easy winner for 12th term
abstract: Representative Thomas Caltagirone received nearly twice as many votes as his Republican challenger, Gregory Garwood, to win his 12th term as the 127th District’s representative in the state House. Garwood was pleased he did as well as he did considering Republicans are outnumbered 3-1 in the district, and he said he believes Republicans are making some headway. Caltagirone will push for more state funding of public schools, but he has not yet ruled out running for mayor.

headline: It's only a $125 ad, but in Iowa
abstract: There has been speculation about Governor Ridge’s national political aspirations, and his campaign purchased a $125 ad in a program honoring Terry Branstad, who is Governor of Iowa, where the first presidential caucuses begin.

headline: Specter: Put off Clinton pursuit
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter said the past election, which cost Republicans five House seats, is proof that the American public doesn’t want to see President Clinton go through the impeachment process. He said Republicans should listen to the public by not continuing the impeachment inquiry in favor of prosecuting Clinton for perjury and obstruction of justice charges once he leaves office. Specter fears the impeachment process could detract from other important issues, but the House Judiciary Committee has said it will continue with the case and could potentially move towards impeachment.

headline: Veep used company card for massages, limos and dinners with hubby
abstract: Deborah Perry Estrin has been summoned to appear before the Philadelphia City Council's finance committee to answer for what the council calls a pattern of questionable expenses by the city owned gas company, Philadelphia Gas Works. Estrin, Vice President for Human Resources, did pay the company back for limo rides, massages, robes and expensive dinners with her husband that she had charged to her company card. In the midst of the controversy, PGW CEO James Hawes resigned. The City's District Attorney is also investigating the matter.

headline: House will begin work on budget for coming year
abstract: The PA House of Representatives will begin working on the 1998-99 budget today and has set a goal of finishing the process by Thursday at the latest. But members of the Berks County delegation to the House said they aren't living under the delusion that what they pass the week will be the final spending plan.

headline: VISION partners top 100
abstract: The Tamaqua Area School District signed on to become the 100th Schuylkill County VISION partner, and the article contains a list of the others. VISION’s executive director, Denise Schlegel, said she was "elated," but she hopes to have 250 partners by May. One of the issues the school district wants to pursue as a partner is special education funding, and the article details some of the efforts by VISION to attract partners.

headline: Valley farmers support proposal on milk pricing
abstract: Federal Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman proposed a plan to consolidate the 31 federal milk marketing orders, which determine the price paid by processors to dairy farmers, to 11. Glickman said that 70 percent of dairy farmers wouldn’t see major price fluctuations; though he proposed a transition period with artificially high prices to help areas that could see reduced prices. Two Valley dairy farmers were interviewed and backed the proposal.

headline: The true cost of higher ed
abstract: Guest editorial by Lisa March, president of Wells College. Both our public and private colleges and universities face economic challenges today that threaten to end many of our long-held beliefs about access to education. Much of the higher education news we read is about costs. This is a reflection of public concern. Too many college choices are based on affordability. She gives tips on crucial aspects on the college selection process.

headline: Congress stabs us on DUI issues
abstract: The US Senate voted to extort the states into accepting a nationwide blood alcohol content level for determining drunken driving. Senator Arlen Specter voted for this assaulted to state rights, and US Senator Rick Santorum voted against it. If the state that don't have the .08 BAC limit don't reduce their limits they will lose some of their federal highway grants. The paper is strongly against the bill.

headline: A dent in Big Tobacco
abstract: PA will receive $11 billion in a nationawide legal suit against tobacco company marketing techniques.

headline: Specter observes the pitfalls of unexpected teen pregnancy
abstract: U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter visited St. Luke's Hospital to discuss abstinence education with about 20 Lehigh Valley teens.  Earlier, Specter visited American Legion Post 367 in the Fullerton section of Whitehall Township assuring about 30 post members and spouses that veterans' benefits are a high priority on his legislative agenda.  In his visit to St. Luke's the senator recognized the Lehigh Valley Coalition to Prevent Teen Pregnancy, which recently won a grant from the state Department of Health to develop and coordinate abstinence education programs aimed at children ages 9 to 14 in Allentown, Bethlehem and Easton.

headline: Aim of game is big pay, stiff odds - Officials bet new lotto hits jackpot starting Sept. 12
abstract: PA Lottery officials have been working to design a new jackpot game to replace Keystone Jackpot and Wild Card Lotto, and they conducted extensive research into players’ preferences. Super 6, which will have 1 in 39.9 million odds of someone winning the jackpot, is expected to debut September 16, and it will run twice a week, beginning with a $3 million jackpot that increases $1 million each time someone fails to hit the winning number. Lottery officials hope the new game will eliminate the $40 million sales decline from last year, and a new type of game will likely be developed in about three years.

headline: Campaign 98
abstract: Profile of Jim Connors including age, address, party, current employment, family, education, and community service.

headline: Jacuzzi wants budget surplus used to boost military training
abstract: The US military is inadequately funded and 14 consecutive years of Defense Department budget cuts are taking their toll on personnel and equipment, Republican congressional candidate Joe Jacuzzi said Thursday. Jacuzzi said he supports legislation that uses a portion of any federal budget surplus to increase military training and readiness.

headline: Spend money to make money
abstract: A rundown of the money raised and spent by Friends of PA Governor Tom Ridge between Jan. 1 1995 and Nov. 24 1997.

headline: Volunteerism in area thrives - There are signs that corporations heeded the call of the U.S. presidents who gathered here a year ago.
abstract: As part of a presidential summit on volunteerism one year ago, corporations across the county vowed to use their resources to help the nation’s youth, and in Philadelphia, many companies appear to be trying to make a difference. While there are still many critical needs that must be met, Philadelphia’s Promise, a temporary organization set up to manage a three-year campaign to coordinate volunteering efforts in the city, said there are signs of progress, and most companies that made pledges a year ago are on schedule to deliver on their promises. The article details efforts by numerous companies in the region to provide volunteer opportunities and reach out to the region’s youth, and according to a report by Philadelphia’s Promise, businesses and trade unions were actively responsible for 38 percent of the programs that reached out to thousands of the region’s youth.

headline: How long can we go on property taxes?
abstract: Citizen's Voice criticizes statlawmakers for their proerty tax proposals and suggets that lawmakers begin to get together and really create property tax relief for residents.

headline: Women's Vote Project plots road map to polls
abstract: According to a study conducted by the Institute for Women’s Policy Research, PA ranks 47th among the 50 states in female detachment from the political system based on voter registration, the percentage of women who vote, the number of women in statewide and national elected offices and the presence of three key female institutions. One political scientist said the political environment in PA is hostile to females, and the state’s high incumbency rates make it difficult for women to win elections, which state Senator Melissa Hart agreed with but doesn’t expect to change anytime soon. Women’s groups across the state have formed the PA Women’s Vote Project, and while they don’t expect to attract significantly more female voters in the next election, they are hoping to implement several strategies to encourage more female voters in time for the 2000 presidential election.

headline: Weather takes a bite out of state apple crop
abstract: PA frost and drought cause the apple market to suffer. This year yielded less product for consurmers and less profit for producers.

headline: The Value of education. California University pumps $71.2 million into local economies
abstract: The State System of Higher Education paid for a study to be done on how its 14 universities impact Pennsylvania’s economy. The study found that all the universities combined contributed $2.2 billion into the state’s economy, directly employed 11,600 people and indirectly created jobs for 23,108 others. California University of PA contributed $71.2 million into the economies of Washington and Fayette counties, directly employed 738 people and was responsible fore creating 1,091 other jobs in the area.

headline: Construction catch-up
abstract: PennDOT will spend more than $50 million in road improvements in Washington County. Other counties could see long awaited improvements coming through.

headline: A Local Look at Juvenile Crime
abstract: Here are the number of juvenile arrests for murder, manslaughter, rape, robbery, aggravated and simple assaults. While the juvenile population has increased since 1985, it has not increased at nearly the rate that crime has increased.

headline: Sportsmen talk up Ridge at Butler courthouse stop
abstract: The Sportsmen for Ridge Caravan, a three week tour by sportsmen and gun owners who support Governor Ridge for reelection, spoke at Butler County Courthouse; however, turnout was poor. Two field representatives from the National Rifle Association pledged their support of Ridge because of his commitment to hear important issues and remain informed via the Governor’s Sportsmen’s Advisory Council.

headline: Airline changes may help Phila.
abstract: Two major developments in the airline industry, the loosening of restrictions on flights to Japan and the alliance between Continental and Northwest, could provide benefits for Philadelphia’s airport. The U.S. government signed a new treaty with Japan that will increase the number of flights between the two countries, and US Airways, Philadelphia’s dominant airline, could potentially be awarded the right to fly directly from Philadelphia to Japan and other parts of Asia. However, the far more likely scenario would be for US Airways to form a partnership with another airline that already flies to Japan, which the Continental-Northwest alliance provides an even greater incentive for US Airways to pursue.

headline: Campaign calls outrageous
abstract: Patriot News talks about lawmakers using telemarketing firms for campaigning during elections. The Patriot News does not like this practice ans feels lawmakers show called resident pesonally is they have important issues to discuss.

headline: Jarolin backer says vote stolen
abstract: A deputy warden of the Luzerne County prison sneaked into the voting booth as a man was voting and pulled the lever for a candidate the man did not want, several election officials said. He apparently thought the man needed assistance despite the fact his registration card does not indicate he does.

headline: Spring Democratic dinner is usually brief, sedate event
abstract: The Westmoreland County Democratic Committee dinner had no guest speaker and did nothing to bolst enthusiam for the party and upcoming elections.

headline: Voters can force board to cut taxes
abstract: If voters want tax changes and school districts do not, then voters can have a referendum to reduce property taxes. The process of doing this is explored.

headline: Last minute is too late
abstract: Barbara Hafer wona court battle to stop previous Department of Treasuer Secretary from binding her to a contract with Boston's State Street Bank & Trust Co.

headline: Worship watch advanced
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Goodling is a cosponsor of the Freedom from Religious Persecution Act, which passed the House and will now move to the Senate. If passed, it would create an Office for Religious Persecution Monitoring to evaluate whether other countries are persecuting their citizens because of religion, and possible sanctions could be imposed against countries that do. Goodling spoke to a Christian church about his bill, and he also criticized President Clinton for not being tough enough on China, especially in response to the massacre of students in Tiananmen Square.

headline: Americans deserve first try at tech jobs
abstract: US Rep. Ron Klink doubts the assessments conducted by the IT industry, claiming a shortage of qualified workers and instead requesting an expansion of the H-1B program which grants visas to foreign workers in those fields. Klink cites a report by the US General Accounting Office which finds weaknesses in the industry's findings. The House bill to raise the cap on visas should include protections for American workers. The IT industry should spend more time training American workers to do the kinds of jobs in question.

headline: Topics abound at PIAA meetings
abstract: There are several discussion but no immediate action taken by PIAA officials at the Board of Control meetings. The discussion were more centered around arcane policy and massive reports than day-to-day business despite looming presence of state Senate concern.

headline: Danville group files suit over tunnel plan
abstract: Danville Historic Distric group has filed a law suit against state and federal departments of transportation to stop a bridge project that would create a tunnel in the middle of the historical district.

headline: A prison by any other name
abstract: According to PA Department of Corrections Secretary Martin Horn, the newly established SCI Pine Grove, which is located near Indiana, PA, should properly be referred to as a correctional institute or prison. Although the inmates who will live in the prison are young, they were handed adult convictions by the courts, so it’s improper to call them juveniles. There is also a photo above the article which depicts PA Department of Corrections Deputy Secretary Thomas Fulcomer, two other individuals from Indiana University of PA and an architect's drawing of the prison.

headline: Stae's high court rejects bid to gove Lambert appeal immediate attention
abstract: PA Supremem Court has rejecte, convicted murderer, Lisa Lambert's appeal without issuing an opinion on the matter.

headline: Allegheny, three other counties declared major disaster areas
abstract: President Clinton declared Allegheny, Somerset, Berks and Wyoming Counties to be major disaster areas after the June 2 tornadoes which destroyed 126 homes and damaged hundreds of others. The declaration will allow the Federal Emergency Management Agency to provide loans of up to $200,000 for rebuilding a home and $40,000 for replacing private property. The sites of disaster relief centers will be announced later today for each county, the Red Cross and Salvation Army are also involved in recovery efforts, and the state will pursue federal funds for municipalities and counties.

headline: Campaign donations returned: Contributions from developers totaling $1,100 were sent back by Representative Charles McIlhinney
abstract: PA Representative Charles McIlhinney Jr. returned $1,100 in campaign contributions to four developers after he and four of his challengers said they do not accept contributions from developers. He said  the money was accepted because he considered the developers to be friends; however, he would return it because he is fighting for legislation to restrict development in areas which are growing too rapidly, and he doesn’t want to accept money from the other side. Richard Gaver, who is challenging McIlhinney in the upcoming primary, criticized him for taking the money in the first place and for having an advantage due to support from the county and state GOP, which McIlhinney denied.

headline: Jim Connors proud to run on his record
abstract: Republican Jim Connors says his rivals for Congress in the 10th district can talk all they wish about their plans once they get to Capitol Hill. He just wants voters to remember he has a record in public office to back up his words. H is one of eight candidates seeking the GOP nomination to succeed 18-term US Representative Joseph McRae.

headline: Staff needs geography lesson
abstract: The authors of the editorial believe that Governor Tom Ridge made an embarrassing mistake by sending a greeting to Dubious Volunteer Fire Department instead of Dubois. They say a geography error in the 1994 U.S. Senate race cost Senator Harris Wofford votes to the winner, U.S. Senator Rick Santorum. The authors claim Ridge is lucky that his election is over.

headline: Voters can scrap ancient systems
abstract: The 200 year long Allegheny County government could be history if voters choose a new home rule charter government in the coming election.

headline: Latest interest-rate cut suggests more are coming
abstract: With its surprise interest-rate cut, the Federal Reserve is signaling it will reduce rates repeatedly if necessary to prevent the world economic slump from toppling the US economy into recession. The Federal cut the benchmark federal funds rate on overnight loans between banks by a quarter percentage point, to 5 percent. The move came only 16 days after the central bank engineered the first cut in nearly three years, also a quarter point. This underscores how seriously policy-makers perceive the risks to the US economic expansion.

headline: $100 million loan OK'd for Allegheny
abstract: The Allegheny health system, which filed for bankruptcy for eight of its nine Philadelphia-area hospitals, its physician practice group and several of its schools, was granted an emergency $100 million loan to pay employees. The loan was approved in a hearing in front of U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Bruce McCullough, where Joseph Dionisio, a chief financial officer of Allegheny, spoke to a crowd of over 60 people, many of whom were lawyers representing Allegheny’s creditors. Dionisio broke down the components of a proposal from Vanguard Health Systems Inc. to purchase many of the Philadelphia-area hospitals, listed other bidders and tried to ease concerns from creditors.

headline: Amish say federal labor law threatens cultural heritage
abstract: The U.S. Labor Department has been fining several Amish families for violating child labor laws by allowing children to work in dangerous environments such as sawmills. The Amish shun most modern conveniences and live in relative isolation from most aspects of society, so they are asking for an exemption from labor laws, claiming they are not putting children into dangerous or exploitative situations and the work experience is an important part of their cultural and religious heritage. U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts, whose district is home to over 20,000 Amish, favors the exemption, but the Labor Department said it has an obligation to protect all young workers regardless of any other factors.

headline: Trustees may vote to oust university president after financial flap
abstract: The 36 trustees of Lincoln University, the nation’s oldest historically black college, will vote at their September 19 meeting on whether Niara Sudarkasa should be forced out of her position as president of the university. She is currently being investigated by the auditor general due to allegations of misconduct over her spending of state funds, and PA Senator Hardy Williams, who is a trustee, said her situation has become an embarrassment for the university. The university is encountering financial difficulties because the state has withheld its annual $11 million in funding, and state Senator Robert Thompson doesn’t see the money being released until questions on how money has been spent are answered.

headline: Conyngham Twp. Will participate in PennDOT's 'Agility Project'
abstract: The 'agility project' will have Pennsylvania Department of Transportation and a municipality switch out hihway maintenance servies on state and local roads. Several townships have joined in on the project.

headline: Abolish jury commissioners: Courthouse personnel can perform selection task; voters can eliminate leftover from patronage days
abstract: The editorial board urges voters in Dauphin and York counties to vote to abolish the office of jury commissioner. They believe the position doesn’t make sense anymore because the court administrator’s office can perform the work done by jury commissioners.

headline: Starr subpoenas head of Clinton security detail
abstract: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr subpoenaed Special Agent Larry Cockell, head of President Clinton’s security detail, and four other uniformed Secret Service officers to testify in an attempt to see if the agents observed anything that could be useful in Starr’s investigation into possible perjury and obstruction of justice charges against Clinton for allegedly trying to cover up his sexual relationship with Monica Lewinski. The Secret Service and the Justice Department are worried about the impact of the subpoenas, and they fear that if the president cannot trust his security team, he will push them away, which could leave him susceptible to a possible assassination attempt. A three judge federal appeals court panel agreed with Starr; however, their decision has been appealed to the full U.S. Court of Appeals.

headline: AlliedSignal moves ahead with AMP takeover
abstract: AlliedSignal, an aerospace and automotive parts maker, made a hostile bid to takeover AMP, which makes electronic connectors in Harrisburg, PA. AMP’s stock rose 1 Ľ due to speculation that it is seeking a friendly buyer to acquire it at a better price. AlliedSignal’s plan calls for 17 outside directors to be elected, who would call for a special shareholders meeting to approve the offer; though it could be difficult to do so considering PA has some of the toughest anti-takeover laws in the country.

headline: Campaign donations rise again: Congressional candidates raised a record $575 million. The pace was a bit slower this year
abstract: Fundraising by congressional candidates for this year’s election has reached an all time record of $575 million, but the rate of increase since 1996 is substantially smaller than the rate of increase between 1994 and 1996. The smaller rate increase can likely be attributed to there being less competitive elections this year and the increased spending of "soft money," which is money spent on ads that indirectly benefit a candidate but do not show up on their spending reports. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter raised nearly $5.8 million for his race which isn’t close, and in PA, the top fundraising House candidates were Representative Jon Fox, Don Sherwood and Representative Bud Shuster.

headline: Language on legislative vacancies again faces rejection
abstract: The legislature has failed to pass a bill that would prevent legislative vacanies from becoming a partisan political game.

headline: Starr Claims 'Pattern of Obstruction' by Clinton
abstract: Independent counsel Kenneth Starr defended his investigation into President Clinton at a public hearing in front of the House Judiciary Committee, and he opened with a statement summarizing times when Clinton obstructed justice and perjured himself, but he largely avoided sexually explicit language and focused heavily on words such as "truth" and "lying." While Democrats made no real effort to dispute the findings of Starr’s investigation, they criticized his conduct, whereas Republicans asked mostly friendly questions and voted to protect him from a longer cross examination by one of Clinton’s attorneys. Starr did exonerate Clinton from two separate charges stemming from actions in 1993 and 1996; however, he was forced to respond to many accusations from Democrats about his involvement in the Paula Jones lawsuit, the handling of an evening where investigators tried to get Lewinski to cooperate and the leaking of information to the public.

headline: Voters could get another say on property tax reform
abstract: Local tax reform may be voted on once again by Pennsylvania residents. Plans for a study commission on how the reform would affect school districts and residents are being made.

headline: Lawmakers approve reform bill
abstract: House and Senate votes are noted for local tax reform bill.

headline: $100 million loan OK'd for Allegheny
abstract: The financially stricken Allegheny health system is promising to pay its Philadelphia area employees today after a federal bankruptcy judge last night approved a $100 million emergency financing plan.  Because of the lateness of the approval, the $100 million loan technically isn't available today.  However, Melon Bank, which handles checking for Allegheny, gave Allegheny permission for an "intentional overdraft" of $2 million to $3 million dollars to meet payroll.

headline: Blackwell leads call for money to treat addicts - The councilwoman said that treatment programs were at stake, and that Gov. Ridge was responsible
abstract: Philadelphia City Councilwoman Jannie Blackwell, her husband, former Congressman Lucien Blackwell, PA Senator Hardy Williams and others held a press conference to criticize Governor Tom Ridge for cutting funding for drug and alcohol addiction treatment programs for people who’ve lost welfare benefits. Mrs. Blackwell criticized Ridge for using the move as a political boost for possible presidential aspirations, but Ridge, who recently announced he would seek reelection for governor, said he was dumbfounded by the press conference because he had approved funding for the program. Apparently, welfare officials had promised the money; however, Blackwell and the others scheduled the press conference in response to an internal memo that was never intended to become public, so instead, they used the press conference to seek additional funding.

headline: Tuition program proves sucessful
abstract: Pennsylvnia State Tution Account Program is doing  great job in providing funds for students to go to college. Valley Dispatch News praises the program.

headline: Council to enlist help in hunt for salt dome location
abstract: Over 186 people signed a petition urging the Franklin Park Council not to build a salt dome that would store up to 4,000 tons of salt near the new borough hall. Council members said they will write to PA Senator Melissa Hart and Representative Jane Orie to see if they can locate the new dome on land owned by the PA Department of Transportation, which has already said the site isn’t large enough.

headline: Acquitted of charges, lawmaker fights overzealous prosecutions
abstract: After his acquittal on charges of bribery and racketeering, PA Rep. Joseph McDade is continuing his fight against the PA Justice Department in the PA House. A panel endorsed his proposal to give citizens recourse against overzealous federal prosecutors. In a voice vote, members of the House Appropriations Committee inserted the measure into an amendment covering the Justice Department's budget. The provision requires the attorney general to punish prosecutors who act unfairly to defendants and create an independent body to review disputes.

headline: Starting in July, suspects culd be videotaped
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner John Timoney, Mayor Ed Rendell and District Attorney Lynne Abraham gathered for a news briefing on a new program that will allow murder confessions to be videotaped, and after a one year trial period, videotaped confessions could be extended to other violent crimes. Rendell said juries sometimes believe confessions may have been coerced by police, and he believes videotapes would help clear up their skepticism. Dorothe Ernest, whose daughter’s alleged murderers were acquitted after the defense attorney accused police of coercing their confessions, pushed for the program and personally thanked Rendell.

headline: AlliedSignal: Let shareholders decide
abstract: As AMP Inc. mounts legal and legislative assaults on AlliedSignal Inc.'s $10 billion acquisition attempt, the Morristown, NJ company is calling on AMP to conduct a special conduct a special shareholders meeting to resolve their disputes. Larry Bossidy, AlliedSignal's chairman and chief executive officer, wrote a letter to AMP's board yesterday, asking it to allow shareholders to vote on issues relating to AlliedSignal's hostile $44.50-a-share offer for the embattle Swatara Twp.-based electronic connectors company. AMP has rejected the offer as inadequate.

headline: Campaign financing and politics
abstract: Senator Arlen Spector discusses why no action has come from the $3.5 million campaign finance abuse investigation.

headline: Late-Term Abortion Issue Pulls Republicans in Two Directions
abstract: Top Republicans are meeting in California today with the chief objective of defeating a resolution to withhold party money from candidates who oppose bans on late-term abortions, but even if the resolution fails as predicted, the split within the party over the issue of abortion is likely to increase. A special election in California for an open U.S. House seat between Tom Bordonaro, a Republican who supports the resolution, and Democrat Lois Capps is expected to deepen the divide, and party leader are concerned the resolution will scare off moderates, including important donors. House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott again supported bans on late-term abortions, but they avoided mentioning the resolution.

headline: Starr draws GOP heat: Specter, Thornburgh assail wider inquiry
abstract: While U.S. Senator Patrick Leahy has called for the resignation of independent council Kenneth Starr, U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and former Attorney General Dick Thornburgh resisted because Attorney General Janet Reno hasn't taken any action against Starr; though they did feel he made a mistake by demanding that Sidney Blumenthal appear in front of a grand jury. Blumenthal, a former reporter for the New York Times, was questioned by Starr; however, he cited executive-privilege and refused to answer a number of questions. Starr called Blumenthal to testify in the obstruction of justice investigation into whether President Clinton asked Monica Lewinski to cover up their alleged affair, and White house officials were critical of Starr, yet they didn’t demand his resignation.

headline: Wecht tempted to run
abstract: Dr. Cyril H. Wecht explores the possibilty of running for Allegheny County Executive Post.

headline: Lloyd supports business incentives
abstract: In testimony before the House Appropriations Committee, PA Representative Bill Lloyd said the new state budget package should contain significant financial incentives to encourage businesses to locate or expand in counties with well above average unemployment rates. According to the December 1997 statistics from the state Department of Labor and Industry, Pa's unemployment rate is slightly below the national average, but 25 counties have unemployment rates at least 2 percentage points above the statewide average.

headline: A new breed of doctor specializes in hospital care
abstract: A new breed of doctor -- the hospitalist --- movement has spawned a new medical society -- the National Association for Inpatient Physicians.  The group estimates that 2,500 hospitalist are in practice, including 600 to 800 who started work just last year.  This emerging system seems to be achieving a rare thing in modern health care.

headline: Costs trouble meeting planners - Convention officials blame the unions. Labor officials say no. Local leaders worry about future business.
abstract: In the last year or two, the Convention Center has developed a reputation as being one of the most expensive and difficult facilities in the country to hold an event, and out of the 23 major conventions and trade shows that used the center in 1998, one-third said they wouldn’t come back unless some major changes are made. According to industry officials, the unions’ strict adherence to work rules creates an intimidating atmosphere and can make the simplest tasks require multiple union workers, which drives up costs. Several people have complained of rude treatment from union employees that borders on abusive, and Convention officials fear they will continue to lose business if these problems aren’t corrected.

headline: Two teacher unions move toward merger
abstract: The nation’s two largest teachers unions, the National Education Association and the American Federation of Teachers, have targeted a merger for 2002. The merger would result in 80% of the nation’s teaching force being represented by one union, which could make it a powerful lobbyist in Congress. The Center for Education Reform’s president is against the merger and feels it will prevent efforts to create charter schools and eliminate teacher tenure.

headline: County to state: Thanks for money, where's the rest? - County receives $190,000 for airport
abstract: Washington County commissioners will receive a $190,000 mock check today from Elizabeth Voras, the PA Department of Transportation’s secretary for aviation, and they will take the opportunity to talk to Voras about future plans for the airport in North Franklin and South Franklin townships. They plan to ask her about the other $1.5 million they’ve requested to complete an instrument landing system that would allow pilots to land when visibility is poor. The airport will use the $190,000 in state funds, $83,000 in county funds and $1.6 million in federal money for several different projects.

headline: Adams County to borrow $2 million
abstract: The Adams County Commissioners are expected to approve taking a $2 million bank loan because over $900,000 in state funding has yet to arrive, and the county has encountered unexpected costs due to its overcrowded prison and changes in Medicare. Governor Tom Ridge wouldn’t comment on the issue until having a chance to review the material, but he said increased county funding is not always the solution. State Representative Steve Maitland said he understands the county’s frustration over not yet receiving funds for its Children and Youth Services, and he said funding for the county’s new judge would definitely come through this fall.

headline: State Attorney general takes role in shooting
abstract: PA state Attorney General Mike Fisher will assume jursidiction over the shooting case of a Honesdale man shot by a police officer.

headline: AlliedSignal's Offer for AMP Hangs on Vote
abstract: AlliedSignal Inc Chairman Lawrence Zbossidy said he will shelve his hostile bid for AMP Inc if the PA Legislature passes a law hindering the takeover. State lawmakers are expected to vote Tuesday on a bill that would bar a vote-by-mail procedure known as a consent solicitation for 12 months after a hostile bid. AlliedSignal's strategy hinges on using such a vote by shareholders to seize control of AMP's board.

headline: Campaign staff always running
abstract: Friends of PA Governor Tom Ridge has never stopped operating, even though he has not run for office since 1995.

headline: Lawmaker wants to get IRA tax laws on same page
abstract: The federal government’s passage of the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 created Roth and Education Individual Retirement Accounts. These two accounts would allow people to save money, which would be exempt from federal taxes, to use later towards the purchase of a home or a child’s college expenses. PA Representative Thomas Druce introduced legislation that would make the state law equal to the federal law regarding Individual Retirement Accounts to encourage savings by making the process more simple.

headline: Starr report cuts Democrats' goals for retaking House
abstract: Democrats could have election trouble due to the recent Clinton scandal and some Democratic party problems.

headline: Where the dollars are
abstract: According to the most recent figures available, here's how the more than 12.1 million tourists spent money in the eight counties of Southeast PA in 1996: Dauphin County $470.36, Lancaster County $400.41 million, York County $176.93 million, Cumberland County $137.92, Adams County $80.37 million, Franklin County $76.27 million, Lebanon County $40.64 million, and Perry County $14.58 million.

headline: Major lauds new state budget
abstract: Tax cuts for families and businesses and more than $42 million in state funding for schools in Sullivan, Susquehanna and Wyoming counties highlight the $18 billion state budget for fiscal year 1998-99. The budget and tax reduction plan was overwhelming approved by the General Assembly and signed by PA Governor Tom Ridge 10 weeks ahead of the June 30 deadline.

headline: A rising force in managed-care debate
abstract: As part of the 1997 Balanced Budget Act, the Federal government is trying to get more senior citizens on Medicaid into HMOs and reduce costs by $116 billion by limiting the annual reimbursement increases HMOs get to 2 percent; however, medical costs are rising by 5 percent, so HMOs will have to either charge more or reduce options to continue making a profit. A Consumers Union study highlighted problems with Medicare HMOs, and a recent merger collapsed, which forced United HealthCare Corporation to drop its unprofitable Medicare HMOs. A lobbyist for the American Association of Retired Persons said the seniors will push for reform of HMOs, and the issue could become one of the most important topics in the upcoming 2000 presidential election.

headline: Hey, leislators, if it ain't broke, then why fix it?
abstract: Margo Madden is worried that proposed House Bill 1800, would adversly affect the Office of Vocational Rehabilitation.

headline: Tyrone Area scrambles to fund project
abstract: The Tyrone Area School Board, which is struggling financially after having $26.2 million of its investments frozen, approved moving money from separate funds towards two construction projects. Tyrone and over 50 other school districts that had investments managed by John Black had their funds frozen by the U.S. Securities Commission in what the agency reported could be the biggest case of municipal fraud in the history of PA. Tyrone is hoping to get more money back after a report is released by former Governor Richard Thornburgh, and PA Representative Camille George has called on Governor Ridge to help the school districts.

headline: Coy wants I-81 repaired now
abstract: PA Representative Jeff Coy gathered 1,500 petitions to begin repairs on Interstate-81 right away, and he delivered them to Governor Tom Ridge’s office. The PA Department of Transportation has announced it would spend close to $21 million to rebuild I-81 between Exit 8 and the Cumberland County line, but it won’t begin work until 2000 or 2001, which Coy believes is far too late. Coy partly blamed the delay on Ridge’s gas tax legislation, which can shortchange roads that are heavily travelled.

headline: Adopted individuals speak for and against national registry
abstract: U.S. Senator Carl Levin sponsored legislation to create a national adoption registry that would allow a person to locate another if both individuals register and consent to be found. The Senate already passed the bill, and at a hearing in front of a House subcommittee, one adopted man testified in favor of the bill, while an adopted woman opposed it. Critics of the bill, including U.S. Senator Robert Bennett, are afraid the registry will end up violating privacy rights of people who don’t want to be found, which could affect the number of people who chose to give up their children for adoption.

headline: State Capitol Rounds - REP. RONALD MARSICO  105th DISTRICT
abstract: The PA House Education Committee unanimously approved a bill introduced by Representative Frank Serafini that would require schools to compile various types of data, including test scores, graduation rates and class sizes, to be distributed as a school report card to taxpayers, parents and students. The Senate Aging and Youth Committee approved a bill introduced by Representative Jim Lynch that calls for the creation of a Senior Citizen Advisory Committee to prevent crimes against the elderly and help elderly crime victims. In addition, the House Majority Policy Committee plans to hold a public meeting on underage drinking, which will be organized by Representative Roy Cornell.

headline: AMP and AlliedSignal square off in a federal courtroom tomorrow
abstract: For nearly two months, AMP Inc and AlliedSignal Inc. have squared off with news releases, bylaw changes, tender offers, full-page advertisements, lobbying on Capitol Hill, and fancy presentations to large investors. But tomorrow the two companies enter one of the more important arenas, a federal courtroom. At issue are legal disputes over AMP's shareholder rights plan and AlliedSignal's plan to seek shareholders' approval to increase the AMP board membership so its $10 billion acquisition of AMP can be approved. AlliedSignal needs AMP's poison pill dismantled so it can pursue its bid.

headline: Campaign-finance enforcement
abstract: Representative Curt Weldon write to the Inquirer about the need for government to enforce the current campaign-finance laws and later think about reform.

headline: Lawmakers closed with a rush
abstract: The PA Legislature approved 67 bills for Governor Tom Ridge’s signature during the final days of the legislative session; however, they failed to address high profile issues like school vouchers, a referendum on gambling, the privatization of liquor stores, a halt on landfill expansions and improved training for teachers. Republicans, including Ridge and House Majority Leader John Perzel, still claimed the entire session had been successful, citing a number of different bills that passed, whereas Democrats, such as House Minority Leader Bill DeWeese, took a more critical stance, especially on property tax reform. The article provides a list of some of the bills that gained final approval, which deal with a variety of different issues.

headline: Starr Submits Report to House   Delivery Comes Without Warning as House Leaders Scramble
abstract: After an eight-month investigation, independent counsel Kenneth Starr sent his report to the House of Representatives, and in the report, there is evidence of obstruction of justice, perjury and abuse of power in Clinton’s attempts to cover up of his extramarital affair with Monica Lewinski, which Starr believes could warrant his impeachment. House members were caught off guard because they didn’t expect the report quite so early, and they are working to develop a plan of action for review and release of the report as well as 36 boxes of grand jury material. House Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde and various other Congressmen are quoted in the article, and the evidence could lead to the nation’s third impeachment in its history.

headline: Clinton controversy could cost Fox among blacks
abstract: Represntative John Fox faces critzim and a lack of support from the blach community in Montgomery County, PA. His former supports may turn against him and support his oponnent, Joseph Heoffel, because of Fox's response to the Clinton scandal.

headline: McHale trashes tax scheme, says roads deserve budget surplus
abstract: Representative Paul McHale does not want to use part of the national surplus to give back to consumers, he wants to invest the surplus.

headline: A shot of reality  Campus binge drinking won't end if it's kept secret.
abstract: According to a national survey, 38 percent of the 12.3 million undergraduates reported they binge drink, and the authors of the editorial cite some recent alcohol-related deaths to highlight the problem of drinking at colleges throughout the country. College administrators are beginning to take more action to stop excessive drinking, but the authors of the editorial argue the real challenge will be changing the culture of drinking at college. The authors believe the goal should be to make excessive drinking as culturally unacceptable as the recent anti-smoking trend is becoming, and they argue parents need to stop denying that there is a problem.

headline: House bill would eliminate overtime for some salespeople
abstract: The Sales Incentive Compensation Act exempts "inside salespeople" who use modern communications technology to sell their products from required overtime payments, in addition to those for whom overtime pay is already limited. The measures is opposed by most Democrats, labor organizations and President Clinton, who argue employers could use the legislation to force employees to work extra hours for commissions alone. However, 43 democrats voted for the bill, including New Jersey Rep. Robert Andrews. HR 2888 has yet to be considered by the US Senate.

headline: Universities assail Hickok for criticism The education secretary wrote a preface to a report that calls core classes "trendy"
abstract: Members of the State System of Higher Education’s Board of Governors are angry at PA Education Secretary Eugene Hickok for writing the preface for a report written by former state Representative Colleen Sheehan. The report criticized the 14 state-owned and four heavily state-subsidized universities for replacing traditional, important core courses for a bachelor of arts degree with "trendy" classes. Hickok won't apologize for writing the preface, and critics of the report claim these courses may have trendy names, but they do cover substantive material.

headline: Crow's Run next step in highway link
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation halted the idea proposed by US Rep. Ron Klink, to run a northern bypass through Cranberry as part of the Crows Run highway project. Editors don't blame Klink for trying. Klink hopes to build a better highway along Route 228 across the southern tier of Butler County. Editors believe his vision has merit, according to recent job growth predictions. Editors believe in Klink's vision.

headline: Adoptees fighting for their rights
abstract: Representative Chris Sainato's office is crowed with adoptees and birth mothers demanding rights to original birth information and adoption informations. Citing a new Oregon law, unsealing adoption records, the individuals suggest the need for legislation unsealing PA records.

headline: State drops appeal bid for new trial
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher withdrawls his appeal of a Supreme Court decision Giving Patricia Carbone a new trial.

headline: AMP extends offer to buy own stock
abstract: AMP Inc said it has extended until November 25 offer to purchase 30 million shares of its stock for $55 each. The self-tender offer had been scheduled to expire at midnight Friday. Swatara Towndhip-based AMP said it extended the offer to align its expiration with the expected completion of financing, which totals about $1.65 billion.

headline: Can ya' spare a ruffed grouse?
abstract: 741 people sent their proposed designs for a new quarter that will be minted by the U.S. Department of Treasury to commemorate Pennsylvania’s heritage. The Liberty Bell was a predictable submission, yet many unique proposals were sent, such as the ruffed grouse, Pennsylvania’s state bird. A special committee will recommend three to five finalists to the governor by early march.

headline: Lawmakers getting less for expenses
abstract: Thanks to a cut in federal funding, state legislators will have to do with lesser per diems. That does not bother either PA Reps. Lisa Boscola or Craig Dally. PA Senate members however, may seek reimbursement for whatever it is they spend. PA Rep. John Lawless predicts lawmakers will spend less time in Harrisburg however, especially on Thursdays when the Legislature is not in session and committee meetings are held. The cut is a result of a survey conducted by the US General Services Administration.

headline: State affirmative action opponents stymied
abstract: Sam Howe Verhovek who reported on the issue of affirmative action for the New York Times, used data obtained from the Nation Conference of State Legislatures. However, it appears the data was misinterpreted. Although a number of states considered such legislation, on most occasions it died in committee or was indefinitely postponed. Affirmative action is most likely secure in the northeast as well.

headline: County population projected to drop 14.2%
abstract: PA State Data center expect the population of Beaver County to drop by 14.2%  and the population of Allegheny County to drop by 16.2%. Additional statistics and population drops are noted for other counties.

headline: Moynihan: Let worker invest tax in pension
abstract: US Sen. Daniel Moynihan offered an amendment in the debate over Social Security which would cut payroll taxes, reduce the annual cost-of-living adjustment and encourage workers to establish personal savings accounts for retirement. The proposal would allow workers to divert 15 percent of payroll taxes to personal savings accounts. Republicans and wall street execs are suggesting Social Security taxes be invested in the stock market. Moynihan hopes to preserve Social Security through compromises that appeal to both liberals and conservatives.

headline: A top official leaving Allegheny   Harvey Levy was a major player in the growth of the health system in the area. It is now retreating.
abstract: The Allegheny health system announced it would sell off six of its nine hospitals in the Philadelphia area, and Harvey Levy, the chief operating officer of Allegheny University Medical Practices, announced his resignation, but neither he nor Allegheny officials gave any specific details. Before Levi arrived, nearly all primary-care doctors in the Philadelphia area owned their own practices, but Levi helped change the city’s climate by purchasing 274 primary-care doctors and 36 specialists between 1991 and 1997, and as of now, only 40-50 percent of primary-care doctors are estimated to own their own practices. Levi became friends with Allegheny’s chief executive, Sherif Abdelhak, which led him to sell his own physician practices to Allegheny in 1991, and while his aggressive tactics helped expand Allegheny, he has had two lawsuits filed against him.

headline: Incumbents, foes address labor issues
abstract: When three incumbents, six challengers and a congressman's representative gathered worker's compensation, unemployment and labor unions were the unavoidable topics. They were attending the Schuylkill County Labor Council Meet the Candidates. Attendees were mainly union members.

headline: Untapped Cohorts Of Teachers
abstract: The president of the American Federation of Teachers said that America will need to hire an additional 2 million teachers in the future, but there could be a shortage of teachers because many are being lured away by the promise of higher paying careers; however, Emily Feistritzer claims the problem isn’t a shortage of teachers but is a matter of putting teachers in the right positions. She claims most graduates aren’t interested in teaching in rural areas or inner cities, where teachers are most badly needed, so there are large numbers of teachers competing for the other open positions. In order to get more teachers for cities, she proposes a program called "Troops for Teachers," which certifies former soldiers and could help put teachers into places where they are desperately needed.

headline: Delegation to present its vision of Erie County's higway priorities
abstract: Erie County officials and PennDOT are working out a plan to decrease traffic congestion on Peach Street Corridor and other various transportation problems in the county.

headline: Adoption Agencies Worried
abstract: Statewide adoption network faces budgeting issues because of the increase in PA adoption rate. The state may not be able to cover the cost of the agency deficits.

headline: State grant will help fight against violence
abstract: A $140,000 state grant is awarded to Cambria County, PA to aid justice system officials when working on domestic violence issues.

headline: AMP offers to buy back 30 million shares to counter takeover offer
abstract: Some investors are skeptical about AMP's Inc's offer to buy back 30 million shares of its stock at $55 in cash per share to counter AlliedSignal Inc's takeover bid of $44.50 per share. The company made the announcement, shortly before AMP Chairman Robert Ripp and about 500 employees gathered for a rally in the state Capitol Rotunda to urge the General Assembly to pass an AMP-drafted bill would help protect the company from its unwanted suitor.

headline: Candidates agree on most issues
abstract: U.S. Representative Phil English and Democratic challenger Larry Klemens had their first debate, but for the most part, the candidates seemed to agree on issues. The biggest disagreement was over abortion, which English was opposed to, whereas Klemens made clear his pro-choice stance. The two agreed on the following issues: the need to reform campaign financing, putting at least some of the federal budget surplus towards Social Security, the North America Free Trade Agreement has hurt the 21st Congressional District, the U.S. should not send ground troops into Kosovo and the government should support farmers who are struggling despite the thriving economy.

headline: Lawmakers Rally Around the White House
abstract: The four Congressional leaders, Republicans Newt Gingrich and Trent Lott and Democrats Richard Gephardt and Thomas Daschle, expressed their commitment to supporting President Clinton’s handling of diplomatic efforts to force Iraqi President Saddam Hussein to allow weapons inspections to resume. The four leaders feared that Congress’s inability to adopt a resolution could threaten Clinton’s diplomatic efforts, and they have agreed on three main points: Hussein is a menace, military action is justified if diplomacy fail, and a consensus is developing for a more long term solution. However, many lawmakers still hold doubts, including Representative Curt Weldon of PA.

headline: State audit criticizes YDC administrators
abstract: PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. released an audit that found  the state-run Loysville Complex overpaid staff members for mileage and gave over 100 hours of free vacation time. The report also found problems at three other juvenile rehabilitation facilities in Weaverstown, Allentown and Coatesville. Casey criticized the state Department of Public Welfare’s administrators at the Loysville Complex, and a spokeswoman for the agency said they’re working hard to make sure the problems don’t happen again.

headline: Fattah Honors Legancy Of Black Local Congressmen
abstract: Congressman Chaka Fattah gave a tribute to Robert Nix, William Gray, and Lucien Blackwell for their congressional service and honorable leadership activities in the public sector.

headline: Municipal Official Predicts Tax Reform
abstract: Christopher Moonis, legislative affairs director for the PA League of Cities and Municipalities, expects the state Legislature to approve tax reform before the end of the current session, and he also expects the state House to introduce a bill shortly; though he’s unsure how it will compare to the Senate-passed version. He said the league is pushing to allow more alternate taxing options for school districts, counties and municipalities, and it is against a provision supported by Governor Tom Ridge in the Senate bill that would require a referendum every time property taxes are increased by more than the state’s average wage increases. Moonis addressed the league’s preference on several other provisions and separate bills, including municipal service fees, the Keystone Opportunity Zone Initiative and two pieces of federal legislation that are being considered.

headline: A veiled threat
abstract: A house bill passes, granting protections to millions of managed care plan customers.

headline: Labor parade's union theme: 'Nabisco's got to go'  - Annual event marches on despite threat of driving rain
abstract: Thousands of union workers marched through Downtown streets during Pittsburgh’s annual Labor Day Parade, which the Allegheny County Labor Council claims is the second largest Labor Day parade in the nation. Governor Tom Ridge took part in the festivities, and Allegheny County Commissioners Larry Dunn and Mike Dawida were pleased with the turnout, especially considering there was a huge thunderstorm in the area an hour before. A unifying theme of the parade was a protest against Nabisco, which announced it would be closing its Pittsburgh bakery and eliminating 350 jobs.

headline: Vote tallies vary from day to day
abstract: According to the editorial, head counting becomes common in the final days of the legislative session, and it appears Governor Tom Ridge’s plans for school vouchers, an expansion of gambling in PA and state funding for stadiums don’t have enough votes to pass.

headline: Demolition not a big comedown
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation workers are talking about the demolition of their old transportation building that will take place soon.

headline: Adult time as a punishment presents the nation a dilemma
abstract: When arrests for violent crimes by juveniles began escalating a decade ago, legislators nationwide reacted. Legislators shifted from a rehabilitative, protective focus to getting tough and sending young people to jail. Now the nation is debating if that is helping or hurting. All those surveyed agree the laws do not nearly enough address the problem.

headline: State lawmakers to consider True's child-protection bill
abstract: The PA Legislature returns the week to consider bills motivated by the death of 16-month-old Maxwell Fisher, a toddler who suffered repeated abuse that led to his death in December 1996. One of the two laws to be voted on was introduced by Katie True. The bills include several provisions required under the federal Adoption and Safe Families Act of 1997. The state is trying to go further than federal mandates.

headline: AMP Stock
abstract: Daily closing prices for the past four months.

headline: Candidates discuss student involvement, apathy
abstract: Bill Belitskus, Scott Conklin, Bill Lloyd and Glenn Thompson, who are all running for different national and state offices in the upcoming election, attended the Candidate Forum held in the HUB Ballroom last night. The candidates expressed concern over the lack of students who showed up to the event, and they answered a question on how they planned to deal with tuition increases for the universities throughout the state, which is a major concern for many Penn State students.

headline: Lawmakers to PIAA boss: Step down
abstract: PA Interscholastic Athletic Association chief Bradley Cashman said he has no intention of resigning, no matter how much some fired-up PA Senators demand it. A confident Caahman also said he doubted the legislature can push him out of the organization he has run for nearly 20 years. He didn't even budge when Senators asked him to resign.

headline: State committee races show rifts
abstract: The Mainstream Republicans, led by Ted Meehan, will run 19 candidates for the PA state Republican committee because they believe the party is willing to endorse candidates who don’t reflect Republican values. Meehan has been especially critical of U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and blames his support on county chairmen telling their committee people how to vote, whereas some party members have said they support Specter because of his record and "winability," while they also criticized the Mainstream Republicans for being "radicals." State Democratic Chairman Cliff Wilson faces more of a political battle than ideological, and seven candidates who oppose him will be running against his endorsed candidates for the state committee.

headline: Festive march highlights George Clay anniversary
abstract: A parade and festivities, which included 120 fire trucks, picnics and a party that lasted long into the evening, were held in West Conshohocken to celebrate the 100th anniversary of George Clay Fire Company. Congressman Jon Fox, along with many other politicians, took part in the festivities. Representative Connie Williams praised the George Clay Fire Company for often being the first to respond to accidents on nearby highways, and awards were handed out by the Delaware Valley Judges Association.

headline: New for '99: Some can tell the taxman to charge it
abstract: In 1999, the Internal Revenue Service will begin allowing Americans to pay their taxes by credit card.

headline: Advocates cite danger at Norristown State
abstract: In the midst of the heat wave sweeping the region, mental health advocates are protesting what they say are life-threatening conditions for patients at Norristown State Hospital.  A state-enforced lockdown has forced most of the hospital's 650 patients to stay inside the primarily non-air-conditioned facility --- a danger with temperatures forecasted near 100 today, said the Mental Health Association of Southeastern Pennsylvania.  The Association will hold a press conference today at 11am, to demand that the state remedy the situation immediately.

headline: Law may hurt local job training
abstract: A proposed overhaul of PA's job training programs is raising concern that local folks may soon have to go out of town for the job training they need. In an unusual move, commissioners from Franklin and Adams counties have issued a joint statement. It calls proposed state legislation, Workforce Development Act, bad policy. Area businesses and economic share the worries. There's a possible loss of face-to-face training and delays in decision-making by officials on a local level.

headline: Voucher decision draws cheers
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court decided yesterday not to review a Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling to allow publicly funded vouchers to give financial aid to parents who want to send their students to private schools, including religious ones. Byron Mundy, a member of the Southeast Delco School Board, saw the decision as a victory for vouchers, and he said the board is deciding whether to appeal a ruling by Judge Joseph Battle that the school board’s proposed voucher plan violates PA law.

headline: Dilution by diversion
abstract: Despite Pennsylvania’s plans to pave about 6,000 miles of state-maintained roads, the authors of the editorial believe these results, if not more, are to be expected, considering the state raised the gasoline tax by 3.5 cents per gallon and increased vehicle registration fees. They cite Peter Spencer’s online report that in 1994, the federal government diverted over half of the money it collected from road revenue towards non-highway uses. The authors believe the benefits of adequately funded highways far outweigh any costs, and they claim all taxpayers should expect revenue collected from highways to be used to build and maintain the highways from which they are collected.

headline: After rape charges are dropped, teacher reflects on ordeal
abstract: Picking up the pieces of a life shattered by a rape charge that proved unfounded, teacher Michael Gallagher vows to try to spare others from false accusations. Gallagher plans to work for legislation to make it a felony, instead of a misdemeanor, to falsely accused someone of a crime. He was accused of raping a student in his fifth grade class, but this was eventually proved false.

headline: State police gear up for gun permit change
abstract: Buying a gun just isn't what it used to be.  The entire process changes on July 1 when the controversial Pennsylvania Instant Check System, commonly known as PICS, goes into effect.  At that time, buyers of handguns and gun permits will undergo a PICS review aimed at weeding out individuals who have committed any one of 32 violent crimes.

headline: Amusement machines pay off in Valley
abstract: Regardless of which form of entertainment you choose, that coin-operated amusement device puts money in the coffers of Valley communities.  Arnold estimates the machines bring in the equivalent of half a million in property taxes.  In Verona and Tarentum, the machines generate nearly a full million worth of revenue.  Some municipalities charge an annual license fee for machines --sometimes depending on the type or number of machines.  Others charge a blanket licensing fee, making it difficult to determine how many machines of a particular type are in town.

headline: Candidates speak out: Itkin
abstract: The newspaper asked all the gubernatorial candidates to respond to questions, and this article provides Democratic candidate Ivan Itkin’s responses. He says his priorities as governor would include cutting property taxes in half, giving schools more funding, repairing Interstate 81 and creating jobs that stay in PA. He tells Shippensburg residents what to expect from him as governor, criticizes incumbent Governor Ridge for catering to big businesses and explains his personal qualifications, which includes 25 years as a PA House member.

headline: Lawyer to seek GOP nod in 4th District
abstract: Allegheny County lawyer Mike Turzai plans to seek the Republican nomination to challenge incumbent U.S. Representative Ron Klink. He will be the first Republican to formally announce candidacy and will likely face Paul Adametz, who lost to Klink in the 1996 election. Turzai said that strong showings by U.S. Senator Rick Santorum, Governor Ridge, and other Republicans prove that a Republican can win the election, and he believe that Klink hasn’t been challenge by a well-funded opponent yet.

headline: State congressman won't join Navy
abstract: U.S. Representative Paul McHale of PA decided not to wait for a senior-level Pentagon position, and he accepted two jobs in his Lehigh Valley district for after his Congressional term expires. He had been considered by senior defense officials for the Navy Secretary position, but no offer was made because current secretary, John Dalton, doesn’t plan to leave the position anytime in the near future.

headline: Gekas gives greetings to firefighters
abstract: Representative George Gekas visit Harrisburg, PA and wishes local firefighters a Merry Christmas.

headline: No sales tax on hot dog, fries
abstract: A 6% sales tax on vendor items at sports games has been repealed. The amount of money lost by this tax repeal is minimum.

headline: Advocates for blind: State faltering on services
abstract: The Pennsylvania Association for the Blind has been sugffering from budget cuts and services are not being rendered as needed to the blind.

headline: Maximum mischief
abstract: In 1987, a Democrat functionary in the US House of Representatives and Senate gave a frank preview of party strategy for pushing the minimum wage. 11 years later, proponents of another minimum wage boost continue to throw numbers out hoping to neutralize the negative impact of inconvenient data on their ambitions to play politics with people's livelihoods. Editorial claims minimum wage is unconstitutional.

headline: Vouchers on a roll
abstract: The Wisconsin Legislature, led by Representative Polly Williams, passed a law that provides state tuition vouchers for some of the state’s poorest children to attend 81 religious and 31 nonreligious private schools. The Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled the program was legal, but opponents, such as the teacher unions, the American Civil Liberties Union and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, appealed the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, which ultimately decided not to hear the case. In the author’s opinion, the Supreme Court’s decision to not hear the case represents a victory for voucher programs across the country, and he hopes the rest of the country follows Wisconsin’s example.

headline: Doctors oppose helmet repeal
abstract: Doctors and health experts met in Harrisburg to ask Govenor Tom Ridge to veto the propsed repeal of the motorcycle helmet law.

headline: Aiming to keep guns out of criminals' hands
abstract: Gun-control advocates, including Philadelphia Mayor Rendell and other big-city mayors, pushing for laws to limit handgun purchases to one month per buyer. The effort is aimed at cracking down on the small but virulent segment of the gun trade that uses legal purchases to put guns in the hands of criminals. 69 percent of Americans favor the idea.

headline: State police skip 'verbal judo'
abstract: The author compares the training of State troopers to the training of deputy game wardens, which the PA Game Commission relies heavily on, and he believes that the training for deputy game wardens is highly insufficient. He discusses a proposal by State Senator Melissa Hart to remove deputies of search and seizure powers, as well as a proposal by State Representative David Levdansky to create a tier system that would relegate less intense duties to deputies with limited training. Ultimately, he believes that these deputies have become an embarrassment, and he would like to see the deputy system eliminated.

headline: AT&T-TCI deal may bring jobs - Merger could precipitate communications advances
abstract: AT&T and TeleCommunications Incorporated, the dominant cable television provider in the Pittsburgh region, have signed a merger agreement worth about $42 billion. The merger could potentially create more jobs, and customers can expect some upgrades in equipment, such as cable television connections. While the full impact of the merger on local operations is still unknown, Pittsburgh City Councilman Dan Cohen hopes to obtain better rates and better customer service from AT&T if the deal goes through.

headline: Candidates square off on issues
abstract: PA House members and their opponents attended the Candidates Night forum, which was sponsored by the League of Women voters, and they answered six questions that were selected from submissions by audience members and radio listeners. Representative Tim Pesci in the 60th District believes Governor Ridge should allocate some of the state’s budget surplus to schools in order to reduce property taxes, whereas his challenger, Samuel Sulkosky, favored closing loopholes in sales tax purchases. Representative Sara Steelman of the 62nd District battled with her challenger, David Frick, over tax issues, and other questions involving funding for Indiana University of PA, school violence and abortion were also debated at the event.

headline: Lawyer will run for judge: Bloom's James in race, Gordner out
abstract: Bloomsburg attorney Thomas James Jr. will seek election as judge in the joint courts of Columbia and Montour counties, a position that should be open because Judge Keller is expected to retire. While any interested candidates have until March 9 to file nominating petitions, PA Representative John Gordner has already announced he would not seek the position. James was an unsuccessful judicial candidate in 1991, and he vows not to use negative ads in the upcoming election.

headline: State considers next step after judge allows removal of feeding  tube
abstract: Virginia Governor Jim Gilmore filed a motion to prevent Michele Finn from removing a feeding tube that has been sustaining the life of her husband, who has been in a vegetative stage since a car accident three and a half years ago. Under Virginia law, life-sustaining treatment can be stopped if a person is in a vegetative state, and Prince William Circuit Judge Frank Hoss Jr. rejected the state’s motion and agreed that Mrs. Finn had the right to remove the tube. There has been disagreement between Mrs. Finn and some of her husband’s family members, and Gilmore said that he was approached by a relative to intervene.

headline: Local football heroes saluted in Harrisburg   Central Bucks West High School's championship football team was honored in the state capital on Monday, along with Doyle Elementary School's Nicole Flego
abstract: The Central Bucks West High School football team, which became the first team in PA history to win a second AAAA state championship, was honored in Harrisburg. They were also featured on a box of cheerios, which Senator Joe Conti of Doylestown sent to Senator Tim Murphy, whose district includes Upper St. Clair, the team that lost the championship game. Representative Tom Druce offered praise to Dave Armstrong, the team’s star senior, Representative Tim Hennessey praised Coach Mike Pettine and Nicole Flego, a fourth grader, was also honored for winning a national football skills competition.

headline: On taxes, Ridge favors minority rule
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge is supporting the idea of forcing legislators to get 60% of residents votes before being able to increase taxes. Scranton Tribune is not in favor of this rule as it creates more user fees and gives 40% of lawmakers too much power.

headline: AGH moves on lining up financial partners
