abstract: Allegheny General Hospital and its affiliates are searching for financial partners, and Highmark Blue Cross and Blue Shield and the Community Hospital Alliance have both indicated that they would consider. The hospitals are struggling financially because their parent foundation, the Allegheny Health Education and Research Foundation, took millions from their reserves to support their bankrupt Philadelphia-area hospitals. Many creditors are pushing the foundation to sell off their Pittsburgh hospitals because they received very little from the sale of their hospitals in Philadelphia.

headline: Mining's Deadly Dust
abstract: When deep mining's heyday passed and coal harvesting moved to strip mines of the surface, everyone assumed it would be a safer profession.  Strip mining still involved hard labor under sometimes tough conditions, but miners, mine operators and the federal government thought the open air would disperse the rock dust that so often coated the lung of deep miners.  They were wrong.  A series of multi-agency studies this decade have found that rates of silicosis, a type of lung disease caused by breathing rock dust, are actually higher in surface miners, especially drillers and heavy-machine operators, than in any other mining profession.

headline: Vouchers: Ridge to have the last word
abstract: Delaware County Judge Joseph Battle ruled that Southeast Delco School District’s program to provide vouchers to pay for students to attend private schools is illegal because it violates the state schools code. However, the judge didn’t rule vouchers unconstitutional, so if the PA Legislature passes a new school code, which mayoral candidate and Representative Dwight Evans wants to do, vouchers could become legal in the future. Anti-school voucher advocates see the judge’s ruling as a temporary victory, but there is speculation that Governor Tom Ridge, a strong supporter of vouchers, may push for voucher legislation after the November 3 elections.

headline: Doctors urge Ridge to veto helmet repeal bill
abstract: PA Senator Jack Wagner and 50 doctors, nurses and EMS crewmembers gathered in Harrisburg to urge Governor Ridge to veto legislation that would repeal Pennsylvania’s mandatory helmet law and make it optional for motorcyclists over the age of 21 to wear helmets. According to the PA Emergency Health Services Council, statistics show that there are less deaths and serious injuries for people who wear helmets. The Alliance of Bikers Aimed Toward Education has called the statistics exaggerated; however, there is a lot of evidence that suggests states with no mandatory helmet laws suffer twice as many deaths from head injuries as states that do have them.

headline: Alienated and angry, teens get a 'rush' from crime
abstract: A gas station attendant in suburban New Jersey was cuffed to a tree and terrorized with a sawed-off shotgun during a robbery last year. Brenda Hall, then 18, a round-faced redhead with no criminal past, is now in jail for her part in the crime. In an interview, she explained that she did it for the rush. This is now a trend seen in teen criminals. Parents have a much harder time than ever.

headline: State slashes budget in half for local gun-safety program
abstract: Robert Flipping plans to tell pupils at Acmetonia Elementary School about gun safety Wednesday because he knows the grief that comes with an accident involving a firearm.  For the past two years, Flipping has worked in the Allegheny County Health Department, where he teaches gun-safety program as part of his job as a violence-prevention community educator.  But next year, the health department will receive about half as much federal money funneled through the state Department of Health which means fewer children will hear the message, said Guillermo Cole, a spokesmen for the county health department.

headline: ATM fee not "convenience"
abstract: When automatic teller machines, or ATMs, were first installed in the 1970s, they were touted as convenient and money saving because they replaced human tellers. They now claim they have to charge user fees to save even more money. These fees are not approved by the paper.

headline: Car event steers funds to children - 2,000 come out for Corvette show
abstract: Sixteen-year-old Kelly Brightbill, who has cerebral palsy, was this year’s spokesperson for the 13th annual Corvette for Kids show, which raises money for children and their families to pay for medical bills and other expenses. Over 2,000 people and 230 Corvettes were at the event, and there was also an auction to raise money. PA Representative Dennis Leh of the 130th District cited the event for its chartable work.

headline: Leadership by example
abstract: Vincent and Vance Moss founded the Youth Leadership Initiative Campaign in Washington, but they introduced the campaign in Philadelphia in 1996 after arriving to attend Temple University School of Medicine. The purpose of the campaign is to show African Americans that there are many career opportunities out there for them by introducing them to people in their chosen fields and helping them determine how to reach their goals. PA Representative Robert Flick befriended the two men and introduced them to District Attorney Lynne Abraham, who helped them organize peace rallies.

headline: State Democrats rally for Clinton
abstract: State Democrats held a rally in Harrisburg to support Clinton and urge Republican lawmakers to focus on the real issues effecting the public.

headline: Looking for Rep. Linda Blair
abstract: Exorcist Baron Decon stood on the capital steps with a Bible and a Cross trying to expel the demons from the building and government officials.

headline: On the tax reform front, nothing is certain
abstract: Since the Homestead Exemption Act was passed by Pennsylvania voters, no one has been certain what taxes would be cut and what taxes would be increased. Lawmakers continue to debate the issue of tax reform as it falls under the Act.

headline: AGH parent documents subpoenaed
abstract: Pittsburgh’s U.S. attorney has subpoenaed records from Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation and its western PA affiliates, including Allegheny University Medical Practices, Allegheny University Hospital, Allegheny Health Insurance Providers Inc., and Jellico Inc. The foundation claimed bankruptcy with $1.3 billion in debts and has been under review by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for possible security fraud and by the PA Attorney General’s Office for possible illicit use of donors’ money. U.S. Bankruptcy Judge M. Bruce McCullough is reviewing the foundation’s financial records, and the proposed sale of eight Philadelphia hospitals has run into some problems.

headline: N.J. shipyard workers hope Kvaerner spells jobs
abstract: When the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard closed in 1995, thousands of people lost their jobs, and in the past, about 30 percent of the Shipyard’s workforce came from New Jersey and the remainder came from PA. These percentages are expected to remain similar when Kvaerner ASA, a European shipbuilder, reopens the Shipyard, and out of the 1,500 job applicants, Kvaerner will be encouraged to hire former workers. PA and Philadelphia contributed substantially more than New Jersey to attract Kvaerner, but nonetheless, in addition to direct jobs from the shipyard’s reopening, it is also expected to generate an additional $100 million in business for Gloucester, New Jersey.

headline: West End library gets $300,000 grant for new building
abstract: Western Pocono Community Library received a $300,000 grant from the PA Department of Education to help construct a new $1.5 million library. The library has over 17,000 card members, and its director said the current building doesn’t have enough room to hold the library’s entire collection. The library hopes to raise another $250,000 from community efforts, and State Representative Craig Dally said the grant will go a long way in helping build the new library.

headline: Driver training center appeals debarment
abstract: The owner of the Moon Township truck center is awaiting word on a court appeal to stop a massive driver retesting program until the center can respond to charges leading to its closure. PA Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory announced a cancellation of the state's contract with West Hills which allowed it to test drivers for their commercial licenses. Twenty-five drivers received passing marks on CDL exams without taking the required tests. The center acknowledges that two examiners were found to have improperly administered tests.

headline: Allentown firearm exchange draws gun enthusiasts' ire
abstract: In a year when past critics of Allentown's annual gun exchange helped plan this year's event , there's talk of a protest, including burning in effigy the mayor, police chief and health director.    A coalition of firearms enthusiasts and local gun clubs have discussed methods to end what they perceive as "anti-gun rhetoric" that comes in the weeks leading up to Allentown's gun exchange program, when officials try to raise awareness, said Andy Barniskis of the Keystone Firearms Coalition.  The group is based in Southampton, Bucks County, but is affiliated with gun clubs in the Lehigh Valley, Berniskis said.

headline: State Supreme Court lets '86 death sentence stand
abstract: U.S. Supreme Court denies convicted murderer and death row inmate, Frederic Jermyn, a new trial after evidence of his mental instability was presented.

headline: Bank branches to close
abstract: Several local First Union and Corestates bank branches will close in October, following the byout of Corestates by First Union..

headline: Casey breaks silence, rebuts Ridge attacks
abstract: Former PA Governor Robert Casey had declined to comment on the performance of his successor, Tom Ridge, in the past; however, he responded angrily over comments that Ridge made recently during speeches for his reelection campaign. Ridge, who spoke of Casey favorably during his first election bid, criticized the Casey Administration for making PA a hostile place for businesses and for being reluctant to sign death warrants. Casey defended his record and cited a number of accomplishments as governor, including the creation of the Children’s Health Insurance Program and his ability to leave Ridge with a $400 million surplus.

headline: Legislation puts new teeth in Sunshine Law
abstract: Sunshine Law reform will require government entities to disclose information and take public comments on matters before voting. If this is not done the entitiy will face financial penalities.

headline: State Demos to reorganize troubled Lehigh County
abstract: The Democratic State Committee will help reorganize Lehigh County Democratic Party. A new party chair person is scheduled to be announced.

headline: May 19 vote could be real killer
abstract: If the new home rule charter passes in Allegheny County, there could be side effects tht the public does not expect, including taxes and political changes, and possible minority discrimination.

headline: Peterson: impeachment possibility fills Congress with fear, trepidation
abstract: U.S. Representative John Peterson said Congress will be hesitant to impeach President Clinton, who is set to testify on his relationship with Monica Lewinsky, and Peterson criticized Vice President Gore’s support of the Kyoto treaty, which calls for a reduction in the use of fossil fuels, because Peterson doesn’t believe there is proof of global warming and the treaty would hurt America’s economy. According to Peterson, there’s no agreement in Congress on how to spend the $80 billion budget surplus, but a new tax code should be implemented by 2001, and he expects some minor tax cuts. In addition to addressing highways, in-lieu-of-tax payments and his impression on his first 18 months in office, Peterson said he agrees with U.S. Senator Rick Santorum’s call to overhaul the Social Security system, and he favors allowing people to invest a portion of their funds.

headline: AGH parent rolled dice with risky purchases
abstract: If the bankruptcy parent of Allegheny General Hospital were a bank or a grocery store in a stagnant market, few would be questioning its strategy.  Confronted with industry-wide overcapacity and flat to declining per-patient revenue, the Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation carved out a niche in academic medicine and got bigger.  It bought a medical school in Philadelphia, opening the door to the influential and once-lucrative world of research and teaching.

headline: Notice served
abstract: In response to the Oct 7 letter titled Fast-Track author would like to say the workers of the 57th Legislative District are well aware of their jobs being moved to Mexico. They also have noticed the lack of concern, leadership and responsibility, along with the do-nothing attitude of Representative Tom Tangretti for 10 years. Meanwhile, he has received pay increases that are equal to or more than the minimum-wages jobs the citizens are forced to take.

headline: Why area schools can't find, keep leaders
abstract: Schools in the Philadelphia region have been facing a significant drop in the number of applications for superintendant positions, there have been high turnover rates, and the interest in high-ranking teachers to move up has been declining in recent years, which is troubling for many school boards that find it difficult to implement new policies and new curriculum when there’s a gap in the school’s leadership position. Superintendants can often obtain much higher salaries in the private sector, and some have retired because of new pension incentives offered by a bill that passed the PA Legislature in 1993. Superintendants often face the wrath of the angry parents and angry taxpayers, so the stress and demands of the job are other explanations for the decline in interest for superintendant positions.

headline: Driving a hard bargain
abstract: Vehicle accidents are the leading cause of death for people between the ages of 15 and 20, and in 1996, 6,300 teen-agers were killed and 600,000 others injured in teen-related crashes. PA Representative Rick Geist, who is chairman of the House’s Transportation Committee, is working on a bill that would require teens to gain more driving experience before getting their licenses and would make driver’s education courses mandatory. The PA American Automobile Association has proposed a graduated driver license program that would include three different stages, and in order to gain a full unrestricted license, a person would have to fulfill all previous requirements, be at least 18 years old and pass a final road test.

headline: Amendment levels the playing field for victims
abstract: The positive benefits of the proposed consitutional referendums on crime are given.

headline: State to release sentencing data on county judges
abstract: Statistics revealing the sentences handed down by county judges statewide for defendants who commit crimes from retail theft to murder will soon be made public, following a decision by the Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing.  The move by the commission to release the data next week has sparked strong opposition from judges' chambers and state and local bar associations.  The information will be 1996 data.

headline: Bank merger impact eyed
abstract: First Union Corp. announced that it would cut some 4,400 jobs and close 172 bank branches in the tri-state area once its proposed takeover of Corestates Financial Corp. is finalized. The Charlotte bank cushioned the blow with a $13 billion promise to the community, which includes $10 billion for small business lending. Wary lawmakers and consumer groups had been pressing First Union for more details on the $16 billion deal that was announced three months ago.

headline: Casey Jr. angrily denies leak came from his office
abstract: Auditotr General Robert Casey and the auditor general's office was accussed of releasing tax information about election candidate Joe Cullen. Casey and the office deny the allegation.

headline: Legislators back with re-election on their minds - Possible tax cut one issues on a fairly busy agenda
abstract: The PA Legislature began its new session today, and many of the legislators, as well as Governor Tom Ridge, will have re-election thoughts in the back of their minds this year. The House plans to vote on separate bills dealing with prisoners’ frivolous lawsuits and lottery winnings for individuals who default on state-provided student loans, whereas the Senate may tackle a bill that would ban sex clubs and another pertaining to health maintenance organizations. With the booming economy creating a surplus, the Legislature will consider tax cuts, and Ridge is set to give his budget proposal for the upcoming fiscal year.

headline: State gave blessing to county agency's non-union post   Public relations positions are automatic exceptions, an official said
abstract: James Kinney was appointed to a newly created non-union position, and the PA Department of Aging said he was exempted from the state’s civil service system due to automatic exemptions that are given for public relations positions. Kinney will conduct many public relations duties, but he will also take over the duties left vacant by Charles Kane, who left his union position as director of the Bucks County Area Agency on Aging, which is responsible for many different programs and services for senior citizens. The union representing workers in the area is considering filing a grievance because they claim the position was created to bypass the union by making it a political appointment.

headline: New Voice of the NRA Sounds Familiar
abstract: The NRA installed Charlton Heston as its new president and loudly applauded his pledge to steer the organization back to the political mainstream from what Heston described as the fringe of American life. The choice of Heston is in response to the public relations problems the NRA has been having. He has already attacked Clinton.

headline: Plan offers tax credit for charity support
abstract: Charitable donatuon to the poor, under new legislation, could qualify individuals for tax-credit and exemptions.

headline: AGH parent sells 6 losing hospitals in Philadelphia
abstract: Less than a month after assuring its Philadelphia employees that it remained committed to the Eastern Pennsylvania market, the parent of Allegheny General Hospital yesterday said it planned to sell six of its nine hospitals there to Vanguard Health Systems, an upstart for-profit health care company.  Pending board and regulatory approvals, Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation will sell all the hospitals acquired when it took over the struggling Graduate Health System in mid-1996 as well as two community hospitals it had acquired earlier.

headline: Officials, Fox push youth job programs
abstract: Us Representative Jon Fox said he is leading the charge in Washington to ensure restoration of a youth-oriented program to the federal budget. And the Montgomery County Commissioners have voted unanimously to urge Congress to continue funding the federal Summer Youth Employment and Training Program. The program targets 14 and 15 year olds who are too young to work in a private job sector job and low-income youth, who have limited opportunities.

headline: Year-round terms vary
abstract: Definitions outlined for the term year round education. The are an extended school year, a single track year-round school, and multi-track year-round school.

headline: Driving under the influence: current vs. proposed laws
abstract: List of proposed laws to stop drinking and driving.

headline: Amid profuse praise, Saylor sworn in to Supreme Court
abstract: Through more than a half-hour of glowing praise, Supreme Court Justice Thomas G. Saylor kept calm at his swearing in yesterday at The Forum.  Gov. Tom Ridge said it was a historic day for the Camp Hill native and the region.  The last mid-stater to win a Supreme Court election was former state House Majority Leader and Justice Herbert B. Cohen of York in 1957.

headline: Stiff penalities proposed for having gun in school
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher along with state lawmakers, seek to impose harsher penalities on juveniles who carry firearms onto school campuses, including felony and adult charges.

headline: Bank merger in U.S. fuels angry debate
abstract: Debate between lawmakers, bankers, and consumers continues as First Union Corp. plans a take over of CoreStates Corp.

headline: Casey Jr. visits the Valley
abstract: PA Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. visited the Lehigh Valley to endorse two Democratic candidates for the House, Steve Samuelson and Rich Grucela. He went door to door meeting with voters.

headline: Legislators' use of telemarketers raises concerns
abstract: Two years ago, PA House Republicans began a taxpayer-funded telemarketing program to call constituents, and the program has become so popular that House Democrats began their own telemarketing campaign. Lawmakers claim telemarketing is no different than sending out taxpayer-funded newsletters, and they claim the calls are strictly for government reasons, not for politics, and both parties agreed to end their programs 60 days before the election. However, critics believe the programs are being used as campaigning tools in an election year, and they provide an unfair advantage for incumbents.

headline: State GOP ads stir the 89th pot
abstract: The Bob Thomas campaign has gone where the Time Bittle campaign went two years ago. In an effort to unseat state Representative Jeff Coy, the Thomas campaign has enlisted the help of the Republican State Committee. The committee is running a television advertisement charging Coy with over stating his mileage on trips between his home and the Capitol to claim fatter reimbursement checks. Some call it negative campaigning others believe the ads address the issue of integrity.

headline: Not a lady in waiting - She finally collects her pageant title
abstract: After six months, Rita Roley will finally be awarded the title of Mrs. Pennsylvania. Rhonda Lewan had previously been awarded the title, but six contestants filed a lawsuit alleging the contest was rigged. The Lancaster Country District Attorney’s Office joined the investigation, and after filing criminal charges against the pageant’s director and others, Lewan gave up her crown.

headline: Property tax relief possible
abstract: If statelawmakers pass the porposed property tax reform bill, residents would get tax relief and school districts would change the way they collect taxes.

headline: AHERF files a bitter pill
abstract: The Allegheny Health Education and Research Foundation (AHERF) filed for federal bankruptcy protection from creditors that are owed an estimated $1.3 billion, and the filing could potentially cost jobs and raise health insurance premiums for insurance companies affiliated with AHERF. U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Bruce McCollough must decide whether to approve a proposed $502 million sale of AHERF’s Philadelphia hospitals to Vanguard Health Systems as well as $50 million in interim financing to help pay for immediate expenses, including payroll. A debt rating agency lowered the bond ratings for Allegheny General Hospital, which was not included in the bankruptcy filing, because creditors may seek money from the hospital to help recoup some losses, and the article provides a table of the creditors AHERF owes the most money.

headline: Panel approves plan to boost work force
abstract: The Workforce Deveolpment bill passed the House Intergovernmental Affairs Committee. The bill establishes a statewide council to oversee various job related programs.

headline: Yo, Philly: Dump the teachers; keep the cop
abstract: The author believes the city should renew the contract of Police Commissioner John Timoney, but it should replace District Schools Superintendant David Hornbeck. Both were hired to enact reforms; however, the author believes Timoney has worked well with both critics and supporters to enact serious reform that has made the city safer, whereas Hornbeck has alienated countless people and has yet to deliver better education for the city’s public school children. According to the author, Hornbeck’s battle with the PA Legislature put the district in the potential position of being taken over by the state, and the city’s next mayor will be unable to fix the school system with Hornbeck in charge.

headline: Drunken Driving Bill Endangered
abstract: When a proposal to create a national drunken driving standard was quietly strangled in a US House committee March 31, its advocates called the maneuver an outrage and said Republican leaders were doping the bidding of liquor and restaurant lobbyists. Backers of the new .08 standard were cheered, because the change had sailed through the Senate and had the President's backing. Reality is far more complex. The standard may have a hard time surviving. The .08 proposal makes states adhere to the .08 standard or lost 10% of their highway funding.

headline: An increase in Juvenile Crime
abstract: Though the nation's juvenile population increased by 10 percent between 1986 to 1996, the number of crimes committed by the same age group typically increased by a larger amount. And a graph shows the increase.

headline: Stop debating gun control and reduce gun violence
abstract: Too many people in our cities are dying from gun violence. Some people believe the primary reason for gun homicide is criminal misuse of guns and insufficient enforcement of current gun control laws. Something real must be done to reduce the mayhem. Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell and the NRA began to something last week. They pledged to work together to seek federal money to crack down on gun criminals in the city.

headline: Bank of New York makes $23 billion hostile bid for Mellon Bank
abstract: Bank of New York launched a $23.2 billion dollar hostile bid today for Mellon Bank Corp. The two sides had failed to negotiate a merger agreement. The proposed combined bank would be called Mellon Bank of New York and would have $106.4 billion dollars in combined assets. A merger would make them a bigger player in the banking industry, but the combined banks would still rank far behind some of those that would be created in a spate of deals announced earlier this month.

headline: Casey prepared for November battle
abstract: Democrat Patrick Casey vowed to fight Republican Don Sherwood "for every vote in every corner of the district" in the campaign for Congress. He is fighting for working families, for children, born and unborn, and for seniors.

headline: Lehigh commissioners elect Josephine Kraft to position
abstract: Lehigh County commissioners appointed Josephine Kraft of Salisbury Township as the commissioner from Distric 3. The Democratic Committee did not agree with the appointment.

headline: STATE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES - House will face tax reform, other key issues in '98
abstract: According to PA Representative Robert Godshall, the state House will tackle three major issues in the new legislative session, implementing local property tax reform, improving job training and rebuilding the state’s urban education system. In light of voters’ overwhelming support of the Homestead Amendment last November, Godshall said the House would search for property tax reform that would spread the burden of local taxes to all classes, and he also advocated changing the structure of Pennsylvania’s job training programs. State Representative Joseph Gladeck said the House would focus on implementing recommendations from a special Legislative Commission on Urban Education, and legislation allowing the privatization of small-scale liquor stores would be another priority.

headline: Packed Stadium
abstract: Forget baseball's spring training and college basketball's March Madness. Gus Felder and Southern Columbia football were the talk at the Capitol Building yesterday. Officials, about 20 of them, PA Interscholastic Athletic Association were in town. The House of Representatives question the PIAA members for three hours on high school sports.

headline: Putting state money to good use
abstract: For about a year, Pennsylvanians heard an ongoing debate about what to do with the large budget surplus that exists. While the gas tax and car registration were raised last year, the surplus sat waiting for a rainy day. For some, it was difficult to understand. For others it was an outrage. PA Governor Tom Ridge used the money allotted for the budget is productive ways when he raised the income level under which families owe no state income taxes.

headline: AHERF finds errors by auditors in '97 records
abstract: The parent foundation of Allegheny General Hospital yesterday said it has uncovered errors in its audited 1997 financial statements and that the statements are unreliable and shouldn't be used.  The disclosure came as the Allegheny Health Education and Research Foundation, along with its former outside auditors, are reviewing old financial statements for irregularities that may have presented a false picture of its financial condition.  So far, that review has found at least two discrepancies that boosted  the year foundation's bottom line in the fiscal year that ended June 30, 1997.

headline: Pennsylvanians limp ahead by 3 cents an hour in 8 years on job
abstract: PA worker's average wages adjusted for inflation, have climbed a miserly three cents per hour in eight years, says a new study that calls for new state policies to ensure prosperity is shared is more evenly. Wages were up last year for the second year in a row. The wage increases have been very small.

headline: null
abstract: According to PA Representative Tim Hennessey, Chester County residents can contact the state Department of Environmental Protection about the radon, a gas which is found in all PA counties and is known to cause lung cancer, by calling a toll free hotline.

headline: DUI cases need more help than prison provides
abstract: The sobering story of Curtis Ireland, the West View man has been convicted eight times of drunken driving, has inspired several makers to introduce a bill that would toughen punishments for drunken drivers. But harsher punishments address only part of the problem for people who are repeatedly caught drinking and driving. We need to help them with their alcohol addiction as well.

headline: Anguished wait
abstract: There are only three full time judges in Allegheny County's juveile court system. The judges have large caseloads and families are forced to wait hours and sometimmes days for their case to make it to a judge.

headline: Stop statutory rape
abstract: It's an important message in a dramatic package. The PA Coalition Against Rape is launching a controversial new public awareness campaign with the release of a compact disc featuring midstate musicians, a teen magazine, posters and Internet banners. The subject matter is statutory rape. The ads are being banned because people are made uncomfortable by the ads. Posters will appear on bus and subway stops.

headline: Bank takeover bill stalls in House
abstract: House Majority leader John Perzel does not call up to vote a bill to prevent Mellon Bank Corp. from a takeover. This bill has passed by a huge margin but does not seem likely to move out of the House.

headline: Casey: State health department has many flaws
abstract: In his first term Pennsylvania auditor general Robert P. Casey Jr. has tackled suspected waste, fraud and mismanagement.  He detailed his department’s  investigation into problems at nursing homes and its performance reviews of school districts and spoke about his future plans during an interview with Publisher Pamela Mayer; Editor Dave M. Levine; Pete Bosak, reporter: and Bruce Wissinger, editor of the editorial page.

headline: Lemmond Announces Re-election Bid
abstract: Republican PA Senator Charles Lemmond Jr. will seek reelection for a seat to represent the 20th senatorial district. He said that he will move forward on a number of different projects, and a top priority will be to continue to provide first-class constituent services to make government more accessible to the people of the district.

headline: State House Races Now Drawing Interest
abstract: Although much attention has been focused on PA Representative Anthony Hardy Williams, who is running to claim his recently retired father’s 8th Senatorial District seat, there are a number of interesting races developing for State House seats in the upcoming Democratic Primary. Representative James Roebuck and Representative Frank Oliver, who represent the 188th and 195th Districts, respectively, face stiff challengers. Representative Andrew Carn could be vulnerable in the 197th District, and several other races are briefly mentioned.

headline: PIAA finds ally in Hershey company
abstract: Jay Feaster, vice president of the Hershey Entertainment and Sports Company (HERCO), sent a letter to SportsFever publisher Gorden Blain to notify him that the company was pulling its advertising from the magazine because of Blain’s criticism of the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association (PIAA). Blain testified during the May 5 hearing before the Senate Special Committee on Interscholastic Athletics, which is expected to have a third hearing on the PIAA’s decision to move the state football finals from Altoona to Hershey. The committees chairman, Senator James Rhoads, is upset over the decision to pull the advertising, and Senators Robert Jubelirer and William Slocum are also mentioned in the article as not being pleased with actions undertaken by HERCO.

headline: Retirees oppose Ridge's tax reform bill
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge recently signed a new tax reform bill, Act 50, that the American Association of Retired Professionals says is unfair an creates a class welfare system.

headline: AHERF looks at sale, bankruptcy options
abstract: With its cash crisis growing worse by the day and pressure mounting to either sell its ailing Philadelphia operations or put them into bankruptcy, Allegheny General Hospital's parent foundation yesterday discussed new sale possibilities that could split the troubled institutions among several owners.  Along with Nashville-based Vanguard Health Systems Inc., the for-profit company that last month made a failed bid to acquire six of the Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation's nine Philadelphia hospitals, there are two nonprofit health care institutions discussing possible deals.

headline: Pitts, Specter at odds over Amish labor bill
abstract: Representative Joseph Pitts and Senator Arlen Spector have different views on a proposed bill to allow Amish youth to work in woodworking shops.

headline: 21st century report has 20th century woe
abstract: The 21st Century Environmental Commission decided to use a computer and a projector to present its report outlining key state environmental issues and 240 recommendations for solving them to the House Environmental Protection Committee, but unfortunately, there was a technological problem that forced the laptop’s screen to go dark. The state also awarded $500,000 in grants for youth mentoring programs.

headline: Endangered bat has I-99 extension on hold
abstract: Construction on I-99 extension has ben stopped after the Army Corps of Engineers noted an endagered species, the Indiana bat, resides in the area.

headline: Anti-pornography law will not change lives of county inmates
abstract: Governor Ridge signed a bill sponsored by PA Representative John Lawless which makes it illegal for inmates in PA’s state and county prisons to receive pornographic materials. According to a spokesman from the state Department of Corrections, prison censors will have to evaluate certain material on a case by case basis. Lawless was also angry that many prisons allow prisoners to purchase cable television, but Chester County Warden John Masters, who already does not permit pornography in his prison, has no plans to ban TV and will also continue to allow smoking in the prison.

headline: Study: Curfews do not reduce juvenile crime
abstract: Curfews have been touted as the solution to juvenile crime, but they actually have no effect on the rate according to a study by the Justice Policy Institute. Juvenile crime rate for misdemeanors and went up among white and Asian-American youth.

headline: Banks 'cry wolf' with ATM fee ban
abstract: Several years ago, banks across the nation adopted a new way of serving customers, a high-technology machine designed to make banking available to anyone at any time. Banks said they would save money by not having to employ as many bank tellers, but now they want to charge a ATM fee. The editorial board says Congress is calling the banks out and trying to ban ATM fees.

headline: Cash can buy air time, but not truth
abstract: According to State Democratic Leader Robert Mellow, Governor Ridge misled voters to believe that Pennsylvania’s economy was in terrible shape before being elected, and he took credit for cutting taxes that former Governor Casey actually signed into law. Mellow is especially critical of Ridge for misleading voters on the issue of jobs, and he cites a report from the Pittsburgh High Technology Council that portrays the job market much more differently than Ridge’s campaign commercials have done. Mellow also provides statistics on some critical areas where PA is not ranked particularly high nationally, and he says that he believes PA can do better than a governor who caters to big corporations while small businesses struggle.

headline: Levdansky keeps seat: Democratic incumbent champions numerous environmental issues
abstract: PA Representative David Levdansky was reelected to represent the 39th Legislative District over Republican challenger Gregory Ribovich. Levdansky made environmental issues a major concern and said he helped bring $30 million in funding to the district to help attract economic development.

headline: State interns get most from experiences: Summer assignments provide students access to different opportunities
abstract: Amanda Goodman, a communications major at Slippery Rock University, is an intern at the state Attorney General’s office, representing one of nearly 2,300 young people who spent the summer as interns throughout PA. These interns can provide students with valuable experience, and Representative John Gordner believes it’s mutually beneficial to have them on his staff. Over 2,000 interns worked for the various departments and agencies in the executive branch, there were 208 interns in legislators’ offices and the thirty six legal interns were the highest paid.

headline: State bans fund-raiser for 5 years
abstract: Soliciter company M. Charles Productions Inc. of Miami are banned from PA for 5 years, after misrepresenting informtion to solicit donations for police officers and firefighters.

headline: Rep. Shuster: Where in the world is America's economy?
abstract: Representative Bud Shuster writes to the Progress to let readers understand how the economy is growing.

headline: AHERF retrenches
abstract: Some of the uncertainty involving the Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation (AHERF) ended after it announced it would sell six of its nine Philadelphia-area hospitals to Vanguard Health Systems Inc. for $300 million. However, the authors claim AHERF still faces many challenges, especially from employees at Allegheny General Hospital in Pittsburgh, who feel AHERF tried to save the Philadelphia investments at their hospital's expense.  While the author’s believe tough challenges still remain, at least AHERF took a step in the right direction by announcing they would sell some of their Philadelphia-area hospitals.

headline: Scranton hospital workers vote on union
abstract: Approximately 1,400 employees of Mercy Hospital of Scranton took to the polls Wednesday to vote on whether or not they should unionize with District 1199P/Serivice Employees International Union, Pennsylvania's Health Care Workers' Union.  Mercy-Scranton's skilled maintenance workers voted by a 24-6 margin to organize the union, according to a press release issued by District 1199P/SEIU.  Nearly 1,300 ballots, representing the votes of the majority of the hospital workforce, were impounded without being counted as a result of the Hospital's appeal.

headline: A lush renewal for Pa. forests.  Forests ravaged by logging are rejuvenated. Animals are back. Can they survive new threats?
abstract: By the early 20th century, settlers had depleted much of the forests across Northern PA and the Northeast, which also caused the populations of a number of species to dwindle; however, the human population in many areas began decreasing, and both the forests and many of the original species have made remarkable comebacks in the region. Unfortunately, there are many other species that aren’t thriving, and there are still many serious challenges to the wellbeing of the forests and other wildlife, including acid rain, development, logging, climate change, insects and the deer population, which many worry is growing too high. Increasingly, loggers are using more sustainable logging practices, and PA has the most environmentally certified forest land in the nation, yet there are still millions of acres of unprotected land.

headline: Engineer sees bridge at its worst
abstract: Pennsylvania Department of Transportation views problem bridges that need repairs.

headline: Art earns Lykens 5th-grader a cover
abstract: Jill Adley wins a $500 bond, lunch with Attorney General Mike Fisher, and her drawing is the cover for a new campaign to "Team Up Against Drugs."

headline: Supreme Court's moderate 'gentleman' Powell dies at 90
abstract: Retired US Supreme Court justice Lewis Powell died at the age of 90, after serving 15 years as a moderate on the Supreme Court. President Clinton said of Powell that he approached each case without an ideological agenda. Chief Justice William Rehnquist called Powell the very embodiment of justice. Powell sat on the Bakke "reverse discrimination case" which instituted affirmative action.

headline: Banks don't need added protection
abstract: A propsed bill, with bank taveove guidelines takes critcism as an attempt to micro-manage business.

headline: Cash-rich Gov. Ridge has cash bar in victory
abstract: After his unchallanged primary victory, Govenor Ridge hosted a party at a pizza parlor where only pizza and soda was free; all other items had to purchased by induividuals.

headline: Lewinsky toll sparks heightened concerns among Democrats
abstract: House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt said that while Clinton’s actions involving his relationship with Monica Lewinski were wrong, he preferred not to make any judgments on impeachment until after Democratic leaders had a chance to review Independent Counsel Kenneth Starr’s report. After seven months of claiming he didn’t have a sexual relationship with Lewinski, Clinton admitted to an inappropriate relationship with her and called to end the controversy; however, Gephardt’s comments suggest Democrats will follow Starr’s report over what the President says. The Democratic Party is also trying to distance itself form President Clinton in the upcoming election, where they need 11 seats to retake the House.

headline: State lawmakers do holiday grab
abstract: Editors blame perks for the reason why politicians have poor reputations. Per diems given to lawmakers were tied to an amount determined by the US General Services Administration. The rate has been decreased from $108 to $80. In the US Senate, a loophole in an IRS code will allow Senators to collect up to $113. The taxpayers are going to be the ones closing the spending gap in this case.

headline: State stops God scam
abstract: PA Attorney General's office wants to ban Florida based Global Ministries from promoting their investmet progrma in the state. It appears that the program is a religious twist to a Ponzi Scheme.

headline: Ridge demands taxpayer approval of reform bill
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge pledges to veto tax reform bills that do not have provision to allow the oublic to vote on them twice.

headline: AHERF's auction: Eight Philadelphia hospitals are unloaded in fire sale
abstract: U.S. Bankruptcy Court tentatively approved a deal for Tenet Healthcare Corp. to purchase eight Philadelphia hospitals from the Allegheny Health Education and Research Foundation (AHERF), but the money will only bring in $345 million towards the $1.5 billion which is owed to creditors. While much uncertainty still remains for the Philadelphia hospitals and AHERF’s remaining Pittsburgh hospitals, the authors of the article believe the sale, at the very least, will allow AHERF to concentrate on fixing the remainder of its system. The authors believe that competition provided by AHERF hospitals in Pittsburgh is good for the community, and they claim more public oversight over health care decisions is necessary in the future.

headline: SEPTA and union on the outs at visit's brink - The Democratic Convention site selectors arrive tomorrow. A feud of the two sides may imperil a deal.
abstract: Two months after the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority and the Transport Workers Union reached a tentative contract agreement that ended a 40-day strike, the two sides are still fighting over details of the contract, and the union has threatened to picket the Democratic National Committee’s convention site-selection team when it arrives tomorrow. Both the Republican and Democratic National Committees are considering Philadelphia for their national conventions in 2000; however, Democrats cut their previous visit short because of the strike, while the union took no action during the Republicans second visit. The union and SEPTA are arguing over worker-compensation benefits and the hiring of part-time workers, and Mayor Ed Rendell has refused to get involved this time.

headline: A Vigil for Victims   Group highlights the dangers of polluted environs
abstract: The Alliance for a Clean Environment (ACE) sponsored a candlelight vigil as part of the national "Day of Action," which is commemorating the 20th anniversary of Love Canal, where local residents suffered from a number of different diseases caused by a toxic waste site and were eventually evacuated by the government. ACE is fighting against Waste Management Company, and it wants the state Department of Health as well the Montgomery County Department of Health to conduct more thorough studies on the effects of Waste Management’s Pottstown landfill. ACE’s president cited a study which found the areas surrounding the landfill have significantly higher rates of several different types of cancer, and parents of children who died or are suffering from serious illnesses believed to be environmentally caused also spoke at the vigil.

headline: Exit 12 project ditched
abstract: The improvement project for Exit 12 on Interstate 81 has fallen through, and the financial backers of the project have pulled out for now.

headline: Ask and you shall be arrested
abstract: Walk into any PA county courthouse and you can discover how much your neighbor paid for his house, whether he pays taxes, is divorced or ever inherited any money. But ask if he is licensed to carry a gun and you could be arrested. Last April, the PA General Assembly passed a bill that contained a little-noticed amendment to the 1995 firearms law that makes it a felony for anyone to request from state police or county sheriffs any information contained in concealed weapons permits. A second amendment levies a $1,000 or more in civil damages and attorneys fees against anyone involved in transferring information about licensed gun owners. The bill and amendment escaped the notice of journalists, gun control advocates and even some lawmakers.

headline: Surprising turn in bid to widen police hiring
abstract: Since John Timoney became the Commissioner of the Philadelphia Police Department, he has been asking to search for policemen outside the city; however, there is a city regulation that requires a civil-service employee must reside in Philadelphia for at least one year before they can begin working. The City Council was considering taking action to allow Timoney to search military bases to recruit police officers, but it was pointed out that the Civil Service Commission can enact the action on its own by a simple vote. City Personnel Director Linda Seya will recommend the military exemption to the Commission, and they will almost certainly approve it.

headline: Bethlehem Steel boosts its offer for Lukens
abstract: Bethlehem Steel Corp struck back boosting its offer for Lukens Inc by 20 percent in a takeover battle for the nation's oldest continuously operated steel firm. The $30-a-share offer, with a total value of $740 million, is the third for the Coatesville steelmaker since mid-December. The $30 would be paid in cash and stock. The takeover fight shows how vigorously US Steel companies are responding to the worldwide economic forces reshaping their fragmented industry.

headline: Cawley Earns Gift with Kindness
abstract: Democrat state Representative. Gaynor Cawley is just about certain that he will be elected to a 10th two-year term this year. He has no opponent, but his campaign manager wants him to be elected as the Republican nominee as well ensuring he will have no opponent.

headline: License bill to prickly, say tattooists, piercers
abstract: PA Representative Anthony DeLuca introduced legislation that would require all body-piercing and tattoo parlors to be licensed and regulated by the state, but 75 parlors joined the PA Coalition of Professional Tattooists and Body Piercers to oppose the bill. DeLuca said he wants greater regulation to ensure diseases aren’t transmitted through unsafe needle use; however, members of the coalition said the industry already regulates itself to ensure cleanliness, and several members expressed concerns about the possibility of facing increased taxes as well as the bill’s ambiguous language. In addition, members said they were concerned about a provision banning facial tattoos, and the coalition’s president plans to meet with state Senator Clarence Bell to discuss the bill.

headline: State Legislators To Blame for High Teachers' Salaries
abstract: The giant increase in teachers salaries is not entirely the teachers fault. The state legislators in Harrisburg are also to blame.

headline: The Harley Boys
abstract: The photo depicts Governor Tom Ridge with Wisconsin Governor Tommy Thompson. Thompson is riding to York, PA, to celebrate the 95th anniversary of the Harley-Davidson company.

headline: Ridge proposal will help rival: Luksik can expect income tax cut
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge has proposed a tax emption policy that would benefit Peg Luksik, who won 13 percent of the 1994 gubernatorial vote as the Constitutional Party candidate. His proposal would exempt families from paying the 2.8 percent state income tax if their income is less than their total tax credits, which would apply to Luksik’s family. Luksik said she was glad to get the tax cut, but it wouldn’t change her plans, and she still expects to run for governor this year.

headline: Aid sought for center's patients   Lawmaker says state doing 'terrible job' with released mentally retarded
abstract: PA Representative Leo Trich heard testimony about the difficulties former residents of Western Center, an institution for the mentally retarded that is set to be closed, encounter while trying to integrate into community living, and he introduced a bill that would require any facility that treats the mentally retarded to notify the state when a patient is moved to another address. State Representative Russell Fairchild is heading a House task force that offered a number of proposals pertaining to care for the mentally disabled, and the County Commissioners Association is trying to temporarily bring a halt to discharges from the Western Center. While Trich, Fairchild and many county commissioners are concerned that mental health patients are being released into the community before they’re ready, many mental health advocates oppose their proposals, and the state Department of Public Welfare has said that Western Center is still set to close.

headline: SEPTA, union trade accusation - State Rep. Dwight Evans said parties were not far apart. A strike threatened Monday.
abstract: Officials for the Transport Workers Union Local 234 and the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority both blamed each other in press conferences for the breakdown in contract negotiations, which haven’t taken place for nine days. The union has threatened to strike if it doesn’t receive a new contract shortly. At a union press conference, PA Representative Dwight Evans urged SEPTA to demonstrate greater flexibility, citing a union analysis reporting the difference between each side’s contract proposal is only $12 million, which SEPTA’s chief labor strategist denied.

headline: Abandoned factory to become golf course
abstract: Transit America Inc. will turn an abandoned factory site, which is located on 214 acres of land between Northeast Philadelphia and Lower Moreland Township, into an 18-hole public golf course. The PA Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) is pleased that the site is going to be cleaned up, and it benefits the company because it gets out of its environmental liability problem. The agreement between the two was made possible by the DEP’s Land Recycling Program, which helps recycle land by freeing industries from the liability of purchasing polluted land.

headline: Faded plates may be replaced - State official says peeling tags give a rustbelt image to Pa.
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation is considering a proposal to require a new license plate reissuance for all vehicles with pre-1987 plates. Proponents claim fading license plates are difficult for police officers to read, and according to Eric Bugaile, director of the House Transportation Committee, these old license plates can present a bad image of the state. Transportation officials estimate PA has between 600,000 and 800,000 vehicles with tags between 10 and 20 years old, and they are considering whether motorists should be charged for new plates; though they are leaning towards reissuing them for free.

headline: At Graterford Prison, art therapy turns cells into studios
abstract: For the last eight years, art therapy has been taught to inmates at Graterford Prison by Will Ursprung, the only certified art therapist working within the PA prison system. Some of the inmates in the article have learned to channel their emotions into their artwork and have learned to express themselves in healthy ways. There is now an exhibit of their artwork on display at Ursinus College, and inmates can either give their artwork to family or sell it to pay for more supplies.

headline: Survey studies crime at public schools: Only 10% reported serious violence in first-of-its-kind national report
abstract: President Clinton will release the first-ever national estimate of crime and violence in schools, which was produced from surveys of 1,200 public schools by the National Center on Education Statistics. 57 percent of schools reported crimes committed on school grounds, and 10 percent reported serious crimes, including 4,100 rapes or sexual assaults, 7,100 robberies and 11,000 fights with weapons. The rate of serious crimes seems small since there are 54 million students in public schools, and when compared to national studies on crime, schools appear safer than the neighborhoods they are located in.

headline: Bidding war
abstract: Terms of the offers for Lukens Inc by Bethlehem Steel and Allegheny Teledyne including total price, price per share, businesses to be combined, businesses to be sold or closed, layoffs expected, and operating savings after merger.

headline: Census update shows Pa. may lose 2 House seats
abstract: The 2000 census may show statistic that will cause Pennsylvania to losse 2 congressional house seats, as southern states will probably gain those seats.

headline: Most of state's congressmen fail to answer issues survey
abstract: Project Vote Smart sent out its biennial survey, which asks candidates from around the country to answer questions pertaining to a number of important issues, but the group’s president, Richard Kimball, said he was worried about what’s going on in PA because only 53 percent of that state’s congressional candidates returned the survey before the deadline. U.S. Representative William Coyne did not fill it out, U.S. Senator Arlen Specter said he’s in the process of filling it out and U.S. Representatives Chaka Fattah and Robert Borski completed the survey. Only seven of the state’s twenty congressional incumbents filled it out, and while Governor Ridge and his challenger Ivan Itkin completed the survey, only 30 percent of the candidates for the PA General Assembly responded.

headline: State of covered bridges
abstract: A new House bill would provide Pennslyvania with funding to protect and preseve historical covered bridges.

headline: Ridge seeks tax cuts for businesses
abstract: PA Governor Ridge proposed a $17.8 billion spending plan for the next fiscal year the cuts taxes for business and the state's poorest workers and increases funding for education. It does not bail out the financially strapped Philadelphia School District, which is facing a $140 million short fall. Buoyed by an election-year surplus, the governors proposal would modestly boost funding in many programs, such as welfare-to-work programs. Past budgets have cut funding for welfare, but that is absent this time.

headline: AIDS and Medicaid
abstract: Anna Forbes, from Working Groups on HealthChoice and HIV, thanks the Inquirer for news coverage on PA's lack of Medicaid coverage for HIV/AIDS infected people.

headline: Severance pay should not be taxed
abstract: PA Representative Louise Bishop of Philadelphia, introduced legislation which would exempt the severance pay of workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own from the state income tax. It is intelligent and compassionate legislation that provides assistance to people who lose their jobs because of layoffs caused by the current trends or corporate mergers and downsizing. They need financial help.

headline: Airport tries hunt to end deer problem
abstract: There was a controlled hunt that killed three deer and caused at least two deer to run out of an opened gate at Wilkes-Barre/Scranton International Airport. Airport officials had the hunt and repaired holes in the surrounding fence because planes have struck two deer in the past month. Airport officials have also contacted the federal Department of Agriculture for advice, and Letter for Animals, which writes letters to defend animal rights, was displeased with the killings.

headline: Family sues over Swinick gas sickness
abstract: A Dunmore family is suing PA Department of Transportation after being sickened by carbon monoxide. The family claims that the PennDOT blasting of the Lackawanna Valley Industrial Highway caused the sickness.

headline: Attempt to plug loophole draws fire
abstract: Mark Titus was a dangerous man in the yes of Luzerne County prosecutors. The convicted rapist had previously served time for arson and simple assault, and prosecutor Ingrid Cronin wanted him evaluated as a sexuality violent predator under PA's Megan Law. But Titus never faced a predator hearing because of a legal technicality. In fact the vast majority of current prisoners never faced it.

headline: Switching sides   Federal agents sometimes fall prey to the lurid lifestyles of their informants
abstract: The article describes several cases in which federal agents used informants to obtain information on criminals; however, these agents often ignored the crimes of their informants, offered them protection in return for information and in some cases even engaged in criminal behavior themselves. While the article describes a number of agents from the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) whose use of informants could be considered highly unethical, if not illegal, the article’s main story focuses on FBI Special Agent Lindley DeVecchio. DeVecchio used Gregory Scarpa Sr., one of New York’s most ruthless gangsters, as an informant, and DeVecchio is accused of fabricating evidence against Scarpa’s enemies, ignoring murders, accepting gifts from Scarpa and actively protecting him from being arrested for his crimes.

headline: Bill would allow cider to flow: Lawmakers are considering law changes to allow hard cider to be sold like beer.
abstract: The PA House approved a bill to change the legal classification of cider from a wine to a malt or brewed beverage, which would change the tax rate on cider and allow it to be sold in beer stores and taverns. The Independent State Store Union is trying to prevent Governor Ridge from privatizing state liquor stores, and it sees this legislation as a step in that direction. The bill awaits the Senate’s vote, and it was first introduced by Senator David Brightbill at the request of Stroh Brewery Company, owner of the Woodchuck cider brands.

headline: CITIZENSHIP AWARD
abstract: The photo depicts Floyd Zimmerman, the recipient of the Tamaqua Area Chamber of Commerce’s annual Citizenship Award. The photo also includes four other individuals, including PA Representative David Argall, who made a special presentation to Zimmerman.

headline: Livingston Seals Speakership Bid
abstract: U.S. Representative Bob Livingston’s only competitor to become speaker, Christopher Cox, dropped out of the race, so Livingston will almost certainly succeed Newt Gingrich, and in the Senate, Assistant Majority Leader Don Nickles vowed not to challenge Majority Leader Trent Lott. Other leading House Republicans, including Majority Leader Richard Armey and Conference chairman John Boehner, are fighting off challengers emboldened by the party’s disappointing showing in last week’s congressional elections. Livingston met with Armey, but he refused to endorse anyone for the majority leadership position, and despite challenges from Steve Largent, Jennifer Dunn and possibly Howard McKeon, Armey remains confident that he will be re-elected when House Republicans meet next week to choose their new leaders.

headline: State of indecision: Puerto Rico is not ready to become a state
abstract: The authors of the editorial claim that Puerto Rico is not ready to become a state despite the efforts of its governor, Pedro Rossello, who has been lobbying for statehood in Congress. The authors believe Congress is rightfully hesitant to allow its statehood because it would more likely than not put a huge burden on the federal government to raise standards up to those of other states. In addition, the authors claim that residents of the island rejected statehood in two nonbinding votes and don’t want to risk losing their culture and language by assimilating into the mainland.

headline: Ridge to add extra budget initiatives
abstract: When PA Governor Tom Ridge unveils his budget proposal, it will include new funding for food banks for the poor, a $39 million to start unifying the state court system. These are in addition to $147 million targeted tax cuts and program expansions Ridge previously announced.

headline: All must work for health-care parity
abstract: PA Representative Nicholas Micozzie, who is also chairman of the state insurance committee, is writing in response to a letter written by Mary Rehrman, director of policy for the Alliance for the Mentally Ill of PA, in which she criticized Micozzie and his committee for not passing legislation that would provide the same health coverage for mental illness that is covered for physical illness. Micozzie cites numerous attempts by his committee to hold public hearings and introduce bills that address the issue to offer full parity for those suffering from mental illness. Micozzie asks Rehrman to take a role in the process, while also claiming that it is his duty to evaluate policy to try to make sure that quality health care is accessible and affordable to all Pennsylvanians.

headline: Shipyard College willl open to banking workers
abstract: Shipyard College Gateway Project is created to assist employees who will lose their jobs as a result of CoreStates Corp being purchased by First Union Corp. Funding is being provided by First Union Corp.

headline: Arsenal of gear helps officer keep poachers in his sights
abstract: Despite patrols and high-tech equipment, Mike Doherty, a Chester County Game Commission officer, said that his most important tool for stopping poachers, which he describes in practical terms as anyone who hunts illegally, is people who call in to report illegal hunting activity. Last year, Chester County racked up 178 prosecutions against violators of hunting laws; however, Doherty said that poachers are still winning and must be stopped to protect the safety of humans and deer. Doherty is trying to work closer with local law enforcement agencies, and he urges people who witness illegal hunting to call immediately.

headline: Farm, Highway Bills Erode GOP Unity
abstract: In this election year, Republicans are experiencing difficulties uniting. A landmark $216 million transportation bill that was passed was diminished by the fight over a smaller $2 billion bill that would use savings in the food-stamp program to provide needed crop-insurance money and restore nutrition benefits for legal immigrants cut from welfare rolls last spring. The result was embarrassing for Majority Leader Dick Armey. An 11th hour bid allowed the provision to be stricken. President Clinton supports the transportation bill despite its reputation as pork barrel spending.

headline: Attorney contests tobacco settlement
abstract: A Kansas lawyer is challenging a provision in the recent $206 billion settlement with the tobacco industry that can prevent the public from knowing how much lawyers are being paid who worked on the case. However, PA Attorney General Mike Fisher released the state’s contract with two law firms. The contracts will split $50 million from the settlement between the two firms, and although the amount is far less than what some attorneys are asking for in other states, Governor Ridge and some others have questioned Fisher.

headline: Tackling Domestic Violence from a Different Angle
abstract: A personal story of dometic abuse from the victim's perspective;  facts and Statisics on the current domestice violence situation.

headline: Bills ante up against online gambling
abstract: A the online kitty for bettors and bookmakers piled up, the Pennsylvania Legislature put its cards on the table last week and joined an expanding crackdown on Internet gambling. Two bills proposed by Republican Reps. Thomas Gannon of Delaware County and Paul Clymer of Bucks County, would give state law enforcement authorities jurisdiction to go after online wagering.  Both have the support of Attorney General Mike Fisher.

headline: CITY CORPS - Republicans seek to free local agencies from red tape to fight urban decay
abstract: The authors of the editorial claim the nation’s cities have faced serious challenges, and efforts to revive them have provided no surefire solutions. The authors are pleased that Republicans in Congress, including U.S. Representatives Joseph Pitts and Phil English, have come together to form the Renewal Alliance to search for ways to help cities; however, they hope the group avoids the issue of public funding for private-school students. The authors agree that strong local leadership is extremely important, and while improvements still need to be made in Harrisburg, they praise Mayor Stephen Reed for the progress that’s been made.

headline: Lobby reform in limbo
abstract: A bill to toughen lobbying reporting requirements is not considered during the House summer session and may not be cosidered in the Fall.

headline: State of Union-Pa.
abstract: The article provides quotes from U.S. Representatives Jon Fox, Ron Klink, Paul McHale, Joseph Pitts and Bud Shuster, who all represent PA in the U.S. House. The comments are in response to the president’s State of the Union address.

headline: Ridge's budget loosens fiscal screws
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge proposed a $17.8 billion state budget for 1998-1999 that boosts funding in many areas, from basic education to children's health programs to various business initiatives. The budget would boost the state Collections Department over the billion-dollar mark for the first time and would send nearly $1 million to the city of Harrisburg for fire protection of the Capitol complex.

headline: Allegheny in turmoil: The causes, the diagnosis, the treatment and the aftershocks
abstract: Once touted as the largest healthcare system on the East Coast with a value of $5 billion, its nine hospitals in the Philadelphia region are now valued at $502 million by Vanguard Health System.  The remaining debt will be tied up in bankruptcy court in Pittsburgh, affecting tens of thousands of lives and businesses for years to come.  Many are the suspects: the board of trustees and former chief executive officer Sherif S. Abdelhak, whose buying binge of hospitals and medical practices proved to be the wrong strategy and the wrong time.

headline: Significant impact of job loss expected
abstract: The takeover of CoreStates Corp. by First Union Corp. is anticipated to bring huge job loss for CoreStaes employees.

headline: Baltimore wants 50 million gallons daily from watershed  Nuclear plant, Susquehanna fish could be harmed
abstract: The city of Baltimore is expected to ask the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, which regulates the use of water from the river, for permission to pump 50 million gallons of water a day out of the Susquehanna River above the Conowingo Dam. However, the Peach Bottom Nuclear Power Plant could be forced to close if that withdrawal resulted in the water level dropping 8 feet in an area known as the Conowingo pool. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is also concerned about the proposal's impact on aquatic life, especially the American shad fish, and over 25 people will testify on behalf of several different PA agencies at the proposal’s hearing.

headline: Farmers: Keep the Bridge
abstract: Franklin County Farmers passed a resolution to oppose the demolition of Walker Road Bridge.

headline: Attorneys general press to settle tobacco-industry lawsuits
abstract: State Attorney Generals seek damages from the tobacco industry's commercial advertising practices. Pa could get as much as $11 billion in damages.

headline: Tattoo Youths
abstract: In Pennsylvania, it’s illegal to tattoo anyone under 18 without parental consent.  Commercial tattoo parlors abide by the law, but many teens get around it by hiring tattoo artists to come to their homes.  The law is not widely enforced because not many cases are reported, which may be attributed to the fact that most parents are not aware of the law.

headline: Bills ante up against online gambling
abstract: Two bills proposed by Republican Reps. Thomas Gannon and Paul Clymer, would give state law enforcement authorities jurisdiction to go after online wagering. Clymer's bill focuses on operators, authorizing the state to charge businesses that accept bets over the Internet with a first-degree misdemeanor. Gannon's bill would make it a summary offense to place wagers over the Internet.

headline: City grows lax on rules spurred by Abscam - Officials have to report sources of income. Some failed to meet this year's deadline.
abstract: After the 1980’s Abscam bribery scandal involving three City Council members and two local congressmen, officials toughened the city’s ethics code and requirements for full disclosure of outside incomes. However, the Board of Ethics has become increasingly less active in enforcing these rules, and six Council members and two of Mayor Ed Rendell’s key administrators failed to disclose their outside financial interests this year. Ethics Board chairman Mark Aronchick said activity has declined largely due to Rendell’s executive order prohibiting employees from accepting gifts from individuals who conduct business with the city, and he said the city solicitor is better prepared to advise city employees on legal issues.

headline: Lobby reform law in limbo   House majority leader sees little chance of vote
abstract: PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer sponsored one of the Senate’s top priorities, a lobby reform law, and it overwhelmingly passed the Senate in March; however, House Majority Leader John Perzel indicated that it would be unlikely for the House to vote on the bill until after the summer recess, much to the dismay of reform groups. Lobbying is an estimated $80 million industry, but Pennsylvania’s lobbyist disclosure requirements are considered among the weakest in the nation, so only $600,000 in spending was reported last year. The bill would toughen reporting requirements and increase violation penalties, and State Representatives Al Masland and Paul Clymer both hope the bill will be voted on as soon as possible.

headline: State official urges townships to participate in 2000 census
abstract: James Lombardo of the PA Department of Community and Economic Development addressed the Lawrence County Association of Township Officials, and he urged them to participate in the 2000 census to ensure all municipalities are counted correctly and receive their fair share of federal funding. James Wheeler of the PA State Association of Township Supervisors also addressed the crowd, and he explained why they should oppose House Bill 1173, which would establish a statewide building code, and why they should support pending legislation that would prevent frivolous lawsuits from being filed against governing bodies. State Representative Frank LaGrotta, who voted to pass a tax reform bill expected to be signed by Governor Tom Ridge, explained his disappointment upon realizing the bill will only help school districts.

headline: Robust job growth returns unemployment rate to 24-year low
abstract: Robust job growth fueled by low interest rates and mild winter weather returned that nation's unemployment rate to a 24-year low of 4.6 percent in February. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declined from 4.7 percent in January and December the lowest since October 1973 the US Labor Department said.

headline: Allegheny leaders shifted millions from endowments
abstract: In the months before the Allegheny health system put its Philadelphia operations in bankruptcy, its executives removed millions of dollars from restricted medical endowments.  And no one is saying where it went.  Allegheny officials in Philadelphia withdrew money from several funds restricted for research, education and patient care because their system was floundering and they had nowhere else to turn for cash, according to interviews with Allegheny administrators, researchers and physicians.

headline: State presents grant to county labor-management committee
abstract: PA Labor and Industry Secretary Johnny Butler presented a $40,000 grant on Governor Ridge’s behalf to the Westmoreland County Area Labor-Management Committee. Statistics show improved labor-management relations have resulted in the lowest number of labor disputes since 1970, and injuries have fallen substantially. Butler praised the work of the Labor-Management Committee for its work in improving labor-management cooperation.

headline: Bay Governors Differ on Waste Limits
abstract: Virginia Governor James Gilmore, Washington D.C. Mayor Marion Barry, Maryland Governor Parris Glendering, PA Governor Tom Ridge and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency signed an agreement at the Baltimore Aquarium which calls for a number of new initiatives aimed at cleaning up the Chesapeake Bay. Gilmore said that voluntary cooperative efforts should be sufficient, whereas Glendering has been a proponent of mandatory regulations. Despite optimistic speeches, officials acknowledged that several key goals set the year before will not be met due to constant increases in population growth and automobile use.

headline: Fatalies
abstract: Number of motor vehicle deaths among US teens

headline: Author denies manipulating Smith trial
abstract: Former convicted murderer Jay Smith sues the state police and prosecution for illegaly handeling his case. They are accussed of having a book deal in the works with Joseph Wambaugh, who testifies at the civil trial.

headline: Teen birth rates fall
abstract: Teen birth rates and pregnancies have dropped sharply throughout the 1990’s as educational, abstinence, and contraceptive campaigns seem to be taking hold, government health officials said.  The rate of girls ages 15-19 giving birth declined by nearly 12 percent nationally from 1991 to 1996, the National Center for Health Statistics reported; Allegheny County’s teen birth rate dropped by 15 percent in the same period, from 38.6 births for every 1,000 to 33 births.  The improvements we especially striking among black females, though they still stand a much greater likelihood than whites of becoming young mothers.

headline: Bob Uguccioni reappointed as vice chair of Governor's Travel and Tourism Council
abstract: PA Governor Tom Ridge announced the reappointment of Robert Uguccioni, executive director of the Poconos Mountains Vacation Bureau Inc as vice chair of the Governor's Travel and Tourism council, a public-private advisory group the advises him on tourism issues and provides him with policy input. Advisory functions include marketing, hospitality, cultural tourism, communication, development of policy, event financing and targeting and coordination of the state infrastructure.

headline: City, auditor general resolve pension fund dispute
abstract: Auditor Genral Robert Casey and the City of Erie, PA have resolved a dispute. The auditor general's office threatened to withhold state pension funds for the city of Erie if the city did not follow state law about pension dispersment.

headline: Lobbyist law tougher, will track money trail
abstract: A lobbying reform bill signed by PA Gov. Tom Ridge will shift oversight of the industry from the General Assembly to an independent State Ethics Commission. PA is regarded as having the nation's most lax attitude towards lobbying. Now lobbyists must report whom and what they are attempting to influence. Robert Stern of the Center for Government Studies says PA doesn't score well on detailed reporting of restrictions and gifts. Common Cause praises the law. Former senator David Heckler, who resigned after being elected Bucks County judge, was on hand to watch Ridge sign the bill into law.

headline: State Panel to Conduct Hearing Here
abstract: The PA House Intergovernmental Affairs Committee will hold a public hearing on proposed workforce-development legislation. House Bill 1800, sponsored by PA Representative Robert Flick proposes to revamp the workforce-development system to raise performance standards and improve efficiency.

headline: Shoppers don't buy into the use tax - Sales-tax free Delaware is a haven for out-of-state bargain hunters. But Pa. and N.J. are missing the money, and more
