abstract: Countless shoppers cross the border into Delaware from New Jersey, PA and other surrounding states because Delaware doesn’t have a sales-tax, and while all purchasers are technically supposed to reimburse their home state for a use-tax, most don’t realize the tax exists or choose to ignore it. Delaware promotes its sale-tax free status to lure shoppers, and the survival of many businesses in the state depend on selling tax-free merchandise, yet their business is costing PA and New Jersey millions of dollars a year. A spokesman for the PA Department of Revenue admitted there’s not much they can do to collect on use-taxes; however, tax officials in states that do impose a sales tax are lobbying Congress to make it easier for them to collect revenue.

headline: Allegheny looks for financing in N.Y.
abstract: The chief executive officer of the Allegheny health system, Anthony Sanzo, was in the New York area yesterday looking for financing that could make or break a deal to rescue the system's failing Philadelphia-area operations.  In a meeting that could decide the fate of their eastern holdings, Allegheny board members in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia are scheduled to hold a joint meeting today over a video network linking the system's two main headquarters.  High on the agenda will be an offer from Vanguard Health Systems Inc. to buy all nine Allegheny hospitals in the Philadelphia region.

headline: Unions help build the boom
abstract: After seven years of economic hardships, the Philadelphia area’s construction industry is headed towards one of its best building seasons ever, and according to the business manager for the Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council, all 70,000 union members will be fully employed for at least the next eight months. While the boom can be partially attributed to the surging economy, labor and management officials claim responsibility for being more aggressive in pursuing new construction projects and more cooperative with business and political leaders in bringing new businesses to the region. In addition, unions have adopted a new drug and alcohol testing program, offered more training opportunities, accepted many new members, increased productivity and reduced injury rates.

headline: Beauty or the Beast?
abstract: How you feel about the whitetail deer probably determines whether you think it's a problem, and, if it is, the type of solution you favor to correct it.  Officials at the state Game Commission and those responsible for maintaining parks in various parts of the commonwealth certainly agree there is an overabundance of deer.  And even if you don't agree with them, one chance meeting between your car and a deer on some dark road late at night can be enough to change your mind in a hurry.

headline: Fatalities rose under Pa.'s 65 mph speed limit
abstract: According to PA Department of Transportation records, traffic fatalities increased by 13 percent when the speed limit was raised to 65 mph. PA Sen. Roy Afflerbach voted against the initial increase in 1995, arguing it would cause motorists to increase their own personal speed limit. However PennDOT Secretary Brad Mallory is satisfied with the results of the increase. Ted Leonard, general manager of the PA AAA Federation also believes the results are positive. Fred Straub, a member of the Central PA Chapter of the American Society of Safety Engineers opposed the increase.

headline: 'Bad law' in Pa. looks to have only a short life - A change in divorce and support rules was a mistake, and it could be reversed this week.
abstract: The PA Legislature passed a bill containing a three-word change that gives courts the power to lessen or halt financial awards in divorce cases if either spouse has a sexual affair after the couple separated. However, state Representative Stanley Saylor claims he wrote the bill to prevent victims of domestic violence from having to pay alimony to their abusers, and he never intended the bill to apply to extramarital affairs. State Representative Joseph Corpora had previously questioned Saylor about the bill’s language, though it was never changed, and Saylor has now agreed to change the wording of the bill to fix the problem.

headline: Teen drinking
abstract: Number of US teens who had five or more drinks in a row during the two weeks prior to this 1996 survey.

headline: Boeing jobs fly to U.K.
abstract: Ridley township will see more than 400 Boeing jobs move overseas to Britian. More job loss is expected by the end of 1999.

headline: Clinton ads by GOP seen as big gamble
abstract: This is the midterm congressional election that once was billed as offering Democrats a shot at taking back the House. Then it was going to be a Republican blowout because of President Clinton's affair. Republicans started making big plans if they could get a filibuster proof majority. Then the Democrats earned sympathy for the intense investigations by Republicans. Now no one knows which way the election will fall.

headline: Lobbyists politicked for AMP
abstract: When now House Maj. Leader John Perzel was first elected as such, he scheduled a meeting with the region's largest employer, AMP Inc. He was curtly told AMP had no need for state government relations. It is ironic now, that AMP CEO Robert Ripp was rebuffed by Perzel when he attempted to seek state legislation to strengthen antiprotection legislation to fend off a takeover of AMP by AlliedSignal Inc. Legislation successfully passed the Senate, but was crippled by an amendment in the House after intense lobbying efforts.

headline: State races in county, but none for Pitts, Gekas
abstract: Six of Lancaster County’s lawmakers in the PA General Assembly will face challengers in the upcoming election. A potential challenger to U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts will not be on the ballot, so both Pitts and U.S. Representative George Gekas will run unopposed to represent Lancaster in the U.S. House. Candidates for the six state races are described in the article.

headline: State budget focused on job creation
abstract: It's interesting to compare the political differences and similarities between President Clinton's federal budget plan and the state budget unveiled by PA Governor Tom Ridge. Both are dealing with budget surpluses. And both find themselves trying to fend off members of the opposing parties who want to spend the surpluses. The big difference is that the state surplus is real.

headline: Allegheny looks to slash high salaries
abstract: The Allegheny health system, seeking to prevent its financial crisis from worsening, is preparing to slash the pay of hundreds to top earners by at least 10 percent.  New appointed chief executive Anthony Sanzo has proposed to reduce the salaries of numerous employees who earn more than $100,000 a year an Allegheny spokesman said last night.  But Sanzo first needs to obtain approval from Allegheny's board and legal counsel, the spokesman said.

headline: University officials want work force input
abstract: State Universities want to part take in the discussions between Governor Tom Ridge and House Republicans regarding workforce development.

headline: Blaze sparked legislative changes
abstract: According to Delaware County Judge Joseph Battle, in 1978 there were hardly any environmental laws; however, two environmental disasters, the Wade Dump fire in PA and Love Canal in New York, led to the passage of federal environmental regulations, including the Superfund act. Former U.S. Representatives Bob Edgar and Jim Florio and U.S. Senator John Heinz visited the Wade Dump site and helped push for the Superfund legislation, which ultimately helped clean up the site five years later.

headline: Foes want Exit 7 booted from county master plan
abstract: There is debate between Franklin County and Greentownship over proposed transportation contruction in the area.

headline: Ballot issue on nonjury trial a case of overkill, foes say
abstract: There is a proposed amendment to the PA Constitution that would allow prosecutors to veto a defendant’s request for a nonjury trial, which proponents claim is necessary to counterbalance attempts by the defense to delay the trial or look for a lenient judge. Representative Samuel Rohrer feels that changing the constitution is not the right solution, as do many other critics who believe prosecutors could use the power to manipulate the system or force financially strapped defendants to take a plea deal. Attorney General Mike Fisher supports the amendment, whereas his predecessor does not, and there is another amendment that is being debated.

headline: Tests planned of system to track protection orders
abstract: New internet database helps domestce violence agencies and caseworkers to track court protection orders. The database also includes various information about individual cases.

headline: Car insurance dropping in most states
abstract: For decades, auto insurance companies apparently were unaware of the credo that what goes up, must come down.  But now, premiums in at least 43 states and the District of Columbia are declining for the first time since the late 1970s.  The average policy is expected to decline 1 percent this year to $642 annually according to the Insurance Information Institute, a Washington-based company that tracks rates.

headline: Clinton and Gore Appeal To GOP for Compromise  Swing Members Are Lining Up for Impeachment
abstract: President Clinton is trying to convince Republican House leaders to consider a compromise to avoid the impeachment process; however, House Majority Leader Richard Armey said they planned to continue with plans for impeachment and were not considering an alternative censure option. Three Democrats said they are likely to vote for impeachment, whereas five Republicans indicated they’d go the other way, so in order for Clinton to avoid being impeached, he would have to sway nine additional Republicans while convincing the remaining Democrats stay on his side. The situation is beginning to worsen after 12 of the 34 Republicans identified as potential targets announced they’d vote for impeachment, and another Democrat is considering switching sides; however, Vice President Gore, numerous interest groups and actor Robert DeNiro are fighting to win over the other representatives.

headline: Local candidate wasn't invited to Democratic Leadership Summit
abstract: While PA Democrats have made the Lehigh Valley a focus for the fall campaign, targeting five local House seats for victory, the party's interest apparently does not extend as far west as Macungle. Democratic candidate Arlene Dabrow, who is challenging eighth-term incumbent Paul Semmel in November, says she and other Democrats in the 187th District have been abandoned by their party.

headline: State Rep. Tom Druce introduces political candidacy legislation
abstract: PA Representative Tom Druce introduced legislation that would prevent candidates from seeking nominations for more than one public office. Druce believes that if a candidate wins more than one election, it could leave the people in some areas without adequate representation.

headline: State court nixes stock-option tax
abstract: Courts decided that taxing an executive's stock options is an investment income tax, and is not permitted under state law.

headline: Allegheny To Sell 6 Area Hospitals   The buyer is a for-profit health firm
abstract: The Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation, which may have overextended itself recently, is planning to sell six of its nine hospitals in the Philadelphia area for $300 million to the for-profit Vanguard Health Systems; though Allegheny will still hold onto its university system. While other hospital groups are concerned about the potential new competition, one professor believes the sale won’t seriously affect consumers; however, some wonder how Vanguard will be able to adapt to make money in light of Philadelphia’s tough hospital market. Vanguard named David Cohen, former chief of staff for Mayor Rendell, as chairman of the board, and the company is developing a plan to potentially consolidate while still retaining and possibly adding new jobs.

headline: Visiting wood shop, Specter considering Amish labor bill
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter visited an Amish woodworking shop, and he said he may introduce legislation that would allow the Amish to circumvent child labor laws. However, he warned the legislation introduced by U.S. Representative Joseph Pitts has flaws and may be unconstitutional. Specter’s three Amish hosts told him youths aged 14 to 17, whose religion prohibits them from attending school, should be able to do work in woodworking shops and sawmills to keep them occupied.

headline: Brooklyn celebrates one year of recycling
abstract: People gathered on November 14 in the Brooklyn municipal building to celebrate the first anniversary of the Recycling Center, and Donna Williams, the volunteer recycling coordinator, thanked all other volunteers. Susquehanna County Commissioner Lee Smith spoke about a new recycling center that is expected to open in Montrose in December, and a representative for Sandy Major, a PA Representative, offered congratulations from the Farm Bureau and Major. Kathy Tuttle, the County’s Recycling/Solid Waste Coordinator, spoke about recycling options for residents and new initiatives that are being developed.

headline: Funds OK'd for trucker training site
abstract: Representative Bud Shuster helps pass a higway bill that allow an area of the Turnpike to be turned into a trucker drivier training facility. There are accussations that Shuster pushed for this bill so it could be managed by a family campaign contributor.

headline: Ballot question divides lawyers
abstract: Allegheny County District Attorney does not support the proposed constitutional referendums on crime.

headline: The crime report: Make it 'uniform'
abstract: Bucks County Courier Times argues there I a need for a Uniform crime report, as the current practice of reporting does not make an accurate account of Pennsylvania crime. There are currently no standards regarding how the reports are calculated or that it be mandatory.

headline: Cashman Finds Business is Booming
abstract: PIAA executive director Bradley Cashman knows his view of his job is not always a popular one. Cashman claimed it was just business when he move the PIAA football championships from Altoona to Hershey.

headline: Clinton backers here plan show of solidarity
abstract: As Kenneth Starr continues to pursue his investigation of President Clinton over allegations into his sexual relationship with Monica Lewinski, his supporters seem to have been reinvigorated and continue to show their support. Clinton will attend a party in Philadelphia that is expected to raise about $300,000 for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee from 30 of the city’s most wealthy Democrats. The support seems to reflect national polls, which found that the President’s approval rating has increased by 10 points within 10 days, and many people support the President’s performance in office, despite allegations into personal conduct.

headline: Local Democrats pledge Clinton support
abstract: U.S. Representatives Frank Mascara, Ron Klink and William Coyne, who are all from PA, commented after the release of Kenneth Starr’s report on President Clinton. The report and evidence could ultimately lead to Clinton’s impeachment, but local Democrats vowed not to make any judgments until after hearing all the evidence.

headline: State Representative 105th District Larry Knapp
abstract: Larry Knapp, who is a lifetime resident of the area, has announced that he will be running for the 105th District’s seat in the PA House, a position currently held by PA Representative Ron Marsico. He is concerned with the working class and senior citizens, as well as growing traffic problems and controlling the cost of services in the district.  He cited a number of traffic problems that deserve attention and criticized the state government for ignoring the needs of the District.

headline: State Democrats: Apply surplus to property tax
abstract: Democrats are proposing to use the anticpated state surplus to lower property taxes for residents. Govenor Tom Ridge and the Republican party are scehduled to announce their surplus proposal shortly.

headline: Allegheny Valley rejects bankruptcy talk: Hospital reportedly operating in black in second half of year
abstract: Moody’s Investor Services lowered the bond rating for the western PA hospitals, including Allegheny Valley Hospital, under the Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation, citing among other reasons the foundation’s $1.3 billion bankruptcy. The foundation had to sell eight Philadelphia area hospitals last month; however, the presidents of the hospital and foundation thought the ratings in western PA were unfair and didn’t reflect the reality of the situation. The foundation claims three of the hospitals, including Allegheny Valley, have cut operating expenses by $3 million the past year, and are financially sound.

headline: A look at Teacher Preparedness
abstract: Students planning careers in teaching are, on average, lower scorers on the SAT. Many end up teaching outside their field of training.

headline: Commission's decision to sit on surplus misses the target
abstract: For the second consecutive year the Pennsylvania Game Commission has snubbed the advice of its professional wildlife biologists and forbade the sale of surplus (formerly bonus) anterless deer licenses.  At its summer meeting last week in Harrisburg, the Commission voted 4-4 on southwestern commissioner Dennis Frederick's motion to return to the system last used in 1996 that allowed the hunters already holding an anterless license to apply for additional tags in counties where they remained available.  Since the sale of surplus tags had been suspended the previous year, the deadlock killed Frederick's initiative.

headline: George a step closer to two-way
abstract: PA Department of Transportation is behind York city officials decision to change George Street into a two-way traffic street. This project is a small part to a larger redevelopment plan for the city.

headline: Ballot questions on crime aren't that simple
abstract: There are concerns and questions on the two proposed constitutional referendums on crime.

headline: THE STATE SHOULD NOT RUSH TO PAROLE VIOLENT PRISONERS
abstract: The PA Board of Probation and Parole decided to release James Stone early from his sentence because they claimed he had been rehabilitated; however, the police officer who was assaulted by Stone and the county prosecutor sued, which led to a Commonwealth Court judge reversing the parole board’s decision. A parolee who was released early two years ago ended up killing a police officer within two weeks of his parole, and a report offered some recommendations on how to better review parole cases and monitor parolees. According to the opinion expressed in the article, early release can be a good incentive to encourage good behavior in prison, but releasing a violent criminal too early could be disastrous, and ultimately, corrections officials should remember that their primary goal must be punishment, not rehabilitation.

headline: Chaste or chased?
abstract: PA Senator Vince Fumo is a co-sponsor of a resolution declaring May 3-9 "Chastity Awareness Week" in PA. However, his spokesman said he was unavailable for comment when the newspaper asked whether he was chaste before his marriage.

headline: Clinton pays a visit on fund-raising tour
abstract: Bill Clinton visits Philadelphia to help fund raising efforts. The city hopes to raise $500,000 to host the Democratic convention in 1999.

headline: Local legislator to serve on community advisory board
abstract: PA Representative Fred McIlhattan was selected to serve on Governor Tom Ridge’s Community Service Advisory Board, known as PennSERVE. House Majority Leader John Perzel said McIlhattan’s long history of volunteering and commitment to the community led to his appointment. The group serves as a link between the state and the federally-funded Corporation for National Service to ensure the AmeriCorps and Learn and Serve programs are being run responsibly.

headline: State Republican leaders challenge ruling on "Pippy Law"
abstract: Republican leaders have decided not to wait for a final court ruling on the constitutionality of what Democrats called the "Pippy Law" before filing an appeal to the state Supreme Court. Passed along largely a party-line vote in February, Act 18 was designed to eliminate the right of citizens to challenge in court the constitutional qualifications of legislative candidates prior to an election.  It gave exclusive right to judge it members to the House and Senate.

headline: State House Democrats outline tax-cutting plan
abstract: The PA Legislature continues to debate property tax reform mandated by a statewide referendum held last year, and some House Democrats, including Minority Leader William DeWeese, gubernatorial candidate Ivan Itkin and Representative Phyllis Mundy, support a bill that would cut school district property taxes by 50 percent over five years. Proponents of the plan argue that if Governor Tom Ridge gave $3 billion in tax cuts to businesses since taking office, homeowners also deserve a tax break, which would be possible with careful spending and use of the state’s growing surplus. They also believe the Senate’s tax reform bill would be ineffective because it simply calls for lost revenue from property taxes to be shifted to a county sales tax or increases in earned income taxes.

headline: Apparently no smoke detector in burned cabin - The fatal blaze that claimed 11 has Pa. officials examining the need for a mandatory state law.
abstract: No evidence of a smoke detector was found in the remains of the mountain cabin where 11 young people died of asphyxiation from a fire, but the incident could push the PA Legislature to consider two pending bills, including one sponsored by Senator Edwin Holl. A long-debated bill to create a statewide building code requiring smoke-detectors be installed in all new homes has already passed the state House; however, Holl’s bill would apply to older structures, and he would push to ensure it applies to all cabins as well. Meanwhile, Line Mountain High School, where eight people who died in the fire attended school, mourned their deaths, and others mourned in Lititz, Lancaster County, where three of the victims had grown up.

headline: $71G loss an expensive lesson
abstract: Dozens of school districts lost an estimated $71 million last year in investments handled by John Black through Devon Management, and the Securities and Exchange Commission froze $233 million in assets. He allegedly misled school officials and lost most of his money investing in Collateralized Mortgage Obligations, which are susceptible to economic downturns. Some people have called on banning these types of investments of taxpayers’ dollars, but some defended their use if invested properly.

headline: Busy with hunting issues
abstract: United Sportsmen of Pennsylvania has looked at a proposed hunting calendar that would provide more time afield for both senior and junior hunters and which would avoid some problems that exist under the current calendar.  The use of the crossbow is an issue concerning many USP members.  Data from Ohio and Arkansas do not show crossbows to be a better weapon.

headline: Get to know PennDOT better
abstract: PA Department of Transportation will hold a free seminar to municipal officials to help officials become more familiar with PennDOT.

headline: Bar members say PG series 'misleading'
abstract: Allegheny County judges were criticized in a previous Post-Gazette article. County Bar Assosiation does not believe the criticism was fair.

headline: The State Supreme Court Rules For County On Privatization of Prison
abstract: The PA Supreme Court ruled that Delaware County can continue to use the services of a private company to run its County Prison, which local officials estimate is saving the county about $3 million a year. The guards’ union had sued the county on claims that the privatization was a union-busting technique, and won an appeal to the Commonwealth Court. However, Chief Justice John P. Flaherty wrote that the lower court had made a mistake and found that the county was within its legal rights, a decision that cannot be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.

headline: Chronology
abstract: The Daily News Summarizes its findings after investigating the finances of the Philadelphia Gas Works' senior management team. The company is facing $350,000 in company credit card charges for personal expenses. The company violated city laws requiring performance standards for raises, which did not exist when bonuses were awarded. PGW has also spent hundreds of thousands in relocation costs. The former President James Hawes III was accused of violating a conflict-of-interest policy in addition to giving money from the company to his alma mater, Morehouse College.

headline: Clinton reportedly acknowledges affair with Gennifer Flowers
abstract: President Clinton reportedly acknowledged that he did have a sexual affair with Gennifer Flowers in the 1970’s. He reportedly made the statement during a six-hour deposition in the Paula Jones sexual harassment lawsuit. He had denied the affair during his 1992 presidential election campaign.

headline: Locally, electorate backed consensus
abstract: Republicans did poorly in the past election, and the authors of the editorial are concerned about exit polls, which showed the nation is deeply divided based on their political party over the questions which were asked. Some are claiming that political opinions are too fragmented to seek a middle ground, however, the authors believe that the three local candidates who won handily, Congressman Tom Holden and State Representatives Bob Allen and Dave Argall, all favor non-ideological issues and are seeking a consensus. The authors believe national politicians need to work towards compromise instead of continuing along their paths of partisanship.

headline: State running city?   Legislature may revamp City Council
abstract: PA legislative leaders are discussing a measure that would change the structure of Philadelphia’s districts for electing city councilmen and would shift City Council elections to non-mayoral election years. Several political sources say state Senator Vince Fumo is behind the proposal because he believe restructuring the districts could lead to more middle-class, conservative-to-moderates winning seats in the City Council, and the other argument is that by moving Council elections to non-mayoral election years, they would receive the attention they deserve and would help increase voter turnout for statewide judicial elections. Although the measure is still a big question mark, City Council members, including President John Street, are not pleased about the prospect of having the state interfere in local matters.

headline: State Senate wrangles on tax-break legislation
abstract: Republicans and Democrats clashed in the Senate over how to cut taxes for PA's fiscal year that opens July 1. The Republican Senate majority eventually exempts the poorest working families in PA from any tax obligations. Passage of that came after protected and acrimonious debate over Democratic proposals to cut the personal income tax, to provide tax credits to offset local property tax payments to local school districts and to give tax relief to working single parents.

headline: At very least, a change for the better, workers say
abstract: Tenet Healthcare Corporation bought the bankrupt Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation’s Philadelphia hospitals and the Allegheny University of the Health Sciences. Most people seemed to be pleased with the takeover and felt like things probably couldn’t have gotten any worse than under the previous leadership; though a number of questions still remain and doctors are still concerned about their futures. Students at MCP-Hahnemann School of Medicine, which was saved from the possibility of closing, held a rally of 200 students to welcome the deal, and generally, people appear to be excited about the change of leadership and the prospects for the future.

headline: 3 districts forced to educate more young inmates
abstract: The PA Legislature passed an amendment to the state’s Public School Code that requires school districts to provide education of 20 hours a week for students in jail up to the age of 21, as opposed to the previous age of 17. School administrators in West Perry, Cumberland Valley and Central Dauphin say that the requirement is a burden on budgets as well as staff, and officials claim that it causes too much paperwork, and it can be difficult to find teachers who are willing to go to prisons to teach. The efforts of each district to comply with the law are discussed in the article.

headline: Case being made for too many deer
abstract: The PA Game Commission’s Deer Management Outreach Committee conducted a tour of Game Lands 44, where deer enclosures were erected three years ago to keep deer away from specific areas, to prove its point that too many deer exist in certain parts of PA. The difference between the enclosures and the areas where deer had access were clearly noticeable, and the committee is convinced that deer need to be removed to allow plants to regenerate and the habitat to recover. Several sportsmen agreed with the assessment, as did state Representative David Levdansky; though he did criticize the Game Commission for not dedicating more funds for fencing.

headline: Get tough on reckless teen drivers - Notification policy is overdue
abstract: The authors support the PA Department of Transportation’s recent announcement that beginning in August, parents or guardians will be notified when their teen-agers with learners’ permits are cited for serious traffic violations. The authors also agree with many lawmakers that this is only the first step, and they urge the state and school districts to reinstate driver training programs. In addition, they urge parents to play a more active role in training their children to drive safely and monitor their driving habits once they receive their licenses.

headline: Berwick native fights extradition
abstract: A Berwick native who returned home only to be arrested in January as a fugitive parolee from armed robberies in Florida is fighting his extradition south. He claims he has already passed the 30-day deadline required for Florida to take action on seeking extradition. That deadline was extended for another 60 days when the governor's warrants were not received within 30 days of his arrest.

headline: The taxpayers will still have to pay
abstract: Observer-Reporter talks about the difficluties of integrating Pennsylvania court systems and suggests that the financial burden of the intergation will fall on tax payers.

headline: City may take a gamble
abstract: If legislation is approved by Harrisburg, a floating casino someday could be docked on the Stonycreek River in Johnstown. State Rep. Dwight Evans's plan to fund stadium projects and educational initiatives with riverboat gambling is sinking in the capital. Gov. Tom Ridge has shown no interest in the proposal and Johnstown area lawmakers aren't convinced the plan will float.

headline: Clinton scandal a complicated topic for political cartoonists
abstract: Some of the details coming from Kenneth Starr’s report on the affair between President Clinton and Monica Lewinski are far too vulgar to be incorporated into political cartoons, and many political cartoonists are walking a fine line between what is acceptable and what is not for a newspaper. The scandal is pushing the line further than before, yet many cartoons are still rejected by newspaper editors, so many cartoonists have to find a way to subtly depict the scandal.

headline: Lone Woman Running for 10th District Seat Touts Common Sense
abstract: Mary Rogan claims the reason she will do well in elections is because she speaks the language of the people. She is CEO of the Rogan family. She is running for the 10th District Congressional Seat. Her plan is to win via a grassroots effort.

headline: State: Hot lottery tickets can lead to jail jackpot
abstract: The thieves who stole lottery tickets from two Allentown-area outlets are unlikely to win anything. According to Robert Herb, security director for the PA Lottery, there is a built in security feature that allows stolen tickets to be registered as stolen. If anyone attempts to cash in on winning tickets, they may find their prize is an arrest.

headline: State surplus prompts talk of tax cuts
abstract: The Ridge administration brought the budget tidings of comfort and joy, predicting a surplus of $273 million and promising no tax increases next year. Budget Secretary Robert Bittenbender indicated the state is looking to further reduce business taxes He distance himself from any cut in the personal income tax, then stressed no final decision has been made. House majority leader is very much in favor.

headline: Attorney general wants say in AHERF bankruptcy case
abstract: State Attorney General Mike Fisher formally bid Monday to become a player in the bankruptcy filing of the Pittsburgh-based Allegheny Health, Education and Research Foundation and its subsidiaries, citing a need to protect charitable assets.  The attorney general's office asked for the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for authority to review a proposed sale of the foundation's nine Philadelphia hospitals to a for-profit Tennessee corporation.  The deal has consumer groups in Philadelphia worried that the quality of care may suffer in the hands of a for-profit enterprise.

headline: A beat-up PIAA finds itself stuck in crossfire
abstract: Some members of the state's General Assembly, as well as some of the PIAA's member schools, want to know more about the organization governing interscholastic athletics involving nearly 230,000 students from more than 1,300 junior and senior high schools. They want to know more about how PIAA manages its money; how it implements policies it admits cannot fully be enforced; and how it decides on picking among communities vying for the financial boom that comes with hosting the state's football, basketball and wrestling championships.

headline: City Receives $58,759 Sewage Planning Grant
abstract: According to PA Representative Teresa Brown, Titusville has received a $58,759 sewage planning grant from the PA Department of Environmental Protection. The money will be used to cover half the cost of preparing the city’s official sewage plan. City Manager Carolyne Ford claims the money will be used for a number of different studies and will allow the city to comply with state regulations required under the Sewage Facilities Act.

headline: Graduated licensing supported
abstract: The author describes an accident he had years ago shortly after receiving his driver’s permit, and he discusses the role of graduated licensing systems, which can phase novice young drivers from limited driving privileges to full driving privileges. According to the author, the basis for graduated licensing systems is that young drivers have a disproportionately high rate of accidents when compared to other states, and PA does have a partial graduated system. However, the American Automobile Association has proposed a much tougher system that includes three different phases in which a person wouldn’t receive unrestricted driving privileges until they are at least 18, have completed stage 2 requirements and have passed a final road test.

headline: Bill on prisoner lawsuits puts inmates in legal strait jackets
abstract: The number of inmates who file appeals has been rising steadily, which is causing a burden on the judicial system, so the PA Senate overwhelmingly adopted a bill that will allow judges to throw out lawsuits with no merit early in the process. The author, however, argues that provisions were added on that are extremely unfair to prisoners, such as not allowing an inmate to file a lawsuit ever again after three priors are thrown out, the imposition of a fee for all lawsuits and another fee that manages to punish successful lawsuits. The author argues the provisions are another way to punish inmates, and he argues an emphasis on treatment and prevention of crime could yield better results.

headline: Timoney already mapping changes
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner John Timoney, who was appointed yesterday by Mayor Ed Rendell, hasn’t waited long in proposing changes to the city’s police department, and during a press conference, he said he wants to improve training, rate commanders based on performance in high-crime areas and get rid of a rule that essentially prevents the department from recruiting officers from outside of Philadelphia. Timoney wants to get rid of the city’s one-year residency requirement to become an officer, which would likely be approved by the city’s Civil Service Commission, and he also said he favors merging police from the Housing Authority and the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority into his department. In addition, he wants to replace the department’s promotion system by expanding the number of appointments he can make and by rating commanders based on the difficulty of assignments they’ve handled.

headline: Congress considers reform act
abstract: A new bill passed in the house will put stricter limits and requirements on individuals wishing to file for bankruptcy.

headline: Clinton Team Says Hill May See Backlash    Tape Described as Complex
abstract: The media has been gearing up for the release of President Clinton’s over four hour long videotaped grand jury testimony, and White House officials, including Chief of Staff, John Podesta, and congressional Democrats said that the release of the video is unnecessary, but they expect people will actually feel sorry for the President. According to people familiar with the content of the video, Clinton admits to an inappropriate sexual relationship with Monica Lewinski, he exhibits a wide array of different emotions, he tries to explain away some ambiguous answers due to memory loss, and he vows not answer any specific questions about their sexual contact due to privacy concerns. While Senator John Kerry wants Clinton to testify in front of the Judiciary Committee to get the ordeal over with, Senator John Ashcroft blamed Clinton for bringing the problems on himself, and Representative Lindsey Graham didn’t think the video would change too many peoples’ opinions of the President.

headline: Lott Floats Plan for Swift Test Vote   Senate Would Decide First If Alleged Clinton Offenses Justify Removal
abstract: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott is distributing a proposal he received that would have the Senate vote on whether the impeachment charges against President Clinton, if they are proven, would warrant his removal from office, and if a two-thirds majority votes yes, the trial would continue and witnesses could be called in. It is widely agreed that the Senate doesn’t have the two-thirds majority needed to remove Clinton from office, so this proposal is seen as a way to quickly end the trial, and allow Senators to develop a censure of the President afterwards. However, House prosecutors are concerned about a vote being undertaken without the Senate being able to hear all the evidence, and the proposal is being challenged by several conservative Republicans who oppose a censure as well as conservative leaders from the community.

headline: State's feel term limits' effects
abstract: A number of state are enacted Congressional term limits for state congrerssional members. Each state has or proposes different conditions.

headline: Stocks tax upheld, but it's not last work
abstract: PA courts ruled that exempting stocks from taxes is unconstitutional. However, the case is being brought to the U.S. Supreme Court.

headline: Audit critical of youth health-insurance program
abstract: An audit of the PA state's Children's Health Insurance Program showed that less then one-fourth of the children enrolled are actually received the promised health care.

headline: A Column from the Senate by Senator Jeffrey Piccola
abstract: This column is written by PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola to explain the federally funded Robert C. Byrd Honors Program. The program awards scholarships to high school seniors who have demonstrated academic achievement and are continuing their education by going to college. To be considered eligible, students must, among other things, rank in the top 5% of their graduating class, meet residency requirements, score high enough on college placement tests and have a grade point average of 3.5.

headline: Clearing up confusion about antlerless licenses
abstract: Many hunters believe there are fewer deer on public lands. However, game biologists have preached and actually documented the need for the sale of surplus licenses to keep the deer herd numbers in control. But when hunters go out of public lands and don't see a deer behind every tree they gripe loudly and the commissioners, sensitive to complaints of constituents, lean toward satisfying the hunters rather than the biologists.

headline: Greene seeking upgrade of Route 21
abstract: Greene County is looking to get much needed transportation improvements to Route 21.

headline: Bill seeks rules for disposal of guns
abstract: State Rep. David Mayernik doesn't care whether guns are confiscated by police are destroyed or given to police training programs --- he just wants to make sure the guns don't wind up back on the streets.  To that end, Mayernik, D.-29th of West View, will introduce a bill next week that would set statewide gun disposal standards.  The bill would require police departments to apply for a court order specifying what is to be done with each within 30 days of the expiration of the last appeal in each criminal case.

headline: Timoney reveals changes for police - He's made 44 top-level transfers, including naming the first woman to head a division.
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner John Timoney named police inspector Patricia Giorgio-Fox as the city’s first female to head a division, and she will be in charge of all patrol officers in South Philadelphia. The move came as part of a large organizational restructuring by Timoney, which involves 10 inspectors, 31 captains and also resulted in new leadership for the Northeast and West Police Divisions. When Giorgio-Fox was promoted to inspector nine months ago, Evelyn Heath was also named inspector in another groundbreaking move by Mayor Ed Rendell.

headline: Consumers assail Allegheny's bankruptcy filing: State Attorney General Mike Fisher will seek to keep Allegheny's charitable assets from creditors, a spokesman said.
abstract: Allegheny health system filed for bankruptcy, but members of the Coalition for Patients Not Profits said that filing for bankruptcy was unnecessary and was simply a way to bypass normal state regulations. Normally, when a nonprofit company is sold to a for-profit company, the nonprofit’s value is determined by the PA Attorney General and put into a charitable foundation; however, Allegheny, which plans to sell nine of its Philadelphia area hospitals to Vanguard Health Systems Inc., claims they are so far in debt that there would be no money left from the sale to put into a foundation. State Attorney General Mike Fisher will try to protect the charitable assets.

headline: Clinton's Problems Don't Seem to Affect Democrats Declarations of Candidacy
abstract: President Bill Clinton’s scandal seems to have had little impact on the Democratic Party’s attempts to recruit top candidates to challenge for seats in the U.S. House; though Republicans claim otherwise. The Democrats still have a tough task ahead of them as they must gain 12 seats to recapture the House, and their candidates hope that they will be judged on their own merit; not by Clinton’s problems. The article describes a number of Democratic candidates, including Patrick Casey, who has a chance of winning the House seat from Scranton.

headline: Lott tells Bill to drop Massiah-Jackson
abstract: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R.-Miss., yesterday called on President Clinton to withdraw the nomination of Philadelphia Common Pleas Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson to the federal bench, and agreed to hold off a vote on the troubled nomination.  Lott said Massiah-Jackson's nomination to U.S. District Court in Philadelphia would be held up until she could respond to allegations to Pennsylvania prosecutors that she is lenient on criminals.  Later this month, she will most likely have another hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee - a highly unusual step.

headline: States see Washington trying to grab power: Lawmakers say promise of shift in authority has not been fulfilled
abstract: While states have won control over a number of federal programs during the Clinton Administration’s six years, state lawmakers from across the country that gathered for their annual meeting in Las Vegas were disappointed the trend was slowing down, if not reversing itself. Lawmakers feel that President Clinton hasn’t fulfilled his obligations to transfer more federal powers to the states, and they cited a recent proposal to establish national drunken driving standards as a prime example of the federal government trying to intrude into state affairs. Despite their lobbying efforts, many believe the issue will be best handled by the courts.

headline: Strong economy produces state budget surplus
abstract: PA is not alone. Buoyed by a strong US economy, states governments nationwide are experiencing record budget surpluses. That's a big change from the early 1990's. State revenues are tightly tied to economic conditions. Results of what state legislatures are doing with the surpluses are detailed.

headline: Auditor: Pa. nursing homes run almost unchecked
abstract: Proposed legislation in Cogress tries to address the Health Department failures noted in the audit investigation by Auditor General Robert Casey.

headline: A lesson in mediocrity: How teachers are trained and chosen
abstract: Last month, the MA Board of Education announced that 59% of prospective teachers failed a new literacy exam. Their tests were filled with spelling mistakes, poor sentence structures, and words used the wrong way. In Philadelphia high numbers of prospective teachers don't pass the essay portion of the school district's three part exam, a requirement for a permanent position. Nearly one-third of applicants for elementary teaching jobs flunked the essay test. These are people who had been certified to teach by the state.

headline: Clinton County will be home to about 40 "wapiti"
abstract: State Game officials plan to trap 40 elk from their traditional haunts in Cameron and Elk counties and release them into western Clinton County. Shawnee Indians called the elk "wapiti" meaning pale deer or white deer. Scientists will draw blood from the animals trapped this winter for genetic studies.

headline: Hanover discusses co-op agreement with PennDOT
abstract: PennDOT and Hanover township officials met to discuss the possibility of implementing the Agility Program, which would trade services between the two.

headline: Bill would help ill children
abstract: U.S. Representative Phil English sponsored a bill written by Representative Clay Shaw Jr. that would allow children with life threatening illnesses to receive cash gifts of up to $2,000 from tax-exempt organizations without having money deducted in taxes. The authors of the editorial believe there is something terribly wrong with the current law, and they support the new bill.

headline: To protect their kids, moms ask about guns
abstract: Now the gruesome toll of school shootings involving children who gained access to guns is leading some parents to add another, potentially awkward question about guns to the list.  After all, guns, mostly handguns are present in an estimated 40 percent of U.S. households.  And according to the National Center for Health Statistics, 5,285 kids aged 19 years and under died gun-related deaths in 1995, the most recent year for which statistics are available.

headline: CoreStates is selling 95 bank offices
abstract: Core States bank sells 95 branch offices to Sovereign Bancorp. In Berks County, PA. As part if the sellout agreement, 800 CoreStates employees will keep their job.

headline: Clinton's support hurts candidate's chances, poll finds
abstract: John Zogby released an independent poll after Kenneth Starr’s report on President Clinton and Monica Lewinski was released that shows Clinton’s support of Democratic candidates in the upcoming election could actually hurt their chances of winning. Nearly three times as many people said they’d be less likely to vote for a congressional candidate who Clinton campaigns for than those who said they’d be more likely to support such a candidate, and if this holds true, Democrats may put pressure on Clinton to resign before the election. While other polls show Clinton more favorably, those polls were mostly done by random sampling, whereas Zogby’s poll sampled likely voters, which he claims gives a more accurate reading of the impact on voters.

headline: Loughran named new president judge
abstract: It was a job no one wanted.  Only after 90 minutes of arm-twisting did Westmoreland County Judge Charles Loughran emerge from his jury room to announce he had accepted a five-year term as president judge.  The county's ten judges met Thursday afternoon to elect a replacement for the late Judge Bernard Scherer as president judge. Loughran served as acting president judge after Scherer's death.

headline: State's teacher unions plan continued cooperation
abstract: Two fueling Pennsylvania state teachers unions will continue working together on issues, despite the rejection of merger with the National education Association.

headline: Surplus filling state's coffers all over U.S.
abstract: Many state have received more revenue then expected, but the projected supluses in these states does not mean tax breaks for residents.

headline: Bill gives public say on closings of institutions   Western Center supporters hail votes
abstract: Parents and guardians of residents at Western Center, a facility for the mentally disabled that the PA Department of Public Welfare announced would be closing, lobbied to postpone its closure until after they could voice their concerns. In response state Representative Russell Fairchild sponsored the Mental Facility Closure Act, which passed the state Legislature and awaits Governor Tom Ridge’s signature. The bill would require a public hearing be held within 60 days of an announced closure of any state-run facilities for the mentally disabled, and it is supported by state Senator Tim Murphy.

headline: A measure of success for Phila. Schools Under Superintendent Hornbeck's accountability system, more than half met their two-year performance goals
abstract: Over half of the Philadelphia public schools met their two-year performance goals under School Superintendent David Hornbeck’s new accountability system, both teacher and student absentee rates dropped, the rate of on-time graduation increased, and nearly all schools showed improvement in test scores, which will be released later today. Hornbeck plans to have a celebration to give $5.5 million in additional funds for schools that met their goals; however, the district is still far from its 12-year goal of having 95 percent of students performing at proficient levels, and high school results were still fairly dismal. Hornbeck and Mayor Ed Rendell have been pleading for additional funds, which led to an earlier confrontation with the state Legislature, and Hornbeck hopes the performance results will influence the state to increase funding to close the $150 million deficit the district appears to be facing next year.

headline: Clinton County will be home to about 40 'waipiti'
abstract: State Game Commission officials plan to trap 40 animals from their traditional haunts in Cameron and Elk counties and release them into western Clinton County.  As of Thursday, 27 animals were being held in  a 3.2 acre pen near Bitumen.

headline: Has Shuster switched? Will 219 plan suffer?
abstract: Representative Bud Shuster remains quiet about the Continental One Alliance and proposed plans for Route corriders.

headline: Bill would require screening for domestic violence
abstract: A bill will be introduced in the PA Legislature within two weeks requiring health care providers to screen women for a history of spousal or partner abuse. The bill for universal screening would make it mandatory for hospitals, emergency rooms and physicians to question women about domestic violence even in visits that may appear unrelated to domestic violence. At this time, no penalties are being proposed for non-compliance.

headline: Tobacco litigation deal nears fruition
abstract: PA hopes to receive $11 million dollars from a legal settlement with the tabacoo industry.

headline: County's visitors to pay room tax
abstract: Indiana County visitors will begin to pay a 1-2% tax increase on their stays in the county at hotels, motels, and other lodging places. The tax is to be used for the purpoe of promoting tourism.

headline: Clout  The Mayoral Watch   Q&A with Happy Fernandez
abstract: The article provides the responses to eight questions that were asked to Gladys "Happy" Fernandez, who is the first female mayoral candidate for Philadelphia to run as a major party candidate. Among other things, she defended her record as a City Council member and said school reform, job creation and improving the quality of life in Philadelphia’s neighborhoods would be her top priorities. She also spoke about her past role as a member of the Gas Commission, and the article provides a humorous "if they were mayor" scenario for how six mayoral candidates would act if they were mayor during the 2000 Republican National Convention that current Mayor Ed Rendell was able to bring to the city.

headline: Low-key Clyborn unafraid to "get in your case."
abstract: U.S. Representative James Clyburn, the first black to represent South Carolina in Congress this century, was elected chairman of the Congressional Black Caucus, replacing Representative Maxine Waters. His personality and style is far more low-key than Waters; however, he vowed to be aggressive and articulate when necessary, and many caucus members believe he is well suited for the leadership position. Despite being a minority caucus within the minority Democratic Party, the caucus has achieved several recent legislative victories in Congress and will continue to work with the rest of the Democrats to build on the party’s success in the recent election.

headline: Step by step, how judge decided to withdraw   Massiah-Jackson wanted to "fight it out" but believes she did what was best for her.
abstract: Common Pleas Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson, who had been nominated by President Clinton to become a U.S. District Court judge, gave her first interview since deciding to withdraw her name from consideration before the Senate had its confirmation vote. Philadelphia District Attorney Lynne Abraham, a potential 1999 mayoral candidate,  tried to show that she shouldn’t be confirmed by citing over 50 past cases, and Massiah-Jackson endured a grueling process, including a 3 ˝ hour question session in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee as well as criticism over legal advice she gave her brother. After finding out her confirmation could possibly be rejected by as many as 70 senators, she ultimately, after struggling with indecision, chose to withdraw her name from consideration.

headline: Tax complexity pushed reform
abstract: New Castle News criticizes the Federal tax Code for its complexity and urges that Congress begin taking measures to curb the issue.

headline: Bill to regulate HMOs is passed
abstract: With the fall election ahead, lawmakers left town for the summer yesterday confident that they had addressed one of their constituents' major gripes: managed health care.  After more than a year of debate, the legislature granted final passage to measure that would make Pennsylvania the latest of about a dozen states to enact a broad set of rules designed to protect patients from poor treatment at the hands of HMOs.  The comprehensive managed-care "patients' bill of rights" emerged yesterday from weeks of secret drafting as a composite of two bills that had been the subject of numerous hearings.

headline: A school for Dr. Haye
abstract: After the death of Ruth Wright Hayre, a trailblazing African American teacher and principal at William Penn of the School District of Philadelphia, school officials want to rename the school in her honor. However, they must invite public comment. Editors believe enough has been named in Penn's name and that the school should be renamed.

headline: Commission fee increases faces uncertain future
abstract: Mike Koegler, a former marine, told a house panel he won't buy a new hunting license until the Legislature puts some controls on the Pennsylvania Game Commission. It remains unclear whether the Game Commission will get the Legislature to approve a license fee boost after the November election. But legislators say it has become increasingly clear that the agency won't get a revenue increase without some significant changes in the way it does business.

headline: Hasay: Ban rigs on Route 437 - Lawmaker wants trucks off busy roadway linking Mountaintop to White Haven area
abstract: PA Representative George Hasay and Mountaintop area residents are trying to ban heavy truck traffic on Route 437, which comes after an employee for the PA Department of Transportation was seriously injured after being struck by a truck driver. Over 50 residents have signed a petition that claims trucks pose a serious safety hazard, and Habay is trying to convince PennDOT to require trucks to bypass the area by getting on Route 309 instead. However, PennDOT officials claim they have tried to encourage truckers to use the alternate route, but Route 437 does not violate either of the two criteria needed to ban trucks, so there’s nothing the agency can do.

headline: Blow-by-blow account of justice in action
abstract: The article provides the court transcripts for an incident when Assistant District Attorney Brian Grady got into a fistfight with lawyer Joseph Stanton in Common Pleas Court.

headline: Trial without jury threatened
abstract: The Eagle Times urges voters to reject the two constitutional referendums on crime.

headline: Cranmer still optimistic on Plan B deal
abstract: Allegheny County Comissioner Cranmer and Steelers President Dan Rooney negotiate on funding for Plan B stadium construction. Rooney thinks the Steelers are taking on too much of the debt.

headline: Coast-to-coast banking
abstract: Banking market shares by state.

headline: Luksik faithful hear her speak
abstract: Gubernatorial candidate Peg Luksik spoke to a small crowd of supporters at Boyce Park ski lodge last week, where she criticized the large size of the bureaucracy of Governor Ridge’s administration. She supports the elimination of the inheritance tax, wants to focus on eliminating political corruption, is strongly pro-life,  and is a proponent of protecting the right to have guns. According to Luksik, she doesn’t consider herself to be a third-party candidate, claiming she has raised more money than Democratic challenger PA Representative Ivan Itkin.

headline: Street camp worth a million
abstract: Even though the Democratic primary for the upcoming mayoral election won’t begin for over a year, City Council President John Street has already raised over $1 million. He is by far the leader in raising money, which some experts believe is due to the power he has as City Council President. Street expects to raise over $2 million; however, his competitors, including City Councilwoman Happy Fernandez, Former Housing Chief John White Jr. and State Representative Dwight Evans, all seemed to downplay his monetary advantage and said that money is only half the battle.

headline: Tax reform bill needs adjustments
abstract: According to the authors, there are serious flaws in the tax-reform bill passed by the PA Legislature that would allow school districts to cut property taxes in return for raising the local earned income tax. They argue the earned income tax should be expanded to all tax earnings, including stocks and bonds, and they believe local governments should also have the ability to implement the new tax changes. In addition, they are against a provision that would require voter approval to raise property taxes in the future.

headline: Bill would allow doctors to be patient advocates
abstract: The state House of Representatives this week is expected to vote on a bill that would allow doctors and hospitals to act as advocates for their patients when managed-care plans question medical treatments.  Under the bill, proposed by Rep. Patricia Vance (R. Cumberland), doctors could appeal decisions made by business that review cases for managed-care plans and questions medical treatments.  State regulators would certify the businesses.

headline: ABSENTEEISM   City schools failing to educate approximately half of their students
abstract: According to the editorial, Harrisburg School District has one of the worst absentee rates in that state, considering that on an average school day over 31% of Harrisburg’s middle school and high school students are absent, and some school officials estimate half of all high-school students are absent on a regular basis. The authors of the editorial believe this is unacceptable, and they urge the School District to implement much tougher truancy policies. The authors say it is impossible to properly educate students if they don’t attend school, and they believe failure to address the problem could lead to greater societal problems in the future.

headline: Commission head gets hefty raise
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission has quietly awarded executive director Don Madi an $8000 pay hike -raising his annual salary to almost $90,000.  The boost comes as the agency has cut back spending on hunter-related programs as it lobbies the legislature for a license fee increase. It comes amid calls by legislators for increased accountability at the Game Commission, which doesn't bother to keep track of public complaints against game officers

headline: Hearing held on intersection project
abstract: West Mahanoy residents will begin to see improvement on the inersection of Route 924 and Pennsylvania Avenue. PA Department of Transportation has decided to take on the project.

headline: Blue Ridge Mountain volunteers recognized for their service
abstract: Representative Pat Flagler attended a banquet at the Blue Ridge Mountain Fire and Rescue Company to hand out awards and praise the work of volunteers. He gave citations of merit from the House of Representatives to William Sellers, chief of the ambulance squad, and Jim Meek, chief of the fire company. Fleagle also honored fundraisers, and some other awards were handed out.

headline: True unveils child welafre reform proposals.
abstract: State lawmakers introduce legislation to protect children in foster care by changing current rules for parental rights and increasing information sharing between counties

headline: Credit Crunch
abstract: U.S. Supreme Court overturns the National Credition Union Administration's practices.

headline: Coin toss decides new member of RAD board
abstract: RAD member, spilt 3-3 on a vote to fill a vacancy. To decide the vote, a third party filpped a coin and candidiate Wesley Blaha won.

headline: Luksik keeps crusade for values alive
abstract: Peg Luksik, the most successful third party gubernatorial candidate in Pennsylvania since 1910, is running on the Constitutional Party ticket, a party she founded in 1994 after rejecting the Republican party for being to interested in "politics as usual."  Luksik runs on a pro-life ticket and also recieves support from anti-gun control groups, and those who support abolishing the inheritance tax, privatizing elderly care, and increasing regulation of factory farms.  Although not projected to win the Gubanatorial bid against Gov. Tom Ridge (R) and Ivan Itkin (D), she remains hopeful.

headline: Street's sidewalk-behavior bill brings fire colleagues
abstract: City Council President John Street’s proposed sidewalk-behavior bill would ban people from sitting or lying on sidewalks; however, homeless people and their advocates have expressed outrage over the bill, and Street has been harshly criticized by several colleagues, including Councilman David Cohen. Many people have attacked the proposal as a political maneuver to improve Street’s chances of winning the 1999 mayoral election, and another mayoral candidate, John White Jr., joined efforts opposing the bill. Street’s candidacy could be given a boost if the bill helps persuade Mayor Ed Rendell to spend an additional $6 million on new programs for the homeless.

headline: Tax reform measure passed
abstract: Votes by Congressmen are listed for legislation invoving the Local tax reform bill, Managed care Regulation, and Keystone Opporunity Zones.

headline: Bill would allow patients to examine doctor backgrounds
abstract: Medical groups are giving mixed reviews to help consumers learn more about their doctors.  The so-called "Medical Practice Disclosure Act" was the subject of more than two hours of testimony yesterday before the House Professional Licensure Committee.  The Pennsylvania Academy of Family Physicians and the Pennsylvania Medical Society were among the groups that offered their input.

headline: Alternative to district breakup offered - State Sen. Allyson Schwartz said dividing the Phila. School system will not help children
abstract: PA Senator Allyson Schwartz and several advocacy groups urged Governor Tom Ridge and the state Legislature not to consider the breakup of the Philadelphia School District into 22 smaller entities with separate elected school boards. Proponents of the breakup, including state Representative George Kenney, believe it would create more accountability; however, Schwartz proposed a different plan to improve accountability by having the mayor appoint schools board members for the same amount of time he is serving and by creating a state oversight board. In return for these changes, Schwartz believes the district should get an additional $150 million in funding to prevent schools from being shut down, which Superintendant David Hornbeck, state Senator Vincent Fumo and state House Speaker John Perzel have threatened to do if additional funding isn’t provided.

headline: Commission practices questioned by hunters
abstract: Whitetail deer management in Pennsylvania has always caused controversy between hunters and the game commission. There is a vast difference in whitetail deer population across the state, with a tide of deer problems moving across the Commonwealth. The game commission has spent money on studies and management, but farmers, foresters and insurance companies are still filing complaints.

headline: Helmet fans, foes buffet Ridge
abstract: Govenor Tom Ridge has only 4 weeks to sign or veto a bill to repeal the helmet law. Pennslyvania supports and oponnets have been expressing their opinions on the subject.

headline: Board applicants should be public
abstract: Southeast Delco School Board is not releasing the names of applicants to district residents for vacant board positions. This practice seems to be in violation of the Sunshine Law.

headline: U.S. Senate accepts 2 for federal bench
abstract: Commonwealth Secretary Yvette Kane and Lackawanna James M. Munley yesterday were confirmed by the U.S. Senate to serve as federal judges for the Middle District of Pennsylvania.  Kane, a Hampden Twp. Resident, was nominated for the post by President Clinton on June 4.  She will be sworn in next week.

headline: Credit union law needed
abstract: Representative Ron Klink writes to the Butler Eagle to tell readers how important the new credit union law is.

headline: Commentator sees McHale as VP nominee-for GOP
abstract: Conservative commentator Bill Kristol made a surprising prediction that outgoing U.S. Representative Paul McHale, a Democrat, would receive the 2000 vice presidential nomination for the Republican Party. While McHale does share some common viewpoints with Republicans in terms of national defense and was one of the first Democrats to call for President Clinton’s resignation, he said he expects to remain a Democrat and cannot envision being a candidate for any office in 2000. He will begin work in the private sector, but he did say he would, if chosen, serve in an appointed position at the Pentagon.

headline: Luksik keeps crusade for values alive
abstract: Peg Luksik, third party candidate for Governor,  went to attend a community meet with local Latino media and community leaders, but the event coordinator had forgotten to call everyone. She got all the information and did it herself, which shows why she is the most popular third party candidate in a long time. Her campaign talks openly about religion in politics. She believes in changing the way government runs.

headline: Sunshine Law needs more improvement
abstract: The Valey Dusoatch News says that changes in the new Sunshine Law are expected to benefit taxpayer and the general public, however, the changes could have been better and more beneficial .

headline: Tax reform sounds like tax shift
abstract: With property taxes increasing by about 10 percent a year over the past decade in PA, voters approved a constitutional amendment last November called the Homestead Exemption that would allow residential property to be taxed at a different rate than commercial and industrial properties. A key focus of the new legislative session will be tax reform, and the PA House Finance Committee has already received a Senate version of tax reform, which the committee’s chairman, Representative Karl Boyes, hopes to deal with this spring. Representative Raymond Bunt, a member of the Finance Committee, said the general consensus in the Legislature is that income taxes, not property taxes, should be used to fund education; however, there are still three major areas of disagreement over the Senate’s bill.

headline: Bill: Cigarette tax hike would fund anti-smoking ads
abstract: PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf has proposed increasing the state’s cigarette tax by five cents a pack to raise an estimated $50 million that would be used to fund an advertising campaign against tobacco. He also suggests some of the money be put towards a help line to help smokers quit as well as police departments, so they can hire more officers to enforce the law preventing tobacco sales to minors. Pennsylvania’s cigarette tax is below the national average, and Greenleaf claims this tax, unlike a federal bill that was just rejected, wouldn’t cause an excessive financial burden on smokers.

headline: At a charter school in Phila., the test begins
abstract: The library still had no books or shelves and some of the offices were bare. But that barely registered with Kevin Williams as he waited for his stepson outside the new West Oak Lane Charter School. The new charter school is a chance for students to have smaller classes and more attention. Skeptics don't believe this is the answer to the problems with public schools.

headline: Compromise will expand opportunities for junior hunters
abstract: The Game Commission reached a compromise on its controversial initiative to allow junior hunters to kill antlerless deer during the buck season. the commission voted unanimously to allow junior hunters to shoot antlerless deer on both Saturdays of the traditional two-week buck season. The ambitious proposal was rooted in a belief that providing more opportunities for young hunters to harvest deer would help to cement a lifelong interest in hunting among its younger participants.

headline: Helmets should stay mandatory
abstract: The authors of the editorial are against a bill that would repeal the law requiring all motorcyclists to wear a helmet. A similar bill was passed in Maryland that led to a significant increase in deaths from motorcycle accidents, and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration predicted that if it passes, it could cost the state more than $32 million a year because of increased medical costs and injury-related expenses stemming from accidents. While motorcyclists say helmet laws infringe on their individual rights, the authors claim it is unfair for taxpayers to have to pay for these rights, and they hope Governor Ridge chooses to veto the bill.

headline: Borski bill protects elders
abstract: US Representative Robert Borski is supporting legislation in Congress to address the growing problem of elder abuse. In an effort to comfort this complex issue, Borski is cosponsoring the Older Women's Protection Act of 1998." The legislation will help protect people from elder abuse, including domestic violence and sexual assault, as well as institutional and community violence.

headline: Underage drinking campaign gets boost
abstract: PA Liquor Control Board gets $400,000 grant to help curb underage drinking in PA.

headline: Credit union law needed
abstract: U.S. Representative Ron Klink addressing the public about House Resoltuion 1151, to protect concumers who enjoy credit union membership.

headline: Comments from Pennsylvania lawmakers about State of the Union address:
abstract: The article provides numerous quotes from PA Congressmen in response to President Clinton’s State of the Union address, including U.S. Representatives Bob Borski, William Coyne, Mike Doyle, Jon Fox, George Gekas, William Goodling, James Greenwood, Ron Klink, Frank Mascara, Paul McHale, John Murtha, John Peterson, Joseph Pitts and Bud Shuster. Clinton’s proposals on fixing Social Security, spending surpluses, balancing the budget, Medicare, lowering taxes, education funding, health care reform and foreign policy were topics discussed by the congressmen. Some of the congressmen’s quotes are also in reference to sexual allegations against Clinton.

headline: Luksik presents more than 75,000 petition signatures
abstract: The Constitutional Party’s gubernatorial candidate, Peg Luksik, submitted three times as many signatures as she needed to run as a third-party candidate, which she attributed to the strength of her campaign. She said it was important for her to obtain more signatures than she did four years ago in her run for governor because of a bill Governor Ridge ultimately vetoed under public pressure that would have significantly raised the number of signatures required for third-party candidates. Republicans and Democrats already have notable advantages in the number of signatures required, and Luksik saw it as an attempt to prevent her from running again.

headline: Surprising 43 apply to join City Council
abstract: Forty three Harrisburg residents have applied to the City Council, which is by far the most that have run for city office, but only one will be selected to replace Frank DeGarcia, who resigned. Three council members will privately narrow the list down to three to five applicants who will then be interviewed in a public session. Mayor Stephen Reed felt like the entire process should be done publicly, and the article provides the names and brief descriptions of 14 of the applicants.

headline: Budget surplus can lower debt
abstract: The nearly $800 billion in tax cuts proposed by the Republicans can be used to reduce debt if they remained in the fedral as surpluses.

headline: Bill to bail farmers not enough for Holden
abstract: Congressman Holden(D) criticized the $ 69 billion appropriations for operations of USDA. The $1.2 billion drought bill was insufficient as the losses in PA due to drought was estimated to be $ 1.3 billion.

headline: School vouchers may survive Senate vote
abstract: House Republicans have said their first vote on tuition vouchers is likely to pass an Academic Recovery proposal. Senate Majority Leader Loeper said that if the House passes the proposal the Senate would also work towards the same and keep the vouchers in it.

headline: Local legislators wait for data on car cell phones
abstract: State legislation may ban cell phone use in cars that has several talking and many legislators from Chester County ambivalent over whether to endorse it.  A conservative Republican group from Chester County said they wanted to see facts and figures before deciding whether they should regulate cell phone use in cars.

headline: Ex-law clerk says judge threatened her
abstract: Attorney Beth Boris said the five years she spent working as the law clerk and staff for Luzerne County Judge Ann H. Lokuta were the most harrowing of her life.  Boris believed that she had to endure Lokuta's alleged repeated sexual advances because the judge had her convinced that she would make sure no one would hire her.  Boris eventually quit in 1997 and moved to Florida and this week confirmed that she has filed a report with the Judicial Conduct Board.

headline: Giles: Downtown stadium's odds '50-50'
abstract: Outgoing Phillies chairman Bill Giles said that the odds that the Phillies new ballpark stadium would go at Broad and Spring Garden streets are at 50-50, which is more pessimistic than Mayor Rendell expressed previously.  A unanimous city council demanded that the Phillies and Eagles provide them precise information as soon as possible on where the teams plan to build new stadiums and how much the city is expected to contribute.

headline: Sherwood introduces legislation
abstract: Congress Dan Sherwood introduced legislation to bring fair treatment to families of victims involved in airline disasters over international waters.  The Airline Disaster Relief Act would allow families who have lost loved ones in aviation disasters over international waters to seek fair compensation.  It addresses inequities faced by families like those in Montoursville who lost loved ones in the TWA Flight 800 disaster in July 1996.

headline: Dancing in the Legislature
abstract: The Pennsylvania Lottery is teaming up with tax collectors for a promotional program that simultaneously takes money from Pennsylvanians while giving them a chance to win some of it back.  Officials from the state Revenue Department and Internal Revenue Service will be visiting 10 shopping malls around the State to promote a system that allows people to file tax returns by telephone.  Taxpayers who bring their financial records to the designated malls can file their returns in just 10 to 15 minutes.

headline: Reenact a mayor's worst nightmares
abstract: Opinion article saying that forum's are not really showing who the mayoral candidates for Philadelphia are yet a role playing exercise would show who they are better.  Role playing as though they would be going through real life situations as the mayor.  Article discusses 4 situations to role play.

headline: Ridge dismisses consideration of special session
