abstract: Governor Ridge has dismissed a call to convene the state legislature for a special session on property tax reform saying that he prefers instead to wait until 2001 to gauge the results of Act 50.  State Senator Lisa Boscola, Democrat-18th, urged Ridge to convene the special session saying that waiting will only result in a mish-mash of taxation in Pennsylvania.

headline: Bush goes on the stump fresh from tax-cut victory
abstract: Texas Governor George Bush saw the Legislature approve tax cuts worth about $1.85 billion, less than he asked for but enough to claim bragging rights.  It was $800 million less than what Bush wanted, just over one-forth the $6.4 billion budget surplus.  Democrts said Bush ducked the tough issues like teacher pay and children's health insurance.

headline: Bunt unveils $ 173 M farm aid plan
abstract: State Rep Raymond Buntun viels a $ 173 million plan to provide farmers with drought assistance. This legilation will address the immediate and long term needs of farmers.

headline: School, vouchers are risky on financialm educational grounds
abstract: The authors writes that support for vouchers comes from economic and not from educational interests. The author also tells us that public schools are better than private schools in every way and the  supporters for the voucher program want to believe otherwise.

headline: Pa. highway plan includes Monroe bypass
abstract: The $68 million Marshalls Creek bypass and several other projects to ease traffic congestion in Monroe County have top priority on the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's new blueprint for priority work.  The Transportation Commission vowed to keep the bypass project on a path to completion by 2003.

headline: Fathers fight for custody rights
abstract: Members of the Greater Pittsburgh Chapter of the National Congress for Fathers and Children and other pro-fathers groups staged the Father's Day rally at the City-County building in Pittsburgh.  Speakers said that dads who want to take an active role in raising their children are often forced into legal battles to achieve even limited custody.

headline: Give tax freeze plan a warmer reception
abstract: School board members of Council Rock have shown litter interest in land preservation which is a shame for development ravaged communities like Netown, Northhampton and Upper Makefield townships. Three times this ,month the board stepped away from offering land preservation incentives provided by the state's Act 153.  All four municipalities have asked the board to adopt the measure.  School districts can freeze the taxes of landowners who agree to protect their properties from development through conservation easements.

headline: Some regulation is warranted to improve sweepstakes mailings
abstract: The United States Congress is investigation the sweepstakes industry which sends mailings to residents stating that they have won a grand prize.  Sweepstakes can be a successful marketing tool but consumers should be informed of the odds of winning rather than putting such information in small print that the elderly have trouble seeing.

headline: David Duke Misses Louisiana Runoff but Has Strong Showing
abstract: David Duke, a Republican campaigning for the first Congressional District in Louisiana, received one of every five votes in the District despite being a former Ku Klux Klan leader and self styled defender of the rights of European Americans.  Duke's strong showing fell short of qualilfying for the House seat yet caused some anxiety to the party as they try to broaden their appeal among minorites.  In Louisiana Republicans and Democrats run against one another in a first primary.  If no clear candidate wins a majority, the top two compete in a runoff.

headline: Reform Party
abstract: The Reform Party's presidential nominating convention will be August 10 - 13 in Long Beach, California.  The 8 to 3 vote by the party's executive committee was a setback for Minnesota Governor Jesse Ventura, the party's highest elected official, who had been pushing his state.  Michael Farris, presidential nomination committee, said Long Beach submitted a detailed proposal while Minnesota officials still were deciding among four possible cities.

headline: School district lowers school taxes
abstract: Low-income homeowners could get a break in the amount of school taxes they pay by freezing their taxes as long as they live in their homes under a reform plan adopted by the Pennsylvania legislature.  Coatesville Area School district is the first in the state to adopt the measure on a one-year trial basis.

headline: Capitol Chimes
abstract: Pennsylvania state sales taxes are approximately $6.3 billion a year or about a third of the state's general fund taxes.  This tax is threatened by purchases made online via the Internet.  Under state law, a person buying on the Internet from out of state and receiving the goods in Pennsylvania without sales tax is under an obligation to pay a use tax.

headline: Candian kids aim letter at Hegins shoot
abstract: Article discusses Canadian children's disgust at Prince Charles School in Saskatchewan with an annual pigeon shooting event written about in a book written by Pennsylvania author Jerry Spinelli.  The book is called "Wringer" and discusses an annual pigeon shooting event at a fictional town called "Waymer" where people shoot pigeons and boys break the necks of the pigeons that are shot but have not died.  The boys were called "trapper boys."

headline: Schools cool to Ridge's local voucher plan
abstract: Local school officials say that they don't foresee the creation of local school voucher program even if they are authorized by a compromise choice school bill facing a final showdown at the state Capitol.

headline: Local officials testify for Route 219
abstract: State Representative Bob Bastian, Republican-Somerset, and Somerset County Commissioner Brad Cober testified before the state Transportation Commission on the importance of Route 219 to the county's economy.  Bastian says the lack of a north-south highway has hampered efforts to revitalize the economy.

headline: Fault fortress

Senator Santorum was headed to York that day and the school worked in a 45-minute session with the high school students.

abstract: State Legislators are considering a bill that would lock the cars owned by people with three convictions for drunken driving. Supporters of this legislation say that this would keep chronic DUI drivers pff the road.

headline: Fingerprinting
abstract: Law enforcement has depended on fingerprints for identification believing that no two are alike.  Fingerprints also give law enforcement one foolproof tool against the rising incidence of check fraud.  It is a tool that should be made available to all including businesses using check card terminology.

abstract: Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board Chairman John E. Jones III announced an immediate ban on all retail sales of grain alcohol from its 648 state stores as a move he says to try and reduce binge drinking on the state's college campuses.  Grain alcohol is a clear tasteless beverage that at 190 proof has a much higher alcohol content than most commercial liquors and been long used as a base for potent punches mixed in bulk and quaffed at college parties.

abstract: Gary Bauer, in his run for the presidential election nomination of the republican party, is concerned that after he officially announces his candidacy he will get "put into a box" of being labled a religious conversative.  He will try to delicately move to gain more voter support although few know him outside his circle.

Bill "Whitey" Coolbaugh, rescue Chief for Reliance, had been trying to get one of the cameras since seeing it in firefighting magazines and at trade shows but the cost made it out of reach. Street, mayoral candidates for Philadelphia, were both responding to the Eastern Philadelphia Organizing Project to make the removal of abandoned vehicles, and other quality of life issues, a priority in their mayoral administrations. He proposed making a category of police officers to target quality of life issues in the neighborhoods.

Rendell is barred by city charter from seeking a third consecutive term.

headline: Crop Concern
abstract: Article discusses the condiitions of two family farms in Pulaski Township which are at opposite ends of Cheriwood Road.  The Anderson farm, despite the drought, is having a fairly successful crop because hit and miss rains have actually fallen just right for them to benefit.  The Mijavec farm, by contrast which is less than a mile from the Anderson farm, is "getting by."  They are expecting a lesser yield due to how dry the soil is.  Some cornstalks are only four feet high when they should be six feet high.  The Mijavec's planted only 35 acres of sweetcorn on a 120 acre farm.  Both farmers are saying that if they both don't get rain soon the summer growing season will over.

Now the Transportation Department wants to add 5 overhead message boards during next year's $51.1 million reconstruction of Interstate 81.

headline: State surplus should benefit homeowners, schools not businesses
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is pushing business tax cuts that benefit mostly big corporations with little or no relief for working families.  Under the Ridge plan, Pennsylvania will have cut business taxes by nearly $3.9 billion since 1994.  This represents a fifth of all general fund tax revenues collected by the state in the current fiscal year.  Despite a recod budget surplus brought on by a robust economy working families in the state have received little in the way of tax relief during the past four years.  By comparison to New Jersey and Texas there have not been significant tax cuts like in those states for working families of Pennsylvania.  In fact, most residents have been paying higher taxes since Governor Ridge took office.

headline: DEMOCRATS FIND CANDIDATE TO RUN FOR SEYFER SEAT
abstract: Erie County Democratic Chairman Pat Cappabianca believes he has found a candidate for the 5th District House seat in Crawford Candidate.  Karen Mulkearn is a well known businesswoman from Sadsbury Township on the outskirts of Conneaut Lake and has been active in Democratic politics in Crawford County.  Seyfer, a Republican was indicted in November on criminal charges and is not seeking reelection.  Her seat has been held by Republicans for more than 20 years.

abstract: Pennsylvania House Democratic Leader William DeWeese, Democrat-Green/Fayette/Washington, appointed Representative Mike Hanna to one of four Democratic seats on the 10-member Select Committee on Rules Review.  One of Hanna's top priorities is reforming the way the House does the people's business in Harrisburg.

abstract: The Local Taxpayers Bill of Rights, part of the purported tax reform law approved last year by the Pennsylvania legislature, is not popular with many local officials.  Mike Christopher, Washington Township manager, called Act 50 a well intended law that went off track and is of no use to taxpayers.

abstract: Philadelphia in 1991 was a financial basked case and not even Ed Rendell would make a hard commitment not to raise taxes.  Eight years later balanced budgets are not even an issue.  The five mayoral democratic candidates debate whether a $150 million tax cut would be enough.  Marty Weinberg has proposed the most aggressive tax-cut by proposing to lower the wage tax to 4 percent to stay competitive with the suburban communities.

headline: Democrats call for emergency legislative session on drought
abstract: Pennsylvania House Democrats, in response to a drought that a Clinton administration official said could cost farmerrs half their net cash income, called for a special session of the Legislature.  Undersecretary for foreign and farm services at the Depatment of Agriculture, Gus Schumacher, said that this is probably the worst drought to hit Pennsylvania farmers in a century.  Schumacher testified in front of a House Democratic Policy Committee on the drought that came with a mini political storm as the Democrats accused the Ridge administration of trying to squelch Schumacher's appearance.  The Governor's administration was concerned that the hearings would be too partisan.

Movement on the issue does not seem likely as Republicans, who are in the majority in the House, and Governor Ridge are focused on school vouchers and summer break.

abstract: State Representative Daryl Metcalfe, Republican-Cranberry, has proposed rewriting Pennsylvania's Urban Renewal Law to greatly limit the authority of local government to seize private property for redevelopment purposes.  Metcalfe all but admitted his aim is to stop Pittsburgh from using eminent domain authority to seize property for the so-called Fifth and Forbes in the downtown area.

abstract: Ron Culpepper of the Ohio Consumers' Council said he could help stop unwelcome telemarketing calls.  The Council recommends that consumers should tell a telemarketer to have their name removed from that company's "selling list" as it will not only remove the name from the company's do not call list but will not allow that same company to sell it to another telemarketing firm.

William DeWeese, Democrat-Greene, told members of the Alliance of Bikers Aimed Toward Education that it's not whether you get knocked down but if you get back up in regards to their efforts to repeal the state's helmet law.  A bill that would have lifted the requirement for motorcyclists over 21 who have at least two years of riding experience made it through the House of Representatives but died in a 26-24 Senate vote.

headline: Republican Convention Plans Revealed
abstract: State and national Republican leaders are already deep into planning next summer's national party convention at Philadelphia's First Union Center and are marshaling a force of thousands to pull it off.  It will be the first convention in Philadelphia since 1948.  Attendance is expected to reach about 45,000 people, including 5,000 state party delegates, 15,000 reporters and between 8,000 and 10,000 volunteers.  It is expected to raise $125 million in direct revenues and another $200 million in indirect revenues.

headline: Verna earns respect
abstract: Philadelphia City Council President Anna Cibotti Verna replaced John Street and was thought be little more than a caretaker and no more than political referee by some on the Council.  Out from under John Street and Ed Rendell leaving office it was thought city council might run amok but consensus and peace emerged.

headline: Fed raises interest rates;economist expect more
abstract: The Federal Reseve raised the interest rate by a quarter point it signalled that it would keep the inflation under control. Ecconomists are better on higher hikes later during the year.

headline: Drought help for farmers delayed
abstract: United States Representative Ron Klink, Democrat - Murrysville, and federal Department of Agriculture undersecretary Gus Shumaker encouraged farmers by saying that relief could be on the way soon for farmers hard hit by the drought.  The relief, however, won't be available until fall at the earliest because of the Senate's rejection of a Democrat-backed $11 billion farm emergency bill last week.  Klink now hopes for aid to come in the fall when Congress reconvenes.  During meetings last week, Klink and Shumaker, plan to work out a proposal to bring more relief to farmers.

headline: Tax credit, school accedd on the agenda
abstract: The PA Public School Acces bill would require schole districts to permit home schoolers participate in certain extra curricular activities. This bill was introduced by state reperesentatuve McNaughton.

headline: Next debate: driver's ed
abstract: Teen driving safety advocates are now focusing their attention on driver education which some believe would complete the state's step toward graduated licensing.  If Governor Ridge signs a proposed bill, it would create a 14-member task force of state officials that will look at funding and mandating driver education in all school districts.

headline: Hearings in Phila to focus on umproving school safety
abstract: The Republican Policy Committee of the PA House of Representatives will hold a hearing on how to make  PA schools safer. In particluar focus will be the schools in Philadelphia.

headline: Industrial park gets a big shot in the arm
abstract: The Adams County Economic Development Corporation received a $1 million infrastructure development grant Friday with the promise of $5.5 million more to assist with the development of the Adams Commerce Center.  The Adams Commerce Center is a planned 182-acre light industrial and manufacturing park to be built at routes 30 and 15.  The $7.1 million project could bring about 1,400 jobs to the county.  Tracy Vernon of the Governor's Action Committee presented the Adams County Economic Development Corporation executive director Catherine Cresswell with a $1 million check from the Department of Economic and Community Development during a government picnic for government and business officials at the site of the future Adams Commerce Park.

headline: Tentative settlements offfered by the bank  in John Gardners Black case
abstract: Tentative settlement of $ 30 million was offered by the bank which sued John Gardner Black in the alleged municipal fraud case. The settlement was approved by Blair County Judge Hiram Carpenter 3.

headline: DEMS HOPING FOR MAJORITY
abstract: State Representative Steve Stetler, D-York is glad that his Democratic colleague, T.J. Rooney is not running for U.S. Congress. He is keeping his job as the Operations Chairman of the House Democratic Campaign Committee.  Democrats have targeted seats in Lackawanna, Erie, and York counties.

headline: Republicans see tonight's debate in N.H. as Bush's big test
abstract: George Bush will share a stage with his republican candidates which he hoped to avoid until at least a year later.His lead in the polls has vanished because he refused to participate in town hall meetings and debates with candidates.  His number one opponent is John McCain.  Pressure is on Bush to break out and make an impression.

headline: Voice opinion at tax-reform forum
abstract: The Pocono Record is hosting discussions on tax reform, suggestions for lawmakers, and concerns over rising property tax bills.  State Representative Joseph Battisto, business leaders and Pocono Mountain School Superintendent David Krauser will be there to share perspectives on issues.

headline: Few calls are heard for tax cuts
abstract: State Rep Greenwood asks for his constituents in Bensalem to speak their minds. Greenwood says the the economy and the lack of understanding of the budget by the public are foiling the GOP proposal.

headline: Drought makes 'farm crisis' a hot topic in D.C.
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers who did not previously pay attention to farmer's needs due to the drought they have endured are suddenly racing to have their districts declared disasater areas.  Farm advocates are worred that Washington will simply throw a few billion dollars at the problem and ignore the real issues that are causing the problem.  The real issues, despite the immense lack of rain, are the Asian financial meltdown, trade imbalances, productivity patterns and young people fleeing from the sight of barns.  Farming is changing in America.  Throwing money at a problem so that it the situation can go back to its original state may not address the real needs.  Aid will not reach farmers in time to buy feed for starving animals.  Senator Lugar, Republican - Indiana, warned payments will not get to farmers anytime soon.

headline: Teacher Quality Targeted
abstract: State legislative committee in Richmond approved a bill which adopted the carrot stick approach for teachers. According to this teachers who show good performance would be rewarded with monetary gains and extra training for in experienced and struggling teachers.

headline: Ohio should copy Pa.'s license law
abstract: People were relieved when Governor Ridge signed into law a bill that will toughen the standards for young drivers in the state.  Ohio, and all states, should enact law like this because it is just common sense.

headline: Heidnik moves closer to death
abstract: A federal judge refused to the consider the appeals of Heidnik's daughter to save her father's life.   Heidnik  had tortured women and killed others in his basement by lethal injection.

headline: It's an investment, it's not an expense
abstract: An editorial emphasizing the distinct meaning between an expense and an investment.  The stadium funding bill the Legislature passed is an investment for the state.

headline: The deal must clear reviews
abstract: The announcement of a merger between Pennsylvania Energy Company and Chicago's Unicom Corporation is only the first in a process that is sure to keep scores of lawyers busy.  The proposed merger faces review by at least four federal or state agencies.  The hardest investigation is expected to come from the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Dems seek a few good candidates
abstract: Within 10 months for the 2000 primaries Democratic Candidates are on the look out for candidates in Erie County, Washington and Harrisburg to run for the Senate and the Congress.

headline: Republicans Seem Poised to Call Witnesses, Risk Bipartisanship
abstract: After a flurry of high-pressure, closed-door talks among Senate Republican Leaders and the House Republican "managers," Republicans appeared poised yesterday to keep the impeachment trial of President Clinton going beyond this week and to depose witnesses, including Monica S. Lewinsky.  By keeping the trial going may be contributing to the realization that Clinton will escape without any punishment at all.  The Senate is about to make it more difficult for the House Republican leaders to make their case that Clinton deserves to be removed from office by denying them far-ranging latitude to call witnesses.

headline: Voters to decide state tax reform question
abstract: Five school districts out of 500 in Pennsylvania are offering a tax reform plan that will shift the burden from property owners to wage earners.  The law allows districts to increase their earned income and net profits tax by as much as 1 percent, but they would have to eliminate nuisance taxes and reduce property taxes.

headline: Free filing on Web debuts
abstract: Just as Pennsylvania residents are gearing up for the new year the Department of Revenue is preparing to send out more than six million reminders of the old one.  Tax payers should not count on any 'year 2000' problems to conflict with income tax forms from arriving their mailboxes.  In keeping with moving into the future the state is continuing to move toward paperless tax returns with the introduction of free Internet filing.

headline: Drought Relief
abstract: A spokesman for the United States Department of Agriculture said that Pennsylvania's request for drought emergency aid was being processed and could be approved soon.  Many counties are eligible for relief because they border counties that have already been declared primary disaster areas.

headline: Teaching is more than just money
abstract: PA had certified 14000 new teachers to fill 3000-4000 jobs last year. Teaching in rural and poor urban areas do not have  teachers, as many are refusing to work in schools based  in those area due to dangerous environment and lack of facilities.

headline: Pa. gets tougher on teen drivers
abstract: Pennsylvania's new teen driving laws make the driver's license process for teens tougher and of longer duration.  A 16 or 17 year old with a learner's permit will have to wait at least six months before he or she can take a driver's test and get a junior license.  The state Department of Transportation is issuing new guides for parents and teens.

headline: Heroin abuse on the rise in Philadelphia
abstract: Heroin abuse is on the rise in Philadelphia because of lower prices and high purity levels that is hooking a new generation of addicts.  Drug treatment centers are reporting a surge of youths seeking help for heroin addiction.  Police say they are arresting more teen-agers for heroin possession.

headline: 'Lead by example,' Argall says
abstract: Representative David G. Argall, Republican-124, says the state must lead by example at the "Sound Land Use Forum" at Pottsville's Quality Hotel.  He suggested 3 ways: enact his downtown location law, have the state consider heating with anthracite, and pass Argall's proposed $675 million "Growing Greener" state bond issue.

headline: The son rises, the son also falls- The story of Rite Aid
abstract: The exit of Martin L.Grass from  the Rite Aid empire,  the stock falling from $ 50 to $ 10, the $2.7 billion debt that the bankers hold brought down the curtain on a major business drama.

headline: Dems seek wider women's role in capitol race
abstract: With control of the legislature on the line next year, state Democrats are pulling out all the stops to make sure the Capitol is in their hands when the dust settles after next year's statewide elections.  Part of that effort includes reaching out to two segments of the party's traditional power base - young voters and women.

headline: Republicans set agenda for fall session
abstract: The Pennsylvania General Assembly went back to Harrisburg to introduce their initiatives before the end-of-the-year break.  Local Representative Larry Sather and House Majority leader Donald Snyder met with the Daily News to state that the Republicans who control the House have an ambitious agenda focusing on school safety and farmland preservation.

headline: What Candidates say about tax cuts
abstract: Ed Rendell has done some good things to move Philadelphia forward however the city remains the one of the most heavily taxed cities in the nation making it difficult to attract new business.  Job growth has been minimal and resident are leaving at a rate faster than in any other major U.S. city.  Basil Whiting, an urban affairs consultant who recently studied Philadelphia for the Pew Charitable Trusts, says "Philadelphia is stagnant."  The candidates for mayor, Sam Katz and John Street, both say taxes should be cut but differ on how much and how deep.  Street says cuts should be gradual and modest.  Katz says time is up and would reduce the wage tax from 4.6 percent to 4 percent.

headline: Give back more to state's littlle guys
abstract: Gov.Ridge's proposed tax cuts aims at job creation and a marginal decrease in personal income tax. The main focus will be reduce corporate stock,franchise tax and corporate income tax.

headline: Drought-relief program passes
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives have passage to a $65.6 million drought-relief program that earmarks $60 million in grants to help farmers recoup 1999 crop losses and $5.6 million in crop insurance incentives for next year.  Backers noted that the state money will combine with an estimated $75 million in federal aid to bring the total for drought relief in Pennsylvania to $135 million.

headline: Teaching standards cause legal battle
abstract: Groups representing teachers and educational professionals filed a lawsuit in Commonwealth Courts to block easier teaching standards in PA.

headline: Pa. Senate delays teen driver reforms
abstract: To tighten licensing requirements for teen driver, the Pennsylvania Senate may to vote to create a special trucking permit for oversized loads of "float glass or flat glass."  This provision, tailored to benefit PPG Industries, is one of several amendments tacked onto the teen-driving bill by the Senate.

headline: High court orders new trials, throws out wiretaps
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ordered new trials for Joseph Metts who was convicted of first-degree murder in Fayette County, and Tony Ardestani, who was convicted of trying to hire someone to kill his wife in Allegheny County.  Justice Zappala said wiretaps of the men's comments violated the state constitution's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures.

headline: KOZ entices two businesses to area sites
abstract: The Keystone Opportunity Zone redevelopment initiative has enticed two businesses to the Clearfield-Curwensville sub zone development sites.  The businesses are Lezzer Trust System and Elmco Pennsylvania, Incorporated.

headline: Trustees back center county vistors center
abstract: The nations governors would be among the first to visit Center County's vistors center. The final plan was aproved by Penn State Board of Trustees at the Great Valley Campus.

headline: Dems try to oust convicted lawmaker
abstract: A day after the Republican leadership in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives protected Representative Frank Serafini from being expelled as a convicted felon a government reform group said it may seek an injunction to prevent Serafini from performing duties as a public official.  Barry Kaufman, executive director of Common Cause Pennsylvania, explains that they have a solid legal case.

headline: Republicans set agenda for fall session
abstract: The Pennsylvania General Assembly will return to Harrisburg for 23 legislatives days in the fall touting their initiatives to be considered prior to the end of the year break.  Republican Representative Sather and House Majority Whip Snyder stated that Republicans control the House and have an ambitious agenda.  Majority leader Perzel has asked members to focus on school safety, preserving farmland, and repair damage done by to Pennsylvania's Megan's Law.

headline: What size is the right size for future Philadelphia?
abstract: What should the size, shape, and scope of city government be in the next century?  Philadelphia of the early 1900s resembled the Philadelphia of today in one startling and important way: population.  Philadelphia's population at the end of the 20th century will be about 1.4 million people but the government designed in the 1950s was set up to handle about 2 million people.

headline: Goodling played major role
abstract: US Rep Goodling(R) was one of the 12 members of the Congress appointed to the joint committee charged with developing a tax-cut plan that would strike a balance between the House and the Senate versions.

headline: Farm aid outlook pessimistic
abstract: Gov Tom Ridge and eight other East Coast Governors wrote to the Congressional leaders of the inadequte drought aid plan. State farm lobbyists also voiced the gloomy situation at Washington.

headline: Test Time
abstract: Educators voice concerns about  The Pennsylvania State System of Assessment(PSSA) as students prepare to take up the test. Educators feel that the state tests may not give necessarily refelect the overall potential of a student.

headline: Parents thank Ridge for pickup rider bill
abstract: Martin and Susan Couglin of Lake Harmony in Carbon County worked with Senator Hal Mowery, a Republican of Camp Hill, for four years to pass a law to make it illegal for children to ride in the back of pickup trucks because their 16 year old son Matthew was killed when thrown from the back of a truck.  Governor Ridge signed Mowery's bill into law which bans children 18 and under from riding in open truck beds, regardless of speed.

headline: Hitler death day heightens school alerts
abstract: School districts across the region wew on heightened aletr for trouble of several bomb threats and persistant rumors of school violence, some of which were tied to the death anniversary of Adolf Hitler.

headline: Kvaerner reported selling its shipyards
abstract: Kvaerner Group, the European company planning to build a major new shipyard at the former Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, will announce a major restructuring that could include selling all or part of its shipbuilding division.  A Norwegian daily newspaper reported a deal on the table to buy Kvaerner's shipbuilding operations for $650 to $680 million.

headline: Vote on gambling should be close
abstract: Supporters and opponnets neck to neck on the controversial trio gambling question: whether to legalize riverboat gambling;allow slots at the four horse racing tracks and whether to permit vieo poker machines in bars. The bill goes to the Senate for voting.

headline: Dems try to oust convicted lawmaker
abstract: State Representative Frank Serafini, Republican-Lackawanna-was convicted last August of perjury for lying to a federal grand jury about an illegal campaign finance scheme.  House Republicans who control the chamber by a narrow 3-seat majority, said they weren't required to take any action until he was sentenced.  Serafini was sentenced to five months in prison however that was delayed by the judge because of an appeal.  Democrats wasted little time trying to get him sent back to Lackawanna County.  Democratic House Leader H. William DeWeese attempted to suspend the House rules so members could consider a resolution to expel Serafini, but was blocked 95-92.  It was a partisan vote that Serafini was permitted to vote on.

headline: REPUBLICANS WORRY ABOUT LOSING CONTROL OF LEGISLATURE
abstract: According to state Representative Sam Smith, next year's state elections could determine which party control PA for a decade.  He said that Republican control of the Legislature is essential in 2000 because of the federal Census and subsequent shifting of boundaries of state districts.

headline: A Parent-Child Adventure
abstract: Superior Court Judge Corry Stevens and his 16 year old son participated and completed an eight-day parent-child course at the North Carolina Outward Bound School.  Outward Bound challenges individuals to push beyond themselves by living in the wilderness, learning how to navigate with a compass and a map, and respect for the environment.

headline: Goodling supports tax-cut plan
abstract: US Rep Goodling(R) supported the $ 864 billion tax cut proposal saying  this would support middle income American families.

headline: Farm aid package leaves out drought
abstract: By the passage of a $7.4 billion farm assistance package, tobaccco subsidies took precedence over the agricultural disaster which threatened livelihood of thousands of farmers. Sen Santorum fought for extra funding for speciality crops.

headline: Testing is a multiple choice answer
abstract: York suburban school districts starts  testing in grade 2. By the time York school district students graduate from high schools they would answered 100's of multiple choice questions, state assessments supplemented with private assessment. School use all these assessment to guage student skills and sharpen curriculum.

headline: PennDOT approves I-81 sounds barriers
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation announced areas that qualify for sound barriers on the east shore in three Lower Paxton Township neighborhoods.  To qualify, neighborhoods had to pass a three-pronged test with noise levels exceeding 66 decibels.

headline: Home and School must face violence
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher and Secretary of Education Hickok observe that violence at school could also be due to home environment. At the same time they do not blame all acts of violence on home and say that the whole environment in which the student interacts must be taken into considetation.

headline: Land use forum makes its way to Pottstown
abstract: Residents of the Pottstown area are going to speak their minds regarding the suburban sprawl issue they are facing at the Ramada Inn where Steve Morgan will be present who is the spokesperson for the Governor's Center for Local Government Services, a division of the Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development.  There will be 50 of these land use forums around the state.  The purpose of the forums is to find out what land use solutions work across the state.

headline: Wage increase is a non-state funded benefit
abstract: The National Federation of Independent Businesses which is voice for all small businesses. The Delaware chapter will take up the cause for Senate Bill 2 as this increases the state minimum wages from $5.15 to  $ 5.65.

headline: Disappointed Democrats Offer Chance for Bradley
abstract: Article gathering opinions from people on why the like Bill Bradley for president as opposed to Al Gore.  People are still feeling as though Gore is attached to Clinton and Bradley is separate enough.  Others feel that building a base that is anti-Clinton is not enough for Bradley to win the 2000 presidential election.

headline: Request for ouster has precedent in municipal case, attorney general says
abstract: State Attorney General Mike Fisher plans to use a legal maneuver that successfully ousted a township supervisor to remove convicted Frank Serafini if he refuses to resign.  Serafini has refused to resign while his case is under appeal and house democrats tried to remove him by a vote that was blocked.  Fisher set a deadline for Serafini to resign or face court action to remove him from office.  The attorney general cited a constitutional ban that prevents those  convicted of perjury and other crimes from serving in the General Assembly.

headline: A whirlwind of awards bringing Bush to Phila.
abstract: Michael Dannenhauer, chief of staff to former President George H. W. Bush, comments that the President will give two distinguished Americans honors and receive them himself on a two-day trip to Philadelphia in the span of 36 hours.  Bush will present awards to Walter H. Annenberg at the National Constitution Center and to Colin L. Powell, former chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, the Eishenhower Medal.

headline: GOP leaders urging rebels back to fold for big tax cut
abstract: With a vote for the biggest tax cut since 1981,  moderators have been pushing for a scale back  in the tax cutting package. Republican moderators lead by Rep Castle have proposed a packe no more than $ 514 billion.  A group of social conservatives are also pushing for the tax package to be changed.

headline: Farm bill opposed by Holden
abstract: US Rep Holden was forced to vote against $61 billion agriculture appropriations bill. The Republicans cuts in the measure would hurt vital programs in Holden's district. However, Rep Holden is confident that the cuts will be restored by the Senate or the Conference Committee.

headline: The Carnival has left Harrisburg
abstract: Governor Ridge's school-voucher program was not successful in the state general assembly and the Grower Greener initiative did no better.  Philadelphia Senator Vince Fumo made the new $400 million stadium for the Phillies disappear.

headline: PennDOT gears up to fight tag thefts
abstract: Authorities say that a black market for stolen license plates is thriving in Philadelphia.  The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is now proposing a series of tough measures to deal with the problem.  A task force is expected to recommend to the General Assembly to raise the fine for driving a vehicle with a stolen license plate from $75 to $1,000.

headline: Hospital stay over, Phoenix arraigned
abstract: Harrisburg City Councilman Zane Phoenix was arraigned on charges that he beat his girlfriend who then stabbed him in self-defense.  Dauphin County District Justice Joseph Solomon relapsed Phoenix on a $10,000 unsecured bond and set the preliminary hearing for January 11.

headline: Land-use forum elicits passionate words from crowd
abstract: The Ridge administration held its land-use forum in Chester county which is the under the most development pressure of Philadelphia's seven suburban counties in two states.  The turnout was high and the passion intense.  Bill Fulton, the county planning director, expalains that they are using all their resources toward the sprawl problem.

headline: Water limits binding drought-stricken states
abstract: Drought continues to be problematic for most of the east coast.  The heat is blamed for claiming at least 256 lives since mid-July.  Dave Ondrejiak, Service Hydrologist at the National Weather Service in State College, Pennsylvania, said that it takes a long time to get into a drought and a long time to get out of one.  Just about the only way to get out a drought like this is to have a tropical storm.  Governor Ridge has declared drought emergencies for 55 of 67 counties.

headline: District 1 candidates wage spirited campaign
abstract: Ronald Francis Jr., the Republican candidate for Allegheny County Council's District 1, made a speech at Stone Mansion Restaurant in Franklin Park and used the opportunity to slam his Democratic opponent Louis Coccoli Jr.  Francis said that Coccoli was Cyril Wecht's water boy, owner of a company that operates bars and restaurants at airports across the country, and running for a $9000 a year job hoping that it would benefit him personally.  Article discusses both candidates histories and backgrounds.

headline: Resolution approved to change date of election
abstract: The PA Senate has approved a Resolution sponsored by Senator Mowery that calls for a review of the current primary election system with the intention of moving the date to september.

headline: After surgery, Rendell relaxing at the Shore
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell is recovering at his house on the New Jersey shore following an hour-long hernia operation at Thomas Jefferson University Hospital.  The operation on his right inguinal hernia was routine and his surgeon states he his recovering nicely.  Rendell has previously undergone 4 hernia operations.

headline: GOP Senate Losers in Wisconsin Sees his  Passion To Reduce National Debt Embraced by 2 Parties.
abstract: GOP Senate loser Rep Neumann sees his passion for the reduction of national debt and is embraced by both the parties.Mr Neuman's electoral plans remain hazy. He has become a certified investment adviser as he wants to advise people to make good decisions.

headline: Farm groups call for law providing tax benefits, lawmaker seeks delay
abstract: Representative Scott Chadwick, Republican-Bradford, announced that he would introduce legislation to delay provisions of a new law designed to provide tax breaks to farmers so that impact of the changes on other taxpayers could be studied.  As the law is now, it could cause severe problems for local governments unless adequate plans are made to find other ways to make up the lost tax revenue.

headline: Under bill, parents would pay to school expelled students
abstract: A plan to make parents pay to their expelled children, eventhough would makle sense would be difficult to implement. This bill being sponsored by State Representative Egolf paased the House Education Committee.

headline: PennDOT road managers, assistants take the hot seat
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation maintenance managers and their assistants in all 67 counties will man the fix-it road hotline which is normally done by office personnel or recorded on voice mail.  Transportation Secretary Bradley Mallory states customers will have the opportunity to talk first hand with the people in charge of maintaining the roads.

headline: House adopts Semmel's resolution declaring Fire Prevention Week in Pa.
abstract: House members unanimously adopted a resolution introduced by Representative Paul W. Semmel, Republican-187, to declare October 3-9 as Fire Prevention Week in Pennsylvania.  As chair of the House Veterans Affairs and Emergency Preparedness Committee Semmel wants to raise public awareness to help prevent fire-related loss of life.

headline: Land-use reform nears vote
abstract: The state senate is expected to vote on Senate Bill 300, sponsored by Senator Gerlach, Republican-144th, that would empower municipalities to control sprawl with new planning and zoning tools.  Currently communities find themselves with few options for coping with issues like increased traffic on overburdened highways.  Gerlach says the legislation is needed to protect communities' way of life for existing residents.  One major tool to curb sprawl which would give municipalities relief from having to zone for every use within their own borders.

headline: Water Plentiful in Somerset despite drought, geologist says
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge says water rationing is still needed in Somerset County, but a geologist who has studied the issue says the county is awash in water.  James R. Casselberry, the groundwater geologist, said that there is more than enough water to supply the need it is just that the county needs to tap the water that is already there.  The problem is that the county has too many small suppliers that cannot cope with the cost of drilling, purifying it and getting it to the customers.

headline: District's new lawmaker sworn in
abstract: Jake Corman, Republican-Bellefonte, succeeds his father J. Doyle Corman who held the 34th District Senate seat for 20 years.  Jake remarks on attending all of his father's swearing in ceremonies and plans to push for more money for state universities.

headline: Restless Radicals
abstract: In 1994, the Republicans won control of both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years yet Newt Gingrich behaved like the leaders of a thuggish revolution rather than the winners of an election.  The Republican party is already right wing and it's already the party of mega-corporations and the ultra rich.  Republicans are right wing enough and need to remember a more moderate base.

headline: Capitol springs a leak
abstract: A broken water pipe flooded the Senate chamber and other parts of the state Capitol sending preservationists scurrying to prevent further damage.  Two state senators' offices and a staff office were ruined by the flooding, said Senate Chief Clerk Russell Faber.

headline: If Elected, Bush says, He'll Oppose Tax Increase
abstract: Texas Governor George Bush has been in the practice of keeping controversial issues under wraps but has announced that if elected he will try to block any proposed tax increase.  Opposing tax increases has been a staple for republicans in the New Hampshire primary.

headline: Farm groups unite on behalf of agriculture and rural Pennsylvania
abstract: US Congressman Klink (D), State Senators O'Pake(D), Steelman(D and State Rep Miller(D)along with the three main farm groups in PA discuss to bring to end the farm crisis due to drought of 1999.

headline: The teacher shortage
abstract: The long and costly teacher certification program is one of the main detterents to filling up PA growing teacher vacacies. PA has 169 different teaching licenses broken down into different categories.

headline: Pennsylvania Lemon law, whether consumers know it or not
abstract: Ron Barnes, a resident near Pittsburgh, bought a 1996 Chevy Blazer for $25,000. The Blazer's front end shook so bad that the customer could be barely take his eyes off the road.  The vehicle spent 70 days of the first six months in the garage under repair.  Barnes didn't know about the state's lemon law which is considered to be one of the most consumer-friendly in the country.

headline: House approves school safety measure
abstract: According to bill approved 195-0 in the House all the 501 school districts would require to submit detailed plans on how they are going to counter violence. This bill goes to the Senate for consideration.

headline: Latest stadium plan is better, but it's still flawed
abstract: Pennsylvania's professional sports team owners should be pay their players what they themselves can afford to pay and leave the tax payer out of it.  If team owner's cannot control their costs putting them on par with player salaries of other teams then why should costs spread to taxpayers?  All of this is in light of Governor Ridge proposing to raise the debt ceiling to $650 million.

headline: Water restrictions may be imminent
abstract: Susan Rickens, spokeswoman for the deparment of environmental protection, said that they are planning for a worst case scenario as most of Pennsylvania's counties are on a drought emergency status enforcing mandatory water restrictions.  Governor Tom Ridge is expected to make a major announcement in regards to the drought and the state's drought emergency task force recommended that the governor declare a drought emergency for up to 55 counties.  Other than sporadic rains, there has not been enough rain in terms of amount and frequency needed to add to the declining water tables.  Suan Obleski, spokeswoman for the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, said that conditions are worse now than they had been since the last drought like this in 1964.

headline: Dividing Point
abstract: Pennsylvanians will find out soon if the state courts hold that the law applies equally to everyone or if they decide that there are two classes of citizens, namely lawyers and non-lawyers.  Lawyers are challenging the Lobbyist Disclosure Act which is set to take effect August 1 where they are contending that the law unconstitutionally regulates the practice of law.  Lawyer-lobbyists seek to avoid disclosure of the amount of funds spent to influence legislation by hiding behind a claim of lawyer-client privilege.

headline: Retiring mayor takes shot at Goldie
abstract: McKeesport Mayor Lou Washowich announced yesterday that he is going to take an early retirement. As he announced that he also took shots at Council member Mary Ann Goldie claiming that she "has a record as a tax scofflaw." These attacks were in response to attacks that Goldie had made earlier towards the Mayor and his family.

headline: Chamberlain began wowing peers, fans in high school
abstract: Tony Daversa recalls his memories of playing basketball against Wilt Chamberlain who played for Overbrook High School and took the school to three public school championships and two all-city titles before graduating in 1955.  When the news spread of Chamberlains' death, Daversa described him as the greatest player in basketball who stood 7 feet 1 inches.

headline: Hastert Looks at Easing Spending Limits
abstract: House Speaker Hasert opened doors for Republicans to loosen spending restraints that helped the first balanced budget in a generation. The search for new resources especially Defense and Education parallels a GOP effort to pass big tax cut.

headline: Farm hosts visit by local, state officials
abstract: Local farms in Hershey host Sen Santorum, Sen Specter, Sen Wenger and Rep Gekas to demonstrate the effect of drought. Sen Santorum announces $7.4 billion farm assistance fund.

headline: The voucher solution
abstract: The writer says that the courts have ruled that the voucher would go to a student and not to the relegious order. He allo writes that most of the arguments against the voucher did not seem to stem from the minority groups as people would expect it.

headline: Pennsylvania not listed as state with worst roads
abstract: According to Overdrive magazine, Pennsylvania is now for the first time in nine years not the state with the worst roads in the nation.  The state tied for Illinois with the worst highways which are rated by truck drivers.  Governor Ridge lobbied for a year before obtaining an increase in gasoline taxes and vehicle registration fees in 1997 to increase state money for maintenance of state roads.

headline: House rejects efforts to do away with executions

headline: Lawmaker will revise sprawl bill
abstract: State Senator Jim Gerlach, Chester County, said that he would drop language that would permit local officials to delay development plan approvals until key traffic improvements are completed in the hotly debated land-use bill scheduled for a senate vote in order to salvage the proposed legislation.  The concurrency clause was designed to help the state's fastest-growing areas deal with their growing pains.  As proposed, the measure would have allowed municipal officials to delay approval of housing developments for as many as 5 years while required highway improvements are made if located in a high growth county and have a master plan.

headline: We're all in drought together
abstract: Citizen's response to Governor Tom Ridge's drought-emergency declaration have been positive.  It has, however, spurned a number of calls from citizens in the Pittsburg area to the local office of the Department of Environmental Protection for clarification of the water restriction rules.  The aim of Ridge's water restriction declaration was to reduce water usage.  If citizens are seen violating the declaration officers have been asked to use discretion where first time violators will most likely receive a warning.  Article discusses further how the "warning first" approach by police makes them appear to citizens.

headline: Dixie Coup - Democrats rise again, give GOP revolution quite a turn in South

headline: Conservatives Attack Pat Robertson's Clinton Remark

There were indications that conservatives were in fact pulling back from impeachment as the stronger detractors of the President were not making remarks to remove him during the Conservative Political Action Conference.

headline: Farmers can get grants for hay crop losses
abstract: Livestock farmers devastated by this year's drought can now apply for state aid under a $5 million Hay Assistance Program.  The program, initiated by Governor Tom Ridge last month, will partially reimburse qualifying farmers who lost most of their hay crop used to feed livestock.  How much each farmer gets will be determined by the number of applicants, but, not all livestock farmers will receive aid according to Bill Steel, President of the Pennsylvania State Grange. The cuts include nearly $400 million in reductions in business and consumer taxes, tax forgiveness, for low-income Pennsylvanians and a property tax rebate for some senior citizens.  The measure will now return to the Senate for voting.

Scores in the most fundamental area - reading - rose across the board.  On the other side, middle-school students are in danger of losing ground because math and science scores went down.

In 1997 Kingston passed an ordinance banning bring your own beer clubs to prevent nude dance clubs.  State law does not allow nude dancing in an establishment where there is a Pennsylvania liquor license.  Jules Greenberg, owner of the club that featurs partial nudity, has applied to de-license a part of his club to allow full nude dancing.  The liquor control board approved his request. Bunt, author of the largest of the aide plans, invited both parties to weigh in on the drought-relief package, which will be coordinated by the House and Senate Agriculture Committee staffs.

The repair facility would secure thousands of jobs and ensure that Pittsburgh remains the airline's major maintenance hub.

Her resignation from president as head of the red cross was seen as in informal sign that she will run.  Fund-raising will be a problem.  Dole served as labor secretary under Bush Senior and transportation secretary under Reagan.

headline: Farmers wait for drought relief funds
abstract: Representative Raymond Bunt, Republican - Schwenksville and chairman of the House Agricultural and Rural affairs committee, said that the agricultural community may know as early as next Monday which counties may qualify for federal disaster relief funds due to the drought.  Federal disaster relief is made by a county-by-county basis and in this case crop losses must exceed 30%.  Governor Ridge would also have to make a formal request for aid to the United State secretary of agriculture.

Anne Franchak, executive director of the Coalition, says that the Transportation department has been aware of the program as they have been advocating for it since 1992.

headline: Killer of officer slain in prison
abstract: Robert "Mudman" Simon was convicted to a life sentence after killing Franklin Township (New Jersey) police officer Ippolito Gonzalez.  He was serving his life sentence in the New Jersey State prison and was killed there by a fellow death row inmate at the Trenton facility.  Simon had originally served 12.5 years in prison in the Pennsylvania State Correctional Institution at Graterford in 1974 for killing his girlfriend, Beth Ann Dusenber, 19, because she refused to have sex with fellow Warlocks motorcycle gang members.  Simon was convicted of second degree murder and become eligible for parole and was released in 1994.  Two months after the murder Pennsylvania changed the second degree murder penalty to life without parole.

headline: Legislators head back to business
abstract: State Representative Gary Haluska, Democrat-Patton, states that Governor Ridge has made a big issue of stadium funding and wants to obtain $300 million for new stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  Haluska mentioned mixed views of supporting the endeavor as he stated he would have trouble looking people in the eyes who do not have safe water to drink and have to collect water to flush commodes.  He would support low-interest loans to support the program.

State Representative Samuel E. Rohrer said that the speech was unifying, and that is good, yet there was little detail.  State Senator Micheal A. O'Pake, a democrat from Reading, agreed that the speech was unifying but if the Governor really wants to be unifying he should propose tax cuts in property and personal income so that working families can enjoy the budge surplus.

headline: Farmland Preservation Criticized
abstract: James H. Broussard, of Citizens Against Higher Taxes, states that the Democratic candidates for Bucks county commissioner have a plan to spend the county reserves on farmland preservation which would wipe out the county surplus.  Sandra Miller and Christopher Serpico's plan, according to Broussard, would be to spend $10 million of the $18 million on farmland perservation.  Democrats say they never said that, only that they would consider spending up to that amount.

abstract: Pittsburgh Chief City Magistrate Williams Simmons says that the PA State Legislature should tighten  licensing laws, and the punishment for an induvidual driving with a suspended license should be more severe.

About $103,000 was spent in overtime and about $10,200 in helicopter equipment costs during the search.

headline: Legislators help locate owners of unlcaimed property
abstract: Nearly 160 state lawmakers participated in a bipartisan program aimed at finding people who have unclaimed property.  The Treasury Department's Bureau of Unclaimed Property is responsible for reuniting people with forgotten loot from sources like abandoned bank accounts, security deposits, or tax refunds.  The amount of unclaimed property in the state's possession totals $500 million.  State Treasurer Barabara Hafer suggests that everyone check the records because even though someone may be certain they have no unclaimed property, they might be heirs to some.  There is no time limit for claiming forgotten property.

headline: Bill would give some WWII vets diplomas
abstract: Senator Raphael Musto, Democrat-Luzerne, introduced a bill that would give high school diplomas to veterans who left high school early to serve in World War II.  The bill would be patterned off of Massachusetts' similar program and called Operation Recognition.

abstract: Elizabeth Dole will announce next Wednesday that she is forming an exploratory committee toward seeking the republican nomination for president in 2000.  The committee will allow her to explore fund-raising and organizing efforts.  Polls indicate that she is the strongest female candidate for the presidency in history.

abstract: Republican House Representatives are pushing for a proposal to reduce the personal income tax to middle-income constituents. Treasurer Barbara Hafer takes the position that anyone who withdraws from the program gets back the money they deposited minus the program's enrollment fees.  Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr. said the law mandates that those opting out of the program receive only 90 percent of the account's value, or 90 percent of the tuition for the number of of tuition credits purchased, whichever is less.  In one case an account holder was refunded nearly $500 more than required.

Philadelphia's lead lawyer told the judge that things had gotten much better in its prisons but got in trouble when asked about progress towards replacing the aging House of Correction with a new facility.

abstract: The Central Philadelphia Development Corporation wants more office workers because the more tax revenue the city can generate through business growth, the faster it can cut wage and business tax rates while maintaining, or even increasing, spending on schools and neighborhoods.  They have prepared analysis of building size and projected revenues.

The Guard would only step in when other organizations could not provide the service.

abstract: Faced with the prospect of delaying aid to farmers until next year due to loss of crop to the drought, the House of Representatives voted 138-54 to accept a Senate plan to authorize $65.6 million in drought assistance. headline: Lawmakers map out plans for tax reforms
abstract: Just as the current tax filing session is complete lawmakers are looking ahead to revamp taxes for 1999 and beyond. Tax suggestions offered by lawmakers include breaks for working parents, easing on senoir citizens and trimming the income tax rate.

headline: Law that could give wealthy a tax break reconsidered
abstract: State Representative Scott Chadwick said that the Pennsylvania House of Representatives Agricultural Committee will consider suspending implementation of recently passed legislation that may award an unfair tax break to mini-estates and wealthy land developers at the expense of the majority of taxpayers.  Act 156 of 1998 changed the manner in which properties qualify for Clean and Green tax breaks.

headline: Tuition rise for 14 state universities awaits voice
abstract: Tuition could increase by a $150 for under graduate students attending the 14 state universities. The proposed hike of 4.3 percent is consistent with the hike since 1993-94

headline: Proposals for new drivers make sense
abstract: The shocking deaths of five Delaware County girls in a car driven by a 16-year old reinforces a call by Governor Ridge for better training of young motorists.  There is no fool proof way to teach caution but an intelligent licensing program should at least attempt to make them mindful of the risks and get them off to a good start.

headline: Judiciary hearings to probe breakouts
abstract: After Martin F. Horn took over as Pennsylvania's prison commissioner he set a no-nonsense tone and initiated a massive and highly publicized drug and weapons sweep at Graterford which is considered to be the most corrupt prison in the state.  In the four years since that search Horn has earned widespread praise for cleaning up the system.  Now with the escapes of Norman Johnston along with McCloskey and Yang his leadership is under new criticism.

headline: Lynch: price tag for new stadiums rising
abstract: State Representative Jim Lynch states that Governor Ridge has already exceeded the plan to spend $500 million on new sports stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  Lynch reports the Ridge administration as having sought out $650 million in new spending for stadiums and other projects.

headline: Congressman seeks pay hike, boost in morale for military
abstract: United State Representative Pat Toomey is supporting more funding for the military as Marines in a peacekeeping force in Australia prepare for deployment to East Timor.  Toomey supports the National Defense Authorization act for fiscal year 2000 which contains more money for the military.

headline: Duties of state legislatures growing
abstract: The most revitalized and changed government institutions in America are state legislatures.  This claim is from William T. Pound who is the executive director of the National Conference of State Legislatures, the trade association for those lawmakers and their staffs.  Congress has even changed too in that it has moved from the top-down leadership style of Wright and Gingrich to leadership with strong committee and subcommittee chairman.

headline: Rudy in Reverse
abstract: Article fictionally theorizing what Rudy Giuliani, Mayor of New York City, is thinking about Hillary Clinton who are both running for the U.S. Senate in 2000.  Giuliani is deposed as someone who thinks Clinton is campaigning on the idea of being a victim of her husband so he, in turn, will show New Yorkers how he is in fact a worse off victim than her.

headline: Loved ones say farewell at sea
abstract: A Navy destroyer carried family members to a ceremony to scatter the ashes of John F. Kennedy, Junior, his wife, and sister-in-law at a site not far from where they died.  A group of 15 family members scattered their ashes off the United States Ship Briscoe off of Martha's Vineyard about three miles from where their bodies were discovered.

headline: Lawmakers, governor must decide how to spend tobacco money
abstract: The Pennsylvania General Assembly must decide how to allocate about $18 billion for the state's budget and will also have to decide what to do when the first installment of an $11.3 billion settlement with the tobacco industry.  Pennsylvania will receive fluctuating payments that will range from $369 million to $482 million annually for 25 years.

headline: Legislation passed to help drought-stricken farmers
abstract: Legislation that would provide financial assistance to Pennsylvania's  50,000 farm families to help them recover from $700 million in crop losses due to the recent drought has been approved by a legislative committee, accoring to Represenatative Raymond Bunt, Jr., Republican - Montgomery.  The legislature would work in concert with federal assitance to provide grants, rebates, subsidies and incentives to farmers to help them recover from the drought.

headline: Tuition to increase at state owned universities
abstract: The Board of Governors are likely to vote on a 4.3 percent hike in the tuition in the 14 state owned universities. The hike comes against a backdrop of a continued legislative effort to attach some form of accountablity for the higher system of education.

headline: Rail Service
abstract: In 1997 the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation announced that is planned to purchase nine state-of-the-art diesel train set for the 104-mile Harrisburg to Philadelphia service, capable of reaching speeds of 110 miler per hour, and reducing the travel time from 2 hours to 90 minutes.  The service was expected to go into effect in summer 1999 but negotiations with Pittsburgh-based Adtranz, the sole bidder on the new equipment, remain stalled over price.

headline: Jumping the Gun?
abstract: The tobacco lawsuit settlement has spawned a new wave of suits against the gun industry inspiring mass-injury litigation.  A group of antigun lawyers have mounted a serious threat to the way the gun industry does business.  Lawyers from the tobacco settlement say they do not see an analogy between tobacco and guns.

headline: Make sinking homes a federal case
abstract: The sinking homes crisis in Wissinoming in June was quickly resolved when the city stepped in to compensate each of the 25 homeowners who were evacuated.  City Councilman Marion Tasco says the Logan area, which is experiencing a similar problem, ought to be expanded to include several more blocks so that all affected persons can receive assistance whose homes are sinking.

headline: Deal on A-Test Ban Stalls As Senate Vote Approaches
abstract: The United States Senate stalled on voting on a treaty to ban underground nuclear tests because Republicans wanted to avoid having the pact become a campaign issue in 2000 with the Democrat's desire to keep the issue alive next year.  Both sides of the aisle, however, are urged to shelve the issue to avert a political and diplomatic embarrassment.

headline: EDITORIAL:  THE PARTIES' PARTY WEEKEND IS ALL BUSINESS
abstract: Started more than 100 years ago by transplanted Pennsylvanian's who wanted to keep in touch with their home state, is the Pennsylvania Society in New York City.  Every December a select group of elected officials from PA travel to New York City (this year at the Waldorf Astoria) for a formal dinner paid for by regional corporal leaders and lobbyists.  There are complaints from law makers that other fundraising events in Pennsylvania are interfering with this year's PA Society dinner.

headline: Rules reform hearing in Pa.
abstract: Representative Ken Lee quit his post of over four years due to being tired of voting on issues that he knew little about because the Pennsylvania House is run by a small collection of leaders who often force rank-and-file members to vote with little time to research legislation.  Representative Greg Vitali, Republican-Delaware, supported this claim saying that it is a big problem and that it has to change.  Vitali sits on the House Select Committee on Rules Reform.

headline: Making the Case for Hands-On Courts
abstract: Biography of Judge Judith S. Kaye of New York on her ambitions after law school and  challenges she faced as a woman in 1962.  In 1999 she serves as New York's chief judge as head of a branch of government with more than 15,000 employees and 4 million new cases a year.

headline: Local lawmakers back state budget
abstract: Local lawmakers gave their support for Gov. Ridge's 1999-2000 state budget. State Representative Nickol and (R) and State Representative Platts(R) applauded the Governor for the $ 273 million in tax cuts which was mainly aimed at businesses, increase in funding for special education, libraries, agriculture and highway maintenance.

headline: Legislators and agencies must act to protect welfare of all Pennsylvanians, come rain or shine
abstract: Representative Victor J. Lescovitz, Chairman of the House Democratic Policy Committee, submitted a response to a letter the editor wrote in regards to the drought that was seriously affecting Pennsylvania farmers.  Lescovitz said the editor made a comment that two days of drought hearings serve no one of interest and countered by saying that those who testified offered solid legislative and administrative suggestions.

headline: United House Democrats vow to influence assembly
abstract: Bill DeWeese insisted that Democrats in the Pennsylvania House were more united than they have bee in the past and are pushing an agenda of school property tax cuts, more funding for school districts, and colleges, expanded benefits for senior citizens, and a higher minimum wage.  Democratic leadership claimed that their push for a 50% school property tax cut over five years has shifted debate away from business toward middle class Pennsylvanians.

headline: 'Random' retests screen state drivers over 45 years of age
abstract: The Mature Driver Re-exam program seeks out those drivers over age 45 whose licenses are up for the annual four-year renewal.  In a random, statewide pool, 1,650 drivers are chose monthly to be tested for vision and general physical wellness.  The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation may also require a driver's examination.

headline: Keep the prisoners in; don't shut the public out
abstract: Although it seemed somewhat easy for three inmates to break out of two of the state's prisons, it seems harder for concerned citizens to get at the truth about security measures at Jackson Township facility.  State Department Corrections officials compromised security at the Dallas prison by closing watchtowers, ignored the concerns by the prison's Citizens Advisory Group and misled the public about the efficiency of new systems and procedures that were to make the towers obsolete.

headline: Mayor travels to Harrisburg in search of grant money
abstract: While Scranton may lose a $10 million state grant for the Hotel Casey for failing to comply with 15 conditions, Wilkes-Barre Mayor Tom McGroarty was careful to follow the state's rules on a grant-seeking trip in Harrisburg.  McGroarty met with Governor Ridge and asked for an appropriation of $24 million in grants taking with him the list of 15 conditions to receive state funds to revitalize the deteriorating downtown.

headline: Democrats Ready for Senate Fight to Save Test Ban Treaty
abstract: The White House and Senate Democrats are ready for a fight with the Republican controlled Senate to save a Clinton administration top foreign policy goal of banning nuclear testing.  Unless Republicans agree to hold hearings this year in the Senate on the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which 152 nations have signed, Democrats are threatening to Congress to standstill.

headline: Editorial: Roddey for executive
abstract: Allegheny County has seen turmoil and dissension and a new chance for new leadership is in Jim Roddey.  Discusses Roddey's politcal career history in support of his campaign for county executive of Allegheny County.

headline: Ruling bolsters christian group
abstract: In a victory for the beleagured Christian Coalition, a Federal Judge rejected most charges in a  lawsuit that accused the group of illegaly distributing millions of worker guides and mailer guides to prmomote Republican Candidates.

headline: Noteworthy:
abstract: Governor Ridge will introduce Washington Post political reporter and columnist David Broder, of whom he has said "he is the best, the best," today during a session of Pennsylvania National Bank Day at the Chautauqua Institution in New York.

headline: Lottery born of crisis, savvy
abstract: In 1971, Pennsylvania experienced an unprecedented financial crisis leaving state Senator Patrick Stapleton to face a challenging vote which was to create the state's first ever income tax.  Despite reservations, Stapleton voted for the 2.3 percent tax and the Senate approved the bill a day after the House voted.

headline: Legislators rally to aid drought hit PA farmers
abstract: Lawmakers continue to push for drought relief bill. State Rep Maitland (R) and State Sen.Boscola push for different bills which would aid PA farmers.

headline: Voucher advocates, opponents should think before taking sides
abstract: The author talks abou the voucher program. He feels the a modest voucher of $ 1500 would hardly pay tuition especially when transportation is  involved. The author also tells us the private schools have be careful before they can let the government meddle with them. He says both the pros and the cons should be considered before it can be made available to the school districts.

headline: Reform bill on 'fast track'
abstract: Legislation to change the way teenagers get their licenses in Pennsylvania is on a fast track to approval and should be signed by the Governor by the June recess.  Representative Steven Nickol, Republican-Hanover, states that there will need to be some fine-tuning to the bill before it goes to the Governor on issues like how it proposes to deal with teenagers who are out after 11:00 pm due to a late night job.

headline: Lawmakers ask for punitive damages for Swissair victims
abstract: Lawyers for Swissair asked a federal judge to decide whether families of the 229 people killed in last year's crash off the coast of Nova Scotia are punitive damages as the parties seek to negotiate a settlement.  The families are asking United States District Judge James T. Giles to reject a $300 million package because it would limit an estimated $1 billion in punitive damages.

headline: Mayors visit D.C. to talk community
abstract: Steelton Mayor George Hartwick at a roundtable discussion in Washington, D.C. came away from the meeting with a sense of reassurance that the borough of almost 5,000 people is on the right path as it works to rejuvenate its downtown and find businesses to replace long-departed steel companies.  Hartwick commented that what they are doing in Steelton is similar to what other cities around the country are doing.

headline: Gekas, Pitts fault Kosovo goals
abstract: Lancaster County's two Congressional Republicans did not support President Clinton's policies in Kosovo and do not praise the peace deal.  Representative George Gekas said that while the bombing removed the Serbs from Kosovo it has opened up other problems like the refugee matter that may not be solvable.

headline: Education tops list of public concerns in poll
abstract: As a new legislative year begins education, health care, social security, Medicare, and the aging population are ranking issues that are priorities for the United States Congress and will be significant in President Clinton's state of the union address.  Clinton's impeachment seems to be low on the public's mind as indicated by USA Today/CNN/Gallup Polls and Vice President Al Gore and Texas Governor George Bush are lead contenders for the next presidential election.

headline: Salvatore: Bill would stem vote fraud
abstract: State Senator Frank A. (Hank) Salvatore (R-5), has introduced legislation to stem voter fraud by establishing a statewide voter registry and making other improvements to the registration system. He said his bill would create a statewide voter registry, to better protect against duplicate registration and more easily track voters when they move.

headline: 'Numbers' becomes fourth major movie to film in Pennsylvania
abstract: Governor Ridge announced that a movie will be filmed in the state for the fourth time in 1999.  The movie is called "Numbers" and stars John Travolta and will begin principal photography on location in Harrisburg.  It also stars Lisa Kudrow, Bill Pullman, Ed O'Neill, Tim Roth, and Michael Weston among others.

headline: Municipal friendly budget plan backed.
abstract: The House Appropriations Committee approved the 1999-2000 budget. The resulted in the restoration of the $ 44 million for state police patrol coverage and $ 46.3 million for the Growing Greener initiative.

headline: Local legislator outlines state drought-relief efforts for local farmers
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives took action to help the State's farmers as they felt the federal government did not do enough.  The drought hit farmers in the worst time of the year because it hit during the growing season.  The House, to summarize, adopted three bills which would direct grants to farmers equivalent to 20 percent of their federal crop loss assessment; subsidized hay and roughage bought to replace homegrown crops; refunds of 10 to 20 percent of farmers' 1999 "out-of-pocket" costs for seed, fertilizer, and weed and pest control; and cost sharing incentives to plant cover crops and small grains for late-fall or early-spring roughage.

headline: Voucher debate going over many people's heads, survey finds
abstract: As politicians and educsators debate about voucher programs and charter schools a national survery said that 63% of the adults knew little or nothing about the voucher plans. The public were even more mystified about charter schools as 81% of adults answered negative for charter schools knowledge.

headline: Reform's goal: making teen drivers responsible
abstract: State Representative Stephen Barrar, 160th legislative district, urges citizens in light of the five young girls killed in an automobile accident to listen to the statistics involving teenage auto-accident deaths.  To make our teenagers safe we must pass teen driving reform.

headline: Lawmakers look to make changes
abstract: State Representative Larry Sather, Republican-McConnellstown, states that as he sits on the committee looking at the way the state Department of Corrections is looking at future improvement as well as past blunders.
