abstract: More than a year after Governor Ridge signed Act 58 into law, a bill designed to crack down on dead beat parents to pay child support with provision like suspension of hunting, fishing and driver's licenses, several hundred thousand parents who are not paying support still have not lost their licenses.  The Act is working in part because it is helping enforcement officers find people they have been looking for, for years to pay support.

headline: Phila. must do stadium the right way
abstract: The proposal that city officials decide to build the Phillies' new baseball stadium at Broad and Pattison in South Philadelphia is beneficial.  With two preseason games and a mere eight in the regular season, any economic development claim made for football is laughable.  Baseball, on the other hand, has more than 80 home games and potential to generate some foot traffic for local businesses.

headline: VFW Celebrates 100th Anniversary, Honor Lynch
abstract: State Representative Jim Lynch, Republican-Warren, spoke at the Veterans of Foreign War's 100th anniversary celebration held in Altoona.  Lynch praised the organization for their 100 years of service to the nation with loyalty, commitment, and strong sense of patriotism.

headline: Flap Bytes Evans but boosts Street
abstract: Dwight Evans, candidate for Philadelphia's mayoral office, had to fire an aide for a fake internet site that was a scandal on Philadelphia's Demcratic mayoral primary.  This allowed John Street and perhaps John White to gain some lead over the other candidates.  A former college classmate of David Sirota, who was Evans Depputy campaign manager, had ties to a website called www.white99.com which highlighted a controversial statement that White, "The black and brown, if we unite, we're going to control this city."  Evans fired Sirota and was also accepting the resignation of Chestnut Hill businessman Jack Fugett.

headline: Senator vs. Senator
abstract: Jeffrey Toobin, a writer for the New Yorker, said that Bill Clinton was considering running for the senate in 2002 from his home state in Arkansas.  His wife Hillary Clinton is considering running for the Senate from another state.  If that happens this would be the first connubial Senate team.  The column progresses to discuss how this would be a negative experience for voters.

headline: State democrats tout proposal to refund surpluses as tax relief
abstract: State Sen Bodack(D) said that the Home - STAR or the Home Owner School Tax Relief Plan, where the home owners would get a part of the school property tax relief plan calls for the home owners to share the state's budget surpluses.

headline: Some Pennsylvania Pigeons Finally Can Look Forward to Labor Day
abstract: Hegins, Pennsylvania, a tiny corn and cabbage town in eastern Pennsylvania, cancelled its 66th annual pigeon shooting event because last July the Pennsylvania Supreme Court issued a ruling giving officers of the Pennsylvania Society for the Prevention of the Cruelty to animals to cite pigeon shooters for cruelty.  This has ended a 13-year dispute with animal-rights activists.  Robert Tobash, one of the shooting event organizers, said they would still hold the event except just without the shooting.

headline: Boscola says Ridge promise is garbage
abstract: State Senator Lisa Boscola wants tougher measure to keep out-of-state trash out of Pennsylvania.  Boscola, Democrat - 18th District, and Rich Grucela, Democract - 137th District, both criticized Governor Tom Ridge during at press conference Tuesday in Bangor because the State Department of Environmental Protection recently issued size landfill permits that increase the amount of out-of-state trash hauled into Pennsylvania.  The approval of the permits comes a few months after Ridge called for a moratorium on out-of-state trash.  Ridge wanted a three-year freeze on permits for municipal waste landfills and limits on the amount of trash allowed in existing landfills.  But, due to the department of environmental protection's recent act, it opens the door wider to accepting trash.

headline: The real risk
abstract: The National Transportation Safety Board announced findings that seat belts would not improve safety on buses.  Buses are designed differently and they react differently in crashes, according to the Board.

headline: No charges expected in discovery of fetuses at doctor's offices
abstract: Four fetuses were discovered in dusty glass bottles in the office of Burgettstown doctor Glenn Roberts who left town six months ago with amphetamines and steroids.  Washington County District Attorney John Pettit said there was no evidence Roberts had any of them illegally and may have had a medical purpose.

headline: Philadelphia shipyard not to be affected by divestiture
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge and Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell moved quickly to allay fears over the Philadelphia Shipyard's future as well as the state and city investments in that facility.  Kvaerner ASA may potentially sell all or part of its shipbuilding operations has generated strong criticism from state Senator Leonard Bodack, a Pittsburgh Democrat.

headline: Area code conversion produces some hang-ups
abstract: An out of state reporter called the Wilkes-Barre area and encountered a problem because their phone was not registered to recognize a new area code that had been installed.  570, the new area code installed in northeastern Pennsylvania, had been scattered throughout the area.

headline: Flights of Fancy
abstract: An opinion article criticizing state Representative H. William DeWeese, a Democrat from Greene County, for the number of tax payer funded flights that he took between July 1998 and June 1999 to go to and from his district, Harrisburg, Reading, Trenton, New Jersey, Youngstown, Ohio, and others.  On two of the trips DeWeese's wife, a Harrisburg lobbyist, accompanied him.  A spokesman for DeWeese states that all of his trips were for legislature business and his wife was fully covered by personal funds.  If an elected representative wants to stay in the public trust they must follow cost-efficient policies and employ a staff that books travel far enough in advance to utilize discounted airfare like that offered by US Airways.  Spur of the moment trips are not sensible.

headline: Senators Divided on Key Issues
abstract: Despite all of their talk on bipartisanship, United States House Representatives and Senators remain split not only on key issues such as whether to call witnesses or to consider censure but also on the more fundamental questions about whether the allegations against Clinton are serious enough to remove a president from office for the first time in history.  Presidential jurors will attmept to maintain the civility that brought them together for a 100 to 0 approval of procedures on Friday.  To achieve that accord, the senators proposed the critical decisions on whether to hear live testimony on the floor from Monica S. Lewinsky and others involved in the case.

headline: State legislators shouldn't wish upon Home-STAR
abstract: Pennsylvania Senate Democrats propose to give homeowners a tax cut that is seen as popular and progressive, however, it is a bad idea because despite repeat budget surpluses in recent years the state still has not put away enough cash reserves to weather the next recession.  Instead, senators are pushing the Homeowner School Tax Relief plan, commonly known as Home-STAR, which is a more streamlined measure than Act 50 for reducing local property taxes.  This would be a local option proposal invoked by school board and the voters.  It would be a statewide tax cut triggered by a state surplus exceeding 1 percent of the budget in a give year.  Half the surplus would be returned to homeowners as a credit against their school taxes.

headline: Specter gets the dirt from farmers
abstract: Local farmers painted a bleak picture for US Sen Specter. Gov Ridge ask the US Agricultural Secretary to declare PA a drought stricken state and make assistance available for 50,000 families.

headline: Commission's Link Program well worth the paperwork
abstract: Pennsylvania's Game Commission "Link Program" is a great idea, however, link everything else it will require effort from those who could benefit the most and consequently the very reason why it could be doomed.  The program is the product of Game Commissioner George J. Venesky and is intended to link landowners to hunters and trappers who have had their property suffer too much from wildlife.  The problem is that the paperwork process linking the two participants is so lengthy that it may take too long to show results.

headline: Tighter license rules passed
abstract: After a two-hour debate the Pennsylvania House of Representatives voted in favor of passing teen driver's license reform by a vote of 131-66.  The bill will now go to the Senate where supports of it say that this legislation is a strong step towards dealing with inexperience of new drivers.

headline: No early release
abstract: It is important for law abiding citizens that violent criminals shoulf serve 85% of their sentences. The scourge of drunken drivinf in this nation required that judges set the harsh penalties and stick by them.

headline: Phoenix Steel Co foundry project can move forward, thanks to local co-opration
abstract: A financial hurdle that threatened the completion of the Phoenixville showcase project was cleared with help from the county's Department of Community and Economic Development.

headline: AT&T uses deceptive ads, Bell claims
abstract: The president of Bell Atlantic has accused AT&T Corporation of mounting a smear campaign against Bell a week before an expected landmark state Public Utility Commission vote on local telephone competition.  They are claiming that AT&T and Pennsylvania's for Local Competition are running advertisements in newspapers and electronic media.

headline: Flourtown Ophthalmologist seeks Republican bid to take 13th District seat
abstract: Melissa Brown, a Flourtown Republican, will run against State Senator Stewart J. Greenleaf for the 13th District Congressional seat currently by Joseph M. Hoeffel the 3rd.  Brown closed her medical practice two weeks ago to show she's committed and in hopes of getting the GOP endorsement.

headline: Senators look for alternatives to independent counsel act
abstract: Senator Carl Levin, who authored the Independent Counsel Act said the law may be beyond rescue as a result of Kenneth Star's investigation of the White House.  Levin proposed that the Justice Department be given new tools to investigate possible wrongdoing within the government.

headline: State manages quite well, thank you
abstract: A national study showed that Pennsylvania tax payers can rest assured that a $18.6 billion state budget that is supported by state sales tax, personal income tax, business taxes, and various state fees are receiving better-managed state programs than two-thirds of other states.  The Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs at Syracuse University gave Pennsylvania state government an average "B" grade in its study.  Only five other states had better grades.

headline: State House, Senate pass separate drought relief packages
abstract: State and House passed opposing versions for the drough relief packages. It is upto Sen Slocum and Rep Bunt to agree on the final package. Gov. Ridge's office is waiting for the Federal Aid on the same.

headline: Bureau of Forestry focuses efforts on dump eradication
abstract: Thank to the enactment of the Forest Lands Beautification Act late last year the Rothrock Forest District in Huntingdon County will see a number of unsightly trash dumps cleaned up in the months ahead.  Governor Tom Ridge signed into law in 1998 the new legislation which will provide up to $7.5 million over the next five years for the cleanup of trash dumps on state forest land and park lands.  Around 30 trash dumps have been indentified in the Rothrock District Forest to be cleaned up.

headline: Time for drivers to hang up phones
abstract: A 2-year-old Bucks County girl has been killed by a driver plowing into another car after being distracted by dialing her cell phone.  The state Legislature finally appears willing to tackle the issue of whether it should be illegal to use a cell phone while driving.

headline: No Title
abstract: Governor Ridge will deliver the deliver the Republican response to President Clinton's address. Governor Ridge has been the designated Republican person to talk on curbing violence in schools.

headline: Pirates get $45 million loan for expenses
abstract: The Pirates newest loan from Boston-based Fleet Financial Group for $45 million is a sign of health, not economic duress, according Dick Freeman, the team's executive vice president and chief operations officer.  The Pirates will use most of the money for $40 million of the cost of a new baseball stadium that will open in April 2001.

headline: Bell Atlantic appeals PUC order to high court
abstract: Bell Atlantic appealed directly to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court to stay and then overturn the landmark order by the state Public Utility Commission on local telephone competition.  Bell's petition seeks to bypass Commonwealth Court by having the Supreme Court exercise King's Bench Review, a controversial and little-used procedure in which the high court takes jurisdiction of a case from a county or lower-level appellate court.

headline: Foes set in primary for attorney general
abstract: John Morganelli and Jim Eisenhower are the remaining Democratic candidates for Pennsylvania Attorney General now that Claude A.L. "Cal" Shields has announced he will drop out in favor of Morganelli.  Morganelli has tried to force Governor Robert P. Casey to deny a federal judgeship to Philadelphia Judge Frederica Massiah-Jackson whom Eisenhower supports.

headline: Senators struggle with votes 'for all time'
abstract: The Senate's impechment deliberations began to burst out into the open regarding hearings of President Clinton.  Clinton's impeachment fate was not in doubt however some last minute soul searching was evident by republicans.  Senator Richard Shelby, Republican-Alabama, carreid a copy of the federal statutes on perjury and obstruction of justice, heavily highlighted, into an afternoon session.  Shelby is one of a handful of republicans whose vote will answer the only real remaining question.  Will either article of impeachment win even a simple majority?  This is in doubt.

headline: State Poltics with a national spin
abstract: With the Texas legislature beginning again, which it only does once every other year for 140 days, it is easy a budge surplus as are many other states.  The outgoing democratic governor also introduced incoming repupblican governor George W. Bush as the country's next president.  Governors like Reagan, Dukakis, and Clinton have all found out that actions taken in their statehouses can cast a disprportionately large shadow in the nation stage.  Bush will have to take into account his actions in Austin, Texas as they may impact his actions if he is elected President of the United States.

headline: Toomey lobbies House for federal drought relied for state's farmers
abstract: Lehigh Valley Congressman Pat Toomey(R) writes to the House Speaker asking for Federal relief for PA farmers devasted by drought. The loss according to PA Dept of Agriculture was estimated to be $ 500 million.

headline: Can Old Allegheny Co. law control landfills?
abstract: David Black, Jefferson County Commissioner, says that a way of controlling the proliferation of landfills may have been at hand for 60 years.  The state legislature granted certain powers to second-class counties in 1933 that amounted to local control of landfills.  Allegheny County is the only second class county in the state.  It enjoys the power of licensing landfills, levying fees and the power to revoke a permit.  Black says that the law has been tested in Court and has never been repealed.  He thinks that is Pennyslvania is serious about controlling landfills all it has to do is amend the code to all counties.

headline: Tough seat belt laws necessary to save lives
abstract: A strong primary seat belt law, which makes it mandatory to buckle up, has proven to increase belt use on average by 15 percent.  National Child Passenger Safety Week, and The Air Bag & Seat Belt Safety Campaign and the National Safety Council, are sponsoring a program in which children meet with congressional representatives to push for stronger seat belt laws.

headline: Officials close highschools over rumors of violence
abstract: Bucks County high school will remain closed due to rumored threat of violence, one of the many cases reported after the Littleton School massacre.

headline: Pirates turn first shovel for new park
abstract: The Pirates broke ground yesterday for PNC Park, a majestic $228 million steel-and-limestone baseball stadium expected to lead the team to modern-day profits while evoking nostalgic memories of smaller arenas like Wrigley Field.  Pirates owner Kevin McClatchy, Governor Ridge, Mayor Tom Murphy and others grabbed silver shovels and turned a pile of dirt for the event.

headline: Bell Atlantic offers new national service
abstract: Bell Atlantic Corporation has introduced national 411 service in response to people saying that no one can help Pennsylvanian's telephone customers needing directory assistance.  By dialing 411 customers can now receive assistance for both local and long-distance numbers, regardless of which company provides long distance service.

headline: For new mayor, a party for every pocketbook
abstract: After being elected mayor John Street is attending dinner fund-raising parties that range from $10,000 per couple to $50 per plate to non-alcoholic celebrations in "faith communities."  Street's former campaign manager Lana Felton-Ghee planned the parties and is also a professional planner.  She has also been a part of democratic campaign planning for 20 years.

headline: Serafini fracas is about holding on to majority, not about justice
abstract: House Speaker Matt Ryan is scrambling for ways to justify why convicted representative Frank Serafini is still able to hold on to his office.  He first cited the American principle of innocent until proven guilty, however, Serafini has been convicted and sentenced but is still out on appeal.  The state constitution clearly states that anyone convicted of a crime cannot hold public office.  Ryan is now attempting to subvert the intent of the constitution.  He says that the constitution actually is on his side as it prescribes no means of ouster of a member, permitting such authority to gravitate to the General Assembly itself, under its rule-making authority.  In other words, Ryan says, the Attorney General may represent the people of the state but the speaker's interest is in protecting the fundamental constitutional duties vested in the chamber.

headline: State representatives tout tax reform
abstract: Five Lehigh Valley state Representatives said senior citizens and other property owners deserve a piece of Pennsylvania's $773 million budge surplus.  For the past three years the state has been accumulating an increasing surplus where 15% of it goes into a rainy day fund which stands at about $1 billion.

headline: Till the cows come home
abstract: Sen Edwin wants cows to return to Norristown Farm Park which houses other livestocks as a part of the unique feature of the park.

headline: Clinton, Centre counties get 'green' money
abstract: An environmental program called "Keystone Land Trust" will provide clean and green money to Clinton and Centre counties.  Governor Ridge announced the awards recently as part of a series of 28 grants totalling $5 million to land-trust organizations and coservacies.  The money will be used to plan and protect critical habitat and open space across the Commonwealth.

headline: Tougher licensing steps would save young lives
abstract: Of all the things that Governor Ridge would like to be remembered for like a robust economy, welfare, education reform, and perhaps even stadium funding, he may actually be remembered for meddling with one of the most sacred rites of passage of all - the teen-age driver's license.  Ridge wanted significant changes to the in the way driver's licenses are awarded to the drivers with the worst overall driving record and the highest fatality rate.

headline: Officials oppose planned fee for state police coverage
abstract: A group of 21 township and state officials met Thursday for an informal roundtable discussion on Governor Tom Ridge's plan to charge for the police coverage.  State lawmakers said the plan to charge probably won't fly in the pending budget - but even if it is defeated now, it will likely be brought back next year.  Ridge wants to charge communities with 5,000 or more residents $35 per head for the rest of this year and $70 a person next year to continue full-time state police coverage.  The governor has proposed variations on the plan twice before.  The current version could bring about $14 million into the state's general budget.  Some officials say that Ridge is not seeking revenue as much as trying to force municipalities to provide local police service.

headline: Pittsburgh needs a marina to take advantage of the rivers
abstract: Despite the many things Pittsburgh has that would attract a marina like world famous Three Rivers, one of the nation's largest inland ports, and a boat regatta drawing more than a million people they do not have a marina.  The unrealized potential is upsetting to Port Authority chairman George Ross.

headline: Bell Atlantic to offer area tests of new DSL service
abstract: Bell Atlantic has been signing people up to test its Infospeed DSL service in Harrisburg, Lancaster, and East Petersburg.  People who had expressed an interest over the Bell website in these areas are being contacted to see if they are still interested.

headline: For Religious Right, It's a crowded field
abstract: Some conservative republicans are beginnig to worry that there are too many hard-right conservatives vying for the party's Presidential nomination.  They fear a splintering of conservative clout, especially that of social and religious conservatives, who account for at least a third of the party's membership in many states and, when cohesive, can sometimes steer things their way.

headline: Serafini wins procedural fight to keep his seat
abstract: Representative Frank Serafini was granted a stay of political execution after delivering an emotional speech on the House floor asking for support and vowing his innocence.  House Democratic Leader H. William DeWeese, Democrat-Greene, could not line up enough votes for a motion that would have cleared the way for the House to consider an expulsion resolution.

headline: State tax filings by home computers on the rise
abstract: People who are filing their tax returns are doing it more so online than by submitting the traditional paper return.  People are using their home computers to file and tabulating a count of 17,500 in 1999.  By comparison to the previous year the total was only 204.  The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue said that more than 800,000 returns had been submitted by computer or telephone.  Most of the 401,000 computer-filed returns were submitted through tax preparers and all online filing required a joint submission with federal returns, said Revenue Department spokesman Wendi Taylor.

headline: Wine Welfare
abstract: PA's mild winters and long growing seasons are ideal for growing great wine. The PA Liquor Control Board says that liquor consumption has increased from 2000 gallons to 3000 gallons in 1999 which encourages the market to look at increasing wine production.

headline: Colleges push wise water use
abstract: Kutztown University students are being asked to cut their shower time to three minutes or less this fall in an effort to conserve water due to the drought.  Richard Morrison, director of public relations at Kutztown, said students will be greeted by about 500 posters promoting water conservation.  About 3,200 of the school's 7,800 students live in residence halls.

headline: Train opponent promises answers about service
abstract: Executive Director Frank Reilly of the Morris County, New Jersey Department of Transportation is spearheading a bi-state effort to regain rail service from northeast Pennsylvania to New York City.  United States Senator Arlen Specter said the results of the third and final federal rail study will be released next month answering all questions surrounding passenger service.

headline: Oh, brother! Ex-Phila. man gets unclaimed $1.4 million
abstract: A former Philadelphia resident has received $1.4 million in stock that he inherited years ago but never claimed.  The award came from the state Treasury Department, which returns lost or unclaimed property to Pennsylvania residents, and it is by far the largest single return ever made.  The larger the amount of money returned the more likely the person or company is likely to ask that their name be withheld from the public.  Pennsylvania law requires that unclaimed property reverts to the Treasury Department after seven years.  The department then acts as a huge lost and found, using various programs to return property.

headline: Plan aimed at urban sprawl hurts quality of life
abstract: The Sierra Club has undertaken a national campaign against something it calls sprawl.  Members prefer that people who live in suburban areas be persuaded, or coerced if necessary, back towards the central city.  The result is the popularization of "infill" develoment.  This is great when it is taking out ugly, abandoned warehouses and strip shopping centers, and restoring run-down areas.  But it is highly overrated when the result is that urban pockets of green are eaten by development.

headline: Bell's status in Pennsylvania awaits outcome of dispute over state decision
abstract: Federal regulators have allowed Bell Atlantic to offer long-distance service in New York state but the company's status in Pennsylvania is still up for grabs.  Pennsylvania's Public Utility Chairman John Quain has been conducting talks with Bell, other companies, and consumer advocacy organizations in the hope of eliminating a long extensive court battle over a broad-ranging court order setting conditions on telephone conditions in the state.

headline: For Rendell, a bigger stage, a big break
abstract: Mayor Ed Rendell who is an aspiring Governor is the chairman of the National Democratic Committee. He will be the one voice of the two major parties.

headline: Serafini's Done
abstract: Applause was mentioned for attorney general Mike Fisher for giving Serafini, a house republican representative who was convicted by a federal jury and sentenced to five months yet is still free due to filing appeals, a deadline to leave office today or face legal action by his office.  Gover Ridge also asked Serafini to resign but in a very indirect way.  With both of these peole asking Serafini to resign the time must be here to do it.

headline: State's standing on new ecomony.
abstract: PA was ranked 24th overall in the new economy.

headline: You may not have a friend in Pennsylvania
abstract: Opinion article criticizing the Senate for not approving enough aid in its return bill to the House in regards to the hardships Pennsylvania farmers are facing due to the drought in the summer.  The Senate cut nearly $200 million out of the bill the House sent to them for aid to farmers.  Article makes the point that if we do not help our farmers when they are in need then what will we have left.

headline: Committees to meet to weigh various bills
abstract: The Senate Appropriations Committee will meet to discuss the "growing greener" bill.  Growing Greener is the Ridge administration's answer for a host of environmental woes, from abandoned mine clean-up to open-space preservation.

headline: Transit at forefront of race
abstract: The first Allegheny county executive is expected to make a high speed transit stop between downtown Pittsburgh and the International Airport a priority.  The four candidates are generally happy satisfied with Port Authority, two favor replacing authority board chairman Neal Holmes.

headline: Orie targets violent sex offenders
abstract: State Representative Candless called on Governor Ridge to convene a special sessions of the legislature to crack down on bills that would target down on sexually violent offenders.

headline: Plan B user fee
abstract: Most Pennsylvanians have a strong opinion about whether the state should play a role in funding construction of new sports stadiums.  Supporters contend that stadiums are crucial to keeping teams in the state, create jobs and encourage economic development.  Detractors say that is it really the taxpayers' responsibility to fund the stadiums when the vast majority of citizens will never attend an event at any of the stadiums?  State Senator Jim Gerlach proposed these questions.

headline: Bill to protect firms from web business deals
abstract: State Representative Lescovitz said the The Electronic Commerce Security Act would protect businesses by extending legal protection to electronic and digital signatures thus making e-commerce more secure.

headline: For Superior Court
abstract: Two open seats on Pennsylvania's Superior Court are up for election and sought after by two Republicans and two Democrats.  The Republicans are Richard B. Klein, a Philadelphia Common Court of Pleas Court Judge and Superior Court Judge Maureen E. Lally-Green of Butler County. The Democrats are Berle M. Schiller of Montgomery County on the Superior Court as an appointee and Debra Todd form Allegheny County, a trial lawyer of 17 years' tenure.  This paper has endorsed Schiller and Klein.

headline: Seven of eight charges against Murphy dropped
abstract: District Justice Wendy Dennis said that prosecutor Jack Heneks has dropped seven of the eight charges of voter fraud on absentee ballots against U.S. Representative Austin Murphy.  The only charge remaining is one misdemeanor cout of violating the state election code.  Defense attorneys met with the prosecutor for about an hour

headline: Study: 3 jobless for each job open in area
abstract: A Keystone Research Center report shows that Pennsylvania's unemployed outnumber available jobs in the state by a 2 - 1 ratio.  In Philadelphia the ratio is 3 - 1.  Family supported employment, defined as a job earning a minimum of between $8.83 and $12.29 per hour, depending upon family size and location, is even more scare.  Job seekers statewide outnumber those jobs 4 - 1.

headline: Young farm agent knows hard times
abstract: Article discussing Dwayne Miller's personal experiences of watching the drought in Pennsylvania have a deep impact on farmers.  His occupation is at an extension office of Pennsylvania State University in education which provides research taken to the public for the benefit of farmers, county planners, homeowners, government officials, and anyone else.  Miller grew up on a family farm and can relate to the experiences farmers are having during the drought.

headline: Congress may weigh in on 10-year fight by states vs. trash imports
abstract: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani says that the States should be more willing to accept trash to go in landfills from the nation's cultural center.  This statement has brought up the arugment again that state's should have more control over interstate waste shipments.  Tom Bliley, United States House Commerce Committee Chairman, has had a long standing issue against allowing state's having control over accepting trash from other states.  New legislation to allow states to regulate waste shipments is expected to be introduced into the House within two weeks.  The legislation is modeled after a 1993 bill that would prohibit receiving out-of-state waste without local government aproval.  Governors Ridge and Pataki of New York are joing together on the issue which may cause probems for Mayor Giuliani.

headline: Transportation Plan
abstract: An article listing the new projects approved in the state's 12-year transportation plan, which was released by the Transportation Commission.  The articles lists the highway names, what is being done, whether it was on the 12-year program before in 12 counties in the state.

headline: Our own legislator cast vote for tyranny
abstract: United States Representative Bud Shuster voted for the House to pass legislation instructing the Treasury Department to publish an annual list of international drug kingpins, whose assets in this country would be seized by the government.  Shustre is criticized because assets should only be seized after charges are brought, and guilt is proved to a neutral third party.  As the bill is written a person would not be able to go to court to defend against the seizure.

headline: Plan B Victory
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature voted to provide $150 million in desperately sought funding for Pittsburgh's professional sports stadiums.  City of Pittsburgh and Allegheny County officials have cobbled together an $809 million blueprint, dubbed Plan B, that provides a mix of public and private funding to build the stadiums and enlarge the Convention Center.

headline: Bills aim to ensure phone competition
abstract: Senators Vincent Fumo, Democrat-Philadelphia, Roger Madigan, Republican-Towanda, and Mary Jo White, Republican-Venango, introduced legislation they hope will bring cheaper and better telecommunications service to Pennsylvania which is aimed at Bell Atlantic, the dominant telephone company in the state.  One of the bills has 25 co-sponsors and would prohibit the proposed merger of Bell and GTE in Pennsylvania as uncompetitive.

headline: Forbes goes beyond flat tax
abstract: Republican candidate for president, Steve Forbes, has announced that he will run his entire candidacy on the Internet.  Forbes finished fourth in the Iowa caucuses and New Hampshire primary.  Democratic candidate Al Gore is hypothetically expected to trounce Forbes in the polls.

headline: Seyfert answers charges
abstract: State Representative Tracy Seyfert has sent a letter to new media in response to the Federal Bureau of Investigations charges that have been made against her.  The statement addressed charges by former staffer Marilyn Soltis that the state legislator has a strong interest in witchcraft.  Seyfert expressed her faith in Christianity, proclaming belief in Jesus Christ, and denied any involvment with being a witch.  Seyfert acknowledged that she loaned to Soltis tapes on the mind-body relationship due a physical condition Soltis had.  Seyfert is a licensed psychologist.

headline: Surplus may mean tax cuts
abstract: State officials are looking at a year-to-date tax revenue surplus of $ 21 million. With the Rainy Day fund approaching $ 1billion and 2000 being an election year Democrats will make the case that the additional money should be sent to the school districts to fund property taxes cuts.

headline: A Big Step
abstract: The author writes that PA has lower worker compensation premium when compared to the other states.Governor Ridge made this his goal during his first term in office.

headline: Congressman Peterson Announces Funds Available To Clean Up Streams
abstract: Congressman Peterson announced a new federal initiative that makes available $750,000 for clean up of acid mine drainage from streams.  The funds are available to Appalachian states organizations, especially small watershed organizations for local acid mine drainage projects.

headline: Turbulence at Takeoff
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Bob Cranmer said he might withhold his support from the airport authority he helped create after a large campaign contributor to Mike Dawida was elected to lead its board.  The fallout from the board elections represents the first major split between Republican Cranmer and Democrat Dawida who teamed almost two years ago to run the government.

headline: PA has executed only two people since 1963
abstract: PA has seldom put to use the dealth penalty sentence. Since Gov. Ridge took over office in 1994, he has vowed to sign more death warrants.

headline: Plan B Wins Big
abstract: The Pennsylvania legislature overwhelmingly approved a package allowing Governor Ridge to allocate $320 million for new sports stadiums in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.  This move is intended to keep the major baseball and football teams in place for 30 years.

headline: Cable TV and the Internet, Too
abstract: Comcast Corporation and Mediaone Group Incorporated have left the impression that cable television is passé as the nation's two biggest cable companies have struck a $53 billion deal.  Bell Atlantic is still an important rival to Comcast-Mediaone yet just offering cable television is not as glamorous as offering data services, broadband and the Internet.

headline: Former state assemblyman Ed Johnson dies at age 77
abstract: Former Republican state representative Edwin George Johnson, 77, died at University Medical Center in Las Vegas.  He is remembered as listening to the local communities and acting in accordance with their needs.

headline: Seyfert can continue to hold office
abstract: Despite an indictment, Representative Tracy Seyfert will still hold on to her seat in the General Assembly and would not become ineligible to hold it unless she was convicted of a felony and then sentenced.  Seyfert's more immediate concern is running for re-election to a third two-year term and Republicans in Erie and Harrisburg are concerned for her viability in the 2000 election.  Seyfert denies reports that the Republican party has pressured her to step down.

headline: Targeting PA tax cuts makes sense
abstract: Anticipation over Gov. Tom Ridge proposed budget is whether the personal income tax should be cut. The last 3 budgets from the Governor has helped the low income families. A complementary tax cut of .1 percent was reveiled by the House Republicans.

headline: American workers have stepped backward
abstract: State Representative Surra writes that the contributions of the American worker have not been recognized recently both in terms of working conditions and sharing the corporate prosperiety they help to produce.

headline: Danville to take reins in times of drought
abstract: Danville Council got its first look at the borough municipal authority's proposed plan which sets a river level at which the borough should ask folks to start conserving, and another at which the borough will demand that they do so.  The plan establishes river levels for three stages of dry weather.

headline: Vanity license plate would help Scouts
abstract: Representative Sara Steelman is proposing to direct the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation to design a Boy and Girl Scouts of America vehicle registration plate.  The legislation would create a Scouting Fund in the Treasury to which $15 of the $35 registration plate fee would be deposited.

headline: PA House targets playground drug dealing
abstract: State Rep Roebuck intorduced a bill that would combat drug dealing in areas frequented by children. The areas would include recreation centers, parks and play grounds too.

headline: Plan B, cont'd.
abstract: With the start of the 1999-2000 legislative session Governor Ridge has proposed raising the state's borrowing limit by $500 million with the purpose of providing the one-third funding from the state for new stadiums.  Lawmakers who would benefits most by having the new stadiums in their communities must vote for it and not just enjoy the benefits.

headline: Cable TV industry defends its pricing, service
abstract: William Cologie, president of the Pennsylvania Cable and Television Communications Association, defended the industry from complaints about high pricing and poor service during a legislative hearing both explanations got a poor reception from some lawmakers.  He states the cost of cable in Pennsylvania is quite reasonable considering the ever increasing programming costs faced by cable operators.

headline: Fox campaing has raised $9,000
abstract: Former U.S. Representative Jon Fox, Republican for the 13th District has barely $9,000 in his campaign fund.  Fox's opponents State Senator Stewart Greenleaf, Republican of Willow Grove, raised $58,000 and Floutown opthalmologist Melissa Brown dropped $100,000 of her own money.

headline: SEYFERT SEAT DRAWING INTEREST
abstract: PA Representative Tracy Seyfert (R-5) announced she will not see re-election to a third term.  She has been charged with illegally acquiring government surplus property.  T.K. Stover, chairman of the Crawford County Republicans said that there are already 6 Republicans who have expressed an interest in the seat.

headline: Tax Cuts Gives GOP Little Momentum
abstract: Economist feel that GOP tax cuts gather little momentum as the country is admist prosperous times and there is speculation whether the country needs the added boost at this time. Economists feel that this surplus can be used to pay the debt.

headline: Bill could stop Pittsburgh Works
abstract: The state Senate unanimously approved a measure that would ban worker residency requirements in construction projects awarded by municipalities, including those for football and baseball stadiums in Pittsburgh.  Senator John Wozniak, sponsored the bill and aimed it at negating Pittsburg Works, a referendum approved by city voters requiring city construction contracts greater than $200,000 use city residents for 35% of the jobs.

headline: Costlier hunting tags now available
abstract: Depsite speculation and concern over the increase in the price of the Pennsylvania Game Commission licenses Richard Irvin of the Huntingdon County Treasurer's Office says that they are the same old licenses.  There are a few new categories that the Game Commissioner authorized be added which are combination licenses.  The combination licenses for resident and nonresident juniors combine hunting, furtaking, archery, and muzzleloader for one price.

headline: Warner, Lott Try to Temper Push For Additional Flights at National
abstract: Republican Senator John Warner of Virginia introduced a bill yesterday that would implement the agreement with Senator John McCain last summer to limit the number of takeoffs and landings to 24.  Majority Leader Trent Lott sough this week to defuse a potential floor fight by calling on the Senate to scale back McCain's new proposal.

headline: Pa. fixing to save 500G
abstract: Pennsylvania state troopers like their Chevrolet Caprice cop cars so much they're giving them the ultimate vote of confidence.  Rather than auction the old cars when they hit the 100,000 mile mark and switch to Ford's Crown Victoria, state police plan to keep some of their old Caprices and give them complete makeovers.  They intend to refurbish 65 high-mileage vehicles to add as much as 100,000 miles to the life of the car.  Chevrolet discontinued the Caprice in 1996, leaving the new full-size police cruiser market exclusively to Ford with its Crown Victoria .  A new patrol car costs about $21,000.  By spending about $12,000 to refurbish a Caprice the department could save as much as $500,000 according to Police Chief Evanko.

headline: Plan B, finis?
abstract: Pennsylvania House majority leader John Perzel stated that the House would likely never vote to raise the commonwealth debt ceiling to provide one-third of the funding to new stadiums each in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.  Governor Ridge has offered to spend more than $300 million in non-stadium economic development projects.

headline: Communities urged to rehearse for Y2K
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Schweiker's spokesperson announced that Thursday would be PA2K day which would create an awareness amongst citizens about the Y2K issue.

headline: Fray Brewing for GOP nod in auditor general contest
abstract: GOP primary fight over auditor general was rasied in the Republican State Committee weekend. State Representative Katie True vies against Lehigh executive Jane Baker.  The contention being abortion rights for which Baker like Ridge is a supporter.

headline: Shades of '68: Bush is unifying his party, or at least his rivals
abstract: The current presidential race has similarities with former vice president Nixon running for office.  When in Florida he declaired that he had enough delegates to get the nomination on the first ballot.  He was challenged, however, by popular and longtime nemesis New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller and California Governor Ronald Reagan, who announced his candidacy on the opening day of the convention.  Nixon found himself squeezed from both the left and the right.  Nixon eaked out a narrow first ballot victory and is similar to Bush in the current election race.

headline: Tax-cut consensus may be in reach
abstract: House Majority leader John Perzel stated that he might consider a property tax cut instead of a personal income tax cut which signals some common ground on the idea of a tax cut.  Another idea is to give senior citizens a break through the property tax rebate program.

headline: Breaking down barriers
abstract: Representative Pat Brown, Republican-Lehigh, is sponsoring a bill tha twould give employers financial incentives to hire disabled persons.  The bill is designed to help more people in vocational rehabilitation programs more easily find work.  Each full-time job created for a disabled person or welfare recipient would give the company a $5,700 credit against what it owes the state and what it owes in corporate tax.

headline: Court panel sides with state's decision to withhold audit
abstract: The Commonwealth Court, by a ruling of 4 to 3, has rejected an attempt to force release of the report on damages sustained by Envirotest Partners after Governor Tom Ridge canceled the company's statewide contract to perform centralized automobile testing.  The audit that paid out over $145 million will remain confidential.  The state hired the auditing firm of Ernst and Young to prepare the report when Envirotest sued the state in 1995 for cancelling the contract.  The case was settled for $145 million seven months later.  Two years later, in 1997, Democratic Senators LaValle and Kusinic asked the Governor's general counsel, Paul Tufano, for a copy of the audit report and were refused because Tufano says that they have a policy of not releasing legal research used to defend the state.

headline: Waugh seeks repeal of right-lane decree
abstract: State Senator Mike Waugh, Republican-Shrewsbury, has introduced a measure that would repeal an amendment to the state vehicle code that was recently signed into law as part of the new teen driver legislation.  The amendment requires all vehicles to be drive in the furthest right lane of limited access highways, except when passing, or preparing for a left hand turn.

headline: Pa. groups' tobacco appeal may jeopardize settlement
abstract: Antitobacco groups and at least one Pennsylvania county are appealing a Philadelphia judge's approval of the tobacco settlement in an effort to assure their ability to sue cigarette makers.  The appeals could threaten or delay the nationwide settlement that would give Pennsylvania $1.3 billion over the next 25 years.

headline: Planned growth a must in our region
abstract: Wayne and Pike counties are two of the fastest growing counties in the state.  Many of the open spaces people are accustomed to have become housing developments and strip malls.  Some may like the growth but it strains infrastructure like roads and sewers that municipalities are not prepared to deal with nor with the necessary funds.  Development should only occur when the infrastructure is already planned out and present to handle it.

headline: Computer co-ordination center ready to identify Y2K hoaxes
abstract: CERT/CC formely known as the Computer Emergency Response Team is ready to identify whatever bugs creep into world's computer network especially when the calendar changes from 1999 to 2000.

headline: Freshman lawmakers take an oath of office
abstract: This year's swearing in of the new Pennsylvania legislature indicates its most experienced group ever as five Senators and thirteen House members were sworn in.  Five of the eighteen newcomers are returning as they have recently completed prior terms and have won re-election back to the legislature.

headline: Sharing the Wealth
abstract: President Clinton made a bold statement by proposing to invest billions of taxpayer dollars in the stock market and create a government-sponsored 401(K) type individual plan for taxpayers.  The plan drew immediate and harsh criticism from congressional republicans.

headline: Tax-cut details delay Assembly's budget approval
abstract: Governor Ridge's office said that Republicans and Democrats agreed on the $ 18.6 billion spending plan which included tax cuts for the businesses, seniors, low-income families and property tax cuts.

headline: Buoyant for shipyard jobs
abstract: The new Kvaerner Philadelphia shipyard held a job fair at the Navy shipyard where more than 1,500 people came for one of about 1,000 jobs.  The jobs will be available once Kvaerner rebuilds the decommissioned military base into a state-of-the-art shipbuilding center.

headline: Debating Clean and Green
abstract: State Rep Chadwick(R) and County Commissioners are against the bill which could lead to  tax increase for residents not enrolled in Clean and Green.

headline: Wecht pledges to dismantle panel
abstract: Cyril Wecht, democratic candidate for the Allegheny County executive, announced that if elected he would take apart the Allegheny County Airport Authority.  Wecht also ridiculed a plan to accept a lump-sum $12.4 million payment from the Authority for relinquishing future airport development.  Wecht in a critic of the airport authority formed in June by County Commissioners Mike Dawida and Bob Cranmer.  Jim Roddey supports the Authority.

headline: Pa. hailed for prison anti-drug effort
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Corrections has taken dramatic efforts to enforce their zero tolerance policy in its prisons.  The National Institute of Justice praised their efforts by announcing that the number of Pennsylvania inmates who tested positive for illegal drugs decreased nearly 80 percent over the last two years.

headline: Planners clear way to build PNC Park
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Planning Commission moved forward on plans for new stadiums for baseball and football despite uncertainty in Harrisburg.  The panel approved zoning and design changes for the $228 million PNC Park, the new Pirates stadium to be built on the North Shore if the Legislature decides to provide the necessary funding.

headline: Confident government officials are planning precautions anyway
abstract: PA and NJ officials say that the states are fully inoculated for the Y2K bug. Agencies at Federal, State and Local Levels also concur.

headline: From No-Show To Also-Rain?
abstract: Since 1976 no presidential candidate has won either the New Hampshire primary or his own party's presidential nomination without finishing first, second, or third in the Iowa caucuses.  By his decision not to compete in Iowa, McCain, probably the most popular candidate in both parties among the political press corps, could well be sentencing himself to a media blackout in that critical three-week period before the New-Hampshire primary and to also-ran status in the 2000 race.

headline: Sheehan tapped for top attorney, helped Ridge with voucher effort
abstract: Governor Ridge announced Carlisle native James Sheehan will be his next general counsel to replace outgoing Paul Tufano.  Sheeha, 53 years old, was chief counsel for the state Education Department since 1995 and was intimately involved in the governor's plan to attempt passing a school voucher program through the general assembly.

headline: Taxpayers still waiting for meaningful reform
abstract: Democratic lawmakers are proposing to refund part of the state's surplus to homeowners in the form of property tax rebates.  The plan would require that any time the state's budget surplus exceeds 1 percent of the budget, half of the surplus would go to property owners as a credit against school taxes.

headline: Coal's once dominant role in Indiana County shrinks further with Consol's closing of complexes employing nearly 1,000
abstract: Consol Energy will close two mining complexes by the end of the year that employed 1,000 people in Indiana County.  The United Mine Workers of America says the closures may cost just as many jobs in trucking, mining equipment and other support industries.  The layoffs mark fall in line with the overall mining decline in central Pennsylvania.  The state Deparment of Labor and Industry says that since 1982 the state has lost about 4,000 coal jobs.  Robert Marcus, chairman of the Indiana County Chamber of Commerce, says the layoffs may double the county's unemployment rate which was at 5.5% in September.

headline: Deer and their impact
abstract: Over 200 people gathered in Harrisburg at a conference on the impact of white-tailed deer on the biodiversity and economy of Pennsylvania to discuss deer and their impacts on people and the landscape they share.  Conference organizers presented the issue that there is growing agreement among wildlife biologists, land managers, ecologists, foresters, and others that white-tailed deer are over-populated with profound negative consequences for both humans and the other plants and animals that share the deer's world.  Until recently it was normal for hunters to travel into north-central Pennsylvania to hunt the deer and see large populations of them.  But in the 1980s and 1990s deer populations increased rapidly in agricultural and urban regions outside their traditional primary range.

headline: Wecht says airport authority not ready to fly
abstract: Democratic county executive candidate Cyril Wecht criticized recent airport-related agreements crafted by the current Allegheny County administration and continued his attack on the authority formed to take over airport management.  Wecht contends that the new airport authority had forsaken the broader regional approach to airport development.

headline: Paying for Protection
abstract: An idea that has been cancelled at least twice before is that of Governor Tom Ridge's proposal to collect a protection fee from towns that use state troopers for their primary police coverage.  Political leaders say the bill most likely will die this year as it did in 1991 and 1996.  Officials in places like Middletown and Concord - Delaware County's more affluent areas - are worried that the proposal's presistence is a sign that it may become law someday.  If it does, those two municipalities and more than 40 similar ones across the state will be confronted with an unpleasant decision.  They would have to start paying a hefty sum for a service they now get for nothing or pay to start their police departments.

headline: Port Richmond site added
abstract: A new site proposal has been added to the list of possible sites for the Philadelphia Phillies.  A group headed by state Senator Vincent Fumo, Democrat-Philadelphia, and state Representative Marie A. Ledere have proposed the Phillies build their new park on Port Richmond on the site of the existing Conrail train yard.  The site is 240 acres of blighted land.

headline: Don't fall prey to Y2K
abstract: State Representative Clymer urges the public to be aware of Y2K con artistes and use to common sense in dealing with their bank accounts and  stocks. He also assured the public that PA was Y2K compliant in every way and there was no need to be apprehensive about loss of money and services.

headline: 'Fun Filing' fund-raiser to help fill Robbin's campaign coffers
abstract: State Senator Robert D. Robbins was easily re-elected last fall but he is already campaigning for funds for his re-election for his 50th District Senate seat for 2002.  Campaign funds have reached around $500,000 with some even topping $1,000,000.  Goes on to talk about other senators who are already raising funds for re-election as well.

headline: SHOT IN THE ARM FOR POLITICS
abstract: Pennsylvania Democrats are forming a political action committee called New Century Democrats that will seek to enroll colege students and other young people who want to get involved with politics but do not know how.  This age group is not known to be as interested in public affairs as other groups such as retirees.

headline: The Pennsylvania 'sales tax' guide: It's always good for a few laughs
abstract: Who would have thought we would find a laugh in 'A guide to Pennsylvania's State Sales Tax?'  Early on when the sales tax was first enacted, politicians tried to lean heavy on the rich by taxing luxury items and exempt necessities to go easy on the poor as is indicated in the first 20 pages of the guide.  In addition there is the theory that items that are to be discouraged are taxed and those that are encouraged are exempted.  The article continues to list taxable and exmpet items that are humorous to the author's opinion.

headline: Gov. Ridge to open Fayette Career Link Center
abstract: Governor Ridge along with Leiteunant Governor Schweiker will "virtually" cut a ribbon as a part of Fayette's Career Link Center which is the second one stop chartered career development center to operate in PA.

headline: Democrats blast Growing Greener
abstract: Pennsylvania House Democrats criticized Governor Tom Ridge's plan to fund Growing Greener by diverting money from popular programs for recycling, hazardous waste cleanups and landfills.  They called Ridge's $1.3 billion proposal a shell game that promotes one set of environmental goals at the expense of others.

headline: Who gets the bucks?
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation and planning groups are preparing Program 2001, a biennial update of the state's 12-year transportation plan, including the more important 2001-2004 component from which new projects will flow.  Seven hearings will be held throughout the state to hear what the public thinks.

headline: Phila tops in making traditional form of meth
abstract: The US Drug Enforcement Administration released a report that Philadelphia is still the leader of the East Coast in making traditional form of methamphetamine.

headline: Private funding for stadiums should increase
abstract: Currently the plan to fund new sports stadiums in Pennsylvania stands at about 75 - 80% public funding and the rest from private sources.  If Governor Ridge is serious about rallying support for his pledge to fund stadiums at one-third of public funding then he should push corporate leaders to raise a larger portion of costs from private sources.

headline: E-Commerce tax questions have yet to be answered
abstract: Governor Ridge questioned about the relationship of taxes to e-commerce . Officials in Washingrton said that PA was behind the curve in e-commerce as PA had not taken steps to reduce the telecommunication taxes which is related to e-commerce.

headline: Fund-raiser exceeds expectations
abstract: Republican Bill Ravotti, who organized a fund-raising event for Pat Buchanan set a goal of raising $7,500 and exceeded the goal they set by $1,500.  The cost was $100 per person for the buffet, however, George Bush and Al Gore host luncheons charging $1,000 per person.

headline: Should conservatives leave the GOP on pure principle?
abstract: New Hampshire Senator Bob Smith left the presidential election race for 2000 and left the republican party. Article goes on to discuss how Smith has gone to the U.S. Taxpayers party, who although small and registering less than one percent of the vote, can be influential in pulling votes away from other candidates.  Cites the example of Ross Perot's Reform Party siphoning votes away from George Bush and Bob Dole helping Bill Clinton become elected.

headline: Time for a 30% tax cut
abstract: Mr.Dan Quayle former Vice President of the United States voiced his opinion against President Clinton's tax releif, as felt that that the government should be using the tax releif for the Americans to succeed and save more.  He also proposed the Freedom Accounts where the which would allow Americans to contribute dollars for tax free build up for use after retirement.

headline: Help needed
abstract: State lawmakers should increase the wage for the low end worker. The proposal that was introduced by the House would increase the state's wages by 50 cents every May 1 until it equals the federal poverty level for a family of three.

headline: DEP Receives 50-60 letters
abstract: The Department of Environmental Protection held a public hearing at the DuBois Ramada Inn and now has plenty of local testimony agianst a landfill in their area.  The Department is considering the application from Eagle Environment for a train-to-truck trash transfer station to be located near the proposed Happy Landing landfill four miles north of DuBois along Route 219 in Washington Township, Jefferson County.  Despite having its application suspended indefinitely, Eagle has not withdrawn its petition.  The construction of the transfer station could not happen without the development of a landfill.

headline: Young driver reform scrutinized
abstract: Lawmakers say that Governor Ridge's plan to make teen-agers wait longer and practice more to get a driver's license is a good idea but deserves some scrutiny.  The plan requires a teen to hold a permit for six months prior to getting a license and must have 50 hours of practice before receiving it as well.  The executive directors of both House and Senate transportation committees say their colleagues have received phone calls from complaining constituents and expect debate in both chambers.

headline: Philly: Is NYC law the wheal deal?
abstract: New York City's mayor Rudy Giuliani has allowed police officers to seize the vehicles of drunk drivers and to keep the vehicle when convicted.  Mayor Rendell of Philadelphia brushed off the question of whether he would ever do something like that with a gruff "no comment."

headline: Project put in High Gear- VAIL INDUSTRIAL PARK
abstract: Local lawmakers announced that the Vail Industrial Park would receive an additional $ 3 milllion in state funding to help pay for its project.

headline: Extending electronic handshake
abstract: Governor Ridge backs  legislation which would consummate a legally binding contract through digital signatures between two paries with out even meeting,

headline: Gekas says 67 votes to convict was not goal in trial
abstract: United States Representative George Gekas, Republican-Harrisburg, is read to move after the five-month impeachment ordeal of President Clinton.  His fellow House members only had to deal with the issue of impeaching President Clinton for a few days and members of the Senate served in jurors in the trial for six weeks.  Gekas' legislative and personal life has been on hold since August.

headline: Showy Bandwagon No Free Ride Toward Bush Nomination
abstract: Texas Governor George W. Bush has signed up more elected officials and endorsements that anyone in the republican field for the 2000 presidential election.  Despite all the support he will still have to go out and earn the vote.  Republican National Chairman Haley Barbour is the leader of Bush's exploratory committee and has ticked off a number of factors that have impelled half the GOP governors and hundreds of officeholders to pledge their support to Bush even before announcing his candidacy.

headline: Two districts cry foul over plan to abolish amusement tax
abstract: If the Pennsylvania Senate votes to cut the amusement tax in Pennsylvania, Conestoga Valley School District and East Lampeter Township might be forced to raise taxes.  The House previously voted 109-89 to cut the amusement tax that 50 school districts collect from amusement parks, movie theaters, golf courses and other recreational facilities.

headline: House Democrats try to force action on $1 minimum wage increase
abstract: US Representative Bonior and the House Democrats tried to hasten the republicans to vote on the minimum wage increase. The House Democrats accused the House Republicans of stalling.

headline: DEP video honored with pair of awards
abstract: A video about the Department of Environmental Protection's friendly Harrisburg Regional Office Building has won two multimedia awards for the cable program "GreenWorks for Pennsylvania."  The monthly television program won second prize in the 1999 Unites States International Film and Video Festival, and a bronze statuette in the 1999 national Telly Award competition.

headline: Yudichak to state: Build new bridge now
abstract: State Representative John Yudichak, 119th District, commended the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation for its quick response to the Carey Avenue bridge closure.  Yudichak is now asking the transportation department for a long term solution by building a new bridge.

headline: Police ask for radar guns
abstract: Whitehall Township police officers, who monitor over 55,000 motorists each day by the mall, are having to use stopwatches to monitor their speed.  Whitehall officials, police and representatives held a conference at the township municipal building to advocate legislation to use radar guns.

headline: PSU offers rural development model
abstract: State lawmakers learned that there is a new tool to help municipalities and concerned citizens groups in their districts predict how new development will affect specific rural areas.  State Representative Sheila Miller, chairwoman of the Center for Rural Pennsylvania, and Representative David Argall staged a special program for key legislative leaders to unveil the Pennsylvania State University's Community Impact Model.

headline: False claims earn hefty fine for telemarketers
abstract: A $2.4 million judgment was intered against Canadian telemarketers who conned United State consumers into purchasing bogus foreign lottery chances, falsely claiming that the odds of winning the large cash prize were 1 in 6.  United State District Court Chief Judge Sylvia Rambo of the Middle District in Harrisburg ordered Systems 3 Marketing Incorporated and two of its officials to pay $1.75 million in consumer restitution, and $630,000 in civil penalties and investigative costs.  In Pennsylvania, 131 consumers were awarded refunds.  Attorney General Mike Fisher filed a lawsuit in December saying the defendants violated the federal telemarketing act and other laws.

headline: Gekas, Santorum insist witnesses necessary for finding truth
abstract: Pennsylvania Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum voted with fellow Republicans agianst ending the impeachment case against President Clinton and want to issue subpoenas to witnesses.  Despite limiting their testimony to three witnesses and offering no guarantees of live testimony on the Senate floor, the votes lifted the spirits of United States Representative Geroge Gekas, Republican of Harrisburg, and other House impeachment managers.

headline: Siamese Senators
abstract: A satirical and comical article featuring Hillary Rodham Clinton and Rudolph Giuliani as they campaign against each for the U.S. Senate race.  The article depicts them each staying up late at night writing out statements and criticisms of each other.

headline: Unemployment rate hold steady at 4.1 percent in November
abstract: The US Labor Department said the unemployment rate stayed at a 4.1% and matched the October rate. Employers have also added 234,000 jobs jobs in November.Economists feel that this job growth and could be a recipe for inflation.

headline: Layoffs of 450 at health system
abstract: The University of Pennsylvania Health System announced it is laying off 450 people, mostly in administration, to trim 9% of its workforce.  Chief Executive Officer William N. Kelley said the region's largest health-care system was making the deepest cuts of his decade-long tenure by eliminating 1,100 full-time positions, more than half of which are vacant.

headline: Earth Moving
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge tried to hold the state Senate lawmakers back from taking an even bigger gallop at the State's environmental challenges that he wanted.  The Senate voted unanimously to approve a bill that would spend $623 million over five years to preserve farmlands, clean polluted streams and mines, and aid other environmental chores.  It is a more ambitious agenda than the Governor wanted, but the bill sponsored by Senator Mary Jo White of Venango, locks in dedicated funding.  Ridge did not want this.  It earmark's part of the state's real estate transfer tax and redirects $175 million from recycling and hazardous cleanups for the work.  Environmental groups hailed the Senate's action.

headline: 2 Phila. Officers get a lesson in security
abstract: Philadelphia police officers got a first hand look at violent demonstrations in Seattle that will likely benefit city officers with security at the Republican National Convention coming to the city in July.  Inspector Robert Muhly and Lieutenant Christopher Werner are on the Department's convention-planning staff and observed dignitary protection methods at the invitation of the Secret Service.

headline: Police discontinue sales of old guns
abstract: As no people are buying the Philadelphia Police Department's old guns it is halting sales of them back into public circulation and will likely start melting down outdated guns.  The new policy only came to light after Republican mayoral candidate Sam Katz wrote to mayor Ed Rendell asking that the practice be stopped.

headline: Public wants controls on development in the state
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge recently signed into law his $645.9 million Growing Greener bill.  With matching county and municipal funds, Pennsylvania governments will have more than $1.3 billion to buy land and developmental rights to slow growth largely in suburban townships that surround Philadelphia and in Lancaster and York counties.  What brought lawmakers together to pass this?  Public referendum.  14 Pennsylvania and southern New Jersey townships approved by solid majorities public referenda to raise their own taxes to buy open space and arrest development.  If Harrisburg faile dto fund Growing Greener, Harrisbug would have had open space or their heads handed to them next November.

headline: For whom the Bells toll
abstract: Pennsylvanian's utility regulators are intent on disrupting what's left of dinnertime peace as the Public Utility Commission may be fostering a truly competitive market in local phone service.  After years of waiting for the benefits of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 how much longer must Pennsylvanians wait for the promised deregulation.

headline: Ger Ready Now for the November Election
abstract: Editorial that discusses the campaign for Philadelphia's mayoral election saying that the lead white Democratic candidate, Marty Weinburg, unwittingly picked who would be the leading African-American Democratic candidate, John Street, by singeling him out to be the man to beat.  Says that under Ed Rendell's watch, while still mayor, he and Street moved the city forward and helped it to progress.

headline: Stadium, gambling lobbyist don’t have to tell
abstract: A lobbying disclosure law is designed to close loopholes that have enabled many of the 850 registered lobbyists here to avoid reporting what they really spend on wining and dining lawmakers or running public relations to influence bills.  The new law that Governor Ridge signed won't go into affect until the first half of this year's legislative session is over.

headline: Untitled
abstract: Sean Duffy, head of the Commonwealth Foundation felt that that a 15%-17% could be taken out every departmental budget in Harrisburg.

headline: Mold Base Industries Union, Form Partnership
abstract: A unique partnership was established between Mold Base Industries, International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers Union. This patnership would identify issues vital to workplace and businesses. State Senator Piccola and State Representative Tulli were present during the signing.

headline: Emissions audit looms as campaign issue
abstract: Governor Ridge and his administration lawyers have stonewalled on releasing the details of a $145 million buyout of Pennsylvania's contract for a never-implemented, centralized auto emission inspection program.  The program used public money but the Governor says that he has the right not to disclose the details due to attorney-client privilege.  The seven judges of the Commonwealth Court are deciding if the issue should be declard public.

headline: A sure-fire encore for Ed Rendell
abstract: A guest opinion article asking that Ed Rendell become the lead person in a nationwide gun-control campaign to enact the strictest legislation there is.  Rendell is applauded for being a successful mayor and asks that all the law firms and lobbyists who supported him and benefited from the renaissance that he brought to Philadelphia to contribute their support one more time in support of stricter gun-control laws.

headline: Police union calls for boycott over Mumia-supporting band's concert
abstract: The Philadelphia police union is calling for a boycott of all businesses involved in the rock concert supporting cop-killer and death row inmate Mumia Abu- Jamal.

headline: Questions about over steel use for stadium
abstract: Governor Ridge is criticized for favoritism for public funding of new sports stadiums in Pittsburgh where it was thought that the public bidding process on stadium projects was suspended in the name of saving money.  The no-bid process allowed the Public Auditorium Authority to conduct non-public bidding and private negotiations on projects that are two-thirds funded with state tax dollars.

headline: Free Markets Online to enable state to purchase goods online
abstract: Free Markets Online Inc, a company that uses a proprietary software to purchase and sell products in an auction manner said that it would help PA sell and purchase goods in its 3 month pilot program. This announcement was made during Governor Ridge's budget address.

headline: Get over Clinton, candidates wooing conservatives say
abstract: Republican presidential hopefuls for the 2000 election said it was time to move past Bill Clinton and focus on attacking George W. Bush with his father's record and 1992 loss for reelection, and former cabinet secretary Elizabeth Dole with her husband's shortcomings as the party's losing 1996 nominee.

headline: Sparks fly at forum
abstract: Philadelphia's mayoral candidates squared off at the Daly News / Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce for an 80 minute event to speak on issues like schools, the city wage, and also through political jabs to knock an opponent down a per or two.  Sam Katz, Marty Weinberg, John Street, Dwight Evans, John White, and Happy Fernandez squared off to debate.

headline: Use state surplus to cut state taxes
abstract: The author voices his opinion on how the budget surpluses could be used. The author suggests using the state surplus to decrease state income tax. He also writes that the State cannot reduce property taxes as this falls under the jurdisction of the counties and the local school districts.

headline: More pay for care workers pursued
abstract: State Representatives Lescovitz and Solobay say they will support legislation to increase wages for direct care workers at private homes caring for the mentally ill and retarded throughout Pennsylvania.  The legislation will direct $90 million into paychecks of workers at community-based mental health/mental retardation programs.

headline: Endangered fish list focus of hearing
abstract: An endangered long-head darter was brought in for show at a public hearing in Meadville in regards toe the controversial issue of expanding the state's listing of endangered fish.  The darter was collected from French Creek near Meadville.  Andrew Shiels, the fish commission's nongame and endangered species coordinator said that they are trying to show how conservation and development could live together.  The state Fish and Boat Commission's proposal would add eight native species endangered species list.  Representatives of the mining, river dredging and oil drilling industries and local political leaders insisted that adding to the state's endangered fish list would result in habitat protections that could stop or limit their business activities.

headline: A year after rioting, State College girds for arts fest
abstract: Men convicted for their part in the riots last July 12 put on bright-orange construction vests and replanted lights posts they pulled up during the riots at State College.  This visible punishment was meant to send the message that an encore performance will not be welcome as the town prepares for the Central Pennsylvania's Festival of the Arts.

headline: Policy punishes families
abstract: Families pay twice as much as the going rate to receive a collect call from a family member or someone they know calling them collect from prison.  Prison advocacy programs like Citizens United for Rehabilitation of Errants are complaining to the Public Utility Commission that the prison rate is so exorbitant as to constitute a restriction of free speech.

headline: Ready, Action
abstract: In its budget, the Ridge administration proposed to redirect a quarter of the environmental dollars spent by the state and link infrastructure grant money to smart growth policies.  Legislation is again being introduced in the General Assembly to provide local communities with tools to better plan growth and protect open space.  Ridge's 21st Century Environmental Commission identified suburban sprawl as the state's most pressing environmental problem.

headline: House panel opens hearings into internet commerce
abstract: House sub committee will examine the millions of dollars of state tax revenue draning away into cyberspace. Since none of the sales on internet have any sales tax this could lead to some controversy with the businesses.

headline: Gigliotti a no-show at campaign meeting
abstract: Frank Gigliotti, a Pennsylvania House Representative, was a no-show at a meeting to plan strategy with his fellow Allegheny County legislative democrats at Piccolo Piccolo Ristorante.  Gigliotti is under investigation by federal authorities and are not revealing the reasons for their investigations.

headline: Specter partially lifts self-imposed gag order
abstract: Senator Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania partially lifted his self-imposed gag order to talk with reporters about procedural hurdles in the ongoing impeachment trial of President Clinton.  The Senator had previously declard on January 15 that he would make no further statements on the matter.  Specter limited his remarks to procedural questions and refused to answer two questions that he deemed were fact-finding in nature.

headline: Vote on state budget scheduled for today
abstract: The legislature is expected to vote on the 1999-2000 state budget that calls for no tax increases, $400 million in tax cuts and targets money for the Governor Ridge tuition voucher program.  The $19 billion budget is slightly higher than the $18.6 billion spending plan Governor Ridge presented to the legislature.
