headline: New Labor legislation would allow Amish youth to work
abstract: A bill introduced by Congressman Joseph Pitts, PA-16, passed the House Education and the Workforce Committee unanimously which modifies the Department of Labor policies that are negatively affecting Amish constituencies.  The bill would allow Amish youth to be employed with adult supervision in the places where machinery is used to process wood products.

headline: Environmentalist law suits a bet against casinos
abstract: Even though casinos have spread over the country bringing in revenue and jobs, environmentalists are slapping law suits staring with Missouri. They feel the casinos encourage damage of the environment.

headline: A year in prison changes Preate, a former prosecutor
abstract: Ernie Preate, formerly the state's top prosecutor and once defended the state's death penalty to the United States Supreme Court, had time to think about prison when he spent a year there in 1995 after pleading guilty to mail fraud in connection with a $20,000 campaign fundraising violaiton.  The article provides further discussion on prison overcrowding and Preate's criticism of the death penalty.

headline: Politics and pardons
abstract: As members of the state Board of Pardons, Pennsylvania's lieutenant governor Mark Schweiker and attorney general Mike Fisher, helped approve pardon recommendations for seven convicted shoplifters, a person guilty of disorderly conduct, and another carrying a concealed weapon.  One pardon they would not give was for Rudy Thomas.  Thomas helped a friend find a nurse to have an abortion when it was illegal to do so.  Now, post 1973 when the United States Supreme Court has issued its decision in Roe v. Wade, it is a constitutional right of Americans.  What was really on the minds of Schweiker and Fisher was their politics and morality of abortion.  It is wrong to hold someone in prison when your own politcal/moral agenda is in conflict with the law of the land.

headline: Regional planners see population shift continuing into 2025
abstract: The Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission predicts that over the next 25 years as more and more people will continue to move from Philadelphia to the suburban fringes which is distressing officials there who want to control sprawl.  The needed tax dollars to repair roads, sewer systems, and schools in the urban areas are disappering.

headline: Internet measure puts Pa. at regulatory ground zero
abstract: Legislation before the House Consumer Affairs Committee would have far-reaching effect for consumers and the cable television, Internet and telephone industries in Pennsylvania and elsewhere.  It would force cable companies to sell their high speed broadband to any other Internet service provider that requests it, at the same terms they would sell it to any affiliate.

headline: Gigliotti met with state, firm
abstract: Representative Frank Gigliotti, under investigation for his ties to a painting contractor, met late last year with the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation and the president of the Anastasios Corporation regarding plans to ban the company from doing state work.  The West Mifflin painting company later was debarred from state contracts for alleged labor law and health violations.  That matter, now under appeal, was pending when the meeting occurred.  Gigliotti disclosed to Representatives James Casorio and Don Walko that federal prosecutors were investigating his alleged relationship with a painting contractor.

headline: Specter says he will stay silent
abstract: Senator Arlen Spector of Pennsylvania has appeared on dozens of television talk shows in recent weeks to discuss President Clinton's impeachment trial and issued the unexpected statement that he would have no more to say.  This reversed his previous willingness to speak on the topic.  He was one of the Senate's unofficial spokesmen on countless radio broadcasts and television shows speaking on the matter.

headline: Web site seeks ideas on how to use cash
abstract: Pennsylvania state Senator Jay Costa is gathering public opinion on how to use the $11.3 billion share of the tobacco settlement money by using an online poll.  The survey lets people choose from a list of suggested spending options.

headline: Penn State Geisinger spent half-million fighting off labor unions
abstract: Penn State Geisinger spent almost a half-million to help fight off labor unions in its first year of existence.  The money was paid to Subelt Organization Services of Arizona for roughly six months work to prevent unions from organizing at Geisinger Medical Center in Danville and the Wyoming Valley Medical Center near Wilkes-Barre.

headline: Envirotest buyout to be decided by judges
abstract: Senators Richard Kasunic, Democrat-Dunbar, and Geral LaValle, Democrat-Beaver, filed a suit trying to force the governor to open the books on the state's expensive Envirotest Inc. buyout which is now in the Commonwealth Court.  It deals with whether an audit commissioned by the governor's office and used in negotiations with Envirotest is protected by attorney-client privilege.  LaValle says the audit and buyout were paid for with public money.  Governor Ridge's office says that the audit and other research done by the administration to prepare itself against a lawsuit should remain private because releasing the documents could set bad precedent for future lawsuits.

headline: Abu-Jamal lawyers file appeal
abstract: Lawyers for the death- sentenced inmate  Mumia Abu-Jamal filed a appeal saying that every aspect of the trial was unfair.

headline: Prison influx slowing
abstract: The number of inmates that are coming into Pennsylvania's prisons is starting to slow and is a trend that is taking place on the national level.  Pennsylvania's state prison system saw a 4% growth from 1998 to 1999 which is about 2% lower that the average annual growth rate of the state's prison system of 6.3% since 1990.

headline: Rendell suggests ticket tax to raise money for stadiums
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell and Governor Tom Ridge spent time yesterday selling the benefits of new sports stadiums for Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  Rendell has suggested a tax on game tickets as a way to raise money for the projects.

headline: Is a web political poll reliable ? Yes ? No ? Maybe ?
abstract: Researchers at Harris Black International Ltd. Sayt internet polling is less expensive, faster and offfers high response rates than telephone surveys. But the flip side to this ix most of the peole who go on these polls are a self selected pool. Some crtics also say the internet users are all too white and educated and relfect only a certain part of the society.

headline: Gigliotti probe rooted in painter's problems
abstract: For years, competitors of painting contractor Ernest Smalis wondered how he managed to secure local, state and federal jobs despite his dismal record for violations of federal labor and environmental regulations.  Smalis is the same person who five years ago was ordered to pay the largest single fine in the history of the United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration after his workers were exposed to toxic doses of lead dust while workers on Tarentum Bridge.  Smalis' ability to obtain his contracts also caught the attention of federal prosecutors as well.  Representative Frank Gigliotti is expected to have been peddling contracts to Smalis.

headline: Specter turns dean of moderate Senate
abstract: United States Senator Arlen Specter became the dean of the Senate's liberal Republicans.  With the death of Senator John Chafee, Republican-Rhode Island, Specter is the most senior of a group of fiscal conservatives on moderate social issues.

headline: Which PA tax should be cut ?
abstract: Debate in the House and Senate as to which PA tax should eleminated -  personal income tax, school tax or  gross receipts tax. Gov.Ridge pushes for gross receipt tax and business tax.

headline: Philadelphia loses high paying jobs to suburbs
abstract: Workers in Montgomery County, a county bordering Philadelphia, earned an average of $34,751 which was 5% more than the average wage in the city according to the United States Bureau of Economic Analysis figures.  Workers in West Chester earned an average of 4% more than workers in Philadelphia.

headline: EPA wants changes in autos and fuel
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency will propose a new package of tighter auto-emission and fuel standards that will cost billions of dollars and put two powerful Washington lobbies - the auto and oil industries - against each other in a fight over who should be responsible for reducing smog.  The rule could add as much as $200 to the cost of a new car and 5 cents to a gallon of gas.  Officials will likely say that 90% of sulfur must be removed from gasoline, force sport utility vehicles to abide by regular passenger car emission standards, tighten overall emission limits, make diesel cars and small trucks meet passenger car emission standards.

headline: Abu-Jamal supporters cite letter to debunk alleged confession
abstract: Supporters of death row inmate said that Abu-Jamal said a former prison volunteer lied about Abu-Jamal admitting to murdering a Philadelphia police officer.

headline: Prison site to be picked before August
abstract: Martin Horn, secretary of the state Corrections Department, stated he is waiting on tests from several sites within 50 miles of Pittsburgh to decide where to put a prison to replace the 117-year-old state prison which is along the Ohio River.  Once the site is picked crews will need three years to build the maximum security prison.

headline: Rendell's primary concern is looming
abstract: Philadelphia mayor Ed Rendell is waiting to seek the City Council's approval until after the spring primary election.  Although this is his plan, there is only a slight chance this will happen because pressure to answer how, why and where the Philadelphia stadium will be is building.

headline: Lawmakers inundated with e-mails over false rumors of e-mail fees
abstract: US Representaive English and State Reps say that they have received hundreds of e-mails over the possiblity of the Federal Communications Commissions putting a charge on e-mails.

headline: Giuliana Lingers in Arizona with a New Political Friend
abstract: Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani exntended his trip to Phoenix, Arizona to be with Senator John McCain.  Giuliani is considering running for a senate seat and McCain is running for the presidency.  Giuliani was at a fundraiser for conservatives and stayed longer at the invitation of McCain.

headline: Specter wants president to testify
abstract: Breaking two weeks of self-imposed silence Senator Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania said he not only wants witnesses to testify in the impeachment tiral of President Clinton but he wants the President to testify as well.  He quickly noted; however, that he did not think he could get the 51 votes for live witnesses or for the President to testify.  In a case of this magnitude there should be witnesses, Specter felt.

headline: 2 more staffers sue state agency over race bias
abstract: Kimberly Davis and Cheryl Williams charge racial discrimination by the Bureau of Contract Administration.  The suits filed allege allegations similar to those charged in a lawsuit filed by former analyst Madie Maddox who claimed the Ridge administration was trying to roll back Affirmative Action programs.  The state paid Maddox more than $70,000 to settle two lawsuits she filed in 1996 and 1998 alleging sexual and racial harassment.

headline: Ridge to announce unemployment tax cut
abstract: Governor Ridge's office announced that unemployment taxes will be cut by $ 20 million  for the next year due to a strong economy. Unemployment benefits will also be paid to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of theirs.

headline: Ex-Game Commissioner chief won't be prosecuted
abstract: Donald Madl, former executive director of the Pennsylvania Game Commission will not be prosecuted for alleged game code violations spanning 10 years because the statute of limitations has expired.  However, other allegations made in a State Inspector General's report, including the misuse of state supplies and using state emloyees for personal work, have been forwarded to Attorney General Mike Fisher.  Vern Ross has replaced Madl.  Madl's attorney, Al Lindsay, said his client has been smeared by the allegations and is appalled by Game Commission and Inspector General's office for making the accusations without notifying his client of the specific nature of the charges.

headline: Abuse of an 'Awesome Power'
abstract: Jeff Kumer, owner of Pittsburgh Wool Co., writes in response to an editorial that discussed how his company was a near victim of the abuse of eminent domain.  He states that few realize that property rights abuses often start with a bogus designation of blight that is easy to receive, nearly impossible to change, and put into motion the first stages of government taking property.

headline: Private Pensions?
abstract: Many outside entities are coming into Pennsylvania trying to build private prisons while Attorney General Mike Fisher is seeking to address this immediately as he states this is not allowed as a matter of law, not policy.  He told Cornell Corrections Incorporated, of Houston, Texas, to stop construction of a site in Clearfield County which they were contracted to build by the Federal Bureau of Prisons.  Fisher argues that there is no statute allowing private prisons in the state.

headline: Residency requirements for contracts questioned
abstract: Two western Pennsylvania lawmakers introduced legislation this week that would bar residency requirements in the awarding of municipal building contracts.  The legislation would earn the enmity of Pittsburgh city officials who are asking voters to approve a referendum requiring that 35% of all jobs on publicly funded construction projects more of than $200,000 go to city residents.

headline: Lawmakers question proposed telemarketing changes
abstract: Plans to crackdown on telemarketers in Pennsylvania is raising questions among lawmakers that could hamper their ability to do political polling via the telephone.  The House Consumer Affairs Committee held a hearing on a bill sponsored by Representative Lynn Hermann, Republican-Centre, that would toughen the state's 1996 telemarketing law.

headline: Giuliani vs. Giuliani
abstract: Hillary Clinton is having a good month running for the U.S. Senate seat against Rudolph Giuliani.  All she has to do is let Giuliani be Giuliani.  He lost 20 points in the polls due to handling the issue of Amadou Diallo, a west african immigrant who was shot 19 times and fired at by four white police officers 41 times.  The police were looking for a rapist, thought this was him, and thought he was armed.  Previously a haitian immigrant, Abner Louima, accused the police of torturing her.  In both cases Giuliani dismissed the crticism of the police as political opportunists.  He is seen as the mayor of a white only New York.

headline: Specter's non-moment
abstract: People had hoped that Senator Arlen Spector would take the lead in the impeachment process of President Clinton and extricate the nation from this demeaning process.  When votes were counted Specter's was one of the votes that was with Democrats not to allow Clinton from being impeached.  Specter found a middle ground by saying "guilty" or "not-guilty" - but "not proved" and therefore guilty.

headline: Abortion clinic plan stalled by state regs
abstract: Planned Parenthood's proposal to perform abortions in Lancaster is on indefinite hold after the state Department of Health notified the agency it must have a transfer agreement with a local hospital before it can begin to offer the service.  The clinic had originally planned to begin performing abortions in September, but is now uncertain when if ever_ it will be able to do so.

headline: State auditor's report cited in Yough bus driver dispute
abstract: The state Auditor General recommended cutting transportation and health benefit costs and may have been the catalyst for a dispute between the Yough School District and its union bus drivers.  The bus drivers presented testimony to the Pennsylvania Labor Relations Board stating that the district did not bargain collectively in good faith.  The dispute arose from the school district's decisioin in August 1998 to subcontract bus services to Laidlaw Transit Inc. rather than offer a new contract to the district's 23 drivers and two mechanics.  School district Solicitor Terrance Faye stated at the hearing that the district was under pressure from Governor Tom Ridge's office to reduce transportation and health care costs.

headline: Federal appeals court decides ozone levels are within standards
abstract: In the spring the Environmental Protection Agency issued stricter ozone pollution standards which caused cities in the Lehigh valley region to exceed limits.  In contrast, however, the United State Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia set aside those tougher standards.  The Court was responding to an appeal from the industry and two of the three judges on the panel determined that the stricter standards loosely enacted and unconstitutional.  The Environmental Protection Agency has appealed the ruling.  Depending on which standard for pollution is applied will determine if the Lehigh vally is compliant.  Before the Court case, ozone concentrations above 124 parts per billion were illegal, after they were 84 parts per billion.

headline: Abuse of an 'Awesome Power'
abstract: Jeff Kumer, owner of Pittsburgh Wool Company, responds to a December 14 editorial where his company was mentioned as a near victim of eminent domain.  He explains that few people realize that property rights abuses often start with a bogus designation of "blight."

headline: Private prison must not burden local public
abstract: People are publicly opposing and endorsing the building of a private prison in Morris and Decatur townships.  Attorney General Mike Fisher has stopped the project altogether as he claims it is not in the state's laws to do so.  State Representative Camille 'Bud' George authored this article and presses for more facts and figures before any decisions for or against are made.

headline: Residents of sinking homes may get aid
abstract: Anne Whiston Spirn, professor of landscape architecture and co-director of the urban studies program at the University of Pennsylvania, explained that at the beginning of the century it was common practice for homes to be built over stream beds and flood plains.  In 1987 the city paid about $20 million to bail out homeowners in the city's Logan section after about 1,000 homes were sinking.

headline: Melissa virus forces Democrats to shut down computers
abstract: The Melissa computer virus has infiltrated the House Democrats' computer system and forced the party to shut-down e-mail and Internet service for all Democratic lawmakers and staffers.  In the middle of budget negotiations and debates on other bills, House Democrats discovered that they could not access the state's computer system to get meeting schedules or information on bills.  The Republicans however have a computer system with a better virus protection so it was not affected.

headline: Glitch can affect election outcome
abstract: Sandy Township voters may not be able to elect all five supervisors.  A state law glitch allows candidates to file for more than one supervisor's post if two terms of differing lengths are to be filled in a given election.  State Representative Dan Surra, Democrat from Sandy Township, is trying to get the law changed.

headline: Split Decision Sets Stage for Battles
abstract: Elected officials and census experts said that the Supreme Court's decision is vurtually certain to lead to fierce battles in Congress, state legislatures and courts nationwide over what census figures should be used to draw lines and to distribute Federal money.  The court said in its 5-4 ruling today that the Clinton Administration could not use sampling, a scientific polling technique, to adjust the 2000 census to apportion seats in the House of Representatives among the 50 states.  The court did; however, leave the door open for states to use adjusted census data when they draw new lines for Congressional, legislative and other political seats in 2000 and after.

headline: Aiming for Sunday
abstract: Opinion article explaining that it used to be the case that people in Lancaster county did not work on Sundays and the rare exception were police, hospital staff, and turnpike workers.  Now people not only shop on Sundays but they hunt as well, which is legal.  The limitation, however, was that deer, bear, turkey, and small game could not be hunted.  Dan Surra, 75th District, has introduced a bill, House Bill 1237, that would permit Sunday hunting during the regular antlered deer season.

headline: Statewide school health care could help defuse labor strife
abstract: Although Pennsylvania has not had an unusual amount of labor strikes, the ones it has have been rancorous enough that they have gained national attention causing the state to gain the reputation as a "labor strife" state causing business in the state to suffer greatly.  The Heinz Foundation, chaired by Teresa Heinz, is underwriting a new approach to bring together disparate state school administrators, school business officials, the Pennsylvania Federation of Teachers, and the School Boards Association to work out health care costs and quality.

headline: Federal money may make sewer system affordable for township
abstract: United States Representative Bud Shuster, Republican-Everett, announced that Metal Township could get a $500,000 Environmental Protection Agency waste water grant.  The sewer will serve about 160 homes in the township which has one of the highest poverty rates in Franklin County.  The grant still needs approval of the Unites States Senate and President Clinton.

headline: Advocates question proposed changes to domestic abuse laws
abstract: The PA Coalition Against Domestic Violence told the legislative task force to tighten the language in the pair of bills which was on domestic abuse and violence.

headline: Professor criticizes DNA-test legislation
abstract: Barbara Woodhouse, a University of Pennsylvania law professor, charged that proposed bills to expand the use of DNA testing in paternity cases would be detrimental to children and the legal system.  Woodhouse testified during a House Judiciary Committee hearing on legislation to change a law requiring an Amity Township man to pay support for a child despite having DNA tests prove he is not the biological father.

headline: Residents to state: Ease development pains
abstract: Perry Count was the last site for the forum held with Pennsylvania citizens (there were a total of 53) by the Department of Community and Economic Development's Governor's Center for Local Government Services which will be used for a report sent to the Governor's office.  Issued raised at the forum ranged from education to open space concerns.

headline: Merger essential for AT&T
abstract: AT&T chief executive officer Michael Armstrong stated that it was more important that it acquire MediaOne than for Comcast to do it because it faced more risks and had fewer options to achieve its goals.  Speaking at an e-commerce conference conducted by the World Affairs Council Armstrong stated that he has congressmen in every district in the state expecting AT&T to deliver service.

headline: GOOD NEWS: COMPUTER ACCESS TO CAMPAIGN FINANCE RECORDS PASSES
abstract: The Free Press supported a pojrect to establish a database for public access to all campaign finance records. Gov. Tom Ridge's 1999-2000 state budget includes a $398,000 allocation for such a project which will make more than 100,000 pages of campaign finance report records accessible to the public through the Internet and will include records for PA House and Senate members, judges and elected executive office holders.

headline: STATE DEMOCRATS VISIT ERIE
abstract: State Senate Democrats visited Erie to promote campaign finance reform that they say will allow candidates to spend more time on the issues rather than raising money according to Senate Minority Leader Robet Mellow of Lackawanna County.  Other Democratic Senators on hand included Ralphael Musto of Luzerne County, Vincent Hughes of Philadelphia, and Jay Costa, Jr. of Pittsburgh.

headline: Amendement nixes domestic partner benefits
abstract: State Representative Egolf succeeded in passing an amendment which oulf prevent state supported universities and colleges from granting health benefits to unmarried couples. The amendment was inspired out of the contreversy at Penn State and University of Pittsburgh relating to health benefits for gay and lesbian couples.

headline: Times-Tribune wins state safety award
abstract: Lieutenant. Governor Schweiker presented PENNSAFE- Pennsylvania Safety First award, a workplace initiative to to Times-Tribune in Scranton.

headline: Game Commission talks turkey
abstract: The wild turkey in Pennsylvania is the premier game management success story owing much of its thanks to the Wild Turkey Super Fund that the National Wild Turkey Federation created in 1985.  National Wild Turkey Federation volunteers in Pennsylvania have spent more than $1.6 million of Super Fund money on nearly 800 projects across the state.  Every state has a Super Fund, however, few have seen as much activity as the Pennsylvania state chapter and local chapters in Pennsylvania have generated.

headline: After shootings in Colorado and Georgia schools across the country tighten security
abstract: After 2 shooting incidents schools across the country are tightening security at schools. Some of the measures that have been taken are using metal detectors, closed video circuit for monitoring and forging close relationships with the Police SWAT team.

headline: Proposed State Police service fee assailed
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge's proposal to charge some municipalities for state police services got a cool reception from some municipal officials yesterday, but no one was particularly surprised.  Ridge wants to charge townships with 5,000 or more residents and no police force $35 per resident for the last part of 1999 and $70 per resident in 2000.  In the midstate, townships are on a list distributed by the state: South Middleton in Cumberland County and Jackson in Lebanon County.  In both places the proposal would mean increased taxes, to the tune of about 16 million.

headline: Ridge listening to opposition to business park
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is contributing his opinion to building a business park in Moosic Mountain.  Ridge's spokesperson, Jerry Feaser, says the Governor has close concerns to the issue.  The state Department of Environmental Protection and the Department of Conserviation and Natural Resources have raised objections to the park project, along with the United States Environmental Protection Agency and Department of Interior.  Interest groups have alread stopped construction of a federal prison at Moosic Mountian.

headline: Motion would set performance standards
abstract: In addition to approving the merger of Bell Atlantic Corporation and GTE Corporation, state Public Utility Commission Chairman John Quain offered a motion setting performance standards that Bell Atlantic-Pennsylvania Incorporated must meet as it open its local telephone network to competition.  The motion addresses topics of high importance to potential Bell Atlantic competitors.

headline: GOP Battle Lines Growing Sharper
abstract: Texas Governor George Bush was the Iowa straw poll for the 2000 presidential election marking his rivals' efforts to increase their attacks on him.  Several opponents were saying they would use tactics of vague and evasive on critical issues, and lacking the preparation and temperament needed to be president.  Bush finished the poll with 31 percent of the vote in a field of 9 contenders.

headline: State GOP blunders couldn't have come at more critical time
abstract: The Pennsylvania House has had to deal with Scranton Representative Frank Serafini's ongoing perjury trial and allegations that Representative Joseph Gladeck became involved in an altercation with his girlfriend during a Memorial Day party.  In the Senate, Erie Senator William Slocum's indictment on charges that he violated the Federal Clean Water Act by allegedly allowing raw sewage to flow into the Brokenstraw Creek when he was borough manager of Youngsville in Warren County.

headline: Battle lines being drawn on school prayer bill
abstract: Towanda based political group wants to give the option of making school prayers mandatory. The PA Alliance for Democracy led by Clark Moeller wants the House Bill 1726 to fail. Mr.Moeller feels that children should not be forced to follow relegious practices that could be contradictory to ones practiced at home.

headline: Why is Bill Goodling bottling up the right to work bill ?
abstract: The current federal labor law forces  millions of Americans to pay their union dues, without which they could lose their jobs. PA has no right to work law and the Keystone union  base has shrunk considerably since the 1960s. State Rep Goodling refuses to see the union issue and feels that the situation is not yet ripe for the Senate to consider.

headline: Game Commission will study role of conservation officers
abstract: Due to controversy over wildlife conservation officer's law enforcement efforts the state House Game and Fisheries Committee has set up a committee to review the role of its deputies.  The committee is charged with reviewing all areas of the deputy program and to bring forward recommendations designed to enhance public perception, develop an increased awareness of human relations skills, and increase the understanding of constitutional issues and concerns of individual rights.  Deputy training will be part of the committee's focus.

headline: An Amendment undone
abstract: The Commonwealth Court has done Pennsylvania a favor by scuttling a constitutional amendment that would have made it vitually impossible to reduce the prison sentences of convicted murderers.  At issue is a constitutional amendment approved by state voters in 1997.  Its principal features were 1) a requirement that the five-member Board of Pardons unanimously approve any recommendation for a reduction in a convicted murderer's sentence (previously only a majority vote was required) and 2) a change in the nature of gubernatorial appointees to the Pardons Board, abolishing requirements that the board include a penologist and a lawyer and creating the new requirement that one member be a crime victim.  The 1997 amendment took away a convicted murderer's hope at clemency.

headline: Protect business from lawsuits
abstract: State Senator Bob Thompson has introduced legislation that is putting lawsuit abuse of businesses with key provisions to avoid costly fines to companies.  There is growing support across the state to give judges the power to impose penalties against people, businesses, and lawyers who bring frivolous lawsuits against companies.

headline: Ridge trading votes to get stadium money?
abstract: Governor Ridge has plans to double the amount of money to be borrowed for development projects in counties outside the state's major metropolitan areas in an effort to get support for new sports facilities in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  Rural legislators are calling it a budget buster while Republican Representative Larry Sather is waiting to see if it materializes.

headline: Needed to make a call: Tenacity and 10 digits
abstract: Problems are anticipated with the introduction of two new area codes and the death of seven-digit phone numbers that will spread into the Philadelphia area in a few days.  The two new area codes, 215 and 610, will require that any call made to these area codes will require the entire number to be dialed which also includes cell phones.

headline: GOP bigwigs impressed by Ridge, Philadelphia
abstract: Pennsylvania Republican Chairman Alan Novak said that the Republican National Convention's summertime meeting was held in Philadelphia and met with several people from all over the country who all said they had positive impressions of Tom Ridge, Governor.  Philadelphia will be the host city for the 2000 Republican National Convention.

headline: State GOP gunning for Battisto's 189th District seat
abstract: Pennsylvania House Republican leaders have targeted Representative Joe Battisto's 189th District seat and have asked Monroe County Controller Kelly Lewis to be their candidate in 2000.  Lewis is a Republican who just won re-election to a four year term as controller is considering running against Battisto and is meting with House Majority leader John Perzel.

headline: Bill Bradley's Challenge
abstract: Bill Bradley, speaking at the Wollman Lounge at Cooper Union and the second democratic candidate for nomination, spoke without jokes or turns of phrase in issues such as race and the crowd listened intently.  To move beyond racial inequality he said that we must vanquish it from our hearts and minds, well beyond civil rights or affirmative action.

headline: "Never" Ridge says to ending voucher fight
abstract: Governor Ridge said that he would never stop fighting for the parents and children of PA after his third defeat of the voucher program with the House of Representatives.

headline: Giuliani responds to state's paper protest
abstract: Pennsylvania House Democrats were angered by New York City Mahor Rudolph Giuliani by his comment that states should be willing to accept trash from New York state.  In response they filled 50 trash bags of shredded paper and sent it to his office.  Giuliani's argument was that other states should be willing to accept their trash because of the cultural entertainment the city provides to everyone.  Representative Todd Eachus, Democrat - Luzerne, was angered with Giuliani.  New York has shipped 3.3 million tons of trash to Pennsylvania in 1997 according to the state Department of Environmental Protection.  Pennsylvania is the nation's lead importer of trash.

headline: Area legislator sponsors bill for more support volunteer fire companies
abstract: State Representative Sam Smith, Republican - Punxsutawney, is sponsoring a House resolution in response to a report concerning state aid to Volunteer Firefighters' Relief Association sissued by the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee.  The resolution will be a survey of Pennsylvania's more than 2,400 volunteer fire fighters.  The resolution passed the House unanimously and directed the Center for Local Government Services to conduct the survey and report its findings to the House within six months.

headline: Punish vandals more; strengthen state legislation
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives has unanimously approved a bill to stiffen penalties for graffiti artists and other vandals.  Urge the State Senate and Governor Ridge to approve the bill as well.

headline: Ridge wants big boost from unions on Plan B
abstract: Governor Ridge will ask about two dozen union leaders in the construction trades tomorrow to get behind a renewed push for legislation to fund major league sports stadiums and other big-ticket projects.  The meeting in one of a series that are to generate support for delivering state funds to build ballparks in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, among other projects.

headline: Open Purse
abstract: The press release from Gov.Ridge's Office says that technology would be placed center stage in the 1999-2000 budget.  This includes the $ 132 million Link-to-Learn program and the establishment of the PA Technology Investment Authority which would enable PA to be a leader in technology.

headline: GOP candidates can't ignore abortion issue
abstract: Republican presidential campaigning for the 2000 election has produced debate on two issues: policy crisis in the Balkans and abortion.  The GOP's hard-line stance against abortion may change in hopes of bringing it more in line with the majority of republican voters and not seem unsympathetic to women's rights.

headline: State House leaders still arguing over embattled legislator
abstract: Despite legislative matters being wrapped up for 1999, Democrats and Republicans are still debating what to do with Representative Frank Serafini who was convicted of perjury.  House Democrats released a letter to Attorney General Mike Fisher to continue his probe into whether Serafini should be removed from his 114th District seat which he has held for more than two decades.

headline: Bipartisan Poll Shows Bush Gains With Women, Hispanics
abstract: Texas Governor George Bush has made significant ground amongst women and hispanic voters against vice president Al Gore and threatens to neutralize the Democratic Party's traditional advantage on such key issues as education and protecting the middle class, according to a bipartisan poll released yesterday.

headline: 10 more schools get walk-through metal detectors
abstract: By September students at 13 Philadelphia schools will have airport style walk-through metal detectors in order to get into the building.  School officials for Miller and Benjamin Franklin schools said the program was so successful that they decided to expand the program to other schools.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: Heard on the Hill: "We have managed to get ourselves $3 million in debt serving 950 customers, and we have no water." - Newport Water Authority Chairman James Williamson, testifying before the House Democratic Policy Committee.

headline: Area police support radar gun bill
abstract: Pennsylvania is the only state that does not allow municipal police officers to use radars and lasers to detect speeding motorists.  The Senate Transportation Committee introduced a bill last week that allows trained municipal police offers to use them.

headline: Ratings problems hoped to be in the past
abstract: The Chairman of the Pennsylvania Bar Assocation, Micheal Bloom, states that the judicial candidate rating panel will be improved and will not repeat the problems they experienced in 1997.  In 1997 three of the six candidates, who were Republican, were rated as "not recommended" which triggered a political firestorm.

headline: Ridge, House leaders and team owners agree on new stadium funding plan
abstract: Governor Ridge and House legislative leaders agreed to a plan that would allow $320 million to finance new stadium construction in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  The teams would have to collect an equal amount in state taxes during the next 30 years.  If that tax revenue falls short then team owners would have to pay the difference out of their own pockets at 10-year intervals.

headline: PA "Y2k" ready
abstract: Thanks to Governor Ridge and team efforts the PA2K is ready. This makes PA  one of the best prepared states in the nation to tackle the Y2K event. The PA2K website has a wealth of information on how to be prepared for Y2K.

headline: GOP HAS MAJOR PLANS FOR FUNDS FROM DINNER
abstract: The House Republican Campaign Committee had a fund-raiser at the Four Seasons Hotel in Philadelphia.  They expect to raise $600,000 from the event and end the year with more than $1 million dollars.  The GOP holds a 103-100 edge but face a tough fight to retain the majority in light of Representative Frank Serafini's (R-Lackawanna) convinction for perjury.

headline: State lobbyists reveal what they pay for influence
abstract: Pennsylvania's Lobbying Disclosure Act revealed that lobbyists spend about $5.3 million influencing state officials and is higher than in recent years.  Even during August, when state government is generally slower lobbyists still spent hundreds of thousands of dollars.

headline: Black Democrats incensed by party's all-white slate
abstract: Jackie Hill, political action director of the Pittsburgh branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People stated that they are encouraging the African-American community to vote only for African-Americans.  Tim Stevens, NAACP president, and former president Harvey Adams reacted to the Democratic Committee for choosing an all white slate for countywide elections.

headline: 1000 rally for vouchers
abstract: PA would become the second state to enact a voucher program followed by Florida. About 1000 packed the Capitol to voice their support for the voucher plan.Governor Ridge said that PA 's parents should be given a choice.

headline: Government Moves to Conserve Remote Areas of National Forest
abstract: The Clinton Administration stopped logging in the undeveloped areas of the national forests which shifted forest policy toward conservation after a year of heated public debate.  The move sets the stage for a broader review of long-term forest policy.  The administration will study not only the remote areas affected by the suspension, but also other undeveloped areas excluded from the moratorium and the larger expanses crisscrossed by an estimated 400,000 miles of roads.

headline: Attorney general setting legislative priorities
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher unveiled an agenda of laws he would like to see enacted ranging a wide list from indecent email and voilent behavior in schools.  His initiatives include a four year bill package to impose a one year minimum sentence for those convicted, bills to toughen state regulation of home improvement contractors and to toughen penalties, openly identify obsentiy in email so that it can be blocked, and gjve the attorney genral greater power to review hospital mergers.

headline: Rep. Argall's school violence measure advances in House
abstract: According to a legislation introduced by State Representative Argall would require the Department of Education to provide parents and educators of the crime status in their school districts. Young people would also be better informed of the dire consequences of a committing a crime.

headline: Ridge's tax cuts would bring more investment and jobs to Pennsylvania
abstract: Gov. Ridge's tax cut proposal of $273 million aims to increase employment and bring in more investment and businesses to the state.

headline: PA joins internet business venture
abstract: PA has joined a group of industrial and technology companies to develop a system which allow  to create and colloborate products on the internet.

headline: GOP in a Mood to Compromise
abstract: Congressional Republicans are having to reach out to the Clinton administration to find compromise solutions to problems that would have been untouchable at the height of the impeachment trial of President Clinton.  After failing to remove Clinton from office, Republicans feel they can find common ground on issues like Social Security, taxes and national defense.

headline: State Politicians gearing up for 2000
abstract: Several Democrats who are already preparing for the 2000 general election are seeking Rick Santorum's seat in the U.S. Senate who has held it for the past five years.  Polls show he may have a difficult time holding on to his position.  Pennsylvanian's are saying they are not hearing enough about him or the things he's accomplished since taking office.

headline: Black lawmakers push bill requiring racial study of police stops
abstract: The Pennsylvania House will consider legislation that would require the attorney general to conduct a study assessing racial aspects of traffic stops by police. Representative Harold James, Democrat and former Philadelphia police officer, sponsored the bill.

headline: 3 B's mean A+ program for schools
abstract: Community Education Partners is a private-for-profit education organization that removes disruptive or failing students to special schools where behavioral and academic problems are addressed.  These bad actors return to regular school only after mastering the three R's and three B's which are: Be here, Behave, and Be learning.

headline: Government wants to spend more to rid Lae Erie of dangerous chemical
abstract: Francine Norling, manager of the Environmental Protection Agency's Region V Lake Erie Team said that they want to focus their efforts on ridding Lake Erie of dangerous polychlorinated biphenyls or PCBs.  Production of polychlorinated biphenyls was banned in 1979 because of evidence that the toxic compounds caused deformities in fish-eating birds and over concern about possible harm to people who eat fish from polychlorinated biphenyl tainted waters.  Other problems noted at Lake Erie were diminishing wetlands and declining quality of wetlands, changing populations of yellow perch, walleye and other fish, changes to the ecosystem, and changing levels of phosphorus.

headline: Beer sales come under scrutiny in probes of opening-day brawl
abstract: A fist fight a the Phillies' home opener has opened an investigation into whether there was under-age sale of alcohol to minors.  The state police Bureau of Liquor Control Enforcement and the City Recreation Department that operates the stadium are conducting probes into the possibility that beer was served to minors.  Ogden Entertainment operates stadium concessions.

headline: Reports may be ploy for fugitive
abstract: Norman Johnston's friends may be throwing police officers off the trail of the escaped murderer with phony sightings, dusting off tactics used to foil law enforcement.  Johnston escaped more than a week ago and police in three different states have been swamped with calls regarding the Chester County killer.

headline: Rockledge receives grant for building
abstract: Sen. Greenleaf(R) announced  Rockledge borough would receive $300,000.00 from the state to construct new municipal buildings. The Department of Community and Economic Development will fund the project allows municipals and police officials to conduct business in a safer environment.

headline: Pa. deal expected soon on merger of phone firms
abstract: The Pennsylvania Attorney General is expected to announce so that is has reached an agreement with Bell Atlantic and GTE on the merger of the two local phone companies.  The agreement is expected to include financial and other concessions favorable to consumers and businesses in GTE's local phone markets and not expected to include concessions on Bell Atlantic's markets.

headline: GOP leaders want to meet with Seyfert, discuss her political future
abstract: Erie County's Republican Chairman and Leader of the House of Republicans both want to discuss with Representative Tracy Seyfert about her political future.  They are most concerned to know whether she wants to run for re-election despite her federal indictment.

headline: State Representative Gigliotti indicted
abstract: According to a 27-count federal indictment Representative Frank Gigliotti has supplemented his state income with cash and trips to Florida by shaking down companies that sought public contracts.  Gigliotti hid payments totalling $36,352 in cash and trips from the Internal Revenue Service.  A key figure in the indictment was Ernest Smalis, a painting contractor who has been cooperating with federal investigators since October 1997.  Smalis plead guilty to six federal charges unrelated to the Gigliotti indictment and wore an electronic recording device during conversations with Gigliotti and used money provided by the Federal Bureau of Investigations to pay $15,000 in bribes to him.

headline: Black voters must choose their leaders
abstract: Leadership for the black community in Pittsburgh is being sucked up.  The lback community has a sorry recent history of being fractured politically - polarized by lcass, separated by geography and paralyzed by ingorance.  A group of collaborates including former state House Speaker K. Leroy Irvis, Urban League president and CEO Esther Bush and others are trying to make sure black political power does not quickly devolve into a lowest common denominator.

headline: A child-health hazard escapes inspection
abstract: A preschool classroom at Temple Beth Hillel-Beth El, tested for lead hazards more than 10 times recommended safety levels and abated the immediate hazard by painting over flaky lead based paint on walls, doorways, and window frames.  The incident underscores the fact that no government agency requires inspections for lead hazards at preschools.  The United State Environmental Protection Agency calls lead poisoning the most serious environmental hazard facing children.

headline: Gov't has to stop flow of garbage into PA
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge is correct when he asserts that the Constitution precludes him from stopping the flow of out-of-state garbage into Pennsylvania dumps.  State legislators, however, should do whatever they can to limit out-of-state garbage from coming in to make the state as inhospitable as possible to it.  A pending House bill, for example, would cap waster disposal capacity, impose fees on haulers to finance an expanded waster-truck inspection program and require that agreements that local governments are forged before the state issues permits to dumps.  Until Congress can act on this matter the state should do what it can to limit out-of-state garbage from coming in.

headline: Beware of Vehicle Cloning in PA
abstract: Vehicle cloning is making its way through the Commonwealth. Vehicle cloning involves breaking into a vehicle and stealing registration and identification information.

headline: Ridge Appoints Judicial Candidate Review Board
abstract: Governer Tom Ridge appoints six people to a judicial advisory commision to recommend a candidate to serve as Clarion County interim judge.  They are Maria Battista Kerle, Richard W. Dooman, Cassandra M. Neely, Ray H. Scott, Fred Anderson, and Ronald J. Wilshire.  The position will run to the end of 1999.

headline: Rooney throws flag on Specter plan for stadium financing bill
abstract: United States Senator Arlen Specter drafted a plan to require the National Football League to pay half the cost of new football stadiums.  Pittsburgh Steelers vice president Art Rooney II says that they have done their fair share to finance a new stadium in Pittsburgh.

headline: Personal Technology
abstract: This article gives a chronology of events as to what dates and times the author's Microsoft Windows crashed. The author states that the makers of software programs should improve at the source.

headline: GOP moderates say party must soften language, agenda
abstract: The Republican Main Street Partnership, which is a moderate Republican group, states that the party must soften its language and push a centrist agenda featuring compassion as well as prudence or face losing control of Congress in the 2000 elections.  Republicans failed to improve its 55-45 Senate edge and lost five House seats leaving it with a precarious 11 seat House margin and big questions about how to prepare for the 2000 presidential and congressional races.

headline: State representative targets foul language
abstract: For politicians in Harrisburg credit is like currency and they will do anything to get it especially if it helps them get re-elected.  State Representative Steven Nikol, Republican-York county, demanded credit for doing nothing.  He spoke on the House floor sponsoring a bill that does nothing more than clean up and move some archaic language around in the county code.

headline: Boot
abstract: Governor Ridge is for signing into law a bill that exempts state universities and colleges from being forced by local and anti-discrimination ordinances to provide medical benefits to partners of gay and lesbian employees.

headline: A knuckle rapping
abstract: The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers has given the Philadelphia School District a deadline of Friday to pay hundreds of employees who have gone without pay since August because of a computer foul up.  The $26 million computer system is however paying dead and former employees.

headline: Green, as in G.O.P
abstract: Robert C. Smith of New Hampshire was chosen to succeed John Chafee as chairman of the Senate Environment of Public Committee.  Chafee, who died last month, stood up well to well financed efforts promoted by polluting industries.  He continued a tradition of crafting bipartisan environmental policy.  Robert Smith, was recently an independent running for U.S. presidential election, and criticized republicans as being conciliatory.  Smith would do well to respect a bipartisan tradition.

headline: Bill would ban unmarked cop cars
abstract: State lawmakers want to prohibit police from making routine traffic stops from unmarked police cars.  Legislators say they want to protect motorists from criminals who impersonate police.  State police, however, oppose the controversial legislation, which was reintroduced this week by state Representative Jim Lynch, Republican - 65th, as House Bill 782.  Lou Southard, a spokesperson for the Pennsylvania State Police in Harrisburg stated that they felt unmarked police cars are a very beneficial tool for us for enforcement purposes.

headline: Ridge calls on America to make schools safe
abstract: In the aftermath of the Littleton, Colorado massacre, Governor Ridge at a local school in PA called on all schools to for a safer environment for children. He also asked the educators to identify students who could be potential violators.

headline: Sen. Coroman: Urges passage of statewide building code
abstract: People assume that when they enter a building that the structure is safe. However, of the approximately 2,600 municipalities in the Commonwealth, nearly half do not have minimum construction standards.  This poses a particular degree of risk for firefighters who must worry about structural soundness and the quality of building materials when fighting fires.

headline: Phone companies' merger plan blasted
abstract: Judge Morris Solomon, an administrative law judge of the Public Utility Commission, has rejected the proposed Bell Atlantic-GTE merger on the grounds that it is anti-competitive and of no benefit to consumers.  Solomon pointed out that bonuses that Bell and GTE Corporation executives would receive if the merger is completed is not in the interests of Pennsylvania consumers.

headline: GOP Must Beware the 'Polk Factor'
abstract: An underappreciated aspect of political parties is the influence that third parties can have in influencing the election.  Traditionally these were for voters who wanted to protest against a party or discipline them for straying from their party principles.

headline: State senator hospitalized after stomach trouble on plane
abstract: State Senator Vincent Fumo was taken to a hospital by ambulance after being stricken with abdominal pains and vomiting on a plane from France.  He was admitted to Thomas Jefferson University Hospital where he was reported in stable condition.  Doctors said he had an intestinal virus.

headline: Bradley benchmark should be followed
abstract: Bill Bradley, presidential hopeful for the 2000 presidential election, made a challenging statement on race to the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People saying that if he is elected he will work to reduce african american childhood poverty and appoint people to his administration that reflects the talent of the African American community.  It was a challenge to engage Bush and Gore.

headline: A radical plan for training teachers
abstract: State Education Secretary Hickok proposed a plan that no one under 30 years should be allowed to teach in public schools and no one should be hired to teach at the 14 teacher preparatory schools without 2 years of training. This plan was proposed to  use the tax money wisely towards education.

headline: Groups to take on trespassing wildlife
abstract: Vern Ross, of the Pennsylvania Game Commission, explains that they are setting up a pilot program called the "The Link Program" to connect hunters and trappers with landowners who are having trouble with trespassing wildlife.  Dr. Gary Alt, head of the Game Commission's deer management section, said the program will "empower landowners" to protect their property and help hunters access private lands that otherwise would be off-limits.

headline: Bill would end or limit state executions
abstract: State Senator Helfrick who is a staunch opponent of death penalty has introduced a six- bill package that would end or limit death sentences in PA.

headline: Ridge police plan has merit, but only if no hidden agenda exists
abstract: At the heart of the debate about whether the state should require payment from some municipalities for state police protection is municipalities' being allowed to make their own decision on establishing - or not establishing- a police force.  Municipalities say they should not be forced to establish police departments because of financial pressures imposed by the state.  The governor should continue to press forward with his agenda if there are no hidden issues for municipalities and would also undermine the state police department.

headline: Senate passes bill for managing development
abstract: Senate passage of a bill giving local officials more ability to manage development, sponsored by Jim Gerlach, Republican-Chester, reach a legislative point, but, that legislation has become more notable for the provisions left out of it than those in it.  Left out of the bill is a provision giving municipal officials the power know as concurrency to require that roads be installed before new subdivisions can be approved.  It also makes the mention of education impact fees.

headline: Phone settlement talks start slowly
abstract: Negotiations aimed at settling litigation brought by Bell Atlantic Corporation against the state Public Utility Commission over the local telephone competition court order got off to a rocky start.  The talks may be key to whether the state gets real competition in the local telephone market.

headline: GOP NOT DOOMED BY IMPEACHMENT
abstract: Political analysist speculate that Republicans could lose control of Congress because of public disgust over the excesses of the impeachment prosecution of President Clinton.  In the tri-county area there is little coattail effect of impeachment more than a year later.  Performance, positions and character of local elected officials is more relevant than the vote on impeachment.

headline: State Senator to run for U.S. Senate
abstract: Discusses the election race for the U.S. Senate between, Allyson Schwartz, Marjorie Margolis-Mezvinsky, and Rick Santorum.  Highlights Schwartz saying that Santorum does not represent the mainstream values of Pennsylvania families.

headline: Can GOP make room for gays?
abstract: Richard Tafel became "Mr. Gay Republican" when he became executive director of Log Cabin Republicans, the Washington-based group that speaks for gays and lesbians within the party.  The vast majority of gays vote democratic causing questions to the motives of Tafel's devotion to the party of Pat Buchanan and Gary Bauer.

headline: Academic Recovery Act would abandonstate's public schools
abstract: Tom Bigler professor of communications at Wilkes University says the assumption of the Academic Recovery Act that public and private schools serve the same ends is false. Bigler opnions that the beneficiaries of this act would be politics and ideology.

headline: Hatchery trout may be tainted by PCBs
abstract: The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission is warning that the 350,000 trout that were stocked in the eastern and south-central part of the state may be tainted by cancer causing polychlorinated biphenyls.  Low levels of polychlorinated biphenyls have been detected in samples of fish now in the Huntsdale Fish Culture Station in Penn Township near Carlisle.  Polychlorinated biphenyls are a mand-made petroleum-based product often used as a lubricant or a coolant in machines and electrical transformers.  The use of this lubricant was outlawed in the 1970s.  Officials do not yet know the source of the contaminants in the rivers.

headline: Bill would help guard police in traffic stops
abstract: Representative Susan Laughlin, Democrat-Beaver, introduced a bill that would require drivers who are stopped by police to illuminate the interiors of their vehicles and place their hands on the steering wheel.  The bill is designed to extend additional safety to police officers.

headline: Ridge stands firm on prison review
abstract: Even though the three escaped prison inmates are back behind bars Governor Ridge says he has not changed his mind about an outside review of security at all 24 of Pennsylvania's state prisons.  Escaped killers Norman Johnston,  Michael McCloskey and arsonist Anthony Yang were captured within hours of each other late Thursday and early Friday.

headline: Senate passes building bill
abstract: Pennsylvania is one of the last states not to impose a minimum building code on its municipalities.  Of the roughly 2,600 municipalities in the state more than 40% have no minimum standards for construction.  Lawmakers hailed the passage of the state Senate's passage of a proposal to hold all Pennsylvania municipalities to minimum building standards.

headline: Proposed Bell Atlantic-GTE merger sparks a debate
abstract: The Public Utility Commission was urged to take the interests of customers into account as it considers the proposed merger of Bell Atlantic and GTE.  But there was not a consensus on what those interests are.  The main issue is that consumers should share in the economic benefits reaped if the companies are allowed to join.

headline: GOP officials cite unity in their sweep in Montco
abstract: Montgomery County Republican Party Chairman Frank Bartle said the election for county commissioner was a tremendous victory for the party who showed Republican candidates Marino and Matthews winning by 30,000 votes.  This puts the Republican party back to the kind of voter turnout they had not seen since 1987.  The incumbent Democrats declined to seek reelection.

headline: State Spends $67 million on advertising campaigns
abstract: Pennsylvania government will spend more than $66.8 million on advertising this year to raise awareness of government programs and boost commerce, a large part is aimed at changing behaviors.  State agencies would like us stop smoking, regrain from drinking and driving, buy a dog license, wear your seat belt, recycle your garbage, vacation in the state, and buy more lottery tickets.  Sean Duffy, executive director of the Commonwealth Foundation, says the expectation from the advertising is increased revenues.

headline: Councilman wants to send message of peace to Klan
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council President Bob O'Connor wants to combat the Ku Klux Klan's rally to be held in front of the City-County Building by having a rally within earshot of religious leaders and church choirs spreading a message of love and peace in opposition to their message of hate.  O'Connor's chief of staff states that this will be a test of the communities faith.

headline: Academic Study
abstract: State Representative Druce led the review of the higher education which begins with the ultimate aim of tying state financial assistance for colleges and universities to accountability standards.

headline: Hearing to be held on fish-list proposal
abstract: The Fish and Boat Commission followed the normal procedure to propose expanding the state's endangered fish list by publishing it in the Pennsylvania Bulletin and also in the Department of Environmental Protection's newsletter "The Update."  The proposal, however, which adds 13 species to the endangered list went unnoticed by lawmakers and business men affected by it and now the Senate Game and Fisheries Committee plan to have a public hearing on the matter.  Senator William Slocum, Republican - Cameron, explained that something this important could create economic havoc for some of our businesses.

headline: Bill would require new leaves for women employees
abstract: According to PA Coaltion Against Domestic Violence women would be granted 30 extra days of leave to recoup from a abusive relationship. This law would apply to businesses with 50 or more employees.

headline: Rights and Wrongs
abstract: The Parental Rights Bill is about the respects of parents and decisions on how to raise chilren. The author feels that supporters and the public should keep an eye on the fine print on any subsequent legislations which can be pased in connection with this bill.

headline: Senate passes building code bill
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate passed legislation setting minimum standards for new construction establishing statewide building codes.  The bill passed 40-8 and replaces a hodgepodge of local ordinances with a state code pegged to set by the Building Officials and Code Administrators, a national nonprofit group of building inspectors.

headline: PUC decision will not stand, Bell CEO says
abstract: Bell Atlantic Chairman Ivan G. Seidenberg said he believes his company will eventually have the decision by the Public Utility Commission overturned.  Bell is planning a court appeal which lowered prices competitors may pay to lease pieces of the Bell network and ordered Bell to separate into wholesale and retail companies.

headline: GOP Presidential Prospect interviewed
abstract: Religious consevative leaders from the Committee to Restore American Values interviewed the potential presidential candidates for the 2000 election.  George Bush declined the invitation to be interviewed.

headline: States move to earilier primary mixed blessing
abstract: State lawmakers voted last week to move the primary elections from April 25 to April 4 to avoid conflict with Easter weekend and theJewish Passover. Governor Tom Ridge is expected to sign the bill.

headline: Counting on Latinos in 2000
abstract: Over 30 community leaders met in Harrisburg last week to tell latinos to stand up be counted in upcoming census.  The United States Bureau of the Census estimates that as many as 8.4 million people nationwide were not counted in the previous census and of those approxiamately 1 million latinos.  Lupe Pierce, executive director of Allentown's Hispanic American Organization, and George Ramos of the South Bethlehem Neighborhood Center, are striving to prevent that from happening again.

headline: Allow time to learn
abstract: Education received additional funding from the Pennsylvania legislature at a time when the state's coffers are brimming.  Yet the state's anti-education welfare reform policy forces women to drop out of college and specialty training programs.

headline: Hearings end on Sunday hunting
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Game and Fisheries Commmittee has finished holding its series of three public hearings on the issue of whether to have hunting on two of the Sundays in the regular hunting season.  The opinion in York and Meadville was overwhelmingly against Sunday hunting while the opinion in Jermyn favored it.  Those opposed to the idea of Sunday hunting cited noise and safety concerns as well as the distraction it would cause Sunday church activities.  Farmers, private land owners, and some sportsmen groups have lined up solidly agianst the measure.

headline: Bills' fates up in air as session nears end
abstract: A dominant political issue for Governor George Bush of Texas was a hate-crimes bill named for James Byrd, Junior who has dragged to death in a racially motivated crime in Jasper, Texas.  The bill, would have added penalties for crimes born of bias, including bias against lesbians and gay men, died without a final vote.  Bush was criticized for declining to vote for the controversial legislation.

headline: Santorum backs broad durg-fighting bill
abstract: Senator Santorum backs the federal Drug Free Country Act which would fund community education projects and other methods to battle drugs sale and use.

headline: Sixth time charmed?
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge publicly blasted Scranton Mayor Jim Connors, a fellow Republican, for well-documented "mismanagement and lack of leadership" regarding the downtown Scranton hotel and convention center project.  The Governor did however extend the deadline for a $10 million grant to help develop the project noting that the city's residents should not have to pay the price of a lost grant for the administration's incompetence.

headline: PUC opens the way to local-phone rivalry
abstract: After three years of debate the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission approved dramatic and sweeping rules to promote competition in the state's $3.7 billion local phone market.  The commission's rules would give consumers and businesses new choices when they select a company to provide local phone service and more access to advanced telecommunications services.

headline: GOP re-elects RNC leader
abstract: Jim Nicholson re-elected to the Republican National Committee said that the setback that the Republicans faced due to the impeachement of President Clinton was only temperory.

headline: State's open records law weakened by restrictions, omissions
abstract: Boss rule came to an end in Pennsylvania nearly 42 years ago after a landmark law opened some government financial records to the public.  A House Bill commonly called the Right to Know Law was approved by a 196-6 vote and already approved by the Senate which changes the way government operated by making it more accountable to the public.

headline: Courting religion
abstract: The United States Supreme Court has let stand a Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling that outlawed sales tax exemptions for religious literature.  That decision means that the commonwealth must end a 43-year policy of exempting the Christian Bible, the Jewish Talmud, the Muslim Koran and the Book of Mormon, among other materials.  The state high court ruled in April that the commonwealth should not be in the business of supporting religion through tax breaks or any other means.  As for encouraing the reading of religious material, that should not be a government function, especially through the application of a tax exemption.

headline: An appeal to sense
abstract: According to Sean Duffy, president of the Commonwealth Foundation The Charter School Appeal Board should aggresively and failry push for choices to thousands of families who would benefit from new charter schools in a new century.

headline: Helping trees weather drought newer plantings at most risk
abstract: Discusses citizen awareness of the livelihood of trees during a drought and highlights a locust tree at 33rd and race streets in West Philadelphia which received special irrigation attention.  Mary E. Buckno, a coordinator for the Pennsylvana Horticutural Society's Philadelphia Green project, comments that it is amazing to her that peole do not think of trees in hot weather.

headline: Bills target johns on wheels
abstract: State Representative Stephen Stetler, Democrat-York, introduced a package of bills targeted at those who patronize prostitutes.  His package includes suspending a convicted "john's" driver's license, requiring courts on a second offense to order forfeiting a vehicle used to promote or patronize prostitutes, allowing police to impound such vehicles and requiring the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation to suspend a vehicle's registration.

headline: Santorum: Private prisons, yes; out-of-state trash imports, no
abstract: United States Senator Rick Santorum believes that private prisons are a way to deal with problems that is cost-effective for taxpayers.  Santorum says that having to accept trash from other states is an issue before the Congress which has ruled that states must accept the trash due to the interstate commerce clause.

headline: Slush fund lives under a new name
abstract: Delaware county will receive $2 million state grant for their community projects. The Community Revitalization Program will  amount to little more than the slush funds for key legislators projects.

headline: Punish threats in cyberspace
abstract: State Senators  Dent and Boscola say that threats via the internet should be met with severe punishment. There has been sevearl instances of internet threat throughout PA.

headline: GOP Sen. Gerlach touted as Casey foe
abstract: Republican activist have asked state Senator Gerlach to challenge incumben auditor general Casey in 2000.

headline: Statewide effort nets Morganelli local challenge
abstract: John Morganelli, district attorney of Northampton County, may seek Democratic nomination to challenge Attorney General Mike Fisher, the Republican incumbent.  Cal Shields, Schuykill County District Attorney, and former law school friend at Villanova University will run agianst him as Republican.  Former Northampton GOP chairman called Mike Fisher to mention that Morganelli would run unopposed unless they promoted someone to run against.

headline: Fearful words that won't go away
abstract: Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee appointed Republican crony Doctor Fay Boozman as the top state health official.  Boozman, an eye surgeon and former state senator, lost his bid for re-election after he declared that fear-induced hormonal changes could block a rape victim's ability to conceive.  Because of such a phenomenon, Boozman said, rape and incest victims rarely get pregnant and felt safe in backing abortion rights for them.  He states his findings are not scientific but based on observation.

headline: An appeal to sense
abstract: According to Sean Duffy, president of the Commonwealth Foundation The Charter School Appeal Board should aggresively and failry push for choices to thousands of families who would benefit from new charter schools in a new century.

headline: Heritage 21 Alliance plans rally at Capitol
abstract: The Hertiage 21 Alliance, a coalition of 21 environmental groups backing the borrowing of $1 billion for environmental efforts, is planning a rally for the Capitol tomorrow.  The coalition has a tough sell on its hands.  Governor Tom Ridge has made it clear that he does not want to borrow any huge sums of money for open-space preservation or any other major environmental initiatives.  Ridge wants to fund his "Growing Greener" initiative with funds from new money, funds that are unused, or funds that are underused.

headline: Birmelin bill sets up community input in justice system
abstract: A bill that would issue community service to low level lawbreakers in return for having a clean record was unanimously passed by the state House of Representatives.  The bill was sponsored by Representative Jerry Birmelin, Republican-189th, which would establish eight-person boards offering community service instead of facing charges in court.

headline: School policies cover weapons, body parts
abstract: Most schools have dress codes and many are looking at uniforms and clear back packs so that teachers can monitor the students for any kind of weapons. This is to make the school a safer place for children to learn in a safer environment.

headline: Smart politics but dumb
abstract: Vice President Al Gore has a plan called "smart growth" for America's suburbs.  It adds up to a strategy for Washington to direct the way people live.  It might preserve farm land, cut down on distance for commuting, and reduce auto emissions.  But peole flock to the suburbs for larger homes and yard space.  The result will be smaller homes in high density neighborhoods.  The real fault of the plan is the instrusion from the federal government.  Local leaders have to be responsive to their constituents so that they can tailor their plans to specific issues in their regions and that communities can learn from each other.

headline: Rep.Mc.Call legislation to protect children
abstract: State Representative McCall has gained the bi-partisan support for his legislation which would protect minors from Internet access in libraries.

headline: GOP Senate Seats on the Line
abstract: After President Clinton's impeachment and acquittal trial, democratic strategists have marked 10 republican senate seats for re-election.  The democrats are determined to portray these incumbents as trapped in a renegade party controlled by an ideological right wing and defiant of voters who twice elected Clinton.  All 10 senators represent state that cast 1996 pluralities or majorities for Clinton.

headline: Steelworker Hopes to face Toomey
abstract: United Steelworker's leader Ed O'Brien will run for Congress as a Democrat with a desire to represent the working class on issues such as the minimum wage, school vouchers, and patient rights.  O'Brien will run for the 15th District seat currenly held by Republican Pat Toomey.

headline: Flag bill still burns
abstract: As the country celebrates the 222nd anniversary of Flag Day there is a constitutional amendment that remains before Congress that would give that body the power to ban the flag's desecration.  Senator's Arlen Spector and Rick Santorum say that banning flag burning is a necessary limitation of free speech.

headline: Application for Byrd honors acholarship program is available
abstract: State Representative Baker said that Byrd Honors scholarship for high school students was available for application.

headline: House Bill would recycle smaller scrap tire piles
abstract: House lawmakers are considering legislation to expand the scope of a state program that rids the landscape of scrap tires.  A bill, sponsored by Representative David Argall, Republican-124, would extend cleanup up efforts to include scrap piles containg fewer than 10,000 tires.  The bill faces a vote in the House Environmental Resources Committee.  The state's current tire cleanup program is aimed at removing piles of scrap tires containing more than 10,000 tires.  State officials made this legislation a priority after several scrap piles forced the evacuation of neighboring residents.

headline: Casey slams Ridge for  not releasing school violence information
abstract: Auditor General Casey has blamed the Ridge Administration for not releasing on school violence.

headline: School violence
abstract: State Representative Major said that the House passed a number of bill after the Columbine School massacre, but was rejected by the Senate. The Safe and Secure School Act will make money available to schools to counter violence. The grant will be funded through a $ 20 million appropriation in the state budget.

headline: Stadium proponents ignore voter verdict
abstract: Every mayor and governor seems to be convinced that a new stadium is just the ticket for local economic growth.  Although it seems the state's no risk to taxpayers is good a idea to fund the four new stadiums Jake Haulk of the Allegheny Institute points out that the monitoring and tracking of this is going to be terribly complicated and the state has no leverage if a team comes up short to pay.

headline: Repub;icans Plan to Offer a Party Line To the Internet
abstract: The Republican National Committee plans to begin offer subscriptions to a family friendly internet service which will deliver party messages instantly.

headline: GOP Senators show more hesitation over witnesses
abstract: The United State senate is resuming President Clinton's impeachment trial and faces crucial decision that could detemrine how muc hlonger th trial lasts and whether a condemnation accompanies Clinton's expected acquittal.
