abstract: "Downtown Corporate Elite" are the words that County Commissioner Larry Dunn repeated like a mantra and said goodbye to the candidacy of his former running mate Bob Cranmer while describing the issues that he claims will bring him the GOP nomination and victory in November for Allegheny County executive.  Dunn wants voters to know he is against Downtown corporate interests and campaign strategy rests on two assumptions.  He must convince voters that the election is about ordinary folks against millinionaire ball players and criticism of the county's property tax assessment system which attracted voters four years previously.

headline: State probe of standoff nears end
abstract: The fatal hostage standoff at the Norristown State Hospital has prompted review of state policy and after three months of work appears to be coming to an end.  Denis Czajkowski was a former psychiatric nurse at Norristown State Hospital and shot two hostages and killed one of them after police threw a rock through a office window.

headline: State ignores call on sprawl
abstract: Pennsylvania continues to sell off former state hospital tracts for development in suburban Philadelphia counties.  This does not seem to square with high-minded hopes of limiting sprawl.  The 21st Century Environmental Commission, a blue ribbon-panel, appointed by Governor Ridge, came up with a fat report that basically pointed to suburban sprawl as the environmental problem heading into the 21st century.  The problem was shortly thereafter the state's Department of General Services proudly announced it was selling the old Eastern State School and Hospital tract in Bucks County to private developers for several million dollars.

headline: Musical Politics
abstract: Governor Ridge will tour Asia with the Philadelphia Orchestra along with PA's 14 technology companies. The goal of this tour will be to emphasize on PA's techonological capabilities.

headline: Hart buys home in Bardford Woods.  Move could give lawmaker leverage in bid for Congress.
abstract: State Senator Melissa Hart has moved to a new home in Bradford Woods, which is in the 4th Congressional District, to run against Ron Klink.  Hart, 38, is in the middle of her third, four-year term in the State senate.  If she is not elected she could still finish out her term in the State senate.

headline: THE EVOLUTION OF REPRESENTATIVE PLATTS
abstract: Todd Platts was elected to the PA State House of Representatives in 1993 as a Republican.  He has gone against the party and made leadership angry but has won a few minor reform victories and one piece of legislation that has become law.  He is being accused of abandoing reforms but denies this and proposes that his shift comes down to a split with reformers like Ed Krebs, Republican from Lebanon County, on how to approach reforms.

headline: Student Portfolios Challenged as an Alternative to State Tests
abstract: The state assessment panel in New York will evaluate if students can use portfolios if they fail their Regents. This decision created a stir among the parents and educators supported by the Schools Chancellor Rudy Crew.

headline: PA House Bill 970
abstract: A bill introduced by Representative David Argall would protect clothing preference at work under the Human Relations Act.  Sexual preference or orientation is currently not protected under the state's Human Relation's Act.  Essentially the act gives the right to freedom from discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations if your individuality is defined as a protected class.

headline: Class action
abstract: Hiring good teachers is one of the most effective school reforms.  The search for good teaching requires a flexible attitude that neither slavishly defends the status quo nor mindlessly seeks to blow it up.

headline: No change to doe season
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission narrowly rejected a proposal to control deer populations by extending the doe hunting season and will remain at three days statewide.  Commissioner Robert J. Gilford of Clarion County has proposed that regions vary the length of the season depending on their deer populations.  His proposal, however, was struck down by a 4 to 3 vote.  In a separate vote, commissioners decided to issue the same number of votes as last year standing at 890,000.

headline: Inaugurate an agenda for new year
abstract: At Governor Ridge's second inaugural party which will be a two-day event several events will be arranged for children.  Lynn Lawson, spokeswoman for the gubernatorial inaugural committee says that much of what Ridge has done in his first term is dedicdated to better opportunities for children.  Children wil be affected more so by what state leaders decide this year.  Two issues that repeatedly surface are financial assistance from the state for new sports stadiums in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia and state-funded vouchers for private and parochial schools.  Other concerns are land-use, welfare, and education.

headline: State tally of schools finds drop in violence
abstract: Schools in and around Harrisburg saw a slight decline in the violence rates when compared to the last year. Governor Tom Ridge announced that 54 school districts in PA will receive Safe School Grants to keep their class rooms safe.

headline: State ignoring its own report
abstract: Pennsylvania continues to sell off former state hospital tracts for development in suburban Philadelphia counties.  Obviously the last thing either the state or the township people are thinking about is stopping sprawl or preserving open space.

headline: Polls fear for Kvaerner deal
abstract: Pennsylvania Senators Specter and Santorum are against passing a trade bill unless it exempts the United State from a worldwide ban on shipbuilding subsidies.  Any ban on subsidies could have implications for the ongoing development of the Kvaerner shipyard in Philadelphia.

headline: HENRY ROWAN FILES LIBEL SUIT
abstract: Buckingham Supervisor Henry Rowan filed a lawsuit in Bucks County Court accusing state Representative Charles McIlhinney Jr., and GOP party chief Harry Fawkes of libeling him during the 1998 election for the 143rd District state House seat.  The suit stems from a last-minute campaign brochure that accused Rowan of failing to pay his property taxes.  After the brochure was mailed, it was determined that the mortgage company was at fault and he was only one of a number of residents whose property taxes were paid late because of computer error.

headline: The Friends of John McCain
abstract: Interest Groups such as the National Rifle Association, National Right to life Committiee, American Conservative Union, and the Christian Coalition are attacking John McCain for his recent stance on campaign finance reform in the New Hampshire and South Carolina Primaries.  These groups claim that limits their free speech rights.

headline: Students asked to discuss crow droppings at conference
abstract: Teacher Mary Pat Evans wondered whether state officials' efforts to scare crows away from government office buildings and asked her students to come up with a way to test if the loud barrage of noise being used was indeed working.  The procedure the students came up with was to count bird droppings to determine a decrease in the birds.  The students took photos of a sidewalk near where the birds nested and their conclusion was that the noises were working.

headline: Pitt Subpoenas two city council members to fight over same sex
abstract: Two city council members were subpoenaed by the University of Pittsburgh as a part  of the school's defense in a complaint by the employees who said they were discriminated against because of their sexual orientation.

headline: Clinton, Governors assess efforts to improve education
abstract: President Clinton meet with the Governors at the third education summit to set and discuss goals for 2000. The President urged them to set loftier goals for schools to raise the academic standards. He also conveyed the message that he would like see American among the tiop nations leading in math and science.

headline: Noteworthy:
abstract: Colonel Paul J. Evanko, chief of the state police, said he would tell troopers to use discretion in enforcing restrictions on water use in the midstate and 55 counties.  First-time violaters will likely get a warning, he said as top state officials met yesterday to formally enact the drought emergency declaration by Governor Ridge.

headline: Iowa's straw poll persuades Alexander to quit GOP race
abstract: Former Tennessee Governor and education secretary Lamar Alexander withdrew his nomination for the 2000 presidential republican nomination at the Iowa caucus.  This was due in large part to the straw poll.

headline: State wants to keep ticket money
abstract: State lawmakers are looking at ways to make state police coverage more cost-efficient, to make sure the state does not lose out on the costs of providing protection for communities without their own police forces.  The problem is that some municipalities, including some in Adams County, may wind up losing out instead.  A legislative task force has endorsed a new plan to divert fines issued by state police for various traffic violations and minor criminal offenses to the unit of government whose police whose police force made the arrest.

headline: State Labor secretary says development key to future
abstract: For Butler County to remain competitive it must add to work force development to its business expansions, according to John Butler, state Secretary of Labor and Industry while speaking at the Community Development Corporation.  Butler lauded the development corporation as being one of the most efficient economic development agencies in the state.

headline: Revving up his trade pitch
abstract: President Clinton was speaking at a Harley Davidson plant at the Springetsbury Township plant wearing one their distinguished jackets trying to associate with blue collar workers as a means to associate Americans with his efforts to show them that foreign trade can benefit Americans.  Clinton is trying to win Americans support before going to talks at the World Trade Organization next month.  His visit to Harley Davidson was also an attempt to show how good relations between labor and management can make companies more competitive.

headline: Hillary Clinton Begins Noncampaign Offensive
abstract: Hillary Clinton, campaigning for a U.S. senate seat in New York, began a two day tour Manhattan and Long Island praising the state's history and culture.  She had a 12 hour day of speeches, dinners, photo sessions and a news conference.  She stands out in contrast to Rudolph Giuliani, also running for the senate seat, on school vouchers.  Clinton states that they are a threat to the nation's public education system where Giuliani embraces the idea of private school vouchers.  Giuliani has criticized Rodham-Clinton on being a political opportunist because she has never lived in New York.

headline: The lawyer lobby
abstract: Two Harrisburg lawyer's are trying to dismantle the new Lobbyist Disclosure Act before the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court even before it takes effect on the issue of when a person is acting in the capacity as a lobbyist and when they are acting as a lawyer.  Under the state constitution the Pennsylvania Supreme Court alone has the power to police members of the legal profession whether they are acting as barristers on behalf of clients or as hired guns for clients who want to see the law changed.

headline: Students taught to take the right PATH
abstract: First Lady Michele Ridge was at Harrisburg's Foose Elementary School to promote Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies(PATH) which would help first through fifth graders to to control their internal emotions and be able  to manage their  feelings instead of acting things out. This is funded by the Ridge administration through the Community Partnership Program.

headline: Police Profiling Debate: Acting on Experience, or on Bias
abstract: Profiling, which is the use of race and ethnicity as clues to criminality, is at the heart of federal and state investigations into police behavior in New Jersey and New York City.  It is the subtext of the outrage over the fatal shooting two months ago of Amadou Diallo, an unarmed West African immigrant, by four white New York Officers in the Bronx.

headline: Colleges offer deal to faculty
abstract: The State System of Higher Education offered it tems to the college union. The terms of the contract was refused by the college union. The only asssurance that students got was that classes would begin as scheduled.

headline: Open houses to tackle Pa. deer problem
abstract: The issue of how to best manage deer - the population stood at 1.2 million last fall - has polarized Pennsylvanians since the beginning of the century, when deer were stocked to augment a depressed population.  Throughout the years, many hunters generally have wanted more deer, while farmers, foresters and landowners have complained of increasing property destruction because of them.  The Game Commission - an eight member appointed board that has drawn fire for frequently ignoring the recommendations of agency-biologists - has held formal public hearings and meetings on deer management.  Each open house will feature five stations focusing on issues and possible solutions to management problems.

headline: IRS looks at how PIAA officials charged expenses
abstract: State Senator Mellow said that Internal Revenue Services has launched an investigation in to the Pennsylvania Interscholastic Atheletic Association because they have been keeping money  they were supposed to use for their travel expenses.

headline: Stop Waging War on Hemp Growing
abstract: State Legislature does nothing to ease the ban on hemp growing. The White House Office of the National Drug Control Policy fears that marijuana crops could be hidden among hemp.

headline: State plays ball
abstract: State lawmakers could not approve the new stadium funding bill where they borrowed $650 million without some political cover like a long list of development projects in other areas.  The tax revenue generated by new stadiums - which the state would receive anyway - probably will exceed the amounts of the state contributions.

headline: Ridge promotes state rail firms
abstract: Governor Ridge looks at a poster of a train in Mexico. The National Train Co. in Mexico recently bought 125 trains that were made in PA.

headline: Hillary Clinton plans move into new house around first of the year
abstract: First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton hopes to move into her new house in New York around the first of the year.  Clinton is preparing for a Senate run in New York next year.  She made the remark during a campaign visit to Syracuse yesterday.  She plans to move into the new house in Westchester County just north of New York City before or after New Year's Day.

headline: The return of 3M?
abstract: So far, state Senator Allyson Schwartz, D-Philadelphia, is the only declared Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate seat held by Republican Rick Santorum.

headline: Students, residents gauge progress through school portfolio reviews
abstract: The Pittsburgh Council of Public Education is promoting the use of portfolios apart from the test scores for an overall assesment of the students and the school. The use of portfolios in assessment is still in its infancy in Pittsburgh.

headline: 'Populist' Hypocrite
abstract: Opinion article citing Pat Buchanan's position on Hitler and auditioning for the Reform Party makes him a fraud.  Buchanan was upset that white Christians were not better represented by the Harvard studenty body.  He appeared on Face the Nation and was asked about his remarks yet tried to deny and down play them.

headline: Conservancy acquires farm that inspired Wyeth
abstract: The Kuerner Farm wher Andrew Wyeth painted more than 1000 works has been acquired by the Brandywine Conservancy to be preserved as a museum.

headline: Opinion: Throw your money in the water
abstract: People think they are getting a bad deal from the Fish and Boat Commission and are now no longer buying fishing licenses who had done so for as much as 30 or 40 years.  People would pay a base price for a license and then more to fish for trout.  Fisherman are able to fish for some trout but also shrinking waterways.  A few years ago the state "blew up" Stump Pond, which was one of the few remaining public-access fisheries left in the county.  With shrinking waterways people wonder what their license fees are paying for and the speculation is that they are funding projects in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh which they will never know about or see.

headline: Is the Lottery's Number Up?
abstract: Pennsylvania recorded lower lottery sales than the previous year indicating a trend that is matching 14 other states.  Proceeds from the lottery go to programs benefiting older Pennsylvanians such as property tax rebates, free bus transportation and discounts on prescription drugs.

headline: Sue cracks dealers just like carmakers, coffee- servers.
abstract: House Bill 478, the Drug Dealer Laibility Act will allow unduviduals to sue crack dealers for anything that goes wrong even if it is one's own fault.

headline: State Policymakers praise VISION
abstract: Schuylkill County's VISION initiative, a compilation of goals developed through focus groups, a Citizens Summit, task force meetings, and town meetings, was praised at the Legislative Office for Research Liaison Conference on state policy issues held at the state Capitol.  Mercer County's visions were nothing in terms of what Schuylkill County has done with its vision.

headline: Steel makes its case against imports
abstract: Despite improved conditions the steel industry's problems are far from over. PA's republican senators Santorum and Specter suggested that quota legislations introduced in Congress would roll imports from all countries prior to the steep rise in imported steel in 1998.

headline: His Legacy Continues
abstract: It was a bold statement to say that Philadelphia should have a black mayor by 1977 when John White, Sr. said it.  White was only off by six years when Wilson Goode was elected the first black mayor of Philadelphia in 1983.

headline: The unbuttoning of Al Gore: Act 1
abstract: Al Gore, in Concord, New Hampshire, is going to a home with 40 guests to gather support for his presidential race.  Despite being vice president, 16 years in Congress, authoring a book yet people still do not know who he is.  Article goes on to discuss how his intelluctual mindset casts him as boring.

headline: Study to help 14 state owned universities tailor offerings
abstract: The State System of Higher Education is taking up a study that would determine what PA companies need from the workforce. This study is approved by the Board of Governors and will be used at state universitites to meet the companies needs.

headline: PRDC Forum : Recognizing dealing with hate crimes
abstract: Captain Robert P. Hague of the Office of Heritage Bureau of Criminal Investigation examined the identification of hate groups and hate based crimes in PA.

headline: Controversy plans to threaten school voucher program
abstract: If Governor Ridge's voucher plan overcomes the odds and makes it to the PA General Assembly, the governor has proposed 2 voucher plans which would improve PA's quality of education substantially. But the voucher programs is embroiled with constitutional, political and educational controversies.

headline: Panel weighs passing the buck
abstract: The Quaker "blue laws" saw to it that no one in Pennsylvania hunted on Sundays.  Now some are saying that these laws are outdated and do not represent modern citizen want to hunt on the Sabbath.  The Pennsylvania House Game and Fisheries Committee is conducting a series of hearings on the matter for the public.  Dan Surra, Republican Representative from western Pennsylvania, has sponsored a bill that would allow hunting during two Sundays of the regular season.  He intentionally picked the time during buck season to introduce the bill because he was sure it would spark discussion.

headline: Lawmakers consider alterning primary date
abstract: State lawmakers are considering chanfging the primary date and to discuss whether its possible to have a  pair of primaries in the presidential election years. PA's spring primaries have long been criticized due to PA's inability to make a good selection for the presidential candidates.

headline: Task force on abuse to hold hearing today
abstract: The Domestic Violence Victims Address Confidentiality Act sponsored by State Rep. True would allow victims of domestic violence to obtain a confidential substitute address. The task force on domestic relations will hold a meeting in Landsville to discuss the same.

headline: State's economic situation on upswing. Schweiker says
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Schweiker said that PA was on the move economically and educationally at the Schuykill Chamber of Commerce. He also added that PA was the highest job creating state.

headline: Trade agreements complicate sale of Great Lakes water
abstract: Environmentalists and members of the United States Congress told a United States-Canadian panel that moving great lakes water by the tankerload to Asia or Africa may be prohibitively expensive for years to come, so this is a good time for Canada and the United States to consider export policies.  The International Joint Commission is preparing a report to advise the two nations on what they ought to do before the next exportation proposal is devised.  As part of the task the commissioners are in a 12-city fact-finding mission that included hearing in Toronto, Detroit, Ottawa, and Washington.  Export costs are so great that anything done commercially is extremely remote.

headline: Hobgoblins of Harrisburg
abstract: Pennsylvania lobbyists are compared to Halloween trick-or-treaters where people do not know who could be coming to their door just as lobbyists in Harrisburg parade around the capital disguised as special interests.  The new Lobbyist Disclosure Act was supposed to unmask the lobbyists so that everyone would know who was influence the legislature.  The problem is that instead of unmaking lobbyists it has turned every state interest into a special interest.

headline: The Wrong Way
abstract: A United States Census Bureau study revealed that Pennsylvania's fastest growing age group is people 85 and older.  The number of people in the oldest category jumped 31 percent between April 1990 and July 1998.  This is positive because it means that Pennsylvania residents are living longer because they are healthier.

headline: Summer school makes a return
abstract: The Philadelphia School District has launched a summer school program aimed at struggling students with the goal of ending social promotion.  Officials estimate that between 8,100 and 9,600 students will attend the classes.  The program offers support to students before they are held to higher academic standards.

headline: Privacy for sale
abstract: A California company named VIE says that it has a deal with Pennsylvania to buy personal financial data, employment histories, and income information submitted to the state by law.  The state department of labor and industry has agreed to provide that information to VIE which will then forward that information on to mortgage companies and lending institutions.  Supposedly this will speed up the loan approval process which normally takes weeks.  The state should not be in the business of raising money by violating the privacy, and more importantly, the trust of its citizens.

headline: Council approves Civil War Museum.
abstract: City Council approved Harrisburg's civil war museum. Gov. Ridge is expected to release a $ 14.9 million grant from the state for the museum construction.

headline: Philadelphia: Erect buildings that don’t damage environment
abstract: Philadelphia should build green because its buildings are polluting the air and water.  All buildings pollute but pollution comes not directly from pipes or chimneys rather the energy used to heat, cool and light our buildings.  Buildings are responsible for 33 to 40 percent of air pollution.

headline: Lawmakers discuss campaign reform
abstract: The day after the Senate rejected th campaign finance reform, members of the House State Government Committee discussed a legislation sponsored by State Representative Ledansky and a bill sponsored by State Representative Vitali. Both offer significant measures to alternative ways of campaign financing in PA.

headline: Taxpayers pay price for justice
abstract: The 1999-2000 state budget approved by the legislature will spend a record $1.1 billion to keep a burgeoning prison population behind bars at 24 state prisons and one boot camp.  The amount spent is more than double what the state spends on health programs and is 19 times more than the state will spend on libraries.  The state Department of Corrections projects a slight increase over the next 5 years which is already at 42% over capacity.

headline: Statewide building code clears Pa. House
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved a statewide building code that would set minimum construction standards for new homes and commercial structures while giving cities and towns some leeway to impose their own, more stringent rules.  The bill passed, 180-16, then goes back to the Senate, which passed a similar version.

headline: US, China must give, take to make trade deal work
abstract: The trade agreement signed between China and US in Washigngton,  remove trade barriers that have put American Companies at a disadvantage. The piracy hope treaty brings relief to American companies.

headline: Hoeffel, Greenwood vote for campaign reform
abstract: Congress may be closer to closing loopholes in campaign- finance law. U.S. Representatives Hoefel and Greenwood voted for the Shays- Meehan campaign bill that eliminates soft money and eliminates sham commercials.

headline: Third Democrat enters race for county executive
abstract: Community activist David Tessitor is seeking his the democratic party's nomination who is the third candidate seeking election for Allegheny County executive.  Tessitor, the one-time chair of the Citizen Advisory Panel of the Southwestern Pennsylvania Commission, has campaigned against suburban sprawl for years.

headline: Surviving spouses fight state for cost-of-living adjustments
abstract: A surviving spouse of a 40-year Pennsylvania school teacher is upset that the pension benefits that once increased with cost-of-living-adjustments are now frozen because the spouse has died.  The General Assembly has approved three cost-of-living adjustments since 1998 however those person's whose spouse was the recipient of the pension funds that died have seen no increase in benefits.

headline: Promoting Religion
abstract: Anyone who purchases a Bible or other religious articles and publications sold by religious organizations in Pennsylvania might take a second look at the sales receipt.  In Pennsylvania, those items are not subjected to sales tax.  The exemption, which dates back to 1956, is a gift from a government that considered the exemption a natural extension of the tax exemptions granted to religious institutions.  The exemption is multi-denominational.

headline: Court flunks voucher plan
abstract: Commonweallth Courts ruled that local school districts cannot enact their own voucher plan until state lawmakers give them the power to do so. The ruling means that only legislators can authorize school districts to funnel tax dollars to families who send their children to non - public schools.

headline: Plan for water cleanup unveiled
abstract: Pennsylvania House Democrats unveiled a six-bill legislative package to tackle the state's biggest water problems, incluidng drainage from abandoned coal mines, by floating some $500 million in bonds.  The plan, dubbed H-2000 by primary sponsor Representative Camille George, Democrat - Clearfield, also targets flooding, improving access to drinking water in rural areas, and giving local government more control over the use of sewage sludge on land.  The keystone of the H-2000 package is a $450 million fund to clean up acid drainage from the state's coal regions.  The bonds would have to be apporved by voters in a referendum.

headline: Legislature closes, showering Ridge with new bills
abstract: Governor Ridge commented on the number of bills that he signed into law because the legislature passed more than three dozen of them to him for signature before the conclusion of the two year session.  A pair of controversial school choice bills, later merged into one compromise package, was Ridge's number-one priority and the push largely eclipsed most other legislative action.

headline: Teaming up by Rendell and NRA leads to launch of gun crackdown
abstract: Philadelphia is a city where eight out of ten murders are committed with guns - the highest rate of any major United States city - federal and local authorities are teaming up to prosecute hundreds of gun-possession cases in federal court, where sentences are tougher, cases move faster, and defendants often are jailed while awaiting trial.  The program is modeled on one in Richmond, Virginia that is credited with cutting gun homicides in that city by 40%.

headline: Steelman sticks to guns on stadium vote
abstract: If Governor Ridge wants Representative Sara Steelman's support for his revised stadium-funding plan, he's going to have to release more state money for smaller projects that directly benefit smaller communities in her district.  Steelman, Democrat-Indiana, said she won't support the governor's plan if it only provides more state dollars for big civic projects even if one of those projects is the construction of a multi-million dollar new home for the Jimmy Stewart Museum in Indiana.

headline: We're losing the trade war
abstract: Steel lawmakes led by US Representative Traficant plan to introduce ledialations to bring relief to the US steel industry. Lawmakers feel that its easy to win House support. US Senator Santorum feels that the Senate is hard to sell.

headline: Hornbeck and guns fuel fiery session
abstract: The Pennsylvania legislature wraps up its year with controversy over convicted felon Representative Frank Serafini, Republican-Scranton, and a resolution seeking to dump Philadelphia Schools Superintendent David Hornbeck for saying state school funding is racist.  It is also working on a gun bill combining trigger locks with a ban on municipal lawsuits against gun makers.

headline: Time for progress for state, county
abstract: Just after taking the oath of office Governor Tom Ridge delivered his second inauguration address that is summed up by saying it is time to put away our differences and emphasize the common good.  His speech was a blueprint for people in Schuylkill County and across the state.  Ridge sees his mandate as one to make the state more civilized, unified, and prosperous and promoted lessons that should be applied.

headline: Rocky mountain states resisting move to broaden hate crime laws
abstract: Lawmakers in Colorado, Idaho, Montana Utah have defeated the bill that would add sexual orientation to hate crime laws.

headline: Cowell to start on new chapter
abstract: Ron Cowell, House Democratic Education Committee chairman, is retiring at the end of the term yet wants to stay involved in children's policy issues.  To do that officials from foundations that support education have asked him to fill a long-overlooked gap in state education by leading the newly formed "The Education Policy and Leadership Center."  The intent is to help lawmakers and policy and education czars use the research and information churned out annually to help students learn.  Some of Cowell's notable achievements are being the framer of the state's early invention program which helps disabled and the most needy youngsters get remedial services to prepare them for school.

headline: Power plants report chemical emissions
abstract: Residents living near power plants will know what types of pollution they are putting into the air because this year they have to report them to the federal Enivronmental Protection Agency which will make the numbers public.  They must produce the Toxics Release Inventory that is due the Environmental Protection Agency no later than July 1.  The inventory traces about 650 chemicals of which only six apply to coal burning electrical plants.  The Lehigh Valley is home to two coal burning plants in Lower Mount Bethel Township and Upper Mount Bethel Township.

headline: It's official: The GOP is coming here in 2000
abstract: The Republican National Convention officially chose Philadelphia at the site of the Republican's political convention in 2000.  Site-selection committee chairman Jan Larimer promised her fellow Republicans that Philadelphia would be great and urged them to ratify the committee's recommendation.

headline: The children's well-being must guide decision-making in abuse and neglect cases
abstract: Child welfare systems in the Pennsylvania and nationwide have significant barriers that impeded the goals of ensuring the health, safety and due process rights of parents and children.  Serious analysis of all county systems in Pennsylvania may be in order, as each county has its own set of challenges and strengths.

headline: Steely Resolve
abstract: Pittsburgh Pirate's owner Kevin McClatchy made it clear that if the state Legislature did not pass a stadium funding bill he would move the team.  McClatchy seemed to have some leverage that the Phillies and Eagles did not have according to Bill Giles, chairman of the Phillies.

headline: Court upholds deportation order for ex-Nazi guard
abstract: A federal appeals court has upheld the deportation of an 80-year-old Buck County man who served as a concentration camp guard for the Nazis during World War II.  Nikolaus Schiffer, was born in Philadelphia but raised in Romania and joined the Romanian army and later became part of the German Waffen SS, the elite branch of Hitler's army.

headline: House approves bill to move 2000 primary
abstract: The PA pimary will be moved from April 25 to May 2 according to a bill signed by the State House of Representatives. This bill was introduced by State Representative DeWeese.

headline: Time to start workign on our sales pitch
abstract: Governor Ridge was trying to gather support amongst fellow state governors to attend the next National Governor's Association, which will be held in State College, while at the current event in St. Louis and joined by their families, staff, and volunteers.  One hurdle the Governor recognizes is that next summer's Democratic and Republican conventions may divet governor's attention away from Happy Valley.  In particular the republican convention will be held in Philadelphia just two weeks after the national governor's meeting.

headline: Same-sex couples face parental challenges in Pennsylvania and beyond
abstract: Gay couples with children present challenges to the state's legal system that makes decisions off of traditions established in a mom, dad, two kids, and a dog.  It has become increasingly common for gay and lesbian couples to establish a common household and complete the family unity by having children avoiding marriage as it is illegal in the United States.

headline: Cyberstarting Too Young
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge wants to spend $1.6 million to give free on-line access to 4,000 licensed day-care centers so preschoolers can become familiar with the Internet before starting school.  Gail Menapace, director of the Columbia Child Development Center says that she does not think it is wonderful for children to be exposed in all our classrooms because of their age.  Proponents of the plan think it is a valuable teaching tool for children.

headline: Prevent pollution and save money
abstract: Pennsylvania's Office of Pollution Prevention and Compliance Assistance is touting its new grant and loan programs for small business as part of National Pollution Prevention Week.  Pennsylvania businesses with up to 100 employees are eligible for the money.  The goal is to get business people to realize the benefits with pollution prevention according to Robert Barkanic who is the agency's secretary.

headline: It's over.  There's a lesson
abstract: House Judiciary Chairman Henry Hyde issued a statement that the House of Representatives should not try to impeach President Clinton because they would not succeed in getting the required 67 votes from the Senate and the American people did not have the will or desire to remove him either.  Although Clinton did not escape punishment.

headline: The Flaw in Bush's Tax Plan
abstract: Bush's tax plan would allow married couples who both work to deduct up to $30,000 of the lower earning spouse resulting in an annual savings of $300.  Currently non-married couples living together fair better under the tax plan than married couples.  Criticism of it is that the proposal ignores lower-income families while delivering a special benefit to more affluent families.  The plan does nothing for one income single parent households.  Married couples with one income cannot currently split the income of the one earner to gain the rewards of a two income tax break married couple.

headline: Street, Katz both pledge to fine $37 million to aid Logan section
abstract: Sam Katz and John Street both say they would raise $37 million to repair the sinking homes of Philadelphia's Logan section and rebuild the area.  $37 million would more than double the amount already spent on the homes.  It was discovered in 1986 that about 1,000 homes were sinking into ash weakened by a creek.  Philadelphia Interfaith Action, a nonpartisan civic action group that includes 40 churches and synagogues, want the additional money to be used not only to buy out the remaining 50 homeowners but also to restore the blighted area.

headline: From Russia with gov.: County hosts foreign visitors
abstract: Five Russians toured Montgomery County's prothonotary, district attorney office and public defender office to learn about democratic government.  They were part of a 2,000 member contingent visiting the United States.

headline: House bill honors Irvis
abstract: K. Leroy Irvis, former speaker of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, will be honored with a tribute with the passage of a bill to name the East Wing of the State Capitol Building after him.  Irvis was the first African-American to be elected speaker of a state legislative body.  The building was built in the 1980s.

headline: To have voice heard, move PA primary up
abstract: By the time PA's primary eletions loom, the presidential nominations would have been done. By moviing up the primay election date there could be less campaign time for the candidates. PA needs to move its primary every fourth year to be recognized as a keepeer of promises and to be noticed in the presidential race.

headline: Same-sex couples face parental challenges in Pennsylvania and beyond
abstract: Same sex couples with children present challenges to a staid legal system that based its traditions on families consisting of a mom and a dad with two kids and a dog. Same sex parents are increasingly having children all of which happens without marriage as it is illegal in the United States.  Most Pennsylvania trial courts have not rejected same-sex adoptions because the Commonwealth does not recognize same-sex marriages.

headline: Data shows amount spent higher per pupil
abstract: The Pittsburgh Board of Public Education spends more money per student than other similarly sized urban school due to the presence of a large budget. This was attributed to high labor cost. Pittsburgh School Teachers ean about $65700 annually.

headline: Program cleans up 500th industrial site in four years
abstract: Governor Ridge says that a Pennsylvania program has cleaned up 500 industrial sites in four years making the state a leader in replacing them new business.  Roughly 15 thousand people are now working at sites once deemed decaying and dirty "brownfields."  Jeff Schmidt of the Sierra club says that some sites were covered up but not cleaned because many of the 500 sites were treated under the state's Land Recycling Act which protects new property owners from lawsuits because of hidden pollution.

headline: It's take the money and run for mayor
abstract: Campaign fundraising has increased significantly since Ed Rendell was mayor of Philadelphia in 1991.  Rendell had $411,000 available for the mayoral race and all democratic candidates combined had $773,000.  Now, candidates are receiving contributions that Ed Rendell would not see until after he won the democratic primary.  By candidate the following have raised these amounts for the Philadelphia mayoral race: Dwight Evan, $800,000; Happy Fernandez, $920,000; John Street, $200,000; Mary Weignburg, $200,000; John White, Jr., $750,000; Sam Katz over $1 million.

headline: The tale of 2 prison breaks: Cut bars, dummies in beds
abstract: Two inmates who escaped from a state prison in Luzerne County apparently fled late Sunday night or early Monday after smashing a window and cutting away a prison bar covering it.  The escape by convicted killer Michael McCloskey and his arsonist cellmate, Anthony Yang in a way mirrors the August 2 breakout by Chester County murderer Norman Johnston from another state prison.

headline: Streetnows involvement on stadums
abstract: When mayor-elect John F. Street returns from vacation he will meet with friend and political ally mayor Ed Rendell to discuss negotiations for building sports stadiums in Philadelphia.  The Phillies and Eagles are aggresively seeking lease deals for their teams focusing on South Philadelphia.  Center city was too hot to consider and Street says that he has no preference other than what is right for the citizens and taxpayers of the city.

headline: Gathering honors detained teacher
abstract: Dickinson College students and staff and faculty turned out in a rally to support Yongyi Song and his wife who have been detained by the Chinese government on suspicions of illicit attempt to steal state secrets.

headline: House honors late basketball star, dissenter laments sex legacy
abstract: The Pennsylvania House voted 195-1 to approve a resolution recognizing the achievements and honoring the legacy of Wilt Chamberlain.  Representative Steve Samuelson, Democrat-Northampton, stated his vote was cast with mixed feelings as honoring someone who says in his own autobiography that he had sex with thousands of women.

headline: Top Race Glance
abstract: A overview of the election canditates and the summary of different PA races

headline: Senate tries again to pass late-term abortion ban
abstract: The United States Senate is resuming an emotional debate over legislation that would ban some late-term abortions, opening the way for another presidential veto.  Opponents have condemned the legislation as unconstitutional and designed to boost Republican election prospects next year at the expense of pregnant women whose lives and health are in danger.

headline: Day-care bill fiasco risks kids' safety
abstract: All day-care centers in Pennsylvania, regardless of size, should be subject to unannounced inspections.  For years, Representative Robert Godshall, Republican-Hatfield, has been trying to pass legislation that would make these two requirements the law.

headline: Puzzling policy
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Protection is being penny wise and pound foolish by proposing to cut grants to clean up tire dumps.  Just five yeas ago firefighters from virtually every volunteer department in Monroe County battled a tire fire at Trophy Tire Company in Stroud Township when a 100,000-tire stockpile mysteriously went up in flames.  The fire burned for days and polluted a nearby stream.  Lawmakers from across the state the Department rethink its misguided position.

headline: It's time for Bush to open up
abstract: Opinion article challenging George Bush on coming clean on his record of drug use, not to politicize abortion, and a change to make things right with his father.

headline: There's safety in firepower
abstract: Frenzied bidding over a TV Show " Homicide: Life in Schools" occurs for cancellations and renewals.This show has a fictionary school district where it is legal to carry fire arms and superior fire wins over the inferior one.

headline: Swinging for Broad Street
abstract: Mayor Rendell announced that he would not seek to introduce new stadium legislation for the Phillies and Eagles before leaving office because there is too little time for City Council to review the plans and have a bill submitted on time.  With the responsibility being passed off to mayor-elect John Street this might bring back the possibility of having the Phillies stadium at Broad and Spring Garden streets.

headline: Gore pays campaign visit to New Hampshire
abstract: The vice president paid visits to a diner and a house party, discussing Kosova and welfare, in the first-primary state.  At a house party he discussed his views on Yugoslav president Milosevic and denounced him as a leader but said that he would not support sending troops the region.  The NATO air strikes would be effective.

headline: House Members Say They Want to Call 15 Witnesses, Including Clinton Aides
abstract: United States House Representatives stated they want to use as many as 15 witnesses, including not just Monica Lewinsky, but also an array of current and former Presidential advisers in the impeachment trial of President Bill Clinton.  The House members acknowledged that if Senate leaders allowed them less time for witnesses than the two weeks they had requested, they might have to winnow the list to as few as five people.  The 13 House prosecutors from the House Judiciary Committee said they were intent on bringing many of the players who have occupied center stage in the Lewinsky drama back.

headline: Tories Turning to GOP for Tips
abstract: Despite hard times for Republicans in the United States Congress, William Hague who heads Britain's Conservative Party is still a fan of them despite his own setbacks with a downtrodden institution.  Hague is traveling to Washington to take some courses from well known Congressional Republicans on conservative politics.

headline: Slaying sparks calls for expansion of hate crimes law
abstract: Representatie Cohen and Senator Conti called for the expansion of state crime laws that would add sexual orientation, disability and ancestery to the list. The bills are supported by various gay and lesbian and civil rights groups.

headline: Day-care workers receive low pay
abstract: A legislative report compiled form a survey of 541 licensed child-care centers and 122 group child-care homes across the state found that average salaries for day-care workers are so low that often the people who depend on care for their children earn less than the poverty level.  While many members of the Pennsylvania joint Legislative Budget and Finance Committee said they were not surprised but must take a closer look to see if those salaries could be boosted.

headline: Remember legal details tomorrow
abstract: A discussion on the details of deer hunting season for hunters to remember things like wearing at least 250 square inches of flourescent orange, positively identify your target, be in shape to drag dead deer back to your vehicle, and no hunting within 150 yards of an occupied building without the occupant's permission.  If a dead deer that has been tagged is found to have infection after killing it contact the closest commission regional office to find out if a replacement tag is available.

headline: It's time to computerize voting
abstract: Opinion article written by Dennis Ness who is advocating Governor Ridge to move Pennsylvania into the future by doing away with old mechanical voter machines and advancing to computerized voting.  Column goes on to show how this would be a benefit to citizens.

headline: Tobacco funds sought for firefighting
abstract: Representative Jerry Nailor of Mechanicsburg wants part of the tobacco settlement money coming to the state to be spent on firefighting services.  Nailor states that smoking related fires are the lead cause of fire fatalities in the United States and one of the leading causes of property damage.

headline: Taking another swing at stadiums
abstract: Democratic Representatives Andrew Carn of Philadelphia and Representative William Robinson of Pittsburgh have introduced legislation that is a long-shot but would free up money that may be beneficial to all parties.  The legislation is different from other legislation where it would create a state authority which the stadium-construction money would be funneled to the teams.

headline: Koreans sue seven U.S. chemical companies for Agent Orange exposure
abstract: 20 victims in South Korea have claimed that they and their families have suffered an array of cancers, deformities, and birth defects after being exposed to toxins found in the demilitarized zone.  A group of Koreans have filed a federal lawsuit demanding potentially millions in compensation for the damage suffered after United States manufactured defoliants like Agent Orange that were sprayed in South Korea's demilitarized zone.

headline: HOUSE PANEL CONTINUES CAMPAIGN FINANCE HEARINGS
abstract: Rep Asa Hutchinson (R-ARK) said that his campaign finance reform bill has a better chance of passing this year.  His bill bans soft money (unlimited unregulated donations that are supposed to used only for political party activities) at the federal level only.  A similar bill was rejected by the Sentate earlier.

headline: Trust the people
abstract: People living around the Philadelphia region have told pollsters that they are enjoying living there now than in any time in the last five years.  Elected officials receive the credit because residents are less likely to cite crime and drugs as major problems than in recent years.

headline: Speakers urge renewed action by all citizens
abstract: Hundreds gathered to honor the work of Revered Martin Luther King, Junior.  Lawrence Wilson, president of Ambler Olympic Club is this year's recipient of the Reverend Doctor Martin Luther King, Junior award.

headline: Democrats criticize governor's school- choice measure
abstract: State Representative Colafella said the voucher program is actually a bailout for the schools and not a school choice bill.  He also stressed the fact that even if the bill passed Ridge would face constitutional challenges as to whether public dollars can be used for private schools.

headline: Ridge asks N.Y. to honor trash promise
abstract: Governor Ridge has sent a letter to New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani stating that a survey of nearly 70% of Pennsylvania's communities who have landfills and incinerators do not want trash from New York City.  Ridge asked Giuliani to keep his promise not to send the trash to communities that do not want it.  New York City's deputy mayor of operations, Joseph Lhota, said that New York City would never its waste to a community that does not want it.

headline: It's time to tame our legislative beasts
abstract: Pennsylvania residents charge our state representatives with the job of enacting policy that will better conditions in our great state but sometimes their actions confuse us.  A law banning sex with animals was inadvertently deleted from the books in 1995 and legislators felt they had to act.  A bill has passed both the House and the Senate and is on its way to the Governor to sign the bill into law.

headline: Tobacco Windfall Begins Tug-Of-War Among Lawmakers
abstract: State legislatures nationwide are debating how to use the settlement monies from the tobacco industry on things like health care, antismoking campaigns, schools, jails, state debs, or even sidewalks.  Over the next 25 years, all 50 states and some cities will receive almost $246 billion from cigarette producers as a result of the lawsuits brought against the tobacco industry to recover Medicaid money.

headline: Tax-free zones can be tool to curb sprawl
abstract: State officials went throughout Pennsylvania to announce the approval of 12 tax free business zones to prompt economic development.  Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker visited Lehigh Valley and stated that this is particularly good here because the Keystone Opportunity Zone will help curb suburban sprawl.

headline: McCain Harshly Criticized Clinton Policies
abstract: Senator John McCain was critical of President Clinton on his views on Kosovo to the Middle East to international trade.  He made his speech bringing together his views on foreign policy at a National Press Lunch Club gathering.

headline: House panel Oks foundation grant-watchdog proposal
abstract: The House State Government Committee approved a bill designed to shed more light on the activities on nonprofit foundations.  The bill would force state agencies accepting grant money from private entities for the establishment of a new program to run that program through a state regulatory review before accepting the funds.  The bill was sponsored by Berks County Republican Samuel Rohrer.

headline: Trust, race, and a city
abstract: John F. Street, the second ever African-American elected as the mayor of Philadelphia, won the race by fewer than 6,000 votes.  Street did not hold much of an edge to white Republican opponent Sam Katz, a businessman, with little public sector experience.  The question of Trust for political elections is discussed in regards to the wide range of Democratic voters and narrow range of Republican voters in Philadelphia and how Street appealed to them to win.

headline: State bill allows colleges to refuse same-sex benefit
abstract: House bill on training moved to the Senate after adding some advanced language that state financed colleges will have the right to refuse health insurance to same sex partners even if the municipality requires coverage.

headline: Denver teacher to try out merit pay
abstract: Denver teachers will have merit pay based on their students performance. The 2 year pilot program will explore whether monetory incentives for teachers will lead to better test scores amonst students.

headline: Ridge call N.Y. bluff on landfills
abstract: New York City Deputy Mayor Joseph Lhota says his town won't send trash where it's not wanted.  Governor Tom Ridge yesterday ordered the Department of Environmental Protection to canvass Pennsylvania communities that are hosts to landfills and other waste disposal centers to find out if they want New York City's trash.  Communities that answer "No" will be put on a list and sent to Mayor Rudolph Giuliani.  Governor Ridge is saying that they are asking New York City to comply with policy set by Pennsylvania's local communities and an attempt to get New York City officials to accept responsibility for their actions.

headline: Jesse Jackson Will Skip 2000 Race, Advisors Say
abstract: Reverend Jesse L. Jackson does not intend to run a third time for the presidential election in 2000.  Jackson commands a loyal following of liberal Democrats and would have complicated the race for Al Gore is he had run.  Jackson said on Black Entertainment Television that there challenges trying to raise money for minorities by pressing Wall Street.

headline: Two men escape from Scranton halfway house
abstract: Police were looking for Carl Caum and Kevin Frisbie who both escaped from a halfway house in Scranton.  Both were discovered missing about 4 a.m. and police provided detailed physical descriptions, possible vehicles they may be in and possible whereabouts.

headline: The great stadium debate
abstract: Jerry Boyer, President of the Allegheny Institute, a Pittsburgh based watchdog group, says that no matter how you look at it the deal the state made to fund four new sports stadiums is a bad one.  The legislature's approval vote was based on the belief that the stadium funds build the local economy but most economist do not buy this argument.

headline: Pitts believes trip was step toward peace
abstract: United States Representative Joseph R. Pitts returned from a trip to Vienna with 10 other congressmen hopeful that they hammered out a framework for a peace agreement with Yugoslavia.  The members met with members from the Russian Duma, which is Russia's legislative body.

headline: House Team Opens Trial by Likening Clinton to 'Cancer'
abstract: House prosecutors denounced President Clinton as a leader who has put himself above the law and must be excised like a cancer from the body.  The tough rhetoric, carrying echoes of Watergate a quarter-century ago, opened what will be three days of arguments by a team of House Republicans seeking the president's ouster.  The extraordinary proceeding is only the second of its kind in the nation's history.  Clinton stand accused of perjury and obstruction of justic for his role in trying to conceal his relationship with former White House intern Monica Lewinsky.

headline: Turbulence at Takeoff
abstract: Allegheny County Commissioner Bob Cranmer was incensed that the elections of Robert Lewis, who contributed funds to Mike Dawida's campaign, funds to his own campaign and state Representative David Mayernik, tainted Pittsburgh International Airport with the kind of politics he wanted out.  Cranmer said the political appointment played directly into the hands of the critics who maintained that the authority would be little more than a political dumping ground.

headline: State's Right to Know law antiquated, ineffective
abstract: Several county commissioners and local police departments were recently asked for documents that according to the state's 42 year old Right to Know Act are supposed to be quickly and easily available to any Pennsylvania citizen received grades ranging from "A" to "F".  Various officials were asked for things like phone records, animal control ordinances, high school principal salaries, police logs and court commissioner meeting minutes.

headline: Did effort on vouchers hurt Ridge or not?
abstract: Governor Ridge states that ending his battle for school vouchers a few votes short of legislative passage is nothing more than a learning experience yet his critics say it could affect his national ambitions and future effectiveness.  Ridge is still pushing to put the program in place that Governors of Wisconsin and Ohio have already put in place in Milwaukee and Cleveland.

headline: Ridge keeps denying water line grant
abstract: Sewickly township officials say that their constituents are unable to tap into the community revitalization program controlled by Gov. Ridge to obtain drinking water from natural resources.

headline: Jim Roddey, politician
abstract: Jim Roddey is the first elected Allegheny County chief executive with strong business and organization skill and works well with people.  Roddey says he doesn't know much about politics and is not a politician.  Article goes on to discuss three reasons why politics will be hard to keep out of his office.

headline: Up in smoke
abstract: What was seen as a dumb move, Allegheny Court Commissioners Mike Dawida and Bob Cranmer have withdrawn their lawsuit challenging the $11.3 billion settlement between Pennsylvania and the tobacco industry.  The county had jumped in trying to secure what it considered its rightful share of the $1.3 billion of the state settlement.

headline: The growth challenge
abstract: Measures that only work halfway to curb sprawl will not work and is the challenge before lawmakers, Governor Ridge, municipal officials, environmental groups and the development community as they debate the details of it.  Due to the pace of sprawl going slow will not work.

headline: Senator: Open Cuba to travel
abstract: Senator Patrick Leahy is using a trip to Cuba, where the Baltimore Orioles played Cuba's baseball team, as a means to call for an end to the travel ban on American tourists from visiting the island.  The United States treasury department regulates that United States citizens cannot spend money in Cuba.  Leahy, the ranking Democrat on the foreign operations subcomittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee, brought the first major league team there since 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power.

headline: How Big Labor Plans to Save Gore
abstract: Vice President Al Gore's support for the 2000 presidential election is coming from union leader Gerald McEntee.  McEntee is working hard to make sure the AFL-CIO endorses Gore.  Gore is desparate for support as his candidacy sinks deeper due to his guilt-by-association to Clinton.  Only one other candidate has been endorsed this early by the AFL-CIO, Walter Mondale.  Gore's most fervent backers are public-sector unions.

headline: Ture colors of Mike McGeehan
abstract: A former Republican candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives 173 Legislative District, Daniel Sansoni, is firing back at Mike McGeehan, whom he lost to in the election race for the seat, for criticizing the Northeast Times.  Sansoni calls McGeehan a racist and that he wants people to believe he will base his reasons for choosing a mayor on Section 8, reform of L&I, public schools, and the wage tax.  Yet Sansoni says McGeehan has personally done nothing about these issues

headline: Student publications are not the place to advertise alcohol
abstract: Students at the University of Pittsbugh have filed a lawsuit in an attempt to reverse a law prohibited alcohol advertisement in educational institutions. The law is not perfect but should remain intact.

headline: District scrambles for staff
abstract: Philadelphia School District has less than a month to go before school starts with 500 teaching positions it needs to fill.  It is optimistic that it can reduce the number to about 150 vacancies which is better than how it started the previous year.  Increased recruitment and hiring incentives have led to more applications and inquiries.

headline: Ridge to speak at 2020 conference in April
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge will be the guest speaker at  Chester County's 2020 event.  David E. Davis, chairman of Chester County, says that the Governor is coming because he recognizes the county's model of land preservation and use is perfect for the state.  Ridge has commended the county through a press release on uniting government, development, and environmental groups to improve its towns and villages.

headline: Job growth, development top priorities for Boscola
abstract: Lisa Boscola was sworn into office in the Pennsylvania Senate by Chief Justice John P. Flaherty.  Boscola, a Democrat, succeeded Republican Joe Uliana, who gave up his seat after an unsuccessful run for Congress, and beat Republican candidate Len Gruppo for the seat.

headline: Violence: A catholic school issue too
abstract: Robert Paserba diocesan superintendent of schools, eventhough the violence rates is low due the moral education that students receive, Catholic Schools are not exempt from violence and face the same issues as others. Closed video circuits and locked doors after the classes begin are some measures that schools are taking.

headline: The region's best, on display under one roof
abstract: The Gateway Visitors Center in Philadelphia will be a tourist portal to the entire promoting Independence Hall and attractions as far afield as Valley Forge and the Amish Country.  The building is designed to be a one-stop planning destination where visitors can get information, tickets, reservations for restaurants, museums, and historical sites.

headline: Terrorism experts urge regional plan
abstract: The Central PA Counter Terrorism Task Force sponsored a series of seminars and workshops on how groups in Central PA can react better to terrorism  when they happen locally.

headline: How Henry Hyde's Resolve Was Shaped Against Clinton
abstract: United States Representative Henry Hyde stated that President Bill Clinton should not be impeached for having a peccadillo and that he would not be impeached with bipartisan support.  Hyde also said that House Judiciary Committee proceedings would bring honor to Congress and not fall into partisan bickering.  Democrats were pleased with this until he opposed a Democratic proposal that would have limited the inquiry and instead toyed with expanding it.  He opposed a censure option, which Republicans do not want as well, and presided over hearing dominated by partisan attacks.  Hyde was angered by Clinton's cavalier attitude toward the law, the investigation and the committee.  Boxed in by Democrats Hyde felt he had no choice but to push for impeachment.

headline: Two answers to every convention question
abstract: In Los Angeles, the Democrats are excited about how their $35 million political convention will be paid for by private funds.  In Philadelphia organizers of the $35 million plus Republican convention are bragging about a public-private investment in the region's economic future that will have taxpayers footing at least one-third of the convention bill.

headline: Suit may cause counselors to think twice before advising about advising abortion
abstract: Planned Parenthood National Foundation Director Gloria Fledt stated that the lawsuit against the Hatboro-Horsham School District, which alleges that a school counselor urged a student to have an abortion, claims this is just another attempt to limit the vulnerable, young, and poor's reproductive choice.  An attorney for the anti-abortion American Center for Law and Justice is representing the family filing the suit against the school district.

headline: Don't endanger our rights in name of school safety
abstract: State Representative Sheila Miller wants to amend the state's Sunshine Law to add security issues to the list that may be debated in closed door sessions in public schools.  Miller argues that public discussion of security arrangements would aid people with not the best intentions.

headline: Ridge to televise zebra mussel woes
abstract: From the round goby to the zebra mussel, Governor Tom Ridge will tell the nation about the problems of non-native species invading the Great Lakes and the efforts to prevent future invasions in a documentary to be broadcast on CNBC in August.  Ridge will be speaking not only as the governor of Pennsylvania but as chairman of the Council of Great Lakes Governors'.  The council supports numerous programs to combat invasive species such as the zebra mussell.  A major inititiative of the council is to prevent additional exotic species from hitchng a ride in the ballast of ocean-going freighters that enter the lake.  That is how the zebra mussell and other invasive species arrived.

headline: We can't ignore the growth of prisons
abstract: An opinion article explaining that citizens need to pay attention to the overcrowding prison issue now rather than waiting until one of our family members winds up in prison and pay attention to it then.  Former attorney general Ernie Preate was convicted of mail fraud and after spending time in prison became an advocate for prison inmates after his release.

headline: The stadiums folly
abstract: As Governor Tom Ridge was sworn in for his second term questions are raised as to which governor he will present himself as.  Will he be orator of political catch-phrases or the politician who insists on using tax dollars to perpetuate welfare?  Ridge has wedged himself into the middle of the long-running debate over taxpayer-funded sports stadiums  where he has promised state tax receipts to cover one-third of the costs of new stadium funding.

headline: Well now, look who's arming China
abstract: China's army conducted a military exercise with simulated missile firings against Taiwan and also for the first time conducted mock attacks on United States troops in the region.  With the mock attacks, China is sending the message that they will return Taiwan back to their ownership even if it means war with the United States.

headline: How mayoral hopefuls would cultivate city's arts
abstract: The mayoral candidates for Philadelphia's mayor have experience with or participate in the fine arts but some are concerned if the new mayor will fund the arts as copiously as Mayor Rendell did.  Rendell has been a key figure raising money for the arts.  He and John Street started the Philadelphia Cultural Fund and has so convincingly argued for the support of the arts that his successors for mayor are already tuned in to the issues.

headline: Two more Democrats join the race to replace Rep. Klink in 4th District
abstract: Lawrence Mangino, Lawrence County District Attorney, and Terry Van Horne, Democratic New Castle Representative, will both run for Representative Ron Klink's 4th District seat in Congress.  Van Horne is giving up his State House seat for the congressional bid.  Mangino stressed education and public-private partnerships to provide full college scholarships.

headline: The Problem: Philadelphia's way of dealing with its diversity may be preventing the city -and many of its citizens- from reaching full potential
abstract: Article discusses in three parts what Philadelphia should do to work on diversity.  1.  Build Dialogue: build connections amount neighborhoods, promote cultural diversity education, and combat damaging stereotypes.  2.  Level the Playing Field: Leave ethnic groups alone to develop their own institutions, economic capital and political clout.  Ethnic groups are much more likely to get along when they feel they can determine their own destiny.  3.  Equality of Opportunity:  Create and enforce equal opportunity in education, business and politics.  Equal opportunity for high education is the first priority.

headline: Doubts about schools widen the voucher debate
abstract: Opinions are divided amongst the various ethnic and relegious groups.  Most American Jews remain steadfast in their support for public education. Relegious Catholic schools see this as a means of filling up empty classrooms.

headline: Ridge urges GOP to have aggressive locally-based environmental program
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge announced to the Coalition of Republican Environmental Advocacy that current environmental regulation was holding things back from progressing faster.  Ridge wants a locally-oriented approach that is profitable and environmentally reponsible but doing that would require the GOP ending the "enforcement first" mentality that dominates much of the current thinking on the subject.  To highlight his idea, the Pennsylvania Land Recycling Program releases parties who clean up the environment when they have damaged it and creates new jobs.  The coalition gave Ridge its Theodore Roosevelt Award to raise money for next year's national election.

headline: Wielding Veto, President Presses Hate Crime Issue
abstract: President Clinton is trying to add homosexuals to the list of persons identified under hate crimes in effect broadening the federal law.  The proposal would authorize federal prosecution of persons accused of violent crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, gender or disability.

headline: The work of the city
abstract: Employment hit rock bottom in Philadelphia in 1996 and has been slowing edging up since then.  Mayor Rendell has exploited the cities new Convention Center and historic infrastructure.  Republican candidate Sam Katz insists that he can cut the wage tax from 4.6 percent to 4.  Democractic John Street nominee says he can reduce it to 4.4 percent.

headline: Annual GOP picnic offers plenty of food for thought
abstract: The annual Montour County GOP picnic provided for a lot of opportunities for the political leaders to talk.

headline: HOW TO STOP PLAYING POLITICS
abstract: Lee B. Horne, an auditor in the State Auditor General's Office in Philadelphia responds to comments made in a previous edition by Steven Van Dyck who proposed that "democracy is only for the people who can afford to pay the money to sit at the table." Horne observes that the Founding Fathers attempted to bring a new government based on freedoms, rights and privileges and proposes that only individual donations should be allowed (and capped); campaigning should be limited to 6 months; and elected and government officials should not accept meals, airfare, vations, or other non-monetary gifts.

headline: Two States Retain Roles in Shaping Presidential Race
abstract: The presidential primary enters a frantic pace for the Iowa caucuses and New Hampshire primary.  Some analysts thought it would not be as important because California and New York moved up their dates for their primaries.  Candidates have not downplayed Iowa's and New Hampshire's importance by sending TV and radio ads.  Mentions John McCain, George Bush, and Bill Bradley.

headline: The state legilsature bashes gays - again
abstract: Governor Ridge will sign a bill which will ban same sex employee benefits. This law states that if same sex benefits would not available to partners working in public universities. The American Civili Liberties Union said that they would would fight this law in court.

headline: Ed-Flex ;aws hasn't cut all strings on school aid
abstract: The Ed-Flex law signed by President Clinton is aimed at reducing red-tapism in school's federal aid and easing the administrative burden. Local school officils say that coping with the state rules is more difficult than the federal ones.

headline: Ridge's green plan outlined.
abstract: The State Department of Environmental Protection said the Governor Ridge wants to shfit $ 1.3 billion from the lesser used funds to a local level to the growing greener initiative of the environment.

headline: null
abstract: United States Senator Rick Santorum, Republican-Pennsylvania, states that now is the time to save Social Security for present and future generations.  Santorum supported President Clinton that the time for reform is now, private sector investment is viable, and personal retirement accounts are crucial.

headline: Three of the four lawmakers representing county vote no
abstract: Only Lawrence County's state Representative Frank LaGrotta voted in favor of the state funding four new sports stadiums in Pennsylvania.  State Representative Chris Sainato, and state Senators Gerald LaValle and Mary Jo White opposed it.

headline: Annual GOP picnic offers plenty of food for thought
abstract: The annual Montour County GOP picnic provided for a lot of opportunities for the political leaders to talk.

headline: In His Words
abstract: At his annual year-in-review press conference Friday, Governor Tom Ridge covered topics ranging from his convictions about school vouchers to the conviction of Representative Frank Serafini, Republican - Lackawanna, for perjury in federal court.  The article illustrates quotes on his views on school vouchers, education, capital stock and franchise tax, using the budge surplus to fund property tax rebates, House members' legal problems, Serafini's conviction, privatizing state liqour stores, and New Year's resolutions.

headline: Unease over Gore coloring impeachment, polls indicate
abstract: Voters expressed their views that a third of independent voters for a general election stated that they would not be in favor of Al Gore becoming the next president of the United States.  Voters doubts are being quantified through some well-known republicans like George W. Bush and Elizabeth Dole.

headline: Three women sue state police for sexual and racial harassment
abstract: Several civil rights advocates joined three women in calling for a formal investigation of alleged racial and sexual abuse of the women by their state police co-workers.  Kathy Kidd and Edwina Clarkson said they were sexually harassed by colleagues of the Bureau of Liquor Enforcement.  Clarkson and Sharon Williams, who are black, also allege racial discrimination on the part of the bureau denying them promotional training and accusing them of stealing in their Philadelphia office.  The women are suing for loss of wages and punitive damages.

headline: Education Official: City fails
abstract: Ridge administration is fighting an uphill battle with the voucher program Education Secretary Hickok said the voucher plan can help parents get their children out of schools that do not work. The Pennsylvania State Education Union feels that the voucher program will not work as it offers no assistance or additional resources.

headline: Ridge's 'green' plan robs Peter to pay Paul
abstract: Opinion article stating that Governor Tom Ridge has made one thing clear that he can "deliver the goods" to the kingpins who bankrolled his campaigns while not advancing the environment.  Yet by contradiction, he is pushing his Growing Greener Initiative.  The author claims that this is to head off criticism from a coalition of conservation, cultural and environmental organizations called the Heritage 21 initiative.  The problem with this is that to fund this Ridge is having to take away funds from already existing environmental programs.  This has been a pattern neglecting and underfunding environment programs so that a "surplus" would emerge to fund his new initiative Grower Greener.

headline: 11th-Hour Push Forges Social Security Plan
abstract: A key question for one of President Clinton's state of the union addresses was how to address Social Security in his speech, which dealt with how much of the budget surplus would go to saving the program from insolvency.  Even Clinton's top economic advisors could not come to a consensus on how the funds should be spent, how much, and how much criticism from republicans they were willing to risk.

headline: Tougher building codes coming
abstract: Broomall Fire Chief Tom Murray remembers when Marple Township's stringent building codes were directly responsible for saving the lives of three people trapped by fire.  The house had a sprinkler system installed that put out a fire which spread rapidly while a master bath was being finished.

headline: 2 more Pa. lawmakers are subjects of federal investigations
abstract: In a rough year for Pennsylvania lawmakers the Senate majority leader's home and office were searched by federal agents, a western state senator was indicted, and a Scranton lawmaker was convicted of perjury.  Leon Rodriguez, and United States Attorney and Tracy Seyfert also came under investigation by federal law enforcement.

headline: In Mayor's race, a push to sway the swing voter
abstract: Both mayoral candidates for Philadelphia changed their advertising tactics from nice guy approaches to appeals to swing voters that crossed racial and party lines.  Sam Katz is using an endorsement from African American John F. Street, Jr. while John F. Street is showing Mayor Ed Rendell who was just annointed chairman of the Democratic National Committee.  Katz and Street are both trying to to get the endorsement of Henry Nicholas, head of the National Union of Hospital and Health Care Employees, District 1199c.

headline: Veon's claim irks GOP House leaders
abstract: State House Minority leader Mike Veon, Democrat-14, sent out a letter identifying himself as the majority leader of the next century which quickly upset the Republican majority.
