abstract: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt promised to have the controversial Gettysburg Battlefield Tower, a 310-foot metal structure, torn down within two years even if it meant taking the private property by eminent domain.  The tower desecrates the memory of the Americans who died on the battlefield.

headline: Paying for Parity
abstract: No one argues against insurance coverage parity for the mentally ill on the grounds that it isn't needed or isn't appropriate.  The argument is that it would cost too much.  Accomplishing real fairness will require plugging the loophole in the 1996 Mental Health Parity Act that has allowed insurers to impose high co-pays and tightly restrict hospital days or outpatient visits for mental illness.

headline: Penn State Sprawl
abstract: Group of 25 higher education campsuses wrote to the State Education Secretary protesting his approval for Penn State expansion saying that tax payers are paying for Penn State to come into their communities and duplicate their course offerings thus threatening their existence.

headline: Bill aims to reduce highway fatalities, crashes, by 25 percent
abstract: An area teenager in Mechanicsburg thinks that West Virginia should be the example to follow in terms of teen driver licensing requirements where teens there are learning to drive at 15 and getting their licenses at 16.  Pending legislation in the Pennsylvania General Assembly would restrict driving by six months at both the permit and junior levels .

headline: Administration proposing to help communities with 'smart growth'
abstract: The Clinton administration is proposing a $1 billion-a-year program to help develop "smart growth strategies" for communities plagued by dirty air, traffic congestion and suburban sprawl.  The proposals are aimed at addressing a growing concern among many Americans - and one that may have political payoff - that unbridles growth is contributing to a decline in quality of life.

headline: Jet stream blockage equals drought, or does it?
abstract: A storm that recently came through the Pennsylvania region this week knocked down trees and power lines yet the rain it brought did not do much good because it was not a soaking rain.  Bill Drzal, a hydrologist at the National Weather Service's Pittsburg office, said that because things have been so dry what they need to have a helpful impact is a soaking rain.  Otherwise the rain just runs off and is ineffective.  The jet stream being further north that it usually is, is also a factor.

headline: Campaign oversight lax for 2000
abstract: The Federal Election Commissiononer Scott Thomas told the press that he is expecting an unusally high number of complaints. He also said that the agency is dropping  cases due to lack of staff. The FEC caseload rose from 93 in 1998 to 106 in 1999 which is  a 14% increase.

headline: NOTEWORTHY
abstract: U.S. Rep. Jack Murtha, D-Johnstonw, dean of the PA Democratic congressional delegation, has lent his names to two friends seeking statewide office in 2000.  He has agreed to serve as honorary chairman of the campaings of Treasurer candidate Catherine Baker Knoll and U.S. Senate hopeful, Ron Klink, a Democratic congressman from Westmoreland County.

headline: Township park celebrates grand opening
abstract: Shippensburg Township officials along with family and friends celebrated the opening of the new Shippensburg Township Park.  This site was only a dream a few years ago but now is a place where parents can bring children for picnics, playground fun, basketball, and eventually swimming.  Township Supervisor Galen Asper set the celebration in motion.

headline: Payment for body parts is ethically shaky
abstract: Pennsylvania is taking a step in an unknown direction by paying donors' families $300 toward the funeral expenses of each organ donor.  Federal law prohibits the sale of organs and body tissues but the Organ Donor Advisory Committee thinks it can circumvent that prohibition by paying money directly to the organization handling the funeral.

headline: Pennsylvania teacher would have to go back to school to stay in school
abstract: House bill would force PA teachers to get classroom training periodically in order to maintain their certification. Eventhough the Ridge Administration refuses to support the bill Education officials want stricter standards enforced.

headline: Bill would hike speeding fines
abstract: State Representative Steve Samuelson is proposing a plan to hit Interstate 78 speeders in their wallets as he is introducing legislation that would double fines statewide for speeding in 65 miles per hour zones.  The bill would also post more speed limit signs.

headline: Adult movie theater owner fights city urban renewal plan
abstract: George Androtsakis states he supports renewing a seedy section of Pittsburgh's north side, however, the city's attempt to take away his adult movie theater is a violation of his first amendment rights.  He supports his claim saying that politicians fall all over themselves to be the first to say they oppose pornography when before they tried to be the first to oppose communism.

headline: Jet stream blockage equals drought, or does it?
abstract: A storm that recently came through the Pennsylvania region this week knocked down trees and power lines yet the rain it brought did not do much good because it was not a soaking rain.  Bill Drzal, a hydrologist at the National Weather Service's Pittsburg office, said that because things have been so dry what they need to have a helpful impact is a soaking rain.  Otherwise the rain just runs off and is ineffective.  The jet stream being further north that it usually is, is also a factor.

headline: Campaign-cash suit is dismissed by judge
abstract: George Bochetto, a former republican candidate for mayor in 1998, filed a law suit in the Philadelphia Common Pleas Court seeking to strip Democratic candidates John Street and Happy Fernandez of hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign cash.  The law suit was dismissed.  Bochetto charged that Street and Hernandez raised funds to run for the mayor's office while still members of the City Council, City Charter forbids one to run for another office while still in one.  Judge Pamela P. Dembe dismissed the law suit.  The issue came down to whether fund-raising alone could be construed as an admission of candidacy.  The charter the judge said was intended to prevent fund-raising activities from becoming "a hammer which officials use to demand tribute from those who need jobs, services, or the opportunity to contract with the city on a fair basis."

headline: Noteworthy:
abstract: Education Secretary Hickok has been appointed by Governor Ridge to the Team Pennsylvania board of directors.  Team Pennsylvania is a public-private partnership formed to improve the state's economic and community development efforts.  Compiled by Charles Thompson.

headline: Use tax money to pay for repairs at Gettysburg park
abstract: State Representative Harry Readshaw has tried publicly to raise awareness on the issue of allowing Gettysburg National Military Park to deteriorate.  He has raised approximately $100,000 for the cause and asks the state legislature to commit funds to restore the state monuments in Gettysburg.

headline: Pennsylvania seeks ethical line
abstract: Organ donation can be interpreted as a matter of economics where 66,000 people in demand of donations are vying for 5,500 organs in supply.  Organ donation was kept out of the marketplace but now the state department of health is beginning a three-year program to pay donors' families $300  toward funeral costs.  State officials insist they are not in the organ buying business.

headline: Pennsylvania to hold 13th annual Financial Aid hotline
abstract: State Representative McGill announced that the PA Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators would hold its 13th Financial Aid hotline during the week of June 25th.

headline: Brooken's next hurdle: To regain union confidence
abstract: Transport Union Workers President Steve Brooken lead a 40-day strike and won reelection now must work to restore his credibility because his union is divided over whether he can lead it.  Some employees of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Association fear another strike when their current contract expires in 2001.

headline: Agency to monitor 12 tax-break zones
abstract: The Allegheny Institute for Public Policy will monitor and analyze the progress of Governor Tom Ridge's Keystone Opportunity Zone program.  The Institute, a nonpartisan conservative think-tank in Pittsburgh, was supportive of the program.

headline: Judge clarifies ruling;horsemen must pay PN
abstract: Dauphin County Court Judge Joseph Kleinfelter clarified his ruling that in the dispute between Penn National Race Course and Horsemen's Association, Horsemen's Association has to pay PN $600000 as horse boarding fees to receive 60 day extension on an eviction notice.

headline: CAMPAIGNING TO PUT EXPENSES ONLINE
abstract: The Ridge administration wants the state to spend $398,000 to make campaing expense reports for legislative candidates more accessible by putting them on the Internet.  State Representative Greg Vitalie (D-Delaware) who has pushed for such a measure said he was encouraged by such a request.  Currently campaign expense reports for condidates for governor and lieutenant governor are posted on the Internet and previous efforts to do so for Legislative candidates has been resisted by the General Assembly.

headline: Nuts or Guts?
abstract: Opinion Article discussing presidential candidate John McCain ability after being tortured in a Vietcong prison camp for five and a half years.  Article questions whether he can be an effective candidate despite what had happened to him during the war.  McCain replies with jokes and states any criticism like this is ludicrous and just revenge tactics for doing well in the polls in New Hampshire.  Some criticisms came from the George Bush campaign.

headline: Wills House could still be purchased, congressman says
abstract: Regardless of a pending park management plan the Wills House in downtown Gettysburg could be included in the battlefield boundaries, according to Ron Klink, Democrat-Westermoreland County.  Klink's attempts to block National Park Service plans to build a new visitor center has not effect on legislation to annex the Wills House into park boundaries.

headline: Penny-wise, pound-foolish on mental care Pa. drops the ball on mental health funding
abstract: An article criticizing the amount of money spent on mental health and retardation services in Pennsylvania illustrated that 90 percent of funding at the state level is from Harrisburg.  The state fails to provide adequate funding to meet the growing demand for the kind of services that keep people out of the hospitals.  The state's Department of Public Welfare has failed to provide the county's mental health and retardation services with fair funding.

headline: Pennsylvania's 1800s vouchers want of folly of revisiting  them
abstract: The writer who is a professor at Lehigh University writes that the current voucher plan is similar to the ones that PA tried to adopt in the 1800s. The write says that the current voucher system reinvents the pauper school system and there would be no accountability from public schools.

headline: Car seats protect tots from injury
abstract: All children should be restrained at all times in a vehicle.  Each year, approximately 1,800 children ages 14 and under are killed in motor vehicles and more than 280,000 are injured.  Car safety seats, when correctly installed and used, are very effective in saving children's lives.  The Pennsylvania Safety Traffic Injury Prevention Project provides specific information on safety belts.

headline: Apartments felled to make way for stadium
abstract: After $228 million was secured to build a riverside ballpark for the Pittsburgh Pirates, the biggest obstacle to construction was a six-story building where 100 older people lived.  The residents will be moved to nearby apartments and Three Rivers Plaza was felled with dynamite in 8 seconds.

headline: Lawmakers bubbly over champagne?
abstract: A New Year's Eve party without champagne just cannot be done when one of the sponsors of the event is the Official Champagne of the Millennium.  Millennium Philadelphia was in danger due to the state's liquor control laws because under the code only formally licensed retailers can sell champagne by the glass and even then cannot sell after 2 a.m.

headline: Campaigns, money and reforms
abstract: Presidential candidates are running for election earlier than they ever have before and candidates who wish they could run based on eligibility cannot due to financial constraints.  Article discusses the complexity and extent a person would have to go to raise the financing necessary to compete in a current presidential election.  It goes on to discuss ways to lessen spending.

headline: Nutter back John White
abstract: City Councilman Michael Nutter, who represents the Fouth Distric and serves as Democratic leader of the 52nd Ward, yesterday endorsed former Philadelphia housing chief John White Jr. for Mayor.  White is one of three black mayoral candidates running in the May 18 Democratic primary.  In most polls White is behind John Street.

headline: Abolish real estate taxes, Dawida says
abstract: Fed up with Allegheny County's beleaguered property assessment system, Commissioner Mike Dawida will present proposals to abolish real estate taxes altogether and to get rid of the turmoil-plagued assessment board.  Dawida also plan to offer legislation to abolish the assessment board, which has been plagued by infighting the past year.

headline: Petition targets staffing concerns at nursing homes
abstract: Joan Chiampi, a concerned resident of Kingston, is asking state legislatures to review state guidelines as they apply to Pennsylvania's nursing homes.  She is particularly concerned about nursing home care in regards to patients with Alzheimer's Disease, a debilitating affliction characterized by memory loss, confusion and disorientation.

headline: Philadelphia schools awarded $3.5 million for improvements
abstract: Certain Philadelphia schools who have shown improvement on standardized test scores will receive about $3.5 million in reward money from the state.  This is proportionally a greater share than the state's public school population as Philadelphia has 212,000 students representing roughly 11.7% of Pennsylvania's public school students.

headline: Cell-phone legislation pushes some buttons
abstract: Senator Joe Conti, Republican-Bucks, has proposed legislation that would fine drivers $250 and assess them three points against their driving record for using a wireless phone when driving.  Though he already introduced the bill earlier this year, focus on the legislation has been heightened by the death of a 2-year-old girl who was killed in an automobile accident by a man who was dialing a cell phone while driving through an intersection.

headline: Arena glorious steppingstone to our dreams
abstract: State Representative Kevin Blaum, Democrat-Wilkes-Barre, chairman of the Luzerne County Convention Center Authority, makes his remarks in regards to the grand opening of the new facility in Wilkes-Barre Township.  The people on the Luzerne County Convention Center Authority will always have ultimate responsibility for the operation of the convention center.

headline: Lawmakers mull service report cards
abstract: Current Senate bills for consideration would require state agencies to issue report cards on public schools, nursing homes and health maintenance organizations.  The argument is that if the public is better informed about the quality of education at their local school, the services provided to nursing home residents or the health care provided, they will make better decision as consumers.

headline: Candidates just toddling on campaign finance reform
abstract: All Democrats vying the to opppose the U.S. Senator Santorum say that the campaign fund raising system is broke. Candidates also say that Bush and Ridge also pursue policies that reward industries and wealthy induviduals.

headline: Official: Weinberg campaign 'racist'
abstract: State representative W. Curtis Thomas is speaking out against the negative campaigning by the Marty Weinberg campaign saying that it is "negative, racist, and divisive campaigning" through television advertising and special mailing.  Weinberg's ads were against John Street and insinuated that police lives would be in jeopardy should a particular African American mayoral candidate be elected.

headline: Airport tax giveback financing explored
abstract: Allegheny County is looking at creating a large tax increment financing a district near Pittsburgh International Airport to raise much of the $90 million in local funding it believes is needed to build a $604.5 million US Airways maintenance complex.  County Economic Development Director Mulugetta Birru said yesterday that the district would build a planned business park, cargo center, and proposed office complex.

headline: Pharmacies Say Rates Paid by Rite Aid Unit Are Doing Them In
abstract: Local pharmacies in the Philadelphia area are having trouble with the low reimbursement rate from Medicaid for prescriptions in the city.  The rates are so low that independent drugstores have failed or sold out in the past two years, and many that remain simply refuse to fill some or all Medicaid prescriptions.

headline: PIAA aide's copmments are amusing
abstract: The PA Interscholastic Atheletic Association's executive director told the Altoona Mirror that she was impressed with the field condition of the Hershey Park Stadium. In contrary to her statement other soccer coaches said that the field was in bad shape especially after the november 20 match.

headline: City losing old trolleys to Scranton museum
abstract: Three of Philadelphia's old trolley cars will be the first of 23 to come from Philadelphia, Bucks County, and New Jersey to be taken to Scranton and placed in a museum.  The museum is scheduled to open this summer.

headline: Argall to apear on PCN
abstract: State Representative David G. Argall, Republican-124, who will appear on Pennsylvania's Cable Network, will join Representative Tom Tangretti, Democrat-57, to discuss the Historic Home and Neighborhood legislation they sponsored to preserve Pennsylvania's neighborhoods through tax incentives for the rehabilitation of historic homes.  The legislation earned unanimous support from the House Finance committee.  The bill offers tax incentives that will make th ehome more affordable and the community and the state will benefit from the increased value of the properties once they rehabilitate.

headline: Lawmakers try to stop legislation restricting wine sales
abstract: George Radovich, a winemaker and congressman, is trying to persuade his colleagues to defeat legislation that would limit mail-order and Internet sales of alcohol.  The Senator, however, passed the juvenile crime bill which touted curbing alcohol sales to minors and also works against mail-order and internet sales of alcohol.

headline: Candidates seek key to 'gold mine' of youth
abstract: As the 2000 presidential race intensifies the republican and democratic candidates are reaching out the young voters and on college campuses.  There were 25 million eligible voters aged 18 to 24 according to the U.S. Census bureau estimates.

headline: Officials question legislator's pay
abstract: Inquiries into the business dealings of Senate Majority Leader Joseph Loeper by the Federal Bureau of Investigation have caused more to pay attention to what the laws are.  Currently they state that a lawmaker only need to disclose who the money is from and not how much or why it was given.  Legislators feel this is inadequate but think the details of their donor's sources should be private.  Loeper's dealings with a company called the Municipal Tax Bureau have been scrutinized by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.  According to the State Ethics Board lawmakers must disclose the source of any income of $1,300 or more; the holders of any debt of $6,500 or more; the source of any gifts exceeding $250; and any gifts of lodging, transportation or hospitality exceeding $650.

headline: Amusement tax cheered, feared
abstract: The Wilkes-Barre Township Council has voted to impose a 5% amusement tax aimed primarily at the fledgling Luzerne County Arena but designed to help repay $5.2 million the board owes for sewer projects.  The vote drew applause from the residents in attendance.

headline: Prognosis Better For Medicare; Social Security
abstract: The Clinton administration released a financial report that shows Medicare resting on far more solid fiscal ground than previously expected.  This forecast could undermine the changes that Congress will reform either of the nation's main retirement programs.  The fund that pays hospital bills is expected to last for 16 more years, seven years longer than predicted just a year ago.

headline: PIAA in step with most Senate recommendations
abstract: The Pennsylvania Interscholastic Association is poised to heed the advice of the state Senate. Out of the 18 recommendations put forth only one was rejected. The lone one rejected was to create a standing board of appeald for eligibility cases.

headline: Conti: Disconnect drivers
abstract: Senator Joe Conti, Republican-Bucks, would like to see a $250 fine and three license points levied against motorists who use cell phones while driving.  The move was prompted by the death of a 2-year-old Upper Bucks girl.

headline: Argall's right, will eventually prevail
abstract: Regardless of how tough state representative David G. Argall's Downtown Location law is or isn't, the state General Services Department could no doubt circumvent it if it were determined to do so.  If the bill is endorsed by the House Urban Affairs Committee, passed by the General Assembly and signed by Governor Tom Ridge, the law, will advise General Services to site state facilities in a way that will help downtown-and community-renewal efforts.

headline: Legalized gaming measure not a dead issue
abstract: The gaming issue was not killed despite the headlines and the analysis by the pundits.The plan to legalize gambling is a pinch bill which would squeeze every special interest dollar into the Democratic and Republican campaign without delivering anything.

headline: CANDIDATES' SPENDING MATCHED BY INTEREST GROUPS, POLITICAL PARTIES
abstract: A study of 16 of the most competitive congressional races last fall found political parties and outside interest groups spend almost as much as the candidate did.  The study funded by the Pew Charitable Trusts found that parties and interest groups spent at least $67 million dollars and the 32 major party candidates in the 16 races spent $70 million dollars.

headline: One Challenge for Bush: Remaking Image of Divided GOP
abstract: George Bush's aides have prepared a fresh stump speech that they hope will show his "compassionate conservative" side.  This change will require more to bring a divided republican party together.  The hope is that Bush's candidacy will reshape and unite the party.

headline: BCC hold line on mileage
abstract: Bradford County Commissioners voted unanimously to maintain the property tax at 5.9 mills for 2000 at their meeting in the Bradford County Courthouse.  Commissioner Tina Picket explained that through careful spending and cooperation they were able to avoid an increase.

headline: Program to win drinking wins grant
abstract: The Late Night Penn State grant has been a leader in the alcohol abuse program and has won a $75000 grant to study and research the effect of binge drinking.

headline: PIAA leadership continues  to fumble the ball
abstract: The Senate committee which includes Senator Robbins want the PA Interscholastic Atheletic Associationto demonstrate why PIAA should be allowed to operate as an independent organization. The directors of PIAA was its worst enemy..

headline: County yields airport control
abstract: Two Allegheny County Commissioners gave final clearance yesterday to their plan to turn over the county's control of two airports to a quasi-autonomous authority.  Pittsburgh International Airport and Allegheny County Airport had both of their operations control switched over to the Allegheny County Airport Authority to operate.

headline: As State ponders growth issue, some communities act on their own
abstract: In Lancaster, Pennsylvania residents piled into the Manheim Township municipal building with checks to buy 16.4 acres of land to prevent a developer from putting up high density townhomes.  In 30 days, the neighborhood and the township teamed up to raise $325,000 needed to buy the property.  Thanks to the resident's initiative the township is now taking the steps to acquire the land and add it to an adjacent park.  Manheim township is not alone in this endeavor.  Several townships across Pennsylvania are doing this to stop "suburban sprawl."

headline: Legislation would curb telemarketing
abstract: The Pennsylvania House Consumer Affairs Committee held a public hearing recently on legislation, sponsored by state Representative Lynn B. Herman, Republican-77, that would curb calls by telemarketers.  The legislation would strengthen the 1996 act Pennsylvania already has regulating telemarketers.

headline: Candidates still awaiting decision from some bigs
abstract: Happy Fernandez, who finished fourth in the Democratic primary with about 6 percet of the vote for the Philadelphia mayoral race said she is being pulled by both John Street and Sam Katz to give them her endorsement.  The Fraternal Order of Police said they will not endorse either candidate.  The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers will not endorse either candidate as well.  City Councilman Michael Nutter endorsed John White over Street.  District Attorney Lynne Abraham said she will hold off on endorsing either candidate.  City Councilwoman Marian Tasco chose John White over Street.

headline: Out-of-Town contributions play key role in Philly mayoral race
abstract: People living just outside of Philadelphia are becoming a force in the upcoming November election for Philadelphia's mayor as they are filling the war chests of the six candiates.  About 59 percent of the campaign funds for all six candidates has been funded by people living as out-of-towners.

headline: Benefits of Large Multi-Municipal Bond to Be Studied
abstract: Delta Development Group, a Camp Hill consulting firm, approached the Clinton County Economic Partnership about the possibility of a pooled bond financing program for Clinton County with the idea that larger bond issues receive better interest rates.  Delta did a similar study and program in Greene County, securing significant funding for various projects.

headline: Providers leaving Aetna, voicing dissatisfaction
abstract: Hospitals and doctors around the country have walked away from millions in patient revenues from Aetna United States Healthcare in a series of unusually public rifts.  The issue is what hospitals and doctors allege are unacceptable reimbursement rates, delays and denials of payment, and a mandate that they participate in all Aetna plans.

headline: PIAA Schools Reject Senate Reforms
abstract: The member schools of the Pennsylvania InterScholastic Atheletic Association reject the so called restitution rule put forth by the Senate. The rule requires a number of schools that engage in or join unsuccessful litigation against PIAA to pay the legal fees incurred by the PIAA in defending the action.

headline: Coy proposes making ATV helmets mandatory
abstract: Representative Jeffrey W. Coy, Democrat-Shippensburg, announced he will introduce legislation that would require mandatory helmet use for all terrain vehicle operators and passengers.  Operators must only wear helmets when on a road open to vehicular, all terrain vehicle, or snowmobile traffic.

headline: Authority close to finalizing leases for new stadiums
abstract: The Public Auditorium Authority is nearing completion of leases with the Pirates and Steelers for the teams' new stadiums.  The agreements could be ready for approval at the authority's October 25 meeting, said authority spokesman Greg Yesko.

headline: Lemieux asks for another extension of sale deadline
abstract: Marion Lemieux's attorneys have asked the judge for a third delay in the closing of the sale of the Pittsburgh Penguins.  Lemieux needed more time to finalize settlement agreements with investors.

headline: Candidates take to Web
abstract: The internet became a campaign tool when Bob Dole announced his website at the end of a debate with Bill Clinton in 1996.  Mike Cornfield of George Washington University said of 1998 that 89 percent of all candidates running for governor or the U.S. senate nationwide has Web sites.

headline: Pa. attorney general gives lawmaker an ultimatum
abstract: Pennsylvania House Republicans appear to be headed for a showdown with the state Attorney General because Frank Serafini has refused to give up his seat as a state Representative.  Attorney General Mike Fisher gave Serafini until noon Monday to resign to avoid a Constitutional crisis or he would go to court to remove him.

headline: Council moves ahead with plan for raises in pay
abstract: Harrisburg City Council is moving ahead to give its members raises of $5,000 effective in 2002, following a brief public hearing that drew no members of the public.  The council will vote on increasing member's salaries from $10,000 to $15,000 and would make Harrisburg City Council the third highest paid body in the state.

headline: PSGHS to announce layoffs
abstract: Penn State Geisinger Health System expects to publicly announce a first round of layoffs in mid-November after employees are informed of them.  Departmental review teams have recommended cost-saving moves to improve the system and save $35 million.

headline: PIAA will not delay start of season
abstract: Despite dry, hard athletic field conditions, the Pennsylvania Interscholastic Athletic Association has no current plan to delay the start of the fall athletic season, said assitant executive director Melissa Nash.  The organization did ask school officials to give their schools permission to water their fields to prevent injuries that could be caused by drought conditions.  Susan Rickens, of the state Department of Environmental protection, said that state officials not bound by regulations that would prevent lawn watering exemption for school districts and athletic fields.

headline: Cranmer confident airport will land needed funding
abstract: The federal government should be able to provide about $100 million to help finance a new US Airways maintenance and training center at the Pittsburgh International Airport.  Bob Cranmer, Allegheny County Commissioner, led a delegation of county officials and local labor leaders to Washington, D.C. to meet with the state's congressional delegation and United States Labor Department representatives.

headline: Bidding critics don’t buy explanation
abstract: The Ridge administration says language regulating bidding on new stadiums, approved by the Legislature as part of the Capital Budget bill in June, simply reiterates language on state books since 1993.  State Senator Leonard Bodac, Democrat-Lawrenceville, and several other Pittsburgh area legislators are not buy it and say they will visit the bidding issue when the Legislature returns in September.

headline: Lemieux hits snag with SMG on Pens deal
abstract: The Penguins are set to run out of operating money and Mario Lemieux's ownership has not yet finalized a deal with SMG, the civic arena landlord.  With a three-pronged agreement, of which the first two tenets were agreed to, the third part has agreed to invest $5 million in Lemieux's ownership with provisions that would give SMG a seat on the team's board of directors and allow the firm to withdraw its money or be bought out in three years.

headline: Capital Hill Bordello
abstract: Article that discusses prostitution on television, its role in politics, and comparisons of prostitution to behaviors of legsilators in Congress.  Mentions Senator John McCain of Arizona trying to reform campaign financing who is also trying to run for the republican national primary.

headline: Pa. eyes Saidel's legal bills
abstract: City Controller Jonathan Saidel may be in politcal trouble again as his campaign finance reports show his election fund paid $47,908 in legal bills for Diana Roca (Saidel's ex-lover and aide).  An aide to state attorney general Mike Fisher, who is prosecuting Roca, said their office is already making plans to look into the new expenditures.  The issue is whether campaign funds can be used to pay legal fees when state election law states that campaign funds can only be spent on "influencing the outcome of an election" or on staff and vendors.  The attorney for Saidel's campaign committee, Gregory Harvey who is an election law expert, said the federal courts have permitted campaign money to pay for alleged crimes and that there was no effort to conceal these funds in this matter.

headline: Council clears raft of bills, bids colleague adieu
abstract: Philadelphia City Council acted in harmony for four years to approve city budgets, spur economic development with tax breaks, and regulate quality of life on city streets by passing 86 bills.  Council members renewed the cable-TV franchise for Wade Cablevision, authorized a health-care advocacy office, and increased tax abatements for new residential construction.

headline: PSU, Geisinger split
abstract: Citing a clash of cultures between the two institutions, the 18 members of the board of directors voted unanimously to dissolve the 1997 merger of Hershey Medical Center and Geisinger Health System.  The motion to dissolve came from Edward Junker III, president of Penn State's board of trustees.

headline: Piccola defends his record on education
abstract: Senator Piccola says that the school choice program is an opportunity for every child in PA and says this could be one of the best means to improve the education in PA.

headline: Cross County Metro gets aid from state
abstract: Pennsylvania's capital budget includes a $1.67 million allocation for engineering, infrastructure and vehicles for the proposed 53-mile commuter rail route that would link Bucks, Montgomery and Chester counties.  State Senator Stewart Greenleaf, Republican-12th District, announced that the project is now being included in other state capitol projects.

headline: Bill gives hope to York's dreams
abstract: Although York was not directly involved with the major initiative to fund the four professional sports teams in the state it was relieve, however, when the state did vote to raise the debt ceiling.  York hopes to bring a minor league baseball team to its city and with the lift in the debt ceiling several projects across the state, like York's effort to bring baseball to its city, were cleared.

headline: Lynch Praises Ridge Plan To Cut Taxes For Families
abstract: State Representative Lynch (R) said that the 1999-2000 state budget provides tax cuts for working families and small businesses. The $ 18.6 billion state budget increased spending by less than 3% and cuts taxes by $ 273 million especially geared towards working and low income families.

headline: Capitol Ideas
abstract: Reprensentative T.J. Rooney, Democrat-Northampton/Lehigh, was cited for ghost voting which is when members leave the chamber to use the restroom or meet with constituents and ask colleagues to press their electronic voting buttons for them.  Rooney explains that he and four other colleagues were at a news conference on gun control across the capital complex while there was a vote taking place on drought assistance to farmers.  Rooney admitted he made a technical violation of House rules.  Critics also cite that 'ghost voting' skews the records of legislatorsby allowing others to vote for them on positions for which they never actually took a stance.

headline: Pa. House strong contender for most ethically bankrupt body
abstract: An editorial citing that the Pennsylvania House Republicans would qualify in the Guiness Book of World Records as the most morally and ethically bankrupt legislative body there is.  One of them, Frank Serafini, has been convicted of perjury by a federal jury.  All Republican representatives refused to remove him.  Allowing Serafini to make an appeal to the House members until his appeals in Court are exhausted goes against the letter and spirit of the constitution.  The only reason Republican representatives did this was to hold on to their slim 103-100 majority.  Ethics and morality be damned.

headline: Counties need to comply with Clean and Green
abstract: Discusses the potentiality of corporations or individuals having to pay higher taxes yet not having to pay them on time.  Representative Raymond Bunt, Jr., Republican - Bradford, says that counties are doing just that.  They are being assessed a higher tax rate yet, under the Clean and Green Act, they are able to hold off on paying the tax until several years later.  Discusses property like housing developments and shopping centers being taxed at their potential rather than their performance.  Counties by contrast are taxing farmers at their potential when they should be taxed at their performance.  The Clean and Green act is allowing counties to tax farmer through loopholes in the system to raiser greater fees.

headline: Public offers ways to slice tobacco pie
abstract: Local hospitals in Pennsylvania are hoping that the billions coming to the state will help them recover the costs they spent on treating people without health care insurance.  Citizens voiced their opinion stating that the money should be spent on everything from training people to work in nursing homes to preventing young men from chewing smokeless tobacco.

headline: Pledge, sign or nothing
abstract: A state lawmaker who feels classrooms are lacking patriotism has introduced a bill that would require school to offer students an opportunity to recite the Pledge of Allegiance or sing the National Anthem at the start of each school day.  State Representative Allan Egolf, Republican-Perry, introduced his measure to coincide with Flag Day and Flag week which would not mandate participation though schools would have to offer it.

headline: Dent asks limit on teens in car
abstract: Senator Charlie Dent, Republican-Lehigh, has introduced a bill to toughen a law waiting to take effect in which drivers under 18 would be prohibited from having more than two passengers under 21 in their vehicle unless an adult is present.  Dent's rationale is that a car crowded with teenagers poses a safety risk.

headline: Bill would funnel state funding
abstract: The bill providing $320 million for baseball and football stadiums in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia also included $330 million for redevelopment assistance projects across the state.  Governor Ridge pushed for the measure and signed it into law February 9.

headline: Marino won't block Mario
abstract: Penguins co-owner Roger Marino's attorney stated that he is willing to let go of the team if Mario Lemieux has a plan to buy the franchise out of bankruptcy.  National Hockey League Commissioner Gary Bettman will meet with potential Penguins investors and Lemieux is the only one expected to have a plan.

headline: Cappabianca cites constitution in fight to save Serafini's job
abstract: State Representatve Italo Cappabianca has asked the speaker of the house to launch a legal counter offensive to state Attorney General Mike Fisher who is trying to oust Frank Serafini.  Cappabianca is a Scranton area republican as Serafini is and also Serafini's best friend.  Serafini has been in the public eye since his federal conviction in November for contributions connected to the 1996 presidential campaign of Bob Dole.  Fisher gave Serafini a deadline to get out of office or face legal action.

headline: Pa. senator's opinions go against the flow of most of their colleagues
abstract: 96-year old Strom Thurmond of South Carolina expressed rejection to having Monica Lewinsky testify before the Senate in the impeachment trial of President Clinton.  Thurmond's opinion prevailed with a 70-30 vote in favor of ending the impeachment trial of a popular President.  His opinion; however, was different from that of Pennsylvania Sentors.  Rick Santorum and Arlen Specter stuck to their views that a full impeachment trial was a fair impeachment trial and voted to have Lewinsky appear before the Senate.

headline: County challenges home's bid for tax exemption
abstract: Adam county commissioners say that law through which Brethren Home Community is attempting to acquire property tax exemptions is unconstituional. How ever, state senators Nickol and Maitland argue that the law is constituional.

headline: Quick action expected on HMO law
abstract: The General Assembly is expected to act quickly on legislation requiring health maintenance organization "report cards" which is a follow up from the prior session's Patient's Rights Act.  House Insurance Committee Chair, Nick Miccozie, Republican of Delaware, has begun hearings on the measure.

headline: Prime time for after-school care
abstract: About 10,000 children attend 650 supervised after-school programs in the city, according to Philadelphia Citizens for Children and Youth.  This year, for the first time after-school programs have become an important issue for Democratic Candidates John Street and Happy Fernandez, urging large increases in city expenditures.

headline: Developers make proposal at state commission hearing
abstract: Developer Hugh McHugh and architect Steve Victor made a proposal to the state Department of Transportation Commission in hopes of straightening the S-curve on Noblestown road in Collier Township.  Victor told the commission that straightening the road would make for a smoother flow of traffic.

headline: Bill would stem suburban sprawl
abstract: Legislation that would stem sprawl was voted our of the Senate Local Government Committee yesterday.  The bill, sponsored by Senator James Girlish, Republican-Chester, would encourage planning and require municipalities to provide for every land use.  It also would look at land planning and zoning among local municipalities, counties and the state.

headline: Nabisco plant offer expected within a week
abstract: The city of Pittsburgh, Allegheny County and the Steel Valley Authority will offer to buy the Nabisco Holdings Corp. The bid will be backed by $ 3 million from the city and the council and will have additional investments from the banking companies.

headline: Caring Closer to Home
abstract: Republicans are going to learn how to talk to Americans someday and sweep the competition, but, until they do Democrats who speak of concern for the problems of average people and seem to offer the soft balm of caring are leading.  Republicans balk at the therapeutic approach to politics and lament the loss of frontier fortitude in the citizenry.  Just notice how many Republican's distanced themselves from Governor George Bush's "compassionate conservatism."

headline: PAC IT IN
abstract: In recent elections, a new type of ideology-based politcal action committee has become influential known as the leadership committee.  It was first used by House Speaker Newt Gingrich who used the committees to help Republican party candidates win the majority in 1994.  In York County, donor by donor favored ideological political action committees for conservative causes but dollar for dollar, a Democratic leadership committee won York County's largest individual contribution in 1997-98.

headline: County wants role in airport growth
abstract: Economic Development Director Mulugetta Birru is upset over a plan that he says could restrict or eliminate his agency's role in developing property near Pittsburgh International Airport.  The proposed transfer of authority gives his agency no stated role in developing county-owned land near the airport.

headline: Report: Pa. should alter long-term care rules
abstract: The Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Council on Long-Term Care report says that the state should define and regulate assisted living facilities-residences that offer fewer services than nursing homes-and change state law to allow more Medicaid dollars to pay for support services there and at home.  The Council's Executive Director Dale Laninga says that they are looking for a wider array of options and some that offer more consumer choice.

headline: Professors union closer to striking
abstract: The faculty union for the PA's stated owned universities have come close to a strike.The union's negotiating team recommended to the union's executive leadership that the union go on strike.

headline: Drinker asked to consider consequences
abstract: State Senator  Helfrick sponsor of the Driving Under Influence law in PA appeals to the citizens on the havoc drunken driving can cause.

headline: Bipartisan Bills targeting suburban sprawl
abstract: Local municipalities would have more say in controlling development and curtaling suburban sprawl under a package of bills introduced by a bipartisan group of lawmakers.  State Representative David Steil, Republican-Bucks, says the trio of bills he has drafted promote "smart growth" and avoid one-size-fits-all solution to sprawl.  The objective is provide municipalities, as well as builders and developers, with a variety of options so they can decide what works best for them, Steil says.

headline: New Jersey Court Approves Rate Cut On Auto Insurance
abstract: The New Jersey State Supreme Court approved an across-the-board rate cut that regulators say will save drivers at least 13% on their annual auto-insurance costs.  Auto-insurance rates in New Jersey surpass those of any other state in the country.

headline: Case before high court may set redistricting rules
abstract: The United States Supreme court may be providing new guidelines for policing the map-making efforts of the state and local lawmakers.  Arguments were heard in a North Carolina case where the justices wrestled with the key issue: How much evidence is needed to conclude that an election district is the product of unlawful gerrymandering because racial considerations played too large a role.

headline: Parties talk compromise, but prospects seem remote
abstract: Some bipartisan agreement is apparent at the end of the impeachment trial of President Clinton but the chance of agreement between both parties on major issues seems more remote.  Republicans are eager to move on issues like tax cuts, Social Security, defense and education to try and erase the notion that all they have been concerned over is Clinton's impeachment.  Clinton himself may also want to move on those issues to save what he can of his presidency with less than two years left.

headline: CV panel says "no" to state tax-reform law
abstract: Act 50 would mean lower taxes for some residents including farmers and retired homeowners, but it would mean higher taxes for about an equal number of others including homeowners with moderate incomes and renters.  The Act allows districts to enact a new tax of 1.5% on residents' earned incomes in exchange for eliminating so called nuisance taxes and reducing property taxes.

headline: Require retractable syringes
abstract: Some medical changes that are simple to see the benefits should be made immediately.  Lynda Arnold has asked state legislators to require hospitals to use retractable syringes to avoid people being accidentally stuck with syringes that have the AIDS virus.

headline: Program expansion sought by educator
abstract: The State System Chancellor McCormick would like to see the academic pasport go which allows students to transfer from community colleges to state owned universities without losing credits. He wants this transfer to be expanded to state related universities like Penn State, Pitt and Temple. He called this the Pennsylvania Passport program

headline: Driver license suspension should be publicized
abstract: Legislative correction needed to  tighten laws on suspended license drivers, who drive all the same. Suspended drivers should be publicized to make the community more aware. Motor vehicles kill around 40,000 people and injure millions when some one disregards traffic rules.

headline: Borough wins opportunity zoning
abstract: Downingtown was awarded with one of the 12 new Keystone Opportunity Zones where $750,000 in state and local taxes will be forgiven to stimulate job creation and community renewal.  With the designation and the cooperation of taxing agencies, all state and local taxes are eliminated for 12 years.

headline: New law facilitates e-commerce in state
abstract: The House and the Senate unanimously passed a bill which supports e-coomerce and electronic signatures in business contracts in PA. The bill awaits Governor Ridge's approval.

headline: Cash in Hand, Forbes Reaches to Right
abstract: Steve Forbes, presidential candidate seeking republican nomination in 2000, has asked the former chairman of the Iowa republican party, Steve Grubbs, to recruit him to his campaign.  Forbes' effort to recruit him was part of a larger strategy to address the central weakness of his failed 1996 campaign bid for the republican presidential nomination.  Then, Forbes spent $37 million of his own money on a media campaign that faded because he had no organization on the ground and he alienated supporters of the Christian right.

headline: Party like aura pervades legislators' swearing-in
abstract: 18 new members joined the state Senate and House as Pennsylvania's General Assembly opened its 183rd session.  Stephen J. McEwen Junior, president judge of the state superior court judge gave the oaths of office while 202 members were sworn into office.

headline: Delay in mailing form costs taxpayers $5,000
abstract: Norristown County Commissioners changed their minds and decided to go ahead and send out 220,000 forms to area residents of which they were hoping to save $75,000. Because they waited it will cost one cent per stamp more totaling $80,000.  The form is needed to sign up for the potential tax reduction under the Homestead Act.

headline: Ridge nominates new Health secretary
abstract: Robert S. Zimmerman, a 28-year state employee, has been nominated by Governor Ridge to run the state health department which provides medical assistance payments to more than one million Pennsylvania residents.  Currently Zimmerman serves as deputy secretary for medical assistance programs in the Department of Public Welfare and must be confirmed by the state Senate prior to taking office.

headline: Proposed bill on guns in schools is demagogic
abstract: Representative Alan Butkovitz is introducing a bill into the state legislature that would make school administrators liable for damages caused by students caught with a weapon twice in a year.  His idea is criticized as one that would not prevent the violence endemic in some neighborhoods from overflowing in public schools.  Butkovitz's idea would just make school officials' jobs even more tenuous.

headline: E-Zpass to be installed on Pennsylvania Turnpike
abstract: Pennsylvania's Turnpike Commission will start phasing in the E-Zpass system next fall on sections connecting the Lehigh Valley and Mid-County interchanges and from Harrisburg to the Delaware River Bridge.  Spokeswoman Kathy Liebler said that there will be 17 interchanges that will represent about 64% of all customers.

headline: Budget supported by Senate slates $88.6 million for Berks.
abstract: State Senate passes $ 88.6 million budget bill for Berks County projects. State Sen O'Pake says its upto the county to decide on key project to receive this funding.

headline: No case for merger
abstract: The only benefit for ratepayers to the proposed merger between the Pennsylvania Electric Company and Unicom Corporation is alleged better service.  Without guaranteed benefits for electricity customers, the two energy companies should be stopped.

headline: Census 2000 a high-stakes question for Western Pa.
abstract: Government worker Zilla Thompson recalls that when collecting census data residents in Greene and Fayette counties in April of 1990 that she was confronted by people asking point blank why she wanted their names, ages, and relationships and races.  Thompson says they were not hostile yet leery of giving information.  This time, in 2000, Thompson says things will be different.  She will inform people and groups that the census is about counting people and that for people who want to stay hidden the information is not shared with another agency.

headline: Pay raise for state legislators explained
abstract: Matthew Seagrist is attempting to clarify that the rumored pay raise for the Governor and his cabinet is not true.  What was within a bill in question was a cost of living adjustment each year for lawmakers.  The percentage of change was based on state department of labor's consumer index statistics.

headline: Democrats offer plan to lower property tax
abstract: Democratic State Representatives Rich Grucela, Democratic-Northampton, and T.J. Rooney, 133rd District, have a plan to reduce school property tax by 50% over the next five years.  Democrats across the state are hearing similar concerns yet Republicans control both houses in the legislature.

headline: Ridge signs bill requiring public hearings before closing centers
abstract: Governor Ridge signed a law requiring that state welfare officials meet with the public when they make decisions to close or downsize institutions for the mentally disabled.  Ridge vetoed this legislation the first time it landed his desk last December yet this time Ridge agreed to a compromise worked out with Representative Fairchild, a Republican of Union.

headline: Proposed Pocono arts center would be waste of state funds.
abstract: Governor Ridge may flush $ 17.5 million from the 1999-2000 capital budget in a misguided effort to help the performing arts center in Pike County.

headline: E-ZPass weekday: Confusion and lines
abstract: E-ZPass is getting off to a rough start after mailing out approximately 20,000 electronic toll passes as commuters heading into Philadelphia sat on the Delaware River Bridges due to incorrect pass readings, traffic snarls and confusion. Delaware River Port Authority spokesperson Joseph Diemer said they had congestion on all four bridges but when a new system is tried delays are expected.

headline: Budget, stadium plans on deck
abstract: The Pennsylvania House is expected to approve a plan to provide $320 million to finance new stadiums in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh.  Owners of the professional sports teams would not have to repay public funding under the plan announced yesterday but would need to collect an equal amount in state taxes during the next 30 years.

headline: No Dice
abstract: Majority of the State Senators killed the gambling referendum bill to PA's benefit. The Senators feel that gambling takes in more from the community rather than giving back.

headline: Census Pact May Be Reached in Spring, But New Partisan Fights Loom Later
abstract: Republicans will not extend funding for fiscal year 1999 past June 15 to fund the Commerce Department, which contains the census bureau, who wants to use statistical sampling to help count the hardest-to-find Americans which is a something that most generally believe will boost population figures in areas that tend to vote Democratic.  The Census Bureau's budget is tied to the State and Justice departments and Republicans say they cannot take shutting down those agencies during the Kosovo conflict.  The Census will then likely be funded until September.

headline: Payback time ?
abstract: Lehigh Valley Democrats rejoice when Philadelphia Mayor Rendell chairman of the Democratic Nartional Committee.

headline: Democrats still pushing to cut property taxes
abstract: Pennsylvania Democrats are still pushing a plan to send the schools more money so that they can reduce property taxes. However, the plan has little change of passing the Republican dominated legislature.  State Representative Jeffrey Coy, Democrat-Shippensburg, said the plan would not preclude school districts from taking the new money and raising property tax rates anyway by saying rising costs outpaced the increase in state funding.

headline: Save the Kids, Fight Tobacco
abstract: The most promising health intervention today would be to invest part of the $246 billion tobacco settlement funds in prevention programs for our nation's children from smoking.  Congress and the states could work together in protecting children from becoming victims of tobacco-related diseases.

headline: PSU chief visits county to spur solid partnerships
abstract: Penn State University's president Spanier visited Lancaster County to learn more about the county, school districts, agriculture and workforce so that the University's partnership with the county could be increased.

headline: Financing for airline center still in dispute
abstract: Three US Airways representatives met with state and county officials at Pittsburgh International Airport to discuss the state's proposed financial contribution to the proposed maintenance facilities at the airport.  Steve Aaron, spokesperson for Governor Ridge, stated the talks went well but there was still separation on how much the state would contribute.

headline: Build parks for all
abstract: House Democratic Leader William DeWeese asks why doesn't Governor Tom Ridge support taxpayer-finance bonds to build professional sports stadiums but rejects borrowing to protect the environment?  Other states are investing to preserve open.  Why not Pennsylvania?

headline: No Sure Bet
abstract: Race tracks in West Virginia are not allowed to have slot machines. This shows that PA should keep its eyes open if it passes a legislation to go down the same road as West Virginia.

headline: Changing times allow first ladies to mold their roles
abstract: The challenges of being the first lady to a governor involve not being elected but expected to serve and not opinionated but should have an agenda.  Looking at other first lady models like Hilary Clinton and Elizabeth Dole both were expected to have future careers in politics.  First lady Terry Ventura was upset that she had to quit her job and felt that the first lady should be paid.  Ellen Casey, wife of former Governor Bob Casey of Pennsylvania, was more than ready to return to private life.

headline: Pennsylvania candidacies for 2000 begin
abstract: New candidates have begun to emerge for PA primaries> Apart from helping to choose a candidate for the presidential election, PA voters will also be asked to vote to retain or replace first term US Senator Santorum.

headline: Democrats take poke at Ridge's tax reform
abstract: Governor Ridge has characterized Act 50 as a historic tax reform but if Democrats have their way it will not see another year.  House Minority Whip Mike Veon, Democrat-Beaver Falls, described it as a bogus tax reform law that provided nothing but political cover for the majority Republicans.

headline: School Health
abstract: The Heinz Foundation tries to tackle issues of healthcare cost and quality in PA schools. Working with state wide organizations the goal is to get all the public schools in PA to collectively purchase health insurances while maintaining quality and decreasing costs.

headline: Relief on campus follows pact
abstract: Negotiators representing 5500 professors and the 14 universities in the State System of Higher Education struck a 3 year contract. The SSHE was charged with high tuition rates which were attribute to the high salaries.

headline: For safety's sake, limiting phone use in cars worth a try
abstract: Senator Joe Conti, Republican-Bucks, was struck particularly hard by the tragedy of a 2-year-old being killed in an automobile accident by a driver dialing a cell phone because last spring he withdrew a legislative amendment that would have banned the use of cellular phones while the vehicle is in motion.  Conti withdrew it because the amendment would have bee to the teen-driving legislation and keeping it in would have delayed its passage.

headline: Carn back at-bat again for stadium
abstract: State Representative Andrew Carn, Democrat-Philadelphia, saw a bill that would have forced a regional referendum on stadium funding on the fall-election ballot defeated earlier in the month.  Carn is announcing that he will try a similar version of a bill again but this time it is a referendum on the location of a new baseball stadium for the Phillies.

headline: Noteworthy
abstract: Pennsylvanians who saw their properties pummeled by Hurricane Floyd would get a tax break this year under a bill introduced in the House.  Representative Mario Civera, Republican - Delaware, has sponsored legislation that would allow municipalities and school districts to abate 1999 real estate taxes for property damaged or destroyed by flooding caused by Floyd.  The amount would have to be proportionate to the amount of property damage and could not exceed $30,000 for a property.

headline: Cheaper government
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker said the PRIME initiative has resulted in the carrying out of 315 changes in state government, worth $314 million in internal savings, since the Improvement Management Performance and Cost Control Task Force commission unveiled its report in February 1996.  Schweiker did say that there were some mistakes and some things were not done like selling off the state run liquor control system.

headline: Personal becomes political
abstract: Editorial pushing for Texas Governor George Bush's personal life regarding drug abuse to be forgotten and that the question posed to anyone seeking a position high within a federal post not to have used illegal drugs in the past 25 years apply and forget his record.  States that Bush has given tacit admission of drug use yet the dates, times, amounts, and doses should not be revealed.

headline: Dems unveil property-tax plan
abstract: State Senate Democrats from Southwestern Pennsylvania unveiled legislation that would bring much needed property tax relief to Pennsylvania's 3 million homeowners.  The Homeowner School Tax Relief (STAR) would use a portion of the state's budget surplus to give homeowners a tax credit on their school district property taxes.

headline: Schwartz bill would improve nursing home care
abstract: State Senator Allyson Schwartz, Democrat-4th District, has introduced legislature that would establish new minimum staffing levels at long-term care facilities in Pennsylvania.  Specifically it would establish minimum ratios of residents-to-nurse aides for each shift and residents-to-registered nurses or licensed practical nurses for each shift.

headline: Rendell says U.S. falls way short on subsidizing the arts
abstract: Mayor Rendell states the federal government should subsidize costs for arts and culture as other countries do.  He criticized the federal government and called for a federal arts community-development block-grant program.

headline: Free ride may soon be over for turnpike drivers
abstract: Motorists have been enjoying free rides between the Breezewood and Bedford exits to encourage traffic away from a stretch of United States Route 30 that is being widened.  The one-exit trip used to cost 80 cents for cars and more for truckers.  Turnpike Commission records show that when the program began more than $1 million of the $3.1 million allocated had been spent.

headline: Chamber to host legislative breakfast
abstract: State Senator Charles Lemmond and State Representative Sandra Major will be guest speakers at the Wyoming County Chamber of Commerce.  They will address the group on issue affecting the local business community there with emphasis on any pending legislation regarding land use, taxes or unemployment.

headline: Official:Funds should go elsewhere. GOP pushing to block Dawida grant
abstract: State Rep Habay(R) and GOP seek to block state  grant worth $900,00.00 received by Mike Dawida (D) for his institute. Various State Representatives and Senators feel  the grant should be awarded to more worthy trade organizations. Critcs contend that Gov.Tom Ridge used the grant to award to persons who support his agenda.

headline: City race moves to airwaves
abstract: The Democratic primary for mayor has poured onto television this week with John  F. Street joined by two of his four rivals in broadcasting hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign ads.  Philadelphia's police union backed Marty Weinberg and a gay coalition backed Street.

headline: Phillly phobia' continues
abstract: The remaining candidates for the two open seats on the Superior Court are both from Pittsburgh.  Article mentions how there is a phobia of electing candidates from Philadelphia.  The two candidates still in the running are Republican and Democrat.

headline: Floods of cash swamp coffers
abstract: The $ 703 million according to Gov.Ridge's budget office is the state's largest single budget surplus. The surplus would be used to payback the taxpayers, transferred to the Rainy Day Fund and a new property tax relief program would be put in place.

headline: Searching for Cover
abstract: After 34 years of the federal Medicare program one of its most criticized and most immutable features is on the table that of paying for outpatient drug costs.  The reason is that companies would oppose price controls that would surely result.  Now, however, the drug industry released a statement saying it now favors Medicare to cover the cost of outpatient prescription drugs under certain circumstances.

headline: Republican education reforms put parents and children first
abstract: Newspaper column that summarizes Governor Tom Ridge's National Radio Address.  Education is government's most important responsibility to our children, and our greatest opportunity.  If we provide our children with a quality education, then I believe there is no challenge that we cannot overcome.

headline: From outlaw to lobbyist
abstract: Comparisons of old and new biker stereotypes are of the old one who lived on the outskirts of the law and today's version who struggles with the role that he wants the law to play in his life.  Two bills currently in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives deal with an attempt to repeal the state's mandatory helmet law and to ban discrimination in employment because of motorcycle ownership or operation.

headline: Check back with us in a decade…
abstract: Pennsylvania House Speaker John Perzel stated that the taxpayer is protected from the funding plan put into place for Pennsylvania major baseball and football teams as it calls for tax revenues generated from the stadiums which will go to repay the $320 million debt.  The plan is criticized because it is believed that the stadium developments will pay for themselves leaving the legislature to easily slip a small rider bill forgiving the debt.

headline: Our Viewpoint: Gambling not a free ride
abstract: The writer says that the gambling money is not new found money, but money which has already been circulating in the economy that induviduals put back for gamling.

headline: City's top Dem rips sign regs
abstract: The all-republican city council in Chester is enforcing a 25 year old ban which bans the posting of campaign posters on telephone polls, trees, and city buidlings.  Representative Thaddeus Kirkland, Democrat - 159, says this is "a political stunt, an effort to keep the community in the dark about the political process."  Mayor Dominic Pileggi and city council members Patricia Lewis-West and Monir Ahmed are up for re-election.

headline: Philly Republican Hopes to follow GOP wins in New York, L.A.
abstract: If Sam Katz wins the mayoral election for Philadelphia he will become the first GOP candidate in 52 years to win it.  Terry Madonna, a political science professor of Millersville University, states that the race relations have improved signficantly in this election race although they have played a large part in determining the election outcome in the past.  Ed Rendell, has endorsed John Street, who is known for bringing the nation's fifth largest city back from bankruptcy.  Of the few issues they differ on, Katz is for public school vouches whereas Street is against them.

headline: Ford City: 'Withering and dying' or ready to rebound?
abstract: A company town without a company is counting on an infusion of government money to help it reduce high unemployment, cope with malaise and deal with a population that's mostly elderly.  The city likened to a town in Florida where Ford City, which sits along the Allegheny River has 40% of its people 55 years and older.

headline: Senate agrees to 4-Day HMO debate
abstract: The United State Senate has taken up "patients' rights" legislation that would set new controls on health maintenance organizations and other and other managed care plans.  Polls show that people who have not even had any experience with such an organization fear that they care they will one day receive will be denied by the insurance company trying to save money.

This example encapsulates the program Governor Ridge is trying to push through yet has been promoting unsuccessfully.

This represents a 74% boost over last year's plan.  County Commissioner Terry Kauffman states that this is basically a million dollars a week invested in the county's infrastructure.

abstract: State Representative Tim Solobay, Democrat-Canonsburg, believes that the vote the legislature made to fund four new sports stadiums in Pennsylvania is one of the most important votes of the century.  Once the taxpayers safeguards were in the revised plan a surge of economic development resulted.

abstract: Pennsylvania residents are aware that state law prohibits them from bringing in alcohol from another state.  The state wants to keep its monoply because it's big business but state government shouldn't be involved in the sale of alcohol.  State beer taxes bring in about $25 million annually and sales of wine bring in another $136 million annually.  Pennsylvania's liquor stores should be sold in private enterprise, as such stores are operated in most other states.

He states that it is not a legal practice if they are speaking and acting in their roles as heads of congregations.  They cannot engage in partisan political activity but can remain non-partisan and encourage voting without pushing specific candidates.

headline: Plan C?
