abstract: The name of state House District 35 candidate Marc J. Gergely will remain on the May 21 Democratic primary ballot.  Commonwealth Court Judge James R. Kelly this week denied a petition that sought to remove Gergely's name because of residency question.  Gergely said the McKeesport Republican Committee instigated the petition, a claim the local chairman denied.

headline: Rendell Interview
abstract: The following is a transcript of an interview with gubernatorial hopeful Ed Rendell. The various topics discussed include property taxes and education.

headline: Confessions of a City Budget Cutter
abstract: The Competitive Contracting Program allowed Philadelphia to contract out services provided by the city. It helped lower the budget, but still provide quality services. It also required that Philadelphia perform an economic analysis of the work and notify unions when considering contracting out.

headline: Some flu cases found in state
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Health has confirmed 11 cases of influenza in the state, none in the Harrisburg region. The confirmations are the result of tests samples forwarded by doctors participating in the department's program to monitor flu strains.

headline: Tax reform may hinge on residents getting veto
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker wants Pennsylvanians to have the same taxpayer protection that people in most states have - - the right to vote on many school spending increases.  He called on lawmakers to pass legislation that would require school boards to secure voter approval if they want "to increase spending higher than the cost of living with enrollment increases factored in."  The idea of giving taxpayers more control over school spending is incorporated into several of the legislative proposals expected to be considered in the special session.

headline: Budget hearing turns to bickering
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Lynne M. Abraham has pushed for the death penalty and during her era, her prosecutors have sent 77 people to death row. Some question if the death penalty is being overly applied.

headline: Hershey Trust reorganizes board, hires four locals
abstract: The Hershey Foods Corporation Charitable Trust has been reorganized. Pennsylvania Attorney General Mike Fisher has announced that the board will have four new members that will help to restore the Hershey community and school.

headline: City gets its best shot on TV worldwide
abstract: State capitals will be featured on military TV instead of commercials aired on regular television shows. The time for Harrisburg will showcase the Capitol, the new National Civil War Museum, the Doll House Museum, and the large picture of Pickett's Charge in the State Museum.

headline: Judge who ruled on redistricting break status quo
abstract: It was the court ruling that reverberated throughout Pennsylvania, a decision so bold it is deeply affecting this year's state and federal elections.  But it should not have been a surprise that federal Judges Richard Nygaard and Sylvia Rambo would have the strength to shatter the status quo.  Even before their congressional redistricting decision last Monday, Nygaard and Rambo had  taken forceful, independent positions on other issues.

headline: Rendell meets prospective supporters
abstract: Rendell, who wants to be Pennsylvania's next governor, told the people he wants to make "common sense" changes in the state.  He wants to double the cigarette tax, keep medical malpractice insurance reasonable, and expand prescription drug coverage for senior citizens.  Rendell spoke Sunday at a cocktail party hosted by residents of the age-restricted community Village of Neshaminy Falls.

headline: Council members force Verna to set hearing on redistricting
abstract: Using legislative procedure as a weapon, a renegade faction of nine City Council members forced Council President Anna C. Verna to schedule a hearing on a redistricting plan that she and her allies do not like. A City Council hearing broke down into any angry yelling match during the maneuver, which came one day after mayor Street vetoed a redistricting plan shepherded by Verna. The move signaled that Street had succeeded in solidifying a group of members willing to work with him against Verna.

headline: State House approves tobacco penalties
abstract: There was an attempt to overturn a current tough Allegheny County law against selling tobacco to minors, but anti-smoking forces fought it off. The state House did approve a provision that would prevent local governments from enacting such laws in the future.

headline: Testing the test: Looking at PSSAs
abstract: The Pennsylvania System of School Assessment Tests has been coming under harsh criticize. Many critics say the test should not be the only measure of student success. Pennsylvania Governo-Electr Ed Rendell is supporting alternatives methods to be used in conjunction with testing.

headline: Bush to Seek Tougher Penalties In Assault on Corporate Fraud
abstract: President Bush will call today for tougher criminal penalties for corporate executives convicted of fraud, an initiative that he hopes will ease a crisis of investor confidence with out inviting an avalanche of new legislation.  The new penalties for fraud could include longer prison sentences for corporate officers, either by extending the maximum penalties under current law or by allowing judges to require those convicted to serve longer portions of their sentences, a senior administration official said.  The president also is expected to renew his call for legislation requiring top executives to swear to the veracity of public financial disclosures.

headline: Horse industry lobbies for slots
abstract: With horse racing continuing to decline in New Jersey, breeders and owners urged legislators to allow slot machines at the few remaining tracks.  The extra revenue, they argued yesterday, would allow tracks to increase purses.  That, in turn, would bring better horses, helping the tracks compete with neighboring states, and could add race days, which add more pay days.  Supporters of a proposed constitutional amendment allowing slots outside Atlantic City casinos insisted that casino industry misgivings are unfounded.

headline: City politician fishing for votes
abstract: Al Taubenberger is seeking the Republican nomination for the 13th Congressional District, the newly drawn district. His primary opponent is Melissa Brown and the winner of the primary will face US Representative Joe Hoeffel.

headline: Judge, row officers sworn in for new terms
abstract: Cumberland County Judge J. Wesley Oler and other county elected officials took the oath of office Saturday morning in the Old Courthouse in Carlisle in a ceremony joined by J. Michael Eakin, a county native recently elected to the state Supreme Court. William S. Daniels introduced Oler, who was approved by voters in November for a second 10-year term on Cumberland County Court of Common Pleas.

headline: Rendell names Cohen to run transition team
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell said that David L. Cohen, who served as his chief of staff in City Hall, would be General Chairman of his transition team charged with building a new state administration in Harrisburg.

headline: Council mulls changes in taxes, residency, salaries
abstract: Allentown City Council will review six charter changes to put before voters in November's election, including: one that would allow the solicitor to live outside the city, one to hike council salaries and one to make it easier for lawmakers to raise or set taxes. Other proposals would allow council members or the controller to work for the city after leaving office and to adjust the fiscal year.  Council's three-member Legal and Legislative Committee unanimously recommended the proposals Monday night.  The full panel of lawmakers is expected to vote on the suggested changes at council's June 19 meeting.

headline: State improving with heart patients
abstract: Mortality rates for coronary artery bypass graft surgery dropped by 13 percent since 1995 in more than 55 Pennsylvania hospitals. 45 hospitals had their mortality rates in the expected range which takes into account the high risk involved in the surgery and the fact the patients are among the most sick.

headline: Think large for river
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed has come up with an idea for a new museum on City Island and wants to put a public display of the archaeological material in it. Reed's idea has been considered to be "germ" because the mayor has aimed too low to appreciate the richness and history of artifacts by not considering Harrisburg, the largest city on the Susquehanna as a location for a museum.

headline: Chandra Levy's remains found in D.C.
abstract: The skeletal remains of Chandra Levy, a Washington intern who had been missing for more than a year, were found in a wooded area of Rock Creek Park.  The case had drawn attention because of Levy's relationship with US Representative Gary A. Condit.  Levy was last seen in 2001 when she ended her membership at a gym in Washington's DuPont Circle neighborhood.  Her disappearance drew national media focus after Condit, acknowledged to police that he had an intimate relationship with her.

headline: House passes bill to discourage future sale of Hershey Foods
abstract: The PA State House of Representatives has passed a bill that would allow the PA State Attorney General to require a court verdict on any prospective sale of Hershey Foods Corporation.

headline: Coleman to appear on CNN's Inside Politics
abstract: State Representative Jeff Coleman, will make his debut on CNN's Inside Politics on Tuesday, May 21st at 4:00 p.m.  Coleman will discuss education funding reform and property tax reform.  Coleman is the youngest member of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives.

headline: Judges let elections go as planned
abstract: Three federal judges ruled that the May 21st primary will go on as scheduled. Two weeks ago, legislative leaders wanted to reschedule the primary for June or July so they could enact the new congressional districts.

headline: Rendell No. 1 in leftover campaign signs
abstract: Columnist Bill White writes about the number of remaining political signs still in the area from the gubernatorial campaign. White traveled 139 miles around Lehigh Valley counting the number of political signs left over in public areas and found that Rendell had the most with 38 signs.

headline: Council on board with new blight bill
abstract: Mayor Street won a major political victory when nine City Council members signed on  to a new bill that will enable him to issue $295 million in bonds to eradicate blight. The bill, to be introduced by Majority Leader Jannie Blackwell, provides for a board degree of City Council oversight. Oversight was the issue that separated the mayor and Council when he refused to sign or veto a blight bill that City Council President Anna Verna had pushed through Council in December.

headline: State lawmakers push for another special session to tackle malpractice insurance
abstract: Bucks County lawmakers Charles McIlhinney, R-143, Kathy Watson, R-144 and Paul Clymer, R-145, began circulating a petition calling for a special session to address medical malpractice insurance reform three days ago.  The GOP lawmakers say medical malpractice insurance rates continue to increase at a rate that is driving physicians to leave Pennsylvania in favor of others states with cheaper rates.  Local doctors say the malpractice  premiums have risen anywhere from 20 percent to 90 percent in the last year.

headline: Timeline in the school takeover saga
abstract: Despite the deal struck in December between the city and state, Philadelphia schools are still waiting for lawmakers to approve millions in new money.  Some key dates in the saga: March 21-City Council approves $45 million in new funding for schools but balks at paying for a $300 million school bond.  June 10- The school district says it will run out of cash on this date without the $300 million.

headline: Charles T. Strickland shot a burglar in self-defense, but was given a life sentence
abstract: Charles T. Strickland shot a burglar in self-defense, but was given a life sentence. Governor Casey Sr. signed his pardon. Strickland will vote for Casey's son, Robert P. Casey Jr., as he tries to win the Democratic nomination for governor.

headline: House rejects bill to allow bingo at Wal-Mart
abstract: The State House of Representatives have rejected legislation that would enable Wal-Mart and other business to host free bingo games. Lawmakers from York County complained that the measure would set a bad precedent and would expose communities to too much gambling. Some even said it was a bad business practice.

headline: Colleagues say judge not remorseful for drinking problem
abstract: Colleagues have claim that Allegheny County President Judge Patrick McFalls has shown no remorse for his alcohol abuse. McFalls is on leaving for being drunk on the bench. His colleagues want some form of remedial sanction on McFalls.

headline: Kanjorski camp scoffs at Barletta challenge
abstract: Hazleton Mayor Louis Barletta has filed a nominating petition to run against US Representative Paul Kanjorski. Kanjorski is vulnerable due to the revelation that he has steered millions in federal money to family-owned businesses and to purchase land owned by his family.

headline: Rendell picks up key big-city endorsements
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell has received the support of both the Pittsburgh and Philadelphia mayors in his pursuit of the Democratic nomination for Governor. State Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr., his opponent, has support from rural Pennsylvania. Rendell will need both cities to have good turnouts in order to win.

headline: Despite criticism from Street, Saidel to push his tax package
abstract: City Controller Jonathan Saidel said he would attempt to get a majority on City Council to pass a wage and property tax reform package proposed by Mayor Street. Saidel's lobbying effort would put him directly at odds with Street, who is moving to eliminate planned wage-tax cuts. Street's aides also have sharply criticized Saidel's ambitious proposal to cut wage taxes and to overhaul the way the city taxes property and businesses.

headline: State looks at pre-empting laws regulating tobacco
abstract: Pre-emption bills are being discussed nationwide. The history of pre-emption bills in PA are discussed and new bills on regulating tobacco are currently being proposed.

headline: Times running short for school reform in Philadelphia
abstract: Philadelphia's school privatization plan is still far from complete, prompting concerns for the fall.  The city announced in April that it would overhaul management of 70 of its 264 schools, turning over at least 51 to a handful of private companies and nonprofit groups and replacing teachers and principals at the rest.  Yet, with the summer at hand, the city has yet to sign contracts defining the role private companies will play in running the 200,000 -student district, the nation's seventh largest.

headline: Child testimony bill passes House
abstract: Child advocates won a victory in the state Legislature when the House passed a bill that would let abused children submit videotaped testimony or testify via closed-circuit television to avoid facing their accused attackers in court. But one advocacy group said the bill creates problems because it also applies to adult witnesses. The Senate passed the House 190-3, despite attempts to narrow its focus and add on an amendment to expel convicted lawmakers from the Legislature.

headline: Insures defend big reserves as vital
abstract: The scene at Wednesday's hearing before the state Insurance Department was a familiar one: a series of high-ranking corporate executives wearing dark suits and serious expressions, answering questions about their business practices to government officials.  But unlike recent hearings in Washington into bankruptcies and corporate ethics, the top brass from Pennsylvania's four Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations were called to Harrisburg Wednesday to explain why they had so much money.  The four companies- Blue Cross of Northeastern Pennsylvanian, Highmark, Capital Blue Cross and Independence Blue Cross - at the end of 2001, had a combined $3.8 billion in surplus funds, nearly quadruple the total minimum set by the Insurance Department.

headline: Color-coded confusion
abstract: Homeland Security Director Tom Ridge unveiled his Homeland Security Advisory System. It is a set of color-coded warnings based on the military's defense condition. The colors go from green (low condition) to red (severe).

headline: Kanjorski launches ad counterattack
abstract: U.S. Representative Paul Kanjorski's campaign has launched a television counterattack on Hazleton Mayor Lou Barletta. Barletta had accused Kanjorski of arranging federal grants to go into companies owned by his nephew and daughters. The commercial accuses Barletta of favoring the privatization of social security, which would allow the creation of personal savings accounts and investments in stock market.

headline: Rendell pulls ad touting medals
abstract: Democratic governor candidate Ed Rendell has altered a television ad for his campaign amid criticism by state Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr. The original advertisement contained a shot of medals on a uniform that Rendell has never received while in the Army Reserve.

headline: Council gives its final OK to tax bill
abstract: Without debate but with applause from the audience, City Council yesterday gave final approval to a bill ensuring that Philadelphia will continue to cut the wage tax for at least five more years.  The bill allows small cuts in the wage tax every year, and would implement accelerated cuts if the economy does well. The 15-0 vote brought to an end the epic battle over tax policy that pitted a majority of Council, business groups, and the city's financial watchdogs against Street, who insisted that it was better to cut business taxes than the wage tax.

headline: State to rent Polyclinic
abstract: A vacant part of the Polyclinic Hospital in Harrisburg will be renovated into 300,000 square feet of office space, according to Harrisburg Mayor Reed. The new office will become the Penn Center Harrisburg building which will house state agencies and other various organizations.

headline: Tips for city school - business program
abstract: A Philadelphia task force has studied the school-business relationships in Philadelphia districts and has found them to be unfocused and uncoordinated. The task force has stated the need for a revision in the partnerships and the creation of a business advisory council with representatives from the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce, the Greater Philadelphia first, individual school districts and other business organizations.

headline: Child-rape law toughened
abstract: PA Governor Mark Schweiker has signed into law a bill that will increase the penalties for rape of a child and increase the penalty for causing serious bodily injury to the child. The bill came about after the sexual assault of a 5-year old Dauphin County girl where the attacker got only 2 1/2 to 5 years in prison.

headline: Interest bill clears House
abstract: Business could earn interest on bank checking accounts under a bill sponsored by U.S. Rep. Pat Toomey that passed the House on Tuesday.  A 1933 law prohibits banks from paying interest on commercial checking accounts.  The law was intended to keep banks from becoming too aggressive in seeking customers at a time when many banks were failing.  Toomey, R-15th District, said his bill (H.R. 1009), which passed on a voice vote, would give small business the ability to earn returns on idle money held primarily at smaller community banks.

headline: Commentary was character assasination
abstract: Young Adam Schott's commentary concerning my candidacy for lieutenant governor was little more than character assassination with little or no facts. Mr. Schott provides no evidence as to his knowledge of my 12-year voting record as a member of the General Assembly.

headline: Kanjorski spends four times more than Barletta
abstract: U.S. Representative Paul Kanjorski has outspent his Republican opponent Lou Barletta in his campaign to retain his House seat. The two candidates have already spent a combined $964,309 this year, according to financial statements filed with the Federal Election Commission.

headline: Rendell records show him rolling in dough
abstract: PA Gubernatorial candidate Ed Rendell's campaign has painted him as the average man, but his finances indicate otherwise. The financial records of nominee Ed Rendell and his wife show that the family has financial assets valued between $2 million and $5.2 million.

headline: Council panel Ox limits on tax hikes
abstract: The tax-assessment board will join city council to provide immediate relief to homeowners. A Philadelphia council committee has given a preliminary approval to several bills that would freeze or cap recent property-tax increases.

headline: Supreme Court rules execution of the mentally retarded is unconstitutional
abstract: The US Supreme Court has ruled that executing the mentally retarded is unconstitutional, as it is cruel. The 6-3 ruling will affect 20 states that allow for this type of execution.

headline: Tougher GED test debuts
abstract: Nationwide, GED testing in 2001 climbed by as much as 30 percent according to the American Council on Education, a nonprofit Washington, D.C. group. The test was last updated 14 years ago. The new test has several significant changes, including greater emphasis on higher math skills.

headline: Cigarette craving- Smokers find bargains outside state
abstract: Jim Price, the 44-year old South Beaver Township man can drive from his home to the Pennsylvania-Ohio line within minutes and save almost 50 cents in tax for each pack of cigarettes he buys. But as a Pennsylvania resident, Price knows he has to stay within the legal limits of the state's cigarette tax laws, or face the penalties.  The state's cigarette tax laws limit the number of cigarettes a Pennsylvania resident can buy in another state to 10 packs or one carton.  Cigarettes bought outside Pennsylvania can be identified because they do not have the state stamp on them.

headline: Judge approves bankrupt cetury-old brewery's plans to end production
abstract: A bankrupt 96-year-old beer company can shut its brewery and contract production with another brewery, a federal judge said. The ruling by U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Judith K. Fitzgerald means Jones Brewing Co.'s Stoney beer will be brewed by Pittsburgh Brewing Co., which makes Iron City and other beers. Jones filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in November 2000, saying it was difficult to compete for a reasonable share of the market.

headline: County seeks explanation of $100M pension loss
abstract: There has been $100 million lost in Allegheny County's pension fund and three investment firms had to explain their losses to the retirement board. Two of the firms were responsible for half of the losses. There was enough in the fund to pay for all of the retirees.

headline: Kanjorski won't commit yet to debate congressional foes
abstract: Debates that would give local residents a chance to learn about their candidates for Congress remain uncertain as his opponents wait for U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski to commit to a date.  The League of Women Voters of Lackawanna County has tentatively set an Oct. 23 debate at the University of Scranton.  Republican candidate Lou Barletta and Reform Party candidate Thomas McLaughlin plan to be there, but it's unclear whether Mr. Kanjorski will be.

headline: Rendell rocks and rolls across the state, turning liabilities into assets
abstract: This is what Fisher faces in the fall election, a charismatic politician who plays well to the crowds, who does have a sort of "rock star" quality about him - - a quality Fisher does not possess.  Considering recent polls and the momentum Rendell has been building on since his smashing victory in the primary, the November 5 election would seem to be his to lose.  However, a day  can be a lifetime in political campaigns, and with 15 weeks before the election, anything can happen.

headline: Council vote forces Street to do about face
abstract: Last January, Mayor Street may have blundered when he proposed to freeze future wage tax cuts, but he knows how to count votes, assess damage and move on.  And on a day when City Council gave preliminary approval to a bill that would re-impose $120 million in wage tax cuts that he had wanted to stop, Street was nimble.  Council is expected to vote next week on final approval of the proposal, which would continue small yearly reductions in the tax, currently at 4.54 percent for city residents and 3.96 percent for nonresidents.

headline: The cost of smoking
abstract: Taxes on a pack of cigarettes in Pennsylvania have been raised from 31 cents to a dollar, bringing the cost of a pack of cigarettes to over four dollars.  But will that affect the amount that teens smoke?  According to Gene Terry, spokesperson for the American Cancer Society, higher prices do deter teens from smoking as much.

headline: Town-gown friction eased by community meeting
abstract: Community activists are trying to have better relations between Shippensburg residents and those who attend the university. The Community/University Relating Better organization will work hard to control their streets from troublesome college students.

headline: City Council proposes centralizing cases moved from Magistrates Court
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council wants to keep cases from Magistrates Court in one central location if the court should be dissolved.  If the state eliminates the court, elected district justices would take over the work -  nearly 40,000 cases per year, not including traffic violations.

headline: Judge slams Hershey Foods sale decision
abstract: The potential sale of Hershey Foods Corp. appears to be "excessive and unnecessary," and claims that the sale is only an option are "an affront to the intelligence," a Dauphin County Court judge wrote in a scathing opinion yesterday.  In a 16-page opinion, Orphan's Court Judge Warren G. Morgan outlined his reasoning behind last week's decision temporarily barring a sale while the legal case continues, and he continually called into question why the potential sale was even being considered.  Morgan blasted the Hershey Trust Co. - - created to oversee the Milton Hershey School and which has a controlling interest in Hershey Foods - - at one point saying the trustees' actions appear "so unreasonable as it relates to their duty to the school trust that is amounts to a capriciousness that is an abuse of their discretion."

headline: County split into six districts
abstract: The state was forced to give up two of its 21 congressional seats because Pennsylvania's population did not grow as fast as that of other states, according to the 2000 U.S. Census statistics. Under the redistricting plan finalized Thursday, Montgomery County would be served by six congressional districts instead of the current five. Of Montgomery County's 62 municipalities, six would be represented by two congressional districts including Abington, Marlborough, Plymouth, Upper Dublin, Upper Moreland, and Whitemarsh.

headline: Kanjorski: Lawyers cleared involvement
abstract: Facing mounting questions about whether he improperly channeled $9.4 million in federal funds to two companies run by his nephews, U.S. Rep Paul Kanjorski said he cleared his involvement with lawyers from the U.S. House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct. The U.S. House of Representatives Ethics Manual prohibits members from voting on legislation that benefits themselves or their families more than it benefits anyone else in the same class of people.

headline: Rendell routs Fisher.
abstract: Ed Rendell has become Pennsylvania's governor-elect with 1,573,414 votes or 54% beating his opponent Mike Fisher who had 1,258,405 votes, or 43% votes.

headline: Council votes no to living wage
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council voted to eliminated the city's living wage law right before it was going into effect. The Mayor opposed the pay requirement. Supporters want to get a ballot referendum.

headline: The unhealthy state of health care
abstract: Clifford A. Rieders, president of the Pennsylvania Trial Lawyers Association, claims that the reason malpractice insurance premiums are rising is due to trends in the insurance business cycle and the malpractice delivery system; not the influx of malpractice suits. Rieders also suggests that clinics are not closing and doctors are not retiring early, in fact, the number of doctors in Pennsylvania is growing at rate four times faster than the state's population. Rieders believes that the medical community cannot police itself as it asserts and that doctors should be held accountable for their medical errors.

headline: Tuition increases in state headed toward collision with economics
abstract: For years, Pennsylvania has deliberately pursued a high-tuition, high-student-debt strategy for public higher education. In terms of direct aid to the state's public universities per student, the state ranks near the bottom. Nerveless, with many highly regarded public and private institutions; Pennsylvania continues to attract many more out-of-state students than it sends of its own residents elsewhere for a college or university education.

headline: City finds new headquarters for sex crimes unit
abstract: Philadelphia city signed a 10 year $245,000 annual lease with Temple university health systems to renovate a building for the police sex crime unit. An 80-officer squad will likely move in to the building in the year 2000 with an estimated cost of $1.5 million for the renovation.

headline: Kirkland rips city harness-racing track proposal
abstract: State Rep. Thaddeus Kirkland yesterday criticized the proposal for a harness-racing track on the city's Delaware River waterfront as a "really bad idea" and questioned its potential for economic development.  Chester Downs and Marina L.L.C., headed by former Montgomery County state legislator Joseph A. Lashinger Jr., plans to transform the former site of Sun Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Co. into a harness-racing track, marina, restaurant and amphitheater.  Kirkland's opponent in the Senate race, Republican Chester Mayor Dominic F. Pileggi, said last week that the proposal fits with the city's long-range plan for the riverfront.  He did not return a call yesterday.

headline: Court calls off hearing on revised congressional redistricting
abstract: A federal court panel will not hold a hearing on the constitutionality of a Pennsylvania redistricting plan. The panel previous rejected a new map of congressional districts.

headline: Kanjorski: Visionary, or just trying to cash in?
abstract: State Representative Paul Kanjorski blasted the incumbent during his first campaign and now is running for his 10th term. People are accusing him of funneling millions to companies owned by family members and backing projects for his and his family's benefits. He claims it's just disgruntled former employees.

headline: Rendell schoo plan draws Casey's fire Auditor general assailed on campaign ads
abstract: Bob Casey Jr. charged that his rival's education proposal would lead to a massive tax increase while Ed Rendell assailed Casey over campaign tactics in the lates head-to-head enocunter of their race of the Democratic nomination for governor.  The contenders met for an hour -long debate on Pittsburgh's WPXI television one month before the tenative date of their primary face-off.  Due to litigation over the state's new congressional districts, a question mark hangs over that date, however, a fact that both candidates bemoaned yesterday.

headline: County residents thrown out by judge
abstract: US District Judge Ralph Cindrich ruled that a reapportionment plan passed by Allegheny City Council was in violation of Allegheny County Administrative Code. Republicans filed a suit against the plan which was designed by a Democrat.

headline: The Word from Harrisburg
abstract: Doctors and hospitals are being hurt by malpractice lawsuits. The high costs of insurance have forced doctors to move to other states. The state house is working towards three basic and fundamental reform.

headline: Tutoring dollars are going to waste
abstract: For all the fighting over extra school funding in Pennsylvania, there are millions of dollars that the Department of Education hasn't been able to give away.  The state allotted nearly $24 million last school year for grants up to $500 to parents whose children in grades three through six scored less than "proficient" on certain standardized tests.  Under the program, called Classroom Plus, parents must use the money for tutoring designed to boost their children's reading and math knowledge.

headline: City gets more time for trials to be held prosecutors will have two more months to bring some cases to court. Defense lawyers say the plan is unfair.
abstract: Starting January 1, a new rule by a Philadelphia court will give prosecutors an extra two months to bring misdemeanor cases to court. The limit was extended to 180 days instead of 120 days between arrest and trial.

headline: Law provides buying option for wine
abstract: Chairman of the House Liquor Control Committee disagrees with the Patriot News' editorial 'Online wine law goes dry.' The legislature passed a law which would allow Pennsylvanians to purchase hard to find wine online.

headline: Court grants stay, primary will be May 21
abstract: The May 21 primary will take place as scheduled, after a federal court on Tuesday agreed to allow this year's congressional elections to move ahead using a map initially adopted by the General Assembly in January and later declared unconstitutional by the court.  The same three-judge federal panel that initially denied the Legislature's request for a stay has now granted one, saying the state can hold elections using the first st of congressional maps, known as Act 1, for 2002 only.  The court also set a May 8 hearing in Harrisburg to determine whether the second set of maps adopted earlier  this month, known as Act 34, passes constituitonal muster.

headline: Keeping it relatively connected
abstract: U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski encouraged relatives to start several high-tech-related companies, then steered at least $9.4 million in federal research and development contracts to two of those companies. The sister companies are only the latest in a decade long progression of Kanjorski-backed high-tech ventures, which have spawned a network of family-owned businesses and left a trail of fractured relationships and questions about secrecy, abuse of authority and self-interest. It is illegal for members of Congress to contract with the federal government. U.S. House ethics rules prohibit members from voting on legislation that benefits themselves or their families more than it benefits anyone else in the same class of people.

headline: Rendell seeks donations for his inaugural
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor-Elect Ed Rendell has plans to raise $2 million to cover the costs of his inaugural events that will include, a parade, a public ball, and a reception for donors.

headline: Cumberland County plans tax on cell towers
abstract: The operators of cellular phone towers and other such communications sites in Cumberland County will face something new in 2003: a property tax bill.  For years those towers - - there are at least 80 cell in the county - - have gone untaxed by the county and its municipalities and school districts because they haven't been logged onto the property tax rolls.  County commissioners have resolved to change that and have hired an East Shore firm for $25,000 to find all sites and establish valuations for them.  The tax gain for the county, townships and boroughs and schools should be substantial, said Bonnie Mahoney, county chief assessor.

headline: Thumbs Up
abstract: Officials at Lower Bucks Hospital are planning a $10 million expansion that will double the size of the emergency room and increase cardiac services. PA Governor Mark Schweiker has come up with half of the needed money via a state grant.

headline: TV ads brush up city schools' image
abstract: In the midst of accusations about mismanagement and credit card misuse, a threatened divorce between the school board and the superintendent, and stinging criticism from some big financial supporters, Pittsburgh Public Schools is launching an ad campaign full of happy faces and affirmation.  The school board tonight is scheduled to vote on funding for the "Pride of Pittsburgh Public Schools" marketing campaign, which was first proposed more than a year ago, according to district spokeswoman Pat Crawford.  While the television commercials are a wrap and the ads already have time slots on KDKA-TV beginning next month, the board still needs to approve a $42,000 donation from the three corporations that have agreed to pay for the first spots.

headline: City tosses more than half of all cases
abstract: When someone is accused of a major crime in Philadelphia there is a 53% chance that the case will be dismissed. Under John F. Timoney as commissioner, Philadelphia police made a record number of arrests. But as the number of cases has rose, so has the number of dismissals. These are cases that die at preliminary hearing level.

headline: Lawsuit abuse reform good for Pennsylvania
abstract: President of the PA Chamber of Business and Industry talks about the PA Joint and Several Liability law and urges state lawmakers to do something about it.

headline: Court overturns redistricting
abstract: A federal court ruled Monday that the Republican-backed plan adopted by the state Legislature for remapping the state into 19 congressional districts is unconstitutional.  In a 2-1 vote, the three-judge U.S. District Court panel ruled that the redistricting plan's difference of 19 persons between the populations of the largest and the smallest of the new congressional districts violated the "one man, one vote" principle.  However, in a dissent, U.S. District Judge William H. Yohn Jr. said the 19-person deviation was justified by a legitimate objective of avoiding splitting voter precincts among districts.

headline: Keller weighs in politics
abstract: Ed Keller, executive director of the 66,000-member Local 13 of the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees, was an architect of Gov. Bob Casey's 1986 election. A year after Casey became governor, a state law made most state employees dues-paying union members from the day they were hired.

headline: Rendell sounding like Casey
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ed Rendell unveiled his healthcare plan which is very similar to his opponent, Robert P. Casey's plan. Rendell's plan would use part of the state tobacco settlement fund and federal funds to insure 48,000 Pennsylvanians.

headline: District hears tax reform proposal
abstract: Proposed legislation would make the state pay for a bigger share of public school funding and the property owners would pay less in real estate taxes. The Pennsylvania School Reform Network believes in that plan will be a transformational change.

headline: Tobacco foes burn over state budget
abstract: Public health advocates are troubled by a growing trend that finds states using money from a nationwide tobacco settlement to close budget gaps and pay for non-health-related programs. Governor Mark Schweiker proposed using $182 million from Pennsylvania's share to pay for tax cuts and new spending. Health-care advocates, such as Alice Dalla Palu, executive director of the Coalition for a Smoke-Free Valley, prefer the money stay in the specific health-related programs for which it was originally allocated.

headline: U.S. Department of Education to investigate Edison contract
abstract: The U.S. Department of Education said it will investigate how Edison Schools Inc. obtained a contract to run 20 low-performing city schools.  The probe was requested by U.S. Rep. Chaka Fattah, a Philadelphia Democrat who wants to know whether the for-profit company and state Education Secretary Charles Zogby conspired to influence the bidding process.  Edison denied wrongdoing and said it is being unfairly singled out, while a spokeswoman for Zogby said he acted appropriately.

headline: City, state ready for Fourth of July with heightened
abstract: A million people - and Secretary of State Colin Powell - are coming here to celebrate the Fourth of July - a possible juicy target for terrorists who might want to disrupt and icon of American history.  But the city is ready, said Police Commissioner Sylvester Johnson at a press conference in front of police headquarters yesterday.

headline: Legislation unable to stop all unsolicited calls
abstract: A handful of telemarketing companies and the firms that sell their services by cold-calling are downplaying the effect Pennsylvania's do-not-call law will have on their business.  The law is not designed to eliminate all unsolicited phone calls.  Newspapers and publications that have been in business for more than two years are exempt.  The local cable company can't call to try to get you to install cable service, but it's allowed to pitch upgrades to customers.

headline: Court rules redistricting map unconstitutional
abstract: A federal court on Monday dropped a bombshell on lawmakers, overturning the Legislature's congressional redistricting plan just six weeks before the May 21 primary election.  The Republican-controlled Legislature was given three weeks to develop a new map.  The state is prohibited under the decision from using the current maps.

headline: Keller, Besch forgo bid for re-election
abstract: Cumberland County Commissioners Nancy Besch and Earl Keller have announced that they will not seek a fourth term in their positions. The announcement has opened the door for more PA Republican candidates to join the race.

headline: Rep. Hoeffel has $190,000 more than Brown in 13th District race
abstract: Democratic incumbent Joe Hoeffel has extended his fund-raising advantage over Republican challenger Melissa Brown in the 13th Congressional District race.  Hoeffel had $501,000 to Brown's $311,000 on June 30, the end of the latest reporting period.  The $190,000 difference is substantially larger than $79,000 edge Hoeffel had when the period began May 2.  The gap would have been even larger if Brown hadn't lent $85,000 to her campaign on June 29.

headline: Districts blame tax rises on state
abstract: Educating children is becoming more and more expensive. For property owners in Cumberland and Perry counties, it's likely tax payers are being asked to pay more of the bill.  Nine of the 10 public school districts in Cumberland County plan to raise their property tax rates in 2002-03.  In Perry County, three of four districts plan to do likewise.

headline: Tobacco law enforcement still months off
abstract: Allegheny County's controversial tobacco law takes effect today, however, enforcement of the law won't start for several months, according to Health Department spokesman, Guillermo Cole.  The DOH states the law will be phased in by sending out notices to the 1,700 state-license tobacco retailers in the county advising them that the new law is in effect.

headline: U.S. targets 2 city schools for improvement
abstract: The federal government has stated they want to improve the Fort Pitt and Reizenstein Middle Schools which it says its academic performance is inadequate. Fort Pitt has low math scores, but parents of students of the school believe it is making gains.

headline: Clearfield County commissioners spurn bid to remove 10 Commandments courthouse marker
abstract: The agenda for the Clearfield County commissioners' biweekly meeting carried a demand from an organization of area atheists to clear the courthouse steps of a 30-year-old marker bearing the Ten Commandments.  More than 300 people squeezed into the county's main courtroom.  And when the assembly opened with the Pledge of Allegiance, the crowd fairly shouted the phrase "under God."  When it was all over three hours later - - after the last of 74 people spoke his piece- - the three commissioners agreed that despite threats of a lawsuit, the Commission will stay.

headline: Legislator ponders big store's fallout
abstract: State Representative Sheila M. Miller is not certain about the building of a $35 million sporting-goods store in Bethel Township. The store would be built on valuable farmland and could drive local hunting and fishing supply stores out of business. She is concerned about the impact.

headline: Court ruling ends nonsense
abstract: Three federal judges ruled that the May 21st primary will proceed as scheduled. The congressional redistricting will be resolved later. The upcoming primary is an important one with two major Democratic gubernatorial candidates.

headline: Knoll seeks blessing
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor-Elect Catherine Baker Knoll is the co-chairwoman of Governor-Elect Ed Rendell's transition team.

headline: Rep. Waters knocks lone challenger of primary ballot.
abstract: Rep. Ronald Waters (D-Philadelphia) secured his re-election Monday after Commonwealth Court ordered his only challenger removed from May 21st primary ballot.  The court ruled that challenger Anthony D. Jackson did not have the 300 valid signatures required on nomination petitions for House races.  The legal challenge to his petitions was filed by Waters.

headline: Duel of the tax relief plans
abstract: While death and taxes may be the only things one can be certain of, just how those taxes should be paid  - and how much should be paid - has become the hottest, most divisive issue in the contest for the state Senate between Tommy Tomlinson and Peter Kostmayer.  Both men say they can cut people's property taxes by about half.  Tomlinson, the two-term Republican incumbent, says the fairest, most fiscally sound way to do so is to raise income taxes while slashing property taxes and putting a limit on how much schools can spend.  Kostmayer, the Democratic challenger and former Bucks County congressman, says he can replace every dollar the state loses from cutting property taxes by increasing fees on cigarettes, imported waste, slot machines and by slashing government waste.

headline: Tobacco money aim: Put end to smoking
abstract: Beaver County will receive $1.25 million over the next three years to spend on programs aimed at getting longtime smokers to quit and getting young people to avoid smoking in the first place.  That share is just a portion of the state's expected $11 billion in tobacco settlement funds, which will be disbursed over the next 25 years.  About 12 percent of that money will be dedicated to tobacco-use cessation and prevention programs, according to the state Department of Health.

headline: Uncertainties about start of school year underscore need for serious tax reform
abstract: Summer is over and it's time for the four Rs: Reading, 'riting, rithmetic and tax reform.  Just as Pennsylvania's 1.8 million school children head to classes this week, the state's 253 lawmakers return to Harrisburg for a special session on property tax reform.  For many of the school children and lawmakers, it's an uncertain proposition.

headline: Commandments compromise will be discussed at hearing
abstract: The great debate over the Ten Commandments plaque on the façade of Chester County courthouse shifted yesterday from the bronze tablet to topics less glamorous: drill holes and hang wires.  The county said yesterday that the American Civil Liberties Union erred when it told a federal judge on Tuesday that the county commissioners were ready to install a tableau of historical texts around the plaques by drilling holes in the courthouse wall.  Still, the county said it wants to pursue the idea of a tableau at a Monday hearing in U.S. District Court.

headline: Lessons from Georgia
abstract: Proposed legislation would set statewide crematory standards. A crematory in Georgia had given powdered cement as ashes while keeping the corpses.

headline: Dad's values drove Fisher as a reliable, steady youth
abstract: Charles Thompson of Harrisburg Patriot News reports about State Attorney General Mike Fisher's regular childhood, his prep school days, and how his father's values that drove him to becoming a man of steadiness and reliability.

headline: Knoll stumps for votes in Hazleton
abstract: Catherine Baker Knoll is running for lieutenant governor on the Democratic ticket.  Knoll told residents of Hazleton that she and gubernatorial candidate Ed Rendell and can make a difference in the community and work to help residents of the area.

headline: Report criticizes state's spending
abstract: A conservative-leaning national organization of state legislators says that as state officials wrestle with the biggest economic bears they've seen in more than a decade, they've got only themselves to blame. That's the overriding message in "Crisis in State Spending," a 92-page handbook issued by the American Legislative Exchange council this week.

headline: Election year tax reform 'unlikely'
abstract: There's more noise in the Legislature about property tax reform than any year during the past decade, but a final solution may still provide elusive because this is an election year. Tax reform generally means shifting from property taxes to income-based taxes. Pennsylvania lawmakers have wrestled unsuccessfully with ways to replace the property tax for about 30 years.

headline: 'Tort reform" in health care is bad law for the wrong patient
abstract: A war is being waged over inadequate medical care in Pennsylvania. The enemy in this war is the incompetent physicians, not the courts, jurors, or competent physicians. The fix that is required is the placement of accountability on incompetent physicians and their insurance carriers.

headline: Union irate over plan for schools
abstract: Philadelphia Federation of Teachers president Ted Kirsch vows to fight any move by the city's School Reform Commission that would take schools out of the union and give them to private firms to run.  Kirsch's comments came after the School Reform Commission last week said it planned to use privatization as one of five new management models to improve as many as 75 low-performing district schools.  While privatization has been talked about for months, it was only last week that commission officials said union contracts would not have to be honored under that model.

headline: Complex portrait of Jaffe emerges
abstract: For a man fond of neatness and order, Judge Joseph Jaffe was disheveled and shaky when he ushered his former wife into his Upper St. Clair home.  After he had been snared in an FBI sting that caught him accepting $13,000 in cash from a lawyer with cases pending before him, Jaffe made his first telephone call. It had gone to his ex-wife.  It's urgent he told her.  Jaffe, an Allegheny County Common Pleas Court judge since 1986, is so tidy that he organizes his socks by color in a dresser drawer, Fleck said.  Now he faces the messy reality of a growing FBI investigation into his life and the way he presided over his courtroom.

headline: Local start-ups cross fingers as investors give fair a chance
abstract: Scouts will be crawling all over Heinz Field on Tuesday and Wednesday.  These scouts will be venture capitalists from Pittsburgh, as well as high-tech strongholds of Boston, Philadelphia and Washington, D.C.  They will be putting entrepreneurs from 31 start-up companies through their paces--- examining business plans for hot new technologies, evaluating the nimbleness of management teams and judging the size of the potential market for new products and services.

headline: Darling, Rendell
abstract: "Darling" by the Beach Boys is Ed Rendell and his wife's special song. The Beach Boys played the song at a Rendell function, but his wife Midge was not allowed to attend because she is a federal judge.

headline: Kukovich to finish campaign in Greensburg
abstract: Allen Kukovich will end his campaign for the Democratic nomination for lieutenant governor in Westmoreland County. He will campaign at a few other places southwestern Pennsylvania before heading to Greensburg. He has also started to air television ads in western Pennsylvania.

headline: Report was no knock on Ridge
abstract: Mr. Berkowitz, Vice President of the Heritage Foundation, claims that a recent report on homeland security "was in no way intended as a criticism" of Pennsylvania Governor Ridge. Mr. Berkowitz continues to explain that the report was a laundry list of sorts that lists preparations that need to be addressed to avoid another September 11th and that Governor Ridge should not and is not being attacked by the Heritage Foundation.

headline: Few stand neutral on property tax form
abstract: State Representative Daryl Metcalfe has been working to eliminating property tax. Along with bills to abolish property tax, bills aimed at protecting seniors, bills on school equity will be addressed in the special session of the legislature which was called by state Rep. Lisa Boscola.

headline: West Nile hits 2 in York County
abstract: Two York County residents yesterday were diagnosed with the West Nile virus, along with five other people in Pennsylvania, state Health Department officials said.  To date, 18 people in the state have tested positive virus, said Amy Kelchner, state Health Department spokeswoman.  The two York County residents who tested positive yesterday were identified only as a 28-year-old man and a 50-year-old woman.  Three Pennsylvania residents, including a Lancaster County man, have died as a result of the virus, which is typically transmitted through mosquitoes.

headline: Universities worry about reductions in state aid
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Mark Schweiker's budget for the fiscal year reduces aid by 5 percent to Penn State, Lincoln, Pittsburgh, and Temple. Schweiker is also proposing a 3 percent reduction for the 14 universities that make up the State System of Higher Education. State Education Department officials have said some cuts were necessary to balance the budget amid a recession and a projected a $622 million revenue shortfall.

headline: Court rejects lawsuit over cost of inmate phone calls
abstract: A Commonwealth Court judge dropped the lawsuit by the Citizens United for Rehabilitation of Errants of Pennsylvania against the state prison system. The inmates' rights group claimed that the cost of collect calls by inmates were excessive.

headline: Local trustees prove key
abstract: Three of the four Hershey Trust Co. board members who live in central Pennsylvania were among the majority that voted Tuesday to call off the sale of Hershey Foods Corp.  The fourth local resident, William L. Lepley, lame duck president and chief executive officer of the Milton Hershey School, voted against rejecting two bids for the sale of the Derry Twp. candymaker.

headline: Daschle anti-recession plan challenges GOP's
abstract: Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle, accused by Republicans of blocking a plan to stimulate the economy, say the nation needs a broader anti-recession plan and blames President Bush's tax cuts for limiting lawmaker's options. Daschel says the $1.35 million tax-cut package Bush won from Congress was responsible for the disappearance of projected federal budget surplus and the government's return to annual deficits and borrowing. Republicans say Daschle's proposal amounts to more new spending and lays the groundwork for a tax increase.

headline: Labor official fired after release of audit
abstract: Robert E. Moore, former PA State Labor and Industry Department Secretary, has been fired after allegations of $200,000 in wasteful spending came up in an agency audit.

headline: Report: Democrats solicited blanks
abstract: Allegheny County Elections Board investigated allegations of absentee ballot voter fraud in Kennedy and found that rate of absentee voting in Kennedy  was higher than the county average. A large portion of the Kennedy's absentee ballots were hand carried to the county Election division. The Board also found that the absentee ballots from the 1999 primary are missing and believed to be stolen or accidentally destroyed.

headline: Fire, rescue grant gets panel's support
abstract: A Carlisle official wants the state to find room in its $20 billion annual budget for volunteer fire companies next year and his council peers agree.  Councilman Timothy Scott has drafted a letter asking state Sen. Hal Mowery, R-31, and state Rep Will Gabig, R-199, to "do everything within scope of their powers" to restore a popular  $25 million grant program for volunteer fire and rescue units throughout the state.  Council on Thursday adopted a resolution in support of Scott's letter.

headline: Youth tobacco use disheartens legislator
abstract: Despite decades of warnings about the dangers of tobacco use, Rep. Babette Josephs says statistics show minors are still lighting up.  At a public roundtable hearing last week on how to stop rampant sales of tobacco products to minors, the Philadelphia Democrat said the facts on youth tobacco use are disheartening.  But Josephs says Pennsylvania can draw from the work of other states that have increased their state taxes on cigarettes and cracked down on retailers who sell tobacco illegally to minors.

headline: University gets $6 million to build statewide bioterror warning system
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh has been awarded a $6 million grant to develop a statewide, computer-based system that would provide early warning of a bioterrorist attack.  The funds will expand as system already in place in 25 hospitals in southwestern Pennsylvania that alert medical and emergency officials of any spike in symptoms that could be related to a biological attack.  The University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University jointly operate the Biomedical Security Institute and the Real-time Outbreak Disease Surveillance system.

headline: Corman's bill to limit email SPAM
abstract: State Senator Jake Corman has introduced a bill they would limit the amount of SPAM that a computer user received by allowing SPAM recipients to sue for actual damages per message received.

headline: Loose Change: Fisher has tackled Hershey nonprofit before.
abstract: When the boards of big Pennsylvania companies such as CoreStates, Conrail, AMP and Peco voted to sell themselves to big out-of-state companies, state officials declined to try to stop them.  Elected officials might not like it when thousands of constituents lose their jobs, but they're also reluctant to second-guess corporate boards, as Commerce Secretary Samuel A. McCullough said on the eve of CoreStates' 1998 sale to First Union Corp., a deal that vaporized more jobs in the Philadelphia area than Hershey Foods Corp. employs in the state.  But if state officials don't feel it's their place to meddle with corporate destiny, nonprofits are another matter.  In Dauphin County Orphans Court today, Attorney General Mike Fisher will try to help block the Hershey board's proposed sale of Hershey Foods.

headline: DeAngelis announces candidacy for Republican Party ticket
abstract: Kenneth DeAngelis recently announced his candidacy for the Republican nomination for the office of State Representative for the 134th District.  He is currently serving in his second term as Township Supervisor for Lower Macungie Township.  He is also employed by the township as the Director of Finance and Administration.

headline: Latest I'm sorry didn't do a Lott of good
abstract: U.S. Senator Trent Lott has been under criticism for his association with racist remarks. Columnist John Baer writes to make fun of Lott's appearance on the television show BET. Baer says Lott need to resign from his position in office.

headline: Reprieve
abstract: The budget by Governor Mark Schweiker has an accounting maneuver which will help school districts from paying sharply higher pension costs. The reprieve may be temporary. The better the Pennsylvania School Employees Retirement System's investments do, the less school districts have to chip in to cover employee pension costs.

headline: Fisher talks business at Pennsylvania Press Club, says there should be no delay in Capitol Stock and Franchise Tax phase out
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher is the Republican candidate for Governor and has criticized his Democratic opponents saying their plans will spend money, but will not create jobs. Fisher also commented on Ed Rendell's gambling plan.

headline: Barletta makes hay of 'anti-farm' vote
abstract: United States Representative Paul Kanjorski's voted against permanent repeal of the federal estate tax.  Republican congressional candidate and Hazelton Mayor Lou Barletta says it was a slap at family-owned farms and small businesses in Northeastern Pennsylvania.  Barletta also said the tax is unfair because it taxes assets already taxed at least once through income and other taxes.

headline: Up to half of teacher candidates failing tests
abstract: Between one-third and one-half of Pennsylvania's prospective math and science teachers failed certification tests last yea. These numbers are causing education officials to question whether the state's colleges and universities are doing a good enough job educating their students. The tests were taken by soon-to-graduate college students and recent graduates during the 2000-01 fiscal year.

headline: Could rash be psychosomatic?
abstract: Pinpointing the cause of a rash break out in Bucks and Montgomery County is proving to be tricky. The rashes, which have afflicted both teachers and students, have not been accompanied by serious symptoms such as fever, nausea, or swollen glands. The cause of some rash epidemics is all in the head in other words hysteria.

headline: Make gambling pay, state poll says
abstract: With lawmakers seeking a solution to pay for property tax reductions, a new statewide poll released today shows Pennsylvanians favor expanded gambling and so-called sin taxes rather than general tax increases to raise new revenue.  Accentuating the reason why lawmakers have been unable to resolve so-called tax reform for more than four decades, the poll by the Pennsylvania Economy League, a nonpartisan research group, shows strong opposition to raising state income, sales or gas taxes or highway tolls as new revenue sources.  Lawmakers say new forms of gambling don't bring in enough revenue to drastically cut property taxes statewide.

headline: Dear John
abstract: PA House Majority Leader John Perzel has supported legislation that has reduced the power of Philadelphia city officials and has allowed the state to take control over the PA Convention Center in Center City. The Inquirer says Perzel has done a disservice to his city and hopes that Governor-Elect Ed Rendell will fix the mess.

headline: Law firm has paid Rendell $500,000 over two years
abstract: Democratic candidate for PA governor, Ed Rendell has yet to make public his 2001 income tax return, which he promised to do. Rendell was paid about $500,000 by a law firm after leaving the Philadelphia mayor's office and is expected to have stocks with liquid holdings worth $1.3 million and $5 million.

headline: Republican aspirants vie for a chance to take on Joe Hoeffel
abstract: Republican Melissa Brown is running for the 13th Congressional District and has been endorsed by committees for both areas. She also has support from US Representative Jon D. Fox and state Senator Stewert Greenleaf. Her opponent is Al Taubenberger.

headline: For Pittsburgh leaders, 'the devil is in the details'
abstract: Pittsburgh faces a $20 million budget shortfall, a 50-year decline in population and an ongoing debate on how to jump-start its downtown retail corridor. Mayor Tom Murphy is proposing to make Pittsburgh a cleaner and safer city. To accomplish this Mayor Murphy has introduced the Pittsburgh Clean Neighborhoods Collaborative and increased the enforcement of jaywalking and obscene language on city buses and trolleys.

headline: Bill seeks cleanliness at petting zoos, fairs
abstract: Proposed legislation would require petting zoos and agricultural fairs to provide adequate hand washing facilities on exhibition grounds. The bill was created after the death of a 4 year old who contracted E. coli from the Montgomery County petting zoo.

headline: Vallas will need the patience of a saint in Philly
abstract: It's an apt metaphor for what Paul Vallas is trying to do as the new CEO of the school district: educate thousands of kids with very limited resources.  That's hard enough for any human, as decades of failure have proven.  But Vallas is additionally burdened by the mounting impression that he's the school district's long-awaited savior.

headline: County to oversee tobacco money
abstract: The Lebanon County Commissioners will be the primary contractor to oversee the tobacco-use prevention and cessation program in Lebanon County. $280,000 will be administered for the next three years by the county's Commission on Drug and Alcohol Abuse.

headline: Malpractice insurers fleeing Pa.
abstract: Various state malpractice insurers have left the state or collapsed. State regulators blame mismanagement, but the companies are having to pay out more in claims than they are receiving in premiums.

headline: Debate is chance to learn more about Battisto, Scavello
abstract: Two highly qualified candidates are running for state representative in the brand-new 176th District in Monroe County, and residents should use the chance to meet and hear them both tonight.  Former state representative Joseph Battisto, a Democrat, and Monroe County Commissioner Chairman Mario Scavello, a Republican, will face off from 7-8 p.m. in a debate at the Pocono Township Volunteer Fire Company fire hall.

headline: law hastens public access to government records
abstract: A law designed to hasten the public's access to government documents has taken effect. The law forces state agencies to answer record requests within 10 days. Municipal and county governments must respond within five days.

headline: Republicans deny while the cock crows
abstract: Recent polls indicate that what people fear the most in the country is not Iraq; it is the state of the economy. The media has focused on terrorism, the upcoming war with Iraq, the Maryland sniper and other issues that marks an ideal scenario for Republican strategists who have been criticized for ignoring the current state of economy.

headline: Gloves off in Roddey, Flaherty tax battle
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Jim Roddey accused city Controller Tom Flaherty of illegally using Roddey's confidential tax information to take a political potshot. Flaherty branded Roddey a hypocrite for suggesting a shift away from property taxes to wage or income taxes after Roddey took a $2,555 write-off on his city and school wage taxes last year.

headline: Coalition efforts helped defeat farm bill
abstract: A Coalition of PA Environmental groups and family farmers helped to stop passage of a bill that would have allowed factory farms to operate without many state regulations.

headline: Vallas: Fixing libraries, labs top to-do-list
abstract: Renovating high school libraries and science technology labs will be a top priority, Philadelphia School District Chief Executive Officer Paul Vallas said yesterday.  Vallas made the pledge following the School Reform Commission's meeting at which two Strawberry Mansion High students testified that their library is sub-par and has no librarian.  Tyshia Brame presented a letter she wrote to first Lady Laura Bush asking for help.  Mrs. Bush wrote back commending her effort and suggested that she speak with school district administrators.

headline: Court looks at hearings for troopers
abstract: The state Supreme Court heard both sides on whether new state troopers on probation deserve hearings if they are terminated. The Pennsylvania State Troopers Association and the state Labor Relations Board argued that the state police unilaterally cut off hearings for probationary troopers. The state police say they should be able to fire troopers during the probationary period for any reason without a hearing.

headline: Merger
abstract: One of the difficult tasks that local governments face in Pennsylvania is trying to restructure to become efficient. The  state needs to provide financial incentives to encourage the merger of municipalities. Municipal debt, different pension systems and the possible loss of jobs and offices can all impede the accomplishment of a merger.

headline: Debate shows capable, competent candidates
abstract: Three major party candidates for governor, two Democrats and one Republican, squared off in the first gubernatorial debate at an event sponsored by the Pennsylvania Newspaper Association. All three candidates, former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr., the Democrats, and Attorney General Mike Fisher, a Republican, were articulate about the issues and masterful in their knowledge of the state. According to Brad Bumsted, a reporter for the tribune, it reinforced the view that Pennsylvania's can't lose.

headline: Law ignored as local voting districts unchanged
abstract: Council wards must redraw their lines every ten years just like Congressional districts and state legislative districts. City Councils and township boards rarely deal with boundary changes. Some population shifts may cause wards to redraw boundaries.

headline: Republicans downplay Hafer's endorsement
abstract: Republicans state Treasurer Barbara Hafer, who cried foul when state GOP leaders endorsed Mike Fisher for governor over her, will throw her support behind the Democratic nominee, Edward Rendell.  Hafer made her announcement Wednesday at the City-County Building in Pittsburgh, after which she was scheduled to accompany Rendell on a plane tour through Harrisburg to Philadelphia, with news conferences scheduled at every stop.  She said the endorsement reflects Rendell's superior qualifications, not any grudge against Fisher or the party leaders who rebuffed her a year ago, and "transcends party interests."

headline: House hopefuls focus on school taxes. Samuelson, Strunk target same issue in 135th district race
abstract: Candidates for the PA 135th House Seat are all emphasizing lower school property tax in their campaigns. PA State Representative Steve Samuelson wants to continue allowing schools to tax properties, but would ease that burden with more state money. His Republican opponent Keith Strunk would want to throw out property tax entirely.

headline: Continuing drought taking a toll on dairy farmers
abstract: Marlene and Rodney Reese have raised dairy cattle for decades near Port Matilda, west of State College in Centre County.  But this year they're doing something they've never done before - - buying corn for silage.  Until, this year, the Reeses had always grown enough corn and hay to feed their cattle, but the rainy spring and the drought that followed have forced them to buy their feed this year.

headline: We must do our homework on school funding
abstract: Most taxpayers' highest priority for how their money is spent is on the education of children. The quality of that education will determine the future of the community, state, the nation, and even the world. Senator James J. Rhoades of Schuylkill County is calling on the state to fund the cost of public education from an increase in the state income tax.

headline: Court overrules badge sentence
abstract: Regina Zimmerman was ordered in January 2001 to wear a badge reading "convicted shoplifter" when she went into stores.  Last week, the state Superior Court stepped in and threw out her sentence, returning the case to Judge Bradford Charles. She never wore the 4-inch red badge because someone else did her shopping during that six-month period. The case got international publicity.

headline: Movie producers eyeing film studio at Fayette County
abstract: A group of movie producers say they want to turn a Fayette County amphitheater into the state's first movie studio.  Fayette Films spelled out their proposal to use the vacant Great Meadows Amphitheater to county commissioners this week.  The group wants to develop the 130-acre site and sign a five-year 540-thousand dollar lease.

headline: Debate: Special Election
abstract: Democrat Bruce Beardsley kept the pressure on Republican Gibson C. Armstrong Thursday night during the candidates' one debate before July 16 special election to fill the unexpired term of former state Rep. John E. Barley.  Armstrong, a Strasburg resident and former Marine captain, chose a Spartan approach, emphasizing from the beginning his leadership abilities, his conservative attitude toward government and his local roots.  Beardsley, a Paradise Township resident and retired businessman, drew applause and laughter during the hour-long debate at the Strasburg Township municipal building.

headline: Lawless outraged over pay increase
abstract: State representative John Lawless has said he is outraged by the $10,000 raise that 3 members of the PA Securities Commission got. It was put in a 41 page bill designed to protect the agency's rules and regulations.

headline: Republicans roar
abstract: PA Republican lawmakers increased their majority in the PA House of Representatives and reclaimed undisputed control of the senate by garnering a 51-member majority. CBS News anchor Dan Rather called the election results a "Bushification " of America.

headline: Judge: Voting map violates county code
abstract: A federal judge ruled against County Council Democrats saying they forced the council to approve a voting map which would strengthen the party's election hopes. The county's Administrative Code requires Pittsburgh to be divided by population which would be four council districts, but instead the city was divided into six.

headline: Farm bill could help local dairies
abstract: Dairy farmers in Pennsylvania would receive federal help in a farm bill passed in the U.S. Senate. The bill would create a milk price support system similar to the Northeast Dairy Compact, which expired last year before Pennsylvania was able to gain admission. The House version of the measure contains no comparable dairy provision and it remains to be seen if it can survive conference committee negotiations.

headline: What to do about cyber schools
abstract: The original charter school law did not address or contemplate the idea of educating children through a modem. The state Department of Education simply picked a school district that will give a charter, enroll students, and send the school a bill. The Schweiker administration and the General Assembly need to address the law.

headline: Court to decide whether cops can monitor e-mail without warrant
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has agreed to decide whether police may look at a suspect's e-mail and instant messages without first obtaining a court order. The case involves a former Lehigh County police office who used the Internet to solicit sex from a 15-year old girl. Though federal law only requires the consent of one person before a telephone call or Internet communication can be recorded, Pennsylvania and 11 other states require the consent of all parties.

headline: Nestle reported to have bid for Hershey Foods, Nestle declines comment
abstract: Swiss food and beverage giant Nestle is offering about $11.5 billion fro Hershey Foods, the biggest U.S. candymaker, USA Today reported in Monday's editions.  But Nestle, whose brands include Crunch candy bars, Taster's Choice coffee and Perrier water, declined to comment on the report.  A call to Pennsylvania-based Hershey Foods before business hours was answered by a recording.

headline: Democrat Gergely takes contest in 35th District
abstract: Marc Gergely of White Oak won the Democratic primary for the 35th District in the state House, beating out challengers Lori Spando and Christopher M. Terrick. With 70 of 74 precincts reporting, Gergely had nearly 38 percent of the vote, over Spando's 32 percent and Terrick's 30 percent.  The results are unofficial. Gergely will be the de facto winner in the fall since there are no Republican candidates who filed for the vacant seat.

headline: Lawless vigilant for Erin's Law
abstract: Pennsylvania Representative John Lawless (D., Montgomery) mentions Erin Jacob’s name on the House floor every time he gets a chance. Erin Jacob contracted the E. coli virus when visiting a farm to pick pumpkins in 1999. Lawless is attempting to pass a bill that would establish sanitation standards for petting zoos and mandatory reporting of E. coli infections to the state Health Department.

headline: Republicans sue to block voting district plan
abstract: Allegheny County Republicans sued Thursday to block County Council Democrats from pushing through a revamped voting district plan and have a judge create a map instead  The lawsuit, filed in Common Pleas Court, argues the voting map proposed for council's 13 districts is illegal because it missed a deadline established under the county's Administrative Code, according to Tom Hardiman, the county Republican Party treasurer who is handling the lawsuit.  Common Pleas Judge Joseph James will meet with lawyers from both sides at 11 a.m. today, Hardiman said.

headline: Lawmakers should consider 'boutique' taxes
abstract: Recently, USA Today wrote about efforts in Seattle to raise money for social  services.  In the city synonymous with coffee - the headquarters of Starbucks, no less - voters will decide they want to pay a 10-cent tax on every cappuccino, latte and mocha they buy.  Proponents say the tax on espresso drinks could raise as much as $10 million a year to pay for child care.

headline: Farm bill's opponents watchful for passage
abstract: A number of environmental activist groups are hoping to stop PA Senate Bill 1413 from passing before the end of the legislative session. The bill would alter the way in which municipalities could crack down on agricultural operations.

headline: When kids need to learn a lesson
abstract: Community Education Partners schools educate disruptive and low-performing youth. CEP schools are for profit and strike to improve attendance, classroom behavior, and learning. Ideally, the students would return to their neighborhood public school.

headline: DA defends molester legislation
abstract: Authorities must be allowed to notify Montgomery County residents if there's a sexually violent, child predator living in their neighborhoods to protect communities, prosecutors wrote in court paper delivered to Pennsylvania's highest court last week. The state Supreme Court previously agreed to hear the appeal and prosecutors had until this week to file written arguments supporting their position.  It hasn't been determined if attorneys will have to appear before the high court in person to argue the constitutional issue.

headline: No decision on sale of Hershey yet, trust's CEO says
