abstract: Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Joseph A. Jaffe is the target of a federal investigation and has been temporarily relieved of his judicial duties.  Jaffe has not been charged by authorities.  Although authorities refused to comment on the case, sources close to the investigation said that it centered on a meeting last week between Jaffe and Joel Persky, a Downtown lawyer, in which the judge accepted $13,000.

headline: Senate passes bill to discourage future sale of Hershey foods
abstract: The State Senate  has passed a bill that would require any future sale of Hershey Foods Corporation to be approved by the courts. A sale must first be recommended by the state attorney general.

headline: Desire to help people makes Henderson run
abstract: Candidates for the PA 120th district seat were asked in a forum to tell why they are the best candidate for the office. Henderson responded by saying that he got into the race for the 120th district with an intention of helping people and that he will best serve the people of the district in a beneficial manner.

headline: Let's hope tempest remains in teapot
abstract: The two candidates for the 176th House District, Mario Scavello and Joseph Battisto, are upset with each other over issues brought up in the campaign. The Monrow County Commissioner Scavello has questioned Battisto's age (70), while former state Representative Battisto has brought up Scavello's mayoral record.

headline: Santorum ridicules Kanjorski's ethics gripe
abstract: U.S. Sen. Rick Santorum on Wednesday defended a Republican research project aimed at determining the party affiliation and political contributions of Washington lobbyists and encouraging them to hire more Republicans.  Mr. Santorum also said his limited role in the so-called "K Street Project" falls far short of U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski's ethical lapses.  Mr. Kanjorski, the focus of criticism for steering millions of dollars in federal money to two companies controlled by his family, issued a statement Friday denouncing Mr. Santorum's role in the K Street Project.  On Wednesday, he accused Mr. Santorum of "extreme partisanship" and conduct "out of character" for a senator.

headline: Roddey presents tax proposals
abstract: With a growing belief among some lawmakers that a long-tern solution on tax-shifting may be out of reach before the end of a special session, Allegheny County Executive Jim Roddey presented legislative leaders with several ideas for a short-term solution, including tax breaks for senior citizens and controlling school district costs.  It comes as some leaders maintain that an increase in the state income or sales tax to replace property tax cuts appears unlikely before the Nov. 5 election.  The special session ends Nov. 30.

headline: Gov. Schweiker's budget disregards emergency services
abstract: According to State Rep. Tim Solobay, Governor Schweiker's budget address outline budgetary cuts that shockingly left out some important programs. The most important program ignored was a $45 million grant program for volunteer and municipal emergency services departments. Representative Solobay insists that studies estimate that volunteer emergency services departments save municipal taxpayers roughly $6 million per year.

headline: Hershey Foods strike is over
abstract: Striking workers at two Hershey Foods Corporation plants voted by a margin of 9 to 1 to approve the company's contract offer. This vote ended the longest work stoppage in the history of the nation's number one candy manufacturer.  The 2,700 workers accepted lower wage increases in exchange for keeping their employee health premium contributions at 6% over the contract's four years.

headline: Drought rules hold firm despite rain
abstract: Dauphin County commissioners are reminding residents to conserve water despite the recent rains. Commissioners say that the drought is still in PA and residents are urged to conserve water by at least 15%. A Penalty may be imposed if residents do not abide by the conservation order.

headline: Judge McFalls agrees to terms of program
abstract: Suspended Common Plea Judge Patrick McFalls was the 120th defendant to get his assignment to the Acerlerated Rehabilitative Disposition hearing for a drunk driving offense.

headline: Shanksville: Final flirt 93 search
abstract: The last search for debris and human remains from the crash of United Airlines Flight 93 turned out 125 people. The area was not completely canvassed in the fall. A five gallon bucket was filled with various metals and remains.

headline: Despite House rules change, itemized telephone records remain exempt from public view
abstract: The public is now able to view documentation to justify state Representatives' expenditures, however, the documentation is only in Harrisburg and may not be complete. House members will be notified when documents are being reviewed, and copies of such documents are not allowed.

headline: Libertarian adds spice to debate
abstract: Voters who watched the first televised debate of the gubernatorial campaign Thursday night didn't see anything memorable from Democrat Ed Rendell or Republican Mike Fisher.  Instead the candidate who stole Thursday's show was Libertarian Ken Krawchuck, whose acerbic one-liners and single-minded ideological clarity made the mainstream candidates bland.  Rendell acknowledged his closing statement the Libertarian had been responsible for most of the evening's fun, and after the debate Rendell's son Jesse cell-phoned his dad to say he was voting for Krawchuck.

headline: Scavello easily wins full term
abstract: PA State Representative Mario Scavello won a full term in office by defeating his Democrat challenger, Gratz Washenik for the 17th District seat.

headline: Saidel report: City shouldn't be hiring
abstract: Philadelphia City Controller Jonathan Saidel suggests Mayor Street should put city government on a diet in his annual mid-year report of the city's economic and financial well-being. The Daily News reports that the city's work force has grown by more than 350 since Street became mayor. Even though the city's population has declined in the last decade, the city's number of employees on payroll has increased.

headline: Greensburg Diocese remove another priest
abstract: Roman Catholic officials in Greensburg have permanently removed a fourth priest because of sexual abuse allegations.  The diocese declined to identify the priest, who was removed Tuesday.  Officials said the priest was not working in a parish and the allegations against him surfaced after the diocese began a review of church records in February.

headline: Miners hope new Quecreek probe will provide answers
abstract: The U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration have reopened their investigation into the Quecreek Mine accident. The Untied Mine Worker Union says that investigative results will have to show safety improvements before mine workers can get back to work.

headline: Dumping trash and cash
abstract: Landfill towns are debating the benefits of landfill money versus the effect of having the landfill in the town. A review of Plainfield township, Ferris, TX, and Tully town landfill and towns is done.

headline: Judge to retire in deal with state discipline court
abstract: An Allegheny County judge accused of being drunk on the bench and dropping his pants in public has agreed to resign, his attorney said.  Judge H. Patrick McFalls, 59, faced more than three dozen charges brought by the state's Judicial Conduct Board.  The board, which decides if there is enough evidence to bring a case to the Court of Judicial Discipline, has agreed to dismiss all charges against McFalls, according to a source at the Court of Judicial Discipline who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

headline: Slot machine proponenants are betting on new support this year.
abstract: Supporters of expanding gambling in Pennsylvania say they like the odds this year for adding slots to racetracks. Because of the $600 million budget hole the state faces; the number of surrounding states embracing gambling and three gubernatorial candidates open to the idea, advocates say there is growing interest in the idea among lawmakers.

headline: DeWeese: Republicans took a meat cleaver to our district!'
abstract: The new congressional reapportionment plan reduces the number of congressional representatives from 21 to 19 for the hills of Aleppo and the city of Johnstown. The plan was passed 28-22 by the Senate and 132-59 in the House. The Democrats are appalled by the congressional reapportionment plan.

headline: Lieutenant governor nominee visits county
abstract: Democratic lieutenant governor candidate Catherine Baker Knoll visited Scranton to help open her and Ed Rendell's area campaign office.

headline: Scavello victorious in 176th district. State representative thanks supporters in win over Washenik
abstract: PA State Representative Mario Scavello won the election on Tuesday by beating Democrat Gratz Washenik. Scavello's campaign focused on property tax reform .

headline: School funding focus of panel
abstract: A state House committee on public education is considering the idea of increasing the state's personal income tax to 4 percent and reducing the local school property tax by 50 percent. The committee is not close to any real decision on property tax reform.

headline: Gun-rights groups aim to boost Casey
abstract: Ed Rendell's position on gun control is to limit handguns to one a month. It is expected that the state's gun owners to  back Bob Casey Jr. in the Democratic primary. Guns have not been a major issue in the campaign, but are important to select groups.

headline: Miracle in the Mine Shaft
abstract: Blaine Mayhugh was one of the nine miners who were rescued after being trapped 240 feet below ground for more than three days.  Mayhugh knew the job was dangerous.  But the job paid $15 an hour- double that of most positions in Somerset County.

headline: Emissions tests changing
abstract: The state has changed how it measures emissions in vehicles. Some lawmakers feel the tests are a waste of time and target vehicles less likely to pollute. In 1997, the state began emissions testing in  highly populated areas.

headline: Judge to step aside in some cases over relationship to Lt. Gov.
abstract: Commonwealth Judge Renee Cohn will disqualify herself when the court hears cases dealing with the state senate or the Schweiker administration, said Lt. Gov. Robert C. Jubelirer, who is engaged to Cohn. The judge was elected to the court in November and will serve a 10-year term. The court hears cases involving the state and serves as an appeals court interpreting the meaning of actions taken by the Legislature.

headline: Slotsa luck: Philly Park may get one-armed bandits
abstract: All four of Pennsylvania's tracks are prohibited from having by law slot machines. Pennsylvania's track owners want to add slot machines at their tracks to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue. Sal Debund, vice president of the Pennsylvania Thoroughbred Horsemen's Association, fears that unless any of the several pending bills in the state legislature make it into law, Philadelphia Park will suffer the same fate as the old Liberty Bell harness in the Northeast.

headline: DiCicco-Mariano feud over redistricting heats up
abstract: There's definitely bad blood between former buddies Frank DiCicco and Rick Mariano, a couple of dapper City Council Democrats who've been warring for months over redistricting plans. The point of contention between Mariano and DiCicco has been the 23rd Ward. The Daily News newspaper has offered to hire a certified polygraph operator who would administer a detailed test to both of them.

headline: Life inside county GOP not a party
abstract: Two Republicans were elected to the state House of Representatives and Republicans won 14 of 18 municipal races. The chairperson for the Monroe County Republican Committee is facing tough competition.

headline: Scavello, Battisto agree on something: Don't believe everything you see on TV
abstract: Republican Mario Scavello and Democrat Joe Battisto are each crying foul over television commercials, paid for by their represenative state committees, that have flooded the airwaves over the past week.  Battisto's commercials have accused Scavello of raising taxes five of the six years Scavello served as mayor of Mount Pocono, and for squandering a $6 million reserve fund over the past two years as a Monroe County commissioner.  Scavello's commercials have accused Battisto, a nine-term represenative for the 189th District, of voting for more than 20 tax increases and for bringing back little in funding for local road projects.

headline: School mulls Act 24
abstract: School officials had good news and bad news for Lewisburg taxpayers. The good news is that occupational tax is officially gone. The bad news is that without the occupational tax the district is facing a projected deficit over the next five years that would require a 12.7 million tax increase to balance the budget.

headline: Hearing on whether plaque can stay for now
abstract: The battle over the Ten Commandments plaque at the Chester County Courthouse returns to federal court today as a judge considers whether to order its immediate removal.  U.S. District Judge Stewart Dalzell will hold a hearing to consider the county's position that removing the plaque from the 155-year-old building will cause irreparable damage to the building wall.  The county and the American Civil Liberties Union, which is suing on behalf of local atheists to have the plaque removed, will present testimony from engineers on the technical aspects of removing the plaque.

headline: Nuclear workers waiting for funds
abstract: Sickened nuclear weapons plant employees who have filed claims for $150,000 in compensation from a newly established federal program are beginning to wonder whether they'll ever see the money, but the agency administering the program is asking claimants to be patient. The compensation act, known as the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program, was launched on July 31 and is managed by the U.S. Department of Labor. The act is supposed to compensate workers who handled uranium, plutonium, beryllium and other cancerous or toxic agents while building weapons components and conducting nuclear experiments in the '40s, '50s, and '60s.

headline: EPA offers consent decrees for sewer repairs
abstract: Federal environmental regulators announced that they want 83 Allegheny County municipalities to agree to fix $2 billion worth of sewer overflow problems or face millions of dollars in fines. The consent agreement would waive fines from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for past pollution and give municipalities until 2007 to monitor, inspect, and repair their sewer systems. The EPA offered the consent agreement as an alternative to fining municipalities that violate pollution standards.

headline: Judicial Center
abstract: Pennsylvania is one of the few states that doesn't have a centralized judicial system in its state capital. Rather, appellate judges - except for Commonwealth Court- and the judicial administrative staff are scattered around the commonwealth.  The high cost and inefficiency of this ancient arrangement is recognized in plans for a Pennsylvania Judicial Center to be built in the Capitol Complex to house Commonwealth Court, now located in the South Office Building, the administrative offices of the three appellate courts, the Judicial Conduct Board and Court of Judicial Discipline.

headline: Smokers have time to buy cigarettes at current prices
abstract: Cigarette smokers in Pennsylvania who want to stock up before the 69-cent-a-pack tax increase takes effect have some time to do so.  The tax of $1 a pack, which takes effect July 15, is more than triple the current tax of 31 cents.  The money helps fund a $20.7 billion state budget that contains the state's largest tax increase in 11 years.

headline: Did Barley have too much power?
abstract: As Republican lawmakers search for the next House Appropriations chairman, a would-be successor to state Rep. John Barley has promised to separate the two roles that gave Barley - -the outgoing chairman - -much of his political clout.  GOP state Rep. Jess Stairs, responding to rumors circulating Capitol Hill about Barley's resignation, said he wants to eliminate any links between the powerful House Appropriations Committee and the House Republican Campaign Committee, the fund raising arm of the Republican Party.

headline: most of gubernatorial candidates contribution were under $500
abstract: Of the 22,000 contributions that gubernatorial candidates Ed Rendell and Mike Fisher received in the past two years, more than 60% were form people giving $500 or less.

headline: School pension fund may be staggering to Bethlehem taxpayers
abstract: Due to stock market problems, pension funds for PA school teachers and employees has lost $10 billion. Taxpayers will mostly likely be force to pay for the money lost in the PA Public School Employees Retirement System. Local officials are speaking out and blaming state lawmakers for the problem and not the stock markets.

headline: Schools officials brace for severe financial shortfall
abstract: Various school districts are struggling to balance their budget with little help coming from Harrisburg. Local property taxes will have to increase greatly to help compensate. Some residents have rallied in Harrisburg for more money.

headline: Heightened security still rules the day
abstract: Six months after the terrorist attacks of September 11th, heightened security remains. The state Army National Guard, state police and airport security continue to patrol airports, nuclear power plants, and other facilities throughout Luzerne County. People are starting to travel again.

headline: Pension agency to take over LTV pensions
abstract: A federal insurance corporation on Monday will assume responsibility for three under funded LTV Steel Co. pension plans that cover about 82,000 former employees and retirees of the bankrupt steelmaker.  The termination of the three plans is by far the largest and most costly in the 27-year history of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp., the federal agency that guarantees employers' defined benefit pension plans said yesterday.  The plans together have liabilities of $4.4 billion and combined assets of almost $2.2 billion, meaning they are under funded by approximately $2.2 billion, according to PBGC estimates.

headline: Expert: Deer hunting depends on management
abstract: Dr. Gary Alt studies and manages the state's black bear population. He now is trying to help the deer herd by changing the state's antler restrictions to three or more as the minimum number of points per antler to legally kill a deer.

headline: Jury selected in 1969 races riot trial
abstract: An all-white jury has been selected in the trial of three white men charged with murder in the death of a young black woman during York's 1969 race riots.  The six women and six men have little recall of the 10 days in July, except for one woman who lived across the street from a white police officer fatally shot during the upheaval.  That woman, who was 8 years old during the riots, remembers the curfews police placed on the city and the three days her mother took her out of the city to avoid the violence.  Standing trial in the July 21, 1969, death of Lillie Belle Allen are Charlie Robertson, who for eight years was the mayor of the city of 41,000, and two men prosecutors say were members of white gangs that ambushed Allen's car.

headline: Some get relief, others are wondering
abstract: A letter, delivered by Federal Express, from Chase Manhattan Mortgage Corp., informed a home owner that the mortgage on his home in A Pocono Country Place would be reduced to reflect the home's true value.  The Chase plan, which could soon turn the Pocono dream of home ownership into more pleasant, stress-free reality.  But hundred of others, duped into buying homes at inflated prices, are still hoping for relief a year after the Pocono Record published a three-day investigative series entitled 'A Price Too High' detailing extensive real estate fraud.

headline: Did Rendell really save Philadelphia?
abstract: Ed Rendell's mayoral record in Philadelphia is reviewed to gage Rendell as a potential governor. Rendell was able to approach Philadelphia's budget crisis and surrounded himself with competent people. One things that Rendell would not have as a governor is the Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, which was a tool that Rendell used in getting concessions from labor unions.

headline: Lisotto in the 56th
abstract: Republican candidate Susanna Lissoto is running against Democrat  Representative James Casorio in the PA State House race for the 56th district.

headline: School-panel interviews continue
abstract: Former Philadelphia school board member and prominent business leader Rosemarie Greco was one of six candidates interviewed yesterday for a spot on the new state School Reform Commission overseeing city schools. Greco, who emerged from the interview at Governor Schweiker's Center City office, said she was not sure she would accept the post if it were offered.

headline: Schweiker plea opens tax session
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker said yesterday that voters should have strong new controls over local school board spending decisions as part of any comprehensive school property tax reforms.  The session, prompted by lawmaker petitions, marks the Legislature's latest attempt to solve the $7 billion Rubik's Cube the school property tax issue has become.  Most legislators agree that the state relies too heavily on the property tax to pay for public schools, but to date- -despite 30 years of effort- - there has been no consensus on how to replace that funding system.

headline: High Court Reaffirms 'Truth in Sentencing' Capital-Case Jurors Must Know Options
abstract: The Supreme Court, in a split decision, reaffirmed that courts must tell jurors that life without parole is an alternative to the death penalty in capital murder cases where the defendant's future dangerousness is at issue. The court's 5 to 4 ruling marked the first time it had applied a "truth in sentencing" principle it laid down in 1994 to a case where prosecutor did not explicitly argue that the defendant would be a public menace in the future but rather used language, such as "murderers will be murderers," that arguably implied the defendant would be a threat even if sentenced to prison.

headline: Some state jobless funds struggling to stay solvent
abstract: The House passed an economic-stimulus bill that packaged a 13-week benefit extension with health care assistance and corporate tax breaks.  Employers finance unemployment compensation by paying federal and state taxes on their payrolls. The federal portion, which funds the loan pool for states with shortfalls, also would pay for the proposed 13-week extension.

headline: Family who owned drilling site offers hospitality in ordeal
abstract: The man from the state Department of Environmental Protection stopped by Bill and Lori Arnold's farm yesterday and told the world that, before too long, the place would be looking like new.  That place would be the six acres of gully where six bulls and 14 heifers last week were doing what bull and heifers do.  That was before the equipment moved in, tons and tons of equipment: drills and cranes and earthmovers, all set down on a newly pitched base of softball-sized shale.  It was there that they cleared and drilled and forced air down a shaft where nine miners were stuck 240 feet underground.

headline: Law grad assigned lesson in lockup
abstract: A law school graduate who failed to report for jury duty in Dauphin County this week got a refresher course in civil service- - the top judge ordered her locked up for three days.  Angela Hlatky, a former law review member from Widener University, was taken into custody Tuesday at her job in the legal division of the state Worker's Compensation Appeal Board.  Sheriff's deputies were sent to her North Seventh Street office after calling Hlatky unsuccessfully for two days to ask why she had not appeared in court as ordered.

headline: State relaxes some drought designations
abstract: Governor Schweiker lifted a drought emergency in six central and eastern counties and normalized the drought status of 14 other counties.  Fourteen central and eastern counties remain in a drought emergency. Residents are asked to cut back on up to 15% of water usage.

headline: Differences: True, Blair debate
abstract: Monday night's debat between Republican candidates Steve Blair and Katie True for the new 41st District House seat turned into a verbal boxing match.  Before a packed house at the East Hempfield Township municipal building, Blair, the attorney, and True, the former state lawmaker, wasted no time going after each other's credibility, integrity, and, to a lesser degree, stance on thei issues.  The event sponsored by the Lancaster County League of Women Voters, was moderated by former league president Edwina Coder.

headline: Lobbying donations may fade from view
abstract: Lt. Gov. Robert Jubelirer (R. Blair) and his chief of staff each got a $400 ticket to the 2002 Super Bowl in New Orleans, courtesy of Anheuser-Busch.  Rep. Susan Laughlin (D., Allegheny) was one of several lawmakers to receive a $2,400 preseason pass to the slopes from the Pennsylvania Ski Areas Association during 2000.  And Rep. Tom Gannon (R., Delaware) got a pair of tickets to a performance of Nutcracker in December 2000, a $568 gift from the Pennsylvania Ballet.  But the public might not be able to view such information about state government much longer now that the Pennsylvania Supreme Court has nullified the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

headline: Schools to compensate for pension-fund losses
abstract: The PA State Legislature passed a bill to soften the blow of pension fund losses to school district taxpayers. The school-districts will pay annually to the Public School Employees Retirement System, the $43 billion pension fund for the retired public school workers.

headline: Seizing the moment while city's wage tax is a hot issue
abstract: Mayor Street is against any wage-tax reduction and wants to scrap the program of mini-cuts set by the former Mayor. City Councilman Michael Nutter is pushing a bill which would cut the tax for residents and commuters.

headline: House panel approves $8 million for Pennsylvania National Guard
abstract: The House Appropriations Committee has approved Congressman George Gekas' request for $8 million in counter terrorism and counter drug funds for the PA National Guard.

headline: Street unfazed by balking union
abstract: Mayor Street isn't discouraged by the carpenters union's rejection of key labor reforms proposed for the city's troubled Convention Center.  The carpenters union, which provides the largest work force at the Convention Center, said it did not support a unified labor pool proposed to end labor strife.  The Teamsters union, according to today's Inquirer, also has rejected the unified-work-force proposal with Teamsters Local 107 President Bill Hamilton stipulating, "We're not against a combined type of work force that makes sense."

headline: Federal OK given to reopen Quecreek
abstract: Pennsylvania state and federal regulators have approved a plan for the resumption of mine operations at Quecreek. The U.S. Department of Environmental Protection will issue their final report on the mine and perhaps a reopening of the mine can occur.

headline: Lawmaker: Ban executions of retarded
abstract: State Senator Edward W. Helfrick want Pennsylvania to ban the execution of mentally retarded death row inmates. The Senate Judiciary Committee heard from Helfrick and various other experts on the issue.

headline: State store reform not swaying many voters
abstract: One issue that unites every single person in Pennsylvania is state store reform. PA Attorney General Mike Fisher's promise to abolish state stores and selling them to private industries, to finance public education, has not seemed to get him any votes in his bid for PA governor.

headline: Director is grateful for chance
abstract: Ridge has been in his high-profile job as the nation's first homeland security director for six months.  During that time, the former Pennsylvania governor, has experienced what many have called an impossible task.  Ridge begins most days with the White House senior staff meeting, followed by intelligence briefings with the FBI, CIA and other agencies.  When President Bush is in town, they often meet.

headline: Local TV stations get political-ad windfall
abstract: You might find them boring or even annoying, but the deluge of campaign advertisements flitting across your tube form now until Election Day means big bucks for local television stations.  The stations increase their rates as demand for air times soars, and some critics accuse local stations of colluding to artificially boost the cost of ad purchases near elections.  The problem is worse in the five-station Wilkes-Barre/Scranton media market, in which election-cycle advertising rates "are probably two or three times more than in other markets its size," said a veteran campaign operative, who did not want to be named.

headline: Schuykill controller won't challenge Allen Gary
abstract: Schuykill County Controller Gary Hornberger announced that he will not run for the 125th District state House seat. Hornberger, a Republican serving his second term, said he considered challenging state Rep. Bob Allen, R-Schuykill, in the May primarybut decided not to do so after finding little political support.

headline: Senator proposes cut in Philadelphia wage tax
abstract: Proposed legislation would cut the Philadelphia wage tax so residents would pay 3.5 percent and nonresidents would pay 3.04 percent. Many are pushing for tax cuts because the city has the highest wage tax of all major cities.

headline: House passes bill to limit monetary liability in lawsuits
abstract: The state House has passed a tort reform bill that small businesses, manufacturers, hospitals and other groups have praised as a major step toward reining in lawsuit abuse.  Lawmakers voted 117-78 for a "Fair Share Act" that will limit a defendants liability for monetary damages in a civil suit to its share of responsibility for causing the injury, as determined by a jury.  The bill now goes to the Senate for approval.  Proponents said the bill will help correct a state legal climate that is causing hospitals to discontinue certain services and businesses to expand in other states.

headline: Tentative agreement to save troubled airline $465 million
abstract: U.S. Airways and its pilots union have tentatively agreed on a package of wage and benefit concessions -- a major breakthrough in the hobbled airline's attempt to slash labor costs and avoid filing for bankruptcy protection.  Negotiators for the Air Line Pilots Association agreed to $465 million in annual wage and benefit concessions over the next year 6 1/2 years, ALPA spokesman Roy Freundlich said yesterday.  The figure represents about 85 percent of the $547 million in concessions that the company requested in its most recent offer to unionized pilots, down from management's initial request in May of $595 million over 7 1/2 years.

headline: Fee increase won't deter trash imports
abstract: The Patriot News characterizes a $5 tax on the tipping fee at Pennsylvania's solid waste disposal sites as a way of discouraging the influx of out-of-state waste.  There is no economic evidence to support that conclusion.  Based on figures just released by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, there is hard economic data to support the conclusion that Pennsylvanians generate 14.2 million tons of municipal and residual waste each year which is disposed at Pennsylvania landfills and the $5 tax will cost them $71 million annually.

headline: Lawyers line up for bench
abstract: Nine lawyers will screen before the Bucks County Bar Association for the vacancy on the Bucks County Court. The judge that left was Judge Cynthia Weaver Rufe who was confirmed by the US Senate last week to fill a vacancy on the US District Court in Philadelphia.

headline: State stores take spotlight
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher and former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell have debated on how much to change state laws on liquor sales and lawsuit liability.  The two disagreed but also praised each other in their first face-off as their parties' nominees in a 45-minute forum in the Penn Starter Conference Center, sponsored by the Chamber of Business & Industry of Centre County.

headline: Disappointed by Casey, impressed by Rendell
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey Jr. has alienated voters with his television commercials. He has bashed Ed Rendell, his opponent. Geoffrey Brace of North Whitehall Township wants candidates to talk about their ideas.

headline: Long odds for third parties
abstract: The major-party candidates for Pennsylvania governor have been campaigning for months, but some candidates have to work for a living, Green Party nominee Michael Morrill said through the static crackle of a long-distance, pay-phone call.  Rendell, the Democratic former mayor of Philadelphia, and Fisher, the Republican attorney general, have run high-profile campaigns, raising money measured in the millions.  Meanwhile, Morrill and Libertarian candidate Ken Krawchuk have been running grass-roots campaigns, with finds measured in the thousands.  The odds of Morrill or Krawchuk winning are particularly grim this year, analysts say, because the election season offers nothing that would push a third-party candidate to the forefront.

headline: Schweiker enjoys record approval rating
abstract: The Republican governor's approval ratings have soared to 66 percent, according to a poll released yesterday.  A July poll showed Schweiker with only a 50 percent approval rating.  But that poll was taken just before Schweiker garnered national celebrity status for his roll in the rescue of nine trapped miners in Somerset County.  In the span of just a few days, the former Bucks County commissioner went from "Governor who?" to a political celebrity drawing comparisons to New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani after Sept. 11.

headline: Shortfall due in city schools no matter who is in charge
abstract: Even with extra money from the city and state, Philadelphia School District could be facing a budget hole of $100 million in just three years. City Council heard the district's proposed $1.72 billion spending proposal to restore its finances.

headline: House passes final version  of lawsuit-reform bill
abstract: The PA House of Representatives have approved a bill that will hold defendants responsible for only their share of damages or harm done to a plaintiff. This lawsuit-reform bill restrict the previous concept of joint and several liability.

headline: The 'living wage' - Economically bankrupt
abstract: Pittsburgh's new law requires an hourly wage of $9.12 for those with health insurance and $10.62 for those without. Mayor Tom Murphy will introduce legislation that would kill Pittsburgh's living wage law. Murphy believes that the law will create a less-competitive environment.

headline: Flood of hog manure gushes into stream
abstract: Hog manure overflowed from a 770,000-gallon pit at Fulton County, Pa., farm and coursed into a steam 150 yards away, turning it black, state officials said yesterday.  The amount spilled at the south-central Pennsylvania pig farm was unknown, since investigators do not know how long the manure was overflowing before it was first reported Friday.  George Geisler, the agency's regional manger of law enforcement, predicted "significant" environmental damage and said the farm's owner might face criminal charges.

headline: Lewis: Special interests tainted appraisal measure
abstract: A bill aimed at tightening oversight of Pennsylvania appraisers has lost the support of PA State Representative Kelly Lewis. The bill contained new legislation giving the PA attorney general the jurisdiction to prosecute appraisers under the Unfair Trade Practices Act. The bill also called for the creation of two new board positions, to be filled by a representative from the PA attorney general's office and by a citizen not aligned with real estate.

headline: State targets Amish for unlicensed feeds
abstract: The state Department of Agriculture says that the Amish are violating the law by cooking and selling meals to tourists. It is a violation because the Amish are not licensed to serve food to the public in their homes according to the state health and zoning laws.

headline: Disappointing?
abstract: The PA State Legislative session has ended for the year without passing a reform bill on medical malpractice or on property tax. Pennsylvania State Representative Stephen Cappelli says the legislature wasted a lot of time and made little progress. Other lawmakers agree.

headline: 'Long Overdue' Move to Update to Open Records Law Impresses Local Legislature
abstract: Local lawmakers say the state's new open records bill better defines what documents citizens can peruse and provides improved prosecutorial powers for those who are wronged.  Rep. Steven W . Cappelli, R-Williamsport, said the new legislation would define who and what are subject to the law and what recourse they have.  He was among the overwhelming number of House members who voted in favor of the legislation earlier this week.  The bill now goes before the state Senate.

headline: Schweiker Oks session on tax reform
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker Wednesday evening ended weeks of anticipation when he announced he would convene a special session of the Legislature Sept. 4 aimed at reducing local property taxes.  Schweiker was required to call the session because Sen. Lisa Boscola, D.-Northampton, collected a majority of state legislators' signatures on a petition seeking the session.  All 11 Democratic state legislators representing Luzerne and Lackawanna counties signed the petition, which marks the first use of an obscure constitutional provision allowing the General Assembly to force the governor to call a special session.

headline: Some city residents appeal increased property taxes
abstract: Chairman of the Board of Revision of Taxes, David Glacey has stated that the number of appeals filed for increased property taxes was not significantly higher than last year. Typically 20% of those who file property tax appeals do usually receive some tax relief.

headline: Perspectives: She brings business sense to aging county agency
abstract: Prior to impending release of tobacco settlement funds, the Pennsylvania Lottery was the principle source of financing for services to the aging. With relatively flat income from the Lottery and a steadily increasing demand for services, the Allegheny County Area Agency on Aging is challenged to maintain high levels of services to county seniors. In an attempt to be more entrepreneurial, the agency is planning to charge "customers" for certain services that it can uniquely provide.

headline: Threat to close to site during talks violates state law, labor board says
abstract: The state Labor Relations Board has ruled that the Dauphin County commissioners violated state labor law by threatening to close the Schaffner Youth Center in the course of contract negotiations. A two-page decision overturns an administrative decision issued by the board's secretary holding that the commissioners did no wrong. The ruling is not expected to have any direct effect on the center's proposed closing but could become a factor in lawsuits after it closes.

headline: Forum on the Mon Fayette Expressway: Stay out of the city
abstract: The Group Against Smog and Pollution opposes of the Mon-Fayette Expressway into Pittsburgh. We see this extension, landing around Bates Street in South Oakland, as likely to have serious adverse effects on human and natural environments in and near the city. GASP's primary mission has always been to restrain pollution of the environment.

headline: License scam suspects face deportation
abstract: Legal battles for the 15 of the 21 Middle Eastern men arrested last year in a license-selling scam won't be over after their criminal cases are resolved in U.S. District Court here.  The U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service then will conduct hearings to determine if the 15 men should not be deported, officials said. Six of the defendants are naturalized U.S. citizens and will not face deportation.

headline: State telemarketing bill advances
abstract: The state Senate Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure Committee yesterday unanimously endorsed legislation that would toughen regulation on telemarketing. Committee members sent the bill on to the full senate. H.B. 1469 would require the state attorney general's office to offer a free "do not call" list of consumers that would be maintained by a nonprofit organization.

headline: Do you know who your congressman is?
abstract: Redistricting has left many voters to be put in new districts. Every 10 years, districts are redrawn by politicians in Harrisburg. Often neighborhoods are split.

headline: Looking ahead
abstract: The Joint PA State Government Commission's task force is scheduled to meet.

headline: Schweiker receives 51% approval rating from Pennsylvanians
abstract: After eight months on the job, a majority of Pennsylvanians think Governor Mark Schweiker is performing well.  Fifty-one percent responded in a poll that they approved of the way Schweiker is handling his job as Governor.  Ten percent did not approve and thirty-nine percent had no opinion.

headline: Sources: Street taking new tack on tax cuts
abstract: Philadelphia's Democratic Mayor Street will address the city council today regarding tax cuts and a proposal for the city's budget.  Street's proposal for continued gross-receipts tax cuts are an extension from former Mayor Rendell's administration. Street will not continue Rendell's wage tax cuts, which generates over half of the city's general-fund tax revenue. Street's budget proposal will include cutting personnel budgets of various city departments and deferring funds to the municipal pension fund.

headline: Protesters seek Santorum's help
abstract: Protesters rallied outside the federal courthouse in Allentown on Monday and demanded that U.S. Sen. Rick Santorum support legislation that would fund at-home care for people with disabilities.  Carrying signs and handing out fliers, the protesters picketed the courthouse at 504 Hamilton St. because Santorum, R-Pa, has an office in the federal building.  Peggy Dougherty of Easton said she and the rest of the protesters wanted Santorum's support in writing for Senate Bill 1298, which would allow anyone receiving Social Security disability payments to use the money for attendant care inside the home.

headline: Threat of injury or death just part of the business, ironworkers say
abstract: One ironworker perished and two others were injured at an U.S. Steel Coke Works in Clairton. Since the late 1990's, the federal Occupational Health and Safety Administration have required ironworkers to wear a full-body harness. The two ironworkers injured in a structural collapse were left dangling by their safety harness about 100 feet above the ground as the truss where they were working fell.

headline: Game Commission rebuffed in vote on elk-, deer-farming
abstract: The state Game Commission believes that a deadly neurological disease will be able to strike the wild deer herd more if the commission loses its regulatory oversight of elk and red deer for commercial purposes. Proposed legislation would exclude elk and red deer kept in livestock operations from the definition of game animals.

headline: Local authorities praise Oley outcome
abstract: Faced with an occupied school bus being commandeered off its regular route, local school and police officials said they could do little more than what authorities did in the same situation. An extensive search covering the township of Oley, the county, and the state was issued by state police in an emergency message across the Commonwealth Law Enforcement Assistance network. Governor Mark Schweiker thanked authorities for their efforts.

headline: State to use young people in search for liquor-law violator
abstract: The state of PA has passed a new law that will allow liquor law compliance checks to be done by police officers aged 18-20. The compliance law will allow teenagers and young adults to go into liquor and tobacco businesses and check to see if they will sell to an underage person.

headline: Doctor's ad campaign baseless
abstract: Soaring premiums are the reason for many doctors to leave Pennsylvania. Doctors have created many advertisements stated this, but some have found that the situation is not as bad as they claim. Statistics show that the campaign's theme to be unfounded.

headline: Looking for an edge
abstract: Pennsylvania GOP Representative John M. Perzel, majority leader of the state House, tapped into the public's money (special leadership fund) to acquire U.S. Census data from researchers at Carnegie Mellon University.  Perzel used these funds to navigate the re-drawing of the state's legislative boundaries to enhance the Republican party's control of Pennsylvania politics. Democrats did not have the same access to this data even though Carnegie Mellon officials insisted that state House Republicans had guaranteed that the data would also be made available to Democrats.

headline: Schweiker says he tried to be state's CEO(, people's governor
abstract: PA Governor Mark Schweiker, in an interview, has stated that his term as governor will end with few regrets and no plans to run for future public office. A brief review of Schweiker's time in politics is also given.

headline: State AARP marks new territory with property tax activism
abstract: The American Association of Retired Persons would like to see property taxes cut and school quality raised at the same time. The AARP's 1.8 million members will receive a voter guide that includes property tax questions posed to gubernatorial candidates Mike Fisher and Ed Rendell. The AARP does not endorse political candidates and has not endorsed and property tax alternative.

headline: Sather urges seniors to attend expo
abstract: State Rep. Larry Sather, R. Huntingdon, is encouraging seniors to attend his third annual Senior Expo from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Thursday at the Standing Stone Senior Center.  The expo will feature more than a dozen exhibitors to provide information on services and agencies available to seniors, as well as free admission, refreshments, door przes, entertainment by Dan and Galla and more.

headline: Union dues
abstract: The Pennsylvania Convention Center is an expensive place to do business and losing business because of these high costs and union workers bad mouthing customers. Mayor Street needs to address these issues with union officials, but is hesitating because they are key political allies of his.

headline: Game Commission sets ban
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission announced Tuesday it is banning the importation of live deer and elk into the state as part of its efforts to prevent Chronic Wasting Disease from spreading here.  The fatal neurological disorder --- similar to Mad Cow Disease in bovines and Creutzfeldt-Jacob Disease in humans --- has run rampant across Western states in recent years. There is no evidence of Chronic Wasting Disease in Pennsylvania, and game commission officials want to keep it that way.

headline: Malpractice issue may not be about money, study says
abstract: A recent study by Judges John W. Herron and Albert W. Sheppard Jr. found that the number of big-money jury awards in malpractice cases dropped by one-third last year. The study sparked an immediate reaction from both sides of the malpractice issue. Lawmakers hope to have the malpractice-insurance package ready for Gov. Schweikers's signature next week.

headline: State warns of telemarketing scam
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher has issued a warning about an alleged Canadian-based telemarketing scam.  The scam claims to stop all telemarketing calls to a person's home for 10 years for a payment of $3.99 a month or a one-time fee of $299.

headline: Does poll mean lead for Rendell?
abstract: According to a SurveyUSA computer-response poll for television stations in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, Edward G. Rendell has pulled ahead of Robert P. Casey Jr. for the first time in the Democratic primary for governor.  But many experts in polling cast doubts on the technique used in the survey.  Both campaigns said they believe that the race is tightening, though not to the extent shown in the SurveyUSA poll.

headline: low voters turnout predicted
abstract: Voters registration in Westmoreland County is at an all-time high with 239,304 registered voters. Local officials, however, suspect that turnout for the PA gubernatorial election will be far below expectations.

headline: Schweiker to offer tax reform guides
abstract: On the first day of a special session today on changing the property tax system, Gov. Mark Schweiker said he will offer state lawmakers general guidelines for achieving reform but will not focus on specifics of how to change the tax structure.  Schweiker will address a joint session of the House and Senate this afternoon.  The governor called the special session in response to a petition from a majority of state lawmakers.

headline: State action on tax reform not near Luzerne County is grappling with reassessment, and it appears unlikely that Harrisburg will make moves on its own
abstract: Luzerne County commissioners will hold a public meeting in the courthouse to discuss reassessment, but they say the real solution to the county's problems lies in Harrisburg. Although most state lawmakers agree there are serious problems with the property tax-bases system on which counties, municipalities and most school districts rely, efforts to change it have proved unsuccessful.

headline: Senior citizens might eventually be able to keep their assets and have Uncle Sam help out more with their nursing home care
abstract: The state House approved a bill which would allow senior citizens and disabled people to use federal government assistance without having to first use their own funds for long-term care. Before the bill, seniors would have to use all of their savings and sell all of their assets before they can receive government assistance.

headline: Workers' compensation dispute focuses on part-time employment
abstract: Charles Snyder Jr. had a workplace accident which rendered him a quadriplegic. He is trying to get the state Supreme Court to restore his workers' compensation to higher levels. Previously a Commonwealth Court panel ruled that his part-time wages should be included in the equation to figure out his compensation.

headline: Game commission shakes up tradition
abstract: The state Game Commission has changed the rules for buck and doe seasons which has caused on uprising. Hunters are encouraged to kill does rather than wait for the three-day bonus hunt. It will not take long to tell if the Commission has made the right decision.

headline: Many local police departments have not reported crime statistics
abstract: About 400 of the state's 1,126 police departments have still not reported their 2001 crime figures.

headline: States are taking a look at Andersen's accounting
abstract: The accounting firm of Arthur Andersen is under investigation by state regulators who hold the power to take away its right to practice. States rarely revoke a large firm's license, but some regulators are considering the possibility in Andersen's case because of the size and devastation wrought by Enron Corp.'s bankruptcy.  Andersen signed off on Enron's books, including questionable partnership deals that contributed to its collapse.

headline: Dolusio dropped job-bias suit
abstract: Former Bethlehem Area School District technology coordinator Angelo Speziale has dropped his federal court allegations against Superintendent Thomas Doluisio. Speziale is claiming he was wrongfully fired and that Doluisio forced him to extract campaign contributions from district vendors.

headline: Lynch holds off challenger
abstract: State Representative Jim Lynch will run unopposed for reelection in November.  Lynch defeated Warren real estate business owner David Kell in the Republican Primary Election for state representative of the 65th District.  There were no state representative candidates on the ballot in the Democratic Primary, but both Kell and Rutherford campaigned for the write-in votes.

headline: Schweiker; leaders hold talks on budget
abstract: Governor Mark Schweiker and state legislative leaders held a meeting to discuss the 2002-2003 budget. The meeting did not leave any participant feeling like progress was made or anyone was satisfied with finacial decisions.

headline: State lawmakers offer good news on property taxes
abstract: After weeks of dire warnings and bleak school-budget projections, millions of Pennsylvania's property owners finally have received some good news: It looks as though their taxes won't be going up as much as they thought.  However, school officials warned yesterday, the price for a tax break now might mutate into a fiscal nightmare later.  By a unanimous vote late Tuesday night, the state House and Senate passed a bill that greatly reduced the amount that school districts have to pay into the state pension plan for teachers, which suffered tremendous losses in the last two years.

headline: Smashing success of complete failure?
abstract: The state legislature enacted welfare reform that would enforce regulations and cut the state's welfare rolls in half. Critics claim the growing economy helped cut welfare rolls. Others say it has reduced welfare rolls, but hasn't helped reduce poverty.

headline: Workers' compensation rates are increasing as pool of insurers is shrinking
abstract: The state House Labor Relations Committee researched how workers' compensation rates have been affected by the terrorist attacks of 2001. The rates have been increasing even before 9-11. Businesses are struggling to get insurance.

headline: Game official pitches antler restrictions
abstract: The state Game Commission's Deer Management Section supervisor is promoting a two-week concurrent antlered and antlerless white-tailed deer season and an early pre-rut hunt. The game commission's Board of Commissioners gave preliminary approval of the recommended four or more points her antler restrictions.

headline: McFalls' drinking may cost him his job
abstract: The state Judicial Conduct Board has accused Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge H. Patrick McFalls Jr. on 35 counts of abusing alcohol and neglecting his duties. They have asked that he be suspended without pay while awaiting a trial, that could result in his removal from the bench.  The complaint was the second lodged against McFalls by the board. The new complaint alleges that McFalls presided over official business while under the influence of alcohol, postponed official business because of this drinking, appeared intoxicated in public, partially disrobed in public, was arrested and charged with drunken driving and failed to file proper reports with the state Supreme Court on cases pending before him.

headline: Strip club spending scrutinized by auditors
abstract: The embattled former head of the Delaware River and Bay Authority is the main target of an investigation into employees frequenting Philadelphia strip clubs and spending public money at massage parlors, officials said Wednesday.  A spokesman for Delaware Gov. Ruth Ann Minner has called revelations of the illicit excursions only the "tip of the iceberg."  State and federal officials are investigating.

headline: Domestic issues trump war in congressional races
abstract: According to a USA today survey, candidates for PA House and Senate seats' campaigns have reflected the issues voters cared most about including, jobs, the economy, retirement security, and prescription-drug costs.

headline: Lynch won't rearrange schedule 'for some cowboy event' debate
abstract: Two of the three candidates for the PA 65th district seat in the PA State House, Alan Kiser and Sheila Brooker, will debate at the Knights of Columbus Hall. PA State Representative Jim Lynch, the incumbent and third candidate, has refused to attend the debate and said he is not willing to change his schedule for the event.

headline: Scramble on to redraw maps
abstract: Top Republicans in the state Legislature cleared the way yesterday for a vote next week to redraw the state's congressional districts, necessary because the map approved in January was thrown out by a panel of federal judges on Monday.  If a new plan is approved,  it could make it unnecessary to push the planned May 21 primary election until September, as some lawmakers have suggested.  Republican leaders of the state House and Senate said yesterday they will go ahead and redraw the confessional district boundaries - - set in January because of the 2000 U.S. Census - - while they appeal  the ruling of a special three-judge federal court panel that found the current map to be unconstitutional.

headline: State passes tax collector bill
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker has signed a bill that will make it easier for small towns to have local tax collectors when nobody wants the job, a measure sponsored by state Rep. Steven Nickol.  The bill allows neighboring municipalities to form "joint tax collection districts" to share the same tax collector.  Nickol (R-Hanover) said he thought of the concept after hearing about Railroad Borough and several other towns in Pennsylvania contracting out their tax collection services because they couldn't find someone to do the job.

headline: Social Security fight heats up
abstract: Seizing on poll data, indicating current and future retirees don’t trust Republicans on social security, Democrats across the country are hammering opponents who favor diverting money from social security into personal investment accounts. Democrats suggest that Republicans can't manage the economy and have misguided the priorities.

headline: Workers on farms fear talk of unions
abstract: Hispanic workers in the state's $352 million mushroom industry will not talk about union support out of fear of being fired. However, workers at the Kaolin Mushroom Farm in Kennett Square signed a collective bargaining agreement. They are the only mushroom union in the state.

headline: Gas-spill residents hold 'roast' for EPA
abstract: According to Laurel Gardens residents, the US Environmental Protection Agency has not responded appropriately to a 50,000 to 900,000 gallon fuel spill. The community is seeking expert help to determine the aspects of the situation.

headline: McFalls' judicial superiors outline 5 steps for his return
abstract: Judge McFalls has had a second alcoholic relapse. Two fellow Allegheny County Common Pleas Court judges recommended that when Judge McFalls should abstain from alcohol, submit to and pay for weekly random blood tests, attend AA, attend "relapse prevention therapy" sessions and participate in an aftercare program.

headline: Student loan agency's leader plans to retire
abstract: Michael Hershock, President of the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency, has announced that he is retiring. He has served in PHEAA during the greatest period of growth for the agency. He will be replaced by the current chief operator, Richard Willey.

headline: Dozen Democrats vie for second place
abstract: Very few knew Mark Schweiker was Governor Tom Ridge's Lieutenant Governor, but now that President Bush has appointed Ridge as homeland security chief, Schweiker will become Governor of Pennsylvania. State Senator Jack Wagner is running to become Lieutenant Governor and keep his senate seat.

headline: Mackereth, Cooper vie for 196th district
abstract: Candidates in the race for the PA State House of Representatives seat in the 196th district share similar views on many issues. Democrat Leo Cooper and Republican Beverly Mackereth both back full-day kindergarten programs.

headline: Security at Capitol remains hush-hush
abstract: Mum's the word when it comes to security at Pennsylvania's state Capitol.  The four-year fire, safety and security upgrade project for the Capitol building has produced a few visible changes, but Samantha Elliot, press secretary for the Department of General Services, said there's more than meets the eye.  Next year's budget includes an additional $53 million for the project - -bringing its total to $263 million - - but Elliot would not comment much on where, exactly, that money will go or how much is being spent specifically on security upgrades.  During the past year, workers erected concrete bollards - -sturdy poles designed to keep car and truck bombs away from a building - - around parts of the Capitol Building.

headline: Tax reform
abstract: A citizens group to monitor the Lewisburg Area School District is a good idea.  The first act of such a group should be to revisit the dueling tax reform acts.  Organizers of the grass-roots effort to put Act 50 of 1998 on the ballot are interested in challenging the school board's decision to implement Act 24 of 2001.

headline: Social Security takes a back seat
abstract: Social Security watch dogs are worried about slipping back into the habit of routinely tapping trust fund revenues to avoid making hard choices on spending and taxes. And since this is an election year, Democrats and Republicans are battling to show which party is more likely to get the country back in the black faster without Social Security. Robert Bixby, director of the bipartisan Concord Coalition, which lobbies for balanced budgets, said running deficits now might be an appropriate response to war and recession.

headline: Board gives Einstein list of directives
abstract: There is a cyber charter school which has been issued written directives from the Morrisville School Board. They ordered the cyber school to keep a skeleton staff in Morrisville, replace Tutorbots as the school's management company, hire a business manager, provide copies of all financial documents to Morrisville, and hire an independent auditor.

headline: Green for green
abstract: I commend the Legislature's restoration of funding for the Growing Greener program in the state budget ("Tax-Hike Turnabout," July 2).  Since its inception, Growing Greener has made a huge impact, actively restoring 370 miles of polluted streams, plugging over 1,000 oil and gas wells and protecting more than 40,000 acres of farmland, in addition to improving many state parks and forests.  The restoration of funding means that urgent conservation work will be able to continue across the state.

headline: McFalls vows to fight judges 'big time'
abstract: Embattled Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Patrick McFalls vowed to fight efforts by two of his fellow judges to suspend him from the bench. The Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts filed a petition with the state Supreme Court. McFalls was previously placed on paid administrative leave after his fired staff filed federal lawsuits accusing him of abusing alcohol.

headline: Suddenly, Philadelphia's a showbiz darling
abstract: We may never be know as "Hollywood on the Schuylkill," but the heads of regional film offices nationwide would kill to be in Philadelphia right now.  At a time when other cities are desperate to attract any kind of movie work, M Night Shyamalan's thriller Signs- set and shot in Bucks County - opened Friday to huge box office, bringing more attention to the area's already-thriving filmmaking industry.  Revenues from local production this year are expected to exceed 2001's record of $108 million by as much as $10 million.

headline: Earll's challenge
abstract: I met Sen. Jane Earll, R-Erie, for the first time recently.  I found her to be professional, intelligent and articulate.  She obviously is a person who can think for herself, and willingly and openly shares her opinions about issues.  She is running for office as lieutenant governor, and has expended a large amount of time and effort working hard to make sure people know what she stands for.

headline: Maitland wins in landslide
abstract: PA State Representative Steve Miatland defeated Democrat Mark Berg for the 91st PA district seat in the State House. Maitland said he supports a system that gives individual school districts the ability to choose their method of taxation. He also supports a reduction in property taxes, but wants the solution to be local.

headline: Senate hopeful says he is smeared
abstract: State Senate candidate Robert Wonderling says his opponent Brian O'Neill has created a telephone poll which smeared his reputation instead of doing a scientific survey. The questions asked were designed to gauge his strengths and weaknesses.

headline: Street calls halt to cuts in wage tax
abstract: Philadelphia will end its tiny but much-heralded cuts in the wage tax next year, the result of Mayor Street's decision to put schools, new sports stadiums, and neighborhood transformation at the top of his priority list. Street, following Rendell’s formula, continued to trim the tax in his first year in office. In his second budget proposal, the mayor proposed a second small trim. The trim would mean the typical Philadelphia taxpayer, one earning $50,000 yearly, would see his or her tax bill fall 9 percent.

headline: Social services may see more than 30% of budget
abstract: Sam Noble, executive director of Occupational Services Inc. in Chambersburg, was glad to see $33 million in Gov. Mark Schweiker's proposed budget allocated for recruitment and retention of people who work with the disabled. Schweiker's $20.9 billion plan includes about $7.3 billion in spending for social services, the second largest chunk in the budget after education. In addition to increases for programs that work with the disabled, the county also stands to benefit from proposed hikes for early childhood services such as Head Start and medical assistance programs for women.

headline: $75M school aid draws fire
abstract: Philadelphia is being given an additional $75 million to help the Philadelphia school district. Some believe that is too much while others say it will not help the schools. Others are angered because Philadelphia schools have received a 4 to 5 percent funding increase while other school districts will only receive 1 percent more.

headline: Harley wins Governor's Award
abstract: Harley-Davidson is one of 41 Pennsylvania companies to take home a Governor's Award for Environmental Excellence.  On Wednesday, Gov. Mark Schweiker honored business for positively affecting the state's environment.  Harley-Davidson was the sole York County company to win the award.

headline: Megan Law labels stalker
abstract: Louis Rocco used only words to wound his victims, but prosecutors believe he deserves to be placed in the same category as sexual predators who use physical violence.  The Scranton man who used notes, letters and phone calls to terrorize women has been declared a sexually violent predator under the state's Megan's Law, even though he never had physical contact with any of his victims.  Prosecutors in Lackawanna County said they believe this is the first time in state history that the label has been applied to someone who never physically contacted a victim.

headline: Sunday liquor bill wins final approval
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Mark Schweiker is expected to sign a bill that will allow state-owned liquor stores to sell alcohol on Sundays. The PA House and Senate passed the bill and some members speak out about the success of the bill.

headline: Former legislator back as parking attendant
abstract: Former state Rep. Frank Gigliotti of Brookline, who resigned from the House in June 2000 after pleading guilty to extortion and other charges, is out of prison and working for Alco Parking Co., the city's largest operator of lots and garages.  Alco President Merrill Stable said he'd known Gigliotti for years and that Gigliotti's brother, Tony Gigliotti, who's worked for Alco for more than 40 years, inquired about job possibilities for him.  Stabile described Gigliotti's current work status as "floating," meaning he fills in for sick or vacationing workers at Alco's 30 lots and garages.

headline: Make change, elect Sabatine in 18th District
abstract: Voters from Northampton County feel that the campaign in PA's 18th Senate district is about more than school taxes. The district wants a senator who can take on and understand all new issues, who forms opinions on issues and use them to support, amend or oppose legislation. Voters think Nick Sabatine would be a better choice over incumbent PA Senator Lisa Boscola.

headline: Senate Judiciary Committee sends Pennsylvania judge's nomination
abstract: Three Senate Democrats voted to send one of President George W. Bush's judicial nominees to the full Senate for consideration, despite critics' questions about him.  The nomination of U.S. District Judge D. Brooks Smith to the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia was approved 12-7 by the Senate Judiciary Committee.

headline: Street recognizes budget realities
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street is pushing for budget-cuts in the city. Street has predicted a $612 million budget deficit for the city in 2007. Street has been spending money on the Safe Streets program and for school improvements, but it seems that there is no money in the city for such initiatives.

headline: Talking to the man in charge about welfare
abstract: Gloria Guard had the opportunity to discuss with President Bush while she was in a Secret Service limo.  Guard was the entrepreneur who built Powelton's People Emergency Center, one of the most respected homeless services centers in Philadelphia. Guard shared her views on Bush's welfare reform proposal.

headline: 17 W. Pa. schools are given troubled rating
abstract: Seventeen Western Pennsylvania schools were identified yesterday as being academically troubled under federal law because of low students test scores, and in most cases, they will have to offer families the choice of sending their children to other schools in the fall.  That may prove to be a difficult task, however, for school districts such as Wilkinsburg and Sto-Rox, where all of the elementary school have been placed on the list, leaving families with no places to send their children within the districts.  While those pupils could be sent to neighboring districts, that can happen only if the other districts agree to take them.

headline: Huge crowd backs state's proposal to protect bucks from overharvesting
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission's deer management section is proposing a statewide antler restriction on hunters. The Game Commission will vote in April on restricting hunters from hunting male white-tailed deer with three or more points on one antler in Luzerne County this year. Biologist Gary Alt, who heads the Pennsylvania Game Commission's deer management section, appears to have the support of the general public and the Game Commission in this statewide initiative.

headline: Megan's law requirement for Indiana man upheld
abstract: The PA Superior court has upheld the lifetime registration requirement for sex offenders, as stated under Megan's law. The decision came from the case of Timothy Scott Fleming.

headline: Telemarketer fined
abstract: A Canadian telemarketing firm must pay the state of PA $20,000 in penalities after deceiving PA customers by claiming that donated money would go to a state firefighters association. The PA State Attorney General's Office investigated the matter and found the firm in violation of several Acts.

headline: Druce gets month to answer suit
abstract: A Dauphin County judge had given former state Rep. Thomas W. Druce a month to answer a lawsuit that will decide how much coverage his insurance company owes him.  Judge Richard A. Lewis needs to response from Druce to move closer to deciding it Druce's guilty plea to leaving the scene of an accident that killed Harrisburg resident Kenneth R. Cains invalidated parts of his insurance policy with Mutual Benefits Insurance Company of Huntingdon.  Druce, of Bucks County, also pleaded guilty to trying to cover up his involvement in the July 27, 1999, accident on Cameron Street.

headline: Make children's issues, action part of Pa. campaigns
abstract: "Hey, what about the kids?" With this rallying cry, a statewide campaign called Focus Five for Kids seeks to infuse the 2002 Pennsylvania elections with a passionate concern for the needs of children.  The Children's Coalition of the Lehigh Valley has joined this campaign and shares its belief that investment in children is a top priority in promoting the long-term prosperity of the region and the state.  To build a better Pennsylvania, the CCLV and Focus Five call upon the state to embrace an agenda of five connected issues.

headline: Senate panel recommends confirmation for Altoona's Smith
abstract: The US Senate Judiciary Committee voted 12-7 yesterday to recommend confirmation of U.S. District Judge D. Brooks Smith of Altoona to the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.  Smith's supporters say they believe he will win confirmation easily in the Senate where a number of Democrats are expected to join all 49 Republicans to vote for him.  The Senate has 50 Democrats, 49 Republicans and one independent.

headline: Street, confident and expansive, touts successes
abstract: Mayor Street wants to reform or eliminate the Section 8 rental program. Section 8 subsidizes rent payments for tenants unable to acquire affordable housing. Mayor Street wants the renters to become property owners.

headline: White House Watch: Welfare reform forever
abstract: Welfare rolls are down from 1994, but still one third of all American children live below or just above the poverty line. President Bush is looking to make welfare reforms. The Democrats in Congress feel his plan ignores the need of hardworking, taxpaying immigrants.

headline: 2 execs eyed to reform schools
abstract: A local university and a corporate executive are among the leading candidates for seats on the new commission in charge of Philadelphia schools. Governor Schweiker reportedly has been talking with both James P. Gallagher, president of Philadelphia University and chairman of the state Board of Education, and Daniel J. Whelan, president of Verizon Pennsylvania. The School Reform Commission has replaced the board of education in managing the school district's affairs.

headline: Hunters flock to Cambria County, stalking wild boar
abstract: There are wild boars wandering the western Cambria County mountains. Officials with the state game commission and Agriculture Department figure that the boars escaped from an fenced in game preserve. One hunter said 250 hours in the woods got him one boar.

headline: Men seek 'paternity fraud' law
abstract: New Jersey lawmaker Neil Cohen has sponsored legislation allowing men to use DNA tests to disprove paternity and end financial support to a child. The bill recently came out of committee and faces a vote from the General Assembly.

headline: Timber industry raps proposed legislation
abstract: Representatives of the area timber industry used a recent legislative hearing on the use of state-owned land to express their disapproval of a proposed House bill which would call for environmental impact statements and public hearings on state land use.  Paul Lyskava, executive director of the Hardwood Lumber Manufacturers Association, and Edward Kocjancic, proprietor, asked state Reps. Jim Lynch of Warren County and Scott Hutchinson of Venango County, who attended the hearing, to oppose the bill. Neither Lynch nor Hutchinson introduced House Bill 2799, better known as the Pennsylvania Environmental Policy Act.

headline: Druce, insurer battle over policy
abstract: A judge has given former state Rep. Thomas Druce a month to respond to a lawsuit that will decide how much, if any, coverage his insurance company owes him and whether he owes money to the company.  Druce, who represented the 144th District in the House of Representatives, was sentenced to two hours to four years in prison after pleading guilty to leaving the scene of the July 1999 accident on a Harrisburg street that killed a man.  Druce has appealed his sentence to the state Supreme Court.  He was released on $600,000 bail just before Christmas 2000 pending the outcomes of that appeal.

headline: Making a historic quest
abstract: The campaigns for Auditor General Bob Casey Jr. and former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell have been the most costly. The race has been very high profile. The winner will face Republican state Attorney General Mike Fisher.

headline: Senate panel to vote today on Altoona's Smith
abstract: President George W. Bush's controversial nomination of U.S. District Judge D. Brooks Smith, of Altoona, to the federal appeals court bench will be decided today by the Senate Judiciary Committee.  The committee has 10 Democrats and nine Republicans. All nine Republicans are likely to support Smith, unless the 10 panel Democrats to kill Smith's nomination.

headline: Tax issues gain approval
abstract: Voters in Philadelphia have approved a ballot question that sets up a Tax Review Commission that will examine the city's tax structure and issue a report each year in November. State voters also approved a $100 million bond issue to help volunteer fire companies.

headline: Young Pennsylvanians' families watching, waiting for Children's First Act
abstract: Child care in Pennsylvania, as elsewhere in the nation, can be costly. Consequently, the federal Child Care Development Block Grant, the primary source of support for families who otherwise can't afford child care and the major funding source for state child care programs, is critical.  CCDBG, authorized under the welfare reform law of 1996, provides financial assistance to 45,000 lower middle class working families in Pennsylvania and supports households striving to make the transition from welfare to work.

headline: 6 charter schools expected to open
abstract: Six new charter schools are likely to open in September under action taken by Philadelphia's School Reform Commission yesterday.  That would raise the number of charter schools in the city to 45.  The approval came as Paul G. Vallas, new chief executive officer of Philadelphia schools, noted that the commission had charged him with developing a tougher set of standards for charter schools to ensure that they perform at high levels.  Charter schools, Vallas said, should not perform worse than neighborhood schools, as is the case with some charters.

headline: Judge: Oks settlements
abstract: A Lancaster County judge Monday approved settlements that end lawsuits filed by a citizen's group against Manor Township and Lancaster County Solid Waste Management.  Judge Paul K. Allison signed off on the agreements People Against Landfill Expansion (PALE) reached last week with both the township and the authority.
