PALE sued the two entities over a controversial effort to expand the county landfill in Manor Township.

headline: National briefing: Mid-Atlantic
abstract: A PA State Superior Court has ruled that the former lesbian partner of a woman who has five children must pay child support. The children were granted visitation with the former partner.

headline: Tracks are hot, but racing is not
abstract: Race tracks are popping up nationwide and particularly in PA. While race tracks are increasing in number, the interest in horse racing is decreasing. Race tracks are being used as a way to get legal gambling into areas of the state and the country.

headline: Dumeyer: County Republicans
abstract: The Lancaster County Republican Committee has chosen Dave Dumeye as the new local party chairman. An overview of the election process and parties involved is given.

headline: Making a List
abstract: Already in line to become the No. 3 Republican in the House next year, Rep. Roy Blunt (Mo.) is lending a helping hand to dozens of GOP candidates in an effort to make sure that his new title will be Majority, not Minority, Whip.  A memo sent from Blunt's Rely On Your Beliefs Fund - commonly referred to as the ROYB Fund - outlines "A" and "B" lists of incumbents, challengers and open seat races that Blunt is urging supporters to help fund and offers a glimpse into House Republicans' internal handicapping of the 2002 elections.  The memo was sent Aug. 1 to Blunt's "most active supporters and folks looking to direct resources to the most competitive campaigns," according to KerriAnn Hayes, director of finance for the Fund.

headline: Senate rules make a crooked ethical yardstick
abstract: PA State Senator Lisa Boscola, in her re-election campaign, has sent out a mailer that headlined efforts to help PA firefighters. Her mailer essentially calls on voters to support a ballot question that would provide $100 million in aid to volunteer fire and emergency services. The premise may go against the ethical standards of the PA Senate's rules.

headline: The big-issue: Education
abstract: Paying for education has become the hot issue in the race for governor. The percentage of education costs funded by the state is down, forcing local property taxes up. Both candidates, Ed Rendell and Mike Fisher agree that the state should not depend on local property taxes to pay for public education. Rendell wants to find state money to replace the property taxes whereas Fisher is proposing local taxes, on income or sales, to fill the gap.

headline: 9th district covers a vast area
abstract: Stretching from the base of the Commodore Barry Bridge to the Lancaster County line, Pennsylvania' 9th Senatorial District takes in this city, Delaware County's most historic and blighted community; Chester County's still-substantial horse and mushroom farms; and all manner of suburbia in between.  Many of the issues topping people's legislative agendas are the same throughout the district, according to interviews with several self-identified registered voters last week.   Residents of Chester and Delaware counties named sprawl, unfair property taxes, high prescription-drug prices and the medical-malpractice-insurance crisis as the most important problems facing the state.

headline: 75 schools targeted for possible overhaul
abstract: Philadelphia's School Reform Commission yesterday said it would put as many as 75 of the district's low-performing schools under a new governance structure by September.  The commission will look at five models for governance, several of which would involve outside management firms, such as Edison Schools Inc.  The most drastic change is the privatization model, which could allow an outside firm to take over, bring in its own staff and principal, and honor union contracts or not.

headline: Law already updated to limit the role of authorities
abstract: I would like to clarify several points made in your editorial (July 16) about the role of municipal authorities.  While most of the piece dealt with issues surrounding Forum Place, the implication was that all authorities may engage in similar real estate practices.  This, in fact, is not true, and has never been true of the 2,000 authorities that exist in Pennsylvania.  The vast majority of authorities are created for a specific purpose in a specific geographic area, mostly to provide public infrastructure services such as sewer treatment, drinking water, solid waste disposal and recreation.

headline: New law dubbed victory for victims' rights
abstract: A new law, prompted by Bucks County officials, requires victims of crime to be notified and given an opportunity to provide comment when the court recommends that a defendant participate in a motivational boot camp program.  The change also would require victims to be notified of the offender's date of release from a boot camp.  The legislation last week was passed by both the House and Senate and signed into law by Gov. Mark Schweiker.

headline: Tribal represenatives to meet governor's staff
abstract: A Canadian-based group of Indian tribes known as Six Nations Confederacy will meet with Gov. Mark Schweiker's staff this morning to talk about casino gambling. The group is looking at Fayette County, but their intentions are not clear since they would need to be recognized both by the state and federal governments to seek approval to open a casino on a reservation. And Pennsylvania has no Indian reservations.

headline: Dumeyer: Makes 2 appointments
abstract: Dave Dumeyer, the newly elected chairman of the Lancaster County Republican Committee, marked his first full week in office Wednesday by issuing several announcements.  Dumeyer was elected by a narrow margin last week over former chairman Chet Beiler.  Dumeyer's winning ticket included vice chairwoman Linda Gordon, secretary Cindy Zinn and treasurer Keith Greiner.

headline: Mansion candidates' camps spar before televised debate
abstract: Pennsylvania Republican and Democratic party supporters shouted and argued outside an auditorium prior to a televised gubernatorial candidate debate. Mike Fisher, Ed Rendell, Michael Morril, and Ken Krawchuck participated in the debate. Both the Republican and Democratic candidate have over $100 million to spend on the race.

headline: Senator hopes to continue unexpected political rise
abstract: Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Fisher has picked State Senator Jane Earll to be his running mate as a candidate for lieutenant governor. There are parallels between Earll and former Governor Tom Ridge. Both are from Erie from working-class families. They are both lawyers and Catholics who support abortion rights.

headline: The Campaign for Tax Reform
abstract: Nicholas Sabatine supports a plan devised by Rep. Kelly Lewis, R-Monroe.  The plan would eliminate local school taxes and raise more than $7 billion by: Increasing the state personal income tax from 2.8 percent to 3.9 percent, increasing state sales tax from 6 percent to 7 percent and creating an independent commission to determine how best to eliminate tax breaks for business to raise another $3 billion.  State Sen. Lisa Boscola, D-Northampton, said she will not introduce her options until Monday, but will give state lawmakers the option of eliminating local school taxes by choosing $7 billion in options among the following $9.4 billion in options.

headline: A preservation group hangs on, looks ahead
abstract: The Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia is trying to help save historic buildings with a radial approach. They want to co-opt the techniques of private developers by investing in rundown properties, renovating them and selling them for profit. The approach failed and the group has new plans.

headline: 89th candidates offer different plans to fund education
abstract: PA State Representative Jeff Coy and his opponent Chris Sheffield are running for the 89th district seat and have very different views on school funding. Coy would keep the basics of the current system, and make it law that the general assembly fund schools at 50%. Sheffied would eliminate property tax and dedicate 1% of sales tax to fund schools.

headline: Lax security exposes lethal chemical supplies
abstract: Despite repeated warnings from federal intelligence agencies to keep intruders away from tanks holding lethal chemicals, a Pittsburgh Tribune-Review investigation shows that six months after the Sept. 11 attacks, anyone has unfettered access to more than two dozen potentially dangerous plants in the region.  The security was so lax at 30 sites that in broad daylight a Tribune reporter--- wearing a press pass and carrying a camera--- could walk or drive right up to tanks, pipes and control rooms considered key targets for terrorists.  A derailed train, a .50-caliber bullet or a pipe bomb: Each could turn a local neighborhood into an industrial disaster area, based on paperwork filed with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency by the chemical manufacturers, shippers and users themselves.

headline: New lawyer is appointed for Einhorn
abstract: A veteran homicide defense lawyer has been appointed by a court to handle Ira Einhorn's murder trial. William "Bill" Cannon was notified that he will represent the former fugitive and hippie guru in a second trial on charges that Einhorn killed girlfriend Holly Maddux in 1977 and stashed her body in a trunk in the couple's Powetlton Village apartment. Common Pleas Court Judge D. Webster Keogh, criminal division supervising judge, sought an experienced, capable lawyer and chose Cannon because of merit, according to the judge's staff.

headline: Trust company seeks approval for a sale; Nestle bid reported
abstract: Amid reports that potential suitors for Hershey Foods Corp. may be submitting or preparing bids, the Hershey Trust Co. yesterday asked a judge to throw out state Attorney General Mike Fisher's objections to a sale.  Fisher, who on Friday asked Dauphin County Orphans Court to block the trust company's proposed sale of the candymaker, is trying to "destroy the status quo, not restore it," the trust company said in its court response yesterday.  Judge Warren G. Morgan yesterday scheduled a hearing for 10 a.m. Sept. 3 but did not order the trust company or Hershey Foods to stop the sale process before then.  Fisher contends a sale would cause "irreplaceable harm" to the community.

headline: Eating on the run
abstract: For Pennsylvania's gubernatorial candidates, meals are a low priority on the campaign trail, but food does play a part in how they polish their images. Reporters describe candidate Ed Rendell as a compulsive eater who will try anything, anywhere. He has been called "biggest tater known to man."

headline: Many aren't helped by state pension plan
abstract: The article that was written about how the state pension plan will help in the long run is untrue. The article was written by officers of PSEA and have a deal with Governor Ridge. School districts have not saved money to increase their contributions towards the pension fund.

headline: Senator Mellow defeats Scavo by big margin
abstract: PA State Senator Robert Mellow has beat Republican Frank Scavo for the 22nd PA district seat. Mellow will be serving his ninth term, winning about 72% of the votes.

headline: The Mayor's Mid-Term Report Card
abstract: Philadelphia's mayor Street is given an A for his work on improving Philadelphia neighborhoods. However, Street received a B for his work on bringing Philadelphia a new stadium and his staff appointments, and a B- for his work on city finances. Street received an Incomplete for his work to improve the school system as it is too early to gauge the success of the new his newly appointed Board of Education and the re-negotiation of teacher’s contracts.  Street's weak points are in communication and political schmoozing, where he received D's.

headline: Advocacy group objects to county's hiring of lobbying firm
abstract: An advocacy group is objecting to Beaver County's decision to hire a lobbying firm, through the county says it needs help getting federal funding for local water and sewer projects.  County commissioners recently approved a one-year, $60,000 contract with Bucephalus LLC, a Pittsburgh lobbying firm headed by former Democratic Congressman Ron Klink.  The commissioners say they were hoping to elicit more federal funding for county projects such as installing water and sewer lines along Route 60 to spur development.

headline: A Charter-School Showdown
abstract: A public charter school did not have funding when it began which lead to many problems. When the funding was given, it was immediately taken away due to the problems that had arisen when the school had no funds. It is a catch-22 for the school.

headline: Legislation would phase out use of MTBE
abstract: The PA State senate Committee on Environmental Resources is considering a bill that would phase out the use of Lethyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE) as a gasoline additive. The MTBE additive has been the cause of groundwater contamination.

headline: News in brief from central Pennsylvania
abstract: A onetime escapee from Centre County Prison almost got away again last month when someone sent his jailers a forged sentencing order saying that his time behind bars was up. Officials at the Lincoln-Edison Charter School are at odds with the York school board over how much access city officials should have to school records. Osram Sylvania said it might expand operations at its incandescent light bulb plant in Tioga County as it closes factories elsewhere in the country.

headline: U.S. tariffs hurt area firm that relies on French plate steel
abstract: The 30 percent tariffs President Bush imposed on steel imports are supposed to protect American workers.  Don't try telling that to the 100 employees, including 67 members of the United Steelworkers union, who work at Precision-Marshall Steel in Washington, Pa.  Tariffs have been slapped on the small steel processor's best-selling product.

headline: Ed shows he's good sport to keep PHA post
abstract: When Ed Rendell left the mayor's office, he remained chairman of the five-member board of the Philadelphia Housing Authority. Rendell and then-City Council President John Street joined the board in 1993 at the request of federal officials, who urged the direct involvement of the city's top political leaders to save the troubled housing authority. Rendell said that Street asked him to remain on the PHA board because of his relationship with President Clinton and top officials in Washington.

headline: Map mischief
abstract: The primary election will happen on May 21st and it would be unfair to the Democratic gubernatorial candidates who are in a costly race. A new redistricting map was created and could have gone into affect for the election, but it would have had to been delayed.

headline: Sept. 11 Attacks Prompt House Bids by Pilots, Flight Attendant
abstract: Chris Redmond, a commercial airline pilot, was friends with Jason Dahl, one of the pilots on the ill-fated United Flight 93 that crashed on Sept. 11. Redmond has decided to run for Congress in order to bring his voice as a member of the airline industry to the House. Redmond is one in a handful of House candidates from both parties with experience as either commercial airline pilots or flight attendants who have made the decision to run for Congress this year.

headline: They Fled to Greener Pa$ture$
abstract: Philadelphia has a high wage tax which is causing some residents to leave to the suburbs. Mayor Street is trying to cut the tax which was begun by former Mayor Ed Rendell.

headline: Another store closes in Pittsburgh's Fifth-Forbes area
abstract: Another store in Pittsburgh's Fifth and Forbes retail corridor has closed. McDonald's joins a list of stores that have closed in recent months.  A committee is working on renovating downtown's retail area.

headline: Divining a Q&A for state's QB
abstract: John Baer, an Inquirer Columnist, pokes fun at PA Governor Mark Schweiker's possibility of heading the Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce. Baer creates a fake interview between Schweiker and Philadelphia officials.

headline: A new library record: 7.2 million
abstract: More than seven million items were checked out of the Philadelphia Free Library in the last fiscal year, besting a 1964 record.  For the year that ended June 30, about 7.2 million items were checked out, library spokeswoman Linda Carroll-Pitts said.  The previous record of 6,716,174 items was set in 1964, when the city had a half-million more residents than it does today.  Of course, these days, customers are checking out a large number of audio books, videotapes, music recordings and DVDs.

headline: Local support growing for proposed deer program
abstract: Pennsylvania Game Commission deer biologist Gary Alt has proposed antler restrictions for the upcoming hunting season in attempts to cut the buck harvest in half. He modeled it after the bear management program. He believes it will result in more and bigger bucks.

headline: NRA gives Gekas an A+. Magazine provides edge to Holden's A
abstract: The National Rifle Association rated U.S. Congressman Gekas' record on guns owner's right as an  A+, while giving opponent Holden an A. Both had previously been rated A but the NRA said they took into account an amendment that Gekas sponsored in the 1993 crime bill, and his position on the House Judiciary committee to give him a better grade than Holden.

headline: US Steel reports $83 million loss in first quarter
abstract: US Steel released its first quarter financial report and reportedly lost $83 million. Sales fell 8.3% in the first quarter.

headline: Edison boss calls report questioning firm's revenue 'irresponsible'
abstract: A story reported by Bloomsberg News, said Edison's Schools boosts its revenue by more than $96 million annually by counting teacher's salaries and other expenses as revenue. Investors have grown increasingly skeptical of corporate accounting practices since the collapse of energy trader Enron. Edison's CFO Adam Field said the company's practice of recognizing revenue was consistent with generally accepted accounting principles.

headline: Mapping suit heads for court
abstract: The legal challenge to Pennsylvania's congressional redistricting plan will play out in a two-day trial next month. Three federal judges will hear evidence on the plan that places Schuylkill County in a new 17th Congressional District wit Dauphin and Lebanon counties and parts of Perry and northern Berks counties. The outcome may determine the re-election bid for U.S. Rep. T. Timothy Holden.

headline: Sept. 11 may taint Clinton's legacy
abstract: Until the terrorists struck on American soil, it appeared that Bill Clinton would be enshrined in history as the politically gifted, personally flawed president who survived impeachment and governed an affluent nation at peace with the world. There is now a debate whether Clinton should be judged in the context of his times - as a president preoccupied with domestic issues in a decade when few deemed terrorism a top priority - or judged harshly with benefit of hindsight - as a weak commander-in-chief who allowed a lethal enemy to spin a global web.

headline: They want to market Philly, too
abstract: A number of news-readers have been pushing for a new effort to market Philadelphia as a great city to move into. Columnist Carla Anderson writes in response to resident's efforts and argues that the city of Philadelphia can grow and propose if resident take a proactive stand.

headline: Bill could hinder open space preservation effort
abstract: The PA State Legislature is considering a bill that would make it harder for local communities to preserve open space and make it easier for developers to build homes. The bill was introduced by PA State Senator James Gerlach.

headline: Lawless will pass on PSU Sex Fair
abstract: Last year Rep. John Lawless attacked Pennsylvania State University for allowing a sexual health fair event which he attended and at one point called to cut off its state funding. This year the Montgomery Democrat, who is running for his party's nomination for lieutenant governor, said he will not attend this year’s faire. Womyns's Concerns, a feminist student group, is the organizer of the event.

headline: A sober effort on campuses
abstract: Universities around the nation are turning to increased enforcement, early intensive counseling, intervention, and social norms advertising to tell students that fewer school students drink than they might think. It is a new method of alcohol prevention among students.

headline: Mining policies protested
abstract: Residents of western Pennsylvania coal fields called on legislators to pass legislation aimed at strengthening protections for homes and roads from damage caused by longwall mining. The Coal Communities Fairness Act, drafted by state Rep. Camille George, D-Clearfield/Centre counties, would expand current laws restricting mining beneath schools, public buildings and hospitals to include historic structures and public utility lines. The Sierra Group and other environmental groups joined about 30 residents from Washington and Greene counties who have had or expect to have mining occur beneath their homes at a rally inside the Capitol Rotunda.

headline: Numbers aside, officials agree violence is problem
abstract: The statistics were in debate, but the problem was not: Violent attacks and other crimes committed by students in Philadelphia schools must be stopped.  The school district and Harvey Rice, the state's safe-schools advocate, do not agree on the numbers in a report he released Friday.  Rice says there were 5,287 serious or violent incidents in city schools last year, and one-third of the 1,122 weapons offenses were never reported to police.

headline: Usher deems tariffs necessary for steel industry's survival
abstract: The US Steel Corporation believes any tariff less than 40 percent will greatly hurt the American steel industry. President Bush must decide if he wants to impose a tariff on imported steel. US Steel also wants to consolidate the steel industry.

headline: Editorial: The right medicine / A bitter pill for trial lawyers is a healthy step
abstract: At opposite ends of an argument over malpractice insurance, and speaking the fervent language of self-interest, doctors and trial lawyers both held rallies in Harrisburg. HB 1802, which passed the House by a decisive 164-32 margin and is now before the Senate, attacks the problem on several fronts, and includes a good dose of old-fashioned tort reform. The trial lawyers argue that the rights of patients injured by malpractice are severely restricted by this bill -- a position that the Post-Gazette would dispute.

headline: Mark Berg to challenge Maitland
abstract: Mark Berg announced his desire to win the Democrat's nomination for the 91st District state representative. The District is very conservative and he lost previous by a landslide. He wants to help preserve the rural area's power in the state legislature.

headline: Seven In House Get Free Rides
abstract: Seven of Philadelphia's 27 state Representatives will not face opposition in the upcoming primary. The filling deadline has passed.

headline: Tricky property-tax politics
abstract: A comparison between the wage-tax revolt and the current property-tax debate is made. The Daily News says that Philadelphia Mayor Street and the city's council members are not doing a good job at making home assessment rates fair. The lack of fair property assessments should be addressed before property-taxes increase.

headline: Bill would increase oversight of appraisers
abstract: The House Professional Licensure Committee has voted to approve a bill, with amendments, that would tighten state oversight of real estate appraisers.  The legislation provides safeguards to ensure that home appraisals are done honestly and gives the state attorney general more power to prosecute fraudulent appraisals.

headline: Rendell surprised Gore won't run
abstract: PA Governor-Elect Ed Rendell has stated that he is disappointed that former Vice President AL Gore has decided not to run for President in 2004. Rendell was surprised by the decision.

headline: Ambitious agenda
abstract: The proposals from new Philadelphia schools CEO Paul Vallas are coming so fast, he's barely leaving time for the public to catch its breath.  That's not a bad thing. Mr. Vallas' can-do barrage of ideas has changed the tone and substance of the conversation regarding the nation's eighth-largest school district.  Mr. Vallas' stint as head of Chicago's school reform effort obviously has helped him size up quickly some of his new district's most pressing problems, including the need to expand summer remedial course dramatically.  It is farcical that in a district in which so many of the 200,000 students struggle to master the basics, only 9,280 attend summer programs.

headline: Museum had map needed at Quecreek mine.
abstract: The map that could have prevented the accident where nine miners became trapped in a water-filled underground chamber of Quecreek mine last summer, was present in the museum storage drawer 30 miles away.

headline: Officer's gun goes off during show-and-tell
abstract: Shortly after a Philadelphia policewoman passed around a loaded handgun among students during a show-and-tell at a Germantown charter school, the weapon accidentally discharged grazing a 10-year-old boy in the face. the student received five stitches and returned home last night in good condition. The officer, Vanessa Carter-Moragne, was removed from street duty and is now the subject of an Internal Affairs investigation.

headline: Why are media exempt?
abstract: Journalists are the only ones to be able to exercise freedom of speech. Private citizens, groups, or candidates have to pay for space in newspapers. News and entertainment media is exempt from government restriction due to a federal law. Their stories are not regulated.

headline: Education, economy focus of Rendell's Armstrong campaign
abstract: If elected as Governor of Pennsylvania, Ed Rendell does not plan on sitting in Harrisburg. During a campaign stop in Armstrong, he focused on public education and finding a way to change it.

headline: Mascara ads draw fire from NRA
abstract: US Representative Frank Mascara changed a newspaper ad because the National Rifle Association harshly criticized it. The ad used the NRA's trademark phrase 'I am the NRA.' The group claims they do not endorse Mascara, but instead endorse his opponent US Representative John Murtha.

headline: Shady strategy
abstract: Bucks County Sheriff Larry Michaels is leaving his post just six months after being reelected to his sixth term. Michaels will undergo dialysis treatments which are very physically draining. There is a controversy since he began dialysis a year ago and reassured voters his health did not affect his job performance.

headline: Where have all the young people gone?
abstract: While Bucks County's population exploded between 1990 and 2000, growing by 56,461, the number of people ages 20 to 34 declined by 26,657. Experts like Lynn Bush, executive director of the Bucks County Planning Commission, are not convinced the youth drain has to do with the high cost of living in Bucks. Bush believes Buck's neighbors are faring better because those counties are home to huge pharmaceutical and financial corporations that attract people fresh out of college and graduate school.

headline: Committee discusses impact of federal election legislation on Pennsylvania
abstract: A piece of federal legislation that would reform Pennsylvania's electoral system by mandating new voting machines, using provisional ballots, and changing identification requirements has passed Congress. The legislation is awaiting President George W. Bush's signature.

headline: 2002 state budget: State budget has less for the arts
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker's proposed 2002-03 budget, will reduce funding for the Council on the Arts for the first time in 10 years.  The council was among the beneficiaries during the boom times of the 1990s, when then Gov. Tom Ridge presided over a budget that bulged with surplus funds.  The council, which received $9 million in 1995, was budgeted to receive $15.4 million this fiscal year.

headline: Another cyber school prepares to hit scene
abstract: Grace Academy is a for-profit, private cyber school. It is religious based and offers curriculum for grades K-12.

headline: Noteworthy
abstract: Rep. Dan Surra, D-Elks, soon plans to introduce a House resolution condemning New York City's decision to suspend the recycling of plastics for one year and glass for two years because he believes it will generate more garbage for Pennsylvania's landfills.

headline: Officials eye CPI for fire training
abstract: Local officials are exploring the option of putting Centre County's new firefighter-training site at the Central Pennsylvania Institute of Science and Technology in Pleasant Gap, state Rep. Kerry Benninghoff said Tuesday.  If the training facility were built at the school instead of on 15-acre plot in Benner Township, CPI students might help in construction of the project.  Additionally, firefighters-in-training would be close to classroom space that's frequently vacant on weekends - - the time when many courses conducted, Benninghoff said.

headline: Why slots at tracks make sense for state
abstract: The debate in Pennsylvania has shifted to what kind of gaming should be allowed and how it should be managed. It is being argued that slot machines will save horse racing in the state and will generate large funds for the state without raising taxes and bring new jobs to Pennsylvania.

headline: Electing to accent positive
abstract: Democrat Ed Rendell has said he and Republican Mike Fisher have agreed to be positive gubernatorial candidates. They're going to talk about issues and not use playground banter of "did so" or "did not." Rendell wants the campaigns to be about what they would do for Pennsylvania.

headline: Mascara puts 'Texas mudslinger' on team
abstract: US Representative Frank Mascara has hired a Texas political consultant, Billy Horton, to help with his re-election campaign against US Representative John Murtha. Horton has helped on numerous campaigns at all levels. Congressional redistricting has caused the two Representatives to have their districts combined.

headline: Shame on You, Ed, on tax news
abstract: John Baer of Philadelphia Daily News writes that gubernatorial candidate Ed Rendell's tax returns put a stain on his campaign.

headline: Wage-tax cuts are 'positive message'
abstract: The cost of schools, stadiums, blight removal, and the lingering effects of a recession prompted Mayor Street to announce a proposal to halt the incremental wage tax cuts as of July 1. 2003. To partially compensate, Street wants to speed up cuts in the gross receipts tax on businesses, a much criticized levy that requires every firm to fork over money based on gross revenue. The wage tax is widely considered a major contributor to Philadelphia's loss of jobs and population in recent decades.

headline: Committee slots could draw crowd
abstract: Party committee jobs may be farther down the political food chain than governor and state Legislature. But the party committees have a lot to do with picking the candidates for those top-of-the-ticket races. This year, both major political parties will elect new slates of committee members in each of the country's 225 voting districts.

headline: A Budget for Pennsylvania's Future
abstract: The annual state budget crafted by the General Assembly does more than just determine how much money will be invested in state initiatives in any given fiscal year.  It sets the tone for the state's role in supporting public education, improving public safety and emergency services, attracting new jobs, and helping working families and senior citizens afford the necessities of life.  With revenues coming in at levels far below estimates, this year more than ever lawmakers must remain focused on what is best for the future of our Commonwealth and its citizens while crafting the budget.

headline: Are disabled students served by assessment tests?
abstract: By state and federal law, all students must participate in statewide testing.  In Pennsylvania, these more severely retarded or physically limited children can now take a specially developed test, called the Pennsylvania Alternate System of Assessment, or PASA.  The requirement exists partly because, years ago, some schools were accused of discouraging special education students or lower achievers from taking standardized tests so they could improve their schools' test scores.

headline: On the first day of deer season, the town of Claysville gets its shot
abstract: In Washington County, the city of Claysville, PA always gets an influx of hunters on the opening of deer season. Local business in the city are happy to get the increased business.

headline: Only limit is on justice
abstract: A state law requires child sexual abuse victims to come forward before the age of 20. A man has his lawsuit thrown out because he was 27. The statue of limitations of the law should be raised.

headline: Wyomissing company becomes national gaming power
abstract: A gambling empire that has sprung up from a rural eastern Pennsylvania horse race track is about to go Hollywood.  Penn National Gaming Corp. expects to nearly double its revenues with the expected closing of its $780 million purchase of Hollywood Casino Corp. early next year, Chief Executive Officer Peter M. Carlino said.  The deal will mean name changes for the riverboat and on-land casinos Wyomissing-based Penn National already owns in Mississippi, Louisiana and Colorado.

headline: Election '02: Special interests chose hopefuls
abstract: The money behind the two candidates for state representative in the 18th District could suggest who has what to gain in the coming election.  What one man might call an act of motherly love, another man calls a campaign contribution.  Scott Blacker and the Democratic candidate for state representative in the 18th District included cookies and balloons, donated by his mom, in the more than $7,402 "favors" or in-kind contributions to his campaign this year.

headline: Mascara says he may run against Murtha
abstract: Congressman Frank Mascara says he may challenge fellow congressman John Murtha in a newly developed seat taken from the districts they represent. Because of the redistricting, much of Mascara's Washington County district will become part of the 12th district, where Murtha of Johnstown is the incumbent. The two met yesterday at a United Mine Workers gathering in Washington but there was no talk of campaigning against each other.

headline: She was a pioneer in Pennsylvania and national politics
abstract: Chrystal Bird Fauset, considered a pioneer in politics, is a Pennsylvania lawmaker who was the first black woman to be elected to a state legislature.  Born in 1893, she was elected as Philadelphia's Democratic Representative in 1938.  She worked on Franklin D. Roosevelt's campaigns, was a race relations advisor to New York's mayor LaGuardia, and--before her death in 1965--she earned two Meritorious Service Medals.

headline: Wage-tax skirmish is tiny step in larger war
abstract: Bucking the mayor and the odds, a pro-growth, pro-competitiveness coalition came together and stopped the city from taking a misguided backward step on the city wage tax.  It's understandable that there should be some confusion on this point.  People who believe Philadelphia can grown and thrive don't get many chances to savor victory - even a victory as admittedly modest as the City Council's vote to keep cutting little tiny bits out of the much-loathed wage tax.

headline: Congress stymied by party fighters
abstract: Both political parties in U.S. Congress supported President George W. Bush's authority to go to war against Iraq, but differed on every issue of consequence this year. Issues ranged from enacting prescription drug coverage for the elderly, to establishing a Department of Homeland Security, to funding education reform at authorized levels.

headline: As budget nears a vote, Democrats cry foul
abstract: Some PA State Democratic lawmakers are complaining about Governor Schweiker and Republican lawmakers' budget. Democrats say they were left out of the negotiations process and are angry about parts of the proposed budget including: the rainy day fund, school funding, landfill tipping fees, business taxes and cigarette taxes.

headline: At 11 schools: Cash for tip-offs
abstract: At some Philadelphia public schools, students will soon be able to cash in on crime tips about violent incidents that occur in their classrooms and hallways.  The program, patterned after a national Crime Stoppers effort, will involve 11 schools.  Students will be eligible for financial rewards if they provide information that leads to the arrest of student violators.

headline: Overdue taxes, unpaid bills stir debate
abstract: The Pennsylvania-American Water Company will turn off the DuPont Borough water for the fire hydrants if the bill wasn't paid. The administration has been trying to get a reduced rate for fire hydrants. The Borough still owes thousands to the IRS and state and local taxes.

headline: Pa.'s internet child-porn law raises doubts
abstract: A new state law requires internet service providers to block child porn on their sites after being put on notice by state law enforcement authorities. Some applaud the government's efforts, while others have doubts if it will be able to be enforced.

headline: You may tint your windows- - With the Law in Mind
abstract: Are you considering tinting the windows of your new car to give it a sporty look or to cut down on glare from the sun?  Before you go to your local window detailer, make that Pennsylvania law regulates automobile window tint levels.  With some exceptions, light transmittance through all vehicle windows must be greater than 70 percent.  Any motorist who operates a vehicle with windows that do not conform to the Pennsylvania standards may be subject to a citation.  Attorney General Mike Fisher wants to alert you that some businesses may try to defraud consumers by selling illegal window tint.

headline: Election 2002 shows the ugly side of politics
abstract: Claims of dirty tricks and distortions continued in PA up until Election day. The Pennsylvania Election Code does not address alleged misinterpretations, distortions, or lies in campaign, according to PA State Department Commissioner Richard Filling.

headline: Mayor Street delays vacation to attend talks
abstract: Philadelphia's Mayor Street has postponed his vacation to preside over intensive negotiations to resolve the labor & management problems plaguing the Pennsylvania Convention Center.  Negotiations begin this morning, and it was just a week ago that a top official of the Carpenter's Union rejected the idea of a unified labor force recommended in a report on how to clean up the convention center mess.  The Mayor has already been working behind the scenes, and while he still supports the labor model specified in the consultant's report, a different scenario that achieves the same result would be acceptable.

headline: She works for city, she doesn't work for city
abstract: Naomi Post, wife of Mayor Street, is paid $115,000 a year to run nonprofit social service agency under an arrangement that keeps her on the city payroll and permits her to continue accruing municipal pension benefits.  The money to pay for Post's salary comes from Philadelphia Safe and Sound Inc., the child-advocacy charity that is largely funded by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.  Under the arrangement, Safe and Sound, and not the city, determines what Post's salary will be.  It then channels funds through the city treasury to pay Post.  Mayor Street's latest financial disclosure form, filed April 30, identifies Post's employer as Philadelphia Safe and Sound Inc., and her job title as "executive director."

headline: What's this wage tax stuff all about
abstract: Is the wage tax killing our city, sending Philly's jobs and residents to the suburbs-or farther away?  Or would wage-tax cuts mean drastic reductions in city services and city jobs?  A question and answer to help sort out the great debate over the city's prime source of funds.

headline: Congressman Borski may be a lame duck
abstract: U.S. Representative Robert Borski last week outlined the proposed new makeup of his congressional district. Pennsylvania is losing two seats because of the sluggish population growth in the 1990s, and Republicans are using the opportunity to make sure that the two seats that will be eliminated belong to Democrats. Under the most optimistic GOP plan, 14 of the 19 seats will be won by Republicans.

headline: At least, adversaries are talking again about closing state's budget gap
abstract: State lawmakers have until June 30 to pass a state budget, or the state will not be allowed to spend any money. The budget is facing a deficit and the Morning Call thinks that cigarette tax and tipping fees and the rainy day fund could help lawmakers solve the budget crisis.

headline: Barnes wins grant for inventory
abstract: The Barnes Foundation has received a $14,167 state grant to help finance an inventory of its papers and world-renowned art collection, State Sen. Constance H Williams (D., Montgomery) announced Tuesday.  The grant from the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission will enable the foundation to hire a part-time archival assistant to sort through correspondence left by millionaire Albert C. Barnes, founder of the museum.

headline: PA Supreme Court upholds governor's power to fire game commissioner
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has upheld a lower court ruling that found former Gov. Tom Ridge was within his administrative powers to fire former Game Commissioner George Venesky.  Ridge fired Venesky from the Game Commission in December, 2000, after Venesky had completed just 2 -1/2 years of an eight-year term that was due to expire in mid-2006.  Venesky sued, arguing Ridge lacked the authority to dismiss him, even though Ridge nominated Venesky to the job.

headline: Panel wants to open hearings
abstract: A PA State advisory committee has endorsed giving the public access to hearings for abused and neglected children. The  PA Joint State Commission's Task Force on Services to Children and Youth announced in their report that a number of new changes to the system are coming.

headline: America honors its veterans
abstract: The nation will observe Veterans Day on Monday in memory of all the Vietnam war veterans. In Sommerset County, the flight 93 Memorial chapel will unveil an outdoor metal sculpture, named the Memorial Torch of Liberty, in memory of the passengers and crew of flight 93.

headline: Election-day mopes dampen democracy
abstract: Who wins when voter's don't vote?  It's a question that primary elections raise because so few voters cast ballots in primaries.  Many just let the party decide what their choices will be in the fall.  So whom should they blame if they don't like the choices in the fall?

headline: Maza may join senate race
abstract: Borough attorney and former Montgomery County commissioner James W. Maza said he intends to explore over the next three weeks whether he has what it takes to run for state senate. Maza, 53, chairman of the Marlborough Township Board of Supervisors, said he is interested in running as a Democratic candidate for the 24th Senatorial District only if current Republican Senator Edwin G. Holl of Landsdale opts not to run for re-election.

headline: Sheriff, Roddey face off on pay for employees
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Jim Roddey is warning that he will withhold paychecks from about 60 sheriff's department employees, effective next payday, even if they continue to work.  But Sheriff Pete DeFazio is keeping his entire staff on the job.  He said he is prepared to take Roddey to court if the chief executive refuses to sign the paychecks at the end of the current two-week pay period, which began yesterday.  The Sheriff's Department is on pace to be $2.8 million over its $9.9 million budget allocation this year.  That prompted Roddey to threaten to block the paychecks for about one-third of DeFazio's employees.

headline: Why county is wary of new voting machines
abstract: Lake Shore County officials have gathered information on voting systems over the past two years and have found that the systems range in cost from $1.6 million to 4.8 million. County officials are reluctant to spend that amount of money on new voting systems.

headline: Congressman fires volley at critics of his 71 years
abstract: US Representative George W. Gekas has challenged anyone who thinks he is too old for Congress to a game of tennis. Gekas is 71 and has responded to questions regarding his age.

headline: Being tough on crime is tough on budget
abstract: Pennsylvania has not found it necessary to give prison inmates early releases in order to balance the budget. PA Governor-Elect Ed Rendell has said that the state could be facing a budget deficit of in the billions if something isn't done to curb the problem.

headline: Bill bans spanking in school
abstract: A leading state lawmaker wants to take the paddle out of teachers' hands.  State Rep. Mike Veon of Beaver County is introducing legislation that would forbid corporal punishment in Pennsylvania public schools.  The Pennsylvania School Code permits physical reprimands in the state's 501 school districts.

headline: Pa. alters hunting targets
abstract: Deer hunters this season will again target antler-less deer. The season will go on for two weeks instead of two or three days. Forests have about 930,000 deer, which is about 400,000 more than what they can support and the state is issuing about 1.03 million "antler-less" licenses this fall, which is up by 32% from last year.

headline: PennDOT examiner pleads guilty to selling bogus truck driver's licenses
abstract: Robert Ferrari, a former Pennsylvania driver's license examiner who sold fraudulent licenses in exchange for bribes, pleaded guilty and faces a prison term of 18 to 24 months when he is sentenced by U.S. District Judge Robert Cindrich. Ferrari was able to strike a deal with prosecutors because of his cooperation with federal agents in the investigation of 20 Middle Eastern men who bought bogus commercial driver's licenses and permits to haul hazardous materials. After Sept. 11 attacks, Ferrari provided information about the men, most of the Iraqi refugees, and the FBI immediately detained them out of fear they might be terrorists planning further mayhem.

headline: Bush planning to topple Hussein
abstract: President Bush has decided to oust Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein from power and ordered the CIA, the Pentagon and other agencies to devise a combination of military, diplomatic and covert steps to achieve that goal. No military strike is imminent, but Bush has concluded that Hussein and his nuclear, chemical and biological weapons programs are such a threat to U.S. security that the Iraqi dictator must be removed.

headline: Elections 2002
abstract: The November 5, election day will see voters deciding on PA governor, U.S. congressional candidates, PA state legislative candidates and on a ballot question that would authorize as much as $100 million in borrowing to buy equipment for volunteer firefighters, ambulance operators and other emergency services crew.

headline: McHale's role gives worrywarts much to consider
abstract: Former U.S. Congressman Paul McHale is expected to be named Assistant Secretary of Defense. Writer Paul Carpenter says even with McHale's accomplishments there are still reasons to worry about his placement in the Department of Defense. Carpenter also says that in the process of fighting terrorism, federal agencies cannot disregard the Constitution.

headline: Sherwood lobbied to keep county intact
abstract: U.S. Representative Don Sherwood said Thursday he did his best to keep all of Lackawanna County in his congressional district and he wishes Scranton was still part of it. But as much as he or aides privately lobbied for the status quo, Sherwood said he couldn't change the minds of state General Assembly Republicans who controlled the redistricting process. Senate GOP counsel Stephen MacNett confirmed Mr. Sherwood made clear to Republican redistricters a desire to have all of heavily Democratic Lackawanna County or at least as much as possible.

headline: Why we can't afford to cut the wage tax
abstract: While some believe reducing the wage tax will help with Philadelphia's major problems- job and population losses, it provides very little in savings to the typical family. It would cost the city $120 million in lost revenue.

headline: Congressman to visit Penn state on Monday
abstract: U.S. Representative Harold Ford , Centre County Commissioner Scott Conklin and candidate for PA State Representative Rodney Nusser are scheduled to visit Pennsylvania State University.

headline: Budget bills call for referendum on firefighting funds
abstract: Because the Haneyville Fire Co. receives no tax money for its $20,000 budget, its 25 members depend heavily on community goodwill to keep the department running, said Bill McCoy, chief of the Lycoming County company.  Gov. Mark S. Schweiker has included ways the state can offer some help in the $20.7 billion budget he signed on Saturday.  A tax code bill in the budget package calls for a November referendum on whether the state should borrow up to $100 million to create a program that would improve volunteer fire and emergency services.

headline: Casey, Rendell slugfest centers on education
abstract: The two Democratic candidates running for governor have battled each other in television commercials, debating on how well or poor Ed Rendell did to improve the quality of Philadelphia schools. Rendell wants to improve the state's chare of education funding while Casey is criticizing Rendell's approach and proposed a tax rebate.

headline: Padoubles landfill capacity despite outcry over trash imports
abstract: Pennsylvania, the nation’s largest importer of garbage, has doubled its capacity for trash from 1995 to 2000. The industry provides 19,000 jobs and $100 million in revenue to municipal and county governments. Both environmentalists groups and lawmakers are trying to pass legislation to rein in this industry.

headline: Pennsylvania announces new witness protection program
abstract: Law enforcement officials are hoping that an offer to help Pennsylvania witnesses find safe homes will yield more information about unsolved crimes and put more criminals behind bars. Attorney General Mike Fisher said a new state witness protection program is not only necessary in making arrests and convicting criminals, but is vital for the safety of the witnesses. So far, officials say the program has helped two witnesses relocate.

headline: Bush: Pittsburgh on front line in war against bioterror
abstract: President Bush and the Oakland academic establishment were a study in mutual admiration during a visit that was part seminar and part sales pitch for a vast increase in spending to combat terrorism. Bush detailed his plans for spending on public health while putting them in the perspective of the struggle against terrorism. He said that by the end of this year the nation would have enough medicine stockpiled to shield as many as 20 million people against disease like anthrax and plague.

headline: Embattled legislator quitting House seat, cites "campaign to destroy me, my family'; supporters, foes "shocked"
abstract: State Representative John E. Barley has decided to quit his campaign and resign from his seat. He previous had left the race do to harassment of himself and family, but decided to come back again to try for his tenth term. He has decided again to drop out citing harassment as the reason.

headline: Mcllhinney looks to hold seat.In 143rd district, early results have him with nearly 3,000 vote edge
abstract: Unofficial early returns in the 143rd district election had PA State Representative Charles McIlhinney with 9,525 votes and Betsy Helsel with 6,790. Both are Republicans, but Helsel's name appeared on the Democratic ballot.

headline: Shuster calls redistricting ruling 'irrational decision'
abstract: Congressman Bill Shuster called a federal court ruling overturning the state's congressional redistricting plan on "irrational decision" on Wednesday.  A three-judge U.S. District Court panel found that Pennsylvania Republicans, in putting together a plan with congressional districts that varied by no more than 10 people from the average district of 646, 371 people, had too wide a deviation for an allowable plan.  The widest deviation between any two districts was 19 people.

headline: Zoning upheld
abstract: The US Supreme Court has ruled that local governments due have the power to impose land-use controls on private property. Last year, the court ruled that a property owner might be entitled to compensation even if he knew when he bought the land that development was restricted. The Fifth Amendment prohibits the government from taking private property without just compensation.

headline: Consultant predicts difficulty in Philadelphia for Fisher
abstract: Gubernatorial candidate Mike Fisher intends to campaign in every part of the state, but Philadelphia and its suburban counties. Those areas are considered a major obstacle for him to overcome if he is to defeat Democrat Ed Rendell.

headline: Budget expected to avoid tax hike
abstract: The state General Assembly is expected to pass a budget that does not have an income tax increase despite a projected growing deficit. The budget will be $677 million short for the current fiscal year.

headline: Cleveland focus of voucher debate
abstract: The US Supreme Court will decide if Cleveland's voucher program violates the constitutional separation of church and state. Former Governor Tom Ridge attempted and failed three times to get a voucher program through the PA General Assembly.

headline: Penn DOT offering timbered land in exchange for I-99 sites
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation is offering to give up 3 acres of timbered land for each of the 68 acres it wants to seize from the PA State Game Commission. Penn DOT plans to buy more than 200 acres of nearby land to give it to the Game Commission as an exchange.

headline: Philadelphia police plan new anti-drug push
abstract: The new goal of the Philadelphia Police Department is prevention and deterrence rather than arrests. It is the largest anti-drug operation launched by the Department. The operation will take as long as it needs.

headline: Drivers needed for trips to VA medical centers
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of the Disabled American Veterans is seeking volunteers with a strong sense of duty.  The PDDAV needs drivers willing to spend a few hours a week to take disabled military veterans to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs medical centers.  Locally, the Department of Disabled American Veterans has about a quarter as many volunteer drivers as it needs to provide free transportation to the VA center in Lebanon, the main veterans' hospital serving the mid-state.

headline: Embattled venture won't seek reelection
abstract: Governor of Minnesota, Jesse Ventura, has announced that he will not seek reelection. This decision comes after he has fallen in the polls and his family has been receiving negative media attention.

headline: Media mayor spearheads rally supporting Rendell
abstract: Mayor Bob McMahon led a rally of borough lawmakers, teachers and parents supporting Democratic gubernatorial candidate Edward G. Rendell yesterday, and questioning Republican candidate Mike Fisher's education reform plan - or lack thereof.  Similar rallies up and down the eastern part of the state took place simultaneously yesterday to show parents the differences between Rendell and Fisher's education reform philosophies.

headline: Shuster captures GOP nomination
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Shuster has defeated challengers David E. Bahr and David S. Keller for the Republican nomination in the 9th District in Tuesday's primary election.  With 100% of precincts reporting, Shuster had 33,293 votes; Keller had 6,288 votes; and Bahr trailed with 5,413 votes.  Shuster will face Democrat John Henry in November.

headline: Billionaire publisher and philanthropist Walter Annenberg dies at 94
abstract: Walter Annenberg who launched national TV guide magazine and served as ambassador to Great Britain has died from pneumonia at age 94. Annenberg built Triangle publications and was listed as one of the wealthiest Americans by Forbes magazine. He also donated a collection of masterpieces of art worth $1 billion to New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art.

headline: Democrats approve Council redistricting; Republicans upset
abstract: Democrats on Allegheny County Council mustered enough votes yesterday to approve a reapportionment map drawn by their party.  The new map closely resembles one that U.S. District Judge Robert Cindrich threw out in March after hearing a Republican lawsuit.  But the new version divides Pittsburgh voters among only four districts, squarely addressing the judge's finding that the earlier map spread the city among six districts, two more than allowed by county law.

headline: Budget lets lawmakers work in secret
abstract: Lawmakers have loaded the state's capital budget for the next year with $12billion in pet projects and there is no record available to the public to find out which legislators sponsored projects included in the capital budget.

headline: Bush's visit expected to back security plans
abstract: Research at the University of Pittsburgh will provide the framework today for President Bush to promote his plan to spend nearly double on homeland security next year. One program of special interest to Bush is University of Pittsburgh's BioMedical Security Institute, which is developing a system to recognize early signs of bioterror attacks. White House spokesman Scott Stanzel Bush’s visit to the University of Pittsburgh will give him a platform to outline the need for dedicating more money into fighting bioterrorism.

headline: Pennsylvanians must focus on demands of rare winter drought
abstract: Tuesday, Gov. Mark Schweiker declared a rare wintertime drought emergency for 24 counties, including Lehigh Valley.  Under his declaration, residents in those eastern and south-central counties face mandatory restrictions on "nonessential" water use, such as watering lawns and washing cars.  Winter is the time of year when nature recharges reservoirs, but when nature fails to do the job, its up to people to adjust.

headline: Pittsburgh police start issuing fines for littering
abstract: Pittsburg police spent two weeks warning scores of residents not to litter, but the opening day of the city's litter crackdown got off to a slow start yesterday.  Police are now issuing 15-dollar fines to people who toss a cigarette butt or throw a coffee cup.  But because of staffing shortages and cool weather, few fines issued yesterday.

headline: Flag makes it's way from Ground Zero to Pentagon
abstract: Runners are hand delivering a special flag from the Pentagon to Ground Zero in New York City.  The Relay runners left the Pentagon at about 2 a-m Sunday, carrying an American flag that flew at a field location in Afghanistan and at the Pentagon.  The runners will cover more than 400 miles as they head to the Pennsylvania crash site at Shenksville before moving on to Ground Zero in New York.

headline: Enron collapse had minimal impact on state investments, lawmakers told
abstract: The state of Pennsylvania lost $87 million due to Enron's financial collapse. Treasurer Barbara Hafer told the state lawmakers that it was only a small percentage of the state's investments.

headline: Mellow for senate
abstract: People want to endorse PA State Senator Robert Mellow, a democrat who is a minority chairman in the Senate, because they believe that he will be in a good position to deliver for the people,  in the likely event that voters elect Ed Rendell as governor.

headline: Shuster moving on up in the House
abstract: U.S. Representative Bill Shuster has been named Assistant Majority Whip in the House. The position shows that Shuster is on the move up in the Congress and could bring great benefits to that state of PA.

headline: Bucks to see 'Signs' earlier than others
abstract: Clarence Berger is looking forward to the weekend when the film "Signs" opens in theaters.  The movie, starring Mel Gibson and directed by Hollywood thriller master M. Night Shyamalan, was filmed mostly in Bucks County in the fall.  On Thursday, Gov. Mark Schweiker, a former Bucks County commissioner, will be host to a sneak preview party at 7 p.m. at the Michener Art Museum and the County Theater in Doylestown to benefit Network of Victim Assistance, a crime victims' advocacy group in Bucks County.

headline: Contractor accused of illegal campaign contributors
abstract: A defense contractor is accused of seeking to influence five members of Congress --- including Democrat John Murtha of Pennsylvania -- with illegal campaign contributions, according to a federal indictment unsealed Tuesday.  The president of Science and Applied Technology Inc. solicited employees and others to make illegal contributions to Republican Rep. Randy "Duke" Cunningham of California, Democratic Sen. John Kerry of Massachusetts and three other congressmen, according to the indictment.  The contributions, totaling more than $75,000 over eight years, were intended to help the company win lucrative U.S. government contracts for an air-to-ground missile system, the indictment alleges.

headline: Budget plan slashes river spending
abstract: President Bush's proposal to slash about 13 percent from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers fiscal year 2003 budget could mean a $1.83 million cut for maintenance and operations of Allegheny River locks and dams. Lawmakers and lobbyists are confident, despite Bush's insistence that money is needed for the war on terrorism, that Congress will restore most of the money Bush hopes to cut. Bush's proposed budget won't affect progress on the cleanup of the nuclear waste burial grounds in Parks.

headline: Candidates pressured to reform school funding
abstract: People from across the state are protesting the high property taxes which are used to fund the public schools. Rallies have been held to call for changes to school funding. Some want the state to pay for over half of the funding.

headline: Picking the trash for more money
abstract: State Representative Kate Harper has proposed a bill to raise the tipping fee for waste deposited in landfills. A number of other proposals are being made to get the money for state lawmakers to fund their own Green projects.

headline: Pittsburgh settles last 32 police abuse suits for $275,000
abstract: The city of Pittsburgh has agreed to settle 32 pending police abuse lawsuits, totaling damages in the amount of $275,000. Pittsburgh City council must approve the deal. It was designed to save the taxpayer the expense of trial.

headline: Kanjorski fighting to save veterans benefits
abstract: U.S Representative Paul Kanjorski, a co-sponsor of the Retired Pay Restoration Act, has said that more than 25,000 military veterans have signed a petition urging the government to provide quality medical care to all veterans. The administration is arguing that the veterans should not be able to "double dip" retirement benefits and disability benefits at the same time.

headline: 'Erin's Law' finally passes committee
abstract: The General Assembly passed 'Erin's Law' which would regulate petting zoos. Rick Jacobs' daughter died after contracting E. Coli at a petting zoo. Jacobs threatened to run for the state Senate if the bill was not passed.

headline: Mellow is regional chair for Rendell
abstract: Luzerne County Controller Steve Flood has been supporting Ed Rendell for PA governor. State Senator Robert Mellow has been named the Northeast regional chair of Rendell's general election.

headline: Signed into Law
abstract: PA Governor Mark Schweiker has signed several bills into law including bills that allow Sunday liquor sales, that require the Pledge of Allegiance to be said in schools, that require hand-washing stations at petting zoos, that let the government burden certain religious freedoms, that provide safe havens for newborn drop-offs, and that allow Bucks County officials to increase taxes.

headline: Cell phones are bad, crybaby colleges day
abstract: The Daily News writes on the most ridiculous items around the county including: a ban of cell phone at colleges to save money, parents who tied up their daughter to stop her from dating a married man, commercials being better then television programs, and a New York strip club billboard.

headline: Convention bid may lack appeal this time around
abstract: After the success of the Republican National Convention in Philadelphia in 2000, Mayor Street is pushing for a bid for hosting the Democratic National Convention in 2004. The deadline is approaching, but the city is unsure if it can put together another convention.

headline: Budget shortfall: Cutting through the smoke of the tobacco deal
abstract: Several Democrat lawmakers pounced on Republican Gov. Mark Schweiker for dipping into the tobacco fund to help balance the state budget. Unlike the last seven years under Schweiker's predecessor, Republican Gov. Tom Ridge, when state coffers were flush with cash, the commonwealth faces a budget shortfall of at least $670 million. One of the ways Schweiker balanced the budget was transferring $182 million from the state's tobacco settlement fund.

headline: Charter school closing backed, protested
abstract: Thurgood Marshall Academy Charter School families urged the Wilkinsburg school board to keep their school open at least until June. The state Charter School Appeal Board said the school board has more than enough justification to close the school. The appeal board, which unanimously rejected the academy’s appeal last month, left the date of the closing up to the school district, which has unanimously voted to close the academy January 25th.

headline: Platts decries environmental rating
abstract: US Representative Todd Platts said his low approval rating from the League of Conversation Voters, a nonprofit group with environmental ties,  is unfair and misleading.

headline: Plan omits city magisterial courts
abstract: The state Supreme Court has received two proposals to change the boundaries of minor judiciary districts in Allegheny County. One proposal involves eliminating Pittsburgh's magistrates court.

headline: Murtha seeks turf Mascara calls his
abstract: US Representative Jack Murtha handed a $1 million check to Washington and Jefferson University to establish a training center for National Guard personnel. Representative Frank Mascara wants to challenge Murtha after his district was combined with Murtha's. Both men are popular in the area.

headline: Ethics question dogs Kanjorski. Research funds helped family firm. he says benefit was incidental
abstract: U.S. Representative Paul Kanjorski is taking ethical hit. He is accused of arranging the federal budget that brought more than $7 million to Cornerstone Technologies, which is partly owned by his family members. Most recently he added a line to a defense appropriation bill that funds the development of 'material micronization' which benefits Cornerstone Technologies.

headline: Memo shows Enron CEO heard of problems in August
abstract: An employee of Enron Corp. warned its chairman last summer that the now-bankrupt energy company could "implode in a wave of accounting scandals" and that disgruntled employees knew enough about Enron's financial books "to get us into trouble." The warning, in a memo that congressional investigators obtained, raises questions about senior Enron officers became aware of the dubious bookkeeping practices that led to the company's collapse.

headline: Silence reigns on final day of Barley's career
abstract: John E. Barley's resignation from the state House becomes official today, a quiet and uneventful end to a 17-year legislative career that had become enveloped in controversy.  Barley has not commented publicly since his March 23 announcement, and officials in Harrisburg won't speculate on his decision.  Barley is being paid for one day of service in April about $237 gross, according to the House Office of the Chief Clerk.

headline: Dan Rooney back in the air after crash landing plane
abstract: Dan Rooney walked in the front door of his North Side home shortly after he set his Beechcraft Bonanza down on its belly at Allegheny County Airport Wednesday night and proudly declared to his wife, " I just made by best landing."  Flying has been a passion for Rooney, the Steelers' 70-year-old president, for the past 27 years - - despite his family's concerns about it - - but he never had an experience quite like the emergency landing in West Mifflin.  His crash landing did not prevent an uninjured Rooney from climbing into a rented Cessna yesterday afternoon to fly himself and two others back to Latrobe to watch his team practice at St. Vincent College.

headline: Convention Center candidate emerges
abstract: Former state Revenue Secretary Robert Judge has become the frontrunner for the next chief of the Philadelphia Convention Center. The current president plans to resign for medical reasons. The names of candidates will be released this spring.

headline: Budget vote expected this week
abstract: State lawmakers and the Schweiker administration have reached a state budget agreement. Three quarters of the Rainy Day fund will be used to cover a deficit and a cigarette and trash tax will be increased.

headline: Charter School Pupils Struggle on Pa. tests
abstract: A study by the Tribune Review showed that 69% of PA charter elementary public schools and 46% of charter middle schools scored below the bottom fifth of all public schools in the state. Changing the course for charter schools, the discipline of charter schools, the problems/obstacles of charter schools, and performances by PA charter schools in the study are examined.

headline: Playing by different rules
abstract: Local watershed organizations are encouraged to focus their energies on "non-point" sources of pollution. Coal companies pollute streams and subsided pools fill in with several feet of sediment, but instead of being punished the government says the streams will recover.

headline: Pol wants no deadline on priest-abuse cases
abstract: Proposed legislation would lift the criminal statute of limitations that bars prosecution for child sexual abuse unless the victim comes forward by age 23. Civil law keeps dockets clear of suits against priests and dioceses. The Pennsylvania Catholic Conference does not oppose the bill.

headline: President courts three U.N. Security Council members as he opens international lobbying on Iraq
abstract: President Bush, taking his anti-Iraq public relations campaign overseas, telephoned leaders of China, Russia and France on Friday in hopes of softening their opposition to action against Saddam Hussein.  In a round of early morning calls from the Oval Office, Bush talked with Presidents Jacques Chirac of France, Jiang Zemin of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia.  Each could use their votes on the United Nations Security Council to veto resolutions aimed at Saddam.

headline: Ex-Chairman of Enron Cancels Hill Testimony
abstract: Former Enron chairman Kenneth L. Lay abruptly cancelled a much-anticipated appearance before a Senate panel in the wake of a scathing report on the management failures and self-dealing that led his company's spectacular collapse. Key members of Congress, reacting to the report said top officials of the bankrupt energy trader may have engaged in securities fraud in booking $1 billion in non-existent profits over the past 15 months. The Justice Department is conducting an investigation into Enron's collapse.

headline: Midstate Recap and State Recap
abstract: The results of the PA State House and Senate races as well as the results of U.S House races are listed.

headline: Six of seven legislators say they support Casey
abstract: Bob Casey Jr. released a statement saying 61 or the 98 state House Democrats have endorsed him instead of Ed Rendell for the Democratic primary for governor. The state House Democratic Whip Michael Veon came out and endorsed Rendell.

headline: Dennis W. Kanouff/State's top Elk keeping very busy
abstract: Dennis W. Kanouff's new responsibilities as president of the Pennsylvania Elks State Association will be keeping him on state roads this year, tracking the activities of Pennsylvania's 60,000 Elks members.  But Kanouff still is committed to his Monday morning ritual of making ham salad and dicing onions in his kitchen for Monday night bingo at his own lodge, Oakmont Elks Lodge 1668.

headline: Convention center opening gets chair
abstract: Ann McGuinn has been appointed to the chair position of the new David L. Lawrence Convention Center.

headline: Bush Budget Underscores His Priorities
abstract: President Bush will propose budget that would keep funding nearly flat for the departments of Agriculture, Commerce, Education, Interior and Justice, as well as the environmental-protection and space agencies, while sharply cutting the budgets of the Labor Department and Army Corps of Engineers. Bush and his aides have been publicly trumpeting the big increases proposed for defense and homeland security for fiscal year 2003. The thick budget books also attempt to focus attention on that time; their covers are emblazoned with a waving American flag.

headline: Charter schools get sudden support
abstract: With $75 million in funding at stake, Philadelphia School Reform Commission chairman James Nevels heads to Harrisburg today prepared to outline an expanded school-reform plan.  In an interview with The Inquirer, Nevels said that at least three high schools would be added to the list of 70 low-performing elementary and middle schools targeted for overhaul.  The schools, to be overseen by outside managers, are expected to be identified this week.

headline: Port, maritime officials blast report critical of dredging plan
abstract: Supporters of the Delaware river shipping channel project say a report questioning the economic benefits of dredging the channel is misleading and wrong. Officials from the Port of Wilmington and the Maritime Exchange for the Delaware River and Bay want to deepen the channel by five feet.

headline: Police: Wanna-be hero of 9/11 exploits tragedy
abstract: Bill Bresnahan, a retired Philadelphia police officer, drove from Chester County to New York to help after September 11th. He has been known as a a hero, but he is now profiting off of his stories. He has since been charged with theft by deception which is a felony.

headline: Supreme court says it will take up Agent Orange case
abstract: The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to decide if two cancer-stricken Vietnam veterans, Stephenson and Issacson, can reopen a challenge against chemical companies over exposure to Agent Orange. Agent Orange was the chemical used by U.S armed forces in the 1960s and 1970s to clear dense jungle growth in Vietnam.

headline: Executive race cost Ervin campaign $1.70 per vote
abstract: The two candidates in the Nov. 6 election for Lehigh County executive reported a combined $63, 240 in campaign spending from June to November. Lehigh County Executive Jane R. Ervin, a Republican elected with 53 percent of the vote, reported her campaign was responsible for $42, 275 in spending, almost 67 percent of the spending total. Democrat Matthew Croslis reported his campaign committee spent $19,779 from June to November.

headline: Mifflin County's Clark drops out of race for 81st District seat
abstract: Larry Clark, the only Democratic nominee for the state House of Representatives 81st District, recently announced his decision to withdraw from the race.  Clark, of McVeytown, said he's leaving the race with over 40 days until the election because signatures on his petitions for candidacy were challenged.  Clark said he decided not to fight the challenge because he would need to hire a lawyer, something he is not willing to do.

headline: Six Reform Party stalwarts gather to prepare for upcoming races
abstract: Six true believers gathered in a side room of the Hampton Inn on a rainy night.  That was the setting for Wednesday might's reorganization meeting of the Reform Party of Monroe County.  Party members selected representatives for county and state committee, and prepared to support Tom McLaughlin, of Bartonsville, in his Congressional campaign this fall.

headline: It's a coin toss for Schweiker
abstract: Governor Schweiker has to decide whether to go the Steelers or Eagles NFL playoff game. Either choice will potentially cost Pennsylvania taxpayers.

headline: Coolbaugh Dem replaces Battisto in state race
abstract: Coolbaugh Township Supervisor Gratz Washenik will replace Joseph Battisto in the race for the 176th District state House seat, the Monroe County Democratic Committee announced Thursday.  Washenik. 44, will face Republican Mario Scavello, who won a special election in April to fill the new Monroe County seat until the end of the year.  Among those who attend the committee meeting were Battisto and state Sen. Lisa Boscola, whose 18th District includes part of Monroe, Northampton and Lehigh counties.

headline: Bush considers factoring inflation for tax break
abstract: President's Bush senior advisers are debating a capital gains tax cut that would let taxpayers subtract the effect of inflation from profits on the sale of stocks, real estate or other assets.  Bush has not decided whether to go ahead with it, administration and congressional sources say.  It is sure to encounter resistance on Capitol Hill.  The proposal is one of several Bush is considering to restore investor confidence in Wall Street and the economy.

headline: Charter schools OKs are put on hold
abstract: The applications of 25 groups to open new charter schools in Philadelphia in September were put on hold until November by the School Reform Commission. The surprise vote left charter school advocates angry and disappointed that they had no chance to talk to the commission before the decision was made. The vote to push back the 25 applications passed unanimously with no discussion at the commission meeting.

headline: Proposed changes in deer hunting hit nerves
abstract: The state Game Commission is deciding whether or not it should approve of changes to the deer hunting season. It wants to impose antler restrictions, which would limit the killing of younger bucks. The new policy would allow only bucks with four or more points on one side to be hunted.

headline: Politics trounces reason in gun control debate
abstract: The Justice Department wants to change the Second Amendment which states a 'right to bear arms.'
