The department told the Supreme Court that its previous rulings have been wrong which claimed the Second Amendment focuses on state militia's and not private individuals. The departments wants to make personal gun possession a constitutional right.

headline: Unloaded and unready
abstract: National Guard troops are patrolling Pennsylvania airports and nuclear power stations with unloaded weapons, suggesting that commanders don't trust their soldiers to act responsibly.  Requiring soldiers to keep their ammunition out of their weapon unless ordered otherwise defeats the very purpose of placing these troops at locations thought to be possible terrorist targets.

headline: Ex-mayor built on his reputation in Philly area
abstract: Rendell first trailed by 10 points in polls, and unions were questioning his integrity and accomplishments at the staet of his campaign.  Six months later, his popularity has given him a fortress in the region that already knew him as a leader, Philadelphia.

headline: Mike Diven trips out on Cuba
abstract: Democratic state House member Michael Diven is planning a U.S. Cuba Sister Cities Conference. Representative Diven invited fellow House members to make the trip to bolster Pennsylvania's trade status with the Communist island regime. This might be a bad idea noting the United States still maintains an embargo on most trade with Cuba.

headline: Something went doggone wrong
abstract: The author of this article, John Baer, contends that President Bush's dogs are probable suspects in a recent pretzel-trauma, in which Bush chocked on a pretzel while watching the NFL.

headline: New York millionaire gives $750,000 to Harrisburg
abstract: Mortimer Levitt, a New York City millionaire, is donating $750,000 to have Harrisburg's amphitheater upgraded. He has donated to 22 cities in order to have sites named after him.

headline: Council Rock contract does not include a pay raise
abstract: The tentative contract for teachers in the state's highest-paid school district does not include a pay raise in the first year, union members said.  Members of the Council Rock Education Association, who went on strike for three days last week, met Sunday to discuss the deal, which was struck early Friday morning.  Union members, who asked not to be identified, said the agreement does not include a salary increase in the first year.

headline: Bush invites ideas about the economy
abstract: Hoping to bolster confidence in the sputtering economy, President Bush has invited a diverse group of investors, workers, corporate executives, students and economists to Texas on Tuesday to share ideas about promoting economic growth.  The high profile gathering at Baylor University in Waco is part of a White House campaign to reassure Americans that the economy is on track and in capable hands.  Most experts agree that there is little any president can do short-term to reinvigorate a weak economy, but Bush will be held to account for it anyway.

headline: Charter school's principal resigns
abstract: Harrisburg's largest charter school is facing its first crises in its two-year history, refusing to pay the for-profit company that manages it and receiving the resignation of its principal.  The Ronald H. Brown Charter School has not paid Mosaica Education Inc., the New York-based company that provides management and curriculum, as the result of a dispute that the company and the school's local board of trustees would not discuss.  The dispute comes at a time when the midtown school, the largest of two Harrisburg charter schools with more than 500 students, has expanded to eight grades and is considering the addition of grades 9 through 12.

headline: Proposed state budget cuts could affect environmental grants
abstract: Two environmental grant programs for projects in Luzerne and Lackawanna counties could be cut after proposed budget cuts for the upcoming year. Other environmental programs have had their funding cut by 50 percent.

headline: Preventable tragedy
abstract: Alexandra Wake, 14, her mother Sandra Watkins, and her maternal grandparents, Jimmy and Juanita Watkins, were all hot to death at their Ardmore home by Sandra's husband of four years Michael Burgess. Burgess, suffering from depression, purchased the gun after the police had been called to the house for domestic violence earlier in the year. Pennsylvania, like most states, only restricts persons that are involuntary committed with a mental illness from purchasing a gun. If Pennsylvania had a law such as Connecticut does, Watkins' friends or family could have had the gun removed from the Watkins home.

headline: Veterans to get local cemetery
abstract: Federal officials have finally struck a multimillion-dollar land deal with two Washington County farmers that will clear a place for western Pennsylvania veterans to be buried closer to home.  The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs said Thursday that after two years, brothers William and Robert Morgan, of Cecil Township, have agreed to accept "several million dollars" for their adjoining dairy farms just south of the Allegheny County line.  The sale is one of the final steps in turning 275 acres of farmland into a $40 million national veterans cemetery, the site of 15,000 graves.

headline: Experts say fisher must change strategy
abstract: Political experts are saying that Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Fisher needs to avoid attacks on Ed Rendell and focus more on promoting his key policy issues if he hopes to close the 15-point gap between them in the polls.

headline: Minnesotans glad Ventura isn't running
abstract: The vast majority of Minnesotans seem to think Governor Jesse Ventura's decision not to seek a second term is good for the state.  That's according to a new poll, which finds that two-thirds of respondents agree with the decision of the wrestler-turned-politician.  The survey also gave Ventura a 44 percent approval rating, down from 73 percent just two years ago.

headline: Son of Philadelphia mayor to try hand at politics
abstract: The eldest son of Philadelphia Mayor John Street, Sharif Street, is running for office against a veteran Democratic state representative who supported his father.  Sharif Street promised to run a grass-roots campaign in the 195th District, which Oliver has represented for 19 years.

headline: Philanthropic media baron Walter Annenberg dies
abstract: Walter Annenberg, an American billionaire, philanthropist, publisher, and a diplomat died on October 1. He was 94 years old.

headline: Council's vote for tax cuts marks Street's biggest defeat
abstract: With defeat looming, Mayor Street asked his fellow Democrat to postpone the vote on his measure to continue the wage-tax trims that Street wanted to halt.  That way, the pair could fashion a joint statement signifying that they had reached an accord. Nutter declined to go along. The time for lobbying was over.

headline: Bush's budget projects deficits
abstract: Undeterred by a return to deficits for the first time since 1997, President Bush plans to propose a 2003 budget next month that would give a boost to defense and leave the government $80 billion in the red. White House budget director Mitch Daniels said that Bush will ask Congress to give the Pentagon a $48 million or 15% hike, including a "war reserve" for the next phase of the U.S. campaign against terrorism.

headline: Chester school system mulling severing ties with Edison
abstract: Chester County Schools, one of the PA's poorest school districts, has hired Edison schools to rescue their troubled school system but is considering severing ties with the company. Edison schools won a five-year $60 million contract to operate 20 Philadelphia schools.

headline: Quecreek Mine Report: Executive Summary
abstract: The Governor's Commission on Abandoned Mine Voids and Mine Safety have released their report on broad issues surrounding the Quecreek Mine. A copy of the Governor's missions and functions for the Commission are outlined in the article as well as the recommendations by the Commission.

headline: Principle of shared liability challenged
abstract: A legal doctrine which gives joint and several liability has created a civil-suit system which encourages plaintiffs to search for the deepest pocket. One company had to pay a settlement because someone was shot on the store parking lot. Stakeholderds are looking to change the law.

headline: Windber quietly buries war hero and adopted son
abstract: Air Force Tech. Sgt. John Chapman was one of the first Americans to die in Afghanistan. More than 1000 people attended the viewing. His wife and two children attended the funereal where John was considered a hero.

headline: Ex-principal running for 9th District
abstract: Fresh from his stint as principal of Octorara Area High School, Henry "Hank" Detering announced recently that he will throw his hat into the race for the General Assembly, specifically the state senatorial seat for the 9th District.  The seat had been held by longtime state Sen. Clarence Bell, of Media, who recently passed away.  A special election to fill the seat for the remainder of this year is scheduled for Oct. 1.

headline: Minority leader DeWeese hires 2 policy advisors
abstract: The PA House Majority Leader Bill Deweese has hired Edward Haines and Audrey Powell to fill vacancies as policy advisors to the party.

headline: State legislators enabled big rip-off
abstract: The state pension system lost $106 million from the collapse of Enron. The state lawmakers helped to create bogus accounting practices which led to Enron's crash. A 1995 law allowed Enron to authorize dubious "forward looking" accounting.

headline: We gave $2.4 billion - - where did the money go?
abstract: The checks poured in for months after Sept. 11 - - the biggest charity drive in American history.  Nationwide, donors gave at least $2.42 billion, and the amount continues to grow.  Midstate charity drives alone generated about $4 million, according to a survey by The Patriot-News.  No other fund-raising effort comes close.  Seven of every 10 Americans contributed to Sept. 11 causes, studies show.

headline: County ethics code toothless, ignored and un-enforced; no watchdog panel named
abstract: Allegheny County Council has approved an ethics code but has yet to appoint an ethics commission. There is currently not commission to accept and investigate reports of ethics violations. Council President James Simms says the issue of property assessment got in the way.

headline: Bush's new economy of words
abstract: President Bush, mindful of rising jobless rates and Americans' growing worries about their finances, is turning his attention from the war on terrorism to the economy. Bush has renamed his package of tax cuts, extended jobless benefits, and subsidized health-insurance coverage from "economic stimulus" to "economic security." By casting his economic plan as a matter of national security, Bush hopes to generate public pressure on Democrats to take action.

headline: Chicagoan likely to be schools CEO
abstract: Philadelphia's School Reform Commission has chosen former Chicago public schools chief Paul G. Vallas to be the district's chief executive officer, a source close to the reform process said yesterday.  Vallas, 49, who ran Chicago's public schools for six years and recently lost a Democratic bid for Illinois governor, declined to comment yesterday.  He met with Mayor Street in Philadelphia yesterday and later with Gov. Schweiker in Harrisburg.

headline: Quecreek story leads visitors to Tour-Ed Mine's educational vein
abstract: The Quecreek Mine accident near Somerset made people around the world want to avoid going into coal mines - - including some of those nine rescued miners.  But at the Tour-Ed Mine near Tarentum, the curious have been queuing up to go deep.  The Tour-Ed -- "Ed" as in "educational" - -  Mine and Museum is an otherwise sleepy little tourist attraction on the northern fringe of Allegheny County. With Quecreek putting mining so miraculously on the map, so many more visitors than usual have been taking the plunge that Tour-Ed has decided to extend its season past the usual Labor Day closing and stay open on the weekends through October.

headline: Prisoner unlocks hepatitis C epidemic
abstract: One spring morning in 1992, inmate Rob Lassen reported to the infirmary at a state prison in Pittsburgh for routine blood work.  A prison nurse delivered the good news a few days later.  He didn't have HIV.  But the bad news took four years to get to him: Lassen had tested positive for hepatitis C, a blood-borne virus that attacks the liver and can destroy it.  Lassen is one of the reasons that Pennsylvania - unlike New Jersey and most other states - is aggressively tackling the hepatitis C epidemic within its prisons.

headline: Biotechnology gets big shot in arm
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker yesterday pointed to that joint effort as an example of how Pennsylvania-based brain power and scientific research can translate to an industry he hopes will become the foundation of the state's future economic success: biotechnology.  He did so while announcing the release of $100 million to fund three life-sciences "greenhouses" intended to spur development of the biotechnology industry across the state.  Schweiker said the investment will position Pennsylvania as a national leader in biotechnology, which involves the scientific manipulation of living organisms to create useful products.

headline: Ex-Rep. Brandt sues Armstrong over 'booze cruise' quote
abstract: The legislative career of state Representative Tom Armstrong may be ending this year, but legal troubles from his failed re-election bid are just beginning.  Before former state Rep. John E. Barley dropped his lawsuit against Armstrong, Carolyn Hetrick, an Elizabethtown attorney representing former state Rep. Kenneth Brandt, filed a writ of summons against Armstrong on May 24.  The writ was filed to notify Armstrong he is being sued by Brandt.

headline: Mixed reaction in Rendell victory
abstract: Ed Rendell, the governor-elect of Pennsylvania, represents different things to York County political leaders. In York County, PA Attorney General Mike Fisher beat Rendell 64% to 33%. Statewide, with 96& of precincts reporting, however, Rendell has 53% of the vote.

headline: Snyder man, SU graduate to square off
abstract: A Snyder County resident and a Susquehanna University alumnus will square off in the fall election for the 82nd District House seat, according to unofficial election results.  C. Adam Harris of Mifflintown won the Republican nomination, coming in first with 1,954 votes.  The other candidates for the Republican seat were: Frank Berrier, 1,792; Beth Reifsnyder, 1,755; and Jerry Leach, 1,571.

headline: County plans to keep voting machines
abstract: Westmoreland County officials have said the more than 700 lever voting machines are not broken and do not need to be replaced with a high-tech alternative. President George W. Bush signed into law the Help America Vote Act that authorizes $3.9 billion in federal spending to states for upgrades of voting machines.

headline: Candidates in 11th district focus on taxes
abstract: PA State Representative Guy Travaglio is facing Brian Ellis for the PA 11th district seat in the State House. Both candidates have different views on how to make up for the lost money in the state budget as a result of cutting property taxes. Travaglio sees slot machines as the way to create new source of income whereas Ellis sees an increase in state sales tax and personal income tax as the solution.

headline: City offers to help reform the schools
abstract: The School Reform Commission, in charge of city schools since the seized the troubled system, will release the names of the groups that are vying to provide a host of consulting services to the central administration. In a related matter, a coalition of unionized school employees and community groups refilled a complaint in state Supreme Court seeking to have the reform commission dissolved and the takeover declared unconstitutional. Last month the commission asked interested parties to submit their qualifications to help improve virtually every operation of the school district's central administration.

headline: Residents slow to follow septic law
abstract: More than 20 percent of township residents with septic systems are in violation of an ordinance requiring the pumping of those systems every 3 years. Approximately 350 residents haven't pumped their systems since the ordinance passed in December of 1998, meaning they'll soon be receiving notification from the township of that lapse. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection adopted its own policy calling for pumping every three years in 1989 and has in recent years been encouraging municipalities to follow suit.

headline: Private prison back on track for Philipsburgh after three-year stall
abstract: A three-year stall over the constitutionality of a private company housing PA prisoners seems to be coming to an end as issues surrounding the prison are being settled. Cornell Corrections, the proposed prison site, would bring a number of jobs to the area and be a great asset to the state.

headline: Committee discusses funding to provide newspaper stories to the blind
abstract: A state legislative committee is considering a bill that would use a telephone surcharge to fund a service for the blind to obtain newspaper stories using a touch-tone phone.  Representative Linda Bebko-Jones says she wants to provide a permanent state funding source for Newsline.  It's a nationwide newspaper service established by the National Federation for the Blind.

headline: FBI launches probe into Kennedy election
abstract: The Federal Bureau of Investigations began an investigation into possible voter fraud allegations related to Kennedy Township elections. The FBI has submitted all the related documents and the Weinsteins have denied the allegations against them.

headline: Montco divided in redistricting proposal
abstract: State legislative leaders revealed a compromise for cutting the number of congressional districts that would give the Republicans a substantial edge but preserve the seat of Pennsylvania's most senior Democrat. Republicans hope to stretch their current one-seat advantage to at least seven seats under the plan, which is expected to go to the General Assembly for a vote. The proposal also would create a new predominantly Republican 6th District in Chester, Berks and Montgomery counties and strengthen the GOP's position in the western part of the state.

headline: Sources: Feds probe Kanjorski
abstract: Several sources say federal investigators are looking at U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski's involvement in obtaining millions of federal dollars for the company Cornerstone Technologies partly owned by his nephew. Although the congressman holds no ownership in Cornerstone, a former employee said Kanjorski takes an active interest in the company. Federal law prohibits federal officials from being involved in companies to which they direct funding.

headline: Rendell takes mock election in a landslide
abstract: There were 505 students at Holland Middle School who cast mock ballots for PA governor. Of the votes casts, 352 said Ed Rendell would be their choice to be Pennsylvania's next Governor.

headline: Cash from WAM still flows
abstract: The budget is so tight that more than $309 million in state spending has been frozen. Despite being $622 million short of expected tax collections, the Governor hopes to release the remaining rounds of grants for the 2002 fiscal year.

headline: City school funding cutoff provokes calls for a shakeup
abstract: Government and community leaders across Pittsburgh said yesterday that they hope a decision by three local foundations to suspend all funding to the city schools will lead to a shakeup in how the district is run.  Richard Flanagan, youth development coordinator for the Bloomfield-Garfield Corp. and former school board member, agreed that the move by the Pittsburgh Foundation, The Heinz Endowments and the Grable Foundation should be an impetus for local leaders to become more involved in the city schools.

headline: Safe Drilling
abstract: The State House of Representatives has approved a bill that would license, certify, and regulate drillers and set standards for well construction. House bill 1519, which is in the Senate, raises concerns regarding the ability of the state to ensure that well drillers are doing what is needed to prevent contamination and related health problems.

headline: Probation given for phone threat
abstract: One year of probation was the punishment handed down last week to the man accused of threatening Betsy Helsel, a political candidate and Plumstead supervisor, in an anonymous telephone call in January.  Carl Smith, 52, of Danboro, was identified by his voice on Helsel's answering machine.  Smith will not face trial because prosecutors allowed him to enroll in Accelerated Terroristic-threat charges were dropped Wednesday, and Smith's criminal record will be expunged if he completes probation and has no contact with Helsel, First Assistant District Attorney David Zellis said.

headline: 'Do-Not-Call' law begins: Sales out, politics in
abstract: Pennsylvanians can now make their phone numbers off-limits to telemarketers pushing goods and services, but they remain powerless under the new "Do-Not-Call" law to block those pushing candidates, charities or causes.  Details of the program were announced yesterday by state Attorney General Mike Fisher, the Republican candidate for governor, who was asked whether his own campaign would voluntarily refrain from unsolicited calling.  "The answer to that question is 'No,' " Fisher said.

headline: Federal grant money awarded to three Pennsylvania groups
abstract: Three Pennsylvania organizations are collecting more than half-million dollars from the federal government. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has awarded a 195 thousand dollar grant to Community First Fund. The Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency got a 60 thousand dollar grant from the U.S. Department of Justice. The Justice Department is offering up to 300 thousand dollars to state and local government agencies and victim advocacy groups.

headline: Montgomery autoworker leads Poole for nomination
abstract: Montgomery County autoworker Rick Jacobs was the front-runner in the Democratic nomination for the open 44th state Senate seat.  Jacobs received 6,955 votes while Douglass Township farmer Kevin G. Poole got 3,281 votes. The campaign was low-key, but the candidates did differ on abortion and expanding legalized gambling.

headline: Sources: Johnson to become 'permanent'
abstract: Three months after he named Sylvester Johnson interim police commissioner, Mayor Street has decided to make the appointment permanent, sources said.  It could be not determined when Street intends to inform the public of his decision.  His office denied that the mayor has made up his mind to promote Johnson.

headline: Rendell talks homeland security, tax reform during Fayette visit
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ed Rendell praised local efforts when he toured rescue operations during Saturday's Fayette County Emergency Management and 911 Center's annual open house in downtown Uniontown.  But Rendell said more work needs to be done.  Arriving on his campaign bus early Saturday afternoon, Rendell examined displays that were set up in the parking lot next to the 911 center, located on Main Street, the exhibits featured special weapons, rescue equipment and canines used by Fayette County rescue personnel.

headline: Caucus floats tax proposal
abstract: The House Local Tax Policy Caucus released a three-part proposal to help reduce school's reliance on property taxes by shifting to income taxes. The proposal wants the state to assume control and provide all funding for special education. A local personal income tax would be created to pay for 3/4 of the budget.

headline: City's pilot reading program is a success
abstract: An experimental after-school literacy program run out of religious institutions boosted children's reading skills by an average of two grade levels, according to a  panel of civic and philanthropic leaders. Philadelphia youngsters who participated for 90 days in the Youth education for Tomorrow program advanced by 1.4 grade levels, and those who stayed with the program for a year advanced by two grades, according to figures released at a City Hall press conference. The YET technique engages children for 90 minutes a day in oral-language skills, listening, composition, and book reading.

headline: Senator revives prposed bill to punish 'eco-terrorists'
abstract: A state senator representing counties around the Allegheny National Forest said he will introduce an "eco-terrorism" law aimed at making environmental advocates pay if their protests disrupt that area's timber business. Although environmental activists said the bill is an attempt to intimidate them by tarring legitimate protests as terrorism, state Sen. Joseph Scarnati, R-Brockway, said his intention is to support the timber industry in northwestern Pennsylvania and ensure its long-term survival.

headline: Punxsutawney Phil to be well-guarded
abstract: With the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks as a backdrop, Pennsylvania State Police and the National Guard will provide extra security for the 30,000-plus people expected to gather on Feb. 2 for Groundhog Day and the appearance of the famous weather prognosticator, Punxsutawney Phil. Organizers anticipate that this year's crowd will be the largest yet. Sate Police and National Guard troops, who normally handle crowd control at the event, will search and secure the area with a bomb-sniffing dog.

headline: Echoes of slavery at Liberty Bell site
abstract: Historians claim the site of the $9 million Liberty Bell pavilion is the exact location of George Washington's House, which is where he kept his slaves. Some believe the sign of freedom should not be on the grounds where slaves were held.

headline: Female Erie senator named Fisher's running mate
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher, the GOP nominee for governor, named Senator Jane Earll of Erie as his running mate on the Republican ticket.  Earll would be the first woman elected lieutenant governor in the state if she wins the primary and general election.  Fisher will ask the members of the republican State Committee to endorse Earll for lieutenant governor at its February 9 meeting.

headline: More races mean more debates
abstract: Campaign debates, or forums, or whatever you want to call them, may never have been the sole province of the League of Women Voters, but the league did stage most of them.  Now, possibly because there are so many races and only so much league money to go around, more community groups are sponsoring candidate nights.  One of the biggest of this campaign season will be held Oct. 14 by the Penn Manor Education Foundation, the Lancaster Foundation for Educational Enrichment and the Hempfield Education Foundation.

headline: South Philly politics gets nastier yet
abstract: Philadelphia Union Leader John Dougherty and PA State Senator Vincent Fumo have been feuding for quite some time. The battle continues to get even nastier then before and some fear the two are fighting over small things that don't matter in the long-term. Philadelphia official are getting stuck in the battle.

headline: Rendell tax return shows big stock gain
abstract: PA gubernatorial candidate Ed Rendell was one of the 12 big-name political figures appointed to the Board of Comnet Ericsso and reportedly made $279,000 through options in its sale. The tax returns which he released shows that he and his wife, made $903,000 during the year and that Rendell has begun receiving a $73,000 a year pension from the city of Philadelphia.

headline: Cigarette tax could double
abstract: State lawmakers are expected to debate increases in cigarette taxes and waste-hauler tipping fees, as well as cuts in education and environmental programs. A projected $1.2 billion deficit for the fiscal year has lawmakers considering significant withdrawals from the state's Rainy Day Fund and reductions in proposed tax cuts.  Schweiker has already frozen more than $300 million in this year's budget, including $50 million slated for the environmental Growing Greener program.

headline: Civil war collection to remain in Philly under proposed pact
abstract: The collection of a civil war museum founded by Ulysses S. Grant and other Union Army leaders will be kept in a new museum in Philadelphia and will not be moved to another state, as a tentative agreement.

headline: Starr tire deal goes to pieces
abstract: A firm that received a $3.2 million state loan to remove and recycle millions of tires on Max and Martha Starr's property backed out of the deal after taking the money. The Starrs' are suing, but the company says the tires could damage their equipment.

headline: Putting police where drugs are
abstract: Mayor Street of Philadelphia is starting a new tough policy on drugs, Operation Safe Streets. The crackdown will target 300 open-air drug markets and is unprecedented. Hundreds of police officers will be deployed to known drug corners and blocks.

headline: Internet domain names become big issue for state
abstract: Take the reaction of Montoursville resident Bill Hall, an Internet businessman who was on the receiving end of a 400-page civil complaint alleging the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is the rightful owner of PA PowerPort.com, a name Hall registered on the Internet two years ago.  From Hall's perspective, the fat legal document that landed at his home - a document which wasn't filed in a state or federal court but in Switzerland - illustrates why business people have concerns about government and the Internet.  From the state's perspective, the cheapest and fastest route was taken to arbitrate an intellectual property concern.

headline: Ferlo campaigns in Valley
abstract: The 38th District which is based in Pittsburgh was expanded to include a large portion of the Valley. The state senator for the area is retiring so many candidates have popped up for the position.

headline: Most smokers say they'll keep puffing
abstract: The Times Leader asked 10 smokers on Public Square how the possibility of paying significantly more for a pack of cigarettes would affect their habit.  While all were unhappy about the prospect of paying more money for cigarettes, 7 out of 10 said they will still but them no matter what the cost.

headline: Spanish enters political arsenal
abstract: The Republican National Convention will launch a monthly Spanish-language TV show. House Democrats got together for an hour long Spanish lesson. The Republicans also finished a 10 day Spanish course for state party officials and will pay tuition for other party leaders. Both parties realize they must woo the Latino vote.

headline: Rendell unwilling to give up on region
abstract: Campaign officials say Ed Rendell is not conceding any part of southwestern Pennsylvania to Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. in the Democratic primary campaign for governor. Rendell has strong support among the state's mayors. Casey and Rendell will battle for the nomination in a race that political consultants believe will be very expensive.

headline: Deficit even worse than thought, state told
abstract: The deficit is projected to be at $1.2 billion at the end of the current fiscal year. The state's tax collections were less than expected due to a slumping economy and after September 11th, the tax collections went sharply down.

headline: College funds keeps on giving City graduates get financial aid from 1940 trust
abstract: The neediest students in Harrisburg and immediate suburbs are getting help with college and/or other post-secondary education from the Ray Shoemaker Scholarship.  A spokesman for Mellon Bank stated that award notifications were mailed last week to more than 100 students who will get scholarship awards totaling more than $200,000.

headline: State delays auction for leases to gas-drilling rights
abstract: State officials delayed the auction of natural-gas drilling rights on public forest land. The state environmental advisory panel recommended postponing the auction so the public would have a chance to comment on the issue.

headline: Red-light cameras roll right through Senate committee
abstract: State Senators Stewart Greenleaf and Clarence Bell have introduced a bill that would allow municipalities to install red-light cameras to catch violators. The bill has gotten approval in the Senate committee and awaits approve from the full Senate.

headline: Internet filters on library computers: protection or censorship?
abstract: Library officials and free-speech advocates claim that porn-blocking strategy maintained by the Children's Internet Protection Act of 2000 is inadvertently blocking access to important information on health, sexuality, and social issues. The trial will be heard by the US District Court.

headline: Few incumbents face primary challenge
abstract: Most incumbents will not be challenged in the upcoming primary election. There are a few challengers for US Representative Bill Shuster and US Representative Todd Platts. In the fall election, two current US Representatives will face each other since their districts were combined.

headline: Murphy: I'm staying
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy has announced that he has no intention of leaving the city to take a job with PA Governor-Elect Ed Rendell. Murphy's mayoral term ends in 2005.

headline: Special interests take a hit
abstract: President Bush grudgingly signed a new law to scale back the impact of big money in US politics. The soft money loophole has allowed for millions to contributed which would normally be considered an illegal contribution. The loophole is now closed.

headline: Rendell wants district to lead state Democrats
abstract: Ed Rendell says he will recommend a candidate from the southwestern part of the state to succeed state Senator Christine Tartaglione, the Democratic party chair.  The Democratic nominee for governor said this week that he had not yet settled on a particular candidate but among the likely choices, however, is state Representative Mike Veon.  Veon, the second-ranking Democrat in the state House and a respected party strategist, supported Rendell in the primary.

headline: Dfense buildup proposed by Bush
abstract: President Bush has sent a $2.13 trillion budget proposal to Congress that would deliver the largest increase in defense spending in 20 years and nearly double funding for homeland security while returning to deficits and cutting popular programs. The reorienting of the nation's priorities is necessary to continue the war on terrorism and better protect Americans at home as a result of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, Bush told lawmakers in a message at the front of the budget.

headline: College students face 'sizeable' tuition hikes
abstract: Under the latest budget, state-owned colleges face a cut from their state subsidy. This could mean the largest tuition hike in years. The hikes could be up to 10 percent for 17 state schools. Economic downturns have caused the Governor to make budget cuts.

headline: State may tax trash
abstract: Gov. Mark Warner and leaders of the Republican-controlled General Assembly stand poised to officially adopt that view during a one-day session April 17.  Warner announced a proposal to levy a $5 state tax on every ton of trash dumped in Virginia.  State and local fees in Virginia are among the lowest in the Mid-Atlantic; the new charge would change that - - and could cause interstate trash haulers to look elsewhere.

headline: Referendum aims to aid firefighters
abstract: Pennsylvania State Representative Jeffrey Coy urged voters to support the volunteer firefighter referendum when they go to the polls. The ballot question asked whether the state should issue a $100 million bond to assist emergency first responders in their effort to save lives property.

headline: Last Call
abstract: Politicians and professional alarmists went nuts recently when NBC broke what had been a 50-year voluntary ban on advertising hard liquor.  They claimed the ads would encourage kids to drink, and tempt recovering alcoholics to jump off the wagon.  The network was forced to back off.

headline: Finally, Open Records Law Nearer to Passage
abstract: To examine public records in Pennsylvania, no matter how obvious the legitimacy, is expensive, time consuming and bureaucracy ridden. For the first time since the 1960's, the governor and the legislature appear ready to substantially upgrade the Commonwealth Open Records law.  A House committee voted favorably on the reform bill, sending it to the full House for a vote. Gov. Mark Schweikers' office has made it clear that he is committed to this reform.

headline: Murtha beats Mascara in battle of incumbents
abstract: U.S. Representative John P. Murtha got a victory over U.S. Rep. Frank R. Mascara in the race for the Democratic nomination in the newly drawn 12th Congressional District.  Murtha won by about a 2-1 margin over Mascara. After a bitter campaign, Murtha said he was in no mood to extend a post-election olive branch to Mascara.

headline: Special legislative session on taxes has potential to break Harrisburg inertia
abstract: One way or another, it looks like the Pennsylvania General Assembly will hold a special session to deal with property tax reform and the way Pennsylvanians fund their public schools.  Both gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Ed Rendell and Republican Mike Fisher, say they'll call one if elected.  And last week, state Sen. Lisa Boscola, D-Northampton and Monroe, filed a petition with Gov. Mark Schweiker's office calling for one.

headline: Rendell widens lead over Fisher in race for government
abstract: The keystone poll, a telephone survey of 573 registered voters, found that 45% of residents would vote for Ed Rendell and 30% would vote for Mike Fisher. Democrat Ed Rendell currently holds a 15-point lead over Republican Mike Fisher.

headline: 'Dreadful' March puts state deficit near $ 1 billion
abstract: Years of plenty, it appears, are giving way to year of want as state officials are starting to fear at least a $ 1 billion deficit.  To date, Pennsylvania is about $749 million in the hole, this following March's dismal revenue collections - - 8.8 percent less than anticipated for that month; down 4.9 percent for the 2001-02 fiscal year that ends June 30.

headline: Colleges warn of steep rise in tuition
abstract: Public universities in Pennsylvania and New Jersey could face a possible double digit increase in tuition costs. The upcoming budget shows a 5 percent cutback on funds for Penn State ,Temple, and Lincoln, while the 14 state-run universities would face a 3 percent cut.

headline: State officials concerned huge catfish could take over river
abstract: State officials are calling on all fisherman for their help riding the Susquehanna River of a pesky fish that doesn't belong there.  Fish and boat officials want the anglers to keep and kill all flathead catfish they catch in the river or its tributaries, no matter how large or small the fish are.  Otherwise, one-hundred pound flathead catfish could eventually take over the Susquehanna River and disrupt its ecosystem.

headline: Religious sect targets prison policy on worship
abstract: A group of attorney for the Jehovah's Witnesses is targeting the York County Prison of their ban on Bible study groups at the prison. The attorneys are claiming that York County Prison religious policy is not in compliance with the law.

headline: Legislators urge cut in Verizon's phone rates
abstract: PA State legislators are calling upon the PA State Public Utility Commission to reduce Verizon Communications Corp's wholesale telephone rates. Lawmakers want to bring Pennsylvania rates down so that they are in line with rates in New York, New Jersey, and Ohio.

headline: First lady Laura Bush visits Pennsylvania
abstract: First lady Laura Bush was among hundreds of people honoring former Pennsylvania first lady Michele Ridge on Thursday night for her work in youth violence prevention.  About 600 people turned out for the program at the Hershey Lodge & Convention Center, including Pennsylvania's current first lady Kathy Schweiker.  It was part of the annual conference of the Governor's Community Partnership for Safe Children.

headline: Murtha, Mascara in battle for funds
abstract: U.S. Rep. John Murtha has raised more money than his probable primary election opponent, fellow Democratic Rep. Frank Mascara, but Mascara has more money in the bank, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission.  Murtha raised $240,000 during the first three months of 2002 and has $230,000 in the bank.  Mascara raised $189,400 during that period , through $100,000 was from a loan, and has $273,000 in the bank.

headline: Special Report: How a Street appointee's influential union has run afoul of federal labor laws.
abstract: John Dougherty, leader of Local 98 of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers helped elect the mayor, holds a position in his administration, and is a Democratic Party star. A National Labor Relations Board Lawyer argued in successfully prosecuting Local 98 for illegally blockading a United Parcel Service warehouse in 1999. Over the last six years, the NRLB, which enforces federal labor laws, has found that Local 98 violated those laws in more than a dozen episodes involving more than 16 companies.

headline: Rendell will live on less as governor
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell will give up his partnership in a Philadelphia law firm and his membership on three corporate boards to take the position as governor. Rendell will earn far less as a governor then he did in his other jobs. Rendell's finances and assets are briefly discussed.

headline: DV tax increase cut to just $1 a month
abstract: The Delaware Valley School District Board of Directors, on July 19 reduced the tax increase adopted in June from 2.34 percent to 0.57 percent, which is just over half of one percent.  At a regular meeting held at DV campus on Routes 6 and 209, the board reduced the tax rate from 84.34 mills to 82.88 mills.  The newly adopted mileage means that the average household will see a DV school tax increase of only $1 per month, the smallest tax increase in 18 years.  Two years ago the board adopted a no tax increase budget.

headline: Confederate flags banned at Butler schools
abstract: Edward Fink, Superintendent of Butler Area School District, said that high schools will be prohibited from displaying Confederate flags on clothing or other items on campus. The ban comes after some parents voiced concerns. The ban applies to both high school and the District's intermediate school for grades 9 and 10.

headline: State says no to plan for tires as fuel
abstract: PA Environmental officials have rejected Kimberly-Clark Corporation's plan to burn millions of tires as fuel, citing that the burning could increase toxic emissions in the Chester area. The PA Department of Environmental Protection took three years to study the matter before ruling on it.

headline: Rendell aide has conviction record
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor-Elect Ed Rendell's personal aid, Charles Breslin, and driver has been released from jail after being charged with heroin possession and reckless endangerment. Rendell has admitted to knowing Breslin had a past with drugs but thought he had changed. Breslin will no longer be a part of his staff.

headline: Pa. funds Philadelphia area biotech greenhouse
abstract: Gov. Schweiker announced yesterday that Philadelphia would receive $33.8 million to create a biotechnology "greenhouse" in Southeastern Pennsylvania.  The amount is less than the $45 million that local backers of the economic development initiative had wanted.  But several hundred people gathered in West Philadelphia to hear the governor's announcement, and many were enthusiastic about the potential for the greenhouse program.

headline: First television attack in governor's race airs
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Bob Casey Jr. aired his first negative television ad against his opponent former Philadelphia mayor Ed Rendell. Casey claims that Rendell did little to help the Philadelphia school district and left them in such bad shape that the state had to take them over.

headline: Need new way to draw districts
abstract: Congressional redistricting is the most partisan political endeavors and is in need of radical reconstruction. Though state legislatures do a remarkable job of getting all the districts in their state to be equal in population, there are still potential violations of the premise of one person, one vote. Switching the basis for reapportionment from census figures to voting numbers may make a lot of sense.

headline: Special Senate election set for October
abstract: Provoking outrage from Democrats, Lt. Gov. Robert C. Jubelirer yesterday ordered a special election Oct. 1 to replace the late state Sen. Clarence D. Bell.  Balloting in the 9th Senatorial District will take place five weeks before the Nov. 5 gubernatorial election pitting former Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell against state Attorney General Mike Fisher.  Jubelirer, a Republican, cited the need to have a new senator in place for the flurry of end-of-session lawmaking that could include property-tax reform this year.  The special election winner could be seated before Nov. 1 Republicans currently hold a 29-20 majority in the Senate.

headline: Rendell, Casey Jr. donors split
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Robert Casey Jr. banked his largest campaign contributions from organized labor and business, while his opponent, Ed Rendell, relied on Philadelphia law firms and businesses.  Two unions, Service Employees International and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, gave Casey $925, 000 through Jan. 31.  Rendell's largest donor was his law firm, Ballard Spahr Andrews & Ingersoll of Philadelphia, with $110,276.

headline: Editorial: Fiscal Freezeout / State budget cuts hit the good and the bad
abstract: Faced with a potential deficit of $622 million by the end of the fiscal year, the Schweiker administration has had to make tough choices that are preliminary to more budget cuts. The reason is Pennsylvania's revenue collections are below estimates due to economic turndown. Schweiker's budget cuts were directed at in environmental initiatives and to Pennsylvania colleges.

headline: Council OKs bills to oversee school takeover
abstract: City Council passed bills to give itself and parents of schoolchildren some power in the process of reforming the city's children. One bill says 75 percent of the parents of students at a public school must approve a private company's plan to take over the school. The other bills gives Council the power to approve any contracts or agreements issued by the School Reform Commission, which took control of the school district as part of the state takeover.

headline: State to consider water use plan
abstract: The PA General Assembly is working towards passing legislation that will start a five year process of inventorying the state's water resources. The Water Resources Planning Act comes after the a number of droughts have been affecting the state.

headline: Rendell aide released, races drug and endangerment charges
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor-Elect Ed Rendell's personal aid and driver, Charles Breslin, has been released from jail after being charged with heroin possession and reckless endangerment. Rendell has announced that Breslin will no longer be a part of his staff.

headline: Pa. House bill to allow Internet wine sales
abstract: Governor Mark Schweiker is expected to sign off on a bill that would allow Pennsylvanians to buy wine over the Internet. Pennsylvania would join 14 other states in permitting Internet sales. Residents will be allowed to buy one case of wine per month as long as state stores don't carry the brand.

headline: Fisher blasts Rendell stock windfall. Dem's camp scoffs at try to link their man to corporate scandals
abstract: PA Gubernatorial candidate Mike Fisher has tried to tie his opponent Ed Rendell to America's corporate scandals, as income tax returns revealed Rendell reaped $279,000 in stock windfall from a company once run by his top campaign contributor. Rendell's campaign scoffed at the notion, saying the candidate had done nothing improper or illegal.

headline: Nepotism stalled after hearing
abstract: Philadelphia City Councilman Michael Nutter is proposing a bill that will ban city officials from hiring their relatives. Nutter's bill is being debated even as Mayor Street's wide, Naomi Post, was withdrawing her name as a candidate for deputy managing director for social services. The Post situation was not discussed during the hearing, and Nutter said he introduced the bill before learning that she would be considered for a top job.

headline: Special session will focus on state tax reform
abstract: State lawmakers return to Harrisburg Wednesday after a two-month summer session on property taxes - an issue that for years has bounced around the Capitol like a beach ball losing air.  But many legislators, who were forced into the special session by a freshman senator who capitalized on an obscure clause of the state Constitution, caution that this special session may not result in significant reforms.  Gov. Mark Schweiker has yet to rally around a specific reform plan, and some expect to see superficial political posturing as lawmakers gear up for high stakes gubernatorial and legislative elections in November.

headline: Rendell's Democrats woo Casey supporters
abstract: Democrats are trying to unite for the gubernatorial election in November.  House Democratic Leader H. Williams DeWeese has sent a letter to Democratic state lawmakers this week urging them to get behind Ed Rendell.  The extent to which that's accomplished could determine who is elected governor.  Most of the party's legislators supported Rendell's opponent, Bob Casey Jr., in the primary.

headline: 'Fake budget' is rhetorical rite of passage for state lawmakers
abstract: State House lawmakers will vote on 275 amendments to Governor Mark Schweiker's proposed budget for fiscal year 2002-2003. This is known as the 'fake budget' because the state Senate will work on the real spending plan.

headline: Despite economic challenges, state hopes more grads will stay
abstract: Governor Mark Schweiker will deliver the commencement speeches at seven college campuses asking graduates to stay in Pennsylvania. Some students say it has been difficult finding employment in the state and are being forced to look elsewhere. A "Stay Invent the Future" initiative is trying to change college graduates' perceptions that Pennsylvania has little to offer and raising the profiles of thriving companies that have job openings.

headline: State's reintroduction program began in '83
abstract: The state Game Commission began a bald eagle reintroduction program in 1983. They removed 12 bald eagles from Canada where they were flourishing and placed them in man-made nesting structures in Pike and Dauphin counties. The bald eagles have made great gains in the state.

headline: Rendell aims to become gun owners' pal
abstract: Writer Peter DeCoursey talks about Ed Rendell's run for governor. DeCoursey says Rendell must reassure gun owners in order to win because he has a gun-control nut label on him.

headline: Parents worry about kids' access to adult chat rooms
abstract: An increasing number of teens are using computers to explore pornographic chat rooms. The Internet's easy access into adult chat rooms has created problems for parents and teens say many parents need more information. One 13-year old former Carlynton student disappeared on New Year's Day after meeting a man on the Internet and was found restrained in Washington D.C. suburban townhouse.

headline: Fisher camp takes campaign on the road in gigantic RV
abstract: With Democrat Ed Rendell's big, red, whit and blue bus having so far received all the attention in this gubernatorial campaign, Republican Mike Fisher is now out and about in his own vehicle, and RV that's almost as big as a bus, with visages of him, his running mate Jane Earll, and his family.  Fisher spokesman Kevin Harley said the decision to get the RV - last used in a campaign by GOP Gov. John Engler of Michigan --- was not made to counter Rendell's bus.

headline: New district will bring clash of ideas
abstract: Republican candidate for Congress Melissa Brown believes she understands the key issue of Campaign 2002, and that she's the right candidate to address it. The new 13th Congressional District, created with the merger of Montgomery County and the bulk of the Northeast, has a much older demographic mix than the old 13th District. Brown will have to address section 8 housing, problems with violence in public education, and weak job growth forcing seniors into early retirement.

headline: Specter of job losses could cost him vital support in midstate
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher's much-disputed role in the potential sale of Hershey Foods Corp. has become a high-stakes venture for his gubernatorial campaign.  Job creation and retention is the top issue in voter surveys.  Many analysts believe a potential sale of the candy company could cost the midstate white-collar and blue-collar jobs, and the special character of its best-know community.  That makes the deal unpopular in the midstate, where Republican Fisher needs at least 65 percent of the vote to defeat Democrat Ed Rendell, analysts said.

headline: Rendell's first political test: Cabinet appointees.
abstract: PA Governor-Elect Ed Rendell's first task is to decide upon cabinet members for his administration. The Centre Times says that for those cabinet nominations that will require PA Senate approval, Rendell must proceed with caution and go about it in a bipartisan manner.

headline: Gekas, Holden debate economy
abstract: US Representative George W. Gekas attacked US Representative Tim Holden saying Holden does not support an economic stimulus package which would help the downturning economy. Holden claims he supports half of the package, but is against a part that would eliminate the alternative minimum tax.

headline: Cyberschool pitches its package
abstract: Parents of students enrolled in charter schools download their child's daily lessons from the online school and oversee the children as they work on hands-on projects or field trips. The school provides students with computers, monitors, printers, Internet access and dozens of hands-on items such as books, building blocks, paint brushes, and tambourines. If a child enrolls in a charter cyberschool, the public school district he would normally attend is required by state law to cover 80 percent of the child's costs.

headline: Study will set sewage priorities
abstract: The National research Council will come to southwestern PA to help find solutions to the $10 billion sewage crisis. The regions water quality and septic system are in jeopardy.

headline: Rendell vows more cash for fire companies
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Ed Rendell made a quick stop at the Newtown Fire Co.'s fund raising festival to open the annual event and to tout his plan for fire companies statewide.  Rendell said that last year a $25 million state grant program to help fire companies with equipment costs, train volunteers and repay loans was eliminated from the budget.  At the same time, Rendell said, the state's "Rainy Day Fund" was high.  Rendell said he plans to insert that grant money back into the budget.

headline: PUC might set cost of phone competition
abstract: The Public Utility Commission has been trying to implement laws that will allow telephone competition. The push comes in the face of opposing demands from Verizon, which wants rates to be maintained or raised as opposed to AT&T and MCI World Com which want a law to require that rates be cut. Similar laws have been passed in New Jersey and Ohio.

headline: Fisher gets a welcome boost
abstract: Republican nominee Mike Fisher is running unopposed in the May primary for governor. He has been able to spend the time in his campaign sending a positive message and appealing to Republicans, meanwhile, the two Democratic nominees are spending millions for negative ads against one another.

headline: New electoral map, no election data
abstract: The state Senate and House have reached agreement on a plan that shifts 73,000 people among the state's 19 districts.  The decision came a week after a three-judge federal panel rejected the Republican redistricting plan signed into law in January because it violated the principle of "one man, one vote" by creating districts that varied by as many as 19 people.  The new Senate plan, approved yesterday, included an amendment moving the May 21 primary to July 16, to allow time to reopen petitioning.

headline: Specter stumps for Gannon
abstract: Pennsylvania State Representative Tom Gannon will face Democrat Sara Lynn Petrosky for the 161st district election. Gannon voiced his support for local control of public schools and his opposition to income tax increases. Gannon also has support from U.S. Senator Arlen Specter.

headline: Rendell's lead in Northeast Pennsylvania slim, poll says
abstract: Four months after native son Bob Casey Jr. suffered a resounding defeat in the Democratic primary for governor, Northeast Pennsylvanians have been slow to support the man who defeated him, according to poll released Wednesday.  The Quinnipiac University poll showed Democrat Ed Rendell leading Republican Mike Fisher by1 percent point - 49 percent to 48 percent (with 4 percent undecided) - among likely voters in the heavily Democratic Northeast.

headline: GOP must balance state budget and reelection hopes
abstract: Governor Mark Schweiker and Republican state lawmakers are trying to find a way to close PA's worst budget deficit in more than 10 years. A balanced budget must be adopted by June 30. A number of proposals are on the table.

headline: Diploma seal plan a lesson in controversy
abstract: Many students do not take performance tests very seriously. A state plan is considering putting a special seal on diplomas depending on how the student performed on these tests. Opponents argue that the seals do not reflect students' achievements.

headline: Swans' best defense? Maybe offense
abstract: Two national animal-welfare groups are preparing a campaign for tundra swans because they believe the state Game Commission is considering having a swan hunting season. The groups are trying to draw attention to the bird in hopes of gaining support against a hunting season.

headline: Rep. Argall supports additional funding for volunteer firefighters, rescue workers
abstract: Rep. David G. Argall (R-124) announced he supports more funding for volunteer firefighters and rescue workers in Pennsylvania and throughout Schuylkill and Berks counties.  According to Argall, as part of the recently adopted 2002-03 budget, he voted for House Bill 1848 that calls for a voter referendum to appear on the ballot in November for a $100 million bond issue to fund volunteer fire companies and volunteer emergency services in Pennsylvania.

headline: State complies with subpoena
abstract: PA Governor Schweiker's administration has agreed to comply with subpoenas requesting documents related to the award of a $228 million state telecommunications contract to a consortium led by Adelphia Business Solutions.

headline: Fisher gets GOP nod for Pennsylvania governor
abstract: Republican state Attorney General Mike Fisher accepted his party's formal blessing for governor, promising to build on seven years of GOP rule and to guide the state into an economically strong future. The event was another occasion for Republican Pennsylvanian leaders and the party faithful to sell the message they've been peddling for weeks: Pennsylvanians need to support GOP candidates and reject the tax-and-spend Democrats who would return the state to the economic doldrums of the early 1990's.

headline: New state bond issue up for consideration
abstract: State budget negotiators are looking into a new bond issuance to finance spending needs in the state.  On the list of possibilities are volunteer fire companies and the PA Game Commission. A number of individuals and groups have something to say on the matter.

headline: Specter will run in 2004, may face GOP primary challenge
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Spector has announced that he will seek re-election in 2004. PA State Representative Pat Toomey may decided to run against Spector in the Republican primary.

headline: Rendell's party has big hopes for House Democrats say his popularity in the region should help them gain the majority.  GOP leaders say think again.
abstract: The regional popularity of former Philadelphia mayor Ed Rendell, who is running for governor on the Democratic ticket, provides an opening to take control of the state House for the first time in nine years. Democrats hope Rendell will bring in Democratic candidates in some of the 26 Republican-controlled House districts in the territory from Allentown to Coatsville.

headline: Gov's budget combines creative financing with tax cuts, anti-terror spending
abstract: Facing a recession, Gov. Mark S. Schweiker asked lawmakers to approve a $20.9 billion budget that contains modest tax cuts and spending increases for anti-terrorism, offset largely by a reserve-fund withdrawal and new borrowing by an independent agency. Schweiker's first and only budget during his 15-month tenure would limit the growth of spending to less than 1 percent. Although, this is the smallest increase in at least a decade, it requires a fiscal juggling act that is likely to be intensely scrutinized in this gubernatorial election year.

headline: District's new CEO outlines his goals
abstract: New Philadelphia schools chief Paul G. Vallas has carved out an ambitious agenda.  Within a month he expects to unveil a four-year financial plan for the district, announce a timeline for crafting an educational blueprint, and wrap up negotiations with outside education managers.  His top priority is making sure all 264 city schools are ready to open in September.

headline: Tapped out: Drought has region's wells going dry
abstract: Governor Mark Schweiker believes groundwater levels are dangerously low and conservation measures are needed to avert a major shortage this summer. Unusually low amounts of rainfall and little snow this winter have caused record-low stream and groundwater levels. Responding to the call for conservation, Perrier voluntarily reduced water withdrawals by 10 percent at its Hoffman Springs plant in Lynn Township.

headline: Rep. Peterson votes in favor of tougher business penalties
abstract: U.S. Rep. John Peterson (R-5) voted Tuesday to increase penalties for corporate executives who engage in manipulative accounting and other fraudulent practices.  The Corporate Fraud Accountability Act of 2002 (H. R. 5118), which passed the House of Representatives on Tuesday, increases penalties for activities like mail and wire fraud from five to 20 years and provides additional tools for prosecutors to crack down on corporate criminals.

headline: Universities computer system hits snag
abstract: A $96 million project to unify the computing systems of the 14 state-owned universities may have run into a glitch. The German-based software company SAP who is the subcontractor for the project assures that a recent layoff will not affect its contract with the state.

headline: Fisher hopes for an upset in election
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher, who spent 22 years as a legislative member, faces a daunting task in trying to crack his opponents Ed Rendell's popularity in the PA governor's race. Rendell is popular among voters in suburbs. If Fisher does win a suburb, chances are, it would be Chester County.

headline: New vote machines worry Rendell camp
abstract: The Rendell camp isn't thrilled that the city's first use of its new voting machines comes in an election in which he is counting on a huge Philadelphia margin.  Election officials point out that the city chose the Danaher electronics machines precisely because they're most like the machines voters here are used to.  They're "full-face ballot" machines, meaning voters don't have to scroll through multiple pages.  The look is similar to the old mechanical machines, with electronic buttons and indicator lights replacing the old levers.

headline: Spector lauds Bush, warns Saddam during visit here
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Spector, while speaking at a fund raising breakfast, stated that the U.S. Senate should work to pass a homeland security bill. Spector supports President George W. Bush and does believed that Saddam has weapons of mass destruction.

headline: Rendell's primary win rewrites state political clichés
abstract: Learning theorists tell us that learning "the hard way" may actually be the easy way.  If that's true, the 2002 gubernatorial primary should be charging us all continuing education tuition fees.  The New Deal Coalition has finally unraveled in Pennsylvania.

headline: Grucela talks about shifting tax burdens
abstract: State Rep. Richard Grucela, D-Northampton, talked about major issues and bills related to the hot topic of property tax reform Thursday during a public meeting for Nazareth area residents.  Grucela's talk, held at the Upper Nazareth Township Municipal building, was based on input from a bi-partisan committee he served  on to come up with a reform plan.

headline: Edison gets funding to open schools
abstract: Edison Schools Inc., the publicly held company that is to run 20 of Philadelphia's public schools, told analysts yesterday that it had restructured its senior management team in a quest for profitability, and predicted that it would reach that goal in the quarter that begins April 1.   And in the last moments of the five-hour investors' conference, chief executive officer H. Christopher Whittle said the company had just closed on a $40 million financing package needed to open its Philadelphia schools.  Benno C. Schmidt Jr., chairman of Edison's board, and several other top executives were late to yesterday's session because they had just wrapped up the deal.

headline: Township says homes threatened by abandoned mine flooding.
abstract: Jackson township supervisors have said that three dozen homes could be in danger of being flooded with sulfuric water from an abandoned mine in Johstown. The PA State Department of Environmental Protection does not believe there is much water in the mine.

headline: Report: Pa. crime down but murder, rape up
abstract: There was good news and bad news in the annual Uniform Crime Report, released yesterday.  Serious crime dropped more than 6 percent last year in Pennsylvania, the report says, but the number of murders and rapes both increased.  The number of serious crimes reported to police dropped to 320,737 in 2001 and some offenses such as robbery, theft and burglary dropped to their lowest levels in more than 20 years.  But the number of murders increased 12 percent to 646 last year, and forcible rapes increased 3.1 percent to 3,139.

headline: A hardhearted approach to solving big steel's troubles
abstract: President Bush imposed tariffs on imported steel which helped steel unions, but hurt trade relations with foreign countries. Economists doubt the tariffs will help the struggling steel industry.

headline: Fisher hops aboard pro-business theme
abstract: Attorney General Mike Fisher tried to cloak himself in the warm feelings many Pennsylvanians still hold for former Governor Tom Ridge, and tout himself as the gubernatorial candidate of continuity. The 2001-02 recession has stuck around, and the state's general fund has a projected $1.2 billion revenue shortfall this year.  Despite the changed circumstances, Fisher said last week he sees nothing wrong with the continuity theme, especially as it pertains to jobs and economic development.

headline: New whistleblower try
abstract: State lawmakers are considering a new "whistleblower" bill that would presumably help state and local authorities root out fraud in government contracting. Its advocates, particularly prosecutors, say the federal law does not allow authorities to pursue civil penalties against those who defraud state and local governments. The only York County lawmaker to co-sponsor the bill was state Representative Bruce Smith.

headline: Spector supports Bush bill
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Spector, while speaking on a York College campus, said that he supports President George W. Bush's plan to develop a new Department of Homeland Security. Spector also discussed terrorism, education, and local issue while at the college.

headline: Rendell's wife couldn’t campaign because she's a federal judge
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell's wife Marjorie Rendell could not campaign for her husband because she serves as a federal appellate court judge and ethics restrictions prevent her from politicking in any way. Rendell could not even use her photograph.

headline: House Congress Taxes Roll Call, 140
abstract: Pennsylvania's portion of the 213-188 roll call Wednesday by which the House defeated a bill to make permanent the education-related parts of the 10-year, $1.35 trillion tax cut enacted last year.  A two-thirds majority was needed to pass the bill.

headline: Edison Schools' Stock Halts Dive
abstract: Shares of Edison schools fell by almost half of it's value before keeping steady at the end of the week. The addition of 20 schools would not raise the revenues of the company as high as they had previously led Wall Street to expect. Edison is the largest for-profit operator of public schools.

headline: Trash bills likely to increase
abstract: Pennsylvanians' trash bills probably will increase by about $4 this year. Waste haulers will be required to pay an additional $4-per-ton fee to dump trash in Pennsylvania landfills under legislation signed into law by the governor last week.  The previous fee was $3.25 per ton of waste.  The increase, originally proposed in legislation by Republican state Rep. Kate Harper of Lower Gwynedd Montgomery County, was included as an amendment to the state budget, which was adopted Saturday by lawmakers.

headline: Ridge: Fight won't end with al-Qaida U.S. will keep its guard up, official vows
abstract: The end of al-Qaida won't mean the end of the United States' battle against terrorism, according to Homeland Security Director Tom Ridge. Ridge compared it to the continuing wars on drugs and crime. Ridge said al-Qaida cells or sympathizers probably were still in the United States.

headline: Bush imposes steel tariffs
abstract: President Bush has decided to impose 30 percent tariffs on steel imports. The struggling American steel industry wanted 40 percent tariffs. The tariffs will be in place for the next three years and Bush hopes that the industry will be able to restructure itself in that time.

headline: Fisher meets with Dubya
abstract: State Attorney General Mike Fisher has meet with President George W. Bush at the White House for a photo opportunity. The meeting was confirmed by spokesman Kevin Harley.

headline: Newcomer Petri upends Cherkin
abstract: Republican first time candidate Scott Petri got a 2,000 vote lead over Democrat challenger Carl Cherkin for the 178th PA House district election.

headline: Spector, Santorum not ready to fold up Trent
abstract: U.S. Senator Trent Lott has been criticized for recent racist remarks that he made. U.S. Senators Rick Santorum and Arlen Spector are standing behind Lott and do not support a movement toward resignation for Lott.

headline: Rep. Brooks holding open house
abstract: State Rep. Wallis Brooks (R., Montgomery) will host an open house on Saturday at her new district office in Upper Merion.  Residents of the 149th Legislative District are invited to attend.  The office is at 192 E. Dekalb Pike.

headline: House Oks Schweiker budget, rejects spending cut
abstract: The state House of Representatives approved the amended version of Governor Schweiker's $20.9 billion budget. The final version must be in place by July 1st. The budget will limit the growth in spending by less than 1 percent.

headline: Edison to run 20 Philadelphia schools
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street says the city's School Reform Commission went "too far, too fast" in today's decision to private 70 elementary and middle schools.  But reform commission member Daniel Whelan says the schools need aggressive reform, immediately.  Today's three-to-two vote turns over 20 schools to Edison Schools Incorporated.

headline: Vigilance urged by state on West Nile
abstract: Calling it a "war on mosquitoes," state officials have stepped up efforts to combat the deadly West Nile virus and are enlisting the help of residents to prevent its spread.  The virus is spread by the bite of an infected mosquito.  David Hess, secretary of the state Department of Environmental Protection, said the battle has gotten a little tougher this year because, thanks to heavy rains this spring, Pennsylvania has about eight times more mosquitoes than it did a year ago.

headline: Rural townships deny ski resort bid for a liquor sales
abstract: Voters in a rural section of Western Pennsylvania have rejected efforts by a ski resort to sell alcohol in areas where sprawling slopes cross into dry townships.  Residents of rural Middle Creek Township and Saltlick Township voted 481-412 to keep dry sections of the Seven Springs Mountain Resort that cross into the dry townships.  Alcohol is sold in other parts of the resort.

headline: Center to focus on trade
abstract: The South-central Pennsylvania International Network announced that Harrisburg will gets its own world trade center.  It won't be twin towers or any other kind of building, at least to start according to Tina Weyant, executive director of the network, which has been renamed World Trade Center - Harrisburg. It will help local businesses find international customers and increase exports by providing a global network of expertise.

headline: Fisher picks 'ceiling breaker' for No. 2 spot in governors race
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Fisher has tapped a state senator from Erie as his choice for his lieutenant governor. Fisher is expected to lock up the party's nomination now that state Treasurer Barbara Hafer has withdrawn from the race.

headline: News from the Pennsylvania General Assembly
abstract: A number of legislative developments are discussed including: the state budget, sexual abuse of minors, rallies on state aid to schools, nursing, public utilities, retirement, and senior centers.

headline: Spread the 'Wealth'
abstract: So it was all just a big misunderstanding.  The governor never meant to funnel most of the reform money to his favorite private providers.  At least, that's the latest plot twist in Harrisburg's headlong rush to privatize everything in sight.  Before Gov. Schweiker's hasty retrenchment there was a stealth move to make sure $55 million of $83 million in additional Harrisburg funding would benefit only those 45 schools set to be run by private managers.  The biggest beneficiary, of course, was to Edison Schools Inc.

headline: Rep. Freeman to seek ninth term
abstract: State Representative Robert Freeman will seek his ninth two year term in the state House of Representatives. His seniority allows him to be a candidate for a chair of a commission. He is the lone candidate so far.

headline: House panel ducks tough tax issues
abstract: After more than a year of work and 16 public hearings across the state featuring testimony from 180 witnesses, the highly touted state House Select Committee on Public Education Funding yesterday released what one lawmaker derided as a "pass the buck" report on what to do about property taxes.  The committee recommended that a seven-member commission be appointed by the governor and legislative leaders to tackle the thorny issues of tax reform: how to cut property taxes fairly; which state taxes should increase to offset that cut; how large school budgets should be and how to fund them fairly; and how to keep property taxes from creeping back up in the future.  The commission should finish that work in April, well after the entire House has stood for re-election and a new governor is in office, the select committee decided.

headline: Editorial: Be part of reform
abstract: Everybody knows that the Philadelphia schools are being "privatized" and turned over to Edison Schools Inc.  No doubt, blind faith that "Edison is The Answer" drove former Gov. Tom Ridge and new Gov. Schweiker during last fall's school-takeover talks.  Their boundless trust in Chris Whittle's company produced, in fine Newtonian fashion, an equal and opposite reaction from city activists.  These two hyperboles have become the poles that frame much of the news coverage and public debate.

headline: Warmer weather burns utilities
abstract: Businesses throughout the state have been hurt by the warmer weather. They have not been able to sell winter weather equipment and supplies with temperatures well above freezing throughout November to February.

headline: Scavello to push for use of radar by local police
abstract: Pennsylvania State Representative Mario Scavello plans to request a transfer to the Transportation Committee in order to push for the legalized use of speed radars by local police. Radar use has been opposed by both Pennsylvania police unions as well as the State Police due to concerns about radar guns causing cancer said Stroud Regional Lt. Jack Rundle.

headline: Forum on American steel: Preserve our industry by stopping unfair competition from abroad
abstract: Foreign nations are proceeding with guarding the law which has hurt hardworking men and women and the communities in which they live. President Bush must decided whether or not to impose a steel tariff to help the struggling American steel industry.

headline: Fisher plan targets corporate fraud
abstract: State Attorney General Mike Fisher yesterday proposed stiffer state penalties and an expanded role for his office in corporate fraud cases.  Citing the need to improve investor confidence and protect pension investments, Fisher, the Republican candidate for governor in the November election, weighed in on the corporate earnings scandal that has recently rocked the stock market.  Fisher wants to make violations of the Pennsylvania Securities Act a racketeering offense, which would give the state attorney general concurrent jurisdiction with district attorneys to investigate and prosecute these offenses

headline: News from the Pennsylvania General Assembly
abstract: Erin's law has had its name changed to remove 'Erin,' the girl it was named after. Erin contracted E. coli from a petting zoo. Democrats believe Republicans are playing partisan politics because Erin's father is running for Montgomery County's 44th District.

headline: Squabbling schoolboys bring race to Pa.'s largest TV market
