abstract: There is a feud between state Senator Vince Fumo and Mayor Street of Philadelphia. Fumo supports Casey in the governor's race, while Street backs Rendell. Street is an ally of City Councilman Rick Mariano, but Fumo writes negative letters on Mariano. Now the two sides are fighting over who will represent the new stadium special-services district of Philadelphia.

headline: Old ally gives Rendell a helping hand
abstract: Mayor Street of Philadelphia gave his endorsement to former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell as he seeks to win the Democratic nomination for Governor. Street is planning on doing whatever it takes to make sure Rendell receives the support from Philadelphia.

headline: Stern will seek another state house term
abstract: The 2000 census required that Pennsylvania redraw their district figures. Part of the 81st District were put into the 80th District which is where state Representative Jerry Stern represents. Stern has vowed to meet the needs of the new parts and seek reelection.

headline: State fund dries up
abstract: It took six years for Pennsylvania to build a sizable economic safety net, a Rainy Day Fund that now totals $1.1 billion and is nearly 20 times larger than it was in 1995. Governor Mark Schweiker will deliver his annual budget address and ask the Legislature to tap the Rainy Day Fund for a total of $550 million, which would be used to cover an expected budget deficit for this year and pass a budget for next year that does not raise taxes. The Schweiker administration is touting its upcoming budget plan as the first that does not raise taxes during a recession in recent memory.

headline: Hey, Harrisburg: We told you so on school $ $
abstract: So it is about the money, after all.  For years, state government has refused to connect the poor performance of Philadelphia's public schools with lousy funding from Harrisburg.  The problem, they sniffed wasn't that suburban schools got more bucks per student than city schools did.  It was that the city school district frittered away the money it had.

headline: Nuclear power plants not protected against air crashes
abstract: Government regulators stated that the 103 operating nuclear reactors would not be able to withstand the impact of an airplane the size of the ones used in the terrorist attacks of September 11th. Most plants are not designed to withstand an accidental crash including Three Mile Island.

headline: Thou shalt appeal
abstract: The Chester County commissioners passed a resolution declaring Judge Steward Dalzell's order to remove the Ten Commandments plague from the Courthouse to be "in error" and directed the solicitor's office to appeal. They said the Ten Commandments has a secular and historical purpose.

headline: 97th: State House race
abstract: Roy Baldwin will face newcomer William Robert Hagen, a Green Party Member in the PA State House race for the 97th district. Both candidates believe that the current system of the state funding for education is flawed and needs to be reformed.

headline: Funds vary in House contest
abstract: Some Republican candidates have chosen to use billboards in their campaign. There are eight Republican candidates for the new 47th District and each are trying to find a way to set themselves apart.

headline: On the street, a reaction of disgust
abstract: Three days after President Bush said that the business stories in American newspapers "should not read like a scandal sheet," they again do.  Young and other passers-by has a few clues that something big - - allegations of another corporate scandal - - had taken place inside the building.   About 20 reporters and photographers swarmed Grass and three of his former Rite Aid colleagues as they left the building separately after standing shoulder to shoulder inside to enter not-guilty pleas to charges related to the drugstore chain's allegedly fraudulent accounting practices.

headline: Strange bedfellows in 100th
abstract: Dr. G Terry Maddona on whether the Democrat could win in 100th. Special election to finish Barley's term is Tuesday.  Besides facing a feisty Demon in Beardsley, Armstrong faces foes in his own GOP, who resent him for challenging Barley.

headline: State to freeze millions in budget
abstract: PA Governor Schweiker's administration has announced that they will freeze $270 million in state spending and remove $50 million from the Rainy Day Fund to help balance to 2002-2003 state budget deficit. The Schweiker administration is citing the poor economy as the reason for the budget shortfalls.

headline: Hourglass Foundation to host education reform
abstract: The Hourglass Foundation will host a forum on public education, featuring three individuals who figure prominently in education issues. State Sen. James J. Rhoades, chairman of the Senate Education Committee, will speak about the Legislature's view of public education in Pennsylvania and the commonwealth's recent initiatives to improve the performance of public schools. Benno C. Schmidt, chairman of Edison Schools Inc., will describe the experiences, the promise and problems of private enterprise school management.

headline: Nuclear Route
abstract: The U.S. Senate voted last night to make a mountain in Nevada the country's one-stop depository for nuclear waste generated by America's power plants.  And though Bucks was not mentioned by name during the debate, this county's roads would likely become the route for transporting 77,000 tons of radioactive material to the nuclear dump site in the desert.  The federal Department of Energy has proposed that the spent fuel be moved to Yucca Mountain, Nev., along the Pennsylvania Turnpike.

headline: Tobacco settlement tops Fisher's achievements
abstract: PA Attorney General Mike Fisher, in his 6 years as attorney general, has received law-and-order credentials and has steered $206 billion deal to Pennsylvania as a part of national tobacco settlement. Some public policy advocates suggest that Fisher's office has missed other opportunities by not placing more emphasis on consumer-related and environmental issues.

headline: 98th race turns into a slugfest
abstract: The Armstrong-Hickernell debate between two 98th District candidates have inflicted plenty of damage on each other.  But no one has landed a knockout blow, although Armstrong has been throwing some haymakers in the late rounds.

headline: Gabig declines Muniz's 'odd' debate proposal
abstract: U.S. Representative Todd Platts has declined an invitation to moderate a debate between State Representatives Will Gabig and Christian Muniz. Platts is running his own campaign for re-election and bowed out.

headline: Once full of political promise, Cadue fades into history
abstract: Columnist Bob Groff writes about Monroe County Commissioner Jim Cadue and his political ambition that seems to be a thing of the past. Cadue will seek reelection re-election and Groff writes on the potential problems in Caude will face in another election.

headline: Strategists sketch race for governor
abstract: A Republican strategist expects that Attorney General Mike Fisher, the Republican nominee for governor, will be able to get thousands of conservative Democrats to support him. Rendell is expected to get his base by portraying Fisher as a hard-right conservative who is bad for the state economy and education.  Fisher will seek to define Rendell as out of touch with the voters of a rural state with a long history of playing it safe.

headline: Taxes help smokers snub a habit
abstract: Higher cigarette taxes are driving some smokers to give up the habit.  This month, Pennsylvania increased its cigarette tax from 31 cents to $1 a pack and New Jersey's went from 80 cents to $1.50, causing many smokers to rethink their lifestyles.  They are part of a nationwide trend: Four states raised cigarette taxes in 2001, and 16 states, New York City and Puerto Rico increased their taxes this year.

headline: House approves bill to boost school sign-language classes
abstract: The State House of Representatives has passed a bill that will allow school districts to offer American sign language as a substitute for a foreign language. The sign language credits will count toward high school graduation credit.

headline: Officials to discuss Salem nuclear plant's safety
abstract: Staff from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission will meet with PPL Susquehanna staff Tuesday, April 16, to discuss the plant's annual safety performance.  The meeting is open to the public.  NRC staff will answer questions from the audience.  Officials will address the plant's safety record from April 1 of 2001 to Dec. 31 of 2001.

headline: Toughen the rules for personal care homes
abstract: A grand jury has released a report calling upon the State Legislature to change the way Pennsylvania regulates personal care homes. The report comes after the case involving the death of William Neff at a Bucks County Personal Care facility. Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare (DPW) released its newly proposed regulations on personal care facilities. The new regulations are awaiting public comment within a 30-day period during which time the House chaired by Representative George Kenney will be studying them.

headline: A capitolwire.com analysis: Is the "Casey legacy" fair fodder in the gubernatorial campaign?
abstract: Auditor General Bob Casey Jr. has used his father's name in campaigns. Robert Casey Sr. was a well liked and respected Governor of Pennsylvania. Ed Rendell, a gubernatorial contender of Casey, has used Casey's name as well, but in a negative way. This has caused a rift between the two Democrats.

headline: Gannon, Petrosky go by party lines on property taxes
abstract: Pennsylvania State Representative Thomas Gannon and Sara Lynn Petrosky, candidates in the 16st District State House race, lined up behind their parties gubernatorial candidates on the issue of school taxes. Gannon supported the tow bills while Petoskey believes property takes should eventually be abandoned.

headline: Once rivals, Rendell and Casey unite
abstract: State Auditor general Bob Casey Jr. has endorsed his once opponent, Governor Ed Rendell. Casey wants to focus on common ground and unite democrats statewide to get things done for the state.

headline: Straw poll gives no hint of leader
abstract: Candidates for the 100th House District got little to cheer about when the Lancaster County Republican Committee released the results of its latest straw poll. The pre-endorsement poll was taken by members of the Solanco, Penn Manor, and Pequea Valley Republican committees. Of the 35 members present, 23 chose not to endorse anyone.

headline: Taxes take biggest rise since 1991
abstract: Late Friday and early yesterday, the Republican-controlled Legislature and Gov. Mark Schweiker raised cigarette taxes to $1 a pack and landfill dumping fees by $4 a ton to balance and pass a $20.7 billion budget.  Taken together, it marks the largest tax increase since the $3 billion increase Republicans lambasted Democrats for passing in 1991.  Schweiker and Republicans said they turned to taxes out of necessity, and only after drawing down $750 million from a $1.05 billion Rainy Day Fund because of a poor economy.

headline: House committee to consider easing home schooling regulations
abstract: A bill that would revise Pennsylvania's home schooling law is scheduled for consideration by the PA House Education Committee. The measure, sponsored by PA Representative Samuel Rohrer, would not require home schooling families to keep records of student work, to obtain year end evaluations from a teacher, or to have their children undergo standardized testing.

headline: PGW to file for increase in gas rates
abstract: Philadelphia Gas Works will ask for a rate increase of up to $50 million because of lower gas sales caused by warm winter weather. If approved by state regulators, PGW will be allowed to increase rates by $85 a year for the average customer. The request for the increase is the first since October, when the state gave PGW half of the $65 million it wanted.

headline: Underage drinking is under fire in Pa.
abstract: In a recent report, Clinton County, Pa., authorities revealed 15 percent of sixth-graders, 30 percent of eighth-graders, 50 percent of 10th-graders, and 85 percent of 12th-graders said they were regularly using alcohol. Pennsylvania legislators have now taken the problem under advisement with two pending bills that propose to curb teen-agers' ability to get alcohol. Senate Bill 222 is aimed at social hosts, people who buy kegs of beer and give kids access to alcohol, and involves keg tagging.

headline: A capitolwire.com Q & A with House Appropriations Committee Chairman David Argall
abstract: Rep. David Argall now knows the meaning of the old saying about being careful for what you wish.  This month the Schuylkill County Republican was named chairman of the powerful House Appropriations Committee after former Rep. John Barley left office.  But he takes the job just as the state faces what some projects as a looming $1 billion revenue shortfall and one of the toughest budgets in Pennsylvania history.

headline: Gardner tapped for federal judge
abstract: President Bush will nominate Lehigh County Judge James Knoll Gardner to serve as a federal judge in Allentown, filling a void created more than three years ago, U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter said Monday.  Specter, R-Pa., made the disclosure to a reporter moments after appearing at an unrelated event in Allentown.  U.S. Senators rarely, if ever, announce presidential nominations before the president does.  Specter said he made an exception with this one because it has been pending so long.

headline: One last time for Battisto, Scavello
abstract: Republican Mario Scavello and Democrat Joe Battisto, spoke to more than 250 people assembled about the problems facing the new district , and their vision for the future.  Spirited discussion on school property taxes, jobs and transportation issues highlighted the hour-long debate, which was sponsored by the Pocono Record.

headline: Street backing son against state rep
abstract: Mayor Street is backing his son, Sharif, against state Rep. Oliver because, according to Oliver, the mayor heard that Oliver was talking trash about him. Oliver denied the accusation and suspected Street's anger was over his decision not to take a city commissioner job offered to him by the mayor. Oliver, who's been in the House since 1974, announced his re-election bid last night.

headline: Taxes: Dozens of Changes
abstract: Lower income taxes, a bigger child tax credit, new breaks for education and enhanced retirement savings are only a few of the dozens of changes awaiting taxpayers in 2002 as a result of the sweeping tax law enacted last year. In all, the 10-year, $1.35 trillion tax cut passed by Congress and signed by President Bush last June made 441 tax law changes, according to H&R Block Inc. Most will be gradually phased in over the decade, but some important ones are already in effect.

headline: Hurdles remain for vouchers in state
abstract: Forget the immediate problem- which is, the state doesn't have the money - in offering parents tuition vouchers to send their children to the school of their choice.  There's the problem of changing Pennsylvania's Constitution to allow the state to offer vouchers.  According to the American Civil Liberties Union, Article III, Section 29 prohibits the state from making any grants to parents to pay for elementary or secondary religious or private schools.  A constitutional change could take at least two years because an amendment must pass the Legislature in two consecutive sessions and then must be approved by voters in a referendum.

headline: Quecreek commission says better maps are a must
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Schweiker's Commission on Abandoned Mine Voids and Mine Safety has released their report on the Quecreek Mine accident. There are 48 recommendations that should be implemented by the state to avoid another mining accident. One of those recommendations is mine maps.

headline: Union opposition leads Dauphin Co. to shut juvenile facility
abstract: Dauphin County commissioners voted to close a youth detention center after union officials opposed efforts to privatize the facility. Despite concerns from the county's president judge, the commissioners approved a plan to close the Schaffer Youth Center in Swatara Township. The 5-year-old, $4.3 million facility can house up to 50 juvenile offenders awaiting sentencing and 15 abandoned youths.

headline: A capitolwire.com Q&A with House Majority Leader John Perzel
abstract: House Majority John Perzel has weathered some tough times the last two years, almost losing his eat in 2000 and losing a close friend, lobbyist Tom McCormac. Now the Philadelphia Republican is facing his toughest budget since becoming majority leader in 1995.

headline: Gekas adopts Holden communication style
abstract: The glossy newsletters with color photos began showing up in midstate mailboxes in recent weeks.  In the past few months, central Pennsylvanians may have a much better sense of what U.S. Rep. George Gekas believes are some of his greatest accomplishments, thanks to the newsletters printed and mailed at taxpayer expense.  Gekas, R-Harrisburg, spent $123,279 in mailings through Aug. 7 - - a 2,524 percent increase over his average of the past five years - - telling voters his accomplishments.

headline: One year later, Ridge sees a country better prepared
abstract: Tom Ridge, the man President Bush called to Washington to become the first director of homeland security, believes that the country is now better prepared than it was a year ago to repel or prevent an attack and then to care for the people and places harmed if terrorists strike again.  Mr. Ridge's job did not exist before the Sept. 11 attacks, and it is a sign of its importance that in the event of another attack, the first person to get the call from the president is likely to be Mr. Ridge.  The former Pennsylvania governor believes that his new office has been sufficiently accepted by the government and the country at large since he arrived in Washington 10 months ago.

headline: Street election $ used for trip
abstract: Mayor Street's campaign organization used $4,237 in political donations to buy roundtrip air fares to Rome for the mayor's wife, son, sister-in-law and niece, according to campaign expense records.  Campaign-finance experts contacted by the Daily News questioned the legality of using campaign funds to pay for the air fares.  Under state law, campaign expenditures must be made "for the purpose of influencing the outcome of an election."

headline: Taxing and spending: The Rainy Day Fund
abstract: Mark Schweiker says tapping the Rainy Day Fund for $550 million to help prevent a tax hike marks the first time in the 10 recessions since World War II that Pennsylvania will have avoided raising taxes. The phase-out of the Capital Stock and Franchise Tax continues under Mr. Schweiker's budgetary proposal. It is beyond dispute that lower taxes stimulate creation of wealth by the private sector, which in turn creates more revenue for the government, which may in turn reduce tax rates further.

headline: In city's toughest schools, educator teaches success
abstract: Bridging Worlds is a program which is used in Philadelphia's toughest schools. It helps boost critical thinking and confidence through reading and writing literature, guest speakers, plays environmental field trips, and constant parental contact.

headline: Rescue drama boosts chance for postage stamp honoring miners
abstract: The dramatic rescue of nine trapped miners in Somerset County has increased interest in efforts to have a postage stamp issued in honor of coal miners.  For 16, years John Vengien has been writing letters and gathering hundreds of signatures in support of the stamp.  But for years, he was told that coal miners lack a key requirement, national interest.  Vengien, 84, a former coal miner from Plymouth in Luzerne County, was recently notified along with other supporters that the coal miner stamp is under consideration for possible issuance in 2005.

headline: Unions feel pressure on wage tax
abstract: Mayor Street wants to freeze wage tax cuts, but has admitted that it could hurt city workers. Unions for the city police and firefighters have been fighting the bill. Their contracts expire this year and the loss of revenue from the wage tax would be less money for the police and firefighters.

headline: A confusing start to GOP congressional primary
abstract: Melissa Brown is running as the GOP congressional canidate, as she did in 1998, for the 13th District (Montgomery) of Pennsylvania.  The Brown campaign released a letter to the media signed by House majority leader John M. Perzel (R-172) which indicated that Brown had the backing of State Represenatives George Kenney (R-170), John Taylor (R-177), and Dennis O'Brien (R-169). Unfortunatley, the State Represenatives did not give their blessing for such a letter or their endorsement of Brown. Represenative Keeney was under particular distress because a life-long friend of his, Al Taubenberger, might run for the same seat.

headline: Gekas and Holden search for winning issues in showdown of incumbents
abstract: With three months still to go before Election Day, national political groups have begun pouring money into one the nation's hottest congressional races, the showdown between incumbent U.S. Reps. George Gekas and Tim Holden.  The AFL-CIO began airing a television spot in mid July, attacking the Republican Gekas for supporting "fast track" trade legislation giving the president the power to negotiate foreign trade deals without congressional approval.  The ads claimed that free trade agreements led to the loss of tends of thousands of jobs in Pennsylvania.

headline: O'Pake says commission should redraw boundaries
abstract: A state commission should take over redrawing congressional boundaries from the state Legislature, Senate Minority Whip Michael A. O'Pake said Wednesday.  O'Pake, a Reading Democrat, drafted a constitutional amendment that would allow the five-member Legislative Reappointment Commission to handle congressional redistricting.  Senate Republicans said that 2005 would be the earliest that voters could approve such a constitutional amendment.

headline: Street mum as critics question job for wife
abstract: Mayor Street pointedly refuses to discuss the possible hiring of his wife, Naomi Post, to a top city job as critics continued to argue against it. State ethics law would prohibit Street from playing any role in the hiring of his wife. Some observers are not convinced that Post could be hired legally.

headline: Unemployment rate drops to 5.7 percent in August, with significant new hiring in the service sector
abstract: The nation's unemployment rate unexpectedly fell to 5.7 percent in August and companies added 39,000 new jobs, the fourth consecutive monthly increase.  Last month's jobless rate fell by 0.2 percentage point after remaining stuck at 5.9 percent for the two previous months.  Analysts had expected the rate to stay at 5.0 percent or edge up slightly for August.

headline: In higher education, costs climbing faster than state aid
abstract: Pennsylvania is in a fiscal squeeze so severe that Gov. Mark Schweiker has proposed cutting campus funding for Pitt, Penn State and the other public universities by 3 percent to 5 percent.  Leaders of some of those schools have answered with predictions of double-digit tuition increases in a state where public universities already are a third most expensive in the nation.  If they're right, increases this fall would approach $700 at some schools, not including increases in books, student fees, room and board and other living expenses.

headline: Security boosted at nuke facilities
abstract: The Bush administration has decided to tighten security at nuclear power facilities based on documents and information obtained from al Qaeda terrorists. The terrorists had been gaining information on various nuclear power plants but there are no plans to raise the national threat level.

headline: Unwed couples can adopt kids
abstract: A state Supreme Court ruling that unmarried couples can legally adopt children will affect hundreds of same-sex couples in Pennsylvania who have children and want to both be listed legally as parents.  The state Supreme Court ruled Tuesday in a 6-0 decision with one justice abstaining that one partner in a gay or lesbian relationship can adopt a child without forcing the other partner to give up parental rights.  Previously, the parent would have had to give up rights to the child for the adoption to proceed.

headline: A farm-show celebration for a big-city governor
abstract: PA Governor-Elect Ed Rendell plans to hold his inaugural concert and ball at the PA State Farm show complex.

headline: Gekas bids House goodbye
abstract: George W. Gekas has been a U.S. Representative for 20 years. Gekas was defeated by U.S. Representative Tom Holden. Gekas is moving out of his office and thinking about what his next public move will be.

headline: Out-of-state donors spur election spending
abstract: Out-of-state money accounted for more than 25% of the $20 million that former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell and state Auditor General Bob Casey Jr. have raised between November of 2000 and April of 2002. Rendell was able to raise money out of state because of his relationships with wealth donors and Casey was able to because of national organized-labor groups.

headline: Street will endorse Rendell over Casey
abstract: Mayor Street of Philadelphia will give his endorsement to former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell in the upcoming Democratic primary race for Governor. There is overwhelming public support in the city for Rendell over state Auditor General Robert P. Casey Jr., his opponent. Street has received a pledge from Rendell to be a chairman for Street's reelection campaign.

headline: Warning to state Democrats: 'The Butcher' is at work
abstract: Shield your eyes. Fall in homage.  If you're Mayor Street, count your fingers. The butcher is at work.  Passage of a state budget, expected today or tonight, shows his talents and his power grabbing prowess.

headline: In hunt for teachers, challenges arise
abstract: Tom Lynskey, 43, is the kind of the teacher Philadelphia wants - a male who is certified to teach in elementary grades, a former computer programmer, someone who has spent time volunteering in a city school, and a regular substitute teacher in his home district of Council Rock.  Recently, Lynskey was called in by the school district to pick a school for September, but before the morning was over, both he and the school district ended up disappointed.  With the first day of school just three weeks away, Philadelphia still must fill 211 teaching vacancies.  On top of that, about 1,200 teachers -- 10 percent of the workforce -- now hold emergency certification, meaning they have yet to finish courses or pass certification exams.

headline: Senators siphon heart out of fuel efficiency
abstract: The US Senate rejected increasing fuel efficiency standards. America should increase their standards since the law only requires 24 miles per gallon in American vehicles.

headline: Visa violators or terrorists?
abstract: Mohamed Rifaey is in solitary confinement in York County Pennsylvania. Rifaey is an illegal alien from Egypt and has been in custody for four months and is among hundreds of people caught on the wrong side of the domestic war on terrorism. The huge York County prison houses one of the East Coast's largest INS detention centers, with more than 700 detainees.

headline: A golden opportunity: Extinguish 'The Torch'
abstract: The independent counsel for the Whitewater investigations is running in New Jersey for the Republican nomination for the US Senate. Two other challenges will be running in the state which has not elected a Republican Senator since 1972.

headline: Gekas gets the credit, but who got the money?
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Mark Schweiker has singled out U.S. Representative George W. Gekas for helping secure $100 million for the Pennsylvania National Guard. The fight over who actually deserves credit for the money has become a theme as Gekas and U.S. Representative Tim Holden want to claim credit during their election campaign.

headline: PA Supreme Court rejects Lawless' lawsuit against Jubelirer
abstract: A divided Pennsylvania Supreme Court has upheld a lower court ruling that allows Lt. Gov. Robert Jubelirer to continue serving  in his Senate seat.  The court released a one-page order Thursday affirming a decision issued by Commonwealth Court last December in a lawsuit brought against Jubelirer by Rep. John Lawless (D-Montgomery).  But Chief Justice Stephen Zappala issued a six-page dissenting statement, in which Justice Russell Nogro joined, urging the court to hear arguments on the merits of the case.

headline: Street's worry: Reform plan confusing & hasty
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street has sent a long personal letter to Governor Schweiker, expressing his worries that city school reform has become too confusing and too quick.  The Street administration wouldn't release the letter the mayor sent last week, saying it was "private."  Sources familiar with it say Street had expressed concern that there had been little information shared about how the proposed reforms would happen or who would be held responsible if they failed.

headline: A chance to work
abstract: Heinz Field, PNC Park, and David L. Lawrence Convention Center have positive signs during construction, but have been criticized for no providing some business to minority and women owned businesses. Plan B was created to share the construction work with minority and women owned businesses, but the program failed.

headline: Increase in state subsidy a morsel for area schools
abstract: The $156 million state legislators added to the education budget this weekend sounds like a lot of money.  Though they're thankful for every extra dollar they get, some local public school officials said Monday their share of the additional cash is peanuts.  Meeting into the wee hours of Saturday morning, the state's General Assembly approved the 2002-03 budget, including $4.1 billion for education -- 3 percent more than originally proposed.

headline: State begins cleaning up Whitpain gas leak
abstract: After one of the region's worst gas leaks, state officials will begin cleanup efforts expected to last for decades. Contractors will drill wells, lay pipe lines, and construct a treatment plant in order to remove the 12 to 15 thousand gallons of gas in the groundwater.

headline: Voters to answer $100 million question on volunteer firefighting
abstract: Voters will be asked to decide if the state of PA should borrow up to $100 million to create programs that would help volunteer firefighters and emergency rescuers finance improvements and equipment. Though the referendum is not binding, it would be difficult for lawmakers to ignore a passing vote, according to L. Savage III, the head of Pennsylvania Fire and Emergency services Institute in Harrisburg.

headline: A lawless race for Democrats
abstract: The Pennsylvania Democratic Party has no fewer than a dozen candidates considering making the race for lieutenant governor. Montgomery County representative John Lawless is a candidate and has recently changed his registration from Republican to Democrat. Adam Scott, a member of the Pennsylvania Democratic State Committee and Penn State University senior, believes Lawless is not a not a worthy candidate and that lawless switched parties to run for lieutenant governor.

headline: Gekas vs. Holden: Their records
abstract: U.S. Representatives George W. Gekas and Tim Holden are campaigning against each other in the redrawn 17th congressional district. Gekas is proclaiming himself to be a leader on important national policies, while Holden is emphasizing to the voters his efforts to improve local communities.

headline: Pa. court upholds legislative remapping
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has given its seal of approval to the state legislative reapportionment plan, thereby laying the legal foundation for a special election this spring in the 176th House District being transplanted to Monroe County. The court rejected a number of legal challenges to the plan approved last fall by the Legislative Reapportionment Commission. The court said the plan is in compliance with the state and federal constitutions.

headline: Summer primary readied by GOP
abstract: If federal judges don't blink next week, Pennsylvania will postpone its scheduled May 21 primary election until this summer, Senate Majority Leader David J. Brightbill, R-Lebanon, said yesterday.  Brightbill said legislative leaders and Gov. Mark Schweiker have agreed to rewrite the state's congressional districts to make their populations equal, as required by a federal court panel Tuesday.  But they will move the primary date unless federal judges suspend their order requiring the Legislature to redraw the state's 19 congressional districts by the primary date, Brightbill said.

headline: Altoona changes outside material policy after ACLU challenge
abstract: The Altoona School District will no longer allow private groups to distribute written materials on campus after the American Civil Liberties Union challenged a flyer for religious study groups. Under the change the district will now only distribute materials related to school events. The policy revision is just the latest in a string of changes, dating back to 1999 when a Baptist preacher filed a request to display the 10 Commandments.

headline: Judge considers arguments over cyber school's funding
abstract: The Einstein Academy Charter School is trying to get the Commonwealth Court to restore its state funding after the state Education Department decided to withhold its funds due to multiple problems at the cyber school. The Department wants to make sure it can legally withhold funds.

headline: State reduces land in gas-drilling lease sale by more than half
abstract: The State Legislature has scaled back a proposal by reducing the amount of land to be used in a gas-drilling leasing deal. This comes after harsh negative public reaction to the original proposal.

headline: War on terrorism impacts war on drugs
abstract: Following increased security after September 11th, drug markets started drying up and drug seizures fell. Increased security means more searches and many feel it is no longer worth the risk. Drugs are now being carried to others using the postal service.

headline: A positive work ethic, leadership with Rendell
abstract: Jeffrey Warren of Forks Township is impressed with Ed Rendell's campaign. He believes Rendell brings leadership, real ideas, and a positive work ethic.

headline: Gekas, Holden fight turf battle
abstract: U.S. Reps. George W. Gekas and Tim Holden have spent countless hours in unfamiliar territory, courting politicos and senior citizens, attending picnics and talking with any groups offering invites.  During several dozen trips to Schuylkill and Berks counties, Gekas, R-Harrisburg, assures voters that he would be as attentive to them as Holden has been. Meanwhile, during meetings with individuals and groups in Dauphin, Lebanon and Perry counties, Holden, D-Schuylkill, emphasizes his record of bringing home federal projects and his growing seniority on committees that can deliver more money.

headline: Pa. Dems heading toward rift
abstract: A rift between two top state Democratic Party leaders goes public in a battle over who, if anyone, should get the party's endorsement for governor in the May primary. State Representative T.J. Rooney, vice chairman of the state party, will personally endorse former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell and call for an open primary with no party endorsement. Rooney will also criticize state Senator Tina Tartaglione, the party's chairwoman, who has been steering the party toward an endorsement of Auditor General Bob Casey Jr. for governor.

headline: Sunny dispositions rule at Labor Day parade
abstract: As the annual Labor Day parade wended its way down Liberty Avenue yesterday, Dottie Hauger sat near a flower bed waving to luminaries and other marchers in the celebration.  Nearly 200 different unions, marching bands and marching groups participated in the parade, which began at Mellon Arena and ended at Point State Park.  For nearly three hours, thousands lined the streets as teachers, steamfitters, and other unionists swaggered by, displaying worker solidarity.

headline: Bill would restrict who is able to nominate churches as historic
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman Bob O'Conner will introduce a bill that will free churches and other religious structures from some of the city's historic preservation regulations. A review of the bill and its provisions are given.

headline: Judge rips Einstein
abstract: A Commonwealth Court Judge has not decided if the shortcomings of the Einstein Academy cyber school are worth the state withholding future payments. There have been many complaints about the school. There has been great mismanagement. The founder's husband's company which was in charge of supplying the school's programming and curriculum got paid $3 million while the teachers went unpaid.

headline: Study charts fall in residential electric prices
abstract: Residential electricity rates have dropped in 48 states since restructuring of the industry began in 1996, according to a study released yesterday by the Penn Future public policy group in Harrisburg.  John Hanger, president and chief executive officer of Penn Future and a former member of the state Public Utility Commission, said the average price drop for residential customers is 15.4 percent, adjusted for inflation.  Only Vermont and Hawaii have not seen residential electricity rates fall.

headline: Wheatley pled guilty to 1992 felony theft
abstract: The endorsed Democratic candidate opposing state Rep. Bill Robinson in the primary acknowledged Monday he pleaded guilty to charges of larceny and assault and battery a decade ago in Michigan.  But Jake Wheatley Jr., 30, of the Hill District, dismissed his criminal record as the result of a youthful fistfight and said the convictions --- a felony for larceny and a misdemeanor for assault and battery --- redirected his life towards positive goals.  In a plea agreement, Wheatley pleaded guilty to the lesser charges and received two years' probation, which he completed without incident, spokeswoman Debbie Carley said.

headline: A sense of unease grows
abstract: Columnist John Baer talks to Tom Ridge, Director of Homeland Security, about sniper and organized terrorism. Tom Ridge compares the sniper and organized terrorism to anthrax murders, which remain unsolved and also expresses that not having a Department of Homeland Security might be the greatest disappointment to the country.

headline: Gekas, Holden racing to fill their war chests
abstract: U.S. Reps. George W. Gekas and Tim Holden are racing to fill their campaign war chests against a midnight deadline that will serve as a key barometer of their campaigns' success.  National campaign committees, lobbyists, major donors, interest groups and analysts who rate congressional races will pay close attention to the results of midyear finance reports that the two candidates for the 17th Congressional District will file.  Among the things they will look for is whether or by how much Gekas, R-Harrisburg, has been able to narrow-- or even surpass-- Holden, who has maintained a greater than 2-1 funding advantage.

headline: Pennsylvania Governor, Lieutenant Governor races
abstract: The profiles of gubernatorial candidates Mike Fisher, Ed Rendell, Ken Krawchuk and Michael Morril and profiles of Lieutenant Governor candidates, Jane Earll, Catherine Baker Knoll, Henry Haller III and Vicki J. Smedley are presented. Candidates responses to the question- what can state government do to ensure equitable funding so that all of our public schools can provide children with the best public education? are also given.

headline: Superior Court backs dismissal of developer's suit against Rep. Lewis
abstract: The state Superior Court has agreed with the dismissal of a defamation lawsuit against state Rep. Kelly Lewis by developer Gene Percudani, saying there was "no merit to the issues raised on appeal."  The suit, filed last year, claimed that Lewis made libelous statements against Percudani and two of his businesses, Raintree Homes and Chapel Creek Mortgage Banker.  Judge John Lavelle, acting on preliminary objections filed by Lewis that his comments were not directed toward any specific individual or builder, dismissed the suit in December.

headline: Bush to sign 'born-alive' bill in Pittsburgh
abstract: During President Bush's visit here today to meet the Quecreek miners and raise money for state Attorney General Mike Fisher's run for governor, he will sign the Born-Alive Infants Protection Act.  While anti-abortion activists have championed the measure as a way to protect babies, abortion rights proponents see it as a step toward outlawing abortion.  Congress last month gave final approval to the act, which states an infant is considered "born alive" if it is completely extracted or expelled from the mother, breathes, has a beating heart and voluntary muscle movement.

headline: Kukovich: Special session on education is needed
abstract: State Senator Allen G. Kukovich wants to hold a special session on education. He held a news conference with many state Representatives and Senators. A Special Session has been called 36 times since the first in 1791, all to discuss important issues relating to Pennsylvania.

headline: The Private Sector: Power Plays
abstract: The courts have established the validity of deregulation efforts of the energy markets, but the marketplace will determine the validity of the courts ruling. The government comes in at times and tries to interfere with the marketplace. The marketplace will also go up and down.

headline: Witness describes police action at van
abstract: A witness describes a dramatic scene in suburban Richmond, Virginia involving state police chasing a white van which may be connected to the sniper shootings.

headline: A unique political award day for some
abstract: Gar Joseph of Philadelphia Daily News writes about the post-election scenario that had few Representatives like Melissa Brown who lost by a wide margin. Republican PA State Representative John Taylor defeated his democratic opponent 78% to 22%.

headline: Gekas, Holden throw verbal punches at forum
abstract: US Congressman George W. Gekas and opponent Tim Holden throw verbal punches at each other at candidates' forum over the issues related to marriage penalty tax, estate tax, inheritance tax and prescription drug plans. Internal polling showed that Holden has a 48-35 percent advantage over Gekas.

headline: Pennsylvania Governor: Candidates worlds apart on abortion, gun control
abstract: The two Democratic candidates for governor have very different opinions on certain issues. Ed Rendell is for abortion rights while Bob Casey Jr. is against abortion. Rendell wants additional control on handguns, while Casey feels the laws are sufficient. Republican candidate Mike Fisher holds views similar to Casey.

headline: Supervisor races
abstract: Londonberry and Middle Paxton townships will expand their boards from three members to five after voters in November overwhelmingly approved referendums for expansion. Already, the field of candidates is becoming crowded in Londonberry as five Republicans and one Democrat have announced their candidacy for the new supervisor seats. In Middle Paxton, no one has officially announced their candidacy.

headline: Erie council passes anti-discrimination law covering gays
abstract: Erie County has approved an anti-discrimination ordinance which would protect the rights of homosexuals. Equal rights activists have praise the decision, but conservative groups feel it is a step in the wrong direction.

headline: LCB expands prevention effort
abstract: Grants to fight underage drinking by college students will be made available to municipalities by the state Liquor Control Board. The municipal grants are modeled on a program in which the LCB since 1999 has awarded more than $219,000 to 72 colleges and universities to develop coalitions and implement strategies to prevent alcohol abuse among their students. The grants include a two-year $12,000 grant to the Susquehanna Valley Consortium, a group of 13 mid-state colleges and universities.

headline: TMIA plays valuable role; Freedom to criticize entrenched power is essential in providing balance and scrutiny in democracy
abstract: Celebrating 25 years in existence, Three Mile Island Alert is an enduring local activist organization that has kept the various owners and governmental oversees of the local nuclear power station on their toes. Predating the accident at Unit 2 on March 28, 1979, TMIA served as a rallying point for local concern in the wake of that worst of all cases of things that could go wrong at a U.S. commercial nuclear reactor.  Ever since, it has served as a self-appointed watchdog over TMI that often has been in the forefront of such national issues as nuclear plant security and safety.

headline: York County Prison inmates decry conditions
abstract: The York County Prison is trying to extend its contract with the U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Services.  However, the prison is coming under criticism as prisoners complain that they are not getting enough food in prison and are subject to substandard medical care.

headline: Action delayed on court bailout
abstract: Allegheny County Council last night put off voting on a bailout for the county's criminal court system, which has run out of money to pay the court-appointed attorneys who represent indigent defendants.  Also at last night's meeting, the council's Republican minority managed to temporarily block a Democratic plan for holding public hearings on yet another reapportionment proposal.  Council intends to schedule a meeting of its Budget and Finance Committee sometime next week to consider bailout alternatives for the Common Pleas courts, which have already exhausted their $1.04 million allotment for court-appointed defense lawyers this year.

headline: Gekas-Holden race attracts big spenders
abstract: The race for the 17th Congressional District is starting to heat up, but not because of anything that U.S. Reps George W. Gekas, R-Harrisburg, and Tim Holden, D-Schuylkill, are doing.  In action that is likely to intensify through the fall campaign, outside interests are spending thousands of dollars on television and radio advertisements to influence the outcome.  Single-issue groups, coalition and the national political parties have spent more than $300,000 on advertising this month, and campaign officials and political insiders suggest the total could easily reach $2 million to $3 million by November.

headline: Pennsylvania House of Representatives Races
abstract: A list of all candidates in the state House races. The list includes what political party they are and their education, occupation, and qualifications.

headline: Supreme court refuses to accept suit over districts
abstract: The PA Supreme Court has refused to consider multiple cases over Pennsylvania's unequally-sized congressional districts. The Court acknowledged that it is difficult to redraw the state since it has lost 2 of the 21 congressional districts due to slow population growth.

headline: Greetings, cardinals!
abstract: A memo from the faithful Catholics in Philadelphia to the American cardinals visiting the city. There are various greetings from people all over the Philadelphia metro area.

headline: Learning the basics
abstract: With 90 percent of American children relying on public schools, Washington lawmakers were right to buttress the bridges linking the nation's capital and the country's classrooms. The Elementary and Secondary Education Act that President Bush signed aims at improving accountability for whether students learn, setting academic benchmarks for what we as a nation feel every child should know. Each state will have 12 years to bring all of its students up to academic proficiency, showing incremental progress along the way.

headline: Boyes enters airport impasse
abstract: Karl Boyes, a veteran PA state legislator is sponsoring a meeting between Erie Regional House Delegation and PA Department of Transportation hoping that legislators would listen and help solve airport runway extension conflicts.

headline: York residents grapple with verdict
abstract: An all white jury in York found Robert Messer Smith, the leader of Newberry Street Boys, and Gregory Neff, member of another youth gang, guilty of murder in Lillie Belle Allen's death. The third defendant, former York Mayor Charles Robertson, was acquitted in relation to the murder. The African-American community was disappointed.

headline: Activist is off and running with PAC
abstract: Activist Ron Harper, Jr. is plunging into Lancaster County politics without even running for office. Instead, Harper has created a new political action committee, CleanHouse Pac.com, devoted to open and accountable government. The nonpartisan PAC aims to raise money to encourage grass-roots efforts among people who might not otherwise participate in the political process.

headline: Gekas-Holden race tests GOP'S remap art
abstract: U.S. Representative George W. Gekas is facing a tough competition from Tim Holden for the 1th Congressional seat.  Gekas has been defending his position on social security and about the redistricting cycle.

headline: Pennsylvania House races
abstract: The articles presents the profiles of all the candidates for Pennsylvania House of Representatives and their response to three questions asked: (1) how can the state best meet its constitutional obligations to fund public education? (2) what are your top three legislative priorities? and (3) what is your position on developing a system of merit selection for appellate judges to replace the present elective system?

headline: Survey shows Rendell with 12 point lead over Fisher
abstract: In the PA gubernatorial race, Ed Rendell shows a 12 point lead over Attorney general Mike Fisher in resident polls. There are still a number of undecided voters but the Rendell campaign is happy about their position thus far.

headline: House approves modest expansion of state's open records laws
abstract: The state House of Representative has approved a bill that would expand the state's open records law. The bill would set time limits for responding to requests, impose fines on agencies or officials that improperly deny those requests, and provide residents with an explanation why a record is not considered public.

headline: Learning tug-of-war
abstract: Harrisburg school district, which granted Ronald Brown its charter, will send a team to review Brown's operations and determine if its charter should be renewed in the next two years. This comes after an increase in the rate of charter school drop outs has occurred..

headline: $120 million jet maintenance facility 'a little short' of funds
abstract: According to Allegheny County Executive Jim Roddey, all but about $10 million has been identified to fund construction of a $120 million publicly owned jet maintenance facility at Pittsburgh International Airport. Roddey said funding for the project, which he said will help solidify the jobs of 3,000 mechanics and related workers, should be resolved within 60 days. Those jobs would be lost if US Airways, which would lease the facility from the country, were to maintain its fleet in another city.

headline: After-school activities
abstract: The Boys and Girls is one of the busiest spots on Berry Hill Street.  Every weekday afternoon it provides services and activities to kids who don't have access to Scouts, league sports and shopping malls.  Most of these "latchkey" kids, a social category that has its roots in welfare reform rules that require able-bodied parents to work.  That often means able-bodied single parents.  As a consequence the two-to three-hour period between the end of the school day and the end of the usual work day is placing more responsibility on non-family caretaking.

headline: All agree either Democratic gubernatorial candidate could win
abstract: The two Democratic gubernatorial candidates are in a tight race and have raised nearly $25 million since April. Both have launched negative attacks on one another. Rendell will focus on southeastern Pennsylvania and Casey is concentrating on the western and northeastern part of the state.

headline: Getting a boost
abstract: U.S. Rep. Charles Stenholm, D-Texas, is the ranking minority member on House of Representatives Agriculture Committee.  If Democrats manage to pick up eight more seats in the House, he could become chairman.  So even though he faces opposition at home in the 17th District of Texas, Stenholm was stumping Pennsylvania's 17th District yesterday with Rep. Tim Holden, D-Schuylkill, who is trying to pick up one of those seats.  Holden faces a more difficult re-election challenge than Stenholm, having been forced by redistricting into a race with incumbent Rep. George W. Gekas, R-Harrisburg, in a district that gives Gekas a voter registration edge.

headline: Pollsters not down for count
abstract: Pennsylvania Democrats and Republicans are discussing polling results from before the gubernatorial election between Mike Fisher and Ed Rendell. Republicans say the polls ended up hurting Fisher in the race and Democrats say that the only poll that mattered was the results of the votes on election days.

headline: Take the political process away from the politicians
abstract: The Republicans want to move the primary until July in order to put their new reapportionment plan. The Democrats want their incumbents to have a better chance of winning. Voters should take the election process away from the legislature.

headline: Inside the Capital
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union has asked PA Governor Mark Schweiker to veto the Religious Freedom Protection Act, citing that it is flawed and actually end up hurting the free expression of religion.

headline: Legislators hike local school subsidies
abstract: Members of the state General Assembly substantially increased funding for Pennsylvania's 501 public school districts, compared to what Governor Mark Schweiker proposed in February, in the final budget passed last week.  The governor had proposed across-the-board increases of one percent for all school districts.  The state association representing school boards lobbied successfully for additional funding.

headline: A Bargain: $221.7 million sounds like a lot, but an updated airport will be worth it
abstract: The most outstanding thing about the proposed new Harrisburg International Airport redevelopment is its price.  At a breathtaking $221.7 million, it will be a one of the most expensive capital projects yet undertaken in central Pennsylvania.  Fortunately, Harrisburg International's managers over the years prudently had assembled available lands on its periphery, and as a result a sweeping new 283,000-square-foot terminal (twice the size of the current facility), a multimodal transportation center, an Amtrak stop with moving sidewalks and various on-field improvements can be developed on existing airport land holdings.

headline: Amish families serving meals in home run risk with law
abstract: Roughly 15 Amish families have been charging tourists for meals served in their homes. The practice is illegal to operate a public eating or drinking place without a license. The homes must be inspected for safety reasons if the families plan on serving to the public for profit.

headline: All's quiet on primary election front
abstract: The expensive and bloody Democratic fight for the gubernatorial nomination will likely stir some voter interest in the May 21 primary.  But virtually no other contests for major-party nominations will appear on the ballots that Centre County voters will open in less than seven weeks.  It costs the county- - and thus the county taxpayers- - about $50,000 to stage a primary election.  That cost won't change this year, but it looks like it will mostly pay for idle polling places and the sound of silence.

headline: Gillespie chosen to lead 'Democrats for Barletta'
abstract: Hazleton's Republican Mayor Louis Barletta will face a tough battle if he plans to unseat US Representative Paul Kanjorski. In an attempt to get crossover votes, Barletta named former county District Attorney Bob Gillespie as director of "Democrats for Barletta."

headline: Pol's role in rezoning questioned
abstract: State Sen. Tina Tartglione last year urged the city Zoning Board of Adjustment to approve a proposed prison in her district without revealing her family ties to the project.  The company behind the deal, Par Economic Development Corp., is owned by the husband-wife team of Carlos Matos and Renee Tartaglione.  Besides her brother-in-law, Matos is Tina Tartaglione's $43,000 administrative assistant and a ward leader in her district.  Renee, Tina's sister, is a $151,000 deputy city commissioner who works for their mother, City Commissioner Marge Tartaglione.  Sen. Tartaglione's role in rezoning the property at Erie and Whitaker avenues, and her failure to disclose her personal connections raise ethical questions about her conduct.

headline: Takeover ignites challenge in teacher's union
abstract: With unrest running high among teachers in the state-run Philadelphia School District, a fight is on for the leadership of the teacher's union. Philadelphia Federation of Teachers president Ted Kirsch is trying to fend off a challenge by an insurgent group that says the union has not fought hard enough to ward off privatization. The results could effect the implementation of Gov. Schweiker's school reform plan, with cooperation and morale of teachers and their union leaders being paramount under any circumstances.

headline: Judge strikes down ordinance requiring permits for speech
abstract: U.S. District Judge William W. Caldwell has struck down a Harrisburg City ordinance that requires people to obtain permits before distributing leaflets or making speeches in city parks. Caldwell cited the ordinance violated free speech rights.

headline: Legislators raise fairness questions about $75 million for Phila. Schools
abstract: Pennsylvania legislators have said that they are reluctant to give more money to Philadelphia schools when other districts across the state also faced a budget crunch. State Representative Phyllis Mundy gave her opinion on the matter after meetings with James Nevels, chairman of the Philadelphia School Reform Commission.

headline: Agencies move to ease commuting as the outskirts get more populated
abstract: SEPTA only has a public transportation stop mid-county in Upper Bucks and Montgomery Counties. Those who commute from those areas have longs trips into Center City Philadelphia. SEPTA is looking to adding a commuting line from Landsdale to Quakertown plus adding a Metro line.

headline: Bill offers tax relief to elderly
abstract: Proposed legislation that passed in the state House will provide property tax relief to low-income working families and senior citizens. The rebate could be up to $500 for 1 million Pennsylvanians.

headline: Ambitious new capitol visitor's center coming
abstract: Work has begun on a new visitor's center in one of the most ambitious building projects in the U.S. Capitol's 200-year history.  When finished in 2005, the three-level underground facility on the east side of the Capitol will include a dining room for 600, two 250-seat theaters, gift shops, exhibitions and a first aid center.  More than 3 million people visited the Capitol in 2000.

headline: Gingrich wins by 64 votes in 101st
abstract: Former Palmyra Borough Council President Mauree Gingrich beat out Lebanon businessman Bruce Golgowski in a five-candidate race for the Republican nomination for the 101st District state House seat.  Gingrich's unofficial total of votes was 1,863.

headline: Push for reform now
abstract: The U.S. House faces showdown votes this week on campaign finance reform, specifically the Shays-Meehan bill. Shays-Meehan would stop the corrupting torrent of unregulated "soft money" that flows from unions, corporations and well-heeled individuals to the two major parties. The bill would also ban most phony issue ads within 60 days of an election.

headline: Tax reform remains elusive
abstract: The state Legislature will come back early from its summer recess to begin an historic special session Wednesday dedicated to local property tax reform.  The session will seek remedies to high property tax rates and to the public school funding that causes them.  About half of all public school funds in the state come through local property taxes, and many homeowners want relief.

headline: Lawmaker proposes safeguards for religions
abstract: State Representative Mike Veon, is proposing a religious freedoms protection act to allow religious organizations to hire in accord with their mission, preserve the ability of health-care and social service agencies to meet their ethical and moral standards.

headline: Lender offers fee-free student loans
abstract: Pennsylvania State Employees Credit Union has become the first lender in the state to offer student loans with no up-front fees. Most student loans require payment of origination fees, or "points," equal to 3 percent of the loan. With most federally insured student loans, one point each is paid by the lender, the student and the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency. The credit union offers to pick up the student's share.

headline: Airport soldiers' guns were unloaded
abstract: For seven months, more than 80 National Guard troops watched almost 12 million passengers walk through the gates and security checkpoints at Philadelphia International Airport.  The soldiers stood ready, dressed in Army fatigues, their 9mm pistols strapped to their sides but the guns had no bullets.  At 16 airports across Pennsylvania, National Guard troops were banned from patrolling with loaded weapons, according to some guardsmen stationed in Philadelphia.

headline: Bush undercuts welfare reform
abstract: Back during Bush's first term as an anti-big-government Republican governor, he proposed a revolutionary reform of Texas' welfare system.  A few years later, when Bush ran for president as a "compassionate conservative," he hawked a "faith-based imitative" that would have given religious organizations billions of federal tax dollars  to run a broad array of government services including welfare-to-work programs.  It was a centerpiece of the less-government-is-good-government mantra that he chanted on his way to capturing the White House.

headline: Analysts say race in 12th District is Murtha's to lose
abstract: Two incumbent Representatives are fighting for a newly drawn district. John Murtha and Fran Mascara are battling for the 12th District. Murtha has the advantage as the state's "quarterback" in Congress.

headline: Good intentions, but
abstract: Legislation now awaiting Gov. Mark Schweiker's signature would set time limits for municipalities to act on developers' projects. Ambiguity of the bill's time limits for responding to more complex developer challenges could spell trouble and prove disastrous to communities.

headline: Pa. ranks 47th, given F in records openess
abstract: Pennsylvania ranks 47th among the 50 states in citizens access to government records, accordig to a new national study.  The Chicago-based Better Government Association gave Pennsylvania's open-records law a grade of F.  Only South Dakota, Alabama, and Montana fared worse than Pennsylvania in the study, which appears in the cuurent issue of The IRE Journal, a journalism trade publication.

headline: Teacher strike title goes to Illinois
abstract: Illinois had two more school employees strikes last year than Pennsylvania, which has long been considered the public school strike capital of America.  The seven strikes of public school teachers or support staff in Pennsylvania is the same number as recorded the previous year and is the second lowest number in the state in the past 10 years.  Pennsylvania has been home to about a quarter or more of all strikes, according to Pennsylvania School Boards Association data.

headline: Men, women both needed in politics
abstract: State Rep. Patricia Vance, R-87, spoke during a Women's Political Summit sponsored by Pi Sigma Alpha, Shippensburg University's political science honor society.  Titled "Women in Pennsylvania Politics," the summit was presented in conjunction with National Women's History Month.  Court of Common Pleas Judge Carol L. Van Horn of Franklin and Fulton counties and Monroe County Republican Committee Chairwoman Linda S. Womer joined Vance on the panel.

headline: Lewis: Local schools need $27M more
abstract: Monroe County will need $27 million more in state funding to avoid a double digit increase in school property taxes. The four school districts will lobby for more aid. The current budget allowed for a $310,340 increase.

headline: 'Alisha's Justice' passes House
abstract: The state House yesterday approved legislation that stiffens penalties for reckless drivers who kill someone -- a measure named for a York County girl killed in a 1999 crash.  The proposal is part of a lengthy transportation bill that also creates a controversial pilot program for cameras to catch red-light violators in Philadelphia. The reckless driving bill has been dubbed Alisha's Justice, for Alisha Kay Diehl of Dover.

headline: Child-care problems persist
abstract: About 50 people turned out Thursday to hear representatives from the state Department of Public Welfare, Child Care Network and United Way's Success by 6 offer options for more child care in the area.  In the end they learned there is no quick solution to replacing child-care services lost when four providers were cited this summer for caring for more than three children without being registered.

headline: Appointment to be test case of blacklist
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker will provide the first test case of whether the threats of House Minority Leader H. Williams DeWeese against a prominent lobbyist will be carried out.  DeWeese and Senate Minority Leader Bob Mellow, D-Lackawanna, had already jointly nominated lobbyist Steve Wojdak to the important Philadelphia Convention Center Board, before the DeWeese-Wojdak feud blew up recently.  Schweiker will now decide if DeWeese's threatened blacklist of Wojdak starts with this appointment.

headline: GOP already looking unbeatable in Bucks congressional races
abstract: Democratic leaders in Bucks County have all but conceded the 2002 congressional contest to longtime incumbent James C. Greenwood. While Democrats have never come close to beating Greenwood they have never failed to slate a candidate against him. Democratic Chairman John Murray said it is likely that Republican incumbents will not face challengers in four Upper Bucks districts in the State Legislature.

headline: Pa. Senate: Ferlo wins Senate nod in first run for state office
abstract: Jim Ferlo in his first run for state office, easily defeated Highland Park financial planner Bonnie DiCarlo to capture the Democratic nomination in the 38th Senatorial District.  The victory in the district has given Ferlo an inside track to the seat held for 24 years by Leonard Bodack, who is retiring.

headline: Tell Sen. Specter to protect Arctic wildlife refuge
abstract: The future of the Artic wildlife refuge is under great debate. The Senate is looking into opening the refuge for oil drilling. US Senator Arlen Specter has not said publicly which way he will vote.

headline: Scary proposal
abstract: The PA Senate voted to approve the Religious Freedom Protection Act, which will allow the free practice of religion. The Act can be used to justify a number of behaviors. The Patriot News says the Act is a violation of the U.S. Constitution and urges the PA House of Representatives not to support the bill.

headline: Little change in school realignment plan
abstract: The Pittsburgh Public Schools reapportionment plan is now available for public review. There have been few changes proposed in the plan.

headline: Amish Tickets
abstract: The state House of Representatives rejected a measure that would have exempted ultraconservative Amish sect from a state law that requires reflective orange triangles on horse-drawn buggies and other slow-moving vehicles.  On Thursday, the House deleted from a transportation bill language that would allow animal-drawn vehicles to use gray reflective tape instead of the triangles, which are the subject of a legal dispute between the state and the Swartzentruber sect.  The amended bill was passed 174-23 and was returned to the Senate.

headline: Church day-care centers may face new state regulations
abstract: The child-care center Bustleton UMC has an affiliation with the Methodist Church. The child-care center also has a certification of compliance from the state Department of Public Welfare. The pastor believes the regulations from the state do not interfere with its ability to be religiously affiliated.

headline: Area GOP rally for Fisher/ Earll
abstract: Lackawana County GOP Chairman Paul Catalano believes a United Republican party can elect PA Attorney General Mike Fisher as the next governor of Pennsylvania. Catalano says Fisher's experience in the PA House and work with environmental issues brought in 400,000 new jobs to the state and can do more if elected governor.

headline: GOP attempts to limit Lott damage, starting with new leader
abstract: U.S. Republican Senators are working to limit the damage that U.S. Senator Trent Lott's words had on the party's efforts to attract minority voters. Republicans hope for a fresh start with new incoming Republican leader U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell.

headline: Pa. special session ends as a footnote
abstract: PA State lawmakers introduced more than 80 bills during the special session. Of all the bills proposed, there was not a single one that become law or even made it to a floor vote. Bills presented included, property tax reform, senior citizen tax breaks, school tax referendums, and statewide teacher salary contract.

headline: The 102nd district
abstract: Pennsylvania State Representative Pete Zug is running for re-election in the 102nd House District against his second cousin Raymond Ondrusek. Ondrusek said his concerns are school taxes, cutting down state spending, eliminating the state income tax, and ending parole for violent offenders.

headline: Sham contracts undercut minority goals
abstract: A report by the Sports & Exhibition Authority found that contractors routinely undermined efforts to involve minorities and women owned businesses in the $1 billion stadium and convention center projects. There were recommended changes, but the time has already passed for minority and female opportunities.

headline: Magazine reports Pennsylvania lags in preschool funding
abstract: Barb Willard, vice president of children and youth services for the Heritage Health Foundation, stands in the preschool room at the 4Kids Child Care Center in Braddock. The cost of caring for a child at one of the $Kids centers is about $7200 a year. Thousands of children in Pennsylvania enter the first grade lagging behind their peers because they did not go to a good preschool, and many of those children will never catch up, local and national experts said Monday.

headline: Amtrak, confronting subsidy cuts, threatens to cut Pittsburgh service
abstract: The latest threat to Amtrak's operations surfaced this week as the Bush administration released a budget proposal that provides $521 million for Amtrak. The Amtrak Reform Council, a congressional committee, is scheduled to release a report recommending that the government break up the railroad and open passenger rail travel to competition. Amtrak must give 180 days' notice before it curtails service on any routes.

headline: Gekas vows Social Security benefit protection
abstract: U.S. Rep. George W. Gekas marked the 67th birthday of Social Security by assuring senior citizens that Congress would never allow the program to be cut back.  He made no mention of proposals to allow workers to invest a portion of their Social Security taxes in the stock market, a controversial issue that he and other Republicans now are being accused of trying to avoid.  Gekas, R-Harrisburg, pledged last month not to support Social Security privatization.  But an April 22 poll, financed by his campaign and National Republicans, stated that he believes people 50 and under should be able to invest Social Security funds to potentially earn higher returns.

headline: Area, happy with incumbent, wonders what Gekas can offer
abstract: U.S. Representative Time Holden, D-Pottsville, has represented the 6th District, including all of Schuylkill and Berks county since 1992. The latest congressional redistricting has sliced up the 6th District adding Schuylkill and western Berks counties to the 17th District of U.S. Representative George W. Gekas, R-Harrisburg. Holden is weighing whether to seek re-election against Gekas in the new district, where Republicans outnumber Democrats 189,098 to 135, 482.

headline: GOP challenges candidacy of Earl's only foe for nomination for lieutenant governor
abstract: The qualifications of former Bellefonte Mayor Candace Dannaker are being questioned in her run for become lieutenant governor. The state Republican's top executive is challenging her nominating petition claiming she did not receive enough signatures.

headline: Pa. Supreme court in a shameful stonewall
abstract: The PA State Supreme Court has put the citizens of Pennsylvania in the dark about how much special interests spend to influence public policy in Pennsylvania. The Court has refused to re hear argument on its deadlocked decision regarding the PA's Lobbyist Disclosure Act.

headline: The art of compromise is essential if homeland security is to progress
abstract: The scope of a new homeland security department is huge.  President Bush wants to merge 22 federal agencies and their 170,000 employees.  The most extensive federal government reorganization in about 50 years would include all or part of major government agencies such as the Coast Guard, Customs Service, and Immigration and Naturalization Service.

headline: State's rural and urban voters less divided than expected, study says
abstract: Rural and urban Pennsylvanians are less divided on politically sensitive issues such as abortion and gay rights than most people believe, according to survey data compiled by Millersville University. The data show that 50 percent of both rural and urban voters believe abortion should be legal, but with restrictions. While 20 percent of both groups oppose it in all circumstances. Twenty percent of both groups also oppose equal rights for homosexuals.

headline: Many city teachers hear bell ringing as uncertainty looms, they're fleeing, retiring
abstract: As a graduate student, Amy McNally wrote her thesis on the Philadelphia School District's problem of losing new teachers, discovering that many quit after about fiver years on the job.  She is becoming her own statistic, by shopping her resume to the suburbs, due to the upheaval caused by the state's takeover of Philly schools.  At the same time, a parade of retirement-aged teachers, are calling it quits rather than grappling with the uncertainty of reform.

headline: Ban driving while under the influence of a phone
abstract: PA State Senator Joe Conti has repeatedly tried to pass legislation that would restrict the use of handheld cell phones on PA state roads and highways. The Courier Times wants Conti to continue to fight for the bill despite other lawmakers' failure to support it.

headline: Legislation could boost or bail out single parents, farm families, retirees
abstract: As far as state Rep. Samuel E. Rohrer is concerned, proposed legislation to amend Pennsylvania's 65-year-old "industrial homework" law is a matter of common sense.  The Berks County Republican, a primary sponsor of House Bill 1682, recognizes the timeliness of amendments to permit single mothers and welfare-to-work parents to earn money from home, and to give struggling farm families a way to raise their incomes.  In addition, according to Macungie resident Barbara Mills, who has lobbied for the bill, it could help people whose retirement funds have been eroded by the stock market dip.

headline: Argall called front-runner for Appropriations chair
abstract: State Representative David G. Argall is a candidate for the chairman of the House Appropriations Committee. The House will vote for the position the following week. The former chairman surprisingly resigned after he was confronted with unspecified allegations.

headline: GOP finds duplicate voting
abstract: A survey by the Republican National Committee has found nearly 50,000 cases of improper duplicate voter registrations in Pennsylvania.  Under their database, Republicans found 17,276 cases of individuals who were apparently  registered in two different jurisdictions within the state and at least 32,000 cases where individuals were registered concurrently in Pennsylvania and another state.

headline: PA-house-contested
abstract: A summary of the latest, unofficial results of the PA State House elections is given, with 94 democratic seats and 109 GOP seats.

headline: The candidates- North
abstract: Listed is the unofficial list of candidates for the primary election for state House and senate seats from the northern Pittsburgh area.

headline: Street talk hits a nerve on race
abstract: Stirring up debate on the airwaves and in politicians' offices was Street's unvarnished rhetoric Saturday during a NAACP northeast regional training conference in Center City.  In a 25 -minute rambling speech, Street, speaking without a text, touted the accomplishments of his mayoralty: towing thousands of abandoned cars, raising millions to fight blight, helping improve Center City.  Extolling the NAACP's history of fighting discrimination, the mayor listed the many African Americans serving in senior positions in his administration.

headline: Masch has jobs but no degree
abstract: One of Mayor Street's picks for the new School Reform Commission has two decades of budget savvy and an Ivy League job, but does not have a college degree. Masch, a vice president at the University of Pennsylvania, confirmed that he never graduated from that school or Temple University. Masch said he did not tell the mayor's staff that the had the degrees or review the press release before it was issued.

headline: Bridge users slam traffic, tolls, E-Z Pass
abstract: Residents at a Phillipsburg meeting voiced their concerns about traffic. They demanded that the Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission give them relief from higher toll fees and traffic congestion from the E-Z Pass lane on Interstate 78 and Route 22 bridges.

headline: Pa. considers dropping welfare  ban
