Representative Henry Waxman of California highlighted 17 points on which the Cheney energy policy either dovetail's with Enron's positions or benefits the company.

headline: Hart launches re-election bid
abstract: U.S. Rep. Melissa Hart launched her re-election campaign with four-stop swing through the 4th Congressional District. Before joining Congress in 2000, Hart served in the state Senate for 10 years, where she chaired the Finance Committee.

headline: Poll says Rendell is leading Fisher
abstract: Republican candidate for governor Mike Fisher said he is counting on his Democratic opponent to emerge "battered and broke" from a nasty primary battle. The ordeal seems to have helped Ed Rendell, according to a poll released yesterday by Quinnipiac University.  It showed an early 45 to 37 percent lead for the former mayor of Philadelphia.

headline: Washenik's character considered key in House race
abstract: Democratic party leaders have decided to replace PA State representative Joe Battisto with Gratz Washenik in the election for the 176th state seat. Gratz will run against Republican Mario Scalvello. His supporters say his fiery character will be his biggest asset.

headline: Health care threatened by out-of-control costs
abstract: Spurred by soaring malpractice awards, runaway insurance rates are forcing doctors to cut back. They have less money to invest in new medical equipment, are forced to close smaller offices, and must trim office staff. The upshot is a downswing in available health care services. According to a recent Pennsylvania Medical Society survey, 72 percent of doctors said they have deferred buying new medical equipment or hiring new staff due to sudden increases in liability insurance.

headline: School bond plan revised; New hope seen for $300M aid
abstract: City Council President Anna Verna appeared to have struck a deal with School Reform Commission Chairman James Nevels yesterday to improve the odds for a $300 million bond to keep the district financially afloat.  Verna and Nutter spoke approvingly of the revised bond deal, which will now be  discussed in a hearing April 10 and could be first voted on by Council on April 11with a final approval vote on April 18.  The deal calls for Council to approve $45 million in new annual funding for the district.

headline: Second defendant pleads guilty in driver's license charges
abstract: A native of Iraq pleaded guilty in federal court Monday to illegally obtaining a driver's license that allowed him to transport hazardous materials. A total of 20 men of Middle Eastern descent have been charged with bribing a former Pennsylvania Department of Transportation official to bypass state examinations for truckers who carry dangerous payloads. Prosecutors said the truck drivers, many of whom were immigrants, used a middleman to pay off Pennsylvania Department of Transportation license examiner Robert Ferrari Sr.

headline: Rendell visits Latrobe, outlines economic plan
abstract: With the decaying buildings of the former Valley-Vulcan Mold Co. serving as a backdrop, Ed Rendell announced his plan to economically revitalize the state's smaller communities. Rendell is promising to local officials that his administration would help the state's small cities, boroughs and township get a fair share of financial help. Rendell, who served two terms as Philadelphia mayor, said his hometown and Pittsburg have been reborn mainly because of state grants.

headline: Bush signs law creating memorial for victims of hijacked plans
abstract: President Bush signed legislation Tuesday creating a national memorial to honor those who died on the hijacked plane that crashed into the Pennsylvania countryside Sept. 11 - men and woman he has repeatedly lauded as a new breed of American hero.  Many in Washington believe they owe their lives to those on board United Flight 93.  It is believed the hijackers intended to fly the plane into the White House or the Capitol, but that some passengers and crew fought back and perhaps forced the plane into the field near Shanksville, Pa.  All 44 people aboard, including the four hijackers died.

headline: Haste fills commissioner post
abstract: Jeff Haste, former PA State Representative and current Chief Clerk for Dauphin County, will complete the remaining 11 months of the Dauphin County Commissioner position, vacated by John Payne.

headline: Poll shows Rendell-Fisher race tightening
abstract: The gubernatorial race between Democrat Edward G. Rendell and Republican Mike Fisher has tightened up in recent weeks, according to a poll released Wednesday.  The independent survey by Quinnipiac University Polling Institute in Hamden, Conn., showed Rendell is the choice of 47 percent of registered voters and Fisher favored by 39 percent. That compares to 49 percent for Rendell and 36 percent for Fisher in a Quinnipiac poll released July 24.

headline: We demonstrate our commitment to country by voting
abstract: The Pocono Record appeals to the thousands of Pennsylvanians who will enter the voting booth to elect a state representative, a senator, a congressman, and a governor to remind voters of the key role voting plays in PA official's ability to make good decisions.

headline: Health insurance reserves
abstract: What are Pennsylvania's Blue Cross and Blue Shield plans doing with an estimated $3 billion in reserves even as they have been raising premiums by double-digit amounts?  That question has come to be raised enough times by enough people, including some state lawmakers, that Insurance Commissioner Diane Koken recently invited officials at "the Blues" to offer explanations at public hearings to be held in early September.  The reserves held by the Blues, which provide health insurance for more than half the state's population, are several times what the insurance department requires.

headline: School consultants hired, but the questions remain
abstract: School Reform Commission chairman James Nevels promises: "We're going to have a better-run school district next September."  The commission voted last week to hire Edison Schools Inc. and 11 other private firms and groups as consultants, seeking advice on services from school safety to food service to teacher recruitment.  It was the first step in what the commission expects will be a long road toward reshaping public education in Philadelphia.

headline: Region
abstract: A public meeting will be held by the Port Authority of Allegheny County is find out what residents think about a proposed $390 million tunnel beneath the Allegheny River linking downtown and the North Shore via light rail.

headline: Rendell, Fisher lay out economic plans
abstract: Gubernatorial candidates Ed Rendell and State Attorney General Mike Fisher will be releasing their economic plans. Fisher unveiled his property tax reform program while Rendell's economic plan focused on reducing business taxes, investing federal money to lure private capital investment and buying and rehabilitating blighted properties and infrastructures.

headline: Bush to campaign for Gekas at HIA
abstract: President George W. Bush will rally at Harrisburg International Airport to campaign for U.S. Congressman Gekas's reelection campaign. Bush had made 59 trips for political events thus far, raising $145 million, according to CBC news.

headline: Heard on the hill
abstract: "Unfortunately, the majority of tax-shifting 'reform' plans coming out of the General Assembly are based on two myths - that the schools are under funded and that they are under-funded because the state has failed to pay its 'fair share.' "

headline: Poll worker pay hikes sought
abstract: Proposed legislation would allow counties to pay poll workers more. There are 60,000 workers at 9400 voting precincts.

headline: We've got bigger things to worry about than a few months' rent
abstract: Governor Tom Ridge of Pennsylvania left his position as Governor to become the country's first director of the federal Office of Homeland Security. Ridge stayed in the Governor's mansion four months after he resigned and a state Senator wants Ridge to reimburse the state for the lodging costs. However, some feel this should not even be a real issue.

headline: Health-care industry should get real
abstract: Richard D. Gorski, a lawyer from Bethlehem, Pa., would like the health-care people to agree to abolish the Pennsylvania Peer Review statute, which lets hospitals investigate physicians who have committed acts ranging from malpractice to criminal behavior and then sweep their findings under the carpet. According to Gorski, plaintiffs are not allowed access to these investigations even if a patient has died due to neglect, reckless, or criminal behavior.

headline: School cuts may help win extra aid
abstract: The Philadelphia School Reform Commission cut hundreds of administrative jobs which could help the school district receive $75 million from the state legislature. The commission took over the Philadelphia School District.

headline: Regional agency backs $4 billion plan for Mon-Fayette Expressway/Southern Beltway
abstract: The Southwest Pennsylvania Commission voted in favor of endorsing a financing plan for the expensive road project Mon-Fayette Expressway/Southern Beltway is a 100 miles from West Virginia to Pittsburgh. The project is still $2.5 billion short.

headline: Rendell, Fisher offer arena funding views
abstract: Democratic gubernatorial nominee Ed Rendell has proposed his funding views for state, claiming if elected he would limit state aid for Pittsburgh Penguins. His opponent, State Attorney General Mike Fisher, says the funding should hinge on how much funding Pittsburgh gives to the Penguins.

headline: Bush will stump for GOP hopefuls
abstract: President George W. Bush is scheduled to fly into the Philadelphia area to support Republican candidates Mike Fisher and PA State Senator James Gerlac in their election campaigns.

headline: Heard on the hill
abstract: "We have urged people to look to Pennsylvania as a model, and so I think the legislation that's just been passed is very, very good."

headline: Poll: economy top election issue, but Dems don't benefit
abstract: The CBS-New York Times poll showed that the economy and jobs were the top issues on voters minds when deciding who to vote for gubernatorial elections. The nest important issues were terrorism, national defense, and then education. The poll also showed that Democrats have not convinced voters that they have a clear plan for the country if they gain control of Congress.

headline: What has Barley done?  Republicans who yanked support say they don't know
abstract: When 24 Republican committee people signed a letter stating that Rep. John E. Barley, R-Conestoga, had committed a transgression so grave thata they could no longer support him, most had no idea what the transgression was.  The Lancaster County Republican committee members said they were operating primarily out of faith in Kim Rankin, Barley's former campaign manager and, until recently, his biggest booster.  It was Rankin's announcement last week that she had information that made it impossible for her to continue to support Barley's re-election campaign that prompted the House Appropriations chairman to announce he would end his campaign and resign, effective Tuesday.

headline: Helping Seniors Afford Prescription Drugs
abstract: Local readers of  The New York Times were no doubt take aback by a recent article" Pennsylvania drug plan in need of care."  It was a classic good news-bad news report.  The good: Pennsylvania's program to help low -income elderly people buy prescription drugs (PACE) is the largest in the nation and extremely popular.  The bad: Revenues from the State Lottery, which funds the program, can't keep up with soaring costs

headline: School directors seek more funding
abstract: More than 50 superintendents and board members protested in Harrisburg demanding that the state provide them with more funds. If no further assistance is provided, many school districts will be forced to raise property taxes. Governor Schweiker's budget provides $6.6 billion for schools. The Ridge/Schweiker administration has increase the state's share of funding by $1.7 billion over the past seven years.

headline: Republican Dent says he has feel for area's needs
abstract: State Senator Charles Dent says he has a good feeling about the Pocono and West End area needs. Dent says infrastructure plans in the area will be a top priority, including the $2 million project on PA Department of Transportation's 12 year plan on bad traffic spots in Chestnuthill Township.

headline: Save space while you can
abstract: Voters in five municipalities have approved open-space initiatives, in most cases by overwhelming margins.  In addition, voters in Lehigh County approved a non-binding resolution to borrow $30 million over 10 years for open-space preservation.  Voters in the southeast, already the most heavily developed region of the state, have shown substantial willingness to tax themselves in order to preserve what open space remains.

headline: Bush, Fisher raise $1 M for campaign
abstract: President Bush barnstormed into Pittsburgh on Monday, giving state Attorney General Mike Fisher's campaign for governor a boost by helping to raise more than $1 million in campaign funds.  Bush also used the Fisher campaign event at the Pittsburgh Hilton & Towers, Downtown, to restate his faith in the economy and his determination to win the war on terrorism.  Saying the nation was making progress in the war on terrorism, Bush pledged that America would root out terrorist leaders.

headline: Heard on the hill
abstract: State Treasurer Barbara Hafer is quoted asking former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak, at a pitch to the board of the Public School Employee's Retirement System yesterday on investing in security and defense technologies, if he could help coordinate the CIA and the FBI.

headline: Poll: Many willing to trust Bush
abstract: A USA Today/CNN Gallup Poll indicates that the public feels the Bush administration is not responsible for any wrong doing in the Enron scandal. Enron and its executives have donated 1 million dollars to President Bush throughout his career.  Some political scholars claim that the public might be looking past any possible wrong doing of the Bush administration with the Enron fiasco in light of President Bush's leadership on the war on terror.

headline: What politicians might offer us this April Fool's Day
abstract: The White House today announced a compromise with Congress in the controversy over funding to keep America safe.  Homeland Security director Tom Ridge agreed to testify before Congressional committees if committee members agree to dress in the color-of-the-day as determined by Ridge's color-coded security alert system.  Congressional leaders said many members are comfortable with the plan, especially if the country remains on its current color-alert status-yellow.

headline: House passes malpractice bill
abstract: The state House voted 144-53 last night to pass a sweeping medical malpractice reform bill, trading new restrictions on malpractice claims for better tracking of medical errors. The sweep of the House bill's tort reforms stunned some advocates for patients' rights, especially a clause giving doctors the right to ask patients to agree to a cap on non-economic damages before treating them. Larry Frankel, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Pennsylvania, voiced concern that the clause will lead to unequal treatment between patients who sign and those who do not.

headline: School district has $10 million deficit, faces steep budget cuts
abstract: A budget hearing was held at Coatesville Area School District. The administrators want to make $12.7 million in budget cuts. Chester County school district is in a $10 million deficit and wants to cut 79 teaching positions.

headline: Resident calls maglev routes 'inconsiderate'
abstract: Westmoreland County residents who went to an open house on maglev trains state their concerns. The major concern is that the proposed train routes are inconsiderate of the location to their homes. Some residents have even receive eminent domain letters.

headline: Schweiker still mulling convention center reform bill
abstract: PA Governor Mark Schweiker has announced that he will sign a bill that would change the management of the PA Convention Center in Philadelphia, only if he can be convinced that it offers drastic improvements in its operations.

headline: Bush, in Pa., pushes bioterror budget
abstract: President Bush prodded Congress to approve his $5.9 billion bioterrorism budget, saying the investment would pay off in better security and better health care. A day after releasing his $2.13 trillion federal budget for fiscal 2003, Bush toured a medical research center at the University of Pittsburg to promote his plan for defeating bioterrorists. The bioterrorism budget includes money to improve and expand medical early-warning systems to detect infectious outbreaks.

headline: Helsel move angers GOP and Dems
abstract: Plumstead Township Supervisor Betsy Helsel almost lost the Republican primary for the 143rd District seat. Helsel pulled off a write-in victory for the Democratic nomination. Democratic supporters of Helsel worked the polls and urged party members to cast write-in votes for the Republican.  No Democrat was on the ballot.

headline: Poll: Rendell, Casey clawing for an edge
abstract: Ed Rendell has a four point edge over his Democratic rival for governor. A quarter of Democrats were unsure of how they would vote. The director of the Muhlenberg Institute of Public Opinion said the race is a dead heat with no real frontrunner.

headline: Where's Catherine?
abstract: The past two previous Lieutenant Governors have had to become the Governor due to illness and the promotion of one Governor to a federal position. There are three realistic candidates for the new lieutenant governor. Former Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll is the frontrunner, but is conducting a low-profile campaign.

headline: How much aid can we afford to give seniors?
abstract: Senate Democrats this week are pushing for a vote on a proposal that elevates prescription drugs for seniors over all other domestic needs.  The plan is so expensive that if it ever passed, it could squeeze out the party's other priorities - - such as education or health coverage for the uninsured - - for years.  Compounding the problem, the Senate Democrats haven't identified how they would pay for this big new expense because they are still unwilling to challenge President Bush's huge tax cut.

headline: School districts exhale in pension-funding relief
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker is expected this week to sign into law a bill that has local school district official breathing a little easier as they prepare their 2002-03 budgets.  The bill, passed by both the state House and Senate last week, would boost pensions of state and school retirees and also lower the contributions made by school districts to fund those retirement plans.  The measure raises cost-of-living allowances for state retirees by more than $1.7 billion over 10 years, while saving school districts about $220 million a year.

headline: Restoring driving privileges comes at a price
abstract: A state law requires offenders with two DUIs to wait two years to get back their license or pay $1000 to install an ignition interlock device. Some lawyers argue that the ignition interlock device is unconstitutional because it creates an unfair standard. Those who choose to install the device must still wait a year before they can receive their driving privileges.

headline: Seeking a spot for a memorial
abstract: While New York City plans to create a large-scale memorial at the site of the world trade center, the desire to pay tribute to victims is no less strong in the township of Lower Makefield. Eight families lost relatives, making  Lower Makefield the most severely affected community in the Philadelphia area. Township supervisors decided to build a memorial almost immediately after September 11.

headline: Bush: Thousands of terrorists are poised to strike
abstract: President Bush called upon Congress to join him in a dual war on terrorism and the recession. Bush made clear that the swift victory in Afghanistan against al-Qaeda terrorists and their Taliban protectors is only the first front in a war that will be fought on other battlegrounds. The president, who was interrupted 77 times by applause, said nations that sponsor terrorism will face the consequences.

headline: Hempfield GOP chairman enters race for county party's top post
abstract: Dave Dumeyer, the Hempfield GOP chairman, has announced his candidacy for county party chairman.  Dumeyer will challenge incumbent Chet Beiler for the unpaid position.  Beiler has been chairman of the county's dominant political organization for the past two years.  Dumeyer is a Republican research staff member with the state House of Representatives in Harrisburg.

headline: Polls are threat in both races for governor
abstract: PA gubernatorial candidates Ed Rendell and Mike Fisher are entering the final days of the race and are battling against two opposite perspectives, dangers posed by polls and media expectations. Recent polls show that Rendell has a double digit lead over Fisher.

headline: Where's Catherine?
abstract: The two previous lieutenant governor's have at some point the power. Governor Robert P. Casey was recovering from a heart/liver transplant when Lt. Governor Mark Singel took over. Lt. Governor Mark Schweiker became Governor when Governor Ridge was appointed the Homeland Security Director. The frontrunner for becoming lieutenant governor is former Treasurer Catherine Baker Knoll.

headline: Incarceration in Florida exacerbates problems for aggressive, mentally ill boy, 17
abstract: A juvenile court judge ordered specialized mental health treatment in a locked facility for 17-year-old Michael Durkin after he was thrown out of an Erie County group home for hitting a staff member. The trouble is Pennsylvania has no such facility. Therefore, Durkin boarded a jet and headed for a psychiatric hospital in Florida panhandle, where his care will cost Allegheny County $265 per day.

headline: School districts reap a modest windfall
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker signed a budget yesterday that will give school districts a little extra money to work with in the coming school year.  Schweiker had proposed increasing the basic education subsidy by 1 percent, and school boards, which were required to approve their budgets by today, based their plans on that figure.  But state lawmakers working into the early hours yesterday negotiated a 3 percent increase in the basic education subsidy, to a $4.1 billion.

headline: Rockville Bridge marks 100th anniversary this spring
abstract: The Rockville Bridge will be 100 years old this year. In 1902, the bridge was built out of necessity. Two other bridges were there before, but the wooden and iron ones became outdated so the current one was built.

headline: Shuster backs county plan
abstract: Ambitious plans by a local developer to restore Bedford Springs Hotel received a major setback yesterday when U.S. Rep. Bill Shuster, R-Hollidaysburg, refused to endorse the proposal.  Instead, Shuster threw his support behind county officials and their decision to hire an Atlanta-based hotel development company to prepare preliminary designs for the $90 million restoration project.  A master-development contract between Stormont Hospitality of Atlanta and Bedford County Redevelopment Authority is expected to be in place by the end of June.

headline: Business lobby supports Nailor
abstract: State Rep. Jerry Nailor, R-88, has been endorsed by the political action committee of the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry.  Nailor faces Democrat Chris Adams in the November election.  Chamber PAC supports incumbent state legislators and other candidates who "back the Pennsylvania Chamber's legislative program, promote the tenets of the free enterprise system and pledge to make Pennsylvania a better place in which to do business."

headline: Herman to speak at fire banquet
abstract: Rep. Lynn B. Herman, R-77 of Philipsburg, will speak at Philipsburg's Hope Fire Co. banquet scheduled for 7 p.m. Saturday.  Rep. Herman will discuss legislation of interest to firefighters and review other developments in state government affecting the Philipsburg area.  Rep. Herman is chairman of the House of Local Government Committee.

headline: Pols uneasy about mayor hiring his wife
abstract: Having sought the advice of neither the city solicitor nor the State Ethics Commission about potential nepotism issues, Mayor Street may approve the appointment of his wife, Naomi Post, to the high-level city job of social services director as soon as next week. Street got a taste of the likely reaction yesterday, as he was peppered with questions from reporters, and one civic leader warned the appointment could violate the state ethics law.

headline: White House plotted GOP win
abstract: President George W. Bush and his administration threw themselves into helping Republicans gain full control of Congress. The President and his aides chose the candidates and the President himself became his party's main campaign asset.

headline: Lawmakers must ease nursing home job ban
abstract: The state should change the flaw in the Older Adults Protective Service Act. The Act prevents criminals from working at nursing homes, but does not allow a person who has long since reformed from being able to work at these homes.

headline: School districts rip budget figures
abstract: Already sagging under the weight of recession, Lehigh valley taxpayers got more bad economic news from the state capital that they might have to shoulder higher school taxes next year. The state's Basic Education Subsidy, which averaged a 2 to 4 percent increase over the last decade, will go up by only 1 percent in he proposed 2002-3 budget. State Budget Secretary Robert Bittenbender conceded that the state subsidy, which does not match the rate of inflation, would force some districts to raise taxes.

headline: Rooney unhurt in emergency plane landing
abstract: Pittsburgh Steelers President Dan Rooney escaped injury Wednesday night when the small airplane he was piloting made an emergency belly landing at Allegheny County Airport in West Mifflin.  Rooney was flying alone when the landing gear on his Beech Bonanza aircraft failed to deploy, and he was forced to land the craft on its belly in a grassy area off an airport runaway at 8:45 p.m., said JoAnn Jenny of the Allegheny County Airport Authority.  The plane did not catch fire.

headline: Shweiker Oks time limits on zoning decisions
abstract: Governor Mark Schweiker signed a new state law Friday that gives developers more of an advantage in some legal proceedings over local zoning issues. Schweiker acted after getting appeals during the past week from business groups to sign the bill and counter-appeals from local officials in his native Bucks County to veto the bill. The law contains provisions supported by builders and developers that set timetables for local officials to act on development proposals rather than let cases go for months or even years without a decision.

headline: Cabinet office would combing 170,000 workers from 8 agencies
abstract: President Bush has proposed one of the most sweeping reorganizations of the federal government in decades. He will create a Cabinet-level Department of Homeland Security that will likely be headed by former Pennsylvania Governor Tom Ridge.  Bush has asked Congress to join in creating a single permanent department, with an overriding and urgent mission: securing Americans homeland and protecting the American people.

headline: Hershey Foods sale debate could raise Fisher's profile
abstract: Mike Fisher's days and nights were already crammed with activities related to his job as state attorney general and his campaign for governor when news broke that the venerable Hershey Foods Corp. was up for sale.  Since then, Fisher, as the state's top law enforcement officer, has been hip deep in the very prickly issue of corporate reality versus hometown jobs, with the likelihood that his performance will reflect on his image with voters.  Saying he feared the loss of jobs and tax base if a faraway corporation took over, Fisher first asked the trustees who own the controlling stake in the candymaker to reconsider.  Then, when he was rebuffed, Fisher involved the courts in an effort to scare off potential suitors and impede a sale.

headline: Poor turnout for debate not a good harbinger
abstract: Republican candidate for the 176th District Mario Scavello and Democratic candidate Joe Battisto debated at East Stroudsburg University. There were few people who turned out for the debate. Both political sides worry about a low voter turnout.

headline: Why can't Pa. reduce legislature?
abstract: The state is reducing the size of its legislature by one-fourth, trimming 25 seats in the state House and 12 in the Senate.  Why is this so noteworthy? Because it doesn't happen every decade, and because it couldn't happen without legislative approval.  The lawmakers had to agree to slit their own throats. Not a surprisingly, it wasn't easy to get them to do so.  It took a big pay raise (the carrot) and a massive scandal in their own ranks (the stick) to get their attention.  And in the years since the voters ratified the measure, back in 1994, various senators and representatives have been trying to undo it.

headline: Lawmakers target nursing home refunds
abstract: State lawmakers are looking into a piece of legislation which would prohibit nursing homes from charging more than necessary after a resident dies. The legislation is in response after a family member tried to collect the security deposit after her aunt died. The nursing home refused because she did not give proper notice.

headline: School drug testing ignored
abstract: Although the U.S. Supreme Court has given school districts the go-ahead to test some students for illegal drug use, most districts are saying no to drug testing for now.  One exception is the Seneca Valley School District in Butler County, which tests student athletes and students who drive to school.  Advocates of drug testing said they believe it can reduce drug use, both by identifying students who use drugs and discouraging others from starting.

headline: Rumbling trash rigs take toll on signs, intersections
abstract: To try to eliminate some of the truck traffic in Newville, the local landfill has devised a route from Interstate 81 onto the north-south road that makes trucks turn onto other roads before they reach the borough. If truck does not follow this route and is caught by Newville police, the landfill takes action. A similar restriction applies on the east-west road for tractor trailers. If they are found three times on that route, they are banned from dumping at the landfill again.

headline: Some richer, some poorer
abstract: Most of Philadelphia's suburbs grew even richer than the rest of Pennsylvania during the 1990s but the inflation-adjusted household income dropped almost 4 percent.  Some nearby older suburbs were also caught in the downdraft, making it a disappointing decade for towns that are home to half of the region's 3.85 million people. Counting just the suburbs, however, 7 out of every 10 people lived in towns with rising incomes, according to new census figures released yesterday.

headline: Caltagirone accused of removing rival's signs. The campaign manager of the state legislator's opponent is cited for stapling a campaign advertisement to a utility pole
abstract: Theft and criminal mischief charges were filed against PA State Representative Thomas R. Caltagirone alleging he was caught on videotape tearing down campaign signs of his opponent, Francis Acosta.

headline: Hibernians honor a favorite son
abstract: When state Rep. Tom Corrigan received an award last week from the Ancient Order of Hibernians' national leader, he took a bow for 40-years of service to his community, his friends said.  The award honors Corrigan's participation in the state Legislature's Irish Caucus and his work in promoting Irish culture in Bucks County.  Corrigan, D-140, who's running unopposed this fall, is getting ready to start his ninth term.

headline: Possible plot to kill Florida Gov. Jeb Bush under investigation
abstract: The Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the FBI are investigating a possible plot to kill Gov. Jeb Bush with a truck bomb in Tallahassee, law enforcement officials confirmed Thursday. The story about the alleged plot came from a confidential informant, jailed in Broward County, who said at least four men with Arab names were trying to contact someone to drive a truckload of explosives to Tallahassee today and blow up the governor.

headline: why don’t city blacks hold high political office?
abstract: Fifty five percent of the population is Harrisburg are African-Americans who continue to be the Democratic party's most reliable voters. The city has never been represented by a black mayor which may be due to low voter turnouts, party politics, and difficulty in finding influential candidates.

headline: Legislators seek health care cure
abstract: Officials warn that the quality of medical care is threatened even though there has not been a mass exodus of physicians to other states like that seen in eastern portions of Pennsylvania.  United States Congressman John Peterson, State Senator Joe Scarnati and State Representatives Sam Smith and Dan Surra recently met with leaders and hospital administrators in Dubois to see how the region is faring in light of soaring medical malpractice insurance rates and declining reimbursements for services.

headline: School issue dogs Reed
abstract: Mayor Stephen R. Reed's unprecedented sixth term was supposed to be the time when he finally fixed the Harrisburg School District, the sharpest and deepest thorn in the city's side, completing Harrisburg's long-gestating revival. Problem is, even a Reed foretold great things for the 7600-pupil school system in his inaugural address, he acknowledged his hands could be tied if the courts give back control of the district to the elected school board.

headline: Safe 80 seeks federal grant for I-80 study
abstract: The safe 80 Task Force continues its search for deep pockets to fund a $5 million feasibility study that would examine a 25-mile stretch of Interstate 80. State Rep. Kelly Lewis (R-189) said the latest attempt to acquire the financing has come in form of an appropriations request to U.S. Sen. Rick Santorum. In other safe 80 news, a $500,000 congestion grant was awarded last December, which covers Route 611 from the Delaware Water Gap to Bartonsville.

headline: State budget funds appropriated for rural communities
abstract: Due to the efforts of state Rep. Dan Surra, D-Elk/Clearfield, Pennsylvania's 2002-03 General Fund budget contains funding for programs important to rural Pennsylvania.  Amendments added by Surra early in the budget debate remained in the version finalized in the early morning hours last Saturday.  The budget restores a $640,000 appropriation to the Department of Community and Economic Development for local development districts, including the North Central Pennsylvania Regional Planning and Development Commission.

headline: Campaign 2002: Rendell, Casey eye slow Pa. growth
abstract: Both Democratic candidates for the gubernatorial election, Bob Casey Jr. and Ed Rendell, agree that Pennsylvania is lagging on the pace of economic growth. They both recognize that the next governor's most important job is to implement policies that lead to more and better jobs.

headline: His family name forces Casey to walk a tightrope
abstract: Bob Casey Jr. spoke at a rally about restoring old-time Democratic values and fighting for the working families. The Casey family is popular in Pennsylvania politics. 7 percent of those who plan to vote for Casey are doing so because the late Governor Robert P. Casey Sr.

headline: Post-debate fireworks in race for No. 2 post
abstract: The lieutenant governor candidates' debate yesterday was a cordial, question-and-answer-style forum - until the cameras stopped rolling.  During the forum, Democrat Ed Rendell's running mate, Catherine Baker Knoll, fended off a panelist's question about a 1994 scandal involving a campaign aide during her tenure as state treasurer. Knoll said she saw no reason for her to accept responsibility for a scandal involving someone who was not a state employee.

headline: WHY IT'S WRONG, WRONG, WRONG
abstract: Mark Alan Hughes, a teacher in Penn's Fox Leadership Program, believes that Mayor Street's wife, Naomi Post, should not be considered for a job as the head of social services in Philadelphia. In the murky world of Philadelphia legal technicalities, it is permanently unclear whether the mayor would be breaking a law to appoint his wife. Various fig leaves have been held up to cover the Street-Post intimacy - but the legal arguments for and against the hire don't matter.

headline: Local hospitals seeking Rx for medical errors
abstract: A study conducted by the federal Institute of Medicine shows that medical errors account for between 44,000 and 98,000 deaths per year nationwide. The state legislature approved legislation which will create a patient safety board to reduce medical mistakes.

headline: School panel may revel reform plan
abstract: The School Reform Commission is the new governing body for Philadelphia School District. They have unveiled a plan to allow parents and students more input in the reform process. The commission will create 10 education reform committees made up of parents, students, staff, and community members.

headline: Safe 80 Task Force hopes its message sticks
abstract: The Safe 80 Task Force stepped up its public relations campaign Thursday with the introduction of a new bumper sticker encouraging motorists to drive safely.  Approximately 10,000 bumper stickers will be distributed with the message of zero tolerance for speeding, unsafe driving, tailgating and drunken driving.  Task force chairman state Rep. Kelly Lewis, R-189, said the cost of producing the bumper stickers was paid by private citizens and private companies.  He said none of the money came from taxpayers.

headline: Street says blight bill will lead to 'world-class neighborhoods'
abstract: Mayor Street sign his $295 million anti-blight bill. The Mayor is now allowed to issue bonds to clear tracts of land for future development.

headline: Campaign a war of words--and money
abstract: Congressmen John Murtha and Frank Mascara are battling each other over the newly drawn 12th Congressional District. Murtha claims to have brought in $96 million worth of federal grants which created 1002 jobs. Mascara says he has brought $379.3 million in grants.

headline: Hoeffel denies charge he used tax money for political fliers
abstract: To her patients, Republican congressional candidate Melissa Brown is know as a doctor of ophthalmology.  Her opponent in the November election, U.S. Rep. Joe Hoeffel, says Brown's political specialization is best described as "doctor of distortion."  At a news conference Monday, Hoeffel, D-13th, said Brown's criticisms of him are the most inaccurate portrayal of his record in a political career that has spanned races for the state Legislature, the Montgomery County Commissioners and 10 Republican opponents.  Until Monday, Hoeffel has responded piecemeal to what he's called unfounded attacks by Brown.

headline: Powell may get his own day
abstract: With Secretary of State Colin Powell to get this year's Philadelphia Liberty Medal on July 4, Rep. Michael Horsey has proposed a resolution designating that date as Colin Powell Day in Pennsylvania. Powell was the first black chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and is the first black secretary of state.

headline: Will 'Fish' pull a 'Torch'
abstract: A Fox Philadelphia keystone poll showed on possible governor candidate in the next election show that acting Governor Mark Schweiker would lead Ed Rendell and Mike Fisher. Philadelphia Inquirer columnist Gar Joseph says that Republicans might need to find new candidates.

headline: Malpractice bill passes state House
abstract: In an effort to help lower skyrocketing malpractice premiums for doctors, the state House approved a controversial bill that would allow doctors to negotiate a cap on damages with their patients before the treat them. The bill, which passed the House 164-32, now moves to the Senate for consideration. The House squashed two amendments offered by democrats to remove the language about the cap from the bill and refer it back to the judiciary committee.

headline: School reform panel recommends scaling back management plan
abstract: The School Reform Commission backed off a plan that would privatize of 42 low-performing public schools in Philadelphia. Teachers and students spoke out against privatization which could mean teachers and principals would be out of a job. Seven outside entities will operate the 42 low performers.

headline: Santorum to Put Additional Money on 'List of Priorities'
abstract: Santorum said some $25 billion is available through the federal Highway Trust Fund for a number of transportation projects.  However, he warned Lycoming County officials and others gathered for his visit to Williamsport Tuesday morning that the battle for transportation money is highly competitive.  He reminded everyone that U.S. Rep. John Peterson , R-Titusville, whose congressional district touches on much of the local area, serves on the Appropriations Committee, which doles out vital funding for projects.

headline: Task force unveils sweeping plans for downtown Pittsburgh
abstract: A task force wants to do a $363 million redevelopment plan for ailing downtown Pittsburgh. The plan includes a marketplace, high-end hotel, apartments and condos, and room for parking and retail stores. The task forces hopes to attract new businesses while retaining historic structures.

headline: Campaign condemning bill doesn't hold water
abstract: Supporters of legislation usually tout what a bill will do in order to make the case for passage.  But in the case of a bill to set state standards for the drilling of water wells, many lawmakers who voted for it last fall are busy telling constituents what the bill won't do.  The lawmakers are trying to counter and anonymous disinformation campaign against the bill that has rolled across Pennsylvania's northern tier in recent months.

headline: Hoeffel finds himself in a nice spot
abstract: US Representative Joseph M. Hoeffel has fought hard for his seat in the US House of Representatives. The Republicans redrew the districts and had him going up against popular US Representative Robert Borski. Borski has decided to step down as Representative which has allowed Hoeffel to become the favorite for the District.

headline: Preparing to get elected
abstract: One is a Republican two-term state senator with a dozen years of legislative experience, but all of it in Harrisburg.  The other is the son of a former U.S. senator who has worked behind the scenes in the state and national Democratic Party for 25 years, but never held elective office.  But similarities or differences aside, both men - - Republican Jim Gerlach and Democrat Dan Wofford - - have roughly three months to convince voters that they are the best for the job of representing the newly created 6th Congressional District.

headline: Will Katz challenge again for the GOP nomination
abstract: Republican Sam Katz has stated that he has not yet made a decision about whether he will run for Philadelphia mayor in the next election. Katz previously ran for the position in 1999 and loss by a narrow margin.

headline: Malpractice bill please doctors
abstract: Some Indiana County physicians say they are generally pleased with the Pennsylvania House's passage of a bill to reform the medical-malpractice system. Supporters say the bill would help control the rising cost of malpractice insurance, make substantial improvements to the malpractice legal system and provide a mechanism for reducing the number of medical treatment mistakes that lead to law-suits. Mark Phenicie, the legislative counsel for the Pennsylvania Trial lawyers Association said that his group is pleased the state House has begun the debate on medical-malpractice reform but that he hopes the bill the House passed is changed.

headline: School shuts after mysterious rash infects more students
abstract: A Bucks County elementary school has been closed after dozens of students came down with a mysterious rash for the third straight school day. School officials initially speculated that the skin condition might have been caused by a reaction between chemicals in a carpet cleaning solution. The St. Luke Quakertown Hospital treated 54 students for the rash.

headline: Schweiker backs beltway project
abstract: Gov. Mark Schweiker Wednesday urged the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission to quickly begin construction of the Findlay Connector, part of the $900 million Southern Beltway project.  Schweiker recommended that the commission earmark the $175 million needed to finish the project.  The Findlay Connector, a roughly six mile four-lane highway that will stretch from Route 60 at Pittsburgh International Airport south to Route 22 in Robinson Township, Washington County, is currently in final design, which will be finished by the end of the year, Bill Capone, a spokesman of the Turnpike Commission, said.

headline: The opening Act
abstract: Hershey's $75 million Giant Center is facing tough competition from Philadelphia's First Union Center, Pittsburgh's Mellon Arena, and Penn State University's Bryce Jordan Center. The main tenant of the Hershey arena will be the Hershey Bears hockey team.

headline: Campaign finance bill due vote
abstract: A bill that would limit contributions and set up taxpayer-financed governor and lieutenant governor campaigns is scheduled for a vote in the state House. State Rep. Greg Vitali's bill would limit contributions to $2,500 per election and provide public financing of up to $7.8 million for governor candidates who voluntarily agree to spend no more than $12 million. Pennsylvania has no limits on contributions to state and local campaigns and all campaigns are funded by private contributions.

headline: Hoeffel slams Brown over flier
abstract: U.S. Congressman Joe Hoeffel has accused his opponent Melissa Brown, of playing racial fears in her bid to unseat him in the 13th congressional District.

headline: President Bush to Campaign for Fisher in Pennsylvania
abstract: President George W. Bush will visit the state to support Attorney General Mike Fisher's campaign for Governor.. Fisher says he is honored by Bush's endorsement.

headline: With bells on, Street reemerges
abstract: Philadelphia is suffering from major financial problems. Columnist Tom Ferrick Jr. writes to make fun of Philadelphia Mayor Street who attended a City Council meeting to discuss financial matters. Ferrick says the speech sounded more like a reelection campaign for Mayor Street had begun and less like a solution to the financial problems.

headline: Malpractice concerns far-flung. Large majorities in Pa. fear medical care's cost will rise while access shrinks, a survey found
abstract: A survey conducted by Princeton Survey Research Associates for the project on medical liability in Pennsylvania revealed that nearly 51% of 1,100 people and 58% of 600 small-business leaders say that the failure of state legislatures to pass laws reducing malpractice rates is a major reason for the rising cost of malpractice insurance.

headline: School study: Bigger budget doesn't bring better scores
abstract: Standard & Poor's report states that school districts must pay more attention to how they spend their funds. School districts will receive a small increase in funds, but that will not necessarily means better student achievement.

headline: Senate approves lowered drunken-driving limit
abstract: Pennsylvania State Senators have passed a bill that will lower the blood-alcohol content needed to be classified as legal drunk to 0.08. The previous level was 0.10.

headline: Voicemail threat won't stop her anti-sprawl fight
abstract: A township supervisor published criticisms of developers, state lawmakers, and county Republican leaders. She is leading an anti-sprawl movement. Her vocal opinion has caused her to have threats against her and her family.

headline: Campaign finance reform tops 8th District debate veteran Republican Greenwood called 'hypocrite' by Dem foe.
abstract: Democrat Timothy Reece has stated that U.S Representative James Greenwood accepted more than $30,000 in political contributions from executives in the health care industry, a business that Greenwood's house committee regulates

headline: Hoeffel-Brown race has hard edge. Dem incumbent, newcomer in 13th District trade jabs throughout the campaign
abstract: U.S Representative Joe Hoeffel and Republican Melissa Brown have been campaigning against each other for five months for 13th District election. The tone of the race is snippy, with both accusing each other of various political wrong doings..

headline: Presidential prerogatives, national security and industry
abstract: An introduction into the situation between former President Harry S. Truman and his seizure of US steel mills is given. The Truman situation is described as a precedent for President George W. Bush's possible war in Iraq. The constitutional situations are strikingly similar.

headline: With Mike & Ikes, a sweet comparison
abstract: At each seat on the dais at the Republican State Committee meeting lay a movie-concession-size box of Mike & Ike candies. The boxes of candy were placed in an attempt to make a subtle link between Attorney General Mike Fisher, the party's candidate for governor this year, and President Dwight D. Eisenhower.

headline: Malpractice insurance crisis temporarily averted
abstract: Physicians who feared they would be unable to practice medicine in the new year because of skyrocketing insurance premiums will continue to care for patients, at least temporarily, due to a series of stopgap measures intended to hold the line until the Legislature convenes. Some doctors in high-risk specialties whose malpractice liability insurance was set to run out have acquired temporary, and costly, last minute coverage. Governor Schweiker said that he would give state-insured doctors until April 30 to pay surcharges on their 2002 premiums.

headline: School taxes are on the increase
abstract: Most of the region's school districts will have to increase school taxes. School budget planners did appreciate the state Legislature's elimination of a five-fold increase in what districts were preparing to invest next school year for teacher pensions.

headline: SEPTA union's finances probed
abstract: A federal grand jury is conducting a review of the Transport Workers Union Local 234's finances dating back to 1996. Documents subpoenaed include charge receipts for a union American Express card; bank records for four union bank accounts; and all bookkeeping records, including expense vouchers. Local 234 is SEPTA's (Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority) largest union and were taken over by international union leaders last year.

headline: Will Convention center's problems stunt his growth?
abstract: State lawmakers says they are in no hurry to authorize a $232 million proposal to expand the Convention center before the summer begins. This comes as the Convention center is mangled in labor and management troubles.

headline: Campaign spending piles on the calories
abstract: Republican state Sen. Joe Conti, whose family used to own a popular Doylestown restaurant, frequently takes political contributors out to dinner, and that doesn't mean Burger King.  Conti's campaign committee spent $58,258 in the last 2 1/2 years on American Express credit card charges, according to financial reports filed with the state.  While the reports list the spending only as "expenses," Conti said the charges represent the tab for dozens of restaurant meals with potential campaign contributors.

headline: Hoeffel's win wasn’t easy
abstract: Democrat Joseph M. Hoeffel III was re-elected to win his third term in the U.S. House of Representatives. Hoeffel narrowly defeated Melissa Brown with 50.8% of the vote to Brown's 47.5%.

headline: Pretzel Logic
abstract: Auditor General Bob Casey Jr. is jeopardizing possible support for lieutenant governor by fellow Democrats if he does not choose state Senator Allen Kukvich as his running mate. Casey already has the support of the Democratic State Committee, but has waived off the committee in endorsing his running mate. Kukvich is sure to be chosen as Casey's running mate noting he has the backing of labor and state lawmakers and Democrats in both the Southeast and Northeast.

headline: With no apologies, Casey relies on ads to get out his message
abstract: Robert P. Casey Jr has ran a campaign for governor by showing many television commercials. He has attacked his opponent former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell. Some complain he should focus on the issues, but he makes no apologies for how he has run his $11 million campaign.

headline: Malpractice panel pick was sued in related case
abstract: Carolyn F. Scanlan, one of PA Governor Ed Rendell's insurance task force members, has been sued by the Insurance Department citing that she ignored signs of fiscal problems in PHICO.

headline: Schoolkids won't take tests? Pay 'em!
abstract: Ronnie Polaneczky, a columnist for the Philadelphia Daily News, suggests paying student in the Philadelphia school district to take the PSSA and SAT-9 tests. The PSSA and SAT-9 tests are standardized, mandatory tests given to select grades to track academic achievement. Schools with improved test results receive financial rewards from Harrisburg.

headline: Show on the road
abstract: State. Sen. Allen Kukovich has taken his show on the road in his quest for the Democrat nomination for lieutenant governor.  Kukovich last week hit nine counties in the eastern part of the state, where he racked up endorsements and raised money.  Kukovich has been campaigning in train stations, bus stops and at receptions.

headline: Will the levies break?
abstract: Larry Eichel, a guest writer for the Philadelphia Inquirer claims that Mayor Street has "sought to develop a plan to eliminate blight and encourage neighborhood transformation. Working with the governor, he's hammered out a city-state partnership intended to bring stability and solvency to the public schools. Eichel believes Street's views on city government as "more in terms of the good it can do through services delivered than of damage through taxes imposed."

headline: Campaigns pull out the stops - and the votes
abstract: The get-out-the-vote push for Bob Casey Jr.'s campaign included five Scranton teenagers waving handmade signs at a busy Wilkes-Barre intersection.  At the same time in Hazleton, Luzerne County Controller Steve Flood was on a three-county sweep of polling places.  Flood  had managed Ed Rendell's gubernatorial campaign in Luzerne, Lackawanna and Wyoming counties.  He said getting Democrats to the polls was crucial.  Flood said 200 to 300 Rendell volunteers also phoned voters throughout the day.

headline: Holden blasts Gekas
abstract: U.S. Representative Timothy Holden attacked his opponent U.S. Representative George Gekas for mailing brochures that misrepresented Holden's record on senior citizens issues. Gekas supported a pharmaceutical plan and said Holden voted against senior citizens four times. Holden disputes the information and is accusing Gekas of using a nasty tone during his campaign.

headline: Primary could change power balance
abstract: Janet Reno's battle for the Democratic nomination for Florida governor was too close to call Wednesday, a day after problems with the state's new election system led to delayed votes and confusion.  New Hampshire U.S. Sen. Bob Smith lost his GOP primary and Elizabeth Dole won easily in North Carolina's Republican Senate primary.  Voters in 12 states on Tuesday determined fall lineups for six open governor's offices, three of the most competitive Senate seats and a few House seats that could influence control of Congress and the shape of the remainder of President Bush's administration.

headline: With primary opponent out, Fisher runs like it's the fall
abstract: Republican Mike Fisher campaigned to an industrial park a pro-business message and criticized his Democratic opponents. He has no Republican opponents so he is starting to campaign like it was the fall.

headline: Malpractice reform bills wins passage
abstract: A package bill was approved in the state Senate and House. The package hopes to stabilize the malpractice market and lower insurance costs. It would create an 11 member authority which would review reports of serious medical errors and make recommendations for improvements.

headline: Schools' $75M just 'plaster'
abstract: Columnist John Baer write on the state's aid to Philadelphia public schools in the amount of $75 million. Baer says the money will simply fix holes in the walls and not fix the problem in schools. State Senator Vince Fumo agrees.

headline: State expands rural transit program
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation has begun to institute a public transportation program that will transport riders with disabilities in rural parts of the state. It will include an expansion into Dauphin, Lancaster, Lycoming, Snyder, and Union counties.

headline: A baby step on alcohol
abstract: The PA House and Senate have proposed bills to allow a two-year pilot program which would allow 10% of PA liquor stores to be open in Sundays. The Patriot News says that PA lawmakers are making progress and should encourage the alcohol industry to be an adult experience and not be monopolistic.

headline: Can split congress sidestep gridlock? Analyst say lawmakers may make gains on some bills despite discord
abstract: The U.S. Congress will remain divided equally between Democrats and Republicans, a recipe for gridlock on big issues such as tax cuts and social security. Hopeful officials fear voter backlash in 2004 which already has White House officials and Democratic moderates envisioning modest successes on health care, energy, and welfare legislation.

headline: Holden camp rips GOP  on mailer, TV spot
abstract: Democrats supporting Representative Tim Holden have accused Pennsylvania Republicans of waging a "sleazy" congressional campaign for US Representative George Gekas. A mailing funded by the state GOP claims Holden "consistently voted to force senior citizens" to choose between food and medicine for which republicans offered no apologies.

headline: Primary set for May 21
abstract: York County's director of elections and voter registration John Scott was relieved the May 21st primary will go on as planned. Scott had all preparations on schedule for May 21st. Keeping the date will save the county at least $100,000.

headline: Wofford asks Gerlach to pull 'dishonest' ad
abstract: U.S 6th district candidate Dan Wofford has publicly asked his opponent, U.S. Congressman Jim Gerlach, to withdraw one of his campaign ads. Wofford calls the ad desperate and dishonest. Gerlach is unapologetic about the commercial which claims Wofford "tried to profit from high costs of prescriptions through thousands of dollars in drug company stocks".

headline: Malpractice reform passes House
abstract: Lawmakers have responded a crisis in the Pennsylvania insurance market by passing legislation that would alter Pennsylvania laws governing who's forced to pay damages in lawsuits involving medical errors, faulty products and drunken driving.  The measure, which goes to the Senate for consideration, seeks to limit practice of targeting the richest party in a civil lawsuit for payments out of proportion to that party's share of the blame for a death or serious injury.

headline: Schools list consultant needs
abstract: The state-controlled Philadelphia School District yesterday invited all interested parties to compete for the job of providing a mountain of consulting services, while making clear that it prefers to hire one company. In a detailed request for qualifications, the School Reform Commission described pages of services needed to improve the district's central administration. The qualifications range from the recruitment of a new district chief executive officer to the evaluation of food service.

headline: Sources: SEPTA treasurer to be named new GM
abstract: Faye Moore, SEPTA's treasurer and chief financial officer, is to be named general manager of the transit agency. Moore, a certified public accountant, would be the first woman and the first African-American to run SEPTA. Moore is credited with helping to keep SEPTA operating within budget just about every year since she was hired in 1995.

headline: After 'Miracle', new lives, mixed emotions
abstract: The site where September 11 terrorists crashed Flight 93 and the hole where nine men emerged alive from a flooded coal mine have become tourists spots in Somerset. The sites have been attracting a number of tourists and the media.

headline: Candidate backs theater, urban projects state Senator hopefuls see Easton as key spot in 24th district
abstract: Pennsylvania State Senate candidate Rob Wonderling is facing James Maza in the 24th district election. Wonderling said he will work to secure funding for urban revitalizing projects in the district's cities. Both candidates are set to convince voters of Easton, the only city in the redrawn 24th senate district, that they will represent Easton and its surrounding communities well in Harrisburg.

headline: Holden files petitions to run in new territory
abstract: Monday morning brought a long line of candidates waiting to submit their nominating petitions for the May primary ballot. US Representative Tim Holden waited as well to turn in his petition with 1000 signatures which he collected himself.

headline: Profiles
abstract: Representing Pennsylvania's 84th district is the simple, yet seemingly complete gentleman Brett Feese, who has served his constituents for four consecutive terms.  The story of this man begins as a child in Montoursville where he enjoyed athletics, predominately football and basketball during high school.  As a child, Brett accompanied his father, a court stenographer, to many local cases where he became inspired by courtroom drama.

headline: Wonderling, Boscola, Dent win
abstract: Rob Wonderling has won the election for the 24th PA district seat by defeating Democrat Jim Maza by a 45% - 55% margin. Democrat Lisa Boscola won re-election to the 18th PA State Senate District. Republican incumbent Charles Dent won re-election in the 16th PA Senate District, according to unofficial results.

headline: Malpractice reprieve short-lived
abstract: Doctors are urging Harrisburg to act before their insurance policies lapse again or the big premiums come due. On January 1, the nine orthopedic surgeons of Willow Grove's Orthopedic Specialty Center were going to be without malpractice insurance. This would effectively close Abington Memorial Hospital's trauma center, as nine of the center's 10 orthopedic surgeons come from this one practice.

headline: Schools losing out on expected $49M
abstract: State House Majority Leader John Perzel wants to take $45 million from the Philadelphia Parking Authority to help pay for the financially troubled Philadelphia school district. The state Supreme Court has halted the action of Perzel's takeover bill.

headline: State lawmakers at crossroads over Flight 93 memorial highway
abstract: State Representative Keith McCall introduced legislation to have Route 93 to be named Flight 93 Remembrance Highway, but state Representative Bob Bastian wants to have a highway in Somerset County to be named the Flight 93 Remembrance Highway. Somerset County is the located of the crash.

headline: At least one Pa. snack-maker is in touch with community
abstract: For nearly a century two Pennsylvania products, Tastykakes and Hershey bars, have been icons of pride- as well as business success - in our community.  But as the Tasty Baking Co. is reinforcing its place in Pennsylvania, the charitable trust running Hershey Foods Corp. is doing exactly the opposite.  Meanwhile, over the shocked protests of central Pennsylvania residents, the Hershey Trust has placed Milton Hershey's beloved chocolate company on the auction block.

headline: Candidate requests debates
abstract: David Bahr, one of three Republican candidates for the 9th Congressional District seat held by Rep. Bill Shuster, has called for a series of debates with opponents.  While contender David Keller said he thinks it's a great idea, the campaign manager for Shuster said they haven't decided.  Bahr, a U.S. Air Force veteran and retired federal executive who lives in Greene Township, said the debates are necessary.

headline: Holden to challenge Gekas in redrawn 17th District
abstract: Representative Tim Holden plans to challenge Republican representative George Gekas in his newly redrawn 17th district in central Pennsylvania.  Holden, 41, is a Democrat from Schuykill County who is serving his fifth term while Gekas, 71, is a Republican serving his 10th term.  Holden was thrown into Gekas' district by a congressional redistricting plan crafted by Republicans who control the State Senate.

headline: Property tax issue taxing incumbent Mario Scavello in 176th state house race. His opponent, Gratz Washenik, has made levy focus of the race.
abstract: PA State Representative Mario Scavello is trying to win a full term in the State House by touting his ability to bring money to Monroe County. His Democratic challenger Gratz Washenik has placed taxes at the center of the election campaign. Both are running for 176th seat.

headline: Worker shortage predicted for city
abstract: The problem, analysts say, is the sum of several factors.  The region's population is aging and shrinking, its students aren't adequately prepared to work in the most-in-demand fields and employers in those fields fear they won't be able to sustain themselves without a skilled and plentiful workforce.  The worker shortage in certain occupations is so severe that some companies are looking outside of the regionand in some cases, outside of the country.

headline: Malpractice task force has 1 month
abstract: PA Governor-Elect Ed Rendell's medical malpractice insurance task force met in Philadelphia but did not have anything substantial to report on. The task force will report on their overall findings in less than a month to deliver recommendations about malpractice insurance reform.

headline: Schools start year under state control
abstract: The state government took control of the city school district on Dec 21, the seventh-largest in the nation, after four months of seesaw negotiations between city and state officials.  In the largest and boldest experiment in the history of urban public education, the 200,000 Philadelphia students aren't expected to see any immediate differences. The School Reform Commission will have the authority to approve partnerships with community groups or politicians who will team up with private management companies like Edison Schools, Inc.

headline: State Senate: Katlynn's Law Introduced
abstract: State Senator Jay Costa Jr has introduced a bill that would established a zero-tolerance drunk driving standard for school bus/van drivers. The bill is known as Katelynn's law in honor of an 8 year old girl who was injured by a drunk school van driver.

headline: Attempting to sell Hershey cost the firm $17.3million.
abstract: Hershey Foods Corporation has spent $17.3 million on the auction process that ended when its controlling shareholder decided not to sell the company. Despite those expenses and a 2.3% decline in sales. The third-quarter profit rose to 1.9% because of cost-cutting and the company's focus on its most profitable brands.

headline: Candidates address hot topics
abstract: The candidates for the 157th State House District gave Phoenixville Area Chamber of Commerce members a preview of some of the hot-button issues that will surface in their campaigns in the next two months.  While voter apathy numbers are usually high in the area, it appears this race has at least spurred some interest.  Phoenixville Borough Councilman Anthony DiGirolomo (D-Middle) and State Rep. Carole Rubley (R-157) shared their views with the largest crowd to ever attend the breakfast, which had to be moved to the larger banquet room in Columbia Station.

headline: Holden tossing hat in Gekas' ring
abstract: Setting the stage for a competitive congressional battle in central Pennsylvania U.S. Rep. Tim Holden, D-6th, will announce his intent to challenge U.S. Rep. George W. Gekas, R-17th. State lawmakers in Harrisburg adopted a congressional map forcing Holden and Gekas, both popular incumbents, into the same political subdivision. The new 17th District, created as part of the congressional reappointment, favors Gekas heavily.

headline: Punxsutawney to predict Super Bowl outcome
abstract: The Punxsutawney Groundhog Club's Inner Circle believes that Punxsutawney Phil will not only predict the weather this year, but will also predict the if the Steelers will win the Super Bowl.

headline: Write-in challenges Representative Lewis
abstract: Hamilton Township Democrat Liz LaBar will challenge PA State Representative Kelly Lewis for the 189th house district seat. LaBar, who operates a senior citizen care service, has criticized Lewis for failing on his promises to help the elderly in the state, especially where it concerns school property taxes.

headline: Medical aid plan changes thwarted
abstract: The Earnests and many other Pennsylvanian parents who have children with severe disabilities no longer have to worry about finding a way to pay a large portion of their child's medical care.  State lawmakers forestalled a Schweiker administration budget proposal that would have rendered some children ineligible for state medical assistance based on their parent's income.  Under the plan, a family of four with an annual income of $100,000 would have been ineligible for the state aid.

headline: Schools to require vaccines
abstract: On Sept. 1, Pennsylvania becomes one of more than 30 states that require school children to be immunized against chickenpox.  All children entering kindergarten, first grade or seventh grade must have immunization or proof they've already had chickenpox.  Another new law requires students attending colleges or universities in Pennsylvania who live in dormitories to be immunized against meningitis.

headline: State to use Web to market properties near airports
abstract: The state of PA is using the internet to help attract businesses to PA. The Airport Properties Development can now be accessed through the PA Department of Transportation.

headline: Bankruptcy judge approves sale of LTV steel operations
abstract: A court approved WL Ross  & Company's bit to buy LTV's steel operations. WL Ross will assume environmental costs and liabilities. LTV previous sought bankruptcy.

headline: Candidates air views on trash
abstract: As the year pass, the flow of out-of-state trash into Pennsylvania keeps increasing and Congress keeps refusing to allow states to impose limits.  Republican congressional candidate Lou Barletta says it's partly the fault of incumbent U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski, the Democrat whose job Mr. Barletta is seeking.  Mr. Kanjorski says he's tried, but the Republican-controlled Congress repeatedly refused to let bills he's co-sponsoring come up for a vote.

headline: Holly, Ed to marry
abstract: PA Lobbyist Holly Kinser will marry Ed Linsley. They got engaged at Swann Foundation in Logan Circle.

headline: Q&A with Pennsylvania's Homeland Security Director Earl Freilino
abstract: Capitol Wire.com has interviewed the state's Homeland Security Director Early Freilino. He describes his job description as well as what the state Homeland Security Department does.

headline: York mayor endorses Casey for governor
abstract: Former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell can't claim all of Pennsylvania's mayoral endorsements in his bid for governor, through his campaign said he has so far received at least 60.  York's Mayor John Brenner, who was elected last year, recently threw his support behind Casey, citing the auditor general's conservative fiscal philosophy as his reason.

headline: Medical experts dispute Mezvinsky defense
abstract: The government dispute former congressman Edward Mezvinsky's claim of mental-health diseases for his trial. Experts were brought in to go against his claim of bipolar disorder.

headline: Schools: Must reopen budgets
abstract: After months of hand wringing and number crunching, local school districts have something they had not planned for- more money.  The state budget signed into law by Gov. Mark Schweiker over the weekend calls for an increase of up to 3 percent, instead of the expected 1 percent, in basic education subsidies.  District officials now have to decide how to use the money and what changes can be made to their budgets.

headline: State 'visibly intoxicated' law test bars
abstract: The State Police Liquor Control Enforcement is looking into a tavern that may have served alcohol to a Sellersville man who was visibly intoxicated. The man then crashed his car and killed himself and three others. He was twice the legal driving limit and had marijuana in his system.

headline: Battle for Hershey Foods Corp. not over
abstract: Talk of a sale has been swept dramatically off the table by the trustees who control Hershey Foods Corp., and the mess remains following the 55 days in which it was publicly known they were seeking bids on the candy maker.  Besides petitions that are still circulating in the 13,000-population Hershey calling for the trustees to be removed, the Hershey Trust Co. faces a hostile executive board at the nation's largest candy maker.  In addition, the state attorney general's office and Legislature are still drafting what they hope will be a state law to prevent the trust from selling its controlling stake in Hershey Foods without court approval.  There's also the wildcard possibility of a shareholders' lawsuit.

headline: Candidates courting Erie's fickle voters
abstract: Democratic candidate Ian Murray will face State Senator Jane Earll in Pennsylvania Governor's race. Both democrats and republicans see Erie's link to the next governor as crucial to the city's future.

headline: Holman criticizes Goodman
abstract: Clyde C. Holman, GOP candidate for the 123rd district addressed a group of supporters at Middleport American Legion. He criticized his opponent Neal P. Goodman for going to the courts to extend the tax increase as Mahanoy city councilman in 1993.

headline: Quote worthy
abstract: State Senator Stephen MacNett is quoted on the intention to spend more of the Rainy Day fun then proposed in Governor Schweiker's budget.

headline: Young GOP taps Enola resident
abstract: Nate Silcox, an Enola resident, has been elected executive director of the PA Young Republicans. He is the legislative assistant to State Senator Bob Robbins.

headline: Medical insurance reform OK'd
abstract: The state legislature passed a medical malpractice reform bill. Some believe the bill will help doctors in Pennsylvania reduce their insurance premiums by 15 to 20 percent. Still some believe it will not solve the problem.

headline: Schweiker details early-education plan
abstract: A report released by PA Governor Mark Schweiker's appointed task force of child care and education experts has made 14 recommendations including,  early-education planning, dropping the compulsory school attendance age from 8 to 6, instituting full-day kindergarten, and making preschool available for parents on a voluntary basis. The plan has won strong praise from law enforcement officials.

headline: State's road salt supply runnet over
abstract: Nick Martino, Philadelphia's County manager of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, said he is praying for snow because he has a surplus of salt and no place to put it. PennDOT already has 116,256 tons of salt in 36 storage depots. The amount of salt is enough to handle three average winters in the five county region.

headline: Blue laws and green beer
abstract: The local-tavern industry does not plan to open on St. Patrick's Day which falls on a Sunday. State liquor law's prevent taverns from doing business on Sundays which is a reminder of the Blue Laws. The Blue Laws prevented most commerce from occurring on Sundays.

headline: Candidates differ on property tax solution
abstract: U.S. Representative Susan Lughlin, is running against Republican Ron Eggert to keep her PA 16th legislative district. Both the candidates differ on a property tax solution.

headline: Homeland
abstract: President George W. Bush has been able to get the U.S. Congress to approve the establishment of the Federal Department of Homeland Security. The Patriot News says the new department will have a difficult time getting agencies incorporated into it, but if done properly, can be a vital agency for the country.

headline: Race in the 148th features two
abstract: Two Lower Merion residents are vying for the Democratic nomination for the 148th legislative district. The winner will go against unchallenged Republican Melissa Murphy Weber. The incumbent decided to not run again.

headline: Zappala lobbyist hits Harrisburg
abstract: District Attorney Stephen A. Zappala Jr. is a possible candidate for the state Attorney General. He has hired a former congressional aide to be a lobbyist for the Allegheny County District Attorney's Office. Some believe the lobbyist was hired to promote Zappala, but Zappala claims he has no interest in running for a higher position.

headline: Medical malpractice insurance reform: Yes
abstract: Malpractice insurance has skyrocketed by 40 percent this previous year. This could affect the quality of health care in Pennsylvania. Longer waits to see specialty doctors and elimination of high risk surgeries are some of the negatives attached to the higher insurance.

headline: Schweiker visits school 'organized for learning'
abstract: Philadelphia's first Community Education Partners school has 40 percent of the students on probation. The school, however, is extremely safe and is organized for learning. CEP schools believe in second chances.

headline: Take 581 instead of the Turnpike
abstract: When I first saw the newly completed Turnpike Administration building in Highspire, its architectural features brought to mind an airport control tower, which seemed somewhat unusual for its function.  Little did I realize that in the future it would enable the planning staff of the Commission a bird's-eye view of the Friday night eastbound traffic jam created by the total inadequacy of the Exit 19 facility.

headline: Bush's exclusion of legacy costs could kill US Steel mega merger
abstract: President Bush has increased tariffs on imported steel to 30 percent over the next three years in attempts to aid domestic steelmakers.
