abstract: Teresa Heinz Kerry, the Heinz Ketchup heiress whose husband John Kerry is running for President, is receiving speculative media attention regarding her role in the campaign. The answers to questions regarding the Heinz fortune, her passion for the progressive cause, and Teresa's ability to relate to the American middle-class will unfold in the next few months.

headline: Blood clots send Veon to hospital
abstract: PA Representative Mike Veon, the Democratic House minority whip, was hospitalized with a blood clot problem in his legs. Veon expects the issue to be resolved shortly so that he can return to the Capitol and vote on upcoming gambling, PACENET prescription drug program, and medical malpractice reform legislation.

headline: Budgeting For Schools A Struggle
abstract: The Carbondale Area School District will be receiving nearly $200,000 in a refund of overpayments for special education but still faces the prospect of taking out loans to cover expenses if the PA legislature and PA Governor Ed Rendell do not resolve budget differences soon.

headline: County battles for more funds for seniors
abstract: The Monroe County Area Agency on Aging faces the prospect of cutting services as they fail to secure the funding necessary to provide help for a growing population of elderly citizens in the Poconos. Monroe County Area Agency on Aging Executive Director Dorothy Kaufman has asked the PA Department of Aging to give special consideration to PA's fast-growing counties in 2003-04 budget allocations, citing the use of outdated US Census data from 1990 as a reason for the funding shortage.

headline: Kessler's new job
abstract: PA Governor Rendell named Alan Kessler, a long time fundraiser for him and Al Gore, as the Democratic Party's state finance chairman

headline: Budget crunch hurts programs
abstract: The PA budget dispute has harmed the human service providers in the mental health field who await word on how much funding they will receive from the state. Westmoreland County health centers have been operating with $1.2 million less in funding, forcing staff and service cutbacks.

headline: Business leaders faulting boards for low test scores
abstract: The Allegheny Conference on Community Development attributed their perceived failures of the PA schools to the respective school boards of each school district, faulting the elected members for poor test scores. The Conference graded elementary schools in Allegheny and surrounding counties.

headline: Cruel cuts in store for county
abstract: Budget cuts for the 2003-2004 fiscal year have caused the PA Department of Public Welfare to reduce aid given to several county agencies, such as the Lancaster County Drug & Alcohol Commission. Rick Kasnter, Drug & Alcohol Commission executive director with the aid of groups such as County Commissioners Association of PA are lobbying state legislators to restore social service funds or create a supplemental budget to fund the agencies.

headline: Lawmaker seeks to make all convention center workers become state employees
abstract: PA Representative Dwight Evans, D-Philadelphia, will introduce legislation to make convention center employees in Philadelphia employees of the state in order to end the dispute between labor organizations and the center's management board. The state took over the convention center in 2002 at the behest of PA House Speaker John Perzel, who has been unsuccessful in his efforts to negotiate a new labor deal.

headline: Budgetary injustice
abstract: Leslie Hurtig, assistant vice president for addictions services at the Philadelphia Health Management Corporation, opposes the planned budget cuts to drug and alcohol treatment programs. Not only will recovering addicts suffer, but children stand to suffer from cuts to residential treatment facilities.

headline: C-H hires teachers to ensure smaller class sizes…
abstract: The Chartiers-Houston School Board voted to hire additional teachers to have smaller classes for kindergarten through second grade, resulting in what Superintendent Charles Mahoney described as a "philosophical change." The board had delayed its decision on hopes that the state Legislature would pass a state budget on July 1. The board's decision is in line with PA Governor Ed Rendell's plan to permit smaller classes by more state funding to education.

headline: No more free rides
abstract: Harry Corbett, a senior citizen from East Liberty, writes regarding Port Authority's chief executive officer Paul Skoutelas proposed suspension of night and weekend bus service. Corbett suggests eliminating the policy which gives senior citizens free rides, and establishing a reduced-fare policy for senior citizens.

headline: Lawsuits against Teamsters, others over beating dismissed
abstract: A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit filed by Don Adams against the Teamsters, former Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, and others in connection to a beating he and his sister took from union members during a rally for President Clinton in 1998.  District Judge William H. Yohn Jr. said that Adams and his sister Theresa failed to prove the violation of their civil rights.

headline: By the numbers
abstract: According to the PA Department of Health, more than 84 percent of PA nurses were very or somewhat satisfied with their careers.  However, 45.6 percent said they plan to end their careers within the next 10 years, which could be problematic considering there are 10 percent less nurses in Pennsylvania than 10 years ago, bringing the total from 77.000 in 1993 to 69,000 in 2003.

headline: City schools budget to eat at surplus
abstract: Pittsburgh City Schools Superintendent John Thompson delivered a proposal for the 2004 budget which included an $8.5 million tax cut, a call to use part of the surplus the school's have accumulated, and for the city to close and consolidate schools to lower costs. The School Board has already approved the hiring of a consulting firm for the school closures, which were one of the key provisions Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy's Commission on Public Education recommended.

headline: No reason to delay action on PACE bill
abstract: The author argues for the PA Senate to pass a bill for additional prescription assistance for the elderly which the PA House of Representatives has already passed. The Senate is anticipated to approve the bill but they are waiting to see if the US government takes any action before the end of the year. However, everyone has already agreed that the PACE program should be expanded so the authors argue the bill should pass now to get needed assistance to PA's elderly.

headline: Left facing the music after voting to elect Ed Rendell
abstract: The author criticizes the early results of PA Governor Ed Rendell's administration as the state struggles to pass a budget and human service industries experience funding cuts.

headline: Chi-Chi's lawsuits withdrawn
abstract: Three lawsuits against Chi-Chi's restaurant were withdrawn as lawyers question whether to involve the suppliers of green onions that may have been at the source of the hepatitis A outbreak in Beaver County.

headline: Colleges may lose millions in state aid
abstract: The education spending bill negotiated by PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA House of Representatives stands to cost community colleges approximately $16.6 million in funding . Governor Rendell and company are seeking to cut spending but community colleges are seeking to have the funding reinstated, fearing they will have to cut services just as enrollment is rising.

headline: Prevent cuts to disabled
abstract: Walter Chezik of Bensalem asks fellow citizens to write to their local representatives to oppose PA Governor Ed Rendell's planned cuts to state funding for the mentally challenged and physically disabled. He suggests Rendell "walk in the shoes of the clients who...are on waiting lists to move to group homes or community-living arrangements."

headline: Legislators don't skimp on autos
abstract: The authors of this article condemn PA legislators for cutting state programs while maintaining an $850,000 budget for travel-related expenses, including the leasing of vehicles and the reimbursement for mileage. While the authors thank some local representatives for choosing the most economical option of using a state-owned vehicle, they also find that in general the legislature has proved over-indulgent in the use of taxpayer money for automobiles, especially in comparison to other states.

headline: Chi-Chi's seeks OK to pay off victims
abstract: Chi-Chi's restaurant is seeking permission in bankruptcy court to pay a $500,000 insurance deductible that would allow the chain, at the center of a hepatitis A outbreak that has killed 3, to free up to $51 million to pay claims. The PA Department of Health has confirmed 540 cases, who Chi-Chi's is seeking to reimburse for expenses and lost time but the reimbursement requires clearance due to Chi-Chi's status in US bankruptcy court.

headline: Danville eyeing switch to all-day kindergarten
abstract: Danville School District is examining the possibility of all-day kindergarten, preferring to make the switch for academic reasons but concerned over the financial implications. Danville may seek to receive additional state money as PA Governor Ed Rendell supports all-day kindergarten.

headline: Social service agencies say they're pinched by budget cuts
abstract: Fifteen social-service officials descended on Harrisburg in an effort to have $150 million in funding restored by PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA legislature. Debate is ongoing between Rendell and legislators over how much money to spend on educational programming, with restoration of some funding likely once a compromise can be reached. In the meantime, social service agencies are struggling to maintain services, taking advantage of what grants they can receive such as short-term funding from the PA Department of Public Welfare and county aid.

headline: Legislators look after themselves
abstract: Dennis Glembock of Maidencreek Township blasts Steven E. Fischer, business manager for the Brandywine School District, stating that he is in the norm for elected officials who talk about tax reform but only seem to increase their pensions. Glembock is "sick and angry that they do nothing," but reminds readers that motorcyclists no longer have to wear helmets. This is in response to a recently-passed piece of legislation.

headline: Childrens' asks state to restore funding
abstract: The Children's Hospital in Pittsburgh is urging PA Governor Ed Rendell to restore $6.7 million the hospital could lose in Medicaid funding. Statewide, cuts could lead to hospitals losing $89 million and, because of the loss of federal matching funds, nearly $250 million in all. The state is receiving $900 million in the next two years from the federal government, and Governor Rendell's office has said some of that is slated to be used for Medicaid funding.

headline: Cuts threaten library service
abstract: Libraries in Cambria, Somerset, and Bedford will be forced to cut hours and layoff workers, disrupting service to the community because of PA Governor Ed Rendell's budget plan, which cuts public library funding by 50 percent. Cambria County System Director Lyn Meek promised to voice opposition along with Library System Directors in other counties. Executive Director of the Pennsylvania Library Association Glen Miller said there is a chance to regain funds in Rendell's second budget proposal.

headline: Board could eye finances
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell named Joe Vignola as chair of a task force to examine Pittsburgh's municipal financial woes in December, and the task force is due to report their findings by Monday. Pittsburgh has a projected deficit of $60 million this year, and the PA General Assembly gets the final say on whether the city may institute Mayor Tom Murphy's proposed tax increases to pay off the debt. Vignola is head of the PA Intergovernmental Cooperative Authority, which was created in 1991 and issued bonds to Philadelphia to help its deficit.

headline: Legislature passes bill to ease pension costs for Pa., schools
abstract: A bill increasing the amortization period for the two state-controlled pension funds meant to quell the skyrocketing employer contribution costs faced by PA and PA's school districts passed both the PA House of Representatives and the PA Senate unanimously. In the short-term, the move should save the state and school districts $550 million in contributions to the PA State Employees' Retirement System and the Public School Employees' Retirement System. Long-term the contributions will cost the state more due to the lack of a beginning balance on which the contributions could earn interest.

headline: Children's yoga
abstract: It was nice to see that in article about children's yoga the American Academy of Pediatrics response was shown to cont the American Yoga Association believes. The AYA believes that yoga can be harmful to children. However, children's yoga is done differently than adult yoga and there is no medical evidence to show that it can cause harm.

headline: Cutting money for education? It's a tough choice and a bad one
abstract: The author, a professor at West Chester University of PA, condemns the PA government for cuts in higher education funding for the 14 state-funded universities and for the cuts in education funding generally. The cuts are harming the quality of a higher-education, the author opines, and will cause long-term damage to PA.

headline: A regional 'road-map'
abstract: Addressing Philadelphia's 'Road Map to Regional Growth,' the author finds positives in the possibilities in the report. The 'Road Map' is an effort from Innovation Philadelphia, a city initiative, and the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce to identify Philadelphia's strengths and determine ways to develop them to compete globally. The author argues the region needs to change its habits and become more collaborative, bringing together educational institutions, business interests, and government to enhance areas of strength like pharmaceuticals and health care as well as emergent industries like nanotechnology.

headline: Legislature wants Rendell to call special session on medical malpractice.
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell said that he would not call a special session to reduce property taxes unless he needs to focus the Legislature on the issue, but would support such a session for dealing with medical malpractice, following PA Representative Kerry Benninghoff's circulation of a petition urging him to do so. Benninghoff, a former hospital worker and county coroner, included in the petition a provision to declare the issue an emergency, which would allow the Legislature to bypass the constitutional rule requiring any change to the constitution be approved in two consecutive legislative sessions before voters can decide whether to approve it.

headline: Counties don't have resources to fill gaps in state funds for social services
abstract: The editors believe taxpayers are willing to continue paying for the mental retardation and illness and drug and alcohol programs PA Governor Ed Rendell proposed to cut in the state budget. Ronald Heckman, Northampton County's director of human services says there is no give in the budget for continued funding, despite that programs are cheaper ways of dealing with social ills than prison or other solutions. Lehigh County President Judge William Platt is arguing for restoration of the funds.

headline: District appeals for local leaders' support
abstract: Allentown School District Superintendent Karen Angello is pressuring local officials and community leaders in the Allentown area to support PA Governor Ed Rendell's education reform initiative. The Governor's education reforms would provide funding for school districts, especially important in Allentown as they face a ten percent increase in property tax in order to fund the city's schools.

headline: Arts Walk awarded $2 million to get project running
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell presented Allentown with a $2 million check for the city's Arts Walk program, which is meant to help with the city's economic revitalization. The financial support was advocated by the city, Lehigh County, arts organizations, and legislators such as state Representative Jennifer L. Mann and state Senator Charles W. Dent. As mayor of Philadelphia, Rendell undertook a similar initiative in Philadelphia's Avenue of the Arts.

headline: Librarians upset at lack of state funding
abstract: PA's librarians were upset and shocked as the PA House of Representatives restored some funding to many programs in the latest budget but did not do so for libraries. The funding should be partially restored still as negotiations for passage go on in the PA Senate, with lawmakers acknowledging that the restoration is likely.

headline: Damage control
abstract: Having gained first-hand experience from their time as a home-care nurse and hospital chaplain, the author says the PA law requiring helmets should be maintained due to the societal costs of caring for quadriplegics and paraplegics as well as the impact the loss of loved ones has on family members.

headline: Districts chafe at narrow shortfalls
abstract: Across the Philadelphia area, school districts are scrambling for possible appeals to citations for failing to meet state and federal goals for student achievement, despite making good to excellent scores on the math and reading tests.  Schools like Faust Elementary School are put on the list for having attendance .01 percent off the 95 percent bar set by the PA Department of Education.  26 districts already have filed appeals after falling on the "needs improvement" list.

headline: Authority to give $1.3M to bayfront hotel builder
abstract: A bayfront hotel next to the proposed convention center in Erie, PA will receive up to $1.3 million from the Erie County Convention Center Authority if they pay the prevailing wage for building. The convention center is seeking a state grant to assist in building and the bayfront hotel is considered critical to the success of their grant proposal. The $1.3 million represents a repayment of money the developer will lose by paying the prevailing wage.

headline: Libraries hope for their share of state money
abstract: PA's librarians were upset and shocked as the PA House of Representatives restored some funding to many programs in the latest budget but did not do so for libraries. The funding should be partially restored still as negotiations for passage go on in the PA Senate, with lawmakers acknowledging that the restoration is likely.

headline: Day-care insurance bill introduced by DeWeese passed by state House of Representatives
abstract: Legislation introduced by PA Representative H. William DeWeese has passed the PA House of Representatives and would alter current state law to require family day-care homes with six or fewer children to have liability insurance. The legislation was spurred by the tragic death of a toddler in a Greene County day-care center, which resulted in the stricken family carrying the burden for related expenses.

headline: Don't blame pro skater
abstract: Skateboarder Bam Margera gets a bad rap when people say he is bringing bad publicity to his hometown of West Chester. He never represents himself as a role model and it is not his fault when young adults partake in stupid activities while trying to mimic him.

headline: Big shots and fans offer sub stories of their own
abstract: The Philadelphia Eagles have banned bringing food into their stadiums as a safety precaution. PA Governor Ed Rendell, a "noted junk-food gourmand," favors the ban as people could disguise dangerous material in food packaging. The article includes a list of letters, emails and faxes, in one of which Philadelphia City Councilman Frank Rizzo states that the plan is meant to sell more concessions at the stadium.

headline: Lieutenant governor asks Easton voters to back Corpora
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Catherine Baker Knoll campaigned in Easton, PA in support of Democratic candidate for mayor Dan Corpora, who is challenging Republican candidate Phil Mitman. Corpora pledged his time as mayor would be spent on quality of life issues and financial control.

headline: Blue Mountain gets $60,000 state grant
abstract: Blue Mountain School District Superintendent William H. Hall announced that the district will receive a grant from the PA Department of Education. He said that the funds will be used for "life skills" in classes, such as the installation of a sink, refrigerator, washer and dryer in one classroom. More funds will be used to build a greenhouse and to by laptop computers, among other projects.

headline: Racetrack list narrowed down to five
abstract: The PA Horse Racing Commission met in Philadelphia and announced they have narrowed the list of applicant's for PA's remaining thoroughbred license to five following an influx of applications in light of the legalization of slots gambling at PA racetracks.

headline: Pennsylvania's war weary pocketbook voters pick Kerry
abstract: Political analysts argue that Senator Kerry's victory over President Bush in Pennsylvania was due to voter unrest over the Iraq War and the conomy.   President Bush was unable to fair well in the once Republican suburbs of Philadelphia--a failure that many say cost him the 21 electoral votes of the state.

headline: Board OK's new contract with faculty of state-owned universities
abstract: The board of the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education approved a new four-year contract for faculty at state-owned universities. The deal had already been approved by the Association of PA State College and University Faculty and represents a compromise between improved benefits and salaries while not becoming cost-prohibitive for the state.

headline: Raceway in running for slots license
abstract: Dr. Joseph Mattioli, owner of the Pocono Raceway, wants a license to open a slots parlor, and state Senator Robert Mellow will appeal to the board which issues the licenses on his behalf. Mattioli stated that the raceway has adequate space and facilities, and that slots would help the raceway keep its National Association for Stock Car Auto Racing events and compete with Dover International Speedway in Delaware. The members of the PA Gaming Control Board will announce the winners of the 14 available slot licenses next year.

headline: Murphy has 8,000 vote lead over Gerlach
abstract: In the Pennsylvania 6th District Congressional Race, Democrat Louis Murphy maintains an 8,000 vote lead over incumbent U.S. Representative Jim Gerlach.  Although the results are unofficial, it is clear that this is one of the most competitive congressional contests in the country.

headline: CASD changes program for fall
abstract: Children entering kindergarten programs in the Connellsville Area School District will be in class for a full-day session beginning in the fall. This has come to a pleasant surprise to many of those involved.

headline: Record profits fill U.S. Steel's till
abstract: Pittsburgh-based U.S. Steel reported record third-quarter profits which have lead to a $1 billion cash reserve, leading to speculation they may seek to acquire new assets though they indicated they will first settle in-house debt issues.

headline: Clymer positioned to win 13th term in state House
abstract: According to unofficial results, veteran state legislator Paul Clymer is well on his way to winning his 13th term in the PA House of Representatives.  Clymer is running against political newcomer John Norvaisas, who claims that he will run against Clymer again if he is not successful this time around.  Clymer, who is 67, has no intention of retiring anytime soon and says he may stick around long enough to make sure gambling does not get legalized.

headline: City, teachers' union continue negotiating
abstract: Negotiators for the York City Education Association and the York City School District reached no agreement during a meeting on Monday. Despite the "cordial" discussions, so termed by YCEA president Mary Ann Swalgin, a fact-finder appointed by the PA Labor Relations Board will soon hold a hearing and shortly thereafter release a list of recommendations. York City School Board president Jeff Kirkland said contract negotiations include extending the length of elementary school teachers' work days.

headline: Recruiting for the home team
abstract: This article argues that PA Governor Ed Rendell's economic stimulus package will receive a boost from the Citizen's Job Bank, an initiative from Citizen's Bank to offer low-interest loans to manufacturing firms in exchange for the creation of new jobs.

headline: Casey wins in a landslide
abstract: Democrat Robert P. Casey Jr. won a landslide victory in the state treasurer's race on Tuesday.  With the victory, many are wondering if Casey, the former Auditor General, will seek higher political office in the near future.

headline: Colleges boosting tuition
abstract: College tuition at Drexel University, the University of PA, St. Joseph's University and Temple University is increasing. Temple President David Adamany said that Temple's increase was the lowest necessary to continue improvements at the university, while a spokesman for St. Joseph's said that enrollment and increased demand for facilities and technology drove costs up. According to the National Association of Independent Colleges and Universities, tuition increases are a national trend. The PA State System of Higher Education was to vote on a tuition increase, but PA Governor Ed Rendell said that they hadn't made a convincing enough argument as to why the increase was necessary.

headline: Rendell acts to keep slots gambling clean
abstract: The editorial board supports PA Governor Ed Rendell's efforts to avoid problems associated with gambling.

headline: Kanjorski wins 11th term in House of Representatives
abstract: Congressman Paul E. Kanjorski easily defeated a minor party candidate on Tuesday to secure his 11th term in the United States House of Representatives.  Representative Kanjorski hopes to use his seniority to strengthen laws in the insurance and real estate industries and to increase economic development in Luzerne and Lackawanna counties.

headline: Community college receives $50,000 grant to use at county education center
abstract: The PA Department of Community and Economic Development gave a $50,000 grant to the Westmoreland County Community College following efforts by PA State Representative William DeWeese. The funding will go towards furniture for the College's Greene County Education Center.

headline: Rendell administration is granted two more months to respond to Delaware Nation lawsuit
abstract: The Rendell administration has been granted two more months to file a response to a federal lawsuit that seeks to allow the Delaware Nation to pursue casino gambling in Pennsylvania. The state wants to coordinate legal efforts among the defendants.

headline: GOP flexes muscle
abstract: With President Bush's election to a second term and gains in both the Senate and House of Representatives, the Republican Party achieved major victories on Tuesday and siezed more power over the nation's domestic and foreign agendas.  President Bush won the election with the biggest vote total of any president in US history and viewed the outcome as a mandate for his policy agenda--an agenda that will be carried out more easily with increased Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress.

headline: Cornell disinfecting could cost $150,000
abstract: Following a stomach illness that sickened nearly 180 students, staff, and family members, cleaning and disinfecting the Cornell Education Center could cost nearly $150,000, the school board recently learned. The district may take out a loan to cover the expenses and then seek federal or state assistance in repaying the debt.

headline: Rendell hoping for action on economic development bills
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell hopes that the state Legislature will complete work on his plan to expand and attract businesses to the state. The program, financed by Citizens Bank of PA, will create loans which will require borrowers to create at least one full-time job for every $25,000 borrowed within three years after borrowing the money. Citizens Bank chairman and CEO Stephen D. Steinour believes the plan will help the state invigorate small- and medium-sized businesses.

headline: Few problems reported in PA Voting
abstract: Although Pennsylvania did not endure major voting irregularities on Tuesday, high levels of turnout forced voting dealays and caused some polls to remain open beyond 8pm.  In addition to high turnout, party lawyers, in their quest to challenge fradulent registrations and voter intimidation, slowed the voting process down.

headline: Critics targeting federal measure
abstract: While President Bush is marking the two-year anniversary of the No Child Left Behind Act as positive, critics are saying the federal mandates are illogical, inflexible, inconsistent, and unfunded.  Both the Central Bucks and Reading School Districts, the former representing the richest and the latter representing the poorest of the state's districts, face sanctions for violating some part of the law's myriad requirements.

headline: Rendell requests detailed plan before giving arts center money
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell said that the state will not bail out the Mountain Laurel Center for the Performing Arts near Bushkill unless the center comes up with a business plan guaranteed to bring in revenues. The center has not yet approached the state. The center is also funded by bonds from the Pike County Industrial and Commercial Development Authority.

headline: Local poll workers deal with heavy turnout
abstract: In Pennsylvania, Tuesday's election went off without any major problems.  The biggest problem officials encountered was high turnout.  This forced many precincts to stay open beyond 8pm for all votes to be cast.

headline: Cutoff of data worries group
abstract: The PA Association of School Retirees is now being denied the names of new retirees from the PA School Employees Retirement System, hurting their recruitment of new members for the agency which acts as a lobbying group. The association claims they are being punished by the PA State Education Association, the largest teachers union in the state, which holds four seats on the retirement system's board.

headline: Rendell stands behind gambling board pick
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell defended his choice of former Philadelphia police officer Frank Friel as chairman of the PA Gaming Control Board despite reports Friel had been the subject of a corruption investigation in 1974. Rendell also disputed claims he would name PA State Treasurer Barbara Hafer to the Board.

headline: A little help goes a long way
abstract: The PA House passed legislation that would provide a statewide system of services to help families care for children who are physically, but not mentally, disabled.  This legislation would help with home care and would provide much needed assistance to families with a physically-disabled child.

headline: Deer Lakes School Board approves study of full-day kindergarten
abstract: A group of parents formed and convinced the Deer Lakes school district to explore offering full-day kindergarten, estimating the cost to be $278,000.

headline: Republican legislators vow to fix slot law 'flaws'
abstract: PA Republican legislators are vowing to make amendments to the law authorizing expanded gambling in PA, seeking to enhance law enforcement provisions and the participation of the PA Attorney General's office. The legislators will also seek to remove a provision allowing state and local officials to own up to 1% of a casino.

headline: Rendell to sign job tax
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell is expected to sign a bill that will allow municipalities across the state to raise their occupational privilege tax.  The bill is designed to increase municipal revenues and stave off municipal layoffs and budgetary shortfalls.  The bill also includes a tax reform plan for the city of Pittsburgh.

headline: Downingtown teachers to vote on tentative contract
abstract: Downingtown School District teachers will vote on a contract that includes a wage increase as well as an increase in their share of medical premium co-payments. Downingtown is one of four Chester County school districts in the midst of labor negotiations, and the agreement would mark the largest percentage increase for Chester County teachers in the past 2 years.

headline: Sheetz officials sink their teeth into a public relations problem
abstract: Stan Sheetz, president of Sheetz Incorporated, was one of many corporate officials to visit the company's convenience stores following calls from the PA Department of Agriculture reporting an outbreak of Javiana salmonella, linked to Roma tomatoes. The company quickly removed all tomatoes and lettuce from their stores and warehouses, and had employees sanitize each store. The PA Department of Health confirmed 70 cases in the outbreak as of Friday.

headline: New city tax dead: Commuter levy won't be revived, Rendell promises
abstract: Even though a Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reporter claimed that Governor Rendell might impose a commutter tax on Pittsburgh, he insists that he has no plans to seek a commutter tax and that his comments were misunderstood and misconstrued by a reporter who was evesdropping on his conversation with City Council members.  Governor Rendell argued that the a commutter tax is not necessary, as Pittsburgh's financial bailout legislation will raise enough revenue to balance the city's budget.

headline: Education nominee would face big test
abstract: Francis Barnes, nominated to be PA's Secretary of Education, will be tested should he be confirmed as he seeks to secure support from PA Republican legislators for the agenda of PA Governor Ed Rendell. Barnes is seeking to overcome the funding gap that has separated legislators and the governor's administration as Republicans resist increased spending, preferring that schools and the state put current funding to better use.

headline: Slots bill shaping up as bad law, and is based on dishonest rationale
abstract: The editorial accuses the slots bill that is to be passed in the PA Legislature next week as being seriously flawed. The legislation calls for four or five non-horsetrack sites, which lets down the PA public because it expands the amount of officially sanctioned gambling Pennsylvanians will tolerate beyond the PA Lottery and betting at horsetracks. The editorial board calls the bill dishonest also because PA Governor Edward G. Rendell had originally said that the purpose of slot-machine gambling in the first place was to provide thrivingtracks where PA agriculture can thrive. However, only 18 percent of the revenue at the tracks will go to horsemen while most will go to track owners and the state. The board also believes the property-tax reduction related to the slots bill will be detrimental to public education.

headline: One Pay Raise Most Generous
abstract: State lawmakers failed to pass legislation that would have given them a 20 percent pay raise.  The legislation didn't go to the floor for a vote because Governor Rendell demanded approval of legislation he favored in exchange for his signing off on the pay raise.  Republican lawmakers refused to concede and headed for home with one week remaining in the current legislative session.

headline: Farm kids contend with No Child
abstract: Because of the federal No Child Left Behind Act, the Bermudian Springs School District only allows nine days of absence for its students, with the risk of parental fine for any student who goes over.  This is a problem for students like 11-year-old Hannah Grim, who will likely miss three days of school attending the Pennsylvania Farm Show.  Parents like Greg Grim, Hannah's father, wish there was more flexibility in the No Child Left Behind Act.

headline: Slots bills give political leaders control of board
abstract: Proposed gambling legislation in Pennsylvania would differ from other states, in that four leaders of the General Assembly, and not the Governor, would appoint members to the state gaming control board.  There is intense behind-the-scenes negotiations of the proposal to grant 14 slot machine licenses statewide, with Governor Rendell and gambling supporters saying that a tax on slot machine profits can generate $1 billion in revenues to curb school property taxes by 20 percent.

headline: Tens of thousands of students affected by SEPTA strike
abstract: More than 58,000 Philadelphia students who use SEPTA to get to and from school were asleep when transit workers walked off the job in the wee hours of the morning yesterday. School District of Philadelphia spokesman Fernando Gallard, says the district is anticipating that a number of students will not make it to school. If a student can't make it to school as a result of the strike, officials say, homework and lessons will be available for pickup at schools and regional offices.

headline: Route 22 set to reopen today
abstract: Residents and business owners is Murrysville, PA are glad that Route 22 will be opening back up today.  The 3 to 4 mile stretch of Route 22 that runs through Murrysville has been under construction and closed for nearly two years.

headline: Few students are left behind here
abstract: Nearly all of the 16 school districts in Lancaster County are meeting federal standards for reading and math, according to the test results recently released by the PA Department of Education.  65 of the county's 74 elementary schools have met or exceeded expectations, along with 16 of 20 middle schools and 14 of 16 high schools doing the same.

headline: Slots debate in Pa., Md. brings issue of influence
abstract: PA's lack of campaign finance restrictions has enabled gambling companies to heavily contribute to recent campaigns, leading to accusations that the government has been unduly influenced due to the impending legalization in PA. The Maryland legislature has also considered slots legislation but ultimately turned it down after far less was spent by gambling companies on campaign contributions.

headline: 16 year old sought in fatal shooting
abstract: Jalil Speaks, a 16 year old sophomore at Strawberry Mansion High School, was killed on Monday in a gun fight that injured three other students.  Investigators believe that Speaks was killed because he failed to pay 50 dollars he lost in a rap contest.  Authorities have approved an arrest warrant for the 16 year old boy who they believe killed Speaks.

headline: For a better state education policy, start with cost of a good education
abstract: This article addresses the education policy of PA Governor Ed Rendell, feeling that too little was done prior to the budget negotiations and eventual compromise to guarantee that Rendell's campaign promises of smaller class sizes, full day kindergarten, and increased state funding to ease the property tax burden could have been achieved. The article argues that the state should establish a baseline cost for a good education by appointing an independent commission to investigate and analyze education expenditures in state.

headline: Slots finally get green light
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell signed into law a bill legalizing slot machine gambling in the state, as well as another bill allocating $1 billion of revenue from the slots to offset property tax reductions. The PA House of Representatives had approved both bills from the Senate, as well as the state's $23 billion budget. The City of Chester and Delaware County are expected to bring in about $10 million per year once slots are up and running, although PA Representative Thaddeus Kirkland fears placing slots in low-income areas such as Chester. According to the American Gaming Association, PA is the 18th state to legalize slot machine gambling.

headline: Saving baseball project is a long shot, but a long shot worth taking
abstract: Governor Rendell and the PA state Legislature could not come to an agreement on local funding plans for the proposed minor-league baseball stadium in Allentown.  Currently, the state is providing a 12 million dollar grant for stadium construction--a grant that, under current plans, must be matched by Lehigh County.  Two proposals--a hotel tax and a tax-shifting plan--are designed to raise the 12 million dollars for the local share, but Governor Rendell and the legislature could not agree on a proposal for local funding.

headline: Forum: Brown vs. Board of Education -- a work in progress
abstract: Ken Gormley writes about the 50th anniversary of Thurgood Marshall's arguing before the US Supreme Court the case of Brown vs. Board of Education. He writes that although the country's schools are integrated, inner-city public schools still remain segregated, large achievement gaps exist between whites and black, and African-American graduation rates are shockingly low. Gormley asserts that there is still much work to be done to fully integrate American schools, and that Thurgood Marshall would not be satisfied with the progress made since the decision in 1954.

headline: Slots looking likely
abstract: PA Senator Robert "Tommy" Tomlinson, among other PA legislators, have said they believe they have reached a deal to bring slot machines to Pennsylvania. The proposal calls for a mix of up to 12 racetrack and freestanding casinos, including one at Penn National in Grantville, PA, as well as two licenses for smaller casinos at resorts with overnight lodging and other amenities. Lawmakers hope to pass the slots bill, which will only be voted on if legislators can produce a companion measure to cut property taxes, with the passage of the 2004-2005 state budget before the fiscal year ends next Wednesday. Kate Philips, press secretary for PA Governor Edward G. Rendell who supports the passage of the bill, said the administration believes they are "closer than ever" to signing slots legislation.

headline: County certifies vote results; Kerry squeaks past president by 552
abstract: Three weeks after the presidential election, Washington County certified its official election results, with Democratic Senator John Kerry maintaining a slim lead over President George Bush.  The margin of victory was only 552 votes.

headline: Full-day classes welcome addition
abstract: The editorial board lauds South Middleton School Board for establishing full-day kindergartens. Despite there being more teachers, the net cost is zero due to PA Governor Ed Rendell's education initiative which funds early childhood education. Although it is possible that the state subsidies might stop at anytime, Rendell and the state Legislature would suffer severe criticism by removing the funding.

headline: Some who sell beer prefer not to tap into day of rest
abstract: With legislation pending that could allow beer distributors to be open on Sundays, some owners are claiming they are unsure if the added hours are positive. The change is being pursued to ensure PA keeps tax dollars in state on beer sales, with support from most corners other than PA restaurants that stand to lose revenues earned on Sunday six-pack sales.

headline: Officials: Victim encounteres suspect hours before death
abstract: Authorities report that Lee Sullivan, the 25 year old medical student who was fatally attacked on Sunday afternoon, came face to face with her killer, Nader Ali, hours before her attack.  Ali was a former classmate of Sullivans and came to her apartment building hours before he attacked Sullivan.  After the crime, Ali fled to North Jersey; he is being held without bail in Bergen County and extradition proceedings have begun.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: PA Education Secretary Vicki Phillips told the PA Senate Education Committee that she will send notices to school districts about the new Accountability Block Grant program based on the $175 million that legislators and PA Governor Ed Rendell agreed upon in December. However, last week she told the PA Senate Appropriations committee that she would send notices based on the $250 million that Rendell desired. Her actions drew criticism from Republican senators who stated that her plan was at risk of violating the law that created the block grant program.

headline: State contracts with gambling consultants
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell's administration hired a PA-based consultant and two others to find the best way to monitor slots revenue and to conduct background checks.

headline: A long scandalous tale
abstract: In October 1999, Philadelphia public school libraries made national news for having books with outdated information.  In response to this report, Mayor Street and former Philadelphia School Superintendent David Hornbeck said they were going to set up a panel to examine the problem.  The panel never met.

headline: Grading minority graduation rates
abstract: Allentown School District officials are focusing on ninth-graders in belief that if freshmen feel more connected with their teachers, fewer minority students will drop out. A joint report by the Urban Institute and the Civil Rights Project at Harvard University shows that high school dropout rates across the country are generally lower than the federal government estimates. Luis A. Ramos, a member of Allentown School District's oversight committee and a member of the state Board of Education contends that the state is not doing enough to help minority students. The US Department of Education requires that minority graduation rates be lumped together with those for white students.

headline: State hires consultants to develop slots systems
abstract: Seeking the best way to implement the expansion of gambling, PA Governor Ed Rendell's administration has hired gambling consultants to help the PA Department of Revenue choose a computer system to track all of the state's slots machines. The consultants will also work with the PA State Police's Office of Gaming Enforcement in conducting background checks.

headline: Flaherty says plan to abolish row offices is Onorato power grab
abstract: According to Democrats, Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato's row office reduction plan represents nothing more than a Republican power grab.  Democrats currently hold all 10 row-office seats, and under the row-office reduction plan 8 of those 10 seats will be eliminated.  Chief Executive Onorato defends his proposal, claiming that it is not just a Republican issue.  Many Democrats have proposed row-office consolidation as well.

headline: Home-schoolers chafe at state law
abstract: Four lawsuits are being pursued seeking the end of restrictive policies of Pennsylvania's home-schooling law, with the lawsuits particularly focusing on the disparity between the home-schooling regulations and the Religious Freedom Protection Act. The lawsuits and other critics allege that PA has the most restrictive policies in the nation, requiring assessment testing and reporting of intent to home-school.

headline: State House to consider damage caps
abstract: A bill regarding caps on awards in medical malpractice cases passed in the PA Senate and will go on to the PA House, but a statewide referendum and implementation are not likely to happen for a while. The measure would require changing the state constitution, which requires voter approval. PA specialists such as surgeons and gynecologists saw their insurance rates increase from 130-165% from 1999-2002, according to the General Accounting Office.

headline: Fund private racetrack with private cash only
abstract: Governor Rendell is considering a 2.5 million dollar grant for a car racetrack in the Poconos.  This project is essentially a country club for the rich and will not benefit the community at large.  It should not be funded with our tax dollars.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: School districts across PA will receive $200 million in state grants for full-day kindergarten programs, literacy and math coaches for teachers, and materials to improve test scores of minority, low-income, English as a second language, and/or special education students. PA Governor Ed Rendell had hoped for more money, but "legislative sources" say that the Republican-controlled General Assembly didn't want to give Rendell, a Democrat, such a victory. When Rendell signed the state budget on July 4, he planned to move money from discretionary community development grants to his school program.

headline: The Flood of '04: Flood insurance often falls short
abstract: In the wake of flooding on September 17, homeowners in flood zones are examining the possibility of federally-subsidized flood insurance while those with damage seeking claims are learning the coverage is full of loopholes. The PA Department of Emergency Management and the Federal Emergency Management Agency are working to resolve claims with private insurers.

headline: County Bureau of Elections now cleaning up voter rolls
abstract: With the 2004 elections over, the Luzerne County Bureau of Elections has begun focusing on voter registration and roll maintenance, as well as updating the county-wide voting system to meet the standards of the Help America Vote Act.  This process entails updating voter rolls to reflect change of address requests, deceased voters, and inactive voters.  The final part of this process is implementing electronic voting machines and precinct consolidation.

headline: Legislators defend hidden PIAA bill
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell signed into a law a bill creating the PA Athletic Oversight Committee, a panel of legislators to oversee the PA Interscholastic Athletic Association. However, many legislators were unaware of its creation, as the provision was included at the last minute. Previously, there existed the PA Interscholastic Athletic Council, which featured state legislators but was run through the PA Department of Education.

headline: Study touts role of manufacturers in region, cites growth in advanced technology arenas
abstract: A study sponsored by Catalyst Connection, PA's Industrial Resource Centers and the TEAM PA Foundation showed that manufacturing played a crucial role in the state's economy, despite the retrenchment of the steel industry in the 1970's and 1980's. Kevin Lane, spokesman for the Pittsburgh Technology Council, states that manufacturing was considered "dirty, dingy, unsafe and unhealthy" when it was equated with the steel industry. Deloitte, a consulting firm which conducted the report, determined that manufacturing contributes about $64 billion annually to PA's economy.

headline: Leaders miss the bus cut meeting
abstract: Unless federal and state legislators intervene, York County's Rabbit Transit Authority is planning to cut transportation services by 25 percent.  Approximately 60 local resdients attended a public hearing during which Richard Farr, Rabbittransit's executive director, explained the reasons for the cuts.  In response, citizens expressed their displeasure, stating that service cuts will affect their ability to travel to work and school.  The cuts will go into effect, however, unless one of the two bills under consideration in the state House and Seante---bills that would provide relief across the state--is passed.

headline: Let sun shine on law school meetings
abstract: The editorial encourages the Pennsylvania Senate to pass a bill to force The Penn State Dickinson School of Law's governing board to meet in public because the decisions it is discussing are of critical public interest. A closed task force is studying the merits of building a new law school campus in State College. PA Senator Hal Mowery has introduced and built support for a bill that would amend the definition of the word "agency" in the state's Sunshine Act so that it includes the type of board under which Dickinson functions. The editorial board believes it is unfair to the taxpayers in Pennsylvania and state legislators for the board to hold private meetings and the Legislature should pass Mowery's bill to force the board to meet in public.

headline: There's a world out there, and it needs our help
abstract: Tony Norman expresses his frustration with specifically right-wing talk radio hosts and those who write letters to city newspapers who blame President Bush for directing tax dollars to the tsunami victims while those victims are the ones who have "steal" US manufacturing jobs.  Norman claims that PA Governor Ed Rendell and Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato have kept the victims of the local flood in Carnegie, Pennsylvania on their minds and has credited President Bush with understanding the severity of the disaster in Sri Lanka.

headline: Bill OK to boost fine for school-zone speeding
abstract: A bill that would dramatically increase the fines and penalties for speeding in a school zone passed unanimously in the state House yesterday.  The School Zone Saftey Act, sponsored by Representative George Kenney and House Speaker John Perzel, raises the maximum fine for speeding and also carries a license suspension for repeat offfenders.  The bill is a response to measures implemented in Philadelphia that have drastically reduced illegal parking and reckless driving around schools.

headline: Libraries need your support
abstract: A letter writer points out that the recent reduced funding for state libraries hurts all communities, and there are two ways to help this problem.  After citizens petition legislators in Harrisburg to reprioritize library funding in the future, they should also consider private donations to the libraries.  The writer adds that Pennsylvania ranks 40th out of all the states in terms of library services, and that is contradictory to the legacy of Benjamin Franklin.

headline: U.S. Steel posts best quarter in years
abstract: U.S. Steel announced a profit of $221 million in the April-June quarter, its most profitable since 1991 and one that exceeded its previous three-month best, according to chairman Thomas Usher. Other steelmakers, such as Allegheny Technologies and Universal Stainless & Alloy Products posted higher profits. The weaker US dollar and high demand for steel in developing countries such as China are fuelling the rise in profits.

headline: Onorato angers some fellow Democrats with plan to eliminate eight elective posts
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato formally presentd a proposal to eliminate eight of the county's 10 elected row offices.  Under his proposal, voters would decide--via referendum--if the offices should be eliminated.  To get the referendum on the ballot, however, Onorato needs the support of at least on Democrat in City Council--a vote that may hard to come by since all but one of the row offices are filled by Democrats.

headline: Limit funding promises, education secretary told
abstract: PA Senate Appropriations Committee Chairman Robert Thompson and Senate Education Committee Chairman James Rhoades informed PA Education Secretary Vicki Phillips that notices she is about to send to school districts regarding state block grant money would violate the Public School Code. The notices promise school districts more funding than the law permits, which could create confusion. Phillips was aware of the funding limit, but recognized that PA Governor Ed Rendell was trying to increase funding, by which school districts would receive more money if they told the Department of Education how they would use the money, said Stinson Stroup of the PA Association of School Administrators.

headline: US Airways chief abruptly quits
abstract: US Airways chief and executive president David Siegel resigned amidst strong opposition from airline unions to wage cuts which the airline felt were necessary to remain competitive as Southwest Airlines moves into Philadelphia International Airport. The wage cuts represent another effort by US Airways to remain competitive with industry-high operating costs hurting revenues while other low-fare airlines simultaneously force US Airways to cut their fares.

headline: Turmoil in Allentown City Hall isn't in troubled community's best interests
abstract: Reports are surfacing that Allentown Mayor Roy Afflerbach has been discussing a job at the PA Public Utility Commission with Harrisburg Democrats.  Although insiders say Afflerbach is interested in filling a vacant seat on the commission, he has downplayed his intrerest in the new job.  Afflerbach has 13 months left on his mayoral term and has still not announced his intentions for re-election next year.  Both the public and the City Council deserve to know Mayor Afflerbach's intentions; the city needs and deserves cooperation and commitment from its elected officials.

headline: Mold gone, school to reopen
abstract: Halifax Elementary School was finally opened after being closed for weeks as mold and mildew were removed. The school has applied to the PA Department of Education for students to receive credit for missed class time at the very beginning of the closure. Students had been taking classes at local churches while the clean-up was underway.

headline: US Airways says repair jobs can be saved
abstract: US Airways Chief Executive Officer Bruce Lakefield wants to keep the airline's 1,700 maintenance jobs in the Pittsburgh area, and at a private meeting with US Representative Tim Murphy stressed that his company could end up in bankruptcy again. In 2002, then-Allegheny County Chief Executive Jim Roddy asked Harrisburg to help the company to build a maintenance center which the county would own and the airline would lease. US Airways is also seeking union concessions, but the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers is strongly resistant to the concessions. PA Governor Ed Rendell continues to work with US Airways to preserve jobs in the state.

headline: John Grogan: So thankful for this turkey shoot
abstract: An Inquirer columnists gives thanks to several of Pennsylvania's politicians for giving him so much political scandal and intrigue to write about.  Among the PA political lumanaries mentioned are Governor "fast Eddie" Rendell, Senator Vince Fumo, House Speaker John Perzel and Representative Thomas Druce.

headline: New program to help schools cut into 'achievement gap'
abstract: The PA Department of Education announced 16 schools that would be targeted in the PA Achievement Gap Effort that aims to reduce the achievement gap between white and minority students in PA. Three southwestern PA schools were chosen for the initiative which will last approximately three years and be funded by state grants, foundation grants, and private donations.

headline: When the money comes rolling in
abstract: The author argues for removal of the provision of the slots legislation allowing PA legislators to own up to 1% of a gambling enterprise in the state as well as enhanced protections to prevent other forms of proprietorship for public officials. PA House Democratic leaders William DeWeese and Mike Veon are decried for their claims that the 1% stake is reasonable due to a lack of restrictions in other business ventures on public officials.

headline: A recess strands would-be judges
abstract: With seven days remaining in the 2003-04 legislative session, lawmakers have decided to take a recess, leaving nine judicial nominees poised for Senate confirmation in abeyance.  Since lawmakers did not adjourn, they could conceivably return to vote on nominees, but it is unclear whether or not they will do so.  If the nominees are not voted on before the end of the current legislative session, Governor Rendell will have to re-nominate them in the next legislative session.

headline: No reason for teachers to challenge EITC
abstract: Naturally many teachers disapprove of the Educational Improvement Tax Credit which provides state funds to private institutions. However, this program provides benefits to those whom could not afford it. It allows children who work better in smaller environments to obtain a more beneficial classroom environment when they would have been able to otherwise.

headline: Bomb claims two guardsmen from Pa. unit
abstract: Two PA National Guardsmen from Erie County passed away in Iraq, the first two from their unit to pass away from combat since World War II. Each will posthumously receive the PA Distinguished Service Medal from PA Governor Ed Rendell.

headline: Politics: Playing it again in Harrisburg
abstract: During the final days of the legislative session, there was a great deal of politics going on that prevented the resolution of several important issues currently under consideration.  In one sense, this was good because legislators went home without voting themselves a pay raise, but at the same time there remains unfinished legislative business with slot-machine regulation, emergency funding for Philadelphia's public transit system, open-space preservation, and industrial-site cleanup measures.  Although legislators may reconvene before the session officially ends, this is unlikely.

headline: Online schools grow more popular in PA
abstract: Students in PA enrolled in cyber-schools are expected to increase by 50% this year to nearly 10,000 and three new cyber-schools will open. Parents are seeking alternatives for their children that allow greater flexibility but school districts have been slow to accept the new option, resisting pressure to pay student fees for them to attend the cyber-schools.

headline: Governors keep politics at bay on war casualties
abstract: The articles cites New Jersey Governor James McGreevey and PA Governor Edward G. Rendell and their actions towards the families of soldiers that have died in the Iraq war as examples of ways to leave politics out of responding to war casualties. McGreevey's role in response to deaths from the war is dependent upon the family's wishes, spokesman Micah Rasmussen said. Kate Philips, spokeswoman for Rendell, said Rendell decided early in the conflict that he would not attend funerals so as to keep politics out of the tragedies of war. Rendell did attend the funeral of Sgt. Sherwood R. Baker because his mother had worked in Rendell's administration when he was mayor of Philadelphia. Instead of attending funerals, Rendell orders flags in the soldier's home county to be flown at half staff and sends each family a personal sympathy note.

headline: Lawmakers ease threat of winter utility shut-offs
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers passed a bill that protects the poor, seniors and families with children from utility shutoffs during the cold winter months.  The bill prevents gas and electric companies from shutting off utilities to customers whose income falls below 25 percent of the federal poverty level.  Also, the bill prevents companies from shutting off service to households that include people over the age of 65 or children 12 and under.

headline: Parents want all students bused
abstract: Parents are asking the Waynesboro Area school district to begin busing all elementary age students, a practice currently not in place due to a state policy which disallows state reimbursement for busing of children within 1.5 miles of schools. At the school's request, the PA Department of Transportation has determined safe walking patterns for students in the Hawbaker Avenue area, which is an area of particular concern to many of the parents.

headline: Local firm awarded military contract
abstract: US Representative John Murtha paid a visit to United Defense Industries Incorporated in Uniontown, in order to present the company with a check establishing a contract with the US Army. UDII will remanufacture Bradley fighting vehicles, which Deborah Fox, the plant's manager, said will help troops serving in Operation Iraqi Freedom. During an address at the plant, Murtha said that troops in Iraq had inadequate body armor and there was a shortage of Bradleys.

headline: Turnpike toll takers might strike
abstract: Pennsylvania Turnpike toll collectors and other nonunionized workers might go on strike the day before Thanksgiving--traditionally one of the busiest days of the year.  If a strike occurs, tolls at every turnpike exit will cost two dollars for passenger vehicles and 15 dollars for commercial vehicles.  The Turnpike workers most recent contract is set to expire in September.

headline: Pennsylvania universities 2nd costliest in U.S.
abstract: An analysis by a pair of higher education groups showed that Pennsylvania's public universities are the second most expensive in the country, behind only Vermont. Tuition is up as much as 65 percent at some state schools. Schools are also to blame for the increase in tuition, they are spending a lot more money per student than they had in the past.

headline: A Dell Deal: Computer giant lands contract with state
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell announced that PA had reached a deal with computer manufacturer Dell to be the sole provider of computers to the state government, a deal which Rendell says will save taxpayers $19.1 million a year. The four year contract is part of Rendell's strategic sourcing initiative, a process of awarding state contracts to low, single bidders in hopes of saving taxpayers $100 million a year.

headline: School district to study grading procedures
abstract: The West Chester Area School District is planning to examine college admissions procedures and other school districts' policies in order to determine if they should switch to a different grading system.  Many parents feel that their children are at a disadvantage in the college admissions process because the West Chester district does not use a 10-point grading scale--awarding A's only to students who score a 93 or higher.

headline: Philips named to post in Oregon
abstract: PA State Education Secretary Vicki Phillips has accepted the Superintendent position for Oregon's largest school district, leaving PA amidst speculation as to the reason for her departure. The move was speculated to be due to a perception that Governor Rendell has not been as committed as promised to education policy while others felt it was a better opportunity. Phillips has also come under scrutiny from state politicians for her role in awarding grants to school districts as well as facing PA auditor general and Federal Bureau of Investigation queries regarding the finances of the Lancaster School District where Philips was previously employed.

headline: Toll grows for cell-phone surcharges
abstract: The opinion article by columnist Jeff Gelles addresses how the complaints cell phone customers have about the increasing fees, taxes and surcharges they face on monthly bills. Gelles cites Barbara P., a Malvern resident, and her T-Mobile bill that charged her three extra fees in a matter of four months as an example. The Federal Communications Commission recently received a petition about the deceptive nature of carrier charges. Gelles says two of the three new charges to Barbara P. are Pennsylvania's telephone gross-receipts tax and a new fee to support enhanced-911 emergency system, both charges that Gelles believes will not be repealed. The most controversial of the charges is T-Mobile's "Regulatory Programs Fee".

headline: Lack of tax breaks halts Comcast move
abstract: Comcast Corporation is seeking tax breaks in exchange for moving its headquarters to Philadelphia, and claims that it would not be as willing to expand its corporate operations in Pennsylvania without tax breaks.  The PA General Assembly closed its two-year legislative session without approving a bill that would grant the desired tax breaks to Comcast.  Many legislators object to giving tax-free living to one of the largest companies in the country.

headline: Pitt makes funding pitch to state
abstract: Te Pitt Alumni Association and University of Pittsburgh Chancellor Mark Nordenberg visited Harrisburg to tout the school's accomplishments and to lobby for more state financial aid.

headline: Four States Seek Out Of New Trade Rules
abstract: The governors of Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, and PA have asked US trade negotiators to resist deals which would override state laws offering preference to in-state industries. US trade representatives have asked states to consider extending an agreement allowing countries to compete for contracts in the US but the four governors have resisted, citing a struggling manufacturing sector in PA Governor Ed Rendell's case.

headline: Naming Rights
abstract: There is a debate about whether allegations of corruption and fraud should preclude the Philadelphia Housing authority from naming a new building after Ron White.  This is the wrong debate to have; even if Ron White had an unblemished legacy, there are several candidates who are more deserving.

headline: Pittsburgh schools to announce closings
abstract: Pittsburgh superintendent John Thompson announced that the district plans to close several schools. He said the closings would enhance the quality of education and strengthen the district's financial future. He had warned of school closings when he announced the preliminary budget in November.

headline: Pa. takes first steps for trade with Cuba
abstract: Pennsylvania became the first state, and Philadelphia the first port in the Northeast corridor, to sign formal trade commitments with Cuba after PA companies signed trade agreements for $35,000 worth of apples and cattle. PA Agriculture Secretary Dennis Wolff said that trade agreements with Cuba make sense and that, as part of the agreement, state officials would urge PA's Congressional delegation in Washington, DC to remove the US travel embargo. US Senator Rick Santorum joined President George W. Bush in remaining opposed to removing the trade and travel embargos.

headline: Preschool program gets $100,000 gift
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed accepted a $100,000 private donation for Harrisburg School District to expand early education initiatives, while requesting that more local money be donated. Reynolds Construction, which will receive a tax credit for the contribution, designated the gift for the city's rapidly expanding all-day early childhood classes.

headline: 199th District
abstract: The author profiles the candidates in the race for the 199th District seat in the PA House of Representatives, Republican PA State Representative Will Gabig and Democratic challenger Christian Muniz. The focus of the analysis is the candidate's differing views on reducing the property tax burden, with Gabig preferring a lower but broader sales tax while Muniz favors an increase in the state income tax. The author, on behalf of the Patriot-News, endorses Muniz for the seat.

headline: Acquisition helps firm bolster online training
abstract: Knowledge Planet, formerly Knowledge Soft of Mechanicsburg, announced yesterday that it acquired Massachusetts-based company Knowledge Impact, another player in the online learning field.

headline: Referendums not smart, say Pa. school officials
abstract: School superintendents in the Lehigh Valley, such as John Reinhart of Bangor Area School District, oppose state legislation that would allow referenda on school district budgets. The bill, House Bill 113, increases state funding to districts and requires that districts which increase property taxes above the state average subject their plans to voter approval. Local school administrators state there are "too many underfunded mandates," such as the federal No Child Left Behind Act.

headline: A night for Dems to celebrate Clinton, Carter & Gore
abstract: Gar Joseph recounts the Democratic National Convention's first night, describing it as an "infomercial aimed at convincing Americans they can do better than President Bush." Speeches were given by former presidents Bill Clinton and Jimmy Carter, as well as former vice president Al Gore. PA Governor Ed Rendell attended the convention, and defended Teresa Heinz Kerry's telling a reporter to "shove it." Rendell stated she was polite compared to US Vice President Dick Cheney.

headline: BLOCK THE RAISE
abstract: Although critical issues have been left unresolved, legislators have found time before the end of the current legislative session to plan a pay raise.  This raise is undeserved and Governor Rendell should veto any pay-raise proposal that lands on his desk.

headline: Region's schools are ranked 8th in U.S.
abstract: Expansion Management magazine ranked Pittsburgh area school districts as the eighth best for publicly funded secondary education in the US amongst larger metropolitan areas. Harrisburg, Lancaster, and Allentown areas all fared well in the rankings amongst smaller metropolitan areas.

headline: A street-smart master of connections
abstract: The article is a feature article about the professional and personal lives of Ronald A. White,  a successful and influential Philadelphia lawyer from a difficult housing project in North Philadelphia. Despite his fatherless upbringing and his juvenile run-ins with the law, White worked hard to earn undergraduate and law degrees and has connections with many officials throughout the City of Philadelphia. Now he is being investigated as part of a federal corruption probe, has received a letter that he is likely to be charged, and those people that previously had tapped into him as a resource for connections have severed their ties with him.

headline: State Senate passes alternative energy bill
abstract: A bill passed in the state Senate on Thursday requires that utilities provide 18 percent of the electricity used in PA from alternative sources such as wind, solar and waste coal.  Utilities must meet this goal by 2020.  The bill still requires approval by the House.

headline: Rendell made good choice for education chief
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is applauded by the author for his nomination for PA Secretary of Education, Francis Barnes. The author has personal experience working with Barnes at the school board level.

headline: A unity Cabinet
abstract: The author says the partisan differences over foreign policy issues could be resolved if presidential candidate US Senator John Kerry were to announce a Cabinet that would include prominent Republican legislators.

headline: Rendell, Hickernell still at loggerheads on ed funding
abstract: PA Governor Edward G. Rendell has vowed to stand his ground against legislation that would require the state to fund school districts at a previous year's spending level if the Legislature has not passed a budget by August 15 of any given year. PA Representative Dave Hickernell, who introduced the bill, sent a letter to Rendell asking him to reconsider his veto threat in the interest of Pennsylvania's children. Hickernell sponsored the legislation that would establish the Emergency Basic Education Subsidy Fund in response to the 2003 state budget impasse that delayed state funding to PA's 501 school districts until late December. Abe Amoros, deputy spokesman for Rendell, said the governor intends to veto the bill.

headline: Absent Rendell hurting party in primaries
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has largely stayed out of the Democratic Party primary election campaigns after having difficulty securing support from Democrats for his own gubernatorial campaign two years prior and gaining help with his budget from Republicans, promising not to campaign against them in the process. PA State Representative Bill DeWeese has called for Rendell to help on the primary trail but Rendell has resisted as he seeks to secure passage of his agenda through a Republican-controlled PA Congress.

headline: Changing Skyline: Barriers remain to public at Water Works and trail
abstract: The city of Philadelphia recently completed two related projects--the Schuykill River Park trail and the renovation of the adjacent Fairmount Water Works.  Both projects were popular successes, but full public access to these public amenities is not guaranteed.  The partk trail is blocked by CSX railroad tracks and the restaurants and establishments that will soon inhabit Water Works may be too exclusive and expensive to reach a wide spectrum of people.  Access to both should be broad and inclusive and steps need to be taken to make this a reality.

headline: Rendell: Should get involved in politics
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell visited Ambridge Area High School, who's marching band he had supported in their bid to perform at the Annual Tournament of Roses Parade in California, and urged students to participate in their political system.

headline: Ad war narrows to 14 states
abstract: With the election less than a month away, presidential candidates George W. Bush and US Senator John Kerry have narrowed the focus of their campaigns to key battleground states and pulled advertisements from states where one candidate is comfortable ahead.

headline: County may get 10th judge
abstract: On Thursday, the House of Representative unanimously passed legislation that authorizes 15 new judgeships statewide, including one for the 11th judicial district of Luzerne County.  The bill now goes back to the Senate Judiciary Committee and then to the full Senate for passage before being referred to Governor Ed Rendell.

headline: School districts racing state clock
abstract: School districts such as East Stroudsburg are racing to borrow money ahead of the implementation of the Homeowner Tax Relief Act, which will force school districts to put tax increases that exceed the rate of inflation on the ballot as a voter referendum. School districts are looking to secure funding even if the money is not immediately needed, as they fret over the viability of provisions to allow fast-growing districts to bypass the referendums.

headline: All in the (divided) family
abstract: The author offers a personal anecdote to illustrate the divisiveness created by the presidential race between incumbent President George W. Bush and US Senator John Kerry.

headline: Transit looks for a tow from state
abstract: Insiders say that a permanent fix that would eliminate the possibility of service reductions and fare increase for the Southeastern PA Transportation Authority and the Port Authority of Allegheny County is ulikely to occur before the end of this legislative session.  More realistic is another stop-gap measure that would keep buses and trains running at the two largest transit agencies in the state.

headline: School officials: PSSA error raises accuracy question
abstract: The PA Department of Education revealed that an error on the PA System of School Assessment standardized tests used to measure student progress, leading school officials to express concerns the numbers are not reliable. The Department has said that the error will not affect the scores.

headline: Anti-Kerry movie to be shown in Montgomery County
abstract: The film Stolen Honor: Wounds that Never Heal, which is critical of US Senator and presidential candidate John Kerry's record in the Vietnam War, was screened in Harrisburg by a Young Republican group and will be shown again in Montgomery County.

headline: Officials urge residents to return tax relief forms
abstract: Officials are urging property owners in the region to return tax-relief forms by December 31st.
