abstract: The author examines the nominees for the Lehigh Valley minor-league baseball franchise stadium site, focusing on the increasing likelihood a partially-built stadium in Williams Township will be chosen as the site by PA Governor Ed Rendell. The author prefers Rendell choose the Williams Township site and investors unless other investors at a separate site are able to attract a high-level minor league team.

headline: Airline unions: Was no sickout
abstract: Union leaders argue that chronic understaffing by US Airways, not a staged "sickout" by airline employees, is to blame for the company's Christmas meltdown.  Of approximately 1,675 flight attendants scheduled to work over the three busy travel days, about 300 called in sick daily, which was much higher than anticipated.

headline: Institutions show signs of strain
abstract: Pennsylvania'a community college system is showing signs of strain.  Schools are faced with increasing community needs and surging enrollments, but struggle to keep pace due to shortages in state funding.  Governor Rendell is setting aside 20 million for community colleges this year, and his administration is working with community colleges to identify the schools' most pressing needs.

headline: Brightbill expects costly liability fight
abstract: In response to the issue of capping awards on medial-malpractice lawsuits, PA Senator David J. "Chip" Brightbill said he believes a statewide referendum on the issue will probably be held during the May 2005 primary elections. Brightbill, the Senate Majority Leader, commented on medical-malpractice measures during the annual Berks County Chamber of Commerce legislative breakfast. The issue has been discussed in other states as well, including Texas and Oregon where about $15 million has been spent in the past year campaigning for a medical-malpractice cap. PA doctors hail caps as the solution to soaring medical-malpractice rates. PA Representative Douglas G. Reichley of Lehigh County said the insurance costs affect doctors, hospitals and all sectors of the economy.

headline: State eyes downtown W-B
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry is planning to relocate within Wilkes-Barre city limits, as its lease on offices in Wilkes-Barre Township is about to expire. DLI spokesperson DLI press secretary Frank Kane stated that the department prefers downtown locations, and that the Rendell administration is committed to helping the agency revitalize downtown locations. Furthermore, with a 1% city wage tax, the city could generate more income. Neither the mayor nor council chairwoman Kathy Kane were available to comment.

headline: States will tweak jobless benefits, taxes
abstract: Due to recession-induced job losses, the Pennsylvania unemployment trust fund does not have enough funding to remain solvent.  As such, the Department of Labor and Industry is raising the taxes paid by businesses to support unemployment benefits and reducing the benefits that unemployed workers receive.

headline: Appointment to gambling board prompts lawsuit
abstract: State Representative Jeffrey Coy resigned his legislative post to accept an appointment to the PA Gaming Control Board.  In response to Coy's appointment, the state attorney general's office filed suit--arguing that the state constitution prohibits lawmakers from being appointed to paid state government jobs during the terms for which they were elected.

headline: City man gets $825,000 award
abstract: Elmer Varner of Harrisburg was awarded $825,000 in a medical malpractice suit after complications from heart surgery left him disabled. The award comes as debate continues on the necessity of caps on malpractice awards, which physician groups have expressed a desire to see passed.

headline: South Side tech firm to add 100 jobs over next 3 years
abstract: Akustica Inc., a firm in Pittsburgh, announced they will expand on the same day the PA Department of Community and Economic Development announced $1 million in state aid for the company.

headline: 2 firms hired to search for executives for state gaming board
abstract: The new Gaming Control Board of Pennsylvania has hired two head-hunting firms to help round up candidates for its three top administrative and legal jobs.  The board waived the usual requirement for competitive bidding in the hiring of executive search firms, arguing that the tight time frame it is under to implement the new gambling expansion law justified an emergency waiver.

headline: Flood victims gauge loss
abstract: Floodwaters from Hurricane Ivan deluged portions of Pennsylvania and New Jersey--prompting Governor Rendell to expand his request for federal disaster relief to 47 of the 67 counties affected by the floods.  So far 19 counties have received federal disaster relief.

headline: Critical shortage of flu vaccine drives prices 'beyond reason'
abstract: Prices for the flu vaccine have skyrocketed after the shortage was announced, as demand increases and wholesalers seek to maximize profits.

headline: Stadium consultant rounds the bases
abstract: A stadium consultant hired by PA Governor Ed Rendell visited four proposed baseball stadium sites in Allentown, Bethlehem, and Williams Township with municipal officials and members of the Lehigh Valley Chamber of Commerce. The consultant will provide a report to Governor Rendell on the four sites before the Governor chooses the site to receive a $12 million state grant which must be matched by the local government.

headline: Lansdowne mulls OK for same-sex benefits
abstract: William Smith, chair of the Lansdowne Borough's finance and administrtation committee, is expected to introduce two resolutions that would ban sexual-orientation based discrimination in the workplace.  The first proposal bans discrimination based on sexual oreintation in employment, and the second provides gay and lesbian borough employees with domestic partnership benefits.  Both proposals are expected to pass, making Lansdowne the first municipality in Delaware County to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation.

headline: Region sits inside hurricane corridor
abstract: Over the past 50 years, remnants of at least 14 hurricanes and tropical storms have caused major flooding and damage in Northeastern PA.  The Northeast corner of the state sits in a corridor often traveled by tropical storms, and because of this meteorologists say that this region will always be at some risk.

headline: Doctors' proposal gets nod at MCP
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter and PA Governor Ed Rendell appeared together to support the effort of a group of doctors to take control of the Medical College of PA and run it as a full-service hospital. Tenet Healthcare Corp. owns the hospital but is looking to pull out with multiple proposals on the table, including ones from Temple University and Drexel University.

headline: State building standards kick in, apply to all
abstract: PA's Uniform Construction Code goes into effect, increasing the debate between rural Pennsylvanians and "city slickers from Pittsburgh and Philadelphia." The article features a series of questions and answers about the code, such as its development history under former Governor Tom Ridge, regulation enforcement by municipalities or the state Department of Labor and Industry, and changes made in the state Legislature. PA Governor Ed Rendell has not yet signed those changes into law. The state DLI and the PA Builders Association contributed to the article.

headline: 20 Years later, US far from head of math class
abstract: More than 20 years after the education report, A Nation at Risk, labeled the American educational system mediocre, results from a 2003 study confirm that the American educational system has not improved much since that time--especially in reagrds to math and science education.  Although American students were above average in the age ranges evaluated, they were still nowhere near the top ranks in math and science literacy.

headline: Pilots stand by veto of offer
abstract: Two pilots' union members stand by their decision to veto U.S. Airways' concession proposal and say they will veto any proposal that they view as anti-labor.  The members believe that the company is not bargaining in good faith and is engaging in union busting.  Many are concerned that U.S. Airways will not be able to reach negotiated settlements with its unions, thus making it impossible for the company to attract new investors and emerge from bankruptcy.

headline: Drexel doctors to use mediation to resolve malpractice complaints
abstract: The faculty of Drexel University College of Medicine will start to use mediation to resolve malpractice complaints before they can go to the court. Medical school dean Steven Klasko said that the school would rather deal with a case now than in four years. PA Governor Ed Rendell's malpractice task force had recommended mediation, while the state Supreme Court's malpractice task force is considering requiring a mediation plan in every county.

headline: State officials promote preservation plan
abstract: PA Agriculture Secretary Dennis Wolff and General Services Administration Secretary Don Cunningham are offering their support for PA Governor Ed Rendell's $800 million Growing Greener II proposal and examining farmland that could be preserved from development through use of the funding. Governor Rendell would like to have the proposal before voters in the November election. If approved, the Governor's plan calls for an increase in waste disposal fees, an aspect of the proposal which will likely face condemnation in the PA legislature as damaging to business interests.

headline: Philly to move juvenile lockup to make room for Barnes
abstract: The Barnes Foundation art gallery in Lower Merion Township contains one of the world's deepest collections of impressionist and post-impressionist paintings.  A recent court decision approved the Barnes Foundation's request to move the gallery from its secluded and exclusive location in Lower Merion Township to a new museum in Center City Philadelphia.  This decision has disappointed art students and enthusiasts alike, as they feel that the new setting lacks intamacy and is not true to the wishes of Dr. Barnes--the original owner of the collection.

headline: State quietly opens facility for young sex offenders
abstract: Pennsylvania has opened a treatment unit at Torrance State Hospital in Derry Township to confine violent young sexual predators who have served their sentences but are too dangerous to be released.  The offenders--all of whom were convicted as juveniles--will be held until they respond to treatment.  Derry township residents and officials are concerned that the facility will pose a problem and have met with state officials to discuss security at the facility.

headline: Flu-shot supplies are cut in half
abstract: Worries of a flu epidemic increased as it was announced the US would receive half of it's normal amount of flu vaccines, leading to calls for only the most vulnerable to receive the shot. PA Department of Health officials and local health department officials all will have shortages, creating fears that the flu may claim more lives this year.

headline: State still mulling whether to construct office building downtown
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry has expressed an interest in relocating its current offices in Wilkes-Barre Township to a new building in Wilkes-Barre City that may be built on a site called the "hole in the ground", Frank Kane, spokesmen for the Department, said. Kane said the agency is in line with the plans of PA Governor Edward G. Rendell to locate state offices in urban areas by encouraging revitalization of the commonwealth's downtowns. The state offices that would be housed in the new facility would include the Bureau of Workers Compensation, Unemployment Compensation Board of Review and Board of Disability Determination.

headline: Street moving fast on home for the Barnes
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street chose the the location for the new Barnes Foundation art collection.  The collection will be housed in a museum built where the Youth Study Center currently resides.  According to Mayor Street, the Youth Study Center will be demolished and the temporarily displaced juveniles will stay at a detention facility at 17th and Cambria streets until a new juvenile center is completed in West Philadelphia.

headline: So, Rendell's had it as guv?
abstract: Reporters respond to Governor Rendell's remarks about not running for re-election next year and wanting to give up politics to be a sportscaster.  A spokesperson for Governor Rendell said he was just blowing off steam and the comments were toungue in cheek.

headline: Focus on the needs of older Americans this month
abstract: As the nation celebrates Older Americans Month, the author, Lehigh County executive Jane Ervin, supports the implementation of programs nationwide and locally through the PA's 52 Agencies on Aging that help the elderly to live independently. She also urges the legislature to maintain adequate funding for the programs.

headline: State sues in alleged housing fraud
abstract: PA Attorney General Jerry Pappert's office filed suit in PA Commonwealth Court against 20 real estate companies and appraisers in the Poconos, accusing them of preying on first-time home buyers by overstating property values and offering low-monthly mortgages. The lawsuit seeks $2.7 million and the banning of those involved from real estate practices.

headline: Allentown stadium deal collapses under weight of bigger plan
abstract: Although Lehigh County Executive Jane Ervin thought that she and Governor Rendell had struck an economic revitalization deal that would bring a baseball stadium,  a major office complex, a hotel, and an industiral park to Allentown, it was her desire to procure funding for more than just a baseball stadium that caused the whole deal to collapse.  Allentown's revitalization plan was thwarted by legislators from Northampton County; legislators opposed the economic revitalization because it did not benefit Northampton County, and because the deal would have increased the hotel room tax.

headline: Ronnie Polaneczky: She made us proud of our city
abstract: Ronnie Polaneczky, the former University of Pennsylvania president credited with leading the effort to transform the neighborhoods surrounding the Penn campus, will receive the Philadelphia Award.

headline: From the Capitol: Midge Rendell's doctor 'goes west'
abstract: At a news conference, PA Governor Ed Rendell announced several proposals to deal with the state's medical malpractice insurance crisis. He also noted that the surgeon who successfully operated on his wife Midge Rendell's herniated disc was among those leaving the state. That surgeon, Steven Dante, relocated to Cincinnati, according to the PA Medical Society.

headline: Tax base growth swings out to suburbs
abstract: A study from the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission confirmed that rural and suburban communities are experiencing strong growth while urban areas continue to see a depleting tax base. In the Lehigh Valley, Allenton, Bethlehem, and Easton all saw plummeting land values while suburban areas were witnessing surging tax bases.

headline: Not all may share in slots-revenue windfall
abstract: School districts across Pennsylvania are deciding whether to sign up for a share of the estimated 1 billion dollars in annual gambling revenue.  Districts are concerned because there are several strings attached to the money.  For example, accepting the gambling money will make raising property taxes in the future more difficult, and it also mandates that districts increase their local earned income tax by .1 percent--something that could have a negative impact on local economies.

headline: Local businesses optimistic about economy
abstract: The PNC Economic Outlook survey shows that business owners in central PA are cautiously optimistic about the economy.  A number of uncertaintites--such as rising health costs, increased energy and raw material costs, and terrorism--could shift the region's economic outlook, however.

headline: Gaming abuse
abstract: The author, the President of the PA Family Institute, lauds PA Governor Ed Rendell for encouraging parents to speak with their kids to prevent drug and alcohol abuse but questions why Rendell did not also address gambling addiction.

headline: The green for Schenley Plaza
abstract: As part of his economic stimulus package, PA Governor Ed Rendell presented the Pittsburgh Parks Conservancy with a $5 million check for the transformation of Schenley Plaza in Pittsburgh from a parking lot into a park. According to Governor Rendell and Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato, the renovations are necessary in order to attract young professionals to an area that is the state's third largest commercial district. The project will be located next to the University of Pittsburgh in an area known as the Oakland plaza.

headline: Bridge panel plans to borrow 40 million
abstract: Even though it will be running a 115 million dollar surplus next year, the Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission plans to borrow 40 million for unspecified construction and road projects.  While many have criticized the move, Frank G. McCartney, the commission executive director, claims that it makes better financial sense to borrow the money at current low interest rates than to use future toll profits or borrow at a significantly higher rate later.

headline: Old hand guiding Kerry's PA effort
abstract: Terry Podesta, the strategist who handled Bill Clinton's successful campaigns in Pennsylvania in 1992 and 1996, is now Senator John Kerry's top strategist in PA.  Politicians in PA lobbied to have him as the top strategist because of his connections, his ability to react quickly and his ability to keep Washington bigwigs from meddling.

headline: Health costs emerging as election issue
abstract: US Representative Tim Murphy and Democratic challenger Mark Boles have turned to medical care issues in their race to be the US Representative for the 18th District in PA. Murphy advocates a program to modernize health care practices while Boles is seeking a more active government role in regulating the profits of insurance companies.

headline: Times sure are tough for Comcast
abstract: The opinion article by Eric Heyl ridicules the comments by Comcast that it cannot afford to reduce rates in Pennsylvania if it receives state and local tax breaks to build a skyscraper in Philadelphia. Comcast wants to build a new corporate building at a site in the Keystone Opportunity Improvement Zone, which would exempt the company from paying business taxes for 15 years. PA Governor Edward G. Rendell supports the Comcast tax abatement, the reason for which Comcast executive vice president David Cohen, who was Rendell's chief of staff when he was mayor of Philadelphia, says has nothing to do with their past relationship. Heyl mocks comments by Cohen about the inability of the company to rollback a recent 6 percent rate increase when it has experienced incredible growth in the past year.

headline: Incentives needed for young workers
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature spends too much time working on salary increases and personal issues and not enough time trying to figure out a way to keep graduates of Pennsylvania colleges and universities in the state after graduation.  While our legislature has created many incentives for seniors to move and stay in the state, it has done nothing to encourage young workers to stay in the state after college to seek employment here.

headline: County faces 1.25 million bill for voting machines
abstract: Because of a mandated switchover from lever-style voting machines to electronic ones, Fayette County must come up with 1.25 million dollars to fund the new machines.  Fayette County is fuding the switchover partially with state grants, but officials are uncertain as to how they will raise the remaining 1.25 million.

headline: Health fair seeks to help area's Mexicans
abstract: Binational Health Week will be marked by a health fair in Kennett Square that aims to bring free medical help to the growing Mexican community. Chester County Commissioner Andrew Dinniman estimated that there were approximately 25,000 Mexicans in Chester County, though the official tally is 16,000.

headline: Towers Perrin to remain in Phila.
abstract: Towers Perrin, a major management consulting firm has decided to keep a facility in Center City Philadelphia, rather than move to New Jersey, and renewed its lease. City and state officials coordinated a campaign to convince the firm to stay, including a personal phone call from PA Governor Ed Rendell to Towers Perrin real estate director David Duncan. Rendell and Philadelphia Mayor John Street, both at the Democratic National Convention, joined Towers Perrin's announcement by video conference from Boston.

headline: On Barnes plans, lessons in success and failure
abstract: Although some are concerned that the new Barnes Foundation musuem will ultimately fail, the Barnes has a few elements that recently failed museums lacked.  First, the museum will be home to hundreds of impressionist paintings.  Second,  the foundation has the support of the Philadelphia region's civic and political leaders and the backing of three large charitable organizations.

headline: PUC decision anticipated in showdown on electricity deregulation
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission is scheduled to meet with the Duquesne Light Company to determine how the company's 587,000 customers will purchase electricity in a deregulated market.  The terms and conditions of how power will be sold after deregulation has pitted the Duquesne Light Company, Governor Rendell and big business against the Public Utility Commission.

headline: Health plan is held as a cure-all
abstract: The Federal Employee Health Benefits plan is again being lauded by politicians as a model to look to in efforts to reform the US health care system, with both President George W. Bush and presidential candidate US Senator John Kerry citing it as their blueprint. Kerry has proposed an expansion of the system to cover small businesses,  focusing on the ability of the system to encourage competition amongst health care providers.

headline: UGI gas tank now gone from Allentown skyline
abstract: Allentown Mayor Roy Afflerbach joined UGI Corporation to mark the end of the removal of the UGI gas tank that had been part of the Allentown skyline for more than 70 years. The property has been marked for redevelopment, possibly as parking for the proposed baseball stadium for a minor league team in Allentown.

headline: Passport upgrade needs more work
abstract: The United States is implementing new technology that will make electronic data gathering part of the passport and visa process.  A tiny chip on passports and visas will be used to transmit information through the air to a reading device.  Because the data is transmitted via radio signal, however, many worry that the data will be gathered by unauthorized persons and lead to identity theft.

headline: The Mayor and City Unions Enough of False Choices
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street is presenting the public with a false choice: pursue tax reforms or give workers fair raises.  The city has room in its budget to achieve both objectives, and the big question is how to balance these two goals--something difficult, but not impossible.

headline: Hundreds line up for flu vaccine
abstract: Lehigh Valley Hospital and Health Network sponsored a community immunization clinic with hundreds of people attending, seeking reclusive flu shots. The Hospital had decided to forego there typical round of clinics when news got out that there was a shortage of flu immunization shots this year. Members of the Allentown Bureau of Health were also on hand.

headline: Valley lawmakers back away from stadium funding idea
abstract: Legislators and local officials in the Lehigh Valley are debating the means to pay for a minor league baseball stadium, with the proposed increase in the hotel tax meeting opposition from those who want to use slot revenues. Stadium backers of proposed plans must provide an outline of who will play in the stadium and how the stadium will be financed to PA Governor Ed Rendell, who will ultimately decide the site.

headline: Victaulic workers donate flu shots
abstract: Employees of Victaulic Corporation of America donated a portion of their flu vaccines to residents of the Praxis Alzheimer's facility.  This was extremely helpful, as the supply of flu shots was dramatically limited this year.

headline: Municipalities ask for flood help
abstract: Greene County residents attempting to repair flood-damaged homes may apply for grants through the Federal Emergency Management Agency.  Local government bodies and agencies are also eligible for federal grants, but some costs and damages associated with the flood--costs such as overtime hours, damage to public buildings, damage to roads and equiptment--is not reimbursable yet.

headline: Insurance increases could hurt districts
abstract: PA school districts will pay 30% more for health insurance on average, according to the PA School Boards Association. The Shippensburg School District was told to expect a 90% increase, however, said Superintendent David Landis. The costs to Shippensburg and other school districts such as Big Spring are attributed to increased costs for medical services and prescriptions.

headline: Ace Ltd.'s latest hurricane: Probe of industry
abstract: New York Attorney General Eliot Spitzer's office is investigating the insurance industry, challenging the growth of Philadelphia-based commercial insurer Ace Ltd. The investigation was predicted to slow business and squeeze premiums.

headline: Lieutenant governor must be at top of game
abstract: This article questions the competence of PA lieutenant governor Catherine Baker Knoll and speculates on whether she will run for re-election in 2006.  Lieutenant governor Knoll seems unable to perform her job without a lot of help, and frequently confuses names and titles.  This is problematic for someone presiding over the state Senate.

headline: 20 steps to make way to school safer
abstract: The number of Philadelphia school children hit by cars has doubled in recent years.  In response to this trend,  City Councilman Jim Kenney compiled a 154-page report containing 20 recommendations to make school zones safer.  One major recommendation is that the school district take over the crossing-guard program from the Philadelphia Police Department.

headline: Lawmaker unrelenting in push for workplace smoking ban
abstract: PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf is pursuing support for legislation he introduced which will ban smoking in public buildings in PA, including restaurants, lobbies, schools, and even the recently-legalized casinos. Greenleaf acknowledges the legislation may not survive opponents who deride it as intrusive but feels public acceptance is growing, opening the door for possible breakthroughs.

headline: Betting against State House: Is this the month for gambling in PA?
abstract: The editorial addresses whether or not the PA Legislature will make gambling legal in the state in response to a proposal by PA Governor Edward G. Rendell. State Police Commissioner Jeffrey Miller said he is concerned about security at the casinos and about organized crime, so he is already preparing by hoping to set up a 279-man unit for gaming enforcement. The editorial board believes that the proposal will be approved before the June 30 recess of the Legislature because of the significant amount of revenue gambling will generate for the state, but it is worried about the question of where in Philadelphia casinos will be placed.

headline: A tax too far/The city schools should cut excess capacity first
abstract: Pittsburgh school superintendent John Thompson has proposed a 22.5 percent jump in school property taxes by 2006.  Before it contemplates raising taxes, the school district should take a look at its spending, and an obvious starting point is reducing excess school capacity.

headline: Why Doctors are leaving
abstract: Many physicians are leaving Pennsylvania because of high malpractice premiums.  Although Governor Rendell talks a good game when it comes to tort reform, the fact remains that he received a large contribution from the Philadelphia Trial Lawyers Association and has failed to enact real reforms that could keep doctors in the state.

headline: Lawmakers hear complaints over soaring health care costs
abstract: Marilyn Landis, a small business representative from Basic Business Concepts, was joined by farmers, unions and the uninsured at a hearing on rising health care costs at a hearing at the PA House Majority Policy Committee yesterday. Gabe Morgan, a local director for the Service Employees International Union, predicted larger strikes while Bruce Hottle of Eagle Concrete Products lamented the rising cost of family health-care coverage in his company. Also in attendance were Pittsburgh's Local 5 of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers and the PA Farm Bureau. The PA Health Care Cost Containment Council at the same time released reasons for the increase in costs.

headline: Bettis carries slots issue to Black Caucus
abstract: Steelers running back Jerome Bettis met with members of the General Assembly's Black Caucus endorsing a proposed Pittsburgh track and slot machine parlor, an activity that may be against the National Football League's rule prohibiting gambling activities by players. PA legislators said they understand that Bettis has a financial arrangement with developer C.J. Betters on the Pittsburgh Palisades Park, which includes the track, slot parlor and housing and retail development. PA Representative Jake Wheatley said Bettis, Betters and representatives from four horse racing tracks met with the Black Caucus to discuss plans for including minorities in all levels of the gambling industry. PA Senator Jay Costa called Bettis' involvement an "excellent move" and an example of inclusion, though it may go against NFL rules governing gambling.

headline: Williams' baseball hopes dim
abstract: Although Governor Rendell did not name the recipient of a 12 million dollar baseball stadium grant, it seems unlikely that the Williams Township stadium proposal will get Governor Rendell's approval.  The governor has expressed concern about the debt developers would take on to finish the Williams Township stadium, but sources say Governor Rendell also has misgivings about the Allentown proposal.

headline: In dead heat, Ohio poised to be another Florida
abstract: Ohio--like other key swing states such as Pennsylvania and Florida--is likely to have a strong impact on the 2004 presidential election.  Although the state is crucial to electoral success, it seems poised for the kind of embarrassing uncertainty that plagued Florida after the 2000 presidential election; almost three quarters of Ohio still use punch-card ballots.

headline: Medical malpractice crisis
abstract: PA senators discussed a proposed constitutional change placing caps on awards in medical malpractice lawsuits yesterday, while Drexel University College of Medicine and Abington Memorial Hospital are practicing mediation as a solution to malpractice cases. Mediation, a confidential process, involves patients or loved ones being invited to a mediation session with the hospital to discuss alternative outcomes to the situation. The editorial board considers mediation a "smart step" in the direction of solving PA's medical malpractice crisis.

headline: Bidding plan draws fire
abstract: Pete Tartline, president of the Technology Council of Central PA and Kevin L Shivers, state director of the National Federation of Independent Business, said that the Rendell administration's plan to save money by having firms bid for contracts will have negative long-term effects. They say that the contracts will end up going to large-scale corporations at the expense of small, locally-owned businesses. Tartline and Shivers note that the federal government began bundling contracts 12 years ago, and in the process only 19% of contracts were awarded to small businesses.

headline: Turnpike, workers to resume pact talks
abstract: PA Turnpike workers have been without a contract since September 30th.  Talks are scheduled to resume today between the Teamsters Locals 250 and 77 and the PA Turnpike Commission.  A strike is not anticipated, though it remains a possibility.

headline: Waynesburg residents scrub away Ivan's muck
abstract: Heavy rain from Hurricane Ivan led to flooding in the low-lying areas of Waynesburg.

headline: Medical malpractice resolution tabled by senators
abstract: The PA Senate Judiciary Committee voted to table a measure to amend the state's constitution to cap pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits. The measure is mostly opposed by Democrats. Physicians contend that frivolous jury awards are driving up the cost of medical malpractice insurance, causing an exodus of doctors from the state.

headline: Bronner: No rescuers for US Airways
abstract: US Airways chairman David Bronner predicts that if the airline needs to file a second bankruptcy claim within the next month they may be doomed, as he does not envision any possible help on the horizon in that scenario. US Airways is attempting to avoid defaulting on a federally-backed loan, requesting a reduction by the U.S. Internal Revenue Service.

headline: School zone speeding bill a hit in W. PA
abstract: Many across the state support legislation currently under consideration in the state Senate that would increase penalties for those that speed in school zones.  The School Zone Saftey Act is designed to increase child saftey and lower the number of children hit by cars in schools zones.

headline: It was total chaos
abstract: Over the weekend, flooding caused by former Hurricane Ivan's tropical moisture wreaked havoc throughout central Pennsylvania.  Some of the worst damage came a day before in Dauphin County, however, where residents had little time to react to the surging waters of Stony Creek.

headline: Meeting to focus on suicide prevention
abstract: The author conducted an interview with the executive director for the PA Alliance for the Mentally Ill, who will be visiting Pittsburgh to speak at a conference on suicide. The transcript of the interview is included.

headline: Cities can't enforce zoning, planning rules on casinos
abstract: The new slots legislation does not include measures allowing local government's to enforce zoning or planning regulations, an aspect of the bill PA State Senator Vincent Fumo's office say is necessary to allow the state to maximize the profit from tax revenues. While the slots bill will allow greater latitude for the casinos to secure beneficial locations, it does not allow state or local officials to claim land through eminent domain as well as allowing local officials a 2-month period wherein they may comment on possible sites to the PA Gaming Board.

headline: Lame Ducks
abstract: For far too long, legislators in Pennsylvania have manipulated the system with late-night votes and lame-ducks sessions.  Yet again, legislators are hiding behind a lame-duck session to enact a pay raise.  Only when the legislature stops its duplicity will it earn the respect of the public.

headline: Rendell Appoints Phila. Judge, The Only Woman in Slots Board
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell appointed Philadelphia Common Pleas Court judge Mary D. Collins to the state Gaming Board.  She is the final appointment to the board and the only female member.

headline: Needed changes in long-term care
abstract: The Executive Director and the Senior Executive Policy Specialist for PA Governor Ed Rendell's Office of Health Care Reform address the need for a long-term care policy which reflects the wishes of Pennsylvanians to stay in their homes as long as possible before moving to assisted-living facilities. The article supports Governor Rendell's initiative as it is rolled out in a few areas around the state, including Philadelphia.

headline: CMU administrator picked for gambling commission
abstract: Carnegie Mellon University's assistant vice-president of enrollment Sanford Rivers was named by PA Governor Ed Rendell as a member of PA's Gaming Control Board. Rivers said he was surprised but would serve full-time in the position, realizing the difficulty the Board will face with no history of gambling regulations in PA.

headline: Who's policing the cops?
abstract: Philadelphia mayor John Street has had a year to appoint members to the city's Police Advisory Commission and has failed to do so.  His failure to make appointments promopted City Council to pass a resolution urging the mayor to make the appointments, but Mayor Street has not yet selected the 7 members of the commission.  There is some urgency here, as citizens continue to file complaints with the commission.

headline: Low-cost airlines tiptoeing into Pittsburgh market
abstract: Traditionally, Pittsburgh International Airport had very few low-fare carriers, but this trend seems to be changing with the financial troubles of U.S. Airways and its decision to close its hub at PIA.  The airport has been working with Allegheny County officials to bring new service to Pittsburgh, but experts say that the expansion of low-fare service ultimately depends on what happens to U.S. Airways and its impending bankruptcy.

headline: News from the Pennsylvania General Assembly
abstract: A bill passed by the House 192-4 exempts existing one-family and two-family homes undergoing repairs from the Pennsylvania's Uniform Construction Code, which PA Representative Sam Smith calls an "administrative nightmare for small, rural municipalities." PA Representative Curt Schroder said he introduced a resolution to force the House Judiciary Committee to release a bill that would allow limits on pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits. A bill to extend the deadline for dentists to pass a clinical evaluation and office inspection before obtaining a permit to administer anesthesia passed in the PA House 200-0 and goes to the PA Senate. PA Representative Matthew Good sponsored a bill that was passed in the House 193-8 that would set aside more than $1.8 million in state funding for Lake Erie College of Osteopathic Medicine.

headline: Deal reached for IP site
abstract: It is highly likely that MTR Gaming Group Incorporated will build a horse racetrack on the former International Paper Company in Erie, while local officials are pushing for state funding to develop the former IP site to include a movie theater and access to Lake Erie. PA Governor Ed Rendell is committed to providing that money as long as the state Legislature acts on his economic-stimulus package which includes legalizing slot machines at horse racetracks. MTR also plans to build racetracks in Summit or McKean townships, pending approval from the PA Horse Racing Commission.

headline: More to guiding teens than no
abstract: Parents, teachers and religious leaders need to realize that keeping our children safe requires more than just telling them "no" or giving them a list of "don'ts."  If all we do is tell them no, we run the risk of rendering our message meaningless.  We therefore must find a balance that allows us to take some mystery out of the forbidden--those things we don’t want our children to do--without condoning those very things.

headline: Beleaguered gaming chair nominee says his record manifests integrity
abstract: Frank Friel, a former Philadelphia cop appointed by Governor Rendell to head PA's Gaming Control Board, accuses the Philadelphia Daily news of exacting payback against him for his testimony in a libel suit against the newspaper.  The Daily News ran a series of stories questioning Friel's character--focusing on unsubstantiated allegations and acting as if there was a smoking gun where there wasn't one.  Friel claims he hasn't done anything wrong and would not change his actions.

headline: No large decline in doctors leaving state
abstract: The alleged increase in doctors leaving PA due to high malpractice premiums was not reflected in statistics released by the PA Insurance Department and the Pennsylvania Medical Society. Researchers for the Pennsylvania Medical Society attributed the lack of a sizable decline to increased demand through the growing population, which should have necessitated a substantial increase in doctors. The Medical Society has argued for a cap on malpractice suit awards but patient advocate and lawyers have argued against it.

headline: Don't bet on big tax relief, Senate study says
abstract: On the proposal to pay property tax rebates with gambling revenue, PA Senate Republicans released a study which showed reductions for citizens property tax bills but also not nearly to the degree most envision, according to PA Senate Appropriations Chairman Robert Thompson. The study is the latest in the ongoing debate for the limited legalization of slots in the state in order to generate a new revenue source, a proposal backed by PA Governor Ed Rendell. Some PA Republicans have questioned the promise of the proposal and the figures released by Governor Rendell and the debate figures to heat up after the primary on April 27th.

headline: Letters urge Rendell to snub club
abstract: Developer Richard Muller Jr. is seeking a state grant for his Alpine Rose Resorts project--a project that would include a race course and country club.  Muller claims that the project merits state funding because it will benefit the local and regional economy, but local residents and the Blue Mountain Preservation Association claim that the project will only benefit the rich and has no social value.  For this reason, the association has appealed the Eldred Township supervisors' decision to grant preliminary approval to Alpine Rose.

headline: PA county may be the nation's recreation capital
abstract: Pennsylvania's most sparsely populated county--Forest County--leads the country in recreational homes.  Three out of every four dwellings are used occassionally--as second homes--according to the U.S. Census Bureau.  Most part-time residents do not consider making the county their full-time home because job opportunities are sparse.

headline: Numbers disputed in debate over caps
abstract: Those in support of a $250,000 cap on awards for pain and suffering in medical malpractice lawsuits state that most malpractice insurers have left PA, making it even more difficult for doctors to gain coverage, but those opposed point to the fact that 17 new insurers obtained approval form the PA Insurance Department, nine of which are risk-retention groups. Joseph Brady of the Professional Casualty Association hopes his group will become "the premier writer for Pennsylvania doctors." Nonetheless, a doctor representing the PA Medical Society told a state Senate committee that the number of malpractice insurers is only 3.

headline: Ex-mayor set to retire specialist job
abstract: Bill Gamble, a former Oakdale mayor and a state specialist in municipal police merges, is retiring after 24 years as a state employee and the past 17 years with the Governor's center for Local Government Services. Gamble said he believes it is the responsibility of the Legislature to call for merging or sharing police departments. Gamble said his retirement plans include perhaps going into private consulting. Greg Morgan, spokesman for the PA Department of Economic and Community Development, said the state is committed to keeping the regional office in which Gamble worked but will miss the resources that Gamble provided.

headline: Officials seek to beef up use of convention center
abstract: In response to several complaints from local businesses, state and city officials are holding a public hearing on Friday to find ways to imporve and increase business at Pittsburgh's David L. Lawrence Convention Center.

headline: Governor Rendell's anger toward reporters glosses over flaws in gaming law
abstract: Governor Rendell criticized the press for unfairly treating  Frank Friel, his nominee to head up the new state Gaming Control Board.  The media raised public attention to certain elements of Friel's past, ultimately causing him to resign his post.  Mr. Friel's background does create a cloud of doubt and suspicion, and the media were right to make this information available to the public.

headline: Proposed amendment only part of solution
abstract: A plan sponsored by PA Senator James Rhoades was approved after 12 hours of negotiation, taking the first steps to a constitutional amendment limiting pain and suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits in the state. The editorial board believes this is only one small step in the solution to the medical malpractice insurance crisis, in which doctors claim large awards are driving up the cost of their insurance. The board considers a few other complementary solutions, such as one suggested by PA Governor Ed Rendell that the PA Supreme Court "should adopt a rule that would bar attorneys from bringing a malpractice suit without obtaining a certificate of merit from an independent physician."

headline: Foes of Sheetz beer plan pack hearing
abstract: Ministers such as the Reverend Gary Dull and members of the Malt Beverage Distributors Association of PA spoke before the PA Liquor Control Board in opposition to a Sheetz convenience store selling beer. PLCB examiner Tom Miller will have 60 days to review the testimony before making a recommendation to the board. Dull contends that the decision to allow beer sale should be up to the state Legislature, while David A. Shipula of the MBDA of PA contends that Sheetz will begin to compete with beer distributors.

headline: A record 600 million spent on presidential campaign ads
abstract: During the 2004 election, Senator John Kerry and President George Bush spent a combined 600 million dollars on political advertising.  That figure is triple the amount spent on radio and television ads in 2000, making the 2004 election the most expensive in history.

headline: Thompson demands bonuses
abstract: John W. Thompson, Superintendent of Pittsburgh Public Schools, claims that he is owed as much as 70,000 dollars in bonus pay.  Both he and the school board acknowledge that the matter might go to arbitration if the board refuses to pay.

headline: Report: malpractice crisis driven by economic climate
abstract: A report released by Public Citizen contends that there is no correlation between increasing malpractice insurance costs and the number of malpractice lawsuits or amounts of settlements, but rather reflect the current economic status. Frank Clemente, director of Congress Watch, a Public Citizen project, stated that a proposed amendment currently before the state Senate to cap pain and suffering damages at $250,000 would hurt patients who suffered from negligent medical treatment. The report also showed the number of cases filed in Philadelphia dropped by more than half in 2003 due to a PA Supreme Court measure mandating malpractice lawsuits occur in the counties where the treatment occurred.

headline: Harness-racing applicant touts benefits of mile track
abstract: The PA Harness Racing Commission heard testimony from Bedford Downs, applicants for the state's final harness-racing license, who said their longer racetrack will serve to provide more competitive races and safer elements for the horses. There is one other applicant for the license, which will likely be used to also set up a slots gambling operation.

headline: Election picks/A recap of the Post-Gazette's endorsements
abstract: This editorial reiterates the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette's endorsements for the 2004 state and federal elections.  It covers endorsements for presidential elections, U.S. Senate, State Auditor General, State Attorney General, State Treasurer, U.S. House, State Senate, and the State House of Representatives.

headline: Waiting list for health care surges in PA
abstract: Pennsylvania's adultBasic insurance program, which is designed to provide health insurance to poor, uninsured adults, has a waiting list of over 100,000 people.  The list has gone up a third since February--due mostly to increases in insurance costs--and has beomce a major theme in the U.S. Senate race between Arlen Specter and Joseph M. Hoeffel.  Hoeffel wants a comprhensive solution that would give the working poor access to the health insurance plan members of Congress have, while Specter wants to improve upon our current market-based system of health care.

headline: Report: PA helping to insure children
abstract: A report by the Pennsylvania Partnerships for Children, an independent nonpartisan group that evaluates the health, education and well-being of PA's children, stated that though PA does a good job of enrolling uninsured children in health insurance programs, it fails in relation to providing equitable education programs. According to the State of the Child in PA 2004 report, one in six children under the age of 5 lives in poverty while parents of 60 percent of children under age 5 work. A study by the National Institute for Early Education Research found that PA pre-kindergarten falls short on seven of 10 quality standards. PA Representative Robert J. Thompson of West Goshen said he believed the state's public schools' funding formula needs to be changed but lawmakers are unsure how to do so.

headline: Hart's legislation aims to boost metals industry
abstract: US Representative Melissa Hart and US Steel President and Chief Operating Officer John P. Surma Jr. joined forces to plea for increased federal funding for metals industry research because funding for the Metals Initiative and the Manufacturing Extension Partnership is tied up in the US Congress. Hart and Surma were joined at a US Steel Tower news conference by Lisa Roudabush, manager of US Steel's research efforts, American Iron and Steel Institute President Andrew G. Sharkey and Pittsburgh Technology Council Chief Executive Steve Zylstra. The Metals Initiative funds research to reduce energy consumption and pollution and boost competitiveness, and a bill introduced by Hart would provide $10 million annually for the program. A majority of the money ends up in Western Pennsylvania.

headline: Senate race hinges on recognition
abstract: Although he has spent only 2 million less than Senator Arlen Specter, U.S. Representative JoeHoeffel is still unknown to more than half of Pennsylvania's voters.  Senator Specter has the type of name recognition that comes from 24 years of national service--something that will be hard for Congressman Hoeffel and others to overcome on election day.

headline: Gar Joseph Kerry Fundraiser here is up in the air
abstract: Efforts by local Democratic leaders to hold a rally and fund raiser for presidential hopeful John Kerry were stalled.  The Kerry campaign is disorganized and failed to coordinate its efforts through Philadelphia's Democratic City Committee.  As a result, leaders have not been able to pin down Senator Kerry's schedule.

headline: School districts can't keep footing benefits bill
abstract: Many of PA's school districts are facing rising health care costs, forcing them to either cut expenses or raise taxes. Furthermore, many school districts are reporting difficulty in implementing the federal No Child Left Behind Act, because they cannot stretch tax dollars to cover the act's expenses. Some districts are exploring other means to cover health care costs, such as the Nazareth Area School District, which is self-insured.

headline: Hooters Air could wing into Pittsburgh
abstract: The President of Hooters Air announced that the airline is looking at moving shortly into a Pennsylvania airport, possibly Pittsburgh. The airline is also examining Philadelphia and Allentown as potential PA markets, and will decide based on existing air service in the community, the economy and world events. Pittsburgh has been aggressively trying to attract new carriers to the Pittsburgh International Airport and had sent a proposal previously to Hooters Air.

headline: Kerry doesn't have answers
abstract: Senator John Kerry is not a suitable choice for president of the United States.  He does not understand Islamic fundamentalism or how to keep us safe--like Bush does--and his voting record and opinions on taxation, abortion, gay marriage and the poor are out of touch with reality.

headline: CHIP carries potential to save children's lives
abstract: The PA Crime Prevention Association and the Freemasons have introduced their Child Identification Program throughout the Blue Mountain school district.  The program is designed to help authorities by providing them with critical information should a child go missing.  Parents are provided with a full set of fingerprints, as well as a DNA sample; all of this information is stored on a disc that parents can take to police in event of an emergency.

headline: Smoke-free for PA
abstract: PA State Senator Stewart Greenleaf is commended by the author for introducing legislation that would ban smoking in all PA workplaces.

headline: House cautions on slots changes
abstract: Legislation to amend the slots bill passed the PA Senate but has stalled in the PA House of Representatives as members are reluctant to embrace the totality of a bill which features expanded attorney general powers, a ban on state lawmakers ability to own a stake in gambling enterprises, and a reduction of the commission's power to override local zoning ordinances.

headline: Economists as lost as pollsters
abstract: Both Senator Kerry and President Bush are using the economy to their advantage--trying to garner votes by claiming that our current economic woes are the fault of the other party.  University and public sector economists across PA argue that neither candidate can really use the economy to his advantage, however, because the economy is in stasis.

headline: Arena-carnated
abstract: Bits and pieces of Veterans Stadium, such as the turf and lights, were sold and/or donated to sports organizations in and around Philadelphia.

headline: Specter making push to get $344M released for state nursing homes
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter said in a visit to Wilkes-Barre that he is urging the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services to release $344 million to protect nursing homes from closure and seniors from losing Medicaid benefits. Specter pointed out that, if re-elected, he would be in line to become Senate Appropriations Chairman, a key position in gaining funding and position he could use to guarantee nursing home funding.

headline: If US Airways keeps bad credit mark, jet plan may evaporate
abstract: US Airways faces the prospect of paying creditors more than $150 million in cancellation fees as their credit rating dips, with the company seeking to cut costs and lower wages and benefits for employees to avoid even further debt.

headline: Comfort aspect key for voters
abstract: The election between Senator John Kerry and President George Bush is shaping up to be one of the most deeply divded elections in U.S. history.  What this election is most about--and what people are deeply divided over--is character.  In the end, this election will come down to which candidate Ameircans feel comfortable with and can trust.

headline: Rendell Makes it Clear: Driscoll is his choice for Congress
abstract: After state Senator Charlie Dent ran an ad showing PA Governor Ed Rendell praising him, the governor quickly reaffirmed his endorsement of Dent's Democratic challenger, Joe Driscoll.  Governor Rendell claims that Driscoll will be an independent voice in Congress.

headline: State Senate Oks limit on medical malpractice
abstract: The PA Senate voted in favor of legislation limiting pain and suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits, and the bill will now go to the PA House of Representatives. Senator Jay Costa stated that he was disappointed with the passing of the bill, and that he would have preferred alterations he made allowing exceptions in the case of death and severe impairment. The bill was passed when three Democrats initially opposed to the bill voted "yes" after Senator James Rhoades amended the bill. PA Governor Ed Rendell has stated that he has "philosophical differences" with supporters of the bill, but that he could eventually be swayed.

headline: Legislation would use the sales tax to fun schools
abstract: PA Representative Samuel Roher will soon introduce legislation to eliminate property taxes across the state, a bill co-sponsored by Representative Paul Clymer. PA Senator Rob Wonderling, cautious about PA Governor Ed Rendell's plan to legalize gambling to generate revenue for the state, expressed support for Roher's plan. Roher's plan calls for giving up sales tax exemptions on food and clothing, but lowering the tax rate.

headline: Young voters eye change
abstract: This article gathers opinions from Temple University students on the upcoming presdiential election and the importance of voting.

headline: A new day for school saftey
abstract: The Philadelphia Parking Authority began its crackdown on illegally parked cars in school zones.  The crackdown comes in response to dramatic increases in the number of school children hit by cars, and was a suggestion by the task force on school-zone traffic dangers.

headline: Time to step back from malpractice
abstract: This article argues the recent reports showing the mass doctor exodus from PA to be untrue should lead to a calm period wherein the legislation enacted on behalf of doctors will be allowed to take affect. Rather than a knee-jerk reaction to the reports and a return to the prior circumstances, the article argues that changes such as taxpayer support of doctor insurance premiums were long overdue. The unsettled issue of a cap on medical malpractice claims should be left unsettled for the time being, in doing so preventing a time-consuming and contentious battle, the article contends.

headline: Legislators can own share of slot-machine parlors
abstract: PA's state legislators will be permitted to own up to 1% in any of the state's planned slot machine parlors that became legal after PA Governor Ed Rendell signed a bill into law on Monday. The law, which allocates $1 billion per year from gambling revenues to the state to fund property tax relief, came under fire from PA Representative John Maher who said there were not enough anti-corruption safeguards. The law also prohibits members of the PA Gaming Board from working for a gaming company for one year after leaving office, but Barry Kauffman of the PA chapter of Common Cause said there is still an opportunity to fix the law.

headline: A new rival for a ticket giant
abstract: Comcast-Spectacor, owner of the Philadelphia 76ers and Philadelphia Flyers, will venture into the ticket business when its contract with Ticketmaster expires in 2006.  The deal is not expected to lower ticket prices, but will allow for more variable pricing for certain events and reduce processing and servicing fees.  This venture will put Comcast-Spectacor in competition with Ticketmaster.

headline: Health care hangs up contract
abstract: Although some progress has been made in contract talks between the Cumberland County School District and its teacher's union, no progress has been made on health care--the main sticking point in negotiations.

headline: Tiny lifelines
abstract: The US Food and Drug Administration has increasingly approved the use of stents to treat blocked blood vessels throughout the body rather than exclusively in the heart. Advances in stent technology, including the use of drug-coated stents, have prevented many previous side effects, enhancing an already widely used technology.

headline: Let's hope board keeps slots fair
abstract: Columnist Tom Ferrick writes about the appointment of Joseph W. Marshall III, whose manta is "open, fair, forthright and honest," to PA's new Gaming Control Board. After PA Governor Ed Rendell signed the state's gambling law, PA House Speaker John Perzel named Marshall to the board. Marshall has been appointed by members of both political parties to various offices, and he does not consider himself a gambling man. Ferrick suggests Marshall hire a professional staff, without regard for politics, make the GCB's work transparent, and choose experienced companies to run the slot parlors. Lastly, Ferrick points out that the state's current "gaming industry," the state Lottery which benefits the elderly, is relatively free of scandal.

headline: Phone legislation draws opposition
abstract: State Senator Vincent Fumo and Democrats are opposing House Bill 30--legislation on broadband internet development that they claim is a giveaway to Verison Communications.  The controversy is primarily over a feature in the legislation that would allow telephone companies to raise rates beyond what the law currently allows, a provision that Democrats say disproportionately benefits Verizon.

headline: Those with mental retardation push awareness of voting rights
abstract: Dauphin County is putting together a voter registration drive to help register mentally retarded residents.  Since the 1993 Motor Voter Law, which required disability service organizations to provide voter registration services, the focus has been primarily on accommodating and registering those with physical disabilities.  Only recently has the focus shifted to those with cognitive impairments--a trend that County Commissioner George Hartwick III says will continue in Dauphin County.

headline: Unequal prenatal care blamed in high black-baby death rule
abstract: More than 400 newborn black babies who died in Pittsburgh since 1970 would have survived if their mothers had been afforded the same care as white women, a doctor at Magee-Women's Hospital said.

headline: May I take your bags?
abstract: Hundreds of farmers, homebuyers and "blueblood horse owners" visit the PA Farm Show complex every year, and developers are considering building a hotel on the complex's grounds. The PA Department of General Services warned developers about water mains and flooding at a presentation, but encouraged them to consider what can be done on the grounds. Rich Heaney, director of the Mayor's Office of Economic Development believes the planned hotel would continue the resurgence of Harrisburg's hospitality and tourism industry.

headline: Specter will win this fight, too
abstract: On the day following George Bush's reelection, an election won mostly by Bush's championing of strong moral values, Senator Arlen Specter made a critical mistake that drew the ire of the religious right.  Specter, who is in line to chair the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee, told reporters that it is unlikely that judges who would outlaw abortion would be confirmed in the Senate.  This comment has created a targeted effort to deny him the chairmanship, but his support of pro-life judges in the past--such as Clarence Thomas--makes it unlikely that these efforts will be successful.

headline: Secret deal keys cry of favoritism
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street made a secret deal with District Council 47 union leader Tom Cronin that bailed out the union's troubled health and welfare fund.  District Council 33, the blue-collar counterpart of District Council 47, is facing the same problems but received no such bailout.  The actions of Mayor Street have angered District Council 33 leader Pere Matthews.

headline: Vaccine plant to triple output
abstract: MedImmune Vaccines, Inc. in North Philadelphia are working to produce an additional two million flu vaccines after word arrived that a London-based provider would not be able to send shots, creating a massive shortage. The company produces a nasal mist that can not be used by the elderly or children, two of the most at-risk groups.

headline: N.J. company next in line to run arts center
abstract: The Mount Laurel Center for the Performing Arts is negotiating to bring in a new company to run the center, which is nearly bankrupt and facing a state audit. The Center is owned by the Pike County Commercial and Industrial Development Authority.

headline: City hall to be cast in whole new light
abstract: For the first time in its history, the exterior of Philadelphia's City Hall will lit up at night.  This comes from the efforts of the Center City District--the private service organization responsible for lighting the façade of the Art Museum and the Benjamin Franklin Parkway.

headline: Farmers facing problems
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell vetoed HB 1222, a bill in the 2003 legislative session which would have addressed the growing number of local, municipal ordinances which regulated farming. The author argues the bill is necessary in order to protect the rights of farmers from ordinances while also protecting townships from frivolous lawsuits. The author was disappointed that Governor Rendell vetoed the legislation and worries that it could signal the decline of farming in Pennsylvania.

headline: NY gambling study packed with information- good and bad
abstract: Provides a breakdown of a study related to gambling legalization in New York with an emphasis on the Sullivan County region.

headline: Senate confirms education chief nominee
abstract: Education Secretary nominee Francis Barnes appeared before the Senate Education committee on Tuesday to defend his department's decision to relax federal No-Child-Left behind criteria for adequate yearly progess.  Although some senators questioned his department's decision to lower standards, Barnes was unanimously confirmed by both the Education committee and the full Senate.

headline: Fresh produce new frontier of foodborne illness
abstract: Another wave of food poisoning has been traced to the use of fresh produce, leading to concerns that the US Food and Drug Administration needs to set tougher standards on imported produce, something international and domestic law currently precludes.

headline: Pa. slots law change clears state Senate
abstract: The PA Senate passed legislation approving changes to the slots law, returning power over the location of the slots parlors to local officials. The changes proved contentious as Senate Republicans invoked a rarely used maneuver to cut-off debate, invoking an angry retort from PA State Senator Vince Fumo. The legislation also removes the provision allowing state officials to own up to 1 percent of gambling enterprises.

headline: Drug maker gives county 10,000 doses of flu vaccine
abstract: In response to a law suit filed by the Gloucester County Freeholders, drug maker Aventis Pasteur delivered 10,000 doses of influenza vaccine to Gloucester County.  The law suit was filed to compel Aventis to honor its contract with the county--a contract made prior to the national vaccine shortage.  Aventis denies allegations that it bowed to legal pressure and claims that the 10,000 doses were part of a distribution plan developed by the Centers for Disease Control.

headline: Maybe Kerry can pull a Bulworth
abstract: The author wonders if Senator John Kerry would benefit from a Bulworth moment, wherein he tells the truth about himself, his roots and politics in general.  In such a moment, he would tell voters that both major parties are subsidiaries of special interests and that he is rich and has nothing in common with most voters.  Truth telling seems to help in the polls; it certainly will help more than windsurfing.

headline: Fresh-produce voucher program opens
abstract: Eligible seniors and participants in the Women, Infants & Children nutrition program in Pennsylvania can participate in the Farmer's Market Nutrition Program by receiving $5 vouchers for fresh fruits and vegetables grown locally. PA Secretary of Agriculture Dennis Wolff said the state received $1.5 million in grants from the US Department of Agriculture, which will help serve 144,000 people in Pennsylvania while helping local farmers markets. PA Secretary of Aging Nora Dowd Eisenhower said the program will help older Pennsylvanians be able to stretch their budgets and buy nutritious food. Barry Shutt, director of the PA Department of Agriculture Bureau of Donated Food, said that last year the program helped 163,000 WIC recipients and 137,000 senior citizens.

headline: Payoff on slots bill could come tonight
abstract: PA Senators said they would vote tonight to legalize slot machine gambling in Pennsylvania, although some members of the PA Legislature say they do not have enough information about how gambling revenue will benefit their districts to vote accordingly, said Bill Patton, spokesman for House Democrats. PA Representative Katharine Wilson said she has not yet run the numbers to discover the benefits of the gambling bill for her district in Bucks County. The bill calls for gambling halls to pay five percent of their revenue into an economic-development fund. Part of the plan negotiated within the Legislature includes fully funding the expansion of the Philadelphia Convention Center with $636 million in gambling tax revenue. Gary Tuma, spokesman for PA Senator Vincent Fumo, said an agreement was also made to cut the Philadelphia city wage tax.

headline: US turnout sets record; young voters surge
abstract: Motivated primarily by strong feelings about President Bush and the Iraq War, record numbers of Americans voted yesterday.  Experts predict that 114 to 121 million people voted--the largest turnout in US electoral history.  This increase in turnout was fueled primarily by new voters--most of whom are young--and is expected to carry over into subsequent elections.

headline: Rally can't scare up a crowd
abstract: In honor of national preparedness month, PA Homeland Security Director Keith Martin gave a speech at the Luzerne County Courthouse.  Unfortunately, the public and the local press were informed of the event just 66 minutes before it took place.  As such, turnout was poor.

headline: Rain damage to crops detected in patches
abstract: Agriculture producers in PA and NJ are suffering from excessive rain, which is damaging crops and encouraging crop diseases.

headline: Pennsylvania keeps consumers in dark about lending violators
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell may seek to change a PA state law that prevents consumers from accessing PA Banking Department records of violations by mortgage banks and brokers. Foreclosures in PA occur at the sixth-highest rate in the country, part of the reason the Mortgage Bankers Association of PA believes greater disclosure could spur public confidence in the institutions.

headline: A county in PA leads hotline's list of voter complaints
abstract: A new voter-complaint hotline was set up for the 2004 elections.  Surprisingly, Pittsburgh's Allegheny County had more voter complaint phone calls than any other county in the country.  The complaints were primarily related to voter registration, as many residents failed to receive voter registration cards and did not know where to vote.

headline: Termites can be a concern, but some are really awful
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has declared the week of May 9 through May 16 as "Termite Awareness Week" and the author provides suggestions on ways to prevent termite damage.

headline: Pennsylvanians expected to flock to new Monticello casino
abstract: Joyce Fox of Canaan Township was one of many Pennsylvanians at the grand opening of the Monticello Raceway's video-slot parlor in New York State, and exclaimed that PA Governor Ed Rendell should "bring these to Pennsylvania." Many of the patrons of the casino came from Northeastern PA.

headline: Paucity of polling place pranks
abstract: Although many anticipated voter intimidation and disenfranchisement to run rampant in Philadelphia during the 2004 elections, there were surprisingly few, if any, allegations of wide-spread fraud.  Most of the problems in Philadelphia and elsewhere involved isolated incidents of voter intimidation and misinformation dissemination.  There were no major suits filed for vote fraud, however.

headline: 6 Donegan kindergarten classes moving to Fountain Hill
abstract: Six kindergarten classes from Donegan Elementary School in Bethlehem will be moved to space leased from the former Holy Ghost Catholic School in Fountain Hill. At a meeting of the Bethlehem Area School Board's Curriculum Committee on Monday, Superintendent Joseph Lewis stated the increased enrollment caused the classes to have to move. The school district needs new construction and wants to add full-day kindergarten programs, and PA Governor Ed Rendell's education initiatives were partially accounted for in a state budget with money for educational block grants.

headline: Pilots make new pitch to US Airways
abstract: The US Airways pilots union have sent the airline a cost-cutting proposal, with the airline seeking concessions as they lower fares and the airline also provides notice that they may not be able to comply with the terms of federally-backed loans, meaning they may soon fall back into bankruptcy.

headline: Piccola easily defeats Epstein to take 3rd term
abstract: In the Pennsylvania State Senate's 15th-District race, Jeffery Piccola--the Susquehanna Township Republican--overwhelmingly defeated Democrat Eric J. Epstein.

headline: A threat to community colleges
abstract: James J. Linksz, president of Bucks County Community College, writes about dwindling state funding to community colleges. The state did not meet its community college funds obligations in the 2003-2004 fiscal year, and despite PA Governor Ed Rendell's support for community colleges, is not likely to meet its obligations in 2004-2005. The state needs to continue funding community colleges if it is to remain competitive and keep members of the workforce in the state.

headline: Pippy to seek limits on slot site ownership
abstract: PA Senator John Pippy plans to introduce legislation to prohibit state and local elected officials from holding financial interest in slot machine companies when the PA General Assembly reconvenes in September. The Pittsburgh City Council gave preliminary approval to a similar ordinance that was introduced by council president Gene Ricciardi. Under the state's slot machine law passed on July 4, state officials may own up to 1% interest in a gambling company.

headline: Republicans hold leads in 2 races
abstract: In two northern York County legislative districts, incumbents hold commanding leads.  With only 36 percent of the ballots counted, Republican Burce Smith had a comfortable lead ove Democrat Mike Kelly, and Republican Stephen Nickol was far ahead of Green-Party challenger Thomas Marti.

headline: As enrollment rises, community colleges could see aid cut
abstract: Budget negotiations between PA Governor Ed Rendell and PA House of Representatives leaders led to cuts in funding for community colleges in PA, leading to concerns that the colleges may have to cut services just as they are seeing increased enrollment. The PA Senate will be considering the legislation which passed the House of Representatives, which could remove $16 million in community college funding.

headline: Property tax relief, slots bill co-dependent
abstract: PA legislators will meet next week to vote on whether to allow 61,000 slot machines at up to 14 locations in PA to try to raise $1 billion a year to finance property tax relief. Gambling proponents say they have enough votes in both the PA House and Senate to get it passed, but the twin property tax relief bill was still being negotiated as of Friday. PA Senator Gerald LaValle said he believes the package of bills he will vote on this week is as good as it can possibly be, and he will vote for the bills because they include tracks in his district. PA Governor Edward G. Rendell has always supported slots legislation as a means of property tax relief, spokesman Chuck Ardo said. PA Representative Paul Clymer is part of the group that opposes gambling but was unsure if he will oppose the tax-relief bill.

headline: 2004 bears some resemblance to 2000
abstract: The 2004 presidential election bore some resemblence to the election of 2000, with the same key battleground states of Florida, Iowa, Wisconsin and Michigan figuring prominently in the outcome.

headline: Bill proposes vouchers for special-ed students
abstract: A bill sponsored by PA Representative Daryl Metcalfe will allow parents of special-needs and gifted students to send their children to another school with state funds was introduced yesterday. Opponents of the program say that the program would produce little savings for districts. Former PA Governor Tom Ridge attempted 3 times to broaden the state's voucher plan, but failed each time. The Commonwealth Foundation supports the bill.

headline: Proposal could sink local slots
abstract: PA Senator Vincent Fumo is proposing to limit companies to owning only one horse-racing track with a gaming parlor, which would affect Penn National Gaming Inc. that owns Penn National and the Downs at Pocono. Under the proposal, Penn National may not be able to own two tracks in PA if it wants to operate slots. Abe Amoros, spokesman for PA Governor Edward G. Rendell, said the negotiations for the slots bill are still being discusses and the governor is confident of a compromise. PA Senator Raphael Musto, a supporter of the slots at the Downs, said it is difficult to say when the slots bill will be passed and with which stipulations, but there are numerous safeguards proposed to prevent monopolistic control of slots.

headline: PA House: Roberts hangs on to state House seat
abstract: This article reviews the outcomes of several state House elections and focuses heavily on the victory of state Representative Larry Roberts.  Representative Roberts overcame a state grand jury investigation, a messy divorce and a severe bout of hiccups to win re-election in the 51st district last night.

headline: Nativity-scene thefts baffle community
abstract: Nativity-scene thefts hit communities nationally. The Catholic League for Religious and Civil Rights reports that more than 40 incidents of theft have occurred in the United States in the last year. Police authorities suggest that mounting nativity scene to the ground will deter theft. William Donohue, President of the Catholic League for Religious and Civil Rights, believes cameras will discourage theft.

headline: Two high schools again fail to meet a target
abstract: All school districts within Berks County except Reading School District met the standards set by the No Child Left Behind Act for the 2004-2005 year.  Both Tulpehocken and Wilson high schools failed to meet the target for mathematics for special education students for the second year in a row.  The state law requires that 45% of students perform at grade level in reading and math.

headline: Area job growth great progress
abstract: A series of announcements about nearly 1,000 new jobs in the region indicate that the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre area might be reaping some dividends from its geography within the expanding Northeast and from a great deal of hard work in building and marketing a strong infrastructure for business development. Opportunities seem endless.

headline: Choosing a state cookie: Is the process crumbling?
abstract: PA Rep.
