Gaynor Cawley had the PA Legislative Reference Bureau draft a bill on behalf of 9-year-old George Conrad to designate the oatmeal chocolate chip cookie as the state's official cookie to go along with the state's official state drink. When the legislative term expired, Cawley resubmitted the bill. However Common Cause PA Executive Director Barry Kauffman thinks Cawley should focus on more important issues. PA Sen. Robert Thomas has introduced legislation to designate the chocolate chip cookie as the state's official cookie.

headline: Toward more transparency
abstract: This editorial praises PA Senator Vincent Fumo and Pennsylvania Common Cause director Barry Kauffman for promoting reform in how the PA Legislature does business.  The article claims that the rules are in place from the state constitution, but the legislators need to respect and follow these rules.  It compliments Fumo and Kauffman's proposals of posting daily transcripts on the chamber's actions and votes being readily available to the public.

headline: Religious right and GOP split on tactics
abstract: Political analyst Dick Polman sees potential problem for the GOP and its base. President Bush tried to portray religion as personal, while Pat Robertson, a leader of the religious right, suggested the gradual erosion of conservative consensus is that nation's biggest threat. Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist attempted to mediate the positions of Democrats, to which Robertson responded he could not see Frist as a future president. The director of Robertson's legal arm, Jay Sekulow, is one of 3 strategists entrusted with shepherding White House judicial nominees through the Senate.

headline: US Report Card: Young readers make big gains
abstract: Nine-year-olds in the US are reading at a higher level than ever, while there has been no change for 17 year olds according to the National Assessment of Educational Progress.  Kati Haycock of the Education Trust said the study proves that achievement gaps are not inevitable between white students and students of color.  The US Education Secretary, Margaret Spellings, said that the report proves that No Child Left Behind was working.

headline: Bethlehem gets grants for study on reviving corridor
abstract: Bethlehem city officials announced a $85,000 grant to study the revitalization of the Stefko Boulevard corridor. Mayor John Callahan also announced a grant to revitalize the business district.

headline: City drops investment firm
abstract: Philadelphia, Allegheny County, and the state of Ohio all have fired MDL Capital Management Incorporated as their personal money-management firm due to what they claim to be lower-than-expected returns on their investments.  Despite these claims, many state agencies still invest their money in the firm, as the state as more than $600 million and the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority has $34 million invested with MDL.  MDL has historically donated to political candidates such as Barbara Hafer, Bob Casey Jr. and Mayor of Philadelphia John Street.

headline: Urgency in force changes should be to get it right
abstract: Keith Martin, a senior adviser to PA Governor Edward Rendell for homeland security and a member of the Overseas Commission, is writing to remind people to not lose sight of the Base Realignment and Closure Commission’s process to help the country. He reminds people that the BRAC commission was chartered by Congress to offer an assessment of the structure and positioning of US forces inside and outside the US. In their final report they found that Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s vision is comprehensive, commendable, and supported by sound planning.

headline: Senators want to rally around the flag
abstract: The national anthem reminds Americans that "our flag was still there" and so is legislation that would compel PA public schools to start each day by saluting Old Glory. It also allows students to opt out for religious or personal reasons. The American Civil Liberties Union is opposing the legislation.

headline: Weatherly Area opts out of Act 72
abstract: Calling the legislation confusing and contradictory, Weatherly became the first school district in Carbon County to opt out of Act 72, the state law that aims to reduce property taxes with revenue from slots parlors using an increased income tax. School Director Gary Makuch said the law rewards districts with high property tax rates and low student achievements while punishing those with low millage and high student achievement. Under the Act, a school's budget could not exceed the rate of inflation without a referendum. The Act benefits senior citizens most.

headline: Bliley Technologies, Sunburst Electronics appoint Cline new chief executive officer
abstract: John Cline will take over as the chief executive officer of Bliley Technologies Incorporated and its subsidiary Sunburst Electronics Incorporated.  Bliley recently received a $1.36 financial package from PA Governor Ed Rendell to start the development of its high-performance quartz crystals and create 40 jobs.  Sunburst has recently acquired $2 million of loans by working with the Economic Development Corporation of Erie County, Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority, Erie County Industrial Development Agency and the Northwest Regional Planning Commission.

headline: City ponders ways to permit lobbyists
abstract: The city ethic board has sent Philadelphia mayor John Street a draft ordance that would require Lobbyists and anyone using them on city officials to register within two weeks of undertaking lobbying. No such lobbyist registration law exists as of yet in PA but they have been growing in popularity around the country. .

headline: Vote against Udin traced to his Murphy ties
abstract: The referendum on Tom Murphy put Bob O'Connor in the Democratic driver's seat for Pittsburgh mayor and Murphy ally Sala Udin on the way out after 10 years in City Council. Udin holds impeccable government credentials, however his main challenger, Tonya Payne, had only to tie him to Murphy to cause his downfall in the Democratic primary. Udin said the vote was a reprimand for tough decisions made, including a vote for a contract with the firefighters union that closed a fire station. In other races Tuesday, Murphy allies either lost or his foes won.

headline: Street to expand minority contract agency's power
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John street wishes to grant sweeping new powers to the city agency that ensures businesses owned by minorities, women, and the disabled receive a share of city contract work. One of these stipulations include that all city departments submit their contracts to the Minority Business Enterprise Council to make sure that all professions required for the contract reflect diverse ethinicites and backgrounds. The changes will become law as soons as the mayoral executive order is released.

headline: West York Area students learned about healthy habits from Jared the Subway guy
abstract: Jared Fogle, "Jaredy the Subway Guy", who was discovered after having lost over 245 pounds on a diet of subway sandwiches, is touring the area educating students about his own struggle with obesity and the choices he made to take charge of his situation. Jared wants to start a nonprofit foundation to fight childhood obesity. He is pictured talking to students of West York Area Middle School.

headline: Brownsville getting inspected for renovations
abstract: PA Governor Edward Rendell personally presented to the Fayette County Redevelopment Authority a $150,000 state grant to fund the Brownsville Revitalization Initiative for a Great Tomorrow (B.R.I.G.H.T).

headline: City ponders ways to regulate lobbyists
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street has pledged to change the laws regarding lobbying within the city, and the city Ethics Board has proposed a ordinance that requires lobbyists and those employing lobbyists to register them within two weeks of undertaking in the practice.  The firms that are using the lobbying practices would have to complete quarterly reports on the lobbying expenses but does not force the lobbyists to report expenses.  David Grandeau, director of the New York State Lobbying Commission, supports the rule that would force public officials to disclose any gifts, but he feels that lobbyists should be forced to disclose how much they are being paid for their services.

headline: Vote of praise for those who said no to money
abstract: 131 of the 201 PA state House members took the controversial raises early as unvouchered expenses, but PA Representatives Tom Quigley and Carole Rubley did not accept the money. The PA House approved the bill 119 to 79 and the PA Senate approved the bill 27 to 23 and PA Governor Edward Rendell signed the pay raise into law.

headline: Street to expand minority contract agency's powers
abstract: Mayor Street of Philadelphia has ordered that all city departments and non-profit organizations that receive city money to submit to the Minority Business Enterprise Council all their contracts in order to ensure that there is sufficient diversity in the business transactions.  Michael Williams, director of the council, reported that the contracting levels in the past year were 10.65% for minorities and 6.03% for women, which represents an increase from the previous year.  Councilwoman Marian Tasco has openly admitted to being offended by the mayor's approach to encouraging diversity within business.

headline: Will lawsuit stop Penn State
abstract: Penn State is being sued by three members of Dickinson Law School’s Board of Governors. The plaintiffs, G. Thomas Miller, Tom P. Monteverde, and Leslie Ann Miller want the court to stop the split of the law into two locations. PA Governor Rendell remains the students and communities last chance in keeping costs down.

headline: Casino zoning plan unveiled
abstract: Pittsburgh City planners presented a plan to allow a slot machine casino in one of four neighborhoods where current zoning laws prohibit it.  Susan Golomb Pittsburgh's director of planning said changing zoning would speed up the process once a location is selected.

headline: Clark has earned trust on the bench
abstract: Due to the outrageous actions by our state legislators, Corky Goldsten feels compelled to remind voters specifically not to let that conduct and our great anger overshadow our fair evaluation and clear thinking in regard to the retention of Judge Lawrence Clark for Dauphin County bench. He has served with distinction and earned our respect and trust.

headline: Vote them out
abstract: The author of the letter disapproves of the 16% legislative pay raise and calls on legislators to justify their raises or donate it to programs in their districts which need funding.  She notes Governor Ed Rendell's refusal of a raise.

headline: The Lightning Round Wrapped Up in Old Glory
abstract: This editorial comments on various political events that took place recently including its disapproval of the US Congress wasting its time on trying to create an amendment against burning of the US flag.  It also criticizes PA Representative John Perzel for making a comment on a mandatory African-American history course in Philadelphia, a delayed sentencing on a former Klu Klux Klan member and Adelphia Communications founder's banking fraud.  It does compliment PA Governor Ed Rendell's creation of 200,000 jobs within the state and the Philadelphia City Council's increased funding to provide for the homeless.

headline: Will lawsuit stop Penn State?
abstract: Dickinson Law School board of governors are battling out details with Penn State for a merger. Students and community seem to be ignored. With the plans constantly changing state funds have not yet been released.

headline: Building played key role in luring tortilla making firm to Crestwoood Industrial Park
abstract: Mission Foods is the world's leader in corn and flour tortillas. The mexican-based firm will manufacture, warehouse, and distribute its corn and flour products in a new 110,000 square foot facility in Crestwood Industrial Park, PA. The speculative building was formely owned by real estate developer Robert Mericle, who claims the project has granted Northeastern PA with a strategic economic advantage over its neighbors.

headline: Congress too busy to take on T.O.
abstract: This editorial compliments PA Governor Ed Rendell for discussing prescription drug assistance for the elderly rather than meddling in the controversy for his favorite football team, the Philadelphia Eagles, and their star player, Terrell Owens.  It criticizes US Senator Arlen Specter for suggesting the Judiciary Committee investigate into the matter rather than paying more attention to the pressing issues of the Supreme Court nominee Samuel Alito or the prewar intelligence for Iraq.  It feels Owens can find legal help on his own if needs it, and the lawmakers should be more concerned with more important matters.

headline: Voter turnout in area ranged from low to abysmal
abstract: Betty Hillwig, Lehigh county election board chief clerk, reported that about 17 percent of registered voters showed up at the polls for Tuesday's primary. Races included county executive, judge and mayor. Chairman of the Lehigh County Democratic Committee Charles Smith called the low turnout unfortunate. Election Director of Carbon County, Ken Leffler, estimated turnout at 30 percent.

headline: The scent of a man appeals to gays
abstract: A study examining areas of the brain which are stimulated by a chemical scent in testosterone, which stimulates areas of the brain in gay men but not in straight men, appears to suggest that homosexuality is biological, not learned. The study was published in "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences." Charles Wysocki, who conducted a similar study in Philadelphia, appears to have reached the same conclusions.

headline: Will teacher quality rules help our kids?
abstract: Baruch Kintisch, an attorney with the Education Law Center in Philadelphia, criticizes the PA Board of Education's recent decision to allow teachers to be qualified to teach a class if they had taken in some cases as little as one single class in college in the subject.  Concerned parents Colleen Tomko and Gay Vroble both feel that low expectations for teachers will only harm their children's education.  Kintisch claims that the state needs require teachers to take new college classes and school districts have to stop teachers from teaching three or four subjects and allow them to specialize in a certain topic.

headline: Check, Please
abstract: Today, Governor Rendell is expected to present a $16 million check that marks the first phase of the expansion of the Pennsylvania Convention Center. By nearly doubling the size of the current center, Philadelphia should be able to increase both the number and the size of the conventions it can host. Each new convention represents millions of dollars in economic impact for the city. Previously the state has been concerned with how well the project will be managed; we hope this check signals a new vote of confidence.

headline: Continue lawsuits or raise will come back to haunt us
abstract: Pennsylvanians have done a great job in showing their anger over the legislative pay raises. However, they cannot stop now because than the lawmakers could go back to their old ways. They must continue holding them to a high accountability.

headline: Women's conference to inspire, educate
abstract: PA first lady Marjorie Rendell is inviting Western PA women to trek out to Philadelphia in November for what she calls a life-changing conference. The annual PA Governor's Conference for Women, which began last year and attracted more than 3,000 people,, will be a day full of high-profile speakers, networking opportunities and inspiration, Rendell says. Speakers will include retiring US Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, TV personality Lisa Ling and actress-playwright Sarah Jones.

headline: 2003 mental-health study credited with opening doors
abstract: A 2003 mental health study funded by Chester County, the Chester County Community Foundation, and the Chester County United Way justified the need to create more mental health resources. A mental-health facility for children and adolecents was opened in Kennett Square in response to the study. The survey found that people 19 and under were not receiving available services due to poor accesibilty. Since the publication of the study, Chester County has increased facilities and availablity of counselors creating greater access to mental-health resources.

headline: Will teacher quality rules help our kids?
abstract: The requirement for the state of Pennsylvania to have licensed teachers in all schoolc subjects has been hard to fullfill given the fail-rate of teachers on the license tests, called Praxis exams. The state board of education has implemented two policies to then reduce the standards of licensing teachers, known as bridge one and more recently, bridge two. These programs allow teachers to be licensed in many subjects deemed as "highly qualifed" simply because they may have taken a class or two on the subject in college. Concerned parents and other citizens are concerned about the quality of our teachers, saying that they want to change the system but not by demanding less from our teachers.

headline: City bucking for bite of $1.5B
abstract: The Salvation Army in Pittsburgh is currently generating a proposal to acquire money from the $1.5 billion gift from Joan B. Kroc to The Salvation Army in order to build a $40 million recreation center in the North Side of Pittsburgh.  Even with the Kroc donation, the center would cost about $1 to $2 million a year to operate although deputy mayor and Urban Redevelopment Authority chairman Tom Cox said it is too early to discuss the final details, but Pete Bellisario of the Brighton Heights Citizens Federation expects mild opposition due to traffic problems.

headline: Contributors may take heat for pay grab
abstract: PACleanSweep, a Harrisburg-based watchdog, is planning boycott all businesses that donate to incumbent legislators after the General Assembly recently passed a pay raise for themselves.  The pay raise, which goes around a constitutional prohibition and was signed into law by PA Governor Ed Rendell, allows lawmakers to receive unvouchered expenses equal to the raises.  Dave Majernik, a PA Republican committeeman, is critical of both the pay raise and the boycott and feels a more effective solution would be to build a legislative consensus to rescind the pay raise.

headline: Voters Oust a Supreme Court Justice
abstract: Justice Russell Nigro, who got 49 percent of the vote Tuesday, was the first statewide judge to be turned out of office in a yes-or-no retention election in the 36 years such elections have been held. Justice Sandra Schultz Newman won a second term with 54 percent of the vote. The results are a sign of the public's anger at lawmakers for pushing through a pay raise last summer. Rendell will appoint a temporary successor in January, when Nigro's term is over.

headline: 2003 mental-health study credited with opening doors
abstract: A mental health study funded by Chester County, the Chester County Community Foundation, and the Chester County United Way found that only 5% of those nineteen years or younger in certain parts of the county receive the mental health services to which they are entitled. The Chester County Department of Health and Services reported this problem with access to necessary services. In response, the Coatesville Area School District became the first in the state to have mental health counselors available in all its schools and a mental health center for children was opened.

headline: "Green" plan advancing
abstract: An $800 million bond issue to pay for PA state-wide enviornmental improvements may be coming in the near future. A group of house republicans have formulated a proposal entitled "Green PA", which would borrow $800 million over the next seven years to improve forests, clean hazardous mines and waste sites, and other enviornmental projects. The borrowing will be paid off by the current $4.25 per ton tax on municipalities and commercial waste haulers to dump trash in landfills.

headline: City to begin using state grant cash
abstract: Barbara Kowitz, director of the Easton Redevelopment Authority, is planning to apply to withdraw $1 million from a grant given by PA Governor Ed Rendell last year to redevelop the Bushkill Creek corridor.  She has been in contact with the PA Department of Community and Economic Development to ensure the authority gets the money within 8-12 weeks.  The grant will retire $1 million loan with Lafayette Ambassador Bank for the purchase of the Moon property at 1250 Bushkill Drive.

headline: Cortes expected at Amani Festival
abstract: The Secretary of the Commonwealth Pedro A. Cortes, Pennsylvania's first Latino cabinet member, will be attending the 11th annual Amani Festival.

headline: Voting system switch bogus?
abstract: After reviewing results from last week's primary, county officials said results from paper ballots were similar to those of the recently banned electronic voting system. Testing administrator Michael Shamos however said officials were making invalid comparisons. Shamos found the system had a higher than normal undervote rate, which occurs when the number of votes cast in a particular race is less than those cast in an entire election. Beaver County Commissioner Charlie Camp insisted on the accuracy of the system.

headline: A new test to pass
abstract: Jon Dale, PA Department of Health director of school health, reported that once Body Mass Index screenings were done in schools two years ago, 40% of children were reported as being overweight, and as a result, almost all public elementary schools will be using the system this year.  Beth Trapani, the spokeswoman for the Pennsylvania Advocates for Nutrition and Activity, said that this method is for protection of the children's health as well as for raising awareness of the situation.  Despite successes with the BMI Initiative in states like Arkansas, there were many phone calls, up to 100 in Arkansas, complaining that the government overstepped its bounds by reporting the results.

headline: $625M question gets support
abstract: Montgomery County commissioners voted unanimously to support the Growing Greener II legislation in the upcoming primary election. The bill allows the state to borrow $625 million for environmental restoration and conservation.

headline: City unveils slot site plan
abstract: Mayor Street's Gaming Advisory Task Force has recommended that Penn's Landing and 8th and Market street be closed to casino development. In a 436-page report, the task force said two proposed slots parlors placed at a variety of other locations would generate some $750 million in annual revenue and create thousands of jobs. Those locations are in Center City, along Delaware Avenue, near the Schuykill Expressway-Roosevelt Boulevard Intersection and at the Navy Yard.

headline: Councilman to run for Pittsburgh mayor
abstract: Former Pittsburgh Councilman Bob O’Connor will run for Pittsburgh mayor. O’Connor hopes to replace Mayor Tom Murphy. Allegheny County Prothonotary Michael Lamb will seek the Democratic nomination and City Councilman Bill Peduto may run too.

headline: Watchdog group calls 13 Congress's most corrupt; Rick Santorum is on list
abstract: A watchdog group named Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington  recently released a report naming the 13 most corrupt members in the US Congress, which included US Rick Santorum from Pennsylvania.  Melanie Sloan, executive director of CREW, criticized both parties for failing to police the ethics problems present in Washington.  The report accuses Santorum of being corrupt in the controversy that Pennsylvania taxpayers paid for his children's schooling while they lived in Virginia.

headline: AIDS still threatens US, too
abstract: This editorial taken from the San Diego Union-Tribune warns readers about the continuing threat of AIDS even in a developed country like the United States.  It cites the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's statistic that over 1 million people are now infected with the disease.  It also encourages every level of government to strengthen their efforts to prevent the disease as well as treat the disease, especially in minority communities.

headline: 625 million reasons to cast your vote on May 17
abstract: The editorial board urges its readers to register to vote so that they can vote on the referendum regarding the Growing Greener Environmental Stewardess and Watershed Protection Act. It is an act put forward by Governor Ed Rendell and the state legislature over whether or not to borrow $625 million for environmental conservation and restoration projects.

headline: City's No. 2 high-rise is sold
abstract: One Mellon Center in Pittsburgh was bought by Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. from Philip Morris Capital Corp for $185 Million.  Pittsburgh was recently ranked among America's worst real estate markets.  If the building is reassessed and matches the sale price, the county's tax bill could drop.

headline: Councilman to run for Pittsburgh mayor
abstract: Former Pittsburgh councilman Bob O'Connor has announced that he's running for mayor. O'Connor, who will run for the Democratic nomination, hopes to replace Mayor Tom Murphy, who's already said he will not run for a third term.

headline: W-B native sues over state pay-raise law
abstract: Gene Stilp, a political activist, is filing a lawsuit against the state legislatures pay-raise law in Commonwealth Court. Stilp notes that the state Constitution specifically prohibits members of the General Assembly from receiving a salary increase in the same term that they are sitting and the lawsuit names PA Governor Edward Rendell, Treasurer Robert P. Casey Jr., PA House Speaker John M. Perzel and PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert C. Jubelirer. State lawmakers claim that they are not accepting salary hikes but are accepting checks for unvouchered expenses and that this was previously upheld by the PA state Supreme Court.

headline: Alarms raised on hospital infections
abstract: The PA Health Care Cost Containment Council released a report saying that over 11,000 patients acquired infections during hospital stays last year.  Mark Volavka, executive director of the organization called the report the "tip of the iceberg," while Roger Baumgarten, spokesman for the Hospital and Healthsystem Association of PA believes the number is lower because the estimate included problems that didn't turn on to be infections and infections acquired before hospital stays.  Baumgarten also said the numbers may be different because the reporting system is "evolving."

headline: Bay Renewal
abstract: Pennsylvania and the other tributary states to Chesapeake Bay have until 2010 to make significant reductions in the amount of nitrogen, phosphorus and sediment flowing into the nation's largest estuary. The Rendell administration is leading the effort in Pennsylvania, which contributes 50 percent of the freshwater to the bay, through a newly announced strategy that includes limiting expansion of sewage treatment facilities and upgrading existing facilities.

headline: Comcast unveils plans for new headquarters
abstract: Construction on the Comcast Center, which when finished will be Philadelphia's tallest building, is set to begin this month.  PA Governor Ed Rendell thanked Comcast Corporation for staying put in Philadelphia by granting them an aid package of $42.75 million, and the PA Department of Community and Economic Development gave another $12.75 million in grants and tax credits for Comcast's promise to create at least 600 jobs.  Dave Campoli, president of the Center City Owners Association, fought against the state subsidies because he claims the taxpayers are paying for something that the company can already afford.

headline: County chamber pans legislators' pay hikes
abstract: The York County Chamber of Commerce is not happy with the PA state Legislature’s ways of conducting business. The Chamber specifically does not like the way that lawmakers approved pay raises for themselves; Chamber president Thomas Donley sent a letter to local lawmakers detailing the group’s concerns and that they were shocked with the use of unvouchered expenses to skirt the law. The Chamber is backing a bill from PA Representative Will Gabig to prevent the use of unvouchered expenses or mid-term raises  and Donley is urging lawmakers not to accept the early raise through the expense system and to support the legislation.

headline: well so much for independence
abstract: A staff member from the PA state senate has claimed that a slots parlor in the Lehigh Valley area is almost a near certainty. License decisions however, are to be made by the state's new gaming controll board, which is suppose to be a politically independent body, even though 4 of its members have already been named without a confirmation process by the republican and democratic parties.

headline: Alternative medicine gaining acceptance
abstract: Alternative medicine is slowly becoming accepted by the health-care establishment. A growing number of health insurers are starting to cover the $30 billion industry. Medicare seniors can get a $25 voucher to try alternative care.

headline: Breathing Easy
abstract: A year after vehicle emissions testing arrived in south-central philadelphia amid a cloud of confusion, frustrationl and fear, a sense of acceptance and gradual decline of fees have settled in. According to the Pennsylvania department of transportation, citizens are getting more acclimated to the system requirements and implementation has gone seamless across the board. Across the midstate, the average cost of a test has declined 5.7 percent.

headline: Comcast unveils plans for new headquarters
abstract: Philadelphia's newest skyscraper wil be its tallest, a 975 foot tower built by Comcast Corp, justly called the Comcast center. The company has enjoyed millions of dollars in state and local tax breaks and grants through taking advantage of its strong connection with PA governor Ed Rendell. This November Rendell created a deal that didn't require the legislature's approval which granted Comcast even more government subsidies. Comcast in turn has promised 600 new jobs, with as much as 1000-2000 in then next decade, although their tax breaks has caused much complaint from rival office landlords who dislike public subsidies in fear of their own businesses.

headline: County scrambles to keep Aventis
abstract: Monroe County Commissioner Chairwoman Donna Asure claims that the county will borrow money against their annual Community Development Block Grant totaling $3 million to contribute to the $40 million needed for a new sewer system.  This sewer system will convince Aventis Pasteur to continue a $160 million expansion of their flu vaccine plant in the county after they gave a deadline to PA Governor Ed Rendell to commit to funding the sewer project.  Pocono Township Supervisor L. Patrick Ross has asked US Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum and US Representative Paul Kanjorski for federal money but they have not responded enthusiastically.

headline: Well, so much for independence
abstract: A staffer of PA Senator Vincent Fumo, Christopher Craig, reported that a slots parlor will definitely be constructed in the Lehigh Valley because of the lucrative market.  The decisions to license will be made by the PA Gaming Control Board, which is planning on becoming a politically independent body.  However, four members of this board have been appointed without confirmation by bipartisan caucus leader of the PA Legislature.

headline: Alternative medicine gaining acceptance
abstract: With more than an third of Americans using alternative medicine, health insurers are embracing the $30 billion industry by offering discounts to members for complimentary and alternative forms of care. Brian Berman, a physician believes complimentary-alternative medicines should be held to the same standard as clinical effectiveness. Pharmacist Robert Fishman, on the other hand, is suspicious of Berman’s conclusion.

headline: Breathing easy
abstract: Anthony Haubert of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation claims that customers and automobile service stations are getting more accustomed to the vehicle emissions testing that started a year ago in Pennsylvania.  The average cost of a test has fallen 5.7% since last year, but PA Governor Ed Rendell is considering adding a $2 sticker fee for vehicles that have passed the test.  There was originally a lot of controversy over the tests after Pennsylvania Department of Transportation originally calculated the cost of a test at $13.76.

headline: Connell Park on comeback trial
abstract: State Representative Fred Belardi announced that $250,000 in state legislative initiative grants will go towards renovating Scranton's Connell Park. Mayor Chris Doherty announced that the city will match the grant with federal Community Development Block Grant funds.

headline: county to name vendor for voting machines by November
abstract: The Luzerne County Electronic Voting Machine Committee held an exposition of voting machines from vendors that are competing for the county’s business. Under the 2002 Help America Vote Act passed by Congress to prevent difficulties experienced during the 2000 presidential election states must be using electronic voting machines in the 2006 primary election.

headline: West Shore voters guide: Carlisle Mayor
abstract: Democrat Charles Andrews is focusing on downtown Carlisle in his challenge to longtime Republican Mayor Kirk Wilson. Andrews contends that police enforcement of downtown traffic and pedestrian safety has declined under Wilson. Wilson does not believe that this is the case; he also believes he has already made important political connections that give him an advantage over Andrews.

headline: An effort to boost Hispanic children's health
abstract: An annual conference was held for La Raza, a nationwide Hispanic civil rights and advocacy group.  The article discusses high volumes of health problems for Hispanics, along with a lack of health insurance.  It also cites that many may not know that their children are eligible for the State Children's Health Insurance Programs.

headline: Commissioners urge voters to support Growing Greener II
abstract: West Chester County Commissioners are urging residents to authorize the state to borrow $625 million for environmental initiatives. Commissioner Andrew Dinniman noted the state's previous Growing Greener initiative more than doubled money the county invested in environmental projects. The county's fund is almost empty however, and continued funding is vital to the survival of its Landscapes, Linking Landscapes and Watershed program. Commissioner Carol Aichele agreed.  A rally on the courthouse steps will include state representatives and environmental groups.

headline: Connellsville to take part in revitalization effort
abstract: Mayor Judy reed announced that Connellsville will be one of the 22 PA locations to be selected for the Blueprint Community program which entitles the city to receive some intense training to help them set goals and objectives where you want the community to go. Reed applauded PA Governor Edward Rendell for his role in supporting the initiative because Rendell is very interested in the revitalization of older communities like Connellsville. The Federal Home Loan Bank of Pittsburgh began the development of the Blueprint Communities program.

headline: Dallas Oks feasibility studies for district wide project
abstract: The Dallas School Board decided to hire two firms, Borton Lawson Architecture and Quad3, for a total of $27,000 for two studies that examine the practicality of a district wide renovation and construction project.  However, the three minority members who are poised to become the majority in two months, Dennis Gochoel, Maureen Matiska and James Richardson were not involved in the meeting while the current majority met behind closed doors.  Dan Nulton, board members, reported that the study will most likely lead to a project that will cost approximately $30 million.

headline: Will Specter save the GOP from itself?
abstract: The editorial board criticizes Republicans in the United States legislature threatening to vote to get rid of the ability to filibuster. They hope that Senator Specter will vote with the Democrats to keep filibusters.

headline: Area team watches stem-cell debate
abstract: The US House of Representatives voted to expand federal funding for stem cell research, with US Senators voicing support. However, President Bush has promised a veto. In 2001, Bush banned the use of federal funds for research, though privately funded research may continue. At Penn State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center, Kent Vrana hopes to get a $350,000 federal grant for additional studies. The state's Abortion Control Act makes it a third degree felony to perform some medical procedures or experiments on an "unborn child," without defining what constitutes an unborn child.

headline: Cast vote for health
abstract: This editorial encourages voters in New Jersey to vote for the initiative that would use 20% of the corporate tax to reimburse bus and truck operators who have to reduce diesel emissions and overhaul the fleets.  This comes after New Jersey Governor Richard Codey signed into law a 10-year control plan on diesel-engine emissions from publicly and privately owned garbage trucks and transit buses.  The article reports that emissions will be reduced by 500 tons  per year and save up to $1.4 billion in health care costs every year.

headline: County airs 12 development proposals
abstract: Luzerne county commissioners discovered more than $64 million in economic development projects in the works for 2005. Development professionals and local leaders summonned the commissoners on Thursday seeking the funds from the office of community development to finance portions for their own projects.

headline: Decision delayed on racing license
abstract: The PA Harness Racing Commission will delay its decision on the awarding of a harness racing license to either Ambrosia Enterprise or Centaur Incorporated because Ambrosia recently changed its financial backer to Innovation Capital Holding Limited Liability Company.  Jeffrey Smith of Centaur criticized this decision citing the fact that his own company is ready to being the project while their competitors are still delaying the process and aren't completely ready.

headline: Wise re-nominated to Monroe's bench
abstract: Jennifer Wise, a Democratic Scotrun attorney, has been nominated for the second time by PA Governor Ed Rendell for the vacant judge seat in Monroe County.  Wise's name was pulled after being nominated by Rendell the first time at the request of PA Senator Robert Mellow because of a delay on approval of Democratic judges by a Republican-dominated Senate.  Art Zulick, a Republican Stroudsburg attorney, Republican Stroudsburg Mayor Jonathan Mark and Mount Pocono lawyer Timothy Fisher Junior have all announced they are running for the seats as well.

headline: Atrium case goes to jury
abstract: The US District Court listened to closing arguments from Assistant US Attorney Leo Dillon and defense attorneys in the trial of Martha F. Bell and the Ronald Reagan Atrium I Nursing and Rehabilitation Center. Bell and the nursing home she once ran in Robinson are charged with defrauding Medicare and Medicaid of more than $7 million and making false statements to hide the fraud and poor care of patients, many who had Alzheimer’s disease.

headline: Cattle farmer's conservation practices generate national recognition
abstract: Robert and Kate Boyce, of Lower Frankford Township, and their Li’l Ponderosa Enterprises, which is a Black Angus cow/calf operation, thoroughbred horse business and farm products business, were named the regional winners in a National Cattlemen’s Beef Association environmental program. The Boyces were nominated by the PA Cattlemen’s Association for the practice of matching plant life to their soil and using conservation practices such as rotational grazing, brush management, stream bank fencing, stream crossings.

headline: County airs 12 development proposals
abstract: Many local interest groups, leaders and development professionals are petitioning the Luzerne County commissioners for financing from the Office of Community Development after the commissioners discovered more than $64 million  in economic development projects will be given to the county in 2005.  Commissioners Todd Vonderheid and Greg Skrepenak reported 12 pitches were made that total to $5,124,000, and a majority of the projects are listed in the article in detail.

headline: Democratic reform must begin at home
abstract: In an effort to promote democracy aboard the new Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice says Russia needs an independent press in order for Russia to flourish. However, while the Freedom of Information Act and Patriot Act is legal in America and reporters and editors can be prosecuted for refusing to reveal their sources, the promotion of democracy should be carried out in the United States.

headline: Wise re-nominated to Monroe's bench
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell renominated Scotrun attorney Jennifer Wise, a democrat, for Monroe County's vacant judicial job seat. The former Judge, Pazuhanich (no first name given), a republican, was ousted 3 weeks after his election after a public drunkuness incident where he also plead no contest to molesting his daughter at the concert they attended. Wise now need 2/3 thirds of the 50 member PA state senate for approval, which most people are confident she will receive.

headline: Blues to fund low cost insurance
abstract: PA Governor Rendell announced that Pennsylvania’s Blue Cross/Blue Shield plans have agreed to grant $150 million toward health care for low-income and other Pennsylvania residents for the next six years. The funding is projected to include $85 million a year to enroll 29,000 people in adultBasic. Pennsylvania’s Blue Cross/Blue Shield has also been criticized by PA state lawmakers for maintaining billions in cash reserves and surpluses despite the companies non-profit status.

headline: CDC report criticizes plan to dump nerve-agent waste in Delaware River
abstract: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are recommending that the plan to treat the toxic nerve agent VX and dump it into the Delaware River not go forward.

headline: County will sue city, Pa. agencies.
abstract: Lancaster County Commissioners Dick Shllenberger and Molly Henderson voted to sue the Redevelopment Authority of Lancaster,, the State Department of Community and Economic Development and its secretary, Dennis Yablonsky over it's use of a state funding program, Act 23, to build a hotel/convention center in downtown Lancaster.  Commissioner Pete Shaub voted against the lawsuit.  Previously, the county filed a complaint with the state Department of Community and Economic Development claiming that it's illegal for private developers to pass property tax payments to city government.  Attorney Clarence Kegal, representing the county, said that the commissioners filed the suit because they don't know how the state will rule on the complaint.

headline: Democratic reform must being at home
abstract: New Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice took an eight day trip to Europe and found out Russia isn't measuring up to the US concept of a democracy. We are backsliding back to the cold war and we must take measures at home to keep this from happening.

headline: Your Opinion: how would you rate Rendell
abstract: The author of the opinion is asking the newspaper's readers their opinion of PA Governor Ed Rendell since he is about to be halfway past his term as governor.

headline: Blues to fund low-cost insurance
abstract: The state's Blue Cross/ Blue shield plans, the subject of recent criticism about their cash revenues, have agreed to give $150 million a year toward health care programs for low-income residents and other Pennsylvanians. The funding includes $85 million a year to enroll another 29,000 people in adult Basic, the state's low-cost health insurance program for the poor.

headline: Cleaner vehicle program closer for Pennsylvania
abstract: Louie Lease, owner of Louie's Auto Service and Gurreri Towing in Springettsbury Township, remembers the 1960's, when you had to get your car tuned up in the spring and the fall to get it through the year. He remembers the 1970's when car manufacturers used to produce different cars for use in different altitudes because the different air density could affect their performance. If PA does make the transition to a model of car with stricter emission standards come 200 Lease doubts the changeover will send shockwaves through the industry.

headline: Custom Patio
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell gave Custom Patio Rooms Inc. with $916,000 from the state Department of Community and Economic Development. The money comes from a Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority loan and Job Creation Tax Credits. The money is expected to create 193 jobs.

headline: Democrats talk up high minimum wages in PA
abstract: PA House democrats are claiming that for the first time in years the state legislature will have serious deliberations concerning raising the minimum wage from $5.15/hr to the proposed $7.15/hr. Democrats claim that the current wage is not nearly enough to survive on in this day and age but the proposal faces harsh opposition from the state GOP and the governor himself, Ed Rendell.

headline: Your opinion: How would you rate Rendell?
abstract: This article calls for citizens to rate PA Governor Ed Rendell as he has reaches the halfway point for his gubernatorial term.  The article leaves an address, fax number and email for readers to contact with their rating of Rendell and how they want to improve the government.

headline: Budget limits some Medicaid care, but calls for no eligibility changes
abstract: Medicaid patients would face new limits on drugs, hospital admissions and doctor visits under Gov. Rendell's proposed state budget. The cuts are a way to fill a $400 million hole in the welfare department budget created by decreased federal support for the program, growing enrollment, and increasing health-care costs.

headline: Controlling deer
abstract: This editorial sides with Pennsylvania hunters by saying that there are an overpopulation of deer within the state that are causing crop damage, destroying their own food source and preventing tree growth.  However, it does say the solution to solving the overpopulation should be a group effort between environmentalists and hunters.  Although it doesn't claim to have the answer, the editorial suggests lengthening the hunting season.

headline: Downtown developer sets sights on Crate & Barrel
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor-elect Bob O' Connor is excited that developer Madison Marquette is interested in using Crate & Barrel and Tiffany & Company as retailers for the renovations of lower Fifth Avenue.  The developer is working with the Pittsburgh Task Force, which is headed by the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership, on the plans for residential and retail complexes.  PNC Financial Services Group has also planned a $170 million office on Fifth Avenue as part of a widespread development of the area.

headline: Democrats want voters to revive Act 72
abstract: Democrats in the PA Legislature such as PA Representative William DeWeese have proposed a referendum in the 390 districts currently not participating in Act 72 to allow voters to decide whether or not to join.  This referendum would also eliminate a 0.1% income tax increase due to disapproval from wealthy property owners but still has the support of PA Governor Ed Rendell.  PA Senator Robert Jubelirer did not think that the plan will be voted on before the summer recess, however.

headline: 9/11 monument forged in metal, born in grief
abstract: Montgomery County Commissioner Jim Matthews helped push for the completion of a new World Trade Center memorial outside of the Montgomery County Courthouse.  The memorial contains a beam from the wreckage and is dedicated to both the victims and the rescue workers.  The artist, Sassona Norton, put it in $90,000 of her own money even after the memorial was given a $100,000 grant.

headline: Budget limits some Medicard care, but calls for no eligibility changes
abstract: PA Governor Rendell’s proposed state budget for 2005-06 will limit some Medicaid care, which will result in hardships for Pennsylvania seniors and disabled persons. The proposed changes will increase prescription drug costs, limit hospital admissions to two times a year, and reduce doctor visits. Kate Sorenson, health director for Citizens for Consumer Justice believes Pennsylvania’s elderly and disabled persons will be negatively effected, leaving hospitals to find solutions in giving them care.

headline: County scrambles to keep Aventis
abstract: Monroe county applied for a $3 million loan to contriubute to the $40 million needed for a new sewer-system to to satisfy Aventis Pasteur, which is threatening to terminate a major expansion of its flu-vaccine plant there. Aventis Pasteur is a French-based vaccine company and is the sole supplier of injectable Flu vaccine to the United States, manfacturing about 50 million doses per year. The firm sent a letter to PA Governor Ed Rendell stating that if the new sewer project does not happen the company will be forced to move its expansion to Toronto or France, costing the region hundreds of future and current jobs.

headline: Editorial…Pa. Growing Greener II First Step to recovery
abstract: Editors believe voters should authorize the state to borrow $625 million for its Growing Greener II initiative. The money will be directed toward various environmental projects around the state. PA Governor Ed Rendell and the legislature have settled on this figure after Rendell's initial $800 million proposal in his 2004 budget address. Recognizing the state's needs, Montgomery County Commissioner passed a resolution urging voters to approve the initiative. The Brookings Institution noted PA has natural assets which could aid in its prosperity. Voters should take advantage of them.

headline: Dems reward pay raise backers
abstract: House Democratic Leaders H. William DeWeese and Mike Veon deny that stripping 15 House members of their subcommittee leadership positions was a punishment for them not voting for a legislative pay raise.  Governor Ed Rendell said he'll contact the leaders regarding the issue.

headline: Book recalls worst flood along Delaware River
abstract: The 50th anniversary of the 1955 flood of the Delaware River are being commemorated, which were a result of Hurricane Connie and Diane, through personal tales of 100 survivors.

headline: Cancer research survives cuts
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell wanted to redirect 6& of the money earmarked for medical research, but the legislature and Philadelphia's National Cancer Institutes were against it.

headline: Deer scarce on some Pa. land
abstract: The Pennsylvania Game Commission has been hunting deer to reduce their population. However, the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources reported a study that shows that too many deer have been killed and they are scarce in some areas.

headline: Federal funding in tug-of-war
abstract: The federal Abandoned Mine Land Program has been thrown into disarray and with PA’s nearly quarter of a million acres of abandoned-mine land its federal remediation allocations do not come close to keeping pace because the state’s coal industry has stagnated.

headline: Depot supporters seeks more jobs
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum said there would be no jobs lost at Letterkenny Army Depot (LEAD) through the Base Closure and Realignment Commission at a briefing for opportunity 05.  The briefing was used for organizing local support for the BRAC hearing in D.C. Congressmen Bill Shuster said he will press for more work to be relocated to LEAD.  Governor Ed Rendell and Dave Sciamanna, director of the Greater Chambersburg Chamber of Commerce were also present.

headline: Briefly Noted
abstract: H.F. Gerry Lenfest matched $4.5 million in donations to the Gettysburg National Battlefield Museum Foundation, while Jody McDonald will hose New York's ESPN station from 10am to 1pm.

headline: Cancer screening bill helps early detection
abstract: Governor Rendell signed a bill unanimously approved by Legislature that expands the pool of women eligible for free breast and cervical cancer screenings. It clears the way for uninsured and underinsured women between the ages of 40 and 49 to receive free annual mammograms and Pap smears. This brings the state program in line with the National Institutes of Health recommendations that annual mammograms begin at age 40.

headline: DEP project plows ahead
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection said that pollution caused by mining in the past along Burma Road is a major concern and has allowed its Abandoned Mine Reclamation Program to reclaim the mine.  William Tomayko, the project manager for the landfill, said the reclamation is significant because it allows the DEP to control the storm water and acid mine drainage that is mixed into outside water sources.  The department is waiting on the local municipalities' response to two concerns: toxic waste produced from a proposed landfill and waste infection of a stream that runs through the proposed site.

headline: Financial crisis looms
abstract: Erie Mayor Rick Filippi warned that there could be police layoffs, department shutdowns and firehouse closings because of a budget crisis.  He wants City Council to approve $2 million to counteract this despite many in the Council feeling that $2.6 million would be the least amount of money needed to solve the crisis.  Councilwoman Jessica Horan-Kunco expressed apprehension about a $2 million transfer because she feels the reserve money is needed for emergencies.

headline: Derr's whining about vote is hypocritical
abstract: The writer is expressing his opinion over the tactics of politicians in the state of Pennsylvania. He is upset that Lehigh county commissioner Kurt Derr (Democrat) is complaining that the commissioner's republican majority elected a republican as board chairman. To the author, it is not only normal for parties to elect their own members to an office, but even expected. He continues his rant involving the state legislature and even Governor Ed Rendell.

headline: Chance of closing looms over county's care home
abstract: 80 people enjoying music, food and each other's company during a county fair in the recreation room at Dauphin County's Spring Creek nursing home, Judy Doutrich grew troubled at the prospect that her home of almost two years could close. Closing Spring Creek or making drastic cutbacks are among options the county commissioners are considering to control rising costs. The tipping point came this month when the home's 2006 budget called for $2 million more than anticipated.

headline: Conquering the killers
abstract: The article talks about the advances in vaccines against infectious diseases, the problems that still exist, and the struggles we're likely to face in the future.

headline: DEP to develop way to muzzle mercury emissions
abstract: The PA State Department of Environmental Protection received the “OK” to develop tougher regulations for power-plant mercury emissions. The Environmental Quality Board, an independent panel for approving changes to state regulations, agreed that the PA Environmental Protection Department could draft tougher standards for mercury emissions. New national mercury emissions regulation, imposed by the US Environmental Protection Agency went into effect but both the PA Department of Environmental Protection and PennFuture say that the standards aren’t tough enough.

headline: Financing sewer projects a complicated equation
abstract: New sewer projects being constructed in various Mon Valley communities are costing citizens a wide range of prices depending on how their local legislators decide to pay for the projects.  Despite loans and grants being available from the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority, the residents often have to pay a tap-in fee according to Rostraver Township commissioner Nick Lorenzo, whose county's projected tap-in fee will cost $1,000 for homeowners.  Michele Cathers, secretary of the Smithton borough's sewer authority,  was able to secure a $750,000 Community Development Block Grant and a $250,000 PennVEST grant, which allows users to pay only a $39 monthly fee.

headline: Derr's whining about vote is hypocritical
abstract: This opinion piece by Bill White criticizes Lehigh County Commissioner Kurt Derr, who complained recently about a Republican-led group of commissioners elected a Republican Jim Kelly as the board chairman.  White makes the point that politicians usually elect members of their own party to offices, and he also states that Derr's wife was hired for a clerk's position in the Allentown Police Department despite mass layoffs from Mayor Afflerbach.  He also comments that local legislators who want PA Governor Ed Rendell to design projects based on local recommendations is no better than allowing politicians to use Walking Around Money on their accord.

headline: Delaware River flooding approaches worst ever
abstract: Pennsylvania Emergency management Agency Director reported that the flooding of the Delaware River due to a hurricane is the worst since Hurricane Diane in 1995. Governor Ed Rendell declared a state of emergency and will allow municipalities to apply for state funding to cover 25% of the cost of the flooding. Easton Mayor Phil Mitman has declared a state of emergency in his region.

headline: Co-pays for health insurance:
abstract: Co-pays for health insurance are a critical issue in seven school districts in and around the Lehigh Valley that have not reached an agreement on new teacher contracts. The author believes that the teacher’s union is unrealistic when it comes to health-care and the spokesman for the PA State Education Association, the union the represents most Valley teachers, said that the health care costs shouldn’t fall on the backs of the teachers.

headline: Don't dump on your neighbors
abstract: This editorial believes that large landfill proposed by Resource Recovery and approved by the Lancaster County's Board of Supervisors should not be built without the construction of an interchange midway, which officials have denied. It feels the highway right now cannot handle the increase of garbage trucks that would pass through I-80 to get to the landfill and negative effects would be drastic to the county and its neighbors.

headline: For next trick? Cut taxes
abstract: The editorial board calls Philadelphia's Mayor Street's projection of $50 million in new revenue a "magic trick."  The PA Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, which overseas the local budget, threatened to stop Street's spending plan before the projected revenue.  Street claimed the money would come from real estate transfer taxes.  Street convinced City Council that decreasing his budget plan would be a problem, and executive director of PICA, Joseph Vignola, said Street was "playing council members for fools."

headline: Did you know? There's an election Tuesday
abstract: Expectations for Tuesday's primary election when Republicans and Democrats will choose their nominees for municipal government. In Harrisburg, the winner of a three-way primary between incumbent Stephen Reed, Ernie Napoli and Jason Smith, will be the next mayor, with no Republican opponent. Penn State Harrisburg Professor Matthew Woessner says voters have not yet recovered from the exhausting Bush-Kerry battle last year.

headline: Editorial…Keep tight focus on a good plan
abstract: Editors say it is too bad the city's judges, who fill vacancies by state law, did not use an opportunity to recruit new blood. A year ago, Fairmount Park Commission president Robert N.C. Nix 3d announced a strategic plan for Fairmount Park. Yet the Philadelphia Parks Alliance has just released a report saying the strategic plan has dropped out of view. Author Bill Hangley Jr. says the plan's future is unclear without a political champion or financial backing. Interim Park Director Karen Borski has announced her departure. Neither park nor Mayor Street's officials are moving fast enough to save the park.

headline: County wants more Mental Health Funds
abstract: Should the Harrisburg, PA State Hospital close, locals from around the area want to make sure the state will provide a long-term program so the community does not become the victim. Furthermore, there is a shortage of state hospital beds which also results in the county prison not being able to move troubled innmates, even worsening the situation.  The hospital has 260 patients with 539 employees and serves Dauphin, Adams, York, Cumberland, Perry, Franklin and Fulton counties.

headline: Dry spell leads county to  ban outdoor burning
abstract: At the request of the county Emergency Management Agency, Dauphin County Commissioners Jeff Haste, Nick DiFrancesco, and George P. Hartwick III passed a ban on outdoor burning because of a long spell of dry weather.

headline: Good signs in region's job report
abstract: Reports by the state Department of Labor and Industry show that job growth was flat last year, but this year there is significant job growth in spite of a small spike in unemployment in March.

headline: Don't count on that raise just yet
abstract: Many citizens have been petitioning and writing to their Pennsylvania lawmakers such as PA House Speaker John Perzel and PA Governor Ed Rendell to try and influence them to repeal the recent legislative pay raises.  PA Senator Jeff Piccola claims to have voted against the pay raise and will vote for any bill that will repeal the raises.  The two candidates for the US Senate position have differing views as incumbent Rick Santorum feels the raises are for the local and state government to decide and State Treasurer Robert Casey Jr. wants to change the rules on unvouchered expenses and base any raise on the increase in the cost-of-living increases.

headline: Federal, state officials get first look at area's flood damage
abstract: Luzerne County emergency managers took officials of the Federal Emergency Management Agency and Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency through several townships so they could assess the damage done by severe flooding. The assessment with determine if victims of the flooding receive any federal aid.

headline: County wants more mental health funds
abstract: The PA Department of Public Welfare will announce the closing of Harrisburg State Hospital that would take place at the end of the year and send many patients home for treatment.  A meeting of Dauphin County commissioners discussed the possibility of the state government providing more long-term funding in order to make sure taxpayers won't have to pay for the transfer of patients and their home care.  Dauphin County District Attorney Edward M. Marsico Junior also is worried about the cutting of funding too much as the county relies heavily on Mayview State Hospital in Pittsburgh.

headline: Environmental group seeks limit on mercury
abstract: A statewide environmental group, Citizens for Pennsylvania’s Future, will urge the PA state Department of Environmental Protection to move forward with stricter mercury regulations, even though three legislators say they’re not necessary. The letter was sent by the chairmen of both the PA House and Senate Environmental Resources and Energy committees questions the need for state-specified regulations when the federal Environmental Protection Agency introduced new standards. The PA state DEP filed a federal lawsuit claiming that the federal rule is not strong enough and will not protect the public health.

headline: Governor outlines fall objectives
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has reported that he wants to increase penalties for sex offenders and curb the production of methamphetamine by putting certain pharmaceutical products behind the counter.  He also wants to increase benefits for National Guard personnel and pass an economic development proposal, the Redevelopment Assistance Capital Program.  PA Representative David Argall claimed that the Republican legislators largely agree with these proposals.

headline: Don't gamble your future on the lottery
abstract: Gregory Karp writes urging people to not waste their money on lottery tickets as the lottery is becoming increasingly popular with a 28-state Powerball jackpot reaching $340 million.  He cites a Consumer Federation of America study that cited many Americans of low and middle incomes think they have a better chance of saving for retirement by playing the lottery rather than saving and investing.  Karp cites the odds of winning the Powerball lottery as being 1 in 146 million and calls the lottery a "tax on the hopeless."

headline: Flood teaches valuable lesson in disaster prepardeness
abstract: Allegheny County is more prepared to deal with emergencies, due to the devastating floods in the previous year. The volunteer organization, Southwestern PA Long term Recovery Task Force, rose from the post-flood mess and would coordinate charitable relief the next time an emergency comes and the state is counting on the group to serve as a model to the rest of PA, according to Martin Miller of the PA Emergency Management Agency.

headline: Cut Viagra from Medicaid
abstract: This editorial compliments the Pennsylvania Legislature for not allowing sex offenders to receive Medicare-funded Viagra medication.  However, resulting from PA Auditor General Jack Wagner's statement that this may have been an accident, the editorial encourages the state government to make sure that there are no loopholes in the law.  Finally, it says the government should go as far as to not allow any impotence drugs be funded by Medicare.

headline: Environmental plans tossed around in state's 'green' war
abstract: PA State Democrats with Governor Rendell and State Republicans disagree over funding and who will take credit for environmental plans for the state. Last year, Governor Rendell proposed an $800 bond program to continue former Governor Tom Ridge’s Growing Greener program. At the start of the 2005 legislative session, the Republicans in the General Assembly proposed their own environmental plan called Green PA. Both sides agree on preserving the environment, saving open space, and cleaning up pollution.

headline: Home again
abstract: When too many Philadelphians can't find affordable housing, we all pay the cost. The city spends $67 million a year on temporary shelter and emergency services for the homeless; disabled people who can't find wheelchair-accessible housing end up in institutions; older homes are abandoned when owners can't make repairs cost millions to demolish. A housing trust fund is a common-sense investment.

headline: Down the aisle, at the governor's
abstract: 76ers president Billy King will be married at Governor Ed Rendell's home, with his wife, federal judge Marjorie O. Rendell officiating.

headline: Flooding damage might sink state's boating season
abstract: The Boat Owners Assocation of the Untied States reported that recreational boat losses from Hurricanes Frances and Ivan totaled $450 million.  Andy Talento, president of the Pennsylvania Boating Association, said that about 20% of boaters won't be able to return to the water this year.

headline: Disabled worry lives not valued
abstract: People with mental or physical impairments and those who advocate for them say a history of feeling their lives were devalued by the medical community made them all the more alarmed at a June symposium of the Task Force for Quality at the End of Life in Pennsylvania. The symposium spend all day discussing different end of life issues but never acknowledged special problems of people with disabilities.

headline: Environmental plans tossed around in state's 'green' war
abstract: The battleground once again is in the halls of the state Capitol in Harrisburg, and at stake once again is a high-priority quality of life issue for residents of PA. This time the issue is the environment and politicians are fighting over who gets credit for the environment changes. Governor Rendell has proposed $800 million bond program to continue the work of further governor Tom ridge's Growing greener program.

headline: Information consolidated on website
abstract: Cumberland County government has launched a new website to promote economic development. It has information on different programs that provide resources for people to create a business. The event included speakers from Community First Fund, SEDA Council of Governments, and Cumberland Area Economic Development Corp., which are organizations working to increase economic growth in Cumberland County.

headline: Drawing the line on gerrymanders
abstract: For all the justified public anger in PA over the unconscionable conduct of the state legislature, voters will have an opportunity to exercise that wrath in the voting booth. It's not just because the lawmakers enriched themselves nearly 18 months before the next legislative general elections with the hope that voters will have a short memory lapse. Incumbents have gifted themselves with a wide aray of advantages over would-be challengers. Th elist in impressive, from the nation's worst public information and lobbying dislcosure laws, to unlimited campaign contributions, to free production and mailing of public-interest newletters, videos and public-service announcements.

headline: Front and center
abstract: Charles Tarbox, a Civil War re-enactor, is proud that the National Park Service decided to build a new museum and visitors' center for the Gettysburg National Military Park on Hunt Avenue, named after former Union General Henry Jackson Hunt.  John McKenna of the National Park Service said that the location was chosen because it was further away from the actual battlefields and the silence and reverence of these fields could be preserved.

headline: Doctors finding bigger is better to reduce costs
abstract: In the past doctors have been plagued by low insurance reminbursements, high malpractice costs, and lack of control over patient care. No more in today's day and age, where doctos have formed new mega-practices with several different doctors to offset the costs of overhead in addition to being able to treat a signifcant amount of more patients.

headline: Financing sewer projects a complicated Equation.
abstract: In a number of Mon Valley communities in Pennsylvania, including Washingtown township and Fayette county, there is growing tension over who should pay for state-mandated sewage maintanece and planning. While the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority grants low-interest, multi-year loans for sewer projects, local residents are angry that they end up paying too oftern- and most defintely too much.

headline: Kansas City woos Penguins
abstract: Paul McGannon, the president of NHL 21, which is a group of 100 civic leaders trying to bring hockey to Kansas City, has invited the Pittsburgh Penguins to play an exhibition game in the new stadium in Kansas City in an attempt to persuade them to move to the Midwestern city.  Mario Lemieux, owner of the Penguins, has consistently expressed doubts the team can stay in Pittsburgh after his meeting with Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato, Mayor Tom Murphy and Mayor-elect Bob O' Connor did not win him support for a new arena.  Houston, Las Vegas and Seattle are all attempting to woo the Penguins to move to their cities as well.

headline: Early competition for Pa.'s Lt. Gov
abstract: Valerie Mcdonald Roerts, the recorder of deeds for Pittsburgh's Allegheny County, is planning to announce that she will be taking on Pennsylvania's Lt. Gov. Katherine Baker Knoll in next years election. Rendell has stated that Knoll will be his running mate.

headline: Grant opens door for open space
abstract: The PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources has issued a $625,000 Growing Greener Grant to Northampton County  to purchase 160 acres of land that is owned by the Totts Gap Medical Research Center.  Northampton County Public Works Director Ed Boscola has credited Parks Superintendent Gordon Geller for starting the movement for the purchase 15 years ago.  Council Ron Angle is skeptical still about the purchase because the purchased land was already protected and feels the preservationists should protect surrounding lands instead.

headline: Doctors finding bigger is better to reduce costs
abstract: This article uses obstetrician Nancy Roberts to illustrate the growing trend in doctors who join private mega-practices to decrease annual malpractice costs, which ran Roberts about $118,000 at her old Lankenau Hospital.  Philip Armstrong, administrator for the Oregon Clinic, states that smaller practices have difficulty handling requirements of Medicare and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act.  Stephen Krell, of the Women's Health Care Group in Pennsylvania joined 40 gynecologists and obstetricians to reduce his malpractice insurance premium from $100,000 to $80,000.

headline: Fine didn't trash trash firm's rep
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental protection fined Browning Ferris Industries $250,000 for waste violations. Philadelphia Mayor Street recently sent a bill to City Council which proposes that BFI, owned by Allied Waste Industries, be given 44 percent of the city's waste removal services, with the potential for contract renewal for up to three years. In defense, Street's Department deputy commissioner said BFI's violations were due to problems with a subcontractor. Carlton Williams maintained that the problems have been corrected and the company is being watched by the administration.

headline: Lehigh County has a good stadium deal if final details can be completed in time
abstract: There's temptation to get excited about the signing of a stadium lease to bring professional baseball to Allentown. But years of experience tying to lure minor league baseball to the Lehigh Valley also urges circumspection. After all, what does a lease for a baseball stadium that isn't built yet mean? A lot of work still needs to be done, so people should not start celebrating yet.

headline: Ed for judges' raise, wants minimum up
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell reported that he supports judicial pay raises under any circumstances but only will approve a legislative payraise if the state lawmakers raise the minimum wage to $7.15 over a course of time.  Many Democrats in the Legislature support the idea, such as PA Representative William DeWeese, who wants the minimum wage to be $7.15 per hour by 2007.  PA Representative Sam Smith, a Republican, does not want to link a legislative pay raise to minimum wage, claiming that they should be done on merit.

headline: Horseback riders concerned Allegheny forest may ban open riding
abstract: Allegheny National Forest officials are considering a ban on open riding in the forest and restrict it to marked trails as part of the park’s new long-term plan. The officials say that this doesn’t mean that horseback riding will be outlawed because there are four different plans for regulating horseback riding being considered.

headline: Doctors hoping countersuits stem tide of malpractice claims
abstract: Activist doctors have opened a new front in their war with trial lawyers, a campaign of countersuits to be filed against attorneys, plaintiffs and others who bring frivolous medical malpractice suits against physicians. They has been pushing hard for reforms to the state's medical liability system. Jury awards are driving up the cost of malpractice insurance.

headline: Firms truck in harmful sludge
abstract: The author is writing about the lack of information that farmers have about the “free fertilizer” they are spreading that is spreading sludge. They ask why if the sludge is safe large out-of-state companies are paying for cleaning their sludge and hauling it to PA for free. The writer thinks that the homeowners should be worrying about the effects of the sludge.

headline: Lehigh Valley region riding housing price rocket
abstract: The Lehigh Valley housing market is the hottest in PA. Lehigh Valley home prices surged nearly 17 percent over the past year, according to recent study that examined spring home prices. The compares with about 13 percent for both PA and the United States. The region's housing appreciation stems from a spillover of demand from higher-priced areas in New York and New Jersey, according to a report released by the Federal Deposit Housing Enterprise Oversight.

headline: Editorial: Stealth raise/The outcry over the state pay hike is justified
abstract: The editorial board disapproves of a legislative pay raise, especially when the state has yet to see property tax relief from slots and when $240 million have been cut in medical assistance for the poor.

headline: House funds study of '04 flood areas
abstract: The US House authorized the Army Corps of Engineers to conduct a study of ways to reduce flooding in South PA.  Shaler Manager Tim Rogers said the flooding after Hurricane Ivan took it's toll on residents.

headline: Doctors hoping countersuits stem tide of malpractice claims
abstract: Politically active doctors have started a campaign of countersuits against lawyers and plaintiffs who have bring frivolous medical malpractice suits against physicians. The Politically Active Physicians Association believes such suits are driving up the cost of malpractice insurance. Dan Fee, spokesman for the trail lawyer-backed Pennsylvania Citizens for Fairness, believes the campaign is an attempt to deter people from filing medical malpractice suits.

headline: Flawed Growing Greener bond plan better than nothing
abstract: Editors call Growing Greener II a painful compromise in the primary. The amount of funding requested is inadequate; $200 million alone will go to the Game and Fish and Boat Commissions to oversee it, not to mention other agencies. Republicans in the legislature blocked PA Governor Rendell's efforts to pay for the initiative with fee hikes and bonds in addition to having not firmly decided whether they will need more than the initial $625,000 to fund the initiative. Nevertheless however, editors agree with Wildlands Conservancy of Emmaus President Tom Kerr, some money is better than none at all.

headline: Nordstrom may finally be coming here
abstract: At the spring convention of the International Council of Shopping Centers in Las Vegas, a display by Simon Property Group included plans for a Nordstrom as an anchor for its Ross Park Mall in North Hills. However, Nordstrom denied that it was planning a new location. No other sources could confirm. Pittsburgh Mayor had tried to bring Nordstrom in to revitalize the city's deteriorated retail corridor with no success in the past.
