headline: Editorial: Texas Ferlo/ Politcians should let Sheehan make her own case
abstract: Cindy Sheehan has been holding a wartime vigil outside President Bush’s Crawford, Texas ranch and PA state Senator Jim Ferlo, an outspoken critic of the Iraq war, has joined Ms. Sheehan. The editors bring up the fact that the presence of a politician risks alienating those who suspect that the protest has cynical motives at work. The editors believe that Cindy has the moral standing to be there asking hard questions of President Bush but they are wary of those who rush there to share the limelight.

headline: Ivan's damage could take two years to undo
abstract: It will cost Pennsylvania millions of dollars and perhaps as long as two years to rebuild portions of the Delaware Canal State Park ravaged by remnants of Hurricane Ivan. The state department of conservation and natural resources completed the canal towpath in the spring of 2004 and now it is completely destroyed due to Ivan. Cleanup and restoration of the affected areas in Northampton and Bucks counties may amount to as much as $9 million, accordng to the department of conservation and natural resources, and the department has said that they should know with four to six weeks how much funding they will receive from FEMA, which should cover 75% of the total cost.

headline: Don't cut cessation
abstract: Money from a tobacco settlement has been used by the Sadler Health Center of Carlisle to create programs helping people quit tobacco. Howeve,r Governor Ed Rendell is decreasing funding for these programs in the budget and putting it elsewhere. A woman from Partnership for a Healthier Community Carlisle wrote in to the newspaper to tell people to encourage Rendell not to cut any funding from the programs.

headline: Funding cutbacks portend an austere year
abstract: The state's environmental and natural resources departments are facing austere budgets that despite some adroit fiscal maneuvering will leave visitors to parks and forests slapping themselves and looking for some privacy behind a tree. The Department of Environmental Protection, faced with almost an 11 percent decrease of $19.43 million in its general fund budget, has eliminated its $4.4 million black fly spraying program.

headline: Loan to help pay for renovations
abstract: The PA Industrial Development Authority has approved a $1.35 million loan to help a company buy and renovate the former Susquehanna Center nursing home. The property is being acquired by 44 Harrisburg Associates and will be renovated by Hersha Hospitality Management. The project is expected to retain 60 jobs and create 25 new jobs, according to the PIDA application. Most of the existing jobs will be shifted from Hersha's operations in Fairview Twp.

headline: Editorials
abstract: The newspaper responded to reader requests by posting recent editorials in the print edition of the paper in an online database.  This list outlines each editorial from recent issues briefly and includes links to these articles online.  The editorials included are encouraging stem-cell research, reforming PA Governor Ed Rendell's plan for Act 72, Congress forcing rules upon sports leagues, declaring a recent law to mandate a constitution class unconstitutional, giving sound advice at commencements, and mandating seat belt use in school buses.

headline: Ivan's damage could take two years to undo
abstract: The PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources has estimated that rebuilding of a part of the Delaware Canal will cost up to $9.2 million after being damaged by Hurricane Ivan.  The Federal Emergency Management Agency is assessing the damage currently and will cover up to 75% of the costs.  Two groups, Friends of the Delaware Canal and the Historic Delaware Canal Improvement Corporation have raised $102,176 in order to repair a 110-foot section of the canal already.

headline: Electronic medical records the goal of Murphy's bill
abstract: US Rep. Tim Murphy for PA proposed legislation yesterday with bipartisan support to provide grants and loans to develop electronic medical records systems to reduce medical errors and health care costs. The 21st Century Health Information Act, HR 2234, is supported by Sen. Hillary Clinton as well as Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist and Rep. Patrick Kennedy. Murphy noted the Pittsburgh Regional Healthcare Initiative as a model for the kind of nonprofit organization that might develop such systems.

headline: Funding cutbacks portend and austere year
abstract: Pennsylvania’s Department of Environmental Protection and Department of Conservation and Natural Resources will face hefty budget cuts for the next year. The funding cuts will result in a reduction in employment positions and operational expenses.

headline: Money mounts for Lehigh Valley baseball
abstract: The PA Legislature have acquired additional money for a Class AAA baseball stadium as well as Joe Finley and Craig Stein, Gracie Baseball partners, depositing $750,000 to begin construction.  Because the Legislature has raised the top amount the state can borrow for capital projects, PA Governor Ed Rendell is permitted to donate another $5 million to the $34 million project in addition to the $12 million Rendell has promised.  The construction of the stadium is planned to begin in September 2006.

headline: Eminent Domain
abstract: The government's powers of eminent domain are in need of serious reform, an issue that rightly belongs on the state Legislature's front burner. Two and a half hours of testimony is not enough research for the committee vote on Monday ad the full Senate vote on Wednesday. Eminent domain can be a positive force for good beyond the usual application to obtain rights f way for highways ad utilities.

headline: Layers of government, individual families tally costs of flooding
abstract: State and county officials will begin conducting damage assessments to determine how much damage was done by the massive flooding of the Delaware River. Once the assessments are compiled, Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency Director Adrian King will recommend to Governor Ed Rendell whether or not he should seek assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Easton Mayor Phil Mittman is hiring contractors to help city officials assess the damage.

headline: Drug costs run free under New York Medicaid
abstract: New York frequently pays many times more for drugs than Medicaid programs in other states. For years, New York Medicaid has been great for drug companies and their wares. Prescriptions that are severely restricted in many states are often dispensed freely here, and at higher prices, costing taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars. New York has adopted a bill which would limit the drugs a doctor can prescribe.

headline: Game Commission investigates shooting on season's last day
abstract: The PA Game Commission will investigate one man who was shot and injured by another on private property in Greenwood Township while both were hunting on the last day of the season.  Jerry Feaser, Game Commission spokesman, reported 17 people shot during the two-week deer season with only two being fatal.  He also claimed that there has been a significant decrease in hunting accidents since mandatory hunter safety education programs and mandatory fluorescent orange hunting outfits.

headline: New arena must be local priority
abstract: Guy Junker discusses his views on various sporting issues including PA Governor Ed Rendell's statement that Pittsburgh's proposed new hockey arena cannot become a priority in the state government unless the local officials in Pittsburgh make it a priority.  Despite this, he believes Rendell's consistent public support of Philadelphia sports teams could be political suicide if he doesn't show the same support for Pittsburgh teams.  Junker also discusses the reasons behind the lack of enthusiasm behind the Pittsburgh Pirates and lower television ratings as well.

headline: End slush fund
abstract: The author is angry that the PA Legislature continues to put funds away for their own use and they have done so for fifteen years, accumulating to what they call a $135 million “political slush fund.” They also say that governors have used this tactic of storing money away too, including former PA Governor Robert P. Casey. At the end the author asks what will PA voters do about the bad behavior of the Legislators.

headline: More evacuee flights to Pa. unlikely
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell reported that the state is not likely to receive more Hurricane Katrina evacuees from the federally organized flights.  The Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency said that the state currently houses 1,000 families, who mostly arrived on their own accord.  Pennsylvania officials plan to conduct criminal background checks on the evacuees.

headline: Family doctors coming up short on flu vaccine orders
abstract: Health bureaus have it. Hospitals have it. But a number of area doctors can't get flu vaccine this year and are sick about it. The problem affects small practices that only need a small amount of the vaccine. The larger organizations have contracts with the companies distributing, but have ordered more this year because they ran out last year and couldn't get more.

headline: 'Green' plan advancing
abstract: Republicans in the PA House of Representatives have proposed an $800 million bond issue over 7 years in order to preserve farms, clean up old mines and improving state forests among other environmental projects.  The funding for the project would come from a current $4.25 per ton tipping fee that municipalities and other commercial waste management companies pay to dump trash in various landfills.  PA Governor Ed Rendell has proposed that this plan be funded by increasing the tipping fees and imposing toxic emission taxes on industries.

headline: New Jersey franchise headed to State College
abstract: Construction of the new bill park is moving along. Now, State College appears to have a team to put in it. Altoona Curve management reached a sales agreement with the New Jersey Cardinals of the New York-Penn League. The single- A minor league franchise, pending approval from various organizations, will become the to-be-named State College Professional Baseball Club.

headline: Ethics is on agenda; is Mariano voting?
abstract: Philadelphia City Councilman will return to the Council chamber to vote on ethics legislation after he was indicted on corruption charges this past October.  Mariano met with Mayor John Street and other Council members in order to discuss and support Street's ethics agenda.  Mariano does not feel that his voting on ethics legislation while being indicted for retaliation against witnesses for firing his previous chief of staff as well as using his friends' businesses to pay various bills.

headline: Rendell opens emergency center to help agencies cope with flooding
abstract: Due to expected flooding, Governor Ed Rendell opened an emergency center to help emergency agencies. It will be staffed by members of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, State Police, the Public Utility Commission and other agencies.

headline: Family dreads Medicaid cutback
abstract: Governor Rendell’s proposed changes to the Medical Assistance program may hurt the elderly and persons with disabilities. The changes will not alter Medicaid eligibility, but will place limits on some of the services many adults receive. Jonathan Stein, general counsel for Community Legal Services, a Philadelphia Agency, believes the health care changes will hurt Pennsylvania’s sickest people.

headline: Growing Greener alternative offered
abstract: House republicans announced a new proposal to the growing greener preservation program Wednesday. The alternative, entitled Green PA, is similar to PA governor Ed rendell's original growing green plan, but includes greater funds and a longer state- commitment. Many legislators believe the governor will pass the $800 million enviornmental conservation program very soon.

headline: Next renaissance / Three cheers from the city for Three PNC Plaza
abstract: This editorial applauds the proposed $170 million Three PNC Plaza skyscraper that will be built on Fifth Avenue in Pittsburgh in hopes it will help spur development in the area.  It also supports the financing plan that is a combination of $122 million in private money and $48 million in state money and local tax breaks.  Despite the editorial's wish that it were closer to the David L. Lawrence Convention Center, it feels the skyscraper will be a welcome addition to other construction projects in the area.

headline: Evans not ready to declare for '07
abstract: Opinion piece about PA Rep. Dwight Evans possible announcement to run for Philadelphia mayor in 2007. Evans says he will make an announcement by May 2005. His decision to run could prompt other potential Democratic candidates, including City Councilman Michael Nutter and U.S. Rep Chaka Fattah, into announcing their intentions to run. Included is a follow-up piece about the Mike Stake Jr. case involving allegations of forgery on nominating positions. The case stalled over whether an out-of-district judge should preside over the hearing. The original ruling stating an out-of-district judge was needed given Starks connections was upheld this week.

headline: Strikers want unions to boycott garages
abstract: Teamsters Local 926, which represents 230 parking attendants throughout Pittsburgh, are trying to organize a boycott of the lots and garages owned by Alco Parking Corporation and the Pittsburgh Parking Authority, the two biggest operators.  Parking Authority Director David Onorato and Alco Parking President Merrill Stabile both said a boycott would not change their position on the issues.  Teamsters recently rejected Alco's most recent offer of a 50 cent raise over three years because of the lack of coverage on health care premiums.

headline: Family dreads Medicaid cutback
abstract: If the Governor's proposals are implemented, people would have to share in the cost of the services he now receives for free. When children become adults, the services could be scaled back. Many low-income, elderly and disabled people would be limited to two inpatient hospital admissions a year. They would face a $5,000 limit on medical equipment, like wheelchairs, and other limits on prescription drugs and outpatient medical services.

headline: Growing Greener alternative offered
abstract: Republicans in the PA House of Representatives have proposed a new environmental program called Green PA to take the place of PA Governor Ed Rendell's current Growing Greener environmental program that will expire in 2012.  The new plan would last for 28 years with a $2 billion investment and would add hazardous site cleanup coverage to the plan.  PA Representative Mike Veon does not support the proposal because it takes money from current environmental programs to fund other programs.

headline: Novavax announces milestones
abstract: This article reviews various business announcements from within the area including Novavax Incorporated's recent announcement that it received the US Food and Drug Administration's approval to manufacture its new drug Estrasorb and reduced debt.  It also mentions that Aqua America Incorporated has acquired Saddlewood Estates development in Texas through its subsidiary, Aqua Texas Incorporated.  It finishes with the story that PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Department of Community and Economic Development gave Gamesa Incorporated a $9.31 million package to build a new wind turbine manufacturing plant in Cambria County.

headline: Evans not ready to declare for '07
abstract: The columnist predicts that state Representative Dwight Evans will run for mayor of Philadelphia in 2007. United States Representative Chakah Fattah may also run for mayor, and current Mayor Street has encouraged him. City Councilman Michael Nutter may also run. The columnist also reports that ward leader Mike State Jr., father of State Senator Mike State the 3rd, were indicted by the state Attorney General's Office for forgery on nomination petitions.

headline: Board Eys tax changes
abstract: The Cumberland County School Board is meeting to discuss substituting a $10 tax ($5 per capita and $5 per residence) with a same value real estate tax. Supporters of the switch claim the costs of collection would decrease if the tax is rolled into property taxes. The opposition argues taxpayers are against higher property taxes to fund schools. Tax collectors argue changing the tax cuts cheats them out of wages promised by the district.

headline: Flu season: so far, so good
abstract: Despite two manufacturers of the flu vaccine not providing the vaccine this flu season, John Lines, spokesman for Lancaster General Hospital reports that the number of flu patients is below average this year.  Officials have only reported 100 cases of the flu within Pennsylvania, although many expect that number to increase.  The US Centers for Disease Control have distributed later shipments of the vaccine and emergency vaccines will be given to high-risk patients within Lancaster County this week.

headline: Growing Greener may be on spring primary ballot
abstract: Environmentalists groups such as Chester County 2020 Trust hope that state Senators will vote to put Growing Greener II on the primary ballot. Governor Ed Rendell wants to put the legislation to referendum as well.

headline: Officials exonerate care home inspector
abstract: PA Department of Public Welfare officials exonerated Deb Avery after she was accused of negligence in the inspection of a personal care home. The inspection returned a clean finding of the facility in September after complaints the Lebanon Veterans Administration Medical Center said a county detective. The home was later closed in March by the county district attorney. A department spokesman reiterated that inspection officials must evaluate the home on the basis of what they see during their visit, and in September, there was no cause for concern during the visit.

headline: Evolution Slate Outpolls Rivals
abstract: All eight members up for re-election to the Pennsylvania school board that had been sued for introducing the teaching of intelligent design as an alternative to evolution in biology class were swept out of office yesterday by a slate of challengers who campaigned against the intelligent design policy. The election results were a repudiation of the first school district in the nation to order the introduction of intelligent design in a science class curriculum.

headline: "Mini-City Hall" funding an open secret
abstract: The PA Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, which must certify Philadelphia's budget balanced - said it was concerned about off the books obligations regarding Mayor Streets plan to possibly close a "mini town hall."  Republican City Councilman Jack Kelly wanted to include it in the budget but Democrat Joan L. Krajewski said it would be solved behind the scenes.

headline: Flu Season: So far, So good
abstract: There has been much discussion this year over how bad the flu season will hit not only Pennsylvania, but the nation as a whole. The country's supply of the flu vaccine has been scarce, but so have the cases and patients who have reported catching the flu. PA has only documented 100 confirmed cases, although the flu season does not take full effect untill later this month.

headline: Hunting fees
abstract: This editorial encourages the PA Game Commission to actively persuade the PA Legislature to approve a $10 increase in hunting license fees to $29 as they do not receive any state funds.  It also calls for a combining of the game and fish commissions into a PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources to promote other animals than deer to be hunter.  While it urges the Game Commission to acquire more funds, it asserts that there is in fact a deer overpopulation problem that the commission needs to deal with, possibly by increasing their revenue through higher license fees.

headline: Optimism in news on jobs in Valley
abstract: The 1990's were the god old days for Lehigh Valley according to market researcher Kamran Afshar. The optimism about finding good jobs spilled over into the year 2000, but in 2001 the outlook changed dramatically. A series of developments this winter point to better times.

headline: Executive changes on tap
abstract: Charles "Wick" Moorman has been named CEO of Norfolk Southern Corp, effective Nov 1. He will succeed David Goode, who will continue as chairman until retiring in early 2006. Bret Wise will become the new president and chief operating officer at York-based Dentsply International Inc on Jan 1 replacing Thomas Whiting, who intends to retie.

headline: $92 million Great Wolf resort opens in Poconos
abstract: The big smile that spread across the face of the Poconos' chief tourism official spoke volumes at the opening of the Great Wolf Lodge in Scotrun. A throng of state and local officials filled the expansive lobby to watch as Great Wolf executives turned a ceremonial spigot to the resort's 78,000-square-foot indoor water park in Monroe County proclaiming Great Wolf open for business. It’s the first new resort to open in the Poconos in 30 years.

headline: Fourth human case of West Nile in state
abstract: A 50-year-old woman in Allegheny County is the fourth human case of West Nile virus confirmed in PA for the year Department of Health officials said.

headline: In other areas…
abstract: Rendell's plan would also provide a $22 million increase for the state police, to support a record number of troopers and cut the state Department of Environmental Protection and the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

headline: Options put cars in the back seat
abstract: The city government of Bethlehem and the Economic Development Corporation are beginning a 5 month study on how to best create alternative transportation for students and citizens alike particularly in the South Side.  The $25,000 study was funded by the Keystone Innovation Zone, an initiative from PA Governor Ed Rendell that intends to partner businesses and universities to develop technology.  Rendell hopes that this initiative will help reduce the fleeing of recent graduates from Pennsylvania to find better jobs in other states.

headline: Executive puts $5 million down for mayoral race
abstract: Insurance executive Tom Knox transferred $5 million to his new political committee in what amounts to the largest single campaign donation in city history. His campaign staff is moving into a Center City headquarters this week as he gets ready to launch his campaign. His donation certainly raises the financial stakes for other candidates. Knox wanted to show to people that he's serious about this and that he can't be bought.

headline: A tree marks the spot
abstract: Streetscapes improvements continue in the 100 block of Bridge Street with flair and style. The official borough of Phoenixville emblem has been stampled on and incorporated into, the recently installed tree grates in the Ironworks District, adding a one of a kind touch to the project. Don Edwards, borough manager and engineer, said this week that the distinctive emblem is also used on borough letterhead, police cars and borough vehicles.

headline: G. Fred Dibona, head of Independence blue cross, dies
abstract: G. Fred Dibona, a south philadelphia native and scion of a Philadelphia political family, died early this morning after a 2 year fight with cancer. Dibona was the president and chief executive officer of Independence Blue Cross and lead the region's largest insurer for 15 years. The article is a memoir to his life and mentions his most famous achievements.

headline: Keep looking to determine where the deer roam
abstract: Hunters have criticized the number of antlerless deer hunting licenses the Pennsylvania Game Commission has issued, saying it has decreased the deer population too drastically. An aerial survey confirms this, but the editorial board says that only 2% of forested areas were surveyed and that more information is needed.

headline: Owner, Coatesville see no end to fight over land
abstract: The city of Coatesville is still trying to condemn 31 acres of land in Valley township in order to create 5 more holes for a proposed golf course. Dick Saha, the owner of the land, has been fighting the motion for 4 years now, and as the publicity of his case grows more and more lawsuits have been followed favoring potentially crippling limitations on the City Council's power, specifically their ability to acquire lands beyond the city limits.

headline: Expectations high for Quakertown's big parade
abstract: Quakertown borough is turning 150 years old, and parade committee chairman Ken White hopes to make its sesquicentennial Celebration Parade the biggest the borough has seen. Special guests will include Miss Pennsylvania 2004 Victori Bechtold, 1955 Centennial Queen Abby V. Brown-Watson and radio and personality Sally Starr. PA Governor Ed Rendell was also invited. The county's democratic leadership is confident Rendell will attend the parade. Bucks County Democratic Chairman John F. Cordisco said Bucks County appreciates it anytime Rendell visits.

headline: Act 72 uncertainty rife in Pine Grove
abstract: Pine Grove Area School District must decide by May 30th whether or not to opt in to Act 72, a property tax relief act. School districts who participate must lower the property tax, but will receive revenue from newly legalized gambling. Pine Grove held a meeting for school officials, county officials and residents about the issue. Jay Hines, the director of Pennsylvania Association of School Business Officials, spoke.

headline: G. Fred DiBona, head of Independence Blue Cross, dies
abstract: The president and chief executive officer of Independence Blue Cross, G. Fred DiBona died of cancer this morning after leading Blue Cross for 15 years from $1.3 billion insurer to a $9.1 billion managed care company.  DiBona was reportedly most proud of his Caring Foundation for Children and his nursing scholarship program because of his desire for every citizen to have health care.  He was the child of a Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge and rose through the ranks of the Philadelphia Zoning Board of Adjustment, Philadelphia Port Corporation and the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce.

headline: Know @ noon
abstract: PA Governor Rendell’s plan will increase funding to the state police and decrease funding to the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and Department of Conservation and Natural Resources. Rendell hopes PA lawmakers will agree to allow PA voters to approve the Growing Greener II program.

headline: Owner, Coatesville see no end to fight over land
abstract: Valley Township landowner Dick Saha is still fighting against the City of Coatesville, which has taken 31 of his 40 acres of land since 2000.  The city is taking over mass amounts of land throughout the township as part of a $700 million revitalization plan in the area.  The law suits will take place in Chester County Court on February 7, but both sides expect further delays to this ongoing battle.

headline: Ex-steeler brings political game to town
abstract: Pittsburgh Steeler legend Lynn Swann flew into town for a tailgate campaign, said Gov. Ed Rendell is dictating an unpopular school tax relief plan, and called the legislative pay raise an insulting thing to the people. Celebrity candidate Swann leads a field of four Republicans who are nosing around the banquet halls and barbecue grills of PA for support for theirs party's nomination to challenge Rendell for governor. A day after Rendell proposed mandating school district participation in Act 72 property tax relief, Swann suggested the governor was trying to take advantage of state lawmakers who are reeling from anger over pay raise.

headline: Act 72: S. Side wants in
abstract: The South Side Area School Board approved Act 72 legislation to reduce property taxes. The district is the second in Beaver County to opt in to the plan to reduce property taxes by accepting revenue from slot machines. As a result, the county's income tax will rise by .1 percent. District director of finance Lori Byron said the district will balance its increased budget with state aid in response to a property tax appeal two years ago by FirstEnergy Corp. Byron noted the aid will eventually run out however, and with the district's increasing budget, taxes will eventually need to be raised.

headline: Geisinger plan details large-scale facility
abstract: The Geisinger medical clinic at Interstate 99’s Grays Woods interchange would be able to increase health-care giant’s physical presence in Sate College with five construction phases. The clinic would be nearly 90 percent of the current size of Mount Nittany Medical Center and the new clinic would be the “bull’s-eye” of a seven-county central PA service area.

headline: Landfill plans ignite uproar
abstract: In Boggs township, Clearfield County, Pennsylvania, local residents are angered over the approval for construction of a 560-acre landfill. Botch mining and landfill operations have decimated the amount of fish in the area and corrupted the groundwater according to one resident, Bill Albert. Bill Dickinson, board of supervisors chairman, said that supervisors did not solicit a landfill for the area but at the agreed up on $2/ton, the township will able to double its annual budget in just 40 days.

headline: PA development group seeks local input
abstract: The Pennsylvania Rural Development Group is hosting forums in rural counties to bridge the gap between the public and private sector. The forums are designed to address the needs of rural communities, which are often neglected by state and federal programs. Members of Gov. Ed Rendell’s administration will meet with local community members to discuss issues including community development, health care, economic development, education and infrastructure.

headline: Ex-Steelers player among 7 elected to county court
abstract: Former Steeler Dwayne Woodruff will join six other lawyers in filling the seven seats on the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas. The candidates were elected from a field of 10

headline: Act 72's backers weigh in
abstract: It looks as if Pittston School District favors Act 72, with Pittston Superintendent Frank Serino calling it the first legislation the state has ever offered as an avenue to property tax relief. The board voted to opt in to the Homeowner tax Relief Act, passed by the PA Legislature as a companion bill to the state's gambling legislation. School boards that participate in Act 72 will be required to hold voter referendums if any further school budgets introduce a tax increase above the cost of living adjustment.

headline: Health courts would reduce legal costs
abstract: William Lander, president of the Pennsylvania Medical Society discusses how unpredictable and often outrageous jury verdicts have become commonplace in malpractice cases, this has caused payouts for malpractice claims against doctors in Pennsylvania to climb to an all time high in 2004 - $448 million. Doctors are now faced with increased liability and high malpractice premiums; this is causing some of them give up the practice ob  medicine altogether. Pennsylvania needs a more comprehensive solution; the idea of special health courts is becoming a popular idea.

headline: Landfill plans ignite uproar
abstract: PA Waste Limited Liability Company is proposing the construction of a 560-acre landfill in Boggs Township that will collect 5,000 tons of trash a day.  The company has initially offered to buy all property within a mile of the landfill that amounts to 2,000 total acres.  PA Representative Camille George was the first person to discover the landfill proposal that was approved by Boggs Township supervisors.  Bill Dickson of the Board of Supervisors did not ask for this landfill but agreed upon $2 a ton, which doubles the township's budget.

headline: Pa. development group seeks local input
abstract: The Pennsylvania Rural Development Council will be holding a town meeting in which members of state agencies and Rendell's administration can discuss its plans, and take questions and comments from locals.

headline: Faith-Based Politics
abstract: The writer of the article argues that even after his victory over Senator John Kerry in the 2004 election, President George Bush has little influence. Many of his efforts have been shot down by the United States Senate.

headline: Aide: Street favored White's deals
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street's finance director will tell a jury that when it came to handing out city business, Street instructed her to favor companies recommended by Ronald A. White, the now deceased lawyer at the heart of the city hall corruption scandal investigated by the FBI. Street has not yet been charged of any wrong-doing but the Bureau has said they need time gather evidence and formulate a case.

headline: Health insurance deal draws fire
abstract: Last week, state officials and Pennsylvania four Blue Cross0 Blue Shied plans said they will use contributions from the Blues to provide health insurance to 29,000 people without coverage. Some business groups and Republican legislators view the plan as an extra business tax and predict it will backfire by prompting more businesses to drop coverage, leading to more people without insurance. Gov. Ed Rendell argues that health insurance is unaffordable for employers and the changes should help.

headline: Let harness racing commission do its job
abstract: State Rep. Frank Lagrotta wants the three Harness Racing Commissioners to resume deliberations and choose between two applicants that they unanimously rejected. The Commission serves all of Pennsylvania and it should award the licenses to a qualified applicant, even if that takes another two years of deliberation.

headline: Pa. pols must OK eminent-domain protections
abstract: A U.S. Supreme Court decision ruled that it was OK for the city of New London, Conn., to seize 15 homes in a working-class neighborhood so a private developer could build a riverfront hotel and office complex. They felt that the city's need for greater tax revenue was sufficient for it to take over the homes of its residents. Pennsylvania Legislature enacted a law to prevent municipalities from straying outside their boundaries to take over someone's property. A bill is being sponsored to overturn that law; the Senate must agree on a bill that gives municipalities rights, but not to the degree in Connecticut.

headline: Farewell to a 'great American'
abstract: You know someone's made a huge difference in the world when the Rev. Jesse Jackson gives her eulogy, and Al Gore is on hand to call her a four-star general in the army of the righteous. Heavy weights throughout the political and entertainment worlds came together to say a final goodbye to native Philadelphian and political siren C. Delores Tucker during a service at Deliverance Evangelistic Church in North Philadelphia.

headline: All eyes on school board tally as Act 72 deadline nears
abstract: Local school boards are faced with the choice to provide property tax relief created under Act 72. Those districts opting out of Act 72 have done so by a 2-1 margin. Out of the state's 501 districts, only about 100 have made a decision. Act 72 would link school budgets to slots revenue, shifting to local income tax increases for revenue and subjecting future increases in property tax relief to voter referendum.  PA Governor Rendell and lawmakers will have some decisions to make when voting is completed. What will be done with the slots money if no one wants it?

headline: Health plans reduce costs, raise financial risk
abstract: As the cost of health insurance rises, employers urge workers to choose their healthcare plans wisely, but the Employee Benefit Research Institute reports that only 8 percent of workers feel comfortable doing so. Some employers and employees are turning to health savings accounts. The Kaiser Family Foundation reports that health insurance costs have increased on average by 11 percent in the past year, for the fourth consecutive year of double-digit increases.

headline: Litter removal scheduled across state
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Protection, along with three other agencies, are sponsoring the Great Pennsylvania Cleanup. Numerous groups will pick up litter and trash from roadways, parks, forests, riverbanks and neighborhoods.

headline: Pittsburgh may have too much oversight
abstract: PA Representative Frank Dermody, a Democrat, is impressed that many Republicans who helped to create the state oversight board now feel it should be dissolved.  While some Republicans support its dissolution, other, such as PA Representative Tom Stevenson feels the board should complete its job of auditing city water and parking authorities and supports it lawsuit against the Act 47 recovery team that has a five-year contract with firefighters.  These two boards, Act 47 recovery team and the state oversight board, will cost $3.8 million this year but cannot find common ground over city finances.

headline: Feds eye Wisc. Dental-care firm's ties to PA. Polls
abstract: Federal Investigators are studying why Doral Dental Services hired Philadelphia fundraisers Ronald A. White and Robert M. Feldman (who fundraised for Governor Ed Rendell).  The company had been collecting millions in tax dollars for dental work for the poor.  Many other issues with Doral's finances including payments from improper funds and inconsistent payments have been reported.

headline: Argument rages on gains, costs of a Wal-Mart
abstract: A hearing was held where the North Cornwall township supervisors heard from supporters and opponents of developing a Wal-Mart South of Lebanon.  Wal-Marts engineer Chris Dellinger said Lebanon County, the township and Cornwall-Lebanon School District would share at Lease $12,320 per year.  Attorney Dwight Yoder, on behalf of Wal-Mart opponents said they may need to hire additional police.

headline: Hospitals Battling Infections
abstract: A report was released be the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council indicating that thousand of people acquired infections at PA hospitals, and that several facilities reported no infections.  State Representative George Kenney, Chairman of the House Health and Human Services Committee said he found no infections unlikely.  He said the Committee may need to consider a bill proposed by state Representative Tony DeLuca, requiring that hospitals post the number of infections acquired there.  Roger Baumgarten, of the Hospital and Healthsystem Association of PA said they have no taken a position on the bill

headline: Luzerne County about to get a little Greener
abstract: Luzerne County will receive $1.75 million in state money to use for environmental projects from Gov. Ed Rendell's Growing Greener II initiative.  Commissioner Todd Vonderheld said there are plenty of projects that could benefit. Growing Greener will fund a variety of projects.  Money has been allotted to the Department of Environmental Resources and the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.  The article also lists projects which plan to use the funds.

headline: Pittsburgh Tuesday takes
abstract: This editorial encourages the public to stop PNC Financial Services Group from receiving a $18 million as a tax break in a tax-increment financing package.  Furthermore, it complains about the proponents who want the Pittsburgh Hilton & Towers to be turned into a taxpayer-subsidized convention center hotel because it feels there is no market for new hotel rooms in the Golden Triangle.  It also doubts that the proposal from PA Senator John Pippy to reduce the size of the General Assembly will see an honest vote where the Republican leaders will try their hardest to ensure no one shows up to the hearing.

headline: Feeling OK after seeing shrink
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell and his wife Midge sang the national anthem as part of a bet against Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney over the New England Patriot's Super Bowl victory over the Eagles.

headline: 'Back to the drawing board'
abstract: Dan Onorato, Allegheny County Chief Executive, plans to appeal a ruling by Common Pleas Judge R. Stanton that declares Onorato's plan to cap increases in the taxable value of property and reassess property differently unconstitutional.  Onorato wants to start the 2006 tax year by using property values calculated in 2002 and adjust them according to sales, assessment appeal results, and inflation among other factors.  Despite Onorato's claim that current assessments leave Allegheny County at a competitive disadvantage, Judge Stanton ruled against it because he felt it did not treat all taxpayers equally.

headline: Hospitals' mortality rate higher than expected
abstract: A report by the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council revealed that four local hospitals have higher morality rates than expected for certain procedures.  Moses Taylor Hospital had more patients die than expected for nonsurgical heart attack treatment, blood poisoning and gallbladder removals.  Council Executive Director Marc Volavka reported that overall patient mortality is declining but called for more preventative care as readmission increases are rising.

headline: 'Miracle' fix to be tested on I-99
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection approved a 4,000 ton shipment of Bauxol, a highly alkalinic "red mud" left over from the process of manufacturing aluminum, to an acid rock drainage hazard site on I-99. Testing procedures have yet to be approved, but will need to determine whether the PA Department of Transportation's planned massive injections of Bauxol will prevent acid drainage into nearby water sources. A Penn State scientist estimated the cost of the initial shipment at $16 million.

headline: Production facility planned
abstract: Carlisle Companies Inc. said its construction materials unit will build a 200,000 square-foot manufacturing plant in Smithfield. It will be the company's sixth US roofing-insulation facility to make products for commercial and industrial projects. Production is expected to begin in early 2006.

headline: Feeling OK after seeing shrink
abstract: The Philadelphia 76ers pulled off a narrow 97-93 victory against the Boston Celtics yesterday. Though the Sixers were up 26 points in the first quarter, the Celtics ma-naged to come within 3 points of victory in the last 72 seconds. The Sixers maintained their No. 8 spot in the NBA’s Eastern Conference thanks to 38 points from Allen Iverson and 19 steals. Gov. Ed Rendell and his wife sang the national anthem after losing a bet to Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney.

headline: Bill to overhaul water rates grabs Council's attention
abstract: Currently, water rates in Philadelphia are set by the mayor's water commissioner, but city Councilman Brian O'Neill introduced a bill that would give the council the final say on rate hikes.

headline: How hospitals compare
abstract: This article directs readers to the report from the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council by providing the link: www.thetimes-tribune.com or www.phc4.com.  It also lists higher-than-expected mortality ratings for the following Northeastern Pennsylvania hospitals: Geisinger Wyoming Valley Medical Center, Marian Community Hospital in Carbondale, Mercy Hospital in Wilkes-Barre and Moses Taylor Hospital in Scranton.

headline: Missing out
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell and state Senate Republicans broke the deadlock on Rendell's Growing Greener II proposal. Voters will decide by referendum on May 17th whether or not to allow the state to borrow $625 million for environmental cleanup and land preservation. The editorial board urges everyone to vote for this measure. The editorial board also agrees with Rendell that this should be partly funded by raising trash hauling fees.

headline: Rendell brings $525, 000 to region
abstract: PA Governor Rendell has brought $525,000, from the state’s Home Town Streets and Safe Routes to Schools Programs, to four Centre County Municipalities. The grants will be used to install new sidewalks, street lights or curbs to revitalize their downtown areas.

headline: Few problems with paper ballots
abstract: Election officials in 3 western PA counties opted for paper ballots after their voting machines were decertified by the Department of State. Democratic committeeman Bob Schmetzer said it was easy to use paper. PA policy director for the Association of Communities Organized for Reform Now, Celeste Taylor, noted there were still enough problems in Allegheny County elections to be concerned. The system was changed after a study revealed the "undercount," the difference between the number of voters who cast ballots and the total votes counted, was significantly higher in all three PA counties.

headline: Bill would provide tax relief for homeowners
abstract: State Representative Sean Ramaley spoke about his proposal for property tax relief.  He wants to create a property tax fund in the state treasury, and when it reached $100 million, it would be distributed to school districts for the purpose of lowering property taxes.

headline: How serious a threat is avian flu?
abstract: Bird flu, or specifically avian flu, that is. Suddenly, you can't turn on your TV set without seeing a report on the possibility of deadly flu epidemic that might reach the US. The threat of a new flu epidemic seems to have energized the federal government, which is still reeling from charges it was way too slow to respond to the disaster of Hurricane Katrina. But how serious a threat is avian flu? It is a cause for a heightened state of alert, or just another public health issue like SARS or West Nile virus that will generate more alarm here in America that actual cases of serious illness.

headline: Mouse is hunter's deadly weapon
abstract: Democratic state Rep. Mark Gergely, who is an avid hunter, sponsored a bill which got rid of internet sites that allow you to have animals killed by the click of the mouse. These sits claim they help handicapped sportsmen. Gergley believes that is non-sense, he says that there are plenty of state-sponsored programs for handicapped hunters, which can assist them in hunting safely.

headline: Rendell brings $525,000 to region
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell brought more than $525,000 to town with him to help four Centre County municipalities install new sidewalks, street lights or curbs to reinvigorate their downtown areas. The money, from the state's Home Town Streets and Safe Routes to School programs, will be used to help revitalize the communities and restore a hometown atmosphere.

headline: Firefighters endorse GOP hopeful
abstract: Firefighters Local 1 Union President Joe King reported that the firefighters are supporting Republican mayoral candidate Joe Weinroth due to a unanimous vote at a meeting on Friday.  King said that this is the first time the fire department has supported a Republican candidate ever in the mayor election.  Democratic mayoral candidate Bob O' Connor said he was confused about the decision as he has put public safety first and supported the firefighters.

headline: Black-Market Business booming in city
abstract: In Pittsburgh, like many other cities, there is a huge black market for a many different items. Often times thieves will steal an array of items ranging from deodorant to plasma TV's and sell them for just pennies on the dollar. Pittsburgh police reported 919 retail theft cases in 2004.

headline: Hundreds affected by county decision
abstract: Approximately 180 elderly people learned they would lose their place to live when Luzerne County Commissioners announced Valley Crest Nursing would close. Another 270 people will be out of work when the Plains Township facility shuts down. It will not close until every resident has a bed in another facility. That process is expect to take at least 6 months.

headline: MTR's shares plummet
abstract: MTR Gaming Group Inc's shares fell m ore than 10 percent after the company said it expected third-quarter profits to fall about $3 million below the same period last year because of a drop in traffic and higher than anticipated costs at its properties. Net income for the quarter ending Sept. 30 is expected to be $2.8 million to 43 million, or 10 cents per share, on revenues of $97.5 million to $98 million. MTR's third-quarter profit in 2004 was $5.9 million or 20 cents per share.

headline: Rendell to visit FC
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell will visit Ford City for an economic development announcement.

headline: First Perzel's race, then maybe her own
abstract: Kelly Preski, who works on PA House Speaker John Perzel's campaign and wife of his chief of stuff Brian, is considering a run for a Philadelphia City Council seat in 2007.  While she lives in Councilman Rick Mariano's district, she will move to another district where Councilman Brian O' Neill is responsible.  She is considering an at-large bid for that reason.

headline: Blue, white and gray
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell and his wife attended the Penn State Blue and White game. He is in the area to encourage the Centre County school district to support his property tax-relief plan Act 72. While in Centre County he was asked how he felt about the disappearance of Centre County District Attorney Ray Gricar, and he responded that he was distressed over it and hoped for the best.

headline: Injunction sought to block Altoona Center closing
abstract: 40 Altoona Center residents and their families still plan to seek an injunction in U.S. District Court in Johnstown to block the center's closing. The center provides care for people with mental and physical disabilities. The families contend the move is illegal under federal law because the state cannot duplicate the care and programs the residents are receiving in the Altoona Center.

headline: Murphy proposes creation of panel to clean up city
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy announced a proposed Clean Pittsburgh Commission to clean up litter, dumpsites and abandoned cars in the city.  The commission would consist of Representatives of city departments, the PA Resources council, PA Cleanways and other organizations.  Legislation about the commission was sponsored by Councilman Doug Shilds and will go to City Council.

headline: Rendell visiting Allentown today to deliver funds
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell is expected to appear at Center Square this afternoon to deliver a $1.25 million check, bringing the Allentown Parking Authority and its partners within one funding step of building a downtown transportation hub after more than four years of planning. What remains is the approval of borrowing through city-guaranteed bonds, which City Council will begin to discuss Wednesday night.

headline: Four years after 9/11 and we weren't ready
abstract: This editorial questions the readiness of the state of Pennsylvania after reviewing how Federal Emergency Management Agency head Michael Brown, Mayor of New Orleans Ray Nagin and Louisiana Governor Kathleen Blanco failed to effectively deal with Hurricane Katrina.  It also criticizes the White House for its lack of efficient communication with these public officials.  It does say that Pennsylvania is more prepared than most with 20,000 National Guardsmen,  two search and rescue teams and state police to assist in case of a disaster, but it still encourages PA Governor Ed Rendell and Mayor John Street to develop a plan because FEMA cannot be trusted.

headline: Boone opts for tax relief program
abstract: Daniel Boone School Board voted to opt in to Act 72, but also approved a budget that calls for an 11.3 percent tax increase. Act 72 is designed to give property owners tax relief. Henceforth, the district will be required to seek a referendum to raise its budget above the rate of inflation. Act 72 was designed to discount property taxes in exchange for an increase in income tax. Taxpayers voiced their support for education regardless of what happens with Act 72.

headline: Insurers split on health insurance legislation
abstract: Small business owners continue to suffer from rising health insurance premiums, but insurers disagree on the effectiveness of bills before the PA legislature that might address the problem by changing the way premiums are set. The latest measure of discontent came from the National association for the Self-Employed, which released a survey showing more than 50% of businesses with 10 or fewer employees do not offer health insurance, primarily because of cost.  Four bills have been introduced in the PA legislature the would address the situation by changing the rules for how insurers set small business premiums.

headline: No skiing this year at Laurel Mountain, state says
abstract: The state Department of Conservation and Natural Resources confirmed that Laurel Mountain will be closed this winter. They are negotiating to reopen it in 2006, officials said. Somerst Trust acquired Laurel Mountain Ski Resort last year through foreclosure on a $1 million loan taken out by the former owner and his partnership.

headline: Residents discuss visions of change
abstract: About a dozen Connelsville residents met with community leaders to talk about the city's opportunities for development under the "Blueprint Community" banner. Lucinda Robbins, an educator with the Pen State Cooperative extension, led the group through exercises to focus the city's version for change. As a Blueprint Community, the city joined 21 other municipalities in PA chosen to make comprehensive change happen. The designation could mean additional money and opportunities for development.

headline: Fumo blasts House use of public money for politics
abstract: PA Senator Vincent Fumo has condemned the government's use of public money to fund campaign commercials as The Morning Call investigated and revealed that PA Representative Sam Smith and William DeWeese spend a total of $3.4 million in the last seven months of 2004.  While many critics claim that the funds used are taxpayer dollars that incumbents use to their advantage, spokespeople for the legislators say the ads and polls are used to inform constituents about important issues.  Fumo feels that money used for these types of ads need to be drawn from campaign funds.

headline: Borough holds line on taxes
abstract: Shenandoah Township Borough Manager Joseph Palubinsky reported that health care costs will rise 15% in the coming year and warned that these rising costs will be tough to maintain without raising other taxes and fees.  However, the 2006 budget still maintains the property tax at 17 mills.  In other issues, West Mahanoy Township and the Shenandoah Sewer Authority are in the process of agreeing to connect residents in Shenandoah Heights to the treatment system.

headline: Legal group: Poor families are buying insurance they can get free
abstract: Community Legal Services, an investigation group concerned with Pennsylvania's four Blue Cross and Blue Shield health insurers, claims that 8,500 children currently paying for low-cost insurance qualify for free insurance from the PA Children's Health Insurance Program.  Jonathan Stein, of the group, has not yet found any evidence that the insurer deliberately misinformed the families but did a poor job of informing them of their options.

headline: Oil spill is rated 2d worst on river
abstract: The most recent oil spill totaling 265,000 gallons from the pierced Greek tanker Athos 1 took place in the Delaware River in November, but Captain Jonathan Sarubbi, the Coast Guard's head of the Port of Philadelphia, reported this number can only be an estimate at this point in time.  The spill was caused by a large 15-foot hunk of metal found on the river bottom that officials are trying to identify.  The spill affected a 57-mile stretch of shoreline from the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge to the Smyrna River in Delaware.

headline: Secretary of Economic Ignorance
abstract: The author is responding to a letter from the secretary of the PA Department of Community and Economic Development, Dennis Yablonsky, who said that the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review did not understand the PA Governor Edward Rendell’s administration’s economic development policy. The author believes that he was trying to protect his own position and that he failed to address the number of lost jobs from corporations leaving the state because of high business taxes, high fuel taxes and increased insurance rates.

headline: Fun with numbers and daily expenses: State legislators keep cashing in
abstract: While most of the public anger has been focused on state lawmakers' dead-of-night pay grab in July, there are some other benefits they get that are quietly increasing. For instance those who live 50 miles or more from Harrisburg can claim a reimbursement known as per diem; they can also claim a $141 daily deduction on their federal income taxes for traveling expenses under what's known as the "four day rule."

headline: Bridge agency to hire two
abstract: The Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission will hire a chief financial officer and a deputy executive director of communications. Chairman Philip Mugavero said both new positions will be essential as the commission moves forward with its $640 million capital improvement program. Currently, a controller and various financial consultants handle the commission's fiscal affairs.

headline: Many oppose closing county nursing home
abstract: More than 130 family members and about 30 Spring Creek Rehabilitation and Health Care Center residents attended a closed-to-t public sessions with the three commissioners, who said ballooning costs are causing the board to consider options for the 308-bed facility, including closure or sale. The board is concerned from the news that this year's expenses would top $7 million, instead of the $4.2 million budgeted.

headline: Oil Spill is Rated 2nd worse on River
abstract: A ship called the Greek Tanker Athos 1 released 265,000 gallons of oil into the Delaware River last week, making it the 2nd worst spill in the history of the Delaware River. Coast Guard officials said the number was an accurate estimate, and that identifying the cause of the spill and cleanup could take several months.

headline: Slots law revenue cap ripped by officials
abstract: East Hanover Township Supervisor Becki Oller complained to the PA House of Representatives House Tourism and Recreational Development Committee that having the Penn National slots casino will double the budget and revenues from the parlor will not be enough to cover the increase.  PA Representative Ronald Marisco proposed an amendment that the PA Legislature is not expected to vote on until after summer recess that eliminates the law that limits a host's share of revenue to 50% of the township budget.  PA Representative Mario Scavello estimated the cost of police increasing to $1.4 million where the township only has a budget of $1 million.

headline: Gambling hot issue in Bethlehem City Council race
abstract: As the race for Bethlehem City Council winds down, the three incumbents and three challengers are being asked a lot of questions concerning the casinos. Other issues include zoning laws to city debt. The six candidates all offer their own unique experiences.

headline: Budget cuts in art areas spark protest
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street announced his budget, which must be approved by the City Council, and it received much protest. He wants to cut taxes for businesses, and the group Good Jobs First said that business taxes should not be decreased if it means cutting essential programs and services, such as the ones the Philadelphia Museum of Art provides. The group Philadelphia Forward, however, is arguing for reduced taxes on businesses.

headline: Medicaid mess / The governor and the GOP have better options
abstract: This editorial encourages Republican lawmakers to discuss Medicaid reform with PA Governor Ed Rendell rather than simply insulting his recently rejected $500 million proposal.  While Rendell's plan did reduce reimbursements for care providers, increase co-pays and reduced benefits, the editorial did applaud Rendell's efforts to keep 1.8 million poor, disabled and elderly in the program.  It proposes amendments to this proposal, however, such as a tax on smokeless tobacco or using some of the surplus funds.

headline: Pa. plan to turn waste coal into diesel
abstract: Waste Management and Processors Incorporated is planning to build the first commercial plant to convert waste coal into zero-sulfur diesel fuel and home-heating oil.  The plant, which will cost $612 million, is expected to use about 258 million tons of culm that are piled on 8,500 acres of land in southwestern Pennsylvania.  PA Environmental Protection Secretary Kathleen McGinty and PA Governor Ed Rendell both said that this will solve an environmental problem for the state as well as providing a product for which there is a large demand.

headline: So what can we expect next from BIO?
abstract: This article is an interview with Fritz Bittenbender, president of the PA Biotechnology Industry Organization, after their annual meeting in Philadelphia.  He explains that the industry is trying to attract more investments for research and create industry partnerships.  He also cites that the industry is responsible for about 1500 to 2000 jobs solely within the southeastern part of Pennsylvania.  He did express the need for a better tax code for businesses in the state as well as more public funding.

headline: Gaming board plans ethics policy
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board Chairman Thomas Decker discussed a the ethics policy for commissioners where after slots applications are turned in, there will be 60-day period afterward where no lobbyists or gambling officials can talk to the member board that grants licenses.  Commissioner Joseph Marshall III explained that this policy is to ensure the legality and ethicality of the process.  While PA Representative Paul Clymer accused the process of only increasing skepticism within the public, PA Representative Jake Wheatley claimed it will allow for more minority and women-owned businesses to be involved.

headline: City could get $2.6 million from job tax
abstract: In Harrisburg, PA the city council voted and passed the emergency services, or job tax, which will take into effect this year. The enactment calls for an increase from $10 to the state maximum of $52 tax per year on the city's employees, which number about 60,000 people.

headline: MH/MR appeals are over
abstract: Susan J. Dellock, former Mental Health/Mental Retardation program director, won an appeal with the state Civil Service Commission that challenged her termination from the service by county solicitor Paul J. Datte. The county was forced to remove the termination from her record and pay her two months salary.

headline: Pa. voter approval of Greener II bond issue and beginning
abstract: Unless voters approve the ballot initiative, Growing Greener II, PA's extensive environmental efforts will dwindle if not disappear because of lack of funding. Members of PA Governor Rendell's administration have traversed the state urging voters to authorize the initiative, which enjoyed bi-partisan support in the PA House. PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources Secretary Michael DiBerardinis, who recently delivered money to Allegheny County from the state's Growing Greener program, said the initiative tracks with other voter approved acts.

headline: State aid for projects awaits approval of bond issue
abstract: The Commonwealth Financing Authority agreed to fund 34 economic development projects in the state but couldn't agree how to borrow.  The Authority was developed by Governor Ed Rendell and the legislature approved it last Fall.  When funding is available, Pittsburgh projects include: the Tech 21 Research Park in Marshall, a Regional Industrial Development Corp.  Urban Redevelopment Authority work for transit oriented development and the Pier Point professional center, two Washington County projects and a Beaver County Project.

headline: Gaming 'witchhunt' hurts fire companies
abstract: James Krammes Senior of Cressona writes a letter to the editor expressing her disappointment that the citizens of Pennsylvania elect officials who takeaway volunteer organizations' ability to fundraise.  She cites the example of the video poker machines that the government is attempting to remove from the volunteer fire houses, which use the machines as means to fund their operation.  While she acknowledges that the machines are illegal, she claims that the government money that these volunteer organizations receive  does not suffice.

headline: City could get $2.6 million from jobs tax
abstract: Harrisburg City Council recently voted to institute a $52 job tax on the 68,000 employees within Harrisburg to replace a $10 occupational privilege tax in order to create property tax relief.  Employers can collect the tax over a three month period or all in one chunk, according to their discretion.  The city is expected to make a $2.6 million windfall this year as a result of this tax.

headline: MH/MR appeals are over
abstract: The personnel problems of Mental Health/ Mental Retardation crisis of 2004 are resolved. Susan J. Dellock, former MH/MR program director, won an appeal with the PA Civil Service Commission for wrongful termination. Former administrative assistant Mary Ann Link also filed an appeal, but lost. Allegations of overspending and poor financial record keeping within the program resulted in a outside investigation and the layoff of several MH/MR employees. County officials still claim service providers were overpaid and are seeking reimbursement.

headline: Peak Outrage
abstract: In support of the Clean Water Protection Act introduced by US Reps. Frank Pallone and Christopher Shays, editors urge their local congressman to support the legislation to end mountaintop mining. The practice is rape of the central Appalachian landscape, threatening both the environment and residents. It takes jobs too because it does not require the labor that traditional mining does. The five counties in which it is practiced are among the poorest in West Virginia.

headline: State aid helps Beaver County plants keep jobs
abstract: The Rendell Administration granted aid to two of PA's largest manufacturers. Regional director of the Governor's Action Team, Frank Horrigan, noted Anchor Hocking and Horsehead Corp. were essential manufacturing components of the PA economy. Horsehead landed in bankruptcy court in 2002 and since restructured. The Team secured an Opportunity Grant from the PA Machinery and Equipment Loan Fund for Anchor. President of one of the United Steelworkers locals at the plant, John Poskosky, noted 200 people lost jobs in restructuring.

headline: Gen. Rendell
abstract: The author of the letter finds Governor Ed Rendell to be anti-military.

headline: City's fiscal watchdog growling
abstract: Pittsburgh's state-appointed fiscal watchdogs signaled that they may send Mayor Tom Murphy's proposed 2006 budget back for revisions. An area of concern is the proposed contribution of nonprofit organizations. The budgets calls for $5.67 mill in contributions, but so far they have pledged $3.89 million for next year. City Councilman Doug Shields argued against counting on any contribution from nonprofit groups, saying the city has no legal ability to get these groups.

headline: Montco looking to be ready for bird flu
abstract: The Montgomery County health department is putting together a Pandemic Crisis Committee that will create a plan in response to an outbreak of avian flu or other deadly contagious diseases. Those asked to send representatives to sit on the committee cover a wide range of specialties, from public health to law enforcement, to veterinarians.

headline: Power outage kills 300,000 trout
abstract: A scheduled power outage at the US Fish and Wildlife hatchery in Warren was followed by a surge that blew out the hatchery's backup generator, killing 300,000 lake trout that were to stock Lake Erie and Ontario this year. Approximately 50 percent of the hatchery was killed. Program supervisor Bill Archambault noted the power outage prevented oxygen from reaching the fish. More could die as a result of the stress of the seven hour loss of power. The real impact of the loss will be felt several year down the road, when the fish were supposed to have matured.

headline: State aid to make steel parcel shovel ready
abstract: PA governor Ed Rendell announced Wednesday $15 million in state grants and loans to help clean up and develop 1,000 acres of former Bethlehem Steel Corp land. Lehigh Valley Industrial Park Inc is receiving the grants to develop its seventh industrial park in the area. The new park is expected to bring 6,000 to 10,000 new jobs.

headline: Gibbons' former foe gears up for a rematch
abstract: In 2001, Terry Houck came close to defeating his former boss for district attorney of Bucks County. Now, Houck is running against Diane Gibbons, who is unopposed in the primary. His Democratic rival is Lawrence Otter. Both men believe they have better experience, with Houck having served as a Philadelphia police officer. Otter once worked as deputy attorney general. Both have criticized Gibbons, who attributes the close previous election to the fact that she is a prosecutor, not a politician.

headline: Council should consider term limits
abstract: City council resumed work, but it wasn't exactly business as usual. A Council committee convened hearings into the impact of the steep PGW rate hike on city residents, but the consistent protector of the city's underclass was missing, David Cohen. He is fondly remembered for this, but his life is giving others to lesson leaving the spotlight of politics after a certain age, because he was beginning to ramble in speeches and puzzle people.

headline: Neighborhood groups push for return of curfew center
abstract: Lawrenceville United is lobbying for the return of the youth curfew center, urging for Pittsburgh to establish a holding facility. District 2 Councilman Gene Ricciardi said that he is committed to having $250,000 allocated for a new center. The city opened a curfew center in 1996 in the Public Safety Building but stopped funding it last summer. The center was set up so that trained social service professionals could intervene and help families solve the problems that led to the curfew violations.

headline: PPL to face DEP action over leak
abstract: The PA state Department of Environmental Protection has said that enforcement action will be taken as testing and cleanup continue after the fly ash leak at PPL Corporation’s Martin’s Creek power plant. The DEP is conducting biological assessments on the river and have noted that river testing so far has not indicated problems for water treatment facilities downstream.

headline: State aid to make Steel parcel 'shovel-ready'
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell recently announced that Lehigh Valley Industrial Park Incorporated will receive a $5 million grant and a $10 million loan in order to build a new industrial park that will create 6,000 to 10,000 jobs.  The money is a result of a pool of grants and loans totaling $300 million in the Pennsylvania's Building in Our Sites initiative.  Mayors John Callahan, Roy Afflerbach and Phil Mitman all spoke highly of Rendell's development promotion in the Lehigh Valley.

headline: Give Pennsylvanians access to more information
abstract: There are Sunshine laws written by the Legislature, which allows the public to access meetings and records of its public officials. However, the Legislature has exempted itself from many of its provisions and honor it only when they feel forced to. Until citizens are provided Sunshine rights within the Pennsylvania constitution, lawmakers will continue to regard their citizens as inconsequential.

headline: Council tentatively Oks 20% tax hike
abstract: Homeowners in the Highspire Borough will face a 20% increase in their municipal property taxes in 2006 as well as a $10 increase in sewer bills as well.  John McHale, borough manager, reported that this will increase the average homeowner's annual taxes by $113, and Highspire Borough Council President Marie Hoch said that this biggest tax increase since her 12 years on the council is necessary for the borough.  McHale attributes the $1.4 million budget to rising health insurance, pension and fuel costs.

headline: New life for old hospitals
abstract: Polygon Partners, a New York developer, plans to use the vacant Mount Sinai Hospital and develop it into residential condominiums as well as some townhomes.  This one of a few plans that are taking vacant hospital buildings and redeveloping them, for example, the Metro Club condominiums that were built in the former Metropolitan Hospital building.  Moreland Development has also publicized plans to build a supermarket plaza across from the entrance to the Germantown Hospital, which is another vacant hospital.

headline: Putting down roads
abstract: Organizers of a massive tree-planting effort scheduled for Saturday at Stroud Preserve are looking for a few good diggers. The preserve, located on North Creek Road at the former Georgia Farm location, will be the new home for 6,000 trees planted alongside Taylor Run, a tributary of the East Branch of the Bradywine Creek. The trees were provided by TreeVitalize, a partnership of state government and private organizations whose goal is to plant more than 20,000 trees and shrubs in southeastern PA this fall.

headline: State awards money to Allentown
abstract: Allentown's Commercial and Industrial Development Authority has been awarded 1.9 million in state grants and loans to proceed with plans for an industrial shell building adjacent to its Bridgeworks business incubator. The funding will be used for its site remediation, utilities, and other things. The 90,000 square foot building would provide flexible industrial/commercial space in Allentown in a Keystone Opportunity Zone that is free from most local and state taxes.

headline: Goal is to repeal raise, don't 'screw it up worse'
abstract: State lawmakers are determined to get the 2005 pay raise fiasco settled by Thanksgiving. House and Senate leaders said they have the same goal; to repeal the 16 percent to 54 percent raises that lawmakers granted themselves and the executive and judicial branches. The constitution prevents judges' salaries from being reduced, which is making the agreement difficult.

headline: County schools reject Act 72
abstract: The Manheim Township school board voted against participating in Act 72. School board president Hannah Bartges called it faulty. Not a single Lancaster County school district has opted in to Act 72. Thus far, 24 percent of the state's districts have opted in for a total of 85 districts participating. 269 districts have opted out. The state legislation would grant property tax reductions in exchange for slots revenue and higher income taxes. Further efforts to increase property taxes above the rate of inflation will be subject to referendum. This morning Lancaster School District's vote is expected to be close.

headline: Diet and Exercise Help Gov. Rendell Trim Off 40 Pounds
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell has lost about 40 pounds and is aiming to get down to 200 pounds.

headline: New service cuts through prescription confusion
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell commended a program operated by the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America trade group, called the Partnership for Prescription Assistance, which guides low income residents with no prescription health care plan through the complex process of obtaining coverage. Most of those eligible are senior citizens. Industry insiders say companies motives in being involved in the program are tax deductibles, good publicity, and avoidance of federal overhaul of the system by Congress.

headline: Recycling could save $17 million controller says
abstract: A report by Philadelphia City Controller Jonathan A. Saidel says that the city’s low-performing recycling program could save $17 million a year with weekly collection because more recycling results in less trash collected and reduces the amount spent on landfill dumping fees. The Philadelphia Streets Department responded that this savings is overstated because collecting recyclables is more labor and capital intensive.

headline: State has its eye on city Horst building
abstract: The Stephen Girard estate trust in Philadelphia may be close to buying the Horst building at 29 E. King Street. The plan is for the state to lease space and move the Department of Labor and Industry office there from 60 W. Walnut St. The edifice is a Lancaster landmark; it was the site of the former Garvin's Department Store until it closed.

headline: God and Sex
abstract: The American Civil Liberties Union filed suit against the US Department of Health and Human Services for allowing "The Silver Ring Thing" abstinence-only program to teach on the taxpayers' dime. The Silver Ring Thing noted it counted the task as an opportunity to communicate the "Good News of the Gospel." Editors note US Sens. Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum have been major benefactors of "The Silver Ring Thing," questioning whether taxpayers want their tax dollars spent that way.

headline: DCED offers grim Union outlook
abstract: Union Township is expected to end the year with a budget shortfall even though the supervisors disbanded the local police department to cut costs. The deficit could run as high as $175,000 an official with the PA state Department of Community and Economic Development predicts. Mike Foreman of the DCED’s Center for Local Government Services said that its consultant looked over the township’s expenses and found no evidence that the township officials have been hiding money.

headline: Nursing shortage prompts union to ask state for help
abstract: About 1,500 other union nurses at state-run PA prisons, hospitals, nursing homes and health departments are calling on Gov. Ed Rendell to aggressively recruit more nurses. They are concerned that upcoming retirements could cause a staffing crisis, especially at prisons, where it's often been difficult to hire and retain nurses.

headline: Region on the verge of a building boom
abstract: More than $3 billion worth of projects are planned for the Pittsburgh region, launching the area into a building boom.  The boom will help alleviate the standstill in construction employment as it is down this year by about 3,000 jobs, hovering around 55,100 construction workers total.  About half of the $3 billion will fund three major projects: $575 million to a new children's hospital, $200 million to new Veterans' Administration facilities and $800 million to Greene Energy Resource Recovery Project, which will clean highly polluted acidic water.

headline: State loans and grants sought
abstract: Plymouth Township has asked the PA Department of Community and Economic Development for $510,000 in loans a $16,000 in loans because of its financial problems and total debt of $525,629.  Solicitor Joe Lach added other problems during a recent hearing including laying off its police department and getting hit by two floods this past April.
